on Elsevier eBooks+: 22 Videos and 1 Client Information Sheet.

Gathering Information Before the
Veterinarian Enters the Exam Room
The physical examination begins before the veterinarian ever touches
the animal.1-3 The traditional teachings of look, smell, and listen are
as important as ever. Excellent veterinarians avoid making
diagnostic decisions driven by laboratory-derived data that bypass
the physical examination. This chapter is founded on the concept
that veterinarians must bring together data from the history,
physical examination, and diagnostic tests to care for an animal in
the context of its life—including the expectations the owner envisions
for the pet (ch. 1). Algorithms alone are of limited value without an
excellent history (ch. 2) and physical examination. Increasing

reliance on “artificial intelligence” is not recommended in favor of
this traditional approach.
When possible, the animal’s temperature and weight should be
recorded before the veterinarian enters the examination room. This
provides the nursing staff the chance to communicate with the pet’s
owner (client, caretaker), gather pertinent information, note changes
in weight over time, and identify the owner’s primary concerns or
request(s). The veterinarian may review these findings with the
owner if there are questions about the history or why the pet is being
presented for examination. Unskilled staff should not be doing
“TPRs” (measuring temperature, pulse, and respiration) since
mistakes can be made and the veterinarian and nurses/technicians
may lose valuable information such as the anal tone, skin around the
perianal region, incorrect weight, etc. Also, skilled technicians know
how to talk to the owner and the animal and help to relax rather than
frighten the pet.
This is a good time for the staff to record current medications and
dosages being administered, prophylactic agents being utilized (e.g.,
for heartworm disease, ectoparasites, internal parasites), and herbal
or other supplements being administered (ch. 2). The animal’s
vaccination and reproductive status (i.e., spayed, neutered, or last
heat cycle) should be identified in the record. Knowing the current
diet and amount being fed can save valuable doctor time and should
be recorded (ch. 145). Notation of medications should always be
accompanied by the owner’s perception of their efficacy since this
information may influence future treatment and prognosis. Nursing
staff may also utilize this time to provide valuable information to the
pet owner on subjects the veterinarian may have limited time to
discuss. Examples include new vaccine programs, wellness
programs, microchipping information, behavior, and products to aid
in training and health as well as office financial policies. Having
discussed these topics allows the veterinarian to concentrate on
medicine rather than finances. Problems here should be noted in the
medical record by the nursing staff.
It is important to always attempt to provide the pet owner with an
on-time, efficient examination. Reading material (magazines of
interest to a wide variety of pet owners and their children) should be
available if there is a likelihood of the owner having to wait. Pet
owners should be given an indication of the doctor’s schedule and

the length of a delay, if any is anticipated. Providing the owner with
this information can offset frustration, anger, or anxiety. If the
hospital has brochures for new pet owners or information about
hospital services, this is a good time to deliver these and to allow the
owner to browse through the material. Likewise, instructional video
recordings may be of interest to the owner (ch. 1).

Observing the Pet and Meeting the
Caretaker
The process of performing a physical exam often is described as an
isolated event that takes place only between the veterinarian and the
animal. However, a physical examination also is a type of ritual that
demonstrates to an owner how the veterinarian will interact with the
patient. This is as true in veterinary medicine as in human medicine:
“When a sick patient is examined with skill, it goes a long way in
earning trust and authority.”4 A pet owner’s confidence in the
veterinarian allows a dialog to emerge regarding physical exam
findings, the owner’s interest and experience around health concerns
brought up by physical exam findings, and the veterinarian and the
owner’s perspectives on investigating physical exam abnormalities.

FIGURE 3.1 When Dr. Ettinger enters the exam
room he greets the owner and pet. When both are
provided the opportunity to feel relaxed, the balance
of the examination is likely to be more successful.

Gaining the Owner’s and the Pet’s Trust
Every veterinarian approaches a pet in his or her own way. With
time, it becomes second nature. It is important to develop proper
animal handling skills. Owners observe a great deal during this
process and may determine long before any recommendations are
made just how trusting they will be. Gentle care, compassion,
concern, and attention cannot be overemphasized. It is good for the
veterinarian to restate the owner’s concerns in the context of the
physical exam because this allows the pet’s owner to know that the
veterinarian has been listening and is being attentive to them at the
same time as the veterinarian is evaluating the patient (ch. 1).
Alternatively, the veterinarian may repeat to the owner what the

nursing staff has written on the examination sheet to assure the
owner that the owner’s concerns about pet have been heard. It may
be quite different from what was written earlier!
The process begins as the veterinarian enters the examination area
(Figure 3.1) where the owner and pet are waiting. A friendly
greeting and a small but appropriate amount of banter are often
appreciated. An occasional owner makes it clear that the veterinarian
should get down to business. People appreciate being greeted and
particularly like being acknowledged (ch. 1) (Figure 3.2). If the
case is a referral, noting the distance traveled or offering a kind word
about the trip and the referring veterinarian acknowledges the owner
in an important way. It is not a technique easily taught, and it is not
difficult to see whether the veterinarian “gets it” quickly and learns to
communicate or simply turns away from such contact. Similarly,
owners like to see that the veterinarian notices their pet by name or
with a gentle touch. These elements allow a physical exam to take
place in a context with less tension and a greater focus on the value
of the exam.
The importance of letting each pet owner know that the
veterinarian cares about him or her and the pet cannot be
overemphasized. This must be done in a genuine way, reflected in
dialog, attention, body language, and actions. Such a sense of
“community” is far more likely to be appreciated and will be
recognized as more genuine than superficial attempts like having
“We Care” or some other logo stamped on hospital leashes or
stationery. Owners value compassion as much as (and often much
more than) possession of knowledge.5 Every successful veterinarian
can relate tales about brilliant doctors whom owners dislike! The
smartest veterinarian may never have the opportunity to
demonstrate his or her skills if concern and caring are not expressed
in a way that is meaningful to the owner. In fact, human patients are
more likely to be antagonistic toward physicians who fail to express
compassion6 and the same appears to apply to veterinarians.
Complaints are likely to be made much more frequently about an
arrogant doctor than about one who is poorly trained or medically
inadequate but friendly and compassionate.7 Ultimately, an excellent
veterinarian approaches the case with both medical skill and
personal empathy. Professionals with a disproportionately higher

number of malpractice claims may be readily separated from those
with fewer claims by evaluation of their examination room
attitude.7,8

FIGURE 3.2 Patient and owner in exam room.
Comments about the pet or the owner help to break
the silence and relieve some of the owner anxiety
that likely is associated with the veterinary hospital
visit. “That’s a nice little comb. Where did you get
it?”
If there has been a delay, it is paramount that the veterinarian
acknowledge this upon entering the room. The veterinarian should

show pet owners the courtesy of recognizing that they have been
waiting. Unnecessary interruptions should be minimized, and every
hospital should have a policy in this regard. In a large critical care
setting, delays and interruptions do occur, but these should be
limited. Phone calls should be restricted to those that are
professionally relevant or urgent. When such calls interrupt me
(SJE) with owners, I explain that I need to speak with another
concerned owner about their hospitalized pet, for example. I do try
to make it clear that I am focusing on their pet’s problems.

The Doctor Must Listen
A skilled veterinarian understands that no part of the examination is
as important as carefully listening to the owner (ch. 1). Therefore,
adequate time must be allowed for this interaction in an
environment that enhances the process. Examination rooms should
be comfortable and inviting. Privacy for owners is necessary because
the situation may be a difficult one for them. The owner may
perceive diagnoses or recommendations that may seem routine or
minor to the practicing veterinarian as quite serious and worrisome.9
Owners that “mindread” may already be anxious and worried
because in their mind the pet already has a fatal disease! This initial
period of acquaintance and contact conveys the owner’s perceptions
to the veterinarian. In this way, the beginning of the physical
examination is interwoven with obtaining part of the medical history
and establishing a rapport with the pet’s owner. I find that this can
be the most useful time of the examination process. I can touch the
pet, gently stroke it, observe the quality of the hair coat and skin,
determine the hydration status, and generally gain an impression of
certain key aspects of the animal’s health status (e.g., debilitated or
thriving, obese or thin, noting visible abnormalities the owner may
ask about such as cutaneous/subcutaneous masses) while
understanding the pet’s context and the owner’s mindset (

Video

3.1 and Figures 3.3 and 3.4). Odors such as that of exhaled ketones
in a diabetic animal10 or uremic halitosis (ch. 46) or halitosis
associated with chronic liver disease (fetor hepaticus)11 may be

apparent even upon entering the exam room. This is also a
convenient time to gently examine some pets without the animal
being fearful, especially for those pets that are more aware of the
owner’s talking than of the veterinarian’s gentle palpation. Pets
generally seem less fearful while I am at their eye level (at an
appropriate distance) and when I refer to them by name.

FIGURE 3.3 Observing the animal from a slight
distance also gives the veterinarian a chance to note
other abnormalities—masses, deformities, and
difficulty standing or walking. This dog is weak, has a
plantigrade stance in the hind limbs and is
uncomfortable standing or walking.
In order to place physical exam findings in their proper context, it
is important to get the owners’ version of the history and not one
that has been “dictated” to them (ch. 2). For example, when
questioned, the owners may acknowledge that a friend, family
member or referring veterinarian told them about the supposed
problem. Further questioning may determine that the owners
themselves have not noted any clinical signs that warrant concern.

Computers are commonly used for recordkeeping during the
history and examination process. Whether the physical exam
findings are entered electronically or on paper, it is important to
maintain eye contact with the owner as much as possible while
recording information.12 If the owner feels that the computer takes
precedence over their impressions, an important component of the
examination and history may be lost. Worse, the owner may feel
disregarded and dissatisfied. Benefits of computer tablets include
being portable and easily used while facing the pet owner (Figure
3.5).

The Examination Begins
There is no single technique for the examination process. Because
this chapter is intended to explain my method of examination, I
(SJE) will delineate the regimen I follow, a process learned over
decades of experience. When possible, I try to make eye and physical
contact with the pet. First, I make a brief attempt at greeting the
animal by extending the back of my hand toward its face.14 For this,
cats and smaller dogs can be placed on the examination room table
(Figure 3.6, A and B). Usually, with medium to large dogs, I kneel
on the examination room floor to greet the animal (Figure 3.7). Of
course, some dogs and cats (those that are fearful/aggressive
[Figure 3.8, A and B], in cages, or tightly held by the owner) may
let me know beforehand whether or not they are ready for such a
greeting. If not, I bypass the greeting and make a light comment to
the owners about the situation (“After all,” I say, “who likes going to
the doctor?”). This begins a conversation with the owner that
acknowledges the possibility of the pet being fearful and allows the
owner(s) to let me know how they feel about the process or about
previous veterinary experiences. Thus, the physical examination
often overlaps with the latter part of the history being taken.
Frequently it is easier to do the initial examination of a cat while he
or she is still in the carrying case if it opens from the top or side
(Figure 3.9, A and B). While not as thorough, it avoids difficulty
handling a fractious pet, something most owners do not like to view.
Another useful technique is to examine the cat in a blanket-covered

basket. This often settles the anxious cat (Figure 3.9, C). Dogs or
cats that are known to be fearful +/– aggressive in advance of the
appointment may benefit from pretreatment with an anxiolytic,
provided the animal does not have a medical contraindication to it.15
Gabapentin has emerged as an excellent option for cats and many
dogs,16 and other medications such as trazodone likewise can make
the appointment much less stressful for the patient, and therefore for
the owner and veterinarian. A veterinarian-client-patient
relationship must exist in order to prescribe medications, so this can
be considered for follow-up visits, not the initial appointment.

FIGURE 3.4 Observing the dog or cat from a
distance allows the veterinarian to note evidence of
an enlarged abdomen (in this case due to ascites)
and dyspnea, which would allow questioning and
examination to move along in a more specific
direction.

FIGURE 3.5 Computer tablets allow the owner
and the veterinarian to face each other while the
veterinarian enters information. In a 2017 study, 71%
of human patients preferred to interact with a
physician without a stationary computer; patients
perceived their physicians to be more
compassionate, better communicators, and more
professional (all P ≤0.001) when the physician was
not interacting with a stationary computer in the
exam room.13

FIGURE 3.6 A, The exam room table is best
covered with a soft towel, cloth, or ideally a nonskid
pad or mat. B, Stainless steel is very intimidating,
slippery, cold, and unfriendly.

FIGURE 3.7 For larger dogs, I (SJE) like to
examine them on the floor and be at eye level with
them. I often kneel on a gardener’s pad to be more
comfortable.
Pet owners often wish to share what they know, think, or
understand about their pet’s problems. Regardless of how clearly and
confidently owners relate their interpretation of their companion’s
issues, it is essential for the veterinarian to “go back to square one” in
order to provide an objective assessment. Thus, the owner’s opinion
and the veterinarian’s analysis may run in parallel. Enough
confidence must be placed in the owner’s story to solidify the trust
being developed during this important part of the examination but
the veterinarian must also think independently enough to avoid

being led down an incorrect path of deduction. I like to give owners a
few minutes to express themselves, regardless of relevance, because
what they have to say is likely to be important to the ultimate
outcome. For example, owners may refuse to acknowledge how sick
the pet is, or they may be worried about “cancer” or may focus on
something that may not be pertinent (“can we also empty the anal
sacs and trim the toenails?” in an acute heart failure patient).
Owners’ comments provide valuable insight into their personality,
their understanding of veterinary medicine, as well as their concerns
and goals. There are different levels of owner commitment to pets,
and this will influence choices they make regarding the pet’s care.
During this time, the veterinarian also is observing the animal and
seeing its mentation, responsiveness to surroundings, behavior,
respiratory pattern, and other important parameters that will be
altered once the hands-on physical exam begins.
Many owners offer information obtained from friends, breeders, or
other sources, especially online sources of varying degrees of
credibility and accuracy. They may wish to have the veterinarian go
over printed material but that should be kept for the end of the
examination. A reasonable technique that precludes taking time
away from the office call is to acknowledge the request and inform
the caretaker that material will be reviewed at the end of the
examination to allow the doctor to thoroughly complete the
evaluation. “Dr. Google” has become a regular but silent partner in
the examination room.17 Dr. Google often will be consulted
immediately upon the owner’s having online access after the
examination, and very often even before the appointment begins.18
Refusing to acknowledge this is not wise; rather, hearing the owner’s
beliefs and level of knowledge provides an entry point for the
veterinarian to understand how the owner may interpret, and choose
to act on, information obtained from the history and physical exam.
In turn, this can have direct benefits for the patient.19
Conversely, sometimes an owner might volunteer almost no
information and present an attitude that is more blunt or
standoffish. If an owner implies: “OK, you are the doctor, so you tell
me what is wrong,” a different tack then becomes necessary. The
approach changes from open-ended questioning, such as “tell me
what you have observed,” to focused, closed-ended questioning like

“it appears that your dog (or cat) has been losing weight; tell me, has
this been a recent occurrence?” Or, “have you always been able to
feel your dog’s spine this clearly?” (ch. 1). Comments or questions
like this may be all that is necessary to have owners begin talking
about their pet.
Not every owner-veterinarian experience is informative. All
valuable and relevant acquired facts should be noted in the medical
record. If an owner refuses to provide information or begins to
verbally attack another individual, the record should be so-noted.
The record provides not only a potential legal defense but also a
guide to further owner communication (ch. 1).

FIGURE 3.8 A, If a cat or dog is aggressive, it
sometimes helps to examine the pet away from the
owner. The veterinarian can do this by explaining to
the owner that he/she is going to walk the pet to the
treatment area (B) where the pet is likely to
experience less fear because of not feeling the need
to protect its owner.

FIGURE 3.9 A, Some anxious cats are best left in
their carrier and examined at a distance initially to
allow them to overcome anxiety or fear (B). C,
Placing a cat, even those that are agitated, in an open
basket such as this often provides enough calming
effect that a physical examination can then be
completed. C, Courtesy Mark E. Peterson, DVM,
New York.
Inquiring in an unobtrusive manner about the owners’ needs,
financial concerns and expectations helps to define their wishes and
permits the veterinarian to provide options from which the owners
can choose.
It is not always possible to begin the examination under optimal
conditions as described above, and I (SJE) do not make a distinct
effort to perform every examination this way. For example, if the dog
or cat is sitting anxiously (e.g., protectively or in a frightened
manner) in the owner’s lap, I avoid interacting with the pet at first
and instead, I dwell on the pet’s and the owner’s story. Pets often
relax during this period and are less fearful of me as time goes by. A
truly frightened or fractious animal presents a different situation,
which may require the use of a muzzle or Elizabethan collar for
protection. Before muzzling any dog, it is strongly recommended to
attempt an examination away from the owner (Figure 3.8, A and
B)—for example, while taking a dog to a scale outside the
examination room or to an environment that no longer requires the
pet to feel protective of the owner.14 It is important to remember that
owners should not be allowed to hold their pets during any part of

the examination process that entails a likelihood of injury to anyone,
as could occur with touching a frightened or injured pet. This
remains a chronically differing point of view among veterinarians
(but not insurance companies). Many owners wish to hold their own
pet, yet the veterinarian is legally liable for examination room
injuries. Too, some pets are more likely to be irritable and protective
while being held. On the other hand, many owners feel
uncomfortable not holding their pet. Thus, the examining doctor
must use caution, experience, and the cues provided by the owner
and the animal to determine the best approach. Most importantly,
one must always work to avoid situations likely to result in a bite
wound or other injury to the owner, the veterinarian, or anyone else.
When a dog or cat reacts adversely to the veterinarian, it is important
to back off slowly, reassess the process, and move forward in a
manner that is safe for all involved. Usually, the owner recognizes
the need for this.
A severely sick or crisis presentation requires an entirely different
approach from a routine outpatient visit. In a critical context, a brief
examination for triage is performed (ch. 119), and a complete
physical exam follows when the patient is stabilized. Pet owners also
must be observed and evaluated, since many people are
understandably anxious in severe or life-threatening situations.
Owner anxiety, however, may manifest in a wide variety of responses
(ranging from a quiet, stunned composure to intense displays of
emotion). Skilled veterinarians assess these factors when beginning
to talk with an owner.
Some owners feel (and say) that their pet needs immediate
medical attention before the veterinarian has had the opportunity to
perform the physical exam. In such situations, comprehensive
questioning and a detailed physical exam in front of the owner are
likely inappropriate. Instead, it may be wise to advise the owner that
the pet is being taken to the treatment area so that a more thorough
examination may be completed, and medications initiated as needed.
It is imperative to advise the owner that either the veterinarian or the
veterinary assistant will be back shortly to brief them on the pet’s
condition, and then to do so (Figure 3.10 and

Video 3.2).

The Physical Examination: Initial
Observation
The physical examination commences when the veterinarian first
sees, smells, and hears the patient. This is the so-called “distant
exam” and it is extremely informative. Usually, this takes place in the
examination room, where the pet’s mentation, general appearance,
odor, and any irregularities are noted (Figure 3.3).
While observing the patient, the veterinarian should listen for
abnormal breathing sounds and watch for labored respirations,
suggesting either respiratory or systemic disorders (

Video 3.3;

see also Videos 37.1, 37.2, 37.3, and 37.4). The animal’s body size and
posture also should be observed: for example, a plantigrade stance
could suggest a neuropathy if affecting the hind limb (ch. 292;
Video 292.1) or ligament injury if affecting the forelimb, and flaccid
ventroflexion of the neck in a cat suggests hypokalemia or thiamine
deficiency (Figure 3.11) (ch. 256) (

Video 68.1). Overweight

pets (Figure 3.12) may be overfed (ch. 150), inactive (ch. 20), or
much less commonly, hypothyroid (ch. 285). Emaciated animals
may be systemically ill or underfed (Figure 3.13) (ch. 145). It is
true that owners may point out these concerns, but they may
misinterpret such changes or may simply not be cognizant of their
significance. Dogs and cats with ascites may appear to have gained
weight to the owner while in fact they are cachectic (Figure 3.10
and

Video 3.2; ch. 21).

In a desire to “wish well” for the pet, the owner sometimes can fail
to provide information for fear of its significance. The veterinarian
has the responsibility to seek out this information. Examples of
owner concerns and signs the veterinarian may observe are
presented in chs. 10 through 56 of this textbook. The examination
process must not be so quick or expedient as to result in an obvious
underlying condition being overlooked.
If the animal is ambulatory and has a history of lameness, a
neurologic deficit, or weakness, it is essential that the veterinarian

watch the animal move (Figure 3.14 and

Video 3.4; chs. 31, 43,

and 241).20 This may be done before or after the hands-on physical
examination. For dogs, this may require having the pet walk on a
surface with adequate traction, preferably with the owner as the
handler. Lameness, signs of neurologic deficits, or other
irregularities in gait or conformation (chs. 41, 43, 241) may become
critically important to the ultimate diagnosis (Figure 3.15 and
Video 3.5). Furthermore, as the physical examination continues, the
veterinarian should attempt to localize the source of any observed
lameness or visible abnormality (e.g., patella luxation, stifle cranial
drawer sign, elbow pain).

FIGURE 3.10 Weight loss associated with
sarcopenia (muscle wasting) may be confused with
weight gain by the owner if ascites is present.

A review of previous examination notes or itemized assessments
from the SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, and Plan—i.e.,
the entries in the medical record) regarding prior issues can aid in
the clinical assessment. For example, comparing the size of a
subcutaneous mass with previous findings is something owners may
appreciate as a sign of continuity of care and attention to detail,
particularly if the record clearly identifies prior dimensions,
appearance, and location. Measurement of lesions with calipers or a
ruler is good for review and trending purposes (Figure 3.16). The
nearly universal availability of digital photography makes good use of
these tools for the veterinarian and the owner, particularly if digital
images can be attached to the medical record. The front desk staff
can be trained to ask pet owners to videorecord their pet’s clinical
signs at home on their cell phone prior to the appointment if
possible, if the signs are intermittent. This can produce very valuable
information and can shorten the physical examination time
considerably.
Neurologic signs, such as diminished proprioception, diminished
muscle tone, limb dragging, or unusual evidence of pain during
compression of the muscles or manipulation of the vertebral column,
are noted and could require further investigation to point to a
diagnosis (Figure 3.17) (ch. 241). Noting any area that appears
painful is important since it can provide clues to the veterinarian,
and an owner who mentioned pain as a concern will appreciate
seeing that it was acknowledged and examined.
Every seasoned veterinarian has developed his or her own method
of performing the hands-on portion of the physical examination,
derived from experience. For example, many animals are frightened
by a large figure looming overhead and are less anxious when
approached at eye level. I (SJE) prefer to kneel on the examination
room floor to perform the physical examination (Figure 3.7), except
for cats and small- to medium-sized dogs on the examination table. I
find I am better able to perform thoracic auscultation in large-breed
dogs completely and more thoroughly in this manner (Figure 3.18).
Medium-, large-, and giant-breed dogs standing on the floor, rather
than the examination table, are almost always more relaxed, making
it easier to palpate thoroughly while having a good presence with the
pet. Whenever possible, animals should be in the same position
(table or floor; standing) each time they are examined.

FIGURE 3.11 A, Dog plantigrade in stance (R>L)
associated with weakness and pain caused by
multijoint osteoarthritis. Performing a gentle flexion
test on this dog’s right carpal joint made the dog
ambulate awkwardly and with a visible lameness,
suggesting joint pain. B, Cat with flaccid neck
ventroflexion. The veterinarian could lift the cat’s
head with no resistance but the cat was unable to do
so itself, nor to hold the head up without assistance.
The cat was profoundly hypokalemic (K+ = 2.8
mg/dL) at the time.

FIGURE 3.12 Obese dogs (A) (19.5 kg [42.5 lb])
and cats (B) (15.5 kg [34.5 lb]) require an
appropriate medical diagnosis first and then
nutritional discussion based upon the cause (medical
or dietary) of the weight gain. (C) 1.6 kg (3.5 lb)
weight loss brought this overweight pug down to a
healthy weight, resolved most of his respiratory
distress without medication and helped him regain a
normal walking pattern.

Head, Neck, and Skin
After observation, I prefer to stroke the pet to gain a more general
knowledge of the overall body status through touch (

Videos 3.1,

3.6 and 3.7). The body condition score (BCS) is assessed (endsheets

and inside covers; ch. 72), as well as the hair coat. Skin and coat
changes must be evaluated in context of the animal’s living
environment. Indoor pets should not have foreign material in the
hair coat (unless some other pets in the household are both indoor
and outdoor pets). Hair loss can be a clue to cutaneous or systemic
disease and should be noted (ch. 12). Hair loss should be assessed as
unilateral or bilateral, symmetrical or asymmetrical, patchy or
generalized, and pruritic/associated with secondary lesions (e.g.,
redness, evidence of self-trauma) or not. Coat changes may correlate
with thyroid or adrenocortical diseases (chs. 285, 293, and 294).
Skin abnormalities may be better understood with cultures,
scrapings, biopsy, or allergy testing (ch. 83). Fleas, flea dirt, ticks,
and other ectoparasites should not be present. Pets living outdoors
are more likely to have ectoparasites, weather-related hair coat
changes, or bite wounds. In cold regions, outdoor pets may have
white hair at ear tips due to frost bite. As with the indoor pet, an
attempt can be made to find correlations between a skin condition
and the owner’s concerns or other issues. Recommendations can
then be made accordingly. Hair coats with a strong odor of perfume,
skunk, oil, or smoke could suggest to the veterinarian possible
problems regarding allergies, toxic exposure, skin or lung disease,
reactive airways, or an animal that has been in or around a fire with
subsequent smoke inhalation (ch. 33).

FIGURE 3.15 Rhodesian Ridgeback presented
after treatment by the family veterinarian for
generalized muscle wasting and atrophy, joint
swelling, and extremely painful assisted walking.
Note the prominent left zygomatic arch due to
profound loss of muscle mass of the head. The
response to steroid and antibiotic therapy and
physical rehabilitation provided this dog with an
additional 2 excellent years of life with only
intermittent bouts of lameness. Immune-mediated
muscle disease and polyarthritis were assumed to be
the cause of this dog’s muscle wasting and
recumbency at the time of entry to the hospital.

FIGURE 3.16 Measuring skin lesions (or other
palpable abnormalities) provides the owner with an
opportunity to follow up and can be utilized to
compare changes in size, shape, or color to previous
examinations. Utilizing handheld devices to
photograph such lesions and include them in the
medical record is advisable.

FIGURE 3.17 Note the proprioceptive deficit in
the left hind limb in this dog with degenerative
myelopathy. The right hind limb is similarly affected.
This patient underwent thorough orthopedic and
neurologic examinations as the first step toward
determining the etiology of the proprioceptive
deficits.

FIGURE 3.18 Examination of the heart and lungs
in my hands (SJE) in a medium- to large-sized dog is
best done on the floor, where the animal remains less
anxious and provides a better setting for this critical
examination. Others may prefer to do this exam on a
table but whatever you choose, use the same
technique each time.
The skin tent test involves gently pinching a fold of skin on the
animal’s thorax, abdomen, or neck between the veterinarian’s thumb
and index finger, painlessly lifting it 3-5 cm (1-2 inches), and then
releasing it.21 The skin should snap back to being flat immediately,
and a delay is usually attributed to dehydration. However, the result
of the skin tent test should be interpreted in light of other findings in
the patient. In addition to dehydration, age-related changes of the
skin can falsely increase the skin tent (in animals older than 10-12
years) whereas obesity and normal breed variation can decrease the
skin’s ability to be lifted and cause a false negative test.
Swellings in the form of edema or fluid collections are correlated
with other changes. Subcutaneous edema (ch. 30) is identified as

being generalized or localized to one region. In an animal with
subcutaneous edema, it is important to note whether there is also
abdominal distension due to free abdominal fluid, in which case high
hydrostatic pressure (e.g., congestive heart failure) is most likely.
Edema should be described as: painful or not, pitting or not, cold or
warm, and oozing or not (

Videos 3.8 and 30.1).

The head should be examined superficially for hair loss, muscle
wasting (Figures 3.13 and 3.15), swelling, or asymmetry. Pain on
dorsiflexion or ventroflexion or lateral movement of the head and
neck may be indicative of local discomfort such as cervical disc
disease, shoulder muscle disorder, or a more distant issue (ch. 241).
Flaccid neck ventroflexion in cats (Figure 3.11, B) may indicate
hypokalemia (ch. 68), thiamine deficiency (ch. 14), or myasthenia
gravis (ch. 253).
Oral and conjunctival mucous membranes should be moist,
smooth, and glistening. Tacky or dry mucous membranes may be
due to dehydration, but also can occur with local drying, as with
panting (oral) or keratoconjunctivitis sicca (conjunctival).
Conversely, mucous membranes may appear slimy in dehydrated
animals that are nauseated (oral) or with serous ocular discharge
(conjunctival). Color and capillary refill time of the oral mucosa
should be assessed (chs. 25-29 and Figures 3.19, 3.20, and 3.21).
Pallor gives reason to suspect anemia (ch. 57), hypoperfusion, or
hypoxemia (ch. 123); muddy (ashen, pale pink to greyish) mucous
membranes occur with heart failure (ch. 229), pulmonary
hypertension (ch. 218), and various lung diseases (ch. 217); and
cyanosis occurs with right-to-left cardiovascular shunting (ch. 231),
respiratory diseases (chs. 215, 216, and 217), and hematologic
intoxications (Figures 3.22, 3.19, and 3.20) (ch. 138).
I then note the appearance of the oral cavity, pharynx, lips, gums
and teeth (Figures 3.21 and 3.23).22,23 Drooling (ptyalism,
hypersalivation), oral discharge, or malodor (ch. 46) can be
significant and should be noted if present. It is important for the
veterinarian to speak to the owner about the condition of the pet’s
teeth and gums; it also is important for the owner to see, if possible,
any area of concern in the oral cavity (Figure 3.24). Alignment of
the jaw bite (dental occlusion; Figure 3.25, A and B) should be

assessed (ch. 258). The presence of oral mucosal ulcers, mass
lesions, and any discoloration in the oral cavity should be checked.
The teeth are examined for calculus, fractures, displacement, or
discoloration. Abnormalities, including missing or persistent
deciduous teeth are recorded and mentioned to the owner. Drooping
of the tongue to one side suggests a loss of teeth in that part of the
mouth (Figure 3.26). Signs of dental wear due to fence biting or
rock chewing should be noted, as well as any resulting sensitivity.
Gingival hyperplasia, masses, gingivitis, foreign bodies, or ulcers
may correlate with other clinical signs. During the first-time puppy
or kitten examination, evaluation for cleft palate or other congenital
defects is required (ch. 258). With an uncooperative or fractious
animal, examination of the oral cavity can be a daunting procedure.
When the pet resists such an examination, removing the pet from the
owner often allows a more complete examination without difficulty.
Special care is required for aggressive patients and may require
sedation. If ptyalism or a behavioral change is mentioned, concern
for a rabid patient is always paramount (ch. 202).
A complete neurologic examination (ch. 241) is not usually a
component of the routine physical examination unless clinical signs
warrant such. However, a brief examination for cranial nerve deficits
should be included during this portion of the examination. The
posture of the head (e.g., head tilt, Figure 3.27), masticatory muscle
mass and tone, and the appearance of the eyes may be important
clues that there is a neurological problem.
Similarly, a complete ophthalmic examination is not performed on
every patient, but the veterinarian should be able to do so in the
exam room when necessary (ch. 13).24 The globes and the
periorbital region should be assessed for superficial and deep
changes. Ophthalmic sensitivity (Figure 3.28),
squinting/blepharospasm, or any other evidence of photophobia is
noted. Unusual sensitivities are also noted. Lips and facial skin folds,
especially in brachycephalic breeds, may be sources of inflammation,
moist exudates, and a foul odor (Figure 3.29; ch. 33).
Enophthalmos can be a sign of periorbital fat loss or of myositis,
weight loss, cachexia, or a primary ophthalmic process.
Exophthalmos can be caused by orbital disease (neoplasm,
inflammation, arteriovenous malformation), tooth root abscess

(concurrent pain likely when opening the mouth), zygomatic
mucocele, or there may be pseudoexophthalmos due to a shallow
orbit in brachycephalic breeds. Any ocular discharge should be
described as to color, composition, volume, and whether the
discharge is unilateral or bilateral. The examination continues with
assessment for signs of conjunctival color changes, inflammation,
masses, or foreign bodies. Pupillary size, symmetry, and integrity are
noted, as is the pupillary light response, both direct and consensual.
Sensation of the eyelids and the surrounding tissue is observed as are
masses involving the eyelids, noting their size and whether they are
irritating the cornea. Abnormalities that are regularly noted when
examining the eyes include dry eyes; abnormal tearing; corneal
ulcers, especially in brachycephalic dogs and cats; discoloration of
the conjunctiva, cornea, and sclera; and nuclear sclerosis or
cataracts. Corneal lesions should be noted in the record, particularly
the size, shape and depth of corneal ulcerations. Digital pictures of
such lesions may be included in the record for comparison in future
examinations. Specific assessments with Schirmer tear testing,
fluorescein staining (confirm nasolacrimal duct patency with
appearance of fluorescein at the nares), and intraocular pressure
measurement can be performed if indicated. If nystagmus (
Video 3.9) or strabismus (Figure 3.30) is noted, this suggests the
need for a more thorough neuro-ophthalmic examination (ch. 241).

and associated with a BB-shot or thready pulse that
may also be described as quick to rise and quick to

The appearance of the skull, the muscles of mastication, and the
other muscles of the head and neck are noted (Figure 3.31). Owners
can be concerned that a mass has developed on the skull, which is in
fact the external occipital protuberance. Increased prominence is
associated with generalized muscle catabolism (corticosteroid
treatment in dogs, any systemic catabolic state; ch. 18) or specific
loss of temporalis muscle mass (e.g., masticatory myositis; ch. 258),
making the protuberance obvious (Figure 3.32). In puppies,

particularly those with disproportionately large heads, examination
of the fontanelles as a clue suggesting hydrocephalus should be part
of the examination (Figure 3.33). Pain, swelling, or heat of the face
and periorbital regions is noted if present, most often representing
infection or noninfectious inflammation (e.g., peritumoral). More
detailed examination of the eyes, including direct and/or indirect
ophthalmoscopy may be required (ch. 13). In the event that a more
detailed examination is required, dark room adaptation and the
cursory fundic examination can usually be completed without
sedation but time must be allotted. A slower approach will provide
time for iris adaptation (usually about 3 minutes) and a better
ophthalmic examination. Even if the patient is being referred to an
ophthalmologist, the veterinarian should note all relevant findings
and assist in scheduling an appointment (or delivering diagnostic
tests and treatment if there is no referral) as quickly as possible in
the event that it is a serious problem threatening the health of the
eye.

FIGURE 3.23 Chronic dental tartar and gingivitis
is common in middle-aged to older dogs and cats
and should be identified as a treatable problem.
Chronic periodontal disease leads to other medical
problems as dogs and cats age and it should not be
neglected.

FIGURE 3.24 A cat with a granulomatous
sublingual lesion and persistent deciduous teeth
initially presented for loss of appetite, drooling and
an inability to eat. The lesions were biopsied
(pyogranuloma), and the lesions regressed after
removal of much of the affected tissue.
Examination of the ears (pinnae and ear canals) is expected by the
owner and is an important part of every veterinary physical
examination (Figure 3.34). Evidence of ear mites, inflammation,
discharge, or abnormal odor is particularly relevant in the new
puppy or kitten. In adult dogs, it is more common but by no means
absolute to see ear disease in those with long floppy pinnae that
cover the ear canal. An owner may report that a pet has difficulty

eating or chewing when the problem in fact is caused by pain from
one or both ear canals. Aural discharge, unusual “yeasty” odor (ch.
33), or discoloration of the canal tissue may be noted (Figure 3.35;
ch. 82). Owners are likely to notice abnormal conditions of the
pinnae (e.g., aural hematoma). Superficial examination of the ear
canal can usually be accomplished in the examination room without
difficulty, allowing the veterinarian to discuss chronic ear disease
with the owners while showing them any abnormality. Otoscopic
examination is indicated if there is a suspicion of an underlying
lesion in the canal (e.g., causing excessive headshaking or buildup of
otic discharge). Video otoscopy is a preferred technique by some
veterinarians to show the caregiver changes in the ear canal (
Video 3.10; ch. 82). Cats likewise are prone to ear disease,
particularly when they are outdoor cats or in a household with many
cats. Scratching at the ear is likely to leave them with crusts and
excoriations at the base of the pinna. Swabs taken from the external
ear canal and observed microscopically identify ear mites and
Malassezia yeasts. Aural hematomas occur in cats but much less
frequently than in dogs. Careful cleaning of a dirty ear canal is
warranted; however, if it is too aggressive, the tympanic membrane
may be damaged, leaving the patient with a short-term head tilt and
occasionally permanent hearing loss. In either dogs or cats
presenting with significant disease of the ear canal, sedation may be
required to properly clean and evaluate the external ear canal and
the tympanic membrane. Gentle rinsing of the ear canal is strongly
recommended rather than pushing more wax and debris further into
it, to avoid iatrogenic problems. Creeping mites (Cheyletiella) are
another cause for scratching at the neck and base of the head. If the
scratching persists, empirical use of an appropriate topical
parasiticide will be sufficient to quickly kill them (ch. 142). Some cat
owners may be concerned about the normal thinness of the hair coat
cranial and ventral to the pinnae. In the absence of scratching and of
lesions of the skin or ear canal, this alone is neither a problem nor a
condition that requires treatment.
Airflow through the nostrils can be assessed quickly using a
stethoscope and contralateral occlusion of the nares. Otherwise, one
may utilize a wisp of cotton in front of each nostril to assess airflow (

Video 36.2) or watch the pet exhale onto a metal surface (e.g.,
the top of an exam table in most examination rooms) or chilled glass
microscope slide to observe for fogging as evidence of nostril
patency. While seemingly basic, such examinations can be
challenging to perform if the patient is dyspneic and uncooperative
due to difficulty breathing through the nose. The veterinarian’s
familiarity with a normal result through experience will help make
this assessment brief and accurate.
Evaluation of the oropharyngeal region is often limited to external
palpation during the physical examination. The laryngeal region
should be checked for sensitivity, pain, masses, and the gag reflex
(ch. 47). Detection of visible or palpable deformities and monitoring
of the laryngeal apparatus may yet be possible without sedation (ch.
214). Palpation for changes in the salivary glands and the
submandibular lymph nodes is important and it is equally important
to distinguish between these two organs. Enlargement of the
submandibular or sublingual salivary glands is particularly relevant
when there are signs of localized pain or chronic drooling/ptyalism.
Distinguishing between the submandibular salivary glands and
lymph nodes can be challenging. These are both usually palpable but
small under normal conditions. The lymph nodes may be more
superficial and mobile than the adjacent salivary glands, but even so,
fine-needle aspiration of many a palpably “enlarged submandibular
lymph node” has returned cytologic results of normal salivary gland
tissue.

jaws should be evaluated, especially in newly
purchased dogs and cats, particularly if they are
intended to be show animals or used for breeding. A,
A normal bite is shown in this young dog, whereas
(B) this dog has a maxillary brachycephalic bite
(prognathism) that is already impeding bone growth
and formation. The owner should be made aware of
such abnormalities at this time, since in many breeds
of dogs and cats, such a condition would eliminate
them from being shown.

FIGURE 3.26 Drooping of the tongue out of the
mouth, especially to one side in older smaller breed
dogs and cats, occurs frequently. It is commonly seen
after either extraction or loss of major teeth that hold
the tongue in place.
Examining the oral cavity begins by opening the patient’s mouth.
In cats, this can be accomplished by placing the fingernail of the
veterinarian’s index finger between the incisors to prompt the cat to
open its own mouth (Figure 3.24). In dogs, reaching over the
maxilla with one hand allows the veterinarian to press the maxillary
lips inward between the rows of teeth using the fingertips of that
hand, and this pressure can prompt the dog to open its mouth. Often,
the mouth will be open only briefly before the patient wishes to close

it, and the period of examination can be short but essential. Good
lighting conditions (exam lamp, or at least a well-lit exam room)
optimize visualization of oral structures. Mass lesions, evidence of
trauma, mucosal abnormalities, foreign bodies, and evidence of bony
changes should be identified. Palpation of the hard palate may be
performed without holding the mouth open, to identify bony changes
in any animal with chronic mucopurulent or bloody nasal discharge.
In some dogs and rarely cats, pressing down on the base of the
tongue with an index finger when the animal’s mouth is open allows
visualization of the tonsils and oropharynx. While complete
visualization is usually not possible, visualization of the roof of the
mouth, caudal oral cavity (including tonsillar crypts), tongue,
sublingual area, and cheek pouches should be a component of every
physical examination. If there is indication of an abnormality, a more
thorough examination under sedation is indicated. For every sedated
oral/pharyngeal exam, an endotracheal tube should be immediately
on hand in the event of upper airway obstruction during the
procedure. This is particularly necessary in brachycephalic animals
and those with severe upper respiratory distress (chs. 37, 123). A
discussion with the owner in advance of sedation should take place
to determine which steps to take (corrective surgery, tracheostomy,
euthanasia) in the event that intubation becomes necessary and then
persistent airway obstruction makes extubation impossible.

idiopathic vestibular disease, chronic pulmonary
hypertension, and degenerative myxomatous mitral
valve disease.

identifies ophthalmic sensitivity associated

FIGURE 3.29 Moist, foul-smelling skin folds
around the eyes, nose, and mouth occur in all breeds.
Skin fold dermatitis is particularly common in
brachycephalic breeds.
Continuing to the ventral cervical region, palpation of the trachea
may reveal tracheal sensitivity if a cough is induced (

Video 3.11),

which may be the cause for the pet being brought in for an
examination (ch. 34). An inducible cough is a subjective finding that
depends on the amount of pressure applied and it is anatomically
nonspecific, because tracheal (ch. 215), bronchial (chs. 214 and
215), and pulmonary (ch. 216) disorders can cause it. The ventral
cervical region is also palpated for the size and position of the
thyroid glands. Normal thyroid glands are not palpable in dogs or
cats. In the middle-aged to older cat, noting a “thyroid slip” as the

veterinarian gently slides his/her thumb and forefinger along the
trachea, from the thyroid cartilage to the thoracic inlet, best
identifies an enlarged thyroid

(Video 287.2).25 In short-haired

dogs and cats, the external jugular veins may be observed for
pathological distention, which is consistent with right-sided
congestive heart failure (ch. 229). Jugular distension has the
appearance of a jugular vein that is being raised for phlebotomy but
in the absence of manual pressure. Muscular twitching and
transmission of the carotid pulse through the jugular vein (especially
in thin, muscular dogs) are impostors for jugular pulsation. If
spontaneous jugular distension is present, applying pressure to the
abdomen while the patient is in lateral recumbency may induce
further jugular distension due to hepatojugular reflux, indicating
right-sided heart disease or cardiac tamponade as the most likely
causes. Palpation at the thoracic inlet can reveal superficial cervical
(prescapular) lymph node enlargement, crepitus (subcutaneous air
leakage/emphysema), or masses.

normal eye position due to one of many disorders of
cranial nerves or extraocular muscles. In this case,
the ventral strabismus affecting the right eye
required a further neuro-ophthalmic examination to
