Examination of the Thorax
After having observed respirations and thoracic conformation as a
distance, I examine the thorax by touch, trying to gain an impression
of any surface irregularity, notably bumps, lumps, and other
abnormalities. Asymmetry of the thorax (scapulae, muscles, rib cage,
masses, or fat accumulation) should be correlated with signs, as
should kyphosis or sternal deformities. Breathing difficulty can be
associated with changes in the appearance of chest wall movements
(ch. 37). Fluid accumulation in the thoracic cavity (ch. 220),
significant pulmonary disease (ch. 216), and some muscle disorders
may cause the rib cage to feel or appear abnormal. A large cranial
mediastinal mass may make the cranial thorax less compressible in
cats. Congenital thoracic deformities may cause respiratory signs.

Peritoneopericardial diaphragmatic hernia (ch. 235) may be
associated with deformities of the xiphoid region of the sternum,
such that the veterinarian can insert a finger into a rent involving the
caudal sternebrae, and actually touch the beating heart. Other
concerns on initial examination of the thorax may include lymph
node enlargement, swelling (fluid, masses, fat, distention, tympany,
pain), discomfort, and skin abnormalities (changes in the hair coat,
open wounds, fleas, dirt, ticks, or other abnormalities).

FIGURE 3.32 Temporal and masseter muscle
atrophy is associated with immune-mediated
masticatory myositis, chronic corticosteroid
administration, as well as aging in older pets. The
muscles of mastication atrophy. This may cause
difficulty chewing, opening the mouth, pain, and
enophthalmos.

FIGURE 3.33 Examination of the skull may
identify open fontanelles (at the tip of the index
finger), a congenital defect where the bones of the
skull fail to fuse after birth. In young dogs, this may
be associated with clinical signs of hydrocephalus. In
this 12-year-old Chinese Crested Dog, there were no
problems during her lifetime associated with the
open fontanelles. She did present for signs of
unrelated degenerative myxomatous mitral valve
disease at a younger age than would normally be
expected.

FIGURE 3.34 Examination of the pinna is always
important as all forms of ear problems represent a
large percentage of daily clinical practice. This is a
normal pinna but slightly dirty due to external otitis
that required attention (Figure 3.35).

FIGURE 3.35 The routine physical examination is
never complete without looking at the ears and the
external ear canal. This dog presented with a “yeasty”
odor emanating from the ears, along with a waxy
moist debris suggesting Malassezia, which was
confirmed on microscopic examination of a slide
swabbed with the debris from the ear canal.
The veterinarian then palpates the cardiac apical impulse, noting
its location. Normally this is over the left fifth to sixth intercostal
space at the level of the costochondral junction. Deviations are
consistent with pathologic cardiac chamber enlargement, pleural
effusions, thoracic cavity masses or, rarely, situs inversus. Also
important are the heart rate, rhythm, and strength of the cardiac

apex beat, and its synchrony with the femoral pulse palpated
simultaneously. A prominent or excessively strong apex beat needs
to be identified as physiologic (excited or nervous animal) or
pathologic (anemia, outflow tract obstruction, other cardiac disease,
systemic disorder such as pheochromocytoma) and this distinction is
helped by the rest of the physical examination, notably cardiac
auscultation for a murmur.
My preference (SJE) is usually to complete the entire physical
examination before ausculting the heart and lungs (

Video 3.12).

I return to palpating the cardiac apex beat, noting whether there is a
precordial thrill. A thrill is indicative of a loud heart murmur (grade
5/6 or 6/6). Cardiac thrills should be described in terms of point of
maximal intensity (PMI) and timing. It is important to recall that
cardiac thrills indicate substantial turbulence in blood flow, but a
guarded prognosis does not apply to 100% of these patients. For
example, in dogs with myxomatous mitral valve disease, the general
probability of congestive heart failure is higher if the dog has a thrill
(loud murmur) at the PMI, but at the same time, 8% of dogs with a
thrill have only minor (stage B1) disease.26
Cardiac auscultation begins where the cardiac apex beat is
palpable: the veterinarian should place the stethoscope head where
he or she feels the heartbeat. The process of complete auscultation of
the heart proceeds cranially from the cardiac apex to cover all
regions of the heart valves. The veterinarian auscults over the region
of the cardiac apex beat for several seconds, then moves the
stethoscope dorsally (mid-thorax, just dorsal to the costochondral
junction) and auscults there for several seconds, then returns
ventrally but slightly cranial to the previous location and auscults
there for several seconds, and so forth. This alternance from
ventralmost thorax to just dorsal to the costochondral junction for
stethoscope position progresses cranially to ultimately cover the
entire region over the heart (precordium) on the left. The
auscultation for that side is complete when the stethoscope is in the
patient’s left axilla and the normal heart sounds are no longer
audible, which is usually much farther cranially than intuition might
suggest. A complete cardiac auscultation like this almost always
requires extension or abduction of the patient’s ipsilateral forelimb

in order to capture the heart sounds that are best heard in the axilla.
The process is repeated on the right side. In dogs with barrel-chested
thoracic conformations and in cats, the heart needs to be ausculted
over the sternum, from caudal to cranial, as some focal murmurs are
only audible there. Auscultation at the thoracic inlet is valuable for
identifying murmurs that radiate cranially, such as the murmur of
moderate or severe subaortic stenosis. Auscultation over the carotid
arteries has been proposed for the same reason, although the
veterinarian must be careful to avoid applying too much pressure
with the stethoscope over the carotid arteries and in so doing, create
an audible bruit (murmur in the carotid artery) iatrogenically. In cats
and very small dogs, and any small puppy or a kitten, the stethoscope
may cover most of the heart valve regions in one location and only a
general description such as “parasternal” (adjacent to the sternum) is
possible for describing the PMI of a murmur. Cardiac auscultation
should identify the rate, rhythm and presence or absence of a heart
murmur. The first and second heart sounds should always be
present. These sounds indicate the closing of the mitral and tricuspid
(S1) and aortic and pulmonic (S2) valves. During auscultation,
moving the stethoscope cranially should change the proportional
intensity of heart sounds, with S1 being as loud as or louder than S2
over the mitral valve region, to S2 being louder than S1 when the
stethoscope is correctly over the aortic and pulmonic valves. This is a
useful indicator of the completeness of cardiac auscultation. The
third and fourth heart sounds (gallop sounds) are too quiet to hear
normally but when present they suggest structural cardiac disease
that may be substantial (ch. 38). Murmurs provide the veterinarian
with clues as to turbulence within the heart, and their timing, grade,
and PMI allow the veterinarian to create a differential diagnosis for
their cause (ch. 38). In addition, there are other abnormal sounds
including whoops, clicks, ejection sounds, gallop sounds and
splitting of the first and/or second heart sounds that need to be
identified if present (ch. 38). Decreased heart sounds may be a
normal variant (obesity, thick hair coat) or may indicate pleural or
pericardial effusion or hypovolemia.
Alterations of the cardiac rate and rhythm are another irregularity
to note. They are suggestive of either physiologic variation (e.g.,
sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, respiratory sinus arrhythmia)
or pathologic disruptions (electrical conduction block, premature

beats, etc.). There are both primary cardiac and extracardiac causes
for arrhythmias (ch. 230).
Systematic auscultation of the lungs should cover each hemithorax
completely. A proper auscultation requires dogs to be prevented
from panting by having their mouth held closed, and cats to be
prevented from purring. Moving large-breed, anxious, thick-coated
dogs to an area with cooler air or outdoors can reduce the drive to
pant, and holding cats near a source of running water stops purring
most of the time (81% success rate).27 The veterinarian should note
regions where breath sounds are absent (pleural effusion [ch. 220],
pneumothorax [ch. 220], mass lesion [ch. 222]). Loud
bronchovesicular sounds, wheezes, and rhonchi (airway gurgling
sounds) typically are associated with abnormalities of the small and
large airways (chs. 215 and 216). Pulmonary crackles (crepitations,
râles) are associated with interstitial disorders such as pulmonary
fibrosis (usually minimal dyspnea) and cardiogenic pulmonary
edema (usually visible dyspnea, possibly severe). Referred upper
airway sounds can interfere with auscultation and can be normal,
such as with panting, or indicative of partial upper airway
obstruction.

Abdomen and Abdominal Cavity
Progressing caudally to the abdomen, the veterinarian first should
note whether the abdominal wall is pumping rapidly, a possible sign
of anxiety, tachypnea, or dyspnea. Initially, tachypnea, dyspnea, or
abdominal breathing should be observed while standing back from
the pet (ch. 37).
Examination of the abdomen, as with all other parts of the body,
should be performed systematically (

Video 3.13). The

veterinarian examines the abdomen and spinal column
independently. This allows the veterinarian to avoid being misled by
apparent sensitivity in one area that is, in fact, derived from another.
As with the thorax, the abdominal examination begins with
superficial palpation of the abdominal wall, noting asymmetry,
cutaneous or subcutaneous mass lesions, evidence of discharge or
wounds, and evidence of superficial pain. Dogs with chronic airway

diseases like chronic sterile bronchitis can have prominent and
palpable hypertrophy of the external abdominal oblique muscles,
presumably due to chronic expiratory push, analogous to the “heaves
line” of a horse with similar disease. Symmetric enlargement of the
fat pads of the lumbar region (“love handles”) are commonly seen in
an older pet, particularly if it is gaining weight and should not be
confused with subcutaneous masses (Figure 3.36). This finding
needs to be taken in context of the patient’s body condition (ch. 72)
and weight management implemented as needed (ch. 150).
Examination of the mammary glands (

Video 3.14) should be

thorough, moving up and down both right and left chains probing for
masses, irregularities, and evidence of enlarged glands. Enlarged
glands producing small amounts of fluid may be an indication of a
false pregnancy, a near-term pregnancy, or an infection in that gland.
Mammary masses are usually easily palpated but can be confused or
mistaken for subcutaneous lesions. Small masses may not be noted
unless one dedicates a few moments to carefully assess the area.
Masses should be noted as to size, shape, and texture (Figure 3.37)
so that these characteristics can be tracked over time. Hot, ulcerated
or rapidly growing masses always should be considered for surgical
removal.
Distention of the abdomen (ch. 21) requires attention. Four major
causes of abdominal enlargement are free fluid, fat, muscle laxity,
and abdominal organ enlargement (Figure 3.4 and Table 21.1).
Abdominal distension must be assessed in the context of owner
observations and additional factors, including the animal’s age,
breed, sex, neuter status, clinical signs, palpable (ballotable) fluid
collection, pregnancy, neurologic status, obesity and the presence of
masses. The evaluation of abdominal distension begins with gentle
ballottement

(Video 21.1) to determine whether enlargement is

likely to be associated with fluid accumulation or other disorder.
Correlating the findings of this examination with other history and
laboratory tests allows the veterinarian to consider potential causes.

FIGURE 3.36 Large subcutaneous deposits, often
firm, are noted in many older dogs and may be
thought by the pet’s owner to be malignant growths
even when benign.

FIGURE 3.37 Examination of each mammary
gland and the entire left and right chains should be
completed, noting masses, texture, size and any
ulceration present. Size and appearance should be
noted in the record for comparison at the next health
care visit. This firm, irregular nodule is measured
and noted in the record.
Evidence of pain on deep palpation of the abdomen is a significant
finding. However, abdominal guarding and resentment of palpation
is common in virtually all pets being examined (Figure 3.38;
Video 3.15). The veterinarian needs to distinguish tensing of the
abdomen in a normal apprehensive patient from referred spinal

pain, primary abdominal pain, or systemic pain. Triggered pain
impostors are minimized by applying gentle, steady pressure to avoid
eliciting a tense reaction, and moving the fingers slowly, to avoid
anything the animal could perceive as jabbing. Accuracy is further
improved with a gradual approach to palpation that begins with
superficial touch and gradually progresses to deeper palpation. This
portion of the examination requires gentle but firm pressure using
both hands and moving from dorsal to ventral and cranial to caudal.
Adequate palpation includes utilizing ipsilateral fingers in line or
touching with thumbs aligned as the abdomen is carefully traversed.

FIGURE 3.38 Frightened cats will often present
with the pinnae directed dorsally and laterally,
dilated pupils and an anxious facial expression. A
tense abdomen, and resentment of palpation, should
not automatically be interpreted as evidence of
abdominal pain in these cases.
Acute abdomen (ch. 126) needs correlation with laboratory
testing and clinical signs. Pain should be localized, if possible, as
cranial, mid-abdominal, caudal, or generalized. Palpation for masses
and the detection of enlarged viscera comprise an art that is not
replaced by more sophisticated, expensive, and complicated tests.
Pain in the abdomen is a clear indicator for further testing, such as
radiographs, sonographic imaging (ch. 73), and/or laboratory
analyses. It also must be correlated with the clinical history. Malaise,

failure to move or change position, fever, and nausea may be
explained by abdominal or back pain.
It is generally easier to perform a complete abdominal palpation
on cats and smaller dogs than on large dogs. In cats, it is frequently
possible to palpate the small intestine, spleen, both kidneys, colon,
and bladder. In larger companion animals this may not be as easily
accomplished, but enlargement of abdominal organs, masses, and
fluid accumulations should still be apparent.
Palpation of the abdomen is an individually determined technique.
I (SJE) like to examine animals both from behind and from the side.
When examining the abdomen from behind, I am able to palpate free
fluid, one or both kidneys, the small intestine, the colon, midabdominal masses (normal or abnormal), and the urinary bladder.
Diffuse hepatomegaly is palpable as a convex surface protruding
caudally from the costal arch. The spleen is palpable cranially on the
left and it can course caudally or cross ventrally over the midline. In
dogs, palpable splenic masses are neoplastic or nonneoplastic (chs.
21 and 182). In cats, palpation of an enlarged spleen often is a sign
suggesting mast cell disease (ch. 327), lymphoma (ch. 322), or
another neoplastic process. A folded spleen is a common impostor
for an abdominal mass in dogs. Differentiation from other
abdominal masses can be done initially through the physical
examination and later via imaging (ch. 73). Urinary bladder
distention should be defined as normal or due to abdominal disease
or neurological disease (i.e., upper or lower motor neuron). Both
kidneys are not always palpable in healthy dogs; the left kidney is
easier to feel while only the caudal pole of the right kidney might be
palpable, or the right kidney might only be palpable when it is
enlarged or displaced. When bilaterally enlarged, both kidneys in
dogs may be palpated. When an otherwise healthy dog is obese, it
may not be possible to feel either kidney. A very large or painful
prostate in a dog may be palpable transabdominally, and this should
be noted and correlated with clinical signs.

FIGURE 3.39 Lifting the pet up so that the
abdominal organs shift caudally sometimes allows
the veterinarian to be more thorough in palpation of
the abdominal organs or in identifying the presence
of free abdominal fluid that has collected at the most
ventral level.
Lateral palpation provides another perspective regarding any
structure: liver, spleen, bowel, urinary bladder, prostate, etc.
Occasionally it is helpful to have an assistant pick up the pet (Figure
3.39) and allow it to stand on the hind limbs so that the abdominal
viscera or free fluid shift caudally, permitting yet another
perspective.

Rectal Palpation
Rectal examination is a component of palpating the caudal abdomen
that should be part of every physical examination in medium-and
large-breed dogs (Figure 3.40). This may require separating the
dog or cat from the owner to limit squirming or crying. While
examining the perineum, the veterinarian should check the animal
for evidence of constipation, obstipation, or generally dry, hard
stools via abdominal palpation (ch. 51). Such problems lead to
difficulty defecating. The perianal region should be examined for
fecal staining, anal sphincter integrity, masses and, particularly when
straining to defecate occurs, for perineal hernia, either unilateral or
bilateral. Perineal hernias (

Videos 3.16A and 3.16B; ch. 264)

are detected on rectal palpation by laterally deflecting the index
finger immediately after entering the anus (i.e., no farther than the
first or second joint of the inserted finger). If the veterinarian probes
too deeply past that point, this important lesion will be missed.
Rectal prolapse must be differentiated from ileocolic intussusception
because of different etiologies and treatments. Prolapse is associated
with the inability to pass a blunt instrument or digit alongside the
everted viscus per rectum beyond the level of the pelvic inlet.
Perianal fistulas are readily identified on the physical examination
provided the tail can be elevated; however, they are often so painful
that examination of this area is made much simpler and more
comfortable with sedation and analgesia. Perianal masses (Figure
3.41) should be evaluated for changes in size, and appearance.
During this portion of the examination, the tail is checked for skin
lesions and for pain on rotation and extension/dorsiflexion. Animals
experiencing tail pain, and occasionally urinary and/or anal
sphincter problems, should be examined with injury to the tail region
in mind. Tail injuries due to being caught in doors or otherwise
pulled aggressively (more common in the cat) can be associated with
neurologic problems involving the urinary bladder, anal sphincter,
and/or the ability to move the tail. A recent report suggests that
surgical treatment of neurologic bladder dysfunction can be
successful, offering an opportunity beyond the previous, limited
options of tail amputation, converting the cat into an outdoor-only
pet, or euthanasia.28

FIGURE 3.40 Digital rectal examination is
regularly performed as part of the physical
examination if there is reason to be suspicious of
prostatic, colonic, or perianal disease as well as to
examine the anal sacs and sphincter. Palpation of the
perianal region, as shown, is also informative and
may be the only option in cats and small dogs.

FIGURE 3.41 Perianal masses are likely to be
painful, irritated and often covered with stool,
making them difficult to examine without being
gently but well cleaned. This cat presented with an
ulcerated mass just ventral and to the right of the
anal sphincter.
In older male dogs or when signs suggest colorectal dysfunction,
lower urinary tract problems, prostate concerns, or hind end
disorders of an orthopedic or neurologic nature, the findings on
rectal palpation gain even greater importance. With the increased
use of abdominal sonography, palpation gains value because lesions
within the pelvic canal often do not image well. Prostatic
abnormalities are likely to be palpated per rectum in all but larger

male dogs. Correct palpation of the prostate is done with the index
finger of one hand in the rectum while the other hand, externally, is
providing dorsocaudal upward counterpressure at the level of the
caudal abdomen to elevate the prostate gland toward the palpating
finger. This is especially useful for larger dogs and/or the palpator
with a short index finger. A normal rectal examination (ch. 264)
identifies a symmetric, bilobed, nonpainful, rubbery-textured
prostate with a median raphe that clearly separates two lobes (ch.
314). Palpation of the surrounding tissue should evoke no pain nor
reveal any irregularity along the canal wall or the bony pelvic
structure surrounding the gland. The urethra is a thin, flat tube
usually overlying the pelvic symphysis and palpable along the full
length of the symphysis. A thickened, ropy urethra may be felt in
cases of urethritis or transitional cell carcinoma. Rotation of the
palpating hand 180° so the palm points dorsally then allows the
veterinarian to palpate the aortic trifurcation and aortic pulse, and
may rarely allow the palpation of sacral (sublumbar) lymph nodes if
very enlarged. Rotation of the wrist maximally in the other direction
(45-90° past midline) is warranted, to identify masses or other
abnormalities within the pelvic canal.
With the index finger still in the rectum, the veterinarian palpates
the anal sacs at the 4 and 8 o’clock positions to determine whether
they are enlarged and if they can be readily expressed. The ease with
which these sacs can be expressed, and the type of fluid released, aid
in the evaluation for anal sac disease. Many owners worry
considerably about “full” anal sacs, and it is important to identify
problems if they exist. It could be necessary to alter a diet’s fiber
content in some dogs to improve natural anal sac compression and
expression with each bowel movement. Serious anal sac disease does
occur in cats, especially if overweight or obese, although anal sac
disorders in cats are less common than in dogs. Expression from
outside the anus is preferred over transrectal expression in small
dogs and cats (Figure 3.40). The rectal mucosa should be neither
rough nor painful and no blood should be noted on the examination
finger when removed from the anus. It is important to note the
presence of mucus or blood specks (red or black), particularly if there
are complaints regarding stool appearance at home.

Genitalia
The testicles and scrotum should be examined in the intact male for
pain, skin lesions, and variability in testicular size and shape. The
scrotum of a neutered male should be examined for masses or
ulcerations. The presence of one or no scrotal testicles in an intact
male is an important diagnostic finding (cryptorchidism). Retention
and/or neoplasia of one or both testicles may correlate with the
presenting clinical signs. In the puppy examination, the presence or
absence of testicles may indicate a congenital defect and must be
identified to the pet owner because the purchase agreement may
need to be reviewed. It is important to note the presence of an
inguinal (flanker) testicle because showing and breeding would not
be allowed, and the pet may be infertile. Explanation of such a
finding for the new puppy owner is relevant, particularly if the pet
was purchased for breeding purposes. Being a heritable defect,
neutering will eliminate the ability to transmit this problem to
offspring.

FIGURE 3.42 Normal discharge from the prepuce
of a male adult dog (arrow). Owners often are
disturbed when they notice this discharge and may
believe there is an infection in the penis or urinary
system.
Changes in and around the prepuce may be identified. Preputial
discharge (smegma), a small amount of a thick yellowish fluid that is
normal, might not be readily seen unless the pet is placed in lateral
recumbency (Figure 3.42). Extruding the penis to appreciate
changes in the mucosa or structure of the penis and prepuce (
Video 3.17) may explain abnormal findings of pathological preputial
discharge or a history of chronic licking. The presence of the os penis
in dogs should allow the penis to be easily and painlessly extruded
and evaluated: with the dog in left lateral recumbency, for example,
the veterinarian grasps the base of the penis and prepuce together in
his/her right hand and pushes the base of the penis (and os penis)
cranially while using the left hand to retract the prepuce caudally
over the penis. The prepuce needs to be pushed back completely,

meaning the bulbus glandis should be exposed, for a complete
evaluation of the preputial cavity. In the male cat (

Video 3.18),

evaluation of the penis and its surrounding area is important,
particularly in cases of suspected feline lower urinary tract disease.
Neutered tomcats have small to no “spines” present on the penis
(Figure 3.43), in contrast to the obvious spines seen in intact
tomcats.
In females, examination of the vulvar region is important in
determining the presence of discharge, the state of estrus, and the
presence of skin conditions that may be responsible for licking or
irritability of the hind region (ch. 101) or urinary tract infection.
Asking questions that relate to the timing of the last or latest heat
cycle may elicit insightful information relevant to pseudopregnancy
or pyometra. It is worth remembering that not every spayed female
has been completely spayed and estrous cycles and stump pyometra
remain on the differential diagnosis until proven otherwise. Vaginal
swabs taken to evaluate the state of the mucosa are a quick, easy way
to determine the presence of pus or red cells in the canal as well as
the hormonal status of the bitch (ch. 101). Examination of the hood
region (

Video 3.19) may provide a cause for odors and irritation

due to the accumulation of mucus or pus, and for recurrent urinary
tract infections. Females usually tolerate gentle palpation of the
vulva and vestibule, regardless of neuter status or stage of estrous
cycle. However, in healthy spayed dogs, vaginal palpation (

Video

56.1) is not a routine component of the physical examination. Some
disorders are quite painful, requiring additional restraint or sedation
for digital examination.

FIGURE 3.43 Penis of a neutered tomcat showing
no spines on the penile surface in contrast to an
intact tomcat.

Spine and Limbs
Prior to examining the limbs, particularly in cases of lameness, the
examining veterinarian evaluates the mobility and flexibility of the
head and neck (

Video 3.20; ch. 241). Particularly in larger

breeds of dogs, cervical conditions can cause neck guarding, failure
to thrive, nondescript signs of acute painful crying, lameness, and
malaise. Intermittent or recurrent problems may not be immediately

obvious on the physical examination. Animals that are difficult to
examine or painful may be better evaluated utilizing sedation and
analgesia. In cases that do not have an obvious abnormality, it is
often wise to suggest to the owner that they videorecord the distress
at home and send it in, so the veterinarian can see and evaluate the
results. This may help immediately identify a lesion or deficit not
observed in the exam room.
Hind limb pain, weakness, and ataxia may be signs of a
musculoskeletal or neurologic disorder, such as cervical,
thoracolumbar, and/or lumbosacral disease. The physical
examination should include compression of the tissues along the
spinal column and the lumbosacral region to assess for signs of pain
(

Videos 3.21A, 3.21B, 3.21C and 3.21D). Sensitivity alone may be

inadequate grounds for making a diagnosis and may only point to
one of several conditions in the differential diagnosis. Neurologic
deficits, including altered postural tone, proprioceptive deficits, or
muscle atrophy, assist the process of defining the differential
diagnosis for disease states (Figure 3.44;

Video 3.21; ch. 241).

Evaluation and examination of the limbs, including bilateral
femoral pulses, lymph nodes, joints, paw pads, and interdigital
regions, can reveal important clues to the presence of medical
problems. Joint disease, often silent or less than immediately
obvious, is easily overlooked unless specific attention is paid to joint
swelling or discomfort (Figures 3.45 and 3.46; ch. 177). Ch. 32
provides a summary of the assessment of joint effusion and pain, and
ch. 31 describes the orthopedic examination. Nutritional and
hereditary causes of osteopenia and pathologic fractures are
discussed in ch. 162. The veterinarian should flex each of the
patient’s carpi with moderate force to assess for signs of joint pain
that would otherwise not be recognized (chs. 31 and 32); animals
with nonspecific signs, especially suggesting intermittent neck or
back pain, may be found to have polyarthritis (ch. 177). As noted at
the beginning of this chapter, it is important to observe cats with any
gait deficit or suspicion of neurologic or musculoskeletal dysfunction
out of their carrier, on the floor in a safe, escape-proof room. Many
cats will not ambulate in the veterinary clinic, and it is good to
suggest that the owner videorecord such abnormalities at home

when the cat is less inclined to remain static (

Video 3.22).

Swelling, heat, and pain in one or more joints can explain many
signs, including lameness, malaise, and fever. Swelling of the
adjacent subcutaneous tissues provides reason for further
evaluation. Claudication, painful or non-weight-bearing lameness
directs the veterinarian to the affected limb. Thorough examination
of the limbs for differentiation of warmth, pulses, or swellings may
yield a direct clue to the cause of lameness. Embolization is usually
associated with pain when the embolism is arterial (ch. 238) in
contrast to acute paresis with fibrocartilaginous embolism (FCE; ch.
251). Noting a disparity in the circumference of the joints, muscle
mass of the limbs, or the presence of atrophy in the shoulders or
muscles of the scapula may more readily help to identify a source of
lameness (Figure 3.47).

FIGURE 3.44 The patient presents with evidence
of pain, difficulty walking and hind limb weakness.
His body posture (hunching of the spine—kyphosis)
suggests pain in the limbs or back. Deep pain
perception is present, as are patellar and withdrawal
reflexes. He is a candidate for a complete
neurological and orthopedic examination to establish
a differential diagnosis.

FIGURE 3.45 Joint swelling may be associated
with a single joint or multiple joints. The swollen left
tarsal joint carries a multitude of differential
diagnoses and should be approached as such unless
an obvious cause is identified at the time of the
physical examination (ch. 32). This enlarged joint
was firm, cool and only minimally painful on
palpation and was associated with chronic
degenerative joint disease. The discoloration of the
hair implies that the dog is chronically licking at his
enlarged joint suggesting that sensory discomfort is
present.

FIGURE 3.46 Measuring an enlarged joint to
compare with the opposite limb may assist in
following progression of the disease and also helps to
identify to the owner the initial disproportionate size
of the joint. Owner follow-up is more likely to be
successful if they recognize the difference in joint
size themselves.

FIGURE 3.47 The discrepancy of the size of the
left tarsal joint in comparison to the right provides
the veterinarian with more likely evidence as to
where the lesion is. Likewise, atrophy of muscle mass
on one side of the body compared to the other may
be an indication of disuse or underuse because of
pain or nerve damage.
Deep palpation of the bony tissue provides information relevant to
both medical and orthopedic problems. Considering the age and
health of the animal is relevant, because some diseases are specific to
young, growing dogs (panosteitis, hypertrophic osteodystrophy),
whereas others would be expected in older, overweight dogs (cranial
cruciate rupture, osteoarthritis, bone cancer). Cats are usually easier
to palpate than dogs, and larger-breed dogs may be difficult to
examine without sedation. Prior to sedation and clinical studies, it is
important to gait the animal to evaluate pain, lameness or
proprioceptive deficits at a walk and a trot (

Video 3.5). It may be

advantageous to discuss the benefits of sedation or anesthesia with

the owner for a more thorough physical examination, diagnostic
imaging, and/or joint tap (arthrocentesis) (chs. 87 and 32).
Palpation of the hips and evaluation for coxofemoral disease must
distinguish this from lumbosacral and stifle disorders. A cranial
drawer sign and meniscal clicking are indications of internal stifle
abnormalities such as cruciate ligament tears, sprains, and meniscal
tears. The opportunity to evaluate these findings in greater detail
may need to be conducted with the patient sedated. When a limb is
to be imaged, the veterinarian should exercise the benefit of
evaluating both limbs to evaluate the significance of the changes
noted by comparing symmetry. Some orthopedic problems,
including patellar disease in small to mid-size dogs, are often
identified without sedation.

FIGURE 3.48 A small lesion on the footpad of this
Boxer dog was identified. Interdigital and footpad
cysts, granulomatous masses, neoplasms, ulcers and
foreign bodies should always be considered when
unidentified lameness is noted.
No lameness examination is complete without evaluation of the
paw pads and interdigital regions. It is of paramount importance to
examine these tissues carefully for infiltrating problems, foreign
bodies, interdigital cysts, tumors, or other paw pad lesions (Figure
3.48). Lengthy claws, sometimes so long that they curl around and
re-enter the skin, can be a cause of significant lameness, easily
diagnosed by observation and then treated with toenail trimming.

Completing the Physical Examination
Every hospital has its own set of digital or paper records (ch. 2). This
is the time to complete a well-written medical record. The traditional
SOAP method provides the entire hospital and others with your
record of the physical examination, history, findings, and the plan for
moving forward with the pet’s care.
No physical examination is complete until the results are listed in
the examination report and an assessment is made of the findings.
The veterinarian should identify in the records his or her
recommendations for proceeding with the case. It is here that the
owner or caregiver can once again participate. The veterinarian
needs to summarize the findings, note the pertinent points, and
identify how care might proceed. Noting the findings alone without
recommending a course of action does not complete the process. The
veterinarian should also note in the record, in addition to the
subjective and objective findings, the likely differential diagnoses
and tentative clinical assessment. A definitive diagnosis need not be
made at this time but identifying the most plausible possibilities
helps to portray a thought process in progress. The owner must be
informed of the possible courses of action, the advantages and
drawbacks of each, and the estimated cost of such work. If the
prognosis is potentially poor or guarded, the veterinarian should
discuss this with the owner at this point and note in the record that
this has been done. Owners who fail to “hear” bad news or who later
recall a much more optimistic picture than what was really discussed
may be very surprised to see that the veterinarian had written the
discussion about it in the record one or more times during record
keeping. From the outset, regularly discussing serious findings with
the owner ensures better practitioner-client communication. In the
plan, the veterinarian should identify the course of action to be
followed so that he/she or another veterinarian may continue the
examination process one step at a time if that is how the owner
wishes to proceed. Recommendations for further evaluation noted
along with the owner’s response is important. Estimates provided for
care should become part of the medical record as well, including
owners’ responses to them. Medical records should be time- and
date-stamped with additional commentary provided and date or time
of follow up discussions also recorded. From a medical-legal point of

view, keeping the owner informed and up to date is necessary for
maintaining good doctor-client relations and communication.
Commentary of this nature need not be extensive but should be
thorough enough to be a complete record of what was seen, done,
and recommended.

Client Information
The Physical Examination of the Dog and Cat
Except under emergency situations, the two most important parts of
the visit to your veterinarian (DVM is a term indicating doctor of
veterinary medicine that can include many other abbreviations
depending upon the school and country where the doctor trained to
become a veterinarian) includes asking about the history and the
physical examination. Despite the fact that you may describe the
signs that your pet is exhibiting, it is important for the veterinarian
to fully examine the dog or cat so that he/she is familiar with all of

the body organ systems and their potential for relating to the
problem(s) described.
A thorough history needs to be taken so that the doctor can define
what areas of the body are necessary to pay specific attention to.
Often, while the owner is able to describe a single or multiple signs,
the history will lead the DVM to examine multiple organ systems to
help locate the initiating cause of the signs described. Examples of
this includes excessive thirst or water drinking that might arise from
any disorder within the entire urinary system as well as other
metabolic and anatomical defects outside the kidneys that frequently
cause increased thirst and urinating (diabetes is an example, as is the
administration of some drugs).
Usually the DVM will be concerned about the most prominent
features the pet is being presented for; seemingly unimportant
information can be left out that would provide the doctor with hints
as to the cause of the clinical signs. An example would be travel
outside of your non-heartworm region and the dog not being
protected against heartworms or travel to places where certain
infectious diseases may be more prevalent than where you live at
home, e.g., leptospirosis, a contagious disease involving multiple
body organs.
After taking the history the DVM will want to examine your pet.
Usually the examination is very thorough but sometimes the signs
are sufficiently specific that the doctor will go directly to that area to
understand what the problem is; an example is an acutely lame dog
that was out running the previous day and now is holding one of the
rear legs up, not placing weight on that limb and showing signs of
significant discomfort and pain in the stifle (knee region). A specific
diagnosis may be suspected and then the DVM can follow through to
be sure that other organ systems are well so that safe sedation can be
given to further examine the knee (or other body part). The same is
true in an emergency situation such as a dog becoming acutely
paralyzed, requiring immediate care including a vascular catheter, a
multi organ blood examination and medications to prevent shock
and swelling of the spinal cord. Once stabilized then the doctor will
return to completing the examination to look for other changes of
significance. The same is true in cases of suspected or known
poisoning where it is essential to either remove the ingested poison
or to neutralize it before permanent damage to vital organs occurs

(i.e., rat poison, snail bait or antifreeze ingestion). These compounds
can be fatal if not treated quickly.
The routine physical examination should where possible be
completed in a quiet area so that the pet is as relaxed as possible
during a visit to the clinic. Your veterinarian will want to observe the
pet to look for significant weight change, skin appearance or the
presence of parasites (fleas) that might relate the signs reported.
Some problems are more obvious and easier to detect than others
(e.g., chronic ear wax and infection) but that does not make them
easier to treat. Those of a chronic nature require more thorough
treatment that can only be determined during the physical
examination. An example, otitis (ear infection) might resolve with a
mild cleaning of the ear canal but a chronic otitis may involve
significant injury to the tissues of the ear canal requiring sedation
and evaluation and treatment, a more time consuming process
including more aggressive home care.
After a superficial examination of the skin, hair coat, general
appearance and weight of the pet, the doctor may want to observe
any gait abnormalities (if lameness is a problem) or he/she may
proceed with a thorough examination of the body systems beginning
at one end of the body, examining the different tissues and organs.
An example would be to examine the oral cavity for mucous
membrane color for signs of inadequate oxygenation to the body
parts, poor dental hygiene, a foreign body or growth in the mouth or
under the tongue. Abnormal breathing sounds from the nasal region
or fluids emanating from the mouth or nostrils would be another
point where the DVM may stop to further evaluate these to
determine a potential cause for such changes. Proceeding from head
to tail, the doctor will palpate the region of the larynx (or voice box),
the neck and the thyroid glands for signs of tissue enlargement.
Likewise there are multiple peripheral lymph nodes that can be
enlarged due to infection, inflammation or cancer.
Continuing the examination, the chest (thorax) will be examined,
manually first and then with a stethoscope to listen for changes in
the heart sounds (murmurs, irregularities, abnormal sounds) and the
lungs sounds. Abnormal breathing sounds are not normal.
Evaluation of coughing can also be performed at this time since often
the windpipe (trachea) may be sensitive, allowing the doctor to
initiate a cough. Weight changes may affect the animal’s ability to

breathe comfortably as well. Excessive weight is unhealthy and
restrictive to normal breathing.
Palpation of the abdomen (belly) is very important as the liver,
stomach, spleen, kidneys, bladder and multiple other organs are in
this cavity and clinical signs may point to changes within these
organs. Likewise the intestines make up the bulk of the tissue in the
abdomen, and when vomiting, diarrhea or chronic intestinal signs
are present it may be possible to feel irregularities in these tissues,
giving the DVM the opportunity to focus on that area for further
examination (x-rays, blood, urine tests and ultrasound) where the
clinician can look inside the body non-invasively and characterize the
tissues as normal or not.
This brief information sheet cannot fully describe the entire
physical examination; however, it may help to introduce the client to
the reasons for a thorough evaluation. Based upon the history
provided and the physical examination, your veterinarian will then
make recommendations regarding the care of your pet. Most often
this is straightforward and the animal may be sent home with
medications and instructions for home care. Other situations may be
more complex and the DVM will identify these problems to you and
make suggestions as to what can be done to further care for existent
problems and how they may be approached. This is the part of the
examination that requires full participation of the pet keeper and the
veterinarian. Hopefully you understand what has been identified;
you should be able to discuss this with your veterinarian and be able
to ask relevant questions that he or she can explain. If you are
uncertain or have further questions, please be sure to ask your
veterinarian. The veterinary support staff should also be able to help
in this regard but it is important that you are informed of the process
being provided to care for your pet.
Stephen J. Ettinger (Laguna Beach, California), Edward C.
Feldman (Davis, California), and Etienne Côté (Charlottetown,
Prince Edward Island, Canada)

Why Every Clinician Needs to
Incorporate Evidence-Based Medicine
into Their Practice
One of the largest challenges facing today’s veterinarian is
attempting to stay current amongst the rapidly increasing and
changing veterinary literature. Additionally, despite the wealth of
available (and accessible) information for veterinarians,
incorporating this information into the day-to-day clinical decisionmaking process can be difficult. Further, attempting to do so when
there is limited or conflicting veterinary literature (i.e., no clear,
established answer) can be even more challenging—and stressful.
Evidence-based veterinary medicine (EBVM) provides the
framework and tools to address these various challenges, yet EBVM
is often poorly understood and is minimally utilized by veterinary
practitioners. Some veterinarians may believe that when they speak
to colleagues about challenging cases, consult a discussion board, or

perform an internet search on a topic, they are practicing EBVM.
Although these practices are elements of EBVM, they fall far short of
all the practical aids that EBVM has to offer to the busy and
dedicated clinician. Along these lines, practitioners may believe
EBVM is too complicated (and time-consuming) to warrant its
inclusion in day-to-day practice. However, the EBVM framework and
key concepts are basic, easy to follow steps that every practitioner
can implement for the purpose of improving their practice.
Incorporation of EBVM will save time, assist in decision-making, and
result in optimized outcomes for patients and clients.
Today, information is readily available to everyone—clients
included. This accessibility (and client accountability) further
increases veterinarian ease (and need) for EBVM decision-making.
In 2019, a manifesto, “EBVM for better health,” was proposed and
endorsed globally by many veterinary institutions. The creation and
overwhelming endorsement of this manifesto highlights the strong,
perceived need for further incorporation of EBVM in daily clinical
practice.1

What is Evidence-Based Veterinary
Medicine?
EBVM can be defined as the use of the best relevant evidence in
conjunction with clinical expertise to make the best possible decision
about a veterinary patient.2 Central to the EBVM process is a
structured approach, incorporating the individual circumstances of
the patient and client, values of the client, and appreciation for the
many forms of evidence (and variability in strength of evidence)
when making clinical decisions.
The EBVM process can be distilled to five key steps—termed the 5
A’s (Table 4.1)3—Ask, Access (acquire), Appraise, Apply, and Assess
(audit). The process starts and ends with the patient. It is important
to remember that evidence obtained through the EBVM process does
not by itself make a decision, but rather informs and supports
decisions regarding a patient. An online module is available that

guides clinicians through the EBVM process and provides additional
information and practical examples (cases).4

The Five Steps in the Ebvm Process
1. Ask an Answerable Clinical Question.
The EBVM process starts with formulating a clinical question arising
from a patient (e.g., prognosis, diagnosis, treatment, prevention). As
an example, “Should I prescribe an antimicrobial (e.g.,
metronidazole) for my otherwise clinically well canine patient with
acute idiopathic diarrhea to decrease time to resolution of clinical
signs?” (Table 4.1).
As the wording of the clinical question forms the basis for the
EBVM process, it is strongly encouraged to use a particular format
(termed PICO(T)—outlined below and in the provided example
[Table 4.1]) in developing a clinical question. Using the PICO(T)
format encourages a well-developed clinical question that will assist
with a focused literature search (step 2 [Acquire] in the EBVM
process) that generates evidence for specific clinical knowledge
needs, i.e., for the patient or client.
• P: Patient/Population/Problem. What is the group of patients
to which the current patient belongs? This would include
relevant clinical characteristics (e.g., signalment, primary
problem, geography). The aim is to include an appropriate
level of patient detail (if too specific, it may be difficult to
locate evidence related to your case; if too vague, you may be
overwhelmed with evidence not related to your case).
• I: Intervention/Exposure/Diagnostic test/Prognostic
factor/Prevention you are considering for your patient. Are
you considering prescribing a drug, ordering a diagnostic test,
recommending a surgical procedure, or vaccine?
• C: Comparison of intervention/exposure (e.g., reference
intervention) by which the intended intervention (“I” above) is
compared. What is the alternative to “I”? Are there two (or
more) different drugs, therapy regimens or diagnostics
between which you are trying to decide?

• O: Outcome of interest to patient, client, you. Is your primary
objective to eliminate/reduce clinical signs, improve function,
performance, quality of life, or increase survival time?
• T: Timeframe relevant to your patient/client. Is it short-term
(days to weeks) or long-term (years, lifelong)? This is an
optional component of PICO as not all clinical questions may
require a “T.”

2. Access (and Acquire) Evidence to Help Answer the
Clinical Question.
This step can be the most challenging for clinicians as many of us
were not taught these techniques. We have all used internet searches
in one form or another and may feel our current searching
techniques are adequate for EBVM needs. However, without a
systematic, proven search strategy, it is impossible to know if a
search that produces minimal evidence is due to an absence of
existing evidence or is simply due to performing a poor search.
Further, non-systematic searches can be difficult to focus and result
in retrieving a high number of irrelevant results. To improve
confidence and focus in search results, the following steps can be
followed (Table 4.1)5:
• Use the developed PICO(T) to identify key search terms.
• Identify additional terms (synonyms) for each search term.
• Create a search string by combing the terms with connectors
[OR between synonyms; AND between different
concepts/topics—components of the PICO(T)] and place into a
literature search database.
There are a number of reliable search databases available to
clinicians. Each database is populated with literature specific to a
given discipline; PubMed (Medline)
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) and CAB Direct
(https://www.cabdirect.org/) are the most commonly used for
clinical veterinary medicine. Individuals should become familiar with
the database(s) best suited for their needs, noting specific shortcuts
and “tricks,” such as searches of keywords vs. subject headings (e.g.,
MeSH in PubMed), wildcards/truncation (e.g., canine∗ returns

canine and canines), and limits (e.g., date range, language). General
internet search engines are discouraged (including refined engines
such as Google Scholar) as these are difficult to impose search limits
and prone to bias by previously performed searches by the user
(“filter bubbles”), often resulting in a high number of results poorly
aligned with the clinical question.

3. Appraise the Acquired Evidence in an Unbiased,
Systematic Manner.
The strength of available evidence is often highly variable (i.e.,
ranging from opinions to well constructed evidence summaries, such
as guidelines or consensus statements). Veterinary professionals
must be able to differentiate between the varying strength of
evidence levels. Additionally, they must understand that low levels of
evidence (e.g., opinions, textbooks) should generally have a lower
contribution towards clinical decision-making, while higher levels of
evidence (e.g., appropriately conducted randomized controlled trials)
should have more impact on decisions. The strength of evidence for a
given clinical question is directly related to the type of evidence
(Figure 4.1), quality of the evidence (e.g., strengths/weakness in the
studies) and how well aligned the evidence addresses the clinical
question.

Types of Evidence
Evidence ranges from opinions and textbooks (low level) to
evidence-guided summaries, such as consensus statements and
guidelines (high level) (Figure 4.1). In veterinary medicine, the
reality is that not all types of evidence will be available for a given
clinical question.
The reader is likely familiar with most types of evidence
(summarized elsewhere as needed)6-8; however, there are a few
relatively newer types of evidence that deserve mention (Figure
4.1). These include summaries (e.g., consensus statements,
guidelines) that integrate the best available evidence to provide a
range of evidence (and ideally strength of evidence rankings) about
management options for a given health problem. A number of such
summaries are currently available, including position

statements/guidelines from national and international veterinary
organizations.9-13 Evidence syntheses (e.g., systematic reviews,
meta-analyses) summarize the available evidence on a topic through
a formal search and appraisal of the primary research.5,8 These
should not be confused with narrative reviews, as these types of
reviews do not follow the formal search/appraisal methodology of
evidence syntheses, and are at a greater risk for biases, and are a
lower level of evidence. Synopses of studies, sometimes referred to as
critically appraised topics (CATs), are evidence-based abstracts of
primary studies. This type of evidence (CATs) has become very useful
for clinicians through the unrestricted online access of frequently
published (and regularly updated) “Knowledge Summaries” and
“BestBETS for vets,” both of which are focused on common clinical
questions.5,14,15

FIGURE 4.1 Hierarchy of the strength of evidence
that may be available when acquiring and assessing
evidence. Summaries: evidence-based consensus
statements, guidelines. Syntheses: systematic
reviews, meta-analyses. Synopses of studies:
evidence-based abstracts of primary studies (e.g.,
critically appraised topics). RCT, Randomized
controlled (blinded) trial.
All levels of evidence are useful, and it is important to
systematically incorporate these varying levels of evidence into the
EBVM process to aid clinical decision-making. As an example, this
textbook (as is true for all textbooks) represents a relatively low level
of evidence. However, textbooks serve as an important entry point
for a succinct summary of information on a topic and contain a
bibliography that represents a selection of references from an expert
in the field. Applying EBVM principles to each chapter allows the
reader to optimize and grow their practice acumen from the material
as new studies are published that alter clinical decision-making.

Quality of the Evidence
Although there is an inherent hierarchy in evidence type, even
amongst peer-reviewed articles there is great variability in the
quality of published studies (e.g., sound methodology, results clearly
presented without bias, conclusions supported by results, all forms of
bias limited). As an example, one study evaluating the methods of
randomization in 114 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published
in five veterinary journals found 7% did not use appropriate methods
and 47% did not report the method used.16 As effective
randomization is crucial to a successful RCT, these findings highlight
the importance of critical literature evaluation when reviewing
evidence. A high evidence type with many weaknesses may be
internally evaluated by a reader as weaker evidence than a wellconstructed low evidence type study. Several reader checklists have
been developed to assist individuals in critically evaluating the
literature.17-20 Use of these checklists should be incorporated into
the EBVM process.

4. Apply the Best Evidence.
This is done by combining the available evidence (i.e., that which has
been accessed/acquired [step 2] and appraised [step 3]) with other
relevant information about the individual case/client to make and
act on the best decision for this unique patient. For example, after
review of the identified evidence (two RCTs21,22) addressing your
clinical question (metronidazole administration in a dog with
idiopathic diarrhea [Table 4.1])3 you and the client elect not to
administer an antimicrobial due to potential health risks and
absence of clear benefits.

5. Assess (Audit) Your Practice.
Evaluate your EBVM performance with this patient, critically
evaluating the outcome of the decision, along with benefits to the
patient and client. Additionally, audit your practice actions beyond
this one patient. This would include retrospectively/prospectively
checking your actual practice “actions” against “best” evidence-based
practice.

The goal of EBVM is to systematically and appropriately
incorporate evidence into clinical decision-making to optimize
patient and client outcomes. Clinical experience and expertise
remain vital components in the decision-making process but should
not be overshadowed by higher types of evidence; EBVM and clinical
experience should complement each other towards improved patient
(and practice) outcomes. For the EBVM process to be optimized,
clinicians must learn to incorporate the 5 EBVM steps into their
decision-making process. Once comfortable with the process,
clinicians will find EBVM to be efficient and note a reduction in
patient management errors and broaden their awareness and
comfort with the available veterinary literature. This will provide
clinicians and clients with greater confidence in patient decisionmaking, and optimize individualized outcomes for patients, clients
and clinicians.

Chapter 5: Biomedical Statistics and
Veterinary Literature
John D. Bonagura, and James B. Robertson

This brief chapter is directed to the clinician wanting a non-mathematical overview of basic statistical
concepts and procedures. It is written to foster critical reading of published literature. For
straightforward explanations of statistics and related errors, the textbooks of Motulsky,1 Campbell,2
Glantz,3 and Fields4 are recommended. Some useful web resources and links to the extensive reviews by
Bland and Altman (in the British Medical Journal) and a series in Deutsches Ärzteblatt International
are listed in Table 5.1. Some basic steps involved with evaluating a study design and data analysis are
summarized in Box 5.1. Additionally, clinical and preclinical investigators should be familiar with
guidelines relating to the statistical reporting of research as summarized at EQUATOR network,
CONSORT, and STROBE-VET.5-8 The nomenclature associated with experimental design and
inferential statistics involved with hypothesis testing and regression slightly differs across the biologic,
social, and physical sciences. Some relevant terms for clinicians are italicized in this chapter. Unfamiliar
definitions can be found through online searching (Table 5.1).

Concepts and Definitions
Research data are analyzed through the application of statistical models or tests. One can envision a
statistical model as a mathematical (algebraic) expression that uses symbols and mathematical
operators to relate the predictor (independent) variables to the outcome (dependent) variables.4 Much
as a realistic model toy car resembles the actual item, the best statistical models predict the outcome
data while yielding the smallest (unexplained) error. An ideal statistical model incorporates the smallest
number of needed predictors to explain the outcome (parsimony). The statistical test selected is based
largely on the study design and characteristics of the independent and the dependent variables. Deciding
on which study variables to include in a model depends on biologic issues related to the study questions.
Treatment or exposures are frequent independent variables in clinical studies. Thus, when investigators
report that a t-test, analysis of variance ( ANOVA), linear regression, or a chi-square test of association
was performed, they are explaining the statistical model selected. If the wrong statistical test is selected,
the reported conclusions might be invalid.

Data sets demonstrate central tendencies and distributions. These can appear normal (bell-shaped) or
be skewed to the left or the right. Named distributions include the normal or Gaussian, lognormal
(often mistaken for a normal distribution with outliers), binomial (based on heads-or-tails outcomes),
and the Poisson observed with count data.1,9 One of the first steps of data analysis involves generating
summary or descriptive statistics and graphs. This involves plotting the raw data, inspecting and testing
data points or residuals (the difference between data points and mean values) for distribution,
identifying any skewness or kurtosis, calculating central tendencies (the arithmetic or geometric mean
and the median), and quantifying the sample distribution. Beyond actual data, test statistics such as Z,
t′, F, and chi-square also exhibit unique distributions, related in part to sample size. Typically, the
extreme 5% of values for the probability distributions of a statistic defines statistical significance.

Null Hypothesis Testing and Statistical Significance
Research studies are initiated to address observations or questions pertinent to disease pathogenesis,
diagnosis, staging, treatment, outcomes, or prevention. A research hypothesis (in statistics: the
alternative hypothesis, HA) is generated based on clinical experience, ideas, controversies, or other
theories. However, this hypothesis is in opposition to the statistical or null hypothesis (H0) of no
difference, which constitutes the basis of null-hypothesis significance testing (NHST).1-4 A common
medical scenario involves sampling and comparing groups of patients exposed to different treatments or
disease-altering factors such as a diet, carcinogen, drug, or surgical treatment. The research goal (HA) is
focused on identifying samples derived from truly different populations, such as the populations of
untreated versus treated hypertensive patients (Figure 5.1). Accepting the HA requires that one reject
the H0 within some specified probability or P-value, most often set at P<0.05, although this convention
is arbitrary. Failing to reject the H0 indicates insufficient evidence to consider the samples as different.
In this regard, the P-value “reflects the measure of evidence against the null hypothesis.”10 In contrast,
rejecting the H0 supports the research hypothesis of a true difference between the groups (i.e., different
populations). The probability of erroneously rejecting H0 and calling the groups different (when they are
not) is termed the Type I or alpha error. This probability—as it is not a certainty—assumes some value
between 0.0 and 1.0. For instance, a P-value of 0.02 indicates that if 2 groups were truly not different,
observing a difference between means or medians larger than that found in the study would only occur
2% of the time. Thus, using a significance cutoff of 0.02 indicates a Type I error would occur only 2%
(one-fiftieth) of the time. A focus of NHST is setting an arbitrary level of statistical significance and
controlling the false positive rate (alpha error) for differences in either direction (a 2-tailed test)
(Figure 5.1). Sometimes the Type I error is focused on 1 direction (a 1-tailed test) and this is acceptable
if a difference can only occur in that direction (or if the directional difference is the only focus, as with
sudden death). The NHST approach can seem backwards, but it is an essential feature for defining
statistical errors. Bayesian theory and inferential modeling offer alternatives, ignoring the binary
reject/do not reject NHST approach, while also considering pretest probabilities of a condition plus
other pertinent factors.11

Statistical Power
The trade-off for maintaining the Type I error at alpha=0.05 (or less) is a higher chance for a false
negative discovery rate. This represents a failure to detect a true difference between samples derived
from different populations and is called the Type II or beta error. It relates to the statistical power of a
test (Figure 5.1, bottom panel), where statistical power is a proportion equal to (1 − beta).3,10 Low
statistical power is a major issue in veterinary medicine, where small sample sizes with wide biologic
variability are common; these 2 conditions make a Type II error more likely. The predetermined power
for detecting a difference between outcome variables (ideally power ≥0.8 or 80%) should be reported
along with the assumptions that were made in that calculation. Statistical power depends on setting the
alpha error (0.05) and estimating the population variability in dependent variables from past studies.
The investigator must state the size of the detectable difference or treatment effect; this is a clinical
decision. Power is also reduced by attempts to find small, statistically significant effect sizes (or
differences) between groups. The key point is that a failure to find differences might simply indicate low
statistical power.1-3,10 Before a reader accepts an abstract conclusion of “no significant difference” or “no
treatment effect,” the power of the hypothesis tests should be assessed, graphical and tabular data
studied, and potential for Type II errors considered.

Point Estimates and Variability
Biologic sampling aims to estimate an otherwise unknown population parameter for a stated variable
through the selection and testing of individuals (or specimens) with specific characteristics of that
population.1-4,9,10 As an example, investigators might want to know about blood pressure (BP) and its
variability in the population of healthy, 4 to 8 year-old cats compared to an otherwise similar population
of cats with subclinical kidney disease. Such comparisons are often done by comparing the group means
(the average values in a sample) or medians (the middle values). These are termed point estimates of the
true population parameters.9 Although subtracting the difference between group means or medians is
clinically relevant, simple arithmetic differences in the sample means can stem from the vagaries of
random sampling. To exclude this possibility, within a defined probability, variation within and between
the samples must be quantified. Sample deviations, sums of squared differences, variance and
standard deviation (SD) are statistical terms describing related methods for quantifying
variability.2,9,12,13 These measures of variability are used in statistics employing linear models such as
linear regression, t-tests, and ANOVA. Estimates of variance components are also essential to linearmixed procedures. Thus, for meaningful statistical comparisons, the variability within different samples
must be considered along with their point estimates. Repeated sampling of a population rarely yields
identical values for the mean and SD. This uncertainty of the point estimates is often expressed by the
standard error of the mean (SEM) or by the related 95% confidence interval (CI) for the mean (or
median). This is in contrast to the SD, a statistical parameter describing individual data variability
(variance) within a normally distributed sample or population. Samples with a larger SD indicate
greater variation between individual data points, as does a wider interquartile range when reported
around a median (useful when data are not normally distributed). Importantly, the sample SD is much
greater than the SEM, but these parameters are related as SEM = (SD/√n), where n is the sample size.
Therefore, a large SD when combined with small sample sizes causes greater uncertainty about the point
estimates, making it more difficult to reject the null hypothesis of no difference.

Research Variables
Research studies deal with variables,1,9,11-13 a quantity or data item capable of assuming some set of
values (Table 5.2), and that can be measured, controlled, or manipulated in a research study. They are
included as independent (predictor) or dependent (outcome or response) variables in the statistical
model. Variables can be named (categorical or nominal), ranked (ordinal), or numeric (discrete or
continuous). Independent variables are manipulated by the investigator in experimental studies, but are
coincidental in observational studies. Dependent variables are measured or calculated. Investigators
should focus a data analysis on the main outcome variables. The inclusion of multiple independent
variables in a study can complicate the research design, statistical analysis, and study conclusions. A
shotgun approach that incorporates too many independent and dependent variables increases the
likelihood of both false positive (Type I error) and false negative (Type II) errors. Such approaches can
also entrap a reader in the minor outcomes, potentially missing the proverbial forest for the trees.
Additionally, independent variables can demonstrate interactions with each other that cloud the
interpretation of results.4 A recurring concern in the veterinary literature is the apparent disregard of
independent variables exhibiting multi-collinearity.14 For example, if one tries to correlate blood
viscosity to independent variables packed cell volume and hemoglobin concentration, it is likely that
each will exhibit significant predictive properties as they are strongly related (collinear) to each other.
This has been observed, for example, in studies of canine mitral valve disease when the collinear left
ventricular and left atrial dimensions are used as predictors. Typically, only one predictor survives the
multivariate analysis to be retained in the model. However, this does not mean that the other predictor
was not significant. The influence of multiple predictors, and the order in which they are entered into
the multiple regression equation, can yield widely disparate results. Another issue in multiple regression
is over-specifying a model with too many independent variables. While debated, a rule of thumb is to
include (at least) 10 to 20 subjects for each independent variable in the multiple regression
equation.15,16 Testing for collinearity and scaling the number of predictors are important considerations
when performing multiple or proportionate hazards regression. Confusing the characteristics and

statistical treatment of ratio, interval, continuous, and ordinal variables is also relatively common
(Table 5.2).1

Study Designs and Statistical Tests
To address a research hypothesis, a study design is needed and a statistical model (or test) is selected
based on the predictor and outcome variables and data distribution.1-4,12,13 This design should address a
discrete number of specific aims or objectives related to the hypothesis (Box 5.1). Unfortunately, many
veterinary studies meander, trying to evaluate too many independent and dependent variables using too
few subjects. Disappointment often results, caused by a complicated study design with insufficient
statistical power to find any true differences.Analytical studies in veterinary medicine are usually
classified as observational, experimental, or clinical trials, which can be observational or
experimental.1,2 Some general nomenclature related to clinically related research studies and reports is
summarized in Tables 5.3 and 5.4. Studies that analyze previously collected data are called
retrospective while those that collect new data in a planned manner are termed prospective. Clinical and
experimental studies involving therapy should be blinded (masked) to investigators and participants and
prospective because confounders are better controlled by randomization to treatments. Small,
retrospective case-control studies are often flawed, because establishing balanced, randomized groups is
nearly impossible.
Many textbooks and reviews focus on formal study designs such as “randomized blocks,” “Latin
squares,” or “split-plots,” and the reader is referred to additional resources for more information on
these. Common terms used in clinical research include cohorts, case-controls, and cross-sectional study
designs. Cohort studies involve groups that are defined based on an exposure to a risk factor or
treatment; these subjects are followed prospectively to an outcome and analyzed. The attributable risk is
calculated as the difference in outcome proportions within the exposed group. The relative risk is
calculated as the ratio of the two proportions between treated and placebo, or exposed and unexposed
(Table 5.4A). As with other effect sizes, CIs are calculated around the relative risk, and ideally the
number of animals needed to treat to prevent an event is determined.1,17 In contrast, in a case-control
study, the groups are identified as diseased or as unaffected (controls) and the investigators look
retrospectively to key factors that might have influenced the observed outcomes (Table 5.4B). These
studies depend on finding suitable historical controls, which can be challenging and often inaccurate due
to unmeasured confounders. Statistical treatment involves calculating the odds (ratio) as: odds = [odds
of exposure in affected cases/odds of exposure in unaffected controls] or the ratio of the probabilities.
Since the number of controls can be altered, the calculations of relative risk and odds will not always
yield the same results.1,17 In cross-sectional studies, the data are collected at the same time. In contrast,
longitudinal studies are observational studies wherein data are collected over time.
The selection of a statistical test can be viewed simplistically as the intersection of study elements,
including: (1) the number of study groups; (2) the type and number of independent variables or
predictors; (3) the measurement scale used for the dependent variables; (4) the distribution of the
dependent variables (or residuals); and (5) the number of measurements obtained per subject.1-3,12,13
These considerations lead to selecting the most relevant statistical model. Models that are more
advanced also consider various random elements and hierarchical designs. The statistical analysis
logically follows from these aspects of the study. One important consideration relates to handling
longitudinal or correlated data.18 Related samples, typically longitudinal or repeated measurements
within the same subjects, must be treated differently statistically as these designs defy the assumption of
independence of sampling (Table 5.3).
Generally, the reader or reviewer of a scientific paper can consult a textbook of statistics1-4,13 to
determine if an appropriate parametric or nonparametric model has been applied to the data (Tables
5.3 and 5.4). Approaches can vary. Consider a comparison of different antihypertensive treatments in 2
groups of cats with chronic kidney disease selected using the same criteria. The cats are randomized to
receive 1 of the 2 treatments and reassessed 3 weeks later. Suitable predictor and response variables are
selected (Table 5.2), BP data are collected, and the results tabulated, graphed, and analyzed through a
statistical test. Depending on the study focus, different but reasonable approaches could be undertaken.
A simple approach for comparing BP at the study’s end could involve Student’s t-tests for independent
groups (or a comparable Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon rank-sum test for non-normal data). A more

complicated and informative approach could involve a fixed and random-effects,13 linear-mixed
procedure comparing BP changes over time, differences in BP between the 2 treatments, and the impact
of baseline serum creatinine (a covariant) on treatment results. Readers should expect reporting
investigators to specify precisely what statistical approaches and corrections were applied in their data
analysis. Furthermore, if multiple comparison testing was performed, suitable statistical
