There are other considerations. We want results that are generalizable to the intended population.
This might not occur if only small convenience samples are obtained, or if only cats with extreme values
of hypertension are studied because rechecks of BP would likely show a reduction towards the true
population mean regardless of treatment (regression to the mean). Furthermore, although P-values
offer a probability estimate for detecting statistical differences between groups, significant P-values
falling just below 0.05 are frequently not reproducible.19,20 Even in the setting of a “highly-significant”
P-value (for example, P<0.005), the absolute differences between mean or median values for the
treatments and the 95% CI of the difference tell more about the clinical significance of the results.1,10,21
This assessment is made by the investigators and readers; it is not entirely a statistical matter. Similarly,
wide 95% CIs for point estimates or for differences between groups, especially approaching 0 (or 1.0 for
hazard and odds ratios) can indicate marked sample variability or small sample sizes, offering a lower
“confidence” about the repeatability of the study results. One practical check involves reviewing
quantitative features of graphs, figures, and tables. These are often more useful for assessing the clinical
impact.

Common Errors and Pitfalls of Data Analysis
Scientific abstracts provide an efficient repository for scanning research studies, but are limited to
identifying papers that should be read fully before deciding if the study conclusions should alter clinical
practice. Results reported as “statistically significant” are frequently of little clinical importance or else
limited in their generalization to other patients.1,9,10,19-21 Results reported as “not statistically
significant” often suffer from low statistical power or inappropriate statistical modeling and are
therefore inconclusive. Observational studies are especially prone to misleading conclusions related to
confounders or retrospective study designs—limitations compounded by small sample sizes and
overblown statistical treatments. It can be argued that observational studies are better evaluated
through perusal of the tabular and graphical presentations and by considering alternatives to NHST
such as propensity scoring and Bayesian analysis.22Pocock and colleagues21 have listed 4 key steps in
data analysis, namely: “(1) Displaying results in tables and figures; (2) Quantifying any associations (e.g.,
estimates of treatment differences in patient outcomes); (3) Expressing the uncertainty in those
associations by use of confidence intervals (CIs); and (4) Assessing the strength of evidence that the
association is ‘real’ (i.e., more than could be expected by chance) by using P values (statistical tests of
significance).” Within and beyond these 4 steps are pitfalls that can weaken the value of an
experimental, observational, or clinical study as summarized in Table 5.5.

Ultimately, consumers of scientific literature must decide if a published study simply demonstrates a
trend or yields a more conclusive positive or negative result sufficient to alter clinical practices. Our
assessment of available literature should be based on many factors, not simply statistical results.
Nevertheless, sound study design and statistical treatment of the data are critical aspects to addressing
the aforementioned questions. Understanding principles of biostatistics, appreciating common errors
and pitfalls in design and data analysis, and assessing results within a clinical and biologic context are
essentials to becoming a critical reader of our literature.

Pain Medicine is Integral to The Practice
of Good Medicine
This chapter’s position in the first section of the textbook reflects
how fundamental pain assessment and management are to the
practice of good medicine. Dramatic changes in cultural attitudes
about the moral status of companion animals and advances in pain
neurobiology have focused attention on pain management as both a

welfare imperative and a client demand. Pain, as a domain in the
practice of medicine for all species, has been an underrecognized and
undertreated public health problem1 for decades, leading to elevation
of pain as the fourth veterinary vital sign.2 Between 20% and 38% of
dogs presenting to veterinary teaching hospitals were identified as
painful in a series of cross sectional studies,3-5 making pain a very
common reason to seek veterinary care.
The World Small Animal Veterinary Association (WSAVA)
Guidelines for Recognition, Assessment, and Treatment of Pain
characterized pain management as “our moral and ethical duty to
mitigate this suffering to the best of our ability.”2 Globally,
veterinarians voice an overwhelming belief in the importance of pain
management and pain prevention in companion animals (for
example, 99% of surveyed UK and French veterinarians),6 solidifying
pain management as fundamental to veterinary practice.

Why Treat Pain?
Treatment of pain achieves important medical goals, besides
fulfilling the ethical and professional obligation to prevent and
relieve suffering of animals. In contrast to the common, but undue
concern that treatment of pain is risky, the dangers of avoiding pain
management are not well known. Pain has a reciprocal relationship
with biological and emotional stress, as both cause and effect. Pain
can result from emotional distress, besides clearly causing it, because
anxiety and fear lower the nociceptive threshold (i.e., stimulation
needed to activate pain receptors) and amplify pain perception. Pain
also produces biologic stress—an attempt to preserve bodily
functioning in the face of environmental, emotional, or physical
threats to homeostasis.7 Untreated or undertreated pain causes
neurohumoral, immunological, and hematological effects.8 The
pathophysiologic consequences of pain can include increased cardiac
work and oxygen demand, vagal inhibition, hypoxemia, hypercarbia,
atelectasis, ileus, nausea, vomiting, oliguria, thromboembolism,
fatigue, sedation, and fear.8 Many of these effects are due to pain’s

ability to stimulate an autonomic response. Additionally, pain causes
dysfunction in the immune system due to neuroendocrine-mediated
pathways.9 Poorly treated pain increases complications, delays
recovery, increases costs, and prolongs hospital stays in people8 and
veterinary patients.6,10
Recent attention has been paid to the relationship between pain
and behavior problems,11 an intuitively obvious connection (ch. 11).
A consensus among behavior experts is that suspected pain should
be treated before a behavior problem rather than waiting until
behavioral therapy fails.11
Possibly the most important reason to treat acute pain promptly
and comprehensively is for prevention of chronic pain syndromes. A
history of pain, particularly under-/untreated pain or pain early in
life, is the only modifiable factor in the development of debilitating
and difficult-to-treat chronic pain and persistent post-surgical
pain.12,13 Exposure to undertreated pain also has negative behavioral
and cognitive impacts on animals.13
Effective pain management is undoubtedly beneficial to veterinary
patients. However, it may also be beneficial to the veterinarian, in an
indirect but important way.14 Attention to, and relief of, patient
suffering generates positive feelings about practicing and reduces
workplace ethical distress.

Physiology and pathophysiology of
Nociception and Pain
The globally used International Association for the Study of Pain
(IASP) definition of pain is: “An unpleasant sensory and emotional
experience associated with, or resembling that associated with,
actual or potential tissue damage.”15 A functional categorization of
pain types into 3 distinct entities (Figure 6.1) helps clinical
understanding of this broad definition: Nociceptive pain, or the
protective warning system that generates avoidance behaviors from
potentially damaging noxious stimuli; Inflammatory (or acute)

pain, or the protective and adaptive pain that occurs after tissue
injury and assists in healing; and Pathological pain (including
neuropathic pain and dysfunctional pain), or chronic pain that is
maladaptive with no protective function.16 Note that pathologic
chronic pain is not simply inflammatory pain that persists beyond
expected healing or a defined length of time.16,17 Inflammatory pain
is characterized by hypersensitivity to peripheral noxious stimuli,
while pathologic or chronic pain is a disease state of the nervous
system itself, uncoupled from peripheral disease, and characterized
by altered processing of neural signals.16,18 Chronic pain can appear
after tissue damage is healed, without tissue damage, or without
known etiology.19 The implication of this pathophysiologic sequence
is that a detectable peripheral lesion may be minor or non-existent,
challenging the veterinarian looking for a cause.

FIGURE 6.1 Pain classified into 3 main
categories. From Woolf CJ. What is this thing called

pain? J Clin Invest. 2010;120(11):3742-3744.
Pain perception results from the heavily modified summation of
complex processes at multiple neuroanatomic, subcellular, and
molecular levels. The basic steps are: nociception, transduction of
the signal into an action potential, transmission of the information
from the periphery to the spinal cord, modulation of the information
within the spinal cord including regional exchanges within the dorsal
horn, ascending and descending projections from the spinal cord to
the brain and lastly, perception of pain.18,20,21 At each step, the
encoded information is so extensively altered (including by cognitive
and emotional processes22) that there is rarely a linear relationship
between noxious stimulation and pain perception23 (Figure 6.2).
Nociception is the biological process by which thermal,
mechanical, environmental, and endogenous noxious stimuli (i.e.,
those capable of producing tissue damage) are detected by unique,
bidirectional sensory receptors called nociceptors.18 Nociception is
required for pain perception, but does not always lead to an
experience of pain.16 Both peripheral nervous system (PNS) and
central nervous system (CNS) components of the pain system have
life-long, enormous capacity for change (plasticity) in response to
noxious stimuli.18,23 The cellular and molecular mechanisms of
plasticity both explain the profound difference between acute and
chronic pain18 and provide specific therapeutic targets, since many
endogenous and exogenous analgesics act on descending modulatory
pathways.22 The bidirectional signaling of nociceptors changes in
response to noxious stimuli (i.e., peripheral sensitization) while
central sensitization results from similar changes in the spinal cord
and brain.16 Initially, inflammatory pain provokes allodynia (i.e.,
when normally non-noxious stimuli cause pain) and hyperalgesia
(i.e., noxious stimuli produces more intense pain than before) which
normally resolve, but can persist and amplify as nervous system
dysfunction in chronic maladaptive pain.18
The always subjective experience of pain has a sensory (intensity)
and an affective (unpleasant or aversive) dimension.24 Recent work

in human22 and animal subjects25 has revealed that cognitive and
emotional states have deep, complex, and reciprocal influences on
pain. For example, positive emotional states and certain cognitive
processes can decrease pain, but negative emotional states can
increase pain. All of these processes work in concert, in feedback
loops, to modify the perception of pain.22 Because of pain’s highly
subjective nature and affective dimension, perception of pain IS
pain.

FIGURE 6.2 Simplified steps in pain signaling
from nociception to perception.Clockwise from
upper left: transduction to perception. NMDA, Nmethyl-D-aspartate. From Russo MM,
Sundaramurthi T. An overview of cancer pain:
epidemiology and pathophysiology. Semin Oncol
Nurs. 2019;35(3):223-228.

Pain Assessment
Animal pain assessment is often assumed to be difficult and
inaccurate, although there is evidence that this mindset is changing.6
Veterinarians still report assessment as a major obstacle to adequate
treatment of pain,26 citing difficulties ranging from self-doubt to
patients’ hiding of signs. Pain is a subjective experience, so without
self-reporting, absolute accuracy cannot be expected. However,
practitioners’ familiarity with animal behavior and solid
observational skills provide the most important tools needed for pain
assessment by proxy. The basic requirements for accurate pain
assessment are knowledge of species-specific normal behavior, an
understanding of pain physiology, and observation. Pain provokes
physiological, behavioral, and emotional responses,10 so
consideration of all 3 factors improves the precision of pain
identification.
Nociception and pain processing are evolutionarily well conserved,
so a reasonable starting point for pain identification is the
“anthropomorphic method”: an assumption that events known to
cause pain in people are likely to also cause pain in animals.25
Despite the practicality of this approach, clearly different behavioral
and emotive components of pain compel a species-specific
refinement of this assessment method.10 Pain identification in
animals requires consciously using common clinical observations
collected from every patient that the veterinarian often notes
subconsciously. Pain can be indirectly expressed by abnormal
behaviors and/or the change in, or absence of, normal
behaviors.10,27,28 Any prior knowledge of the patient’s posture, facial
expression, reactions to handling, vocalizations, and gait are
tremendously helpful, because recognition of deviation from normal
is easier. For example, noticing that a cat no longer makes a greeting
noise when approached could be a subtle but important clue to
discomfort.
By letting go of common assumptions, veterinarians can access
their existing skill at pain assessment:

• Trying to observe postures and behaviors without
simultaneously interpreting. Using a “beginner’s mind”29 to
re-see the familiar.
• Not assuming that pain behaviors are consistent between
patients or even within the same patient at different times.
• Rejecting common myths and prejudices about animal pain.
Evidence shows that patients who can be distracted may still
be painful, that vocal and/or pediatric2 patients might be
feeling more pain than average, not less, and that anxiety and
fear make pain worse.
Pain assessment should be included in every patient
evaluation.2,28 See accompanying videos for examples of pain
assessment in animals with post-operative abdominal pain (
Video 6.1), long-bone fracture (Video 6.2), bite wounds (Video 6.3),
and systemic infection (feline infectious peritonitis; Video 6.4). By
performing pain assessments, veterinary staff can quickly gain
knowledge of pain behaviors (Box 6.1) and build skill. These
assessments can be brief and include only pain intensity (for
example, numerical rating scales) or validated, multidimensional
tools designed for acute/post-operative pain assessment like the
Glasgow Composite Pain Measuring Scale27 (chs. 44, 125) or
chronic pain (e.g., Canine Brief Pain Inventory27). See Figure 6.3
for a simple approach to acute pain identification. Links to canine
and feline pain scoring tools can be found in the references for this
chapter.2,10,30,31 Regardless of the method chosen, regular and
frequent assessments will maximize the utility of the results.
However, the observer matters: variability between observers can be
high in the clinic setting, home caregivers provide more accurate
reporting of chronic pain,27 and surprisingly, pet owners may not be
able to accurately predict behavioral responses to acute pain.32
Helpful factors to consider when assessing pain include
evolution,33 socialization, personality,32 and the full integration of
emotion, cognitive state and pain in the brain of vertebrates.22

Evolutionary history as a predator or prey species influences how
much a patient will try to hide pain from an observer. Socialization to
people significantly impacts showing (or maybe experiencing) pain
in animals. For example, well socialized dogs may display less pain
behavior when handled. Personality, or the individual variations in
behavioral response that are constant over situations, may have
some impact on pain behaviors32; however, there is no evidence that
assumptions about breed-specific pain tolerance are scientifically
valid.34 Emotion and pain perception are inextricably linked both in
neural locations and processing,35 providing complex interaction.
This means that anxiety, fear, and distress directly impact pain
levels. It also means that non-painful causes of distress, like nausea,
a full bladder, hunger, frustration, and restrictive bandages, can
mimic signs of pain. Attention to potential causes of non-painful
distress will improve assessment and treatment accuracy.

Key Points for The Identification of
Chronic Pain
The diagnosis of chronic pain is hampered by the typical outpatient
setting of a single snapshot observation. Fortunately, veterinarians
have a useful skill available: history taking (ch. 2). Home caregivers’
long-term observations on changes in mobility, social behavior, and
other determinants of daily function provide the best evidence for
chronic pain.36 All patient assessments should include a screening
question for chronic pain (e.g., “Can you tell me about any changes in
your pet’s ability to move or do normal activities like groom or
play?”) (ch. 1). Further investigation can be done by using an already
validated questionnaire for caregivers or adapting one for
standardized use in practice; see references for available
options.27,37-39

Treatment of Acute and Chronic Pain
Pain management becomes an art form in the adjustment of the
therapeutic plan to each individual patient’s unique and subjective
pain. General goals of acute pain management are: (1) maximize
comfort, (2) normalize physiologic homeostasis, (3) reduce the risk
of future chronic pain and (4) minimize adverse effects of pain
management. Although counterintuitive to the usual practice of
medicine, effective pain management requires a willingness to treat
pain without certainty it exists. Without purely objective ways to
confirm the presence of pain, veterinarians should put trust in their
observation of the response to treatment as a practical way to
diagnose pain. See Box 6.2: Key Principles of Pain Management for
broad concepts.

Making A Treatment Plan
To meet these goals, a flexible treatment plan is needed. Treatment
plans should be updated regularly, guided by pain assessments,
especially when response is inadequate, or when unexpected

responses are noted. Start with standardized strategies for mild,
moderate, and severe pain for efficiency, then consider patient
specific factors (see the WSAVA pain guidelines for protocol
examples2). Considerations when individualizing a plan are species,
age, general health and body condition, temperament, pain history,
expected course of treatment, and inpatient or outpatient status.
Incorporation of caregivers’ capabilities is needed since financial
constraints, compliance and expectations will impact plan success.
Becoming comfortable with typical responses to commonly used
therapies provides some degree of predictability and an ability to
identify atypical outcomes.
For moderate to severe pain or difficult-to-treat pain,
multimodal analgesia improves effectiveness while reducing risk
of adverse effects and subsequent chronic pain. The rationale is that
combining therapies with diverse modes of action (drugs and/or
non-pharmacological therapy) is synergistic because each treatment
targets different events in the pain signaling system.2 Multimodal
analgesia can also reduce risk of adverse events by decreasing the use
or dose of drugs with higher risk.2
Some obstacles to pain management persist in the form of
misinformation or little-known ideas. For example, the idea that the
benefits of limited activity from withholding analgesia outweigh the
negative consequences on healing has long been discredited, but it
endures in practice.2 Not well known is the idea that chronic disease
may respond better to treatment if associated chronic pain (a disease
state itself) receives directed therapy as well.

Analgesic Therapy: Nsaids and Opioids
Systemic analgesia using non-steroidal anti-inflammatory
drugs (NSAIDs) or opioids, given orally or parenterally, is the
traditional foundation of pain management. Significant differences
exist in the licensing and regulation of specific drugs in different
countries. Supply chain problems unpredictably complicate selection
of analgesics, so the veterinarian should consult local veterinary
associations and regulatory bodies for up to date information and to
be prepared with knowledge of alternatives for standard protocols.

BOX 6.2 K e y Princ ip l e s of Pain Manage me nt
• Reject the idea that patients need to prove they are in pain
before initiating treatment.
• Make an individualized treatment plan for every patient.
• Use response to treatment as a guide for adjustment of the plan.
• Start treatment promptly since pain is more resistant when
treatment is delayed.
• For better response, don’t start gradually, especially if pain is
severe or longstanding.
• If typical treatment fails, reassess for different causes, adverse
events and compliance.
• Don’t forget to look for signs of visceral pain with abdominal or
thoracic cavity disease.
• Dose analgesics “to effect.”
• Consider lower dosages of analgesics for geriatric patients.
• Anything other than simple, mild to moderate intensity acute
pain will benefit from multimodal therapy.
• Use preventative analgesia to reduce post-operative pain and
persistent post-operative pain.
• Employ non-pharmacological methods to enhance treatment
success.
• Treat expected pain from procedures and trauma proportionally
to expected intensity and duration of pain.
• Don’t neglect treatment of pain in common conditions, such as
otitis externa, severe dermatitis or pancreatitis.
• Make use of information about prior pain and anesthesia
episodes to tailor therapy.
• Remember to consider and prevent pain during and after
diagnostic procedures.
• Recognize that chronic pain states may consist of several types of
pain.
• Look for changes in the source(s) of pain as chronic pain and/or
chronic disease progresses.

• Discontinue NSAIDs if GI adverse events occur, but not
necessarily other analgesics, whose side-effects might be safely
managed.
• Rule out unresponsive visceral pain before blaming GI signs on
analgesics since they may look the same.
NSAIDs are highly effective against acute, and sometimes chronic,
pain due to their powerful anti-inflammatory effects (ch. 143).
NSAIDs are widely used because their efficacy far outweighs the risks
in the majority of cases.2 All NSAIDs work via inhibition of
inflammation, but by varied molecular mechanisms of action with
different adverse event profiles. Consequently, one NSAID may work
better in a particular patient than another. NSAIDs can provide
effective analgesia when given short-term or as single doses, thereby
avoiding much of the risks of chronic use.
Well-known adverse effects of NSAIDs include gastrointestinal
(GI) impacts ranging from nausea to perforating duodenal ulcers and
idiosyncratic hepatotoxicosis. Systematic review did not yield an
incidence of NSAID adverse events, although vomiting and diarrhea
is the most common adverse event in dogs.40 However, the data do
support some practical suggestions to minimize toxicosis: use only
NSAIDs approved for use in the target species, do not administer
with other anti-inflammatory drugs or corticosteroids, and avoid
using in patients with pre-existing GI, hepatic, or renal
disfunction.40,41 Fortunately, hepatotoxicosis appears to be rare and
usually idiosyncratic (i.e., unpredictable and not dose dependent),
and renal toxicosis is uncommon.40,42
Opioids are naturally occurring (opiates), synthetic, or semisynthetic chemicals that bind to opioid receptors in the PNS and CNS
and inhibit pain signals.2,43 Each opioid has a specific profile of
interaction with different types of opioid receptors (e.g., mu, kappa,
and delta types) leading to variations in levels of sedation, analgesia,
and other diverse drug effects.43 Opioids are widely used in
perioperative and emergency/critical care settings in veterinary
medicine, and less so in chronic outpatient pain management, except

perhaps for the synthetic opioid tramadol. Overall, the human opioid
addiction crisis has discouraged chronic use in veterinary patients
due to diversion fears and legal prescribing obstacles, as have global
shortages.
Current understanding of opioid neurobiology has led to novel
delivery methods (e.g., transmucosal and transdermal), new clinical
uses, and reduction in unwanted effects. For hospitalized patients,
injected opioids (starting doses, e.g., methadone 0.2-0.7 mg/kg IV or
IM in dogs and 0.1-0.6 mg/kg IV or IM in cats, or hydromorphone
0.025-0.1 mg/kg IV or IM in dogs; in cats, buprenorphine 0.02
mg/kg IV or PO transmucosally) are usually given as bolus doses.
Although IV constant-rate infusion (CRI) use is often relegated to
patients with severe pain, it may help avoid adverse effects in
patients with less severe pain. Combining opioids of different
functional classes often occurs in veterinary patients, but the effects
are unpredictable.2,44 Layering of opioids from the same class (i.e.,
oral or bolus dosing of morphine in addition to a fentanyl CRI) can
allow for fine-tuning of pain control and adverse effect management.
Although oral tramadol is used commonly, evidence to support
efficacy in dogs is poor44 and palatability in cats often prevents use.
Other oral opioids may have a valid role in chronic and cancer pain
management,45 but clinical data are sparse, so use has been
anecdotal only.
Opioids have few or manageable cardiovascular effects, are largely
reversible, and are readily titrated to effect.2,44 Common side-effects
include vomiting, nausea, salivation, hypothermia, panting,
respiratory depression (with high IV doses) and bradycardia.2 Less
common side-effects include urinary retention, hyperthermia,
constipation and very rarely, opioid-induced hyperalgesia.46 Perhaps
the most common adverse event is excessive sedation or dysphoria
that delays discharge from the hospital. Predictable sedation and
mental depression should be avoided because they can lead to the
potentially life-threatening (i.e., euthanasia-triggering)
misperception of deterioration by a family member. Knowledge of
the patient’s past reactions to analgesics and sedatives helps with
dose adjustments. If oversedation is a common problem, it is
prudent to start with lower dosages of opioids and sedatives as a rule.

Use of shorter-acting opioids, like fentanyl, can help as well. Some
opioids are associated with less sedation or dysphoria; methadone
and buprenorphine are examples.
Sedation might be a welcome effect immediately post-op and
usually does not require treatment. If oversedation or dysphoria
requires treatment, then opioids can be partially reversed with low
dosages of butorphanol (starting at 0.05 mg/kg IV) or titrated mureceptor antagonists (e.g., naloxone 0.002-0.01 mg/kg IV, diluted
and titrated to effect to avoid abrupt and full reversal of analgesia).

Other Analgesic Therapies
Necessity produced a flourishing of creativity in veterinary pain
management, incorporating ideas from basic pain research and
innovation in human pain medicine. Huge advances in pain
pathophysiology research revealed new therapeutic targets, which
are just beginning to yield new treatment options, such as antinerve
growth factor monoclonal antibodies.47
Novel analgesia delivery systems like sustained-release drugs
and continuous wound infusion have become routine in veterinary
surgical practice. Loco-regional anesthesia and analgesia are
considered standard for all surgical procedures due to efficacy and a
dramatic ability to reduce unwanted side-effects (like sedation) of
systemic analgesics2 (see references for video and protocol
instructions2,48-50).
Non-pharmacological therapies can provide analgesia, at
least in part, via manipulation of endogenous pain-inhibitory
systems.51,52 Moderate weight loss (ch. 150) and increased exercise
(ch. 256) have evidence-based strong benefits in patients with
degenerative joint disease52,53 (ch. 226) and can lead to positive
feedback in endogenous analgesia circuits.
Patients who can be distracted from distress are often assumed,
incorrectly, to lack pain (

Video 6.1). In fact, compassionate

nursing care and diversion are well understood methods of invoking
endogenous analgesia.54 Widely used examples of non-

pharmacologic treatments include manipulative therapies like
massage, thermal treatments, acupuncture, and physiotherapy,
among many others. Published studies establishing clinical success
of many of these methodologies remain sparse despite significant
progress in the elucidation of mechanisms of action in experimental
settings.53 Anecdotally, these methods can augment analgesia and
reduce the need for (or dosages of) drugs, making them excellent
options or adjuncts in cases when adverse effects are feared.
Increasing veterinary use of non-traditional and adjunctive
analgesics has paralleled rising attention to pain medicine. Due to a
lack of evidenced-based recommendations for many of these
therapies, systematic reviews45,51-53 and ethical guidelines for the
use of novel therapies55 provide practical help in trialing new
therapies in practice.
A few common non-traditional analgesics bear mention here.
Acetaminophen (paracetamol) may provide analgesia without
anti-inflammatory effects and minimal GI impact in the dog (e.g., 1015 mg/kg PO q12-24h, in dogs ONLY), despite being highly toxic to
cats.2 Gabapentin and pregabalin, related antiepileptic drugs
with anti-hyperalgesic and anxiolytic effects, may have a role in the
management of acute and chronic pain (e.g., for gabapentin in dogs,
for short-term acute analgesia and possibly anxiolysis, in
gabapentin-naïve patients: dogs 10-20 mg/kg PO q8-12h and cats 510 mg/kg PO q8-12h; and for pregabalin: 1-2 mg/kg PO q12h for cats
and 2-4 mg/kg PO q12h in dogs, but probably best used for chronic
pain).51,52 There are pharmacokinetic data for gabapentin and
pregabalin in dogs and cats, but limited investigation as analgesics.51
It seems likely that some of the sedative and anxiolytic effects can be
beneficial in acute pain management in addition to any analgesic
effects. Sedation and ataxia are common, but may decline with
continued therapy.53 N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptor
antagonists (e.g., ketamine, amantadine, methadone) have wellstudied benefits as part of balanced anesthesia and may be helpful
analgesics outside the perioperative period. Amantadine (3-5
mg/kg PO q12-24h) showed clinical benefit in dogs with

musculoskeletal pain in one small study53 and has been used
anecdotally for neuropathic pain.45
Antidepressants (i.e., drugs that inhibit the re-uptake for
serotonin and/or norepinephrine in the CNS, such as amitriptyline
and fluoxetine) are standard therapy for chronic pain in humans.
Despite the potential for drug interaction and adverse effects,2,45
they may be the best options for refractory chronic pain, including
visceral pain.

Special Notes on Chronic Pain
Management
Understanding key ideas about the nature of chronic pain and
communicating them clearly to caregivers reduces obstacles to
treatment success. Caregivers and veterinarians may be skeptical of a
diagnosis of chronic pain without a convincing peripheral source
unless chronic pain is understood to be a disease of the pain nervous
system. Unrealistic expectations, such as a rapid response, also
instigate frustration. Chronic pain and the attendant disability are
resistant to simple interventions and poorly responsive when
approached as a succession of acute events rather than a chronic
illness. Multimodal treatment plans and the use of non-traditional
analgesics and non-pharmacological therapies are generally required
for efficacious treatment of significant chronic pain.52,53 Since
chronic pain is often incurable and progressive, client education and
the setting of shared goals and expectations are imperative to
outcome success. Shifting the goals of treatment from clinical sign
changes (like reduced lameness) to better function56 (such as, more
interest in playing or going for a walk) focuses efforts on the patient’s
overall well-being and the human-animal bond.
Effective management depends upon thorough investigation since
chronic pain is a complex syndrome of different pain types and
comorbidities.17 Identification of client- and patient-specific
outcome measures derived from initial surveys and visits are key to
gauging progress or lack thereof. Having owners keep a daily journal
consisting of 4-5 simple, personalized questions can be useful,

particularly for those clients who have difficulty identifying changes.
Incorporating personalized outcome measures in the diary (e.g., “did
your pet get on their favorite chair today without assistance?”) and
instructing clients to answer at about the same time daily are useful
measures. Clients’ perceptions of pain may be skewed if monitoring
is persistent and uninterrupted; thus, clients may benefit from
pausing assessments periodically, in order to have a fresh and more
objective perspective when they resume.
Recheck exams, rather than phone or electronic updates, can
identify subtle changes and potential caregiver placebo effects. Visits
help cement the partnership between the caregiver and the
veterinarian in the goal directed health care approach.
Chronic musculoskeletal pain has rightly received extensive
attention as the most common type of chronic pain.2,36,52 Visceral
and neuropathic chronic pain, although more nebulous, deserve
consideration. Visceral and neuropathic pain are often episodic,
difficult to localize, spontaneous, and may be not provoked upon
palpation. Chronic visceral and neuropathic pain may be challenging
to diagnose and treat, but attention to them may improve outcome in
chronic illness that is poorly responsive otherwise. Neuropathic pain
is a contributor to degenerative joint disease and cancer pain,
requiring particular therapy to treat.17,57
Cancer pain etiology is different,58 often more complex, and
resistant to treatment than other types of pain (ch. 331). The
specific sources and mechanisms of pain generation morph during
the course of cancer proliferation, invasion and metastasis;
accordingly, pain management must be adjusted while the disease
course is changing.12 Excellent reviews of cancer pain
pathophysiology12,58,59 can assist in adapting pain management
strategies for cancer pain.

Introduction
Antimicrobial therapy is arguably one of the most important medical
discoveries of the 20th century. Apart from the direct impact on
patient (human and animal) care through treating infections,
effective antimicrobials have allowed medicine to advance. Without
ways to prevent and treat bacterial infections, fields such as surgery
and chemotherapy would look nothing like they do now. However, as
antimicrobials are heavily used (and often misused or overused), the
emergence and dissemination of antimicrobial resistance (AMR)
compromise these gains.
AMR has been called the global health crisis of our time and has
been compared to climate change and armed conflict as a leading
global threat. Sometimes described as an insidious pandemic, AMR
has been allowed to increase, largely unchecked. While the impact is

hard to quantify, AMR is clearly a problem in companion animals
and antimicrobial usage (AMU) in all animal species is coming under
increasing scrutiny. Emergence and dissemination of pathogens like
methicillin-resistant staphylococci, extended spectrum betalactamase (ESBL) producing Enterobacterales and multidrug
resistant Pseudomonas and Enterococcus clearly impact veterinary
patient care. Without effective interventions, it is reasonable to
assume that existing AMR threats will become more common and
new or rare resistant pathogens (e.g., carbapenemase producing
Enterobacterales [CPE])1 will continue to emerge.

Antimicrobial Stewardship
Antimicrobial stewardship is (or should be) a patient-centric,
coordinated approach to optimize the use of antimicrobials and
maximize patient care, while minimizing the risk of resistance,
toxicosis or other adverse events. This involves a multifaceted
approach to determine when to prescribe antimicrobials, which drug,
dosage and duration should be used, how they are administered,
whether other approaches are needed in addition to or in lieu of
antimicrobials (e.g., surgery, wound care, management of underlying
disease; ch. 227) and ongoing assessment.
The field of antimicrobial stewardship is relatively new,
particularly in veterinary medicine, but aspects of stewardship are
applied daily by veterinarians. An antimicrobial stewardship
program (ASP) is an effort to coordinate and optimize these daily
decisions, add depth to decisions, provide decision-making support,
provide a means for assessment of antimicrobial use and educate all
members of the use pathway (prescribers, dispensers, owners). It
may be perceived that an ASP is restrictive and will negatively impact
the practice of veterinary medicine. While some aspects of an ASP
may implement controls, an ASP is not meant to complicate patient
care, remove access to needed antimicrobials or decrease practice
efficiency. Rather, a well-structured and functioning ASP can
improve patient care and facilitate timely and effective treatment,
improving patient outcomes and clinician satisfaction.
In human medicine, the field of antimicrobial stewardship has
evolved into comprehensive programs run by people specializing in

the field, sometimes dedicated solely to operation of the program.
This can include multidisciplinary teams of infectious disease
specialists, microbiologists and pharmacists, working together on
activities ranging from broad programmatic efforts (e.g., formularies,
training, audits) to patient-level approaches (e.g., reviews, targeted
evaluation points during treatment). In contrast, there has been
limited specific implementation of ASPs in veterinary clinics and
limited practice- or patient-level guidance. Reasons for this include
smaller facilities, less access to specialized personnel (e.g., infectious
disease clinicians, infectious disease pharmacists), less institutional
support, a smaller profession overall with more of a focus on
community care and less directly evident role of AMR on patient
care. Regardless, AMR is clearly a relevant clinical issue, AMU and
AMR in animals can have public health consequences, and there are
initiatives that virtually any veterinary clinic can undertake to
improve AMU. Further, as there is increased scrutiny on AMR and
AMU in veterinary medicine, development and implementation of
practical ASPs will be necessary as a method of due diligence, to help
ensure that veterinarians continue to have relatively unfettered
access to antimicrobials.

Components of an Antimicrobial
Stewardship Program
Virtually all clinicians practice some form of antimicrobial
stewardship on a daily basis, through decisions about when and how
to use antimicrobials, and through measures taken to reduce the risk
of disease. Therefore, implementation of an ASP should not be
approached as a paradigm shift, but rather an evolution of core
principles of medicine that fosters communication and education of
all players in the prescribing cascade (attending clinician, diagnostic
laboratory, pharmacy, owner) to facilitate optimal use and remove
pressures to use antimicrobials in situations where they are not
indicated.

Selected Examples of Applied
Antimicrobial Stewardship Concepts
There are many potential ASP components (Box 7.1). The
importance, feasibility and potential benefits of these vary, with
some representing rather easy-to-implement and potentially high
yield measures, and others being more complex or lower priority.

De-escalation
De-escalation is an important stewardship concept that is easy to
apply but typically under-used in veterinary medicine. Essentially, it
is a process to decrease the number of antimicrobials and overall
spectrum of treatment, as indicated by diagnostic testing and clinical
response. For example, a patient might be initially treated with
clindamycin and a fluoroquinolone for severe pneumonia.2 However,
with good clinical improvement and airway culture results, one of the
initial drugs can likely be discontinued within a few days.
De-escalation can reduce costs, reduce adverse event risks,
facilitate transition to outpatient care, facilitate compliance and
reduce antimicrobial selection pressure. The main barriers are
simply thinking about it, lack of culture results, lack of confidence in
narrowing the spectrum and reluctance to change. The latter is
particularly common, and excessively long or broad antimicrobial
treatment is a classic demonstration of ‘defensive medicine.’3
In addition to fostering a culture where the antimicrobial regimen
is constantly re-assessed, there are various formal approaches that
can be added. For example, mandatory review points can be
implemented, whereby use of all antimicrobials or selected drugs or
combinations must be re-evaluated (and treatment orders re-issued)
after a specified timepoint (e.g., 48 h). This prevents unnecessary
continuation of treatment simply because no one took the active
measure of saying ‘stop.’ Similarly, mandatory stop orders can
dictate cessation of treatment after specific times, with the ability to
re-initiate treatment. Making continuation of treatment an active
component can facilitate re-assessment and transition to narrower
spectrum treatment, as opposed to situations where the active step is
stopping treatment.

Delayed Prescribing

Delayed prescribing is an approach to situations where
antimicrobials are not likely indicated at the time of examination but
might be reasonable based on the course of disease (clinical signs
and/or timing). A delayed prescribing approach is an indication to
the pet owner that antimicrobials are not yet recommended but will
be made available under certain situations, in the absence of a need
for further examination of the animal. This can consist of providing
an actual, post-dated prescription (to be filled elsewhere) or an
indication that if the stated criteria are met, the client can simply
pick up the antimicrobial or be sent a prescription. This facilitates
efficient patient care and owner communications (ch. 1), while
avoiding antimicrobials in situations where they are not indicated.
Syndromes where delayed prescribing might be most beneficial in
small animal veterinary medicine include acute diarrhea (chs. 49,
262) and upper respiratory tract infection (chs. 203, 205). An
example is a dog with acute diarrhea that is otherwise clinically
normal. A delayed prescribing approach could involve making a
dietary recommendation and providing time for disease to selfresolve, indicating that an antimicrobial (e.g., metronidazole) will be
provided should disease persist for a certain period of time (e.g., >3
days).
In human medicine, delayed prescribing has been investigated in
conditions such as otitis media, acute pharyngitis, acute bronchitis
and rhinosinusitis.4 For example, for acute otitis media (which is
likely viral), patients are provided with a post-dated prescription that
they can fill in 2-3 days if pain persists. This has been shown to
substantially reduce AMU while having no impact on ultimate
patient outcome or complication rates.5 Patient satisfaction with
delayed prescribing can be similar to that from immediate
prescribing, both being greater than when no antibiotics are
prescribed.4 From a psychological standpoint, patients can be more
satisfied because delayed prescribing reduces apparent hassles or
time commitments, provides a recognition by the clinician that a
disease is present and demonstrates a clear path forward.
Delayed prescribing should be used with caution or avoided in
patients where there is less certainty in the diagnosis, where owner
observation or follow-up may be poor or where the patient is likely at
higher risk for complications.

Treatment Guidelines
Clinical treatment guidelines are increasingly available. These
include international disease-specific diagnosis and treatment
guidelines,2,6-9 as well as various national prescribing guidelines.
Small animal treatment guidelines are typically based on low levels
of evidence because of limitations in the current scientific literature.
However, well-developed treatment guidelines can be useful tools to
improve diagnosis and management of infectious diseases.

Antimicrobial Tiering
Tiering of antimicrobials is a basic awareness tool to indicate drugs
that are of greater concern for specific reasons. Typically, this is
based on importance of the drug in human medicine and the
potential impacts of use in animals on resistance in human
pathogens. Various systems are used internationally, such as those
described by the World Health Organization (WHO)
(https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241515528)
or European Medicines Agency (EMA)
(https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/news/categorisationantibiotics-used-animals-promotes-responsible-useprotect-public-animal-health). These provide different
categories for drugs, something that can be useful to consider during
drug selection. Attention tends to be focused on 3rd generation
cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones, 2 drug classes that are
commonly used in veterinary medicine and important in human
medicine. They are classified as ‘highest priority critically important
antimicrobials’ by the WHO and as ‘Category B/Restrict’ by the
EMA. Use of drugs in these higher tier categories may be
appropriate, but consideration of tiering is useful when choosing
between different drug options, with a goal to use the lowest tier that
is appropriate for the individual patient. Measures such as
infographics, lists of drugs and their categories or labelling of drug
containers (e.g., a red sticker on fluoroquinolone bottles, a yellow
sticker on potentiated penicillins and a green sticker on
tetracyclines) can be simple and cost-free approaches to provide
basic education and awareness.

Formulary Restriction
Formulary restriction essentially means evaluation of all
antimicrobials that are stocked by a clinic and restricting access to
other antimicrobials. It can also involve restrictions on use of certain
drugs that are present in the clinic.
For internal restrictions, this can be a formal requirement to meet
certain criteria (e.g., Box 7.2), complete a form to document and
explain use or otherwise take some active measure to be able to use a
restricted drug (e.g., vancomycin). For use of drugs not in the
formulary, this can require completion of a form that justifies use
and indicates where proper dosing information was obtained.
These approaches are relatively straightforward and require
limited time but can help reduce unnecessary or improper (e.g.,
inadequate dosing of an uncommon drug) AMU. These steps permit
use of uncommon or restricted drugs, maintaining patient care,
while trying to reduce those occurrences and providing clear
documentation of such situations.

Audit and Feedback
Audit and feedback is a means of providing periodic assessment and
review of antimicrobial decisions. This must be approached with
sensitivity as people may resist the perception of being evaluated.
However, it can provide an important contact point to discuss
individual case decisions and broad use practices. It can be peer-topeer, akin to case rounds, or a more formal assessment by someone
with expertise in antimicrobial stewardship. Retrospective review of
AMU can be part of this, using medical records to assess selection
and dosing regimens. However, care must be taken to consider
differences in clinician case populations (e.g., a clinician that sees
more dermatology patients will likely have different overall use
practices than others). If approached collegially, with a focus on
discussion and education, audit can be a very useful tool, allowing
clinicians to consider their specific and broad use practices.

Automated Decision Support
While not currently widely (if ever) used in veterinary medicine,
automatic decision support is a potential approach whereby predetermined default treatment options are facilitated. For example, if
a clinician entered an ‘acute bacterial cystitis’ diagnosis code in the
electronic medical record, a pop-up box can ask if the default
prescription is desired (e.g., ‘Would you like amoxicillin, 15 mg/kg
PO q12h for 5 d? That will be one 125 mg tablet twice a day’).
Alternate drugs and regimens can be used, but require an active
change. Accepting the clinic’s pre-determined choice is the passive
(easier), default approach. This can provide education about the
recommended treatment regimen and, as people typically take the
path of least resistance, unless there are compelling clinical reasons,
it is likely that the default treatment will be accepted.

Checklists
Checklists can be used in targeted situations to confirm steps in the
decision-making process. Surgical checklists typically have questions
about antimicrobials to confirm whether antimicrobials are needed,

whether they have been administered and what time further intraoperative dosing is required (when indicated). Errors in
antimicrobial administration and timing are among the most
commonly detected issues with veterinary surgical checklists,10 and
a properly designed checklist is an effective, quick and essentially nocost antimicrobial stewardship tool.

Conclusion
Antimicrobial stewardship applies to every veterinary practice,
regardless of size or scope. A patient-centric approach aiming to
support clinicians in AMU practices, optimizing patient care while
reducing adverse event and resistance risks, should be incorporated
into every veterinarian’s daily practices.

Information Sheet.
Traveling with pets is increasing and pet owners need to be aware of the requirements for travel
within the continental United States (US), to Hawaii and Guam, and to countries outside the US. This
chapter will focus upon the travel of dogs and cats originating from the continental US. For domestic
and international travel, airlines require a health certificate for the transport of dogs or cats. The health
certificate is a controlled government document signed by a United States Department of Agriculture
(USDA) accredited veterinarian. It attests that a dog or cat was examined and is free of any infectious or
contagious disease. For domestic travel, learn the requirements of the destination state. Depending upon
the state, the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) Form 7001 (“Health Certificate” or
“Certificate of Veterinary Inspection”) may or may not be used; however, an electronic certificate of
veterinary inspection (eCVI) or a state-specific health certificate may be required. If traveling to rabiesfree regions such as Hawaii or Guam, be aware that additional state requirements are needed to allow
entry from the continental US. For international travel, the APHIS Form 7001 is required by the airline,
and additional destination-specific requirements are needed to show proof that a dog or cat is free of
infectious or contagious diseases.
Dogs and cats can host or harbor vectors of diseases that are endemic in the United States (ch. 9).
These diseases may be foreign to an international destination and could impact the health of animals
and people. To mitigate risk, each international destination has its own dog and cat entry requirements.
Compliance with the entry requirements is mandatory and may take several days to months. Upon
arrival to the destination, the pet owner will be held responsible for their dog or cat meeting the entry
requirements. Non-compliance can lead to denial of entry (and return to the country of origin at the
expense of the pet owner), mandatory quarantine, or humane euthanasia.
Service animals are not exempt from the entry requirements and may require additional
documentation. For clients with service animals, consider asking questions regarding future travel to
assist them with meeting the entry requirements.

What Can Veterinarians Do to Help Prepare Pets for
International Travel?
To assist pet owners, the following are needed:
1. Documentation completed by an “official or authorized” veterinarian, meaning the veterinarian
needs to be a USDA accredited veterinarian or military veterinarian. See the USDA Veterinary
Accreditation Program (USDA APHIS | National Veterinary Accreditation Program),
to determine your accreditation status, how to become accredited, and to locate an accredited
veterinarian.1
2. The dog or cat is declared medically fit for travel. Stress associated with travel can exacerbate
pre-existing medical conditions. Pets with medical conditions (such as cardiorespiratory
disease, diabetes, seizure disorders, separation anxiety, etc.) or pets that require routine
medication, could respond negatively to air travel.
3. Promotion of animal welfare and safety during air transportation. Encourage the pet owner to
purchase a dog or cat travel crate that complies with the current International Air
Transportation Association Live Animals Regulations (IATA-LAR). Pet container requirements
(container requirement 1) can be found at www.iata.org/pets.2 Additionally, the crate must
be large enough to allow the pet to sit upright, lie down, and stand and turn about without
touching the top and sides inside the crate. The crate must also have food and water receptacles
accessible without opening the crate door and absorbable bedding.3
4. For safety during travel, encourage pet owners to comply with the airlines’ animal transportation
policies. The policies vary by airline, and may include the following restrictions: Certain breeds
(brachycephalic breeds and/or breeds with inherent strength); length of travel; temperature
limits or seasonal embargoes; crate size embargoes; limits on the number of connecting flights;
and sedation. Note: According to the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA),
sedation is not advised for air travel of dogs and cats. Sedation impairs the natural ability to
balance equilibrium, brace to prevent injury, and impairs the ability of the respiratory and
cardiovascular systems to respond to altitude pressures.4
5. Facilitate the pet’s departure and return to the United States. Prior to departure, ensure the
destination entry requirements are valid, and do not expire prior to their arrival in the
destination. Pet owners must also be aware that upon their return to the United States their
dog or cat must meet the entry requirements mandated by the Centers for Disease Control and
Prevention (CDC). Note: If CDC deems the country a high-risk rabies endemic country,
additional entry requirements will apply.

DETERMINING The Dog or Cat Entry Requirements for The
International Destination
The entry requirements vary by international destination and can range from incredibly detailed to
minimal. The USDA Pet Travel Website (USDA APHIS | APHIS Pet Travel) is a great resource that
provides the dog and cat entry requirements for most destinations.5 If the entry requirements are not
available via the website, contact the animal health officials of the destination.6 If a pet owner decides to
travel to multiple countries during international travel, the pet must meet the entry requirements for
each country they visit.

Common entry Requirements (Table 8.1)
1. Microchipping
Microchips are the global standard for the identification of companion animals, recognized by the World
Small Animal Veterinary Association and the AVMA.7,8 For international travel, dogs and cats are to be
microchipped with an International Organization for Standardization (ISO)-compliant microchip, which
contains 15 digits and operates at a frequency of 134.2 kHz. There are brands of non-ISO-compliant

microchips that operate at frequencies of 125 kHz and 128 kHz. Please check with your microchip
manufacturer to ensure ISO compliance. If a chip is non-compliant, it may be necessary to administer a
microchip that complies. If the country accepts non-ISO compliant microchips, the pet owner will be
required to travel with a microchip reader capable of identifying the microchip. The microchip number
must be written on all health documents, diagnostic tests, etc. An error in transcribing the microchip
number could lead to a denial of entry.

2. Animal Health Documentation Requirements
As an entry requirement, one or more of the following documents are needed: Import Permit/License
(IP); Country-specific animal health certificate (CSAHC); Valid Rabies Vaccination Certificate (RVC);
Electronic Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (eCVI) or an APHIS 7001 form. The destination will
determine the documents required for dog or cat entry. Once all of the requirements are met,
documentation must be signed by a USDA accredited veterinarian and endorsed by the USDA APHIS
Veterinary Services office in your region (USDA APHIS | APHIS Veterinary Services
Endorsement Offices).9 Some countries will allow US active-duty military veterinarians to sign the
documents and, in those cases, endorsement by USDA APHIS Veterinary Services is not required. To
expedite the process, use USDA’s Veterinary Export Health Certificate System (VEHCS), which allows
the entry requirements to be electronically signed by a USDA accredited veterinarian and submitted to
USDA APHIS Veterinary Services for endorsement.10 Countries fall into 3 categories for use of VEHCS:
Full (allows electronic signatures and digital endorsement); Partial (allows electronic signatures, but
does NOT allow digital endorsement); No VEHCS (does NOT allow electronic signatures or digital
endorsement).

3. Rabies and Other Vaccinations
Rabies vaccination is required for entry to most destinations (ch. 202). The number of rabies
vaccinations administered, the earliest age at which the vaccination is given, and post-rabies vaccination
waiting periods are features which impact the entry into an international destination. A destination can
deny the entry of dogs and cats that are not vaccinated or fully immunized against rabies. A destination
may also require all dogs or cats to receive all core vaccines and non-core vaccines (ch. 185 and inside
cover).

4. Rabies Titer and Other Infectious Disease Diagnostic Tests
A Rabies Neutralizing Antibody Titer Test, with a titer value of 0.5 IU/mL or above, and other infectious
disease diagnostic tests, may be required (ch. 202). All diagnostic tests must be performed at an
approved laboratory. See the CDC website for a list of approved laboratories for Rabies serologic testing
by country at: https://www.cdc.gov/importation/bringing-an-animal-into-the-unitedstates/approved-labs.html.11 Consult with the destination for approved laboratories for the other
required diagnostic tests.

5. Anti-Parasite Treatments
To protect animals in international destinations and to protect dogs and cats against parasites that they
are not exposed to in the United States, anti-parasitic treatments may be required (ch. 142). Multiple
treatments, with products approved by the international destination, may be needed for the treatment of
external parasites, intestinal parasites, and blood parasites.

6. Quarantine
Upon entry, pets may be placed in mandatory quarantine for a time determined by the destination.
Mandatory quarantine arrangements must be made by the pet owner prior to arrival. Also, if not in

compliance with the entry requirements, pets may be placed under quarantine. All quarantining will be
at the pet owner’s expense.

7. Prohibited Breeds
Some countries prohibit the entry of domestic-wild hybrids (such as wolf hybrids or Savannah cats) and
dog breeds considered to be dangerous due to their history of being bred for fighting.

Chapter 9: Health Concerns of Imported
Pets
Vanessa R. Barrs

AC RO N YM S
PETS Pet Travel Scheme
UK United Kingdom
US United States
VBD vector-borne disease

This chapter is enhanced with the following electronic assets on Elsevier eBooks+: 6 Tables.
The purpose of this chapter is to assist clinicians to rapidly assess whether a recently traveled or
imported animal presenting with illness is sick as a consequence of the journey, has contracted an
infectious disease from the place of importation, or has an ailment that is unrelated to travel. The
examining veterinarian should be aware of notifiable exotic infectious diseases in their jurisdiction by
consulting the web-pages of the relevant regulatory animal health agencies (ch. 8). A notifiable disease
is one for which there is a legal obligation to report its diagnosis or suspicion of diagnosis to the
regulatory authorities.

Patient History and Pre-Examination Considerations
Obtaining a thorough history from the owner or agent (ch. 2) is the first step in the investigation of a
sick imported animal or one with a recent travel history, and should include the following: 1)
confirmation of the patient signalment; 2) major presenting signs and the date of their onset; 3)
vaccination and parasite prophylaxis/treatment timeline (ch. 185); 4) dietary history (ch. 145); 5)
previous medical history, current medications and timeline of administration; 6) past and recent travel
history—time spent in region/country of origin, other regions/countries visited, duration and dates of
travel (departure, arrival, transit), access to food and water; 7) mode and duration of transportation; 8)
source of origin (e.g., shelter, breeder, pet shop), dietary and lifestyle factors in region/country of origin
including access to the outdoors (e.g., hunting, sporting activities); 9) exposures to insects (mosquitoes,
sandflies/flies, ticks, other), prey and other animals (rodents, small mammals, farm animals), natural
habitats (woodlands, grasslands, bodies of water), and environmental disruptions (e.g., construction
sites).
Vaccination certificates (ch. 8) should be checked carefully to assess whether an animal is likely to be
adequately immunized based on the frequency and types of vaccinations administered (ch. 185).
Whether the primary vaccination course was completed and compliant with international guidelines
such as the World Small Animal Veterinary Association (WSAVA) vaccination guidelines,1 should be
determined. If the presentation is consistent with an infectious disease that the animal is allegedly
vaccinated against, the possibility of vaccination failure or a fraudulent vaccination certificate should
also be considered. In 2021, the United States (US) Centers for Disease Control and Prevention banned
importation of dogs from 113 countries for at least 1 year because of an upsurge in the detection of

fraudulent rabies vaccination certificates.2 Similar concerns regarding issuing of fake vaccination
certificates have been raised in other countries, such as the United Kingdom (UK).
Before examining the animal, be aware of major infectious diseases endemic to the region from which
the animal has travelled. These are summarized by geographic region in Tables 9.1 to 9.4.3-54 It should
also be borne in mind that vector prevalence varies geographically. The time of year in which the same
species of tick is most active may differ from one country to another due to differences in temperature,
precipitation, and humidity. For example, Dermacentor reticulatus is most active in the UK in winter,55
while in Berlin it is generally active year-round.56 Even within a country, tick activity may vary. For
example, Ixodes scapularis ticks, vectors of Borrelia burgdorferi and of Anaplasma phagocytophilum,
are most active in fall and winter in the southeastern US while in the northern US they are additionally
active in the spring.57 Similarly, sandfly population densities, although generally lowest during the
coldest and/or driest seasons of the year, may be high year-round in tropical regions.58

Eu Pet Travel Scheme
The Pet Travel Scheme (PETS), introduced by the European Union in 2001, enabled travel for
microchipped, rabies-vaccinated pet dogs, cats, and ferrets from member countries without the need for
quarantine. Over time, the scheme was also rolled out to other countries/regions including the US,
Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Singapore, Hong Kong, Malaysia and rabies-free islands (ch.
202). The increased numbers of traveling and imported companion animals resulting from the
introduction of this scheme raised concerns soon afterwards about the introduction of canine
leishmaniosis into non-endemic areas, such as the UK.59 While this has not been documented to date
since the phlebotomine sandfly vector remains exotic to the UK, increasing numbers of canine
leishmaniosis cases have been diagnosed in traveled dogs and imported rescued dogs returning to nonendemic areas including the UK, Germany, Romania and Poland, creating a potential reservoir of
infected animals.60-63

Reason for Travel and Lifestyle Factors
The reason why an animal has been imported can provide important clues about possible infectious
diseases that the animal may have contracted before travel. For example, Brucella canis infection should
be considered as a differential diagnosis for a breeding bitch presenting with spinal pain, if imported
from an endemic country. Animals imported by rescue organizations present the risk of concurrent
importation of emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases. For example, Brucella canis is not
endemic in the Netherlands; however, brucellosis was diagnosed in 15 rescue dogs imported from
Eastern Europe between 2016 and 2018.15 Similarly, the H3N2 canine influenza virus now circulating in
the US was first introduced in 2015, most likely in association with the importation of rescue dogs to
Chicago from live animal markets or meat dog farms in South Korea. A subsequent reintroduction was
associated with importation of dogs from China.64,65
Other lifestyle factors such as swimming or exposure to wildlife through sporting or hunting activities
can aid in the development of differential diagnoses depending on the clinical presentation. A dog
imported from Australia with a history of hunting feral boar is at risk of Brucella suis infection (Table
9.1)

Nutritional Assessment
A complete nutritional assessment should be performed to rule out the possibility of a nutritional
deficiency, intoxication, or metabolic disease and to determine whether caloric intake has been
appropriate for the animal (https://wsava.org/global-guidelines/global-nutrition-guidelines/
and the 2021 American Animal Hospital Association Nutrition and Weight Guidelines for Dogs and
Cats66) (ch. 145). Recalls of pet foods in the animal’s place of origin should be checked for (Box 9.1).

Physical Examination
A complete physical examination is the next step to help assess whether the animal’s illness is most
likely a result of the journey (e.g., dehydration, fatigue, stress) and to determine whether signs are
referrable to a particular organ system or systems (ch. 3). A thorough search for vectors or hallmarks of
their recent presence (e.g., ticks, tick-craters) should be performed including otoscopic examination and
examination of all skin-folds and mucocutaneous junctions. The most common tick bite locations on
dogs and cats are the head and neck, especially in/around the ears, eyes, muzzle, face and chin.67 Ticks
can attach anywhere on the body, and sites such as the interdigital areas and tail should not be
overlooked. There are multiple reports of alien tick importation on dogs traveling to different
countries.68,69 The most commonly identified alien tick on dogs traveling to the UK and Europe is
Rhipicephalus sanguineus,which has been found on dogs traveling from endemic regions in Europe,
Africa (Sudan, Zambia), the Middle-East (Iran, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates), Canada, and
the US.68,69 Ixodes ricinus ticks have been detected on cats traveling to the UK from Romania and
Hungary.68 Dogs imported into the US carrying Haemaphysalis longicornis ticks have been implicated
as having a critical role in the establishment of endemic populations of this tick in the US since 2017.70

Alien ticks should be correctly identified since ticks are not only vectors of infectious diseases, but
some species can cause intoxications. Gravid Ixodes species of hard-bodied ticks endemic to Australia,
especially Ixodes holocyclus and I. cornuatus inject neurotoxins produced in their salivary glands during
blood-feeding that cause an ascending flaccid paralysis in dogs and cats. Tick paralysis (ch. 253) is a
common disease in Australia and was also reported in a dog imported to the UK from Australia through
the PETS scheme even though the dog had been treated with an acaricide and examined by veterinarians
prior to travel.71 Dermacentor species ticks in the Pacific Northwest and Atlantic Southeast of the US,
including D. andersoni and D. variabilis, have been reported to cause severe paralysis in dogs,
infrequently.72
Consideration should also be given as to whether the animal could be suffering from a primary acute
infection or whether the presentation could be a manifestation of chronic infection resulting from
exposure months, or even years, previously. Animals at risk for the latter include those in which a preexisting medical condition or its treatment could be associated with immunosuppression, e.g.,
hyperadrenocorticism or atopic dermatitis (chs. 180, 227). For example, dogs subclinically infected
with Leishmania infantum may develop severe clinical disease if they become immunosuppressed.73
Similarly, animals can be subclinically infected with Cryptococcus species and could develop clinical
disease years later in the face of immunosuppression.74

Testing
For animals in which ticks or tick-craters are identified, a complete blood count including peripheral
blood smear examination, serum biochemistry panel and vector-borne disease (VBD) testing panels are
indicated (ch. 184). Even though the incubation period of a VBD may not have elapsed since the period
of tick attachment, previous tick attachment is possible to likely. Dogs entering the UK have been
diagnosed with clinically significant Hepatozoon canis infections after their owners presented them for
treatment of tick infestations observed on arrival following importation from endemic areas.75
Removed ticks from imported animals should be submitted to agencies offering identification
services. In the UK, ticks can be submitted to Public Health England’s Tick Surveillance Scheme for
identification (https://www.gov.uk/guidance/tick-surveillance-scheme). In the US, many state
government agencies offer tick identification services.
If a notifiable disease is suspected, the relevant government agency should be contacted immediately
to file a report, and to receive advice about testing and isolation. Precautions should be taken if
collecting samples for diagnostic tests for zoonotic diseases, including wearing of appropriate personal
protective equipment. For detailed information about specific tests and how to perform them, the reader
is referred to the Infectious Disease section of this textbook in chs. 183 to 211 (Table 9.5, E-Tables
9.6 to 9.11).76-101
