Chapter 10: “Ain’t Doin’
Right”
The Nonspecific Chief Concern of Ill Thrift
Etienne Côté, Stephen J. Ettinger, and Edward C. Feldman

Ill thrift refers to a vague change in activity level, mental arousal,
behavior, or some combination thereof. Often, it is difficult for
clients/pet owners, caretakers, and family members to describe it
clearly, and they simply can characterize the situation as “He’s not
himself” or “She ain’t doin’ right” (ADR). Subjectively, it is a frequent
reason for veterinary consultations and it can be caused by a disorder
of essentially any organ system.
The hallmark of ill thrift is its nonspecific nature: instead of a
discrete clinical sign like coughing or inappetence, ill thrift is a
poorly defined decrease in vitality. A second characteristic is the
wide variability in severity of the underlying cause. Ill thrift can be
associated with trivial disorders requiring no treatment, or it can be
the first manifestation of disorders that progress to life-threatening
states. In some cases, it is further complicated by the nature of the
concern, the client voicing the concern, and the reality of the
situation. Usually, these are real concerns, but in other situations
they are totally benign processes misidentified by a client with a
heightened sense of anxiety, or some combination of both.
Regardless of the veterinarian’s feelings about a patient who “ain’t
doin’ right,” the concern should always be taken seriously and
investigated in such a way that the patient’s health is addressed
correctly and the client is guided appropriately.1 Clients are sincere
in their belief, and questions or thoughts should not be pushed off
with a wave of the hand saying, “Everything’s OK—don’t worry.”

Virtually any disorder in veterinary internal medicine can cause ill
thrift as its clinical expression. The goal of evaluating the patient
with ill thrift is foremost to determine severity. When the underlying
cause is benign and self-resolving, efforts can focus on exclusion of
more serious disorders, on client reassurance, and on monitoring
parameters and milestones. When the underlying cause seems likely
to be harmful to the patient, the veterinarian’s efforts should focus
on defining the extent of the problem and on more intensive and
immediate intervention.
Since the range of possible diagnoses for ill thrift is broad, the first
step necessarily should be a review of the patient’s signalment and
medical history.

Signalment
Signalment (ch. 3) is an important general guide, beginning with the
patient’s age. Young animals are more likely to have ill thrift due to
congenital malformations, parasitoses, trauma from being
unsupervised, or ingested foreign bodies or substances, for example.
Conversely, mature dogs and cats have a higher prevalence of
degenerative diseases and neoplasia. A patient’s somatotype is
important: large-breed dogs have a higher prevalence of
osteosarcoma, splenic and cardiac neoplasia, and many other
disorders. Small-breed dogs are overrepresented with respect to
degenerative/myxomatous mitral valve disease, chronic pancreatitis,
and others. Chondrodystrophic breeds have a higher prevalence of
intervertebral disc disease, which can manifest with nonspecific
signs that a client interprets as not feeling normal. Sex has an
obvious link to the prevalence of reproductive disorders like
pyometra and prostatitis, but also to certain disorders like immunemediated polyarthritis, which has a higher prevalence in females.
Any of these disorders first can manifest with vague signs of ill thrift.
Importantly, these broad generalizations are nonspecific, and
conclusions drawn from a patient’s signalment must be kept loose
and amenable to change because these guidelines, like the clinical
algorithms included in most chapters of this textbook, are only
meant to offer the clinician a starting point and preliminary
orientation.

Medical History
A detailed review of the medical history is the next important step
(ch. 2). Experience suggests that ill thrift notoriously can trigger
suspicions in a client’s mind that can be unfounded, such as
poisoning by a neighbor, or concerns about infectious disease
outbreaks triggered by news headlines or social media activity. These
represent a client’s rationalization of observed signs within the limits
of his or her understanding (ch. 15): the immediate environment,
the animal’s typical behavior, and increasingly, the most readily
available information on the Internet. Such interpretations can be
useful, or can be misleading, and a skilled veterinarian should
consider the client’s insistence and convictions with a suitable
balance of internal skepticism and willingness to hear what matters
to that person.
Just as importantly, key items of the history could be overlooked
by the client and only become apparent on careful questioning.
Therefore, the medical history should be explored in a way that is not
leading or suggestive, to avoid miscommunication with clients, but in
a way that also is thorough and insightful (ch. 1).
Key aspects of the medical history in patients with ill thrift include:
• Frame of reference. A client who is a first-time pet owner
might not be familiar with species-appropriate physiology and
behavior, or normal interindividual variations in energy and
stamina among dogs or cats. By contrast, an experienced and
astute client can identify important, subtle signs that are not
even apparent to the veterinarian initially. Although the
client’s experience with animal health is important to
consider, a limitation in this regard is that clients’ selfdescribed level of expertise can be much lower or higher than
their actual proficiency.
• Duration and course. The client should be asked when the pet
last was normal, and how the concern evolved over time.
Medically important ill thrift can be of any duration. If the
condition seems to have continued without change for days to
weeks or more, two important possibilities should be
considered. A chronic disorder could be present, which could
be producing obvious physical abnormalities (e.g., morbid

obesity, severe osteoarthritis) that might not be as obvious to
the client as to the veterinarian and the client simply feels that
the pet “ain’t doin’ right.” Alternatively, the client might be
misinterpreting the animal’s normal state as being abnormal.
The latter possibility is more challenging to confirm and
generally emerges as a diagnosis of exclusion after completion
of diagnostic testing. An important third possibility is a
disease that follows a waxing-waning course, and information
about whether clinical signs have varied this way must be
elicited during the collection of the medical history.
• Exposure, environment, and habits. An adult dog that has
never been inquisitive and does not like to mouth objects is
unlikely to have ill thrift from intestinal obstruction due to
ingestion of a foreign body, for example. Similarly, an indoor
cat is unlikely to be exposed to toxic substances that are found
outdoors. The client’s habits can be informative: dropped
(human) medication tablets, missing sewing needles or
thread, remodeling of an older home (lead poisoning), the
possibility of outdoor exposures (spider bites, plant foreign
bodies, encounters with wildlife), use or misuse of nutritional
supplements and nontraditional diets and remedies, and a
home with a garage (where the animal can have ingested
ethylene glycol antifreeze) are examples of important clues.
Simple but crucial day-to-day aspects must not be overlooked,
because they may provide the answer to the pet’s concern: has
the food being fed changed, or has a new bag of food just been
opened? Has the pet been in a different environment where
activity, feeding, and risk of exposure to harmful substances is
different?
• Vital functions. The veterinarian should ask about the pet’s
alertness and responsiveness lately; energy level, willingness
to perform usual activities, and stamina; respiratory effort at
home; appetite, and ability to prehend and swallow food;
about any changes in elimination of feces and urine; and about
change in diet, including dietary indiscretion.

Physical Examination

Together, the findings from the signalment and medical history can
allow the clinician to create an initial, often general, differential
diagnosis list. In all cases, this information then is refined through
interpretation of physical examination findings. The physical exam,
which always begins with a hands-off observation of the animal’s
mentation and gait, is described in detail in ch. 3. The process, and
the application of physical examination findings, is as relevant to
patients with ill thrift as to patients with any general presenting
concern, including a wellness examination.

Diagnostic Tests
Often, a conclusive diagnosis is not reached with signalment, history,
and physical exam findings alone. Additional, objective information
can be obtained with diagnostic testing. Diagnostic tests provide
information on two levels: abnormal results suggest—or conclusively
identify—the causative problem, whereas normal results increase the
level of reassurance that a serious problem is less likely.
Test selection for patients with ill thrift can be considered
according to whether the patient is considered a serious case or a
nonserious case.2 Serious cases have one or more of the following
characteristics: presence of overt systemic signs that suggest
hypovolemia or hemodynamic instability (e.g., poor perfusion,
weak/absent pulse, pathological and very rapid or very slow cardiac
arrhythmia, evidence of dehydration), neurologic compromise (e.g.,
depressed mentation, locomotor deficits, generalized weakness),
respiratory difficulty (e.g., dyspnea, inappropriate tachypnea), or
persistent pain (e.g., change in mentation, subdued behavior,
guarding). Obvious, externally visible abnormalities such as wounds
or spontaneous hemorrhage of course can be evidence of serious
disorders, but these specific findings lie outside the realm of ill thrift
as a poorly defined, general state of malaise. Nonserious cases have
none of the characteristics listed above. Specifically, nonserious cases
have normal (or, in the veterinarian’s opinion, insignificantly
abnormal) physical exam findings for all body systems, notably the
cardiovascular, neurologic, and respiratory systems. When the
distinction is unclear as to whether a patient is a serious or
nonserious case, both the veterinarian’s concern and the client’s

concern (and the client’s logistical, financial, and emotional factors)
are used for guiding the degree of diagnostic testing to be pursued.
In nonserious cases, basic tests are implemented according to the
information obtained in the history and physical examination. A first
tier of tests that applies to many situations includes a packed cell
volume and total solids, blood glucose, estimation of blood urea
nitrogen (e.g., Azostix), urine specific gravity, and a urine dipstick
profile. Often, this information and much more can be obtained with
the same blood and urine samples, and only a marginally higher cost
to the client, via a complete blood count, serum biochemical profile,
and complete urinalysis. Clients who make an appointment for their
pet to be evaluated for nonspecific malaise should be encouraged to
bring a sample of the pet’s urine, collected at home in a clean and
sealed container. Simple analysis can be performed prior to meeting
the client and seeing the patient, which immediately informs the
clinician of some important diagnoses (e.g., diabetes mellitus, renal
concentrating capacity if the urine specific gravity is >1.035, various
causes of discolored urine). A serum total thyroxine level can be
considered for adult cats, and retroviral testing for all cats. A
serologic titer for heartworm disease is warranted in endemic areas.
Thoracic radiographs and an abdominal ultrasound exam have value
if the signalment, history, and physical exam suggest a structural
lesion in the thorax or abdomen as the leading differential diagnosis.
In serious cases, these same tests are indicated, and often are
followed by a second tier of tests. These additional tests can
investigate abnormalities found on the first tier of tests, or they can
explore the most likely remaining differential diagnoses given the
disorders that have been ruled out by normal results on the first
tests. Importantly, serious cases are more likely to produce
diagnostic test abnormalities that give a clear direction to the
treatment that is necessary.
Depending on the context, including the client’s ability and desire
to monitor the animal at home, perceived importance of
hospitalization for observation, cost of testing, and the client’s
history of similar situations with other pets, the client may wish to
forgo any diagnostic testing and monitor the animal at home. In
nonserious cases, such an approach is acceptable, and monitoring
typically should involve client assessments of mentation, appetite,
ambulation, respiration, digestion, water intake (which the client can

measure at home if there is a concern about polydipsia; normal is
<100 mL/kg/24 hours in dogs [usually <80 mL/kg/24 hours]3 and
<200 mL/cat/24 hours4 or <50 mL/kg/day5 in cats), and general
responsiveness. Persistent abnormality or worsening of any of these
parameters warrants reevaluation and diagnostic testing. The
veterinarian should explain to the client both the advantages and the
drawbacks of not pursuing testing initially if this direction is chosen.
The explanation should be informative without eliciting a sense of
guilt in the client, nor the perception of the veterinarian trying to
force the client to commit to testing. Importantly, the veterinarian
needs to outline how he or she expects the patient’s situation to
evolve if the situation improves versus how it is expected to evolve if
the problem is worsening. This type of explanation helps the client
feel the veterinarian cares, and it empowers the client to pursue tests
and treatment with the veterinarian if deterioration occurs, rather
than being left with the impression that the veterinarian lost interest
because the full array of tests was not pursued.1 A useful option is to
give the client a sheet of paper with the hospital’s contact
information on it and a broad, written plan, e.g., (1) Exam and
history; (2) Blood panel; (3) If not better in 7 days or worse anytime,
radiographs (X-rays); (4) If no answers and the problem persists,
ultrasound/referral/other; etc. This gives the client a continuum of
what could be necessary and the client may then ask for all of it to be
done, some of it, or none of it. A copy in the medical record is useful
for continuity if colleagues care for the animal later, and for
medicolegal purposes. A follow-up phone call from a staff member in
24-48 hours helps the client understand that the veterinarian cares,
and provides early troubleshooting if the problem is worsening.
Should the client not perceive an improvement in the signs, it would
be advisable to follow up with an additional appointment. Once
again, this shows the message that “my veterinarian cares.”
In serious cases, if the client declines diagnostic testing, the
veterinarian needs to provide monitoring guidelines that include
indicators of suffering; describe risks that could be posed to the
client, including zoonosis, bite wound injuries, and the like, where
applicable; and provide recommendations for supportive care. This
information needs to be accompanied by a frank discussion on

prognosis, neither too grim nor too upbeat, if over time the client
sees that the clinical signs are not improving.

Treatment
Treatment of patients with ill thrift depends on the inciting cause.
When none is found, supportive care can be provided, either by the
veterinarian and his or her staff in the hospital or by the client at
home. Some clients express dissatisfaction when no treatment is
administered in the face of an open diagnosis because, in their view,
“nothing was done.” The veterinarian should have both the client’s
and the pet’s well-being in mind when navigating this situation, and
deciding whether to discharge a nonserious case with a mild,
nonspecific supportive treatment such as subcutaneous fluids for
mild dehydration, analgesia (at a dosage that will not produce
sedative effects) for any perceived discomfort, and the like.
Treatment might need to be implemented sooner, or the patient
might be more likely to require hospitalization, in serious compared
to nonserious cases.

Ill Thrift That is Not A Sign of Disease
An important element that helps differentiate medically serious from
medically nonserious cases of ill thrift is background information
that could be affecting the client’s perception of the animal’s quality
of life. The recent loss of another pet or other member of the family,
recent illness in the family, forthcoming travel where the pet is being
left behind, and other sources of anxiety, tension, and guilt can
trigger a heightened level of concern and lead the client to believe
that the animal is experiencing ill thrift. This is a common situation
in small animal practice and it must neither be suspected excessively
nor discounted too quickly. Without being intrusive, the veterinarian
should be mindful of the critical role of these types of circumstances
and assess whether the intensity of the client’s response might place
“overinterpretation of normal signs” on the differential diagnosis,
rather than a true medical disorder. Client overinterpretation, then,
becomes a diagnosis of exclusion. A complete physical examination

and evaluation according to the serious/nonserious approach
described above can identify important problems when they are
present, or can be reassuring to the client when results are within
normal limits. Follow-up, both to identify emerging disease and to
create an atmosphere of support for a concerned client, becomes
especially important in this context.
Another example of “relative” ill thrift that can reflect normal
variation is the natural decrease in spontaneous activity often
associated with aging in an animal with no historical or physical
abnormalities to indicate cognitive dysfunction, neurologic or
musculoskeletal disease, or other internal disorder. Often, a client
compares a pet to its former self, or to a fellow animal, and identifies
“ill thrift” not associated with any existing or emerging disease. Such
situations simply can reflect normal maturation and its associated
behavioral and physical changes that remain within normal limits. If
no abnormalities are present on physical exam or diagnostic tests, or
if abnormalities emerge that are considered too mild to explain the
client’s concern, then having the client videorecord the clinical signs
when they occur can be valuable, as can specific laboratory testing
guided by the features of the history and physical exam. Ultimately,
this diagnosis is reached through a combination of the veterinarian
disclosing the findings of the physical examination, elimination of
serious causes with diagnostic testing, and passage of time with no
visible progression of the signs.

Resolution
Follow-through for patients who “ain’t doin’ right” is important.
Nonserious cases that fully respond to nonspecific treatment or
whose clinical signs simply normalize with time still should be
addressed. Veterinarians should request that the client communicate
an update to the veterinary hospital staff. Such feedback then needs
to be entered in the animal’s medical record. This way, the client
understands that the veterinarian cares enough about the patient’s
outcome to stay informed on how the situation evolved, and the
client bears some of the responsibility for communicating with the
veterinary hospital after discharge. Cases that worsen at home
instead of improving, or serious cases that are discharged, should be

followed more closely, with telephone updates and return visits for
reevaluation as dictated by the patient’s signs, response to treatment,
and perceived severity of the underlying problem. Typically, such
deterioration also triggers the emergence of new physical signs that
can be more specific, leading to additional diagnostic testing,
treatment, and/or referral to a specialist.

Disorders From Medical Disorders
Diane Frank

A C RO N YM

This chapter is enhanced with the following electronic assets on Elsevier

Introduction
Distinguishing behavioral disorders from medical disorders can be challenging. Owners
will often report that their animal is ill because of behavioral changes.1 Behavioral
“problems” of animals can be subdivided into undesirable normal behaviors (speciesappropriate behaviors that humans dislike) or undesirable abnormal behaviors
(behavioral disorder, behavioral illness) (Figure 11.1). Behavioral disorders typically
have one or several of the following characteristics: (1) the behavior is inappropriate for
the context (i.e., one cannot justify the behavior in that situation); (2) the behavioral
sequence is altered; (3) the frequency is excessive for the context; (4) the severity and/or
duration is excessive for the context; (5) the animal exhibits signs compatible with
anxiety in one or several contexts; (6) with primary behavioral disorders, the patient
usually has a normal neurologic examination (ch. 241). However, it should be noted
that in certain cases of structural brain disease, behavioral changes can sometimes
precede neurological changes.
Medical disorders or painful conditions can have one or several of the following:
inappropriate behaviors for the context, altered behavioral sequences, increased
frequency and/or duration of behaviors. For example, a dog with a brain tumor could be
presented for veterinary care due to sudden-onset aggressive behavior that is not
appropriate for the context; a dog or cat that self-mutilates because of pain can have an
altered behavior sequence because the animal does not stop the chewing/biting
behavior and eventually causes self-injury; and a pruritic cat or dog will lick or groom
itself more frequently or for longer periods than normal.
Therefore, certain changes in behavior are nonspecific. Other behavioral changes that
can be associated with either medical or behavioral disorders could include appearance

of a new behavior (e.g., hiding) or disappearance of a normal behavior (e.g., no longer
playing), inappropriate behavior (e.g., aggression “out of the blue”), and changes in
frequency and/or duration of normal behaviors.
Truly behavioral disorders (“mental illness”) could therefore be defined as behaviors
that are inappropriate for the context, have an altered sequence, are excessive in
duration and/or frequency, occur in the absence of other identifiable medical disorders,
or some combination of these features. It is important to remember that comorbidity of
medical and behavioral disorders also occurs, perhaps more often than is recognized. In
a study of 72 dogs with anxiety disorders, 21 dogs (29%) had concomitant
gastrointestinal (GI) signs/disease, 19 dogs (26%) had dermatologic signs/disease, and
10 dogs (14%) had musculoskeletal signs/disease.2
In addition to this overlap of signs for medical and behavioral disorders, many terms
used in behavioral medicine as diagnoses are in fact nonspecific signs. Examples could
include urine marking, inappropriate elimination, and all of the repetitive behaviors
(also called “obsessive compulsive disorders” or “compulsive disorders”), including but
not limited to pica, fly-biting, circling, and tail chasing. Finally, signs compatible with
anxiety overlap with signs of pain, discomfort, or medical conditions.3 Some examples
(Table 11.1) could include restlessness, pacing, vocalizing, panting, licking lips, and
repetitive swallowing. Furthermore, pain can exacerbate anxiety and anxiety can
exacerbate pain (ch. 6).

FIGURE 11.1 Differential diagnosis algorithm for behavioral
signs. int. med., Internal medicine.

Behavioral Disorders
Anxiety is a dominant feature of many behavioral disorders and can be an important
characteristic for differentiating behavioral from medical disorders. Anxiety is defined
as an emotional state associated with adaptive physiological and behavioral responses.
Anxiety becomes a disorder when it is exhibited in contextually inappropriate situations
or in natural ones but at a level that impairs adaptive responses.4 Anxiety disorders in
companion animals generally are characterized by heightened arousal (increased
vigilance) and increased reactivity.5 The normal dog spends most of its time in a calm,
non-vigilant, non-reactive state. The reactive/anxious dog spends most of its time being
vigilant (unable to relax even though, in some cases, the dog is totally exhausted) and
overly reactive (

Video 11.1). An affected dog might startle more easily even at the

sound of day-to-day “regular” noises (Video 11.5). This dog in specific situations could
exhibit piloerection more rapidly and more frequently, could be difficult to interrupt

(e.g., the dog “seems unable to hear” the owner), and requires more time to return to
“normal” baseline behaviors after an event of inappropriate or undesirable behavior.

Age of Onset of Signs
Behavioral disorders generally are observed in young animals,6,7 although some
exceptions occur. Behavioral disorders such as redirected aggression, interdog
aggression, and impulse-control aggression (formerly called dominance aggression) are
commonly described in dogs aged 18 to 24 months.8,9 Similarly, in cats, anxiety-related
disorders such as intercat aggression or status-related aggression typically appear when
the cat is a young adult (2 to 4 years of age).10 Anxiety disorders other than aggression
can also be observed earlier in life (e.g., 6 to 18 months).7 This prevalence by age group
can help to raise or lower the likelihood of a behavioral disorder as the cause of clinical
signs in an individual patient. Occasionally, the context in which a behavior occurs along
with typical body postures can alert to a behavioral condition. For example, submissive
urination usually occurs strictly in specific contexts such as a person approaching,
reaching or bending over, petting, speaking loudly or in a high-pitched voice, staring at,
or scolding the dog.11 The posture will be lowered (head, body, tail) and in some cases,
the dog may even lie on its side with an elevated limb. Dogs diagnosed with excitement
urination do so when aroused or excited (context-specific). They usually do not squat or
lift a hindlimb and often seem unaware of dribbling. These examples illustrate the
importance of collecting information on context.

Increased reactivity includes signs such as piloerection, long recovery time after an
event, propensity to startle easily, appearance of a dog that seems “unable to hear”
owner instructions during undesirable behavior (aggression) as opposed to a dog that
does not want to obey. See Video 11.5.

Increased vigilance includes signs such as constant visual scanning, inability to relax,
keeping eyes half closed (i.e., the dog is exhausted, different from eyes half closed due to
pain/globe retraction). See

Video 11.1.

Two studies12,13 showed that the behaviors of approximately 10% of puppies were
significantly different from the behaviors of their peers. One study described puppy
behavior in the veterinary clinic.12 One hundred and two 8- to 16-week-old puppies (46

males, 56 females) that had been adopted at least 1 week prior to evaluation were
observed and videorecorded. The evaluation was divided into 3 different parts: (1) freefloor assessment; (2) physical examination; and (3) specific manipulations. Most
puppies (free on the floor) behaved in a similar fashion. They were very active and
oriented to the environment (exploring), silent, and not panting. They interacted little
with the veterinarian. However, about 10% of puppies were outliers that did not explore,
were panting, were vocal (whining or barking), and sought active interaction (jumping
up and barking) with the veterinarian. During the physical examination with pups
placed on a table, the “outliers” actively tried to avoid the physical examination, panted,
and held their ears drawn back. These “outliers” also licked their lips and yawned during
both the physical examination and manipulations on the floor. Many behaviors
expressed by the “outliers” were compatible with recognized signs of anxiety such as
panting, excessive motor activity (pacing), active avoidance, vocalization, decreased
exploration, flattened ear position, lip licking, and yawning. This study illustrated that
some individuals behave very differently at a young age.
In another study,13 32 puppies (16 males, 16 females), ranging in age from 50 to 118
days (mean 82 days) were videorecorded at home alone for 60 minutes. The recording
process was repeated after 1 and 2 months, yielding a total of 3 recordings per puppy.
Puppies were mainly inactive, resting, or sleeping. Vocalization, lip licking, and oral
behaviors (chewing, biting, destroying items), which are signs compatible with stressrelated/anxious behaviors and tended to cluster together in the dogs of this study, were
apparent in 3/32 (10%) of puppies. Although this study did not follow up on all puppies’
future behaviors, 1 of the 3 “anxious” puppies did exhibit separation anxiety as an adult
and required treatment. Overall, these findings support the clinical experience of an
early-age onset of behavioral disorders. They suggest that careful history-taking can
detect signs compatible with anxiety at an early age in puppies, and that such elements
in a thorough medical history can be valuable in helping to differentiate behavioral from
medical causes of clinical signs.

Potential Medical Disorders in Dogs
Oral Repetitive Behaviors, Including PICA, Surface Licking,
Fly-Biting, Air Licking, Flank Sucking, and Self-Mutilation
In general, these oral repetitive behaviors are most likely signs of medical disorders in
isolation, or possibly with concomitant behavioral conditions. Historically, oral
repetitive behaviors were considered almost universally to be of primary behavioral
origin, but newer investigations have identified direct causal associations between some
of these signs and primary GI and other abdominal disorders. These signs could be
heightened by anxiety and coexisting behavioral disorders, but in general, oral repetitive
behaviors should carry a broader differential diagnosis than primary behavioral
disorders alone.
Pica is defined as the ingestion of non-food items. Owners generally do not
distinguish between destruction and pica. If destruction occurs during the owner’s
absence, the dog should be filmed home alone before diagnosing separation anxiety.
One destructive dog tentatively diagnosed with separation anxiety was filmed home
alone and slept during the entire duration of the owner’s absence. The destruction was
associated with pica and the dog also had a history of intermittent diarrhea. Following
medical investigation, the dog was diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

With a change in diet and treatment with prednisone, both the diarrhea and pica
improved. Whenever the prednisone dosage was decreased, the dog resumed pica. This
case illustrates the importance of obtaining GI biopsies when performing surgery for GI
foreign body removal in dogs (chs. 261 and 262), particularly in cases of “repeat
offenders,” because the foreign body ingestion may be the consequence of primary GI
disease; in turn, such GI disease may be escaping detection if it is manifesting through
clinical signs that are misinterpreted as being purely behavioral in origin.
Based on preliminary studies and case reports, GI disease can manifest with unusual
behavioral signs, including excessive licking of surfaces,14 fly-biting,15 and stargazing.16 In general, there are also other subtle signs of GI disease, such as presence of
flatulence, borborygmus, eructation, lip licking, repetitive swallowing, or drooling,
although not always (

Videos 11.1, 11.2, 11.3, 11.4, 11.5, 11.6). Owners will not

necessarily report these subtle GI signs unless asked about them specifically.
In a study of dogs licking surfaces (floors, walls, blankets, sofas, etc.) excessively,14
where patients received concurrent evaluations by a behavioral medicine service and an
internal medicine service, 14/19 dogs (74%) had GI disorders, including eosinophilic or
lymphoplasmacytic GI infiltration, delayed gastric emptying, irritable bowel syndrome,
chronic pancreatitis, giardiasis, and a gastric foreign body. Mean duration of the
“behavior” problem (e.g., how long the dog had been licking surfaces) was 32 months
(range 0.08 to 82). Sixteen of the 19 dogs licked surfaces daily. Following treatment for
the underlying condition, complete resolution of signs was achieved at 90 days in 53%
(9/17) and in 59% (10/17) at 180 days (unpublished results). Three dogs showed a
decrease (more than 50%) both in duration and in frequency of licking bouts at 180
days. Therefore, 76% of dogs (13/17) improved significantly clinically over the 6-month
follow-up. Of the 5 dogs without GI abnormalities and treated non-specifically
(hydrolysed protein diet), 2 dogs stopped licking by day 90. One of the surface-licking
dogs was also air licking (repetitive horizontal tongue movement in and out of the
mouth), retching, and closing its eyes partially; endoscopy revealed a 12-inch (30-cm)
piece of twine in the stomach, which had been present for an estimated 6 months prior
to presentation. Treatment included endoscopic removal of the foreign body and a
switch to a hydrolysed protein diet, and both the GI signs (air licking, surface licking,
and retching) and the pain-related sign (eyes partially closed)17 ceased once this
treatment was implemented (
Videos 11.6A and 11.6B).
Fly-biting is defined as an activity where the dog appears to be snapping at imaginary
flies.18 In 1 case series, medical investigation of 7 fly-biting dogs15 revealed that the
onset of fly-biting occurred within the wide age range of 6 months to 10 years. At the
time of presentation, dogs had exhibited fly-biting from 6 days to 4 years. The frequency
of bouts varied from once daily to once hourly. The duration of a single bout varied from
seconds to 1 hour. At home, fly-biting was more frequent following feeding in 3 dogs.
The most significant finding was the occurrence of head-raising and neck extension
preceding jaw snapping in all dogs. Clinical presentation was similar for all seven dogs.
In 2 cases, raising the head and extending the neck occurred more frequently than
snapping. Underlying medical abnormalities included gastric and/or duodenal
eosinophilic or lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, and delayed gastric emptying. Two dogs
had gastroesophageal reflux during endoscopy. One dog had no histological
abnormalities but presented a very flaccid and distended stomach on ultrasonographic

and endoscopic examination. Medical treatment of the underlying GI disease resulted in
complete resolution of fly-biting in 5/6 dogs (within 30 days for 4 dogs, including 1 dog
that had been fly-biting for 2 years). Four dogs also presented behavioral changes
compatible with anxiety (pacing, panting, hiding, increased attention-seeking) along
with the fly-biting episodes. These signs disappeared once the underlying GI disease was
treated (

Videos 11.3, 11.4A, and 11.4B).

Some of the repetitive behaviors also labeled as obsessive-compulsive disorders, such
as “flank sucking,” “self-mutilation,” and “checking,” could in fact be secondary to
somatic or visceral neuropathic pain. Inflammatory bowel disease could, in some cases,
be causing anal sac disease.19 Therefore, “checking behaviors” reported in Miniature
Schnauzers and “flank sucking” in Dobermans should include GI disease in the
differential. These dogs could be experiencing pain or discomfort and are therefore
looking repeatedly (“checking”) at the hind end or sucking the flank. Similarly, in cats, 1
case series identified that a majority (16/21 cats; 76%) suspected of having psychogenic
alopecia in fact had an underlying medical cause.20
Self-mutilation should always alert the veterinarian to the possibility of pain. Pain can
be local or neurogenic (ch. 6). However, animals should still be assessed for behavioral
disorders when pain is suspected. Neuropathic pain often is worsened by stimuli that
evoke a sympathetic response, such as the startle response and emotional arousal.21
Therefore, the increased arousal and reactivity often seen in anxiety disorders can
contribute to neuropathic pain.

Summary
• Typically, behavioral disorders are seen in young animals. Dogs suffering from
anxiety disorders tend to be more vigilant and reactive.
• For oral repetitive behaviors, owners should always be questioned about more
subtle GI signs such as flatulence, borborygmi, eructation, neck extension and
stretching, lip licking, tongue flicking, repetitive swallowing, or drooling, in
addition to more obvious signs such as vomiting (ch. 48), diarrhea (ch. 49), or
tenesmus (ch. 51).
• Gastrointestinal biopsies should always be taken when performing surgery for GI
foreign body removal in dogs, particularly in cases of “repeat offenders.”
• Medical and behavioral disorders may occur concomitantly. A thorough history
of all signs will help distinguish medical from behavioral disorders and identify
patients with concurrent disorders.

Client Information
Distinguishing Behavioral Disorders From Medical Disorders
Determining whether an animal shows symptoms caused by a medical disorder,
versus a behavioral or “psychological” disorder, can be extremely challenging in
veterinary medicine. Yet, this determination is of critical importance because the way of
approaching each, the treatments, and the expected outcomes all depend on accurately
pinpointing the cause of the problem.

Signs More Typical of Behavioral Disorders
In dogs and cats, anxiety is a dominant feature of many behavioral disorders and can be
an important characteristic for differentiating behavioral from medical disorders.
Anxiety is defined as the anticipation of a future danger, either real or imaginary.
Anticipation of real danger is normal. Anxiety becomes an illness (disorder) when the
animal is in a constant state of anxiety or is anticipating imaginary dangers. Anxiety
disorders in dogs and cats are often characterized by increased reactivity (heightened
arousal) and increased vigilance. The reactive/anxious dog or cat spends most of his or
her time being reactive and vigilant (unable to relax even though often the animal is
totally exhausted). The reactive dog or cat may startle more easily even at the sound of
day-to-day “regular” noises. This dog or cat in specific situations may in some cases
exhibit piloerection (hair raised on end, hackles raised) more rapidly and more
frequently. People sometimes describe that affected dogs or cats are difficult to interrupt
(e.g., “seems unable to hear” you because of fixating on something else) and require
more time to return to “normal” baseline behaviors after an event of inappropriate or
undesirable behavior. Anxious dogs or cats also have difficulty adapting to change, and
therefore any change in daily routine or environment can exacerbate signs of anxiety.
They sometimes seem unable to distinguish between real danger and perceived danger
(imaginary danger). Everything is thus interpreted as “dangerous.” Your observation of
such signs, and describing them to your veterinarian, can be very helpful in determining
the exact nature of your pet’s condition.

Signs Compatible With Medical or Behavioral Disorders
Signs of behavioral (“psychological”) and medical (“internal disease”) conditions can
overlap. Appearance of behaviors such as repeated lip licking, panting, pacing,
trembling, aggression, agitation, hiding, withdrawal, and vocalizing can be seen in
anxious animals with behavioral disorders, but also in sick or painful animals with
internal illness. Disappearance of behaviors such as playing, social interaction, and selfgrooming can also be seen in anxious, sick, or painful patients. It is therefore crucial to
distinguish between medical, painful, and behavioral disorders, because treatment and
outcome will differ depending on the underlying cause.

Age of Onset
Behavioral disorders are generally observed in young animals (6 to 18 months),
although some exceptions occur. Thunderstorm or firework phobia can appear later in

life. Signs of anxiety can be recognized in puppies as early as 2 to 4 months of age.
Sudden appearance of new behaviors (swallowing non-digestible items, aggression,
anxious behaviors, etc.), especially in middle-aged or older animals, generally are
indicative of an underlying internal medical condition.
Your observation of these features is an essential component of understanding the
nature of a pet’s problem and obtaining the correct diagnosis.

Next Steps if Your Animal is Behaving Differently
Ideally, the underlying cause must be identified in order to implement an appropriate
treatment plan. A film is worth a thousand words, so when possible, capturing the
unusual or undesirable behavior on video is often very useful. The behaviors and
symptoms that your veterinarian sees on the film can help orient tests necessary for
investigation of the following conditions: neurological, digestive, dermatological, or
urinary, or the findings observed on the video can point to typical behavioral disorders.
Keeping a log or diary of the undesirable events is also recommended. Important
information to record can include the animal’s body language, facial expression, and
frequency and duration of the behavior.
Diane Frank (St-Hyacinthe, Québec, Canada)

Manifestations of Systemic
Disease
Karen Campbell-Motsinger

Sheet.
The skin is the largest and most visible organ of the body.1
Dermatologic manifestations (Box 12.1) are often helpful in the
diagnosis of a systemic disease. When affected, skin is easily
accessible for obtaining samples for cytology, culture,
histopathology, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and other tests
useful in diagnoses of disease (ch. 83).

Systemic Diseases Associated with Skin
Color Changes
Erythema (Redness)
Pathologic conditions resulting in erythema/red skin include
vasodilation (ch. 26) and erythrocyte extravasation (petechiae or

ecchymoses).1 These can be differentiated by diascopy (

Video

12.1) using a glass slide to apply skin pressure, observing for
blanching (indicating that the erythema is due to inflammation.)
Cutaneous flushing is seen with pheochromocytoma episodically
(ch. 298). Localized or multifocal areas of erythema are seen with
allergies, ectoparasites, infections, immune-mediated diseases,
adverse drug reactions (erythema multiforme; ch. 178), neoplasia
(most commonly associated with mast cell tumors and cutaneous
lymphoma) and trauma.1 Darier’s sign: eliciting erythema and an
urticarial wheal by rubbing a lesion, is consistent with mast cell
tumors, systemic mastocytosis or urticaria pigmentosa. Petechiae
and ecchymoses (ch. 29) are seen with vasculitis (ch. 181) and/or
thrombocytopenia and are consistent with immune-mediated
diseases and infections (e.g., ehrlichiosis, Rocky Mountain spotted
fever; ch. 193).

Yellow Skin
The most common cause of skin turning a yellow color is jaundice
(icterus), which is the accumulation of bilirubin pigments in some
liver diseases or with hemolysis (ch. 28). Accumulation of
carotenoid pigments in the skin will also result in a yellow color.
BOX 1 2 .1
In this chapter, systemic diseases with cutaneous manifestations
are grouped into the following categories of presenting signs:
• Color changes
• Alopecia
• Thin skin/skin fragility
• Thick skin
• Scales and/or crusts
• Plaques and/or nodules

Pallor/White Skin/White
Hair/Hypopigmentation
Pallor (ch. 25) can be seen with severe anemia or inadequate
perfusion due to hypovolemia or cardiac failure. A loss of skin
pigment (leukoderma) and/or hair pigment (leukotrichia) can be due
to failure of melanin production (destruction of melanocytes or
tyrosine deficiency) or due to inflammation disrupting melanin
transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes. Causes include vitiligo,
cutaneous lupus (ch. 178), uveo-dermatological disease (E-Figure
12.1),2 hypoadrenocortism (ch. 296),3 and cutaneous lymphoma
(E-Figure 12.2; ch. 322).1 Partial oculocutaneous albinism and a
blue smoke coat color in Persian cats is a marker for ChédiakHigashi syndrome, an autosomal recessive disease with abnormal
granulocytes and platelets resulting in recurrent infections and
hemorrhage (ch. 176). A gray coat color and light-colored nose is a
marker for canine cyclic hematopoiesis, an autosomal recessive
disease in Collies where coat color is linked with a dysfunction of
pluripotential stem cells in the bone marrow (ch. 180).1

syndrome. B, Close-up of left eye showing
depigmentation of eyelids and uveitis. C, Close-up of
nose showing areas of depigmentation and
ulceration.

E-FIGURE 12.2 A, Patchy leukoderma and

Black/Blue Skin Lesions
Skin hyperpigmentation is commonly a sequela to cutaneous
inflammation. Pigmented viral plaques (E-Figure 12.3) due to
papillomavirus infection may progress to squamous cell
carcinomas.4 Melanomas may be pigmented or non-pigmented.
Cutaneous hemangiomas may be red or black in color. Blue cysts and
nodules may be apocrine gland cysts or tumors (E-Figure 12.4).1
Generalized blueness (cyanosis) occurs with reduced oxygenation
(ch. 27).

E-FIGURE 12.3 Pigmented viral plaques caused
by papillomavirus infection in an 8-month-old
Pomeranian dog.

E-FIGURE 12.4 Ear pinna of Domestic Shorthair
cat with apocrine cystadenomatosis.

Systemic Diseases Associated with
Alopecia
Overview
The differential diagnoses for alopecia are extensive. The classical
systemic diseases associated with generalized alopecia are the
endocrinopathies. It is important to rule out other causes of
generalized alopecia, including demodicosis, dermatophytosis,
bacterial folliculitis, pattern baldness, follicular dysplasias,
congenital hypotrichosis, telogen effluvium, color dilution alopecia,
sebaceous adenitis, and epitheliotrophic lymphoma. Feline
paraneoplastic alopecia is a cutaneous manifestation of pancreatic
and hepatic carcinomas.

Hypothyroidism (Chs. 285 AND 286)
Thyroid hormones are necessary for the initiation of the anagen
phase of the hair follicle cycle. Hair loss usually begins over the
bridge of the nose, ear pinnae, tail and elbows.1

Hyperadrenocorticism (Chs. 293 AND
294)
The skin is a sensitive indicator of hyperadrenocorticism. Early
findings include a thin, dull haircoat. Over time the skin also
becomes thin and may develop hyperpigmentation, bruises,
phlebectasias, striae, poor wound healing, secondary infections
and/or calcinosis cutis.1

Hyperestrogenism
Hyperestrogenism may develop in female dogs as a result of
polycystic ovaries or ovarian neoplasia. Cutaneous signs include
bilaterally symmetric alopecia, enlarged vulva and nipples, and a
history of abnormal estrous cycles. Male dogs develop
hyperestrogenism as a result of an estrogen-secreting testicular
tumor (most commonly a Sertoli cell tumor of cryptorchid testes).
Clinical signs include alopecia (E-Figure 12.5), nipple enlargement,
pendulous prepuce, ventral hyperpigmentation, attraction of other
male dogs, and atrophy of the non-neoplastic testicle. Any dog can
develop iatrogenic hyperestrogenism from estrogen-containing
compounds administered for treatment of urinary incontinence or
from contact with or licking creams or patches intended for human
use.5 A unique cutaneous manifestation of hyperestrogenism in male
dogs is linear preputial dermatosis—a linear, erythematous or
hyperpigmented narrow band of skin located between the preputial
orifice and the scrotum.6

E-FIGURE 12.5 Truncal alopecia in a 6-year-old
cryptorchid Poodle-mix dog with a Sertoli cell tumor.

Pituitary Dwarfism (CHS. 280 AND 281)
Pituitary dwarfism has been reported as an autosomal recessive
disorder in the German Shepherd Dog and Karelian Bear Dog (ch.
22). Affected dogs develop a bilaterally symmetric alopecia (EFigure 12.6), proportionate dwarfism, and delayed eruption of
permanent teeth.1

E-FIGURE 12.6 German Shepherd Dog with
pituitary dwarfism exhibiting generalized thinning of
the hair coat.

Feline Paraneoplastic Alopecia
Rapid development of extensive alopecia in an older cat may be the
first sign of underlying pancreatic or hepatic neoplasia; most
commonly the etiology is pancreatic adenocarcinoma, but a few have
had hepatic carcinoma or biliary cholangiocarcinoma.1,7 Hair loss
often begins periocularly and rapidly progresses to involve the
ventral neck, abdomen and legs (Figure 12.7). Hairs epilate easily
and the alopecic skin appears shiny but is not fragile. Secondary
Malassezia infection may cause excessive grooming. Some cats also
have dry, scaly footpads.

Systemic Diseases with Thin Skin/Skin
Fragility
Cutaneous Asthenia (Ehlers Danlos Syndrome,
Dermatosparaxis)
Cutaneous asthenia, a hereditary disease that causes defective
formation of connective tissue, results in skin hyperextensibility (EFigure 12.8) and fragility. Some dogs have joint hyperlaxity and
luxations, hernias (diaphragmatic, perianal), periodontal disease,
subcutaneous hematomas and vascular complications.8 Several
forms occur in animals and humans.9 A defect in procollagen
peptidase was identified in one cat.10

E-FIGURE 12.8 Hyperextensibility of the skin of a
mixed breed dog with cutaneous asthenia.

Feline Skin Fragility

Acquired skin fragility is most often seen in cats with
hyperadrenocorticism secondary to adrenal tumors or iatrogenic
administration of glucocorticoids or progestational compounds (ch.
294).1 Skin fragility has been reported uncommonly secondary to
feline infectious peritonitis, hepatic lipidosis, or hepatic
neoplasia.11,12

Systemic Diseases with Thick Skin
Mucinosis
Excessive amounts of mucin in the dermis causing thick skin is a
breed-associated characteristic of Chinese Shar-Pei dogs and is
occasionally seen in hypothyroid dogs (ch. 285).1

Acromegaly (CHS. 280, 281)
Cutaneous changes associated with acromegaly include thickened
myxedematous skin with excessive skin folds, hypertrichosis and
thick hard claws. Hypersecretion of growth hormone may be a result
of pituitary neoplasia or hyperprogesteronism.1

Systemic Diseases with Scales and/or
Crusts
Canine Distemper (Ch. 204)
The classic skin manifestation of canine distemper is “hard pad
disease” with hyperkeratosis of the footpads and planum nasale.
Superficial pustules (impetigo) may be seen during the acute phase
of the disease.1

FIGURE 12.7 A, Domestic Shorthair cat with
paraneoplastic alopecia associated with pancreatic
adenocarcinoma. Note the distribution of lesions
affecting face, legs, neck and ventral abdomen. B,
Close-up of leg showing the characteristic shiny
appearance of the alopecic skin.

Dermatomyositis
Dermatomyositis, a genetic disease affecting skin and/or muscle, is
most commonly diagnosed in Collies and Shetland Sheepdogs. Initial
skin lesions are usually small focal areas of crusting, scaling and
alopecia on the face, lower extremities and tail (E-Figure 12.9).
Over time the skin becomes atrophic. Concurrent muscle disease
may result in dysphagia and gait abnormalities. Affected dogs may
also develop megaesophagus. The disease is thought to be autosomal
dominant with incomplete penetrance in Collies.1 A study of linkage
disequilibrium mapping in Shelties had evidence of a microsatellite
marker on canine chromosome 35.13 This disorder has also been
classified as an ischemic dermatopathy.14

E-FIGURE 12.9 A, Shetland Sheepdog puppy with
dermatomyositis with alopecia, scaling and crusting
of periocular and dorsal nasal skin. B, Severe
alopecia with scales and crusts on the tail of the
Shetland Sheepdog puppy in A.

Epitheliotropic (Cutaneous) T-cell
Lymphoma (CH. 322)
This form of lymphoma can cause a variety of cutaneous
manifestations (see E-Figure 12.2), including erythroderma,
alopecia, variable pruritus, scales, crusts, plaques, nodules,
leukoderma, leukotrichia, mucocutaneous ulcers, and depigmented,
ulcerated or hyperkeratotic footpads. A few affected animals also
have neoplastic lymphocytes in circulation (Sezary syndrome).1

Feline Thymoma-Associated Exfoliative
Dermatitis
Skin lesions of erythema, crusting and scaling with alopecia (EFigure 12.10) may be the first sign of disease in cats with
thymomas. Secondary infections with Malassezia may result in
pruritus. Affected cats may also have signs of coughing, dyspnea,
anorexia, and weight loss.1,15,16

E-FIGURE 12.10 Thymoma-associated exfoliative
dermatitis in a neutered male Domestic Shorthair cat
with generalized crusts and scales.

Leishmaniasis (Ch. 197)
Skin lesions are seen in >80% of dogs with visceral leishmaniasis,
most commonly silvery white scales over the head, pinnae and limbs.

Nasodigital hyperkeratosis may be present and periocular alopecia is
common. Other findings include onychogryposis, paronychia, nasal
depigmentation, and nodular dermatitis. Systemic signs include
lethargy, weight loss, generalized lymphadenopathy,
hepatosplenomegaly, muscle wasting, cachexia, fever, epistaxis and
lameness. Associated renal failure may cause polyuria and
polydipsia.1

Lethal Acral Dermatitis/Acrodermatitis
Bull Terriers may be affected by an autosomal recessive condition
caused by a MKLN1 splicing defect on chromosome 14 that results in
defective zinc and copper metabolism and altered production of 13
liver proteins.17 Affected puppies have lighter than normal skin
pigmentation, often have difficulty chewing/swallowing, and develop
splaying of the digits, crusting and cracking of their footpads (EFigure 12.11), and ulcerated crusted lesions on the ear pinnae and
mucocutaneous junctions. Foot lesions progress to onychodystrophy,
paronychia and interdigital pyoderma. Systemic signs may include
diarrhea and respiratory infections. Most succumb to secondary
infections before 7 months of age.1,17 Genetic testing is available
through several laboratories.

E-FIGURE 12.11 Left hind limb of 6-week-old Bull
Terrier puppy with lethal acrodermatitis. Note the
splaying of the digits and hyperkeratosis of the
footpads and posterior surface of the leg.

Lupus Erythematosus (Ch. 179)
Lupus erythematosus is an autoimmune, inflammatory disorder with
several forms.18 Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) causes skin
lesions of the face, particularly the planum nasale and dorsal surface
of the nose (ch. 178). Severely affected dogs may have nasal
turbinate involvement with epistaxis and secondary infections.1
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), a multisystem disease with
variable clinical presentations, causes skin lesions in 40% to 50% of
cases that vary from mild scaling and/or alopecia of the face and
dorsum to severe ulcerations. Other findings may include fever,
malaise, anemia, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, lameness,
depression and/or behavioral changes. Exfoliative cutaneous lupus
erythematosus (ECLE) is a familial form primarily affecting German

Shorthaired Pointer dogs.18,19 Skin lesions are often the first
abnormality noted and include excessive scaling and crusting of the
muzzle, pinnae and dorsum (E-Figure 12.12). As the disease
progresses, most dogs develop severe lameness, renal disease, and
are euthanized before 4 years of age.18,19 Genetic studies of affected
dogs have identified a homozygous missense variant in the Cterminal tail of UNC93B1 that restricts TLR7-mediated
autoimmunity via interactions with syndecan binding protein.19

E-FIGURE 12.12 German Shorthaired Pointer
with exfoliative cutaneous lupus erythematosus
exhibiting generalized cutaneous scaling.

Paraneoplastic Pemphigus (Chs. 178 AND
331)
Paraneoplastic pemphigus has been reported in dogs in association
with thymic lymphoma and splenic sarcoma. Clinical signs include

scaling and crusting associated with vesiculobullous and ulcerative
lesions affecting the face and clawfolds. Autoantibodies in affected
dogs have targeted desmoplakin, envoplakin, periplakin, desmoglein
1 and desmoglein 3.20

Superficial Necrolytic Dermatitis (SND;
Hepatocutaneous Disease) (CH. 274)
Skin lesions in dogs with SND include ulceration and crusting of
mucocutaneous junctions, face, footpads and pressure points
(Figure 12.13) due to degeneration of keratinocytes resulting in
epidermal edema and necrosis. The degeneration of keratinocytes is
believed to be due to hypoaminoacidemia resulting in inadequate
nutrients to maintain a viable epidermis. The underlying cause in
most affected dogs is liver disease; only a few have glucagonoma.21,22
Most affected dogs also have a non-regenerative anemia, mild
hyperglycemia, and increased liver enzyme activities (ch. 269). The
disease in cats has been associated with pancreatic tumors and
chronic liver disease.23,24

Zinc-Responsive Dermatitis (ch. 160)
Skin lesions associated with zinc deficiency or zinc-responsive
dermatitis include areas of erythema, alopecia, scales and crusts
starting on the face, mucocutaneous junctions, feet and footpads.
Other findings may include depressed appetite, weight loss, impaired
wound healing and increased susceptibility to secondary infections.
Alaskan Malamutes and Siberian Huskies are most often affected
and may have a decrease in intestinal absorption of zinc.25,26
Pharaoh Hounds have also been reported with a severe form of the
disease.27

FIGURE 12.13 Doberman Pinscher mixed breed
dog with superficial necrolytic dermatitis associated
with liver disease. A, Pustules and crusts are present
on ventral thorax, abdomen and limbs. B,
Ulcerations and crusts of lower leg and footpads of
dog in A. C, Ulceration and crusting over hock of

dog in A, note the intense erythema of the skin
adjacent to the crusts.

Systemic Diseases with Cutaneous
Plaques and/or Nodules
Calcinosis Cutis
Lesions of calcinosis cutis appear as granular plaques in the skin (EFigure 12.14), most commonly over the dorsum or in the inguinal
region. Apatite crystals are usually found deposited in the dermis in
association with collagen or elastin fibers. Metastatic calcification
occurs as a result of excesses in circulating calcium and/or
phosphorus in dogs with renal failure or systemic blastomycosis or
paecilomycosis. “Dystrophic calcification” is thought to be the result
of alterations to collagen fibers in dogs with hyperadrenocorticism or
as a result of inflammatory diseases such as leptospirosis, follicular
cysts, foreign body granulomas, interdigital pyoderma, demodicosis
or pilomatrixomas. Iatrogenic calcinosis cutis has been reported
secondary to percutaneous absorption or injection of calciumcontaining products. Calcinosis circumscripta lesions develop over
pressure points or areas of trauma (including the tongue and
footpads) of young dogs during the stage of life when serum levels of
phosphorus and calcium are elevated.28

E-FIGURE 12.14 Calcinosis cutis forming plaques
on the dorsal neck of a mixed breed dog with
iatrogenic hyperadrenocorticism.

Eosinophilic Plaques
Eosinophilic plaques develop in cats in association with underlying
allergies (parasitic, dietary or environmental).1

Feline Viral Diseases (Chs. 199 AND 205)
Feline herpesvirus 1 (rhinotracheitis) can cause cutaneous and oral
ulcers in cats and occasionally results in severe pruritus. Feline
calicivirus can result in oral vesicles and ulcers.1 Feline poxvirus
causes cutaneous nodules that ulcerate and can also result in
systemic signs, including fever, anorexia, depression, diarrhea and
pneumonia.29 Cats with feline leukemia virus infections may exhibit
chronic or recurrent gingivitis, pyoderma, poor wound healing,
seborrhea, exfoliative dermatitis, pruritus, cutaneous horns, giant

cell dermatosis and/or secondary infections with bacteria, Demodex,
dermatophytes and other fungal infections.1

Hyperpigmented Viral Plaques
Canine viral plaques are a manifestation of papillomaviral infection
that appear as pigmented lesions on the ventral abdomen (see EFigure 12.3) or in the axillary region. On occasion, papillomavirusassociated viral plaques progress to squamous cell carcinomas.1,4

Infectious/Pyogranulomatous Nodules
Cutaneous nodules and/or ulcerated draining lesions develop
commonly in animals with blastomycosis (ch. 209),
coccidioidomycosis (ch. 208), cryptococcosis (ch. 207),
histoplasmosis (ch. 209), aspergillosis (ch. 211), lagenidiosis or
mycobacterial infections (ch. 188). Nodules typically develop
following hematogenous dissemination of the organism from
another site (pulmonary, nasal, gastrointestinal) to the skin and less
commonly following direct inoculation of fungal, oomyces or
bacterial organisms into the skin.1

Nodular Dermatofibromas
German Shepherd and related dogs have an autosomal dominant
genetic disease due to mutations in the folliculin gene (FLCN)
causing multiple cutaneous nodules, cysts and kidney
cystadenocarcinomas.30,31 Females may also develop uterine
leiomyomas and leiomyosarcomas.1

Sterile Nodular Panniculitis (SNP)—
Pancreatic Panniculitis Variant

Sterile nodular panniculitis is characterized by sterile subcutaneous
inflammatory nodules that may ulcerate and drain a purulent or oily
exudate. While uncommon, pancreatitis (ch. 277) and pancreatic
tumors have been associated with panniculitis (E-Figure 12.15).3234
Other differentials for nodular panniculitis include foreign bodies,
immune-mediated reactions, infections, vitamin E deficiency
(pansteatitis in cats eating diets high in red tuna or fed excess cod
liver oil), serum alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, injection reactions,
burns and trauma.1

E-FIGURE 12.15 Panniculitis with ulcerations on
the back of a dog with pancreatic adenocarcinoma
(area has been shaved).

Xanthomas
Xanthomas appear as yellow-white papules, nodules or plaques
located on the head, limbs, feet and/or over bony prominences (EFigure 12.16). Xanthomas develop in animals with hyperlipidemia

(ch. 156) due to hereditary hyperlipoproteinemia, diabetes mellitus,
hyperadrenocorticism, treatment with progestational compounds or
following consumption of high-fat foods and treats.35-38

E-FIGURE 12.16 Xanthomas on the posterior
surface of hindlegs of a 2-year-old Domestic
Shorthair cat with familial hyperlipidemia.

Client Information
Dermatologic Manifestations of Systemic
Disease
We understand that you have many questions regarding the
recommendations being made for evaluation of your pet’s general
health when your concern is that your pet has been losing hair and
developing excessive “dandruff.” Additionally, your pet has been
licking its legs and has had a decreased appetite lately. The reason we
are recommending an extensive evaluation is because there are many
possible causes for hair loss, “dandruff” and decreased appetite. Here
is a summary of the tests we are recommending and what we will be
looking for in each test.
• Skin scrapings: these involve using a dull blade to remove a
small sample of skin to examine for mites that could be
responsible for the hair loss and irritation that is causing your
pet to lick excessively.
• Skin cytology: we will apply a piece of clear tape to your pet’s
skin to remove any organisms on the surface of the skin. This
will enable us to determine if your pet has a bacterial or yeast
infection in the skin that could be making it itchy.
• Wood’s light examination: this is a screening test for one type
of ringworm that pets are susceptible to and that can cause
hair loss.
• Dermatophyte culture: not all types of ringworm show up on a
Wood’s light examination, therefore we recommend also doing
a culture for ringworm to be certain that your pet is not
infected with one of these organisms.
• Serum biochemistry profile: animals may develop may develop
many problems such as diabetes mellitus, liver disease or
kidney disease that could be affecting your pet’s appetite and
overall health; a serum biochemistry profile will help us in
detecting any problems with these organs.
• Thyroid hormone testing: animals sometimes experience a
dysregulation in thyroid hormone production. Most
commonly in older cats an overproduction of thyroid
hormones can result in overgrooming and hair loss. Dogs are

more likely to have problems associated with a decrease in
thyroid hormone secretion.
• Adrenal function testing: pets sometimes develop an
overproduction of cortisol that can result in hair loss; we may
need to do a series of blood tests known as “dexamethasone
suppression testing” to determine whether there is a
dysregulation in cortisol production.
• Skin biopsy: taking a couple of small pieces of your pet’s skin
can be easily done using a local anesthetic and can provide us
with important information regarding the cause of hair loss
and excessive scaling and itching.
• Abdominal ultrasound: one of the possible causes of hair loss
and other skin lesions in animals is liver disease or a tumor in
pancreas or liver; an ultrasound exam of the abdomen may
detect whether there is a tumor in the pancreas or liver and
will also allow us to examine other organs, including the
adrenal glands and kidneys.
We understand that this is a lot of information and that you may
well be surprised that there are so many possible reasons for hair
loss, scaling and a decreased appetite. We would be happy to discuss
any questions that you may have regarding our recommendations
and to help you prioritize the list of diagnostic tests if you decide not
to have all the tests performed in the same visit. We anticipate that
performing all of these tests will give us the best opportunity to
determine why your pet is showing the signs of hair loss and
inappetence and will enable us to provide you with the best
recommendations on how to help your pet. We thank you for the
confidence that you have shown in bringing your pet to our clinic.
Karen Campbell-Motsinger (Wentzville, Missouri; Urbana,
Illinois; Columbia, Missouri)

on Elsevier eBooks+: 4 Videos and 3 Client Information Sheets.

Introduction
A thorough ophthalmic examination is an important part of a
physical examination in every patient. The clinician has the unique
opportunity to directly visualize blood vessels as well as neurologic
tissue (the optic nerve) in the fundus of the eye. Abundant blood
supply to the iris and choroid makes these tissues susceptible to
spread of infectious organisms or neoplastic cells to these tissues
with inflammation of the iris, ciliary body and choroid as a result.

Other parts of the eye may be affected by various systemic diseases
as well. This chapter will first describe ophthalmic examination
techniques, followed by ocular manifestations of systemic disease in
the various parts of the eye.

Ophthalmic Examination
Proper restraint is important for ophthalmic examination and
measurement of intraocular pressure (

Videos 13.1 and 13.2).

Examination of the anterior segment of the eye is best performed
using a bright light source. A slit lamp biomicroscope is ideal for
examination of the anterior segment, as it provides illumination and
magnification at the same time (Figure 13.1). The slit lamp function
allows further localization of lesions by providing optical crosssections of the anterior segment of the eye. Most penlights are not
bright enough for a thorough examination. A Finoff transilluminator
will provide a focal bright light beam. Magnification and illumination
can be obtained at the same time by using an otoscope. The eyelids
are evaluated for function, anatomy and the presence of abnormal
ciliae. Normal conjunctiva is thin and has scant blood vessels.
Hyperemia and swelling of the conjunctiva (chemosis) are commonly
seen abnormalities. A normal cornea has a glossy appearance and is
transparent. The anterior chamber is best evaluated for the presence
of aqueous flare by focusing a small light beam on the cornea and
observing light scattering on proteins and cells in the anterior
chamber if present (

Video 13.3). A normal lens is transparent

and located between the iris and the vitreous cavity. The fundus can
be examined by either direct or indirect ophthalmoscopy. Direct
ophthalmoscopy is easy to learn and the equipment is often readily
available (Figure 13.2). It provides high magnification of a small
portion of the fundus. Indirect ophthalmoscopy is the preferred
choice for evaluating a large part of the retina at one time at a
relatively low magnification (

Video 13.4). Equipment needed

includes a focal bright light source and an indirect viewing lens
(Figure 13.2). Popular lenses include the panretinal 2.2 lens, as well

as a 20 or 28 diopter lens. The Welch Allyn Panoptic
ophthalmoscope combines the ease of use of a direct
ophthalmoscope with a relatively large area of the fundus evaluated
at one time.

Interpretation of Fundus Lesions
One of the questions to ask when observing a lesion in the fundus is
whether it is an active or inactive lesion. Inactive lesions are common
incidental findings that have little clinical significance. The presence
of active fundus lesions may help determine diagnostic plans for
current diseases in the patient. Evaluating the color and reflectivity
of a lesion in the tapetal area of the fundus can help determine
whether a lesion is active or inactive. Focal areas of chorioretinitis
over time will result in thinning of the retina, exposing the reflective
tapetum to a greater degree than normal. The result is a focal
hyperreflective area in the tapetum, which is consistent with an
inactive lesion. If a tapetal lesion involves the retinal pigment
epithelium in the deepest part of the retina, focal hyperpigmentation
is a common result (Figure 13.3). Clinically this is seen as a
hyperreflective lesion with a dark center. If the color of the
underlying tapetum in an active lesion appears to have changed little
compared to the surrounding tapetum, clear fluid is present in the
lesion. This can be seen with (early) systemic hypertension (ch. 236)
and secondary retinal edema. If the color of the underlying tapetum
has changed, this indicates the presence of cells in the lesion. This
could be either hemorrhage or other cellular infiltrates such as white
blood cells or neoplastic cells. Figure 13.4 is a flowchart for
evaluating tapetal fundus lesions.

Eyelids and Conjunctiva
Blepharitis, inflammation of the eyelids, can be a disease in itself, or
be part of a generalized dermatologic problem. The eyelids have
numerous meibomian glands, which are an important part of the
tear film as they secrete the oily surface part of the tear film. These
glands can become impacted and secondary infection with

Staphylococcus spp. may result in painful, swollen eyelids. Infection
with Demodex spp. may result in alopecia of the eyelids. Immunemediated diseases such as uveodermatologic syndrome or
pemphigoid diseases may affect the eyelids and mucocutaneous
junctions (ch. 178).1 Infectious diseases, such as leishmaniasis (ch.
197) can manifest themselves in the eyelids.2 The etiology for
blepharitis in a retrospective study of 102 dogs found allergic disease
to be most common (52%), followed by infectious/parasitic (21.5%),
autoimmune (17.7%) and neoplastic disease (4.9%).3
Inflammation of the conjunctiva (conjunctivitis) is common in
cats. Hyperemia of the conjunctiva, chemosis, blepharospasm and
epiphora are common signs. Infection with feline herpesvirus 1
(FHV-1) is a common cause of conjunctivitis in cats and is often selflimiting in nature (ch. 205). Primary infections with this virus are
often associated with upper respiratory signs. Recrudescent
infections often involve the eye(s) only. Supportive care with a
topical antibiotic ointment 3 to 4 times a day is indicated to prevent
secondary bacterial infections. In cats with a weak immune system,
antiviral therapy is often needed to help resolve the clinical signs.
This can be either topical (0.5% cidofovir twice a day, vidarabine,
trifluridine or idoxuridine 4 times a day) or systemic by using oral
famciclovir. The recommended dosage for famciclovir has a broad
range: from 8 mg/kg once daily to 140 mg/kg 3 times daily.4 A
placebo-controlled study showed efficacy of famciclovir against FHV1 infection at 90 mg/kg 3 times daily.5 A subsequent study revealed
that 40 mg/kg 3 times daily resulted in tear penciclovir
concentration that were suggested to be high enough to be effective
against FHV-1.6 A more recent pharmacokinetic study recommends
that famciclovir should be given to cats at 90 mg/kg twice a
day.7 Chlamydophila felis and Mycoplasma felis are conjunctival
pathogens in cats although less common than FHV-1 (ch. 205).
Conjunctival and nictitating membrane involvement has been
reported in disseminated histoplasmosis in cats (ch. 209).8
Conjunctivitis in dogs is often secondary to a decrease in tear
production (keratoconjunctivitis sicca [KCS]) or systemic allergies.

Infectious causes of conjunctivitis such as canine herpesvirus are
rare in dogs.9
