Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca
A decrease in tear production is a very common cause of redness,
irritation and discharge in dogs. An immune-mediated destruction of
the tear gland is the most common cause for KCS in dogs. Other
causes for KCS in dogs include endocrine disorders (diabetes
mellitus; ch. 291),10,11 neurogenic, iatrogenic (excision of the gland
of the nictitating membrane, radiation therapy), distemper infection
(ch. 204), and chronic blepharoconjunctivitis.3 Clinical signs
include redness and (mucoid) discharge, especially in the morning.
In acute KCS, corneal ulceration is common. Medications such as
oral sulfonamides and etodolac have also been associated with KCS

in dogs.12,13 Oral antihistamines commonly used in management of
atopy in dogs can cause a decrease in tear production as well.
Special consideration needs to be given to dogs that are sick
enough to be hospitalized. A study evaluating tear production in dogs
admitted to an intensive care unit found a significant decrease in tear
production in these dogs.14 This may predispose to the development
of painful corneal ulcerations. Application of lubricating artificial
tear ointment several times a day may help prevent surface ocular
disease in sick dogs.
KCS is rare in cats, and clinical signs are different in cats than in
dogs. A transient decrease in tear production is often seen in FHV-1
infection (ch. 205). This decrease may become permanent in some
cats. The most common clinical sign of KCS in the author’s
experience is blepharospasm that is fairly mild but persistent.
Mucoid discharge as seen in dogs is not usually present, and
conjunctival hyperemia is often subtle. Corneal changes such as
fibrosis/pigmentation/vascularization are not usually present in KCS
in cats. Diagnosis of KCS in cats can be challenging as normal cats
can have a low Schirmer tear test (STT) reading secondary to stress.
Presence of clinical signs in combination with response to therapy
(viscous artificial tear solution 2 to 3 times a day) often confirms the
diagnosis of KCS in cats.

Cornea
A normal cornea is transparent, devoid of blood vessels and pigment,
and is in a constant state of dehydration. The cornea receives its
nutrition from the aqueous humor and the tear film. Multiple
different abnormalities can be seen within the cornea. Table 13.1
lists corneal changes and their characteristic appearance and most
common causes. Lipid keratopathy is a unilateral or bilateral lipid
infiltration secondary to systemic disease. Common diseases include
hypothyroidism (ch. 285), diabetes mellitus (ch. 291), pancreatitis
(ch. 277), and any condition causing an increase in serum lipid
concentrations (ch. 156).15 The opacity may be in the central or
paracentral or peripheral cornea. It may be focal, or arc shaped along
the limbus, often with a clear area between the limbus and the lesion.

Calcium infiltrate in the cornea in dogs is associated with ocular or
systemic disease and is most commonly seen in older dogs. Systemic
disorders associated with corneal calcium infiltrates include
hypophosphatemia, hypercalcemia, hypervitaminosis D, and uremia.
Treatment consists of topical 1-3% NaEDTA solution or ointment, or
diamond burr debridement.16 Intrastromal corneal hemorrhages can
be seen in older dogs.17 Systemic disease including diabetes mellitus
(ch. 291), hyperadrenocorticism (ch. 293), hypothyroidism (ch.
285), and systemic hypertension (ch. 236) is present in the
majority of affected dogs.

Iris
The anterior uvea of the eye consists of the iris and ciliary body. The
ciliary body is continuous with the choroid, and inflammation of the
anterior uvea is often associated with inflammation of the choroid as
well. The uveal tract is a highly vascular area and is often affected by
systemic diseases. Inflammation of the uveal tract results in a
breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier. This is clinically visible as
aqueous flare when proteins and/or cells enter the aqueous humor. (
Video 13.3). A decrease in production of aqueous humor by the
ciliary body in combination with increased resorption through the
inflamed uveal tract results in a decrease in intraocular pressure.
Spasm of the ciliary body muscles may result in a painful miosis.
Other clinical signs seen in anterior uveitis include conjunctival and
scleral hyperemia and a decrease in vision or loss of vision if
inflammation is severe.
Anterior uveitis has many causes in both dogs and cats.18 The
most common causes in cats include infection with feline leukemia
virus (ch. 199), feline immunodeficiency virus (ch. 198), feline
infectious peritonitis (ch. 200), Toxoplasma gondii (ch. 197), the
various systemic fungal diseases (chs. 207, 208, 209) and
neoplasia.19 The role of Bartonella henselae in anterior uveitis in
cats is still debated (ch. 191). Numerous etiologies exist in dogs.
They include ocular (trauma, lens-induced uveitis) and systemic
diseases including infectious organisms such as bacterial, fungal,

rickettsial, protozoal, parasitic, viral diseases and immune mediated
and neoplastic diseases.20-25 Uveodermatologic disease is an
immune-mediated destruction of pigment in the eye and the skin
resulting in uveitis and loss of pigmentation in skin and hair (chs. 12
and 178).1 Diagnostic workup includes testing for the various
infectious diseases. Aqueocentesis is not diagnostic in anterior
uveitis cases with a non-neoplastic etiology. It can be useful in the
diagnosis of lymphoma in dogs and cats.26-28 Lipemic uveitis is the
accumulation of lipoproteins in the anterior chamber. Miniature
Schnauzers and Yorkshire Terriers were overrepresented in a study
of 75 cases. Ophthalmic disease was present in 43% of cases.
Systemic disease was present in 72% of cases with diabetes mellitus
(ch. 291), hyperadrenocorticism (ch. 293) and hypothyroidism
(ch. 285) the most common diseases. The combination of
hyperlipidemia and uveitis needs to be present for lipid flare to be
visible in the anterior chamber.29 Pigmentary uveitis is an inherited
disease in Golden Retrievers. Pigmentary uveitis is not associated
with other ocular or systemic diseases. Iris hyperpigmentation,
fibrinous material deposits within the anterior chamber and
pigmentation on the anterior lens capsule are visible. Pigmentary
uveitis can result in secondary cataract formation, glaucoma and
blindness.30 A cause may not always be found for anterior uveitis in
dogs and cats but nevertheless, treatment is indicated in these
animals. Management of uveitis consists of treatment of the
underlying disease if possible as well as treatment of the uveitis
itself. Treatment of anterior uveitis consists of topical corticosteroids
such as 1% prednisolone acetate, 0.1% dexamethasone solution or
0.05% difluprednate.31 The frequency of application depends on the
severity of the disease. A painful miosis is often present and is best
treated with application of topical 1% atropine solution or ointment.
Topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications such as 0.03%
flurbiprofen, 0.1% diclofenac or 0.5% ketorolac are especially useful
if the presence of a corneal ulceration precludes the use of topical
corticosteroids. Systemic corticosteroids or other
immunosuppressive medications (ch. 144) are indicated in
treatment of severe anterior uveitis or if the choroid is involved in
the disease process as well. Careful monitoring of the intraocular

pressure is indicated, as secondary glaucoma may occur in anterior
uveitis.

Lens
The lens is an avascular structure, and abnormalities of the lens are
limited to cataract formation and lens luxation. The most common
reason for cataract formation in the dog is a hereditary abnormality.
The second most common cause is diabetes mellitus32 (Figure 13.5;
ch. 291). The onset of diabetic cataracts is often very sudden and
affected dogs may lose their vision within days to weeks.33 The high
concentration of glucose in the lens is metabolized through aldose
reductase into sorbitol which accumulates in the lens. This results in
an accumulation of water in the lens with subsequent lens fiber
damage and cataract formation. The lens can become much larger
than normal (intumescent cataract) and secondary spontaneous lens
capsule rupture has been reported in diabetic dogs.34 The window of
opportunity for successful cataract surgery is much shorter in
diabetic dogs than in dogs with genetic cataracts and surgery should
be performed soon after the onset of cataract formation if possible.
Focal cataract formation in the lens can be seen in dogs with
hypocalcemia. The most common cause for cataract formation in
cats is chronic anterior uveitis.

Choroid and Retina
It is uncommon for diseases to affect the choroid and/or retina
without affecting the anterior uvea as well. The causes for
choroiditis, retinitis, and chorioretinitis are similar to the causes for
anterior uveitis in dogs and cats.35,36 Clinical signs of chorioretinitis
may include retinal edema, retinal vascular changes such as
tortuosity or vasculitis, intraretinal, preretinal or vitreal
hemorrhages, and retinal detachment. Vision may be impaired if
changes are severe. Diagnosis and treatment of chorioretinitis is
similar to the diagnosis and treatment of anterior uveitis. Topically
applied medications, however, are not effective in treating
chorioretinitis, and systemic treatment is indicated. Punctate retinal
hemorrhages were identified in a study in 119 eyes of 83 dogs.

Concurrent ophthalmic diseases were present in 66% of eyes.
Systemic disease was present in 60% of affected dogs, with diabetes
mellitus (ch. 291), multiple myeloma (ch. 322) and systemic
hypertension (ch. 236) the most common diseases present.37

FIGURE 13.5 Diabetic cataract. Being a mature
cataract, it prevents visualization of the fundus and
is associated with absence of vision in that eye. This
is different from nuclear sclerosis, which is a normal
aging change where the fundus is visible through the
aging lens, and where vision is present.
The optic nerve is the only part of the central nervous system that
can be observed and evaluated directly in the conscious patient. A
normal optic nerve in a dog is variable in size and shape, depending
on the amount of myelin present (Figure 13.6). The edges of a
normal optic nerve are well-defined. Edema of the optic nerve and
inflammation of the optic nerve can have a similar appearance. The
optic nerve is swollen and protruding into the vitreous cavity, the
edges are hazy and indistinct, and there may be edema present in the
area immediately adjacent to the optic nerve (Figure 13.7). Optic

nerve edema may be associated with an increase in intracranial
pressure. Evaluation of the optic nerve prior to collection of
cerebrospinal fluid is indicated (ch. 109). Vision may not be affected
when optic nerve edema is present. Inflammation of the optic nerve
(optic neuritis) is usually associated with a mydriatic pupil and loss
of vision. Optic neuritis should be considered part of a neurologic
disease, and appropriate diagnostic workup for neurologic disease is
indicated (chs. 14 and 242).

Sudden Acquired Retinal Degeneration Syndrome
Sudden acquired retinal degeneration (SARD) is a common cause of
irreversible blindness in dogs.38 It most commonly affects female
dogs of middle to older age, and small breeds are predisposed.39,40
Clinical signs include sudden loss of vision sometimes preceded by a
decrease in night vision. Vision loss develops over a period of days to
weeks. Systemic abnormalities are often present and may precede
the vision loss. They include polyuria/polydipsia, polyphagia, and
weight gain. Routine labwork often reveals an increase in liver
enzyme activities and a stress leukogram. Clinical signs that precede
the vision loss may mimic Cushing’s disease41 (ch. 293).
Ophthalmic examination is unremarkable with a clinically normal
appearing retina. The diagnosis is confirmed by an
electroretinogram, which will show extinguished retinal function.
Chromatic pupillary light response (PLR) testing using a bright red
and blue light source typically results in a lack of, or severely
diminished, PLR using the red light source and a normal PLR using
the blue light source. On histopathologic examination, the
photoreceptor outer segments show acute degeneration with the
remainder of the retina being relatively normal. The etiology of
SARD continues to be poorly understood. An immune-mediated
etiology has been suggested.42 Various immunosuppressive
therapies have been attempted, but none has proven to be
consistently successful to date.43

variable in size and shape, pink in color, and has
well-defined edges.

areas adjacent to the optic nerve.

Orbital Disease
Inflammatory or neoplastic diseases of the orbit are often local
diseases and not associated with systemic disease. Signs of orbital
disease may include exophthalmos, protrusion of the third eyelid,
decreased retropulsion of the globe into the orbit, and loss of vision
and pain upon opening of the mouth. Abscess formation in the orbit
of dogs may be associated with dental disease, foreign body
penetration through the mouth or conjunctival surfaces, or rarely be
a consequence of abscess formation elsewhere in the body. Orbital
inflammatory disease often has an acute onset, is very painful, and
general malaise is usually present. Masticatory myositis is an
immune-mediated inflammation of the masticatory muscles and may

result in bilateral painful orbital disease.44 Diagnosis is confirmed by
testing for type 2M fiber-specific autoantibodies against masticatory
muscle myosin heavy and light chains (ch. 258). Treatment is aimed
at immune suppression and should be long-term to avoid relapse of
the disease. Extraocular polymyositis is a disease that is most
commonly seen in young Golden Retrievers. Swelling of all
extraocular muscles results in bilateral exophthalmos; however,
retropulsion in the orbit is normal. The sclera is visible 360°, which
gives these dogs a distinct look. Diagnosis is confirmed by the
presence of enlarged extraocular muscles on computed tomography
scan or magnetic resonance imaging. Treatment is aimed at immune
suppression.

FIGURE 13.8 Hypertensive retinopathy in a cat.
Focal areas of retinal edema are present.

FIGURE 13.9 Hypertensive retinopathy in a cat.
Extensive vitreal and retinal hemorrhage is present.
Orbital neoplasia can be primary orbital neoplasia or secondary
from extension from adjacent tissues (most commonly the nasal
cavity) or metastatic spread from elsewhere. Orbital neoplasia is
usually malignant in both dogs and cats.

Systemic Hypertension
Ocular manifestations of systemic hypertension include hyphema,
iris aneurysms, vitreal hemorrhage, retinal hemorrhage, retinal
vascular tortuosity, retinal edema, retinal detachment, and loss of
vision45-47 (Figures 13.8 and 13.9). Secondary to the loss of retinal
function, the pupil becomes mydriatic, which is often noted by the
owner. Similar clinical signs can be seen in dogs with hyperviscosity
syndrome.48 The reader is referred to chs. 91 and 236 for diagnosis

and treatment of systemic hypertension. Treatment of hypertensive
retinopathy consists of treatment of the hypertension. If hyphema is
present, use of topical corticosteroids such as 1% prednisolone
acetate or 0.1% dexamethasone is indicated 2 to 4 times a day. The
intraocular pressure needs to be monitored as these eyes are at risk
for development of glaucoma. The prognosis for return of vision
depends on the ease with which the hypertension can be managed as
well as the severity of the ocular abnormalities present. In a study
evaluating 88 cats with hypertensive chorioretinopathy, 61% of cats
were blind in both eyes at presentation. Of these, 58% regained some
vision with treatment.49
The etiology of hyphema includes both systemic and ocular
diseases. Systemic diseases include systemic hypertension as well as
any disease resulting in a bleeding disorder (ch. 171). The most
common ophthalmic diseases associated with hyphema include
trauma, chronic uveitis, retinal detachment and intraocular
neoplasia.50 Post-sterilization hyphema is a rare occurrence in
cats.51

Metastatic Neoplasia
The uvea is a highly vascular structure within the eye that acts as a
filter for pathogens and neoplastic cells in the body. Metastatic
neoplasia can be seen in the iris and choroid of dogs and cats. The
most common metastatic neoplasia found in the iris is lymphoma.5254
Lymphoma (ch. 322) in the iris of cats is usually a focal pink
raised lesion in the iris. Performing an aqueocentesis and submitting
the aqueous humor sample for cytospin and cytologic evaluation (ch.
71) may help aid in the diagnosis of lymphoma in cats. Lymphoma in
the iris in dogs more commonly manifests itself as an anterior uveitis
with or without focal nodules in the iris. Involvement of the uveal
tract indicates systemic involvement, especially in dogs. Debate still
exists as to whether primary ocular lymphoma without systemic
involvement exists in dogs and cats or not.55 Treatment of ocular
lymphoma consists of systemic treatment of the lymphoma. The iris
lesions can resolve completely in response to chemotherapeutic

agents. Topical corticosteroids are indicated if systemic disease
cannot be adequately controlled with chemotherapeutic agents.

Client Information
Topical Corticosteroid Information
After a thorough examination, your pet has been prescribed an eye
drop or ointment, which contains a corticosteroid. Topical
corticosteroid medication can be very useful for treating some eye
conditions. It can, however, be the wrong medication in other
situations.

Use This Medication Only As Directed
This medication may have to be discontinued if the eye condition
changes. Please watch for persistent squinting, redness, or excessive
discharge or tearing. If any of these signs are noted, please call your
veterinarian or have your pet treated by an emergency service as
soon as possible.
DO NOT use this medication for other pets in the family or for
future eye problems your pet may develop. This may harm the eye.
Using this and all medications according to directions is the best
way to help your veterinarian, you and your pet.
This information in not intended to cover all possible uses,
directions, precautions, drug interactions, or adverse effects. If you
have questions about this or other medications or would like more
information, check with your veterinarian or pharmacist.
Alexandra van der Woerdt (New York, New York)

Client Information
Anterior Uveitis/Chorioretinitis
Your dog or cat has been diagnosed with anterior uveitis and/or
chorioretinitis. Anterior uveitis is inflammation of the iris (the
colored part of the eye) and ciliary body. Chorioretinitis refers to
inflammation of the tissues in the back of the eye, which may include
the retina. Symptoms you may have noticed include redness of the
conjunctiva (the tissues that line the eye) and haziness of the cornea
(the surface of the eye) because of corneal edema (increased fluid
retention within the cornea). If the inflammation is severe, the eye
may be uncomfortable, your pet may not be feeling well and vision
can be decreased.
Anterior uveitis and chorioretinitis are often associated with
diseases elsewhere in the body. Your veterinarian may recommend
diagnostic tests to determine the cause of the uveitis. These tests may
include bloodwork to test for various infectious diseases, radiographs
(X-rays) of the chest and/or ultrasound scan of the abdomen and
other diagnostic tests as may be deemed appropriate. It is not always
possible to determine the cause of the uveitis, at which time it is
referred to as “idiopathic.”
Treatment for anterior uveitis and chorioretinitis consists of 2
parts: Treatment of the underlying disease if possible and treatment
of the ocular symptoms. Treatment of the underlying disease varies
with the disease process involved. Treatment of the ocular symptoms
may include one or more of the following medications:
• Topical corticosteroid medications. Examples of these include
1% prednisolone acetate and 0.1% dexamethasone solution.
These are anti-inflammatory medications to help treat the
inflammation in the eye. These medications may have to be
discontinued if the eye condition changes. Please watch for
persistent squinting, redness, or excessive discharge or
tearing. If any of these signs are noted, please contact your
veterinarian as soon as possible.
• Topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications.
Examples of these include 0.03% flurbiprofen and 0.1%
diclofenac ophthalmic solution. These anti-inflammatory
medications are often used if topical corticosteroids need to be

avoided, such as in diabetic patients or if a corneal ulcer is
present.
• Topical atropine or tropicamide. These medications help to
dilate the pupil and relieve pain if a painful pupillary spasm is
present.
• Topical glaucoma medications may sometimes be prescribed if
the intraocular pressure is higher than normal. Examples
include 2% dorzolamide and 0.5% timolol maleate ophthalmic
solution.
• In severe cases, treatment with oral corticosteroids or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications may be needed.
It is important to continue using the medications until the
scheduled follow-up examination. Eyes affected with anterior uveitis
and/or chorioretinitis need to be examined on a regular basis to
assess the response to the medications and to monitor the
intraocular pressure as glaucoma (high intraocular pressure) can be
a complication of anterior uveitis.
Alexandra van der Woerdt (New York, New York)

Client Information
Cataract
Cataract is an opacification of the lens of the eye. The lens is the
crystalline structure within the eye that focuses the light onto the
retina inside the eye. The lens is normally transparent. As the animal
ages, the lens becomes more dense, which can be visible as a hazy
appearance of the eye. This is a normal aging change that should not
be mistaken for a cataract. A cataract is a true opacity in the lens. If
the cataract is small, vision may not be affected. If the cataract
involves a large portion of the lens, then the ability to see may be
reduced.
The most common reason for cataract formation in the dog is a
genetic predisposition for cataract development. The second most
common reason is cataract formation secondary to diabetes mellitus.
The progression (change over time) of cataracts caused by a genetic
predisposition is variable and may be unpredictable. Cataract
formation secondary to diabetes mellitus may develop very quickly

A thorough history (ch. 2) and physical examination (ch. 3) may
reveal abnormalities attributed to a systemic disease that is causing
neurologic signs. Conversely, neurologic signs may be the only
manifestation of a systemic disease. Neurologic signs from systemic
disease usually originate in the cerebral cortex or the peripheral
nervous system (PNS). However, white matter changes, brainstem
and cerebellar signs have also been documented secondary to
systemic conditions.

Diseases Causing Central Nervous System
(CNS) Signs (Table 14.1)
Hypoxia From Systemic Disease
Decreased arterial oxygen tension or reduced cerebral blood flow can
lead to hypoxic encephalopathy. Hypoxia can occur secondary to an
anesthetic accident, hematologic disorders (especially anemia), or
cardiovascular and respiratory failure. Autoregulatory mechanisms
providing a relatively constant cerebral blood flow despite changes in
systemic arterial pressure fail when mean arterial blood pressure is
<50 mm Hg. Some areas are more susceptible to energy deprivation.
Increased release of the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate in cell
injury leads to increased cellular influx of calcium and neuronal
death. Global ischemia may cause bilateral infarcts in the “watershed
zones” between areas supplied by major arteries. Changes in blood
flow to the brain may occur secondary to the hyperviscosity
associated with polycythemia (relative or absolute),
hypercholesterolemia/hyperlipidemia (familial hyperlipidemia [ch.
156], hyperadrenocorticism [ch. 293], hypothyroidism [ch. 285]),
immune-mediated disease (ch. 175), sepsis (ch. 128),
coagulopathies (ch. 170), and hyperglobulinemia (ch. 60).
Hyperviscosity can also cause ischemic infarcts due to embolism.1
The clinical signs reflect the area of the brain affected. Acute vision
loss in cats after a cerebrovascular accident may be due to misuse of
a mouth gag that occludes the maxillary arteries and reduces blood
flow to the brain.2 Cytotoxic edema in the white matter can be
detected on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Steroids are

contraindicated and may cause further brain damage. Recovery is
slow, taking weeks to months, and residual neurologic signs may
persist after severe injuries.

SYSTEMIC HYPERTENSION
During rapid and sustained rises in blood pressure the
autoregulatory mechanisms for maintaining blood flow fail, resulting
in hypertensive encephalopathy (ch. 236, Table 14.1). Neurologic
signs occur at a lower blood pressure (170 mm Hg) if hypertension
develops rapidly.3 Common neurologic signs are seizures, ataxia,
stupor, and blindness. Postmortem findings may include cerebral
edema, cerebellar herniation, arteriolar hyalinosis, hyperplastic
arteriosclerosis, ischemia, and necrosis. Cerebral microbleeds
possibly secondary to hypertension have been reported on MRI and
necropsy in dogs.1 MRI results in dogs and cats with hypertensive
encephalopathy have been described and ischemic optic neuropathy
with acute blindness has been described in a dog.4,5 Hyaline
arteriopathy in cats secondary to hypertension may result in
thrombosis with signs of cervical myelopathy or encephalopathy.6

Endocrine/Metabolic Causes
Hepatic Encephalopathy
Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) can be caused by portosystemic shunt
(PSS; ch. 267), microvascular dysplasia (ch. 267), idiopathic
noncirrhotic portal hypertension (ch. 267), or other causes of liver
failure (ch. 266). Neurologic manifestations occur in 95% of dogs
with PSS, with waxing-waning clinical signs that might be more
obvious after a meal.7 The neurologic signs are typical of diffuse
cerebral disease and vary from mild (an inability to learn new things
and behavioral changes) to more severe (head pressing, blindness,
mentation changes, seizures, and rarely brainstem and cerebellar
signs). Brain MRI results in PSS dogs have shown hyperintense non–

contrast-enhancing lesions in the lentiform nuclei and widened
sulci.8
The pathogenesis of HE is not fully understood.
Hyperammonemia, >120 mcmol/L, due to urea cycle enzyme
deficiency has been documented in young Irish Wolfhounds without
PSS.9 Increased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) concentrations of
ammonia, glutamine, quinolinic acid, tryptophan, and tryptophan
metabolites have been found in dogs diagnosed with a PSS.10,11
Activation of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptors due to
increases in endogenous benzodiazepines may contribute to the
clinical signs of HE, and a withdrawal effect may cause postsurgical
seizures.12 Medical therapy can reduce neurologic signs (ch. 266).13
Phenobarbital should be used with caution since it is protein-bound
and metabolized by the liver. Benzodiazepines may not prevent
postsurgical “withdrawal” seizures.14 Surgical correction of
congenital PSS before 2 years of age carries a better prognosis for
postoperative survival and neurologic morbidity.14 Dogs with signs
of HE before surgery are more likely to have seizures
postoperatively.14,15

Renal Encephalopathy
Toxic substances not excreted due to kidney failure can cause
encephalopathic signs similar to those of HE. It has been suggested
that increased concentrations of parathyroid hormone (PTH) and
subsequent hypercalcemia have a role in renal encephalopathy.16
Treating hypertension can lower the risk for hypertensive
encephalopathy (ch. 236).5

Hypothyroidism
Acute or chronic progressive central vestibular signs may be the sole
clinical sign in dogs with hypothyroidism (ch. 285). The
pathogenetic mechanisms of hypothyroidism-associated
abnormalities are likely multifactorial, and include atherosclerosis
with hypercholesterol-induced or hypertriglyceride-induced
microthrombi causing infarcts or transient ischemic attacks,
segmental demyelination, dysfunction of brain metabolic pathways,
and metabolic derangement of neuronal or glial cell populations.17
Abnormalities may be detected on brain auditory-evoked response
(BAER) or electroencephalogram (EEG).17 Transient ischemic
attacks cause intermittent vestibular signs, but without changes on
MRI or histology. Increases in protein may be noted on CSF analysis.

Treatment with thyroxin usually resolves neurologic signs.
Myxedema coma, a rare but life-threatening manifestation of
hypothyroidism, can cause brain-edema-induced mentation changes,
hypothermia without shivering, nonpitting skin edema, and
bradycardia. Hyponatremia and hypoventilatory hypoxia can worsen
neurologic status. Clinical improvement is usually seen within 24
hours of treatment; however, mortality is high.18
Congenital hypothyroidism has been described in numerous dog
breeds (ch. 285) as well as in cats (ch. 286). Clinical signs include
disproportionate dwarfism, abnormal hair coat, lethargy, a
stiff/stilted gait and abnormal mentation. Histologically, there is
hypomyelination in the corpus callosum, corona radiata, pons,
pyramids, and the lateral funiculi of the spinal cord.19

Hyperthyroidism
Cats with hyperthyroidism may show mild CNS signs: hyperactivity,
change in sleep/wake cycle, aggression, or obtundation (ch. 287).
Neurologic signs improve and may completely resolve with
treatment.20

Pituitary Dependent Hyperadrenocorticism (PDH)
Direct compression from a pituitary macroadenoma can cause mild
to severe neurologic signs in about 15-30% of dogs with PDH (ch.
293).21 Early clinical signs of macroadenoma include inappetence,
mild obtundation, disorientation, and pacing. Severe signs
associated with masses >1.5 cm in diameter include obtundation,
circling, tetraparesis, ataxia, and seizures. Blindness is rare. Infarcts
may be caused by hyperlipidemia.

Hypoglycemia
The brain is dependent on blood glucose (about 100 g/day) for
normal cellular metabolism (ch. 61). Persistent hypoglycemia causes
vascular constriction and hypoxia and can occur in dogs and cats
secondary to a variety of conditions, including simple poor nutrition
(chs. 147, 148), insulinoma (ch. 289), liver failure (ch. 266),

hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296), nonislet cell tumors producing
insulin-like growth factors, large metabolically active tumors
(leiomyosarcoma), severe polycythemia (ch. 57), sepsis (ch. 128)
and as a paraneoplastic syndrome (ch. 331).22 Hypoglycemia can
also be associated with exogenous insulin overdose (chs. 291, 292).
Neurologic signs wax and wane with episodes of obtundation,
weakness, disorientation, tremors, partial or generalized seizures,
blindness, and coma (

Videos 42.3, 61.1). There is no correlation

between the severity or frequency of clinical signs, degree of
hypoglycemia, and survival time posttreatment. Permanent brain
damage from neuronal death can cause permanent neurologic
abnormalities.23

Thiamine Deficiency
Thiamine is essential for decarboxylation of pyruvic acid and other
alpha-keto acids. Thiamine deficiency decreases utilization of
pyruvic acid and some amino acids, increases use of fats, and causes
aciduria. Thiamine deficiency occurs in cats and dogs fed meat
preserved with sulfur dioxide, food low in thiamine due to
processing, or thiaminase-containing fish. Histopathologic
abnormalities are typical of polioencephalomalacia with bilateral
symmetrical spongiosis, necrosis, and hemorrhage in the medial
vestibular nuclei, caudal colliculi, cerebellar nodulus, and the
subcortical grey matter.24 Experimental thiamine deficiency in cats
led to learning deficits with lesions in the hippocampal formation.25
Neurologic signs of thiamine deficiency reflect lesions in the
cerebrum and vestibular nuclei. On MRI, lesions are hyperintense on
T2-weighted and fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR)
sequences and contrast enhance with gadolinium. Treatment results
in resolution of clinical signs after weeks to months.24

Irradiated Diets
Leukoencephalomyelopathy has been described in colonies of cats
fed irradiated diets. The cats became ataxic after several months on
these diets. Histopathology showed brain and spinal cord Wallerian

degeneration, perhaps caused by oxidative stress. Cats recover when
fed a balanced diet or if treated with cobalamine (vitamin B12).26

Electrolyte Abnormalities
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia (ch. 69) has, rarely, been thought to cause seizures
via poorly understood mechanisms.

Hypocalcemia
Hypocalcemia (ch. 69) in lactating pets (eclampsia) or in those with
chronic kidney disease (CKD) or primary hypoparathyroidism causes
increased membrane excitability in both CNS and muscles that can
result in generalized tetany and seizures.27 Hypocalcemia may be
associated with coagulopathies.27

Hypernatremia/Hyponatremia
Severe hyponatremia (ch. 67) can cause cerebral edema and lifethreatening, diffuse encephalopathy.28 Overaggressive correction of
hyponatremia in dogs may cause CNS signs due to cerebral edema,
central pontine myelinolysis, and loss of oligodendroglial cells 2 to
several days after treatment.29 MRI shows bilateral symmetrical
hyperintense areas on T2-weighted images in the central thalamic
nuclei. Correction of hyponatremia should be gradual to prevent
these lesions (ch. 120). Aggressive saline fluid administration in
symptomatic pets with hyponatremia of less than 24-hour duration
may be successful without causing neurologic signs.
Hypernatremia (ch. 67) results in osmotic movement of water
out of brain cells, which can lead to reduced brain volume, rupture of
cerebral vessels, and focal hemorrhage. Severity of neurologic signs
is related to rapid development of hypernatremia rather than its
magnitude.28 In chronic hypernatremia the brain adapts to
hypertonicity by producing idiogenic osmoles, which prevent cellular
dehydration. Rapid correction of hypernatremia results in movement

of water into idiogenic-osmole-containing cells, causing cerebral
edema. Mild hypernatremia can be corrected by offering water but
more severe hypernatremia requires intravenous (IV) therapy (ch.
120).

Neoplasia
Neoplasia can cause neurologic signs from direct invasion or
metastasis, or secondary to ischemic and hemorrhagic infarcts.
Diagnosis is made by MRI, by CSF analysis, and by identifying the
primary neoplasm. Paraneoplastic syndromes (ch. 331), such as
hypoglycemia induced by an insulin-producing tumor and
hypercalcemia secondary to lymphoma, thymoma, and apocrine
adenocarcinoma directly affect the CNS.

Hyperthermia
The canine brain has intrinsic thermal resistance. The origin of
neurologic dysfunction in dogs and cats with hyperthermia is not
from direct effects of increased temperature, but from secondary
changes such as hepatocellular degeneration, disseminated
intravascular coagulation, respiratory alkalosis, and reduction in
mean arterial pressure.30

Diseases Causing Peripheral Nervous
System (PNS) Signs (Table 14.1)
Hypoxia
Aortic thromboembolism in dogs (ch. 238) usually occurs secondary
to protein-losing nephropathy, hyperadrenocorticism, neoplasia,
disseminated intravascular coagulation, sepsis, atherosclerosis, or
immune-mediated hemolytic anemia. Neurologic signs may include
chronic exercise intolerance, pelvic limb weakness, or more acute
symmetric or asymmetric pelvic limb ataxia, paresis, or plegia. Such
neurologic signs are due to an ischemic myopathy, neuropathy, or

myelopathy.31 Cats usually have peracute signs that include
tachypnea, hypothermia, paraparesis, or plegia (ch. 238).
Underlying causes are cardiomyopathy, hyperthyroidism, and
neoplasia.32

Metabolic/Endocrine Disorders
Hypothyroidism
Thyroxine (T4) stimulates mitochondrial respiratory activity, thus
facilitating production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). In
hypothyroidism (chs. 285, 286), ATP deficiency impairs Na+/K+
pump activity, reducing axonal transport and causing axonal
degeneration and demyelination. Myopathy has also been described
secondary to hypothyroidism. In rare circumstances, neurologic
signs may be the only manifestation of hypothyroidism. Neurologic
signs include generalized weakness and focal signs, such as laryngeal
paralysis (ch. 214), facial paralysis (ch. 249), megaesophagus (ch.
259), or a vestibular syndrome (ch. 248). Electrodiagnostic
abnormalities and histopathologic abnormalities on muscle and
nerve biopsies are typical of demyelination and axonal loss (ch. 111).
Signs may resolve after months of treatment. Electrodiagnostic
changes may partially improve.33

Hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism in cats (ch. 287) can cause neuromuscular
weakness with ventroflexion of the neck, a plantigrade stance, and
exercise intolerance. The clinical signs are reversible with treatment
of the hyperthyroidism.20

Hyperadrenocorticism
Hyperadrenocorticism (chs. 293, 294) is usually associated with
muscle weakness. In rare cases, dogs have fibrotic myopathy or
polyneuropathy. Fibrotic myopathy may cause a stiff, stilted gait;

generalized muscle atrophy; and difficulty flexing the limbs (
Videos 14.1, 293.2). The clinical signs of polyneuropathy include
general weakness and muscle atrophy. Diagnosis is made on
electrodiagnostic testing (electromyogram [EMG] and nerve
conduction [ch. 111]) and muscle and nerve biopsies (ch. 110). Type
II myofiber atrophy is common. In dogs with fibrosis the stiffness
rarely improves with treatment.34 Steroid myopathy has also been
described secondary to treatment with exogenous glucocorticoids.

Hypoadrenocorticism
Hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296) can result in episodes of lethargy,
weakness, tremors, and collapse. Painful muscle cramps are
extremely rare.35 Secondary hypoglycemia occasionally contributes
to the weakness. Treatment results in full clinical recovery.35

Diabetes Mellitus (DM)
Peripheral nerves are dependent on glucose for metabolism. A
sensorimotor polyneuropathy, a late complication of DM, may be
caused by either metabolic derangements or vascular changes (ch.
292).36 Clinical signs are most prominent in the pelvic limbs of cats
with a plantigrade stance, difficulty jumping, postural reaction
deficits, decreased tendon reflexes, and muscle atrophy (Videos 14.2,
292.1

). Such abnormalities are rare in DM dogs. Abnormalities

on nerve conduction studies and EMG are found in both thoracic and
pelvic limbs (ch. 111). Histopathologic findings include
demyelination, splitting and ballooning of the myelin sheath, and
axonal injury. Microvascular pathology included increased capillary
size, capillary luminal size, and basement membrane thickness.36,37
Permanent deficits are common.

Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
Dogs and cats with CKD (ch. 301) may have weakness associated
with renal secondary hyperparathyroidism, which causes a

peripheral neuropathy and myopathy. Inositol phosphates, protein
kinase C, and cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), among other
regulatory enzymes and signal-transducing systems in muscle cells,
are affected by calcitriol directly. The PTH-mediated uremic
myopathy may be reversible when treated with calcitriol. Excess PTH
also partially affects motor nerve conduction velocities. Nerve
excitability is modulated by calcitriol, which also affects the synthesis
of nerve growth factors. Changes can be found on electromyography
and nerve conduction studies (ch. 111).

Electrolyte Abnormalities
Hypokalemia
Hypokalemia (ch. 68) can be caused by reduced intake, excess renal
or gastrointenstinal (GI) losses, and rarely secondary to an adrenal
tumor causing primary hyperaldosteronism or adrenal-dependent
hyperadrenocorticism. A genetic potassium-wasting nephropathy
has been described in Burmese cats.38 Hypokalemia alters the
resting muscle cell membrane potential and can result in generalized
muscular weakness in dogs and cats and ventroflexion of the neck in
cats (ch. 3,

Video 68.1). These signs are not pathognomonic for

any condition.

Paraneoplastic Syndromes
Paraneoplastic syndromes (ch. 331) cause neurologic signs due to a
remote effect of cancer and can affect both the CNS and the PNS.
Neurologic signs can develop months to years before a tumor is
detected. Lack of specific diagnostic tests makes recognition of the
syndrome difficult. Removal of the tumors may result in resolution
of the neurologic signs. Thymoma (chs. 222, 253) is a common
cause of myasthenia gravis in humans and cats and less common in
dogs. Neurologic signs can be focal (megaesophagus) or generalized.
The myasthenia gravis may improve with removal of the mass.39,40

Client Information
Neurologic Manifestations of Systemic Disease
Brain Disorder

Your dog/cat has neurologic signs originating from the brain.
Sometimes diseases in the body, outside the brain, cause clinical
signs from the brain. These could be things like liver or kidney
dysfunction, high blood pressure, low blood sugar, electrolyte
abnormalities (calcium, sodium, potassium), or endocrine disorders
(problems with the thyroid gland or the adrenal glands) such as
hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, Cushing’s disease or Addison’s
disease. In order to rule out these diseases we would like to do some
blood work including a complete blood count (CBC) and chemistry
panel, a thyroid (T4) panel, and check the blood pressure. A
urinalysis would also help in assessing the kidney function.
Additional specific blood tests may be necessary if any of the tests are
abnormal.
Cancer can start in the brain, but can also spread from other parts
of the body (metastasis). The blood work helps us to evaluate the
function of the organs. In addition, chest radiographs and an
abdominal ultrasound will help us discover structural changes in the
internal organs from an infection or a cancer.
If none of the above mentioned tests explain the cause of the brain
signs, or show changes that make us worried about anesthetizing
your pet, we would recommend a magnetic resonance image (MRI)
of the brain. The MRI shows the structure of the brain and we can
detect infections, inflammations, infarcts (strokes) and cancer. A
cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis can help us. The spinal tap helps
us in further characterizing what we see on the MRI, for example we
can detect inflammatory cells, infectious organisms and on rare
occasions cancer cells. The MRI and spinal tap are done under
general anesthesia.

Neuromuscular Disorder
Your dog/cat has been diagnosed with a neuromuscular problem,
which means a problem in the nerves, the muscles, or the junction
between the nerves and muscles. There are many causes of
neuromuscular diseases. Many times muscle and nerve changes
occur from a systemic illness, which means a general disease
affecting the body. Sometimes there are no other signs of this
primary disease but the neuromuscular signs.

Disease that can cause signs from the nerves and muscles are liver
and kidney problems, electrolyte imbalances, endocrine diseases
such as a problem with the thyroid function or the adrenal glands or
diabetes. In order to rule out these conditions, we recommend some
blood work to be done. Initially this would include a CBC and
chemistry panel. A urinalysis would also help in assessing the kidney
function. Additional specific blood tests may be necessary if any of
the tests are abnormal.
Sometimes cancer elsewhere in the body can cause neuromuscular
weakness. Cancer can also set off the immune system to produce
antibodies against itself (autoimmune disease). In order to rule out
cancer, we recommend chest radiographs and an abdominal
ultrasound.
If all these tests are normal, or do not explain the neuromuscular
disease, the next step would be to explore the nerves and muscles.
The tests are called electrodiagnostic tests and are done under
anesthesia. Needles are placed in the muscles to assess the muscles
(electromyography [EMG]) and along the nerves in the forelimbs
and hindlimbs to assess nerve function (nerve conduction velocity
[NCV]). Since these are only functional tests, they do not give us a
specific diagnosis. Biopsies of some muscles and nerves can help us
to get a better idea of the cause of the neuromuscular disease.
Helena Rylander (Madison, Wisconsin)

Chapter 15: Intoxication Versus Acute
Nontoxicologic Illness: Differentiating the
Two
Mark Edward Hitt

AC RO N YM
DDx differential diagnosis(es)
The decision to add toxicosis to a list of differential diagnoses (DDx) is the combined result of being
clinically suspicious and keeping in mind the basic tenets of toxicology. An optimal approach involves
the veterinary diagnostician thinking logically and diagnosing poisoning sooner rather than later, but
not being swayed towards poisoning by an undue suspicion that turns out to be incorrect. So, how
should veterinarians make the clinical decision to purposefully add toxicosis/poisoning to their
diagnostic thoughts? What helps increase or decrease the accuracy of that suspicion as the case evolves?

Toxicosis/Poisoning
A goal of this chapter is to help the veterinarian decide whether a patient presenting with a pattern of
clinical findings, ranging from acute to chronic in duration and having a variably complete medical
history, has been exposed to something toxic. It is a process of gathering facts and making observations
with an open mind (ch. 4).1,2 The attending clinician needs to assess the validity and relevance of the
information (ch. 2), continuously correlating the clinical findings (ch. 3) with the DDx and avoiding
either over- or undervaluation of information.3,4 This is followed by seeking an appropriate supportive
care plan and a diagnosis-specific treatment plan. Finally, the veterinarian monitors the patient and
makes reassessments to adapt the ensuing responses.1
Most cases of toxicosis are not the result of intentional poisoning. However, because malicious
situations still occur, the concepts of intentional injury and litigious implications remain relevant. The
sometimes strong emotions that can be associated with this scenario, whether real or imagined, should
not distort the veterinarian’s objective assessment using judicious, non-leading questions (chs. 1 and 2).
If there is a concern that a patient has been purposely harmed, then reporting such to the appropriate
regulatory body (e.g., state board of veterinary medicine in the United States) for guidance or contacting
a veterinary toxicologist for forensic input can be advised. In some US states, the veterinarian may be
required to report situations of potential intention to harm as animal abuse.5-7

Process of Discriminating Toxic from Non-Toxic Differential
Diagnoses and the Art of Making Decisions
Toxicoses can be on a DDx list from the beginning of a case or may be added later.4 The patient’s recent
geographic and environmental exposures, signalment, and any available elements of the medical history
are gathered and reviewed. A relatively acute and/or severe or progressive presence of clinical findings
adds urgency to the process. To help with categorizing syndromes in clinical toxicology and narrow DDx
lists, the concept of toxidromes was introduced in the 1980s.

Toxidromes
In the context of toxicoses/poisonings, the collection of a clustered set of clinical findings is called a
“toxidrome” and it serves as a mental shortcut to facilitate more rapid decision-making. The term
toxidrome blends the terminology of a clinical syndrome with toxicosis. Similar chemicals or drug
classes create a toxidrome of similar clinical toxic effects (Table 15.1).4,8-12 Therefore, a veterinarian
who suspects that a patient has been exposed to a toxic substance should look for other manifestations
within a possible toxidrome; the presence of such additional signs reinforces the likelihood of toxicosis,
whereas single clinical signs that are unaccompanied by other signs within a toxidrome, or the presence
of unrelated signs, suggest that toxicosis is less likely. There can be exceptions of toxins that do not fit a
specific toxidrome or that have symptoms which overlap more than one toxidrome’s definition.

Process of Reaching a Diagnosis: Gathering Information
The medical history is discussed in detail in ch. 2, and techniques for obtaining information from clients
and caretakers are described in ch. 1. This process can require more time when the veterinarian engages
the client in both open- and closed-ended questions and uses reflective listening techniques. Obtaining
the owner’s version of the pet’s anamnesis can be more challenging where the patient has had periods of
not being observed. Nevertheless, the client’s observations can provide pivotal information for helping
the veterinarian reach a diagnosis. The client should be asked about the patient’s environment, and
multiple members of the household queried for clues as appropriate. The occurrence of similar clinical
signs in other animals within the environment makes a toxicologic cause more likely. Points of interest
that are more suggestive of intoxication can include the presence in the pet’s environment of missing or
chewed upon pill containers (pet or owner), risk of lost/dropped human medications, discovery of
recreational drugs, dietary ingestion risks (e.g., possible exposure to raisins, grapes [ch. 135], xylitol
[ch. 134], environmental chemicals, etc.; an animal that manifests pica or that is known to chew or
ingest objects or substances inappropriately; the presence of improperly stored human or animal food;
spoiled foods or carcasses [ch. 190]), observed growth of mushrooms in accessible areas, the presence
of environmental molds, ongoing home renovations (construction materials, leaded paint [ch. 133]),
access to indoor or outdoor plants, and access to brackish or stagnant pond water (blue-green algae
[cyanobacteria, ch. 134]). Information about environmental chemical exposures in geographic areas of
potential pet exposure (e.g., pesticides, herbicides) is also pursued. Questioning of clients becomes more
rapidly focused when the features of a toxidrome begin to emerge from the physical exam findings and
available history. Information for specific toxicants can also be searched via material safety data sheets
and appropriate labels on containers when exposures to known chemicals are suspected. Calling poison
control centers is common to help in suspected or known cases of toxication/poisoning. In North
America, the national American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) Animal
Poison Control is an excellent resource (888-426-4435), as are the toll-free phone lines for
manufacturers of various products.

A review of the patient’s general health background is essential, because it provides context for the
patient’s physical exam findings and helps the veterinarian clarify whether toxicologic or nontoxicologic
illness is more likely to be present. This should include checking for stresses creating comorbid health
conditions (e.g., crowding or inadequate shelter, malnutrition), pharmacogenetics (e.g., the MDR-1
mutation), hydration status, and extremes of ambient temperature and humidity.
When intoxication with a specific substance is suspected, dosage of possible exposure and timing since
possible exposure must also be considered. Some toxins from the same source can be very toxic on one
day or from one site, and less so the next day or as found at a different location/source (e.g., blue-green
algae toxin from multiple farm ponds). Some toxins can be less concerning as patients develop tolerance
with repeated exposures (e.g., habitual toad poisonings) while others gradually worsen with repeated
exposures and accumulation of the toxicant in the body (e.g., chlorinated hydrocarbons, heavy metals).
Intoxications can occur as acute, subacute, or chronic (persistent or relapsing) situations. Therefore, it is
very important to assess how these findings fall on a timeline of clinical signs and window of time for
possible exposure because incompatible timing can rule out toxicosis. For example, a dog with epistaxis
who could only have been exposed to anticoagulant rodenticides in the preceding 12 hours cannot have
that exposure to rodenticide as the cause of the current epistaxis.

Process of Reaching a Diagnosis: Analysis
In considering toxicosis versus nontoxicologic illness, it is useful to remember that toxicosis is a less
common event compared to the breadth of all diseases found in dogs and cats. Although toxicoses are
familiar clinical subjects, they may fall to the bottom of DDx lists unless a conscious effort is made to
consider them. The process of formulating the DDx and making a diagnosis of toxicologic or
nontoxicologic illness is akin to other forms of decision making and problem solving in daily life.3,13
Classically, making a diagnosis starts with the problem-oriented medical approach and the use of
problem-based medical records (chs. 2 and 4). A common acronym used for remembering and ranking
disease processes is DAMN IT. This acronym refers to diseases originating from developmental,
degenerative, anomalous, mental, mechanical, metabolic, nutritional, neoplastic, inflammatory,
infectious, ischemic, immune mediated, inherited, idiopathic, traumatic, and toxic mechanisms. With
these disease categories in mind, the clinician considers the information gathered from the signalment,

available history, and physical exam as noted above. Looking for a pattern of clinical findings that may
fit a toxidrome is part of this exploratory process and if such a pattern is not apparent, toxicosis remains
possible but other disease processes in the DAMN IT concept must be considered further. When making
diagnoses, probability is also factored in, partially based on personal clinical experiences, the facts of the
case, and the appropriate literature or texts. The clinician’s mind constantly moves up and down an
evolving differential list via clinical reassessment of the facts of the case.
One essential goal should be to avoid the premature closure of a DDx list. If the question has arisen
about whether the animal is experiencing toxicosis or nontoxicologic illness, then this question must be
asked repeatedly through the steps of case management until the veterinarian has a satisfactory answer.
A flow plan might include information gathering (above), the patient’s signalment, overall health status,
the clinical history, clinical findings, potential effects of and type of environment in which a prospective
toxin is found, and consideration of the type of compounds/toxicoses that could be considered for the
setting (i.e., does a toxidrome fit?). If toxicosis is likely, next steps should include the process of toxicant
identification, provision of supportive care and treatments to enhance elimination of the suspected
substance, blockage of further absorption/exposure, and selection of an antidote if available, together
with monitoring of response to treatment. Conversely, if nontoxicologic illness is likely, then selection of
confirmatory tests (if needed), delivery of supportive care and specific treatments, and monitoring are
prioritized. When a case evolves such that nontoxicologic illness is more likely, toxicosis usually remains
on the DDx list initially because subsequent developments could alter the prioritization within the
DAMN IT concept and make toxicosis more likely later on.

Clinical Decision-Making
The process of making clinical decisions in medicine is complicated. It includes topics taken from
psychology that help meld the human process of decision-making with that of problem solving.12
Problem solving represents a creative activity. The steps of problem solving around a clinical decision
about toxicologic versus nontoxicologic disease are similar to the mental path used when working
through clinical problems with the problem-based medical record system (ch. 2): the veterinarian
identifies a problem or set of problems, clarifies the importance for the patient of each problem,
organizes the information, forms a strategy, allocates resources, monitors for progress/correctness, and
then re-evaluates results/responses. This is the basis of the system using heuristics, which are mental
shortcuts that can be helpful when there is a large volume of information and time is of the essence.14,15
The problem solving strategy starts with forming a plan for action.16 A foundation regarding the use of
heuristics in medical decision making deals with judgment under situations of uncertainty and considers
the roles of heuristics and bias.17 Such paths can use type I or type II decision-making.
Type I decisions rely heavily upon use of prior experience and inference which might be termed, “gut
instinct.” The ability to make quick decisions also relies upon prior training as almost a reflex like
response. This facilitates our ability to react with rapid emergency responses. But it also introduces the
potential for unwanted biases. For more complex problems, when we have more time or need for more
thorough analysis, we fall to Type II decision making. Type II thinking adds logical paths of thought
such as an algorithm (creating a flow chart, decision tree, or cascading paths based on positive and
negative answers to questions). Baseline processes are familiar to most veterinarians, beginning with
trial and error and followed by the use of simple algorithms for assessment of results, often forming
conditional probabilities (Bayesian medicine). This involves using a system of mental questions based
on limiting binary terms of “and, not, or, both,” which is a cognitive skill. This system of logic is most
familiar via computer search programs that operate using these operatives in Boolean logic.
Type I decision processes emerge instinctually, reflexively, often in a situation of acute need for
decisions and action. Veterinarians must make decisions under conditions of “uncertainty” and often
under the constraints of limited time, and type I decision making offers a path for making an educated
best guess. Heuristics are efficient cognitive processes, conscious and unconscious.Because heuristics
save time, it can be that greater errors might occur. We accept this risk and use these mental shortcuts
when we believe the limited initial information is adequate to act upon. These are ingrained, and as with
many thoughts, they are subject to a plethora of cognitive biases. Heuristics make it possible to use
“rules of thumb” concepts, allowing frequency or probability judgments to be made based on “the ease
with which instances or occurrences can be brought to mind.” Heuristics facilitate rapid decisionmaking in the face of emergencies, overloads of information, multiple concurrent decisions of lesser

importance, and conversely, when there is little verified information available. However, utilizing
heuristics risks introducing bias through simplification. Each individual’s past experiences and existing
knowledge (the biases and fallacies that must be taken into consideration) influence the assessment of
incoming data.15,16 The most common forms of heuristics include observer, availability, anchoring,
representativeness, confirmation bias, overconfidence, bandwagon, and omission.17 Heuristics have
evolved because of the evolutionary need for fast responses/decisions. Heuristics are advantageous in
these settings, but if they are used without self-vigilance, they also come with risk of a premature or
incorrect diagnosis. As a bias, these reflexive heuristics have the potential for shutting down exploration
of further differential diagnoses or seeking out the odd permutations that are possible in clinical
situations. A reflexive desire to believe in our rapidly formed judgment could then impair moving on to
type II decision making as a more logical, but slower, process of critical analysis (e.g., following the
complete problem-based medical record protocol).
Type II decision making involves the more deliberate thought processes of sequential questions and
monitoring of “fit” to the situation. It involves breaking the information down into multiple smaller
steps or questions while seeking a clarity of the inter-relatedness of the findings. Type II decision
making most often occurs either following a burst of type I thinking or when there is no urgency to the
quest.
A logical fallacy is a faulty argument that has replaced quality logic. Over 50 such cognitive biases have
been named,15 from ad hoc bias to Zebra retreat (the author’s favorite). This large number is a reminder
that human weaknesses abound in the process of making a diagnostic decision,18 and that the process of
clinical decision-making needs to include an acknowledgment of conscious and unconscious personal
biases and assorted types of logical fallacies.19,20
The author finds it helpful, when faced with a situation of possible poisoning, and a lack of confirmed
toxicant identification, to accept that he may never be finished asking questions. The diagnosis is based
upon probability at some level of the assessment of the history and clinical findings. The intent behind
developing more experience and more openness to considering other possibilities is that it is more likely
a correct diagnosis will be achieved. However, this is not clear cut. Having experience may inject more
bias if a veterinarian is not self-aware to look for cognitive errors that are often coexistent.21 Hence,
experienced clinicians need to value their earned knowledge, but remain humble and vigilant. Newer
clinicians and students may not have a bank of experiences to draw on. This leads to their greater
reliance on the strengths of using the problem-based medical record approach. A basic understanding of
the paths of type I and type II medical decision making can help identify cognitive blind spots.
Veterinarians can strive to avoid the pitfalls of many cognitive biases and fallacies by being open minded
to new thoughts, adding new or updated data, clarifying the validity and appropriateness of such data,
and seeking outside input in a collegial environment. This process is supplemented by maintaining high
standards for continuous learning.
During the process of making a diagnosis, the patient is supported and stabilized (chs. 119 and 132).
Attention to the ABCs of critical care and triage comes first (ch. 119), and in critical patients, principles
of triage almost always need to be applied before a diagnosis is known. If a toxic etiology is suspected,
then ongoing reassessments and new directions help the veterinarian refine that consideration. As a
specific toxidrome, or suspicion of toxicosis as a DDx, is emerging during the assessment, then the
attending doctor can try to anticipate the patient’s situation and potential organ system dysfunctions.
Immediate laboratory data is sought and often includes a first (and sequential) complete blood count,
serum biochemistry profile(s), electrolytes, blood pressure, urinalysis, and imaging as warranted.
Provision of supportive care is ongoing. If intoxication is suspected, then efforts for decontamination
and enhanced elimination, and cytoprotection of organ systems, are pursued concurrently (ch. 132).
The collection and storage of clinical samples such as pre-treatment serum, whole blood, stomach
contents, and even hair samples can be done as a precautionary step and follow-up submission of
specimens for toxicant identification pursued if desired. A plan for submission of testing samples can
include looking for alkaloids, organophosphates, rodenticides, heavy metals, blood cholinesterase levels,
other chemical compounds/toxicants, and specific poisons as may be suspected. Consideration is also
given towards potential of adverse drug reactions (ADRs) and drug overdoses as may be suggested by
toxidromic findings. The art of medical decision making, combined with the use of toxidromes, will
hopefully allow for successful diagnosis and treatment of cases of toxicosis.
