Defining Fever, Hyperthermia, and Fever of
Unknown Origin
Body temperature can be increased because of fever (pyrexia) or
hyperthermia (Figure 16.1). For the purposes of this chapter, fever is
defined as an increased body temperature associated with a raised (and

often more variable) thermoregulatory set point in the anterior
hypothalamus that is secondary to the release of pyrogens (feverinducing substances). Hyperthermia, in contrast, is not associated with
an alteration in the thermoregulatory set point. The hyperthermic animal
therefore will make more efforts (physiologically and behaviorally) to
cool itself when compared to a pyrexic animal at the same temperature.
Hyperthermia most frequently arises from exposure to an increased
environmental temperature, which is addressed in ch. 130.
Hyperthermia can also arise due to exercise (especially in hot, humid
environments by overweight dogs and those with respiratory
impairment), seizures, hypermetabolic disorders (e.g., hyperthyroidism,
hypocalcemia), certain drugs (e.g., opioids, ketamine and phenobarbital
in cats, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in dogs and cats),
intoxications (e.g., cocaine in dogs), malignant hyperthermia, and stress
(including associated with visiting a veterinary clinic).1-10
Fever of unknown origin (FUO) is a term used relatively frequently in
veterinary medicine11,12 and definitions vary, as they have done in human
medicine.13,14 Extrapolating from the definition of classic FUO in
humans,13 FUO in dogs and cats could be defined as a temperature of
>39.2°C (102.5°F) of at least 3 weeks’ duration in which no obvious cause
is apparent following at least 3 visits to the veterinarian and/or 3 days of
hospitalization including a basic evaluation of history, clinical signs,
clinical (physical) examination and minimal diagnostic testing (complete
blood count, serum biochemistry, urine analysis). Additionally, FUO in
dogs and cats has often only been considered after a short (5-10 days,
although typically 7 days) course of an antibacterial agent has not
resolved the fever.6,15-17 In human medicine over 200 diseases have been
associated with FUO.14 However, as a cause is found in many so-called
“FUO” cases, and as the causes of fever and FUO are not sufficiently
different, it is suggested that cases of FUO should be considered within a
continuum of “fever.” Perhaps in the future the term FUO should be
reserved for those cases that truly remain unknown, despite the extensive
investigations for fever outlined below? This chapter will focus on the
pathophysiologic mechanisms, differential diagnoses and clinical
approach to fever, including FUO, in dogs and cats.

Pathogenesis of Fever

Fever is an important part of the nonspecific adaptive response of the
body to a disease process. The response has benefits and risks, the
balance of which changes with time and the particular process and
patient.18 Similar to other adaptive processes, the animal usually gains
short-term benefits from the process, but in the long term starts to
develop unwanted complications.
Pyrogens may be classified into internal (endogenous) and external
(exogenous) groups; however, exogenous pyrogens often exert most of
their pyrogenic activity via endogenous routes.19 Endogenous pyrogens,
particularly the cytokines interleukin-1 (IL-1), interleukin-6 (IL-6) and
tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha), are released from neutrophils,
monocytes and many other cells and activate the arachidonic acid
cascade.20 This arachidonic acid cascade increases prostaglandin E2,
which acts on thermoregulatory neurons and raises the hypothalamic set
point. More recent research has also suggested an important role for
neural rather than humoral pathways for the initiation of the febrile
response.21
Equally, the body produces endogenous anti-pyretics, including
glucocorticoids, neuropeptides and certain cytokines (such as
interleukin-10 [IL-10]), to protect the body against the effects of fever.22
It is even possible that at high temperatures pyrogens (such as TNFalpha) act as cryogens, limiting the severity of fever.18 For these reasons,
true fevers rarely exceed 41.1°C (106°F).

Benefits of Fever
In evolutionary terms, fever is a very old (at least 360 million years)
response by the body to infection.20 The conservation of this response
suggests that possessing the ability to develop a fever confers significant
evolutionary advantages. The proposed benefits of fever include:
1. Improved survival. Several studies, both in human medicine and
experimental, have shown that those patients that develop a fever
are less likely to die and the higher the fever, up to a limit, the
better the chances of survival.23 A good veterinary example is the
association between survival and the development of fever in
rabbits with Pasteurella infections.24 However, not all studies in

human medicine have shown similar results, resulting in
controversy.
2. Shorter duration of illness. Several studies have shown that fever
reduces the symptomatic phase of illness and may reduce viral and
parasitic excretion.25,26

FIGURE 16.1 Schematic diagram illustrating the
important difference between hyperthermia (A) and
fever (B). Set point refers to thermoregulatory set
point in the hypothalamus. IL-1, Interleukin-1; TNFα, tumor necrosis factor-alpha.
3. Improved immune system function. Neutrophil mobility and
phagocytic abilities are initially enhanced by fever, as are
macrophage function and lymphocyte proliferation.20 However,
not all immune cell functions are improved by fever, and natural
killer cells are less active at fever temperatures.20 At temperatures

>41.1°C (106°F), neutrophil and monocyte functions are
impaired.20
4. Production of heat shock and acute phase proteins. These are
important free-radical scavengers as well as preservers of cellular
components.27
One widespread fallacy is that fever kills bacteria. In fact, the bacteria
most commonly associated with infections continue to multiply and
survive well above temperatures that would prove fatal to an animal.24
Fever has evolved as a response to infection rather than occurring as a
result of infection: the host is trying to improve its response to infection
rather than directly kill the bacteria.

Costs of Fever
The proposed costs of fever include:
1. Increased number and severity of clinical signs, leading to a
reduction in animal welfare and increased owner concerns.
However, there is very little evidence that mild clinical signs of
fever are actually harmful.28
2. Increased metabolic rate: typically the resting energy requirement
is increased up to 1.3 times.29,30 If this exceeds the energy intake
of the host, energy deficits will occur in critical tissues with
increased oxygen demand and increased carbon dioxide
production.
3. Reduction in some constitutive processes; for example,
hemoglobin’s oxygen binding affinity is reduced by fever, so at the
very time that the peripheral tissues have an increased oxygen
demand, the hemoglobin is less able to deliver oxygen.31
The published evidence to date suggests the benefits of fever are often
limited to those with less severe disease, and in more severe diseases or
more severe (or prolonged) fevers the side-effects start to outweigh these
benefits.23

Measurement of Temperature

Invasive contact devices such as esophageal and pulmonary artery
thermistors are considered the gold standard for assessing core body
temperature32; however, these are not suitable for conscious veterinary
patients and are reserved for anesthetized or critical care cases.33 Good
agreement has been shown between rectal and core body temperatures in
dogs.33,34 Similar studies have not been performed in cats. However, it
can be difficult to obtain rectal temperatures, particularly in fractious
patients or in those with rectal or perianal disease. Rectal thermometers
are also a potential source of cross-contamination and rectal injury. In
addition, the accuracy and repeatability of rectal temperature
measurements can be negatively affected by depth of measurement, the
presence of feces, and conditions affecting local blood flow.34,35
There have been several studies examining the validity of measuring
auricular or axillary temperatures as an alternative to rectal
temperatures.33-45 Auricular temperatures may be measured using
dedicated thermometers which use pyroelectric sensors to measure
infrared radiation emanating from the tympanic membrane (TM).
Auricular TM thermometers are quicker and better tolerated than rectal
thermometers. However, they show greater variability between
measurements than rectal temperatures.35,39,40 Axillary temperatures
may be measured with a standard rectal thermometer and are well
tolerated (

Video 16.1) but are less reliable than rectal

temperatures,43,44 especially in overweight animals and animals with
thick or longhaired coats.36,37,39,43,45 Although the various studies have
produced conflicting results, most authors agree that TM and axillary
temperatures should not be used interchangeably with rectal
temperatures, and rectal temperatures remain the most accurate
method.46 When rectal temperature measurement is not possible in
dogs, then TM temperature is recommended over axillary temperature as
it is better tolerated, shows better agreement with the rectal
temperature,45 and significantly fewer dogs have clinically unacceptable
differences of >0.5°C (0.9°F).39 Body surface temperature measurement
by non-contact infrared thermometer (e.g., on gums, ears) shows clinical
potential in reflecting rectal temperature,47,48 and may be a technique
used to remotely measure temperature in the future. When rectal
temperature measurement is not possible in cats, then axillary

temperature is recommended over TM temperature, as it is better
tolerated, and significantly fewer cats have clinically unacceptable
differences of >0.5°C (0.9°F)41,42; one study suggested that rectal
temperatures could be roughly approximated by adding 0.9°C (1.6°F) to
the axillary reading in cats.43 Contrary to the belief of some dog owners,
assessing a dog’s temperature simply by palpating its nose is not reliable:
there is no correlation between thermographically measured nose
temperature and rectal temperature in dogs, and tactile assessment of
noses as being warm has a sensitivity of 29.4% and a specificity of 79.5%
for detecting rectal hyperthermia.49

Normal Temperature
Although published reference ranges vary,50 normal cats and dogs have a
rectal temperature generally in the range of 38.0°C (100.5°F) to 39.2°C
(102.5°F), but normal dogs and cats can reach as high as 39.7°C (103.5°F)
and 39.7°C (103.4°F) respectively in the consulting room.10,51 One study
evaluated the rectal temperatures of healthy adult cats measured indoors
in climate-controlled conditions and found them to be lower than
commonly reported.50 Studies on the repeatability of temperature
measurements have shown that rectal temperatures measured in the
morning in hospitalized dogs can fluctuate about 0.7°C (1.3°F) day to
day.52 Exercise may increase the rectal temperature of a normal Labrador
as high as 42.2°C (108.0°F), and most dogs can reach 41.1°C (106.0°F)
immediately after exercise.53,54
Body temperatures that exceed 41.1°C (106°F) are life-threatening as
they can result in neurological damage, disseminated intravascular
coagulation (DIC) and metabolic abnormalities. Such levels are more
likely to occur in hyperthermic patients (ch. 130), and active cooling is
required as immediate treatment.

Severity of Fever
Clinical experience suggests that there is little correlation between the
absolute temperature and the clinical signs of fever. It may be that it is
not the absolute temperature that determines the severity of clinical signs
but rather the rate of change. The terms “mild” and “severe” fever should

therefore only be used to refer to the clinical signs rather than any
temperature range.

Differential Diagnoses for Fever
Causes of fever, and especially FUO, can be broadly divided into
infectious, immune-mediated, neoplastic, inflammatory and
miscellaneous categories17,55 (ch. 183). In dogs, infectious, immunemediated, and neoplastic causes are important.11,12,16,17 One study of 66
dogs with fever in a UK referral center described 33% of cases to be
immune-mediated/inflammatory, 27% infectious, 8% neoplastic, 9%
miscellaneous and 23% were undiagnosed.11 By contrast, an earlier study,
also from the UK, of 101 referred cases of canine FUO described 22% of
cases to be immune-mediated, 16% infectious, 9.5% neoplastic, 11.5%
miscellaneous and 19% undiagnosed. In this study, 22% of cases were
classified as being primary bone marrow diseases but these largely were
of a neoplastic etiology; the higher overall prevalence of neoplasia in this
study was attributed to an oncology bias within that particular center at
that time.12 Another study of 50 dogs with fever that presented to a
university veterinary hospital found that 48% of cases were due to socalled non-infectious inflammatory diseases (which included immunemediated diseases), with only 18% of cases being infectious in origin and
6% neoplastic.56 A referral case series explored the causes of fever
specifically in juvenile dogs (<18 months of age)57; in this series of 140
cases, non-infectious inflammatory disease was the most common
category of diagnosis (65.0%) followed by infectious (13.6%), congenital
(2.9%), neoplasia (0.7%) and undiagnosed (17.9%). In the non-infectious
inflammatory disease group, Beagles, Border Collies, Cocker Spaniels and
Whippets were over-represented and 60% were diagnosed with steroidresponsive meningitis arteritis (SRMA). Additionally, SRMA was
suspected, although not confirmed, in many of the dogs in the
undiagnosed group.
It has long been believed that infectious causes are more common than
immune-mediated diseases or neoplasia as causes of fever in the
cat,6,15,17 in contrast to the importance of immune-mediated disease in
dogs with fever. This was confirmed in a retrospective study of 106
referred feline cases with fever58 where infectious disease was the most
common disease category (36.7% of all cats), and feline infectious

peritonitis was the most common diagnosis (20.8% of all cats). In this
study, the next most common category of disease was non-infectious
inflammatory such as pancreatitis (17.9%), then neoplasia (12.3%),
miscellaneous (10.4%), no diagnosis reached despite extensive
investigations (15.1%), then immune-mediated (5.7%).
Studies evaluating the causes of fever in dogs and cats presenting to
primary care clinics have not yet been performed.
Box 16.1 lists conditions that have been associated with fever in dogs
and cats and so may be considered as differential diagnoses. It is worth
highlighting that although many of the infectious conditions are
associated with fever, they can also present in the absence of fever (ch.
183); for example, only 21% of myocarditis (chs. 233, 234),59 40%-43%
of endocarditis (ch. 232)60,61 and up to 30% of discospondylitis (ch.
250)62 dog cases present with fever. Thus, although Box 16.1 highlights
conditions that can present with fever, one must understand that not all
cases with these etiologies have fever.

Approach to a Fever
Firstly, it is important to distinguish between fever and hyperthermia
(Figure 16.2) as hyperthermia may require urgent therapy to reduce
body temperature (ch. 130). History is the most important method of
identifying hyperthermia, as exposure to heat will have occurred very
recently and, before heat exposure, the animal will either have been well
or showing other clinical signs associated with another problem. Fever is
a common clinical finding in small animal practice, but owners usually
report non-specific signs (ch. 10) such as lethargy, anorexia, depression,
hyperpnea and stiffness.
The initial consultation can provide important clues as to the etiology
of the fever, and these may either lead to a diagnosis themselves or point
to diagnostic investigations that should help confirm a diagnosis. Figure
16.3 shows algorithms depicting information based on signalment,
history (ch. 2) and clinical examination (ch. 3; including ophthalmic
[ch. 13] and neurologic [ch. 241] examinations) that can be important
to consider when first presented with fever in a cat (Figure 16.3, A) or a
dog (Figure 16.3, B). The first presentation of an animal with fever can
usually be dealt with relatively easily. Many causes of fever can be
identified during a thorough clinical (physical) examination, e.g., bite
wound, upper respiratory tract infection, dental abscess (Box 16.1).

These should be treated appropriately, and further diagnostic
investigations may not be required.

If localizing signs are not evident and the effects of the fever are
relatively mild, and the temperature is <41.1°C (106°F), then detailed
diagnostic investigations may not be necessary as the underlying cause
may become readily apparent. The fever should be monitored, and the
patient supported appropriately. A question that may arise at this stage is
whether to give anti-pyretic and/or antibacterial therapy without a
definitive diagnosis. Discussion of this is given in the Treatment of Fever
section later. However, if the fever causes severe side-effects, then early
investigation may be warranted.
If the cause of the fever is not apparent on clinical examination within
5 days, then a diagnostic plan is formulated. This will usually include a
complete blood cell count, serum biochemistry panel and urinalysis, with
feline leukemia virus antigen and feline immunodeficiency virus antibody
testing in cats at risk of these infections (Figure 16.4 and Table 16.1).
Consideration of feline infectious peritonitis is also important in younger
cats and, as well as assessment with the above tests, the addition of an
ocular examination and other tests such as diagnostic imaging and serum
alpha-1 glycoprotein measurement can be performed (ch. 200). Whilst
these tests are ongoing, a short course (5 days) of empirical antibacterial
therapy can be considered for cases in which a bacterial infection is likely.
However, guidelines for antibacterial stewardship and the appropriate
use of antimicrobials to limit antimicrobial resistance63 suggest that
strong consideration be given to a move to earlier diagnostic intervention
instead of empirical use of antibacterials (ch. 7). It is of note that over
80% of the cats reported in a retrospective series of referred feline

pyrexia cases had had antibacterial therapy before referral,58 showing the
widespread use of antibacterial drugs in fever. Anti-pyretic therapy may
also be considered but its use should primarily be based on the severity of
the clinical signs rather than the severity of the fever. If the fever persists
despite such treatment(s) (and therefore has persisted for more than 12
days) then other diagnostic investigations can be planned according to
the clinical findings or the results of initial diagnostic investigations,
especially if the fever can be localized to a body system or region.

FIGURE 16.2 Algorithm for the general approach to
increased body temperature. CBC, Complete blood
count; FNA, fine needle aspirate.
Table 16.1 lists the diagnostic tests that can be used in the
investigation of fever. It is important to repeat diagnostic investigations,
particularly thorough clinical (physical) examinations, as new

abnormalities can develop in cases that may provide important clues to
the etiology or localization of the fever (Figure 16.4). Subsequent
examinations may reveal pain (e.g., in the neck or joints) or changes in
ophthalmic (ch. 13) or neurologic (ch. 241) examinations. In cases
where the etiology of the fever remains elusive, despite the above tests,
then a sequential series of investigations which could include urine
culture, blood culture (ch. 184), bacterial and fungal cultures of any
discharges or lesions (ch. 184), arthrocentesis (ch. 87), cerebrospinal
fluid collection (ch. 109), fine needle aspirates of any masses and some
lymph nodes (even if normal on palpation; ch. 88), ultrasonography
(particularly of the abdomen in cats), radiography (thoracic, abdominal,
limbs and vertebrae), echocardiography (ch. 97), serology (ch. 184)
and/or bone marrow samples should be started.11,12,58 Cytology can be
helpful in diagnosis, even in cases showing no clinical abnormalities of
the body systems sampled (ch. 85).11,12 Indeed, a recent study56 found
that cytology, or histopathology, were the most useful tests in
determining the etiology of fever in a group of dogs, and other studies
similarly have found cytology to be useful in enabling a diagnosis in both
dogs and cats.11,12,58 There may also be a role for nuclear imaging in
some cases. The exact order of diagnostic tests will depend on individual
patient factors and consideration of regional variations in disease
prevalence. As in human medicine, it is probable that there is no
uniformly useful diagnostic algorithm for the further investigation of
fever beyond the initial clinical examination,14 although machine
learning methods on large datasets are being used to help create tools to
help clinicians diagnose cases of FUO in people.64
If all of the above tests have been performed and the cause of the fever
is still unknown, then it is reasonable to term this FUO but until then the
distinction of fever and FUO in terms of differential diagnoses and
investigations is unclear and the two conditions should be regarded as a
continuum. Assuming that only a small fraction of cases of fever are
referred for investigation, then cases of true FUO are rare; out of 217 dogs
referred to specialist centers, no diagnosis was achieved in 48 (22%) and
some of these belonged to owners who did not wish to pursue all
diagnostic options.11,12,56 In the case series of fever in 140 juvenile
dogs,57 25 (17.9%) dogs were undiagnosed. The undiagnosed group
comprised mainly dogs which had shown resolution of clinical signs
during hospitalization rather than being dogs in which no diagnosis was
made despite testing.

Amongst 104 cats referred to specialist centers, no diagnosis was
reached in 15.1%.58 Most humans who develop true FUO will eventually
recover spontaneously, and this may occur in dogs as well.11,12,65

Treatment of Fever
The treatment of fever assumes that fever is, at least in part, noxious and
that its suppression will reduce the noxious effects. Yet, despite many
attempts, there is no evidence to suggest that specific treatment of fever
actually improves survival or worsens the prognosis.66 In one study it
was shown that treatment of fevers delays diagnosis in dogs,11 although
this was not found to be the case in a study of juvenile pyrexic dogs.57
Patients treated with anti-pyretics undoubtedly look (and probably feel)
better and are at less risk of fever related complications ranging from the
mild (e.g., inappetence) to the potentially life threatening (e.g., DIC).
However, such treatment prevents any of the benefits of fever described
earlier. Many of the clinical improvements seen from anti-pyretic
therapies may be due to the concomitant analgesic and/or antiinflammatory actions of these drugs.
Therefore, anti-pyretic therapy ideally should be reserved for severe or
prolonged fever. Mild acute fevers for which no cause has been identified
are probably better left untreated. It may be more appropriate to educate
clients that fever is often good for the animal and the use of drugs may
delay the development of important clinical signs that may help to
identify the cause of the fever.

Physical Cooling
Active cooling of patients (as described in ch. 130) with fans, cool water
and other methods is not required unless the patient’s temperature is
>41.1°C (106°F), when a degree of hyperthermia can be assumed. Obese
patients or those with upper respiratory tract compromise are more
prone to this situation and therefore should be monitored more closely.

Fluid Therapy
Fever increases insensible water losses and may reduce water
consumption. Dehydration is therefore more common in pyrexic animals.

Intravenous fluid therapy may be required, and at the very least, careful
attention needs to be paid to monitoring the hydration status of an
animal with fever.

Antibacterial Therapy
Antibiotics (ch. 140) should be administered to all dogs and cats with
fever and signs of bacterial infection. The prevalence of systemic or
unidentified bacterial infections in cases of fever is sufficiently high to
warrant consideration of antibacterial treatment for animals that have an
unexplained fever of more than 5 days’ duration. Such therapy should use
a single antibacterial agent with adequate penetration into most of the
common sites of infection considered likely in that case. As such,
clavulanate-potentiated amoxicillin is a logical choice, though by no
means exclusively so. In areas where vector-borne pathogens are
common, then doxycycline may be a preferred alternative. Most
authorities would regard fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides and later
generations of the cephalosporins as being inappropriate first-line
choices (ch. 7). The administration of multiple antibacterials in rapid
succession over several days is unlikely to be successful and can increase
antibacterial resistance.63,67 The duration of antibacterial treatment
required for treatment of the various bacterial causes of fever in
veterinary species has not been investigated, other than for urinary tract
infections (ch. 307), but should be as short as possible; short duration
reduces exposure of commensal bacteria to antibacterial drugs, can
improve client compliance, and reduces costs and likelihood of drug sideeffects.63

Non-Steroidal Therapy
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) have been at the
forefront of anti-pyretic therapy for many years (ch. 143).28 They reduce

the synthesis of thromboxane and prostaglandins from arachidonic acid
in the hypothalamus by directly inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX)
enzymes and downregulating their expression.66 This returns the
thermoregulatory set point to its normal level. There is also evidence that
NSAIDs may exert a variety of non-COX-dependent actions on the
pyrogenic cascade, such as by suppressing tissue inflammation, reducing
pyrogenic cytokine production, or through enhanced expression of
endogenous anti-pyretics.66 They also have analgesic characteristics,
such that they are capable of mollifying many clinical signs of illness and
thereby improve patient welfare. However, NSAIDs are associated with a
small number of undesirable side-effects, including renal and hepatic
impairment (which can in rare cases lead to kidney and liver failure),
gastrointestinal ulceration, vomiting, and blood dyscrasias. Repeated use
of NSAIDs increases the risks of many of these undesirable side-effects.68

Steroids
Glucocorticoids are potent anti-pyretic drugs and they act in many
different ways (ch. 144), including some of the same ways as NSAIDs.
However, their use is associated with more side-effects than NSAIDs and,
in addition, they reduce the chances of successful diagnosis and, for some
conditions, successful treatment.11 Therefore, they are indicated only
once a diagnosis (such as an immune-mediated disease) has been
established. However, on those occasions when it is difficult to
differentiate primary immune-mediated from infectious causes of pyrexia
in cats (e.g., some arthropod-borne blood infections) that may also have a
secondary immune-mediated disease, then steroid administration
alongside an effective antibacterial (such as doxycycline) is unlikely to
exacerbate such diseases, and will help control pyrexia and other clinical
manifestations of disease (ch. 227).6 The concept of “relative adrenal
insufficiency” has been largely and substantially discredited in human
medicine and should not be used as a generalized justification for the
administration of steroids to a patient with pyrexia, even if associated
with sepsis.69,70

Client Information
Fever
Your veterinarian has diagnosed fever in your pet, which means that
your pet’s body temperature is increased because of disease. This leaflet
will help you understand this problem and tell you what to do about it.
You should read all the leaflet and ask a member of the veterinarian’s
team if there is something that you do not understand. This leaflet is only
intended for general guidance and is not intended to replace the specific
advice that your veterinarian has provided for your pet.

What is Fever?
An increase in body temperatures is caused by a wide range of diseases of
which infections are the most common. Other important causes include

immune-mediated diseases (this is when the body’s immune system
wrongly attacks part of the body), non-infectious inflammatory diseases
(especially affecting joints and the brain in dogs) and, rarely, some
tumors. As such a wide range of diseases exist, many different diagnostic
tests (from simple blood and urine tests through to more complicated
scans and joint fluid sampling) may be needed to determine the cause of
your pet’s fever.
Fever is caused by small molecules in the body increasing the
“thermostat” in the brain. Fever is a normal and important reaction to the
disease present and helps animals recover from it.
Signs that your pet is suffering from a fever may include a loss of
appetite, lethargy/tiredness, stiffness, panting, breathing faster than
usual and curling up to keep warm. If your pet shows any other signs
when having a fever, then please tell your veterinarian.
The body temperature, when measured with a thermometer, will be
increased in fever. Normal cats and dogs have a rectal temperature in the
range of 100.5°F (38.0°C) to 102.5°F (39.2°C) but even normal animals
can reach 103.0°F (39.4°C). Exercise can increase temperature, so it is
important not to measure your pet’s temperature within 30 minutes of
strenuous exercise.

Is Fever Dangerous to my Pet?
Fever is not particularly dangerous. Indeed, there are many benefits
(such as getting better quicker) to having a fever. For this reason, any
drugs that are used to reduce the effects and signs of fever should be used
sparingly and only when really needed (for example, after several days of
not eating).

How Should i Monitor my Pet’s Fever?
It is important that your pet’s temperature is checked frequently if fever
has been identified. Your veterinarian may wish to do this themself or
may show you how to do this. Do not worry if the temperature rises and
falls a little during the day—a difference of 0.7°C (1.3°F) is normal day to
day variation for dogs. Contact your veterinarian immediately if your
pet’s temperature rises above 41.1°C (106.0°F), as immediate action will
need to be taken to reduce the temperature. However, most pets with
fever never get as hot as this.

How Should i Look After my Pet With a Fever?

It is very important to maintain your pet’s water balance (hydration) so
add small extra quantities of water to your pet’s food. Make sure that
clean fresh water is always available to your pet and they do not have to
walk to get to it (remember they may not feel like walking if they have a
fever).

What Should i Feed my Pet with a Fever?
Feed your pet its normal food but try to encourage it to eat more than
normal. This is not the right time to diet your pet. If your pet is not eating
well then add small, tasty morsels of nice (maybe warmed) food to
encourage your pet to eat, and if this does not work, consult your
veterinarian again.

Should i Exercise my Pet with a Fever?
Pets with fevers do not feel well and therefore probably do not feel like
doing much exercise. Rest is an important part of recovery from most
diseases so you should not encourage your pet to exercise. A return to
normal activity levels is a good sign that the fever is improving.

What Drugs can be Used to Treat Fevers?
If your veterinarian has been able to diagnose the disease that is causing
fever in your pet, then treatment of that disease should resolve the fever.
However, sometimes the underlying disease is not known or your
veterinarian may want to try and treat the fever directly for another
reason (e.g., whilst diagnostic tests are being performed). Anti-fever
drugs (anti-pyretics), typically non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
(NSAIDs), and antibacterials are the most commonly used drugs, but
many others exist.
Anti-pyretic Drugs
These can reduce the signs of fever and make animals feel better but do
not usually treat the underlying disease causing the fever. Anti-pyretics
should only been used for short courses (a few days).
Antibacterial Drugs
These may be used to treat a known or highly suspected infectious cause
of fever caused by a bacterial infection. They may need to be given for
several days before an improvement in your pet is seen and may need to
be continued for some time after the signs of infection have disappeared,

depending on the type of infection and where it is present in your pet.
Your veterinarian will advise on the duration of antibacterial treatment
needed as this can be very variable. It is important that you complete the
full course of antibacterial treatment even if your pet seems to be well. If
your pet is still unwell at the end of the course, or fails to improve during
the treatment course, then you should see your veterinarian as soon as
possible.

Whom do i Contact if i Want to Know More?
If you have any questions about fever, or concerns about your pet’s
health, contact your own veterinarian. They will know your pet’s medical
history and will know about specific diseases and treatments.
Séverine Tasker (Solihull, United Kingdom) and Ian K. Ramsey
(Glasgow, Scotland)

Chapter 17: Anorexia
María Dolores Pérez Alenza

A C RO N YM S
BCS body condition score
CKD chronic kidney disease
FDA U.S. Food and Drug Administration
MCS muscle condition score
RER resting energy requirements

Introduction
Reduced food intake is a common clinical sign and owner concern in
dogs and cats. Decreased appetite can be caused by many acute and
chronic diseases. A clinical survey identified inappetence as the third
most common clinical sign reported (3.9%) and the most common
presenting problem overall (8.5%) in primary care practices.1
Decreased appetite was more commonly observed in cats (5.8%)
than dogs (2.2%).1 This clinical sign can be easily diagnosed and
managed, or it can be a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge that can
decrease quality of life and ultimately survival. Reduced caloric
intake at time of hospital admission was associated with a higher risk
of death in dogs.2 Proactive diagnosis and management of this
problem is needed, since it can be frustrating and upsetting for
owners and its complications can include weight loss, cachexia,

sarcopenia, immune system suppression and multiple organ
dysfunction.

Definitions: Hyporexia Versus Anorexia
Terminology
Terminology related to appetite and food intake can be confusing.
Common terms include hyporexia, poor appetite, inappetence, and
anorexia. Standardized terminology allows clinicians to be more
precise when describing dogs and cats with reduced
appetites.3 Adequate food intake indicates voluntary consumption of
enough food to maintain body weight or to reach ideal body weight.
Hyporexia is consumption of inadequate calories to maintain body
weight or to reach ideal body weight. Anorexia is the complete
absence of voluntary food intake. Dysrexia describes abnormal
patterns of food intake, such as cyclic or unpredictable appetites
observed in some pets with a chronic disease.

Key Initial Considerations
An inability to eat, rather than a reduction in appetite, must always
be the first consideration and can be caused by various problems,
such as oral foreign body, dental disease, nasal or retrobulbar
conditions, masticatory myositis or physical barriers (Elizabethan
collar). A complete history should include a thorough description (or
a video) of the pet eating. Review previous and current illnesses,
medications, or changes in environment. Inflammation caused by
illness, injury, or surgery, mediated by cytokines, can alter neural
regulation of appetite, as can some medications, altered
gastrointestinal motility, or changed taste perceptions. Stress related
to the novel environment of being hospitalized can diminish appetite
in any pet.4

Diagnostic approach

General History
After “inability to eat” is dismissed as the explanation for decreased
appetite, causes remain numerous (Box 17.1). A logical, costeffective, and practical diagnostic approach is recommended
(Figure 17.1). Signalment and complete clinical history are the first
pieces of information needed when evaluating a dog or cat with
reduced food intake. Clinical signs may be subtle, subjective, patient
specific, and all are dependent on client observation. Detailed
questioning of clients is crucial to accurately assess duration and
severity of the reduced appetite.5 The decreased appetite in cancer
patients receiving antineoplastic drugs is graded from 1 to 5. This
calculation includes duration and amount of weight lost.6

Nutritional Assessment
A complete nutritional assessment is critically important. The diet
history should begin with the quality and quantity of the primary diet
being given (ch. 145). All treats, other food sources and
supplements should be reviewed (diet forms are available; ch.
145).7,8 Is the pet being over fed? Body condition and muscle
condition scores (see inside covers) should be estimated. Resting
energy requirements (RER) could be calculated and compared with
the pet’s RER to establish the presence of hyporexia vs. anorexia.
Admittedly, such specificity is not often used in private practice. RER
can be calculated using the following formulas (chs. 147, 148):3
RER (pets weighing 3 to 25 kg) = (30 × body weight in kg) + 70
RER (used for pets of any weight) = 70 × body weight in kg0.75
During the history, the clinician should try to determine whether
the pet has interest in food, is there evidence of nausea (ch. 48), are
treats or flavors added to encourage the pet to eat the primary diet.
Has anyone force-fed the pet? Has there been an interest in and then

loss of interest in any diet after a few days? Consider dysrexia versus
hyporexia. Food aversion must be assessed and avoided in the
management of any pet (chs. 151 and 163). Food aversion is caused
by the association of a food with an unpleasant event: illness, pain,
fever, nausea, vomiting or medications and can be exacerbated by
force-feeding.3,9
A complete and detailed physical examination (ch. 3) should
include careful palpation of the oral, ocular, cervical, and nasal areas.
Problems in any of these areas can adversely influence appetite.
Thoracic, abdominal, and rectal examinations should be routine.9
Body condition and muscle condition scores (BCS, MCS) should be
estimated using standardized scales (see ch. 72 and inside covers).10
In pets suspected of having reduced food intake due to chronic pain,
orthopedic (ch. 31) and neurologic (ch. 241) examinations should
be completed. A minimum database (complete blood count, serum
biochemistry, urinalysis, blood pressure) should be considered. After
assessing this information, radiology, ultrasonography, serology or
other testing (cytology, fecal exam, advanced imaging) may be
indicated (Figure 17.1).

Treatment
Management of a dog or cat with reduced food caloric intake should
always be based upon the underlying cause.9 Intervention depends
on severity (hyporexia-to-anorexia), duration, and consequences of
the reduced caloric intake on BCS and MCS. Initially, suggest
avoidance of environmental stressors to improve food acceptance,
especially in cats. One should avoid any association between feeding
and unpleasant situations (drug administration, unknown people,
visiting animals, noise at certain times, or temperatures too hot or
cold). One may resolve the problem by changing the feeding location
or using a food dish made of different material. Feeding should be a
pleasant event. Remove barriers to eating (Elizabethan collar) or
place food on a bench for dogs with neck or other orthopedic issues.3
Consideration should be given to improving diet palatability. This
may involve warming or changing the texture of the food, adding
flavors or aromas, and/or increasing moisture and ensuring
freshness (ch. 157). Some dogs and cats prefer home-cooked foods.
Consultation with a veterinary nutritionist is recommended when
formulating home-made diets to ensure that balance and adequate
nutrition are achieved (ch. 167).3
Use of an appetite stimulant may be considered with or without
making a specific diagnosis. Stimulants represent an important tool
for managing dogs and cats with chronic diseases that decrease
appetite. Common chronic diseases include chronic kidney disease
(CKD, ch. 301), pancreatitis (chs. 277, 278), chronic inflammatory
bowel diseases (ch. 262), or cancers. Frequently proposed appetite
stimulants include benzodiazepines (diazepam), serotonin
antagonists (cyproheptadine), anabolic steroids (nandrolone),
anesthetics (low dose propofol), anticonvulsants, analgesics
(gabapentin), serotonin receptor antagonists (mirtazapine), and
ghrelin receptor agonists (capromorelin)4,11-18 Treating CKD cats
with mirtazapine (1.88 mg PO q24-48h) has been shown to stimulate
appetite, promote weight gain and reduce vomiting.12 In one study,
cats with unintended weight loss were treated with either placebo or
2 mg of transdermal mirtazapine, daily. The mirtazapine group had
greater weight gain.13 In cats, transdermal mirtazapine has been

approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as an
appetite stimulant (Miratraz, Kindred Biosciences Inc.) and is
considered a “gold standard” treatment. In a recent study,
compounded transdermal mirtazapine administered at 3.75 mg/cat
and at 1.88 mg/cat resulted in significant increases in weight and
appetite, but individual cats may excessively vocalize when given
excessive doses.14 It is important to note that dosing and
administration of the approved product (Miratraz) is lower (2
mg/cat) than the dose used in the latter study. In another
prospective clinical trial, the administration of either mirtazapine at
1.88 mg/cat PO or gabapentin at 5 mg/kg PO increased food intake
in healthy cats hospitalized for ovariectomy.4

Capromorelin, a potent orally active growth hormone secretagogue
receptor agonist, acts directly on the hunger centers of the
hypothalamus to stimulate appetite and enhance food
consumption.15 The FDA approved oral capromorelin (ENTYCE,
Aratana Therapeutics, Leawood, KS) has been effective in increasing
food consumption and body weight in healthy Beagle dogs given 3
mg/kg PO over 4 days.14 ENTYCE given for 4 days significantly
increased appetite and body weight in a population of hyporexic dogs
while decreasing the incidence of adverse reactions (vomiting,
diarrhea, hypersalivation, or polydipsia).16 Additional studies are
needed to learn the long-term efficacy and safety of capromorelin
administration in dogs. In cats, acute exposure to capromorelin can
lead to suppression of insulin secretion causing glucose intolerance
for as long as 30 days.18 Further studies are needed regarding its
effect on glucose intolerance in cats.
It is generally accepted that dogs and cats consuming less than
their RER for more than 3-5 days benefit from an assisted refeeding
plan. The timing for introducing a refeeding plan depends on BCS,

MCS, and the severity and nature of any underlying disease. Certain
conditions benefit from immediate intervention (e.g., feline hepatic
lipidosis; chs. 269 and 271).4 Assisted feeding plans require
placement of feeding tubes (Figures 17.2 and 17.3; ch. 81).

Background
Weight loss may be intentional or unintentional. Intentional weight
loss in animals occurs as a result of caloric restriction dictated by a
voluntary (or prescribed) dieting program (ch. 150). Unintentional
weight loss, the focus of this chapter, is a frequent owner concern
and can be associated with serious disease. Maintenance of body
weight is a reflection of nutrient intake, absorption, and utilization.
These factors may be impacted by age, health status, and
environment (diet, food availability, etc.). In people, unintentional
loss of ≥5% body weight over 6-12 months warrants investigation.1
While clinically relevant weight loss has not been defined for dogs
and cats, ∼5% is a reasonable benchmark. Weight loss is also
common in human illnesses; unintentional weight loss is reported in

as many as 65% of geriatric patients.2 The high prevalence of
unintentional weight loss in clinical illness underscores the need to
carefully monitor weight in dogs and cats as a part of their general
health assessment.

History
Appetite, Diet, Environment, Exercise
Dogs and cats may be brought to a veterinarian with weight loss as a
primary or sole complaint. More commonly, it accompanies other
signs associated with an underlying condition. Careful history-taking
(chs. 2, 3) should include questions about appetite, caloric intake,
daily exercise, and environment. Appetite is variable in animals with
weight loss and may be reported as reduced, normal, or increased.
Appetite may be preserved or increased when malnutrition results
from starvation, malabsorption, or maldigestion. However, appetite
is reduced (hyporexia) or suppressed completely (anorexia) by many
systemic illnesses, leading to unintentional weight loss. Whenever an
owner mentions the possibility of weight loss, the dietary history
should be carefully reviewed: quality and quantity of food offered
(including any dietary supplements provided), ease of food
availability for the pet, the possibility that other pets might be
competing for food, and the pet’s appetite. A medication history
should be obtained, since some medications can depress appetite or
might even alter taste or smell sensations. It is important to
distinguish those animals that have an appetite but cannot prehend
or swallow food from those who have no appetite but can chew and
swallow normally. Diagnostic considerations suggested by various
patient history findings are presented in Box 18.1.

Mechanisms that Lead to Weight Loss
Common mechanisms leading to weight loss include decreased
caloric intake, increased metabolic demand, accelerated energy loss,
inability to utilize ingested calories, and inappetence. Specific
etiologies usually cause weight loss through several mechanisms,
each of which may need to be evaluated if weight loss is to be

understood and treated. Some cancers cause severe weight loss
because the tumor mass interferes with food intake or nutrient
processing. Some cancers cause severe weight loss via the production
of humoral factors that impair metabolism. For example, oral cancer
may impede mastication or swallowing while gastrointestinal (GI)
neoplasia may interfere with digestion and absorption of nutrients or
cause nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea. Some cancers synthesize
substances that cause anorexia or induce cachexia.

Gastrointestinal and Endocrine Causes of
Weight Loss
In humans, GI disorders are the leading non-neoplastic cause of
unintended weight loss; the same may be true for dogs and cats. Oral
and dental diseases (ch. 258), megaesophagus (ch. 259), chronic
gastroenteritis (chs. 261-263), inflammatory bowel disease (IBD;
ch. 262), pancreatitis (chs. 277, 278), dysmotility (ch. 254), and
other disorders can produce weight loss through a variety of
mechanisms that include induction of nausea, inappetence, protein
loss, maldigestion, and malabsorption. Several endocrine disorders
are associated with weight loss. Hyperthyroidism causes weight loss,
in part, due to increases in metabolic rate (ch. 287). Diabetes
mellitus, a condition associated with an absolute or relative
deficiency of insulin, causes weight loss due to an inability to utilize
nutrients (chs. 291, 292). Both these conditions are usually
associated with increases in appetite. Other endocrine conditions,
such as hypoadrenocorticism and hyperparathyroidism, commonly
cause weight loss and are associated with a reduction in appetite.

Cardiac, Respiratory, Kidney, Infectious,
Inflammatory, and Neurologic Concerns
Chronic bacterial or fungal infection, especially those accompanied
by persistent systemic inflammation, are associated with weight loss
(chs. 187-197, 207-209, 211). Likewise, the persistent systemic
inflammation of connective tissue disorders, such as systemic

immune-mediated conditions, may cause weight loss through similar
mechanisms (chs. 176-179, 181). Both cardiac and respiratory
disorders can lead to an increase in metabolic demands and induce
cachexia (ch. 151). Indeed, heart failure caused by chronic valvular
disease or cardiomyopathy is a frequent cause of cachexia (cardiac
cachexia) in dogs (ch. 151).3 Uremia secondary to chronic kidney
disease (CKD) commonly leads to nausea, gastric ulceration, and
vomiting that, in turn, decreases appetite and reduces caloric intake
(ch. 301). Some neurological disorders reduce appetite that leads to
weight loss; others decrease food intake by impairing mastication or
swallowing. The neurologic disorders that impair autonomic
function or cause dysmotility may cause GI dysfunction and weight
loss (ch. 254). Cognitive dysfunction and psychiatric disorders are
present in a substantial proportion of people with weight loss but the
role of similar neurologic disorders in dogs and cats is unknown.

Cachexia vs. Starvation
No standard definition for cachexia exists (ch. 151). In clinical
practice, cachexia is the term used to describe the weight loss, loss of
muscle, and anorexia that accompany many chronic disease
conditions.3 However, cachexia is not simply caused by inadequate
nutrient intake. Cachexia and starvation are not equivalent
physiologic processes. Two biochemical features distinguish
malnutrition caused by cachexia from that caused by starvation.4
First, unlike starvation, inflammation is a consistent feature of
cachexia. Cachexia causes marked activation of the inflammatory
cascade, characterized by a pronounced acute phase inflammatory
response and excessive production of proinflammatory cytokines
such as interleukins (IL-1 and IL-6, among others) and tumor
necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) (ch. 60).5 These cytokines
stimulate the ubiquitin pathway, a central pathway in protein
turnover.6 Ubiquitin complexes with target cellular proteins and
stimulates their metabolism via the proteasome system. Second,

cachexia is associated with a rise in resting energy expenditure,
which increases as a consequence of altered protein, fat, and
carbohydrate metabolism. Loss of body muscle and adipose tissues is
marked and an insulin-resistant state may develop. Despite a similar
clinical appearance, activation of the ubiquitin-proteasome system
and increased energy expenditure are not features of starvation. A
diagnosis of cachexia should be considered for any dog or cat with
marked weight loss, severe muscle loss, and decreased appetite in the
setting of a chronic inflammatory response or cancer.3 By this
definition, cachexia is not a specific diagnosis but a state of
disordered metabolism that can be caused by a variety of diseases.

Physical Examination (PE) and
Laboratory Testing
Weight Loss is a Clinical Sign, not a Specific
Diagnosis
Suspected weight loss should be verified, when possible, by
comparing current weight with that previously recorded. Owner
perception of weight loss may not be accurate. Suboptimal body
weight, loss of subcutaneous (SQ) fat with prominent underlying
skeletal structures, an emaciated appearance, and a low body
condition score (BCS) support the suspicion of weight loss (ch. 72).
It must be borne in mind that substantial weight loss may occur
without obvious physical changes. Some pets have a normal BCS,
despite significant weight loss. Marked loss of body condition is a
characteristic finding of severe cachexia in which muscle loss may be
disproportionate to fat loss. In many cases, a diagnosis may be
apparent after completion of the PE. If not, a directed PE (e.g.,
neurologic [ch. 241] or orthopedic [ch. 31] examination) and/or
laboratory testing may be indicated.

Laboratory Testing
Laboratory findings in animals with unintended weight loss are
neither specific nor consistent. Test results typically reflect the

primary pathologic processes responsible for weight loss but may be
unremarkable. In cachexia, laboratory findings may show
characteristic yet nonspecific changes.5 Serum protein
concentrations vary even in the presence of a systemic inflammatory
response. For example, elevated fibrinogen concentrations (as a
component of the acute phase response) in humans with neoplasia
may be offset by reduced albumin synthesis. Increases in hormone
concentrations, such as cortisol and insulin, may be observed in
animals with cachexia; these changes may result from or be the cause
of cachexia-induced alterations in metabolism. In general, as for
other forms of unintended weight loss, results of PE and laboratory
findings will reflect the underlying disease rather than specific
indicators of cachexia. No compelling reasons exist to perform
specific laboratory tests to make a diagnosis of cachexia. Instead,
cachexia is largely a clinical diagnosis made when appropriate
physical findings are present in a dog or cat with a disease associated
with a chronic inflammatory response.

Diagnostic Plan (Figure 18.1)
A general algorithm for making a diagnosis of a condition causing
unintended weight loss begins with demonstrating >5% loss of
weight over a period of less than 12 months in any pet. A suitable and
tailored diagnostic plan based on PE and laboratory findings should
be developed. It is important to recognize cachexia because animals
with this condition may not respond as expected to therapeutic
interventions and nutritional support. In humans, a diagnostic workup may fail to uncover an etiology in as many as 30% of individuals
with a complaint of unintended weight loss.1 Some dogs and cats
with weight loss can be expected to have an unrewarding diagnostic
evaluation. More commonly, an underlying condition can be
confirmed.

FIGURE 18.1 Algorithm for making a diagnosis of
cachexia.+, Diagnostic testing identified a disorder
associated with weight loss; −, diagnostic testing did
not identify a disorder associated with weight loss;
GI, gastrointestinal.

Treatment
Successful therapy or resolution of the primary disorder is the most
efficacious means to address unintended weight loss. Therapy will
ameliorate or reverse the underlying factors contributing to weight
loss and body weight may be restored with nutritional support.

When weight loss is due to cachexia, nutritional support remains the
cornerstone treatment; however, additional considerations must be
given to designing the nutritional plan (ch. 145). Hypercaloric
feeding is intended to supply the dog or cat with sufficient calories to
meet increased maintenance caloric needs (because of
hypermetabolism), prevent additional weight loss, and promote
weight gain. Unfortunately, hypercaloric feeding alone may not be
sufficient therapy for animals with true cachexia. People with
cachexia who receive hypercaloric feeding gain weight, but the
increase in body weight is almost exclusively the result of an increase
in adipose tissue without change in lean body mass. Thus, simply
feeding more may not be sufficient to reverse the abnormal protein
catabolism that accompanies cachexia. Pharmacologic therapies that
have been used for cachexia in humans that may prove useful for the
treatment of animals include nutritional supplements (including fish
oils), appetite stimulants, anabolic agents, anti-inflammatory drugs,
and cytokine inhibitors. Although some of these drugs have been
extensively used for appetite support and other indications in small
animals, information is limited about their efficacy when used for
cachexia.7 Specific inhibitors of the ubiquitin system, which inhibit
the effects of cachexia at the molecular level, may eventually be
developed.8
It is less clear which steps should be taken when a patient with
weight loss has a non-diagnostic work-up. Failing to confirm a
cancer is the most serious concern for clinicians. While published
information regarding dogs and cats is lacking, as mentioned above,
a specific cause is not identified in about 30% of humans evaluated
for weight loss. Some of these people have been monitored and
tested for as long as 2.5 years without a diagnosis.1 Studies of
humans with unexpected weight loss suggest it may be prudent to
adopt a wait-and-see strategy whenever a dog or cat with weight loss
has a negative PE and unremarkable laboratory and imaging results.
Wait-and-see takes a strategy of serial monitoring over time rather
than immediate continued non-directed efforts that might involve
use of medications, employment of more expensive or invasive
diagnostics, or simply the pursuit of an unlikely diagnosis.

Client Information
Unintentional Weight Loss

Why is Weight Loss a Concern?
Body weight is a readily measured indicator of a pet’s general health
and nutritional status. Body weight is maintained in healthy pets
when nutritional intake, metabolic needs, and energy expenditure
are in balance. Weight loss that is intentional, as part of a diet or

conditioning regimen, is not of concern, so long as weight reduction
is accomplished safely. However, unintended weight loss is a
potential concern in dogs and cats that may reflect the presence of
illness. In some pets, weight loss is accompanied by other concerns,
such as decreased appetite, vomiting, or altered water consumption,
but it is also possible for a pet to suffer severe weight loss in the
absence of obvious signs of illness. Pets that experience severe
weight loss may appear gaunt, thin or have a loss of body condition.
Often there is loss of muscle tissue and bony structures appear
prominent such that the pet has a “starved” appearance. Weight loss
often follows a decrease in appetite but it must be noted that it may
occur in the presence of a normal or even increased appetite. A pet
noticed to have unintentional weight loss should be evaluated by a
veterinarian.

Possible Causes for Unintended Weight Loss
It is important to recognize that unintentional weight loss is
considered a sign of illness and is not by itself considered a specific
disorder. There are numerous causes for weight loss in dogs and cats.
Possible causes include nutritional deficiencies, related to care,
feeding, or housing practices. For example, underfeeding or feeding a
nutritionally incomplete diet may lead to malnutrition and weight
loss. Competition between pets for limited amounts of food or
housing that prevents access to food are examples of management
problems that may produce weight loss even when the diet fed is
nutritionally balanced. In other cases, weight loss is due to specific
medical disorders. Any disorder that leads to impaired food intake,
reduced nutrient absorption or metabolism, or accelerated nutrient
loss can produce weight loss. For example, poor dentition that
impairs the ability to chew or swallow food may result in weight loss.
Likewise, gastrointestinal problems such as parasite infections,
stomach and bowel diseases, or pancreatic disorders may produce
nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea leading to weight loss. Diabetes
mellitus in dogs and cats and hyperthyroidism in cats are endocrine
disorders that may cause weight loss. Inflammation and other
metabolic disruptions caused by certain cancers, autoimmune
disorders, chronic kidney, lung, or cardiac disorders or by infection

with various bacterial and fungal agents may produce weight loss in
some affected dogs and cats.

Determining the Cause of Unintended Weight Loss
Diagnosis of unintended weight loss in a dog or cat can be difficult.
The work-up begins with a thorough medical history that includes
complete dietary information, past and ongoing medical problems,
and investigation of current complaint. A complete physical
examination may identify abnormalities that provide insight into the
cause for weight loss. Diagnostic tests are usually needed to confirm
a cause for weight loss. Since there are so many possible causes for
weight loss, the recommended diagnostic plan will vary for each
patient. Initial diagnostic tests that may be helpful for dogs or cats
with weight loss include a complete blood count, biochemistry panel,
urinalysis, fecal parasite examination, virus screening (cats), and
thyroid hormone level (cats). Radiographic or sonographic studies
may provide additional information. Depending on the results of the
initial diagnostic tests, additional special laboratory tests or
advanced imaging studies may be needed to further investigate
possible diagnoses.

Treatment of Unintended Weight Loss
No single treatment is effective for all causes of unintended weight
loss in dogs and cats. Reversal of weight loss is best accomplished
when the primary diagnosis (i.e., the cause of unintended weight
loss) is determined and effectively treated. Many dogs and cats with
weight loss will benefit from nutritional therapy that aims to restore
optimal body weight but is not needed in all cases. It is important to
work with a veterinarian to develop a comprehensive plan for
addressing the cause and treatment of unintended weight loss in
pets.
Thomas Schermerhorn (Manhattan, Kansas)

Chapter 19: Polyphagia

Overview
Polyphagia refers to excessive consumption of food, which may be a
physiologic response to increased energy requirements (e.g.,
pregnancy, lactation) or a sign of a systemic disease. As satiety and
hunger are controlled by the central nervous system (CNS),
polyphagia can be classified as primary (i.e., CNS disease) or
secondary (i.e., a systemic problem affecting the CNS). Secondary
polyphagia is much more common and often accompanied by other
signs of underlying disease. Food intake, body weight (BW), and
energy balance are closely connected. Determining whether BW

changes have occurred is an important step in the diagnostic
evaluation of any polyphagic pet.

Physiology and Pathophysiology
In healthy physiologic conditions, energy intake is balanced with
energy expenditure to maintain stable body composition and BW.
The complex regulation of appetite involves endocrine and
neurological signaling from the brain, pituitary, gastrointestinal (GI)
tract and adipose tissue to the hypothalamus and other areas of the
CNS. After arriving in the CNS, signals are integrated to produce
sensations of hunger or satiation. Simply put, some areas of the
hypothalamus are considered the “feeding (hunger) center” and
others the “satiety center.”1,2 Stimulation of the “feeding center” in
the lateral nuclei of the hypothalamus leads to voracious eating.
Destroying these cells leads to loss of appetite.1 The “satiety center”
in the ventromedial nuclei of the hypothalamus is responsible for
sending inhibitory signals to the feeding center, leading to
nutritional satisfaction. If stimulated, animals refuse to eat, and if
ablated, animals develop a voracious appetite and extreme obesity.1
The paraventricular nuclei, dorsomedial nuclei, and arcuate nuclei of
the hypothalamus have similar impacts on food intake. Disturbances
in the first two lead to either augmented appetite (paraventricular
nuclei) or reduced appetite (dorsomedial nuclei). In the arcuate
nuclei, hormonal signals from adipose tissue and the GI tract
converge to control food intake and energy balance.1
Interplay within and between various hypothalamic centers
influence secretion of adrenal, thyroid, and pancreatic islet
hormones.1 The feeding-regulating neurons within the hypothalamus
also receive neurogenic signals from the GI tract (gastric filling) via
the vagus nerve, signals from hematogenous nutrients (amino acids,
fatty acids, glucose), hormonal signals from the GI tract and adipose
tissues, and neurogenic signals from the cortex cerebri (sight, smell,
taste).1-7 Ultimately, the forebrain integrates all this information and
induces feeding behavior via the motor nervous system.

Some important mediators involved in hypothalamic signaling
include alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH) and
the cocaine- and amphetamine-related transcript (CART).1,8,9 Both
are produced by pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons. The
orexigenic neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related protein (AGRP)
are produced by other neurons.1,8,10 Many peripheral hormones (e.g.
leptin, insulin, cholecystokinin, ghrelin) target the POMC/CART and
AGRP/NPY neurons, influencing appetite and satiety.1,7 Dysfunction
in these pathways can cause disease: e.g., mutations in the POMC or
melanocortin-4 receptors (binds alpha-MSH) lead to severe
obesity.1,9 Conversely, activation of the melanocortin system is
thought to contribute to loss of appetite in infectious disease, cancer,
or uremia.1

Differential Diagnosis
Primary Versus Secondary Causes
The cause of polyphagia can be primary or secondary (Table 19.1).
Primary polyphagia is triggered by lesions in the brain or
psychogenic factors. Secondary polyphagia is much more common
and is either physiologic (e.g., during pregnancy), induced by
medication, or pathologic. In the latter case, polyphagia is induced
by increasing metabolism or reducing energy supply through loss,
malassimilation, reduced intake, or unknown causes.

Historical Findings
Crucial Questions
A complete and thorough history (ch. 2) is of critical importance
when evaluating a pet whose owner is concerned about polyphagia. A
few questions to ask include:
• Age?
• Some young growing puppies and kittens are surprisingly
hungry.
• GI parasites in some young puppies and kittens cause an
increased appetite.
• Duration and progression of appetite change: worsening,
stable, improving?
• If female, is pregnancy possible?
• Duration and progression of body weight changes: worsening,
stable, improving?
• Type, amount, and quality of food being given?
• Was food changed recently, and did this lead to a change in
appetite or body weight?
• Environmental factors which may stress the pet?
• What is the animal’s environment?
• Is there competition for the food? Can the pet consistently
reach the food?
• Does the animal live outside or inside or both?
• Review all medications and supplements, including topicals.
• Are there any other clinical signs which could point toward a
specific disease?

Body Weight (BW) Changes

The trend in BW can be an important clue (Figure 19.1). Primary
and drug-induced polyphagia usually lead to BW gain, as there is no
energy loss or metabolic hyperfunction. Healthy increases in
metabolism (e.g., due to growth, pregnancy) which cause polyphagia
will also lead to weight gain if quality and quantity of food is
adequate. Unhealthy increases in metabolism (e.g., hyperthyroidism)
may result in weight loss despite the increased quantity and quality
of food consumed. Diseases that cause a loss of nutrients (e.g.,
diabetes mellitus), malabsorption (e.g., parasites), or maldigestion
(e.g., pancreatic exocrine insufficiency) are also each associated with
weight loss, as increased food intake cannot make up for the energy
loss.

Physical Examination

Primary Polyphagia
Dogs and cats with primary polyphagia due to a CNS lesion can show
neurological deficits depending on the area affected. Exhibited signs
may include ataxia, proprioceptive deficits, blindness,
polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD), and circling. Pets with primary
polyphagia due to environmental factors may only exhibit weight
gain.

Secondary Polyphagia
Pets suffering from secondary polyphagia caused by an underlying
disease may exhibit any of a variety of clinical signs. Dogs and cats
with diabetes mellitus typically have weight loss and are PU/PD.
Dogs with Cushing’s syndrome (iatrogenic or naturally occurring)
often exhibit PU/PD, exercise intolerance, hair and skin changes,
panting, and an enlarged abdomen. Hyperthyroidism may lead to
weight loss, PU/PD, hyperactivity, and personality changes (these
cats usually have a palpable cervical mass). Disproportionate growth
of the head, paws, belly, and skin are consistent with acromegaly.
Large-volume, malodorous, soft stools may be seen with pancreatic
exocrine insufficiency. Other GI signs (e.g., diarrhea, melena) may be
associated with infiltrative bowel disease, lymphangiectasis, or
parasites. Animals with megaesophagus often have a history of
regurgitation. Pets with a congenital portosystemic shunt or hepatic
encephalopathy can show neurologic abnormalities, ascites, or
retarded growth. Blind dogs with “sudden acquired retinal
degeneration syndrome” (SARDS) are often polyphagic, resembling
Cushing’s syndrome.

Diagnostic Approach
Initial Decisions
After determining age, growth stage, deworming history, and
possibility of pregnancy, the clinician should carefully weigh the pet
and assess any possible psychogenic (stress), environmental (cold,
exercise), or dietary (low-calorie diet, diet change) factors that could
result in an abnormally increased appetite. If these are ruled out, a

minimum database that includes a complete blood count, chemistry
profile (with a total thyroxine [TT4] in cats), and urinalysis is
recommended. If a pet with an unknown history of deworming has
polyphagia, weight loss, and appears to be in good health, it should
at least have a fecal examination (ch. 80) and a deworming trial
(ch. 142).

Further Diagnostics
Any additional testing should be considered after reviewing history,
signs, physical examination, and database results. Diagnostic
imaging (especially thoracic radiographs and abdominal ultrasound)
is non-invasive and informative, whether or not abnormalities are
identified. Results may be as simple as confirming a pregnancy or as
complicated as identifying enlarged adrenals, unexpected masses
within the thorax/abdomen/pancreas, an abnormal liver, visible
shunt vessels, enlarged esophagus, abnormalities within the GI tract,
or enlarged lymph nodes.
Areas of concern may then point to additional tests for
consideration. For example, to check for the presence of an
insulinoma, one should consider measuring circulating insulin
concentrations when the blood glucose concentration is low and
computerized tomography (CT) of the abdomen (chs. 61 and 289).
Acromegaly can be confirmed by finding appropriately increased
insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) concentrations and evidence of a
pituitary mass on CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans
(ch. 280). If there is a suspicion of naturally occurring Cushing’s
syndrome, adrenal testing is indicated (ch. 293). The suspicion of a
portosystemic shunt or other liver dysfunction may lead to
considering liver function tests, liver biopsy, and/or abdominal
advanced imaging scan (chs. 267 and 268). If pancreatic exocrine
insufficiency is suspected, serum trypsin-like immunoreactivity (TLI)
and cobalamin determination should be considered (ch. 279); to
diagnose other malassimilation syndromes, intestinal biopsies may
be necessary (ch. 293). Finally, if primary polyphagia is suspected,
further diagnostics might include advanced imaging of the head (ch.
112) together with examination of the cerebrospinal fluid (ch. 109).

Management
Treatment of polyphagia depends on the underlying disease.
Physiological reasons for polyphagia are usually transient and should
be treated with increasing the amount of food offered. If a
psychogenic cause is suspected, the trigger factor(s) should be
identified and eradicated. If that is not possible, an environmental
change or the consultation with a behavioral therapist may help. In
drug-induced polyphagia, the side effects of this drug therapy should
be explained to the owner, and the treatment regimen should then be
changed, reduced, or, if possible and not dangerous, stopped. If an
underlying disease can be identified and treated, the polyphagia
often disappears or improves. In some animals, however, the
increased appetite persists even though the disease seems well
controlled. This is often observed in dogs with Cushing’s syndrome
and cats with diabetes mellitus (and acromegaly).
