CHAPTER 20: Weight Gain
Alexander J German

A C RO N YM S
BCS body condition score
CT computed tomography

Reasons FOR Weight Gain
Weight gain typically arises from accumulation of fluid or body
tissue, which includes both adipose tissue and lean tissue (e.g.,
skeletal structures and soft tissues such as internal organs and
muscle). Fluid accumulation (within body cavities and
subcutaneously) typically occurs over days to weeks, whereas weight
gain from accumulation of body tissue mass usually occurs slowly,
over weeks to months.
Obesity (ch. 150) is overwhelmingly the most common cause of
weight gain in dogs and cats, and is now recognized as a disease by
the veterinary profession.1 Accumulation of adipose tissue and, to a
lesser extent, lean tissue mass (increased abdominal organ size and
muscle mass) are associated with adverse effects on health, lifespan
and quality of life.2 Although obesity is assumed when a dog or cat is
>30% above its ideal weight, in reality, there is a continuum with
lesser amounts of body fat accumulation of >10% above ideal weight
being classed as “overweight.”1 Obesity is ultimately the result of
imbalance between energy intake and energy use, with multiple risk
factors recognized, including genetics, dietary factors, owner factors,

comorbidities, environmental factors, and neutering (ch. 150).
Concurrent drug therapy can result in weight gain by stimulating
appetite, with examples including corticosteroids, anticonvulsants
(phenobarbital and potassium bromide) and progestins. Some
comorbidities can also affect energy balance, like musculoskeletal
diseases which cause decreased energy expenditure through
immobility (ch. 226).

FIGURE 20.1 Algorithm for a suggested approach
to the investigation and management of weight gain.
ACTH, Adrenocorticotropic hormone; BCS, body
condition score; CBC, complete blood count; cTSH,
canine thyroid-stimulating hormone; IGF-1, insulinlike growth factor 1; LDDST, low-dose
dexamethasone suppression test; MCS, muscle
condition score; T4, thyroxine.
Some endocrinopathies can also cause weight gain, including
hypothyroidism (dogs, ch. 285), hyperadrenocorticism (dogs and
cats, chs. 293 and 294), insulinoma (dogs, ch. 289) and
acromegaly (cats, ch. 280). Acromegaly and hyperadrenocorticism
cause weight gain through a combination of increasing food intake,
promoting fat redistribution, and organomegaly; the weight gain
associated with hypothyroidism is the result of decreased
metabolism, whereby energy intake is unaltered. Finally, weight gain

can also arise from large tumors, most likely arising within the
abdominal cavity (ch. 21).

Signalment and History
Obesity develops at any age, but its peak is in early to middle-aged
adult life, with neutered animals and certain breeds (e.g., Labrador
Retrievers, Golden Retrievers, brachycephalic breeds and Beagles)
being at increased risk.3 Endocrinopathies tend to occur during
middle-aged years; depending upon the condition, there are again
known breed predispositions (e.g., Doberman Pinscher, Golden
Retriever and Irish Setter in hypothyroidism; Poodles, Dachshunds,
Boxers and small terriers in hyperadrenocorticism).
Both the magnitude (percentage change in body weight, which can
be calculated from historical weight measurements) and duration of
weight gain should be determined. Rapid increases in body weight
suggest fluid accumulation and the clinician should then look for
possible cardiac, hepatic, infectious, inflammatory, or protein-losing
conditions; more gradual weight gain suggests increased body tissue,
and the clinician should instead look for obesity, a possible
endocrinopathy or an abdominal mass.
Polyphagia (ch. 19) can be associated with endocrinopathies (e.g.,
hyperadrenocorticism, insulinoma or acromegaly), usually in
association with other signs depending on the disease. For example,
polyuria, polydipsia, lethargy, exercise intolerance, and excess
panting might be seen with hyperadrenocorticism, whereas seizures
and other neurological signs might be present with insulinoma. In
contrast, the polyphagia in feline acromegaly is usually due to
concurrent diabetes mellitus, and other typical signs would be
expected (e.g., polydipsia and polyuria). Finally, weight gain without
polyphagia in a middle-aged dog could suggest hypothyroidism and
again, there might be other signs such as lethargy and cold
intolerance.
Where obesity is suspected, detailed information should be
gathered about food intake (both main meal and additional food
from treats and table scraps), feeding habits and details of the family
unit including other pets (chs. 145, 150). The amount and intensity
of physical activity should also be recorded, as should the details of

drug therapy and comorbidities (that might reduce exercise
capabilities).

Physical Examination
Clinicians should carefully evaluate the patient for ascites, pleural
effusion, and subcutaneous edema (ch. 30); if present, pulse
characteristics (rate, rhythm and volume), capillary refill time, and
thoracic auscultation might further suggest underlying cardiac
disease. With abdominal palpation, masses, organomegaly, and
enlargement can be identified (ch. 21). Hyperadrenocorticism can
be associated with a pot-bellied appearance as a result of
hepatomegaly, centripetal fat redistribution, and abdominal muscle
weakness. Further, examination of the skin and hair coat can reveal
changes consistent with endocrinopathies such as
hyperadrenocorticism and hypothyroidism (ch. 12); these include
alopecia, scale, myxedema, thin skin, hyperpigmentation and
comedones. Finally, acromegaly in cats results in increased soft
tissue mass, manifesting as abdominal organomegaly (e.g.,
renomegaly) and also coarsened facial features.
Body condition score (BCS; ch. 72 and inside textbook covers) and
muscle condition score (MCS)4 are vital measurements where weight
gain is present, enabling the nature of any body tissue gain to be
elucidated. The World Small Animal Veterinary Association
(WSAVA) recommend the 9-point BCS system,5 whereby scores of 67 and 8-9 represent overweight (10-20% above ideal) and obese (3040% above ideal) condition, respectively. However, many dogs and
cats are “beyond the scale,” whereby their excess adiposity is greater
than that depicted by BCS 9. Finally, measuring bodyweight, using
calibrated electronic scales, is vital.6 Practices should consider
weighing dogs and cats every at every visit, since this enables an
individualized record to be created, thereby facilitating the early
detection of bodyweight changes.6 Given that BCS systems are not
validated for puppies and kittens, regular weight measurements are
the best way of monitoring weight gain during growth, with reference
to evidence-based growth standards (ch. 146).7 Such standards

confirm whether rate of weight gain is appropriate or excessive,
enabling corrective measures to be implemented.8

Further Investigations
A suggested diagnostic approach to weight gain is shown in Figure
20.1. History and physical examination can narrow the differential
diagnosis, but further investigations are often necessary. Possible
laboratory analyses include complete blood count, serum
biochemistry, urinalysis and testing for endocrine disease including
thyroxine (T4) and canine thyroid-stimulating hormone (cTSH),
adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation test, low-dose
dexamethasone suppression test, and insulin-like growth factor-1
(IGF-1) measurement. Diagnostic imaging can be also helpful:
thoracic radiography and ultrasonography (including
echocardiography) can identify cardiac disorders and pleural
effusion; abdominal radiography and ultrasonography are useful for
possible abdominal neoplasia, organomegaly, adrenal gland changes
and ascites. Further, whole-body computed tomography (CT) is often
preferred for assessing body cavities in large dogs, radiography or CT
of the musculoskeletal system is indicated where orthopedic causes
of weight gain are suspected, and either magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) or CT can also be used to identify possible pituitary masses.
Finally, in cases of obesity, body fat mass can be quantified using
dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry9 or CT.10

Enlargement
Emilia Bourassi

A C RO N YM S
FIP feline infectious peritonitis
GI gastrointestinal

Overview
Abdominal enlargement is commonly seen in small animals. It can
either be the presenting concern or an incidental finding during the
physical examination. Causes of abdominal enlargement can be
classified in categories based on a mnemonic adapted from human
medicine (the 7 F’s): Fat, Fluid, Firm, Food, Flatulence, Flabby,
Fetus (Table 21.1).1
Fat accumulation can be diffuse secondary to obesity (ch. 150) or
localized as a mass (lipoma). Peripheral fat redistribution to the
mesentery, seen with hyperadrenocorticism (ch. 293), can also
contribute to abdominal distention.
Fluid can accumulate in organs such as the gastrointestinal (GI)
tract (functional ileus or mechanical ileus/obstruction), the kidneys
and/or ureters, the urinary bladder (urethral obstruction or
neurologic causes of urinary retention) or the uterus (pyometra or
hydrometra). It can also collect in cysts or abscesses. Fluid in the
peritoneal or retroperitoneal space is a common cause of abdominal

distention and can be separated in different categories based on the
underlying mechanism (ch. 71).
A mass effect can be present secondary to the enlargement of any
organ in the abdomen, intra-abdominal lymphadenomegaly, or
granuloma. Organomegaly can be due to congestion (mainly spleen
and liver), torsion, or infiltration (neoplasia most commonly).
Granulomas have been reported with foreign bodies, fungal disease,
parasites, and pythiosis.
Increase of the volume content of the GI tract may cause
abdominal enlargement. This can be physiologic in the postprandial
period, or due to overeating, obstruction or functional ileus of the
intestines, constipation or megacolon (ch. 51). A high worm burden,
especially in kittens and puppies, is also a common cause of
abdominal distention.
Gas can accumulate in the GI tract (gastric dilation +/– volvulus,
ileus, obstruction, torsion) or in other organs, secondary to
emphysematous bacterial infections (liver, gallbladder, urinary
bladder). Free gas can be present secondary to GI perforation, gasproducing bacteria in septic peritonitis, trauma, or post-surgery.
Abdominal musculature weakness can lead to the appearance of
abdominal enlargement and is usually associated with
hyperadrenocorticism but is possible with any muscle-wasting
disease.
Pregnancy should be considered in any intact female. Fetal
retention and subsequent uterine rupture have also been reported as
a cause of abdominal distention post-partum.2

Diagnostic Approach (Figure 21.1)
Triage
The first step in the approach of abdominal distention is to
determine if it is an emergency. Some of the clinical signs that should
alert the clinician to the possibility of an emergent situation include
lethargy, weakness, dyspnea, tachycardia, pale mucous membranes,
poor pulses, a capillary refill time >2 seconds, unproductive retching,
or severe abdominal pain (ch. 126). A history of an acute onset

should also raise concern as this is more likely due to an active
process such as active bleeding.

History
The patient may be presented for decreased appetite (ch. 17),
lethargy (ch. 10), weakness (ch. 23), weight gain (ch. 20),
increased respiratory effort (ch. 37), abdominal pain or more
specific signs related to the underlying cause (e.g., unproductive
retching with gastric dilation and volvulus). A thorough history is
vital, not only to help determine the urgency of the situation but also
to develop a complete differential diagnosis list (ch. 2). Information
obtained from the history should include duration and description of
clinical signs, previous medical history, drug history, travel history as
well as a description of the patient’s environment.

Physical Examination (ch. 3)
Body and muscle condition scores (ch. 72 and textbook’s inside
covers) can help rule out obesity or muscle-wasting disease as
differentials. A thorough examination of the abdomen might reveal
organomegaly, distention of a hollow organ, pregnancy, the presence
of a fluid wave on ballottement (

Video 21.1), the presence of gas

on percussion, or signs of pain (ch. 6). Other abnormalities of the
physical examination depend on the underlying cause.

Diagnostic Procedures
Minimum Database
In most cases, a minimum database should be performed. A
complete blood count might show evidence of a septic process or
bleeding. A serum biochemistry profile and urinalysis are useful to
identify organ involvement or to rule out or rule in certain disease
processes such as protein-losing enteropathies, protein-losing
nephropathies, and liver dysfunction.

Abdominal +/– Thoracic Imaging
Diagnostic imaging is often needed to determine the cause of
abdominal distention and a combination of modalities may be
necessary. Survey radiographs have better sensitivity to detect the
presence of gas, and they are also useful for detection of masses or
obstructive patterns.3 Abdominal ultrasound is very useful in finding
fluid (

Videos 21.2A and 21.2B; ch. 73), masses, cysts, enlarged

lymph nodes or any structural abnormalities. Thoracic imaging
should also be performed as it is not uncommon to have either both
cavities affected or the primary cause localized to the thorax.
Computed tomography scanning is sometimes warranted, especially
when vascular abnormalities are suspected.

Tissue Sampling

Any abnormal structure or organ should be sampled if deemed safe.
Fine needle aspirates may be sufficient to reach a diagnosis but
biopsies (ultrasound-guided or surgical) might be needed.

Abdominocentesis
Abdominocentesis (ch. 86) and analysis of peritoneal fluid (ch. 71)
is essential and can provide either a final diagnosis or useful
information concerning the possible underlying causes.
The different categories of abdominal fluid are based on the
underlying mechanism (ch. 71) and can help narrow the differential
diagnosis list.
Transudates can develop secondary to changes in plasma
hydrostatic pressure or oncotic pressure. In the past, transudates
were classified as “pure” or “modified” but a classification between
low- and high-protein transudates is more helpful in determining the
underlying cause (ch. 71). Low-protein transudates are caused either
by severe hypoalbuminemia or presinusoidal portal hypertension.
Causes include protein-losing enteropathies (ch. 262), proteinlosing nephropathies (ch. 302), liver vascular anomalies (ch. 267),
hepatic cirrhosis (ch. 270), or burn injuries. High-protein
transudates are usually caused by sinusoidal or post-sinusoidal
portal hypertension. Causes include congestive heart failure (ch.
229), liver disease (ch. 270), caudal vena cava thrombosis (ch.
171), Budd-Chiari syndrome (ch. 239), and neoplasia.
Exudates develop as a result of either increased vascular
permeability due to inflammatory mediators or vessel or viscus
injury/leakage4 (ch. 71). They usually contain both increased
protein and cell counts. Based on a recent retrospective study on
canine peritoneal effusion, 3000 cells/microL might be a preferred
cut-off value to differentiate transudates from exudates.5 Exudates
are caused by infectious (bacterial, viral, fungal, protozoal) or
noninfectious (pancreatitis, neoplasia, bile, urine, foreign body)
disorders and can be septic or not. Most cases of peritonitis will
present with an exudate.4 In addition to cytology and bacterial
culture, measurement of glucose and lactate in the effusion might be
of use to determine if septic peritonitis is present (ch. 265).

Chylous peritoneal effusion is uncommon in dogs and cats.6 One
retrospective study in cats showed a prevalence of 6.7% among all
peritoneal effusions whereas in a retrospective study on 107 dogs
there were no cases of chylous effusion.5,7 The most common cause
reported in both dogs and cats is neoplasia, particularly carcinoma.
Other causes reported in cats include cardiovascular disease, feline
infectious peritonitis (FIP), biliary cirrhosis, liver steatosis, and
lymphatic rupture or leakage.6,8 In dogs, other causes include rightsided heart failure and lymphatic obstruction, rupture or leakage.6,9
Hemorrhagic effusion (hemoperitoneum, hemoabdomen) can
occur secondary to trauma or be considered spontaneous.
Spontaneous hemoperitoneum in cats is uncommon; causes are
evenly distributed between neoplastic and non-neoplastic diseases
(46% and 54%, respectively).10 Liver disease is the most common
cause for hemoperitoneum in cats. Among neoplastic causes,
hemangiosarcoma is the most common (18/30 cats). Among nonneoplastic causes, coagulopathies (23%) and liver necrosis (23%) are
the most common. In dogs, similar causes have been found but
neoplasia is the most common cause of spontaneous hemorrhagic
effusion.11 It is of interest to note that causes and origin of
hemorrhage vary between small and large dogs, with small dogs
having a lower prevalence of splenic hemorrhage (43.2% versus
61.3%) and a higher prevalence of hemorrhage from the liver or
other locations.12 Anaphylaxis-related hemoperitoneum has also
been reported in dogs (ch. 73) and should be considered if the
history and physical examination findings are consistent and no
other causes can be found.13
Uroabdomen is a consequence of rupture of the urinary tract at
any level (ch. 127). The most common site of rupture in both dogs
and cats is the bladder, followed by the urethra, while rupture at the
level of the kidneys or ureters is uncommonly reported.14,15 The
most common cause of urinary tract rupture is vehicular or other
blunt trauma. Other causes include urinary tract obstruction,
traumatic bladder expression or catheterization, bladder neoplasia,
urethral catheterization and post-operative leakage.16 Contrast

studies are needed in most patients to determine the source of urine
leakage and the best treatment options.

FIGURE 21.1 Algorithm for the diagnostic
approach of abdominal enlargement. FIP, Feline
infectious peritonitis; GI, gastrointestinal; US,
ultrasound.
Biliary effusion results from disruption of the biliary tract, either
at the level of the biliary duct or the gallbladder. It can be due to

trauma or secondary to obstructive lesions (cholelithiasis),
inflammation (necrotizing cholecystitis) or neoplasia. Although in
most cases biliary effusion can be diagnosed by comparing serum
and effusion bilirubin concentrations, in rare cases dogs can have a
ruptured gallbladder without icterus and with low peritoneal fluid
bilirubin concentration. Measurement of bile acids in both serum
and effusion can be useful in these cases (40-fold higher
concentration in effusion in one reported case).17
Neoplasia is the most common cause of peritoneal effusion in
small animals.6,7 Protein and cell count are not helpful to classify
neoplastic effusions because different mechanisms can lead to
effusion in patients with cancer, including compression of
lymphatics, rupture of an organ, and inflammation. Tumor cells are
not always identifiable in the fluid, as not all types of tumor exfoliate
into effusions. For most abdominal neoplasms causing peritoneal
effusion in dogs and cats, the diagnosis is obtained through
histopathologic evaluation of tissue. Common tumors causing
effusion include lymphoma, adenocarcinoma, and carcinoma.
Additional testing can be performed on the peritoneal fluid,
depending on the disease suspected. Peritoneal cPLI concentration
was 100% sensitive and 94.7% specific in diagnosing canine acute
pancreatitis in one study.18 Flow cytometry and PARR (polymerase
chain reaction for antigen receptor rearrangements) can be useful if
neoplasia is suspected but not confirmed on cytology. The Rivalta’s
test can be used for ruling out FIP and a reverse transcriptase
polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) test can be performed on the
fluid to confirm a suspicion of FIP (ch. 200).

Measurement of Abdominal Pressure
Many causes of abdominal distention can lead to abdominal
compartment syndrome, where sustained intra-abdominal
hypertension results in multiple organ dysfunction as well as
detrimental effects on respiratory, cardiovascular and nervous
systems.19,20 Measurement of abdominal pressure should be
considered in patients considered at risk, such as those with an acute
onset of abdominal distention or abdominal effusion that develops
post-operatively.

Treatment
Treatment will vary, as it should be aimed at the underlying cause.
Palliative treatment such as abdominal drainage may be needed if a
patient is experiencing respiratory difficulties or discomfort,
especially in cases where definitive treatment is not possible.

Client Information
Abdominal Enlargement

What are the Causes of Abdominal Enlargement?
Abdominal enlargement refers to the belly becoming larger than
usual. You may have noticed your pet’s belly becoming rounder over
a long period of time or discovered a sudden bulge in the belly area.
Abdominal distention is another term frequently used as well.
There are many causes of abdominal enlargement, ranging from
benign causes to serious disease. Some of the common causes
include:
• Pregnancy
• Weight gain
• Worms, in particular in kittens and puppies
• Enlarged organs: organs in the abdomen can become increased
in size due to infection, inflammation, cancer
• Free fluid: accumulation of fluid in the abdomen can be due to
many causes such as the rupture of an organ or a mass, cancer,
heart disease, liver disease, kidney disease.
• Gas in organs or in the abdomen: a common cause is stomach
dilation and torsion (gastric dilation volvulus [GDV], “bloat”),
especially in large deep-chested dogs. A blockage in the
intestines due to a foreign body can also cause accumulation of
gas in the intestines.
• Cushing’s disease: This is a disease of hormonal imbalance
affecting the adrenal glands where dogs will have an enlarged
belly due to a bigger liver, more fat in the abdomen and
weakened belly muscles.

Should i be Concerned if i Notice My Pet’s Belly
Looking Bigger?
Some causes of abdominal enlargement require emergency care.
Signs that should prompt emergency consultation include weakness
or collapse, retching or vomiting, difficulties breathing or rapid
breathing, pale gums, and signs of pain.

How to Determine the Cause of Abdominal
Enlargement
A detailed history (when the veterinarian or nurse asks you questions
to better understand what you have noticed and what has happened
so far) and a thorough physical examination will be very valuable to
establish a list of possible causes. It is important to have as much
information as possible about the abdominal enlargement: how long
it has been present, how quickly it appeared, and any changes that
happened before you noticed the change, for example.
It will usually be necessary to perform diagnostic tests, and these
may include screening tests such as bloodwork, urinalysis and
diagnostic imaging of the abdomen and chest (x-rays and ultrasound
are the most commonly used). Based on the results of these tests,
treatment may be recommended or additional tests may be
warranted, such as specific blood tests, evaluation of heart function,
collection of the fluid in the belly for microscopic analysis, aspiration
of a mass or an organ with a fine needle, or biopsies.

What is the Treatment for Abdominal Enlargement?
Treatment will vary with the underlying cause. Some causes can be
cured, such as worms or intestinal obstruction. Other causes will
require long-term management with diet or medications.
Surgery is sometimes necessary, such as when a tumor is present
or bleeding inside the belly needs to be stopped. If a cause is not
found or is not treatable, then supportive care such as pain
medications or regular drainage of fluid build-up can provide relief.
Emilia Bourassi (Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, Canada)

Chapter 22: Failure to Grow
Hans S Kooistra

A C RO N YM S
GH growth hormone
IGF-1 insulin-like growth factor-1
IGF-BP insulin-like growth factor-binding protein
TSH thyroid stimulating hormone

Introduction
Dogs and cats grow rapidly over a relatively short period of time
during the early stages of life. Linear (vertical) growth primarily
occurs during the first 6 to 9 months of life but can continue in some
dogs until about 2 years of age. Growth in long bone length is limited
to the growth plates and occurs via the process of enchondral
ossification. Linear growth halts when the growth plates close. No
species has as much variation in body size as the dog, which may
make it difficult to determine whether failure to grow is really a
problem.
Failure to grow is defined as not growing at the anticipated rate or
to a normal extent. Failure to grow may be an owner’s chief concern
or may be identified by a veterinarian during routine physical
examination (PE). Usually there is good correlation between parental
height and that of their offspring. Thus, if possible, the size of the

dog with supposed failure to grow should be compared with parental
and sibling height. The possibility should be considered that an
apparent dwarf may simply be a small individual whose size is within
normal biological variation. Alternatively, the individual may be the
offspring of an unexpected or unwanted mating with a small sire.

Pathophysiology
Genetic factors play a major role in linear growth, with numerous
genes involved in its regulation. After domestication of the dog,
selection of such genes by humans has resulted in a wide variety of
breeds with a wide variety of body sizes and growth rates. The
chondrodystrophic dog breeds are examples of selection by people
for the genes that give rise to angular limb formation and short
limbs. As these breeds have been created intentionally, they are
usually not considered as having a problem with failure to grow.
To meet its full (genetic) potential for growth, any animal must
consume adequate calories and nutrients (chs. 147, 148). Following
consumption, food must be digested, absorbed, transported to
necessary tissues and used for metabolic maintenance and growth.
The causes of failure to grow can be subdivided in three major
groups: (1) inadequate intake of calories and nutrients, (2) increased
use of calories and nutrients, and (3) loss of energy generated by
consumed calories and nutrients. Because several hormones are
important determinants of linear growth, it may be helpful to
differentiate endocrine and non-endocrine causes of failure to grow.

Endocrine Causes of Failure to Grow
Growth Hormone (GH) and Insulin-Like Growth
Factor-1 (IGF-1) Deficiencies
Growth hormone (GH), originating from the pituitary anterior lobe,
plays a central role in the modulation of growth (ch. 281). Healthy
puppies and kittens may secrete large amounts of GH, i.e., juvenile
hypersomatotropism, an important determinant of linear growth.1
Serial measurements of plasma GH demonstrated that the increased

concentrations documented in Great Dane puppies decrease to
“adult” concentrations by about 6 months of age.2 In Beagles, GH
secretion is increased only until about 7 weeks of age.1 In Miniature
Poodles, GH concentrations do not change significantly with time
and values in young animals are within adult reference ranges.3
In the total absence of GH, linear growth occurs at about a third to
a quarter of the normal rate. Growth hormone deficiency in a young
animal affects the growth of almost all tissues, resulting in
“proportionate dwarfism”: all body components are equally small.
Although GH has a direct effect on several tissues, its primary
growth-promoting actions are mediated by insulin-like growth
factor-1 (IGF-1). GH stimulates the synthesis and secretion of IGF-1
by the liver. In the systemic circulation, IGF-1 is bound to “carriers”:
IGF-binding proteins (IGF-BPs). Binding to IGF-BPs prolongs the
half-life of IGF-1, consistent with its long-term growth-promoting
action. Once hepatic IGF-1 reaches target cells via the circulation, it
stimulates anabolic processes, e.g., protein synthesis,
chondrogenesis, and growth. In addition to its endocrine effects, GH
also stimulates “local” production of IGF-1. Locally synthesized IGF1 stimulates anabolic processes in a paracrine or autocrine manner
and linear growth is largely dependent on local production of IGF-1
within growth plates. In adult dogs, there is a strong linear
correlation between plasma IGF-1 concentration and body size, while
basal plasma GH concentrations are quite similar among various
breeds. This reduces the value of assessing GH and further implies
that breed-specific IGF-1 reference ranges must be established to aid
in determining the cause for a dog that has failed to grow.

Juvenile Hypothyroidism
Adequate circulating thyroid hormone concentrations appear to be
an absolute prerequisite for normal growth (ch. 285) because total
absence leads to an almost complete cessation of linear growth.
Thyroid hormone exerts direct effects on cell metabolism. Further,
the action of IGF-1 on cartilage cells is dependent on thyroid
hormone. Because skeletal growth depends on thyroid hormones
that promote chondrogenesis, in synergy with GH and IGF-1,

juvenile hypothyroidism is associated with delayed epiphyseal
closure, retarded epiphyseal growth, reduced long bone growth, and
“disproportionate dwarfism.”4

Insulin Deficiency (Juvenile Diabetes
Mellitus)
Insulin has strong anabolic actions separate from its effect on
carbohydrate metabolism. These actions include stimulation of
protein synthesis and cell division. Consequently, insulin deficiency,
i.e., juvenile diabetes mellitus (ch. 291), is associated with growth
retardation. Failure of normal growth is also associated with a
decrease in insulin-dependent transportation of glucose and fatty
acids into muscle and fat cells. Some glucose (energy) is lost in the
urine of diabetics.

Glucocorticoid Excess
The catabolic effects of the glucocorticoids are characterized by
increased gluconeogenesis, decreased uptake of glucose by muscle
and fat cells, increased protein breakdown, and lipolysis. In addition,
glucocorticoid excess suppresses pituitary GH secretion, mainly due
to stimulation of hypothalamic somatostatin release (ch. 293).
Consequently, long-term administration of glucocorticoids to young,
growing animals may result in growth retardation.

Gonadal Steroid Excess
Gonadal androgens and estrogens also affect linear growth.
Prepubertal gonadectomy may result in taller individuals.5
Administration of androgens or estrogens at an early age may result
in stunted growth due to premature closure of the growth plates.

Other Endocrine Deficiencies

Hypoadrenocorticism may occur at any age (ch. 296). The Nova
Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever is a breed recognized to occasionally
develop primary hypoadrenocorticism at an early age.
Hypoadrenocorticism is often associated with a decrease in appetite,
and vomiting and diarrhea. These problems result in reduced
nutrient intake, which may give rise to a failure to grow.
Hypoparathyroidism may also occur at a young age. Parathyroid
hormone (PTH) has an important role in bone metabolism and its
deficiency may result in growth retardation. Disorders associated
with severe polydipsia, such as central diabetes insipidus, may result
in impaired appetite and failure to grow normally.

Non-Endocrine Causes of Failure to Grow
Nutrition
In addition to genotype, another important factor affecting growth is
intake of insufficient calories and nutrients. Nutritional deprivation
severely impairs growth. Selective deficiencies in vitamins or
minerals may also cause abnormalities of growth. The quality and
palatability of food should be taken into consideration (chs. 145 and
146).

Oropharyngeal, Gastrointestinal,
Pancreatic Exocrine Disorders
A poor appetite, e.g., due to a systemic disease, may result in less
food intake (ch. 17). Oropharyngeal disorders may cause hyporexia
(ch. 259). Regurgitation or vomiting could cause insufficient
nutrients reaching the intestines (ch. 48). A vascular ring anomaly,
due to a persistent right aortic arch, should be considered in puppies
with stunted growth and chronic regurgitation, especially after
weaning (ch. 259). Maldigestion, e.g., due to exocrine pancreatic
insufficiency (ch. 279), and malabsorption, e.g., due to an intestinal
wall disorder (ch. 262), can result in decreased uptake of nutrients.
Intestinal parasites are a frequent cause of inadequate uptake of
nutrients in puppies and kittens (ch. 262).

FIGURE 22.1 Algorithm depicting the diagnostic
approach to a dog or cat who appears to be failing to
grow as expected.CBC, Complete blood count; EPI,
exocrine pancreatic insufficiency; GH, growth

hormone; PU/PD, polyuria/polydipsia; TLI, trypsinlike immunoreactivity.

Inflammation, Heart, Kidney, Liver
Catabolic processes, such as those associated with inflammatory
processes and fever (ch. 16), will result in increased use of energy.
Congenital heart anomalies (ch. 231) and endocarditis (ch. 232)
may be associated with tachycardia which, in turn, utilizes excess
energy, leaving fewer calories for growth. Disorders involving organs
that play a central role in metabolism, i.e., the liver and the kidneys,
may result in failure to grow. Both congenital and acquired kidney
disorders can result in stunted growth. Portosystemic shunting
resulting in hepatic encephalopathy is the most common liver
disorder associated with failure to grow (ch. 267). Hepatitis and
glycogen storage disease have also been associated with failure to
grow (ch. 269). Growth failure in chronically anemic young
individuals (ch. 57) may be associated with impaired oxygen
delivery to tissues as well as increased cardiovascular effort.
Glucosuria is most commonly seen in juvenile diabetics that also fail
to grow (ch. 291). Glucosuria can be the consequence of abnormal
renal proximal tubules (ch. 303). Persistent proteinuria (ch. 302)
and protein-losing enteropathies (ch. 262) decrease growth
potential.

Diagnostic Approach (Figure 22.1)
History and Physical Examination
A detailed nutritional history should be obtained in order to obtain
information regarding the amount, quality and palatability of food
consumed (ch. 145). A poor appetite, despite the feeding of a
palatable, high-quality food suggests a disorder of the
gastrointestinal tract or the presence of systemic disease. Stunted
growth in pets with very good or ravenous appetites may point to

maldigestion, malabsorption or loss of energy. History-taking may
also reveal treatment with steroids for an unrelated problem.
Concurrent clinical signs may help identify an underlying cause for
failure to grow. Diarrhea or voluminous stools may point to
maldigestion or malabsorption. Polyuria may point to renal disease,
hepatic disease, diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus or other
conditions. Mental dullness may point to hypothyroidism or hepatic
or renal encephalopathy. Symmetrical truncal alopecia can be seen in
dogs with GH deficiency or hypothyroidism. Regurgitation since
weaning may point to vascular ring anomaly or megaesophagus.
Body proportions must be carefully evaluated in dogs or cats who
fail to grow. Relatively short limbs compared to the trunk suggest
either juvenile hypothyroidism or chondrodystrophy. Growth
hormone deficiency, in contrast, causes proportionate dwarfism. It is
also important to note the ratio of height to weight. An animal with
stunted growth that is overweight for height is more likely to have an
endocrine disorder such as GH deficiency or hypothyroidism.
Malnutrition or systemic disorders are more likely to result in
underweight animals with stunted growth.
A thorough physical examination is essential in animals with
failure to grow, as specific physical findings may point to a specific
disorder. For example, dogs with hypothyroidism usually will have a
weak pulse. A heart murmur may disclose a cardiac abnormality. The
presence of ocular changes in a dwarfed dog may point to inherited
oculo-skeletal dysplasia, an autosomal recessive disorder that has
been identified in Labrador Retrievers, Samoyed dogs and Northern
Inuit dogs.

Basic Laboratory Evaluations
Laboratory evaluations should include multiple fecal examinations
for intestinal parasites, e.g., Giardia (ch. 80). Fecal examination
may also provide information regarding digestion and absorption.
Urinalysis (ch. 70) may reveal proteinuria, glucosuria or
hyposthenuria. Indications for pyelonephritis may be found in the
urine sediment. A complete blood count (CBC) should be evaluated
for anemia, inflammation or eosinophilia. Remember that puppies
and kittens normally have lower red blood cell counts as compared

with adults. Eosinophilia may point to parasitism or
hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296). Results of a routine serum
biochemistry profile can help to identify renal disease (chs. 301305), hepatic disease (chs. 266-271) diabetes mellitus (ch. 291) or
hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296). Decreased serum protein
concentrations may point to hepatic disease (chs. 267, 268),
protein-losing enteropathy (ch. 262) or protein-losing nephropathy
(chs. 302, 305). Decreases in serum trypsin-like immunoreactivity
(TLI) in a fasted dog confirms exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI;
ch. 279). Serum cobalamin and folate concentrations may suggest
intestinal abnormalities causing maldigestion and malabsorption
(ch. 262).

Specific Tests, Imaging, Genetic Testing
Specific tests may be required to diagnose endocrine disorders.
Growth hormone deficiency can be diagnosed indirectly by
measuring and finding low serum IGF-1 concentrations. Absence of a
significant increase in circulating GH concentration after IV
administration of GH-releasing hormone also implicates GH
deficiency. Decreases in serum thyroxine concentration together with
a clear increase in thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration
may confirm hypothyroidism. A TSH-stimulation test can be used to
secure the diagnosis in dogs whose TSH concentrations are not
increased. The diagnosis of hypoadrenocorticism should be based on
the results of an adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation
test.
Diagnostic imaging may reveal skeletal abnormalities (ch. 162).
Ultrasonography may be helpful to detect structural abnormalities of
the internal organs or identify portosystemic shunting. Ultrasoundguided biopsies may be needed if renal or liver disease is suspected.
For several inherited disorders the genetic cause of failure to grow
has been identified, which allows for genetic testing. For example,
pituitary dwarfism in Shepherd dogs is usually caused by a mutation
in a gene that encodes for the transcription factor LHX3.6 The
availability of a diagnostic DNA test not only allows for proper
diagnosis of dogs with pituitary dwarfism due to this mutation, but
also enables breeders to prevent dwarfs from being born by

identifying carriers of the LHX3 mutation. If all breeding animals
were genetically tested for the presence of the LHX3 mutation and a
correct breeding policy would be implemented, this disease could be
eradicated completely.

Treatment
The treatment is dependent on the underlying disorder. Some
disorders can be well managed medically, whereas others may
require surgical correction. If the underlying disorder is diagnosed
and treated early, “catch-up” in growth is usually seen.

Client Information
Failure to Grow
Growth is a complex yet tightly regulated process. Growth is
mainly determined by the genetic composition of the animal and
regulated by multiple hormones. To meet its full (genetic) potential
for growth, any animal must consume sufficient calories and
nutrients. Following consumption, food must be digested, absorbed,
and the nutrients transported to the necessary tissues and used for
metabolic maintenance and growth. An abnormality in one or more
of these processes or a hormonal dysfunction may result in failure to
grow. Failure to grow, in this context, is defined as not growing at the
anticipated rate or to a normal extent.
In addition to genotype, another important factor affecting growth
is intake of insufficient calories and nutrients. Therefore, your
veterinarian will ask you for a detailed nutritional history regarding
the amount, quality and palatability of food consumed. Historytaking is also important because additional symptoms may help
determine any underlying cause of failure to grow. For example,
disorders associated with vomiting could cause insufficient nutrients
to reach the intestines.
A thorough physical examination is essential in animals with
failure to grow, as certain physical findings may point to a specific
disorder. A heart problem may be associated with a high heart
frequency, which, in turn, utilizes excess energy, leaving fewer
calories for growth. Therefore, if a heart disorder is suspected in an
animal with failure to grow, it will need to be examined thoroughly.
A normally functioning pancreas and gastrointestinal tract are
essential for digestion and absorption of nutrients, whereas the
kidneys and liver play a central role in the metabolism of the
nutrients. Consequently, a disorder of any of these organs may
require testing. Intestinal parasites are a frequent cause of
inadequate uptake of nutrients in puppies and kittens. Your
veterinarian, therefore, may request multiple stool samples to see if
there is evidence of parasites. Fecal examination may also provide
information regarding abnormalities in the digestion or absorption
of nutrients in the gastrointestinal tract. Urinalysis may reveal the
presence of too much protein or sugar in the urine, which may
disclose conditions commonly associated with poor growth. A

complete blood count (CBC) may reveal anemia, an inflammatory
process or provide information pointing to a parasitic infection.
Blood tests may also be required to determine whether or not kidney,
liver, or pancreas disease is likely. A low protein concentration in the
blood may point to liver disease, an intestinal disorder or kidney
disease. A decrease in serum trypsin-like immunoreactivity (TLI) in a
fasted dog confirms a condition called “exocrine pancreatic
insufficiency (EPI).” Serum cobalamin and folate concentrations are
useful for assessing intestinal abnormalities causing maldigestion
and malabsorption.
Hormonal dysfunctions that may result in failure to grow include
growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus and
adrenocortical insufficiency. Specific tests are required to confirm
the presence of one or more of these conditions. To diagnose growth
hormone deficiency the blood insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1)
concentration has to be determined. For the diagnosis of
hypothyroidism the blood concentrations of thyroid hormone (T4)
and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) are required. The diagnosis
adrenocortical insufficiency should be based on the results of an
adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation test.
Diagnostic imaging with radiographs (X-rays) may reveal skeletal
abnormalities that can contribute to a diagnosis. Ultrasonography
may be helpful to detect structural abnormalities of the internal
organs. Biopsies may be needed if renal or liver disease is identified.
Genetic testing may be helpful for the inherited disorders for
which the genetic cause of failure to grow has been identified.
Hans S. Kooistra (Utrecht, The Netherlands)

Chapter 23: Weakness
Sean E Hulsebosch

A C RO N YM
PE physical examination

Introduction
General Observations
Weakness is a common presenting complaint in dogs and cats.
Animals can have an acute onset of weakness or chronic weakness,
and it may be persistent or episodic. The list of differential diagnoses
for weakness is vast, and therefore its explanation can be a challenge
or, at times, obvious.

Importance of the History and Physical
Examination
A detailed history is essential given the vague nature of this
presenting problem. The onset, duration, and progression of clinical
signs should be noted. Alternative terms a client might use for
“weakness” include lethargy, listlessness, lack of energy, slow,
difficulty rising, dull, cannot complete a typical walk, and, depending
on severity, collapse. One should determine if the observed weakness

is persistent or episodic; between periods of episodic weakness, most
pets appear healthy. Is the pet limp or stiff during episodes?
“Stiffness” would be consistent with hypocalcemia or a seizure, for
example, while a pet that appears episodically “limp” could have an
arrhythmia or syncope. Health of the other household pets should be
reviewed. The clinician must query the owner regarding
environment, potential toxin exposure, diet and treats, medications,
vaccination status, and then complete a comprehensive systems
review. Episodes of weakness captured with video by a client can be
informative (chs. 2 and 41;

Video 61.1).

A thorough physical examination (PE, ch. 3) is critically
important when trying to narrow a list of differential diagnoses, with
special attention given to vital parameters, mentation, hydration
status, mucous membrane color, capillary refill time, cardiothoracic
auscultation, abdominal palpation, and pulse rate, rhythm, and
quality. Careful orthopedic (ch. 31) and neurologic (ch. 241)
examinations may be indicated, especially when vital and perfusion
parameters are unremarkable. The clinician should attempt to
discriminate true weakness, strictly defined as lack of strength, from
“apparent weakness” due to pain or lameness

(Videos 23.1,

23.2). Be certain the pet is visual, as acutely blind pets are not
necessarily weak, but they can be reluctant to walk. Fundic
examination is indicated especially in pets with a fever or with an
otherwise unremarkable PE (ch. 13). The mechanistic and body
systems approach to weakness that follows can help in creating a list
of differential diagnoses.

Mechanisms of Weakness
Hematologic
Anemia, a common cause of acute and chronic weakness in dogs and
cats, results in mucous membrane pallor (ch. 25). If the anemia is
severe (hematocrit < 20% in dogs, < 15% in cats), tachycardia or a
physiologic heart murmur may be detected on PE. There are myriad
causes of anemia, which is never a final diagnosis but is invariably
the result of a primary condition. The clinician must first determine

if the anemia is regenerative or non-regenerative (ch. 57). Pets with
a regenerative anemia commonly have a brief history of illness, and
their anemia can be subdivided as caused by blood loss (decreased
total solids and non-pigmented plasma) or hemolysis (normal total
solids with icteric or hemolyzed plasma). Identifying spherocytes on
red blood cell morphology (dogs) or auto-agglutination is consistent
with immune-mediated hemolysis (ch. 174). Heinz bodies are noted
in red blood cells after oxidative damage (ch. 138), schistocytes are
consistent with microangiopathic hemolysis, and hemoparasites are
noted with some hemolytic anemias (chs. 194, 197). Evidence of
blood loss on PE (melena, hematochezia, hematuria, epistaxis, or
evidence of echogenic cavitary effusion) may reveal where blood is
being lost. Remember blood loss into the thorax or abdomen is
commonly auto-transfused back into circulation, but blood lost into
the gastrointestinal or urinary tract is not recovered.
Non-regenerative anemias (ch. 172) are the result of primary bone
marrow disease or secondary to systemic disease.1 Bone marrow
aspirate or core biopsy (ch. 84) can be used to assess bone marrow
health while laboratory testing and imaging are used to assess for
systemic disease. Bone marrow disorders commonly associated with
non-regenerative anemias include myelofibrosis, myelodysplasia,
precursor immune-mediated anemia (PIMA), pure red cell aplasia
(PRCA), aplastic anemia, bone marrow infection (e.g., chronic
ehrlichiosis, feline leukemia virus), and round cell neoplasia.
Systemic diseases associated with non-regenerative anemia include
chronic kidney disease (ch. 301), chronic inflammatory diseases,
iron deficiency, hypothyroidism (ch. 285), hypoadrenocorticism
(ch. 296), and extra-medullary neoplasia (ch. 57).

Metabolic and Electrolyte Abnormalities
Metabolic derangements that can cause systemic weakness include
hypoglycemia, uremia, hepatic encephalopathy, hypocalcemia,
hypokalemia, and hyperkalemia. Hypoglycemia leads to
neuroglycopenia, often causing weakness or stumbling before
twitching, or convulsions are noted

(chs. 61, 289; Videos 42.3,

61.1). Uremic encephalopathy secondary to severe azotemia, the

accumulation of uremic toxins, and possibly gamma-aminobutyric
acid (GABA)–related mechanisms, causes mental dullness and
weakness (ch. 300).2 Hepatic encephalopathy due to
hyperammonemia and other endogenous toxins, especially postprandial or when combined with gastrointestinal bleeding, can lead
to neurologic signs

(Video 269.1), including weakness. Severe

hypokalemia can lead to muscle weakness (Video 68.1) via effects on
muscle and nerve membrane polarization.3 Severe hyperkalemia (>7
mmol/L) can cause bradycardia, decreased cardiac output, and
weakness.

Hemodynamic Mechanisms
Hypovolemia due to severe dehydration, internal or external
hemorrhage, or third space fluid loss (ch. 60) can result in
weakness. Distributive shock due to sepsis, thromboembolic disease,
or gastric-dilatation-volvulus will result in weakness.4 PE
abnormalities consistent with hemodynamic compromise include
dull mentation, pallor, delayed capillary refill time, poor pulse
quality, tachycardia or bradycardia (especially in cats), hypothermia,
core and extremity temperature difference, and delayed skin turgor
(ch. 121).

Endocrine Disorders
In dogs, hypothyroidism, hypercortisolism, hypoadrenocorticism,
hypoglycemia (iatrogenic or naturally occurring),
hyperparathyroidism, and hypoparathyroidism can cause weakness.
Hypothyroidism in dogs (ch. 285) commonly causes lethargy, but it
also causes weight gain, mild non-regenerative anemia, and
hyperlipidemia, which conspire to compound weakness.5 Chronic
hypercortisolism (chs. 293, 294) causes appendicular muscle
atrophy and weakness. Hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296) causes
weakness through malnutrition, hypovolemia, and/or hyperkalemia.
Hypercalcemia- mediated hyperpolarization of nerve and muscle

membranes, regardless of cause, leads to weakness (ch. 69).6,7
Hypocalcemia (ch. 69) alters calcium-mediated nerve excitability,
and pets that seem weak to an owner often have muscle cramping,
stiffness, and lameness.8 Insulinoma (ch. 289) causes hypoglycemia
and associated weakness, identical to the clinical signs associated
with exogenous insulin overdose in a diabetic dog

(Video 42.3).

Cats commonly develop one of two endocrine disorders that can
cause weakness. About 10% of diabetic cats have clinical signs of
weakness due to peripheral neuropathy, causing difficulty jumping
as well as the classic “plantigrade stance”

(ch. 292, Video

292.1). Almost 75% of diabetic cats have evidence of neuronal
degeneration on histopathology.9 Overzealous insulin therapy and
hypoglycemia can cause any diabetic to become weak.
Hyperthyroidism (ch. 287) commonly causes weakness in cats,
noted by owners when cats have difficulty jumping.

Cardiac Disorders
The 4 primary mechanisms of cardiac-induced weakness include
arrhythmias, congestive heart failure, thromboembolic disease, and
pericardial effusion. Arrhythmias resulting in poor cardiac output
and signs of weakness or collapse can be the result of cardiac or noncardiac disease, including electrolyte derangements, adrenergic
stimulation, drug-induced alterations, splenic disease, and gastricdilatation volvulus. Causes of bradyarrhythmias and weakness
include atrio-ventricular block, sick sinus syndrome, and atrial
standstill. Tachyarrhythmias that cause weakness include
supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular
tachycardia (ch. 230). Left-sided congestive heart failure with
pulmonary edema predisposes to hypoxia-induced weakness (ch.
229). Arterial thromboembolism occurs in approximately 15% of
cats with cardiomyopathy. Affected cats may appear weak to owners
that are not aware of the cat’s painful limbs; on PE, abnormalities
include decreased to absent pulses in affected limbs, and cyanotic
appearance of nail beds (ch. 238).10,11 Pericardial effusion resulting

in cardiac tamponade can cause weakness due to forward heart
failure and, if severe, collapse (ch. 235).

Respiratory Disorders
Respiratory diseases can lead to weakness via 4 main mechanisms:
hypoxia, hypercapnia, pulmonary hypertension, or vasovagal
syncope from coughing. On PE, affected pets may exhibit respiratory
distress, tachypnea, cough, stridor, stertor, or cyanosis. Inspiratory
difficulty is usually indicative of extra-thoracic disease, while
expiratory difficulty typically indicates intra-thoracic disease (ch.
212). In addition to careful laryngeal and thoracic auscultation,
cervical and thoracic radiographs are useful to identify many
respiratory diseases. Arterial blood gas analysis can determine the
presence of hypoxemia (PaO2 < 80 mm Hg) or hypercapnia (PaCO2
> 45 mm Hg) (ch. 123). Echocardiography can help determine
presence and degree of pulmonary hypertension. Moderate-to-severe
pulmonary hypertension can lead to collapse and weakness (ch.
218). Radiography, complete blood count, heartworm testing, and
bronchoscopy are among the tests used to help determine the cause
of coughing in dogs and cats.

FIGURE 23.1 Flow-chart of episodic or persistent
weakness. CBC, Complete blood count; ECG,
electrocardiogram; UA, urinalysis.
Common causes of respiratory-induced hypoxemia include
laryngeal paralysis (ch. 214), severe tracheal collapse (ch. 215),
airway foreign body (ch. 215), aspiration or bronchopneumonia (ch.
217), and pulmonary thromboembolism (ch. 219). Hypercapnia can
result from a laryngeal or tracheal foreign body, pneumothorax,
pleural effusion, or hypoventilation (ch. 220). Common diseases
leading to pulmonary hypertension include left-sided congestive
heart failure, heartworm disease, chronic inflammatory pulmonary
disease, pulmonary fibrosis, and pulmonary thromboembolism.
Vasovagal syncope can be observed in dogs with advanced airway
collapse and severe paroxysmal coughing (ch. 34).12

Neurologic Disorders
A thorough neurological examination is essential for neuroanatomic
localization (ch. 241). Neuromuscular disorders (neuropathy,
myopathy, or junctionopathy) are commonly associated with
weakness

(Videos 23.1, 241.2, 252.3, 252.4). Peripheral

neuropathies, unless peracute, may manifest with lower motor
neuron signs of flaccid limbs, altered sensation, and/or severe
muscle atrophy. Neuromuscular junction disorders (ch. 253), such

as myasthenia gravis, may appear similar to peripheral neuropathies
except that reflexes and sensation are intact, muscle atrophy is
minimal, and weakness may worsen with exercise

(Video 253.1).

Myopathies may be suspected in pets with normal spinal reflexes,
proprioceptive positioning, and sensation, but they often have
increases in serum creatine kinase concentrations (ch. 66). Central
nervous system disorders (brain or spinal cord disease, chs. 242251) may cause reduced voluntary limb movement rather than true
weakness. Other clinical signs such as changes in mentation, cranial
nerve deficits, seizures, and/or ataxia may be noted with intracranial
disease. Paresis, ataxia, vertebral column pain may be noted with
spinal cord disorders.

Orthopedic Disorders and
ARTHROPATHIES
Unlike most causes of weakness, dogs and cats with orthopedicrelated weakness often exhibit pain on PE. A complete orthopedic
examination and observation of gait can help localize the area of
concern (ch. 31). Fractures, diffuse osteoarthritis, immunemediated polyarthritis (ch. 177), septic arthritis, developmental
bone and joint disorders (e.g., hip dysplasia), and skeletal neoplasia
(ch. 326) are some of the orthopedic conditions that cause weakness
or apparent weakness (

Video 23.2).

Toxins
Dogs and cats exposed to a toxin frequently have dull mentation,
lethargy, ataxia, ptyalism, nausea, and sometimes vomiting and/or
diarrhea. Common toxins that can cause weakness or disorientation
include marijuana, opioids, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, ethylene
glycol (peracute phase), xylitol, alcohol, anti-depressant medications,
and macrocyclic lactones (ch. 133).13

Miscellaneous
Miscellaneous causes of weakness include severe obesity (ch. 150),
malnutrition, late-term pregnancy, pyometra, sarcopenia (ch. 151),
thiamine deficiency (ch. 14), medication side effects, sedation, and
post-anesthesia.

Persistent VS. Episodic weakness (Figure
23.1)
Discriminating pets with episodic weakness from those with
persistent weakness can aid in arriving at a diagnosis. In general,
pets with severe infection, inflammation, neoplasia, or chronic
disease have persistent weakness. In contrast, hypoglycemia,
hypocalcemia, bleeding tumors (e.g., hemangiosarcoma), and postprandial hepatic encephalopathy are examples of conditions that
cause episodic weakness.

Diagnostics
As emphasized above, a complete history and PE are of paramount
importance given the vague nature of “weakness” and they determine
the choice of diagnostics necessary to identify a final diagnosis. The
“minimum database” of diagnostics might include complete blood
count, serum chemistry panel, and urinalysis. Further specific testing
may then be indicated as well as thoracic and/or abdominal imaging,
and possibly vertebral or limb radiographs (Figure 23.1).

Chapter 24: Restlessness
Michael D Willard

Overview
While recognized as an important behavioral problem, restlessness
has not received much focused attention as an internal medicine
issue. Many veterinarians either do not recognize restlessness when
it occurs, ignore it because they are unsure what to do when it is
mentioned, or automatically assume restlessness is a behavior issue
(ch. 11). Restlessness may represent a sign of major, even lifethreatening, disease. Failure to consider medical causes of
restlessness may place a pet at unnecessary risk. Granted, it can
sometimes be difficult to diagnose the cause of restlessness. It may
be appropriate to tell an owner that there is no doubt that the
behavior they describe is real, but it can be difficult (and sometimes
costly) to ascertain the cause.

History
The history (ch. 2) is key in detecting and determining the
significance of restlessness. While some clients will use the term
“restless,” many use words like “agitated,” “anxious,” “nervous,”
“pacing,” “uncomfortable,” or that their pet has been constantly
“seeking attention.” Restlessness in animals who have been placed in
a new environment (e.g., a boarding facility) is not generally worth
pursuing because it is likely a result of being placed in an unfamiliar
environment. It is much more likely to have medical significance
when the owner reports atypical “restlessness” when in familiar
surroundings. One should be aware of breed behavioral
characteristics since some (especially working breeds like Border
Collies) may “seem” restless. It is helpful to know if the restlessness
is constant or episodic. For example, some dogs with congestive
heart failure are restless at night, a reflection of respiratory difficulty
associated with being recumbent. Dogs and cats with pleural effusion
or pulmonary edema may seem “restless” due to respiratory distress,
underscoring need for careful auscultation and thoracic imaging.
Dogs with pheochromocytoma have been described as having
paroxysmal episodes of restlessness. Females in heat, males that
sense a female in heat, and polyuric animals seeking to go outside
may all seem restless.
If a restless pet has other prominent concerns, those should be the
initial focus of a diagnostic evaluation, especially if any have more
clearly defined rule-outs (e.g., cranial nerve deficits, muscle
weakness, vomiting, diarrhea, weight loss, localized pain, etc.; ch. 6;
Figure 24.1). Here, placing a lower priority on the restlessness is
usually appropriate, efficient, and cost-effective. An example would
be restlessness in a cat that is possibly hyperthyroid, a condition
diagnosed from history (e.g., weight loss despite a ravenous
appetite), physical examination (e.g., palpable thyroid nodule), and a
serum thyroxine (T4) concentration.
If restlessness cannot be explained by an obvious “other problem,”
or if it is the only major complaint with no localizing findings on
history or physical examination (PE), then one should further
characterize the owners’ observations. Quantify the degree of
restlessness (i.e., mild, moderate, severe), how abruptly it began,

how persistent it is (e.g., <10% of the time [episodic?], about half the
time, >90% of the time) and whether it is static, getting better, or
becoming worse. Are the owners aware of any stimulus that
consistently results in the restlessness? Selected causes of
restlessness are listed in Box 24.1 and the general approach to this
concern is provided in Figure 24.1. Some causes (e.g., shock,
dyspnea) may be identified from the history and/or PE because
evidence of an underlying illness could be obvious and localizing;
these causes will not be discussed further.

Intoxications and Drugs
Description of the signs and their onset gains importance if no cause
is apparent from history and PE. If the restlessness is sudden,
intoxication or drug-induced effect are a major consideration.
Restlessness sometimes occurs before more serious signs of
intoxication are noticed (ch. 15). Restlessness can be seen after a pet
ingests and/or absorbs a recreational drug (e.g., amphetamines,1
cocaine2), metaldehyde,3 chocolate, tremorgens (i.e., mycotoxins
from Penicillium spp.),4 zinc phosphide, etc. Environment is
important. For example, metaldehyde is particularly common in
areas where snails are a “garden pest.” Access to chocolate or “any
drug” should be reviewed. Being envenomated by an arachnid or
insect (e.g., black widow spider bite,5 scorpion, wasp) may cause
pain mimicking restlessness (chs. 132 and 133). Diagnosis, in
some, may require appropriate toxicological analysis.
“Intoxication” includes adverse drug effects. Drug-induced
restlessness can be expected or surprising. A classic drug-induced
cause of restlessness in dogs is excess thyroid medication.6 Pets with
diabetes mellitus being given excess insulin may exhibit restlessness
as an early sign of

hypoglycemia (Video 61.1).7

Sympathomimetics (e.g., ephedrine, phenylpropanolamine,
albuterol), metoclopramide8 (especially if given as an intravenous
[IV] bolus), methylxanthines (e.g., theophylline [especially if given
with enrofloxacin, which increases blood levels of theophylline],

theobromine, aminophylline, caffeine), atropine, lidocaine (when
given IV), and prostaglandins are recognized by most veterinarians
as potential causes of restlessness. While the most common central
nervous system (CNS) adverse effect of many drugs is drowsiness or
sedation (e.g., antipsychotic drugs, analgesic drugs), some can have
paradoxical effects if they “disinhibit” behaviors. Antihistamines,
cyproheptadine, benzodiazepines, buspirone, mirtazapine,
haloperidol, phenothiazines (especially perphenazine), amantadine,
phenobarbital, levetiracetam, and selegiline can cause restlessness.
Glucocorticoids are recognized for altering behavior in people and
can occasionally cause restlessness in dogs. If a drug effect is
suspected, the drug should be withheld and the pet observed for
several days.

FIGURE 24.1 Suggested diagnostic approach to
the problem of restlessness in the dog and cat.
CBC,Complete blood count; CNS, central nervous
system; CT, computed tomography; MRI, magnetic
resonance imaging; TT4, total thyroxine.
The “serotonin syndrome” is a potentially fatal intoxication in
which restlessness is prominent. Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs)
and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) can cause
restlessness. If such drugs are combined with other medications that
increase serotonin (e.g., monoamine oxidase inhibitors [MAOIs],
such as amitraz), restlessness can result.9,10 S-adenosyl-Lmethionine, metoclopramide, dextromethorphan, and 5hydroxytryptophan (a nutritional supplement) should be used
cautiously or avoided in pets receiving a TCA or an SSRI. St. John’s
wort, used extensively in complementary medicine, should not be

used in conjunction with TCA or SSRI drugs. L-deprenyl, alone, is an
MAOI that can cause restlessness.

Pain or Discomfort
Once intoxications and drugs are tentatively eliminated as a cause of
restlessness, one should consider pain, discomfort, or
encephalopathies. Pain can cause restlessness as an acute or gradual
and subacute condition (ch. 6). Detecting pain varies from easy to
quite difficult, depending upon cause, how stoic the pet is, and how
adept the veterinarian is at PE (ch. 3).11 Diffuse abdominal pain or
generalized muscular discomfort can be especially difficult to
localize. Be sure that anti-inflammatory or analgesic drugs are not
being given, as either could make detection and localization of pain
difficult. Pets receiving such drugs should be re-examined after drug
effects are likely to have dissipated. One may need to repeat the
physical examination several times before recognizing pain. The
“feline hyperesthesia syndrome” has numerous causes and is a
diagnostic challenge.12 Leukocytosis may be indicative of
inflammation that can cause pain, supporting the need for a
complete blood count (CBC) in most pets with this concern.

Metabolic
The restlessness associated with encephalopathies may be acute in
onset or insidious-and-chronic. Metabolic encephalopathies (i.e.,
hepatic encephalopathy [chs. 266, 267, 269], hypoglycemia,
hypocalcemia) may initially produce restlessness as the only
discernible clinical sign. Review of a serum biochemistry panel
(preferably obtained while the pet is displaying restlessness) is
important. Hypoglycemia causing restlessness is common in pets
overdosed with insulin and in those with an insulin-secreting tumor,
hepatic failure, or hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 61). It may be valuable
to measure both ionized and total calcium concentrations (ch. 69).
Abdominal imaging (radiographs ± ultrasound) should be
considered regardless of serum biochemistry findings. The finding of

an adrenal mass in a pet described as having episodic restlessness
may be consistent with pheochromocytoma (ch. 298).
While hypoglycemia and hypocalcemia are relatively straightforward, hepatic encephalopathy can be difficult. Congenital
portosystemic shunts (PSS), the major cause of hepatic
encephalopathy in dogs and probably cats, can occasionally be a
major diagnostic challenge (chs. 267 and 268). Clues for an
underlying hepatic cause of signs include decreases in albumin,
glucose, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and/or cholesterol on serum
chemistry profiles. However, some dogs with congenital PSS may not
show signs of encephalopathy until 7-12 years of age. Those dogs
often have normal serum biochemistry profiles, urinalysis,
fasting/post-prandial serum bile acids and resting blood ammonia
concentrations. A surprising number of dogs with PSS have a
normal-sized liver on abdominal imaging and the shunting vessel or
vessels may not be identified even by highly experienced
ultrasonographers. Therefore, it is sometimes worth re-measuring
serum bile acid and blood ammonia concentrations in pets with
undiagnosed restlessness. The ammonia tolerance test is thought by
some to be more sensitive for congenital PSS than serum bile acids.
Protein C determinations may reveal unsuspected hepatic
insufficiency. If no explanation for restlessness is identified after
extensive testing, advanced imaging may be worth considering.

Primary Intracranial Conditions
Restlessness may be the only sign of primary CNS disease (chs. 14,
242-247). Cranial nerve deficits, postural deficits, and seizure
activity are absent in some animals afflicted with major CNS disease.
Restlessness in these pets may have an acute onset or develop and
progress insidiously. In epileptic animals, restlessness can be a preictal event or even the primary seizure event (ch. 247). Dogs with
pituitary dependent hyperadrenocorticism (PDH) and a pituitary
macro-tumor are often described as “restless” or “wandering
aimlessly.” Thus, if a dog with PDH develops signs of restlessness,
first ask about use of L-deprenyl (metabolized to amphetamine) and
then appreciate that dogs with a pituitary macro-tumor may have
changes appreciated by an owner but not obvious to the veterinarian
(ch. 293). Lesions in various areas of the brain can cause
restlessness (

Video 24.1). Advanced imaging scans (ch. 112) and

cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis (ch. 109) may aid in identifying
or confirming a diagnosis.

Need for a Behaviorist?
Intoxications, pain/discomfort and altered
mentation/encephalopathy are particularly important because they
may be caused by diseases that can progress rapidly and cause
serious injury or death. Only after these have been considered and
tentatively or definitively eliminated should restlessness be
attributed to behavior and a behaviorist consulted (ch. 11).

Definition and Identification of Pallor
Mucous Membrane Color
Pallor is defined as unusual or extreme paleness. In dogs and cats,
mucous membrane color is utilized to determine presence of pallor.
Pallor can be generalized (e.g., the entire body) or regional (involving
only certain areas). Evaluation of mucous membrane color and
moisture is part of any routine physical examination (PE [ch. 3]),
providing a glimpse into the hemostatic and cardiovascular state.
The gums, conjunctiva, lips, tongue, and inner pinnae are available
for assessment of color, depending on pigmentation. Vaginal,
preputial, and anal mucous membranes should also be assessed,
especially if mucous membranes of the head are pale. Occasionally,
the paws or paw pads can be assessed.
Assessment of pallor is subjective, as it is “measured” relative to
what would be considered “normal” pink mucous membranes.
Mucous membrane color is determined by perfusion and hematocrit.
More specifically, color is determined by the amount of oxygenated

hemoglobin present within the capillaries of the area being assessed.
The high concentration of capillaries within mucous membranes
allows for an easy and relatively reliable measure of hematocrit and
perfusion. With pallor comes suspicion of anemia or
vasoconstriction. Pallor is relative and must be judged individually.
Dark mucous membrane pigmentation in some dogs and cats can
obscure assessment. Accumulation of other pigments (e.g., bilirubin,
myoglobin) in blood can also obscure evaluation for pallor.

Generalized VS. Regional pallor
Generalized pallor, due to anemia or cardiovascular disease, is more
common than regional. Regional pallor is usually due to inadequate
perfusion of a specific area, such as an embolic episode at the
bifurcation of the aorta causing lack of perfusion and pallor to the
hind limbs (ch. 238) or right to left shunting of blood in the heart,
which can cause pallor in the rear portion of the body but healthy
color to the head. Generalized pallor is usually easily seen when a
dog or cat has a hematocrit <25%. Thus, mild anemia may not result
in obvious pallor. Also, the definition of a “normal” hematocrit varies
between dogs and cats. Healthy young animals have lower
hematocrits as compared with adults (ch. 57). It is important to avoid
overinterpretation of pallor in young animals or when comparing
dogs with cats.

FIGURE 25.1 An algorithm based on physical
examination findings and preliminary diagnostic
results. The chart shows a path to determining
causes of pallor and illustrates the possibility of more
than one cause/overlapping etiologies. CRT,
Capillary refill time; MM, mucous membranes; PCV,
packed cell volume; US, ultrasound.

Etiology and Duration of Anemia, and
Their Effect on Mucous Membrane Color
Acute and chronic anemias are common in dogs and cats and are
caused by a large number of conditions (chs. 57, 172, 174).
Chronicity and mechanisms causing anemia may affect ease of seeing
pallor on PE. Acute hemorrhage may or may not lead to pallor. Poor
cardiac output due to hypovolemia slows circulation and can cause
pallor. Other causes of decreased cardiac output and abnormal
mucous membrane color include severe tachycardia or bradycardia,
pathologic tachyarrhythmias (ch. 230), cardiac tamponade (ch.

235), severe myocardial failure (chs. 233, 234), various types of
shock (ch. 121), pulmonary arterial hypertension (ch. 218), and
severe systemic hypotension. Vasoconstriction, the immediate
response to a severe decrease in blood volume, initially maintains
perfusion with blood containing a near normal hematocrit. Soon,
hypovolemia is sensed by the kidneys, stimulating the reninangiotensin-aldosterone system to cause retention of fluid by the
kidneys. Retained fluid progressively dilutes the blood to restore
volume at the expense of hematocrit, allowing its recognition.
Following a precipitous drop in hematocrit/hemoglobin, pallor may
be noted at a higher hematocrit in some dogs and cats than is typical.

patient Assessment and Differential
Diagnoses (Figure 25.1)
History and Physical Examination (PE)
Given the potentially life-threatening nature of some causes for
worrisome pallor, a rapid yet thorough history (ch. 2) and PE (ch.
3) are crucial. Pre-existing conditions; recent illness, trauma,
surgery; recent and current medications and/or nutraceuticals might
begin to explain the current condition. Initial PE results may be
similar in dogs and cats that have severe anemia and those with
compromised cardiac output. In addition to pallor, pets with severe
anemia, shock, or heart failure often exhibit lethargy, poor pulse
quality, tachycardia, increased respiratory rate and/or effort, and/or
a heart murmur on auscultation.

Capillary Refill Time (CRT) and Pulse
Quality
PE parameters may aid in differentiating an anemic patient from one
with compromised cardiac output. CRT, normally 1-2 seconds in
duration, is assessed by observing the color of the gums in the
maxillary area above the area of a canine tooth and then pressing

gently but firmly on that area for a few seconds. After releasing
pressure, observe how long it takes for the initial color to return. If
the mucous membranes appear almost white (severe pallor), CRT
may not be able to be assessed because there is no color return.
Prolonged CRT suggests decreased capillary perfusion pressure,
most commonly due to decreased cardiac output or shock. Anemic
pets are much less likely to have an abnormal CRT, especially if the
anemia is chronic, but they may have pallor. By contrast, acute
severe hemorrhage can cause prolonged CRT due to hypovolemic
shock. While CRT can be helpful in determining the cause of pallor,
it is not foolproof and should be used in context of PE, history, and
laboratory results.
Palpating the “quality” and “strength” of arterial pulses can be
helpful in assessing a pet as well as in determining a cause of pallor
(ch. 39). Animals with significant anemia often exhibit an increased
gap between systolic and diastolic arterial pressures, but this is not
pathognomonic. Pulse quality that feels decreased or of “poor
quality” is consistent with decreased cardiac output due to primary
cardiac or pericardial disease resulting in cardiac tamponade,
preventing normal diastolic filling of the chambers. Less volume in
the chambers of the heart means there is decreased cardiac output
and poor perfusion. Quick assessment of pulse quality and strength
should be a component of every PE, performed while auscultating
the heart. This allows identification of pulse quality, deficits, and
arrhythmias. Further evaluation of the heart and pericardial space
may be warranted in pets with decreased pulse quality. Remember,
good pulse quality does not rule out decreased cardiac output.

Packed Cell Volume (PCV), Total Solids
(TS), and Serum Color
Treatment of severe anemia involves administration of blood
products (ch. 124) while dogs and cats with heart disease often
require specific medications or interventions (chs. 229, 230, 235,
238). The incorrect therapy could be detrimental or catastrophic,
emphasizing the importance of understanding the cause of a pet’s
illness before beginning treatment. Laboratory test results should be
interpreted in the context of the history and PE. PCV and TS are used

to determine the presence of anemia. These parameters are not
reliable in pets with severe acute hemorrhage because the
physiologic response, as previously discussed, includes
vasoconstriction and transient maintenance of PCV/TS
concentrations. With time, fluid retention to restore blood volume
reveals the anemia. When assessing PCV/TS, serum color should
also be noted. Icteric serum usually suggests hemolysis or hepatic
disease, but a bleeding disorder causing hemorrhage is possible
(chs. 28, 171).
If no evidence of acute hemorrhage is appreciated, the presence of
a normal PCV and TS usually rules out anemia as the cause of pallor.
Thorough cardiovascular evaluation may be warranted since
emergency therapy may be necessary. An electrocardiogram (ch.
96), arterial blood pressure (ch. 91), thoracic radiographs, and/or
evaluation of the pleural and pericardial spaces via ultrasound (ch.
73) should be considered. If no significant abnormalities are noted,
an echocardiogram (ch. 97) and additional advanced diagnostics
may be considered.
