Chapter 26: Hyperemia
Anthony C.G. Abrams-Ogg

A C RO N YM S
CRT capillary refill time
NO nitric oxide
Hyperemia is defined as increased blood within tissue vasculature. It
may be active or passive. Active hyperemia refers to increased
arteriolar (pre-capillary) blood flow to a tissue. It is a normal
physiologic response to increased metabolic activity, as in exercising
muscle, where hyperemia delivers more oxygen and nutrients.1
Active hyperemia is also a key pathophysiologic response in
inflammation.2 The main clinical sign of active hyperemia is
erythema, which results from increased perfusion of capillary beds
with oxygenated blood. Passive hyperemia refers to congestion,
resulting from decreased removal of post-capillary blood, which does
not cause erythema. This chapter addresses generalized active
hyperemia of peripheral mucous membranes (referred to here on in
as hyperemia), which are sentinel tissues for circulatory status
because of rich vascular supply and ease of examination (Figure
26.1). Hyperemia is usually initially recognized as gingival and
conjunctival erythema during examination. It is important to ensure
that these are not caused by gingivitis or conjunctivitis (local
hyperemia). If gingivitis is present, the buccal mucosa should be
examined. Hyperemia may also be recognized in the genitalia. In
some cases, cutaneous erythema may also be found, especially in
breeds with thin hair coats, melanin dilution, or large upright ears.
The term “injected mucous membranes” is variably used as a

synonym for hyperemia/erythema or to refer to conditions
characterized by brick-red mucous membranes, most often
associated with sepsis, overheating, or hypoadrenocorticism.
Although “hyperemic” and “erythematous” are not identical, these
terms are sometimes used interchangeably. Erythema not due to
hyperemia may be caused by erythrocytosis, hemoglobinemia, and
Oxyglobin™ treatment, which may be ruled-out by history and a
hemogram. Conversely, erythema is less obvious in an anemic
animal. Neonatal mucosa is also dark compared to color at around 6
weeks of age due to high fetal mean corpuscular volume (

Video

26.1).3 Experimentally, carbon monoxide and cyanide poisoning may
cause bright red mucous membranes. In the former this is due to
carboxyhemoglobin formation; in the latter it is because oxygen is
not extracted from hemoglobin; and in both cases there is likely a
hyperdynamic response.4 Carbon monoxide and cyanide poisoning
are most often encountered in dogs and cats with smoke inhalation,
where red mucous membranes are inconsistently reported and other
signs predominate.5-7 These poisons may also be used for malicious
poisoning and extended suicide.8

FIGURE 26.1 Algorithm for diagnosing the cause
of hyperemic mucous membranes in a dog. The
algorithm may also be used for cats but hyperemia is
less frequently recognized.
As with other tissues, blood flow through mucous membranes is
determined by cardiac output and arteriolar vascular tone.
Hyperemia cannot occur without vasodilation, and as such the
causes of hyperemia will be causes of vasodilation, although not all
causes of vasodilation will cause hyperemia. Vasomotor tone is under
complex local (intrinsic) and extrinsic control. Local control signals
include metabolic products, endothelin-1, nitric oxide (NO),
thromboxane A2, prostacyclin, histamine, and bradykinin.1,9 The
main extrinsic control mechanisms are neurohormonal reflexes of
the autonomic nervous system (secretion of acetylcholine,
epinephrine and norepinephrine), some of which are mediated by
intrinsic mechanisms.1,9 Noticeable waxing and waning change in

gingival color has been seen in healthy and clinically stable
Doberman Pinschers, Golden Retrievers, and other breeds during
the course of physical examination or short observation, attributed to
excitement-induced vasoconstriction.
Capillary refill time (CRT) is a measure of distal capillary
perfusion, and is typically determined while examining gingival
mucosa. The subjectivity, inconsistency and various causes of altered
CRT has brought its utility into question in human medicine.10 These
factors likely affect judgment of CRT in animals as well, but it
remains a standard component of physical examination. When
testing CRT, light pressure for 1-2 sec to blanch the tissue should be
used. Excessive or prolonged pressure, and repeated testing in one
area, may result in an exaggerated response from reactive
hyperemia, an increase to above normal blood flow following
transient vascular occlusion. The CRT is not a stand-alone test and
interpretation should be in the context of other clinical signs. For
hyperemic mucous membranes, the CRT will be normal (0.5-2 sec)
to fast (<0.5 sec) if there is normal-to-increased cardiac output.
Prolonged CRT (>2-3 sec) in hyperemic mucous membranes
indicates severe vasodilation and risk for associated hypotension.
Hyperemia is recognized less often in cats compared to dogs,
probably because of lower hematocrit, lower relative blood volume,
and lower prevalence of disorders that cause hyperemia, and
possibly because of high sympathetic tone in stressful conditions
promoting vasoconstriction, and lack of routine examination of
genitalia. Recognition of hyperemia in cats may also be complicated
by the common occurrence of gingivitis.
The most common cause of hyperemia in the dog is the normal
physiologic response to increased heat (

Video 26.2; ch. 130).

Increased heat may be internal or external. One function of the
circulatory system is the transport of normal products of metabolism
for elimination, and internal heat above what is needed to maintain
normal body temperature is one of these products.1 Vasodilation
results from several mechanisms.1,9,11 The increased blood flow to
the skin will increase convective cooling in the dog to some extent,
but panting is the main mechanism to increase evaporative cooling,
which is facilitated by oral mucosal hyperemia. Increased physical

activity will increase heat production from skeletal muscle. Causes
include situation-related normal or abnormal behavior, status
epilepticus, metaldehyde poisoning, and the work of breathing
associated with polyradiculoneuritis (Coonhound paralysis).12-14
Increased external heat comes from high ambient temperature or
external warming sources, and external heat stress will exacerbate
internal heat load (ch. 130). Increased ambient humidity will also
exacerbate heat stress as it reduces the effectiveness of evaporative
cooling. Cats that are overexcited and/or subjected to a high ambient
temperature may also pant and be hyperemic.
Overheating will be initially associated with normal CRT, but with
increasing heat stress will progress to rapid CRT, and then to heat
stroke and shock, with pallor and prolonged CRT.15
Fever (ch. 16) is an adaptive response and does not in-itself cause
hyperemia. However, fever is often due to sepsis, which may cause
hyperemia. Unlike hyperthermia, where vasodilation is appropriate,
inflammatory mediators in sepsis cause inappropriate vasodilation (
Video 26.3).16,17 The hyperdynamic phase of septic shock
(infrequently recognized in cats) is characterized by fever,
hyperemia, normal-to-increased CRT, and tachycardia. It may
progress to hypodynamic shock characterized initially by prolonged
CRT, followed by pallor and hypothermia.16,17
Certain drugs and toxins may cause hyperemia. These include
acepromazine, phenoxybenzamine, and prazosin (but not
tamsulosin), which block alpha-adrenergic receptors; animals with
hyperemia will typically be sedated. Ethanol may cause peripheral
vasodilation; the mechanism may be modulation of extrinsic
vasomotor control mechanisms.18 Animals with ethanol-induced
hyperemia will probably be ataxic. Ethanol ingestion may result from
malicious/accidental poisoning, bread dough ingestion, or treatment
of ethylene glycol poisoning (ch. 132).19 Hypercapnia caused by
rebreathing during anesthesia may directly cause peripheral
vasodilation. If blood pressure and oxygenation are adequate, the
mucous membranes may be hyperemic. The animal may also be
hyperventilating. It is emphasized that hypercapnia may occur
without these signs.20

Some dogs with atypical and classical hypoadrenocorticism (ch.
296) have presented with profound hyperemia with prolonged CRT,
and in some cases have initially been misdiagnosed as septic.21
Cortisol is necessary for a normal response to adrenaline and inhibits
NO synthesis; therefore, cortisol deficiency results in vasodilation.
Dogs with hypoadrenocorticism may also present with pallor from
volume contraction and peripheral vasoconstriction, and the variable
circulatory findings are one more reason this disorder is “the great
pretender.” Low sodium:potassium ratio and/or absence of a stress
leukogram will often be present, but protracted vomiting may lower
the serum potassium concentration, and unrelated inflammation
may mimic a stress leukogram. Hypoadrenocorticism may also
occasionally cause a fever.22 Measuring basal cortisol level or
performing an ACTH stimulation test should be considered in cases
with unexplained hyperemia, but in interpreting results in this
scenario the possibility of critical illness-related corticosteroid
insufficiency must also be considered.23
Histamine is a potent vasodilator, and dogs with mast cell tumors
(ch. 327) will occasionally present with periodic self-limiting
hyperemia not associated with increased activity or ambient
temperatures. Intermittent exposure to an allergen could also cause
this sign. If history does not reveal repetitive allergen exposure and
thorough examination of the skin does not reveal a mass, then
imaging and/or aspiration of the spleen, liver and bone marrow
should be considered.
Blushing is an emotionally-triggered hyperemia in humans. It is
not recognizable in most dogs and cats probably because of fur,
melanin and fewer social triggers. However, Pharaoh Hounds, which
have thin facial fur and melanin dilution, have a recognized blushing
response with intra-breed variability. Variable blushing responses
have also been seen anecdotally in Ibizan Hounds and Sphynx cats.
Blushing is attributed by owners to perceived happiness.
Altered NO mechanisms are involved in menopausal vasomotor
symptoms in humans. An animal model of vasodilation in the tail of
forced exercise ovarioectomized rats exists, but postovariohysterectomy vasomotor signs have not been recognized in
dogs and cats.24

Hyperemia
A. Your dog’s gums are hyperemic. This means that they are more
pink or red than usual. The most common causes of this are:
1. Gingivitis (inflammation of the gums). The most common
cause of gingivitis is dental disease. If there does not appear
to be another cause of red gums or gingivitis, then dental
cleaning will be recommended.
2. Being overheated. More blood flows through the mouth to
help with cooling. It is normal for your dog’s gums to
become pinker after exercise or when it is warm outside
(the same as a person becoming flushed). It is not a concern
on its own, but if your dog is weak or seems to be having
trouble breathing, you should get him or her to a cool place
as quickly as possible and contact a veterinarian.
3. Increased number of red blood cells. This can be diagnosed
with a simple blood test. If red blood cells are increased you
will be given additional information.
B. If your dog is very sick and has dark red gums (“injected
mucous membranes”), then a veterinarian will be concerned
about infection, heat stroke, and less often Addison’s disease.
These are all emergencies. You will be asked questions about
possible causes of infections and overheating, temperature will
be taken to see if there is a fever, and blood pressure will be
measured to see if it is low. Addison’s disease is a disorder
where the body does not produce enough of the hormone
cortisol (one of the stress hormones). Usually dogs with
Addison’s disease have had some mild abnormalities for a
while before becoming very sick. Blood tests that will help to
diagnose infection and Addison’s disease include a complete
blood count (to examine red and white blood cells), and an

ACTH stimulation test, which is used to measure the body’s
production of cortisol. Bacterial cultures may be taken of urine,
wounds, the lungs, blood or other organs to try to identify an
infection and the best antibiotic with which to treat it.
C. There are some drugs and poisons that can make gums turn
red. Normally you or your veterinarian knows that your dog
has been given a drug or has eaten something unusual, but
occasionally these are given by mistake or to poison a dog.
Poisoned dogs will be tired or uncoordinated.
D. If your dog has recurrent flushing (which you may also notice
with the eyes becoming red), it is possible that he or she is
getting an allergic reaction to something being eaten or to
something in the environment, including wasp or bee stings.
This happens because histamine is secreted by cells during an
allergic reaction (and is why antihistamines are prescribed for
allergies). It is also possible that your dog has a mast cell
tumor. This tumor makes histamine, and when the tumor
releases histamine it mimics an allergic reaction. Your
veterinarian will examine your dog’s skin closely for a lump,
and if one is found, then a biopsy will be recommended. If no
lump is found, and if you and your veterinarian think an
allergic reaction is unlikely, then your veterinarian may
recommend some X-rays, ultrasound exams or some blood and
bone marrow tests to help rule-out this tumor. Pharaoh
Hounds may flush without increased exercise or illness.
Spayed female dogs do not get hot flashes.
Anthony C.G. Abrams-Ogg (Guelph, Ontario, Canada)

Chapter 27: Cyanosis
Jared A. Jaffey

Introduction
Cyanosis is derived from the Greek word kuaneos, meaning dark
blue, and refers to the blue discoloration of skin or mucosa caused by
high concentrations of deoxygenated hemoglobin (Hb) circulating in
superficial capillaries. Cyanosis is readily identified in regions with
rich superficial vasculature and thin overlying tissue such as the
nasal planum, pinna, oral cavity, penis, vulva, nail beds, and

footpads. Cyanosis is classified as being either central or peripheral,
with the former being more common. Central cyanosis is most
commonly caused by a reduced arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2)
secondary to cardiopulmonary diseases, or by hemoglobinopathies
that do not adequately transport oxygen (O2).1 Conversely,
peripheral cyanosis is characterized by a normal SaO2 and results
from vasoconstriction and diminished peripheral blood flow.1

Physiology and Pathophysiology
Oxygen is transported in the blood in two forms: dissolved in plasma
and bound to Hb. Normal arterial oxygen tension (PaO2) in an
individual breathing room air (fraction of inspired oxygen [FiO2],
21%) at sea level (atmospheric pressure 760 mm Hg) is 80-100 mm
Hg.2 The amount of dissolved O2 comprises just 1-2% of the total O2
concentration of blood, but it is this fraction that is measured
clinically on blood gas analysis with PaO2.2 In contrast, the majority
of O2 in blood is combined with Hb and the amount bound is directly
related to the PaO2, a relationship illustrated in the O2 dissociation
curve (Figure 27.1).2 Hypoxemia is generally defined as an SaO2 of
<95% or PaO2 of <80 mm Hg.3 Severe, potentially life-threatening
hypoxemia is defined as an SaO2 of <90% or a PaO2 of <60 mm Hg;
however, animals with chronic respiratory disease develop
compensatory mechanisms which can lessen the severity of
respiratory signs at a given PaO2.3 Oxygen delivery to tissues is
dependent upon mean arterial pressure, which is a product of
cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance.
Cyanosis is detectable only when the concentration of
deoxygenated Hb in capillary blood exceeds 5 g/dL, which equates to
3 g/dL of deoxyhemoglobin of arterial blood.4 Dogs and cats with

normal Hb concentrations (dog: 14-20 g/dL, cat: 11-16 g/dL)5 will
have cyanosis observed at SaO2 levels below 79-85% (PaO2 <44-50
mm Hg) and 73-81% (PaO2 <39-45 mm Hg), respectively. However,
the amount of deoxygenated Hb required to produce the same
amount of cyanosis varies considerably depending on the total Hb
concentration. Because of this, cyanosis may not be detected in
anemic animals with severe hypoxemia but is more readily apparent
in those with erythrocytosis or polycythemia at a higher SaO2. For
example, an anemic animal with a Hb concentration of 6 g/dL
(hematocrit: 18%) will not exhibit cyanosis until a critically low SaO2
of 50% (PaO2 <27 mm Hg) is reached; conversely, an animal with
polycythemia or erythrocytosis and a Hb concentration of 24 g/dL
(hematocrit: 72%) will have cyanosis identified at an SaO2 of 87%
(PaO2 <53 mm Hg). As a result, cyanosis is an insensitive marker of
total blood O2 concentration. The calculation used for estimating the
SaO2 required to observe cyanosis at a given Hb concentration is
provided by: SaO2 = 100 − ([3/Hb concentration g/dL] × 100).
The detection of cyanosis can also be affected by dark pigmented
skin or mucosa, daylight or artificial light sources simulating the
spectral composition of daylight, and physiologic factors that alter
the affinity of Hb for O2 (i.e., shifts the O2 dissociation curve).6,7
Factors that shift the curve to the left (i.e., increased O2 affinity)
reduce the concentration of deoxygenated Hb at a given PaO2,
therefore lowering the PaO2 at which cyanosis is first detected.
Conversely, factors that shift the curve to the right will have the
opposite effect.

Classification and Causes
Central cyanosis is present on cutaneous and mucosal surfaces
throughout the body, and is most commonly caused by respiratory or
cardiovascular diseases resulting in hypoxemia and occasionally by

the presence of abnormal Hb. There is a vast heterogeneity in the
distribution of cardiopulmonary disorders with the potential to
result in hypoxemia. Cardiopulmonary disorders that decrease SaO2
do so by five broad mechanisms: (1) reduced inspired oxygen tension
(PiO2), (2) hypoventilation, (3) ventilation-perfusion (V/Q)
mismatch, (4) diffusion impairment, and (5) right-to-left shunting
(ch. 123).2

Reduced PIO2
A reduction in PiO2 will decrease the alveolar oxygen tension (PAO2)
and result in hypoxemia by decreasing the alveolus-to-capillary O2
gradient. A reduced PiO2 is most commonly associated with high
altitude but is rarely the primary cause for hypoxemia because of
physiologic compensatory mechanisms.

Hypoventilation
Reduced global ventilation results in an increase in both arterial
(PaCO2) and alveolar (PACO2) carbon dioxide tension, which leads to
a proportional reduction in PAO2 and subsequent hypoxemia.
Characteristic features of hypoventilation include a normal alveolararterial oxygen gradient (i.e., <10-15 mm Hg), hypercapnia, and a
good response to oxygen supplementation.2 Mechanistic causes for
hypoventilation include impaired central drive, cervical spinal cord
injury, neuromuscular junction diseases (ch. 253), myopathies,
severe abdominal distension (ch. 21), and defects in the chest wall
(chs. 123 and 222).

FIGURE 27.1 Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation
curve. Hemoglobin-bound O2 (O2 saturation)
increases progressively as PaO2 increases. Modified
from Hall JE. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical
Physiology. 13th ed. Elsevier; 2016:530.

V/Q Mismatch
Ventilation-perfusion mismatch refers to an imbalance of ventilation
and blood flow in the lung that compromises gas exchange and
consequently results in hypoxemia. It is the most common cause for
hypoxemia and there are many potential underlying causes such as
diseases of the pulmonary parenchyma (e.g., pneumonia,
noncardiogenic edema, neoplasia, interstitial lung disease,
hemorrhage; ch. 217), airways (e.g., laryngeal paralysis [ch. 214],
tracheal collapse [ch. 215], brachycephalic obstructive airway
syndrome [chs. 213 and 221], bronchomalacia [chs. 215 and 216],
asthma [cats]), pleural space (e.g., effusion, mass/soft tissue,

pneumothorax, diaphragmatic hernia; chs. 222, 235), and
cardiovascular system (e.g., pulmonary hypertension [ch. 218],
pulmonary embolism [ch. 219], and systemic hypotension [ch.
121]).

Diffusion Impairment
Diffusion impairment results when alveolocapillary O2 transport is
impaired as a consequence of alveolar inflammation, interstitial lung
disease, or edema. It is rarely a primary cause of hypoxemia while at
rest because red blood cell (RBC) transit through the pulmonary
capillary is slow enough to allow complete Hb saturation.2,8
However, many of the diseases that cause diffusion impairment also
result in V/Q mismatch which, when combined, have the potential to
amplify the magnitude of Hb desaturation.8

Right-To-Left Shunting
Intrapulmonary shunting refers to an extreme V/Q mismatch in
which there is perfusion to unventilated alveoli resulting in a V/Q
ratio of 0.8 The net effect is that a high proportion of blood passes
through the lungs without being oxygenated and is distributed to
systemic circulation. Examples of disorders where intrapulmonary
shunting can occur include severe diffuse pneumonia, left-sided
congestive heart failure, pleural space disease, acute respiratory
distress syndrome, complete intraluminal/extraluminal obstruction
of the trachea or mainstem/lobar bronchi, and pulmonary
arteriovenous malformation.8 Extrapulmonary right-to-left shunting
refers to cyanotic congenital heart diseases with defects that result in
deoxygenated blood that flows into the systemic circulation, leading
to hypoxemia. This can occur secondary to defects like tetralogy of
Fallot, an atrial or ventricular septal defect with concurrent
pulmonary hypertension, or transposition of the great vessels (rare)
(ch. 231). Eisenmenger syndrome refers to large intra- or
extracardiac defects that begin as systemic-to-pulmonary (left-toright) shunts and, due to development of severe elevations of

pulmonary vascular resistance with time, progress to reversal
(pulmonary-to-systemic, right-to-left, “reverse”) or bidirectional
shunting causing cyanosis and secondary erythrocytosis.9
Differential cyanosis can occur in animals with a reverse patent
ductus arteriosus and is characterized by cyanosis of the caudal
portion of the body, while the cranial section remains pink (ch. 231).
The phenomenon is often transient and made more apparent with
light exercise in some animals.

Erythrocytosis
This refers to an increase in RBC count because of either increased
RBC mass or reduced plasma volume (ch. 173). Cardiopulmonary
diseases and hemoglobinopathies can result in a secondary
erythrocytosis as a physiologic response to tissue hypoxia, which
functions to increase O2 concentration of blood but also drastically
increases blood viscosity. The increase in blood viscosity can impair
tissue perfusion, which can contribute to the visualization of cyanosis
by two mechanisms: (1) increased proportion of deoxygenated Hb in
capillaries, and (2) development of pulmonary hypertension.10

Hemoglobinopathy
This refers to abnormalities in Hb that interfere with normal binding
of O2 molecules, which decreases O2 transport to tissues (i.e.,
hypoxia). Most hemoglobinopathies decrease the total O2 blood
concentration but do not result in hypoxemia because the dissolved
O2 content in plasma remains unaffected (and hypoxemia is a low
concentration of dissolved O2, i.e., low measured PaO2). Therefore, a
hemoglobinopathy should be considered in animals with cyanosis
and a normal PaO2.11 Methemoglobinemia refers to an accumulation
of methemoglobin (MetHb) that exceeds 2-3% of total Hb
concentration and it is the most common hemoglobinopathy.12
Acquired methemoglobinemia is most common and occurs after

exposure to exogenous oxidative toxins (e.g., acetaminophen, skunk
musk, hydroxyurea, benzocaine, and nitrites/nitrates).13 Affected
animals have an acute onset of cyanosis, usually a concurrent Heinzbody hemolytic anemia, and demonstrate obvious signs associated
with tissue hypoxia (ch. 138).13 Hereditary methemoglobinemia is
rare and is most commonly the result of cytochrome b5 reductase
deficiency, the primary pathway by which MetHb is reduced back to
Hb.12,14 In contrast to acquired methemoglobinemia, animals with
the hereditary form exhibit persistent cyanosis, typically have a
secondary erythrocytosis, and clinical signs are generally mild and
well-tolerated in the absence of comorbid diseases or oxidant
exposure (Figure 27.2).12
Peripheral cyanosis occurs due to inadequate oxygenation of
peripheral capillary blood that results from vasoconstriction,
diminished perfusion, or as an extension of central cyanosis.15
Peripheral cyanosis can occur secondary to diseases that impede
arterial (e.g., arterial tumor embolism or thromboembolism [ch.
238]) or venous (e.g., thrombosis, iatrogenic external occlusion)
blood flow as well as erythrocytosis, hypothermia, or hypotension.
Systemic SaO2 is typically normal and cyanosis is limited to distal
extremities unless there is concurrent central cyanosis.

FIGURE 27.2 Cyanosis of the nasal planum,
muzzle, and tongue in a dog with hereditary
methemoglobinemia at (A) baseline, and (B)
resolution of cyanosis in the same dog after
normalization of methemoglobin levels with oral
methylene blue therapy.

Clinical Evaluation
The evaluation begins with a detailed review of the clinical history
(chs. 1 and 2) and physical examination (ch. 3), which usually guide
the clinician to the etiology of cyanosis. Clinicopathologic test results
and imaging findings such as complete blood count, arterial blood
gas, pulse oximetry, thoracic radiographs, and echocardiography
facilitate confirmation of clinical suspicions. Details in the history
(e.g., pre-existing conditions, vomiting/regurgitation, trauma, toxin
exposure) can provide insight as to the cause of cyanosis and allow
for prompt intervention. Physical examination should assess the
extent of cyanosis (i.e., distal extremity/extremities only, diffuse,
differential), thoracic wall for defects (ch. 222), respiratory pattern
(ch. 37), cardiothoracic auscultatory abnormalities (chs. 38, 212,
217), palpation of pulses (ch. 39), neurologic abnormalities (ch.
241), abdominal palpation, and for evidence of trauma (ch. 119).

The primary initial focus should be on the assessment of respiratory
distress (chs. 37, 123) for two reasons: (1) delay in diagnosis and
treatment can have life-threatening implications, and (2) its absence
generally indicates cyanotic congenital heart disease,
hemoglobinopathy, erythrocytosis, or peripheral cyanosis as the
underlying cause. Respiratory patterns and audible breathing sounds
can be used to localize the anatomic region of disease in animals with
respiratory distress, which can help differentiate respiratory from
cardiogenic etiologies.3 Cardiogenic pulmonary edema should be
suspected in animals with respiratory distress and either crackles or
wheezes and a concurrent murmur.16 However, the absence of a
murmur does not rule out cardiac disease (ch. 229). In cats, the
presence of a gallop sound, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypothermia
is suggestive of an underlying cardiogenic etiology for respiratory
distress (ch. 234).17 Arrhythmias should also be noted as they could
suggest cardiac disease in the absence of a murmur (ch. 230).

Arterial Blood Gas Analysis
The determination of the PaO2 remains the gold standard criterion
for the diagnosis of hypoxemia; however, it is not commonly
performed because it is not widely available, it requires special
training, and some animals require sedation to acquire the sample
(ch. 74).

Pulse Oximetry
Pulse oximetry provides a noninvasive and continuous estimation of
SaO2 and thus PaO2 by way of the O2 dissociation curve. Similar to
SaO2, normal O2 saturation measured by pulse oximetry (SpO2) is
defined as >95%. Importantly, pulse oximetry is an estimation and
does not uniformly correlate with true SaO2 and with it, PaO2.18-20
Pulse oximetry measurements correlate well with SaO2 at higher
ranges (i.e., >90%) but tend to overestimate the SaO2 and the

magnitude of error worsens at low SpO2 ranges (i.e., <70-80%).18-21
Other factors that can affect the accuracy of pulse oximetry include
pigmentation, perfusion, severe anemia, and the presence of
dyshemoglobins.18,19 Methemoglobinemia will yield SpO2
measurements between 75% and 85% in the absence of comorbid
conditions.11,14,22

Pulse Co-Oximetry
Pulse CO-oximetry utilizes similar spectrophotometric technology as
standard pulse oximetry; however, a CO-oximeter measures light
absorbance at multiple wavelengths as opposed to the two measured
by standard pulse oximetry. The broadened wavelength detection
neutralizes the effect of dyshemoglobins on SpO2.23 Pulse COoximetry also has the added benefit of noninvasively and
continuously estimating total blood Hb concentration.23

Spot Test
This is performed by placing 1-3 drops of the cyanotic animal’s blood
on white filter paper and comparing it to a similarly prepared sample
from a normal species control. Blood containing high concentrations
of MetHb will appear chocolate brown compared to the bright red
control.22 Blood from animals with hypoxemia will initially appear
dark red/violet but will turn bright red when exposed to atmospheric
O2. Arterial blood samples provide the best results, but venous blood
can also be used.

Glucose Concentrations
Delta-Glu (i.e., difference in blood glucose concentrations between
systemic and peripheral affected limbs) at cutoffs of 30 mg/dL (1.67

mmol/L) and 16 mg/dL (0.9 mmol/L) in cats and dogs, respectively,
are useful in diagnosing arterial thromboembolism.24

Point-of-Care N-Terminal B-Type
Natriuretic Peptide (BNP)
This can be used for differentiating cardiac from noncardiac causes
for respiratory distress in cats.25

Thoracic Radiography
Radiographic examination of the lung fields may reveal evidence of
parenchymal disease, obstructive airway disease, arterial vascular
pattern, pleural space disease, or abnormalities that support the
presence of cardiac disease.

Thoracic Computed Tomography
This facilitates a diagnosis of pulmonary thromboembolism and can
provide useful information regarding respiratory causes for
hypoxemia (ch. 212).26,27

Echocardiography
This represents the gold standard criterion to exclude or confirm
structural cardiac disease (ch. 97). Contrast echocardiography or a
“bubble study” can be used to diagnose right-to-left shunts (ch.
231).28

Management
Central cyanosis with concurrent respiratory distress requires urgent
therapeutic intervention (ch. 123). Oxygen supplementation should
be administered immediately to all cases; however, this will not be

helpful in cases with right-to-left shunting. Heart failure should be
recognized early and therapy tailored to the type of underlying
disease (ch. 229). Thoracentesis to remove fluid or air should be
performed in cases with pleural space disease (ch. 92). Pulmonary
parenchymal and airway diseases require disease-specific therapies;
however, establishment of airway patency and assisted ventilation
may be needed in cases with inadequate response to O2 or with
fatigue (ch. 123). Most animals with cyanotic congenital heart
disease are comfortable at rest and do not require emergency
intervention. Therapy for acquired methemoglobinemia necessitates
removal of the toxin in addition to either methylene blue, Nacetylcysteine, or blood transfusion.11,29-32 Oxygen therapy will be of
little use because MetHb cannot bind O2. Uncomplicated hereditary
methemoglobinemia does not require emergency therapy.12
Peripheral cyanosis is often suggestive of serious pathologic
conditions; however, it is rarely life-threatening and therapy is
directed toward resolution of the underlying disease process.

Hyperbilirubinemia vs. Jaundice
(Icterus)
“Jaundice” is defined as yellow discoloration of the sclera, skin, and
mucous membranes due to deposition of the pigment bilirubin.
“Hyperbilirubinemia” is the term applied whenever the serum
bilirubin exceeds reference limits, but mild increases do not usually
cause the yellow membrane hue. Jaundice usually becomes apparent

when the serum bilirubin is >2.5 mg/dL (>43 micromol/L).1
Jaundice in a pet with only mild bilirubin increases usually suggests
that higher concentrations had been present earlier. It takes days for
jaundice to clear because it acts as a stain. “Jaundice” is not a disease
or a diagnosis; rather, it is a clinical manifestation of various primary
diseases. Understanding bilirubin metabolism and excretion is
essential for a logical clinical assessment and diagnostic approach.

Pathophysiology
Bilirubin is the terminal product of heme metabolism.2 Most heme is
liberated from hemoglobin when senescent or damaged erythrocytes
are removed from blood via the mononuclear phagocytic system of
the spleen, liver, and bone marrow.3 Within the mononuclear cell,
the red oxygen-carrying pigment, heme, is cleaved by hemeoxygenase, forming the green pigment biliverdin.2,4 Biliverdin is
reduced by biliverdin-reductase to bilirubin, excreted into the blood
in its unconjugated lipophilic form, and transported to the liver
bound to albumin.4,5 Some aging red blood cells are destroyed
intravascularly (IV) with hemoglobin released directly into the blood.
Free hemoglobin, bound to haptoglobin, is delivered as a complex to
the hepatic reticuloendothelial system for degradation to
unconjugated bilirubin.6
Bilirubin passes through the sinusoidal surface membranes into
hepatocytes by passive diffusion in combination with active transport
mediated by several sinusoidal transporters.5 Once within
hepatocytes, bilirubin is bound to ligandin and transported to the
endoplasmic reticulum where it is “conjugated” into a water soluble
form via glucuronidation.5 Most of this water soluble conjugated
bilirubin is excreted into bile canaliculi by an adenosine triphosphate
(ATP)-dependent active transporter. A small amount is secreted into
sinusoidal capillaries and recycled eventually back to hepatocytes for
final excretion into the bile.5 Conjugated bilirubin is incorporated
into bile, stored in the gallbladder, and excreted into the duodenum
via the common bile duct. Within the intestinal tract, bilirubin is

converted by bacterial flora into urobilinogen (colorless), urobilin
(orange-red), stercobilinogen, and, finally, stercobilin, the pigment
that imparts the brown color to feces. In complete biliary
obstruction, feces lack these pigments and are grey- or clay-colored,
termed “acholic.” The liver and biliary system process and excrete all
bilirubin produced via heme metabolism. If the system becomes
overwhelmed or deranged, jaundice may result.

Causes of Jaundice
Jaundice results from one of 3 conditions: moderate to severe
hemolysis (pre-hepatic), inability of hepatocytes to process and
transport bilirubin (hepatic), and obstruction of the biliary tract
(post-hepatic) (Box 28.1).

Pre-Hepatic Jaundice
Pre-hepatic jaundice is usually the result of excessive extravascular
hemolysis (intravascular hemolysis produces only small amounts of
bilirubin). Excessive production of bilirubin overwhelms hepatic
absorption, processing, and excretion. Bilirubin then accumulates in
the blood, where it is transported throughout the body, adding its
color to all tissues. The most common cause of pre-hepatic jaundice
in dogs is immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA, ch. 174).7
Infectious disease and immune-mediated destruction of erythrocytes
are common causes of hemolysis in cats.7 Feline red blood cells are
particularly sensitive to oxidative damage, which leads to hemolysis,
as in hepatic lipidosis.8 In both dogs and cats, intoxications (zinc,
onions, acetaminophen; ch. 138), genetic disorders (pyruvate kinase
deficiency, osmotic fragility syndrome, etc.), and hypophosphatemia
are less common causes of hemolytic anemia.7,9-12

Hepatic Jaundice

Hepatic hyperbilirubinemia is associated with hepatocellular
dysfunction and may be due to idiosyncratic drug reaction
(carprofen, methimazole, phenobarbital), environmental toxins
(Amanita spp., blue green algae, aflatoxin, xylitol; ch. 138),
immune-mediated or inflammatory conditions (ch. 174), infectious
diseases (bacterial, fungal, protozoal, viral), neoplasia, or genetic
abnormalities in copper metabolism (copper-associated hepatitis;
ch. 269).13-19 Hepatic lipidosis is a common cause of jaundice and
hepatic dysfunction in cats (ch. 274).8 Lipidosis follows rapid
mobilization of peripheral fat to the liver, overwhelming hepatocyte
capabilities and cell function is compromised.8 Mild
hyperbilirubinemia has been reported in cats with significant
systemic inflammatory disease, especially sepsis.20 However, clinical
jaundice is rarely noted as the serum bilirubin concentration is
typically <2 mg/dL (<34 micromol/L).2

Post-Hepatic Jaundice
Post-hepatic jaundice can follow intraluminal obstruction of the
biliary system or abnormal compression of the biliary tree (chs. 272
and 273). Obstructions may be partial or complete. Intraluminal
causes of extrahepatic biliary duct obstruction (EHBDO) include

biliary mucocele, cholelithiasis, strictures, parasites (flukes),
infection, or neoplasia.21 Infectious cholangitis causing partial or
complete obstruction is more common in cats than in dogs. Biliary
mucoceles are rare in cats.21 Extraluminal causes of EHBDO include
pancreatitis, neoplasia, enlarged lymph nodes, or a duodenal foreign
body at the level of the papilla.21 Regardless of cause, complete
obstruction of the biliary system is an emergency requiring
reestablishment of bile drainage.21-24

Clinical Approach to A Dog or Cat with
Jaundice (Figure 28.1)
Signalment, History, Physical Examination
Certain breeds are predisposed to genetic disorders such as pyruvate
kinase deficiency or copper storage disease.10,11,16-19 Age is
important, e.g., an adult dog is far less likely to have canine
adenoviral hepatitis than is an unvaccinated puppy. A complete
history (ch. 2) should include travel (ch. 9), ectoparasite exposure,
current medications, possible environmental toxins, and vaccination
history. A variety of drugs may cause hemolytic anemia (ch. 138) or
liver toxicosis (ch. 134).13 Descriptions of appetite, water intake,
urination, defecation, and stool appearance may help elucidate the
underlying problem. Establishing duration and progression of
clinical signs may prove to be important, e.g., a dog with acute
vomiting and sudden onset of jaundice is more likely to have a biliary
obstruction or IMHA than copper-associated hepatitis.
Results of a complete physical examination (ch. 3) may further
narrow the focus of any investigation. Careful attention to mucous
membrane color (ch. 25), heart rate, and pulse quality are useful in
diagnosing anemia. Abdominal palpation may reveal hepatomegaly,
cranial abdominal pain, masses, or effusion. Fever (ch. 16) is
consistent with an infectious or inflammatory process, e.g., IMHA,
pancreatitis, bacterial cholangitis, or a ruptured gallbladder.
Bleeding abnormalities can be associated with IMHA, hepatic failure,
and severe cholestasis. Close inspection of the skin and mucous

membranes may reveal petechiae or ecchymoses (ch. 29). Rectal
palpation may reveal melena or evidence of gastrointestinal (GI)
bleeding secondary to drug exposure (e.g., carprofen) and/or liver
failure. A neurologic exam may be indicated (ch. 241), as hepatic
encephalopathy may occur with hepatic lipidosis, acute failure or
cirrhosis.
Information gathered from signalment, history, and physical
examination should aid in developing a prioritized list of differential
diagnoses. For example, pale mucous membranes, tachycardia,
weakness, tachypnea, and bounding pulses should lead the clinician
to assess the hematocrit. Evidence of cranial abdominal pain,
vomiting, fever, and dehydration are typical of biliary obstruction or
pancreatitis and warrant thorough diagnostic evaluation.

Diagnostic Plan
CBC, Chemistry Profile
The classic “minimum database” should be collected in any
jaundiced pet. The complete blood count (CBC) can identify and
characterize any anemia. Hemolysis typically causes a macrocytic,
hypochromic, regenerative anemia, while a microcytic,
normochromic non-regenerative anemia may result from chronic
liver disease (ch. 57).7-12,16 Cats with hepatic lipidosis can have a
regenerative Heinz body anemia (ch. 274).8 Spherocytosis and
autoagglutination confirm immune-mediated destruction of
erythrocytes (leukocytosis secondary to inflammation is common),
and an inflammatory leukogram is often present (ch. 174).7
Thrombocytopenia (ch. 59) may be noted with IMHA or
disseminated intravascular coagulopathy secondary to liver failure or
severe inflammation, e.g., pancreatitis or bile peritonitis.

FIGURE 28.1 Algorithm for the diagnostic
approach to a patient with jaundice. HCT,
Hematocrit; IMHA, immune-mediated hemolytic
anemia; Retic, reticulocyte count; tBili, total serum
bilirubin concentration; u/s, ultrasound.
The chemistry panel should include liver enzymes (alkaline
phosphatase [ALP], alanine aminotransferase [ALT], aspartate
aminotransferase [AST], gamma-glutamyl transferase [GGT]), and
liver function tests (cholesterol, blood-urea-nitrogen [BUN],
albumin, glucose, and bilirubin) (ch. 65). Post-hepatic jaundice is
often associated with moderate to marked hyperbilirubinemia,
marked increase in cholestatic enzyme activities (ALP, GGT),
moderate to marked hypercholesterolemia, and mild to moderate
increases in “hepatocellular leakage enzyme activities” (ALT, AST).21
Other than bilirubin, liver function test results are unremarkable

unless other co-morbidities exist.21 Pets with hepatic jaundice have
moderate to marked increases in ALT and AST activities, variable
cholestatic enzyme activities, and abnormal liver function test
results.8,13-16 IMHA may also increase hepatic enzyme activity.7
Markedly elevated ALP values and mildly to markedly elevated ALT
values coupled with a normal GGT in an obese, jaundiced cat are
typical for hepatic lipidosis.8 Bilirubinuria, proteinuria, glycosuria,
or renal tubular casts may suggest multi-organ dysfunction requiring
further investigation.

Imaging
Abdominal radiographs may reveal a metallic gastric foreign body
(coin; ch. 138), mass lesions, small liver, or choleliths.7,16,21
Ultrasound (US) provides a non-invasive chance to evaluate the
gallbladder (content, wall thickness), liver morphology, biliary tree,
pancreas, surrounding mesentery, and local lymph nodes. 7,16,21
Splenomegaly (ch. 182) is common in hemolytic anemias.7
Unexpected findings (e.g., a mass) may re-direct the diagnostic plan.
A persistently dilated common bile duct, worsening
hyperbilirubinemia, biliary mucocele, gallbladder rupture, or
cholelithiasis with evidence of obstruction, are each supportive of
immediate exploratory laparotomy.21 Percutaneous US-guided
biliary drainage in pets with EHBDO secondary to pancreatitis has
been beneficial.22,23 Endoscopic biliary stenting may provide a
minimally invasive treatment option for certain causes of EHBDO.24
With no evidence of complete biliary obstruction, pets with
suspected cholangitis or pancreatitis are treated medically, but if
cholangitis is suspected, US-guided cholecystocentesis for bile
culture can guide choice of antimicrobial (ch. 272).23,24 If primary
hepatic dysfunction is suspected to be the cause of jaundice, USguided fine-needle aspirate (FNA) of the liver for cytology should be
considered (ch. 85). Cytology is most useful in diagnosing neoplasia
and hepatic lipidosis.25-27 Liver biopsy may be warranted if imaging
and cytology results are inconclusive.14,28-30

Jaundice in any patient indicates a significant underlying
pathologic process. The veterinary clinician is encouraged to
consider all aspects of the condition before recommending any tests.
Often, with a logical approach and basic understanding of the
underlying processes, it is possible to identify the cause and
therefore make appropriate recommendations regarding treatment
and prognosis.

Client Information
Jaundice: Why It Happens and What to Expect
at Your Vet
What is Jaundice?
“Jaundice” is a term used to describe a yellow discoloration of the
skin, eyes, and gums. The terms jaundice and icterus are used
interchangeably. This may be the reason you brought your pet to see
your veterinarian, or it could be an abnormal finding your
veterinarian detected when performing a physical exam on your pet.
What Causes Jaundice?
Bilirubin, a yellow pigment, is made from the natural breakdown of
old or damaged red blood cells. Bilirubin is then taken to the liver for
processing, stored as a component of bile in the gallbladder, and is
finally excreted into the small intestine through the bile duct. We see
“jaundice” when an excessive amount of bilirubin builds up in the
blood due to 1 of 3 major problems: too much of it is being made, the
liver can’t process it properly, or there is an obstruction blocking bile
from exiting the bile duct.
Too Much Bilirubin Is Being Made
Destruction of red blood cells leads to large amounts of bilirubin in
the blood. Common causes include the immune system attacking the
red blood cells (“immune-mediated hemolytic anemia” or “IMHA”),
infection, or certain toxins (acetaminophen, zinc, onions).
Uncommon causes include genetic diseases or low phosphorus
levels.

Liver Unable to Process Bilirubin
Anything that causes enough damage, inflammation, or scarring of
the liver can cause jaundice. Common causes of liver disease include
toxins, infections, cirrhosis, immune-mediated or inflammatory
disease (“chronic hepatitis”), cancer, and fatty liver (“hepatic
lipidosis”).
Bile Duct Obstruction
Diseases that cause blockage of the bile duct include gallstones,
biliary mucocele (in dogs), pancreatitis, other types of inflammation,
infection, and cancer.
What Happens Now?
Your veterinarian will be recommending a series of tests to help
differentiate between these different diseases because treatment of
each is different. Understanding the underlying cause is essential for
treatment recommendations and prognosis. Laboratory testing—
including a complete blood count, chemistry panel, and urinalysis—
will be one of the first steps. Your veterinarian may also recommend
an abdominal ultrasound to look at the liver and the biliary system.
Adjunctive tests will be based on the results of these initial
diagnostics. Such testing may include infectious disease screening
tests (usually blood tests), radiographs (x-rays), fine-needle aspirates
(FNA) of the liver or gallbladder, cytology, biopsies of the liver, and
cultures of the bile, liver, or urine. Depending on the findings, other
ancillary tests may be recommended. In the case of an obstructed
biliary system, your pet may require emergency surgery.
Additionally, your veterinarian may be recommending supportive
care for your pet while they continue investigating the underlying
cause of your pet’s jaundice.
It is quite important to understand that jaundice is always a
serious concern. If your pet is jaundiced, action for diagnosing and
treating the problem is warranted.
Christina A. Bradbury (Meadow Vista, California)

Chapter 29: Petechiae and
Ecchymoses
Marie-Claude Blais

Petechiae and ecchymoses are red to purple discolorations of the
skin or mucous membranes that result from small blood vessel
bleeding. A small, well-defined punctiform lesion (<3 mm) is
referred to as a petechia, and petechiae usually appear secondary to
superficial capillary bleeding. In human medicine, the term purpura
is used when petechiae have coalesced and become bigger and
irregular. An ecchymosis refers to a larger blood collection (often >1
cm), usually occurring deeper in the dermal layers secondary to
small arterioles and venules bleeding. Erythema, which will
disappear on finger pressure (blanching; Video 12.1

), should not

be mistaken for such hemorrhagic lesions. Thrombocytopenia is the
most common cause of mucocutaneous bleeding like petechiae and
ecchymoses, although other primary hemostatic disorders such as

vascular abnormalities (ch. 181), von Willebrand disease (vWD)
(ch. 175), and platelet dysfunction (ch. 175) or even a more global
bleeding condition (chs. 124 and 171) can be responsible.
The severity of systemic bleeding is determined by the extent of its
underlying disorder. For example, mild cases of primary (plateletbased) hemostatic defects like thrombocytopenia or
thrombocytopathia can produce minimal bleeding whereas severe penia or -pathia can produce ongoing, extensive hemorrhage. The
same spectrum is true for secondary (coagulation factor deficiencybased) hemostatic defects and associated clinical signs: mild
deficiencies can be subclinical, and severe deficiencies can be lifethreatening. Mucocutaneous bleeding (petechiae/ecchymoses)
strongly suggests a primary hemostatic disorder, and similarly “late
bleeding,” that is, bleeding that occurs hours to several days after a
challenge, is mainly characteristic of disorders of fibrin formation or
fibrinolysis. However, the presence of frank hemorrhage or blood
loss causing critical bleeding is nonspecific and does not allow for
distinguishing between primary and secondary hemostatic disorders.
Overall, clinical signs of bleeding are not specific for a certain
bleeding disorder and detailed laboratory testing is always needed
for a definitive diagnosis.1

Pathophysiology
Under normal conditions, platelets do not interact with the intact
vessel wall. However, upon vascular injury, the subendothelial
extracellular matrix is exposed to the blood, to which platelets
promptly adhere in order to limit hemorrhage and promote tissue
healing. This matrix contains several adhesive macromolecules
including collagen and von Willebrand factor (vWF).2 Platelet
adhesion triggers a signaling cascade mediated by tyrosine kinases
and G-protein coupled receptors, which guide full platelet activation
and concomitant granule release. In turn, this results in recruitment
and activation of even more platelets. Platelet aggregation follows,
with the presentation of a procoagulant surface promoting the
formation of a fibrin-rich hemostatic plug at the injured site.3 The
pivotal role of platelet-vascular interactions in maintaining

hemostasis is illustrated in both quantitative and qualitative primary
hemostatic disorders, which clinically tend to manifest as mucosal
bleeding, including petechiae and ecchymoses.

Differential Diagnosis
Thrombocytopenia
Acquired thrombocytopenia can occur through several mechanisms,
including increased platelet destruction, consumption, or
sequestration, or from decreased bone marrow production (ch. 175).
Immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (ITP) is the most commonly
acquired disorder of primary hemostasis in dogs,4 although it is
seldom reported in cats.5 ITP is now recognized as a complex and
heterogeneous syndrome that results from a combination of
antibody-mediated destruction and cell-mediated attacks on
platelets peripherally and, to a lesser degree, megakaryocytes in the
bone marrow.4 As reported in a recent study including 61
thrombocytopenic dogs with platelet counts <50,000/mcL, ITP is
most often primary or idiopathic (57%), but may be secondary (28%)
to several conditions such as neoplastic, inflammatory, or infectious
disease, or drug exposure.6
The remaining dogs (15%) in that study were diagnosed with a
non-immune thrombocytopenia attributed to either bone marrow
aplasia or consumptive coagulopathy.6 Indeed, disseminated
intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a serious complication that occurs
in association with a wide variety of diseases, including infection,
inflammation, neoplasia and trauma (ch. 171). DIC usually
contributes to morbidity and mortality through systemic
microvascular thrombosis associated with a hypercoagulable state.
However, the disorder can progress to a consumptive coagulopathy,
resulting clinically in petechiae, ecchymoses and overt bleeding.7
Other causes of thrombocytopenia typically do not cause
hemorrhage unless thrombocytopathia or another, additional
disorder is present. For instance, mild to moderate
thrombocytopenia has been reported in 10% of all dogs with cancer

at a university hospital, but without clinical signs (ch. 331).8
Decreased bone marrow platelet production can be secondary to
infectious agents, drugs, neoplasia or bone marrow disease such as
myelodysplasia, and is usually associated with other cytopenias (chs.
172, 176). Finally, sequestration (splenomegaly or within the
pulmonary circulation secondary to sepsis or endotoxemia) and loss
(massive hemorrhage) can cause mild to moderate
thrombocytopenia.3

Thrombopathia
Abnormal platelet function may be inherited or acquired (ch. 175)
and should be suspected in animals with an adequate platelet count
and evidence of primary hemostatic bleeding.
Several congenital platelet disorders have been described in dogs
of specific breeds, including German Shepherd (Scott syndrome and
kindlin-3 mutation), Grey Collie (cyclic hematopoiesis), American
Cocker Spaniel (dense granule defects), Great Pyrénées and
Otterhound (Glanzmann thrombasthenia), Greater Swiss Mountain
Dog (P2Y12 defect), and Basset Hound and Spitz dogs (intrinsic
platelet defect).3,9-12 In addition to petechiae, ecchymoses, and
mucosal bleeding, excessive bleeding during permanent tooth
eruption may be the first indication of these congenital
thrombopathias.3
Acquired thrombopathia may be secondary to uremia, liver
disease, neoplasia, or infectious disease (e.g., rickettsial infections),
but the exact mechanisms are mostly unclear. Aspirin and
clopidogrel therapy will intentionally alter platelet function but are
rarely associated with spontaneous hemorrhage.13 Finally, several
drugs have been reported to alter platelet function in vitro, with
limited clinical relevance, including other non-steroidal antiinflammatory agents, certain antibiotics, hydroxyethyl starch
solutions, chondroprotective agents and omega fatty acids.3,14,15

Von Willebrand Disease

vWD is the most common inherited bleeding disorder in dogs, with a
particularly high prevalence in Doberman Pinschers (type 1) (ch.
175). That said, this inherited coagulopathy has been described in
>50 breeds, with variable bleeding tendencies, notably according to
the type of vWD (type 1: partial quantitative deficiency; type 2: rare
qualitative defect; type 3: most severe, virtual absence of vWF).
Some dogs have no clinical signs, whereas others may have bleeding
from the nose, vulva, urinary bladder, or oral mucous membranes,
and less frequently subcutaneous hematomas and hemarthrosis.
Disease signs are usually evident during even minor surgical
procedures or after trauma.16,17 In cats, vWD is extremely rare, with
few case reports published.18

Vascular Disorders
Vasculitis results from an aberrant immune response directed
toward blood vessels either as a primary immune-mediated
condition or triggered by an underlying factor such as a variety of
medications, infections, or neoplastic conditions (ch. 181). Early
signs include petechiae, ecchymoses, and edema, while the condition
often progresses to skin necrosis, ulcerations, pain and systemic
signs.19

Diagnostic Approach
The presence of petechiae and ecchymoses is highly suggestive of a
primary hemostatic defect. In addition to the animal’s signalment, a
complete and detailed history (ch. 2) can help narrow down the list
of differential diagnoses. For example, age, breed, and patient or
family history of bleeding tendencies may be suggestive of an
inherited platelet disorder. Travel history (ch. 9), flea/tick or toxin
exposure, recent vaccination, or drug administration can modulate
the suspicion of an underlying trigger.
Similarly, a thorough physical examination (ch. 3) is essential not
only to determine the extent of hemorrhage, but also of signs of
underlying disease. Petechiae and ecchymoses can readily be

appreciated on the ventral abdominal and inguinal skin (Figure
29.1). In addition, petechiae are often found on the inner pinnae as
well as the mucous membranes of the oral cavity and genitalia,
whereas ecchymoses commonly appear over recent venipuncture
sites (Figure 29.2). Other clinical signs reported in primary
hemostatic disorders include oral, intraocular, urinary and
gastrointestinal bleeding (including occult blood loss, hematemesis,
hematochezia and melena), epistaxis, and even potentially lifethreatening pulmonary and intracranial hemorrhage.6 As such, a
bleeding score metric has been developed in dogs with ITP and it
may prove to be a useful tool in predicting patient outcome.6
When petechiae and ecchymoses raise the possibility of a primary
hemostatic disorder, the first laboratory test to perform is a platelet
count (Figure 29.3; ch. 59). Ideally, jugular venipuncture should
be avoided in such patients, due to the potential of large hematoma
formation afterward despite manual compression. Automated
thrombocytopenia needs to be confirmed by a manual platelet count
based on the examination of a stained blood smear, particularly in
feline patients. In the emergency setting, a rough platelet estimate
can be obtained by multiplying the number of platelets present per
high powered field by 15,000-20,000/mcL. Thrombocytopenia tends
to be more severe (<20,000 platelets/mcL) in dogs with ITP, even
when comparing primary versus secondary ITP.6,20 The risk of
spontaneous bleeding progressively increases as the platelet count
declines below 30,000/mcL, but paradoxically not all ITP patients
bleed, and the platelet count alone does not reliably predict bleeding
outcomes.4,21

ventral abdominal and inguinal skin of a dog with

FIGURE 29.2 Ecchymoses over the jugular vein
following venipuncture in a dog with immune

Careful examination of the blood smear and complete blood count
may provide additional pertinent information. For instance, a high
mean platelet volume (MPV; >12 fL) has a 96% positive predictive
value for a normal or hyperplastic bone marrow megakaryocyte
population.22 As such, an increased MPV is supportive of ITP,
although a normal to low MPV does not exclude the diagnosis.4,23
Concurrent anemia may reflect blood loss secondary to the

thrombocytopenia, but Evans syndrome (combined immunemediated hemolytic anemia [IMHA]) and ITP) and bone marrow
disease should also be considered. The presence of spherocytes,
erythrocyte ghosts and/or a positive saline agglutination test is/are
suggestive of concurrent IMHA, notably if the anemia is
regenerative.24 Although insensitive, careful blood smear
examination may identify the presence of vector-borne pathogens.24
Pancytopenia (ch. 176) is indicative of bone marrow disease,
whereas the presence of schistocytes may be suggestive of DIC (ch.
171).25

Coagulation tests should be performed to investigate the
possibility of DIC, namely prolonged activated partial
thromboplastin time (aPTT) and prothrombin time (PT), and
elevated concentrations of fibrinogen degradation products,
fibrinogen or D-dimers (ch. 170).7,26
Bone marrow evaluation (ch. 84) is not typically performed in
cases of thrombocytopenia, unless there is a suspicion of an
underlying marrow disease, or the patient has a poor response to
therapy. Indeed, in most cases of ITP, cytologic evaluation of bone
marrow does not provide additional diagnostic or prognostic
information,4,21 although finding megakaryocytic hypoplasia is
associated with bleeding and non-survival.27 That said, severe
thrombocytopenia is not a contraindication to bone marrow
investigation, especially if the sample consists of a simple sternal
marrow aspirate.4,28
A thorough investigation for underlying causes of ITP or DIC
should also include a serum biochemistry profile, urinalysis, vectorborne disease screening, and imaging to rule out neoplasia. Plateletassociated antibodies and immunoglobulin assays, notably using
flow cytometry, may aid in the diagnosis of ITP but have limited
capacity to distinguish primary ITP from other causes.20,29
Platelet function disorders should be suspected in animals with an
adequate platelet count and evidence of primary hemostatic
bleeding. Buccal mucosa bleeding time (BMBT), which evaluates
in vivo platelet-vascular interactions, can easily be performed in any
clinical setting (ch. 79). In animals with normal platelet counts,
BMBT prolongation suggests thrombopathia, vWD (ch. 175), or
vascular disorders (ch. 181). Given its relatively high prevalence,
vWD should be excluded first, usually using a vWF antigen assay.
The platelet function analyzer (PFA-100, PFA-200) is an automated
point-of-care instrument that may rapidly assess primary
hemostasis.30 Differentiation between thrombopathia and vWD can
be deduced by simply replacing the patient’s plasma with that from a

normal dog (i.e., source of vWF), thereafter normalizing the result in
cases of vWD.30 Platelet function disorders are further assessed by
platelet aggregation, flow cytometry, platelet dense granule release
and/or content; such specialized assays are not widely available and
often require fresh samples. Genetic testing is available for vWD and
some platelet defects (ch. 175).3

Treatment
The therapeutic approach to platelet diseases varies depending on
the underlying cause, emphasizing the importance of thorough
diagnostic investigation. The cornerstone of the treatment of ITP is
immunosuppressive therapy, but treatment must be selected
appropriately. For example, doxycycline is often added while
awaiting results of vector-borne disease screening depending on the
level of suspicion and geographic location. Medications that can
cause thrombocytopenia/-pathia should be discontinued. Similarly,
in cases of neoplasia, a surgical approach or the initiation of
chemotherapy may be necessary. Thrombopoietin-mimetic drugs
will likely join the therapeutic arsenal against ITP in the future but
currently are rarely used in veterinary medicine.4,31
Platelet-rich plasma and concentrate are stored at room
temperature for a maximum of 5 days. During ITP, administered
platelets are rapidly destroyed, and the benefit of the transfusion is
very short-lived. Thus, platelet transfusions are usually limited to
patients with life-threatening bleeding, especially suspected central
nervous system or pulmonary hemorrhage, or as prophylaxis around
surgery.
Lyophilized derivatives of canine platelets, which have a long
shelf-life and can be easily transported, have recently been
commercialized, solving the need for emergency access to fresh
blood donors.32 When vWD is responsible for clinical signs,
cryoprecipitate transfusion is ideal, although fresh frozen plasma
could also be used.

Chapter 30: Peripheral Edema
Jessica Ward

Pathophysiology of Edema Formation
Peripheral edema refers to a visually recognizable and palpable accumulation of fluid within
the dermal interstitium. The balance of body fluid distribution between intravascular and
extravascular (interstitial) compartments is governed by the Starling equation1,2: Q = Kf ([Pc –
Pi] – σ [πc – πi]), where Q is the net fluid movement between vascular and interstitial
compartments; Kf is the filtration coefficient (indicative of vascular permeability); Pc and Pi
are the hydrostatic pressures within the capillary and interstitium, respectively; σ is the
osmotic reflection coefficient; and πc and πi are the oncotic pressures within the capillary
(vessel) and interstitium, respectively. In normal physiologic states, the hydrostatic pressure
difference (Pc – Pi) is greater than the net oncotic pressure difference (πc – πi) such that there
is a small net movement of fluid from intravascular to interstitial spaces. This fluid is then
taken up by the lymphatic system and returned to systemic venous circulation.
Several physiologic mechanisms normally function to limit excessive accumulation of fluid
in the interstitium. This interstitial matrix is a dense connective tissue meshwork consisting of
collagen and elastin fibers, glycosaminoglycans, and hyaluronan that normally contains very
little fluid.3,4 With increased fluid filtration, connective tissue fibers provide tension that
compresses the interstitial matrix and increases interstitial hydrostatic pressure, limiting
further edema formation. Finally, the lymphatic system responds to increased fluid
accumulation by increasing lymphatic uptake. Peripheral edema can occur when these
compensatory mechanisms become overwhelmed or are dysfunctional.

Mechanisms and Etiologies Causing Peripheral Edema
General mechanisms of peripheral edema formation are classically categorized as (1)
decreased plasma oncotic pressure; (2) increased intravascular hydrostatic pressure; (3)
increased vascular permeability; and (4) lymphatic dysfunction (Table 30.1). Certain
mechanisms preferentially cause peripheral edema that is either generalized or localized,
while others can cause both; some disease processes involve multiple mechanisms. Though
theoretically possible, changes in oncotic or hydrostatic pressure within the interstitium are
not implicated in clinical disease.
A common cause of generalized peripheral edema reported in small animals is decreased
plasma oncotic pressure due to hypoalbuminemia (ch. 60), as a result of either protein loss
(e.g., protein-losing nephropathy [ch. 302]5 or enteropathy [ch. 262]6;) or decreased
protein synthesis (e.g., hepatic failure,7 malnutrition8; chs. 266 and 270). The degree of
hypoproteinemia must be severe (serum albumin <2.0 g/dL [<20 g/L]) in order to cause overt

edema in the absence of other factors.2 Also note that hypoproteinemia in small animals more
commonly manifests as cavitary effusions (particularly ascites; ch. 21), instead of (or in
conjunction with) peripheral edema.
The category of increased intravascular hydrostatic pressure includes diseases that lead to
volume expansion of the entire systemic venous system, such as right-sided congestive heart
failure, as well as diseases that cause local increase in intravascular hydrostatic pressure due
to venous obstruction or fistulation. Although peripheral edema is a common manifestation of
right-sided congestive heart failure in humans and large animals, it is rare in small animals,
and is almost always accompanied by cavitary effusions (particularly ascites)9 (chs. 228 and
229). Obstruction of the cranial vena cava (so-called “cranial vena cava syndrome”) results in
peripheral edema of the forelimbs and ventral cervical and thoracic regions, and can be due to
extraluminal compression from a cranial mediastinal mass or intraluminal obstruction from
thrombosis, stricture, or pacemaker lead.10 Obstruction of the caudal vena cava (so-called
“Budd-Chiari syndrome”) results in peripheral edema of the ventral caudal abdomen and
hindlimbs, and can also be due to extraluminal compression from caudal abdominal masses or
intraluminal obstruction from thrombosis or neoplastic invasion of the caudal vena cava.11
Arteriovenous fistulas can cause peripheral edema in the area of the vascular malformation
due to a localized increase in intravascular hydrostatic pressure12 (ch. 239).
Increased vascular permeability is the major mechanism of peripheral edema formation in
inflammatory states, including hypersensitivity (allergic) reactions and systemic inflammatory
response syndromes (chs. 128, 129, and 181). Mechanisms affecting vascular permeability are
numerous, including inflammatory cytokines, histamine, vasodilatory prostaglandins, and
nitric oxide.2 Peripheral edema has been reported as a clinical sign in small animals with
vasculitis13 and systemic inflammatory response syndrome,14 and is occasionally reported as a
clinical sign in various bacterial and parasitic infectious diseases in small animals, usually
localized to the site of infection.15,16 Local increases in vascular permeability with resultant
peripheral edema can also occur with direct cell damage caused by surgery17,18 or by
mechanical, chemical, or thermal trauma (burns).19 Increased vascular permeability is also
the presumed mechanism for peripheral edema in sterile inflammatory dermatopathies
(Wells-like syndrome and Sweet-like syndrome)20 (ch. 178).
Peripheral edema secondary to lymphatic dysfunction is termed lymphedema. Lymphedema
is typically localized, and can represent a primary or secondary disease process21 (ch. 239).
The most common cause of lymphedema in small animals is acquired destruction of a regional
lymphatic system due to neoplasia, particularly lymphoma or lymphangiosarcoma.22,23 Other
causes of acquired lymphedema include prior surgery or trauma.24 Congenital lymphedema
(lymph node hypoplasia or aplasia) is rare in dogs and cats.25,26 Affected animals typically
present within the first weeks or months of life; hindlimb edema is most common and may be
asymmetric, although cranial body areas may also be affected.27

Patients may also develop peripheral edema due to a combination of these mechanisms. For
example, a patient with protein-losing nephropathy may develop peripheral edema due to
hypoalbuminemia (decreased plasma oncotic pressure) or because of venous thrombosis
secondary to renal loss of endogenous anticoagulant proteins (increased intravascular
hydrostatic pressure), or both (ch. 302). The clinical syndrome of myxedema, a manifestation
of severe hypothyroidism, can cause generalized non-pitting edema due to a combination of
increased vascular permeability, hypoproteinemia, and decreased lymphatic drainage28 (ch.
285).

Diagnostic Evaluation of Peripheral Edema
The first step in the diagnostic evaluation of peripheral edema is assessing the distribution of
fluid accumulation (Figure 30.1). Generalized edema is more likely the result of disease
processes that affect the entire blood pool or vasculature, such as hypoproteinemia, systemic
inflammatory response syndrome, myxedema, or right-sided congestive heart failure.
Localized edema is more likely due to processes that affect a specific vascular or lymphatic bed
(Table 30.1). In general, peripheral edema will be most severe in gravity-dependent (ventral)
body regions.
Differentiating between pitting and non-pitting edema can also be diagnostically useful.
Pitting edema is recognized by a persistent depression in the skin after firm digital pressure
has been applied (

Video 3.8). Pitting edema suggests that fluid is being displaced within

the interstitial space, while non-pitting edema suggests that fluid exists primarily within cells
(intracellular swelling) or that clotted fibrinogen is preventing fluid displacement within the
interstitium.29 Most mechanisms and diseases discussed previously will result in pitting
edema. Causes of non-pitting edema can include angioedema (because fluid accumulation
occurs in deeper subdermal layers), post-surgical or traumatic swelling, lymphangiosarcoma,
and myxedema. Chronic lymphedema can transform into a non-pitting state as chronic
collagen deposition eventually results in interstitial fibrosis.21
The diagnostic approach to the edematous patient is guided by signalment, history, and
physical examination findings. Owners should be questioned about recent trauma, surgery,
vaccination, envenomation, toxin exposure, or drug therapy. Generalized peripheral edema in
the presence of ascites or pleural effusion would increase index of suspicion for
hypoalbuminemia or right-sided congestive heart failure. Right-sided congestive heart failure
would be supported by physical examination findings of jugular venous distension (ch. 228;
Videos 229.1, 237.3) and a cardiac murmur (ch. 38) or arrhythmia (ch. 230). Physical
examination findings suggestive of systemic inflammation (fever [ch. 16], circulatory shock
[ch. 121]) would increase suspicion for vasculitis (ch. 181) or systemic inflammatory
response syndrome. Arteriovenous fistulas are associated with a focal palpable swelling and
bruit (ch. 239). Congenital lymphedema may be suspected based on patient signalment and
absent or hypoplastic lymph nodes on palpation (ch. 239).
Basic screening lab work (complete blood count, serum chemistry profile, serum thyroxine
concentration, and urinalysis) can confirm some relevant differential diagnoses for peripheral
edema and rule out many others. For patients with edema primarily affecting the cranial or
caudal half of the body, diagnostic imaging (radiographs, ultrasound, computed tomography)
is indicated to screen for venous obstruction or compressive masses. For localized non-pitting
edema where a focal infectious or inflammatory process is suspected, aspiration of the area
may be diagnostically useful to identify organisms or a predominant inflammatory cell type.13
In most cases, the cause of peripheral edema can be determined through a combination of
the above tests. Direct imaging of lymphatics and lymph nodes is rarely indicated, and
requires specialized techniques.30,31 Historically, lymphangiography via direct lymphatic
cannulation was the only method for evaluating the lymphatic system. This cumbersome
technique has largely been replaced by advanced imaging such as computed tomography,
scintigraphy, and magnetic resonance imaging.

FIGURE 30.1 Diagnostic algorithms for determining etiology of
peripheral edema in small animals. CBC, Complete blood count; Chem,
serum chemistry panel; CT, computed tomography; PLE, protein-losing
enteropathy; PLN, protein-losing nephropathy; R-CHF, right-sided
congestive heart failure; SIRS, systemic inflammatory response
syndrome; UA, urinalysis; UPC, urine protein to creatinine ratio.
In general, the underlying cause of edema formation should be treated specifically. There is
no effective directed treatment for the peripheral edema itself. Physical removal of fluid is not
effective or practical (in contrast to centesis for cavitary effusions). Diuretics can potentially
palliate edema caused by increased hydrostatic pressure, but are contraindicated for most
other etiologies of peripheral edema. Chronic bandaging, surgery, or medical therapy with
rutin have been suggested as palliative treatments for underlying diseases with no definitive
therapy (such as chronic lymphedema),27 though these treatments have not been scientifically
evaluated. Prognosis for peripheral edema varies widely depending on underlying etiology,
from excellent (e.g., hypersensitivity reaction) to good with treatment (e.g., protein-losing
enteropathy) to poor (e.g., lymphangiosarcoma).
