Chapter 31: Orthopedic
Manifestations of Systemic
Disease
Bing Yun Zhu

A C RO N YM S
CKD chronic kidney disease
PE physical examination

Overview
Dogs and cats with systemic disease causing changes in mobility may
not present to the veterinarian for a complaint of “illness,” but
instead for lameness, abnormal gait, difficulty rising or even more
subtle signs such as unwillingness or reduced ability to jump up onto
furniture or into a car. Maintaining an open mind regarding the
various causes for orthopedic signs provides the most efficient means
of reaching an accurate diagnosis and efficacious therapeutic plan.
Since various underlying systemic diseases can cause orthopedic
signs in dogs and cats of any age, empirically prescribed medications
might be contraindicated, such as giving immunosuppressive drugs
to a pet with an infectious condition. Some empirical therapies may
delay the ability to safely provide appropriate treatment, such as
administering non-steroidal anti-inflammatories to a patient who in
fact requires steroidal therapy as soon as possible. Close or
concurrent administration of these drug classes may damage the

gastrointestinal lining. Therefore, steroidal therapy may need to be
withheld until the non-steroidal medications and effects are
eliminated (ch. 143).

Diagnostic Approach to Orthopedic
Manifestations of Systemic Disease
(Figure 31.1)
Signalment
The process of prioritizing diagnoses begins with knowing the
patient’s age, sex, neuter status, and breed. In turn, they provide the
initial roadmap for choosing diagnostic tests. This may gain
importance in circumstances where finances are limited and higher
yield tests may be preferred. For example, crush injury is a concern
in nursing puppies or kittens while the probability of neoplasia
increases as pets age. Large and giant breed dogs are predisposed to
primary orthopedic conditions such as dysplasia and degenerative
joint diseases while immune-mediated diseases occur more
commonly in middle-aged female dogs (ch. 177). Primary immunemediated polyarthropathies are rare in cats.1 Male dogs but not male
cats may develop lameness secondary to discospondylitis (ch. 250)
or prostatic disease (ch. 314).2

FIGURE 31.1 Diagnostic algorithm for orthopedic
manifestations of systemic disease. CK, Creatine
kinase.

History
Commonly, the clinician allows the owner to express their primary
concern and observations without too much interruption (ch. 1).
Then, the owner is informed that a review of their pet’s entire history
will be discussed before more focused questioning of their main
concern (ch. 2). From the foundation history, one may inquire about
trauma earlier in life or about the presence of similar issues in
littermates or related pets. Does the pet roam free in a forest or are
they confined to an apartment in a high-rise building? Review recent
and previous travel, especially into areas known for ticks (rickettsiae,
protozoa, bacteria, spirochetes), fungal disease (histoplasmosis,
blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, cryptococcosis), or leishmaniasis
(ch. 9). Seasonality and environment should be considered since

warm weather marks the onset of tick and snake activity, whose bites
may cause rapid onset paresis and paralysis. Cats thought to have
difficulty jumping but also noted to have polyuria, polydipsia,
increase in appetite, and/or weight loss may be hyperthyroid (ch.
287) or diabetic (ch. 292). Some diabetic cats exhibit signs of
neuropathy such as a plantigrade stance and dramatic reduction in
jumping ability (Videos 14.2, 292.1

). Certain medications may

“trigger” orthopedic signs. Glucocorticoids cause muscle weakness.
Antibiotics, such as trimethoprim-sulfur, may induce immune
mediated polyarthritis that can cause difficulty rising and reduced
ability to ambulate or jump.

Physical Examination (PE)
When an animal is presented for possible orthopedic issues, the PE
should begin when first meeting owner and patient (ch. 3). One
should carefully observe the dog’s ability to rise and their gait,
perhaps as the owner walks the dog into the examination room.
Ideally, veterinarians should also assess walking and trotting gaits on
a non-slip surface, while the dog is being led by its owner. Cats
should be allowed to explore the examination room as the history is
taken, allowing the clinician to observe their gait and ability to jump
onto a chair or counter.
After the general PE, a full orthopedic examination should be
performed. If one limb appears painful, it is always valuable to first
closely examine the opposite (non-painful) limb or perhaps all 3
other limbs to gain pet and owner trust. Comparing limbs may allow
the veterinarian to gain insight into a pet’s stoicism or sensitivity, as
well as possibly identify pain or swelling in areas not previously
suspected. An orthopedic examination should include palpation of
long bones and the vertebral column, including lumbosacral
palpation via digital rectal examination (ch. 3). Peripheral joints
should be manipulated gently and then carefully palpated for
effusion (ch. 32; Video 177.1

). Stifles should be assessed for

ligament laxity and the jaw should be opened and closed to assess
the temporomandibular joints (ch. 258). Any muscle atrophy

should also be noted. By this juncture, one should have determined if
lameness is associated with one or multiple limbs. The orthopedic
evaluation should be followed by testing proprioceptive placement
reflexes in all four limbs. Abnormalities in proprioceptive placement,
gait, or mentation indicate need for a full neurological examination
(ch. 241). Fundic examinations (ch. 13) may be valuable indicators
of hypertension (ch. 236), fungal disease (chs. 207-209) or other
systemic inflammatory or infectious conditions.

Differential Diagnosis
The Initial Approach
One method for remembering and categorizing possible differential
diagnoses is to focus on histopathological processes. While these
categories are exclusive of other conditions, they provide a starting
point in the quest for a diagnosis.

Diseases of Bone
Degeneration, Tissue Injury, and Death
Fractures can be due to significant trauma or secondary to an
underlying condition that causes weakened bone structure, in which
relatively minor activities can cause a bone to break (ch. 162). Weak
bones are not usually painful but are more susceptible to fractures
(obvious or subtle). Some bone diseases cause focal pain, such as
with infection (osteomyelitis) or neoplasia (ch. 326). Some systemic
diseases can cause diffuse bony changes: for example, the increased
osteoclastic activity associated with excess parathyroid hormone
from primary, nutritional secondary, or renal secondary
hyperparathyroidism (ch. 162).3-5 Disuse osteoporosis begins
within weeks.6 Osteoporosis has also been associated with vitamin D
deficiency, whether from inadequate dietary intake or malabsorptive
conditions.7,8
Inflammation (Infectious or Sterile)
Pain associated with osteomyelitis commonly causes lameness and
often results in decreased appetite and/or apparent “lethargy.”

Severe disease can lead to pathological fractures. Bacterial
osteomyelitis can follow hematogenous spread, direct trauma and
inoculation, or surgical intervention.9 Fungal causes of osteomyelitis
include blastomycosis (ch. 209), systemic aspergillosis (ch. 211),
cryptococcosis (ch. 207), histoplasmosis (ch. 209), and
coccidioidomycosis (ch. 208). Panosteitis is a disease of medullary
adipocytes associated with eosinophilic granular degeneration that
affects young dogs of medium, large and giant breeds. Clinical signs
include lameness, difficulty rising, and pain on palpation of long
bones (ch. 162).
Disorders of Cell Growth (Abnormal Growth and
Neoplasia)
Disorders of cell growth can be categorized as deviations in normal
growth or secondary to a benign or malignant neoplastic process
(chs. 22, 280, 281, and 326). Abnormal growth of bone can cause
discomfort when bearing weight or pain in surrounding tissues. If
abnormal bone growth occurs in or near the vertebral column, nerve
root or spinal cord compression can cause pain, paresis or paralysis.
Neoplasia of bone can be primary (osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma,
fibrosarcoma, hemangiosarcoma, myeloma) or metastatic (ch.
326).10 Common cancers that spread to bone include mammary
carcinoma, urinary tract carcinomas (including prostate),
lymphoma, melanoma and mast cell tumor.11 Benign neoplasia of
bone (osteochondromas, bone cysts, multiple cartilaginous
exostoses) can cause lameness.10
Systemic diseases that can cause abnormal skeletal development in
growing dogs and cats (ch. 22) include pituitary dwarfism (chs.
280, 281), congenital hypothyroidism (chs. 285, 286), and
nutritional imbalances such as hypovitaminosis D (rickets in growing
animals), copper deficiency, and calcium or phosphorus deficiencies
(ch. 162).12 Hypervitaminosis A, as can occur in cats fed liver diets,
can cause multiple bone exostoses, enthesiophytes, joint laxity, and
nerve impingements resulting in spinal cord or peripheral nerve and
plexus disorders (ch. 162).13 Mucopolysaccharidoses are inherited
storage diseases that can cause long bone and/or vertebral column
malformations resulting in a “crouching” gait, paresis, or paralysis

(ch. 162).14,15 Metachromatic granules in peripheral blood smear
leukocytes are a clue for possible mucopolysaccharidosis.
Primary diseases of bone development include osteogenesis
imperfecta (ch. 162) and osteochondrodysplasia syndromes.
Various skeletal structures can be affected, increasing susceptibility
to fractures and/or signs of lameness.16 Physeal dysplasia in cats can
lead to slipped capital femoral epiphyses.17 Hypertrophic
osteodystrophy (HOD) is a painful idiopathic disease of young,
growing, large-breed dogs affecting the metaphyses of long bones.
Hypertrophic osteopathy (HO) causing painful periosteal reaction
along appendicular bones may occur secondary to pulmonary
neoplasia or systemic infections in adult dogs and cats.18,19
Vascular Disturbances
Avascular femoral head necrosis is a well-documented condition
seen in young small breed dogs. Ischemic necrosis has been reported
less commonly in other locations.20,21 Medullary bone infarcts are
rare and usually associated with neoplasia or surgical
intervention.22,23

Diseases of Joints
Degeneration, Tissue Injury, and Death
Degenerative joint disease and its associated inflammation are
common in dogs and cats. Combinations of conformational
abnormalities and degenerative changes to ligamentous structures
that provide joint stability can precipitate degenerative joint diseases
that include cranial cruciate ligament rupture and patellar luxation.
Both conditions are relatively common in smaller dogs. Degenerative
arthropathies can also occur secondary to abnormal bone growth,
such as in congenital hypothyroidism or acromegaly (chs. 280 and
285).24,25
Inflammation
Inflamed joints may be sterile or septic. In either, pain is common.

Sterile
Sterile immune mediated inflammatory joint diseases usually involve
multiple distal joints (carpus and tarsus; ch. 177). Most are
diagnosed in young-to-middle-aged female dogs. Their joint disease
is not erosive, and the diagnosis is “idiopathic” or associated with a
primary auto-immune disorder (ch. 179). Less commonly,
polyarthritis may be secondary to infectious or neoplastic diseases.26
The presence of erosion in more than one sterile inflamed joint is
suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis. Drugs such as trimethoprimsulfur may induce sterile inflammatory polyarthritis, underscoring
the importance of a thorough drug history as well as screening for
underlying disease.
Septic
Septic (bacterial) arthritis typically results from hematogenous
spread or direct inoculation by the nails of a cat, a bite wound or a
foreign body. Single joint inflammation, especially of a proximal
joint, should raise suspicion for septic arthritis. Joint infections have
been associated with systemic fungal disease (coccidioidomycosis
[ch. 208], blastomycosis [ch. 209], cryptococcosis [ch. 207],
sporotrichosis, and aspergillosis [ch. 211]), rickettsiae (Rocky
Mountain spotted fever [ch. 193], ehrlichiosis [ch. 193],
anaplasmosis [ch. 193]), spirochetes (Lyme disease [ch. 187]),
viruses (feline calicivirus [ch. 205] and coronavirus [ch. 200]) and
protozoal diseases (leishmaniasis, hepatozoonosis, babesiosis; ch.
197). Confirming the presence of infectious arthritis can be
problematic and frustrating. Despite being infected, joint fluid does
not often “culture positive” nor does it often contain adequate
numbers of organisms for cytologic detection.27 Blood culture and
serology may be of value in these scenarios. Bacterial or fungal
infection of intervertebral spaces can cause discospondylitis (ch.
250).2
Disorders of Cell Growth (Abnormal Growth and
Neoplasia)
Abnormal growth and conformation of joints can lead to
degenerative joint disease. These are described in detail in

orthopedic textbooks and include conformational dysplasia of hips
and elbows as well as abnormal cartilage development with
osteochondrosis. Many breeds are known for their congenital
malformations. Primary joint tumors causing joint deformities
include histiocytic sarcoma, synovial cell sarcoma, synovial
myxomas, fibrosarcoma and chondrosarcoma (ch. 326).28
Vascular Disturbance
Primary ischemic joint disease is uncommon, but any systemic
bleeding disorder could lead to bleeding into the joint space
(hemarthrosis), causing pain. Bleeding can be caused by genetic
factor deficiencies (hemophilia) or acquired (rodenticide
intoxication) (ch. 171).
Pigmentation and Tissue Deposits
Joint swelling and pain can be associated with systemic amyloidosis,
most commonly in Shar-Pei dogs.29,30 Calcinosis circumscripta (ch.
12), an uncommon syndrome of calcium salt deposition in soft tissue
that can include joints, may be idiopathic, develop secondary to
neoplasia or, rarely, chronic kidney disease (CKD). Calcinosis in dogs
and cats with CKD usually involves footpads rather than joints.31

Diseases of Muscle
Degeneration, Atrophy or Dysfunction
Distinct from primary “muscular dystrophy,” muscle atrophy or
weakness can be caused by either decreased innervation or systemic
conditions (ch. 14). Glucocorticoid or thyroid hormone excess,
whether naturally occurring or iatrogenic, cause muscle catabolism
and weakness. Muscle weakness due to glucocorticoid treatment may
be observed in a matter of weeks. Hypokalemia causes generalized
muscle weakness due to altered electrical activity (ch. 68; Video 68.1
). Hypocalcemia alters nerve and muscular function, leading to
painful muscle cramping and rigidity (“tetany”) that owners may
misinterpret as “weakness.” (ch. 69; Videos 69.1, 284.1, 284.2

)

Hypercalcemia commonly causes mild weakness. Myolysis can follow

exertion (rhabdomyolysis) or snake envenomation of myolysins.
Primary muscular dystrophies are rare in dogs and cats.32,33
Inflammation (Infectious or Sterile)
Many protozoal infections (Toxoplasma gondii, Neospora caninum,
Hepatozoon canis, Cytauxzoon felis and Leishmania) cause painful
myositis. Blood tests are available to aid in identifying these
infections (ch. 197). Microscopic evaluation of muscle biopsy is
required to discriminate non-infectious from infectious myopathies
(ch. 110). Diagnosis may require special analyses for neuromuscular
junctionopathies and inflammatory myopathies.
Disorders of Cell Growth (Neoplasia)
Muscle tumors that cause changes in mobility are usually large,
painful or impact nerves. Otherwise, muscular neoplasia may only be
detected as a palpable non-painful mass. Types of neoplasia that can
arise from muscle include varieties of soft tissue sarcoma (ch. 324),
hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325), histiocytic sarcoma (ch. 328), and
leiomyoma.
Vascular Disturbance
Thromboembolic disease can cause acute, extreme pain due to
ischemic muscle injury (ch. 238). Embolism can involve large blood
vessels, such as in cats with aortic thromboembolism, or small
vessels in the distal extremities of either dogs or cats. Affected limbs
are cool to touch and exhibit reduced pulse quality. A search for the
cause of hypercoagulability should be undertaken (ch. 171).

Diseases of Nerves
It is difficult to break down the various nerve disorders into
histopathological processes because many conditions are functional
(ch. 252). Of note, systemic conditions that manifest as changes in
mobility include diabetic neuropathy in cats (ch. 292; Videos 14.1,
292.1

), hypothyroid-associated neuropathies (chs. 14, 285),

insulinoma (ch. 289) or other neoplasia-induced neuropathy (ch.

331), hypo- and hyperkalemia (ch. 68) and hypo- and
hypercalcemia (ch. 69).

Other Causes of “Orthopedic Signs”
Conditions unrelated to the musculoskeletal system can cause
lameness, difficulty rising or a slow gait. Both infection and cancer of
the prostate can be painful. Either can spread to the vertebral
column causing discomfort and pain (ch. 314). Disease affecting
paw pads such as superficial necrolytic dermatitis and plasma cell
pododermatitis can appear as lameness to an owner (ch. 12).

Diagnostic testing
After completing a thorough history and PE, one should begin to
consider most likely differential diagnoses. Clinicians may or may
not be suspicious of a specific condition or lesion causing orthopedic
signs. Bone and joint diseases are often best assessed by
radiography. Joint fluid obtained for cytology (± culture) can be an
extremely valuable diagnostic aid (chs. 32 and 87). Complete blood
cell count, serum biochemistry profile, urinalysis and urine culture
are more strongly indicated in animals exhibiting not only
orthopedic signs, but also systemic signs. These include lethargy,
decreased appetite, fever, vomiting, diarrhea, weight loss, coughing,
polyuria and polydipsia. Some dogs and cats have peripheral lymph
node enlargement on PE warranting needle aspiration (ch. 88).
Further diagnostics should be pursued as dictated by radiographic
and laboratory findings. This may include specific infectious disease
screening (especially before use of immunosuppressive agents),
congenital disease testing or investigation of coagulopathies. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are frequently used for orthopedic
analgesia, but their potential nephrotoxicity means that kidney
function should be assessed before prescribing these drugs.

Chapter 32: Swollen Joints
and Joint Pain
Jonathan David Dear

A C RO N YM S
DJD degenerative joint disease
FeLV feline leukemia virus
IMPA immune-mediated polyarthritis
PE physical examination
RF rheumatoid factor
SLE systemic lupus erythematosus

Owner Observations (History) and
Definitions
Lameness and gait abnormalities are common presenting concerns
for dog and cat owners. Signs may be the result of trauma,
developmental orthopedic condition, neoplasia, or infectious bone
disease. This chapter focuses on atraumatic inflammatory joint
diseases. A pet with degenerative joint disease (DJD) may appear to
have intermittent or shifting leg lameness and is generally healthy,
lacking signs of systemic disease. Those with inflammatory joint
disease, by contrast, are not often considered lame, but many have
lethargy, decreased appetite, and a fever.1 In these animals the

practitioner may be the first individual to detect lameness or joint
disease.
Inflammatory joint diseases can be subdivided into septic and
nonseptic etiologies. Further, arthropathies are often characterized
by the number of affected joints: monoarthropathy (single joint) or
polyarthropathy (multiple joints).

Physical Examination (PE)
Before beginning to develop a list of differential diagnoses, a
thorough PE should be completed, followed by orthopedic (ch. 31)
and neurologic (ch. 241) examinations. The practitioner should
observe the pet within the exam room in addition to evaluating gait
from a distance (i.e., within a hallway; ch. 3). Different surfaces or
speeds may reveal subtle ambulatory disturbances. Some pets that
seem “stiff” in an examination room (particularly cats) may simply
be reluctant to move. Each appendicular joint should be palpated for
warmth, effusion, and sensitivity before assessing flexion, extension,
and range of motion. Typically, DJD affects a few joints while
immune-mediated and hematogenous arthropathies affect many
joints.2 Distal joints such as the carpus and tarsus are specifically
targeted by immune-mediated diseases, whereas larger, proximal
joints are more often affected by DJD. Cervical pain or pain when
manipulating the jaw might also alert the practitioner to presence of
a polyarthropathy.

Pathophysiology
Joints, comprised of two or more articulating bones with articular
cartilage, synovium and synovial fluid, are found throughout the
body, including the appendicular skeleton (such as the carpus or
stifle) and axial skeleton (such as the vertebral articulations or the
temporomandibular joint). Joint pain or lameness is associated with
the appendicular skeleton. Due to their vascular anatomy, joints are
particularly susceptible to emboli. Emboli to the synovium can be
bacteria (as with septic arthritis) or antibody-antigen complexes (as
in immune-mediated polyarthritis [IMPA; ch. 177]). IMPA is the

most common inflammatory joint disease and is generally
considered to be a type III hypersensitivity reaction. The diagnostic
approach to joint swelling and pain begins with assessing clinical
signs and PE, before considering blood tests, radiographs, and joint
fluid analysis as guides in making a diagnosis (Figure 32.1) (ch.
87).

FIGURE 32.1 Algorithm for diagnostic approach
to polyarthritis. Blue background indicates
intermediate steps; mauve background indicates
final diagnoses. FNA, Fine-needle aspirate; GI,
gastrointestinal; IMPA, immune-mediated
polyarthritis; SLE, systemic lupus erythematosus.

Septic Arthritis
Septic arthritis can affect single joints, as with post-operative joint
infections, penetrating wounds, or foreign bodies, and it can affect
multiple joints when caused by bacteremia. A septic process should
be a top consideration when a single proximal joint is affected (stifle,
elbow, shoulder, or hip). Recent history of trauma or surgical
intervention or pre-existing osteoarthritis may also increase
suspicion of septic inflammation.3 Neutrophilic inflammation is seen
in both septic and immune-mediated arthritis, though degenerative
neutrophils or the presence of intracellular bacteria suggests
infection. Joint culture should be performed when septic
inflammation is suspected, though the sensitivity of joint cultures is
disappointingly low.3-5 Septic joints can be lavaged or managed
medically empirically with systemic antimicrobial therapy while
awaiting joint or other culture results.

Immune-Mediated Polyarthritis
IMPA is the most common inflammatory joint disease in dogs (chs.
177 and 179). Affected dogs often present for cyclic lethargy (often
associated with fever), anorexia, shifting leg lameness, or apparent
hyperesthesia. Some are described as “walking on eggshells.” As with
any immune-mediated disease, IMPA can be either primary
(autoimmune) or secondary to either endogenous or exogenous
triggers. Notable triggers of secondary IMPA include vector-borne
disease (specifically Borrelia burgdorferi; ch. 187) and as an
adverse reaction to “sulfa-containing” medications (e.g.,
trimethoprim-sulfa given to Doberman Pinschers). IMPAs are
classified radiographically as either erosive or non-erosive to bone.
Cartilaginous lytic and proliferative changes are erosive. These
categories can be further subdivided based on other diagnostic
criteria (chs. 177 and 179).

FIGURE 32.2 A demonstration of the method to
grossly assess joint fluid viscosity. A drop is placed
on a glass slide. It is gently touched with a fingertip
that is then slowly moved away. The reader should
note the strand of viscous fluid typical for normal
joint fluid viscosity.

Erosive Polyarthritis
Overview
Erosive polyarthritis is characterized radiographically. Progressive
osteolysis and proliferation of periarticular joint surfaces may be
seen. Initially, mild soft tissue swelling and joint effusion may be the
only radiographic markers of erosive disease. As the condition
progresses, evidence of erosive disease can include decreased opacity
of perichondral and subchondral bone, narrowing of the joint space,
and enthesiophytosis or osteophytosis with either luxation or
subluxation.6 In dogs, both septic and rheumatoid arthritis can be

erosive. Since radiographic changes are not specific, it is critical to
analyze joint fluid and to consider culture to aid in diagnosis.

Rheumatoid Arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis in either dogs or cats is catalyzed by antibody
production directed at IgA, IgG, and IgM—called rheumatoid factor
(RF).7 These antibody complexes circulate and can be deposited
within synovial tissue, leading to intense inflammatory reactions.8
Progressive cartilage and bone destruction take place over months to
years. In some, the chronic inflammation has been so destructive and
poorly responsive to medical therapy that bone deformation and
subluxations occur.2,6 The underlying cause for development of
these autoantibodies is not understood. Though the diagnosis of
rheumatoid arthritis in humans follows a rigorous algorithm
involving a host of criteria and factors, similar criteria have not been
established in veterinary medicine. Plasma RF can be measured but
is neither sensitive nor specific for this diagnosis (chs. 169, 177, and
179).

Feline Periosteal Proliferative Polyarthritis
Erosive polyarthropathies are uncommon in cats but are occasionally
diagnosed in male cats that develop a progressive polyarthropathy
and osteopathy that involves periosteal proliferation and
subchondral osteolysis that may progress to ankylosis.9 Soft-tissue
edema and joint effusion are typical. Cytologic analysis of joint fluid
reveals aseptic neutrophilic inflammation, which in time may
become lymphoplasmacytic. Radiographic features of this disease
include intense periosteal proliferation, which may develop
characteristic trabecular patterns and subchondral bone
destruction.10

Nonerosive Polyarthritis
The inflammation associated with IMPA causes joint pain and soft
tissue swelling without damaging the synovium or cartilaginous

interfaces (chs. 169, 177, and 179). As a type III hypersensitivity
reaction, the disease often stems from an antibody production
response to chronic antigenic stimulation, but the source of this
stimulation is rarely identified, and the disease is termed idiopathic
polyarthritis.11 When identified, inciting causes include neoplasia
(particularly hemic neoplasia [ch. 322]), chronic infection (such as
deep mycoses [chs. 207-209], discospondylitis [ch. 250], or
endocarditis [ch. 232]), primary immune disease (such as systemic
lupus erythematosus [SLE; ch. 179]), or administration of certain
drugs and vaccines.12 Less frequently, enteropathic polyarthropathy
can result from either acute or chronic inflammatory gastrointestinal
disease.13
Dogs and cats with nonerosive polyarthritis often are seen by
veterinarians for an intermittent, shifting leg lameness or for
generalized nonspecific systemic signs such as lethargy and anorexia.
PE often reveals fever (ch. 16) as well as warmth and effusion
involving multiple distal joints. The tissue around affected joints may
appear edematous, and local lymph nodes may be enlarged as a
consequence of the systemic immune reaction. Though IMPA
appears to favor distal joints, other joints such as the
temporomandibular joint and vertebral articulations may be
affected, leading to the clinical appearance of odynophagia,
dysphagia, neck or back pain. Vaccine-induced polyarthritis usually
develops within 1-2 weeks of a first or booster vaccination, less
commonly longer (ch. 185). Implicated vaccines include canine
distemper and Lyme. The most common drug-induced polyarthritis
follows administration of sulfa-containing drugs (e.g., trimethoprimsulfonamide [TMS]) to Doberman Pinschers.14,15 The penicillins and
cephalosporins have also been implicated. Other causes of
nonerosive polyarthritis include juvenile-onset polyarthritis of Akitas
and the familial swollen hock syndrome in Chinese Shar-Peis.
Concurrent steroid-responsive meningitis-arteritis and IMPA has
been reported most commonly in large-breed dogs.16,17

Other Causes of Mono- or
Polyarthropathies
Hemarthrosis is an uncommon cause of single or multileg lameness
and is usually caused by thrombocytopenia or other bleeding
disorders. Most skeletal system malignancies spare the joints,
though neoplasia of the synovium or round cell tumors (specifically
lymphoma or histiocytic sarcoma) can affect the joint and its
articulating bone and cartilage (ch. 326).

Arthrocentesis
Arthrocentesis is the single most important diagnostic aid in patients
suspected of having an inflammatory joint disease. It can usually be
easily performed in most small animals (ch. 87). Joint aspiration
should be performed under heavy sedation or anesthesia, using
aseptic technique. When immune-mediated disease is suspected,
multiple distal joints (including carpi and tarsi) should be aspirated
and samples submitted individually for cytologic analysis. Remaining
samples can be pooled for culture. In pets with suspected
monoarthropathy, arthrocentesis of multiple joints can “reveal”
unsuspected multiple-joint involvement.

FIGURE 32.3 These photomicrographs are joint
fluid cytology specimens typical of a normal (A) and
a sterile inflamed joint (B). Normal joint fluid is
relatively acellular, thick, and proteinaceous with a
small number of large, with rarer small,
mononuclear cells. Joint fluid from a dog with
immune-mediated polyarthritis contains a larger
number of nondegenerate neutrophils and may
contain lupus erythematosus (LE) cells (indicated by
the arrow) in cases of systemic lupus erythematosus
(SLE). Courtesy A. Adedeji, DVM, William Pritchard
Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital, UC Davis.

Joint Fluid Analysis
Normal synovial fluid is present in small volumes and is clear,
viscous, and with low cellularity. A crude test for viscosity can be
performed by placing a small drop between thumb and forefinger to
see if the fluid “strings” 4-5 cm as the fingers are pulled apart
(Figure 32.2). Fluid from diseased joints often lacks this viscosity,
and it may be turbid or discolored. Samples contaminated with blood
from superficial vessels, while entering or withdrawing the needle
from the joint, usually have red discoloration. Normal joint fluid also
has a relatively small population of large mononuclear cells as
“housekeepers.” Normal cell counts are less than 3000/mcL. In
IMPA, individual joint cell counts can exceed 50,000/mcL and are
primarily nondegenerate neutrophils. Septic joints tend to have
similar neutrophil numbers, although the joint fluid might have signs

of the septic process: degenerate neutrophils, intracellular
organisms, and/or a positive bacterial culture (Figure 32.3).
Ancillary joint fluid testing provides little clinically useful
information, but in cats, when obtaining aerobic and anaerobic
cultures, Mycoplasma culture or polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
should also be requested. Mycoplasma have been associated with a
form of septic arthritis that causes nondegenerate joint
inflammation.18,19 This organism is difficult to culture using
conventional microbiologic methods.

Additional Testing
Septic arthritis may be suspected in a joint despite the absence of an
obvious wound or pathway for introduction of bacteria (i.e., recent
orthopedic surgery, trauma, or penetrating wound). In such a case,
the clinician should investigate the possibility of hematogenous
spread of bacteria to the synovium. Specific conditions associated
with bacteremia include endocarditis (including Bartonella spp.; ch.
232), discospondylitis (ch. 250), pyelonephritis (ch. 304), or
prostatitis (ch. 314). Diagnostic imaging and blood or urine cultures
(ch. 184) may be considered to confirm or deny the presence of
these conditions.
IMPA is thought to arise from chronic antigenic stimulation, often
stemming from chronic infection, inflammation, neoplasia, or drug
and vaccine exposures. Pets suspected of having IMPA should be
evaluated for such immune system triggers, starting with a detailed
medical history (ch. 2), paying close attention to the pet’s home
environment as well as recent travel (ch. 9), medications, or
vaccination. A thorough PE (ch. 3) should help identify
comorbidities that may relate to the current condition and help
understand the number of joints involved. Particular attention
should be paid to assessing the fundus (ch. 13), thoracic
auscultation (ch. 38), axial skeleton palpation, rectal examination,
and lymph node size.
A comprehensive medical evaluation should determine the
animal’s overall health and aid in identifying any inciting disease
prior to initiating therapy. A complete blood count (CBC), serum
biochemistry profile, and urinalysis with culture should be

performed. Serologic testing for endemic infectious diseases
associated with polyarthritis (such as Ehrlichia canis [ch. 193],
Borrelia burgdorferi [ch. 187], Anaplasma phagocytophilum [ch.
193], or systemic mycoses [chs. 207-209]) should be performed
according to geographic location. When erosive disease is suspected,
radiographs of the affected and contralateral joints should be
obtained to determine the extent of disease. In order to rule out
neoplastic disease and other infectious or inflammatory disease,
diagnostic imaging of the thorax and abdomen should be performed.
Additional testing such as blood cultures (ch. 184), echocardiogram
(ch. 97), vertebral radiographs, or cerebrospinal fluid analysis (ch.
109) should be considered on a case by case basis. Serum
concentrations of C-reactive protein, an acute phase protein and
biomarker of systemic inflammation, are usually elevated in dogs
with uncontrolled IMPA and can be used to differentiate the disease
from DJD.20,21
All cats with polyarthritis should be tested for both feline
immunodeficiency virus (FIV, ch. 198) and feline leukemia virus
(FeLV, ch. 199). Immunosuppression may play a role in disease
development or susceptibility to other infections, and FeLV has been
implicated in the pathogenesis of periosteal proliferative
polyarthritis.
Markers of immune disease such as a Coombs’ test, anti-nuclear
antibody, or RF can bolster the suspicion for immune disease,
though both sensitivity and specificity of these tests are
controversial. Positive results do not exclude the possibility of
secondary disease.
In the absence of other diseases inciting polyarthritis, a diagnosis
of idiopathic or primary IMPA is reached (ch. 177). This disease may
affect patients individually or along with other immune diseases such
as glomerulonephritis or SLE (chs. 175-179).

Chapter 33: Body Odors
Darren Berger

A classic definition of odor is a perceived sense through olfaction,
which is stimulated via volatile chemical compounds and may be
interpreted as pleasant or unpleasant. However, many people fail to
take into consideration that the situation, a person’s culture, and
their experiences are important factors that determine individual
perception of an odor.1 Besides these contextual references,
interindividual variations in odor sensitivity or thresholds exist.
These interindividual variations have long been observed by
olfactory researchers and are influenced by age, sex, personality,
cognitive function, and health status.2-4 These differences in odor
threshold, sensitivity, and perception are important to comprehend,
as clinicians may not be able to detect the malodor that a client (pet
owner) is describing or vice versa, even when a medical condition is
present. A relevant clinical example exists in patients with diabetic
ketoacidosis, where only a percentage of people can detect the
presence of ketones, and those that do may describe the odor
differently as either nail polish remover or fruity. Due to these
differences in perception, many terms are used to described odors
such as aroma, fragrance, scent, stink, stench, reek, malodor, or
essence. Understanding these terms and their connotations can be
useful to a clinician in picking up subtle clues from clients regarding
possible concerns and in appropriately conveying messages to a pet’s
owner in a delicate or blunt manner (ch. 1).

Identifying and Treating Body Odor in
Patients
Many factors contribute to the overall odor of an animal. It is
important to be aware of the factors that can contribute to the
complaint of a malodorous pet so that the clinician can determine if
it is the result of 1) a normal pet, 2) a healthy pet with an obvious
non-medical cause, or 3) a pet with an underlying disease.
Regardless, it is the clinician’s responsibility to either correct the
underlying disease process or make the pet’s odor more acceptable to
the owner.
The first step in addressing a patient with a primary concern of
malodor is to get a thorough history. Most owners are keen to the
normal odors of their animal. This awareness to the scent of their pet
was highlighted in an investigation that demonstrated 89% of
participants were able to distinguish their dog’s odor from that of
another dog.5 Given this and clinical experience, many owners are
keenly aware of changes in the normal odor associated with their pet,
when it occurred, and events that were associated with the change.
This information is helpful in differentiating between the various
possibilities for a pet’s presentation.
Once a thorough history has been acquired, all patients require a
complete physical examination (ch. 3), which includes actually
smelling the patient from rostral muzzle to tail to identify if an
abnormal odor is perceptible. Many patients that present for
abnormal odor will have Malassezia dermatitis, active pyoderma, or
otitis externa. To help identify these patients, the clinician should
pay particular attention to subtle clinical signs and body locations.
Clinical signs suggesting a secondary infection is present include:
erythema, alopecia, abnormal or excessive exudate, papules,
pustules, epidermal collarettes, crusting, or excessive scale (dander)
formation. Specific anatomic locations where meticulous attention
should be directed include: the ear canals, facial folds (Figure 33.1),
mandibular lip folds (Figure 33.2), around collars and bandages,
interdigital areas, and the perivulvar or perianal regions (Figure
33.3).

FIGURE 33.1 Facial fold erythema with increased
tan-to-brown keratosebaceous debris secondary to
bacterial overgrowth in an English Bulldog,
highlighting the importance of separating skin folds
when they are present in a patient who is being
evaluated for a complaint of malodor around the
face.

FIGURE 33.2 Mandibular lip fold erythema and
fur discoloration secondary to Malassezia spp.
overgrowth in a Cavalier King Charles Spaniel. This
is a common location of secondary infections that are
normally overlooked, which results in facial pruritus
and the misconception of odor originating from the
oral cavity.

Normal Pet Odors
Natural body odor is the result of epidermal lipid production, gland
secretions (sebaceous, epitrichial, atrichial, ceruminous, and anal
gland) and their decomposition by lipase-producing microbes into
unsaturated and aromatic fatty acids, which produce the perceived
unpleasant scent.6 Glandular density is highest near mucocutaneous
junctions, paws, dorsal neck, rump, and specific portions of the tail
and are areas where normal odors predominate. Natural pet odor is
also dependent on the species, breed, age, sexual status, and overall

health of the individual. Specific examples of a pet’s signalment
impacting its natural odor include: members of the hound or spaniel
family having a muskier odor; dogs with oilier coats (i.e., Labrador
Retrievers) having increased odor; intact male cats compared to their
castrated counterparts; animals with excessive skin folds (e.g.,
English Bulldog); and those that drool excessively such as the
Mastiff, Saint Bernard, and Newfoundland.

FIGURE 33.3 Perianal fistulas in a German
Shepherd Dog (ch. 264). The area is erythemic and
hyperpigmented, and the surrounding fur is
discolored due to licking and serosanguineous
discharge from the draining tracts. Additionally,
there is fecal material present. All contributed to the
owner’s chief concern, which was increased odor
from the rear end of this patient.
If the pet is deemed healthy with no obvious abnormal odor, client
education is required along with management strategies to improve

or mask what the client finds offensive. This may require a change in
grooming habits or frequencies, shampoo choice, use of conditioners,
and fragrance sprays. This would be similar to the approach upon
which the entire cosmetic industry is built, and in some cases, it is
simply what the client wants. In other circumstances this may not be
enough and a second choice of topical agents with different
ingredients may be needed, as some owners will find the components
of products noxious. Finally, diet has been suggested to influence a
pet’s odor, specifically by proponents of raw dog foods, although
studies documenting this are lacking.7 Despite this, the most
common anecdotal report of diet contributing to body odor has been
observed with dogs predominantly fed fish-based diets.8 In cases
where no cause can be determined, it may be worth changing the diet
to investigate whether a diet containing different ingredients
improves the patient’s odor.

Normal Pet With an Obvious NonMedical Cause
The second category encountered is patients who lack a primary
medical condition but an obvious cause for the odor exists. One
example would be in patients with long, dense, or corded hair coats
that are not maintained or allowed to dry properly. This is seen with
dogs that swim frequently, drool excessively, or in animals whose
hair coat needs more intensive grooming (e.g., Old English
Sheepdogs). In all of these circumstances, client education, improved
grooming habits, or shaving the hair coat will eliminate the problem.
However, it is important to keep in mind that shaving the hair coat
may create a more significant cosmetic issue for some clients. In
other cases, an animal’s behavior may be the source of the abnormal
odor. This is particularly true with dogs that roll in feces or decaying
material. These patients require changes in grooming or more
frequent bathing similar to that of normal patients without
identifiable causes. Other pets may liberally express their anal sacs
due to being easily frightened or for other reasons. Dietary changes,
behavior modification, or surgical excision may be required in these
instances. Finally, pets may come across wildlife such as skunks, and

during this unfortunate incident, they may be sprayed during the
encounter. It is important to note that it may take days to weeks to
completely eliminate the skunk odor and commercial as well as
home remedies are available to address these patients.8

FIGURE 33.4 Algorithm for a patient presenting
with a complaint of body odor. dz, Disease; FIV,
feline immunodeficiency virus.

Primary Medical Condition Resulting in
Pet Malodor
The vast majority of patients presenting with a complaint of body
odor are those with a primary medical condition or skin disease.
These conditions are outlined in Figure 33.4. Thorough historical
information, physical examination and appropriate diagnostics
should result in identification of the underlying condition and
secondary problems. For specific management recommendations of
these conditions, the author encourages the reader to refer to other
chapters within this textbook, or when required, Muller and Kirk’s
Small Animal Dermatology.6,8 Regardless of the cause, targeted
therapy against the primary condition and secondary infections
present are required to resolve the issue and prevent recurrence.

Client Information
Body Odors
Dogs and cats, like humans, have a natural body odor. In animals,
this odor is the result of skin oils and gland secretions along with
their by-products, which are important for recognition, social
interactions, and mate selection. These normal odors are most
pronounced around the ears, paws, back, tail and anus of the animal
where certain glands are in highest numbers. These odors vary by
species (cats vs. dogs), breed (hounds vs. other breeds), and sexual
status of the animal (neutered vs. not). In addition, dogs and cats
have two scent or anal sacs (“anal glands”) that open to the surface
near their anus. These sacs produce a normal secretion that may vary
from watery and yellow to thick and grayish in consistency. A small
amount of this material is normally secreted when an animal
defecates or a larger amount may be expressed when the animal is
frightened. The anal sac secretion can be very pungent and
overpowering, creating a worrisome smell for people who are not
familiar with this odor. In special cases, prescription diets or surgical
excision of the anal sacs may be needed when pets excessively
express these sacs, creating an intolerable situation in the home. In
other cases, an animal’s odor is the result of poor grooming, rolling
in decomposing and decaying material, or interactions with wildlife
such as skunks. In all of these cases, changes in grooming habits,
shaving of the hair coat, or the use of topical shampoos, conditioners,
or sprays will resolve the problem at first, and avoidance of the cause
is needed for longer-term prevention.
In other cases the odor may be due to issues with poor selfgrooming, fecal, or urinary issues. These problems arise as a result of
debilitating arthritis or severe illness. However, the most common
reason for an abnormal or change in a pet’s body odor is a secondary
skin or ear infection. These infections may be the result of bacteria or
yeast and are usually associated with another primary medical

condition. Regardless, once an infection is identified, topical or oral
medications are required to correct the problem. In addition, the
primary disease causing the infection also needs to be addressed to
prevent recurrence of the abnormal body odor. The primary medical
condition is identified from the pet’s history, physical examination
and special diagnostics or tests.
Darren Berger (Ames, Iowa)

Chapter 34: Cough
Luca Ferasin

MMVD myxomatous mitral valve disease

Cough is a vital defensive physiological function frequently observed
in both people and small animals. The cough reflex prevents
aspiration of foreign or noxious material and preserves the normal
health of the respiratory system by inducing a rapid and forceful
removal of harmful substances, such as inhaled foreign particles,
pathogens, tissue debris or excessive bronchial secretions from the
airways. Excessive and inappropriate coughing can emerge as a
primary presenting sign of many airway diseases but can also
represent an important sign of an underlying disease not strictly
associated with the airways, like post-nasal drip syndrome (PNDS)
or gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and can even potentially
become a harmful sign when it becomes persistent.1 An old Yiddish
proverb states: “three things cannot be hidden: coughing, poverty,
and love.”2 Indeed, once initiated, the cough reflex cannot be easily
interrupted and due to its typical loud sound during the explosive

expiratory phase, the cough is readily observed by pet owners. When
persistent, cough can also affect quality of life by interfering with
sleeping, breathing, exercise, eating and drinking. Approximately 1 in
3 people are woken up by a bout of cough every year and, similarly,
many coughing dogs and cats can keep their owners awake at night,
prompting a visit to their veterinarian. This is especially true of pets
that might sleep in their owners’ bedroom. Occasionally cough can
cause syncope (Video 34.1

), urinary and fecal incontinence, signs

of muscle pain and exhaustion. The frequent and noticeable
presentation of coughing makes this sign a very common concern
reported to physicians and veterinarians worldwide.3-5

COUGHING MECHANISMS
The typical coughing reflex (CR), also known as “tracheobronchial
cough,” is characterized by an initial deep breath, followed by a rapid
and powerful expiratory act against the closed glottis and finally
opening of the glottis, closing of the nasopharynx and forceful
expiration through the mouth, accompanied by a typical vocalization
caused by the vibration of the vocal cords. Cough can be evoked by
stimulation of coughing receptors localized in the larynx, trachea, or
bronchi, whereas irritation of bronchioles and alveoli does not elicit
coughing.6,7 The expiration reflex (ER), also referred to as “laryngeal
cough,” is a similar defensive mechanism, which is induced by
stimulation of the vocal cords or trachea and consists of forced
expiratory effort against a closed glottis but is not preceded by a deep
inspiration.7 This reflex is often observed in dogs and sounds like a
“huff” sound. The distinction between laryngeal cough and
tracheobronchial cough is important since their physiological
functions are different: laryngeal cough protects the airways from
airway aspiration, while tracheobronchial cough provides airway
clearance and maintenance of the mucociliary apparatus.8 Therefore,
the presence of tracheobronchial cough would suggest lower airway
stimulation, such as in bronchial disease (Videos 34.2, 215.16, 215.17
), whereas laryngeal cough is more commonly associated with

upper airway irritation (Video 34.3). The sneezing reflex (SR) is a
third protective reflex in the respiratory tract (ch. 35). Sneezing is
somewhat similar to coughing but it is primarily evoked from the
nasal mucosa; its expulsion phase occurs mostly through the nose in
order to eliminate the provoking stimulus and, in contrast to the
coughing reflex, it cannot be initiated voluntarily.9,10 Co-expression
of coughing and sneezing can be observed in cats. This is
characterized by enhanced muscle recruitment, offering an improved
airway defense.10 (Video 34.4

). When all these reflexes are

ineffective, such as in diabetic patients, stroke or neurodegenerative
disease patients, or those with muscular dystrophy, recurrent
pneumonia can occur.10

HISTORY
History alone rarely provides sufficient information to determine the
underlying cause of coughing. Nevertheless, a careful history (ch. 2)
should include questioning relating to the duration, characteristics
and timing of the cough. Pet owners often fail to use a correct
terminology or accurate description of the sign and therefore audiovideo recording of their coughing pet can be invaluable, even when
obtained with a mobile phone camera (Video 34.5

). “Nocturnal

cough” is often reported by pet owners, but this information could be
misleading because their animal sleeps in the same bedroom, while
the pet may be unsupervised for the rest of the day. Finally, severity
of coughing may be perceived differently by different pet owners, and
therefore appropriate questions should be asked once the problem
has been identified. Classification of cough based on its duration is
rather arbitrary. A cough lasting less than 3 weeks is termed “acute.”
It usually results from viral upper respiratory tract infection (URTI;
e.g., “kennel cough”; ch. 203) and often resolves spontaneously,
although post-infective cough can sometimes persist for a longer
period of time. A cough present for at least 8 weeks is defined as
“chronic” and clinicians should also recognize a “sub-acute” overlap
period of between 3 and 8 weeks.7 Cough can be classified as

“productive,” “wet” or “chesty” when it is associated with
expectoration of large amounts of sputum (phlegm), often swallowed
after coughing. Conversely, a “dry,” “honking” or “hacking” cough is
characterized by little or no production of phlegm. However, there
are substantial overlaps between these two forms and coughing pets
can display both types of cough at the same time (i.e., productive
cough followed by dry cough after expectoration). Furthermore, the
character and timing of a cough are not diagnostically helpful since
the diagnostic approach and outcome are almost identical, whether
the cough is productive or not. Conversely, a history of hemoptysis
(coughing up blood) should prompt urgent investigations since it
could be the first clue to the presence of lung tumors (ch. 217),
bleeding disorders (ch. 171), pulmonary thromboembolism (ch.
219), heartworm disease (HWD, ch. 237), or lungworms (ch. 215).
Information relating to home environment and animals’ habits may
also provide useful elements for a successful diagnosis. Indoor pets
can be exposed to compounds that could cause coughing, such as
dust mites, molds, fireplace ash, dandruff, litter tray dust, sprays,
deodorants, and cigarette smoke. Histological bronchial changes
have been reported in several animal models following experimental
chronic cigarette smoke inhalation, and biochemical evidence of
exposure to passive cigarette smoke has been demonstrated both in
privately-owned dogs and cats.11-14 The medical history may also
reveal exposure to boarding kennels, grooming parlors, dog parks
and general contact with other dogs in the few days preceding the
onset of an acute cough, suggesting infectious disease, especially in
young unvaccinated animals (chs. 203, 204). Coughing pets living
in endemic areas for Dirofilaria immitis (HWD, ch. 237),
Angiostrongylus vasorum (French heartworm, ch. 215) or
Aelurostrongylus abstrusus (cat lungworm, ch. 215), should be
tested or empirically treated for these parasites. The geographical
presence of these parasites changes rapidly and it is important to
know their potential prevalence in different regions.15

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS FOR
COUGHING

Cough is mostly induced by stimuli originating in the airways, with
upper airways more frequently involved than lower airways. In dogs,
dynamic and static airway collapse is one of the most common
causes of coughing and this disease process can affect different tracts
of the trachea, as well as major bronchi. The lesions are mostly
associated with weakness of the tracheal or bronchial wall, in an
isolated tract or extended tracts (i.e., tracheomalacia,
bronchomalacia and trachea-bronchomalacia; ch. 215). Dogs
affected by airway collapse typically present with a persistent, dry,
paroxysmal “honking” cough and can also be affected by varying
degrees of dyspnea16,17 (ch. 37).
In cats, one of the most common causes of cough is lower airway
inflammatory disease, mostly caused by feline asthma (ch. 215) or
HWD (ch. 237). Cats affected by small airway disease commonly
present with paroxysmal coughing, which resembles hacking-up
hairballs and can inadvertently lead to gastrointestinal investigations
rather than respiratory workups. Clinical signs can often escalate
into bronchospasm associated with severe dyspnea (asthmatic crisis)
(chs. 37, 123).18,19
Since irritation of bronchioles and alveoli does not elicit coughing,
parenchymal conditions, such as pneumonia, may not induce cough
unless the noxious process extends to the airways (e.g.,
bronchopneumonia with sputum production). Similarly, converse to
inaccurate former reports and opinions, cardiogenic and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema do not cause coughing.8,20-22 This
can be easily extrapolated, once again, by the fact that cough reflex is
not present in the deeper respiratory tract. Patients with pulmonary
edema will rather present with tachypnea/dyspnea, although they
may occasionally cough if there is concomitant airway irritation or if
the amount of fluid in the alveolar space is severe enough to reach
higher airways and stimulate coughing receptors, as occasionally
observed in large breed dogs with fulminant pulmonary edema.
Cardiomegaly, especially with left atrial enlargement (LAE), is
associated with an increased risk of cough in dogs with myxomatous
mitral valve disease (MMVD), and there is a ten-fold increased risk
of coughing if LAE and airway disease coexist. There seems to be a
weak association between LAE and airway collapse in dogs with

MMVD and therefore underlying airway inflammation might
represent the major cause of coughing in such patients.21-23
GERD, PNDS, and use of angiotensin-converting enzyme
inhibitors (ACEi) or beta-blockers are common causes of coughing in
people but are less commonly reported in animals.24-31 Risk factors
for cough are listed in Table 34.1.

CLINICAL ASSESSMENT
The physical examination of the coughing dog or cat may reveal a
potential underlying cause (ch. 3). Nasal and ocular discharge
accompanied by frequent licking and swallowing could be an
indication of PNDS associated with rhinitis and sinusitis. A cough
easily elicited by gentle tracheal palpation or chest compression
suggests that coughing receptors are already stimulated by an
underlying condition, where the pathological stimulus is not
sufficient to reach a threshold for more persistent coughing (Videos
34.4 and 34.6

). Therefore the widely used concept of “positive

tracheal pinch” is misleading because this maneuver does not
provide a “positive/negative” response.4 Auscultation over the larynx
and trachea can reveal stridor or clicks in coughing animals with
laryngeal paralysis or tracheal collapse. Thoracic auscultation may
reveal stridor, rhonchi, crackles and wheezes, which are suggestive of
airway disease at different levels in the respiratory tract. Inspiratory
crackles can be present in coughing dogs with chronic interstitial
lung disease (ILD), especially in West Highland White Terriers and
other terrier breeds (ch. 217).32 An association between ILD and
coughing has also been reported in cats.33 The exact mechanism of
cough in ILD is elusive but may be related to upregulation of airway
sensory receptors, increased cough sensitivity and chest wall
vibration.34 Although crackles are commonly reported in the
veterinary literature as an indication of alveolar pulmonary edema,
the most likely mechanism of crackle generation is sudden airway
closing during expiration and sudden airway reopening during
inspiration, as it happens more commonly in pneumonia and ILD.35-

37

Furthermore, rhonchi associated with bronchial disease can be
mistakenly described as crackles by some clinicians. Chest
percussion can reveal a horizontal line of dullness consistent with
pleural effusion, sometimes associated with cough both in dogs and
in cats. Finally, thoracic masses, often responsible for cough by
mechanical compression, can sometimes be identified by chest
percussion.

CLINICAL INVESTIGATIONS
Laboratory tests should include differential white cell count, which
may reveal neutrophilia in inflammatory diseases or eosinophilia
and basophilia in parasitic or fungal infections. Fecal Baermann
testing should be considered to attempt identification of lungworms
(ch. 80). Serological tests are available for detection of Dirofilaria
immitis (ch. 237) and Angiostrongylus vasorum (ch. 217) and
their use is recommended in all coughing animals living in endemic
areas. In chronic cases, thoracic radiographs should be considered
prior to other more invasive diagnostic tests since significant
abnormalities will alter the diagnostic plan and avoid unnecessary
further investigations. However, the poor sensitivity of standard

radiographic exams in identifying dynamic airway collapse,
infectious tracheobronchitis or parasitic infections should be borne
in mind.38-40 Bronchoscopy (ch. 93) can be considered at a later
stage for further evaluation of coughing patients, although diagnostic
yield from bronchoscopy in the routine evaluation of chronic cough
tends to be low. Bronchoscopy may have a higher diagnostic
potential in selected cases, such as inhaled foreign bodies, dynamic
or static airway collapse, chronic bronchitis and lungworms.
Furthermore, bronchoscopy provides the opportunity for airway
sampling by either mucosal biopsy or bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL).
Transtracheal wash (TTW) can be considered as an alternative
sampling technique although it provides a lower diagnostic yield.
Thoracic CT scanning is becoming widely available in veterinary
medicine and this technology allows more accurate diagnoses of
diffuse parenchymal lung disease, bronchial disease, and foreign
bodies, which may have not been identified on thoracic radiographs.
Additional diagnostic investigations may include fluoroscopy (ch.
259), GI endoscopy (ch. 107), rhinoscopy (ch. 89), allergy testing,
etc. An algorithm for clinical approach is presented in Figure 34.1.
It is also important to remember that a definitive diagnosis is not
always necessary and if a clinician reaches a series of differential
diagnoses that do not alter the outcome for the patient, additional
testing is unnecessary and could be costly or potentially harmful.41

CLINICAL MANAGEMENT
Cough that occurs very acutely may indicate a serious underlying
problem (foreign body inhalation, severe airway obstruction, neardrowning, smoke inhalation, etc.); otherwise acute cough is usually
self-limiting and treatment, if any, should be directed at the cause
rather than the clinical sign of cough. Indeed, cough is a protective
mechanism and should not be suppressed, unless it affects the
patient’s quality of life which, in coughing humans, can be assessed
by validated questionnaires, such as the Leicester Cough
Questionnaire.42 A similar objective assessment is not routinely used
for coughing dogs and cats, so quality of life is considered affected
when cough interferes with respiration, eating, drinking, exercise

and sleeping. The pet owner’s sleeping pattern can also be affected if
the dog sleeps in the same room. Cough can also spread infections
and, by further irritating the airways, it may initiate a vicious circle
of cough-induced cough. Cough suppression should be reserved for
use only in the above situations. Ideally, when a primary cause can
be identified, removal of the underlying etiology should be
considered first (removal of inhaled foreign body, antibiotic
treatment in bacterial infections, etc.).4

NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL APPROACH
The initial approach can be empirical and aimed at controlling
cough, relieving airway obstruction and reducing the source of

irritation, as indicated below:
1. Cigarette smoke, dust, spray cleaners and deodorants, should
be avoided. Carpets should be vacuumed frequently. Cleaned
cotton sheets should be used to cover the pet’s bed.
2. Gentle and long walks are more indicated than short intense
runs. Light exercise can assist in dislodging bronchial mucus
and may help opening small airways.
3. A harness should be worn instead of a collar when the dog is
walked on a leash.
4. In animals that are overweight or obese (ch. 150), weight
reduction will improve respiration, exercise capacity, and
cardiovascular functions with dramatic results. Indeed, fat
tends to accumulate in the thorax and reduce lung volume.
This can cause compression of the airways and stimulate
cough.
5. Humidification of the environment favors expectoration from
the deeper airways, bronchi, and trachea because it thins the
mucus and lubricates the irritated respiratory tract.
Ultrasound humidifiers (“cool mist”) are available in many
health & beauty shops and they can be activated overnight in
the room where the animal sleeps. Repeated gentle coupage
may help dislodge some of the deeper secretions.

PHARMACOLOGICAL APPROACH
If improvement is not observed following empiric interventions, an
antitussive approach can be considered, although it should be noted
that scientific evidence in dogs and cats is lacking.
1. Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS, ch. 90) (e.g., fluticasone,
beclomethasone, budesonide) act directly on the airway
mucosa reducing local inflammation. Since ICS are minimally
absorbed, negligible side-effects are expected. ICS are
administered using dedicated spacers with a mask.
2. Expectorants (e.g., guaifenesin, potassium iodide) work by
increasing the volume and reducing the viscosity of airway
secretions, therefore improving the efficiency of cough to

remove such secretions. However, there is limited information
about their utility in coughing pets.
3. Mucolytics (e.g., acetylcysteine, ambroxol, bromhexine) modify
the structure of mucus glycoproteins and reduce mucus
viscosity. Their use should be restricted to a few special
instances, such as liquefying thick, tenacious, mucopurulent
secretions.
4. Cough suppressants (e.g., butorphanol, codeine, hydrocodone,
dextromethorphan) are centrally acting antitussives, which
inhibit the cough reflex by acting on the medullary cough
center. Most cough suppressants have sedative effects, which
might be desirable in painful, persistent cough. The clinical
usefulness of dextromethorphan in coughing children has been
questioned and little information is available about its efficacy
in small animals.43
5. Bronchodilators (e.g., inhaled salbutamol/albuterol,
theophylline, aminophylline, and terbutaline) relax the smooth
muscle of contracted airways. Therefore, they are only useful
during bronchospasm, such as in feline asthma (ch. 215).
Inhaled bronchodilators are preferred over systemic
medications. Naturally-occurring bronchospasm has not been
convincingly demonstrated in dogs; therefore, in addition to
the larger airways found in this species, the clinical utility of
bronchodilators in dogs remains highly controversial.44
6. Neuromodulating medications (e.g., baclofen, gabapentin)
seem to reduce cough frequency and severity in human
patients, improving their quality of life. However, there is no
available information about their efficacy in dogs and cats at
this time.45-48

CLIENT INFORMATION
Cough

WHAT IS COUGH?
Cough is a wonderful natural reflex that protects your pet’s lungs.
Every time that a potential “offender” (foreign bodies, smoke, dust,
etc.) penetrates your pet’s airways, cough pushes it out with a

forceful and loud expiration called “cough.” To improve this
protective mechanism, cough teams up with another defensive
system called the “mucociliary escalator,” which is formed by mucus,
a slimy substance that entraps small particles like bacteria and
viruses, and cilia, which are tiny, hair-like projections in the
respiratory tract that beat constantly in order to move mucus and
debris up and out of the respiratory tree in order to protect the lung
from infection or irritation.

WHEN DOES COUGH BECOME A PROBLEM?
Occasional cough is hardly ever a problem and a few isolated
coughing episodes during the day can be completely normal.
However, if cough becomes persistent and starts affecting your pet’s
quality of life by interfering with normal daily activity, like eating,
drinking, exercising, and sleeping, a visit to your veterinarian is
recommended. Persistent cough can also indicate an underlying
disease and can potentially spread infections, which might be
important if you have other pets in your household. Please note that
transmission of infectious diseases from pets to humans by coughing
is very rare.

WHAT ARE THE CAUSES OF PERSISTENT
COUGHING?
The most common cause of coughing in young dogs and cats are
infectious diseases of the upper airways, like “kennel cough” in dogs
and “feline flu” in cats. The onset of this cough is usually sudden, but
tends to be a self-limiting condition, comparable to a human cold.
Only occasionally this cough persists for more than a few weeks.
Another common cause of cough in cats is “feline asthma.” Asthma
can occasionally be accompanied by labored breathing caused by
bronchospasm, which is an abnormal contraction of the smooth
muscle of the bronchi. This condition requires prompt medical
attention by your veterinarian.
In middle-age and geriatric patients cough can be caused by
degenerative conditions, such as tracheal and bronchial collapse,
which more frequently affects small and toy-breed dogs, or chronic
bronchitis. Chronic bronchitis is a chronic inflammation of the

airways accompanied by excessive mucus production, and there
seems to be an increased prevalence in some canine breeds, like
terriers, Labradors, Golden Retrievers, Springer Spaniels, and
Cocker Spaniels. Although cardiac disease is often reported as a
primary cause of coughing in dogs, this is not entirely accurate since
advanced cardiac disease can aggravate underlying airway diseases,
rather than causing cough directly. In older patients, lung tumors
can certainly be a cause of coughing, but this is usually accompanied
by other signs, like lethargy, weight loss and difficult breathing.

WHAT TESTS ARE NEEDED?
A thorough physical exam is usually sufficient to identify the primary
cause of persistent cough, and conservative management can be
opted by your veterinarian, like most doctors do with people with a
cold. However, when needed, your veterinarian may recommend a
blood test, a fecal exam or chest X-rays. In some selected cases,
advanced diagnostic tests or specialist referral may be discussed.

WHAT TREATMENT CAN BE USED?
If cough is persistent, your veterinarian will try to identify and
eliminate the underlying cause. Cough should not be suppressed
unless it is interfering with your pet’s quality of life. Several nonpharmacological interventions can be considered in the first instance
for the management of persistent cough, as follows:
1. Avoidance of irritants. Cigarette smoke, dust, sprays from
deodorants, perfumes, and house cleaning products are all
potential irritants. If present in the house, carpets should be
vacuumed frequently. Cleaned cotton sheets should be used to
cover the pet’s bed and changed frequently.
2. Avoidance of excessive, strenuous exercise in dogs. Gentle and
long walks are more indicated than fast short runs. Light
exercise can assist in dislodging bronchial mucus and helps
open small airways by promoting increased lung volumes
associated with a standing position.
3. A harness should be worn instead of a collar when the dog is
walked on a leash.

4. Weight control. Fat tends to accumulate in the chest and
reduce the lung volume. This can cause compression of the
airways and stimulate cough. Weight reduction will improve
respiration, exercise capacity, and cardio-vascular functions
with dramatic results.
5. Relief of airway obstruction. Humidification favors
expectoration from the deeper airways, bronchi, and trachea
because it thins the mucus and lubricates the irritated
respiratory tract. Ultrasound humidifiers (“cool mist”) are
available in many health & beauty shops and they can be
activated overnight in the room where the animal sleeps.
During, or immediately after, humidification the owner can
perform “coupage.” This maneuver seems to dislodge some of
the deeper secretions and helps them move into the airways,
causing initially more cough that will remove mucus from the
chest.
If your pet does not improve following the above conservative
interventions, pharmacological treatment (e.g., inhaled steroids,
antibiotics, antitussives) should be discussed with your veterinarian.
Luca Ferasin (Alton, Hampshire, United Kingdom)

Nasal Discharge
Julio López

This chapter is enhanced with the following electronic assets
on Elsevier eBooks+: 5 Videos.
Sneezing is an involuntary, protective reflex that expels air from
the lungs through the nose and mouth in a sudden, explosive manner
to clear the upper airways. It is triggered when chemical or physical
irritants stimulate the subepithelial receptors in the nose. Sneezing
or nasal discharge may occur in diseases of the nose, sinuses and
nasopharynx (Box 35.1) or may be secondary to lower airway or
systemic disease (Box 35.2).

Clinical Presentations
Most patients with nasal disease will present for evaluation of nasal
discharge or sneezing. Signs of caudal nasal cavity disease include

stertor, reverse sneezing, excessive swallowing, gagging (ch. 47),
coughing (ch. 34), dysphagia (ch. 47), and changes in phonation.
Clinical signs are not usually pathognomonic for a particular disease
and various ancillary tests are required to reach a diagnosis.

Stertor
This term refers to a snorting/snoring respiratory sound indicating
an obstruction to airflow at the nasopharynx that usually resolves
with open-mouth breathing (ch. 212). Nasal discharge, mass
lesions, and nasopharyngeal swelling can cause it and it is classically
heard in brachycephalic breeds due to an elongated soft palate,
excessive nasopharyngeal tissue, and airway stenosis (

Video

35.1).

Reverse Sneezing
Reverse sneezing is a loud, sometimes violent, inspiratory snoring
sound that occurs without warning. Lasting seconds to minutes, it
may give clients the impression that respiratory distress is occurring.
Irritation of the nasopharyngeal mucosa triggers spasms of the
pharyngeal muscles, leading to obstruction of air passage to the
larynx and transfer of secretions and foreign material to the
oropharynx for swallowing. It is common, and usually of no
consequence (

Video 35.2). Nasopharyngeal disorders such as a

foreign body, the nasal mite (Pneumonyssoides caninum), viral
infection, allergic rhinitis or epiglottic entrapment of the soft palate
should be investigated when reverse sneezing is new or increases in
occurrence.

Nasal Discharge
The location and character of nasal discharge may help formulate a
list of differential diagnoses, keeping in mind the tremendous
overlap amongst diseases that cause it.1 Discharge is typically

unilateral with foreign bodies, oronasal fistulas, aspergillosis, and
neoplasia (ch. 213), and bilateral in inflammatory, infectious, or
allergic disease. It is classified as: serous, mucoid, mucopurulent,
purulent, sanguineous (containing blood), epistaxis (frank
hemorrhage), or food-containing. Nasal discharge may not be noted
in nasopharyngeal disease, as secretions tend to be swallowed.
Serous discharge is watery, clear, and can be a normal finding. If
excessive, it may be a sign of noninfectious inflammatory disease or a
viral upper respiratory tract infection in cats.
Mucopurulent discharge is more viscous and opaque, usually
having a white, yellow, or green coloration. Any nasal disease that
causes inflammation and secondary bacterial infection can present
with this type of discharge, thus making it nonspecific (

Video

35.3).
A sanguineous discharge occurs from damaged nasal mucosa and
may be brought on by continuous sneezing alone. Significant nasal
turbinate destruction or erosion of nasal vascular structures caused
by craniofacial trauma, mycotic infection, or neoplasia can cause a
sanguineous nasal discharge or epistaxis2 (

Video 35.4). It can

also be caused by systemic diseases (hypertension) or hemostatic
disorders (thrombocytopenia, thrombocytopathia, vasculitides, or a
coagulopathy; ch. 171).2
Food material in the nasal cavity suggests a congenital
abnormality such as a cleft palate, a dysphagic condition in a young
animal, or an oronasal fistula in an older animal (ch. 258).

Diagnostic Approach
Signalment
Young animals are more likely to have congenital or infectious causes
of nasal discharge. Conversely, neoplasia and dental disease are
more frequent occurrences in older animals. Animals housed
together or stressed (shows, shelters, kennels, new home), or those
exposed to regional outdoor environments (mycotic infection), are
more susceptible to infectious diseases.

Brachycephalic dogs commonly have conformational causes of
upper airway disease (ch. 213) and less frequently nasal neoplasia,
while brachycephalic cats are at increased risk of fungal rhinitis.3,4
Dolichocephalic breeds are overrepresented with respect to nasal
disease, likely related to the greater surface area of their mucous
membranes increasing exposure to inhaled irritants and allergens.
They also have a higher incidence of fungal rhinitis (ch. 210) and
nasal tumors (ch. 213).3
In cats, nonspecific inflammatory rhinosinusitis is likely the
sequela of upper respiratory viral infection (ch. 205). They alter
normal nasal anatomy and defense mechanisms, causing a
predisposition to secondary bacterial infections and an abnormal
immune response. Cats with neoplasia are more likely to be older,
have dyspnea, or hemorrhagic or unilateral nasal discharge.5
