History
A thorough history (ch. 2) may assist in prioritizing diagnostic tests
and treatments. The pet owner should be questioned about
attendance at shows/kennels, trauma, travel (ch. 9), outdoor
activities (exposure to foxtails/grass awns, fungal organisms) and
recent anesthetic procedures (nasopharyngeal gastric reflux, dental
extractions) (

Videos 35.4 and 35.5). The presence of

gastrointestinal (GI) signs such as appetite changes, vomiting,
retching, eructation or borborygmus may suggest GI disease as an
underlying cause of chronic idiopathic lymphoplasmacytic rhinitis
(ch. 221).6
Another diagnostic aid is the time frame of the onset of clinical
signs (peracute, acute, chronic). Paroxysmal sneezing in a dog that
was recently outdoors might indicate a plant-origin nasal foreign
body (

Video 35.5), especially if accompanied by pawing at the

face. In contrast, acute sneezing in cats is commonly from a viral
etiology. It is less likely from foreign body inhalation due to the
smaller opening of the external nares in cats. Nasopharyngeal
foreign bodies may occur secondary to vomiting or regurgitation of
grass or fur into the nasopharynx. Clients may report reverse
sneezing, increased swallowing or gagging (postnasal drip),
coughing, or audible breathing noises (stertor) in pets with caudal
nasal cavity disease.

Physical Examination
Clinical suspicion of nasal disease can be confirmed by a thorough
physical exam (ch. 3), although at times no abnormalities may be
noted even though significant disease exists. The nose is examined

for the presence of discharge, ulceration/crusting around the nares,
depigmentation of the nares (nasal aspergillosis; ch. 210),
asymmetry of the nose and/or face (nasal neoplasia [ch. 213],
cryptococcosis [ch. 207]), and evidence of pain over the dorsum of
the nose (nasal aspergillosis/neoplasia). Placing a glass slide, a few
hairs or a wisp of cotton in front of each naris and noting
condensation or movement, respectively, assesses patency of the
nasal passages (Video 36.2). In a quiet area, listen for nasal stertor
while keeping the patient’s mouth closed (

Video 35.1).

A thorough oral exam, usually necessitating anesthesia, is
performed as part of a complete evaluation (ch. 258). Mucosal
ulceration (feline calicivirus), fractured teeth, oronasal fistula, cleft
palate, inability to depress the soft palate or a ventral displacement
(nasopharyngeal space-occupying lesion) may be noted. Halitosis
may indicate dental disease, oronasal fistula, or a foreign body.
Exophthalmos, prolapse of the nictitans, deformity of the facial
bones, or inability to retropulse the eye should lead to suspicion for a
retrobulbar mass; disease of the extraocular muscles is a differential
diagnosis. Epiphora may be a sign of nasolacrimal duct occlusion.
Fundic examination (ch. 13) may reveal chorioretinitis (neoplastic
or infectious diseases) or tortuous retinal vessels, retinal
hemorrhages, or retinal detachment (systemic hypertension, ch.
236).
Nasal disease extending beyond the cribriform plate
(neoplasia/aspergillosis) may affect the central nervous system and
therefore, a neurological exam should be performed (ch. 241).
Primary thoracic diseases may cause secondary nasal signs from
secretions coughed into the nasopharynx. Crusting of the nares with
the absence of sneezing or nasal discharge suggests
keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS) or primary dermatoses such as
discoid lupus erythematosus (ch. 178).
Epistaxis (ch. 36) is the most common clinical sign associated
with thrombocytopenia. If petechiae, ecchymoses (ch. 29), or
melena are noted, a hemostatic disorder should be the primary
consideration (chs. 124, 171).

Diagnostic Plan
Using the information gained from the chief concern, signalment,
history, and physical examination, an appropriate systematic
diagnostic plan can be formulated (Figure 35.1). Despite thorough
evaluation, 36.3% of cases of nasal disease in dogs remain
undiagnosed and 23.7% of dogs and 64% of cats are diagnosed with
nonspecific rhinitis.7,8 Likely contributing to these numbers are
cases of early neoplasia or foreign bodies, where repeated testing
would probably lead to a diagnosis. Testing should also be repeated
in patients with chronic rhinosinusitis that have worsening of clinical
signs, to investigate the development of a second disease process.
In most cases of nasal disease, complete blood count and
chemistry panels are not usually helpful in determining a diagnosis.

Despite this, they must be performed to screen for systemic diseases
manifesting with nasal signs and before undergoing diagnostics that
require general anesthesia. Cryptococcal serology titers should be
performed in cats (ch. 207). Aspergillus serologic testing by agar gl
immunodiffusion test may support a diagnosis of fungal rhinitis, as it
was shown to be highly specific (98%) but not sensitive (i.e., a
negative result does not rule out the disease) (ch. 210).9 Fungal
culture as a sole means of diagnosing fungal rhinitis is not
recommended due to the possibility of nonclinical transient fungal
organisms.10 Testing for respiratory viruses (feline calicivirus, feline
herpesvirus-1; ch. 205) by immunodiffusion, enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assay, or polymerase chain reaction is of no use in
most situations due to the high prevalence in healthy cats.11 In cases
of epistaxis (ch. 36), a platelet count, coagulation times
(prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time) or levels
of proteins induced by the antagonism or absence of vitamin K (ch.
170), and blood pressure (ch. 91) should be assessed, and, if
indicated, a buccal mucosal bleeding time (BMBT) should be
performed (ch.79).
Cytologic evaluation of nasal secretions usually reveals nonspecific
inflammation. Occasionally, fungal organisms (Cryptococcus sp.),
parasitic ova (Eucoleus boehmi) or neoplastic cells are noted.
Samples obtained by swabbing, brushing, flushing, or impression
smears of tissue fragments can be used (chs. 89 and 212). Facial or
nasal swellings and enlarged lymph nodes should be sampled by fine
needle aspiration or biopsy (needle core [Tru-Cut] or punch).
Bacterial culture of nasal discharge or the nasal cavity (deep
swabbing or biopsy) is generally considered of little value as it
commonly yields a mixed growth of normal commensal microflora
(ch. 213). Although primary bacterial rhinitis is rare, notable
exceptions include Pasteurella multocida (dogs), Bordetella
bronchiseptica (dogs and cats) and Mycoplasma spp. (cats).12,13
Further assessment beyond these initial steps requires general
anesthesia and should begin with an examination of the oral cavity
(ch. 258). If dental disease is suspected, dental radiographs should
be acquired. Imaging studies should be obtained before performing
dental probing or endoscopic procedures to avoid causing

hemorrhage within the nose that will affect visualization. Regardless
of the diagnostic method chosen, it cannot be stressed enough that
bilateral examination and sampling of the nose should always occur
even when unilateral disease is suspected.

Skull Radiographs
Although not the ideal imaging modality when investigating nasal
disease, routine radiography may reveal the extent and character of
the disease and help direct biopsy sampling. Advantages are that it is
widely available and relatively inexpensive. Disadvantages include
the need for general anesthesia for proper patient positioning and
the inability to detect subtle changes within the nasal cavity.
Superimposition of structures or accumulated fluid may obscure
abnormalities and can be minimized by obtaining intraoral
dorsoventral and/or open-mouth ventrodorsal views, the latter
allowing assessment of the cribriform plate. Lateral oblique views
and rostrocaudal views allow visualization of the dental arcade and
frontal sinuses, respectively.
Rhinitis in dogs and cats, regardless of cause, can have a variable
radiographic appearance depending on chronicity and severity.
Destruction of conchae can be a feature of both rhinitis
(fungal/other) and neoplasia. This finding along with soft tissue
swelling, bony invasion and ipsilateral sinus opacity are more
commonly noted in nasal neoplasia.14,15 In cats, Cryptococcus
neoformans does not usually cause bony destruction. Radiopaque
foreign bodies may be identified. Radiolucent foreign bodies can be
localized by the appearance of a soft tissue opacity caused by
secondary inflammation and discharge.

FIGURE 35.1 Sneezing and nasal discharge in
dogs and cats. From Brown NL. Sneezing and nasal
discharge. In: Ettinger SJ, Feldman EC, eds.
Textbook of Veterinary Internal Medicine . 7th ed.
Saunders Elsevier; 2010.

Computed Tomography (CT)
In contrast to skull radiographs, CT is much quicker to perform and
provides vastly superior, detailed images without the problem of
superimposition.15-17 It also allows for visualization of areas

inaccessible by endoscopy, provides guidance for biopsy
procurement, and helps plan therapeutic strategies for fungal rhinitis
(cribriform plate integrity) or neoplasia (radiation therapy).
Disadvantages include availability and the need for general
anesthesia, although it is becoming more accessible and, with newer
units, sedation may be sufficient. While cost can be a factor, the
superior images obtained may lead to an expedited, cost-effective
diagnosis.
Although CT provides a reasonably accurate differentiation
between neoplastic and nonneoplastic disease in dogs, confirmation
via biopsy should always be performed. Neoplasia is typically
associated with a soft-tissue density and extensive turbinate
destruction, whereas normal to moderate destruction, with or
without soft-tissue densities, is more typical of inflammatory
rhinitis.18 Fungal rhinitis is associated with extensive turbinate
destruction and hyperlucency of the nasal passages.17,19,20 In cats,
features overlap between nasal neoplasia and fungal rhinitis.21
Contrast enhancement may differentiate fluid from vascularized soft
tissue, although it cannot determine the nature of the lesion.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
Although studies show the ability of MRI to diagnose neoplastic
versus inflammatory nasal disease, it is currently not the advanced
imaging modality of choice. In dogs with nasal neoplasia or
aspergillosis, studies have failed to demonstrate an advantage of
MRI over CT.20,22 The lack of a mass effect was significantly
associated with inflammatory disease and a mass effect along with
vomer bone lysis, cribriform plate erosion, paranasal bone
destruction, and invasion of the mass into the sphenoid sinus or
nasopharynx was significantly associated with neoplasia.23
Disadvantages of MRI include prolonged anesthesia due to the time
required to obtain images, the expense, and availability compared to
CT. In cases of undiagnosed chronic nasal disease, MRI may be of
value.

Rhinoscopy/Nasopharyngoscopy (chs.
89, 213)
The nasal cavities, nasopharynx, and, in some cases, the frontal
sinuses can be directly visualized with endoscopic equipment. The
procedures require expertise and moderately expensive equipment.
Small rigid or flexible endoscopes provide adequate visualization of
the nasal cavities. A flexible endoscope is required for access to the
nasopharynx and frontal sinus, although sinuscopy may require
trephination.24 Rigid scopes have better optics and are easier to
maneuver, while flexible scopes are associated with less mechanical
trauma to the tissue. Nasopharyngoscopy should be performed first,
as hemorrhage from rhinoscopy may pool in the nasopharynx and
impair visualization. In addition to endoscopic assessment of the
airways, in cases where signs of GI disease are present, performing
upper GI endoscopy (oropharynx, esophagus, stomach, and
duodenum) concurrently is recommended.6
The procedure can be diagnostic (visualization of fungal plaques,
foreign bodies, nasal polyps, mass lesions, nasal mites,
nasopharyngeal stenosis) as well as therapeutic (removal of foreign
bodies, fungal plaques, flushing/suctioning excessive secretions). It
allows for biopsy procurement under direct visualization. Endoscopy
was superior to nasal radiographs in achieving a diagnosis in dogs
with persistent nasal disease.25 Evaluation of the choanae correctly
identified nasal neoplasia in 26 of 34 animals where biopsies were
obtained.26

Nasal Biopsy (chs. 86, 213)
Several biopsies from each nasal cavity should be procured from all
dogs and cats with chronic nasal disease even if etiology appears to
be unilateral, is obvious (foreign body), or no apparent lesion is
noted. Rhinoscope-guided biopsies are preferred, as visualization
ensures that specific lesions are sampled. Blind biopsy techniques
can also be used, although in order to avoid inadvertent penetration
of the cribriform plate, the clinician should measure the distance

from the tip of the nose to the medial canthus of the eye and ensure
the biopsy instrument does not pass this distance. A CT can
determine the length the biopsy instrument must be advanced to
reach the affected area. Biopsies may also be acquired via traumatic
nasal flush or via rhinotomy.
Cytology of impression smears from biopsy samples may provide a
fast tentative diagnosis.27 If Cryptococcus spp. are detected,
serologic testing should be obtained to determine asymptomatic
carriage from true infection (positive result) and to help monitor
treatment. Hemorrhage (which can be life-threatening) and
aspiration of blood are complications that should be expected.

Treatment/Outcome
The diagnosis and treatment of nasal disease can be frustrating for
both the veterinarian and pet owner. Despite a systematic and
extensive investigation, an etiologic diagnosis remains elusive in
many cases. More often, a descriptive diagnosis based on
inflammatory infiltrates is provided (nonspecific rhinitis) with
management based on symptomatic therapies to alleviate clinical
signs. Specific treatments are available for neoplasia, fungal rhinitis,
foreign bodies, most congenital abnormalities, parasites, GI disease
and dental disease. Prior to undergoing an extensive and costly
investigation, educating the client of possible outcomes and the
potential for lifelong management will help minimize unrealistic
expectations and frustration.

Epistaxis
Initial Approach
Epistaxis is hemorrhage from the nose due to one or more of a
variety of etiologies (Box 36.1). Knowledge of the animal’s
environment and signalment can assist in recognition of the source
of hemorrhage (chs. 2 and 3). Trauma, intranasal transmissible
venereal tumors (TVT; ch. 330), and parasitic (ch. 213), rickettsial

(ch. 193), and fungal (ch. 207) infections are more often seen in
dogs and cats allowed outside. Foreign bodies are generally inhaled
plant material observed in dogs allowed to roam.8 While rodenticide
ingestion (ch. 138) is associated with roaming, it can also occur in
pets kept indoors. Purebred dogs are more commonly affected with
immune-mediated diseases (chs. 169 and 175), von Willebrand
disease (vWD; ch. 175), or congenital coagulation factor deficiencies
(ch. 171). Nasal tumors in dogs are more common in older,
dolichocephalic animals (ch. 213). Nasopharyngeal polyps occur
more often in young cats (ch. 213), while brachycephalic felines are
more susceptible to chronic viral respiratory infections (ch. 205).

History and Physical Examination
A complete history (ch. 2) and physical exam (ch. 3) can provide
essential information. Bleeding that occurs after elective surgery or
minor trauma might indicate a congenital coagulation factor
deficiency or platelet disorder (ch. 171). Epistaxis from foreign body
inhalation is acute in onset and often accompanied by sneezing,
agitation and pawing at the face (

Video 35.5). Foreign objects

lodged in the nasal cavity for long periods of time are associated with
a cellular and chronic nasal discharge (chs. 35, 213). Patients
receiving vitamin K antagonists or platelet inhibitors should have
those dosages reassessed, along with diet, and concurrent
medications (ch. 171). Platelet dysfunction is seen with nonsteroidal
anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) administration (ch. 143).
Immune-mediated platelet dysfunction is seen with vaccines and
some drugs (ch. 175). Estrogens, phenylbutazone, and many
cytotoxic chemotherapy agents can cause thrombocytopenia (chs.
175 and 321).
Nasal trauma results in acute-onset bleeding that resolves with
supportive measures and does not recur. There are usually other
signs of trauma and, due to the proximity of the brain, patients
should be closely monitored for signs of increased intracranial
pressure or focal intracranial hemorrhage (ch. 246).
Seasonal epistaxis might be the result of allergic rhinitis (ch. 213).
Low humidity, especially change from a humid to dry climate, can

dry nasal mucous membranes and result in mild epistaxis. Recurring
episodes of epistaxis are seen with oronasal fistulas, fungal (ch. 210)
and bacterial rhinitis, and nasal tumors (ch. 213). Travel to endemic
areas for fungal and rickettsial organisms, such as ehrlichiosis (ch.
193), leishmaniasis (ch. 197), and hepatozoonosis (ch. 197), can
help rank differential diagnoses and refine the diagnostic plan.
The initial physical examination should prioritize patient
hemodynamics and tissue oxygenation (ch. 119). While emergency
diagnostics are indicated to identify specific treatments, the
possibility of extensive hemorrhage should be assumed since it is
difficult to know the volume of blood lost prior to presentation (ch.
124). The patient’s heart rate, mucous membrane color, capillary
refill time, pulse quality, and blood pressure should be assessed.
Patients with epistaxis as part of a systemic bleeding disorder might
also be bleeding into the lungs or other body cavities. Auscultation of
the chest can identify evidence of intrapleural or intrapulmonary
hemorrhage. Muffled heart sounds might indicate hemopericardium.
Patients with petechiae, mucosal bleeding, melena, or fundic
hemorrhage are likely to have a defect of primary hemostasis
(platelets), whereas those with hemarthrosis, hematomas, or
bleeding into the chest, lungs, or abdomen are likely to have a defect
of secondary hemostasis (coagulation factors).

Treatment of The Unstable Patient
With any evidence of hypovolemia, vascular access should begin with
a peripheral intravenous catheter or intraosseous system (chs. 74
and 76). Before beginning fluid administration, blood samples
should be collected for coagulation testing, packed cell volume,
complete blood count, blood type, and biochemical profile. In a
patient with epistaxis, it is wise to draw blood from peripheral veins
until systemic coagulation status is known, so a pressure wrap can be
applied after phlebotomy if hemostasis is compromised. Rapid
restoration of vascular volume should begin while awaiting results.
Anemic patients showing signs of shock should receive a
transfusion of red blood cells (ch. 124). Patients with prolonged
clotting times should receive a unit of fresh frozen plasma or fresh
whole blood. Plasma is always indicated in the presence of clinically

significant hemorrhage and an abnormal coagulation profile. The
decision to use whole blood should be guided by available
component blood products and the patient’s need for red blood cells.
Blood loss can be minimized by anesthetizing the patient, protecting
the airway with a cuffed endotracheal tube, and occluding the nares
and oropharynx with appropriately sized Foley catheters to create
tamponade (

Video 36.1). Targeted arterial embolization with

interventional radiology techniques is a viable treatment for
intractable epistaxis.1

Further Evaluation and Differential
Diagnosis
When the patient is stable, it is important to inspect the nares,
maxilla, and regions of the paranasal sinuses. Holding a few strands
of cotton or a glass slide in front of the nose can assess nasal patency
and airflow (

Video 36.2). Many intranasal diseases, such as

nasal tumors, begin with unilateral epistaxis that can become
bilateral as the disease progresses and the nasal septum is displaced

or breached. Although bilateral epistaxis might indicate “extranasal”
causes such as coagulopathies, hypertension, thrombocytopenia, and
thrombocytopathia, sometimes epistaxis is unilateral with extranasal
disorders.
Ulceration and depigmentation of the nasal planum can be seen
with immune-mediated disease (ch. 178), fungal infections
(particularly sinonasal aspergillosis, ch. 210), or neoplasia.
Asymmetry of the nose is most often associated with neoplasia. Cats
with nasal cryptococcosis (ch. 207) often have a convexity of the
bridge of the nose referred to as “Roman nose.” Polypoid masses
extending from the nares can be seen with rhinosporidiosis (ch. 211)
and cryptococcosis.
Careful examination of the mouth for severe dental disease,
oronasal fistulas, loose teeth, palate deformity, or masses should be
performed (ch. 258). In addition to facial deformities, nasal tumors
can extend in other directions, causing hard palate deformity. A
fundic examination (ch. 13) might reveal chorioretinitis with
systemic inflammatory diseases, or signs of hypertensive retinopathy
such as retinal hemorrhage or retinal edema and detachment
(especially in cats; ch. 236). Nasal masses can make retropulsing
the globe difficult if they extend into the orbit and can cause
epiphora. Regional lymph nodes should be examined and possibly
aspirated, looking for reactivity, infectious organisms, or metastatic
neoplasia. Melena (ch. 50) and hematemesis can occur when blood
from the nasopharynx is swallowed. Central nervous system (CNS)
dysfunction might occur with hyperviscosity syndromes or nasal
tumors invading the brain (ch. 245).
Intranasal processes are the most common cause of epistaxis, with
nasal tumors the most common cause of epistaxis in older pets (ch.
213). Animals with severe dental disease and/or oronasal fistulas
can have nasal discharge or epistaxis. Much less commonly,
arteriovenous malformations can rupture, causing severe, acute
epistaxis. Primary bacterial rhinitis is uncommon, but usually
involves agents ubiquitous to the respiratory tract like Bordetella,
Pasteurella, and Mycoplasma spp. Aspergillosis in dogs(ch. 210)
and nasal cryptococcosis in cats (ch. 207) are the most common
fungal causes of epistaxis. Cats with upper respiratory infections (ch.
205) can develop sneezing, chronic nasal discharge, mucosal
damage, and intermittent epistaxis.

Systemic causes of epistaxis most often involve clotting disorders.
Primary hemostatic defects (platelet plug formation) include
thrombocytopenia or thrombocytopathia (ch. 175). Decreased
platelet production, abnormal platelet destruction, platelet
sequestration, and increased platelet consumption will lower platelet
numbers. Mild, moderate and severe clinical hemorrhage is possible
with platelet counts less than 25,000 platelets/mcL, 10,000
platelets/mcL, and 5,000 platelets/mcL, respectively.2 Spontaneous
bleeding is uncommon with platelet counts over 50,000/mcL, unless
there is a concurrent platelet function defect. Decreased production
of platelets occurs secondary to infections, myelophthisic neoplasia,
drug reactions, or immune-mediated disorders. Increased
destruction of platelets can be immune-mediated or related to
microangiopathic changes observed with diseases such as
hemangiosarcoma. Sequestration of platelets in the spleen, liver,
large vascular tumors, or following rattlesnake envenomation can
result in a circulating thrombocytopenia. Increased platelet
consumption is seen with disseminated intravascular coagulopathy
(DIC; ch. 171), vasculitis (ch. 181), and hemorrhage (ch. 124).
vWD is the most common cause of primary thrombocytopathia (ch.
175). Secondary thrombocytopathias are more common than
hereditary diseases and can occur with nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug (NSAID) administration (ch. 143), neoplasia
(ch. 331), DIC, liver disease (ch. 266), and dysproteinemias such as
those seen with ehrlichiosis (ch. 193). Thrombocytopathia can occur
with end-stage renal disease due to uremic toxins.3
Hemophilia A and B are uncommon congenital coagulopathies
that vary in severity (ch. 171). Acquired coagulopathies affecting
clotting factors include anticoagulant rodenticide intoxication (chs.
124 and 138) and decreased coagulation factor production
secondary to hepatic failure. Another, less common, systemic cause
of epistaxis is increased capillary fragility, which can result from
systemic hypertension, invasive neoplasia, hyperviscosity
syndromes, hyperlipidemia, and thromboembolic disease.

Clinicopathologic Testing

Regenerative anemia indicates a bone marrow response to blood
loss. It can take a few days to complete the normal regenerative
response to blood loss, making acute hemorrhage appear nonregenerative (ch. 57). A nonregenerative, iron deficiency anemia can
also be seen with chronic epistaxis (ch. 172). Schistocytes can be
observed with microangiopathic diseases such as hemangiosarcoma
and DIC. Leukocytosis occurs with chronic inflammation, infection,
or a regenerative marrow response to blood loss. Leukopenia can be
seen with chronic ehrlichiosis, cytotoxic drug administration, sepsis,
and infections such as Salmonella and canine parvoviral enteritis
(ch. 201). A blood smear can assess platelet numbers.
Thrombocytopathia should be investigated if platelet numbers are
above 100,000/mcL. Buccal mucosal bleeding time (BMBT) is a
useful in-hospital screening test of platelet function (ch. 79). When
abnormal despite a normal platelet count, specific tests such as a von
Willebrand titer are indicated. Coagulation studies, such as activated
partial thromboplastin time (APTT), prothrombin time (PT), and
activated clotting time (ACT), should be performed in cases of
epistaxis in which thrombocytopathia and severe thrombocytopenia
(<10,000/mcL) have been ruled out. If abnormal, a factor-deficiency
coagulopathy should be assumed (ch. 171). Further investigation
into the cause of the coagulation defect can include testing for
anticoagulant rodenticides, evaluation of hepatic and post-hepatic
conditions affecting vitamin K production, and testing for specific
factor deficiencies. Additional tests for consumptive coagulopathies
might include fibrinogen, fibrin degradation products (FDPs), and
antithrombin concentration. Thromboelastography (ch. 170)
evaluates the efficiency of blood coagulation and can assess factors,
such as platelet function, clot strength, and fibrinolysis, that PT,
APTT, and ACT tests cannot.4
Panhypoproteinemia might develop with chronic blood loss.
Hyperglobulinemia is associated with neoplasia or chronic infections
(ch. 183). Serum protein electrophoresis can assist in distinguishing
between monoclonal or polyclonal gammopathy. Monoclonal
gammopathies occur with multiple myeloma, chronic ehrlichiosis,
lymphoma, leukemias, and macroglobulinemia (ch. 60). Azotemia is
essentially always present if a patient has uremia-associated
vasculitis. Hepatic dysfunction can lead to decreased production of

clotting factors and might be evidenced by increased bilirubin and
hepatocellular enzyme activities, or decreased albumin and glucose.
Rickettsial causes of thrombocytopenia, such as ehrlichiosis and
Rocky Mountain spotted fever, are diagnosed serologically (ch. 193).
Aspergillus spp. titers indicate exposure, but correlate poorly with
active infection (ch. 210). Latex agglutination tests for Cryptococcus
spp. capsular antigen are useful for diagnosis and therapeutic
monitoring (ch. 207). Feline leukemia virus (FeLV; ch. 199) and
feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV; ch. 198) tests are indicated in
cats with systemic illness.

Diagnostic Imaging, Endoscopy
The goal of imaging in epistaxis is to localize the disease, determine
the severity, and guide biopsy procedures (ch. 213). Imaging studies
should be performed prior to rhinoscopy and probing bad teeth or
oronasal fistulas. Anything causing iatrogenic hemorrhage might
complicate interpretation of the images. Nasal radiographs should
include lateral, oblique, open-mouth, ventrodorsal, intraoral, and
frontal sinus views. Computed tomography (CT) is superior to
radiographs for nasal disease because it allows visualization of bony
and soft tissue lesions and it images all areas including turbinates,
nasal septum, cribriform plate, and sinuses. Imaging studies should
be examined for asymmetry and bone lysis. Contrast enhancement
can distinguish tumors from an abscess or mucus accumulation.
Rhinoscopy (ch. 89) is performed after a systemic bleeding
disorder has been ruled out, with the animal anesthetized and
intubated with a cuffed endotracheal tube to prevent aspiration of
blood. With the animal in sternal recumbency, the least-affected side
is examined first. Thorough evaluation of the oropharynx and oral
cavity should be performed. Rigid arthroscopes are the most useful
for visualizing the rostral nasal passages. The distance from the
medial canthus to the end of the nostril should be marked on the
instrument prior to entry into the nose to avoid penetration of a
diseased cribriform plate. An otoscope could also be used to view the
rostral nasal passages, especially in cases with a foreign body or large
tumor. A flexible bronchoscope is best suited to visualize the caudal
nasal cavity and nasopharynx. If a rigid scope is used, a spay hook

can be employed to retract the soft palate so that structures in the
nasopharynx can be viewed with a dental mirror and light source.
The entire nasal cavity should be examined for masses, foreign
bodies, polyps, and fungal or inflammatory plaques.

Diagnostic Sampling
Nasal swabs are limited in their utility. The presence of bacteria and
even fungal hyphae is not definitive evidence of a primary infectious
process. Culture of rostral nasal secretions also has limited value.
Cryptococcus infections can be diagnosed cytologically using
standard stains or India ink because of their characteristic thick,
non-staining capsule (ch. 207). Before flushing the nasal cavity or
taking biopsies, the cuff of the endotracheal tube should be checked,
and the oropharynx packed with gauze sponges. Ventroflexing the
head and neck and working from below the level of the nose will help
lavage fluid and blood come out the nose and mouth, protecting the
airway. Saline can be flushed through the nares using the rigid scope,
a feeding tube, or catheter attached to a large syringe. The liquid
recovered should be collected and examined for foreign bodies,
accumulations of cellular debris, and even abnormal tissue and
parasitic ova. Fluids can also be flushed from the nasopharynx
through the nasal passages with a flexible endoscope or large feeding
tube. Multiple biopsies should be obtained from suspicious areas
identified on rhinoscopy. Complications of rhinoscopy and nasal
biopsy include severe hemorrhage, aspiration of blood, and
neurologic signs if the rostral brain is damaged.

Next Steps
Primary bacterial rhinitis is rare, but secondary infection is common.
Antibiotic treatment might improve clinical signs by resolving
secondary infections. If the primary disease is not addressed, it will
likely recur. Deep tissue cultures taken during rhinoscopy are the
most likely to yield primary pathogens in cases with bacterial
infection. If a foreign body is too large to remove or if rhinoscopy,

flushing, and biopsies fail to aid in diagnosis, exploratory rhinotomy
should be considered.

Hemoptysis
Initial Approach
Hemoptysis (from Greek hamia, “blood” + ptysis, “spitting”) is the
expectoration of blood or bloody mucus from the respiratory tract at
or below the larynx (Box 36.2). As with epistaxis, environment and
signalment can indicate the source of hemorrhage. Animals that
roam are susceptible to trauma, rodenticide intoxication, inhalation,
and parasitic, rickettsial, and fungal infections. Young animals might
be inclined to chew electric cords or play with small objects that
could occlude their airway. Older pets are more likely to suffer from
left-sided heart failure and primary lung or metastatic neoplasia.
Furthermore, fungal and heartworm disease have endemic regions
where animals are more likely to be affected.

History
Information regarding cardiac and pulmonary abnormalities,
medications (including heartworm preventative), toxin exposure,
and travel history are essential (ch. 9). Owners should be questioned
about whether the pet has shown signs of exercise intolerance,
dyspnea (ch. 37), syncope (ch. 40), and cough (ch. 34). They
should be asked about recent trips to a groomer or other potentially
stressful events that could trigger non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema
(acute-onset hemoptysis, dyspnea) or that could have been a source
of airborne infection (onset of hemoptysis and cough typically
occurring days after exposure). Since hematemesis can be confused
with hemoptysis, a careful history of gastrointestinal problems might
be necessary. Recent surgery, trauma, or systemic disease can
predispose patients to pulmonary thromboembolism. Prior bleeding
episodes suggest a bleeding disorder. Animals with a history of cough
prior to onset of hemoptysis might have chronic disease, such as
bronchitis, neoplasia, heartworm disease, or left-sided heart failure.
If blood is mixed with inflammatory sputum, more suppurative

problems, such as bronchopneumonia or chronic bronchitis, are
likely. Pulmonary edema fluid is usually bloody, with a frothier
character, while bright red blood is likely to be active arterial
hemorrhage.

Iatrogenic: Endotracheal intubation, complication of lung
biopsy/aspirate, transtracheal wash, or bronchoscopy

Physical Examination
As with epistaxis, the initial physical examination should prioritize
patient hemodynamics and oxygenation (ch. 119). Small amounts of
blood in the lower airways can cause ventilation/perfusion mismatch
and moderate or marked hypoxemia. Supplemental oxygen is usually
indicated especially if the mucous membranes are pale, gray, or
cyanotic (ch. 123). If oxygen by face mask, nasal cannula, oxygen
hood, or oxygen cage is not sufficient, the patient can be intubated
and mechanically ventilated. Hemoptysis secondary to thoracic
trauma is indicative of pulmonary contusions. Contusions are best
managed with cautious fluid therapy and attention to coagulation
function (chs. 123 and 217). Auscultation of the airways might reveal
fixed stridor over the region of an airway foreign body. Dynamic
stridor over the larynx, more pronounced on inspiration, is common
with severe laryngeal paralysis (ch. 214). Auscultation of the chest
might reveal a regurgitant murmur with mitral insufficiency, moist
crackles with pulmonary edema, or evidence of a fluid line with
pleural effusion (ch. 38).

Treatment of The Unstable Patient and
Initial Diagnostic Testing
Vascular access should be established, though fluid therapy should
be approached cautiously. Pre-treatment blood samples should be
collected for coagulation testing, packed cell volume, complete blood
count, and biochemical profile. If a systemic bleeding disorder is
possible, it is wise to draw blood from peripheral veins until systemic
coagulation status is known, so a pressure wrap can be applied after
phlebotomy if hemostasis is compromised. Specific treatment for
left-sided heart failure should be instituted if this is suspected (chs.
123 and 229). Diuretics should be used with caution in hypotensive
or hypovolemic patients.

Differential Diagnosis
Pulmonary edema, secondary to either left heart failure (ch. 229) or
non-cardiogenic causes (ch. 217), can result in expectoration of
blood and pink froth. Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema is
associated with a variety of acutely stressful events, including
electrocution, near drowning, airway obstruction (inhaled foreign
bodies, strangulation, laryngeal paralysis), and seizures.5 Platelet
defects are less likely to cause hemoptysis, whereas acquired
coagulopathies, like anticoagulant rodenticide intoxication, can
present with hemoptysis.
Heartworm disease can cause hemoptysis in dogs and cats (ch.
237). In dogs, exercise after adulticide therapy can result in worm
embolization, inflammation of the pulmonary vasculature and
parenchyma, and hemoptysis. Parasites, including Capillaria,
Aelurostrongylus, and Paragonimus spp., cause pulmonary lesions
that can bleed into airways (ch. 217). Chronic bronchitis (including
feline asthma), bronchiectasis, and eosinophilic
bronchopneumopathy can inflame the mucosa, causing bleeding
during coughing (ch. 215). Infiltrative bacterial and fungal
(Blastomyces [ch. 209], Histoplasma [ch. 209], Coccidioides [ch.
208] spp.) pneumonia, lung abscesses and invasive neoplasia can all
result in hemoptysis (ch. 217). Less common causes of hemoptysis

include pulmonary thromboembolism (ch. 219), pulmonary
hypertension (ch. 218), ruptured arteriovenous malformations (ch.
239), bacterial endocarditis (ch. 232), and lung lobe torsion (ch.
220).
Pneumonic plague caused by Yersinia pestis is a rare but serious
infectious cause of hemoptysis that has recently been reported in
dogs.6 In one case report, the diagnosis of plague was delayed,
resulting in potential exposure of staff, veterinary students, visitors,
and other patients due to the unusual occurrence in this species, the
clinical presentation, and the time of year.6,7

Further Evaluation
In addition to the minimum database above, evaluation for systemic
disease should include arterial blood gas analysis, urinalysis, and
three-view thoracic radiographs. Blood gas results can help identify
hypoxemia and hypoventilation that might require intensive oxygen
support and mechanical ventilation. Proteinuria or a fixed urine
specific gravity could suggest renal or endocrine causes of pulmonary
thromboembolism. Thoracic radiographs should be carefully
evaluated for evidence of cardiac enlargement, pulmonary vascular
congestion, pulmonary edema, traumatic rib fractures and
contusions, pleural effusion, pneumonia, primary or metastatic
neoplasia, foreign objects, and evidence of heartworm disease. If
radiographs localize infiltrates to one lobe, the patient should be
positioned with that side dependent during hospitalization, both for
intrapulmonary hemostasis and for improved oxygenation.
Heartworm testing should be performed in dogs and cats from
endemic areas (ch. 237). An echocardiogram can help characterize
cardiogenic pulmonary edema and diagnose pulmonary
hypertension (ch. 97). Parenchymal lesions in the lung can require
the additional detail of a CT or magnetic resonance imaging scan of
the thorax.

Next Steps

Pulmonary edema, arterial hemorrhage from an invasive lesion, and
traumatic pulmonary contusions are the most serious causes of
hemoptysis. Sedation and supplemental oxygen after treating the
cause of non-cardiogenic edema is usually sufficient. Cardiogenic
edema can be managed with diuretics alone (ch. 229), though
severe cases might require additional support (ch. 123). Traumatic
pulmonary contusions present a therapeutic challenge, as intensive
fluid therapy might exacerbate bleeding. Careful attention to blood
pressure, patient temperature, blood calcium concentration, and
arterial pH will help identify other treatable causes of bleeding in the
trauma patient. Fortunately, most other causes of hemoptysis are
self-limiting with mild sedation and cage rest.

Dyspnea and Respiratory

This chapter is enhanced with the following electronic assets
on Elsevier eBooks+: 4 Videos and 1 Client Information Sheet.
The term dyspnea is frequently used to refer to difficult or labored
breathing, though it more precisely refers to the conscious sensation
of shortness of breath.1 Respiratory distress is therefore perhaps a
more accurate term for what may be observed clinically in our
veterinary patients and it appropriately highlights the seriousness of

this finding. Orthopnea refers to dyspnea that is positional,
specifically present when the patient is recumbent or lying down
(positions other than standing or sitting upright).2 Tachypnea refers
to an increased rate of respiration, which may occur with or without
respiratory distress. These clinical signs are most commonly
associated with disorders affecting the respiratory system, pleural
space, or thoracic wall, though occasionally they may be due to nonrespiratory conditions, such as metabolic or electrolyte disturbances,
central nervous system disease, endocrine disorders, hypotension,
and pharmacologic interventions.3 In dogs, tachypnea should be
differentiated from panting, which is rapid and shallow open-mouth
breathing without respiratory distress and which is most often
associated with thermoregulation, anxiety, or pain, and more rarely
with other medical conditions.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Control of breathing involves the integration of three main elements:
1. Sensors that gather data, 2. The respiratory control center in the
brain that coordinates the data and sends impulses to the 3. Effector
muscles (diaphragm, intercostal, and abdominal muscles).4 The
main sensors include central and peripheral chemoreceptors, which
are sensitive to changes in arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide
(PaCO2), and both arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) and
PaCO2, respectively. Under normal conditions, PaCO2 sensed by the
central chemoreceptors is the most important stimulus for
ventilation and is very tightly controlled. Under abnormal
conditions, hypoxemia sensed by peripheral chemoreceptors
becomes an important driver of ventilation, and the response is
heightened by concurrent hypercarbia.4 By the time respiratory
distress is present, there is typically significant hypoxemia or
hypercarbia (often PaO2 <60 mm Hg or PaCO2 >50 mm Hg,
depending on duration).3,4 Causes of hypoxemia include: 1.
Decreased fraction of inspired O2, 2. Hypoventilation, 3. Diffusion
impairment, 4. Right-to-left cardiovascular shunt, 5. Ventilation-

perfusion (VQ) inequality, and 6. Abnormal hemoglobin. The main
causes of hypercarbia include: 1. Hypoventilation, and 2. VQ
inequality.5

INITIAL ASSESSMENT OF THE
DYSPNEIC PATIENT (ch. 123)
Respiratory distress is a common presenting complaint that
necessitates immediate evaluation and attention, as respiratory
compromise can very rapidly deteriorate to respiratory failure or
arrest (ch. 123). Since stress and anxiety can contribute to this
deterioration, these patients should be handled minimally and
judiciously. Oxygen therapy should be immediately administered via
face mask, flow-by, nasal prongs, nasal cannula, hood, or cage. The
choice of delivery method necessitates balancing the invasiveness of
the technique with the inspired oxygen levels achieved for the given
patient’s condition and temperament. While oxygen is being
administered, much information can be gained from observing the
patient at a distance (ch. 3). It is important to note posture, mental
alertness and behavior, and respiratory pattern, including rate,
regularity, depth, and effort (both degree and timing with the
respiratory phase). This information, in conjunction with more
detailed physical exam findings, may be used for assessing severity
and localizing the problem to the upper airways (chs. 213, 214),
lower airways (ch. 215), pulmonary parenchyma (ch. 217), pleural
space (ch. 220), or thoracic wall (ch. 222).3,6,7 Labored breathing
that results in exaggeration or prolongation of a phase of the
respiratory cycle is described as obstructive, and can further be
characterized as having more inspiratory effort (suggesting an upper
airway disorder) (

Video 37.1), more expiratory effort (suggesting

a lower airway disorder) (

Video 37.2), or both (mixed) (Videos

37.3 and 37.4; Figure 37.1). Labored breathing that results in
shorter, rapid, shallow breaths is described as restrictive, and may be
seen with pulmonary parenchymal or pleural space disease which
may be differentiated using additional physical examination features

(Figure 37.1). Localization of dyspnea becomes important in
selecting the most appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic actions.
Markedly hypoxemic animals will appear panicked, often with
elbows abducted, head and neck extended, nostrils flared, and with a
glazed expression as they are focused on breathing (

Video 37.4).

It is important to promptly recognize upper airway obstruction
(exaggerated inspiratory effort with little to no air movement) as
sedation and intubation may be necessary immediately. Also
important to recognize is the paradoxical or inverse breathing
pattern, where during inspiration, the caudal intercostal muscles and
ribs are noted to collapse inward with diaphragmatic contraction and
the abdomen is noted to move outward as the cranial abdominal
contents are forced caudally (

Video 37.3).1,6 This pattern

indicates greatly increased work of breathing and respiratory muscle
fatigue,1 and has been significantly associated with pleural space
disease in both dogs and cats.6,8 A thorax that is barrel-shaped or
increased in size with expansion of the thoracic wall may indicate
tension pneumothorax or marked pleural effusion, although breedassociated thoracic conformation can have an important
confounding effect.9 Two or more fractures of two or more adjacent
ribs may result in flail chest, recognized as a segment of thoracic wall
moving in during inspiration and out on expiration (chs. 220,
222).3,9

FIGURE 37.1 Algorithm for localization and
diagnostic approach to the dyspneic patient. BAL,
Bronchoalveolar lavage; CBC, complete blood count;
CT, computed tomography; FB, foreign body; FNA,
fine needle aspirate; HW, heartworm; MRI,

magnetic resonance imaging; PTE, pulmonary
thromboembolism; TTW, transtracheal wash.
Some patients will require other immediate therapy in addition to
oxygen supplementation (ch. 123). This may include sedation to
reduce anxiety and work of breathing or to facilitate intubation.
Opioids (e.g., butorphanol 0.1-0.2 mg/kg intramuscular [IM] or
intravenous [IV]) and benzodiazepines (e.g., midazolam 0.1-0.2
mg/kg IM or IV) alone or in combination tend to be effective and
have a good safety profile.3,9 Cooling may be necessary as patients
frequently become hyperthermic from the work of breathing,
particularly those with upper airway obstruction (ch. 130).3,9,10
Techniques include using a fan, shaving fur, applying cool wet
towels, and administering IV fluids. If airway obstruction or
imminent respiratory arrest is anticipated, then endotracheal (ET)
intubation should be performed. Manual or mechanical ventilation
may then be instituted if necessary depending on blood gas analysis
and work of breathing. If intubation cannot be achieved due to the
presence of a physical or functional obstruction (e.g., laryngeal
paralysis or mass), a tracheotomy may be necessary. A red rubber
feeding tube or jugular catheter can sometimes be passed beyond the
obstruction to deliver oxygen while preparing for a tracheotomy.9 If
pleural effusion or pneumothorax is suspected, thoracocentesis
should be performed and fluid samples saved for cytologic evaluation
and microbial culture (ch. 92).

HISTORY
Signalment can be very relevant for identifying breed and age
predispositions. Young dogs may be presented more commonly for
breed-associated upper respiratory tract obstruction (ch. 213) and
pleural space disorders secondary to trauma (ch. 220).7 Other
breed- and age-associated conditions include brachycephalic breeds
like Bulldogs and brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome
(BOAS, ch. 213); smaller-breed dogs like Yorkshire Terriers and
Pomeranians and collapsing trachea (ch. 215); older, small-breed
dogs and congestive heart failure due to myxomatous mitral valve

disease (MMVD, ch. 232); older, larger-breed dogs and laryngeal
paralysis ch. 214; West Highland White Terriers and pulmonary
fibrosis ch. 217; young to middle-aged cats and asthma ch. 215; and
middle-aged to older cats and pleural effusion ch. 220.7,11-17
Historical information of importance (chs. 1 and 2) includes the
duration and progression of clinical signs,7 and the presence of
concurrent respiratory signs like coughing, wheezing, sneezing,
snoring, nasal or ocular discharge, or change in tonality of bark or
meow. Also of importance is the presence of other systemic signs
that may point to involvement of other body systems (weakness,
exercise intolerance, collapse, vomiting, regurgitation, seizures) or
the presence of known pre-existing disorders (respiratory, cardiac,
neuromuscular, metabolic, immune-mediated, inflammatory).
Thorough questioning on possible exposure to trauma, toxins (e.g.,
rodenticides), allergens, smoke, other environmental conditions,
electrocution, other dogs or cats, and ticks should be performed.
Information on heartworm status and prophylaxis in endemic areas
and travel history should also be collected.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Complete and thorough physical examination remains the mainstay
of accurate patient assessment and initial diagnosis (ch. 3). As
mentioned above, of primary importance is noting the respiratory
pattern, including rate, depth, and timing and degree of effort, to aid
in localization (Figure 37.1). During examination of the head,
symmetry of the face and nose should be noted, because asymmetry
may suggest space-occupying lesions or traumatic injuries. Patency
of nasal air flow should be assessed by differential occlusion of the
nostrils and listening or watching for air flow through the patent
nostril, or holding a chilled microscope slide up to the nose and
observing for steaming (

Video 36.2). Ocular and nasal discharge

(ch. 35) may indicate an infectious process, and precautions to avoid
spread to other patients ± isolation protocols may be warranted.
Loud respiratory noise, including stertor (snoring-type inspiratory
sounds) or stridor (high-pitched, whistling-type inspiratory sounds),

is indicative of upper airway obstruction.6 Oral mucous membrane
color provides an indication of oxygenation and crude perfusion
(cyanosis, pallor). An exam of the oral cavity for electrocution burn
wounds, or obvious mass, foreign body (FB), or blood in the mouth
or pharynx is warranted, though a complete exam may not be
achievable until the patient is sedated (ch. 258). Light sedation is
certainly necessary to properly examine laryngeal function (
Video 214.1). The neck should be palpated for signs of trauma or
esophageal FB.
The thorax should be palpated for signs of trauma, rib fractures, or
cardiac thrills. In cats, compressibility of the cranial thorax should be
assessed, as lack thereof may suggest the presence of a cranial
thoracic or mediastinal mass.18 Thoracic auscultation is of central
importance. The identification of murmurs, gallops, or arrhythmias
on cardiac auscultation (ch. 38) supports the presence of cardiac
disease that may be responsible for respiratory distress. It is
important to recognize, however, that the same geriatric small breed
dogs that are predisposed to MMVD may also be predisposed to
airway diseases such as chronic bronchitis or collapsing trachea, and
cats may have physiologic murmurs; therefore, the presence of a
heart murmur does not automatically indicate the dyspnea is cardiac
in origin. Conversely, the absence of a murmur in a cat or a large
breed dog does not rule out cardiac disease as the cause of dyspnea
given their predisposition to cardiomyopathies. The presence of an
audible gallop (third heart sound), tachycardia, and hypothermia has
been demonstrated to be highly suggestive of cardiac cause for
dyspnea in cats.19 Displaced or muffled heart sounds may indicate
the presence of a mass, diaphragmatic hernia, and/or effusion.
Pulmonary auscultation may reveal increased bronchovesicular (BV)
sounds as a result of airway narrowing by constriction or secretions
causing flow turbulence. Tracheal auscultation should be performed
to determine whether the source of increased BV sounds is indeed
the lower airways or is referred from the upper airway. Crackles or
wheezes may be heard with lower airway or pulmonary parenchymal
disorders. Crackles, also called rales, are discontinuous popping
sounds resulting from air bubbling through fluid (not just
cardiogenic edema) or from rapid opening of stiff airways. Wheezes

are high-pitched continuous musical sounds indicating air
movement through very narrowed airways. Decreased to absent lung
sounds indicate the presence of something preventing transmission
of lung sounds through the thoracic wall. If decreased ventrally,
pleural effusion or a space-occupying mass may be present, whereas
if decreased dorsally, pneumothorax may be present. Thoracic
percussion would tend to yield dullness and increased resonance
with free fluid and air, respectively.
Abdominal palpation should be performed and may reveal
discomfort or pain, ascites (suggesting cardiac disease, portal
hypertension, neoplasia, or hypoproteinemia; ch. 21), or distension
from aerophagia. Femoral pulse quality (ch. 39) may reveal
additional information referable to cardiovascular status.

LOCALIZATION AND DIFFERENTIAL
DIAGNOSIS
UPPER AIRWAY (chs. 213-215)
The upper airway is composed of the nasal passages, pharynx,
larynx, and extra-thoracic trachea. Patients with upper airway
obstruction exhibit inspiratory dyspnea characterized by effort
during a long inspiratory phase and inspiratory noise (

Video

37.1).6 Patients with upper airway disorders may have noisy stertor
(snoring) if there is partial obstruction of the nasal passages or
nasopharynx (ch. 3).3 Differential diagnoses in this case may
include stenotic nares, nasal FB, neoplasia, rhinitis (infectious or
inflammatory), or nasopharyngeal polyp (ch. 213). Dyspnea may be
accompanied by stridor (a harsh, high-pitched inspiratory sound) in
the case of laryngeal or tracheal obstruction (chs. 214 and 215).3
Common differential diagnoses include laryngeal paralysis,
neoplasia, FB, BOAS, and extra-thoracic tracheal collapse. Additional
signs with upper respiratory obstruction may include choking,
retching, pawing at the face, or a honking cough (in the case of
tracheal collapse).

LOWER AIRWAY (chs. 215 and 216)
The lower airways include the intrathoracic trachea, bronchi, and
bronchioles. Patients with lower airway disease typically exhibit
expiratory dyspnea, characterized by a shorter inspiratory phase and
longer expiratory phase with effort or push, sometimes involving the
abdomen (

Video 37.2).3,6 Increased BV sounds, wheezes, or

crackles (inspiratory and/or expiratory) may be heard on
auscultation. Common differential diagnoses for larger airway
disease include tracheal and/or bronchial collapse or
tracheobronchitis (ch. 215), and for the smaller lower airways
include feline asthma in cats, chronic bronchitis, eosinophilic
bronchopneumopathy, smoke inhalation, and bronchopneumonia
(chs. 215, 216).

PULMONARY PARENCHYMA (ch. 217)
Disease involving the alveolar ducts and alveoli, pulmonary
interstitium, or pulmonary vasculature may result in mixed
inspiratory and expiratory dyspnea (

Videos 37.3 and 37.4).

Alternatively, these patients may have a restrictive pattern with rapid
and shallow breathing if the disease prevents the lungs from fully
expanding. Increased BV sounds and often crackles are noted on
auscultation.3,6 Differential diagnoses may include cardiogenic
pulmonary edema, non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (secondary to
strangulation/upper airway obstruction, electrocution, head trauma,
post-seizure, vasculitis), pneumonia (viral, bacterial, fungal),
hemorrhage, neoplasia, parasitic disease, pulmonary
thromboembolism, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, the acute
respiratory distress syndrome, or pulmonary contusions (trauma)
(ch. 217). This extensive (yet still incomplete) list of differentials
emphasizes the importance of identifying and considering other
historical and physical exam data including history or evidence of
cardiac disease, history of vomiting or regurgitation to suggest
aspiration pneumonia, history of trauma, electrocution, heartworm
status, and travel. Distribution of pulmonary changes on thoracic

radiographs can be helpful in narrowing these differential
diagnoses.10

PLEURAL SPACE (ch. 220)
Patients with pleural space disease may have a restrictive breathing
pattern characterized by rapid and shallow respirations due to an
inability of the lungs to expand, or they may have mixed inspiratory
and expiratory dyspnea. As mentioned above, paradoxical breathing
(caudal thorax moving inward and abdomen moving outward on
inspiration) has been correlated with pleural space disease in both
dogs and cats.6,8 Lung sounds tend to be muffled at least ventrally
with pleural effusion and dorsally with pneumothorax. If significant
air or fluid in the pleural space is suspected to be causing dyspnea,
thoracocentesis should be performed (ch. 92). Differential
diagnoses for pleural space disease include pneumothorax,
pyothorax, hemothorax, chylothorax, masses, diaphragmatic hernia,
and transudative pleural effusion due to a variety of causes including
neoplastic disease, cardiac disease, lung lobe torsion, or
hypoproteinemia.

THORACIC WALL (ch. 222)
Patients with disorders of the thoracic wall tend to hypoventilate due
to failure of the normal respiratory apparatus. They exhibit
respiratory distress in the face of decreased thoracic wall movement,
lacking intercostal, diaphragmatic, and abdominal assistance during
respiration. They may or may not have signs of trauma. This pattern
may be a result of neuromuscular disease (peripheral neuropathies,
brain disorders, spinal cord disease between C1-C4, phrenic
innervation abnormalities) or trauma (rib fractures, flail chest,
penetrating wounds). Therapy in these patients typically necessitates
intubation and ventilation.

DIAGNOSTIC INVESTIGATION

Further diagnostic tests are typically necessary to obtain a definitive
diagnosis. However, the necessity and timing of these tests must be
balanced with patient safety and stability. When instituted in a
dyspneic patient, they are best done in an interrupted fashion to
allow the patient to return to oxygen and to rest. Suggestions for
diagnostic work-up based on initial assessment are outlined in
Figure 37.1. Preliminary thoracic imaging often includes thoracic
radiography and/or thoracic focused assessment with sonography
for triage and trauma (TFAST; ch. 73).20,21 N-terminal pro-B-type
natriuretic peptide may also be used to aid in differentiation of
cardiac and respiratory causes of dyspnea.22-24 Cardiac evaluation
including echocardiography (ch. 97) and electrocardiography (ch.
96) may be indicated. Pleural fluid analysis and culture should be
performed if pleural effusion is present (ch. 71). More directed
respiratory evaluations, including oral and laryngeal examination
(chs. 217, 258), rhinoscopy (ch. 89), fluoroscopy for tracheal or
bronchial collapse (ch. 212), transtracheal wash (ch. 93),
bronchoscopy and lavage (ch. 93), computed tomography,25 and
fine needle pulmonary or mass aspirates, among others, may be
pursued as indicated (ch. 212). While awaiting diagnostic results,
empirical therapy for common causes of respiratory distress is often
administered, at least as single doses (e.g., furosemide for heart
failure, bronchodilator and corticosteroid for feline asthma or
chronic bronchitis), particularly when there is evidence to support
these on history or physical exam.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Your pet has been diagnosed with a condition that places him/her at
risk of labored breathing (dyspnea) and/or fast breathing
(tachypnea). These conditions can lead to severe respiratory distress
in some cases; therefore, recognition of developing problems is
important. In addition to administering all medication as per your
veterinarian’s recommendations, you can play an active role in your
pet’s care by monitoring their breathing on a daily basis, paying
particular attention to rate and effort. You can also take efforts to
minimize stress or anxiety in your pet’s environment, as these factors
can exacerbate breathing difficulties.
How to Count Your Pet’s Breathing Rate
Breathing rate is best counted when your pet is at complete rest.
Observe your pet’s chest wall movements and note that the chest
expands outward with each breath in, then back down with each
breath out. This outward then inward chest movement represents
one breath cycle. Count the number of breath cycles in 15 seconds
and multiply by 4 to get the per minute breathing rate. Normal
resting breathing rate for dogs and cats is less than 30 breaths per
minute. It can be helpful to trend your pet’s breathing rate on a daily
to weekly basis.
Additional Important Signs to Watch For
• Increased breathing effort
• Shallow, rapid breathing
• Open-mouth breathing (to be differentiated from panting)
• Noisy breathing

• Discomfort lying down or increased breathing difficulties when
lying down
• Restlessness at night
• Decreased activity level or decreased tolerance of usual
exercise
• Weakness or collapse
• Blue gum color (it is best to observe the gums, not the tongue)
When to Call Your Veterinarian and/or Seek Veterinary
Attention
• Breathing rate consistently >35 breaths per minute at rest
• Breathing that appears labored, difficult, or uncomfortable in
any way
• Inability to lie down comfortably
• Collapse episode
• Blue gum color
• Any other signs that have you concerned
M. Lynne O’Sullivan (Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island,
Canada)

Sounds and Heart Murmurs
