This chapter is enhanced with the following electronic assets
on Elsevier eBooks+: 1 Video and 18 Audios.
Cardiac auscultation is an important tool in the clinician’s
armamentarium.1-7 Interpretation of heart and lung sounds is
predicated on the clinician’s understanding of their genesis in health

and a variety of clinical disorders. Cardiovascular sounds of short
duration are referred to as transient heart sounds and include the
normally heard first heart sound (S1) and second heart sound (S2)
(Audio 38.1

). Heart murmurs (synonym: cardiac murmurs) are

auditory vibrations of longer duration created when laminar flow is
disrupted.
Implementing good technique with a quality stethoscope is
fundamental. During auscultation the animal should be standing or
sitting in a quiet environment.4 Both sides of the thorax should be
carefully auscultated using the stethoscope’s diaphragm and bell,
with special attention to the areas overlying the cardiac valves. The
clinician should correlate the various heart sounds to the events of
the cardiac cycle (Figure 38.1). A good point of reference is palpation
of the precordial impulse (left apex beat) that occurs just after S1,
and the arterial pulse that is felt between S1 and S2.

Normal Heart Sounds
The first heart sound (Figure 38.1) is associated with closure and
tensing of the atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid) at the
onset of systole, typically coinciding with the QRS complex on the
electrocardiogram. S1 is longer, louder, and lower pitched than S2.
Causes of increased intensity of S1 include thin chest wall,
tachycardia, high sympathetic tone, systemic arterial hypertension
(ch. 236), and anemia (ch. 57). Diminished intensity of S1 may be
auscultated in animals with obesity (ch. 150), pleural (ch. 220) or
pericardial (ch. 235) effusion, diaphragmatic hernia (chs. 222,
235), dilated cardiomyopathy (ch. 233), hypovolemia (ch. 121),
emphysema, or a prolonged P-R interval. Splitting of S1 is
occasionally auscultated at the cardiac apex in healthy, large-breed
dogs or may result from electrical disturbances (ectopic beats,
bundle branch blocks, cardiac pacing; ch. 230) or mechanical
factors (tricuspid or mitral stenosis; ch. 231).

The second heart sound (Figure 38.1) is associated with closure
of the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonic) at the end of systole,
typically following the T wave on the electrocardiogram. In dogs and
cats, pulmonic valve (P2) closure follows aortic valve (A2) closure by
a very short interval, which causes S2 to be heard as a single sound.
On occasion an audible, split S2 may be seen in healthy, large-breed
dogs during inspiration due to a longer right ventricular ejection
period. Pathologic splitting of S2 due to delayed P2 can occur with
heartworm disease (ch. 238; Audio 38.2

), primary pulmonary

hypertension (ch. 218) and right-to-left patent ductus arteriosus
(ch. 231).

FIGURE 38.1 Murmur shapes and descriptions
with some common examples.The upper tracing is
an electrocardiogram; the shaded areas for each
murmur correspond to the phonocardiographic
appearance (“shape”) of the respective sounds. The
line diagram at the bottom is also a
phonocardiogram, depicting normal and transient

heart sounds. Also depicted are normal and
abnormal transient heart sounds and their location
within the cardiac cycle. A2, Aortic valve closure; AV, atrioventricular; meso, mid; P2, pulmonic valve
closure; proto, early; S1, first heart sound; S2, second
heart sound; S3, third heart sound; S4, fourth heart
sound; tele, late; VSD, ventricular septal defect.
Pathologic splitting of S2 (due to delayed closure of P2) also occurs
with left-to-right intracardiac shunts (notably large atrial septal
defects), pulmonic stenosis, right bundle branch block, ectopic beats,
and ventricular pacing. Less commonly, S2 splitting can occur due to
premature A2, as with certain cases of mitral insufficiency and mitral
stenosis. Paradoxical splitting of S2 results from delayed closure of
the aortic valve and is sometimes audible in dogs with aortic
stenosis, left bundle branch block, ectopic beats, and systemic
hypertension.

ADDITIONAL HEART SOUNDS
The Third (S 3 ) and Fourth (S 4 ) Heart Sounds
The third and fourth heart sounds occur during diastole and are not
audible in normal dogs and cats. S3 and S4 heart sounds are of lower
frequency than S1 and S2 and are usually best heard with the bell of
the stethoscope. When heard, S3 and S4 may sound like the triple
cadence of a galloping horse (Audio 38.3

).

The term gallop rhythm should probably be avoided because the
presence of an audible S3 or S4 has nothing to do with the heart’s
underlying electrical rhythm. Rapid ventricular filling generates the
S3 sound, also known as S3 gallop, protodiastolic gallop, or
ventricular gallop. An audible S3 (Audio 38.4

) is most

commonly heard with diastolic volume overloading as in dilated
cardiomyopathy (ch. 233), patent ductus arteriosus (ch. 231), and
mitral insufficiency (ch. 232). In dogs with mitral insufficiency, the
S3 gallop may be mistaken for the second heart sound if a loud
pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur extends through the second heart
sound. Protodiastolic gallop sounds in cats are most commonly
associated with dilated cardiomyopathy, anemia, and
hyperthyroidism.
The presystolic gallop, also called S4 gallop or atrial gallop, is
heard just before S1 and occurs just after the P wave on the
electrocardiogram. This low-frequency sound is generated by blood
flow into the ventricles during atrial contraction; hence the absence
of S4 gallops with atrial fibrillation. An audible S4 (Audio 38.5

)

in the cat and dog is usually associated with increased ventricular
hypertrophy and stiffness and is sometimes audible in animals with
third-degree atrioventricular block.
At fast heart rates, rapid ventricular filling and atrial systole occur
very close together, which makes differentiation between S3 and S4
impossible. The resulting single accentuated sound is referred to as a
summation gallop.8,9

Ejection Sounds, Systolic Clicks, Opening
Snaps, and Pericardial Knocks
Ejection sounds are left basilar high-frequency sounds generated by
opening of the semilunar valves or dilatation of the great vessels and
they occur during early systole. These sounds are occasionally noted
in pulmonic stenosis, aortic stenosis, tetralogy of Fallot, and
heartworm disease.
BOX 38.1 Grading o f C ar diac Mu rmu rs
Grade 1: Very soft, localized murmur detected in a quiet room
after intently listening for a minute or more

Grade 2: Soft murmur but easily heard after a few seconds
Grade 3: Moderate-intensity murmur
Grade 4: Loud murmur but not accompanied by a palpable
thrill (vibration)
Grade 5: Loud murmur accompanied by a palpable thrill
Grade 6: Very loud murmur that produces a palpable thrill
and is still audible after stethoscope is removed 1 cm from the
thoracic wall
Systolic clicks are mid to late high frequency sounds usually heard
best over the mitral valve area (Audio 38.6

).10,11 Systolic clicks

are occasionally associated with degenerative valvular disease, mitral
valve prolapse, and mitral dysplasia. The genesis of the sound in
dogs is uncertain but is likely caused by the sudden tensing of
redundant valve leaflets or elongated chordae tendineae as they
buckle into the left atrium. A systolic click should be differentiated
from a split (Audio 38.2) or gallop heart sound (Audio 38.3

).

Opening snaps are the audible manifestation of early-diastolic
opening of a stenotic mitral valve. They are rarely documented in
dogs or cats. Pericardial knocks are uncommon early diastolic
sounds caused by constrictive pericardial disease. Timing of the
sound is similar to S3 and appears to be generated by abrupt
restriction to ventricular filling by a diseased pericardium. See
Figure 38.1 for timing of transient heart sounds and description of
murmurs.

Cardiac Murmurs
Cardiac murmurs represent sounds of longer duration than the
transient heart sounds. Cardiac murmurs are caused by turbulent
blood flow in the heart or adjacent blood vessels created upon
disruption of normal laminar flow. The development of turbulent
blood flow can be created by high-velocity flow, flow from narrow
restricted area into a larger area, or low blood viscosity. The
relationship of cardiac murmurs and flow velocity, vessel size, and

blood viscosity is defined by the Reynolds number. When the
number reaches a critical high level, blood flow becomes turbulent.

Murmurs can be characterized and described by their timing
within the cardiac cycle (systolic, diastolic, portions thereof),
location (point of maximal intensity [PMI]) on the surface of the
body, radiation away from the PMI, intensity (loudness), shape, and
frequency (pitch).

Timing
Systolic murmurs may start immediately at the first (S1) heart sound
and last through the second (S2) heart sound (pansystolic murmur),
may start immediately after S1 and last until S2 (holosystolic), or may
occur in early (protosystolic), mid (mesosystolic), or late
(telesystolic) systole. Diastolic murmurs most commonly occur in
early diastole (protodiastolic), throughout diastole (holodiastolic), or
can occasionally be audible only at the end of diastole (presystolic).

Location and Radiation
The location of a murmur refers to the valve area at which the
murmur is heard best (PMI). Alternatively, location can be described
simply by the terms apex or base (e.g., left apex or mitral valve area).
Some murmurs may also radiate to other areas, yielding important
clues as to the source of the murmur. For example, the murmur of
subvalvular aortic stenosis (PMI at left heart base) may radiate to the
ventral neck area due to turbulence in the carotid arteries and may
also be heard on the right cranial thorax (ch. 231).

Intensity (Loudness)

The intensity of the murmur is commonly graded on a 1 to 6 scale,
with grade 1 murmur the softest and grade 6 the loudest (Box
38.1).12
A grade 1 murmur is the faintest murmur and is heard in a quiet
environment with particular effort, whereas grade 5 and 6 murmurs
are associated with palpable vibrations on the chest wall (palpable
thrill). The intensity of the murmur at its origin is determined by
blood flow velocity and the rate of flow (velocity × flow = force). The
intensity of the murmur at the body surface is affected by direction of
the turbulent jet, character of tissue between auscultation area and
the turbulent jet, and the frequency of the murmur. Often the
intensity of a heart murmur is not directly correlated with the
severity of a lesion. However, describing the loudness of a murmur is
important for serial examinations, and in certain heart diseases at
least a rough correlation exists.

Pitch (Frequency)
A murmur’s quality and pitch relate to its frequency components,
which may be high, medium, low, or mixed. Most murmurs consist
of midrange mixed-frequency sounds. On occasion, high-frequency
musical tones or low-frequency “honks” are auscultated. Musical
murmurs (whoops) are most commonly identified in dogs with
modest mitral valve disease.

Shape
Heart murmurs are often described by their frequency profile within
the cardiac cycle in relation to their shape on a phonocardiogram
(Figure 38.1). Terms that are commonly used include plateau- or
band-shaped murmurs for those murmurs of equal intensity
throughout their duration; decrescendo for murmurs that gradually
taper off from an initial peak; and crescendo decrescendo (diamondshaped, ejection murmur) for murmurs that build up to a peak
intensity and then taper in intensity.

Systolic Heart Murmurs
Mitral Insufficiency
The murmur of mitral insufficiency is best heard at the left apex
(mitral valve area) and commonly radiates dorsally and to the right
thorax, making a reliable diagnosis of tricuspid regurgitation
difficult.
The characteristic murmur is plateau- (band-) shaped and
holosystolic; however, in its early stages the murmur may be
protosystolic or with mitral valve prolapse the murmur may develop
in mid- to late-systole. A mitral insufficiency murmur is typically of
mixed frequency and harsh sounding (Audio 38.7

), but it may be

high-pitched or musical (whooping) in quality, typically in mild cases
(Audio 38.8).
Mitral insufficiency can be caused by chronic degenerative valvular
disease (myxomatous valvular heart disease, ch. 232), endocarditis
(ch. 232), hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (ch. 234),
congenital malformations (ch. 231), and diseases that cause left
heart enlargement and dilation of the mitral annulus (e.g., patent
ductus arteriosus [ch. 231], dilated cardiomyopathy [ch. 233]).

Tricuspid Insufficiency
The murmur of tricuspid insufficiency sounds similar to that of
mitral insufficiency but is loudest over the right apex (tricuspid valve
area - right hemithorax). It is often difficult to distinguish tricuspid
insufficiency from a radiating murmur of mitral insufficiency.
Tricuspid murmurs might be a different pitch compared with a
radiating mitral regurgitant murmur and can be accompanied by
jugular pulsations (Videos 229.1, 237.3

). Tricuspid insufficiency

can result from congenital malformations of the valve (ch. 231),
chronic degenerative valve disease (ch. 232), or any disorders that
cause marked right heart enlargement and valve annulus distention,
such as pulmonary hypertension (ch. 218) and arrhythmogenic
right ventricular cardiomyopathy (chs. 233, 234). Tricuspid valve
endocarditis is extremely rare in dogs and cats.

Aortic Stenosis
Valvular and subvalvular aortic stenosis (SAS) produce a systolic
ejection (crescendo-decrescendo) murmur that is usually best heard
at the left heart base (Audio 38.9; ch 231

).

The murmur is usually of mixed frequency and harsh, and it
sometimes radiates towards the right cranial thorax and up the neck
along the carotid arteries. Mild obstructions cause soft murmurs that
are difficult to distinguish from innocent or functional murmurs.
Murmurs that vary dramatically in intensity with exercise or
excitement should prompt consideration of a dynamic left
ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Dynamic outflow tract
obstruction is the most common type of ejection murmur in cats with
hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and its onset and duration coincide
with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve (Audio 38.10; ch.
234

). Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction occurs

uncommonly in dogs as an isolated abnormality or in association
with mitral valve dysplasia or hypertrophy of the interventricular
septum (chs. 231, 233).

Pulmonic Stenosis
The pulmonic stenosis murmur is typically a high-frequency
crescendo-decrescendo (ejection) holosystolic murmur, best heard at
the left heart base over the pulmonic valve (Audio 38.11; ch. 231
). The murmur can be very similar to the aortic stenosis murmur
(Audio 38.9) described above but should not radiate along the
carotid arteries. As the pressure gradient between the right ventricle
and pulmonary artery increases, the murmur intensity becomes
louder and peaks later in systole.

Ventricular Septal Defect
Ventricular septal defects (VSDs) produce murmurs that vary
tremendously in shape and quality. Most often the murmur is a

harsh, mid- to high-frequency holosystolic murmur best heard on
the right cranial thorax (Audio 38.12

).

Murmur intensity may be reduced when the VSD is large and as
pulmonary hypertension develops. With severe pulmonary
hypertension, the murmur may be entirely absent and splitting of the
second heart sound is noted (Audio 38.2)

.

Atrial Septal Defect
Heart murmurs in dogs and cats with an atrial septal defect (ASD)
result from increased flow across the pulmonic valve as a result of
the left to right shunting. Thus, the murmur resembles that of mild
pulmonic stenosis but is often accompanied by a fixed splitting of the
second heart sound. Flow across the atrial septal defect is usually not
audible.

FIGURE 38.2 Algorithm for differentiating causes
of abnormal heart sounds and murmurs. S1, First
heart sound; S2, second heart sound; S3, third heart
sound; S4, fourth heart sound.

Physiologic and Innocent Murmurs
Functional (physiologic) murmurs are usually caused by decreased
blood viscosity or increased cardiac output. Physiologic murmurs are
most often noted in animals with anemia, fever, pregnancy,
hyperthyroidism, thin thoracic walls, and increased sympathetic
tone. These murmurs usually are proto- to mesosystolic, soft to
moderate intensity (grade 1/6 to 3/6), and loudest at the left heart
base (Audio 38.13

). They tend not to radiate extensively.

Innocent murmurs should disappear as the puppy or kitten
matures. They appear to be the result of or relative anemia13 or

larger stroke volumes for the size of the great vessels in comparison
with adults, the lower viscosity of blood associated with lower
hematocrits in puppies and kittens, or both.
In some cats, turbulent blood flow can be noted in the region of the
right ventricular outflow tract, often causing a soft systolic apical
sternal murmur ranging in grades from 1/6 to 3/6, with no evidence
of structural heart disease and little clinical consequence (Audio
38.14

).14,15

Diastolic Heart Murmurs
Aortic Insufficiency
The murmur of isolated aortic insufficiency (valvular aortic
regurgitation) is typically a decrescendo murmur starting at the time
of S2 and extending variably into diastole (Audio 38.15

).

In young dogs, aortic insufficiency can occur as an isolated defect
or in combination with subaortic stenosis or a ventricular septal
defect (ch. 231). Detection of aortic insufficiency in an adult dog or
cat should prompt consideration of bacterial endocarditis (ch. 232).
When the regurgitant volume is large, the diastolic murmur is
often accompanied by a soft mesosystolic ejection murmur, creating
a distinct “to-and-fro” murmur (Audio 38.16

).

The systolic ejection component tapers off in late systole and
allows recognition of S2 and differentiation from a continuous
murmur. Other causes of “to-and-fro” murmurs include ventricular
septal defects that cause loss of aortic root support and pulmonic
valve stenosis and significant pulmonic insufficiency (rare).
Occasionally massive aortic regurgitation causes premature closure
of the mitral valve, producing functional mitral stenosis and a
diastolic murmur referred to as an Austin Flint murmur.

Pulmonic Insufficiency

The murmur of pulmonic insufficiency is similar to that of aortic
insufficiency; however, clinically significant pulmonic insufficiency is
uncommon. It is sometimes detected in animals with pulmonary
hypertension, pulmonic valve dysplasia, or idiopathic dilation of the
pulmonary artery.

Mitral Stenosis
The diastolic murmur of mitral stenosis (ch. 231) is difficult to
recognize in dogs and cats. This low-frequency murmur begins in
mesodiastole and has presystolic accentuation due to atrial
contraction (Audio 38.17

). Mitral stenosis might be accompanied

by other cardiac malformations, which cause murmurs such as
valvular or subvalvular aortic stenosis (ch. 232). In dogs, mitral
stenosis may be more common in breeds that are prone to congenital
mitral valve malformations such as the Bull Terrier breed, in which it
is often associated with aortic stenosis (ch. 231).

Continuous Murmurs
The most common cause of a continuous murmur at the left heart
base is patent ductus arteriosus (PDA; ch. 231). This classic
“machinery-like” murmur of a PDA is usually audible throughout the
cardiac cycle, with peak intensity near S2 (Audio 38.18 and Video
38.1

).

The intensity of the murmur is diminished in late diastole in dogs
with very slow heart rates and the diastolic component can also
disappear with the development of pulmonary hypertension. Less
common causes of continuous murmurs include aorticopulmonary
windows, ruptured aneurysms of sinus of Valsalva, and coronary
arteriovenous fistulas.

Auscultation and Beyond

Historical findings may suggest underlying heart disease; however, a
thorough auscultation with identification and understanding of
abnormal heart sounds and their genesis will permit recognition of
the most likely cause (Figure 38.2).
As important a tool as cardiac auscultation is, it should be one part
of a complete physical exam that integrates evaluation of lung fields,
jugular veins, arterial pulses, and peripheral circulation (ch. 3).
Increasingly the affordability and availability of next-generation
electronic stethoscopes will allow the clinician to pick up difficult-tohear heart sounds and other body sounds.
Additionally, other diagnostic tests might be needed to further
classify and define the animal’s abnormality, and in some cases
differentiate a pathologic from a physiologic murmur (especially
cats).

OVERVIEW
Pulse palpation (feeling of the pulses with the fingers) is a key
component of the physical examination. It provides direct and
indirect evidence of circulatory sufficiency or insufficiency, and when
combined with other physical examination findings, such as a heart
murmur, it can narrow the differential diagnosis considerably.1 It is
inexpensive, readily available, and easily/rapidly obtained in most
patients. True expertise in pulse palpation can only be obtained
through practice on patients, preferably with experienced guidance.
This chapter will focus on peripheral arterial pulses, as central pulses
are not evaluable without catheterization and venous pulses are
generally not palpable due to the lower pulse pressure although they
may occasionally be seen in short haired breeds (Video 229.1) or in
those animals that have had their hair clipped over the near central
veins

(Video 237.3). Normal pulse generation, pulse alterations

that are commonly encountered in practice, and some specific pulse
abnormalities are reviewed.

Obtaining the Pulse
There are several pulses that may be palpable on dogs and cats, but
the easiest, most reliable and most commonly palpated is the femoral
arterial pulse. This artery is large and easily palpated in most
patients due to its course on the medial aspect of the hind limbs in
the femoral triangle. Generally, two or three fingers are lightly placed
over the dorsomedial aspect of the hindlimbs; it is ideal to start with
both femoral pulses simultaneously to assess synchronicity and
similarity. A weaker or absent pulse in a limb may be indicative of
obstruction; this is uncommon outside of cats presenting for
cardiogenic arterial thromboembolism (CATE), but may occur in
dogs (ch. 238).2-4
After assessing the pulses for presence and similarity, it is ideal to
auscultate the heart while feeling the pulse. Heart rate, arrhythmias,
rhythmic alterations in pulse strength, and absence or presence of
pulses during auscultation may be assessed. These are all important
aspects of obtaining a working diagnosis, which can assist in
determining the urgency of the situation as well as the next most
appropriate diagnostic or therapeutic step. Other pulses that are
typically palpable in dogs include the dorsal pedal, carotid and
brachial pulses, though the latter typically require more thorough
palpation. Dorsal pedal (metatarsal) pulses are palpable on the
dorsal and slightly medial surface of the metatarsus, distal to the
tarsometatarsal joint, and are occasionally the easiest to palpate
unless hypotensive. In fact, the lack of a palpable dorsal pedal pulse
may be evidence of hypotension.5 Carotid pulses may be palpable
lateral and dorsal to the trachea, though they are quite deep in most
patients. While the femoral pulses are typically easily palpated,
obesity, excess hair or mats, or shivering/shaking may make pulses
difficult to palpate. Chondrodystrophic breeds (such as bulldogs or
dachshunds) may also have pulses that are difficult to palpate.

Normal Pulse
It is important to realize that the strength of the pulse is determined
by the difference between the systolic and diastolic blood pressures
(called the “pulse pressure” for this reason) and not the absolute
value of the blood pressure (BP). For example, a normal or weak
pulse may be palpated in hypertensive patients that have a normal or
smaller than usual difference between the systolic and diastolic BP.
This is demonstrated in Figure 39.1. In hypotensive patients, the
pulse pressure tends to decline as the pressures drop; thus,
hypotensive patients typically have weaker pulses. However, the
pulse may remain normal or close to normal until the mean BP drops
dramatically.6 A normal pulse pressure is approximately 40 mm Hg
(120 mm Hg systolic – 80 mm Hg diastolic pressures); this may
increase during activity due to an increase in ventricular stroke
volume, which increases systolic pressures in excess of diastolic
pressures.
The strength of a pulse is dependent on both the vascular
compliance and the ventricular stroke volume; intrathoracic pressure
plays a role as well.7,13 The stroke volume, in turn, is dependent on
preload, afterload, and contractility (ch. 228). More detailed
information on this topic may be found in the chapters on BP (ch.
236) and cardiac function (ch. 228). In short, preload is a measure
of the amount of blood returning to the heart (when considering the
arterial pulse, the left ventricle). Afterload can be considered as the
resistance to blood flow out of the heart (typically due to vascular
resistance). Contractility describes the strength of cardiac
contraction. All of these variables affect pulse strength in
complicated ways, but as a general rule pulse strength is augmented
by increases in preload and contractility, and is diminished by
factors that decrease contractility or preload. Commonly
encountered conditions reducing contractility include sepsis (ch.
128), cardiomyopathy (chs. 233, 234), and anesthesia. Common
causes of reduced preload include hemorrhage, hypovolemia from
vomiting/diarrhea (ch. 121), tachycardia or pericardial effusion (ch.
235).
Conditions that increase the cardiac output while maintaining or
decreasing diastolic pressure will typically result in the strongest

pulses (systemic diseases, congenital heart disease). These have been
described as “bounding” or “waterhammer” pulses, and are clinically
encountered with some regularity. Weak pulses are commonly
associated with volume loss, tachycardia, and/or impaired heart
muscle function. These conditions are summarized in Box 39.1.
The upstroke of the pulse is termed the “anacrotic limb,” and the
downstroke of the pulse is called the “dicrotic limb.” The anacrotic
limb is generated during systole following the isovolumic contraction
of the left ventricle. The pressure rises, and ejection begins when
ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure and causes opening of
the aortic valve. Pressure continues to rise as ejection occurs during
systole, then begins to fall as ejection declines. Active relaxation of
the ventricle begins, causing a rapid fall in ventricular and aortic
pressures (dicrotic limb) during diastole. The aortic valve closes
when ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure, which is
temporally associated with the dicrotic notch. The pressure
continues to fall during diastole due to runoff into the peripheral
vasculature. This fall is typically slight unless the aortic valve is
incompetent or an arteriovenous fistula is present (most commonly a
patent ductus arteriosus [PDA]).

FIGURE 39.1 Normal and abnormal arterial
pressure tracings. The strength of the palpable pulse
depends on the pulse pressure: the difference
between systolic and diastolic arterial pressures.
Blue: in a normal individual, the peak systolic
pressure may be 120 mm Hg and the lowest diastolic
pressure 80 mm Hg. The normal pulse therefore
reflects a pulse pressure of 120 − 80 = 40 mm Hg.
Purple: in a hypertensive patient, the peak systolic
pressure may be 160 mm Hg and the lowest diastolic
pressure 120 mm Hg. The pulse pressure is still 40
mm Hg (160 − 120 mm Hg) so the pulse quality is
normal. Green: in patent ductus arteriosus (PDA),
diastolic runoff through the ductus greatly reduces
diastolic pressures. The peak systolic pressure is 120
mm Hg, but the lowest diastolic pressure is 40 mm
Hg. The pulse pressure is very high (120 − 40 = 80
mm Hg), which explains the bounding or

“waterhammer” pulse that is characteristic of PDA.
Orange: in moderate hypotension, both systolic and
diastolic pressures can be low but again the pulse
pressure may still be normal. If the pressures are
very low, a very weak or “thready” pulse will be felt, if
any pulse is palpable at all. (Courtesy Dr. Etienne
Côté.)

Exercise
The cause of pulse alterations can be better determined when
combined with auscultatory findings. The presence or absence of a
murmur may be helpful, particularly in younger patients. For
example, a basilar murmur is present in the most common
congenital heart diseases in dogs: a PDA, subaortic stenosis (SAS)
and pulmonic stenosis (PS) (chs. 38 and 231).8 While a PDA may
be differentiated based on the continuous character of the murmur,
in some cases this is difficult to hear. Pulse characteristics can be
quite helpful in determining which is most likely, prior to obtaining a
definitive diagnosis with echocardiography. A PDA will be associated
with bounding pulses due to the widened pulse pressure (Figure
39.1). This is due to a normal or high systolic pressure and a low
diastolic pressure due to runoff through the PDA during diastole.
Severe SAS, on the other hand, is associated with pulsus parvus et
tardus due to the slow systolic upstroke and prolonged ejection time
through the stenotic orifice, which results in a narrow pulse pressure.
Severe PS does not cause pulse alterations in the systemic arteries
(normal pulses), as the disease affects flow to the pulmonary arteries.
By assessing the pulse and murmur simultaneously, a preliminary
diagnosis may be made in the exam room with the owner present
prior to confirmation with more expensive and extensive diagnostics.

Patterns of Pulse Alterations
Strong pulses are those with a wide pulse pressure, and are present
with conditions that increase systolic pressure, decrease diastolic
pressure, or both. Weak pulses are present in conditions that reduce
the systolic pressure with a disproportionate (lesser) decrease in
diastolic pressure. Pulse deficits are most commonly due to
arrhythmias, typically premature beats of ventricular (and less
commonly atrial) origin. This occurs due to inadequate filling time
for the ventricles, which reduces contractile strength (due to the
Frank-Starling mechanism). The resulting contraction may be
insufficient to produce ejection if the pressure does not rise
sufficiently to exceed aortic pressure. Pulsus alternans is a pulse that

varies in strength from beat to beat, and is infrequently encountered
in clinical small animal medicine; it is reportedly most common with
ventricular dysfunction (typically dilated cardiomyopathy). A more
common arrhythmia that is palpably similar is pulsus bigeminus, the
beat-to-beat variation in strength is due to a ventricular (or less
commonly atrial) bigeminy. Pulsus paradoxus is a classical finding
in cardiac tamponade (pericardial effusion sufficient to impair right
atrial filling). The pulse strength falls or disappears completely
during inspiration and increases during expiration, and is an
exaggeration of the typical (small, <10 mm Hg) fall in pulse pressure
during inspiration due to alterations in intrathoracic pressure.
Venous return to the right heart is augmented during inspiration.
Normally, this is accompanied by a fall in right atrial and ventricular
pressures; however, in patients with tamponade, the right atrial and
ventricular pressures rise due to elevated intrapericardial pressure
(the right atrium and ventricle are not able to expand normally). The
resulting increase in right-sided heart pressures impinges on the left
atrial and ventricular filling (reducing preload) when the pressure in
the pericardial space is excessive, thus reducing pulse pressure.
Other mechanisms may also play a role.9

Pulse Rate and Rhythm
One of the most valuable pieces of information obtained via pulse
palpation is the rate and rhythm. Healthy dogs have heart rates
between 60-180 beats/minute in the hospital, and are lower at home
in a comfortable environment.10 The heart rhythm in healthy dogs
tends to vary cyclically with the breathing, a pattern called
respiratory sinus arrhythmia (ch. 230). This variability is reduced in
dogs with advanced heart disease, hemorrhage, or other causes of
reduced BP that result in elevated heart rates.11,12 This is not
typically present in cats in the hospital due to elevated sympathetic
tone, but has been documented on ambulatory ECG monitoring in
healthy cats at home.13 The heart rate can provide information
regarding clinical status, but is nonspecific and best combined with
other information to obtain a working diagnosis.

Arrhythmias affect pulse strength via alterations in filling time,
which consequently reduce both preload and contractility (reducing
stroke volume). This effect varies greatly with timing; typically,
premature beats with a short cycle length reduce or eliminate the
pulse entirely, whereas long cycle lengths may not affect pulse
strength at all. Sustained tachycardia results in weak pulses
primarily due to reductions in preload. If sustained at high rates for
long periods of time, tachycardias may result in
tachycardiomyopathy. The reduction in contractility further weakens
pulse strength. Atrial fibrillation is an irregularly irregular rhythm
that results in variable pulse strength on a beat to beat basis due to
constantly varying filling intervals (ch. 230). This may be difficult to
appreciate if the heart rate is very high (>250 bpm) or low (<120
bpm). Bradycardias (heart rate <60 bpm), on the other hand, are
frequently associated with strong pulses due to long filling times and
high stroke volumes.
The characteristics, rate, and rhythm of the pulse can be assessed
rapidly and easily in most patients. When combined with
auscultation, they can provide the clinician with an assessment of
hemodynamic status. An understanding of the basic factors that
comprise pulse strength, as well as an understanding of pulse
pressure, can then assist in determining the next most useful
diagnostic and therapeutic steps.

Chapter 40: Syncope

A C RO N YM S

ILRs insertable loop recorders
VT ventricular tachycardia
Collapse is a broad, generic term, defined as a sudden loss of
postural tone, not necessarily with a loss of consciousness; it may be
of any duration. Syncope is a subset of collapse that involves a
transient loss of consciousness (TLOC), resulting from insufficient
blood flow to the brain. There is an associated abrupt transient
reduction in delivery of oxygen and nutrients, which is of short
duration and is followed by a good recovery to normal.1 A partial loss
of consciousness can result in a brief period of ataxia or stumbling,
which is termed pre-syncope. It is of paramount importance to
differentiate syncope from non-syncopal causes of collapse,
particularly neurological causes such as epileptic seizures (ch. 45).
In a clinical audit of human patients presenting to an emergency
department with a history of syncope, the diagnostic accuracy of the
initial treating physician was 65%.2 In another review of human
patients referred to an epilepsy clinic, with a diagnosis of epilepsy,
12.9% ultimately had a diagnosis of neurocardiogenic syncope.3 It
would seem likely that the accuracy of diagnoses or misdiagnosis
would be similar in veterinary medicine. The diagnostic rate for
animals that present with collapse, of all causes, has been reported as
67% in one study of 743 dogs,4 which seems relatively high, but

many of these animals had abnormalities to find on physical
examination or diagnostic tests that led to a diagnosis. Furthermore,
of the 153 dogs in which the collapse was undiagnosed, 42% resolved,
23% continued to collapse, 24% died and 11% were subsequently
diagnosed.4

FIGURE 40.1 Algorithm for syncope and nonsyncopal collapse. This algorithm provides guidelines
and broad differential groups for managing animals
presenting with syncope and non-syncopal collapse,
with the aims of assisting the veterinarian in how to
approach this type of case. AV, Atrioventricular;
BUAS , brachycephalic upper airway syndrome.
If an animal presents in a state of collapse, the opportunity for a
physical examination, with a methodical approach, during the
episode may allow the affected body system to be determined.
However, when the animal presents with a history of collapse but
walks into the clinic without clinical signs, then a diagnosis becomes
challenging.

MECHANISMS AND CAUSES OF
SYNCOPE

It is essential to have an understanding of the pathophysiological
mechanism of syncope so that a targeted history can be teased from
the owner (chs. 1 and 2) (Figure 40.1). Since syncope, by definition,
is associated with a transient reduction in blood flow to the brain,
then cardiogenic disorders dominate, associated with cardiac
arrhythmias or neurocardiogenic reflexes. It is only by reaching a
diagnosis that appropriate treatment can be provided. For example,
it may be that patients with intermittent bradyarrhythmias might
need pacemaker implantation or those with tachyarrhythmias may
require antiarrhythmic therapy (ch. 230).5 Likewise, inappropriate
empirical (best guess) treatments have the potential to lead to poor
outcomes.

CARDIOGENIC SYNCOPE
Cardiogenic syncope occurs when there is intermittent, profound
and abrupt hypotension that results in a marked reduction in blood
flow to the brain. It is estimated that blood pressure has to fall by
50% before unconsciousness develops,6 and blood pressure is
usually much lower than this during syncope.7 Therefore, for any
arrhythmia to result in this degree of systemic arterial hypotension,
it has to be abrupt, profound and sustained. Blood pressure will fall
quickest when the heart stops suddenly, such as with an arrhythmia
that results in asystole like sinus arrest or ventricular standstill,
whereas a slower reduction in blood pressure will occur with rapid
ventricular tachycardia (VT) (ch. 230). Additionally, the duration of
a sustained arrhythmia that causes sufficient hypotension to induce
syncope has to be a minimum of 10-30 seconds, depending upon the
activity level (metabolic demand) of the animal and the presence or
absence of structural heart disease. In the majority of cases the
arrhythmia abates, hence the intermittent nature of syncope; if it did
not, then death would likely occur.
The most common arrhythmias8-13 that cause sufficient
hypotension to result in syncope are bradyarrhythmias that result in
asystole such as sinus arrest or high-grade atrioventricular block
with periods of ventricular standstill. Tachyarrhythmias, which have
a marked effect on stroke volume, such as rapid VT, can also lead to

hypotension and syncope (ch. 230). Atrioventricular block is usually
evident at the time of examination, although rarely it can occur
intermittently, particularly in cats with cardiomyopathy.14 Sinus
arrest or ventricular tachycardia can be intermittent and might only
be detected on prolonged Holter monitoring or cardiac event
recordings (Videos 40.1, 40.2, 40.3, and 40.4

). Ventricular

tachycardia does not always produce syncope, but at higher rates
there will usually be a degree of hypotension; it tends to be the more
rapid VT that is associated with syncope. If an arrhythmia is
diagnosed, this should prompt further investigations to determine if
there is an underlying cause of the arrhythmia associated with either
cardiac or extracardiac diseases such as cardiomyopathy (chs. 233,
234), pericardial effusion (ch. 235), myocarditis (chs. 233, 234),
neoplasia (ch. 235), systemic or metabolic disorders, sepsis,
toxemia, shock, or drug-related causes (chs. 233, 234). In animals
fitted with pacemakers, checking for intermittent pacing failure, such
as lead displacement or high pacing thresholds, needs consideration
(ch. 230), and in some cases Holter monitoring may be required to
reach a diagnosis (ch. 96).
Arrhythmias that produce a lesser degree of hypotension tend to
result in episodic weakness rather than syncope. Such arrhythmias
might include less-rapid VT or rapid supraventricular tachycardia, or
less profound bradyarrhythmias. However, the combination of
structural heart disease or pulmonary hypertension (which is severe
enough to limit cardiac output) with the additional transient
hypotension associated with these arrhythmias, can result in
syncope, particularly following excitement or exertion.15
Importantly, there are several structural cardiac diseases that are
known to be associated with a high incidence of arrhythmia, such as
the various cardiomyopathies (chs. 233, 234), pericardial effusion
(ch. 235) and myocarditis (chs. 233, 234). Echocardiography is
therefore nearly always indicated in animals with syncope (ch. 97).

NEUROCARDIOGENIC SYNCOPE

There are many synonyms that describe this type of disorder,
including vasovagal syncope, neurally mediated syncope and
vasodepressor syncope. Neurocardiogenic syncope occurs due to
profound and abrupt hypotension caused by the combination of a
bradyarrhythmia and inappropriate reflex vasodilation. It is
characterized by sudden autonomic nervous system failure: there is
withdrawal of sympathetic tone with abrupt increase in vagal tone,16
although the exact mechanism remains unclear.17 The triggering
events are variable and determined by which afferent nerve or
receptor is stimulated.18
Vasovagal syncope, first described in 1932 by Lewis,19 is probably
the most well-known form of neurocardiogenic syncope in small
animals, particularly in young Boxer dogs4; the trigger is usually
intense excitement such as greeting the owner or play activity,
resulting in triggering the neurocardiogenic reflex described above,
leading to syncope. Vasovagal syncope also seems to be exacerbated
by concurrent gastrointestinal or abdominal conditions, and syncope
may resolve when the abdominal disorder resolves.20 The presence
of structural heart disease such as aortic stenosis or hypertrophic
obstructive cardiomyopathy can exacerbate high left ventricular
pressures, stimulating ventricular pressure receptors and triggering
this neurocardiogenic reflex; this is termed the Bezold-Jarisch
reflex.21 This reflex originates in cardiac sensory receptors that have
an augmented response to mechanical or chemical stimuli, relayed to
the brain through C-fibre afferents. In the brain these inhibit efferent
vasoconstrictor sympathetic outflow resulting in vasodilation and
bradycardia and thus an abrupt hypotension producing syncope.
This reflex is also triggered in animals suffering rapid, severe
hemorrhage; vigorous contraction of the left ventricle around a
volume-depleted ventricular chamber producing a paradoxical
increase in firing of these receptors results in a reflex bradycardia
and vasodilation.21
It is also well-known that some small breed dogs with degenerative
mitral valve disease can present with syncope. The mechanism of the
syncope in this setting remains unclear, but includes vasovagal
syncope, arrhythmias, and pulmonary hypertension.22 Situational

syncope occurs when the neurocardiogenic reflex is triggered by
activities such as coughing (tussive syncope; Video 34.1

),23

vomiting, sneezing, micturition, defecating,24 swallowing, or visceral
pain.1,25 Tussive syncope is common in dogs with either cardiac or
respiratory disease; the mechanism remains unclear but may be
associated with an increase in intrathoracic pressure during
coughing inhibiting venous return or possibly a neurocardiogenic
reflex vasodepressor-bradycardia response to cough.23

NON-SYNCOPAL COLLAPSE
It is difficult to differentiate syncope from the many causes of nonsyncopal collapse (that are not associated with a reduction in blood
flow to the brain). Conditions to consider would include neurological
conditions such as epileptic seizures (ch. 45; Video 45.2

),

narcolepsy (ch. 244), paroxysmal movement disorders (ch. 41),
neuromuscular disease (ch. 253) or exercise-induced collapse (EIC;
ch. 253).3,26 Animals with profound hypoxemia, such as those with
severe respiratory disease (ch. 217), pulmonary hypertension (ch.
218), or transient upper airway obstructive conditions (chs. 213,
214), can present with intermittent collapse particularly following
excitement or exertion.25-27 In a recent study of dogs with
pulmonary hypertension28 the most common presenting concern
was syncope (64%). Coughing, common with respiratory conditions,
can also lead to tussive syncope (

Video 34.1).29

HISTORY-TAKING
When an animal is presented for evaluation of collapse, it can be very
difficult to differentiate between syncope and seizures. Owners often
will recall events in an array of descriptions, misleading analogies, or
misunderstood terminology. It is critical that the clinician use
analytical questioning to obtain as good an original description of the

collapse as possible; this, therefore, also has to be from the person
who witnessed the collapse. Differentiation between syncope and
non-syncopal collapse is often difficult, and therefore keeping an
open mind to a wide range of causes of transient collapse is prudent.
History-taking for collapse is a particularly difficult and challenging
task for the clinician, which requires considerable time and
experience. Obtaining movies from owners of their animal during a
collapse can be invaluable in these situations.
Determining if an animal was unconscious or not, from an owner,
is difficult. Additionally, “unconscious” is a symptom, as opposed to
a clinical sign. A client is usually unaware that the eyes often remain
open when unconscious and this can be misinterpreted as being
conscious (their pet was “staring at them”). It is more appropriate to
ask questions around how responsive their animal was: did their pet
react or move in response to touch or calling? Loss of bladder and/or
bowel control with urination or defecation is not only seen with
epileptic seizures but can also be seen with cardiogenic syncope
(Video 40.4

). Animals with cardiogenic syncope are often

initially motionless (sleep-like) with flaccid limb and body tone.
However, some that are partially unconscious can flail the limbs (as
if struggling to get up), such that this can mimic epileptic seizures;
detailed questioning is therefore needed to differentiate semiconscious “leg-flailing” (

Video 40.3) from repetitive paddling

(swimming) movement of the limbs (more suggestive of epileptic
seizures). Additionally, dogs with cardiogenic syncope that is
prolonged or severe can develop profound cerebral hypoxia which
results in a period of opisthotonos (forelimbs extended and stiff, with
the head and neck extended dorsally), which seems to be uncommon
with epileptic seizures (

Videos 40.4 and 45.1). Epileptic seizures

often are characterized by jaw chopping or chattering of the teeth,
and salivation, followed by exhaustion on recovery (see ch. 45
videos

). Syncope may have a trigger event such as excitement or

the onset of exercise, whereas epileptic seizures usually occur at rest
or from sleep with no acute trigger, often have a pre-ictal period of
anxiety or odd behavior, and also can be associated with facial

muscle twitching. Cats can have cardiogenic syncope that mimics
brief focal seizures.30,31 Cardiogenic syncope typically is short in
duration, and the animal should generally return to normal within a
few seconds to up to a minute. Epileptic seizures can be followed by a
post-ictal period of up to hours where the animal may be confused,
anxious, or display localizing neurologic signs (ch. 241).

DIAGNOSTIC TESTS
Comprehensive blood work is important (complete blood count,
serum biochemistry profile including serum electrolyte, fasted
glucose concentrations, thyroid status); if hemorrhage is suspected,
repeated blood tests may be necessary 12-24 hours later to reveal
evidence of blood loss. If hypoadrenocorticism is suspected, an
adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation (ACTH) test should be
performed (ch. 296). Serum cardiac troponin I (cTnI)
concentrations were shown32 to differentiate dogs with cardiogenic
syncope from those with epileptic seizures with a sensitivity of 75%
and specificity of 80%; unfortunately, there was a significant overlap
in the results, suggesting this might have a low discriminatory value
for individual cases.
An electrocardiogram (ECG) is always indicated (ch. 96);
however, a normal resting ECG does not exclude an intermittent
arrhythmia. Ideally the ECG needs to be performed when the
syncopal event occurs. Additionally, it is important to rule out an
arrhythmia prior to considering general anesthesia for diagnostic
investigations such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the
brain.
Continuous ambulatory electrocardiography (Holter monitoring)
has become a key diagnostic test to screen for intermittent
arrhythmias in syncopal animals. It is important when using a Holter
monitor that the timing of the event is accurately and reliably
recorded, and this is really only achieved by ensuring the client
presses the “event button” on the Holter monitor (ch. 96). Many
animals may not have a syncopal event while the Holter monitor is
being worn, so attempts to induce syncope can be encouraged, in
view of the importance of reaching a diagnosis so that the correct

treatment can be chosen (provided such attempts do not pose undue
risk to the patient). From the history, it should be determined if
there is a trigger for the syncope; if there is, then this behavior or
routine can be encouraged in moderation during the Holter
recording, once the animal’s owner understands the risk-to-benefit
ratio of such an approach and provides informed consent. Holter
monitoring is typically for 24 hours for an arrhythmia count;
however, in animals with syncope, the Holter monitor ideally needs
to be worn until there is an episode of collapse; this can take several
days, or potentially longer, depending upon the frequency of
syncope. If worn for only 24-48 hours the diagnostic rate of a Holter
monitor in syncopal dogs is low.33
Cardiac event loop recorders can be an alternative option; one
study10 documented a 75.5% success rate to rule in/out an
arrhythmia as the cause of syncope in animals without structural
heart disease and 95.6% success rate for those with underlying heart
disease. For the vast majority of animals (58 of 60), the event
recorder was worn for less than 1 week. Equally, most Holter
monitors can be worn for 5-7 days and therefore are likely to give
similar success rates.
Implantable loop recorders (ILRs) are cardiac event devices that
are placed surgically in the subcutaneous tissues of the left thorax,
overlying the heart. These provide an alternative option for animals
that fail to have a syncopal event following prolonged Holter
monitoring. Studies have shown a good success rate (48 to 66%) in
diagnosing the presence or absence of intermittent arrhythmias as
the causes of collapse.34-36 However, failure to identify a cause of the
collapse was due to the animals no longer collapsing or the owner
failing to manually trigger a recording.
In the majority of cases, echocardiography is indicated to screen
for structural heart disease, or for conditions that might be
associated with arrhythmias (ch. 97). Thoracic radiographs might
reveal changes consistent with cardiac or respiratory disease;
occasionally, they might be indicative of hypovolemic shock
(microcardia, small caudal vena cava, hypovascular lung fields)
warranting an investigation for underlying causes, including blood
work and abdominal ultrasonography in search of abdominal disease
such as hemoabdomen.

If the results of all of the above evaluations are still inconclusive,
then the key step remains prolonged Holter monitoring to document
if intermittent sustained arrhythmias are the cause of collapse or not;
this may need to be repeated a few times or ILRs considered.
Alternative options include teaching the client to examine the
mucosa for pallor (lips and gums are more reliable than the tongue),
or palpating or even ausculting the heart during syncope (although
this can be difficult if the duration of syncope is short). The use of a
smartphone-based ECG device can seem attractive; however, in the
time taken to obtain a recording, the event has usually passed (
Videos 40.2 and 40.3). Instructing the owner to take a movie of the
collapse can be particularly useful in providing the opportunity for
the clinician to observe the event and decide if this is syncopal or
non-syncopal collapse and potentially the body system involved.

SUMMARY
Collapse is a broad generic term, defined as a sudden loss of postural
tone, but not necessarily with a loss of consciousness. Syncope is a
subset of collapse that is characterized by unconsciousness, due to a
transient reduction in blood flow to the brain, which is of short
duration followed by a rapid recovery to normal. The common causes
of syncope are classified as cardiogenic or neurocardiogenic. It is of
paramount importance to differentiate syncope from the large
number of non-syncopal causes of collapse, particularly epileptic
seizures and paroxysmal movement disorders. Cardiovascular
conditions dominate the differentials for syncope, most commonly as
a consequence of hypotension associated with cardiac disease or
neurocardiogenic reflexes. If abnormalities are found on physical
examination, these might identify the body system requiring further
investigation. If no abnormality is found on physical examination,
then a meticulous history becomes the most important part of the
assessment. If initial diagnostic tests are inconclusive, then the key
step is documenting an episode of collapse, which is often best
performed by prolonged Holter recording over a 5-7 day period,
ensuring the owner presses the event button to unambiguously link
the timing of the collapse to the ECG recorded. Once a diagnosis is

reached, then further investigations can be performed in order to
provide appropriate treatment.
For management or treatment to be successful in animals with
syncope, it is imperative to pursue the diagnosis.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Syncope and Seizures: Understanding the Causes of Faints, Fits and
Falls in Animals
Collapse is a general term to describe an animal that has an
episode of falling down (or “recumbency”), which can either be brief
or prolonged. The causes of collapse in dog and cats range from
abnormal heart rhythm disorders, such as the heart temporarily
stopping (faint/syncope), and conditions affecting the brain or
nervous system (seizures/fits), to medical conditions such as an
internal bleed, low blood glucose or an imbalance in blood electrolyte
levels.
It is important to be aware that there is an overlap in the outward
appearance of collapsing due to any of these conditions. Abnormal
movements that characterize seizures can be similar to the abnormal
movements associated with a heart rhythm disorder (syncope). In
seizures, there tends to be rapid paddling/swimming movements,
jaw chomping, and excessive salivation (drooling). With some heart
rhythm disorders, the signs can range from motionlessness (sleeplike) to spasms/stiffening of the front legs and arching back of the
head and neck (which can mimic seizures). It is estimated in human
medicine that 20% of people initially diagnosed with seizures are
later found to have a heart rhythm disorder; this is likely to be
similar in veterinary medicine. It is also very much preferable to rule
out a heart problem, before contemplating an anesthetic for a brain
scan.

WHAT CAN YOU DO?
A good description from the person that has witnessed the event, or
preferably, movies of the collapse, can be immensely useful. It can be
useful to check the color of the inside of the lips and gums during the
collapse to see if they are a normal pink color or have changed to
become white versus blue, provided doing so does not pose a risk of

being bitten or injured. Keeping a note of the duration of the
collapse, and whether it was triggered by something like excitement
or a certain time of day, is useful. Try to note if your pet reacts to
touch or calling its name during the collapse; this helps identify
whether consciousness was maintained. Note, however, that the eyes
can remain open and staring during unconsciousness, so observing
that the eyes stay open does not determine the nature of the
problem.

WHAT CAN YOUR VETERINARIAN DO?
Following a description of the events, the next step is a physical
examination by your veterinarian to check for any clues that might
explain the collapse, and that guide which diagnostic tests need to be
performed. A heart rhythm disorder would warrant further tests on
the heart such as an electrocardiogram (ECG, EKG) or
echocardiogram (ultrasound scan of the heart). If there is a swollen
belly (abdomen), it might be due to fluid or internal bleed, which
would warrant an ultrasound scan of the abdomen. A neurological
examination is needed to check for any brain, spinal or nerve
conduction problems. Complete blood tests often are necessary to
screen for medical causes of collapse or seizure, such as liver disease,
abnormally low blood glucose (sugar), imbalance in the electrolytes,
or loss of blood (anemia). Repeated blood tests might be needed in
some cases, as some changes might not show in a blood test for the
first 24 hours.
In animals with intermittent collapse, the cause of the problem
might not be apparent at the first examination. There might be an
intermittent pause in the heart rhythm or an abnormally fast, racing
heartbeat, but identification of these when infrequent requires an
ECG during the collapse. This can be achieved by your pet wearing a
heart monitor (Holter) for a few days to capture an ECG recording if
the collapse happens when this is worn. It is only by diagnosing
whether or not a heart rhythm disorder was the cause of the collapse
that treatment can be decided on. For example, if the heart has
intermittent racing episodes, then medication might help to prevent
that from happening. Or if the heart is temporarily stopping, then a
pacemaker would be able to keep it beating and prevent collapse. If
your pet does not collapse when wearing the Holter monitor, then it

is difficult to rule out an abnormal rhythm disorder because it may
be occurring only sporadically (but still be of concern). In this case,
Holter monitoring may need to be repeated when the collapsing
becomes more frequent. Alternatively, a smaller recording device
(insertable loop recorder [ILR]) can be surgically inserted under the
skin near the heart for many weeks to months of ECG monitoring.
In summary, do your best to remember an accurate description of
the event, a movie recording is immensely useful, and check the color
of the lip/gums if you can safely do so. Your vet will examine your
pet for any persisting symptoms, but some initial tests are usually
needed such as bloodwork, an ECG and an ultrasound scan. Often,
more advanced tests such as having the dog or cat wear a Holter
monitor for several days is commonly needed in these types of cases.
But for the correct treatment to be successful in animals with
collapsing, it is imperative to pursue and obtain a diagnosis.
Mike Martin (Kenilworth, United Kingdom)

DEFINITIONS
“Movement Disorders” (MDs), an umbrella term used in humans,
helps to classify different neurologic conditions in which there is
either excess or paucity of voluntary and automatic movements
unrelated to weakness or spasticity.1 Applying criteria used in people

to dog and cat MDs does not translate well, especially since many of
the common diseases in humans are either rare or unreported in
veterinary medicine. In veterinary medicine, the physiology and
pathogenesis of paroxysmal movement disorders (PMDs) are being
clarified.2,3 MDs in dogs and cats are categorized as either
hypokinetic (decreased amplitude of movement) or hyperkinetic
(excessive movement). The terms bradykinesia (slow movement) and
akinesia (loss of movement) are also used.1 Hypokinetic MDs are
uncommon while dyskinetic (unnatural movements) and abnormal
involuntary movement conditions are more common.1

RECOGNITION OF PATTERNS
PATTERNS USED TO INITIALLY ESTABLISH
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES
Initial diagnosis of most MDs is based on clinical signs. It is crucial
to observe typical episodes, looking for major clinical patterns
(“phenotypical” patterns).4 Pattern recognition aids in establishing
the appropriate differential diagnoses used in choosing a practical,
logical, and cost effective diagnostic strategy.5 Different types of
involuntary movements may occur concurrently, making the
recognition of specific patterns more difficult.6 Paroxysmal
dyskinesias (PDs) occasionally include tremors and/or myoclonus.

MYOCLONUS
Myoclonus is a sudden, brief, shock-like involuntary muscle
contraction causing movement of that area of the body4 (Videos 41.1
and 41.2

). It can be classified according to the muscles involved,

as focal, multifocal, segmental, or generalized.4 Myoclonus can result
from neuronal lesions or as an uncommon expression of epileptic

activity.4,7 In epilepsy, myoclonus can be spontaneous or triggered
by visual and/or auditory stimuli4 (Video 41.3

).

TREMORS (CH. 42)
“Tremor” is an involuntary, rhythmic, oscillatory movement of an
affected body area.6 Noting “rhythmicity” is the key for
discriminating tremors from other MDs, although sometimes this
can be difficult.3 Pets with tremors exhibit regularly repeated
oscillatory movements, although the amplitude of each movement
may vary8 (Videos 41.4 and 41.5

). In dogs and cats, tremors are

sub-classified as action-related and further divided into postural
(occurring during antigravitational posture) or kinetic (occurring
during active movement)8 (Video 41.6). Tremors can also be a
component of more complex PMDs, e.g., the idiopathic head tremor
(Video 41.7

) in some breeds (English Bulldog and Doberman) is

considered a PMD.

DYSTONIA
Dystonia is defined as a “sustained muscle contraction, frequently
causing twisting and repetitive movements, or abnormal postures”
because agonist and antagonist muscles contract simultaneously9
(Video 41.8

). Affected humans often exhibit sustained

contraction of the same muscle groups that persists longer than is
typical of other MDs. These, in some cases, can be initiated or
exacerbated by voluntary movements.10,11 Dystonia is typical of PD.
In many PDs, sustained contraction of a single limb is observed,
which can progress to involve other limbs. Ultimately, the pet may
lose its balance and fall.

PAROXYSMAL MOVEMENT DISORDERS
(PMDs; PAROXYSMAL DYSKINESIAS)
CLASSIFICATIONS
PMDs, also termed paroxysmal dyskinesias, are characterized by
abrupt episodes of self-limiting abnormal movement. Use of video
recordings by owners has increased veterinary awareness of this
heterogenous group of MDs. In humans, PDs are classified according
to a combination of trigger, age, and duration:12
1. paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia (PKD), precipitated by
sudden movement or being startled
2. paroxysmal nonkinesigenic dyskinesia (PNKD), related to
stress, alcohol, or caffeine
3. paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia (PED), associated
with prolonged heavy exercise
Classifications are less specific for dogs and cats. Those used in
people are not helpful. Most PDs in dogs and cats would be classified
as PNKD in humans. A veterinary classification scheme based on
clinical features with subclassifications based on likely diagnoses has
been proposed.2 The best described PDs in dogs have been related to
genetics, diet, or are drug-induced. The most common differential
diagnosis is epilepsy. Discussions focus on the relationship between
PDs and epilepsy because a pet can have both conditions.
Coexistence of PD and epilepsy has been documented in Chinook
dogs.13

CLINICAL APPROACH AND
PHENOTYPIC CHARACTERIZATIONS
(FIGURE 41.1)
PDs should be differentiated from epileptic seizures (ch. 45). In
humans, this is based on results of electroencephalography (EEG).
Since EEGs are not performed in general veterinary practices,

reaching a proper diagnosis can be challenging. Typically, pets with
PDs do not lose consciousness nor do they exhibit autonomic signs of
hypersalivation or fecal and urinary incontinence. Duration of
episodes is variable, from seconds to hours (Video 41.9

).

Termination of the “attack” is usually abrupt, with no post-ictal
phase. Owners in most instances are not able to interrupt episodes.
During an episode, dogs may exhibit signs of discomfort, not overt
pain. Unfortunately, it is difficult to distinguish a PD from a focal
seizure. Both occur without loss of consciousness, autonomic signs,
and can be brief, although episodes of much longer duration are
typical of PDs. Episodes invariably end without evidence of a postictal phase.3

ETIOLOGY
A classification scheme has been proposed to separate canine PDs by
cause, including genetics, diet, drugs, or secondary to other
diseases.2 Genetic etiologies include two disorders in which a
causative genetic mutation was identified: episodic falling syndrome
(EFS) in Cavalier King Charles Spaniel (CKCS) and PD in Soft Coated
Wheaten Terriers (SCWT)14-16 (Videos 41.10 and 4.11

). Some

other PDs, including PD in Chinook dogs13 (Video 41.12

),

“Scottie cramp” (SC) in Scottish Terriers17 (Video 41.13), PDs in
Norwich Terriers (NT)18 (Video 41.14), Labrador Retrievers, Jack
Russell Terriers, and Maltese dogs have suspected genetic
origins.19,20 Gluten-sensitive PDs have been identified in Border
Terriers21,22 (Video 41.15

). Phenobarbital administration

reportedly caused PD in a Chow Chow and propofol caused PD in a
Golden Retriever.23,24 PD has also been occasionally reported in
dogs suffering from intracranial neurological disease, including
meningoencephalitis of unknown etiology (MUE).2 There have been
sporadic reports of PDs affecting other dog breeds, including Bichon

Frisé, German Shorthaired Pointer, Boxer, and Dalmatian.25-28 PDs
have also been observed in mixed-breed dogs (personal observation)
(Video 41.9; Video 41.16

).

PATHOGENESIS
The pathophysiology of PDs in people, after review of functional
imaging and pathologic study results, demonstrates evidence of
abnormalities in the basal nuclei and related thalamocortical
network.29 Lesions in the basal nuclei have been documented in
secondary PDs.30 The identification of genetic mutations involving
ion channel function supports the theory that many PDs result from
“channelopathies.” Despite some PDs having a genetic basis, their
pathogenesis involves multiple mechanisms, as confirmed by finding
non-ion channel mutations.2 A genome-wide association study
(GWAS) on Border Terriers diagnosed as having canine epileptoid
cramping syndrome failed to detect significant chromosomal
alterations in the study group. Nevertheless, pedigree analysis
supported the hypothesis of an underlying complex inherited
disorder triggered by gluten exposure.22

DIAGNOSIS (FIGURE 41.1)
The diagnosis of PDs, in many instances, is challenging due to their
complex clinical signs and similarities with epilepsy. Each patient
must be properly described clinically, because advanced imaging
(MRI, CT, et al.) results are often non-specific and used to exclude
structural neurologic diseases.2,5 Results of MRI scans performed on
dogs with idiopathic epilepsy (IE) and those with PDs are similar and
consistent with the non-structural nature of these disorders. The
interictal patterns on EEG can be useful in differentiating IE from
PD, but this tool is rarely available in clinical practices. Thus,
signalment, history, and characterizing the episodes are important
when identifying PDs not associated with other neurological

disorders.3 Hematology, serum chemistries and urinalysis are used
to rule out obvious systemic disorders that can cause signs, such as
muscle cramping associated with hypocalcemia (chs. 69 and 284).

FIGURE 41.1 Clinical approach to a dog with
suspected paroxysmal dyskinesia. CBC, Complete
blood count; CSF, cerebrospinal fluid; EEG,
electroencephalography; MRI, magnetic resonance
imaging.

TREATMENT
Many PD episodes are self-limiting, raising the question of whether
improvement following treatment is due to the therapy or simply a
reflection of the typical clinical course. Different drugs have been
used to treat PDs with varying results. When related to stress or
other triggers, owners may be able to reduce episode frequency by
improving or changing the environment.

SPECIFIC BREED-RELATED
PAROXySMAL DYSKINESIAS
EPISODIC FALLING SYNDROME (EFS) IN
CAVALIER KING CHARLES SPANIELS (CKCS)
EFS in CKCS, one of the first recognized and best-known dog PDs, is
usually first observed in the first 4 years of life.3,15,31,32 EFS in CKCS
is an autosomal-recessive inherited disorder caused by mutation of
the brevican (BCAN) gene, resulting in a disturbance of axonal
conduction and synaptic stability.2,15 Episodes resemble PNKD
triggered by exercise, stress, or excitement and are characterized by
progressive limb hypertonicity, arching of the back, and lowering of
the head. The result is a “deer-stalking” posture before falling.
Episodes last seconds to minutes.3 (Video 41.10

). Diagnosis is

based on clinical suspicion and confirmed with genetic testing.
Treatment has not been rewarding, although clonazepam (0.5-2
mg/kg q8h) or acetazolamide have each been beneficial in some.
Drug tolerance may develop.33

SCOTTIE CRAMP (SC) IN SCOTTISH
TERRIERS
SC was first described in the 1940s and is clinically similar to EFS in
CKCS. It can be triggered by stress, exercise or excitement.3,17,34 SC

was considered an autosomal-recessive inherited disorder, but a
recent study demonstrated that almost three-fourths of all females
are affected, suggesting a complex genetic pathogenesis.17 First
episodes are usually observed during the first 6 months of life,
although rarely seen as late as 7 years of age. Most episodes are
similar to EFS: progressive dystonia of the hind limbs, generalized
hypertonicity producing a stiff stilted gait that progresses to a “deerstalking” posture and then falling with the back arched and flexion of
the neck and tail17 (Video 41.13

). Dogs appear conscious during

episodes. Milder episodes of hind limb spasticity and bunny-hopping
have been reported.17 Attacks usually have a duration of 5 to 10
minutes, but some last as long as 20 minutes. Dogs appear healthy
between episodes and diagnosis relies on signalment and clinical
signs. Fluoxetine and diazepam are considered beneficial.31 Signs
usually decrease in severity over time, some following a regimen of
behavior modification and avoidance of triggering factors.

PAROXYSMAL DYSKINESIA IN
CHINOOK DOGS
PD in Chinook dogs is a presumed autosomal-recessive inherited
disorder. For years, this condition was known as “Chinook seizures”;
now it is classified as a PMD.13 A minority of Chinook dogs exhibit
both PDs and generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS).3,13 Episodes
resemble a PNKD, as they are not triggered by sudden movements.
Clinical signs are first seen between 2 months to 5 years of age and
consistently include inability to stand, dystonia (hypertonic flexion of
one or more limbs), chorea-like (repetitive small-range) movements,
and ballismus-like movements (flailing or kicking limbs).13 Fine
head tremors have been observed. As with other PDs, autonomic
signs or loss of consciousness are not seen. Episodes vary in
frequency, from several episodes in a day to only occurring every few
months. Episode duration varies from minutes to an hour (

Video

41.12). Diagnosis is dependent on signalment and clinical signs.

PAROXYSMAL GLUTEN-SENSITIVE
DYSKINESIA IN BORDER TERRIERS
Formerly known as “canine epileptoid cramping syndrome” and
considered a type of epilepsy due to the presence of “autonomic
signs” (borborygmi, vomiting, diarrhea) between episodes, this
condition is now thought to have a dietary etiology.21 Paroxysmal
episodes are characterized by gait abnormalities: from
incoordination to inability to stand; dystonia of limbs, head, and/or
neck; and tremors (Video 41.15

). The duration of most episodes

ranges from 2 to 120 minutes.35 The median age when clinical signs
are first seen is 2 to 3 years.22 Diagnosis is based on breed and
videos. Diagnosis can then be confirmed with positive test results for
anti-gliadin and -transglutaminase-2 antibodies. Antibody tests are
only reliable when dogs have not had appropriate dietary changes.2
Affected dogs respond well to a gluten-free diet, which significantly
decreases frequency and severity of episodes. Remission has been
achieved in some. Anti-gliadin and -transglutaminase-2 antibodies
should be monitored every 3 months to ensure that the levels are
returning to baseline.2

PAROXYSMAL DYSKINESIA IN SOFT
COATED WHEATEN TERRIERS
An autosomal-recessive inherited PD associated with a missense
mutation of the PIGN gene has been described in SCWT.16 These
episodes are similar to PNKD since they are not associated with
exercise and are sometimes triggered by excitement. Episodes, single
or multiple, share the typical features of PDs and can last from
minutes to as long as 4 hours. Typical episodes include dystonic
rapidly alternating or synchronous flexion and extension of the hind
limbs, with varying degrees of truncal dystonia. Severe cases also
have front limb involvement16 (

Video 41.11). Treatment with

anti-epileptic drugs, including benzodiazepines, has not been
beneficial. The disease has the tendency to worsen with age and
some dogs are euthanized due to increasing frequency and severity of
the episodes.16

PAROXYSMAL DYSKINESIA IN
MALTESE DOGS
Male Maltese dogs seem overrepresented and the frequency of
episodes varies from daily clusters to isolated events.20 The median
age of the first episode was 5.4 years and most owners observe their
dogs seeking reassurance before onset.20 Paroxysmal episodes are
characterized by dystonia starting in the front limbs and progressing
to involve the hind limbs and generalized body tremors. Dogs remain
conscious and, typically, do not exhibit autonomic signs. Treatment
includes acetazolamide, fluoxetine, and a gluten-free diet.
Interestingly, some dogs empirically placed on gluten-free diets have
a resolution of clinical signs.20

PAROXYSMAL DYSKINESIA IN
NORWICH TERRIERS
PD in NT was first reported in 1984 but has since been better
characterized.18,30,36 The median age at first episode is about 3 years
and duration of episodes ranges from 2 to 30 minutes. In some dogs,
stress, excitement, anxiety, exercise, change in weather or
temperature seem to trigger episodes of sustained hypertonicity
variously affecting the hind limbs (

Video 41.14). Some dogs also

show dystonia of the front limbs, trunk, and tail. Most dogs are
unable to stand during episodes.18 PD in NTs is not considered a
progressive disease.

EPISODIC HEAD TREMOR SYNDROME
(“HEAD BOBBING”)
This is a breed-associated disorder in the English Bulldog (Video
41.7; Video 41.17

), Doberman Pinscher (Video 41.18), and a few

other breeds.37-39 While considered a form of PD due to the brief
duration with an abrupt onset and end, they are also considered a
“tremor.”

MYOCLONIC DISORDERS
In veterinary medicine, myoclonus events are classified as epileptic
or nonepileptic.4 Nonepileptic myoclonus in dogs is a common
consequence of distemper encephalomyelitis. Myoclonus may
develop after other types of encephalitis. In distemper, constant,
repetitive myoclonus is better appreciated during rest and sleep. It
affects primarily limb and facial muscles (Videos 41.1 and 41.2

).

Myoclonic contractions appear to originate from functional lesions in
lower motor neurons that produce an autonomous pacemaker,
resulting in rhythmic muscle contractions.7 Epileptic myoclonus has
primarily been documented in dogs suffering from Lafora Disease
(LD) and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and in cats with audiogenic
reflex seizures.4,40-42 LD is a genetic, autosomal recessive,
neurodegenerative disease affecting several dog breeds including
Miniature Wirehaired Dachshund (MWHD), Beagle, Miniature and
Standard Poodle, Welsh Corgi, and Pointer.4 LD is the result of an
EPM2b gene mutation, is usually diagnosed in 6- to 13-year-olds,
and is characterized by jerky movements of the head triggered by
auditory and visual stimuli (

Video 41.3). Some progress to

GTCS.4,41 Other signs include hypnotic myoclonus, jaw smacking,
fly-catching, and panic attacks.41 Diagnosis of LD is made when
brain MRI (ch. 112) demonstrates generalized cortical atrophy

together with positive genetic testing.41 Treatment, consisting of oral
levetiracetam administration (20 mg/kg q8h), can be initially
successful but myoclonus becomes progressively more severe.41
Juvenile-onset myoclonic epilepsy has been described in Rhodesian
Ridgebacks due to a fully penetrant recessive mutation in the
DIRAS1 gene.42 Levetiracetam-responsive reflex myoclonic
audiogenic seizures have been recently described in a population of
older cats (median age 15 years). This late-onset epilepsy of unknown
origin is non-progressive and affected cats, besides reflex myoclonic
seizures, can exhibit hearing disturbances, GTCS, weight loss, and
reduced interaction.41
