Tremor is an involuntary, rhythmic, oscillatory movement of a
body part produced by alternating contractions of reciprocally
innervated muscles.1 Tremor is easy to see but more difficult to
categorize and treat. It may be seen in isolation or in conjunction
with other neurological conditions—for example, with movement
disorders such as paroxysmal dyskinesia (ch. 41).2,3

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF TREMOR
Achieving coordinated movement requires reciprocal innervation
(Sherrington’s Second Law), i.e., a premotor neuron sends excitatory
projections to the motor neurons innervating the agonist muscle

group (for example, the joint extensors) and to the inhibitory neuron
innervating the motor neuron for the antagonist muscle group (for
example, the joint flexors).4 This reciprocal innervation is controlled
by neural circuits in the thalamus, inferior olive nucleus, cerebrum,
and cerebellum.5 The dentate-rubro-olivary tract linking the dentate
nucleus of the cerebellum with the contralateral red nucleus and the
inferior olive nucleus is of pivotal importance.6 These circuits, with
their complex feedback loops, are inherently unstable. If neural
membrane excitability increases or if inhibition is reduced, then the
circuit begins to oscillate. These rhythmic oscillations manifest as
tremor.5

NEUROTRANSMITTERS AND
TREMORLYTIC DRUGS
The cerebellar Purkinje neurons (or cells which synapse on them) are
implicated in many tremor syndromes.5,7 Purkinje cells are
inhibitory GABAergic, influencing the outflow of the deep cerebellar
nuclei such as the dentate nuclei. Excitatory noradrenergic neurons
of the locus coeruleus influence these Purkinje cells and are other
important neuron groups implicated in tremor.8 Decreased
GABAergic inhibition of deep cerebellar neurons disinhibits their
pacemaker activity, resulting in rhythmical activity of the thalamic
and thalamocortical circuits.9 Consequently, many types of tremor
respond to drugs that enhance post-synaptic GABA-mediated
inhibition, such as phenobarbital and primidone. Drugs which have a
membrane-stabilizing effect such as propranolol, gabapentin and
topiramate can also be effective.5,7,10,11 Consequently, these drugs
are the mainstay for treatment of many human tremor conditions
(for example, essential tremor) and can be of benefit in some
veterinary tremor syndromes.12-14 Parkinsonian tremor is related to
basal nuclei dopaminergic degeneration and abnormalities of striatal
acetylcholine signaling.15 The mainstay of treatment of Parkinson’s
disease is drugs affecting dopaminergic neurotransmission such as

L-dopa (increases striatal dopamine), dopamine agonists, and
inhibitors of monoamine oxidase (block dopamine degradation).11 In
addition, symptoms are relieved by anticholinergics.11,15 With the
exception of inherited canine multiple system degeneration, which is
not associated with resting tremor,16 conditions comparable to
Parkinson’s disease are not yet recognized in domestic small animals
and use of these drugs for tremor syndromes has not been reported.
In veterinary medicine, methocarbamol, a carbamate with centrally
acting muscle relaxant properties, is also used in severe generalized
tremor disorders (40-50 mg/kg IV slowly until resolution or near
resolution of tremor; repeat as necessary or follow with 8.8-12.2
mg/kg/h IV constant rate infusion [CRI], titrated to effect but not to
exceed 2 mL/min; monitor for hypotension, profound central
nervous system [CNS] depression, seizures).17

CLASSIFICATION
A veterinary consensus on categorization of tremor is not available.
Consequently, veterinarians often refer to the Consensus Statement
on the Classification of Tremors from the International Parkinson
and Movement Disorder Society.1 Tremor may be classified
according to clinical features (axis 1) or etiology (axis 2) (Table
42.1). This system overcomes the difficulty of how to classify tremor
types that have multiple etiologies or tremor syndromes that have
more than one type of tremor.

INVESTIGATION OF TREMOR
HISTORICAL FEATURES
The veterinarian should explore historical features such as: age of
onset, temporal evolution, familial history, medical and medication
history (ch. 2; Video 42.1

) and possible exposure to toxins. Like

many neurological conditions, features such as insidious onset and
progressive course are suggestive of degenerative conditions (ch.

244) whereas acute-onset generalized tremor is more suggestive of a
metabolic, drug-based, toxic, or immune-mediated etiology (ch.
242).

TREMOR CHARACTERISTICS
A tremor can be categorized by: 1) anatomical distribution and body
parts that are affected (for example: generalized, head, pelvic limbs,
ocular (Video 42.2

) or jaw); 2) tremor frequency (see

Electrophysiology, below); and 3) how the tremor is activated, for
which the broad classification is rest or action (Table 42.2). Action
tremor is further subdivided into postural, kinetic, isometric and (in
humans) task-specific. Resting tremor is tremor without voluntary
activation, i.e., in a body part that has no voluntary muscle
contraction and is completely supported against gravity (Video 42.1
). Resting tremors are uncommon in veterinary medicine. Action
tremors are associated with voluntary muscle contraction, such as
while maintaining a position against gravity (postural and
orthostatic tremor); muscle contraction against a rigid stationary
object such as jaw clenching (isometric tremor); or during voluntary
movement (kinetic tremor).1 Kinetic tremor is further subdivided
into simple (tremor is roughly the same throughout a movement)
and intention (crescendo increase in tremor as the affected body part
approaches its visual target; associated with cerebellar disease).
Orthostatic tremor is defined as tremor in the limbs and trunk
evoked during standing and is considered a distinct clinical entity
under axis 2 (Table 42.1).

ASSOCIATED SIGNS
Physical (ch. 3) and neurological (ch. 241) exams should focus on
identification of associated or concomitant signs that may aid in
establishing the clinical diagnosis. An isolated tremor is a syndrome
where tremor is the only abnormal sign, whereas in combined
tremor there are other abnormal neurological (e.g., cerebellar ataxia,
dystonic postures, or rigidity) or systemic (e.g., weakness, vomiting,
diarrhea) signs.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTS
Laboratory Tests
A complete blood count and serum biochemistry profile are essential
in the workup of a tremulous animal, especially with acute-onset
generalized tremor. Metabolic causes of tremor include
hypoglycemia (ch. 61), hypocalcemia (ch. 69), hepatic
encephalopathy (ch. 267), thiamine deficiency (ch. 14),
thyrotoxicosis (ch. 287), hyperchloremic metabolic alkalosis,
hypophosphatemia (ch. 69), and hypodipsic hypernatremia (ch.
67).

Toxicology
Inappropriate ingestion of a tremorgenic substance is the most
common cause of acute-onset generalized tremor and is usually
combined with other neurological and systemic signs (Mycotoxicosis
and Other Tremorgenic Intoxications, below; ch. 133). Many
laboratories offer toxicology screening assays of the suspected
contaminated material, vomitus or stomach contents, urine, and
blood. Depending on the nature of the toxin, there may be other
diagnostic options, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based
identification of mushrooms.18

Electrophysiology
Tremor frequency is determined by electromyography (EMG; ch.
111) or, in humans, computerized tremor analysis with

accelerometers attached to body parts.19 However, even in humans,
analyzing tremor frequency has limited usefulness because the
frequency of most pathological tremors is 4 to 8 Hz. The important
exception to this is primary orthostatic tremor, which classically has
a frequency of 13 to 18 Hz (Figure 42.1). Electrophysiologic testing
may also be useful to rule out concomitant neuromuscular disease.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI; ch. 112) is useful to identify
neurological diseases with (combined) tremor that result in
structural changes, such as infectious and non-infectious
inflammatory diseases, leukoencephalopathies (white matter
disease), degenerative diseases resulting in cerebellar atrophy, and
developmental cerebellar disease (Figure 42.2). Most isolated
tremor disorders will not result in structural MRI changes in the
brain.

Aspirational Diagnostic Tests
In human medicine, positron emission tomography (PET), single
photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) imaging
techniques, and transcranial sonography of the nigrostriatal
dopaminergic system, basal nuclei and cerebellum can distinguish
essential, parkinsonism, orthostatic, neuropathic, drug-induced and
dystonic tremors and help improve understanding of the
pathophysiology of tremor.

ACUTE-ONSET GENERALIZED TREMOR
SYNDROMES
PHYSIOLOGICAL AND ENHANCED
PHYSIOLOGICAL TREMOR
Physiological tremor is a barely visible tremor that occurs in healthy
individuals and may be enhanced in certain situations such as
loading (muscle fatigue), stress, drugs and toxins, metabolic diseases

(for example, thyrotoxicosis, hypoglycemia [Video 42.3

],

hypocalcemia, and other electrolyte disorders), and
thermoregulatory shivering.20 Enhanced physiological tremor is
reversible if the cause of the tremor is eliminated.1

MYCOTOXICOSIS AND OTHER
TREMORGENIC INTOXICATIONS
Mycotoxins are toxic secondary metabolites produced by fungi and
molds. Ingestion of tremorgenic mycotoxins, particularly the
Penicillium toxins penitrem A and roquefortine, is one of the most
common causes of acute-onset generalized tremor in veterinary
medicine Table 42.3.21 A whole-body tremor is present at rest and
is exacerbated by effort and anxiety. Affected animals may also show
mydriasis, vestibular signs, facial myoclonus, generalized seizures,
hyperesthesia, hyperthermia, tachycardia and gastrointestinal signs
(vomiting, diarrhea, flatulence).21,22 The most important differential

diagnoses are other intoxications (ch. 133). Management of
tremorgenic intoxication is outlined in Figure 42.3. In a rodent
model, tremorgenic mycotoxins decreased GABAergic inhibitory
outflow and increased release of glutamate (excitotoxicity).23,24
Therefore, drugs affecting these targets are appropriate for
management. However, the tremors are often resistant to
intravenous benzodiazepines,21 possibly due to intracellular chloride
ion accumulation secondary to excitotoxicity.25 Mycotoxins are
highly lipid soluble, which explains their excellent ability to
penetrate the brain. Using intravenous lipid emulsion (Intralipid
20%) can shorten the median time to clinical improvement to 4
hours from 24-96 hours.17 Use of other drugs varies between
clinicians. The author prefers dexmedetomidine as a first-line agent
(375-500 mcg/m2 IV; repeat as necessary q4h or follow with 25
mcg/m2/h IV CRI) followed, if necessary, by anti-epilepsy drugs (ch.
247).22 Dexmedetomidine is a central alpha2-adrenoreceptor
agonist with a site of action at the locus coeruleus, influencing
Purkinje cell and GABAergic output.26 A CRI of the centrally acting
muscle relaxant methocarbamol is also described to be useful (see
dosage, above).17 Most dogs make a complete recovery within a few
days but persistent ataxia for months or years has been reported.27

IDIOPATHIC GENERALIZED TREMOR
SYNDROME
Idiopathic generalized tremor syndrome (IGTS) historically was
referred to as white shakers, because of a tendency to occur in white
breeds like West Highland White Terriers and Maltese dogs.
However, IGTS may occur in any dog breed or cross (rare in large
breeds) and is also reported in cats.28,29 It occurs in young adult
dogs; other diseases are more likely in dogs aged 5 years and older.
The etiology is undetermined but histopathological studies and
response to immunosuppressive doses of corticosteroids suggest that
it is a noninfectious, immune-mediated disease. Anecdotally, some
dogs have concomitant gastrointestinal disease. Affected dogs have a
whole-body tremor that worsens with anxiety (Video 42.4

).

Associated signs include hyperthermia, hyperesthesia, opsoclonus
(ocular tremor; Video 42.2), and mild cerebellovestibular signs such
as head tilt and ataxia. There are no structural abnormalities on MRI
of the brain. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis may be normal or
suggest mild mononuclear or lymphocytic pleocytosis. Management
is by immunosuppression, typically with prednisolone monotherapy
starting at 1-2 mg/kg PO q12-24h. In most cases, the tremor
improves in 3-10 days. After the tremor resolves, the corticosteroid
dosage is tapered slowly, usually over 6 months or more. The
prognosis is good, although relapses can occur, and, in some
patients, low-dose corticosteroids must be continued for many
months. In poorly responding or relapsing cases, or where the
adverse effects of corticosteroids are poorly tolerated, the author
adds mycophenolate at 10 mg/kg PO q24h (every 12 hours for the
first 7 days of therapy) (chs. 144 and 169).

COMBINED TREMOR WITH CENTRAL
NERVOUS SYSTEM INFECTIOUS AND
NON-INFECTIOUS INFLAMMATORY
DISEASE

Any CNS disease that involves the cerebellum or the neural circuits
between the thalamus, inferior olive nucleus, cerebrum, and
cerebellum can present with tremor (Figure 42.2). However, unlike
IGTS, where generalized tremor is the predominant sign, in other
CNS inflammatory diseases the tremor is combined with other
neurological signs. If there is associated meningitis, then pain will be
a predominant feature. The most important differential diagnoses for
IGTS are cerebellitis; meningoencephalomyelitis of unknown origin
(Video 42.5

) (including granulomatous

meningoencephalomyelitis and necrotizing
meningoencephalomyelitis); viral encephalitis (for example,
Aujeszky disease virus30); and protozoal encephalitis (Video 42.6
; ch. 242).

CHRONIC GENERALIZED TREMOR
SYNDROMES
CEREBELLAR TREMOR
The cerebellum regulates movement by adjusting the output of the
descending motor system of the brain. It acts as a “comparator,”
compensating for errors of movement by comparing intended with
actual performance.30 The hallmark of cerebellar disease is intention
tremor (Videos 42.6 and 42.7

) although many animals with

cerebellar disease will also have postural tremor, particularly of the
head, and a rhythmic postural sway (truncal tremor) (Video 42.8
).31 There are many causes of cerebellar disease, including
spinocerebellar ataxias and other (inherited) degenerative, metabolic
(

Video 42.7), or inflammatory disorders (Videos 42.4 and 42.5).

DYSMYELINATION AND
HYPOMYELINATION DISORDERS
(SHAKER PUP SYNDROME)
Inherited developmental disorders of central myelination may result
in shaker pup syndrome. From approximately 10 days of age,
affected animals show a gross generalized tremor, particularly when
aroused. Many affected dogs recover by 5 months of age.32 The
condition is recognized in many breeds including the Springer
Spaniel (autosomal recessive, sex-linked: males have a more severe
and fatal phenotype33), Weimaraner (mutation in folliculininteracting protein 2 gene32;
Video 41.4), Chow Chow, Bernese
Mountain Dog, Samoyed, and Siamese cats. Quantitative MRI
demonstrates that the white matter of affected pups resembles the
myelin pattern of newborns, with altered signal intensity compared
to age-matched controls.34

LEUKODYSTROPHIES AND
LEUKOENCEPHALOPATHIES
Leukodystrophies are degenerative disorders that primarily involve
the brain white matter and destruction of initially normal myelin
(ch. 244). Examples with combined tremor include globoid cell
leukodystrophy, hereditary leukodystrophy in Standard Schnauzer
puppies (TSEN54 missense variant35), spongiform
leukoencephalomyelopathy in Border Terriers,36 Alexander’s
disease, and leukoencephalopathy associated with parvovirus
infection in Cretan hound puppies.37 MRI findings vary with the
specific disease entity but in general, leukodystrophy is suggested by
diffuse bilateral and symmetrical or almost symmetrical white
matter disease (hyperintense on T2-weighted [T2W]) without mass
effect (Figure 42.2; Video 42.9

).

ORTHOSTATIC TREMOR (LIMB
SHAKING WHEN STANDING)
Orthostatic tremor is a tremor of the limbs and trunk evoked during
standing and which disappears during voluntary movement and
when the patient is recumbent (Video 42.10

). In humans, an

important differential for orthostatic tremor is orthostatic
myoclonus, which is characterized by action myoclonus when
standing and irregular myoclonic EMG bursts with a median
duration of 38 to 62 ms and a median frequency of 6 to 12 Hz.38 This
is not reported in veterinary medicine, possibly because it has not
been considered.

Benign Orthostatic Tremor (Senile Tremor)
A benign syndrome of pelvic limb tremor is recognized, particularly
in older dogs.14 Occasionally the thoracic limbs may be affected.
There are anecdotal reports in cats. Although the tremor may
become more pronounced with time, it does not appear to cause
distress or interfere with function. If treatment is required, then the
author’s first choice is gabapentin 10-20 mg/kg PO q8-12h or as for
primary orthostatic tremor (below).

Primary Orthostatic Tremor
A condition described as a primary orthostatic tremor has been
detailed in young adult Great Danes and Scottish Deerhounds.12,13
Tremor with high-frequency EMG discharges (13-18 Hz; ch. 111)
appears when the dog stands or when moving from one static
posture to another—for example, from standing to sitting or
posturing to eat, drink, or defecate (Figure 42.1). The tremor
disappears on walking and when recumbent. If forced to stand, then
the dog tends to shift weight between the limbs looking
uncomfortable and distressed. Function is compromised as the dog
seems to have difficulty moving from one static posture to another.
Auscultation of the muscle with a stethoscope may reveal a
helicopter-like sound. The condition is progressive over years. The

condition has been compared to primary orthostatic tremor in
humans (shaky legs syndrome) which is also characterized by a highfrequency tremor (13-18 Hz) triggered during isometric contraction
of the limb muscles or during standing. However, in humans the
tremor often is not visible and may only be apparent on palpation,
auscultation of muscle with a stethoscope, or EMG. The diagnosis is
suspected from the subjective description of feeling unsteady when
standing and relief on sitting.1 By comparison, in dogs the tremor is
visible, gross, and severe (Video 42.11

). First-line therapy in dogs

is phenobarbital (2-3 mg/kg PO q12h). Second-line therapy, usually
in combination, is gabapentin (10-20 mg/kg PO q8-12h). By
comparison, first-line therapy in humans is clonazepam. Second-line
therapies, either as monotherapy or in combination, include
gabapentin, primidone, sodium valproate, carbamazepine and
phenobarbital.39

TREMORS ASSOCIATED WITH
MOVEMENT DISORDERS (MYOCLONUS,
DYSTONIA, PAROXYSMAL
DYSKINESIAS)
Myoclonus describes a sudden, brief involuntary twitching or jerking
of a muscle or group of muscles (Videos 42.12 and 42.13

; ch.

41). Dystonia is an involuntary abnormal co-contraction of
antagonistic muscles, which may cause sustained abnormal postures
or twisting and repetitive movements.2 Paroxysmal dyskinesias in
the dog are characterized by episodes of rapid flexion and extension
of the limbs, usually altering between limbs but sometimes involving
more than one limb (ch. 41; Videos

41.8-41.12). The trunk is

often dystonic (for example, kyphotic posture) and the head often
weaves from side to side. The dog remains conscious, with variable
autonomic signs (for example, vomiting). Tremulous movements

may be observed as part of these movement disorders or be the
predominant sign3 (Table 42.2 and Video 42.14

).

IDIOPATHIC HEAD TREMOR
SYNDROME (IHTS)
IHTS is characterized by paroxysmal rhythmic head movements and
is most likely a paroxysmal tremulous dystonia or myoclonus (Video
42.15

). It is most common in English and French Bulldogs,

Doberman Pinschers, Boxers, Staffordshire Bull Terriers and
Labrador Retrievers, but it can occur in many purebred and mixedbreed dogs.40 Affected dogs may have a yes-yes (vertical) or no-no
(horizonal) action. It is very unusual to see both no-no and yes-yes in
an individual dog and the direction of movement does not change
during an episode.41 There may be a subtle head tilt (dystonia). The
first episode is generally when the dog is a young adult (before 48
months of age) but it may occur in older dogs.40 Episodes vary in
duration from a few seconds to several hours, with much variation in
frequency and length of time between episodes.41 Anxiety may be a
trigger in some dogs and episodes are more likely (but not
exclusively) from rest or sleep.42 The owners may be able to
interrupt mild episodes, such as by offering food or turning the head.
The dog may try to stop the action by pressing its head into an object
or its paws. Most dogs do not respond to anti-epileptic drugs
(phenobarbital, bromide, diazepam, imepitoin).40,43 However, there
can be many months between episodes and the syndrome may
resolve spontaneously in older animals.42

TREMOR ASSOCIATED WITH
PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY
An animal may present with a tremulous limb associated with
weakness from a peripheral neuropathy (ch. 252) or ventral horn
cell (spinal cord) damage (Video 42.16

).14,44 Occasionally, the

tremor may be disproportionate to the weakness and in humans it
has been suggested that in some demyelinating neuropathies there
may be a central component.45

CLIENT INFORMATION
Idiopathic Generalized Tremor Syndrome (IGTS)/White Shakers

WHAT IS IDIOPATHIC GENERALIZED TREMOR
SYNDROME (IGTS)?
Tremor (shake, tremble or shiver) can be a normal body function
(e.g., shivering with cold or anxiety) but sometimes it is seen as part
of a neurological disease. IGTS is a disease characterized by a severe
whole-body tremor. The onset occurs over hours to days and is
thought to be due to inflammation which causes a problem in brain
neurotransmission.

WHAT TYPE OF ANIMAL CAN BE AFFECTED AND
WHAT ARE THE CLINICAL SIGNS?
IGTS is sometimes referred to as White Shakers, because of a
tendency to occur in white breeds like West Highland White Terriers
and Maltese dogs. However, IGTS may occur in any dog breed (or
cross) and is also reported in cats. It is more common in small dogs
and is rare in dogs that weigh more than 20 kg. It generally occurs in
young adult dogs (typically 2 years old). Other diseases are more
likely in dogs aged 5 years and older. Affected dogs have a wholebody shake that worsens with anxiety or stress. They may also have
elevated body temperature, increased sensitivity to sounds and touch
and have poor balance. They can sometimes have a tremor of the
eyeball and jaw causing jerky eye movements and teeth chattering.
Although their ability to walk is compromised they remain mentally
aware. It is not a painful condition although it can be distressing.

WHAT CAUSES IGTS AND HOW CAN IT BE
DIAGNOSED?
The cause of IGTS is unknown. Studies suggest that it is a noninfectious central nervous system inflammatory disease. Diagnostic
tests such as magnetic resonance imaging and cerebrospinal fluid
analysis may be normal or suggest mild inflammation (encephalitis).
IGTS is considered an auto-immune disease, i.e., a condition where
an overzealous immune system attacks normal cells mistaking them
for an infection.

WHAT IS THE PROGNOSIS AND TREATMENT?

IGTS is treated by suppressing the immune system with
corticosteroids, typically prednisolone or methylprednisolone. The
pet is started on a high dose and after the tremor has resolved the
dose will be tapered slowly, usually over 6 months or more. Your
veterinarian will want to examine your pet at regular intervals to
monitor the response to treatment. In most cases the tremor
improves in 3-10 days. Prognosis is good although relapses can
occur, and, in some patients, a low dose of corticosteroids must be
continued for a long time. In some cases, other immunosuppressive
drugs such as mycophenolate or leflunomide may be given in
combination with the corticosteroids.

DOES THE TREATMENT HAVE ANY SIDE
EFFECTS?
It is important that the corticosteroids are not stopped too quickly
because the body becomes adapted to their presence and the dog or
cat can become very ill if they are withdrawn suddenly.
Unfortunately corticosteroids do have side effects which are detailed
below.
Common Side Effects That Are Dose Dependant
These side effects improve as the dose of drug is reduced.
• Increase in thirst, urine volume and urination frequency. Some
housebroken dogs produce so much urine that they cannot
wait to be taken outside and urinate in the home.
• Increase in hunger. Corticosteroids send a message to the brain
that the dog or the cat should eat despite there being no need
for extra calories. Consequently there is a tendency for weight
gain which can be challenging to avoid. Try feeding more of a
reduced calorie food and presenting the food in ways to
prolong mealtime; for example, using a maze food bowl.
• Panting
• Lethargy
• Poor hair growth from any clipped sites (for example, where
there was an intravenous catheter)

Common Side Effects That Are Duration of Therapy
Dependant
These side effects may be seen after several weeks of corticosteroids.
• Muscle weakness
• Poor exercise tolerance and lethargy
• Hair loss in the trunk area (usually not from the head or limbs)
• Pot-bellied appearance
• Susceptibility to infection (for example, skin or bladder
infections)
• Delayed wound healing
Rare but More Serious Side Effects
Generally if your pet has signs that concern you then call to discuss
with your veterinarian as soon as possible.
• Mood changes such as increased anxiety
• Vomiting and diarrhea
• Gastrointestinal bleeding. In this instance the feces will appear
tarry black. Contact your veterinarian immediately.
• Life-threatening infection
• Increased susceptibility to diabetes mellitus
• Increased susceptibility to embolism (where blood flow in an
artery is blocked by a blood clot)

Paresis, and Paralysis

Ataxia, paresis, and paralysis are clinical signs commonly seen in
various diseases of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. The
main difference between ataxia and paresis is that ataxia affects
coordination without affecting strength, while paresis affects only
strength. These clinical signs provide fundamental information for
lesion localization; therefore, it is important to be familiar with their
presentation, clinical significance, and main causes. The discussion
that follows, combined with the videos and algorithms, aim to assist
the reader achieve this goal.

ATAXIA
Ataxia means incoordination. It comes from the Greek word a taxis,
which means without order or without coordination. It is one of the
most important neurologic signs to recognize due to its importance

in localizing lesions within the nervous system. Ataxia is an inability
for the patient to coordinate the position of its head, trunk, and
limbs in space.1 Ataxia is a sensory, not motor, dysfunction that can
only be identified when the patient moves.2-4 The type of the ataxia
is characterized through a complete neurologic examination (mental
status, gait and posture, postural reactions, evaluation of cranial
nerves and spinal reflexes, and pain perception; ch. 241). Special
attention should be given to the gait and posture. Mild forms of
ataxia may be difficult to recognize. The animal’s gait should be
carefully evaluated in a room large enough to allow the animal to
move freely. The animal should also be walked, at a slow pace,
toward and away from the examiner in an area with nonslippery
floors. Ataxia is mainly a sign of a neurologic disturbance. It is often
confused with weakness (discussed below) but they are quite
distinct. Systemic conditions can cause ataxia, but more commonly
cause weakness without ataxia. Examples of systemic conditions
causing ataxia are hypocalcemia causing cerebellar ataxia and
thiamine deficiency causing vestibular ataxia.1 Many other systemic
diseases can cause transient ataxia, such as hypoglycemia,
hypotension, and certain intoxications.

TYPES OF ATAXIA
There are three types of ataxia, namely proprioceptive, cerebellar,
and vestibular.1,4 Vestibular ataxia is the easiest to recognize (ch.
248;

Video 43.1). Vestibular ataxia is characterized

predominantly by a head tilt.5 Usually, the side of the head tilt
indicates the side of the lesion. Other common signs of vestibular
ataxia are leaning, falling, rolling, occasionally circling, strabismus,
and nystagmus. The severity of vestibular signs depends on a
number of factors, but it is usually worse in the acute phase of the
disease, while the patient still has spontaneous nystagmus. It is
important to differentiate between central and peripheral vestibular
disease because the differential diagnoses and prognoses differ
greatly. Patients with central vestibular disease have changes in

mental status (most commonly somnolence) and deficits in
proprioceptive positioning and/or hopping. Nonambulatory
tetraparesis is also commonly associated with central disease.
Vertical nystagmus or positional nystagmus (one that changes
direction when altering the head position) may also be seen. The
proprioceptive positioning deficits are ipsilateral to the head tilt,
except in cases of paradoxical vestibular syndrome, where
proprioceptive deficits are contralateral to the head tilt. Central
vestibular signs are associated with rostral medullary lesions
(brainstem) or with lesions in the flocculonodular lobe of the
cerebellum and are commonly caused by encephalitis or tumors. In
peripheral vestibular disease, as the lesion involves the inner ear
receptors located outside the brain (petrosal portion of temporal
bone), the patient does not display changes in mental status nor
proprioceptive positioning deficits. The nystagmus is always in the
same direction, either horizontal or rotatory, but not vertical. Both
central (brainstem) and peripheral (inner ear) vestibular disease are
common. It is important to emphasize that idiopathic vestibular
disease is always peripheral. If the patient has signs suggestive of
central or paradoxical vestibular disease, further specific
neurodiagnostic tests to investigate the brain are warranted (chs.
109 and 112).5 The most frequent causes of vestibular, cerebellar,
and proprioceptive ataxias are presented in Box 43.1.
Cerebellar ataxia is characterized by dysmetria (inability to control
the rate and range of stepping movements), which is usually
manifested by hypermetria (exaggerated step) (ch. 241;

Videos

41.6, 42.5, 42.6, 43.2).2 It is normally easier to recognize a
hypermetric gait in the thoracic limbs. It is important to differentiate
this sign from thoracic limb spasticity or hypertonicity, which often
accompanies proprioceptive ataxia secondary to cervical
myelopathies. Hypermetria is manifested by a prolonged flexion of
the step (protraction), while spasticity causes the thoracic limbs to
appear rigid or spastic. Other signs characteristic of cerebellar ataxia
are head and whole-body tremors, intention tremors, and wide pelvic
limb stance and gait. Patients with pure cerebellar ataxia do not
display weakness (paresis) nor proprioceptive positioning deficits, as
they have no involvement of the upper motor neurons or conscious

proprioceptive (CP) tracts, respectively. This can be very useful in
distinguishing cerebellar from proprioceptive ataxia. Due to the close
anatomic and functional relationships, occasionally patients present
with a combination of vestibular and cerebellar ataxia, which
indicates a central lesion.

Proprioceptive ataxia is the type primarily related to spinal cord
diseases (chs. 250 and 251).1,4 This ataxia can be differentiated from
vestibular and cerebellar ataxias by the absence of head involvement
(tremor or tilt) (Figure 43.1;

Video 43.3) (ch. 241).

Proprioceptive ataxia may be seen with brain lesions (brainstem,
thalamus, basal nuclei, or cortex) but is much milder, and other
brain signs (somnolence, behavior changes, cranial nerve
involvement, circling, seizures) are usually more obvious than the
ataxia. When evaluating an animal with proprioceptive ataxia, it is
important to rule out the influence of any drug (e.g., sedatives) or
metabolic disorder (e.g., severe anemia) that may be causing ataxia.
As proprioceptive ataxia is commonly associated with spinal cord
diseases, this discussion will focus on this aspect. Proprioceptive
ataxia is a phenomenon of the spinal cord’s white matter, reflecting a
dysfunction of the sensory tracts carrying unconscious
proprioception (dorsal, ventral, and cranial spinocerebellar tracts, as
well as the cuneocerebellar tract).3 Clinical signs seen with
proprioceptive ataxia are truncal sway (wobbliness) and abnormal
limb stance and gait such as circumduction, abduction, or adduction
with the limbs crossing with each other as the animal walks. Some
animals also display a delay in initiating the protraction phase of the
gait with a slight hyperflexion of the limb and a longer stride than
normal. Proprioceptive ataxia is seen early in the course of
compressive myelopathies, and may or may not be accompanied by
proprioceptive positioning deficits (CP deficits or “knuckling”).
Usually, patients with spinal cord disease have ataxia associated with
proprioceptive deficits; however, dogs with chronic spinal cord
disease display ataxia without CP deficits. This can be explained by
the fact that the tracts carrying fibers involved in conscious
proprioception (fasciculus cuneatus for the thoracic limbs and

spinomedullary tract/fasciculus gracilis for the pelvic limbs) are
different from those involved in unconscious proprioception and are
responsible for ataxia.2,4 Therefore, it is the gait examination
(presence or absence of proprioceptive ataxia) and not the evaluation
of proprioception (knuckling) that conclusively defines the
involvement of the spinal cord (ch. 241). As the spinal cord lesion
worsens, paresis appears.

PARESIS AND PARALYSIS
Paresis means partial loss of motor function, which is usually
manifested as weakness. Paralysis (plegia) refers to the complete loss
of motor function. The terms plegia or paresis can be used in
association with a prefix to specify which limb(s) are involved.
Tetra-, para-, hemi-, or mono-paresis/-plegia refers to involvement
of all four limbs, pelvic limbs, ipsilateral limbs, or a single limb,
respectively.4 It is important to make the distinction between
ambulatory and non-ambulatory paresis and plegia (
Video
43.4). A “down” dog can have non-ambulatory paraparesis and if
appropriate treatment is established, dogs with paresis will typically
recover faster than those with paralysis (plegia). Paresis and
proprioceptive ataxia are common signs in patients with spinal cord
diseases (chs. 250, 251). The more severe the spinal cord
involvement, the weaker the patient becomes, until the point of
paralysis. Paresis can be seen with brain (cortical or thalamic)
lesions, but it is usually mild and always contralateral to the lesion.
More severe paresis can be seen with lesions caudal to the midbrain,
and in these cases the involvement is ipsilateral.6 Paresis or paralysis
can also be seen with involvement of the peripheral nerves,
neuromuscular junction, and muscle (ch. 252). It is important to
establish whether the patient has paresis with or without ataxia.
Paresis without ataxia indicates that the lesion is located outside the
central nervous system and is therefore not affecting the spinal
cord.7,8 Clinical examples of this presentation are polyneuropathies
and polymyopathies, where the patient shows variable degrees of
weakness in all four limbs (tetraparesis) but does not have ataxia. A

careful evaluation of cranial nerves, postural reactions, and spinal
reflexes will assist to establish whether the problem is in the
peripheral nerves, neuromuscular junction, or muscle (ch. 241). In a
tetraparetic patient, if the reflexes are decreased or absent, a
neuropathy or neuritis (e.g., Coonhound paralysis) is likely (chs.
252, 253).7,8 Myopathies cause only mild decrease in spinal
reflexes.

FIGURE 43.1 Algorithm for clinical evaluation of
patients with ataxia.
The clinical approach for a weak patient should first exclude
systemic or metabolic causes of weakness (ch. 23). Several systemic
conditions can cause weakness. Examples include anemia, metabolic
diseases such as hypoadrenocorticism and hypothyroidism,
electrolyte imbalances such as hypocalcemia and hypokalemia,
cardiovascular diseases such as pericardial effusion or conditions
associated with hypotension, and nutritional derangements such as
thiamine deficiency. A thorough physical examination (ch. 3) along
with complete blood work and biochemistry profile may reveal
evidence of metabolic or neoplastic diseases, which may cause either
neuropathies (e.g., diabetes mellitus in cats) or myopathies (e.g.,
hyperadrenocorticism in dogs). Further tests such as a thyroid
profile, and a complete cardiac work-up may also be recommended
depending on the case.8

If the patient is paralyzed, the lesion is within the spinal cord or
somewhere along the peripheral nervous system. It is important to
localize the spinal lesion as closely as possible to concentrate
diagnostic efforts on the affected region (ch. 241). The principles of
upper motor neuron (UMN) and lower motor neuron (LMN) are
used to localize lesions within the spinal cord. 2,4,6,7 Upper motor
neuron is a term used to designate a group of motor tracts
originating from the brain and terminating within the spinal cord.
The most important tracts forming the UMN are the corticospinal,
rubrospinal, reticulospinal, and vestibulospinal tracts. Basically, the
combined function of the UMN is to facilitate gait in animals,
inhibiting extensor muscles of the limbs while facilitating flexor
muscles. As such, when the animal has an UMN spinal cord lesion,
there is paresis or paralysis with increased extensor tone of the limbs
(due to the lack of UMN inhibition). The hallmarks of UMN signs are
paralysis or paresis with increased extensor tone (spasticity or
hypertonus), normal to increased spinal reflexes (hyperreflexia), and
slowly progressive muscle atrophy from disuse.6 On the other hand,
LMN is formed by a group of neurons that originate in the ventral
grey horn of the spinal cord or in nuclei of the brainstem, to give
origin to peripheral or cranial nerves that then innervate the target
muscle(s). LMN is also known as the final common pathway because
any motor activity to be displayed has to go through the LMN. When
the patient has a lesion somewhere along the LMN pathway, such as
in the spinal cord enlargement (ventral grey horn), nerve roots,
spinal nerve, peripheral nerve, or neuromuscular junction, LMN
dysfunction occurs. Clinical signs of LMN dysfunction are basically
the opposite of those seen with UMN lesions: paresis or paralysis
with absent to decreased extensor tone (flaccidity or hypotonus),
decreased or absent spinal reflexes (hyporeflexia or areflexia,
respectively), and rapid and severe (neurogenic) muscle atrophy.7
The presence of UMN or LMN signs dictates the location of the
lesion within the spinal cord (ch. 241).
Clinically, the spinal cord can be divided into four regions: cervical
(C1-5), cervicothoracic (C6-T2), thoracolumbar (T3-L3), and
lumbosacral (L4-S3). Involvement of all four limbs suggests a lesion
at either C1-C5 or C6-T2. Assuming increased tone and reflexes in
the pelvic limbs, normal to increased tone and reflexes (UMN signs)

in the thoracic limbs indicate a lesion at C1-5, while decreased to
absent tone and reflexes (LMN signs) suggest a lesion at C6-T2
(Figure 43.2). 2,4,9
Paraplegia or paraparesis indicates a lesion caudal to T2. Normal
to increased reflexes and muscle tone point to a T3-L3 lesion, the
most common site for spinal lesions (

Video 43.5). More specific

lesion localization within the T3-L3 segment can be achieved using
the cutaneous trunci reflex and spinal palpation (ch. 241).
Decreased tone and reflexes suggest an L4-S3 lesion (Figure 43.2).
It is important to note that the lumbosacral spinal cord segments do
not match with their corresponding vertebrae. The entire lumbar
enlargement (L4-S3) is located within the vertebrae L4-L5 in most
dogs, and L5-L6 in cats. Lesions involving the vertebral areas L6, L7,
and S1 in dogs affect the nerve roots for the pelvic limbs, perineal
region, sphincters, and tail (reflecting involvement of sciatic,
pudendal, pelvic, and caudal nerves). As there is no spinal cord in
this region, no proprioceptive ataxia is observed (although
proprioceptive positioning deficits may be seen), but paraparesis and
pain in the lumbosacral area are present. The flexor and perineal
reflexes display LMN signs. Box 43.1 presents common diagnoses
according to lesion localization. 9,10

FIGURE 43.2 Algorithm for lesion localization in
patients with paresis or paralysis. LMN, Lower
motor neuron; UMN, upper motor neuron.
Two notable exceptions exist in regards to lesion localization
within the spinal cord based on the principles of UMN and LMN. The
so-called Schiff-Sherrington phenomenon occurs in patients with
severe thoracolumbar lesions (T2-L7) damaging the propriospinal
tract, which is inhibitory to the extensor muscles of the thoracic
limbs. These patients are paraplegic with normal thoracic limb gait,
but display, when laterally recumbent, thoracic limb spasticity.
Spinal shock can also pose a diagnostic challenge. It is seen in dogs
with peracute T3-L3 myelopathies causing decrease extensor tone
and decreased flexor reflexes, usually with normal patellar reflexes,
in the first 24 hours post-injury. After 24-48 hours, the pelvic limb
reflexes show the expected UMN signs. 2
In a paralyzed animal, it is important to establish whether or not
nociception (pain perception) is intact. A noxious stimulus such as
pinching at one of the toes or at the nail bed should elicit a
withdrawal of the limb accompanied by a behavioral response, such
as vocalization. If the patient flexes the limb but does not have
conscious perception of the painful stimulus, this indicates a severe
spinal cord lesion and carries a guarded to poor prognosis,
particularly if the patient had external spinal trauma, is paralyzed for
many days, and displays LMN signs. 4

DEFINITIONS
Consciousness refers to a mental state generated through the normal
functions of the intracranial nervous system which allows one to be
able to recognize and respond to a variety of internal and external
stimuli.1 Abnormal levels of consciousness are described on a
spectrum of severity, with stupor and coma being the most severe

states. Stupor is a rousable unconsciousness, characterized by a state
in which the animal appears to be unconscious but can be roused by
a noxious stimulus. When the stimulus is withdrawn, the animal will
lapse back into the unresponsive state. Coma is an unrousable
unconsciousness, characterized by a state of unconsciousness from
which the animal cannot be roused even by a noxious stimulus. It is
important to recognize that the withdrawal movement of limbs from
noxious stimuli is a spinal reflex, which is different from a behavioral
response demonstrating awareness or purposeful avoidance
indicative of consciousness (e.g., eye opening, crying, biting) (Videos
44.1, 245.3

). Stupor and coma indicate an acute, life-threatening

emergency requiring prompt intervention for preservation of life and
brain function.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Consciousness is generated in the cerebral cortex and modulated by
the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS). The reticular
formation is a net-like aggregation of neurons in the upper
brainstem with descending tracts modulating sensory, motor, and
autonomic functions, while the ARAS modulates arousal and
awareness integral for consciousness. The ARAS receives sensory
input at the reticular formation in the pons and midbrain, and relays
this information through the thalamus and basal forebrain to
activate the cerebral cortex via cholinergic stimulation. The ARAS
also connects through the hypothalamus to regulate sleep and
arousal via monoaminergic and hypocretin systems.2
Stupor and coma can result from a variety of different conditions
(Box 44.1).3-17 The principal causes of stupor and coma are (1)
compressive or destructive lesions affecting the ARAS at its origin in
the pontine and midbrain regions of the brainstem, (2) bilateral and
diffuse damage of both cerebral hemispheres (or if unilateral, the
effect must be large enough to exert compression on the contralateral
hemisphere or brainstem), or (3) suppression of cerebral function
due to metabolic derangements, drugs, or toxins, which either

impairs oxygen or substrate delivery altering cerebral metabolism, or
interferes with neuronal excitability and/or synaptic function.18
Cerebral edema may develop secondary to intracranial lesions or
metabolic derangements, and can impair consciousness by (1)
further distorting neural tissue affecting the ARAS or its forebrain
targets, (2) causing increased intracranial pressure (ICP) to the point
of impairing cerebral blood flow (CBF), and/or (3) causing
herniation. Cerebral edema can be classified into cellular and
extracellular edema.19 Cellular (or cytotoxic) edema is characterized
by cell swelling and oncotic death of neurons (e.g., hypoxia,
neuroglycopenia).20 Extracellular edema can be classified into four
types: vasogenic, hydrocephalic, hydrostatic, and ionic. Vasogenic
edema is due to increased permeability of the blood-brain barrier
causing extravasation of protein and fluid into the extracellular space
(e.g., brain mass).19-21 Hydrocephalic (or interstitial) edema involves
an outflow obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) causing the CSF
to permeate through the ventricle wall. Hydrostatic edema occurs
secondary to systemic hypertension elevating cerebral capillary
pressures, resulting in transudation of fluid from the vasculature to
brain tissue. Ionic (or osmotic) edema develops when the osmolality
of brain tissue exceeds that of the plasma, leading to fluid movement
into the parenchyma by osmosis (e.g., water intoxication, rapid
correction of hyperosmolar states).21 As cerebral edema develops
and extends, different types of edema can occur simultaneously due
to progressive cellular and extracellular injury.19,21
Increased ICP can occur due to cerebral edema or intracranial
lesions (e.g., mass, hemorrhage, hydrocephalus). The Monro-Kellie
doctrine dictates that the cranial vault contains a fixed volume of
brain parenchyma, blood, and CSF. Intracranial compliance
maintains these components in a balanced dynamic equilibrium such
that an increase in one component results in reciprocal decreases in
the others. When the limits of intracranial compliance are
overwhelmed, ICP increases, which decreases cerebral perfusion
pressure (CPP) and leads to cerebral ischemia. The Cushing reflex, or
cerebral ischemic response, is triggered by a severe acute increase in
ICP. It causes systemic hypertension in order to maintain a normal
CPP, and a concurrent, vagally-mediated reflex bradycardia. This

condition requires immediate treatment as it signifies potentially
life-threatening intracranial hypertension with imminent brain
herniation.

There are numerous types of brain herniation, of which those most
commonly known to cause loss of consciousness include
transtentorial and tonsillar herniations due to compression of the
ARAS in the brainstem. Caudal transtentorial herniation (central and
uncal) causes downward (ventral) displacement of brain tissue
through the tentorial notch, leading to sequential compression of the
midbrain, then pons, and finally medulla. Upward (dorsal)
transtentorial herniation occurs due to an infratentorial lesion
forcing the midbrain up through the tentorial notch. Tonsillar
herniation, which can be a sequela of transtentorial herniation,
occurs when the cerebellar tonsils are pushed downward through the
foramen magnum, causing compression of the medulla, and often
leading to respiratory arrest and death.

ASSESSMENT
Patients presenting with stupor or coma initially should be assessed
and treated for immediate life-threatening conditions, such as shock,
hemorrhage, and hypoxemia (ch. 119). If the Cushing reflex is noted
(bradycardia with hypertension), immediate treatment for increased
ICP should be initiated (see below). A thorough history should be
obtained regarding the onset and progression of clinical signs,
previous illness or injury, and drug or toxin exposure (ch. 2).
Complete physical (ch. 3) and neurologic (ch. 241) examinations
should be performed, and a baseline score using the Modified
Glasgow Coma Scale can be obtained to categorize patient severity
and estimate prognosis (Videos 44.2; 125.1, 246.1, 246.2;

Box

125.1).22 Asymmetrical neurologic signs suggest a lateralized
structural lesion, while symmetrical abnormalities indicate a more

diffuse, toxic, or metabolic process. Specific abnormalities which aid
in assessment and neurolocalization in the unconscious patient
include alterations to breathing pattern, skeletal motor responses,
pupil size and reactivity, and reflexive ocular movements.

ALTERED RESPIRATION
Breathing is involuntarily controlled in the upper brainstem by the
respiratory center, which consists of the dorsal and ventral
respiratory groups in the medulla, and the pneumotaxic and
apneustic centers in the pons. From the respiratory center, nerve
impulses are sent to the intercostal muscles and diaphragm,
adjusting the rate and tidal volume based on blood pH and arterial
partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) detected by central and
peripheral chemoreceptors. A metabolic derangement or brain lesion
disrupting the respiratory center can result in a number of abnormal
breathing patterns in association with an alteration in consciousness
(ch. 123).
Kussmaul breathing is a rapid, deep, and labored breathing
pattern typically associated with severe metabolic acidosis, which
stimulates central chemoreceptors to increase respiration. This
generates a compensatory respiratory alkalosis. Cheyne-Stokes
respiration is a cyclical pattern of apnea and hyperpnea with a
crescendo-decrescendo pattern due to fluctuation of PaCO2 below
and above the apneic threshold. It can be indicative of a lesion in the
diencephalon or pons, or bilateral cerebral hemisphere dysfunction
(e.g., increased ICP, metabolic encephalopathy). Central neurogenic
hyperventilation is persistent deep and rapid breathing, often due to
lesions in the pons or medulla triggering uninhibited stimulation of
both inspiration and expiration. With apneustic breathing, there is a
prolonged inspiration with a breath hold, followed by rapid
exhalation with a prolonged expiratory pause. It occurs with damage
to the pneumotaxic center in the upper pons, impeding the
termination of inspiration. Ataxic respiration consists of completely
irregular breaths and pauses caused by damage to the medulla; if this
is noted, intubation and mechanical ventilation should be provided
to prevent impending respiratory arrest. Agonal breathing is a

brainstem reflex that occurs from anoxic brain injury, and is seen as
shallow irregular gasps that do not effectively move air into or out of
the respiratory tract. In most instances, it progresses rapidly to
apnea and death. Early recognition of any abnormal respiratory
pattern allows the clinician to act promptly to prevent further
deterioration of the patient’s condition.

SKELETAL MOTOR RESPONSES
Voluntary motor activity does not occur with unconsciousness, due
to absent cortical function. However, stuporous or comatose patients
may display abnormal posturing, with involuntary flexion or
extension of the limbs, if there is an injury to the descending motor
tracts (ch. 241). A decerebrate posture is characterized by extensor
rigidity of all 4 limbs due to loss of descending input from the
cerebrum to the red nucleus in the midbrain, which is the relay
center for motor pathways that affect limb flexion. This posture
indicates a lesion in the midbrain, rostral pons, or bilateral cerebral
hemispheric dysfunction. Stupor or coma is present with decerebrate
rigidity, and opisthotonos (extension of the head and neck) may also
be present if the rostral lobes of the cerebellum are damaged
(Figure 44.1). A decerebellate posture is different in that it does not
affect consciousness, and is characterized by opisthotonos, forelimb
extension, and pelvic and hindlimb flexion when caused by rostral
lesions of the cerebellum. If the lesion involves the ventral aspect of
the cerebellum, extension of all 4 limbs is seen. Intermittent
increased extensor tone in forelimbs, hindlimbs, and neck can occur
when an unconscious patient is moved. This is due to unopposed
stimulation of extensor postural muscles in response to impulses
from the vestibular system.23 Involuntary movements, such as
twitching or paddling, may indicate seizure activity resulting from
increased ICP, toxins, or metabolic disturbances, and should be
treated accordingly (chs. 45 and 125).

ALTERED PUPIL FUNCTION
The size of the pupils and the pupillary light reflex (PLR) are useful
assessments for neurolocalization in an unconscious patient (ch.
241). A normal PLR requires an intact retina, optic nerve, optic
chiasm, optic tract, midbrain (pretectal nucleus and Edinger-

Westphal nucleus), oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve [CN] III), ciliary
ganglion, short ciliary nerve, and sphincter muscles of the iris.
Lesions along this neural pathway cause characteristic abnormalities
in pupil size and light reactivity specific to the lesion’s location.
Bilateral, small, reactive pupils are typically seen when there is
metabolic encephalopathy or bilateral diencephalic injury (which
occurs with central transtentorial herniation). Pinpoint pupils occur
from injury to the pons, with destruction of the descending
sympathetic pathways. Fixed pupils occur with bilateral damage to
CN III or its nuclei in the midbrain, and are either dilated if the
descending sympathetic tracts are preserved or midposition if they
are not. A unilateral fixed pupil may be caused by an ipsilateral
midbrain lesion or unilateral compression of CN III (as occurs in
uncal transtentorial herniation). It is important to remember that
direct (either blunt or penetrating) trauma to the eye can alter pupil
size and response; this confounder needs to be taken into
consideration when assessing the pupils of a stuporous or comatose
patient. If pupil size and reactivity are normal in a comatose patient,
midbrain function must be intact, thus indicating either widespread
structural lesions or metabolic suppression of cerebral function as
the cause for unconsciousness.

OCULAR MOVEMENTS
The oculomotor pathways lie in close association with the brainstem
ARAS, so structural causes of stupor and coma that affect this region
are likely to cause abnormalities of ocular movements. Physiologic
nystagmus is a normal conjugate eye movement in response to
vestibular input (ch. 241). It requires the integrity of the peripheral
(vestibular branch of CN VIII and labyrinth of the inner ear) and
central vestibular pathways involving the cerebellum
(flocculonodular lobe) and brainstem (vestibular nuclei and medial
longitudinal fasciculus connecting the nuclei of CN III, IV, and VI).
Spontaneous or positional nystagmus (rotary, horizontal, or vertical)
can indicate disruption along this pathway due to pathologic lesions,
intoxications, or metabolic conditions (

Video 125.1). Physiologic

nystagmus is tested with the oculocephalic (doll’s eye) reflex by

briskly moving the head in a horizontal or vertical direction, with a
normal reflex occurring when the eyes conjugately deviate to the
direction opposite the head rotation with a fast correction toward the
head movement (ch. 241). In trauma patients, it is essential to first
rule out a cervical fracture or dislocation before moving the head. If
nystagmus continues after the head motion stops, a lesion in the
vestibular system is probable. If the oculocephalic reflex is absent in
a comatose patient (eyes stay fixed mid-orbit), brainstem injury
should be suspected. In contrast, patients with metabolic
encephalopathy (e.g., hepatic failure) may have exaggerated or very
brisk oculocephalic responses. If the oculocephalic reflex is intact,
the coma is unlikely to be due to a structural brainstem lesion.4

DIAGNOSTIC PLAN
The causes for stupor and coma are numerous and, in some
instances, there may be more than one factor contributing to the
patient’s unconsciousness. A spot blood glucose should be checked to
rule out hypoglycemia (ch. 61), and a blood pressure should be
taken to ensure severe hypo- or hypertension is not present in
connection with the patient’s neurologic status (chs. 91 and 236).
Ophthalmic and retinal evaluations (ch. 13) may help to identify
changes consistent with high ICP (papilledema) or infectious disease.
Routine lab work (complete blood count, serum biochemistry profile,
urinalysis) should be performed to rule out metabolic causes of
altered consciousness. If metabolic or endocrine disease is present or
suspected, additional lab work can include blood gas, serum bile
acids, blood ammonia, thyroid hormone, and adrenocorticotropic
hormone (ACTH) stimulation testing as indicated. Thoracic
radiographs and abdominal ultrasound may be indicated to rule out
metastatic, infectious, or inflammatory disease. If a systemic cause is
not identified from this initial diagnostic workup, then advanced
imaging of the brain with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or
computed tomography (CT) scan is indicated to look for an
intracranial lesion (ch. 112). CSF analysis can help determine if
neoplastic, infectious, or inflammatory central nervous system
disease is present (ch. 109), although CSF tap should be avoided if
high ICP is suspected or impending herniation is determined from

advanced imaging. General anesthesia may not be necessary in the
comatose patient, and if needed, it carries some risk of further
destabilizing the patient.

TREATMENT
The first priority is to stabilize the patient by treatment of any lifethreatening conditions (ch. 119). Ensure a patent airway is present
with adequate respiration, along with normoxia, normocarbia, and
normotension. Assess for hypo- or hyperthermia and manage as
appropriate (ch. 130). Use the history, physical examination, and
laboratory findings to diagnose and treat any metabolic
disturbances, administering intravenous fluids and medications as
indicated (ch. 120). Seizures can be controlled with injectable
anticonvulsants such as diazepam or midazolam, phenobarbital, or
levetiracetam (ch. 247). Cerebral edema can be treated with
mannitol, hypertonic saline, and if traumatic brain injury is
excluded,24 injectable corticosteroids (ch. 125). Patients suffering
an acute neurologic deterioration can be hyperventilated to a PaCO2
of 30 mm Hg while additional medical or surgical stabilization is
initiated. Hyperventilation should be brief, since the resulting
cerebral vasoconstriction not only decreases cerebral blood volume
and ICP, but globally decreases CBF and perpetuates ischemia.
Keeping the head elevated to a 30° angle reduces ICP by facilitating
venous drainage from the brain.25 Nursing care should provide clean
and dry bedding, frequent turning, and physical therapy (passive
range of motion and massage of limbs; ch. 256) to prevent urine
scalding, pressure sores, and limb contracture, respectively. Ocular
lubrication, nutritional support, and urinary care (bladder
evacuation or an indwelling urinary catheter) are important to
optimize patient management.
Patients with stupor or coma may have rapid changes occur in
their stability, so serial evaluations of neurologic status and
monitoring parameters are imperative to identify any acute
neurologic decline. The technical staff should also be instructed to
observe for and report any sudden changes, as immediate treatment
may be necessary. Compression of the brainstem can result in abrupt

changes in breathing pattern, heart rate, blood pressure, pupil size
and reactivity, and can quickly result in death. Intensive therapy may
need to be instituted to counteract brain herniation if these changes
are observed.

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis for animals with stupor or coma will depend on the
underlying cause, concurrent comorbidities, the location and severity
of the injury, and the response to treatment. If metabolic
derangements or intoxications are the inciting cause, once corrected
the animal may return to normal consciousness (

Video 125.1). If

the condition is due to traumatic brain injury, the animal may have a
chance of recovery if secondary brain injury is prevented and the
primary injury does not cause debilitating permanent damage. Dogs
and cats have a remarkable ability to compensate for loss of cerebral
tissue, so it can be important to not reach hasty prognostic
conclusions.26 However, the prognosis generally is poor if brainstem
involvement is the cause for coma. Serial neurologic evaluations and
scoring using the Modified Glasgow Coma Scale (Box 125.1) should
be performed as an objective assessment of changes in neurologic
status to help the clinician with decisions in case management and
prognostication (

Video 44.2). Electroencephalography (EEG),

bispectral index (BIS), and brainstem auditory evoked response
(BAER) can be used to detect brain death, and continuous EEG can
also monitor for non-convulsive seizure activity.27-30 Clients should
be informed of the potential for permanent neurologic deficits,
seizures, and the need for long-term nursing care in patients with
stupor and coma.

CHAPTER 45: Seizures
Karen R. Muñana

AC RO N YM S
CSF cerebrospinal fluid
EEG electroencephalography
MRI magnetic resonance imaging

Seizures are the most common neurologic condition encountered in small animal practice, with an
estimated prevalence in the general population of 0.82% in dogs1 and up to 0.16% in cats.2 Seizures are
transient paroxysmal disturbances in brain function due to an imbalance between excitatory and
inhibitory neurotransmission resulting in hyperexcitable, hypersynchronous neuronal activity. The
abnormal neuronal function can be identified by distinctive epileptiform activity on
electroencephalography (EEG), and is typically characterized by its clinical manifestations. Clinical
features can include impairment of consciousness, behavioral changes, involuntary motor activity, and
alterations in autonomic nervous system function such as mydriasis, salivation, vomiting, urination, and
defecation. Seizures can be preceded by a preictal or prodromal phase hours to days in duration, during
which the animal will display atypical behavior such as restlessness, anxiety, attention-seeking, or
attempting to hide. The postictal phase immediately follows a seizure, and can present as fatigue,
disorientation, restlessness, compulsive walking, aggression, ataxia, hunger, or blindness. Postictal signs
can persist for minutes to days, and the degree of postictal impairment does not necessarily correlate
with the severity or duration of the seizure itself.

SEIZURE CLASSIFICATION
Seizures are classified as either generalized or focal, based on the EEG activity present at the onset of the
seizure and the clinical manifestations of the neuronal disturbance. Generalized seizures are
characterized by abnormal neuronal activity that originates from both cerebral hemispheres at the onset
of the episode, and most often manifest in dogs and cats as symmetric tonic, clonic, or tonic-clonic
contractions of somatic muscles, loss of consciousness, and autonomic signs of salivation, urination
and/or defecation (Video 45.1

). Generalized myoclonic seizures, that manifest as brief spasms of a

muscle or group of muscles, and atonic seizures, in which there is episodic loss of muscle tone causing
the animal to collapse, are seen less frequently (Video 45.2

). Focal seizures originate within

neuronal networks in a discrete region of the cerebrum or thalamus, and manifest as focal motor activity
(Videos 45.3 and 45.4

), autonomic signs, and/or behavioral abnormalities (Video 45.5). Also see ch.

11. Focal seizures can secondarily generalize, in which the seizure event rapidly spreads to involve both
cerebral hemispheres.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH
The general approach to the diagnostic evaluation of an animal with seizures is outlined in Figure 45.1.

HISTORICAL FINDINGS
Seizures, being episodic events, frequently are not witnessed by the clinician. Because of this, it is
imperative that an accurate description of the episode be obtained from the pet owner to determine
whether or not a seizure disorder is considered likely. Episodic disorders that can be confused with
seizures include syncope (ch. 40), narcolepsy/cataplexy (ch. 244), transient vestibular dysfunction
(ch. 248), behavioral disorders (chs. 11 and 244), idiopathic head tremor (chs. 41, 42) and
paroxysmal movement disorders (ch. 41). Differentiating between these disorders is sometimes
difficult, although discerning a few key characteristics of the episode can be helpful. The owner should
be questioned regarding the animal’s behavior immediately prior to, and immediately after, the episode,
and whether the animal is normal between episodes. In addition, the owner should be queried as to
whether the episodes typically occur while the animal is at rest or during activity, and if there are any
events that tend to trigger the episodes, such as eating or excitement. Finally, the owner should be asked
to describe specifics of the episode, including whether or not the animal maintains normal
consciousness (this can be assessed by determining whether the animal looks at or otherwise responds
to the owner when its name is called), details regarding the animal’s posture, whether muscle tone is
increased or decreased, if autonomic signs are observed, and the duration of the episode. Characteristic
features that can assist in differentiating seizures from other episodic disorders are summarized in
Table 45.1.
Cats can present with focal seizures that have atypical clinical features. Episodes are characterized by
orofacial motor signs such as lip smacking, chewing, licking and/or swallowing in addition to behavioral
aberrations such as vocalization, piloerection, aggression, motionless staring, startling and running3 and
may not be immediately recognized as a seizure (ch. 255). The presence of other clinical signs that are
characteristic of seizure disorders, such as facial twitching, salivation, mydriasis, and urination or
defecation, often aid in the determination. In some cases, these focal seizures will secondarily generalize,
and the cat will display characteristic tonic, clonic, or tonic-clonic motor activity immediately after the
orofacial and behavioral changes. These seizures are associated with a specific form of epilepsy (ch.
247).
If an episode proves difficult to characterize based on the description alone, it can be helpful to have
the owner record an event on video for review. The clinician should review the video with the discerning
characteristics of a seizure in mind, in order to make a determination as to whether or not the episode is
likely to be a seizure. However, even with a detailed description and video recording of the event,
discriminating seizures from other episodic disorders can remain challenging in some cases. For
example, cardiovascular disorders that produce syncope can also cause a transient decrease in cerebral
blood flow, triggering hypoxic-anoxic seizures.4 Intermittent episodes with features that are consistent
with both seizures and syncope can be investigated using Holter or cardiac event monitoring (chs. 40
and 96) before considering general anesthesia for CSF collection and/or neuroimaging. EEG is routinely
used in human medicine to confirm a diagnosis of seizures, but this testing is not readily available in
veterinary practice. In such instances, additional support for a diagnosis can be obtained by initiating a
therapeutic trial with an antiseizure drug (ch. 247) and monitoring for a decrease in the occurrence of
episodes; however, such a trial is only feasible for episodes that are occurring regularly and with an
established frequency.

EXAMINATION FINDINGS
A general physical examination is useful in evaluating for any evidence of cardiovascular or respiratory
disease, as well as any signs of systemic disease that can provide clues as to the underlying cause of
seizures (ch. 3). In addition, a complete neurological examination (ch. 241) should be performed to
assess for any signs of forebrain disease, such as changes in mentation or behavior, abnormal posture or
gait, altered vision, or postural reaction deficits.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Seizures can be categorized based on etiology (Box 45.1). Reactive seizures result from extracranial
causes, in which metabolic (endogenous) or toxic (exogenous) disturbances secondarily impair normal

brain function. Reactive seizures are not considered a form of epilepsy, because the brain is otherwise
healthy and seizures typically resolve once the disturbance is corrected. The term epilepsy is reserved to
describe a disease of the brain characterized by an enduring predisposition to generate epileptic
seizures, which is interpreted clinically as the presence of 2 or more unprovoked seizures at least 24
hours apart.5 Epilepsy can be further classified according to etiology. Idiopathic epilepsy is the most
common form of epilepsy in dogs, and is diagnosed in over half of all dogs with recurrent, unprovoked
seizures.6-8 It is a disorder characterized by recurrent seizures with no underlying cause other than a
confirmed or presumed genetic predisposition that is believed to result from a functional defect within
neurons. Structural epilepsy is characterized by recurrent seizures that are caused by a congenital or
acquired lesion of the brain, such as hydrocephalus, encephalitis, cerebrovascular disease, trauma or
neoplasia. Epilepsy of unknown cause refers to a condition of recurrent seizures in which a genetic cause
is determined unlikely based on age of onset or examination findings, but a structural cause is not
identified. It is also used to denote instances where a through diagnostic investigation has not been
performed to look for an underlying cause. A detailed discussion of epilepsy is provided in ch. 247.

DIAGNOSTIC PLAN
As a general rule, the initial diagnostic plan for an animal with seizures should focus on identifying any
potential extracranial causes. Accordingly, any animal with seizures should have a complete blood count,
serum biochemistry profile, urinalysis, and serum bile acid concentrations measured. If intoxication
seems likely based on the history, then specific tests for toxin exposure are recommended (ch. 133).
Additional testing for systemic disease might be warranted based on examination and initial laboratory
findings. Cats should be evaluated for serologic evidence of infectious disease, including feline

immunodeficiency virus infection (ch. 198), feline leukemia virus infection (ch. 199), toxoplasmosis
(ch. 197), and cryptococcosis (ch. 207).
If extracranial causes of seizures are excluded, then intracranial disease must be explored. When
considering differential diagnoses for intracranial causes in dogs, it is often helpful to take into account
the likelihood of diseases based on the age at onset of seizures. Dogs with an onset of seizures between 6
months and 6 years of age have a high probability of being diagnosed with idiopathic epilepsy, with this
diagnosis accounting for up to 75% of cases in this age category.8 Idiopathic epilepsy is an exclusion
diagnosis that is made based on the presence of compatible clinical features, including typical age of
onset of seizures, a normal interictal physical and neurological examination, and a normal diagnostic
evaluation. The International Veterinary Epilepsy Task Force (IVETF) has proposed that a diagnosis of
idiopathic epilepsy be made based on a tiered system with increasing degrees of confidence determined
by the extent of the diagnostic evaluation.9 This is discussed further in ch. 247. In brief, if laboratory
evaluation for extracranial causes produces negative results, and the signalment, history, and
examination are compatible with idiopathic epilepsy, then a presumptive diagnosis of idiopathic
epilepsy with a tier I level of confidence can be made. However, if an owner desires stronger confidence
in the diagnosis (tier II level), then magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain (ch. 112) and
cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis (ch. 109) are indicated. In addition, if seizures prove refractory to
treatment in a dog diagnosed with idiopathic epilepsy based on a tier I level of confidence, or if interictal
neurological signs develop that cannot be attributed to antiseizure drugs, then MRI and CSF analysis
should be considered to evaluate for structural brain disease.
For dogs with an onset of seizures outside the typical age range for idiopathic epilepsy, structural
epilepsy assumes a greater likelihood. Although idiopathic epilepsy remains the most likely diagnosis in
dogs with seizure onset less than 1 year of age,10 structural epilepsy due to brain anomalies and
infectious etiologies also has a high probability.11 Because of this, a more extensive diagnostic evaluation
is warranted in these dogs. Ultrasound of the brain through an open fontanelle can demonstrate the
presence of ventriculomegaly in a patient with hydrocephalus (ch. 244). Infectious disease testing,
particularly in an unvaccinated animal, can be performed to raise suspicion for a diagnosis of
encephalitis. However, CSF analysis is necessary to confirm infectious causes, and MRI of the brain is
required to identify most structural abnormalities aside from hydrocephalus.
In dogs with an onset of seizures at greater than 6 to 7 years of age, a diagnosis of structural epilepsy is
most likely.11-13 Furthermore, the likelihood of a diagnosis of structural epilepsy increases in prevalence
with increasing age within this older population of dogs.12 Neoplasia is the most likely cause of
structural epilepsy in this age group, but cerebrovascular disease, encephalitis, and degenerative
conditions should also be considered. Serial blood pressure measurements are routinely recommended
in these cases (chs. 91 and 236), and the animal can be screened for neoplasia with thoracic radiographs
and abdominal ultrasound. If findings are unremarkable, further evaluation with brain MRI (ch. 112)
and CSF analysis (ch. 109) is recommended. It should be noted that an underlying structural cause is
not identified in a substantial proportion of older dogs that undergo a thorough neurodiagnostic
evaluation12,13; these dogs are diagnosed with epilepsy of unknown cause.
Seizures in cats warrant a somewhat different approach. Idiopathic epilepsy occurs in cats, but it is
proportionally less frequent than in dogs, with structural epilepsy diagnosed in up to two-thirds of all
cats with recurrent seizures.14,15 Similar to dogs, infectious and congenital causes are most common in
cats less than 1 year of age,16 and neoplasia is often identified as the etiology in older cats.14 Since
seizures in cats are often associated with an underlying cause, it is recommended that cats with
recurrent seizures undergo MRI and CSF analysis to evaluate for an intracranial cause, regardless of age.

Lenin Arturo Villamizar Martinez
