HALITOSIS
Halitosis is an acute or chronic offensive odor that may have an
intra- or extraoral origin. Intraoral halitosis is linked to bacterial
endogenous and exogenous proteolytic action on food debris, blood
components, saliva, exfoliated oropharyngeal lining cells, and
gingival crevicular fluid (inflammatory exudate at the gingival
sulcus). The end product of bacterial metabolism over these
substrates is considered the primary pathway for producing volatile
sulfur compounds (VSCs) and other proteolytic byproducts
(cadaverine, putrescine, indole, and skatole) responsible for oral
malodor.1
Disruption of the oral mucosa, palate, or tongue due to
inflammatory, neoplastic, or ulcerative conditions, or deep
periodontal pockets in patients suffering from periodontitis, along
with lack of oral hygiene, are factors that together lead to bacterial

proliferation and subsequent increase of VSCs and other bacterial
end-products in the mouth (Figure 46.1).2 In humans, it has been
demonstrated that the irregular surface of the dorsal aspect of the
tongue, cavities, dry mouth (xerostomia), and habits such as
smoking or chewing tobacco-based products can also contribute to
having bad breath.3
Periodontal disease is the most common cause of intraoral
halitosis in veterinary patients, due to the proliferation of blackpigmented Gram-negative anaerobic rods associated with the
destructive inflammatory reaction of periodontal tissue.4,5 The
prevalence of periodontal disease in dogs evaluated under general
anesthesia is 44-100%, depending on study design, breed, body
weight, age, and the patient’s immune system status.6,7
Microorganisms associated with periodontitis in humans, such as
Porphyromonas spp., Prevotella spp., Fusobacterium spp.,
Veillonella spp., and Bacteroides spp., have also been associated
with elevated production of VSCs.3
Deep palate rugae in brachycephalic dogs may predispose to food
debris, hair, and bacteria accumulation, leading to mucositis and
bleeding. Foreign bodies entrapped in the rugae or at any location of
the oropharyngeal region may cause local inflammation and tissue
necrosis, which is the perfect substrate for bacterial buildup and
their proteolytic effect.8
Although the oral cavity has been considered the primary source of
bad breath (halitosis), extraoral conditions such as upper and lower
respiratory infection, gastrointestinal (GI) disorders, or systemic
illness have also been linked to it (ch. 33). Patients with kidney
disease can show uremic breath and oral ulceration, while ketotic
diabetic dogs and cats may display a sweet or fruity breath smell.
Patients suffering from liver disease may have bad breath due to
recurrent episodes of vomiting.9-11 Figure 46.2 displays the most
common causes of intra- and extraoral halitosis in dogs and cats.

CLINICAL SIGNS

The main clinical sign is an offensive odor from the mouth.
Depending on the underlying condition responsible for the halitosis,
other clinical signs may be present, such as difficulty chewing and
swallowing food (ch. 47), maxillary or mandibular swelling, labial
mucocutaneous ulceration (ch. 178), lip fold dermatitis (ch. 33),
mandibular lymph node enlargement, mucopurulent or blood-tinged
oral discharge, ptyalism, and evidence of pain on palpation.9 Clinical
signs associated with upper or lower respiratory, GI, or systemic
diseases may vary and should be correlated depending on the
affected organ (e.g., mucopurulent or bloody nasal discharge may be
due to an infectious or neoplastic nasal disorder, whereas
regurgitation, loss of appetite, exaggerated or frequent swallowing,
and weight loss may be associated with megaesophagus).9,12

PHYSICAL EXAM AND DIAGNOSIS
Even though bad breath may be erroneously considered normal
during the physical exam in dogs and cats, its finding should not be
underestimated. The physical exam must be focused on revealing the
primary local or systemic origin of the halitosis (ch. 3). Visual
assessment of the intraoral structures must be performed to identify
the presence of ulcerative lesions or necrotic tissue associated with
traumatic, inflammatory, or neoplastic disorders. A complete patient
history including tooth-brushing, chewing activity, dental toys, and
previous dental procedures must be recorded.13
The status of the gingiva, teeth, and the presence of dental calculus
and gingivitis may be initially assessed on an awake patient.
However, the gold standard technique for evaluating teeth and
periodontal structures is that it must be performed with the patient
under general anesthesia (ch. 258). Periodontal probing and
intraoral dental radiographs are mandatory for objectively assessing
the periodontium.4,14 A complete oral assessment including the
buccal mucosa, soft and hard palate, tonsils, tongue, and oropharynx
is necessary to rule out other oral conditions. A complete blood count
(CBC), serum biochemistry panel, and other diagnostic tests such as
thoracic radiographs, computed tomography (CT) scan, or
ultrasound may be necessary if a systemic disease is suspected. If

ulcerative or neoplastic tissue is observed in the oropharyngeal
region, fine needle aspiration and incisional or excisional biopsies
may be required.
A diagnosis of halitosis is performed subjectively by organoleptic
assessment (smelling) or objectively using a halimeter, a portable
VSC monitor.15,16 Previous studies performed in dogs demonstrated
that this is a reliable method of assessment that might help measure
the concentration of VSCs in veterinary patients. However, its use
and the relation between the production of VSCs and specific
bacteria associated with periodontal disease in dogs and cats must be
evaluated and validated in a clinical setting.17

Diffuse severe dental calculus (asterisks), gingivitis

TREATMENT
Treatment is focused on the triggering pathologic condition of
halitosis. In oral halitosis, improving oral hygiene is the key to
decreasing bacteria load and end products. Professional dental
cleaning, which includes supra- and subgingival scaling and

polishing, antiseptic rinses such as 0.12% chlorhexidine, and zinc
ascorbate, along with consistent tooth-brushing, aim to reduce the
bacterial load and bacterial subproducts in patients affected by
periodontal disease.3

PTYALISM
The oral cavity is constantly rinsed by saliva produced from the
major and minor salivary glands. The major salivary glands in dogs
and cats are the mandibular, monostomatic and polystomatic
sublingual, zygomatic, and parotid. The minor salivary tissue
corresponds to microscopic salivary glands dispersed throughout the
oral mucosa. In the cat, a small nodular gland located at the
linguodistal aspect of each mandibular first molar tooth has been
described. However, its salivary function has not been established.18
In contrast with the parotid salivary gland, which produces a
serous salivary secretion, the rest of the salivary glands produce
mixed serous and mucous saliva. The function of the primary saliva
is to lubricate the food bolus through the oral cavity before
deglutition. Although it was previously considered that saliva in the
dog initiates food breakdown, some studies have shown deficient
alpha-amylase concentrations in the saliva of this species, which
suggests that digestion does not begin in the mouth.19,20
Antimicrobial, antifungal, and antiviral action have also been
attributed to the saliva thanks to its biochemical components
(enzymes, lysosomes, and immunoglobulins), as well as the constant
rinsing action over the dental and intraoral soft tissue surfaces,
which removes microorganisms and food debris. In humans, saliva
flow reduction or absence has been associated with infection of the
oral mucosa, and dental decay.21
Cholinergic and adrenergic pathways of the parasympathetic and
sympathetic systems regulate saliva production and its composition,
respectively. This biochemical mechanism maintains a continuous
basal flow rate of saliva that is necessary to preserve intraoral
moisture. Postganglionic nerve endings of the facial and
glossopharyngeal cranial nerves are mostly responsible for saliva
production. Stimulation of these nerves is associated with increased

low-protein, watery, serous saliva, as seen during food stimulation or
mastication. On the other hand, macromolecule secretion from
sympathetic stimulation results in a thick and ropy saliva, as
observed in stressed or excited animals.22-24 In dogs, saliva overflow
plays an essential physiological role in thermoregulation. High body
temperature is reflected in more saliva production, improving
evaporative heat loss during panting.25

FIGURE 46.2 Algorithm showing the most
common intra- and extraoral disorders associated
with halitosis in dogs and cats.
Ptyalism, also called polysialia, hypersalivation, or sialorrhea, is an
overflow of saliva in the oral cavity. It is associated with increased
saliva production or the inability to swallow the usual saliva
produced under normal conditions (pseudoptyalism). Excessive
drooling, as seen in some large breeds such as the Saint Bernard,
Mastiff, Newfoundland, and Basset Hound, is associated with the
inability to keep the saliva in the mouth due to the particular
anatomical conformation of the lower lip (excessive lower lip fold).
Salivary gland disorders such as sialocele, sialadenitis,
sialadenosis, necrotizing sialometaplasia, and salivary gland cancer
(ch. 258) may directly increase saliva production.26 Neoplastic,
inflammatory, infectious, or obstructive conditions of the alimentary
tract or the inability to close the mouth due to mandibular fracture,
open-mouth jaw locking, or trigeminal neuropathy could result in
pseudoptyalism (Figure 46.3). Dogs and cats suffering from intense
pain or sepsis may have an increase in saliva production due to the
high sensitivity of the salivary gland tissue to autonomic
neurotransmitters. Swallowing or exposure to chemical agents,
including insecticides, medications, caustic substances, toxic plants,
or animal venom, can also be causes of ptyalism.27,28 Dogs
displaying excessive drooling and neurologic signs such as seizures,
paralysis, fever, and/or other behavioral disorders must be suspected
of rabies (ch. 202).29 Figure 46.4 displays the most common
causes of ptyalism in dogs and cats.

FIGURE 46.3 Dogs showing temporary ptyalism.
A, Ropy saliva in an excited adult Boxer playing in a
dog park. B, Hypersalivation associated with the
inability to close the mouth in an adult dog with
bilateral mandibular fracture. C, Ptyalism observed
in a dog due to intravenous administration of
ketamine as part of its anesthetic induction protocol.

CLINICAL SIGNS

The main clinical sign is intermittent or continuous, mild to severe
drooling. Depending on the cause of ptyalism, the saliva may show a
clear, blood-tinged, or purulent appearance. Other clinical signs such
as halitosis, difficulty swallowing, vomiting, regurgitation, anorexia,
depression, weight loss, fever, pawing at the face, or neurological
deficits, must be evaluated to determine the primary cause.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Previous to the physical examination (ch. 3), a complete history
must be obtained (ch. 2). The history must include age, vaccination
status, acute or chronic presentation of clinical signs, history of
trauma, toxic substance exposure, drug administration, and other GI
signs. Although several systemic disorders may result in
hypersalivation, the initial approach must focus on the maxillofacial
structures and oropharyngeal region. Visual and systematic gentle
palpation of the extraoral soft and bony tissue structures are
necessary to identify tenderness or asymmetry of the masticatory
muscles (masseter and temporalis) or mandibular or parotid salivary
glands. Jaw tone and the ability to close the mouth must also be
established at this time.
A thorough intraoral exam includes assessing gingiva and teeth,
oral mucosa, tongue, hard and soft palate, tonsils, and
mucocutaneous junction (ch. 258). Severe periodontal disease,
stomatitis, neoplastic or traumatic lesions, the presence of foreign
bodies, mucocutaneous junction ulceration, and neurological signs
such as ptosis and mandibular paralysis must be recorded as possible
causes, or indicators of the cause, of hypersalivation.13

DIAGNOSIS
Ptyalism may be a clinical sign of neurologic, metabolic, or GI
disease. Its diagnosis is based on the medical history and the
physical examination. A CBC and serum biochemistry panel should
be included in the initial diagnostics to assess systemic health (e.g.,
liver and kidney status). A thorough physical exam of the oral cavity
and the maxillofacial structures aims to determine if the

hypersalivation is associated with an increase in saliva production or
dysphagia (ch. 259), leading to the inability to swallow average
amounts of saliva. A neurologic exam (ch. 241) must also be
included to rule out alterations of the central nervous system and
cranial nerves (e.g., trigeminal and facial).

FIGURE 46.4 Algorithm showing the most
common clinical conditions associated with ptyalism.
If the primary cause of hypersalivation remains unknown, other
diagnostic tests may be required, such as fine-needle aspiration,
biopsy, CT scan, or magnetic resonance imaging to assess the
salivary glands and maxillofacial structures; biopsy of neoplastic or
inflammatory lesions of the oral cavity; and specific diagnostic
evaluation for a portosystemic shunt in patients in whom it is
suspected (ch. 267).30 Radiographic exam, fluoroscopy, endoscopy,
or blood test in cases suspicious of myasthenia gravis (ch. 253) may
be required to diagnose megaesophagus (ch. 259).

TREATMENT
Treatment is focused on the underlying pathologic condition causing
the hypersalivation. Since ptyalism may have a systemic or localized,
metabolic, neurologic, or traumatic origin, the treatment can range
from medication administration to surgery of the affected organ. For
example, surgical lip correction may be required in dogs with
abnormal lip anatomic conformation leading to excessive drooling
and lip fold dermatitis (cheiloplasty).
Surgical treatment to reduce the flow of saliva can include
anything from salivary gland excision to ligation of the salivary gland
ducts.31-35 It has been reported that excision or ligation of the
salivary gland ducts of the parotid, mandibular, and sublingual may
reduce the overflow of saliva into the mouth without postoperative
complications such as dry mouth (xerostomia). Anti-inflammatory
and antibiotic medications (based on culture and sensitivity testing)
have been recommended to treat sialadenitis. Other drugs such as
phenobarbital (1-2 mg/kg orally q12h) have been suggested to treat
sialadenosis and necrotizing sialometaplasia (ch. 258).26

CHAPTER 47: Gagging and
Dysphagia
Megan Grobman

A C RO N YM S
CN cranial nerve
GERD gastroesophageal reflux disease
GI gastrointestinal
LES lower esophageal sphincter
LES-AS lower esophageal sphincter achalasia-like syndrome
VFSS videofluoroscopic swallow studies
At its most broad, the term dysphagia (swallowing impairment) can
be used for describing a defect in any of the phases of swallowing
(i.e., oral preparatory, pharyngeal/cricopharyngeal, and
esophageal/gastroesophageal). For the purposes of this chapter, the
term pharyngeal dysphagia will include cricopharyngeal dysphagia,
and esophageal dysphagia will include gastroesophageal dysphagia.
It is important to recognize that dysphagia is a clinical finding rather
than a diagnosis. It is equally important to note that idiopathic
conditions such as primary megaesophagus and idiopathic
esophageal dysmotility (IED) are diagnoses of exclusion, and
identification of the underlying cause, wherever possible, is needed
to optimize treatment and outcome. The clinical signs that are
suggestive of dysphagia are broad (

Table 47.1) and may include such client concerns as a “gag.” The
gag reflex is an airway protective behavior initiated to prevent
aspiration of foreign material (e.g., food, oral cavity/nasal secretions,
etc.) into the respiratory tract. Testing for a gag reflex is also a part of
any thorough cranial nerve (CN) examination (ch. 241). The
presence of clinical gagging may be suggestive of dysphagia;
however, the significance of an absent gag reflex on a physical
examination is less clear. In people, the absence of a gag reflex
during physical examination was not found to be predictive of
dysphagia.1-3 A similar relationship is suspected in dogs, though
currently this is anecdotal. As such, a “gag” must be interpreted in
the context of the entire clinical presentation; what clients refer to as
“gagging” or “choking” in fact may be reverse sneezing,
expectoration, or other signs. Conscious clinical recognition of
dysphagia as a cause of both respiratory and alimentary signs,
including a gag, is necessary to identify affected patients.

ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY
SWALLOW MECHANISM
Swallowing is a complicated motor activity that can be considered
both a feeding and an airway protective behavior (ch. 221). The
swallow is classically divided into three sequential phases: oral
preparatory, pharyngeal, and esophageal. The oral preparatory phase
is voluntary and it encompasses prehension, mastication, and
formation of a food bolus within the valleculae. The valleculae are
formed by the soft palate, elevated epiglottis, and the base of the
tongue (Figure 47.1).4 Afferent and efferent pathways involved in
this process are mediated by CNs V, VII, and XII. All subsequent
phases of swallowing are considered involuntary and irreversible
once triggered. The pharyngeal phase can either follow the oral
preparatory phase (i.e., feeding) or occur spontaneously (i.e.,
reflexive swallowing of oral secretions).5,6 Chemical and mechanical
stimulation of the larynx and pharynx are relayed via the cranial
laryngeal nerve, and to a lesser degree the glossopharyngeal (CN IX)
and recurrent laryngeal nerves, to the swallow pattern generators to

initiate downstream pharyngeal contraction.4,7 A pharyngeal
swallow triggers the esophageal phase of swallowing by initiating
primary esophageal peristalsis. This and secondary esophageal
peristalsis, triggered by esophageal distention, conduct a bolus down
the esophagus through the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). This is
followed by LES closure, with transient hypertonicity, to prevent
reflux.6 It is worth noting that the motor endplates of striated muscle
demonstrate complex co-innervation between extrinsic vagal
cholinergic, intrinsic nitrergic, peptidergic, and monoaminergic
neurons. This complexity allows for modulation of esophageal
musculature including esophageal striated muscle by myenteric
neurons. This may provide an explanation for common diseases (e.g.,
megaesophagus) despite species-specific differences in the
esophageal musculature (e.g., smooth vs. striated muscle).6,8

GAG REFLEX
The gag reflex, or pharyngeal reflex, is a reaction to tactile
stimulation of several intra-oral structures including the base of the
tongue, palate, epiglottis, and caudal pharynx (ch. 241).9 It is
considered a normal protective behavior against penetration or
aspiration of foreign material into the larynx, pharynx, or trachea. It
should not be elicited during a normal swallow. Afferent signaling is
conducted via CN V (sensory) and IX to the medulla oblongata.
Subsequent efferent signaling via CN X results in oropharyngeal
contraction, and spasmodic, retrograde peristalsis, which forces air
over the glottis, clearing the material, and producing a characteristic
“retching” noise.10-12 The region of the medulla oblongata that
coordinates gagging is near the salivary, vomiting, and cardiac
control centers. As such, stimulation of the center controlling
gagging may result in changes corresponding to these regions (e.g.,
ptyalism, retching, and vomiting). While the presence of an
inappropriate gag (i.e., during normal swallowing) may be suggestive
of dysphagia, the absence of a gag reflex in more than 13% of nondysphagic adult humans has called its clinical relevancy as a
screening tool into question.1

Retching frequently accompanies a gag, and in people the
combination is considered a more severe form of gagging (i.e., hypergag) where gagging is combined with part of the emetic response.13
Retching is an unsuccessful attempt to expel gastric contents and
may appear as a rhythmic heaving. Retching is thought to provide 3
functions: 1) triggering vomiting, 2) provide rostral momentum to a
bolus prior to vomiting, and 3) mixing and buffering gastric
contents.14,15 This does not imply that gagging, retching, and
vomiting are irrevocably linked and must occur in sequence. Each
process may, and often does, occur independently. Rather, these
processes may occur in combination due to common anatomy and
triggering stimuli. Anecdotally, retching may also be seen in dogs
attempting to clear a retained esophageal bolus and it is often
preceded by repetitive swallowing and ptyalism. Expectoration,
defined as the clearance of mucoid secretions from the airways, may
appear as “hacking” that is mistaken for gagging and retching.
Expectoration may occur in combination with gagging and retching
in the absence of triggering gastrointestinal (GI) disease. A gag, and
retch occurring at the end of a paroxysm of coughing (“terminal
retch”), may suggest respiratory rather than GI disease.

CLINICAL EVALUATION
SIGNALMENT
Because the conditions capable of causing dysphagia and/or gag are
very broad, considering signalment is important for organizing lists

of potential differentials (Table 47.2). As would be expected,
patients with congenital defects often present with evidence of
disease from birth or weaning (e.g., vascular ring anomaly, ch. 259)
while those with acquired disease tend to be middle-aged or older.
However, it is worth noting that esophageal motility may continue to
develop until 1 year of age.16,17 Therefore, discretion should be used
before ascribing pathologic significance to mild-moderate deficits in
esophageal motility in pediatric and juvenile patients. Breed and
familial predispositions have been reported and are provided in
Table 47.3. Dysphagia is more commonly recognized in dogs
compared to cats,18 though careful questioning of cat owners may be
needed to distinguish cough from retching/gagging.

HISTORY
A strong emphasis must be placed on taking a thorough history to
identify dysphagic patients (ch. 2). Small animal patients with
dysphagia often have subtle clinical signs that are not noticed by
their owners, and “occult” aerodigestive disease may be common in
small animals, as it is in humans.19 In addition to general questions
related to vaccination status, appetite, access to toxins/foreign
material, and disease progression, attempts should be made to
identify occult dysphagia (dysphagia in the absence of GI signs; ch.
221). This is particularly important for cases where a patient has
recurrent pneumonias, laryngeal dysfunction, coughing while eating
and drinking, and/or in cases of cough with normal thoracic
radiographs. When more overt clinical signs are present, attention
should be paid to gaining information that will aid in
identifying/localizing a swallowing defect (e.g., distinguishing
between regurgitation and vomiting [ch. 48]). Vaccination status is
of particular importance as patients with rabies may present with
dysphagia (chs. 47, 202). Travel history and geography (ch. 9) are
important as certain causes of dysphagia often show specific
geographic ranges. For example, spirocercosis (ch. 259), tick
paralysis (ch. 253), and dysautonomia (ch. 254) may be
appropriate differentials for dysphagia in patients in endemic
areas.20,21 For patients with gagging as a presenting concern,

attention should be paid to timing of the gagging episodes and the
relationship to swallowing and respiratory signs. A patient that gags
during normal swallowing may suggest dysphagia while a patient
that gags after a coughing paroxysm (ch. 34), or with a history of
nasal disease (ch. 213), or reverse sneezing (ch. 35), may require
further evaluation for respiratory disease (ch. 212).

CLINICAL SIGNS
Clinical signs tend to be reflective of the anatomic site of the
swallowing defect. However, overlapping clinical signs, and a disease
process that can affect more than one area, make diagnosing
dysphagia very challenging based on clinical signs alone. A table of
commonly encountered clinical signs is provided (Table 47.1).
Careful attention should be paid to the timing of clinical signs. For
example, gagging and/or repetitive swallowing while eating and
drinking may be suggestive of pharyngeal dysphagia. However, this
same behavior observed spontaneously without a preceding oral
preparatory phase (i.e., reflexive swallows) may be suggestive of
gastroesophageal reflux (GER) or a retained esophageal bolus. This
swallowing reflex arc reflects attempts to clear the esophagus, buffer
gastric acid with bicarbonate-rich saliva, and protect against
aspiration of gastric contents.22,23 For those with concurrent signs of
nasal disease, post-nasal drip may also result in a gag and repetitive
reflexive swallow. Patients with pharyngeal dysfunction, including
weakness and spontaneous inappropriate opening of the upper
esophageal sphincter, may also demonstrate substantial aerophagia
and bloating.

DIAGNOSTICS
Initial Evaluation
Correctly identifying the cause of dysphagia relies upon a thorough
history and physical examination (ch. 3), as well as observation of
feeding. A thorough physical examination in this case should include
a complete neurologic examination (ch. 241) that includes
evaluating for generalized neuromuscular disorders and CN deficits
caused by lesions that could impact specific phases of swallowing. As
was mentioned previously, further research is needed to determine
the significance of an absent gag reflex in dogs; however, the absence
of a gag reflex should prompt additional evaluation in dogs with
other clinical signs that are supportive of dysphagia. A thorough
examination of the oral cavity is recommended for all patients with
suspected oral preparatory phase dysphagia (ch. 258). Specific
physical exam findings are variable and depend on duration of
clinical signs, presence of systemic illness, and the underlying
etiology.
A minimum database (e.g., complete blood count, serum
biochemical profile, and urinalysis) frequently is unremarkable but
may help identify those patients with evidence of systemic disease
(e.g., basophilic stippling with lead intoxication or electrolyte
abnormalities with hypoadrenocorticism). Ideally, specific disease
testing should be performed based on the anatomic location of the
swallowing defect and considered in the context of the specific

patient. For example, a dog with oral preparatory phase dysphagia is
unlikely to benefit from an adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
stimulation test to investigate the possibility of hypoadrenocorticism.
However, this may be entirely appropriate in a dog with esophageal
hypomotility. Patients with evidence of pharyngeal and esophageal
dysphagia are likely to benefit from laryngeal function examination
(ch. 214) due to common innervations between the larynx, pharynx,
and proximal esophagus (e.g., CN IX, X, and interior branch of XI).
For example, concurrent dysfunction between the pharynx, larynx,
and esophagus is reported in dogs with laryngeal paralysis,
increasing the risk of aspiration-related pulmonary syndromes in
this population.24,25
Thoracic radiographs (minimum 3 views) should be performed in
all patients with dysphagia, particularly those with suspected
esophageal dysfunction. Thoracic radiographs are the diagnostic test
of choice to identify patients with megaesophagus, although the
degree of dilation has no role in determining the underlying disease
process, and radiographs do not provide functional information
necessary to classify conditions such as lower esophageal sphincter
achalasia-like syndrome (LES-AS).26 Cervical radiographs are
recommended for those animals suspected of having abnormalities
rostral to the thoracic inlet. Regardless of the cause of dysphagia,
thoracic radiographs are recommended to assess for concurrent
aspiration pneumonia/pneumonitis (ch. 217), which are common
and life-threatening sequelae to dysphagia.27,28 It is important to
note that patients with aerophagia may have transient dilation of the
esophagus, and this should not be mistaken for megaesophagus,
which requires concurrent disturbances in motility (ch. 259).
Unfortunately, radiography provides very little functional
information on the swallow mechanism. In these cases, additional
testing is recommended (i.e., videofluoroscopic swallow studies
[VFSS]).

Advanced Testing
Observation of feeding is a critical part of evaluating a patient for
dysphagia. A superficial evaluation may be performed by feeding the
patient in the clinic or having a client record the patient eating and

drinking at home. However, VFSS remain the criterion standard for
evaluation of dysphagia in dogs and cats (

Videos 47.1, 47.2, and

47.3).29 This technique allows continuous, real-time assessment of
the oral preparatory, pharyngeal, and esophageal phases of
swallowing. The method of performing these studies has changed in
recent years. Historically, animals were held in lateral recumbency
and force fed. This has several limitations, including an unacceptable
risk of aspiration and non-physiologic bolus sizes, which can impact
swallowing parameters, including esophageal transit.30 Recent
studies have proposed a free-feeding, free-standing VFSS protocol
that addresses these limitations and reduces the risk of aspiration to
what the patient would experience while eating and drinking at
home.29 This allows for evaluation of patients where VFSS would
have been relatively contraindicated (e.g., megaesophagus). This
modified technique led to the identification of LES-AS in a
subpopulation of dogs with esophageal dysphagia that has been
subsequently shown to respond to targeted intervention.28,31
Esophagoscopy is rarely helpful in diagnosing functional
dysphagia. However, it is invaluable when mechanical
obstructions/defects are suspected (ch. 107). It also provides a
means of targeted intervention for patients with esophageal
strictures, esophageal foreign bodies, and LES-AS, as well as the
ability to collect biopsy samples as needed. Assessing reflux by
endoscopy is challenging because of changes in LES tone secondary
to anesthesia. Additionally, non-erosive reflux, which is thought to
contribute to 50-85% of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
cases in people,32 does not cause overt mucosal lesions. As such,
these cases may be missed by an over-reliance on observing mucosal
changes by endoscopy. In cases where GERD is suspected, a VFSS is
recommended to both detect and gauge the significance of the reflux
(i.e., physiologic vs. pathologic).
A limitation of VFSS is the ability to detect microscopic reflux and
aspiration events. Nuclear scintigraphy, used for evaluating
mucociliary clearance in dogs,33 has recently been adapted to detect
reflux and aspiration events. This has the benefit of not being reliant

on pH, is non-invasive, and can be performed without anesthesia.34
However, it is not widely available. Other ancillary tests include
manometry. Though this provides valuable information on
esophageal pressurization, its currently very limited availability
makes it more academic than clinically actionable.35

TREATMENT
Appropriate management depends on identifying and treating the
underlying disease where possible, optimizing caloric intake, and
preventing/limiting aspiration. Recently, two studies evaluating dogs
with esophageal dysphagia have reported positive responses to
targeted intervention at the LES. The first was in dogs with general
megaesophagus and sildenafil,36 and the second in dogs with LESAS.28 In both cases, thorough patient evaluation and
characterization of dysphagia led to specific interventions and
improved outcomes. In cases of idiopathic forms of dysphagia,
disease treatment is limited to supportive care. Feeding strategies
should be tailored to the specific patient. Dogs with pharyngeal
disease may benefit from having a food bowl elevated to the level of
the point of the shoulder. A Bailey chair and fully upright feeding is
recommended in dogs with esophageal dysphagia including
megaesophagus (ch. 259). Food trials evaluating different
consistencies may be recommended, as no one consistency is
superior in all cases. In dogs where feeding by mouth is not possible,
feeding tubes should be considered (ch. 81). The feeding tube
should bypass the site of dysphagia (e.g., gastrostomy/percutaneous
endoscopic gastrostomy [PEG] tube for dogs with megaesophagus).
Esophageal feeding tubes are not recommended for patients with
esophageal dysphagia.

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis in dogs with gag and dysphagia is dependent entirely
on the underlying etiology, the ability to ensure appropriate caloric

intake, and prevent aspiration-associated respiratory syndromes
(Figure 47.2).

and Vomiting
Alex Gallagher

Vomiting is a common presenting concern in cats and dogs. While
the majority of time the patient is truly vomiting, it may actually be
regurgitation in some cases as owners are often unaware of the
difference. The clinician must distinguish between these two clinical
signs as the differential diagnoses and diagnostic evaluation are quite
different for each.

DIFFERENTIATING REGURGITATION
FROM VOMITING

A complete history (ch. 2) and thorough physical examination (ch.
3) will usually allow differentiation of regurgitation from vomiting
(Table 48.1; Videos 48.1 and 48.2)

. Asking owners to describe

the episodes is helpful, as a description of abdominal contractions
(retching) or bile in the vomitus is specific for vomiting. In rare
instances, bile may be present in regurgitation due to reflux of bile
from the stomach into the esophagus prior to regurgitation.
Additionally, vomiting is often associated with prodromal signs of
nausea such as salivation or lip-smacking. With regurgitation,
owners typically report that the animal simply lowers its head and
material is expelled.
Other factors such as timing of the episode in relation to feeding or
the amount of material produced are not distinguishing factors.
Animals may vomit undigested food or regurgitate digestedappearing food. The pH of the expulsed material has been considered
a possible differentiating test. Vomited material is expected to have a
low pH and regurgitated material to have a more neutral or high pH.
However, some animals may regurgitate stomach contents (such as
in reflux esophagitis) and some may vomit bicarbonate-rich fluid
refluxed from the duodenum, making pH a poor indicator.
In some instances, the owner may not have witnessed the episode,
but only report finding food or fluid on the floor. In other cases, the
description of the episodes may not allow obvious distinction. In
these cases, the rest of the history and physical examination should
be used to determine if vomiting or regurgitation is more likely. As
regurgitation is uncommon in cats, episodes can often be assumed to
be vomiting in this species. If possible, having the owner capture an
episode on video may be helpful. While uncommon, both vomiting
and regurgitation may be present concurrently.

CLINICAL SIGN

REGURGITATION
Regurgitation is the passive expulsion of food, fluid, or other
material from the pharynx or esophagus. It must be differentiated
from expectoration, which is the expulsion of material from the
respiratory tract associated with coughing (chs. 34, 47).
Regurgitation may be followed by a terminal retch or gag which
owners may confuse with cough, and regurgitation can lead to
aspiration pneumonia resulting in a true cough.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
The esophagus is a long tubular organ bordered proximally by the
upper esophageal sphincter and distally by the lower esophageal
sphincter. The muscular composition of the esophagus differs
between dogs and cats. In dogs, the esophageal body is fully
composed of striated muscle. In the cat, the distal one third to one
half of the esophagus is composed of smooth muscle. In both species,
during swallowing, the upper esophageal sphincter relaxes to allow
passage of the food or liquid into the proximal esophagus (ch. 47). A
primary peristaltic wave is initiated, which moves food distally to the
stomach. Secondary peristaltic waves are generated as a response to

intraluminal distension to clear remaining material. The lower
esophageal sphincter relaxes as the food bolus approaches, allowing
passage into the stomach. Diseases that result in inflammation,
obstruction, or hypomotility in the esophagus interrupt this normal
process and can result in regurgitation (ch. 259).

CLINICAL SIGNS
The regurgitant may include undigested food, digested food, or clear,
frothy fluid. Weight loss and polyphagia may occur due to
inadequate nutrition. In some cases, dilation of the cervical
esophagus may be apparent. Signs of aspiration pneumonia
including lethargy, anorexia, cough, or dyspnea may be present (ch.
217). A neurological examination should be performed (ch. 241) to
evaluate for deficits consistent with generalized neuromuscular
dysfunction.

DIAGNOSIS
Initial evaluation consists of cervical and thoracic radiographs to
assess for generalized (megaesophagus) or focal (vascular ring
anomaly, stricture) esophageal dilation, foreign bodies, intra- or
extraluminal masses, and aspiration pneumonia (Figure 48.1).
Contrast radiography (esophagram) provides further assessment if
survey radiographs are non-diagnostic. Use of video fluoroscopy is
beneficial to better assess esophageal motility. Endoscopy can
confirm radiographic findings, provide treatment for foreign bodies
or strictures, allow biopsy of mass lesions, and identify esophagitis
(ch. 259).
A minimum database including complete blood count, serum
biochemistry profile, and urinalysis is warranted when systemic
illness or megaesophagus is present. Adrenocorticotropic hormone
(ACTH) stimulation, thyroid tests, acetylcholine receptor (AchR)
antibody test, and blood lead assay should be considered in cases
with megaesophagus or esophageal hypomotility.

TREATMENT
Specific therapy should be used for any underlying disease as well as
aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217), if present. Management strategies
to reduce frequency of regurgitation are used when primary disease
is not identified or is unresponsive to therapy. Dietary management
includes small, frequent meals and elevated feeding (ch. 259).
Maintaining the patient in an upright position for 5-10 minutes after
feeding may allow gravity to help esophageal transit. A Bailey chair
can be used for this purpose. Owners should experiment with
different food textures such as liquids, gruels, canned, or dry foods to
determine which one works best for their pet. If gastroesophageal
(GI) reflux disease is present, acid reducers and prokinetics may
reduce the risk of esophagitis. Cisapride (cats) and bethanechol
(dogs) may improve esophageal motility. Increasing the lower
esophageal sphincter tone can exacerbate regurgitation in some
cases.

VOMITING
Vomiting is one of the most common reasons dogs and cats are
presented to a clinician for evaluation. It is an active expulsion of
ingesta from the stomach and sometimes duodenum through the
mouth. In contrast to regurgitation, vomiting involves a centrally
mediated reflex with coordinated closure of the nasopharynx and
glottis to protect the airway, reducing the risk of aspiration
pneumonia. Like regurgitation, it must be differentiated from
expectoration.
Vomiting evolved as protection against the ingestion of toxic or
noxious substances, which explains its activation by both neural and
humoral stimuli. It is most often associated with primary GI
disorders, but may also occur due to non-GI diseases such as
metabolic or neurological disorders. Severe or prolonged vomiting
can have significant consequences, including volume depletion, acidbase and electrolyte derangements, aspiration pneumonia, and
esophagitis.

FIGURE 48.1 Diagnostic approach to
regurgitation. AchR Ab, Acetylcholine receptor
antibody; ACTH, adrenocorticotropic hormone; BE
tube, balloon esophagostomy tube; PEG,
percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Vomiting is a complex reflex initiated by the emetic center, which is
composed of a group of nuclei located in the medulla oblongata of
the brain stem (Figure 48.2). Within this area are serotonergic
(5HT1) and alpha2 adrenergic receptors. In addition, neurokinergic

(NK1) receptors are located in the adjacent nucleus tractus solitarii,
which can stimulate the emetic center. Activation of these receptors
may occur indirectly by humoral pathways via the chemoreceptor
trigger zone (CRTZ) or directly through neural pathways from the GI
tract, cerebral cortex, or vestibular system.
The CRTZ is located in the area postrema in the floor of the fourth
ventricle and lacks a blood-brain barrier, allowing it to sample
chemical stimuli in the blood. Stimulants include endogenous
(uremic or hepatoencephalopathic toxins) and exogenous substances
(drugs, toxins). Dopaminergic (D2), histaminergic (H1), alpha2
adrenergic, serotonergic (5HT3), cholinergic (M1), enkephalinergic
(ENK-mu, delta), and NK1 receptors are present in the CRTZ, but
there are species differences (Figure 48.2). Apomorphine (D1 and
D2 agonist) is a potent stimulator of emesis in dogs but has little to
no effect in cats, suggesting a lack of D2 receptors in this species.1,2
However, xylazine (alpha2 agonist) is an effective emetic in cats,
signifying that alpha2 receptors may be more important.3,4 Visceral
rather than central 5HT3 receptors appear to be more important in
cisplatin-induced emesis in the dog.5

FIGURE 48.2 Physiology and pharmacology of
vomiting. alpha2, Alpha-2 adrenergic receptor; D2,
dopamine-2 receptor; ENKμ,δ, enkephalinergic mu,
delta receptor; H1, histamine-1 receptor; 5-HT, 5hydroxytryptamine (serotonin) receptor; M,
muscarinic cholinergic receptor; MOT, motilin
receptor; NK1, neurokinin-1 receptor; NMDA, Nmethyl-d-aspartate; NTS, nucleus tractus solitarius;
omega2, omega-2 receptor. (From Washabau RJ,
Day MJ. Canine and Feline Gastroenterology.
Elsevier; 2012:169.)
Neural stimulation of the emetic center occurs via afferent vagal,
sympathetic, vestibular, and cerebrocortical pathways (Figure
48.2). GI diseases can directly cause vomiting by stimulating release
of serotonin from enterochromaffin cells that binds to 5HT3
receptors on afferent vagal nerves (dog) or the CRTZ (cat). Vestibular
stimulation feeds into the CRTZ before activating the emetic center
in the dog, but appears to act directly on the emetic center in the cat.

CLINICAL APPROACH
The initial approach starts with a thorough history (ch. 2). A
description of the vomiting episodes is essential to differentiate from
coughing or regurgitation. The owner should be asked to describe the
frequency, duration, relation to eating or drinking, and the character
of the vomitus. Vomiting may be acute or chronic (>1-2 weeks in
duration). In some cases, vomiting may be sporadic, making it
difficult to determine if it is chronic versus intermittent acute
disease. Vomiting food more than 8 hours after ingestion suggests
delayed gastric emptying due to either gastric outflow obstruction or
gastric hypomotility, while the presence of bile suggests patency of
gastric outflow. The presence of either fresh or digested blood
(“coffee grounds”) indicates GI erosions or ulcers, but could be due
to ingestion of blood from other sources such as the respiratory tract.
A complete diet history (ch. 145) should be obtained including
past and current diets for planning possible diet trials. Recent diet
changes or opening a new bag or can of food may be the cause of
vomiting. Medication history must include asking about drugs,
supplements, nutraceuticals, and alternative therapies that could be
associated with vomiting. The owner should also be questioned
about possible exposure to toxins or foreign body ingestion (ch.
136). Vaccination status, travel history (ch. 9), and exposure to
other animals are important for determining risk of infectious
diseases, which are more common in young animals (ch. 183).
Physical examination (ch. 3) should start with an overall
assessment of patient demeanor. Oral exam (ch. 258) may reveal
ulcers associated with uremia or toxin ingestion, or sublingual linear
foreign bodies (particularly in cats). Icteric mucous membranes
suggest liver disease. Cardiac arrhythmias can indicate metabolic
derangements or toxin ingestion. The abdomen should be palpated
for evidence of pain (pancreatitis, obstruction), effusion (peritonitis),
gas distension (obstruction, gastric dilatation-volvulus), or
organomegaly. Rectal exam may reveal evidence of melena,
constipation, or material consistent with foreign body ingestion.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH

The diagnostic approach differs based on classification of the
vomiting as acute or chronic (Figures 48.3 and 48.4). Acute
vomiting with mild clinical signs is often self-resolving. As such, a
minimalistic approach is usually appropriate. Fecal examination (ch.
80) may identify parasitic causes of vomiting. Abdominal
radiographs are performed if there is a clinical suspicion of surgical
disease (e.g., suspected foreign body ingestion) or if vomiting does
not resolve with initial therapy.
Conversely, severe or life-threatening signs indicate a more
thorough evaluation should be done. Complete blood count, serum
biochemistry profile, and urinalysis allow identification of systemic
or metabolic diseases. Metabolic alkalosis is suggestive of gastric
outflow or proximal duodenal obstruction and is often associated
with hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and hypochloremia. Abdominal
radiographs +/− abdominal ultrasound are used to evaluate for
surgical diseases such as foreign body, obstruction, gastric
dilatation-volvulus, or intussusception.

FIGURE 48.3 Algorithm for diagnosis of acute
vomiting. GDV, Gastric dilatation-volvulus.
Chronic vomiting requires further investigation so definitive
therapy can be prescribed. Complete blood count, serum
biochemistry profile, and urinalysis should be performed. In
addition, cats should be tested for feline leukemia and feline
immunodeficiency viruses (chs. 198, 199) and those over 5 years of
age should be evaluated for hyperthyroidism by serum total
thyroxine (T4) assay (ch. 287). If a cause is not found, additional
diagnostic testing including ultrasonography, heartworm testing
(cats), bile acids profile, pancreatic lipase testing, and ACTH
stimulation testing should be considered. If a non-GI cause for the
vomiting is not identified, further evaluation of the GI tract is
needed. Contrast radiography may be helpful, particularly if
ultrasonography is not available or the stomach is poorly visualized
due to intraluminal gas. Diet trials should be considered in stable
animals to exclude diet responsive disease prior to more invasive
testing (ch. 152). Endoscopic or surgical biopsy is required to

identify inflammatory disease such as chronic gastritis, Helicobacter
gastritis, or inflammatory bowel disease or neoplasia (chs.
261, 262).

FIGURE 48.4 Algorithm for diagnosis of chronic
vomiting. ACTH, Adrenocorticotropic hormone; GI,
gastrointestinal; T4, thyroxine.

TREATMENT
Initial treatment should be aimed at the primary disease, which often
results in resolution of vomiting (Box 48.1). Acute, self-limiting
vomiting usually resolves with fluid replacement and fasting for 1224 hours. Acute cases with protracted or severe vomiting may benefit
from antiemetic therapy (Table 48.2). Caution should be used as

antiemetics may mask underlying disease that has not yet been
identified. Chronic cases are best treated by identifying the
underlying cause. Antiemetic therapy can be considered to improve
comfort and nutrition, and prevent excessive fluid losses.

CLIENT INFORMATION

Regurgitation and Vomiting

HOW ARE REGURGITATION AND VOMITING
DIFFERENT?
Regurgitation is the passive expulsion of food or fluid. Often there is
no warning that regurgitation will happen. Your pet may simply
lower his or her head and material will seem to fall out. In contrast,
vomiting is an active expulsion of ingesta from the stomach. Pets will
often show signs of nausea such as lip-licking prior. Vomiting is set
apart from regurgitation by the retching or abdominal contractions
that occur before ingesta is expulsed. Yellow coloration signifying the
presence of bile is more consistent with vomiting rather than
regurgitation.

WHY IS IT NECESSARY TO DISTINGUISH
BETWEEN REGURGITATION AND VOMITING?
The anatomic location of disease, potential causes, and diagnostic
tests are different between regurgitation and vomiting. Most
commonly regurgitation is due to disorders of the esophagus which
affect the normal motility such as megaesophagus, esophagitis,
foreign body, and strictures. Vomiting may be due to disorders of the
stomach or duodenum, but can also occur due to disease of other
abdominal organs such as the liver or kidneys, ingestion of drugs or
toxins, or other causes.

WHAT TESTING IS NEEDED IN PETS WITH
REGURGITATION?
Initial testing includes chest radiographs (x-rays). If a specific cause
is not found, then further imaging of the esophagus with contrast
(dye) studies or endoscopy may be needed. There are systemic
diseases that may secondarily affect esophageal function. Blood tests
can be used to screen for these conditions.

WHAT TESTING IS NEEDED IN PETS WITH
VOMITING?

Testing will depend on the duration and severity of vomiting. Pets
with acute, mild vomiting may not need testing initially. Common
testing may include complete blood count (CBC), chemistry,
urinalysis, fecal examination, and abdominal radiographs. Further
imaging with contrast studies, ultrasonography, and endoscopy may
also be performed. Additional blood tests may be needed for specific
disorders such as hypoadrenocorticism or pancreatitis.

WHEN SHOULD I CALL MY VETERINARIAN?
If your pet only vomits once or twice, is still bright and alert, and
able to drink water, you may be able to monitor at home for
resolution. Withholding food for 12-24 hours may help. If vomiting
continues, is severe, contains blood, and/or is associated with
lethargy or unwillingness to eat or drink, you should contact your
veterinarian as soon as possible as examination and diagnostic
testing are likely needed. Pets with chronic vomiting should be
evaluated by your veterinarian so the underlying cause can be
identified and specific therapy started.
Alex Gallagher (Columbia, South Carolina)

INTRODUCTION
Diarrhea is the most common manifestation of intestinal disease,
characterized by increased frequency, fluidity, and/or volume of bowel
movements.1 It occurs secondary to disease processes either within or outside
the gastrointestinal (GI) tract that alter intestinal absorption, secretion,
permeability and/or motility. In most patients, multiple pathomechanisms
contribute to clinical signs concurrently, so etiologic categories such as
infectious, neoplastic, endocrine, structural, and non-infectious
inflammatory, are used for organizing the differential list. A systematic
approach helps to mitigate a one-size-fits-all approach to diarrheic patients,
which could delay diagnosis and result in unintended side-effects. A
comprehensive workup is not feasible for all clients.2 For this reason, priority
should be placed on ruling out diseases unlikely to improve with typical
empiric therapies and those that could result in patient decompensation if
not recognized (e.g., hypoadrenocorticism).

SIGNALMENT
Consideration of patient signalment may help prioritize differentials in the
diarrheic patient. Parvovirus and panleukopenia (ch. 201) must be
considered in dogs and cats, respectively, that have unknown or incomplete
vaccination histories or for whom maternal antibody protection is waning. It
is generally safe to assume that all puppies harbor ascarids, so anthelmintics
may be prescribed with or without corroborating fecal tests (chs. 80, 142).
Neoplasia is of greater concern in older patients, realizing that infectious
diseases can affect this population as well. Conditions thought to be immunemediated, such as chronic inflammatory enteropathy (CIE), typically present
in early adulthood (ch. 262). Endocrine disorders can be stealthy causes of
diarrhea, and typically develop in adult animals, though dogs as young as 4
months old have been diagnosed with hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296).3 In
young cats, feline infectious peritonitis (FIP, ch. 200) and tritrichomoniasis
(ch. 262) are important differentials to consider.
Knowledge of breed predispositions can reorder the differential list and
streamline the workup. Examples include exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
(EPI, ch. 279) in German Shepherds, Rough-Coated Collies, and Cavalier
King Charles Spaniels3; lymphangiectasia (ch. 262) in Yorkshire Terriers,
Maltese and Chow Chows4; E. coli-associated granulomatous colitis (GC, ch.
263) in Boxers and French Bulldogs5,6; and protothecosis (ch. 263) in
Rough-Coated Collies and Boxers.7,8 Abyssinian and Bengal cats are more
susceptible to FIP (ch. 200)9 and tritrichomoniasis (ch. 262).10,11

HISTORY (ch. 2)
It should be readily apparent whether diarrhea is an acute, first-time offense,
or a chronic (observed for ≥3 weeks) or recurrent issue. Asking when patient
was last “normal” may help link onset of signs to changes in the environment,
diet, or medication regimen. Animals with long-standing signs that remain
clinically well are less likely to have aggressive enteric infections or neoplasia.
Characterization of the consistency, frequency, and presence of substances
like blood (digested or fresh; ch. 50) or mucus in the feces, as well as
concurrent clinical signs, help to localize diarrhea to the small or large bowel
(synonym, small or large intestine; Figure 49.1). Inappropriate defecation
suggests urgency, orthopedic or neurologic problems impairing ability to get
outside or to the litter box, or cognitive dysfunction (ch. 51). Observing
defecation directly or via owner-obtained video may uncover tenesmus,
dyschezia, difficulties posturing, and/or urinary abnormalities (ch. 54).

Pictorial fecal scoring charts are especially useful in plotting response to
therapy.
Other historical features help round out the clinical picture. These include
travel history (consider regional prevalence of infectious agents, ch. 9),
clinical signs in other animals in the household, exposure to animals outside
the household (doggie day care, dog shows, field trials), and use of parasite
prophylaxis (ch. 142).
It is important to obtain a comprehensive history (ch. 2), and ensure the
client describes all noteworthy clinical signs, such as regurgitation, vomiting,
change in appetite, thirst and/or urination, weight loss, abdominal distension
and/or pain. At times, the patient is presented for a primary concern of
diarrhea, but a careful history identifies a different problem that is more lifethreatening or has fewer differentials.

PHYSICAL EXAM
Given the myriad disease processes resulting in diarrhea, a complete physical
exam is crucial (ch. 3). Special attention should be paid to hydration status,
body condition score and peripheral lymph nodes. Careful abdominal
palpation may reveal evidence of pain, mass effects, abnormal loops of bowel,
and/or a fluid wave (ch. 21) (Video 21.1). Cats should be examined for a
thyroid slip (Video 287.2

). A digital rectal exam is essential in dogs with

diarrhea; for cats, this is pursued on a case-by-case basis. This may uncover
rectal masses or strictures, mucosal irregularities, intrapelvic
lymphadenomegaly, pelvic canal boney abnormalities, and/or anal sac
masses (ch. 264). Fecal and rectal scrape samples can also be readily
obtained for cytologic evaluation (Table 49.1). Many animals will have fairly
unremarkable physical exams despite intractable diarrhea.

DIAGNOSTIC TEST SELECTION
After a thorough history and physical exam, it should be clear whether the
animal is clinically well or unwell, and whether the diarrhea is acute or
chronic.

ACUTE DIARRHEA
In many cases of acute diarrhea, the underlying cause is not identified and
signs resolve without specific treatment. In clinically well animals with
normal vital parameters, diagnostic tests may not be warranted. Treatments

unlikely to do harm, with some probability of reducing the severity or
duration of clinical signs, are reasonable. Leading considerations include
deworming, feeding of a bland diet, probiotic supplementation,12 and
subcutaneous fluids. Antibiotics such as metronidazole and tylosin are
commonly prescribed to animals with acute diarrhea,13 but their potential
benefit14 must be balanced with drawbacks such as disruption of the native
microbiota15,16 and promotion of antimicrobial resistance.17 Metronidazole
has also been shown to cause DNA damage in feline lymphocytes,18 and so
should not be considered a benign anti-diarrheal drug in this species.
Indications for antibiotic administration include signs of sepsis or the
systemic inflammatory response syndrome (ch. 128), neutropenia, or
documented infection with an enteropathogen that is not responding to
supportive care.19 Anti-diarrheals such as loperamide and bismuth should be
avoided in cases of uncharacterized acute diarrhea, as they could impede the
body’s pathogen clearance efforts.
Unwell animals should be evaluated with a minimum database consisting
of a complete blood count (CBC), serum biochemistry panel, urinalysis, and
fecal parasite screen (ch. 80). This may reveal abnormalities of immediate
concern (e.g., neutropenia, hepatic synthetic dysfunction, azotemia) which
would shift the focus of case management and guide further workup and
treatment decisions.

CHRONIC DIARRHEA
Animals with diarrhea persisting ≥3 weeks merit a CBC, serum biochemistry
panel, urinalysis, and fecal parasite screen (ch. 80). These general diagnostic
tests screen for the presence of protein-losing enteropathy (PLE, ch. 262)
and/or signs pointing to an extra-GI cause of diarrhea. In the absence of
either, a general approach to animals with chronic diarrhea is depicted in
Figure 49.1.
For non-anorexic animals with small- or large-bowel diarrhea, it is
reasonable to consider a diet trial early on (ch. 152). Considerations include
easily digestible, novel protein, or hydrolyzed protein prescription diets, as
well as high-quality over-the-counter (OTC) diets. Since undeclared proteins
have been documented in many OTC “limited ingredient” pet foods
analyzed,21,22 prescription diets are preferred. A majority of dogs with CIE

will have improvement in their clinical signs with change in diet.23,24 It is
challenging to predict which diet will benefit an individual patient, though
ultra-low-fat diets are prioritized in non-anorexic dogs with
hypoalbuminemia +/– hypocholesterolemia.25 In general, multiple dedicated
diet trials (exclusive feeding for ≥2 weeks) are completed in chronic diarrhea
patients prior to advanced diagnostics.
A trial with supplemental fiber is typically instituted early on in patients
with predominantly large bowel signs26 (ch. 165). Psyllium husk powder
contains both soluble and insoluble fibers, which have prebiotic properties
and can help normalize fecal consistency. Potential adverse effects of fiber
supplementation include delayed gastric emptying and worsened flatulence.
Starting low and gradually increasing the dose is advised. When diet
modulation fails to improve clinical signs, the author returns to the
differential diagnosis list (chs. 262 and 263), revisiting infectious, structural,
and endocrine etiologies for chronic diarrhea not apparent on initial workup.

Infectious Agent Testing
Testing for infectious agents in patients with diarrhea is most effective when
one has a specific infectious etiology in mind with clinical manifestations that
match those of the patient (Table 49.2). Broad overlap exists in PCRpositivity between healthy and diarrheic patients,27,28 so simply identifying
an organism (particularly bacterial) in the feces does not prove that that
organism is the cause of the patient’s clinical signs. This knowledge helps one
resist the urge of premature closure and resultant over-treatment.

Other Diagnostic Tests
Major concepts for the interpretation of diagnostic tests in patients with
diarrhea are summarized in Table 49.1. Some animals require
histopathologic analysis of intestinal biopsies to achieve a definitive
diagnosis. Endoscopy (ch. 107) offers a minimally invasive means of
examining and sampling the gut mucosal lining. Exploratory laparotomy
allows for collection of full-thickness biopsies, required for focal or jejunal
lesions. The risk of dehiscence, particularly in hypoalbuminemic and
otherwise debilitated animals,29 makes endoscopy the preferred option in the
vast majority of cases. Inflammatory infiltrates in the gut are common and
non-specific. Therefore, it is of paramount importance that biopsies be
interpreted within the context of the patient’s overall clinical picture and that
aforementioned etiologies (e.g., EPI, hypoadrenocorticism, infections able to
be diagnosed without GI biopsies) have already been ruled out. Biopsy is
most important in animals with PLE, anorexic animals not amenable to diet

trials, and those with a high suspicion of neoplasia, E. coli-associated GC, or
atypical infection. Placement of an esophageal feeding tube can be considered
under the same anesthetic event (ch. 81).

CHAPTER 50: Melena and
Hematochezia
Karen Michele Tefft

A C RO N YM S
BUN blood urea nitrogen
CBC complete blood count
GI gastrointestinal

Witnessing blood in the stool of their pet is distressing for many
owners and thus often prompts an urgent visit to their veterinarian’s
office. The presence of blood in the stool may or may not indicate a
life-threatening disorder, however. In addition, the source of the
blood may not be gastrointestinal (GI) in origin. The veterinarian
must localize the source and seriousness of the hemorrhage by
careful evaluation of history, physical examination, and diagnostic
test findings.

MELENA
DEFINITION
Melena refers to feces that are black and tarry due to the presence of
hematin and other hemochromes from the bacterial degradation of
hemoglobin (Figure 50.1). While classically this is thought to be

due to hemorrhage originating from the small intestine or orad, the
length of time blood spends in the intestinal tract is more important
than the site of bleeding.1

CAUSES
Sites of hemorrhage to consider in patients with melena include both
the upper and lower respiratory tract, where blood from epistaxis or
hemoptysis (ch. 36) can be swallowed, and the GI tract, including
the oral cavity, esophagus, stomach, and small intestine. Rarely, the
cecum and colon may also be considered as a source for melena,
particularly if intestinal motility is decreased. Melena can also result
from blood ingested as part of a raw diet. The absence of melena
does not rule out GI bleeding. In humans, it has been experimentally
determined that at least 50 to 100 mL of blood must be ingested
before melanic stool is appreciated.2 Important mimics of melena
that will cause black stool include ingestion of activated charcoal,
iron supplements, anti-diarrheal medications containing bismuth, or
large amounts of blueberries.
Many diseases have the potential to cause melena (Box 50.1). The
majority of these conditions result in GI hemorrhage by directly or
indirectly disrupting mucosal barriers to injury.3 Defense
mechanisms utilized by the GI mucosa include: an adherent mucus
layer, hydrophobic nature of epithelial cells, epithelial secretion of
bicarbonate, rapid repair of the epithelial layer by restitution, a high
rate of mucosal blood flow, prostaglandins and nitric oxide (chs.
261-263).

CLINICAL EVALUATION
History
A careful assessment of the history is the first step in the evaluation
of a patient presenting with melena (ch. 2). The clinician should not
ask leading questions about the patient’s stool color, but instead let
the owner use his or her own descriptors. Ideally, owners can be
shown a set of swatches from which to select which color best

represents their pet’s fecal color, as inconsistencies have been shown
in subjective color reporting as compared to selecting a color off a
scorecard.4 The owner should be asked specific questions concerning
diet, drug administration, and potential exposure to toxic substances
(ch. 136); the veterinarian uses this information to determine
immediately if the owner had administered a bismuth-containing
medication or any other compound that can cause black stool.
Determining the patient’s diet, and specifically whether they eat a
raw meat diet, or receive liver or spleen, or eat a diet that
incorporates bones in the food, directly addresses this category of
causes of melena (ch. 167).
After ruling out causes of black stool other than respiratory or GI
tract hemorrhage, the focus of the history collection can shift
towards these pathologic causes. Additional clinical signs such as
exercise intolerance, stridor, coughing, or dyspnea raise suspicion for
respiratory tract disease (ch. 212), while anorexia, regurgitation,
vomiting, or diarrhea raise suspicion for GI tract disease (ch. 257).
The owners should be asked about any other instances of observed
bleeding; epistaxis or hemoptysis can indicate primary respiratory
tract disease and hematemesis may indicate primary GI tract disease.
However, the clinician should remain mindful that a systemic
bleeding disorder might alternatively be the cause, particularly if
hematuria or ecchymosis is reported (chs. 171, 261, 262).

It is important to question the owners specifically about
administration of corticosteroids and non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs (chs. 143, 144). Both of these classes of drugs
reduce the production of protective prostaglandins, leading to gastric
mucosal injury.5 The history should address whether the patient had
any opportunity to ingest anticoagulant rodenticides, corrosive

compounds or foreign objects (ch. 138). The patient’s travel history
can suggest the possibility of specific infectious diseases (ch. 9).

Physical Examination
While particular attention should be paid to the respiratory and
digestive systems, a thorough physical examination is still necessary
in the patient with melena (ch. 3). Inspection of the skin, mucous
membranes, and sclera can reveal petechiae or ecchymoses (ch. 29),
which can indicate a bleeding disorder or jaundice to suggest
hepatobiliary disease. A fundic examination (ch. 13) is important to
identify retinal hemorrhages, which can indicate a bleeding disorder,
hyperviscosity, or systemic hypertension (ch. 236). Examination of
the skin, mucocutaneous junctions and nail beds can reveal masses,
which may indicate mast cell disease (ch. 327). A thorough
examination of the nares and oral cavity is warranted, for active
hemorrhage or lesions with the potential to bleed (ch. 258). Patients
with moderate to severe blood loss will display mucous membrane
pallor (ch. 25). Careful auscultation of the lung fields is warranted,
and abnormal sounds could support the presence of pulmonary
disease. Thorough palpation of the abdomen can allow the
veterinarian to identify signs of pain, organomegaly, or masses. A
digital rectal exam must be included to confirm the presence of
melena, to obtain a stool sample for fecal testing, and to assess for
mucosal abnormalities and sublumbar lymph node enlargement.

Diagnostic Evaluation
After confirming the presence of melena, the clinician then should
move to diagnostic testing to provide objective support for
abnormalities detected on physical examination and to begin ruling
in and out differential diagnoses (Figure 50.2). The initial
diagnostic work-up at a minimum includes a complete blood count
(CBC), serum biochemistry panel, urinalysis, prothrombin time,
activated partial thromboplastin time, and fecal flotation (ch. 80).
Anemia is the most common finding on the CBC of a patient with
melena (ch. 57). The anemia can be mild to severe, and a
regenerative response may be evident if sufficient time has elapsed
since blood loss began and suitable regenerative capacity exists.
Chronic, low-grade hemorrhage can result in iron deficiency that

ultimately can cause a microcytic, hypochromic non-regenerative
anemia (ch. 173). Thrombocytopenia, if moderate to severe, can be
the primary cause of melena (chs. 59, 171). Mild thrombocytopenia
likely is a secondary finding resulting from consumption of platelets
at the site of acute hemorrhage. Thrombocytosis can be seen with
chronic GI hemorrhage. Leukocyte counts may be decreased, within
normal range, or increased based on the underlying disease, and a
left shift may or may not be present (ch. 58). Eosinophilia can be
caused by a variety of diseases that can result in GI hemorrhage,
such as parasitism, systemic mycosis, mast cell tumor, eosinophilic
gastritis or hypereosinophilic syndrome. Common abnormalities on
the serum biochemistry profile include disproportionately elevated
blood urea nitrogen (BUN) concentration compared to creatinine
(ch. 62), and hypoproteinemia (ch. 60). A BUN/creatinine ratio
>30 (when both are measured in mg/dL; metric equivalent: >0.12) is
consistent with upper GI hemorrhage, but the development of an
elevated ratio is dependent upon several factors such as the amount
of blood lost, time since hemorrhage, GI transit time, and volemic
status.6,7 Elevated hepatic enzyme activities (ch. 65) or azotemia
should raise suspicions for liver or renal disease, respectively.
Hyponatremia in conjunction with hyperkalemia should raise the
suspicion of hypoadrenocorticism, although salmonellosis and
whipworm infections can occasionally cause
pseudohypoadrenocorticism (chs. 68 and 296). A urinalysis is
performed for evaluation of concurrent disease, including
differentiating causes of azotemia (ch. 70). Prolonged coagulation
times will aid in diagnosing cases of rodenticide intoxication or
disseminated intravascular coagulation (ch. 170). A fecal flotation
can identify parasite ova (ch. 80).

FIGURE 50.2 Diagnostic approach to melena.
CBC, Complete blood count; CT, computed
tomography; PT/PTT, prothrombin time/partial
thromboplastin time.

The next phase of diagnostic testing, which may be performed
concurrently with the previously described tests or subsequently, is
imaging. Radiographic imaging of the thorax and abdomen can help
further differentiate between respiratory and GI sources of melena.
Clearly definable abnormal lung patterns likely will be present in
cases with clinically significant hemoptysis. Thoracic radiographs
also are useful to screen for metastatic disease if a mass has been
palpated in the abdomen. Relevant abdominal radiographic
abnormalities can include radiopaque foreign bodies, abnormal size
or shape of abdominal organs, mass effects, and abnormal gas and
fluid patterns within the GI tract. Abdominal ultrasound can further
evaluate for foreign bodies, abnormal organ architecture including
intestinal wall layering, masses, lymphadenopathy, or
intussusception. It is more sensitive than radiography at identifying
non-perforated GI ulcers.8
Definitive diagnosis of the underlying cause of melena often
requires advanced diagnostic techniques, which may include specific
serologic testing, fecal cultures, computed tomography, rhinoscopy
(chs. 89 and 213), bronchoscopy (chs. 93 and 212), GI endoscopy
(ch. 107), and exploratory laparotomy.

TREATMENT
Specific treatment for patients presenting with melena will vary
dependent upon the underlying cause. However, given that GI
ulceration is the underlying etiology in most cases of melena, it is
reasonable to start therapy that addresses ulceration while a
definitive diagnosis is pursued. Pharmaceuticals used in the
treatment of GI ulceration work by decreasing intraluminal acidity
and promoting mucosal defense mechanisms. Proton-pump
inhibitors, synthetic prostaglandin analogues, and sucralfate are
commonly used in combination to treat GI ulceration (ch. 261).5

HEMATOCHEZIA
DEFINITION
Hematochezia refers to the passage of bright-red colored stools due
to the presence of hemoglobin (Figure 50.3). While classically this
is thought to be due to hemorrhage originating from the colon, the
length of time blood spends in the intestinal tract is more important
than the site of bleeding.

CAUSES
Some overlap exists between potential causes of melena and
hematochezia; however, sites of hemorrhage to typically consider as
causes of hematochezia include the cecum, colon, rectum, and anus.
Small intestinal hemorrhage may present with hematochezia if
intestinal motility is increased. Mimics of hematochezia that can
cause red stool include ingestion of foods or treats containing red
food coloring or large amounts of beets. In addition, owners
sometimes mistake bleeding from a perineal bite wound or anal sac
abscess as hematochezia. Many diseases have the potential to cause
hematochezia (Box 50.2).

CLINICAL EVALUATION
History
The majority of questions for the owner of a patient with melena also
apply for hematochezia, with the exception of questions pertaining to
the respiratory tract. Additional questions specific to the lower GI
tract include inquiring about the patient’s bowel habits, including
whether dyschezia, tenesmus, “scooting,” or frequent attempts at
defecation producing only small amounts of stool or mucus is
present. It is useful to ask if the feces are entirely red or marooncolored, suggesting a proximal colonic lesion, or if they are otherwise
normal in color with frank blood only on the surface, suggesting an
anorectal lesion. Asking the owner if the patient may have
experienced recent stress or an abrupt dietary change or indiscretion
is useful, as these are frequent triggers for self-limiting colitis.

Physical Examination
While particular attention should be paid to abdominal and rectal
palpation, a thorough physical examination is still necessary in the
patient with hematochezia as described for the patient with melena,
above (ch. 3). Thorough palpation of the abdomen is needed for
signs of pain, organomegaly or masses. A digital rectal exam must be
included to confirm the presence of hematochezia, to obtain a stool
sample for fecal testing, and for assessment of mucosal
abnormalities such as masses or strictures, sublumbar lymph node
enlargement, pelvic fracture or other perianal abnormalities such as
fistulas or ulceration. The anal sacs should be palpated for the
presence of nodules or cellulitis, and expressed for evaluation of their
contents. The clinician should be cautious in performing rectal
palpation as an underlying disease process could make it painful for
the patient.

Diagnostic Evaluation
In a patient presenting with simple, acute hematochezia
characterized by blood streaking on the surface of the feces and no
other clinical signs or physical examination abnormalities, a fecal
flotation and direct saline preparation are the only diagnostic tests
initially indicated (ch. 80). Patients with severe hematochezia (i.e.,
feces that look like “raspberry jam”), chronic hematochezia, and/or
other clinical signs should have a diagnostic work-up as described for
patients with melena.

TREATMENT
Specific treatment for patients presenting with hematochezia will
vary dependent on the underlying cause. In a patient presenting with
simple, acute hematochezia as described above, empiric treatment
with a broad-spectrum anthelmintic, a probiotic, and a bland diet
containing soluble fiber is often successful (chs. 152, 165, and 263).
