CLIENT INFORMATION
Melena

WHAT IS MELENA?
Melena is the medical term to describe bowel movements that are
black and tarry due to the presence of digested blood. Melena is not a

disease in itself, but rather is a symptom of an underlying condition
that can range in severity from serious to minor and self-resolving.

WHAT CAUSES MELENA?
Melena is most commonly caused by a source of bleeding in the
upper portion of the digestive system, such as from the esophagus,
stomach or small intestines. Less commonly it can be caused by
blood from the nose, mouth or lungs that the dog or cat swallows.
Melena can also result from blood ingested as part of a raw diet. If a
dog or a cat is given certain medications (e.g., activated charcoal,
iron supplements or anti-diarrheal medications containing bismuth)
their stool may turn black in color, but this is not true melena. Some
of the more common causes of melena include:
• Stomach ulcers
• Parasitic infections
• Intestinal foreign object
• Inflammatory bowel disease
• Steroid or anti-inflammatory medications
• Kidney failure
• Liver disease
• Pancreatitis
• Cancer of the respiratory or digestive systems
• Anticoagulant rodenticide (“rat bait”) intoxication

WHAT SYMPTOMS CAN BE SEEN WITH MELENA?
If your pet has experienced enough blood loss to become anemic
(i.e., a decreased number of red blood cells), they may experience
weakness and pale gums. Other symptoms that your pet may have
while experiencing melena relate to the underlying cause of the
melena and the source of the bleeding.
In pets with bleeding from the digestive system, the following
symptoms may also be seen:
• Loss of appetite
• Vomit containing blood or material that looks like coffee
grounds
• Diarrhea

• Weight loss
In pets with bleeding from the respiratory system, the following
symptoms may also be seen:
• Nose bleed
• Sneezing
• Coughing up blood
• Difficulty breathing
In pets with bleeding due to a problem with blood clotting, such as
from anticoagulant rodenticide intoxication, the following symptoms
may also be seen:
• Nose bleed
• Blood in urine
• Blood in the eye
• Bruising

WHAT TESTS ARE NEEDED?
Your veterinarian will ask you many questions detailing your pet’s
overall health, diet, previous vaccinations, current medications and
supplements, and travel history. They will also ask you about the
onset of melena, how long it has been present, any other symptoms
you have noted, and any possible inciting incidents. The answers you
provide to these questions will help your veterinarian determine the
source of bleeding. Next, your veterinarian will perform a complete
physical examination, including a rectal examination.
Standard laboratory tests that your veterinarian will begin with
include a complete blood count (CBC), biochemistry profile, a
urinalysis, fecal exam, and coagulation profile. The CBC will evaluate
whether the bleeding has been significant enough to cause anemia, a
decreased number of red blood cells. The CBC also evaluates if your
pet has enough platelets. Platelets are necessary for the first step of
forming a blood clot. Some conditions can cause decreased numbers
of platelets; if platelets are decreased sufficiently, spontaneous
bleeding can occur. The biochemistry profile will screen for diseases
such as kidney failure or liver disease, which can lead to the
formation of stomach ulcers. The urinalysis will also help evaluate

for kidney disease and will look for blood in the urine, which can be
seen in patients with problems with blood clotting. The fecal exam
will evaluate for a variety of parasites and other organisms that can
cause melena. A coagulation profile directly measures the ability of
your pet to form a blood clot.
Radiographs (“x-rays”) and potentially ultrasound are also useful
tests to try to non-invasively look inside your pet to determine the
source of bleeding. Radiographs of the abdomen will look for foreign
objects that may have been swallowed, masses, and abnormalities in
the size or shape of organs. An ultrasound of the abdomen is
complimentary to radiographs. It can further evaluate for foreign
objects that might not be visible on radiographs, masses and
abnormal internal architecture of the organs. Radiographs of the
thorax (“chest”) will look for masses or other abnormalities of the
lungs or esophagus.
The above-described tests may be sufficient to diagnose the
underlying cause of your pet’s melena. However, there still may be
additional tests needed to pinpoint the exact underlying cause or to
help guide treatment. Some of these tests include endoscopy,
computed tomography (CT scan) or specialized bloodwork. With
endoscopy, a flexible tube with a camera is passed into your pet’s
nose, lungs or digestive tract while they are under anesthesia. Via the
endoscope, masses, foreign objects, infections, or ulcers can be
directly visualized and biopsied. The endoscope may even be able to
remove the foreign object if one is present. A CT scan can evaluate
for masses or abnormal structures in areas that are not amenable to
ultrasound (such as the nose) and can look for abnormal blood
vessels that may be causing the bleeding. The specialized bloodwork
may vary based upon what your veterinarian suspects.

WHAT TREATMENT IS NEEDED?
In patients that have become severely anemic from their blood loss, a
blood transfusion may be necessary. Other specific treatment for
dogs and cats with melena will vary dependent upon the underlying
cause. However, since stomach ulcers are the underlying cause in the
majority of cases, your veterinarian may start your pet on ulcer
therapy while diagnostic tests are being performed. Medications
used in the treatment of stomach ulcers usually consist of a

combination of an antacid to decreased acid production by the
stomach and sucralfate which coats and covers ulcerated areas.
Karen Michele Tefft (Raleigh, North Carolina)

CLIENT INFORMATION
Hematochezia

WHAT IS HEMATOCHEZIA?
Hematochezia is the medical term to describe bowel movements
with frank blood. The blood may be mixed with the stool giving it an
overall red or maroon color. Alternatively, there may be bright red
blood streaking on the surface of otherwise normal colored feces.
Hematochezia is not a disease in itself, but rather a symptom of an
underlying condition that can range in severity from serious to minor
and self-resolving.

WHAT CAUSES HEMATOCHEZIA?
Hematochezia is most commonly caused by a source of bleeding in
the lower portion of the digestive system, such as from the colon,
rectum or anus. Less commonly it can be caused by blood from the
upper portion of the digestive system. If a dog or a cat receives food
or treats containing red food coloring, their stool may turn red in
color, but this is not true hematochezia. Occasionally bleeding from a
bite wound to the hindquarters or bloody discharge from an infected
anal sac may initially be thought to be hematochezia until the patient
is more closely examined. Some of the more common causes of
hematochezia include:
• Colitis
• Parasitic infections
• Acute hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome (AHDS)
• Steroid or anti-inflammatory medications
• Fractured pelvis
• Liver disease
• Pancreatitis
• Cancer

WHAT SYMPTOMS CAN BE SEEN WITH
HEMATOCHEZIA?
Many pets remain alert and active despite having hematochezia and
display no other symptoms. However, dependent upon the
underlying cause of the hematochezia, other symptoms that your pet
may have include:
• Straining to defecate
• Increased frequency of defecation
• Crying or whimpering during defecation
• Scooting
• Mucous-covered stools
• Vomiting
• Loss of appetite

WHAT TESTS ARE NEEDED?
Your veterinarian will ask you many questions detailing your pet’s
overall health, diet, previous vaccinations, current medications and
supplements, and travel history. They will also ask you about the
onset of hematochezia, how long it has been present, any other
symptoms you have noted, and any possible inciting incidents. Next,
your veterinarian will perform a complete physical examination,
including a rectal examination.
In a dog or a cat with sudden onset of frank blood streaking on the
surface of otherwise normal colored feces and no other symptoms or
abnormalities found on physical examination, your veterinarian may
only recommend a fecal exam to start. The fecal exam will evaluate
for a variety of parasites and other organisms that can cause
hematochezia. For dogs or cats with severe hematochezia (i.e., feces
that looks like “raspberry jam”), other symptoms such as vomiting or
that have had long-standing hematochezia additional tests will be
recommended.
Additional laboratory tests that your veterinarian will recommend
include a complete blood count (CBC), biochemistry profile, and a
urinalysis. The CBC will evaluate whether the red blood cells count
has become increased, which can commonly be seen with AHDS. The
CBC also evaluates the white blood cell count, which may be affected

by some infections. The biochemistry profile will screen for diseases
such as kidney or liver disease, which can contribute to
hematochezia. The urinalysis will also help evaluate for kidney
disease and will look for blood in the urine, which can be seen in
patients with problems with blood clotting.
Radiographs (“x-rays”) and potentially ultrasound are also useful
tests to try to non-invasively look inside your pet to determine the
cause of the hematochezia. Radiographs of the abdomen will look for
foreign objects that may have been swallowed, masses, and
abnormalities in the size or shape of organs. An ultrasound of the
abdomen is complimentary to radiographs. It can further evaluate
for foreign objects that might not be visible on radiographs, masses
and abnormal internal architecture of the organs.
The above-described tests may be sufficient to diagnose the
underlying cause of your pet’s hematochezia. However, there still
may be additional tests needed to pinpoint the exact underlying
cause or to help guide treatment. Some of these tests include
colonoscopy or specialized bloodwork. With colonoscopy, a flexible
tube with a camera is passed into your pet’s colon while they are
under anesthesia. During colonoscopy, masses or foreign objects can
be directly visualized and biopsied. The endoscope may even be able
to remove the foreign object if one is present. The specialized
bloodwork may vary based upon what your veterinarian suspects.

WHAT TREATMENT IS NEEDED?
Specific treatment for dogs and cats with hematochezia will vary
dependent upon the underlying cause. However, in a dog or a cat
with sudden onset of frank blood streaking on the surface of
otherwise normal colored feces and no other symptoms or
abnormalities found on physical examination, your veterinarian may
recommend symptomatic treatment to start. This treatment may
consist of a broad-spectrum dewormer, a probiotic, and a bland diet
containing soluble fiber.
Karen Michele Tefft (Raleigh, North Carolina)

Tenesmus, Dyschezia, and
Fecal Incontinence
Emily N. Gould

INTRODUCTION
Constipation refers to the reduced frequency or absence of
defecation due to retention of hard, dry feces in the colon. Total fecal
volume is also often decreased. Obstipation occurs when the ability
to defecate is impossible without medical intervention, and typically
results from prolonged constipation (ch. 263). It is a common
misconception that constipation and obstipation are synonymous,
but not all constipated animals become obstipated. Tenesmus is
repeated, nonproductive straining by which the animal attempts to
defecate or urinate (Video 51.1

). As it relates to distal intestinal

disorders, tenesmus is often accompanied by signs of large intestinal
(LI) disease (e.g., hematochezia, mucus, increased frequency of
defecation with reduced fecal volume). Tenesmus and constipation
are frequently confused and used interchangeably by owners.
Dyschezia means painful defecation, and commonly results from an
anorectal rather than solely colonic abnormality. Tenesmus and
dyschezia often occur together. Fecal incontinence is the failure to
retain feces in the colon and/or rectum, resulting in unconscious
“leakage” of fecal material. Both neurogenic and non-neurogenic
causes of fecal incontinence exist, and differentiating between the
two is important for developing a diagnostic plan.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES
Constipation: Causes of constipation can be divided into
functional versus mechanical etiologies. Within these categories,
differentials include nutritional, metabolic, neurologic, and
endocrine disorders; trauma to the pelvis, colon, or rectum; and
primary inflammatory or neoplastic disorders of the colon or
anorectum. Diets low in insoluble fiber will decrease colonic
motility,1 as will hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia,
prolonged states of dehydration, and pica (e.g., consumption of
bones, hair, wool, cat litter, or plant material). It is common for
animals with diseases causing polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD) (e.g.,
chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, hyperthyroidism; ch. 53)
to develop constipation. Pica often occurs secondary to a behavioral

disorder or chronic enteropathy (CE). Pets with congenital sacral
spinal cord (i.e., breed related in Manx cats and certain
brachycephalic dogs) and rectoanal (i.e., atresia ani) abnormalities
are predisposed to constipation. Trauma to the lumbar and sacral
spinal segments or pelvic canal commonly results in constipation
with tenesmus. Severe prostatomegaly might cause extraluminal
obstruction. Dysautonomia is a rare condition more often seen in
cats, but has also been documented in dogs (ch. 254).2 Hypothyroid
dogs and cats (especially kittens with the congenital form) can
become constipated due to the effect of thyroid hormone on normal
gut motility (chs. 285 and 286).3 Obesity (ch. 150),4 along with
prolonged inactivity, also slows colonic transit time. Cases for which
a primary etiology is not found are considered idiopathic. Feline
idiopathic megacolon (Figure 51.1) initially manifests as recurrent
constipation with eventual progression to obstipation.5
Tenesmus and dyschezia: Tenesmus and dyschezia also
develop from either mechanical or functional disorders of the colon
and/or anorectum. The presence of dyschezia without tenesmus
often localizes disease to the anorectum without colonic
involvement, as tenesmus is typically present with colonic disorders.
Lower urinary tract (LUT) disease should be ruled out prior to a
workup for colorectal disease. Mechanical intraluminal (e.g.,
neoplasia, foreign body [FB], strictures) and extraluminal (e.g.,
compressive abdominal mass or organomegaly, pelvic fractures,
pseudocoprostasis) obstructions should be eliminated prior to
pursuing functional problems. Many animals with concurrent
chronic, intermittent LI diarrhea have an underlying CE or parasitic
infection (i.e., Trichuris, Ancylostoma spp.). Fiber-responsive large
bowel diarrhea (FRLBD) and food-responsive enteropathies (FREs)
are more likely to affect the LI in both cats6 and dogs.7,8 Acute-onset
clinical signs often arise from dietary indiscretion or “stress colitis”
(dogs only). Cats with Tritrichomonas foetus (T. foetus) are usually
presented for tenesmus, dyschezia, and foul-smelling, LI diarrhea
(ch. 196). While pythiosis (ch. 263), histoplasmosis (ch. 209), and
protothecosis (ch. 263) often also affect the small bowel, all can
cause marked colonic disease.9-11 Puppies and kittens that develop
tenesmus shortly after birth should be inspected for atresia ani, to

which Poodles and Boston Terriers are predisposed.12 While any
breed of dog can develop perianal fistulas, German Shepherd Dogs
(GSDs) are overrepresented (ch. 264). Any cause of anal sacculitis
can result in tenesmus and dyschezia, as do perianal hernias.
Chronic tenesmus might also result in perineal herniation.
Fecal incontinence: Causes of fecal incontinence are divided
into neurogenic (e.g., upper motor neuron [UMN] sphincter
incompetence, intervertebral disc disease [IVDD] and diffuse lower
motor neuron [LMN] disease, discospondylitis, cauda equina
syndrome) and non-neurogenic (e.g., reservoir incontinence,
external sphincter incompetence from aging, behavioral disorders,
trauma, or neoplasia). Both focal (e.g., arachnoid cysts, IVDD,
masses) and diffuse systemic (e.g., inflammatory central nervous
system [CNS] disorders, dysautonomia) diseases cause UMN
sphincter incompetence. Degenerative myelopathy (DM, ch. 250)
should be a rule out for GSDs, and potentially Pembroke Welsh
Corgis,13 with concurrent pelvic limb paresis, ataxia, and reduced
motor function to the tail. Cats with sacrocaudal luxations (“tail-pull”
injuries) often have damage to multiple nerves innervating the anal
sphincter.14,15 Reservoir incontinence results in an inability to store
feces for normal periods of time. It is commonly associated with
either severe inflammation of the colon and/or rectum, or seen in
animals following subtotal colectomy. Aging reduces anal sphincter
integrity,16 and might be responsible for fecal incontinence in
geriatric pets. Rarely, intoxications (e.g., vincristine, macadamia
nuts) can cause transient peripheral neuropathies.

FIGURE 51.1 Impacted feces in the colon of a
constipated cat with idiopathic megacolon. Right
lateral radiograph pictured. Not every constipated
cat will develop megacolon (which is a radiographic

HISTORY
Questions of importance in the medical history (ch. 2) are
summarized in Box 51.1, and further expanded upon below. A
primary goal of the clinician must always be to elicit if LUT signs are
present, prior to developing a diagnostic plan.
Constipation: Owners of chronically constipated animals often
describe intermittent episodes of hematochezia or diarrhea, likely
secondary to retained feces causing mucosal irritation. Thus, it is
common for owners to mistake constipation with diarrhea, or vice
versa. Constipated cats are sometimes reported to sit in the litter box
for prolonged periods of time without attempting to defecate.

Concurrent LUT signs in males should increase suspicion of a
prostatic disorder. As PU/PD contributes to constipation due to
dehydration, pointed questions should help elicit if the owner is
performing certain duties with increased frequency (Box 51.1).
Tenesmus and dyschezia: LUT signs increase the likelihood
that lower urinary tract stones, a urinary tract infection (UTI),
neoplasia (bladder, urethral) or a prostatic disorder is present.
Determining the timing of tenesmus in relation to evacuation is
necessary, as tenesmus usually precedes defecation in animals with
obstructive diseases, whereas those with inflammatory disorders
often strain following defecation. A dietary history (ch. 145) and
known response(s) to previous diet trials are important, as is
documentation of administration of flavored monthly antiparasitics.
Dogs that have recently been boarded or kenneled might be
experiencing self-limiting “stress” colitis. Stools that are “ribbonlike” or “narrowed” in shape imply luminal narrowing of the colon or
rectum. Dogs with granulomatous colitis (GC) often exhibit profound
weight loss along with exclusively LI diarrhea, with Boxers and
French Bulldogs overrepresented (ch. 263).17,18 Young, purebred
cats for which T. foetus is a concern might be more likely to have
been obtained from a cattery or shelter situation and have affected
housemates. Clinical improvement but failure to completely clear
diarrhea following metronidazole administration is a classic history
for cats with T. foetus.

Fecal incontinence: An accurate history is paramount in
discerning animals with permanent lack of sphincter tone from those
with reversible causes of incontinence. Intermittent episodes of
incontinence and/or conscious awareness of defecation occur more
often with behavioral problems, colitis, or reservoir incontinence
rather than permanent sphincter damage. Any recent trauma or
colonic, pelvic, lumbosacral, or perineal surgery should be
documented.

PHYSICAL EXAM
Physical exam (PE; ch. 3) tasks that should always be performed
include notation of hydration status, abdominal palpation, and rectal
and neurologic examinations (ch. 241). The clinician should also
watch the animal urinate and, ideally, defecate. In particularly
painful or reactive pets, rectal exam should only be performed under
heavy sedation or general anesthesia. If a complete rectal is not
possible without first evacuating feces, enemas should be
administered.
Constipation: Careful attention should be paid to the
appearance of the anus and surrounding tissues for
pseudocoprostasis (obstruction due to matted hair stuff), masses,
and/or perianal fistulas. Digital rectal palpation might allow
detection of pelvic fractures, colonic and/or rectal strictures or
masses, perineal hernias, and potentially colonic FBs. In dogs,
prostatomegaly is often palpable if severe enough to cause
constipation. Animals with dysautonomia typically have concurrent
urinary retention and/or incontinence, regurgitation, nictitating
membrane prolapse, and bradycardia (ch. 254). The pets’ body
condition score (BCS, ch. 72; see inside covers of textbook), muscle
condition score (MCS; see inside covers of textbook), and any

dermatologic abnormalities (e.g., “rat tail,” poor haircoat) raising
suspicion for a chronic systemic disease or endocrinopathy should be
noted. Kittens with congenital hypothyroidism often have a
“juvenile” haircoat, macroglossia, and might be hypothermic on
PE3,19 (ch. 286).
Tenesmus and dyschezia: The urinary, reproductive, and
gastrointestinal (GI) tracts must be evaluated as completely as
possible. Visible reproductive structures (i.e., penis, vulva) should be
inspected for masses or discharge indicating a urogenital problem.
Inspection of the perineal region and anal sacs can identify hernias,
masses, fistulas, and abscesses. Young animals with atresia ani might
have perianal swelling or “ballooning” from fecal impaction.12 An
erythematous perianal region might indicate excessive licking, as is
commonly seen with FRE or anal sac disorders. Rectal exam
sometimes allows for detection of obstructive processes (e.g., masses,
polyps, colonic strictures), pelvic fractures, prostatomegaly, and
urethral thickening. Inflammatory disorders of the LI often result in
a scant amount, or absence of, feces on rectal palpation, with or
without mucus and hematochezia. Pets with severe inflammation of
the colon or rectum, masses, perineal hernias or strictures might
require general anesthesia for thorough abdominal palpation or
rectal exam. It is common for cats with T. foetus to develop rectal
prolapse, which might be apparent on PE (chs. 196, 263).
Protothecosis is rare, but should be considered in dogs with
concurrent systemic disease (e.g., weight loss, vomiting, lethargy),
especially those with ocular or CNS involvement (ch. 263).11
Fecal incontinence: A thorough neurologic exam, including
assessment of the anal reflex and strength of anal tone, is paramount
(ch. 241). Assessment of the anal reflex is accomplished by gently
“pinching” the perianal skin and watching for sphincter contraction.
Tone is best assessed via digital rectal, or gentle “probing” with a
thermometer, hemostat, or cotton-tipped applicator. Those with
reservoir incontinence should have normal tone and reflexes, but
might be uncomfortable during rectal palpation if significant
inflammation of the colon and/or rectum is present. Animals with
fractures (vertebral, pelvic) or discospondylitis will often exhibit
signs of pain during rectal or abdominal palpation, especially with
pressure applied to the dorsal vertebral column. Anal tone is

commonly reduced with external sphincter incompetence but normal
with UMN disorders. Many pets with neurogenic causes of
incontinence will also display one or more of the following
abnormalities: hind limb paresis, lumbosacral pain, diminished
reflexes, and/or bladder atony. Evidence of systemic weakness
should prompt diagnostic evaluation for diffuse neuromuscular
disease (ch. 252).

DIAGNOSTIC PLAN
For all clinical syndromes, a complete blood count (CBC), serum
biochemistry panel including electrolytes and calcium, and urinalysis
(UA) are all warranted. This provides baseline screening for systemic
disorders and guides decision making for advanced tier diagnostics
(Figure 51.2).
Constipation: Though often unrewarding, a minimum database
might raise suspicion for systemic disease or an underlying
endocrinopathy, as well as assessing for comorbidities. Abdominal
radiographs are especially useful for determining colon size (Figure
51.1), and for identifying the amount of feces and radiopaque foreign
material in the colon, prostatomegaly, abdominal lymphadenopathy,
fractures of the pelvis and/or vertebral canal, and sometimes intraor extraluminal masses. Contrast studies or fluoroscopy might be
required to assess for the presence of colonic or rectal strictures. If
no underlying cause is identified following plain film radiography,
abdominal ultrasound (AUS) and colonoscopy/proctoscopy would be
next steps for obtaining a definitive diagnosis.
Tenesmus and dyschezia: Routine fecal examination is
indicated to look for LI parasites (i.e., Trichuris, Ancylostoma; ch.
80). Abdominal radiographs and AUS are warranted to evaluate for
colonic FBs, masses, polyps, abdominal lymphadenopathy, abnormal
colonic wall layering, and assessment of the urogenital tract. Rectal
scrapings are sometimes diagnostic for infiltrative histoplasmosis,
pythiosis, or protothecosis. The gold standard diagnostic test for T.
foetus is fecal polymerase chain reaction (PCR).20 While not
typically viewed as a “diagnostic test,” a minimum of two exclusion
diet trials (altered fiber, novel or hydrolyzed protein) should be part
of the plan prior to colonoscopy (chs. 152, 165). Unlike

dermatologic food trials, most animals with FRLBD and FRE will
show clinical and clinicopathologic improvement within 2 weeks.7,21
Indoor/outdoor cats should be kept indoors for the duration of the
food trial. Colonoscopy is indicated if the pet fails two diet trials
and/or structural disease is suspected. This diagnostic allows for
visualization of the entire colon and rectum with a retroflex
maneuver (ch. 107). If predominantly anorectal disease is
suspected, colonoscopy is likely of limited utility, and proctoscopy
should be performed instead.
Fecal incontinence: Differentiating between neurogenic and
non-neurogenic causes is usually possible with acquisition of a
complete history and PE. Abdominal radiographs, computed
tomography and/or magnetic resonance imaging are often necessary
to diagnose lumbosacral lesions and diffuse, inflammatory CNS
diseases. Specialized diagnostics such as sphincter
electromyography22 and/or anorectal manometry23 can be used to
confirm sphincter incompetence, but they are rarely necessary. If
reservoir incontinence is suspected secondary to FRLBD or FRE, a
diet trial is indicated. Referral to a behaviorist might be necessary for
cases in which other differentials have been eliminated, or a
behavioral cause is felt more likely (ch. 11; Figure 51.2).

CHAPTER 52: Flatulence
Genevieve Mak

A C RO N YM
GI gastrointestinal
Flatulence is gas, or flatus, that is generated from the gastrointestinal
(GI) tract and expelled through the anus. Dogs and cats, regardless of
age or sex, normally pass flatus multiple times a day; an average
number of what is considered normal has not been determined.
From an observational standpoint, flatulence is noted more
obviously in dogs compared to cats. In most cases, pet owners are
not too concerned when their pets have flatulence as an isolated
entity, although the odor can be bothersome enough to prompt a
veterinary appointment.

PHYSIOLOGY AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
The source of gas in the GI tract typically occurs from aerophagia,
production by gut bacteria, diffusion of gas from blood vessels, or
chemical reactions between acid and bicarbonate. This gas is then
expelled via eructation, expelled as flatulence, consumed by bacteria,
or absorbed back into the blood. More than 99% of GI gas is
composed of these 5 odorless gases: carbon dioxide, hydrogen,
methane, nitrogen, and oxygen, in varying percentages.1 Nitrogen
and oxygen are derived from aerophagia or excessive panting. Less
than 1% of gases are sulfur based, and these are the gases that are
odiferous. Bacterial production of gas accounts for the majority of

flatulence, and approximately 75% of flatus is hydrogen, methane,
and carbon dioxide.2
Both the small and large intestines play a role in generating
flatulence through bacterial fermentation. The composition of the
bacteria—as well as the volume and frequency of flatus—is in turn
influenced by the type of diet consumed. Dietary fiber plays an
important role in patients with GI disorders (ch. 165). Fiber acts on
the GI tract through several mechanisms. One of these mechanisms
is increasing fecal mass with mechanical stimulation or irritation of
the colonic mucosa, which in turn results in increasing secretion and
peristalsis. Fermentation byproducts of dietary fiber—particularly
short-chain fatty acids—also have an impact on the intestinal
microbiota, immune system, and the neuroendocrine system of the
GI tract.3
Based on physical and chemical structures, dietary fiber can be
classified as soluble vs. insoluble, fermentable vs. non-fermentable,
or as short-chain vs. long-chain carbohydrates. Soluble fiber can also
be subdivided into viscous vs. non-viscous. These distinctions are
important, as the composition of fiber can influence the volume and
frequency of gas evacuation. Foods containing the following
fermentable carbohydrates are poorly absorbed in the small
intestine: oligosaccharides, galactooligosaccharides, disaccharides,
monosaccharides, and polyols. These highly fermentable, shortchain, and soluble fibers lead to an increase in intestinal osmolality
and result in higher gas production, while also increasing the volume
of fluid that is delivered to the colon. In contrast, long-chain,
intermediate viscous, soluble, and moderately fermentable dietary
fiber results in low gas production.3 This leads to the absence of
clinical signs related to excessive gas production. The colon harbors a
large amount of bacteria that may ferment these products, thereby
releasing hydrogen and carbon dioxide into the GI tract. However,
other groups of colonic bacteria—particularly sulfate-reducing
bacteria, acetogenic bacteria, and methanogenic archaea—consume a
large proportion of the gases produced by fermentation.4

SIGNALMENT

While excessive flatulence can be observed in any breed of dog,
brachycephalic breeds have been identified as having a higher
frequency of flatus and also having feces with a stronger odor.5 The
anatomy of brachycephalic breeds predisposes them to aerophagia,
which in turn results in increased gas production. This gas
production is associated with a higher presence of non-assimilated
substrates, resulting in flatulence and odorous feces.6

HISTORY AND PHYSICAL
EXAMINATION
A complete dietary history of the patient should be obtained,
including types and composition of food, treats, and table scraps
given (ch. 145). Medications and supplements being administered
should also be noted. The owner should be questioned about
duration and frequency of clinical signs, along with any association
with the diet or recent changes to the diet. Excessive flatulence is a
clinical sign that is reported most frequently in conjunction with
borborygmi, perceived bloating or abdominal distension, weight loss,
vomiting, diarrhea, and/or constipation. Aside from these clinical
findings and history, the physical examination of a dog or cat with
excessive flatulence may be relatively normal. Regardless, a thorough
examination, including abdominal palpation and rectal examination,
should still be performed (ch. 3).

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
Since flatulence is most often reported in conjunction with other GI
clinical signs, initial diagnostic testing should include a minimum
database of a complete blood count, serum biochemistry panel,
urinalysis, and fecal parasite screening (ch. 80). Thoracic and
abdominal radiographs, abdominal ultrasound, and/or additional
blood work to measure serum cobalamin, folate, trypsin-like
immunoreactivity (TLI), and pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity
(PLI) levels may also be warranted based on initial physical
examination findings and diagnostic test results. While

gastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy are rarely indicated in dogs
and cats presenting solely for flatulence, they may be recommended
as part of the diagnostic work up if there is concurrent weight loss,
vomiting, or diarrhea.

MANAGEMENT
There are several different treatment options suggested in the
management of flatulence (Figure 52.1). However, there is no
general consensus as to which treatment is most effective for the
individual. In patients with excessive flatulence, a diet change is a
reasonable first step (ch. 152). Diets and treats with ingredients that
contain fermentable oligo-, di-, mono-saccharides, and polyols (so
called FODMAPs) should be avoided. Wheat, rye, leeks, and zucchini
are examples of foods that contain oligosaccharides. Dairy products
that contain lactose are composed of disaccharides. Fruits such as
apples, pears, peaches, mangoes, and apricots are rich in
monosaccharides and polyols. Galactooligosaccharides, which are
found in lentils, other legumes, cabbage, brussels sprouts, and green
beans, can also result in excess GI gas production. There are many
different prescription and homemade diets available that are
marketed for patients with GI disease. Trial and error with these
different diets—fed exclusively for a minimum of 6 to 8 weeks per
diet—can be attempted to see which one works best for the
individual.

FIGURE 52.1 Algorithm for management of
flatulence. Modified from Guilford WG. Flatulence
and borborygmus. In Ettinger SJ, Feldman EC, eds.
Textbook of Veterinary Internal Medicine. 4th ed.
WB Saunders; 1995:132 and Mak G. Flatulence. In:

Veterinary Internal Medicine. 8th ed. Elsevier;
2017:177, Figure 51.1 .
Probiotics are live beneficial bacteria that, when given in adequate
amounts, may exert positive health benefits. Currently there are
several strains and combination of strains of bacteria in probiotics
composed mainly of Bifidobacterium species, Lactobacillus species,
Enterococcus faecium, and Streptococcus thermophiles. There are
numerous studies on various probiotics with conflicting results as to
whether or not probiotics improve flatulence, bloating, stool
consistency, and overall quality of life. Some studies showed no clear
evidence for benefit of probiotics,6 while others demonstrated

significant short- and long-term reduction in flatulence and
bloating.7
Prebiotics are substrates that are selectively utilized by host
microorganisms to confer a health benefit. Prebiotics are already
present in pet foods, and the most common ones include
galactooligosaccharides, mannan-oligosaccharides,
fructooligosaccharides, and beta glucans. The main function of
prebiotics is the modulation of native host microbiota by stimulating
beneficial bacterial growth and/or activating their metabolism in the
intestinal tract.8 While there may be concern that prebiotics can
result in excessive flatulence based on their composition, studies
have shown that the addition of prebiotics had no effect on total stool
production, fecal pH, fecal quality, or nutrient digestibility. Instead,
prebiotics have resulted in beneficial shifts in fecal metabolites that
may support gut health and improve the immunity of healthy dogs.9
In humans with bloating, abdominal pain, or flatulence who received
a prebiotic galactooligosaccharide mixture containing bifidobacteria,
improvement in their clinical signs were reported after 2 weeks.10
Yucca schidigera is a flowering plant with an extract that is used in
the livestock industry to bind ammonia and decrease odors from pig
and poultry wastes.11 This extract is present in some pet foods,
treats, and supplements for dogs and cats and is marketed for
reducing fecal odor. In one study, when Yucca schidigera extract was
fed to dogs and cats, fecal odor was improved.12 Saponins—the active
ingredient present in Yucca schidigera extract—are believed to
reduce fecal odor by blocking urease inhibition, binding ammonia,
modifying the colonic microflora, and increasing intestinal
metabolism or absorption by altering intestinal permeability.11
However, total gas production and number and frequency of
flatulent episodes in dogs fed this extract are unchanged.
Activated charcoal is effective in binding sulfur gases to reduce
odor, but it does not decrease the amount of gas production. In
humans, charcoal seat cushions or underwear are used to absorb
bothersome odors. These devices are obviously not practical or
beneficial for dogs and cats. Charcoal-based treats are available on

the market for dogs, but their efficacy for reducing flatulence is not
documented.
Simethicone is an anti-foaming agent that decreases the surface
tension of gas bubbles, causing them to merge into larger bubbles in
the GI tract for easier expulsion. This theoretically reduces bloating
and flatulence. No studies are available for its efficacy in dogs and
cats. However, simethicone is available over the counter in various
products. The dosage of simethicone is 20-200 mg per dog PO given
up to every 6 hours.
Antibiotic use for flatulence has been studied in people, specifically
with rifaximin and metronidazole. While studies in humans showed
improvement of flatulence with the use of antibiotics,13 it is
important to note that the subjects were also suffering from
inflammatory bowel disease and small intestinal bacterial
overgrowth, conditions that predisposed them to having flatus.
Antibiotic use for dogs and cats with excessive flatulence as the sole
complaint is therefore not recommended, as non-discriminant use
contributes to antibiotic resistance (ch. 7).

DEFINITIONS
Polyuria (PU) and polydipsia (PD) are common presenting concerns
in small animal practice. PD is generally defined as water intake

>90-100 mL/kg/day in dogs and >50 mL/kg/day in cats. PU is
defined in both species as urine output greater than 50 mL/kg/day.

ENVIRONMENTAL AND DIETARY
INFLUENCES ON WATER INTAKE
In health, water intake is increased with high environmental
temperature, exercise and feeding. Both dogs and cats fed dry food
have greater water intake than those fed canned food, but the
increase is less marked in cats.1 Diets with greater digestibility and
those higher in protein or salt increase water intake. The type of
water source (still or flowing) can influence intake in some cats.2

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
OVERVIEW
PU results from excessive intake of water (primary polydipsia) or
decreased urinary concentrating ability (primary polyuria) (Box
53.1). PU/PD are consistent features of some diseases (e.g., diabetes
mellitus [chs. 291, 292], chronic kidney disease [CKD; ch. 301],
hyperthyroidism [chs. 287, 288]) while the association is more
tenuous in those based on small case series or extrapolated from
human medicine or experimental models.

PRIMARY POLYDIPSIA (PP)
“PP” represents a group of disorders in which increased thirst is the
driving (primary) mechanism for PU (PD causes PU). The secondary
PU is an essential physiological response to avoid volume overload
and osmotic consequences. Because some people diagnosed with PP
have psychiatric conditions, the term “psychogenic polydipsia” is
sometimes used in veterinary medicine.3 In dogs and cats,
behavioral disorders or those suspected of having altered function of
the hypothalamic thirst center due to primary disease or secondary
to osmoregulatory or neural abnormalities may be suspected but

difficult to confirm. It has been proposed that PP contributes to the
PU in hyperthyroidism and hepatic failure. An association between
PP and gastrointestinal disease has been reported in dogs.4

PRIMARY POLYURIA
Overview
Arginine vasopressin (AVP; antidiuretic hormone [ADH]) is the
main hormone responsible for water homeostasis, acting within
renal collecting ducts to increase cell permeability to water. AVP
stimulates osmotic reabsorption of water from the hypotonic tubular
lumen into the hypertonic medullary interstitium, from which it is
returned to the circulation. Disrupting any of these steps can lead to
PU and secondary PD (PU causes PD). Secondary PD is an essential
physiological response to avoid volume depletion and osmotic
consequences.

Diabetes Insipidus (DI): Central and Nephrogenic
Central DI (CDI; ch. 282) is a condition resulting from complete or
partial deficiencies in AVP and can be due to neoplasia,
inflammation, trauma, or developmental defects.5,6 Some cases are
idiopathic. Absolute AVP deficiencies are more commonly
diagnosed, perhaps because the PU/PD is profound. Nephrogenic DI
(NDI) is defined as a complete or partial inability of the kidneys to
respond to AVP. Primary NDI is a rare hereditary disorder that
results in severe PU/PD at an early age.7 Secondary NDI, the most
common cause of PU/PD in small animals, is caused by several
diseases and can be the result of drugs that cause hyposthenuria,
isosthenuria or minimally concentrated urine specific gravity (USG).

Disruption of the Osmotic Gradient

The abnormal presence of osmotically active agents in the renal
tubular lumen can disrupt the osmotic gradient and impair water
reabsorption. This is the mechanism responsible for PU in diabetes
mellitus, CKD, renal tubular disorders (such as primary renal
glycosuria and Fanconi syndrome), post-obstructive diuresis, the
syndrome of inappropriate diuresis (SIAD), and diuretics such as
mannitol. Since the solute in the glomerular filtrate drives loss of
water, hyposthenuria should not be observed in these conditions.
The osmotic gradient required for reabsorption of water could be
disrupted by reduced renal medullary tonicity, a condition called
“medullary washout” that may be seen in pets with prolonged
PU/PD, after prolonged IV fluid therapy, or chronic use of diuretics.
Low renal interstitial tonicity may also occur in dogs fed severely
protein- or salt-restricted diets, or in diseases associated with
decreases in sodium or blood urea nitrogen (BUN).

Other Mechanisms
Increased intravascular volume and/or pressure may contribute to
PU observed in some dogs with SIAD or pheochromocytoma.8
Although the mechanism is not understood, PU has been described
in a few dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma and gastrointestinal
leiomyosarcoma.9,10

Multiple Mechanisms
Classifying the causes of PU/PD into discrete categories can be
misleading because many affected pets have multiple issues. For
example, pets with CKD have reduced numbers of functional
nephrons capable of responding to AVP, decreased renal medullary
tonicity, and increased distal tubular osmolality. Despite the
limitations, a discrete classification system is useful during
diagnostic investigation (Box 53.1).

POLYURIA AND POLYDIPSIA IN CATS
Several of the diseases listed in Box 53.1 have not been reported to
cause PU/PD in cats. PU/PD is not often reported by cat owners

despite consistently low USGs. Cats may be resistant to PU because
of their greater urine concentrating ability and tolerance to
dehydration. Water consumption and urine output are often difficult
to quantify due to outdoor access and/or use of multiple water
sources. Furthermore, outdoor access and the use of litter trays make
all but extreme PU less obvious to cat owners. PU/PD is common in
cats with CKD, diabetes mellitus, hyperthyroidism and CDI.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH
In many dogs and cats, identifying the cause of PU/PD is
straightforward since they have other clinical or routine
clinicopathologic features. By contrast, the diagnosis can be
challenging in some and others may have more than one
contributing condition. In these pets, a logical and sequential
approach can be beneficial for achieving a diagnosis (Figure 53.1).

FIGURE 53.1 Diagnostic algorithm for the
investigation of polyuria and polydipsia. SG, Specific
gravity.

STEP 1: ENSURE POLYURIA AND
POLYDIPSIA ARE PRESENT
Before embarking on diagnostic testing, it is critically important to
ensure the presence of PU/PD. A thorough history should aid in

distinguishing PU from a behavioral issue, incontinence, or
pollakiuria. PD without PU may be seen in pets with non-urinary
water loss (e.g., diarrhea or excessive panting). PD is usually
confirmed by having owners measure water intake at home. Known
quantities of water are provided over a 24-hour period and intake
calculated by subtracting residual volumes. Access to water from
non-measurable sources must be restricted with no other changes to
the environment, especially the usual water sources (still or flowing)
for cats.2 Calculation of water intake can be difficult in pets from
multi-pet households or when outdoor access is unavoidable.
Measurement during hospitalization is not reliable because drinking
patterns may be altered outside of the home.
It is not usually practical or necessary to quantify urine volume
since presence of consistently dilute urine suggests PU. Urine
volume can be estimated by weighing cat litter in single-cat
households. Osmolality is the “gold standard” measure of urine
concentration but is not widely available or needed. Measuring USG
by refractometer is common and there is usually good agreement
between the 2 methods. Results may vary between individual
refractometers.11,12 The abnormal presence of osmotically active
particles also increases USG; for example, USG increases about
0.004 for each g/dL of glucose. The magnitude of effect has been
shown to be more variable in clinical samples, with as much as 0.008
increase in dilute urine after 2.4 g/dL (133 mmol/L) of glucose was
added.13
The USG in health can vary markedly, ranging from 1.006 to 1.050
in dogs and 1.005 to 1.090 in cats.14,15 In general, USG is lower in
healthy dogs than healthy cats (1.033 versus 1.050, respectively). In
dogs but not cats, the USG of morning samples is typically higher
than evening samples. It is recommended that owners collect
multiple urine samples at home over several days to determine the
range in values. Results consistently >1.030 in dogs and >1.035 in
cats is strong evidence against PU unless there is glycosuria or the
PU is intermittent. Randomly obtained low USG values can be
normal.

STEP 2: SIGNALMENT, HISTORY,
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (PE)
Although unlikely to lead to a definitive diagnosis, age, breed, sex
and neuter status may be useful in refining the differential diagnosis
list for PU/PD. For example, females may have pyometra,
hyperthyroidism is more common in older cats, and primary NDI
can be excluded unless the animal is very young. Since
glucocorticoids, diuretics and phenobarbital commonly cause
PU/PD, recently administered medications should be reviewed.
When possible, drugs should be discontinued, or doses reduced
before investing in diagnostic tests. A complete PE is essential.
Animals with diseases such as hyperadrenocorticism,
hyperthyroidism, pyometra and liver disease often have additional
findings that allow rapid diagnosis or refinement of the differential
list.

STEP 3: CBC, SERUM BIOCHEMISTRY
AND URINALYSIS
Routine complete blood count (CBC) and biochemistry with
electrolytes may allow exclusion of erythrocytosis, hypokalemia,
hypoadrenocorticism, diabetes mellitus and SIAD. Most dogs and
cats with hyperadrenocorticism, hyperthyroidism, hypercalcemia,
hyperaldosteronism, liver disease, CKD or pyelonephritis provide
clues to their underlying condition on PE, CBC, or serum
biochemistry profile. As many as one third of dogs with increased
ionized calcium concentrations have total calcium concentrations
within reference interval.16,17
Although inconsistently identified, PP can decrease plasma
osmolality, a dilutional effect caused by PD. Osmolality is ideally
determined from measures of freezing-point or vapor-pressure
depression, but this is rarely available in clinical practice. As an
alternative, serum osmolality can be estimated. Use of serum
osmolality is based on the concept that pets with underlying PD
dilute their plasma while those with underlying PU concentrate their
plasma. The following formula (using conventional units; for SI

units, remove the denominators from glucose and BUN) has been
reliable in both cats and dogs, even when hyperglycemia and/or
azotemia are present:18-20

UA should be repeated at the time of blood testing even if
previously performed, to confirm the presence of PU. USG can aid
differentiating renal from pre-renal azotemia. Isosthenuria or
minimally concentrated urine is characteristic of renal azotemia
(e.g., CKD) and concentrated urine is a feature of pre-renal azotemia
(e.g., dehydration). Dogs and cats with an underlying condition
causing PU may not be able to concentrate urine despite severe
hypovolemia or dehydration. Pre-renal azotemia with low USG is
common in dogs with hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296).21,22
Disorders such as hypercalcemia, hyperthyroidism and
hyperaldosteronism may contribute to development or progression
of CKD (ch. 301). In dogs, marked hyposthenuria (USG <1.006) is
most commonly due to hyperadrenocorticism, CDI, hypercalcemia,
hypoadrenocorticism, liver disease or PP. The presence of
hyposthenuria allows exclusion of CKD and other osmotic causes of
PU. Identification of glycosuria confirms diabetes mellitus or renal
tubular disease, provided stress hyperglycemia is not present (cats).

STEP 4: ADDITIONAL TESTING
Urine Culture
Urine culture, in dogs and cats with PU/PD, is frequently
recommended because pyelonephritis may be a causative or
complicating factor. Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are common in
dogs with diabetes mellitus and hyperadrenocorticism. UTIs are not
common in cats with hyperthyroidism.23-25 Routine urine bacterial
culture in “all animals with PU” has been questioned.26,27 The

International Society for Companion Animal Infectious Diseases
(ISCAID) guidelines recommend against urine culture in the absence
of lower urinary tract signs since treatment of asymptomatic
bacteriuria is not advocated.28 By contrast, urine culture is advised
when pyelonephritis is suspected (ch. 304).28 Pyelonephritis can be
difficult to exclude because affected animals may have non-specific
clinical signs and unremarkable routine clinicopathologic and
diagnostic imaging results.29 Thus, urine culture may be indicated to
exclude this differential. When performed, samples should be
collected by cystocentesis and results interpreted carefully prior to
therapy (chs. 70 and 98).30,31

Other Tests
If a definitive diagnosis has not been achieved, the selection of
additional tests is largely dependent upon clinical suspicion.
Abdominal ultrasonography is often performed because changes may
be observed with adrenal, liver and kidney diseases, and it is
sensitive for identifying pyometra and masses such as splenic
hemangiosarcoma and intestinal leiomyosarcoma. Specific testing
for liver function (ch. 266), hyperadrenocorticism (ch. 293),
hyperthyroidism (ch. 287), or acromegaly (chs. 280, 281) may be
indicated (Figure 53.1).32,33 Pyelocentesis can be performed if
pyelonephritis is suspected on abdominal imaging or results of UA
(ch. 304). However, in most cases a presumptive diagnosis is made
based upon abdominal imaging and cystocentesis culture results.
Exclusion of early kidney disease can be challenging because loss of
renal concentrating ability may precede azotemia. Urine
concentrating ability starts to decline after losing about two thirds of
functional nephrons while creatinine concentrations do not increase
until approximately 75% are lost. In such cases, measurement of
glomerular filtration rate or serum symmetric dimethyl arginine
(SDMA) concentrations may confirm renal dysfunction (chs. 62 and
299).34,35 Leptospirosis (ch. 192) has been described as a potential
cause of PU/PD without hepatic or renal injury, based largely upon
resistance of renal tubular cells to AVP in experimental models.36,37
This is likely rare because development of PU prior to the

characteristic clinical and clinicopathologic features of leptospirosis
has only been described in a single dog.38 Advanced imaging such as
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is indicated if brain disease is
suspected (ch. 112). In dogs with no identifiable cause of PU/PD,
changing the diet is easy and possibly beneficial.

STEP 5: MODIFIED WATER
DEPRIVATION TEST OR
DESMOPRESSIN TRIAL
The modified water deprivation test is designed to distinguish
between PP, CDI and primary NDI. It is essential to ensure that all
other differential diagnoses have been excluded prior to commencing
this test or a desmopressin trial. The modified water deprivation test
is time-consuming, labor-intensive and associated with a risk of
severe hypertonic dehydration, which can be fatal. In cats, primary
NDI has not been reported. One cat in the literature may have had
PP.39 For these reasons, some authors propose trial therapy with
desmopressin as an alternative to the water deprivation test (ch.
282).

CHAPTER 54: Pollakiuria,
Stranguria, and Urinary
Incontinence
Mary Anna Labato

A C RO N YM
FIC feline idiopathic cystitis

Disorders of urination are quite common and inappropriate
urinations are a leading cause of a pet being presented for medical
evaluation or worse, resulting in relinquishment of ownership or
euthanasia (ch. 11). Differentiations must be made between polyuria
(an increased urine volume) and pollakiuria, stranguria, and urinary
incontinence. The differential diagnoses for these latter three
conditions are often diseases of the lower urinary or genital tract.

DEFINITIONS
Urinary incontinence is defined as an involuntary escape of urine
during the storage phase of the urinary cycle. This can appear
clinically in a variety of ways; the most common presentation is
intermittent or continuous dribbling of urine combined with
episodes of normal voiding. Causes of urinary incontinence include
urethral sphincter mechanism incompetence (ch. 310), an anatomic

abnormality in the termination of the ureter(s) (ch. 313), inability of
the bladder to expand in capacity (ch. 310), spasms of the bladder
(ch. 310), and nerve damage (ch. 310).1-4
Detrusor hyperspasticity or instability is defined as spontaneous
and uninhibited detrusor muscle contractions (i.e., an overactive
bladder). It is characterized by involuntary bladder contractions
resulting in the frequent voiding of small volumes of urine. This
results in urinary incontinence, although more commonly clinical
signs resemble pollakiuria. Most often, animals with detrusor
hyperspasticity have an underlying cystitis. This must be
differentiated from isolated cases of bacterial infection (ch. 307),
inflammation, cystic calculi (canine [ch. 308], feline [ch. 309]),
polypoid cystitis, neoplasia (ch. 330;

Video 54.1), or drugs.

Cases in which no underlying cause is determined are referred to as
having idiopathic detrusor instability.4,5 The syndrome is commonly
seen in cats with cystitis or feline idiopathic cystitis (FIC; Pandora
syndrome) (ch. 311).
Pollakiuria is defined as abnormally frequent passage of small
amounts of urine.6 Common causes are urinary tract infection (ch.
307), inflammatory diseases of the bladder or urethra (ch. 312),
polypoid cystitis, cystic calculi (canine [ch. 308], feline [ch. 309]),
neoplasia (ch. 330), or drugs.
Stranguria is defined as a slow and painful discharge of urine
produced by spasmodic muscular contraction of the urethra and
bladder.6 This may be described as difficulty urinating, where the
owner describes that urine is being passed only drop by drop with
signs of pain and even tenesmus. The common causes are similar to
those of pollakiuria and include urinary tract infection (ch. 307),
inflammatory diseases of the bladder or urethra (Video 54.2),
urethral stricture (ch. 312;

Video 54.3), polypoid cystitis, cystic

calculi (canine [ch. 308], feline [ch. 309]), and neoplasia (ch.
330).
Dysuria is defined as difficult or painful urinations and is often
used as a “catch-all” term to describe stranguria or pollakiuria (ch.
310). It is important when obtaining a thorough history and direct

observation of the animal urinating to distinguish between these
conditions.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Bladder function is primarily under the influence of smooth muscle.
The body of the bladder contains smooth muscle (the detrusor
muscle). The outlet conduit is composed of the trigone and proximal
urethra. The smooth muscle fibers of the detrusor continue into the
proximal urethra, forming a functional internal urethral sphincter.
The distal urethra is composed of striated muscle and it functions as
an external sphincter.
During the storage phase of micturition, the bladder functions as a
low-resistance, high-capacity vessel. The urethra functions as a highresistance barrier. The reverse is true during the voiding phase: the
bladder acts as a muscular pump and the urethra as a low-resistance
vessel.
In male dogs, prostatic disease can involve the urethra and
bladder, producing dysuria (ch. 314).7

NERVOUS CONTROL
Nervous control of the bladder and urethra is a combination of
autonomic and somatic interactions (ch. 310).
Parasympathetic innervation is supplied to the detrusor by the
pelvic nerve, which arises from sacral spinal cord segments S1-S3
(ch. 241). Stimulation of the pelvic nerve results in detrusor
contraction.
Sympathetic innervation is supplied via the hypogastric nerve,
which is composed of preganglionic fibers exiting the lumbar spinal
cord at L1-L4 (dogs) and L2-L5 (cats) and synapses in the caudal
mesenteric ganglion. Sympathetic innervation is supplied to both the
detrusor and urethral smooth muscles and high sympathetic tone
characterizes the storage phase of micturition. Alpha-adrenergic
fibers synapse in smooth muscle in both the trigone and urethra.
Stimulation results in contraction of these muscles and forms a
functional internal urethral sphincter. There are also alpha-

adrenergic fibers that have a modulating effect on the external
urethral sphincter. Beta-adrenergic fibers synapse in the detrusor
muscle; stimulation results in relaxation.
Somatic innervation is supplied via the pudendal nerve, which
arises from sacral spinal cord segments S1-S3, providing stimulation
to the striated urethral musculature.
For voluntary control of micturition to occur, there must be
integration between the cerebral cortex, pons, and the spinoreticular
tract (ch. 241).8,9 A second pathway from the cerebral cortex to the
sacral nuclei coordinates voluntary sphincter control. Additionally,
cerebellar neurons inhibit nervous transmission to the reticulospinal
pathways in the pons.

Sensory receptors are located in the bladder mucosa and are
numerous at the ureterovesicular junction and in the trigone.
Inflammation of the mucosa or bladder contraction may cause pain,
an urgency to urinate even with a small bladder volume, detrusor
spasm, or a “burning” sensation. Sensory receptors in the urethra
respond to flow, urethral sensation and traction on the trigone.
Inflammation or irritation of the urethra causes pain, burning
sensation and spasms of the urethral sphincter.

CAUSES OF CLINICAL SIGNS
Diseases of the lower urinary tract (urethra and bladder) or lower
genital tract (prostate or vagina) may result in mucosal irritation or
inflammation and result in frequent or painful urinations. Many of
the causes of pollakiuria (Box 54.1) and stranguria (Box 54.2) are
associated with pyuria, hematuria or both (ch. 55). The main
differential diagnosis for urge incontinence (Box 54.3) is cystitis in
dogs and FIC/Pandora syndrome in cats (ch. 311). Once other
causes are ruled out, a diagnosis of detrusor hyperspasticity may be
established. This is confirmed by a urethral pressure profile that
demonstrates uninhibited detrusor contractions, or response to
treatment with an antispasmodic if a urodynamic study is
unavailable.

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP (Figure 54.1)
A complete history (ch. 2) is essential for the diagnostic workup for
any patient presenting for pollakiuria, stranguria, or urge
incontinence. This should include the reproductive status; age at
neutering; age at the onset of the problem; previous medical
problems, especially those involving the urogenital system; previous
history of trauma; and an accurate description of the abnormality.
How frequent is urination? What is the volume of urine that is being
passed? Pollakiuria may be associated with large or small volumes of
urine. Is there stranguria, and if so, is any urine being passed?
Stranguria is more frequently associated with voiding of small
amounts of urine, or the owner may report that a normal volume is
ultimately produced after multiple attempts to urinate with small
volumes passed each time. If there is incontinence, is it continuous
or intermittent? Is the animal aware of the incontinence? Does it
occur only at rest/during sleep or while the animal is awake and
moving? Urge incontinence is most frequently associated with
spontaneous voiding while the dog or cat is awake. Owners may
report it as purposeful voiding.
Complete physical (ch. 3) and neurologic (ch. 241) examinations
should be performed, with particular attention paid to the urogenital
system. The bladder should be palpated carefully before and
immediately after voiding to evaluate the extent of distension, tone,
and the ease with which the bladder can be expressed manually.
Lower motor neuron lesions generally are associated with reduced
sphincter tone and, therefore, easy manual expression of the bladder.

Upper motor neuron lesions generally are associated with increased
sphincter tone and difficult manual expression. In the neurologic
examination, the innervation of the urogenital system should be
evaluated. The perineal reflex evaluates the pudendal nerve. The
bulbospongiosus reflex evaluates the integrity of both the pudendal
nerve and the sacral spinal segments. Pollakiuria is commonly
associated with a medium to small bladder size and with normal to
small amounts of urine being passed. Stranguria is commonly
associated with a medium to large bladder if there is a partial
obstruction and variable (normal to moderate to small) amounts of
urine being passed if the stranguria is associated with infection or
inflammation without an obstructive process. With urge
incontinence, the bladder is often small on palpation.
A rectal examination (ch. 3) should be done to evaluate the
prostate gland, pelvic diaphragm, and anal tone. Observing the
animal urinating can help characterize the micturition abnormality (
Videos 54.1, 54.2, 54.3). This can be challenging in cats and shy
dogs; in these cases, having the owner video record it can provide
useful information. The residual urine volume should be measured.
The animal is allowed to void until urine is no longer passed, the
bladder is catheterized, and the volume of any remaining urine is
measured. In a normal animal, the residual volume should not
exceed 0.4 mL/kg. Catheterization of the bladder also assesses the
patency of the urethra. This will help to rule in or rule out a complete
or partial obstruction secondary to calculi, stricture or neoplasia.
Ultimately, a contrast cystourethrogram, ultrasound examination or
cystoscopy (ch. 100) may need to be performed to further
characterize the lesion unless the cause of the obstruction is a
radiopaque calculus.

The diagnostic workup should include a complete blood count and
serum biochemistry profile. Typically, the serum biochemistry
profile will be normal if there is infection or inflammation confined
to the lower urinary tract. Obstructive lesions in the lower urinary
tract can result in azotemia, hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia.
If there is concurrent infection in the upper urinary tract, there may
be azotemia. A complete blood count may demonstrate a
leukocytosis if upper tract infection is present, but not typically with
lower tract infection except in cases of acute prostatitis or a prostatic
abscess.
A urinalysis is one of the most important tests that can be
performed (ch. 70). Hematuria, pyuria and proteinuria indicate
inflammation within the urinary tract. These are nonspecific
findings, which may be associated with both infectious and
noninfectious processes. It may be possible to visualize bacteria,
fungal organisms or parasitic ova while examining the urine
sediment. The presence of these organisms, however, may not
represent infection (ch. 307). Quantitative urine culture and
sensitivity are the definitive way of identifying actual infection. High
bacterial numbers in a properly collected sample indicate true
infection. Small numbers may indicate contamination.
Crystalluria may be seen in normal patients, those with
urolithiasis, or those with disorders unassociated with the urinary
tract such as portosystemic shunts (ch. 267). The presence of
crystals in urine sediment must be interpreted cautiously. Urine is
best evaluated for the presence of crystals shortly after being
obtained. In cats with FIC, crystalluria, hematuria and proteinuria
occur, while pyuria of any significance is uncommon.10
The presence of neoplastic cells in urine sediment indicates the
presence of urinary tract neoplasia (ch. 330). However, it may be
difficult to diagnose neoplasia based solely on urine sediment
examination. Atypical epithelial cells arising from inflammation or
extremes in urine pH or osmolality are difficult to differentiate from

neoplasia.10 Cytological examination of prostatic fluid may be
helpful in identifying prostatitis, abscess or neoplasia (ch. 314).
Imaging of the urinary tract is especially beneficial in
differentiating the various causes of pollakiuria, stranguria, and urge
incontinence. Survey radiographs are helpful in identifying
urocystolithiasis. Abdominal ultrasound is a very helpful diagnostic
tool, providing the ability to visualize wall thickness, presence or
absence of urocystoliths, and soft-tissue masses in the bladder or
portions of the urethra. Contrast radiographs, such as an excretory
urogram (intravenous pyelogram), or double contrast
cystourethrogram may be helpful in determining the presence of
calculi or a space-occupying mass, especially those causing a partial
obstruction. Finally, cystoscopy can be used for visualizing the
urethra, bladder and, in females, the vagina. Biopsy and brush
sampling for cytologic analysis can be performed via cystoscopy to
help in identifying the underlying cause of the dysuria.
While causes of pollakiuria and stranguria are quite common and
the diagnosis can be straightforward based upon history, signalment,
physical exam findings and diagnostic workup, urge incontinence is a
diagnosis of exclusion. Urge incontinence may be diagnosed via a
complete history, observation of the animal urinating, imaging
modalities, and urodynamic studies such as a cystometrogram and
urethral pressure profile. Causes of inflammatory cystitis or
urethritis must be eliminated first as the source of urgency. If it is
possible to perform a urodynamic study, uninhibited contractions of
the detrusor confirm detrusor hyperspasticity. Otherwise, response
to therapy is the diagnostic test and treatment of choice.

TREATMENT
Treatment of pollakiuria, stranguria and urge incontinence is
dictated by the underlying cause. When a urinary tract infection (ch.
307) is the cause of pollakiuria, the diagnosis is relatively easy and
treatment with an antibiotic should be based on culture and
sensitivity results. If the underlying cause of pollakiuria is an
inflammatory condition, treatment with analgesic agents (e.g.,
opioids) may be necessary if there is evidence of pain associated with
the stranguria. If urocystoliths are the source of pollakiuria, then a

variety of options is available, ranging from antibiotics (chs. 308 and
309) and dissolution diets (ch. 159), to minimally invasive
procedures (ch. 117) such as voiding urohydropropulsion,
cystoscopy with basket retrieval, lithotripsy, percutaneous
cystolithotomy,11 or surgery. Neoplasia may be treated with
chemotherapy, surgery, radiation therapy or a combination of
modalities depending upon the type of cancer (ch. 330). Diseases of
the prostate or vagina may be treated with a range of modalities
depending upon the underlying cause but may involve medical
management (hormonal replacement therapy, hormonal limiting
therapy), to medical management of prostatic infections or vaginitis,
to surgical interventions.
Treatment for the multiple causes of stranguria ranges from
medical management utilizing antibiotics, antispasmodics, and
interventional therapy (laser lithotripsy/ablation, stent placement,
cystostomy tubes) to the management of cancer.
Urge incontinence is best treated by identifying and then
addressing the underlying cause. If the problem is secondary to
idiopathic detrusor hyperspasticity, then an antispasmodic agent
such as flavoxate hydrochloride, oxybutynin, tolterodine or
dicyclomine is indicated. If the condition is recognized in cats with
FIC, then multimodality treatment is often indicated (ch. 311).

Pollakiuria, Stranguria and Urge
Incontinence—Feline
IS YOUR CAT HAVING PROBLEMS URINATING?
Your cat has been showing signs of frequent visits to the litterbox
(pollakiuria), straining to urinate (stranguria) or inappropriate
urinations. This indicates that something is going on in the urinary
tract. All 3 of these clinical signs may be a sign of 1) a bacterial
infection of the lower urinary tract, 2) stone disease, 3) feline
idiopathic cystitis (FIC), an inflammatory condition of the bladder
and urethra, or 4) in the older cat, a mass or tumor in the bladder.
FIC is a self-limiting condition, and is most frequently seen in
young and middle age cats, between the ages of 1 and 6 years old
typically. Most cats with FIC will need to urinate frequently and only

pass small amounts of urine each time. There may be blood in the
urine or inappropriate urinations (in the bathtub or sink). It occurs
with equal frequency in males and females, but may become a lifethreatening emergency in male cats that develop a plug of crystals
and mucus that becomes lodged in the narrowed penile urethra. If
your cat shows signs of straining to urinate and not passing any urine
at the litter box, vocalizing frequently and sounding painful, this may
indicate a urethral obstruction that requires immediate medical
attention to relieve the obstruction before kidney damage occurs. A
common misperception is that your cat is constipated. If you see
these signs your cat should be checked out immediately. FIC is a selflimiting disease and usually resolves in a few days, although it can be
a recurring problem. To diagnose this condition, other conditions
will need to be ruled out. Usually this involves a urinalysis and
perhaps an X-ray.
Urinary tract infections are common in kittens and in senior cats.
As your cat ages, their immune system ages as well and they become
more susceptible to urinary tract infections. Other diseases seen in
the older cat that may predispose them to bacterial infections include
diabetes, chronic kidney disease, having bladder stones or a bladder
tumor. Bladder tumors are rare in cats but do occur; special testing
may be needed to make that diagnosis.
In middle age to geriatric cats a common cause of the clinical signs
of straining to urinate, frequent urinations, inappropriate urinations
and perhaps even blood in the urine (in addition to infection), is the
presence of bladder stones. The most common stone types are
struvite and calcium oxalate. These stones are easily seen with the
help of an X-ray. Struvite stones can often be dissolved if your cat
will eat a special diet. Depending upon the size and number this
process may take weeks to months. If after a month there is no
change in the appearance of the stones on an X-ray, they are most
likely calcium oxalate stones or a mixture of stone types. A minimally
invasive surgical or surgical procedure for removal is then going to
be the treatment of choice. Some stones are small enough that they
become lodged in the urethra and cause either a complete or partial
blockage. When this happens, it is an emergency situation and your
cat needs to be unblocked as quickly as possible.
The causes listed above for creating the clinical signs of straining
to urinate, frequent urinations or a sense of urgency to urinate, or

inappropriate urinations may be diagnosed by one or more of the
following tests: a urinalysis, culture, X-ray, contrast dye study, or
ultrasound examination.
Treatment for these conditions may include antibiotics, antiinflammatory medication, pain relief, anti-spasmodics, special diets,
extra water in the diet, behavioral/environmental enrichment, and a
surgical or minimally invasive surgical procedure.
Mary Anna Labato (North Grafton, Massachusetts)

Pollakiuria, Stranguria and Urge
Incontinence—Canine
IS YOUR DOG HAVING PROBLEMS
URINATING?
Your dog has been showing signs of frequent urinations
(pollakiuria), straining to urinate (stranguria) or loss of
bladder control (urge incontinence). This indicates that something
is going on in the urinary tract. All 3 of these clinical signs may be a
sign of 1) a bacterial infection of the lower urinary tract, 2) bladder
stones, 3) inflammation in the bladder or urethra, 4) in the older
dog, a mass or tumor in the bladder or urethra, or 5) a neurological
problem causing a sense of urgency and loss of bladder control with a
start/stop type of urinating that allows a small amount of urine to
pass after posturing and trying to urinate and then a quick stop of
the urine stream.
Frequent needing to go outside to urinate and urinating a small to
typical amount of urine is called pollakiuria. It indicates a sense of
need to urinate repeatedly. It may be caused by an infection, or by an
irritation in the bladder, urethra or even in the vagina in females.
Other causes may be from irritation triggered by bladder stones or a
mass in the bladder.
When your dog strains to urinate, this is referred to with the
medical term stranguria. Straining may indicate a burning sensation
when urine is passed or may indicate that your dog is having
difficulty passing urine. This difficulty may be caused by swelling in
the urethra, or a blockage from a stone or mass in the urethra or
neck of the bladder.

Urge incontinence is when your dog has to urinate and cannot wait
until she/he gets outside. It can be confused with inappropriate
urination (your dog stops and pees in a place they should not, but are
aware that they are doing it). With urge incontinence they just lose
control. This is often due to marked irritation/inflammation in the
bladder or urethra or to a neurological problem.
Urinary tract infections are common in puppies and in female
dogs. These are usually simple infections that will be treated with a
short course of antibiotics. Older female dogs and male dogs that
have frequent bladder infections may have an underlying disease
that will make treatment more difficult. These are called complicated
urinary tract infections and require more testing to find out what is
causing the underlying problem and most often require a long course
of antibiotics. These infections may be associated with other diseases
such as chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, Cushing’s disease
or a mechanical problem such as a stone or tumor.
In middle age to geriatric dogs a common cause of the clinical
signs of straining to urinate, frequent urinations, inappropriate
urinations and perhaps even blood in the urine (in addition to
infection), is the presence of bladder stones. The most common stone
types are struvite and calcium oxalate. These stones are easily seen
with the help of an X-ray. Struvite stones can often be dissolved by
treating the underlying infection and a special diet. Depending upon
the size and number of stones, this process may take weeks to
months. If after a month there is no change in the appearance of the
stones on an X-ray, and you have been successful with administering
the antibiotic and diet, then the stone is of another type. Surgical
removal or a minimally invasive interventional procedure is then
going to be the treatment of choice. Some stones are small enough
that they become lodged in the urethra and cause either a complete
or partial blockage. When this happens, it is an emergency situation
and your dog needs to be unblocked as quickly as possible.
The causes listed above for creating the clinical signs of straining
to urinate, frequent urinations or a sense of urgency to urinate, or
inappropriate urinations may be diagnosed by one or more of the
following tests: a urinalysis, culture, X-ray, contrast dye study, or
ultrasound examination. In some cases we may need to pass a small
scope up the urethra and into the bladder to diagnose and even treat
the problem.

Treatment for these conditions may include antibiotics, antiinflammatory medication, pain relief, anti-spasmodics, special diets,
extra water in the diet, behavioral/environmental enrichment, and a
surgical or minimally invasive surgical procedure.
Mary Anna Labato (North Grafton, Massachusetts)
