CHAPTER 55: Hematuria and
Other Conditions Causing
Discolored Urine
Thierry Francey

A C RO N YM S
CK creatine kinase
UA urinalysis

OVERVIEW
Visual inspection of urine is the first step in performing a standard
urinalysis (UA). It aims at evaluating color and turbidity, which can
provide useful clinical information. Abnormal urine color is
occasionally recognized by the pet owner and it may represent the
only reason for a consultation, especially when the urine is overtly
red. Abnormal urine color indicates presence of endogenous or
exogenous pigments and is usually associated with a clinical
problem. However, significant systemic or urinary tract disease may
exist despite normal colored urine. Urine discoloration is
nonspecific, but should prompt completion of a thorough history,
including current diet, medications, environment, and collection
technique. Thorough physical examination is important, examining
the urogenital areas last before approaching the “problem area.”
Laboratory testing is often warranted, including a detailed urine
sediment examination. Knowledge of urine color may also be

important in interpreting dipstick colorimetric test results since
discolored urine may interfere with those assays.

NORMAL URINE
Normal urine is typically transparent and light yellow, yellow, or
amber in color. The intensity of the yellow color of normal urine
varies primarily with degree of urine concentration or dilution
(Figure 55.1, A).1 The yellow color is primarily associated with renal
excretion of plasma urochrome, a yellow sulfur-containing oxidation
product of a colorless urochromogen. The daily urinary excretion of
urochrome is relatively constant, and the intensity of the urine color
provides an estimate of the degree of urine concentration. Highly
concentrated urine will thus be amber in color, while dilute urine
may be light yellow or almost colorless.1 Production of urochrome
does depend to some extent on the metabolic rate. Increased
quantities of urochrome are excreted as a result of fever, catabolism,
or starvation. Urochrome may further darken when exposed to light,
giving false impression that the urine is concentrated. Small
quantities of the endogenous orange-brown heme degradation
pigment urobilin may contribute further to the yellow color of urine.
Urobilin is the oxidation product of its colorless precursor
urobilinogen, a bacterial degradation product of intestinal bilirubin
that is reabsorbed into the bloodstream. Increased bilirubin in the
urine may give it an intense yellow color, similar to that of
concentrated urine (Figure 55.1, B). When exposed to light, it may
oxidize and turn brown to almost black.

DISCOLORED URINE
WHAT IS ABNORMAL?
Any urine color other than yellow or amber is abnormal. There are
many potential causes of discolored urine (Table 55.1). The most
common abnormal urine colors in dogs and cats are red, brown, or
black. These colors may be caused by hematuria, hemoglobinuria,

myoglobinuria, and possibly bilirubinuria (Figures 55.1, C and
55.2).2-4

PALE YELLOW URINE
Pale yellow or clear urine may be normal or indicative of polyuria
(Figure 55.1, A; ch. 53). Pale urine usually indicates a urine
specific gravity of less than 1.015. Urine may be appropriately dilute
if it is associated with recent consumption of water, administration
of fluids, consumption of a low-protein or high-salt diet, or
administration of diuretics, barbiturates, or glucocorticoids.5 Dilute
urine is inappropriate if the pet is dehydrated, indicating failure of
physiological water sparing mechanisms. Renal diseases (chs. 300305), hyperthyroidism (chs. 287, 288), diabetes insipidus (ch.
282), hyperadrenocorticism (chs. 293, 294), hypoadrenocorticism
(ch. 296), pyometra or other infections with lipopolysaccharideproducing bacteria (ch. 128), hypokalemia (ch. 68), and
hypercalcemia (ch. 69) may be associated with persistently dilute
urine. However, dogs and cats with severe polyuria from
uncomplicated diabetes mellitus usually have urine specific gravities
of 1.025 to 1.035 due to the presence of glucose in the urine. Their
urine often appears deeper yellow in color.
A simple test to determine whether polyuria is persistent is to
determine the specific gravity of several owner-collected morning
urine samples or to compare the specific gravity from different urine
samples collected throughout the day.6 Based on dilute urine, the
clinician may recommend a serum biochemical analysis and a
complete UA. A complete blood count, abdominal imaging,
assessment of thyroid and adrenal function, or monitoring urine
specific gravity after several days of desmopressin administration
(ch. 53) may be considered (ch. 282).

RED, BROWN, OR BLACK URINE
Test Strip Positive for Blood

Freshly collected urine that is red, brown, or black suggests the
presence of blood, hemoglobin, myoglobin, or some of their
degradation products (Figure 55.1, C). The quantity of blood, the
amount of time urine has been in contact with blood, urine
concentration, and pH all affect color. Red blood cells progressively
disintegrate and release hemoglobin in urine. This may be oxidized
to methemoglobin and result in a brown or black urine color. A thin
layer of black urine viewed under a bright light usually appears
brown or deep reddish-brown. Hematuria, hemoglobinuria, and
myoglobinuria cause the test for blood on reagent strips to read
positive. “Blood” indicates presence of a globin with a heme group.
Additional investigations are required to differentiate these
possibilities (Figure 55.2).3,5

FIGURE 55.1 Urine color, concentration and
turbidity. A, Influence of the urine concentration on
its color—a concentrated urine sample (right)
displays a deeper yellow color than a more dilute
sample (left), due to different concentrations of the
endogenous pigment urochrome. B, The presence of
bilirubinuria (right) gives the urine sample a deep
yellow to amber color and thus the wrong impression
of concentrated urine. C, The visual inspection of a
non-centrifuged red-brown urine sample often
allows the distinction between hematuria (center,
turbid) and hemoglobinuria (right, transparent).
Centrifugation further indicates a clear supernatant
on a red blood cell pellet in hematuria (left) and an

Test Strip Negative for Blood Despite the Urine
Being Red, Black, or Brown
This suggests presence of a chromogen other than hemoglobin or
myoglobin.2,7 Oxidized bilirubin should be ruled out first. An intense
yellow coloration of the plasma suggests hyperbilirubinemia, which
can be quantified by measuring serum bilirubin concentration.
Hyperbilirubinemia may result from pre-hepatic hemolysis, liver
failure, post-hepatic obstruction, or rupture of the biliary tract (ch.
28).

Urine Sediment: Red Blood Cells Present?
A positive reagent strip test for blood should be followed by analysis
of the urine sediment. If the discoloration is due to hematuria, there
will be numerous red blood cells and increased turbidity. In contrast,
urine remains transparent when color change is due to
hemoglobinuria (Figure 55.1, C).

Myoglobinuria and Clear Plasma
If no red blood cells are seen on microscopic examination of the
urine sediment, hemoglobin or myoglobin should be suspected.
Examination of the plasma color may aid in differentiating these
potential explanations. If urine is discolored due to myoglobin, the
plasma will usually be clear because little myoglobin is bound to
protein and it is rapidly excreted. Myoglobinuria is indicative of
severe muscle damage, and serum creatine kinase (CK) activity is
usually markedly increased (ch. 66). CK concentrations are used to
help confirm myoglobinuria rather than characterizing the urinary
heme proteins using immunoassays. The serum CK activity offers the
additional advantage of being cleared slowly from the blood, which
may allow a delayed diagnosis.

Pink Plasma
If plasma from a non-traumatic venipuncture sample is pink, it is
suggestive of hemoglobinemia. When present in small quantities in
the circulation, hemoglobin is bound to haptoglobin, hindering its
glomerular filtration. If the binding capacity of haptoglobin is
exceeded, free hemoglobin is filtered and appears in the urine.
Hemoglobinemia and hemoglobinuria are therefore indicative of
significant intravascular hemolysis, resulting from immune-,
parasite-, or drug-mediated destruction of red blood cells or from
fragmentation due to microangiopathic conditions (ch. 57). A
marked red-brown discoloration of the urine may also cause falsepositive reactions on other urine dipstick test pads and should be
considered in their interpretation.

MILKY WHITE URINE
Milky white–colored urine may be due to presence of white blood
cells (pyuria), lipid, or crystals. The more concentrated the urine, the
more opaque it may appear. The presence of pyuria secondary to
bacterial urinary tract infection is the most common cause of cloudyto-milky white urine (Figure 55.1, D). However, pyuria may also
occur due to non-infectious inflammations. The presence of lipid
droplets in the urine of healthy animals usually remains a
microscopic observation. However, lipid droplets could contribute to
urine turbidity. Lipiduria may be increased in cats with hepatic
lipidosis. Crystalluria, if heavy and present in a concentrated urine
sample, may also result in milky white urine color. Microscopic
examination of urine sediment will aid in the differentiation of these
causes.

Preputial Discharge
Jeffrey de Gier

INTRODUCTION
This discussion will focus on non-physiological (worrisome) vaginal
or preputial discharges and will not include disorders of the
urological tract and/or perineal disorders which may cause
“pseudovaginal discharge,” e.g., as occurs with an anal sac abscess or
perivulvar dermatitis. Physiological (non-worrisome) vaginal
discharges are common in bitches during pro-estrus, pregnancy,
parturition, and the days to weeks following parturition. Vaginal
discharge is seen in some cats during and after parturition.
Mucopurulent discharge from the prepuce of males, without clinical
signs, is considered physiological and of little consequence.

VAGINAL DISCHARGES
OVERVIEW
A thorough history should include the pet’s age, the nature of the
discharge (e.g., serosanguineous, mucoid, or mucopurulent), and
whether the pet is intact or has an ovariectomy or
ovariohysterectomy been previously performed? In intact animals,
time of the most recent estrus is relevant. A complete physical
examination (PE) should be completed before assessing the genital
tract with abdominal palpation and if indicated, digital palpation of
the vaginal vault (Video 56.1

), vaginoscopy (Video 56.2), or

vaginal cytology obtained to evaluate for estrogen influence (ch. 101;
E-Figure 56.1). Invasive examination is not usually feasible in
awake cats and prepubertal bitches. Additional testing may be
warranted to assess for inflammation, bone marrow hypoplasia, the
pituitary-gonadal axis, abdominal ultrasonography (US), cytology of
a fine needle aspirate (FNA) or histologic assessment of a tissue
sample.1

E-FIGURE 56.1 Vestibular cytology showing
estrogen influence in a bitch; examples of superficial
cells (arrows) and erythrocytes (arrowheads).

SEROSANGUINEOUS VAGINAL
DISCHARGE IN INTACT BITCHES AND
QUEENS (FIGURE 56.2)
Young Dogs
In young bitches, during their first or second estrus, prolonged
estrogen influence or “split heats” are relatively common. Prolonged
exposure to estrogen can result in a persistent sanguineous discharge
which can be confirmed with vaginal cytology (E-Figure 56.1)
and/or vaginoscopy (Video 56.3

; ch. 101). “Split heats” are

thought to result from a failure to ovulate, as demonstrated by
persistently low plasma progesterone concentrations. Other causes
of prolonged proestrus include cystic ovarian follicles, portosystemic
shunts (ch. 267), or exposure to exogenous estrogen.

Middle-Aged or Older Dogs
In middle-aged or older dogs, the most common cause for prolonged
sanguineous discharge in the absence of estrogen influence is
endometritis or neoplasia of the urogenital tract (E-Figure 56.3;
Video 56.4

; ch. 330). Vaginal tumors are often benign (e.g.,

leiomyoma, fibroma) and cytologic or histopathologic evaluation
may be of value before surgical removal is attempted.

E-FIGURE 56.3 Vaginoscopy in a bitch showing a
small and probably benign tumor (asterisk),
protruding into the cranial end of the tubular
speculum.

Subinvolution of Placental Sites (SIPS)
SIPS can result in prolonged bloody vaginal discharge (longer than
2-3 weeks) in otherwise healthy bitches after parturition (ch. 101).
Vaginal smears from a dog with SIPS show erythrocytes, occasional
neutrophils, and vacuolated giant cells (E-Figures 56.4 and 56.5).

SEROSANGUINEOUS VAGINAL
DISCHARGE DESPITE PREVIOUS
OVARIECTOMY (FIGURE 56.2)
Serosanguineous discharge due to estrogen influence in a previously
ovariectomized bitch is usually caused by functional remnant ovarian
tissue. Estrogen influence can be confirmed with appropriate
changes, such as vulvar swelling, vaginal cytology, vaginoscopy
(Video 56.5

; ch. 101) and/or if the plasma progesterone

concentration is >2 ng/mL. If no estrogen influence is observed and
the plasma progesterone concentration is <2 ng/mL, then
determination of anti-mullerian hormone concentrations or a
gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) stimulation test may be

necessary to confirm a diagnosis. Determination of basal plasma
luteinizing hormone (LH) concentrations, alone, is not reliable due
to changes in the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis after an
incomplete ovariectomy.3-5 Serosanguineous discharge after
ovariectomy may also be caused by long-term administration of
estrogens, e.g., for urinary incontinence.6 Further causes of bloody
discharge after ovariectomy, without the presence of estrogen
influence, include endometritis of the uterine stump due to the
administration of progestins, neoplasia of the urogenital tract (more
frequently malignant than in intact bitches), or uterine stump
hemorrhage in the 1-2 weeks after ovariohysterectomy. Rarely,
trauma, hemorrhagic diathesis or a foreign body may cause bloody
discharge.

MUCOPURULENT VAGINAL
DISCHARGE IN INTACT BITCHES AND
QUEENS (FIGURE 56.7)
Adults
Clear to opaque mucous vaginal discharge is sometimes seen about
day 30 of normal pregnancy (E-Figure 56.8). Mucopurulent
vaginal discharge in the intact bitch at the onset of diestrus may be
physiological as well (E-Figure 56.9). The most common
pathological cause of mucopurulent vaginal discharge in the intact
bitch after estrus or parturition is endometritis. The vaginal
discharge in association with abortion is often dark green.
Vestibulitis/vaginitis may cause mucopurulent discharge. Primary
vaginitis is not seen in the cat. The etiology of vaginitis and/or
vestibulitis may be better understood by appreciating that the area
immediately proximal to the urethral opening is the caudal aspect of
the internal genitalia which fuses during development with the
external genitalia caudal to the urethral opening. Age and the stage
of the estrous cycle may be important. Infrequently, inflammation
within the vestibule may be due to an infection, e.g., with canine
herpesvirus.

Puppies
Hormonal and immunological factors may play a major role in
“vaginitis/vestibulitis” in young dogs, whose clinical signs are often
restricted to mucous discharge and attracting males. Prepubertal
“puppy vaginitis” and “vaginitis/vestibulitis” after the first or
second estrus are most common in large and brachycephalic breeds,
sometimes as early as 3 months of age. This condition is
characterized by a slightly swollen vulva, mucoid white or yellow
discharge and/or attraction of male dogs. Vaginoscopy may reveal an
exudate, mucosal lesions primarily in the vestibule, and concomitant
lymphoid follicle hyperplasia (E-Figure 56.10). Vaginoscopy
performed when a healthy bitch is in diestrus shows a patchwork of
white and red areas. Red areas in these dogs should not be mistaken
for inflammation if mucosal lesions are not present (E-Figure
56.11; Video 56.6

). Vaginal discharge in young dogs is usually

self-limiting, disappearing after the first estrous cycle or after the
second or third luteal phases. Treatment of “puppy vaginitis” prior to
the first estrus is not recommended. Local or parenteral antibiotics

will not alleviate signs, application of ointments or other medications
are not well tolerated, and the general health and fertility of the bitch
are usually unaffected.

of bitches. A, Non-hyperplastic. B, Lymphoid follicle

E-FIGURE 56.11 Vaginoscopic view of vaginal

Vaginitis/Vestibulitis After First or Second Estrus
In this scenario, topical ointments containing glucocorticoids may
alleviate signs and if helpful, supports the concept of an underlying
immunological etiology. If vaginal discharge is noted with concurrent
urological problems (e.g., cystitis and/or pyelonephritis), more
intensive therapy may be needed. Bacterial culture of the vagina
usually demonstrates normal flora and does not have significant
value. However, if antibiotic treatment is being considered, culture
and sensitivity testing should be performed. “Vestibulitis/vaginitis”
may recur, but the problem is usually self-limiting with the end of
the luteal phase or with advancing age.

Vaginitis in the Mature Bitch
Vaginitis in an adult bitch is usually secondary to problems such as a
foreign body or vaginal neoplasia. Rarely, anatomic deformities may
lead to accumulation of secretions or urine, leading to inflammation
and vaginal discharge. Vestibulitis with discharge may also be caused
by urinary incontinence, e.g., after ovariectomy. Vesicles may be
transiently observed along the mucosa of the vestibule if a bitch has a
herpes infection. Remnant ovarian tissue in a bitch, after
hysterectomy, may lead to non-bloody vaginal discharge, mostly of
shed superficial cells and not to be mistaken for purulent discharge.
(E-Figure 56.12; Video 56.7

).

DISCHARGE AFTER OVARIECTOMY

Mucopurulent discharge after ovariectomy without estrogen
influence may be caused by neoplasia in the genital tract or “stump

endometritis” due to progesterone secretion from remnant ovarian
tissue (E-Figure 56.13) or may follow progestin administration.
Progestin administration is always contraindicated after
ovariectomy. If, after ovariectomy, cystic endometrial hyperplasia is
present in the uterine tissue, and progestins have not been
administered, then remnant ovarian tissue is the most probable
cause.

PREPUTIAL DISCHARGES (FIGURE
56.14)
Preputial discharge may be composed of fluid and cells that originate
from the urinary bladder, prostate gland, testicles, epididymis,
urethra, and/or mucosa of the penis and penile sheath (prepuce).

Preputial discharge is often present in intact male dogs but is less
commonly seen in castrated dogs. Preputial discharge is extremely
uncommon in tomcats. Rarely, generalized mucosal disease or
hemorrhagic diathesis may cause preputial discharge. “Normal”
discharge in the intact male is characterized by a small amount of
grayish-white to yellow mucopurulent material that may be seen at
the preputial orifice as moist or dried exudate. Abnormal discharges
may be mucopurulent (E-Figure 56.15) or serosanguineous (EFigure 56.16). It is important to consider age, breed, reproductive
status, duration and character of the discharge. Systemic signs that
precede or are associated with preputial discharge may accompany
inflammatory conditions, infection, neoplasia, trauma, or exposure
to a toxin. Penile tumors are rare (E-Figure 56.17). The prevalence
of transmissible venereal tumor (TVT) varies with geographical
location (E-Figure 56.16). A complete PE (ch. 3), including the
male reproductive tract, should be performed.7 Examination of the
penis (Videos 3.17, 56.8

) and preputial space (preputioscopy)

may be indicated to assess the entire mucosal surface (E-Figure
56.18).

In dogs and cats castrated prior to puberty, penile tissue may
appear less developed and the penis may be more difficult to
completely extrude in cats. Based on the appearance of the preputial
discharge, historical information, and PE findings, a list of possible
diagnoses can be generated (Figure 56.14). Further evaluation
might include a complete blood count, serum biochemical profile,
and urinalysis, as well as US examination of the testicles, prostate, or
urinary bladder. Evaluation of testicular or prostatic secretions may
be possible through semen collection or prostatic massage (ch. 104).

Additional diagnostics may include bacterial culture and sensitivity
testing, fine needle aspiration, or biopsy. Test results may lead to a
definitive diagnosis. In the absence of definitive findings, the male
should be re-evaluated at a later date. Comparison of subsequent
findings with the original data may lead to a definitive diagnosis or
management plan.

CHAPTER 57: Anemia and
Erythrocytosis
Tracy Stokol

A C RO N YM S
CBC complete blood count
HCT hematocrit
HB hemoglobin
IMHA immune-mediated hemolytic anemia
MCV mean cell volume
PCV packed cell volume
RBC red blood cell
Anemia is defined as reduced red blood cell (RBC) mass and is
recognized by a packed cell volume (PCV), hematocrit (HCT),
hemoglobin (HB) concentration, or RBC count below the lower limit
of established reference intervals for that species. Conversely,
erythrocytosis is defined as increased RBC mass and is recognized by
values that are higher than the upper reference limit for these tests.
Although polycythemia and erythrocytosis have been used
interchangeably, they are not identical. Polycythemia refers to
increases in any cell in blood (RBCs, leukocytes, platelets), whereas
polycythemia vera is a chronic myeloproliferative disease, specifically
chronic erythroid leukemia (ch. 173). Erythrocytosis specifically
means an absolute increase in RBCs (or a true increase in RBC mass)
and will be used herein. In veterinary medicine, we typically use the
PCV or HCT (the default applied herein) as the main indicator of

RBC mass, whereas HB concentration is standard in human
medicine. The reason for the discrepancy between disciplines is
unclear; however, it may be related to the higher likelihood of
postprandial lipemia in small animal patients, which can result in
false increases in HB concentration. It should be noted that although
PCV and HCT are used synonymously, they represent 2 different
measurements. The PCV is a directly measured value from a
centrifuged microhematocrit tube whereas the HCT is a calculated
result from a hematology analyzer that uses mean cell volume (MCV)
and RBC count (HCT = MCV × RBC). Thus, the HCT will be
influenced by artifactual or real changes in the MCV, such as storageassociated RBC swelling,1 which are less likely to affect the PCV.
Internal studies done at the author’s institution with the ADVIA 120
hematology analyzer showed that the PCV is generally lower than the
HCT, with a median difference (PCV− HCT) of −0.02 L/L (range,
−0.06 to 0.03 L/L) and −0.03 L/L (range, −0.06 to 0 L/L) in
clinically healthy dogs (n = 64) and cats (n = 69), respectively.
The first step in interpretation of HCT results is to decide whether
the result is abnormal for that individual animal and due to a disease
process versus an expected physiologic change, i.e., results should be
interpreted in context of patient signalment (breed, age, sex,
reproductive status). The use of reference intervals can be misleading
because they are usually established from presumably healthy adult
animals of various breeds and will be insensitive to breed- and agespecific changes.2-6 For instance, a HCT of 0.45 L/L (45%) is within
established reference intervals for most laboratories, but would be
compatible with anemia in Greyhounds, which typically have higher
HCTs than other breeds.3 Reference intervals can be broad and may
be insensitive to changes in an individual animal that are beyond
analytic or biologic variation. Thus, the author considers it
worthwhile to obtain baseline hemogram (complete blood count
[CBC]) and clinical chemistry results when a dog or cat has reached
adulthood (around 12 months of age in small or medium dog breeds
and cats and 2 years of age in large dog breeds), so that individualspecific abnormalities can be identified using a reference change
value or critical difference approach.7 Reference change values have
been established for hematologic measurands in dogs and cats.8,9

However, these values are dependent on the cohort of animals (lower
variation is expected with laboratory-bred animals), instrument, and
analytical method used in the study. Ultimately, clinicians use their
own judgment to determine if the degree of change from an
established baseline is excessive for an individual animal. Once
anemia or erythrocytosis has been conclusively identified, a systemic
approach can be used to determine the pathophysiologic
mechanism(s) and, hopefully, the underlying cause for the
abnormalities.

ANEMIA
Anemia is the most common hematologic abnormality encountered
in veterinary clinical practice. It can be the cause of disease (e.g.,
immune-mediated hemolytic anemia [IMHA]) or a marker of
underlying disease (e.g., cancer, chronic kidney disease). There are
three main pathophysiologic mechanisms for anemia: hemorrhage
(loss), hemolysis (decreased lifespan), and decreased production.
Distinguishing between these mechanisms is important for
identifying the underlying disease or cause of anemia (Box 57.1) and
is best accomplished using a combination of signalment, historical
information, clinical signs, imaging findings, and clinical pathologic
results. Anemia can be multifactorial in origin, which can complicate
discovery of the underlying cause. There are always going to be those
challenging and potentially frustrating cases, where the mechanism
and cause of the anemia remain ambiguous.

MECHANISMS OF ANEMIA
If an anemia is “adequately” regenerative (see approach below), the
underlying mechanism is hemorrhage or hemolysis. Distinguishing
between these 2 mechanisms relies on identifying a source of
hemorrhage or a cause for hemolysis on a blood smear examination
(Figures 57.1 and 57.2; Box 57.1). In some cases, the anemia may
be due to a combination of hemorrhage and hemolysis, with one
process being the main cause.

Hemorrhage
This can be internal (into a body cavity) or external (“lost” from the
body, e.g., from gastrointestinal hemorrhage). A low total protein
concentration (especially the combination of low albumin and
globulins) would support the conclusion that an anemia is due to
hemorrhage, but it is not specific for hemorrhage. A normal total
protein concentration also does not rule out hemorrhage, since
peracute hemorrhage, internal bleeding, or chronic intermittent
external blood loss may not decrease total protein concentrations. If
external hemorrhage is chronic and occult, iron deficiency can ensue
once iron stores are depleted. Iron deficiency should be suspected if
hypochromic RBCs are seen on a blood smear (Figure 57.2) and a
CBC shows microcytic hypochromic RBC indices. Iron
concentrations and percentage saturation of transferrin are usually
quite low in serum or plasma with iron deficiency anemia, but can
also be decreased with inflammatory disease.10 Newer diagnostic
tests for HB content in reticulocytes (e.g., reticulocyte hemoglobin
content [CHr]; ch. 172) can help support a diagnosis of iron
deficiency anemia in dogs but these results are not usually provided
as part of a routine CBC and are not specific for iron deficiency,
being abnormal in dogs with inflammatory disease, portosystemic
shunts, or breed-associated microcytosis.10,11

Hemolysis (ch. 174)
A hemolytic anemia is due to premature phagocytosis of RBCs by
macrophages in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow, called
extravascular hemolysis (because it is occurring “outside” vessels in
tissues). Extravascular hemolysis is occurring in all cases of
hemolytic anemia. However, with certain causes, there may be a
concurrent intravascular component, where the RBC membrane
physically ruptures within the circulation, liberating free HB. It is
important to identify which animals with a hemolytic anemia are
suffering from concurrent intravascular hemolysis, because this
helps narrow down the differential diagnosis (Box 57.1) and has
negative prognostic implications. Intravascular hemolysis is
characterized by hemoglobinemia and hemoglobinuria. Ghost RBCs
and relevant RBC changes (e.g., Heinz bodies reflecting oxidant

injury; Figure 57.2) or infectious organisms (e.g., Babesia canis)
may be seen on blood smears, but should not be relied upon for
distinguishing intravascular from extravascular hemolysis. Ghost
RBCs are not specific for intravascular hemolysis, being more
commonly seen with any cause of in vitro or artifactual hemolysis
(e.g., lysis of cells in stored blood) or as a consequence of blood
smear preparation. A hemolytic anemia is usually secondary to RBC
abnormalities, such as membrane-bound immunoglobulins or
complement in IMHA, although abnormally activated or neoplastic
macrophages in histiocytic disorders can inappropriately remove
normal RBCs (ch. 328).12 Hemolytic anemia is typically associated
with a normal or high total protein concentration and can result in
bilirubinemia, especially due to unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin.
However, cholestasis with increases in conjugated (direct) bilirubin
may occur and the latter may even dominate in dogs with IMHA and
sick anorectic cats (presumably due to bile sludging). Liver enzyme
activities may be increased from hypoxic injury but can be normal.
Iron concentrations and percentage saturation of transferrin are
consistently increased in the plasma or serum of dogs and cats with
hemolytic anemia, and siderocytes (RBCs with faint iron inclusions;
Figure 57.2) may be seen on a blood smear. None of these results is
specific for hemolytic anemia and should be considered as
supportive, not confirmatory, results. The lack of these findings does
not rule out hemolysis either.

Decreased Production (ch. 172)
If the anemia is not acute and is non-regenerative or “inadequately”
regenerative, this indicates a problem with RBC production in the
bone marrow, of which there are many causes (Box 57.1). Clues as
to the mechanism of a non-regenerative anemia can be gleaned from
the severity of the anemia, RBC indices, and other hematologic
findings, particularly concurrent cytopenias (specifically,
neutropenia and thrombocytopenia) and abnormal (neoplastic) cells
in blood smears (Figure 57.3). A mild to moderate normocytic
normochromic anemia is the most common form of nonregenerative anemia and is usually due to extramedullary disease,
particularly anemia of inflammatory disease (used to be called
anemia of chronic disease) and cancer-associated anemia (which is

multifactorial, but does involve inflammatory cytokines).13,14
Suppressed RBC production in the bone marrow from concurrent
disease or inflammation can dampen the regenerative response to a
primarily hemorrhagic or hemolytic anemia so that it becomes less
regenerative than expected or even “inadequately” regenerative. The
most common causes of a severe non-regenerative anemia, without
other cytopenias, are immune-mediated conditions in dogs and
immune-mediated conditions and feline leukemia virus infection in
cats (ch. 199).13,14 Feline leukemia virus-associated hematologic
disorders are infrequent since the advent of vaccination.

A MECHANISTIC APPROACH TO
ANEMIA
A stepwise approach can be used for distinguishing between
mechanisms of anemia and is based on asking these 4 questions
(Box 57.2):
1. How acute is the anemia? This is important for assessing
whether an anemia is regenerative or not (question 2, below).
The bone marrow takes approximately 3-5 days to mount a
regenerative response. An anemia of acute onset may appear
“non-regenerative” if the bone marrow has had insufficient
time to respond (termed pre-regenerative). Clinical signs and
history can help with determining duration of anemia, but
anemia frequently manifests with vague clinical signs that may
be missed by the owner. Unless there has been a known
traumatic event, a regenerative response should be manifest by
the time of presentation in most patients. The expected
marrow response will also depend on the degree of anemia and
erythropoietic stimulus. A robust regenerative response is
expected in a moderate to severe anemia; however, a weaker
response would be expected in a mild anemia.

hemolysis is always accompanied by extravascular
hemolysis (phagocytosis of RBCs by macrophages)
whereas extravascular hemolysis can occur alone. Causes
of intravascular hemolysis are bolded.
∗∗
Ghost cells will only be seen when the hemolytic anemia
has a component of intravascular hemolysis (i.e., is not
only due to extravascular hemolysis). However, ghost
cells in blood smears may be a consequence of smear
preparation or in vitro or “within tube” (artifactual)
hemolysis from issues associated with sample collection,
handling, and storage.
∗

2. Is the anemia regenerative? The bone marrow responds to
an anemia by releasing immature anucleated RBCs, which are
characterized by increased RNA content. These immature
RBCs can be identified using intravital dyes, which precipitate
RNA and can be visualized on smears (e.g., new methylene
blue), or dyes that bind to RNA/DNA and are detected with
automated hematology analyzers. When identified with these
dyes, the immature anucleated RBCs are called reticulocytes
and are quantified as a percentage of the RBC count (only
aggregate reticulocytes or immature anucleated RBCs that
contain aggregates or large amounts of RNA are quantified in
cats). Due to their higher RNA content, immature anucleated
RBCs can be recognized as polychromatophilic (purple) RBCs
on Romanowsky-stained blood smears (Diff-Quik, Wright’s
stain) and regeneration can be subjectively estimated from the
degree of polychromasia in well-made blood smears from both
dogs and cats (Figure 57.4). As an example, all RBCs can be
averaged in two 100× oil immersion fields in the monolayer of
a blood smear using a 10× objective. Then polychromatophilic
RBCs can be counted and averaged across ten 100× oil
immersion fields and divided by the average number of all
RBCs to obtain a percentage.15 The latter technique correlates

well (correlation coefficient >0.9) in dogs with automated
reticulocyte counts >5% but does not fare as well (correlation
coefficient <0.7) with lower reticulocyte counts. The manual
smear estimate underestimates the automated absolute
reticulocyte count (as much as 3-fold), because punctate
reticulocytes would be counted by hematologic analyzers but
would not be polychromatophilic on blood smears. Regardless,
with any manual or automated reticulocyte count, a high
reticulocyte percentage alone or the presence of
polychromatophilic RBCs in a blood smear does not
necessarily mean that the bone marrow is responding
appropriately to the anemia, and the severity of anemia must
be taken into consideration. Therefore, various formulae are
available to assess “adequacy” of regeneration by accounting
for the severity of anemia, including the absolute reticulocyte
count, corrected reticulocyte percentage (which is handy for
practitioners because it is based on PCV and does not require a
RBC count) and the reticulocyte maturation index. Which
formula is used is a matter of personal preference; however,
the author and others use the absolute reticulocyte count
(values above the upper limit for the laboratory’s established
reference intervals support a regenerative anemia).13,15-17 If an
automated reticulocyte count is not available, we rely on smear
estimates to assess adequacy of regeneration, which is
subjective. Dogs and cats with normal HCTs can have absolute
reticulocyte counts above the laboratory’s upper reference
limit, although many laboratories only provide a reticulocyte
count in anemic animals (HCT below the lower reference
limit). Differential diagnoses for an animal with a normal HCT
and high absolute reticulocyte count include variation of
normal (particularly if the HCT is in the mid- to upper
reference interval), hypoxic or non-hypoxic stimulus for
erythropoietin release (e.g., cardiac or pulmonary disease),
compensated hemolytic anemia, and resolved anemia. On
blood smear examination of an anemic patient, if there is
moderate to marked polychromasia (>7 RBCs/100× oil
immersion field),17 the anemia is likely regenerative,
regardless of severity. However, with mild polychromasia (<3

RBCs/100× oil immersion field), the judgment of “adequate”
regeneration is far more difficult to make, particularly in
moderate to severe anemias. Note that nucleated RBCs
(nRBCs) and Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear fragments) may be
seen in blood smears of animals with a regenerative anemia
but are not used for evaluating the regenerative response
because they occur in other conditions (e.g., heatstroke,
chemotherapeutic drug administration).18,19 Also, with newer
hematology analyzers, the MCV and mean corpuscular HB
concentration are usually normal in a regenerative anemia
(i.e., the anemia is not macrocytic and hypochromic) and
should not be relied upon as an indicator of regeneration.17 If
an anemia is adequately regenerative (i.e., absolute
reticulocyte count sufficiently above the reference interval for
the degree of anemia), then the anemia is likely due to
hemorrhage or hemolysis and decreased erythropoiesis is
unlikely to be the main cause for the anemia, although the
latter may still “dampen” the erythropoietic response. If the
anemia is non-regenerative (i.e., absolute reticulocyte count is
within reference intervals, even if the percentage of
reticulocytes is increased) or inadequately regenerative and the
bone marrow has had time to respond, mechanisms of
decreased RBC production are operative and effort should be
placed on identifying the underlying cause (Box 57.1).

BOX 5 7 .2 A Qu e s tio n-Bas e d A p p r oach t o
A ne mia
1. How acute is the anemia?
2. Is the anemia regenerative?
3. Is a cause identifiable from a blood smear?
4. Which additional tests are indicated?
3. Is a cause for the anemia evident on a blood smear?
Blood smear examination is an essential part of assessment of
an anemic patient and it provides a wealth of information.
Preparing a high-quality blood smear (Video 57.1

) and

optimally staining the smear are essential tools in a clinician’s
armamentarium in the diagnostic evaluation of sick patients.
Videos on these procedures and tips on how to examine a
blood smear also are available online.20 Changes in
morphologic features of RBCs (and other cell lineages) and
detection of infectious organisms or neoplastic cells can
provide clues as to, or specifically identify, the cause of an
anemia (Figure 57.2, Boxes 57.1 and 57.3). Finding
abnormal RBC morphologic features in a blood smear does not
necessarily mean they are of pathologic relevance. Relevance is
subjective and depends on both the type and number of
abnormalities and should always be determined in context of
the patient. For example, a few RBC fragments (schistocytes,
keratocytes and acanthocytes) may be a result of mechanical
fragility in iron deficiency anemia, whereas in a critically ill
patient with thrombocytopenia, the presence of these RBCs
could reflect and trigger additional testing for underlying
disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). The
identification of these RBC abnormalities is highly dependent
on the skill of the observer.

4. Which additional tests are indicated? Results of
complete clinical pathologic testing (CBC, clinical chemistry,
urinalysis) and imaging, combined with cytologic or histologic
assessment of tissues, is essential in all anemic patients for
identifying extramedullary disease that could be causing the
anemia or suppressing the bone marrow’s response. Testing
for infectious diseases is worthwhile in animals with an
unexplained regenerative or non-regenerative anemia, because
blood smear examination can be insensitive for organism
detection. Even if a cause of the anemia is identified on a blood
smear, additional testing is frequently performed for
confirmatory purposes, e.g., Coombs test for IMHA,21
antinuclear antibody testing for systemic lupus erythematosus,
or genetic or serologic-based tests for infectious organisms. In
general, bone marrow aspiration is not indicated in a
regenerative anemia or mild non-regenerative anemia, unless
specifically investigating occult infection (e.g., Leishmania sp.)
or underlying neoplasms (e.g., multiple myeloma, lymphoma).
Pancytopenia (defined as a non-regenerative anemia,
neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia, regardless of severity of
the anemia; ch. 172) and a severe non-regenerative anemia
(alone or with other cytopenias) usually indicate a bone
marrow problem and bone marrow aspiration is warranted in
affected patients (ch. 84), particularly if a primary disorder is
not identified from other testing (e.g., imaging, infectious
disease testing). Similarly, bone marrow aspiration is
worthwhile in animals with suspect or definitive neoplastic
cells in circulation (for staging lymphoma or confirmatory
diagnosis of leukemia). Bone marrow aspiration with Prussian
blue staining for iron is the gold standard test for confirmation
of iron deficiency in dogs, but not cats (stainable iron is absent
in the bone marrow of healthy cats). However, bone marrow
aspiration rarely is performed for the latter purpose.
BOX 5 7 .3 U s e fu l R BC A b nor malitie s in a
Bl ood Sme ar ( Figu re 5 7. 2 )

DIC, Disseminated intravascular coagulation; EDTA,
ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid; HB, hemoglobin; IMHA,
immune-mediated hemolytic anemia; RBC, red blood cell.
Acanthocytes: Fragmentation injury, iron deficiency
anemia (mechanical fragility), vascular neoplasms (e.g.,
hemangiosarcoma),63 liver disease,64 DIC. Usually seen
with keratocytes and schistocytes. Of unclear diagnostic
relevance in various diseases63 or, rarely, a non-relevant
finding in healthy young animals (presumptive, congenital
or inherited disorder).
Agglutination: IMHA,21 EDTA-dependent pseudoagglutination,65 cold agglutinins.66 Must be differentiated
from rouleaux (recommended: microscopic examination
of a 1:4 to 1:10 dilution with saline; macroscopic slide tests
are less reliable). Cold agglutinins will dissipate when the
blood is warmed to 37°C.
Eccentrocytes: Oxidant injury. Low numbers may be
seen in various diseases without indicating an oxidantinduced hemolytic anemia.67 Can be seen with keratocytes
and pyknocytes (remnants of eccentrocytes, which
resemble spherocytes).68
Elliptocytes: Usually secondary to precursor-directed
immune-mediated anemia or pure red cell aplasia in dogs
(indicates myelofibrosis in these disorders16) and liver
disease in cats (particularly lipidosis).64 Inherited in dogs
(rare).69
Heinz bodies: Indicate oxidant injury. Single small
Heinz bodies can be normal in cats and may not result in
anemia.70 Large or multiple Heinz bodies in cats or any
size Heinz bodies in dogs support an oxidant-induced
hemolytic anemia. Can be seen concurrently with
eccentrocytes, ghost cells, pyknocytes and
methemoglobinemia, depending on the oxidant.
Hypochromasia: Absolute iron deficiency (e.g., chronic
external blood loss), abnormal iron metabolism or

inhibition of HB (heme) synthesis (e.g., shunts, lead
poisoning, vitamin B6 deficiency). Siderocytes can be seen
with inhibition of or abnormal heme synthesis.
Keratocytes: Fragmentation injury (vasculitis, DIC, iron
deficiency; seen with acanthocytes and schistocytes) or
oxidant injury (seen with eccentrocytes ± Heinz bodies).
Determine which mechanism is operative by other evident
RBC abnormalities (e.g., keratocytes and eccentrocytes
support oxidant over fragmentation injury). Low numbers
may be normal in cats.
Poikilocytes: RBCs with various shapes can be seen in
cats with liver disease,64 but may not result in anemia.
Rouleaux formation: Increased fibrinogen or
immunoglobulins (polyclonal) secondary to inflammation
(e.g., feline infectious peritonitis) or increased
immunoglobulins with antigenic stimulation (polyclonal,
e.g., chronic liver disease) or B cell or plasma cell
neoplasia (monoclonal, e.g., chronic lymphocytic
leukemia, multiple myeloma). Serum protein
electrophoresis is helpful (ch. 60).
Schistocytes: Fragmentation injury. Often concurrent
with acanthocytes and keratocytes.
Siderocytes: Hemolytic anemia, lead toxicosis, drugs
(e.g., hydralazine), portosystemic shunts, myelodysplastic
syndrome (cats).60
Spherocytes: The presence of moderate to many
spherocytes is usually diagnostic of IMHA.21 Can be seen
concurrently with siderocytes (increased RBC turnover)
and ghost cells (if intravascular hemolysis). Partial
spherocytes (smaller RBCs with a small amount of central
pallor; Figure 57.4B) can be seen in dogs with precursordirected immune-mediated anemia.57 A few spherocytes
can be seen with fragmentation injury, and transfused
RBCs can be sphered. Spherocytes are difficult to detect in
cats because feline RBCs normally lack central pallor.

ERYTHROCYTOSIS
An increased RBC count or HCT is occasionally seen in dogs and is
quite rare in cats. A high HCT may be normal for specific breeds of
dogs3,22 and has been observed in individual animals of certain
breeds (Jack Russell Terriers and German Shepherd Dogs) by the
author. Hence, breed-specific associations should be excluded before
evaluating an animal for pathologic causes of a high RBC
count/HCT. Similar to anemia, a sequential mechanistic approach
can be used for diagnostic evaluation of an animal with a high HCT
(Figure 57.5).

RELATIVE INCREASE IN RBCs
Erythrocytosis refers to an absolute or true increase in RBC mass and
not just increased RBC numbers. A HCT (or RBC count) may be seen
as a relative change, i.e., change in RBC numbers in relation to water
content. A relative increase in HCT is due to a decrease in body water
(e.g., dehydration) or RBC release from the spleen. Up to one third of
RBCs are stored in the splenic red pulp and can be released with
splenic contraction under the influence of epinephrine, although this
is uncommon in dogs and cats. Measurement of total protein
concentrations (high results expected) and rehydration of a
dehydrated animal with sequential testing to confirm persistence of a
high HCT are tools that can help distinguish between a relative and
absolute increase in HCT.

MECHANISMS OF ERYTHROCYTOSIS
Erythrocytosis is a true increase in RBC mass due to increased RBC
production (also called absolute increase in HCT). This can be
separated into a primary or secondary erythrocytosis. Primary
erythrocytosis can be inherited in some species (not dogs or cats) or
an acquired chronic myeloproliferative disorder, called polycythemia
vera. The latter is quite rare in dogs and cats (ch. 173).23,24 Up to
90% of human patients with polycythemia vera have a point
mutation in amino acid 617 (valine switched for phenylalanine) in

the JAK2 non-receptor tyrosine kinase, which is downstream of the
erythropoietin receptor.25 The mutation drives constitutive, usually
erythropoietin-independent, stimulation of erythropoiesis. Testing
for the JAK2 mutation is considered a major criterion for diagnosis
of polycythemia vera in the 2016 revised World Health Organization
scheme.26 A mutation in JAK2 has been identified in a dog with
polycythemia vera and may facilitate diagnosis of this rare disease23
(which is usually a diagnosis of exclusion; Figure 57.5). Secondary
erythrocytosis due to increased erythropoietin is a more common
cause of an increased HCT in dogs and cats than polycythemia vera.
Secondary erythrocytosis can be subclassified as appropriate or
inappropriate, which refers to the stimulus for erythropoietin
release. Appropriate release of erythropoietin occurs in hypoxic
conditions and can result in secondary erythrocytosis in dogs and
cats with respiratory or cardiac conditions.27 An inappropriate
release of erythropoietin is most frequently seen in renal disease but
it also is seen as a paraneoplastic response with renal and non-renal
neoplasia.28-31 High erythropoietin concentrations support a
diagnosis of secondary erythrocytosis but studies have shown an
overlap in erythropoietin concentrations with different causes of
erythrocytosis, limiting the usefulness of the test.32,33 Bone marrow
aspirates will not be informative because they will reveal an
erythroid hyperplasia with any cause of erythrocytosis (whether
primary or secondary), although core biopsies in humans with
polycythemia vera may show helpful features, such as
hypercellularity involving all lineages, hyperlobulation and
anisokaryosis of megakaryocytes, and lack of marrow iron.34
However, these features are not well-described for dogs or cats with
this neoplasm. Thus, differentiating between causes of erythrocytosis
requires other diagnostic tests geared at ruling out relative or
secondary causes.

INTRODUCTION
Peripheral blood leukocytes are primary components of the innate and
adaptive immune systems. As such, their numbers are dynamic and
affected by a large variety of stimuli. These stimuli include but are not
limited to: infection, inflammation, autoimmune disease, tissue damage,
parasitic infestation, and hormones. Leukocytes are produced

continuously, in a series of steps, from hematopoietic stem cells in the
bone marrow (ch. 176). These initially pluripotent stem cells are selfrenewing, but reproduce infrequently. They give rise to a variety of
common lymphoid and myeloid cell lines after progression from
hematopoietic stem cells to their respective progenitor cells,
differentiating further to result in more determined and restricted cell
lines. The bone marrow microenvironment of the precursor cells,
essential for hematopoiesis, is composed of endothelial cells, stromal
cells, adipocytes, osteoblasts, macrophages, lymphocytes, extracellular
matrix, and growth factors. The correct microenvironment, cell
interactions, and extracellular matrix attachments are requisite to
optimal proliferation, differentiation, and survival of hematopoietic stem
cells. Alterations to the microenvironment can dramatically impact
hematopoiesis.
Neutrophils in the bone marrow are included in two pools: a mitotic
pool and a maturation and storage pool. Myeloblast maturation and
release from the bone marrow generally takes about 6-9 days, but
maturation is expedited by certain inflammatory signals. Interleukins
(ILs)-1, 2, 3, 6 and 11; granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor
(GM-CSF); granulocyte colony stimulating factor (G-CSF); and stem cell
factor (SCF) are inflammatory mediators that stimulate neutrophil
production while GM-CSF, G-CSF, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and C5a
mediate release from the bone marrow. Monocytes originate from the
granulocyte-monocyte progenitor cell under the influence of IL-3, IL-34,
GM-CSF, and macrophage colony stimulating factor (M-CSF). Monocytes
are produced more quickly than granulocytes, and there is minimal
reserve in the marrow; replication rather than rapid release is responsible
for increases in monocyte numbers in the blood. Eosinophils are derived
from the eosinophil progenitor line under the influence of GM-CSF, IL-3
and IL-5 produced by activated T helper 2 (Th2) lymphocytes. Basophils
are produced from the bipotential basophil-mast cell progenitor under
the influence of IL-3, IL-5, GM-CSF, transforming growth factor-beta
(TGF-beta), and nerve growth factor. In addition to microenvironment
and cytokines, the role of microRNAs is under active study in regulation
of inflammation and hematopoiesis.
B lymphocytes, T lymphocytes and natural killer (NK) cells are derived
from combined lymphocyte progenitor cells under the influence of SCF,
FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3 ligand (Flt3L), insulin-like growth factor
(IGF) and IL-7. The Notch gene plays an important role in the B cell T
cell lineage switch. Lymphoblasts leave the marrow and migrate to the
thymus where they develop into T lymphocytes because of stimulation

from compounds in the thymic microenvironment, Notch gene product,
and growth factors including Flt3L and IL-7. NK cell production is not
entirely understood, but is thought to be stimulated by IL-2, IL-7, IL-15
and SCF. NK cells are produced in the bone marrow in approximately 7
days, and also can arise from the lymph nodes, liver and spleen.
The peripheral white blood cell count is a function of the rate of
production in the bone marrow, release from the bone marrow, the
proportion of cells in the marginated versus circulating pools, and the
rate of egress of white cells from the blood into the tissues. Peripheral
blood leukocytes are divided into approximately equal circulating and
marginated pools, although there is some species variation in the ratio.
The marginated cells are found rolling along the endothelium, preparing
to exit the circulation and migrate to target tissues. Marginated cells
interact with the vascular endothelium through interactions between Lselectins on leukocytes and P- and E-selectins on endothelial cells as well
as other cellular receptors. Marginated cells can return to the circulation
during times of increased blood velocity or due to the effects of cortisol or
epinephrine. Changes in the relative ratio of marginated to circulating
pools of cells will alter the white blood cell count, as only the central or
circulating pool is evaluated in the complete blood count (CBC).

LEUKOCYTOSIS
Because they are the most numerous and dynamic populations of white
cells, neutrophils and to a lesser extent lymphocytes are the cell lines
most commonly responsible for leukocytosis. Rarely, other cell lines
expand sufficiently to result in a leukocytosis. Exercise, epinephrine and
cortisol are associated with a mild to moderate increase in circulating
neutrophil count, largely due to shifts of cells from the marginal to the
circulating pools with a rapid return to baseline cell counts. The
neutrophil count should not be greater than twice the upper limit of its
reference interval, nor should it produce a left shift, from these
physiologic effects alone. Infection, inflammation and neoplasia are
associated with neutrophilia of varying magnitude with no clear cut-off
that is discriminatory between each category of disease.
As the inflammatory processes continue, increased demand for
neutrophils triggers an early release of neutrophils from the maturation
pool, resulting in a left shift toward more immature forms of neutrophils.
If the number of mature forms exceeds immature forms, the pattern is
known as a regenerative response. When the demand for neutrophils
exceeds the marrow’s capacity to provide mature neutrophils, increasing

ratios of immature forms are released, resulting in a degenerative left
shift. In both dogs and cats, degenerative left shift is most commonly
caused by infection and is associated with a more guarded prognosis,1-3
with a hazard ratio for the risk of death or euthanasia of 1.9 in affected
dogs1 and 1.75 in affected cats.3
Toxic changes are morphologic changes of neutrophils caused by
accelerated maturation. They may include: cytoplasmic basophilia, Döhle
bodies, increased vacuolization, decreased nuclear condensation and
increased granules (Figure 58.1). Neutrophilic leukocytosis with left
shift and/or toxic changes should raise suspicion of infection such as
peritonitis, pleuritis and pneumonia; however, the absence of a left shift
or toxic changes does not exclude infection, and non-infectious
inflammatory disease such as severe pancreatitis or hemolytic anemia
and others can be associated with neutrophilia, left shift, and toxic
change.
Severe leukocytosis (>35,000 cells/mcL) is often termed a leukemoid
response, although this term has generally fallen out of favor.4 Typically,
neutrophils are the predominant cell type involved with severe
leukocytosis, although other cells could be involved. The most common
causes of severe neutrophilic leukocytosis include infection, tissue
necrosis, neoplasia and immune-mediated disease (Table 58.1) (ch.
176).2,4,5 Other important differential diagnoses would include leukocyte
adhesion deficiency,6 paraneoplastic leukocytosis,7-9 Babesia
infection,10 Hepatozoon canis infection,11,12 immune-mediated
hemolytic anemia,13 and bacterial prostatitis.14
Lymphocytosis sometimes can be so profound as to cause a
leukocytosis. Physiologic lymphocytosis usually is mild. Increased
circulating concentrations of epinephrine, but not cortisol, results in a
lymphocytosis. Cats are more likely than are dogs to have reactive
lymphocytosis in response to inflammation.15,16 Lymphocytosis
secondary to inflammation is usually mild but can be 2-3 times the upper
limit of the reference interval.15 Lymphocytosis can occasionally be
associated with chronic infectious etiologies such as feline leukemia
virus, feline immunodeficiency virus, toxoplasmosis and Ehrlichia
canis.17 Hypoadrenocorticism is associated with lymphocytosis, but due
to concomitant neutropenia rarely results in leukocytosis. Lymphoma,
chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and acute lymphocytic leukemia
(ALL) can all be associated with marked leukocytosis (ch. 322). Because

the cells in CLL are mature, distinction between reactive lymphocytosis
and CLL may require advanced techniques like immunophenotyping or
clonality testing via polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for antigen receptor
rearrangements (PARR). Leukemic lymphoma can be difficult to
distinguish from ALL, though nodal infiltration is less common with ALL
and the lymphocyte count associated with ALL tends to be greater.
Eosinophilia and monocytosis are an uncommon causes of leukocytosis.
The main categories of disease resulting in eosinophilia are parasitism,
hypersensitivity reactions, mastocytic disease, hypoadrenocorticism,
hypereosinophilic syndrome, and occasionally lymphoid neoplasia.
Chronic granulomatous disease can cause moderate to severe
monocytosis. Other causes of monocytosis include chronic infections.
Myelomonocytic leukemia is a rare cause of leukocytosis and frequently is
associated with concurrent neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.

LEUKOPENIA
Because neutrophils make up the largest fraction of the white cell count,
leukopenias most commonly are secondary to neutropenia. Though

reference ranges vary by lab, neutropenia is generally a neutrophil count
<3000 cells/mcL (<3 × 109 cells/L, <3 × 106 cells/mL).16 Neutropenia is
classified as mild when the neutrophil count is 1500-3000 cells/mcL,
moderate if it is 500-1500 cells/mcL, and severe if it is <500 cells/mcL.
Severe neutropenia frequently is associated with fever and opportunistic
infection, since neutrophils are first-line defenders against a variety of
pathogens. Therefore, any animal with moderate to severe neutropenia
and a fever should be treated emergently. Conversely, severe infections
can cause neutropenia, making cause-and-effect sometimes challenging
to discern. Increased demand of neutrophils secondary to pneumonia,
peritonitis, ulcerative dermatitis, and viral and fungal infections all have
been identified as causes of neutropenia in dogs and cats (Table 58.2).18
General mechanistic causes of neutropenia include decreased marrow
production, increased peripheral usage, vascular sequestration
(anaphylaxis and sepsis), and immune-mediated destruction of either
mature neutrophils in the periphery or in marrow reserves, or immature
precursors (E-Figure 58.2).19 Causes of peripheral neutrophil usage
include severe infections (bacterial, viral or fungal), and specifically,
septic peritonitis, pyometra, pyothorax and enteric salmonellosis among
others.20 Inflammatory diseases like pancreatitis, bile peritonitis, organ
torsion or tissue infarction also can cause neutrophil migration. Most of
these conditions can result in neutrophilia; however, if demand exceeds
production of neutrophils, neutropenia could result.18 Neutrophils follow
a cytokine and haptenic pathway composed of C5a, CXCL-8, leukotriene
B4, and platelet activating factor among other signals to the site of
inflammation.21,22 Decreased bone marrow production of neutrophils or
other cell lines occurs secondary to failure of the elements of the
hematopoietic niche. Drugs like chloramphenicol, azathioprine,
phenobarbital, phenylbutazone, methimazole, sulfa derivatives and
others have been linked to neutropenia and other cytopenias.23
Additionally, chemotherapy or neoplastic infiltration of the bone marrow
results in marrow hematopoietic suppression or collapse.24-26 Chronic
idiopathic or benign neutropenia in cats can result in mild to moderate
neutropenia occasionally with counts less than 1000/mcL but should not
be associated with a left shift, toxic changes, clinical signs, or evidence of
recurrent infection.

Lymphopenia is rarely a cause of leukopenia but could contribute to a
reduction in leukocyte count. Lymphopenia is most commonly due to
viral infection, or the effect of glucocorticoids in ill animals. A decrease in
circulating monocytes, eosinophils or basophils rarely result in
leukopenia because they account for a minor percentage of leukocytes.

APPROACH TO EVALUATION OF
LEUKOCYTOSIS AND LEUKOPENIA
Leukocytosis and leukopenia are common findings on the CBC.
Therefore, a systematic approach to assessing leukocytosis or leukopenia
is essential. Changes in white blood cell counts generally are nonspecific
findings and rarely indicate a particular disease process. Rather, these
changes help alert the clinician of possible disease. Additionally, a normal
white blood cell count does not rule out infection, inflammation,
autoimmune disease or neoplasia.
The first step in assessment of the peripheral blood white cell count
should always include evaluation of hematology analyzer scattergrams,
overall absolute cell count, a cell differential count, and morphologic
description of the cells. Machine-generated differential cell counts can be
inaccurate; therefore, evaluation of the blood smear to determine a
differential cell count and evaluate cellular morphology is an
indispensable step in the diagnostic evaluation for any animal with

leukocytosis or leukopenia. Evaluation for possible causes of machine
interferences resulting in erroneous leukocytosis (e.g., Heinz bodies,
nucleated red blood cells, giant platelets, platelet clumps, cryoglobulins,
microorganisms) or leukopenia (e.g., leukocyte aggregation) should be
performed. During the initiation of inflammation, often a transient
leukopenia develops, either due to a shift in the leukocyte pool or when,
in cases of overwhelming inflammation, the demand for leukocytes
transiently exceeds the supply. Care should be taken to identify if
leukopenia is transient or persistent by serially evaluating white blood
cell count, the differential count, and morphology of the leukocytes. In
general, transient leukopenia due to acute inflammation resolves within
4-24 hours.

Discriminating among the possible causes of leukocytosis and
leukopenia (E-Figure 58.2) requires identification of the specific
pattern of cells affected, coupled with the clinical history (ch. 2) and
physical examination findings (ch. 3). A complete history (clinical signs,
past or recent illnesses, exposure to toxic substances, medications,
trauma, travel [ch. 9], vaccination [ch. 185], infection exposure) and
completion of a thorough physical examination allow the clinician to
prioritize differential diagnoses. Exam findings of fever or hypothermia,
scleral injection, lymphadenomegaly, organomegaly, effusions, abscesses,
or heart murmurs are particularly important. A serum biochemical
profile and urinalysis should be reviewed to look for clues not identified
on physical examination. Based on the information gained, a list of likely
differential diagnoses can be assembled. Then, a logical approach can be
planned for additional diagnostics such as imaging with radiographs,
ultrasound, or computed tomography; serologic titers; aspiration or
biopsy of enlarged or morphologically altered organs or effusions; cardiac
ultrasound; microbial cultures of blood, urine, effusions, or purulent
material; or bone marrow aspiration for cytologic evaluation or core
biopsy for histologic assessment, as indicated. Bone marrow aspiration or
biopsy (ch. 84) frequently is indicated in instances of suspected
leukemia or when persistent leukopenia, bicytopenia, or pancytopenia is
identified. Specialized tests like flow cytometry, PARR, and antineutrophil antibody testing can be employed to identify neoplasia or
immune-mediated neutropenia if indicated.27,28 The diagnosis of chronic
idiopathic or benign neutropenia in cats should only be considered after

ruling out retroviral infections and other causes of neutropenia if
indicated. In the absence of retroviral infection or other indicators of
disease, bone marrow assessment is not indicated, as no abnormalities
are typically found in cats with chronic idiopathic or benign neutropenia.

CHAPTER 59:
Thrombocytopenia,
Thrombocytosis
Marjory B. Brooks

A C RO N YM S
DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation
ITP immune-mediated thrombocytopenia
MPV mean platelet volume
TPO thrombopoietin
Quantitative defects of platelet number are detected as increased or
decreased platelet count in the hemogram and blood smear. A
consistent diagnostic strategy helps streamline differentiation among
the many primary and secondary disease processes that influence
platelet number.

PLATELET LIFE CYCLE
Platelets are small anucleate cell fragments produced from bone
marrow megakaryocytes. Platelets circulate for approximately 5 to 9
days in dogs and cats. The cytokine thrombopoietin (TPO) is the
major regulator of megakaryocyte maturation; however, additional
growth factors act synergistically with TPO.1,2 The liver is the
primary site of TPO synthesis, which upon release binds to a ligand
(c-Mpl) expressed on megakaryocytes and platelets. As platelet count

falls, free TPO levels increase to stimulate thrombopoiesis.
Conversely, as platelet count rises, free TPO falls and thrombopoiesis
slows. Platelet mass is further regulated through clearance of
senescent platelets lacking sialic acid residues by engagement with
hepatocyte Ashwell-Morell receptors and subsequent increased TPO
production.3
Platelets in circulation undergo transient splenic sequestration.
Approximately one third of total platelet mass is compartmentalized
within the spleen in healthy individuals.2 Prothrombotic and
inflammatory stimuli induce platelet activation and incorporation
into a hemostatic plug or egress into tissues from the
microvasculature. Non-activated platelets undergo gradual apoptotic
death and subsequent clearance by hepatic and splenic
macrophages.4
Disease processes that upset the balance of platelet production,
activation, and clearance result in an increase or decrease in platelet
count. Thrombocytopenia is among the most common acquired
bleeding disorders in small animal practice, whereas thrombocytosis
is typically identified as a laboratory abnormality without specific
clinical signs.

DIAGNOSIS OF THROMBOCYTOPENIA
CLINICAL SIGNS
The characteristic signs of thrombocytopenia include petechiae,
ecchymoses, mucosal hemorrhage (e.g., epistaxis, hematemesis,
hematuria, melena; ch. 29) and prolonged bleeding after injury
(chs. 29 and 124). Signs may overlap with those of acquired or
hereditary platelet dysfunction (ch. 175), coagulopathies (ch. 171),
von Willebrand disease (ch. 175), vasculopathies (ch. 181), or
vascular injury. A platelet count is indicated to confirm
thrombocytopenia and guide subsequent testing. While risk of
bleeding is not strictly correlated with platelet count,
thrombocytopenia is rarely the sole cause of severe or spontaneous
hemorrhage at counts above 30,000/mcL. Hemorrhage may be
exacerbated, however, by concurrent coagulation disorders or
vascular defects.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
Platelet Count and Blood Smear Examination
Platelet number for healthy dogs and cats ranges from approximately
200,000 to 500,000/mcL.1,2,5 Hematology analyzers also measure
mean platelet volume (MPV), an indicator of platelet size that may be
useful in characterizing and monitoring thrombocytopenia. Speciesspecific reference intervals should be developed for in-house
methods or provided by each testing laboratory (Table 59.1).
Thrombocytopenia detected by manual or automated count should
prompt a careful blood smear examination.
Blood smear examination confirms a low platelet number and
rules out spurious thrombocytopenia. Platelets are highly reactive
and subject to activation and clumping in the process of blood
collection or storage.6 These artifacts are minimized by atraumatic
venipuncture, blood collection directly into anticoagulant, limited
storage time, and avoidance of cold temperatures. After review of the
smear edges to detect platelet margination, platelet count is
estimated from counting 10 oil immersion fields (100×) on the blood
film monolayer as follows: platelet count (per mcL) = average
platelets/field × 15,000.2

Ancillary Diagnostics
Hemogram and blood smear review should be followed by thorough
drug and travel history (ch. 9), physical examination (ch. 3) to
include funduscopic examination (ch. 13), and evaluation of spleen,
liver, and lymph nodes. Subsequent work-up may include bone
marrow examination (ch. 84), serologic or direct detection of
pathogens (ch. 183), imaging with collection of cytology or biopsy
specimens, and coagulation testing (ch. 170; Table 59.2).

CLASSIFICATION OF
THROMBOCYTOPENIA (FIGURE 59.1)
Patients with a variety of systemic diseases may develop transient,
mild to moderate thrombocytopenia (platelet count 100,000 to
150,000/mcL) that resolves as the patient recovers.7,8 In contrast,
persistent or progressive thrombocytopenia indicates ongoing
imbalance in platelet production or consumption, or more complex
combined defects.

Production Defects
Thrombocytopenia combined with leukopenia and/or anemia is
often an indicator of defective hematopoiesis caused by an
underlying bone marrow disorder.2,7,9 High MPV and thiazole
orange-stained or “reticulated” platelets are characteristic of newly

released platelets; however, direct examination of the bone marrow
is the best means to evaluate thrombopoiesis.8-10
• Infiltrative disorders: bone marrow infiltration by neoplastic
cells typically results in hematopoietic failure and systemic
signs resulting from thrombocytopenic hemorrhage. The
clinical course, hemogram, and bone marrow examination are
used for classification of acute versus chronic leukemia and
lymphoid versus myeloid leukemia (ch. 322).2,9,11 Beyond
cell morphology, immunophenotyping to define cell surface
markers provides more detailed classification.5,10 Bone
marrow exam may reveal non-leukemic neoplastic infiltrates,
e.g., lymphoma, multiple myeloma, mast cells, histiocytes, and
metastatic carcinoma.9,12 Clonal expansion of hematopoietic
precursors (myelodysplasia) also causes dysregulated cell
maturation and cytopenias.12
• Myelofibrosis describes a non-cellular, fibrous matrix that
replaces bone marrow stroma. Myelofibrosis results from
excessive proliferation of bone marrow fibroblasts in response
to injury. Inciting causes of myelofibrosis include chronic drug
therapy, hemolytic anemia, bone marrow neoplasia, and
prolonged inflammation.
• Drug toxicosis: drug-induced thrombocytopenia may result
from bone marrow suppression or immune-mediated
destruction (chs. 138, 175, 176).13 Drugs with stem cell toxic
effects cause pancytopenias, although signs of
thrombocytopenia may develop first. Thrombocytopenia is a
known side-effect of many chemotherapeutic agents (ch.
321), and is a complication of drugs such as estrogen,
chloramphenicol, methimazole, penicillin, procainamide, and
sulfa antibiotics13,14 (Box 59.1).
• Infectious thrombocytopenias: infectious agents may cause
bone marrow suppression, peripheral platelet activation or
sequestration, and immune-mediated destruction (ch. 183).
The prevalence of infectious thrombocytopenias is increasing

due to pet-friendly travel and international pet adoption (ch.
9), suburbanization, and climate change–induced vector
range expansion15-17 (Box 59.2). In addition to
thrombocytopenia, infectious agents often cause systemic
illness. Disease diagnosis is based on these physical exam and
laboratory abnormalities and pathogen-detection (e.g.,
antigen assays, PCR amplification, isolation and culture, direct
visualization) and/or antibody assays that measure host
immune response to the infectious agent.
• Endocrine disorders: estrogen is bone marrow suppressive in
dogs and may cause severe thrombocytopenia or
pancytopenia.14 Functional ovarian granulosa cell tumors and
Sertoli cell tumors produce excess endogenous estrogen and
are typically diagnosed and treated through examination and
surgical excision (ch. 315). Although now uncommon, drug
history may reveal exogenous estrogen prescribed for
pseudopregnancy, mismating, incontinence, or prostatic
hypertrophy. Hypothyroidism is associated with general bone
marrow depression; however, clinically relevant
thrombocytopenia is unlikely to occur due to thyroid
insufficiency alone (ch. 285).
• Hereditary thrombocytopenias (ch. 169): a large survey of
Greyhounds revealed a subclinical, mild reduction in platelet
count.18 A more severe hereditary macrothrombocytopenia of
Cavalier King Charles Spaniels is caused by aberrant platelet
microtubule assembly due to a point mutation in the beta1
tubulin gene.19 The same mutation has been identified in
other, unrelated breeds including Chihuahuas, Labrador
Retrievers, and Shih Tzus. Homozygotes have high MPV and
platelet counts from 25,000 to 75,000/mcL. A second, distinct
beta1 tubulin mutation was found in Norfolk and Cairn
Terriers.20 A beta1 tubulin structural variant unique to felids
is also speculated to cause the relatively wide variation in
platelet size and count in domestic cats.21 In spite of low
count, platelet mass is preserved in macrothrombocytopenic
defects and the traits do not cause a bleeding tendency or
require therapy.

FIGURE 59.1 Algorithm for low platelet count.
CBC, Complete blood count.

Destruction and Consumption Defects

Excessive platelet activation, sequestration, or targeted destruction
may exceed the bone marrow’s capacity to maintain platelet
numbers. Among these mechanisms, immune-mediated destruction
is often associated with the most severe thrombocytopenia (<
20,000/mcL).7,9,22
• Immune mediated destruction: primary immune-mediated
thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune disorder with
production of antibodies directed against normal, “self”
platelet antigens (ch. 175).22,23 Secondary immune
thrombocytopenias are associated with an underlying disorder
(e.g., infection, neoplasia, drug exposure, transfusion) that
introduces neoantigens or upsets the host’s immune
balance.7,24 Anti-platelet antibody assays screen for
antibodies bound to the patient’s platelets (platelet surface
immunoglobulin [PsAIg]) or circulating antibodies capable of
binding platelets.25 However, these assays do not differentiate
primary from secondary ITP, and non-specific platelet
antibody binding further limits their clinical utility. Primary
ITP is uncommon in cats. Case series of canine ITP indicate a
disease of middle-aged dogs, over-representation of females,
and breed predispositions (Cocker Spaniels, Poodles, Old
English Sheepdogs).22,26 The diagnosis is typically based on
combined clinical and laboratory criteria: exclusion of
underlying disease, severe thrombocytopenia (<
50,000/mcL), normal to increased megakaryopoiesis, and
response to immunosuppressive therapy.
• Platelet activation and consumption defects: platelet activation
and depletion accompany infectious and non-infectious
vasculitides through thrombus formation and egress from the
vascular space (ch. 181). Hemophagocytic syndrome refers to
a non-neoplastic expansion of activated macrophages and
lymphocytes leading to cytokine-mediated cell destruction.
Thrombocytopenia is a common feature of endotheliotropic
pathogens and is often present in cats with feline coronavirus
immune-complex vasculitis (ch. 200).25,27 Snake venoms

may directly activate platelets and indirectly result in
activation and clearance due to tissue injury and vascular
leakage.28 Progressive platelet consumption is a feature of
disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC; ch. 171).28,29
Diagnosis of consumptive and activation defects usually
involves characterization of a DIC process through coagulation
testing and screening for an underlying infectious agent,
neoplastic disorder, or inflammatory syndrome. Although
uncommon in companion animals, ex vivo platelet activation
and thrombocytopenia may result from extracorporeal
circulation procedures.30,31
