• Sequestration defects: diseases that cause splenic enlargement
may result in platelet sequestration and clearance, or
hypersplenism (ch. 182).2,7 Diagnostic efforts are based on
the differentials for splenomegaly such as infectious agents,
neoplasia (often mast cell, lymphoma, hemangiosarcoma),
and congestion secondary to portal hypertension or heart
failure.

Dilutional Defects
Rapid administration of high volume resuscitation fluids, plasma
expanders and massive transfusion with plasma or packed cells
(replacement of > 1 blood volume in 1 day, > 50% blood volume in 4
hours) may result in decreased platelet count.32 Although
uncommon, dilutional thrombocytopenia may be severe enough to
impair in vivo hemostasis.

DIAGNOSIS OF THROMBOCYTOSIS
(FIGURE 59.2)

Mild to moderate increases in platelet count often develop as a
“reactive” bone marrow response to chronic blood loss or
inflammation that is mediated by cytokine release. Paraneoplastic
thrombocytosis may also develop in response to tumor-origin
cytokines.33,34 Reactive thrombocytosis requires no treatment
beyond correction of the underlying disorder. Autonomous (primary)
thrombocythemia is characterized by marked elevation in platelet
count (>900,000/mcL) and is a feature of rare, potentially fatal
myeloproliferative disease. Essential thrombocythemia refers to a
clonal disorder specifically affecting megakaryocyte maturation.35,36

CLINICAL SIGNS
Signs of primary, essential thrombocythemia typically include fever,
splenomegaly, anemia, thrombosis, and hemorrhage. In contrast,
reactive thrombocytosis is characterized by the inciting disease
process with no specific signs caused by the high platelet count.37,38

DIAGNOSIS OF THROMBOCYTOSIS
The presence of thrombocytosis should first be confirmed by a repeat
hemogram and review of blood smear, followed by appropriate workup to identify an underlying disorder.34,37-39 Non-pathologic high
platelet counts may persist after splenectomy. Primary
thrombocythemia is diagnosed by bone marrow examination, often
with assessment of iron stores to rule out iron deficiency. In human
medicine, molecular genetic analyses of growth-promoting
oncogenes are included in the work-up of myeloproliferative
disorders, and similar analyses may prove useful in veterinary
medicine.36,40

CLASSIFICATION OF
THROMBOCYTOSIS

Primary (Essential) Thrombocythemia
Essential thrombocythemia refers to an isolated increase in platelet
count; however, thrombocytosis may be a prominent feature of other
myeloproliferative disorders including myeloid leukemias (ch. 322),
polycythemia (ch. 173), and myelodysplastic syndrome (ch.
176).35,36 The presence of driver mutations in JAK2, CALR, and
MPL are common to all of these syndromes.

Secondary (Reactive) Thrombocytosis
A general upregulation of cytokine growth factors, including TPO, is
the presumed cause of reactive thrombocytosis.1,34 Chronic blood
loss, infection, inflammation, malignancy, and tissue necrosis are
among the disease processes associated with this response. Occult
neoplasia and gastrointestinal or urinary blood loss may require
concerted diagnostic efforts including careful imaging to identify the
inciting cause of persistent thrombocytosis.

THE MAJOR CIRCULATING PROTEINS
Plasma proteins are responsible for maintaining oncotic pressure
and acting as “blood carriers” for hormones, metals, ions, bilirubin,
fatty acids, drugs, and other insoluble organic substances. Transient
binding to proteins (usually albumin) allows substances to be carried
throughout the body via the vasculature. Plasma proteins have
significant roles in inflammation and immune responses. Plasma
proteins responsible for coagulation (primarily fibrinogen) are not
present in serum, which is the fluid obtained after clotted blood is
removed.

ALBUMIN
Albumin, the most abundant blood protein, comprises about half of
all plasma protein in health. It is synthesized in the liver, accounts
for roughly 80% of colloid oncotic pressure, and is the primary blood
carrier protein. Albumin assists in maintaining acid-base balance,
acting as a plasma buffer.

GLOBULINS
Non-albumin blood proteins are primarily “globulins,” which are not
measured in most routine serum biochemistry profiles.
Concentrations are determined by subtracting measured albumin
from measured total protein. There are several common globulin
categories of interest to internists, especially the alpha, beta, and
gamma globulins, each of which can be measured quantitatively by
serum protein electrophoresis (SPE).

ACUTE PHASE PROTEINS
Infectious or immune-mediated processes, acute or chronic
inflammation, trauma, or neoplasia can stimulate macrophage
release of cytokines, including interleukin-1, interleukin-6, and
tumor necrosis factor-alpha. These cytokines upregulate production
of a set of globulins referred to as “acute phase reactant proteins”
that include fibrinogen, C-reactive protein, serum amyloid A,
ceruloplasmin, haptoglobin, and others. These cytokines
simultaneously suppress production of negative acute phase
proteins, such as albumin and transferrin. Consequently, acute phase
reactions can be associated with a mild reduction in albumin
concentration and mild to moderate increases in total globulin
concentration. Clinically, acute phase responses are characterized
systemically by fever, leukocytosis, hypercortisolemia, decreased
thyroid hormones, and other metabolic changes.1

PATHOLOGICAL ALTERATIONS IN
PROTEINS
HEMORRHAGE AND PROTEIN-LOSING
ENTEROPATHIES (PLEs)
Hemorrhage (ch. 124) is given separate attention in this chapter
because it is always a consideration with plasma protein
abnormalities. Hemorrhage implies the simultaneous loss of all
contents of blood. Proteins remaining in the circulation maintain
their ratios. If after losing blood, a pet is rehydrated with saline, for
example, all blood proteins are equally diluted and equally
decreased. Decreases in both albumin and globulins are also noted in
some PLEs (ch. 262). Maintenance of “normal” albumin/globulin
ratios is of value to note, since in most disease conditions albumin
and/or globulin concentrations may increase or decrease, but not
often in the same direction.

HYPOALBUMINEMIA (Figure 60.1)
Leakage From the Vasculature
Abnormally low circulating albumin concentrations result from
excess loss or decreased production. Rarely, albumin may be
decreased secondary to overhydration. As the smallest protein,
albumin is lost from the circulation in far greater quantities than
other proteins in many conditions. Significant decreases in serum
albumin concentration (<1.5 g/dL [<15 g/L]) lower the plasma
oncotic pressure, allowing fluid (water) to leak from the vasculature.
Severe hypoalbuminemia can result in pleural effusion (ch. 220) or
ascites (ch. 21), sometimes both. Less commonly, water can leak
from the vasculature into the subcutaneous space, creating pitting
edema (ch. 30). Albumin can leak through diseased gastrointestinal
(GI) surfaces (ch. 262), abnormally porous glomeruli (ch. 302),
severe exudative skin lesions including burns, vasculature altered by
inflammation (vasculitis, ch. 181), or into fluid accumulating in the
thoracic or abdominal cavities (“third spacing”).

Antithrombin
Loss of albumin is typically accompanied by loss of the similarlysized antithrombin (AT), placing pets with marked
hypoalbuminemia at risk for thromboembolic complications (ch.
171).

Decreased Production
Decreased albumin production is usually observed when >80% of
healthy hepatocytes are lost. Severe hepatic dysfunction is associated
with portosystemic shunt (PSS, ch. 267), cirrhosis (ch. 270), cancer
(ch. 275), chronic hepatitis (ch. 270), and other conditions.2,3
Although PSS is commonly diagnosed in young animals, some are
older when diagnosed, explaining why it should remain a differential
diagnosis in adults with hypoalbuminemia.2 Mild to moderate
hypoalbuminemia may be seen with chronic underfeeding or due to
downregulation of production as occurs with increases in acute
phase proteins or secondary to hyperviscosity syndrome (HVS).

Specific Causes
A pet with PLE or protein-losing nephropathy (PLN) may have
profound hypoalbuminemia (<2 g/dL [<20 g/L]) and complications
that include ascites, pleural effusion, peripheral edema, or
thromboembolic complications due to the concurrent loss of AT. GI
loss of albumin is common in pets with acute hemorrhagic diarrhea
syndrome (“hemorrhagic gastroenteritis”), parvoviral enteritis,
severe endoparasitism, or after severe acute vomiting and diarrhea.
Hypoadrenocorticism is commonly associated with mild to moderate
hypoalbuminemia, but occasionally its severity is similar to that in
PLE.5-7 Most pets with a glomerulopathy exhibit low serum albumin
and AT concentrations.
If a pet has “third-spacing” of fluid, one must depend on severity of
hypoalbuminemia together with analysis of the fluid protein content
to differentiate whether an effusion is the cause or the result of low
albumin concentrations. Serum albumin concentrations >1.5-2
mg/dL (>15-20 g/dL) usually do not result in significant effusion
unless concurrent portal hypertension is present. Effusions due to

hypoalbuminemia typically have a extremely low total protein values.
Fluid protein concentrations >2.5-3 g/dL (>25-30 g/L) are
consistent with an exudative process, mild hypoalbuminemia due to
third spacing and vasculitis (ch. 71).

Diagnosis
The diagnostic approach to hypoalbuminemia includes ruling out
obvious causes, e.g., exudative skin lesions, and careful evaluation of
the complete blood count, serum chemistry profile, and urinalysis
(Figure 60.1). Albumin concentrations <2.5 and >2.1 g/dL (<25
and >21 g/L) are considered mildly low, values 1.5-2.0 g/dL (15-20
g/L) are moderately low, and concentrations <1.5 g/dL (<15 g/L) are
severely low. Hypocholesterolemia may be seen with PLE, hepatic
dysfunction, and hypoadrenocorticism.3,6,8,9 Some PLN are
associated with hypercholesterolemia.10 PLN can be ruled out if the
urine protein to creatinine ratio is <2.0. Hypoadrenocorticism is
unlikely if the baseline serum cortisol concentration is >2 mcg/dL
(>55 nmol/L). If <2.0 mcg/dL (<55 nmol/L), an adrenocorticotropic
hormone (ACTH) stimulation test may be indicated. Significant liver
disease including PSS can be identified using postprandial serum
bile acids and/or blood ammonia. Intestinal loss can be difficult to
rule out even in the absence of GI signs and testing fecal alpha-1
protease or obtaining GI biopsies may be indicated (ch. 262).8,9

HYPOGLOBULINEMIA
Decreased globulin concentrations are seen in juveniles if adult
reference ranges are used. Low globulin concentrations are also seen
with specific immune deficiencies (ch. 180). SPE can be utilized as a
diagnostic aid in humoral immunodeficiencies.

HYPERPROTEINEMIA
Hyperalbuminemia

“Apparent” increases in albumin occur secondary to volume
contraction or dehydration, but pathological hyperalbuminemia is
not a distinct entity.

Hyperglobulinemia
Most pets with hyperproteinemia have hyperglobulinemia.
Hyperglobulinemia has been reported in Basenji dogs with
immunoproliferative enteropathy and in dogs with intestinal
histoplasmosis.11 Pets with multiple myeloma or infectious causes of
glomerulonephritis (GN), e.g., Lyme nephritis or ehrlichiosis, may
have increased serum globulin concentrations.10 Potential
mechanisms for excess globulins include the release of acute phase
proteins and any systemic antigen stimulation. These cause
“polyclonal gammopathies,” which are to be distinguished from
excess production of a single globulin, called “monoclonal
gammopathies” (Figure 60.2). The classic monoclonal
gammopathy is caused by multiple myeloma. Less commonly,
inflammatory or infectious diseases that are usually associated with a
polyclonal gammopathy develop, instead, a monoclonal gammopathy
(Figure 60.3).12,13
Performing a SPE may be indicated when hyperglobulinemia
cannot be attributed to an obvious cause or when extreme (>5.0
mg/dL [50 g/L]). SPE separates proteins based on size and electrical
charge into four fractions: albumin, alpha globulins, beta globulins,
and gamma globulins. SPE result should include an image of the
tracing (electrophoretogram) and the specific concentrations of each
protein. Although SPE results do not provide a definitive diagnosis,
identifying the fraction(s) most increased can help focus the
diagnostic approach. Polyclonal gammopathies have a broad peak
made up of beta and gamma globulins, consistent with acute phase
protein elevations, or an inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic, or
immune-mediated process. A monoclonal gammopathy has a narrow
peak or “spike” in the beta or gamma region, most commonly
associated with lymphocyte or plasma cell neoplasms (multiple
myeloma, macroglobulinemia, lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic
leukemia). After identification of a monoclonal or polyclonal
gammopathy, the diagnostic approach can be tailored to include

specific infectious disease testing or obtaining bone marrow, lymph
node, liver or spleen aspirates or biopsies to make a definitive
diagnosis.

reduced flow to tissues. Complications of HVS include hemorrhage,
often manifested as epistaxis, bleeding from the gums, retinal
hemorrhage, hyphema, or neurological signs of depressed mentation,
ataxia, or seizures.14,15

HYPOGLYCEMIA
IS THE TEST RESULT ACCURATE?
Proper Collection
Blood glucose (BG) measurement at a veterinary diagnostic reference
laboratory is the gold standard. Serum or plasma must be separated
promptly from blood cells or blood should be collected in fluoride
oxalate or citrate buffer tubes to prevent continued in vitro glucose
utilization by red and white blood cells (Figure 61.1).1

Low Blood Glucose (BG) Test Result
A common reason for an inaccurately low BG is prolonged sample
storage in serum or lithium heparin tubes prior to centrifugation.
Results will also be decreased if either fluoride oxalate or citrate
buffer tubes are not filled to the draw line. Capillary tubes are

recommended for small volumes. Use of benchtop in-clinic
biochemistry analyzers can facilitate processing of samples to avoid
in vitro decreases, but these analyzers are not subject to the same
quality control as those in a reference laboratory and results might
not be reliable. Severe polycythemia or leukocytosis may also be
associated with in vitro hypoglycemia.

Low BG on a Portable Blood Glucose Meter (PBGM)
Any dog or cat identified as hypoglycemic with a PBGM should have
its blood retested with a reference analyzer before pursuing further
diagnostic investigation. PBGMs designed for human blood often
underestimate the true BG concentration (BGc) in dogs and cats,
with the difference increasing as BG increases (chs. 78, 291, 292).2
Veterinary PBGMs provide more accurate results for dog and cat
blood than those designed for humans, but can falsely give
euglycemic results despite the presence of hypoglycemia. Other
factors that can affect accuracy of PBGMs include problems with test
strips, inadequate test strip filling or covering, medications such as
acetaminophen, and endogenous factors such as icterus and
hypertriglyceridemia. Anemia can be associated with a falsely
increased BG, potentially masking hypoglycemia, whereas
dehydration can result in falsely low BGs.

Low Fructosamine Result
Fructosamine is a measure of glycated plasma proteins that provides
an estimation of the average BGc over the preceding 2-3 weeks. Only
validated assay results from reference veterinary diagnostic
laboratories should be used because bench-top biochemistry
analyzer assays are less reliable. There also may be substantial
variation in results between reference laboratories. Any condition
that affects plasma albumin production or turnover can alter
fructosamine results. Results from lipemic and/or hemolyzed
samples are not reliable. Decreased fructosamine results are
obtained from samples contaminated with EDTA, citrate, or fluoride
oxalate; therefore, it is important to fill serum or heparin sample
tubes first.3

Low Glycated Hemoglobin Result
Glycated hemoglobin concentrations provide an estimate of the
mean BGc during the lifetime of erythrocytes (approximately 16
weeks in dogs and 10 weeks in cats). Results are provided as a
percentage of total hemoglobin and should be interpreted in context
of the packed cell volume (PCV) and/or routine hematology. Anemia
likely increases glycated hemoglobin results.

FIGURE 61.1 Variation of glucose concentration
in samples from healthy human subjects stored

Adv Clin Chem 2018;84:101-123.

Low Interstitial Glucose (IG) Result

Glucose concentrations in blood and interstitial fluid are not always
the same. Rapid changes in BG are not immediately reflected in IG
concentrations. IG monitor results have been reported to be less
“accurate” than BGc (ch. 78). While of some use in monitoring
diabetics, results with IG devices have not reliably discriminated
between euglycemia and hypoglycemia (Figure 61.2).4,5 The
devices do detect periods of low BG that might have been missed by
intermittent BG testing.6 Any low or unexpected result should be
rechecked by measuring BGc.

CLINICAL SIGNS OF HYPOGLYCEMIA
Potential presenting signs of hypoglycemia in dogs and cats are listed
in Box 61.1 and examples are provided in Videos 61.1, 61.2,7 and
61.3

.8 Signs may be acute or intermittent/episodic (ch. 289).

Individual episodes can vary dramatically. In healthy animals,
hypoglycemia initially causes an autonomic nervous system
response, which may manifest as tremor, anxiety, panting, or
hunger. If hypoglycemia persists, neuroglycopenic signs develop.
Hypoglycemic events with insulin treatment are now known to be
more common than previously realized because most are subclinical
(chs. 291, 292). Individuals experiencing frequent hypoglycemia,
even if episodes do not cause clinical signs, might lose their
“protective” autonomic response (hypoglycemic unawareness) and
neuroglycopenic signs may then develop quickly without warning.
Dogs and cats usually recover to normal after clinical hypoglycemia,
although transient or permanent brain damage can result from
severe episodes (Figure 61.3) and there is risk of death due to
misadventure or brain damage.

TREATING ACUTE HYPOGLYCEMIA
Dogs and cats in an acute hypoglycemic crisis require prompt
treatment to increase their BGc before any diagnostic investigation
can proceed. Treatment options include IV, trans-mucosal, or oral
administration of glucose/dextrose boluses to resolve signs, followed

by feeding (dogs) and/or constant rate IV infusion of
glucose/dextrose if needed (chs. 119, 155, 289). In contrast to
recommending that dogs be fed following a hypoglycemic episode,
feeding has not reliably increased the BGc in cats. Glucose syrup can
be added to cat food as cats cannot taste sweet foods.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Potential causes of hypoglycemia in dogs and cats are listed in Table
61.1. The differential diagnoses in physiologically normal and
diabetic animals can usually be established after learning the history;
their hypoglycemia usually resolves with time, but treatment to
increase BG is preferred. Thorough investigations are required for
pathologic causes of hypoglycemia (Figure 61.4). Suspicion of a
hypoglycemic episode 30 minutes to a few hours earlier is usually
based on learning owner observations. It is not always possible to
confirm earlier hypoglycemia after a pet has recovered, since their
hypoglycemia may have resolved or become less worrisome.
Diagnostic investigation for pathologic causes of hypoglycemia
should begin with screening via history, physical exam (PE),
hematology (complete blood count), serum biochemistry profile, and
urinalysis. Initially, one should focus on the most likely diagnoses
(Table 61.1), which might prompt tests such as an ACTH
stimulation test, bile acid test, or urine microbial culture (chs. 266,
289). Frequently, all results may be unremarkable, including
confirmation of hypoglycemia. Fructosamine or glycated hemoglobin
measurement might be helpful in those cases. If hyperinsulinism is
suspected, assay of serum/plasma insulin from the same blood
sample in which hypoglycemia was confirmed is indicated.9 This
may require a period of carefully monitored fasting (ch. 289).
Insulin assays should only be run at reference veterinary diagnostic
laboratories that participate in an external endocrine quality
assessment program. Each laboratory should establish its own
insulin reference intervals.

HYPERGLYCEMIA
INCIDENTAL HYPERGLYCEMIA
Mild hyperglycemia (100-180 mg/mL, 5-10 mmol/L) is typically
clinically silent and may be an incidental finding. While insulin
treatment is not required, mild hyperglycemia might indicate
subclinical diabetes mellitus (“pre-diabetes”) and warrant follow-up
monitoring (chs. 291 and 292). More severe hyperglycemia is
usually associated with one or more of the clinical signs of diabetes
mellitus (polydipsia, polyuria, polyphagia, weight loss), although
sometimes such signs are not reported before hyperglycemia is
identified. Potential causes of hyperglycemia in dogs and cats are
listed in Table 61.2.

DIAGNOSIS OF DIABETES MELLITUS
Current criteria developed by international consensus for diagnosis
of diabetes mellitus in dogs and cats (chs. 291, 292) are provided in
Box 61.2.10 Differentiation of stress hyperglycemia from diabetes
mellitus can sometimes be difficult, especially in cats. Measurement
with a PBGM of an ear prick sample obtained using minimal
restraint before further examination of a cat might provide a more
reliable result than laboratory testing of a venous sample collected
after examination and restraint. It is important to document both
persistent hyperglycemia and glucosuria to establish a diagnosis of
diabetes mellitus, because hyperglycemia differentiates diabetes
mellitus from primary renal glucosuria, whereas glucosuria
differentiates diabetes mellitus from other causes of hyperglycemia
(Table 61.2). Documenting an increase in serum fructosamine
concentration and/or glycated hemoglobin supports the presence of
sustained hyperglycemia; however, results within the reference
interval can occur in animals with clinical diabetes if the duration of
their disease is brief. IG monitoring may provide another option for
confirming persistent hyperglycemia (ch. 78).

GLYCEMIC VARIABILITY (BOTH
HYPOGLYCEMIA AND
HYPERGLYCEMIA) IN INSULINTREATED PATIENTS
The “Somogyi effect” is the term often used in veterinary medicine to
explain periods when both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia occur in
association with insulin treatment. A more appropriate term,
adopted in human medicine, is “glycemic variability.”11 There is no
evidence to support the proposed theory of “rebound” hyperglycemia
due to secretion of excessive counter-regulatory hormones following
hypoglycemia.12 Periods of hypoglycemia are likely caused by excess
exogenous insulin, whereas the mechanism(s) for the periods of
hyperglycemia are poorly understood and probably relate to the
multiple causes of hyperglycemia and insulin resistance in diabetes
mellitus. Dogs and cats with increased glycemic variability may
exhibit poor diabetic control due to the occurrence of frequent
hyperglycemia, whereas most of the hypoglycemic events are
associated with no clinical signs and would be missed by standard
intermittent BG monitoring. Nevertheless, the frequent
hypoglycemia can induce physiologic unawareness of hypoglycemia
and impaired glucose counter-regulation, which in turn predisposes
to increased risk of neuroglycopenia.13

ALIVE∗ Criteria for Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus in
Dogs
Diabetes mellitus in dogs is diagnosed:
1. In a patient with a random (fasted or unfasted) blood glucose
concentration ≥ 200 mg/dL (≥ 11 mmol/L) with classic
clinical signs of hyperglycemia (with no other plausible cause)
or hyperglycemic crisis
• In some cases clinical signs may not have been reported by
the owner.
• In cases with uncertainty over presence/absence of clinical
signs, diagnosis should be confirmed by repeat blood
glucose measurement and/or documentation of alternative
glycemic parameters such as increased glycated proteins
and/or glucosuria.
2. In some patients with fasting blood glucose concentration >
125 mg/dL to ≤ 200 mg/dL (> 7 mmol/L to ≤ 11 mmol/L)
with or without clinical signs of hyperglycemia or

hyperglycemic crisis, diabetes mellitus is differentiated from
stress hyperglycemia by documentation of persistent fasting
hyperglycemia for more than 24 hours or increased serum
glycated protein concentration.
ALIVE∗ Criteria for Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus in
Cats
The potential for stress hyperglycemia warrants caution in
interpretation of hyperglycemia of any magnitude in cats.
Diabetes mellitus in cats is diagnosed:
1. In a patient with a random (fasted or unfasted) blood glucose
concentration ≥ 270 mg/dL (≥ 15 mmol/L) with classic
clinical signs of hyperglycemia (with no other plausible cause)
or hyperglycemic crisis AND at least one of the following
criteria:
• increased serum glycated protein concentration
• glucosuria on more than one occasion on a naturally voided
sample acquired in a home environment at least 2 days
after any stressful events
In some cases clinical signs may not have been reported by the
owner.
2. In a patient with random (fasted or unfasted) blood glucose
concentration > 125 mg/dL to ≤ 270 mg/dL (> 7 mmol/L to ≤
15 mmol/L) and at least two of the following:
• classic clinical signs of hyperglycemia (with no other
plausible cause) or hyperglycemic crisis
• increased serum glycated protein concentration
• glucosuria on more than one occasion on a naturally voided
sample acquired in a home environment at least 2 days
after any stressful events
Applying the above ALIVE∗ criteria permits the possible
existence of a subpopulation of cats where diabetes mellitus or
stress hyperglycemia cannot be confidently confirmed or excluded;
if concerns over presence of diabetes mellitus persist, periodic reevaluation is warranted.

∗

Project ALIVE (Agreeing Language In Veterinary
Endocrinology) was founded by the European Society of
Veterinary Endocrinology in 2016 and endorsed by the Society
for Comparative Endocrinology in 2017, and focuses on
creating agreement over the definition of common terminology
in veterinary endocrinology.8

INTRODUCTION
Biomarkers are commonly used for early identification of
abnormalities within numerous body systems. For the urinary tract,
the gold standard for estimation of renal function is measurement of
the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) via inulin clearance or other

substances such as iohexol. Because measuring GFR is not widely
available, is costly, and is clinically cumbersome, endogenous
biomarkers have been identified to estimate GFR. These biomarkers
include blood urea nitrogen (BUN), serum creatinine (sCr), and
more recently, symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA). The ideal
properties of a renal biomarker include constant rate of production,
narrow biologic variability, complete filtration through the
glomerulus, no protein binding, no tubular secretion or reabsorption,
no non-renal metabolism, easy measurability, and cost-effectiveness.
None of the current renal biomarkers fit these criteria perfectly;
however, they still have significant clinical application despite their
drawbacks. Therefore, it is imperative to know the origins and
limitations of each endogenous biomarker in order to understand
their applicability in clinical practice.
Elevated concentrations of nitrogenous waste products such as
BUN and sCr above the reference interval is termed azotemia (chs.
299, 300, 301). The collection of clinical signs associated with
severe azotemia, such as nausea, vomiting, lethargy, hypothermia,
oral mucosal and gastrointestinal (GI) ulceration, melena,
encephalopathy, and seizures, is termed uremia. For the purposes of
this chapter, increases in all renal biomarkers will be referred to as
azotemia unless otherwise noted despite the fact that this term is not
truly inclusive of SDMA.

PHYSIOLOGY AND NON-RENAL
INFLUENCES
CREATININE
Creatinine is a breakdown product of creatine and creatine
phosphate in skeletal muscle. Its production rate is constant but is
dependent upon muscle mass of the individual patient. Thus breeds
with increased muscle mass (such as Greyhounds) will have higher
baseline creatinine values, and breeds or conditions with low muscle
mass (such as cachexia or sarcopenia) will cause lower baseline
creatinine values. Because muscle mass has such a large influence on
sCr, the sensitivity of detecting early azotemia can be confounded by
changes in muscle mass. Additional factors that may influence

baseline sCr include age (pediatric and geriatric), body size, and
thyroidal illness. Thyroidal illness may lead to higher sCr in
untreated hypothyroid dogs (ch. 285) and lower sCr in untreated
hyperthyroid cats (ch. 287).
Creatinine is freely filtered by the glomerulus, with no tubular
reabsorption in dogs and cats, although male dogs have small
quantities secreted by the renal tubules.1,2 Small quantities of sCr are
also excreted via the GI tract. Although most creatinine within the GI
tract is degraded by the enteric microbiome, small amounts of
previously excreted or dietary sources of creatinine are absorbed but
are unlikely to be clinically significant.3 Because of these properties,
creatinine is considered a more accurate estimation of GFR than is
BUN. In human medicine, formulae exist to calculate GFR using sCr
but attempts in veterinary medicine have proven to be inaccurate
due to significant breed and sex variations.4
Analytical challenges are present with interpreting sCr values
when performed on different analyzers or by different laboratories.
Accurate trending over time should be performed on the same
analyzer whenever possible to reduce variability of results.

BLOOD UREA NITROGEN (BUN)
Urea is a product of hepatic metabolism of endogenous sources of
ammonia, primarily consisting of digestion of dietary proteins and
breakdown of tissue proteins. It is freely filtered by the glomerulus,
but there is significant proximal tubular reabsorption of
approximately 60-65% of filtered urea. This is exacerbated under
conditions of slow tubular flow rates, allowing for greater
reabsorption. In the distal tubule, urea reabsorption is exacerbated
by increased tubular permeability to urea by the actions of
antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Urea is excreted into the intestinal
lumen where it is converted to amino acids and ammonia by the
intestinal microbiota. Other smaller sources of urea excretion occur
in saliva and sweat. Although these limitations as well as non-renal
influences discussed below make BUN a non-specific marker of GFR,
this process is paramount to establishing medullary hyperosmolality
for renal concentrating ability.

Non-renal influences that may lead to significant changes in
measured BUN concentration include increased protein metabolism
and uptake by the GI tract as well as catabolic processes leading to
increased urea synthesis by the liver. Increased GI absorption
includes both high protein diets as well as GI hemorrhage. Catabolic
diseases causing increased BUN concentrations include infection,
prolonged exercise, rhabdomyolysis, fever, glucocorticoid
administration, tissue necrosis, and starvation. These causes should
be investigated especially when there is a disproportionately
increased BUN concentration compared to creatinine. Diseases that
decrease BUN concentration primarily involve hepatic insufficiency
such as portosystemic shunts, cirrhosis, and prolonged acute liver
failure, or causes of polyuria.

SYMMETRIC DIMETHYLARGININE
(SDMA)
SDMA is synthesized by all nucleated cells by methylation of arginine
and is subsequently released into circulation. More than 90% of
SDMA is renally excreted via glomerular filtration, with no
significant tubular reabsorption or secretion, whereas the remainder
is thought to undergo enzymatic degradation.5 Studies have
established that SDMA inversely correlates with GFR measured by
inulin clearance and directly correlates with sCr in partially
nephrectomized dogs, making it a good candidate for use as an
endogenous biomarker.6 An advantage of SDMA as a renal
biomarker compared to sCr is that there is less interindividual
variability of SDMA compared to sCr in both dogs and cats. This
makes a single SDMA result more clinically useful when compared
against population-derived reference intervals.7,8
An advantage of SDMA is the lack of significant known non-renal
influences on SDMA concentration. Studies have demonstrated that
SDMA is minimally affected by mitral regurgitation, pancreatitis,
hyperthyroidism, changes in muscle mass, age, sex, and breed,9-16
with mild changes but further investigation needed for
hypothyroidism.17 Further investigation is necessary for non-renal

influences in veterinary species as non-renal influences such as
hepatic clearance in people18 and GI absorption in rats19 have been
documented.

GENERAL APPROACH TO BIOMARKER
ABNORMALITIES
Localizing disease source can aid in narrowing the differential list as
well as focusing diagnostic priorities. Localizing the cause of
azotemia is in reference to the nephron. Pre-renal (and non-renal)
azotemia is due to processes occurring proximal to the nephron,
renal azotemia includes the nephron, and post-renal azotemia
involves disorders occurring distal to the nephron. Differentiating
among these categories in an azotemic patient typically starts with
evaluation of the urinalysis and urine specific gravity (USG), which
reflect the ability of the kidneys to appropriately concentrate urine in
light of the current intravascular volume and hydration status of the
patient (ch. 70). Azotemia with a USG that is “appropriate” for the
current volume and hydration status of a patient indicates pre-renal
azotemia, whereas isosthenuria (USG of 1.008-1.012) or
inappropriate concentrating ability (USG <1.030 in the dog or
<1.035 in the cat) indicates renal azotemia. It is important to
acknowledge that the cause of azotemia may be multifactorial and
patients may have concurrent disease within multiple localizing
categories. Further evaluation of the urinalysis may provide
additional insight into the cause of azotemia based on the presence
or absence of proteinuria, glucosuria without hyperglycemia,
bilirubinuria, cylindruria, bacteriuria, and pyuria, although these
findings cannot be used definitively for localization of azotemia
(Figure 62.1).
Importantly, evaluation of the urinalysis alone does not provide
insight into non-renal and post-renal causes of azotemia. Ruling in
or out these categories necessitates incorporation of additional
biochemical, physical exam, historical, and diagnostic imaging
findings which will be discussed in later sections of this chapter.

PRE-RENAL CAUSES OF BIOMARKER
CHANGES
Pre-renal and non-renal causes of azotemia can be considered within
the same category but non-renal causes will not be discussed here as
they were previously covered. All causes of pre-renal azotemia
(excluding non-renal causes) share a common mechanism consisting
of reduced renal blood flow and subsequently GFR without intrinsic
renal disease. Decreased GFR reduces clearance of BUN, sCr, and
SDMA. In these states, USG will most commonly be high when renal
function is still adequate as these diseases typically cause
simultaneous ADH release and therefore water reabsorption in the
collecting ducts. Keep in mind that with diseases that cause pre-renal
azotemia, prolonged reduction in renal blood flow can eventually
cause renal damage secondary to renal hypoxia, leading to acute
kidney injury (AKI) and thereby adding a renal cause to the current
azotemia (ch. 300).
Broad mechanisms of reduced renal blood flow and thereby
decreased GFR include hypovolemia, decreased cardiac output, and
altered vasomotor tone leading to poor renal perfusion. Causes of
hypovolemia include dehydration, hemorrhage, shock, or loss of
fluids through mechanisms such as vomiting, diarrhea, thirdspacing, hypoadrenocorticism, and severe burns (ch. 119). Causes of
decreased cardiac output include cardiomyopathies (such as dilated
cardiomyopathy), sepsis, severe brady- or tachyarrhythmias,
anaphylaxis, and hypoadrenocorticism. Causes of altered vascular
tone primarily include sepsis and anaphylaxis. Despite pre-renal
azotemia being commonly viewed as a correctable problem, recent
data from human medicine has suggested a change in terminology to
“volume-responsive acute kidney injury” since these patients have
worse outcomes despite the absence of a renal source of azotemia
(ch. 300).20,21 Further investigation is warranted to know if this
finding is applicable to veterinary species, although initial
investigations utilizing this terminology have begun.22,23

BLOOD UREA NITROGEN (BUN) TO
SERUM CREATININE (sCR) RATIOS
Because there is a significant amount of urea reabsorption from the
tubules, especially in times of low tubular flow rate, BUN can
increase earlier and with a higher magnitude than creatinine. This
can be demonstrated by the BUN/sCr ratio; however, there are too
many factors that can alter this ratio to make it clinically relevant.

SDMA-SPECIFIC CONSIDERATIONS
There are minimal data specifically addressing the use of SDMA in
pre-renal causes of biomarker elevation. Because SDMA is a more
sensitive marker for decreased GFR, its circulating concentration will
also be elevated along with BUN and sCr, but to date there are no
studies to suggest additional benefit of measuring SDMA along with
the traditional markers of azotemia.

RENAL CAUSES OF BIOMARKER
CHANGES
Any disease process that results in reduction of renal functional mass
will cause reduction of GFR over time and ultimately azotemia.
Previous studies have documented an approximate 75% reduction in
renal functional mass necessary to result in azotemia.24-26 Azotemia
typically occurs after loss of concentrating ability of the renal
tubules, thereby resulting in an inadequate USG for the patient’s
current volume and hydration status. However, one study documents
that this relationship may not always be true in cats that can retain
concentrating ability despite the presence of renal azotemia.27,28
Categorical causes include loss of nephrons, decreased glomerular
patency, increased interstitial pressure, increased intratubular
pressure, or intravascular obstructive lesions.
Diseases to be considered with renal azotemia include chronic
kidney diseases (CKDs) (including glomerulonephritis and
interstitial nephritis) (ch. 301), AKI (causes include intoxications,

infectious diseases, pyelonephritis, sepsis) (ch. 300), embolic
disease (thromboembolism, septic emboli, neoplastic emboli; ch.
238), renal edema, and venous occlusive diseases such as neoplastic
invasion of the renal veins or caudal vena cava, caval thrombi, and
venous extraluminal compression. Further discussion of these
diseases can be sought in other chapters for more in-depth
discussion of pathophysiology, diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment.

BUN-SPECIFIC CONSIDERATIONS
BUN is reabsorbed by the tubules and also has significant extra-renal
influences that contribute to the final measured serum or plasma

values. Because of these factors, BUN is an insensitive and
nonspecific indicator of renal azotemia.

CREATININE-SPECIFIC
CONSIDERATIONS
Creatinine is the most commonly used renal biomarker to estimate
GFR, due to its increased specificity compared to BUN. However,
75% of functional renal mass must be lost prior to significant
changes to sCr, which corresponds to an average decrease in GFR in
dogs of 48%.10 This makes sCr an insensitive biomarker of renal
function. The International Renal Interest Society (IRIS) currently
uses creatinine as the primary marker for staging of CKD as well as
AKI (chs. 300, 301). Use of IRIS guidelines provides valuable
information regarding monitoring, treatment, and prognostication
for patients with either CKD or AKI. For patients with AKI, small
changes in sCr even within the reference interval can be indicative of
declining GFR even though sCr is an insensitive indicator of
declining GFR. For early detection of CKD, trending sCr over time
can improve the sensitivity by establishing a patient-specific baseline
(provided that muscle mass remains stable) because the intraindividual variability of sCr is lower than inter-individual
variability.29,30

SDMA-SPECIFIC CONSIDERATIONS
Studies have demonstrated that SDMA can increase with as little as
20-40% reduction in GFR.10 Therefore, SDMA is currently
considered a more sensitive indicator of declining GFR. It will
increase prior to changes in sCr and is independent of changes in
muscle mass.11,31 SDMA values increase above the reference interval,
on average, 17 months in cats and 9.8 months in dogs earlier than
increases in sCr for CKD patients.12,32 The IRIS has updated
guidelines to incorporate SDMA in staging of CKD but recommends
measurement concurrently with sCr (ch. 301). This

recommendation is supported by recent evidence that measuring
both SDMA and sCr identifies more patients with decreased GFR
than with either biomarker alone.33 Despite the current lack of
incorporation of SDMA into IRIS AKI staging guidelines, it can be
used for diagnosis of both CKD and AKI but is not able to
differentiate between the two.14

POST-RENAL CAUSES OF BIOMARKER
CHANGES
Post-renal azotemia indicates that the cause is distal to the
functional nephron. Categorical causes of post-renal azotemia
include obstructive diseases or leakage of urine from the urinary
tract where the urine is retained within the body (chs. 127, 306).
Mechanisms of azotemia secondary to obstructive diseases include
increased hydrostatic pressure within the glomerular capsule as well
as release of vasoactive substances such as prostaglandins and
angiotensin, which cause reductions in renal blood flow, all resulting
in decreased GFR. The mechanism of azotemia secondary to leakage
of urine is via passive reabsorption of creatinine and BUN, most
commonly across the peritoneal membrane.
Obstructive diseases can be diagnosed at the level of the renal
pelvis, ureters, ureterovesicular junction, and urethra (chs. 117, 306,
312). Ureteral occlusions are increasingly commonly recognized due
to advances in diagnostic imaging availability as well as increased
clinical awareness. Causes of ureteral occlusion in dogs and cats
include ureterolithiasis, blood calculi, iatrogenic ligation of ureters
during intra-abdominal procedures, and neoplasia. The
ureterovesicular junction can become occluded, most commonly by
neoplasia such as transitional cell carcinomas (TCC; ch. 330).
Urethral obstructive causes include calculi, urethral plugs in cats,
neoplasia such as TCC and prostatic carcinomas, herniation of the
urinary bladder through perineal hernias, or iatrogenic surgical
ligation, most commonly encountered during attempts to perform
orchiectomies of cryptorchid animals.
Urine leakage can occur from all levels of the urinary tract. Causes
include rupture secondary to trauma or prolonged obstruction,

iatrogenic surgical trauma (ligation of a ureter or urethra), renal
avulsion from trauma, or renal neoplasia.
The diagnosis of post-renal causes of azotemia is commonly made
by diagnostic imaging, physical exam findings (ch. 3), history (ch.
2), and evaluation of free peritoneal or retroperitoneal fluid (ch. 71).
Clinically, patients may be anuric or oliguric, but urine production
does not rule out post-renal azotemia. Likewise, the presence of
anuria/oliguria is not pathognomonic for post-renal azotemia as this
can be seen with some renal causes like AKI (chs. 299, 300).
Abdominal radiographs or an abdominal ultrasound exam
performed by a skilled ultrasonographer is typically sufficient for the
diagnosis, although cross-sectional imaging such as computed
tomography is occasionally necessary. When peritoneal or
retroperitoneal effusion is diagnosed, comparing fluid to blood
concentrations of creatinine and potassium can provide the
diagnosis of uroperitoneum/uroretroperitoneum. The fluid-to-blood
creatinine ratio is usually >2:1 with 86% sensitivity and 100%
specificity in dogs with uroperitoneum. A fluid-to-blood potassium
ratio is diagnostic of uroperitoneum with 100% sensitivity and
specificity if >1.4:1 in dogs or >1.9:1 in cats.34,35 Sensitivity and
specificity is not reported for abdominal fluid to blood ratios in cats.
When there is leakage of urine in areas of the body other than a body
cavity, as is the case with some urethral tears, sufficient free fluid
may not be obtainable but positive contrast urethrography is usually
adequate for the diagnosis. BUN is not used for the diagnosis of
urine leakage because it equilibrates among body compartments
more readily than creatinine. SDMA will be increased with postrenal causes of azotemia but has not been further investigated; thus,
any potential clinical advantage of measuring SDMA in this context
is currently unknown.

VLDL very low-density lipoprotein

DEFINITIONS AND TERMINOLOGY
Disorders of lipid metabolism are more common in dogs than in cats.
The term hyperlipidemia refers to an increased concentration of lipids
(i.e., triglycerides, cholesterol, or both) in the blood (serum or plasma).
Specifically, an increased blood concentration of triglycerides is
referred to as hypertriglyceridemia, while an increased blood
concentration of cholesterol is referred to as hypercholesterolemia.
Both triglycerides and cholesterol are transported in the blood
combined with specific proteins called apoproteins. The lipid-protein
complex is referred to as lipoprotein or apolipoprotein and the term
hyperlipoproteinemia is often used interchangeably with the term
hyperlipidemia. The term lipemia is used to describe the grossly visible
turbid or lactescent appearance of serum or plasma (Figure 63.1).
Lipemia is a result of moderate and severe hypertriglyceridemia
(typically > 200-300 mg/dL [>2.3-3.4 mmol/L]), but not
hypercholesterolemia or very mild hypertriglyceridemia. The terms
hypotriglyceridemia and hypocholesterolemia refer to decreased
concentrations of triglycerides or cholesterol in the blood, respectively.
Finally, the term dyslipidemia is a more general term, the use of which

is not limited to describing increases in blood lipid concentrations, but
rather any kind of disturbance in the quality and/or quantity of blood
lipids and/or lipoproteins.

FOUR CLASSES OF LIPOPROTEINS
Canine and feline lipoproteins can be divided into four major classes
based on their hydrated density after ultracentrifugation:
chylomicrons, very low-density lipoproteins (VLDLs), low-density
lipoproteins (LDLs), and high-density lipoproteins (HDLs).1-3 An
intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL) likely exists in cats. Several
subclasses of these major classes of lipoproteins exist in dogs and cats,
but their nature and clinical significance have not been fully elucidated.

METHODS AND ASSAYS
The most basic laboratory procedures for detection and evaluation of
lipid disorders are determinations of serum triglyceride and total
cholesterol concentrations typically measured with spectrophotometric
or enzymatic methods. Other tests have occasionally been used to
further characterize or investigate hyperlipidemia (mainly primary
hyperlipidemia). The chylomicron test is used to determine if lipemia is
due to chylomicrons, VLDL, or both (Figure 63.2). Lipemic serum
samples are left for 12 hrs undisturbed at 4°C. Due to their lower
density, chylomicrons (if present) float to the top and form a cream
layer.1,2 Absence of a cream layer indicates absence of chylomicrons. If
the serum below the cream layer is clear, hyperlipidemia is only due to
increased chylomicrons; turbidity indicates an excess of VLDL.

FIGURE 63.1 Lipemia. Serum samples with normal
triglyceride concentrations are clear (A). As the serum
triglyceride concentration increases, serum becomes
turbid (B) and ultimately lactescent (C). From

FIGURE 63.2 Chylomicron test. A, Lipemic serum
sample from an animal with hypertriglyceridemia
immediately after separation of the serum from the
clot. B, The same sample after overnight refrigeration
(chylomicron test). The formation of a cream layer due
to hyperchylomicronemia is obvious. The remaining

For the indirect measurement of plasma lipoprotein lipase activity,
serum triglyceride concentrations are measured before and 10 minutes

after giving 40-90 IU/kg heparin, IV.4 Heparin stimulates the release
of lipoprotein lipase from the capillary endothelium, leading to a
transient increase in the hydrolysis of chylomicrons and VLDLs. If
there is an obvious decrease in plasma triglyceride concentrations after
the administration of heparin, lipoprotein lipase is functional. No
change is an indirect indicator of decreased or absent lipoprotein lipase
activity.
Other tools for investigating lipids include lipoprotein
electrophoresis,5 ultracentrifugation,5,6 and measurement of specific
apoproteins. Lipoprotein electrophoresis and ultracentrifugation can
be performed in-clinic. Since apoprotein assays are not routinely
available, they are not discussed in detail. Commercially available
genetic testing for inherited forms of hyperlipidemia is not currently
available.

HYPERLIPIDEMIA (Table 63.1)
POSTPRANDIAL, PRIMARY VERSUS
SECONDARY
Postprandial hyperlipidemia is physiologic and usually resolves within
7-12 hrs after a meal.1,2 Therefore, serum lipid concentrations should
only be determined after a fast of at least 12 hrs and even longer might
be needed when assessing serum triglycerides.7 Persistent fasting
hyperlipidemia is abnormal and can be either primary or secondary to
other diseases or secondary to administration of some drugs.
Secondary hyperlipidemia is the most common pathologic form of
hyperlipidemia in both dogs and cats, usually the result of an endocrine
disorder, e.g., hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus (DM), or
hyperadrenocorticism (chs. 285, 291, 293).1,2,8-10 Hyperlipidemia can
also be the result of pancreatitis in dogs (ch. 276).1,11 When
concurrent diseases such as DM and hypothyroidism or use of certain
drugs are excluded, hypertriglyceridemia and hypercholesterolemia
occur infrequently (18% and 24%, respectively) as a result of
pancreatitis and are typically mild.12 Therefore, fasting hyperlipidemia

(especially when severe) in dogs with pancreatitis likely reflects
concurrent hyperlipidemia (primary or secondary). Several other
causes of secondary hyperlipidemia have been reported in dogs.1,3

PRIMARY LIPID ABNORMALITIES IN
DOGS
Primary lipid abnormalities in dogs are usually, but not always,
associated with certain breeds. Genetic differences in breeds from
different geographic regions is also important. Primary hyperlipidemia
is common in Miniature Schnauzers in the United States and Japan
(>30% of Miniature Schnauzers are affected based on one U.S.
study).13,14 Anecdotally, hyperlipidemia in Schnauzers is considerably
less common in Europe. Primary hyperlipidemia in the Miniature
Schnauzer is typically characterized by hypertriglyceridemia with or
without hypercholesterolemia.6 Primary hyperlipidemias have also
been reported in Shetland Sheepdogs (in Japan and possibly other

countries),14,15 Beagles,16 Briards,17 Rough-Coated Collies (United
Kingdom),18 and anecdotally in Doberman Pinschers and Rottweilers.

LIPID ABNORMALITIES IN CATS
Feline hyperlipidemia can be post-prandial, primary or secondary.2
Conditions responsible for secondary hyperlipidemia in cats are similar
to those in dogs: DM (ch. 292), obesity (ch. 150), nephrotic
syndrome (ch. 302), hypothyroidism (ch. 286),
hyperadrenocorticism (ch. 294), cholestasis, hepatic lipidosis (ch.
275), and other conditions (e.g., neoplasia).2 Corticosteroid or
megestrol acetate can induce hyperlipidemia. The primary
hyperlipidemias reported in cats include a form of inherited
hyperchylomicronemia (mainly reported in related colony cats) and
characterized by decreased lipoprotein lipase activity.19-21 Transient
hyperlipidemia in kittens is characterized by massive increases in
serum chylomicron and VLDL concentrations and sometimes
anemia.22,23 Hyperlipidemia of Burmese cats is characterized mainly
by postprandial hyperlipidemia.24,25

CLINICAL SIGNS AND SIGNIFICANCE OF
HYPERLIPIDEMIA
A systematic diagnostic approach is required to understand and
appropriately treat dogs with hyperlipidemia. Although hyperlipidemia
might not directly cause obvious clinical signs, it has been shown to be
associated with development of other diseases that are clinically
important and potentially life-threatening (Table 63.2), e.g., severe
hypertriglyceridemia is a risk factor for canine, but not feline,
pancreatitis.26,27 Diffuse vacuolar hepatopathy (ch. 274) and
gallbladder mucocele (ch. 273) may result from hyperlipidemia in
dogs.1,15 Primary hypertriglyceridemia was associated with increased
liver enzyme activities in clinically healthy Miniature Schnauzers.28 In
cats with severe primary hyperchylomicronemia, histologic evaluation
of the liver revealed discrete hepatic xanthomata and a vacuolar

hepatopathy characterized by accumulation of triglycerides in
hepatocellular and Kupffer cells,29,30 but their importance is not
known. About 50% of cats with DM and secondary hyperlipidemia also
have increased serum hepatic enzyme activities, presumably due to
lipid accumulation in hepatocytes.31
Another potential complication of hypertriglyceridemia in dogs is
insulin resistance, which has been reported in Miniature Schnauzers.32
In cats, there is evidence that both naturally occurring and
experimentally-induced hyperlipidemia causes insulin resistance as in
humans and dogs.33,34 Other potential complications of
hyperlipidemia in dogs include atherosclerosis (mainly as a result of
secondary hypercholesterolemia due to endocrinopathies),35 ocular
disease (e.g., lipemia retinalis, lipemic aqueous, lipid keratopathy, solid
intraocular xanthogranuloma in hyperlipidemic Miniature
Schnauzers),36,37 seizures, and other neurologic signs,38,39
xanthomatosis and lipomas.29,30

DIAGNOSIS
BACKGROUND
Hyperlipidemia is typically diagnosed after noting increased fasting
serum triglyceride and/or cholesterol concentrations on routine serum
biochemistry profiles. Because hyperlipidemia is often secondary, it
can serve as a clue to primary conditions in dogs. Hyperlipidemia is
often the only abnormality in dogs with primary hyperlipidemia. In
order not to miss existing hyperlipidemia, both serum cholesterol and
triglyceride concentrations should be included in all routine
biochemistry profiles. Moderate and severe hypertriglyceridemia (but
not mild hypertriglyceridemia or hypercholesterolemia) can be
suspected by inspecting serum or plasma that has a turbid or lactescent
appearance (Figure 63.1). However, even these pets should have their
serum triglyceride and cholesterol concentrations assayed to reach an
accurate assessment. In some, a meal challenge to diagnose
postprandial hyperlipidemia might be indicated but experience with
this test is limited.7 In Burmese cats, clinically important lipid

disorders demonstrated with oral fat tolerance tests can exist despite
normal serum triglyceride concentrations.24,25

PRIMARY VERSUS SECONDARY
HYPERLIPIDEMIA (Figure 63.3)
After diagnosing hyperlipidemia, the next step is distinguishing
primary from secondary. In secondary hyperlipidemia, the underlying
condition should be treated. After secondary hyperlipidemia is
excluded, a tentative diagnosis of a primary lipid disorder can be made.
Regardless, a detailed history should be obtained (ch. 2) and physical
examination performed (ch. 3). These steps are crucial because dogs
and cats with secondary (not primary) hyperlipidemias typically
exhibit clinical signs of the underlying disease (e.g., polyuria and
polydipsia in pets with DM or hyperadrenocorticism, hypoactivity and
hair loss in hypothyroidism). Signs can help prioritize diagnostic tests
and lead the way to an appropriate diagnosis in a practical and costefficient manner. Testing of all hyperlipidemic dogs and cats should
include a CBC, serum biochemistry profile, and urinalysis. Then,
measuring serum total (TT4) and free thyroxin (fT4), TSH, pancreaticlipase immunoreactivity, serum bile acids, urine protein:creatinine
ratio, and screening tests for hyperadrenocorticism can be
recommended as indicated. A more general and wide selection of tests
might be necessary for pets with vague or no clinical signs.

MINIATURE SCHNAUZERS AND OTHER
PRIMARY HYPERLIPIDEMIAS
Primary hyperlipidemia is common in Miniature Schnauzers from
certain geographic regions. A detailed diagnostic investigation of
hyperlipidemia might not be necessary in this breed in the absence of
clinical signs suggesting an underlying cause. When
hypercholesterolemia is the main abnormality (without or with only
mild hypertriglyceridemia), secondary hyperlipidemia is more likely.
When primary hyperlipidemia is suspected, there is little more that can
be done to identify the cause. Tests used to further investigate the
cause of primary hyperlipidemia in dogs and cats are not usually
commercially available.

HYPOCHOLESTEROLEMIA AND
HYPOTRIGLYCERIDEMIA
The main causes of hypocholesterolemia in dogs and cats include
protein-losing enteropathy (e.g., severe inflammatory bowel disease,
intestinal lymphoma, lymphangiectasia; ch. 262), hepatic
insufficiency (e.g., cirrhosis [ch. 270], portosystemic shunts [ch.
267]), and selected malignancies. History, and clinical and
clinicopathological findings usually provide adequate information to
identify the primary cause of hypocholesterolemia. In cases where it is
unclear, additional diagnostics might be needed, including ultrasound,
serum bile acids, fecal alpha-1-proteinase inhibitor, endoscopy or
laparoscopy with biopsies, etc. Severe deficiencies in caloric intake may
also lead to hypocholesterolemia. With the possible exception of
severely deficient caloric intake, hypotriglyceridemia is not known to
be clearly associated with any disease.

CHAPTER 64: Amylase and
Lipase
Jörg M. Steiner, and Harry Cridge

INTRODUCTION
Pancreatic acinar cells synthesize and secrete digestive enzymes,
inactive preforms of digestive enzymes (i.e., zymogens), in addition
to other molecules, such as colipase and intrinsic factor. Under
physiologic conditions, these are all stored in zymogen granules, and
very little of these molecules enter the systemic circulation; however,
during pancreatitis, acinar cell damage causes the molecules to enter
the vascular space. In theory, any of these molecules could serve as a
biomarker for pancreatitis. The optimal biomarker would be one
exclusively present in acinar cells, one that is not excreted through
the kidneys (so that kidney disease is not associated with false
increases), and one that does not get scavenged by other molecules in

the serum (e.g., trypsin is scavenged by alpha2-macroglobulin). Even
a marker fulfilling these criteria must then be quantified by an assay
that exclusively measures that molecule, with no cross-reactivity, to
maintain diagnostic accuracy.

SERUM AMYLASE ACTIVITY
Serum amylase activity has been used for several decades to diagnose
pancreatitis. Unfortunately, assays for serum amylase activity are
neither specific for measurement of pancreatic amylase, nor sensitive
for a diagnosis of pancreatitis (chs. 277, 278). The lack of specificity
is evidenced by the presence of significant serum amylase activity in
dogs after total pancreatectomy and by increased serum amylase
activity in many non-pancreatic diseases, such as renal, hepatic,
intestinal, and neoplastic disease.1,2 Thus, serum amylase activity is
not clinically useful for the diagnosis of pancreatitis.

SERUM LIPASE ACTIVITY
There are many lipases in the body, some of which originate from the
exocrine pancreas. One of the most important lipases is classical
pancreatic lipase, but many others exist, including gastric lipase,
hepatic lipase, lipoprotein lipase, pancreatic lipase related protein 2,
and many others. In principle, lipases can be measured by enzymatic
(i.e., serum lipase activity) or immunologic (i.e., serum pancreatic
lipase immunoreactivity [PLI]) assays. Immunologic assays use
antibodies that will only bind pancreatic lipase, thus being highly
specific for the measurement of pancreatic lipase. In contrast,
enzymatic assays are based on the hydrolysis of a variety of
substrates by lipases in a serum sample. Given the shared function of
many lipases, the substrate selected has a significant effect on the
specificity of each assay. Assays based on three substrates are
commonly available, but none are truly specific for pancreatic lipase.

1,2-DIGLYCERIDE (1,2 DiG)-BASED
ASSAYS
Original enzymatic assays were based on the hydrolysis of 1,2 DiG,
resulting in a color change. While these assays offered improvement
over earlier serum lipase assays, the sensitivity for pancreatitis was
low and the specificity was limited relative to other assays.3

1,2-o-DILAURYL-rac-GLYCERO-3GLUTARIC ACID(6′METHYLRESORUFIN) ESTER
(DGGR)-BASED ASSAYS
Over the last 20 years, DGGR has been used as an alternative
substrate in lipase activity determination and various assays utilize
this substrate (e.g., PSL, Antech Diagnostics, Irvine, CA). Overall, the
clinical utility and specificity of DGGR-based assays are likely better
than those based on 1,2 DiG, but recent studies note a lack of
substrate specificity.3-7 Also, in a recent study, heparin
administration led to significant increases in serum lipase activity as
measured by a DGGR-based assay, but not by the PLI assay.6 This
indicates that the DGGR-lipase assay detected lipases of nonpancreatic origin, as heparinization leads to the release of hepatic
and lipoprotein lipases. A large retrospective study also documented
a high prevalence of DGGR-hyperlipasemia in many non-pancreatic
disorders such as renal disease.7

TRIOLEIN-BASED ASSAY
A point of care assay utilizing triolein as a substrate (i.e., V-Lip, Fuji,
Tokyo, Japan) has been described; however, hemolysis and icterus
significantly alter results, limiting its diagnostic utility.8
Additionally, only 58% of dogs with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
(EPI) have lipase activity in the lower 20% of the reference interval,

suggesting that this assay is non-specific and also measures lipases of
non-pancreatic origin.8

PANCREATIC LIPASE
IMMUNOREACTIVITY (PLI)
Assays for the measurement of PLI in dogs and cats (cPLI and fPLI,
respectively) are frequently utilized in veterinary medicine. Serum
cPLI concentrations were non-detectable or severely decreased in
dogs with EPI, indicating that cPLI measured in serum solely
originates from the exocrine pancreas.9 Serum cPLI is also not raised
above the reference interval in dogs with experimentally induced
renal disease, another key feature of an optimal biomarker.10
Several assays for the measurement of PLI concentration are
available. Importantly, the Spec cPL and Spec fPL assays (IDEXX
Laboratories, Westbrook, ME) have undergone analytical validation,
while other assays have not undergone analytical validation or have
failed validation studies (cPLI and fPLI by Laboklin, Bad Kissingen,
Germany; VetScan cPL by Zoetis, Parsippany, NJ; Vcheck cPL and
fPL by Bionote, Hwaseong-si, Korea).11,12 The Spec cPL assay has
also been shown to be analytically precise and unaffected by
transportation variables in clinical samples.13 Several clinical studies
have shown that the measurements of PLI concentration by Spec cPL
and Spec fPL assays are the most sensitive and specific diagnostic
tests for canine and feline pancreatitis currently available.14,15
However, it should be noted that the sensitivity reported varies
widely between studies, ranging between 33% and 100%.16
Sensitivities likely range based on the population studied and
whether a clinical diagnosis or histopathologic evaluation of tissue
specimens was used as the gold standard diagnostic test. The
sensitivity for acute severe disease is higher than that for chronic
mild disease, and as such, inclusion criteria likely influence the
sensitivity reported in each study. It is also important to note that
inflammation of extrapancreatic abdominal organs or hypoperfusion
of the pancreas may also lead to acinar cell damage that may be

associated with an increase in serum PLI concentration. It is crucial
that these conditions are properly diagnosed in the face of secondary
pancreatic damage and/or inflammation. Suspected secondary
pancreatic damage and/or inflammation has been suspected in
certain cardiac, infectious, neurological, endocrine, and renal
diseases.
Semiquantitative patient-side test kits (SNAP cPL and SNAP-fPL,
IDEXX Laboratories, Westbrook, ME) have also undergone analytic
validation.14,15 These patient-side assays are intended for a rapid
rule-out of pancreatitis. A normal result indicates that serum
pancreatic lipase concentration is within the reference interval and
that pancreatitis is unlikely. A positive result, in contrast, indicates
that serum Spec PL concentration is either within the questionable
range (“grey zone”) or suggestive of pancreatitis and additional
testing (e.g., a quantitative PLI) is indicated. Failure to perform a
quantitative PLI and utilizing the SNAP cPL assay as a definitive
diagnostic can result in false positive results.14 The baseline PLI
value may also be useful for disease monitoring.
Of note, no diagnostic test is 100% sensitive and/or specific and
careful integration of history, physical examination, general clinical
pathologic findings, imaging, and specific disease markers is
imperative to arrive at the most appropriate diagnosis.

OVERVIEW
Enzymes catalyze biochemical reactions in every cell in the body.
Substrate specificity is manipulated to detect and quantify enzyme
activity.1 To be clinically relevant markers of disease, there must be
correlation between changes in circulating enzyme concentrations and
changes in the tissue of interest. Since many factors affect enzymatic
activity in vivo and in vitro (pH, temperature, salt or protein
concentration, ionic strength, cofactor concentration, inhibitors),
interpretation also requires accurate assays. Serum or heparinized
plasma samples are used in enzyme assays. Citrate complexes divalent

cations and ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) inhibits activity of
almost all enzymes; neither should be used for enzyme analysis.1

SERUM LIVER ENZYMES USED AS
BIOMARKERS IN DOGS AND CATS
BACKGROUND
Although numerous hepatic enzymes exist, only 4 are routinely used as
biomarkers for hepatobiliary disease in dogs and cats: alanine
aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline
phosphatase (ALP), and gamma-glutamyl transferase or transpeptidase
(GGT, GGTP).2,3 These enzymes have relatively stable circulating
concentrations that may increase with membrane injury, whether
reversible or irreversible (cell death). Increases could be associated with
increased rates of synthesis (transcription and translation), cell
proliferation (neoplasia or hyperplasia [e.g., bile duct]), decreased
clearance, or, although not yet described in veterinary medicine, enzymeautoantibody complexes (macroenzymes), which extend enzyme halflife.1,4,5 Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), commonly used with other
species, is an oxidoreductase that catalyzes conversion of lactate to
pyruvate. LDH resides in the cytoplasm of all cells and is of little value as
a marker of liver disease in dogs or cats.

WHAT LIVER ENZYMES TELL US AND
WHAT THEY CANNOT TELL US
Serum liver enzyme activities aid in the identification, differentiation,
and monitoring of liver disease. They are broadly classified as
“hepatocellular leakage enzymes” (ALT, AST) or “cholestatic enzymes”
(ALP, GGT) based on their subcellular location and response to
hepatocellular injury, but none measures liver function (Figure
65.1).2,3,6 ALT and AST reside predominantly in cytosol, although a
mitochondrial AST isoenzyme exists in cats and dogs.7 The cytosolic
enzymes are the first to leak into the peri-sinusoidal space and enter the
systemic circulation secondary to hepatic necroinflammation that
damages plasma membranes. ALP and GGT are associated with the
hepatocyte canalicular membranes and, in the case of GGT,

cholangiocytes. These enzymes are released as a result of bile acid
membrane solubilization or cleavage of the membrane binding domain
(GGT) during cholestatic injury.2,8,9
While increases in liver enzyme activity are commonly identified on
biochemical screening tests, they do not definitively identify underlying
liver disease (Table 65.1).10 None of the aforementioned enzymes is
entirely liver-specific and isoenzymes exist. Further, the hepatic enzyme
induction phenomenon may cause marked increases without histologic
evidence of liver lesions.2,11-13 Isoenzymes, or “isozymes,” catalyze the
same reactions but have different amino acid sequences (ALT), varying
subunit combinations (LDH), or unique post-translational modifications
(ALP) or protein structure (AST).14 Enzymes modified by serum
proteases to slightly different forms are called isoforms.1 For example:
the intestinal ALP isoenzyme has a different protein structure than the
tissue-nonspecific renal, liver, and bone isoenzymes, which have identical
amino acid sequences but different carbohydrate composition.1,11

Miscellaneous

Serum enzyme activities are indicators of pathologic processes, not of
specific diseases. Abnormalities must be interpreted in the context of pet
signalment, history (that includes previous and current medications; ch.
2), physical examination (ch. 3), exposure to hepatotoxins (ch. 134) or
infectious organisms (ch. 9), and comorbidities. Sequential monitoring
of enzyme activity is needed to map the course of disease with attention
to duration of the increase (acute, chronic), stability (increasing,
decreasing, waxing and waning), and pattern (cholestatic,
necroinflammatory, induced). For example, increased activities after an
acute hepatic injury due to hepatotoxin exposure may rapidly return to
reference limits (ch. 269).15 However, enzyme values that progressively
increase or that wax and wane may reflect chronic and/or progressive

necroinflammatory disease (ch. 266).16 Decreased enzyme activities are
not usually diagnostically relevant.

THE LEAKAGE ENZYMES: THE
AMINOTRANSFERASES, ALT AND AST
OVERVIEW
ALT and AST catalyze the transfer of the alpha-amino group of alanine or
aspartic acid to alpha-ketoglutarate, resulting in the formation of
glutamic acid and pyruvate or oxaloacetic acid, respectively.2 These
enzymes are integral components of the glucose alanine cycle. ALT and
AST require pyridoxal 5′ phosphate (P5P), the active metabolite of
vitamin B6, as a cofactor. Alanine reacts with P5P to yield pyruvate plus
pyridoxine.3,5 Pyridoxine reacts with alpha-ketoglutarate resulting in
glutamate and regenerated P5P. Decreased transaminase activities can be
observed if systemic vitamin B6 concentrations are low due to disease or
drug administration (cephalosporin, cyclosporine, d-penicillamine, and
isoniazid).17 ALT and AST are cleared by adsorptive endocytosis in
sinusoidal hepatocytes, and clearance rates may be altered in severe liver
disease and in sinusoidal hypoperfusion (ischemia, portosystemic
vascular anomalies).18,19
ALT and AST rise within 24 to 48 hours of acute hepatocellular injury,
most markedly with necrosis (ch. 269). While there is a direct
correlation between the degree of aminotransferase increase and the
number of hepatocytes injured (mild, <5-fold high normal reference
range value; moderate, 5- to 10-fold; severe, >10-fold), this information
alone is not prognostic. Rather, monitoring of serum enzyme activities,
albumin, cholesterol, coagulation factors, and bilirubin concentrations
are needed. Generally, following acute hepatic insult, transaminase
activities increase quickly, begin to decrease within 2 to 3 days, and
normalize in 2 to 3 weeks. Waxing and waning transaminase values are
seen with chronic inflammatory conditions (chs. 270-273).16,20,21 A
reduction in liver enzyme activity in a dog or cat with chronic liver
disease may be due either to improvement in the disease process or
conversely, to diminished hepatocyte numbers.

ALANINE AMINOTRANSFERASE
ALT, while regarded as “liver-specific” in the cat and dog, is also present
in lesser intracellular quantities in heart, kidney, and skeletal muscle.
Dogs, and possibly cats, have two isoenzymes: ALT1 in the liver and
skeletal muscle and ALT2 in skeletal muscle.14 The ALT half-life in dogs
is 40-60 hours and in cats about 3-4 hours.3,5 Mild to moderate increases
may be seen with vacuolar hepatopathy (ch. 274), portosystemic
vascular anomalies (ch. 267), and passive hepatic congestion (chs. 228,
229, 266). In dogs, while ALT transcription may be induced by
glucocorticoids, glucocorticoid-treated cultured canine hepatocytes do
not have significant increases in ALT production.19,22 In cats, ALT
increase may occur secondary to hemolysis (ch. 174), hyperthyroidism
(ch. 287), or acute rhabdomyolysis due to dystrophin deficiency.3,5
Muscular dystrophy in dogs causes variable ALT elevations.3 Increased
serum ALT activities in dogs have the highest sensitivity (80-100%) for
hepatic necrosis and hepatic failure but are less sensitive (45-80%) in
hepatitis, cirrhosis, vacuolar hepatopathy, passive hepatic congestion, or
portosystemic vascular anomalies (chs. 266, 267, and 270).19 In cats,
ALT is 80-100% sensitive for extrahepatic bile duct occlusion and
cholangitis/cholangiohepatitis.23 ALT cannot differentiate types of liver
disease, but diagnostic accuracy improves when targeting canine
populations with suspected hepatitis.24 The largest ALT increases are
seen in necroinflammatory diseases.16 Acute necroinflammatory hepatic
injury may follow drug intake, toxin ingestion (heavy metals, amanita
toxin, cycads, xylitol) or infectious/inflammatory disease (leptospirosis,
toxoplasmosis, copper-associated hepatopathy, autoimmune disease)
(Box 65.1).5,16,25 Not all cases of hepatic necrosis result in transaminase
activity elevation. Aflatoxin B1 inhibits hepatic biosynthesis of ALT and
AST. These transaminases cannot be used as liver disease biomarkers
following intoxication.26

ASPARTATE AMINOTRANSFERASE
The greatest concentrations of AST are found in skeletal muscle, cardiac
myocytes, and the kidneys. AST is also present in brain, small intestine,
spleen, liver, and erythrocytes. A muscular isoenzyme may be considered

as the source of increases in AST activity if there are concurrent increases
in creatine kinase (CK) concentrations (ch. 66); however, in chronic
myopathy, the shorter half-life of CK may not allow differentiation.3 AST
is located in 2 hepatocyte subcellular sites: the cytosol (80%) and
mitochondria (20%) (Figure 65.1). Cytosolic AST is most important in
veterinary medicine.27 Its half-life in dogs is thought to be 22 hours or
longer and in cats about 77 minutes.3,5 As a soluble cytosolic liver
enzyme, serum AST activities mirror ALT activities. However, AST is a
smaller entity, diffusing into the sinusoidal circulation more rapidly after
plasma membrane disruption.28 It may also become quiescent earlier
than ALT due to its shorter half-life. In the cat, AST is the more sensitive
indicator of hepatocellular damage, particularly in hepatic necrosis,
cholangiohepatitis, myeloproliferative diseases, infiltrative lymphoma,
and chronic bile duct obstruction.19
