THE CHOLESTATIC ENZYMES: ALKALINE
PHOSPHATASE AND GAMMA-GLUTAMYL
TRANSFERASE OR TRANSPEPTIDASE
SERUM ALKALINE PHOSPHATASE (ALP)
ALP is a membrane-bound glycoprotein that hydrolyzes phosphate esters
at an alkaline pH.1 In dogs and cats, ALP resides within cells of the renal
cortices, placenta, intestine, bone, and liver.5 Two ALP isoenzymes have
been identified: intestinal and tissue nonspecific.29,30 The liver, bone,
and kidney isoforms are transcribed from the tissue-nonspecific gene
locus. Differential glycosylation of the gene product generates tissuespecific isoforms. In the dog, glucocorticoid-induced ALP (G-ALP) is a
product of the intestinal ALP gene expressed in hepatocytes and the
biliary epithelium (ch. 293). Transcription of G-ALP is delayed
approximately 10 days after beginning exogenous steroid administration.
It may continue to rise with ongoing treatment.11 The dog is unique in the
expression of two hepatic canalicular membrane ALP isoenzymes.30 The
liver isoenzyme (L-ALP) is also inducible by glucocorticoids and is the
first isoenzyme to be serologically detected. Although transcription of LALP plateaus after about 10 days of prednisone treatment, the enzyme
continues to be translated, making differentiation of the 2 isoenzymes
irrelevant. The ALP induction phenomenon is not limited to
glucocorticoids. G-ALP activity is also associated with inflammation,
chronic diseases (possibly secondary to increases in endogenous
glucocorticoid secretion), and anticonvulsant drugs.13,27
L-ALP and G-ALP isoenzymes have half-lives of 2-3 days in dogs.3
Canine placental, renal, and intestinal ALP half-lives are <6 minutes. The
half-life of feline L-ALP is brief (6 hours) while the feline intestinal ALP
half-life is <2 minutes. The placental isoenzyme is detected in late term
pregnancy. L-ALP, G-ALP, and bone isoenzyme (B-ALP) are the three
primary isozymes in the dog. Cats do not express G-ALP. B-ALP is
present in growing dogs and cats up to 7 months of age. It is also seen in
renal secondary hyperparathyroidism (chs. 162, 301), bone tumors

(negative prognostic indicator for osteosarcoma; ch. 326), mammary
carcinoma (ch. 329), osteomyelitis (ch. 31), and feline hyperthyroidism
(ch. 287), the latter partly due to increased osteoblastic activity
stimulated by T3 and T4.12,30,31
Increased serum ALP activity is one of the most common biochemical
abnormalities in dogs. ALP has a high sensitivity but low specificity for
hepatobiliary disease. If a concurrent GGT elevation is identified, an
increase in ALP is more likely due to liver disease in both dogs and
cats.8,9 Canine serum ALP activity may increase with necroinflammatory
or cholestatic injury, and with primary or metastatic neoplasia. The
degree of ALP activity has not proven to be helpful in distinguishing
between intra- and extrahepatic cholestasis. Enzyme synthesis may be
induced (e.g., secondary to inflammatory mediators or
endogenous/exogenous glucocorticoids) or the enzyme can be released
from the hepatic canaliculi via bile acid solubilization. Vacuolar
hepatopathy associated with mild to severely increased ALP activity and
cytosolic glycogen accumulation was long considered a benign
manifestation of steroidogenic hormones (cortisol and sex steroids) and a
multitude of non-adrenal diseases (ch. 274). It was suggested that excess
glycogen accumulation could become pathologic, but this is not likely a
clinical concern.32 Breed-related hyperphosphatasemia (G-ALP) exists in
Scottish Terriers and has been correlated with cholestasis due to
progressive vacuolar hepatopathy, adrenal dysfunction, and
hepatocellular carcinoma.33-36
An increase in serum ALP activity is less specific in cats but still
clinically relevant. This is particularly important in feline hepatic
lipidosis, where increases tend to predominate over increases in other
liver enzyme activities except in cats with underlying cholangitis /
cholangiohepatitis. Hepatocellular swelling, altered osmotic influx, and
cholestasis due to cellular swelling likely cause the marked increases in
ALP activity associated with feline hepatic lipidosis.37 In cats, increased
ALP activity occurs with intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary injury due
to cholestasis and bile duct hyperplasia.19 Feline serum ALP activity
elevation is not typically caused by anticonvulsant or glucocorticoid
therapy.

GAMMA-GLUTAMYLTRANSFERASE OR
TRANSPEPTIDASE (GGT)
GGT catalyzes transfer of the gamma-glutamyl group from glutathione
(GSH) to an acceptor, forming glutamate. This enzyme regulates amino
acid transport across cell membranes and is critical for the cellular redox
pathway. GGT is found in cell membranes of kidney, pancreas, biliary
epithelium, hepatocytes (zone 1, periportal), intestine, spleen, heart,
lungs, skeletal muscle, and erythrocytes.5
In dogs, GGT has its largest tissue concentration in the proximal renal
tubules and pancreas.3 However, its epithelial location in these tissues
results in loss into urine or the pancreatic lumen, rather than into the
circulation. Microsomal enzyme induction has been observed in dogs
treated with glucocorticoids but this was not repeated in cultured
hepatocytes and has not been identified in the cat.22,38 Mild increases
may be seen with phenobarbital administration, which increase further if
hepatotoxicosis develops.39 Hepatobiliary or pancreatic carcinogenesis
moderately increases GGT activity. Canine neonates exhibit markedly
increased GGT activities during the first 1-3 days of life secondary to
colostrum intake, while only a minimal increase is observed in kittens.40
An increase in GGT expression also occurs in conditions of oxidative
stress. GGT is a cholestatic liver enzyme and its activity increases when it
is cleaved from its plasma membrane anchor by bile acid solubilization.
GGT is not a sensitive marker of liver disease in the dog (40%) but it has
a higher specificity than ALP.9 In cats, sensitivity (55%) exceeds
specificity of ALP for detecting inflammatory diseases and GGT activity is
most markedly increased in necroinflammatory diseases of the portal
tract, biliary tree, and pancreas.8 GGT is minimally elevated in canine
and feline hepatic necrosis affecting zones 2 and 3.3 Extrahepatic bile
duct obstruction causes moderate to severe increases, typically greater in
dogs than cats. Reportedly, cats with underlying necroinflammatory liver
disease and bile duct obstruction or cholestasis may develop a higher-fold
increase in GGT than ALP.8,20,23

SUMMARY

Abnormal (usually increased) liver enzyme activities are common in
clinical veterinary practice. Interpretation of liver enzyme abnormalities
requires a complementary approach including bilirubin, paired serum
bile acids, arterial ammonia, and coagulation factors to determine the
next step (Figure 65.2) (ch. 266). Imaging modalities may eliminate
non-hepatic causes of increased liver enzyme activity (thoracic and
abdominal radiographs) or increase suspicion for a specific diagnosis
(abdominal ultrasound, shear wave elastography, or CT) prior to liver
biopsy.41,42 Non-enzymatic blood biomarkers of liver disease validated in
human medicine may enhance non-invasive diagnostic accuracy in
veterinary medicine.43,44

CHAPTER 66: Creatine
Kinase
Robert Mack

A C RO N YM S
CK creatine kinase
[CK] serum creatine kinase concentration
IM intramuscular
PE physical examination

TISSUE DISTRIBUTION AND
IMPORTANCE
Creatine kinase (CK), also referred to as creatine phosphokinase
(CPK), is an enzyme responsible for phosphorylation of adenosine
diphosphate (ADP) from phosphocreatine to generate adenosine
triphosphate (ATP), providing energy for muscle contraction.1 Of the
3 primary isoenzymes of CK identified—CK-MM, CK-MB, and CK-BB
—CK-MM accounts for 100% of activity in skeletal muscle and >90%
of activity in cardiac muscle of dogs and cats. CK-MB, not routinely
measured in dogs or cats, is used as a marker of myocardial
infarction in people. CK-BB accounts for most CK found in the
nervous system and can increase non-specifically in nervous system
diseases, e.g., degenerative disease, epilepsy, inflammatory
conditions, and space occupying lesions.2 Although research on

these isoenzymes and their significance continues, total CK
concentrations ([CK]s) are the most useful diagnostic measurement
in dogs and cats.
CK has a brief serum half-life (2 to 4 hours in dogs) and increased
[CK] can occur in any dog or cat. CK, concentrated in the cytoplasm
of skeletal and cardiac muscle cells, is released into the circulation
within hours of cell damage and returns to reference levels within 48
hours if damage ceases. [CK] increases can persist for days if muscle
damage is severe or ongoing. The most common explanations for
increases in [CK] are direct muscle insult due to blunt trauma,
intramuscular (IM) injection, surgery, or excessive physical restraint.
Other causes include recent excessive exercise, hyperthermia, heat
stroke, chronic recumbency, hereditary myopathy (Golden
Retrievers, Labrador Retrievers, Chow Chows, and Irish Setters),
infectious disease (toxoplasmosis, neosporosis), endocrine disease
(hypothyroidism), immune-mediated conditions (dermatomyositis,
masticatory myositis), nutritional imbalance (hypokalemia in cats),
intoxication (snake/spider envenomation), neurological conditions
(seizures, space-occupying intracranial lesions, meningitis), and
neoplasia. Effective therapy of the underlying disease often leads to a
marked decrease or normalization of [CK] in days. In addition to
specific therapy, some pets have related medical issues, e.g., shock,
sepsis, or dehydration, that compromise their clinical status. These
issues may require additional supportive treatments, pain
medication and good nursing care.

HISTORY AND PHYSICAL
EXAMINATION (PE)
After completing a thorough history (ch. 2) and PE (ch. 3) (Figure
66.1), the underlying cause for an increased [CK] is often identified.
PE findings vary, but most commonly include evidence of obvious
trauma. Other observations may include gait abnormalities (
Video 23.2), evidence of generalized muscle pain, evidence of oral
pain, fever, recumbency, muscle atrophy or hypertrophy, or
ventroflexion of the neck in cats (Video 68.1

). Persistent [CK]

increases in dogs without a history of underlying trauma, metabolic
disease or infection may be due to primary muscle disease, especially
in breeds with hereditary muscular disorders. These dogs often have
signs of muscle weakness, gait abnormalities, and muscle swelling or
atrophy. Increased [CK] should be rechecked in a pet with no
explanation to rule out a false result and, if within reference limits,
no further investigation is indicated. If a previously increased [CK] is
decreasing, further monitoring is recommended. If increasing,
especially in a breed associated with a hereditary myopathy, a muscle
biopsy should be considered (ch. 110).

SAMPLE HANDLING
CK is typically measured in serum as plasma concentrations can be
falsely increased due to platelets releasing small amounts of CK
during clotting.3,4 Serum should be separated from red blood cells
soon after collection to minimize hemolysis. Hyperlipidemia does
not significantly alter results. Serum [CK]s are stable for about 7
days at +4° C (39.2° F) and about 1 month at −20° C (−4° F).4
Samples held longer than 7 days should be frozen. Healthy puppies
and kittens (<8 weeks) often have [CK]s approximately 1.5-2 times
above adult reference values.4,5

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATIONS
Dogs and cats with increased serum [CK]s often have other abnormal
laboratory results dictated by their underlying disease. Since
aspartate transaminase (AST) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) are
enzymes also found in muscle cells, either or both can increase after
muscle insult (ch. 65). Rarely, cats with cervical ventroflexion are
hypokalemic (ch. 68). The complete blood count may be consistent
with inflammation secondary to stress, infection, or immunemediated disease. Eosinophilia can develop secondary to infection,
parasites or immune-mediated (masticatory myositis) disease. After
completing the history and PE, additional diagnostic testing may be
warranted (Figure 66.1), e.g., an acetylcholine receptor antibody

test (myasthenia gravis, ch. 253), 2M antibody test (masticatory
myositis, ch. 258), or serologic titers (toxoplasmosis, isosporiasis;
ch. 197). Persistent [CK] increases without identifying an underlying
disease may suggest need for muscle biopsy to screen for primary
myositis or a hereditary myopathy. Pets with evidence of an
intracranial or spinal cord lesion may require advanced imaging
studies to identify their disorder (ch. 112).

FIGURE 66.1 Increased creatine kinase flowchart.

INCREASED CK CONCENTRATION [CK]
IN CATS
Increased [CK] in cats, like in dogs, is often caused by recent skeletal
muscle damage (trauma, bite wounds, surgery, IM injections,
excessive restraint) and the cause is often clear from history and PE.
However, many clinically ill cats have increases in [CK] without any

obvious explanation. These cats often have a history and clinical
signs that include collapse, dyspnea, abnormal lung sounds,
cyanosis, shock and paraplegia.6 Some have underlying cardiac
disease (with aortic thromboembolism, signs are usually obvious;
ch. 238), bacterial infection, sepsis, or the systemic inflammatory
response syndrome (ch. 128). Clinically ill cats with marked
elevations in [CK], especially above 7500 U/L, have higher mortality
rates, longer hospitalizations and increased cost for treatment when
compared with ill cats that have normal [CK].6 Therefore, confirmed
increases in [CK] in a cat with signs of clinical illness suggest severe
underlying disease. Monitoring both [CK] and response to therapy
may provide prognostic information. Hyperthyroid cats often have
increases in [CK] secondary to their hypermetabolic state,
hypoperfusion, and chronic skeletal muscle ischemia (ch. 287).7
Underlying cardiomyopathy, either primary or secondary to
thyrotoxicosis, may also contribute (ch. 234). Any persistent [CK]
increase in cats is considered significant and warrants further
investigation. A thorough history to assess for recent muscle insult,
anorexia, or weight loss is vital and the PE should include cervical
thyroid palpation (Video 287.2

) and checking for fever (ch. 16),

icterus (ch. 28), and evidence of cardiac or respiratory disease.
Anorexia for almost any reason can lead to increases in [CK],
presumably due to increased muscle catabolism complicated by
illness (ch. 17). Usually, nutritional support and appropriate
treatment of the underlying cause resolves abnormalities in [CK] in 2
days.8

PROGNOSIS
Mild [CK] increases (<5 times reference range) in dogs and cats with
a history and PE suggestive of mild muscle trauma have an excellent
prognosis, with values returning to reference limits in days. The
prognosis for animals with severe muscle trauma or with serious
clinical signs depends on the underlying disease and the response to
therapy. In these more severe clinical cases, monitoring [CK], along

with clinical response to treatment, may provide important
prognostic information.

OVERVIEW
Sodium (Na), the dominant cation in the extracellular fluid (ECF), is
the primary determinant of plasma osmolality (mOsm/kg) (Box
67.1).1 Hypo- or hypernatremia impacts intracellular (IC) electrolyte
concentrations because “water follows Na” unless compensatory
mechanisms adjust the IC milieu. Similarly, conditions such as
hyperglycemia increase “effective osmolality” and decrease Na
concentrations ([Na]) (Box 67.1). Chloride (Cl), the dominant anion
in the ECF, tends to “follow” Na since processes causing hypo- or
hypernatremia typically drive Cl concentrations ([Cl]) in the same
direction.2 Disconnects between [Na] and [Cl] are diagnostically and

therapeutically important, particularly in dogs and cats with acidbase disturbances. Primary derangements in Cl can be identified by
“correcting” for concurrent [Na] (Box 67.1).
The single predictable effect that illness has on circulating
electrolyte concentrations and on total body amounts of any
electrolyte is that they are never predictable. Despite this limitation,
managing an ill dog or cat receiving intravenous (IV) fluid therapy
based in part on addressing serum electrolyte values is critically
important, even knowing that Na and Cl serum concentrations do
not consistently reflect body content. A patient can have normal
serum [Na] and [Cl] despite the presence of significant total body
excesses or depletions. Because of the relationship between Na and
water, patients with hyponatremia have an excess of free water,
regardless of volume status. Conversely, those with hypernatremia
have a free water deficit, even if total body volume is unchanged.
Assessment of volume status helps contextualize Na and Cl
derangements and is an essential component of any diagnostic
evaluation. It is challenging to detect modest volume depletion or
excess (i.e., < 5%).

Key considerations when evaluating abnormalities in [Na] and/or
[Cl] are outlined (Figures 67.1 to 67.4). More than one process
may co-exist, and the role of the clinician is to identify the dominant
influence(s). Injudicious interventions can have substantially
deleterious consequences, including death. Any dog or cat requiring
IV fluid therapy should have their initial serum electrolyte status
determined. Need for reassessment should then be individualized
(chs. 121, 122).

HYPERNATREMIA (Figure 67.1)
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
The most common cause of hypernatremia during illness is loss of
water (with or without lesser amounts of Na). Much less commonly,
it indicates the addition of Na (with or without lesser amounts of
water). Patients with surplus Na are often euvolemic or volumeloaded, whereas those with a pure water or hypotonic fluid loss have
evidence of volume depletion (i.e., hypertonic dehydration).3 By
definition, the dehydrated group is ill and unable or unwilling to
ingest adequate amounts of water or they cannot retain it once
swallowed, as both volume loss and hypernatremia should trigger
thirst as well as the release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
The clinical impact of hypernatremia is influenced by severity and
rate of onset, impacting the likelihood and magnitude of fluid shifts
from the IC compartment.4 For example, hypernatremia secondary
to salt intoxication quickly results in ataxia, disorientation, and
seizures as a result of shrinkage of cells within the central nervous
system.5 Insidious chronic hypernatremia will drive the IC

accumulation of non-ionic organic osmolytes, including amino acids
and polyalcohols.6 These osmotically active molecules attract water,
maintaining IC osmolality and volume in the short-term, protecting
the individual from significant clinical morbidity.

CAUSES OF HYPERNATREMIA
Pseudohypernatremia
Hypoproteinemia can impact reported [Na]; if unexpected,
hypernatremia should be verified using a patient-side device with a
direct ion-selective electrode.1

Iatrogenic
Administration of Na-rich fluids can cause hypernatremia,
particularly if patients are not drinking water voluntarily.4 Volume
status will depend on the underlying condition and the amount of
fluids administered (chs. 121, 122). The impact of IV fluid therapy
on [Na] can be estimated using the formula in Box 67.1.7 Loop
diuretics and mannitol can occasionally result in hypernatremia, but
only at high doses or if the patient is unable or unwilling to drink.8

Pure Water Loss (Urinary or Respiratory)
Disorders associated with polyuria and dilute urine, such as seen
with liver failure or any form of diabetes insipidus, can result in
substantial loss of free water through the kidneys (chs. 266,
282).9,10 Sustained panting or tachypnea could result in substantial
free water loss via the airways. Inadequate compensatory water
intake will result in hypernatremia.

Loss of Hypotonic Fluids
Conditions associated with vomiting, diarrhea, and/or severe
diuresis can result in severe water loss, dehydration, and increased
serum electrolyte concentrations. Common conditions associated
with excess loss of water include gastrointestinal disorders, acute

kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, postobstructive diuresis, and
diabetes mellitus.4 Affected animals typically exhibit signs of volume
depletion, such as a loss of skin elasticity, tachycardia and depressed
mentation.

Third Spacing
Movement of hypotonic fluid into a body cavity uncommonly is
associated with hypernatremia.4

Hypodipsic Disorders
Any disorder from an oral foreign body to a primary neurologic
disease that interferes with an animal’s ability to drink adequately
can result in hypernatremia. Primary hypodipsia is rarely reported in
veterinary patients, and appears to be associated with deranged
osmoregulatory mechanisms +/– malformation of the corpus
callosum.11-13

Hyperaldosteronism and Hypercortisolism
Hypernatremia is not commonly reported in pets with either of these
adrenocortical hormone excess conditions but both are associated
with Na retention, greater in hyperaldosteronism than
hypercortisolism (chs. 293, 295). Na retention leads to water
retention and systemic hypertension can result from the volume
overload (ch. 236).14,15

Salt Intoxication
This should be considered in a hypernatremic patient with acute
neurological compromise.4 Sources of salt can include home-made
playdough or clay.16

HYPONATREMIA (Figure 67.2)
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Hyponatremia is a result of excess water or a loss of Na.17 Since pure
Na loss is not possible, patients may have hypertonic fluid losses or
they may have lost Na-containing fluids (e.g., vomiting or diarrhea)

which were replaced by water (i.e., hypotonic dehydration).18 In the
absence of azotemia, both states result in calculated decreases in
serum osmolality (< 290 mOsm/kg).1 Subnormal [Na] may be the
result of ECF “dilution” by water drawn by conditions such as
hyperglycemia.

CAUSES OF HYPONATREMIA
Pseudohyponatremia
Depending on assay method used, hyperlipidemia and
hyperproteinemia can decrease measured concentrations of [Na]
(Box 67.1).1 Patient-side devices are not typically affected by these
issues.

Dilutional
[Na] is the primary determinant of ECF osmolality and a
compensatory decrease in this electrolyte is expected in severe
hyperglycemia. When the “corrected Na” is within the reference
range (Box 67.1), the hyponatremia should resolve with
management of the underlying problem. The addition of
unmeasured osmoles, such as mannitol or ethylene glycol, also can
trigger a dilutional hyponatremia; affected animals will have an
increased osmolal gap (i.e., measured – calculated osmolality).19

Iatrogenic (e.g., Administration of Water, Diuretics)
Inappropriate use of low-Na replacement fluids or of high-dose
diuretic therapy may result in clinically significant
hyponatremia.8,20

Loss of Na
Fluids lost through vomiting, diarrhea, the urine in pets with renal
disease, or “third spacing” typically contain significant quantities of
Na. This Na loss can be worsened by replacing lost fluids with water.
In health, homeostatic mechanisms maintain both volume and

osmolality within narrow ranges. With illness, osmolality is
sacrificed in favor of maintaining blood volume and perfusion. This
is the most common form of hyponatremia seen in clinical settings
and its clinical impact is determined by both severity and
duration.18,21

FIGURE 67.2 Diagnostic approach to
hyponatremia in dogs and cats. Anticipated volume
status for various conditions is indicated by its
position within the shaded box, but will vary
depending on overall patient status, previous
therapies, concurrent disease, etc. CKD, Chronic
kidney disease; GI, gastrointestinal; Na, sodium;
SIAD, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis.

Retention of Water
Water retention is commonly associated with several conditions,
some common and some rare: examples include congestive heart
failure, liver failure, nephrotic syndrome, and myxedema coma.
These conditions activate the fluid-conserving non-osmotic
stimulation of ADH release and subsequent water retention (in
excess of Na) and hypervolemia.20,22

Hypoadrenocorticism
Aldosterone deficiency results in hyponatremia by increasing the
amount of Na lost through the kidneys.23 Cortisol deficiency is
associated with increased ADH secretion, which contributes to
decreased serum [Na] via water retention and dilution (ch. 296).24
Although patients may present with acute illness, hyponatremia has
likely developed over more time.

Water Intoxication
Actual water intoxication with a rapid drop in [Na] and cerebral
edema is rare in companion animals. It has been reported in dogs
playing in ponds or lakes, and may also occur in dogs with
psychogenic polydipsia given desmopressin.25,26

Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuresis (SIAD)
This term includes patients with inappropriate ADH secretion and
other disorders in which urinary dilution is impaired, with urine
[Na] > 20 mEq/L.27 Affected animals often have underlying
neurologic, neoplastic or inflammatory disorders. SIAD has been
described in a cohort of dogs with babesiosis.28-30

HYPERCHLOREMIA (Figure 67.3)
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Hyperchloremia per se, while not associated with clinical signs,
merits attention. Changes in Cl usually parallel those of Na. If
changes are due to altered free water, the corrected [Cl] (Box 67.1)
is normal and the differential diagnoses for hypernatremia should be
investigated. True hyperchloremia is usually iatrogenic or driven by
acid-base disorders.2,31 As Cl is the most prevalent strong anion in
the ECF, an increase in [Cl] predictably causes metabolic acidosis
with a normal anion gap.32,33

hyperchloremia in dogs and cats. Anticipated volume
status for various conditions is indicated by its
position within the shaded box, but will vary
depending on overall patient status, previous
therapies, concurrent disease, etc. AKI, Acute kidney

CAUSES OF HYPERCHLOREMIA
Spurious / Pseudohyperchloremia
Hemolysis, hyperlipidemia, and bromide therapy can result in
misleading measurements; the first two can be excluded using a

device with a direct ion-selective electrode.2

Iatrogenic
Inappropriate fluid therapy, total parenteral nutrition, or the use of
carbonic anhydrase inhibitors or zonisamide can lead to
hyperchloremia. Prolonged use of fluids with 1:1 Na:Cl content (such
as 0.9% NaCl) will drive up serum [Cl]. Carbonic anhydrase
inhibitors and zonisamide promote hyperchloremia by limiting renal
reabsorption of bicarbonate (HCO3).34

Disproportionate Loss of Sodium
Any condition in which the loss of Na significantly exceeds that of Cl
will result in hyperchloremia. This can occur in patients with various
diarrheic disorders, as intestinal reabsorption of Na may be
disproportionately impacted.35

Metabolic Acidosis
As Cl and HCO3 constitute the bulk of the ECF anions, HCO3 loss will
trigger a compensatory increase in Cl in order to maintain
electroneutrality. Potassium depletion is also associated with
diminished net acid excretion and a hyperchloremic metabolic
acidosis.36

Hemolysis
Hyperchloremia has been reported in dogs with acute babesiosis (ch.
197) and other forms of hemolytic anemia.37,38

HYPOCHLOREMIA (Figure 67.4)
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
A normal corrected Cl in a dog suggests an increase in ECF water,
and the differentials for hyponatremia should be pursued.2 Noniatrogenic, corrected hypochloremia is usually due to acid-base

disturbances, or gastric outflow obstruction and the loss of Cl-rich
fluid.32,39

FIGURE 67.4 Diagnostic approach to
hypochloremia in dogs and cats. Anticipated volume
status for various conditions is indicated by its
position within the shaded box, but will vary
depending on overall patient status, previous
therapies, concurrent disease, etc. Cl, Chloride.

CAUSES OF HYPOCHLOREMIA
Iatrogenic

Glucocorticoids, loop diuretics, and thiazide diuretics promote renal
loss of Cl and may result in hypochloremia.40,41

Gastric Outflow Obstruction
A hyperchloremic metabolic alkalosis is the hallmark of a gastric
outflow obstruction in a vomiting patient.42 Low [Cl] in the renal
tubular fluid limits the excretion of surplus HCO3, resulting in
paradoxical aciduria.

Respiratory Acidosis
Compensatory increases in [HCO3] due to chronic respiratory
acidosis will increase renal excretion of Cl.43

Miscellaneous Considerations
Various disorders, particularly those associated with hyperkalemia
(e.g., trichuriasis, tumor lysis syndrome) are occasionally associated
with hypochloremia.44 Hypochloremia is uncommonly reported in
dogs with hypercortisolism.

POTASSIUM (K+)
OVERVIEW
About 90 to 98% of total body K+ is concentrated within intracellular
fluids (ICFs) and 2 to 10% in the extracellular fluid (ECF). About 75%
of ECF K+ is in bone and 25% in circulation and interstitial fluids.1-5
K+ is vital for the generation and maintenance of physiologic resting
cell membrane potentials, effects of which can be obvious in cardiac
and skeletal muscle. ICF K+ is vital for maintaining cell volume
homeostasis, enzyme reactions, metabolic functions, and action
potential transmission.

PHYSIOLOGY
The Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System
(RAAS)
Mineralocorticoids, primarily aldosterone, are synthesized and
secreted from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex. They
function to control sodium (Na), K+, and water homeostasis;
promoting Na, chloride (Cl), and water reabsorption in the proximal
convoluted renal tubules as well as distal convoluted tubular
reabsorption of Na via exchange with K. Secretion of aldosterone is
primarily under control of the RAAS, whose activities are closely
associated with the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) in the kidneys.
The JGA, a component of every glomerulus, acts as a microscopic
pressure transducer that continuously monitors renal perfusion,
synthesizing and releasing renin in response to perceived decreases
in blood volume. Renin causes release of angiotensin I from the liver;
angiotensin I has 2 amino acids split off by “converting enzyme”
mainly in the lungs, producing the potent vasoconstrictor and
aldosterone stimulant angiotensin II. Resulting increases in
aldosterone concentrations enhance Na retention and K excretion,

expand the ECF volume, increase renal perfusion, and ultimately
suppress the signals for renin release.

Effect of Diet, Hydration, Acid-Base Status, Renal
Perfusion
Dietary intake of K+ is critical for balancing renal and colonic
losses.3,5,6 Various other factors, including insulin and
catecholamines, also influence serum K+ concentration ([K+]) by
increasing cellular uptake.7 Acidosis (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis
[DKA]) can dissociate ICF from ECF K+ causing migration into the
ECF from which it can be lost into urine, stool, and/or vomitus (ch.
290).8 When renal perfusion is compromised, regardless of cause
(e.g., dehydration, poor cardiac output), K+ excretion is
compromised (chs. 300, 301). In this scenario, serum [K+] may be
increased despite a total body depletion, explaining why serum
concentrations do not consistently reflect total body K+ excesses or
deficiencies.9 When [K+]s are abnormal, neuromuscular and cardiac
consequences can be evident.5,6 Abnormal [K+]s were documented
in 27% of dogs and 40% of cats presented to an emergency clinic and
K+ abnormalities were associated with greater mortality.10

Reference Intervals
Reference intervals for dog and cat serum [K+] are usually about 4.0
to 5.5 mEq/L (4.0-5.5 mmol/L) (unit conversion: 1 mEq/L K+ = 1
mmol/L K+). Slight variations among laboratory reference ranges
are expected due to use of different methodologies.2,6

HYPOKALEMIA
Classification; Artifactual Alterations in [K + ]

Low [K+] causes vasoconstriction, disrupts cell function, impairs
protein synthesis, inhibits release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH),
and can dramatically worsen kidney function. Hypokalemia can be
classified as mild (3.0-4.0 mEq/L), moderate (2.5-3.0 mEq/L), or
severe (<2.5 mEq/L).2,5,6 Serum samples may slightly overestimate
[K+] because K+ is released from platelets during the clotting
process.2 Hemolyzed samples may also overestimate [K+] due to K+
release from erythrocytes (red blood cells [RBCs]), which can be
quite dramatic in breeds with high intra-RBC [K+] (e.g., Akita, Shiba
Inu, and English Springer Spaniel).3,11 Artifactual K+ decreases may
occur when photometric methods are used on lipemic or
hyperproteinemic samples. Ion-selective electrodes in most point-ofcare testing units are not so-affected.2,3,6,11 Severe hyperglycemia
(>750 mg/dL [>42 mmol/L]) or azotemia (blood urea nitrogen
[BUN] >115 mg/dL [>41 mmol/L]) can cause pseudohypokalemia.12

Clinical Signs
Clinical signs of hypokalemia, the most obvious being muscle
weakness, depend on severity and the time frame in which the deficit
developed. Occasionally, signs may not correlate with severity of
hypokalemia since they are determined, in part, by the ICF:ECF [K+]
ratio.2,6,7 Clinical signs due to hypokalemia can be expected when
serum concentrations are <3.5 mEq/L in cats and <2.5 mEq/L in
dogs. Most cats and dogs with mild-to-moderate hypokalemia show
no associated clinical signs. Cats seem more susceptible to
hypokalemia.2,5,6,12 Hypokalemia initially causes hyperpolarization
and then hypopolarization of neuromuscular and cardiac cell
membranes.6,12
The classic clinical sign of hypokalemia-induced weakness in cats
is “ventroflexion,” a flaccid neck secondary to hypokalemic myopathy
(Video 68.1

). Generalized muscle weakness, a plantigrade stance

(ch. 292; Videos 14.2, 292.1, 292.2), and hypermetria have been
variably observed.2,5-7 Hypokalemic myopathy may be associated

with increases in serum creatine kinase (CK) activity (ch. 66) and
with electromyographic abnormalities (ch. 111).12 Burmese cats
have a familial disorder characterized by hypokalemic periodic
paralysis; exact mechanism is unknown but possibly secondary to
either acute K+ translocation to the ICF or following a K+-losing
nephropathy.7,13
The cardiac effects of hypokalemia may be dramatic and lifethreatening: reduced myocardial contractility, supraventricular and
ventricular arrhythmias (ch. 230), and decreased cardiac output.
On an electrocardiogram, hypokalemia may cause decreased T-wave
amplitude, shortened S-T segments, prolonged Q-T intervals,
prominent U waves, and/or arrhythmias.2,5,6,12 Severe hypokalemia
(<2 mEq/L) may be associated with rhabdomyolysis and respiratory
muscle paralysis.7 Paralytic ileus (causing abdominal distention,
anorexia, vomiting, and constipation) and polyuria/polydipsia
(PU/PD) are nonspecific issues associated with hypokalemia. PU/PD
is the result of interference with ADH release and a hypokalemic
nephropathy: chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis, impaired renal
function, and azotemia.6,7,12

When Should Serum Potassium Be Assessed?
The one predictable observation about serum electrolyte
concentrations in ill dogs and cats is that they are never predictable.
Recognition of electrolyte abnormalities and their treatment can be
lifesaving. Any dog or cat to be given intravenous (IV) fluids should
have their serum electrolyte concentrations assessed. Any concern
resulting in recommending a serum biochemistry profile should
include serum electrolytes.

Differential Diagnoses (Figure 68.1)
Causes of hypokalemia include: 1) losses into the gastrointestinal
(GI) tract or the urine, 2) reduced intake, 3) iatrogenic, and 4)
excessive or abnormal translocation to the ICF.2,5-7,12 In many
scenarios, more than one mechanism is involved (e.g., DKA).8

Chronic or frequent vomiting or diarrhea may lead to K+ depletion.
Dehydration or hypovolemia activates the RAAS, which can worsen
K+ deficiency by increasing its renal excretion.2,6,9
Primary and secondary renal conditions associated with K+ losses
are diverse. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a common cause of
hypokalemia, especially in cats, due to PU and excess K+
excretion.2,7,9 It has been suggested that a subset of cats has CKD
secondary to primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s syndrome; chs.
295 and 301).14 Excess aldosterone contributes to development of
CKD and promotes excess excretion of K+. Primary
hyperaldosteronism is rare in dogs (ch. 295). Hypercortisolism in
dogs uncommonly causes mild to moderate hypokalemia (ch.
293).5,7 Polyuric conditions secondary to osmotic diuresis and postobstructive diuresis often cause excessive renal K+ losses. Distal
renal tubular acidosis – type 1 is associated with hypokalemia. Risk
of iatrogenic hypokalemia may follow sodium bicarbonate treatment
for proximal renal tubular acidosis – type 2. Assessment of the
fractional urinary excretion of K+ (FEk) may be useful in
discriminating renal from non-renal causes of hypokalemia using the
formula: FEk = (Uk/Sk) / (Ucr/Scr) × 100 (%). The formula correlates
urinary K+ (Uk) and urinary creatinine (Ucr) concentrations with
serum K+ (Sk) in mEq/L and serum creatinine (Scr) in mg/dL.2,6 An
FEk <6% would indicate that K+ loss is not renal. Abnormally
increased results are not specific for excess renal K+ loss.2
Transiently decreased K+ intake does not usually cause changes in
serum electrolyte concentrations. Rarely, hypokalemia can develop
after prolonged anorexia or after feeding diets deficient in K+.
Hypomagnesemia and hyperthyroidism (ch. 287) may cause
hypokalemia.5,12 Hypokalemia is a frequent, potentially lifethreatening complication of IV fluid therapy if the chosen fluid is not
supplemented with sufficient K+, as is the case with short- or long-

term use of fluids containing no K+ (0.45% NaCl, 0.9% NaCl, 5%
dextrose) or fluids containing too little K+ (e.g., Ringer’s solutions
contain 4 mEq/L) (ch. 120).2,6,7,12
Other than use of inadequately supplemented IV fluids, iatrogenic
hypokalemia is seen with administration of diuretics (e.g.,
furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide). Less commonly, administering
glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, penicillin derivatives,
amphotericin B, and sodium bicarbonate may cause
hypokalemia.2,5,7,12 Hypokalemia may develop secondary to
peritoneal dialysis.2,5,7,12 Some drugs (beta-adrenergics, e.g.,
albuterol) or administration of total parenteral nutrition solutions
cause hypokalemia by shifting K+ into cells from the ECF.2,5,12
Insulin, exogenous or endogenous stimulated by glucose
administration, and catecholamines, stimulate K+ uptake by hepatic
and muscle cells (ch. 290).2,5 Hypokalemia has been documented in
some dogs with pheochromocytoma (ch. 298). Hypothermia may be
associated with K+ shift into cells.7 Hypokalemia does not contribute
to development of alkalosis in dogs and cats but metabolic alkalosis
may cause K+ to shift from ECF to ICF.2,7,12 Rattlesnake
envenomation and ingestion of bentonite-containing clay cat litter
are other reported causes of hypokalemia.7

HYPERKALEMIA

Ruling Out Pseudohyperkalemia
Hyperkalemia is usually defined as a concentration >5.5 mEq/L and
is considered severe when >8.0 mEq/L.5,12 When hyperkalemia is
observed, especially with bizarre increases inconsistent with life,
pseudohyperkalemia must first be ruled out. In vitro increases may
be caused by K+ being “released” from within cells.3,11 Recognized
conditions for pseudohyperkalemia include severe leukocytosis
(>100,000 leukocytes/mcL), severe thrombocytosis when K+ is
measured in serum (platelets release K during clotting), hemolysis
(especially in Akitas, Shiba Inus, English Springer Spaniels,
neonates), and samples contaminated with K+ containing fluids (IV
fluids, etheylenediaminetetraacetic acid [EDTA], or oxalate).3,11,12

When Should K+ Be Assessed?
As stated previously, the one predictable observation about serum
electrolyte concentrations in ill dogs and cats is that they are never
predictable. Serum electrolytes should be assessed in any pet with
unexplained anorexia, weakness, GI signs, or bradycardia, not
because results are likely to be diagnostic, but they may reveal
disturbances that require treatment while the search for a diagnosis
continues (chs. 119, 122). Serum [K+] must be assessed in any ill
dog or cat being treated for hyperadrenocorticism and in any pet
suspected as having primary hypoadrenocorticism. Anuria and
oliguria are consistent causes of hyperkalemia, as are urethral or
bilateral ureteral obstruction, uroabdomen, or kidney failure.3,14,15

Clinical Signs
Hyperkalemic cats and dogs may not show clinical signs until
relatively severe increases occur (i.e., >7.5-8 mEq/L).7 The margin
between developing signs and life threatening hyperkalemia is
slim.6,12 Clinical manifestations of hyperkalemia reflect
modifications in cell membrane excitability, and are worse with acute
changes.3,12 Generalized weakness, similar to that observed in

hypokalemia, is the most common clinical sign associated with
hyperkalemia.5-7 Hyperkalemia decreases resting cell membrane
potentials, and impairs repolarization and subsequent action
potentials.3,6,9 Bradycardia is classic for hyperkalemia (decreased
excitability, increased refractory period, slowed conduction).
Electrocardiogram abnormalities that reflect the severity of
hyperkalemia include tall and narrow T waves, decreased P-wave
amplitude, prolonged QRS duration, prolonged P-R intervals, P wave
abolishment, ST segment deviation, heart block, ventricular
arrhythmias, and cardiac arrest (ch. 296).3,6,7,12

Differential Diagnosis (Figure 68.2)
The mechanisms leading to hyperkalemia also outline the differential
diagnoses: 1) decreased renal excretion, 2) GI disease or effusions, 3)
translocation from ICF to ECF, 4) and iatrogenic. More than one
mechanism may be present in a same pet (e.g., CKD).3,6,12

FIGURE 68.2 Algorithm for the evaluation of
hyperkalemia. CKD, Chronic kidney disease; GI,
gastrointestinal. Adapted from Della Maggiore AM.
Potassium, magnesium. In: Ettinger SJ, Feldman
EC, Côté E, eds. Textbook of Veterinary Internal
Medicine. 8th ed. Elsevier; 2017:270-275.
Decreased capacity to excrete K+ through the urine is common in
both acute kidney injury (AKI) or in later stages of CKD (chs. 300,
301). Total urethral or bilateral ureteral obstructions consistently
cause hyperkalemia. Uroabdomen secondary to ruptured ureter or
bladder usually causes hyperkalemia within 48 hours in dogs.3,6,12 A
history of trauma, urinary calculi, or straining to urinate should raise
suspicions for urinary tract rupture in a hyperkalemic pet with a

small or non-palpable bladder. A small bladder is also typical of
anuric/oliguric kidney failure.7
Primary hypoadrenocorticism (Addison’s disease), a disease far
more common in dogs than in cats (ch. 296), involves deficiencies
of mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids. Aldosterone deficiency
causes K+ retention and Na loss, abnormalities worsened with
dehydration, poor renal perfusion, vomiting, diarrhea, and oliguria.
Early in the course of the illness, clinical signs might wax and wane,
with periods of unremarkable electrolyte concentrations. Dogs with
secondary hypoadrenocorticism and a small percentage of dogs with
primary adrenal insufficiency do not have electrolyte abnormalities.
Failure to observe hyperkalemia does not rule out adrenal
insufficiency.16
Some GI diseases (i.e., trichuriasis, salmonellosis, perforated
duodenal ulcer) have caused hyperkalemia. It occurs in some pets
with “third spacing” of fluids (i.e., chylothorax, pleural effusion,
ascites). Uncommonly, Greyhound dogs in late pregnancy may be
hyperkalemic, possibly due to decreased renal excretion secondary to
hypovolemia.3,5
Transcellular K+ shifts from ICF to ECF may occur secondary to
different scenarios. Metabolic and respiratory acidosis can cause K+
translocation to the ECF.7,8 DKA is unique since the osmolality
associated with hyperglycemia may cause water and K+ to shift from
ICF to the ECF. The result is total body K+ depletion but serum
concentrations that are initially within reference limits or even
increased (ch. 290). This is exacerbated by decreased renal
perfusion due to dehydration. Insulin, IV fluids, sodium bicarbonate,
and glucose administration associated with treating DKA can quickly
stimulate cellular uptake of K+ while at the same time, rehydration
improves renal excretion of K. Together, they predispose to severe
hypokalemia.7,8
Massive tissue breakdown such as observed in acute tumor lysis
syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, crush injuries, or reperfusion after a
thromboembolic event (e.g., aortic thromboembolism) may cause
massive K+ translocation to ECF, causing transient but potentially

dangerous hyperkalemia.3,5,7,12 Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis was
reported in a young Pit Bull with episodic weakness.3 Among
iatrogenic causes of hyperkalemia, nonselective beta-blockers (e.g.,
propranolol) and alpha-agonists (e.g., phenylpropanolamine) may
decrease liver and muscle K+ uptake.3,5
Drugs with the potential to induce iatrogenic hyperkalemia are
more likely to do so if combined with other contributing factors, e.g.,
CKD. Excessive oral intake of K+ is extremely uncommon and
unlikely. However, excessive amounts of K+ administered IV,
transfusion of expired RBCs, or K+-containing drugs (e.g., potassium
bromide, potassium citrate) may cause transient hyperkalemia.
Other drugs that may contribute to hyperkalemia by means of
reducing renal K+ excretion are angiotensin converting enzyme
inhibitors (e.g., benazepril), angiotensin receptor blockers (e.g.,
losartan), K+-sparing diuretics (e.g., spironolactone), cardiac
glycosides (e.g., digitalis), prostaglandin inhibitors (e.g.,
nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories), some antibiotics (trimethoprim,
K+ penicillin G), succinylcholine, heparin, and immunomodulators
(e.g., cyclosporine, tacrolimus).3,5,6,7,12 Trilostane administration to
dogs has been associated with mild to severe hyperkalemia, even
death. Suppression of aldosterone synthesis is the likely cause,
although not yet proven.17

MAGNESIUM (Mg++)
PHYSIOLOGY
Mg++ is an abundant but often forgotten intracellular ion.1,5 In dogs,
only 1-2% of the total Mg++ is in ECF and about 60-67% of that Mg++
is stored in bone. Of the remaining Mg++, about two-thirds is in
muscle and one-third in other soft tissues.1,4,7 Like calcium,
circulating Mg++ is present in three forms: biologically active ionized
or free Mg++ (55%), protein-bound (20-30%), and complexed to

anions such as phosphate or bicarbonate (15-25%).18,19 Mg++
homeostasis depends on adequate intestinal absorption (mainly
from the distal small intestine and colon in cats and dogs), bone
stores, and kidney function.1,4,7 No specific hormone has been
identified that regulates Mg++ metabolism. Parathyroid hormone
(PTH) and calcitriol (vitamin D) stimulate intestinal Mg++
absorption. Aldosterone stimulates Mg++ excretion via the
kidneys.1,15 Dietary Mg++ determines the amount absorbed by the
intestines.1 Many other factors also affect Mg++ absorption and
excretion.18,19
Mg++ is required for oxidative phosphorylation and anaerobic
glucose metabolism in mitochondria. It influences DNA metabolism,
protein synthesis, and intracellular messengers, and acts as a
cofactor for most ATPase enzymes. Mg++ has a vital role in almost
every metabolic process by supporting electrolyte movement and
electrochemical gradients.1,4,18,20 These include bone
mineralization, muscle activity, neuronal signal transduction, and
regulation of ICF calcium. Mg++ alters peripheral vascular resistance
by causing vasorelaxation when increased and vasoconstriction when
decreased.18

ASSESSMENT
Mg++ assays measure either the “total” (tMg++) or the ionized
fraction (iMg++).18,20 Since 20-30% is albumin-bound,
hypoalbuminemia may result in decreased results. There is no
consensus regarding the best assay for clinically assessing Mg++
status of a dog or cat. Test results do not consistently correlate with
clinical conditions and the total and ionized fractions do not
consistently provide complementary data.1,4,7 More accurate
techniques to assess body Mg++ content are not routinely used nor
available (e.g., 24-hour urinary excretion or retention, RBC or tissue

Mg++ concentrations).7,18,19 Reported reference ranges vary since
several assay methods have been used. Generally, tMg++ results
between 1.5-3.0 mg/dL (0.6-1.2 mmol/L) or iMg++ results between 11.9 mg/dL (0.4-0.6 mmol/L) are considered acceptable reference
intervals.4,12 Reference intervals for dogs do vary, with tMg++
intervals of 1.7-2.5 mg/dL (0.7-1.03 mmol/L) and iMg++ intervals of
0.51-1.4 mg/dL (0.21-0.58 mmol/L) reported. For cats, tMg++
reported reference intervals are 1.3-2.6 mg/dL (0.53-1.07 mmol/L)
and iMg++ intervals are 1.04-1.53 mg/dL (0.43-0.63 mmol/L).1
Hyper- and hypomagnesemia can be life-threatening.19-22

HYPOMAGNESEMIA
Overview
Hypomagnesemia is likely when serum tMg++ and iMg++ are below
reference ranges. However, tMg++ reflects only 1% of the body’s total
Mg and iMg++ represents only 0.2-0.3%.4,12 Thus, serum results may
be within reference intervals despite ICF deficits. Hypomagnesemia
has been reported as the most common electrolyte disorder in
critically ill pets (54-67%), associated with Na, K+, calcium, and
phosphate deficiencies (chs. 119, 122).5,12,19,20 Mg++ depletion
impairs PTH secretion, increases PTH target-organ resistance, and
decreases calcitriol synthesis. This “transient hypoparathyroidism” is
reversible with Mg++ replacement.23

Clinical Signs
Clinical signs of hypomagnesemia are not usually obvious until
serum tMg++ and iMg++ concentrations are below 1.0 mg/dL and 0.4
mmol/L, respectively. Even then, dogs and cats may have no
associated clinical signs.12 Nonspecific clinical signs of
hypomagnesemia include lethargy, anorexia, muscle

weakness/fasciculations, dysphagia, dyspnea, tetany, ataxia,
seizures, and coma.1,4,12,18-20 Hypomagnesemia decreases resting
membrane potentials, causing Purkinje fiber excitability and
arrhythmias (atrial and/or ventricular fibrillation, supraventricular
and/or ventricular tachycardia).1,12,18 Mg++ depletion has a
permissive effect on K+ exit from cells due to its crucial role as cofactor for most ATPase reactions, such as Na+/K+-ATPase. In this
scenario, ICF K+ enters the circulation and is excreted by the
kidneys, leading to total body deficiencies refractory to
supplementation until Mg++ deficits have been corrected, a common
concern in dogs and cats with DKA.4,5,7,8,12,20

Differential Diagnosis (Figure 68.3)
Causes of hypomagnesemia include decreased oral intake (unlikely if
commercial diets are being fed), prolonged anorexia, decreased GI
absorption, excess loss via the GI tract or kidneys, and ECF Mg++
translocation to ICF.1,7,18 Recognized GI causes for Mg++
malabsorption or loss include chronic diarrhea, malabsorption
conditions, short bowel syndrome, colonic neoplasia, and acute
pancreatitis (chs. 262, 263, 277).4,7 Excessive urinary Mg++ losses
are common in ill pets with diabetes mellitus (chs. 291, 292), DKA
(ch. 290), exposure to other osmotic or diuretic agents (except K+sparing agents), AKI (ch. 300), post-obstructive diuresis (chs. 117,
127, 312), and renal tubular acidosis (ch. 303).18,20 Lactation can
lead to excessive losses of Mg++. Hyperthyroidism (ch. 287) and
primary hyperaldosteronism (ch. 295) increase rates of renal Mg++
excretion.5,12 Causes of a shift of Mg++ into the ICF include
hypothermia, catecholamine excess, insulin or glucose
administration, and alkalosis.1,2,4 Mg++ loss can be associated with
various drugs (e.g., gentamicin, cisplatin, digoxin, cyclosporine,
ticarcillin, carbenicillin, and proton pump inhibitors).4,5,7,18,19,24
Brachycephalic dogs may be predisposed to hypomagnesemia.25

HYPERMAGNESEMIA
Overview

Hypermagnesemia is present when serum tMg++ and iMg++
concentrations exceed reference intervals. Unlike Mg++ depletion,
when serum measurements are less reliable, increases in Mg++
storage do correlate with test results. However, this remains an
uncommon-to-rare medical problem since the kidneys are efficient at
excreting Mg++.1,12,18-20

Clinical Signs
Hypermagnesemia can interfere with neuromuscular function,
leading to the nonspecific clinical signs of lethargy, weakness, and
hypotension.1,4,5,18 It appears that Mg++ values may need to reach 79 times above reference interval to cause clinical signs.18 In humans,
symptoms of hypermagnesemia include loss of deep tendon reflexes,
paresis, paralysis, respiratory depression, nausea, vomiting, and
electrocardiographic derangements.4,12 Serum Mg++ concentrations
>12 mg/dL (>4.9 mmol/L) can block calcium channels and cause
cardiac arrest.26 Mg administration should be carefully titrated in
pets with kidney disease.5,18

Differential Diagnosis (Figure 68.4)
The common causes of increased Mg++ concentrations are renal
failure and urinary tract obstruction. Excessive Mg++ administration
(e.g., Mg++-containing fluids, antacids, cathartics) is the most
common cause of hypermagnesemia.1,18-22 Hypermagnesemia has
been reported in cats with thoracic neoplasia, pleural effusion, or in
association with methylprednisolone acetate administration.7,12
Hypermagnesemia has been reported in dogs with primary
hyperparathyroidism (ch. 283), hypothyroidism (ch. 285), and
hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296) as well as occurring after giving
spironolactone or angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ch.
229).5,7,12,19

CALCIUM (Ca) REGULATION
About 50% of the total serum Ca (tCa) concentration is composed of the physiologically active ionized
(iCa) form while about 40% is protein-bound and 10% is the chelated form complexed with lactate,
citrate and bicarbonate.1 The percentage of Ca in each form can vary, altered by albumin and other
protein concentrations, acid-base balance, and natural chelators present in the circulation. The
hormones involved in regulating Ca metabolism include parathyroid hormone (PTH), 1,25dihydroxyvitamin D (vitD), and calcitonin. PTH, secreted by parathyroid gland chief cells, increases Ca
concentrations by mobilizing Ca from the bone, increasing Ca reabsorption in the distal tubules of
nephrons, and increasing urinary phosphate (phos) excretion. VitD increases Ca concentrations by
increasing gastrointestinal (GI) absorption of Ca, mobilizing Ca from bone and causing Ca to be
reabsorbed in the kidneys. Calcitonin, secreted by thyroid gland C cells, reduces Ca resorption from
bone, thereby lowering Ca concentrations. PTH-related protein (PTHrp) mimics PTH activity and serves
as a marker of malignancy (ch. 331).2 Abnormalities in Ca are observed frequently in small animal
practice. Hypocalcemia (hypoCa) and hypercalcemia (hyperCa) can result in clinical signs; their
detection can be informative during diagnostic evaluations.

ASSAYS USED TO INVESTIGATE CALCIUM METABOLISM
DISORDERS
TOTAL Ca (tCa) AND IONIZED Ca (iCa)
tCa can be measured by spectrophotometric methods using serum or heparinized plasma. Ca cannot be
measured in blood containing anticoagulants ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid [EDTA], citrate or oxalate
as they chelate Ca. iCa concentrations are measured by an ion-specific electrode; results can be
influenced by sample pH. It is advisable to transport samples for iCa anaerobically and to assay as soon
as possible after collection.

PARATHYROID HORMONE (PTH)
Several PTH assays are validated for both dogs and cats. Usually, samples are collected in EDTA tubes,
separated, frozen, and transported frozen, since it is a labile protein (chs. 283 and 284).

PARATHYROID HORMONE-RELATED PROTEIN (PTHrp)
PTHrp assays have been validated in both dogs and cats.2 The majority of hyperCa dogs with an
underlying malignancy have increased plasma PTHrp concentrations. This PTHrp is synthesized by the
cancer (ch. 331).2

VITAMIN D (VitD)
Assaying 25(OH)D provides the best assessment of vitD status, while assays for the biologically active
vitD (1,25[OH]2D) are available. Free 25(OH)D concentrations, which represent the most biologically
available 25(OH)D fraction, can also be measured.3-5

HYPERCALCEMIA (hyperCa)
OVERVIEW
Clinical signs of hyperCa vary depending on its underlying cause. The neuromuscular, GI, renal and
cardiac systems are commonly affected. HyperCa interferes with synthesis of antidiuretic hormone,
leading to an inability to concentrate urine and polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD) (ch. 53). Urine specific
gravity (USG) is often isosthenuric or hyposthenuric. Other clinical signs of hyperCa include lethargy,
muscle weakness, seizures, inappetence, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea and cardiac arrhythmias (ch.
283).

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS OF HYPERCALCEMIA (Box 69.1)
Malignancy-Associated
Lymphoma, the most common malignancy-related cause of hyperCa, is frequently but not invariably
associated with increased concentrations of PTHrp, while normocalcemic (normoCa) dogs with
lymphoma usually have low or undetectable PTHrp concentrations.2 Apocrine gland adenocarcinoma of
the anal sac is a less common cause of malignancy-related hyperCa in dogs. Several other malignancies
are inconsistently associated with hyperCa. Since PTHrp mimics natural PTH, affected dogs have
increases in both tCa and iCa while phos is usually low-normal or normal (Table 69.1) (ch. 331).6

Primary Hyperparathyroidism (PHP)
PHP is a well-recognized cause of hyperCa in dogs (ch. 283). Most have moderate to marked hyperCa
and low-normal or low serum phos (Table 69.1).7

Hypoadrenocorticism
Approximately 30% of dogs with hypoadrenocorticism are hyperCa at time of diagnosis.8,9 Increases in
tCa and iCa tend to be mild (ch. 296). Concentrations of PTH, PTHrp and vitD metabolites are typically
within reference ranges.10,11

Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
Most dogs and cats with CKD are azotemic, hyperphosphatemic (hyperphos), normoCa, and
isosthenuric (ch. 301). A small number are hypoCa and even fewer are hyperCa (Table 69.1; ch. 301).
CKD is associated with decreases in 1-alpha-hydroxylase synthesis and phos retention, which inhibits its
enzymatic action. These lead to reduced concentrations of vitD which, in turn, leads to decreased GI Ca
absorption, subclinical decreases in circulating Ca and stimulation of PTH synthesis. These responses
initially maintain normoCa but as CKD progresses, they may become insufficient and hypoCa can ensue.
While CKD is typically associated with normoCa or hypoCa, a small number of affected animals can
become hyperCa. The etiology of CKD and hyperCa is poorly understood but may be due to autonomous
secretion of PTH, a raised set point for Ca autoregulation, or increased binding of Ca to retained anions
(Table 69.1).

Miscellaneous Causes
Healthy young growing dogs and cats can have mild hyperCa and hyperphos. Ingestion of vitDcontaining rodenticides or of topical ointments containing vitD analogues used in treating people with
psoriasis can cause hyperCa (ch. 134).12 Excess vitD and hyperCa can be the result of overzealous
dietary supplementation or vitD overdose when treating hypoparathyroidism. Excess vitD increases GI
absorption of Ca and phos, leading to hyperCa and hyperphos. HyperCa is occasionally associated with
granulomatous diseases that induce ectopic production of vitD.

HYPERCALCEMIA IN CATS
Most causes of hyperCa are similar in cats and dogs, but there are some important differences (Box
69.1). In cats, CKD and malignancy (especially squamous cell carcinoma) are the most frequent causes
of hyperCa.8,13 Anal sac apocrine gland adenocarcinoma and hypoadrenocorticism are not common in
cats.14 Idiopathic hyperCa is an important differential in cats.15 This diagnosis is reserved for cats where
the underlying cause of the hyperCa cannot be identified despite diagnostic evaluations and long-term
follow-up. Both tCa and iCa are moderately increased, PTH concentrations are normal or low, and
PTHrp concentrations are within reference range. It is important to rule out known causes in cats
suspected of idiopathic hyperCa prior to initiating treatment.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH TO HYPERCALCEMIA
A thorough history and careful physical examination should be performed in any dog or cat with
confirmed or suspected hyperCa (Figure 69.1). The potential for access to toxins or medications
containing vitD should be assessed. Peripheral lymph nodes and anal sacs should be carefully palpated
(ch. 3). Serum biochemistries are almost invariably informative with particular attention to the
electrolytes, albumin, urea, phos and creatinine concentrations. Evaluation of USG in the context of the
serum biochemistries can aid in discriminating kidney disease or hypoadrenocorticism from PTH or
PTHrp-driven hyperCa, but in all the USG is likely to be hypo- or isosthenuric. Consideration should be
given to fine needle aspiration (FNA) or biopsy of any enlarged lymph node (ch. 88) or any worrisome
palpable mass, since malignancies and granulomatous diseases can cause hyperCa. A circulating basal
cortisol should be considered as a screen for hypoadrenocorticism in any hyperCa dog or cat, even if the
classic hyponatremia and hyperkalemia are absent (ch. 296).9,16 Thoracic and abdominal imaging are
used to search for unexpected masses which may be the cause of hyperCa. Ultrasonography of the
ventral neck region may be helpful in detecting parathyroid nodules observed in PHP. Assay of PTH,
PTHrp and vitD metabolites may improve understanding a condition and may be required before a
diagnosis can be confirmed (Figure 69.1).

FIGURE 69.1 Algorithm for the diagnosis of hypercalcemia. ACTH,
Adrenocorticotropic hormone; FNA, fine needle aspiration; PTH, parathyroid
hormone; PTHrp, PTH-related protein.

HYPOCALCEMIA
OVERVIEW
HypoCa, not as common as hyperCa, can be caused by a variety of diseases following impaired PTH
secretion or action, impaired vitD synthesis or action, or Ca precipitation or chelation (Box 69.2) (ch.
284).6 Clinical signs depend on underlying cause. HypoCa can be subclinical although many animals
show signs directly attributable to hypoCa-induced increased neuronal excitability that include
nervousness, behavioral changes, focal muscle twitching (especially ear and facial muscles) (Video 69.1
), facial rubbing (Videos 284.1, 284.2), muscle cramps, stiff gait, tetany (Video 284.2) and seizures
(ch. 284). Exercise, excitement, or stress can induce or worsen signs. Additional abnormalities may
include fever, cataracts, and tachyarrhythmias.

Hypoalbuminemia
Hypoalbuminemia is a common cause of low tCa on serum biochemistry profiles but iCa concentrations
are usually within reference limits (tCa measures low because 40% is protein bound). Low albumin can

occur in pets with protein losing enteropathies (PLEs), protein losing nephropathies, or liver failure (ch.
60). iCa concentrations may be decreased in some dogs with PLE.17

Impaired PTH Secretion
Idiopathic primary hypoparathyroidism, uncommon to rare in dogs and cats, can result in severe
hypoCa.18 Iatrogenic hypoparathyroidism may occur in cats following damage to or removal of the
parathyroid glands during thyroidectomy for hyperthyroidism (ch. 284).

Increased Ca Loss
Eclampsia occurs most commonly in young small dogs. The syndrome is relatively rare in cats. Clinical
signs usually occur 1-5 weeks post-whelping due to a combination of Ca loss through lactation and fetal
drain of Ca during skeleton ossification.

VitD Deficiency
CKD in both dogs and cats may lead to mild hypoCa, usually with normal iCa.19 Reduced GI absorption
of vitD in dogs and cats with a PLE or exocrine pancreatic insufficiency may lead to hypoCa.17

Precipitation or Chelation of Ca
Ethylene glycol intoxication causes Ca binding with oxalic acid in the renal tubules, Ca oxalate
crystalluria, and renal loss of Ca (ch. 135). In acute kidney injury (AKI), rapidly rising phos complexes
with Ca leading to hypoCa. Increased renal tubular loss of Ca exacerbates hypoCa. In urinary tract
obstruction, mild to moderate hypoCa may follow increased binding of Ca with phos. In the “acute
tumor lysis syndrome,” hypoCa may result from phos released from lysed cells binding Ca. In
pancreatitis, hypoCa may result from sequestration of Ca in peripancreatic fat or in soft tissues as a
result of saponification.20 HypoCa after blood transfusion may occur due to citrate chelation of Ca or
hypoCa can follow furosemide administration.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH TO HYPOCALCEMIA
The list of common causes for hypoCa is relatively short. The history, physical examination, hematology
(complete blood count), serum biochemistry profile and urinalysis are often helpful in establishing

cause. Evaluation of liver function and assessing for pancreatitis should be considered in
hypoalbuminemic pets. Abdominal imaging may be helpful in the evaluation of GI, liver, pancreatic and
renal diseases. Measurement of plasma PTH is required to confirm primary hypoparathyroidism.

PHOSPHATE (phos)
Phos, essential for normal cellular function, is the body’s major intracellular anion. Although present in
the plasma as organic and inorganic forms, most clinical laboratories measure inorganic phos. Phos
absorption and excretion is regulated alongside Ca. PTH decreases phos reabsorption in the kidney and
vitD increases GI absorption.

HYPERPHOSPHATEMIA (Hyperphos)
Hyperphos indicates presence of an underlying disease but only rarely causes clinical signs (Box 69.3).
Signs are associated with hypoCa. Hyperphos can occur due to increased GI absorption, decreased
excretion into the urine, or a shift in from intracellular to extracellular compartments. CKD is the most
common cause of hyperphos and less common causes include hypervitaminosis D, urinary tract
obstruction, AKI, hypoparathyroidism and hyperthyroidism.

HYPOPHOSPHATEMIA (Hypophos)
Hypophos can occur due to decreased intestinal absorption, increased renal excretion or transcellular
shifts. Hypophos is commonly associated with hyperCa due to malignancy or PHP (Box 69.4).
Hypophos can follow insulin administration of pets ill with diabetic ketoacidosis. Mild hypophos is not
typically associated with clinical signs. Marked hypophos can be associated with hemolysis, respiratory
distress and neurological abnormalities.

OVERVIEW AND INDICATIONS
The urinalysis (UA) is an inexpensive, easily performed, and major
component of any “minimum database.” It often provides crucial
information in diagnosis and management. Urine, the combined result
of glomerular filtration and renal tubular resorption/secretion,
provides insight into systemic and urinary health. The most obvious
indications for UA are investigating pets with polyuria and polydipsia
(PU/PD) (ch. 53); urination difficulties (chs. 54, 310, 312); urinary
tract disease or infection (ch. 307), acute kidney injury (AKI) (ch.
300), chronic kidney disease (CKD) (ch. 301), current or previous

urolithiasis (chs. 308, 309); or known systemic illness. Fanconi
syndrome, urinary tract cancer, and specific non-urinary conditions
such as diabetes mellitus (DM) (chs. 291, 292), diabetes insipidus (ch.
282), hemolytic diseases (ch. 174), and hepatic dysfunction (ch. 266)
are better understood with UA results. In dogs or cats not showing
clinical signs, dilute urine, proteinuria, or crystalluria can stimulate
changes in management or further investigation. UA results may be
helpful in monitoring many conditions and may be useful in the early
detection of adverse reactions. Interpreting any UA in the context of
serum biochemistry (SB) and complete blood count (CBC) results
enhances the value of each. Results may reflect physiologic or
pathologic states, but one should remember potential influences due to
sample collection method, handling, analytic methodology, and other
interferences to avoid errors in UA-based decisions.

COLLECTION AND CARE OF URINE
SAMPLES
Reliable UA results and interpretation require appropriate sample
collection and handling. For example, urine collected from a table-top
may contain micro-organisms or chemical cleaning agents while
cystocentesis samples, free from environmental and lower urinary tract
contaminants, may include iatrogenic red blood cells (RBCs) (ch. 98).
Ideally, urine should be analyzed within 2 hours of collection. Urine
held at room temperature may develop changes in turbidity, pH,
growth of contaminating bacteria, loss of cellular detail, and cast
disintegration or deterioration. Samples shipped to an external
laboratory should be suitably preserved, particularly if culture is
required. Boric acid helps preserve most aspects of UA, but not pH or
urine specific gravity (USG).

METHODOLOGY, LIMITATIONS, AND
INTERFERENCES (Table 70.1)
PHYSICAL

There is some correlation between depth of urine color and its
concentration (ch. 55). Since pigments like bilirubin can appear as
dark yellow, color is not an absolute predictor of concentration and it
should be interpreted in the context of USG and blood test results.1
USG, the ratio of urine weight to that of distilled water, is estimated by
its refractive index. Any effect of temperature is mitigated by
calibration prior to each use. Veterinary refractometers may have
slightly different scales for cat and dog urine.2,3 Not all refractometers
are equally accurate and their imprecision warrants caution in
interpreting results that are close to thresholds (e.g., 1.035).2-5
Osmolality is a more reliable measure of urine concentration and is
usually recommended in provocative tests (chs. 53 and 282).6 Neither
glucose nor protein has much impact on measured USG; glucose
increases USG by 0.001/270 mg/dL (15 mmol/L).5,7

CHEMICAL
Urine chemistries are typically assessed with a “dipstick” of reagentimpregnated colorimetric test pads. Color changes are assessed by
visual comparison to manufacturer-provided charts or by automated
strip readers, which can improve precision. Highest accuracy is
achieved with reference methods.8-11 Results may vary if the stick is
submerged in urine versus using only enough urine to “drip” onto test
pads.12 It is important to read results at stated time-points. Results
may need to be repeated on supernatant for visibly turbid or bloody
samples. Not all available pads on all dipsticks are suitable for
veterinary use (Table 70.1). Urine dipstick pH pads estimate to the
nearest 0.5 or 1 unit, adequate for most clinical uses although pH
meters should be more accurate. Results are more reliable with fresh
urine13-15 and unusual urine pH may indicate that other UA results
may be unreliable.
Urine protein dipstick test pads have higher sensitivity for albumin
than globulin. Results must be placed in context of USG and pH such
that a “1+” reading would be unlikely to be significant if USG or pH are
high but could be relevant in dilute urine. Quantitative protein analysis
with urine protein to creatinine ratio (UPC) may be indicated to
confirm dipstick-detected proteinuria, if globulinuria is suspected, or

with high pH. Any canine dipstick “++” and “+++” reading should be
repeated. All “+” protein results in samples with USG <1.012 should be
further assessed with UPC. Taking USG into account does not
accurately predict significant proteinuria.16-19 The sulphosalicylic acid
(SSA) test is an alternative to dipstick pads. The UPC is measured on
supernatant using a chemical micro-protein method (e.g., pyrogallol
red or Coomassie brilliant blue) at a reference laboratory or on an inclinic analyser. Results may vary.20 Protein may not be detected if
there is significant pyuria and bacteriuria.21-26
Dipstick glucose technology is based on glucose oxidase. An
alternative copper-reduction confirmatory test (Clinitest tablets) is
available. Ketone test pads utilize nitroprusside, detecting acetone, and
aceto-acetate but not beta-hydroxybutyrate. Only conjugated (“direct”)
bilirubin is water-soluble and able to enter glomerular filtrate.
Unconjugated (“indirect”) bilirubin is protein- bound and is not
filtered. Bilirubin tests are based on diazonium. A more sensitive
confirmatory tablet test is available (Ictotest). Dipstick methodology for
“blood” is based on heme reacting with organic peroxide, resulting in
detection of hematuria, hemoglobinuria, or myoglobinuria at levels that
are not visually apparent; test pad sensitivity is 5-20 RBCs/mcL
compared with the >2500 RBCs/mcL needed for visual recognition.
RBCs without free hemoglobin yield blotchy color changes on the pad.
The leukocyte test pad is neither sensitive nor specific for feline white
blood cells (WBCs) and specific but insensitive for dogs. Positive results
correlate with positive culture results in dogs.19

MICROSCOPIC EXAMINATION
Microscopic examination for RBCs, WBCs, epithelial cells, casts,
crystals, or organisms can be performed using concentrated resuspended sediment on a microscope slide. Reference laboratories use
well mixed non-centrifuged samples allowed to settle on a microtiter
plate and an inverted microscope. Similar techniques are employed by
image analysis urine analysers such as Sedivue (IDEXX Laboratories
Inc.), able to recognize and count certain sediment elements.27
Standardized protocols used in analyzing sediment allow comparison
of results. The number of elements recognized per low- or high-power
microscopic field (/lpf, /hpf) depends on individual microscope

specifications and the coverslip approach employed (Box 70.1). Casts
are generally reported /lpf (also viewed /hpf for identification) and
cellular elements /hpf. Sediment stains can help identify some items
but can dilute and alter semi-quantitative counts. Place a drop each of
unstained and stained sediment on one slide for comparison.
RBCs can usually be distinguished from other round elements, yeast,
or lipid droplets by their uniform size. Lipid droplets float to the
surface and remain at a different focal plane. WBC morphology may
vary depending on pH and USG, often making it difficult to distinguish
different WBCs or tubular epithelial cells. Nuclear characteristics may
be enhanced with sediment stains or by clearing with 2-10% glacial
acetic acid. Cytological examination of stained fixed smears may help
identify cellular criteria of malignancy (ch. 85) but cells seen in urine
are rarely conclusive. Contaminated unpreserved stored urine, bacteria
rendered non-viable by preservation method (excessive boric acid), or
recent antibiotic therapy may result in bacteria seen on sediment but
without growth when cultured. An air-dried drop of urine or resuspended sediment stained with a Romanowsky stain (e.g., Diff-Quik)
is more sensitive for bacteriuria than unstained preparations.28-30 Invitro factors that influence crystal development include USG,
temperature, time to analysis, and pH.31 Some crystals require a
certain pH to form. Altering the pH can make detection of certain
crystals easier and may assist in their identification.

PHYSIOLOGY AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
(Table 70.2)
PHYSICAL
Color, Turbidity, and Odor
Urine pigments may interfere with dipstick test results. Biliverdin
imparts a green color while hematuria, hemoglobinuria,
myoglobinuria, and oxyglobin cause urine to be red, pink, orange, dark
brown, or black (ch. 55). In cats with urethral obstruction, darker red
urine has been associated with greater metabolic derangements.32
Urine turbidity increases with excess WBCs, RBCs, epithelial cells,

sperm, casts, mucus, crystals, bacteria, or lipid. Fresh normal urine has
a slight ammonia odor, which can increase with time or with some
infections. The smell of acetone suggests ketonuria.

Urine Specific Gravity (USG) (Table 70.3)
USG, the only result that provides information on renal function, has
no “reference interval” since healthy kidneys can produce extremely
dilute or extremely concentrated urine (1.001 to >1.075). This is
influenced by hydration and electrolyte status, diet, and the
individual.33,34

CHEMICAL
pH
Urine pH usually reflects total body acid-base and may be influenced
by diet, time of day, and disease. High protein diets acidify while
vegetable or cereal-based diets alkalinize urine (ch. 158). Urine
obtained after a meal is often alkaline due to gastric acid secretion.
Interpretation of urine pH in the context of current blood gas,
electrolyte, and bicarbonate may help identify renal tubular acidoses
and paradoxical aciduria in vomiting. Urinary tract infections (UTIs)
with urease-producing bacteria (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Proteus)
cause alkaline urine.

Proteinuria (Figure 70.1)
Persistent proteinuria is common, affecting almost 20% of elderly
dogs.35 UPCs might be higher from in-hospital samples.36 Proteinuria
can be categorized as pre-renal/overflow, renal (glomerular or tubular),
or post-renal. Interpretation of proteinuria should be made in the
context of the sediment examination, as the presence of RBCs and
WBCs is indicative of renal or post-renal issues and their absence may
suggest renal origin (glomerulonephritis, amyloidosis). Pathological
pre-renal causes of proteinuria include hemolysis (hemoglobin),
rhabdomyolysis (myoglobin) or plasma cell cancers
(immunoglobulins). Clues for these conditions may be found on CBC or
serum biochemistry profile. Functional pre-renal origins include
strenuous exercise, fever and seizure activity. Renal proteinuria may be
functional and transient (e.g., inflammation) or persistent and
pathological. Glomerular proteinuria is associated with loss of albumin,
causing hypoalbuminemia when severe. Damaged or diseased renal
tubules, whether due to congenital defects or an acquired AKI (e.g.,
Fanconi syndrome, gentamicin toxicosis), may cause impaired
resorption of filtered low molecular weight proteins and albumin (chs.
299 to 303).

Glucose (Figure 70.1)
When proximal tubular capacity for reabsorption of filtered glucose is
exceeded, it appears in urine (blood glucose >170-180 mg/dL [>9.4-10
mmol/L] in dogs, >260-310 mg/dL [>14.4-17.2 mmol/L] in cats).

Hyperglycemic glucosuria (DM, stress hyperglycemia [cats],
medication) is much more common than normoglycemic glucosuria
(e.g., primary renal glucosuria, Fanconi syndrome).

Ketones
Ketones accumulate when there is a shift from carbohydrate to fat
metabolism, which is a classic finding in decompensating DM (ch.
290) and certain negative energy balance states. As DM is treated,
beta-hydroxybutyrate synthesis is suppressed; acetone and
acetoacetate (for which urine dipstick reagent pads are more sensitive)
accumulate and may create a false impression of continuing or
worsening illness.

Bilirubin
Bilirubinuria with hyperbilirubinemia is expected with RBC destruction
(hemolysis), intrahepatic disease, cholestasis, and biliary obstruction
(ch. 28). The renal threshold for bilirubin is low in dogs and bilirubin
can be detected in urine before hyperbilirubinemia is noted. Canine
kidneys synthesize bilirubin, so not all is derived from the blood. Low
but detectable bilirubin may be noted in concentrated urine samples
from healthy male dogs. Bilirubinuria in cats is significant.
