Blood (Hematuria, Hemoglobinuria, Myoglobinuria)
(Figure 70.1)
Dipstick assessment of blood must be made in the context of USG,
sediment, serum color, and muscle enzyme concentrations. Hematuria
is common, hemoglobinuria is less common, and myoglobinuria is rare.
Hematuria may be present due to bleeding within the urinary tract
from trauma, uroliths, inflammation, infection, neoplasia, or a bleeding
disorder (ch. 55). Confirmation by sediment examination is
recommended. Extra-urinary (genital) sources of blood are common.
Hemoglobin may be present in urine either as a result of
hemoglobinemia (intravascular hemolysis) or RBCs that have lysed in
dilute or alkaline urine. Hemoglobin appears in urine when
haptoglobin binding capacity in plasma is exceeded and renal tubular
resorption mechanisms are overwhelmed. Myoglobinuria can occur if
there is muscle trauma, ischemia, or necrosis (ch. 66). When urine is
discolored due to myoglobin, it may be described as red/brown rather
than pink/red. Elevations in serum creatine kinase and/or aspartate
aminotransferase activity would be expected with myoglobinuria (chs.
65 and 66).

FIGURE 70.1 Interpretation of dipstick-positive
results for protein, glucose, and blood. +ve, Positive

urinary tract infection; WBCs, white blood cells.

MICROSCOPIC SEDIMENT
EXAMINATION
Hematuria (Figure 70.1)
Small numbers of RBCs may be seen in the urine of normal dogs and
cats. Healthy pets have the fewest RBCs in free catch samples. There
are numerous causes for hematuria (ch. 55).

Pyuria

Small numbers of WBCs may be seen in urine from healthy dogs and
cats, with a ratio to RBCs of about 1:1; neutrophils are the most
common. Large numbers of WBCs are consistent with infectious or
non-infectious inflammation, often accompanied by some degree of
hematuria and/or proteinuria. Failure to see bacteria does not exclude
infection, hence the recommendation to culture pyuric urine. Noninfectious causes of pyuria include neoplasia and uroliths.

Epithelial Cells
The interpretation of epithelial cells depends on type: tubular,
transitional, or squamous. Large numbers of morphologically typical
transitional cells are indicative of inflammation, although mechanical
abrasion, neoplasia, and other causes may be suspected.

Bacteria
Normal urine is sterile but samples may contain bacteria from the
distal urethra or genital tract in voided or catheter samples. Finding
bacteria in urine sediment may or may not be significant. Not
identifying bacteria does not rule out their presence. Large numbers of
bacteria in cystocentesis, or fresh or preserved catheterized samples are
suggestive of UTI, particularly when accompanied by pyuria.
Quantitative urine culture is indicated to confirm UTI, with
significance thresholds dependent on collection method.

Cylindruria (Casts)
Casts are composed of Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein derived from the
loop of Henle, distal tubules, and collecting ducts, in which cellular
material can be trapped to form casts. Casts can indicate inflammation,
hemorrhage, or degradation of renal tubular epithelial cells. Low
numbers (e.g., <2/lpf) of hyaline or granular casts may be observed in
health. Cellular (WBC, epithelial), fatty, and waxy casts likely indicate
significant renal injury/necrosis due to ischemia, inflammation or
toxins. A mixture of WBC and epithelial cell casts may be observed
following acute tubular necrosis. The presence of RBC casts localizes
bleeding to nephrons.

Crystalluria

Struvite, amorphous phosphate, and oxalate crystals are commonly
seen in the urine of healthy animals. Urate, cysteine, or large quantities
of calcium oxalate crystals are usually abnormal (chs. 308 and 309).
Some crystals are indicative of significant abnormalities or a metabolic
disorder, and others may provide preliminary information concerning
the structure of uroliths, if present. Crystalluria does not predict
urolithiasis. Most urinary crystals in dogs and cats are easily recognized
by shape, size, color, and sample pH. A medication history is invaluable
in interpreting unusual crystals.

THORACIC AND ABDOMINAL CAVITY FLUID
Aspiration of fluid with subsequent cytologic analysis is a routine part of the diagnostic
evaluation of patients with pleural or abdominal effusions. The thoracic and abdominal
cavities are bathed in small amounts of fluid that cannot normally be aspirated in small
animals. Therefore, any fluid accumulation is abnormal. Aspiration is a relatively
innocuous, minimally invasive, and inexpensive procedure that can yield clues as to the
cause of the effusion and provide a definitive diagnosis of the underlying disease.

FLUID ANALYSIS
Analysis starts at collection (chs. 86 and 92), with assessment of fluid color and ease of
collection. If the fluid starts off clear and then becomes bloody during collection, or vice
versa, blood contamination is likely. If the fluid remains bloody throughout collection,
then hemorrhage is likely. If the fluid resembles blood, this could be due to severe
hemorrhage or aspiration of a highly vascularized organ, such as the spleen.
Differentiation between these possibilities can be accomplished by placing the bloody
fluid into a non-anticoagulant (red top) tube. Because blood clots and lyses rapidly
in vivo, the absence of a clot supports in vivo hemorrhage versus blood contamination.
In contrast, clots in the fluid in vitro would argue for blood contamination, although
peracute hemorrhage also could be occurring. Visual inspection of fluid color and

clarity after collection also yields other helpful information and can guide smear
preparation and additional diagnostic testing (Box 71.1, Figure 71.1).

Sample Handling, Storage, and Submission
Fluid should be placed into an ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA)-anticoagulated
(purple top) tube for cytologic examination. EDTA inhibits bacterial growth1 and
preserves cellular features. Collection into a non-anticoagulant tube is helpful with
bloody fluids and is always recommended, volume permitting, if biochemical tests or
culture are desired, although submission of the sample in a culture tube is preferred for
the latter. Several smears should be made from fluids immediately after collection
(Video 71.1

) and rapidly air-dried (with a hair dryer on high aimed at the back of

the slides). At the very least, a direct smear from unconcentrated fluid should be made;
however, this can be paucicellular if the total nucleated cell count (TNCC) is low. Thus,
sediment smears (line smears) from centrifuged samples are recommended for fluids
suspected to be of low cellularity (transparent to lightly turbid; Figures 71.1 and 71.2,
Box 71.1). Only a portion of the fluid should be centrifuged, and the remainder should
be left for cell counts, total protein estimation, and preparation of additional smears by
the testing laboratory. Smears and tubes should be labeled with the patient
identification information, collection date, and fluid (and smear) type. A complete
relevant history should be provided. Submission of smears with fluid samples is critical
to avoid storage-associated changes that impact cytologic interpretation and diagnostic
accuracy of fluid analysis. These changes include:

Colorless, transparent: likely low-protein transudate, low cellularity
(sediment and direct smears recommended); assess for low albumin
concentrations in serum and protein-losing conditions and liver disease (portal
hypertension).
Light to moderate yellow, transparent to slightly turbid: likely
transudative effusion (low- or high-protein); low to moderate cellularity
(sediment and direct smears recommended). Various causes.
Light to moderate red to red-yellow, slightly to moderately turbid:
likely transudative effusion (high- or low-protein, but frequently high-protein)
with concurrent hemorrhage or blood contamination; low to moderate
cellularity (sediment and direct smears recommended). Various causes.
Light to moderate yellow, transparent to lightly turbid, viscous,
± fibrin clot (cats only): likely exudative effusion; moderate to high
cellularity (direct smears likely sufficient); high total protein concentration by
refractometer (>2.5 g/dL, >25 g/L); suspect feline infectious peritonitis.
Yellow to yellow-white, opaque to flocculent, may be lightly or
moderately red, supernatant clears after centrifugation: suspect
exudative effusion; high cellularity (direct smears sufficient); culture or

additional testing may be warranted, e.g., total bilirubin or creatinine
concentrations in effusion if suspected biliary or urinary tract rupture or
leakage, respectively.
White to pink to light red, opaque to opalescent with a cream layer
on refrigeration, supernatant opaque after centrifugation: suspect
chylous (transudative) effusion with concurrent hemorrhage or blood
contamination (if red or pink); moderate to high cellularity (direct smears
usually sufficient); additional testing may be warranted, e.g., effusion
triglyceride concentrations.
Green to green-brown, moderately turbid to opaque: likely high
cellularity (direct smears sufficient); suspect bile peritonitis, enterocentesis, or
ruptured GI tract (particularly if flocculent with food or particulate material);
evaluate smear before accepting cell counts (bacteria, food debris counted as
“cells”).
Dark red (mimics blood), opaque, does not clot in a nonanticoagulant tube, measurable packed cell volume: suspect
hemorrhagic effusion (direct smears usually sufficient, although buffy coat
smears are also prepared in laboratories).
Dark red (mimics blood), opaque, clots in a non-anticoagulant tube,
measurable packed cell volume (EDTA): aspiration of the spleen,
peracute hemorrhage from large vessel, splenic, or liver rupture.

FIGURE 71.1 Clarity and color of body cavity effusions yield
clues on cellularity and help guide smear preparation for cytologic
evaluation. Left: light yellow, clear; the writing on the page can be
read easily through the fluid. Such samples are of low cellularity
and require concentration techniques to optimize smear
preparation and cytologic evaluation, ideally cytocentrifugation. In
the absence of a cytocentrifuge, a sediment can be prepared from
the sample with a regular centrifuge and a line smear prepared
from the resuspended pellet to maximally “concentrate” the cells
(Figure 71.2). Middle: light pink, slightly cloudy. The latter
appearance reflects either cells or lipid, with the pink tinge
supporting the presence of red blood cells (RBCs). Optimal smear
preparation would involve concentration via centrifugation,
although smears of unconcentrated fluid (direct smears) will be
more cellular than that from the tube on the left. Centrifugation
would also help discriminate between lipid (would not sediment)
and cells (a sediment would form) or reveal the presence of both
(cloudy supernatant with or without a fat layer plus a cell pellet). If
lipid is present, triglyceride concentrations on the centrifuged fluid
could be measured to help support leakage of chyle as a component
of the effusion. Right: light to medium red, opaque, preventing
visualization of the text on the page behind the tube. The color
indicates the presence of intact RBCs, which will sediment on
centrifugation. Nucleated cellularity (e.g., white blood cells) may
vary from low to high. For this type of sample, a direct smear of

unconcentrated fluid and a sediment smear of a resuspended pellet
of centrifuged fluid would be optimal smear types.
• Deterioration of cells with storage: this affects cell counts and cell identification.
• Swelling of neutrophils: mimics degenerative change.
• In vitro phagocytic activity: phagocytosis of red blood cells (RBCs) and bacteria
can occur within 30-120 minutes of sample collection, due to in vitro cellular
activity.
• Bacterial proliferation: this can lyse cells and falsely increase the TNCC.
To minimize storage-associated changes, fluid samples should be shipped promptly
and kept refrigerated (on ice packs, avoiding direct contact with the pack to prevent
freezing). Smears should be kept at room temperature and shipped in break-proof
containers.

Cytologic Results
Most laboratories provide gross fluid characteristics, TNCC, a total protein estimate,
and cytologic analysis on optimally concentrated smears (the smear type is usually
dictated by the cell counts). Cytologic assessments can be done in-house using quick
stains (e.g., Diff-Quik) and are worthwhile for rapid diagnosis and improving cytologic
interpretation skills (e.g., comparing results to those of a clinical pathologist).

Cell Counts
These can be done with a hemocytometer or automated hematology analyzers,
including those used at point-of-care.2-4 Body cavity fluids can plug analyzers; thus, a
wash cycle should be done after fluid analysis and samples with visible clots or
particulate material ideally should not be analyzed (these samples could be filtered
first, e.g., using a 70-micron filter). Automated TNCC may be inaccurate in fluids with
cell clumping; in one study, hyaluronidase was added to improve accuracy,5 but this is
not routinely done in body cavity fluids, other than synovial fluid. Not all counted or
nucleated cells are leukocytes (they could be mesothelial or cancer cells) and bacteria
and particulate debris can be counted as “cells,” falsely increasing the TNCC.

Total Protein
Estimates are obtained with a refractometer using the fluid supernatant after
centrifugation if the fluid is turbid. A more accurate total protein concentration can be
obtained with chemistry analyzers,6,7 but this approach is more expensive and not
usually required. Laboratories may provide specific gravity in lieu of total protein.

Cytologic Assessment
Smears are examined for the relative proportions of leukocytes, degenerate neutrophils
(supporting bacterial sepsis), cytophagia (RBCs or other cells), and a potential cause,
e.g., neoplastic cells or infectious agents (Figure 71.3). If RBCs are numerous,
platelets would indicate blood contamination or peracute hemorrhage, whereas
erythrophagia, hemosiderophages, or hematoidin crystals support prior hemorrhage

(Figure 71.3). If sample volume is insufficient for all tests, preference should be given
to cytologic assessment, because cell counts can be estimated from direct smears.
Interpretation of effusions based on cell counts and total protein concentration alone
may result in erroneous fluid classification and diagnoses. Automated differential
counts provided by hematology analyzers are generally inaccurate and should not
supplant cytologic assessment of smears.2-4

FIGURE 71.2 A line smear is used for preparing a sample from
poorly cellular fluid either directly from the fluid or from a
centrifuged pellet. A, Using a standard blood (“wedge”) smear
technique, the drop of fluid is moved forward with the spreader
slide until approximately three-fourths of the way down the slide.
Then the forward motion is stopped and the spreader slide is lifted
off (upward black arrows). B, This technique creates a line (arrow),
in which cells are concentrated. To make the end of the smear (the
line) wider, the slide can be tilted by lifting up the edge of the slide
at the line end, allowing the fluid to run a little backwards (not
shown). The smear is then rapidly air-dried. A marker pen can be
used to delineate the location of the line (not shown).

Other Tests
Additional diagnostic tests can be performed on effusion fluid and may be desired, e.g.,
measurement of bilirubin, creatinine, pancreatic-specific lipase immunoreactivity,
lipase activity, lactate, and glucose concentrations or pH.8-12 The latter 3 tests should

be done in-house, because storage will yield erroneous values.13,14 Advanced cancer
diagnostic tests, such as flow cytometric-based immunophenotyping for hematopoietic
neoplasms and clonality tests (ch. 322),15,16 are best done on fresh samples (<48-72
hours old, kept refrigerated). Flow cytometric analysis requires EDTA- or citrateanticoagulated cells in suspension and can be done on residual samples. Autologous
serum (10-20%) can be added to help preserve cells for flow cytometric testing,15 but
this should only be done to a portion of the sample if cytologic assessment is also being
performed. Clonality testing can be done on the same cell suspension used for flow
cytometry or on stained or unstained cytologic smears. Two cellular slides should
ideally be submitted to ensure retrieval of DNA of sufficient quantity and quality.

CLASSIFICATION OF EFFUSIONS
The author uses a mechanistic approach for fluid classification, which differs from the
traditional classification scheme (“pure” transudate, “modified” transudate, exudate).
Fluids accumulate in body cavities due to the following mechanisms: transudation,
exudation, or viscus/vessel rupture (Table 71.1, Figure 71.4).

Transudation
This is the most common type of effusion and is due to alterations in hydrodynamic
forces, typically venous or lymphatic hypertension. Marked decreases in oncotic
pressure from severe hypoalbuminemia (<1.5 g/dL, <15 g/L) can also result in a
transudative effusion (e.g., nephrotic syndrome), but they are rarely the sole cause and
are usually accompanied by venous or lymphatic hypertension. Transudative effusions
are often light to medium yellow, transparent to lightly cloudy, with TNCC <3-5 ×
109/L (<3-5 × 103/mcL) with a total protein concentration usually <5 g/dL (<50 g/L).
RBC counts are variable. A mixture of non-degenerate neutrophils and macrophages,
with fewer lymphocytes and mesothelial cells (rare in cats), are seen in stained smears
(Figure 71.3). RBCs can be due to blood contamination or, less frequently,
hemorrhage. Erythrophagia (and rarely hemosiderophages) will be seen with prior
hemorrhage, unless it is peracute (Figure 71.3). Unfortunately, a cause is frequently
not evident cytologically with transudative effusions. Transudative effusions can be
separated into “low-protein” (<2.5 g/dL, <25 g/L) and “high-protein” (≥2.5 g/dL, ≥25
g/L) transudates. This distinction is most useful for peritoneal fluids because it reveals
the location of the hypertension, which helps narrow down the list of causes (Table
71.1).

Low-Protein (Protein-Poor or Pure) Transudates
These are colorless to light yellow fluids with minimal blood. Prehepatic (mesenteric
lymphatics) or hepatic presinusoidal (portal) or early sinusoidal hypertension causes
leakage of low-protein intestinal lymph. The most common cause is liver disease,
followed by protein-losing conditions.

High-Protein (Protein-Rich or “Modified”) Transudates

These are light to moderate yellow fluids that are often blood-tinged from hemorrhage.
Late sinusoidal or post-sinusoidal hypertension causes leakage of high-protein hepatic
lymph. Common causes are liver disease and cancer (dogs and cats, Figure 71.3), and
congestive heart failure (dogs).

Chylous or Lymphocyte-Rich Effusions
Both of these terms are descriptive and not mechanistic. They are usually applicable to
transudative effusions and neither is considered exudative, with an exception given
below. Classic chylous effusions, which consist of leakage of chylomicron-rich intestinal
lymph, are more common in pleural fluid. Such effusions are usually opaque and white
and frequently blood-tinged (pink to light red). A fat layer may form on standing or
refrigeration due to buoyant chylomicrons (ch. 63: Figure 63.2). The TNCC is
variable (can be >5 × 109/L), consisting mostly of small lymphocytes with fewer nondegenerate neutrophils and macrophages, which may contain cytoplasmic lipid
droplets. In longer-standing chylous effusions, concurrent inflammation may be
present from the irritating effects of chyle. In the latter fluids, neutrophils may
dominate, but lymphocyte proportions are often still high (Figure 71.3). A chylous
effusion can be confirmed by high fluid triglyceride concentrations (>1:1 ratio vs. serum
or >1.1 mmol/L [>100 mg/dL]). Chylous effusions from anorectic animals may not be
grossly lipemic and may have triglyceride concentrations <1.1 mmol/L17; however, they
are usually still lymphocyte-rich. Chylous pleural effusions can be caused by various
conditions (e.g., right-sided heart failure, abscesses, mediastinal granulomas) causing
transudation, but are frequently idiopathic (ch. 220).18 Chylous ascites is rare and is
caused by lymphatic blockage or hypertension (most commonly due to neoplasia, but
also right-sided heart failure) or lymphangiectasia.17 The term chylous effusion is being
supplanted by lymphocyte-rich effusion.19 However, when the fluid is rich in
chylomicrons, the author still uses the term chylous effusion in parentheses, in
conjunction with a mechanistic interpretation of the effusion, e.g., transudative
effusion (chylous effusion).

This classification is based on a combination of total protein concentration, nucleated
and red blood cell (RBC) counts, and cytologic findings and is helpful for narrowing the
differential diagnostic list for the cause of the effusion.
Differentiation of transudates into low- and high-protein effusions helps
identification of location of transudation (e.g., presinusoidal versus sinusoidal or postsinusoidal) for peritoneal effusions.
∗

†

For g/dL, divide by 10.

Exudation

Exudative effusions are caused by increased vascular permeability due to inflammation,
with leakage of serum protein and inflammatory cell chemotaxis. Exudative effusions
are usually yellow to white, lightly to moderately cloudy to opaque or flocculent, with
TNCC >5 × 109/L and total protein >25 g/L (>2.5 g/dL). The supernatant can clear
after centrifugation (cells pellet). Variable proportions of neutrophils and macrophages
with fewer lymphocytes are seen on smears, with clusters of reactive mesothelial cells
(rare in cats). The dominant inflammatory cell will depend on the cause and duration of
the effusion. Neutrophils usually comprise >80% of cells with acute bacterial infections
(Figure 71.3) and sterile peritonitis and can also be seen with cestode infections,20
whereas a mixed inflammatory infiltrate (<80% neutrophils and >20% macrophages)
occurs with longer-duration effusions or specific causes, e.g., bacterial infections
secondary to indwelling thoracostomy tubes,21 fungal infections, pancreatitis, and
cancer. Although degenerate neutrophils are considered evidence of bacterial sepsis,
they can also be seen with sterile inflammation, e.g., bile peritonitis, or feline infectious
peritonitis (FIP).
Culture of the fluid is indicated in animals with an exudative effusion, whether or not
degenerate neutrophils or infectious organisms are seen on smears. There are various
causes of an exudative effusion, including infectious agents (bacteria, fungi, parasites,
coronavirus/FIP), foreign bodies (e.g., retained surgical sponge, penetrating grass
awn), viscus leakage or rupture, and tissue inflammation (e.g., pleuropneumonia,
pancreatitis, steatitis). FIP deserves special mention due to the unique characteristics
of the effusion (ch. 200). Although the effusion is exudative (from vasculitis),
leukocyte chemotaxis is not prominent, yielding a light to moderate yellow viscid fluid,
with fibrin clots, high protein concentration, and a TNCC usually <5 ×109/L. Smears
contain a mixture of mildly degenerate neutrophils with moderate macrophages and
few lymphocytes or mesothelial cells, with protein crescents or precipitated protein in
the background (Figure 71.3). Immunocytochemical staining of effusions, which can
be done with a cell block technique,22 is of 57-100% sensitivity, with a specificity of 71100%.23 A confirmatory diagnosis still relies upon the histopathologic finding of
pyogranulomatous inflammation with positive immunohistochemical staining for feline
coronavirus antigen in macrophages.23,24 Eosinophilic-rich effusions can be
transudative or exudative.25 Although mast cell tumors are a logical explanation for an
eosinophil-rich effusion, the latter can occur with other conditions, including trauma
and infections.25,26

Vessel or Viscus Rupture or Leakage
These can be separated into hemorrhagic effusions, bile peritonitis, uroperitoneum,
and gastrointestinal (GI) leakage or rupture (Table 71.1). Seminoperitoneum, which is
quite rare, can occur secondary to rupture of the genital tract during mating or after
vasectomy.27,28

Hemorrhagic Effusion
These are bloody throughout collection, resemble peripheral blood, do not clot in a
non-anticoagulant tube (Box 71.1), and usually have a packed cell volume >5%. Direct

and buffy coat smears (to concentrate nucleated cells) are usually prepared for
examination. In smears, the fluid resembles blood with blood-associated leukocytes
and variable numbers of mesothelial cells (dogs). There is evidence of chronic or prior
hemorrhage (erythrophagia, hemosiderophages, hematoidin crystals) with no or few
platelets. With peracute hemorrhage, platelets may be seen and the fluid may clot.
Common causes of abdominal hemorrhage are trauma and neoplasia
(hemangiosarcoma),29 with the spleen being the most common site of hemorrhage (ch.
126).30 There are reports of anaphylaxis causing hemoabdomen via an unknown
mechanism.31 Hemorrhagic pleural effusions are uncommon and can be due to trauma,
neoplasia, or parasitic, viral, or bacterial infection (ch. 220).29,32-34 Any animal with
an unexplained hemorrhagic effusion should be tested for an underlying hemostatic
disorder (ch. 170), e.g., anticoagulant rodenticide intoxication (ch. 138).35

cytologic criteria of malignancy, but can be difficult in individual
patients, necessitating additional diagnostic tests.

Bile Peritoneum
Biliary rupture, due to trauma, mucoceles, or necrotizing inflammation, can result in
bile peritonitis (ch. 273).36-38 Depending on the degree of leakage, the fluid can be
transudative but is more typically exudative, with mixed non-degenerate neutrophils

and macrophages. Lipid droplets can be seen in these cells in some patients, suggesting
concurrent steatitis. Free or phagocytized green-brown to yellow bile pigment may be
seen, but small amounts may be missed and can resemble other pigments, e.g.,
hemosiderin. In a few patients, only aggregates of light blue mucus, so-called “white
bile” may be seen37 (Figure 71.3). High effusion bilirubin concentrations (usually ≥2×
serum) can confirm bile peritonitis; however, bilirubin may not be higher in the fluid
versus serum in effusions of dogs with ruptured mucoceles and only “white bile” in the
fluid.37 Note that mucus can also be seen in effusions in animals with mucinous
adenocarcinomas and myxosarcoma,39 and small amounts may be mistaken for fibrin
(or vice versa).

Uroabdomen
In an acute rupture, urine may flood the abdomen, yielding a low-protein transudate;
however with time, a sterile peritonitis will develop (ch. 127). Uroabdomen should be
suspected in animals with azotemia, high serum potassium concentrations, and
abdominal effusion.40 There are no cytologic findings typical of uroabdomen;
confirmation requires finding high creatinine concentrations in the fluid compared to
blood (usually ≥2×).40

Gastrointestinal Leakage or Rupture
This results in a septic peritonitis with free and phagocytized mixed bacteria typical of
gut flora, including Gram-positive cocci in pairs and various Gram-negative rods. If
there is a yeast or bacterial overgrowth, offending organisms may also be seen.
Bacterial phagocytosis is key for differentiating a partial enterocentesis (with aspiration
of abdominal fluid and GI contents) from an acute GI rupture. Intracellular bacteria are
not expected with the former in smears made from freshly collected fluid. If an aspirate
only consists of intestinal contents (food debris and mixed bacteria), enterocentesis is
likely.

Neoplastic Effusions
Tumors cause effusions via multiple mechanisms and more than one mechanism may
be operative in a given patient, e.g., inflammation-induced exudation accompanied by
transudation due to tumor infiltration of lymph nodes. Identification of neoplastic cells
in smears of an effusion can provide an immediate diagnosis. Round or discrete cell
(particularly lymphoma and mast cell tumors) or epithelial (carcinoma) tumors are
more likely to exfoliate and be identified in smears of effusions, whereas neoplastic
cells from sarcomas are rarely seen (unless the primary tumor is directly aspirated). A
potential complication of body cavity fluid aspiration in animals with cancer is tumor
seeding of the needle tract.41 Only select tumors will be discussed more below.

Lymphoma (ch. 322)
Lymphoma is readily diagnosed when there are many individual intermediate to large
discrete cells with high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratios in smears of effusions (Figure
71.3). Low numbers of tumor cells or cells from a small-cell lymphoma are more
difficult to distinguish from reactive and normal counterparts, respectively. Flow

cytometric-or immunocytochemical-based immunophenotyping can be performed on
body cavity fluids to determine the type of lymphoma but should only be done if there
are sufficient tumor cells that can be distinguished from reactive or normal cells. Flow
cytometric-based immunophenotyping is superior to immunocytochemical staining
because more antibodies can be applied to cells; however, it does require live cells in
suspension. Clonality testing can be used to help confirm neoplasia, although
pseudoclonal results can be yielded if sample cellularity is low. Clonality is frequently
used for phenotyping lymphoid tumors, although this is not ideal because B cell tumors
can show clonal T cell rearrangements and vice versa.42 In addition, clonal
rearrangements in T and B cell receptors can be seen in acute myeloid leukemia,43
which can rarely manifest as an effusion in animals. In reality, the clonal
rearrangements in the specific lymphocyte receptor usually match the
immunophenotype of the lymphoid neoplasm in most cases and can be done, with the
above caveats in mind, if cellularity is insufficient or the sample is not appropriate for
immunophenotyping with flow cytometry (e.g., only slides are available). Other tumors
can resemble lymphoma, including acute leukemia, poorly granulated mast cell tumors,
pheochromocytoma, embryonal tumors (e.g., nephroblastoma), and carcinomas.

Mast Cell Tumors (ch. 327)
These individualized cells have lower nuclear to cytoplasmic ratios than large
lymphocytes and contain variable numbers of purple granules dispersed in the
cytoplasm. Accompanying eosinophilic inflammation can be a helpful finding (Figure
71.3), but is also seen with lymphoma,25 particularly T cell neoplasms. Poorly
granulated tumors with less cytoplasm can be difficult to distinguish from a lymphoma
of granular lymphocytes,44,45 without other testing, e.g., tryptase or CD3
immunostaining.

Carcinomas
These exfoliate as variably sized clusters of round to polygonal cells, with individualized
cells (Figure 71.3). The tumor cells must be distinguished from reactive mesothelial
cells, particularly in dogs (reactive mesothelial cells are rare in effusions in cats), and
macrophages (which can be seen in small aggregates in some fluids). Mesothelial cells
can become quite reactive and demonstrate abnormal features (e.g., trinucleation) in
effusions (Figure 71.3). Distinction can be difficult unless the tumor cells are showing
prominent cytologic criteria of malignancy, e.g., marked anisokaryosis, macronucleoli.
Ultimately, the diagnosis of carcinoma may rely upon documentation of the tumor in
internal organs or carcinomatosis, particularly if the cells are bland or mimic
mesothelium.

Mesothelioma (chs. 220, 235)
This tumor is difficult to diagnose with certainty from analysis of an effusion.
Neoplastic mesothelial cells can resemble reactive counterparts (i.e., lack cytologic
criteria of malignancy) and exfoliated carcinoma cells. Even if the cells resemble
mesothelial cells (central nuclei, moderate amounts of cytoplasm with a fringe or
“corona,” Figure 71.3) and are displaying features of malignancy, a diagnosis of
mesothelioma requires documentation of tissue invasion on histopathologic

examination. Because mesothelioma is an uncommon neoplasm, if clusters of cells with
prominent cytologic criteria of malignancy are seen in a fluid, an underlying carcinoma
is far more likely. The presence of multiple body cavity effusions is not specific for
mesothelioma.26,41,46-48

SYNOVIAL FLUID (CHS. 32, 87)
Unlike thoracic and abdominal fluid, synovial fluid can be aspirated from normal
joints. Normal synovial fluid is light yellow and transparent, with no blood, and is quite
viscous due to its hyaluronic acid content. The fluid should be collected into EDTA and
handled similarly as described above for other body cavity fluids, with emphasis placed
on rapid drying of smears (Video 71.2

). This is because cells “ball up” in the viscous

fluid and are difficult to identify, let alone find intracellular structures in neutrophils
that may be informative, e.g., infectious organisms, such as morulae of Ehrlichia
ewingii or Anaplasma phagocytophilum in dogs49,50 or particulate nuclear material in
neutrophils (called “ragocytes”) or “lupus erythematosus cells” in immune-mediated
disorders.51,52
Cytologic analysis of joint fluid usually includes cell counts, total protein by
refractometer, a viscosity estimate, and smear examination. Viscosity is usually
subjectively measured as the length of a “strand” of fluid that forms between a needle
tip and a slide or the edge of the collection tube and the cap of the tube or tip of a
plastic pipette (ch. 32, Figure 32.2). Joint fluid of normal viscosity should form a
strand that is at least 2 cm long (Video 71.3

). For low volume samples, preference is

given to cytologic assessment of well-made smears versus cell counts or total protein
measurement. There are ongoing studies on the utility of inflammatory cytokines,
proteomic profiles, or specific protein concentrations in the diagnosis of joint
diseases53-55; however, none of these tests or procedures is a part of routine synovial
fluid analysis.
Normal TNCC in synovial fluids from dogs range from 0.5 to 3.0 × 109/L (0.5 to 3.0
× 103/mcL) between different joints, with <3.0 × 109/L being used as a general
“normal” upper limit,56 although most fluids have counts <1.0 × 109/L. Counts are
generally <1 × 109/L in cats.57 The total protein by refractometer is <25 g/L (<2.5
g/dL) and should be less than 15 g/L. Total protein results below 25 g/L (the cut-off for
manual refractometers) can be obtained using digital refractometers. On smears, the
fluid consists of large mononuclear cells (macrophages or synoviocytes), with <20%
lymphocytes (also called small mononuclear cells) and <10% neutrophils. The cells are
dispersed in a stippled or stringy pink to purple background from the viscosity. It can
be difficult to distinguish lymphocytes from non-reactive macrophages and
macrophages from synoviocytes; thus, many clinical pathologists use the term “small
and large mononuclear” cells. It is unclear if monocyte or macrophage-appearing cells
are blood-derived or derived from histiocytes within the synovium. Therefore, the
author often uses the terms “macrophages” and “synoviocytes” interchangeably. The
term “reactive” for the macrophages means that the cells have increased cytoplasm that
appears foamy and may contain vacuoles or phagocytic debris versus non-reactive cells,

which lack cytoplasmic vacuolation and have eccentric round to monocytoid nuclei. The
presence of pink to red cytoplasmic granules (presumptive, hyaluronate) in
mononuclear cells is supportive of a synovial origin. Other biochemical analyses are not
usually performed on joint fluids.

CYTOLOGIC INTERPRETATION
Results of joint fluid analysis are rarely specific for a particular disorder and rather fall
into two general categories: non-inflammatory and inflammatory disease. These can be
distinguished by TNCC, total protein concentration, and proportion of cell types in
smears (Figure 71.5). Other disease processes, including primary or metastatic
tumors to the joint,58-60 infectious agents,61 and hemarthrosis can be detected on
cytologic evaluation of synovial fluid, but these conditions are quite uncommon.
Hemarthrosis has been reported with hemostatic disorders (e.g., severe
thrombocytopenia,62 hemophilia A63), parasitic infection,64 and synovial tumors.65

Non-inflammatory Joint Disease
This term is used for joints with degenerative disease, due to musculoskeletal
abnormalities (e.g., osteochondrosis) or trauma. The fluid lacks evidence of active
inflammation (<10% neutrophils) and may be normal or show mild cytologic
abnormalities, such as mildly increased total protein concentration, increased
proportions of reactive macrophages, mildly increased TNCC (<5 × 109/L) and
decreased viscosity alone or in various combinations. There may be evidence of
synovial hyperplasia (multinucleated or aggregates of synoviocytes) or damage to
cartilage (osteoclasts).

Inflammatory Joint Disease
This term applies to joints with active inflammation, specifically a high TNCC (usually
>5 × 109/L) with increased proportions of neutrophils (usually >20%). There are two
general causes—infectious (e.g., Ehrlichia ewingii or Anaplasma
phagocytophilum,49,50 but not Ehrlichia canis66) and immune-mediated disease
(primary or secondary to vasculitis or infectious agents, e.g., Lyme disease [ch. 187]),
with immune-mediated disease being more common in dogs (ch. 177).67-70 In cats,
infectious causes of arthritis (e.g., Mycoplasma, calicivirus infection) are more
common than immune-mediated disease.71 Anaplasma phagocytophilum does occur
in cats and causes limb pain,72 but synovial findings have not been described for this
species.
It is difficult to distinguish between infectious and non-infectious causes of arthritis
based on cytologic assessment alone, because neutrophils are rarely degenerate in
septic joints and unique diagnostic features are often absent (see below). A single
affected joint should raise suspicion for a bacterial infection (e.g., from a penetrating
foreign body), whereas a polyarthropathy involving the carpi and tarsi is highly
suspicious for immune-mediated disease. All animals presenting with an apparent
single affected joint should be carefully examined for involvement of other joints (ch.

32), and the other joints should be aspirated so that a polyarthropathy is not missed
(ch. 87). The author has seen several cases of immune-mediated disease where
aspirated joints did not have an obvious effusion, but neutrophilic inflammation was
still identified on cytologic examination, even with a normal TNCC. It is important to
note that acute joint trauma (e.g., cranial cruciate rupture) can result in mild
inflammation (TNCC up to 12 × 109/L with up to 65% neutrophils73), but this should be
localized to the affected stifle joint. Neutrophils should be carefully examined for
bacteria (e.g., Anaplasma morulae49,50), protozoa (e.g., Leishmania74), fungi,75,76
particulate (ragocytes) or homogenous nuclear material (lupus erythematosus
cells),51,52 but these diagnostic findings are not frequently observed. Concurrent
thrombocytopenia should prompt testing for infectious organisms.49,50,72 Rare cases of
immune-mediated disease are characterized by eosinophilic inflammation77 or, in the
author’s experience, lymphocytic-predominant inflammation. Unfortunately, cytologic
analysis is not usually diagnostic as to the cause of joint inflammation, and other tests
are required for a specific diagnosis, e.g., serologic or genetic-based tests for infectious
organisms. In some cases, the diagnosis relies on an appropriate response to therapy,
e.g., doxycycline treatment for Lyme disease. Bacterial culture, in cases of suspected
septic synovitis, was only positive in 44-63% of cases in two studies by the same
investigators78,79; polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based testing for bacterial 16s RNA
was not significantly more sensitive but was less specific than bacterial culture in one
study of 18 dogs.78

CHAPTER 72: Body and
Muscle Condition Scoring
Kathryn E Michel

A C RO N YM S
BCS body condition score
DEXA dual x-ray absorptiometry
MCS muscle condition score

The literature supports an association of altered body composition
with greater risks of morbidity and mortality. Excess body weight in
dogs and cats is associated with abnormal glucose metabolism, nonallergic skin disease, osteoarthritis, and respiratory problems,1 while
loss of lean body mass is associated with poorer survival times for
companion animals with cancer, heart failure, and chronic kidney
disease.2-4 There are effective strategies and therapies that can be
implemented to mitigate these risks, but for intervention to be
possible, first a patient’s altered body condition must be recognized.
Body composition can be evaluated and quantified through a number
of methods5; however, only the combination of body (BCS) and
muscle (MCS) condition scoring provides a simple, rapid, and when
performed correctly, accurate and reliable approach that can be
employed by the veterinary health care team in a clinical setting.5-9

What is more, this technique can be taught to pet owners so it can be
used as a guide for monitoring a pet’s nutritional status in the home
setting.9
Investigations have shown that these techniques can be
successfully acquired by members of the veterinary health care team
and pet owners alike, and implemented in primary care practices.5,912
Studies have also shown that discrepancies between expert and pet
owner evaluations of pets exist and that acceptance and routine
implementation of BCS and MCS in clinical practice can be variable,
especially with regard to the use of the MCS.10-13 Major veterinary
medical associations (American Animal Hospital Association, World
Small Animal Veterinary Association) have advocated for making
nutritional assessment the 5th vital sign.14,15 The assessment of BCS
and MCS as part of every physical exam should be the standard of
practice. In regard to communicating with a pet owner about their
pet’s nutritional status, investigations that have compared
assessment of body condition by the pet owner with that of an
“expert” have consistently shown that when dogs and cats are
overweight, pet owners are more likely to underscore their pet (score
them as less overweight than the expert).12,13 On the other hand,
when pets are underweight, the same studies have shown that pet
owners are more likely to overscore their pets (score them as less
underweight).12,13

BODY AND MUSCLE CONDITION
SCORING SYSTEMS
There are different BCS scoring systems available for scoring
companion animals.5,9,10 The most commonly used systems in North
America are the 5-point and 9-point systems.10 The 9-point system
has been validated for use in both dogs and cats (see front and back
inside cover figures) and is, in effect, the 5-point system with half
scores. Investigations have shown that the 9-point system is
repeatable and reproducible in the hands of trained observers and

that it is predictive of percent body fat as measured by dual x-ray
absorptiometry (DEXA).6,7
Fewer MCS scoring systems have been described and only one, the
4-point system, has been validated. The 4-point system has also been
found to be repeatable and reproducible, and shows good association
with lean body mass as measured by DEXA and epaxial muscle
thickness as measured by ultrasound.8,16,17

LEARNING TO BODY AND MUSCLE
CONDITION SCORE (Box 72.1)
All the BCS and MCS systems currently in use combine visual
assessment of body silhouette and physical palpation of muscle and
body fat. While the visual assessment can reinforce a decision made
through physical palpation, it can also provide minimal or
misleading information depending upon whether the patient has a
long or thick haircoat or altered body composition. For example, a
previously overweight cat that has experienced dramatic weight loss
will still have what appears to be an abdominal fat pad. However,
upon palpation, that fat pad may simply be loose skin containing
subcutaneous tissue but very little body fat. Therefore, a critical step
in determining a patient’s body and muscle condition is to physically
assess the patient. Clinicians and technicians will have refined their
ability to differentiate tissue types by palpation; however, most pet
owners will require instruction on what they should be discerning
when we tell them to feel for fat over their pet’s ribs.
BOX 72 .1 Le arning Ob je ctive s for Bo dy and
Mu s c le C ond ition Scoring
You should be able to:
• use palpation skills for differentiating the tissue types (skin,
subcutaneous tissue, fat, muscle) requisite for assigning
body condition and muscle condition scores
• demonstrate the techniques for body condition and muscle
condition scoring dogs and cats

• describe the criteria for optimal body and muscle condition
of dogs and cats
The next critical step in learning how to apply a BCS or MCS is to
understand and be able to recognize the criteria for ideal body and
muscle condition. This includes knowing the locations on a dog or
cat one should palpate to evaluate body fat or muscle as well as what
would constitute appropriate fat or muscle mass. The importance of
establishing one’s ability to reliably apply these criteria to a dog or
cat cannot be understated. The application of scores for over- or
underweight pets in the case of assigning a BCS, or for muscle
wasting in the case of assigning a MCS, should be anchored to one’s
ability to recognize what is considered optimal.
The last step in learning how to apply a BCS or MCS is to practice
evaluating dogs and cats and assigning scores based on the criteria
provided in the scoring system. It is useful to practice with one or
more colleagues, where each person independently scores the same
patient. Sharing and discussing one’s findings and reconciling
divergent opinions is a useful way to refine one’s skills and
interpretation of the scoring system criteria. See the accompanying
videos for a brief step-by-step tutorial of BCS and MCS (Videos 72.1
and 72.2)

.

CHALLENGES AND PITFALLS (Box 72.2)
In general, BCS can be more challenging in dogs than cats due to the
large variation in conformation seen across breeds. In a preliminary
study of 19 dogs representing 6 different breeds, body composition
was found to vary with breed and significant differences were found
in the % body fat of dogs of different breeds deemed to be in ideal
body condition.18 Another investigation of show dogs found that
breed standards might influence body condition as breeds whose
standards included reference to muscular or sturdy characteristics
were more likely to have a higher BCS than breeds whose standards
described lean or elegant characteristics.19 These findings are not

altogether surprising given that a breed standard reflects the original
purpose of the breed which might include working in a cold climate
or in conditions of food scarcity. Insufficient research has been done
to be able to make breed-specific recommendations for ideal BCS;
however, the current canine 9-point BCS system considers scores of
4-5/9 ideal (the feline system restricts ideal to 5/9), allowing some
leeway for breed differences. A BCS of 4/9 should be considered
ideal for lean breeds such as sighthounds while stockier breeds might
score a 5/9 as ideal. However, dogs with excess fat over the cranial
rib cage should be scored above ideal regardless of breed or
conformation.
There are several pitfalls to avoid when scoring dogs and cats.
Always physically assess a patient in the proper location for body fat
and muscle mass. When evaluating fat over the rib cage, base the
BCS on the amount of fat accumulated in the cranial as opposed to
the caudal rib cage. When scoring a cat, the BCS should be
determined on the extent of fat both over the ribs and in the inguinal
region. Some cats will have minimal fat over the ribs, yet have a
substantial inguinal fat pad. Remember to always anchor your body
condition assessment to the criteria for ideal BCS, recognizing that
extremely obese animals will exceed the characteristics described for
a 9/9 score. Last, do not neglect to perform a MCS on a dog or cat
with an overweight appearance. While it can take some skill to
evaluate epaxial muscle condition in an overweight animal, it is
critical to do so as a patient experiencing malnutrition or a catabolic
state can present with significant, even severe muscle wasting while
still retaining excess fat.
BOX 72 .2 Common Pitfalls
• Simply visually assessing the patient without also assessing with
physical palpation
• Not physically assessing the patient thoroughly and in the
appropriate locations

• Not anchoring the assignment of body condition scoring or
muscle condition scoring to how they deviate from the criteria
for ideal

ABDOMINAL FLUID SCORING SYSTEM
(Video 73.5 )
The AFAST abdominal fluid scoring system is validated in lateral
recumbency, making each view gravity-unequal and thus serving as
an inherent depth gauge. Abdominal fluid is scored as 0, 1/2, or 1,
with “1/2” being considered a weak positive, and “1” a strong positive
(Figure 73.1) using over and under maximum fluid dimension of 5
mm for cats and 1 cm for dogs.17 Those totaling <3 are considered
small volume bleeder/effusion and those ≥3 as large volume
bleeder/effusion.2,13,15 The HR5th view is similarly scored but not
part of the total score. Patient score helps anticipate the need for
blood transfusion, surgical intervention, and expected degree of
hypovolemia, and thus guides fluid resuscitation and decisionmaking.2,13,15 Knowing this information real-time at triage and
during patient rounds is impactful for case
management.2,3,6,8,13,15,18-20 When bleeding has abated, and
coagulation abnormalities, if present, are corrected, near-resolution
of hemoabdomen within 48 hours can be expected, as a rule of
thumb. Lavage fluid should always be completely removed because
for unknown reasons, it lasts (unlike blood) several days and thus
confounds imaging interpretation. See ch. 21 for more information
on abdominal enlargement and ch. 86 for information on
abdominocentesis.

AFAST EXTRAS
Gallbladder Wall Edema
Gallbladder wall edema (GBWE), mural sonographic striation of
white-black-white, or white-gray-white regardless of thickness, is a
marker for canine anaphylaxis (AX, ch. 129) because the canine

shock organs are the liver and gastrointestinal tract.21 In the setting
of acute weakness or collapse in a previously healthy dog, GBWE
supports AX (“anaphylactic gallbladder”) and right-sided heart
failure (“cardiac gallbladder”), most commonly due to PCE (ch.
235).21-25 However, when PCE is absent, TFAST echocardiography
(echo) is needed. Patients with other causes of GBWE, such as
cholecystitis, pancreatitis, hepatitis, hypoalbuminemia, immunemediated hemolytic anemia, acute hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome,
sepsis, and post-transfusion, typically do not present with acute
collapse.21,24-26 The “cardiac gallbladder” also occurs in cats and
humans.24,27

FIGURE 73.1 Row 1 shows abdominal focused
assessment with sonography for trauma (AFAST) in
right lateral recumbency and its first four views,
which are part of its abdominal fluid scoring system
(AFSS). These four views are obtained in this
standardized order:Diaphragmatico-Hepatic (DH)
view, Spleno-Renal (SR) view, Cysto-Colic (CC) view,
Spleno-Intestino Umbilical (SIU) view. Note each
has its target organs with ascites present evidenced
by the anechoic (black) triangulation of free fluid.
These first 4 views are followed by the Focused
Spleen and Hepato-Renal 5th (HR5th) bonus view
(not shown). Row 2 shows the AFSS and its use for
categorizing small versus large volume
bleeder/effusion. The use of small versus large
volume bleeder/effusion allows for tracking patients
as being static (no change), or improving (lower
score), or worsening (higher score). Row 3 shows a
decision algorithm showing how integrating
information at the DH view in the presence of
gallbladder wall edema (GBWE) helps sort out an
“anaphylactic” from a “cardiac” gallbladder. Note the
gallbladder wall in normalcy is essentially a thin,
hyperechoic (white) line as shown in A. In contrast,
GBWE, the sonographic striation of inner wall, outer
wall, and degrees of edema in between, creates the
halo sign effect as shown in B, C, and D. In the
presence of GBWE, looking past the diaphragm
cranially for pericardial effusion (PCE) is important
(racetrack sign) as well as characterizing the caudal
vena cava (CVC) and its associated hepatic veins to
differentiate a “cardiac” from an “anaphylactic”
gallbladder. In the absence of PCE, a fluid-intolerant
or distended CVC lends support to a “cardiac
gallbladder” and thoracic focused assessment with
sonography for trauma (TFAST) echocardiography
views are indicated. An “anaphylactic gallbladder” is
supported by a clinical profile that fits anaphylaxis
and the absence of PCE and a small attenuated CVC,

i.e., the opposite of what is expected with a “cardiac
gallbladder.” CHF, Congestive heart failure; DCM,
dilated cardiomyopathy; PHT, pulmonary
hypertension; R/O, rule out. (Courtesy and with

Country Veterinary Specialists and FASTVet.com,
Spicewood, Texas.)

Medically Treated, Endogenous Heparin-Induced,
Canine Anaphylactic Hemoabdomen
A unique, recently described canine complication is medicallytreated AX hemoabdomen (ch. 126).22,23 Any dog with a clinical
profile that fits AX including acute collapse, often with
gastrointestinal signs in a previously healthy dog; sonographic
GBWE; a small CVC; absent cavitated mass (e.g., splenic);
hemoconcentration; and a positive AFAST has a medically-treated
AX hemoabdomen until proven otherwise.22,23 Global FAST tracking
with an AFAST assigned fluid score categorizes small versus large
volume bleeder and abdominocentesis with fluid analysis (when
ascites is safely accessible; ch. 86) should be performed for
confirmation. Glucocorticoids and histamine-2 antagonists mitigate
the acquired coagulopathy.22,23,28 Results of traditional coagulation
testing (prothrombin time [PT]; activated partial thromboplastin
[aPTT]) are variable, although theoretically the aPTT should be
discordantly elevated because of heparin release from mast cell
degranulation.21-23 Surgery is not indicated and risky, often fatal
anecdotally, so veterinarians must recognize this newly-described
complication. When bleeding has stopped, and coagulation
abnormalities if present are corrected, it is reasonable to expect near
resolution of the hemoabdomen within 48 hours as a rule of thumb.

Free Air (Video 73.6

)

Ultrasound is extremely sensitive for detecting volumes of free air as
small as 0.2 mL in the peritoneal cavity and retroperitoneal space.

The concept is 3-fold: 1) air rises to the least gravity-dependent
region (SR view in right lateral), 2) free air is continuous with the
peritoneal lining (enhanced peritoneal stripe sign), and 3) any small
anechoic gap (black gap) between the peritoneal lining and the
presumed free air is gastrointestinal tract until proven otherwise
(Figure 73.2).29

Urinary Bladder Volume Estimation
At the CC view, urinary bladder measurements are taken in the
sagittal plane for length (L) (without going into the trigone) and
height (H), and in transverse for width (W). L × H × W (cm) × 0.625
estimates urinary bladder volume (mL) (ch. 307).4 Thus, over time,
clinicians have a non-invasive means to estimate urinary output.

Volume Status
Characterizing the CVC in its sagittal plane as it courses through the
diaphragm (and its associated hepatic veins; Video 73.14

)

estimates patient volume status by its respirophasic height change as
follows: fluid responsive (bounce), a change of 35-50%; fluid
intolerant (FAT), little change (<10%) and an increased maximum
height; and fluid starved/hypovolemic (flat), little change (<10%)
and a decreased maximum height (Figure 73.2).25,30,31 Hepatic
venous distension (“tree trunk sign”) has high sensitivity and
specificity for increased right-sided filling pressures in dogs and cats
positioned in lateral, standing or sternal, and its finding, plus a FAT
CVC is easily recognized by properly trained non-radiologist
veterinarians.3,7,16,25

Gastrointestinal Motility
The stomach/proximal duodenum and the jejunum may be observed
for peristalsis, expecting 4-5 minute-1 and 1-3 minute-1, respectively,
if food is present in the canine gastrointestinal tract. This
observation can help detect the presence or absence of ileus.32 With

food absence, including intentional fasting, ileus occurs in normalcy
and must be placed into clinical context.32

TFAST
TFAST is designed according to the principle that air rises and fluid
falls into gravity-dependent regions called pouches.3,6,8,9 Thus, the
Chest Tube Site (CTS) view is used for PTX (Video 73.19
), and
the Pericardial Site (PCS) views, and DH view for PE and PCE,
cardiac evaluation, including TFAST echo views (Figure 73.2).3,58,13,15

PLEURAL AND PERICARDIAL
EFFUSION (Videos 73.10, 73.11

)

There are basic tenets to accurately diagnose PCE that is contained
and rounded within the pericardial sac (ch. 235), and PE that is
uncontained and unrestrained within the pleural cavity (ch.
220).7,13,15
1. Image the heart at the DH view, where the walls of the
ventricles at the cardiac apex are distinctive, for the “racetrack
sign” of PCE, and from the right PCS view, for the “bull’s eye
sign.” Conversely, PE appears as anechoic
triangulations.7,8,13,15
2. Image cranial (cardiac-cervical pouch) and caudal (cardiacdiaphragmatic pouch) to the heart away from chambers by
using the “TFAST Slide” for the “curtain sign” of PE (Video
73.29

).7,8,13,15

3. Use only the long-axis 4-chamber view, where all 4 chambers
may be identified, and fluid clearly determined to be outside

the heart and contained within the pericardial sac for PCE or
outside the pericardial sac for PE.7,8,13,15
4. Always image the heart in its entirety using the bright white
(hyperechoic) pericardium as a landmark in the far
field.7,8,13,15

FUNDAMENTAL
ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIC VIEWS (
Videos 73.12, 73.13)
TFAST echo views are obtained from the right PCS view and they
include the left ventricular (LV) short-axis “mushroom” view for
volume status and contractility, the short-axis left atrial (LA) to
aortic (Ao) view for left-sided problems (increased LA filling
pressures), the long-axis 4-chamber view for right-sided problems
(increased right ventricular [RV] filling pressures), and the long-axis
LV outflow tract view for the aortic valve (Figure 73.2).3,8,13,15,16,33
These views also serve as a screening test for cardiac-related softtissue abnormalities because the radiographic cardiac silhouette is
unreliable.34,35 Importantly, when the sonographer is unable to
obtain the echo views, the absence of wet lung during Vet BLUE rules
out clinically relevant left-sided congestive heart failure (Video 73.30
), and the absence of a FAT CVC rules out clinically relevant
right-sided congestive heart failure (ch. 229; Video 73.14

).9,10-

13,15,16,25,36 These Global FAST Fallback Views allow an approach

that often is easier (and faster) than echocardiography in the
unstable patient (Figure 73.2).13,15,16

PNEUMOTHORAX, THE LUNG POINT,
AND ITS 1/3s RULE FOR DEGREE AND
MONITORING
The absence of lung sliding with A-lines plus the finding of the “Lung
Point” support the diagnosis of PTX (chs. 123, 220). This is best
evaluated in a standing or sternally-recumbent patient.3,5,8,13,15,16
The TFAST PTX Lung Point 1/3s Rule is as follows: upper 1/3, trivial
to mild; middle 1/3, moderate; and lower 1/3 severe, serving as a tool
for decision-making (thoracocentesis and tube thoracostomy; ch.
92) and tracking for worsening, static, and resolving PTX.5,13,15,16

Reverse Curtain Sign
A newer strategy is to interrogate the transition zone curtain sign of
the pleural and pericardial cavities at its caudodorsal extremity. The
pleural and abdominal cavities move in respirophasic synchrony in
normalcy, whereas in PTX, they move in asynchrony, toward each
other, then away from each other.37,38 Paradoxical abdominal
breathing (ch. 37; Video 37.3

) also causes asynchrony (author,

unpublished data). Artifacts within the curtain should only be Alines in PTX. Reverse sliding is an additional descriptor for the same
phenomenon.37,38

VET BLUE, ITS REGIONAL, PATTERNBASED APPROACH, B-LINE SCORING
SYSTEM, AND VISUAL LUNG
LANGUAGE

Vet BLUE has bilaterally applied transthoracic views named
caudodorsal, perihilar, middle, and cranial lung regions plus the DH
view, providing a deeper acoustic window of the pulmonarydiaphragmatic interface (Figure 73.2, Video 73.17

). By using a

regional, pattern-based approach combined with its visual lung
language, a working diagnosis can be quickly developed in <2
minutes (Figure 73.2, Video 73.31

).8-12 Moreover, the B-line

scoring system, using the highest score over a single intercostal space
at each respective view, is recorded as 1, 2, 3, >3, and infinity, and
then further subdivided into weak (1, 2, 3) and strong positives (>3,
infinity) (Figure 73.2).8-12 Vet BLUE is real-time information used
as a tracking tool that appears to exceed thoracic radiography for wet
lung conditions, and compares well to computed tomography
(Figure 73.2).39-41 Current research is evaluating its imaging
performance regarding forms of lung consolidation. The “wedge
sign” in non-gravity-dependent regions screens for pulmonary
thromboembolism (triggering thrombolytic therapy and/or
thromboprophylaxis if appropriate), and monitors response to
therapy.12,14

GLOBAL FAST
VOLUME STATUS AND LEFT- AND RIGHTSIDED CARDIAC PROBLEMS
Global FAST (Videos 73.21, 73.22, 73.23, 73.24

) integrates

TFAST echo views and its Fallback Views for left- and right-sided
congestive failure (ch. 229) by incorporating lung (Vet BLUE) and
characterization of the CVC and hepatic venous distension (DH view)
(Figure 73.2).3,7,8,13,15,16,25,30 When TFAST echo views are
obtained, the Fallback Views provide additional evidence for leftand right-sided failure. Conversely, if TFAST echo views cannot be
obtained (too risky to obtain, requiring more restraint, patient too
critical), Fallback Views help rule in and rule out left- and right-sided

congestive heart failure.3,7,8,13,15,16,25,30,42 This Global FAST
integrative approach helps dictate the use of loop diuretics,
vasopressors, and inotropes.16

MONITORING
The combined use of Global FAST’s 3 components provides a
tremendous amount of information, with AFAST and its target-organ
approach, its fluid scoring system, its urinary bladder volume
estimation formula, pneumoperitoneum, gastrointestinal motility,
and its examination of the retroperitoneal space; TFAST for PE, PCE,
PTX and its PTX 1/3s Rule, and its echo views for chamber and soft
tissue abnormalities; and Vet BLUE and its regional, pattern-based
approach, B-line scoring system, and visual lung language for a
working diagnosis and monitoring tool (Figure 73.2).13,15,16,43

INTEGRATING INFORMATION
Global FAST (15 unbiased data imaging points of the abdomen and
thorax) prevents common imaging errors such as “satisfaction of
search” and “confirmation bias” errors through selective imaging.43
For example, if a focused cardiac ultrasound patient is determined to
be hypovolemic based on a focused cardiac ultrasound exam and
administered a crystalloid challenge, the intra-abdominal
hemorrhage that is the source of the hypovolemia may be missed if
the evaluation is confined to the thorax. In another example, if the
evaluation is confined to the abdomen, the clinician could incorrectly
conclude that an acutely collapsed dog with GBWE has AX when in
fact the patient has PCE or dilated cardiomyopathy (“cardiac
gallbladder”). Through Global FAST, the clinician automatically
searches for other rule outs similar to imaging strategies such as
EFAST, extended FAST, and rapid ultrasound in shock (RUSH)
exams.42-44

Hs AND Ts OF CPR

The Global FAST approach is used to rapidly determine if the patient
has treatable forms of shock or cause for cardiopulmonary
resuscitation (ch. 131) by the veterinary Hs –
Hypovolemia/Hypotension, Hypokalemia/Hyperkalemia,
Hypocontractility and Hypertension, and Ts – Trauma/Hemorrhage,
Tamponade, Tension PTX, Thromboembolism, and Toxin.42,43
Following return of spontaneous circulation, Global FAST becomes
part of advanced life support and patient monitoring.43

STAGING PATIENTS
Staging patients is important for 2 major reasons: 1) to rapidly
determine if disease is localized versus disseminated, and 2) to
determine potential sampling sites for a diagnosis.43

POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND ADDONS
Other noteworthy POCUS exams include ocular, musculoskeletal,
and brain, always done with Global FAST to avoid imaging errors
and better interpret findings.

CONCLUSION
Global FAST is low-impact, cost-effective, real-time informationgenerating, rapid, radiation-sparing, point-of-care imaging that
allows the veterinarian to “see” their problem list and thus better
direct resuscitation and treatment, and streamline the diagnostic
plan. Global FAST should be used as an extension of the physical
exam on a daily basis for nearly all patients in the clinical setting and
preempt add-on POCUS examinations.

VENIPUNCTURE
Venipuncture, utilized for phlebotomy or intravenous (IV) injections,
is one of the most common invasive procedures in veterinary
medicine. It is also a foundational skill, and developing proficiency in
fundamentals helps to ensure successful advanced skills.

PHLEBOTOMY
The most commonly utilized veins for phlebotomy include the
cephalic, external jugular, femoral (cats), and lateral saphenous
(dogs), but sublingual, pedal, auricular, and abdominal veins have
been utilized (Table 74.1). Hand hygiene both before and after is
essential; the use of non-sterile examination gloves is best practice.
Palpation using gentle pressure allows for determination of the
direction, size, and depth of the vein. The skin should be free of gross

contaminants, clipped of hair if needed, cleansed, and dry. Isopropyl
alcohol can facilitate visualization of the vein, but alcohol
contamination of blood samples may result in hemolysis. Best
practice is to cleanse the skin with a combination of 2%
chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol, ensuring contact
time of at least 30 seconds; the skin should be allowed to dry
completely (about 30 seconds).1
Materials are listed online in Equipment Pull List 1 and a stepwise
approach is shown in

Video 74.1. Venous occlusion should not

last >2 minutes, because prolonged occlusion can cause
hemoconcentration and discomfort.1 In dehydrated or thick- or
loose-skinned patients, the needle may need to be placed through the
skin first, before entering the vein. To enter the vein, the needle
should be centered over the vein with the bevel facing up, then
advanced using a swift, continuous motion until the entire bevel is
within the lumen of the vein. The needle entry angle should be 15°
(superficial veins) to 30° (deeper veins). A slight release in resistance
may be detected when entering the vein. If no blood enters the
syringe, it is appropriate to withdraw, slightly redirect, and advance
the needle, while minimizing the number of such changes to avoid
tissue trauma. The negative pressure applied to the plunger should
be slight and continuous. Hand hygiene should be performed
postprocedure.
Hospital-acquired anemia may be a concern in some small animal
medicine patients; it can be minimized by combining laboratory
tests, utilizing Microtainer vials, and using existing samples for
additional tests.2 A sampling catheter (ch. 75) should be considered
in patients requiring frequent assessment.
Complications are uncommon when phlebotomy is performed
correctly. Bruising or a hematoma may form if the needle is only
partially inserted into the vein, if both the top and bottom walls are
pierced, or if the patient moves during the procedure; if noted, stop
immediately, withdraw the needle, and apply pressure to the site.
Phlebitis can be minimized with aseptic technique and minimal
movement of the needle tip. Referencing anatomic relationships of
veins to nerves can minimize the chance of injury and nerve pain.3

Vasovagal syncope during phlebotomy may be more likely to occur in
patients with cardiac disease. A good maximum number of blood
draw attempts is two, with reasonable certainty of accessing the vein
on each attempt. Some test results may be altered by stress, anxiety,
or fear, and multiple venipuncture attempts increase complications.
A change in personnel, restraint, or technique, or the use of sedation,
may resolve the problem.
Needle stick injury, transmission of disease, and sample
contamination are known risk factors for veterinary personnel. Best
practice can minimize this risk by disposing of the entire device,
having a sharps container within arm’s reach, and avoiding twohanded needle recapping.

PLACEMENT OF PERIPHERAL VENOUS
CATHETERS
A peripheral venous catheter is indicated when ongoing venous
access is required. Selection of a vein for a catheter is dependent on
the indication, expected duration of use (short/long term), and
quantity and type of infusate. Complications include phlebitis,

infiltration, occlusion and dislodgement.3 The first attempt at
catheterization should be as distal on the limb as is practical if
difficulties are expected, so repeat attempts can occur more
proximally. In all but emergent situations, the smallest gauge
catheter adequate for the prescribed therapy should be selected, for
adequate blood flow around the catheter and lower risk of phlebitis.
Central and jugular catheters are described in ch. 75 and
intraosseous catheters in ch. 76. Materials and a stepwise approach
are listed online in Equipment Pull List 2 and demonstrated in
Videos 74.2 and 74.3. Additional considerations are listed in Table
74.2.
Prior to placement, the catheter should be pre-flushed with saline
and spun on the stylet (to ease its advancement off the stylet).
Topical anesthesia or local block may be indicated for patient
comfort. To prevent intravascular catheter-related bloodstream
infections (CRBSIs), a complete, aseptic, surgical preparation of the
skin using >0.5% chlorhexidine with isopropyl alcohol should be
performed.4 Aseptic technique must be maintained throughout.
After successful venipuncture with the catheter and stylet, a blood
flash occurs in the hub. Hypotensive patients may not show this
indicator, requiring aspiration to confirm placement. The entire
bevel of the stylet and 1-2 mm more must be entirely in the lumen of
the vein. Then, the entry angle is reduced to make the catheter
almost parallel to the skin, and the catheter is advanced off the stylet
and into the vein. If resistance is felt, the catheter is repositioned
until free blood flow is obtained, and then catheter advancement off
the stylet is attempted again. The catheter is never pulled back over
the stylet, which can cut the catheter tip off, causing embolization.4
Digital pressure can be applied proximal to the catheter hub to
prevent blood loss during port placement. If the catheter is in the
vein lumen but will not advance farther, a “fluid stylet” can be used:
the steel stylet is removed and replaced with a 3-5 mL saline syringe,
aspiration confirms that the catheter tip is still in the vein, and then
gentle saline infusion allows the catheter to be advanced and
“floated” into place. This is demonstrated in

Video 74.4. Tape

and bandaging material are used for stabilizing, protecting

connection points, and securing the catheter. Catheter maintenance
recommendations are listed in Box 74.1.

• Flushing of the catheter every 4 hours if continuous fluid therapy

The use of peripheral IV cannulae for the collection of blood
samples is within the clinically acceptable range for hematology
(complete blood count) and most blood chemistry profiles but not

recommended for potassium or blood gas analysis.5 To minimize the
risk of nosocomial infection, catheters should be replaced every 4
days, or if soiled, or if any problems are noted during catheter
maintenance.6 The 4 recognized routes for contamination of
catheters in human medicine are: migration of skin organisms at the
insertion site to colonize the catheter tip (most common), direct
contamination of the catheter or catheter hub by contact (hands,
fluids, devices), seeding of catheters from another focus of infection
(less common), and infusate contamination (rare).4 When removing
a catheter, material should be cut away or removed until the
venipuncture site can be visualized. A cotton ball is placed on the
venipuncture site and then the catheter is removed. Moderate
pressure is applied for 1-2 minutes and then a wrap is placed for ∼30
minutes. The catheter should be inspected for signs of damage or
infection.

ARTERIAL PUNCTURE
Arterial puncture is used primarily for assessment of arterial blood
gas (ABG) or acid-base status. The dorsal pedal and femoral arteries
are used most commonly in dogs and cats (Table 74.3) but under
certain circumstances, the palmar, sublingual, coccygeal, radial,
brachial, or aural arteries can be utilized. The choice of artery also
depends on adequate collateral circulation, which, in the rare event
of arterial occlusion, ensures adequate perfusion to the limb. Arterial
puncture is contraindicated in animals with severe bleeding
disorders. In addition to the known complications from
venipuncture, arterial puncture complications also include
arteriospasm. If utilizing a syringe, 1000 units (1 mL) of heparin
should be drawn into the syringe to thoroughly coat the inside
surface, then expelled. No air (falsely lowers PaCO2, falsely elevates
PaO2) or heparin (falsely lowers PaCO2) should be left in the
syringe.5 Use of an ABG syringe precludes the need for this
preparation. Materials and a stepwise approach are listed online in
Equipment Pull List 3 and demonstrated in

Video 74.5. The

preferred technique for arterial palpation is to place two fingers from
the non-dominant hand proximal to the puncture site, to determine
the location, direction, size, and depth of the artery. Use of Doppler
ultrasound may aid localization. Some prefer to hold the syringe and
needle like a dart and place the needle in one movement. Others
prefer to first place the needle under the skin, then as with
venipuncture, advance it into the arterial lumen. A sharper entry
angle (45-60°) minimizes vessel trauma and allows smooth muscle
fibers to occlude the puncture site afterward.7 Bevel up and bevel
down positions are recognized; the current human recommendation
is bevel up. Blood should spontaneously flow into the syringe, but
hypotensive or small animals may require aspiration of the plunger.
Afterward, manual pressure should be applied to the site for >1
minute, or longer if bleeding or a hematoma is seen. Close
monitoring of the site is indicated for at least 5 minutes. Quality
assurance techniques for arterial puncture are similar to
venipuncture. In addition to residual air or heparin artifacts, the
inadvertent submission of venous blood will produce erroneous
results. Any delay in transportation or analysis will affect results. If
assessment of the patient breathing room air is needed, oxygen
therapy should be discontinued 5-10 minutes before collecting an
arterial sample when feasible.8

PLACEMENT OF ARTERIAL CATHETERS
Arterial catheters are placed for serial ABG assessment or
monitoring of arterial blood pressure. Indications and
contraindications include those of arterial puncture and venous
catheterization. Additionally, thrombotic risk factors identified in
humans are: larger catheter size, hypotension, smaller arterial
dimension, multiple arterial sticks, duration of cannulation,
administration of vasopressor and inotropic agents, and the
cannulation site.9 Catheters used for venous catheterization are used
for arterial catheterization, although longer catheters are often
selected. Materials are listed online in Equipment Pull List 4 and a
stepwise approach is demonstrated in

Videos 74.6 and 74.7. The

approach is as described, above, for arterial puncture and venous
catheter placement. Placement should be rapid to avoid arterial
spasm. The bubble test for confirming arterial catheterization is
demonstrated in

Video 74.6. Catheter stabilization, secure

connection points, and protective taping/wrapping are essential for
arterial catheters, as substantial blood loss is possible if the catheter
is dislodged, the connection leaks, or the catheter is removed
prematurely. Arterial catheters must be clearly identified as such to
prevent inadvertent administration of infusates intended for IV
administration. In addition to the venous catheter maintenance list,
arterial catheters should be flushed hourly with heparinized saline
(Box 74.2).10 Arterial catheters should be removed as soon as
possible. When removing an arterial catheter, pressure should be
applied for a minimum of 5 minutes and the limb should then be
bandaged for at least 30 minutes.
