CHAPTER 75: Jugular
Catheterization and Central
Venous Pressure
Measurement
Ricardo Irizarry

A C RO N YM S
CVP central venous pressure
IV intravenous
PICC peripherally inserted central catheter

Jugular catheters are used for central venous pressure (CVP)
measurements, for intermittent or continuous administration of
drugs, for provision of intravenous (IV) fluids and of solutions with
osmolalities greater than 600 mOsm/L, for atraumatic serial blood
sampling, and for long-term (1-2 weeks) venous access in
hospitalized patients. These long catheters also confer less risk of
contamination from vomiting, diarrhea, and urine and are less prone
to flow disturbances than shorter, peripheral venous catheters.1
A risk-to-benefit assessment should be made prior to placement of
a jugular catheter in patients with significant thrombocytopenia or
coagulopathies; patients with disease processes associated with

hypercoagulable states, such as immune-mediated hemolytic
anemia, protein-losing nephropathy, or hyperadrenocorticism; and
in patients suspected of developing elevated intracranial pressures.2
An alternative to jugular catheterization is a peripherally inserted
central catheter (PICC) through the saphenous veins. As long as the
tip of the PICC line is fed into a more centralized portion of the vein
(e.g., caudal vena cava), all aforementioned benefits of a jugular
catheter are obtained by this technique, except reliable CVP
measurements in adult dogs. The risk of overt hemorrhage, clot
formation or decreased cerebral perfusion is minimized by avoiding
a jugular catheter and opting for a PICC line in this subset of
patients.
Various types of central venous catheters exist. They may be
through-the-needle or over-the-needle, single-lumen or multilumen. Multi-lumen catheters are generally preferred over singlelumen catheters as they provide the ability to infuse multiple
solutions simultaneously without worries of incompatibility, provide
additional lumens dedicated for venous sampling and for CVP
measurements, and their costs and placement techniques are
comparable to their single lumen counterparts.
A commonly used technique in the placement of a central venous
catheter is called the Seldinger technique, or the guidewire technique
(Figure 75.1). This technique allows for a smaller catheter or needle
to serve as the introducing catheter, making placement in smaller
patients or hypovolemic patients easier. A long flexible guidewire is
inserted into the vein through the introducer catheter and a central
venous catheter is threaded over the guidewire and into the vessel.
The latter can be single, double, triple or quadruple lumen. This
technique can also be used to exchange central venous catheters
during the patient’s hospital stay, if necessary.

PREPARATION, EQUIPMENT AND
PLACEMENT: SELDINGER TECHNIQUE3
Except in moribund or very cooperative patients, sedation is
beneficial for patient comfort and to be able to carry out the catheter
placement in aseptic fashion. Administer the sedatives prior to

gathering of supplies to allow time for sedation to occur.
Butorphanol 0.2 mg/kg IV to 0.4 mg/kg IM with or without the
addition of midazolam 0.2 mg/kg IV or IM, works well for catheter
placement.
Place the patient in lateral recumbency (Video 75.1).3 Have an
assistant extend the patient’s head and position its forelimbs
caudally

. Placement of a sandbag or rolled towels under the neck

may be helpful to keep the vein elevated toward the operator. The
assistant should then hold off the vein by pressing into the thoracic
inlet, allowing the vein to engorge and “stand up.” The other end of
the vein is immobilized by extending the head. Clip a rectangular
area from the angle of the mandible cranially to the thoracic inlet
caudally and from the ventral cervical midline to the dorsal cervical
midline. This will help prevent contamination of the catheter during
and after placement. Premeasure the distance from the intended
insertion site (approximately one-third of the distance between the
caudal ramus of the mandible and the thoracic inlet) to the 2nd
intercostal space. This will be the length of wire and the length of
catheter that will be inserted into the jugular vein.

FIGURE 75.1 Over-the-needle central catheter kit.
Content includes (in order of usage): (1) surgical
drape; (2) disposable scalpel blade; (3) introducer
catheter; (4) guidewire in coiled plastic sheath, with
J-tip exposed through its introducer straightenersleeve; (5) vascular dilator; (6) sterile 4 × 4 gauzes;
(7) double-lumen catheter with proximal and distal
ports; (8) catheter caps; (9) butterfly adapters; (10)
non-absorbable suture.
Wash hands and aseptically prepare the area in a circular, surgical
scrub motion. Insert a bleb (4 mg/kg) of lidocaine over the proposed
site of catheterization. Wash hands again and don sterile gloves. Fill
all lumens of the jugular catheter and the over-the-needle catheter or
introduction needle with saline. Cap all ports of the multi-lumen
catheter except the one labeled as distal port. This is the port through
which the guidewire will pass. Drape the prepared area. The
guidewire is long and flimsy and will get contaminated easily if the
draped area facing the operator is missing or not long enough. Make
a small (2- to 4-mm) full-thickness facilitative skin incision over the
vein with a #11 blade. Be very careful to not go too deep, which could
lacerate the vein. Place the over-the-needle catheter included in the
kit into the vein through the facilitative incision, oriented toward the

heart. Alternatively, the author prefers to use an 18-gauge 1- to 1.5inch (2.5- to 4-cm) IV catheter for a dog or a 20-gauge 1-inch (2.5cm) IV catheter for a cat as the introducer catheter. With the
assistant once more holding off the vein, insert the introducer
catheter until it is fully seated in the vessel, then remove the stylet.
The catheter should bleed freely. Draw the “J” of the guidewire back
into its introducer straightener-sleeve. Gently seat the introducer
straightener-sleeve into the catheter hub, and thread the wire into
the vessel to the premeasured length. The guidewire has distance
markers on it that assist in determining the appropriate depth of
insertion. Remove the introducer catheter over the guidewire, taking
care to hold the guidewire so it does not slip out and taking care to
not contaminate the guidewire. The wire alone will now remain in
the vessel. Place the vascular dilator over the guidewire, through the
skin and into the vessel to enlarge the opening in the subcutaneous
tissues and the vessel. Tent the skin, holding the dilator as close to
the skin as possible and push with a twisting motion (this will help
facilitate the dilation process). Advance the vessel dilator until its
hub touches the skin. Remove the dilator over the guidewire, being
especially careful to hold the wire so it remains in place. Use direct
pressure with sterile gauzes to control the bleeding from the enlarged
opening of the vessel. Place the catheter over the guidewire and feed
it close to the dilated opening of the vessel. Then pull the wire slowly
out of the vessel and feed it into the catheter. The wire will eventually
appear out of the hub marked “distal port”. At that point, grasp the
wire, and feed the catheter off the wire and into the vessel. Once the
catheter is fed to the premeasured length, aspirate the distal port
with a syringe to confirm blood flow, and then flush with saline until
the line is clean. Attach a needleless port. Repeat for each port to
confirm patency. (Note: aspirating first helps to prevent injection of
air and of clots.) Clean up any blood on the skin, and cover the
central line with a light bandage to keep everything in place. Perform
a lateral thoracic radiograph to confirm the catheter tip is between
the second and third rib space, cranial to the right atrium. Suture the
catheter to the skin at the insertion point using the plastic butterfly
provided. Cover the insertion site with a non-stick gauze pad or
adhesive dressing, and bandage with cast padding, conforming gauze
and VetRap. Bandaging is meant to stabilize the central line, to
prevent it from being pulled out, and to keep the site clean. The

operator should be able to fit 2-3 fingers under the bandage once it is
completed.
When using central lines, wear examination gloves, keep all
injection ports clean, and change the central line bandage as soon as
it becomes soiled or at least every 24 hours.

PEEL-AWAY INTRODUCTION
TECHNIQUE
There are long catheters that use a peel-away introducer to gain
venous access (Figure 75.2) (Video 75.2)

. A sheath with an

inner stylet is inserted into the external jugular vein or the
saphenous vein. The stylet is then removed, leaving the introducer
sheath inside the cannulated vessel. The long catheter is then fed
through the introducer sheath into the desired location. Once the
catheter is in place, the sheath is snapped and gently peeled off the
long catheter. The long catheter is then sutured and bandaged in
place as previously described. This technique can accommodate
single- or multi-lumen catheters (Figure 75.3). The benefits of
these catheters include avoidance of the guidewire placement and of
vessel dilation. The drawbacks include catheter size constraints as
the long catheter must pass through the introducer sheath, thus
limiting its maximum luminal size to that of the diameter of the
sheath.

catheter. The catheter is composed of a sheath with
an inner stylet. Once inserted into the vein, the stylet
is removed, which allows the central catheter to be
fed through the sheath. The sheath is then snapped
and gently peeled off the central catheter.

PERIPHERALLY INSERTED CATHETERS
(PICCs)
Long catheters can be placed via the saphenous vein and threaded all
the way into the caudal vena cava (Video 75.3).

In dogs, the

lateral saphenous is most commonly used, while in cats, the medial
saphenous veins are cannulated. Single- or multi-lumen long
catheters can be inserted using the Seldinger or the peel-away
introducer techniques. A long catheter can also be modified so as to
introduce it through a short peripheral catheter instead of the
introducer needle that normally comes with the long catheter. The

former tends to have a smaller gauge than the introducer needle of
the typical through-the-needle catheters available. For example, a
20-gauge through-the-needle peripheral short catheter will
accommodate a 22-gauge long catheter. This may be advantageous
for cannulation of the saphenous veins of smaller animals. Follow
the procedures and precautions as per the jugular vein
catheterization techniques previously mentioned.

FIGURE 75.4 Water manometer for central
venous pressure measurements. The three-way
stopcock is attached to the manometer and to an IV
extension line. The free end of the extension line gets

CENTRAL VENOUS PRESSURE
MEASUREMENT
The CVP is the pressure measured in the cranial vena cava and is a
reflection of the right atrial and right ventricular pressures when the
tricuspid valve is open (right ventricular end-diastolic pressure).
CVPs are measured in an attempt to predict right ventricular enddiastolic volumes (preload), and right-sided cardiac performance.4
Pressures in the jugular vein are affected by many factors besides
preload and cardiac output.5 In addition, it is the left side of the
heart that supplies the systemic circulation and drains the
pulmonary circulation. Consequently, estimates of volume and of
cardiac performance in the left side are more accurate in guiding
fluid therapy, but their measurement requires use of a pulmonary
artery catheter, which is much more expensive, risky, and technically
challenging.6 Understanding the fundamental limitations of CVP
monitoring, it may still be useful as an adjunct to other
hemodynamic parameters such as arterial blood pressure, heart rate,
capillary refill time, mucous membrane color, serum lactate levels,
and urine output. Patients that may benefit from CVP monitoring
include those that have advanced renal disease (oliguric or anuric
kidney injury), septic shock, and those that have pre-existing heart
disease and are in need of fluid therapy.
There are two methods to measure CVP: with a water manometer
or with an electronic pressure transducer. The water manometer
system is cost-effective and easy; however, it tends to overestimate
the readings, and it does not provide a waveform for analysis.7 For
this technique, a central catheter, a water manometer, an IV
extension set, a three-way stopcock, and saline in a 20-mL syringe or
from a fluid bag attached to an administration set are necessary.
Alternatively, with the electronic method, a blood pressure monitor
can be utilized to display a beat by beat waveform of the central
jugular venous flow into a pressure transducer. Regardless of the
method chosen, it is imperative to obtain the measurements with
accuracy and to do so serially in order to utilize trends in the values
instead of relying on a single reading. The tip of the central catheter
should rest just cranial to the right atrium. In addition, the patient’s

position and the zero reference point must be kept consistently the
same with every measurement. A PICC line inserted into a
saphenous vein and directed cranially to the caudal vena cava may be
used in the cat and puppy as an acceptable substitute for CVP
measurement.8,9

WATER MANOMETER METHOD
To measure CVPs with the water manometer method, first connect
the water manometer in series with the IV extension set and the
syringe or saline bag (Figure 75.4). Prime both the manometer and
the extension set with sterile saline and remove any bubbles. Place
the patient in the desired position and ensure central catheter
patency. Identify the zero reference point that corresponds to the
patient’s right atrium. The sternum, for patients in lateral
recumbency, and the point of the shoulder, for patients in sternal
recumbency, serve as landmarks for this. Use a string to connect the
aforementioned anatomical landmarks to the manometer. The point
of intersection will be the patient’s zero reference point. The CVP
readings obtained will be subtracted from this reference number to
get the final value. After the manometer and extension set are
primed, attach the free end of the extension tubing to the central
catheter. With the stopcock in the “off” position to the syringe, allow
the fluid column in the manometer to equilibrate with the pressure
at the tip of the central catheter. Larger fluctuations in the meniscus
of the water column are associated with respirations, and small,
more frequent fluctuations result from the action of the heart.
Measurement of CVP is performed at the end-expiratory pause just
before inspiration.

ELECTRONIC PRESSURE TRANSDUCER
METHOD
To obtain CVP measurements with the electronic pressure
transducer, the transducer is connected to the blood pressure
monitor and attached to the central catheter with the use of salinefilled arterial blood pressure tubing. The transducer is then placed at

the level of the right atrium following the aforementioned anatomical
landmarks that correspond to the zero reference point. Once the
transducer and the tubing are primed with saline, and the system is
zeroed out, the CVP readings can be read from the monitor on a
continuous, beat by beat basis in the form of a number as well as a
waveform. CVP values in hypovolemic patients may range from −5 to
+3 cm H2O. A normal CVP range is 0-5 cm H2O, with a
measurement of 7-10 cm H2O often indicating adequate fluid loading
in the absence of cardiac failure. An increased CVP can be caused by
volume overload, cardiac failure, pleural or pericardial effusion,
pneumothorax, pulmonary thromboembolism and pulmonary
hypertension.
If a CVP reading is questionable, a test bolus of 20 mL/kg of an
isotonic crystalloid or 5 mL/kg of a synthetic colloid may be given
over 5 minutes or less. The vascular bed is a very compliant system,
able to accommodate changes in volume with minimal changes in
pressure. If the patient has a low CVP due to hypovolemia, the CVP
will show no change or will have a transient rise toward normal, then
rapidly decrease again. The arterial pressure may also increase with
the test bolus, then return toward prebolus measurements. A small
increase of 2 to 4 cm H2O with a return to baseline within 15 minutes
is usually seen in euvolemic patients. A large increase (>4 cm H2O)
and slow return to baseline (>30 minutes) is seen in hypervolemic
animals or those with reduced cardiac compliance.10 In the event
that the patient is suspected of experiencing heart failure, the use of
a test bolus should be unnecessary and might be considered
contraindicated.

CHAPTER 76: Intraosseous
Catheters
Søren Boysen

A C RO N YM S
CPR cardiopulmonary resuscitation
IO intraosseous
IV intravenous

Vascular access is essential in patients needing fluid resuscitation,
airway management, and injectable medications. Placement of
peripheral intravenous (IV) catheters is successful in most cases (ch.
74), although situations may arise where IV catheterization is
difficult due to small patient size, thrombosis, edema, status
epilepticus, obesity, or marked peripheral vasoconstriction and
vascular collapse.1,2 In these settings, manual and automated
intraosseous (IO) devices should be considered.
Advantages of the IO space include: non-collapsible entry point
into the systemic circulation regardless of the state of the vascular
system; no interruption of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)
efforts; medullary cavity diameter larger than equivalent peripheral
veins; and IO placement is usually possible even when peripheral
venous sites become inaccessible (e.g., thrombosis). Automated IO
access is faster than cutdown jugular venotomy catheter placement

in dogs.3 Evidence in dogs also suggests that IO aspirates can be
used as a surrogate for venous blood to assess glucose, lactate,
bicarbonate, pH, PCO2, total solids, sodium, chloride, blood urea
nitrogen, and anion gap, but should not be used for potassium,
packed cell volume, and hematocrit values.4 IO aspirates have been
used for blood typing and cultures in humans.5,6 Studies comparing
IO and venous samples in cats are lacking.

INDICATIONS
In neonatal puppies and kittens IO access is used for resuscitation of
hypothermia, hypoglycemia, and hypovolemia.7-9 In adult small
animals IO access should be considered when peripheral venous
access is difficult, particularly if the patient is unstable and during
cardiac arrest (ch. 131).3,10-12 Difficult IV access is defined as: (1)
more than two unsuccessful attempts to insert an IV line; and/or (2)
no visible or palpable veins following tourniquet placement.13

CONTRAINDICATIONS
Contraindications to IO access include: bone fractures or prior IO
access within the same bone within 48 hours (due to extravasation of
fluid and/or medications); acute infection at the insertion site;
severe pre-existing bone disease, including cancer, osteomyelitis, or
osteoporosis; compartment syndrome or significant vascular injury
in the target extremity; and orthopedic hardware at the insertion
site.14,15 Relative contraindications include cellulitis or burns at the
target site, sepsis or bacteremia, and inability to palpate
landmarks.14,15

IO DEVICES
IO devices include manually placed hypodermic needles and
automated devices (Figure 76.1). There are no clear

recommendations for one device over another and the choice
depends on the age and size of the patient, availability of equipment,
and experience of the clinician placing the device.

MANUAL IO DEVICES
In young animals with a soft bone cortex, regular 18-30 gauge
hypodermic needles or needles with a stylet to prevent
cortical/medullary bone occlusion of the needle during initial
placement (spinal needle, bone marrow aspirate needle) may be used
(Figure 76.1).1 In older patients with a dense bone cortex, manual
Jamshidi devices or IO infusion needles with a central stylet (Cook
Critical Care, Bloomington, IN; Cardinal Health, McGaw Park, IL)
are used (Figure 76.1).2 A newer manual IO device, the 15 G EZ-IO
T.A.L.O.N. (Teleflex, Limerick, PA), has been approved for sternal
and peripheral use in humans; it has not been studied in veterinary
patients.16

AUTOMATED IO DEVICES
Automated devices are either spring-loaded or battery-powered
(Figure 76.1). Spring-loaded devices include the 17 gauge (G)
FAST1 sternal needle (Pyng Medical, Vancouver, BC, Canada), the 15
G (adult) or 18 G (pediatric) Bone Injection Gun (B.I.G.) (PerSys
Medical, Houston, TX) (Figure 76.1), and the spring-loaded 15 G
New Intraosseous (NIO) device (PerSys Medical, Houston,
TX).14,17,18 Spring-loaded devices project the IO needle at high speed
through skin, subcutaneous tissues, and bone cortex to a fixed depth,
which can often be adjusted (Video 76.1

).2 The spring loaded

FAST1 is specifically designed for sternal applications in humans and
has not been studied in veterinary patients. The battery-powered
rotational EZ-IO is reportedly the easiest and most common
automated device for human use,18 which is likely true in veterinary

medicine (Videos 76.2 and 76.3

). EZ-IO needles are 15 G and

available in 15, 25 or 45 mm lengths (Figure 76.1).

MANUAL VS. AUTOMATED IO DEVICES
Human pediatric simulator research reports success rates of 90100% with NIO, EZ-IO, and B.I.G. devices vs. 43% with a Jamshidi
needle.17 A proximal tibial IO study on anesthetized dogs comparing
the B.I.G. device and Jamshidi needle found no difference in
placement success rates (83% vs. 96%) although B.I.G. was faster to
place (22 vs. 42 seconds).12 A feline cadaver study comparing B.I.G.,
EZ-IO and Jamshidi devices found no difference in combined
success rates for proximal tibia and humerus placement (75-96%);
placement times of 72, 87 and 121 seconds for EZ-IO, B.I.G. and
Jamshidi, respectively; and that the EZ-IO was easier to use than the
B.I.G.10

ACCESS SITES AND IO FLUID FLOW
RATES
The ideal IO access site should have minimal subcutaneous tissue,
allowing the bone surface and landmarks to be easily palpable, and
carrying minimal risk of injury to vital structures. Any medullary
space can be used. The sternum, radius, ulna, calcaneus, proximal
medial tibia, tibial tuberosity, ischium, wing of the ilium, greater
tubercle of the humerus, distal femur, and trochanteric fossa of the
femur have all been accessed in human and/or veterinary
medicine.1,2,11,18,19 The experience and preference of the clinician,
patient age, anticipated duration of use, patient mobility, clinical
setting (CPR vs. fluid resuscitation), fluid flow rates, time for drugs
to reach the heart, and first-time success rates will influence the
anatomic site chosen for IO access.

IO ACCESS SITES
The trochanteric fossa of the femur is most commonly used in exotic
and pediatric patients as it is well tolerated, allows mobility, and is
easy to perform.2,11 The risk of sciatic nerve injury can be minimized
by walking the needle off the medial aspect of the greater trochanter
into the trochanteric fossa with the hip joint in a neutral and
internally rotated position.2 In obese patients, identification of
landmarks around the trochanteric fossa can make IO access
challenging, and the trochanteric fossa of adult large-breed dogs
often requires needles ≥25 mm in length, which can be a limitation
of spring loaded devices; long manual or 45 mm EZ-IO needles can
be used.11
In adult cats and dogs, the proximal caudal medial tibia and the
cranial proximal tibia are the most common IO access sites due to
the ease of landmark location and minimal overlying muscle/tissue
(Figure 76.2, Videos 76.1, 76.2, and 76.4

).1,2,10-12 However,

compared to the tibia, the humerus may have higher placement
success rates and shorter placement times, particularly in smallbreed dogs (Figure 76.2, Videos 76.3 and 76.5

).11 Evidence

suggests IO medications injected into the humerus reach the heart
more quickly than those injected into the tibia during closed-chest
CPR.20 The small cross-sectional area and higher flow resistance of
the tibia may explain lower success rates and a higher incidence of
IO fluid extravasation at 300 mm Hg pressure, particularly in small
breed dogs.11 The curved shape of the ilium makes IO access
challenging.11 Use of the sternum has not been studied clinically in
small animals.

FLOW RATES
IO infusion rates are related to needle and bone diameter, viscosity
of the fluid, needle bevel location (against bony cortex), and needle
patency (occluded with bony debris).11,18 IO fluids are administered

via gravity or pressures up to 300 mm Hg. Pressure infusion is
recommended as it overcomes flow resistance due to bone spicules
and helps push medications into the vascular system. Using 300 mm
Hg pressure roughly doubles isotonic crystalloid flow rates compared
to gravity infusion (maximum of 2.1 mL/kg/min via the humerus
and femur in canine cadavers).11 An EZ-IO canine cadaver study
demonstrated IO flow rates of 2.1, 2.1, 1.5, and 0.6 mL/kg/min at
300 mm Hg for the proximal humerus, distal lateral femur, wing of
the ilium, and tibia, respectively.11 The humerus and femur also had
faster IO gravity flow rates.11 IO whole blood infusion is slower
compared to isotonic crystalloids (50 mL/min at 300 mm Hg in
people), although hemolysis is uncommon, with >90% of red blood
cells entering peripheral circulation in healthy dogs.18 There are no
studies investigating IO flow rates in cats, and it is unknown if flow
rates in live animals will be the same as those reported in cadavers. If
higher fluid rates are needed, placement of multiple IO catheters has
been suggested, although they need to be placed in separate bones.

COMPLICATIONS
Evidence suggests that IO cannulation is rapid, easy, safe, and
effective.1,2,10-12,18,19 Cage-side indicators of successful IO
catheterization include loss of resistance when the medullary cavity
is reached, firm seating of the catheter at the insertion site based on
the ability to manipulate the limb via the catheter, slight resistance to
catheter flushing, and the absence of post-flush subcutaneous fluid
accumulation.18 Aspiration of bone marrow (ch. 84) is confirmatory
but may not always be possible, even with correct IO device
placement, and is painful in an awake or sedated patient.21 Once the
IO catheter is stable, radiographs can confirm IO catheter placement
but this step is not mandatory if other findings indicate correct
placement.
Clinical complications in small animals have not been reported.
Complications in humans include minor hemorrhage, fluid
extravasation, skin infection, skin necrosis, bone fracture,
osteomyelitis, fat and air embolization, compartment syndrome, and
pain/discomfort at the injection site.11,14,18 Severe complications
have been reported in human neonates including fractures and limb
ischemia secondary to compartment syndrome severe enough to
require amputation.22 Although studies demonstrate that
administration of IO fluids and drugs does not impair bone growth,
care should be taken in young patients to avoid the epiphyseal
plates.2,22
Needle fracture is reported with the FAST1 and EZ-IO devices,
although needle retention does not appear to cause any long-term
complications.22 Local micro-fractures using the B.I.G. device have
been documented histologically in canine cadavers, although clinical
significance was not evaluated.
IO access can cause pain in conscious patients, especially during
rapid IO fluid administration. In humans, spring-loaded IO needle
placement is considered nearly pain-free; however, local anesthesia
is still recommended in conscious patients.12 Preservative-free 2%
lidocaine at a dosage of 0.5 mg/kg administered via the IO catheter is
reported to manage the discomfort associated with infusions in some

human studies, although other studies fail to support this finding. If
used, it is recommended to wait 60 seconds to achieve effect and
then follow the lidocaine bolus with a 3-10 mL bolus of normal saline
(depending on patient size). Cats are very sensitive to IV lidocaine;
its use is extra-label and not recommended by many clinicians. Sideeffects of IO lidocaine in cats are unknown but should be considered
the same as IV; the clinician is advised to monitor closely for central
nervous system effects and cardiovascular depression, and use lower
(extra-label) dosages (0.25-0.5 mg/kg IO given slowly over 10-15
minutes, can repeat at 0.15-0.25 mg/kg in 5-20 minutes).

FLUIDS AND MEDICATIONS
Current human recommendations support using the same IV and IO
drug and fluid dosages, with similar expected peak effects.14,18,23,24
Therefore blood products, synthetic colloids, hypotonic crystalloids,
isotonic crystalloids, hypertonic saline, parenteral nutrition, opioids,
antibiotics, and most other IV medications can be given IO.14,18,22-24
Extravasation of IO drugs has the same effect as IV extravasation:
there are reports of tissue necrosis with IO extravasation of
hypertonic solutions (hypertonic saline, 10-50% dextrose),
epinephrine, norepinephrine, and sodium bicarbonate. Although
hypertonic solutions can cause histologic evidence of bone marrow
necrosis following administration, the clinical significance of the
necrosis has not been established, and human patients with clinical
cerebral edema tolerate hypertonic IO fluid administration well.15

Chapter 77: Constant Rate
Infusions
Adesola Odunayo

A C RO N YM S
CRI constant rate infusion
IV intravenous
Sedatives, analgesics, antibiotics, catecholamines, anesthetics and
other medications are commonly administered as a continuous or
constant rate infusion (CRI) in human and veterinary medicine.1-4 A
CRI is defined as a controlled method of intravenous (IV)
administration of drugs, given without interruption, as opposed to
bolus administration. A CRI involves the infusion of a parenteral
drug over several hours to days. It usually involves the addition of
medication to a sterile IV solution before administration to the
patient. CRIs may also be utilized in the administration of drugs into
the epidural space through the use of an epidural catheter.5-7
CRIs are superior to intermittent dosing of certain drugs for many
reasons. They allow for maintenance of plasma drug concentrations
within the target therapeutic range, avoiding peaks and troughs in
plasma concentration and thus avoiding variability in drug effects.8
Another advantage of utilizing CRIs is that they allow rapid
alterations in medication dosage to suit the needs of the patient.4
CRIs also allow medications with short half-lives, like remifentanil or
fentanyl, to be utilized for longer periods of time.9 Some studies in
human patients have shown CRIs of beta lactam antibiotics are

superior to intermittent boluses in terms of attaining
pharmacodynamic targets for those drugs, hence the use of CRIs in
critically ill human patients with sepsis.3,10 Examples of medications
that could be administered as a CRI are outlined in Box 77.1. This
chapter will review the indications for utilizing CRIs, as well as
provide an outline for how to set them up.

INDICATIONS FOR UTILIZING
CONSTANT RATE INFUSIONS
ANALGESIA
Since many different types of medications can be utilized as a CRI,
the indications for setting up a CRI are numerous. One of the most
common indications for utilizing a CRI in patient management is
analgesia. CRIs allow clinicians to provide consistent analgesia that
avoids the peaks and troughs associated with intermittent boluses.11
This makes the patient more comfortable, reduces the incidence of
wind-up pain and might allow for faster recovery since the patient’s
pain level is better controlled.12 While not every painful patient
requires CRIs of analgesic medications, the clinician should consider
a CRI as a priority in patients with moderate to severe pain. Opioids
are the drugs that are most commonly utilized as CRIs to treat pain,
although lidocaine, ketamine and dexmedetomidine may also be
utilized as a CRI with opioids to provide multimodal analgesia.4,8
See ch. 6 for more information on pain identification and
management.

SEDATION
CRIs are also commonly utilized for sedation in the ICU, as well as in
patients with moderate to high level of anxiety while hospitalized.
Sedatives like butorphanol, midazolam, diazepam, and
dexmedetomidine are the most common sedatives utilized in the
intensive care unit (ICU). These sedatives can be given as
intermittent boluses; however, the relatively short half-life of their
pharmacologic effect can be extended when they are administered as
CRIs.

HEMODYNAMIC INSTABILITY
Another common use for CRIs is treating patients with
hemodynamic instability. Catecholamines, positive inotropes, and
vasopressors, e.g., dopamine, dobutamine, norepinephrine and
vasopressin, are among the most commonly used medications in
critically ill patients with hypotension and/or poor cardiac output.
These drugs have a short half-life; therefore, the magnitude of the
patients’ hemodynamic response is partially dependent on plasma
concentrations achieved during continuous infusion of these
medications.13

ANTIBIOTICS

Antibiotics, specifically beta-lactams, may also be administered as a
CRI especially in critically ill patients.3 Beta-lactam antibiotics are
time-dependent and studies have shown that optimal efficacy with
these agents is achieved when the free drug concentration is above
the minimum inhibitory concentration of the targeted organism for
an extended duration of the dosing interval (ch. 140). In one
multicenter randomized controlled trial in human patients, the
administration of beta-lactam antibiotics as a continuous infusion
produced higher plasma antibiotic concentrations than intermittent
administration.3 There was also a direct correlation with patient
improvement and clinical cure in that group of patients with severe
sepsis.
In summary, indications for utilizing CRIs primarily center around
maintaining a constant concentration of the drug in the bloodstream.
This makes CRIs ideal for providing analgesia, sedation,
hemodynamic support, ultra-short-acting insulin and certain
antibiotics.

SETTING UP A CONSTANT RATE
INFUSION
CRIs are best administered using infusion pumps (as opposed to
gravity flow). Advances in infusion pump technology have made
continuous infusions easy and practical to administer.14 Depending
on the infusion pump utilized, administration errors may also be
minimized when pre-programmed doses and calculations are
utilized. However, since these infusion pumps are primarily
programmed for use in human patients, veterinary professionals are
expected to verify doses, concentration, delivery rate and delivery
times before each use. Traditional infusion pump types used in the
delivery of CRIs include syringe and large-volume infusion
(peristaltic or volumetric) pumps.
Syringe pumps (Figure 77.1) work off a motor-driven lead screw
or gear mechanism to drive the plunger into the syringe barrel. They
have the advantages of maintenance of precision and accuracy at low
flow rates (they can achieve flow rates as low as 0.01 mL/hr when
very small syringes are used), which can be useful for

neonates/pediatric patients or patients with fluid
intolerance/overload.15 Syringe pumps can function with different
sizes and brands of syringes and do not require expensive
proprietary administration sets, thus reducing the cost per
administration.15 The biggest disadvantage of syringe pumps is their
limited volume, where most can handle 60 mL syringes at the
most.15 Utilization of syringe pumps for large-volume CRIs leads to
frequent interruption in flow as a result of syringe changes. These
interruptions may be significant enough to alter therapeutic drug
concentrations, depending on the drug being used. Changing the
syringe out often may also potentially increase patient exposure to
pathogens.15
Peristaltic pumps (Figure 77.2) propel the fluid either by
compressing the fluid line or using two or more rotary cams.15 They
have the advantage of improved accuracy in fluid volume delivered to
the patient compared to manual or gravity infusion. They can also
handle any volume of fluid, having a broad range of infusion from
0.1-1200 mL/hr.15 Disadvantages of peristaltic pumps include low
accuracy of infusion at low flow rates, as well as deformation of the
fluid line due to constant massaging. Volumetric (cassette) (Figure
77.3) operated pumps work by having a cassette of a measured
chamber volume inside the pump, which infuses a known volume of
fluid with every cycle.15 They have the advantages of allowing a quick
and easy setup and programming, as well as the capacity for
administration of large volumes of fluids (0.1-1200 mL/hr).
Volumetric pumps also have the disadvantage of inaccuracy at lower
volumes, as well as the requirement for needing the manufacturer’s
administration sets,15 which can be expensive.

FIGURE 77.1 Syringe pump set up as a constant
rate infusion. Labelled with additives contained in
the syringe. This pump gives the user the flexibility
of delivering in mL/hr or dose/kg/time.

FIGURE 77.2 Peristaltic fluid pump showing the
metal bar that compresses the fluid line. This pump
can only deliver constant rate infusions in mL/hr so
the operator has to do all the calculations and
determine a rate.

FIGURE 77.3 Volumetric cassette fluid pump with
a constant rate infusion (CRI) setup. This

ways to set up the CRI (mL/hr vs. dose/kg/time). In
this photo, the CRI is labelled with the patient and
additive information. The fluid bag also contains
light-sensitive drugs which are protected by the
green bag.
Newer infusion pumps can be set to deliver CRIs in mL/hr as well
as in drug dose per kg of body weight over a specific period of time
(i.e., mg/kg/hr or mcg/kg/minute or mg/hr). For practices where

programmable infusion pumps (Figures 77.1 and 77.3) are not
available, the veterinary professional can calculate the CRI rate
manually and set the pump to deliver the CRI in mL/hr. In addition,
and as previously mentioned, delivery rates should always be verified
when using programmable pumps, as errors can occur when
programing the device. Thus, the veterinary professional should be
very comfortable with medication calculations.16 Calculation errors
make up a large portion of total medication errors in health care.16
Consistent practice of mathematical skills improves confidence and
reduces the frequency of errors.17 Examples of CRI calculations are
outlined in Box 77.2.
BOX 77.2 C ons tant R ate Infu s io ns Calcu l ations
1. Rosie is a 2.5 kg 5-month-old kitten that is being
treated for hypoglycemia. How many mL of 50%
dextrose should be instilled in a 500 mL bag of LRS to
make a 5% solution?
When creating dilutions from solutions expressed in
percentages, the following formula is helpful
C1V1 = C2V2
C1 = percentage (concentration) of stock solution
V1 = desired volume to be added to the solution
C2 = percentage (concentration) of solution wanted
V2 = current volume of fluid
For this question, the volume of dextrose needed (V1) is solved as
follows
50% × V1 = 5% × 500 mL
V1 = 5% × 500 mL/50%
V1 = 50 mL
In order to make a 5% solution of dextrose in LRS, 50 mL of
LRS should be removed from the bag and 50 mL of dextrose
added. The bag of LRS should be labelled appropriately.

2. Jack, a 20 kg 10-year-old male castrated Labrador
Retriever, is recovering from a tibial plateau leveling
osteotomy (TPLO). He is being treated overnight on a
fentanyl (50 mcg/mL) CRI at 4 mcg/kg/hr. How many
mL of fentanyl should be drawn up for a 12-hour dose
and what rate should the syringe pump be set to?
Jack requires a total fentanyl dose of 80 mcg/hr based on
the 4 mcg/kg/hr dose chosen for providing analgesia (4
mcg/kg/hr × 20 kg equals 80 mcg/hr).
Jack would require a total of 960 mcg for a 12-hour dose
(80 mcg × 12 hours). This is equivalent to a 19.2 mL total
fentanyl volume since the fentanyl concentration is 50
mcg/mL (960 mcg/50 mcg/mL).
Ultimately the syringe pump will need to be set at 1.6
mL/hr to run over a 12-hour period (19.2 mL/12 hours).
The syringe should be labelled appropriately.
Alternatively, Jack needs 80 mcg of fentanyl per hour,
which is equivalent to 1.6 mL/hr (80 mcg/50 mcg/mL).
The total volume of fentanyl required overnight will be 1.6
mL × 12 hours, which amounts to 19.2 mL. The syringe
should be labelled appropriately.
3. Jack, a 20 kg 10-year-old male castrated Labrador
Retriever, is recovering from a TPLO. He is being
treated overnight on a fentanyl (50 mcg/mL) CRI at 4
mcg/kg/hr. There are no syringe pumps available,
only peristaltic fluid pumps. He has a new 500 mL
bag of 0.9% NaCl for his maintenance fluids, which
would run at a rate of 50 mL/hr. How many mL of
fentanyl should be added to the bag to provide a 4
mcg/kg/hr dose?
This question is similar to question 2 above, except that the
CRI of fentanyl is being delivered through intravenous
fluids, rather than as a separate infusion using a syringe
pump. Since Jack’s fluids will be running at 50 mL/hr, it
will take 10 hours to deliver the entire 500 mL bag of 0.9%
sodium chloride.
Jack requires 80 mcg of fentanyl per hour (20 kg × 4
mcg/kg/hr). Thus, 800 mcg or 16 mL of fentanyl (800
mcg/50 mcg/mL) is the final dose and volume required for

a 10-hour period. It is important to remember to remove 16
mL of 0.9% NaCl from the bag before adding 16 mL of
fentanyl. The bag of 0.9% NaCl with the added fentanyl
should also be labelled appropriately.
Alternatively, Jack requires 80 mcg/hr of fentanyl or 1.6
mL/hr. Since the bag of LRS will last for 10 hours, 16 mL
(1.6 mL/hr × 10 hours) of fentanyl should be drawn up and
instilled into the bag of 0.9% sodium chloride. The fentanyl
should be added after 16 mL of 0.9% NaCl has been
removed from the bag and the bag of 0.9% NaCl should be
labelled appropriately.
4. Princess, a 3 kg 10-year-old female spayed Shih Tzu, is
being hospitalized for congestive heart failure. She is
to be started on a furosemide (50 mg/mL) constant
rate infusion at 0.5 mg/kg/hr. There are no syringe
pumps available and the lowest rate the peristaltic
pump can be set to is 1 mL/hr. How many mL of
furosemide need to be added to a 25 mL bag of 0.9%
NaCl so that the prescribed dose runs at 1 mL/hr?
Based on the prescribed dose of 0.5 mg/kg/hr, Princess
requires 1.5 mg/hr of furosemide (0.5 mg/kg/hr × 3 kg).
Since Princess has congestive heart failure, the CRI should
ideally not be run any higher than the lowest rate the pump
can run—1 mL/hr —to reduce the risks of volume overload.
Thus, the 25 mL bag of 0.9% NaCl should last for about 25
hours.
Hence 25 hours × 1.5 mg/hr would yield a total
concentration of 37.5 mg of furosemide. This is equivalent
to 0.75 mL of furosemide (37.5 mg/50 mg/mL). In
conclusion, 0.75 mL of 0.9% NaCl should be removed from
the bag before 0.75 mL of furosemide is added. The bag
should be labelled appropriately. The pump should then be
set to run at 1 mL/hr, which will deliver a total dose of 0.5
mg/kg/hr or 1.5 mg of furosemide.
5. Monkey, a 15 kg 10-year-old Labrador Retriever, is
recovering from a foreign body exploratory surgery
on a dopamine (40 mg/mL) constant rate infusion.
The manufacturer recommends that dopamine be
diluted to 1.6 mg/mL for administration. Describe the

dilution technique required for a 250 mL bag of 0.9%
NaCl. How many mL/hr should the fluid pump be set
at in order to deliver a dose of 10 mcg/kg/minute?
The first step of this problem is to dilute the dopamine to 1.6
mg/mL using the following equation
C1V1 = C2V2
C1 = percentage of stock solution
V1 = desired volume to be added to the solution
C2 = percentage of solution wanted
V2 = current volume of fluid
The initial volume of dopamine needed (V1) is solved as follows
40 mg/mL × V1 = 1.6 mg/mL × 250 mL
V1 = 1.6 mg/mL × 250 mL/40 mg/mL
V1 = 10 mL
This 10 mL of 0.9% NaCl is removed from the 250 mL bag
and 10 mL of dopamine is added to make a 1.6 mg/mL
solution.
The second part of this problem is to figure out the volume
of 1.6 mg/mL of dopamine needed to deliver a dose of 10
mcg/kg/minute.
Since Monkey weighs 15 kg, he would require 150 mcg of
dopamine per minute, or 9000 mcg per hour (150
mcg/minute × 60 minutes). Since the concentration of
dopamine is in mg, 9000 mcg is converted to 9 mg (9000
mcg/1000). Thus, Monkey requires a dopamine dose of 9
mg/hr. To calculate the equivalent volume in mL, (9
mg/hr)/(1.6 mg/mL), which results in a volume of 5.6
mL/hr.
Medications administered as CRIs can be delivered in their
original concentration, diluted to a specific concentration, and/or
mixed with other medications. Some medications also come as
premixed bags ready to administer (dopamine, dobutamine, etc.). It
is important to follow specific manufacturer recommendations when

it comes to dilution and administration of medications. For instance,
catecholamines should be diluted to manufacturers’
recommendations in order to reduce severity of phlebitis that may
occur if they extravasate. In addition, certain catecholamines, like
norepinephrine, should be diluted in a dextrose-containing fluid. In
addition, when instilling drugs into a bag of fluids, it is important to
remove an equivalent volume of the drug from the bag of fluids first,
in order to ensure the drug concentration is accurate (see examples
in Box 77.2). After instilling all the drugs in the bag of fluids, the
bag or syringe should be gently mixed to ensure adequate dispersal
throughout. Lastly, it is strongly recommended that drug
compatibilities be verified when different medications are combined
together for a CRI.
For most drugs, a loading dose should be administered before
starting the CRI, in order to get adequate plasma concentrations
quickly. Table 77.1 highlights commonly used drugs, dosages, and
special considerations. It is important to ensure all fluid bags and
syringes utilized for CRIs are properly labelled. The label should
include the patient’s name, medical record number, medications
added to the fluid bag/syringe and their respective concentrations,
date the CRI was made as well as the name or initials of the
individual who made the CRI up. All light-sensitive medications need
to be covered up in the bag and/or syringe; if the infusion rate is slow
enough, the administration line should also be protected from light.

It is important to note that some drugs are dosed based on body
weight (in kg) per minute, while some are dosed based on body
weight (in kg) per hour or body weight (in kg) per day. In addition,
some drugs are dosed in micrograms while others are dosed in

cause life-threatening errors if mixed up. CRI, Constant rate
infusion; IV, intravenous.

STOPPING A CONSTANT RATE
INFUSION
CRIs can be slowly weaned or abruptly stopped. In general, a gradual
wean is recommended if the patient needs to be monitored for
recurrence of signs, e.g., pain, hypotension, anxiety, seizures. If
concerning signs recur, the CRI can be increased back to the lowest
effective dose. This is a common practice for patients being treated
with catecholamines for hypotension or opioids for pain. Depending
on the medication being administered and clinical circumstances, it
may take minutes to a couple of hours to wean off a CRI. In some
circumstances, such as a patient on a CRI of furosemide for
congestive heart failure, an abrupt termination is reasonable if the
patient had been doing reasonably well in the time leading to
stopping the CRI.

BLOOD GLUCOSE (BG): INDICATIONS,
ASSAY METHODS, METERS

INDICATIONS
Knowing an animal’s blood glucose (BG) concentration (BGc) can be
critical to many diagnostic and therapeutic decisions, particularly
when treating diabetes mellitus (DM; ch. 291, 292) or conditions
which may cause hypoglycemia (ch. 61, ch. 289). It may be of value
to monitor BGc in nondiabetic pets at risk for altered glucose
homeostasis, e.g., critical care patients with any of a variety of
conditions: trauma, sepsis (ch. 128), systemic inflammatory
response syndrome (ch. 128),1-3 insulinoma (ch. 289),4
portosystemic shunt (ch. 267),5 liver failure (ch. 266),6 and
hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296).7 Juvenile dogs and cats are less able
to maintain fasting BG as well as adults.8

PORTABLE BLOOD GLUCOSE METERS
(PBGMs)
Automated chemistry analyzers using the hexokinase method are
considered the “gold standard” for determining BGc. Several
limitations make the use of the hexokinase method impractical.
Therefore, over time many “patient-side” BG monitoring methods
have been developed, including PBGMs and implantable continuous
glucose monitoring sensor systems (CGMSs). PBGMs are designed
for home self-monitoring by people with DM. A PBGM provides BG
results in seconds and is inexpensive, easy, and requires only a drop
of blood. PBGMs are used for BG curves, to obtain single glucose
measurements in pets with DM, and to screen pets for hyperglycemia
or hypoglycemia, if indicated. New commercially available PBGM
devices are being added to the market by various manufacturers.
New meters usually have improved precision and quicker results,
require less blood, and/or reduce dependence on operator technique.

CONTINUOUS GLUCOSE MONITORING
SYSTEMS (CGMSs)

CGMSs were originally designed for humans with diabetes as an athome means of glucose monitoring that circumvents the need for
repeated finger pricks to obtain capillary blood. These devices have
been adopted by veterinarians primarily to monitor BGs in diabetic
dogs and cats. CGMSs measure the subcutaneous (SQ) interstitial
fluid glucose concentration (IGc), demonstrated to correlate well
with hexokinase method results.9 Use of a CGMS avoids the need for
intermittent BGs, hospitalization, restraint, and repeated
phlebotomies. Moreover, IGcs are continuously recorded for
consecutive days, facilitating detection of intra-day and inter-day
glycemic variability. Several CGMSs are commercially available and a
number have been validated for use in dogs and cats.

AUTOMATED CHEMISTRY ANALYZERS
Several methods are currently available for measuring glucose
concentration. The most commonly used enzymatic techniques are
highly specific for glucose or its derivate glucose-6-phosphate.
Glucose concentrations are generally determined using hexokinase,
glucose oxidase or glucose dehydrogenase assays.10 With the
hexokinase method, glucose‐6‐phosphate, formed from glucose and
adenosine triphosphate (ATP) by hexokinase, is oxidized by
nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) in a reaction catalyzed by
glucose‐6‐phosphate dehydrogenase to produce NADH (NAD +
hydrogen), which can be spectrophotometrically quantified and
directly correlated to the amount of glucose in a sample.
To avoid incorrect results, samples should be analyzed
immediately, centrifuged to remove cells, or collected into fluoride
oxalate tubes to prevent continued glucose utilization. If serum or
plasma is not separated from whole blood quickly, BG can decrease
in vitro at a rate of about 5-10% per hour because erythrocytes and
leukocytes in whole blood continue metabolizing glucose.10 This
effect can be marked with severe leukocytosis, polycythemia, sepsis
or bacteremia (e.g., true infection or bacterial sample
contamination). Additional disadvantages associated with using
hexokinase methodology include: need for a larger blood volume,
more time to obtain results, limited availability, and cost.

PORTABLE BLOOD GLUCOSE METERS
(PBGMs)
METHODOLOGIES: REFLECTOMETRIC
TECHNIQUE AND AN IMPEDENZIOMETRIC
ASSAY
PBGMs are small devices designed for whole BG measurement using
an enzymatic reaction which takes place when blood is placed on a
disposable test strip containing glucose oxidase-like enzymes.
Results can be obtained by a reflectometric technique or an
impedenziometric assay. In reflectometric devices, after the drop of
blood is placed on the test strip it spreads into the layer where an
oxidative reaction occurs, culminating in the production of gluconic
acid and hydrogen peroxide. The hydrogen peroxide reacts with the
enzyme peroxidase and oxidizes a reactive dye on the test strip,
producing a color intensity reported as a BGc. In impedenziometric
devices, blood diffuses into an internal layer of the test strip
containing enzymes (glucose oxidase or glucose dehydrogenase) and
electrodes. The enzymes catalyze the conversion of glucose to
gluconic acid and the electrons produced generate a current
calibrated to measure the BGc.11

CODING, CALIBRATION, ACCURACY
Coding and Calibration
Several PBGMs are commercially available, the majority of which are
designed for at-home self-testing by diabetic people. Some models
require coding or calibration to match the PBGM device with the test
strips. This is usually accomplished by inserting a code strip or a
code number into the meter each time a new batch of test strips is
used. If not done correctly, readings may be inaccurate. Other
models automatically calibrate and code each time a test strip is
inserted (“no coding technology”). Given the high number of PBGMs
that are commercially available, only devices evaluated in
independent quality control studies should be considered for clinical
use in dogs and cats. PBGM accuracy is determined according to the

International Standards Organization criteria (ISO 15197:2013) for
humans: ≥95% of the PBGM measurements should fall within ±15
mg/dL (0.84 mmol/L) of the reference method at BG concentrations
<100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) and within ±15% of the reference method
at BG concentrations ≥100 mg/ dL (E-Figure 78.1, A).12 Secondly,
99% of the PBGM results should fall within zones A and B of the
Parkes consensus error grid analysis (EGA; E-Figure 78.1, B).13 The
EGA categorizes errors in BG measurements in terms of clinical risk.
In this analysis, reference glucose results are plotted against the BG
results obtained by the PBGM. The plot is divided into 5 zones
classifying the magnitude of risk derived from the determination: (A)
no effect on clinical action; (B) altered clinical action—little or no
effect on clinical outcome; (C) altered clinical action likely to affect
the clinical outcome; (D) altered clinical action could involve a
significant medical risk; and (E) altered clinical action could have
dangerous consequences. These criteria are meant for humans and
are quite rigid. In veterinary medicine, a wider degree of deviation
from the reference method can be accepted.

E-FIGURE 78.1 A, Bland-Altman plot
representing accuracy of portable blood glucose
meters (PBGM) for International Standards
Organization (ISO) 15197:2013. On the x-axis are the
reference glucose values, plotted against the
differences between the two techniques (y-axis). The
standard required limits are defined by the
symmetric lines: at ±15 mg/dL from the reference
value for glucose determinations <100 mg/dL and at
±15% from the reference for glucose ≥100 mg/dL. To
convert from mg/dL to mmol/L, divide by 18. B,
Error grid analysis: the reference glucose values, on
the x-axis, are plotted against the blood glucose
values obtained by the glucose meter (y-axis). The
different zones designate the magnitude of risk
derived from the determination. The ISO 15197:2013
requires that 99% of the values fall within zones A +
B for a device to be considered accurate. To convert
from mg/dL to mmol/L, divide by 18.

Accuracy of Made-for-Human Meters
Accuracy of commercially available PBGM devices designed for
human use can vary considerably when used on dogs and cats. Some
PBGMs are sufficiently accurate and precise for monitoring BGc in
dogs and cats; however, the majority of PBGMs underestimate the

“true” BG when compared to the laboratory reference method
because they are “plasma calibrated.” The meters use a formula that
calculates the glucose concentration as if it were derived from plasma
and not from capillary whole blood. This facilitates comparisons
between laboratory and PBGM measurements.14-20 Since the
amount of glucose within dog and cat red blood cells (RBCs) is lower
than in humans (12.5% and 7% vs. 50%, respectively),21 those
PBGMs may underestimate BGc. Studies have demonstrated that the
AccuChek Aviva Nano (Roche Diagnostics),19 Accu-Chek compact,22
and Accu-Chek Performa (Roche Diagnostics)23 are among the most
accurate human PBGMs for use in dogs and cats.

Accuracy of Meters Made for Dogs and Cats
The most accurate and precise PBGM for use in dogs and cats was
developed for veterinary use and is marketed as AlphaTRAK (Abbott
Animal Health).17,24 This PBGM is plasma calibrated to account for
the difference in glucose distribution in whole blood in dogs and cats.
Additional advantages of the AlphaTRAK are the small blood
volumes needed (0.3 mcL) and its extended measurement range (20750 mg/dL [1.1-41.7 mmol/L]). However, some BGc readings from
the AlphaTRAK may differ considerably from reference methods.
Those differences increase as the BGc increases. In contrast to many
human PBGMs, which usually give BGc values that are lower than
the reference method, the AlphaTRAK may either under- or
overestimate “true” glucose concentrations.

FIGURE 78.2 Capillary blood sampling using a
lancing device on the carpal pad in a dog (A), oral
mucosa in a dog (B), inner aspect of the pinna in a
dog (C), and lateral ear margin in a cat (D).
In cats, no differences between AlphaTRAK BGc and the reference
method BGc were found in 9% of samples, 51% of results
overestimated the BGc, with a median difference of 4.4 mg/dL (1.872 mg/dL [0.24 mmol/L; 0.1-4 mmol/L]), and 40% of BGc were
underestimated, with a median of −12.6 mg/dL (−1.8 to −122 mg/dL
[0.7 mmol/L; 0.1-6.8 mmol/L]). At a BGc <100 mg/dL (5.6
mmol/L), where exact measurements are most important, the
precision of the meter is better, with 90% of values falling within ±15
mg/dL (0.83 mmol/L) of the reference method.25 In dogs, the
accuracy of AlphaTRAK is good; however, the device may give BGc
values higher or lower than results measured by the reference
method on the same blood samples.17 Because of this lack of
consistency, caution should be used in interpreting the results
obtained with AlphaTRAK. If there is any doubt regarding the

accuracy of a BGc, the measurement should be repeated with the
same meter and, ideally, with the laboratory reference method.

SOURCES OF ERRORS
There are many potential sources of error when using a PBGM.
Reasons for errors may vary slightly from one device to another, but
usually include operator error, e.g., improper machine calibration,
use of outdated reagent strips, improper blood droplet size or
placement; temperature, altitude and humidity26; hematocrit
(Hct)14,15; blood oxygen pressure27; blood pH28; concentrations of
substances such as triglycerides and bilirubin29; and concurrent
drug administration.29 The effect of Hct on PBGM readings can be
clinically significant and should be taken into account, especially in
critically ill pets with a disease causing abnormal RBC counts. In pets
with a low Hct, PBGMs consistently overestimate BGc.14,15,18,30 In
contrast, an increased Hct can result in a decreased BGc result.30
This effect of Hct is thought to be due to a change in the diffusion
rate of plasma to the test strip reagent pad with abnormally
increased or decreased numbers of RBCs.31

SAMPLING SITE AND LANCING
DEVICES
Capillary blood can be collected from several sites, since their
BGcresults do not differ: ear, oral mucosa, or the paw pads (Figure
78.2, A-D).32,33 The best site for collecting the blood should be the
one best tolerated by the dog or cat and which consistently yields
adequate blood. The inner aspect of the pinna is one of the best sites
(Figure 78.2, C; Video 291.5). Some authors prefer using the lateral
ear margin for cats (Figure 78.2, D;

Videos 78.1, 78.2).34 To

facilitate collection of capillary blood, a variety of lancing devices are
available. These spring-loaded devices, when triggered, drive a lancet

through the skin at controlled depth (

Videos 291.6, 291.7).

Devices of different gauge sizes and various depth settings are
available. Choice of lancing device is based on personal preference
and some prefer using a hypodermic needle (Video 78.1

).

Puncturing the vein on the dorsal surface of the lateral ear margin
may result in excessive bleeding or bruising and it is sufficient to be
near rather than in the vein.34 Blood sampling from the oral mucosa
is an option in dogs (Figure 78.2, B; Video
291.6).32 When
using this site, drying the buccal mucosa with dry gauze before
sampling is recommended to avoid dilution causing falsely low
results. Lancing paw pads yields excellent blood samples (Video
291.7

); however, collecting from the metacarpal, metatarsal or

digital pads tends to be uncomfortable and creates risk of infection
with litter box use in cats.34 Lancing the carpal pad (Figure 78.2,
A) alleviates this issue and is generally well tolerated. No pressure is
usually required over lancing sites since bleeding is not typical.

CONTINUOUS GLUCOSE MONITORING
SYSTEMS (CGMSs)
TECHNOLOGY
CGMSs measure IGc using transcutaneous sensors. These devices
have a sterile single-use sensor, a glucose monitor which records
data, and a communication device for data download. Wireless
devices utilize a transmitter to distribute information from the
sensor to the monitor. The first-generation systems allowed only a
retrospective analysis of the IGs after disconnecting the sensor and
uploading the data (retrospective CGMS). Newer devices (real-time
CGMSs) measure and display data immediately, allowing direct
intervention. These systems detect glucose using technologies similar
to the PBGMs.
When using a CGMS, it is important to consider that they measure
IGc not BGc. The interstitial fluid (ISF) glucose–plasma glucose

relationship is explained by a 2-compartment model in which the
capillary wall separating plasma from ISF acts as a barrier to glucose
diffusion.35 In this model, changes in IGc are determined by rate of
glucose diffusion across the capillary wall and the rate of glucose
clearance from the ISF. ISF glucose clearance is determined by
insulin-mediated glucose uptake by the surrounding cells. Clearance
rates are proportional to the IGc and the rate of uptake by cells. If the
rate of glucose uptake by the surrounding cells is negligible and
diffusion rate between plasma and ISF is constant, a steady-state
relationship develops.35,36 However, diffusion of glucose from
plasma into ISF is not immediate, and a corresponding lag phase
exists between rapid changes in BGc and the delayed change in IGc.
The delay has been described as 5 to 12 minutes in dogs35,37 and 11
to 30 minutes in cats.38,39 The lag phase can also be affected by the
diffusion of glucose from the ISF into the sensor; however, available
CGMSs have digital filters designed to compensate for this delay.

COMMERCIALLY AVAILABLE CGMSs
Several made-for-human CGMSs are commercially available. Several
have been studied for use in dogs and cats: iPro (Medtronic),
Guardian Real Time (Medtronic), MiniMed Gold (Medtronic),
GlucoDay (Menarini Diagnostic) and FreeStyle Libre (Abbott).38-45
Most CGMSs have limitations regarding clinical use. They require
calibration 2-3 times/day by measuring the BGc with a PBGM. Thus,
using CGMSs still requires periodically obtaining a drop of blood.
The recording range is 40-400 mg/dL (2.2-22 mmol/L). In order for
results outside this range to be seen, they must be downloaded. If the
BGc is outside this range, the system cannot be calibrated until the
BGc is in the working range. Finally, the sensor is quite expensive
and can be used only for a few days.

FLASH GLUCOSE MONITORING
SYSTEMS (FGMSs)

Technology
FGMSs (FreeStyle Libre, Abbott) have been introduced
commercially. The FGMS is composed of a small, lightweight, disc‐
shaped sensor (35mm×5mm) which measures the IGc by means of a
SQ catheter (0.4mm×5mm). The system has several features which
distinguish it from other existing technologies. It provides
comprehensive glucose data without the need for calibration and can
be worn for up to 14 days. Glucose detection is based on Wired
Enzyme Technology which consists of both enzymatic (glucose
oxidase) and amperometric (electrode) systems.46 Glucose reacting
with glucose oxidase results in generating an electric current with an
intensity proportional to the IGc. The detection limits of the sensor
are between 20 and 500 mg/dL (1.1-27.8 mmol/L); measurements
outside this range are recorded as “LO” and “HI,” respectively.

Function
The sensor begins recording 1 hour after its application and
automatically measures the IGc every minute. Those results are
transferred from the sensor to a hand-held reader when in close
proximity. The reader then displays the current sensor IGc, an IGc
trend arrow, and the IGcs from the preceding 8 hours. The FreeStyle
LibreLink mobile app, available for both Android and iOS operating
systems, can be used as an alternative to the reader. Scanning can be
performed as often as is needed; otherwise, the measurements are
automatically recorded and stored on the sensor (every 15 minutes)
and can be displayed on the reader when scanned. The reader stores
the data for 90 days. At the end of the recording period, the sensor is
disposable; however, the reader can be re-used with a new sensor.
With the LibreView system, the USB port on the reader can be used
for charging and downloading all data onto a computer. This is a
free, secure, cloud-based diabetes management system provided by
Abbott. The system generates summary glucose reports (Ambulatory
Glucose Profile) from the uploaded sensor data and provides a secure
repository for data. Furthermore, using the FreeStyle LibreLink app,
the glucose data can be easily shared with health care professionals
using the same LibreView system, where the data are automatically
uploaded to LibreView when the phone is connected to the internet.

Clinical Application and Materials Required (Figure
78.3; Video 78.3

)

The device is usually well-tolerated in dogs. Mild erythema at the site
of the sensor application has been the only complication
recorded.45,47-49 In dogs with DM, the device has adequate clinical
accuracy with a mean ± standard deviation difference from the
reference hexokinase method of 2.3 ± 46.8 mg/dL (0.1 +/- 2.6
mmol/L). However, the FGMS readings are less accurate for glucose
concentrations <90 mg/dL (5 mmol/L).45,49 Moreover, dogs with
thinner skin show less accurate measurements as compared to dogs
with thicker skin (>5 mm).50 Changes in metabolic variables,
common in dogs with diabetic ketoacidosis (ketosis, acidosis,
hyperlactatemia), do not affect FGMS accuracy.47 However,
dehydration reduces accuracy.49
In cats, FGMS accuracy is good in the euglycemic and
hyperglycemic ranges, but further validation is required for
hypoglycemia.39,51 The relative deviation from the reference
hexokinase method is 9.96%, with slightly higher median values in
the hypoglycemic and normoglycemic ranges (12.3% and 12.6%,
respectively).51 Changes in BGc are not rapidly detected in the ISF by
the FGMS,39 thus making the device less accurate during periods of
rapidly changing glucose levels. The most common complications
encountered with the use of the FGMS in cats is the reduced sensor
lifespan (5.5-8 days) which should be discussed with owners before
considering its use. Extra fixation with glue on the skin-facing
surface of the sensor is strongly advised in cats.

NEW TECHNOLOGIES
A novel long-term implantable CGMS (Eversense XL; Senseonics,
Germantown, MD) has been developed to overcome some of the
limitations of traditional transcutaneous CGMSs. This system
consists of a sensor inserted SQ, a wearable transmitter, and a
mobile application which displays glucose information on a
handheld device.52 The main advantage of Eversense XL is the longterm sensor lifespan; it extends the possible average CGMS wear
time of 7-14 days to up to 180 days.52 This device has further
advantages over transcutaneous CGMSs: frequent sensor insertions
through the skin are not needed and the transmitter can be easily
removed without the need for sensor replacement.53 However,
unlike the transcutaneous CGMS, the sensor of Eversense XL needs
to be implanted and removed from the skin by means of a minimal
surgical procedure performed by a health care professional.52 An
abiotic (non-enzyme) fluorescent glucose-indicating polymer is
grafted to the poly(methyl methacrylate) shell of the sensor. Glucose
binding leads to increased fluorescence intensity which is measured
by the optical components of the sensor. The overlying wearable
transmitter powers the sensor, employing an inductive link that
receives the fluorescence intensity data. The data are converted to
glucose data and then transmitted via Bluetooth for display on the
mobile app.54 To date, no studies on these devices have been
published in veterinary medicine. In our limited experience, this
device has provided good information. The Eversense XL allows
remotely displaying glucose values and graphs results in an
extremely intuitive way. The main disadvantage is that the sensor
might move in the SQ space and lose the connection with the smarttransmitter. In this case, the glucose data are not recorded or

displayed until the transmitter is properly repositioned over the
sensor. In addition, it requires 2 calibrations per day.

CONCLUSION
The use of CGMSs has been demonstrated to be clinically
advantageous in humans with DM, reducing the risk of hypoglycemia
and hyperglycemia as well as glycemic variability, and improving
patient quality of life. In veterinary medicine, while only a few
studies have investigated the clinical utility of these devices, results
are promising.48,55

CLIENT INFORMATION
The Importance of Measuring Glucose
Knowledge of your pet’s blood sugar (glucose) concentration is
critical when treating animals with conditions that may cause low
glucose concentrations and, particularly, when treating animals with
diabetes mellitus. Diabetes mellitus is a disorder characterized by
high blood glucose concentrations. The disease occurs because of a
deficiency of insulin, a hormone produced by the pancreas.
Successful treatment of diabetic pets relies on the observation of
your pet’s symptoms and your pet’s blood glucose periodic rechecks.
One way veterinarians have to regulate your pet’s diabetes is to
perform a blood glucose curve. A glucose curve involves serial
measurements of blood glucose using a handheld blood glucose
meter (glucometer). To obtain a blood glucose curve, dogs and cats

are usually hospitalized for an 8- to 12-hour period, and capillary
blood samples are taken at 1- or 2-hour intervals using lancing
devices or a needle. Alternatively, you can measure your pet’s blood
glucose concentrations at home. Home monitoring has several
advantages. It is less expensive and the blood glucose readings will
not be artificially increased by the stress of hospitalization. If your
pet doesn’t seem well, you can test the blood glucose and know
whether you are dealing with hypoglycemia (dangerously low
glucose) or hyperglycemia (elevated glucose) and respond
accordingly. Based on the blood glucose curve, your veterinarian can
judge whether the daily insulin therapy is adequate or whether it is
necessary to change the dosage or type of insulin. In cats, it can be
particularly important to regulate them quickly since they can go into
diabetic remission. It is highly recommended you do not change the
dosage of insulin without consulting your veterinarian.
Over the last years, new technologies have been developed to make
easier management of diabetes mellitus. Continuous glucose
monitoring systems (CGMSs) were originally designed for human
diabetic patients as an at-home method of glucose monitoring, which
circumvented the need for repeated capillary blood sampling. To
date, these devices can also be routinely used to monitor glucose
concentrations in diabetic dogs and cats. The CGMSs avoid several
limitations of the blood glucose curves, including the intermittent
assessment of glucose concentration, hospitalization, patient
restraint, and repeated blood sampling. Moreover, they allow a
continuous assessment of glucose concentrations for different
consecutive days. To date, the FreeStyle Libre flash glucose
monitoring system (Abbott) is one of the most convenient CGMSs.
The device can be placed by your veterinarian or yourself and allows
the assessment of your pet’s glucose concentrations for up to 14 days.

METHODS OF GLUCOSE MONITORING
Use of Glucometer Devices and Capillary Blood Sampling
There are several glucometers available for humans. To date,
AccuChek Aviva Nano (Roche Diagnostics) and Accu-Chek compact
or Accu-Chek Performa (Roche Diagnostics) are among the most
accurate human glucometers for use in dogs and cats, respectively.
However, the best PBGM for dogs and cats is a veterinary glucometer

specifically validated and calibrated for use in these species called
AlphaTrak (Abbott). This device requires a tiny drop of blood and
gives a reading in a few seconds. Always be sure to read, understand,
and follow the instructions provided with your PBGM and test strips.
For example, the AlphaTrak needs to be coded for that species (dogs
or cats) before using it. When you turn on the glucometer by
inserting the test strip, the word “CODE” and a “code number” will
appear. At this point, you should press the “c” button to scroll
forward or the “m” button to scroll backward until the number
matches the code on the test strip vial for dogs or cats. Your
veterinarian will usually help demonstrate a method of collecting a
blood sample. Capillary blood samples can be collected from various
sites, including the ear, the inside of the upper lip, or the paw pads
(Fig. 1). Testing is relatively quick and painless. The best site to
collect the blood sample is the one that your pet tolerates the best
and which consistently yields an adequate blood sample. In dogs,
one of the best methods of obtaining a drop of blood is to prick the
inner surface of the pinna (Fig. 2). The steps for blood collection
from this site are as follows:
1. Massage with the thumb the inner surface of the pinna to
increase the vascularization of this area.
2. Hold the tip of the ear between your thumb and index finger,
and hold the surface of the ear flat by the rest of your fingers;
with the other hand, place the lancet device on the inner
surface of the pinna and push the release button.
3. Wait a few seconds to obtain a small drop of blood.
4. Place the PBGM with the test strip inserted over the drop of
blood.
5. The blood is automatically absorbed, and after a few seconds,
the blood glucose concentration is displayed.

FIGURE 1 Capillary blood sampling using a
lancing device on the wrist-pad in a dog (A), oral
mucosa in a dog (B), inner aspect of the pinna in a
dog (C), and lateral ear margin in a cat (D).

FIGURE 2 Capillary blood sampling using the
inner aspect of the pinna in a dog. A, The tip of the
ear is held between the thumb and index finger, and
the surface of the pinna is held flat by the rest of the
fingers; with the other hand, the lancet device is
placed on the inner surface of the pinna and the
release button is pushed. B, After a few seconds a
tiny drop of blood is obtained and the proper code
for dogs is set. C, The glucometer is placed over the

absorbed, and after a few seconds, the blood glucose
concentration is displayed.
In cats, one of the easiest methods of obtaining a drop of blood is
to prick the marginal ear vein (Fig. 3). This is a small blood vessel
that runs along the outer edge of the cat’s ear. The steps for blood
collection from this site are as follows:

1. Place a cotton ball or a folded gauze under the pinna to prevent
excessive digital pressure occluding the vessels or piercing
your fingers.
2. Place the lancing device over one of the capillaries close to the
vein (it is important to avoid hitting the vein, which may result
in excessive bleeding or bruising) and push the release button.
For this step, you can also use a needle (Fig. 3).
Steps 3, 4, and 5 are the same described for the previous
procedure.
Another site that can be used in dogs is the inner lip (Fig. 1). In
dogs and cats that allow you to touch their pads, you can also use this
site. In this case, it is advisable to use the wrist-pad (Fig. 1) on the
forelimb because it is more well-tolerated. Usually, no pressure is
needed after the puncturing procedure as no bleeding is expected
after capillary sampling.
