Use of FreeStyle Libre Flash Glucose Monitoring System
FreeStyle Libre flash glucose monitor system is a small sensor that
records your pet’s glucose concentrations continuously throughout
the day and night. You can see your pet’s glucose concentrations by
scanning the sensor with the reader or with your phone (through a
specific app) whenever you want to. The sensor does not measure the
blood glucose concentration; it measures the amount of glucose in
the fluid surrounding the body cells—called interstitial fluid. There is
a small-time delay when checking this fluid, especially after eating or
after insulin injection. So the FreeStyle Libre result is not always
exactly the same as the capillary blood result.
A flash glucose monitoring system has two parts (Fig. 4):

• A disc-shaped sensor which measures your pet’s glucose
concentrations by means of a small, subcutaneous catheter.
The sensor lasts 14 days; after that, you need to put on a new
one.
• A reader that you can swipe over the sensor to get both the
glucose level and the trend of the concentrations. You can also
scan the sensor with your phone using the FreeStyle LibreLink
mobile app, available for Android and iOS operating systems.

FIGURE 4 Diabetic dog wearing FreeStyle Libre
flash glucose monitoring system sensor. The sensor
has been scanned by the reader. The reader shows
the current glucose concentration, the glucose
concentration over the last 8 hours (graph), and the
direction that glucose is heading (arrow).
Each time you scan the sensor, you can access the last 8 hours of
your pet’s sugar concentrations. Scanning can be performed as often
as is needed; otherwise, the measurements are automatically

recorded and stored on the sensor and displayed on the reader when
scanned. The reader stores the data for 90 days. A USB port on the
reader can be used to charge it and to download all the data onto a
computer, using the LibreView system. LibreView is a free, secure,
cloud-based system. It provides a convenient way to view the glucose
data through clear and easy-to-understand reports, which you can
quickly share with your veterinarian. You can upload your pet’s
glucose data easily from the FreeStyle Libre reader by connecting the
reader to an internet-connected PC and following the upload
instructions. The system generates summary glucose reports from
the uploaded sensor data. Alternatively, using the FreeStyle
LibreLink app, the glucose data can be easily shared with health care
professionals using the same LibreView system. In this case, the data
is automatically uploaded to LibreView when the phone is connected
to the internet. In order to use the LibreView system, the following
steps are necessary: 1) Get your free LibreView account by using your
email. 2) Sign up and log into your LibreView account; 3) connect
your glucose device, and 4) follow the on-screen instructions to
upload data. 5) At this point, you can see glucose patterns and trends
to help your veterinarian make informed decisions about your pet’s
glucose levels. The glucose data is stored securely in the cloud, so you
and your veterinarian can view the reports anytime, anywhere (from
most web-connected devices).
The sensor should preferably be placed on the dorsal surface of the
neck (in dogs) or the dorsal or lateral surface of the neck (in cats).
The sensor placement can be done by your veterinarian or by
yourself following these passages:
1. Before starting, make sure to have all the necessary equipment;
in the yellow box, you can find the sensor pack and sensor
applicator and the alcoholic wipes. You also need 3 gauzes with
chlorhexidine and 1 clean gauze to dry the skin and scissors.
2. Trichotomize an area of approximately 5 × 5 cm on the dorsal
or lateral surface of the neck.
3. Next, clean the skin with chlorhexidine (it is advisable to
perform 2 or 3 passages) and the alcoholic wipes provided by
the manufacturer. Let the skin dry.
4. Peel the lid off the sensor pack and unscrew the cap from the
sensor applicator. Place the sensor applicator into the sensor

pack by lining up the mark that is on the applicator with the
dark mark that is on the pack and press down firmly on the
sensor applicator until it comes to a stop. Lift the applicator
out of the sensor pack and the sensor is ready for the
application.
5. Push the applicator over the site and press firmly until it stops.
At this point, secure the sensor further, covering it with an
extra tape.
6. The sensor can now be activated using the reader (or the
mobile phone).
7. Press the home button to turn on the reader, touch “start new
sensor” and scan the sensor. When vibration is perceived the
sensor is activated and it needs 60 minutes to provide glucose
readings.
8. Finally, the sensor is secured with a cotton bandage and with
an elastic bandage.

Chapter 79: Buccal Mucosal
Bleeding Time
Christine Savidge

A C RO N YM S
BMBT buccal mucosal bleeding time
COX-1 cyclooxygenase 1
vWD von Willebrand disease
vWf von Willebrand factor

Buccal mucosal bleeding time (BMBT) is used to screen for
primary hemostatic abnormalities. Primary hemostasis involves the
interactions of functioning platelets, the vascular endothelium, and
von Willebrand factor (vWf) (ch. 170).1 Diseases that are known to
affect primary hemostasis and platelet function in cats and dogs
include thrombocytopenia (ch. 59); von Willebrand disease (vWD),
thrombasthenia, congenital and acquired thrombocytopathies (ch.
175); and vascular disorders (ch. 181).
Initial diagnostic steps to evaluate primary hemostasis in a
bleeding or at-risk patient include a thorough history, physical exam,
complete blood count, serum biochemistry profile, and urinalysis.
The complete blood count should focus on platelet parameters. If
quantitative platelet parameters are normal, a bleeding time can be
used as a screening test for abnormal platelet function.2

The bleeding time is a measure of platelet plug formation using a
standardized incision.3 A prolonged bleeding time can identify
deficiencies in platelet number and vWf or abnormalities in vascular
integrity and platelet function. See chs. 171, 175, and 181for more
information on diseases resulting in abnormal platelet adhesion and
aggregation, or vascular endothelial dysfunction. The BMBT is most
useful in the presence of a normal platelet count. In a
thrombocytopenic patient (<70,000 platelets/mcL), a BMBT
provides no additional information, because the bleeding time will be
prolonged due to the thrombocytopenia. Any prolongation of the
bleeding time does not correlate with the clinical severity of
abnormal primary hemostasis. Not all conditions that cause platelet
dysfunction will result in an abnormal BMBT. Additional qualitative
measures, such as vWf concentration, and in vitro platelet function
tests, such as optical aggregometry, aperture closure time, and flow
cytometry, can be used for complete evaluation of primary
hemostasis (ch. 170).1

PERFORMING A BMBT4
MATERIALS (Figure 79.1):
• Assistance for maintaining the patient in lateral or sternal
recumbency, or chemical restraint
• Fully automated spring-loaded device for a standardized
incision (5 mm long × 1 mm deep)
• Surgicutt Adult template bleeding device (International
Technidyne Corp., Edison, NJ)
• Simplate II (Organon Teknika Corp., Durham, NC)
• 5 cm wide roll gauze
• Blotting paper/filter paper, e.g., Whatman #1 filter disc (Fisher
Scientific Co., Clifton, NJ)
• Stopwatch
The BMBT test (

Video 79.1) can be performed in conscious or

anesthetized dogs and in sedated or anesthetized cats. It is important

for the patient to remain immobile for the full duration of the test
(several minutes) to avoid disrupting the forming clot and nullifying
the test. With the patient in lateral or sternal recumbency, the
maxillary lip is everted and held in place with a gauze strip tied
around the muzzle. The gauze is tied tightly enough to create venous
congestion. In cats or brachycephalic dogs, the gauze is tied caudal to
the ears.
It is important to use a standardized device that creates a 5 mm
long and 1 mm deep incision, because devices that create smaller
incisions, such as Surgicutt Junior or Newborn for people (Kitvia,
Labarthe-Inard, France), or a scalpel blade, can result in different
bleeding times,5 causing an inaccurate result.
After the safety clip is removed, the automated, spring-loaded
blade device is gently and evenly placed against the patient’s labial
mucosa at the level of the maxillary canine tooth, rostral to the
gauze. It is important to avoid visible blood vessels and highly
vascularized areas.6 The incision is made either perpendicular or
parallel to the lip margin.4,6 The device is activated, which
immediately creates an incision, and the stopwatch is started at that
moment. The device is removed and discarded. With blotting paper,
blood droplets are caught 2-4 mm below the incision. It is important
that the incision remain clearly visible, because it is essential to not
disrupt the forming clot. In an awake dog, any blood that reaches the
patient’s mouth or tongue can bother the patient and disrupt the
procedure. Blood droplets continue to be caught on the filter paper,
until the incision is not actively bleeding. As soon as blood oozing
has stopped, the stopwatch is stopped. The bleeding time is defined
as the length of time from the creation of the incision to the time
when bleeding has stopped, which indicates initial platelet plug
formation.3

FIGURE 79.1 Material and equipment for
performing a buccal mucosal bleeding time
(clockwise from top): filter paper (boxed and
unboxed), roll gauze, timer, fully automated springloaded device.

INTERPRETING RESULTS
Published reference intervals for normal BMBT are 1.8-4.7 minutes
in dogs3,6,7 and 0.5-2.5 minutes in cats.8,9 For clinical purposes,
BMBT <4 minutes is considered normal in dogs, and BMBT <3
minutes is considered normal in cats.8 Dogs with thrombopathia,6

thrombasthenia,10 type II or III vWD6 and cats with ChédiakHigashi syndrome9 can have bleeding times >10 minutes. With the
BMBT, intra-operator repeatability can differ by more than a
minute.11
Advantages of the BMBT include that it is a simple, specific and
fairly sensitive test to perform, and that it is sensitive for both
quantitative and qualitative primary hemostatic dysfunctions.7 The
test is essentially painless, non-invasive, and well tolerated in an
easily restrained patient.7 Minimal, inexpensive, and readily
available equipment is required (
Video 79.1).
Limitations to the BMBT include operator-dependence11 and that
it is not sufficiently sensitive to detect mild bleeding disorders.12 In
humans, poor sensitivity is seen with mild type I vWD.13 The BMBT
is not helpful in identifying clotting factor disorders/coagulopathies
and it offers no additional information in a thrombocytopenic
patient. The location and plane, as well as the vascularity and
capillary density, of the chosen site of the incision and the extent of
venocongestion can affect the BMBT.
In screening people for primary hemostatic disorders, bleeding
times have been replaced by platelet function analyzers (e.g., PFA100 assay) with increased reproducibility and improved sensitivity.
While the PFA-100 assay may be superior to BMBT and is ideal when
available, the PFA-100 assay is ideally run within 5 hours of sample
collection12 and equipment is not always accessible to many
practitioners. The BMBT stands as a good screening test for
abnormal primary hemostasis in small animal patients.

CAUSES OF A PROLONGED BMBT
See ch. 175 for a complete list of platelet disorders.
Inherited thrombocytopathies: intrinsic platelet function defects
are less common.

• vWD, which is a hereditary deficiency of vWF that causes
impaired platelet adhesion and aggregation and which has
been reported in various dog breeds and rarely in cats. vWD
can result in a bleeding time >3× normal.6
• Disorders of platelet membranes include Glanzmann’s
thrombasthenia in Otterhounds and Great Pyrénées dogs.10
• Disorders of platelet secretion seen in Spitz14 and Basset
Hound thrombopathy14 and platelet granule storage pool
deficiency in American Cocker Spaniels15 and feline ChédiakHigashi syndrome.9
Acquired thrombocytopathies: platelet function is not consistently
altered.
• Uremia, due to defective platelet adhesion (ch. 301)16
• Hepatic disease (ch. 266), due to decreased platelet
aggregation17
• Anemia (ch. 57)6
• Dysproteinemias (ch. 60) and disseminated intravascular
coagulation (ch. 171) are thought to result from platelet
coating by paraproteins and fibrin degradation products.6
• Infectious causes that may prolong BMBT: leishmaniasis (ch.
197),18 ehrlichiosis (ch. 193), and anaplasmosis (ch. 193)19
• Myeloproliferative diseases (ch. 331) and vasculopathies, e.g.,
vasculitis and inherited vascular defects (ch. 181)1
• Intravenous infusion of dextran 70 in dogs6
• Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents that inhibit
cyclooxygenase 1 (COX-1) result in decreased thromboxane A2,
interfering with platelet function. Aspirin inconsistently
prolongs the canine BMBT20 while COX-1–sparing drugs, like
carprofen and meloxicam, do not (ch. 143).

Cutaneous bleeding times are described as an alternative to BMBT
in dogs.20 Results are not standardized, with great variation in skin
thickness in different breeds. Cuticle bleeding times, performed by
clipping a claw and determining the bleeding time, have been used
for assessing coagulation. These are difficult to standardize, do not
differentiate between primary and secondary hemostasis, and are
painful unless performed under general anesthesia.3 The cutaneous
and cuticle bleeding times are not recommended by the author.
BMBT is a valuable diagnostic test when screening a patient for
moderately to severely delayed primary hemostasis. The BMBT can
be used prior to surgery when there is a concern for acquired or
congenital platelet dysfunction. The BMBT is an important part of
the diagnostic workup for any bleeding patient with normal
quantitative platelet parameters and normal prothrombin and
activated partial thromboplastin times when specific platelet
function tests are not immediately available.

Chapter 80: Fecal
Examination
Byron L. Blagburn, and Lindsay A. Starkey

A C RO N YM S
PCR polymerase chain reaction
qPCR qualitative PCR

Fecal detection of internal parasites is an important component of
veterinary practice as they remain prevalent and important disease
agents in companion animals.1,2 Techniques include gross
examination, fecal smear (wet mount), flotation (both centrifugal
and standing, with or without quantification), Baermann procedure,
sedimentation, fecal culture, fecal immunologic, fecal molecular
biologic, and artificial intelligence imaging. Failure to employ “best
practice” techniques when conducting fecal examination procedures
can result in failure to detect parasite stages or components in fecal
specimens.3-7 It is important to be reminded that feces should be
fresh (to preserve parasite motility, if present) and an appropriate
sample volume (≥1 g formed feces) should be used for optimal
parasite recovery.
It is also important to recall that microscope settings for fecal
flotations are different than those to examine blood smears, tissue
sections, etc. Adjust the sub-stage condenser to provide better

contrast for visualization of parasites. Furthermore, the entire area
under the coverslip should be examined using the 10× objective
(with use of the 40× objective for verification as needed).

GROSS EXAMINATION
Take note of the color and consistency and look for the presence of
blood, mucus or froth (air bubbles), as those are often indicators of
gastrointestinal disease that may be caused by parasites (chs. 49, 51,
262, and 263). In addition, be sure to examine for any parasites that
may be visible macroscopically (e.g., tapeworm proglottids).

FECAL SMEAR (

Video 80.1)

The direct fecal smear or “wet mount” is the technique of choice for
detection of motile parasites such as Giardia, Tritrichomonas,
Pentatrichomonas, amoeba, or larvae that may be damaged by
flotation solution. It is paramount that the sample be fresh if
examining for motility.

FECAL FLOTATION TECHNIQUES
Fecal flotation continues to be the most common fecal procedure
performed in veterinary clinics and laboratories (Figures 80.1 to
80.3). Fecal flotation is intended to separate parasites from other
objects and debris based on their different densities, and that ability
to separate is enhanced using centrifugation.3 Recall that there are
several optional flotation solutions that can be used (e.g., zinc sulfate
[ZnSO4], magnesium sulfate [MgSO4], sodium nitrate [NaNO3],
sodium chloride [NaCl], Sheather’s sucrose), and for a majority of
the parasites, flotation solution selection may not make much of a
difference. However, recovery of certain parasites may be either
enhanced (e.g., ZnSO4 and Giardia cysts; Sheather’s sucrose and
Trichuris, Taenia, and Physaloptera ova) or hindered (NaNO3 and

Giardia cysts) by use of certain solutions.8 Furthermore, specific
gravity of flotation solutions should be checked routinely with a
hydrometer.
Although not historically performed in companion animal
practice, egg quantification techniques should be considered when
evaluating a patient for suspected drug-resistant intestinal parasites
(e.g., hookworms). The ability to quantify eggs per gram of feces is
useful in determining an appropriate response to treatment. The
only difference between a standard centrifugal flotation technique
and an egg quantification procedure is that the latter uses a known
quantity of both feces and flotation solution, while the feces are
typically not weighed with the former.

FIGURE 80.1 Procedure for performing a direct
smear.

FIGURE 80.2 Preparing a fecal specimen for
flotation.

FIGURE 80.3 Materials needed for fecal flotation.

BAERMANN PROCEDURE
The goal of the Baermann procedure is to recover motile larvae of
parasites (e.g., Aelurostrongylus, Strongyloides, etc.) from fresh
fecal specimens. Immobile ova or dead larvae cannot be recovered
with this technique.

FECAL SEDIMENTATION
Sedimentation is used for concentrating eggs or larvae that are too
dense to float in flotation solutions or that might be distorted by the
solutions, keeping in mind that most all parasites and debris will be
present in the sediment. Sedimentation can be performed using
either the standing or centrifugal procedure, but with water or saline
in lieu of flotation solution (Figure 80.4). We prefer to use a
centrifuge because it results in faster movement of parasites to the
bottom of the tube.

FECAL CULTURE
Fecal culture techniques are rarely performed except perhaps to aid
in the detection of Tritrichomonas blagburni in feline fecal samples.
The In Pouch TF-Feline (Biomed Diagnostics) can be inoculated and
either incubated and examined in practice or sent to a referral
laboratory for evaluation. Diamond’s media can also be used to
culture trichomonads.

FECAL IMMUNOLOGIC TECHNIQUES
Fecal antigen-detection platforms are available for use either inclinic or through veterinary diagnostic reference laboratories, with
some reference laboratories offering additional immunologic
techniques for fecal parasites (e.g., immunofluorescent antibody
[IFA]).
In-clinic options include several commercially available Giardia
antigen-detection platforms which can aid in the diagnosis, as
Giardia stages may be difficult to detect using the traditional
aforementioned parasitological techniques.5,9 Use of these
diagnostics as a screening tool for all fecal samples is not
recommended; rather, they can be used when a patient’s history and
clinical signs are indicative of a Giardia infection. Using these tools
in conjunction with ZnSO4 fecal flotation has resulted in enhanced
sensitivity of Giardia detection.9
Antigens from Toxocara spp., Baylisascaris spp., Ancylostoma
spp., Uncinaria spp., Trichuris spp., and Dipylidium caninum in
canine and feline feces can be detected in samples submitted to
IDEXX reference laboratories.10-12 Benefits of antigen-based
diagnostics include the ability to detect pre-patent infections 1-6
weeks before egg-shedding and environmental contamination can
occur, as well as aiding in the determination of spurious versus real
parasitism.10,11 Enhanced sensitivity has been reported by
combining antigen-based diagnostics with traditional flotation
techniques.13

FECAL MOLECULAR BIOLOGIC
TECHNIQUES
Molecular biology continues to expand its presence in diagnostic
parasitology. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) techniques are now
commonplace in many reference laboratories and can be important
additions to other test methods.14 PCR is a technique that duplicates
a specific segment of DNA when a known sequence (primer) is
attached (annealed) to it. The duplicate DNA product (amplicon) is
specific to the parasite DNA to which the primer is attached. The
sequence of DNA subunits (nucleotides) in the DNA product is
compared to known published sequences. This allows identification
of the parasite with a high degree of accuracy.

FIGURE 80.4 Performing a fecal sedimentation
procedure.
PCR is a useful resource when other fecal examination methods
fail or when additional diagnostic information is needed. Some
parasites for which PCR is helpful either in diagnosis or for further

taxonomic analysis include Giardia, Tritrichomonas blagburni,
Cryptosporidium spp., Toxoplasma gondii and taeniid tapeworms
including Echinococcus spp.15-19 PCR is usually combined with
conventional fecal techniques such as flotation or direct smear. If
these tests yield negative or questionable results, additional PCR
testing might be warranted. PCR tests can provide helpful guidance
when selecting appropriate treatments or counseling clients on
prevention of zoonosis.
Fecal PCR tests can include either universal or species-specific
primers. Universal PCR tests are helpful in identifying groups of
parasites at a general level, such as Giardia or Cryptosporidium.
Species-specific PCR tests can identify a particular parasite from a
group of parasites. Species-specific tests can differentiate individual
Giardia assemblages or specific species of Cryptosporidium such as
C. hominis, C. parvum or C. bovis. Likewise, species-specific PCR
tests could identify Tritrichomonas blagburni when similar parasites
such as Giardia or Pentatrichomonas hominis might be present. All
three of these parasites could be present in a pet with diarrhea and
appear similar to persons not trained specifically to recognize them.
Furthermore, tapeworm eggs of Taenia and Echinococcus spp. are
difficult (if not impossible) to differentiate in a fecal flotation
preparation. Species-specific PCR procedures can successfully
identify parasites in the different genera and specific species such as
E. granulosus and E. canadensis within a genus. Other examples
include T. gondii oocysts in feline feces and their similarity to
Hammondia spp., a parasite also found in feline feces but without
the primary or zoonotic disease implications. Similarly, Neospora
caninum and Hammondia spp. are identical in appearance and both
can be present in the feces of dogs. Universal and species-specific
PCR can also help identify gross parasites that are passed in feces.
With all their advantages, molecular procedures are not without
limits or liabilities. PCR procedures require meticulously clean
laboratories, specialized equipment and extensive validation. Tests
can take one or more days to perform, depending on the procedure.
Fecal samples should be as fresh as possible and either kept
refrigerated or fixed in 70% ethanol. Although formalin-fixed
samples can be processed and examined successfully, special
procedures must be used for extracting DNA. If extraction

procedures are not performed properly, the quality of the DNA
sample and the accuracy of the result could be compromised. Also, it
is important to be aware that a negative result does not necessarily
mean that the target parasite is not present in the host nor the cause
of disease. It could simply mean that parasites were not present in
the sample that was analyzed. Sensitivity of PCR tests can be
improved by increasing the amount of sample, or by submitting
multiple samples collected at different time points.
Molecular tests can be important additions to other fecal
examination procedures. If you are considering a PCR test or have
not received specific instructions, it is best to contact the receiving
laboratory in advance. Laboratory personnel can then provide
instruction on amount of sample required, fixation, storage and
shipment.
A real-time PCR (qualitative PCR [qPCR])-based parasite panel is
commercially available from Antech Diagnostics as a screening
alternative to conventional parasite tests. The KeyScreen (TM) GI
Parasite PCR, a multiplex panel with 22 parasite-specific qPCR tests,
includes the differentiation of zoonotic from non-zoonotic Giardia
strains and the detection of benzimidazole-resistant Ancylostoma
hookworm strains. Additional parasites detected include roundworm
with species differentiation, whipworm, Cystoisospora, Eimeria,
Neospora caninum, Cryptosporidium canis and felis, tapeworms
including Taenia, Dipylidium, and Echinococcus, and the catspecific parasites Toxoplasma gondii and Tritrichomonas
blagburni.

ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IMAGING

∗

The utilization of machine learning artificial intelligence in
veterinary medicine has historically focused on assisting medical
decision-making using physical examinations and laboratory test
findings.20,21 More recently, image-based recognition technology has
been applied to in-hospital urine sediment analyzers.21,22
Additionally, use of image recognition to identify intestinal parasite
eggs, cysts, and oocysts in veterinary medicine has been reported.2326
The VETSCAN IMAGYST (Zoetis Inc., Parsippany, NJ) system

was the first commercial diagnostic platform (other companies have
developed similar products) that uses a combination of image
recognition technology and cloud-based artificial intelligence
algorithms to identify Ancylostoma spp., Toxocara spp., Trichuris
vulpis, Cystoisospora canis, C. felis, C. ohioensis, C. rivolta ,
Taeniidae (tapeworms), and Giardia spp. in dog and cat fecal
flotations.26,27 To use the system, 1 g of feces is prepared using a
sample device of 33% zinc sulfate solution (specific gravity, 1.18)
and/or sucrose solution (specific gravity, 1.28), centrifuged for 2
minutes, and transferred to a specialized coverslip that defines the
scan area to ensure that a thorough, complete scan by a specialized
microscope at optimal depths is completed for each sample tested.
The scan and cloud-based analysis are controlled from a user
software interface and/or the practice management software.
Identified parasites are highlighted by a box and viewable at slide
level with user-controlled zoom (Figure 80.5, A), or in a summary
results view (Figure 80.5, B), which can be printed out to share
with the pet owner or saved to the medical record. The system is
integrated with a “deep learning” object detection algorithm, and
with more training, the algorithm can improve its performance and
functionality (e.g., additional parasites) over time. Compared to
“shallow learning” systems, “deep learning” algorithms facilitate the
system to continuously adapt to new data and apply it to new output
classes with fewer examples.28,29

FIGURE 80.5 A, VETSCAN IMAGYST artificial
intelligence identified/boxed Toxocara spp. eggs and
Cystoisospora spp. oocyst. (Image courtesy Zoetis.)
B, Web-based report showing highlighted
identified/boxed parasites user interface.
Artificial intelligence image recognition can provide a reliable and
consistent approach to fecal examination for busy veterinary
practices, while allowing veterinary professionals to review and

confirm the identified parasite images. Since captured photographs
are stored in the cloud or medical record, questionable results or
suspicious objects can be sent for expert evaluation and second
opinion, and the parasite images can also be used for client
education, teaching, or training materials.

Chapter 81: Nasoesophageal,
Esophagostomy,

Placement Techniques
Julio López

A C RO N YM S

G gastrostomy
GI gastrointestinal

OVERVIEW
Assisted feeding via enteral feeding devices is indicated in patients
that are unable or unwilling to take in adequate calories or fluids on
their own but maintain normal digestive and absorptive functions of
their gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Typically, a candidate for tube

placement has lost greater than 10% of his/her body weight or caloric
intake has or will be disrupted for more than 3 days (e.g.,
maxillofacial surgery). Benefits of enteral nutrition include
improvement of immune function as well as decreased duration of
hospitalization, morbidity and mortality.1-4
The most common types of feeding tubes for delivery of enteral
nutrition are nasoesophageal (NE), esophagostomy (E), gastrostomy
(G or percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy [PEG]), and
jejunostomy (J). The narrow diameters of NE and J tubes limit their
use to liquid diets, whereas larger diameters of E and G tubes allows
for feeding of a wider range of properly prepared diets.
Most feeding tubes are made of red rubber, polyurethane or
silicone. These materials have tended to replace the older
polyvinylchloride feeding tubes that tend to stiffen when exposed to
digestive juices and are more irritating to patients, necessitating
frequent tube replacement.4,5 Silicone is softer and more flexible
than other tube materials, with a greater tendency to stretch and
collapse. Polyurethane is stronger than silicone, allowing them to
have thinner walls and thus a larger internal diameter despite being
the same French size as silicone tubes. The flexibility and decreased
internal diameter of silicone tubes may lead to clogging or kinking of
the tube. Both polyurethane and silicone do not rapidly disintegrate
or embrittle in situ, providing a longer “wear.”4 The French (F) unit
measures the outer lumen diameter of a tube (1 French unit is equal
to 0.33 mm). Tubes that are too flexible may be chilled before
placement to increase stiffness.4
Each feeding tube type has its own indications, benefits and
disadvantages. Deciding which type of device to use is primarily
based on the functional status of the specific GI tract segments,
nutrient requirements, patient size, and anticipated duration of
enteral support. Other factors include cost, availability, clinician’s
expertise, anesthesia concerns and capacity for home use by the pet
owner.

ENTERAL FEEDING TUBE DEVICES
NASOESOPHAGEAL TUBES

Overview, Indications and Contraindications
NE tubes are a simple option for providing in-hospital enteral
nutritional support of short-term duration (<7-10 days) in dogs and
cats with a normal nasal cavity (Figure 81.1), pharynx, esophagus
and stomach. Patients with a bleeding disorder, uncontrolled
vomiting or regurgitation, lacking a gag reflex, or with physical or
functional abnormalities along the path of the NE tube are not
candidates.
Materials and Placement Technique
Red rubber tubes or polyvinylchloride are the least expensive,
although polyvinylchloride may harden within 2 weeks and can
ulcerate the pharynx or esophagus.4 Polyurethane tubes are more
expensive but are less irritating, longer lasting and more resistant to
gastric acid if gastric placement is required (e.g., for suctioning of
gastric fluid to prevent distention in patients with
gastroparesis/ileus).4 Tube size is selected by using the largest tube
that will pass through the nares. Generally, 3F tubes are used for
puppies and kittens, 5F tubes for cats and small dogs, and 8F tubes
for dogs >15 kg. A 12-18F tube can be used for giant breed dogs.
The nasal cavity is desensitized by placing 0.5-1 mL of 0.5%
proparacaine hydrochloride or 0.25-0.5 mL of 2% (20 mg/mL)
lidocaine into each nostril while the head is tilted up to allow the
anesthetic to coat the nasal mucosa. A 2% lidocaine topical lubricant
may also be placed over the nares.1 While waiting 1-2 minutes for
this to take effect, the length the tube will be inserted should be
measured and marked with tape. Unless gastric decompression is
also required, the distance is measured from the tip of the nose to the
7th intercostal space to allow the NE tube to terminate in the distal
esophagus. This position reduces the possible risk of reflux and
esophagitis that can occur with gastric placement due to interference
with the lower esophageal sphincter.5,6 The tip of the tube is coated
with lubricating jelly (5% viscous lidocaine jelly can be used). The
patient’s head is restrained at a normal or slightly flexed angle
(Figure 81.2, A) and the tube is directed in a caudoventral-medial
direction into the nostril; occasionally, a patient may need mild
sedation. The tube should pass with minimal resistance via the

ventral meatus (ch. 213); otherwise, the tip may have gone into the
middle meatus and reached the ethmoid turbinate, or if coughing is
noted, placement into the airway has occurred. If this occurs, the
tube should be withdrawn and passage should be re-attempted while
pushing the nasal planum dorsally to open the ventral meatus.
Correct placement of the tube can be checked by various methods
including aspirating with a syringe (negative pressure created if the
tube lies in the esophagus, air easily withdrawn if in the airway),
infusing 5-10 mL of air while auscultating the cranial abdomen for
borborygmus, or by infusing 3-5 mL of sterile saline or water
through the tube and observing for a cough response (although not
all patients will cough), and end tidal CO2 monitor (tubes placed
within the esophagus should yield no CO2).1 Ideally, a lateral
thoracic radiograph should also be obtained to visually verify correct
tube placement in the distal esophagus. Once correct placement is
verified, the tube is secured at one or two additional areas of the skin
with sutures or staples on a tape tab placed on the tube (Figure
81.2, B). In cats, contact with whiskers should be avoided and may
necessitate directing the tube dorsally along the midline and securing
it between the ears and eyes (Figure 81.2, C).
An alternative placement technique has been recently described
and involves a second tube measurement from the nostril to the
thoracic inlet.1 The tube is initially advanced to this marking and
tested for negative pressure with a 12 mL syringe (thus serving as an
early safety check that the tube is within the esophagus and not the
trachea) before advancing the tube to its distal endpoint (second
marking).1
Advantages, Disadvantages and Complications
Advantages of NE tubes include minimal equipment needs as well as
quick and simple placement that does not require general anesthesia.
Patient feeding can also begin immediately via continuous pump
infusion or intermittent bolus feeding schedules. A disadvantage of
NE tubes is that their small diameter only allows the use of liquid
enteral formulas and use is limited to hospitalized patients.
Complications include epistaxis, dacrocystitis, rhinitis, vomiting, and

mispositioning in the airway causing perforation and pneumothorax
or pneumonia.1

ESOPHAGOSTOMY TUBES
Overview, Indications and Contraindications
E tubes are a great, minimally invasive choice for both short- and
medium-term enteric feeding and they give the clinician the ability to
use a variety of dietary options. Using various techniques, they are
easily placed in both cats and dogs while intubated under heavy
sedation or a short general anesthesia. They are used in patients that
are not consuming their required caloric intake due to acute or
chronic disease, as well as for patients with oral, facial, or laryngeal
disorders that prevent normal prehension and swallowing.7 Patients
with esophageal disorders such as megaesophagus, esophagitis or
esophageal stricture are not candidates.

Material and Placement Techniques
Choice of feeding tube material includes red rubber, polyurethane or
silicone catheters that are 10-20F in diameter. Tubes should be
measured and marked to ensure termination of the catheter in the
distal esophagus. Length is assessed by measuring from the site of
entry at the midcervical esophagus to the seventh intercostal space.
An additional 6-8 cm of tube will remain outside the patient and any
additional length should be trimmed distally.
Esophageal feeding tubes are placed with the patient in right
lateral recumbency while intubated and sedated or under general
anesthesia. Hair from the left lateral neck is clipped from the angle of
the mandible to the shoulder and from dorsal to ventral midlines and
the site aseptically prepped. In debilitated patients, prep can be
performed before sedation or anesthesia. It is advised to hold off the
jugular vein before making the stab incision to avoid perforation.

FIGURE 81.1 Nasoesophageal tube placement. A,
The tube is directed dorsally at the entrance of the
naris; if it is then directed medially, it should remain
in the ventral meatus, ventral to the alar fold. B, The
tube is advanced in the ventral meatus. C, The tube
is through the ventral meatus, nasopharynx, and is
advancing through the proximal esophagus. From

gastrostomy, and jejunal tube placement techniques.
In: Ettinger SJ, Feldman EC, Côté E, eds. Textbook
of Veterinary Internal Medicine. 8th ed. Elsevier;
2017:323-332.

FIGURE 81.2 Nasoesophageal tube attachment.
A, When the tube is inserted, the head is kept
horizontal, as shown, or the neck can be slightly
flexed. B, The tube is encircled with suture that is
anchored in the skin of the lateral aspect of the nose
(or tissue glue can be used instead). C, The proximal
part of the tube is fastened with tape (tape

Medicine. 8th ed. Elsevier; 2017:323-332.
There are two basic techniques that can be used based on
preference. The clinician puts on sterile gloves and the sterile paper
wrapper can be used as a sterile field on which to place the #11
scalpel blade.

Forceps (Curved Carmalt, Mixter, or Schnidt)
Technique
With the curved tips pointing up (away from the table), forceps are
advanced as far into the oral cavity as possible, through the pharynx
and into the midcervical esophagus. Once the instrument is in place,
the index finger is used to tilt the proximal end of the forceps up
(away from the table), elevating the curved tip toward the skin where
it can be palpated. With the tips of the forceps in the desired
midcervical location, a stab incision is made with a #11 scalpel blade
through the skin, while avoiding the jugular and maxillofacial veins,
to expose the subcutaneous tissue and esophageal muscle layers. The
forceps are exteriorized through the skin and the scalpel blade is
used to dissect the tissues and esophageal mucosa until the tips of
the forceps protrude through the opening. The forceps tips are
opened to grasp the distal end of the feeding tube, and the forceps
and tube are withdrawn through the oral cavity. The distal tip of the
tube that is protruding from the oral cavity is re-fed back into the
oral cavity and advanced past the pharynx into the esophagus. Slowly
retracting 2-4 cm of the tube protruding at the incision site assists in
advancing the tube from the oral cavity. The forceps can also be used
to help advance the portion of the tube in the oral cavity in an aboral
direction. The clinician will note the exteriorized portion of the tube
at the incision site rotate in a cranial direction as the tube moves
down the esophagus successfully. If further facilitation is required, a
guidewire can be used.
Correct placement of the tube is verified with radiographs,
ensuring that the distal end does not extend beyond the lower
esophageal sphincter because this would predispose the patient to
gastroesophageal reflux.5 Once correct placement is confirmed, the
tube is secured with sutures (Chinese finger-trap suture) at the
incision site. A gauze dressing with antibiotic ointment is placed over
the incision site after making a cut one third to half the width of the
gauze to allow placement. The site and tube are then loosely
bandaged or a specially made cloth cover can also be used. The
incision site should be examined daily during the first week for
evidence of infection or leakage and the stoma site can be cleaned
with topical antiseptic solution. Once the tube is no longer needed, it
can be removed in an awake patient by cutting the anchoring suture

and withdrawing the tube. The wound is allowed to heal via second
intention and sutures or staples are only needed if the skin incision is
unusually large.

Tunneler Technique
This technique requires the use of an esophagostomy feeding tube
tunneler device and a 14 or 18F long-length feeding tube (MILA
International, Erlanger, KY).8 Tube length is measured and the site
prepped as above. The distal end of the feeding tube is advanced
from mouth to the caudal esophagus where resistance should be met.
The Y adapter at the proximal (external) end of the feeding tube is
removed and a cut is made just below where the adapter terminated.
This non-stretched proximal portion of the tube is then snugly fit
onto the long end of the tunneler device. Next, the short-curved end
of the tunneler is advanced through the mouth and into the
esophagus, until it reaches the desired mid-cervical position where it
is used to tent the side of the neck to facilitate making the cervical
skin incision. Once the incision is made and the tunneler is
visualized protruding from the incision site, it can be grasped by
forceps to stabilize it and aid in slowly pulling it through the incision,
eventually revealing the tube. Continue to pull the tube until you feel
and/or see the “flip” and you reach the positioning mark made on the
tube. The external portion of the tube is then cut to the desired
length and the Y adapter replaced. Care and removal occur as
described in the forceps technique section.

Advantages, Disadvantages and Complications
An advantage of esophageal feeding tubes is the variety of dietary
options available and that feeding can begin as soon as the patient
recovers from sedation or anesthesia. The patient can be sent home
with tube in place for at-home feeding and medication
administration. Silicone catheters can last up to 1 year before
needing replacement and thus allow an option for providing much
needed calories in patients with chronic diseases. One drawback is
the need for sedation or anesthesia and thus they may not be ideal
for very debilitated or critical patients.

Aside from the risks of sedation or anesthesia, infection of the
stoma site is a common complication, especially in patients receiving
glucocorticoids or chemotherapy.2,7 One of the more serious
complications is damaging neurovasculature structures with the stab
incision (e.g., external jugular vein).2 Another complication includes
complete or partial dislodgement of the tube, or regurgitation of the
tube causing the distal end to protrude from the oral cavity.2 Most
morbidity is usually resolved by tube removal and although severe
complications are rare, when they do occur, they can lead to patient
euthanasia.7

GASTROSTOMY TUBES
Overview, Indications and Contraindications
PEG tubes are considered when NE or E tube placement is
contraindicated (esophageal dysfunction) or when longer term
(weeks to months) nutritional support is required.9 PEG tubes
should be used with caution in patients with pancreatitis, severe
ascites, adhesions and space-occupying lesions and are
contraindicated in patients with persistent vomiting, mechanical
obstruction or decreased consciousness. In patients with severe
obesity or esophageal disease, endoscopic placement should occur
with caution, with the “blind” technique being contraindicated.

Material and Placement Techniques
There is a variety of PEG tube options including latex, polyurethane,
and silicone and all with various tips including Pezzer mushroom,
balloon, bumper, or silicone dome tips (Figure 81.3). A 16-20F
sized tube is used based on patient size. Brief general anesthesia is
required and the patient is placed in right lateral recumbency to
allow placement of the tube at the greater curvature of the stomach
and left body wall. The skin caudal to the left costal arch is surgically
prepped.

Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy Technique
and Complications
The endoscope is advanced into the stomach where inflation is
initiated until the abdomen is distended but not too tightly. The tip
of the endoscope is used to transilluminate the left body wall to
ensure that the spleen is not trapped between the stomach and body
wall. Palpation of the external wall will verify appropriate location by
visualizing movement/depression of the stomach via endoscopy. A

small incision is made in the skin with a scalpel blade and a 16-18G,
1.5-2 inch long IV catheter is stabbed through the body wall into the
stomach, aimed at the light of the endoscope (Figure 81.4, A). The
stylet is removed and suture (nylon or polyester) is threaded through
the catheter into the stomach. The suture is then grasped with
endoscope biopsy forceps and together with the endoscope is
withdrawn out through the mouth (Figure 81.4, B). The suture is
then tied to the loop at the tapered end of the feeding tube. For tubes
that do not come pre-tapered with a loop for attachment, the end of
the tube must be cut into an arrow shape to allow it to fit into the
wide end of a tomcat catheter. At this same cut end, a 16-gauge
needle is passed through the walls and the suture is passed through
the tapered end of the tomcat catheter and out through the broad
end, passing it through the needle tip that is inserted through the G
tube (Figure 81.4, C). The needle is then removed and the suture is
tied securely. This arrow-shaped end of the feeding tube is fit snugly
into the broad end of the tomcat catheter. To place the PEG tube,
gentle traction is applied to the suture that is exiting the body wall to
allow the feeding tube to be pulled into the mouth, down the
esophagus, into the stomach and out via the body wall incision
(Figure 81.4, D) until the mushroom end draws the stomach wall
against the body wall. The body wall incision may need to be
widened to allow the broad end of the tomcat catheter and PEG tube
to pass. The sutured end of the PEG tube is cut and the tube is
anchored externally against the skin surface using the flange
(Figure 81.4, E). If the tube does not come with a flange, one can
easily be made by cutting the proximal flared end (opposite the
mushroom end). A 5 mm stab incision is made in the mid-body of
this segment and repeated on the opposite wall to allow the tube to
be passed through this opening with the flange resting against the
body wall to prevent migration once the tube is placed. A Chinesefinger-trap suture can also be placed to avoid accidental tube
removal. The endoscope is reinserted into the stomach to verify the
mushroom tip is positioned against the gastric mucosa without
causing blanching, which would indicate excessive tension that needs
to be reduced to avoid ischemic necrosis. Once in position, a plastic
clamp is placed over the tube and it is capped with a Y-port
connector. The tube is marked at the level of the skin with a marker
or tape to help verify position. It is held in position using a

stockinette jacket and an Elizabethan collar may be needed to
prevent tube removal by the patient (Figure 81.4, F).

FIGURE 81.5 One-step low-profile gastrostomy
device. A, One-step low-profile gastrostomy device
(flanges contained within a catheter sleeve) prior to
placement, with 4 silicone spacers. B, Same device
with flanges released after tearing the surrounding
catheter sleeve open by pulling on the attached black
suture. C, Same device once it is separated from
catheter sleeve, showing a single 5-mm silicone
spacer (arrow) inserted over the shaft, and three
other spacers of varying thicknesses. From Marks SL.
Nasoesophageal, esophagostomy, gastrostomy, and
jejunal tube placement techniques. In: Ettinger SJ,
Feldman EC, Côté E, eds. Textbook of Veterinary
Internal Medicine. 8th ed. Elsevier; 2017:323-332.
The tube must remain in place for a minimum of 2 weeks before
replacement with a low-profile tube or removal can be considered.

This allows for the formation of the gastrocutaneous fibrous tissue
tract to surround the tube between the stomach and body wall,
sealing it off from the abdominal cavity and minimizing the risk of
peritonitis when the tube is removed. If enteral nutrition is no longer
needed or the tube needs to be replaced, it is easily removed by
applying gentle traction in a caudal direction angled slightly away
from the body and pulling it through the stoma. Depending on
patient size and tube size, the tube can also be cut at the skin and the
mushroom tip (and internal flange if one was placed) should pass
from the stomach to the GI tract and out during defecation with
minimal risk of obstruction. The skin is sutured closed and the
stomach opening will close 4 to 8 hours after tube removal.
An alternative device is a one-step or “initial placement” lowprofile PEG tube which can be used in lieu of a regular PEG tube or
as a replacement tube (Figure 81.5 A, B, and C). By using the onestep, there is no need to replace the original PEG tube later with a
low-profile device.

Blind Percutaneous Gastrostomy Tube
If endoscopy is not available and surgical placement is not an option,
a blind or radiographically assisted G tube placement technique is
possible.10-12

Advantages, Complications and Disadvantages
An advantage of PEG tubes is their large diameter that provides the
clinician more dietary options using blended diets as well as allowing
at home use. Disadvantages include anesthesia and the need for
specialized equipment or surgery. One must also wait 12-24 hours
before use.
Incorrect placement of the tube can lead to acute complications
such as splenic laceration, gastric hemorrhage, or
pneumoperitoneum.9 Delayed complications can include pressure
necrosis and cellulitis at the stoma site, vomiting, tube extraction,
tube migration and stoma infection.9 To minimize the risk of gastric
pressure necrosis, overzealous PEG tube traction before placement of
the external flange should be avoided. When placing the external

flange, a 1-cm space between the flange and skin should remain and
the PEG tube should be able to be rotated. Use of the “blind”
technique increases the risk of penetrating spleen or omentum if the
stomach is not insufflated with air prior to positioning the tube
against the body wall.9 In dogs heavier than 30 kg the gastropexy
sites should be reinforced with an Entuir secure GI suture anchor set
(Cook Medical Inc., Bloomington, IN) to anchor the anterior
stomach wall to the abdominal wall and reduce risk of gastropexy
site breakdown. Despite placement of an internal flange between the
distal dome of the feeding tube and gastric mucosa, a major
complication noted in large breed dogs has been the detachment of
the silicone dome end of the G tube causing the stomach to fall off
the end of the G tube without knowledge such detachment has
occurred. To minimize this, an internal flange or T-fasteners should
be placed.

FIGURE 81.6 A, Low-profile gastrostomy devices
and obturators used for stretching the dome-shaped

If a PEG tube is removed by the patient or it malfunctions, the type
of replacement depends on the elapsed time since initial placement.

If replacement is needed within 2 weeks of placement (before the
gastrocutaneous tract is established), iodinated contrast material can
be injected via the stoma to determine if the tract is intact and
endoscopy can be used to visualize replacement of the G tube. Once
the tract is well healed, the original tube can be replaced with a lowprofile gastrostomy device (LPGD) or a balloon-type catheter simply
by removing the current tube and inserting the new tube via the
stoma (Figure 81.6 A, B, C and D). Neither anesthesia nor
endoscopy is needed for this. The length of the established
gastrocutaneous tract must be determined with a special stomameasuring device provided in the kit in order to select the
appropriate replacement tube. An advantage of the LPGD is the
decreased likelihood of inadvertent removal by the patient and better
aesthetic appearance for the owner.

JEJUNOSTOMY TUBES
Overview, Indications and Contraindications
In patients with a normally functioning distal small intestine and
where intragastric or intraduodenal feeding is not tolerated or
indicated, a jejunostomy feeding tube should be considered. They are
indicated in patients with uncontrolled gastric vomiting,
gastroparesis, severe pancreatitis, after gastric or biliary surgery and
where there are risks of gastroesophageal reflux and aspiration.3
Jejunostomy or gastrojejunostomy (PEG-J) tubes can be placed
surgically or percutaneously under fluoroscopic or endoscopic
guidance. If access to the stomach for aspiration of gastric luminal
contents will be needed, PEG-J tubes are preferred. Jejunostomy
tubes are contraindicated in patients with unresolved peritonitis,
large-volume peritoneal effusion, high risk of delayed wound healing
or dehiscence of PEG tube site, or where anesthesia is a risk.

Material and Placement Techniques
Jejunostomy tubes are available from various manufacturers in
various lengths and sizes. A 6-12 French diameter is typically used,
with a 65-cm length for cats, while in dogs tube length of at least 95
cm is recommended. The placement of a PEG-J tube can be divided

into four steps: (1) routine PEG placement; (2) passage of guidewire
into the small intestine via endoscope; (3) retraction of endoscope
leaving the guidewire in place; (4) placement of the jejunostomy
feeding tube over the guidewire.3 A PEG tube is placed under
anesthesia in right lateral recumbency with the external portion of
the tube trimmed to a length of 6 inches. A standard loop snare (or
grasping forceps) is passed into the stomach through the PEG tube
where it is opened and the endoscope is advanced through it toward
the pylorus. The patient is then placed in left lateral recumbency and
the endoscope is advanced as far down the intestine as possible. The
accessory channel of the endoscope is flushed with water to facilitate
the passage of the guidewire down the channel into the small
intestine. The endoscope is carefully retracted into the stomach
leaving the guidewire in place, and once the tip of the endoscope is
pulled past the open snare, the snare (or forceps) is closed on the
guidewire, and the endoscope is withdrawn completely. The
proximal portion of the guidewire extends outside the oral cavity.
The closed snare (or biopsy forceps) is then retracted through the
PEG tube revealing the guidewire, which is gently pulled from the
proximal end causing the guidewire to enter the mouth and advance
down the esophagus and into the stomach until it is produced
through the PEG tube, thus leaving the distal (aboral) end in the
small intestine. Fluoroscopy or radiography can be used to confirm
that the distal end of the guidewire has remained in the distal small
intestine. The jejunostomy tube is then flushed with water to activate
an internal lubricant and is threaded over the guidewire under
endoscopic guidance until the proximal end is seated in the PEG
tube. Once the tube is in place, the guidewire can be removed and
abdominal radiographs taken to conform adequate placement. The
tube should extend 40 to 60 cm distal to the pylorus to prevent
retrograde migration into the stomach. The tube is kept patent by
instilling sterile water every 2-4 hours. The jejunostomy portion of
the tube can be removed at any time, while the PEG tube must
remain in place a minimum of 2 weeks before removal. Alternative
short-term options that have been shown to be well tolerated include
placement of endoscopically or fluoroscopic assisted
esophagojejunostomy or nasojejunal feeding tubes.13-15

Advantages, Complications and Disadvantages
An advantage of PEG-J tubes is the ability to bypass diseased areas
of the proximal GI tract, while giving the flexibility of converting to
gastric feeding as the patient condition improves. Complications of
PEG-J tubes are uncommon and occur at similar frequencies to
those of PEG tubes.3 Before use, 12 hours must be allowed to pass
after placement. One disadvantage is that the tube can only be used
while in the hospital, but once the patient is recovering, the
jejunostomy tube portion can be removed and the patient can go
home with the PEG tube in place. Aside from complications affecting
the stoma, other complications can include tube occlusion, tube
migration into the stomach, transient vomiting and diarrhea.3

GENERAL COMPLICATIONS OF
ENTERAL FEEDING
TUBE OBSTRUCTION
Obstruction of the feeding tube is one of the most common
complications of enteral feeding. This usually occurs due to
formula/diet coagulation, but tablet fragments or medication
precipitation as well as tube kinking can contribute. Sucralfate and
acid suppressants have been reported to precipitate with enteral
formulas.11 Due to their small diameter, NE tubes are prone to
obstruction.
Careful rinsing of the feeding tube port with water after each use
helps avoid the drying of food contents. If blockage occurs, most are
relieved by infusion and suction of warm water under gentle
pressure. For those that do not resolve, administration of carbonated
water (Seltzer/club soda/mineral water) into the tube and allowing it
to sit for up to an hour before applying pressure can help dissolve
dried contents. Rarely, an angiographic wire needs to be passed. Use
of elixir forms of medication instead of crushed tablets is advisable
whenever possible; otherwise, tablets should be crushed and
dissolved in water before administration.

LEAKAGE THROUGH OSTOMY SITE
For the first few days following feeding tube placement mild leakage
from the stoma site can occur. Persistent leakage should be
investigated as it may indicate a tube that is too small for the stoma
site, a tube dysfunction, or infection. Signs of inflammation may
indicate an infection which does not always present with discharge or
fever. Topical treatment of simple infections includes cleaning with
dilute povidone-iodine solution and more frequent dressing changes.
Patients with systemic signs of infection should be treated with
antibiotics.

Chapter 82: Otoscopy, Ear

David Stephen Sobel

A C RO N YM
IV intravenous

When one considers the most common presentations by small
animal patients to first opinion general practitioner vets, aural
disease is amongst the top of the list. Clinical signs related to aural
disease are generally quite easy for owners to observe, are frequently
dramatic in their presentation, often are associated with significant
impact on a patient’s quality of life, and can become chronic, causing
long-term illness. Fortunately, aural disease is usually quite readily
diagnosed and, with appropriate and timely intervention, one of the
more rewarding groups of disease to treat in small animal practice.14

Otoendoscopy has tremendous utility in both the general small
animal practice as well as the referral setting. The techniques, both
diagnostic and therapeutic, are simple to learn and perfect, and
present the sort of utility that makes the time and financial
investment in the procedures and equipment tremendously
worthwhile.5

While small animal practitioners have been well accustomed to
using hand-held otoscopes as a diagnostic tool for many decades, the
advent of modern endoscopic equipment and techniques has enabled
the veterinarian to enjoy dramatically improved visualization of
aural anatomy. Additionally, the modality offers the opportunity to
document, monitor and categorize a patient’s disease and the
progress made in management. Perhaps most importantly, the
ability to intervene therapeutically is markedly enhanced with
minimally invasive surgical (MIS) techniques. This chapter will
outline the indications, equipment utilization, and techniques of
otoendoscopy for the small animal practitioner.

INDICATIONS
Otoendoscopy is of great utility in differentiating between diseases of
the outer or external ear (e.g., otitis externa) and its adnexa, and
diseases of the tympanum and middle ear (e.g., otitis media).
Common clinical signs of aural disease include foul aural odor, head
shaking, aural discharge, pain on palpation of the pinna and external
aural structures, pawing at the head and hearing loss. Somewhat less
commonly, owners may observe anorexia or dysphagia, ataxia and
balance problems, and the presence of abnormal resting nystagmus.
Careful and complete neurological (ch. 241) and physical (ch. 3)
exams can reveal peripheral neurological signs and cranial nerve
anomalies.

ADDITIONAL DIAGNOSTIC
MODALITIES
While a full treatment of all of the available modalities to diagnose
and manage aural diseases is beyond the scope of this chapter, it
suffices to say that radiography/fluoroscopy, computed tomography
and magnetic resonance imaging (ch. 112) can also be important in
the diagnostic workup for these patients.

EQUIPMENT

Generally speaking, the equipment includes a video monitor, a
medical grade endoscopic video camera, a rigid otoendoscope, a light
source, and appropriate accessories for the requisite diagnostic
procedures and therapeutic interventions to be performed (Figures
82.1 and 82.2).
Optionally, the kit can include some form of mechanized
irrigation/suction apparatus, devices to record or photograph the
procedure and store the images, and some form of energy for
surgical use (electrosurgery, radiosurgery, laser)6,7 (Figures 82.3
and 82.4).

CLINICAL ANATOMY
A review of the relevant clinical anatomy will prove helpful in
facilitating an efficient and productive otoendoscopic intervention.
The external ear can be delineated by the external pinna, through to
and including the vertical canal. This includes the pinna, the
cartilaginous support structures of the adnexa, and the vertical canal
to the horizontal canal. The beginning of the vertical canal is
generally identified by the intertragic notch, separating the cranial
and caudal cartilaginous ridges. The intertragic notch is a helpful
anatomic landmark for the endoscopist in mapping out the presence
of lesions in the vertical canal. A ridge of firm, minimally compliant
cartilage can serve as a landmark between the vertical and horizontal
canal.
The tympanum is a thin, glistening membrane at the terminus of
the horizontal canal. In the normal ear, its pars flaccida is visualized
dorsally and in most dogs will account for approximately one-third of
the visible field. The pars tensalis occupies the ventral two-thirds of
the visible tympanum. In patients with a normal, lucent tympanum,
a ventral bony ridge separating the tympanic cavity from the bulla
can be seen. Caudodorsally, the manubrium of the malleus in the
middle ear can often be seen through the tympanum. Frequently
when the tympanum is diseased, its opacity limits visualization of
these landmarks. Severe middle ear disease can produce marked
bulging of the tympanum, notably of the pars flaccidum, and
demonstrative of fluid in the middle ear. Should increased pressure
compromise the integrity of the tympanum, it is most commonly the

pars tensalis that is the first portion breached. However, in patients
with tympanic rupture due to underlying middle ear disease, it is
often difficult to differentiate the individual portions of the
tympanum. When the tympanum is ruptured, either due to middle
ear disease or therapeutically, careful cleaning and suction/irrigation
can allow the middle ear structures to be visualized.

OTOENDOSCOPIC EXAM
Following a complete history, physical examination, and
preoperative diagnostic workup, the otoendoscopic exam can
proceed. If the operator suspects or intends to gather samples for
bacterial culture and sensitivity, antibiotic therapy, whether systemic
or topical, should be discontinued at least 1 week prior to the

procedure. If any otoendoscopic intervention is anticipated, general
anesthesia is advised.
Otoendoscopy is best performed on a “wet table” or surgical sink to
minimize the patient’s head lying in the runoff from irrigated fluids
and for easier postoperative clean-up. The patient is placed in lateral
recumbency with the ear of interest on the nondependent side. Some
practitioners perform this procedure with the patient in sternal
recumbency, but in the opinion of this author, lateral recumbency
allows for more complete, easier, and direct examination of the
horizontal canal and tympanum with less traction placed on the
pinna. The endoscopic equipment cart is placed on the side of the
table facing the ventral aspect of the patient. The operator stands on
the dorsal-facing side, near the patient’s shoulder. The monitor is
placed cranial to the patient’s head, facing the operator at ∼30° angle.
This allows the operator to hold the endoscope in a neutral position
relative to the head, and to observe the monitor with structures
displayed in an anatomically correct orientation.
For irrigation, an intravenous (IV) fluid bag and standard IV
administration set are connected to the ingress port of the
endoscope. Gravity flow is usually adequate for keeping the ear canal
patent and free of debris to allow adequate visualization. An
irrigation/aspiration pump can also be employed (see below).
Appropriate irrigants include normal saline, lactated Ringer’s
solution, Normosol, and Plasmalyte.8,9 Irrigants should be at room
temperature or slightly warmer to minimize postoperative caloric
nystagmus or head tilt.
For an otoendoscopic exam on the anesthetized patient, the
procedure begins with a visual exam of the external and visible
portions of the pinna and proximal auditory meatus. If there is
substantial ceruminous otic debris obscuring visualization, a
standard ear cleaning is advised prior to attempting otoendoscopy.
Otoendoscopy attempted on an ear with extensive exudate will prove
frustrating and increase the operative time.

FIGURE 82.5 Otoendoscopy is performed in a
canine patient using a rigid otoendoscope and a
mechanical irrigation and aspiration device. The
flushing procedure is done via the instrument
channel of the endoscope using a tomcat urinary
catheter to accurately direct irrigation and
aspiration.
With the endoscope and associated instrumentation assembled
(endoscope, camera, light guide cable, irrigation fluid, and associated
accessories), the operator holds the endoscope in the dominant
hand. With the nondominant hand, the pinna is grasped and gently
drawn laterally and very slightly caudodorsally (Figure 82.5). This
maneuver opens up the lumen of the vertical canal, facilitating
visualization and insertion of the endoscope. The endoscope is

introduced into the vertical canal at an angle of ∼90° to the patient’s
skull. The flow of irrigant is begun, with minimal pressure, to allow
the gentle dislodging and flushing of any adherent ceruminous
material. Care should be taken to ensure that fluid egress is
approximately equal to ingress; otherwise, excessive pressure in the
aural canal can lead to iatrogenic damage to the tympanum and
middle ear structures. Depending on the particulars of the
equipment setup, air insufflation can be used for cleaning the
endoscope lens and removing blood, cerumen and other material
from the field of view. The bottom of the vertical canal is visualized,
and the horizontal canal can be examined with visualization of the
tympanum in the far field. Care must be taken to avoid excessive
torsion or bending of the shaft of the endoscope as the horizontal
canal is entered. It is deceptively easy to damage small diameter
endoscopes in this manner. Additionally, care must be taken during
insertion of the scope into the horizontal canal to avoid iatrogenic
damage to the canal wall, the tympanum, and the middle ear.6,10-12
Gentle traction, as noted previously, will help flatten the angle
between the vertical and horizontal canals, making approaching the
tympanum easier.
If bacterial cultures are to be taken, instrumentation must be
prepared in strict aseptic manner to minimize contamination.
Culture of aural exudate should be taken as early as possible in the
examination procedure to minimize the risk of contamination from
superficial flora being flushed into the ear canal. Samples for culture
and for cytologic evaluation can be retrieved via flush, directly with a
culture swab, or by sampling the material with a grasping forceps.13
If a biopsy is to be taken, a complete aural examination should be
completed first. Hemorrhage from a punch or excisional biopsy will
make subsequent examination and visualization more difficult.

DEEP EAR CLEANING/AURAL
FLUSHING
A deep cleaning is indicated if there is marked aural discharge that
clinically suggests disease of either the horizontal canal or middle

ear. Essentially, a deep ear cleaning is a continuation of the irrigation
performed with a standard otoscopic examination.
Lavage catheters can be purchased for the purpose of ear flushing,
or a polypropylene tomcat catheter can be employed, cut to a
manageable length. These catheters can be introduced via the
instrument channel of the otoendoscope to afford the operator
excellent visualization of the endoscopic field and the progress of the
lavage.
Lavage solutions should be the same as those used for the standard
otoendoscopic exam. Ceruminolytic or astringent solutions should
never be used when detritus in the ear canal prevents the operator
from ensuring the tympanum is intact.

EXCISION OF AURAL MASSES
The used of lasers of various types, wavelengths and power has
enabled the endoscopist to offer not only a diagnostic study, but in
many cases, a therapeutic one as well (Figure 82.4;

Video

82.1). Laser fibers in various diameters can be used via the
instrument channels of otoendoscopes to ablate, debulk, vaporize, or
resect various types of aural masses. This author favors the use of an
810-980 nm wavelength diode at power settings of 4-8 W. Each laser
will have unique properties necessitating establishment of effective
and safe protocols for each device. “Blended” or multi-wavelength
diodes, new to the veterinary surgical market, allow the operator to
customize the laser settings to achieve specific benefits of each
wavelength. This wavelength of laser light provides excellent tissue
vaporization and cutting in a fluid medium, and is very effective in
the presence of blood, which provides excellent hemostasis and thus
maintains a visible surgical field. While it is unlikely that laser
excision or vaporization provides clean surgical margins in the face
of aggressive neoplastic lesions, the device has great utility in
removing a variety of common benign and neoplastic diseases of the
ear canal (Figure 82.6, A and B).7,14
Electrocautery and associated bipolar or monopolar snares can
also be used to resect polyps and masses in many situations. The
limiting factor can be identifying a pedicle and looping and

advancing the snare deep enough to encircle the stalk. Electrocautery
does have a greater risk of collateral thermal injury although the
walls of the vertical and horizontal canals are relatively forgiving in
this respect.

MYRINGOTOMY
Historically, veterinarians have been reticent to perform
myringotomies. Indeed, iatrogenic myringotomy, when performed
during an otoendoscopic exam, has often been treated as a
substantial surgical complication. Recent studies have demonstrated
the previously underreported pervalence of otitis media in dogs (in
particular) and the utility of myringotomy in the management of
these diseases.15,16
Myringotomy is a simple and safe procedure that can be
performed during the process of a standard otoendoscopic exam (
Videos 82.2, 82.3, and 82.4). Myringotomy should be
considered in any patient with visible endoscopic evidence of
significant disease of the tympanum and/or middle ear. This can be
visualized as decreased opacity of the tympanum and the inability to
identify the normal anatomic structures and integrity of the
tympanum. Bulging of the tympanum into the horizontal canal
suggests clinically significant fluid accumulation in the middle ear
that can benefit from drainage.

FIGURE 82.6 A, Postoperative otoendoscopic
view of the middle ear of a canine patient following
laser endoscopic resection of an aural mass arising
from the middle ear and extending into the tympanic
bulla. A large portion of the tympanum was incised
to allow for adequate exposure of the lesion, with
evident damage to the ossicles. This lesion was
determined histopathologically to be benign,
demonstrating the dramatic middle ear damage that
can result from even benign disease. B,
Otoendoscopic view of an aural mass in a canine
patient. The mass was determined to be arising from
the ventral floor of the horizontal ear canal, adherent
to the pars tensalis of the tympanum. Removal
necessitated a small myringotomy along the ventral
edge of the pars tensalis. The mass was determined
via histopathology to be a benign lymphoplasmacytic
polyp.
Myringotomy can be performed via a simple perforation using a
tomcat catheter with the end cut to a sharp bevel or with a purposedesigned myringotomy knife. One of the great frustrations to the
practitioner performing a myringotomy is the rapidity with which the
tympanum can heal. Myringotomies can begin to heal within 72
hours, leading to chronic otitis media and further chronic injury to
the tympanum, whereas patency should last for at least 7-14 days to
allow for adequate drainage of the middle ear and effective
management of otitis media. Diode lasers are an effective tool for
performing myringotomy, with the added benefit of delayed tissue

healing, as with any form of thermal energy used in surgery. In the
case of otitis media, the delayed healing of the tympanum and the
resulting longer term of patency of the site of puncture allows for a
longer period of drainage of the middle ear and more complete
treatment.
The diode laser is set to very low power, a slender 400- to 600micron fiber is used, and the pars flaccidum of the tympanum is
identified. With empyema behind the tympanum, the most common
region of bulging is the slightly more redundant pars flaccidum. The
tympanum is cut in a cruciate fashion, centered in the pars
flaccidum. The pars tensalis is to be avoided if possible given its
anatomic proximity to the manubrium of the malleus. However,
chronic disease of the tympanum can make clear identification of
regions of the tympanum difficult. When the tympanum is incised, it
is common to see a rush of dark or purulent fluid enter the horizontal
canal from the middle ear (

Video 82.4), which should be

collected directly for bacterial culture and sensitivity and cytologic
examination.

CERUMINOLITHS
Ceruminoliths are concretions that result from impaction and
consolidation of cerumen, hair and other aural discharges. Manual
removal with endoscopic forceps is the method of choice when
simple irrigation does not remove them. Holmium:YAG laser, with a
wavelength of approximately 2100 nm, has been used by this author
to fragment ceruminoliths to facilitate their removal.

COMPLICATIONS OF OTOENDOSCOPY
With a modest degree of experience, otoendoscopy is an extremely
safe procedure associated with minimal surgical morbidity and rare
surgical mortality. Poor technique can result in trauma to the ear
canal. If otitis media is not adequately treated post-myringotomy,
chronically delayed healing can occur. Intensive topical and systemic
antibiotic therapy is important for adequate and timely resolution of
otitis media and healing of the tympanum. Rarely, patients will

experience a transient caloric or pressure-induced head tilt or, even
more rarely nystagmus, Horner’s syndrome, or facial nerve
paresis/paralysis. These complications, when noted, are usually mild
and self-limiting. Rarely, permanent neurological damage can occur.

SKIN SCRAPINGS
Skin scrapings aim to diagnose cutaneous ectoparasites. Superficial
and deep scrapings identify different parasites and differ
substantially in their procedural approach.

SUPERFICIAL SKIN SCRAPINGS
Indication
Superficial skin scrapings detect mites living on the skin surface or
burrowing within the stratum corneum such as Cheyletiella spp.,
Otodectes cynotis, Sarcoptes spp., and (in cats) Demodex gatoi and

Notoedres cati. Both Cheyletiella and Sarcoptes mites can be
difficult to find.1-3 Cats with Notoedres cati typically have abundant
mites. In the dog with suspected scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei), the
elbows, ear margins, lateral hocks, and ventrum are preferred
anatomic sites.3 In cats, Notoedres cati affects the head. In both dogs
and cats, Cheyletiella mites inhabit the dorsal trunk and typically
cause scaling.3 Otodectes cynotis is most frequently associated with
otitis externa but may produce head and neck pruritus and, rarely,
generalized dermatitis. Superficial skin scrapings should be
performed in any scaly or pruritic dog or cat.4 A ventral alopecia
pattern is seen with the superficially located, contagious and short
bodied Demodex (D.) gatoi.5

Procedure
Mineral oil is applied to the affected skin in a thin film to facilitate
the gathering of scale and surface debris and increase the chance of
positive results.1 Non-excoriated scaly and/or papular sites are
selected and a #10 or #20 scalpel blade is used to sample the surface
of a large area (at least 5 × 5 cm). In hairy dogs, the hair should be
clipped from the target area first—use the clippers only in the
direction of hair growth and leave 1-2 mm of hair, i.e., not a surgical
clip—to retain any surface scale or crust. The oil is gently scraped off
the surface, as if “buttering bread” (E-Figure 83.1) in the direction of
hair growth and transferred onto a slide. This “large oil volume”
technique provides multiple slides for examination, increasing the
chance of success (

Video 83.1). To diagnose cheyletiellosis, fecal

flotations, tape preparations and flea combing are alternatives to
superficial skin scraping (E-Table 83.1).6
