Microscopic Technique
A coverslip is applied to distribute the debris evenly—mites may be
missed if covered by debris—and to speed microscopic evaluation by

reducing need for continuous adjustment of focus. Scanning (4×
objective, 10× ocular) power is used and the condenser is lowered to
increase contrast. Skin scrapings for ectoparasites should be
examined within a few hours of collection, because mites can actually
walk off a slide if left too long.

Interpretation
One mite or egg is diagnostic and should be considered reason to
initiate miticidal therapy. A negative scraping does not rule out
presence of mites and “diagnosis via response to therapy” may still
be indicated.18, 19

DEEP SKIN SCRAPINGS
Indication
Deep skin scrapings are performed to detect Demodex mites.6 In the
dog, D. canis lives in hair follicles, and a longer-bodied mite (D.
injai) is suspected to live in the sebaceous gland ducts.7-9 Canine
demodicosis is characterized clinically by alopecia, comedones,
papules, follicular pustules, scales, and crusts and must be
considered in almost any dog with such lesions. Feline demodicosis
is rare, is caused by the long bodied D. cati, and typically occurs in
cats with systemic disease.10-12

Procedure
Ideally, follicular papules or pustules over an area of at least 1 × 1 cm
should be sampled. Mite counts are higher when the skin is squeezed
prior to and during scraping because the mites can be squeezed from
deep follicles.13 Using a mineral-oil-covered #10 or #20 blade, skin
is scraped in the direction of hair growth until capillary bleeding is
observed (Video 83.2

). Trichograms (hair plucks, placed in

mineral oil on a glass slide for examination) are a useful method for

sampling periocular or pedal lesions.13,14 Squeeze tape preparations
and superglue are alternatives (E-Table 83.1).15,16

Interpretation
D. canis is a normal component of the cutaneous fauna and an
occasional mite can be found on the skin scraping of normal dogs. If
only one mite is found, but clinical signs are compatible, further
scrapings, trichograms, or a biopsy are indicated.10 It is important to
note in the clinical record the site of scraping and the relative
numbers of adults, larvae, nymphs, and eggs per low power field.
Assessment of response to therapy is based on comparison of these
numbers at subsequent monthly visits.

FIGURE 83.1 Draw a line on the skin prior to
performing the biopsy in the direction of hair growth
to help orient the laboratory technician. On the trunk
this runs approximately from nose to tail. This
technique has revolutionized the interpretation of
follicular pathology. Do not draw over fragile lesions
like pustules, which may rupture with pressure.

FINE-NEEDLE ASPIRATION (FNA)
INDICATION
Fine-needle aspiration is frequently performed on nodules in the
skin or subcutis as the “first step” when attempting to differentiate
neoplasia from inflammation or infection.

PROCEDURE

The nodule should be firmly fixed between thumb and forefinger; a
20- or 22-gauge needle is then gently inserted into the nodule and
redirected several times without completely withdrawing it from the
nodule. Control of the needle tip should be sufficient to prevent
going through a lesion or missing it entirely, even in lively dogs. A
needle penetrating through a nodule into normal underlying tissue
could transfer neoplastic cells. Upon withdrawal, the cells within the
lumen of the needle are expelled by attaching an air-filled 5 mL
syringe and using it to blow the contents onto a glass slide. If no cells
are obtained using this technique, a “suction method” may be used.
The needle is first attached to a 10 mL syringe before being inserted
into the nodule and aspirated multiple times. Suction should be
interrupted when the needle is redirected and particularly when
being withdrawn, to avoid sucking cells into the syringe where they
may not be retrievable. The needle is then separated from the
syringe, plunger drawn back, needle reattached, the contents
expelled onto a glass slide, spread as with blood smears, dried,
stained with a modified Wright’s stain (Diff-Quik), and examined (
Video 83.3).

INTERPRETATION
If a uniform cell population is identified, then a neoplastic cause is
likely (ch. 323). Characteristics of neoplastic cell populations are
described elsewhere (ch. 88). Histopathology is the gold standard
test to define tumor grade and enable a prognosis and further
treatment decisions. If inflammatory cells such as neutrophils and
macrophages dominate, then infection is possible. The next
diagnostic step is deep tissue bacterial and/or fungal culture (ch.
184). Culture of hair shafts is done if a dermatophyte kerion is
suspected, differentiating sterile inflammation from an infectious
cause.

GETTING THE MOST FROM A SKIN
BIOPSY (E-Box 83.1)

Site selection and biopsy methodology can make the difference
between success and failure in obtaining a specific diagnosis.4,16
Even “inconclusive results” can rule out some differential diagnoses.

SITE SELECTION
A careful examination of the entire animal for the most
representative range of lesions is the first step in biopsy site
selection. In many pustular diseases, erythematous macules develop
into papules, then pustules and finally crusts/erosions. Sampling
each of these stages supplies the widest range of lesions, but
wherever possible, multiple pustules should be sampled.
Depigmenting lesions should be biopsied in an active area (i.e., gray
color) rather than the final stage (i.e., white).
Alopecic areas should be sampled in the center of the most
alopecic area as well as in junctional and adjacent normal areas. On
submission, differentiating these biopsies can be achieved by placing
samples in separate, carefully labeled, bottles of formalin, or through
the use of tissue dyes by marking different lesion types with a
different color (E-Figure 83.2). When assessing alopecia, where
possible, avoid the glabrous (non-haired) areas of the body as they
contain fewer hair follicle units and smaller sebaceous glands. A line
drawn prior to biopsy on the skin in the direction of the hair growth,
using a waterproof pen, indicates the direction the lab technician
should cut in order to section the follicles longitudinally (Figure
83.1).17

E-FIGURE 83.2 Dye can be used to identify
specific skin biopsies. It is spread thinly on the
panniculus surface and must dry before the tissue is
placed in the formalin (allow 1-2 minutes).
In dogs and cats with severe inflammatory disease, clues with
regard to the follicular growth characteristics may be present only in
adjacent normal skin. Ulcerated areas should be avoided, unless
deep dermal or panniculus lesions are suspected. When sampling an
ulcerated lesion, use an elliptical incision either to completely excise
the ulcer with adjacent normal skin or oriented from the center of
the lesion to include adjacent “normal or intact” skin.

SURGICAL TECHNIQUE
Overlying hair should be clipped only in the direction of hair growth
and gently removed to preserve any scale and crusts. Crusts should
be left on the skin and included in the biopsy as they may contain
microorganisms or inflammatory or acantholytic cells that may help

establish a diagnosis. Write “please cut in crusts” on the submission
form. No aseptic preparation is performed, except when excising
solitary nodules. Infection resulting from a lack of surgical
preparation is almost never seen. General anesthesia is indicated for
facial or paw biopsies and may also be necessary for larger excisional
biopsies. Local anesthesia, with or without sedation, is a practical
alternative for many pets with truncal biopsies. Subcutaneous (SQ)
injection of 1 or 2 mL of lidocaine without adrenaline (epinephrine)
usually provides adequate local anesthesia. The maximum amount of
lidocaine used depends on body weight. The selected site is marked
to enable easy localization and the needle entry point should be
outside the marked area to avoid tissue disruption within the
biopsy.17

WEDGE/ELLIPSE VERSUS PUNCH
BIOPSY
The punch biopsy is quick, relatively atraumatic, and often
recommended when infectious, inflammatory, and endocrine
dermatoses are suspected. Use of new disposable 8-mm punches is
preferred. Smaller punches are reserved for biopsies of paw pads,
nasal planum, mucocutaneous junctions, or eyelids.

FIGURE 83.2 A, Rule of thumb—include 100%
lesional or non-lesional skin when sampling with a
punch biopsy. B, The histopathology technician
should section the elliptical biopsy specimen along
the midline of the long axis of the ellipse. Orientation
of the ellipse across the junction between abnormal
and normal tissues will allow the pathologist to view
the skin from affected, through active, to nonaffected
areas and so gain the best possible appreciation of
the stages of the disease and hence the etiology.

Punch Biopsy Sampling
Hold the punch at a 90° angle to the surface of the skin, firmly brace
the surrounding skin, and rotate the punch in one direction with
continuous but relatively little pressure. When the skin no longer
“turns” with the punch rotation, sufficient depth has been reached to
free the dermis from its underlying attachment. Grasp the tissue
gently at the base and sever it from the SQ tissue. Under no
circumstance should the dermis or epidermis be squeezed as this
leads to “crush artefact” and may result in an unreadable sample.
The use of ophthalmic instruments such as iris scissors and forceps
is recommended.

Excisional/Incisional Sampling
The wedge or elliptical biopsy should be employed as an excisional
technique when a deep dermal or panniculus lesion is suspected.
This method should also be used when removing a solitary nodule or
fragile lesion (such as vesicles) or when a range of changes radiating

from the center to the edge of a lesion are present, e.g., central
ulceration or alopecia and adjacent normal tissue can be included in
the ellipse (Figure 83.2, A and B).
With a suspected neoplasm, an incisional biopsy may be indicated.
This allows an accurate diagnosis without concern of contaminating
surrounding tissue or compromising any subsequent surgical
intervention. Incisional biopsies cannot evaluate margins. Cytologic
evaluations may diagnose malignancy without the need for a biopsy,
but they cannot replace the prognostic information obtained from
histopathologic evaluation of biopsy samples. Once the biopsy has
been obtained, the wound is closed routinely.

Fixation of Tissue
The biopsy sample surface should be gently blotted prior to placing it
in formalin. A minimum volume of formalin, approximately 10 times
the sample volume, is needed for adequate fixation. In cold climates,
the addition of 1 part alcohol to 9 parts formalin will prevent freezing
during shipping. Large tissue pieces should be partially sectioned
with 1-cm slices through the epidermal surface, leaving the sections
attached at the base (adipose tissue) to allow adequate formalin
penetration without sectioning through the mass completely. This
retains the deep architecture intact for margin assessment.

SHAVE BIOPSIES
On the pinnae, cartilage is found directly under a thin dermis and the
panniculus is absent. With punch and wedge techniques, cartilage
may inadvertently be damaged and a permanent change in the shape
of the pinna may result. The shave technique, with the pet under
general anesthesia, is only useful for diseases of the epidermis and
upper dermis such as pemphigus or lupus. This is because with
proper technique, the depth of the specimen will not reach below the
mid-follicular level (E-Figure 83.3) and deep dermal changes such as
vasculitis and disease of the cartilage cannot be evaluated.20 The
outside of the ear requires clipping; the concave/inner pinna may
not. The pinna is bent over the index finger of one hand (E-Figure
83.4). On the stretched and bent convex surface, the scalpel blade

enters the skin at an angle of approximately 20°, only to a depth
where capillary bleeding is observed. At that depth, the incision is
continued parallel to the surface of the skin until a specimen,
approximately 5 × 5 mm (0.25 × 0.25 inches), is obtained. This
sliced-out specimen is an extremely thin piece of skin that should be
placed with the dermal surface down on a piece of a tongue
depressor or cardboard to avoid distortion during fixation (E-Figure
83.5). Three minutes of firm digital pressure applied to the biopsy
site, or use of a silver nitrate stick, typically stops hemorrhage and
suturing is neither necessary nor possible. There is typically no
scarring.

E-FIGURE 83.3 Histopathologic appearance of a
shave biopsy will reveal changes of the epidermis
and upper dermis, as the depth of the specimen with
proper technique will only reach the mid-follicular
level.

E-FIGURE 83.4 Shave biopsy: the pinna is bent
over the index finger of one hand and a scalpel or
razor blade is used to obtain the biopsy specimen.

E-FIGURE 83.5 The very thin shave biopsy
specimen is placed with the dermal surface down on
a piece of a tongue depressor or cardboard—allow 1
minute for adhesion and place the tissue side in
contact with the formalin.

INTERPRETATION—MAKING A
DIAGNOSIS
One of the major indications for a skin biopsy is to obtain a
diagnosis. The second aim, even in the absence of a confirmed
diagnosis, is to rule out differential diagnoses. In order for the

pathologist to look for subtle clues and to interpret unusual changes,
a list of clinical lesions and differential diagnoses must be included
with the submission. Choose a pathologist with an active interest in
dermatopathology or a dermatologist with advanced
dermatopathology training.

Chapter 84: Bone Marrow
Aspiration and Biopsy
Valerie MacDonald-Dickinson

A C RO N YM S
CBC complete blood count
EDTA ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid
IO intraosseous
MER myeloid-to-erythroid ratio

OVERVIEW
Abnormal complete blood count (CBC) results that are not
attributable to a known or readily identifiable process are typically
the primary indication for bone marrow evaluation. Unexplained
abnormalities such as non-regenerative anemia (ch. 172),
neutropenia (ch. 176), thrombocytopenia (ch. 175), or alternatively
a finding such as severe leukocytosis (ch. 58) should prompt bone
marrow evaluation. The presence of immature blast cells or atypical
mature cells on a blood smear are additional flags warranting
marrow investigation (ch. 322). Organisms that may cause systemic
infections such as Leishmania (ch. 197), Cytauxzoon (ch. 197), and
Histoplasma (ch. 209) species are sometimes more readily found
with marrow sample evaluation compared to other tissue sites. On

occasion, searching for occult neoplasia may warrant marrow
sampling when pursuing certain initial abnormal findings on
physical examination, radiographs, or serum biochemistry, such as
hypercalcemia, for example. Some forms of cancer are routinely
diagnosed through bone marrow evaluation such as lymphoma,
leukemia, multiple myeloma, and histiocytic sarcoma and these
procedures are also valuable for follow-up of patients undergoing
treatment (ch. 322). With increasing availability of newer
diagnostics such as flow cytometry and polymerase chain reaction
(PCR) for antigen receptor gene rearrangement (PARR) for the
diagnosis and staging of lymphoma or leukemia, clinicians are more
often using these techniques in lieu of traditional bone marrow
evaluation. Iron stores also can be subjectively evaluated by way of
bone marrow aspiration or biopsy, except in the cat, as feline iron
stores typically stain very subtly with routine or special stains.1
Unconventional, yet emerging, indications for bone marrow
collection include isolation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells
(MSC) for the purpose of stem cell therapy in regenerative medicine.
Historically, while stem cells mainly were used experimentally for
orthopedic diseases, the focus is now expanding to other areas,
including therapy for hepatic, renal, and cardiac diseases.2 Aside
from strict marrow collection, the skill of intraosseous (IO) catheter
placement may become more common in general and emergency
practice for diagnostic purposes (ch. 76).3
There are very few contraindications to bone marrow aspiration,
as the risk of bleeding from this procedure is very low.
Thrombocytopenia is not a contraindication and in fact, bone
marrow aspiration is often used to find its underlying cause.
However, a severe coagulopathy involving deficiency or impairment
of coagulation factors is a concern and marrow aspiration should be
delayed until it is controlled. The risk of causing a bone fracture is
low but it may occur if an inappropriately sized needle is used for a
patient or if the bone is already compromised by disease.
Making the decision of whether to do an aspiration versus a
biopsy, or both, may depend upon the clinician’s differential list and
what exactly is being searched for. Many times, aspiration and core
biopsy complement each other, and both may be required for a more
comprehensive picture of the marrow. Individual cell morphology is

best evaluated with cytopathologic examination of marrow aspirate
smears that may highlight few or very small organisms or subtle cell
features that may aid in identification of cell lineages. Bone marrow
core biopsies give information on the architecture of the marrow,
overall cellularity, and the presence of myelofibrosis, necrosis, and
mass lesions within the marrow space.4 Clinicians who obtain
marrow samples and pathologists should be aware that with respect
to the myeloid to erythroid ratio (MER), which is an integral
component to assessing a marrow’s regenerative response,
discordance may be found between histologic and cytologic results.
Likewise, the site of marrow collection has been found to potentially
influence the MER findings in dogs, with MERs from ilial crest
samples being slightly but significantly greater than samples from
the humeri.5

MATERIALS AND EQUIPMENT
To obtain high quality samples, it is important to select appropriate
equipment. The size of the needle should be appropriate to the
patient and the site being aspirated. A Rosenthal needle and the
Illinois sternal/iliac needle are available for a bone marrow aspirate
while the Jamshidi biopsy needle is generally reserved for bone
marrow biopsies, although aspirates can also be obtained with this
instrument (Figure 84.1). This author has used the Illinois needle
for biopsies as well as aspirates, especially in cats and small dogs.
The 15-ga Illinois sternal/iliac needle is most commonly used for
dogs and the 18-ga needle is available for cats and small dogs. A 1inch (2.5 cm) needle can be sufficient for many animals, but a 1.5inch needle (4 cm) is required for large-breed dogs. Jamshidi biopsy
needles are available in 13-ga and the larger 8-ga size, with the latter
being reserved for larger dogs. All needles must be sterile, and all
consist of two pieces—the hollow stainless steel needle and a solid
stylet. The Illinois sternal/iliac needle has a removable plastic cap

and needle guard. It can be re-sterilized for additional use, but the
tip usually becomes dull quickly so one-time use is recommended.
The Jamshidi needle does not have a needle guard and can also be
re-sterilized, but it too might quickly become dull, making future use
more difficult and potentially painful for the patient.6
Several commercially available battery-powered drills have been
used for bone marrow aspiration and biopsy in humans, cats, and
dogs and for IO catheter placement.3,7-9 See ch. 76 for additional
information on this technique.
Because aspiration and biopsy are painful procedures, general
anesthesia or heavy sedation with analgesia is recommended. The
site should be shaved and aseptically prepared, and a local anesthetic
block performed, starting with the periosteum, then the
subcutaneous tissues and finally the skin, using 1 to 2% lidocaine.
Provided it is not contraindicated, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory
drug or gabapentin should be provided for the patient after the
procedure is completed.
Surgical gloves should be worn and all instruments and supplies
kept within a sterile field. A small surgical drape can be used to help
maintain a sterile field. After local anesthesia is performed, a small
stab incision is made in the skin with a #11 scalpel blade. Other
equipment for an aspirate includes microscope slides, 12-mL syringe,
sterile anticoagulant (4% disodium- or dipotassium–
ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid [EDTA]), Petri dish or weigh boat,
and forceps or pipette. For a core biopsy, a jar of formalin will be
needed instead of slides, syringe, anticoagulant, and Petri dish or
weigh boat. An assistant should be available to help, and the slides
should be laid out at an angle before starting the procedure.

PREPARATION AND SITE SELECTION
Before starting the procedure, it is important to ensure that the stylet
is properly aligned within the needle and, if the needle guard is being
used, that all attachments are snug but not overtightened. A secure
grip of the needle should be maintained by holding it in a modified
pencil grip against the palm of the hand (Videos 84.1, 84.2

). The

needle guard on the Illinois sternal iliac needle has a lip on the end
where the finger and thumb can rest. This hold permits the
application of firm pressure away from the operator (into the bone)
and provides stability and precise control for placement of the
instrument into the marrow.
The most common sites for obtaining a sample are the greater
tubercle of the proximal humerus, the iliac crest of the pelvis, and the
trochanteric fossa of the proximal femur. The humerus is generally
the preferred site but may depend upon the clinician and the
patient’s condition and size. The trochanteric fossa may be used in
cats or small dogs, and the iliac crest is most easily accessed in thin
dogs and large cats, where it is easily palpable.10 Sternal bone
marrow aspiration is not commonly performed in dogs despite the
fact that the sternum is easily accessible and associated with less
pain from aspiration compared to other sites. Aspiration of marrow
from this site in normal dogs has been shown to be feasible and safe,
with sample quality that is equivalent to that of samples from the
humerus or ilium.11 Sternal bone marrow aspiration has been
assessed for practicality and efficacy for the diagnosis and
monitoring of canine leishmaniasis.12

PROCEDURE: BONE MARROW
ASPIRATION
It is easiest to sample the patient’s humerus that is the same as the
clinician’s dominant hand (Video 84.1

). The right-handed

clinician stands ventral to the laterally-recumbent patient (patient’s
head pointing to the clinician’s right) and uses the left hand to grasp
the patient’s right forelimb adjacent to the elbow, slightly rotating it
externally to stabilize it. The lateral aspect of the greater tubercle is
the target site for aspiration: a flattened, roughened area of bone
where muscle and fat coverage are minimal, and the needle is least
likely to slip off the bone. The needle should be placed through the
stab incision and aligned along the long axis of the bone. Firm
pressure is applied, with repetitive, back-and-forth twisting motions
to advance the needle through the cortex (Figure 84.2).

For the proximal femur, the animal is likewise placed in lateral
recumbency. The trochanteric fossa is located by palpation of the
greater trochanter. The fossa is located just medial to the trochanter.
The limb should be adducted and rotated medially to minimize the
risk of sciatic nerve damage. The needle is directed so it is parallel to
the shaft of the femur, to allow placement within the marrow cavity
(Figure 84.3).
For the iliac crest, the animal should be in sternal or lateral
recumbency. The clinician should palpate the widest portion of the
dorsal border of the iliac crest. The needle is advanced into the
middle of the crest, aiming slightly caudal to the vertical line through
the iliac crest (Figure 84.4).
Regardless of the chosen site, the procedure of aspiration is
identical, as are the pitfalls. If the needle does not remain solidly
embedded in the cortex, it may be only partially seated within it (or
parallel to it) rather than the needle reaching into the marrow space.
By maintaining a steady forward pressure from the palm of the hand
combined with a twisting back-and-forth rotation, the needle should
successfully penetrate the cortex and advance into the marrow space.
It is important not to go too far through the cavity and come out
through the opposite cortex. Some clinicians may sense a decrease in
resistance that indicates they have entered the marrow cavity but
others may not appreciate this subtle sensation. If the needle is
properly seated, it should not move on its own if it is manipulated
lightly side to side but rather should move in unison with the bone.

FIGURE 84.4 The needle is positioned into the
middle of the widest portion of the dorsal border of
the iliac crest and directed ventrally.

FIGURE 84.5 A, Stained smear containing
marrow spicules surrounded by blood. B,
Microscopic appearance of a bone marrow aspirate.
Several marrow particles surrounded by looser
monolayers of mixed hematopoietic cells.
Once the needle is firmly seated, the cap is removed from the
needle, the stylet is removed, and a 12 mL syringe is attached to the
hub of the needle. The clinician rapidly pulls back the plunger until
the smallest flash of blood is seen, and immediately stops suctioning.
It can be tempting to harvest as much marrow as possible in these
situations but ongoing suction causes hemodilution, reducing sample
quality. The needle is removed (with the syringe attached) from the
bone, and the contents of the syringe and needle are gently expelled
onto glass slides or into a collection dish. Alternatively, the syringe
alone can be removed first and its contents expelled onto glass slides
or into a dish containing EDTA. However, this author believes the
best sample is actually contained within the needle.
If the marrow sample is placed onto glass slides, especially if there
is no EDTA in the syringe, it is important to quickly prepare the
slides to avoid sample clotting. Thus, having an assistant to smear
the samples on the slides is best practice. The slides should be laid
out on an angle on a slide tray prior to collection. The clinician
should quickly place a drop of sample at the top of each slide while

the assistant follows behind placing a second clean slide
perpendicular to the first slide and gently spreading the marrow
spicules across the slides. This is similar to preparing a blood smear
(Video 57.1

).

If using a Petri dish or weigh boat, the clinician should place the
sample in the container, tilt the container to allow the blood to drain
away, and gently pick up the marrow spicules with the end of a
pipette or forceps. The spicules should be placed on a glass slide, and
gently crushed with a second clean glass slide. The marrow and
blood remaining in the container can be transferred to an EDTA vial
in case additional slides need to be prepared.
To ensure an adequate sample has been obtained, the clinician
should stain and examine one slide to look for evidence of cellularity
(Figure 84.5, A) while the patient is still anesthetized or heavily
sedated. A cursory microscopic evaluation should reveal densely
stained marrow particles populated by mixed hematopoietic cells
with variable amounts of fat and hemorrhage (Figure 84.5, B). If
cellularity is low or uncertain, a second attempt should be made to
collect an adequately cellular sample. In some pathologic conditions
like myelofibrosis or aplastic anemia, cellularity will be poor
regardless of the best technique, and in those cases a bone marrow
biopsy should be collected. The slides should be submitted along
with a recent CBC. It is preferable to have the CBC taken on the same
day as the aspirate, as accurate interpretation of the bone marrow
depends on the findings from the peripheral blood.

PROCEDURE: BONE MARROW CORE
BIOPSY
A bone marrow core biopsy (

Video 84.2) can be performed from

the same site or from a completely different site as a bone marrow
aspirate. All of the sites for bone marrow aspiration are the same for
marrow biopsy. One study evaluated a combined technique (using
the same needle and site for the aspirate and biopsy) in comparison
to obtaining a biopsy directly from the opposite humerus.4 The

authors found that the length of the marrow specimen was shorter
and hemorrhage artifact was more common using the combined
technique, but that cellularity, megakaryocyte count, MER, iron
stores, and diagnostic quality were not different.
The needle should be inserted in the same way as for the
aspiration. However, once the needle has been embedded in the
cortex, the stylet is removed. “Embedded” refers to a point where the
needle has advanced into bone and is firmly inserted enough that
gentle side-to-side movement of the needle also moves the bone.
Then, the needle is advanced an additional centimeter (or more in
large dogs) capturing a core of marrow tissue in the needle shaft.
Once the needle has advanced to this point, the clinician breaks the
biopsy fragment loose of its deep attachments by rocking the needle
back and forth 2 or 3 millimeters. The clinician then removes the
biopsy needle from the bone using a corkscrewing motion of the
needle to reduce friction and manual countertraction with the
nondominant hand against the bone. The biopsy sample is removed
from the needle by using a shepherd’s hook to push it retrograde (out
the handle end) with a Jamshidi needle, or using the needle’s own
stylet to push the sample retrograde if using an Illinois needle.13
Before placing the sample in 10% buffered formalin, the clinician
can roll it on a glass slide for cytological analysis. It is important to
avoid placing cytology slides in the same package as formalin
samples, as the formalin will fix the slides and deleteriously affect
their staining.

CHAPTER 85: Cytology of
Internal Organs
Lamberto Viadel Bau

A C RO N YM
FNA fine needle aspiration

BACKGROUND
“Cytology” refers to the microscopic assessment of cells, which can
be obtained from practically any internal organ of dogs and cats.
Most often, cytology samples are obtained via fine needle aspiration
(FNA). This is accomplished by inserting a needle well into the organ
or tissue of concern. Once within the tissue, there are 2 options. In
one, the needle is connected to a syringe and held in place while the
plunger is gently withdrawn, aspirating cells from the tissue into the
needle lumen. Some organs (liver, spleen, kidney, lymph nodes)
provide more intact cells for cytologic evaluation if suction is not
employed. In this scenario, as the needle is inserted, representative
cells are trapped in the needle lumen, remaining as the needle is
withdrawn.1 Sometimes cytology samples are submitted after tissue
has been gently pressed onto a glass slide (impression smear). These
and additional methods of collecting samples are presented in Video

85.1

. The most common internal organ samples submitted for

cytology include liver, spleen, lymph nodes and thyroid.

INDICATIONS AND ADVANTAGES
INFLAMMATION VERSUS NEOPLASIA; BIOPSY
VERSUS CYTOLOGY
The primary objective of an internal organ cytological evaluation is
usually to discriminate between inflammation and neoplasia.
Cytology is often the first and least invasive diagnostic step in
understanding the nature of suspicious or worrisome tissue.
Microscopic evaluation of a biopsy (an actual “piece” of tissue) is
usually more definitive than cytology. In addition to being less
expensive and less invasive than biopsy, about 85% of internal organ
cytological diagnoses correlate with subsequent histological biopsy
diagnosis.2 Cytologic evaluations are available in a short amount of
time, whereas biopsy samples take longer for tissue fixing and
cutting before slides can be stained and assessed.

BEFORE OR AFTER BIOPSY
Quick cytologic examination of tissue obtained via biopsy, prior to
submission, can be used to determine if the sample appears adequate
or if re-biopsy is indicated. Cytology specimens of good quality can
be submitted for appraisal. Cytology can be performed on slides after
tissue impression of FNA. Some cancers can be reliably diagnosed
via cytology (mastocytoma, transmissible venereal tumor, some
lymphomas, carcinomas and melanomas). Other neoplasms
(mesenchymal origin tumors, for example) exfoliate few cells and are
more difficult to identify.

MULTIPLE MASSES, RECURRENCE,
METASTASIS

FNA of suspicious tissue is recommended when multiple masses or
lesions are present, potentially indicating whether there are one or
several processes present. Cytologic examination of each may be of
value in identifying areas for biopsy. Cytologic evaluation of tissue
can be used to confirm the presence of metastases or to demonstrate
local recurrence of a previously treated neoplasia, useful information
when deciding the next step in care.

CYTOLOGY VERSUS “BLIND” BIOPSY:
MAKING THE MOST OF YOUR CLINICAL
PATHOLOGIST
Rather than “blind” removal of a mass, a pre-surgical cytological
diagnosis enables the surgeon to better appreciate what tissue is to
be extirpated. The clinical pathologist should be able to contribute
valuable insight, e.g., by reporting the invasive nature typical of such
masses, finding necrotic tissue, or whether non-surgical therapy
should be considered. Intraoperative cytologic evaluation of
suspicious tissue can aid in deciding whether it should be removed,
what excision margins should be attempted, and/or whether other
sites should be biopsied.

DISADVANTAGES AND LIMITATIONS
Limitations of cytology are recognized, even with the best technique
employed by a person with experience. Owners should be made
aware that cytology is not always informative and that complications,
while quite uncommon, can occur. Some pathological processes
cannot be detected or confirmed by cytology alone. Cytologic
diagnoses are usually non-specific regarding tissue of origin, e.g.,
“carcinoma” but not necessarily “renal carcinoma.” FNA samples do
not allow determination of vascular or lymphatic invasion. Tumors
that do not readily exfoliate make assessment of architecture
difficult. Some benign tumors can imitate malignancy
(histiocytomas, some parathyroid tumors). It can be challenging to
consistently discriminate normal from hyperplasia and it may be

difficult to distinguish hyperplasia from dysplasia or neoplasia.
“False negative” results might occur, e.g., if necrosis seems obvious
cytologically but the sample was obtained from the necrotic area of a
large rapidly growing tumor. Some malignant cancers (welldifferentiated carcinomas, lymphocytic lymphomas) can appear
benign, resulting in “false negative” results. Cytology samples
occasionally contain too few cells, non-representative cells, or are
diluted with blood. Clinician-induced altered cell appearance, due to
poor technique, can become diagnostic traps known as “malignancy
imitating” processes.

COMPLICATIONS AND
CONTRAINDICATIONS
Serious complications secondary to obtaining a sample for cytology
are quite uncommon. Possible complications include hemorrhage,
release of bioactive substances (mastocytomas), organ rupture or
laceration, pneumothorax, and causing infection or spreading
infection, e.g., if an abscess ruptures or leaks or if a needle drains
infected material while being withdrawn. Spread of tumor cells via
the needle’s exit path is extremely uncommon, but has been
documented with splenic hemangiosarcoma, renal carcinoma,
urothelial cell carcinoma,3 pulmonary,4 and ovarian tumors. FNA is
contraindicated if there is high risk of hemorrhage or if anesthesia is
both required but considered too risky.

SPECIMEN PREPARATION

(Video

85.1)
The quality of the cytology specimen is of key importance for correct
diagnosis.5,6 It is important to avoid using poor quality swabs that
can leave “material artifacts” and result in diagnostic errors. After
aspiration is complete and the needle removed from the patient, the
plunger of the syringe should be advanced to expel contents of the
needle and syringe onto a labelled slide. The material should then be

spread like a blood smear to create a smooth single layer of cells.
Being gentle when creating the smear prevents cell distortion or
lysis. Lysis, for example, may lead to unusual staining artifacts or
large numbers of bare nuclei. Liquid obtained on aspiration should
be transferred to an ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) tube,
mixed, and centrifuged for 5 minutes at 1000-1500 rpm. Most
supernatant can then be poured off and the sediment used to create
the cytology smear. No aspirated material should be discarded until
it is demonstrated that there are adequate cells for submission.
Imprints can also be made of tissue, after which slides are dried,
fixed and stained with Diff-Quik (Video 85.2

).

SENDING SAMPLES TO A LABORATORY
The expertise of a clinical pathologist should always be used to
confirm any serious diagnosis. Unstained or stained slides can be
submitted along with the critically important brief clinical review.
Any digital images of interest should also be submitted.7 Clinical
pathologists are trained to recognize artifacts or cell damage caused
by poor sample preparation. Inadequately fixed or hemodiluted
specimens are common. Other frequent issues include insufficient
cells (“dry aspirates”) and artifacts from contamination by
ultrasound gel (purple reddish amorphous material) or by cotton
grains from surgical gloves. Formalin vapors can seriously alter cell
morphology and staining quality. Therefore, formalin and cytology
samples should not be shipped in one container. Adequate packaging
is needed to prevent slides from breaking during transport. Every
specimen should be clearly labelled and accompanied by a written
review of the animal’s clinical history, physical examination, test
results, treatments employed, and treatment responses. The more
informed the clinical pathologist, the better the interpretations and
recommendations. Difficult and complicated cases should be
discussed.

CYTOLOGY OF DIFFERENT INTERNAL
ORGANS
THYROID
Blood contamination of thyroid FNA is usually significant.8
Specimens are usually highly cellular, forming groups of bare nuclei
on a pale blue cytoplasmatic background. Pink (colloid) amorphous
material can be associated with some cell groups. Malignant thyroid
carcinomas in geriatric dogs (ch. 288) commonly invade
surrounding cervical structures and commonly metastasize (EFigure 85.1). Thyroid masses in geriatric cats are usually benign
adenomas (uniform nuclei without population malignancy criteria)
or adenomatous hyperplasia (ch. 287).

E-FIGURE 85.1 (40×). Thyroid carcinoma
(tubular). Highly cellular specimen; isolated cells or
in groups that are usually formed by bare nuclei on a
pale blue cytoplasmatic background without clear
limits. In the center of the image, there is an acinus
with colloid substance inside.

LUNG
Normally, lung cytology consists of ciliated epithelial cells (E-Figure
85.2), mucus-producing cells (caliciform/goblet; E-Figures 85.3
and 85.4), and macrophages (common in bronchoalveolar lavage
specimens and must be distinguished from neoplastic cell; EFigures 85.5 and 85.6). Increased mucus is non-specific. Caution
is required to not mistake groups of alveolar cells (round or cuboidal;
E-Figure 85.7) as neoplastic cells. Blood contamination is common
(erythrophagocytosis is indicative of pathological hemorrhage).
Bacterial infection is usually associated with purulent inflammation.
Pyogranulomatous inflammation is typical of mycotic infection and
culture is advisable. Reactive hyperplasia is common (respiratory
cells with a more cubic morphology). Squamous metaplasia due to

chronic inflammation is difficult to distinguish from squamous
neoplasia. Most pulmonary masses are neoplastic, but primary lung
tumors (usually solitary carcinomas) are uncommon (chs. 212, 217).
Pleural fluid rarely includes tumor cells. Cytology cannot reliably
distinguish primary (large number of epithelial cells in lamina) from
metastatic carcinomas (E-Figures 85.8, 85.9, and 85.10).
Neoplasms of mesenchymal origin in the lung are often metastatic
(E-Figures 85.11 and 85.12). Non-lung tissues aspirated by
accident include lymph node, thymus, fat or abdominal organ tissue
(hepatocytes and mesothelial cells). Care must be taken not to
mistake these cells as being metastatic tumors cells of pulmonary
origin.

pleomorphic cells in an acinar arrangement,
suggesting glandular origin.

E-FIGURE 85.11 (100×). Lung. Metastatic tumor
of mesenchymal origin. Pleomorphic spindle cells.

E-FIGURE 85.12 (100×). Lung. Metastatic tumor
of mesenchymal origin. Pleomorphic spindle cells.

HEART
General anesthesia is usually required to obtain a specimen. Primary
heart tumors are rare. The most often described cardiac tumor,
hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325), is most often located in the right
atrium, is highly malignant, and often causes pericardial effusion.9
Heart base tumors and chemodectomas are less common (EFigures 85.13 and 85.14).

E-FIGURE 85.13 (40×). Heart. Chemodectoma.
Highly cellular specimen with blood contamination
and apparently bare nuclei against a slightly
basophilic background, typical of neuroendocrine
tumors.

E-FIGURE 85.14 (100×). Heart. Chemodectoma.
Highly cellular specimen with blood contamination
and apparently bare nuclei against a slightly
basophilic background, typical of neuroendocrine
tumors.

THYMUS
Cranial mediastinal masses are usually aspirated to distinguish
thymoma (uncommon) from thymic lymphoma (ch. 322).
Thymomas usually appear with large groups of large epithelial cells
and small, medium, and large-sized lymphocytes. Thymic lymphoma
is usually represented by a predominance of medium-sized and large
lymphocytes.

LIVER
FNA cytology of normal liver consists of a moderate number of
hepatocytes (cells in small groups with abundant blue cytoplasm and
a granular appearance; E-Figure 85.15), red blood cells due to

blood contamination,10 and epithelial cells from the biliary tract
(cuboidal, not to be mistaken for neoplastic cells; E-Figure 85.16).
Vacuolar degeneration is due to accumulated fat (feline hepatic
lipidosis; E-Figure 85.17) or accumulation of glycogen and water
(“steroid hepatopathy” in dogs) (ch. 274). Hepatic cytology is not
sensitive for the diagnosis of inflammatory, dysplastic or
hyperplastic processes.11-13 It is important to recognize nodular
hyperplasia (E-Figure 85.18) as distinct from cirrhosis or neoplasia
(ch. 275). In dogs, hepatocellular neoplasia (E-Figures 85.19 and
85.20) is more common than cancers originating from the biliary
system (cholangiocellular; E-Figure 85.21). Primary hepatic
tumors are uncommon. Hepatocellular carcinoma (E-Figure
85.19), the most common liver tumor, is characterized by cell
aggregates. The cytologic features of some well-differentiated
carcinomas and adenomas can appear normal or similar to nodular
hyperplasia. Non-epithelial tumors such as hemangiosarcoma are
less common (Figure 85.22). The most common hemolymphatic
hepatic neoplasm is lymphoma (E-Figure 85.23), generally formed
by lymphoblasts.

poorly defined cell borders. Cell size varies from one
sarcoma to another, from very uniform to marked
anisocytosis and anisokaryosis.

E-FIGURE 85.18 (100×). Liver. Hyperplastic

SPLEEN
Normal splenic cytology includes hemodiluted small and mediumsized lymphocytes, lymphoblasts, plasma cells, stromal cells, and
macrophages (E-Figure 85.24). Macroscopically, hyperplasia may
appear nodular or diffuse. Microscopically, splenic hyperplasia is
consistent with “chronicity”: macrophages, plasma cells and
lymphoblasts. Possible causal agents should be sought within
macrophages (Histoplasma spp. [ch. 209], Leishmania spp. [ch.
197]) and red blood cells (Mycoplasma, Babesia and Cytauxzoon
spp. [chs. 194, 197]). Heinz bodies could indicate toxic damage (ch.
138). Severe plasma cell hyperplasia (E-Figure 85.25) can be
associated with ehrlichiosis, leishmaniasis, extramedullary
plasmacytoma, or multiple myeloma. Lymphoid hyperplasia is seen
with some viral diseases. The presence of extramedullary
hematopoiesis suggests increased erythroid precursors (E-Figure

85.26). Hematomas (relatively common) or extramedullary
hematopoiesis can be associated with hyperplasia or neoplasia. The
most common splenic tumors in dogs are hemangioma and
hemangiosarcoma (E-Figures 85.27 and 85.28) (ch. 325) and in
cats are mastocytomas (E-Figure 85.29) (ch. 327) and lymphoma
(ch. 322). Lymphoma (E-Figures 85.30 and 85.31) and chronic
lymphocytic leukemias can be diagnostic challenges because their
cytological appearance is similar to that of a normal or hyperplastic
spleen.14,15

spleen showing lymphoblasts (L), lymphocytes (l),
neutrophils (nt) and red blood cells (RBC).

E-FIGURE 85.25 (100×). Spleen. Marked plasma
cell hyperplasia.

E-FIGURE 85.26 (100×). Spleen. Extramedullary

of the erythroid line in a spleen with Leishmania

Hemangiosarcoma. Presence of plump, spindle and
highly pleomorphic cells with marked anisokaryosis,
multiple and pleomorphic nuclei.

Hemangiosarcoma. Presence of plump, spindle and
highly pleomorphic cells with marked anisokaryosis,

ADRENAL GLAND
Increasing use of sensitive advanced imaging diagnostic tools is
allowing detection of unsuspected adrenal masses. Identifying an
adrenal “incidentaloma” presents challenges for both clinician and
owner: how aggressive to be after identifying an adrenal mass if
there are no adrenal-related signs (chs. 293-295)? More than 25%
of adrenal tumors are metastases from distant sites, most frequently
melanomas and carcinomas. Cytology results may aid in the decision
process if used in conjunction with clinical signs. Cytologic
evaluation of an adrenal mass usually allows discrimination between
cortical and medullary tissue and may identify metastatic tissue as
opposed to adrenal. Adrenocortical adenomas are common in older
dogs and their FNA cytologic findings are similar to those of normal
adrenocortical cells. Adenocarcinomas are less common and may
invade surrounding tissues and vasculature, often directly into the

vena cava (E-Figure 85.32). Cytologically, most adenocarcinomas
meet criteria for malignancy. Adrenal adenomas and
adenocarcinomas are rare in cats. In dogs, it may be difficult to
differentiate between adrenal adenocarcinoma and
pheochromocytoma. Pheochromocytoma, the most common
medullary tumor (E-Figure 85.33; ch. 298), usually has a classic
neuroendocrine appearance on cytology. It has been suggested that
masses >20 mm and/or invading peripheral structures are more
likely to be malignant. Some studies suggest that ultrasound-guided
FNA of adrenal masses are relatively safe, but other authors are less
convinced.16-18 Aspirating a suspected pheochromocytoma is not
advised since catecholamine release, induced by needle placement,
can lead to morbidity or mortality associated with blood pressure
instability and/or cardiac arrhythmias. Risk of catastrophic
complications to obtain cells for cytology seems less warranted
knowing that cytology does not consistently provide enough
information to discriminate benign from malignant19 nor whether
the tissue is producing any hormone. Many clinicians and clinical
pathologists prefer to focus and rely on history, physical
examination, rate of growth, presence of metastases, and routine
blood, urine, imaging and adrenal test results. Together, these
should determine the recommended course with “incidentalomas.”

E-FIGURE 85.32 (40×). Cortico-adrenal
carcinoma. Aggregate of epithelial cells with
extensive cytoplasm, generally occupied by lipid
vacuoles, with a round nucleus, often centrally
located, with dense clumpy chromatin and discrete
nucleolus. The degree of anisokaryosis is
low. Courtesy Daniel Borràs.

E-FIGURE 85.33 Pheochromocytoma. Adrenal
gland mass of 4.5 × 2 cm of soft consistency and
brown color, with frequent hemorrhagic
areas. Courtesy Daniel Borràs.

KIDNEY
It is preferable to sedate or anesthetize dogs and cats during kidney
FNA to minimize risk of laceration. FNA may be indicated if there is
evidence of atypical renal enlargement or suspicion of a cyst, abscess,
fungal infection or neoplasia (ch. 299). Little information is gained
from aspirating atrophic kidneys. Complications are uncommon but
excessive hemorrhage has been reported. Normal cytologic findings
include round (E-Figure 85.34) or polygonal cells in cords (EFigure 85.35), and fragments of renal tubules, often with some
blood contamination. Metastatic tumors are more common than
primary tumors. Epithelial tumors are most common in older dogs
(mostly carcinomas; E-Figures 85.36 and 85.37). Some tumors

(adenocarcinoma and melanoma) may be bilateral. The most
common renal tumor in cats is lymphoma.20-22

E-FIGURE 85.34 (40×). Cytology of normal
kidney. Epithelial cells from renal tubules (round or
polygonal cells, with round central nucleus and
abundant cytoplasm).

E-FIGURE 85.35 (10×). Cytology of normal
kidney. Fragments of renal tubules.

E-FIGURE 85.36 (100×). Kidney. Renal
adenocarcinoma (clear cell carcinoma).

E-FIGURE 85.37 (100×). Kidney. Renal
adenocarcinoma (clear cell carcinoma).

LYMPH NODES
Aspiration is indicated when a node or nodes are enlarged or
irregular (ch. 88).23 The purpose of cytology is to identify any
neoplastic process. Normal lymph nodes include small lymphocytes
with lesser numbers of lymphoblasts (E-Figure 85.38) and
immunoblasts. In hyperplasia (reactive lymphadenopathy), the
enlarged node may have normal cytological characteristics but
greater cell polymorphism and macrophage counts. Increased
macrophage numbers are also seen in granulomatous lymphadenitis,
but the macrophages tend to form groups (E-Figure 85.39) or may
appear to blend into multinucleate cells. A predominance of plasma
cells (plasmacytic hyperplasia; E-Figure 85.40) typically follows
strong antigen stimulation. Attempts should always be made to
detect parasites such as Leishmania spp. (E-Figure 85.41), but
false negatives are common. As with cytologic evaluation of the
spleen or liver, there can be extramedullary hematopoiesis (E-

Figure 85.42). Lymphoma (primary neoplasia) is cytologically
divided into small- or large-cell (ch. 322). Small-cell lymphoma
(lymphocytic lymphoma) usually appears cytologically as
monotonous populations of well-differentiated small lymphocytes
which often fragment to produce varying sized cytoplasmatic pieces
called lymphoglandular bodies (E-Figure 85.43). Medium-and
large-cell lymphomas, called lymphoblastic lymphoma (E-Figures
85.44 and 85.45), typically include more than 50% lymphoblasts
and abundant lymphoglandular bodies. Fewer lymphoglandular
bodies may aid in distinguishing benign hyperplasia (E-Figure
85.46) from a malignant process. Morphological characteristics can
be affected by fixation and drying techniques. The existence of
lymphoma imitating processes may interfere with establishing a
definitive diagnosis. The most common neoplasms to metastasize to
lymph nodes are carcinomas (E-Figure 85.47), mastocytomas and
malignant melanomas (E-Figure 85.48).

variable.

PROSTATE
Normal prostatic cytologic features include groups of cubic or
cylindrical cells in “beehive” arrangements. In benign prostate
hyperplasia, cells appear normal but with a slightly increased
nucleus/cytoplasm ratio (E-Figure 85.49). Prostatic abscesses have
large numbers of neutrophils, which are often degenerate. In
squamous metaplasia, there are large numbers of squamous cells
which may be difficult to distinguish from contamination with
squamous cells of the distal urethra when samples are obtained by
massage (ch. 104). Prostatic neoplasms are uncommon but often
malignant. Adenocarcinoma, the most common tumor of the
prostate (chs. 314, 330), is difficult to diagnose with cytology (EFigures 85.50 and 85.51). Urothelial cell carcinoma is less
common.24

E-FIGURE 85.49 (40×). Prostate hyperplasia.
Epithelial cells in a “beehive” arrangement, generally
of normal appearance (although there can be some
anisokaryosis and increased cytoplasm).

E-FIGURE 85.50 (100×). Prostate
adenocarcinoma. It can be very difficult to diagnose
by cytology when coexisting with other prostate
diseases.

E-FIGURE 85.51 (40×). Prostate adenocarcinoma
associated with purulent inflammation (neutrophils,
nt).

OTHERS
Pancreas,25,26 ovaries (E-Figures 85.52 through 85.55),27 vagina
(E-Figures 85.56 through 85.59), urethral discharges (ch. 104),
semen, urinary sediment (ch. 70), and traumatic prostate or bladder
aspirates (chs. 100, 104) are each submitted to clinical pathologists
on occasion. Such examinations can be of value.

Chapter 86:
Abdominocentesis
Oriana Daniela Raab

DEFINITION AND PURPOSE
Abdominocentesis is the percutaneous removal of abdominal fluid
using a needle or catheter. The procedure is routinely performed for
diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.
Abdominocentesis can be carried out to obtain fluid for analysis if
there is a high suspicion of effusion based on physical examination
or if imaging indicates its presence. Analysis of abdominal fluid can
aid in the diagnosis of abdominal hemorrhage, neoplasia, sterile or
septic peritonitis, and hollow organ (gallbladder, gastrointestinal
tract, uterine, or urinary tract) rupture.1 Abdominocentesis can also
be performed to remove large amounts of fluid from patients that are
experiencing effusion-related clinical signs such as dyspnea,
inappetence, and signs of abdominal discomfort.

CONTRAINDICATIONS AND
CONSIDERATIONS
Before performing abdominocentesis, the clinician should consider
the benefits versus the risks of the procedure, particularly when a

blind puncture is to be attempted. Abdominocentesis should be
performed with caution in patients with hemostatic abnormalities. In
these cases, percutaneous insertion of the needle or catheter along
the avascular midline using ultrasound guidance can help minimize
bleeding.
Structural impediments to the safe introduction of a needle or
catheter may include the gravid uterus, distended urinary bladder, or
a large abdominal mass. The intestines typically float in abdominal
fluid and generally move safely out of the way of a slowly advancing
catheter.

COMPLICATIONS OF PROCEDURE
Complications, including hemorrhage, local infection or peritonitis,
and intestinal perforation, are uncommon; they can be minimized
further with the use of ultrasound guidance and aseptic technique.
The risk of a subcutaneous hematoma can be lessened by avoiding
needle or catheter placement in the vicinity of the caudal superficial
epigastric vessels, which lie paramedian and adjacent to a
longitudinal line drawn between the nipples.2 The use of an overthe-needle catheter, rather than a hypodermic needle, can also help
to decrease the risk of penetration or laceration of an organ or blood
vessel and minimize the chance of false-positive results3; however,
the use of a catheter in thicker-skinned or obese patients, or those
with extensive body wall movement (e.g., panting dogs) could lead to
kinking of the catheter, making it ineffective.

SEDATION/ANALGESIA
Abdominocentesis is typically performed in conscious animals using
physical restraint. The use of a sedative may be warranted depending
on the patient’s temperament and clinical condition. The
administration of an analgesic or instillation of a local anesthetic in
the region where the needle or catheter is to be placed should be
considered, particularly when large-gauge catheters are utilized or
when therapeutic (large-volume) abdominocentesis is performed.

SAMPLE COLLECTION
Collection tubes that should be available during fluid sampling
include ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) (lavender top) tubes
for cytologic analysis, total nucleated cell count, protein
measurement and packed cell volume; and plain (red top) tubes and
culture swabs for biochemical analysis and bacterial culture and
susceptibility testing. Additional tests can be performed depending
on the clinical circumstances (ch. 21).

PREPARATION, EQUIPMENT AND
TECHNIQUES
There are several acceptable methods for obtaining a sample of
abdominal fluid. Ultrasound should be utilized whenever possible to
confirm the presence of abdominal effusion and to guide needle
placement for fluid aspiration (ch. 73). If ultrasound is unavailable,
a single blind puncture or four-quadrant technique can be
performed. However, it is important to remember that blind
abdominocentesis might be unsuccessful in patients with small
volumes of abdominal fluid or in patients with effusion confined to
the retroperitoneal space.
Regardless of the technique chosen, patient preparation is the
same. The ventral abdomen should be clipped free of fur and
surgically prepared using antiseptic scrub and isopropyl alcohol. The
individual performing the procedure should wear sterile gloves to
ensure asepsis.
Depending on the size of the patient, a sterile 18- to 22-gauge, 1- to
1.5-inch (2.5-4 cm) needle or 16- to 22-gauge over-the-needle
intravenous (IV) catheter may be utilized. If a catheter is utilized,
prior to the procedure, 2 to 3 small fenestrations can be made in
staggered positions at the distal third of the catheter using a sterile
#10 or #11 scalpel blade (

Video 86.1). Fenestrations should be

no larger than one third of the catheter circumference and should be
spaced far enough apart so that they do not weaken the shaft and
lead to catheter breakage.2 The creation of fenestrations lessens the

chance of obstruction of the catheter by loose tissue such as
omentum and increases the likelihood of obtaining a fluid sample.3,4
Additional equipment needed includes an appropriately sized syringe
and collection tubes.

FIGURE 86.1 Equipment needed for therapeutic
abdominocentesis. From left to right (all sterile):
large syringe (here, 35 cc), 3-way stopcock, gloves,
catheter, extension set, scalpel blade.

SIMPLE ULTRASOUND-GUIDED
ABDOMINOCENTESIS
The patient may be placed in dorsal or lateral recumbency. The
ultrasound transducer should be kept sterile via the use of a sterile
sleeve or aseptic preparation. Using ultrasound guidance, a needle
with an attached syringe of appropriate size is directed
percutaneously into a fluid pocket and the contents are gently
aspirated.

SIMPLE BLIND ABDOMINOCENTESIS
The patient may be placed in lateral recumbency or the procedure
may be performed with the patient standing. A needle or over-theneedle catheter of appropriate size is percutaneously inserted on the
ventral midline approximately 2 to 4 cm caudal to the umbilicus.
Alternatively, the needle or catheter is inserted 1 to 2 cm to the right
of the midline to avoid splenic penetration. A syringe of appropriate
size is attached for gentle aspiration (closed method) or the needle or
catheter is inserted, gentle abdominal compression is applied and
fluid is collected from the hub without attaching a syringe (open
method).3

BLIND FOUR-QUADRANT
ABDOMINOCENTESIS
If ultrasound is unavailable and simple blind abdominocentesis is
unsuccessful, a blind, four-quadrant technique may be attempted.
The patient may be placed in dorsal or lateral recumbency.
Alternatively, with cooperative patients, some clinicians perform this
technique with the animal standing to increase fluid yield through
gravitational draw of fluid ventrally. Using the umbilicus as the
center point, a needle or over-the-needle catheter of appropriate size
is inserted into the cranial dependent quadrant, the cranial
nondependent quadrant, the caudal dependent quadrant and the
caudal nondependent quadrant (or equivalent sequence if the patient
is dorsally recumbent or standing). Fluid may be collected via an
open or closed method as described above. Placing needles (without
attached syringes) in more than one quadrant at a time provides an
air vent that may allow fluid to flow. Any positive tap in any quadrant
completes the procedure.2

LARGE VOLUME ABDOMINOCENTESIS
Patients who are hemodynamically stable but experiencing
respiratory compromise or discomfort may have larger amounts of

fluid removed to alleviate their clinical signs. The technique is
identical to that of a simple abdominocentesis described previously,
except that a larger bore over-the-needle fenestrated catheter is used.
Once the catheter is inserted, sterile extension tubing and a syringe
with a 3-way stopcock are attached to permit aspiration and removal
of abdominal fluid (Figure 86.1; Video 86.1

).

The main theoretical safety concern with large-volume
abdominocentesis is hemodynamic changes; blood pressure initially
falls as intra-abdominal pressure decreases.5 However, relief of
intra-abdominal hypertension can confer hemodynamic and clinical
benefits (e.g., improved appetite and demeanor) in patients with
tense effusion.

Chapter 87: Arthrocentesis
Jonathan David Dear

Anatomy and Physiology
Synovial joints consist of two or more articulating bones, a superficial layer of articular cartilage,
synovium, and synovial fluid. Some joints may also contain intra-articular menisci, ligaments, or
fat pads. The synovium is a thin membrane of synoviocytes spanning the articulating bones to
create an enclosed “compartment.” Synoviocytes are characterized as either type A (phagocytic)
or type B that secrete hyaluronan and other components into synovial fluid, a “dialysate of
plasma.” Healthy synovial fluid is relatively acellular and its functions include lubricating
cartilage and delivering nutrients, as these tissues receive little blood supply. The elastic and
thick viscosity of joint fluid contributes to its lubricating qualities. Any condition that causes joint
inflammation may lead to abnormally porous synovial vessels and joint space accumulation of
extracellular fluid, inflammatory mediators, and leukocytes. This process decreases joint fluid
viscosity, causes pain, and increases susceptibility to structural damage and arthritis.1

BACKGROUND AND INDICATIONS
Arthrocentesis (joint fluid aspiration, joint tap) is a technique for obtaining fluid from
appendicular joints. Potentially valuable information gained from gross and cytologic analysis of
joint fluid may aid in determining cause of swollen joints, lameness, fever, or polysystemic
disease. Arthrocentesis is not technically challenging but has a steep learning curve. Once the
clinician performing it is competent and confident, joint fluid analysis can be employed as a
diagnostic aid in a variety of scenarios. It is particularly useful in evaluating dogs with obvious
joint abnormalities, but also for dogs with fever (ch. 16) and those with vague signs of malaise
(ch. 10). Indications for arthrocentesis are thoroughly reviewed (chs. 31, 32, 41, and 58). Joint
fluid analysis is also reviewed (ch. 71).
The goals of this chapter are to review the techniques and approaches to acquiring joint fluid
for cytologic and microbiologic assessment. Results of arthrocentesis can be helpful in
differentiating osteoarthritis from immune-mediated, infectious or neoplastic processes. The
joint fluid analysis should complement information acquired from the history (ch. 2), physical
examination (ch. 3), orthopedic (ch. 31) and neurologic (ch. 241) evaluations, laboratory and
imaging studies. Radiographs, if indicated, should precede arthrocentesis, as development of
hemarthrosis can interfere with radiograph interpretation.

TECHNIQUES
OVERVIEW (VIDEO 87.1

)

Synovial fluid analysis may provide insight into a pet’s disease but rarely provides a definitive
diagnosis. The decision regarding the joint or joints to aspirate should be made using the
information gathered from clinical history, physical exam and orthopedic evaluation. Joints may
not be obviously abnormal in pets with shifting leg lameness, systemic illness, fever, or possible
immune-mediated polyarthritis (ch. 177). In these pets, diagnostic yield is increased if multiple
joints (usually both carpi and tarsi) are aspirated.

PATIENT PREPARATION AND POSITIONING
Since joint disease may be painful, adequate analgesia, sedation or anesthesia should be
provided. Sedation, as a minimum, is not only imperative for fractious or excitable pets, but it
also enhances ability to safely obtain joint fluid from calm pets, minimizing risk of the needle
causing intra-articular harm. Once sedated or anesthetized, the pet is positioned in lateral
recumbency with all 4 limbs accessible. Often the carpal joint is aspirated from the medial aspect,
requiring access to the “dependent” thoracic limb. There is also a technique using a dorsal
approach to the carpal joint. Elbow, stifle and tarsus joints are usually aspirated using a lateral
approach, requiring access to the nondependent limb.
Prior to arthrocentesis, the joints should be clipped and prepped aseptically alternating
chlorhexidine with alcohol. Sterile gloves, needles and syringes should be used. Draping is not
necessary. To reduce chances of joint trauma, blood contamination, or pain, first manipulate the
joint to find the degree of flexion that allows the largest “window” into the synovial space. Flexing
the limb can be done by the veterinarian performing the arthrocentesis or by an assistant. Should
the veterinarian prefer to manipulate the limb and joint, the veterinarian must perform the joint
aspirate with one sterile hand (usually the dominant hand) while the non-sterile hand (usually
the nondominant hand) holds the limb.

SAMPLE ACQUISITION
Small (22-25 gauge) needles are adequate for fluid to enter the attached syringe (usually 3 cc).
Short needles are less likely to cause joint damage. There should be a good seal between needle
and syringe, but the plunger seal should be broken prior to starting the procedure to allow
smooth movement. The needle should be inserted slowly into the joint, perpendicular to the skin.
The carpal joint is shallow, while the elbow, stifle and tarsus joints may require insertion of the
entire needle to retrieve fluid. If bone or cartilage is encountered or no joint fluid aspirated, the
needle should be gently withdrawn slightly and redirected.

FIGURE 87.1 A-F, Sites of canine arthrocentesis (marked with an
X). F, From Evans HE, de Lahunta A . Miller’s Anatomy of the

Dog.

4th ed. Saunders; 2013.

Gentle intermittent negative pressure should be applied with the plunger once the needle has
passed through skin and into the joint space. One may not be able to withdraw more than 0.2 mL
from a normal joint; thus, apparent absence of fluid may be indicative of a healthy joint. While
only a small amount of fluid is required for analysis, sometimes as much as 0.5-1 mL can be
easily aspirated from abnormal joints. Avoid excessive negative pressure, which may lead to
hemorrhage and compromised cytologic results because red blood cells may interfere with
interpretation. Negative pressure should be completely released prior to withdrawing the needle
to avoid blood contamination from the skin or subcutaneous tissues. Discard any needle and
syringe with blood contamination.

ANATOMIC LANDMARKS (Figure 87.1)
The carpus joint (

Video 87.2) is sampled at the proximal radiocarpal (antebrachiocarpal)

joint along either its medial or dorsal aspect. When using the dorsal approach, care should be
taken to avoid the cephalic vein which courses across the joint surface. The tibiotarsal joint (
Video 87.3) is accessed from the lateral aspect along the talus; similarly, care should be taken to
avoid the superficial caudal branch of the lateral saphenous vein in the area. The needle should
be advanced parallel to the axis of the metatarsals, perpendicular to the tibia. The stifle (
Video 87.4) can be aspirated from either a medial or a lateral approach. From either approach, a
longer needle (often 1.5 inches [3.5-4 cm]) is required as the synovial fluid tends to accumulate
caudal to the patellar fat pad.2

FLUID HANDLING
Synovial fluid should be submitted for cytologic analysis in an ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid
(EDTA)-containing tube and/or as prepared slides. This may depend on the volume of fluid
aspirated. Slides can be prepared by dropping a small amount of joint fluid onto a glass slide near
the frosted edge and slowly spreading the sample across the slide using a second slide (Videos
71.2 and 87.2). Joint fluid and/or prepared slides should be evaluated by a clinical pathologist for
color, turbidity, cellularity, differential cell count and cytologic inspection for infectious
organisms or exfoliated neoplastic cells (E-Figures 87.2 through 87.5 and Table 87.1). A
crude test of synovial fluid viscosity can be performed by stringing the sample between the thumb
and index finger (Video 71.3). Normal joint fluid should string 3-5 cm while joint fluid from
affected joints will be less viscous and string shorter lengths. Lack of viscosity is due to lack of
hyaluronan. Assessing viscosity with one’s fingers is subjective and may yield incorrect
impressions. If the sample is of adequate volume and if clinically indicated, synovial fluid should
be submitted for microbial culture and susceptibility testing in a sterile tube or a special culture
tube. If immediate results are needed, basic fluid analysis can be performed by assessing the total
solids, color, turbidity, and microscopic appearance. The nucleated cell count can be roughly
estimated as being normal, mildly to moderately or markedly increased by counting the number
of cells identified mid-slide under 400× magnification.3 While the presence of intracellular
bacteria is compelling evidence for a septic process, many cytologic features of sepsis are subtle.
Since pets with septic arthritis often have non-degenerate neutrophils, care must be used when
interpreting joint fluid (ch. 71).

MONITORING
Dogs and cats recover quickly following sedation reversal or recovery from anesthesia. Though
they might appear slightly more lame for 1-2 days following the procedure, they almost never
have any long-term effects. The development of hemarthrosis, an unusual consequence of
arthrocentesis, can occur and lead to prolonged joint pain. Recheck physical exam and repeat
arthrocentesis can be used to guide treatment, and cytologic changes in joint fluid analysis are
not affected by repeating tapping.4

Chapter 88: Lymph Node
Aspiration and Biopsy
Takuo Ishida

AC RO N YM S
FNA fine needle aspiration
FNB fine needle biopsy
NMB new methylene blue
