BACKGROUND
Lymphadenopathy (enlargement of the lymph node) is a concern because
its differential diagnoses include a wide variety of worrisome pathologies.
Enlarged lymph modes are associated with neoplastic (ch. 322),
infectious (ch. 184), or immunologic (ch. 169) conditions. If multiple
nodes are enlarged it is advisable to sample >1. There are new
technologies for evaluating and “scoring” enlarged nodes, primarily with
use of imaging modalities,1-3 but the gold standard for precise diagnosis
remains microscopic examination. Techniques usually utilized to obtain
samples from any enlarged peripheral or internal node are nonaspiration fine needle biopsy (FNB) or fine needle aspiration (FNA) for
cytologic evaluation. Cytology is both sensitive and specific in diagnosing
neoplasia regardless of whether it is primary or metastatic.4-7 Lymph
node cytology, in combination with specific microbiologic techniques, is
also of potential value for detecting evidence of infectious disease,

including leishmaniasis (ch. 197), ehrlichiosis (ch. 193), cryptococcosis
(ch. 207), neorickettsiosis (ch. 193), mycobacteriosis (ch. 188), and
feline infectious peritonitis (FIP; ch. 200).8-12 Lymph node aspiration is
also used for flow cytometry and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for
antigen receptor rearrangements in which specific lymphocyte
phenotypes are studied for diagnosis and monitoring lymphoproliferative
diseases (ch. 322).13-16
Biopsy or FNA of submandibular lymph nodes is usually avoided if
other nodes are available for sampling. Changes due to oral infection or
from salivary gland cell contamination can make microscopic evaluation
difficult. One should also try to avoid aspirating from the central area of
severely enlarged nodes because of the possible sampling of necrotic
tissue.17 Superficial sampling may give inconclusive results due to central
proliferation of indolent lymphoma cells in the node.18
The gold standard for identifying the cause of lymph node enlargement
is to excise the entire node and have it submitted for histologic
evaluation. Since the main purpose of histopathology is to obtain
information on the tissue architecture, this method should always be
considered if the patient can be safely anesthetized. Needle-core biopsies
of lymph nodes can be attempted using manually operated or automatic
(Tru-Cut type) needles because the techniques are straightforward and
require only sedation or light anesthesia. However, samples obtained in
this manner often fail to provide proper and adequate samples for
histopathologic evaluation. The needle-core technique can be used when
tissue architecture is not important for diagnosis, as in suspected
infectious disease.

LYMPH NODE CYTOLOGY TECHNIQUES
(Video 88.1
)
Initially, one can attempt to obtain cells via non-aspiration FNB of an
enlarged peripheral or intra-abdominal lymph node. A sterile 20- to 22gauge (for large dogs) or 22- to 23-gauge (for small dogs and for cats)
needle is used. The skin over the peripheral lymph node should be gently
cleaned with ethanol or isopropyl alcohol. If the biopsy involves an
internal lymph node, the skin should be “surgically” cleansed. While
grasping the superficial node with one hand or with the ultrasound guide,
the needle is held by the thumb and forefinger of the other hand. The

needle is then inserted into the tissue, pulled back to the cortex without
withdrawing, and redirected again deeper into the gland in a slightly
different direction. Redirection of the needle and probing different areas
is a procedure that should be repeated several times (5 times is excellent).
Cells and fluid will collect within the needle lumen by capillary action
(Figure 88.1, A). The needle is then removed from the node.17
If the tissue to be biopsied resides in the thoracic cavity, FNA should
always be carried out with the needle attached to a 3- or 6-mL sterile
syringe to avoid development of pneumothorax. The technique described
here can also be used if an initial attempt at FNB failed to give adequate
cells for an accurate cytologic diagnosis (Figure 88.1, B). Holding the
lymph node or ultrasound guide with one hand, a sterile needle attached
to a sterile syringe is inserted into the structure of interest. While pulling
back on the plunger to generate a vacuum, the syringe held by the same
hand should then be pulled back slightly. The needle tip should remain in
the cortex area of the node. Then the vacuum pressure is released, and
the needle should be advanced in a different direction before again
generating negative pressure. Needle redirection should be repeated
more than once—5 times whenever possible. When finished, the vacuum
is gently released and the needle gently withdrawn.
The needle should then be removed from the syringe and the syringe
filled with air before being reattached to the needle. For both FNB and
FNA, any material inside the needle should be gently expelled onto a
clean coverslip or slide by gently pushing the plunger of the syringe down
while the needle tip is positioned just above the slide. One should avoid
ejecting a “jet” of material from the syringe, which has been shown to
distort cells. For the coverslip smear preparation, a second clean
coverslip is placed on top of the first. The material between coverslips will
naturally begin to spread after the weight of the upper coverslip is
applied. The tip of each coverslip should be held separately and pulled
apart horizontally just as the spreading sample material reaches the ends
of each coverslip (Figure 88.1, C). Using this technique, fragile juvenile
lymphocytes can be well preserved if 60% horizontal and 40% vertical
motions are applied when separating the coverslips. The coverslips
should be immediately air-dried, or heat can be gently applied while
holding the coverslip.
Similar high-quality smears can be made by using thin pre-cleaned
glass slides. The sample is expelled gently on the first slide one-third of
the distance from the top and a second slide is placed at right angles over
the sample. The sample material will spread with the weight of the top
slide and the top slide is then gently pulled away from the bottom

(Figure 88.1, D). The smear on the bottom slide usually is best for
evaluation. The slide should be immediately air-dried.

FIGURE 88.1 Non-aspiration technique to obtain
samples for cytologic evaluation of lymph nodes using
the needle alone (A) and aspiration technique with the
needle attached to a syringe (B). The smear samples for
cytology are made either with two coverslips (C) or two
glass slides (D).
For “in-house” evaluation of cytology specimens, the air-dried
coverslips or slides are fixed with fresh methanol for 2 to 5 minutes and
stained with Wright-Giemsa stain. It is important that the methanol be
fresh (>95%), that adequate fixation time be allowed, and that the stain
solution is prepared fresh by using a proper phosphate buffer of pH 6.2.
If quick evaluation is required, a Diff-Quik type quick stain or new
methylene blue (NMB) supravital stain (0.1% in normal saline) may be
used. The NMB stain on air-dried unfixed samples always gives superior
results. The final diagnosis should be made on slides stained with
properly prepared Romanowsky-type stains such as Wright-Giemsa or
May-Grünwald-Giemsa.

LYMPH NODE CYTOLOGY
INTERPRETATION
Cytologic evaluation of lymph nodes, in general, will provide one of the
following findings: normal, hyperplasia (reactive), inflammation,
lymphoma, metastatic neoplasm, or extramedullary hematopoiesis.17
Normal lymph node cytologic findings include approximately 90% welldifferentiated small lymphocytes and up to 10% medium and large
lymphocytes (Figure 88.2, A). Plasma cells, histiocytes (macrophages),
and neutrophils are usually present in small numbers. A few mast cells
per slide can also be identified.19
Increased numbers (usually 15-30%) of medium and large lymphocytes
are seen in the reactive or hyperplastic node. A majority of cells from
hyperplastic nodes (>50%) are small lymphocytes (Figure 88.2, B). The
percentage of the medium and large cells can be as high as 50% in some
cytologic specimens. Examination of additional slides or histologic
examination of a biopsy may be needed to differentiate hyperplasia and
neoplasia.20,21 In hyperplasia, the number of plasma cells is frequently
increased and the number of other inflammatory cells mildly increased.
Lymphoid hyperplasia is usually associated with antigenic stimulation
due to one of several etiologies: infection, inflammation, immunemediated disorders and neoplasia. Additional tests may be required to
confirm a diagnosis.
Lymphadenitis is classified as suppurative, eosinophilic, histiocytic, or
pyogranulomatous based on the inflammatory cells seen.22 Suppurative
lymphadenitis is characterized by increased numbers of neutrophils
(>5%). Neutrophil counts >20% are consistent with infection within the
node or with secondary inflammation, perhaps from draining an infected
area. Eosinophilic lymphadenitis is diagnosed if increased numbers of
eosinophils (>3%) are noted. If histiocytes are >3-5% of all cells,
histiocytic lymphadenitis is likely. Pyogranulomatous lymphadenitis has
increases in both histiocytes and neutrophils (Figure 88.2, C).
Pyogranulomatous lymphadenitis is often associated with fungal,
Leishmania, Neorickettsia or Prototheca infections.
Cytologic diagnosis of high-grade lymphomas can be achieved by
detecting >50% medium or large lymphocytes (Figure 88.2, D).
Additional examinations including histopathologic evaluation of biopsy
samples, immunophenotyping and PCR assessment of clonality are
usually used for establishing a diagnosis based on the latest World Health

Organization (WHO) classification.23 Histologic evaluation is best done
with the largest section of a node possible. Nodes from pets with lowgrade lymphoma, on the other hand, are usually composed of an almost
uniform group of small lymphocytes, making diagnosis with cytology
difficult (Figure 88.2, E). Again, histology and other diagnostic
procedures are needed. Some B-cell low grade lymphomas are known to
progress to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, but histologic grading based
on blast cell numbers is not routine in veterinary medicine.24,25 The
presence of cells not normally seen in the lymph node (e.g., epithelial
cells or melanocytes) or the presence of normal component cells in
excessive numbers (e.g., mast cells) confirms a diagnosis of metastatic
neoplasia (Figure 88.2, F).

88.3, F and G), mitotic figures (Figure 88.3, H) and their
abnormalities (Figure 88.3, I and J), and concluded that high scores
and more frequent mitoses were associated with relapse.26

Chapter 89: Rhinoscopy,
Nasal Flush, and Biopsy
Lynelle R. Johnson

Animals with nasal disorders of any etiology typically have clinical
complaints of sneezing and unilateral or bilateral serous, mucoid, or
hemorrhagic nasal discharge (chs. 35, 213). Common etiologies
include foreign body inhalation, infection (fungal or secondary
bacterial most commonly), dental-related nasal disease, or neoplasia,
although in some practices, one of the more common disease
processes identified is idiopathic inflammation, which is a diagnosis
of exclusion. This is often referred to as chronic rhinosinusitis in the
cat and lymphoplasmacytic rhinitis in the dog (chs. 212, 213).
History and physical examination findings can be helpful in ranking
differential diagnoses in the appropriate order; however, many cases
and virtually all cases of chronic nasal disease require advanced
work-up, including imaging (preferably computed tomography [CT])
followed by rhinoscopy. Depending on the capabilities in the practice
and the pet owner’s interest in pursuing specialty intervention,
various techniques can be used to perform rhinoscopic evaluation.
A minimum database (complete blood count [CBC], chemistry
profile, and urinalysis) is typically completed for animals with
chronic nasal discharge because further diagnostic testing will
require general anesthesia. In animals with epistaxis, a platelet count
and coagulation profile should also be obtained prior to rhinoscopy
because the nasal cavity is highly vascular, and disorders of

coagulation increase the risk of fatal hemorrhage (chs. 36, 170).
Blood pressure evaluation should also be considered. Imaging is
typically performed prior to rhinoscopy to avoid induction of
bleeding, which will obscure visualization of lesions. After visual
inspection of the nasal cavity, samples can be collected for culture,
polymerase chain reaction (PCR), or histopathologic evaluation.
Periodontal probing is performed after completion of rhinoscopy and
collection of samples (ch. 258).

FIGURE 89.1 Infraorbital block in a cat using a 25
gauge needle and tuberculin syringe.

RHINOSCOPY TECHNIQUE
General anesthesia with intubation is required to perform
rhinoscopy completely and safely. Examination of the nose is highly
stimulatory and regional anesthesia with a modified infraorbital
block can decrease discomfort during the procedure.1 A needle or
catheter is inserted into the infraorbital canal parallel to the nasal
cavity (Figure 89.1) and topical anesthetic (0.5-2 mL of
bupivacaine or lidocaine) is injected 5-20 minutes prior to
rhinoscopy. Topical anesthesia of the nasopharynx can be

accomplished using lidocaine gel on long handled cotton-tipped
applicators to decrease the gag reflex and facilitate examination of
the nasopharynx.
Rhinoscopy is best performed with a combination of flexible and
rigid endoscopes. The caudal nasopharynx in a dog or cat is
examined first with a flexible endoscope ∼5 mm in outer diameter.
This is an important part of rhinoscopy because mass lesions can be
sampled with flexible biopsy forceps, foreign bodies removed, and
stenotic lesions identified. Two mouth gags should be in place during
this examination to prevent the animal from biting down on the
scope. In cats, these should be kept in place for a minimal period of
time to avoid impinging on retinal blood flow supplied by the
maxillary artery, which can result in blindness.2 To perform the
examination of the nasopharynx, the endoscope is inserted into the
mouth in an unflexed position until it is beyond the soft palate. The
tip of the scope is then flexed to its maximal angle, positioning the
light of the scope above the soft palate (

Video 89.1). Pulling the

scope forward towards the endoscopist will improve the view of the
choanae. It is important to realize that the image will be upside down
and inverted when this view is obtained. To obtain a biopsy from the
nasopharynx, withdraw the endoscope from the nasopharynx and
pass the biopsy instrument through the channel while the scope is
outside the animal. Manipulate the lever on the scope to note that it
will not flex maximally while the biopsy instrument is in place. After
re-positioning the scope in the nasopharynx, extend the biopsy
instrument towards the lesion, take a firm grasp, and quickly pull the
sample from the mucosa. Without withdrawing the biopsy
instrument into the scope, unflex the bend and remove the scope
from the animal. Extend the biopsy forceps out of the scope to
extract the sample, then obtain additional samples as needed. If a
flexible scope is not available, an attempt can be made to visualize
the choanae through cranial retraction of the soft palate and
insertion of a dental mirror and light source into the mouth;
however, it is very challenging to obtain a biopsy from the
nasopharynx with this method.
After examination of the nasopharynx is complete, ensure that the
cuff of the endotracheal tube is fully inflated to protect the airway

and gently pack the oropharynx with a moistened surgical pad to
prevent aspiration of blood or fluid during rostral rhinoscopy (
Video 89.2). Evaluation of the rostral nasal cavity can be performed
using a flexible endoscope 2.8-5.0 mm outer diameter depending on
the size of the animal, a rigid telescope with sheath (∼5 mm), or the
telescope alone (2.8 mm), bearing in mind that the rigid telescope is
fragile and can break if any force is applied along the shaft. The rigid
scope generally provides better visualization than the flexible scope,
and if a sheath is used, also allows suction and flush. If endoscopes
are not available, a video otoscopy unit can be used, or a standard
otoscope head can be employed. The latter provides little
magnification and does not allow visualization of an instrument
while in the nose but it can be used to provide a spatial assessment of
lesions prior to sampling and it can allow identification of foreign
material.
Prior to passing an instrument into the nasal cavity, the position of
the cribriform plate and entrance to the brain should be
approximated on the outside of the skull by measuring to the level of
the medial canthus of the eye and placing tape on the endoscope or
biopsy instrument. This will prevent excessive passage of the
instrument into the nasal cavity, which could result in penetration of
the brain via the dorsal nasal meatus. In the normal nasal cavity, the
ventral, middle, and dorsal nasal meati can be entered but very little
space is present (

Video 89.3). The epithelium of the turbinates is

generally smooth and pale pink, with minor amounts of mucus
present. The ventral meatus is examined first so that if bleeding
develops, it will not obscure visualization of the middle and dorsal
meati. Lesions within the nose are characterized by increased space
in the case of aspergillosis in the dog (ch. 210) and destructive
rhinitis in the cat, or by decreased space due to the presence of a
neoplastic mass lesion (ch. 213) or fungal granuloma associated
with cryptococcosis (ch. 207) or aspergillosis (ch. 210) in the cat. If
mucus or blood obscures visualization, cautious flushing can be used
via the sheath of the scope in order to clear the field. Gentle suction
can also be applied, although this can induce bleeding. If an
endoscope system is not in use, manual flushing with cold saline can
be performed using a syringe inserted around the alar fold into the

nostril or using a red rubber catheter passed into the nasal cavity.
Forceful infusion of saline in increments of 3-5 mL will lift mucus
and debris from the nose (

Video 89.4). This can be followed by

flushing with air to clear the field of view. The laparotomy pad in the
nasopharynx should be removed and replaced periodically to avoid
oversaturation with fluid. It is useful to evaluate material that has
collected on the pad for evidence of tissue or foreign material. Minor
bleeding or tissue swelling can sometimes be managed by instillation
of oxymetazoline drops; however, excess use of an alpha agonist
could be associated with an increase in blood pressure.
Collection of samples for diagnostic testing is performed after
visual inspection of both nasal cavities, and these are best obtained
with direct visualization of any abnormal region (mass or
granuloma). If desired, samples can be obtained from deep within
the nasal cavity for culture (

Video 89.5). In cats that have had

multiple courses of antibiotics, aerobic and mycoplasmal cultures
can sometimes be useful in guiding antimicrobial treatment of
secondary infection associated with inflammatory rhinitis. A sterile
cytology brush (CytoSoft cytology brush; Medical Packaging Corp.,
Camarillo, CA) is useful for collection of material for culture. Nasal
cytologic evaluation can also be performed but often does not
correlate with histopathologic findings. Some clinicians might prefer
collection of a deep nasal flush using a red rubber catheter, but the
brush technique collects cellular material that can contain bacteria
such as Mycoplasma. It is important to note that culture of nasal
discharge is of no value and intra-nasal bacterial cultures are almost
never useful in dogs. However, samples of tissue or plaque-like
material for fungal culture can be of diagnostic value in both dogs
and cats when the lesion is visually identified and sampled. In dogs
with nasal aspergillosis, fungal hyphae were observed in smears of
nasal exudates or in blind swabs of the nasal cavity in only 13-20% of
cases3 but when visualized samples were obtained, 80-100% of
cytology and cultures were positive.4 If a flexible endoscope or
telescope with sheath is used, through-the-scope biopsy forceps
provide the best opportunity for obtaining a visualized sample;
however, the small size of the channel necessitates use of small

flexible biopsy forceps (usually 1.8 mm). If a rigid telescope is
employed, cup biopsy forceps can be inserted along the shaft of the
endoscope and guided to the site of sampling (Figure 89.2). In
Figure 89.2, A, the rigid telescope is in the nasal cavity of the cat as
the biopsy forceps are advanced. Figure 89.2, B, shows a close-up
of both instruments in the nose of the cat, and Figure 89.2, C,
illustrates sampling of the intra-nasal region with visualization. Rigid
cup biopsy forceps 2-4 mm in size can be used in this fashion,
depending on the size of the nasal opening. If a sheath is employed,
through-the-scope flexible biopsy instruments can be used to
visualize and collect a sample.

FIGURE 89.2 Visualized nasal biopsy technique
in a cat. A, The rigid telescope is inside the nasal
cavity with the biopsy forceps tracking along the top
of the scope. B, Both instruments are inside the
nose. C, Visualization of the lesion during sampling.
After obtaining a sample for histopathologic evaluation, it is wise
to make an impression smear in hopes of obtaining an expedient
diagnosis of either neoplastic or fungal disease. The anesthetic plane
should remain deep throughout the biopsy procedure, and
hemorrhage is controlled prior to recovery of the animal using cold
saline intra-nasal flush and applying ice packs to the nose. Any fluid
in the pharynx should be removed prior to extubation, using suction
and postural drainage.

COMPLICATIONS OF RHINOSCOPY
Some degree of hemorrhage is typically encountered with
rhinoscopy, even when small biopsy samples are obtained.
Conditions such as nasal aspergillosis or neoplasia can be associated
with more marked hemorrhage due to tissue erosion by the disease
process or because of invasion of the vasculature. Minor bleeding can
be controlled by avoiding blood pressure spikes during anesthesia
and recovery. Managing anxiety with judicious doses of
acepromazine, and post-anesthetic analgesia are usually effective. Ice
packs on the nose can be employed, as well as intra-nasal infusion of
a vasoconstrictor agent such as oxymetazoline, although with
substantial hemorrhage, the latter is unlikely to contact the
vasculature sufficiently to provide hemostasis. When hemorrhage is
severe, a peripheral packed cell volume (PCV) should be obtained
and the nose can be packed with cotton-tipped applicators, cotton
balls or pledgets, or tampons, for pressure effects. Pressure can also
be applied to the bleeding area using a balloon catheter. All material
must be removed from the nose at the end of the procedure. When
bleeding persists, ligation or embolization of the carotid artery could
be considered.
Various hemostatic materials have been used to control bleeding
following human endoscopic surgery, some of which are absorbable

and some that need to be removed several days after surgery. Also, in
human medicine, intravenous injection of tranexamic acid has
proven beneficial in providing hemostasis,5 and the hemostatic
properties and safety of this agent have been established in canine
patients.6 Another alternative that could be considered is preanesthetic administration of Yunnan Baiyao.7

FIGURE 89.3 Retrograde flush of the nasal cavity.
A, Sagittal section through the skull of a dog. The
yellow oval represents the location for proper
placement of the Foley balloon to block the
nasopharynx during flushing. B, The head is in a
downward position for flushing, and collection of

From Johnson LR. Canine and Feline Respiratory
Medicine. 2nd ed. Wiley-Blackwell; 2020.

TECHNIQUE FOR NASAL FLUSH
Nasal flush can be performed as part of the rhinoscopic procedure, as
a treatment method for suspected foreign body inhalation, or for
removal of excess mucus in the cat with chronic rhinosinusitis. The
procedure requires full anesthesia and intubation. For antegrade
flush, the pharynx is packed off as described previously (Video 89.2),
and a syringe filled with saline is used to lift material off the nasal
mucosa (Video 89.4

). However, some foreign bodies that are

lodged within the nasal cavity will not be expelled by this technique.
When suspicion is high for a foreign body yet nothing is found when
checking the laparotomy sponge from the back of the pharynx, a
retrograde flush can be performed (Figure 89.3). This is most
easily and safely accomplished by placing a Foley catheter dorsal to
the palate and expanding the balloon to flush fluid from the choanae
out the nostrils. Depending on the size and conformation of the dog’s
head, it can be relatively straightforward to fold the Foley onto itself,
grasp it with right-angle forceps, and pass this through the mouth to
wedge it above the palate. Alternately, biopsy forceps or suture
material can be carried into the pharynx via the ventral meatus of the
nasal cavity, the Foley attached, and the forceps or suture material
withdrawn back through the nose to wedge the balloon of the Foley
dorsal to the palate. After the balloon is expanded, a syringe filled
with saline is attached to the catheter for flushing. The dog’s head is

directed ventrally and material that exits the nose is collected to
identify any foreign material.

Chapter 90: Respiratory and
Inhalant Therapy
Laura A. Nafe

A C RO N YM
MDI metered dose inhaler

By definition, respiratory therapy is the administration of
aerosolized treatments for management of acute or chronic
respiratory conditions. In veterinary medicine, administration of
inhaled medications in this manner is limited by dogs’ and cats’
inability to coordinate inspiration with activation of a metered dose
inhaler (MDI) or nebulization device. Methods utilized in human
pediatric respiratory therapy have been adapted to small animal
veterinary medicine with success in appropriate patients.

NEBULIZATION
Nebulization is the delivery of a substance in the form of small
droplets, facilitating delivery of sterile saline or a medication (usually
diluted in saline to facilitate transport) to the respiratory tract
directly. The particle size delivered varies depending on the type of
nebulizer being used, with most devices delivering particles between
0.5 and 10 microns in diameter. Effective penetration of the lower

airways is achieved in most patients with particles <3-5 microns in
diameter.1

TYPES OF NEBULIZERS
Several types of nebulizers are available for the management of
respiratory disorders. Although all nebulizers are capable of
delivering saline or a medication, the power mechanism, portability,
convenience, and particle size delivered vary. Most common
nebulizers are either ultrasonic or gas-pressure–driven. Many
veterinary hospitals and clinics may have a nebulizer to be used for
inpatient care, but these nebulizers may be cumbersome for
outpatient care due to large size. Particle size delivered is important
when considering which region of the respiratory tract is being
targeted. For example, larger particles (2-10 micron diameter) will be
deposited in the upper respiratory tract and are beneficial for upper
airway (nasal, laryngeal, tracheal) inflammatory diseases.1 Smaller
particles will travel farther in the respiratory tract before being
deposited, and are therefore more useful for lower airway diseases.
In general, nebulizers that generate smaller particles and provide
portability are more expensive, typically ranging in cost from $150 to
$250. For long-term nebulization at home, the author prefers the
Omron vibrating mesh nebulizer (Omron Healthcare, Inc., Lake
Forest, IL) (Figure 90.1). In some geographical areas, there may be
a respiratory pharmacy nearby that is willing to rent a nebulizer for a
specified period of time.

BENEFITs OF NEBULIZATION
Nebulization is an important aspect of respiratory therapy for
patients with acute respiratory conditions, providing hydration or
medication delivery directly to the affected area while minimizing
systemic adverse effects. Of particular importance is the delivery of
water droplets to help improve mucociliary clearance of respiratory
secretions and mucus. Nebulization is not commonly performed
chronically at home, but for inpatient care, it plays an important role
in management of common respiratory conditions.

INDICATIONS FOR NEBULIZATION
In order to understand the indications for saline (0.9% NaCl)
nebulization, one must understand the role of mucus present in the
respiratory tract. Mucus is an adhesive gel consisting of water and
glycoproteins mixed with serum, functioning to trap debris and
bacteria to enhance removal from the respiratory tract.2 Clearance of
mucus is an important respiratory defense mechanism accomplished
by an effective mucociliary apparatus and the cough reflex.3 In order
for the airway cilia to function appropriately, there must be a serous
layer to facilitate movement of the cilia, and therefore mucus, in an
upward motion.3 In addition to rehydration of the mucociliary
apparatus with intravenous fluid therapy, nebulization provides
these patients with direct delivery of saline via droplets to the
respiratory tract, thus hydrating the mucous layer to facilitate
expulsion by the patient via mucociliary clearance and coughing.
Saline nebulization is most commonly administered in patients with
aspiration pneumonitis or pneumonia (ch. 227).
Indications for nebulized medications include resistant bacterial
infections, inflammatory airway diseases (ch. 217), and treatment or
prevention of bronchoconstriction (ch. 215) with antimicrobials,
glucocorticoids and bronchodilators being delivered for each
condition, respectively.

HOW TO PERFORM NEBULIZATION
When providing saline nebulization, approximately 3-5 mL of
normal saline (0.9% NaCl) is placed in the nebulization cup and
when powered, the nebulizer will convert this volume of liquid into
saline droplets over a period of time (typically 10-20 minutes). There
are multiple techniques that can be utilized to ensure the nebulized
droplets are directed into the respiratory tract. Since most dogs and
cats breathe through the nose, the nasal turbinates may trap some of
the saline particles. In dogs that are panting, many of these particles
may be trapped in the back of the mouth and/or swallowed due to
the lack of deep inspiration. The author has found a facemask or
small tent to be useful in facilitating delivery in patients that will

tolerate these additions. In most cases, nebulization should be
followed by coupage or light exercise (if tolerated by the patient) to
further improve expulsion of respiratory secretions (

Video 90.1).

Contraindications to coupage include regurgitation, recent thoracic
surgery, and recumbency. If the patient is recumbent, frequent
repositioning to limit atelectasis and improve movement of airway
secretions is an important aspect of patient care.

FIGURE 90.1 Omron vibrating mesh nebulizer
(Omron Healthcare) with facemask attached.

NEBULIZED MEDICATIONS
There is minimal evidence to support the use of nebulized
medications in small animal veterinary medicine. Although most
medications that are water soluble can be administered via
nebulization, the most commonly nebulized drug classes are
antibiotics (e.g., gentamicin), anti-inflammatories (e.g., fluticasone
propionate), and bronchodilators (e.g., albuterol). Epinephrine has
been found to reduce mucosal edema in the upper airway of dogs
with brachycephalic airway syndrome (ch. 213) and may be
beneficial perioperatively in such dogs.4 Other medications that have
been evaluated for nebulization in a research setting include
lidocaine and N-acetylcysteine.
A clinician may consider nebulized aminoglycoside treatment in
canine patients with multi-drug resistant bacterial pneumonia (e.g.,
Bordetella bronchiseptica, Pseudomonas spp.), usually as an adjunct
treatment to systemic antimicrobial therapy. The advantage of
nebulized aminoglycoside therapy is the ability to administer an
appropriate antibiotic with low risk of systemic adverse effects (e.g.,
nephrotoxicosis).5 Clinicians should keep in mind that aerosolized
antibiotics may cause irritation to the airways and dosage calculation
is often approximate, with it being impossible to estimate the
percentage of the drug that will reach the site of infection. The
author administers gentamicin at 6-8 mg/kg diluted in 5-10 mL of
saline administered once daily via facemask. The concentration
should not exceed 25 mg/mL, because this could decrease drug
delivery.
Glucocorticoid agents are more commonly delivered via MDI to
patients with inflammatory airway disease. In medium- or largebreed dogs, nebulization is the preferred method for effectively
targeting the lower airways. Budesonide has been evaluated for
nebulization in humans, although no studies have evaluated
nebulized glucocorticoids in dogs.6 When considering this route of
administration, the clinician must take into account the limitations
of nebulization, especially cost, as these patients will likely require
lifelong therapy.
Like glucocorticoids, bronchodilator agents are most commonly
delivered via MDI. Nebulized albuterol (0.5% albuterol [salbutamol];

1.25 mg/cat diluted in 2 mL of saline repeated q 1-4 h PRN) is
occasionally used as a one-time treatment for feline patients
presenting with status asthmaticus (ch. 215) or as pre-treatment for
those undergoing a procedure that may induce or worsen
bronchoconstriction (e.g., bronchoalveolar lavage; ch. 93). If
available, nebulized albuterol is preferred over MDI for emergency
management of feline status asthmaticus. This is because patients in
respiratory distress are often not taking adequate breaths, which
limits effective delivery to the lower airways when an MDI is used
with a spacer device. Although an injectable bronchodilator (e.g.,
terbutaline) is preferred in these situations, cats with clinically
significant heart disease may not be good candidates for parenteral
beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonists or methylxanthine
bronchodilator agents. Administration of beta-2 adrenergic receptor
agonists is not typically recommended in dogs with respiratory
disease, as bronchoconstriction is not a common feature of canine
respiratory disease. Parenteral and oral administration of
methylxanthine bronchodilator agents is used in feline and canine
respiratory disease, but inhaled therapy has not been evaluated.
Nebulized epinephrine (0.05 mg/kg epinephrine added to 0.9%
saline to make up a 5 mL nebulization solution) delivered via flow-by
manner using a mesh nebulizer at a rate of 0.25 mL/minute over 10
minutes was evaluated in dogs with brachycephalic airway syndrome
as a method of improving upper airway obstruction.4 Adverse events
associated with epinephrine nebulization included excitement and
nausea in 12% of dogs.4 Results of this study suggest that dogs with
severe brachycephalic airway syndrome had improvement of airway
obstruction preoperatively and most treated dogs had reduced
airway obstruction postoperatively.4
Nebulized lidocaine (4% [without preservatives] diluted to 2%; 2
mg/kg q 8 h for 2 weeks) has been evaluated as a potential novel
anti-inflammatory and bronchodilating agent for management of
feline asthma.7 Although no overt adverse effects were observed,
lidocaine was only found to reduce airway hyperresponsiveness and
should not be used as monotherapy for management of asthma.7 In
specific cases, nebulized lidocaine may provide an alternative
bronchodilator option in cats with heart disease.

Xylitol, a five-carbon sugar, is thought to hydrate the mucus layer
and have potential antibacterial properties. As a result, this therapy
has been investigated as a potential management strategy for cystic
fibrosis in humans. A small safety study evaluated nebulized xylitol
administration for 14 consecutive days in research beagle dogs and
found no adverse effects, contrary to well-recognized toxic effects
with oral ingestion (ch. 134).8 The use of nebulized xylitol in
veterinary clinical medicine has not been evaluated and cannot be
recommended until further safety and efficacy information is
available.
N-acetylcysteine, an antioxidant and mucolytic, is occasionally
administered parenterally, orally or via nebulization as a mucolytic
agent. Evidence suggests that nebulized N-acetylcysteine may
promote bronchoconstriction and resultant airflow limitation in cats
with experimentally-induced asthma when delivered via
endotracheal nebulization.9 Diseases that result in excessive mucus
production in dogs (e.g., pneumonia, ciliary dyskinesia) may benefit
from N-acetylcysteine. However, the risk of bronchoconstriction
during or after nebulized N-acetylcysteine is a concern, deterring
most clinicians from using this treatment. It is not recommended by
the author. Pre-treatment with a bronchodilator is recommended if
this treatment is administered.

LIMITATIONS OF NEBULIZATION
Although nebulization of medications is an attractive option for
many patients with respiratory disease, there are limitations that
should be considered. First, there is concern for the amount of drug
that is delivered to the affected area, with particle size playing an
important role in the area being medicated. Second, the expense
associated with purchasing or renting a nebulization device and the
cost of the medication can be substantial. Third, the time required to
deliver the medication appropriately may be labor-intensive for
many caretakers, especially for patients with chronic conditions
requiring multiple treatments per day indefinitely. Lastly, there is
always potential for a medication to cause further irritation to the
airways, in particular with antibiotics and bronchodilator agents. It

is important to consider these limitations when recommending
nebulized medications.

METERED DOSE INHALER
Delivery of medications via pressurized MDI is the standard of care
for management of many human respiratory conditions and is
continuing to gain popularity in veterinary medicine. The main
limitation of MDI therapy in dogs and cats is the inability to
coordinate respiration with the release of the actuation. The use of a
facemask and space chamber improves this limitation and makes
delivery of medications via MDI a good option in small animal
respiratory medicine.

BENEFIT OF MDI
Like nebulization, delivery of medications via MDI allows treatment
of a condition locally while minimizing systemic side-effects of the
medications being used. Unlike nebulization, administration of MDI
is not labor-intensive and is well tolerated by most patients after
appropriate acclimation to the facemask/chamber device. In fact,
many cat owners find inhaled delivery of medications easier than
oral administration.

INDICATIONS FOR MDI
Respiratory diseases that result in inflammation and/or
bronchoconstriction can be managed with MDI therapy. In dogs,
common diseases managed with glucocorticoids delivered via MDI
include chronic bronchitis (ch. 215), eosinophilic
bronchopneumopathy (ch. 215), and potentially tracheal collapse
(ch. 215) and lymphoplasmacytic rhinitis (ch. 213). As mentioned
earlier, dogs do not develop true smooth muscle
bronchoconstriction, and therefore, do not benefit from beta-2
adrenergic receptor agonist medications (e.g., albuterol). In cats,
common diseases managed with medications delivered via MDI

include feline asthma (ch. 215), chronic bronchitis (ch. 215), and
potentially lymphoplasmacytic rhinitis (ch. 213).

HOW TO ADMINISTER MEDICATIONS
VIA MDI
Cats and dogs cannot coordinate inspiration with release of the
aerosolized medication from a MDI, making an aerosol-holding
chamber or spacer device indispensable. Various spacer devices, all
equipped with an exhalation valve, are available for purchase, with
most costing approximately $40-$80/space chamber. The MDI fits
on one end of the spacer, and the other end of the spacer has an
attachment for the facemask. Shaking the MDI prior to delivery is
necessary, as this opens an internal valve within the canister. The
MDI should then be attached to the space chamber with facemask,
and the space chamber should be placed over the nose and mouth of
the patient, ensuring a tight fit to maximize delivery of the
aerosolized medication to the patient’s airways (Figure 90.2; Video
90.2

). With the actuation of the device, the MDI delivers a

precise dose of the aerosol drug into the space chamber. The space
chamber serves as a holding device for the aerosol so that the cat or
dog can inhale it over a period of time. It is important to watch the
patient take 7-10 adequate breaths, as it is natural for the dog or cat
to stop breathing when the facemask is placed over the nose and
mouth.

MEDICATIONS DELIVERED BY MDI
Glucocorticoids are the medications that are most commonly
administered via MDI in small animal respiratory therapy, with
fluticasone propionate being preferred because it is the most potent
(18 times as potent as dexamethasone) and has the longest halflife.10,11 In addition, the majority of inhaled medication
(approximately 70% or more) will be deposited in the oropharynx
after delivery and will be swallowed. Of the corticosteroids available
for inhalation, fluticasone is poorly absorbed in the gastrointestinal

tract, and therefore, minimal systemic side effects will result.10
Fluticasone (110 mcg q 12 h), budesonide (only available as dry
powder MDI) (200 mcg q 12 h), and flunisolide (250 mcg q 12 h)
have been investigated and found to be effective in management of
feline inflammatory airway with minimal systemic adverse effects.1214
Although used often clinically, there is little evidence to support
the use of inhaled glucocorticoids in canine inflammatory airway
diseases.15,16 Fluticasone is often preferred due to availability and
efficacy; an alternative glucocorticoid may be chosen for particular
patients based on ease of dosing, cost, and/or availability.

FIGURE 90.2 Administration of a medication via
metered dose inhaler (MDI), showing the entire
inhalation device, equipped with facemask, space
chamber, and MDI (Aerokat Trudell Medical
International).

Beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist medications (e.g., albuterol)
are delivered via MDI in feline respiratory medicine, most commonly
for management of acute respiratory distress secondary to
bronchoconstriction. Racemic (R,S)-albuterol is not recommended
for chronic management, as the S-enantiomer is associated with
airway hyperreactivity and development of airway inflammation.17 If
chronic bronchodilator therapy via MDI is desired, daily treatment
with levalbuterol, the R-enantiomer of albuterol, is recommended.
The racemic formulation of albuterol can be used for rescue therapy
as needed for respiratory distress.

LIMITATIONS OF MDI
As with nebulization, there are limitations that should be considered
when recommending treatment with inhaled medications. There is
always concern for the amount of drug that is actually delivered to
the lower airway; this is especially true in any patient weighing >7-10
kg. The expense associated with purchasing MDIs can be financially
limiting for owners over time. In humans, inhaled glucocorticoids
can increase the risk of respiratory infections, in particular oral
Candida infections. Lastly, there is always the potential for a
medication to cause further irritation to the airways, in particular
with bronchodilator agents (e.g., racemic albuterol).

INHALED CHEMOTHERAPY AND
IMMUNOTHERAPY
Treatment of primary and metastatic pulmonary neoplasia using
inhaled chemotherapy has been minimally evaluated in small animal
veterinary medicine. This technique offers a method of increasing
exposure of the lung tumor to the chemotherapy agent while
minimizing systemic adverse effects. Delivery of cisplatin to a
specific lung lobe via bronchoscopy with a specialized catheter has
been described in normal, healthy dogs.18 Aerosols of interleukin-2
liposomes have been evaluated in 9 dogs with pulmonary neoplasia
with positive results and minimal toxicosis. This could represent a

promising potential therapy in specific cases.19 Limitations of
inhaled therapy for neoplasia are many, including need for
specialized equipment, anesthesia, risk of human exposure, and
expense. For specific cases (e.g., non-resectable primary lung
tumor), inhaled chemotherapy may be a viable option for animals
belonging to motivated clients.

Chapter 91: Blood Pressure
Measurement
Andrew H. Sparkes

Veterinary Blood Pressure Society

DAP diastolic arterial pressure
HDO “high definition” oscillometric
MAP mean arterial pressure
NIBP non-invasive blood pressure
SAP systolic arterial pressure
TOD target organ damage

Systemic arterial blood pressure (BP) measurement has become
established as a vital technique in small animal practice. The major
indications are monitoring of BP under anesthesia (primarily to
prevent hypotension), the monitoring of BP in conscious patients
(primarily for the diagnosis and monitoring of hypertension), and
the monitoring of hemodynamically unstable patients.
Direct BP measurement through arterial catheterization is
regarded as the “gold standard” for assessing systemic BP, and

because of its accuracy, it may be indicated in some situations such
as hemodynamically unstable critical care patients.1,2 Although
arterial catheterization allows the direct measurement of systolic
(SAP), diastolic (DAP), and mean arterial pressure (MAP), this is an
invasive procedure and not suitable for use in most conscious
veterinary patients,2 which is the focus of this chapter.
Many non-invasive BP (NIBP) monitors are available, allowing
routine indirect measurement of BP in conscious animals. It is
important to recognize that measurements obtained will be
influenced by the type of equipment, the way it is used, the
environment within which it is used, the individual animal, and the
way the animal is handled. Interpretation of individual BP values can
therefore be challenging, but inter- and intra-individual variation in
BP estimates can be minimized by taking a careful and methodical
approach to how patients are assessed.

EQUIPMENT
The two commonly used techniques for NIBP assessment are the
oscillometric method (

Video 91.1) and Doppler

sphygmomanometry (Videos 91.2, 91.3). With oscillometry, a new
generation of “high definition” oscillometric (HDO) monitors has
been developed. They are designed to better enable measurement of
BP in animals with high heart rates and across a wider range of BPs.1
All types of NIBP monitors rely on measuring the pressure in an
inflatable cuff used for occluding the flow of blood through an artery,
with the major difference between the techniques being the method
by which blood flow is detected. The oscillometric method relies on
inflation of the cuff beyond the point of occlusion of arterial blood
flow, and as the cuff slowly deflates the oscillation of the arterial wall
from the return of pulsatile flow of blood is detected within the cuff
and the pressure measured. Equipment-specific algorithms provide
values for SAP, DAP and MAP.1 By contrast, the Doppler method is
based on detection of pulsatile blood flow in an artery using a
Doppler probe placed distal to the site of an inflatable cuff which is
attached to a sphygmomanometer. The cuff is inflated beyond

occlusion of arterial blood flow and then slowly deflated, with the
point at which the return of arterial blood flow is detected taken as
the SAP. Optical plethysmography can also be used for detecting
arterial blood flow, but this technique has rarely been adopted for
use in animals.1

EQUIPMENT ACCURACY
It is well recognized that NIBP methods have inherent inaccuracies
and variances from direct arterial pressure measurements1,2 but, as
in human medicine, this does not negate the value of NIBP
measurement.
In 2007, the American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine
(ACVIM) developed consensus guidelines on the identification and
management of systemic hypertension in dogs and cats.3 Those
guidelines included recommendations to be used for the validation of
NIBP equipment in dogs and cats, proposed by the ACVIM
Hypertension Consensus Panel and the Veterinary Blood Pressure
Society (AHCP-VBPS). These recommendations noted that
validation can only be applied to the device used in animals of the
same species and under the same conditions (e.g., validation of
equipment in a study of dogs cannot be extrapolated and applied to
cats, and validation of equipment in animals under anesthesia
cannot be extrapolated to conscious animals).
From a review of the published literature on validation of NIBP
techniques in animals,4 it is clear that the great majority of studies
have been performed on anesthetized (rather than conscious) dogs
or cats, and with very few exceptions, the studies have failed to reach
the criteria laid out in the AHCP-VBPS recommendations.4 This
emphasizes some of the inherent inaccuracies associated with NIBP
measurement, but it is also clear that some types of equipment
perform better than others in given circumstances and with
particular species.4 This is not surprising, especially with
oscillometric devices where proprietary software and algorithms are
used for determining BP values. Choosing equipment carefully, with
consideration of the results of published independent studies, may

therefore help to reduce equipment-associated inaccuracies,
especially with oscillometric devices.
Although all methods of NIBP measurement are inaccurate
compared with direct BP, and although no equipment has currently
been fully validated (according to the AHCP-VBPS criteria) for use in
conscious dogs or cats, this does not mean the equipment and
techniques are not clinically useful. Inherent inaccuracies need to be
recognized, and caution in the interpretation of BP data is
warranted. With a careful and standardized approach to use in
clinical practice, these methods yield clinically valuable data, as has
been demonstrated clearly in numerous studies. Furthermore, due to
inherent differences between direct and indirect BP assessment, it
has been questioned whether direct BP values are necessarily the
“gold standard” to which NIBP methods should be compared, as this
is not the case in human medicine.4,5

CHOOSING EQUIPMENT TO USE IN
DOGS AND CATS
Although many studies have investigated different NIBP monitors,
compared different monitors with each other, and/or compared the
results of NIBP monitors with direct BP values, there is little
consensus to emerge from these studies and conflicting results are
common, making firm recommendations on the choice and use of
different monitors difficult.
In both dogs and cats, Doppler, oscillometric, and HDO monitors
have all been used successfully, with the cuffs being applied to the
forelimb (typically proximal to the carpus), hindlimb (proximal or
distal to the tarsus) or proximal tail. A Doppler probe generally is
used for detecting blood flow in the common digital artery, dorsal
pedal artery or the coccygeal artery, whereas oscillometric and HDO
cuffs generally measure BP in the radial (or occasionally brachial),
cranial tibial, dorsal pedal or coccygeal artery, depending on location
of cuff placement. As would be expected, results obtained using
different equipment demonstrate appreciably different results, and
this is also true when different oscillometric devices are
compared.4,6-12 This emphasizes not only the need to try to choose

monitors carefully, but also to ensure wherever possible that the
same monitor is used each time, at the same anatomic location, when
repeat measurements are assessed in individual animals.
While oscillometric and HDO devices are able to produce SAP,
MAP and DAP readings, the use of Doppler sphygmomanometry is
generally limited to estimation of SAP because assessment of DAP is
associated with wide interindividual variation due to its subjective
and imprecise nature.2,13 Additionally, there is evidence that
although an HDO monitor has shown good accuracy for use in
conscious cats,14 the reliability also was much better for SAP than for
DAP. Fortunately, in assessment of potential hypertension in
animals these limitations do not present a major problem, as most
hypertensive dogs and cats display systolic hypertension,3,13,15 and
current hypertension guidelines focus on the assessment of SAP
values.3,15,16
The size of cats and small dogs may make traditional oscillometry
more challenging—many studies suggest this method may be
associated with a higher rate of failures and/or take a longer time to
achieve BP readings. This may be as a result of the higher heart rates
in smaller animals and/or the smaller size of their peripheral
arteries.2,10,14 In cats, and smaller dogs, it may therefore be prudent
to consider the use of Doppler sphygmomanometry or HDO rather
than oscillometry.
From numerous studies, it is clear that the level of arousal or
anxiety in both dogs and cats can have a significant effect on
measured BP values,3,16-20 and that the position of the animal and
the site at which BP is measured can also significantly affect results.
Therefore, it is vital that all these variables be taken into
consideration when measuring BP in dogs and cats as efforts to
reduce the influence of external variables will help to make
measurements more reliable.

PROTOCOLS FOR MEASUREMENT OF
BP

Protocols for the measurement of BP in dogs and cats have been
proposed by the ACVIM3,15 and the International Society of Feline
Medicine,16 and these have been widely adopted. For reliable NIBP
assessment in patients, it is recommended that every clinic follow a
standardized protocol with careful recording of details. Based on the
published data, the following procedures can be recommended:

CALIBRATION
It is recommended that NIBP equipment be calibrated every 6
months by the clinic or the manufacturer to ensure pressure in the
inflated cuff is being measured accurately.15

ENVIRONMENT
The animal should be in a calm, quiet room, away from other
animals. Measuring BP in a cage/kennel in a quiet hospitalization
ward may occasionally be appropriate if the animal is sufficiently
relaxed, but this is not optimal, should not be done routinely, and
appropriate caution should be used in interpreting results. With cats,
having them resting on their own bedding (with their own scent)
and/or using a synthetic pheromone (e.g., Feliway Classic or Feliway
Optimum; Ceva) product in the environment or on the bedding may
help reduce stress.

ACCLIMATIZATION
The dog or cat should be allowed a minimum of 5-10 minutes in the
room to acclimatize and relax,15,20,21 including allowing the animal
to explore the room and interact with people if it wants to. For cats, a
carrier with a removable top will allow the cat to stay in the bottom
of the carrier if it prefers.

PERSONNEL

The minimum number of people necessary (usually 2) should be
used for performing a BP assessment. In most cases, having the
owner present to help provide gentle reassurance to the animal and
keep it calm will be helpful.19 Using a trained, experienced individual
to measure BP increases the reliability of the results,7,22 and a nurse
or technician who routinely undertakes the procedure is often better
than a veterinarian.

RESTRAINT AND POSITIONING
Animals should be handled gently, respectfully and with minimal
restraint to avoid inducing anxiety. They should be in a settled,
relaxed, and comfortable position. If animals become anxious or
agitated, or if they will not keep still during the procedure, it is better
to stop and allow them time to settle before trying again. The dog or
cat should remain still and in the same position throughout BP
measurement if at all possible. It is suggested that where possible,
the site of BP measurement should be roughly on the same
horizontal plane as the heart.13 The position of the animal (e.g.,
standing vs. sitting vs. lateral recumbency) can affect the measured
BP.23-25 While different animals may be more comfortable and
relaxed in different positions, for repeatability and reproducibility
within an individual animal, ensuring the same position is adopted
each time BP is measured is important.

CHOICE AND POSITION OF CUFF
The site chosen for BP measurement will depend partly on what is
tolerated best by the animal, in part by the equipment used and in
part by the preference of the person taking the BP. In cats, there is
some evidence that the tail is better tolerated when using HDO, and
produces a higher proportion of valid readings.26
Unless specified differently by the equipment manufacturer, the
cuff width used should be 30-40% of the circumference of the
limb/tail where it is used.2,13,15,27,28 In human medicine it is also

well-recognized that the length of the inflatable portion of the cuff is
important and it is recommended this be approximately 80% of the
circumference of the limb; a short inflatable portion of the cuff will
lead to erroneously high BP readings, and conversely, a long
inflatable portion of the cuff can lead to undermeasurement.29 The
inflatable portion of the cuff must be positioned over the artery to be
occluded, and when not inflated, cuffs should fit snugly but should
not restrict blood flow. Cuffs can be secured with a Velcro fastener or
a piece of tape, but this should never wrap around the limb or tail.
Studies have shown that the results of NIBP estimates vary
significantly depending on the site at which BP is measured.8,9,12,18,24,25,30-32 As with the position of the animal and the
type of equipment used, this means that for practical purposes to
optimize repeatability and reproducibility within an individual
animal, it is important to use the same site for cuff placement and BP
measurement each time.

RECORDING AND USING
MEASUREMENTS
The first BP measurement is usually discarded. Subsequently, ideally
5-7 consecutive and consistent (<20% variability) measurements
should be made and SAP calculated as the mean of these. If there is a
consistent downward (or upward) trend in readings, or >20%
variation, further measurements should be made until 5-7 consistent
readings are achieved. If necessary, the cuff should be adjusted
and/or a different site used to enable consecutive consistent
readings.9,12,15,25 All readings should be recorded, but only the 5-7
consistent readings should be used to calculate BP. If there is doubt
over BP validity, the procedure should be repeated and this can be
done immediately, after further acclimatization, or at a later time.

REFERENCE INTERVALS
In its 2018 consensus guidelines,15 the ACVIM recommended
classification of SAP readings according to the risk of the patient

suffering target organ damage (TOD). Using appropriate equipment,
with experienced personnel and when used under recommended
conditions, the following classification was recommended for both
cats and dogs:
• SAP <140 mm Hg—“Normotensive” with a minimal risk of
TOD
• SAP 140-159 mm Hg—“Prehypertensive” with a low risk of
TOD
• SAP 160-179 mm Hg—“Hypertensive” with a moderate risk of
TOD, and
• SAP ≥180 mm Hg—“Severely hypertensive” with a high risk of
TOD
The use of experienced personnel and appropriate equipment
under recommended conditions is to reduce situational hypertension
and decrease the likelihood of a falsely elevated result. The authors
also pointed out that in the absence of identifiable TOD, in most
cases decisions about classification and treatment of patients should
be based on measurement of BP on more than one occasion, and that
the interval between testing may depend on the values obtained (e.g.,
a shorter period between repeat BP measurement when the risk of
TOD is moderate to high).

CONSISTENCY AND RECORDS
Careful records should always be kept, and these should include the
room/location used, the personnel involved, equipment used, site
and size of the cuff, demeanor of the animal (a subjective assessment
of stress/anxiety levels), and the position of the animal. For
meaningful BP comparisons, assessments for each animal should be
replicated using the same protocols, as far as possible, each time.

ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR
DOPPLER EQUIPMENT (Figure 91.1)

Dampening the hair and skin with isopropyl alcohol and using plenty
of ultrasound gel helps ensure a good contact between the Doppler
probe and the skin for detecting arterial blood flow. Clipping the hair
at the site is not usually needed but is preferred by some.
Inflating (and deflating) the cuff a few times before making
recordings helps the animal get used to the sensation. The Doppler
probe is held on top of, and perpendicular to, the relevant artery
using gentle pressure to avoid occlusion of the artery, and its position
is adjusted slowly until blood flow is heard. Using headphones when
measuring BP avoids loud sounds startling the dog or cat and
causing anxiety.17
The cuff should be inflated to 20-40 mm Hg above the point where
blood flow is no longer heard, and air then allowed to slowly bleed
from the cuff, with SAP taken as the point at which pulsatile blood
flow is first detected again.

ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR
OSCILLOMETRIC AND HDO
EQUIPMENT (Figure 91.2)
Patient movement can cause false or failed BP readings with
oscillometry and HDO, so ensuring the animal stays still is important
and, as noted, using the tail may help reduce the risks of movement
in some animals.26 The cuff should be chosen, placed, and used
according to the manufacturer’s instructions, ensuring the
appropriate portion of the cuff is placed over the artery where
pressure is to be measured.
Where equipment permits (e.g., HDO), the device should always
be linked to a PC or tablet using the supplied software. Visual
inspection of the recording on the monitor allows confirmation that
the deflation of the cuff is linear and that the pulse waves are
smooth, with an outline approximating a bell-shaped curve (see
Figure 91.2). If these criteria are not met, the reading should be
discarded as unreliable.

FIGURE 91.1 Measuring blood pressure in a cat
using Doppler sphygmomanometry. The Doppler
probe is being held over the palmar common digital
artery. Inset shows the manometer.

FIGURE 91.2 Measuring blood pressure in a cat
using “high definition” oscillometry (HDO). The
HDO cuff is placed on the proximal tail. Inset shows
the PC screen demonstrating characteristics of an
acceptable reading.

CONCLUSIONS
Just as in human medicine, the use of NIBP monitors in animals is
associated with certain inherent inaccuracies. However, with
experience, with choosing appropriate equipment, and by adhering
to appropriate protocols, it is possible to measure BP in most
conscious dogs and cats rapidly and to gain BP results that are
meaningful and may provide critical information for the clinical
assessment and management of the patient.
