Chapter 92: Thoracocentesis
and Thoracostomy Tube
Placement
Timothy B. Hackett

A C RO N YM
IV intravenous

Space-occupying lesions in the pleural space reduce tidal volume,
decrease lung compliance, and cause a restrictive breathing pattern.
Restrictive breathing is characterized by rapid, shallow respirations
and dull lung sounds (chs. 37, 212, and 220). In some cases, such as
with tension pneumothorax, increased intrathoracic pressures can
impair venous return to the heart, resulting in circulatory shock and
further compromise of oxygen supply to vital organs. While
emergency ultrasound and radiographs are used to diagnose air and
fluid in the pleural space, in emergency settings these conditions can
be simultaneously diagnosed and treated by rapid thoracocentesis.
Once removed, fluid can be evaluated to determine the likely source
(ch. 71). Diaphragmatic hernia and intrathoracic masses often
require additional imaging for definitive diagnosis. Ultrasonographic
examination is an excellent way to identify pleural fluid (ch. 73).
Pleural air is harder to visualize with ultrasound. Instead, clinicians
can be alerted to air in the pleural space by lack of a glide sign, the

visualization of visceral pleura of the lungs sliding back and forth
against the parietal pleura of the chest wall.1 Along with glide sign,
pneumothorax can be ruled out by seeing a lung pulse, or B lines,
and ruled in by noting the return of a glide sign and/or presence of a
lung point (ch. 73). A novel protocol has been evaluated involving
abnormal curtain signs which can be caused by the presence of free
air within and/or cranial to the costophrenic recess.2

THORACOCENTESIS
OVERVIEW AND PURPOSE
Thoracocentesis (pleurocentesis, chest tap) is a clinical procedure
that can be performed for diagnostic and/or therapeutic purposes.3
Its principal indications are for the withdrawal of free fluid in
patients with pleural effusion4 and free air in patients with
pneumothorax.5

EQUIPMENT AND MATERIALS
Thoracocentesis requires a source of negative pressure and a means
to reach the pleural space.5 All materials must be sterile. The
negative pressure is provided by a syringe (3-12 mL syringes for
diagnostic centesis; 20-60 mL syringes for therapeutic centesis). For
entering the pleural space, some clinicians prefer to use a needle or
butterfly catheter for cats and small- or medium-breed dogs (e.g., 21to 23-gauge), whereas others prefer the safety of a protected needle,
teat cannula or over-the-needle, intravenous (IV)-type catheter with
a removable stylet (18- to 22-gauge). The advantage of a butterfly
catheter is maneuverability and rigidity, which avoids kinking. The
advantage of an IV catheter is its flexible plastic structure, which
makes it atraumatic once the stylet is removed. In giant-breed dogs
and obese patients, the sheer thickness of the body wall and subcutis
could make a butterfly catheter impractical or impossible to use. A
sterile IV fluid extension set, and 3-way stopcock or other 1-way
valve system, are useful when using a needle or IV catheter for

thoracocentesis. Additional materials that are needed are clippers for
removing hair, and aseptic preparation materials such as gauze and
antiseptic for disinfecting the overlying skin. Local anesthetic is
essentially never used, and aseptic draping should not be necessary
provided the hair is sufficiently clipped.

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
In most cases, diagnostic imaging is necessary immediately prior to,
or while, performing thoracocentesis. Thoracic radiographs and
point of care ultrasound are the two methods used most commonly,
and each has its advantages (ch. 73). Performing a thoracocentesis
without any diagnostic imaging (“blind tap”), based on thoracic
percussion or simply as an emergent intervention for a critically
dyspneic patient, comes with substantial risks of iatrogenic
complications (notably lung laceration) if the patient does not in fact
have pleural effusion, or has only a small volume that does not
warrant centesis. Imaging is recommended to confirm (radiographs
or ultrasound) and localize (ultrasound) pleural effusion
immediately prior to thoracocentesis whenever possible.

PROCEDURE
Choose a side of the thorax and location that is farthest from vessels
and viscera as the point of needle/catheter entry. This is easier when
ultrasound is used to identify large pockets of pleural fluid. Without
ultrasound, and in a patient with a uniform distribution of effusion
throughout the pleural space, the 7th to 9th intercostal spaces, dorsal
to the costochondral junction, are farthest from the heart, liver, and
(on the left side) the caudal vena cava.3 The patient is usually in
sternal recumbency for withdrawing effusion, and in sternal or
lateral recumbency (centesis performed on the nondependent side
when in lateral) for pneumothorax. The desired area of entry is
clipped of hair and aseptically prepared, and this area is usually at
least 5 × 5 cm in a cat or small dog and larger in larger patients.
Suitable restraint is necessary, and the degree of restraint must be
extremely judicious to avoid adding stress and worsening respiratory

compromise in a dyspneic patient. Sedation is administered only
rarely, since affected patients may be hemodynamically unstable. If
needed, butorphanol 0.1-0.2 mg/kg IV (single dose) would be a
reasonable first consideration.
The sterile glove wrapper is opened and flattened on a table or
Mayo stand to serve as a sterile field for the syringe and either the
butterfly catheter or the IV catheter and extension tubing. The
hairless skin over the site of entry is aseptically prepared. The
veterinarian dons the sterile gloves and connects the syringe either to
the butterfly needle or to the sterile IV extension tubing that is in
turn connected to the IV catheter and stylet. When large-volume
therapeutic centesis is the goal, a sterile three-way stopcock should
be placed between the syringe and either butterfly or extension
tubing; this allows repeated emptying of the syringe each time it is
full so further fluid withdrawal can be pursued while the
needle/catheter stays in place.
The veterinarian is now ready to enter the pleural space (Video
220.2

). The veterinarian should identify the side of the needle

with the sharp point and the opposite side with the beveled opening.
The goal after insertion and confirmation of pleural air or fluid is to
reposition the needle with the sharp tip against the chest wall and
the open bevel directed toward the lungs. This will allow lung to be
brought back in contact with the chest wall without risking
laceration.
Ideally, in addition to help restraining the animal, two people
should perform the procedure with one manipulating the needle and
the other holding the syringe and stopcock. If only one person is
performing the thoracocentesis, the veterinarian should hold the
syringe in the nondominant hand and the needle/catheter in the
dominant hand. Using the index finger of the dominant hand, the
veterinarian identifies the intercostal space over the desired area of
entry. The veterinarian removes the cap of the needle or catheter and
penetrates the skin over the intercostal space. As soon as the tip of
the needle or catheter is in the subcutis, the veterinarian should
apply negative pressure to the syringe so that the first flashback of
fluid can be observed once the tip enters the pleural space. If the
needle strikes rib, the veterinarian should withdraw by only a
millimeter or two and angle the needle or catheter cranially, then

advance again. This way, it passes into the intercostal space off the
cranial aspect of the rib that was struck, and not the caudal aspect
where intercostal vessels and nerves could be lacerated.
While applying negative pressure to the syringe, the veterinarian
advances the catheter or needle until fluid (pleural effusion) or air
(pneumothorax) begins to be withdrawn (Video 220.3

). At this

time, the veterinarian will advance the butterfly catheter needle
another millimeter or two, or will advance the catheter several
millimeters and withdraw the stylet. In the latter instance, it is
important for the veterinarian to quickly cap the catheter stylet with
a thumb to prevent iatrogenic pneumothorax, then remove the stylet
from the IV tubing and immediately connect the tubing to the
catheter to begin fluid withdrawal. The process of fluid withdrawal is
often intermittent. Chest wall movements can displace the needle or
catheter, can kink IV catheters, and can displace the effusion itself. If
flow stops completely, the needle or catheter may be rotated 90° or
180° or withdrawn by a millimeter or two at a time. A butterfly
catheter needle or steel stylet should never be pivoted in a way that
makes its tip arc inside the patient, because doing that uses the body
wall as a pivot point and can result in profound lung lacerations by
the tip of the needle or stylet. Rather, redirecting a needle or catheter
must always begin with partial withdrawal so the needle or stylet tip
has almost left the pleural space. The volume to be withdrawn is
generally 6 mL for a diagnostic centesis. For a therapeutic centesis
remove the largest amount that can be aspirated with a patient
remaining comfortable. Some clinicians recommend caution when
thoracic radiographs show rounding of lung lobes, indicating chronic
pleural effusion, together with chylous effusion. This combination
suggests that fibrosing pleuritis may be present, and the risk of nonexpandable lung and iatrogenic pneumothorax from overzealous
thoracocentesis, is greater in this situation (ch. 220). When the
desired amount of fluid has been withdrawn, the needle or catheter is
withdrawn in a single, smooth motion and a sterile-gloved finger is
used to rub the skin over the site of entry to help close the needle
tract.

OUTCOME

Repeated centeses are possible, and there is no documented
maximum number of times the procedure can be performed in a dog
or cat that needs it. Typically, a hospitalized animal that requires
centesis several times in a 24-hour period will have thoracostomy
tubes placed for ongoing drainage and a thoracotomy for surgical
management of the cause of persistent or intractable pleural effusion
or pneumothorax may be considered (e.g., penetrating foreign body,
pulmonary bleb, neoplasia, etc.). Possible complications of
thoracocentesis include lung laceration, airway rupture due to
centesis with trapped lung6 (ch. 220), and iatrogenic infection.7

THORACOSTOMY TUBE PLACEMENT
OVERVIEW AND PURPOSE
Thoracostomy tubes are routinely placed in surgery following open
thoracotomy to maintain negative intrapleural pressure. These shortterm thoracostomy tubes allow normal expansion of the lungs as the
visceral pleura of the lungs are brought back in contact with the
parietal pleura of the chest wall. These tubes are not only useful to
maintain negative intrapleural pressure, they also provide a means to
administer repeated applications of intrapleural local anesthetics.
With normal lung tissue and appropriate surgical closure, these
tubes can usually be removed 6 to 12 hours postoperatively after
several repeated negative aspirates. Inexpensive feeding tubes are
often used for short-term postoperative thoracic drainage. The
surgeon will place these while the thorax is still open to confirm
proper positioning.Thoracostomy tubes are also necessary in
patients with intrathoracic disorders requiring repeated
thoracocentesis to maintain negative intrapleural pressure and
normal tidal volume. Examples of diseases requiring thoracostomy
tubes include traumatic and idiopathic pneumothorax, pyothorax,
chylothorax, and neoplastic pleural effusions (ch. 220). Several
types of tubes are available, and their selection is based on clinician
preference and intended use. Most conditions can be managed with a
single tube, though cases of bilateral pyothorax usually require
bilateral tube placement.

FIGURE 92.1 Commonly-used thoracostomy
tubes. A, Thoracostomy tube with trocar stylet. B,
Red rubber feeding tube/urethral catheter.

FIGURE 92.2 Small caliber tubes for chronic
effusion and prolonged use. A, Over-wire
thoracostomy tube with percutaneous introduction
system and wire. B, Turkel safety catheter: a Veress
needle, with spring-loaded intraluminal cap to
prevent iatrogenic laceration of the lung (inset).

BASIC EQUIPMENT AND TYPES OF
THORACOSTOMY TUBES
To place a thoracostomy tube, the disposable materials needed
include a chest tube, a tubing adapter to take the lumen of the tube
down to a standard Luer connection, a three-way stopcock, 20-gauge
orthopedic wire, extension tubing, large caliber suture to maintain
tube position, and large volume syringes. Necessary instruments (all
sterile) include curved forceps or hemostats, a scalpel handle and
blade, towel clamps, and a surgical drape.

Commercially available chest tubes or red rubber catheters can be
used (Figure 92.1; Video 92.1

). The red rubber catheter is the

least expensive, and is often used for short-term, post-thoracotomy
cases. These are flexible, can easily kink, and are more reactive than
polyvinyl chloride commercial tubes, making them undesirable for
long-term use. Red rubber tubes are also nearly impossible to see
radiographically without the use of contrast.
Commercial tubes are available in different sizes, ranging in
diameter from 14 to 40 French (each 3 French = 1 mm, external
diameter). The commercial tubes are usually open at the end and
have oval side holes. They also have a radiopaque line that runs the
length of the tube to the side hole furthest from the tip of tube, which
is important when evaluating tube placement radiographically. All
holes must be within the thoracic cavity. If the side hole furthest
from the tip is under the skin or beyond, air can be aspirated from
outside the chest.
While sizes have traditionally been selected by matching the chest
tube to the diameter of the mainstem bronchus, other factors should
also be considered. Thoracostomy tubes are invasive and painful. If
smaller tubes are sufficient, they might be better choices for chronic
effusions and continuous, or mild, pneumothorax. Larger tubes
should be considered with highly cellular effusions and large volume,
continuous pneumothorax. Studies have compared a variety of
catheters and placement techniques.7
More recently, smaller products have become available, including
over-wire kits and Veress-needle-style, spring-loaded catheter
systems (Figure 92.2; Video 92.1

). Over-wire, smaller caliber

tubes have proven effective in draining inflammatory exudates in
cats and would be appropriate for other small animals.8
The Veress systems have a blunt safety cannula housed within the
sharp, beveled hollow needle and a safety color change indicator.
These systems are potentially safer when there are concerns about
pockets of fluid or concerns about the lung adhering to the parietal
pleura. These systems usually contain small caliber tubes and can be
indicated when palliative tubes are expected to be in place for long
periods of time. The landmarks and technique described in the

following section should be modified based on the localization of
large fluid pockets, which are best assessed with ultrasonographic
examination (ch. 73).

TECHNIQUES
Several techniques have been described to place thoracostomy tubes.
Whenever possible, the procedure is performed under general
anesthesia. Usually, the patient can be stabilized with
thoracocentesis alone, though in some emergency cases tube
placement might be necessary to establish normal tidal volume and
minimize pleural air accumulation. In these cases, the clinician
might place the tube with the patient under sedation and local
anesthesia. In general, patients are held in lateral recumbency and
the lateral chest wall is clipped and prepared aseptically (Videos 92.1
and 92.2

). A skin incision is made over the 9th to 11th intercostal

space, and then the skin is pulled cranially to the site of tube entry at
the level of the mid-thorax. The tip of the curved forceps is inserted
into the skin incision and blunt dissection is used to separate the
intercostal muscles, taking care to avoid the intercostal vessels and
nerves caudal to the rib. If the patient is intubated and ventilated,
there is little concern about air entering the pleural space during the
procedure. Insertion of a tube with an internal stylet into the pleural
space without prior chest wall dissection could put the patient at risk
of iatrogenic injury to intrathoracic structures. Instead, the tube with
internal stylet is gently manipulated through the hole created by
blunt dissection. If a stylet is not used, the tip of the tube is grasped
by the curved forceps and inserted into the hole created by blunt
dissection. The thoracostomy tubes are placed into the chest with the
tip barely reaching the cranioventral thorax. Over-insertion risks
kinking the tube. When the skin is released and retracts caudally, a
subcutaneous tunnel is formed from the skin incision to the point of
entry into the thorax. This prevents air from entering the skin
incision when the thoracostomy tube is removed. If the patient is
intubated and ventilated, there is no reason to mechanically clamp
the tube. Clamping the tube can create small punctures in the tube,
potentially resulting in air leakage into the thoracic cavity. Making

the necessary connections takes little time and insignificant
quantities of air admitted during the procedure can then be removed
easily. Once the connections are secured to the tube, evacuation of
the pleural space can begin immediately. The chest tube should be
attached to the skin with a self-tightening knot and all connections
secured with cerclage wire. Chest tubes are painful and will result in
a restrictive breathing pattern owing to the discomfort felt with
normal respirations. Most patients with indwelling chest tubes
should receive both systemic and regional analgesia.

FIGURE 92.3 A three-chamber pleural evacuation
system. The largest chamber (A) is connected to the
patient’s chest tube and can quantify the volume of
liquid removed. The middle chamber (B) creates a
water seal that prevents air from being drawn back
into the patient if suction is interrupted. Bubbling
noted in this middle chamber indicates air
production from the patient or connected tubing.
The third chamber (C) is connected to the suction
apparatus and moderates the negative pressure
applied to the patient. When suction is applied and
air is seen to bubble in this chamber, the negative

pressure applied to the patient (cm H2O) equals the
depth of this tube.

INTERMITTENT VERSUS CONTINUOUS
SUCTION
Following thoracostomy tube placement, intermittent or continuous
suction techniques can be used. During the first few hours, the
volume of air or fluid should be evaluated through intermittent
aspiration. With small-volume accumulation and appropriate
monitoring, the intermittent technique can be manageable. Another
advantage of the intermittent technique is that it is harder for the
patient to accidentally remove the tube or traumatize it when a light
bandage covers it.
Continuous suction is usually only indicated when there is rapid
accumulation of air leading to repeat and frequent episodes of
respiratory distress. Continuous suction requires a vacuum source
and a closed system. It is important that the negative pressure be
<20 cm H2O and that the system not allow air to enter the patient if
the suction is turned off. Commercially available systems have
replaced the three-bottle system with three separate chambers
(Figure 92.3). The chamber closest to the patient is the largest and
it is used to quantitate fluids coming from the patient. The suction
tube from the patient is connected to this chamber at an opening
near the top. A tube from the top of the first chamber goes from the
top of the chamber into the second chamber, opening approximately
1 cm under water. This is the water seal chamber and it serves two
functions. During continuous suction, any air seen bubbling into this
chamber means air is coming from the patient (or a leak between the
patient and this chamber). The other function is to prevent air being
drawn into the patient if suction is discontinued. The third chamber,
farthest from the patient and closest to the suction device, modulates
the negative pressure. There is a tube from the top of this chamber,
open to outside air, that terminates near the bottom. When water is
added to this chamber and the suction increased until air is drawn
from the top to the bottom (as evidenced by bubbles coming from the

tube), the pressure of the vacuum equals the depth of the tube. For a
desired vacuum of 20 cm H2O, the chamber is filled to 19 cm (the
additional 1 cm of water creates the water seal in the second
chamber).

TROUBLESHOOTING CONTINUOUS AIR
PRODUCTION
Patients that continually produce air from a chest tube 12-24 hours
after placement should be evaluated for leaks within the tubing or
suction system. The system should be investigated between the
pleural space (including radiographs to confirm all the tube side
holes are within the thoracic cavity) and skin incision, and between
the tube connections and the suction apparatus. The most common
sites of leakage are the tube, from either a side hole just under the
skin or a hole placed by a clamp, and the adapter connection closest
to the tube. A small amount of fluid placed in the tube at the adapter
might reveal a leakage site by bubbles drawn into the tube when
negative pressure is applied (Video 92.2

).

The thoracostomy tube is removed when it is no longer indicated.
Patients on continuous suction for a pneumothorax should be
weaned by switching to intermittent aspiration at progressively
longer intervals. Thoracic radiographs are recommended just prior
to removal of the tube to ensure that the disorder has resolved, both
because tube kinking or hole occlusion could be responsible for
cessation of air or fluid flow, and to be sure there are no pockets of
undrained fluid in pyothorax cases in particular. If stable, the animal
is sedated with a combination sedative analgesic, holding sutures are
removed, and the tube is withdrawn in a steady, rapid motion. The
skin incision can be closed or left open, and a light antiseptic
bandage is placed over the hole. Chest tubes placed for effusions
have often been left in until a measured decrease in fluid production
occurs. In addition to decreasing volumes, it is also appropriate to
make the decision based on patient specifics like fluid character,
etiology, patient comfort, and assessment of risks and ongoing
benefits of the tube(s).9

Chapter 93: Transtracheal
Wash and Bronchoscopy
Tekla M. Lee-Fowler

A C RO N YM S
BAL bronchoalveolar lavage
IV intravenous
SC subcutaneous

Bronchoscopy and airway sampling techniques are useful tools for
investigating airway disease. Tracheobronchoscopy allows
visualization of the trachea and airways while providing access for
sample collection. Air way wash techniques, independent of
bronchoscopic guidance, include transtracheal wash, endotracheal
wash, and bronchoalveolar lavage (blind technique). Procedure
choice should be based on patient stability, whether the disease is
focal or diffuse, goals of diagnostics and operator skill level.

TRANSTRACHEAL WASH
OVERVIEW AND INDICATIONS
A transtracheal wash can be performed to obtain samples from the
proximal respiratory tract in medium- to large-size dogs. Results of
this procedure can be quite informative in dogs with diffuse

infectious or inflammatory pulmonary disease. One major advantage
of the transtracheal wash is that the patient is awake-to-minimallysedated. Since they are not anesthetized, patients often cough during
the procedure, increasing sample return and the likelihood of
obtaining material from lower airways. Transtracheal wash is not
suitable for aggressive or extremely anxious dogs. Hemostatic
abnormalities, severe pyoderma of the neck, and respiratory distress
could each be considered contraindications for this procedure.1

PROCEDURE
The dog is placed in sternal recumbency and gently but firmly
restrained by an assistant who is holding the head with the nose
pointing upward (toward the ceiling). The ventral portion of the
neck, beginning at the larynx and including the proximal portion of
the trachea, is clipped of hair and aseptically prepared. With sterile
gloved hands, the target area can be palpated. Needle placement will
be either through the cricothyroid ligament or on midline between
two adjacent tracheal rings. An intradermal and subcutaneous (SC)
injection of 2% lidocaine is administered over the target area. At
least 10 minutes is required for local anesthesia to take effect. The
cricothyroid ligament is located between the thyroid cartilages
cranially and the cricoid cartilage distally. A 16- to 19-gauge throughthe-needle intravenous (IV) catheter is inserted through the target
area and into the tracheal lumen. Once the needle tip reaches the
lumen, the needle should be angled downward (toward the thorax)
and the catheter advanced into the airway and down the trachea.
When the catheter is in place, the needle can be withdrawn from the
trachea and covered with the attached needle guard. Warm sterile
0.9% saline (5-20 mL, based on body size) is infused through the
catheter using a syringe.2 Suction is applied using the syringe
plunger to retrieve as much of this fluid as possible. In the absence of
coughing, coupage can facilitate return of sample. Generally,
recovery of fluid is much less than with other techniques, with 10%
or less of the instilled volume typically recovered.1,2 It may be
necessary to instill additional aliquots of saline until an adequate
sample is retrieved; the total volume instilled will depend on the

dog’s size and respiratory stability. Although the recovered volume
may be small, the amount should be adequate for cytologic
evaluation and bacterial culture and sensitivity.

FIGURE 93.1 Preparation of a red rubber catheter
for endotracheal wash or bronchoalveolar lavage
blind technique. A, Sterile scissors are used to create
an open-ended catheter by removing the distal end
of the catheter just above the lateral openings. B, A
syringe adapter is attached to the proximal end of the
red rubber catheter. C, A prepared catheter with a
preloaded syringe of sterile saline attached.

COMPLICATIONS
Complications of transtracheal wash are uncommon. Transient SC
emphysema is the most frequently described complication. Other
complications include tracheal laceration, endotracheal hemorrhage,
infection at the puncture site, and transient worsening of respiratory
status.

ENDOTRACHEAL WASH

An endotracheal wash can be utilized in dogs and cats, and is
particularly useful in small dogs and cats for which a transtracheal
wash is not suitable. This technique requires general anesthesia,
allows sampling of the proximal respiratory tract, and differs from a
blind bronchoalveolar lavage in that the catheter is only advanced to
the level of the carina. The distance to the carina can be estimated
externally at the start of the procedure by visualizing the distance
from the tip of the nose to the 5th-6th intercostal space. To prepare
the sterile red rubber urinary catheter prior to the procedure, a
sterile blade or scissors is used for creating an open-ended catheter
by removing the distal end of the catheter just above the lateral
openings. A syringe adapter is attached to the proximal end of the
catheter (Figure 93.1 and

Video 93.1).

The patient is intubated with a sterile endotracheal tube, and the
open-ended sterile red rubber urinary catheter is passed through the
endotracheal tube lumen to the approximate level of the carina.
Warm sterile 0.9% saline (5-20 mL) is infused through the red
rubber catheter, via the syringe, and negative pressure is then
applied to retrieve the sample. Coupage may be performed to
facilitate sample collection. The volume of sample recovered is
similar to that of the transtracheal wash. This process may need to be
repeated to obtain adequate sample. Total volume of saline used is
dependent upon the patient size and respiratory status.

BRONCHOALVEOLAR LAVAGE: BLIND
TECHNIQUE
Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) can be performed without endoscopic
guidance when diffuse lung disease is present. This sampling method
differs from those described above by providing sample from the
lower airways. This technique is most successful in small to mediumsized pets. Substitution of the red rubber catheter with a (longer)
feeding tube has been described for larger dogs.3 Preparation of the
red rubber catheter prior to BAL involves using a sterile blade or
scissors to produce an open-ended catheter by cutting the catheter

just above the distal side openings. A syringe adapter is also attached
to the proximal end of the red rubber catheter (see Figure 93.1).
The patient is anesthetized with a short-acting IV anesthetic,
intubated with a sterile endotracheal tube, and placed in lateral
recumbency. If the disease process is more marked on one side, the
patient should be positioned with that side down. An open-ended
sterile red rubber urinary catheter is passed through the
endotracheal tube until it is gently wedged and cannot be advanced
further. Withdrawing the catheter a few millimeters, rotating the
catheter slightly and gently advancing again until wedged will help
ensure that the catheter is wedged within an airway and not
becoming lodged at an airway division. Once the catheter is in place,
warmed sterile 0.9% saline is instilled through the catheter and
immediately aspirated. The volume infused has not been
standardized and recommendations vary from 5-30 mL aliquots to
using 2-5 mL/kg. An additional aliquot may need to be infused to
recover adequate volume. The volume of sample recovered should be
40-50% of the total volume instilled. After the sampling is complete,
the patient is placed on 100% oxygen for about 5-10 minutes.

BRONCHOSCOPY
OVERVIEW
Tracheobronchoscopy, utilizing a flexible bronchoscope, is a tool for
visually inspecting mucosal surfaces of the trachea and lobar
bronchi. Additionally, specific sites for sample acquisition can be
chosen for pets with focal disease. The patient is anesthetized with an
IV anesthetic and maintained with either IV or gas anesthesia. With
the latter option, the bronchoscope is passed through the
endotracheal tube utilizing a T-adapter. However, internal
endotracheal tube diameter becomes a limiting factor in small
patients. In small dogs and cats, IV anesthesia and direct intubation
with the bronchoscope is often necessary. It is helpful to intubate
these patients with a small diameter (5-Fr), sterile, red rubber
catheter alongside the bronchoscope to provide supplemental oxygen
during bronchoscopy. Supplemental oxygen can also be supplied
through the biopsy channel of the bronchoscope.

INITIAL VISUAL EVALUATION
Inspection of the trachea should include assessing appearance of the
mucosa, the amount of secretions present, and any evidence of
collapse. The carina should then be identified and each lung lobe
should be examined systematically (Figure 93.2 and Video 93.2
). The endoscopist must note the presence of abnormalities such
as mucus plugs, mucopurulent debris, hemorrhage, foreign bodies,

static or dynamic collapse of airways, masses or nodules, and
parasites (ch. 215).

BRUSH CATHETER
The airway mucosal surface can be sampled using a bronchoscope
brush catheter. The brush is covered by a retractable plastic sheath.
With the bronchoscope tip in the desired location, this small
sampling brush is passed through the sampling channel. Once the
brush catheter is visualized, the sheath is retracted and the brush is
gently scraped against the mucosa. Then the brush is retracted back
into the sheath, and removed from the scope. The brush can be
cultured and then gently rubbed on a glass slide for cytologic
examination.

BIOPSY
In a similar method, the bronchoscope is placed in the desired
location and the biopsy instrument is inserted into the sampling port
(biopsy channel). The bronchoscope is then used for guiding the
instrument to the desired location and the biopsy is taken. Samples
can be submitted for culture and histopathologic evaluation. This
technique is primarily indicated for sampling proliferative tissues or
masses within the airways. A technique has been described for
transbronchial biopsy of more peripheral tissue, particularly in the
caudal lung lobes; however, complications such as bleeding,
pneumothorax, small sample size and likelihood of sample crush
artifact could outweigh benefits.4

TRANSBRONCHIAL FINE NEEDLE
ASPIRATE
This method is primarily indicated for obtaining samples from lymph
nodes or masses impinging on the airways. While visualizing the
compressed area with the bronchoscope, a transbronchial needle
catheter is passed through the sampling channel. When the needle

catheter is visualized, the needle is uncovered, and advanced through
the mucosa between the cartilage rings of the bronchus and into the
impinging lymph node or mass (ch. 88). A syringe is used for
applying negative pressure to obtain an aspirate. The needle is
withdrawn without suction, recovered, and retracted from the scope.
Samples can be used for cytologic evaluation. Possible complications
are similar to biopsy, including hemorrhage and pneumothorax.

BRONCHOALVEOLAR LAVAGE:
ENDOSCOPIC
This is a commonly used sampling technique to obtain lower airway
cytologic and microbial culture sample. It is performed after all lobes
have been inspected. The bronchoscope is directed into the desired
bronchus and then advanced until it is wedged or is occluding the
airway. With the lumen of the airway centered in the image, warm
sterile 0.9% saline is instilled into the sampling port and
immediately aspirated. Aspiration can be performed by manual
aspiration with a syringe or via suction pump aspiration.5 The
volume of saline to be infused has not been standardized in
veterinary medicine. Aliquot volumes of 10-30 mL or a “dosage” of 25 mL/kg (small to medium-sized dogs and cats) have been
recommended. About 40% to 50% of the sample should be
retrievable. The lightly anesthetized animal may cough, producing a
better sample. Coupage can also be performed during aspiration to
facilitate sample recovery. This procedure can be repeated to obtain
adequate samples depending on volume of saline used, patient size,
and patient respiratory status. In cats, sampling two different lung
segments can provide more accurate cytologic results.6 BAL fluid can
be submitted for culture and sensitivity and cytological evaluation.
Possible complications of BAL include decline in oxygen
saturation, bronchospasm, and pneumothorax. It is advised to
provide supplementation with 100% oxygen to all animals
immediately after BAL. This can usually be discontinued shortly
thereafter. Additionally, animals with significant respiratory disease
may benefit from pre-BAL oxygenation with 100% oxygen.
Bronchospasm as a complication of bronchoscopy and BAL is most

commonly seen in cats. Premedicating cats with suspected lower
airway disease using a bronchodilator may reduce this
complication.7

Chapter 94: Temporary
Tracheostomy Care
Lori S. Waddell

INDICATIONS
A temporary tracheostomy can be needed for a variety of reasons.
These include upper airway obstruction secondary to trauma,
neoplasia, foreign body, or laryngeal paralysis, inability to open the
mouth with the need for general anesthesia, the need for surgical
access to the laryngeal area without an endotracheal tube in place,
and mechanical ventilation when endotracheal intubation is not
practical. A temporary tracheostomy may be used in a ventilated
patient so the patient can be managed with sedation rather than
anesthesia and can allow for spontaneous breathing modes such as
continuous positive airway pressure that aid in weaning from a
ventilator.

FIGURE 94.1 Temporary tracheostomy in an Old
English Sheepdog-cross dog that presented for
inability to open the mouth after a previous history
of facial trauma. Stay sutures are labeled cranial and
caudal, and a Velcro collar is holding the Jackson
stainless steel tracheostomy tube in place.

TRACHEOSTOMY PROCEDURE

The patient is positioned in dorsal recumbency, and a ventral
midline approach is made to the trachea just caudal to the larynx. A
transverse ventral tracheal incision is made, approximately 50-60%
of the tracheal diameter, usually between the third and fourth or
fourth and fifth tracheal rings.1 Stay sutures should be placed around
the tracheal ring above and below the incision and tied in long loops
to facilitate opening of the stoma for replacement of the
tracheostomy tube. These stay sutures must be labeled as either
cranial and caudal or up and down to avoid crisscrossing the stay
sutures when trying to open the stoma if the tube needs to be
replaced. (Figure 94.1) The use of a label maker to identify the stay
sutures is preferred because it makes labels that are easy to clean
when they become dirtied by discharge from the stoma.

TRACHEOSTOMY TUBE TYPES
There are various types of tubes that can be used for a temporary
tracheostomy, and choice is a bit dependent on the reason that the
patient needs the temporary tracheostomy. For patients that will be
anesthetized or are being mechanically ventilated, a cuffed
tracheostomy tube is ideal, to reduce air leak. For those that are
spontaneously breathing, a non-cuffed tube may be preferred. The
cuff makes the tube’s diameter larger, so use of a cuffless tube allows
for a larger diameter tube to be placed. A cuffless tube also allows for
more air flow around the tube in the event that the tube becomes
obstructed. Generally, the tube diameter should be one-half to onethird of the tracheal diameter to minimize iatrogenic tracheal
trauma, reducing the risk of post-intubation stenosis, and to allow
some airflow around the tube in the event of occlusion of the tube. If
the tube is too small, it will cause increased airway resistance and
work of breathing and could lead to hyperthermia, particularly in
dogs.
Tracheostomy tubes also come with or without inner cannulas,
which act as a lining of the inner surface of the tube. Tubes with an
inner cannula are preferable because the cannulas can be removed
and cleaned, reducing the likelihood and frequency of tracheostomy
tube obstruction. However, the presence of an inner cannula makes
the inner diameter of the tube smaller. The smaller the tube size, the

more difficult it is to make a tube with an inner cannula that doesn’t
lose a significant percentage of its diameter and therefore air flow.
Most smaller-diameter tracheostomy tubes do not have inner
cannulas for this reason, with the exception of the metal tubes
discussed below.
There are generally three types of tubes that can be used for
patients with temporary tracheostomies. There are purpose made
tracheostomy tubes for humans and veterinary patients that come in
a variety of sizes. Shiley (Medtronic, Inc., Minneapolis, MN) is a
human medicine product line that makes flexible tracheostomy tubes
for neonates through adults, in sizes ranging from 2.5 mm inner
diameter (ID) and 4.2 mm outer diameter (OD) to 10.0 mm ID and
13.8 mm OD. The smaller sized tubes do not have inner cannulas or
cuffs. Other manufacturers of human-specific products are very
similar. Mila (Mila International, Florence, KY) makes veterinaryspecific tracheostomy tubes from flexible polyvinyl chloride (PVC)
and have a radiopaque stripe. They come in sizes from 2.5 mm ID
and 3.4 mm OD that are non-cuffed and without an inner cannula up
to 8.0 ID and 11 mm OD that are cuffed and have an inner cannula.
Other manufacturers are also available. Endotracheal tubes, which
are cuffed, can also be used as tracheostomy tubes. It is important to
consider the length of the endotracheal tube as it should be much
shorter when inserted in the cervical region, bypassing the upper
airway and oropharynx. It is easy to intubate past the carina and into
one lung lobe if the reduced length of the trachea that is intubated is
not considered. For any tube that is cuffed, a high volume, low
pressure cuff is ideal if the cuff will be inflated for a prolonged period
of time, as in a ventilator patient. This is to prevent pressure necrosis
and tracheal damage. Jackson stainless steel tracheostomy tubes are
also available in a wide variety of sizes, from 00 (1.6 mm ID, 3.4 mm
OD) up to size 10 (11.1 mm ID, 14.3 mm OD). These have inner
cannulas but no cuffs.

SECURING TRACHEOSTOMY TUBES
Traditionally, tracheostomy tubes have been held in place using
umbilical tape that is passed through the fenestrations on either side
of the flange of the tracheostomy tube and then tied behind the

patient’s neck. This very thin band can make it difficult to keep skin
folds out of the way and, if tied too tightly, can cause edema of the
head. For tracheostomy tubes that will be left in for more than a few
hours, purpose made collars such as the Dale collar (Dale Medical
Products, Inc, Franklin, MA) are ideal (Figure 94.1). These come in
widths from 0.75 inch (1.9 cm) up to 1.5 inch (3.8 cm) and lengths to
fit 9-28 inch (23-70 cm) necks, although they can be trimmed to fit
smaller necks. They are made of material with Velcro fastener tabs
that attach to any size tracheostomy tube to limit the movement of
the tracheostomy tube and reduce the risk of accidental
decannulation. The material also wicks away excessive moisture to
reduce irritation to the skin from any bleeding or discharge from the
tracheostomy site. The two-piece neckband is adjustable via Velcro.
This type of tube holder is especially useful in active, awake
tracheostomy patients and those with particularly large necks with
abundant skin folds, such as English Bulldogs.

FIGURE 94.2 Tracheostomy tube cleaning kit,
which contains sterile pipe cleaners and has wells for
hydrogen peroxide and sterile saline used for
cleaning the inner cannula of the tracheostomy tube.

CARE OF A PATIENT WITH A
TEMPORARY TRACHEOSTOMY
Patients with a temporary tracheostomy require constant
supervision. These patients must be housed in an ICU with adequate
staffing to provide constant care if needed. Tracheostomy tube
obstruction with secretions or foreign material can occur at any
moment and can rapidly lead to asphyxiation. Cages should be
prepared so that no loose material such as lint or hair can be
aspirated into the tracheostomy tube. This is especially important for
cats due to litter boxes; only paper strips should be used for litter.
Patients with tracheostomy tubes should be placed in cages that have
the most visibility, and ideally not in oxygen cages. Oxygen cages

make it impossible to hear if the patient’s tube is starting to become
obstructed. The first hints that a patient is developing an obstruction
are often that the patient becomes restless, unable to sleep, and
develops a change in pitch of breathing. Emergency supplies should
be available next to the patient’s cage including an additional
tracheostomy tube of the same size in case the tube needs to be
replaced emergently as well as a tube of the next size down in case
there is difficulty when replacing the tube. Sterile gloves, sterile
suction catheters and a suction source such as wall suction or a
suction unit should also be cageside for quick replacement of the
tube or suctioning. In addition, having propofol or some other drugs
for rapid induction in the event of extubation and the patient
panicking or becoming fractious can be essential.
Frequent inspection and cleaning of the tracheostomy tube and
site should be scheduled. Initially, cleaning may need to occur every
2-4 hours or even more frequently if there is a lot of discharge from
the tube and stoma. If discharge is minimal, cleaning may be
decreased to every 6 hours. The patient should continue to receive
intravenous fluids at a minimum of a maintenance rate, as long as
there is no contraindication to fluids, to ensure proper hydration.
The tracheostomy tube will increase insensible losses from the
respiratory tract because it bypasses the nasal passages and
nasopharynx. In addition, the patient should be nebulized for at least
10-15 minutes every 4-6 hours to moisten the respiratory tract and
keep respiratory secretions looser and less likely to obstruct the
tracheostomy tube. This is particularly important in cats as they
naturally tend to have thicker respiratory secretions and smaller
tracheas than dogs, and so are at increased risk of acute obstruction.
Previously, cats with tracheostomy tubes were reported to have a
higher complication rate than dogs. However, in the most recent
retrospective studies, the complication rates were similar. In cats,
26% of those with a temporary tracheostomy experienced tube
occlusion and 35% experienced tube dislodgement,2 and in dogs,
26% experienced obstruction and 21% experienced tube
dislodgement, with English Bulldogs having an increased frequency
of tube dislodgement compared to other breeds.3
Care of the tracheostomy tube should consist of visually inspecting
the stoma and surrounding skin, listening for any change in the

sounds the patient is making while breathing (particularly the
development of a high-pitched sound), and if the tube has an inner
cannula, regularly removing it and either cleaning it or replacing it
with a new inner cannula (

Video 94.1). This should occur every

4-6 hours or more frequently if needed. Tracheostomy care kits are
commercially available and include sterile gloves, sterile pipe
cleaners and wells for sterile saline and hydrogen peroxide (Figure
94.2). When the inner cannula of the tracheostomy tube needs to be
cleaned, it is placed in the hydrogen peroxide to help loosen any
secretions, the pipe cleaner is used to remove them, and then the
tube is rinsed in sterile saline and dried with sterile gauze before it is
replaced in the tracheostomy tube. If secretions remain in the
tracheostomy tube, the tube can be suctioned using a sterile suction
catheter that is placed down the tube while someone is holding the
patient’s head up. This can be very irritating and may cause coughing
and gagging. It can be done with the inner cannula in place or while
the inner cannula is being cleaned. Suction can also be helpful to
remove secretions from tubes that do not have an inner cannula. The
patient should be pre-oxygenated with flow-by oxygen or via a mask
for several breaths before suctioning and the suctioning should only
be performed for 10-15 seconds at a time. Suctioning should only be
done on an as needed basis due to the irritation that it can cause.
Some patients may not need to have their tubes suctioned the entire
time that it is in place while others, particularly those with
pneumonia and copious respiratory secretions, may need frequent
suctioning. If nebulization is not available, sterile saline can be
instilled directly into the tube to help keep secretions less viscous.
For cats or small dogs, 0.5 mL can be used, and in large dogs, up to 3
mL usually is feasible. Care must be taken not to instill too much
saline nor to contaminate the saline with any bacteria that may have
colonized the outer portion of the tracheostomy tube. The external
portion of the tracheostomy tube and surrounding skin should be
cleaned with 0.05% chlorhexidine solution prior to instillation of the
saline.
The tracheostomy incision also needs to be kept as clean and dry
as possible. The edges of the skin incision are being held apart by the
tube and stay sutures, which can cause mild irritation. The open
wound may have some discharge as well as some oozing of blood

when the tube is first placed. Excessive respiratory secretions often
increase the amount of discharge coming from the site. Cleaning the
area carefully with sterile saline and changing the collar or umbilical
tape as it becomes soiled is important.

COMPLICATIONS
There are several common complications that can occur with a
temporary tracheostomy. These include some that have been
previously discussed, such as tube obstruction or dislodgement.
Additionally, pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema
can develop if air is leaking out of the trachea and into the
surrounding tissues, particularly if the tracheostomy skin incision is
tightly closed when sutured. This would also make replacing the
tracheostomy tube, if needed, much more difficult. Edema of the
tracheostomy site can also occur. If the tube is undersized or is
partially obstructed, the patient may have increased respiratory rate
and effort and can become hyperthermic from the increased work of
breathing.

REMOVING THE TRACHEOSTOMY
TUBE
The tracheostomy tube can be removed when the upper airway is
usable again. For most patients that have had a tracheostomy tube
placed for upper airway surgery, the tube can be removed within 48
hours. The patient should be calm, and a time should be chosen
when a doctor and/or nurse can carefully observe the patient.
Sedation, sterile gloves, and a new tracheostomy tube should be
nearby in case it is needed. The tracheostomy tube can either be
completely removed or, if available, a tube of a smaller diameter can
replace the tube to see if the patient can breathe around it. This can
be repeated with smaller sized tubes and then the tube completely
removed. The patient should be closely observed for at least 15 to 30
minutes after the tube has been removed or downsized and should be
replaced if there is any sign of respiratory distress. Once the tube has
been removed and is no longer needed, the stay sutures are removed

and the tracheostomy site is left to heal by second intention. The area
should be kept clean of any discharge. A bandage should not be
applied to the site as it will increase the risk of subcutaneous
emphysema and pneumomediastinum. While the wound is healing,
the patient should not be bathed or groomed and should not wear a
collar or neck leash. The skin sutures from the cranial and caudal
parts of the incision should be removed in 10-14 days.

Chapter 95:
Pericardiocentesis
SeungWoo Jung

A C RO N YM S
ECG electrocardiogram
IV intravenous

Pericardiocentesis is a life-saving procedure for patients with
cardiac tamponade. Impaired cardiac filling of the right heart is
known as cardiac tamponade and it occurs when intrapericardial
pressure equilibrates with right atrial and right ventricular diastolic
filling pressures (ch. 235). It leads to an increase in systemic venous
pressure, non-collapsing and dilated caudal vena cava, signs of rightsided congestive heart failure (ascites, pleural effusion), depletion of
ventricular filling volume, systemic hypotension, and possible
cardiac death. Muffled heart sounds, weak femoral pulses, and
pulsus paradoxus are common physical examination findings. Sinus
tachycardia, low amplitude QRS complexes, and electrical alternans
can be seen on routine electrocardiograms (ECGs) (Figure 95.1,A).
Diastolic collapse of the right ventricle and the right atrium is an
echocardiographic definition of cardiac tamponade (Figure 95.1,B).
Therapeutic pericardiocentesis is critical for hemodynamic
stabilization and clinical improvement. If a patient is
hemodynamically unstable, intravenous (IV) fluid therapy with 20-

30 mL/kg prior to or during the procedure and supplemental flow-by
oxygen therapy are indicated.1 Diuretic treatment with furosemide is
contraindicated in patients with cardiac tamponade, because of the
risk of worsening systemic hypotension and hypovolemic shock.

FIGURE 95.1 A, Electrical alternans is a
characteristic electrocardiographic abnormality
observed with large-volume pericardial effusion:
every other QRS complex is of lower amplitude. B,
Diastolic collapse of the right ventricle (arrow) is an
echocardiographic definition of cardiac tamponade.
LV, Left ventricle; PE, pericardial effusion; RV, right
ventricle.

FIGURE 95.2 A-B, Supplies needed for
pericardiocentesis include a, a bowl; b, sterile gloves;

The right-sided approach is the standard with the patient
positioned in left lateral recumbency, which minimizes the risk of
inadvertent laceration of the major left coronary arteries (Video
95.1). Chemical restraint is unnecessary in most cases, but
butorphanol or midazolam or both can be used as needed at 0.1-0.3
mg/kg IV.2 Simultaneous ECG monitoring (ch. 96) is advised to
detect ventricular arrhythmia due to contact between the catheter
and the ventricular myocardium. Echocardiographic guidance is
useful to identify the site of catheter insertion, with the largest
pericardial volume between the thoracic wall and the heart (chs. 73
and 97). Alternatively, if ultrasound is not available, the catheter
entry site can be at the 5th intercostal space below the costochondral
junction. The skin is shaved and prepared with aseptic surgical scrub
technique over the right precordium from the 3rd to 7th intercostal
spaces and from sternum to costochondral junction. A local
anesthetic block is applied with 1 mL of 2% lidocaine at the catheter
entry site to minimize patient discomfort: 0.5 mL intradermally and

0.5 mL at intercostal muscle and pleura. Different centesis-catheter
options are available on the basis of body size (Figure 95.2,B): a 14gauge 5.25 inch (13 cm) over-the-needle catheter (MILA
International) for large-size dogs (>20 kg), a 16-gauge 3 inch (7.5
cm) over-the-needle catheter (MILA International) for medium-size
dogs (between 10 and 20 kg), or a 16-gauge 2 inch (5 cm) IV catheter
(Terumo) for cats and small-size dogs (<10 kg).
The catheter is inserted perpendicular to the skin and is slowly
advanced in 1-cm increments until pericardial effusion (typically
hemorrhagic) is seen in the catheter hub. The catheter is then
advanced into the pericardial space all the way to the hub while the
stylet is held steady. The stylet is removed and a bifuse extension set
with one-way valves (ICU Medical) is attached to the catheter. A 60cc syringe is attached to the other end of the extension set as
demonstrated in Figure 95.2,C, and

Video 95.1. The bifuse

extension set with one-way valves is advantageous at preventing a
human error of administering drained-effusion back to the patient
that often occurs with a three-way stopcock and multiple extension
sets. A small sample of pericardial effusion is collected in a plain tube
and a tube containing an anticoagulant for cytologic evaluation and
fluid analysis. Pericardial fluid analysis is often unrewarding in
determining the etiology of pericardial effusion (ch. 235).3 It is
important to watch the plain tube carefully for the presence of a clot.
Pericardial effusion should not clot unless active hemorrhage into
the pericardial space occurs. Clot formation may indicate an active
bleed, but more commonly suggests that the catheter is inserted too
far and into a cardiac chamber as opposed to the pericardial space.
Once it has been confirmed that the retrieved fluid is from the
pericardial space, as much fluid as possible is drained into a
collection bowl. Removal of even a small amount of pericardial
effusion can drastically improve cardiac filling and stroke volume.
The catheter may need to be slightly withdrawn when the catheter
creates a rubbing sensation against the myocardium or ventricular
arrhythmias are observed on ECG. Once all fluid is removed, the
catheter is withdrawn from the pericardial space. The volume of
retrieved fluid is quantitated, and samples are stored in a refrigerator
prior to submission for cytologic and fluid analysis. Resolution of

cardiac tamponade should be verified by a significant reduction in
the amount of pericardial effusion on echocardiogram,
disappearance of electrical alternans and normalization of heart rate
and amplitude of QRS complexes on ECG, and a marked
improvement of audible heart sounds and femoral arterial pulse
quality. Evidence of hemodynamic instability, re-accumulation of
pericardial effusion, active hemorrhage or ventricular arrhythmia
should be closely monitored following the procedure.

Chapter 96:
Electrocardiography
Erin Anderson

A C RO N YM S
ECG (EKG) electrocardiogram
ILR implantable loop recorder

Electrocardiography is a common, non-invasive diagnostic tool
that records the electrical activity of the heart from the body surface.
The resultant recordings, called electrocardiograms (ECGs, EKGs)
provide valuable information about the heart rate, rhythm, function
of the cardiac conduction system, and—with variable sensitivity and
specificity—structural changes to the cardiac chambers.1-3
Indications for obtaining an ECG include audible arrhythmias,
clinical signs that could be caused by arrhythmias (such as lethargy,
exercise intolerance, syncope), and assessment of antiarrhythmic
therapy in patients with pathologic arrhythmias. ECGs also are
commonly monitored in patients undergoing echocardiography or
general anesthesia and in those with critical morbidity who require
intensive monitoring.

THE PHYSICS OF
ELECTROCARDIOGRAPHY
What the ECG documents is the averaged voltage from the action
potentials generated in the myocardium over time. At rest, myocytes
have a negative internal charge with respect to the outside of the cell,
where the charge is positive. As myocytes depolarize, the electrical
charge becomes transiently positive inside the cells and negative
outside the cells, creating a region of opposite charge (or polarity)
compared to the adjacent non-depolarized cells.4,5 This difference in
polarity is called a dipole, and electrical currents flow readily
between dipoles.2 From the surface of the skin, negative and positive
electrodes record the magnitude and orientation of the electrical
wavefronts, which are composed of multiple dipoles between the
electrodes (i.e., the net vector of electrical activity).3-5 Each pair of
one negative and one positive electrode constitutes a lead. Between
one and 12 different leads may be used to record a surface ECG, with
each lead offering a different “vantage point” from which to assess
cardiac electrical activity. When the net vector of electricity moves
parallel to the lead, a large amplitude deflection is recorded. When
the net vector of electricity moves perpendicular to the lead, an
isoelectric deflection is recorded: either flatline, or with equal
amounts of the deflection existing above as below the baseline. In
addition to the orientation of electricity in relation to the lead, the
amplitude of the recorded deflection also depends on the voltage of
the electrical wavefront, the distance of the lead from the source, and
the conducting medium between the source of electricity and the
electrodes.2,3 The polarity of the deflection is determined by whether
the net vector of electricity moves toward the positive or negative
electrode.

LEAD SYSTEMS
Three bipolar (also called “standard”) leads (I, II, and III) and three
augmented leads (aVF, aVL, and aVR) are commonly assessed in
veterinary electrocardiography. The bipolar leads are generated by

the combinations of electrodes on each forelimb and the left
hindlimb, a configuration originally described by Willem Einthoven
and still referred to as Einthoven’s triangle (Figure 96.1).2,3 Leads
I, II, and III are indicated as bipolar because they are created by one
positive and one negative electrode. In contrast, the augmented leads
are unipolar, since they are created by one positive electrode and the
average of the other two electrodes (a neutral reference point). The
augmented leads create smaller deflections because they are
unipolar, but the deflections are amplified by ECG machines (thus,
the term “augmented”). Together, these six leads constitute the
hexaxial system, which illustrates cardiac electrical activity from
various points along the frontal plane of the animal (a plane dividing
the body into a cranial and caudal half). Additionally, precordial
chest leads are available for unipolar measurement of electrical
activity from up to six different points in the transverse plane (a
plane dividing the body into a cranial and caudal half). The
precordial leads are created by these positive electrodes on the
surface of the thorax and one “indifferent electrode” theoretically
produced at the common junction of the three bipolar electrodes.2,3
Recording precordial leads requires placement of one positive
electrode at each of several specific points around the thorax (Table
96.1).6,7 Different precordial lead systems have been described for
use in veterinary patients, including Lannek’s lead system modified
by Detweiler and Patterson, Takahashi’s lead system, and Wilson’s
lead system, the latter being the most common.6-8 Kraus et al.’s
modification to the Wilson system includes a V1 electrode on the
right hemithorax in the fifth intercostal space at the sternochondral
junction that Santilli describes placing more cranially (in the right
first intercostal space at the costochondral junction) to enhance
assessment of right ventricular activation.6
In whole, this creates 12 different recorded leads, all of which
provide unique vantage points for “viewing,” assessing, and
measuring cardiac electrical activity. From these recordings, one can
count the heart rate and identify the heart rhythm. There are also
various reported criteria with variable degrees of sensitivity and
specificity for identifying chamber enlargement and conduction
disturbances (Table 96.2).2,3,6,7,9-13

RECORDING THE
ELECTROCARDIOGRAM
Recording the ECG (Video 96.1

) requires first restraining the

patient in right lateral recumbency. This is the preferred patient
position because the majority of published reference intervals for
measurements of waves, complexes, and the mean electrical axis
were obtained from animals in right lateral recumbency.9-14
Recordings from sternal or left lateral recumbency or a standing
position may be sufficient for interpreting the heart rate and rhythm
in many cases, but the size and orientation of different deflections
are altered to varying degrees.13,14 Importantly, the patient should
be restrained on the floor, a rubber or foam mat, or a non-metal
table and not on a conductive surface (where interference from
electrical signals could introduce artifact into the ECG). One or two
assistants should be behind the patient with arms draped over the
patient’s neck and lateral left limbs, grasping the dependent (right)
fore- and hindlimbs to maintain gentle restraint. The patient’s
forelimbs should be drawn cranially and hindlimbs drawn caudally,
such that the humerus and femur of each fore- and hindlimb,
respectively, are perpendicular to the trunk (Figure 96.2). This
avoids artifactual deviations in recorded parameters that have been
reported in cats that spontaneously “tuck” their limbs.14,15

The recording electrodes are usually incorporated into alligator
clips, small metal plates, or self-adhesive patches, any of which can
be attached directly to the skin. The electrodes are color-coded: the
white electrode is placed on the right forelimb, the black electrode on
the left forelimb, the green electrode on the right hindlimb, and the
red electrode on the left hindlimb. If alligator clips are used, the
forelimb clips are affixed to the skin directly proximal to the elbows,
the hindlimb clips directly over the stifles, and the precordial
electrodes in their respective locations (Table 96.1) (Video 96.2
). When metal plates are used, the flat surface of the plate should
make full contact with the caudal aspect of the metacarpus or
metatarsus. Self-adhesive patches usually are affixed to the palmar
(or plantar) surface of the paw, against the unhaired paw pads, so
that removal of the patch is atraumatic. Contact between the skin
and electrodes of the clips or plates should be optimized by

moistening the skin with a conducting liquid or ECG paste, before or
after affixing the electrodes in their appropriate position.15 The
patient should be encouraged to remain as calm and still as possible
throughout recording in an effort to avoid baseline artifact that
comes from panting, purring, shivering, or other motion. Electrical
interference (such as electrocautery or 60-Hz alternating current)
should be avoided as much as possible by ensuring appropriate
grounding via the use of a grounding electrode and adequate contact
between electrode and skin.3 Another tool for controlling artifactual
electrical interference is the use of ECG filters, which eliminate
signals above (low-pass filters) or below (high-pass filters) a selected
frequency. Filters can unintentionally distort the ECG signal and lead
to an artifactually high frequency response, which reduces the R
wave amplitude (the highest frequency component of the ECG
spectrum) and/or dampens other subtle but clinically important high
frequency features of the ECG (e.g., notching or ST slurring).16,17 In
order to maximize the use of filters in veterinary
electrocardiography, low-pass filter cut-off frequency should be set at
50-70 Hz in dogs and 150 Hz in cats.6

The ECG can be recorded at various paper speeds, most commonly
25 and/or 50 mm/sec on dedicated, calibrated paper. The amplitude
setting can be altered as necessary to produce complexes of optimal
height. Amplitude settings should be optimized to produce
complexes that are easily visible and measurable but do not overlap
with signals recorded in other leads; 10 mm/mV is standard, but 20
mm/mV will make deflections larger (which can be particularly
helpful in cats), and 5 mm/mV will make deflections smaller.
As many leads as possible should be recorded for several
depolarizations or, ideally, for several minutes. Assessing more than
one lead helps the clinician better understand the cardiac electrical
activity (similar to the way thorough evaluation of thoracic
radiographs requires at least two orthogonal projections instead of a
single lateral projection). Assessing the electrocardiographic
recording requires interpreting the heart rate, rhythm, criteria for
chamber enlargement and duration of intervals, and mean electrical
axis. This material is discussed further in ch. 230 (Cardiac
Arrhythmias) with reference intervals reported in Table 96.2.1-3,9-11

AMBULATORY MONITORING
Extended ambulatory ECG monitoring can be achieved with an
external cardiac event monitor, a Holter monitor, or an implantable
loop recorder (ILR).18-23 External cardiac event monitors and Holter
monitors both feature surface electrodes that adhere to the patient’s
skin and are attached to a portable monitor, which is worn by the
patient. Holter monitors continuously record the ECG for 24 or 48
consecutive hours. This is commonly pursued for one of several
purposes: (1) to investigate intermittent clinical signs that are
suspected of having an arrhythmic etiology; (2) to evaluate the extent
and severity of a known arrhythmia; or (3) to investigate the need
for, or efficacy of, antiarrhythmic therapy. An electrocardiographic
adhesive patch monitor has undergone pilot assessment in dogs; it
records a continuous ECG for up to 14 days, and interpretation of the
data is automated but only using software designed for human
patients.24

An external cardiac event monitor will continuously monitor the
ECG but only record it after physical depression of a “trigger” button
on the device.20 In this way, the monitor can be worn for the
duration of battery life (usually 5-7 days); this longer monitoring
period increases the likelihood of recording events that do not occur
daily, potentially offering a higher diagnostic yield than a 24-hour
Holter monitor.20,21 Capturing the ECG during an episode of
collapse can either implicate a cardiac arrhythmia as the inciting
cause or exonerate arrhythmogenic causes if the heart rate and
rhythm are appropriate.
Internal events monitors like ILRs (e.g., Reveal monitor) are
subcutaneously-implanted devices that can be programmed for
manual and/or automatic recording of ECG in animals with very
infrequent episodes of syncope, collapse, or weakness.22,23 The
recording device remains in the subcutaneous space on the thorax
and can be activated via an owner-operated “remote control” device
applied to the thorax when clinical signs arise. The data are retrieved
with the use of software on a pacemaker interrogator, a device that is
in common usage among veterinary cardiologists. These loop
recorders are easy to implant, carry a low risk of complications, and
can be left in place until an event is captured or the end of battery life
(often several months). In veterinary medicine, ILRs have been
reported to provide a diagnostic yield of 48-58% in dogs with
intermittent weakness and/or syncope.22,23
Perhaps the newest devices available for ECG recording involve
mobile phone applications, the first of which was the AliveCor
Veterinary Heart Monitor for use with certain models of Apple
iPhones. The system incorporated wireless electrodes into a
specialized smartphone case and used software to record an ECG
simply by pressing the phone against the left side of the thorax of a
patient restrained in right lateral recumbency. With newer models
(Kardia), a plastic case is optional and they function with virtually
any type of smartphone. Comparison of even the human-specific
application to a standard diagnostic 6-lead ECG in 46 dogs and 23
cats showed identical instantaneous heart rate calculations, very
accurate 15-second rhythm recordings, and high intra-observer
agreement regarding rhythm diagnosis.25 The AliveCor recordings

produced different polarity complexes occasionally in dogs and
frequently in cats.25 Still newer systems (e.g., Beecardia) utilize
small, self-contained ECG recording devices that interface with
mobile apps and cloud-based portals to facilitate ECG recording,
storage, and integration into medical record systems. This method of
wireless ECG offers an innovative and widely available complement
to standard electrocardiography.
