OVERVIEW
INDICATIONS AND DIAGNOSTIC INFORMATION
Echocardiography is the clinical gold standard for the diagnosis and staging (severity assessment) of
virtually all cardiovascular diseases. With a skilled and knowledgeable operator and interpreter, a
complete echocardiographic examination can provide valuable information about cardiac morphology
and pathology, cardiac size, remodeling, systolic function of the ventricles (and atria), diastolic function,
valvular function and competence, and hemodynamics (i.e., noninvasive estimates of pressure gradients,
stroke volume, cardiac output, and vascular resistance).

LIMITATIONS
Understanding the limitations of echocardiography is important. An echocardiographic examination is
only as good as the individual(s) performing and interpreting the study. An echocardiographic
examination of the highest quality can still be misinterpreted, particularly if the clinical context is
unknown or overlooked. Echocardiography cannot provide a definitive diagnosis of congestive heart
failure (CHF; ch. 229), which requires integration of clinical signs with additional imaging of the
thorax. Echocardiography does not reliably detect cardiac inflammation, fibrosis, or subtle neoplastic
infiltration (chs. 233, 234, and 235). It allows visualization of the proximal, but not distal, segments of
great vessels. Echocardiography contributes to assessing anesthetic risk in conjunction with other
clinical findings, not as the sole determinant. Physiologic variation, day-to-day variability, and artifacts
can be misinterpreted as evidence of disease. Understanding of causes of physiologic variation (e.g.,
impact of autonomic tone on echocardiographic indices), the reproducibility of various measurements,
and common ultrasound artifacts (and how to account for them) is recommended.

INSTRUMENTATION SETTINGS
Familiarizing oneself with controls and instrumentation settings (“knobology”) is highly recommended.
Ideally, the echocardiographer/sonographer/operator is thoroughly trained by an applications specialist
specific to their system, as controls and terminology can vary among manufacturers and models.
Understanding at least basic system controls can help the operator with fine-tuning purposes “on the
fly” and for establishing presets. Specific presets tailored for cats, small dogs, medium-sized dogs, and
larger/giant dogs can be programmed and are highly encouraged to aid efficiency. The American Society
of Echocardiography (ASE) offers an excellent resource to help understand instrumentation settings.1

TRANSDUCERS (PROBES) FOR CARDIAC IMAGING
Cardiac transducers have a smaller footprint (region that contacts the skin) that enables imaging within
intercostal acoustic windows. They also generate sound waves as a sector compared to the wider and
slower formats used for abdominal (linear or convex) scanning. Having two, or ideally three or more,
transducers is recommended for a wide range of scanning frequencies to generate high quality cardiac
studies across the range of body sizes encountered in small animal practice. Cats and tiny dogs usually
necessitate 7-12 MHz transducers and larger/giant dogs require lower frequency transducers (3-5 MHz).
Small or medium-sized dogs typically require a third mid-range probe for optimal imaging. In general,

higher frequency transducers provide better image resolution but sacrifice tissue penetration and
therefore imaging depth. The reverse is true for lower frequency transducers. Lower frequency probes
enhance recording sensitivity for Doppler imaging.
Transducers have a reference marker, typically a line, dot, notch, or ridge, which corresponds to one
edge of the two-dimensional (2D) sector image. This helps orient the operator during imaging. This
chapter assumes the operator is holding the transducer with the index marker at their index finger.
Standard practice is to display the reference symbol on the right side of the 2D image. The 2D image can
be inverted left or right using the instrumentation settings.

THE CORE ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIC EXAMINATION
Real-time 2D echocardiography (2DE), supplemented by motion-mode echocardiography (M-mode),
and spectral and color Doppler imaging, serves as the foundation of the echocardiographic examination
(Video 97.1

). The core (basic) 2DE examination readily quantitates cardiac size and function and

identifies most clinically significant cardiac structural abnormalities. Also called brightness (B)-mode
echocardiography, 2DE provides complementary orthogonal and off-angle images recorded for anatomic
detail. Virtually all cardiac structures are routinely visualized and assessed with 2DE. Current
recommendations for performing echocardiography in dogs and cats are limited to imaging planes and
display conventions.2

FIGURE 97.1 A padded echocardiography table with a cutout improves
patient comfort, aids patient restraint, and by allowing imaging from
underneath, improves the exam and image quality for most echocardiographic
examinations.

TECHNIQUE
Patient Preparation
Most dogs and cats can be examined under gentle manual restraint performed by one or two assistants.
However, sedatives should be considered for animals that refuse to lie still, appear overtly anxious, or
are aggressive. For light sedation, opioids such as butorphanol (0.1-0.4 mg/kg IM or IV) or
buprenorphine (0.005-0.01 mg/kg IM or IV) can be utilized. For moderate sedation, higher dosages of
butorphanol or buprenorphine can be utilized or they can be combined with acepromazine (0.02-0.05
mg/kg IM or IV).3-5 Alfaxalone (1-2 mg/kg IM) is recommended for heavy sedation6; the volume of the
injection can be prohibitive in medium or large dogs. Some cats benefit from administration of
gabapentin (100 mg/cat PO) or trazodone (50 mg/cat PO) ∼1 hour prior to arrival.7,8 Sedatives can lead
to withdrawal of sympathetic tone and therefore indirectly decrease heart rate and myocardial function.
These effects are negligible in most patients,3-7 and sedatives should not be withheld for these reasons.
Maintaining air-free contact between the transducer and thorax is important for optimal image
quality. To accomplish this, the operator should palpate the precordial impulse (heartbeat) prior to
transducer placement. This helps identify the acoustic window. Once it is identified, the hair can be
parted and dampened with isopropyl alcohol. Ultrasound gel should be applied to the transducer surface
(or skin) and reapplied as needed throughout scanning. The patient’s hair can be clipped to improve
image quality. Minimal pressure on the chest wall is typically needed if the aforementioned
recommendations are followed.

Patient Positioning
Small animals can be imaged from any position (standing, sitting, sternal or lateral recumbency). The
use of a padded table with a cutout improves patient comfort, enables scanning from underneath
(patient’s dependent side), and aids the exam and image quality (Figure 97.1). Manual restraint by the
assistant(s) seems to be easier when the laterally recumbent animal’s limbs face the sonographer. Once
the patient is positioned, the electrocardiographic (ECG) electrodes are attached and ECG settings
adjusted as necessary (lead, voltage, screen position). Examinations typically start with right parasternal
imaging with the dog or cat in right lateral recumbency and then transition to left parasternal imaging
with the patient in left lateral recumbency.

Transducer Placement and Movements
Standard transducer placement/locations (acoustic windows)2 are as follows: 1) right parasternal—
usually at the 4th or 5th intercostal space, dorsal to the sternum and ventral to the costochondral
junction. When the patient is in right lateral recumbency, the patient’s precordial cardiac impulse can be
easily palpated at this location. 2) Subcostal (subxiphoid)—just caudal to the xiphoid process. The
transducer must be gently pushed into the abdomen and angled craniodorsally to view the heart. 3) Left
apical—caudoventral, usually just caudal to the left apical precordial impulse and close to the sternum.
The transducer can be placed where the left apical impulse is palpated (the liver is often initially
visualized and steep angulation is required to view the heart, with the probe almost parallel to the floor).
4) Left cranial—cranial to the left apical position, typically between the 3rd and 4th left intercostal space
between the sternum and costochondral junction.
Scanning maneuvers are described assuming the operator is imaging from underneath the patient
using a table with a cutout (Figure 97.1). Primary transducer movements are communicated according
to ASE guidelines1 as follows: 1) Positioning or placement—The transducer is placed at the appropriate
parasternal (intercostal) acoustic window location (e.g., right parasternal). 2) Rotate—The transducer
remains stationary while being turned or “twisted” about its length in a clockwise or counterclockwise
manner relative to the ultrasound beam (not the transducer’s footprint); “clockwise” and
“counterclockwise” directions refer to looking from the transducer cable end, facing the thoracic wall. 3)
Tilt—The transducer is tilted or “fanned” in the same position. It maintains the same axis orientation to
the heart but moves to a different imaging plane. 4) Angle—The transducer is kept at the same location
on the chest but the beam is directed to show a new structure. 5) Slide—The transducer moves across the
patient’s skin to a new position.

2-DIMENSIONAL IMAGING
Specific transthoracic 2DE imaging planes are routinely assessed and recorded for evaluation of cardiac
structure and function. However, cardiac abnormalities are not necessarily confined to these planes and
might require hybrid off-angle imaging. The operator must adapt to findings in real time, which requires
skill and knowledge of anatomy and cardiovascular disease. Initially, a focused cardiac ultrasound might
be warranted in the urgent care setting (ch. 73).9,10 This should be followed-up by a more
comprehensive examination once the patient is stabilized. Extracardiac findings, such as pericardial
effusion and/or thickening, mass lesions, pleural effusion, pulmonary edema (B-lines or “lung rockets”),
are important, as are hepatic vein size and Doppler flow patterns, caudal vena cava size and
collapsibility, and presence or absence of ascites (ch. 21), depending on the context.11,12
The recommended standard transthoracic echocardiographic examination (Video 97.1

)2 and

subsequently stored images and videos are defined by the following nomenclature: 1) transducer
location—right or left parasternal, (left) apical, or subcostal (subxiphoid); 2) plane of the ultrasound
beam—long-axis, short-axis, apical, or angled/hybrid; 3) number of chambers or great vessels imaged—
2-, 3-, 4-, or 5-chamber views; and 4) other tomographic features—typically off-angled views named for
the main structure visualized, e.g., left auricular view in cats. M-mode images are named for the primary
anatomic structures being imaged and spectral Doppler studies are named for the blood flow being
evaluated, e.g., transmitral flow. By convention, echocardiographic images are displayed on the viewing
screen with the cranial and dorsal structures to the viewer’s right as they face the screen. Exceptions
include the left apical 4- and 5-chamber views, and the subcostal window, where the left atrium (LA) and
left ventricle (LV) are to the viewer’s right. The core 2DE examination is summarized in Table 97.1.
Additional imaging with hybrid views or slight variations and use of the zoom feature can be utilized
beyond the examination described herein. At least one representative video loop of each imaging plane
or desired anatomic structure capturing at least three cardiac cycles (ideally in sinus rhythm) should be
acquired and stored for analysis. Frozen/still images can be saved as desired.

M-MODE IMAGING
The M-mode echocardiogram is generated from a single line of B-mode ultrasound, which is recorded
from an operator-guided M-line (cursor) across a real-time 2DE template. Motion-mode provides a 1dimensional graphic display of region-specific cardiac motion over time. Only the structures within the
M-line are visualized. It displays time (in seconds) on the x-axis and depth (in cm) from the transducer
face along the y-axis. The system processes returning sound waves from cardiac tissues with a high
sampling rate (>1000 pulses per second). Thus, M-mode’s primary advantage is high temporal
resolution, which aids timing of cardiac events. It is useful to assess rapidly moving structures such as
cardiac valves or ventricular wall motion during rapid heart rates. Modern echocardiography units
usually permit more than adequate temporal resolution by 2DE, which is not hindered by frozen 1dimensional images and is less hindered by off-angle imaging. Therefore, M-mode is less important now
than it once was.
M-mode (Figure 97.2) is mostly commonly used for 1) LV cavity and wall motion at the level of the
chordae tendineae or “high papillary muscle” level along its minor axis, 2) mitral valve motion at the
valve tips—capturing peak diastolic excursion of the anterior (cranial, septal) mitral valve leaflet, and 3)
right ± left ventricular annular motion/excursion along its major axis (longitudinal or basilar-to-apical
plane).

M-Mode of the Left Ventricle
M-mode images of the LV can be acquired from a long-axis projection (right parasternal long-axis 4chamber or 5-chamber view), a short-axis projection (right parasternal short-axis high papillary muscle
view), or both. The short-axis projection is usually preferred in dogs and cats (Figure 97.2, A). The
center of the septal arc is transected with the M-line cursor, bisecting the LV chamber equally between
the two papillary muscles in the far field. It is important to avoid an insonation angle and cursor
placement that are too dorsal and subaortic on the interventricular septum (IVS). This falsely reduces
septal motion (“septal tethering”), underestimating systolic function and overestimating LV size. The LV
does not have to be centered in the middle of the sector for optimal cursor alignment. If the cursor fails
to align perpendicular to the IVS and LV free wall, a measurement with 2DE is preferred.

M-Mode of the Mitral Valve
Similar to M-mode of the LV, short-axis M-mode of mitral valve (MV) motion seems preferred but both
short and long-axis acquisitions are possible. The cursor should transect the center of the anterior
(cranial) MV leaflet and the posterior mitral valve leaflet, if possible, throughout the cardiac cycle(s)
(Figure 97.2, B). In early diastole, the MV rapidly opens widely (“E” for early) bringing the tip of the
anterior leaflet close to the IVS. As diastolic filling slows (diastasis), the MV drifts closed until atrial
contraction occurs (following the P wave on the ECG). Atrial contraction reopens the MV leaflets (“A” for
atrial contraction). At the onset of systole, the leaflets quickly appose and throughout systole the valve
moves progressively toward the transducer, completing the cardiac cycle. Note that the E and A points
fuse with rapid heart rates. The vertical length from the E-point to the IVS, called E-point to septal
separation, serves as a metric of systolic function, and is inversely related to ejection fraction. It has
diagnostic relevance in dilated cardiomyopathy13-16 but can also be increased by mitral stenosis,
eccentric aortic insufficiency, or off-angle imaging.

M-Mode of the Right Ventricle
From an RV focused left apical 4-chamber view, the cursor is positioned through the RV apex directed to
the lateral tricuspid annulus, i.e., the bright (echogenic) tissue of the cardiac fibrous skeleton lateral to
the tricuspid valve (Figure 97.2, C). The cursor should be aligned as parallel as possible to the
longitudinal, base to apex motion of the RV free wall while avoiding the tricuspid valve (TV) leaflets. The
distance or systolic excursion of the TV annulus is the tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion
(TAPSE), which is an index of RV systolic function. From a left apical 4-chamber view, an analogous
acquisition can be performed on the LV to quantitate longitudinal LV systolic function.

DOPPLER ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIC IMAGING
Doppler echocardiography displays the directional movement and velocity of blood flow (or myocardial
tissue) through the cardiac cycle. It is heavily involved in the perivalvular assessment (identifying
regurgitation or stenosis/obstructions to flow) and to help identify shunts and turbulent blood flow,
assess atrial and ventricular function, and estimate hemodynamic variables (stroke volume, pressure
gradients, and resistance to flow). Doppler studies are based on the frequency shift that occurs when
sound waves are reflected back from a moving object (e.g., red blood cells located within the region of
interest [ROI]) to a stationary observation point, namely the transducer. The direction of movement,
either toward the transducer (positive or up) or away (negative or down), determines the sign of the
Doppler frequency shift. Direction and velocity are displayed in either a color-coded format (color
Doppler imaging [CDI]) or in a graphical display of velocity, direction, and timing (spectral Doppler).
Tissue Doppler imaging (TDI) quantitates myocardial motion (velocity and direction). To optimize
Doppler frequency shift back to the transducer and thus avoid underestimating true velocity, Doppler
echocardiography must be performed with the ultrasound beam as parallel to blood flow (or myocardial
motion) as possible. The angle of incidence should be <20°.

Color Doppler Imaging (CDI)
CDI samples Doppler shifts along a series of contiguous lines of ultrasound. These sample volumes are
processed within a large ROI that is overlaid on a live 2DE image. The ROI box size can be adjusted and
directed to the desired area by the operator. Doppler shift data are displayed in colors within the ROI. By
convention, blue represents blood flow away from the transducer and red represents blood flow toward
the transducer. Blood velocity is also semi-quantitated by transitioning from darker shades to lighter
shades as blood velocity increases up to a point. If that point—the Nyquist limit or aliasing velocity—is
surpassed, the signal will alias and transition to the alternate color (from red to blue or from blue to red,
depending on the direction) and from lighter to darker as blood velocity progressively increases (Figure
97.3). This change in color and hue helps draw attention to rapid and potentially turbulent or otherwise
abnormal blood flow. Nyquist limits are usually set fairly low—between 50 to 100 cm/s for this purpose.
Aliasing is common even in healthy dogs and cats because blood flow velocities commonly exceed 100
cm/s, especially in the ventricular outflow tracts. Depending on blood flow velocity, aliasing can be
eliminated by shifting the baseline/zero of the color scale up or down, depending on flow direction, or by
increasing the scale or pulse repetition frequency to increase the Nyquist limit. This is true for both CDI
and pulsed-wave Doppler (PWD). The primary advantage of CDI is to efficiently localize rapid or

potentially abnormal blood flow patterns over relatively large ROIs. If identified, the flow should be
more accurately quantitated with spectral Doppler. CDI is sensitive and aliasing blood flow does not
necessarily indicate an abnormality or flow turbulence. This is dependent on numerous factors such as
instrument settings (e.g., Nyquist limit setting, color velocity scales), flow direction, timing, absolute
velocity, cardiac anatomy, and clinical context. Disadvantages of CDI largely relate to challenges of
timing of blood flow events in real time and its oversensitivity. For example, normal changes in blood
flow associated with valve closure can be mistaken for valve regurgitation. A frame by frame or slowmotion analysis is usually helpful. Also, performing spectral Doppler or, ideally, combining CDI with Mmode (to increase frame rate) will greatly aid the timing of suspected blood flow disturbances.

Spectral Doppler: Pulsed-Wave and Continuous Wave
Spectral Doppler represents PWD and continuous wave Doppler (CWD) imaging (Figure 97.4). These
are processed to display blood flow direction and velocity graphically over time. Pulsed-wave Doppler
sends ultrasound, pauses, and waits to receive the reflected ultrasound waves back from the ROI before
re-emitting ultrasound waves. These pulses of ultrasound enable precise localization of blood velocity
within a discrete ROI, referred to as sample volume. Conversely, CWD continuously sends and receives
ultrasound using multiple independent crystals in the probe. Thus, CWD records all of the Doppler
shifts returned along the line of transmitted ultrasound. This permits quantitation of high-velocity blood
flow that is virtually limitless, which represents CWD’s primary advantage. Like CDI, PWD’s peak
velocity is limited and subject to aliasing. PWD is better for localizing abnormal blood flow to a specific
region, which is its primary advantage. Both utilize a live anatomic 2DE template to guide the sample
volume (PWD) or cursor line (CWD) to anatomic regions. Best results are achieved by first visualizing
CDI over the desired area, then activating PWD or CWD, and guiding the sample volume or cursor to the
region of the brightest color hue or signal aliasing, if present.

FIGURE 97.4 Spectral Doppler imaging: pulsed-wave Doppler (A) and
continuous wave Doppler (B) of the left ventricular outflow tract, showing their

characteristic “hollow” and “filled-in” appearances, respectively. Ao, Aorta; LA,
left atrium; LV, left ventricle.
Both PWD and CWD display flow toward the transducer as positive and above the baseline, and flow
away from the transducer as negative and below the baseline. Because PWD displays velocity at specific
locations, the spectra are more uniform or compact, yielding a hollow-appearing signal or envelope
(Figure 97.4, A). This is because most blood flow velocity is uniform. When flow within the sample
volume is not laminar, spectral dispersion or broadening can be seen. Spectral broadening is suggestive
of turbulence but it can also be related to technical issues or instrument settings such as a large angle of
incidence, a sample volume size that is too large, or overgaining of the Doppler signal. By definition,
CWD exhibits spectral broadening. Hence, the velocity spectra are not congruent and they have a “filled
in” appearance (Figure 97.4, B). Once CWD is activated, a focal zone marker becomes apparent and it
should be placed in the anatomic region of interest for optimal display. The goal with CWD should be to
obtain clearly delineated outer envelopes for accurate assessment of mean or peak velocity. “Fuzzy”
CWD envelopes are usually related to misalignment or overgained signals.

Tissue Doppler Imaging (TDI)
Tissue Doppler imaging (TDI) refers to PWD applied to myocardial tissue. From a left apical 4-chamber
view, longitudinal myocardial velocities are commonly recorded at the lateral mitral annulus and lateral
tricuspid annulus (within the myocardium just apical to atrioventricular junction) (Figure 97.5). From
this plane, the basilar myocardium recoils in early diastole, moving away from the transducer. This is
represented as a negative (downward) tissue velocity in early diastole (e’). Following diastasis, late
diastolic recoil occurs due to atrial contraction (just after the P wave on the ECG), and another less
prominent negative tissue velocity in late diastole (a’) is apparent. During ventricular systole, a positive
(upward) tissue velocity (s’) is displayed as the myocardium contracts and the annulus moves toward the
apex. Tissue velocities are lower relative to blood velocity, usually <20 cm/s. Recording of these
velocities aids assessment of LV and RV diastolic function and filling pressures (particularly e’ relative to
a’) and assessment of regional longitudinal systolic function (s’).

FIGURE 97.5 Tissue Doppler imaging (TDI) applied to the lateral mitral
annulus using pulsed-wave Doppler from a left apical transducer position. Note
the reduced scale (upper right of the image) of TDI compared to blood velocity.
Early diastolic (e’), late diastolic (a’), and systolic (s’) velocities are apparent.

The Doppler Examination
The Doppler examination is usually performed simultaneously with the 2DE examination, with
adjustments and additional acquisitions made as necessary as the 2DE examination progresses. It is also
performed or expanded based on clinical suspicion or if cardiac abnormalities are suspected or
identified. At a minimum, CDI should be used for screening all four valves (i.e., ventricular inflow and
outflow tracts) for leaks and flow disturbances, keeping in mind these are best identified when blood
flow is parallel to the ultrasound beam. If a flow abnormality is identified, spectral Doppler should be
activated to determine flow direction and velocity. Pulsed-wave Doppler is routinely used for recording
transmitral flow velocities from a left apical 4-chamber view (Figure 97.6). These are crucial for
assessment of LV diastolic function and estimating filling pressure. For transmitral flow assessment, the
sample volume is placed within the LV at the tips of the open mitral valve to yield an early filling velocity
(E wave) and a late filling velocity secondary to atrial contraction (A wave). Equivalent transtricuspid
flow velocities can also be recorded for similar reasons. Systolic flow velocities in the proximal
pulmonary artery (PA) and aorta are commonly acquired near their respective valves using PWD. The
sample volume is positioned just distal to the opened valve cusps. Pulmonary valve velocities can be
acquired from any view that best aligns to flow. This is usually a right parasternal short-axis (RPSAX)
basilar right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) view or a left cranial view PA view. Aortic valve velocities
can be acquired from a subcostal view or a left apical 5-chamber LV outflow tract (LVOT) view. The
subcostal view is often preferred in dogs because other views have been shown to underestimate LVOT
velocity in dogs.17 This is of particular relevance for dogs with known or suspected (sub)aortic
stenosis.18 In general, CWD should be performed for suspected high velocity flow or if aliasing is
observed with CDI and especially if aliasing is observed with PWD. Valvular or perivalvular
regurgitation or stenosis usually first identified by 2DE or CDI should always be interrogated with CWD

using whichever acoustic window and imaging plane maximizes velocity and optimizes the flow spectra
(outer envelope). This is of particular relevance for estimating pressure gradients.

FIGURE 97.6 Transmitral flow velocities quantitated with pulsed-wave
Doppler. The sample volume is positioned at the tips of the opened mitral valve
leaflets. Early (E) diastolic filling waves and late diastolic filling waves
associated with atrial contraction (A) are evident. These velocities can fuse
during tachycardia.
Estimating instantaneous pressure gradients (PG) derived from CWD velocity spectra involves the
simplified Bernoulli equation, PG (mm Hg) = 4 × (velocity [m/s])2. It is a powerful tool that enables
noninvasive real-time estimates of cardiac chamber or arterial pressures. The most common application
involves quantitating systolic pressure overloads affecting the LV or RV. For example, if a stenotic
pulmonary valve is identified—usually based on 2DE and aliasing with CDI—and CWD spectra show a
peak transpulmonary velocity of 5.2 m/s, the peak difference in pressure from the RV, across the valve,
to the PA during systole (the systolic PG) is 108 mm Hg (Figure 97.7, A). If PA pressure is assumed to
be normal, at ∼25 mm Hg, RV systolic pressure can be estimated by adding 25 mm Hg to the PG. Thus,
estimated peak RV systolic pressure in this example is 108 mm Hg + 25 mm Hg = 133 mm Hg. Most
cardiologists rely on peak transpulmonary PG as a key metric for determining the severity of the
pulmonary stenosis (ch. 231).19 Similar steps are taken to estimate PG across a stenotic lesion in the
LVOT, i.e., subaortic stenosis.19
Another important application of the simplified Bernoulli equation relates to applying it to CWD
interrogation of AV valve regurgitation. For example, if TV regurgitation is identified with CDI, and
CWD interrogation shows a peak velocity of 4.28 m/s, this regurgitant flow from RV to RA indicates a

peak systolic PG of 4 × 4.282 = 73.4 mm Hg. Right atrial pressure is often negligible (0-5 mm Hg) or at
most 10-15 mm Hg, so the PG corresponds to—or is slightly below—the peak RV systolic pressure. The
peak RV systolic pressure in turn must equal PA systolic pressure, barring an obstruction in the RVOT.
Thus, the peak velocity of TV regurgitation determined with CWD provides an indirect estimate of
systolic PA pressure. Elevated systolic PA pressure, i.e., tricuspid regurgitation velocity or PG, is a key
metric for the diagnosis and severity assessment of pulmonary hypertension (ch. 218).20 Similar steps
can be taken to estimate systemic arterial pressure from mitral regurgitation (MR) velocity.21 As a word
of caution, it is important to only use well-aligned, well-visualized, good quality CWD spectra (with
contour and shape that comply with known hemodynamic principles) to measure velocities and PGs,
especially those that impact clinical decisions. These can be fraught with technical issues, inaccuracies,
and might vary considerably, even within the same examination.22-25 Averaging at least 3 good quality
peak velocity spectra is encouraged.

ADDITIONAL AND ADVANCED IMAGING
Three-dimensional echocardiography (3DE), post-processing analysis using speckle-tracking
echocardiography, and contrast echocardiography continue to emerge and have been evaluated in dogs
and cats.26-28

Three-Dimensional Echocardiography
Three-dimensional echocardiography includes real-time (live) 3DE imaging (Video 97.2

) and post-

processing techniques that generate a 3D model based on a composite of simultaneously captured 2DE
cine loops (Video 97.3

). This rapidly evolving technology will likely improve clinical decision-

making and help guide medical, surgical, or catheter-based treatments. Major hindrances for 3DE
becoming more routine include added cost of specialized transducers and analysis software and dealing
with faster and more variable heart rates of dogs and cats, i.e., stitching multiple cardiac cycles and
required processing speeds.

Strain Imaging
Strain imaging quantitates myocardial deformation resulting from an applied force. It uses speckle
tracking echocardiography, which tracks the movement of specific 2DE speckles within the myocardium
throughout systole (or diastole). Strain is given a negative value if the distance between speckles
shortens and a positive value if the distance between speckles lengthens. Strain can be assessed
regionally, globally, or both simultaneously. It is not dependent of the angle of insonation, and it can
assess myocardial motion in the longitudinal, radial, or circumferential motion planes. Global
longitudinal (systolic) strain of the LV from an apical view represents the most common clinical
application in humans. Strain imaging is largely considered invaluable for systolic ventricular function
assessment in humans due to its ability to detect early, subtle abnormalities in ventricular function prior
to conventional indices. Current algorithms designed for humans are vendor-specific but have been
applied to dogs and cats for assessment of LV, RV, and atrial function (Video 97.4

). Shortcomings

include challenges associated with high heart rates, inadequate tissue tracking, and low reproducibility.
Based on the human experience and some available evidence,29-33 strain imaging appears promising for
early or subclinical detection of myocardial disease/abnormalities (e.g., cardiomyopathies) in dogs and
cats. However, studies that include gold standards or longitudinal data in naturally occurring diseases
are limited.

FIGURE 97.7 Example of applying the simplified Bernoulli equation of
pressure gradient (mm Hg) = 4 × velocity (m/s)2 to velocity spectra acquired
using continuous wave Doppler to estimate peak systolic pressure gradient
across the pulmonary valve in a dog with severe valvar pulmonary stenosis.

Contrast Echocardiography
Contrast echocardiography involves administering a sterile solution intravenously that enhances
acoustic impedance of blood and waiting for it to enter a cardiovascular structure of interest. The
solution typically consists of agitated saline or a gas that generates micro-cavitations or -bubbles. It can
be used to aid delineation of endocardial borders, enhance Doppler signals, assess myocardial perfusion,
or help outline intraluminal masses, e.g., thrombus or tumor. In veterinary medicine, agitated saline
(Video 97.5

) is most commonly utilized to document a right (pulmonary) to left (systemic) shunt

such as a patent foramen ovale, atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect or patent ductus arteriosus.
These can be ambiguous with 2DE and Doppler imaging techniques. Intracardiac right-to-left shunts are
easily documented by observing the agitated saline enter into the RA and RV and then seeing if the
contrast quickly enters into the LA (shunt at the atrial level) or LV (shunt at the ventricular level) (Video
97.6

). In patients without a right-to-left shunt, the contrast is filtered by the pulmonary capillaries

and is not visualized in the left heart (Video 97.7

). Some normal patients might exhibit

intrapulmonary shunting but the contrast entering the left heart should be diminished, significantly
delayed by several cardiac cycles, and originate from a pulmonary vein. Extracardiac right-to-left
shunting of patent ductus arteriosus requires visualizing contrast in the descending aorta (typically the
abdominal aorta) following injection via a peripheral vein (ch. 231).

ASSESSMENT OF CARDIAC STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
ASSESSMENT OF CARDIAC CHAMBER SIZE: GENERAL CONCEPTS

Assessment of cardiac chamber size aids the echocardiographic diagnosis, provides a robust assessment
of chronic disease severity, and aids clinical decision-making regarding treatment intervention,
monitoring, and prognosis.
Cardiac size and function are influenced by physiologic factors such as species, breed and somatotype,
body size, sex, body condition, plasma volume/hydration, heart rate and rhythm, autonomic tone, and
loading conditions (preload, afterload). Non-physiologic factors, such as drugs that impact the
cardiovascular system and echocardiography-related factors such as operator, equipment, and
acquisition and measurement variability (or error), can also influence cardiac chamber size. These
should be considered when interpreting an echocardiogram to avoid erroneous assessments and
misdiagnoses.

Quantitative Measurements of Cardiac Size and Function
Cardiologists rely on a combination of subjective and objective assessments to guide clinical decisions.
Objective measurements should have an important influence. Estimates of cardiac chamber volume
obtained with 2DE can be accurate, available, and cost-effective. These include linear measurements
usually of the minor axis of a chamber (using 2DE or M-mode) (Figure 97.8, A), area tracings of a
chamber (Figure 97.8, B), and volume estimates using a combination of the two, an area-length
measurement using, e.g., Simpson’s method of discs (SMOD) (Figure 97.8, C). Linear measurements
are popular because they are quick, easy, and reproducible. However, they are often insensitive (and less
accurate) to changes in chamber volume because they serve as a 1-dimensional surrogate for a 3D
structure. Area measurements and volume estimates are more time-consuming, demand higher image
quality, and are less reproducible, but they are more accurate. They represent the current standard in
humans.34 In dogs and cats, preferred measurements vary based on species, breed, cardiac chamber,
disease/context, and personal preference.

Normalizing or Indexing Measurements to Body Size
Body size strongly influences cardiac chamber size in dogs. Unless evaluating cardiac chamber size in
the same dog over time, cardiac chamber size should ideally be normalized (indexed) to body size in
some manner to help determine if cardiomegaly is apparent. In veterinary medicine, two popular
methods for normalizing linear cardiac chamber measurements to body size are: 1) normalizing to body
weight using allometric scaling, or 2) indexing to another cardiac structure that should not change, such
as the diameter of the aorta (aortic ratios). Body weight-adjusted aortic ratio indices have also been
reported.35,36
Linear measurements should not simply be indexed to body weight, which is equivalent to a volume
because this relationship is nonlinear. Physical principles reveal that length = volume1/3 (or length3 =
volume). Thus, to correctly index or normalize a linear measurement to body weight, one should divide
the measurement by body weight∼1/3, where 1/3 represents a scaling exponent.37-39 Normalization of
linear measurements to body weight involves the following formula: normalized linear measurement =
linear measurement/body weightscaling exponent. For example, scaling exponents for LV internal
dimension at end-diastole (LVIDd) have been found to be 0.294 to 0.322 or 0.3 if rounded to 1
decimal.37-39 Thus, LVIDd normalized to body weight (LVIDdN) = LVIDd (cm)/body weight (kg)0.3. If a
25 kg dog’s LVIDd measures 4.8 cm, its LVIDdN = 4.8/250.3 = 1.8 cm/kg0.3. Prediction intervals derived
from the aforementioned allometric scaling studies can then be generated and are used clinically to
serve as reference intervals for dogs of any size.

FIGURE 97.8 Measurements of cardiac chamber size: linear measurement of
the minor axis of the left ventricle (LV). A, Area tracing of the endocardial
border of the LV. B, Estimate of LV volume using Simpson’s method of discs. C,
Most ventricular size measurements are performed at end-diastole. LA, Left
atrium; RA, right atrium; RV, right ventricle.
Aortic ratios serve as a convenient method to index linear measurements to body size. They are likely
more reliable than weight-related indices in dogs that are over- or -underconditioned but are flawed if
there is an abnormality of the LVOT. Certain breeds are known to have smaller aortic diameters,
including Boxers and Bull Terriers.40,41 There are two different ways to measure aortic annular
diameter: short-axis (Ao_Sx; measured from the RPSAX basilar view) and long-axis (Ao_Lx; measured
from the RPLAX 5-chamber view).42 The Ao_Sx is always larger because it inevitably incorporates some
of the sinus of Valsalva.
Indexing area and volume measurements to body size is more intuitive and involves indexing to body
surface area (m2) and body weight (kg), respectively. Some volume estimates are indexed to body
surface area, which is common in human echocardiography laboratories. Given the relatively smaller
dispersion of body sizes encountered in domestic cats, indexing cardiac chamber size to body size is
uncommon but should be considered for extremely small or large domestic cats. Lastly, growing puppies
and kittens present challenges with some data available for guidance.43-46

LEFT ATRIAL SIZE
Quantification of LA size is one of the most important measurements to perform (Figure 97.9). Atrial
size assessments are usually performed at maximum size at end- (ventricular) systole and just prior to
atrioventricular valve opening or at the end of the T wave on the ECG. Diseases that increase LA
pressure, volume, or both, and lead to LA dilation, are common in dogs and cats. In the RPLAX
projections, increased LA pressure causes the atrial septum to bow toward the RA and dilation of an
adjacent pulmonary vein is commonly apparent. The LA also appears spheroidal. From the RPSAX
basilar aortic and LA view, subjective enlargement is easy to appreciate. The aortic root serves as a
reference and enlargement of the left auricle also can be visualized. The latter can become especially
prominent in cats. Pulmonary venous enlargement can also be detected in the far field, depending on the
precise imaging plane. Common quantitative 2DE measurements of LA size in dogs include two linear

measurements, namely, LA long-axis dimension (LA_Lx)39,47 and LA short-axis dimension indexed to
the aortic root (LA/Ao_Sx),42,48 and an estimate of LA volume (LAV) using SMOD.49,50 In cats, LA_Lx
and LA/Ao_Sx are used commonly (Table 97.2).51 Also, some 2DE, M-mode, and Doppler indices of
LA pump function have demonstrated clinical utility,52,53 particularly in cats with hypertrophic
cardiomyopathy (HCM) for assessing thromboembolic risk and prognosis.54-56

LEFT VENTRICULAR CHAMBER SIZE AND WALL
THICKNESS
The ventricles exhibit different morphologic adaptations depending on the timing (systolic versus
diastolic wall stress) and chronicity of the disease process or its hemodynamic burden . Clinical
surrogates used for quantitating LV morphologic adaptation and hypertrophy most commonly involve
linear measurements of wall thickness and chamber lumen, respectively, from a frozen 2DE image, the
M-mode examination, or both. Estimates of LV end-diastolic chamber volume ideally using SMOD are
also becoming increasingly important, notably to aid the diagnosis of dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) in
dogs (Table 97.3).14-16 Indices of LV size at end-diastole and end-systole are used for calculating the
clinically important ejection phase indices (fractional shortening [FS] and ejection fraction [EF]).
Subjective features of moderate to severe LV chamber enlargement in the long-axis projections include
increased sphericity and apical rounding, where the minor axis length approaches the major axis length.

LEFT VENTRICULAR SYSTOLIC FUNCTION
Quantitating LV systolic (pump) function is an important component of the echocardiographic
examination. It can provide clinically useful information regarding diagnosis, therapy, and prognosis.
For example, the echocardiographic diagnosis of DCM is defined by the presence of reduced ventricular
systolic function (with subsequent dilation).14-16 In other disease states, such as end-stage feline HCM,
the development of systolic dysfunction might be associated with reduced survival.55,56
Echocardiographic indices of systolic function do not solely quantitate myocardial contractility.
Systolic function is also dependent on preload (diastolic wall stress, affected by blood volume, venous
return, and ventricular compliance, for example) and afterload (systolic wall stress, affected by vascular
resistance, aortic/arterial compliance, and structure of the outflow tract, for example). Heart rate and
rhythm have important direct and indirect (diastolic filling time) influences on systolic function and
these can further complicate assessment. Notably, heart rate increases systolic function up to a point, via
the Bowditch or treppe effect. However, tachyarrhythmias that are sustained over several days/weeks
can lead to a tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy with a DCM phenotype (ch. 233). Also, premature
complexes (short cycle lengths) diminish systolic function but the next contraction is often enhanced,
i.e., post-extrasystolic potentiation. This underscores the importance of quantitating systolic function
during sinus rhythm and averaging multiple cardiac cycles (>3) if the rate varies, such as during sinus
arrhythmia or atrial fibrillation. Thus, interpreting echocardiographic indices of systolic function
requires understanding their key determinants (contractility, preload, afterload, heart rate and rhythm),
drugs that affect these variables, and the clinical context, including the clinical and echocardiographic
diagnoses.
The gold standard to quantitate LV systolic function is ejection fraction (EF), which represents stroke
volume (end-diastolic volume – end-systolic volume) divided by end-diastolic volume. In veterinary
medicine, fractional shortening (FS), a crude surrogate of EF that utilizes linear measurements, is more
routinely used (Table 97.4). When acquired from a well-executed M-mode or 2DE, FS usually provides
for a convenient and reliable metric. However, relying on a single metric to make clinical decisions is
potentially problematic, particularly if a result is considered borderline or low-normal. In addition to EF
and FS, absolute end-systolic LV dimensions and volumes can represent useful indices of systolic
function. There are dozens of additional systolic function indices that might add value including strain
imaging, which has rapidly gained prominence in human echocardiography laboratories. Many of these
indices have been reviewed in more detail in the context of important veterinary diseases such as canine
DCM (ch. 233) and myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) (ch. 232).16,27,57 Body size has a lesser

influence on EF and FS relative to chamber size measurements. However, some studies have reported
weak negative correlations of FS and EF with body weight.39,58 This corroborates clinical experience
suggesting that some larger dogs tend to have lower FS and EF, which can complicate screening for
DCM.

LEFT VENTRICULAR DIASTOLIC FUNCTION
Assessment of diastolic function can be clinically useful, particularly in diseases that directly lead to
impaired LV filling in the subclinical stages, such as HCM.59 Many diseases are eventually affected by
impaired filling, particularly once CHF ensues. Indices of diastolic function and ventricular filling
pressure can be useful to predict CHF in dogs and cats.60-62 Evaluation of diastolic function is complex
and always intertwined with assessment of ventricular filling pressure. It requires assimilation of
numerous technically demanding Doppler echocardiographic variables.59,63

Assessment of systolic function is relative and especially dependent on the clinical context, which
includes the cardiac diagnosis, heart rate and rhythm, presence of systemic disease, blood volume and
hydration status, level of stress, anxiety or sympathetic tone, and drugs and sedatives.
The primary components necessary for assessment of LV diastolic function involve recognizing
patterns and assessing velocities of transmitral flow (E and A waves) and PWD TDI of the mitral annulus
(e’ and a’ waves). Additionally, LA size (used as a surrogate of mean LA pressure) and function,
pulmonary venous flow patterns, isovolumic relaxation time, and E wave deceleration time are
additional indices that can be helpful.59,63 Diastolic dysfunction can be categorized according to
progressively worsening diastolic function based on LA size, E/A, and e’/a’: grade I) impaired relaxation
(relaxation abnormality), II) pseudonormal filling, and III) restrictive filling (which can be reversible or
irreversible).
Grade I diastolic dysfunction is relatively common and expected in elderly, otherwise healthy
patients.64 It suggests a low probability of CHF unless precipitated by overzealous fluid therapy or
sustained tachycardia. E-wave velocities that are within reference intervals suggest normal LV filling
pressure. Grade II diastolic dysfunction, differentiated from normal diastolic function by reduced e’
velocity together with LA enlargement, indicates an increased risk for CHF. Grade III diastolic
dysfunction, characterized by markedly increased E-wave velocities with diminished A-wave and
reduced e’ and a’ velocities, suggests severe diastolic dysfunction and markedly elevated LV filling
pressure. Grade III diastolic dysfunction indicates CHF is present or imminent. Unfortunately, diastolic
functional assessment is impossible or confounding in many patients. For example, tachycardia is
common in many cats and some dogs, leading to fusion of early and late diastolic velocities, which
precludes analysis. Arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation also preclude conventional analysis due to loss
of A and a’ waves. Characterizing diastolic function in small dogs with moderate to severe MMVD is
complicated by the influence of markedly increased preload. Conventional grading often points to
normal or hyperdynamic diastolic function, which limits its value.57 Studies have documented the
clinical value of peak E-wave velocity in dogs with MMVD.53,65-69 E-waves >1.0 m/s in dogs with leftsided cardiomegaly suggest increased risk for heart failure or cardiac death,68 and values >1.2-1.4 m/s
have been associated with reduced survival in dogs with MMVD.53,65,67,69

RIGHT HEART SIZE AND FUNCTION
Despite its challenges, the assessment of right heart size and function is encouraged. Its clinical
importance has been underappreciated but is growing, even in diseases thought to primarily impact the
left heart.70 Quantitative indices of right heart size and function have demonstrated clinical and
prognostic value in many diseases, including MMVD,71,72 HCM,73-76 pulmonary hypertension,77-81
arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy82,83, and pulmonary stenosis.84 The RV can be involved in
diseases that affect the LV because of shared superficial myofibers, a shared septum and pericardium,
and linkage via the pulmonary circulation. Thus, disease of one ventricle, if severe and long-standing,
often impacts the performance of the other. Studies proposing broadly applicable reference intervals for

2DE and M-mode indices of RA size and RV size and function have become available for dogs77,78,85-87
and cats (Table 97.4).73 Consensus-based guidelines for assessment of the right heart in humans are
also available for consultation.88
All imaging planes should be used to gather a subjective impression of right heart size and function to
complement quantitative indices, which do not incorporate the RVOT. Normally the RA appears at least
slightly smaller and certainly not larger than the LA. RV wall thickness usually appears to be one-third
to one-half that of the LV. The RV chamber lumen should not appear larger than the LV, with the minor
dimension usually <50% that of the LV. Moderate to severe dilation of the RV causes loss of its usual
triangular shape in the longitudinal planes (RPLAX and L apical views) and produces apical rounding or
dominates the cardiac apex. The IVS normally should appear rounded toward the RV (convex) in systole
and diastole and not flattened or bowing into the LV. Significant RV pressure overload causes flattening
of the IVS, primarily in systole; RV volume overload causes diastolic septal flattening.

ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY AND CLINICAL DECISION-MAKING
The numbers of echocardiographic measurements, calculations, and assessments are almost limitless.
Regarding cardiac chamber size and function assessment, most routinely rely on linear measurements
and subjective impressions. Area measurements and volume estimates are utilized for specific diseases
or on a case-by-case basis. Even if certain measurements are used commonly, definitive reference
intervals with broad agreement are rare and might not be easily accessible or available for certain
breeds. Deciding normal versus abnormal is particularly challenging when differentiating normal versus
mild disease in patients not showing clinical signs. Some general recommendations when using
echocardiography to aid clinical decision-making are listed below:
a) Two to three cardiac cycles should be averaged for each measurement during sinus rhythm, or 35+ if the rhythm is irregular.
b) Echocardiographic assessments should always involve the clinical context.
c) Reference intervals are not definitive but should serve as a guide. Demonstrating reproducibility
via serial examinations is encouraged for patients with borderline or equivocal findings.
d) If examining a purebred dog or cat, breed-specific reference intervals should be prioritized over
multi-breed reference intervals, if available. Certain dog or cat breeds and potentially specific
measurements within the breed might deviate substantially.89 For example, cardiac chamber
size in most sighthounds and Newfoundlands has been shown to deviate considerably from
cardiac chamber size in other breeds.38
e) Reference intervals of cardiac size that normalize values to body size in some manner should be
prioritized, even within the species or breed (if available).
f) Relying on single measurements for clinical decisions should be avoided, particularly decisions
that have or might have a lasting or costly impact, e.g., breeding, long-term medications,
invasive diagnostics, surgical/interventional procedures, etc. If possible, use of multiple
measurements/indices that incorporate multiple or orthogonal imaging planes is preferred. For
example, documenting LA enlargement with LA/Ao_Sx and LA_Lx or LAV (from RPLAX, left
apical, or both views) should increase confidence that the LA is truly enlarged if more than one
is above the reference interval.

URINE COLLECTION
The goal of a urine collection procedure is to obtain the highest
quality urine sample with lowest risk of complications to the patient.
The method of collection, collection container used, and the method
of handling of the sample are important aspects of the process, as
these will affect both the results and the interpretation of the sample
obtained. The volume of urine collected is another important
consideration. The usual goal is to collect at least 5 mL of urine for
proper urinalysis and storage of a portion of the urine in case the
initial results of the urinalysis lead to further diagnostics testing,
such as measurement of the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or an
aerobic bacterial urine culture (ch. 70).
There are at least three methods to obtain urine from the bladder
that will be reviewed in this section:

• Free catch (normal voiding and manual compression of the
urinary bladder)
• Transurethral catheterization of the bladder
• Cystocentesis
Each method of urine collection has its advantages and
disadvantages; however, for the purpose of urinary diagnostics,
cystocentesis in dogs and cats is highly recommended. “Off the floor”
urine samples are discouraged as these will have the highest number
of contaminants.

FREE CATCH (VIDEO 98.1

)

The free-catch method is the easiest way to obtain a urine sample
and is indicated in patients where cystocentesis or catheterization is
not indicated or possible. Free-catch urine samples are generally not
intended for culture because of the potential for contamination, but
they are adequate for simple urinalysis. Urine should be collected in
a transparent sterile container with a tight-fitting lid that is available
from medical supply companies or from the veterinary facility, to
help reduce further sample contamination. Owners are discouraged
from using containers from home, which may contain contaminants,
such as detergents, food residue, medications, or leaching reagents;
these will alter chemistry results.
Normal voiding method is preferred with the free-catch method. A
mid-stream sample is best, to reduce further sample contamination.
This form of collection is easy to perform in most male dogs as their
posture for urination allows ample space for catching urine
midstream with a sterile container. When collecting urine from
female dogs, a container lid is often easiest. The lid is slid under the
dog a few seconds after she has begun to urinate, at least 5 mL of
urine is collected, and the lid contents are poured into the container
and closed. For cats, nonabsorbent plastic beads or polished gravel
can be placed in a clean litter box instead of the usual litter. After the
cat urinates, the urine can be aspirated into a syringe or decanted
into a clean or sterile container and taken to the practice.
Occasionally, manual compression of the bladder can be very useful

if the patient is small (<5.5 kg), calm, and compliant. However, the
urinary bladder can be traumatized if excessive digital pressure is
applied. It can also be painful to some patients, especially those with
lower urinary tract disease. Because of technical challenges inherent
to this method and the risk to the patient, this method is not
recommended for most situations where a urine sample is desired.1

TRANSURETHRAL CATHETERIZATION
OF THE BLADDER
Transurethral catheterization is the passage of a urinary catheter
from the external urethral orifice into the urinary bladder. The
primary risks are iatrogenic trauma, which is the most common
cause for urethral rupture in cats,2 and urinary tract infection (UTI)
from bacteria introduced during placement; however, with a
standardized collection technique, the risk for infection is low. For
routine urinalysis, this technique is most often performed in male
dogs, rarely in female dogs and male cats, and almost never in female
cats. For indwelling catheter placement purposes, this technique can
be used in dogs and cats, both males and females. Prior to its
placement, the catheter should be inspected, the length of catheter
required to reach the bladder should be estimated, and if using a
Foley catheter, then the patency of the balloon should be verified.
Sedation (as needed), proper patient positioning, and knowledge of
the anatomic location of the urethral opening can help increase the
chance for successful catheter placement.

Female Dogs
Digital Palpation (Blind) Technique (Video 98.2

)

With the patient in lateral, sternal, or dorsal recumbency, this
technique is performed by inserting the lubricated index finger of the
non-dominant hand (in sterile gloves) into the vulva, and the
urethral papilla is identified by palpation. The junction of the
vestibule and the vagina is a muscular thickening, the cingulum, that
is usually palpable as a narrowing of the lumen of the cavity to the

extent that further advancement of the finger is impossible. This
anatomical landmark is usually helpful because the urethral opening
is located just caudal to it. Inserting a finger into this opening
prevents the catheter from advancing into the vagina rather than into
the urethral opening (Figure 98.1). The dominant hand grasps the
catheter near the tip, and inserts it gently between the labia of the
vulva and into the vestibule. The finger of the non-dominant hand
(which is within the vestibule) is placed on the tip of the catheter and
is used for advancing the catheter forward in small millimeter
increments to guide it along the ventral floor of the vestibule to the
urethral opening. The dominant hand keeps the catheter aligned
until it has entered the urethra. Placement in the urethra is verified
by palpating the tissue of the urethral papilla over the catheter. Once
the catheter has entered the urethra, it is advanced until its tip rests
in the bladder. Urine can be collected with a sterile syringe at this
point. If using a Foley catheter, then it is secured by inflating the
balloon; the catheter is then gently pulled caudally to position its tip
at the neck of the bladder. A closed collection system is attached, and
the catheter is secured to prevent excessive traction on it.

FIGURE 98.1 Urethral catheterization of a female
dog. An index finger is placed over the urethral
orifice to guide the catheter ventrally into the
urethra.
Guiding Catheter Technique
In a difficult insertion, a polypropylene catheter can be used for
locating the urethral opening. A Foley catheter can be placed in the

vestibule alongside it, using the polypropylene catheter as a guide.
The polypropylene catheter is then removed.3 This technique is
similar to the novel two-catheter technique recently described in the
literature.4 Finally, an appropriately sized polypropylene catheter
will also fit through the lumen of a Foley catheter to serve as a stylet
and increase its rigidity and make it easier to pass when needed.
Vaginoscopic Technique
This technique can be performed using a speculum or otoscope and
may be less difficult than the digital/blind method because it allows
visualization of the urethral orifice.5 This technique is best
performed with the patient in sternal or lateral recumbency. If
needed, a sterile, lubricated syringe containing 1-3 mL of 2%
lidocaine can be inserted into the vestibule, and the labia are then
pinched to form a seal around the syringe for local anesthetic
infusion. With a speculum, the vulva is gently pulled in the opposite
direction to the anus, while inserting the speculum with the handle
towards the anus. The speculum is held in the non-dominant hand
and opened such that it pushes the soft tissue of the vestibule aside
to visualize the urethral papilla (Figure 98.3). An appropriately
sized urinary Foley catheter and stylet is then inserted into the
visualized papilla with the dominant hand. With the otoscope
technique, an otoscope with a large (wide but short) cone is used to
visualize the urethral orifice. The catheter is inserted through the
cone of the otoscope. Since the flared end of the catheter does not fit
through the cone, it is detached from the light source and left with
the catheter until the catheter is removed from the patient.
A novel urinary catheterization device—a cylindrical structure
made from polypropylene plastic with the end tapered obliquely such
that there is a long and short end—for use in female dogs has been
described recently in the literature,6 but this device has not been
applied for routine urinary collection at this time.

Female Cats
Catheterization of female cats is generally done with the blind
technique but usually requires a 3.5- or 5-French polypropylene
tomcat catheter. Placing gentle traction on the vulvar folds, the vulva

is pulled caudally to open up the area and the urethra. If the urinary
catheter is placed easily on the first attempt, it likely is in the vagina,
and another attempt is recommended. This technique is difficult to
perform and failure is common.

Male Dogs
The patient can be in standing or lateral recumbency for this
procedure (Video 98.3

). Sedation is generally not required. The

penis is extruded from the prepuce and the urethral orifice is wiped
clean, while the penis remains extended. The approximate length of
catheter (tip of penis to pelvic brim) is measured before placement.
The tip of the catheter is then lubricated with sterile jelly, and then
passed gently through the penile urethra to the previously estimated
length of the urethra. A slight pressure is felt almost immediately as
the catheter passes the os penis; upon reaching the ischial rim there
is a slight reduction in the easy movement of the catheter as it begins
its passage around the pelvic bend. For routine urine collection,
sterile gloves are recommended but not needed as long as the
catheter is handled in its package material to keep the procedure as
clean as possible (Figure 98.2). When urine has begun to leak from
the end of the catheter, then the insertion is stopped. The penis can
be released into the prepuce and urine samples collected.

Male Cats
The patient can be in dorsal or lateral recumbency, and sedation is
generally required for this procedure. The penis is extruded by
placing gentle pressure on the prepuce towards the spine. Gauze
sponges may be used to aid in applying traction. A sterile catheter is
coated with sterile lubricating jelly and inserted into the penile
urethra with the dominant hand. The catheter is advanced until
urine is noted in the catheter lumen, or is visible upon aspiration
with a syringe. This procedure is described in further detail in ch.
99, and a technique for placing an indwelling urethral catheter in a
male cat is shown in

Video 98.4.

CYSTOCENTESIS
Cystocentesis is a common clinical technique used to obtain a sample
of urine directly from the urinary bladder of dogs and cats (
Videos 98.5, 98.6). It involves insertion of a 25- to 22-gauge, 0.751.5-inch (2-4 cm) needle, with a sterile 6- or 12-mL syringe attached,
through the abdominal wall and bladder wall to obtain urine. It is the
preferred urine collection technique when a sterile urine sample is
needed for urinalysis or bacterial culture,7 as it prevents
contamination of urine by the urethra, genital tract, or skin and
reduces the risk of obtaining a contaminated sample. This is a major
advantage to this technique. Cystocentesis also may be needed to
decompress a severely overdistended bladder temporarily in an
animal with urethral obstruction (ch. 99). It can be performed with
the patient in dorsal or lateral recumbency (Figure 98.4), or with
the patient standing, or being held standing on its hindlimbs by
elevating its thoracic limbs. Other than inducing mild transient
microscopic hematuria (which may be indistinguishable from
pathological hematuria), cystocentesis has not been associated with
significant side-effects. Rare instances of puncture or laceration of
large vessels (aorta, caudal vena cava) or bladder resulting in
hemoabdomen8,9 and uroabdomen,9,10 respectively, have been
reported. Vasovagal syncope may occur from autonomic stimulation
of the bladder but is also rare.11

FIGURE 98.2 A, Preparation for catheterization
via the feeder method. The distal closed end of the
catheter package is completely transected and
removed (black arrow). The catheter package is cut
3-5 cm from the cut end by making 2 cuts from both
sides of the package without cutting the catheter
(white arrow). The catheter package tab (asterisk) is
then used to feed the catheter. B, Urethral
catheterization of a male dog. A portion of the
catheter’s package is used to aseptically advance the
catheter through the urethra.

FIGURE 98.3 Appearance of urethral orifice in a
female dog as visualized during endoscopic
examination.

FIGURE 98.4 Cystocentesis may be performed
with the patient in dorsal recumbency, particularly if
the procedure is being done when the urinary
bladder cannot be palpated. The site for needle
insertion is generally at a point midway between the
umbilicus and the pelvic brim. Normally, the
clinician’s left hand would be applying pressure to
the abdomen to stabilize the bladder, but the hand is
moved away here to improve visualization.

Bladder Palpation Technique
The hair at the puncture site is clipped and the area is cleaned with
an antiseptic solution before needle insertion. The bladder is
palpated and immobilized. Care should be taken to ensure that the
bladder is not squeezed tightly while the puncture is being made
since this can cause urine to leak from the puncture site into the
abdominal cavity. The needle is inserted at a 45° angle towards the
trigone into the bladder while the plunger is pulled back to create
negative pressure. Upon obtaining the urine sample, the syringe
plunger is released, and the needle removed from the abdomen. If

urine is not obtained, the needle should not be reinserted, to avoid
the risk of penetrating a bowel loop and subsequently inserting the
contaminated needle into the bladder.12
The needle has to be changed before attempting another insertion
into the bladder. If urine is not obtained after three attempts it may
be due to the fact that the bladder is probably small. The patient
should be allowed to rest until the urinary bladder is full, or
ultrasonography should be considered to guide needle placement.

Ultrasound-Guided Technique
An ultrasound machine allows the veterinary team member to
visualize the bladder and watch the needle being inserted during the
procedure, which can be performed with the patient in dorsal or
lateral recumbency (

Videos 98.5, 98.6). The probe marker is

identified, and the probe is placed on the caudal portion of the
abdomen with the marker in the cranial direction (ch. 73). With
ultrasound, urine within the bladder is most commonly anechoic.13 A
needle is inserted at an approximately 15° angle under the probe and
in line with the mark on the probe indicating the cranial aspect. The
screen is monitored to confirm that the needle is inserted accurately.
Urine is aspirated into the syringe until the desired amount is
obtained or urine stops flowing. Aspiration is stopped before
removing the needle from the abdomen. If at any time the patient
begins to move, aspiration is stopped, and the needle removed to
avoid any complications.

URINE SAMPLE MANAGEMENT
Urinalysis results can be affected by sample handling, including
transportation and preparation of the specimen (ch. 70). Once a
sample is collected, urinalysis should be performed within the hour
to avoid artifactual changes that occur as cells and casts
deteriorate.14,15 If the urine cannot be examined within that time, or
will be shipped to a laboratory, the lid should be tightly secured and
the sample refrigerated to slow the rate of artifactual changes.
Refrigerated and sealed samples are valid up to approximately 6

hours.14 Most laboratories suggest shipping the sample with a cold
pack to delay onset of artifactual changes. The vessel used to
transport the urine sample must be clean and free of detergents and
other cleaning agents. A sterile collection tube is preferred if there is
any anticipation of obtaining a urine culture.

URINARY CATHETER MANAGEMENT
Indwelling urinary catheters are important in the management of
patients with a variety of underlying conditions, including
performance of radiographic contrast procedures, upper and lower
urinary tract diseases, trauma, and orthopedic and neurologic
dysfunction. Urinary catheter placement for indwelling purposes is
typically performed in male and female dogs and in male cats with
urethral obstruction. The urinary catheter placement procedures
have been described earlier in this chapter. Problems with indwelling
catheters include kinking of the catheter or tubing, premature
removal of the catheter, obstruction of the catheter with cellular or
crystalline debris, irritation or inflammation of the urethra, or
introduction of organisms that can cause a UTI. The goals of
indwelling urinary catheter care are to maintain patency and
decrease the likelihood of inducing hospital-acquired infections (ch.
186). This infection rate (approximately 10%),15 which has been
lower than previously reported,16 can be attributed to a standardized
placement technique and catheter management protocol as
described here.

SITE CLEANSING
It is required to wear examination gloves and use sterile gauze
sponges to cleanse, alternating between an appropriate dilute skin
antiseptic (e.g., chlorhexidine scrub diluted with sterile saline to 0.52% chlorhexidine, 1:200 povidone iodine/sterile saline) and sterile
saline. For male dogs, the hair is clipped on the prepuce and
surrounding ventral abdomen. The area is cleansed, using at least 3
scrubs with each solution. The prepuce is flushed 3 to 5 times with 2-

12 mL of dilute skin antiseptic (volume depends on size of dog) using
a sterile syringe. An assistant wearing clean examination gloves then
exteriorizes the penis. Any gross debris on the penis is removed and
the entire area is cleansed, using at least 3 scrubs with each solution,
and then flushed with 2-5 mL dilute skin antiseptic. For female dogs,
the vulva and perivulvar area are cleansed, using at least 3 scrubs
with each solution. The vaginal vault is flushed 3 to 5 times with 0.512 mL dilute skin antiseptic (volume depends on size of animal)
using a sterile syringe. For both female and male dogs, a sterile
fenestrated drape is placed over the work area. Hands are properly
washed and gloves are worn. The bulbs of Foley catheters are tested
before placement. The distal catheter is lubricated with sterile
lubricating jelly from a single-use packet, and the catheter is placed
using sterile technique, as described earlier. The catheter is then
connected to a sterile closed collection system. In male cats, the area
around the penis and prepuce is clipped and prepared using
standard aseptic technique.

MANAGING THE CLOSED COLLECTION
SYSTEM
The use of closed urine collection systems, which allow urine to be
removed from the reservoir bag without disconnection from the
urinary catheter, is standard practice in human medicine.17 Although
open urine collection systems, often incorporating recycled,
sterilized IV fluid bags, are still commonly used in veterinary
patients,18 closed collection systems are preferred. The collection
system typically includes the catheter, adapters, sterile tubing, and
collection bag. The collection bag is positioned lower than the patient
to allow urine to flow by gravity. Retrograde flow of urine from the
collection bag back into the patient should be prevented because this
may cause iatrogenic UTIs. Most commercial urine collection bags
have a one-way valve to prevent retrograde urine flow. The collection
system clamp should be closed when the patient is moved or walked
and immediately reopened once the collection bag is again lower
than the patient. The patency of the tubing should be checked hourly.
The external catheter and the collection line should also be wiped

down with a 70% isopropyl alcohol swab. If there is gross
contamination, the collection line should be replaced.
To secure the collection system and prevent displacement, the
catheter should be anchored at multiple points through a
combination of catheter balloon inflation, suturing, and stress loops
on limbs or tail. An Elizabethan collar is worn by the patient.

DAILY MAINTENANCE OF INDWELLING
CATHETERS
Hand hygiene is performed and sterile gloves are worn. Every 24
hours, the junction of the patient and the external portion of the
catheter are cleaned with sterile gauze sponges, alternating between
dilute skin antiseptic solution and sterile saline (≥3 scrubs with each
solution). All urinary catheter connections are kept tight and clean.
The urinary catheter should be checked for occlusions and adequate
urine output every 4 hours.19 When removing urine via a closed
collection system, hands should be washed and examination gloves
worn. The bag’s exterior drainage tubing is placed into a clean
collection chamber, such as a sterile measuring cup. The tubing valve
is opened to allow urine to flow from the bag into the measuring cup.
After all urine has drained, the tubing valve is closed and the tubing
is secured at the appropriate places. All urinary catheter connections
should be tight, and the bag rested on the floor on top of a clean tray.
Whenever the catheter is flushed, the amount of water instilled
should be noted so that it is not included in the total amount of
urine, which would lead to a false urine output reading. Cats and
dogs should be producing 1-2 mL of urine per kg of body weight per
hour when in a normovolemic, normotensive state with adequate
kidney function.20 Urine output volume should never be zero. If no
urine is noted in the collection system then concerns for occlusion
within the system, leak between connections, a displaced catheter, or
oliguria/anuria should be assessed.

URINARY CATHETERS AND
INFECTIONS
UTI is the most common complication of urinary catheter placement.
It most often occurs when bacteria are introduced from the urethra
during placement, following nonsterile placement, repeated
catheterization, bladder trauma or in immunosuppressed patients.21
UTI and subclinical bacterial colonization of the bladder are also
commonly identified in dogs with indwelling urinary catheters.22,23
Yet, oral or topical antimicrobials should be avoided as prophylaxis
for UTI because they can increase the risk of UTI, and when
infections do occur, they have a high degree of antimicrobial
resistance.18 Their use has not been shown to prevent infection
either. Antimicrobial-coated urinary catheters have not proven to be
significantly beneficial in veterinary medicine as they have been in
human medicine.24 Additionally, routinely culturing the urine (via
cystocentesis and never from the collection bag) at the time of
catheter removal is not recommended and is only indicated if there is
evidence of cystitis. Culturing the tip of a removed catheter is also
not recommended, as it is not predictive of UTI risk.17 There is also
no indication for prophylactic antimicrobial therapy following
urinary catheter removal in a patient with no clinical or cytological
evidence of a UTI. Antimicrobials should only be administered for
documented infection. To further reduce the risk of a UTI, the
indwelling urinary catheter should ideally be removed within 4-5
days of placement.25 Other strategies to prevent catheter associated
UTIs include: avoid indiscriminate use of urinary catheters, always
use hand hygiene, avoid open collection systems, avoid urinary
catheters in immunocompromised patients, and be cautious in
patients undergoing diuresis.26
If the patient develops lower urinary tract signs or fever after a
urinary catheter has been placed, then, preferably, the urine catheter
is removed and a cystocentesis is performed to provide a sample for
culture. Otherwise, the original urinary catheter is replaced with a
new one (sterile) and a urine sample is collected through the second
catheter. It is less ideal to sample the urine through the original

catheter, and a sample from the collection bag should never be
used.23,26
