Chapter 99: Unblocking the
Urethra
Edward Cooper

A C RO N YM S
IV intravenous
UO urethral obstruction
UTI urinary tract infection

Urethral obstruction (UO) is a common and potentially lifethreatening emergency affecting both dogs and cats. There are many
aspects of the etiology, pathogenesis, stabilization, and management
of UO that are covered elsewhere (chs. 127, 308, 309, and 312).
The focus of this chapter will be specifically geared toward the
process of unblocking the urethra of small animal patients with UO.
Given their longer and narrower urethra, males have a much higher
incidence of UO compared to females, and so males will be the focus
of the techniques discussed. As there are many techniques utilized
and various opinions regarding how to best approach these patients,
there will be an emphasis on available evidence where applicable.

GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS

The diagnosis of UO is often made based on signalment (male),
history (lower urinary tract signs, ch. 54), and physical exam
(palpation of a moderate to large, firm bladder). In addition to the
diagnosis, assessment of clinical severity is essential in determining
the most important initial interventions. While it is intuitive that
catheterization and alleviating the obstruction should occur as soon
as possible, this will have limited impact in the face of severe
hyperkalemia and bradycardia. Even if deobstruction could occur
instantaneously, it would be hours before the resumption of
glomerular filtration rate (GFR) allowed sufficient excretion to offset
life-threatening hyperkalemia. In these circumstances, emphasis
should be placed on more immediate interventions such as
administration of calcium gluconate, insulin/dextrose, terbutaline,
intravenous (IV) fluids, etc. (chs. 68, 119, 127, 296). Only after the
patient has been stabilized, or if the patient was not in need of
stabilization, should urinary catheterization attempts take priority.
Once there is opportunity to move forward with unblocking the
urethra, there are several aspects that need to be considered:
gathering supplies, sedation/analgesia/anesthesia, whether or not to
perform a decompressive cystocentesis, patient preparation, passing
the urinary catheter (including size and type of catheter to be used
and steps to minimize risk of urethral trauma), and managing
complications/unsuccessful efforts to unblock the urethra.

GATHERING SUPPLIES
It is important that all necessary supplies be obtained prior to
moving ahead with the deobstruction process. This will help to
minimize the time necessary to keep the patient under heavy
sedation/anesthesia for deobstruction. This can be accomplished by
keeping a list available (see online Equipment Pull List:
Materials/Supplies for Unblocking the Urethra) or creating “UO
packs” with supplies already gathered.
For cats, urinary catheter material and size has been a subject of
much consideration. There are several types of catheters than can be
used for unblocking the urethra as well as for indwelling purposes.
These include polypropylene, polyvinyl chloride,
polytetrafluoroethylene, polyurethane, and metal (olive-tip), each

with its potential benefits and drawbacks. Some practitioners
advocate using a 22-gauge or 20-gauge IV catheter (without the
needle stylet) or olive-tipped catheter to initially flush the urethra,
especially for more distal obstructions. A longer, indwelling catheter
then needs to be placed to allow ongoing evacuation of urine.
Polypropylene catheters (traditional “tomcat” catheter) have been
used for the initial unblocking as they are more rigid, though this
could increase the risk of urethral trauma. Further, this material has
been shown to be more reactive compared to polyvinyl when left as
indwelling.1 The combination of these factors, and the availability of
other catheters carrying fewer risks, suggests that use of these
catheters should be limited. Polyvinyl catheters can include closedended (“red rubber”) catheters or open-ended (“Argyle” feeding
tubes). Red rubber catheters are less commonly used for the initial
unblocking as they lack the ability to flush forward, so a different
catheter may be needed initially. Given it is open-ended, an Argyle
feeding tube can be used both to unblock and serve as indwelling. A
study comparing use of these two catheters (3.5 Fr) in 91 cats (58
with Argyle and 33 with red rubber) showed no significant difference
in the rate of re-obstruction.2 Polytetrafluoroethylene (e.g., “Slippery
Sam”) and polyurethane (e.g., Mila Tomcat) catheters are firmer at
room temperature, thereby allowing them to be used in unblocking
efforts. At body temperature they soften, and so they can be left in
place. As such only one catheter passage is needed to both deobstruct and serve as indwelling catheter, so there may be less
urethral trauma. No studies have been performed to directly
compare urethral irritation, but these materials are thought to be less
reactive than polypropylene or polyvinyl.
Regarding catheter size for cats, typically either 3.5 Fr or 5 Fr
catheters are used. Arguments can be made that a larger catheter is
preferred as it may be less likely to become occluded, and there is
less potential for the patient to urinate around the catheter.
Conversely, a smaller catheter may be associated with less urethral
irritation during placement and while indwelling. One retrospective
study showed a decreased incidence of reobstruction when a 3.5 Fr
catheter was used over a 5 Fr catheter (6.7 vs 19%).3 However, this
study included a number of potentially confounding factors. Further,
another study did not identify any difference in the reobstruction

rate related to catheter size.4 As such, the ideal catheter size for cats
remains to be determined.
The urethral catheter selected for dogs is typically a polyvinyl (red
rubber) or polyurethane catheter for initially unblocking the urethra.
These catheters can then be sutured in place for indwelling, or ideally
replaced by a Foley catheter. Foley catheters are often too soft to be
passed without a stylet, making it difficult to retropulse with them
and use them for initial unblocking. Catheter size selection will
depend on the size of the dog and typically ranges from 6 Fr to 10 Fr.
There are no existing data in dogs comparing catheter size or
material in the urethral deobstruction process.

FIGURE 99.1 Supplies used to create a sterile
lubricated flush solution: 18-20 g needle, two 20-30
mL syringes, a three-way stopcock, sterile lubricant
packets, sterile saline.
An additional step that may be of benefit in setting up for
unblocking the urethra is to create sterile lubricated flush. This can
be accomplished by mixing 1 packet of sterile lubricant per 10-15 mL
of sterile 0.9% NaCl across a three-way stopcock (Figure 99.1;

Video 99.1).

The benefit of creating this solution is the

opportunity to deposit lubricant all along the urethra during flushing
efforts, rather than just lubricating the tip of the catheter. This
should be assembled aseptically if the person passing the catheter
will also be flushing. If an assistant will be flushing, extension tubing
to increase distance is recommended and that way the assistant does
not need to maintain asepsis.
Finally, it is important that a sterile, closed collection system be
available to attach once the indwelling catheter has been secured.
Closed systems allow urine production to be quantified and are
associated with less risk of acquired urinary tract infection (UTI).5
Open catheter systems are not recommended.

SEDATION/ANALGESIA/ANESTHESIA
Given the pain and stress associated with UO, sedation and analgesia
are indicated in almost all circumstances prior to catheterization
attempts (perhaps short of the severely debilitated and/or stuporous
to comatose patient). A study that compared propofol to ketamine +
diazepam in a model of experimentally induced feline UO found that
cats receiving propofol recovered more quickly, but the quality of the
recovery was similar between the two groups.6
As such, the protocol chosen should be based on clinical
experience, the stability of the patient (ch. 119), which medications
are available, and potentially the experience level of the person
performing the deobstruction. For unstable patients, medications
with the fewest hemodynamic effects should be used, such as an
opioid and benzodiazepine combination in conjunction with
alfaxalone. For those that are inexperienced at deobstruction, it may
be worthwhile to consider general anesthesia after premedication
and induction. This affords the opportunity to optimize urethral
relaxation and not have to repeatedly re-dose injectable medications
for what is more likely to be a longer time to deobstruct. Similarly,
general anesthesia may be of benefit for obstructed dogs. As dogs are
much more likely to have calculi as the cause of UO, and they often
lodge just proximal to the os penis, maximizing relaxation with

general anesthesia may increase success.7 Potential protocols are
provided in Box 99.1.

Except for epidurals and inhalant anesthetics, the route of
administration for all medications listed is intravenous (IV). If
necessary, acepromazine, methadone, and midazolam can be given
intramuscularly (IM) in stable cats.
As another consideration for cats, a technique for administration
of a coccygeal (caudal) epidural has been described.8 The goal is to
produce regional anesthesia without loss of motor function to the
hind limbs, and help to reduce or remove the need for systemic
administration of medications. A prospective, double-blind
randomized controlled study has investigated the impact of epidural
administration of bupivacaine only or bupivacaine and morphine in
cats with naturally occurring UO.9 The investigators found that
coccygeal epidural could be performed quickly (median 2 minutes),
with significantly less need for propofol administration to facilitate
catheterization (∼2 mg/kg vs 4 mg/kg) and with a longer time until
rescue analgesia was needed (10 hours vs 4 hours) compared to
sham. No complications secondary to the procedure were recognized.
This study would suggest that coccygeal epidural could be a safe and
effective adjunct to catheter placement in obstructed cats.

FIGURE 99.2 A, Cystocentesis supplies: 22 g
needle, extension tubing, three-way stopcock, 10-20
mL syringe. B, Suggested technique for

cystocentesis: needle is entered at a 45° angle toward
the bladder neck. This allows the needle to stay in
the bladder lumen as it becomes smaller.

CYSTOCENTESIS
Though controversial, cystocentesis is something that may be
considered prior to unblocking the urethra. Several potential benefits
of performing cystocentesis have been suggested.10 Cystocentesis
may allow faster relief of bladder pressure and discomfort,
particularly if catheterization is not immediately achievable or for
those less experienced at deobstruction for whom catheter placement
may take longer. Further, less sedation may be needed to perform
cystocentesis compared to catheterization, which may be of benefit
for sicker patients. In addition, reducing bladder size may decrease
the risk of causing overdistention (and potentially rupture) with
flushing in efforts to retropulse and pass the catheter (see below).
Finally, cystocentesis might help to decrease the back-pressure that
has to be overcome to advance the catheter and relieve obstruction,
and thereby reduce the risk of urethral trauma.
Certainly, the biggest concerned raised for performing
cystocentesis in patients with UO is the risk of causing trauma to a
distended, pressurized bladder resulting in urine leakage and/or
bladder rupture. While this concern seems intuitive, there is
significant evidence to suggest that cystocentesis can be performed
safely. A retrospective study of 47 UO cats that had cystocentesis
performed,11 and an observational study of 45 UO cats utilizing serial
ultrasound,12 found no complications. A prospective randomized
study comparing UO cats that had cystocentesis prior to
catheterization to those that did not (44 cats in each group) found no
difference in complications between groups.13 No studies reporting
safety or complication rates for performing cystocentesis in dogs
with UO could be found, and the true level of risk remains to be
determined
While cystocentesis can be performed safely, there is no evidence
to support any of the proposed beneficial effects. The previously

mentioned study13 was designed to determine whether
decompressive cystocentesis increases the ease or decreases the time
for catheter placement. This study found no difference between the
two groups, though it is not clear whether there are specific
circumstances in which cystocentesis might still be of benefit (such
as patients with a very distended bladder or after unsuccessful
attempts to pass a catheter).
If a cystocentesis is going to be performed, appropriate technique
is important to optimize safety. The patient should be appropriately
sedated (see above) to make sure there is no significant movement
during the procedure. Use of extension tubing and a three-way
stopcock adds flexibility to the system and makes it possible to fill
multiple syringes with a single needle stick into the bladder (Figure
99.2, A). With the bladder stabilized with one hand, the needle
should be inserted at a 45° angle toward the bladder neck. Entering
the bladder wall at an angle will help to decrease the potential for
urine to leak, will maximize the ability to empty the bladder, and is
probably safer due to avoiding the apex of the bladder, which would
be the area most likely to be devitalized in severe cases (Figure
99.2, B).

PATIENT PREPARATION
Once an adequate plane of sedation/anesthesia has been achieved,
the patient can be placed in position to facilitate catheter placement.
For male cats this is typically in lateral or dorsal recumbency, and for
male dogs lateral recumbency. The area should then be aseptically
prepared to decrease the risk of bacterial contamination and UTI.

FOR CATS
1. Clip the fur from the prepuce and peripreputial area (Figure
99.3, A).
2. Prep area with 2% chlorhexidine scrub (5 minutes of contact
time) and wipe with alcohol.
3. To help minimize risk of contaminating the catheter, apply a
sterile drape after cutting a hole to match the clipped and

prepped area (Figure 99.3, B).

FOR DOGS
1. Clip any fur away from the preputial orifice and immediately
adjacent skin.
2. Prep with 2% chlorhexidine (allow 5 minutes of contact time)
and wipe with alcohol.
3. Flush the prepuce 3-5 times with dilute chlorhexidine solution
(0.05%).
4. Extrude and aseptically prepare the penis with 0.05%
chlorhexidine solution. Once the area and prepuce have been
prepped, every effort should be made to maintain asepsis and
sterile gloves should be used.

CATHETER PLACEMENT
Every effort should be made to minimize urethral trauma during
catheter placement. This can be achieved by using lubricated
hydropulsion, adequate sedation/anesthesia (see above), the speciesspecific steps indicated below, and by minimizing forceful
advancement of the catheter. Care must also be taken not to
overdistend the bladder with retropulsion efforts (see below).

FIGURE 99.3 A and B, Sterile prep and draping of
a feline patient prior to catheter placement.

FIGURE 99.4 Technique to facilitate unblocking
the feline urethra A, Once the catheter is seated in
the distal urethra, the prepuce is pinched and pulled
caudally and dorsally. This serves to straighten the
angle between pelvic and penile urethra (B).

FOR CATS (Video 99.2

)

1. The catheter length should be measured from bladder neck to
distal tip of the prepuce.
2. The penis is extruded by placing thumb and forefinger on
opposite sides of the prepuce, applying pressure cranially and
sliding dorsally until the penis exposed. This can be done by
the person passing the catheter or by an assistant.
3. The selected catheter is connected to the lubricated flush
syringe and extension tubing (if used) with the system then
primed. Sterile lubricant is applied to the catheter tip.
4. Once the catheter tip is inserted in the urethral orifice, an
initial flush is applied to clear any distal debris/plug before
gently advancing the catheter.
5. After the catheter is well seated in the distal urethra, the
prepuce is relaxed while maintaining gentle pressure on the
catheter. The prepuce can then be gripped and extended in a
caudal-dorsal direction to help straighten the urethra. For
successful passage of the catheter, the urethra should be made
to be parallel with the cat’s vertebral column (Figure 99.4).
6. The catheter is gently advanced while flushing. If resistance is
met, a slight back-and-forth (“chipping”) motion with more
forceful hydropulsion is applied to alleviate the obstruction.
Repeat as needed.
7. Once the UO is relieved, the catheter is advanced to the
measured length and secured in place.

FOR DOGS
1. The catheter length should be measured from bladder neck to
distal tip of the prepuce.
2. The penis is extruded by gripping it at the base and sliding the
prepuce caudally. Pushing the penis from the base can help
further (

Video 3.17). This is typically done by an assistant.

2. The selected catheter is connected to the lubricated flush
syringe and extension tubing (if used) with the system then
primed. Sterile lubricant is applied to the catheter tip.
3. Once its tip is inserted, the catheter is advanced to the point of
obstruction.

4. The tip of the penis is tightly pinched to occlude the distal
urethra and prevent backflow while forceful hydropulsion and
gentle advancement of the catheter is applied.
5. If this is not successful after 2-3 attempts, it may be helpful to
have an assistant apply digital pressure to the proximal urethra
per rectum. During this maneuver, proximal occlusion
increases pressure within the distal segment of the urethra,
distending it; then, abrupt release of the digital urethral
pressure may facilitate retropulsion (Figure 99.5).
6. Repeat as needed, with care not to overdistend the bladder.
7. Once UO is relieved, the catheter is advanced to the measured
length to empty the bladder.
8. If an indwelling catheter is needed, a Foley catheter should
then be placed.
For either species, once the catheter is in place the bladder can be
emptied, with a urine sample obtained as needed. At this stage, many
practitioners would consider flushing the bladder in an effort to clear
debris, clots, grit, etc. with the hope of decreasing the risk of
reobstruction. A recent study in 137 cats failed to find a significant
difference in the rate of in-hospital reobstruction whether the
bladder was lavaged or not (13% vs 19%).14 However, this study may
have been underpowered to detect a significant difference.

UNSUCCESSFUL UNBLOCKING
EFFORTS
If attempts to unblock the urethra are unsuccessful, sedation and
relaxation might be insufficient and/or the cause of the obstruction
might not be moveable by hydropulsion. In these circumstances it
may be worth trying general anesthesia (if not already employed), or
to consider performing a decompressive cystocentesis to decrease
backpressure and bladder distention prior to further attempts,
especially if there is concern the bladder is becoming overdistended.
If catheter attempts are still unsuccessful then it may be necessary to
consider surgical intervention (e.g., urethrostomy), with either
decompressive cystocentesis or a cystostomy tube used for managing

the patient until that can occur. Another potential reason would be
the presence of a urethral tear (whether spontaneous or iatrogenic).
In these circumstances, a contrast urethrogram is performed to make
a definitive diagnosis. Once confirmed, ultrasound- or
fluoroscopically15 guided percutaneous antegrade urethral
catheterization (ch. 117) or surgical intervention may be necessary.

FIGURE 99.5 Technique to facilitate unblocking
the canine urethra. A, After insertion of the catheter
to the level of the obstruction, the tip of the penis is
tightly pinched to occlude the distal urethra and
prevent backflow. At the same time, an assistant
applies digital pressure to the proximal urethra by
way of the rectum. As hydropulsion is applied, there
is greater buildup of pressure such that subsequent
release of the proximal urethra (B) may facilitate
retropulsion.

COMPLICATIONS
Major potential complications of unblocking the urethra in UO
patients include acquired UTI, urethral trauma/tear, and bladder
rupture secondary to overdistention. While aseptic techniques may
help to decrease the risk of acquired UTI, one study showed a 13%
(4/31) incidence of bacteriuria 24 hours after catheter placement in
cats with UO.16 That same study also found that cats are very
unlikely to have UTI at the time of presentation with samples
obtained by cystocentesis (0/34),16 suggesting that empirical use of
antibiotics at the time of urethral catheterization is not warranted.
Antibiotics also do not help to prevent development of a UTI while
the catheter is in place.17,18 Efforts to minimize force and avoid rigid
catheters, along with reliance on adequate sedation/analgesia and
hydropulsion, should help to minimize the risk of urethral tear. Close
monitoring of bladder size, and potentially cystocentesis, can help to
decrease the risk of overdistention and bladder rupture. Should these
occur, additional medical and/or surgical intervention may be
needed (see above).

Chapter 100: Cystoscopy and
Urethroscopy
Andrew J. Specht

A C RO N YM
UTI urinary tract infection

OVERVIEW
Endoscopy of the urethra (urethroscopy) and urinary bladder
(cystoscopy) can be a useful diagnostic tool for visualization of the
surfaces of the lower urinary tract and can also be used to collect
samples for cytologic, histopathologic, microbial, or stone analysis.
Uroendoscopy is performed under general anesthesia, but is
minimally invasive. In addition, it can be used for facilitating
minimally invasive therapeutic interventional procedures including
some that require retrograde access to the upper urinary tract (ch.
117). Anatomic areas assessed by this procedure may include the
vestibule, vagina, urethra, urinary bladder, and ureteral openings.

INDICATIONS
For most patients with evidence of urinary tract disease,
uroendoscopy is typically performed only after some initial

laboratory testing such as a urinalysis and urine culture and noninvasive imaging such as radiography and ultrasound have been
performed. If no obvious underlying cause is identified by these tests
or if the clinical problems persist or recur despite appropriate
treatment, uroendoscopy may help to localize a problem to a specific
part of the urinary tract, to identify whether a specific focal lesion is
present, to determine if there are other concurrent or potentially
contributing abnormalities, to collect samples for further evaluation,
or to treat a problem.
For patients with urinary incontinence, uroendoscopy can help to
identify or rule out congenital or anatomic problems. In particular, it
is useful for identifying ectopic ureters (ch. 313) and around 95% of
these cases are intramural, allowing them to be addressed with a
cystoscopic-guided laser ablation (ch. 117).1,2 Submucosal injection
of urethral bulking agents guided by urethroscopy may be performed
in some cases without such obvious anatomic abnormalities (ch.
117).2,3 For patients with persistent or recurrent urinary tract
infection (UTI; ch. 307), uroendoscopy may help identify a harbor
for bacteria (urolith, mass, diverticulum, etc.) or allow culture of the
tissue.4,5 For patients that have a positive BRAF test or evidence of a
mass on other imaging tests (ch. 330), uroendoscopy offers the
benefit of allowing direct visualization in order to better understand
the extent of the lesion as well as to collect biopsy samples for a
definitive diagnosis. It can be used for facilitating removal of uroliths
by voiding hydropropulsion or basket capture, or lithotripsy (ch.
117). When there are signs of pollakiuria, stranguria, or dysuria of
unknown cause (ch. 54), uroendoscopy allows visualization with
magnification to identify anatomic abnormalities or lesions.
Similarly, for cases with persistent or intermittent hematuria of
unknown cause (ch. 55), uroendoscopy can be used to look for
mucosal lesions and to evaluate the character of the urine coming out
of each ureter as well as helping facilitate treatments.6,7

EQUIPMENT
There are many types and sizes of endoscopes that can be used for
uroendoscopy depending upon the patient and goal of the procedure.

In general, rigid scopes are used for most procedures in female dogs
and cats, while flexible scopes are used in male dogs.8-11 There are
techniques for percutaneous access to the proximal urethra or
bladder that allow for the use of a rigid scope in male patients if
necessary (ch. 117).12 This procedure is uncommonly performed in
male cats, but there are extremely thin (1 mm) flexible or semi-rigid
scopes that can be used.10,11 No single endoscope will work well for
all patients. A large-diameter rigid scope may not fit in the urethra of
a small female dog, while a scope with a smaller diameter may not be
long enough to reach the bladder in a large dog. Some of the most
commonly utilized endoscope types and sizes for uroendoscopy in
dogs and cats are listed in Table 100.1.
In addition to the endoscope itself, a number of other equipment
components, including a light source, camera system, video monitor,
and image capture and storage systems, are needed to complete and
document a uroendoscopy procedure. Endoscopy equipment is
manufactured and sold by several companies so there may be
differences in the specifications of the equipment. Components made
by different manufacturers (or even by the same company at
different times) may not be compatible, so it is important to check
this before purchasing or upgrading equipment.

RIGID SCOPES
There are several components to the rigid instruments that are used
for most uroendoscopy procedures, and these components may be
separate or integrated. The telescope houses glass lenses and
fiberoptics for light transmission. The sheath protects the telescope
and contains the irrigation and operating channels. The bridge is
often integrated with one or both of these parts and has connections
for the light source and camera as well as the instrument port.
Choosing the largest diameter that will comfortably fit in the patient
will maximize light transmission and field of view. In addition to
size, rigid scopes have specific viewing angles ranging from 0° to
120° relative to the tip of the scope. The most commonly utilized in
small animal uroendoscopy is 30° as this provides good visualization
of instruments and allows a broader overall view with minimal

manipulation (Figure 100.1), but there are situations in which a 0°
scope may be preferable.

FLEXIBLE SCOPES
There are two main types of flexible endoscopes. Fiberscopes use
coherent bundles of optical fibers to transmit light and images while
videoendoscopes convert the optical image into an electronic signal
which is then converted to a standard video image by a processor.
Image resolution is generally better with videoendoscopes and there
is no risk of small defects in the image from broken fibers, but they
are typically more expensive. The tip of a flexible scope can be
deflected, which is combined with rotation of the scope to help
visualize a broader area or focus on a specific area.

OTHER
Most rigid and flexible endoscopes have an eyepiece; however,
attaching a camera system is essential for operator comfort, patient
safety during instrument manipulation, and appropriate image
capture and documentation. Additional equipment is also needed to
collect tissue samples or perform interventional procedures. All but
the smallest scope setups have a channel that allows introduction of
instruments such as a biopsy forceps, snare, basket, guidewire,
flexible needle, laser fiber, etc.

TRANSURETHRAL CYSTOSCOPY
PROCEDURE

PATIENT AND EQUIPMENT PREPARATION
Although uroendoscopy can be performed with the patient in lateral,
dorsal, or even sternal recumbency, it is helpful to develop a
consistent approach. The author prefers dorsal recumbency. For
female patients, the hind end should extend past the edge of the
table, allowing the tail to fall down out of the way. The hind limbs
can be loosely secured out of the way if necessary, but this should not
affect the angle of the pelvis. The height should be adjusted to allow
comfortable, ergonomic scope manipulation. The endoscopist may
be seated or standing and this will influence how the scope is
handled.
It is not possible for a urethrocystoscopy procedure to be sterile,
but care is taken to minimize the risk of contamination or iatrogenic
introduction of bacteria into the urinary tract. For females, the hair
of the perivulvar region should be gently clipped and the skin
aseptically prepped. In some cases, especially when there is a
substantial amount of discharge present, the vestibule may be
flushed with a small amount of antiseptic solution. Similarly, for
males, hair at the tip of the prepuce can be clipped away and the
prepuce should be flushed with sterile saline and an antiseptic
solution. The endoscope should be sterilized or disinfected between
procedures. The endoscopist should wear sterile gloves. Full surgical
gowns, caps and masks may be worn in some cases, especially for
procedures that are expected to have a long duration or involve
repeated withdrawal and reintroduction of the scope, but many
practitioners do not use these for simple diagnostic uroendoscopy
procedures. An adhesive aperture drape or a fabric drape with a
small opening cut into it can be placed to help avoid inadvertent
contact with skin. For larger male dogs, placement of a 9.5 Fr
ureteral access sheath in the distal urethra can provide further
protection against contamination.
After the cystoscope is assembled and connected to the light
source and camera, there may be a few additional steps including
adjusting the image size, focus, or white balance. All valves should be
manipulated to check for smooth function. An irrigation solution,
most commonly sterile 0.9% NaCl, is connected to an ingress port
flushed to eliminate air from the channel. Another line is connected
to an egress port. A small Luer sealing cap or Tuohy Borst valve is

placed over the instrument port to facilitate instrument insertion
without leakage. The endoscope sheath should be liberally coated in
a water-based lubricant, avoiding the lens at the tip of the scope.

PROCEDURE (Videos 100.1, 100.2)
For a female patient in dorsal recumbency, the scope

is initially

directed dorsally (downward) to avoid the sub-clitoral fossa, and is
re-directed to a more horizontal position once in the vestibule, while
irrigation solution is allowed to flow through the ingress port with
the egress port closed. The vulvar folds may be gently closed
manually around the scope to aid fluid distension of the chamber
and visualization of the urethral opening. The vestibule is examined
and then the scope is redirected into the opening of the urethra. As
the scope is slowly advanced cranially through the urethra and into
the bladder, care should be taken to avoid scraping the tip along the
mucosa. When using a 30° angled scope, the lumen will not be
centered in the field of view while the scope is being moved (Figure
100.1). Once the tip of the scope is in the bladder, the degree of
bladder distention and clarity of the fluid are assessed. If the fluid is
not clear, urine and sediment can be drained through the egress port
and the bladder can be refilled with the irrigation solution.
Overdistention of the bladder or complete collapse can cause damage
to the mucosal surface and subsequent bleeding can obscure the
view, so care is taken to avoid either scenario. The process of partial
emptying and refilling is repeated until surfaces can be visualized
clearly. The whole bladder wall should be examined. This can be
aided by rotation of the scope and manipulation of the bladder
through the abdominal wall if necessary (Figure 100.1). Both
ureteral openings should be visualized. Their patency can be verified
by waiting to observe pulsatile jets of urine exiting each ureteral
opening. As the scope is withdrawn, the urethra should be carefully
examined. After exiting the urethra, the vestibule and vagina should
be examined.

FIGURE 100.1 A, The field of view for a rigid
telescope with a 30° angle. B, Rotation of the scope
allows a wider field of view. C, When safely
advancing the scope through the urethra, the lumen
will not be centered. D, If the lumen is centered
while the scope is advanced, it will push into and
scrape the surface. E, Once in the bladder lumen,
utilizing the increased field of view achieved by
rotation of the scope can help visualization of the
ureteral openings without having to tilt the scope.
For male patients, the penis should be exteriorized from the
prepuce before placing a ureteral access sheath or inserting the
scope. Irrigation solution is allowed to flow during introduction of
the scope to help dilate the urethra. When using a flexible scope, the
lumen should be centered in the field of view as much as possible.
The bladder, ureteral openings, and urethra should all be evaluated
during the procedure.

Patients should be closely monitored until they have fully
recovered from anesthesia; in most cases, patients who were stable
prior to the procedure are ready to be discharged within a few hours.
Although uroendoscopy is considered minimally invasive, some
patients may experience mild to moderate discomfort for the first 1-2
days and it is reasonable to provide an analgesic medication to be
given if needed during this time. Some practitioners incorporate an
epidural block into the anesthesia protocol. Some patients may have
evidence of hematuria after the procedure, but this is typically selflimiting and rarely lasts more than 1-2 days. These clinical signs may
be more likely in patients that have an intervention during the
endoscopy procedure. All patients should be monitored closely at
home for the first couple of days after the procedure.

NORMAL APPEARANCE AND COMMON
ABNORMALITIES
The mucosa of the vestibule has a smooth, uniform, pale pink
surface. This is a common site for lymphoid follicles in patients with
a history of urinary tract infection or inflammation. The openings to
the vagina and urethra are more easily seen with fluid distention.
The vaginal opening is surrounded by a ridge of tissue called the
cingulum. Although not normal, it is relatively common to see a band
of tissue sometimes called a vestibulovaginal septal remnant or
persistent paramesonephric septal remnant crossing the opening
(ch. 313). These septal remnants can have widely varied
appearances ranging from an extremely thin band to a long vaginal
septum and may be associated with other developmental
abnormalities of the urinary tract. The urethral opening will be
ventral to the vaginal opening. In intact female dogs there may be a
fold of tissue dorsally that partially covers the opening. There are
fossae lateral to the vaginal and urethral openings that can have a
pitted appearance and should not be mistaken for ectopic ureters.
The urethral mucosa should also be smooth and pink. When
relaxed, there will be longitudinal ridges. These will mostly flatten
out with fluid distention, but there may be a dorsal fold that remains
which is especially prominent in female cats. There is no published
information about normal urethral length, but subjectively some

female dogs appear to have extremely short urethras. In male dogs,
many small duct openings may be seen in the wall of the prostatic
urethra and the colliculus seminalis may appear as a mound or ridge
of tissue dorsally. Abnormalities that may be observed in the urethra
include ectopic ureter openings, lymphoid follicles, ulcerations or
erosions, stones, strictures, markedly proliferative irregular surfaces,
and focal or widespread masses, among others (ch. 312).
The bladder wall surface is smooth and pink, and blood vessels can
be seen clearly as the bladder is distended. In rare cases, abdominal
organs such as the spleen can be seen through the wall as it may
become semi-transparent when distended. The ureteral openings
will typically be located in the dorsal wall in the trigone area and
appear as slits surrounded by a slightly raised crescent of tissue with
the openings facing each other. They may be easiest to appreciate
when the bladder is only moderately distended. There is sometimes a
ridge of tissue extending from the cranial aspect of the ureteral
opening that extends to midline. The frequency and appearance of
the urine jets from ureteral openings are variable, but they should be
observed to confirm patency and evaluate for discoloration or
turbidity. Abnormalities that may be observed in the urinary bladder
include abnormalities of the ureteral openings, irregular proliferative
surfaces, lymphoid follicles, ulcerations or erosions, stones,
diverticula, and focal or widespread masses, among others. Stones,
crystals, and mucus or cellular debris will typically settle to the
dependent aspect of the bladder when there is not a high flow rate of
irrigation solution, while air bubbles will rise to the highest point.
Lesions associated with polypoid cystitis typically appear as
pedunculated, irregularly shaped masses arising in the apex. Lesions
associated with transitional cell carcinoma are more commonly
found in the trigone region or urethra and generally have marked
surface irregularity covering a large area or with a wide base (ch.
330).

POTENTIAL COMPLICATIONS AND
TROUBLESHOOTING
One of the main risks of uroendoscopy is development of a UTI.
During the procedure there may be damage to the urothelial surface

and potential introduction of bacteria from the skin or lower
reproductive tract. Some practitioners recommend a single injection
of prophylactic antibiotics during anesthesia or giving oral
antibiotics for 3-7 days after the procedure. The author does not
routinely administer antibiotics unless there is a documented
infection.
Hemorrhage from a lesion or from iatrogenic trauma can
sometimes obscure visibility. In these cases, patience is critical.
Repeated partial emptying and refilling of the bladder with irrigation
solution while being extremely careful to avoid large movements of
the scope and avoiding full distention or collapse may be enough to
restore visibility. If the bleeding persists, a cold irrigation solution
might help vasoconstriction, but it also may significantly reduce the
patient’s body temperature. If the source of the bleeding is a specific
lesion that can be identified and the equipment is available, the
lesion can be removed, ablated, or cauterized.
Some diseases such as urethral strictures, urethral masses, or
proliferative urethritis may completely obscure or obstruct the
urethral lumen, preventing passage of the scope. In some cases,
applying pressure to the bag of ingress fluids may help dilate the
passage enough to see the route more clearly, but it is important to
make sure that this does not lead to overdistention of the bladder. A
flexible guidewire or soft urinary catheter can also be used to help
guide the scope as long as it can be passed easily, but the scope
should never be forced through a tight passage or through tissue
when the lumen cannot be visualized. If the right tools are available,
there may also be an option to balloon a stricture, place a stent to
open the passage, or debulk abnormal tissue and scope afterwards
(ch. 117).
Perforation of the urinary bladder or urethra is rare when this
procedure is performed gently and with caution, but is always a risk.
It can be related to the scope or an introduced instrument
penetrating the wall, or pressure from overdistention. The risk of
perforation seems to be highest when there is severely diseased
tissue or a weak area such as an infiltrative neoplasia, severe
infection, necrotic wall, or site of prior trauma. In cases where the
perforation is large, surgery may be required to correct the defect. In
cases with relatively small perforations, keeping the urinary tract

empty by placing an indwelling catheter for a couple of days may be
enough to allow healing.

VAGINOSCOPY
INDICATIONS
Vaginoscopy enables visual inspection of the canine lower reproductive
tract: clitoral fossa, vestibule, urethral papilla, vestibulovaginal junction,
vagina and the caudal os of the cervix. Vaginoscopy (often with
urethrocystoscopy) can provide important information during the
diagnostic approach to urogenital disorders associated with abnormal
vulvovaginal discharge (ch. 56), excessive vulvar licking/excoriation,
perivulvar dermatitis, dysuria (ch. 54), recurrent cystitis (ch. 307),
urinary incontinence (ch. 54), or difficulty with natural breeding.
Anatomic defects, foreign bodies, mural masses, and mucosal

abnormalities can be characterized and localized. Sampling, removal, or
biopsy under visualization is possible. Vaginoscopy permits
characterization of the vaginal mucosal folds as the female progresses
from anestrus into proestrus, estrus, and then diestrus (Video 101.1

).

In conjunction with vaginal cytology and serial progesterone/luteinizing
hormone (LH) testing, results of vaginoscopy are important contributors
when determining optimal time for breeding. Vaginoscopy allows
transcervical access to the uterine lumen for diagnostics, therapeutics,
and intrauterine artificial insemination (transcervical insemination
[TCI]) (Figure 101.1, A-C).

EQUIPMENT
Relevant Anatomy
The vagina of the bitch is relatively long; the total length from vulva to
cervix is about 10 to 14 cm in length in an 11-kg bitch. The canine cervix is
not accessible by digital palpation per vaginum, nor can it be visualized
with the aid of a speculum. Equipment for visualizing the entire lower
reproductive tract must be long (e.g., up to 29 cm for large breeds and 33
cm for giant breeds) (Figure 101.1, A-C).

Using an Otoscope for Vaginoscopy (NOT
RECOMMENDED)
Vaginoscopy cannot be accomplished with an otoscope; visibility is
limited to the vestibule.

Rigid Pediatric Endoscopes (NOT RECOMMENDED)
Pediatric proctoscopes with air insufflation, suboptimal optics, and
limited ancillary instrumentation (Figure 101.1, C) are no longer
considered satisfactory.

Flexible Endoscopes (NOT RECOMMENDED)
Flexible endoscopes are hampered by the anatomy of the lower
reproductive tract, specifically the mucosal folds in the vaginal lumen, the
vaginal length, and the position of the cervix in the dorsum of the vaginal
fornix.

Vaginal Speculums (NOT RECOMMENDED)
This tool can be used to facilitate in obtaining cells for vaginal cytology or
as an aid in performing vaginal artificial insemination. Most clinicians
find use of vaginal speculums to be cumbersome and unnecessary.

Rigid Endoscopes (RECOMMENDED)
The vaginoscope/cystourethroscope recommended includes a forward
oblique telescope with a 30-degree viewing angle; a protective sheath
with Luer-Lok adapters and obturator; a telescope bridge with an
instrument channel; and a cold light source (Video 101.2

). The 30-

degree angle is optimal for visualization of the dorsally oriented cervix
from the vaginal lumen. The original scope used for vaginal and
transcervical endoscopy has a 3.5-mm forward oblique telescope with a
30-degree viewing angle; a 22F protective sheath with two Luer-Lok
adapters and an obturator; and a telescope bridge with one 10F
instrument channel and a working length (WL) of 29 cm (Hopkins
Telescope, cystoscopy/reproductive sheath with obturator, bridge with
instrument channel [Karl Storz]) (E-Figure 101.2, A). A smaller version
(2.7-mm Multi-Purpose Rigid endoscope, 18-cm length [Karl Storz])
accommodating a 5.5F catheter (such as is used for rhinoscopy) can be
used for very small breeds (less than 4.5 kg). The larger 33-cm WL scope
accommodates a 10F catheter and can be used for giant breeds (B300057-01 Davidson Transcervical Insemination [TCI] Telescope, 30°, 3.5
mm × 40.9 cm [WL], B10-0114-01 TCI Operative Sheath, 23Fr × 33.5 cm
[WL], B10-0121-00, Bridge for TCI Operative Sheath, 13Fr with 5Fr
[Instrument Channel]; Endoscopy Support Services) (E-Figure 101.2,
B).

E-FIGURE 101.2 A, The Storz Telepack Vet X lightemitting diode (LED) mobile transcervical insemination
(TCI) unit with 29-cm vaginoscope. B, The Endoscopy
Support Services Davidson X light-emitting diode (LED)
mobile transcervical insemination (TCI) unit with 33-cm
vaginoscope.
A video camera attached to the endoscope permits enlarged imaging
and recording. Video endoscopy is preferred for TCI as it also allows both
the operator and audience (e.g., the client) to comfortably watch the
procedure. Electronic air pumps for insufflation and suction are not
generally necessary and may be hazardous to friable urogenital tissues,
creating excessive distension of the vagina or bladder. Adequate air
insufflation or suction can be achieved, if needed, by connecting
intravenous tubing and a syringe with a three-way stopcock to one of the
working channels; this arrangement is sometimes useful for insufflation
for routine vaginoscopy in a non-estrual bitch and occasionally for
suctioning copious estrual fluid to allow visualization of the vaginal
lumen. Air distension with an insufflation bulb also works well. Irrigation
with normal saline also improves visualization of the vaginal vault by
distending the vaginal folds in non-estrual bitches. The Storz Telepack
Vet X light-emitting diode (LED) system is a high quality integrated
portable unit permitting mobile TCI with excellent imaging and image
capture. It can be used with any Storz rigid or flexible endoscope (Karl
Storz); the incorporated air insufflation can be used conservatively.
Another TCI endoscope system (MOFA Global) features a camera
platform that is modular in design with multi-connectivity, multi-camera
heads, and LED light source options. The manufacturer provides a
variety of TCI endoscopes. MOFA also provides vaginal shunt and
balloon equipment to stabilize the TCI scope within the vagina and
permit air insufflation without leakage (E-Figure 101.3, A and B).

Ureterorenoscopes (RECOMMENDED)
These scopes are used for vaginoscopy and transcervical catheterization.
They have a 6-degree viewing angle telescope and instrument sheath
combined into a single 8.0-13.5F unit, two Luer-Lok adaptors, a one-way
instrument port with angled eyepiece, and a WL of either 34 or 43 cm.
The instrument channel of the ureterorenoscope accommodates up to a
5.5F catheter or instrument (Ureterorenoscope [Karl Storz]) (E-Figure
101.3, C).

Catheterization of the Cervix

An 8F polypropylene closed-end urinary catheter is appropriate for most
bitches. A 5.5F catheter is sometimes required for small or maiden
bitches (Sovereign, Tyco Healthcare Group). The largest catheter
accommodated usually offers the best rigidity for manipulation through
the cervix while minimizing reflux. An intra-catheter stylet can be placed
if additional rigidity is required. Commercially available catheters in 5.5
and 8F diameters that include a stylet can be employed (Canine TCI
[Transcervical Insemination Catheter], Minitube USA).

Intravaginal and Intrauterine Sample Acquisition
Routine endoscopic biopsy forceps, brushes, and (guarded) culture swabs
can be used (Video 101.3

). Endoscopic retrieval forceps can be used

for vaginoscopic foreign body removal.

Equipment Care and Iatrogenic Infection Concerns
The vaginoscope manufacturer’s directions for cleaning, usually with an
enzymatic product and mild disinfectant, should be adhered to, followed
by thorough rinsing with ionized water and, finally, isopropyl alcohol.
Catheters, sterile when first removed from packaging, should be used
once. Cytology and biopsy instruments should be sterile or disinfected
before use. Culturettes are single use and sterile as packaged (Video 101.3
). Concerns about the introduction of vaginal flora into the uterine
lumen with transcervical catheterization have not been realized. Normal
vaginal flora can translocate into the uterus transiently during proestrus
and estrus. Vaginal flora is commonly introduced into the uterine lumen
during natural breeding with no adverse impact on fertility.1 Intrauterine
cultures performed when a female is in proestrus or estrus must be
interpreted with caution. Lubrication of the endoscope is seldom
necessary in estrual bitches. If a lubricant is used, it should be nonspermicidal, sterile, and water soluble (Priority Care non-spermicidal
sterile lubricating jelly, Priority Inc.) and should be applied only to the
mid-portion of the sheath. Care must be taken to avoid contact with the
lens because it obscures visibility.

PATIENT PREPARATION
Diagnostic Vaginoscopy

This procedure is usually performed in
ovariectomized/ovariohysterectomized bitches or intact bitches in
anestrus. Without the protective effect of estrogen on the vaginal mucosa
(estrogen causes thickening and keratinization), vaginal endoscopy can
be uncomfortable and potentially traumatic. Adequate immobilization
and analgesia usually requires general anesthesia. The dog is then
positioned in padded dorsal or lateral recumbency to facilitate entry into
the vaginal vault with a rigid endoscope. Ventral recumbency, as is
common for cystoscopy, requires hindquarter elevation. Vaginoscopy
under appropriate sedation/anesthesia in nonestrual intact or neutered
bitches is not traumatic with proper technique, despite the inherent
fragility of the vaginal mucosa. Saline insufflation and lubrication of the
body of the scope facilitates these exams. Force is never necessary; if
cranial motion with gentle pressure is not possible, the scope should be
retracted and positioning, lubrication, scope size, anatomy, and presence
of disease re-evaluated. Excessive force can result in perforation of the
vagina, cervix, or bladder (if malpositioned).

Transcervical Diagnostics
Endometrial cytology, culture, and biopsy via vaginoscopy is a “blind”
intrauterine procedure and should only be considered with extreme
caution. General anesthesia is recommended to safely biopsy the uterus.
Perforation of the uterine wall is possible resulting in peritonitis. The
endometrium should not be biopsied if the bitch is in diestrus because
endometritis is likely.2 Attempts to cannulate a closed cervix for
diagnostic or therapeutic (lavage) purposes (e.g., closed pyometra) must
be performed very carefully; risks often outweigh benefit. Entry of the
actual endoscope into the uterus is not required and can be traumatic. If
visualization of the uterine lumen is desired, hysteroscopy can be
performed using rigid instrumentation.

Vaginoscopy During the Estrous Cycle
Observations at this time enhances correct ovulation timing and is used
for TCIa,b (Video 101.2

) (ch. 56).

ANATOMY AND TECHNIQUE

Both vaginoscopy and swabbing for cytology require familiarity with
lower reproductive tract anatomy and its variations during the estrous
cycle (Figures 101.4 and 101.5, B and C). Achieving entry into the vagina
requires passing the scope or swab dorsally just inside the vulva to avoid
the ventrally positioned clitoral fossa and urethral papilla (Figure
101.6, A). It can be surprisingly easy to enter the urethra, differentiated
from the vagina endoscopically by its smoother, more vascular mucosa.
Air or saline insufflation can facilitate forward passage. Once the
vestibulovaginal junction has been crossed, the scope/swab can be moved
horizontally (Figure 101.5). A well-defined mucosal ridge, the dorsal
median fold (DMF) extends cranially from midvagina to paracervix. The
most cranial portion of the vagina forms a blind paracervical fornix. The
DMF has a distinct tubercle where it begins in the midvagina (the “false”
cervix) (Figure 101.5). The actual cervix is 1-2.5 cm cranial, spanning
the uterovaginal junction and positioned craniodorsally. The vaginal
portion of the estrual cervix appears as a large tubercle.
Diameter of the cervical canal varies with estrous cycle stage and
parity. Nonestrual and maiden bitches usually have a narrow cervical
lumen. Orientation of the cervix and appearance of the vaginal mucosa
can vary from day to day during proestrus, estrus and early diestrus. The
vaginal mucosa is edematous and pale pink during proestrus and is
“crenulated” during estrus, when the vaginal lumen becomes cavernous.
Crenulation results after the abrupt decline in estrogen, abruptly
decreases vaginal edema at the time of ovulation (Figure 101.5).
Maximal crenulation occurs during the most fertile period, making
vaginoscopy complementary to cytology and serial progesterone/LH
testing for ovulation timing. It can be used alone. The estrual cervical os
sometimes can be identified by serosanguineous to hemorrhagic fluid of
uterine origin flowing from the cervical canal during estrus, or purulent
fluid if pyometra is present; catheterization is generally straightforward
(Figure 101.5, D and E). Ovariectomized/ovariohysterectomized and
anestrual bitches have distinctly smoother and thinner vaginal mucosa
and a flatter cervix (if present).

FIGURE 101.4 Schematic of anatomic landmarks of
the canine lower reproductive tract. Proper placement of
a swab for vaginal cytology is illustrated. Vaginoscopic
evaluation of the tract should negotiate the anatomic
landmarks similarly.

VAGINAL CYTOLOGY
ACCURATE BIOASSAY
Vaginal cytology (obtained by swabbing the vaginal mucosa) is an
accurate bioassay of exposure to endogenous or exogenous estrogen.
Cytology of vulvovaginal discharges can help identify disease within the
lower reproductive tract. Vaginal cytology is an important component of
ovulation timing: it provides inexpensive, non-invasive, and immediately
available results that are easily interpreted. Vaginal cytology can be used

to indicate when to begin costly serial hormone (progesterone ± LH)
testing (when 80+% superficial cells are seen), and confirms whether
breedings/inseminations are occurring at the optimal time (>90%
superficial cells), too early (proestrus) or too late (diestrus) (Figure
101.6, C-F). Determining the first day of cytologic diestrus permits
prediction of due dates (56-58 days later) and retrospective evaluation of
ovulation timing (LH surge 7-9 days previously). Vaginal cytology in
reportedly ovariectomized/ovariohysterectomized bitches provides
reliable information about endogenous (ovarian remnant syndrome
[ORS]) or exogenous estrogen exposure.

EQUIPMENT AND TECHNIQUE
Equipment for vaginal cytology includes cotton tipped applicators,
routine Diff-Quik stains, frosted-end glass slides, bibulous paper, and a
light microscope. Each slide should be labeled for reference with dog
name and date. Proper technique is important so that the cells obtained
are vaginal cells, representative of hormonal influence. The sample
should be collected from the mid- to cranial vagina because cells from the
clitoral fossa or vestibule are not informative. The technique to access the
vaginal vault for cytology is the same as described above for vaginoscopy
(Figure 101.4). Care should be taken to roll the swab onto a slide
without smearing or overlapping (Figure 101.6, G and H). As estrogen
rises during proestrus, the maturation rate of the epithelial cells
increases, vaginal cytology progresses from immature “parabasal” and
“intermediate” (small then large) cells to keratinized cornified
“superficial” cells. At the same time, the vaginal mucosa becomes
thickened in preparation for breeding. Full cornification continues
throughout estrus until the “diestrual shift” occurs, indicating the end of
the fertile window when the vaginal cytology changes over 24 to 36 hours
from full cornification to 40-60% immature (parabasal and intermediate)
cells, often with neutrophils reappearing. Clients should be advised to
notify the clinic when they first notice a hemorrhagic vulvovaginal
discharge, vulvar swelling, and/or attraction of males. Proestrus can then
confirmed by vaginal cytology, repeated every 2-4 days until the
progression in cornification is seen to be >80% superficial cells. At that
point, serial hormonal testing should begin. Vaginoscopy (degree of
crenulation) is complementary and easy to perform.3,4 Detailed
published descriptions of ovulation timing are provided.c The diagnosis
of ORS is based upon observation of appropriate clinical signs (vulvar

swelling, sanguine-hemorrhagic discharge, attractiveness to dogs),
confirmation of an estrogen effect by vaginal cytology (superficial cells),
localization by further endocrine testing (anti-müllerian hormone [AMH]
assay) and imaging studies (usually ultrasound). Serum estradiol
concentrations >20 pg/mL (illustrated by vaginal cytology) are
associated with clinical signs of estrus. Since vaginal cytology cannot
differentiate a female with an endogenous estrogen source (ORS) from
one with exogenous exposure (transdermal hormone replacement
therapy in a contact person), the AMH assay is of value. Increases in
serum progesterone levels (>2 ng/mL, measured 2-3 weeks after signs of
estrus) may occur in association with luteinization of an ovarian
remnant.5

CLIENT INFORMATION
Vaginoscopic Transcervical Insemination to Increase Puppy Production
Transportation of dogs for breeding purposes is risky, costly, and
logistically difficult, making shipping semen more attractive. Semen can
be collected, processed, and chilled to be sent by overnight shipment
anywhere in the country. Properly handled, the chilled semen remains
quite viable for 48-72 hours depending on the system used. Although
pregnancy can be achieved with vaginal insemination, chilled semen is
subfertile as compared to fresh, making intrauterine insemination
desirable to enhance conception and improve litter size. With both chilled
and frozen semen breedings, ovulation timing is essential to success.
The popularity of canine semen cryopreservation (freezing) has
increased steadily in the last 20 years. Cryopreservation of semen permits
the retention of genetically valuable stock in a kennel beyond the lifespan
of the stud dog and increases the number of breedings available from 1
dog. Successful breedings with semen frozen for over 20 years is not
uncommon. International exchange of semen can improve genetic health

in canine breeding programs, but distance and shipping time necessitate
cryopreservation, as overnight shipping is challenging internationally.
Frozen semen shipped properly arrives frozen. Freezing and subsequent
thawing markedly diminish semen quality, necessitating intrauterine
insemination to have success.
Historically, the anatomy of the canine vagina and cervix hampered
access to the uterus without abdominal surgery. A method of
endoscopically guided insemination through the canine cervix,
transcervical insemination (TCI) has now been developed specifically for
the bitch, by permitting visualization of the vagina and cervix. This
technique uses an elongated rigid cystourethroscope to look at the cervix.
A slender catheter is then gently passed through the endoscope and the
cervix and advanced into the uterine lumen. Chilled or frozen-thawed
semen is then deposited directly into the uterus, closer to the site of
fertilization (the fallopian tubes). The procedure is best accomplished
with bitches standing under light restraint to inhibit sitting. Bitches
tolerate transcervical catheterization very well during estrus.
Participation of the breeder client for restraint and observation is ideal.
Autumn Davidson (Davis, California)

CLIENT INFORMATION
Vaginal Cytology and Vaginoscopy for Ovulation Timing in the Bitch
Left to their own devices, most dogs would breed at an appropriate
time for conception. However, with human intervention resulting in
problematic schedules and geography, and/or use of compromised semen
(chilled, frozen, or subfertile male), or if the bitch’s behavior and cycle do
not match, ovulation timing is critical to enhance conception. The
female’s eggs (ova) are only viable for fertilization in the oviduct for ∼4-5
days during the entire heat cycle, which generally lasts 3 weeks or longer.
Thus, improper timing for breeding is not an uncommon cause for
conception failure. Ovulation timing also enables calculation of the
bitch’s due dates.
There are various ways to monitor relevant hormones in a cycling
bitch, including vaginal cytology, vaginoscopy, progesterone tests, and
luteinizing hormone (LH) tests. With each of these methods, proper
interpretation of the results is key to properly time insemination. It is
also important to combine more than one of the monitoring tools
available to achieve the most accurate assessment of ovulation timing.

Vaginal cytology: Your veterinarian will use a cotton tipped applicator
to gently remove a few cells from your bitch’s vaginal wall and transfer
them to a glass slide. The cells are then stained and examined under a
microscope for a structural change. As estrogen levels rise at the
beginning of the heat cycle, the vaginal walls thicken, from “cornification”
(flatter, older cells with sharper edges) as the vagina prepares for
copulation. Alternatively, when estrogen levels are low, the cells are much
rounder in appearance. This is a relatively easy and inexpensive test to
determine the influence of estrogen; however, this does not necessarily
correlate with the actual fertile period which is triggered later by a surge
of the LH. Breeders and practitioners use vaginal cytology every 2-4 days
until approximately 70-80% of the vaginal cells are cornified and then
start (more expensive) hormonal assays to determine (predict) the exact
fertile period. Vaginal cytology should begin by day 7 of the heat cycle.
Vaginal cytology prevents wasting funds on hormone tests too early in the
cycle.
Progesterone levels: Your veterinarian will obtain a small blood
sample from your bitch every 2 days as she is nearing ovulation and have
it tested for progesterone at a qualified commercial laboratory or with a
validated in clinic test. The first “initial” rise of progesterone above 1.5-3
ng/mL correlates with the day of the LH surge, which is the hormone that
stimulates ovulation 24-48 hours later; an additional 2-3 days are then
required for the eggs to mature and be fertilizable. A bitch should begin
breeding 3-4 days after the initial progesterone rise or LH surge day.
Progesterone should be greater than 5 ng/mL at the time of breeding
(requiring another test after the rise), ranges from 5-22+ ng/mL are
normal at breeding time.
LH levels: It is also possible for your veterinarian to directly measure
LH using a small blood sample. However, the LH surge can occur over a
short period of time (12-24 hours) and be missed even if tested for every
day. LH levels must be measured daily and always require concurrent
progesterone testing in case the surge is missed.
Vaginoscopy: A small scope can be used to visualize the vaginal vault.
As the estrus cycle progresses, the hormones released affect the character
of the vaginal mucosa. The mucosal surface becomes very wrinkled or
“crenulated” as the bitch reaches her period of fertility. The maximum
amount of crenulation is observed during the most fertile period.
Vaginoscopy can provide useful information but is best used in
conjunction with hormonal testing and vaginal cytology.
Other non-reliable methods: It is possible to find reference to many
other methods of ovulation timing that have been used. Unfortunately,

many of these methods are unreliable and inappropriate for the domestic
dog. For example, the Draminski Method evaluating electrical conduction
in the vaginal canal was originally developed to assist researchers
working with foxes; however, the electrical conduction in the vaginal
canal reflects estrogen levels and does not indicate actual ovulation or the
fertile window. The glucose content in vaginal secretions has also been
evaluated and was shown to be an unreliable indicator of ovulation and
the fertile window. Recently, precise ovarian ultrasound techniques have
been documented to visualize ovulation but can require 2-3 examinations
daily to confirm ovulation.
The “BEST” ovulation timing combines vaginal cytology, vaginoscopy,
serum progesterone testing, and sometimes serum LH testing. Checking
the bitch with an intact male dog can confirm timing. Finally, rechecking
vaginal cytology (± vaginoscopy) on the actual breeding days is a great
way to confirm the timing is right.

Autumn Davidson (Davis, California)

Chapter 102: Peritoneal
Dialysis
Alexa M.E. Bersenas

A C RO N YM S
AKI acute kidney injury
IV intravenous
LRS lactated Ringer’s solution
PD peritoneal dialysis

Peritoneal dialysis (PD) uses the surface area of the semipermeable peritoneum for exchange of uremic toxins. PD does not
require specialized equipment (e.g., an extracorporeal machine and
circuit; ch. 103) eliminating the need for anticoagulation and
making it better tolerated by hemodynamically unstable, very-low
body weight, or coagulopathic patients.1 PD also avoids the need for
advanced vascular access. The modality provides slow, efficient
clearance of uremic toxins, with less risk of dialysis disequilibrium
syndrome.1 No differences in mortality have been identified between
extracorporeal therapies and PD in several human studies in acute
kidney injury (AKI) (ch. 300).1-4
PD requires repeat instillation of a hypertonic PD solution into the
abdominal cavity. PD relies on the principles of diffusion,
ultrafiltration and convection for solute and fluid removal. Molecules

in high concentration in the blood diffuse across the peritoneal
membranes into the dialysate solution until equilibrium is reached.
Dialysate solution contains dextrose, to provide an osmotic draw,
which draws fluid from the patient into the peritoneum, termed
ultrafiltration. The ultrafiltration provided by PD is an effective
method of removing excess fluid from fluid- overloaded patients.
This ultrafiltration augments the removal of solutes from the
bloodstream, termed “solvent drag.”
In veterinary medicine, PD is primarily indicated for potentially
reversible AKI (ch. 300). Patients with anuria, or oliguria (urine
production <0.5 mL/kg/hr) following appropriate volume
replacement, and/or patients with volume overload, hyperkalemia or
acidemia in the face of medical management, warrant dialysis.5,6
Earlier initiation of PD for the uremic patient with progressive
clinical signs can be considered; thresholds of creatinine >5 mg/dL
(>442 micromol/L) or BUN >75 mg/dL (>27 mmol/L) have been
suggested.6 More than any numerical value, the progression of the
disease and the clinical condition and prognosis of the patient should
be considered.
PD can also be used for certain dialyzable intoxications (e.g.,
ethylene glycol, ethanol, barbiturate overdose, sodium
monofluoroacetate poisoning, severe hepatic encephalopathy; chs.
132, 266) and for the management of hypo-/hyperthermia (ch.
130), refractory congestive heart failure (ch. 229), and for presurgical management of unstable patients with post-renal azotemia
(ch. 127).5,6

PREPARATION
PD requires an indwelling multi-fenestrated intra-abdominal
catheter. Soft (permanent) PD catheters are preferred and the
Tenckhoff catheter is the most utilized in human medicine.1,5,7 In
veterinary medicine, similar alternative catheters that have been
successfully used include the Jackson Pratt surgical suction drain6
and the Blake silicon drain.8 Other options include semi-rigid acute
PD catheters. These are inserted using a sharp trocar and are

associated with increased risk of bowel perforation, dialysate leak,
and discomfort, and they should not be left in place for more than 72
hours due to high risk of peritonitis.1,5 Other improvised catheters
(thoracostomy tube, nasogastric tube, red rubber tube catheter) are
fraught with rapid occlusion to flow.1,5,6 Commercial PD catheters
have Dacron cuff(s), to be positioned in the rectus muscle +/– the
subcutaneous space. The advantages of cuffs—decreased rates of
infection and dialysate leak due to fibroblast ingrowth—are not
realized in urgent-onset dialysis.

PROCEDURE
Catheters can be placed surgically, percutaneously or
laparoscopically1,7,9 under local or general anesthesia, based on
patient temperament. Surgical placement is recommended in human
pediatric medicine,1 and appears to be most successful in veterinary
medicine.10 A urinary catheter should be placed to ensure the
bladder is empty. A single preoperative dose of prophylactic
antibiotics (e.g., cefazolin) is recommended.1,7,11 A subcutaneous
tunnel is strongly recommended with the PD catheter exiting the
skin approximately 5 cm away from the abdominal access point1,7,11
(Box 102.1).
For mini-surgical PD catheter placement (

Videos 102.1 and

102.2), the patient is positioned in dorsal recumbency with the
ventral abdomen surgically prepared. A 2-3 cm para-umbilical
incision is made to the right of midline. The incision is extended
through the rectus abdominis muscle (external sheath, muscle, and
internal sheath). The parietal peritoneum is definitively identified
and incised (it is discrete from the internal sheath of the rectus
muscle off midline).6 The catheter (with stylet, or aided by
hemostats) is advanced into the caudal abdomen. At the abdominal
entry site, the distal end of the PD catheter is tunneled
subcutaneously before exiting the skin. A small volume of dialysate
(5-10 mL) should be easy to flush and to retrieve; otherwise, catheter

repositioning is warranted.6 Subsequently, snug closure of the rectus
sheath(s) around the catheter with 1 or more pursestring sutures is
necessary to reduce the risk of leakage.7,11 Alternatively, with the use
of a trocar, the PD catheter can be tunneled under the external
sheath of the rectus abdominis muscle (within the rectus muscle), to
exit the skin 5 cm from the abdominal access point.6 This method
allows full closure of the external sheath of the rectus muscle
overlying the PD catheter. Subcutaneous tissues and skin are closed.
The catheter must be secured to the patient to decrease the risk of
inadvertent catheter removal. Fibrin glue has been suggested at the
skin exit site if leaks occur.1 If a laparotomy is warranted or preferred
for PD catheter placement, then an omentectomy is advised.12 This
decreases the likelihood of obstruction to dialysate flow.10

For percutaneous PD catheter placement, the abdomen should be
filled with saline to decrease the likelihood of inadvertent organ
penetration. Following a skin incision, PD catheter placement on
midline through the linea alba using a Seldinger technique with

sequential dilations of the body wall has been reported, in human
medicine, to be fast and to provide successful dialysis.1 However,
percutaneously placed catheters have an increased incidence of
dialysate retention in veterinary medicine.10
Once the catheter is in place, dialysis can begin following strict
aseptic technique. The circuit should be a closed Y-system to
decrease risk of infection. An in-house Y-system can be made with
the PD catheter attached via a 3-way stopcock to: 1) an intravenous
(IV) infusion set from the dialysate solution, and 2) an IV line
attached to a closed collection bag (

Video 102.2). Every line

connection should be covered with chlorhexidine-soaked dressings,
and access ports (dialysate bags, drug vials, PD access) should be
scrubbed with chlorhexidine and alcohol prior to penetration.10,12
Sterile gloves are indicated for any manipulation, and invasion of the
Y-system (e.g., spiking a new dialysate bag) should use the “flush
before fill” technique.12
Commercial peritoneal dialysate solutions are buffered (lactate or
bicarbonate based) balanced electrolyte solutions containing sodium,
magnesium, calcium and chloride at varying concentrations; most
use dextrose as the osmotic agent at concentrations of 1.5, 2.5 and
4.25%. Employing strict aseptic technique, dialysis fluids can be
prepared using IV fluids if commercial products are not available.1,13
Lactated Ringer’s solution (LRS) is the most similar to commercial
dialysate. The concentration of potassium in LRS is 4 mmol/L (4
mEq/L), which generally allows correction of mild to moderate
hyperkalemia, and is ideal once the patient is normokalemic.1
Alternatively, 0.9% NaCl can be used as a potassium-free dialysate
solution for patients with clinical signs of hyperkalemia. In such
instances, sodium bicarbonate should be added to the solution (3045 mmol/L [30-45 mEq/L]). If using non-commercial products,
dextrose supplementation is needed. Using 50% dextrose solution
and adding this to a 1 L bag of dialysate, 30 mL, 50 mL, or 85 mL are
added to make approximately 1.5%, 2.5%, and 4.25% dextrose
solutions, respectively.6 Unfractionated heparin at 500 U/L (range
250-1000 U heparin/L) is recommended for initial PD exchanges

and up to the first 5 days of therapy to decrease the risk of clot
formation and catheter occlusion in urgent start dialysis.6,14 Heparin
is minimally absorbed at this dosage range.5 In the case of confirmed
septic peritonitis, antibiotics as additives to dialysate solution are
preferred.5
Generally a 2.5% dextrose-containing solution is used at the onset
of dialysis to optimize ultrafiltration and solute removal.5 However,
the concentration of dextrose is determined by the fluid status of the
patient. A 4.25% dextrose solution is selected for fluid overloaded
patients. Once the patient is euvolemic, a 1.5% dextrose solution is
continued.
At initiation of PD, dialysate exchanges occur every 1-2 hours,
throughout the 24-hour day.1,6,14 Warmed dialysate is instilled into
the abdomen over 5-10 minutes using a gravity dependent system or
IV infusion pump or PD cycler.1 The in-flow time should be kept to a
minimum to maximize time on dialysis.5 A minimum 30-45 minute
dwell time is allocated, to allow for diffusion and ultrafiltration to
occur. Subsequently the abdomen is emptied, by gravity, over 10-20
minutes.5,6 Recommended dialysate volumes range from 10-40
mL/kg. Early onset dialysis is started at 10 mL/kg.1,15 Dialysate
volumes can be increased over 2-3 days to improve uremic clearance.
During dialysate infusion, and dwell, the patient should be
monitored for respiratory compromise and signs of abdominal
discomfort. A usual acute dialysis session lasts for 48-72 hours,1 with
exchanges continued q1-2 hours, until uremic control is achieved.
Subsequently dwell times can be extended to 4-6 hours.5,14 Ongoing
dialysis is based on patient response. Patients with oliguric/anuric
renal failure will frequently require several days (3-7) of PD before a
positive response in urine production can be noted or assessed.6
During PD, body weight measurements and re-assessment of
hydration are mandatory (every 4-12 hours), with adjustments made
in the PD prescription accordingly. Patient’s “ins” (IV fluids,
medications, enteral feeds) and “outs” (urine production, dialysate
retrieval, vomitus, etc.) should be tabulated every 4-12 hours (ch.
120). Once the patient is euvolemic, “ins” should be matched to

“outs.” Other monitoring includes continuous electrocardiogram
(ECG; ch. 96) and blood pressure (ch. 91) assessments, electrolytes
and blood gas monitoring every 4-12 hours, along with packed cell
volume and total solids every 12-24 hours. Daily serum creatinine
determination is ideal until improvement is well established.

COMPLICATIONS
Catheter malfunction, slow or incomplete outflow, is frequently
noted and may be associated with catheter migration, or omental
wrapping or fibrin clot/occlusion.5,6 Any retention of dialysate
should be promptly addressed. Patient repositioning, delivery of
enema(s), or flushing of the catheter using a prefilled 20 mL syringe
can be attempted. Alternatively, PD catheter systems can be
connected to active continuous suction devices (collection bulbs).8
Other complications include dialysate leak, extravasation of fluid in
tissue compartments (perineal/pelvic limb edema), lack of uremic
control, intra-abdominal hemorrhage, progressive
hypoalbuminemia, pleuroperitoneal communications (pleural
effusion), hyperglycemia, catheter exit-site infections, and
peritonitis.1,6
While PD provides effective reduction in uremic toxins, allowing
renal recovery, it does not treat the renal insult. Prognosis and renal
recovery rely heavily on the underlying cause of renal injury (ch.
300). Veterinary survival reports using PD range from 2480%10,16,17; improved response is noted in patients with AKI
secondary to leptospirosis (ch. 192),17 and urinary obstruction (chs.
117, 306).10 Cats may also have an improved outcome with PD with
reported survival rates in 2 studies of 45% and 83%, respectively.8,10
