OVERVIEW

Extracorporeal blood purification therapies are a collection of
modalities which employ the principals of diffusion, convection and
adhesion to remove uremic toxins, as well as correct patient’s fluid,
electrolytes and acid base balance. They have also been employed to
remove toxins and autoantibodies. In veterinary medicine, these
modalities have primarily been employed in the treatment of acute
kidney injury (AKI); however, they have also been successfully used
for the management of chronic kidney disease (CKD), autoimmune
diseases, and toxin exposures. The most commonly employed
extracorporeal therapies in dogs and cats include intermittent
hemodialysis (IHD), continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT),
and therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE).
The principles of extracorporeal blood purification were first
described in 1914, when Dr. John Able anticoagulated a dog and
directed blood from an artery into an apparatus he called
“vividiffusion.”1 This device divided blood into straw-like
semipermeable membranes, which were bathed in solution. It was
noted that by changing the composition of the solution, the
concentration of solutes in the dog’s blood could be altered.1
Although this vividiffusion apparatus, constructed from a glass
cylinder and hand-made semi-permeable membranes, seems
rudimentary by today’s standards, it has served as the prototype for
all modern dialyzers. Even today, the dialyzer forms the basis of most
extracorporeal blood purification therapies.

BLOOD PURIFICATION
Diffusion is the tendency for molecules in solution to move from an
area where they are in a high concentration to an area where they are
in a lower concentration. As patient blood enters the dialyzer, it is
divided and travels inside thousands of straw-like semipermeable
membranes that are bathed in solution called dialysate. Dialysate
contains precisely measured concentrations of electrolytes and
buffers. Molecules can be made to diffuse out of the blood, across the
membrane and into the dialysate by ensuring that their
concentration in the dialysate is lower than in the blood (e.g.,
creatinine). In addition, beneficial substances can be made to move

from the dialysate into the blood by increasing their concentration in
the dialysate (e.g., bicarbonate). After leaving the dialyzer, exhausted
dialysate is discarded and purified blood is returned to the patient.
The primary limitation of diffusion is the size of the molecule that
will pass through the membrane. Generally, the likelihood that a
molecule will pass across the membrane is inversely proportional to
its size. Thus, small molecules such as urea pass readily while larger
molecules diffuse more slowly or not at all. In addition, because the
movement of molecules is guided by concentration gradients, a
continuous supply of fresh dialysate is needed.
During convection, the patient’s blood enters the dialyzer, is
divided and travels inside thousands of straw-like semipermeable
membranes where it is subjected to a positive transmembrane
pressure. This causes fluid, called ultrafiltrate, to be forced out of the
blood and across the membrane. The ultrafiltrate carries uremic
toxins, electrolytes and other small molecules which are discarded.
As ultrafiltrate is generated, blood traveling within the
semipermeable membranes becomes increasingly
hemoconcentrated. A sterile balanced electrolyte solution is then
added to the patient’s blood to replace the ultrafiltrate. Unlike
diffusion, it is the size of the pores in the semipermeable membrane
that determines which solutes can be removed. All molecules small
enough to fit through the pores of the membrane will pass at the
same rate. Thus, convection can effectively remove an increased
number of larger molecules than diffusion. In addition, convection
can be used to remove fluid in overhydrated patients. Nevertheless,
convection is technically challenging, as the ultrafiltrate must be
replaced with great accuracy or acid/base, electrolyte, and fluid
imbalances can occur.

FIGURE 103.1 Intermittent hemodialysis (IHD).
IHD is primarily a diffusive modality. Blood is
divided into straw-like semi-permeable membranes
which are suspended in dialysate which flows in a
counter current direction. Drawing courtesy
Nicholas J. Acierno.
Adsorption is the tendency of molecules in blood to stick to
surfaces in the extracorporeal circuit and be removed from
circulation. Studies have suggested that certain dialyzer membranes

can remove cytokines associated with sepsis; however, at this time
there is no clinically proven benefit.2 Hemoperfusion involves the
placing of an absorptive substance, often carbon or resins, in the
extracorporeal blood path in order to trap and remove drugs and
toxins. Although first described in the 1940’s, issues with
biocompatibility and finite absorptive capacity have limited its use.3
Nevertheless, recent advances in the technology have led to wider
adoption of hemoperfusion. Veterinary case reports and studies
related to the treatment of intoxications with this technology have
recently been published.4-6

INTERMITTENT HEMODIALYSIS
For decades, IHD has remained the standard of care for human
patients requiring treatment of AKI, CKD, or for the removal of
certain toxins (e.g., ethylene glycol).7 This is the treatment
commonly referred to as “dialysis.” Veterinary patients are treated
for finite periods of time, often 4-6 hours, after which they are
treated as a typical hospitalized patient. In some cases, they can even
be sent home. IHD is primarily a diffusive technology in which blood
enters the dialyzer, is divided in straw-like semipermeable
membranes and flows counter-current to the dialysate (Figure
103.1). Since significant changes in blood composition need to be
made in relatively short periods of time, large amounts of dialysate
need to be produced on-site. As only a thin semipermeable
membrane separates blood and dialysate, the dialysate must be
relatively pure in order to prevent contaminants or endotoxins from
being introduced into the patient’s blood.8 This requires a significant
investment in both equipment and maintenance.8
Manufacturing dialysate requires that ordinary tap water be
specially treated. Water is first passed through a sediment filter to
remove gross contaminants. Then, it is exposed to carbon, which
extracts chlorine and chloramines. A reverse osmosis water filter
removes remaining dissolved solutes. The water is then delivered to
the dialysis machine, which heats the water and mixes it with
bicarbonate and an electrolyte (acid) solution to produce dialysate.

Since the entire fluid pathway is at risk for contamination, a proper
maintenance program involving disinfection and bacterial
surveillance is essential.

FIGURE 103.2 Continuous veno-venous
hemofiltration (CVVH) is a convective modality.
Unlike in slow continuous ultrafiltration (SCUF), the
ultrafiltrate is replaced. This “replacement fluid”
(dashed line) can be added before or after the blood
passes through the dialyzer. Drawing courtesy
Nicholas J. Acierno.

CONTINUOUS RENAL REPLACEMENT
THERAPY
CRRT is a more recent extracorporeal blood purification therapy,
which is primarily employed in the treatment of AKI and some toxin
exposures. It combines the principles of diffusion and convection to
produce 4 different treatment modalities: slow continuous
ultrafiltration (SCUF), continuous veno-venous hemodialysis
(CVVHD), continuous veno-venous hemofiltration (CVVH), and
continuous veno-venous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF).9 Many CRRT
systems can also perform TPE. As its name implies, CRRT is a
continuous modality and once a patient begins treatment, therapy
continues until kidney function returns, the patient is transitioned to
intermittent dialysis (IHD) or the patient is euthanized. Theoretical
advantages of CRRT over IHD include better control of fluid,
acid/base and electrolyte balance in hemodynamically unstable
patients;10,11 however, in veterinary medicine, some of the appeal is
likely due to CRRT’s reliance on pre-packaged fluids, which requires
neither an investment in water purification facilities nor the ongoing
maintenance associated with producing dialysate. The tradeoff is
that CRRT patients require 24-hour-a-day care.

Slow Continuous Ultrafiltration (SCUF)
SCUF is a purely convective modality.9 As the patient’s blood enters
the straw-like semipermeable membranes of the dialyzer, it is
exposed to a positive transmembrane pressure that forces water out
of the blood. The hemoconcentrated blood is then returned to the
patient. While SCUF has been used in the treatment of diureticresistant congestive heart failure in people, its utility in veterinary
medicine is unclear.12

Continuous Veno-venous Hemofiltration (CVVH)
CVVH (Figure 103.2) is also a convective modality; however, the
ultrafiltrate is replaced with a sterile balanced electrolyte solution.1214
The solution can be added to the blood before or after the dialyzer.

When added after the dialyzer, a positive transmembrane pressure
forces fluid and solutes out of the blood, resulting in increasing
hemoconcentration within the straw-like semipermeable membranes
of the dialyzer.12 Prior to returning the patient’s blood, a sterile
balanced electrolyte solution, called “replacement fluid,” is added to
restore the blood to a physiologic packed cell volume. Adding fluid
after the dialyzer is an extremely efficient way to remove uremic
toxins; however, as the blood becomes hemoconcentrated, there is a
risk that the blood will sludge and clot, limiting the amount of fluid
that can be removed.12 Alternatively, “replacement fluids” can be
added to the blood before the dialyzer, resulting in hemodilution.
The excess fluid is then removed in the dialyzer by convection.12 This
is less likely to result in dialyzer clotting but is also significantly less
efficient.15

FIGURE 103.3 Continuous veno-venous
hemodialysis (CVVHD) is a diffusive therapy, similar
to intermittent hemodialysis (IHD). Drawing
courtesy Nicholas J. Acierno.

Continuous Veno-venous Hemodialysis (CVVHD)
CVVHD is a diffusive therapy that closely resembles IHD (Figure
103.3).9 Blood enters the dialyzer, where it is divided and travels

inside thousands of straw-like semi-permeable membranes that are
bathed in dialysate which flows in the opposite direction. Substances
that are in relatively high concentration in the blood leave and enter
the dialysate while substances whose concentration is higher in the
dialysate enter the blood.16 Unlike IHD, the slow continuous nature
of CVVHD allows for the use of prepackaged dialysate, avoiding the
need for water treatment facilities.

Continuous Veno-venous Hemodiafiltration
(CVVHDF)
CVVHDF combines the diffusive aspects of CVVHD with the
convective aspects of CVVH (Figure 103.4).9 Blood flowing
through the dialyzer’s straw-like semipermeable membranes is
bathed in dialysis solution and exposed to a positive transmembrane
pressure so that both diffusion and ultrafiltration guide the
movement of solutes.12 Because the operator can select the amount
of diffusion and ultrafiltration that takes place within the dialyzer,
CVVHDF gives the greatest control over the treatment administered.
For the treatment of AKI patients, it is unclear which CRRT
modality is superior. Convective modalities (CVVH, CVVHDF) have
the advantage of being able to remove larger “middle-sized”
molecules and therefore more closely mimic the function of the
kidney.17 Nevertheless, it is not known what role these molecules
play in the pathogenesis of AKI or uremia. Diffusive modalities
(CVVHD) are equally effective in removing smaller molecules such as
urea and creatinine and are associated with fewer dialyzer
failures.15,18

FIGURE 103.4 Continuous veno-venous
hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF) combines the diffusive
aspects of continuous veno-venous hemodialysis
(CVVHD) with the convective properties of
continuous veno-venous hemofiltration (CVVH).
CVVHDF provides the most flexibility as convection
and diffusion can be manipulated
independently. Drawing courtesy Nicholas J.
Acierno.

THERAPEUTIC PLASMA EXCHANGE
Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is a blood purification modality
in which a patient’s plasma is removed and replaced with a colloid
solution (Figure 103.5). This allows for the effective removal of
protein-bound toxins, immune complexes, and autoantibodies. In
people, TPE is primarily used in the treatment of specific
autoimmune conditions, infectious diseases, and selected
intoxications.19 The veterinary literature includes case reports in
which TPE was successfully utilized in the treatment of autoimmune,
infectious, encephalopathic and paraneoplastic conditions.20-26 A
recent development is the successful use of TPE for the removal of
protein-bound drugs and toxins.27-30 TPE has been well suited for
the removal of toxins that demonstrate a low volume of distribution
(Vd <0.2 L/kg) and are highly protein-bound (>80%). Substances
with a low volume of distribution remain primarily in the
intravascular space where TPE can remove them. Many drugs are
highly protein-bound, which results in longer half-lives but makes
them difficult to remove using IHD.
TPE can be performed in specialized dialyzer-based systems that
employ convection. These dialyzers allow solutes of up to 0.6
microns in diameter to pass through the membranes and are
disposed of as ultrafiltrate. Thus, plasma and its constituents cross
the membrane while the cellular components of blood are retained. A
colloid-based replacement fluid is then mixed with the
hemoconcentrated blood prior to it being returned to the patient. In
theory, any number of colloid solutions could be used including
plasma, albumin, as well as synthetic colloids; however, in human
studies, the use of fresh frozen plasma has been associated with
substantial morbidity and mortality.31 In veterinary medicine,
several colloid solutions have been successfully employed, including
dilute (4%) hydroxyethylstarch, plasma, and
hydroxyethylstarch/plasma/saline combinations.
Dialyzer-based TPE is a convective process. Thus, as the patient’s
plasma is removed, the blood traveling in the straw-like
semipermeable membranes becomes increasingly
hemoconcentrated. As this occurs, the risk of clotting increases.

Therefore, on each pass through the dialyzer, only a portion of the
patient’s plasma is actually removed while the rest is diluted with a
colloid and returned. Because of this, removal of any substance is
limited, as the fraction remaining in the straw-like semipermeable
membranes is continuously being diluted and returned. Therefore,
while an estimated 63% of plasma solutes are removed on the first
plasma volume exchange (PV = [(0.08 ∗ wt/kg) ∗ (1-hematocrit)]),
an additional 1/2 plasma volume exchange removes only an
additional 15% of solutes and each subsequent exchange is
increasingly less efficient.32,33 Therefore, current treatment
recommendations are for 1.5 plasma exchanges over 2-3 hours to
remove approximately 78% of a given molecule from the
intravascular space.33,34

FIGURE 103.5 Therapeutic plasma exchange. In a
filter-based system, blood is divided into straw-like
semi-permeable membranes and convection is
applied. Plasma is forced out of the membranes and
is discarded and a colloid solution is added. The
blood is then returned to the patient. Drawing
courtesy Nicholas J. Acierno.
Some TPE systems utilize real-time continuous centrifugation
rather than a dialyzer. In these systems, blood from the patient

enters a centrifuge that separates it into layers based on density.
Specific fractions of the blood can then be siphoned out prior to the
blood being mixed with a colloid solution and returned to the
patient. Although centrifugation-based systems may offer more
treatment options, dialyzer-based TPE is more commonly available.
This is partially because many CRRT systems also perform TPE and
dialyzer-based systems can be more cost-effective.

ANTICOAGULATION
Despite being made of highly biocompatible materials, the catheter
and extracorporeal circuit will activate the coagulation cascade.35,36
This can lead to issues involving catheter patency, clotting of the
dialyzer circuit, and time during which the patient cannot receive
treatment. Also, the extracorporeal circuit can contain a substantial
portion of a patient’s blood, which will be lost if clotting occurs.
Therefore, appropriate anticoagulation is essential. There are two
commonly employed anticoagulants: heparin and citrate.
A constant rate infusion of heparin has historically been the most
widely employed method of anticoagulation for extracorporeal
procedures. Heparin binds to and causes a conformation change in
antithrombin (ch. 170).37 This increases its activity by as much as
1000 times. Antithrombin inactivates thrombin, factor X, and other
proteases involved in blood clotting.38 Heparin is effective and its
effect is inexpensively monitored using an automated activated
clotting timer. The primary risk of systemic anticoagulation is
uncontrolled hemorrhage. Monitoring activated clotting time and
adjusting the heparin infusion rate can minimize this risk. In people,
type II heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) poses a serious
risk. This condition, which can affect up to 5% of human patients, is
the result of antibodies that can activate platelets and lead to
thromboembolic events. 39 Type II HIT has not been documented to
occur in cats and dogs.
Recently, there has been growing interest in regional
anticoagulation using citrate to chelate calcium in the extracorporeal
circuit.40 Calcium is an important co-factor throughout the clotting

cascade and blood cannot clot in its absence. As blood enters the
extracorporeal circuit, citrate is infused, which chelates calcium. This
renders the blood unable to clot.41 Calcium chloride is then infused
directly to the patient to maintain physiologic serum calcium levels.
The primary benefit of citrate is that the patient is not systemically
anticoagulated; however, there are substantial risks of hypocalcemia,
alkalosis and citrate toxicosis.41 These necessitate frequent calcium
and acid/base monitoring. Although veterinary experience with
citrate has increased, many still utilize heparin.

FIGURE 103.6 Examples of dialysis catheters.
The catheter on the top is a catheter-within-acatheter design. Blood is taken in to the
extracorporeal system by the holes on the side of the
catheter and ejected at the tip. This minimizes
recirculation, the mixing of purified and patient
blood. The catheter on the bottom of the picture is an
example of a “side-by-side” catheter.

VASCULAR ACCESS
Extracorporeal therapies require significant blood flow rates;
therefore, appropriate vascular access is essential. In most patients,
the only vein large enough to provide this access is the external

jugular; therefore, these vessels should not be used for other
purposes (e.g., blood draw) in any patient for which extracorporeal
therapies are being considered. Dialysis catheters are made of highly
biocompatible material such as polyurethane or silicone and
designed so that there is minimal mixing of processed and
unprocessed blood. While there are many variations, most catheters
are either “catheter-within-a-catheter” or “side-by-side” design
(Figure 103.6). In all but the smallest patients, a dual lumen
dialysis catheter can be placed using the modified Seldinger
technique. Typically, an 11-14 Fr catheter is placed in large dogs
while cats and smaller dogs receive a 7 Fr catheter. In the smallest
patients, one single-lumen 5 Fr neonatal dialysis catheter can be
placed in each external jugular vein.

COMPLICATIONS
Problems associated with appropriate anticoagulation and clotting
are perhaps the most challenging aspect of providing extracorporeal
therapies. Issues regarding clotting of the dialysis catheter and
impaired blood flow are common.42,43 In patients receiving CRRT
over long periods of time, the entire extracorporeal circuit can
become rendered unusable because of blood clots. Conversely, some
patients develop bleeding at the catheter site.
Hypotension is potential complication of all extracorporeal
therapies. Although likely multifactorial, it is thought to be partly the
result of the large amount of blood needed in the extracorporeal
circuit.44 In an attempt to address this problem in smaller patients,
pediatric dialyzers and blood lines can be used and the blood
pathway can be primed with colloids or blood.
Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome (DDS) can be a major concern
when treating azotemic veterinary patients using IHD. Although
several theories have been proposed, it seems likely that DDS is
related to urea’s role as an osmotically active particle.45,46 As urea
accumulates in the blood, it diffuses into various tissues throughout
the body. Each of these tissues can accept and lose urea at different
rates. It is believed that as urea is rapidly removed from blood, there
can exist a differential such that the concentration of urea is higher

in some tissues than in the blood.46 The brain is one example of a
tissue that loses urea more slowly than can be removed by IHD. In
this case, urea acts as an osmotically active particle causing brain
swelling, which can result in mentation changes, seizures, coma, or
death.46 Replacing urea in the blood with another osmotically active
molecule (e.g., mannitol) is one strategy to help prevent DDS;
another is to avoid rapid urea reductions. Because of its slow nature,
DDS has not been reported in CRRT.

INDICATIONS
At one time, the primary indication for IHD or CRRT was anuria;
however, this is an outdated paradigm. IHD and CRRT should be
considered whenever an AKI patient is experiencing azotemia,
electrolyte imbalances or fluid overload that does not respond to
conventional therapy. Due to its intensive 24-hour-a-day
requirement, CRRT is most appropriate in cases of AKI where kidney
function is likely to return in a relatively short period of time or when
there is a plan to stabilize and transition a patient to IHD. IHD is
more flexible, offering opportunities to treat AKI as well as CKD
patients and a number of toxicoses. The ability of IHD to remove
toxins is dependent on the substance’s characteristics, including size,
protein binding, and volume of distribution. The larger the molecule,
the more tightly it binds to protein, and the more widely it disperses
throughout the body, the less likely IHD is to be helpful in treating
an exposure.
Therapeutic plasma exchange has been utilized in the treatment of
autoimmune, infectious, encephalopathic, and paraneoplastic
conditions as well as the removal of protein bound toxins. There is
empirical evidence that TPE should be considered in the treatment of
immune-mediated hemolytic anemia that fails to respond to
immunosuppression (ch. 174).

MEASURING EFFICACY
Calculations have been developed to help determine if the therapy
delivered by CRRT and IHD is adequate. Two commonly used

formulas are the urea reduction ratio (URR) and Kt/V. The URR
represents the percent reduction in urea concentration as a result of
the therapy provided. It is simply calculated as [(pre-treatment urea
– post treatment urea) / pretreatment urea] ∗ 100. Its utility lies in
its simplicity and its ability to predict clinical outcomes in people47;
however, it has limitations. The URR ignores urea being generated
by the body during the procedure.48 While this is negligible during
IHD, during CRRT it can be significant. Indeed, after the initial
CRRT treatment period when the circulating urea concentration is
reduced into the normal range and is no longer decreasing, the URR
effectively becomes 0%. Clearly, the body is producing urea and
CRRT continues to remove it, but the URR is unable to account for it.
In addition, URR does not account for urea that is convectively
removed with excess bodily fluids.48 For this reason, while IHD
practitioners typically utilize the URR, CRRT specialists have used
Kt/V for determining treatment adequacy.
Kt/V is closely related to the URR; however, it can more accurately
reflect urea removed by extracorporeal therapies.48 Kt/V is a unitless
number where K is a measurement of urea clearance expressed in
mL/min.49 Total solute removal per period of time is then defined as
the product of K (mL/min) and time (minutes) that the patient
receives treatment. Dividing Kt by the volume of urea distribution
(mL) normalizes this product. Since urea is approximately equally
distributed in all body water compartments, V can be approximated
as 60% of body weight in kilograms.50 Kt/V calculations account for
both urea being generated endogenously and urea that is
convectively removed with excess bodily fluids. Although relevant
studies are lacking, a Kt/V >2.0 appears to be associated with
successful outcomes in companion animals.
Recently, there has been a shift in defining CRRT prescriptions in
terms of effluent flow rate (mL/kg/hr). In both convective and
diffusive modalities, the concentration of low-molecular-weight
solutes in the ultrafiltrate is effectively equivalent to that of plasma.
Therefore, clearance of urea and other low-molecular-weight solutes
is roughly equal to effluent flow for each of the CRRT modalities.
Recommendations for people target an effluent flow rate of 20-25
mL/kg/hr; relevant studies in animals currently are lacking.

ExAMPLE: Target FF of 20% for a 20 kg dog with a Qb of 60
mL/min receiving post filter CVVH with a Hct – 40%

• This calculation should be based on the total amount being
convected, so if you are using the Pre-Blood Pump (white scale)
to deliver pre-filter replacement solution and you are using the
Replacement Pump (purple scale) to deliver a post-filter
solution then the sum of these two rates is your Replacement
Rate (RR)
Replacement Solution
• This is the solution that replaces what is convected off to remove
solutes. When you set the Replacement Rate, you are actually
setting the convection
• This will maintain the patient at a net zero fluid balance
• Despite the name, the machine is not able to give the patient
additional fluids, it can only maintain a zero balance or remove
fluid
Pre-filter Replacement
• Instills replacement solution into the blood before entering the
filter
• Dilutes the patient’s blood in the filter
• Decreased filter clotting
• Decreased efficiency
• Lower risk of hypotension
Post-filter Replacement
• Replacement solution mixes with blood after blood has passed
through the filter
• Blood going through filter is more hemoconcentrated
• Increased risk of clotting
• Increased risk of hypotension since we are using the patient
for source of volume that ultrafiltrate will be drawn
• More efficient. Not likely to be too efficient if doses are
calculated
• Recent recommendations suggest using a combination of both
pre- and post- replacement solution
Patient Fluid Removal
• For patients that are overhydrated
• Fluid is removed by convection so it will slightly improve your
clearance of solutes and does contribute to your total dose

• Should not exceed 10-20 mL/kg/hr
• Can be done slowly unless patient is suffering respiratory
compromise
Calculations
• Typically aim for a blood flow rate (Qb) approximately 2× the
weight in kg when starting
• Build to this rate, so begin at ½ this and bring up rate over
30-60 minutes
• In pediatrics, Qb is typically started at 2-6 mL/kg/min
• After several hours, if the patient is tolerating the treatment
well, and you are trying to improve clearance, you can
increase this
• There are 3 main ways to come up with the rest of the
prescription:
1. Based on a total dose of >35 mL/kg/hr
2. Based on m2 dosing
3. Based on estimated Kt/V
Total Dose Method
• This is based on human data that a total calculated dose (total
effluent) of >35 mL/kg/hr is associated with better outcomes
• This means that the Replacement Rate + Patient Fluid Removal
+ Dialysate Rate all total ≥35 mL/kg/hr
• This can be split between Dialysate and Replacement or just do
one modality
Example: Running CVVHDF on a 20 kg dog
Calculate the target dose = 20 × 35 ≥700 mL
If you split it:
• Replacement Rate = 350 mL/hr
• Set PBP to 150 mL/hr
• Set Post-filter Replacement to 200 mL/hr

• Dialysate Rate = 350 mL/hr
m2 Dosing
• Similar to previous method. A total dose is determined and then
divided between modalities
• Total dose: 2000 mL/1.73 m2/hr (total of replacement fluid +
dialysate)
Kt/V
• This is a common measure of CRRT adequacy and can be used to
calculate your dose as well as evaluate your treatment efficacy.
• K is a measurement of instantaneous urea clearance (removal
rate/concentration)
• Total solute removal per period of time is defined as the product
of instantaneous clearance (K mL/min) and time receiving
CRRT per day
• Product is normalized for the volume of distribution of that
solute (V mL)
• Urea is approximately equally distributed in all body water
compartments so V = total body water OR 60% of body
weight in kg
• Generally estimate actual t = 22 hours = 1320 minutes to
account for pauses for set-up/alarms/filter changes
• Goal in people is Kt/V > 1.2 – 1.4 as it has been shown to be
associated with decreased morbidity and mortality
• Kt/V Formulae
Key
• All terms should be converted into mL/min, mL, min
• Urea is expressed as mg/dL
• Qb = blood flow rate
• QUF = ultrafiltrate rate = replacement rate + patient fluid
removal
• QRR = replacement rate

• Qd = dialysate rate
• Kcalc = calculated (estimate) urea clearance
• Used to estimate K prior to Tx
• Kdel = actual delivered urea clearance
• Used to estimate K during Tx
CVVH (post filter)
• Kcalc = QUF (mL/min)
• Kdel = [ultrafiltrate urea concentration (mg/dL) × QUF
(mL/min)]/pre-dialyzer urea concentration (mg/dL)
CVVH (pre-filter)
• Kcalc = QUF (mL/min)/[1+QRR (mL/min)/Qb (mL/min)]
• Kdel = [ultrafiltrate urea concentration (mg/dL) × QUF
(mL/min)]/pre-dialyzer urea concentration (mg/dL)
cvvhd
• Kcalc = Qd (mL/min)
• Kdel = [post dialyzer dialysate urea concentration (mg/dL) × Qd
(mL/min)]/prefilter blood urea level (mg/dL)
CVVHDF (pre-filter)
• Kcalc = Qd + (QUF/[(QRR/Qb) + 1])
Kdel = ultrafiltrate urea concentration × (QUF + Qd)/predialyzer blood urea level CVVHDF (post-filter)
• Kcalc = QUF (mL/min) + Qd (mL/min)
• Kdel = Ultrafiltrate urea concentration × (QUF + Qd)/pre-dialyzer
blood urea level
If you are doing a combination of pre- and post-filter delivery,
you have to do both formulas for Kcalc and multiply your result by
the proportion that it is contributing, then add the 2 results
together

• i.e., CVVHDF that is receiving 50% pre- and 50%
postreplacement
• calculate both and multiply each result by 0.5, then add the
two results together to get total Kcalc
• For Kdel, the formula is the same for pre- and post-filter
replacement so you only have to do it once
Once you’ve determined K, it can be plugged into the Kt/V
formula
• Remember, V = 0.6 × BW (kg)
• t = 1320 minutes
• Target result is 1.2-1.4
• The most common mistake in all of this math is an error in units
Example: 32 kg Labrador with AKI secondary to heat stroke is
started on post-filter CVVH
• Blood rate (Qb) is set at 100 mL/min and RR is 20 mL/min
• Estimate that patient will receive ∼22 hr Tx/day = 1320 minutes
• K = ultrafiltrate rate or 20 mL/min
• Kcalc = (20 mL/min × 3120 minutes)/19200 mL = 1.37
• To increase to target of 1.4, can increase the blood flow rate and
the ultrafiltrate rate (filtration fraction)
Blood Priming
• The AN69 membrane causes bradykinin release in blood that is
acidic (all stored blood is acidic)
• After priming with saline, double spike the blood bag with an
“arterial” and “venous” line
• Give heparin bolus into the donor blood
• Have the Prismaflex perform convection on it for
approximately 20-30 minutes at ∼20 mL/min, with a 20%
filtration fraction

○ This removes the acidity and bradykinin
○ Use whatever blood is in the circuit as your prime
○ Keep the heparin CRI going throughout the process
Heparin vs. Citrate
• Human medicine debates this issue regularly and the literature
seems to favor citrate due to lack of systemic anti-coagulation
and prolonged circuit life
• However, citrate is associated with much more intense
monitoring of acid/base and calcium as well as ACT, therefore
increasing cost
Heparin Dosing
• Remember: must be entered into the machine as mL/hr
• Most aim for ACT ∼200 seconds (I tend to be on the more
aggressive side and try to maintain around 220 seconds)
• Start of therapy
• In the absence of coagulopathy (ACT > 150) give 25 IU/kg
heparin bolus
• Recheck ACT. If <180, repeat bolus (maximum of 3 total
boluses)
• During CRRT
• Start heparin infusion at 20 IU/kg/hr
• If ACT <180, increase heparin by 1 IU/kg/hr

PALPATION OF THE PROSTATE AND INITIAL
TESTING
Prostatic diseases are common, and some dogs have more than one prostatic
disorder, complicating any diagnosis. The most common conditions encountered
are benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatic metaplasia or neoplasia, prostatitis,
and prostatic abscesses (chs. 314 and 315). A definitive diagnosis can usually be
reached after assessing results of a complete diagnostic workup that begins with a
thorough history (ch. 2) and a complete physical examination (PE, ch. 3). In
dogs suspected of having a prostatic condition, palpation of the prostate should
be the final aspect of the PE. Digital rectal palpation, used alone or in
combination with abdominal palpation, permits prostate evaluation in most dogs.
In medium and large-size dogs, gently compressing the caudal abdomen dorsally
can shift the prostate dorsal and caudal, allowing better opportunity to fully
palpate the caudal and dorsal aspects of the prostate rectally, noting size, shape,
symmetry, mobility, surface texture, and pain (ch. 3). Imaging and collection of
prostatic samples are specific diagnostic techniques. In addition to a complete
blood count (CBC), serum chemistry profile, and urinalysis (UA),
ultrasonography (US) of the prostatic area and obtaining canine prostate-specific

esterase (CPSE) concentrations may aid in diagnosis. In many, urine culture and
prostatic sample collection for bacteriologic and cytologic evaluation are
indicated.

IMAGING
ULTRASONOGRAPHY (US)
Conventional US
Despite the absence of US images that are pathognomonic for any prostatic
disease, US is an extremely valuable diagnostic aid. US is more sensitive in
assessing the prostatic parenchyma than radiography. Any male dog with clinical
signs of prostatic or lower urinary system disease or pain should be evaluated
with US. Conventional US permits visualization of prostate size, internal
architecture, cystic structures, mineralization, presence of gas, and tissues
surrounding the prostate. US can be used to monitor changes over time or
response to treatment. Regional lymph nodes can be evaluated in dogs with
neoplasia or prostatitis. US can be used to guide fine-needle aspiration (FNA),
biopsy, or percutaneous ethanol injection (PEI; chs. 85, 314, and 315).1 7.5- or
10-MHz transducers provide excellent detail of parenchymal texture. Doppler,
and the more accurate power Doppler US, can be employed to evaluate prostatic
perfusion and to correlate findings with the differential diagnosis.2 Examinations
are performed with the dog in lateral or dorsal recumbency with the hind limbs
extended caudally. Obtaining prostatic images and FNAs is usually
straightforward with dogs in lateral recumbency, often without sedation. Having
the dog standing can be useful if the prostate is located within the pelvis. The
transducer is usually placed on the ventral abdomen cranial to the pubis to gain
the best images, although a perineal approach may be useful in “pelvic prostates”
or those in a perineal hernia. In large dogs, a transrectal transducer would likely
provide superior prostatic images but such transducers are not commonly
available in small animal practice. Avoid introducing air into the rectum by
completing digital rectal palpations several hours before or just after US. In dogs
with a pelvic prostate, it may be useful to push the gland cranially via the rectum
to improve US results.
The prostate is located caudal to the urinary bladder and ventral to the
descending colon and rectum.3 The urinary bladder is an important landmark
and it reduces interference caused by the small intestine. Having the intestinal
tract relatively empty is important. Thus, one should provide owners with
instructions on how to prepare their dog for prostatic US, especially withholding
food for 12 hours before the procedure, allowing water at all times, and trying to
have a moderately full bladder by withholding the opportunity to urinate just
before entering the veterinary hospital. In healthy intact dogs, the prostate on US
has medium echogenicity, a homogeneous parenchyma, fine to medium coarse
echotexture, and a smooth capsular margin. On transverse section, the prostate is

symmetrically bilobed, with a hypoechoic vertical median raphe that is
triangularly shaped, contains the prostatic urethra, and in sagittal plane is roundto-ovoid (Figure 104.1).3 After castration, the prostate decreases in size and
echogenicity due to atrophy of glandular parenchyma (E-Figure 104.2). In older
intact dogs, the prostate commonly becomes less homogeneous due to incidental
isoechoic nodules and small cysts, and it grows from puberty to geriatric ages.
Prostate growth throughout adult life in dogs and humans, with US evidence of
hyperplasia, usually does not cause signs and is considered normal. Prostate size
varies according to neuter status, breed, age, and presence of abnormalities. Size
can be measured in both sagittal and transverse planes via US. Prostatic volume
can be calculated using the formula: V (cm3) = [1/2.6 (length × width × height) +
1.8 (cm3).4 The volume obtained can be compared with an estimated normal
resulting from this formula that correlates age (years) and body weight (in kg): V
(cm3) = (0.867 × body weight) + (1.885 × age) + 15.88.5 US measurements are
determined, in part, by the position of the probe (E-Figure 104.3). Prostatic
width and height should be measured from the largest transverse section, usually
symmetrical in shape and perpendicular to the prostatic urethra. Prostatic length
is measured in a median sagittal section in which the urethra is included. The
transverse section can be used for measuring prostatic height. Measurements
obtained from incorrect sections must be avoided. The colon often interferes with
(foreshortens) height measurements (E-Figure 104.4).

FIGURE 104.1 Longitudinal (A) and transverse (B)
abdominal ultrasonographic images of a normal prostate in an
intact dog. The prostatic parenchyma is uniformly medium in
echotexture and moderately hyperechoic compared to
surrounding structures, with a hypoechoic prostatic urethra
(U). Note the anechoic bladder neck (B) and pubic bone
shadow (S) on the longitudinal image. C, Prostatic structure.
Three different components are seen: peritonem; capsule and
stroma, composed of dense connective tissue, elastic fibers and
smooth muscle fibers; and glandular parenchyma in a tubularacinar configuration.

E-FIGURE 104.2 Transverse image of a normal prostate in
a castrated dog. The gland (arrowhead) is decreased in size
and echogenicity due to the atrophy of glandular parenchyma.
C, Colon.

E-FIGURE 104.3 The drawing on the left shows the correct
position of the probe for measuring the width and height of the
prostate. In the right rectangle: correct position to obtain an
orthogonal transverse scan (1); the most common positioning
errors during measurement are obliquity due to rotation (2)
and tilting (3) of the probe axis.

E-FIGURE 104.4 Prostatic width, height, and length
measurement. Transverse image of a largest section,
perpendicular to the prostatic urethra that appears
symmetrical in its shape (A). White interrupted line shows the
prostatic margin and the green arrowed line (with green check
mark) the correct measure of the height. It is important to
account for colon interference (C); otherwise,
undermeasurement would be possible (red arrowed line with
red X). The measurement of the width is taken orthogonally to
the height. The prostatic length is measured in a median
sagittal section where the urethra is visible, on which the
measurement is taken (B). The height can also be measured in
the same section, confirming the measurement obtained in the
cross-section. (C), Colon.
Doppler and Elastography
To overcome Doppler’s limitations, microbubble contrast-enhanced US (CEUS)
and use of contrast harmonic software provide detailed visualization of the
prostatic microcirculatory bed. They are useful for detecting early prostate
disease, for discriminating benign from malignant lesions, and for staging
disease.6,7 Further improving diagnostic imaging, elastography detects
deformities and tissue stiffness and has the potential to become a useful tool for
distinguishing healthy from diseased prostates.7

RADIOGRAPHY
Radiographic images of the prostatic area usually complement US findings but
are less informative. The colon should be empty prior to radiographic
examination. Radiographs can identify prostatic topography, shape, and size, and
location of the urinary bladder and colon. Images of the caudal abdomen that
include pelvis and hindlimbs are quite important because prostatic cancers often

metastasize into the pelvis. Calcification of prostatic parenchyma or alterations to
the prostatic urethra due to neoplasia are easier to appreciate radiographically
than with US. The normal prostate size should not exceed 70% of the distance
from sacral promontory to the pubic brim, measured on a lateral radiographic
view (E-Figure 104.5).8 Prostatic neoplasia, abscessation, or cysts usually cause
the prostatic silhouette to exceed 90% of this distance.9 However, size alone
cannot be used to discriminate among the differential diagnoses nor help in
prognosis.10 Radiographic examination with positive or negative contrast
improves diagnostic yield. Positive contrast urethrocystography, usually requiring
anesthesia, should highlight the urinary bladder, providing a landmark for the
prostate and identifying the prostatic urethra. Urethral surface irregularities and
reflux of the contrast medium into the prostatic parenchyma are seen with
neoplasia, while cysts or abscesses also compress the urethra.10

E-FIGURE 104.5 A, Radiographic evaluation of prostatic
size on the lateral radiograph of a dog. The prostate diameter
(left arrowed line) compared with the distance from sacral
promontory to the pubic brim (right arrowed line). B, Positive
contrast urethrocystogram in a dog with prostatic
adenocarcinoma. The prostatic urethral surface appears
irregular, with a filling defect due to the growth of neoplastic
tissue (arrow).

COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY (CT) AND
MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI)
Use of CT and MRI scans can improve likelihood of making the correct diagnosis,
although both require anesthesia. CT images avoid interference caused by
overlapping tissues, allow detection of small changes in prostate size and shape,

and provide visualization of local lymph nodes. These are not possible with
radiographs or US.11 Image quality is usually better with MRI but image
acquisition time is longer. Even without contrast, cystic and solid lesions can be
distinguished with both CT and MRI. Contrast media can improve the diagnostic
utility of CT by highlighting walls of cystic structures and the vascularity of
neoplasms (chs. 314 and 315).10

PROSTATIC SAMPLE COLLECTION
OVERVIEW
Prostate imaging results may influence suspicions, but a definitive diagnosis of
prostatitis, abscess, neoplasia, or metaplasia usually requires cytology and/or
bacterial culture (chs. 314 and 315). Intraprostatic cysts should be evaluated for
possible urinary content, which is important when choosing therapy. Selecting an
antibiotic should be based on culture and sensitivity results of appropriate
specimens. Prostatic sampling includes semen collection, prostatic massage,
traumatic urethral catheterization, FNA, and biopsy.11-13

SEMEN COLLECTION
Collecting the ejaculate’s “third fraction” for cytologic evaluation and culture is
recommended in suspected prostatitis and/or concomitant cystitis. The first
fraction is clear, small in volume, and produced for only moments; the second
sperm-rich fraction is produced for 30 seconds to 3 minutes during pelvic
thrusting and is cloudy; the third, final, and largest volume fraction is clear
prostatic fluid that can be collected for 2 to 20 minutes or longer. Ejaculation of
the first and second fractions “rinses” the urethra of debris and bacteria normally
present. The third fraction is not contaminated by urethral flora. Samples for
culture are obtained using a sterile disposable tube and sterilized silicone cone,
avoiding contact with the inner surface of the artificial vagina. Bacterial
concentrations <100,000/mL and growth of several bacterial species are
common in healthy males. Semen aerobic cultures containing >10,000 colony
forming units/mL are suggestive of reproductive tract infection.14
Attempting to collect an ejaculate from dogs experiencing pain from prostatitis
is often unrewarding. In painful dogs, gentle massage (below) can be employed to
provide fluid for analysis and culture while minimizing risk of
peritonitis/septicemia. Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be administrated
immediately after the procedure while awaiting results of culture and sensitivity.7
Despite low cellularity, cytologic evaluation of the third fraction should be
assessed because is specific for the prostate.
Collecting ejaculate is needed for any breeding soundness examination,
artificial insemination, sperm preservation, or diagnostic purposes and is

considered completely safe. Materials needed include latex gloves, sterilizable
silicone semen collection cone (artificial vagina), and three sterile graduated
plastic centrifuge tubes. A quiet room with a floor providing good traction is
helpful. Digital manipulation of the penile region is the most common technique
to obtain ejaculate and is usually successful even in untrained males (

Video

104.1). A “teaser bitch” can facilitate collection but is usually not needed. The dog
is allowed to sniff the external genitals of the bitch and mount. With the gloved
hand, the prepuce is pushed caudally to fully expose the penis and bulbus glandis.
Gentle but firm application of pulsating pressure directly around or just proximal
to the bulbus using the thumb and index finger creates a ring, until a partial
erection develops. After several pelvic thrusts, the erection is usually complete
and the second fraction of ejaculate is produced. As the third fraction is produced,
the dog instinctively dismounts by lifting one hind leg over the collector’s arm
and turning 180 degrees in the opposite direction without altering the location of
the penis (penile “flexible rigidity”). While in this tail-to-tail position, the dog
ejaculates the third fraction. At the end of the ejaculation, the erection subsides
and the bulbus and penis are gently placed into the sheath, checking that no hair
has been caught.

PROSTATIC MASSAGE AND TRAUMATIC
CATHETERIZATION
Massage
Prostatic massage is used to obtain prostatic samples for cytologic analysis and
bacterial culture when collecting an ejaculate is not possible.13 The disposable
materials used for the procedure must be sterile (Figure 104.6 and E-Figure
104.7). The technique allows collection of two samples. The pre-massage sample
contains bladder material while the post-massage sample also contains prostatic
material. The pre- and post-massage samples are obtained using equal volumes of
sterile saline to allow easier cytologic and bacterial comparisons. The technique is
performed after allowing the dog to urinate. Proceed with sedation if necessary,
although the procedure is usually accepted without drug restraint. The procedure
begins by emptying the urinary bladder via sterile catheterization. Choose an
appropriately sized polyethylene urinary catheter with a single opening at the tip
(E-Figure 104.7). The bladder is then “washed” using 5-15 mL of sterile saline
(volume depends on the size of the dog) to obtain the first sample (sample A). The
urinary catheter is then partially retracted until its tip is positioned, with digital
rectal palpation, in the prostatic urethra. Prostate massage is performed
transrectally, or abdominally in larger dogs. The massage, lasting about 1 minute,
must be vigorous but not traumatic, especially if cavitary lesions are present.
Perform the second sterile saline wash. During saline infusion, occlude the
urethra with the finger in the rectum caudal to the prostate to avoid retrograde
fluid reflux. The catheter is then completely introduced into the urinary bladder

and the wash liquid aspirated (sample B). The two samples are submitted for
cytologic evaluation and bacterial culture (Figure 104.8). Possible side-effects
of this technique include rupture of cystic cavities or abscesses and translocating
bacteria. Urethral transitional cell carcinoma frequently invades the prostatic
urethra (ch. 330). It is not usually possible to determine whether neoplastic cells
are of prostatic origin.12 Prostate cancers, usually adenocarcinomas, are
uncommon (ch. 314).

E-FIGURE 104.7 Sterile disposable materials used to
perform prostatic massage and traumatic catheterization (A).
Gloves (1), two syringes with an equal volume of sterile saline
(5-15 mL) (2), 50 mL syringe to empty the bladder (3),
polyethylene urinary catheter with a single endhole for
prostatic massage (4), polyethylene urinary catheter with two
lateral openings for prostatic massage (5). Close-up of the
catheters with a single endhole (left) and two lateral openings
(right) (B).

Traumatic Catheterization
Neoplasms located near the prostatic urethra can be sampled by traumatic
catheterization. The procedure is carried out with a urinary catheter that has two
lateral openings near its tip (E-Figure 104.7). The dog with an emptied bladder
is catheterized with sterile technique and a 5 mL syringe is connected to the
catheter. The tip of the catheter is introduced to the prostatic urethra under the
guidance of digital rectal palpation. Aspiration with the syringe during prostatic
massage with and back and forth movements of the catheter allow collection of
samples from the prostate and the surface of the urethra. The catheter is then
removed and flushed with air or saline to dislodge all material collected for
analysis.

FINE-NEEDLE ASPIRATION (FNA)
Indications
US-guided FNA is recommended for cystic conditions. It is possible to collect
fluid or tissue for cytologic evaluation or culture and then drain fluid from cystic
lesions or apply PEI therapy. The collection with this procedure may be more
selective, in terms of lesion (cyst or nodule), in comparison with prostatic
massage. Rupture of cavities or seeding the needle tract with bacteria, with
subsequent peritonitis, are the most frequent contraindications for aspiration of
prostatic abscesses. If prostatic neoplasia is suspected, one should first consider
collecting an ejaculate, prostatic massage, or traumatic catheterization.12,13
Cytologic evaluations from these samples are often diagnostic, but biopsy may be
required in some. Correct diagnoses in one study were obtained in 47% and 67%
of FNA and prostatic biopsies, respectively.13 Biopsy is contraindicated when
prostatitis or abscesses are suspected. The most common side-effects are
hematuria secondary to urethral injury. Less common complications are
peritonitis and seeding of bacteria or neoplastic cells along the instrument tract.

Procedure
FNA is usually performed with abdominal US guidance using a freehand
technique or using a needle guide for the US probe via a transrectal or perirectal
approach. Simultaneous transrectal palpation guides the instrument. “Blind”
FNA techniques are also described.14 Sedation or anesthesia is occasionally
needed. The dog is placed in lateral recumbency. Since the collection should be
sterile, the skin should be prepared with a surgical scrub and the procedure
performed with sterile disposable material (E-Figure 104.9,

Video 104.2).

Based on need, one might use a hypodermic, spinal, or echo-reflective needle. The
needle should be connected to a 5 mL syringe for suction. US is used to identify
the area of interest within the prostate. The needle is inserted and visualized until
it reaches the point of aspiration. During aspiration of cystic lesions, the needle
remains fixed, while for the aspiration of parenchymal or nodular lesions it is best
to move the needle back and forth. The negative pressure created by the syringe
plunger is released prior to the needle being withdrawn. Aspirate all the contents
of the cystic cavities to decompress them and to avoid leakage of fluid after
removing the needle. Collection of more than one sample is recommended.15

FIGURE 104.6 Prostatic massage: step by step illustration.

catheterization.

3. Aspirate it back to obtain the first sample (A).
4. Retract the catheter to the level of the membranous
urethra, guided by rectal palpation. Perform transrectal
prostatic massage for about 1 minute.
5. Occlude the urethral orifice and slowly inject the second
sterile saline to wash the urethra.
6. Advance the catheter into the bladder and aspirate the

PROSTATIC BIOPSY
The procedure is usually performed percutaneously under US guidance with a
needle core biopsy (“Tru-Cut”) instrument (E-Figure 104.10), using a
transabdominal approach. It is also possible to surgically obtain a wedge
resection. For biopsy, the dog must be sedated or anesthetized, placed in lateral
recumbency, and prepared as described for the FNA. A urinary catheter should be
inserted to visualize the urethra during the procedure. Coagulation testing is
strongly recommended before any biopsy is performed (ch. 170). As reported for
FNA, the biopsy instrument is also displayed on the US screen throughout the
sample collection. The tissue collected is preserved in formalin and submitted for
histological examination.

perform transcutaneous prostatic biopsy. Needle core biopsy
instrument (Tru-Cut) (1), gloves (2).

CLIENT INFORMATION
Your veterinarian is concerned about the possibility of a prostatic disorder
(medical problem involving the prostate gland) in your pet. In order to investigate
this, diagnostic tests are needed. These can be noninvasive diagnostic imaging,
like radiographs (X-rays) and ultrasound. Often, it can be necessary to sample the
prostate gland itself during ultrasound, so that prostate cells or tissue can be
examined by the laboratory for more information about the prostatic condition.
The following is information that is relevant to these types of tests.

RADIOGRAPHS
• This exam is simple and safe for your dog, requires no hospitalization and
lasts a short time.
• Fasting (no food) is important before radiographs: avoid feeding your pet
anything for 12 hours prior to the exam; therefore, do not give food after 8
pm the night before.
• Free access to water is permitted at all times.
• The large intestine (colon) should be as empty as possible: take your dog
for a walk within 2 to 3 hours before the study to allow normal passage of
stool (defecation).
• The urinary bladder ideally should be medium to full: please try to prevent
your dog from urinating for 2 to 3 hours leading up to the study,
especially when you come in to the veterinary hospital.
• It could be necessary for us to shave the fur over the area of interest
(usually the caudal abdomen, meaning the part of the belly closest to the
back legs).
• In case it is necessary to perform a fine-needle aspiration or a biopsy,
sedation will be needed. You should discuss any concerns or questions
you have about sedation with your veterinarian. After either procedure
involving the prostate, you may notice small drops of blood from your
pet’s prepuce (penis sheath) for a day or less afterward. If this persists for
more than a day, or is more than a few drops, please contact your
veterinarian.

ULTRASOUND
• This exam is simple and safe for your dog, requires no hospitalization and
lasts a short time.
• Fasting (no food) is important before ultrasound: avoid feeding your pet
anything for 12 hours prior to the exam; therefore, do not give food after 8
pm the night before.
• Free access to water is permitted at all times.
• The large intestine (colon) should be as empty as possible: take your dog
for a walk within 2 to 3 hours before the study to allow normal passage of

stool (defecation).
Daniele Zambelli (Bologna, Italy)

GASTRIC INTUBATION
Placement of a tube through the mouth into the stomach, also known
as orogastric intubation, is performed for the purpose of removing
gastric contents, decompressing a distended stomach (e.g., gastric
dilation-volvulus; ch. 261), lavaging the stomach, and/or
administering medications or diagnostic solutions (e.g., barium).
Although the procedure itself is not difficult, the potential benefits
and risks should be weighed prior to placement of an orogastric tube.

INDICATIONS AND COMPLICATIONS
The primary indications for orogastric intubation include
decompression of a dilated stomach (ch. 261), toxin removal from
the stomach with or without lavage (e.g., potentially lethal toxins,
intoxicated patients with an altered level of consciousness requiring
controlled decontamination, or those that may form a bezoar or

obstruction within the stomach or intestine; ch. 136), and
medication or diagnostic solution administration into the stomach.
Potential complications to consider include esophageal or gastric
wall damage or perforation, regurgitation followed by aspiration of
gastric contents, and adverse effects of general anesthesia. Animals
that are critically ill or severely intoxicated could be at higher risk for
anesthesia-related complications.

PROCEDURE
Once the patient is identified as a candidate for orogastric
intubation, the anesthetic protocol should be chosen according to the
patient’s systemic status. The main supplies necessary are shown in
Figures 105.1 and 105.2.
Once the endotracheal tube is in place, the cuff should be properly
inflated prior to the procedure to help prevent aspiration of stomach
contents or lavage fluid. The orogastric tube should be a singlelumen, semi-rigid tube with a smooth tip to avoid mucosal trauma.
The clinician should choose a tube with the largest diameter possible
for the patient’s esophagus (approximately the same diameter as an
endotracheal tube for the given animal). A 12 Fr red rubber catheter
may be adequate for small puppies, whereas an 18 Fr red rubber
catheter may be used in adults up to 15 kg, and a true orogastric tube
should be used in dogs weighing >15 kg. Measurement of the length
of the tube to be inserted should be performed using the nares and
the last rib as landmarks (Figure 105.3, A) and the tube should be
marked with either a piece of white tape (Figure 105.3, B) or a
permanent marker.
There is some controversy as to whether animals should be
sedated or anesthetized prior to passing the orogastric tube. The
author’s preference is to anesthetize the patient and place an
endotracheal tube with the cuff inflated to help protect the airway in
case the animal regurgitates or vomits during the procedure. An
exception is neonates that are having an orogastric tube passed for
feeding and do not typically exhibit the gag reflex during the
procedure (ch. 146). Suction catheters and additional necessary
equipment should always be available prior to starting the procedure

so the oropharynx can be cleaned prior to extubation, or in the event
of regurgitation or vomiting following orogastric extubation.
Once the patient is anesthetized and the endotracheal tube is
placed, the mouth can be maintained in the open position using
either a mouth gag or roll of tape, if necessary. Water-soluble
lubricant should be applied to the end of the orogastric tube and the
tube advanced slowly into the esophagus, located in the left dorsal
aspect of the pharynx. The other end of the tube should always be
lower than the dog (and inside a collection container) to allow for
gravitational drainage. The tube is advanced gently to the
predetermined length to reach the stomach. Dogs with gastric
dilation-volvulus might require slight forward pressure with a
twisting motion to aid with entry through the cardia into the stomach
(Video 105.1

). If there is continued resistance to passage of the

tube, the operator can blow a small amount of air into the tube while
gently advancing it (it is recommended that a piece of gauze be
placed over the end prior to doing this to avoid contamination of the
operator’s mouth). Animals with severe distention of the stomach
may require percutaneous trocarization of the stomach prior to
successful passing of the orogastric tube. Once the tube is advanced
to the premeasured length, there should be some fluid or gastric
contents apparent in the collection container below the level of the
patient; if not, careful ballottement of the abdomen may increase
pressure and help increase flow through the tube (ch. 21). If gastric
contents are occluding the tube and preventing drainage, 10-30 mL
of warm water can be flushed into the tube to dislodge the
obstruction.

In order to prevent fluid from leaking out of the tube and into the
esophagus or pharynx during removal, the tube should be tightly
kinked ∼10 cm from the operator’s end prior to removal. The kink
should be maintained firmly until the tube is fully removed from the
animal. The mouth and pharynx should be closely inspected for
residual fluid or stomach contents and cleaned with gauze or suction
as needed.

GASTRIC LAVAGE
Removal of gastric contents via orogastric intubation is referred to as
gastric lavage. It is most commonly performed in an attempt to
remove toxic material from the stomach (ch. 132) or to empty the
stomach prior to gastrotomy. It rarely has been used as a cooling
technique or to confirm bleeding from the upper gastrointestinal
(GI) tract.
The American Academy of Clinical Toxicology has concluded that
the poisoned patient should not receive routine GI decontamination
and clinical evidence in humans has shown no clear benefit of gastric
lavage over activated charcoal for the treatment of toxin ingestion.1,2
However, lavage currently is performed at many human hospitals
and it still is a part of the current recommendation for the treatment
of small animals in specific scenarios, despite limited evidence.3-5
Before emesis is induced or gastric lavage is performed, the clinician
should always ensure that Bailey’s “GI decontamination triangle”
questions have been adequately answered6:
1. Is the ingested toxin likely to cause significant effects?

2. Is GI decontamination likely to change the outcome?
3. Do the risks of GI decontamination outweigh the potential
benefits in this particular patient?
Patients that might benefit from gastric lavage include animals
that have ingested a potentially harmful amount of toxin within 1
hour of presentation, but where induction of emesis is not deemed
appropriate due to neurologic impairment (or emesis is not effective
at removing gastric contents; (ch. 132). If animals have ingested a
very small amount of a toxin, or have already vomited prior to
presentation, the potential risks and benefits of gastric lavage should
be considered even more closely because the procedure is not benign,
and activated charcoal administration may prove to be a safer option.
There are exceptions, especially when very large amounts of a
dangerous substance have been ingested. Gastric lavage is not
indicated for the treatment of food bloat (without torsion) nor
ingestion of material that solidifies in the stomach, such as
polyurethane adhesive (e.g., Gorilla Glue, ch. 136); the latter
requires gastrotomy for removal. Gastric lavage is contraindicated in
animals that have ingested caustic or volatile substances because
esophageal reflux, mucosal damage, and aspiration pneumonia could
result. Three canine studies have evaluated the effectiveness of
gastric lavage for reducing the bioavailability of different markers
(sodium salicylate or barium sulfate).7-9 As expected, gastric lavage
at 15 minutes recovered a much greater amount of the marker than
at 30 or 60 minutes. All three studies showed <15% recovery at 1hour post-administration of marker. Another study examined dogs
that were given 500 mg/kg of aspirin, then underwent gastric lavage
and then were given activated charcoal (1.5 g/kg) 30 minutes after
drug administration.10 There was a 37% reduction in peak plasma
salicylate concentration in the treated group compared to the control
group, confirming the fact that early lavage (and charcoal therapy)
may be worthwhile. It is not known how this treatment compares to
induction of emesis in neurologically intact animals that have
ingested non-corrosive toxins.
The primary risks of gastric lavage include anesthesia-related
complications, aspiration of stomach contents, and trauma to (or
perforation of) the esophagus or stomach. The incidence of GI tract

perforation is very low in people,2 and is assumed to be low in small
animals, but there are no definitive data to prove or disprove this
assumption in veterinary medicine. Excessive absorption of
hypotonic lavage fluid could lead to water intoxication with
hyponatremia and hypochloremia, but this is unlikely if a majority of
the fluid is drained following administration. It is helpful to record
the volume of fluid that is infused and retrieved to avoid excessive
water administration. In order to perform gastric lavage, a single- or
double-lumen orogastric tube should be placed as described above,
the animal positioned in lateral recumbency, and the endotracheal
tube cuff checked for inflation. Approximately 10-30 mL/kg of warm
lavage fluid (e.g., isotonic saline or water) is infused into the stomach
using a stomach pump, bilge pump, or gravity flow through a funnel
(note: never use a hose). Once the fluid has been infused, the
operator’s end of the orogastric tube should be directed into the
designated container and the effluent passively drains via gravity
flow (Video 105.2

). While fluid is infused, and when it is being

drained, the stomach should be palpated to monitor for
overdistention and gently balloted to assist with emptying of the
lavage fluid, respectively. Suction should never be used for emptying
the stomach as this may cause mucosal trauma. The retrieved
stomach contents should be examined for foreign material or toxins
and submitted for toxicologic analysis, if indicated. The infuse-drain
cycle should be repeated (typically 5-10 times) in order to effectively
clean out the stomach. The animal can be turned to the opposite
recumbency for additional gastric lavages, as indicated, but it is
important to check the endotracheal tube position and cuff inflation
after repositioning. Following the final lavage cycle, activated
charcoal (1-5 g/kg), with or without a cathartic, can be administered
through the orogastric tube and into the stomach (and flushed in
with water), if indicated. It is important that the stomach not be
distended prior to recovery and extubation, in order to minimize the
chance of vomiting and aspiration. There is no proven advantage to
the use of pre-lavage activated charcoal administration in human
medicine. This was previously thought to decrease intestinal
absorption of toxin that could be advanced into the duodenum
during the lavage.2

Following gastric intubation ± lavage, the animal should remain
endotracheally intubated with the cuff inflated until sternal and
swallowing. Extubation should not be delayed in cats, however, due
to risk of laryngospasm. Therefore, cats should either have a reduced
dose of activated charcoal administered, or it can be given after
recovery. Supplies for oropharyngeal suction should be readily
available during recovery in case there is fluid in the mouth or
pharynx that can be removed easily prior to extubation. The patient
should be monitored closely for evidence of nausea or regurgitation
and treated accordingly.

Chapter 106: Canine Fecal
Microbiota Transplantation
Jennifer Chaitman, and Jan S. Suchodolski

A C RO N YM S
DI dysbiosis index
FMT fecal microbiota transplantation
GI gastrointestinal
IBD inflammatory bowel disease

INTRODUCTION
Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is the transfer of stool from
a healthy donor to a sick patient, with the goal of restoring eubiosis.1
Feces can be transferred orally, by nasogastric tube, gastrointestinal
(GI) endoscopy, colonoscopy, or by enema. All of these methods may
be effective.2 FMT is most commonly performed in dogs with GI
disease. Studies have shown that it is highly successful in treating
Clostridioides difficile infections,3 ameliorating chronic
enteropathies,4 and increasing insulin sensitivity in people with
metabolic syndrome.5 In dogs, FMT primarily has been explored for
the treatment of acute and chronic diarrhea (chs. 49, 262, 263). Its

benefit over probiotics is that it allows for a more complete
restoration of the gut microbiome with all the organisms and
metabolites as opposed to individual bacteria.

MECHANISMS OF ACTION
The GI tract is a complex organ hosting trillions of microorganisms,
including bacteria, archaea, fungi, and viruses. These organisms
support the health of the host by modulating the immune system,
maintaining the intestinal barrier, resisting colonization by
pathogenic bacteria, aiding digestion, and by producing beneficial
metabolites (ch. 260).6 One important beneficial bacterium in dogs
is Clostridium hiranonis. It has 7-alpha-dehydroxylating activity and
it transforms primary into secondary bile acids. C. hiranonis counts
frequently are decreased in dogs with diarrhea and after broadspectrum antibiotic use and they can be restored with FMT. The
response to FMT often is durable in patients with acute diarrhea or
after antibiotic-induced dysbiosis (Figure 106.1).7 In dogs with
chronic diarrhea, the abundance of C. hiranonis usually normalizes
after FMT but the effects may not last. Most likely, relapses are due
to the underlying conditions in the gut that make it inhospitable to
beneficial bacteria. While there is much yet to be discovered about
the mechanisms behind FMT, it is known that C. difficile infections
in people are successfully treated with FMT and that C. difficile
spores are inhibited by secondary bile acids.8 FMT can be considered
for the treatment of diarrhea as an alternative to antibiotics because
commonly used treatments such as metronidazole and tylosin can
have lasting negative effects on the microbiome (Figure 106.2).9

STUDIES IN THE DOG
In acute diarrhea (ch. 262), FMT improved fecal scores more than
metronidazole. Furthermore, FMT normalized the dysbiosis index
(DI) and the abundance of C. hiranonis, which was associated with
normalization of bile acid metabolism. In contrast, metronidazole led

to an increase in the DI and abnormal bile acid conversion (Figure
106.1).7
In puppies with parvoviral enteritis (ch. 201), FMT given as an
enema in addition to standard therapy shortened the duration of
diarrhea and decreased hospitalization time from 6 days to 3 days in
one study.10
For chronic diarrhea (ch. 262), FMT has been shown to improve
fecal consistency and the DI but based on the author’s experience
there can be variable outcomes, which appear to be correlated with
abundances of C. hiranonis (Figure 106.3).11 Some dogs will
develop diarrhea again days to weeks after FMT. Some dogs will not
have a change in their DI but will have a temporary improvement in
fecal scores, and/or it may also be possible to decrease the amount or
number of chronic medications such as corticosteroids or antibiotics
after FMT. In a study of dogs with inflammatory bowel disease
(IBD), adding FMT as an adjunctive treatment improved the mean
canine chronic enteropathy activity index (CCECAI) from 11.4 before
FMT to 7.4 at 1 month and 7.8 at 3 months. Several dogs were able to
be sustained on less medication as a result of repeated FMT.12 A
second study using FMT in 9 dogs with IBD showed a decrease in the
canine IBD activity index and an increase in beneficial
Fusobacteria.13 At this time, it may be best to consider FMT as an
adjunctive therapy in dogs with chronic enteropathy and successive
FMT may be needed for relapses.
Little has been documented in the cat. There is one case report of a
cat with ulcerative colitis who was successfully treated with FMT.14

FMT PROTOCOL VIA ENEMA BASED ON
CHAITMAN ET AL.7 (Video 106.1 )
Materials needed: 0.9% NaCl, 12 or 14 French red rubber catheter,
60 cc catheter-tip syringes, blender and donor stool, nonbacteriostatic lubricant. Sedation is typically not needed. Feces can
be either fresh or frozen (stored at −20°C or −80°C). When freezing
feces, aliquots should contain 10 g of stool, 30-35 mL of 0.9% NaCl,
and 5 mL of glycerol to avoid freeze damage of microorganisms.15

1. Calculate amount of stool needed: approximately 5 g per kg of
body weight, as weighed on gram scale.
2. Add 60 mL 0.9% NaCl to blender, then add fresh or frozen
stool. If using frozen stool that has been prepared with saline
and glycerol, no additional saline may be needed. In large
dogs, saline may be needed to sufficiently liquefy the stool so
that it can pass through the catheter.
3. Blend on high until the stool is liquefied and no large pieces
are seen.
4. Draw up the mixed stool/saline material into one or more 60
cc catheter tip syringes, and attach a 12 or 14 inch French red
rubber catheter.
5. Push some of the material into the syringe until it comes out
the tip so that no air will be introduced into the colon of the
recipient dog.
6. Feed the catheter all the way in to the colon, then administer
enema. The recipient dog does not need to be sedated.
7. If possible, do not feed the recipient dog and restrict the
recipient dog’s activity for 4-6 hours after the transplant, to
lessen the chances of a premature bowel movement.

FORM OF FMT
The fecal slurry above can be given through a nasogastric tube,
through an endoscope, or as an enema. To make fecal capsules,
aspirate fecal material into a small syringe, and working quickly, put
into gel cap, then into a larger gel cap, then freeze immediately
(author’s experience). In a human study comparing FMT given by
oral capsules or colonoscopy for C. difficile infection, capsules were
effective, but in that study, the patients swallowed 40 of them in one
sitting.16 One to two capsules could be considered for daily, longterm administration in dogs or cats with chronic enteropathy. While
the therapeutic amounts for all forms of FMT are yet to be
determined, it is clear that it shows promise as a treatment modality
for dysbiosis in the dog.
