SURVEY RADIOGRAPHY
INDICATIONS AND CONTRAINDICATIONS
Indications for the radiographic examination of the spine include evidence of
spinal pain and neurologic deficits. There are no true contraindications; however,
positional radiographs or “stress views” under flexion and extension of the spine
to evaluate for spinal instability are discouraged as they are likely to result in
additional spinal cord damage and worsening of clinical signs.

TECHNIQUE AND INTERPRETATION10,13
A radiographic examination of the spine follows the same basic principles as the
radiographic examination of other musculoskeletal structures. With few
exceptions (e.g., an obvious bony lesion such as a tumor or spinal instability
evident on the initial image), radiographs are obtained in at least 2 orthogonal
planes. Straight positioning is of utmost importance as even mild obliquity will
render a study nondiagnostic for assessment of vertebral alignment and
intervertebral disc space width. For this reason, sedation is recommended, to
allow optimal patient positioning. The x-ray beam is collimated to the area of
interest, and the field of view should be kept small, as beam divergence at the
edge of a larger field of view will result in distortion of peripheral structures and
the erroneous impression of intervertebral disc space narrowing.
The systematic approach to spinal radiographs includes the assessment of
vertebral anatomy (number and conformation of individual vertebrae, including
expected variations in vertebral size and shape), incidental anatomic variants
(e.g., transitional vertebrae), vertebral alignment, intervertebral disc space width,
size of the intervertebral foramina, and surrounding soft tissues. Abnormalities
evident on radiographs may include congenital vertebral malformations, spinal
malalignment (e.g., atlantoaxial instability, or secondary to trauma), acquired
bone lesions (e.g., discospondylitis, vertebral neoplasia, fractures) (Figure
112.1), intervertebral disc space narrowing with or without presence of mineral
material within the plane of the intervertebral foramen with IVDH, and
occasionally abnormalities of the paraspinal soft tissues.

MYELOGRAPHY
Myelography is a contrast examination technique of the spine that involves
placement of a spinal needle in the subarachnoid space, injection of contrast
medium, and post contrast radiographs (also see ch. 109 and Video 109.3
).10,11,14,21,22 It can be combined with CT for improved detail.23,24 Even though it
is not particularly technically challenging, this procedure should only be
performed in practices/hospitals prepared to follow diagnostic imaging with

appropriate further steps (e.g., surgery in case of identification of an extradural
compressive lesion such as IVDH).

INDICATIONS, CONTRAINDICATIONS, AND
ADVERSE EFFECTS10,11,22
Myelography is indicated when a reason for spinal pain or neurologic deficits is
not evident on survey radiographs of the spine, or when survey radiographs show
a lesion (e.g., vertebral subluxation) but further information is desired for
optimized treatment planning or prognostication (e.g., presence of spinal cord
swelling). The most important contraindication for myelography is an
inflammatory condition within the vertebral canal (meningitis), as the injection of
contrast medium can lead to further spread of infectious organisms throughout
the subarachnoid space and result in marked worsening in neurologic status. A
second contraindication is increased intracranial pressure, as myelography carries
the same risks as a CSF tap including brain herniation in these animals.
Myelography should not be performed in cases of known allergy to iodinated
contrast agents (which is rare in veterinary patients). The most common
complication following myelography is seizures during the recovery period
(reported incidence ranging from 0 to more than 20% using nonionic contrast
media), which are usually successfully managed medically.25 Worsening of the
clinical signs following myelography is common.22 Severe complications such as
intracranial hemorrhage, asystole, and death are rare.26

FIGURE 112.1 Discospondylitis in a 5-year-old Boxer. On
the lateral radiograph of the lumbosacral junction there is
narrowing of the L7-S1 intervertebral disc space with marked
irregular margination and sclerosis of the adjacent endplates,
and nominal new bone formation ventral to the intervertebral
disc space consistent with early spondylosis deformans.

TECHNIQUE AND INTERPRETATION10,11,22
The examination is performed under general anesthesia and after survey
radiographs of the area of interest have been obtained. The injection can be
performed following a cervical (cisterna magna) or lumbar (typically at the level
of lumbar vertebrae 5 and 6) puncture. Following clipping and aseptic
preparation of the injection site, a spinal needle (typically 22G, 1.5-3.5 inch [3-8
cm] length) is placed in the subarachnoid space. While CSF is typically observed
to flow from the needle hub with a cervical puncture, it may or may not with
lumbar puncture. Non-ionic iodinated contrast medium (180-350 mg I/mL) is
injected slowly. The contrast medium dosage ranges from <0.3-0.45 mL/kg
depending on the injection site and lesion location. A lumbar injection under
fluoroscopic monitoring facilitates reduction in contrast medium dose, as the
injection can be halted once a lesion is identified. Following injection, at least

orthogonal (lateral and ventrodorsal) and possibly oblique radiographs are
obtained.
A normal myelogram is characterized by even and homogeneous filling of the
subarachnoid space with contrast medium. Extradural lesions are recognized
by displacement and/or attenuation of at least one contrast column seen in at
least one projection (Figure 112.2, A and B). An intramedullary lesion
results in spinal cord enlargement and subsequently divergence and thinning of
the contrast columns visible on all radiographic projections. An intraduralextramedullary lesion appears as a filling defect within surrounding contrast
medium, with focal widening of the contrast column adjacent to the lesion (“golf
tee sign”). Additional abnormalities that may be evident on a myelogram include
extravasation of contrast medium from the subarachnoid space (e.g., secondary to
trauma), focal dilatation of a contrast column (e.g., due to subarachnoid
diverticula), and contrast staining of spinal cord parenchyma (seen with
myelomalacia). An acute myelopathy such as intervertebral disc extrusion is
usually associated with some degree of attenuation of the contrast columns, while
chronic disease processes (e.g., chronic IVDH or slow-growing tumors) will result
in displacement of the contrast columns without significant attenuation. Not all
spinal diseases will cause myelographic abnormalities. Normal studies are
common with some intramedullary lesions (e.g., FCE, myelitis, and small
tumors), noncompressive disorders of intervertebral discs (e.g., disc degeneration
and early discospondylitis), subtle vertebral lesions (e.g., nondisplaced fractures
or early bone tumors), meningeal disease (e.g., meningitis), and degenerative and
metabolic conditions (e.g., degenerative myelopathy). Myelography is accurate in
the diagnosis of common spinal diseases including IVDH and spinal neoplasia.2729

(“Wobbler’s”) in an approximately 2-year-old Great Dane. (A
and B,) Cervical myelogram. Contrast medium has been

COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY (CT)30,31
CT is an imaging technique in which an x-ray tube rotates around the patient and
creates cross-sectional images. The appearance of different tissues on CT images
is based on their respective x-ray attenuation, similar to conventional
radiography. Even though MRI is considered the diagnostic modality of choice for
cross-sectional imaging of the brain and spine, CT has several important
advantages. It is fast, especially with new or helical/multi-slice scanners. It allows

acquisition of thin (submillimeter) slices without interslice gaps. It is superior to
MRI in the evaluation of bony detail and mineralized lesions, has excellent
capabilities in the diagnosis of intracranial and spinal hemorrhage, and has fair
soft tissue contrast which is improved further with intravenous contrast medium
administration. It allows for multiplanar (sagittal, dorsal and oblique) and 3D
reconstruction of images which may be helpful for improved anatomic
understanding and surgical planning. It may be given preference if the patient is
unable to undergo prolonged anesthesia or if metallic material is present in the
area of interest. Finally, CT may aid in image-guided sampling of lesions observed
on imaging (e.g., bone tumors), can provide baseline images for 3D printing of
surgical templates, and can be used for radiation therapy planning.

INDICATIONS AND CONTRAINDICATIONS
Indications for a CT examination of the brain and spine overlap with indications
for other imaging modalities and include pain and any neurologic abnormalities.
It may be given preference over MRI in cases of patients unable to undergo
anesthesia, metallic material in the area of interest, acute trauma, and for
evaluation of known or suspected bone lesions, suspected mineralized IVDH, or
suspected contrast-enhancing mass lesions.9,14,21,32,33 There are no true
contraindications; however, most brain and some spine CT examinations require
intravenous administration of iodinated contrast medium, which should be
avoided in dehydrated animals and exercised with caution in patients with
multiorgan dysfunction.

GENERAL CT TECHNIQUE AND
INTERPRETATION PRINCIPLES30,31
The examination can typically be performed under sedation although general
anesthesia should be considered for lengthy studies, or if CT-guided tissue
sampling is planned following the diagnostic scan. Following acquisition of a
scout image (“topogram”), the region of interest is determined. Especially with
modern multi-slice scanners, transverse images are obtained with a thin slice
thickness (submillimeter) and subsequently reconstructed into thicker slices (2-3
mm). Images are reconstructed in a sharp (edge-enhancing) and a soft algorithm
for adequate depiction of both osseous and soft-tissue structures. Following
completion of the precontrast scan, the image acquisition may be repeated after
intravenous administration of iodinated contrast medium at a dosage of 800 mg
iodine/kg (usually done for brain studies, occasionally for spine studies). With CT,
tissues have a specific density/attenuation value that correlates with x-ray beam
attenuation within that tissue and is expressed in Hounsfield units (HU). Cortical
bone has an approximate density of 1000 HU, average soft tissue of 30-60 HU,
pure fluid of 0 HU, fat of –70 to –100 HU, and air/gas of –1000 HU. Image
evaluation is performed with different window settings to maximize the contrast

between different tissues. This is accomplished by adjusting the window center
(WC) and window width (WW). A bone window (e.g., WC 600 HU, WW 2400)
provides excellent contrast of osseous structures, while a soft-tissue window (e.g.,
WC 50 HU, WW 350 HU) maximizes density differences between adjacent soft
tissues. Visualization of subtle brain lesions can be further improved by the use of
a modified soft-tissue window with an even lower WC (e.g., 30 HU) and narrower
WW (e.g., 200 HU).

CT OF THE BRAIN9,31,34
The patient is typically positioned in sternal recumbency. The scan field of view
should at least extend from the level of the cribriform plate to the foramen
magnum. If concurrent evaluation of the nasal cavity and regional lymph nodes is
desired, the scan field of view should extend from the nares to the approximate
level of the third cervical vertebra.
The normal brain is fairly symmetric. It is encased by the osseous skull (average
density of cortical bone, 1000 HU). The central white matter tracts are
hypoattenuating (25-35 HU) to surrounding gray matter (35-50 HU). CSF is fluidattenuating (0-5 HU). Most intracranial lesions are hypoattenuating to normal
brain parenchyma on precontrast images; however, notably, hemorrhage in the
acute and subacute stages is hyperattenuating (40-100 HU) and thus easily
depicted on CT. Mineralization (such as can be present in some meningiomas) is
also hyperattenuating. Following contrast medium administration, the pituitary
gland, choroid plexus, trigeminal nerves and to some degree meninges have
physiologic enhancement. The most common brain tumors in dogs and cats are
extra-axial, located outside the blood-brain barrier, and contrast-enhancing. The
sensitivity of contrast-enhanced CT for the identification of canine brain tumors is
therefore quite high (92%).35 Intra-axial lesions may or may not be contrastenhancing, and the ability of CT to detect intra-axial nonenhancing lesions (e.g.,
infarcts, some cases of brain tumors such as glioma, or encephalitis) is limited.36

CT OF THE SPINE12,31
The patient is typically positioned in dorsal recumbency to minimize artifacts
from respiratory motion. The scan field of view is determined by clinical
neurolocalization (ch. 241).
The spine and paraspinal tissues are fairly symmetric on transverse images. The
density of the vertebral cortical bone is approximately 1000 HU. The soft-tissue–
attenuating spinal cord (approximately 40-60 HU) is located within the center of
the vertebral canal. A differentiation of gray and white matter is typically not
possible. A variable amount of epidural fat hypoattenuating to soft tissue
(approximately –100 HU) surrounds the spinal cord. CT evaluation of the spine
includes assessment of the osseous vertebrae, vertebral canal (diameter,
alignment and contents), size and symmetry of the intervertebral foramina, the

spinal cord, spinal nerves, epidural fat, appearance of the intervertebral discs, and
the paraspinal soft tissues (swelling, atrophy, asymmetry, or evidence of
alterations in density). The subarachnoid space is best evaluated on a CT
myelogram, where it appears as a hyperattenuating rim surrounding the spinal
cord (Figure 112.2, C and D). Following contrast medium administration,
physiologic enhancement is observed within the spinal and paraspinal
vasculature.
Overall, non-contrast CT has proven useful in the diagnostic work-up in dogs
with (acute) thoracolumbar myelopathies, with only 7.6% of patients requiring
additional imaging tests (MRI or myelography) following CT.37 Intervertebral disc
disease is the most common spinal disease in dogs and is accurately diagnosed
with CT (81.8-100%).28,29,38 Mineralized IVDH with or without associated
hemorrhage appears as hyperattenuating material within the vertebral canal and
is easily visualized. This material may result in a variable degree of spinal cord
compression. Concurrent attenuation of epidural fat is common in acute cases. A
diagnosis of non-mineralized disc herniation is more challenging and may be
aided by intravenous contrast medium administration or performance of a CT
myelogram.24,39 Other spinal diseases commonly diagnosed on CT include
congenital anomalies/malformations, inflammatory conditions such as
discospondylitis, trauma, vertebral neoplasia, and degenerative diseases such as
caudal cervical spondylomyelopathy and degenerative lumbosacral
stenosis.15,18,32,40-43 While the identification of contrast enhancing lesions within
the vertebral canal (e.g., epidural empyema or extradural neoplasia) is usually
possible, exact localization of a lesion as extradural, intramedullary or intraduralextramedullary is challenging and may require adjunct myelography or MRI.27 As
described for the brain, noncontrast enhancing lesions (e.g., extradural lesions
such as hydrated nucleus pulposus extrusion [HNPE] or intramedullary lesions
such as a glioma or myelitis), and degenerative or metabolic conditions (e.g.,
degenerative myelopathy) are usually not evident on CT and require MRI or other
tests for diagnosis.8,31,37

MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI)
With few exceptions listed above and in Table 112.1, MRI is considered the gold
standard for imaging of the CNS in small animals. The concept of image
generation with MRI is complicated. Generating an MR signal involves
manipulation of hydrogen protons within a patient. Tissue with an abnormal
content or distribution of hydrogen protons exhibits different signal
characteristics from adjacent normal tissue and can be identified on MRI.8,44,45
MRI is supremely sensitive in the identification and classification of soft-tissue
abnormalities.

INDICATIONS AND CONTRAINDICATIONS
The indications for MRI overlap with indications for other imaging tests for the
brain or spine. Contraindications are few, but there are risks associated with MRI
technology a user should be aware of.46 Ferromagnetic material (e.g., scissors,
non-MRI–compatible anesthesia equipment) must never be brought into the scan
room because it would become a projectile that could injure the patient in the
gantry. While metallic material within the patient’s musculoskeletal system (e.g.,
identification microchips or metallic implants) does not typically pose a risk as it
is surrounded and stabilized by fibrosis,47 ferromagnetic material located within
an internal organ (e.g., brain) may be displaced, with potentially fatal
consequences for the patient. Examples in people include ferromagnetic
aneurysm clips (now obsolete), or shrapnel within the cranial vault. Even though
there are no reported severe adverse effects reported in animals, caution should
always be exercised in animals with known metallic material within the body and
with certain implants such as pacemakers. Other possible risks include burns
from tattoos or external material in contact with the patient, and the high noise
level within the scan room. Gadolinium-based contrast agents used in MRI are
considered safe, with only isolated reports of adverse reactions in animals.48

Boston Terrier with a history of Cushing’s disease and recent

GENERAL MRI TECHNIQUE AND
INTERPRETATION PRINCIPLES
There are multiple possible MRI techniques and sequences that provide
complementary information.8,44 Briefly, on T2-weighted (T2-W) images, fluid
and tissues with an increased amount of mobile hydrogen protons will appear
bright (hyperintense), and on T1-W images these tissues will be dark
(hypointense). Fat and contrast enhancement within a normal structure or lesion
will be hyperintense on T1-W images. Proton density (PD) weighting provides
excellent anatomic detail and may have improved imaging capability of cortical
bone than other MRI sequences. With fluid attenuation inversion recovery

(FLAIR) sequences, pure fluid is suppressed, allowing differentiation of cystic
lesions from solid masses and structures containing proteinaceous fluid. This
sequence also increases conspicuity of small T2 hyperintense lesions bordering
the subarachnoid space or ventricular system. A short tau inversion recovery
(STIR) sequence is used to suppress fat, which can aid in the detection of softtissue lesions and allows differentiation of hyperintense bone marrow fat from
pathologic processes. An MR myelogram highlights the subarachnoid space and
allows the same diagnostic approach as a conventional radiographic myelogram
without the need for invasive contrast medium injection.49,50 A T2∗-W gradient
recalled echo sequence has high sensitivity to regional magnetic field
inhomogeneities and will show signal voids in areas of CNS hemorrhage.51
Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) allows identification of areas of restricted
diffusion, which can aid in the identification of ischemic brain or spinal cord
lesions.52 There are multiple additional MRI sequences and techniques which are
described in detail elsewhere.

MRI OF THE BRAIN8,31,44,53,54
The patient may be positioned in dorsal or sternal recumbency. Sequences
commonly used for brain MRI in small animal patients include sagittal T2-W
images, transverse T2-W, T1-W, FLAIR and T2∗-W images, DWI, and
postcontrast T1-W images in at least one plane.
The normal brain is symmetric, and the signal intensity of CSF, gray and white
matter varies with the MRI sequence as well as patient age. Unlike with CT, MRI
allows visualization of not only the ventricular system but also the normal
subarachnoid space. Most (not all) neoplastic, inflammatory,
metabolic/toxic/nutritional and ischemic encephalopathies are T2 hyperintense,
T1 hypointense, and do not fully suppress on FLAIR (Figure 112.3, A-C).
Hemorrhagic lesions have variable imaging characteristics on standard sequences
but are expected to display signal voids on T2∗-W images (susceptibility
artifacts) (Figure 112.3, D). As with CT, lesions not protected by the blood brain
barrier are typically contrast-enhancing (Figure 112.3, E and F). Unlike with
CT, even though intra-axial inflammatory, metabolic or neoplastic lesions may be
non-contrast–enhancing, they can usually be identified on pre-contrast
sequences.

MRI OF THE SPINE8,31,55
The patient is preferentially positioned in dorsal recumbency. Sequences
commonly used for spine MRI in small animal patients include sagittal and
transverse T1 and T2-W images, sagittal STIR, and sagittal MR myelogram. T2∗W and postcontrast sequences may also be acquired.

FIGURE 112.4 Complex craniocervical junction abnormality
in a 5-year-old Yorkshire Terrier. Transverse (A), sagittal (B)
and dorsal (C) multiplanar reconstructed, and 3-D volume
rendered (D) computed tomography images show a short,
abnormally shaped, and incompletely ossified atlas that is
partially fused to the occipital bone and skull base. There is
aplasia of the dens axis, atlantoaxial subluxation,
mineralization of the apical ligament of the dens, and a C2-C3
block vertebra.Additional findings on the sagittal T2-weighted
magnetic resonance image (E) include a dorsal atlantoaxial
fibrous band that results in moderate spinal cord compression
(arrow), and a focal intramedullary T2 hyperintensity at this
level, likely representing focal spinal cord edema or gliosis.
The signal intensity of the spinal cord, subarachnoid space, epidural fat,
vertebrae, and paraspinal soft tissues varies with the MRI sequence. Even subtle
abnormalities such as a decrease in the normally strong T2 hyperintensity of the
nucleus pulposus with early disc degeneration are easily depicted. Herniated
degenerate disc material is hypointense to spinal cord and may result in a variable
degree of spinal cord compression.14,21 In addition to the identification and
localization of IVDH, MRI has some prognostic value, as the presence and length
of a concurrent intramedullary lesion (representing edema, concussion,
hemorrhage, or myelomalacia), and the length of CSF attenuation on MR
myelogram correlate with outcome.56,57 HNPE will result in fluid-intense

material within the vertebral canal, causing spinal cord compression.58 Acute
myelopathies not resulting in spinal cord compression (ANNPE and FCE) are
characterized by a focal intramedullary hyperintensity with or without
noncompressive changes of a nearby intervertebral disc.59 Due to the improved
soft-tissue imaging capabilities of MRI, inflammatory conditions such as
discospondylitis and abnormalities of the paraspinal soft tissues are detected
earlier than with other imaging modalities.15,20 Spinal neoplasia may result in
variable abnormalities.31 Sarcomas and carcinomas tend to result in cortical
destruction, have variable signal intensity changes to the affected vertebrae, and
typically have a rather large associated soft-tissue mass. Round cell tumors
(lymphoma and plasma cell tumor/multiple myeloma) may have cortical sparing
and are best identified on fat-suppressed sequences.16 Intradural-extramedullary
tumors are best identified and classified using MR myelography.50
Intramedullary neoplasia and inflammatory conditions of the spinal cord
(myelitis) typically result in intramedullary hyperintensity with variable contrast
enhancement.60 Despite the excellent diagnostic capabilities of MRI, spinal
studies may be normal with some disease conditions (e.g., degenerative
myelopathy, meningomyelitis), and the ability to distinguish different types of
intramedullary lesions based on their MR characteristics is poor.2

CONCLUSION
All imaging modalities discussed in this chapter play a role in the evaluation of the
small animal neurologic patient. Even though MRI is generally considered the
gold standard, CT is highly valuable as it is fast and highly accurate in the
diagnosis of bony abnormalities, hemorrhage, and mineralized abnormalities
including intervertebral disc extrusion. In fact, CT and MRI are complementary
and commonly used jointly to evaluate patients with complex spinal anomalies
involving both bony and soft tissue structures (Figure 112.4).

INTRODUCTION

Minimally invasive surgical procedures are playing an important and
growing role in veterinary medicine. As these therapies have
developed over the years in human surgery, the benefits in terms of
reduced morbidity, mortality, analgesia, time to recovery,
hospitalization times, and even cost in some circumstances are
beyond dispute. In addition, these therapies have provided the
means to treat underlying conditions not amenable to more
traditional approaches. These same arguments can be made in favor
of the use of these procedures in veterinary patients; however, the
science has not yet caught up to the practice in our profession. The
background on specific diseases is covered elsewhere within the
textbook.

INTERVENTIONAL
RADIOLOGY/INTERVENTIONAL
ENDOSCOPY
Following the description of percutaneous arterial catheterization by
Sven Ivar Seldinger in 1953, angiography developed into a widelyutilized and essential medical diagnostic tool.1 Technological
advances in imaging and medical devices have since helped
transform this once diagnostic modality into a sub-specialization
with enormous therapeutic potential. Interventional radiology (IR)
involves the use of contemporary imaging techniques such as
fluoroscopy and ultrasonography to selectively access vessels and
other structures in order to deliver different materials for therapeutic
reasons. Interventional endoscopy (IE) utilizes the recent advances
in endoscopy to perform image-guided therapy alone or in
conjunction with fluoroscopy. Endourology (ch. 117) and
interventional gastroenterology (ch. 116) are some of the more
common combined uses in which the operator(s) uses endoscopy to
access an orifice such as the ureterovesical junction within the
urinary bladder or the major duodenal papilla to subsequently use IR
techniques under fluoroscopic guidance to access the upper urinary
tract or biliary tract, respectively. Both IR and IE techniques provide
therapeutic options for diseases once deemed untreatable—often
now the standard of care for a variety of human conditions.

ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES
The use of IR and IE techniques in veterinary patients has the
potential to provide a number of advantages compared to more
traditional therapies. These procedures are minimally invasive and
can therefore theoretically lead to reduced perioperative morbidity
and mortality, shorter anesthesia times, and shorter hospital stays.
Examples of such procedures with reported advantages over
traditional open surgical procedures might include treatment for
feline ureteral obstructions or canine intrahepatic shunts.2-6 Some
less equipment-intensive procedures can result in reduced costs as
well. While the equipment necessary to perform these techniques can
often be expensive in terms of disposables and initial capital
investment, the high (and rising) costs of hospitalization in tertiary
referral and specialty hospitals can be dramatically reduced with
these often outpatient or single night stay procedures. The more
traditional “invasive” surgical therapies may be less expensive to
perform; however, the prolonged intensive care unit (ICU) stays,
postoperative care, transfusions, etc. can often add up to even higher
veterinary bills. The majority of the IR/IE procedures performed at
the author’s institution are similar in cost to the comparative surgical
therapy. The exceptions would be a variety of laparoscopic-assisted
procedures (ovariohysterectomy, bladder stone removal, gastropexy,
gastrointestinal biopsies). Perhaps the greatest advantage of these
procedures is the ability to treat conditions for which more
traditional therapies are contraindicated, associated with excessive
morbidity, or unavailable to veterinary patients. Examples include
sclerotherapy for renal hematuria7 or vascular anomalies,8
embolization or chemoembolization of nonresectable tumors,9
stenting for malignant obstructions,10 etc.
The primary disadvantages of IR/IE include the required technical
expertise, which is not currently available at many veterinary
advanced training institutions; the specialized equipment that is
needed (wide range of endoscopes, fluoroscopy with or without
digital subtraction capabilities); and the initial capital investment
necessary to provide a suitable inventory of catheters, guide wires,
balloons, stents and coils. Training labs and courses available at the

major specialty college symposia as well as privately-run training
labs are now commonplace.

EQUIPMENT
OPERATING ROOMS/ANGIOGRAPHY SUITES
As most of these procedures are minimally invasive (performed
through natural orifices or small holes in the skin), traditional sterile
operating rooms (ORs) are not required, but are recommended.
During the learning process, and even for experienced
interventionalists, conversion to an open surgical approach may be
necessary. Performing these procedures within a sterile environment
so open surgical conversions can be performed quickly and
efficiently facilitates this. Additionally, hybrid approaches are often

used in which small surgical approaches are performed to facilitate
access for interventional therapies. In both circumstances, the pet
owners should consent to open procedures prior to the procedure
and the patient should be clipped and prepared for full surgical
access if necessary. More standard, predictable endoscopy and
interventional procedures can be performed in endoscopy or clean
angiography suites, respectively.
Additional equipment needs require larger OR environments.
Aside from common needs such as anesthesia machines, OR tables,
and surgical equipment, the ideal room should provide ample space
for a “crash cart” with emergency drugs and a cardiac defibrillator
(ch. 131), equipment cabinets, lasers, vessel sealing devices,
lithotripters, and movement of the C-arm fluoroscope away from the
table for additional surgical space. A control room station in the OR
is recommended for fully integrated ORs; currently, these are rare in
veterinary medicine but are growing in number due to the flexibility
they offer to perform multiple different therapeutic modalities within
the same space.
For many of the more commonly performed IR procedures, a
traditional fluoroscopy unit is sufficient. Operators wear full lead (or
similar) gowns, thyroid shields, caps, gowns, and masks. The more
common fluoroscopy units currently available in veterinary hospitals
are often “multi-purpose units,” a combination digital radiography
and fluoroscopy unit built into one system. While these are suitable
for general fluoroscopy needs, the relative immobility of these units
to rotate, the non-sterile environments in which they are standardly
installed, and the inability to permit surgeons standing on both sides
of the patient concurrently make them poor choices for many of the
currently performed IR/IE procedures except the more standard
cardiac interventions, or tracheal or urethral stenting.
Alternatively, mobile C-arm units may already be available in the
OR in many larger referral veterinary hospital settings. Often these
units are suitable for the more basic, non-vascular IR procedures and
most endourological procedures. A C-arm fluoroscopy unit has the
advantage of mobility of the image intensifier (II) (or more recently,
the digital flat panel detector [FPD]), permitting multiple tangential
views without moving the patient. In addition, many of these units
may be able to receive software upgrades such as cardiovascular
packages in order to improve performance according to the desired

technique. Compared to the more expensive, larger, fixed (ceiling or
floor-mounted) units which provide superior image resolution, the
mobile C-arms are easily moved from room to room, have fewer
radiation regulations (leaded walls not necessary but this may vary
according to regional legislation), and can be purchased, leased, or
even rented at a fraction of the cost. Recently, combination digital
radiography-fluoroscopy-coned beam computed tomography (CT)
units like the Epica Vimagoa have become available as a lower-cost
option for veterinarians to provide some of these services.
Often overlooked during purchasing of this equipment is the OR
table. While some standard OR tables are sufficiently thin to permit
fluoroscopy when the patients are small and placed at the end of the
table, specially designated “fluoroscopy surgery tables” are available
in a variety of designs. These more expensive fluoroscopy tables are
often equipped with a “floating” tabletop configuration to facilitate
patient positioning without moving the bulkier C-arm.
As these procedures are often performed by surgeons or internists
without recent training in radiation safety, it is important to refresh
one’s knowledge on the rather substantial radiation exposure that
can occur during some of the more prolonged interventional
procedures. The operator is encouraged to review radiation safety
guidelines and reduce exposure as much as possible, minimize
exposure time and beam size, and maximize shielding and distance
from the beam. Non-essential people should not be in the suite
during fluoroscopy, particularly when fluoroscopic “runs” are
performed (series of recorded images, as opposed to single still
frames) as the radiation exposure levels are often increased.
Radiation dosimetry badges should be worn and regularly evaluated
to monitor for increased exposure. A recent survey of radiation safety
practices at veterinary hospitals revealed U.S. federal veterinary
guidelines are often not met.11
Standard fluoroscopy, available on most veterinary multi-purpose
and mobile C-arm units, is acceptable for the more common
respiratory, urinary, and gastrointestinal procedures. While many
might be familiar with the older “II” models, the recent introduction
of FLDs provides equivalent or even better images at lower dose
exposure to the operator, more working room, and reliability as
repair and replacement parts for II machines are becoming

increasingly difficult to find as these machines are largely being
phased out in the human market. Digital subtraction angiography
(DSA) is highly recommended (and some might say required) for
vascular procedures, particularly when performed in small caliber
vessels with overlying bony and/or gas-filled structures that might
otherwise interfere with image resolution. DSA is a computer
software–processing program that takes an initial non-contrast
fluoroscopic image (the “mask”) and subtracts it from subsequent
images during a “run.” This permits improved vascular imaging and
resolution without overlying structures obscuring the view, allows
the operator to access smaller structures more reliably, and requires
much less contrast than would be necessary otherwise (Figure
113.1). DSA is required for super-selective angiograms of small
caliber vessels and vessels in the head or where there is substantial
bone, which makes angiogram visualization difficult. This is
particularly important when delivering toxic (chemotherapy) or
embolic substances that could reflux into, or enter, non-target
vessels leading to vital structures. “Road-mapping” capabilities on
some systems permit saving these contrast studies and placing them
over real-time fluoroscopy images to provide a “vascular map” for
guide wire, catheter, embolic, or stent manipulations.

ENDOSCOPY
The most common endoscopes used during IE procedures are rigid
rod-lens cystoscopes and flexible fiberoptic ureteroscopes. Rigid
cystoscopy using telescope diameters ranging from 1.9 to 6.5 mm is
commonly performed in female animals to aid in urethral, urinary
bladder, and ureteral access (ch. 100). Similar scopes are used for
antegrade rhinoscopy (chs. 89 and 213). The scope sheath provides
a smooth, rounded edge to protect the mucosa and the telescope, as
well as providing three separate ports. These are used for fluid
irrigation, fluid drainage and a working channel for passage of a wide
variety of interventional devices (biopsy forceps, needles, baskets,
laser fibers, guide wires, stents, etc.). The 30° angle of view is the
most commonly used cystoscope/rhinoscope, allowing excellent
visualization of the nasal cavity and bladder wall, as well as the
ureteral orifices. Flexible fiberoptic ureteroscopes (2.5-2.8 mm

diameter with a 1 mm working channel) are used for lower urinary
tract access in male dogs and for ureteral access in dogs >18 kg.
These scopes tend to have considerably diminished image resolution
(compared to the rod-lens technology of rigid scopes), smaller
working channels limiting devices and irrigation, and weaker
illumination. More recent availability of flexible video ureteroscopes
like the Karl Storz Flex XCb have solved some of the limitations of
the older fiberoptic scopes, providing image resolution and
illumination more similar to traditional rigid rod-lens scopes while
still enabling 270° deflection in two directions.

ANCILLARY IMAGING EQUIPMENT
Aside from the endoscopes, a “tower” will be a necessary capital
investment. This is a multi-tiered cart composed of the camera
control box, light source, monitor, and often, data recording devices.
Light sources are typically halogen or xenon, with the latter being
preferred due to closest similarity to natural light. If possible,
multiple monitors (or at least a single monitor on an articulating
arm/platform) are recommended to facilitate observation from
multiple locations around the surgical table as patients vary in size,
positioning, and entry site among the wide variety of procedures
currently performed. Designing the interventional suite with as
much flexibility as possible will maximize the usefulness of the room.
It is much easier to move the monitor than to relocate the oftencumbersome endoscopy towers. Data recording devices have become
routine components, allowing storage of images and videos of the
procedures. It is recommended that these be saved as part of the
patient record, facilitating review at a later date if/when procedures
need to be repeated. Endoscopes are typically gas- (or sometimes
cold-) sterilized; sterilization is necessary prior to any endourological
procedure. Occasionally, ultrasonography is useful for percutaneous
needle access into vessels or other structures such as the renal
pelvis12 or percutaneous urethral access.13

INTERVENTIONAL
RADIOLOGY/INTERVENTIONAL
ENDOSCOPY INSTRUMENTATION
Access
Prior to any interventional procedure, luminal access is necessary.
This is the first and perhaps one of the most important parts of any
interventional procedure, as the chosen access location can make a
difficult procedure easy, or an easy procedure difficult. Venous
access is often performed percutaneously, while vascular cut-down
for access to the femoral artery (or branches) or carotid artery is
performed to permit arterial ligation at procedural completion.
Ligation of the femoral and carotid arteries is safely tolerated in dogs
and prevents post-operative hemorrhage that can be significant in
animals often discharged the same day. In dogs, the deep gluteal
artery is a branch of the internal iliac artery that allows for collateral
perfusion when the femoral artery (or external iliac) is
ligated/obstructed. Although reported otherwise,14 ligation of both
carotid arteries in dogs may not be universally tolerated. Some cats
have safely tolerated ligation of both carotid arteries. Standard
intravenous catheters or entry needles can be used for vascular
access. “Gauge” is defined as the number of needles or catheters that
can be placed next to one another to sum up to 1 inch (2.5 cm);
therefore, needles of a higher gauge have smaller lumens. For
instance, a 22-gauge needle has a smaller lumen than an 18-gauge
needle. Once more experienced in these procedures, the operator will
soon memorize which catheters accommodate suitable guide wire
diameters. A “single-wall puncture” or “modified Seldinger”
technique is preferred for vascular access to avoid double wall vessel
perforation, particularly in patients with bleeding disorders in whom
additional vascular punctures could increase the risk of hematoma
formation.

Guide Wires
Once vascular access is achieved, or a targeted orifice (e.g., the
ureterovesical junction [UVJ]) is identified, guide wire access is

obtained. Standard spring guide wires (polytetrafluoroethylene
[PTFE/Teflon], stainless steel, nitinol, etc.) are available in a wide
range of diameters, lengths, stiffness, tip configurations, and surface
coatings (Figure 113.2). In general, the guide wires currently used
in veterinary patients range from 0.014″ to 0.038″ (0.35 to 1 mm) in
diameter and lengths from 50 cm to 300 cm. For larger vessels or
lumens, access is typically obtained with an 18-gauge catheter
followed by 0.035″ or 0.038″ (0.9 or 1 mm) guide wire placement. In
smaller vessels or lumens, access may be obtained more easily and
safely with a 22-gauge catheter followed by a 0.018″ (0.5 mm) guide
wire. Urethral and ureteral luminal access is often achieved using
similar angled hydrophilic guide wiresc in the 0.018″ to 0.035″ (0.5
to 0.9 mm) diameter range, depending upon patient size.

Introducer Sheath Sets
Introducer setsd are composed of the sheath (basically a catheter),
the associated dilator that is placed within the sheath, a hemostasis
valve, and a side port (Figure 113.3). They are used for almost all
vascular procedures (ch. 115), particularly those in which multiple

devices may be exchanged. They permit safe, controlled dilation of
the entry vessel and subsequent protection from vascular damage or
hemorrhage during the procedure. The side ports permit
simultaneous flushing, sampling, or contrast angiography if
necessary. The check flow diaphragm of the hemostatic valve
prevents back-bleeding through the sheath while permitting
placement of various sized catheters, balloons, stent delivery
systems, or other devices that could otherwise result in trauma to the
vessel or surrounding tissues. Sheaths are unique in that they are
named for their inner diameters (IDs) compared to all other devices
that are named for their outer diameters (ODs). This helps the
operator choose what size sheath will be necessary for placement of a
certain size stent delivery system, for instance. The typical sizes used
range from 4-12 French (Fr). Three Fr is equal to 1 mm; therefore, a
6 Fr sheath has a 6 Fr (2 mm) inner diameter and its outer diameter
will be larger depending upon the thickness of the wall of the sheath.
The author commonly uses introducer sheaths for endourological
procedures as well, placing them in the urethra, up the ureter, and
even percutaneously into the kidney, or into the urethra during
perineal access (ch. 117).

FIGURE 113.4 Selective catheters. A, Marker

Selective Catheters
Selective catheters are used in combination with compatible guide
wires to select different structures in order to perform contrast
studies, obtain samples, or deliver materials (Figure 113.4). Preshaped angiography catheters are routinely 4 or 5 Fr and they taper
to accommodate 0.035″ or 0.038″ (0.9 or 1 mm) guide wires. Most
catheters are end-hole only (to prevent embolic delivery anywhere
besides the tip of the catheter) but some have multiple side-holes;
this is useful for power injection of contrast in high-flow vessels such
as for cardiac angiography (pigtail catheters for instance; ch. 115).
The most commonly used catheter shapes include the hockey stick
tip (Berenstein)e and C-shaped or Cobraf tip. For access into vessels
originating at very acute angles, reverse-curve catheters can be used
in which the tips are angled backwards. Microcathetersg,h (typically
3 Fr or less) are used in combination with microwiresi,j (typically
0.014″-0.018″ [0.35-0.5 mm]) and passed coaxially through the preshaped catheter in order to access second- or third-generation
vessels without causing vessel occlusion or spasm.

Balloons

Occlusion balloons (low pressure, high compliance) are used for
temporary occlusion of a vessel to facilitate angiography or redirect
embolization materials away from a non-target organ. These
balloons can also be used as flow-directed catheters to allow blood
flow to direct the catheter towards sites that are difficult to access,
particularly in cardiovascular interventions (ch. 115). Balloon
angioplasty cathetersk (high pressure, low compliance) are typically
advanced into position and then filled with dilute contrast agent
under pressure in order to dilate and efface strictures or stenoses of
the blood vessels or other lumens such as the esophagus (ch. 116),
rectum (ch. 116), nasopharynx (ch. 114), trachea (ch. 114), or
urethra (ch. 117).

Drainage Catheters
Drainage catheters provide surgical or percutaneous removal of fluid
collections (e.g., pleural fluid, peritonitis, abscess, etc.) or
diversionary procedures (e.g., nephrostomy, cholecystotomy, gastric,
etc.). Both locking- and non–locking-loop conformations are
available and can be placed using a modified Seldinger technique
(over the guide wire) or a trocar technique (direct puncture). The
locking-loop cathetersl are typically preferred due to the suture
locking mechanism that secures the catheter loop, minimizing
premature catheter withdrawal (Figure 113.5). More recently, a
subcutaneous ureteral bypass (SUB)m device has been described,
composed of a locking-loop nephrostomy catheter and cystostomy
catheter connected subcutaneously or intra-abdominally to divert
urine around ureteral obstructions (Figure 113.6) (ch. 117).4,15

Stents
Stents are tubular structures designed to re-establish patency of a
lumen that has become obstructed. They are available in a variety of
materials, shapes, sizes, and designs that define their suitability for a
particular structure or environment.
Stents can be most easily categorized by some of their properties,
including material (metallic versus non-metallic) and design (selfexpanding versus balloon-expandable and/or covered versus

uncovered) (Figure 113.7). An individual stent is typically named
for its diameter and length. Metallic (or similar) stents are typically
supplied pre-mounted within a delivery system (self-expanding
stents) or on a balloon catheter (balloon-expandable stents). Delivery
systems are named for their outer diameters and can sometimes
limit the ability to place the associated stent in our smaller veterinary
patients.
Self-expanding metallic stents (SEMS) are the most commonly
used stents in veterinary medicine and their use has been described
clinically (or experimentally) in the respiratory (ch. 114),
cardiovascular (ch. 115), gastrointestinal (ch. 116), hepatobiliary
(ch. 116), and urinary (ch. 117) tracts of animals. Mesh SEMS,
composed of an interwoven strand (or strands) of fine wire, are most
commonly used for tracheal stenting but can be used elsewhere in
the body (Fig. 113.7, A,B). In general (but not uniformly), mesh
SEMSn are reconstrainable, meaning at some defined point before
complete deployment, the stent can be recaptured within the delivery
system and repositioned or removed. This functionality is
particularly useful when imprecise positioning would be
unacceptable. Unfortunately, these same stents typically undergo a
variable degree of foreshortening during deployment: as the stent
expands during release from the delivery system, it will concurrently
shorten as it assumes its ultimate diameter and length. The amount
of this shortening will depend upon the degree to which the stent
ultimately expands within the lumen and can often be difficult to
predict exactly, particularly by more novice operators.
Reconstrainability and foreshortening must be understood and
anticipated when mesh SEMS are being used. Woven or braided
SEMS are also made from metallic wire but often of much thinner
gauge to create a softer, almost fabric-like stent, and currently are
not widely used in veterinary medicine; however, they have been
used in the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts of veterinary
patients. Laser-cut SEMSo,p are produced from a narrow tube of
metal in which a laser cuts the stent design that is later expanded to
create the ultimate stent dimensions (Figure 113.7, C). Following a
finishing and coating process, the stent is cooled and crimped onto a
low-profile delivery system to permit placement through small entry
sites. Upon reaching body temperature, the crimped nitinol (or

similar shape-memory metal) stent changes properties and resumes
its original stent diameter and length. These characteristics have
revolutionized stent design and the laser-cut stents are one of the
most commonly used SEMS in IR. These stents are rarely
reconstrainable and have minimal foreshortening; this permits
precise placement across focal lesions, although once deployment
from the delivery system begins, the process cannot be reversed. In
veterinary medicine, laser-cut SEMS are most commonly used in the
urethra16 or vasculature.10,17,18 Grafts, or stent grafts, refer to stents
with coatings or coverings (covered stents) such as silicone and
various types of PTFE/Teflon materials placed inside, outside, or
surrounding the underlying metal structures (Fig. 113.7, D, E).
While these stents can be useful to prevent ingrowth of strictures or
tumors through the stent interstices, disadvantages such as
increased cost, larger delivery systems, high migration rates, and risk
of occluding adjacent lumens—particularly in the vascular systems—
generally limit their routine use.

Polyester covered mesh stent graft (Wallgraft,
Boston Scientific Corporation). F, BEMS compressed
onto percutaneous transluminal angioplasty balloon
before dilation. G, Expanded BEMS subsequent to
balloon dilation. From Weisse C, Mayhew P. Basics
of minimally invasive surgery. In: Tobias KM,
Johnston SA, eds. Veterinary Surgery: Small
Animal . Elsevier; 2012.
Balloon-expandable metallic stents (BEMS)q are pre-mounted
(compressed) onto a balloon catheter, positioned across the lesion,
and as the balloon is inflated, the stent expands (Fig. 113.7, F, G).
The balloon is then deflated and removed and the stent remains in
place. BEMS are ideal for precise placement of short, rigid stents in
areas that are not likely to be compressed externally. Disadvantages
include the relatively short lengths available, poor flexibility, and
static response to compression (i.e., if compressed the stent will
remain compressed and not expand). BEMS were routinely used for
nasopharyngeal stenoses (short strictures often surrounded mostly
by bone) but have now largely been replaced by SEMS.19

Non-metallic stents (Figure 113.8) are primarily constructed of
different polyurethane compounds for use in the urinary tract (e.g.,
ureteral stent), bioabsorbable compounds (e.g., polydioxanone, etc.),
or self-expanding plastic stentsr (SEPS) most commonly for
esophageal use).20 Ureteral stentss are available in a variety of sizes,
lengths, configurations, and durometers (a measure of the material
stiffness). These stents are placed over a guide wire and positioned
with the use of a “pusher” catheter that advances over the guide wire
behind the stent. Ureteral stents can be placed surgically,
endoscopically, or percutaneously, and either temporarily (e.g.,
following shockwave lithotripsy of a nephrolith, or after ureteral
reanastomosis) or permanently (e.g., for neoplastic obstruction or
ureteroliths).2,12

ureteral stent (Vet Stent-Ureter, Infiniti Medical,

Embolics
Embolics are compounds or devices used for obstructing blood flow
to a structure in order to reduce hemorrhage, attenuate blood supply,
occlude vascular anomalies, or improve local concentrations of
certain chemical or biological substances via prolonged elution or
delivery. These agents are most commonly classified as mechanical
or particulate, temporary/biodegradable or permanent, and solid or
liquid (ch. 118).
The most commonly used embolics in veterinary patients are the
permanent mechanical devices used for relatively large vessel

occlusion such as thrombogenic embolization coilst and custom
woven nitinol vascular plugs and occludersu (Figure 113.9) (ch.
115). These coils are now available in multiple sizes, wire diameters,
coil conformations (e.g., straight, helical, complex), and detachable
versions. Several more complex occlusion devices that are
reconstrainable, repositionable and removable, are available for
congenital cardiac malformations (e.g., patent ductus arteriosus,
atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect, etc.); they have also
been used elsewhere in the cardiovascular systems of veterinary
patients.21-24 Particulate and liquid embolics are used for embolizing
the higher-order vessels and capillary beds when more distal
embolization is preferred for tumor ablation or vascular
malformations.9 This ensures more definitive distal tissue ischemia
(and reduced risk of revascularization) but increases the risk of
tissue necrosis. The most commonly used permanent particulate
agents include polyvinyl alcohol particlesv and more recently
hydrogel microspheres.w These are available in various particle sizes
ranging from 45 to over 1000 microns and embolization results from
initial mechanical vascular occlusion followed by permanent fibrin
ingrowth. A variety of drug-eluting hydrogel microspheres is
available and these have been demonstrated to provide a controlled
release of doxorubicin for weeks to months.

FIGURE 113.9 Various embolic agents. A and B,
Vascular plugs of various sizes. C, Thrombogenic
embolization coils in delivery catheter and deployed.
D, Polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) embolic particles. E,
Ethiodized oil liquid embolic.
Liquid embolics have the advantage of passing through the
capillary beds of tumors and vascular malformations or lymphatics,
permitting complete tissue destruction through to the venous
circulation (ch. 118). Glue (most commonly n-butyl cyanoacrylate)x
has been used the most and has been reported for use in vascular
arteriovenous fistulas, arteriovenous malformations, and thoracic

duct embolizations25,26 in veterinary patients. When mixed with
ethiodized oil (Lipiodol)y in a 1:1 to 1:4 ratio, the polymerization rate
can be slowed to mimic the speed of blood flow through the vascular
bed; this is important to prevent embolization distal to the target
site. The iodinated oil also lends radiopacity to the mixture. Care
must be taken to avoid gluing the catheter into the vessel being
embolized and additional training is recommended before
attempting one of these procedures. Newer, slower polymerizing
liquid embolic agents such as Onyxz and others are now available as
possibly safer alternatives for more risky embolization
procedures.27,28

Laser
Lasers have become an increasingly important tool in veterinary
surgery and IE for tissue ablation, coagulation, and stone
management. The diode laser is a continuous laser that emits light at
a wavelength of 980 nm. This type of laser energy has a high
simultaneous absorption in water and hemoglobin, making this a
good laser for cutting and coagulating tissues such as during
intramural ectopic ureter laser ablation or cutting the tissue of a
persistent paramesonephric remnant (ch. 117).29 A
holmium:yttrium aluminum garnet (Hol:YAG) pulsed laser falls in
the near infrared portion of the electromagnetic spectrum (2100 nm)
with the energy absorbed in <0.5 mm of fluid, making it an ideal
surgical laser for endourologic applications like laser lithotripsy. The
laser energy is delivered to the surface of the uroliths using flexible
quartz fibers with multiple different diameters (200, 365, 550
microns) guided through the working channel of small-diameter
flexible or rigid cystoscopes/ureteroscopes. The Hol:YAG laser
combines tissue cutting and coagulation properties, as well as the
ability to fragment stones upon contact.30 Although the various
commercial models of lithotripters vary slightly, the pulse duration,
energy, and frequency chosen are based upon the particular
application.

Contrast Agents

Low osmolarity, non-ionic iodinated contrast media such as
iohexolaa are most commonly used in IR. While ionic contrast agents
are less expensive, the hypertonicity and associated cation (often
sodium) can result in problems for those patients with concurrent
renal or cardiac disease. Non-ionic contrast agents are not
hypertonic and do not dissociate in solution and are therefore safer
for intravenous use in compromised patients in particular. The low
osmolality of iohexol compared to ionic contrast media with similar
iodine concentrations should result in fewer osmolality-related sideeffects. Iohexol is available with different iodine concentrations that
should be reported when used; the author typically uses between 240
to 350 mgI/mL and often dilutes 1:1 or 2:1 saline:contrast.
Complications associated with intravascular contrast media are
typically mild and relatively uncommon but can include nausea,
vomiting, pain, anaphylaxis, hemodynamic effects, and most notably
nephrotoxicosis. Contrast-induced nephropathy remains
incompletely understood but likely results from a combination of
direct cytotoxicity and prolonged vasoconstriction and impaired
renal vascular autoregulation.31,32 For high-risk patients,
alternatives to iodinated contrast media such as gadolinium or
carbon dioxide can be considered. Patients should be well-hydrated
before use (iohexol package insert)33 and while a safe dosage has not
been determined, the author tries to use less than 2-3 mL/kg
cumulatively during standard vascular interventional procedures.

Miscellaneous Devices
There are countless ancillary devices designed to facilitate minimally
invasive procedures that are beyond the scope of this chapter.
Examples include baskets and snares for retrieval of vascular or
intraluminal foreign bodies or stones, balloon esophagostomy tubes
(ch. 116) for esophageal strictures, biopsy devices, intra- and
extracorporeal lithotripters, thrombectomy devices, and flowswitches or adapters to help perform coaxial procedures using
microcatheters to name just a few.
