Minimally invasive airway procedures, particularly stent
placement, are becoming commonplace in veterinary medicine.
Hippocrates (460-370 BCE) was perhaps the first to employ an
airway “stent” when he used a reed tube to assist a suffocating

patient.1 The term stent would later be credited to Dr. Charles
Thomas Stent (1807-1885), a British dentist who created dental
impression compounds used for denture making and splints which
would later be sold under the name “Stents.”2 Aptly, the first
reference to describing a tube acting “as a stent for the anastomosis”
was in dogs for experimental biliary reconstruction in 1954.2 In cats
and dogs, airway stents are used predominantly in the trachea for
treatment of tracheal collapse (TC) and in the nasopharynx (NP) for
treatment of nasopharyngeal stenosis (NPS). This chapter will
provide an overview of the indications and techniques for these
applications. Further information on the underlying disease
processes, diagnosis, and medical management of these diseases can
be found elsewhere in the text (chs. 213 and 215). Less commonly,
airway stenting may be used for the treatment of bronchial collapse,
tracheal strictures, or airway obstruction due to neoplasia.

TRACHEAL STENTING
INTRODUCTION
Tracheal stenting for TC was first reported in a dog in 2002 and in 3
cats for obstructive disease in 2007.3 Since that time, tracheal
stenting has largely replaced the surgical placement of extraluminal
prosthetic rings for treatment of TC in dogs due to quicker procedure
times, decreased surgical complications including laryngeal paralysis
and tracheal necrosis, and ability to treat intrathoracic collapse.
However, due to the long-term complications associated with
tracheal stenting, prosthetic rings should still be considered for
young dogs with only cervical or thoracic inlet collapse. Two types of
TC have been described (ch. 215). Traditional TC (TTC) is
characterized by tracheomalacia, a weakened dorsal tracheal
membrane, or both resulting in flaccid flattening of the trachea. A
second type of TC, tracheal malformation (TM), is a static, dorsal
deviation of the ventral aspect of the cartilaginous rings resulting in a
“W”-shaped cross-sectional morphology that most often occurs at
the thoracic inlet.4 Tracheal stenting has been reported in cats,
predominantly for obstructive tracheal disease rather than TC.5,6

INDICATIONS
While there have been many advancements in stent design and
placement in the last 20 years, stenting is still considered a “salvage”
procedure for treatment of TC due to risks of complications. For this
reason, it is typically only recommended in the following scenarios:
1) Failure to respond to intensive medical management, with
persistence of significant clinical signs; 2) Dyspnea or cyanosis not
initiated by cough; 3) Static obstructive lesions such as TM; or 4)
Inability to successfully extubate following anesthesia or acute
respiratory crisis. Dogs with TM are more likely to require stenting
than dogs with TTC.7
Ideally, other concurrent respiratory or cardiac disease should be
assessed and treated prior to stenting as this may alleviate clinical
signs or allow better medical management. Mainstem bronchial
collapse is a common concurrent finding in 70-80% of dogs with
TC.4,8 In the early years, there was concern that stenting for TC in
dogs with concurrent bronchial collapse would result in worsened
outcomes. However, in a recent study of 75 dogs receiving stents for
TC, the presence of bronchial collapse was not associated with worse
survival time.4

DIAGNOSTIC TESTS
Initial diagnostic tests are often focused on the diagnosis of TC.
These tests include thoracic and cervical radiography,
tracheobronchial fluoroscopy, computed tomography (CT), and/or
tracheobronchoscopy (chs. 93 and 215). Prior to stenting, a
complete airway evaluation should be performed to look for
concurrent diseases including nasopharyngeal/pharyngeal collapse,
epiglottic retroversion (ch. 213), laryngeal paralysis (ch. 214),
laryngeal collapse, bronchial collapse (ch. 215), and lower airway
disease (chs. 216 and 217). Tracheal infection is a common finding,
occurring in 50-80% of dogs with TC prior to stent placement.9-11
Hence, endotracheal (ET) wash or brush sampling for cytologic
evaluation and culture is recommended at the time of stent
placement.

STENT PLACEMENT
Tracheal stenting is technically challenging and should be performed
by clinicians with proper training, to reduce risks of complications.
Stent placement is ideally performed under fluoroscopic guidance.
This allows real-time assessment of stent location and length during
deployment. Alternatively, stents can be placed with the use of digital
radiography or endoscopy. Multiple types of stents have been used
for TC in dogs (ch. 113). Currently, woven self-expanding metallic
stents (SEMS) made of nitinol are preferred. Nitinol is a nickeltitanium alloy with an elasticity that is biodynamically similar to the
trachea, with excellent biocompatibility and kink resistance.12
Veterinary-specific stents are available and have undergone design
enhancements over time to facilitate deployment and reduce stent
fractures.13

Stent Sizing
Stent sizing is one of the critical steps in tracheal stenting.
Undersized stents are at risk for migration or poor mucosal contact,
leading to decreased epithelization, increased mucus accumulation,
and increased risk of infections.13 Stents that are significantly
oversized increase the risk of fracture and may increase the risk of
granulation tissue formation.14,15 For tracheal measurements, the
dog is anesthetized, intubated, and placed in lateral recumbency with
the neck ventroflexed to straighten the trachea. Because the dog may
need to be extubated for stent placement, total intravenous
anesthesia techniques are recommended with the ET tube used for
providing oxygen. The ET tube cuff is positioned just caudal to the
larynx, which is easiest to accomplish with fluoroscopic guidance. A
marker catheter is placed in the esophagus over a guidewire or
within a 10 Fr red rubber catheter to calibrate the image for accurate
measurements.
Lateral view images of the complete trachea to include the larynx
and mainstem bronchi are obtained during a positive pressure
breath hold at 20 cm H2O to maximize the tracheal diameter. Images
are obtained with digital radiography or fluoroscopy. With

fluoroscopy, video loops can be recorded during the breath hold, and
an image at time of maximum tracheal distension can be chosen for
measurements (Video 114.1

). The maximum tracheal diameter

should be determined in the cervical, thoracic inlet, and intrathoracic
areas by measuring perpendicular to the tracheal lumen at each site
(Figure 114.1). The tracheas of dogs with TM often do not expand
well at the thoracic inlet and measurements in this area may
underestimate true tracheal diameter. The tracheal length is
measured approximately 1 cm from the caudal aspect of the cricoid
to approximately 1 cm cranial to the carina. This is the tracheal
length that should not be exceeded when selecting stent length and is
typically the goal for stent coverage. However, stents extending to
the cricoid are often well tolerated.
Choosing an appropriately sized stent is critical for reducing shortand long-term complications. Stent diameter is typically chosen to be
2-3 mm larger than the maximum diameter measured, usually
within the cervical trachea. In some dogs, there may be a significant
difference between maximum cervical and intrathoracic
measurements due to tapering of the trachea, which may contribute
to risk of stent fracture. In one study, tracheal taper was quantified
by dividing maximum tracheal diameter by the maximal
intrathoracic tracheal diameter. Dogs with stent fractures had a
larger tracheal taper compared to those that did not (mean 1.45 vs.
1.34).14 A tapered tracheal stent (Duality Vet Stent, Infiniti Medical,
Palo Alto, CA, USA) is available. In a study of 27 dogs with this type
of stent placed, no stent fractures were noted during a median
follow-up of 3 months (range 1-17 months).16

FIGURE 114.1 Lateral fluoroscopic image
obtained during positive pressure breath hold (20
cm H2O). The endotracheal tube is retracted so the
balloon cuff is just caudal to the cricoid (line B). A
marker catheter is present in the esophagus.
Tracheal diameter is measured at the cervical (lines
B and E), thoracic inlet (line C) and intrathoracic
(line D) regions. Tracheal length is determined
directly from the marker catheter.
Tracheal stents come compressed on a delivery device. In the
compressed state, the stent is longer than when it expands to its
maximal diameter. The change in length as the stent is deployed is
referred to as “stent foreshortening,” and it must be considered when
selecting stent length due to oversizing when selecting stent
diameter. For example, if a 12 mm × 52 mm stent is deployed and it
only reaches a diameter of 10 mm, the stent will be 67 mm in length
rather than 52 mm. Hence, the length of stent chosen is often
different than the length of trachea to be stented. Stent manufactures
provide foreshortening charts and these should be referenced when
selecting stent sizes to ensure the selected stent will not be too long.
Due to better spatial resolution, CT has been evaluated for tracheal
measurements. In a study comparing CT and radiographs, CT
measurements were an average of 1 mm greater.17 In a study
comparing CT and fluoroscopy, CT measurements were an average of
0.2 mm greater.18 As these variances are within the typical
oversizing during stent selection, the difference in measurements
with CT is likely not clinically significant. In both studies, assessment
of tracheal length was the same between modalities.

It is ideal to have a variety of stent sizes on hand so the stenting
procedure can be completed during the same anesthetic episode. The
most commonly reported stent sizes used in dogs are 12 × 52, 12 ×
65, 14 × 58, and 14 × 72 (all sizes in mm).4,19 If an appropriate stent
size is not available, the dog should be recovered and the correct
stent ordered, as placement of the incorrect size can increase longterm complications. If the dog cannot be recovered from anesthesia,
the best available stent can be placed temporarily to allow recovery.
The correct-size stent can be ordered and the stents exchanged prior
to development of significant epithelialization (often within a few
days).

Stent Deployment13,20,21
Due to the nature of the delivery devices, stents are deployed from
distal (caudal) to proximal (cranial). As delivery devices may differ
between manufacturers, the instructions should be read prior to use
to ensure proper deployment. Most tracheal stents are
reconstrainable until 75-90% of the length has been deployed, but
this varies by manufacturer and stent length (Video 114.1

). The

operator should refer to the manufacturer’s information for
specifications on the stent being used. Stent handling and
deployment should be performed using sterile technique.
The dog is maintained in lateral recumbency as for the
measurements. A bronchoscopy adapter can be attached to the ET
tube, which allows continued oxygen delivery while inserting and
deploying the stent through the bronchoscopy port. The ET tube
should be unsecured from the patient and the ET tube cuff deflated
prior to deployment because the dog may need to be temporarily
extubated during the procedure to prevent the stent from being
deployed within the ET tube. If the ET tube is too small to
accommodate the delivery device, the dog will need to be extubated.
Placement of a guidewire through the ET tube under fluoroscopic
guidance first can facilitate exchange of the delivery device for the ET
tube over the wire. Removable markers such as tape can be placed on
the fluoroscopic display monitor to mark the cranial and caudal
extents of the trachea for easier visualization during stent
deployment.

With the stent inserted in the trachea, fluoroscopy is used for
visualizing the radio-opaque marker at the distal end of the stent and
aligning this with the distal (caudal) site of stent deployment in the
trachea. It is often easier to start deploying the stent just caudal to
this site and then to pull the stent cranially into position after the
first 1-1.5 cm of stent is deployed. If the distal end of the stent
appears tapered after deployment, it may be located within a
mainstem bronchus and should be repositioned. Once one-third to
one-half of the stent is deployed, the stent should be gently pushed
and pulled to ensure that the stent is of appropriate diameter to
engage the tracheal wall. If the stent slides easily, it is undersized.
The stent should be reconstrained, removed, and a larger diameter
stent placed. If appropriate size, the deployment is continued. Every
few centimeters, the stent should be gently pushed inward
(distally/caudally) to help the stent maximally expand. This is
particularly important in areas of significant tracheal narrowing such
as the thoracic inlet or if TM is present (Video 114.1

).

As the proximal end of the stent is deployed, the ET tube (if
present) should be pulled cranially through the larynx to prevent the
stent from being deployed within the tube. Prior to reaching the
point where the stent cannot be reconstrained, the length of the stent
should be evaluated to ensure that it will not be too long when fully
deployed. If needed, the stent can be reconstrained, removed, and a
shorter stent chosen. If the stent is too far deployed to reconstrain,
the stent can be retracted through the larynx using the delivery
device. If completely deployed and too long, it can usually be
removed using forceps to grasp the proximal end of the stent and
retract it through the larynx.
Once the stent is deployed, the dog can be reintubated if needed by
sliding the ET tube over the delivery device. Care should be taken not
to dislodge the stent. The delivery device is carefully removed under
fluoroscopic guidance, ensuring that the device cone does not engage
the distal end of the stent and dislodge it. Post-deployment, repeat
tracheoscopy is recommended to evaluate stent position and tracheal
wall apposition (ch. 93). Poor apposition (termed “gapping” or
“guttering”) may be due to incomplete expansion of the stent,
particularly in areas of TM. These areas may be dilated using the ET
tube cuff under fluoroscopic guidance and reassessed with

tracheoscopy. If significant areas of poor apposition remain, the
stent may be undersized and should be replaced with a larger stent.
In the case of TM, a second stent may be needed to provide enough
combined radial force to prevent gapping. Epithelialization of the
stent occurs within days to weeks of placement, making it extremely
difficult to expand or remove a stent later. Therefore, issues with
“gutters” are best addressed at the time of initial stenting.
At the end of the procedure, static ventrodorsal and lateral images
of the stent should be obtained to document stent position and
dimensions for future comparisons. Measurement of the length of
the C7 and T4 vertebral bodies can be performed to use in calibrating
future radiographs when a radiographic marker is not present.19

Post-Stent Care
Due to the presence of the stent, and often concurrent airway
disease, medical management with corticosteroids and antitussives is
prescribed (ch. 215). The author routinely prescribes prednisone 1
mg/kg PO q24h for 2-4 weeks and then tapered to the least effective
dose or stopped if possible. These dogs may require long-term antiinflammatory therapy. For cough, the author prefers diphenoxylate
as it can be titrated to higher doses to control coughing without the
sedation seen with other opioids. The initial dosage is 0.2-0.5 mg/kg
PO q6-8h for 2-4 weeks and then is tapered and stopped, or used as
needed for coughing. It is important to control coughing to prevent
stent migration prior to epithelialization and to reduce the risk of
stent fracture. Empiric antibiotic therapy is prescribed pending
results of airway culture. In one study, Escherichia coli and
Pseudomonas spp. were most commonly isolated prior to stent
placement.11 Sedatives or anxiolytics may be needed to prevent
significant excitation, particularly in dogs with concurrent bronchial
collapse.
Chest radiographs are rechecked 1 month post placement, then
every 3 months for the first year, followed by every 3-6 months
thereafter. Radiographs should be also performed any time there is
exacerbation of clinical signs. In addition to traditional views, a
lateral radiograph with the forelimbs retracted caudally should be
obtained to better visualize the area of the thoracic inlet.

Radiographs are evaluated for evidence of stent fracture, migration,
or tissue ingrowth.

COMPLICATIONS
Stent migration is rare unless undersizing of the stent has occurred.
If migration is diagnosed prior to significant epithelialization, the
stent should be removed and a larger diameter stent placed.
Progressive TC cranial or caudal to the stent may occur if long
segments of the trachea are not stented initially. If causing clinical
signs, this can be treated by placement of an additional stent or
placement of extraluminal prosthetic rings for cervical TC.
While changes in stent manufacturing have reduced stent
fractures, these still occur. Rates of 4-22% have been reported in
recent studies.4,22,23 Stent fracture should be differentiated from
stent “fraying,” wherein the end loops of woven wire break. Stent
“fraying” is clinically insignificant in most cases. Fractures more
commonly occur in the caudodorsal aspect of the stent within the
intrathoracic trachea.4,14 As the intrathoracic trachea is often
smaller than the cervical trachea, there is likely excessive oversizing
of the stent in this region, which results in excessive compression
and weakness of the stent, predisposing it to fracture.13,14 In
addition, shear forces created during coughing may also contribute
to fracture at this location.24 These factors underscore the
importance of proper stent sizing and cough suppression poststenting. The use of a variable diameter stent as noted above may
help reduce the risk of fracture.
Stent fractures may result in acute exacerbation of clinical signs
and require treatment with repeat stenting. The cause of the initial
fracture should be determined to prevent recurrence. In order to
ensure the second stent is placed within and not adjacent to the
original stent, a hydrophilic guidewire should be passed under
endoscopic guidance through the lumen of the stent (Video 114.2
) and the stent delivery device inserted over the wire for deployment.
Alternatively, proper placement within the lumen can be evaluated
with orthogonal fluoroscopic or radiographic imaging. In cases of

mild fracture that does not affect stent integrity or result in
worsening TC/clinical signs, the dog may be monitored closely to
determine if restenting is necessary.
Granulomas and granulation tissue formation are common
complications, reported in 17-28% of dogs in larger studies.4,22,23,25
While granulation tissue is reported to occur secondary to stent
placement in people, inflammatory granulomas appear to be more
common in dogs. If they are left untreated, they may result in the
development of firm granulation tissue from fibrous infiltration.26 In
experimental canine and feline models, granulation tissue has been
associated with excessive stent oversizing.15,27 Infections in people
are associated with granulation tissue and are suspected to be the
cause of granulomas in dogs.26,28 Early detection of granulomas
prior to formation of granulation tissue is important for successful
treatment, underscoring the need for routine monitoring of dogs
post-stenting (Figure 114.2). Therapy with anti-inflammatory
dosages of corticosteroids and with antibiotics, ideally based on
culture, is often successful in achieving resolution.4,23,29,30
Treatment with colchicine was reported to be effective in treating
granulomas in one dog.31

FIGURE 114.2 Granuloma in a dog after
placement of a stent for tracheal collapse. A, Lateral
radiograph showing a soft tissue opacity in the
lumen of the trachea (red arrow). The forelimbs are
retracted caudally for better visualization. B,
Endoscopic image of the trachea showing the
granuloma along the right dorsolateral wall of the
trachea (left half of image).
Some dogs with granulomas may present with obstructive airway
disease. Due to significant dyspnea, these cases are not amenable to
medical management alone. Treatment options include restenting to
compress the inflammatory tissue (Figure 114.3 and

Video

114.2) or laser ablation (Video 114.3). The goal is to open the trachea
enough to resolve dyspnea and allow time for medical therapy to be
effective. For restenting, a stent of the same diameter is usually
chosen. Because of the narrowed lumen, there will be less
foreshortening, at least at initial placement, and this difference
should be accounted for when choosing stent length. If granulation
tissue is present, medical management is unlikely to be beneficial,
and restenting or laser ablation should be considered.

OUTCOMES
In the largest published study to date, 75 dogs were followed for a
median of 728 days (range, 0-2119).4 The median survival time was
1005 days from the time of stent placement. Dogs <7.7 years old and

male dogs had longer survival times whereas dogs requiring a second
stent due to fracture had shorter survival times. Clinical scores for
goose-honking/raspy breathing and for dyspnea improved in 89%
and 84% of dogs, respectively. Clinical scores for cough improved in
only 43%, emphasizing that tracheal stenting may not be beneficial
in dogs whose only clinical sign is coughing.
In a subsequent study from the same group, survival times of the
75 stented dogs were compared with 84 dogs receiving medical
management alone.7 The median survival time from initial diagnosis
of TC was 1363 days for medically managed dogs and 1913 days for
stented dogs, but this was not significantly different. Fifty-one
percent of dogs in the stented group had TM versus only 6% in the
medically managed group, suggesting dogs with TM are more likely
to require stenting. In the stented group, dogs with initial severe
clinical scores in all 3 categories had a survival time of 1694 days
versus 776 days for dogs with no severe scores, but these values did
not differ significantly from the median survival time of 1006 days
for all stented dogs. For dogs with severe clinical scores in 2 or more
categories at final evaluation, median survival was significantly
longer for stented dogs (1338 days) than for medically managed dogs
(12 days). These findings support recommendations for stent
placement in dogs with severe clinical disease or those that fail
intensive medical management.

FIGURE 114.3 Lateral fluoroscopic image
immediately post-restenting in a dog with
obstructive granulomas and dyspnea. Note the large
dorsal and small ventral gaps between the two stents
in the distal cervical region where the granulomas
have been compressed against the tracheal wall. This
resulted in improved lumen patency, which resolved
the dog’s dyspnea. The dog was then managed
medically with corticosteroids and antibiotics.

NASOPHARYNGEAL STENTING
INTRODUCTION
Nasopharyngeal stenosis (NPS) is a narrowing of the nasopharynx
(NP) that results in obstruction of airflow. When NPS results in
complete occlusion of the NP, it is termed an “imperforate”
nasopharynx (IN). NPS is an uncommon condition that affects both
dogs and cats. Further information regarding etiology, presentation,
and diagnosis of NPS can be found in ch. 213.

Treatment of NPS may include one or more of several different
procedures. Stenosis has been treated with surgical excision of the
stenotic tissue, dilation of the stenosis using instruments such as
hemostats, or balloon dilation (BD).32-36 The success of these
treatments has been variable and related to species.37 Based on the
literature and clinical experience, cats seem to be more amenable to
a favorable outcome with these techniques in approximately 50% of
cases.35,36,38 In dogs, it is common to have recurrent stenosis when
BD is the only treatment, although some dogs do respond after
multiple dilations.37,39 This has led to the development of NP
stenting techniques.

INDICATIONS FOR NP STENTING
Stenting may be considered as a first-line treatment in cats and dogs
with NPS or used in cases that fail BD alone. Due to the potential
success with BD in cats, BD alone should be considered prior to
stenting unless financial limitations preclude multiple procedures.
Due to the high rate of recurrent NPS, the author recommends
stenting as an initial treatment in dogs, but BD alone may be
considered, particularly when the stenotic membrane is very thin.
When NPS is located near the caudal edge of the soft palate, BD or
surgery should be considered first due to potential complications
associated with placing stents in this region. Cats and dogs with IN
appear to have a higher risk of recurrence after BD alone and the
author recommends stenting in these cases.37

STENT PLACEMENT
Stent Type
Initially, NP stenting was performed with uncovered balloon
expandable metallic stents (BEMS). However, these stents may
collapse or fracture when pressure is applied to the soft palate,
resulting in closure of the NP. SEMS are now commonly used. These
stents may be covered and/or removable. Uncovered stents will

become incorporated into the mucosa, which reduces risk of
migration and infection but the stents are difficult to remove if
needed.37 In some cases, fibrous tissue may grow through the stent.
Anecdotally, this seems to occur most often with IN. Using a covered
stent helps prevent this complication. Many SEMS are made from
woven nitinol and they undergo foreshortening as noted with
tracheal stents. This has to be considered when choosing stent length
and during deployment. A fully covered, removable stent (Infiniti
Medical) is currently available and is preferred by the author to allow
future removal if needed to manage chronic infections. The stent
does not foreshorten, making sizing and deployment easier;
however, this stent is not reconstrainable. Because the stent is fully
covered, stent migration can occur. A T-bar fastener system is
available to help secure the stent through the soft palate. In cats, the
use of a temporary stent made from a 24 Fr or 28 Fr silicone chest
tube and secured via transpalatal suture has been described.40 This
is beneficial in cats as long-term stent implantation is often not
needed and this is a more economical stent. In the author’s
experience, this technique has not worked well in dogs.

Stent Sizing
Proper measurement for stent size is critical and is best determined
from CT imaging. Pre- and post-contrast images are obtained to
distinguish mucus/fluid accumulation from the stenotic tissue. Axial
images should be reformatted into sagittal planes for best
measurement of length of the stenosis (Figure 114.4). The stent
length should allow 5-10 mm of stent to be rostral and caudal to the
area of stenosis when possible. If possible, the stent should not
extend to within 1 cm of the caudal aspect of the soft palate as this
can prevent soft palate closure during swallowing, permitting
nasopharyngeal reflux of food and liquid.
The diameter of the stent can be more difficult to determine. The
NP is typically oval in shape rostrally and circular caudally. Stent size
can be chosen based on the maximal height of the NP caudal to the
stenosis. When the NP is largely oval in the area to be stented, the
author prefers to use height and width measurements rostral and
caudal to the stenosis entered into a formula to convert oval areas to

circular areas and subsequently a diameter (formulas to convert oval
air duct to round air duct can be found online) (Figure 114.5). The
covered stent typically needs minimal oversizing (1-2 mm) as it is
fastened in place. Excessive oversizing of a stent may result in the
development of an oronasal fistula due to pressure necrosis.

FIGURE 114.4 Midline sagittal reconstruction
computed tomography (CT) image of a dog with
nasopharyngeal stenosis (NPS). The yellow bar (12.5
mm) represents the length of the NPS. The green
bars show the distance 1 cm rostral and caudal to the
NPS. The red bar indicates 1 cm from the caudal edge
of the soft palate. Based on the measurements, a
stent length of 35 mm was chosen.

Stent Deployment37,41
Prior to placement, the stenosis needs to be opened, usually by BD.
This is performed under fluoroscopic guidance. A guidewire is
passed through one naris, across the region of stenosis, and down the
esophagus. Conversely, a wire can be passed retrograde through a
retroflexed scope in the NP to exit one naris. Over the wire, a BD
catheter is passed and is centered over the stenosis. High-pressure

balloons (8-30 atm pressure) are recommended as low-pressure
balloons may not have enough force to open the stenosis. Balloon
size is chosen to be 1-2 mm smaller than maximum diameter of the
normal NP. Balloons are expanded using contrast medium under
fluoroscopy in order to assess for complete dilation. Any “waisting”
of the balloon should completely resolve to indicate complete
breakdown of the stenosis (Video 114.4

).

In animals with imperforate NP, a new opening must be created
across the stenosis. This requires a guidewire, introducer sheath, and
a long access trocar needle (e.g., renal access needle). Initially, a
guidewire is passed through a naris to the area of imperforate
stenosis under fluoroscopic guidance. A 5 Fr or larger introducer
sheath with dilator is passed to the stenosis and the dilator removed.
The access needle is passed through the introducer (using it as a
needle guard) to the imperforate membrane. Under fluoroscopic and
endoscopic guidance (retroflex pharyngoscopy), the access needle is
advanced across the membrane into the caudal NP (Video 114.5

).

The needle is removed and a guidewire passed as above. Typically,
the membrane needs to be enlarged with a rigid dilator over the wire
prior to BD as above.
Once the stenosis is resolved, the SEMS can be introduced over the
wire and deployed based on the manufacturer’s instruction under
fluoroscopic guidance (Figure 114.6). The stent should be centered
over the area of stenosis or at least ensuring that it extends 5-10 mm
rostral and caudal to the stenosis. For temporary stenting in cats, the
tubing is pulled retrograde into place from the pharynx using an
endoscopic grasping forceps.40 Covered stents or tubing are secured
in place using transpalatal sutures or T-bar fasteners.

FIGURE 114.5 Sagittal (upper) and axial (lower)
computed tomography (CT) images from the dog in
Figure 114.4. Note the oval appearance to the
nasopharynx rostral to the stenosis (lower left, level
of green bar on sagittal image) compared to the
round appearance caudal to the stenosis (lower right,
level of orange bar on sagittal image). A 12 mm × 35
mm stent was placed based on these measurements.

FIGURE 114.6 Images after stent placement in the
dog in Figures 114.4 and 114.5. A, Lateral

Post-Stent Care and Complications
After stent placement, anti-inflammatory dosages of corticosteroids
(e.g., prednisone 1 mg/kg PO q24h) are prescribed for 2-4 weeks. If
secondary infections are suspected or documented, appropriate
antibiotic therapy should be administered. Temporary stents in cats
are typically removed after 3-4 weeks and the area of stenosis
reassessed endoscopically.40 Chronic infections are a common longterm complication of NP stenting, occurring in 23% of uncovered
stents and 64% of covered stents.37 This may be more common when
covered stents are used because the coating prevents
epithelialization and provides a place for biofilm adherence.
Treatment of chronic infections can be difficult. This may require
regular nasal flushing and repeat cultures to determine best
antibiotic therapy. The author has used long-term gentamicin
nebulization (4-6 mg/kg in saline nebulized q12h) to help control
infections in some dogs (ch. 90).42 Ultimately, removal of the stent

may be needed, which is an advantage of using a covered stent.
Stenosis may recur after stent removal, requiring restenting.
Oronasal fistula has been reported in ∼17% of cases.37 Tissue
ingrowth was reported in 33% of cases treated with an uncovered
stent and none using a covered stent.37

OUTCOME
In the largest published study to date, outcomes were reported in 46
animals (15 dogs and 31 cats).37 Outcome was considered successful
in 78% of animals based on maintenance of airway patency,
complications, and owner satisfaction. Cats had a significantly higher
success rate (87%) compared to dogs (60%). In addition, outcome
was more successful in animals with NPS (89%) compared to
animals with IN (45%). All animals with IN that had a covered stent
placed had a successful outcome.

Angiography (angiocardiography) refers to the administration of
contrast agents into the vascular system with imaging visualization,

to outline and characterize vascular and cardiac structures. In the
middle of the 20th century and until the 1980s, angiography and
cardiac catheterization were performed solely for diagnostic
purposes.1-3 However, the recognition that the veterinarian could
intervene in cardiovascular diseases, guided by fluoroscopic imaging,
became reality with the development of transvenous pacing
systems,4,5 balloon dilation catheters,6,7 and coils/devices for
vascular occlusion.8,9 Interventional cardiology has since expanded
in the breadth and complexity of small animal cardiac diseases that
can be treated by a minimally-invasive, transcatheter approach. This
chapter provides an overview of the equipment required for
cardiovascular intervention, as well as the indications and
therapeutic strategies currently employed in small animal
cardiovascular medicine.

PREPARATION FOR CARDIOVASCULAR
CATHETERIZATION
Performing diagnostic or interventional studies within the heart and
vasculature requires detailed knowledge of the equipment used,
advanced technical skills of catheterization, and an understanding of
thoracic and cardiovascular anatomy. The catheterization laboratory
should be a sterile space, with sufficient storage for a multitude of
commonly used catheters, wires, and devices; high-quality
fluoroscopic imaging; portable ultrasound for vascular access and
transesophageal echocardiography; a power injector for rapid
delivery of iodinated contrast; anesthetic and hemodynamic
monitoring equipment for intravascular pressure recording; a
sufficient number of monitors for visualization of live images and
pertinent hemodynamic parameters; and a safety or crash cart for
stocking of supplies required for emergent intervention, including a
cardioverter-defibrillator (Figure 115.1).
Prior to intervention, an understanding of thoracic anatomy and
image interpretation is important for appropriate diagnosis,
planning, and equipment selection as well as during catheterization
to verify the intervention is being performed at the correct site and to
troubleshoot unexpected findings or complications. The thorax is a

complex 3-dimensional shape with a wide variation in the
radiographic opacity of thoracic structures; furthermore, the heart is
a rapidly moving organ with a complex spatial relationship. These
realities complicate interpretation of a 2-dimensional fluoroscopic
image, which is made more challenging by the high rate of blood flow
within the beating heart that results in a temporally brief period
available for contrast and chamber visualization as contrast agents
are quickly ejected and diluted following injection.
The difficulty in evaluating cardiovascular anatomy due to the
complex structure of the thorax can be mitigated by review of
multiple image planes, selective injection of iodinated contrast
material in specific locations, use of a power injector, and by digitalsubtraction angiography (DSA, ch. 113). Many human
catheterization laboratories, particularly those that are used for the
treatment of congenital heart disease, now employ biplane
fluoroscopic systems that provide real-time imaging of two
orthogonal views to improve anatomic guidance. There are also
fluoroscopic systems that perform rotational angiography to
circumferentially record a single injection from all angles and create
a 3-dimensional reconstruction of the anatomic structure.
Alternatively, some systems have the capability of importing
anatomic landmarks from cross-sectional imaging studies (computed
tomography [CT] or magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]) onto the 2dimensional fluoroscopic image to improve guidance during the
intervention (Figure 115.2). Few veterinary catheterization facilities
have these capabilities, but many veterinary cardiac interventions
can be performed using a portable C-arm–mounted fluoroscope that
easily rotates the field of view around the thorax to numerous
projection angles. The fluoroscopic system chosen should provide
high resolution (at least a 512 × 512 and optimally a 1024 × 1024
matrix), generate sufficient energy to penetrate the thorax of a large
dog, and be capable of displaying and recording fast frame rates (2530 frames per second or higher; ch. 113). The rapid heart rates of
dogs and cats cause contrast filling of the structure of interest to be
temporally brief and a frame-by-frame review of a recorded
angiographic run often is needed to visualize the structures of
interest and perform measurements. Fast frame rates prevent the
operator from “missing” the lesion during contrast injection into a
high-flow organ such as the heart.

Generally, it is not possible by hand injection to achieve a
sufficiently tight bolus of contrast to optimally opacify a chamber of
the heart in medium-sized and larger dogs. Automated power
injectors overcome this limitation by allowing the operator to
program the volume, flow rate, and pressure of an injection to
maximize opacification of the heart or great vessels within 1-2
cardiac cycles. Importantly, angiographic catheters and highpressure tubing should be used if a power injector delivers the
contrast injection. An end-hole catheter is a poor choice for
recording an angiographic study, particularly within the heart, as the
full force of the injection is directed through the single end hole and
catheter recoil is likely. Additionally, if the end hole is against a
vessel wall or the endocardium, a high-pressure injection may
damage the structure of interest. The preferred angiographic
catheter is one with the largest diameter possible for the task, of the
shortest feasible length, and with multiple side holes and a closed or
tapered tip—all to maximize flow, opacify a large chamber quickly,
and minimize trauma. For intracardiac injections and angiographic
studies in large vessels and the cardiac chambers, the author prefers
the Berman or pigtail catheter.

CONTRAST AGENTS
Contrast agents employed for angiocardiography are almost
exclusively iodine-based (carbon dioxide gas rarely is used as a
negative contrast agent). Iodine has a relatively high atomic weight,
which equates to radiodensity, and the degree of opacity with this
agent is directly proportional to the total amount of iodine in the
image. Second-generation contrast agents (developed in the 1970s)
are non-ionic monomers, which attach an amide group to an
iodinated benzoic ring and prevent dissociation in solution. These
agents cause far fewer adverse reactions than did early generation
agents and are termed low-osmolar agents because the particles do
not dissociate once in solution. These agents still have an osmolality
2-3 times that of the blood (e.g., 550-850 mOsm/kg for most
agents); iohexol is an example of a second-generation contrast agent
that is commonly used in veterinary medicine. The only
commercially available third-generation agent is iodixanol, which is

an iso-osmolar dimer made by combining two non-ionic triiodinated benzoic rings together. This arrangement does not
dissociate in solution, has an iodine:particle ratio of 6:1, and has the
same osmolality as blood (290 mOsm/kg). Although no studies are
available in veterinary medicine, a meta-analysis of human patients
at risk for contrast-induced nephropathy found a lower risk of
adverse reaction for iodixanol compared to iohexol.10 The viscosity
of the contrast agent is also important as this affects the flow rate
during injection. Warming the contrast can decrease viscosity and
allow for more rapid injection rates. Last, iodinated contrast agents
are available in various concentrations and smaller volumes are
needed to create comparable degrees of radiopacity if highly
concentrated solutions are used. Rare contrast reactions are reported
in animals and both the agent used as well as the total amount of
contrast given likely are important in the risk of this occurrence.11,12
However, recommendations vary widely and no prospective studies
are available. In general, the author attempts to keep the cumulative
dosage of contrast for a cardiovascular procedure to <720 mg
iodine/kg, but has given animals as much as 2400 mg iodine/kg
without apparent adverse effects. For animals with renal
impairment, more conservative values and concurrent fluid diuresis
should be employed.

IMAGING PLANES
Most contrast studies and interventions for cardiovascular disease
are performed with the animal positioned in right or left lateral
recumbency. Lateral positioning allows the operator to monitor
dorsal-ventral and cranial-caudal motion of catheters and wires as
they are advanced into the thorax. Right-to-left lateral deflection,
however, is less clearly visualized. Although less commonly used
than lateral imaging for cardiac intervention, the ventrodorsal
projection allows visualization of left-to-right laterality and the
cranial-caudal position of catheters introduced into the thorax. The
location of catheters or wires in the dorsal-ventral plane, however, is
challenging from a ventrodorsal projection. Several additional
imaging planes are used in human medicine to highlight and

optimize imaging of cardiac structures. Variations from the
traditional lateral or ventrodorsal projection are typically given by an
angle, which refers to the position of the image intensifier in relation
to the patient’s thorax in a ventrodorsal position. Commonly used
angulations in human medicine include the right and left anterior
obliques (RAO and LAO, respectively) with variable cranial or caudal
angulation. Typically, the image intensifier is rotated 30° to the
patient’s right (RAO) or left (LAO) and a variable 10° to 30° of
cranial or caudal angulation may also be employed. Altering the
angle of the C-arm can elongate structures (e.g., the left ventricular
outflow tract in subaortic stenosis) or provide a more directly
perpendicular visualization plane during device deployment (e.g., the
atrial septum for closure of an atrial septal defect). These viewing
angles have not been standardized in veterinary medicine and are
largely operator- and case-dependent. In practice, adjusting the
angle of the C-arm is most useful to optimize an angiogram for
measurement, such as improving visualization of the minimal ductal
diameter of a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), or to compensate for
suboptimal positioning of the animal on the table.

RIGHT HEART INTERVENTIONS
CARDIAC PACING
Permanent transvenous cardiac pacing is discussed in ch. 230.

BALLOON PULMONARY
VALVULOPLASTY
Congenital valvular pulmonary stenosis (PS, ch. 231) has been
reported as the third most commonly diagnosed congenital heart
defect of dogs in North America,13 though more recent reports from
Europe suggest it is the most common canine congenital heart
defect.14 Without therapy, dogs with moderate or severe valvular PS
are at risk for clinical signs including exercise intolerance, syncope,
sudden cardiac death, congestive heart failure, and cyanosis,

hypoxemia, and hyperviscosity from a right-to-left shunt (ch.
231).15,16
Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty (BPV) was first performed in a
dog in 198017 and reported in a child in 1982.18 There is evidence
that BPV improves the clinical outcome of human and canine
patients with valvular PS, both with a reduction in clinical
symptomatology and an improvement in survival.15,19,20 The
procedure now is routinely performed in clinical canine practice with
low morbidity and mortality for those animals with a severe gradient
and/or the presence of clinical signs referable to their disease.

Preparation
Prior to intervention, an attempt should be made to characterize the
valve morphology and to estimate the balloon size required.
Transthoracic echocardiography with Doppler (ch. 97) is the current
standard of care in veterinary cardiology for evaluation of pulmonary
valve morphology, annular size, and severity of stenosis (Figure
115.3). Valves that are severely dysplastic (redundant tissue, fibrotic
adhesions to the sinotubular junction, annular hypoplasia,
subvalvular fibrous ring, or subvalvular muscular ridge) are less
likely to respond to BPV and clients should be so advised (Figure
115.4). Although consensus guidelines are not available, the author
recommends BPV in cases with evidence of valve fusion or fibrotic
adhesions at the sinotubular junction. For cases with severe valve
thickening, annular hypoplasia, or exuberant fibrous obstruction,
pulmonary valve stent implantation is pursued in the author’s
practice.21,22
Prior to intervention, an estimation of the pressure gradient across
the stenotic valve is obtained by continuous wave spectral Doppler
(ch. 97), guided by color Doppler imaging to optimize alignment
parallel to the direction of the turbulent jet. Most cardiologists
consider PS mild at a gradient of 10-49 mm Hg, moderate at 50-79
mm Hg, and severe when the gradient is ≥80 mm Hg. The decision
to pursue BPV should be made with the pressure gradient in mind,
with greater benefit from the procedure likely in dogs with severe
stenosis. As with all Doppler estimates, the velocity measured is
dependent not only on the orifice of the valve, but also on the flow

across the valve at the time of measurement and the systolic function
of the right ventricle (RV).23,24 Changes in the dog’s sympathetic
tone, intravascular volume status, or intrinsic RV function can alter
the velocity measured.
There are many balloon dilation catheters available on the market,
with varying profiles, materials, sizes, and maximal pressure. The
most commonly used balloon dilation catheters in veterinary
medicine are made by a human pediatric device company and
include the TYSHAK and Z-MED lines of balloon dilation catheters.
TYSHAK balloon dilation catheters are made of a thin, minimallycompliant thermoplastic elastomer and have a relatively low
maximal burst pressure. They are, however, low profile and most
sizes can accommodate a 0.035″ guidewire, making them a
commonly selected catheter for BPV in dogs. Z-MED balloon dilation
catheters are made from a thicker thermoplastic elastomer, which
provides a greater maximal burst pressure, though requiring a larger
introducer size. Even greater burst pressure can be achieved using
the ATLAS or ATLAS GOLD line of high-pressure balloons (HPBs),
as these are designed to withstand burst pressures of 12-18
atmospheres. Notable differences exist between these two types of
HPB dilation catheters. The primary difference is the length of the
shoulders, which is the portion of the balloon that tapers at each end.
The original ATLAS HPB has long shoulders, which result in a total
length almost 3 times the labeled length for the 2 cm and 4 cm
balloons (as each shoulder is approximately the length of the center
core), while in the ATLAS GOLD HPB line the shoulders are shorter
and total length is ∼2× the length of the central core. The ATLAS
GOLD HPB dilation catheter also has a tapered tip and improved
trackability. The author uses the ATLAS GOLD line of balloon
dilation catheters for BPV in dogs with dysplastic valves (thick,
redundant tissue or a subvalvular fibrous ridge) and the TYSHAK
line of balloons for those with pure valve fusion or small dogs whose
vasculature is too small for the required ATLAS introducer size (ch.
113). A pilot study suggested that BPV with the ATLAS HPBs is safe
and resulted in a substantial improvement in transpulmonary
pressure gradient in the initial cohort.25

dogs with pulmonary valve stenosis. Valve

Coronary Arterial Anomalies
The coronary arterial anatomy is of particular importance in
brachycephalic dogs; these dogs are reported to be at risk for
anomalous coronary arterial circulations characterized by either a
single right coronary ostium or single left coronary ostium (ch.
231).26 In such cases, the anomalous coronary artery arises from the
contralateral coronary artery and passes adjacent and cranial to the
pulmonary valve annulus or, rarely, in between the aortic and
pulmonary valve annuli. Evaluation of coronary anatomy in
brachycephalic dogs with PS should include imaging of the coronary
ostia, either by aortic angiography during catheterization or crosssectional imaging such as CT angiography prior to intervention
(Figure 115.5). Performing BPV with a standard size balloon
(balloon-to-annulus ratio of 1.2 to 1.5) in a dog with a coronary artery
anomaly can result in coronary artery avulsion, damage, and/or
death.27 BPV using a more conservative ratio of 0.9 to 1.0 in such
dogs has been reported with some reduction in stenosis severity.28
The long-term benefit of conservative ballooning in these dogs
remains uncertain, but the procedure may be considered. Currently,
the author performs transpulmonary valve stent implantation for
most dogs with coronary artery anomalies.

Procedure

The BPV procedure is performed from a transvenous approach,
either via the external jugular vein or via the femoral vein. The
jugular vein is preferred for small dogs as it affords a larger size
vessel and therefore a larger introducer sheath can be used than
otherwise would be possible if using the femoral vein. The femoral
vein typically is used when an arterial study is desired concurrently
given the close relationship of the femoral artery and vein (Figure
115.6). Percutaneous access with an appropriately-sized introducer
is achieved with the animal in lateral (jugular vein) or dorsal
(femoral vein) recumbency (Video 115.1).

A vascular sheath is

selected that is at least one French (Fr) size larger than what is
required by the anticipated balloon dilation catheter. The right heart
is catheterized and intracardiac pressures are measured to evaluate
starting RV pressure and transpulmonary gradient; alternatively, the
transvalvar pressure gradient can be calculated using
transesophageal Doppler echocardiography. Note: It is always
preferable to cross cardiac valves antegrade with a flow-directed
(balloon-tipped) catheter or one with a J-tip or pigtail.
Theoretically, advancing an end-hold catheter across the valve can
perforate a valve leaflet, ensnare chordae tendineae, or otherwise
damage the valve apparatus. A balloon-tipped or pigtail catheter,
however, will preferentially enter the true valve orifice and
minimize trauma to the valve. Right ventriculography is performed
with an appropriate angiographic catheter (typically a Berman
catheter) and the pulmonary annulus is measured to size the balloon
(Figures 115.4 and 115.7; Video 115.2)

. The angiographic

measurement is compared to the echocardiographic measurement of
pulmonary annulus diameter and a balloon is chosen with a diameter
~1.3-1.5 times the annulus diameter.
Following right ventriculography, a balloon wedge pressure
catheter is floated across the pulmonary valve and out a distal branch
pulmonary artery. The left pulmonary artery (the more dorsal branch
pulmonary artery when viewed from a lateral image) is preferred, as
it provides a smoother and more secure path for advancement of the
balloon dilation catheter as compared to the right pulmonary artery.
Next, a J-tipped exchange-length guidewire (typically >180 cm
length) is selected and advanced through the wedge pressure

catheter and its tip is placed within the distal branch pulmonary
artery. The J-tip is preferred as it will be less traumatic to the distal
pulmonary artery. The diameter and stiffness of the guidewire
chosen will depend on the size of the dog and the stiffness of the
balloon dilation catheter to be used. Guidewires of 0.035″ diameter
in a standard stiffness or super-stiffness are preferred for BPV. In
small dogs or those with severe RV hypertrophy, super-stiff
guidewires place excess pressure on the tricuspid valve and the RV
endocardium, particularly when they are advanced from a jugular
venous approach. For larger dogs, the standard stiffness guidewires
are overly flexible and do not maintain the balloon in a proper
position during inflation; as such, super-stiff or extra-stiff guidewires
are preferred for large dogs or inflexible balloon dilation catheters.
For very small dogs, the chosen balloon dilation catheter may not
accept a 0.035″ guidewire. In such instances, a 0.018″ or 0.025″
guidewire can be used, but such wires provide even less stability
during advancement and inflation of the balloon dilation catheter
and stiffer varieties should be selected when possible.

FIGURE 115.4 Angiographic images from dogs
with pulmonary valve stenosis. Valve morphology
may vary from a relatively thin and fused, doming
valve in a 5-month-old Staffordshire Bull Terrier

The best candidate for balloon pulmonary
valvuloplasty is the fused, doming valve shown in

be expected in the case shown in panel B, while stent

implantation or open surgical resection should be
considered for the dysplastic cases shown in panels C
and D.
The next step is balloon preparation. First, the protective plastic
sheath around the balloon is removed. A three-way stopcock is
attached to the catheter’s balloon port, with a pressure inflation
device connected to one of the stopcock’s ports and a 12 mL Luerlock syringe attached to the other. A mixture of iodinated contrast
and isotonic saline (from 1:1 to 1:3, contrast to saline) is drawn into
the inflation device and 3-4 mL of a similar mixture is drawn into the
syringe. For larger balloons, a lesser proportion of contrast to saline
should be used as the rate of balloon deflation is partially dependent
on the viscosity of the fluid; contrast is necessary to visualize
inflation but results in a slower deflation rate. The balloon dilation
catheter is then purged of air by drawing back through the three-way
stopcock opened to the balloon (aspirating with the syringe against a
collapsed balloon); the syringe should be pointing down so that air
drawn into it from the catheter balloon port is replaced by salinecontrast mixture. Repeating this aspiration 2-3 times while
vigorously tapping the 3-way stopcock replaces air in the catheter
balloon lumen with saline-contrast mixture. The balloon should not
be inflated outside the patient during purging, which would alter the
balloon profile and make it difficult to feed through the hemostatic
valve of the introducer. The central lumen of the balloon dilation
catheter is then flushed with heparinized saline and slowly advanced
over the guidewire to a position spanning the pulmonary valve
annulus. Projecting a reference image of the RV angiogram can aid in
proper positioning of the balloon; platinum marker bands on the
balloon dilation catheter allow the operator to adequately center the
annulus, or site of stenosis, to the balloon. Many cardiologists place
the balloon markers with one-third of the balloon length past the site
of stenosis and two-thirds preceding the stenosis. Even so, the
operator will need to hold traction on the balloon dilation catheter
during balloon inflation to brace against the force of RV systolic
contraction and blood flow, which will tend to extrude the balloon
into the pulmonary trunk. Advancing the guidewire into the catheter
during balloon inflation can also aid balloon stability. Rapid inflation
of the balloon is performed under live fluoroscopy to visualize the

development of a waist at the site of stenosis and to allow
retraction/advancement of the catheter if the position changes
(Figure 115.7; Video 115.3)

. The pressure generated by the

inflation device should be monitored and increased to the nominal
pressure of the balloon. Exceeding this nominal pressure (the
pressure at which the balloon reaches its advertised diameter) is
appropriate if the stenotic waist persists, but the rated burst pressure
of the balloon should not be exceeded. Once the desired pressure is
reached, or if the balloon migrates from the site of stenosis, rapid
deflation of the balloon is performed. The duration of inflation
should not exceed 5-6 seconds. A precipitous drop in systemic
pressure is expected, with recovery rapid within the following 5-10
seconds. The desired outcome with BPV is resolution of the stenotic
waist and a lack of waist on subsequent re-inflations. Typically, 2-4
inflations are performed to confirm the waist was engaged and has
resolved. RV pressures and the transpulmonary gradient are again
measured and, if the result is satisfactory, all equipment is removed.
Hemostasis is typically achieved with a purse-string suture around
the access site as well as 5 minutes of direct manual pressure. A neck
bandage is placed if the jugular vein was the point of access, to keep
the site clean as the animal is recovered. The prognosis for BPV is
generally good if a significant reduction in pressure gradient can be
achieved.15,19,29

HEARTWORM EXTRACTION
Preparation
Dogs with caval syndrome from severe heartworm infection require
emergent intervention to alleviate the mechanical obstruction to
blood flow and halt ongoing hemolysis (Figure 115.8) (ch. 237).
They are poor anesthetic candidates, but extraction of the worms is
the only effective means to improve their clinical condition. In the
most severely affected patients, extraction may be performed with
light sedation and local analgesia to avoid further hemodynamic
compromise from anesthetics. Stabilization of the patient should be
performed during preparation for heartworm extraction, which can
include fluid resuscitation, blood products to normalize bleeding
disorders, and vasopressor medications.

FIGURE 115.7 Fluoroscopic images during
balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty from an 8-monthold Boston Terrier with pulmonary valve stenosis.
Right ventriculography (A) through a Berman
catheter highlights the right ventricular lumen and
the fused, doming pulmonary valve (arrow). A
balloon dilation catheter is advanced over a
guidewire and rapidly inflated, resulting in a stenotic
waist (arrowheads) at the pulmonary annulus (B).
With greater pressure generation in the balloon, the
waist is torn and the valvuloplasty is complete (C).

FIGURE 115.8 Echocardiographic images of a dog
with heartworm disease and caval syndrome in both
long axis (A) and short axis (B) image planes
showing a mass of worms spanning the tricuspid
valve and requiring worm extraction. Ao, Aorta; LA,
left atrium; LV, left ventricle; PV, pulmonary valve;
RA, right atrium; RV, right ventricle.

Procedure
To extract the worms, the dog is placed in left lateral recumbency
and the skin over the right external jugular vein is clipped and
surgically prepped. A 4-5 cm incision is made over the proximal right
external jugular vein and the vein is isolated by blunt dissection.
Suture or vessel loops are placed proximal and distal to the planned
site of venous access to control the vein and limit hemorrhage.
Tenotomy scissors or a #11 blade are used for creating a 2-3 mm
incision in the lateral wall of the jugular vein. The preferred
extraction equipment is then advanced directly into the vein or
through a vascular sheath to control hemostasis. Several techniques
have been reported, including passage of a catheter with a nitinol
gooseneck snare.30 Alternatively, an endoscopic retrieval basket,31
alligator forceps,32 or specially designed flexible forceps33 may be
used. A nitinol gooseneck snare is a loop set at a right angle to the
end of a semi-stiff wire. The extraction device (snare, basket, forceps)
is passed through the catheter and advanced into the right heart. The
device is manipulated under fluoroscopic guidance with the goal of
ensnaring the worms; echocardiographic guidance may be helpful.34
The loop or basket is tightened and the worms are held firmly and
withdrawn at the site of venous access in concert with the extraction
device (Video 115.4

). It is important to apply gradual tension

when tightening the device to avoid lacerating the worms, which
would spill more dirofilarial debris and antigens into the circulation.
Repeated passes into the right heart are performed until several
negative passes have been achieved and/or brief cardiac ultrasound
shows no more worms in the right heart or pulmonary trunk. The
jugular vein is repaired or ligated at the end of the procedure and the
skin incision closed routinely. On recovery, medical stabilization for
hematologic and biochemical derangements is continued and
adulticide treatment is scheduled over the following 1-2 months once
the animal’s clinical status has stabilized. Caval syndrome in the cat
is much less common than in the dog and is associated with a lesser
worm burden. However, similar interventional techniques have been
reported in cats with caval syndrome and heartworm disease
including use of alligator forceps,35 endoscopic basket-type

forceps,36 a horsehair brush,35 and a nitinol snare.30 It is critically
important to avoid damage to the worms during extraction in cats as
severe anaphylactic-like reactions can occur, resulting in
hypotension and death.37

Prognosis
The prognosis for caval syndrome historically has been guarded to
poor. A review of 42 cases found that half of the dogs were
euthanized or discharged with the intention of euthanasia at the time
of diagnosis.31 Of the 21 dogs in which heartworm extraction was
attempted, 2 dogs died during the procedure, 4 dogs died in the
postoperative period, 1 dog had no worms extracted due to distal
migration, and 14 dogs had successful worm extraction and survived
to discharge. Survival in the 14 dogs after successful extraction
ranged from 2-56 months, with a mean of 24 months. Of the 21 dogs
that underwent attempted extraction, 12 had disseminated
intravascular coagulation and 9 of these dogs survived. As such,
heartworm extraction should be considered for all dogs with caval
syndrome and a successful outcome can be possible even for those
with a severe bleeding disorder at the time of diagnosis.

INTRACARDIAC STENTING FOR
CENTRAL VENOUS OBSTRUCTION
In rare cases, intracardiac neoplasia can result in impaired venous
return and obstruction of cranial or caudal vena caval flow, causing
facial swelling or cavitary effusion (chs. 235, 239).38-40
Historically, medical therapy was the preferred therapeutic strategy
for this condition, with variable results. However, deployment of
intracardiac stents now has been reported for this condition and can
palliate disease by restoring normal venous return. In a series of
three cases, stent placement from caudal to cranial venae cavae
resulted in resolution or substantial reduction in clinical signs, with
survival of up to 37 months.40

Preparation
Echocardiography is necessary to establish the diagnosis and
evaluate the degree of venous obstruction (ch. 97; Video 115.5)

.

Cross-sectional imaging with CT angiography or MR angiography
can be useful to characterize the 3-dimensional extent of the tumor
and the vena caval diameter but is not mandatory. Stent selection is
made with the intent to size 5-10% greater than the vena caval
diameter to achieve sufficient purchase of the stent against the wall.
Length is selected to provide anchoring of the stent with 3 cm or
more in both the cranial and caudal caval veins. Both woven and
laser-cut self-expanding stents have been used for this indication and
there are advantages to each. The woven stent allows for
reconstrainment during deployment (ch. 113), but suffers from
foreshortening, while the laser-cut stent must be deployed at one
time but remains the length at which it resides in the delivery
system.

Procedure
The dog typically is placed in dorsal recumbency to allow access to
both the neck and inguinal region and the right external jugular vein
and left femoral vein regions are clipped, aseptically prepped, and
draped. Vascular access is achieved through either jugular or femoral
vein, depending on the site of obstruction, and a large introducer
sheath (10 Fr) is advanced and sutured in place. For cranial vena
caval obstruction, femoral venous access may be preferable due to
swelling in the head and neck. Angiography, often DSA, is performed
proximal and distal to the obstruction and vena caval measurements
are made using a calibrated marker catheter. A guidewire is
advanced across the right atrium, which may require a snare catheter
to facilitate passage to the distal cava. Hemodynamic measurements
may be taken above and below the obstruction to document a
pressure gradient; collateral venous pathways are likely to have
developed in this condition and absence of a pressure gradient
suggests sufficient collaterals are present and stent placement may
not improve clinical signs. The stent is deployed over the guidewire
(Figure 115.9). Transatrial placement helps to avoid stent
migration across the tricuspid valve by securing its position in both

the cranial and caudal caval veins. It also can prevent excessively
large tumor thrombi from dislodging and migrating to the
pulmonary circulation. Following stent deployment, repeat
angiography and pressure gradients should be performed. Tumors of
the right atrium that lead to obstruction might release vasoactive
substances and the anesthesiologist or anesthetist should be
prepared for marked changes in blood pressure or heart rate as the
tumor is compressed by the stent.39 The venous access site is closed
routinely, often by placement of a superficial purse-string suture.
Follow-up depends on the nature of the disease, though repeat stent
implantation has been performed if cavitary effusion recurs.40 The
prognosis is fair, with all reported cases showing improvement in
clinical signs after transatrial stenting. However, this procedure is
merely palliative and progressive disease from the primary tumor is
likely. Survival of several years after stent implantation is possible.

LEFT HEART INTERVENTIONS
PATENT DUCTUS ARTERIOSUS
Historical Background and Patient Selection
Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is a common congenital heart defect
in dogs, reported as the most common defect in some surveys (ch.
231).13,41 It also occurs in cats, albeit less frequently.42 Without
therapy, the prognosis is poor and therefore, closure of the ductus,
either by surgical ligation or interventional occlusion, is
necessary.43,44
Transcatheter therapy for PDA in dogs was first reported in
1994.45 In the initial decade of transcatheter PDA therapy,
transarterial or transvenous coil delivery was the predominant
method used for ductal closure. Thereafter, human implants of
variable design 46-52 were reported for PDA occlusion in dogs and in
2007, a device designed and optimized for canine anatomy came on
the market.53,54 The species-specific device, the Canine Duct
Occluder (CDO), is now the preferred transcatheter device for PDA
occlusion in dogs due to an excellent safety and efficacy record and

ease of deployment.55 There remains a subset of small dogs,
however, for which vascular access of sufficient size to deliver a CDO
is not possible; in these small dogs, coils remain a useful technique to
achieve ductal closure. A nitinol device for small canine PDAs has
been evaluated with good results but was never made commercially
available.56

Procedure: Ductal Occluder
The technique for nearly all cases of transcatheter PDA occlusion
begins with the animal in dorsal recumbency and access to the
femoral triangle (typically the right side is chosen). Dorsal
recumbency is used for ease of access and catheter advancement in
the inguinal region as it results in a straighter femoral-iliac-aortic
orientation than with the dog in lateral recumbency. Once access is
achieved, the animal or fluoroscope can be turned to visualize the
procedure from a lateral imaging plane. For the CDO and
transarterial coil delivery, the femoral artery is typically isolated by
surgical cut-down and a combination of blunt and sharp dissection
(Figure 115.6). Percutaneous access is used for transvenous coil
delivery through the femoral vein. Percutaneous access also is
feasible for a transarterial approach with one study suggesting major
bleeding complications in only 3% of cases managed with manual
compression.57 In most veterinary centers, surgical isolation of the
artery is preferred. The author has used vascular closure devices58,59
successfully in dogs to close percutaneous femoral arterial access;
however, the thin subcutaneous tissue of puppies makes vascular
closure devices more of a challenge in young dogs undergoing PDA
intervention. Arterial access first is achieved with a 22-gauge overthe-needle catheter and a 4-Fr micropuncture set with a 0.018″ wire.
The micropuncture set is exchanged over a 0.035″ angled
hydrophilic guidewire for a long vascular sheath of sufficient internal
diameter to deliver the desired CDO (Table 115.1). The long sheath
is advanced to the aortic isthmus (i.e., a region of the proximal
descending aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery, at the level
of the ductus arteriosus)60 over the guidewire, after which the
guidewire and dilator are removed. Angiography is performed
through the long sheath and it delineates ductal anatomy and

minimal ductal diameter in most dogs (Figure 115.10, A; Video
115.6)

. If sufficient contrast flow cannot be provided through the

sheath, a pigtail catheter is advanced through the vascular sheath
and a power injection is performed in the ascending aorta; in the
author’s experience, this rarely is necessary. A measurement of the
minimal ductal diameter at the pulmonary ostium is made from the
angiographic image and compared to transesophageal measurements
of minimal ductal diameter. An appropriate CDO is chosen with a
central waist that is 1.5-2 times the minimal ductal diameter. The
hydrophilic guidewire and sheath dilator are then placed back into
the vascular sheath and directed across the PDA into the pulmonary
trunk under fluoroscopic guidance, taking care to not engage the
pulmonary valve with the stiff dilator or sheath. The dilator and
guidewire are removed and the device prepared for implantation.
The screw-tip connection of the delivery cable to the CDO should
ideally be tested by removing the device and screwing it back onto
the delivery cable. The device must screw on and off easily or it
should not be implanted in the animal. When tightening, the device
should be turned until it stops (fully tight) and then turned back onehalf turn; it should not be over-tightened. While on the delivery
cable, the CDO is vigorously flushed and purged of all air bubbles by
extruding and reconstraining the device under saline. The CDO is
then advanced into the long sheath and passed out into the
pulmonary trunk, taking care to extrude only the pulmonary artery
disc. The entire system (sheath, delivery cable) is then withdrawn
until the open pulmonary artery disc engages with the pulmonary
ostium of the PDA (Figure 115.10, B). Slight tension is placed on
the system to ensure the disc is flush with the PDA and this tension is
maintained as the sheath is slowly retracted over the delivery cable to
expand the ductal disc within the PDA ampulla (Figure 115.10, C;
Video 115.7)

. It is common to require a slight forward

advancement of the delivery cable after the ductal disc is deployed to
allow it to regain its cupped shape. The position of the device on the
fluoroscopic image should be compared to the prior angiogram to
confirm it is in the correct location of the PDA. Gentle
pushing/pulling on the delivery cable helps to confirm the device is
appropriately seated; however, even an optimally positioned device

can be pushed out or pulled out of the PDA if too great a force is
exerted. It should be possible to gently pull the cable to deliberately
evert the ductal disc, then advance it to return to the proper shape,
without dislodgment. The author typically waits 5 minutes after
deployment and performs an angiogram through the long vascular
sheath to confirm ductal closure (Video 115.7). If a small amount of
central flow is still observed, it will likely close without further
intervention (Figures 115.10, D and E; Video 115.7)

. If

contrast flow is noted cranial or caudal to the waist and around the
device then the device is improperly positioned and should be redeployed. A similar effect, or failure of the CDO to adopt the correct
shape, can be caused by selecting a CDO with a proximal disc that is
too large for the animal’s ductal ampulla. If satisfactorily implanted,
the device is released by counterclockwise rotation of the delivery
cable, using either the supplied pin or a hemostat, and the cable and
sheath are removed (Figure 115.10, F; Video 115.7)

. The

femoral artery is repaired, ligated, or otherwise controlled and the
skin closed. The animal is kept sedated and quiet overnight and
echocardiography is performed the next day to confirm persistent
ductal occlusion.
