Procedure: Intravascular Coils
Transarterial Coils
The procedure for transarterial coil delivery is comparable to that
described for CDO deployment, except a 4-Fr or 5-Fr catheter is used
for vascular access either alone or through an introducer sheath. As
most cases undergoing transarterial coil delivery relate to insufficient
vascular size, the catheter is placed directly into the vessel with a
hemostatic valve or Tuohy-Borst adapter placed on the catheter hub
to control hemorrhage rather than through a sheath. Angiography is
as described above, through the catheter rather than a sheath. Coil
selection is also based on the minimal ductal diameter, with a coil
loop diameter chosen that is twice the minimal angiographic ductal
diameter; 0.038″ or 0.035″ coils are chosen for small dogs. The

catheter tip is positioned in the ductus, the position is verified by
hand contrast injections, and the coil is carefully advanced through
the catheter to the ductal ampulla (Figure 115.11). If detachable
coils are used, they are mounted on the delivery cable and advanced
into the catheter. The catheter is retracted to expose the coil and,
once positioning is appropriate, the coil is released by
counterclockwise rotation of the delivery cable. If non-detachable
coils are used, they are advanced with a straight-tipped guidewire of
the same thickness as the coil. The drawback to non-detachable coils
is that re-capture and repositioning are not possible; as such,
confirmation of appropriate size and location of deployment is
paramount to success. The author reserves transarterial coil delivery
for dogs of small size (typically 2-3.5 kg) and with a narrow ductal
ostium on the pulmonary side, as these cases appear most amenable
to coil occlusion. Reports of smaller coils being deployed in even
smaller dogs (1-2 kg), either from a carotid or femoral arterial
approach, exist in the literature.61,62 If the dog weighs <2.5 kg, the
author typically recommends transvenous coil occlusion or surgical
ligation.

Transvenous Coils
Transvenous coil delivery is possible in small dogs or cats via
retrograde cannulation of the ductus (Figure 115.12; Video 115.8)
.9,52,63 This technique allows for easier vascular access in small
patients as the jugular or femoral vein are larger and more pliable
than is the femoral artery. Catheterization of the PDA from venous
access requires placement of an end-hole catheter into the
pulmonary trunk with a straight-tipped flexible guidewire advanced
across the ductus to the descending aorta. The delivery is comparable
to that described for transarterial coil delivery, though the
detachable coil system is necessary to allow the coil to be exposed in
the descending aorta and then withdrawn into the ductal ampulla.
The delivery cable is then further retracted to the pulmonary trunk,
leaving 1-2 loops of coil spanning the ductal ostium (Figure 115.12).

Prognosis

The prognosis of transcatheter PDA occlusion is very good, with
perioperative survival rates of 90-100% and median survival of >11.5
years.51,54,64,65 Factors reported to have a negative effect on survival
time include the preoperative presence of clinical signs, concurrent
congenital heart disease, large breed, older age, increased weight,
and severe mitral regurgitation documented within 24 hours of
ductal closure.44

BALLOON AORTIC VALVULOPLASTY
Subaortic stenosis (SAS) is a common congenital defect of largebreed dogs; valvular aortic stenosis is more rarely encountered (ch.
231).14,66 Interventional therapy for SAS remains controversial, with
a prospective case-control study showing no survival benefit for
balloon aortic valvuloplasty (BAV) compared to medical therapy
(atenolol) alone.67 Alternate approaches to transcatheter dilation,
including cutting balloon (CB) and HPB valvuloplasty, have also
been attempted in dogs with SAS.68-71 However, long-term results
remain only partially documented 68,72,73 and no comparison to
medical therapy or the natural history of the disease has been made.
Currently, the author advises CB and HPB BAV for SAS in dogs that
display clinical signs (syncope, weakness, congestive heart failure),
as clinical improvement can be seen.74 Dogs with very severe
stenotic gradients (e.g., >150 mm Hg instantaneous pressure
gradient) and a thin, discrete membrane are also reasonable
candidates for CB and HPB BAV though it remains unclear whether
the procedure provides a durable benefit.

FIGURE 115.11 Fluoroscopic images during
transarterial coil occlusion of patent ductus
arteriosus (PDA) in a small dog. An angled (Kumpe)
catheter is advanced to the aortic isthmus and an
angiogram (A) highlights the location and minimal
ductal diameter (arrow) of the PDA. The coil is
delivered to the ductal ampulla and extruded via a
guidewire. Upon delivery, a repeat angiogram (B)
confirms the coil location (arrowhead) and cessation
of ductal flow.

Procedure
The approach for BAV is typically via a carotid artery cut-down. The
dog is positioned in either dorsal or lateral recumbency and the
ventral and lateral neck (either right or left) are clipped, aseptically
prepped, and draped. A 3-4 cm incision is made along the lateral
border of the trachea and blunt and sharp dissection used for
exposing the common carotid artery, which must be carefully
separated from the vagosympathetic trunk. Suture or vessel loops are
passed around the carotid artery, cranial and caudal to the proposed
access site, to stabilize the vessel during access. The author also
obtains jugular venous access at the same time and advances a
temporary pacing lead into the right ventricle. Tachypacing during
BAV is advantageous as rapid heart rates limit cardiac output and
improve seating of the balloon across the desired target. In the dog,

pacing rates of 220 to 240 beats per minute are usually required to
sufficiently limit forward stroke volume during BAV. Arterial
puncture is performed with an 18-gauge over-the-needle catheter or
arterial access needle, and a vascular sheath of 1 to 2 Fr sizes larger
than required by the desired HPB is advanced into the vessel. The
ascending aorta is catheterized and a pigtail catheter used for
performing angiography in the aortic root for a baseline assessment
of aortic insufficiency. The left heart is then catheterized with a
marker pigtail catheter and left ventriculography is performed to
delineate the site of subaortic obstruction as well as left ventricular
size and function, presence of mitral regurgitation, coronary arterial
anatomy, and other concurrent defects (Figure 115.13; Video 115.9)
. The greatest challenge is crossing the aortic valve in these dogs,
as aortic valve excursion is limited by reduced forward flow, and
extensive poststenotic dilation allows the catheter to wander in the
ascending aorta or engage a coronary ostium. Rarely, the pigtail
catheter will advance alone through the valve orifice. Alternatively, a
guidewire with a long and floppy tip can be used for gently probing
the aortic orifice and with repeated attempts will cross in most cases.
Following angiography, the angiographic catheter is removed over a
0.018″ guidewire that is pre-shaped with a 540-720° curve at the
end, which will enable it to seat in the left ventricular apex. Over this
wire the CB is advanced to the level of the subaortic ridge and rapidly
inflated (Video 115.10)

. Selection of CB size is based upon the

minimal stenotic diameter of the left ventricular outflow tract, with a
balloon chosen at a roughly 1:1 ratio to the stenotic diameter.
Currently, the largest size of commercially available CB is 8 mm in
diameter, which is large enough to engage the subaortic ridge of
most, though not all, dogs that have SAS of a severity that justifies
this intervention. After 2-3 inflations, the CB is deflated and removed
from the animal, with the pigtail catheter placed again over the
0.018″ guidewire. The guidewire is exchanged for an ultra-stiff
0.035″ guidewire with a long floppy tip. The end of the 0.035″
guidewire is also pre-shaped with a 540-720° curve and placed in the
left ventricular apex. A HPB is then chosen—typically the ATLAS or
ATLAS GOLD line of HPBs—as these are designed to withstand
pressures of 12-18 atmospheres. The diameter of HPB chosen is

based on the true aortic valve annulus and sized 0.9-1:1 for balloon to
aortic valve diameter. For smaller dogs in which the smallest ATLAS
HPB (12 mm diameter) is too large, the CONQUEST HPB can be
selected, which also has very high burst pressures (up to 30 atm) and
comes in appropriate lengths. The HPB is advanced over the 0.035″
guidewire to the level of the subaortic lesion and rapidly inflated
(Videos 115.10, 115.11)

. As with BPV, successful inflation involves

the appearance of a stenotic waist, which resolves with increased
pressure and is not apparent on subsequent inflations (Figure
115.14; Videos 115.10, 115.11

). Following 2-3 inflations across

the outflow tract, the HPB is removed, pressures are measured, and
the change in gradient evaluated compared to preoperative values.
An aortic root injection is then performed with the same settings as
the initial aortic angiogram to evaluate for any change in the severity
of aortic valve insufficiency. Once satisfactory results are achieved,
the balloon dilation catheter is removed, often requiring constant
negative pressure during retrieval to allow passage through the
sheath, or the sheath and catheter are removed as a unit if excess
tension is encountered during retrieval through the sheath due to the
large profile common to deflated HPBs. The carotid artery is
repaired with 5-0 or 6-0 monofilament suture and the surgical
exposure closed routinely in 3 layers. Care should be taken to allow
the carotid access site to bleed temporarily prior to repair, to be
certain any thrombus around the introducer sheath is removed
through the access site prior to closure. The neck is routinely
bandaged and the dog recovered with monitoring of the cardiac
rhythm and administration of analgesia, sedation, and prophylactic
antibiotics.

FIGURE 115.12 Fluoroscopic images of
transvenous coil occlusion of patent ductus

catheter is advanced to the pulmonary trunk with

(between arrowheads). A wire is advanced retrograde

catheter is advanced over the wire and the coil
extruded into the descending aorta before being
retracted into the ductal ampulla (C). An additional

side of the PDA and once stability is confirmed the

FIGURE 115.14 Fluoroscopic images during highpressure balloon aortic valvuloplasty from a

A similar approach to BAV can be undertaken for dogs with
valvular aortic stenosis. However, the CB is not used; rather standard
angioplasty balloon dilation catheters are utilized as described for
BPV if these dogs have fusion of apparently normal aortic valve cusps
because they do not require scoring and high pressure tearing of the
fibrous tissue that is present in SAS.22 For aortic valvular stenosis
with valve dysplasia (thickened, hypoplastic leaflets), BAV with the
ATLAS or ATLAS GOLD line of HPBs may be required to achieve
sufficient radial force on the valve. The ratio of balloon diameter to
aortic valve annulus for conventional BAV in the setting of valvular
aortic stenosis is chosen as 0.9-1:1 to limit the risk of postoperative
aortic insufficiency.

Prognosis
The prognosis for CB and HPB BAV is unclear, though an interim
analysis of 28 dogs that underwent this procedure for SAS found a

decrease in peak systolic pressure gradient from a mean of 143 mm
Hg to 78 mm Hg at 1 day after BAV, 84 mm Hg at 1 month, 89 mm
Hg at 3 months, 92 mm Hg at 6 months, and 116 mm Hg at 12
months post-BAV.74 Six dogs had died after BAV, including 3 dogs
euthanized for progressive myocardial failure, 1 dog euthanized for
syncope, and 2 dogs that died suddenly.74 In the author’s experience,
a reduction in gradient is achievable and clients report improved
exercise capacity. If the dog had clinical signs (syncope, congestive
heart failure, profound intolerance to exercise) a benefit can be
achieved.73 However, the gradient typically is reduced to the high
moderate range (70-80 mm Hg) and substantial obstruction persists.
The risk for sudden death does not appear to be lessened when CB
and HPB BAV have been performed. As the procedure is costly and
involves arrhythmic and anesthetic risk, the value of performing this
procedure in a dog that is not showing clinical signs is questionable,
although a randomized prospective study is required to answer this
question. In the absence of such a study, the author reserves this
procedure for cases that display clinical signs or that are at high risk
for clinical signs based on the severity of cardiac remodeling and
peak systolic pressure gradient as described above.

SEPTAL DEFECT OCCLUSION
Large defects in the atrial or ventricular septum are associated with
left-to-right shunting of blood, pulmonary overcirculation, and either
pulmonary vascular disease or left-sided congestive heart failure (ch.
231). Closure of such defects is not common in veterinary medicine
due to the scarcity and cost of open-heart surgery. However,
transcatheter options have been described that allow for closure of
both atrial septal defects75,76 (ASDs) and ventricular septal defects7779
(VSDs) by minimally invasive methods and without
cardiopulmonary bypass.

Procedure: Atrial Septal Defect Closure
Transcatheter closure of ASD is performed by a transvenous
approach—either jugular or femoral venous access (Figure 115.15).

Transcatheter techniques can only be applied to ASDs of the ostium
secundum type at this time, as sufficient tissue around the defect is
required to seat and hold the device in place; optimally, the defect
should have septal tissue around 75% of the circumference to
consider transcatheter closure.76 Most cases reported in dogs have
used the Amplatzer septal occluder (ASO), though the author has
successfully closed an ASD in a dog with the Gore CARDIOFORM
Septal Occluder (Figure 115.16). The center with the largest case
experience advises a jugular venous approach for canine ASD
closure,76 though the author has successfully performed the
technique from a femoral venous approach and this was the
approach used in the first reported canine case.75 The defect is sized
by transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography and this size
is confirmed in the catheterization laboratory using a balloon sizing
catheter (Amplatzer sizing balloon II). The device is selected to
match or be minimally larger (0.5-1 mm) than the largest diameter
measured. The optimal imaging planes to determine maximal
dimension by echocardiography have not been determined in
animals; therefore, use of a sizing balloon is advised to determine the
device required. The device is attached to the delivery cable and
carefully purged of air by immersion in saline and repeated
retraction into the delivery system followed by saline flush through
the delivery system.
A delivery sheath, typically supplied by the manufacturer of the
device, is advanced over a guidewire, across the atrial septum and
into the left atrium. Once the left heart is catheterized, the animal is
heparinized with 150 U/kg unfractionated heparin IV to limit
thrombotic risk. The prepared device is advanced into the delivery
sheath, allowing for some back-bleeding through the device to
confirm all air has been removed. The device is then advanced to the
left atrium and the distal retention disc (left atrial disc) is deployed
(Figure 115.15). Careful tension is then placed on the entire
delivery system as the distal retention disc is retracted against the
atrial septum and the central waist is deployed by retracting the
delivery sheath over the delivery cable. In animals with minimal rim
tissue, it is very easy to pull the device through the ASD so gentle
traction and transesophageal guidance are mandatory. If the waist is
appropriately seated in the ostium of the ASD, the proximal

retention disc (right atrial disc) is then deployed (Video 115.12)

.

All planes of the device are investigated by transesophageal
echocardiography to confirm the device is appropriately positioned
and that the distal and proximal discs are on the appropriate side of
the septum (left and right, respectively) in all planes. Minimal
manipulation of the delivery cable can be performed to assess the
stability of the ASO, though as noted above it is easy to dislodge even
an appropriately deployed device. If it is determined that the device
is appropriately positioned and stable, the ASO is released from the
screw tip of the delivery cable by counterclockwise rotation of the
cable, either with the supplied pin or a hemostat, and the cable and
sheath are removed (Video 115.12)

. The femoral access site is

repaired, ligated, or otherwise controlled and the skin closed. The
animal is kept sedated and quiet overnight and echocardiography is
performed the next day to confirm device position and assess ASD
closure.

Procedure: Ventricular Septal Defect Closure
The technique for transcatheter VSD closure is comparable to that
described for transcatheter ASD closure. The type of VSD most
amenable to transcatheter closure is the muscular-type defect,
surrounded entirely by muscular septum on all sides.79 However,
transcatheter closure of membranous-type defects has also been
reported in the dog with specific, asymmetric devices available.78
The author has closed perimembranous VSDs in three dogs using the
CDO device79a—all cases had an aneurysm of the membranous
septum providing sufficient distance from the aortic valve to position
a CDO across the defect.

Outcome and Prognosis
The outcome of transcatheter ASD and VSD closure appears good,
with case reports and case series describing event-free survival in
several dogs.76,79 However, embolization of these devices is a risk
and can be devastating, as surgical retrieval may be required via

advanced surgical techniques that are not available at all veterinary
centers.76,80,81 Additionally, thrombosis of the device is a risk and
therapy with clopidogrel (2 mg/kg PO q24h) is advised for 6 months
post-implantation.

HYBRID INTERVENTIONS
A hybrid procedure refers to a procedure that utilizes a surgical
approach combined with image-guided intervention.82,83 Examples
in veterinary medicine include delivery of balloon dilation catheters
directly through the left atrium via echocardiographic guidance for
treatment of mitral stenosis84 or cor triatriatum sinister85 as well as
perventricular VSD occlusion86 and transatrial ASD occlusion.80
Future options for mitral valve repair or replacement also are likely
to use a hybrid approach given the complexities of left heart access
and the large delivery systems required of these techniques.87

PERVENTRICULAR VENTRICULAR
SEPTAL DEFECT OCCLUSION
As an example of the hybrid approach to cardiac disease, devices
used for closing VSDs described above via a transcatheter approach
can also be delivered directly through the RV wall and guided by
echocardiography.86,88 The indication for such a technique is
dictated by animal size; some transcatheter devices require delivery
systems of 9 Fr diameter and larger, which may be too large for
vascular access in small dogs or cats. In such cases, a right lateral
thoracotomy can be performed to expose the RV free wall and
beating heart. A pursestring suture is placed around the proposed
access site prior to myocardial puncture to control hemorrhage. A
vascular access needle is inserted directly through the RV free wall,
guided by echocardiography, through which a guidewire is placed
and the desired delivery system is advanced (Figure 115.17; Video
115.13)

. Echocardiographic and fluoroscopic guidance can then

proceed similar to the transcatheter delivery of the same device. A
hybrid approach such as this not only overcomes the challenge of
vascular access in a small dog, it also allows for a more direct path to
the defect, which can make deployment of the device more
straightforward than a conventional, percutaneous approach. The
drawback to hybrid techniques is an increased morbidity associated
with the approach, but such morbidity is typically manageable in
dogs.

GASTROINTESTINAL
ESOPHAGEAL BALLOON DILATION,
BOUGIENAGE, AND STENTING
Indications and Background
Esophageal obstructions in dogs and cats are most commonly
associated with a foreign body or an acquired esophageal stricture
(ch. 259). Other causes include esophageal neoplasia and
extraluminal compressions from vascular ring anomalies (ch.
259).1-3 Strictures occur secondary to mucosal injury and this is
commonly the result of severe gastroesophageal reflux, caustic
mucosal damage, or trauma.2-25 Since the esophageal mucosa is
lined with non-keratinized, stratified squamous epithelial cells, the
acid and enzymes in gastric fluid can result in severe mucosal and
muscular injury, leading to circumferential narrowing and an
esophageal stricture.16
Various treatments for esophageal strictures have been reported,
including bougienage, balloon dilation, a one-stage esophageal
balloon dilation feeding tube (BE-Tube) for serial dilation,
esophageal resection and anastomosis, and salvage esophageal
stenting.1-22,26,27 Esophageal strictures are a notoriously frustrating
condition for veterinarians to treat because they often recur and can
be difficult to cure.26 Treatments using topical therapies to decrease
stricture recurrence like triamcinolone injections12,16 or mitomycin
C (MMC)22 have been used. Previous retrospective studies
evaluating esophageal balloon dilation suggest a good outcome in up
to 75% of cases where a gruel diet is tolerated,2,4-9 but only 14-25%
of patients are reported to return to eating normal dry food. In
humans, refractory strictures are those that fail to resolve despite
more than three dilation procedures,13-15 and this is commonly seen
in veterinary patients as well.
Balloon dilation and bougienage historically are the most
commonly considered treatment options in dogs and cats with
esophageal strictures.2-9 More recently, the use of a BE-Tube for

serial balloon dilation done at home, twice daily for 6 weeks, has
improved the ultimate outcome in dogs and cats compared to all the
commonly considered alternatives.27 Esophageal stents (

Video

116.1) have been reserved for those cases where balloon dilation,
bougienage or a BE-Tube fails, and they are usually considered a last
resort.18-21,26 The use of various types of stents was reported
retrospectively26 in a group of 9 dogs: biodegradable, self-expanding
plastic stents (SEPS), self-expanding metallic stents (SEMS), as well
as covered and uncovered stents were described. These stents
ultimately were found to improve dysphagia, but were met with
common complications of discomfort when swallowing, profound
chronic nausea, hypersalivation, and stent migration. Due to the high
likelihood of poor tolerance, this procedure should be considered a
salvage procedure. If a stent is determined to be the best therapeutic
modality, a covered stent is typically recommended so that if the
stent is poorly tolerated, it can be removed endoscopically. Stents
seem to be far better tolerated for malignancies of the esophagus
than for benign strictures.1,23

Equipment
For evaluation of an esophageal obstruction (ch. 259), a standard
flexible gastrointestinal (GI) endoscope is used (ch. 107). Ideally, all
bougie or balloon dilation procedures should be done under
concurrent fluoroscopic guidance. This allows the operator to see
when the entire stricture is effaced, which is not possible with
endoscopic imaging alone (Figure 116.1). Many strictures result in
both mucosal and muscular fibrosis, and even if the fibrous band of
the mucosa is sufficiently effaced, as visualized endoscopically, the
muscular component may remain intact, resulting in recurrence of
the stricture.
Balloon dilation catheters can be variable or fixed in diameter, and
some are placed over a guidewire, while others have a soft tip and
closed end. The authors recommend to always perform balloon
dilation over a guidewire, as that ensures that the tip of the balloon
dilation catheter is not buried within the esophageal wall. If this were
to happen, then a large perforation of the esophagus could ensue. For

proper dilation, an inflation device is required. The amount of force
required to properly efface a fibrous band can be upward of 6-12
atmospheres of pressure (ATM), whereas manual inflation produces
a maximum of 1-4 ATM (Figure 116.2). A wide variety of balloon
sizes should be available (6-30 mm diameter). If only smaller
diameter balloons are available, side-by-side inflation of multiple
balloons can achieve larger dilation diameters.28 Bougies (Figure
116.3) should be used under fluoroscopic guidance as well. In order
to know the size of the bougie or balloon to choose, a contrast study
with air insufflation to demonstrate the esophageal diameter cranial
and caudal to the stricture is ideal. This minimizes the risk of
overdilating the esophagus and potentially causing a tear.

Techniques
Balloon Dilation Procedure
A balloon size is chosen based on the length of the stricture and the
diameter of the normal esophagus. This can be estimated during
endoscopy; however, a more accurate determination is typically done
using a marker catheter, contrast/air, and fluoroscopic imaging (chs.
113 and 115). Once a balloon size is chosen, it is advanced through
the lumen of the stricture with simultaneous endoscopic
visualization. Using a guidewire helps to prevent iatrogenic trauma
or esophageal perforation and is the method of choice. A balloon is
chosen that is at least 2 cm longer than the stenosis, and the
diameter of the balloon should be equivalent to the diameter of the
esophagus caudal to the stenosis, measured using fluoroscopy. If
fluoroscopy is not used, then an estimated diameter is chosen using
the outer diameter of the endoscope for a reference. In this case, it is
typically recommended to start small (~6 mm) and work up in 2 mm
increments until the lesion is visually torn and there is good
apposition of the balloon against the esophageal mucosal wall when
inflated. There is some argument that this is not necessary and
dilating to the known esophageal diameter avoids the need for
multiple balloon sizes to be used. If we are able to measure using
fluoroscopy, which in our practice is standard of care, then we only
choose the appropriate size based on the size of the esophagus. Since
endoscopic visualization is only confirming mucosal effacement of a

stricture, fluoroscopy is always recommended to confirm muscular
effacement as well (Figure 116.4).
Prior to balloon dilation, superficial, local injections of
corticosteroids (triamcinolone) may be utilized to help reduce
stricture re-formation (Figure 116.5). Triamcinolone injections are
done using a 23- to 25-gauge, 4- to 5-mm length endoscopic injection
needle, preloaded with the appropriate dose of triamcinolone (6-8
mg/patient in 0.5 mL aliquots per quadrant up to 0.3 mg/kg). After
injection, a bleb of fluid should be visualized under the mucosal
tissue. There are limited data to support that doing this technique
improves outcomes or slows the recurrence of stricture reformation.29
If balloon dilation is being done under fluoroscopic guidance, the
inflation device is filled with a 50% contrast solution (diluted with
saline) so that the dilation can be visualized but the viscosity of the
contrast mixture is reduced for ease of administration and removal.
If endoscopy is used solely, then saline infusion is acceptable. Once
the balloon is across the stenosis and the stricture is engaged, the
inflation device is used to inflate the balloon to the recommended
nominal balloon pressure while the balloon is tightly held in place at
the mouth. Some degree of superficial mucosal tearing and bleeding
is expected. In general, the procedure is complete when the stricture
is effaced based on fluoroscopy (Figure 116.4), or the mucosal
tearing seen endoscopically extends linearly beyond the stricture,
deep into the submucosa, or excessive bleeding is seen (Figure
116.6). The inflated balloon is often advanced and withdrawn within
the esophagus to judge if the appropriate size had been used (good
contact) and there are no additional strictures present.
A recommended interval between balloon dilations varies per
clinician and institution. No consensus or standard has been
established in either human or veterinary medicine.13-15 There have
been little data to support that frequent, small intervals of balloon
dilation are better, though with the advent of the BE-Tube, where
dilation is performed twice daily for 6 weeks, outcomes have
surpassed those of balloon dilation done intermittently, or as
needed, based on comparisons between publications.2-9,27

Bougienage Procedure3
The bougie size is selected based on estimations of stricture and
normal esophageal diameters, as discussed above for balloon
dilation. The initial bougie is typically 1-2 mm larger than the
stricture meatus, and is subsequently increased in 1-2 mm
increments until the lesion is similar in size to the normal esophagus.
Topical MMC infusions have been performed in cases of refractory
strictures.22 MMC is an antibiotic and antineoplastic drug that is
produced by Streptomyces caespitosus. MMC causes inhibition of
fibroblast proliferation. This has been shown in children with
esophageal strictures to have some benefit in preventing
recurrence.22 In veterinary medicine, if MMC is used, the
recommendation has been to endoscopically place 2.5-5 mL of a
0.1% solution soaked on a gauze sponge over the stricture site
topically for 5 minutes and then the site is flushed with saline. Gloves
should be worn when using this material. There are no data in
veterinary medicine to support that this technique improves
outcomes.

Esophageal Balloon Dilation Feeding Tube (BETube)
An indwelling balloon dilation esophagostomy tube (BE-Tube) has
been used more readily over the past 5-7 years.27 The goal of this
device is to provide a single procedure to repeatedly dilate a
stricture(s) and prevent stricture recurrence. This provides the
advantages of a stent (more prolonged maintenance of effacement)
without the disadvantages (persistent esophageal distension). This
device likely provides cost savings compared to serial balloon
dilation procedures or the placement of a stent. The BE-Tube
(Figure 116.7, A) is a standard esophagostomy tube (Mila, Inc) that
has a non-compliant, high-pressure angioplasty balloon mounted
externally, with a more compliant, low-pressure balloon mounted
outside the inner balloon to maintain a low profile of the device in
the esophagus between inflations. The device has inflation tubing
side-by-side to the E-tube, permitting intermittent inflation of the
balloon rapidly twice daily at home.

Briefly, dogs are placed in lateral recumbency and the entire
esophagus is visualized using both fluoroscopic and endoscopic
guidance. The left lateral aspect of the neck is clipped and aseptically
prepared, as for esophagostomy feeding tube placement (ch. 81).
The esophageal strictures are identified using endoscopy and then a
contrast study is performed to measure the esophageal diameter.
This is done using a marker catheter, iodinated contrast material and
fluoroscopy (Figure 116.4). While insufflating the esophagus with
the endoscope to distend the lumen with air, contrast is also infused,
which highlights the walls of the lumen. Using the marker catheter
for calibration and reference, the diameter of the esophageal lumen
is measured, both cranial and caudal to the stricture. Then the length
of the stricture is determined. This helps to choose a balloon size to
efface the stricture, as described above for esophageal balloon
dilation. Once the entire stricture is effaced (Figure 116.4, C), the
BE-Tube is placed. The size of the BE-Tube is determined based on
the size of the esophagus and the length of the stricture and is
usually the same diameter as the previously used dilation balloon
used to efface the stricture. The tube size options (diameter × length)
are: 10 mm × 12 cm, 15 mm × 15 cm, 20 mm × 20 cm, 25 mm × 25
cm, and 30 mm × 30 cm.

variable sizes.
A Tube passer specifically designed and sized to pass E-tubes (ch.
81) or the BE-Tube (Figure 116.7, C) is inserted into the mouth and
advanced into the cranial esophagus. Using the most aseptic manner
possible, an incision is made over the angled-ball tip just caudal to
the upper esophageal sphincter (UES) (Figure 116.8, A-H). This
location is determined by fluoroscopy and endoscopy. This allows as
much of the balloon to cross the entire length of the esophageal
lumen as possible. The inner stylet of the tube passer is removed and
the non-balloon end of BE-Tube is passed through the sheath, from
the mouth outwards (Figure 116.8, F). Then the passer sheath is
removed from the neck and the balloon end of the BE-Tube is passed
down the esophagus over the guidewire previously used for the
balloon dilation catheter to avoid damaging the previously dilated
esophagus. More explicit details are in the instruction for use manual
of the device according to the manufacturer’s recommendations as
there are nuances that make the procedure different from a standard
E-tube placement. The tube is then secured in the left lateral neck.
Placement is monitored with fluoroscopy to ensure appropriate
coverage across the stricture(s), without interfering with the UES or
lower esophageal sphincter (LES), when possible. With very

proximal or distal strictures, the device can be placed through either
sphincter (as a pharyngostomy tube proximally, or advanced through
the LES distally) when necessary and this can still result in a good
outcome. Once secured, the BE-Tube is inflated with the
recommended volume of air using a digiflator under fluoroscopic
guidance to ensure dilation is uniform across the stricture site.

Postoperatively, all animals are given standard treatment for
esophagitis, based on clinician preference, with medications like a
proton pump inhibitor, antiemetics, sucralfate, and pain
medications, as needed (ch. 259). At home, the owners are
instructed to inflate the device twice daily for 6 weeks. Typically, at 6
weeks post-operatively, the animal has the tube removed and is rescoped to assess for stricture resolution.

Esophageal Stenting
(Video 116.1) For esophageal stent placement, dogs are placed in
lateral recumbency and the entire esophagus is visualized using
fluoroscopic and endoscopic guidance. The left ventrolateral cervical
region of the dog is clipped and aseptically prepared in order to place
tacking sutures on the cranial aspect of the stent to prevent stent
migration. Once the stricture is visualized, the esophagus and
stricture are measured using a guidewire and marker catheter
combination. The stricture is pre-ballooned partially, to permit safe
passage of the endoscope through the lumen to visualize the most
caudal aspect of the abnormal tissue. Length is typically measured to
ensure at least 1-2 cm of non-strictured esophagus is stented both
cranial and caudal to the location of the stricture. The patient is
placed in dorsal recumbency and the C-arm is rotated so that a
lateral image is projected during stent placement to accurately see
stent deployment. If possible, the cranial aspect of the stent is
extended to cross the level of the thoracic inlet so that it can be safely
and easily sutured in place through the esophageal wall to prevent
migration. Sutures can also be placed endoluminally using a doublelumen endoscope. This procedure should not be done unless the
operator is very comfortable understanding various types of stent
deployment (Figures 116.9 and 116.10). Based on limited data26 the
authors recommend a covered stent (Figure 116.10) that is sutured
in place, and then it can be removed if it is poorly tolerated. This
procedure is usually reserved when a BE-Tube technique fails or the
location of the stricture is not easily amendable to using a BE-Tube
(e.g., very proximal, within a couple of centimeters of the UES).

Follow-up

Patients are typically discharged the same day (or the following day
for BE-Tubes) as any esophageal procedure and routinely treated
with a proton pump inhibitor and sucralfate. Repeat balloon dilation
can be performed as needed based on clinical signs of recurrence
after any of the above procedures.

Complications
The most severe complication seen with treatment of esophageal
strictures is esophageal tearing, resulting in a pneumomediastinum,
pneumothorax, and potentially pyothorax. Most tears do not require
surgical correction and will heal by second intention, but require the
placement of a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube
(ch. 81). This is very uncommon if esophageal dilation is done over a
guidewire. Most tears are likely due to the balloon catheter being
passed through the esophageal wall of highly diseased tissues or
immediately after a dilation procedure. Esophageal stricture
recurrence post-dilation is also seen in a majority of dogs with
standard balloon dilation or bougienage.3-9

Outcome
Success rates vary depending on the outcome measures and
technique. Balloon dilation is reported to have a success rate of 7788%,2-9 but the definition of success can include persistent
regurgitation that is <50% of the original presentation, or the
tolerance of specific dietary consistency, including those dogs that
can only be fed liquid or gruel. A study evaluating the use of
bougienage in dogs and cats found a “good” outcome, with tolerance
of solid food and minimal regurgitation, in 70% of dogs and 75% of
cats.3
In the authors’ experience, greater success has been achieved since
utilizing the combination of endoscopy and fluoroscopy to monitor
stricture effacement, since a false sense of success is commonly seen
if endoscopy is utilized alone. The highest success rates are seen, in
the authors’ practice, with a BE-Tube. In one study,30 91.7% of
animals had an improved dysphagia score at the end of the follow-up
period, with more patients showing no evidence of dysphagia along
with fewer anesthetic episodes, when compared to those that
underwent bougienage or balloon dilation alone.

Special Considerations
Esophageal stents should only be considered when traditional
dilation attempts have failed.

Alternatives

The authors have placed an esophageal feeding tube through the
lumen of a stricture after balloon dilation to prevent the edges of the
stricture from coapting. The intent is to maintain a lumen and allow
a mechanism for feeding if the stricture were to recur, without the
need for a gastrostomy tube. This has been helpful when there is a
concern about the lack of nutritional support if another balloon
dilation procedure must be delayed.

GASTROINTESTINAL STENTING
Indications and Background
Obstructions of the GI tract secondary to strictures or tumors occur
most commonly in the descending colon at the colorectal junction
(chs. 263 and 264).25,30-34 Tumors have also been seen at the
gastric cardia, pyloric antrum, and proximal duodenum but can be

anywhere along the intestinal tract.35,36 In humans, stenting of GI
malignant obstructions is commonly reported; it is typically
considered a palliative treatment for nonresectable neoplasia,27 or as
a “bridge” to a more definitive surgery, providing immediate
endoluminal decompression and improved quality of life.32-36 If
surgery is contraindicated, or not possible, stenting is considered a
good long-term solution, with clinical success rates approaching
90%, and technical success rates as high as 92-100%.35,36
Stenting of the stomach or duodenum is not commonly performed
in veterinary medicine. It has been done for malignant obstruction of
the gastric cardia, pyloric outflow tract, and duodenum in the
authors’ practice. Stenting should be reserved for cases where
traditional surgical resection is not recommended. The location of
the major and minor duodenal papillae should be appreciated prior
to duodenal stenting, as compression of a tumor in this region could
result in a biliary or pancreatic duct obstruction. If the lesion is
obstructive, resulting in vomiting and malnutrition, then stents can
be useful.
Feline GI adenocarcinoma is an aggressive form of GI neoplasia,
most commonly found at the colorectal junction (chs. 263 and 264).
It is associated with distal metastasis 75% of the time, making partial
colectomy a difficult treatment option to encourage. If a partial
colectomy is performed, cats with metastasis have had a much lower
median survival time (MST) than if it is not performed (49 and 259
days, respectively).41,42 Affected dogs that have undergone partial
colectomy have had a longer MST (22 months) than those that did
not have surgery (15 months).25
In both dogs and cats, palliative stenting30,31,35,36 can be
considered. It is often chosen over more aggressive surgeries due to
the outpatient nature, minimal morbidity, and low complication
rates. Rectal or colonic stenting will only be useful to treat
obstipation caused by the obstructive lesion.
Colonic strictures have been treated with stents as well.32,33,37,38
Migration is the biggest problem with covered, retrievable stents
(>60%), and stricture recurrence can be seen after stent removal in
∼50% of cases.32,33,37,38 Balloon dilation or digital bougienage are

also treatment options for colonic strictures and have been met with
success, especially with short focal lesions in cats. For post-surgical
strictures, this has not been as successful in the authors’ experience.

Equipment
Standard flexible GI endoscopes are needed except for the more
distal rectal lesions in which a rigid scope can be used (ch. 107). If
the stent is to be placed through the working channel of the
endoscope, then an appropriately sized delivery system must be
used. The scope is used to evaluate and biopsy the lesion, pass a
guidewire (0.035″ hydrophilic angle-tipped 260 to 400 cm long)
through the lumen of the obstruction, and then standard fluoroscopy
is used for monitoring the guidewire and accurately deploying the
stent. A marker catheter, often infused with contrast and air to
distend the viscus, is used for estimating the luminal diameter and
obstruction length so an appropriate stent size can be chosen
(Figure 116.11).

FIGURE 116.11 Colonic stenting in a dog. A,

FIGURE 116.12 A covered gastrointestinal stent.
Notice the dog-bone shape, which prevents
migration.
GI stents are typically woven, metallic (or plastic), and selfexpanding. Some stents are covered and others bare. The bare stents
are typically used for malignant obstructions, whereas a covered
stent is often needed for strictures due to aggressive tissue ingrowth
and the option for removal. Colonic stents often have a flare at the
distal end to prevent aboral migration (Figures 116.11 and 116.12).
Covered stents typically have a string at one end to endoscopically
retrieve or reposition them when necessary.

Techniques
Gastroduodenal Stenting
Gastroduodenal stenting is performed by gaining access across the
obstructive lesion using fluoroscopy and gastroduodenoscopy (ch.
107). A guidewire is advanced through the working channel of the
endoscope, in the GI lumen, and through the lumen of the tumor.
Using fluoroscopic guidance, the wire is advanced aborad beyond the
obstruction. Next, the endoscope is removed over the wire if the stent
delivery system does not fit through the working channel of the
endoscope, and the position of the wire is monitored under
fluoroscopic visualization to ensure it remains across the
obstruction. The wire used should be a stiffened wire to ensure that it
does not pull into the stomach during catheter and stent
advancement. A marker catheter is advanced over the guidewire and
a contrast study is done to measure the diameter of the lumen and
the length of the obstruction for appropriate stent sizing. Once the

stent is chosen, it is deployed under fluoroscopic guidance.
Deploying the stent through the working channel of the endoscope,
when possible given the diameter of the stent delivery system, assists
in confirming accurate stent positioning and decreases the risk for
losing wire access in the duodenum. If this is done without an
endoscope, then after stent deployment either the endoscope is
reintroduced into the GI tract to confirm positioning and patency, or
a catheter is used for performing a contrast study for confirmation.

Colonic Stenting
Colonic stenting (Figures 116.11 and 116.13) is performed using
endoscopic guidance similar to that described above. Using a marker
catheter, a colonogram is performed and an appropriate stent size is
chosen. The stent is then deployed under fluoroscopic guidance,
being careful to prevent it from being caudal to the rectoanal
junction. Once the stent is deployed, the endoscope is advanced into
the colon to ensure proper placement. If the stent is covered, the
distal end of the stent should be sutured to the rectal mucosa to
prevent stent migration.

Follow-up
Patients with gastroduodenal stents should be fed small meals often
for the first few days. For gastric cardia stents, gastric acid reduction
therapy and antiemetics should be continued rigorously. Patients
with colonic stents are treated with a low residue diet, stool
softeners, and 7-10 days of a broad-spectrum antibiotic.

Complications
Tissue ingrowth into an uncovered stent and migration of a covered
stent are the most common complications seen in both human and
veterinary medicine. Fecal incontinence after colorectal stenting can
occur, but is rarely seen if the stent is positioned cranial to the anus.
For colonic tumors, tenesmus can be associated with infiltration of
the pelvic nerves, and despite de-obstipation being successful with
the stent, continued straining and discomfort may be seen.
Other potential complications reported in the human literature
that have not yet been seen in the authors’ experience include GI

perforation, irritation, intractable tenesmus, persistent vomiting,
stent shortening resulting in re-obstruction, and/or hemorrhage.

Outcome
Only a small number of dogs and cats have had stents placed in
either the upper or lower GI tracts. For colonic stenting, the MST for
malignancy in the authors’ subset of cases was ∼6 months (range, 19274 days).31 Patients with malignancy died of distant tumor effects
rather than local disease.

Special Considerations
Stents placed for GI obstructions can benefit the patient, but if the
patient is straining or vomiting due to the presence of the disease
and the local effects on the nerves, rather than a physical
obstruction, then a stent will likely not help.

HEPATOBILIARY
PT(C)E: PERCUTANEOUS TRANSVENOUS
(COIL) EMBOLIZATION
Indications and Background
Portosystemic shunts (PSS) are vascular anomalies connecting the
portal vein to the systemic circulation, resulting in a gamut of clinical
signs (ch. 267). Intrahepatic portosystemic shunts (IHPSS)
represent a more complex surgical correction than that of
extrahepatic portosystemic shunts (EHPSS) due to their large size
and intraparenchymal location.36,37
Pre-operative imaging, including CT angiography, can be very
useful to help plan the surgical or interventional procedure. Various
surgical options36-42 have been described (ch. 267) but this section
will focus on percutaneous transvenous (coil) embolization (PT(C)E)
via the jugular vein for the treatment of both IHPSS and specific
types of EHPSS. Some techniques for PTE use various other devices

for embolization, like vascular plugs, but coils are the most
commonly used device.43-46
Interventional management has become far more common for the
treatment of IHPSS in the last decade due to the relatively higher
complication rates seen with surgical treatment of IHPSS (2977%)38,39,41,42 compared to EHPSS (0-23%).39-41,47 PT(C)E has
been described from various institutions43-46 in the past decade,
with the largest series reporting 100 dogs.43 Similar intravascular
techniques have been described for treatment of both IHPSS and
EHPSS, in both dogs and cats, and for both partial and complete
attenuation.43,48 The perioperative complications rates were much
lower with the PT(C)E procedure, with similar long-term clinical
results as those that were previously reported with surgical
correction for dogs that survived the surgery.

Equipment
Equipment needed for PT(C)E includes a high-quality fluoroscopy
unit that ideally allows digital subtraction angiography (DSA, ch.
113). Various angiographic catheters (Cobra catheter, Berenstein
catheter, marker catheter for measuring, various guidewires, embolic
coils, and SEMS) are needed for this procedure. For cases where
complete vascular occlusion is possible, then a vascular plug or
similar device might be used. The standard coil used is a 0.035″ 8
mm diameter and 5 cm length stainless steel coil. Contrast is
typically used at a dosage of 2-4 mL/kg and is diluted to a 50%
mixture with sterile saline.

FIGURE 116.13 Images of a colonic stent after
deployment and expansion. A, Colonic stent is in
place across the stenosis. This is a covered stent so
the retrieval string is seen on each end (white
arrows). B, Endoscopic image of colonic stent after
deployment. Notice the retrieval string (white arrow)
at the distal end. The colon is now patent. C, A
ventrodorsal image of the colonic stent after
deployment with the retrieval strings (white arrows).

Technique
Patients are placed under general anesthesia using drugs safe in
animals with some liver dysfunction. Perioperative antibiotics are
used before and during the procedure, and broad-spectrum
antibiotics are continued for ∼7 days following the procedure due to
the implantation of foreign material within the portal circulation.
Patients are placed in dorsal recumbency. A radiopaque stent guide
is placed under the dog on the fluoroscopy table to aid in stent
deployment (Figure 116.14). The hair on the neck is clipped and the
skin is aseptically prepared and draped. Percutaneous right jugular
access is obtained through the placement of a vascular access sheath.
A hydrophilic guidewire is advanced through the catheter, into the
cranial vena cava, through the right atrium and then into the caudal

vena cava. Next, the angiographic catheter is advanced over the wire
and the shunting vessel is carefully selected until the portal vein is
cannulated. Digital subtraction venography is performed to confirm
the location and anatomy of the portal vein and shunting vessel.
Then, a marker catheter and guidewire combination is advanced into
the caudal vena cava and a caudal cavagram is performed during
positive pressure ventilation (20 cm H2O) to maximally distend the
abdominal caudal vena cava (Valsalva maneuver). Next, a
simultaneous caudal vena cavagram and portogram without positive
pressure ventilation (respiratory pause) are performed, to identify
the maximal intrathoracic caudal vena cava dimensions as well as the
anatomical opening of the shunt into the vena cava. These
measurements provide the maximal vena cava diameters to measure
for stent size. Portal venous pressures are obtained and compared to
the central venous pressures in the caudal vena cava. If the resting
portal pressure is >15-18 mm Hg or the portal vein to CVP gradient is
>7-9 mm Hg, then the procedure is not performed. If the recorded
pressures are under these parameters, then the portal vein catheter
is removed and the marker catheter is removed over a
polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE, Teflon) guidewire for stent
placement.
Next, the stent is deployed under fluoroscopic guidance in the
caudal vena cava, using the stent guide to mark the appropriate
location. Once the stent is deployed, the catheter is placed into the
portal vein through the stent for a repeat portovenogram, ensuring
proper stent placement across the mouth of the shunt. Then portal
pressures are obtained and if appropriate, another catheter is
advanced into the shunt through the interstices of the stent for coil
deployment, as the portal catheter measures continuous pressures.
Coils are added until the shunt mouth is covered or the shunt
pressures increase by approximately 7 mm Hg or maximal portal
pressures approach 16 mm Hg. Repeat angiography is performed at
the completion of the procedure. Finally, a triple lumen catheter is
placed in the right jugular vein once the sheath is removed to
maintain central venous access if necessary (ch. 75). The patients
are typically discharged the following day.

Follow-up

Patients are continued on all liver dysfunction medications and diet
(ch. 154) for the following month (ch. 267). A proton pump
inhibitor is continued for life. After 1 month, the liver medications
are slowly weaned over the following 1-2 months, and the diet is
transitioned to a normal adult maintenance diet. Bloodwork profiles
are monitored regularly. If clinical signs return, or evidence of liver
dysfunction persists on bloodwork, then medications can be
reinstituted and evaluation for the need of additional coils is
recommended.

Complications
Most of the complications reported for the interventional treatment
of PSS are those pertaining to IHPSS, as there is little published
information on PT(C)E of EHPSS. These complication rates are
relatively low. In the largest study of 100 dogs with IHPSS,43 the
perioperative mortality rate was 5%, with a 13% perioperative
complication rate. During the PT(C)E procedure, coil migration into
the pulmonary circulation is possible; however, this has been
substantially reduced with the addition of a caudal vena cava stent
prior to coil deployment. Additionally, portal hypertension during
embolization is possible, but this too is uncommon clinically after
PT(C)E.

A, A guidewire is in the caudal vena cava (black

through the right hepatic vein. A stent guide is under
the dog (white asterisk). B, A dual angiogram using
digital subtraction angiography (DSA) of the caudal
vena cava (black arrow) and the shunt (white arrow).

Notice where they come together at the caudal vena
cava (black arrowhead). C, Stent on the delivery
system (black asterisk) in the caudal vena cava. D,
Stent after deployment (black asterisks). E, Catheter

An incidence of postoperative seizures of ∼6% has been reported,
similar to that reported previously.43,47 Portal hypertension, which
has been commonly reported for surgical correction of IHPSS, was
very uncommon with PT(C)E.43 This is likely due to the location of
the attenuation. In this study, 20% of dogs required additional coils
to improve shunt attenuation over time, and at some point, before or
after PT(C)E, 20% of dogs demonstrated signs of GI bleeding.43
Severe GI bleeding is the most common complication seen in dogs
with IHPSS, regardless of the treatment modality, and this has
decreased to under 3% since the advent of life-long proton pump
inhibitor therapy.43 There are many theories as to why gastric
ulceration occurs so commonly in untreated dogs with IHPSS
(hypergastrinemia, hypoprostaglandinemia, abnormal intestinal
blood flow, poor mucosal integrity, abnormal mucus production,
abnormal cell turnover), but the etiology is still unclear. In the
preliminary evaluation of serum gastrin levels, hypergastrinemia
does not seem to be the cause.

Outcome
PT(C)E is a safe, fast, and effective therapy for canine IHPSSs when
performed by an operator who is well trained in interventional
techniques.43 PT(C)E resulted in a fair to excellent outcome in >80%
of patients and an MST >6 years. The perioperative mortality rate
was 5%, lower than that reported historically with traditional
surgery.36-42

Special Considerations
Pet owners should be aware that ∼10% of dogs have sufficient portal
vein perfusion found during angiography to allow complete IHPSS
occlusion, which can be done with various devices like vascular
plugs, ductal occluders, or a covered stent.43 Additionally, ∼25% of
dogs have multiple intrahepatic shunts at the time of angiography,
and about 5% have pre-existing elevated portal vein pressures,
precluding the procedure from safely being performed.43,49

HEPATIC ARTERIOVENOUS
MALFORMATIONS
Indications and Background
Hepatic arteriovenous fistulae/malformations (HAVM) are rare
vascular anomalies involving multiple arterial communications to
the portal vein (Figure 116.15) (ch. 267). Since they usually
involve multiple—rather than single—communications, the term
malformation, rather than fistula, is more appropriate. These
communications are usually from the hepatic artery, but have also
been seen to involve the gastroduodenal artery (GDA), left gastric
artery (GA), phrenic artery and others. Due to the high-pressure
arterial blood shunting to the portal vein, there is severe chronic
portal hypertension (often with subsequent massive ascites) that
results in the development of multiple acquired EHPSS to
spontaneously decompress the portal vein.
Treatment options for HAVM include liver lobectomy, ligation of
the nutrient artery, fluoroscopically-guided HAVM glue embolization
(HAVM-GE) of abnormal arterial vessels, or dominant outflow vein
(DOV) occlusion performed with fluoroscopic and surgical
guidance.50,51 Regardless of the therapy chosen for this condition,
75% of dogs will continue to require dietary and/or medical therapy
due to the persistent portosystemic shunting that occurs through the
multiple acquired EHPSSs, which are not always able to be
completely closed.50,52

Equipment
A high-quality fluoroscopy unit with vascular package capabilities,
ideally with the ability to obtain orthogonal views, is necessary to
avoid non-target embolization and ensure all contributing vessels are
embolized. For arterial embolization, femoral or carotid arterial
access is needed. Protective eyewear is required when handling the
glue material. The glue should only be handled on a special
embolization table to ensure that no saline or blood is in contact with
the glue to avoid premature polymerization. Other specific supplies,
aside from standard catheters for selective arteriography, include the
cyanoacrylate glue (1-5 mL), ionized poppyseed oil (Ethiodol), D5W,
and polycarbonate syringes (ch. 113).

Technique
For glue embolization of HAVM, access is typically obtained via the
carotid or femoral artery. Under fluoroscopic guidance, a catheter is
advanced into the hepatic artery. Hepatic arteriography is performed
to demonstrate the location, anatomy, and extent of the HAVM.
Hepatofugal blood flow is seen as the contrast material travels
through the HAVM and enters the portal vein traveling caudally until
it reaches the multiple EHPSS where it travels through the caudal
vena cava cranially. Then, super-selective microcatheter access is
obtained into each contributing branch of the HAVM (Figure
116.15). Glue embolization is performed with cyanoacrylate mixed
(typically 1:1 to 2:1) with Ethiodol, an iodized poppyseed oil that is
radiopaque and slows polymerization of the glue. The glue
polymerizes upon contact with ionic substances such as blood and
occludes the small communications of the malformation. This is
performed with care to avoid reflux into important regional vessels
(hepatic artery, gastroduodenal artery, etc.) or passage of glue into
the systemic circulation after passing through the shunts. Arterial
embolization should be repeated until the HAVM is completely
occluded; otherwise, patency of the HAVM is likely to return. Once
the nidus of the HAVM is embolized, cranial mesenteric
arteriography is performed to demonstrate the portal flow has
become hepatopetal (or is no longer hepatofugal). Upon completion,
the femoral or carotid artery is ligated at the access point and the
incision is closed.

FIGURE 116.15 Digital subtraction angiography
(DSA) during treatment of a hepatic arteriovenous

FIGURE 116.16 Dominant outflow vein (DOV)
occlusion for hepatic arteriovenous malformation
(AVM). Dog’s head to top of image. A, Digital

artery filling of the liver (white circle) with no AVM

For DOV occlusion, the treatment of choice in the authors’
practice, a carotid approach, as described above for hepatic
arteriography, is obtained to confirm the presence of 1 or 2 DOVs.
Then a laparotomy is performed, and a mesenteric vein is
catheterized for portal venography and pressure measurement. The
DOV(s) is/are identified and surgically isolated when possible;
otherwise splenic vein catheterization may be obtained to perform
venous embolization of the DOVs with embolic materials like coils or
plugs (Figure 116.16). If the DOV is surgically isolated, silk ligation
is performed and the arteriogram repeated to confirm complete
HAVM closure. Portal pressures are repeated as well as venous
portography to demonstrate hepatopetal bloodflow and, if portal
pressures allow, acquired shunts can be isolated and ligated to
improve hepatic perfusion.

Follow-up
After HAVM occlusion, improvement in the ascites should be seen
due to the decrease in portal hypertension. Bloodwork is repeated
the day after the procedure and then again at 1, 3, and 6 months and
then every 6 months thereafter. Medications are continued in most
cases as the EHPSS generally remain. Repeat procedures are
recommended if the ascites persists or liver function worsens.

Complications
Complications associated with glue embolization include non-target
embolization (glue entering unintended vessels such as the portal
system, the extrahepatic shunts or pulmonary circulation). Other
locations of non-target embolization include occlusion of proximal
arterial vessels like the common hepatic artery and the
gastroduodenal artery. Additionally, polymerization of the catheter
tip into the vessel wall is possible. Portal vein thrombosis is possible
due to the stagnancy of the blood flow in the portal vein after
decreasing the arterial flow into the HAVM. For DOV occlusion, the
main complications are bleeding associated with surgical dissection

or non-target embolization if a plug or coil is used during
embolization.

Outcome
In one study on dogs with HAVM-GE, perioperative survival was
100%, with or without partial hepatectomy, compared to 75% to 91%
of dogs undergoing surgery alone, but only 4 dogs had HAVM-GE in
this study.50 Patency of arteriovenous communications can return
and recurrence of clinical signs has been seen requiring additional
embolization procedures; this is seen in ∼30% of cases after arterial
embolization. With DOV occlusion, recurrence seems less common.
Long-term survival is considered fair to good with this interventional
technique.52
All patients have persistent acquired EHPSS due to portal
hypertension (except for the rare cases with concurrent IHPSSs), and
these do not regress, resulting in the need for lifelong medical and
dietary management in the majority of cases.

Special Considerations
Glue embolization is considered one of the more complicated
interventional procedures in human medicine, and human
interventionalists undergo specialty training in the use of glue prior
to performing this type of procedure. This should be considered the
case in veterinary medicine as well.

Interventional urology (also known as endourology) refers to the specialty of urology in which
endoscopes, fluoroscopy and other instruments are used for accessing, under direct visualization,
structures inside the urinary tract. As opposed to traditional surgery, access is most commonly
achieved through natural orifices or small incisions and the procedures are done internally. Minimally
invasive approaches have a multitude of advantages over standard surgery such as shorter
hospitalization times, little to no recovery time and less discomfort (ch. 113). Another application of
endourology is for patients in whom traditional therapies are not available, associated with poor
outcomes, contraindicated, or have failed. The authors feel that minimally invasive procedures should
be considered and discussed with owners of pets suffering from urinary tract disorders. While at times
appearing technically simple, these procedures have been associated with serious complications when
performed by inadequately trained personnel and patients should be referred to a formally trained
and experienced specialist to undergo them. There is a learning curve associated with these
procedures and training and experience are critical in obtaining the best outcomes.

EQUIPMENT AND SUPPLIES
Endoscopes

Rigid cystoscopes with a 30° angle are recommended for interventional endoscopic procedures (ch.
100).

Asepsis
Although the prepuce, vagina and distal urethra have a normal bacterial flora, the authors use sterile
drapes and sterile equipment, and thoroughly disinfect the material used between patients. Sterile
waterproof drapes are available that preserve asepsis while working with continuous saline flush.

Imaging and Materials
Fluoroscopy is used in a variety of these procedures and precautions must be taken to ensure safety of
all the personnel involved (ch. 113). The most commonly used contrast agents in veterinary
endourology are low-osmolarity, nonionic contrast media such as iohexol. Stents are designed to
establish patency of a lumen and are available in a variety of materials, shapes, and design (ch. 113).
The most commonly used stents in veterinary medicine are metallic composed of nitinol, a nickeltitanium alloy, but ureteral stents are most often non-metallic, such as urethane double-pigtail stents.
Laser-cut stents are used primarily in the urethra and blood vessels.1 Urethral stents are most
commonly uncovered metallic stents. Covered stents can also be placed in the urethra and have the
advantage of being removable; however, they must be anchored or sutured in place to prevent
migration.

LOWER URINARY TRACT DISORDERS
PERCUTANEOUS ANTEGRADE URETHRAL CATHETERIZATION
Indication
Urethral obstruction when standard retrograde urethral catheterization cannot be achieved (ch. 99).
It is most commonly done in male cats with urethral tears secondary to trauma from serial attempts to
catheterize or in dogs and cats with malignant urethral obstruction (ch. 330).

Equipment
0.035-inch (0.9 mm) hydrophilic angled wire, 5 Fr open-ended urinary catheter (cats), 18-gauge IV
catheter, 3-way stopcock, iodinated contrast medium, fluoroscopy or digital radiography.

Procedure1-3
The patient is placed under general anesthesia in lateral recumbency and the ventrolateral abdomen
and the perineum are clipped/shaved, aseptically prepped, and draped. An empty syringe (for
withdrawing urine) and a syringe containing a 50:50 mixture of saline and contrast are connected to a
3-way stopcock, which is connected to an extension set. An 18-gauge IV catheter is inserted
transcutaneously into the apex of the distended urinary bladder, directing the catheter tip toward the
trigone. The stylet is removed and the extension set is connected to the catheter. A very distended
urinary bladder may need to be partially drained before injecting contrast. Contrast is injected
through the catheter into the bladder under fluoroscopic guidance until the bladder is distended and
the proximal urethra is visible. The stopcock is removed, and a guidewire is inserted through the
catheter and manipulated towards and down the urethra and advanced until it exits through the penis
or vulva (through-and-through access). A urinary catheter with the tip cut off is advanced in a
retrograde manner over the wire and into the urinary bladder. The guidewire is removed by pulling it
through the urinary catheter and the IV catheter is removed from the bladder (Figure 117.1).

FIGURE 117.1 Antegrade urethral catheterization in a male cat with
urethral obstruction. Lateral fluoroscopic view. The bladder is moderately
distended with contrast (A), a catheter is inserted transcutaneously into the
cranial portion of the bladder (B), and a guidewire passed through the
catheter can be seen in the urethra (C). A marker catheter (D) is in the colon
for sizing if a stent needs to be placed in the urethra.

Special Considerations
For urethral tears, the urinary catheter should be left in place for 3-5 days to allow complete healing.

Outcome and Follow-up
In a small study, percutaneous antegrade urethral catheterization was successful in 7/9 male cats.
However, all of these cats underwent perineal urethrostomy for recurrence of urethral obstruction
within 6 weeks.2

Complications
Inability to achieve access (especially when occlusive urethral stones present) and, rarely, bladder
rupture and leakage of urine and contrast into the peritoneal cavity. A small amount of leakage of
contrast around the bladder occurs commonly and is not associated with adverse effects in the
authors’ experience.

Alternatives

Perineal urethrostomy, intermittent cystocentesis, cystostomy tube or urinary catheter placed by
cystotomy.4,5

PERCUTANEOUS CYSTOSTOMY TUBE PLACEMENT
Indications
Functional or mechanical urethral obstruction not amenable to medical therapy (chs. 99 and 312). A
cystostomy tube can be used as a temporary or permanent implant in conditions such as lower urinary
tract neoplasia, proliferative urethritis, urethral stricture, dyssynergia, neurologic disease, and
urethral/bladder trauma.3

Equipment
Locking loop pigtail drainage catheter, hydrophilic angled guidewire, urinary catheter, 3-way
stopcock, extension set, iodinated contrast medium, fluoroscopy or digital radiography.

Procedure
The patient is placed under general anesthesia and in right or left lateral recumbency. The abdomen is
clipped/shaved, ensuring the clipped area extends laterally on the side where the tube will be placed,
and aseptically prepped. The caudal portion of the bladder is palpated and held in position as the
craniolateral aspect of the bladder is accessed with a needle attached to an extension set with a 3-way
stopcock and 2 syringes. One syringe contains contrast and the other is used for withdrawing urine;
the second syringe will be used to withdraw urine as needed following injection contrast to prevent
excessive bladder distension. Contrast is injected into the bladder, the extension set is disconnected,
and a guidewire is passed quickly through the needle. The guidewire is looped in the bladder or can
exit through the urethra (through-and-through access). The needle is withdrawn over the guidewire
and the locking loop pigtail catheter is passed over the wire and into the bladder under fluoroscopic
guidance. The locking loop pigtail catheter is advanced into the bladder so that all fenestrations are
well within the bladder, and then the guidewire is withdrawn. The loop is locked by pulling on the
string and secured through the locking mechanism. The catheter is positioned within the bladder
without tension and secured using a finger trap suture (Figure 117.2).

Tube Withdrawal
The tube should have been in place 10-14 days prior to removal.6 A guidewire is inserted through the
tube under fluoroscopic guidance to ensure that the loop is fully undone and the locking loop catheter
is straight. The catheter is withdrawn with the guidewire, and an occlusive bandage is left in place for
24 hours. Urine leakage through the stoma is normal for 2-3 days following tube removal.3,6

Special Considerations
When placed for neoplastic urinary tract disease, there have been concerns regarding seeding of the
abdominal cavity and skin.
In the author’s experience, it is best to err on the side of a smaller tube as it is better tolerated and
the bladder can be easily drained.

Outcome
Provides an effective means for temporary or long-term bladder emptying.

Follow-up
Bacterial infections only should be treated if the patient shows associated clinical signs, and targeted
antimicrobial therapy based on culture and sensitivity is recommended.

Complications

Recurrent bacterial infections are common and occurred in up to 86% of patients in one study.6
Slipping of the tube out of the bladder can result in uroperitoneum. Obstruction of the tube is
possible; however, flushing the system or passing a guidewire through the tube can help relieve the
obstruction.

Alternatives
Urethral stenting or surgically placed cystostomy tubes.

CYSTOSCOPIC BASKET RETRIEVAL OF LOWER URINARY
TRACT STONES
Indications
Removal of urethral and bladder stones not amenable to medical dissolution (ch. 159) in dogs (ch.
308) or cats (ch. 309), and too large to be evacuated by voiding urohydropulsion (chs. 99 and 308).
Basket retrieval can generally be considered in female dogs with stones <5 mm in diameter, male dogs
with stones <4 mm in diameter, and female cats with stones <3 mm in diameter; however, patient size
will be an important consideration (Table 117.1).3,7 This procedure is not recommended in male cats
due to their small penile urethral lumen.

Equipment
Rigid or flexible cystoscope, stone basket that can be passed through the channel of the cystoscope.

Procedure
The patient is anesthetized and placed in dorsal (females) or lateral (males) recumbency. The
vulva/prepuce and surrounding area are clipped/shaved, aseptically prepped, and draped. Cystoscopy
(ch. 100) is used for visualizing the stone(s). A stone basket is passed through the channel of the
scope and the stone is grasped. Under continuous saline flush, the basket is pulled towards the tip of
the scope and the scope along with the basket are withdrawn. If resistance is felt, the flush pressure
can be increased in order to help dilate the urethral lumen and the basket can be gently rotated. If
resistance is still felt, the basket should be opened to release the stone and another technique used in
order to avoid damage to, or perforation of, the urethra (Video 117.1).

Special Considerations
In the presence of urethral stricture/inflammation, the clinician should be prepared to remove the
stone using another technique. Female cats have fragile urethras and transvesicular percutaneous
cystolithotomy (PCCL; see below) should be considered in female cats with large stones or large stone
burdens.

Follow-up
Stone recurrence is a concern in both dogs (ch. 308) and cats (ch. 309).

Complications
Urethral stricture or perforation is possible during retrieval of embedded or sharp-edged stones.
Performing this procedure in a patient with a urinary tract infection (UTI) is not recommended due to
increased risk of urosepsis. Antibiotic therapy based on culture/sensitivity is recommended for 5-7
days prior to performing this procedure.

Alternatives
Lithotripsy, PCCL, or cystotomy.

INTRACORPOREAL LITHOTRIPSY OF THE LOWER
URINARY TRACT
Indications
Removal of urethral and bladder stones not amenable to medical dissolution and too large to be
removed by cystoscopic-guided basket retrieval (ch. 100).8-11 Male cats, small male dogs or patients

with large stone burdens should undergo PCCL.

Equipment
Rigid or flexible cystoscope, holmium: yttrium aluminum garnet (Ho: YAG) laser with a fiber that can
be passed through the scope channel/electrohydraulic lithotriptor, stone basket (optional).

Procedure
The patient is anesthetized and placed in dorsal (females or males) or lateral (males) recumbency. The
vulva/prepuce and surrounding area are clipped/shaved, aseptically prepped, and draped. Cystoscopy
is used for visualizing the stone (ch. 100). The tip of the laser fiber is placed in direct contact with,
and perpendicular to, the surface of the urolith. The stone is fragmented by the laser’s energy
transmitted directly to the stone, creating a shock wave that induces fragmentation (Video 117.2).
Stones are fragmented until the pieces are small enough to be voided using urohydropulsion (Video
308.5) or removed with a stone retrieval basket (Video 117.1).

Special Considerations
The major challenge is removal of stone fragments from the urinary tract, especially in male dogs.
Success depends on careful patient selection (Table 117.2).

Outcome
The Ho: YAG is effective on all stone types.12 Complete urolith removal is achieved in 100% of dogs
with urethroliths, 83-96% of female dogs with cystoliths, and 68-81% of male dogs with cystoliths.8-11

Complications
Performing this procedure in a patient with a UTI is not recommended due to increased risk of
