procedure. Self-limiting urethral edema, and mild hematuria may be observed. Bladder/urethral
perforation by the laser is a rare occurrence and can be treated by leaving a urinary catheter in place
for 24-48 hours. Risk of incomplete stone fragment removal is higher in males (20-30%) than in
females due to the difficulty in removing stone fragments by voiding urohydropulsion in male dogs.811

Alternatives
PCCL, surgical cystotomy and/or urethrotomy.

TRANSVESICULAR PERCUTANEOUS CYSTOLITHOTOMY
(PCCL)
Indications
Removal of urethral and bladder stones not amenable to medical dissolution and too large or too
numerous to be removed by voiding urohydropulsion, cystoscopy-guided basket retrieval, or
lithotripsy (chs. 308 and 309). This antegrade approach through the bladder apex can also be used
for gaining access to the urethra, bladder, and ureters.3,13,14

Equipment
Urinary catheter, standard surgical instruments, laparoscopic threaded cannula with diaphragm, rigid
and flexible cystoscopes, stone basket.

Procedure13,14
The patient is anesthetized and placed in dorsal recumbency. The ventral aspect of the abdomen and
prepuce/vulva are clipped/shaved, aseptically prepped, and draped. A urinary catheter is placed in
male patients and sterile saline infused until the bladder apex is palpable. In females, if the bladder is
not palpable, a catheter can be placed or ultrasonography used to identify the bladder apex and
location for the surgical approach. A 2 cm ventral midline skin incision is made over the bladder apex.
The incision is extended into the abdominal cavity, the bladder apex is identified, and is grasped with
tissue forceps. Stay sutures are placed and a small stab incision is made at the bladder apex. The
laparoscopic cannula is screwed in place and directed toward the urethral lumen. In females, at this
time a guidewire can be passed through the cannula, out the urethra, and a urinary catheter advanced
retrograde, over-the-wire, into the urinary bladder. To remove sediment/small stones, the diaphragm
of the cannula is removed and the bladder is flushed via the urinary catheter while applying suction to
the lumen of the cannula. A rigid cystoscope (ch. 100) is advanced through the cannula into the
bladder and the remaining stones are identified and removed with the stone basket. Once all bladder
stones are removed, the urethra is examined through anterograde passage (through the cannula) of
the flexible scope in male dogs and cats and the rigid scope (or flexible scope) in female dogs. Stones
in the urethra can be removed with a stone basket or flushed into the bladder and removed. The
cannula is withdrawn and the bladder incision and abdomen are closed. Laser lithotripsy is rarely
required as larger cystoliths may be removed by stretching/extending the bladder incision13,14
(Figure 117.3).

FIGURE 117.3 Percutaneous cystolithotomy in a male dog. A, 1-cm incision
over the bladder apex. B, Trocar inserted into bladder apex. C, Rigid
cystoscope (∗) through trocar under continuous saline irrigation (+). (−),
Outflow. D, Stone (∗) retrieved with basket retrieval device (+) via endoscope
working channel. E, Closed skin incision is small (arrow).

Outcome
Complete stone removal is achieved in 96% of patients.13,14

Follow-up
Stone recurrence is a concern (chs. 308 and 309). Skin sutures can be removed in 10-14 days.

Complications
Wound infection, dehiscence, and uroabdomen are rare potential complications associated with the
transabdominal approach. If a patient has a UTI, antibiotic therapy should be administered prior to
the procedure, due to increased risk of septic peritonitis.

Alternatives
Surgical cystotomy and/or urethrotomy.

URETHRAL STENTING

Indications
Relief of urethral obstruction and restoration of a urine stream in a patient with partial or complete
urethral obstruction (ch. 99). Urethral stents most commonly are placed to relieve obstruction
caused by urethral, trigonal, and/or prostatic neoplasia (ch. 330). Patients with urethral stricture or
proliferative urethritis may require stenting especially if they have failed ballooning and medical
therapy 15-20b (ch. 312).

Equipment
Hydrophilic angled weasel wire, marker catheter, 14 Fr red rubber urinary catheter, appropriately
sized self-expanding laser-cut nitinol urethral stent (covered removable stent can be considered for
benign conditions and urethral strictures), T-fasteners (to secure covered removable stent in place),
Berenstein catheter (males), introducer sheath, iodinated contrast, fluoroscopy or digital radiography.

Procedure
The patient is placed under general anesthesia and in lateral recumbency. The prepuce or vulvar
region is aseptically prepped and draped. A marker catheter is fully inserted in a 14 Fr red rubber
urinary catheter and they are advanced into the terminal portion of the colon under fluoroscopic
guidance. The marker catheter is essential for accurate selection of stent size. A 0.035 inch (0.9 mm)
angled hydrophilic guidewire is introduced into the urethra under fluoroscopic guidance and
advanced until it curls into the bladder. An introducer sheath (usually 8 Fr) is advanced over the
guidewire into the distal urethra in males and up to and advanced gently past the obstruction in
females. A contrast cystourethrogram is performed, using the sheath in females or a Berenstein
catheter advanced over the guidewire and through the sheath in males. A 50:50 mixture of iodinated
contrast and sterile saline is injected to ensure full bladder distension, creating a clear distinction
between the urethra, trigone, and bladder. Contrast is injected continuously while withdrawing the
catheter into the distal urethra under fluoroscopic guidance or injected through the sheath (females).
The size and length of the obstruction can be determined along with measurement of the maximal
urethral diameter. A voiding cystourethrogram (manual compression of the bladder under
fluoroscopic guidance) can further assist in visualizing the obstruction, especially in females.

Stent Selection
A stent with a diameter 0-15% greater than the maximum diameter of the urethra near the obstruction
is selected. The length of the obstruction is calculated and the stent length is chosen in order to ensure
coverage of the entire obstruction along with 0.5-1 cm additional stent length cranial and caudal to the
obstruction. Under fluoroscopic guidance, the stent delivery system is passed over the guidewire, into
position, and the stent is deployed. The stent is not reconstrainable and once deployment has been
initiated, it cannot be stopped. Once patency is confirmed, a repeat urethrogram is performed and the
bladder is manually expressed to confirm patency. The stent delivery system, sheath, guidewire, and
marker catheter are then removed15,17 (Figure 117.4).

Special Considerations17,19,20
For benign urethral obstruction, balloon dilatation may be considered prior to urethral stenting. For
recurrent benign urethral obstruction, a covered stent may be required to prevent tissue ingrowth.
Metallic urethral stents are considered permanent implants. Removable covered urethral stents can
be used for maintaining urethral patency in patients with treatable or temporary conditions (e.g.,
proliferative urethritis).20 These stents must be sutured in place or otherwise anchored in order to
prevent migration.
Unlike in tracheal stenting (ch. 114), where the carina and larynx must be avoided, a urethral stent
can extend to the trigone cranially and “bird beak” out of the papilla and into the vestibule caudally if
the obstruction involves the trigonal outflow tract or urethral papilla, respectively (Figure 117.4).
Placing an inappropriately small stent will increase the risk of migration, especially with covered
stents. Some patients with chronic obstructions can have concurrent bladder atony. Care must be

taken when performing rectal palpation, administering an enema, or taking a rectal temperature, as
the stent could become damaged or dislodged.

Outcome
Urethral stenting has a success rate of 97.5-100% for relief of both benign and neoplastic obstructions.
Survival times vary as a function of the underlying disease.15-19

Follow-up
Regular urinalysis with culture is recommended, as one-third of dogs develop a UTI following stent
placement.15-17

Complications
Urinary incontinence rates of 12.5% are reported in patients undergoing urethral stenting for benign
obstruction17 and 26-41% in patients with neoplastic obstruction.16,17 Neither stent length, diameter,
location nor sex are predictors of incontinence.15-17 Recurrence of obstruction due to tissue growth
(more common with benign strictures) occurs in 12.8-17%, stent migration in 12%, and persistent
dysuria and stranguria in 19% of patients.15-17 Cats may be at risk of ureteral obstruction with
placement of a proximal urethral stent given the location of their ureteral orifices.19

Alternatives
A urinary catheter (ch. 98), urethral resection and anastomosis, urethrostomy, or placement of a
percutaneous cystostomy tube are alternative options. Patients with obstructive neoplasia (ch. 330)
can undergo ultrasound-guided endoscopic diode laser ablation. Benign urethral strictures can be
balloon-dilated. A temporary pigtail or straight catheter sutured to the vestibule or prepuce are other
means of relieving urethral obstruction.

ULTRASOUND-GUIDED ENDOSCOPIC DIODE LASER
ABLATION (UGELAB) OF TRANSITIONAL CELL
CARCINOMA OF THE LOWER URINARY TRACT
Indications
Debulking of bladder and urethral transitional cell carcinoma in dogs (ch. 330). This technique can
also be used for establishing a urine stream in patients with obstructive disease caused by benign
tumors or polyps of the urinary tract.21,22

Equipment
Rigid cystoscope, Foley urinary catheter, diode laser with laser fiber that can be passed through the
scope channel, ultrasonography, and experienced ultrasonographer.

Procedure
The patient is anesthetized and placed in dorsal recumbency. The vulva/prepuce and surrounding
area are shaved/clipped, aseptically prepped, and draped. The cystoscope (ch. 100) is advanced to
within 2-5 mm of the tumor and the region is simultaneously imaged by abdominal ultrasonography.
The ureterovesicular junctions (UVJs) near the trigone must be spared. Laser energy absorbed by the
tumor increases tissue temperature, resulting in protein denaturation and making the tissue
hyperechoic on ultrasound. Ultrasonographic monitoring improves precision, allowing tumor ablation
without penetration of the bladder wall. The resulting denatured, avascular tissue sloughs after
several days. At the end of the procedure, a Foley urinary catheter is often placed in dogs with tumor

in the urethra and trigone to avoid urethral obstruction while waiting for devitalized tissue to slough21
(Figure 117.5).

Special Considerations
This procedure has a steep learning curve for both endoscopist and ultrasonographer. It is considered
palliative, and chemotherapy should be maintained to improve outcome.

Outcome
Rapid resolution of urethral obstruction and improvement in clinical signs are reported, with a mean
survival time of 380 days. Increased survival times have not been reported from laser ablation as
compared to chemotherapy alone; however, improved resolution of clinical signs has been reported
when both treatments are combined.21,22

Follow-up
The urinary catheter is left in place 3-7 days with urethral lesions, and 1-2 days with lesions of the
trigone. 50% of patients develop bacterial cystitis postoperatively.21 Bacterial cystitis or tumor
regrowth/spread should be considered if lower urinary tract signs recur. Patients may undergo
multiple laser treatments and follow-up ultrasonography or cystoscopic examinations can aid in early
identification of tumor recurrence.21

FIGURE 117.4 Cystoscopic images, 9 y.o. F Rottweiler with urethral
obstruction. A, Obstructive soft-tissue mass invading the urethral papilla and
distal urethra (a, vagina; b, urethral lumen; c, mass at the urethral papilla). B,
Guidewire (upper left) passed through the urethral lumen to access the
bladder. C, Urethral stent in place; lumen is patent. D, Distal end of stent
protrudes (“bird beaks”) from the urethral papilla (c) into the vestibule (d). E,
Stent spans the distal two-thirds of the urethra.

Complications
Despite relief of urethral obstruction, many dogs remain persistently dysuric and pollakiuric, which
can improve over time. 34% of dogs demonstrate gross hematuria lasting 1-2 days, and 5% develop
scar tissue at the cystourethral junction, necessitating subsequent laser treatments. Occasionally,
seeding of the tumor to other previously unaffected areas of the urinary tract has been reported.
Urethral and bladder perforation are possible, with subsequent seeding of the abdomen with tumor
cells.21

FIGURE 117.5 A, Transitional cell carcinoma partially obstructing the midurethral lumen (6 to 9 o’clock position) is visualized with a rigid cystoscope.
B-C, A diode laser passes through the working channel to ablate the mass
under continuous saline flush. D, Urethral diameter is substantially increased
following ablation of the mass.

Alternatives
Urethral catheterization (ch. 98), urethral stent placement, urethral resection and anastomosis,
urethrostomy, or placement of a percutaneous cystostomy tube.

TREATMENT WITH URETHRAL BULKING AGENTS FOR
SPHINCTER MECHANISM INCOMPETENCE

Indications
Treatment of urinary incontinence in dogs and cats with urethral sphincter mechanism incompetence
(USMI, ch. 310) refractory to standard medical therapy may benefit from urethral bulking agents.
Submucosal injection of bulking agents in the proximal urethra improves continence by acting as an
additional central filler, which decreases luminal diameter and increases the length of the muscle
fiber, thereby increasing the strength of the sphincter.22a

Equipment
Rigid cystoscope, injection needle furnished by the manufacturer of the bulking agent, cross-linked
bovine collagen (injection needle: 5 Fr 23 ga) or polydimethylsiloxane (injection needle: 5 Fr 20 ga)
with injection device. Other bulking agents such as cross-linked gelatin are also available.23

Procedure
The patient is anesthetized and placed in dorsal recumbency. The vulva/prepuce and surrounding
area are shaved/clipped, aseptically prepped, and draped. The ureterovesicular orifices, trigone, and
proximal urethra are identified by cystoscopy (ch. 100). The cystoscope is withdrawn to the level of
the proximal urethra, approximately 1-1.5 cm caudal to the bladder neck or at the location of the
proximal urethra where the lumen appears to be the smallest. The urethral bulking agent is injected
submucosally in 3-4 locations: at the 2, 6, and 10 o’clock positions, approximately. The needle is
inserted so that its bevel is pointed towards the lumen and inserted superficially into the submucosa.
The bulking agent is injected until a bleb is visualized that approaches midline and blanching of the
mucosa occurs (Figure 117.6). Once the volume has been administered, the needle is held in place
for 60 seconds to allow the compound to congeal, as premature withdrawal of the needle will result in
product leakage into the lumen. At the end of the procedure, the urethral lumen should be closed by
the blebs. In males, a perineal or PCCL approach can be used for gaining access to the proximal
urethra (see Percutaneous Perineal Access for Canine Rigid Male Cystourethroscopy, below).24,25

FIGURE 117.6 Cystoscopically assisted injection of a bulking agent in the
proximal urethra of a female dog with urethral sphincter mechanism
incompetence. A, Tip of injection needle (through working channel of
cystoscope) is inserted into the superficial mucosa. B, Injection of the bulking
agent is intended to create a bleb, which reduces luminal the diameter; here, a
small amount of bulking agent has leaked around the needle. C, Injection of
the bulking agent is continued until a bleb is seen and there is blanching of the
mucosa.

Special Considerations
The major drawbacks are lack of sustained efficacy and therefore, the need for repeated injections.
The authors choose injection of a bulking agent in older female dogs with USMI refractory to medical
therapy given the ease and minimal invasiveness of the technique. An artificial urethral sphincter
(AUS) is chosen in younger dogs (Figure 117.7); it can be placed at the time of spaying and has better
long-term results but more potential complications.

Outcome
Continence rates using collagen in female dogs vary from 53-100%, with a mean duration of 11-46
months. Improved continence rates of 75-100% have been reported in dogs having undergone
collagen injections and treated with an alpha-agonist.23-28

Follow-up
If patients remain incontinent, a second injection of bulking agent can be performed and improved
continence in one study from 87% to 100%.23 Medical therapy consisting of estrogen and/or the use
of alpha-agonists improves response to therapy (ch. 310).

Complications
Persistent incontinence is the main complication. Inability to urinate is infrequent and if it occurs, can
be treated with placement of an indwelling urethral catheter for 24-48 hours. No hypersensitivity
reactions to collagen have been reported in cats and dogs; however, 3 dogs treated with
polydimethylsiloxane experienced an acute allergic reaction (blepharedema and urticaria), managed
successfully with diphenhydramine.28

Alternatives
Diapers, confinement, and limiting the patient to areas that are easy to clean; placement of an AUS;
colposuspension with or without urethroplasty.28

PERCUTANEOUS PERINEAL ACCESS FOR CANINE RIGID
MALE CYSTOURETHROSCOPY29
Indications
Perineal access into the urethra makes rigid cystourethroscopy possible in most male dogs,
dramatically improving visualization of the urethra, bladder and urethrovesical junctions. This
approach is particularly useful for endoscopic ureteral interventions in male dogs (e.g., laser ablation
of ectopic ureters, sclerotherapy or ureteroscopy for idiopathic renal hemorrhage, ureteral stenting).

Equipment
A 2.7 mm rigid cystoscope, ultrasound machine, C-arm fluoroscope, 8 Fr Foley urinary catheter,
injectable contrast material, 18-ga trocar needle/catheter, 0.035″ (0.9 mm) angle-tipped hydrophilic
guidewire, 0.035″ (0.9 mm) Amplatz Super Stiff guidewire, serial vascular dilators (8 Fr, 10 Fr, 12 Fr,
14 Fr), and 14 or 16 Fr peel-away sheath.

Procedure
The perineal approach is performed with the patient in dorsal recumbency and the hindlimbs drawn
cranially (Figure 117.8). The prepuce and perineal areas are shaved/clipped and prepared
aseptically. This positioning allows for both retrograde flexible urethroscopy and perineal urethral
access. Following flexible urethroscopy, an 8 Fr Foley catheter is placed and the urinary bladder is
filled with diluted iohexol (50%). The C-arm fluoroscopy unit is positioned transversely across the dog
in order to project a lateral image. The catheter is pulled back into the ischial urethra; the balloon is
filled with 50% diluted contrast and identified with perineal ultrasound. A 4-5 mm midline skin
incision is made into the pelvic urethra at the level of the ischium. An 18-ga trocar needle/catheter is
placed, under fluoroscopic and ultrasound guidance, into the urethral lumen. The needle is aimed
such that it penetrates the balloon of the Foley catheter. Once the balloon is popped, the sharp stylet is
removed and the hollow trocar is advanced further, into the pelvic urethra; urine return confirms
proper location. Then the 0.035″ angled hydrophilic wire, or Amplatz Super Stiff guidewire, is
advanced and coiled into the urinary bladder under fluoroscopic guidance. The C-arm is rotated into a
dorsoventral projection. The 18-ga trocar/catheter is removed over the wire and serial dilators (8 Fr,
10 Fr, 12 Fr, 14 Fr) are used for dilating the tract to accept a 14 or 16 Fr peel-away sheath (depending
on the outer diameter of the rigid cystoscope). Once the 14 or 16 Fr sheath is in the mid-pelvic urethra,
the dilator is removed. The 2.7 mm rigid cystoscope is placed through the sheath and rigid
urethrocystoscopy is performed (ch. 100). Upon completion of the intervention, the sheath is
removed. The puncture heals by second intention, and the patient is discharged the same day.

FIGURE 117.7 Inflatable artificial urethral sphincter (AUS). A, The cuff has
been placed loosely around the urethra and suture has been passed through
each eyelet. B, Eyelet sutures are attached; cuff encircles urethra (tubing from
cuff is visible). C, Radiographic contrast study (ventrodorsal view), female dog
with AUS. Contrast-filled cuff around urethra (a); contrast-filled tubing
leading to port (b); access port (c); Huber needle (d). D, Same image with
digital subtraction for improved visualization of contrast.

FIGURE 117.8 Percutaneous perineal access in a male dog. A, Dorsal
recumbency, hind limbs drawn cranially; Foley catheter in the
bladder/urethra (not seen); tail wrapped (red bandage material), perineum
aseptically prepared. B, A peel-away urethral access sheath is placed in the
perineal urethra, allowing passage of a rigid cystoscope under continuous
saline flush.

Outcome
In 10 dogs,24 access time typically was <30 minutes, half the cases went home the same day as the
procedure, and the only complication encountered was 1 dog leaking urine through the perineal
incision 6 hours postoperatively, which did not recur. No long-term complications were identified in
any of the dogs, with a median follow-up time of ~7 months and some >3 years.

Follow-up
The patient is recovered with no special treatments for the perineal approach, as treatments are based
on the underlying condition that was treated.

Complications
The most concerning potential complications are hemorrhage from the vascular cavernous tissues of
the ischial urethra and stricture formation, although this is exceedingly rare.24,25 Hemorrhage has not
been a problem to date, likely due to the stretching (dilation) of the tissues rather than tearing or
cutting that occurs during surgical urethral exposure/access. Strictures also are unlikely to occur with
longitudinal incisions, rather than circumferential ones, as has been demonstrated experimentally in
the urethra.31,32

ENDOSCOPIC LASER ABLATION OF VESTIBULOVAGINAL
REMNANTS (CH. 313)

Indications
Female dogs with vestibulovaginal remnants, including persistent paramesonephric remnant (PPMR,
vestibulovaginal septal remnant [VVSR]), vaginal septum (VS), or a dual vagina (DV), can present
with a variety of signs such as natural breeding difficulties, persistent and positional urinary
incontinence, vaginal pooling of urine, chronic recurrent UTI, dysuria, vaginitis, dystocia, and vulvar
dermatitis.33-36 These abnormalities can accompany others and a thorough cystoscopic examination
of the urinary tract is recommended (ch. 100).33,36 As the current implications of these
malformations remain unknown, having an effective, minimally invasive treatment option such as
endoscopically-guided laser ablation is ideal.

Equipment
Rigid cystoscope, saline infusion ideally run on a pressure system to keep the vaginal vault distended,
guidewire, open-ended ureteral catheter (evaluating the length and location of the remnant), laser
fiber, and either a diode or an Ho: YAG laser.

Procedure
The patient is placed in dorsal recumbency and the vulva is clipped/shaved and aseptically prepared.
The cystoscope is advanced into the vestibule using saline irrigation on a pressure irrigation system.
The vaginal opening is identified and each compartment is evaluated endoscopically. The guidewire
and ureteral catheter are advanced into one of the vaginal compartments, either using the working
channel of the cystoscope or guided alongside the cystoscope. Next, the scope is removed over the
wire/catheter combination and re-advanced into the vestibule next to the catheter (Figure 117.9).
The scope can be advanced into the contralateral compartment to evaluate the length of the septum.
Each abnormality is classified as either a PPMR (<1 cm), VS (>1 cm) or DV (entire vagina to the
cervix) based on measurements of the septum with the open-ended ureteral catheter (1 cm marks
throughout its length).
A laser fiber is then placed inside the working channel of the endoscope and the tissues are laserablated from the caudal aspect to the most cranial aspect. The catheter is used for marking the
contralateral vaginal compartment until the vagina is one open tube with a single opening (Figure
117.9). The vestibule is infused topically with a 1:1 mixture of bupivacaine (0.3 mg/kg) and sterile
isotonic saline mixture for local transurethral analgesia.

Special Considerations
Following vaginoscopy, if the anatomic structure is unclear, a fluoroscopically-guided vestibulovaginogram is recommended. Laser-ablating a septum dividing a DV could result in vaginal
perforation.

Outcome
In a recent study, continence scores, vaginitis, and UTIs all were improved after endoscopic guided
laser ablation.34 This finding is difficult to attribute to the correction of the VVSR, as most dogs
underwent treatment of other congenital malformations, like ectopic ureters, concurrently. In 30 dogs
in which this procedure was performed, no dog had recurrence of the VVSR.34

Follow-up
Patients are discharged the same day as the procedure. Owners are provided with an analgesic to be
administered for signs of discomfort as needed. Noting clinical signs, urinalysis and urine culture and
sensitivity may be indicated in patients with chronic UTIs.

Complications
Complications with this procedure are possible and can include urethral tears, vaginal tears, and
unintended mucosal trauma. In a recent study evaluating endoscopic laser abaltion of

vestibulovaginal remnants, 5/36 dogs (14%) had immediate, mild, postoperative dysuria that resolved
in the first 24-72 hours post-endoscopy.34 Laser perforation of the vaginal wall occurred in one dog,
without clinically significant consequences.

Alternatives
The alternative is open surgical resection of the lesion. The authors consider cystoscopic ablation as
the standard of care for the correction of vestibulovaginal remnants.

CYSTOSCOPIC-GUIDED LASER ABLATION OF CANINE
INTRAMURAL ECTOPIC URETERS
Indications
Correction of intramural ectopic ureters in females and males (ch. 313). The diagnosis can be
made/confirmed by cystoscopy (ch. 100) and laser ablation performed at the same time.37-40
Advanced imaging, such as computed tomography, is rarely required unless other upper urinary tract
anomalies are suspected (vascular).37,38

Equipment
Rigid or flexible cystoscope, hydrophilic angled guidewire, open-ended ureteral catheter, iodinated
contrast medium, fluoroscopy or digital radiography, diode or Ho: YAG laser with a fiber that can be
passed through the scope channel.

FIGURE 117.9 Cystoscopy of a female dog (dorsal recumbency) undergoing
laser ablation of persistent paramesonephric remnant (PPMR). A, urethral
opening (yellow asterisk) is just above (ventral to) the vaginal opening, which
is covered by a dorsoventrally-oriented band of tissue, the PPMR (black
arrow). B, Open-ended ureteral catheter (red arrow) through one
compartment of the vaginal opening; laser (small black arrow) is directed onto
the band of tissue (black arrow). C-E, Progressive transection of the PPMR via

laser (thin black arrow) while monitoring both compartments of the vagina
with the ureteral catheter (red arrow). F, The entire remnant is cut, showing 1
vaginal compartment.

Procedure
The patient is anesthetized and placed in dorsal recumbency. The vulva/prepuce and surrounding
area are shaved/clipped, aseptically prepped, and draped. Complete cystoscopy and vaginoscopy are
performed to identify the site of the ectopia and identify concurrent anomalies (ch. 100). Once the
ectopic ureteral orifice is identified, an angled hydrophilic guidewire is advanced through the working
channel of the endoscope and passed into the ureter under fluoroscopic guidance. An open-ended
ureteral catheter is advanced over the guidewire into the distal ureter. The guidewire is then removed
and a retrograde ureteropyelogram is performed using iodinated contrast medium diluted 50:50 with
sterile saline. The intramural path of the ureter can be confirmed and other anomalies of the renal
pelvis and ureter can be assessed. The medial wall of the ectopic ureter is lasered until the ureteral
orifice is situated within the trigone (Video 117.3). Retrograde contrast urethrocystography confirms
correct positioning and ensures that no perforation of the urinary tract has occurred37,38 (Figure
117.10).

Special Considerations
Dogs with ectopic ureters can have various anomalies of the genitourinary tract (ch. 313). For
example, 93% of dogs with ureteral ectopia have a vestibulovaginal remnant, which can be laserablated at the time of correction of the ectopia. Treatment of UTI is recommended prior to cystoscopic
laser ablation.37-39 Laser ablation of ectopic ureters in male dogs is best accomplished by
fluoroscopic-assisted perineal urethral access allowing passage of a rigid scope into the pelvic urethra
(see above).40

Outcome
Cystoscopic laser ablation results in continence rates of 47% in female dogs 6 months following the
procedure, increasing to 77% with the addition of medical therapy for USMI37 (ch. 310). Success
rates are higher in male dogs.40 Persistent incontinence is believed to be secondary to other
concurrent urinary tract anomalies, such as USMI, which is reported in 75-89% of female dogs with
ectopic ureters.41,42

Follow-up
Treatment of USMI if persistent incontinence. Monitoring of clinical signs and urinalysis and culture
as needed, as UTI is identified in 30% of dogs in the 6 months following the procedure.37. Stricture at
the site of lasering is uncommon; however, the authors recommend urinary tract ultrasonography 2
weeks post-laser ablation to check for hydroureter/hydronephrosis.

Complications
Patients can present mild, self-limiting dysuria and pollakiuria. Recurrence of ureteral ectopia has not
been reported. Stricture at the ureterovesicular orifice is very uncommon. Perforation of the lower
urinary tract is a rare occurrence and can be treated by leaving a urinary catheter in place for 24-48
hours. Encrusted cystitis post-laser ablation has been reported.43

FIGURE 117.10 Laser ablation of an ectopic ureter in a female dog. A, An
open-ended ureteral catheter (d) is in the lumen of the ectopic ureter; the
medial (a) and lateral (b) walls of the ectopic ureter, and the lateral wall of the
urethra (c), are visible. B, The laser probe (e) is ablating the medial wall (a) of

Alternatives
Surgical correction of ectopic ureters. The authors consider cystoscopic ablation as the standard of
care for the correction of intramural ectopic ureters.

RENAL DISORDERS AND URETERAL OBSTRUCTIONS
TREATMENT OF NEPHROLITHIASIS
Indications
Removal of nephroliths in canine and feline patients is only indicated if the nephroliths are
considered complex and problematic, e.g., if there is a partial or complete ureteropelvic junction
(UPJ) obstruction resulting in progressive hydronephrosis; renal parenchymal loss due to stone
growth; progressive azotemia with stone growth; severe chronic hematuria; signs of renal pain; or
recurrent UTIs despite appropriate medical management of an infected nephrolith.44 The main

indication for intervention in cats with upper tract uroliths is when the nephrolith moves into the
ureter and becomes an obstructive ureterolith. If this occurs, then ureteral decompression with a
subcutaneous ureteral bypass device (SUB, see below) is recommended over nephrolithotomy.
Options for interventional removal of nephroliths are extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL)
(dogs only)45-48 and endoscopic nephrolithotomy (ENL; percutaneous nephrolithotomy [PCNL] or
surgically-assisted endoscopic nephrolithotomy [SENL] can be performed in both dogs and
cats).39,40,45,49

Equipment
There are many different brands of machines available for ESWL, with the most common being a dry
lithotriptor. These units are mobile and only a few facilities around the world offer this service for
veterinary medicine. The ENL procedure requires a puncture needle for renal pelvic access (18 ga), an
angle-tipped hydrophilic guidewire, and a dilation set that contains a variety of serial dilators or a
balloon dilation kit (18, 24, or 30 Fr). A nephroscope of appropriate size (22 Fr) is necessary for the
lithotriptor to fit within the working channel. The authors prefer the dual-probe ultrasonic
lithotriptor.∗ If a smaller nephroscope is needed, then the Ho: YAG laser, as mentioned above, can be
used for laser lithotripsy. If the procedure is done percutaneously, then a 6 Fr locking-loop pigtail
catheter is used after the procedure. All patients have an appropriately sized ureteral stent placed after
completion of the procedure, to prevent any fragments from causing a temporary ureteral obstruction.
It is typically recommended to stage this procedure in the case of bilateral nephrolithiasis, treating 1
kidney at a time at least 4 weeks apart to avoid excessive procedure duration and allow time for
recovery. Sometimes this is not possible due to cost and convenience.

PROCEDURES
Extracorporeal Shockwave Lithotripsy
Once a patient is placed under general anesthesia, ESWL can be performed by placing the patient in
various oblique positions, using fluoroscopic guidance, so that accurate targeting via the lithotriptor is
possible.50 The hair overlying the entry point of the shock waves is clipped and coupling gel is applied
to ensure transmission of the shockwaves onto the stone, while avoiding air bubbles from attenuating
the shock waves at the skin surface. The urolith is placed in the focal spot using fluoroscopic guidance
and the machine’s integrated targeting system. Shock waves are then delivered to induce urolith
fragmentation and this is gated to the heart rate and rhythm to avoid shock-induced arrhythmias.

Endoscopic Nephrolithotomy (Figures 117.11 and 117.12)
ENL is done either percutaneously (PCNL) or surgically assisted (SENL).45,50 Over the past decade,
the SENL approach has been considered the standard procedure, making it easier to manage the
nephrostomy access site with primary closure while avoiding a percutaneous nephrostomy tube for athome care. This technique is typically reserved for stones that are not amendable to ESWL (>1-1.5 cm
diameter or cystine in composition). For PCNL, the patient is placed in lateral recumbency and the
area of the kidney and the vulva/prepuce are clipped of hair and aseptically prepared. Using
ultrasound guidance, an 18 ga renal access needle is used for puncturing the renal pelvis through the
greater curvature of the kidney. Using fluoroscopic imaging, a ureteropyelogram is performed. Then, a
guidewire is placed antegrade into the renal pelvis, down the ureter, and into the urinary bladder,
where it is then passed out the urethra to obtain through-and-through wire access. A tract is then
dilated over the guidewire into the renal pelvis, through the renal parenchyma, using a balloon/sheath
combination (or serial dilators). This makes it possible for a rigid nephroscope to provide
intracorporeal access to the nephrolith. Next, the nephroscope and lithotripter are used in
combination to fragment the large stone and remove the fragments. This is carefully maneuvered until
the renal pelvis is clear of stone material, which is guided by endoscopy and fluoroscopy. Finally, once
removal is complete, a ureteral stent is placed to ensure postoperative ureteral patency. If this is done
percutaneously, then a locking-loop pigtail nephrostomy tube is also placed into the renal pelvis to
facilitate nephropexy formation and healing of the nephrostomy access tract. If this procedure is done

surgically-assisted (SENL), the same approach is used, but upon completion of the procedure, the
renal access point is closed primarily using a mattress suture, which avoids the need for a
nephrostomy tube.

Special Considerations
Over 95% of kidney stones in dogs and cats are not considered complex, meaning that at this point
they are not considered problematic enough to remove. Careful consideration should be used prior to
deciding to remove kidney stones, as the potential renal damage done to a compromised kidney,
particularly with a surgical nephrotomy, typically does not justify removal. Prior to choosing the best
procedure for nephrolith removal, stone size, patient size, and stone type should be considered.
Exchanging a non-obstructive nephrolith for an obstructive ureterolith is contraindicated and
concurrent ureteral stenting is often necessary to prevent this. Cystine stones are ESWL-resistant, and
ENL should be considered for this stone type when needed. Stone recurrence also is common, so
medical management should be implemented appropriately to reduce this likelihood or frequency
(dogs, ch. 308; cats, ch. 309). The procedures described here, like the other procedures in this
chapter, should only be performed by trained operators.

Outcome
ESWL and ENL are safe, minimally invasive procedures, and can be highly effective when performed
correctly.51,52 ENL typically is more effective (90-100%)51,53 than ESWL (50-80%)52 when a single
treatment is desired, and has been shown in people to have minimal effect on kidney function when
compared to all other options.53 However, it is important to realize that ENL is more difficult to
perform and is more invasive than ESWL. In a report45 of 12 patients (16 renal units) in which ENL
was performed, the median stone diameter was 2.5 cm (0.5-5.7 cm) and the median pre- and 3-month
postoperative serum creatinine concentration were 1.4 mg/dL (123 micromol/L) (range, 0.7-9.1
mg/dL [62-801 micromol/L]) and 1.3 mg/dL (114 micromol/L) (range, 0.5-8.3 mg/dL [44-730
micromol/L]), respectively; the follow-up time was a median of 557 days (range, 4-2490 days).
Successful removal of all stones was documented in 94% of renal units with 1 procedure, and no
patient died from the ENL procedure, similar to results reported in humans.45,51,53 In a series of 140
dogs with nephroliths or ureteroliths treated by ESWL, the most common complication was the
development of ureteral obstruction, occurring in ~10% of dogs.46 The risk of ureteral obstruction has
declined with the use of concurrent endoscopic ureteral stent placement at the time of ESWL.

FIGURE 117.11 A 3.1 kg Yorkshire Terrier undergoing percutaneous
nephrolithotomy. A, Renal access using an 18-ga renal access trocar needle
(white arrow) and ultrasound guidance. B, Guidewire access (red arrows) into

D, Sheath (yellow arrow) passing over the balloon (black arrow). E, Sheath
inside the kidney. F, Scope inside the sheath for nephroscopy.

Follow-up
After ESWL, dogs are treated with IV fluid therapy for 12-36 hours. Abdominal radiographs are
performed at 24 hours to evaluate nephrolith fragmentation, and ultrasonography is performed to
confirm no ureteral obstruction has developed. If a ureteral stent is placed concurrently, dogs often
are discharged the same day as the procedure. After ENL, the patient is hospitalized and receives IV
fluids and pain medications. Patients are discharged within 24-36 hours, and follow-up imaging and

bloodwork are performed 2 weeks later. Once all stone fragments are confirmed to have been
eliminated, the ureteral stent is removed either endoscopically or using fluoroscopic guidance. The
renal pelvis can remain dilated for a few weeks/months, depending on the size of the stone that was
removed and the length of time the stone was present. For PCNL, the nephrostomy tube is assessed
with a urine culture in 5-7 days, and at 1 month it is removed. This should be done over a guidewire
and can be done at the same time as ureteral stent removal.

Complications
The most common complication with ESWL is ureteral obstruction (10%).46 Additional complications
that can occur include pancreatitis, cardiac arrhythmias, transient hemorrhage, and the need for more
than one procedure (15-30%).46 ESWL is not recommended for treatment of nephroliths in cats
because the feline ureter is only 0.3 mm in diameter, whereas a typical nephrolith fragment after
ESWL has a diameter of ~1 mm. Therefore, fragmentation of nephroliths in cats has a high chance of
resulting in ureteral obstruction. In addition, feline kidneys have been reported to hemorrhage more
with ESWL compared to canine kidneys.46
For ENL, the main risks are hemorrhage, ureteral perforation, and urine leakage from the renal
access point. If the procedure is done percutaneously (PCNL), then a nephrostomy tube remains
indwelling for a minimum of 4 weeks to create a nephropexy; otherwise, urine leakage can occur while
the nephrostomy site heals. Nephrostomy tube dislodgement and UTIs should be considered, and
careful monitoring should be implemented. With ENL, the access point is closed with a suture once
the procedure is complete.
Regardless of which procedure is performed, the biggest risk is stone recurrence; this warrants
careful monitoring and appropriate preventive measures.

Alternatives
The alternative to ESWL or ENL is a surgical nephrotomy, nephrectomy, or leaving the stone within
the kidney without intervention. Fewer than 5% of all stones require removal, and care should be
taken when deciding the best approach for each patient. Most patients with large problematic stones
have underlying renal dysfunction and a nephrectomy should be avoided.

TREATMENT OF BENIGN URETERAL OBSTRUCTIONS
Indications
Benign ureteral obstructions are a clinical problem seen with greater frequency in dogs and cats over
the past decade (ch. 306).54-72 This condition is most commonly associated with ureterolithiasis
and/or ureteral strictures in both dogs and cats. Interventional options have become a common
treatment modality due to the lower morbidity and mortality rates reported when compared to
traditional surgical techniques.66-68,70-72 To date, the recommended interventional treatments for

ureteral obstructions are endoscopic ureteral stent placement for dogs and placement of a SUB device
in cats. On rare occasions, a SUB device is used for dogs with benign obstructions.67

FIGURE 117.13 Images of 3 cats after placement of a subcutaneous ureteral
bypass (SUB) device of different iterations. A, SUB 1.0. B, SUB 2.0. C, SUB
3.0.

Equipment
Various rigid and flexible endoscopes are needed for retrograde ureteral stent placement in dogs. This
is possible in any size female dog, and male dogs weighing >6 kg. Guidewires and catheters are
needed for each procedure, and size depends on the size of the stent and catheter that are ultimately
chosen (Table 117.3). The SUB device† is a specialized 6.5 Fr nephrostomy tube that is connected to a
cystostomy tube and a subcutaneous port, creating an artificial ureter. There have been various
iterations of this device since its inception in 2009, consisting of the SUB 1.0, 2.0 and now 3.0
(Figure 117.13). All of these modifications have been adopted to improve ease of placement and
decrease complications associated with the device like kinking, leakage, blood clot occlusion and
mineralization.

Ureteral Stenting
Ureteral stents are most commonly placed cystoscopically in dogs. This is performed in a retrograde
manner via cystourethroscopy, and a guidewire and catheter are advanced up the ureter through the
UVJ. This is considerably more difficult when the obstruction is due to a trigonal tumor covering the
UVJ (see below), as the orifice is often not able to be visualized to obtain guidewire access. For
endoscopic ureteral stent placement, the patient is placed in dorsal recumbency and the vulva or
prepuce is shaved/clipped and aseptically prepared. In a female dog, a 30° cystoscope is used for
routine cystourethroscopy (ch. 100), and an appropriately sized, angle-tipped, hydrophilic
guidewire/ureteral catheter combination are used for cannulating the ureteral orifice. Once the
catheter is advanced over the wire into the distal third of the ureter, the wire is removed, and under
fluoroscopic guidance, a retrograde ureteropyelogram is performed. This allows for visualization of
the ureteral lumen, obstructive lesion, and renal pelvis. In addition, this often dislodges the
obstructive stone and allows easier passage of the wire, catheter, and stent. Next, the wire is readvanced through the catheter lumen and out its tip, up the ureteral lumen, around or through the
obstructive lesion, and coiled inside the renal pelvis (Figure 117.14). The catheter is advanced over
the wire until its tip is in the renal pelvis. The wire is then removed from the catheter and a urine

sample is obtained for analysis and culture. Next, a 50% mixture of iodinated contrast and saline is
injected into the renal pelvis. If there is pyonephrosis, than the renal pelvis is lavaged thoroughly with
sterile saline and contrast to remove the purulent debris. The wire is then re-advanced into the
catheter lumen and coiled within the renal pelvis. The catheter is removed over the guidewire,
monitoring with fluoroscopic guidance to ensure the wire remains coiled within the renal pelvis and is
not inadvertently removed. During this withdrawal, the ureteral length is measured using the catheter
and monitoring the UVJ through the endoscope. Then an appropriately-sized double pigtail ureteral
stent is chosen based on the ureteral diameter, guidewire size, and ureteral length. This double pigtail
ureteral stent is advanced over the guidewire, through the working channel of the endoscope, and up
the ureter. The proximal loop is coiled over the wire in the renal pelvis. Once the pigtail of the stent is
seen in the renal pelvis, then the wire is slowly withdrawn back into the cystoscope. The pusher
catheter is used to push the distal end of the stent out of the working channel of the endoscope and
into the urinary bladder.

SUB Device
The SUB device (Figure 117.13) is typically used for all causes of ureteral obstructions in cats,
whereas in dogs, it is often reserved for when ureteral stenting fails or a malignant obstruction has
been treated via radical cystectomy. Dogs typically tolerate stents very well and a SUB is not indicated
since a stent can be placed endoscopically. The SUB device has simplified the treatment of ureteral
obstructions in cats tremendously, especially those with multiple ureteroliths, very proximal
obstructions, decompensating patients, and ureteral strictures (∼33% of feline ureteral obstructions).
In a recent evaluation of the SUB 3.0, the median procedure time was 35 minutes for unilateral and 45
minutes for bilateral placement.73

The bladder apex and affected kidney are exposed through a ventral midline celiotomy. Using the
modified Seldinger technique, an 18 ga catheter is advanced through the caudal/caudolateral pole of
the kidney and into the renal pelvis. A urine sample is collected for aerobic culture. An antegrade
pyelogram is performed using a 50% mixture of iodinated saline and contrast, and then a 0.035″
angle-tipped hydrophilic guidewire, or a J-tipped 0.035″ guidewire, is advanced through the catheter.
If the pelvis measures <8 mm, the hydrophilic wire is used and the guidewire is placed down the
ureter. If the pelvis measures >8 mm, then the J-wire can be used and coiled in the renal pelvis.
(Figure 117.15). Once wire access is obtained, the 18-ga catheter is removed over the wire, under
fluoroscopic guidance, and the locking-loop nephrostomy catheter is advanced over the wire. If the
catheter is going down the ureter, then the string is cut and removed. If the catheter is coiling within
the pelvis, then the locking mechanism is employed. Once the radiopaque mark is within the renal
pelvis, the Dacron cuff and silicone sleeve are advanced to the renal capsule and glued using sterile
cyanoacrylate glue.

FIGURE 117.16 Subcutaneous ureteral bypass device: placing cystostomy
catheter. A, Pursestring suture at bladder apex. B, Puncture at center of
pursestring into bladder lumen using electrocautery. C, Bladder catheter
advanced with hollow cannula in place; pursestring secured around catheter
and tied. D-E, Dacron cuff glued to bladder. F, Silicone/Dacron cuff sutured

Next, the urinary bladder apex is isolated, and a purse-string suture is placed using 3-0 Monocryl
suture (Figure 117.16). Cautery is used for making a small, full thickness bladder incision in the

center of the purse-string suture and the cystostomy catheter is advanced into the bladder lumen
using the hollow trocar. The purse string is secured. The Dacron cuff is glued to the serosal surface of
the urinary bladder, and Monocryl suture is used to further secure the Dacron/silicone cuff to the
bladder wall (full thickness), using 3 interrupted sutures. Finally, the tubes are connected. For the
SUB 3.0 device, the nephrostomy and cystostomy tubes are connected to the Y-connector intraabdominally and a third actuating tubing is connected to the other male end of the Y-adaptor. The
skin and subcutaneous tissues lateral to the incision, on the ipsilateral side of the obstruction, are
dissected down to the abdominal musculature and the actuating tubing is passed through the body
wall, leaving enough room for the shunting port and some tubing to connect to the male adaptor (~34 cm). This tubing is then passed through the body wall and connected to the subcutaneous port
(Figure 117.17). A leak test is then performed using a non-coring Huber needle to ensure no
connections are leaking any fluid. Then, the port is secured to the body wall using permanent suture
material. Finally, the system is drained of fluid and the system is flushed with contrast using digital
subtraction angiography (DSA) under fluoroscopic guidance to document patency with no leaking and
no kinking. Once patency is confirmed, the subcutaneous tissue is closed and topical bupivacaine is
infused into the pocket. Then, the abdomen is flushed copiously with warm saline and closed
routinely. Final fluoroscopic images (ventrodorsal and lateral) are taken to ensure no kinking of the
catheters is seen prior to complete closure. The routine placement of an esophagostomy tube and a
triple lumen jugular catheter for supportive care is considered in all feline cases.

Special Considerations
Proper training on the use of stents and SUB devices is recommended prior to considering performing
these procedures. Good-quality imaging and endoscopic expertise should be available. Endoscopic
ureteral stenting in male dogs is possible with flexible cystoscopy, but sometimes percutaneous
perineal access for rigid cystoscopy (>8 kg) makes this procedure easier.

FIGURE 117.17 Subcutaneous ureteral bypass device: connection in
abdomen. A, Y-connector connects kidney catheter, bladder catheter, and
actuating tubing going to port. B, Actuating tubing being passed through body
wall, ipsilateral to kidney catheter. C, Actuating tubing cut to ensure it is not
too long, as the length suits the size of the cat’s abdomen well. D, Actuating
tubing being connected to port.

Follow-up
Patients with ureteral stents or SUB devices need to be monitored very carefully. Feline patients are
likely to develop post-obstructive diuresis and if careful fluid replacement therapy is not employed,
fluid overload can occur (ch. 120). Care is taken to maintain an appropriate fluid balance using
enteral hydration when possible; therefore, routine use of an esophagostomy tube is recommended
(ch. 81). Treatment with a fluoroquinolone for 2 weeks is recommended to help prevent
postoperative biofilm development on urinary devices.74 Routine urinary tract ultrasonography and
radiography, focusing on the renal pelvis diameter, stent location, ureteral diameter, presence of any
free fluid, and location of stent/SUB catheters in the urinary bladder, is performed. This is to ensure
there is no evidence of stent/SUB device migration, kinking, occlusion, or encrustation. The authors
recommend performing a SUB device flush with a urine culture every 3-6 months. Each device is
flushed as well prior to discharge, and at the first 1-month recheck.
The SUB device should be flushed using ultrasonographic guidance. This is typically done using a
SUB flush kit‡ where tetrasodium-EDTA is infused into the device each time. This material75 has been
shown to decrease the rate of mineralization and infections after SUB device placement76 (Figure
117.18).

Outcome/Complications
The most successful variable in the interventional treatment of canine and feline patients with
ureteral obstruction is the operator having appropriate training and experience. These are some of the
more difficult interventional radiology/interventional endoscopy cases being performed. In addition,
the anesthetic procedure should be handled with caution, as these patients have renal disease and
often concurrent heart disease.

FIGURE 117.18 Subcutaneous ureteral bypass (SUB) flush kit: A, sterile
gloves and flush kit. B-C, The parts in the SUB flush kit are attached properly
(all sterile). 1, T-port connector; 2, 3-way stopcock; 3, 20 ga Huber needle; 4,
empty 3 mL syringe (1 for discard, 1 for sample collection); 5, 2.5 mL sterile
saline; 6, 2 mL of Tetra-EDTA (T-FloLoc). D, Cat in dorsal recumbency; port
site clipped and aseptically prepared. D-E, Huber needle inserted through
skin into port using strict aseptic technique. F-G, Ultrasound-guided
evaluation of renal pelvis and bladder. SUB noted coming through caudal pole
of kidney (red arrow). H, First urine sample is discarded, followed by sample
collected for analysis (blue arrow). I, Testing patency: saline infused into
system (white arrow), monitoring the kidney with ultrasound guidance. Once
patency is confirmed, then tetra-EDTA (green arrow) is used to flush into the
system, monitoring the kidney with ultrasound.
In a retrospective study66 of 134 obstructed cats with 174 obstructed ureters treated using a SUB
device, the median survival time was 827 days (range, 0.25-2397 days) for all causes of death, and
only 27.6% died of suspected renal causes.60,66 In another retrospective evaluation of 44 dogs (57
ureters) treated with ureteral stents for benign ureteral obstructions, the median survival time was
>1158 days and 68% of dogs were still alive at the time of last follow-up.65 Another study evaluating
13 dogs with pyonephrosis that underwent ureteral stent placement in addition to renal pelvic lavage
demonstrated excellent long-term survival; recurrence of UTI occurred in ∼50% of dogs, nearly all of
which could be cleared without the need for further intervention.64
SUB complications have been separated into 4 categories: procedural (during device placement),
perioperative (within the first week, typically during hospitalization), short-term (1 week to 1 month
postoperatively) and long-term (>1 month postoperatively) (Table 117.4). With the improvement in
the iterations of the SUB device, complication rates have gone down. The SUB 3.0 has been associated
with shorter surgery times and fewer short-term complications than the SUB 2.0.73 There was no

evidence of kinks with the 3.0 (15.5% with the SUB 2.0), 4% had a perioperative blood clot (compared
to 14% with the 2.0), and no device leaked (compared to 2.8% with the 2.0). There was no difference
in the rate of chronic UTIs, as only 1 animal in each group experienced this complication. It is
important to note that the SUB 3.0 has been used primarily since 2019, whereas the SUB 2.0 was used
from 2013-2019, so there are more long-term data on the SUB 2.0 at this time.

Alternatives
The use of a locking-loop nephrostomy tube has been reported for successful ureteral decompression
in dogs and cats prior to definitive treatment of ureteral obstruction.77 These tubes work very well, but
with the advent of the SUB device, surgical time is similar for a definitive intervention (SUB) as
compared to a temporary one (nephrostomy tube). Thus, the locking-loop nephrostomy approach
rarely has been necessary, to date, in the authors’ practice.

TREATMENT OF MALIGNANT URETERAL OBSTRUCTIONS
Indications
Decompression of a ureteral obstruction secondary to trigonal neoplasia that is causing UVJ occlusion
(ch. 330) can be done using an antegrade approach under ultrasonographic and fluoroscopic
guidance.78 In addition, more recently, radical cystourethrectomy with the placement of bilateral SUB
devices has been utilized with an attempt to remove all gross tumor. This results in placing the
cystostomy portion of the catheter into either the vagina/distal urethra (female) or the distal urethra
(male), which leads to urinary incontinence. This has been well-managed by numerous patients and
pet owners. Another investigational option is the use of a neobladder made of silver-impregnated
silicone. This results in the cystostomy portion of the device being connected to a silicone depot,
which is a neobladder.79 This is then connected to a low-profile tube that can be drained through the
body wall, similar to a cystostomy tube. Treated dogs have been continent but they do require urinary
drainage at least 3-4 times per day.

Equipment

Fluoroscopy and ultrasonography, in addition to an 18 ga renal puncture needle or long 2-2.5″ (5-6
cm) over-the-needle IV catheter, iodinated contrast, various guidewires, catheters, access sheaths, and
ureteral stents, are needed for this procedure.

Procedure
The patient is anesthetized and the area of the kidney and vulva or prepuce are shaved/clipped and
aseptically prepared. The patient is placed in lateral recumbency, with the obstructed kidney facing
up. A 3 mm skin stab incision is made where the ultrasound probe shows the best renal access and
orientation to aim down the ureter. Fluoroscopy is lined up over the kidney and proximal ureter. With
ultrasound guidance, an 18 ga renal access trocar needle, or long over-the-needle IV catheter, is used
for puncturing the kidney through the greater curvature toward the UPJ (Figure 117.19). Once the
needle tip is visualized in the renal pelvis, the sharp stylet is removed and a T-port with a 3-way
stopcock connected to one empty and one diluted (50%) contrast-filled syringe (3-6 mL) is connected
to the stopcock. A urine sample is obtained and then contrast is injected to fill the renal pelvis and
proximal ureter under ultrasound and fluoroscopic guidance. Then, a stiffened 0.035″ (0.9 mm)
angle-tipped hydrophilic guidewire is used for cannulating the renal pelvis, angled down the ureter to
the UVJ and into the urinary bladder. This negotiation through the tumor at the UVJ can be difficult
and requires patience. This is monitored with fluoroscopic guidance. Once the tumor is crossed, the
wire is advanced into the urinary bladder, down the urethra, and out the vulva/prepuce, providing
through-and-through access. Then, a 6-7 Fr × 45 cm (female) or 55 cm (male) sheath is advanced
retrograde, up the urethra, into the ureter through the UVJ, and up to the UPJ. Care is taken to ensure
the dilator of the sheath does not puncture the renal parenchyma. Once the sheath is at the UPJ, the
dilator is removed, and a contrast study is performed through the side port of the sheath to obtain a
pyelogram. Then, a second standard angle-tipped hydrophilic guidewire (0.035″ [0.9 mm]) is
advanced up the sheath and coiled into the renal pelvis. The wire is advanced next to the safety wire,
which is through-and-through and coiled inside the renal pelvis. The sheath is then withdrawn from
the UPJ to the UVJ to measure the ureteral length, and then removed over both wires, while
monitoring under fluoroscopic guidance. Finally, the sheath with the dilator is placed again over the
second guidewire, next to the safety wire. The sheath is advanced over the wire, up the ureter, and to
the UPJ. The proper-sized stent is placed over this guidewire, through the sheath. Once a coil is seen
within the renal pelvis, the sheath is withdrawn to the proximal urethra, maintaining the stent within
the renal pelvis using the pusher catheter in the sheath, while carefully monitoring the distal end of
the stent (fluoroscopically) so it is appropriately pushed into the urinary bladder (Figure 117.19).
The guidewire is then withdrawn to the distal aspect of the stent within the urethra and then the
pusher is used to push the distal end of the stent into the bladder. This technique is complicated and
there is more explanation of technical details in other resources.80

FIGURE 117.19 Ureteral stent placement in a female dog with trigonal
transitional cell carcinoma causing ureteral obstruction; lateral recumbency,

the part of the stent in urethra (red arrow) and sheath is only in distal urethra.
K, Ureteral stent (yellow arrows) being pushed into bladder with pusher
catheter (blue arrow); wire (red arrow) crosses junction of stent and pusher to
keep both together. Notice the stent starting to buckle. L, Stent is then pushed
into the urinary bladder (yellow arrow) and pusher catheter (blue arrow) and
safety wire are removed (M).

Special Considerations
Conversion for surgical placement is rare, but one should be prepared to do this if the interventional
procedure is unsuccessful.

Outcome
In 12 dogs (15 ureters), ureteral stents were placed for ureteral obstructive neoplasia and 1 dog
required surgical conversion.80 All survived to discharge and the median survival time from the time
of diagnosis was 285 days (range, 10-1571 days), while survival following stent placement was 57 days
(range, 7-337 days).

Follow-up
The authors recommend waiting a minimum of 1 week before starting, or resuming, chemotherapy,
due to the risk of post-obstructive diuresis and associated dehydration. Urinary tract ultrasound
examinations and urine cultures should be obtained at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, and every 3 months
thereafter. Complete blood counts and serum biochemistry profiles should also be done as
appropriate. All clients should be encouraged to consult with an oncologist. After stent placement, and
if the patient is not azotemic, treatment with chemotherapy and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
has been shown to prolong survival.

Complications
The biggest risk is ureteral perforation, or leakage from the renal puncture site, resulting in
uroabdomen. This is not a problem if the ureteral obstruction is successfully decompressed with a
stent. If stent placement is unsuccessful, surgical conversion is typically required. If a stent is properly
placed, then any puncture should heal within a few days and conversion is not needed as the
obstruction is decompressed. Other potential complications include stent migration, stent irritation,
chronic infections, and stent occlusion. All of these are rare.

FIGURE 117.20 Subcutaneous ureteral bypass (SUB) device for obstructive
neoplasia in a cat and dog. A-B, Bilateral SUBs and a urethral stent in a cat
with trigonal obstructive neoplasia; 3-way shunting port connects 2 kidney
catheters to a bladder catheter. C, Fluoroscopic image of a dog after bilateral
SUBs and a radical cystectomy, with cystostomy catheter placed in urethra.

Alternatives
A SUB system can be used for this application, but it requires surgical placement. For cases where the
tumor is localized to the urinary bladder +/− proximal urethra, the entire bladder and proximal
urethra can be removed via a radical cystectomy and partial ureterectomy and urethrectomy. In this
case, both renal pelvises have a SUB catheter placed. Then, both nephrostomy tubes are connected to
an “X-piece” as part of a SUB 3.0 (Figure 117.20). A third catheter is placed down the distal urethra
or into the vagina. These dogs will be completely incontinent, but if the procedure is done
appropriately, only microscopic disease or less will hopefully remain.

TREATMENT OF IDIOPATHIC RENAL HEMATURIA
Indications
Idiopathic renal hematuria is a rare condition that is seen in young, large-breed dogs, and it has also
been reported in older dogs and cats of various ages. This condition results in persistent port-wine
colored urine, and may be progressive, become bilateral, result in ureteral or urethral obstructions
due to blood clots, or result in progressive anemia.82-85 The lesion usually is of benign origin and may
be an angioma, hemangioma, or ulcerative lesion of the renal pelvis (pyelitis). If any of these
conditions occurs, then treatment using a renal-sparing option like sclerotherapy or ureteroscopy with
endoscopic electrocautery can be considered. Traditionally, ureteronephrectomy had been performed
for treatment of this condition, but >30% of affected animals develop bilateral disease over time;

however, the lesion is nearly always benign and does not involve the nephrons, making nephrectomy
unnecessary, and risky.82-85

Equipment
A cystoscope (rigid or flexible) is needed to diagnose which renal unit is bleeding. Perineal access
should be performed in male dogs (see above) once the diagnosis is made via flexible endoscopy.24 A
UPJ balloon is used for ureteral occlusion sclerotherapy infusions and these come in 5 and 6 Fr sizes;
a stiffened 0.035″ (0.9 mm) angle-tipped hydrophilic guidewire is used for placing this catheter. For
sclerotherapy, a sterilized liquid 0.5-1% silver nitrate solution, in addition to a 1:1:3 ratio of 5%
povidone iodine, 76% meglumine diatrizoate (76MD), and sterile 5% dextrose in water (D5W), is
used.
Instead of saline irrigation during endoscopy, D5W is used. This helps to prevent red blood cell
lysis, improving visibility during cystoscopy. In addition, D5W prevents silver salt development
during sclerotherapy with silver nitrate, and aids conduction during Bugbee electrocautery, if
necessary.

FIGURE 117.21 Cystoscopic image of a dog showing left-sided ureteral
urine jet with severe upper tract hematuria.
For ureteroscopic electrocautery, a 0.035″ (0.9 mm) stiffened angle-tipped hydrophilic guidewire is
used with a ureteral access sheath to advance the flexible ureteroscope. Irrigation with D5W is done
manually through the ureteroscope. Once a lesion is found in the renal pelvis, a Bugbee cautery
electrode (1-2 Fr) is used in either blend or coagulation mode through the working channel of the
ureteroscope to ablate the lesion. This small-diameter electrode maintains the flexibility of the
ureteroscope within the renal pelvis. If necessary, a ureteral access sheath can be used for maintaining
ureteral patency during ureteroscopy. An open-ended ureteral catheter and appropriately sized
ureteral stent are needed at the completion of the procedure.

Procedure
Diagnostic cystoscopy is performed to identify which ureter has blood coming from it (Figure 117.21;
ch. 100). Then, using a rigid cystoscope, a guidewire and open-ended ureteral catheter combination
are used for cannulating the bleeding ureter/kidney. Once the catheter is midway up the ureter, a
retrograde ureteropyelogram using endoscopic and fluoroscopic guidance is performed to assess for
any luminal defects.

Sclerotherapy
Sclerotherapy typically is performed first (Figure 117.22). The contrast material used is 76% MD, as
this is the recommended mixture for povidone iodine to provide cauterization in humans.86 The
guidewire is advanced to the renal pelvis and then a UPJ balloon is advanced over the guidewire. Once
the catheter is in the proximal ureter, the balloon is inflated with air (volume according to balloon
size), occluding the lumen of the ureter. The patient is tilted into a 20° Trendelenburg position
(hindlimbs higher than kidneys) to enhance accumulation of contrast material in the renal pelvis.
Next, the contrast is used for measuring the renal pelvis volume; accurately determining this volume
will allow appropriate renal pelvis filling, and avoid overdistension or parenchymal backfilling. Once
this volume is determined, then 2 infusions of the povidone iodine/MD/D5W solution are performed,
with a dwell time of 10-20 minutes each. Once each dwell is passively drained from the catheter, then
2 more infusions of liquid sterile 0.5-1% silver nitrate solution are administered, with a dwell time of
10-20 minutes each. This is not mixed with any contrast nor diluted with any fluid.87,88 Finally, the
solution is drained and a guidewire is re-advanced up the catheter and coiled in the renal pelvis for a
double pigtail ureteral stent to be placed as described above.

Ureteroscopy with Electrocautery
Ureteroscopy with electrocautery is reserved for dogs weighing >20 kg, and preferably is performed
after a ureteral stent has been in place for at least 1-2 weeks to allow for passive ureteral dilation
which makes navigation in the ureter and renal pelvis easier.89 A guidewire is passed up to the
proximal ureter, avoiding the renal pelvis to prevent iatrogenic trauma. Then, a ureteral access sheath
that can accommodate the flexible ureteroscope is advanced over the guidewire under fluoroscopic
guidance. Once the sheath is in the ureter, then the ureteroscope is advanced over the guidewire, up
the ureter, using D5W for irrigation. Once in the renal pelvis, irrigation is used cautiously to avoid
overdistension. Once a bleeding lesion is seen, the Bugbee cautery electrode probe (Figure 117.23) is
advanced into the working channel of the ureteroscope and the lesion is cauterized using 12-25 W in
contact mode. When complete, a ureteral stent is delivered over a guidewire and placed as described
above.

FIGURE 117.22 Female dog undergoing sclerotherapy for idiopathic renal
hematuria. A, Cystoscopic image of guidewire catheterizing left ureteral
opening. B, Open-ended ureteral catheter being advanced up ureter over
guidewire. C, Fluoroscopic image during ureteropyelogram through ureteral
catheter. D, Ureteropelvic junction balloon catheter (black arrow) occluding
ureteral outflow during sclerotherapy infusion.

FIGURE 117.23 Ureteronephroscopy in a dog with idiopathic renal
hematuria. A, Fluoroscopic image of ureteroscope up the ureter and inside the
renal pelvis. B, Endoscopic image of the ureteral lumen. C, Renal pelvis bleed
visualized (black arrow). D, Electrocautery probe in renal pelvis.

Special Considerations
This procedure should be done by those trained in endourology, ureteral catheterization, and ureteral
stenting. It should not be done without fluoroscopic guidance, which is used for measuring the filling
volume of the renal pelvis.

Outcome
In a study in which sclerotherapy was used for the treatment of idiopathic renal hematuria, complete
cessation of macroscopic hematuria occurred in 4/6 dogs within a median of 6 hours (range,
immediately post-operatively to 7 days).84 The two additional dogs improved, one moderately and
one substantially. None of the dogs required nephrectomy or became anemic. Since this publication
the authors have performed this procedure in ∼40 patients with a success rate of cessation of gross
hematuria in >90% of patients. Ureteroscopy for electrocautery only has been performed in a small
number of patients.

Follow-up
Antibiotics are used for 2 weeks after ureteral stent placement to prevent biofilm formation on the
stent.74 After 2-6 weeks, if the bleeding resolves, the stent should be removed. If the bleeding does not
stop, then retrograde ureteroscopy and nephroscopy can be performed, as the stent would have
allowed for passive ureteral dilation, making this procedure much easier.90

Complications
The most substantial risk is perforating the ureter during cannulation or excessive renal
filling/distension resulting in nephritis or pelvic rupture. By using fluoroscopy and endoscopy
together, the appropriate filling volume of the renal pelvis during sclerotherapy is ensured. Also, the

risk of post-sclerotherapy ureteritis and post-ureteroscopy edema exists, so the operator should be
comfortable with retrograde ureteral stent placement.

Alternatives
Selective renal arterial embolization has been considered for this condition but is not typically needed
unless a vascular anomaly is identified on angiography, which has not yet been the case.
Ureteronephrectomy should be avoided whenever possible.

Interventional radiology (IR) involves the combination of minimally
invasive approaches and contemporary imaging modalities to gain
access to specific organs in order to deliver a variety of devices or
medications for therapeutic purposes (ch. 113). IR techniques are
being increasingly utilized to help manage humans with cancer
(interventional oncology, IO) in which traditional therapies have
failed or have been demonstrated to provide insufficient benefit.

Interventional oncology has been referred to as the “fourth pillar” of
oncological care along with medical, surgical, and radiation
therapies. Veterinarians have traditionally had little to offer patients
with non-resectable or metastatic tumors. Surgery is uncommonly
indicated when resections have a high likelihood of substantial
morbidity and low likelihood of improved survival times. The
relatively limited efficacy of intravenous (IV) chemotherapy for
macroscopic disease, and the cost, occasional morbidity, and tumor
resistance associated with radiation therapy have stimulated the
search for additional therapeutic options. Initial results have been
promising and regional techniques such as palliative stenting for
malignant obstructions, transcatheter chemotherapy, trans-catheter
arterial embolization/chemoembolization, and more recently
percutaneous tumor ablation, are becoming increasingly
investigated.

PALLIATIVE STENTING FOR
MALIGNANT OBSTRUCTIONS
INDICATIONS AND BACKGROUND
Animals are routinely euthanized for local effects of a tumor rather
than the systemic effects associated with a large cancer burden.
While these conditions can occur in any lumen such as those of the
respiratory (ch. 114), gastrointestinal (ch. 116), and cardiovascular
(ch. 115) systems1-5 (Figure 118.1), one of the more common
examples is malignant obstruction of the urinary tract. Lifethreatening signs associated with complete urinary tract obstruction
or perceived diminished quality of life can lead to owner-elected
euthanasia, even when tumor staging confirms localized disease.
Minimally invasive endoluminal urethral stenting,6-8 and endoscopic
or percutaneous ureteral stenting,9 have been performed in dogs and
cats10 to relieve both lower and upper tract obstructions. While
endoscopic-guided laser ablation is a common therapy for the
typically superficial transitional cell carcinomas (TCCs) experienced
in humans, this is not the recommended treatment for the less
common and more aggressive, muscle-invasive TCC. Considering the

reported TCC laser ablation11 complications reported in dogs, cost,
extended hospitalization times, need for repeat procedures (∼47%),
possible limitation to females, and otherwise similar outcomes,
stenting appears to compare favorably. The procedural aspects are
described in detail in ch. 117.

INTRA-ARTERIAL (IA)
CHEMOTHERAPY DELIVERY
INDICATIONS AND BACKGROUND
Current therapies for bulky tumors not amenable to complete
surgical resection include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and
surgical debulking, but none is consistently able to produce durable
remissions. Specific tumor cell lines tend to be more sensitive to
certain chemotherapeutic agents, and increasing the concentration of
these drugs tends to increase both tumor cell death and systemic
toxicosis. Studies confirm both higher concentrations of
chemotherapeutic agent within the targeted tissues as well as
improved tumor remissions in laboratory animals when IR
techniques are used to deliver drugs superselectively.12-14

EQUIPMENT
Equipment that is commonly used for intra-arterial (IA)
chemotherapy delivery is listed in Box 118.1 and Figure 118.2. IA
chemotherapy procedures require a fluoroscopy unit with
exceptional imaging detail to identify very small caliber vessels using
digital subtraction angiography (DSA, ch. 113) and road mapping, as
well as the ability to obtain orthogonal imaging when necessary.
Failure to identify collateral vessels could lead to non-target delivery
and potentially severe consequences.

TECHNIQUE (FIGURE 118.2)

The patient is placed under general anesthesia and the inguinal
region or neck is clipped/shaved and aseptically scrubbed for either
femoral or carotid arterial access via surgical cut-down. A 4 or 5 Fr
introducer sheath15 is placed and a combination 0.035″ (0.9 mm)
angled, hydrophilic guide wire16 and 4 or 5 Fr reverse-curve
catheter17 (femoral) or 4 Fr Berenstein catheter18 (carotid) is
advanced under fluoroscopic guidance to the terminal aorta. A DSA
delineates the vascular anatomy and a microcatheter/microwire
combination is used to gain super-selective access to one of the
terminal arteries feeding the tumor (e.g., prostatic artery or vaginal
artery in the case of lower urinary tract tumors). Standard therapy
involves the total systemic chemotherapy dose mixed with an equal
volume of iohexol contrast injected under fluoroscopic guidance to
ensure flow down the target artery without reflux into non-target
vessels. The catheter and sheath are removed and the femoral or
carotid artery ligated. The cut-down site is closed in three layers and
the patient recovered.

FOLLOW-UP
The patient is typically discharged the same day with the same
medications prescribed following IV use of the same chemotherapies.
Oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are continued
if indicated and typically IA treatments are alternated with IV
therapies to address systemic (non-regional) disease. Restaging is
often performed according to the oncologist’s recommendations.

OUTCOMES AND POSSIBLE
COMPLICATIONS
These techniques have been described in clinical veterinary cases.
Retrospectively, two statistically similar populations of dogs with
urothelial carcinoma received either (1) IV carboplatin and oral
NSAIDs, or (2) super-selective IA carboplatin and IA meloxicam.19
The IA group demonstrated statistically significantly greater
reduction in tumor length, and percent length, width and
unidimensional measurements compared with the IV group. The IA
group was also statistically more likely to achieve a positive tumor
response as characterized by modified RECIST criteria. In addition,
the IA group was statistically significantly less likely to develop
certain adverse events, including anorexia and lethargy, following
chemotherapy compared to the IV group. Complications are
uncommon and typically limited to the same adverse events
anticipated following IV therapy. A follow-up study15 comparing
dose-normalized, intra-arterially versus intravenously administered
chemotherapy in dogs with lower urinary tract cancer demonstrated
certain lower serum values could be achieved following intra-arterial
delivery of carboplatin and mitoxantrone.
