SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS AND
ALTERNATIVES
Although reported to be safe, care must be taken during repeated
carotid access. The author has seen temporary neurological sequelae
(blindness, circling, etc.) following bilateral carotid artery ligation in
dogs, even when staged. Bilateral carotid ligation is uncommonly
necessary, as performing femoral access distally provides ample
opportunity to re-use the femoral artery more proximally on multiple
occasions. The author has successfully used a unilateral femoral
artery up to five times.

TRANS-ARTERIAL EMBOLIZATION
(TAE)/CHEMOEMBOLIZATION (TACE)
INDICATIONS AND BACKGROUND
Embolization refers to the delivery of a device or material to
interrupt blood flow. Chemoembolization involves super-selective
intra-arterial chemotherapy delivery in conjunction with subsequent
particle embolization. Intra-arterial chemotherapy for liver tumors
has been shown to result in a 10- to 50-fold increase in intra-tumoral
drug concentrations when compared to systemic IV chemotherapy
administration.20 Subsequent particle embolization results in tumor

cell necrosis through ischemia and it paralyzes tumor cell excretion
of chemotherapeutic agents, resulting in increased local
concentrations and minimized systemic toxicosis. While TAE and
TACE have been performed in other areas, the liver is the most
commonly treated organ (ch. 275). More recently, prostate artery
embolization for canine prostate tumors (Figure 118.3; ch. 330)
has been evaluated, with early results indicating encouraging local
tumor control rates.21

EQUIPMENT
Common equipment used for TAE/TACE is listed in Box 118.2 and
shown in Figure 118.4. Embolization procedures require a
fluoroscopy unit with exceptional imaging detail to identify very
small caliber vessels using DSA and road mapping, as well as the
ability to obtain orthogonal imaging when necessary. Failure to
identify collateral vessels could lead to non-target delivery and
potentially severe consequences.

TECHNIQUE FOR HEPATIC TAE/TACE
(FIGURE 118.5)
Carotid or femoral artery sheath access followed by a 4 Fr Cobra
catheter (or similar) and 0.035″ (0.9 mm) angled hydrophilic guide
wire (Figure 118.4) are used in combination to select the celiac
artery and common hepatic artery. Common hepatic arteriography is
performed using a 50:50 dilution of iohexol22:saline. A 1.7 to 3 Fr
microcatheterj,k/microwirel,m combination is used to super-select
the particular vessel supplying the tumor bed, ensuring catheter
placement is not occlusive within the often very small caliber vessels.
Super-selection is the goal to minimize non-target embolization.
The appropriate size of polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) or other
embolization particles is chosen on the basis of vascular architecture.
Use of undersized particles carries the risk of extreme distal vascular
occlusion and increases the risk of necrosis and tissue sloughing. The
use of inappropriately large particles carries the risk of proximal
vessel thrombosis, which may allow for development of collateral
vessels that bypass the proximal occlusion and re-establish perfusion
to the tumor. The author has used PVA-200 particlesm (180-300
micron) or 100-300 micron PVA hydrogel microspheresn for liver

embolization. The chosen embolic is prepared as a slurry with
iodinated contrast material and embolization is performed under
fluoroscopic visualization using digital road-mapping software. Care
is taken to prevent reflux of particles into non-target vessels. A
similar technique is used for oily (“conventional” or cTACE) or drugeluting bead (DEB)-TACE; however, the operator should refer to
manufacturer instructions for information regarding handling, drug
loading, and administration. The systemic dose of chemotherapeutic
agent (typically doxorubicin) is selected and either mixed with
iodinated poppyseed oilo to form the oily suspension (cTACE) or
with the drug-eluting beads (DEB-TACE). A lobar treatment can be
performed using the cTACE technique but only superselective access
should be used for DEB-TACE.

Embolization can continue until near-stasis of blood flow if the
treatment is to be repeated; if performed once, complete stasis can
be attempted. Selective arteriography is performed to evaluate the

success of the procedure after all particles are flushed out. If
embolization is successful, no flow is seen in the target artery feeding
the tumor. The microcatheter is withdrawn and repeat common
hepatic (or other) angiography is performed through the 4 Fr
catheter to identify other feeding vessels. If more vessels are found,
the procedure can be repeated or performed subsequently in the
future.
Following embolization, all catheters and sheaths are removed.
Hemostasis is typically achieved with carotid or femoral artery
ligation. All animals recover from anesthesia in an intensive care unit
for monitoring. Perioperative medical management is standard for
these patients.

FOLLOW-UP
The procedure is generally repeated at 6-week intervals and tumor
response (restaging) evaluated following two treatments.

OUTCOMES AND POSSIBLE
COMPLICATIONS
These techniques have demonstrated improved tumor responses and
prolonged survival times when compared to more traditional
therapies in humans with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC, ch.
275).23-25 The author has performed TAE, Lipiodol-based TACE,
and DEB-TACE in dogs with benign and malignant liver tumors in
which surgery was unsuccessful or was declined. In general, stable
disease (∼60%) or partial remissions (∼23%) are anticipated
following therapy, with better responses in more vascular tumors.
These procedures require an intimate knowledge of the local vascular
anatomy to prevent non-target embolization but can otherwise be
expected to result in fewer than 10-15% major complications when
performed by experienced operators. Reported complications26 in
the human literature include hemorrhage at the vascular access site,
non-target embolization complications (skin necrosis, damage to
normal parenchyma), hepatic infarction/abscessation, acute kidney

injury (for liver tumors), and post-embolization syndrome (PES),
which is a collection of clinical signs characterized by malaise, fever,
and pain. The author’s experience over the past 10 years suggests
similar risks in veterinary patients as well as reduced systemic
exposure to chemotherapy, minimal morbidity, and improved tumor
response rates when compared to systemic chemotherapy.27-29 In
general, approximately 25% of dogs demonstrate PES even with
prophylactic medications.30 In a small, prospective, comparative
series of dogs with HCC that received DEB-TACE, the same canine
patients had measurable serum chemotherapy concentrations for
only a median 30-180 minutes (versus 720 minutes following IV
administration) and one-fortieth of the total systemic chemotherapy
exposure (area under the curve) when they received DEB-TACE
compared to when they received the same dose administered
intravenously.29 Chemoembolization has been performed elsewhere
throughout the body and its use will likely expand.

SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS AND
ALTERNATIVES
For smaller tumors, percutaneous, video-assisted, or open ablation
techniques can be considered, although these have not been
extensively performed in veterinary patients.31-33 Radiofrequency
ablation as well as microwave ablation, laser thermal ablation,
cryoablation, and percutaneous ethanol injection tend to be most
effective with a few (<3) small (<4 cm diameter) lesions. These
circumstances are fairly uncommon in the author’s clinical
experience; however, with the routine use of more advanced imaging
techniques in veterinary medicine, lesions of this size and number
may become increasingly apparent during tumor re-staging
procedures, making tumor ablation techniques a reasonable option
in the future. Additionally, veterinary ablation therapies are being
evaluated for extrahepatic disease such as nasal tumors (ch.
213)32,33 and bone tumors (ch. 326).22,34

DEFINITIONS
Triage, derived from the French word trier, refers to the sorting of
patients for treatment priority when resources are insufficient for all
to be treated immediately. “Resources” include the availability of a
veterinarian, technicians, nurses, diagnostic procedures, therapies,
or even hospital space. In an emergency setting, the sorting of
patients is based on medical priority: the sickest animals are treated

first. While “triage” is routinely applied in emergency settings to
identify animals needing immediate life-saving interventions, triage
is also routinely utilized to determine specialist consultation priority,
interventional procedures, extracorporeal therapies, or housing
location within the hospital (e.g., intensive care unit versus the
general wards).
Both rapid and accurate triage is essential for successful
emergency departments. Ideally, triage identifies those patients
likely to benefit from time-critical interventions or that will suffer
harm if a time critical intervention is not provided as compared with
others that do not require immediate attention.1 “Under triage”
occurs when severity of an illness or injury is not recognized,
resulting in delayed treatment which negatively impacts chance of
survival. “Over triage” occurs when a patient is misidentified as being
more ill or injured than is correct and their care is prioritized higher
than others in greater need.2 This may result in delayed treatment to
other more emergent patients and inappropriate consumption of
limited resources (i.e., staff, equipment or space).

THE TRIAGE PROCESS (Figure 119.1)
OVERVIEW
Any pet arriving at an emergency facility should be immediately
assessed to determine priority of care and need for medical
interventions. This initial assessment should be completed by a
veterinarian or nurse/technician specifically educated in triage.
Effective triage is dependent on the skill of the individual (i.e.,
knowledge, experience, ability to ask the right questions). Triage
should be based on combining the presenting concern, visual
assessment, and initial systems assessment. It is inappropriate to
have an inexperienced individual assigned this critically important
task. When multiple emergent animals are presented at the same
time, the veterinary team must determine how long each animal can
safely wait to be managed.3

TRIAGE SYSTEMS UTILIZED FOR
HUMAN EMERGENCIES
Several different triage systems have been developed to improve the
acuity of triage in people: the Emergency Severity Index, Canadian
Triage & Acuity Scale, Australasian Triage Scale, and the Manchester
Triage System.3-5 Each provides clear guidelines on how to assess
the patient’s clinical needs and priority for care based on vital signs
(e.g., heart rate, respiratory rate). Some also utilize a “presenting
complaint algorithm.”6 Triage systems typically use a 5-level colorcoded system of categorization: 1-resuscitation (red), 2-emergent
(orange), 3-urgent (yellow), 4-less urgent (blue), 5-non-urgent
(green). Each level also targets a time before physician assessment;
level 1 patients must be treated immediately.4-7 Triage is to be
performed by a trained nurse or a “rapid assessment team” (nurse
and physician or advanced practice provider).3 The addition of a
physician or advanced practice provider to a team results in
accelerated initial evaluations and therapies, decreasing length of
stay.3,8-11

VETERINARY TRIAGE LIST
Color-Coded Categorization
Adapted from the Manchester Triage Scale, a veterinary triage list
(VTL) was developed and evaluated for use in animals presenting to
an emergency department.12 In this system, each pet is placed into a
color-coded triage category that includes target waiting times: red:
immediate, orange: 15 minutes, yellow: 30-60 minutes and green:
120 minutes, e.g., severe decompensatory shock, exsanguinating
hemorrhage, severe respiratory distress, or seizures would be triaged
red whereas animals with mild respiratory distress, uncontrollable
minor hemorrhage, or history of unconsciousness would be triaged
yellow. In one study, intuitive triage performed by trained veterinary
technicians using medical history and a visual examination was
compared with a retrospective evaluation of the VTL applied by a

veterinary review team. The review team using the VTL was more
efficient at correctly categorizing emergency patients with target
waiting times as compared with intuitive triage by veterinary
technicians.12 Prospective studies are needed to determine if it
outperforms intuitive triage (i.e., “gut feeling”), and whether it
improves outcome. Regardless of triage system used, the individuals
performing triage must receive comprehensive education and
training.

FIGURE 119.1 Triage Flow Chart. In this
approach, first life-threatening airway problems are
assessed and treated first, followed by breathing
problems, and so on. Using this approach, the aim is
to identify life threatening problems and to institute

Initial Assessment, Obtaining Owner Consent,
Needed Supplies
Rapid patient assessment should be done in a dedicated triage area,
usually an area of the waiting room or an examination room. Visual
inspection and evaluation of major body systems (respiratory,
cardiovascular, neurologic, urinary) should be performed while
obtaining presenting complaint and relevant medical history.13
When significant abnormalities are noted, the pet should
immediately and quickly be assessed by the veterinarian, a process
that should take less than 2 minutes.
If immediate medical intervention is indicated, owner consent for
treatment should be obtained and the pet brought to the triage area.
Written consent and cost estimate should cover the initial evaluation,
treatment for shock and pain (including intravenous [IV] catheter
placement and fluids), point-of-care (PoC) bloodwork, PoC
ultrasound (US), blood pressure (BP) measurement,
electrocardiogram (ECG), pulse oximetry, and medication
administration. Resuscitation status of the pet (i.e., “yes” or “no”)
may also be asked, depending on hospital policy. The triage area
should be equipped with adequate supplies for treating critically ill
or injured animals, e.g., oxygen, IV or intraosseous (IO) catheters,

supplies for needle thoracocentesis and pericardiocentesis, IV fluids,
continuous ECG, pulse oximetry, BP equipment, and a crash cart.

The Crash Cart
The crash cart should be stocked with items needed for
cardiopulmonary arrest: endotracheal tubes, laryngoscope, electrical
defibrillator, and drugs (ch. 131). An US unit should be housed in
this area to facilitate PoC assessment. In-house laboratory facilities
should be available for PoC blood testing, including a minimum
database (packed cell volume [PCV], total protein [TP], glucose and
blood urea nitrogen), blood gas evaluation, and lactate. Pets not
requiring immediate treatment must be periodically re-evaluated.

PRIMARY SURVEY
Overview
The “primary survey” refers to evaluating the same organ systems as
performed during the initial veterinary nurse/technician triage. This
time it should be more detailed and may involve both subjective and
objective evaluations, similar to the Airway, Breathing, Circulation,
Disability and Exposure (ABCDE) approach used to assess critically
ill or injured people, with the urinary system added (Figure 119.1).
During the primary survey, assessments and treatments are
simultaneous and continuous. It may be immediately evident during
the primary survey that an animal is critically ill, but the cause may
be unclear. In these situations, life-saving interventions must be
instituted before obtaining a definitive diagnosis.14

Respiratory System
Subjective Assessments
The respiratory system evaluation begins with determination of
airway patency and then identification of breathing problems.
Diseases of the respiratory system should be treated immediately
because they may cause hypoxemia and/or hypoventilation which
can lead to multiple organ failure. Hypercapnia may cause
vasodilation, hypotension and altered mentation due to cerebral

edema.15 Patients that are not breathing should have immediate
endotracheal intubation performed and positive pressure ventilation
initiated (ch. 131). During intubation, the soft palate, oropharynx
and larynx should be quickly evaluated for foreign bodies (e.g.,
rubber ball), masses, or severe inflammation that might be
responsible for the airway obstruction. The presence of stertor or
stridor with increased breathing effort (either inspiratory, expiratory
or both) may indicate an upper airway obstruction (chs. 37, 214). If
possible, although it may not be tolerated in a distressed animal,
briefly evaluate the oropharynx for masses or foreign bodies. Cats
with upper airway conditions often do not have loud upper airway
noise and signs may be subtle, consisting of increased inspiratory
effort and loud or noisy breath sounds on tracheal auscultation. Pets
with suspected upper airway conditions should receive immediate
oxygen supplementation via face mask or “flow-by” to allow
completion of the primary survey. An IV catheter should be placed to
give medications and to obtain PoC bloodwork. Unless
contraindicated, some “stressed/panicked” pets with upper airway
conditions benefit from sedation (e.g., butorphanol given IV or
intramuscularly [IM]; ch. 123). Emergency medications often used
to reduce respiratory signs include furosemide (suspected congestive
heart failure [CHF, ch. 229]) and terbutaline (bronchoconstriction,
ch. 215).
Once the airway has been assessed, the respiratory rate and
breathing effort of the animal should be evaluated (ch. 37).
Tachypnea is defined as a respiratory rate >40 breaths/minute and
any cat that is “open mouth” breathing. The chest wall and abdomen
should move synchronously during inspiration and expiration. An
asynchronous or inverse breathing pattern (chest wall moves out and
abdomen moves in during inspiration) may indicate pleural space
disease (ch. 220).16 The trachea and thorax should be auscultated
for breath sounds and supplemental oxygen given if there is
increased respiratory effort and/or significant abnormalities
detected (dull lung sounds, pulmonary crackles, wheezes). Mucous
membrane color should be assessed in animals with respiratory
signs. Cyanotic (a bluish discoloration) mucous membranes are late
and severe signs of hypoxemia.17 Several conditions may cause
tachypnea without respiratory compromise: hypovolemia, pain,

abdominal distension, hyperthyroidism, fear, and others. These
animals, however, usually do not have an increased breathing effort.

Objective Assessments
In addition to the visual examination and auscultation of breath
sounds, objective assessments of the respiratory system should
include blood oxygen content with pulse oximetry and/or arterial
blood gas analysis. A pulse oximetry reading <95% (corresponding to
a PaO2 of less than 80 mm Hg; ≥95% is normal) indicates
hypoxemia.18 Arterial blood gas analysis, more invasive than pulse
oximetry, is useful in determining if either hypoxemia (PaO2 <80
mm Hg), hypercarbia (PaCO2 >50 mm Hg), or both are present.
However, obtaining arterial blood gas samples can be challenging in
an animal with abnormal tissue perfusion or those requiring
contraindicated manual restraint.

Fragility of Some Patients
Supplemental oxygen therapy (mask, flow-by, O2 cage) should be
instituted immediately in all animals with respiratory signs and their
clinical response then evaluated. Pets with tachypnea or increased
respiratory effort (regardless of pulse oximetry reading) should be
given supplemental oxygen to improve comfort. Cats with respiratory
signs are particularly fragile and may decompensate quickly.
Performing a physical examination or placement of an IV catheter
can lead to cardiopulmonary arrest. Caution should be
exercised! Such cats often benefit from being placed immediately
in an oxygen enriched cage before trying to perform the complete
primary survey and their respiratory signs monitored closely. Once
respiratory signs have improved, the primary survey should be
completed or, if the oxygen cage size allows, the initial assessment of
the cat can be performed in the cage.

Point-of-Care (PoC) Ultrasound (US) Findings and
Emergency Responses

US can provide valuable information regarding the lungs, pleural
space, and heart. It should be performed as soon as possible to guide
stabilizing interventions (ch. 73).19,20 PoC US may or may not
confirm the respiratory system examination findings, e.g., if lung
sounds seem dull, PoC US can assess for presence of pleural space
disease (ch. 220). US may reveal pleural effusion, an absent glide
(pneumothorax), abdominal organs in the thorax, and/or absent
diaphragmatic crura (tear or hernia). In dyspneic animals with
confirmed or suspected pleural effusion or pneumothorax, needle
thoracocentesis should be performed as soon as possible in an
attempt to relieve respiratory signs (ch. 92). If hemorrhage is
suspected as the cause of pleural effusion in an animal with
concurrent tissue perfusion abnormalities (see below for
cardiovascular evaluation), evaluating the coagulation status may
help determine if needle thoracocentesis is safe or contraindicated
(ch. 170).
PoC US is useful in differentiating cardiac (i.e., CHF) from noncardiac causes (e.g., pleural space disease) of respiratory signs. For
example, an evaluation of the left atrial to aortic ratio, cardiac
contractility, and lung is consistent with CHF when the left atrial to
aortic ratio is >1.5:1 and >3 B-lines are apparent on lung US in
multiple windows.21-24 These results are used in determining the
need for immediate treatment with furosemide. The presence of Blines is indicative of interstitial-alveolar disease typical of CHF and
fluid overload but the finding is not specific, and is also seen with
pneumonia, contusions, non-cardiogenic edema, and acute
respiratory distress syndrome (ch. 217). It is important to note that
dogs with mitral valve disease, hospitalized for other conditions, may
have underlying left atrial enlargement and other causes of
interstitial-alveolar disease.24 Therefore, PoC US should not replace
thoracic radiography and echocardiography, but these tests should
not be pursued until the patient is stable.

Cardiovascular System Evaluation
Initial Subjective Assessment
Primary cardiovascular system assessment includes evaluation for
abnormalities in tissue perfusion that may result in shock. Poor

tissue perfusion can be caused by hypovolemia (ch. 121), cardiac
disease (chs. 231–239), cardiac arrhythmias (ch. 230), and
vasodilatory states such as anaphylaxis (ch. 129), sepsis or SIRS
(ch. 128Chapter 121Chapter 129). During the early stages of
compensatory shock, cardiovascular parameters (e.g., heart rate and
pulse quality) may not be significantly abnormal and the pet could be
initially triaged as “lower priority,” delaying treatment. In this
scenario, the decision to delay treatment could allow deterioration
and, subsequently, a worse outcome. Close evaluation in the context
of clinical history and objective measurements (see below) may yield
subtle clues to the cause for alterations in tissue perfusion. Animals
in decompensated shock are clinically easier to recognize as they
usually have marked cardiovascular abnormalities, e.g., tachycardia,
weak pulses. Regardless of the underlying cause, shock states should
be treated emergently.
Physical examination findings (ch. 3) consistent with poor tissue
perfusion include pale mucous membranes, prolonged capillary refill
time, tachycardia (or bradycardia in cats), tall and narrow pulse
profiles, and poor or absent peripheral pulses. Both femoral and
pedal pulses should be assessed. Absent pedal pulses in patients
without suspected arterial thromboembolism is a strong indicator of
hypotension.25,26 Any animal with alterations in systemic perfusion
may have dull mentation, quiet heart sounds, low body temperature,
and cool extremities (ch. 121). A rectal-interdigital (temperature
taken between the 3rd and 4th digit in a pelvic limb) temperature
gradient >11.6 °F (>6.5°C) may be useful in shock identification in
dogs.27

Objective Assessments
Objective cardiovascular assessments include BP (ch. 91), ECG
tracings (chs. 96, 230) to assess for cardiac arrhythmias or
alterations suggestive of severe hyperkalemia, and blood lactate
levels. Shock may be present in dogs and cats when Doppler BP
measurements are <90 mm Hg. A “shock index” (heart rate ÷ BP)
>1.0 is consistent with shock.28-31 Cardiac tachyarrhythmias and
bradyarrhythmias may be identified on ECG tracings and can
develop secondary to many causes, e.g., electrolyte abnormalities,

cardiac ischemia, cardiac disease, central nervous system disease, or
intra-abdominal disease. Isolated ventricular premature contractions
may not require immediate stabilizing treatments (ch. 230).
However, sustained ventricular tachycardia (heart rate >180 bpm) or
severe bradyarrhythmias could adversely effective cardiac output
and may need to be emergently treated. Finally, tissue hypoxia may
develop in shock states when cells switch from aerobic to anerobic
metabolism. This causes lactate production. A blood lactate >2.5
mmol/L may be indicative of systemic hypoperfusion, although other
conditions, such as neoplasia, may also increase lactate
production.32-34

Initial Management
Patients with abnormal tissue perfusion should have an IV catheter
placed and blood samples drawn. Initial PoC bloodwork, in addition
to blood lactate, should include PCV, refractometer TP, electrolytes,
blood urea nitrogen, creatinine and acid base status. This bloodwork
may reveal vital clues as to the underlying cause for the patient’s
condition. For example, a pet with abnormal tissue perfusion,
normal or low PCV, and low TP may have hypovolemia secondary to
hemorrhage. Emergent evaluation of coagulation status may be
indicated when a coagulopathy is suspected (e.g., young animal with
exposure to anticoagulant rodenticide). A venous blood gas analysis
may reveal a metabolic acidosis, changes in blood electrolyte and/or
glucose concentrations, and may guide initial stabilization measures.
After IV catheter placement, determining the BP, and obtaining
PoC blood tests, thoracic and abdominal US should be obtained to
assess for free thoracic, pericardial, peritoneal, or retroperitoneal
effusion (ch. 73). If effusion is identified, it should be sampled
aseptically (chs. 86, 92, 95) and evaluated microscopically (ch.
71). In undifferentiated shock when cardiogenic shock is deemed
unlikely, an IV crystalloid bolus (10-30 mL/kg aliquots over 15-30
minutes) should be administered in an attempt to restore tissue
perfusion (ch. 121). Continuous re-assessment of the patient’s tissue
perfusion parameters (e.g., serial heart rates, mucous membrane
color, capillary refill time, BP measurements, etc.) should be
performed to determine status of the shock condition and guide
additional therapies.

Neurologic System
Initial Evaluation
Evaluating the neurologic system includes the animal’s level of
consciousness (i.e., mentation), brain stem reflexes, and motor
ability. Modified Glasgow Coma Scale scores can be calculated
serially as a tool for comparing responses over time in critically ill
patients with neurologic disease (Video 44.2

).35 Patients with

severely altered mental status or seizures require immediate
stabilization. A full neurologic examination including spinal reflexes
and ambulatory status (ch. 241) should be delayed until the patient
has normal tissue perfusion and oxygenation. A dull or obtunded
mental status may occur secondary to decreases in tissue perfusion
or oxygenation and should improve with stabilizing treatments for
shock and hypoxemia. Severely altered mental status, such as coma
or stupor, may follow increases in intracranial pressure after
traumatic brain injury, meningoencephalitis, or neoplasia, for
example (ch. 44). Extracranial causes of altered mental status
include hepatoencephalopathy, severe hypertension, rapid changes
in blood sodium, hypoglycemia, and intoxications (e.g., ethylene
glycol, ibuprofen overdose). The history should include questions
about potential toxin exposure (ch. 132). On cardiovascular
examination, animals with elevations in intracranial pressure may
exhibit a “Cushing’s reflex” characterized by bradycardia and
hypertension. Abnormalities in pupil size and/or pupillary light
responses may also be identified. Transpalpebral PoC US, in addition
to the physical examination, can be used to evaluate changes in optic
nerve sheath diameter as a marker for intracranial
hypertension.36,37 Prolonged elevations in intracranial pressure can
lead to brain ischemia and herniation, and should be treated
emergently when suspected.

Initial Treatment
Stabilizing therapies for patients with altered mental status may
include administration of IV hyperosmotic agents (i.e., mannitol or
hypertonic saline). These pets can be placed on a “slant board,”
elevating the head and neck 15 to 30° to decrease cerebral blood

volume through venous drainage.38 PoC bloodwork should be
obtained at the time of IV catheter placement to check blood glucose
and electrolytes. A BP measurement (ch. 91) should be obtained to
evaluate for hypo- or hypertension.
In an animal suspected of acute brain herniation (e.g., manifesting
severely altered mentation and decerebrate rigidity), orotracheal
intubation and mechanical ventilation should be instituted to
temporarily lower arterial blood carbon dioxide levels. This can
cause cerebral vasoconstriction, thereby lowering intracranial
pressure and is used for short-term management of marked
elevations in intracranial pressure. Orotracheal intubation may also
be required in patients with cervical myelopathies resulting in
tetraparesis or paralysis and minimal diaphragmatic movement and
chest wall excursions to breathing efforts. This may have already
been identified on the respiratory system evaluation.

Seizures
Animals presenting to the emergency room in status epilepticus or
with a history of recent seizures should also be emergently treated
(ch. 45). Prolonged seizure activity, regardless of cause, may result
in hyperthermia, respiratory complications, cerebral edema, and
irreversible brain injury.39 Administration of a benzodiazepine (IV,
IM or intranasal) is the most effective first line treatment for active
seizure activity. Patients with a history of recent seizures should be
monitored closely in the treatment area for additional seizure
activity. PoC bloodwork should check for hypoglycemia and
electrolyte disorders (sodium abnormalities, hypocalcemia) as these
are important causes of seizures and may alter stabilizing
interventions. A thorough history of possible exposure to poisons
(i.e., medications, plants) that may cause seizures should be obtained
from the pet owner.

Urinary System Evaluation
Acute kidney injury (AKI) or urinary obstruction can lead to
metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, cardiac arrhythmias, and death
(ch. 300). Urethral obstruction is a common emergency condition
primarily affecting male cats (chs. 99, 312).40 Signs of obstruction

can be vague (e.g., vocalizing, lethargy, vomiting) or not observed by
the pet owner (e.g., litter box is in the basement or cat lives
outdoors). Therefore, caregivers of all young to middle-aged male
cats should be carefully questioned regarding the last witnessed
urination. Bladder palpation should be performed as part of the
triage evaluation. A large firm bladder (either in a cat or dog) that is
not easily expressed is worrisome. One should consider an ECG to
assess for cardiac arrhythmias (bradyarrhythmia or
tachyarrhythmia) that may result from hyperkalemia secondary to
urinary obstruction (ch. 68). These animals should have immediate
stabilizing treatments performed, including placement of an IV
catheter, evaluation of serum potassium and kidney values, and
urinary catheterization (ch. 127). An animal with a history of
decreased urination and/or stranguria without a palpable bladder
should be assessed for AKI or uroabdomen.

Additional Considerations
Other conditions that require immediate evaluation by a veterinarian
include: recent ingestion of a toxin/foreign body; or signs of
intoxication, trauma, active bleeding, allergic reactions, prolapsed
organs, reproductive emergencies (e.g., dystocia, priapism,
paraphimosis), recent snake bites, hypo- or hyperthermia, open
wounds, and burns. These patients should have an initial evaluation
as outlined above and stabilizing therapies initiated if indicated.
These animals may also require specific treatments. For example,
animals recently ingesting a toxin or with signs of intoxication
should have decontamination procedures (emesis induction,
activated charcoal administration and/or IV fluid diuresis) initiated
as soon as possible (if deemed appropriate) as treatment delay could
have life-threatening consequences (ch. 132). Animals with active
bleeding or open wounds should have an occlusive bandage placed to
help control hemorrhage and reduce additional contamination of the
wound until definitive treatment can be performed. Analgesics
should be administered during the triage of animals that are
significantly painful (e.g., animals with fractures or neck pain). As is
likely apparent, it is essential that the emergency veterinarian have
an extensive breadth of knowledge of emergent conditions to provide

timely and appropriate treatment. The reader is referred elsewhere
for more details on the treatment of these conditions.

“Ugly. Ugly. Giant. Bags of mostly water.”
Home Soil, Star Trek: the Next Generation
As the un-named silicate lifeforms so bluntly put it, human and animal bodies are composed mostly of
water. About 60% of body weight is water and 40% solid matter.1,2 Understanding body water
deficiencies or excesses is extremely important when managing illnesses. As many as 90% of deaths in
some devastating diseases (e.g., cholera) can be prevented by giving fluids.3 A sodium (Na) and
bicarbonate (HCO3−)-containing fluid, the first intravascular (IV) fluid therapy and a precursor of
modern crystalloids, was given successfully to cholera victims in the mid-1800s to treat their extreme
dehydration.3 Modern crystalloids have evolved from these beginnings to become the mainstay of IV
fluid therapy.

FLUID COMPARTMENTS AND PHYSIOLOGY
COMPARTMENTS
The 60% of body weight that is water can be divided into the intracellular fluid (ICF; two-thirds of body
water; 40% of body weight) and the extracellular fluid (ECF; one-third of body water; 20% of body
weight; Figure 120.1).1,2,4 The ECF includes interstitial fluid (ISF; around cells), IV fluid, and the

transcellular fluids (cerebrospinal, bile, gastrointestinal [GI], and respiratory).1 Fluid movement
between IV and ISF spaces occur at the capillary level and are governed by Starling’s forces (see
below) while water movement between the ECF and the ICF is in response to changes in effective
osmolality.1,2 The main determinant of effective osmolality is the Na concentration. Potassium (K),
chloride (Cl), urea (blood urea nitrogen [BUN]), glucose, and HCO3− can affect osmolality.1 Clinical
deficiencies of the ECF manifest as dehydration and/or hypovolemia.

TRADITIONAL STARLING’S LAW
Movement of fluid between capillary and ISF is governed by Starling’s forces: oncotic and hydrostatic
pressures which pull or push fluids across vascular membranes, respectively.1,2,5 Oncotic pressure,
generated primarily by albumin within capillaries, retains fluid.1,5 IV oncotic pressure is enhanced by
the Gibbs-Donnan effect: positively charged ions (e.g., Na) surround negatively charged albumin
molecules, increasing the number of particles within the vasculature and magnifying oncotic pressure.1
Capillary hydrostatic pressure, generated by blood volume and precapillary sphincter tone, pushes fluid
from the vascular space into the ISF.1,5 The traditional Starling’s law1,5,6 is written as: Jv = Kf[(Pc −
Pi) − σ(Πc − Πi)] where Jv = net filtration out of the capillary, Kf = net permeability of the capillary
wall, Pc = capillary hydrostatic pressure, Pi = interstitial hydrostatic pressure, σ = macromolecule
reflection coefficient of the membrane, Πc = oncotic pressure of the plasma proteins, and Πi = oncotic
pressure of the interstitial proteins.

FIGURE 120.1 Fluid compartments in the body with the accompanying
amount of total body weight and total body water attributed to each fluid
compartment.

REVISED STARLING’S LAW
The revision to traditional Starling’s law takes the endothelial glycocalyx, directly adjacent to the
vascular endothelium, into account.5,6 The glycocalyx, made up of proteoglycans, glycoproteins, and
glycosaminoglycans, is integral to determining fluid fluxes between the IV and ISF spaces, as well as
being important in coagulation and cellular signaling.6 Between the endothelial glycocalyx and capillary
endothelial cells is the protein-free subglycocalyx space. Its oncotic pressure determines fluid
movement, rather than the oncotic pressure in the ISF.5,6 The revision replaces ISF oncotic pressure
with the oncotic pressure of the endothelial subglycocalyx space (Πg): Jv = Kf[(Pc − Pi) − σ(Πc − Πg).5,6
Lack of oncotic pressure in that area (Πg of zero) favors IV fluid retention. In health, the sole
determinant of fluid moving out of a blood vessel is the hydrostatic pressure differential between IV and
ISF: Pc − Pi.5,6 Fluid movement is determined primarily by IV fluid volume and autonomic signals
dilating and constricting the capillaries which create Pc.5,6 Any fluid remaining in the ISF is drained by
lymphatics.5 The glycocalyx resists fluid flow across the endothelium and increases or decreases Kf (i.e.,

changes capillary permeability) by changing junctional proteins in the endothelium.6 Systemic
inflammation, hypoalbuminemia, some medications, and even fluid therapy can damage the endothelial
glycocalyx, leading to greater capillary wall permeability and more fluid flux out of the vessel than
predicted by oncotic and hydrostatic pressures alone.6

CHARACTERIZING FLUID LOSS
HYPOVOLEMIA VS. DEHYDRATION
“Hypovolemia” is defined as loss of volume from the IV compartment resulting from direct losses
(hemorrhage) or after extreme losses from other compartments. Hypovolemia is important to correct
before correcting dehydration (ch. 119). “Dehydration” refers to an abnormal decrease in total body
water but physiologically it signifies decreases in ISF volume.5 Diagnosis of dehydration is based largely
upon historical and physical examination (PE; ch. 3) findings. A diagnosis of dehydration in a patient
usually requires loss of >5% of volume (Table 120.1).

ISOTONIC, HYPERTONIC AND HYPOTONIC DEHYDRATION
Dehydration can result from equal losses of water and electrolytes (isotonic dehydration), loss of water
in excess of electrolytes (hypertonic dehydration), or loss of electrolytes in excess of water loss
(hypotonic dehydration).9 Isotonic fluid losses suggest that the amount lost from each compartment is
proportional (i.e., there are no changes in solute concentrations). In this scenario, water does not move
between ICF and ECF but only within the ECF (as dictated by Starling’s law).1,2,9 Decreasing plasma
volume will decrease Pc and reduce the net movement of water out of the IV space.5 Thus, in isotonic
dehydration the first ECF compartment affected is the ISF. In hypertonic dehydration, loss of free
water leaves behind solute in the fluid compartments, most importantly Na. Starling’s law dictates that
there is no net movement of fluid out of the IV space due to an increase in tonicity and a decrease in Pc
from the dehydration.5 However, fluid will shift from ICF to ECF compartments due to the increasing
concentration of Na and other solutes in the ECF.1,2,9 In hypotonic dehydration, solute
concentrations (most importantly Na) decrease in the fluid compartments. Depending on severity,
hyponatremia can cause movement of water from the ECF to the ICF space1,2,9 with a possible net fluid
flux out of the IV space.1,2,5,9

CALCULATING A FLUID THERAPY PLAN
DEHYDRATION DEFICIT
When developing a fluid plan in a non-hypovolemic dog or cat (Table 120.2), history (ch. 2) and PE
(ch. 3) must be considered, including any indicators of dehydration (Table 120.1).4,7 Both volume and
rate of administration must be determined. Clinical dehydration typically ranges from about 5% (the
earliest it can be detected) to about 10% (the most that can be estimated). Volume of dehydration
(dehydration deficit) in liters (L) is calculated by multiplying body weight (kg) by % estimated
dehydration.4,7 Common timeframes for replacing dehydration deficits range from 6 to 24 hours. The
rate of replacing the volume deficit should be based on clinical status, risk factors for fluid overload (e.g.,
cardiac or renal disease), and practice setting (24 hr monitoring?).

“MAINTENANCE” REQUIREMENTS
The “maintenance” fluid volume is the total required to replace the volume normally lost every 24 hr in
urine, stool, and breathing. Sweating is not a major factor in dogs and cats. Evaporative losses are
“insensible.”7 Several formulas are used to calculate maintenance fluids. Some formulas bundle
estimated insensible losses with metabolic (urine, stool) losses: 40-60 mL/kg/day or 1 mL/lb/hr.7
Another formula uses “calculated metabolic losses” inclusive of insensible losses: the 24 hr water
requirement (regardless of body weight) for metabolism is: 70 × (weight in kg)0.75. Uncommonly,
when insensible losses are believed to be increased (excessive panting or hypermetabolic disease states
like fever or pro-inflammatory disease), additional insensible losses (typically ∼20 mL/kg)4,7 should be
added to the calculated volume. Fluid volumes lost due to continued vomiting, diarrhea, hypersalivation,
and polyuria (e.g., chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, or post-obstructive diuresis) must be
replaced via estimation. It is always extremely valuable to collect all urine produced, obviating need for
“estimating” this important volume. Fluid volume collected from drains or chest tubes should also be
accounted for when calculating replacement fluid volumes.4,7

“INS AND OUTS”
The “ins and outs” approach to fluid management is one version used to manage “ongoing losses”
described above. It assumes that the pet is NOT dehydrated and will not receive concurrent
“maintenance” fluids. Specific scenarios include risk of fluid overload (e.g., oliguric or anuric renal
failure, heart failure [ch. 223]) or when excessive fluid losses are anticipated to continue, e.g., some
abdominal drains or polyuric states, including post-obstructive diuresis. The volume administered is
solely to replace the volumes of urine, drains and other objective losses while estimating fluid volumes of
vomitus, diarrhea and other losses.8 Typically these animals have urinary catheters to facilitate more
precise urine output monitoring. Urine, diarrhea, and vomitus can be estimated by weighing soiled
absorbent pads (1 g of fluid production = 1 mL).8 Losses should be measured at least every 4-6 hours
and replacement fluid needs adjusted as needed (Table 120.2). The total fluid output during the
timeframe since the previous calculation is used to calculate the fluid rate for that next similar time
period (e.g., if there were 100 mL of urine, drain fluid, and vomitus over 4 hours, the animal will receive
25 mL/hr of crystalloids for replacing these losses over the next 4 hours). The theory in this setting is
that the measured loss of fluid in a non-dehydrated animal is the only volume that needs to be replaced
and giving any additional fluids will potentially be in excess of the animal’s needs. Since this approach
does not include insensible (evaporative) losses, some iterations of ins and outs fluid management add
10-20 mL/kg/day to replace evaporative losses.8

CRYSTALLOID FLUIDS

PROPERTIES
The most commonly administered fluids for rehydration, maintenance, and resuscitation are
“crystalloids.” Crystalloids are typically described by their exact components, tonicity, and presence or
lack of a buffer. Commercially available parenteral fluids are described as isotonic (similar osmolarity to
normal ECF: ∼310 mEq/L), hypotonic, or hypertonic (Table 120.3). Crystalloid fluids contain water
and electrolytes (usually Na and Cl). When crystalloids are given IV, Na moves across semipermeable
vascular membranes to the ISF within about 20 to 40 minutes in non-dehydrated and within about 60
minutes in dehydrated pets.10 During redistribution, approximately 75% of the isotonic crystalloid fluid
(water) volume given IV will move out of the vascular space within 25-30 minutes.10

Dextrose is rapidly metabolized once infused into a patient, making it a source of solute-free water.
Therefore, although the osmolarity listed on the fluid bag reflects the presence of the dextrose in the
solution, the functional osmolarity (tonicity) of the solution intravenously is dictated by only the Na and
Cl concentration and is the same as the basal solution (without dextrose).
∗

BUFFERED, UNBUFFERED, ISOTONIC, AND HYPOTONIC
FLUIDS
“Balanced” Fluids
“Balanced” crystalloid fluids are buffered by having Cl ions replaced by organic anions, e.g., lactate or
acetate. These include Plasma-Lyte, Normosol, and lactated Ringer’s solution (LRS). Metabolism of
lactate by the liver or acetate by skeletal muscle, liver, and kidney consumes hydrogen ions and is
thought to increase pH by producing HCO3−.7,11 Thus, buffered fluids are considered “alkalinizing” as
they correct acidemia when metabolized.7 Direct infusion of HCO3− alters pH faster but is unstable in
currently used gas-permeable fluid bags and cannot be added to commercial fluids.11 Saline is
unbuffered and contains only water, Na, and Cl.12

Isotonic Fluids
Isotonic fluids are usually chosen in veterinary medicine for long-term administration as maintenance
fluids, since their tonicity most closely resembles that of the plasma. When selecting isotonic fluids, the
exact type usually is not critical. However, in cases with specific acid-base or electrolyte disorders, the
fluid chosen may be relevant. For example, 0.9% saline is the fluid of choice for pets with hypochloremic
metabolic alkalosis or when attempting to increase serum Na concentrations. Alternatively, PlasmaLyte-148 or Normosol is preferred in liver failure or when hypomagnesemia is present.

Hypotonic Fluids
Hypotonic fluids are usually used to dilute a drug or for hypernatremia. They contain increased amounts
of water versus solute to dilute the Na. In specific and uncommon situations, hypotonic fluids can be
used in maintenance fluid plans.

Hypertonic Fluids
Hypertonic fluids are used almost exclusively for resuscitation (ch. 121). Their increased Na
concentrations increase the osmolality of the ECF space and expand the vascular volume transiently
until the saline particles redistribute.

CRYSTALLOID FLUID ADDITIVES
A pet’s comorbidities may dictate need for additives. The most common comorbidities that can be
managed with additives are hypokalemia (add KCl and/or KPO4; Table 120.4) and hypoglycemia (add
dextrose). Calcium can be added to fluids. When supplementing K at rates >0.5 mEq/kg/hr, cardiac
dysrhythmias can result so this limit should never be exceeded. Serum K concentrations should be
regularly rechecked in any pet receiving IV fluids. Dextrose is hyperosmolar and it should be diluted to
prevent phlebitis when given IV. It is most commonly added to fluids to create either a 2.5% or 5%
solution. The blood glucose should be regularly rechecked (chs. 61, 78). If higher amounts of dextrose
are required, a 7.5% solution is safe to administer peripherally IV and 10% solutions can be given
through a central line (ch. 75) but are rarely needed and are not recommended in some scenarios (ch.
289).

CRYSTALLOID FLUIDS IN HYPERCHLOREMIA
There are concerns regarding use of 0.9% saline (an unbuffered Cl-rich fluid) as a primary resuscitation
and maintenance fluid. Saline promotes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, which experimentally
induces systemic inflammation and acute kidney injury (AKI, ch. 300).11,13 Large studies in both
human medical and surgical intensive care unit (ICU) and non-critically ill emergency patients
demonstrated significantly fewer kidney events and lower mortality in patients receiving balanced
crystalloids versus saline.14,15 While no similar trials have been conducted in animals, it is safe to
assume that not giving Cl-rich unbuffered crystalloids, especially long-term, may reduce risk of AKI in
dogs and cats.

COLLOIDAL FLUIDS
SYNTHETIC COLLOIDS
Synthetic colloid fluids are composed of a diluent (typically 0.9% NaCl or balanced crystalloid) with
suspended high–molecular-weight (MW) molecules that do not easily pass through semipermeable
capillary membranes. These colloids help retain fluid in the IV space by increasing oncotic pressure (i.e.,
increases Πc). Their effects last as long as the colloid molecules remain, with oncotic effects decreasing
as the colloid molecules are excreted or degraded by amylases and other enzymes.16 The most commonly
used synthetic colloid in veterinary medicine is hydroxyethyl starch (HES), made from hydrolysis of
maize amylopectin (e.g., Hetastarch and VetStarch). Other synthetic starch-based colloids consist of
other HES products or dextrans made from bacterial breakdown of sucrose. Alternatively, synthetic
colloids contain protein-based gelatins made from hydrolysis of bovine collagen. Synthetic colloids are
described by their MW, molar substitutions, and C2:C6 ratios. Larger MW products have longer halflives and less oncotic strength per unit volume. Lower MW products have greater oncotic strength per
unit volume but shorter half-lives.16 The molar substitution reflects the average number of HES groups
per glucose molecule while the C2:C6 ratio is the number of HES groups at the carbon 2 (C2) position on
the glucose molecule versus on the carbon 6 (C6) position.16 The higher the molar substitution (greater
C2:C6 ratio), the longer the molecular half-life, e.g., VetStarch is HES 130/0.4: its average MW is 130
kilodaltons (kDa) and its C2:C6 substitution ratio is 0.4. This is a medium particle size and a
comparatively low substitution ratio that gives VetStarch strong oncotic strength but a relatively short
half-life of ∼12 hr in humans.17

NATURAL COLLOIDS
There are 2 commercially available natural colloids for dogs and cats. Plasma contains both albumin and
other suspended proteins that are retained in the IV space after infusion and increase Πc in the
traditional Starling’s equation. Albumin products (typically either human serum albumin 5% or 25% or
canine albumin 5%) are purified albumin products suspended in buffered Na, K and HCO3− containing
solutions (human) or are lyophilized (freeze-dried) and resuspended at the time of use in 0.9% NaCl or
5% dextrose in water solution (D5W) (canine). Dosing of plasma to provide albumin for oncotic effect
follows the rule that 22.5 mL/kg of plasma is required to provide 0.5 g/dL of albumin.18 Dosing of
albumin (ALB) is typically based upon replacing a deficit:
ALB deficit (g) = 10 × [desired ALB (g/dL) − patient ALB (g/dL)] × body weight (kg) × 0.3
However, the actual albumin target and the best concentration of albumin to use to achieve the target
albumin concentration remains controversial.13

EFFECTS OF COLLOIDS

Classically it was believed that simply the size of the colloidal molecules prevented them from passing
through the endothelial membrane out of the blood vessel. However, newer information suggests that
natural colloids have restorative effects on the endothelial glycocalyx, which can contribute to decreased
vascular permeability.6 Albumin is believed to reduce matrix metalloproteinase breakdown of the
glycocalyx. Fresh frozen plasma has been shown to reduce shedding of the glycocalyx and to improve
production of new glycocalyx components.6 Thus, even in conditions where vasculitis disrupts the
endothelial glycocalyx and causes greater fluid flux out of the IV space, plasma and albumin may reduce
these effects. The net result is that albumin or plasma “hold” more fluid within the vasculature by
improving vessel wall integrity (Kf) and providing increased oncotic pressure (Πc). Synthetic colloids
similarly increase Πc and may improve glycocalyx layer health; however, effects on the glycocalyx are
not as well defined nor as potent as those of albumin and fresh frozen plasma.6

USE OF COLLOIDS AND THEIR CONTROVERSIES
Both natural and synthetic colloids had been recommended for volume expansion during resuscitation
and for constant rate infusions to help maintain IV oncotic pressure in both animals and people.16,19,20
Their effectiveness has come into question since giving synthetic or natural colloids does not
convincingly provide a clear benefit above crystalloids, aside from giving lower total fluid volumes to the
patients.20-22 There is some evidence that longer-term infusions of both types of colloids have beneficial
effects to restore the endothelial glycocalyx (natural colloids more so than synthetic colloids) which
might be beneficial in situations with increased vascular permeability, such as sepsis.6 More recently,
negative side-effects associated with administration of both synthetic and natural colloids have emerged,
leading to a shift in their usage. The initial concerns with synthetic colloids centered around induction of
AKI and renal failure, but this has not been definitively demonstrated in humans, dogs, or cats.23-26
Possible coagulation disorders attributed to colloid administration in humans include
thrombocytopathies, decreases in von Willebrand factor and factor VIII concentrations, and enhanced
fibrinolysis.16 However, definitive evidence that synthetic colloids as a bolus or constant rate infusion
cause clinically relevant bleeding disorders in humans or dogs has not been established.23,27-31 Both
synthetic and natural colloids are more expensive than crystalloid fluids and have a greater chance of
inducing hypersensitivity reactions.16

FLUID OVERLOAD
RESULTS OF FLUID OVERLOAD
Fluid overload can be dangerous; it has been shown to increase mortality rates in humans, dogs, and
cats.32-38 Fluid overload occurs in the non-dehydrated patient when volumes administered exceed

volumes being lost from the body.32,37 This may occur when the non-dehydrated pet’s body weight
increases by more than 10% from baseline (with the increase in weight being attributed to fluid).37
Clinically, fluid overload presents as either edema (ch. 30) or cavity effusions (e.g., pleural effusion [ch.
220], peritoneal effusion [ch. 21]), or other types of fluid deposition in the body. Intra-organ edema
can lead to organ failure by direct reduction in perfusion to that organ or by increasing overall intraabdominal pressure and secondarily reducing organ perfusion.39,40

MANAGEMENT OF FLUID OVERLOAD
The best approach to fluid overload is to avoid its occurrence in the first place. The “ROSE” strategy
described for humans should guide fluid therapy: Resuscitation (the animal needs fluids), Optimization
(give colloids, blood products, pressor drugs to ensure cellular perfusion but rely less on crystalloids),
Stabilization (give the animal maintenance crystalloid fluids and replace continuing losses), and
Evacuation (let the animal waste excess fluid).32,40,41 The ROSE strategy inherently makes sense but is
difficult to apply clinically, especially without good techniques to clinically measure cardiac output and
tissue perfusion. The best approach for the veterinary clinician is to provide a volume needed to restore
a perceived deficit based on PE/bedside diagnostic test findings (low blood pressure, poor quality pulses,
decreased mentation, evidence of blood loss or dehydration) and history (trauma or other information
suggestive of shock, vomiting, diarrhea, or other volume loss). As the fluid deficit is corrected, the rate of
administration should be tapered to the volume needed for metabolism (i.e., a “maintenance” rate of
fluids) plus any ongoing losses. Monitoring goals should include a stable body weight and vital
parameters. One anecdotally overlooked measure is how often an animal without renal disease is
urinating while receiving fluids. If the animal is urinating more often than every 3-4 hours, it is likely
evacuating excess fluids and the fluid rate should be reduced.

DEFINITIONS
Circulatory shock, or simply “shock,” is defined as a condition in which decreased cellular adenosine
triphosphate (ATP) production and decreased energy production lead to cellular dysfunction and/or
death. Shock is classically viewed as an imbalance between oxygen delivery (DO2) and oxygen
consumption by the tissues (VO2). In healthy resting animals VO2 is ∼25% of DO2 (also known as
the oxygen extraction fraction). A critical point in failed DO2 occurs when shock is so severe that
VO2 becomes dependent on DO2 and tissues transition to anaerobic metabolism (Figure 121.1).
More recent advances in medicine have also identified altered utilization of oxygen as a contributing
factor to the generation of shock.1

CLASSIFICATION, PATHOPHYSIOLOGY, AND
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES
ETIOLOGY
Background

Common classification schemes categorize circulatory shock on its etiology or its cardiovascular
effects (Table 121.1). Within these origin-based systems, shock is classified as hypovolemic,
distributive, cardiogenic, obstructive, or metabolic/hypoxemic in origin. Specific disease states then
fall into one of these broader categories, realizing that many, e.g., sepsis, may incorporate aspects of
more than one category.

Hypovolemic Shock
Hypovolemic shock is defined as a loss of intravascular (IV) fluid volume leading to altered
perfusion. “Hypovolemia,” loss of IV fluid volume, is differentiated from “dehydration,” decreased
interstitial fluid volume. Severe interstitial dehydration, however, is associated with hypovolemia.
Hemorrhagic shock is a form of hypovolemic shock in which large volumes of blood are lost (ch.
124). Common causes of hypovolemic shock in dogs and cats include hemorrhage, gastrointestinal
(GI) losses (vomiting and diarrhea), renal losses (polyuria), burn wounds, and “third-spacing” of
fluids (ch. 120).

Distributive Shock
Distributive shock is the result of maldistribution of normal blood volume. This condition,
depending on etiology, may be associated with increases or decreases in systemic vascular
resistance. Due to the large capacity of veins, their dilation can accommodate massive volumes of
pooled blood, decreasing venous return to the heart. Distributive shock is commonly associated with
sepsis and the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), which can lead to inappropriate
arterial and venous dilation. Release of exogenous (lipopolysaccharide, lipoteichoic acid, bacterial
DNA, etc.), or endogenous (histones, nuclear DNA, high mobility group box 1 proteins, RNA, etc.)
substances can induce inflammatory cytokine production, especially tumor necrosis factor-alpha,
interleukin 1-beta, and interleukin 6. These, plus other cytokines and neurohormones, increase
nitric oxide production, causing inappropriate vasodilation (ch 128).

Distributive shock, particularly septic shock, classically progresses through two phases. The
hyperdynamic (compensated shock) phase 1 occurs early, with increased cardiac output and
vasodilation predominating. Without intervention, septic cardiomyopathy may ensue, causing the
hypoperfusion of phase 2, known as the hypodynamic or decompensated form of distributive
shock.2 Cats rarely develop the hyperdynamic phase of distributive shock. Anaphylactic shock,
including shock secondary to mast cell degranulation, may be considered a form of distributive
shock. Like sepsis, it has components of other shock forms (ch. 129). Neurogenic shock is a form of
distributive shock where interruption of vasculature neural pathways causes loss of vasomotor tone
and/or excessive catecholamine surges lead to excessive vasoconstriction. Causes include general
anesthesia, spinal anesthesia, and damage to the central nervous system (chs. 44, 125).1

Cardiogenic Shock
Cardiogenic shock occurs when the heart fails as a pump, resulting in decreased forward blood flow
(ch. 229). In dogs and cats, this may occur secondary to dilated cardiomyopathy (ch. 233),
myocarditis (ch. 233), end-stage valvular disease (ch. 232), end-stage feline cardiomyopathies
(ch. 234), congenital anomalies (ch. 231), cardiac arrhythmias (ch. 230), and toxicoses
(anesthetics, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, etc.; ch. 137). Cardiogenic shock secondary
to myocardial infarction is common in humans. It should be noted that most dogs with left-sided
congestive heart failure secondary to myxomatous mitral valve disease are not in cardiogenic shock.

Obstructive Shock
Obstruction of vascular flow that prevents blood return to the heart is obstructive shock. The most
common causes of obstructive shock in small animals include gastric dilatation volvulus (ch. 261),
thromboembolic disease (ch. 238), and cardiac tamponade (ch. 235).

Metabolic and Hypoxemic Shock
While “macrocirculatory” causes of shock are commonly diagnosed and studied, there is increasing
focus on “microcirculatory” causes of shock. Most causes of metabolic shock result from poor tissue
utilization of oxygen rather than poor delivery of oxygen to the tissues. Causes of metabolic shock
include hypoglycemia (ch. 61), cyanide or arsenic toxicosis (ch. 138), mitochondrial dysfunction,
or the cytopathic hypoxia of sepsis (ch. 128). Causes of hypoxemic shock include carbon monoxide
toxicosis, methemoglobinemia, severe anemia, and hypoxemia induced by respiratory disease (chs.
138, 212).2

OTHER CLASSIFICATION SCHEMES
Circulatory shock may also be classified using a temporal perspective. Compensated shock refers to
the early stages of shock, in which activation of the sympathetic nervous systemic, the reninangiotensin-aldosterone system, and release of antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) support blood
volume and prevent marked decreases in cardiac output. If shock continues, these compensatory
mechanisms prove inadequate, resulting in decompensated or progressive shock.1,2 In this stage, if
left untreated, shock progresses to death. It is characterized by myocardial depression secondary to
decreased coronary blood flow, altered capillary permeability, release of toxins by ischemic tissues
and endotoxins from the intestinal microbiota, cellular and mitochondrial dysfunction, acidosis,
vasomotor failure, and altered blood viscosity. Irreversible shock is the final stage of untreated
shock, in which cellular dysfunction and organ failure lead to death regardless of therapeutic
intervention.1
Vasodilatory shock may be used to refer to the hyperdynamic stage of distributive shock in which
decreased vascular resistance results in profound peripheral vasodilation. Decompensated shock
may similarly result in vasodilation secondary to vasoplegia. This may be differentiated from the
vasoconstrictive forms of shock, including hypovolemic shock, cardiogenic shock, and the
hypodynamic stage of distributive shock.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (Table 121.2)
Physical examination (PE; ch. 2) findings depend on both the type and stage of shock encountered.
Generally, the vasoconstrictive forms of shock in the compensatory stage (hypovolemic shock,
cardiogenic shock, the hypodynamic stage of distributive shock, obstructive shock, and most causes
of hypoxemic and metabolic shock) result in dull mentation (ch. 44), pale mucous membranes,
normal-to-prolonged capillary refill time (CRT), tachypnea (ch. 37), hypothermia, adequate or
weak pulse quality (ch. 39), cool extremities, tachycardia in dogs, and tachycardia or bradycardia in
cats (Video 121.1). Heart murmurs and/or cardiac arrhythmias may be detected in cardiogenic
shock. In decompensatory stages, patients may develop obtundation, pale mucous membranes,
weak to absent peripheral pulses, and prolonged CRTs. Vasodilatory shock (the hyperdynamic stage
of distributive shock) results in hyperemic mucous membranes, hyperdynamic peripheral pulses,
fever, warm extremities, rapid CRTs, and tachycardia.2
Since dogs and cats in circulatory shock are unstable, an immediate “triage PE” focused on the
cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological systems should be performed (ch. 119). Once these
life-threatening abnormalities have been identified and addressed, a more thorough PE may be
completed. Since circulatory shock is a dynamic process, PEs should be monitored throughout
stabilization rather than at any pre-determined single or multiple time points.

DIAGNOSTICS
BLOOD, URINE, AND BLOOD PRESSURE TESTING
Overview
The cause for circulatory shock may not be immediately apparent and broad initial testing may be
necessary to identify an etiology. Until stabilization is achieved, ideal testing is non-invasive,
“bedside,” and it provides rapid reliable results that allow continuous reassessment (ch. 122).

Blood Pressure
Blood pressure monitoring is essential for diagnosing circulatory shock and monitoring response to
therapy. Septic shock and its associated hypotension in humans has a mortality rate >50%,
demonstrating the importance of monitoring and correcting hypotension.3 Blood pressure
monitoring may be conducted either invasively or non-invasively. Non-invasive methods are less
accurate in dogs and cats with peripheral vasoconstriction, such as those with circulatory shock (ch.
91).4

Electrocardiogram (ECG)
Continuous or periodic ECG monitoring is important for identifying arrhythmias, alterations
suggestive of specific electrolyte abnormalities, or sudden changes in heart rate, as either the cause
of cardiogenic shock or a sign of systemic disease (ch. 96). ECGs can be vital in monitoring
response to therapy.

Pulse Oximetry
Pulse oximetry is a non-invasive measurement of arterial oxygenation (ch. 122). It should be noted
that pulse oximetry measures pulsatile arterial flow in tissue beds. Therefore, in low flow states,
such as hypotension or anemia, readings may be much less reliable.5

Blood Gas and CO-Oximeter Analysis
Blood gas analysis is essential for identifying issues in need of correction as part of managing
critically ill dogs and cats. Arterial blood gas analysis can be used to rule out hypoxemic shock if
normal arterial oxygen pressure is recorded with normal CO-oximetry readings. CO-oximetry
provides methemoglobin and carboxyhemoglobin levels to identify either as a cause of the current
illness. Metabolic alkalosis may indicate hypovolemia secondary to vomiting with loss of
hydrochloric acid or diuretic therapy. Most types of circulatory shock result in metabolic acidosis
secondary to lactate and hydrogen generation. Neurogenic shock may result in severe respiratory
acidosis, while hypoxemic shock may cause either respiratory acidosis or alkalosis (ch. 122).

Blood Lactate
Lactate measurements are widely available and extremely valuable in diagnosing and monitoring
patients with circulatory shock. A common cause of hyperlactatemia is decreased DO2 from
hypoperfusion, resulting in anaerobic metabolism. Lactate has been extensively studied as a
biomarker for multiple types of circulatory shock and serial measurements have prognostic value in
shock states such as obstructive shock secondary to gastric dilatation volvulus in dogs.6-8 The
Surviving Sepsis 3 guidelines state “hyperlactatemia is a marker of illness severity and mortality.”9
Hyperlactatemia in patients with circulatory dysfunction is non-specific and associated with a
myriad of conditions, including mitochondrial dysfunction secondary to sepsis, hepatic dysfunction,
neoplasia, severe anemia, severe hypoxia, and drug therapy (e.g., catecholamines).2

Full Laboratory Assessment
Complete blood count (CBC), biochemical profile, coagulation testing, and urinalysis (UA) should be
obtained from every patient in circulatory shock to search for an underlying cause of disease and to
identify sequelae secondary to shock (chs. 122 and 170). Differentiation between cardiac and noncardiac causes of shock may involve measurement of biomarkers (e.g., troponin, N-terminal probrain natriuretic peptide).10,11 Hypoadrenocorticism can be ruled out with a basal cortisol
concentration >2 mcg/dL (ch. 296). Thyrotoxicosis or myxedema coma may be ruled out with
thyroid hormone testing (ch. 285).

Microbiological, Cytological, and Infectious Disease Testing
In pets with suspected sepsis or infectious disease, complete microbiological testing is warranted
(ch. 184). A suspected site of infection should be aerobically cultured with susceptibility testing.

Commonly submitted samples include pleural or peritoneal effusions, fluid from subcutaneous
abscesses, joint effusions (ch. 71), urine, blood, cerebrospinal fluid (ch. 109), and fluid from an
endotracheal wash or bronchoalveolar lavage (ch. 93). If the site of infection is unknown or if
endocarditis is suspected, blood cultures should be considered. Any aspirated fluid should be
evaluated cytologically for cellular morphology and infectious agents. Evaluation of packed cell
volume, total solids, lactate, glucose, bilirubin, creatinine, and/or potassium may be indicated for
differentiating among various underlying causes of effusion. Tick-borne disease testing, including
polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and serologic titers, may be indicated, especially for pets with
concurrent hematological disorders. Leptospirosis titers and/or PCR for azotemic patients in
circulatory shock may be indicated (ch. 192). Viral testing may be indicated in subpopulations of
dogs and cats, including parvovirus/panleukopenia (ch. 201), feline leukemia (ch. 199), feline
immunodeficiency virus (ch. 198), and common respiratory pathogens (chs. 203, 205). Testing
for Dirofilaria immitis or GI parasites may be indicated. Fungal testing may be indicated and
involve cytology and/or serology.

IMAGING
The results of imaging studies can be extremely valuable for determining the cause of sepsis. Point
of care ultrasound (US) may be used to identify pleural, pericardial, and peritoneal effusions, left
atrial size, left ventricular systolic function, and pulmonary parenchyma health (ch. 73). Effusion
may not be identified prior to resuscitation and serial US examinations may be required. Sampling
and cytologic evaluation of any effusion (ch. 71) is recommended following coagulation testing.
Radiography, US, echocardiography, and computed tomography (CT) all have indications in various
types of shock. However, stabilization must be achieved prior to any time-consuming imaging study,
especially ones involving significant restraint or anesthesia.

ADVANCED MONITORING
Numerous other tools have been evaluated in human and veterinary medicine for diagnosing and
monitoring circulatory shock. Biomarkers, such as procalcitonin, C-reactive protein, and cell-free
DNA, have been evaluated for identifying sepsis and response to antibiotic therapy.12,13 In people,
there are conflicting opinions regarding the value of central venous pressure, mixed venous oxygen
saturation, DO2, cardiac output, systemic vascular resistance, preload, afterload, and contractility
when determining goals of therapy.14,15 Since most of these tests involve placement of a pulmonary
arterial catheter, they are rarely performed in clinical veterinary medicine. Cardiac output
monitoring via echocardiography may be a less invasive and more clinically viable method in dogs,
though less accurate in hypotensive states.16 Emerging technologies include tissue oxygen
saturation measurement, arterio-venous gradients, pulse pressure variation, and sidestream
darkfield microscopy. These may have roles in the diagnosis of shock, particularly shock secondary
to microvascular disease.

TREATMENT
OVERVIEW
Treatment for circulatory shock should focus on optimizing DO2, which may involve increasing
cardiac output or arterial content of oxygen (CaO2; Box 121.1). With hypovolemic and distributive
shock, initial focus is on correction of preload to increase cardiac output; if the state of circulatory
shock is not corrected with volume, optimization of afterload, restoration of vascular tone, or
correction of hemoglobin concentration may become a secondary focus. In pets with cardiogenic
shock, improving contractility or correction of arrhythmias is usually the priority. Metabolic shock

may require improving partial pressure of oxygen in the arterial blood (PaO2), oxygen saturation, or
hemoglobin concentration to improve CaO2 (ch. 119).

OXYGEN THERAPY
Oxygen therapy (simple and inexpensive) should initially be provided to all pets in circulatory
shock. Oxygen therapy increases the PaO2, resulting in modest increases in DO2. This is due to the
comparatively small contribution that PaO2 makes to arterial oxygen content (Box 121.1).
Prolonged oxygen therapy in patients not hypoxemic should be avoided due to risks associated with
oxygen toxicosis, including non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema.17

VOLUME RESUSCITATION
Volume resuscitation with IV fluids is critically important in order to stabilize most pets in
circulatory shock, outside those in cardiogenic and hypoxemic shock. Crystalloids, synthetic
colloids, and blood products may all have utility in improving preload, stroke volume, and thus DO2
in patients with shock (ch. 120). In pets suspected to be volume-responsive, aliquots of an isotonic
crystalloid bolus representative of a single blood volume (90 mL/kg in dogs, 50 mL/kg in cats) are
administered. Typically, 20-25% of this dose is administered IV over 10-20 minutes. The pet must
be reassessed after each bolus, which is repeated until normal blood pressure is achieved or until the
patient no longer appears fluid-responsive. In dogs and cats in hemorrhagic shock, hypotensive
resuscitation may be performed (ch. 124).18
Hypertonic saline (7-7.5% at 4-6 mL/kg over 10-20 minutes) may be considered for pets in
hypovolemic shock, particularly those with concurrent traumatic brain injury (ch. 246), without
evidence of dehydration or hypernatremia (ch. 125). In hypoalbuminemic pets needing oncotic
support, human or canine serum albumin or synthetic colloids (hydroxyethyl starches) may be
considered (ch. 120). If there is concurrent coagulopathy and need of oncotic support, plasma
transfusion may be considered. Transfusion therapy, including fresh whole blood, packed red blood
cells, and fresh frozen plasma, may be considered for patients with significant hemorrhage.
Hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers, if available, may be used in similar situations when red blood
cells are unavailable or blood incompatibilities exist.18

VASOACTIVE AND INOTROPIC THERAPIES
Persistent hypotension despite correcting the volume deficit likely indicates a need for vasopressor
or inotropic therapy. Dogs and cats with cardiogenic shock may require inotropic support, while

those with distributive shock may require vasopressor and/or inotropic therapy. Dogs and cats in
hypoxemic shock without cardiogenic shock may require afterload reduction. Reassessments should
be performed 10-15 minutes after initiation of vasoactive therapy and after each increase in dosage
until a target blood pressure is achieved (ch. 91).
Vasopressors increase arterial tone and then arterial blood pressure as well as increasing venous
tone. These changes should increase venous return and mean systemic filling pressure. The most
common vasopressors used in veterinary medicine are alpha-1 agonists (norepinephrine, dopamine,
epinephrine, and phenylephrine) and vasopressin-1 agonists (vasopressin, selepressin, and
terlipressin). Norepinephrine is typically considered the first-line vasopressor in humans with
vasodilatory shock, particularly those in septic shock (ch. 128). There is a dearth of evidence-based
guidelines for small animals, but norepinephrine and dopamine are commonly used. Vasopressors
that have mostly been evaluated in human medicine include nitric oxide scavengers (hemoglobinbased oxygen carriers and methylene blue), angiotensin II agonists, and physiologic glucocorticoids
for patients with suspected vasoplegia secondary to critical illness-related corticosteroid
insufficiency.
Inotropic agents increase myocardial contractility either through beta-1 agonism (dobutamine,
dopamine) or through increasing calcium sensitization to troponin (pimobendan, levosimendan,
and milrinone). While inotropes increase cardiac output, they have variable effects on systemic
vascular resistance and blood pressure (Table 121.3).19,20
Afterload reducing agents have two effects. First, they reduce arterial tone, reducing the
resistance the heart must pump against. Second, their venodilatory effects decrease the effective
circulating volume by increasing the unstressed volume of blood in relation to the stressed volume.
In normotensive patients with hypoxemic shock secondary to left-sided congestive heart failure,
afterload reduction may be accomplished with nitric oxide donors (nitroprusside),
phosphodiesterase III inhibitors (pimobendan, milrinone), or calcium channel blockers
(nicardipine, clevidipine) (ch. 229).21

PRIMARY DISEASE MANAGEMENT
Correction and management of underlying disease processes is often paramount in stabilizing
patients in circulatory shock. Correcting metabolic and electrolyte derangements, including glucose
(ch. 61), calcium (ch. 69), and potassium (ch. 68), should be initiated rapidly. For patients with
suspected sepsis, early antibiotic therapy and source control are essential (ch. 128). Control of
hemorrhage should be prioritized in patients with hypovolemic shock (ch. 124).

PROGNOSIS
Prognosis for recovery from circulatory shock depends on the type of shock and the underlying
disease process. Early recognition and treatment of circulatory shock improves survival in humans
and is likely to similarly improve the prognosis in dogs and cats.22
