In the emergency setting, having results of critically important tests
invariably helps to understand the patient’s current status, prioritize
stabilization efforts, and refine differential diagnoses. Test results
can also guide biosecurity measures (e.g., isolating a puppy in
response to a positive fecal parvovirus antigen enzyme linked
immunosorbent assay [ELISA]). Ideally, emergency testing provides
rapid and accurate clinical data to facilitate a timely response. The
accepted minimum emergency laboratory database consists of a
packed cell volume (PCV), total solids (TS), blood glucose (BG),
blood urea nitrogen (BUN), serum electrolytes (sodium [Na],
potassium [K], chloride [Cl], calcium [Ca]), and a blood smear. Blood
gas and acid-base testing can be extremely valuable. Several pointof-care (POC) tests are commercially available, including several
diagnostic imaging modalities. The clinician can have valuable
clinical data to assimilate and quickly apply to managing an
emergency.

EMERGENCY LABORATORY TESTING
HEMATOLOGY
While a complete blood count (CBC) should be performed in any
systemically sick animal, only a few key pieces of clinical data are
needed in a crisis. First, the PCV and TS should be interpreted in
tandem and in the context of the overall clinical picture (e.g., animal
with evidence of poor perfusion; ch. 121). Next, a blood smear
should be evaluated, especially in animals with anemia or signs of

spontaneous bleeding (Video 57.1

). In the anemic animal,

indicators of regeneration (e.g., polychromasia, anisocytosis) and
clues to the underlying disease (e.g., spherocytosis, erythrocyte
parasites) might be readily identified (ch. 57). Additional POC tests
might be considered at this point, including pre-transfusion
compatibility testing (e.g., blood type; ch. 124), retroviral testing in
cats (chs. 198, 199), and saline agglutination (ch. 174).1 An
estimated platelet count can be obtained by counting the average
number of platelets over 10 high power fields with the 100× oil lens
and multiplying by 20,000. If present, thrombocytopenia can
provide insight into possible diagnoses (ch. 59). Platelet clumping
causes pseudothrombocytopenia, especially in cats, and can be a
normal variant in some dog breeds (e.g., macrothrombocytopenia in
Cavalier King Charles Spaniel). Severe thrombocytopenia (e.g.,
<20,000/mcL) is common in immune mediated thrombocytopenia,
bone marrow disease, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC),
and certain infections (e.g., ehrlichiosis, cytauxzoonosis). Moderate
thrombocytopenia (e.g., 50,000-100,000/mcL) is more likely due to
“consumption” (e.g., hemorrhage, thrombosis) or infections (e.g.,
sepsis, infective endocarditis, anaplasmosis). White blood cell
evaluation may suggest a cause (e.g., lymphocytosis in
hypoadrenocorticism,2 neutropenia in a febrile animal) but is not
usually helpful in a crisis (ch. 58). Accuracy of blood smear
evaluation is operator dependent and focused training improves
knowledge and confidence.3,4

BIOCHEMISTRY TESTING
Results of BG, BUN and creatinine are prioritized over other
biochemical variables in an emergency. Gross evaluation of spun
hematocrit tubes (e.g., icteric or lipemic serum) can be informative.

Blood Glucose (BG)
BG is always valuable but is prioritized in some (e.g., collapsed
neonate). Veterinary specific POC glucometers (e.g., AlphaTRAK) are
convenient in a crisis. Compared to serum or plasma samples, whole

BG may be artefactually decreased or increased in hemoconcentrated
and hemodiluted samples, respectively (chs. 61 and 78). Predictive
formulae have been developed to reduce such errors on veterinary
specific devices in dogs [POC glucose + ([1.6 × PCV] − 81.3)] and cats
[POC glucose + ([1.17 × PCV] − 50.2)].5,6 When possible, additional
blood should be collected and serum saved from hypoglycemic
animals prior to dextrose administration in case measuring a serum
insulin concentration becomes indicated. When hyperglycemia is
identified, the clinician must differentiate stress from pathological
hyperglycemia (diabetes mellitus). Stress hyperglycemia is most
common in cats, usually causing BGs of 200-400 mg/dL (11-22
mmol/L). The urine from all other hyperglycemic pets should be
checked for glucose and ketones (chs. 290-292). Acetone and
acetoacetate can be measured on serum, plasma, or urine samples
using urine reagent dipsticks. Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), the most
clinically relevant ketone, can be measured with specific POC ketone
meters.7 Increased BHB concentrations occur in some cats with nondiabetic illnesses (e.g., chronic kidney disease, hyperthyroidism)
suggesting enhanced catabolism.8

BUN and Creatinine
Serum/blood urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations can be
measured with POC devices. Estimating BUN with Azostix reagent
strips is used less commonly. When possible, BUN and creatinine
should be interpreted in the context of a urine specific gravity (USG)
obtained before parenteral fluid administration. If the patient is
azotemic, the clinician should know the body condition score (ch.
72), palpate the urinary bladder, look for ascites, and assess PCV/TS
and electrolytes. One should efficiently determine if the pet has prerenal, renal, or post-renal azotemia (chs. 62, 299). Discordant BUN
and creatinine results are also helpful, since high BUN:creatinine
suggests dehydration, reduced glomerular filtration in animals with
poor muscle mass, or gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding. Low
BUN:creatinine may be seen in liver failure or well-muscled dogs.

SERUM ELECTROLYTE
CONCENTRATIONS
Sodium (Na)
Na derangements usually reflect water imbalance, such that
hyponatremia reflects water excess and hypernatremia water deficit
(chs. 67 and 120). Knowing whether the Na abnormality is acute or
chronic can impact case management. If hyponatremia is recognized,
the clinician should first rule out artifact (e.g., hyperglycemia,
hyperlipidemia, hyperproteinemia). Na can be corrected for the
degree of hyperglycemia using the formula: measured Na +
1.6[(glucose in mg/dL − 100)/100]. Next, the animal’s volume status
should be evaluated. Hypovolemia is a potent stimulus for
antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release, which promotes water
retention by the kidneys and can contribute to hyponatremia.
Hyponatremia without hypovolemia suggests excessive water intake
or a syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (chs. 53, 67).
Hypervolemic hyponatremia occurs in conditions like congestive
heart failure and nephrotic syndrome where the renin-angiotensinaldosterone system is upregulated. Loss of free water (anorexia,
vomiting, diarrhea, polyuria) is the most common cause of
hypernatremia, although the possibility of abnormal Na gain (e.g.,
ingestion of salt water) should be determined. Hypernatremia may
occur in a normovolemic animal with diabetes insipidus or
hypodipsia, while hypovolemic hypernatremia develops secondary to
excessive water loss through the urinary or GI tracts (ch. 120).

Chloride (Cl)
Cl results should be interpreted in the context of changes in plasma
free water (ch. 67). “Corrected” Cl concentrations can be calculated
using the formula: ([mid-normal Na concentration / measured Na] ×
measured Cl). Corrected hypochloremia is the most relevant finding
in a crisis, since it usually develops secondary to vomiting, pyloric
outflow obstruction, or gastric stasis. Corrected hypochloremia can
be seen in pets being given loop diuretics or in corticosteroid excess.
Hyperchloremia may follow infusion of Cl-rich fluids (e.g., 0.9%

NaCl) and is used to characterize metabolic acidosis as discussed
below.

Potassium (K)
Hyperkalemia can be life threatening (chs. 68 and 296).
Hyperkalemia promotes cell excitability by minimizing differences in
resting membrane and threshold potentials, which may cause cardiac
arrhythmias. Characteristic electrocardiogram (ECG) changes
secondary to hyperkalemia are well-documented (e.g., atrial
standstill, tall T waves, wide complex ventricular tachycardia) but
can vary in individuals related to other electrolyte derangements
(e.g., hypocalcemia).9,10 Hyperkalemia typically reflects impaired
urinary excretion (e.g., urethral obstruction, acute kidney injury,
uroperitoneum, hypoadrenocorticism) but may also occur with
transcellular shifts from intracellular stores (e.g., metabolic acidosis,
hypoinsulinemia). Pseudohyperkalemia may be seen in animals with
thrombocytosis and can be dramatic in some dog breeds (ch. 68).
Hypokalemia is often encountered (e.g., secondary to renal and GI
losses) but usually does not require rapid correction, even in a crisis.

Calcium (Ca)
Some POC devices measure ionized Ca (iCa). Hypocalcemia causes
neuromuscular dysfunction (e.g., tetany and tremors; Video 69.1
) more commonly than seizures or arrhythmias in dogs and cats (ch.
69). While low serum iCa is often seen in critically ill animals,
emergent treatment is rarely needed unless signs of hypocalcemia
are evident (e.g., postpartum dog with eclampsia; Video 284.2

).

Hypercalcemia is also an important laboratory abnormality, which
may be noted in animals with a history of polyuria/polydipsia
(PU/PD) or azotemia (ch. 53). Identifying hypercalcemia can
rapidly focus the diagnostic work up (e.g., lymph node aspirates and
thoracic radiographs to assess for a mediastinal mass in a dog with
suspicion of lymphoma), as well as influence therapeutic choices
(e.g., 0.9% NaCl and furosemide administration).

BLOOD GAS ANALYSIS
Some POC devices measure partial pressures of oxygen (PO2) and
carbon dioxide (PCO2). Either arterial or venous blood samples are
acceptable for PCO2 evaluation, but arterial samples are needed
when PO2 is used to quantify pulmonary function (chs. 74, 123,
212). Blood gas analysis should be performed within 2 minutes of
sample collection or samples stored on ice if delays are anticipated.
Obtaining arterial samples can be challenging (e.g., cats, animals
with respiratory distress or vasoconstriction), forcing the clinician to
abort arterial blood gas analysis and to consider pulse oximetry
instead. The alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient is used to quantify
pulmonary function in animals breathing room air at sea level using
the formula: [150 − (1.1 × PaCO2) − PaO2]. The A-a gradient
effectively provides a sense of the ventilatory effort (indicated by the
partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood [PaCO2]) needed
to achieve a certain partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood
(PaO2). A-a gradient values >20 are consistent with decreased
oxygenation efficiency. If animals are receiving supplemental
oxygen, the ratio of PaO2 to the fractional inspired oxygen
(PaO2:FiO2) is used to quantify pulmonary dysfunction. The PaO2
should be 5 times the FiO2 in healthy animals (e.g., PaO2 should be
500 mm Hg when breathing 100% oxygen). PaO2:FiO2 <300
indicates poor gas exchange. Placement of a central venous catheter
(ch. 75) and collecting venous blood for measuring venous oxygen
saturation can be used to assess systemic hemodynamic function but
is not commonly performed in the emergency setting.11

ACID-BASE ANALYSIS
Traditional acid-base analysis is based on the HendersonHasselbalch equation, where blood pH is a measure of hydrogen ion
concentration from the ratio of bicarbonate (HCO3−) (metabolic

component) and PCO2 (respiratory component; Figure 122.1).
After determining whether acidosis or alkalosis is respiratory or
metabolic in nature, it then is necessary to assess whether
appropriate compensation has occurred (consistent with a primary
disorder) or not (consistent with a mixed disorder; Table 122.1). If
primary metabolic acidosis is present, the anion gap should be
calculated: ([Na+ + K+] − [Cl− + HCO3−]). In biological systems,
electroneutrality is maintained, but a small anion gap is seen in
healthy animals since an excess of cations is readily measured using
conventional diagnostic tests. An increased anion gap suggests the
presence of unmeasured anions in the system (e.g., uremic toxins,
ketones, lactate, ethylene glycol) and can help refine patient
management. Hypoalbuminemia may mask the presence of
unmeasured anions. Lactate may be used as a late stage indicator of
tissue hypoperfusion (type A hyperlactatemia) associated with
enhanced anaerobic respiration secondary to impaired oxygen
delivery (e.g., hypovolemia) or increased oxygen utilization (e.g.,
seizures). Non-perfusion associated hyperlactatemia (type B) may
also be encountered (e.g., type B1—sepsis, neoplasia; type B2—
corticosteroids, ethylene glycol; type B3—hereditary mitochondrial
dysfunction). Admission lactate may provide insight into an illness
but cannot be used for determining a prognosis. Serial lactate
measurements are helpful in demonstrating response to therapy.
Lactate clearance can be calculated as ([initial lactate − delayed
lactate] / initial lactate × 100), with higher lactate clearance being
associated with improved outcome in dogs with shock.12
Anion gap metabolic acidosis usually occurs secondary to HCO3−
loss through the kidneys or GI tract and is accompanied by increased
serum Cl (hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis). Non-traditional
approaches to acid-base may provide greater insight into patient
status. The “Stewart approach” takes strong ion differences and
unmeasured anions into account, while the “Stewart-Fencl
approach” considers the influence of free water, Cl, lactate, albumin,
and phosphate.13

HEMOSTASIS TESTING (ch. 170)
Some pets have evidence of bleeding or thrombosis or they are at risk
of developing one of these issues. Traditional hemostatic tests
(platelet count, buccal mucosal bleeding time [BMBT; ch. 79],

prothrombin time [PT], activated partial thromboplastin time
[aPTT]) are used to identify hypocoagulability. A blood smear should
be used to obtain an estimated platelet count as described earlier
(ch. 58; Video 57.1

). Prolonged BMBT (>4 minutes in dogs, >2

minutes in cats) with a normal platelet count suggests an intrinsic
(e.g., hereditary thrombocytopathia) or extrinsic platelet dysfunction
(e.g., von Willebrand disease; ch. 175). POC devices for PT and aPTT
devices are available, but aPTT results are especially prone to
inaccuracy.14 The PT and aPTT should be interpreted together, since
they reflect different components of the clotting cascade (PT—
extrinsic/common pathway, aPTT—intrinsic/common pathways).
Isolated extrinsic pathway defects are recognized by PT prolongation
and normal aPTT, while isolated intrinsic pathway defects (e.g.,
hemophilia A [factor VIII deficiency], Hageman trait [factor XII
deficiency]) are recognized by normal PT and prolonged aPTT (ch.
171). Prolongation of both PT and aPTT reflect changes throughout
the clotting cascade, but identification of PT prolongation in excess
of aPTT suggests vitamin K deficiency (e.g., anticoagulant
rodenticide intoxication, hepatobiliary disease). In the event of
abnormal PT/aPTT or BMBT results, further hemostatic testing (e.g.,
individual factor analysis, von Willebrand factor antigen) may be
considered and, ideally, samples would be collected prior to
transfusion of any plasma products. Viscoelastic tests (e.g.,
thromboelastography, thromboelastometry) have had limited
availability but a POC device has recently been described.15
Viscoelastic tests provide insight into the rate of clot formation, final
clot strength, and rate of clot lysis. Results may suggest
hypocoagulability, hypercoagulability, or hyperfibrinolysis (ch. 170).
Viscoelastic tests have not been ideal in crisis situations since a
standardized 30-minute rest period is recommended before the 90minute test is completed.16 If thrombosis is suspected, diagnostic
imaging to identify thrombosis is generally more helpful than
hemostatic testing.

URINALYSIS (UA), CYTOLOGIC AND
FLUID ANALYSIS (CHS. 70, 71, AND 85)
A complete UA is a secondary tier diagnostic test, but key pieces of
data may be useful in emergencies (e.g., USG, glucose, ketones,
blood, calcium oxalate monohydrate crystals [ethylene glycol
intoxication]). Cytologic evaluation of tissue aspirates (ch. 85),
effusions (ch. 71), and impression smears may provide rapid insight
into the primary disease present but may require a clinical
pathologist. Some definitive diagnoses can be confidently made in an
emergency setting, especially when multiple pieces of clinical data
are utilized together, e.g., septic effusions are readily identified by
lower glucose and higher lactate concentrations compared to
peripheral blood samples, with evidence of septic suppurative
inflammation cytologically in the effusion. Uroperitoneum can be
confidently identified by documenting higher K and creatinine in the
effusion as compared with peripheral samples.

MISCELLANEOUS POC DIAGNOSTIC
LABORATORY TESTS
Although beyond the scope of this chapter, several other POC tests
may be incorporated into emergency practice. This partial list
includes infectious disease testing (e.g., heartworm antigen test; ch.
237), cardiac biomarkers (e.g., N-terminal prohormone of brain
natriuretic peptide [NT-proBNP; ch. 228]), pancreatic lipase
immunoreactivity (ch. 277), blood ammonia (ch. 267), and
toxicological tests (e.g., ethylene glycol; chs. 133-138).

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING (CH. 73)
Plain radiographs remain valuable, widely available, and clinicians
have confidence in their interpretation. Thoracic and abdominal
radiographs should be considered in any systemically sick animal.
Some situations arise, however, where handling and positioning for
radiographs are best avoided (e.g., cat with respiratory distress). In
this instance, POC ultrasound (POCUS) can rapidly and safely be
used to obtain valuable information. Moderate volumes of thoracic

and abdominal effusion are readily identified with POCUS. Limited
echocardiographic views can also be learned quite easily (Figure
122.2), including the recognition of pericardial effusion, left atrial
enlargement (utilizing the left atrial to aortic ratio), and indicators of
volume status (left ventricular size).17 With training and experience,
sonography of the lung (veterinary bedside lung examination or
VET-BLUE) may be useful for recognizing additional characteristics
including B-lines (hyperechoic vertical lines originating from the
lung surface consistent with pulmonary infiltrates), as well as the
glide sign (to-and-fro movement of the lung relative to the thoracic
wall that rules out the presence of a pneumothorax).

FIGURE 122.2 Ultrasound probe positioning at
the right pericardial side to obtain parasternal short
axis views on the left ventricle (LV) (bottom left) and
left atrium (LA):aorta (Ao) (bottom right).

There is growing interest in the use of sedated whole-body
computed tomography (CT) in animals, especially in the context of
polytrauma.18 Apparent advantages include rapid image acquisition
but image interpretation can be time-consuming. When compared to
POCUS, CT was superior for the recognition of pneumothorax and
pleural effusion, yet was similarly effective in identifying abdominal
effusion.19 Radiographs were shown to underestimate the presence
of lung contusions and rib fractures compared to CT in traumatized
dogs.20 Another study demonstrated that functional indicators of
oxygenation by arterial blood gas analysis were well correlated with
CT image findings, suggesting that lesions identified by CT are
clinically relevant.21 The use of sedated whole-body CT in small
animals for non-traumatic emergent conditions is less well described
(ch. 112).

Elizabeth Rozanski

PATTERN RECOGNITION AND
PROFILING
OVERVIEW
Respiratory distress in dogs and cats is common in the emergency
setting. When respiratory distress occurs, it can be fatal. It is
important to recognize when a dog or cat is in respiratory distress
(ch. 37) and to know treatment options that are immediately
available (ch. 212). In crisis there is need for quick recognition of
the most life-threatening problem and to rapidly respond, sometimes
before all the “needed information” is available.

DOGS
Keys to evaluating a dog with respiratory distress include age, breed,
and recent history.1 Breed predilections can be helpful in directing
diagnostics but these are never pathognomonic e.g., brachycephalic
dogs are predisposed to upper airway obstruction (ch. 213), but also
to hiatal hernias (ch. 222), pneumonia (ch. 217), and heart-base
tumors (ch. 235). Doberman Pinschers may develop congestive
heart failure rather quickly, often without a loud murmur (ch. 233).
Yorkshire Terriers develop severe tracheal collapse (chs. 114, 215).
Puppies, particularly Pit Bull Terrier types, seem predisposed to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (ch. 217). Dogs with a history of
pneumonia may be more likely to develop a recurrence (ch. 217).
Older retrievers may have laryngeal paralysis as part of the geriatric
onset laryngeal paralysis polyneuropathy syndrome (GOLPP; chs.
214, 252).2

CATS
As in any pet in respiratory distress, localization may be helpful in
determining the underlying etiology. Cats with upper airway disease
may have open-mouth breathing but are pink and well-perfused.
Cats that are open-mouth breathing may be severely stressed (e.g., a
frightened hyperthyroid cat) or in respiratory distress (

Video

37.4). In young cats, nasopharyngeal polyps maybe present, while in
older cats, neoplastic mass lesions are more likely. A cat of any age
can have upper respiratory infection (ch. 205) or nasopharyngeal
stenosis. Cats that have heart failure are typically hypothermic, and
this results in bradycardia. Many cats with asthma have a history of
coughing (ch. 34).1 N-terminal pro b-type natriuretic peptide (NTproBNP) testing, available as point of care (PoC) for cats, may be
helpful to rule in or rule out heart disease.3 Older cats almost never
develop asthma without prior clinical signs (ch. 215).

BE PREPARED

Being prepared to manage a respiratory crisis includes having
oxygen available, an ability to intubate or perform a tracheostomy,
and an ability to manage pleural space disease. All staff members
should be trained to recognize and intervene if respiratory distress is
detected or suspected. Sometimes a pet being seen for a scheduled
appointment may arrive with or develop in-hospital respiratory
compromise, e.g., an overheated Bulldog.

FIGURE 123.1 A dog receiving supplemental
oxygen at home.

OXYGEN THERAPY
OPTIONS/MAINTAINING INVENTORY
Supplemental oxygen may be provided via a variety of systems,
including flow-by, face mask, nasal oxygen, e-collar oxygen hood or
helmet, oxygen cage, high flow oxygen therapy (HFOT), and
intubation with intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV).4

All hospitals and clinics should have oxygen readily available, either
in tanks or as the less expensive liquid oxygen. Oxygen concentrators
are a viable option. In busy day practices or emergency clinics,
maintaining adequate oxygen stores is vital, including back-up tanks.
Contact information for the oxygen supplier should be readily
available. Long weekends or holidays require special attention.
HFOT, with flow rates of up to 40 L/minute, will deplete an oxygen
tank with 6600 L in <3 hours. If a practice commonly uses HFOT, it
is important to have adequate oxygen available. One major
advantage of HFOT is avoiding the need for mechanical ventilation,
which is a major commitment financially, emotionally, and from a
staffing perspective.5 If transport is a possibility, oxygen tanks to
permit transfer are useful. Some committed owners have oxygen at
home for pets, a helpful option if the pet’s quality of life is otherwise
good (Figure 123.1).

OXYGEN THERAPY AS A BRIDGE TO
SPECIFIC TREATMENTS
Methods of oxygen delivery should be tailored to the underlying
condition of the pet and the staffing of the hospital, e.g., for a pet
with pleural space disease or upper airway obstruction, oxygen
therapy only serves as a bridge to focused therapy (thoracocentesis
[ch. 92], intubation, tracheostomy [ch. 94]). Thoracocentesis
should only be delayed long enough to discuss and gain approval for
treatment with the family while supplies and an assistant are
arranged (ch. 92). If a pet is to be referred, thoracocentesis should
be performed prior to referral to provide relief. Samples of any
effusion removed should then be sent with the pet. Complications of
thoracocentesis are relatively rare. The benefit of lung re-expansion
far outweigh potential risks, prior to travel.

SHORT-TERM VS LONG-TERM OXYGEN
THERAPY

Short-term, oxygen by face mask is usually well-tolerated and
permits delivery of relatively high oxygen concentrations. Longer
term, oxygen cages or nasal oxygen are less labor intensive and less
stressful. While in people, non-invasive ventilation is commonly
pursued, it is less frequently used in dogs and cats due to less
cooperation. The amount of sedation required to tolerate a tightfitting face mask may be contraindicated in an ill pet. A pressurized
oxygen helmet has been described for use in small animals and can
be a method to provide IPPV without intubation.6

INDICATIONS
Oxygen therapy should be initiated if a pet is exhibiting signs of
respiratory difficulty. Pulse oximetry is of little use in conscious pets
and its results should not be used for determining the need for
oxygen therapy, nor should those results be used to determine
whether the oxygen can be discontinued.7 While oxygen cages can
deliver a known amount of oxygen, nasal oxygen and flow-by are
variable. Whatever concentration is needed to keep the pet
comfortable is appropriate. If distress persists at a known inspired
oxygen concentration (FiO2) ≥60%, ventilation or HFOT could be
considered. Oxygen therapy may be stopped when the pet is
breathing comfortably; in many cases, this can require several days.
In animals receiving high oxygen concentrations, it is prudent to
taper supplementation over hours. Dogs receiving oxygen should
have limited walks and should be carried or moved with a gurney
when possible.

POINT OF CARE (PoC) ULTRASOUND
(US)
Use of US has revolutionized the ability to rapidly and effectively
evaluate pets without the stress of conventional radiography (ch.
73).

UPPER AIRWAY OBSTRUCTION
INTUBATION
Indications
Intubation can save lives and in pets with an upper airway
obstruction it should be pursued promptly. Common causes of
airway obstruction include partially round objects, laryngeal masses
(ch. 214), laryngeal paralysis (ch. 214), and brachycephalic airway
syndrome (ch. 213). If one thinks “perhaps I should intubate this
dog,” it is likely the correct decision and should be done. If a dog is
unconscious, apneic, or in cardiac arrest, the dog should be
intubated immediately.

Need for Sedation or Anesthesia
If intubation is urgently needed but the pet is conscious and
struggling, sedation or anesthesia will be required. Ideally, an IV
anesthetic is used to quiet the pet, but if attempted IV catheter
placement stresses the dog or cat further, IM alfaxalone or
ketamine/midazolam may facilitate intubation and/or placement of
an IV catheter. In some, IV propofol administered via a butterfly
catheter can be quickly followed by placing an IV catheter. Clinicians
and emergency and critical care nurses should master “standing”
catheter placement for dogs in distress that do not tolerate being
recumbent.

AIRWAY CAPTURE IN CHALLENGING
SITUATIONS
A situation requiring intubation often requires multiple team
members. Doctors and technicians must never hesitate to call for
help. Asking for unneeded assistance is far preferable to not asking
for needed assistance. When a challenging intubation is anticipated,
a variety of endotracheal tube sizes and stylets should be available as
well as instruments for a tracheostomy. A “modified Seldinger
technique” may need to be employed: insert a long polypropylene
catheter into the larynx and then advance the endotracheal tube over

that catheter. Confirmation of placement can be made by established
ETCO2 readings. Another option is placing a large bore catheter or
needle through the trachea, directed rostrally. Then a guide wire is
advanced through the catheter and out the larynx. Then an
endotracheal tube can be advanced over the guide wire and into the
airway (

Video 123.1) If such attempts require too much time, an

urgent/emergent tracheostomy should be performed (Figure 123.2;
Video 123.2

).

FIGURE 123.2 An emergent tracheostomy
following cardiorespiratory arrest due to severe bite
wounds to the neck. A jugular catheter (ch. 75) was
also placed through the incision extended from bite

wounds. Return of spontaneous circulation and
consciousness occurred after airway capture.

MONITORING
Once a pet with respiratory distress is stabilized, close monitoring is
required to identify any recurrence. Further testing, e.g., thoracic
radiography, echocardiography, and/or cytological evaluations
should be pursued as indicated.1 Respiratory rate and effort are
useful tools. Subtle increases in respiratory rate and effort may
precede severe decline. Limited value of awake pulse oximetry in
dogs has been demonstrated, but pulse oximetry is more accurate
when obtained from an anesthetized dog or cat.7 Arterial blood gas
analysis may be useful, but is technically challenging, painful, and
only provides a single point in time evaluation. PoC US is useful to
evaluate for recurrence of pleural space disease or evidence of
volume depletion: small left ventricle or caudal vena cava (ch. 73).

THERAPY AND CONTINUED CARE
OVERVIEW
Therapy should be directed at the perceived underlying cause,
although sometimes a diagnosis takes hours or days. It is important
not to rush a decision to euthanize if the underlying condition has
not been confirmed. In those pets, therapy should be directed at the
most likely etiology and any therapy that could worsen an unknown
disease avoided.

QUESTIONS TO BE ADDRESSED
Concerns that might be raised include 1) need for antibiotics and
whether samples should be obtained first (e.g., tracheal wash; ch.
93); 2) chances of volume overload/congestive heart failure and
need for diuretics (ch. 229); 3) pulmonary thromboembolism
possibility and need for anticoagulants (ch. 219); 4) evidence of

pulmonary hypertension that might be helped with sildenafil (ch.
218); 5) continued need for ventilatory support; 6) presence of a
condition requiring surgery; 7) need to identify missing historical
observations, e.g., travel (ch. 9) or trauma possibilities; 8) breed
predilections that might help better predict the underlying cause,
e.g., pulmonary fibrosis in West Highland White Terriers.8

ITEMS TO CONSIDER REGARDING PETS
IN RESPIRATORY CRISIS
Try Not to Panic or Forget the Basics
Some animals with respiratory distress may die, but a systematic
approach will help ensure as many as possible do well.

Try Not Placing Too Much Reliance on US
PoC US has revolutionized veterinary medicine (ch. 73). Without
training and practice, it is possible for US observations to be
confusing. Do not use US in place of therapeutics, other diagnostics,
or careful history (ch. 2) and physical examination (ch. 3) review.

Use of Bronchodilators
Bronchodilators in dogs are rarely useful. In contrast to cats, dogs do
not have naturally occurring bronchoconstriction, and
bronchodilators are unlikely to help (ch. 215). Thus, supplemental
oxygen, cough suppressants, anti-inflammatory glucocorticoids, and
antibiotics may have greater value.

Diuretics
Diuretic (e.g., furosemide) use should not be routinely given to all
pets in respiratory distress, even if cardiac function is normal. Try to
identify the source of the distress. PoC NT-proBNP can be useful if
you don’t have immediate access to imaging.

Asthma Diagnosis

Rushing to a diagnosis of asthma in an elderly cat with new onset
respiratory distress can be incorrect. Carefully consider upper airway
disease, such as a laryngeal mass (ch. 214). Don’t be afraid to sedate
for an oral examination but remember to be prepared for potential
challenging intubation.

INITIAL APPROACH TO THE BLEEDING PATIENT
Stabilization of a bleeding pet should be initiated prior to any in-depth diagnostic testing.
Cardiovascular instability is common. It is most likely caused by, and is proportional to, hemorrhagic
hypovolemia (ch. 121). Fluid resuscitation is key for helping these pets (ch. 120). Bleeding into the
respiratory or nervous system causes life-threatening abnormalities. The source and cause of bleeding
should be rapidly identified through targeted physical examination (chs. 3, 119) and point-of-care
ultrasound (ch. 73). Mucous membranes and skin (especially the axillae and inguinal areas) should be
assessed for petechiae or ecchymoses (ch. 29) and a gentle rectal examination is used to check for
hematochezia or melena (chs. 3, 50). Collection of samples in 3.2% sodium citrate and
ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) tubes prior to fluid or blood product administration avoids
obscured results. Pretreatment results may be diagnostic or may clearly establish a differential
diagnosis. Blood samples can be collected via intravenous (IV) catheters or clean peripheral
venipuncture. Jugular sampling should be avoided. Full assessment should be performed once initial
stabilization is underway. Client anamnesis should include questions pertinent to the assessment of a
bleeding pet: travel history (ch. 9), access to toxins (ch. 132), prior surgery, clinical signs in known
relatives (ch. 171), recent vaccinations or medications, preventative healthcare regimen and prior
transfusion history (ch. 2).

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
HEMOSTATIC DISORDERS; PRIMARY VS SECONDARY HEMOSTASIS
The pathways to hemostasis are often divided into the primary phase, secondary phase, and then
fibrinolysis (chs. 29, 170 and 171). Primary hemostasis involves platelet activation by extracellular
matrix components exposed by endothelial damage, culminating in platelet-plug formation. Secondary

hemostasis involves stepwise activation of plasma serine proteases to generate fibrin that stabilizes the
platelet plug. Fibrinolysis is clot dissolution that follows repair of the damaged endothelium.1 These 3
steps in vivo are indistinct, as hemostasis occurs on cell surfaces, and initiation, extension, stabilization
and dissolution of thrombi occur as a continuum.2 Dividing hemostasis into stages may enable the
dysfunctional component to be predicted from history and physical examination findings (Table 124.1),
which aids diagnosis and helps in guiding therapy.

DISORDERS OF PRIMARY HEMOSTASIS
The first rule-out for a primary hemostatic defect is thrombocytopenia (ch. 59), and this diagnosis is
easily achieved through in-house examination of a fresh blood smear made from an EDTA
anticoagulated blood sample (

Video 57.1). Counts <50 × 103/mcL are associated with spontaneous

bleeding but it is important to check for platelet clumps before diagnosing thrombocytopenia. Pets with
a primary hemostatic disorder and a normal platelet count may have acquired or congenital platelet
dysfunction (thrombocytopathia; Table 124.2). Inherited primary hemostasis disorders are rare, with
the exception of von Willebrand disease (vWD) (ch. 175).3 Confirming thrombocytopathia is
challenging (ch. 171)4 since template bleeding time is too variable. The laboratory platelet function
analyzer, platelet aggregometry, or flow cytometry are preferable for investigation of thrombocytopathia.

DISORDERS OF SECONDARY HEMOSTASIS
If clinical signs suggest a secondary hemostatic disorder, then inadequate coagulation factor production,
excessive consumption or both are likely (chs. 170 and 171). Assays of secondary hemostasis include
initial screening tests and unique assays for specific factor deficiencies. Prothrombin and activated
partial thromboplastin times (PT, aPTT) are assessed, often at the point of care. The PT evaluates the
extrinsic and common pathways: factors VII, X, V and II. The aPTT evaluates the intrinsic and common
pathways: factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, and II. Factor activity must be significantly decreased before
test results become prolonged. Mild prolongations of point-of-care tests (<120% normal) may be
clinically inconsequential.

TREATMENT
OVERVIEW
Blood component transfusion tailored to the bleeding disorder is the cornerstone of treating acute
coagulopathies. It minimizes risk of volume overload, polycythemia, and transfusion reactions. Specific
factor concentrates are available for people but not for dogs or cats.5 Desmopressin (DDAVP) has also
been used in management of primary hemostatic bleeding in dogs.6

FIBRINOLYTIC DISORDERS
Fibrinolysis restores vessel patency following hemostasis. It is mediated by plasmin, cleaved from
plasminogen by tissue-type (tPA) and urokinase-type (uPA) plasminogen activators.7 Primary
hyperfibrinolysis results from quantitative or qualitative abnormalities of fibrinolytic pathway proteins
and occurs in the absence of thrombosis. Secondary hyperfibrinolysis occurs when the normal
fibrinolytic system is excessively activated or the clot is abnormally susceptible to lysis. Congenital or
primary hyperfibrinolytic disorders are uncommon in humans8 and rare in small animals. There is a
single case report of a dog with factor XIII deficiency. It is likely that hyperfibrinolysis in Greyhounds is
heritable.9 Acquired hyperfibrinolysis is associated with many syndromes: liver failure, sepsis, snake
envenomation, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute traumatic coagulopathy and cancers.10-12
Assessment of the fibrinolytic system requires specialist assays.13 Viscoelastic tests such as
thromboelastometry and thromboelastography (ch. 170) provide global assessments of coagulation and

fibrinolysis,14 and enable monitoring of response to antifibrinolytic drugs.15 Administration of an
antifibrinolytic agent, epsilon-aminocaproic acid (EACA) or tranexamic acid (TXA), is the primary
therapy for hyperfibrinolytic disorders.16 These drugs are lysine analogues that competitively bind Cterminal sites on plasminogen, preventing plasminogen binding of fibrin, inhibiting plasmin formation.
The recommended EACA dosage in dogs is 100 mg/kg IV or PO q6h or 100 mg/kg IV followed by 15
mg/kg/hr constant rate infusion. Rapid administration may cause hypotension and gastrointestinal (GI)
signs. TXA, 10 times more potent than EACA, may have superior and more sustained antifibrinolytic
activity at a dosage of 10 mg/kg IV q4h. Vomiting is a major side-effect of TXA in dogs, especially at
higher dosages (20 mg/kg). There are few data on feline fibrinolysis and clinicians should be cautious
about use of antifibrinolytics in cats.

TRANSFUSION MEDICINE
Overview
Blood product transfusion, neither benign nor risk-free, is integral to resuscitation and support of
bleeding patients and can be lifesaving (Table 124.3). Transfusing only those pets most likely to benefit
maximizes utility and minimizes risk. Safe transfusions begin with meticulous blood product collection
(Videos 124.1, 124.2), careful processing (

Videos 124.1, 124.3), gentle handling and proper storage

(Video 124.4).

Blood Products and Donation
Most small animal transfusions involve component therapies (Figure 124.1), but fresh whole blood
(FWB) may be required or the only product available. Knowing safe collection protocols is vital (
Videos 124.1, 124.2).17,18 To maximize safety, donors should be screened and blood-typed. Consensus
recommendations for infectious disease screening of blood donors are available and should be carefully
followed.19

Dog Blood Typing
Blood typing involves identifying protein antigens expressed on surfaces of donor and recipient
erythrocytes (red blood cells [RBCs]) that are the targets for anti-erythrocyte antibodies responsible for
immunologic transfusion reactions. Accurate blood typing is critical for safe transfusions using cards, gel
column systems, or immunochromatographic cartridges.20 Canine blood types are classified using the
dog erythrocyte antigen (DEA) system: DEA 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and Dal, although only DEA 1, 4, 5, 7 and
Dal screening are available. Antigens 1, 4 and Dal are associated with development of hemolytic
transfusion reactions, but only screening for DEA 1 is performed routinely. The prevalence of DEA 1 is
∼40-70% and varies with breed and geographical location, while DEA 4 occurs in 98-100% of dogs. The

Dal antigen was recently identified in ∼90% of non-Dalmatian breeds. Dogs do not express
alloantibodies against most DEA antigens including Dal (exceptions are 3, 5 and 7), but administering
non type-specific blood causes alloantibodies that can lead to future life-threatening transfusion
reactions.21 “Universal donors” should be negative for DEA 1, 3, 5 and 7 but positive for DEA 4. This
phenotype is particularly common in Greyhounds.

Cat Blood Typing
Feline blood groups are described by the AB system and include A, B and AB. Type A is the most
common (70-100%) depending on geographical location. Pedigree cat breeds have distinct blood type
frequencies, with some having high frequencies of type B. In contrast to dogs, cats have naturally
occurring alloantibodies to non-self RBC antigens and should always receive type-compatible blood.
Type A cats have weak anti-B alloantibodies, resulting in limited lifespans for transfused type B
erythrocytes. Type B cats have strong anti-A alloantibodies that cause acute severe hemolytic reactions
against type A erythrocytes. Type AB cats are rare and do not possess anti-A or anti-B alloantibodies and
could theoretically receive blood of any type for their first transfusion, although type A is typically
recommended. Additional feline erythrocyte antigens (FEAs) have also been identified,22 and
crossmatching should be considered prior to all feline transfusions.23

Crossmatching
Crossmatching should be performed in any dog or cat given a blood transfusion >3 days previously, if
there is a history of a transfusion reaction, or when the recipient’s transfusion history is unknown.20 The
major crossmatch tests for recipient antibodies to donor erythrocyte antigens, and the minor crossmatch
tests for donor antibodies to recipient erythrocyte antigens.

Red Blood Cell Products
FWB, collected from a donor without any further processing, is ideal for treating acute hemorrhage.
FWB contains RBCs, plasma proteins and some platelets. Since FWB is rarely available, in an
emergency, stored whole blood is an option.24 FWB can be used to treat primary or secondary
hemostatic disorders provided pets are monitored for polycythemia and volume overload. It should also
be recognized that FWB is inefficient in treating isolated deficiencies. Generally, specific component
therapies are preferred. Packed red blood cells (PRBCs), obtained by centrifuging FWB and then stored
at 2-6°C, are indicated for anemia without hypovolemia, anemia with hypovolemia (where the volume
deficit is restored using other fluid types), anemia without deficits in other blood components and
anemia with risk of volume overload. The most accurate formulae for the prediction of the posttransfusion packed cell volume (PCV) in dogs are25:

Plasma Products
Plasma, separated from PRBCs within 6-8 hours of collection by centrifugation, can immediately be
transfused (fresh plasma) or frozen at −20°C. After a year, fresh frozen plasma (FFP) should be
relabeled as frozen plasma (FP). Frozen plasma may have lower concentrations of factors V, VIII and
von Willebrand factor (vWF) compared to FFP.26 The primary indication for FFP administration is
documented coagulopathy with evidence of bleeding. If FFP is thawed and not used, it can be refrozen to
maintain efficacy,27 or refrigerated for use within 7 days.28 Cryoprecipitate is enriched in factors VIII,
XI and XII, fibrinogen and vWF and is the product of choice for hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency),
hypofibrinogenemia and vWD. A unit of cryoprecipitate contains 40-60% of factor VIII and vWF present
in the original FFP. Cryosupernatant, produced when making cryoprecipitate, contains the vitamin-Kdependent coagulation factors albumin and antithrombin. Cryosupernatant can be used for rodenticide
intoxication (ch. 138), hemophilia B (factor IX deficiency; ch 171) and hypoalbuminemia (ch. 60).

FIGURE 124.1 Blood component products algorithm. CryoPpte,
Cryoprecipitate; CryoSuper, cryosupernatant; FFP, fresh frozen plasma; FP,
frozen plasma; Fresh P, fresh plasma; FWB, fresh whole blood; PC, platelet
concentrate; Ppte, precipitate; PRBCs, packed red blood cells; PRP, platelet-rich
plasma; WB, whole blood.

Platelet Products
Platelet transfusions are indicated for management of life-threatening bleeding (into central nervous
system, respiratory system or gastrointestinal tract) accompanied by moderate or severe
thrombocytopenia regardless of cause.29,30 Ideally, all platelet transfusions would be performed with
fresh platelet concentrates, but these have limited availability, a short shelf-life (5-7 days), and are
expensive. Alternative canine platelet products include lyophilized platelets and dimethyl sulfoxide
(DMSO)-stabilized cryopreserved platelet concentrates.30,31 These preserved platelet products likely
contain few viable platelets, but available data suggest hemostatic efficacy.31-33

Blood Product Administration
RBC products should be administered via a 270-micrometer filter to eliminate aggregates or clots (
Video 124.5). Filters are included with blood administration sets or can be purchased separately. Blood
products should be administered within 4 hours, slow initially and increased if no reaction is seen. In
hypovolemic hemorrhagic shock blood products can be administered rapidly, but this should be avoided
unless strictly necessary. Blood products should be given via a dedicated catheter to avoid CPDA-1
incompatibilities. Monitoring is vital for early transfusion reaction identification (E-Appendix 124.1).

Transfusion Reactions
Adverse responses to transfusions occur in ∼3-8% of events and can be acute or delayed, immunological
or non-immunological.18 Signs can be nonspecific, including fever, weakness, agitation, vocalization,
seizures, dyspnea, cardiovascular instability, salivation, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, pruritus, erythema,
hemoglobinuria, angioedema and urticaria (E-Appendix 124.2; ch. 129). All transfusions should be
stopped immediately if a transfusion reaction is suspected, the patient assessed and determinations

made regarding the nature, cause and consequence of the reaction. If the reaction is mild and subsides
with treatment, the transfusion can be restarted. Delayed immunological reactions occur days after
transfusion and generally do not require treatment.

OVERVIEW
Neurologic emergencies can be a primary complaint in an ill dog or
cat, but they also frequently develop in-hospital as sequelae or
complications of another disease. Functional assessment of
neurologic status is imperative, and essential first steps include
identifying and resolving the myriad potential confounding factors
that can affect neurologic assessment. Confounding factors include
cardiovascular instability, complications of trauma, systemic disease,
effects of any medication but certainly sedatives and analgesics.
Some systemic diseases frequently affect the central nervous
system (CNS; e.g., hepatic encephalopathy [ch. 267]) or CNS
structural lesions may develop as an underlying disease complication
(e.g., ischemia after thromboembolism [ch. 238], neuronal death
following persistent hypoglycemia [ch. 61]). CNS signs may or may
not be reversible after managing an underlying disease, can
markedly affect a clinician’s medical plan, or alter the pet’s quality of
life and ultimate outcome. Whether advanced imaging or other
neurodiagnostics might be of assistance and how the neurologic
disease affects the patient’s overall prognosis are critical in any
decision process. Evaluating patients in a stable and ideal
physiologic state permits assessment of any “true” neurologic deficit
(chs. 240, 241). This chapter focuses on neurologic crises
secondary to brain disease and will also review emergent
assessments for myelopathies.

BRAIN DISEASE
TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY (TBI)
Initial Evaluation and Prognosis
The pathophysiology of TBI is discussed in ch. 246. This chapter
reviews prognosis and management aspects of head trauma patients.
A key in managing TBI is avoiding exacerbation of secondary injuries
(edema, hemorrhage), best accomplished by attempting to maintain
all physiologic parameters within reference ranges. Because of
impaired autoregulatory mechanisms, small physiologic changes that
may not be important in an otherwise healthy brain could have

marked sequelae after TBI. Jugular occlusion, hypercapnia, and
lowered head position can each severely increase intracranial
pressures (ICP) up to 100% over baseline.1 Such severe increases in
ICP can be catastrophic in TBI patients where maintenance of
cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is essential (ch. 246).

Modified Glasgow Coma Scale (MGCS; ch. 44)
Scores obtained using the MGCS (Box 125.1) provide an excellent
overall survival prediction for head trauma patients.2-6 Since
prognosis for neurologic disease is initially based on results of the
neurologic examination, reliable evaluations first require systemic
post-trauma stabilization (Figure 125.1). Then, MGCS scores of 3-8
correlate with a poor prognosis, scores of 9-14 have a guarded
prognosis, and scores of 15-18 have a good prognosis.3 Survivors had
a mean score of 14 while non-survivors had a mean of 9.3,4 About
50% of patients with a score of 8 survive.3,4
The MGCS puts a numerical value to the common sense of
neurologic assessment: the more severely affected, the more guarded
the prognosis. A complete neurologic exam (ch. 241) is essential for
accurate neuroanatomical localization but is not always feasible or
safe for the TBI patient. The MGCS utilizes three portions of the
neurologic examination for rapid objective assessment of brain
disease: mentation/level of consciousness, motor activity/gait, and
brainstem reflexes (Box 125.1). Importantly, the MGCS is only valid
for the prognosis of veterinary TBI and should not be used with other
brain conditions.3 Repeated MGCS scores can be a useful tool for
monitoring neurologic improvement or decline (ch. 44). In a cohort
of dogs with altered levels of consciousness due to various etiologies
including non-traumatic brain disease, MGCS compared favorably
with continuous remote monitoring via bispectral index (BIS). There
was a strong correlation between BIS, MGCS, and survival to
discharge.5 In pets with a low MGCS (<8) and no history of trauma,
metabolic assessment and drug/toxin history (ch. 132) become
important to identify potentially reversible causes for stupor or coma
(Video 125.1, ch. 133

).7

Advanced Imaging
Results of computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) scans can be quite valuable (ch. 112). Clinicians must
determine whether the information generated is worth the expense
and risk of decompensation caused by needed sedation or
anesthesia. CT or MRI results from TBI patients have provided
variable correlations between abnormalities seen and patient
outcome. However, when imaging results are compared with MGCS
scores, the most positive outcomes were reported in patients with
higher MGCS scores, regardless of abnormalities noted on imaging
(i.e., prognosis should be based primarily on results of neurologic
exam).6,8-10

Seizures
Development of seizures immediately, short-term, or long-term is
reported in 10-36% of dogs and cats post-TBI.6,8,9,11-13 Seizures in
TBI pets should be managed immediately (Figure 125.2; ch. 45).
However, prophylactic anticonvulsant treatment is not
recommended because it could alter observations when monitoring
the pet.

SEIZURE MANAGEMENT
Acute management of seizures is often a neurologic crisis, as the
clinician attempts to identify possible underlying causes while
stopping the seizures. Etiology and pathophysiology of seizures and
status epilepticus (SE) are presented in ch. 45. Considerations for
acute seizure management are presented in Figure 125.2. Ruling
out obvious systemic or extra-cranial causes (hypoglycemia [
Video 61.3, ch. 61], electrolyte abnormalities, intoxication [ch. 133],
hepatic encephalopathy [ch. 267], etc.) are essential first steps,
followed by controlling the seizure with either an acute seizure
management drug or specific therapy for an identified underlying
cause (e.g., dextrose supplementation for hypoglycemia), or both.
Intravenous (IV), intranasal (IN), and rectal administration of

various anticonvulsant medications have been reported.14-18 IV or
IN benzodiazepines are used for initial seizure management. Studies
on drug therapies for SE or cluster seizures always include at least
bolus benzodiazepines as the initial standard of care.14-17 Injectable
formulations of levetiracetam as adjunctive treatment with
benzodiazepines are reported to improve initial management of
cluster seizures and SE.15,16 After resolving SE or cluster seizures,
consideration should be given to need for long-term anticonvulsant
therapy. If required, phenobarbital (2-5 mg/kg PO q12h) or
imepitoin (15 mg/kg PO q12h) are recommended, with potassium
bromide (40 mg/kg PO q24h) less commonly used. Levetiracetam
and zonisamide are not widely recommended for initial
maintenance.19

NON-CONVULSIVE STATUS
EPILEPTICUS
A particular challenge for functional assessment of patients with SE
or cluster seizures receiving anticonvulsant medications (often
many!) is the limited ability for the clinician to evaluate cerebral
function and to determine whether the seizure activity is continuing.
Patients not twitching or convulsing may continue to have cerebralcortical activity associated with seizures. Generalized tonic-clonic
seizures are easily recognized and treated, but partial seizures and
non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) may have few or no
external manifestations, particularly in sedated pets. Continuing
cerebral seizure activity increases risk of a poor outcome. Functional
assessment of cerebral-cortical activity with electroencephalography
(EEG) permits intervention if electrographic seizures (ES) are
documented. In 20% of a group of dogs and cats managed for
seizures, EEG during hospitalization documented ES activity ranging
from 10 seconds to 10 minutes or more. Pets with ES were 4 times
more likely to die during hospitalization.20

SPINAL CORD DISEASE
INTRODUCTION
Often a sequela of trauma, and sometimes occurring in patients with
systemic disease (e.g., thromboembolic disease, clotting disorders,
etc.), acute myelopathies are common emergencies (ch. 251). In the
polytrauma patient, assessment of the CNS is imperative for
prognosis and for prioritizing the next diagnostic or therapeutic
steps. If there is a known history of trauma in a myelopathy patient,
affixing the animal to a backboard is recommended to minimize any
additional trauma from a fracture or other instability. A limited
neurologic examination with a patient in lateral recumbency is
possible. Similar to TBI, neurologic examination and localization of
the lesion (chs. 241 and 251) after systemic stabilization is the most
reliable assessment for prognosis (Figure 125.1).

FIGURE 125.2 Treatment of cluster seizures and
status epilepticus. AED, Anti-epileptic drug; CRI,
continuous rate infusion; IN , intranasal; IV,
intravenous; KBr, potassium bromide; PR, per

rectum. Courtesy Chrisoula Toupadakis Skouritakis,
PhD.

ASSESSMENT OF NOCICEPTION/PAIN
PERCEPTION
In myelopathy patients, the recognition of a nociceptive stimulus can
be the difference between a good/excellent prognosis (recognition
present) or guarded/poor prognosis (recognition absent), regardless
of imaging findings. Depending on the spinal cord injury location,
acute myelopathy patients may have exaggerated segmental limb
reflexes. Thus, it is imperative for the clinician to differentiate
between reflexive limb movements and conscious recognition of a
noxious stimulus (ch. 241, Video 125.2

). Hemostats are often

used to pinch either the interdigital skin (superficial
nociception/pain sensation) or to clamp a digit or the tail to
stimulate the periosteum (deep nociception). The clinician should be
looking for any reaction or evidence of conscious recognition of the
noxious stimulus (vocalizing, attempts to bite, or trying to move
away from the stimulus;

Video 125.2). In stoic or distracted

patients, these responses can be difficult to assess. Repeating
assessment of pain sensation at a later time, reversing any
medications that might alter response to a noxious stimulus, and
testing an apparently normal limb to determine the patient’s
“baseline reactivity” are methods to better evaluate lack of reaction
to a painful stimulus. Absence of a response to deep nociception in
acute myelopathies in a pet with a vertebral fracture or luxation
carries a poor prognosis for return to function. Those with
intervertebral disc disease have a guarded prognosis.21,22

SPINAL SHOCK
The clinical phenomenon of spinal shock may confound
neuroanatomical localization in acute myelopathy patients. Patients

with spinal shock present clinically with reduced muscle tone and
decreased-to-absent reflexes in one or more limbs caudal to the site
of an acute spinal cord injury. This is the result of transient
physiologic dysfunction of the lower motor neurons (LMNs).23,24 On
neurologic examination, these patients might demonstrate LMN
signs despite having a lesion that does not actually involve the LMN
region of the spinal cord (chs. 241 and 251). Segmental reflexes in
spinal shock gradually improve with time (hours-weeks),23,24
emphasizing the importance of continued re-evaluation of the
acutely myelopathic patient (ch. 43).

WEAKNESS
Generalized weakness results from diseases involving the peripheral
nerves, neuromuscular junction, and/or muscles. The
neuromuscular system is extremely sensitive to metabolic
derangements, particularly electrolyte abnormalities. A thorough
systemic evaluation is essential in pets with acute generalized
weakness (ch. 23). Two potential emergent complications in a dog
or cat with generalized weakness are hypoventilation and aspiration
pneumonia. Pets with severe forms of either process may require
mechanical ventilatory support. In a patient with hypoventilation,
the clinician must utilize the neurologic examination (ch. 241) to
determine whether the ventilatory abnormalities result from
neuromuscular disease/weakness or a cervical spinal cord lesion (C15), since diagnostic approaches and potential treatments are
markedly different for these two localizations (chs. 23 and 251).

CHAPTER 126: Abdominal Crisis
Mark Haworth, and Lisa Smart

INTRODUCTION
Abdominal crisis is frequently encountered by veterinary practitioners and
requires rapid assessment, appropriate analgesia (ch. 6), and stabilization (ch.
119). Abdominal crisis is a time-dependent diagnostic challenge, demanding
rapid decision-making to expedite optimal delivery of therapeutic interventions.
While the basis for decision-making is grounded on evidence, time dependence
often precludes thorough gathering of data initially, making clinical judgment
the integral factor when implementing stabilization (chs. 15, 122). Early,
intensive, yet judicious interventions are keys for optimal outcomes in critically
ill patients.

DEFINITIONS
The terms “acute abdomen” and “abdominal crisis” refer to abdominal disease
causing signs of severe abdominal pain of <24 hours duration. The pain may

originate from within or outside the abdomen (ch. 6). Visceral pain may arise
from inflammation, ischemia, or from acute enlargement of an organ causing
tension of the surrounding capsule.1 Organ enlargement may be the result of
distension of a hollow viscus or enlargement of a solid organ. Thoracic and
spinal pain can mimic abdominal pain and care should be taken to differentiate
these with a thorough physical examination (PE, ch. 3). However, not all lifethreatening intra-abdominal disorders cause obvious signs of pain, especially if
level of consciousness is impaired. Accordingly, any pathological acute illness
causing clinical signs that are abdominal in origin may serve as an alternative
definition of acute abdomen.2 The defining features that may raise this problem
to the level of a crisis include severe pain, compromised tissue perfusion and
metabolic disturbances.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
SEVERE ABDOMINAL PAIN
Stretch, torsion, ischemia or inflammation of any abdominal organ may cause
pain via activation of C-type nerve fibers in visceral organs (ch. 6); this tends to
cause a dull, aching or burning pain that is difficult to localize according to
human sufferers.3 Sharp pain may occur due to activation of A-delta nerve
fibers.3 Pain may also be caused by stretch or inflammation of the peritoneum,
e.g., acute peritoneal fluid accumulation or peritonitis (ch. 265). Severe
abdominal pain may cause nausea, vomiting, and other autonomic effects.4
Active contractions of visceral smooth muscle can cause pain in people.5 Visceral
pain in people can also cause referred muscle pain mimicking back or spinal
pain.4 The urgency of severe abdominal pain is two-fold; amelioration of severe
pain is required for animal welfare and severe abdominal pain often indicates a
life-threatening condition that may compromise local or systemic perfusion. The
effects of pain have been associated with gastrointestinal (GI) ileus and immune
suppression.6,7 Treatment of pain and determining its cause is often urgently
required (chs. 6, 119).

COMPROMISED TISSUE PERFUSION
A crisis as a result of abdominal disease may arise from the development of
circulatory shock or reduced perfusion of individual organs (ch. 121). Although
the underlying abdominal disease may have developed over days to weeks, the
pathophysiological sequelae of the condition may benefit from immediate
action. Circulatory shock in this setting can result from any of 3 mechanisms:
hypovolemia due to loss of fluid or blood, obstruction of blood flow due to

distension of a viscous structure or torsion of major blood vessels, or
vasodilation due to a systemic inflammatory response (chs. 119, 121, and 128).

METABOLIC DISTURBANCES
A major concern in patients with acute abdominal disease is the parallel
development of metabolic disturbances, including electrolyte, acid-base or
glucose abnormalities.2 Diseases that cause severe pain or shock often involve
GI losses (vomiting, diarrhea) which can lead to electrolyte imbalances, e.g.,
hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis due to pyloric outflow obstruction and
vomiting or hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis due to bicarbonate loss in
diarrhea or hypokalemia (ch. 68) due to both vomiting and diarrhea. Some
diseases can alter free water balance, affect serum sodium and chloride
concentrations (ch. 67), interfere with glucose metabolism (ch. 61), or reduce
urine output in a way that raises serum potassium concentrations. Therefore,
metabolic disturbances are common in dogs and cats with acute abdominal pain.

DIAGNOSIS
OVERVIEW
Abdominal crisis in dogs and cats can evolve rapidly. The diagnostic pathway is
usually performed cage-side or within the stabilization area of the emergency
room. Diagnostic tests often include point-of-care (PoC) clinical pathologic tests,
PoC abdominal and thoracic ultrasonography (PoCUS), radiography, computed
tomography (CT), abdominocentesis or diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) with
subsequent fluid analysis, and exploratory celiotomy. With infection, sample
collection for culture and susceptibility should be obtained before antimicrobial
administration, where possible.

SIGNALMENT, HISTORY, AND PHYSICAL
EXAMINATION
Validated principles of triage and assessment should be followed (ch. 119). The
initial history is often truncated when veterinary time is divided between owner
communication and patient stabilization. A more thorough history should
always be completed once the patient is stable (ch. 2). History for the acute
abdomen is often nebulous, including the vague signs of restlessness, lethargy,
vomiting, diarrhea, and anorexia. History including the days or months prior to
the acute event may provide important clues. Previous ingestion of foreign
objects or scavenging, access to toxins that may be hepatotoxic (ch. 134) or
nephrotoxic (ch. 135), current medications, most recent estrus, and waxing or

waning signs are examples of historical findings that can direct and expedite the
diagnostic process.
Clues that a dog or cat needs immediate attention can be gained by following
basic triage principles and include: changes in breathing patterns, signs of
circulatory shock, obtunded mentation, and signs of obvious abdominal pain,
e.g., hunched posture, stilted gait, reluctance to move (chs. 6 and 119). Early
identification of circulatory shock is vital to avoid exacerbating morbidity and
mortality (ch. 121).8 Abnormal perfusion parameters should be addressed
immediately with intravenous (IV) fluid resuscitation, with doses based on
severity of signs (ch. 120). It is prudent to provide analgesia together with IV
fluids for severe abdominal pain. Analgesia can have benefits beyond providing
pain relief: determining if tachycardia is due to pain, facilitating more thorough
abdominal palpation, and allowing PoCUS. As for any emergent case, a
secondary survey with a complete PE should be performed once life-threatening
problems have resolved (ch. 3).

CLINICOPATHOLOGIC TESTING
A complete blood count, including blood smear (ch. 57), biochemical analysis,
and urinalysis (ch. 70), is ideally performed at admission. These tests are not
only for diagnosis, but they can be used to establish baseline values and trends.
Although these samples are best collected prior to any treatment, initial
stabilization (fluid therapy) should not be delayed if sample collection is difficult
(ch. 119). Samples should not be obtained during rapid fluid infusion and
results should be interpreted in context of recent treatments. PoC tests ideally
performed before fluid resuscitation include packed cell volume, total protein
estimation, blood gas, and electrolyte analysis. Repeating tests after
cardiovascular stabilization can be informative in order to track progression,
e.g., detecting significant hemorrhage via a large decrease in packed cell volume
or assessing resolution of the metabolic perturbations of shock. Abdominal fluid
analysis can provide important information (chs. 71 and 86). The SNAP cPL
(canine pancreatic lipase) test can be used to help identify pancreatitis (ch.
277), but pancreatic inflammation can be secondary to other intra-abdominal
disorders, causing false positive test results and potentially diverting diagnostics
away from the primary disorder. A negative test result likely rules out
pancreatitis but follow up diagnostics such as formal abdominal ultrasound are
recommended.9

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
Prioritizing Imaging Modality Use
Results of abdominal imaging can be key to determining the cause of severe
abdominal pain. Multiple modalities are often required to fully evaluate the

patient, including PoCUS and radiography initially. If needed, CT may be
employed once the patient is stable. The order for prioritizing these modalities is
determined according to their advantages and disadvantages, coupled with
patient needs. Many patients presenting with abdominal crisis have clinical
signs that heighten risk for complications caused by obtaining diagnostic
images, e.g., the pet with vomiting or regurgitation and a decreased level of
consciousness is at risk for aspirating gastric contents if radiographic positioning
requires dorsal recumbency. Dorsal recumbency may also exacerbate the
consequences of reduced tissue perfusion.10 Sedation and general anesthesia
can further increase these risks. Thus, PoCUS is often used initially because it
can be performed while the patient is being stabilized, usually without the need
for further sedation.

Ultrasound (US) (ch. 73)
Abdominal focused assessment with sonography for trauma, triage, and tracking
(AFAST) is a standardized PoCUS method, providing a rapid, safe, and costeffective screening method (

Video 126.1). It also can be used to track the

patient’s condition. Although AFAST cannot replace a complete abdominal US
or orthogonal abdominal radiographs, it may be performed as part of the
primary survey to identify relatively small volumes of free fluid, compared to
radiography, or may identify obvious soft tissue abnormalities not detected on
PE.11,12 Serial AFAST during the initial hours of fluid resuscitation can be useful
for detecting development of free fluid following rehydration. A complete US
examination performed by a radiologist is recommended to follow an AFAST
once the patient is stable. US identification of the source of abdominal pain is
likely superior to radiographic examination and has proven sensitive for
identifying soft-tissue masses in dogs with non-traumatic hemoabdomen and
small intestinal mechanical obstructions.13-15

Radiography
Since radiography is widely available, it remains a first line imaging modality in
acute abdominal disorders. Although two-view radiographs may suffice in most
GI diseases, three-view abdominal radiographs may be necessary if the initial
series yields inconclusive results.13 The sequence of projections recommended is
first the left lateral, followed by ventrodorsal, and then right lateral views
allowing evaluation of the pylorus and duodenum, as gas accumulation provides
negative contrast.16 When considering a two-view study, the lateral projection of
preference depends on the clinician’s index of suspicion of the underlying cause.
A left lateral view may be more beneficial for investigation of proximal intestinal
foreign bodies and lesions, especially those of a linear nature.2,17 The right
lateral view is recommended for differentiating between gastric dilatation (GD)

and gastric dilatation and volvulus (GDV; ch. 261), though ambiguity should
prompt additional views. As with AFAST, repeat radiographs are often
performed to track clinical progression. However, the utility of serial
radiographs for GI mechanical obstruction may be poor and subsequent imaging
with US may direct earlier appropriate treatment.18,19
Identification of free peritoneal gas should prompt the clinician to consider GI
perforation and need for urgent exploratory celiotomy, in the absence of
penetrating trauma or iatrogenic causes.20 The left lateral radiographic
projection is sensitive for detecting as little as 2.5 mL of free peritoneal gas.21
However, US consistently has detected smaller air volumes by identifying the
“enhanced peritoneal stripe sign” (EPSS),22 though inexperienced operators
should exercise caution as air-filled bowel may be difficult to differentiate from
intraperitoneal free gas.

ABDOMINOCENTESIS AND FLUID ANALYSIS
Free peritoneal fluid is frequently diagnosed in pets with acute abdominal crisis
(ch. 21). Fluid analysis provides an opportunity for narrowing the differential
diagnosis list (ch. 71). Accessible fluid should be sampled (ch. 86), preferably
with ultrasound guidance (

Video 126.2). A severe coagulopathy could be a

relative contraindication. Even in pets with a coagulopathy, worrisome bleeding
is unlikely to follow careful paracentesis, especially if replacement of coagulation
factors via plasma therapy is imminent. In the absence of US guidance, fourquadrant abdominocentesis can be performed blindly.23 Caution should be
applied if pyometra, organomegaly, or bleeding disorder is suspected to avoid
iatrogenic injury or peritoneal contamination. Two methods for obtaining fluid
are used: closed collection using a needle with syringe attached and open
collection using only a needle and passive flow.23 Although open collection may
reduce risk of needle occlusion due to negative pressure, it may also introduce
air into the abdomen and is not recommended. Diagnostic peritoneal lavage23
may be useful in circumstances where the index of suspicion of septic peritonitis
is high and there is scant free fluid. However, this method is rarely required
when US is used after the patient is adequately hydrated.

This list of diagnostic tests is not exhaustive but aims to include common pointof-care tests performed while stabilizing a patient with abdominal crisis. For
example, advanced imaging may not be included in this list as these tests are
often able to identify the diagnosis, creating a clear therapeutic pathway.
AFAST, Abdominal focused assessment with sonography for trauma, triage, and
tracking; cPLI, canine pancreatic lipase; fPLI, feline pancreatic lipase.

Using plasma rather than whole blood to measure blood glucose to compare
with peritoneal fluid is more sensitive and specific.
Samples should be collected aseptically into ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid
(EDTA) and plain tubes for cytologic and biochemical analysis, and culture (ch.
71). The minimum PoC data obtained from fluid should include packed cell
volume, total protein and cytologic evaluation. Other useful tests include lactate,
glucose, bilirubin, potassium and creatinine, depending on underlying suspicion
for cause of abdominal fluid (Table 126.1). It is prudent to also submit
abdominal fluid for evaluation by a clinical pathologist. These tests, including
fluid cell count, can assist in characterizing the fluid to narrow the differential
diagnosis list (Table 126.1).
The need for urgent surgery in dogs and cats with free abdominal fluid
includes hemoabdomen with ongoing bleeding not related to coagulopathy, bile
peritonitis, uroabdomen, and septic peritonitis. Discriminating among these is
usually straightforward (Table 126.1), but the diagnosis of septic peritonitis can
sometimes be elusive. A delay in diagnosis and in implementing source control
of the infection can be life-threatening, but no single analyte of abdominal fluid
has proven to have both high sensitivity and specificity for identifying septic
peritonitis. When compared to blood concentrations, low abdominal glucose and
high abdominal lactate (Table 126.1) are suggestive of septic peritonitis in
dogs; however, other conditions may similarly affect these parameters.24-28
Ultimately, only intracellular bacteria visualised on microscopic evaluation or
gas accumulation within an organ such as the liver can confidently determine a
need for exploratory celiotomy. The presence of free abdominal gas in the
absence of iatrogenic causes is also a strong indicator for septic peritonitis and
surgery. Submission for microbial identification and antimicrobial susceptibility
testing is also prudent, especially if the patient is at high risk of multidrug
resistant infections (ch. 7).
∗

URGENT INTERVENTIONS/STABILIZATION
Cardiovascular stabilization is paramount to minimize exposure of the patient to
shock and further systemic inflammation (chs. 120, 121, and 128). IV boluses of
isotonic crystalloid fluids are usually the first choice, especially since these
patients are often dehydrated. In acute hemorrhage, blood products may also be
required (ch. 124). Caution should be applied when using synthetic colloid
fluids in pre-surgical candidates, as synthetic colloids may interfere with
hemostasis.29 Endpoints for resuscitation should be closely monitored,
including normalizing perfusion parameters, blood pressure, urine output, and
packed cell volume.
Cardiovascular instability should not preclude early administration of
analgesia. Optimal analgesia plans are often multimodal and may include an Nmethyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist and local anesthetics (ch. 6).

These have the added benefit of reducing general anesthetic drug requirements.
A loading dose of opioid drug followed by a constant-rate infusion is preferred
over intermittent dosing to avoid adverse effects from peak plasma
concentrations and subtherapeutic troughs. Epidural administration of opioid or
local anesthetic drugs should also be considered if the patient is concurrently
undergoing general anaesthesia, especially for conditions associated with severe
abdominal pain.30 Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs should be avoided due
to potential detrimental effects on renal and GI systems in the critically ill.
Another therapeutic consideration early in the assessment of abdominal crisis is
the need for IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, if sepsis is suspected.31,32

CONCLUSION
Often the most pressing clinical question regarding a dog or cat with abdominal
crisis is whether or not to recommend exploratory celiotomy. Avoiding
unnecessary surgery reduces cost and morbidity due to the “second hit effect.”33
This concept essentially states that patients with existing systemic inflammation
(the first hit) that undergo surgical intervention (the second hit) may incur
exacerbation of the inflammation which can result in multiple organ
dysfunction, a potent cause of morbidity and mortality (ch. 128).33 However,
early optimal emergent surgery, where appropriate, will maximize outcomes. It
is important to note that cases initially presenting with a solely medical
diagnosis may evolve to requiring surgery.
Critical illness is implicit with abdominal crisis. Once the stabilization process
has commenced, subsequent identification of the underlying cause is of
paramount importance to focus and optimize treatment. Unfortunately, a
definitive diagnosis may not always be possible, and the clinician will need to
draw on a constellation of markers for guidance. Results of diagnostic tests
should be reconciled with the history, physical exam, and response to treatment.
Despite identification of an underlying etiology and appropriate treatment,
deterioration and complications may arise. Therefore, these cases often benefit
from 24-hour intensive care for both medical and surgical conditions.
