Chapter 127: Lower Urinary
Tract Crisis
Dana Lynn Clarke

A C RO N YM S
AKI acute kidney injury
CT computed tomography
GFR glomerular filtration rates
SUB subcutaneous ureteral bypass
UBDs ureteral bypass devices

OVERVIEW
Disruption of urine flow at the level of the ureter(s), bladder, or
urethra, secondary to either obstruction or leakage, causes
electrolyte and metabolic derangements that can quickly deteriorate
into a life-threatening crisis. Prompt recognition, urine diversion,
patient stabilization, and timely definitive intervention are the keys
to a successful outcome. Common management strategies include
urethral catheterization (chs. 98, 99), percutaneous abdominal
draining (ch. 117), and exploratory laparotomy to repair a leakage
source or obstruction removal/bypass. Image-guided procedures for
minimally invasive urethral and ureteral stenting, subcutaneous (SQ)
ureteral bypass (SUB), and percutaneous antegrade catheterization
are increasingly available for stabilizing a pet rapidly (ch. 117).

URETERAL OBSTRUCTION
CAUSES AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Ureteral obstructions can be secondary to ureterolithiasis, ureteral
strictures, obstructive pyonephrosis, blood clots/dried solidified
blood calculi, iatrogenic ureteral ligation, retroperitoneal fibrosis,
ureteropelvic junction stenosis, and/or neoplasia (ch. 306).1-11
Ureteroliths are the most common cause in small animals. About
98% of feline and 38% of canine ureteroliths contain calcium (chs.
308, 309).12,13 Acute kidney injury (AKI) can follow ureteral
obstruction, the result of inflammation and nephron loss secondary
to reduced renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rates (GFR; ch.
300). Prolonged intra-renal hypertension and unresolved nephron
injury and loss will ultimately cause fibrosis and loss of function (ch.
301).14,15

DIAGNOSIS
Confirmation of ureteral obstruction requires diagnostic imaging,
usually with ultrasound (US), although dried solidified blood stones
may not be visualized.2,5,6,16,17 While marked renal pelvic dilation is
classically associated with ureteral obstruction, pelvic dilation is not
always seen (Figure 127.1).16,18 Radiographs can be helpful in
diagnosing ureterolithiasis. Most stones are in the proximal or midureter (ch. 306).2,4,19 Antegrade pyelography and computed
tomography (CT) may aid in diagnosing and localizing a ureteral
obstruction, but require general anesthesia or heavy sedation for safe
and credible diagnostic studies.2,20-23 Antegrade pyelography has
documented up to 94% of ureteral stones, though complications
include contrast leakage, hemorrhage, and laceration of the renal
pelvis.22,23 In cats, CT has revealed some ureteral calculi that were
not visible on US or radiography, but there is a risk of contrastinduced nephropathy when GFR and renal function are
decreased.2,24

MEDICAL MANAGEMENT
Medical management for ureteral obstruction is similar to that for
other forms of AKI: IV fluids to restore volume deficits and maintain
hydration while avoiding overhydration, correction of electrolyte
abnormalities, supportive care for uremia, and other therapies (chs.
120, 300). Intermittent hemodialysis and continuous renal
replacement therapy (CRRT) may be considered for treating severe
azotemia, refractory hyperkalemia, oligo-or anuria, or to improve
patient stability prior to definitive intervention (ch. 103). However,
none these therapies resolves the obstruction. Renal replacement
therapies may improve the AKI and the patient’s clinical status, but
these techniques require anticoagulation, which can increase the risk
of hemorrhage during surgical or interventional procedures.
Placement of large-bore dialysis catheters is both challenging and
time-consuming, especially in small pets. Definitive interventional
procedures to relieve an obstruction can be performed quickly and
are preferred over extracorporeal therapies.
Additional medical therapies to facilitate passage of obstructive
ureteroliths include amitriptyline, glucagon, amlodipine, and alphablockade. When medical management alone was used in cats, 13%
had significant decreases in creatinine and 60% of those cats passed
the stone. However, creatinine did not improve in 31%, and 13% were
euthanized or died within a month of diagnosis.3

INTERVENTIONAL THERAPIES (ch. 117)
Nephrostomy Tubes
Nephrostomy tubes can provide temporary relief of an obstruction
when definitive intervention for ureteral obstruction is not
immediately available by decompressing the renal pelvis.1,3,25
Locking loop catheters are recommended over red rubber catheters
since their locking mechanism helps secure the catheter in the renal
pelvis. US- or fluoroscopic-guided percutaneous placement is
possible in dogs and cats with significant pelvic dilation. However,
due to the mobility of feline kidneys, surgical placement with

nephropexy is recommended to decrease risk of inadvertent
dislodgement.25

Surgery
Surgical techniques employed for management of ureteral
obstructions include single or multiple ureterotomies, ureteral
resection and anastomosis, ureteral reimplantation, and a modified
Boari flap.1,3,26-28 The most common complication after ureteral
surgery (up to 16%) is urine leakage.1,3,27,29,30

Ureteral Stents
Ureteral stents have been used for both temporary and permanent
urinary diversions (ch. 117). Stents have been used in pets with
obstructive ureteroliths and nephroliths and to aid ureteral healing
after surgery or trauma. Stents can facilitate stone passage after
extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy in dogs. Stents may allow
passage of dried solidified blood stones. Stents allow urine to bypass
ureteral strictures and can prevent ureteral obstruction secondary to
spasm after sclerotherapy for renal hematuria, obstructive
pyonephrosis, and neoplasia.7,8,31,32 In general, ureteral stents are
placed cystoscopically in dogs, surgically in cats with benign ureteral
obstructions, and percutaneously in dogs with obstructive urinary
tract neoplasia. Regardless of the method used for placement,
intraoperative fluoroscopy is recommended to ensure appropriate
positioning.

FIGURE 127.1 Ultrasound image (A) from a
severely azotemic cat showing minimal dilation of

the renal pelvis; however, complete ureteral
obstruction was documented on intra-operative
pyelography (B).

Ureteral Bypass Devices (UBDs)
UBDs were first developed for people with urinary tract neoplasia as
an internalized urinary drainage system to avoid permanent
nephrostomy tubes.33 A similar device (SUB) has been developed for
cats and dogs with ureteral obstructions as an alternative to ureteral
stenting.11,34–36 Placement of the device requires laparotomy, but
does not require ureteral dissection or access, which can be
advantageous when there is no ureteral dilation, especially in cats
(ch. 117). There are no evidence-based guidelines for use of stents vs
SUBs. The SUB device may be preferable for ureteral strictures, as
passive dilation around a ureteral stent is not likely. Also, stents can
become encrusted and cause obstruction.

URETHRAL OBSTRUCTION NOT
AMENABLE TO CATHETERIZATION
CAUSES, SEDATION, ANESTHESIA
Causes
Urethral obstructions can quickly become life-threatening
emergencies, especially if retrograde urethral catheterization (chs.
98, 99) is not possible. The most common causes of urethral
obstruction in dogs and cats are calculi, strictures, feline lower
urinary tract disease (FLUTD), and neoplasia (chs. 308, 309, 312,
330). When catheterization is not possible or if there is concern that
catheterization will cause a urethral tear, alternative means of
urinary drainage are necessary.

Sedation and Epidurals
It is important to ensure the dog or cat is adequately sedated to
facilitate catheterization. Sedation also allows the urethra to relax,

reducing risk of urethral trauma and/or perforation. If sedation is
insufficient to facilitate catheterization, local anesthesia and/or
general anesthesia should be considered. Local anesthesia to the
pudendal and pelvic nerves using a caudal epidural block provides
regional analgesia to the perineum, penis, and urethra. Cats given a
caudal epidural with bupivacaine combined with morphine required
less propofol to facilitate urethral catheterization and the
combination provided a longer time (10 hrs) until rescue analgesia
was needed than bupivacaine (8 hrs) alone (sham injected: 2 hrs).37

TREATMENT OPTIONS
Intermittent Cystocentesis
Intermittent cystocentesis (ch. 98; Videos 98.5 and 98.6) can be
used for short-term bladder decompression. This procedure,
however, is associated with risk of tearing the bladder wall if it is
diseased, with subsequent urine leakage, and of urosepsis if the urine
is infected. There is also risk for peritoneal, body wall, and SQ
seeding of neoplastic cells, particularly transitional cell carcinoma
(TCC; ch. 330).38,39 In one study, 3/15 male cats with urethral
obstruction treated with sedation, analgesia, and decompressive
cystocentesis developed uroabdomen, 1/15 had hemoabdomen, and
11/15 cats were successfully managed without catheterization. This
technique could offer an alternative to euthanasia when financial
constraints prohibit catheterization.38

Hydrophilic Wires
Hydrophilic wires are coated with a water-attracting polymer which
becomes gel-like, reducing friction and facilitating passage (ch. 113).
Such wires are radiopaque for visualization with fluoroscopy or
radiography and are essential for image-guided interventions. They
can be used when urethral access is challenging, e.g., strictures,
stones, or neoplasia (chs. 117, 312, 320). Guidewire tips are angled
or straight to facilitate catheter positioning, device placement, and
therapeutic procedures. The angle-tipped wires are quite helpful for
navigating non-linear anatomies, since the tip can be rotated and

essentially “steered” (Figure 127.2). Hydrophilic wires should never
be advanced backend first. The backend is sharp, stiff, and can
perforate catheters and tissues. A retrograde urethrocystogram can
quickly define urethral location and abnormalities. Fluoroscopy or
repeated digital radiography can be used to help guide the wire,
usually 0.035″ (0.9 mm) in diameter, through the urethra and into
the bladder. Other commonly used wire sizes are 0.018″ (0.5 mm),
0.025″ (0.6 mm), and 0.038″ (1 mm) in diameter. The most
commonly used length is 150 cm. A standard 5 Fr red rubber catheter
with the distal end cut can then be passed over the wire and
positioned in the bladder to relieve the urethral obstruction. The end
of a Foley balloon urinary catheter can be cut to allow wire passage
while still maintaining balloon integrity. However, the lumen of a
balloon catheter is substantially smaller than a non-balloon catheter,
so wire compatibility must be confirmed prior to placement within
the urethra.

FIGURE 127.2 Straight and curved ended
hydrophilic wires.

Cystostomy Tubes
Cystostomy tubes can be helpful when urethral catheterization is not
possible to relieve the obstruction (ch. 117). However, commonly
used cystostomy tubes require laparoscopic or open surgical
placement, which can be challenging in a critically ill and unstable
pet.40,41 Locking loop (pig-tail) catheters can be quickly placed
percutaneously with fluoroscopic guidance to establish drainage.

Since they are placed without cystopexy, there is risk of urine leakage
if the catheter is dislodged. Bladder access is obtained via
cystocentesis with an over-the-needle catheter, contrast is infused in
the bladder to delineate the bladder margins, and a hydrophilic
guidewire is advanced through the catheter into the bladder. The
catheter is removed over the wire, and the locking loop catheter is
passed over the wire into the bladder. The stylet for the locking loop
catheter and the wire are removed and the catheter “locked” into
place using the suture locking mechanism and secured to the skin
with pursestring and finger trap sutures.
In small pets where the bladder is palpable percutaneously,
locking loop catheters can be placed directly transabdominally into
the bladder apex using the sharp stylet after a small skin and body
wall incision has been made with a scalpel blade. In one study, 3/3
cats treated with locking loop cystostomy catheters had partial
dislodgment and urine leakage.42 Locking loop catheters can also be
used for abdominal drainage when placed in the peritoneal cavity.

Interventional Techniques and Antegrade Urethral
Catheterization
Interventional techniques can be used for pets with known urethral
tears or when urethral catheterization is difficult, e.g., small females
and pets with urethral masses or strictures for which retrograde
catheterization is not possible (ch. 117).43 Percutaneous antegrade
urethral catheterization provides rapid bladder decompression in
pets that might otherwise require cystostomy tubes. Using the same
bladder access technique described for locking loop cystostomy
tubes, a hydrophilic guidewire is directed antegrade out the urethra
(Figure 127.3). Once the wire is visualized exiting the urethra, an
open-ended catheter (or cut-tip red rubber catheter) is advanced
over the wire into the urethra and bladder. Once the catheter is
appropriately positioned within the bladder, the wire is withdrawn
and the catheter is secured routinely.43 Depending on the indications
for percutaneous antegrade urethral catheterization, the catheter can
be left in place to facilitate urinary tract healing or until definitive
surgical or interventional management can be performed.

FIGURE 127.3 Hydrophilic wire being directed
antegrade out the urethra during percutaneous
antegrade urethral access to facilitate urethral
catheterization in a cat with a urethral tear.

Cystoscopy (ch. 100)
Cystoscopy can be used to help achieve urethral access, especially in
small females and pets with urethral obstruction secondary to
neoplasia or urethral tears. General anesthesia is required for patient
comfort and positioning, but with practice, cystoscopy can be
performed quickly to guide urethral access.

Urethral Stenting (ch. 117)
Urethral stenting can provide rapid, noninvasive, and permanent
relief of urethral obstructions secondary to urethral or prostatic

neoplasia, urethral stricture, proliferative urethritis, or urethral
compression secondary to organomegaly, such as metastatic lymph
node enlargement.44-46 Urethral stents are placed under general
anesthesia using fluoroscopy or digital radiography with measuring
capabilities. About 25-30% of pets have severe incontinence after
stenting, regardless of sex or length of urethra stented.44-46

URETERAL LEAKAGE
Ureteral leakage may be identified with CT, ureteropyelography, or
via direct visualization during exploratory laparotomy. Either
interventional or surgical options can be considered to repair the
leakage source. Surgical repair options include ureteral resection and
anastomosis, neoureterocystostomy (ureteral reimplantation) for
mid- to distal ureteral lesions, and a modified Boari flap for more
proximal ureteral leakage.8,26-28 Ureteral stents, placed
cystoscopically or surgically, and SUBs are interventional treatment
options (ch. 117). Complications of these procedures are similar to
those encountered when these techniques are used for ureteral
obstructions.

BLADDER OR URETHRAL LEAKAGE
When urine leakage is from the bladder or urethra, diversion and
decompression should be the first steps for patient stabilization. The
management strategies are the same as those used for urethral
obstruction: catheterization, cystostomy tubes, and percutaneous
antegrade catheterization. With urethral tears, retrograde
catheterization with the use of a hydrophilic wire and fluoroscopy
can be useful for navigating past the site of urine leakage. Small
urethral and bladder tears may heal after diversion through urethral
catheterization and continuous bladder decompression. Larger tears
or devitalized tissue in either location may require surgical
debridement and primary repair, which can be challenging within
the pelvic and distal urethra. Urethral strictures can result from

urethral tears that have healed improperly or after urethral surgery;
therefore, long-term monitoring for their occurrence is warranted.

DEFINITIONS
Sepsis is derived from the Greek word meaning “to make rotten” or
“to putrefy.” It is an infection-induced innate antimicrobial response
disorder defined as bacteremia or as a concurrent infection with
evidence that the infection is causing the systemic inflammatory
response syndrome (i.e., SIRS). Immune system dysregulation is the
key pathologic process, not just a pro-inflammatory response and/or
widespread infection (ch. 227). Infection-induced innate
antimicrobial response disorders encompass a wide range of
syndromes including SIRS, the compensatory anti-inflammatory
response syndrome (CARS), mixed antagonist response syndrome
(i.e., concurrent SIRS and CARS) (MARS), the persistent
inflammation and immune suppression catabolism syndrome
(PICS), and the multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS)
(Table 128.1, Box 128.1).

PATHOGENESIS
TRIGGERS OF SEPSIS AND THE INNATE
IMMUNE SYSTEM (IIS)
Triggers
Sepsis is a complex, variable, prolonged host response triggered by
infection (ch. 183). Manifestations of sepsis vary by pathogen (type,
load, virulence, site of inoculation) and host (genetics, site of
infection, comorbidities). In dogs and cats, Gram-negative bacterial
infections are the most common cause of sepsis, with E. coli being
the most common isolate (Figure 128.1).1-10 However, any
pathogen (e.g., fungus, parasite, virus, protozoan) could cause sepsis.
In dogs, sepsis most commonly originates from abdominal and
respiratory tract infections.1,2 In cats, abdominal and pleural space
infections are most common.6-11

Innate Immune System (IIS)

The IIS is predominately responsible for the initial manifestations of
sepsis, activated by danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs),
e.g., pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs; endotoxin
from Gram-negative bacteria; exotoxins, peptidoglycans and
superantigens from Gram-positive bacteria; and fungal cell wall
material from pathogens) and alarmins (e.g., high-mobility group
protein B1 [HMGB-1], S100 proteins, RNA, DNA and histones)
produced by the host. Pattern-recognition receptors of the IIS
recognize DAMPs via toll-like receptors (TLRs), C-type lectin
receptors, retinoic acid inducible gene 1-like receptors, and
nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like receptors to activate
innate immune cells and induce systemic inflammation. For
example, in Gram-negative sepsis, the glycolipid component of
Gram-negative bacteria cell walls (lipopolysaccharide [LPS]) is
released. The lipid A portion of LPS binds to LPS binding protein,
recognized via macrophage cell surface receptors like CD14. The
main function of CD14 is to transfer LPS to TLR-4 and myeloid
differentiation factor-2 (MD-2) for subsequent cellular activation.
Once LPS binds to cell surface receptors, the macrophage or other
cells become activated.
Activation of innate immune cells results in “genomic” and
“cytokine” storms. As numerous genes that encode various
inflammatory mediators, signal transducers, and cellular adhesion
molecules are activated, inflammatory mediators are produced.
Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha, interleukin (IL)-6, chemokine
(C-X-C motif) ligand-8 (CXCL-8), keratinocyte-derived chemokine
(KC)-like chemokine, chemokine (C-C motif) ligand 2 (CCL2),
HMGB-1, nitric oxide and leukotrienes are examples of important
mediators contributing to the pathologic process of sepsis in dogs
and cats.12-19 Production of these inflammatory mediators results in
activation of vascular endothelial cells and upregulation of adhesion
molecules. These inflammatory mediator signals cause neutrophils,
monocytes and/or lymphocytes to travel to the site of infection,
secrete a second wave of inflammatory mediators, and provide
killing mechanisms for microorganism clearabnce. Neutrophils
release extracellular traps, filamentous DNA containing histones and
granular proteins, to enhance bacterial killing and promote
thrombosis. The transition from a localized infection/ inflammation

to sepsis is dependent on the systemic circulation of inflammatory
messages and activation of distant immune cells (Figure 128.1).

THE ADAPTIVE IMMUNE SYSTEM
The adaptive immune system is involved in the pathogenesis of
sepsis. Antigen presenting cells that have ingested a pathogen
activate the adaptive immune response, causing naïve T cells to
proliferate and effector cells to be generated. Naïve T cells
differentiate into Th1/Th17 cells or Th2 cells and pro-inflammatory
cytokines (e.g., TNF, IL-2, IL-12, interferon-gamma, and
leukotrienes or IL-17A) and/or anti-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL4, IL-5, IL-9, IL-10 and IL-13). The balance between the Th1/Th17
and Th2 responses contributes to the clinical manifestations of provs anti-inflammatory shifts.

THE COMPENSATORY ANTIINFLAMMATORY RESPONSE
SYNDROME (CARS)
CARS is characterized by cyclic
immunosuppression/immunoparalysis, a relative failed immune
response to infection.20-22 Immunoparalysis is characterized by
apoptosis of lymphocytes, dendritic cells, endothelial cells,
gastrointestinal (GI) epithelial cells, and thymocytes; production of
IL-10; suppressed CD8+ T cell function; reduced monocytic
production of pro-inflammatory cytokines; expression of inhibitory
receptors on T cells; increases in regulatory T cells; downregulation
of human leukocyte antigen-DR expression; increases in myeloidderived suppressor cells; and immune cell quiescence.21,23,24 The
neuroinflammatory reflex contributes to CARS through multiple
mechanisms, including activation of the cholinergic antiinflammatory pathway, which results in reduced pro-inflammatory
cytokine production. Clinically, immunoparalysis leads to an
inability to fight and eliminate infection and the development of new

infections from opportunistic or otherwise weak organisms.23
Reactivation of latent viruses is another possible development.

Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS): A pulmonary
inflammatory disorder characterized by non-cardiogenic
pulmonary edema, neutrophilic inflammation and hypoxemia.
Bacteremia: The presence of viable bacteria in the blood
stream.
Compensatory anti-inflammatory response syndrome
(CARS): Global deactivation of the immune system resulting
in immunosuppression and immunoparalysis.
Infection-induced innate antimicrobial response disorders:
Umbrella term encompassing the different forms of immune
system dysregulation which develop in response to infection.
Mixed antagonist response syndrome (MARS): SIRS and
CARS existing concurrently during infection; dysequilibrium
of pro- and anti-inflammatory response during infection.

Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS): Altered
function of 2 or more organs secondary to SIRS such that
homeostasis cannot be maintained without intervention.
Persistent inflammation and immune suppression catabolism
syndrome (PICS): Maladaptive, self-perpetuating cycle of
persistent inflammation, reduced effective immunity and
organ injury resulting in loss of muscle mass and function,
altered bone marrow function, failure of metabolic adaption
and chronic critical illness.
Sepsis: 1. Systemic inflammatory response to infection or 2.
Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated
host response to infection.
Septic shock: 1. The systemic inflammatory response to
infection with hypotension despite adequate fluid
resuscitation along with the manifestations of hypoperfusion;
or 2. Subset of sepsis in which underlying circulatory and
cellular/metabolic abnormalities are profound enough to
substantially increase mortality. Generally, this is sepsis with
either persisting hypotension requiring vasopressors to
maintain mean arterial pressure (MAP) 65 mm Hg or a serum
lactate concentration >2 mmol/L despite adequate volume
resuscitation in people.
Severe sepsis: This term has fallen out of favor and is generally
not used.
Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS): A clinical
syndrome caused by systemic inflammation of infectious (i.e.,
sepsis) or non-infectious origin. The diagnosis of SIRS is
based on fulfillment of at least 2 of 4 criteria in dogs:
tachycardia, tachypnea, hypo- or hyperthermia, and
leukocytosis, leucopenia or >5% bands; or 3 of 4 criteria in
cats: bradycardia or tachycardia, tachypnea, hypo- or
hyperthermia, and leukocytosis, leukopenia or >5% bands
(Table 128.1).

PROGRESSION OF SEPSIS

Classically, sepsis was considered the result of systematic
progression through a hyper-inflammatory phase followed by
resolution during hypo-inflammation.21 It is now appreciated that
sepsis is a waxing/waning continuum, where the animal may
vacillate between pro- and anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive
response states. Resolution is an orchestrated independent
process.21,22 Therefore, the response during sepsis could be
activation of resolution pathways and recovery or continued illness
due to a pro-inflammatory response, an antiinflammatory/immunosuppression response and/or
fluctuating/interweaving responses. This concept of vacillating or
concurrent responses is termed MARS. Ultimately, multiple organ
failure and/or opportunistic infections could result in chronic critical
illness or death.23 Lack of resolution and development of chronic
critical illness is termed persistent inflammation and immune
suppression catabolism syndrome (PICS).

CLINICAL OBSERVATIONS
DOGS
Dogs have either hyperdynamic or hypodynamic responses during
sepsis. The hyperdynamic response is characterized by fever, brick
red mucous membranes, tachycardia, and bounding pulses. As the
disease process progresses, a hypodynamic response may be
observed: hypotension, pale mucous membranes and hypothermia.
GI or respiratory signs may be associated with endotoxemia. Hyperor hypoglycemia, hypoalbuminemia, azotemia, hyperbilirubinemia,
increased serum alanine aminotransferase and/or alkaline
phosphatase concentrations, leukocytosis, neutrophilia with a left
shift, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and anemia have been variably
identified in dogs with sepsis. Evidence of coagulopathy (decreased
protein C and antithrombin concentrations, prolonged prothrombin
time and partial thromboplastin time, increased D-dimer
concentrations) have been documented in dogs with naturally
acquired sepsis (ch. 170).1,25 Many dogs with sepsis have
myocardial dysfunction and vasodilation, leading to hypotension.

Poor perfusion, tissue hypoxia and cellular metabolic derangement
can lead to metabolic acidosis.

CATS
Cats with sepsis may develop most of the clinical signs and
clinicopathologic abnormalities observed in dogs with sepsis, but
bradycardia, hypothermia and abdominal pain are frequent, unique,
and poorly understood observations in cats with sepsis.4,9,11 Cats
also appear to develop septic shock more readily than dogs do, and
typically the hyperdynamic phase is not recognized.

MULTIPLE ORGAN DYSFUNCTION
SYNDROME (MODS)
The pathogenesis of MODS is multifactorial, including development
of mitochondrial dysfunction secondary to circulatory collapse,
microcirculatory changes, hypoxemia, and inflammation.26 MODS is
defined in dogs as ≥2 forms of organ dysfunction (Table 128.2) in
an animal with appropriate risk factors. However, criteria for
defining individual forms of organ dysfunction vary and are
conflicting.26,27 The incidence of sepsis-induced MODS is not known
in dogs or cats although cardiovascular, GI, hepatic, renal, endocrine
and respiratory dysfunction/failure have been recognized.28-33

DIAGNOSIS
A complete history (ch. 2), physical examination (ch. 3), blood
pressure (ch. 91), complete blood count, serum biochemical profile,
urinalysis, blood gas analysis, coagulation profile (ch. 170) and
appropriate diagnostic imaging should be performed in any critically
ill patient. In dogs and cats, the diagnosis of sepsis is based on the
presence of infection and systemic inflammation (i.e., SIRS),
although this definition is likely inadequate. Care should be taken to
avoid excluding sepsis as a diagnosis based on a lack of SIRS criteria.
Clinicians should consider sepsis in any animal with infection and
hypotension and/or organ or immune system dysfunction. Infection
may be identified via culture, cytology (ch. 85), histopathology, or
serology. If bacterial infection is suspected, culture and sensitivity
should be performed to identify the best antibiotic. Based on the
clinical findings, specimens should be collected from blood, urine,
wound exudate, peritoneal fluid, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or
synovial fluid (ch. 71) prior to antibiotic administration. Peritoneal
fluid glucose concentration >20 mg/dL (>1.1 mmol/L) below the
blood glucose concentration is diagnostic for septic effusion (ch.

71).3 In some, confirming infection is difficult and/or delayed. Here,
a presumptive diagnosis of infection should be based on all other
information and after considering non-infectious differentials for
SIRS (e.g., acute pancreatitis, autoimmune disease, and
envenomation).

TREATMENT
OVERVIEW
The severity of sepsis varies; some pets need advanced life support
measures to survive while others require less care. The keys to
successful sepsis treatment include: initial hemodynamic
stabilization, alleviating the inciting cause and intensive supportive
care. Sepsis treatment includes the initial resuscitation period (i.e.,
first 1-6 hours) and long-term management (i.e., >6 hours to hospital
discharge).

INITIAL RESUSCITATION:
RESTORATION OF HEMODYNAMIC
STABILITY
Initial resuscitation includes restoration of hemodynamic
homeostasis and alleviating the cause through use of antimicrobial
drugs and/or debridement. There are no standardized resuscitation
protocols for animals; suggested criteria have been extrapolated
from the Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for
Management of Severe Sepsis and Septic Shock in people (Figure
128.2).34 In animals, judicious fluid therapy and vasopressors if
indicated should be administered to improve physiologic parameters
(ch. 120). Clinicians should focus on improving physiologic
parameters including blood pressure, heart rate, tissue perfusion,
oxygenation, blood lactate concentrations and urine production.
Specific resuscitation goals should be tailored to the individual needs
of the patient. Improving physiologic parameters can be
accomplished using intravenous (IV) isotonic crystalloid boluses

(dogs 15-20 mL/kg, cats 10-15 mL/kg) or colloid boluses (dogs 5-10
mL/kg, cats 2-5 mL/kg, IV to effect). Point of care (PoC) cardiac
ultrasound (US) can guide fluid therapy (ch. 73). Use of “shock”
fluid boluses (dogs 90 mL/kg; cats 50 mL/kg) is not recommended
because overhydration is associated with worse outcomes in people
and fluid overload should be avoided (ch. 120). Ongoing fluid
therapy should be tailored to the needs of the patient (ch. 121) and
administration of vasopressors considered as needed in patients that
are unresponsive to fluid resuscitation alone.

FIGURE 128.2 Algorithm reviewing treatment
strategies for sepsis in dogs. CRI, Constant rate
infusion; GI, gastrointestinal; IV, intravenous; MAP,
mean arterial pressure; NMDA, N-methyl-Daspartate; NSAIDs, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory

drugs; PaO2, partial pressure of oxygen; PPN, partial
parenteral nutrition; SpO2, oxygen saturation; TPN,
total parenteral nutrition.
Animals with sepsis have a propensity for interstitial edema (e.g.,
subcutaneous and pulmonary edema) due to increased vascular
permeability and decreased blood colloid osmotic pressure.
Administration of colloid fluids (e.g., hydroxyethyl starch) might
help prevent interstitial edema. However, people with sepsis given
hydroxyethyl starch have an increased risk of acute kidney injury
(AKI). No evidence regarding AKI is available for dogs and cats with
sepsis (ch. 300). However, in a canine model of hemorrhagic shock
and in a randomized clinical trial of dogs admitted to the emergency
and critical care department of a teaching hospital, hydroxyethyl
starch did not increase urine biomarkers of AKI.35,36 An alternative
is 5% lyophilized canine-specific albumin, which raised plasma
albumin concentrations in dogs with abdominal-source sepsis.37,38
Use of 0.9% saline has fallen out of favor in people with sepsis due to
its excess chloride (ch. 120). Administering chloride-rich solutions
induces shock in animal models, promotes metabolic acidemia,
induces a pro-inflammatory shift, reduces renal perfusion, increases
the risk of AKI, and increases mortality in people with sepsis.39
Giving 0.9% saline to dogs reduced renal blood flow and glomerular
filtration rate.40 Use of balanced electrolyte solutions is preferred,
e.g., Plasma-Lyte.
Despite volume resuscitation, some pets require additional
support to maintain normal blood pressure and perfusion. There is
no “best” treatment for dogs or cats with septic shock.
Sympathomimetic drugs should be avoided if possible in
hypovolemic patients. Since the goal of treating septic shock is to
maintain tissue perfusion, medications that cause vasoconstriction
should be used only if necessary. Using point of care cardiac
ultrasound (ch. 73) to identify appropriate patients, positive
inotropic drugs (e.g., dobutamine) may help combat the decreased
cardiac output caused by myocardial dysfunction without inducing
peripheral vasoconstriction. Positive inotropic drugs should not be
given to cats with evidence of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (ch.
234). If volume resuscitation and positive inotropic support have

failed to restore blood pressure, a vasopressor agent (e.g., dopamine,
norepinephrine, epinephrine or vasopressin) could be added (ch.
121). Vasopressors should always be administered as a constant rate
infusion and ideally monitored via direct blood pressure. Criticalillness related corticosteroid insufficiency has been identified in dogs
with sepsis and refractory hypotension.31 Judicious use of
corticosteroids may address therapeutic failure of vasopressor
therapy.

INITIAL RESUSCITATION: ALLEVIATE
THE CAUSE AND USE OF ANTIBIOTICS
A key aspect of treating sepsis centers on the identification and
eradication of the inciting cause. Since pathogens drive immune
stimulation, physiologic responses, and shock, their eradication
should downregulate those responses (ch. 227).41 Clinicians should
implement strategies to improve the rapidity of pathogen clearance
(Table 128.3).41 While attempting to identify the cause of sepsis,
early antimicrobial treatment is critical for survival and should not
be withheld pending culture results. Many clinical features of sepsis
(fever, leukocytosis, abdominal pain, tachypnea, shock) could be the
result of sterile disease. The likelihood of infection should be
carefully considered prior to antibiotic administration. Ideally, broad
spectrum IV bactericidal agents (e.g., fluoroquinolone + penicillin)
should be given within the first 30-60 minutes. The specific
antibiotic selected is based on the most likely organism causing the
infection. The antibiotic chosen can be adjusted after culture and
determination of antibiotic sensitivities. Consideration should be
given to confounding factors that could alter antimicrobial efficacy
(e.g., barrier penetration, inactivation by purulent material, reduced
effectiveness due to acidic environments or hemoglobin, poor
antimicrobial penetration in hypoxic environments, etc.) or
resistance (e.g., hospital vs community acquired infection; recent
antibiotic exposure; ch. 7). Depending upon the source of infection,
surgical debridement can be extremely beneficial.

LONG-TERM MANAGEMENT:
SUPPORTIVE CARE
Tissue Perfusion and Avoiding Organ Failure
Continued therapy should focus on maintaining tissue perfusion and
managing organ failure (Figure 128.2). It is common for
hemodynamic derangements to recur after initial resuscitation, with
relative or absolute hypovolemia and/or poor tissue perfusion. Gut
bacterial translocation contributes to systemic inflammation during
sepsis. Early placement of a feeding tube for enteral nutrition helps
maintain GI barrier function (ch. 81). If the patient is vomiting,
parenteral nutrition should be implemented (ch. 164). Medications
that support GI protective mechanisms can be used (e.g.,
omeprazole, famotidine, sucralfate). Sepsis-induced
nausea/vomiting can be treated with ondansetron or maropitant
(ch. 48). GI motility disorders can be treated with erythromycin,
metoclopramide, or cisapride (chs. 261, 262). Hyperglycemia is a
complication of nutritional therapy, especially parenteral nutrition,
and should be avoided.
Oxygenation, acid-base status, packed cell volume or hemoglobin
concentration, and organ function should be closely monitored.
Along with maintaining good tissue perfusion, maximizing oxygen
delivery and cellular oxygenation help maintain tissue viability. This
may be accomplished by ensuring good oxygen carrying capacity,
providing supplemental oxygen when indicated, and preventing
microthrombi formation. Earlier transfusion triggers should be
considered in patients with sepsis due to the detrimental effects of
hypoxic tissue injury. Typically, acid-base issues are related to lactic
acidosis secondary to poor tissue perfusion and will resolve with
improved tissue perfusion. Bicarbonate is not recommended. When
organ dysfunction occurs, specific therapy aimed at maintaining
homeostasis should be considered. In some cases, peritoneal (ch.
102) or hemodialysis (ch. 103), plasma or blood transfusion (ch.
124), positive inotropic agents and mechanical ventilation may be
necessary.

Comforting the Patient

Management of pain, catheter maintenance, bladder/bowel care and
frequent turning/movement to prevent decubital ulcers are
extremely important. Most patients with sepsis require pain
management (ch. 6). Ketamine and buprenorphine may offer
specific anti-inflammatory advantages during endotoxemia.42,43
Morphine, conversely, augments the inflammatory response to
endotoxins and increases mortality in endotoxemic rats.43,44 It is
unknown if morphine is detrimental when treating sepsis in dogs or
cats.

Anti-Inflammatory Treatment
Sepsis is a systemic inflammatory disease so it is logical that
strategies aimed at halting inflammation have been evaluated. The
only anti-inflammatory therapy with some positive benefit in canine
clinical trials has been polymyxin-E (colistin), which binds to
endotoxins from Gram-negative bacteria, preventing the interaction
between endotoxin and the immune system. In a placebo-controlled
clinical trial, dogs treated with polymyxin-E (colistin) (12,500 IU/kg
IM q12h) had significant improvements in hydration, capillary refill
time, and pulse quality and significantly lower plasma TNF
concentrations compared to controls.14 Although experience in dogs
is limited, polymyxin-E (colistin) may be a potential treatment for
Gram-negative sepsis.

PROGNOSIS
Mortality rates for dogs and cats with sepsis range from 2879%.9,25,31,45-50 Hypotension, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, acidemia,
coagulopathy, multiple organ dysfunction, increased procalcitonin,
hypovitaminosis D, increased ALT, and persistent ionized
hypocalcemia (cats) are associated with a poorer outcome in dogs
and cats.

Chapter 129: Anaphylaxis
Mark Haworth

A C RO N YM S

IV intravenous
PT prothrombin time

DEFINITIONS
Anaphylaxis is the term given to extremely severe allergic reactions.
Though frequently encountered, particularly in some geographic
regions, the prevalence in small animals remains unknown. In
people, an estimated lifetime prevalence between 0.3-5.1% has been
reported depending on the varying definition of anaphylaxis.1 The
World Allergy Organization (WAO) recently proposed a definition for
anaphylaxis: “a serious systemic hypersensitivity reaction that is
usually rapid in onset and may cause death. Severe anaphylaxis is
characterized by potentially life-threatening compromise in
breathing and/or the circulation and may occur without typical
skin features or circulatory shock being present.”2

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

The classic and most frequently encountered type of anaphylaxis is
IgE-mediated.2 Production of IgE antibodies follow initial exposure
to an allergen and bind to high affinity receptors (FcεRI) on mast cell
and basophil surfaces.1,3 Re-exposure to that allergen causes crosslinking of surface-bound IgE releasing preformed mediators, e.g.,
histamine, platelet activating factor (PAF), and leukotrienes as well
as de novo synthesis of other inflammatory mediators.3,4 Non-IgE
mediated anaphylaxis was previously termed anaphylactoid. This
terminology is now discouraged as the clinical presentation is
indistinguishable and treatment identical.1,3

TRIGGERS, TIMING, SEVERITY
Regional differences in trigger profiles have been recognized in
people. This may also be the case for veterinary patients.1 Many
triggers of anaphylaxis have been reported in humans. Most
veterinary reports since 1950 have identified hymenoptera stings,
antimicrobials, vaccinations, food, agents used in anesthesia,
iodinated radiographic contrast agents, and ophthalmic medications
(in cats) as triggers.5-11 Anaphylaxis may also be categorized as
idiopathic.1
Onset of anaphylaxis is usually within minutes of allergen
exposure; uncommonly it may be delayed for hours.1,2,6,11
Progression of clinical signs is uniphasic, biphasic, or protracted.12
Biphasic reactions have been demonstrated in people where initial
recovery is followed by deterioration without further antigen
exposure.13 This usually occurs within 4 to 8 hours but may be up to
72 hrs following initial clinical improvement.13 Risk factors for
biphasic reactions in people include an initial severe reaction,
hypotension, and delay in epinephrine administration.14 Protracted
anaphylaxis has been described either as slowly developing
irreversible hypotension which may last days or anaphylaxis lasting
greater than 5 hours.12,15

The severity of anaphylactic reactions may be mild, moderate, or
severe (Figure 129.1) and it depends on several factors, including
trigger and dose.1 Other factors reported in people include age,
medications, stress, exercise, atopic disease, and comorbidities:
respiratory illness, cardiovascular disease, and acute infections.1
Rapid onset of clinical signs is associated with increased severity.
Mild initial symptoms may swiftly become life-threatening.6,10,11

CLINICAL SIGNS AND LABORATORY
FINDINGS
CUTANEOUS RESPONSES TO ANAPHYLAXIS
Cutaneous signs usually consist of urticaria, angioedema, erythema,
and pruritus (ch. 12). They have been observed in as many as 57% of
dogs and 21% of cats with anaphylaxis.6,8,10,16 While common, these
signs may be subtle, delayed, or short-lived and be difficult to detect
due to fur and pigmentation.8,10 Importantly, a fulminant
manifestation of anaphylaxis could precede development of
cutaneous signs and may be absent at presentation.16

GASTROINTESTINAL (GI) AND HEPATIC
RESPONSES TO ANAPHYLAXIS
GI and hepatic insults are common in animals experiencing
anaphylaxis, with vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, salivation,
and nausea reported in up to 94% and 74% of dogs and cats,
respectively.6,8 Inflammatory mediators, hepatic ischemia, and
hypoxemia likely contribute to increased alanine aminotransferase
(ALT) activities in dogs, though increases may be delayed for 24
hours.8,16 ALT increases are usually mild, but results as high as
10,000 U/L have been observed. Quantity of increase is not
prognostic.7,8,16 Reported sensitivity for increased ALT is 85-100%
and specificity 98%, with increases usually persisting for >24 hours

(chs. 65, 134, 269).7,8,16 In dogs, peracute hepatic arterial
vasodilation together with sinusoidal outlet vasoconstriction can
cause hepatic vascular congestion.17 Subsequent portal hypertension
can impair gallbladder circulation, leading to gallbladder wall edema,
which has a sensitivity of 85 to 93% and specificity of 98% in dogs
with anaphylaxis (ch. 73).8,16,17 The reported mean wall thickness in
one study was 4.7 mm vs a normal of 2-3 mm.8,16,18 Wall thickening
can also be seen with liver disease, right-sided heart failure,
pericardial effusion, hypoalbuminemia, ascites, sepsis, pancreatitis,
and any cause of elevated portal venous pressures.7,8,18

CARDIOVASCULAR RESPONSES,
PERITONEAL EFFUSIONS, AND
RESPIRATORY ISSUES
Cardiovascular signs associated with anaphylaxis include collapse,
obtundation, tachycardia, bradycardia, dysrhythmia, hypotension,
poor peripheral pulses, and mucous membrane pallor with
prolonged capillary refill time.16,19 Rapid fluid extravasation,
vasodilation, hepatic congestion, and cardiac effects contribute to
hypotension, which may be exhibited with vasoconstrictive or
vasodilatory signs. A mixed distributive-hypovolemic shock pattern
may also be observed as concurrent vasoconstrictive and
vasodilatory signs (ch. 121).5,10,19 Shock may be further complicated
by decreased oxygen carrying capacity and loss of vascular volume
arising from spontaneous hemoperitoneum.7,16 A mechanism
postulated is that hemostatic alterations precipitate coagulopathies
in combination with increased vascular permeability.16 Peritoneal
effusion was demonstrated in 65.5% dogs in one study, the majority
of which were hemorrhagic in nature.16 Hypotension was noted at
presentation in 66% of dogs with severe anaphylaxis. Of 10 nonsurvivor dogs, 2 had been normotensive and 1 hypertensive.16 A
sudden and profound state of hypotension may occur due to a

relative bradycardia in combination with vasodilation.19 Here, the
postulated mechanism implicates a neurocardiogenic reflex triggered
by cardiac mechanoreceptors following increased force of
contractions from initial compensatory sympathetic outflow.20
Mediators prevalent during anaphylaxis sensitize these
mechanoreceptors, which in turn signal potentiated central reflexes
to trigger parasympathetic nerve outflow, severely limiting
sympathetic activity.19,20

FIGURE 129.1 Diagnosis and severity scoring for
anaphylaxis in dogs and cats.

Respiratory system involvement is usually indicative of moderate
to severe anaphylaxis with signs of bronchoconstriction, upper
airway edema, and/or bronchorrhea: tachypnea, bradypnea,
dyspnea, wheezing, coughing, cyanosis, stridor, stertor, and/or
respiratory arrest (ch. 123).5,10,16 Life-threatening anaphylaxisinduced respiratory effects have been noted in about 67% of affected
dogs and cats.6,16 It is difficult to interpret respiratory signs in the
retrospective studies, as tachypnea or open-mouth breathing can be
caused by stress, pain, or hypotension.

DIAGNOSIS
The diagnosis of anaphylaxis (Figure 129.1) is dependent on
consistent history and clinicopathologic findings. The history may
reveal previous anaphylactic events or recent exposure to an insect
sting, vaccination, or new medication. There may have been prior
exposure to blood products. While increases in serum histamine and
tryptase concentrations are useful diagnostic markers in people,
their concentrations rise and abate rapidly, sensitivity and specificity
are modest, and serial measurements are recommended.19,21 These
tests are not readily available to veterinarians, and their clinical
utility has yet to be established in small animals.

TREATMENT
INITIAL TREATMENT AND USE OF
EPINEPHRINE
The life-threatening nature of anaphylaxis demands rapid
intervention, constant monitoring, and immediate vascular access
(ch. 119). Treatment should focus on airway patency, breathing, and
circulation. Removing any exposure to the inciting cause, if possible,
is critical (Figure 129.2). Multiple sources emphasize using
epinephrine in treating anaphylaxis.1,22 The adrenergic effects
include decreased mediator release from mast cells and basophils,
vasoconstriction, positive inotropy and chronotropy,

bronchodilation, and decreased mucosal edema, which assists with
upper airway obstructions.22 Following the onset of hypotension in a
group of dogs with experimentally induced anaphylactic shock,
constant rate intravenous (IV) infusion of epinephrine was superior
to bolus dosing subcutaneously, intramuscularly, or intravenously.23
Significant amounts of epinephrine may be required in hypotensive
patients. If bolus dosing is implemented, a subsequent infusion
should be titrated to effect (Figure 129.2).20 As infusion rates vary,
toxic effects can develop as the anaphylaxis resolves, demanding
careful monitoring of pets receiving an infusion.20 Epinephrine
autoinjectors for out-of-hospital use are available but doses are too
large for dogs under 15 kg. In many parts of the world autoinjectors
may be expensive. An alternative may be pre-filled light-protected
syringes, which have been shown to maintain stability and sterility
for up to 90 days.24 Bespoke doses, likely safer than an owner
drawing from a vial in a time of crisis, may be prescribed. Use of outof-hospital epinephrine is at clinician’s discretion and may be
considered. Atropine may also be indicated for hypotension coupled
with bradycardia.

FIGURE 129.2 Anaphylaxis action plan. BP, Blood
pressure; ECG, electrocardiogram; EPI, epinephrine;
ETCO2, end tidal carbon dioxide; IM, intramuscular;
IV, intravenous; SpO2, peripheral oxygen
saturation. Modified from Brown SG. Anaphylaxis:

clinical concepts and research priorities. Emerg

INTRAVENOUS FLUIDS
Large-volume IV fluid bolus using a balanced isotonic crystalloid
may be required to combat hypotension (ch. 120). Careful
reassessment of the patient following each fluid challenge should
focus on heart rate, mucous membrane color, capillary refill time,
pulse quality, mentation, peripheral temperature, and blood
pressure. Fresh frozen plasma or red blood cells may be required if
hemorrhage or coagulopathy exist.7,16 IV glucose should be
administered immediately for hypoglycemia (
Video 61.3) and
monitored (chs. 61 and 289; Figure 129.2).

ANTIHISTAMINES AND
GLUCOCORTICOIDS (CH. 143)
Antihistamines are not a frontline treatment for life-threatening
anaphylaxis and should not delay better immediate treatments.
Cardiovascular responses observed in dogs with experimentally
induced anaphylaxis were not prevented by pretreatment with
antihistamines.25 A Cochrane systematic review of H1
antihistamines was unable to identify any quality evidence for their
use.26 Potential harmful effects may be observed with some
antihistamines: promethazine possesses vasodilatory effects, and
rapid chlorpheniramine infusion may cause hypotension and should
be avoided in severe reactions.1,27 Antihistamines may be useful to
alleviate pruritus and wheals in mild reactions.
While glucocorticoids are commonly utilized, evidence for their
use is lacking.1 Their delayed onset of action, regardless of route of
administration, limits usefulness during the hyperacute phase. Their
use has traditionally centered on minimizing biphasic reactions,

limiting protracted issues, and reducing bronchoconstriction.27,28
However, a review of 31 studies on people found no benefit in
reducing severity of anaphylaxis or biphasic reactions. It was
recommended that routine use be avoided.29

PROGNOSIS
Predictors for death include hypoglycemia, hypocoagulability, and
hyperphosphatemia. Dogs identified as hypoglycemic within 6 hours
of admission were 5.7 times more likely to die.16 Activation of the
coagulation and fibrinolytic pathways produces prolongation in
prothrombin (PT) and partial thromboplastin times (PTT), and
concurrent increases >50% of the reference interval has been
associated with death in dogs.16 One report demonstrated increases
in PT, PTT, or both in 95% of dogs categorized as having severe
anaphylaxis.16 Hyperphosphatemia has been linked with death. Dogs
were 79.6 times more likely to die if serum phosphate values were
>12.0 mg/dL (>3.9 mmol/L).16 Potential mechanisms proposed
include intracellular phosphate release from hepatocellular or
muscle damage. Creatine kinase (CK) activity was increased in 81%
of dogs, implicating some degree of muscle damage.16 Limited data
exists for mortality in small animals, which has been reported as
being as high as 14.9% and 13% in dogs and cats, respectively.6,16

HYPERTHERMIA
DEFINITIONS
Hyperthermia is defined as a non-stressed dog’s or cat’s body
temperature >39.2°C (>102.5°F). Clinicians must differentiate
hyperthermia from fever (ch. 16). In the spectrum of heat-related
injuries identified in humans, heatstroke is most severe.1,2
“Heatstroke” is defined as a core body temperature >40°C (104°F),
neurologic impairment, and multi-organ dysfunction (ch. 129).1,3-5

PATHOGENESIS
Heat Sources
Heat is produced endogenously (cellular metabolism) or exogenously
(external temperature and humidity); aberrations in both, combined
with overwhelming compensatory mechanisms, result in heatstroke.

Heat Dissipation
Heat is dissipated by conduction, convection, radiation, and
evaporation. Conduction occurs through direct physical contact with
a cooler surface and convection occurs with passage of cooler air over
the body. Radiation is passive heat loss into the environment while
evaporation is heat lost by converting liquid to gas. In cats and dogs,
up to 70% of heat is dissipated through radiation and convection.1,5-7
As temperature rises, evaporative loss through panting becomes
essential. When environmental humidity is >80%, evaporation is
impaired.3,6

Heat Shock Proteins (HSP)
Excess heat leads to synthesis of “chaperone molecules”: heat shock
proteins (HSPs). HSPs protect cells from heat-related damage by
reducing production of inflammatory cytokines, maintaining the
antioxidant pool, preventing protein denaturation, and protecting
against cell apoptosis.1,3 In one study, HSP72 concentrations were
lowest 12 hrs after admission and rebounded within 24 hrs to
admission levels only in dogs who survived.8 Increased age, lack of
acclimatization, pre-existing disease, and dehydration can decrease
concentrations of HSPs.3,7,8

CLINICAL SIGNS
Overview
Heatstroke has global effects on the body, causing profound
hypovolemic and vasodilatory shock (ch. 121), multi-organ

dysfunction, and death. Predisposing factors can be classified as
exogenous or endogenous (Table 130.1). Temperatures of 41.542.0°C (106.7-107.6°F) induce apoptosis in liver, spleen, thymus,
and small intestine cell cultures within minutes.1,3,9

Gastrointestinal (GI)
Diarrhea and hematochezia are identified frequently in heatstroke
patients, resulting from direct GI mucosal cytotoxicity and ischemia
in shock states (chs. 49, 50). Patients are at risk for sepsis and
endotoxemia secondary to bacterial translocation.1,3-5,7,9

Cardiovascular
Heatstroke causes both absolute and relative volume deficits.
Dehydration and hypovolemia result primarily from direct
evaporative effects of heat and GI losses. Arrhythmias follow direct
myocyte cytotoxicosis, ischemia from hypoperfusion, and release of
excess free radicals.1,7

Coagulation
In a retrospective analysis of 54 dogs with naturally occurring
heatstroke, thrombocytopenia was identified in 45 dogs and
prolonged prothrombin times (PTs) and activated partial
thromboplastin times (aPTTs) identified in 27/47 dogs (ch. 170).
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), a risk factor for death,
was diagnosed in 52% (ch. 171).6 Early in heatstroke, platelets,
coagulation, and fibrinolysis are activated, resulting in
microthrombosis. This consumptive process, combined with
denaturation of proteins, can cause serious bleeding dyscrasias.1,37,9-11

Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)
AKI is a common sequela of heatstroke; about 33% of dogs have
increased serum creatinine concentrations afterward (ch.
300).1,5,7,9 This is due to a combination of initial ischemic damage

and eventual vasodilation in prolonged shock states. Additionally,
pigment nephropathy can occur as a result of myoglobinuria from
rhabdomyolysis.1,4,5,7,9

Central Nervous System (CNS)
Direct nerve cytotoxicosis occurs in dogs and cats with heatstroke.15,7,9 Cerebral hypoperfusion, free radical accumulation, and
microthrombosis can cause cerebral edema, manifested as altered
mentation, tremors, and seizures.

DIAGNOSIS AND MONITORING
Initial Testing
The diagnosis is made based on history and physical examination.
Normothermia does not exclude heatstroke as a possibility,
especially if cooling had been implemented prior to examination.1,5,9
Initially, results of a complete blood count, blood smear, serum
biochemistry panel, PT, and aPTT should be assessed. Continuous
electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring is recommended (ch. 96).3
One study of 40 dogs with heatstroke documented nucleated red
blood cells (nRBCs), likely due to direct cytotoxic bone marrow
damage, in 90% of blood smears obtained at presentation from dogs
with heatstroke.12 Further, ≥18 nRBCs/100 white blood cells had a
sensitivity of 91% and a specificity of 88% for predicting death. Not
all heatstroke dogs have nRBCs.

Hypoglycemia
Hypoglycemia has been associated with heatstroke, either due to
increased consumption or failure of glycogenolysis. Neuroglycopenia
(<60 mg/dL [<3.3 mmol/L]) can contribute to an altered mental
status and seizure activity (chs. 61, 289; Video 61.3). The presence
of hypoglycemia at admission or its persistence despite appropriate
treatment is associated with increased mortality.6,13

Coagulation Testing
In a study of 30 dogs, abnormalities in platelet count, PT, aPTT, Ddimer, and fibrinogen were detected within 4 hrs of heatstroke (ch.
170). Progressive PT and aPTT prolongation at 12 and 24 hrs after
heatstroke were associated with increased mortality (ch. 170). Nonsurvivors had significantly lower fibrinogen concentrations at 24
hrs.10

TREATMENT
Initial Steps
Treatment of a pet suffering heatstroke begins with rapid cooling,
shock resuscitation, and management of complicating factors
(coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, etc.). Pets should be hospitalized for a
minimum of 24-48 hrs and an “ABC triage” examination should be
completed (ch. 119), remembering that completely and partially
obstructed airways can cause heatstroke.1,3,7 Owners should be

instructed to cool their pets until veterinary care is obtained. The
most effective cooling measures include spraying the dog or cat with
cool water and using a fan to provide a breeze. Ice water or packs
should be avoided because rapid decrease in body temperature can
cause vasoconstriction, potentially trapping heat in the body
core.3,13,14 Studies suggest that evaporative cooling can work twice
as fast at reducing body temperature when compared with more
invasive methods (iced peritoneal or gastric lavage).13,14 Care must
be taken to avoid hypothermia by monitoring the temperature every
5 minutes and stopping all cooling efforts when it reaches 39.539.7°C (103.0-103.5°F).2,3,5,15

IV Fluids
Room temperature IV isotonic crystalloids (dogs: 20 mL/kg; cats: 10
mL/kg) should be administered when hypovolemia is recognized
(ch. 120). These fluid doses should be given over 20 minutes.
Synthetic colloids, such as hetastarch or tetrastarch (5-10 mL/kg IV
boluses) have been given, but concerns have been raised regarding
their potentiating coagulopathies.16 Hemorrhaging pets should be
given fresh frozen plasma (10-20 mL/kg IV). Vasopressor therapy is
indicated in pets not responding to volume resuscitation or
transfusions.

Blood Glucose (BG)
BGs should be repeatedly monitored during the first several hours of
treatment for heatstroke. If hypoglycemia develops, 50% dextrose
should be given at a dose of 0.5-1 mL/kg, which should be diluted 1:3
with saline before being administered as a bolus. Additional
supplementation can be continued with 2.5-5% dextrose as a
constant rate infusion, at doses which avoid hyperglycemia.

Antibiotics
Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy is recommended to prevent sepsis
following bacterial translocation (ch. 140).5,9 Experimental studies
in dogs suggest that endotoxemia is decreased if oral antibiotics are

given prior to heatstroke. Studies have not identified the optimal
antibiotic or a morbidity and mortality benefit of prophylactic
antibiotic administration in naturally occurring heatstroke.4,17
Ampicillin/sulbactam, 30 mg/kg IV q8h, is recommended.

Mannitol
Mannitol administration can serve two purposes: reducing cerebral
edema and forcing diuresis to augment urinary production in
oliguric pets. Mannitol is advocated for pigment nephropathy (0.5-1
g/kg IV, administered over 20 minutes).3,5

Anti-Inflammatory Medications
With widespread systemic inflammation, corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) were theorized to be
beneficial. NSAIDs may increase the production of protective HSPs.3
Since time is required to upregulate HSP production, NSAIDs may
be more beneficial in prophylaxis rather than in the acute treatment
of heatstroke. Given the side-effects of anti-inflammatory drugs,
combined with the GI and renal dysfunctions associated with
heatstroke, use of these medications is not recommended (ch. 143).

PROGNOSIS
Even with hospitalization and intensive treatment, the prognosis for
survival from heatstroke remains between 50-60% in both human
and veterinary medicine.2-6,10 Poor prognostic indictors include
coma (ch. 44), hypoglycemia on presentation (ch. 61), development
of refractory hypoglycemia, increased serum creatinine
concentration at 24 hours, hypothermia, prolonged PT/aPTT at 12
and 24 hours, and decreased fibrinogen concentration at 24
hours.3,6,10,13

HYPOTHERMIA

DEFINITION AND CLASSIFICATION
Hypothermia (body temperature <37.2°C [<99°F]), whether primary
or secondary, occurs when heat dissipation overwhelms metabolic
heat production, resulting from exogenous and endogenous
factors.18-20 Primary or accidental hypothermia is the result of cold
exposure. Hypothermia can be secondary to an underlying disease,
trauma, or drug administration. Anesthesia is the most common
cause of secondary hypothermia.21-24

CLINICAL SIGNS
Physiology
Initially, sympathetic stimulation causes peripheral vasoconstriction
to prevent heat loss and increase cardiac output. Glycogenolysis
results in a mild hyperglycemia, providing an energy source for the
increased metabolic activity caused by shivering.18-20 Animals may
be seen to seek heat. If these compensatory mechanisms are
overwhelmed, untreated hypothermia can progress from mild to
moderate to severe and then to death.

Cardiovascular
As core body temperature decreases, bradycardia and decreased
systemic vascular resistance predominate. Alpha-1 adrenergic
receptors lose affinity for norepinephrine in a temperaturedependent fashion.20 Cardiac pacemaker cells lose automaticity,
compounding the bradycardia. Hypothermia-induced bradycardia is
unresponsive to atropine.19,25 Hypothermic pets can have
ventricular fibrillation or asystole (ch. 131). As many as 50% of dogs
with core temperatures <23.3°C (<74°F) had ventricular
fibrillation.19,20

Kidney
Cold diuresis usually precedes a reduction in core body temperature
due to compensatory peripheral vasoconstriction and increased

glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Severe hypothermia suppresses
antidiuretic hormone secretion, augmenting cold diuresis and
compounding risk of hypovolemia.19,21

Coagulation
Hypothermia produces clinically evident hypocoagulability. This can
be difficult to quantify, as many PT/aPTT analyzers warm samples to
body temperature, producing normal results.19,21,22 When cool
temperatures were maintained while standard clotting analyses were
performed, significant prolongations in clot times were identified.26
Abnormalities in bedside PT/aPTT testing should alert the clinician
to investigate causes of secondary hypothermia, as primary
hypothermia alone would not explain aberrations in these test
results.

TREATMENT
Warming and IV Fluid Therapy
Controlled warming is the key therapy for hypothermia. Drastic
increases in temperature, which can cause peripheral vasodilation to
dissipate heat, should be avoided. Instead, treatment should include
drying wet fur and providing passive surface warming in hydrated
pets with mild hypothermia using blankets, towels, and bubble wrap.
Active surface warming should be considered for dehydrated pets
with moderate to severe hypothermia, using forced-air blankets,
warm water bottles, and heating pads. Active core warming should
be considered in pets with severe hypothermia and cardiovascular
abnormalities using warmed IV fluids (40-42°C [104-107.6°F]),19-21
warmed/humidified air for intubated pets, warm water enemas, and
intracavitary/intravesicular warm water lavages. Judicious volumes
of IV fluids are indicated in hypothermia to correct shock and warm
the pet (ch. 120). Plasma transfusions are not indicated in pets with
primary hypothermia.19 Pets with secondary hypothermia should
receive plasma on a case-by-case basis (e.g., trauma, surgical blood
loss).

Complications of Warming
“After Drop” occurs when a pet’s temperature counterintuitively
drops during the rewarming process. This is explained as secondary
to redistribution of cold blood from the periphery to core.
Rewarming shock occurs as a result of a rapid increase in
temperature triggering peripheral vasodilation and venous stasis.
Moderation in warming with a focus on the patient’s core can
prevent these complications.19,21

PROGNOSIS
There is little information on prognosis in severely hypothermic
people or animals. Patients surviving initial resuscitative efforts
following severe hypothermia often experience significant multiorgan dysfunctions likely secondary to ischemia-reperfusion injury.
A study on hypothermic people suggests that severely increased
serum potassium concentrations (>12 mmol/L) are prognostic for
non-survival. Pronunciation of death due to hypothermia in humans
includes a serum potassium >12 mmol/L, electrocardiogram
analysis, core body temperature, and physical examination.19

DIAGNOSIS OF CARDIOPULMONARY
ARREST
Cardiopulmonary arrest (CPA) is defined as complete cessation of
blood flow, ventilation, and blood oxygenation. Untreated CPA
results in irreversible ischemic injury and death. Treatment,
cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), initially focuses on restoring
blood flow and oxygen delivery to tissues using chest compressions
and positive pressure ventilation. CPR should delay the onset of
ischemic injury to the brain and other vital organs and aims to
achieve return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Rapid
identification of CPA and immediate institution of high-quality CPR
are essential for patient survival. The Reassessment Campaign on
Veterinary Resuscitation (RECOVER) initiative provided evidencebased veterinary CPR guidelines (Figure 131.1).1,2
CPA is a clinical diagnosis made when an animal is acutely nonresponsive and making no attempt to breathe. A rapid (5-10
seconds), standardized, airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC)
assessment, including palpating for a pulse, should be immediately
undertaken. Visual inspection of the airway should identify any
masses, swellings, or foreign objects (a laryngoscope should be
used). Clearance of the airway (e.g., by suction) might be required
and if there is response to manipulation of the airway, CPA has been
ruled out and treatment for respiratory arrest should ensue (ch.
123). The breathing assessment in an unresponsive patient is
targeted at rapid identification of apnea. One should observe chest
excursions, feel for chest movement, and/or auscult for lung sounds.
In obviously apneic patients, the airway exam may be done using a
laryngoscope during intubation (see Basic Life Support [BLS]
below). If uncertainty about the diagnosis of CPA persists after the 10
seconds, CPR should be initiated immediately rather than
performing further diagnostic assessments.1 Evidence suggests a

strong association between delay in initiation of CPR and
mortality.3,4

INITIATION OF CPR
The 2 major aspects of CPR are basic life support (BLS) and
advanced life support (ALS) (Figure 131.1). The goal is to complete
all 5 tasks highlighted at the top of the algorithm, in the order
recommended, within the first 2 minutes.

BASIC LIFE SUPPORT
Definition
BLS is focused on restoration of circulation, ventilation, and arterial
oxygenation. It is the most important component of CPR. In the
absence of good quality BLS, ROSC is unlikely. BLS consists of chest
compressions and positive pressure ventilation.

Chest Compressions
The goals of chest compressions are (1) creation of pulmonary blood
flow to remove carbon dioxide (CO2) and provide oxygen to
pulmonary capillary blood and (2) deliver oxygen to tissues to
maintain cellular metabolism. Even with optimal external chest
compressions, only about 25-40% of normal cardiac output may be
generated.5,6 Therefore, chest compression technique must be
meticulous for CPR to be effective. Usually the animal should be
placed in right or left lateral recumbency and the chest compressed
one-third to one-half its width 100-120 times/minute. Full elastic
recoil of the chest between compressions is important to maximize
blood flow to the heart and brain.7 Because it can take a full minute
of chest compressions to attain steady arterial blood pressures,
compressions should be delivered in uninterrupted 2-minute cycles
when possible.8,9 Rotation to a new compressor after each cycle

reduces rescuer fatigue and helps maintain appropriate compression
quality.10
In medium- and large-breed dogs with round chest conformations
(width and depth of the chest approximately equal, e.g., Labrador
Retrievers, Rottweilers) compressions over the highest point on the
lateral thoracic wall with the patient in lateral recumbency will
maximally compress the chest and increase intrathoracic pressure
(Figure 131.2, A). In contrast, in dogs with a keel-chested
conformation (significantly deeper than wide, e.g., sighthounds)
compressions should be focused directly over the heart (Figure
131.2, B). In markedly broad-chested dogs (chests significantly
wider than deep, e.g., English Bulldogs), placing the patient in dorsal
recumbency and focusing compressions over the mid-sternum may
be most effective (Figure 131.2, C).
Compressor posture also affects chest compression quality. The
compressor should use locked elbows with fingers interlaced and one
hand on top of the other while keeping the shoulders directly above
the hands, which allows compressions to be driven by core
abdominal muscles rather than the arms (Figure 131.3). This
approach reduces fatigue, allowing maximal compression force for a
longer period. To optimize posture, the rescuer should stand on a
stool, kneel on the table behind the patient, or place the patient on
the floor and kneel behind.
Small dogs and cats have higher thoracic compliance due to their
narrow chest conformation. Chest compressions are usually focused
over the heart. Alternatively, a one-handed technique may be
attempted in these patients by wrapping the hand around the chest
at the level of the sternum or by compressing with a single hand
(Figure 131.2, D). Compressions are accomplished by pushing the
thumb against the fingers on the opposing sides of the chest, aiming
to compress from the apex to the base of the heart. Because of the
higher chest compliance of these animals, the one-handed technique
may reduce the risk of over-compressing the chest to more than onehalf its width (Video 131.1

).

FIGURE 131.3 Correct posture during chest
compressions. The arrows indicate the four critical
elements of rescuer posture: (1) the hands are
stacked such that one focal compression point
