Ventilation
The second priority of BLS is positive pressure ventilation. The
RECOVER guidelines recommend initiating ventilation as soon as
possible in dogs and cats with CPA since primary respiratory arrest is
common.1,4 An endotracheal (ET) tube should be placed as soon as
possible. Since intubation in lateral recumbency is easily
accomplished, chest compressions should continue during

placement. Mouth-to-snout or mask-to-snout ventilation is an
acceptable, but inferior alternative if an ET tube is not immediately
available.11 In intubated animals, chest compressions and
ventilations can be administered concurrently, if the ET tube cuff is
inflated. This approach minimizes pauses in chest compressions,
optimizing tissue blood flow. Dogs and cats with an inflated ET tube
cuff in place should receive 1 breath every 6 seconds with an
inspiratory time of 1 second. Excessive ventilation is harmful and
should be avoided (Video 131.2

).12

ADVANCED LIFE SUPPORT (ALS)
Initial Steps
ALS includes therapy with drugs, fluids, and defibrillation. The first
3 steps of ALS listed on the RECOVER CPR algorithm are
attachment of monitoring devices, obtaining vascular access, and
administration of “reversal” agents (Figure 131.1). The CPR team
leader should assign ALS interventions in the order listed on the
algorithm. Many commonly used monitoring devices, such as pulse
oximeters and blood pressure monitors, are of little to no use during
CPR because of motion artifact.13 However, electrocardiogram
(ECG) and end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2) monitors are
recommended and should be attached as soon as possible after the
initiation of BLS.1 Drug and defibrillation decisions are largely
guided by the ECG cardiac rhythm. Therefore, attaching the ECG
leads allows evaluation at the end of each 2-minute cycle of chest
compressions during the brief pause while compressors switch and
motion artifact is not present. Chest compression should not be
interrupted for ECG evaluation once a 2-minute cycle has begun.
ETCO2 reflects the amount of CO2 present in the alveoli and
ETCO2 monitors are not affected by the motion of chest
compressions. ETCO2 monitoring is strongly recommended during
CPR. Because alveolar CO2 arises from the tissues and is delivered to

the lungs by blood, ETCO2 is proportional to pulmonary blood flow
and correlates with cardiac output.14,15 If good blood flow is
generated during chest compressions, the ETCO2 increases. Because
minute ventilation also affects ETCO2, consistent ventilation
according to the BLS guidelines is essential if ETCO2 is to accurately
reflect the effect of BLS on blood flow. If the ETCO2 is <15 mm Hg,
the approach to BLS (including chest compressor position/posture,
hand position, chest compression depth and timing, possible
compressor fatigue, ventilatory rate, and approximate tidal volume)
should be critically evaluated by team members and altered in an
attempt to improve results.16 Another use of ETCO2 during CPR is
early identification of ROSC without stopping compressions. A
sudden substantial rise in ETCO2 may indicate there is increased
blood flow due to ROSC and should prompt rescuers to assess for a
spontaneous pulse.17

Obtain Vascular Access
If the patient has an IV catheter in place, its patency should be
confirmed. In dogs and cats, presence of an IV catheter prior to CPA
is associated with ROSC.4 In patients yet to have IV access, a
catheter should be placed as soon as feasible (chs. 74, 75). Repeated
or prolonged attempts at percutaneous catheterization are not
recommended. Venous cutdown procedures are relatively simple and
facilitate more rapid catheter placement.18 Veins closest to the heart
(cephalic or jugular) should be prioritized over those more distant
(lateral and medial saphenous).19 During chest compressions,
cephalic cutdowns may be less challenging than jugular cutdowns.
The dependent limb is usually easier to access because the vessel
runs medially. Intraosseous (IO) femur catheters are often easy and
quick to place in puppies and kittens (ch. 76).18 In adult animals,
commercial IO drill devices facilitate rapid placement, usually along
the medial, proximal humerus (ch. 76).20

Reversal Agents
Naloxone (0.04 mg/kg IV/IO) may be used to reverse opioids,
flumazenil (0.01 mg/kg IV/IO) for benzodiazepines, and atipamezole
(0.1 mg/kg IV/IO) or yohimbine (0.1 mg/kg IV/IO) for alpha-2
agonists. A drug and dosing chart that includes reversal agent doses
should be readily available (Figure 131.4).

IMPORTANCE AND USE OF THE
ELECTROCARDIOGRAM (ECG)
INTERPRETATION, GOALS, AND ALGORITHM
FOR DIAGNOSIS
Correct ALS therapies can only be chosen if an ECG rhythm is
obtained and interpreted correctly (Figure 131.1). Team members
should individually assess ECG rhythms during the brief pauses
between chest compression cycles. The team leader should call out
the rhythm diagnosis and opposing opinions should be debated after
resuming chest compressions. The primary goal of ECG analysis
during CPR is to differentiate: (1) shockable arrest rhythms, (2) nonshockable arrest rhythms, and (3) perfusing rhythms. A simple
algorithm can be used to quickly (<3-5 seconds) diagnose rhythms
during the inter-cycle pauses in BLS (Figure 131.5). If ROSC is not
obvious, chest compressions should immediately resume. Before
pausing chest compressions, one rescuer should prepare to palpate
for a pulse or apex beat.
When chest compressions pause, it is important to search for
repeated complexes on the ECG, regardless of their shape.
Frequently, more than one type of complex may be identified, but
they should repeat consistently. If there are repeated complexes and
no clear signs of effective circulation (e.g., no apex beat, no pulse,
and ETCO2 <30 mm Hg), the team should quickly estimate the rate.
If the rate is <200 per minute, it is most likely pulseless electrical
activity (PEA), a non-shockable arrest rhythm. If the rate is >200 per
minute, the rhythm is most likely pulseless ventricular tachycardia
(VT), a shockable rhythm. In the absence of consistent, repeated
complexes on the ECG, the shape of the line is assessed. A flat line is

most likely asystole, a non-shockable arrest rhythm. If there is
random, non-flat activity on the ECG, this is most likely ventricular
fibrillation (VF), a shockable rhythm. VF can take on different
appearances, but the random chaotic activity is consistent (Video
131.3

). Regardless of the arrest rhythm, BLS should be resumed

while the correct ALS therapies are administered. At the end of each
2-minute cycle of BLS: (1) the arrest rhythm is diagnosed, (2) BLS
resumed, and (3) correct ALS interventions administered. The 2minute cycles are continued until ROSC is achieved or CPR is
aborted.

ADVANCED LIFE SUPPORT (ALS)
THERAPIES
SHOCKABLE ARREST RHYTHMS
Electrical Defibrillation
Electrical defibrillation is the most efficacious therapy for dogs and
cats with shockable arrest rhythms.21 Other therapies have been
investigated, but in the absence of electrical defibrillation, the
prognosis is grave.22 The goal is to stop uncoordinated ventricular
contractions by simultaneously forcing as many myocardial cells as
possible into a refractory period at the same moment. This provides
an opportunity for the heart to recover synchronized electrical
activity. Electrical defibrillators may be either monophasic or
biphasic. The user experience of both defibrillator types is identical
other than energy dose required. Biphasic defibrillators are preferred
because they use lower currents and VF is terminated more
effectively.21 A chart with recommended dosing schemes for both
types of defibrillators is available (Figure 131.4). If needed,
subsequent defibrillator doses may be increased by 50%. All team
members should be trained on equipment operations and safety
precautions to prevent injury (Video 131.4

). When a shockable

rhythm is identified, chest compressions should continue until the
team is totally ready for defibrillation. Defibrillation should then take

place, even if the 2-minute compression cycle is not complete.
Immediately after defibrillation, chest compressions should resume
for an additional 2-minute cycle until the next rhythm check, as
direct conversion to a perfusing rhythm is not likely. In a prospective
observational study, only 27% of successfully defibrillated dogs and
cats achieved a perfusing rhythm immediately post-shock.4

FIGURE 131.5 Electrocardiogram (ECG) decision
tree to determine the cardiac rhythm relevant for
choosing the correct advanced life support
technique. During cardiopulmonary resuscitation,
the primary goal of ECG analysis is to answer a
single question: is the rhythm shockable or nonshockable? PEA, Pulseless electrical activity; ROSC,
return of spontaneous circulation; VF, ventricular
fibrillation; VT, ventricular tachycardia.

Precordial Thump
If an electrical defibrillator is not available, a precordial thump
(mechanical defibrillation) may be attempted for treatment of
shockable rhythms via a strong blow directly over the heart.
However, reports show a dismal success rate. A precordial thump
should never be used if an electrical defibrillator is available.23

Adjunctive Anti-Arrhythmics
For patients with prolonged CPA with a shockable arrest rhythm
despite multiple defibrillation attempts, adjunctive anti-arrhythmics
can be considered (ch. 230). Amiodarone is the most efficacious

drug for this purpose but only as an adjunct to electrical
defibrillation.21 Lidocaine is less efficacious. The use of a vasopressor
may be considered in patients unresponsive to repeated attempts of
defibrillation to redirect blood flow from the periphery to the core
organs (ch. 121).

NON-SHOCKABLE ARREST RHYTHMS
Vasopressors
By increasing peripheral vascular resistance, vasopressors lead to
preferential distribution of blood flow toward core vital organs (e.g.,
heart, lungs, brain). In contrast to defibrillation, which should be
done every cycle (i.e., every 2 minutes), vasopressors should be given
every other cycle (i.e., every 4 minutes). The best studied CPR
vasopressor is epinephrine, a catecholamine that causes peripheral
vasoconstriction by stimulating alpha-1 receptors.24 Initially, low
doses (0.01 mg/kg IV/IO) are recommended. With prolonged CPR
(greater than 10 minutes), a higher dose (0.1 mg/kg IV/IO) may be
considered but has been associated with lower rates of survival to
discharge and should only be used with that understanding.1
Epinephrine (double dose: 0.02 mg/kg low dose; 0.2 mg/kg high
dose) may be administered intratracheally through a long catheter
(e.g., a red rubber feeding tube) threaded through the ET tube after
the epinephrine dose has been diluted with an appropriate volume
(e.g., 2 mL/10 kg) of sterile isotonic saline or sterile water.
Vasopressin is an alternative to epinephrine during CPR that can
be expected to be of similar or higher efficacy.25 Its vasoconstrictive
effects are achieved via activation of peripheral V1 receptors and it
may be used instead of or in addition to epinephrine during CPR at a
dose of 0.8 U/kg IV/IO. As with epinephrine, it should be
administered every other cycle of BLS (i.e., every 4 minutes).
Vasopressin also can be administered via ET tube using the same
technique as described for epinephrine (dose doubled, diluted,
delivered at level of carina).

Anticholinergics

Studies examining the use of atropine, an anticholinergic drug,
during CPR provide little evidence of beneficial or harmful effects.21
Atropine (0.04 mg/kg IV/IO) may be considered for routine use
during CPR in dogs and cats with non-shockable arrest rhythms. In
dogs and cats with evidence of increased vagal tone at the time of
CPA, it is reasonable to administer atropine as part of ALS. It is given
every other cycle (i.e., every 4 minutes) during CPR in patients with
documented bradycardic arrest or in animals with diseases
predisposing to high vagal tone, such as gastrointestinal, respiratory,
central nervous system, or ophthalmic diseases. Atropine also may
be administered via ET tube (0.08 mg/kg) as outlined previously for
vasopressors.

OTHER ADVANCED LIFE SUPPORT
(ALS) THERAPIES
Intravenous (IV) Fluids
In patients with documented or suspected hypovolemia, boluses of
IV isotonic crystalloid fluid at standard doses (20-30 mL/kg in dogs,
10-20 mL/kg in cats) may improve cardiac output during CPR by
increasing cardiac preload (ch. 120). IV fluids should be avoided in
euvolemic or hypervolemic patients, as they may increase right atrial
pressure with no increase in aortic pressure, decreasing perfusion of
the brain and heart.26

Buffer Therapy
Sodium bicarbonate (1 mEq/kg IV, once) may be beneficial in
patients with preexisting severe acidemia (e.g., pH <7.1) and with
prolonged CPA, as severe tissue acidosis leads to peripheral
vasodilation and metabolic disturbances.26 However, such
disturbances may be rapidly resolved with ROSC. Bicarbonate
should be reserved for prolonged CPA (>10 minutes), ideally only
after documenting severe acidemia (pH <7.0).

Open-Chest CPR (OC-CPR)

While closed-chest CPR generates approximately 30% of a normal
cardiac output, direct cardiac massage via OC-CPR yields markedly
better blood flow, improves ROSC rates, and increases chance of
survival to discharge if implemented in the first few minutes of
CPA.27 Because OC-CPR is more invasive, more expensive, and
requires intensive after-care, clients frequently decline this option. In
patients with pleural space disease, pericardial disease, or significant
thoracic wall defects, OC-CPR should be strongly recommended.
Closed-chest CPR is also unlikely to be effective in giant breed, round
chested dogs. In patients that develop CPA during abdominal or
thoracic surgery, direct cardiac massage is likely the only viable
option for CPR.

PROGNOSIS
Unfortunately, little epidemiological CPR data are available in
veterinary medicine, limiting our ability to infer prognostic
information for dogs and cats with CPA.28,29 Reported survival rates
are very low, but as in human medicine, it is likely that one of the
most important prognostic indicators is the underlying cause.
Patients with untreatable or progressive chronic diseases have a poor
prognosis if they develop CPA. However, dogs and cats developing
CPA in the perianesthetic period have survival to discharge rates
approaching 50%.4,16 Therefore, the circumstances of the arrest are
important. Prompt identification of CPA, rapid initiation of highquality CPR, and adherence to these evidence-based guidelines have
the potential to improve survival rates.

in animals can present with vastly different clinical signs. However, the
mainstays of treatment often utilize similar medications and methods of
decontamination. These processes are often the most effective way to
prevent the development of clinical signs, especially when there are no
effective treatments for the toxin.1

DECONTAMINATION
GENERAL PRINCIPLES AND TRIAGE
Decontamination typically focuses on one of two areas: preventing systemic
absorption of a toxin or enhancing its elimination. Decontamination is most
effectively performed in the patient with few or no clinical signs. Patients

should undergo assessment prior to any type of decontamination to ensure
that they are not showing severe clinical signs (ch. 119). It is essential to
treat any life-threatening problems first. Clinical signs may warrant
treatment even before a toxicologic history can be taken or decontamination
can be initiated. Once the pet is stabilized, a thorough physical exam should
be performed (ch. 3), and a full toxicologic history can be obtained (ch.2).

PREVENTING HUMAN EXPOSURE
When decontaminating a patient, the handler should always wear
appropriate personal protective equipment to prevent relay exposure of the
toxicant.1 Any recommended at-home decontamination should take into
consideration potential exposure to the pet owner. If human exposure is
suspected to have taken place or if recommendations on preventing human
exposure to a toxin are required, a human poison control center should be
contacted (e.g., in the United States: 800-222-1222).

ORAL DECONTAMINATION
Oral decontamination is performed to prevent systemic absorption of orally
ingested toxicants, to make a toxicant less locally irritating or corrosive, or to
enhance the elimination of toxicants. Oral decontamination should be
considered cautiously in an animal that is showing clinical signs, due to the
risk of aspiration if the patient is not able to protect its airway. Toxicokinetic
properties of the agent should be evaluated, as absorption rates and peak
plasma concentrations will vary and affect the window available for oral
decontamination.

Dilution
Dilution is often used to decrease oral and gastric irritation. Dilution
typically involves the oral administration of milk or water (2 mL/kg PO,
maximum 70 mL, in a bowl or via oral syringe in conscious patients only).
Dilution is commonly utilized when pets ingest petroleum distillates,
corrosive or caustic agents, and plants that contain insoluble calcium
oxalates.1 Additionally, the calcium in milk can be beneficial in decreasing
absorption of some toxicants, including fluoride, fluoroquinolones,
tetracyclines, and bisphosphonates.

Emesis

Emesis is used to remove ingested toxicants from the stomach (Video 132.1
). At best, 40-60% of stomach contents are expected to be recovered.2
Vomitus should be closely examined for evidence of the ingested toxicant.
Recovery is most likely to be successful within 30-90 minutes post-ingestion;
however, some agents may take much less or much more time to be
absorbed. Emesis should always be considered on a case by case basis and
should not be attempted without first examining the patient and taking a
history. Factors the veterinarian should consider when deciding whether to
induce emesis include toxicant ingested, time frame since ingestion, whether
emesis will change the kinetics (and therefore the prognosis) of the toxin,
and whether the risk of aspiration is higher than the intended benefit. The
risks and benefits of emesis should be carefully weighed in patients with
underlying medical issues and in patients that are showing clinical signs.
Emesis is contraindicated in patients that have ingested caustic substances
or petroleum distillates.
The emetic center in the dog is regulated by dopamine receptors. These are
found in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CRTZ). Apomorphine (0.03 mg/kg
IV, or in the conjunctival sac) is a centrally-acting emetic and it can be used
to induce emesis in dogs.3-5 Ropinirole (Clevor) eye drops also induce
vomiting by stimulating the dopamine receptors in the CRTZ.6 3% hydrogen
peroxide (0.5 mL/kg PO, up to 50 mL total dose) is a locally-acting emetic
and it can be used for inducing emesis in dogs.1,3,4 It can be repeated once if
no emesis is seen after 10 minutes. 3% hydrogen peroxide is not
recommended for use in cats, due to the potential to cause necroulcerative
hemorrhagic gastritis.7 Dexmedetomidine (7 mcg/kg IV) or xylazine (0.44
mg/kg IM) can be used as an emetic for cats, as their CRTZ is regulated by
alpha receptors.8 Providing additional motion (such as rotating a cat in a
carrier on a desk chair) has been anecdotally suggested to increase the
success rate.

Activated Charcoal
Medical grade activated charcoal is a form of carbon with an intricate pore
structure resulting in a high surface area. It can be a very useful tool to
adsorb toxicants that are still in the gastrointestinal tract or those that
undergo enterohepatic recirculation.1,4 Activated charcoal should be
considered in pets with recent exposures to toxicants with the potential to
cause serious clinical signs but who are not showing clinical signs. The initial
dose is often given with a cathartic to help facilitate the movement of the
activated charcoal and the toxicant through the gastrointestinal tract. It is

important to ensure the timely elimination of the activated charcoal/toxin
complex through the feces, as adsorption is reversible. Multiple doses of
activated charcoal may be indicated for agents that undergo enterohepatic
recirculation.1,4 Subsequent doses are given at half the initial amount and
without sorbitol, or other cathartic. However, recent research has indicated
that multidose activated charcoal may not be more effective than single dose
activated charcoal for some toxicants that undergo enterohepatic
recirculation.9
Activated charcoal does not bind to heavy metals, corrosive agents,
hydrocarbons, fluoride, xylitol, ethanol, and/or petroleum distillates.1,4 The
risk of aspiration should be considered in animals that are unable to swallow
or protect their airway, or in cases of uncontrolled vomiting or
regurgitation.1 Activated charcoal is an osmotic agent and the risk of lifethreatening hypernatremia should be considered prior to administration10;
risk factors include animals that are small, dehydrated, or have ingested
osmotically active substances (such as chocolate, paintballs, or soft chew
medications/supplements). Monitoring serum sodium and administering
fluids or allowing free access to water when activated charcoal is
administered are important steps to detect and prevent hypernatremia.10

Cholestyramine
Cholestyramine is a resin that binds to bile acids in the intestine. It forms an
insoluble complex with the bile acids in the intestine and is excreted in the
feces.4 With the lack of bile acids to aid in resorption from the digestive
tract, certain toxins experience a higher rate of excretion. Cholestyramine
has been used off-label in overdoses of cholecalciferol, sago palm (Cycas
revoluta), blue green algae, and some nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
(NSAIDs). Dosing is 0.3-1 g/kg PO q8h (duration depends on toxin
ingested).

ENEMAS
Warm water enemas (5-10 mL/kg) can be helpful for the elimination of
toxicants from the lower gastrointestinal tract1 (ch. 108).

OCULAR DECONTAMINATION

The goal of ocular decontamination is to decrease the concentration and
contact time of the toxin, two important factors in determining the amount
of ocular injury a toxin will inflict. Ocular decontamination uses large
quantities of flush (eye wash, tepid tap water, artificial tears) over 20-30
minutes.1 Sedation and/or rest periods may be necessary to minimize patient
stress.1 Fluorescein staining should be performed afterwards if there is
potential for corneal injury.

DERMAL DECONTAMINATION
Bathing
Bathing with liquid dishwashing detergent or a follicular flushing shampoo
can be used to remove substances that are oily or oil-soluble. The patient
should be reassessed when dry to see if there is any residue. Bathing may
need to be repeated to fully remove the toxicant from the patient.1,4
Petroleum distillates (e.g., gasoline or paint thinner) should never be used to
remove substances from the skin or fur.1,4 It is important to prevent the
patient from becoming hypothermic secondary to chilling after bathing.

Clipping
Clipping (shaving) the fur may be indicated when a substance has dried and
bathing will no longer be effective for removal (paint, tar, glue, etc.).4

INHALANT DECONTAMINATION
Pets that have been exposed to an inhaled toxin should immediately be
moved to fresh air. Additional treatments may or may not be needed.4

ADVANCED ELIMINATION
Intravenous Lipid Emulsion
Intravenous lipid emulsion (ILE) is a sterile emulsion of soybean oil, egg
phospholipids, and glycerin.11 It has been used, off label, for the treatment of
severe lipophilic medication intoxications. Lipids have been used in the
treatment of intoxications with bupivacaine and other local anesthetics,
moxidectin, ivermectin, calcium channel blockers, baclofen, permethrin,
tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), and ibuprofen.11-17 Dosing uses a 20% lipid

solution, with an initial bolus of 1.5 mL/kg IV, followed by 0.25 mL/kg/min
IV for 30-60 minutes. Dosing should be adjusted in small patients to avoid
volume overload. Doses can be repeated q4-6h if the patient is still showing
clinical signs and is no longer lipemic. Persistent gross lipemia,
hypertriglyceridemia, volume overload, and corneal lipidosis are reported
side-effects of ILE.17

Therapeutic Plasma Exchange
Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) has been used in veterinary medicine to
remove toxicants with high protein binding and low volume of
distribution.18 TPE removes a patient’s plasma and the associated proteinbound toxicant and replaces it with new, “clean” plasma. TPE has been
suggested for use in NSAID exposures (e.g., ibuprofen, meloxicam, and
naproxen).18-20 Potential side-effects include hypotension, bleeding, clot
formation, sepsis, and allergic reaction.18

Hemodialysis and Charcoal Hemoperfusion
Hemodialysis has been used in veterinary medicine to remove toxicants that
are of low molecular weight, have low protein binding and a small volume of
distribution21 (ch. 103). It involves removing the blood from the body and
running it through a membrane to remove toxicants. Hemodialysis has been
used for ethylene glycol and ethanol intoxications.21,22 Charcoal
hemoperfusion is used with toxicants that have a higher molecular weight,
protein binding, and a higher volume of distribution.21,22 In charcoal
hemoperfusion, the blood is removed from the body and run through an
activated charcoal-containing cartridge which has been added to the
hemodialysis machine. Hemoperfusion has been used for treating
theophylline and barbiturate toxicosis. Charcoal hemoperfusion and
hemodialysis can be used individually or together21 (ch. 103). The
combination of hemoperfusion and hemodialysis has been used for baclofen,
metaldehyde, THC, and enrofloxacin toxicoses.22-25

THERAPY FOR TOXIC EXPOSURES
Antidotes are used for changing the kinetics of specific toxicants and will be
discussed with those toxins in their respective chapters. Other medications
are commonly used in the treatment of a variety of different toxins (Table
132.1).

CHAPTER 133: Neurotoxicoses
Cristine Hayes

AC RO N YM S
CNS central nervous system
GI gastrointestinal
PNS peripheral nervous system

This chapter is enhanced with the following electronic asset on Elsevier
eBooks+: 2 Videos.
Neurotoxicants have a wide variety of effects owing to the unique structure and
function of the nervous system. The nervous system’s role in regulating the
function of other organ systems throughout the body may result in secondary
effects on multiple organ systems. The response to a neurotoxicant exposure can
vary depending on the dose and the species involved. See Table 133.1 for a list
of common neurotoxicants in dogs and cats.

APPLIED NEUROANATOMY AND
NEUROPHYSIOLOGY
Intoxications that involve the nervous system directly can have effects in specific
microanatomic locations, triggering clinical signs (chs. 240, 241). Neuronal cell
bodies can be targeted directly by neurotoxicants such as methyl mercury or
carbon monoxide, causing neuronopathies via direct neuronal cell damage or
hypoxic neuronal injury.1 This in turn causes the alteration of protein and
neurotransmitter synthesis or possibly neuronal death, leading to permanent
loss of the neuron. Axons can be targeted selectively by neurotoxicants such as
metronidazole or organophosphorus insecticides, resulting in an axonopathy,
with longer axons in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) at higher risk.2
Wallerian degeneration can occur when the neuronal cell body remains intact

while the axon segment distal to the injury caused by the toxicant degenerates.2
Neuronal sodium channel activity can be enhanced excessively by neurotoxicants
such as grayanotoxins (ch. 137), resulting in repeated depolarizations and
prolonged neurotransmission.1 Sodium channels can be inactivated by
pyrethrins, which increases the duration of depolarizations,3 or sodium channel
recovery after depolarization can be inhibited by local anesthetics such as
lidocaine, decreasing the generation and transmission of action potentials.4
Potassium channels are responsible for repolarization of axonal membranes,
allowing for potassium efflux out of the axon and restoring the resting membrane
potential and can be blocked by neurotoxicants such as 4-aminopyridine.1
Certain neurotoxicants, such as bromethalin, may selectively affect the myelin
sheath, resulting in loss of myelin or myelin edema, known as a myelinopathy.5
The loss of myelin interferes with the rapid transmission of an action potential
down the axon. The blood-brain barrier is formed by endothelial cells that have a
higher concentration of mitochondria compared to endothelial cells elsewhere in
the body, increasing their susceptibility to damage from neurotoxicants that can
cause ischemia and subsequent hypoxemia.6 Carrier-mediated transport systems
may allow passage across the blood-brain barrier into the central nervous system
(CNS), and alterations in these transporters may increase the susceptibility of the
CNS to a neurotoxicant, such as alterations in p-glycoprotein resulting in a
higher risk for ivermectin toxicosis.7

CLINICAL SIGNS
Despite the number of effects neurotoxicants can have on various components of
the nervous system, the clinical signs of exposure are generally divided into two
types: stimulatory or depressant. Patients with neurotoxicosis may progress from
one to the other. Stimulatory signs such as agitation (ch. 24), hyperesthesia, and
seizures (ch. 45) typically originate from stimulation of the CNS or sympathetic
nervous system or inhibition of the parasympathetic nervous system.8 Tremors
(mild [Video 42.1

] to severe [Videos 133.1, 133.2]), tetany, hypermetria, and

myoclonus can originate from the CNS, PNS, or muscles (ch. 42).8 Serotonin
syndrome, a disorder caused by excess serotonin, is characterized by
abnormalities in autonomic nervous system function, neuromuscular function,
gastrointestinal (GI) signs, hyperthermia, and vocalization.9 Depressant signs
such as depression, obtundation, stupor, and coma typically originate from
alterations of the neurotransmitters in the CNS (ch. 44).8 Ataxia, paresis, and
paralysis may indicate muscle weakness, CNS effects, or PNS damage to the
axons or myelin (ch. 43).8 The type of clinical signs is frequently dosedependent, with small exposures resulting in one set of signs and large exposures
potentially resulting in the opposite effect.6 Since the nervous system is
intimately connected to other organ systems, many neurotoxicants also have
effects on other organ systems. Cardiovascular signs may include tachycardia,
bradycardia, arrhythmias, hypertension, or hypotension. Hypersalivation,
vomiting, diarrhea, and ileus may be seen due to stimulation of the
chemoreceptor trigger zone in the CNS. Respiratory signs such as tachypnea,
respiratory depression, or respiratory distress can also occur secondary to
neurotoxicant exposure.

DIAGNOSIS
The diagnosis of neurotoxicosis is based on exposure history, presenting clinical
signs, and diagnostic evaluation (ch. 15). For many neurotoxicants, there is a
known or suspected history of exposure, which can be determined through
careful questioning of the pet owner (ch. 2). In combination with the patient
history, the presenting clinical signs may allow the veterinarian to develop a
differential list (Box 133.1).10,11 While most CNS intoxicants act quickly to
produce clinical signs, there are a few exceptions. Medications (such as
amphetamines or serotonergic agents) that are extended release may have a lag
time of up to 8 hours before clinical signs appear. With the rodenticide
bromethalin, high dosages can cause clinical signs within 12 hours, but with
lower amounts signs may not occur until up to 5 days later. Ingestion of

marijuana products can quickly generate signs, or the onset of signs can be
delayed for a few hours.
Diagnostic tests may be useful in the diagnosis and treatment of certain
neurotoxicants. Radiographs to evaluate for metal opacities followed by serum
lead levels can be evaluated in suspected lead intoxication cases.12 A serum
ethylene glycol test may be used to determine an exposure to ethylene glycol (ch.
135).13 An over-the-counter urine drug screen may be useful in determining if
there has been an exposure to human drugs, such as amphetamines,
barbiturates, benzodiazepines, cocaine, marijuana, lysergic acid diethylamide
(LSD), ecstasy (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine [MDMA]), opioids, or
tricyclic antidepressants.14 Hypernatremia can be seen on serum electrolyte
panels with salt exposures.15

TREATMENT
DECONTAMINATION AND INITIAL TREATMENT
After an exposure to a suspected neurotoxicant, decontamination of the patient
should be considered if the patient is not showing any clinical signs of toxicosis
(ch. 132). A thorough history and minimum diagnostic database are indicated,
including a complete blood count, serum biochemistry profile with electrolyte
concentrations, and ideally blood pressure (ch. 91), particularly in the event of
an exposure to an unknown neurotoxicant.16 If available, blood gas analysis can
be helpful to establish a baseline value, should acid-base disorders or respiratory
complications occur. Because neurotoxicants often affect the cardiovascular
system, balanced electrolyte crystalloid intravenous fluids (IVF; ch. 120) and
other measures, as needed, should be used to address hypotension (ch. 121).
Hypertensive crises also may occur and should be managed if present (ch. 236).
Any abnormalities present on initial diagnostic tests should be addressed,
particularly electrolyte disturbances. If vomiting is present, it may be addressed
with an antiemetic, such as maropitant (1 mg/kg SQ, IV q24h).17 Respiratory
signs such as dyspnea may be present due to direct respiratory effects or
aspiration (ch. 217) and should be addressed with oxygen and ventilatory
support as needed (ch. 123). Organophosphorus and carbamate insecticides
may require the use of atropine (0.02-0.2 mg/kg; one-fourth IV, three-fourths
SQ or IM) for treatment of bradycardia or increased bronchial secretions.18
Thermoregulation may also be needed in patients showing stimulatory signs (ch.
130). Many neurotoxins are lipophilic and may be treated adjunctively with
intravenous lipid emulsion therapy (ILE), although it may reduce the
effectiveness of some therapies used for managing clinical signs (ch. 132). A few

neurotoxins have antidotes to reverse their effects. Chelation may also be needed
for the elimination of metals such as lead. Chelators effective for lead elimination
include succimer (10 mg/kg PO q8h for 10 days), edetate calcium disodium
(CaEDTA, 25 mg/kg SQ q6h for 5 days or 75 mg/kg IV q6h for 2-5 days, diluted
to 10 mg/mL for administration), d-penicillamine (30-110 mg/kg/day PO
divided q6h for 7 days), or dimercaprol (British anti-Lewsite [BAL], 3-6 mg/kg
IM q6-8h)12 in approximate descending order of preference (cost, availability,
and ease of administration influence chelator selection).

STIMULATORY SIGNS/SEIZURES
When possible, the neurotoxicant causing stimulatory CNS signs should be
identified prior to choosing the most appropriate medication. In the
hemodynamically stable patient, acepromazine (0.05-0.1 mg/kg IV initially; can
repeat as needed after allowing 15 minutes to take effect) may be considered for
agitation.19 Diazepam (0.5-1 mg/kg IV as needed) or midazolam (0.1-0.5 mg/kg
IV, IM as needed) may also be used for stimulatory signs, although they can
exacerbate signs with certain toxicants such as amphetamines and other
sympathomimetics and may result in apnea when used to treat isoxazole
mushroom toxicosis.20,21 Seizure activity should be managed with an
anticonvulsant, such as diazepam (0.5-1 mg/kg IV PRN), levetiracetam (30-60
mg/kg IV q8h), midazolam (0.1-0.5 mg/kg IV or IM PRN), phenobarbital (4-8
mg/kg IV slowly over 5 min, repeat 4 mg/kg IV q20min up to a total of 20-24
mg/kg IV), or inhalant anesthesia (chs. 45 and 247).20,22-24

SEROTONIN SYNDROME
Serotonin syndrome is a frequent finding with many neurotoxicants that cause
decreased reuptake or decreased breakdown of serotonin. A serotonin antagonist
such as cyproheptadine (dog: 1.1 mg/kg PO or rectally q6-8h; cat: 2-4 mg/cat PO,
rectally q6-8h) may be used.9 Propranolol (0.02-0.06 mg/kg IV or 0.1-0.2 mg/kg
PO q8h) may also antagonize serotonin activity.25

TREMORS (ch. 42)
It is important to distinguish muscle tremors from trembling or other
stimulatory signs because trembling or stimulatory signs are unlikely to respond
well to muscle relaxants. Muscle tremors are typically characterized as
involuntary, continuous, rhythmic muscle contractions and typically affect the
whole body, although they can potentially be localized to the face, ears, or paws

(Videos 42.1, 133.1,

133.2). They can be treated with methocarbamol (55-220

mg/kg slow IV PRN).26

PROGNOSIS AND MONITORING
The prognosis varies case by case, depending on several factors, including the
neurotoxicant involved, exposure dosage, time since exposure, and presence or
absence of clinical signs. A more negative prognosis is warranted in patients
having seizures that do not respond to anticonvulsants and those that present
with severe hyperthermia. When intubation and ventilation need to occur (ch.
123), a financial discussion should ensue. Most neurotoxicants act quickly; if no
clinical improvement is noted within 48 hours of the start of treatment, the
prognosis worsens.
Monitoring of vital signs and the evolution of neurologic signs (ch. 241) is
important, with special attention paid to oxygenation status. Relapsing signs are
not expected with most neurotoxicants (lead is the exception).

NAPQI N-acetyl-para-benzoquinone imine
Hepatotoxicants are often categorized as intrinsic or extrinsic
(idiosyncratic). Intrinsic toxicants are responsible for the vast
majority of cases of hepatotoxicosis and are caused by a wide range
of toxicants, including heavy metals, commodity chemicals (e.g.,
formaldehyde), food-related compounds (e.g., mycotoxins), plant
toxins, and pharmaceuticals. Intrinsic hepatotoxicosis is
characterized by a fairly consistent and predictable dose-response
among similar populations, although species differences in
susceptibility are common. Conversely, idiosyncratic hepatotoxicosis
is not always dose-dependent and only occurs in a small subset of the
population exposed to concentrations of toxicant that would not
generate adverse effects in the majority of the population.
Idiosyncratic responses are not generally predictable, although the

growing field of pharmacogenetic study is increasing our ability to
identify individuals that might be genetically predisposed. Select
hepatotoxicants of veterinary importance are discussed below and in
Table 134.1.

ACETAMINOPHEN
Acetaminophen (APAP, paracetamol in many countries) is a
synthetic, non-opiate derivative of para-aminophenol (PAP) that is
thought to act centrally to increase the pain threshold and inhibit
pain mediators and prostaglandin synthesis. After oral dosing, peak
plasma levels are reached within 10-60 minutes (60-120 minutes for
extended-release forms). Toxic dosages reported for dogs and cats
are ≥75-100 mg/kg and ≥10 mg/kg, respectively.1,2 APAP-induced
hepatotoxicity is attributed to its toxic metabolite, N-acetyl-parabenzoquinone imine (NAPQI). This metabolite is generated by
cytochrome P450 oxidation in the liver and kidney when the normal
glucuronidation and sulfation pathways are saturated. Intrinsic
antioxidants such as glutathione or cysteine bind NAPQI, preventing
cellular injury, but when these antioxidant systems are depleted,
NAPQI binds to cellular macromolecules, resulting in hepatocellular
injury and death.2 See chapter 138 for more information about the
hemotoxicity of APAP. Hepatotoxicosis is uncommonly seen in cats,
who frequently succumb to the hematologic effects before signs of
liver injury can become apparent.
Onset of clinical effects from APAP toxicosis varies from 2-4 hours
for methemoglobinemia to up to 24-48 hours for liver injury. See
chapter 138 for clinical signs of methemoglobinemia and chapter
269 for additional information on acute hepatic injury. Clinical signs
of hepatotoxicosis include anorexia, nausea, vomiting, lethargy, signs
of abdominal pain, icterus, encephalopathy. Laboratory
abnormalities include elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and
aspartate aminotransferase (AST) activities, elevated bilirubin
concentrations, coagulopathy, and hypoglycemia. Serum for APAP
analysis can be submitted to a human hospital, but nomograms that
would distinguish therapeutic levels from toxic levels are not
available for veterinary species, so the utility of this assay is limited

to verifying exposure to the drug. Facial and/or paw edema has been
reported in both cats and dogs, although it is more common in cats.1
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS) has been reported in dogs.3
Management of APAP overdosage includes assessment and
stabilization of the patient as needed. Dyspneic patients should be
provided supplemental oxygen (ch. 123) and intravenous (IV) fluid
therapy should be instituted (ch. 120). Gastrointestinal
decontamination should be considered based on time since exposure
and condition of the patient (ch. 132). Administration of glutathione
precursors such as n-acetylcysteine (140 mg/kg PO, IV loading dose,
followed by 70 mg/kg q6h for 6 doses) and s-adenosylmethionine
(20 mg/kg PO q24h or divided q8-12h) is recommended to reduce
further oxidative injury to the liver.2 Ascorbic acid (30 mg/kg PO,
SQ, IV q6h) helps reduce methemoglobin to hemoglobin, but it is of
unknown efficacy for liver protection. Supportive care may include
management of hypoglycemia (chs. 61, 289), coagulopathy (chs.
124, 171), hepatic encephalopathy (ch. 266), and renal injury (ch.
300). Monitoring tear production for development of KCS within
24-96 hours after exposure is important; tear replacement therapy
may be required for days to weeks.1 Facial/paw edema does not
respond to antihistamines or corticosteroids but tends to resolve
over 72 hours without specific treatment.

AFLATOXINS
Aflatoxins are mycotoxins produced by a variety of fungi, but are
most commonly associated with Aspergillus spp. Most toxicoses are
associated with aflatoxin B1 (AFB1), which occurs in corn and other
grains, peanuts, soybeans, tree nuts, and cottonseed.4 The toxicity of
AFB1 is due to its biotransformation into toxic epoxides that bind
cellular proteins and nucleic acid, resulting in altered protein
synthesis, energy production, cellular metabolism, enzyme activity,
and nucleic acid transcription and translation. These processes lead
to hepatocellular degeneration, necrosis and apoptosis. The low
levels of toxic metabolites generated under normal circumstances are
dealt with by endogenous antioxidant molecules such as glutathione,
and it is only in the face of excessive exposure that significant cell
injury occurs. Aflatoxin-induced DNA damage can result in genetic
and epigenetic alterations that can persist and lead to chronic liver
injury and carcinogenesis. Compared to most other mammalian
species, dogs and cats have inherently low hepatic glutathione
concentrations and low glutathione-s-transferase activity, making
them more sensitive to aflatoxin-induced liver injury. Although the
acute oral LD50 of AFB1 is 0.5-1 parts per million (ppm) for dogs and
0.3-0.8 ppm for cats, toxicosis and death have occurred in dogs
ingesting dog foods contaminated with 60 parts per billion (ppb) or
more of AFB1.5,6 In the United States, the maximum allowable
aflatoxin concentration in human and most animal foods (including
pet food) is 20 ppb, although some livestock feeds can contain up to
300 ppb. Most canine cases of aflatoxicosis have been associated
with aflatoxin-contaminated commercial dog foods, with levels in the
foods ranging from 150-800 ppb or more. To date there have been
no reports of feed-related aflatoxicosis in cats.
Most cases of aflatoxicosis in dogs present with patients already
experiencing some degree of hepatic insufficiency, and the diagnosis
becomes one of exclusion, leading to testing of the suspect food.
Decontamination of the patient in these cases is generally moot, as
the damage has already been done. Clinical signs of aflatoxicosis may

develop within 1-2 days of ingestion of feeds contaminated with very
high levels of aflatoxin but may be delayed for weeks to months in
cases of chronic exposure to more moderately elevated aflatoxin
concentrations.7 The clinical presentation would be the same as any
acute liver disease patient, with anorexia, lethargy, vomiting, melena,
diarrhea, icterus, and hepatomegaly possible. In severe cases,
patients may experience coagulopathy, encephalopathy,
hypoglycemia, stupor, coma, seizures, and death. Chronic low-level
aflatoxin exposure may lead to insidious and nonspecific signs such
as weight loss, anorexia, and intermittent diarrhea.
There is no specific antidote or treatment for aflatoxicosis. Patients
experiencing clinical effects should be managed supportively with
antiemetics, gastrointestinal protectants (acid reducers, sucralfate),
IV fluid therapy, vitamin K1 (5 mg/kg SC, then 0.8 mg/kg PO q8h or
1.25 mg/kg PO q12h), and others as necessitated by their clinical
presentation. N-acetylcysteine (70 mg/kg PO or IV q6-12h), sadenosylmethionine (20 mg/kg PO q24h or divided q8-12h), or
silymarin (50-250 mg/kg PO q12h) may provide glutathione
precursors and offer some hepatoprotection, but there are no
controlled studies that evaluate their efficacy in canine aflatoxicosis.
The prognosis depends on the severity of the liver injury, time until
medical intervention is obtained, and the overall dose of aflatoxin
ingested. Aflatoxin is a known carcinogen in humans, but its
carcinogenic potential in dogs is not known.

CYANOBACTERIA
Toxin-producing cyanobacteria (formerly blue-green algae) can
cause serious illness and death in animals that drink from and/or
swim in contaminated waters. Although toxin-containing
cyanobacterial blooms are more commonly associated with mid- to
late summer when water temperatures are highest, toxicosis can
occur throughout the year whenever warm spells occur. Cyanotoxins
are not limited to large bodies of water, as livestock and dogs have
been poisoned from drinking out of buckets or troughs containing
contaminated water. Rare instances of dogs and humans developing
hepatotoxicosis following ingestion of over-the-counter “blue-green

algae” nutritional supplements contaminated with cyanotoxins have
been reported.8 There are many cyanobacterial species, most of
which do not produce toxins. Unfortunately, distinguishing between
harmless and potentially toxic cyanobacterial blooms is not possible
from gross visualization. Microcystins and nodularins are the most
commonly encountered hepatotoxic cyanotoxins (HCs) in human
and animal poisonings in the United States.9 These toxins are cyclic
hepta- (microcystins) and penta-(nodularins) peptides with similar
mechanisms of action and clinical effects. HCs are absorbed from the
ileum and are taken up by hepatocytes via a bile acid transporter.
Within the hepatocyte, these peptides bind and disable cytoskeletal
proteins, initiate lipid peroxidation, and bind to and fragment DNA.
The overall cellular effect of HCs is loss of membrane integrity,
decreased protein synthesis, necrosis, and apoptosis leading to
rounding and detachment of hepatocytes from the basement
membrane and intrahepatic “hemorrhage” into areas devoid of
hepatocytes. In severe intoxications, massive loss of hepatocytes
results in pooling of large volumes of blood within the liver, resulting
in hepatomegaly and rapid death due to hypovolemia. Surviving
patients experience acute hepatic insufficiency that can lead to
hepatic failure (ch. 269).
Dogs ingesting HC-contaminated water may acutely collapse and
die with no noticeable signs, may sicken and die within hours of
exposure, or they may display initial vomiting with apparent
recovery for ∼12 hours before signs of liver injury manifest.9 Signs
include weakness, depression, icterus, anxiety, recumbency,
dyspnea, oliguria/anuria, seizures and bleeding due to coagulopathy.
Hepatopathy from HC-contaminated nutritional supplements tends
to develop more insidiously, with nonspecific signs such as anorexia,
abdominal pain, icterus, lethargy, and polyuria. As with other
hepatotoxicants, serum liver enzyme activities, bile acid
concentrations, and bilirubin concentrations are abnormal;
hypoglycemia, hypokalemia and hyperammonemia may occur.
Depending on the degree of hepatic injury, coagulopathy or
encephalopathy may develop. Patients surviving beyond 24 hours
may have elevated blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine values
as renal failure develops (ch. 300).

There is no specific therapy for HC toxicosis, and severely affected
animals may die before veterinary care can be reached or initiated.
Due to the rapidity at which HCs are absorbed and the potential for
abrupt onset of life-threatening signs, induction of emesis is
contraindicated, and activated charcoal is not beneficial.9 Patients
should be assessed and stabilized with fluid and/or blood
replacement therapy (ch. 121), seizure management (chs. 125,
247), dextrose for hypoglycemia (chs. 61, 289), and electrolyte
replacement (ch. 120) as needed. Cholestyramine (300-1000 mg/kg
PO q8h), an ion-exchange resin that blocks bile acid reabsorption,
may reduce enterohepatic recycling of HCs, and should be
considered if the patient’s condition is amenable to oral
administration.10 Hepatoprotection using n-acetylcysteine, sadenosylmethionine, and silymarin may be considered (see above for
dosages). Water-borne cyanotoxins are hazards to humans, so if HC
toxicosis is suspected from exposure to public waterways, public
health authorities should be notified.

CYCADS
Cycads (Cycas revoluta, sago palm, Australian nut palm, iron tree;
Cycas circinalis, fern palm, false sago palm, queen sago; Zamia spp.,
comptie, coontie, Florida arrowroot) are highly toxic, ancient plants
that grow outdoors in the southern United States and are sold as
houseplants in home improvement and department stores
throughout the country.11 Cycasin, the primary hepatotoxin, is
biotransformed in the intestine to methylazoxymethanol (MAM), a
metabolite that is hepatotoxic, neurotoxic, mutagenic, teratogenic,
and carcinogenic. MAM alkylates nucleic acids, impairing cellular
protein synthesis and resulting in cell death. Cats and dogs are
exposed by chewing on the plant and/or its seeds, all of which are
toxic; ingestion of a single seed has been lethal to dogs, while there
have been no published reports of sago palm toxicosis in cats.
Clinical effects may occur within hours of exposure, but in some
cases a lag period of up to 3 days may occur.11 Vomiting is the most
common sign, occurring in 80-90% of dogs, and diarrhea (with or
without blood or melena) occurs in approximately one-third of dogs.

Lethargy, anorexia, hypersalivation, abdominal discomfort, ataxia,
decreased mentation, weakness, proprioceptive deficits,
hyperthermia, hypothermia, and seizures have also been reported.
Icterus, coagulopathy, and other signs consistent with liver
injury/failure develop later in the toxicosis. Clinicopathologic
alterations consistent with liver failure (elevated bilirubin
concentrations, liver enzyme activities, and bile acid concentrations;
elevated coagulation times; hypoglycemia) may take up to 24-48
hours to develop. Azotemia, bilirubinuria, hematuria, and
cylindruria may occur. There is no specific diagnostic test for cycad
intoxication, and the diagnosis is based on clinical signs,
clinicopathologic findings, and a history of access to the plant.
Management of cycad exposures includes decontamination of the
patient by induction of emesis and administration of activated
charcoal (ch. 132).12 As with other cases of hepatotoxicosis,
supportive care including blood replacement therapy (ch. 124), IV
fluids (ch. 120), antiemetics, gastrointestinal protectants, gastric
acid reducers (ch. 261), vitamin K1 (5 mg/kg SC, then 0.8 mg/kg PO
q8h or 1.25 mg/kg PO q12h), dextrose for hypoglycemia (chs. 61,
289), and hepatoprotectants may be necessary (ch. 269). Serum
biochemistry profiles including electrolyte concentrations, and
complete blood counts, should be re-evaluated at least every 24
hours for the first 48 hours, then daily in patients showing clinical
signs of toxicosis. The prognosis depends on the amount of plant
ingested, elapsed time to institution of care, and severity of clinical
signs.

DRUG-INDUCED LIVER INJURY
Drug-induced liver injury can be dose-dependent or idiosyncratic in
nature. Dose-dependent hepatotoxicosis worsens with increasing
dosages, is predictable based on dosage in a given species, and
generally can be resolved by reduction of the dosage of the drug.13
Idiosyncratic drug-induced hepatotoxicosis (IDH) occurs at
therapeutic doses in a small subset of patients, is relatively
unpredictable, and generally requires cessation of administration of
the drug. This section will focus on IDH. IDH can occur due to

individual variation in types or amounts of metabolic or antioxidant
enzymes, dysfunction of hepatic transporters necessary for clearance
or sequestration of reactive metabolites, or immunological responses
triggered by neoantigens formed during hepatic biotransformation of
drugs.14 Variation in metabolic enzymes can result in generation of
excessive levels of harmful intermediates which can damage cellular
macromolecules, and variation in antioxidant enzymes may limit the
ability of the hepatocyte to detoxify these intermediates. Either
mechanism has the potential to predispose to significant
hepatocellular injury, and when they occur in tandem, the enhanced
oxidative stress on the cell may trigger necrosis or apoptosis. In
general, because different areas of the hepatic acinus tend to have
differing enzyme systems, the hepatocellular injury caused by this
type of variation tends to be zonal in nature (ch. 269).
Dysfunctional hepatic transporters can prevent sequestration of
harmful metabolites into lysosomes or their excretion into the bile,
increasing the risk of organelle damage, decreased membrane
fluidity, and cellular degeneration. This type of injury tends to result
in diffuse hepatocellular swelling, cholestasis, and necrosis. Binding
of biotransformation-derived drug moieties to cell membranes can
alter membrane surface proteins, generating neoantigens that are
then recognized by the immune system as foreign and leading to an
immune response against that particular cell. Immune responses
against affected cells result in individual “piecemeal” cell necrosis
associated with lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory infiltrate. A list of
veterinary drugs commonly associated with hepatic injury can be
found in Box 134.1. Management of IDH entails immediate
discontinuation of the drug and provision of supportive care.
Alternate drug therapy using drugs from a different class should be
sought for patients who require continued treatment for their initial
medical condition.

HEPATOTOXIC MUSHROOMS
Hepatotoxic mushrooms include members of the genera Amanita
(including Amanita phalloides, death cap), Conocybe, Galerina,
Lepiota, and Pholiotina, although only a few members of these
genera are hepatotoxic.15 Hepatotoxic mushrooms are distributed
widely throughout the United States and southern Canada. The
cyclopeptide amanitin is responsible for liver injury. Amanitin
inhibits RNA polymerase in cells, interfering with protein synthesis
and resulting in cell death. Target organs for amanitin are the
gastrointestinal tract, liver, and kidney, so the clinical effects are
those of gastrointestinal disturbance, hepatic insufficiency/failure
and renal insufficiency/failure, although effects on the liver tend to
predominate. Most patients are exposed when they ingest
mushrooms growing in the environment.

With massive ingestion, fulminant hepatic necrosis may lead to
acute onset of shock, collapse and death within 24 hours. More
commonly, clinical signs of toxicosis are delayed 6-24 hours,
although initial vomiting and diarrhea may be seen, after which the
patient usually returns to normal behavior for several hours before
vomiting, signs of abdominal discomfort, and diarrhea return, along
with evidence of hepatic injury such as icterus, elevated serum liver
enzyme activities and elevated serum bilirubin concentrations.
Patients surviving the initial phase of illness may appear to recover,
only to present in liver failure 72-96 hours later. Late-stage clinical
signs include gastrointestinal distress, icterus, hypoglycemia,
coagulopathy, behavior abnormalities, delirium, seizures, or other
signs of encephalopathy (ch. 269). Diagnosis of mushroom
hepatotoxicosis is commonly based on clinical signs and history of
exposure. A cage side test (Amatoxtest)15a is now available and some
veterinary diagnostic laboratories can run STAT analyses for
amanitin in serum, urine, gastric contents, suspect mushrooms, liver
or kidneys.15
Management of hepatotoxic mushroom exposures includes
decontamination of the patient by induction of emesis and
administration of activated charcoal (ch. 132). As with other cases of
hepatotoxicosis, supportive care including blood replacement
therapy (ch. 124), IV fluids (ch. 120), antiemetics, gastrointestinal
protectants, gastric acid reducers, vitamin K1 (5 mg/kg SC, then 0.8
mg/kg PO q8h or 1.25 mg/kg PO q12h), dextrose for hypoglycemia
(chs. 61, 289), and hepatoprotectants may be necessary (ch. 269).
Biliary drainage in conjunction with octreotide administration to
reduce enterohepatic recirculation of amanitin has been reportedly
used in some mushroom-intoxicated dogs, although controlled
studies are lacking.16 Serum biochemistry profiles including
electrolyte concentrations, and complete blood counts, should be reevaluated at least every 24 hours for the first 48 hours, then daily
from then on in patients that are showing clinical signs of toxicosis.
The prognosis depends on the amount of mushroom ingested,
elapsed time to institution of veterinary care, and severity of clinical
signs.

XYLITOL
Xylitol is a sugar alcohol used in many sugar-free products such as
gums, candies, and baked goods as well as a wide variety of products
such as toothpastes, cosmetics, and oral medications. Dogs have a
unique physiologic response to xylitol that results in a rapid,
sustained, and dose-dependent rise in insulin release, which in turn
triggers a precipitous drop in blood glucose levels.17,28 The ensuing
hypoglycemia can result in vomiting, weakness, ataxia, depression,
hypokalemia, seizures and coma. Some dogs develop elevated serum
liver enzyme activities following exposure, and a subset of these
progresses to severe hepatic necrosis. The cause of the liver injury
following xylitol ingestion is believed to involve depletion of
hepatocellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP), and/or generation of
reactive oxygen species during xylitol metabolism. Clinical effects of
hypoglycemia generally occur within 30 minutes of ingestion,
although dogs ingesting xylitol-containing gums may not develop
hypoglycemia until 12 hours after exposure, possibly due to the slow
release of xylitol from the gum base as it sits in the digestive tract.17
Changes in serum liver enzyme activities following xylitol ingestion
vary from 4-24 hours, and not all dogs with liver enzyme elevations
go on to develop hepatic failure.
Management of xylitol exposures includes judicious
decontamination of the patient and supportive care. Patients that are
showing clinical signs should be stabilized prior to any
decontamination measures, and a baseline blood glucose
measurement should be performed prior to decontamination as
clinical signs of hypoglycemia occur abruptly and without warning
(ch. 132). Activated charcoal does not appreciably adsorb xylitol.29
Patients should be monitored closely for development of
hypoglycemia and provided frequent small meals. If hypoglycemia
develops, IV dextrose should be bolused followed by a continuousrate infusion (ch. 289). Treatment should continue until the patient
can maintain a normal blood glucose in the absence of
supplementation; in some patients this may take 24 hours or longer,
although many recover more quickly. For patients in which liver
injury is a concern, standard treatment of relevant abnormalities

(e.g., vitamin K1 for coagulopathy, plasma transfusion, antiemetics;
ch. 269) should be administered as appropriate. Hepatoprotectants
are usually recommended, although their efficacy in minimizing
xylitol-induced liver injury has not been demonstrated. The
diagnosis is based on clinical signs, response to therapy, and history
of xylitol-containing products in the dog’s environment. The
prognosis for dogs developing hypoglycemia is very good provided
that prompt and appropriate veterinary care is provided; dogs
showing evidence of liver injury have a more guarded prognosis,
which depends on the extent of liver damage that occurs.

The mammalian kidney is vital to fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base
homeostasis. It ensures proper excretion of waste products and
synthesis of renin and erythropoietin.1 Despite their relatively small
size, the kidneys receive approximately 20% of cardiac output, with
the largest fraction moving through the renal cortex.1 This means
that the cortical structures suffer larger exposures to blood-borne
toxicants than most other parts of the body.1 In addition, renal
tubular cells can metabolize many substances into more toxic
metabolites, and these can become concentrated in the filtrate along
with the urine.1 See Table 135.1 for a summary of the mechanisms

of action of some small animal nephrotoxicants. This chapter
discusses practical management of the most common of these
exposures, with the goal of minimizing kidney injury. For a full
discussion on management of acute kidney injury (AKI), see ch.
300.

CHOLECALCIFEROL
Vitamin D and its analogues have the potential to cause AKI
secondary to hypercalcemia and renal mineralization within 4 days
of the exposure (ch. 300).2 The most common sources include
rodenticides and human medications. Exposed patients should be
decontaminated by induction of emesis followed by a single dose of
activated charcoal (AC).2 The patient should then be started on
cholestyramine resin (ch. 132). Baseline serum total calcium (Ca++),
phosphorus (P), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and creatinine should
be obtained and rechecked daily until 96 hours post-exposure.
Ionized calcium can be monitored as an alternative, but the reference
interval and analyzer should remain consistent for the 96-hour
period. Once the hypercalcemic state develops, treatment becomes
very dynamic and is focused on returning serum Ca++ and P levels to
normal.2 Patients should have daily monitoring of serum Ca++ and
the treatment plan should be adjusted according to those findings.
See Table 135.2 and ch. 283 for management of hypercalcemia.
Once serum Ca++ levels normalize, the patient should be weaned off
saline diuresis and discharged on oral medications. Serum Ca++
should be monitored daily for at least 5-7 days, and then at least 2-3
times per week for 2-3 weeks. If serum Ca++ levels start to rise, reinstitution of saline diuresis and additional bisphosphonate
treatment may be needed. If serum Ca++ levels remain steady, the
patient can be weaned off oral medications during this time.
Treatment may be required for weeks due to the long half-life of
calcidiol.3 The prognosis is good if the exposure is treated promptly.

The prognosis is guarded to poor once hypercalcemia develops and
grave once soft-tissue mineralization develops.3

ETHYLENE GLYCOL
Ethylene glycol (EG) is perhaps one of the most notorious
nephrotoxicants. It is found in automotive antifreeze, de-icers, home
solar units, inks, brake fluids, and snow globe-type decorations. EG
is oxidized to glycoaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADeH),
yielding glycoaldehyde.4 Glycoaldehyde is oxidized by aldehyde
dehydrogenase to glycolic acid (glycolate).4 Glycolic acid is further
oxidized to glyoxylic acid (glyoxylate).4 Glyoxylate is oxidized to
oxalic acid (oxalate).4
In order to promote the best prognosis, antidotal treatment for EG
toxicosis should be started within 8 hours of exposure in dogs and 3
hours of exposure in cats.5,6 The diagnosis of a significant exposure
should therefore be ascertained within these timeframes. If a
diagnosis cannot be established, then empirical treatment should be
initiated. While the gold standard is gas chromatography-mass
spectroscopy quantitative analysis of serum EG levels, cage-side EG
tests are available. They have good sensitivity but are lacking in
specificity. False positives can be seen from the presence of alcohols,
propylene glycol, glycerol, and sorbitol.7-9 Osmolal gap and acidbase testing can be used in conjunction with a cage-side EG test to
best determine the need for treatment. An increased serum osmolal
gap (>20 mOsm/kg) within 1-2 hours of the exposure is indicative of
the presence of an exogenous solute like EG. Osmolal gap is the
measured serum osmolality minus the calculated serum osmolality.
Serum osmolality is calculated using the following formula: 1.86 ×
(Na+ + K+ + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8), assuming Na+ and K+ are in
mEq/L and glucose and BUN are in mg/dL; with metric units (all
mmol/L), the formula is 1.86 × (Na+ + K+ + glucose + BUN).
Sequential acid-base testing can also be helpful. A progressive
increase in the anion gap, or decrease in the blood pH or plasma
bicarbonate over the first several hours post-exposure, should also be

considered suspect for a significant exposure. Patients showing
clinical signs consistent with intoxication and with extremely high
blood lactate levels should also be suspected of having EG
toxicosis.10
The antidotes for EG toxicosis inhibit ADeH. The inhibition of this
enzyme halts the progressive accumulation of toxic metabolites.
Fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole) is the preferred ADeH inhibitor. It
directly inhibits the enzyme and causes less central nervous system
(CNS) depression, diuresis, and acidosis than ethanol does.5,6,11,12
Fomepizole should be continued until at least 36 hours postexposure or until an EG test is negative. Ethanol is still widely used
as an ADeH inhibitor instead. Ethanol does not directly inhibit
ADeH, but rather serves as a competitive substrate for the enzyme.
Ethanol should be continued for at least 24 hours beyond the point
where renal and acid-base values are normal.13,14

• Ethanol (dogs and cats): Using 7% solution, load at 600 mg/kg

Patients should also receive IV isotonic crystalloid fluids at a rate
sufficient to promote diuresis, correct dehydration, and compensate
for ongoing losses (ch. 120). Antiemetics should be administered to
any vomiting patient and any patient with CNS depression (ch. 48).
Clinical hypocalcemia should be treated with IV calcium gluconate
just until signs abate (ch. 284). Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2
or HCO3 <12 mEq/L) should be treated with sodium bicarbonate.
Seizures can be treated with diazepam (ch. 247). Pyridoxine
(vitamin B6; 1-2 mg/kg IV q 6 h) and thiamine (vitamin B1; 50 mg
slow IV over 5 min q 6 h) can help promote the metabolism of
nontoxic end-products from glyoxylic acid.4 Hemodialysis is very
effective at removing EG and its metabolites (ch. 103); however,
ethanol and fomepizole are also dialyzable so their dosages will need
to be increased.16 Renal tubular injury can be reversible, but patients
may require dialysis therapies for weeks to months. It may take up to
a year to regain renal concentrating ability and some patients may
never recover it.4

LILIUM AND HEMEROCALLIS SPP.
Cats are the only species known to consistently suffer
nephrotoxicosis after lily exposure, although there is one case report
of suspected lily toxicosis causing AKI in a meerkat.17 All plants in
the Lilium and Hemerocallis genera are considered toxic (Figure
135.1). The specific toxin remains unknown, but it has been found in
the water-soluble portion of Lilium longiflorum.18 It is suspected
that a toxic metabolite unique to feline physiology is the ultimate
toxicant.19 Exposure to any part of the plant should be considered

toxic, including pollen. Renal injury occurs due to necrosis of the
proximal renal tubular epithelium. The toxin has also caused
degeneration of pancreatic acinar cells.18 The renal tubular
basement membrane often remains intact, making recovery possible
with intensive treatment, including hemodialysis (ch. 103).20
Management of exposures is focused on maintaining urine
production. Cats with dermal exposures should be bathed. Emesis
and AC may be used if large amounts of plant material have been
ingested (ch. 132). The mainstay of treatment is intravenous fluid
diuresis. Cats that are started on diuresis within 18 hours of the
exposure generally have a good prognosis.21 Continuing diuresis for
at least 48 hours is recommended to prevent anuric renal failure (ch.
300).

NONSTEROIDAL ANTI-INFLAMMATORY
DRUGS (NSAIDS)
The toxicity and pharmacokinetics of NSAIDs are species- and
formulation-dependent (Table 135.3). In alert, responsive patients,
decontamination can be attempted (ch. 132), but induction of
emesis is usually unrewarding if not done within an hour of
exposure. An antiemetic should be given after emesis. If the dosage
ingested can cause renal injury, then administration of at least 1 dose
of AC is recommended. If the NSAID undergoes enterohepatic
recirculation, a second dose of AC can be given 6-8 hours after the
first dose. In cases of carprofen overdose, administration of multiple
doses of AC has not been proven to lower serum carprofen levels.22
The bile acid sequestrant cholestyramine has been shown to bind
many NSAIDs and can be used in the first 24-48 h after an
exposure23-26 (ch. 132).

FIGURE 135.1 Lilies and their imposters. Top left:
Lilium sp. (nephrotoxic). Leaves emerge in whorls

directly from the stem. Top right: Hemerocallis sp.
(nephrotoxic). Leaves are long and thin and emerge
in clumps from the base of the plant. Bottom left:
Amaryllis sp. (toxic but GI +/– hepatic, not renal).
Leaves are strap-like and emerge directly from the
bulb. Bottom right: Alstroemeria sp. (nontoxic).
Leaves rotate 180° along long axis just as they
emerge from the stem. Lilium and Hemerocallis
photos courtesy of Dr. Lisa Aileen Paul.
If NSAID intoxication is suspected or known to have occurred, a
baseline urinalysis and renal chemistry profile should be obtained,
and the renal profile should be rechecked daily

(Video 135.1).

Patients should receive isotonic crystalloid fluids at a rate consistent
with twice the daily maintenance requirement (ch. 120).27 The rate
should be adjusted as needed. Faster rates may be indicated for
dehydrated or polyuric patients, while slower rates may be necessary
in patients with cardiac disease. Fluid diuresis should be continued
for at least 48 hours. If azotemia develops, then fluids should be
maintained until the renal values normalize or plateau, and then a
24-hour taper of the fluid rate should commence (ch. 300).
Medications to protect gastrointestinal integrity should be started
upon admission to the hospital. Proton pump inhibitors are
considered the standard of care (e.g., omeprazole 0.85 mg/kg PO or
pantoprazole 1 mg/kg IV q 12 h).28 Additionally, sucralfate and
misoprostol may be of benefit.28 Proton pump inhibitors and
sucralfate are continued for 10-14 days, misoprostol for 3-5 days.
Intravenous lipid emulsion (ch. 132) is a sterile 20% lipid used for
parenteral nutrition. Its use has been described in the treatment of
ibuprofen and naproxen toxicosis in dogs and carprofen toxicosis in
a cat.29-31 Although it may be of benefit, its routine use in lieu of
standard treatments cannot be recommended at this time.32 Total
plasma exchange (TPE), or plasmapheresis, is an extracorporeal
therapy whereby patient plasma (containing toxin-protein
complexes) is removed and replaced with albumin or fresh frozen
plasma. TPE has been used for the treatment of ibuprofen, naproxen,

meloxicam, and carprofen toxicosis.33-35 TPE shows promise as a
useful tool in treating NSAID toxicosis, but more evidence is needed
before it can be recommended in lieu of standard treatments
outlined above. With prompt and thorough treatment, most NSAID
exposures in cats and dogs carry a good prognosis. Patients that
develop bleeding or perforated gastrointestinal ulcers or AKI have a
guarded prognosis.

VITIS SPP. (GRAPES AND RAISINS)
Vitis spp. (grapes, raisins) ingestion in dogs has been associated with
the development of AKI (ch. 300).36 A recent retrospective case
series estimated the prevalence of AKI after Vitis spp. exposure in
dogs to be 6.7%.37 The toxic component is suspected to be tartaric
acid. This compound is found in high levels in some grapes and
raisins, and dogs are uniquely sensitive to its renal effects.38 Renal
lesions in affected patients include necrosis of proximal renal tubules
with basement membranes remaining intact. In some samples,
regeneration of epithelial cells is seen. Mineralized tubular debris or
granular or proteinaceous casts can be present.39
Although AKI has been reported at relatively low dosages, the
individual toxic dose of Vitis spp. has not been established. Ingestion
of any fruit in the Vitis genus should be of concern. Some exposed
dogs will never develop signs. The most common and often initial
sign is spontaneous vomiting. Any patient that develops vomiting
within 48 hours of a grape or raisin exposure should be considered at
risk of AKI and treated intensively. Clinicopathologic findings can
include azotemia, hypercalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, increased
alanine aminotransferase (ALT) activity, hyperglycemia,
hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, isosthenuria, hyposthenuria,
proteinuria, glucosuria, pyuria, crystalluria, and cylindruria.40
If no contraindications to emesis exist, exposed patients should
have emesis induced (ch. 132). Induction of emesis can be
rewarding even up to 12 hours post-exposure. AC should be given
only to patients with large exposures and poor emesis results.
Patients should have a baseline renal chemistry profile and

urinalysis. If decontamination is highly successful and the risk of AKI
is considered low, then patients can be monitored at home. Since
spontaneous vomiting is often the earliest indicator of AKI, if
possible, these patients should not be given an antiemetic prior to
discharge so as not to mask the development of any vomiting.
Patients should have a renal chemistry profile and urinalysis
rechecked at 24-48 hours post exposure or sooner if any clinical
signs develop at home. If decontamination is incompletely
successful, then the patient should be admitted to the hospital for
isotonic crystalloid fluid diuresis for 48 hours. Renal profiles and
urinalyses should still be monitored. Most patients that are promptly
treated with fluid diuresis do not develop AKI. Since the tubular
basement membrane remains intact and epithelial regeneration has
been seen histopathologically, recovery is possible if the condition is
managed proactively. Clinical signs of ataxia, oliguria, and/or
weakness; an elevated Ca × P product; and hyperkalemia have been
correlated with a poorer prognosis.40

IV intravenous
There are numerous toxins that affect the gastrointestinal (GI) system with effects
ranging from mild to severe. Vomiting is common in both dogs and cats. With
severe GI signs, animals can become dehydrated, hypoglycemic (ch. 61),
hypoproteinemic (ch. 60), have electrolyte imbalances and even develop
hypovolemic or hemorrhagic shock (ch. 121). Treatment can range from resting
the GI tract (NPO—nothing per os), to antiemetics, to intravenous (IV) fluids and
blood products. See Table 136.1 for selected GI toxicants in dogs and cats.

ACIDS, ALKALIS
A substance is classified as an acid if when in an aqueous solution, like water, it
donates a proton to a water molecule to form a hydronium ion, H3O. Acidic
substances have a pH below 7 and they include vinegars, hydrochloric acid,
phosphoric acid, sulfuric acid, glycolic acid, and many other acids. These can be
found in toilet bowl cleaners, drain cleaners, metal cleaners, anti-rust compounds,
car battery fluid, facial creams and moisturizers, pool sanitizers and industrial
products. The concentration of acids in various products varies widely.1 Acids with
a pH <2 can cause tissue damage and coagulative necrosis. Contact with strong
acids causes immediate pain, resulting in small ingestions. The absence of ulcers
on the lips, tongue, or oropharyngeal region doesn’t mean there will not be ulcers
in the upper GI tract. At least one source has stated that up to 30% of patients with
esophageal ulcers have no oral lesions.1,2
