A substance is classified as an alkali if the molecule in an aqueous solution
creates more hydroxyl (OH−) ions than hydrogen (H+) ions. Alkaline substances
include alkaline battery fluid, calcium carbide, calcium hydroxide, washing soda,
sodium hydroxide, trisodium phosphate, potassium hydroxide, and many others.
These substances are found in batteries, drain openers, oven cleaners, and
cement.3 Alkalis with a pH >12 cause liquefactive necrosis when tissue contact
occurs. Lesions can be more severe than with acids because nerve endings are
damaged, which results in prolonged contact. Like with acids, the absence of
ulcers in the oral cavity doesn’t preclude ulcers in the upper GI tract. There are
more esophageal lesions with alkali ingestions than with acidic ingestions.2-4
Clinical signs from exposure to either acids or alkalis are similar and they
include ptyalism (ch. 46), vomiting (ch. 48), dysphagia (ch. 47), signs of
abdominal pain, and lethargy, as well as oropharyngeal edema, erythema,
erosions, and ulcerations (ch. 258). The mucosal lesions initially look white (like
a blister), turn grayish in color, and erode. Alkalis may also cause nonfebrile
hyperthermia. Clinical signs typically will be seen between 1-8 hours of exposure
and most ulcers will resolve in 7-14 days.1,2,4
With oral acid/alkali exposure it is important not to induce vomiting, because
induction of vomiting would increase the risk of esophageal burns.1,2,4 Activated
charcoal is ineffective. Dilution with milk or water (0.5 mL/kg PO) is most
effective if given early. Sucralfate slurries (0.25-1 g PO q6-8h) and omeprazole (1
mg/kg PO q12h) should be started for 10-14 days. Severe cases may need IV fluids,
pain control (opioids, ch. 6) and nutritional support (liquid diet, feeding tube; ch.
81).1,2,4

DETERGENTS
Detergents are nonsoap surfactants combined with inorganic ingredients such as
phosphates, silicates, or carbonates. Detergents are classified according to their
charge in solutions: anionic, nonionic, or cationic. While anionic and nonionic
detergents only cause mild GI upset, cationics are more toxic. Cationic detergents
include quaternary ammonium compounds (benzalkonium and benzethonium
chlorides), pyridinium compounds (cetylpyridinium, cetrimonium), and
quinolinium compounds (dequalinium chloride). Cationic detergents are used as
fabric softeners, potpourri oils, hair mousse, antifungals, conditioners, germicides,
and sanitizers. The severity of injury depends on the concentration of the cationic
detergent and the duration of contact. Clinical signs and treatment are similar to
those described for acids and alkalis, above.1,2,4

FERTILIZERS
Fertilizers are products designed to be applied to soil to provide one or more
nutrients needed for plant growth. Fertilizers contain nitrogen, phosphorus, and
potassium (NPK) in different ratios and they can be organic or inorganic. Table
136.2 contains a list of common fertilizer ingredients. Fertilizers can contain
minerals and other additives.5,6 Although ruminants may develop
methemoglobinemia due to ingestion of nitrates, dogs and cats usually only
develop mild self-limiting GI upset. Large ingestions result in more severe
vomiting, diarrhea, and rarely, hind limb weakness or stiffness.
Emesis can be induced to treat recent ingestions (ch. 132). Antiemetics like
maropitant can control vomiting. Activated charcoal does not bind effectively to
fertilizer. IV fluids should be administered if an animal is dehydrated or has
significant vomiting and/or diarrhea. The prognosis is generally good.5,6 Very
large ingestions of bone meal can cause obstipation.

INSOLUBLE CALCIUM OXALATE PLANTS (IO)
Most plants that contain insoluble calcium oxalate (IO) crystals are in the family
Araceae. Table 136.3 includes some of the most common scientific names as well
as common names for IO. All parts of the plant are toxic. The mechanism of action
involves needle-like calcium oxalate crystals (rhaphides) packaged into specialized
cells known as idioblasts. The raphides are found in a gelatinous substance
containing free oxalic acid. When the tip of the idioblast is damaged (such as
biting or chewing on a leaf), water from the sap of the plant or saliva from the
animal flows into the cell, causing the gelatinous material to swell. This propels
the raphides to shoot out of the cell and penetrate the tongue, oral mucosa, and
throat, resulting in mechanical damage and mucosal irritation. The cells may
continue to release the raphides even after the plant material is swallowed.
Proteolytic enzymes stimulate kinin and histamine release. The inflammatory
response aggravates the mechanical damage.7-9

GI, Gastrointestinal.
Clinical signs develop from almost immediately to up to 2-3 hours postexposure. Initial signs typically include head shaking and ptyalism (ch. 46). IO
crystals can cause irritation in the stomach, and diarrhea is possible. Rare reports
of swelling of the oral cavity, pharynx and tongue are found in the medical
literature, but airway obstruction is rare.7,9
Induction of emesis and administration of activated charcoal are not indicated
in IO ingestions. Diluting with a dairy product (milk, yogurt, cottage cheese), and
rinsing the mouth to remove crystals are appropriate. In most cases, GI upset will
resolve within 1-2 hours. If severe vomiting and diarrhea are present, an
antiemetic and fluids can be given. If needed, sucralfate slurries (0.25-1 g PO) may
be used. Calcium oxalate crystals do not reach the kidneys and kidney injury is not
part of this type of intoxication. Therefore, systemic signs aren’t anticipated, and
the prognosis is good.7,9

ORNAMENTAL BULBS
There are numerous plants that grow from bulbs, corms or rhizomes (see Table
136.4). Bulbs can cause a foreign body obstruction and may contain a variety of
potential toxins.10 In most cases, clinical signs include vomiting and diarrhea. The
severity depends on the species of plant, part of plant ingested (foliage vs bulb),
time of year and other factors. If only foliage is ingested, the pet owner can
monitor at home for mild GI upset.10 With bulb ingestion, the clinical signs can be
worse and include hemorrhagic gastroenteritis and potentially hypotension

secondary to hypovolemia (ch. 121). Signs develop within an hour and resolve
within 24 hours.8,10-12

Treatment is supportive, typically involving IV fluids as needed, an antiemetic,
and GI protectants like sucralfate and/or a proton pump inhibitor. If bulbs are
ingested, blood pressure should be monitored (ch. 91) and
hypovolemia/hypotension corrected with fluids or blood products as needed.12 In
most cases, the prognosis is good.

POLYURETHANE ADHESIVES
Polyurethane adhesives are used as glues, tile adhesives, spray foams, and surface
coatings. Polyurethane adhesives that contain isocyanates can expand. See Box
136.1 for some of the chemical names for these adhesives. When animals ingest
the adhesive, the glue expands and polymerizes into a large, friable foreign body in
the stomach. The adhesives are hygroscopic (water-absorbing), and the reaction
proceeds even faster at body temperature. One study documented an 8-fold
increase in volume over 2 hours.13,14
Initial clinical signs include vomiting, lethargy, and possibly signs of abdominal
pain. Signs associated with foreign body obstruction may develop. The expanded
glue is rough and it damages the stomach mucosa, leading to gastric hyperemia,
ulceration, and risk of perforation. Emesis, dilution, and activated charcoal are not
helpful. Abdominal radiographs can be used for determining if a foreign body is
present (as early as 4 hours post-ingestion). On radiographs, there is often a large
mottled radiopacity (frequently resembles a stomach full of kibble). Treatment
involves surgical removal of the foreign body.13

The cardiovascular system has several risk factors for toxin damage. The heart
receives all the systemic circulation and needs a steady supply of nutrients (adenosine
triphosphate [ATP], oxygen, etc.). Any toxin that affects these processes can be
detrimental. The myocardium does not have the ability to regenerate to any
meaningful degree. The lungs receive almost all inhaled toxins. See Table 137.1 for a
list of potential cardiovascular and respiratory toxicants.

ALBUTEROL (CARDIAC)
Albuterol is a bronchodilator used for treating bronchospasm in asthma. It is available
as tablets, solutions for nebulization, and inhalers. In therapeutic doses, albuterol is a
selective beta-2 agonist. Stimulation of beta-2 receptors activates adenyl cyclase in
cellular membranes, leading to increases in cyclic adenosine monophosphate (AMP).
This causes bronchodilation, peripheral vasodilation, and an intracellular shift of
potassium. In an overdose situation, albuterol also stimulates beta-1 activity.1 Beta-1
receptors are primarily located in the myocardium and stimulation increases both
force (inotropy) and rate (chronotropy) of myocardial contractions. Dogs biting into
inhalers is the most common exposure of pets to albuterol. It is well absorbed both
orally and by inhalation.1 Initial agitation followed by depression is common, along
with sinus tachycardia (200-300 bpm), tachypnea, weakness, and death. The longer
sinus tachycardia continues, the more pathological arrhythmias are seen and the
higher the risk of myocardial necrosis.
Emesis and activated charcoal administration (ch. 132) are only effective if done
quickly after tablet ingestion. Intravenous (IV) fluids should be started, and heart rate
and rhythm should be monitored for 12 to 24 hours. If the pet is tachycardic, a non-

selective beta blocker is the drug of choice (e.g., propranolol 0.02-0.06 mg/kg IV;
titrate up as needed to achieve a more contextually-appropriate heart rate, e.g.,
<200/min). Not only will it decrease the heart rate, but it will also help normalize the
serum potassium concentration. If the serum potassium is still <2.5 mEq/L after beta
blocker administration, potassium should be supplemented because hypokalemia
further predisposes to ventricular arrhythmias (ch. 230). Signs usually resolve by 12
hours but can persist up to 48 hours.1 The prognosis is good in most cases but
decreases with the length of time the cardiac signs continue.

ACE, Angiotensin-converting enzyme; AV, atrioventricular; Fab, fragment antigenbinding; IM, intramuscular; IV, intravenous; SA, sinoatrial; SQ, subcutaneous.

CALCIUM CHANNEL BLOCKERS (CCB) (CARDIAC)
Calcium channel blockers (CCBs) are used for treating tachyarrhythmias by slowing
conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node via frequency-dependent channel
blockade at the AV node (nondihydropyridine-type CCBs, e.g., diltiazem, verapamil),
and for treating systemic hypertension via direct action on calcium channels in
smooth muscle (dihydropyridine-type CCBs, e.g., amlodipine, nifedipine). In overdose
situations this leads to bradycardia and severe hypotension, respectively, with ample
crossover of effects possible between types of CCB (severe hypotension being the
predominant concern with either type). Hyperglycemia, hyperkalemia, hypokalemia,
and hypocalcemia are also possible.2
Standard decontamination practices (induction of emesis, administration of
activated charcoal) should be performed in cases of significant exposure. Any patient
ingesting a dose that exceeds the therapeutic dose should be monitored for
bradycardia, hypotension, and related signs. Fluid replacement (ch. 120) and calcium
(calcium chloride or calcium gluconate, ch. 284) administration may help correct
blood pressure and conduction abnormalities.2 IV lipid emulsion therapy (ch. 132)
can be attempted if there is no change in cardiovascular parameters.2,3 Other
therapeutics that can be tried include atropine and isoproterenol for

bradyarrhythmias and norepinephrine, phenylephrine, dopamine, or dobutamine for
hypotension.2 Insulin/dextrose has improved survival in a canine model by improving
cardiac inotropy.4 The prognosis is dependent on dosage and response to therapy.
Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema has been reported in cases of massive overdose.2,5

CARDIAC GLYCOSIDES
Cardiac glycoside (cardenolides) are compounds found in pharmaceuticals (e.g.,
digoxin) along with plants (Table 137.1),6 toads, and fireflies. Cardiac glycosides
inhibit the myocardial cell Na+/K+ ATPase pump. This results in increased
intracellular sodium. The sodium is eliminated by an exchange with calcium. The
sarcoplasmic reticulum binds the excess intracellular calcium and uses it to increase
contractility, leading to more forceful contractions.7 A similar mechanism in the
central nervous system (medulla) increases vagal tone, lowering heart rate. This can
be beneficial in patients with heart disease, but given the narrow therapeutic-toxic
range, can be deadly in overdose situations.
Cardiac effects may include all types of arrhythmias, with first-, second-, or thirddegree AV block, premature atrial or ventricular complexes and atrial or ventricular
tachycardia, and ST segment changes being the most common. In addition to
arrhythmias, extracardiac signs can also be seen. These include vomiting, lethargy,
and inappetence or anorexia.
Emesis can be induced if the animal is not showing clinical signs. Activated charcoal
binds to cardiac glycosides and decreases digoxin absorption by 96%. Cholestyramine
and IV lipid emulsion (ch. 132) have also been shown to be beneficial in
decontamination.8,9 Monitoring for arrhythmias is important (ch. 96) and
antiarrhythmic treatment should be instituted as appropriate (ch. 230). Choose a
non-calcium containing fluid to avoid increasing the risk of arrhythmias. Potassium
levels should be monitored, and insulin/dextrose administered if hyperkalemia is
noted (ch. 296). There is a digoxin-specific immune fragment antigen-binding (Fab)
product available for humans that has been used off label in dogs and cats.10 The
injectable product will bind directly to digoxin, inactivating it. Some studies have
shown cross-reactivity with plant-based cardiac glycosides. It may be cost prohibitive.
The prognosis is good to guarded depending on the severity of clinical signs at
presentation. Clinical signs can last for days due to the long half-life of cardiac
glycosides (digoxin half-life dog: 14.4-56 h; cat: 23.8-42.8 h).11

TOADS (CARDIAC)
While all toads secrete toxins (bufogenins, bufandienolides, bufagins, bufotoxins),
Rhinella marina (the Cane or Giant marine toad, formerly Bufo marinus) and Incilius
alvarius (the Colorado River or Sonoran Desert toad, formerly Bufo alvarius) are the
two species that can cause serious toxic problems in dogs and cats. In the United
States, R. marina is found in Florida, Texas, and Hawaii, while I. alvarius is found in
southern Arizona, southeastern California, and southwestern New Mexico.12 The

toxins are excreted from the parotid glands and act like cardiac glycosides (inhibit the
Na+, K+-ATPase pumps in the myocardial cell membrane).13 Bufogenins may also
have some sodium channel blocking ability. Secondary toxins can affect serotonin and
catecholamines.14 The toxins are contained in the parotid glands and skin. Secretions
may be sufficient to contaminate water sources (water bowls). Most exposures consist
of the animal just “mouthing” the toad, but ingestion may occur. Signs begin almost
immediately and include hypersalivation, vomiting, weakness, lethargy, vocalization,
arrhythmias (brady- and tachyarrhythmias), tachypnea, ataxia, tremors, collapse,
seizures, and death. The severity of the clinical signs is related to the volume of
secretions and the patient’s size.
Decontamination is very important. The mouth should be rinsed from back to front
(point hose or syringe rostrally, to avoid water being swallowed) with tap water. If the
toad was swallowed and the patient is not showing clinical signs, emesis should be
induced or endoscopic or surgical removal should be considered. Treatment for toad
intoxication is the same as for other cardiac glycosides, above. Digoxin immune Fab
may provide antidotal treatment.15 Signs may last 12-36 hours. The prognosis is good
to guarded.

FIREFLIES (CARDIAC)
Firefly (Photinus spp.) toxicosis has been reported in several reptile species, but not
dogs or cats. Fireflies contain lucibufagins, which are related to cardiac glycosides.
Based on experimental studies, approximately 1 firefly per kilogram could be enough
to cause significant cardiovascular abnormalities.16 Clinical signs and treatment are
the same as for cardiac glycosides.

GRAYANOTOXINS (CARDIAC)
Grayanotoxins (andromedotoxins) are compounds found in certain plants (Table
137.1).6 They bind to sodium channels in the excitable cell membranes of nerves and
cardiac and skeletal muscle. This increases the membrane permeability of sodium ions
and maintains the cells in a state of prolonged depolarization. When severe, this
negative chronotropic action decreases sinoatrial node activity, causing arrhythmias
and potentially sinus arrest.17 All animals are susceptible; with non-ruminants, it is
rare that they will eat enough to cause cardiac signs, but vomiting is common. Emesis
can be induced, and activated charcoal can be administered in pets that are not
showing clinical signs. Monitoring heart rate and rhythm is important. Cardiac
arrhythmias may require antiarrhythmic treatment (ch. 230). Signs can last for 1-2
days.17

IMIDAZOLINE DECONGESTANTS (CARDIAC)
Naphazoline, tetrahydrozoline, oxymetazoline, and xylometazoline are imidazoline
decongestants used for the symptomatic relief of rhinitis, sinusitis, or conjunctival

inflammation. They are sympathomimetic agents with primary effects on alphaadrenergic receptors. Ingestion of these compounds can cause vomiting, weakness,
lethargy, bradycardia, respiratory depression, and coma.18
Imidazoline decongestants are readily absorbed via the gastrointestinal (GI) tract
and signs occur within 30 minutes to 4 hours of exposure. Induction of emesis and
administration of activated charcoal are usually not indicated due to the quick onset of
signs. Monitoring should include assessments of heart rate and mentation. Reversal of
clinical signs can be achieved with atipamezole (50 mcg/kg, one-fourth IV, rest IM) or
yohimbine (0.1 mg/kg IV). These medications may need to be repeated in 1-2 hours.18

PARAQUAT (RESPIRATORY)
Paraquat is a bipyridylium herbicide used as a defoliant. Paraquat is actively
transported into the pneumocytes, and it accumulates in the lung due to the diaminepolyamine concentrator system found in alveolar epithelial cells.19,20 In the
pneumocyte, paraquat undergoes reduction by a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide
phosphate (NADPH)-dependent reaction to the monocation radical. This monocation
reacts with oxygen to form a superoxide radical and regenerates the parent compound
to allow this reaction to occur again. This radical production damages cell membranes
and organelles leading to cell death.19,20
Initial clinical signs consist of vomiting. With large ingestions, elevations of renal
and liver values occur 48-72 hours later. As the lung heals by fibrosis, pulmonary signs
occur a week or more after exposure. The severe signs are seen with ingestion of the
concentrated product; when diluted appropriately for use, only GI signs are
expected.20
Treatment needs to be timely and intensive. Paraquat is poorly absorbed from the
GI tract, so induction of emesis and administration of activated charcoal can be given
even to patients who are showing clinical signs. Paraquat levels peak in the lungs 4-5
days after exposure. Hemodialysis gives the best prognosis (ch. 103). Oxygen
increases oxidative injury in the lungs.19 The prognosis is guarded to poor.

PHENYLPROPANOLAMINE (CARDIAC)
Phenylpropanolamine (PPA) is a sympathomimetic agent used in veterinary medicine
for controlling urinary incontinence in dogs. While signs can start with ingestions of 1
mg/kg (which is in the recommended therapeutic dosage range), serious signs appear
at doses above 20 mg/kg. Initially, patients may be agitated and tachycardic, but as
the blood pressure increases (vasoconstriction), they may become lethargic and
bradycardic.21 Piloerection, tremors (ch. 42), and seizures (ch. 45) can also occur.
Signs usually start within 30-90 minutes and may continue up to 48 hours, depending
on dosage ingested.22
Emesis can be induced if the patient is not showing clinical signs. Activated charcoal
should be given if the dosage is of concern. Blood pressure should be closely
monitored (ch. 91) and nitroprusside or other vasodilators can be used to manage

hypertension.21 Atropine is contraindicated in the management of bradycardia as it
can worsen the hypertension. IV fluids should be titrated to promote excretion, protect
renal function, and help with thermoregulation (ch. 120). As with intoxications with
other stimulants, cyproheptadine may be given if signs of serotonin syndrome
develop.21

SULFURYL FLUORIDE (CARDIAC ±
RESPIRATORY)
Sulfuryl fluoride is a fumigant gas used to kill termites.23 It is released into the
environment after tenting a building. Sulfuryl fluoride is colorless and odorless so it is
combined with the lacrimator chloropicrin (related to tear gas). Most small animal
exposures occur with animals returning to a tented home or being trapped in the
crawlspace. When pets inhale the gas, the free fluoride found in sulfuryl fluoride binds
to calcium, leading to hypocalcemia (chs. 69, 284), tetany, seizures, arrhythmias,
and death. The chloropicrin causes respiratory irritation (coughing, nasal and ocular
discharge).
Treatment consists of maintaining ventilation, oxygenation, and correcting the
hypocalcemia.24 Other electrolytes, such as potassium and magnesium, can also be
affected. Lidocaine can be used appropriately for ventricular dysrhythmias (ch.
230).24 Fluids should be used judiciously as pulmonary edema can occur. The
prognosis is poor.

YEW (TAXUS SPP.) (CARDIAC)
Yews are ornamental plants that are commonly used for landscaping as they stay
green year-round. Yews contain taxine alkaloids that have a direct action on cardiac
myocyte ion channels. They inhibit the normal exchange of sodium and calcium across
myocardial cells.25 This depresses cardiac depolarization and leads to arrhythmias
(potentially fatal). All parts of the plant, except for the flesh of the red berry, are toxic.
Sudden death is not uncommon within a few hours after ingestion. Animals may also
experience bradycardia, dyspnea, weakness, ataxia, collapse, and hypothermia.
Activated charcoal will bind taxine alkaloids, but the stress of administration could
potentially worsen clinical signs. Treatment consists of supportive care. Patients that
survive 12 hours are likely to survive the intoxication.25

Many toxicants can affect the blood. In general, these can be divided into those
that cause coagulopathy, those that cause hemolysis and/or
methemoglobinemia, and those that cause cytopenias due to bone marrow
damage.

COAGULOPATHIES
ANTICOAGULANT RODENTICIDES
Several different toxicants can cause coagulopathy and/or
thrombocytopenia/pathia (Table 138.1). The most common cause of toxic
coagulopathies are anticoagulant rodenticides (ARs) These have been a mainstay
of rodent control worldwide for decades. However, in 2017, the U.S.
Environmental Protection Agency banned the over-the-counter sale of several
long-acting ARs, including bromadiolone, brodifacoum, and difethialone;
nevertheless, ARs are still commonly used by pest-control operators and can be
purchased in large buckets for commercial or agricultural uses.1 Warfarin

(Coumadin) is still used as an AR and can also be encountered as a medicinal
anticoagulant.
ARs work by blocking the recycling of vitamin K, principally by inhibiting the
enzyme vitamin K 1,2,3-epoxide reductase. Vitamin K is needed to carboxylate
clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X (ch. 171).2 As these factors are depleted,
spontaneous bleeding can occur 3-7 days after ingestion of AR. Sites of
hemorrhage include the thorax (most commonly), abdomen, joints (especially in
large-breed dogs), subcutis, or central nervous system (CNS). Initial signs may
be vague, such as anorexia and lethargy. These can progress to dyspnea,
lameness, weakness, pale mucous membranes, CNS signs (paralysis, seizures),
and blood-loss anemia (ch. 57).2

Because of disagreement among studies looking at toxicity of ARs, no
definitive toxic dose has been determined. It is recommended that ingestions of
>0.02 mg/kg should receive decontamination and possibly treatment.2 Because
of its lower toxicity and the need for multiple doses, ingestions of <0.5 mg/kg of
warfarin/Coumadin are unlikely to cause bleeding.
Decontamination can be attempted within 4 hours of ingestion (ch. 132).
While emesis is standard, the risks of administering activated charcoal
(aspiration, hypernatremia) may outweigh the benefits and relative safety of
vitamin K1 treatment. After a recent ingestion, treatment can either consist of
monitoring the prothrombin time (PT) or starting vitamin K1.2 Since factor VII
has the shortest half-life in dogs and cats, the PT can become prolonged first,
within 48-72 hours of exposure. Therefore, a single PT assessed between these
hours should be sufficient to determine if treatment is needed. If the PT is
prolonged or a large dose was ingested, vitamin K1 should be started. The
vitamin K1 dosage is 1.5-2.5 mg/kg q12h administered PO with a small fatty
meal.2 In small patients (puppies, kittens), the injectable form can be
administered orally. The duration of treatment depends on the agent ingested.
For warfarin (Coumadin), 14 days; for all other ARs, treatment should continue
for 30 days except for bromadiolone, which is for 21 days.2
If the patient is actively bleeding or has a very prolonged PT, in addition to
starting vitamin K1, plasma (fresh or fresh frozen) should be given to provide
immediately available clotting factors (ch. 124).2 In cases of severe anemia,
whole blood can be administered. If severe dyspnea is present, thoracentesis may
be needed to provide relief (ch. 92). In that case, the red blood cells (RBCs) can
be returned to the patient via autotransfusion but should be run though a filter to
remove any clots. The autotransfused blood will provide oxygen carrying
capacity but no coagulation factors.

FACTOR XA ANTAGONISTS
Recently, new anticoagulant medications have been available for human use,
mainly to prevent deep-vein thrombosis and thrombi associated with atrial
fibrillation. These medications, including apixaban (Eliquis) and rivaroxaban
(Xarelto), are factor Xa reversible inhibitors. They are emerging in veterinary use
for prevention of thromboembolism (ch. 238). The LD50 for apixaban in dogs is
>1500 mg/kg.3 Dogs ingesting the medication may demonstrate prolonged PT
and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) but spontaneous bleeding has not been
seen in dogs even at dosages as high as 27.55 mg/kg.4

HEMOLYSIS
Numerous agents can cause hemolysis and/or methemoglobin (MetHgb) (Table
138.1). Hemolysis may be seen due to direct RBC membrane damage or
secondary to oxidative damage and denaturing of the hemoglobin with the
formation of Heinz bodies. Cats are more susceptible to oxidative hemoglobin
damage because their hemoglobin contains 8 free sulfhydryl groups as compared
to 4 in dogs. Heinz bodies appear as translucent blebs at the periphery of RBC in
Giemsa-stained slides (ch. 57, Figure 57.2); the use of new methylene blue
stain can greatly enhance the identification of Heinz bodies, which appear as
blue-staining RBC inclusion bodies.5
Decontamination of patients who have ingested hemolytic toxins includes
induction of emesis and administration of activated charcoal if appropriate (e.g.,
based on toxin ingested, time frame since ingestion, health history, clinical signs,
and risk of aspiration being greater than the benefit of emesis) (ch. 132). Serial
hematocrits and blood smears looking for Heinz bodies can be monitored for
about 5 days after exposure, as peak effects can be delayed for several days.
Owners should be instructed to monitor for pale mucous membranes, weakness,
and hemoglobinuria.5
If hemolysis has already begun, IV fluid diuresis should be administered to
protect the kidneys from hemoglobinuric nephropathy (ch. 120). Sodium
bicarbonate (2-3 mEq/kg given over several hours in IV fluids) may help to
minimize hemoglobin precipitation in the renal tubules. If the anemia is severe,
transfusions of whole blood or packed RBCs can be used for supplying enough
oxygen carrying capacity to make the patient comfortable (ch. 124).5

ALLIUM spp.
Allium spp. include onions, garlic, leeks, and chives. They are toxic in the raw,
cooked, or dried form. In dogs, ingestion of 15-30 g/kg of raw onions can cause
hemolysis; garlic is about 3× more potent than onions.6 Cats are about 3× more
sensitive to the effects of Allium spp. Changes in hematocrit may be seen in as
little as 12 hours but typically are seen in 2-5 days.

ZINC
Zinc toxicosis is most likely seen after ingestion of metallic-zinc items. US
pennies minted after 1982 are composed of a copper-clad zinc core; other
sources of zinc include galvanized metal and other hardware (nuts, bolts,
screws). These zinc objects are solubilized by stomach acid, with subsequent
absorption of zinc. Zinc causes oxidative damage to the RBC, leading to its
destruction.7 Zinc oxide, commonly found in diaper-rash ointment or

sunscreens, rarely causes hemolysis. Zinc oxide is extremely irritating to the
stomach and generally results in rapid emesis and self-decontamination.
However, cases in which large amounts of ointment are ingested and
decontamination is incomplete, or small quantities are ingested chronically, may
result in hemolysis.
After ingestion of metallic zinc, induction of emesis can be attempted (ch.
132). Activated charcoal is not effective against heavy metals such as zinc.
Radiographs may be useful in locating metallic objects in the gastrointestinal
(GI) tract; however, lack of such objects doesn’t rule out zinc toxicosis as the
metal may have fully dissolved. Blood zinc levels may be measured, and this
requires a purpose-made blood collection tube (royal blue stopper) because
rubber stoppers of all standard blood tubes contain prohibitive amounts of zinc.
If emesis is unsuccessful, then removal of metallic objects via endoscope or
surgery should be attempted.7 The use of proton-pump inhibitors (e.g.,
omeprazole 0.7-1 mg/kg PO q12h) preoperatively may reduce solubilization of
metallic zinc in the stomach. If hemolysis has begun, treatment as outlined above
should be started (ch. 124). Hemolysis may still occur up to 72 hours after
removal of a zinc foreign body from the GI tract. Chelation is rarely needed as
zinc levels will drop rapidly following removal of the metal.7

METHEMOGLOBINEMIA
Methemoglobin (MetHgb) occurs when the iron in hemoglobin is oxidized from
the ferrous form (Fe2+) to the ferric form (Fe3+); the ferric form of iron is
incapable of carrying oxygen (ch. 27). This change reduces the blood’s oxygen
carrying capacity; in animals with MetHgb, the blood appears dark brown and
the mucous membranes take on a “chocolate” or muddy cast. Many toxins may
cause both hemolysis and methemoglobinemia (Table 138.1).
Decontamination consisting of induction of emesis and administration of
activated charcoal can be instituted if appropriate (ch. 132). For
methemoglobinemia, the patient should be monitored for signs of brown- or
muddy-colored gums and dyspnea. Pre-emptive use of antioxidants has not
proven effective for many of the hemolytic agents (except for acetaminophen;
ch. 134). N-acetylcysteine can be administered with a loading dose of 140 mg/kg
PO or IV followed by 70 mg/kg PO q6h for 5-7 additional doses. Also, ascorbic
acid (20-30 mg/kg PO, IM, IV q8h × 3 days) can be given, as it reduces MetHgb
back to hemoglobin.8 Oxygen should be administered as needed (ch. 123).
Methylene blue (1-1.5 mg/kg slow IV) can be used for accelerating the reduction
of MetHgb back to hemoglobin. The use of methylene blue is considered
controversial in cats as it can cause Heinz bodies and MetHgb.9

ACETAMINOPHEN

Acetaminophen (Tylenol, non-aspirin pain reliever, N-acetyl-p-aminophenol
[APAP], paracetamol in many countries) is a synthetic non-opiate derivative of
p-aminophenol (ch. 134). APAP is quickly absorbed and peak plasma levels are
seen at 10-60 minutes (60-120 min for extended release). It is distributed into
most body tissues, with the highest concentrations in the periportal zone of the
liver and the renal medulla. The metabolism of acetaminophen occurs primarily
in the liver.8
A byproduct of acetaminophen metabolism, via phase 1 deacetylation, is paraaminophenol (PAP). It is implicated in the hematotoxic effects seen in cats and
dogs.8 While PAP is rapidly conjugated to glutathione (GSH) or acetate in
laboratory rodents, cats have a reduced capacity for n-acetylation and dogs lack
the hepatic n-acetyltransferase enzyme. GSH becomes depleted in the RBCs, and
hemoglobin is oxidized to MetHgb. MetHgb values increase within 2-4 hours,
followed by Heinz body formation. N-acetylcysteine decreases the half-life of
methemoglobin in cats from 10 to 5 hours.8

NAPHTHALENE MOTHBALLS
Naphthalene mothballs are very toxic, and 1-2 mothballs can cause
methemoglobinemia and hemolysis.10 Not all mothballs are naphthalene and
may instead be paradichlorobenzene (can cause CNS signs). The two can be
differentiated using a saturated salt solution. Three heaping teaspoons (30-40 g)
of table salt are added to 4 ounces (120 mL) of warm water and stirred until no
more salt will dissolve. Then one unknown mothball is dropped into a glass of
plain water and another one into the salt solution. Naphthalene will sink in water
but float in saturated salt solution while paradichlorobenzene will sink in both.10
Decontamination can be considered if the ingestion was recent (naphthalene
mothballs dissolve in the stomach during the first 1-2 hours), via endoscopy or
gastric lavage. Treatment for toxicosis-induced hemolysis is as indicated above.

BONE MARROW SUPPRESSION
Many agents can cause bone marrow suppression or aplasia either from chronic
use or acute overdose (Table 138.1 and ch. 176). Treatment consists of
decontamination of the patient in the earliest stages (subclinical), specific
antidotes if available (e.g., leucovorin for methotrexate), and baseline and serial
monitoring of complete blood counts for 2 weeks or longer depending on the
toxic agent. Filgrastim (1-5 mcg/kg SQ daily) can be administered if severe
neutropenia develops.11 RBC transfusions may be used for treating anemias (ch.
124) and darbepoetin (0.45 mcg/kg)12 or erythropoietin (100 U/kg SQ 3 times a
week to start; concern exists due to autoantibodies if using human

formulation)13 may be helpful in restarting bone marrow erythropoiesis (ch.
172).

ESTROGENS
Estrogens can cause bone marrow damage at high dosages; signs can take up to
14 days to manifest.14 The acute ingestion of 1 mg/kg of estrogens can cause
signs and can be seen with ingestion of high-dose estrogen supplements or
estradiol cypionate used as a “mismating shot.” 4 Most birth control pills contain
estrogen at 20-50 mcg/pill, which would require ingestion of 20-50 tablets/kg,
and so are rarely an issue. Similarly, diethylstilbestrol (for hormone-responsive
urethral sphincter mechanism incompetence; ch. 310) at standard dosages has a
long track record of safety in dogs. Treatment for aplastic anemia is discussed
above and in ch. 176. In addition, lithium carbonate or lithium citrate can
stimulate production of neutrophils.

Pharmacokinetics describe the absorption, distribution, metabolism and
elimination of drugs. For example, morphine is rapidly absorbed into the
plasma from the injection site following intramuscular administration in dogs.
Morphine distributes throughout the body, including the central nervous system
(CNS) where it elicits its analgesic effects. Morphine is metabolized primarily to
the inactive metabolite morphine-3-glucuronide, ending its pharmacologic
effect. The inactive metabolite is primarily eliminated in the urine. In contrast to
dogs, cats metabolize morphine primarily to morphine-3-sulfate, a speciesspecific difference in morphine metabolism.

ABSORPTION
Drug absorption from the site of administration occurs for any extravascular
dose, assuming systemic effects are desired. Per os (PO) oral, intramuscular
(IM), subcutaneous (SC), transdermal (TD) and transmucosal (TM) drug
administration are the most common routes of delivery in dogs and cats.
Drug absorption can occur by passive diffusion (through lipid membranes or
aqueous pores and capillary fenestrations) or through one of many transporters
(e.g., anionic, cationic, and amino acid transporters). Diffusion is directly
proportional to surface area and drug gradient, and lipid diffusion is directly
proportional to the drug’s lipophilicity and inversely proportional to the
thickness of the membrane. Drug absorption by diffusion is not saturable;
therefore, higher doses result in proportionally greater drug absorption.
However, absorption by transporters can be saturated, resulting in decreased
rate or extent of absorption with higher doses (less than proportional) as seen
with gabapentin in dogs.1
Bioavailability is the extent or fraction of drug absorbed after extravascular
administration and the rate of absorption. For the context of this chapter,
bioavailability refers to the extent of drug absorption. Numerous factors can
result in incomplete bioavailability. Bioavailability after IM or SC administration
can be decreased at the injection site by tissue sequestration (e.g., tissue
binding, granuloma formation, scarring etc.), degradation or metabolism,
incomplete release from pharmaceutic formulation, or inadequate blood flow to
site of administration (e.g., shock, or injection into connective tissue).
Oral drug bioavailability may be decreased due to drug degradation or
instability (e.g., acid hydrolysis in the stomach), pre-systemic metabolism,
gastrointestinal (GI) motility dysfunction (ileus or hypermotility), binding to
ingesta or the inability to cross the intestinal epithelium due to low lipid
solubility, ionization, or lack of saturation of appropriate transporters. Oral
bioavailability can also be decreased by transporters pumping drug that was
absorbed back into the intestinal lumen (e.g., p-glycoprotein [p-gp] efflux
pump).2
Tablets, capsules, suspensions, and solutions can all be administered PO.
Solid dosage forms must first disintegrate in the GI fluid and then dissolve into
solution prior to drug absorption. Some drugs are poorly soluble in the GI tract
(e.g., itraconazole) and have low bioavailability. Solid dosage forms may be
formulated to alter the rate of disintegration or dissolution to decrease rate of
absorption (extended release) or target disintegration for a specific part of the
GI tract (delayed release). Most oral delayed- or extended-release formulations
are designed for people and may not be effective or consistent in animals due to
differences in GI anatomy and physiology. These formulations may have
immediate release in animals or may be passed through the GI tract without
releasing the drug. Therefore, delayed- or extended-release formulations may
not produce their desired effects in animals.

The primary site of drug absorption following PO administration is the small
intestine (duodenum and jejunum and to a lesser extent ileum). The large
surface area and presence of active transporters facilitate absorption of drugs
from the intestinal tract. Metabolizing enzymes (both Phase I and Phase II; see
Metabolism, below) are also present in the intestine. These enzymes can
metabolize absorbed drugs before the drugs enter the vasculature, thereby
decreasing oral bioavailability.3 Drugs absorbed from the intestine enter the
portal circulation, which carries the drugs directly to the liver. As the drugs pass
through the liver, they are again exposed to drug metabolizing enzymes (Phase I
and Phase II) which can decrease systemic drug exposure. The sum of intestinal
and hepatic presystemic metabolism is referred to as first-pass metabolism. It is
important to note that the majority of drugs absorbed from the rectum and large
intestine in dogs and cats enters the portal circulation; therefore, they do not
bypass first-pass drug metabolism.4,5
IM and SC drug administration deposits drug in the interstitial fluid in the
musculature or SC space, resulting in absorption into the plasma space through
pores, fenestrations or diffusion, and via absorption into the lymphatics.
Therefore, drugs with low lipophilicity like aminoglycosides can still be absorbed
without diffusion through cell membranes. First-pass metabolism and its effects
on bioavailability are avoided for IM and SC injections. Drugs administered IM
or SC as suspensions (solid particles suspended in a liquid) must first dissolve
prior to absorption. Some suspension formulations may provide prolonged
dosage intervals due to delayed absorption (e.g., procaine penicillin G,
methylprednisolone acetate), but not all suspensions provide sustained effects.
Drugs administered IM or SC as solutions may result in more rapid absorption
compared to suspensions assuming they are small drug molecules capable of
diffusion into the vasculature, but some extended-release formulations are
solutions (e.g., buprenorphine injection, Simbadol). Therefore, the individual
formulation pharmacokinetics should be evaluated to establish a patient’s
dosage.
Pain may occur on injection due to tonicity, inflammation, preservatives such
as benzyl alcohol, solvents, or due to the active ingredient itself. Acidic or
alkaline solutions may result in pain as well, which is the reason adding pH
neutralizers to decrease pain is sometimes recommended (e.g., adding sodium
bicarbonate to lidocaine or fentanyl extravascular injections). Sterile or aseptic
techniques are desired for IM and SC drug administration as introduction of
bacteria or foreign material can result in abscesses, cellulitis and even
septicemia in extreme cases. SC injections may have decreased and erratic
absorption due to dehydration, hypotension, hypothermia and obesity; in these
patients, IM injections are preferred.
Transdermal (TD) and transmucosal (TM) administration avoids first pass
metabolism and may result in greater bioavailability than oral administration
for drugs affected by first pass metabolism. TD drug administration may also
result in a depot effect due to sequestration in the stratum corneum. Drugs have

to be lipophilic and un-ionized to undergo TD and TM absorption, which limits
the number of drugs available for these routes. It is important to note that very
few drugs sold as compounded pluronic lecithin organogel (PLO) formulations
actually undergo TD absorption and most are ineffective. Compounded drugs
are not required to demonstrate safety or efficacy (see Generic and Compounded
Drugs [below]). Some TD PLO methimazole formulations are effective in some
animals (e.g., methimazole in cats), but are more variable than PO administered
drugs. Ideally, specific patient monitoring should be available to document
efficacy of TD formulation (e.g., T4 monitoring in cats treated with TD
methimazole).

DISTRIBUTION
Drug distribution is dependent on many factors including drug lipophilicity,
regional blood flow, anatomic barriers, transporters, drug ionization and plasma
protein binding. Drug lipophilicity is a measure of the drug’s solubility in lipids.
Drugs that are poorly soluble in lipids (low lipophilicity) have little ability to
reach intracellular targets and tend to have restricted distribution (unless active
transporters facilitate movement). For example, aminoglycosides are poorly
lipophilic and as a result are ineffective for intracellular infections or infections
in protected tissues such as the brain and prostate. In contrast, gabapentin is
also poorly lipophilic, but it undergoes active transport into the brain resulting
in antianxiety effects.
Highly perfused tissues are tissues that have a high blood flow to tissue mass
ratio (Table 139.1). Highly perfused tissues have faster equilibration between
plasma and tissue concentrations, often resulting in equilibration at higher drug
concentrations than tissues that are not highly perfused (Figure 139.1). For
example, fentanyl brain concentrations equilibrate more rapidly and at higher
plasma concentrations after IV injection than less highly perfused tissues such
as muscle. As fentanyl continues to distribute into the anatomically large
volumes of muscle (in addition to metabolism), the plasma concentrations
decrease below the CNS concentrations, resulting in fentanyl diffusing out of the
CNS resulting in the loss of central opioid effects. Therefore, the loss of central
opioid effects of fentanyl is due in part to drug redistribution from the CNS to
the plasma.
Anatomic barriers can decrease drug distribution into certain tissues for
poorly lipophilic drugs. The blood-brain barrier acts as a physical barrier;
features include glial cells and tight junctions, which decrease drug penetration
into the CNS. Active transporters (e.g., p-gp efflux pump) remove drug that
penetrates the CNS by pumping the drug back into the vasculature, decreasing
CNS drug concentrations. Animals affected by p-gp mutations or treated with pgp inhibitors can have higher CNS drug concentrations, resulting in pronounced
central effects of p-gp substrates (e.g., ivermectin and loperamide after “normal”
dosages). Enhanced toxicity can occur in animals with normal functioning p-gp

when a p-gp inhibitor is administered concurrently with a p-gp substrate due to
a drug-drug interaction (e.g., ivermectin toxicosis occurring when spinosad, an
inhibitor of p-gp, and ivermectin, a p-gp substrate, are administered
concurrently).

FIGURE 139.1 Theoretical drug concentration versus time
profile of intravenous fentanyl. The orange line represents
plasma drug concentration, the green line represents central
nervous system (CNS) fentanyl concentration, and the blue
line represents muscle drug concentration. Fentanyl is
lipophilic and it rapidly diffuses into the highly perfused CNS
and equilibrates at higher plasma concentrations. However,
less well perfused tissues such as muscle equilibrate later and
at lower drug concentrations. The loss of CNS (analgesic)
effects of fentanyl is due in part to fentanyl redistributing
from the CNS back into the plasma.

The blood-prostate, blood-bronchus and blood-ocular barriers also decrease
drug penetration into those tissues. Drugs with high lipophilicity are needed to
penetrate these tissues as well. Other anatomic barriers occur in tissues such as
the mammary gland, testes, placenta and synovium, but in general they are lesseffective barriers to drug penetration.
Drugs that are highly bound to plasma proteins may have restricted
distribution as the protein drug complex is too big to diffuse out of the plasma.
For example, cefovecin is highly protein-bound, resulting in a low fraction of
cefovecin distributing into the tissues.6 However, it is important to note that
plasma protein binding is reversible and there is always some free drug available
that can diffuse out of the vasculature. Therefore, some drugs that have high
protein binding can still distribute throughout the body. For example,
buprenorphine is highly protein-bound in dogs but it distributes well into the
CNS, producing central opioid effects.7 Many references still caution against
using multiple highly protein-bound drugs concurrently due to protein binding
interactions, but the likelihood of a true interaction is minimal. For a protein
binding interaction to occur, the drugs would have to be administered IV, have
to have a low therapeutic index, and undergo rapid hepatic metabolism.

METABOLISM
Drug metabolism results in chemical changes to the drug molecule to enhance
renal or biliary elimination. A drug may not undergo metabolism (e.g.,
gentamicin is eliminated through glomerular filtration and doxycycline is
eliminated by biliary secretion). A drug may undergo a single metabolic process
(e.g., morphine is primarily metabolized to morphine-3-glucuronide in dogs). A
drug may also undergo multiple metabolism processes (diazepam in dogs is
metabolized to temazepam, temazepam is then metabolized to oxazepam,
followed by oxazepam being metabolized to oxazepam-glucuronide).
Metabolism does not always inactivate a drug. For example, tramadol is
metabolized to O-desmethyltramadol in cats, which has greater opioid effects
than tramadol. Metabolism may also vary by species. For example,
approximately 60% of codeine is metabolized to morphine in humans, but <1%
of codeine is metabolized to morphine in dogs and cats, with codeine-6glucuronide being the major metabolite in dogs, but norcodeine the major
metabolite in cats.8

There are two primary metabolism pathways: Phase I (metabolic) and Phase
II (conjugation) reactions. Phase I, metabolic reactions (oxidation, reduction,
hydrolysis, and hydration) are catalyzed by a variety of enzymes. Cytochrome
P450 (CYP) enzymes are a major group of enzymes commonly involved in Phase
I drug metabolism. CYPs are classified into families (>40% amino acid
homology) designated with a number, subfamilies (>55% amino acid homology)
designated with a letter and the specific enzyme is labeled with a number. For
example, methadone is metabolized by CYP2B11 in dogs, but diazepam is
metabolized by both CYP2B11 and CYP3A12/26 in dogs.
Species similarities and differences occur in CYP substrate and inhibitor
specificity. For example, similar metabolism of midazolam occurs by the canine
CYP3A12/26 and human CYP3A4 orthologs. Similarly, ketoconazole inhibits the
CYP3A enzyme orthologs in dogs and humans. However, substrate/inhibitor
specificity differences also occur. For example, chloramphenicol inhibits
CYP2B11 in dogs, but in humans chloramphenicol inhibits CYP2C19.
Species similarities and differences in metabolite formation can also occur.
For example, tramadol is primarily metabolized to the inactive metabolite ndesmethyltramadol in dogs, but to the active metabolite O-desmethyltramadol
in cats.9 The difference in primary metabolites formed may be due to the
relative amounts of the different CYP isoforms (e.g., cats may have a larger
amount of CYP2D than dogs, which forms the active metabolite, but dogs have a
relatively larger amount of CYP2B11, which forms the inactive metabolite).
Different affinities of the drugs and enzymes, or lack of certain enzymes, can
also contribute to species differences in drug metabolism.
CYP can be inhibited or induced, producing clinically relevant drug
interactions. Clinically relevant drug interactions due to CYP inhibition
(resulting in prolonged effect) are relatively specific and more likely to occur
when a drug is a substrate for a specific CYP (not metabolized by multiple CYPs)
and has a low therapeutic index. Clinically relevant drug interactions due to CYP
induction (resulting in decreased/shortened effect) typically occur due to
increase in CYP content (more metabolizing enzymes) resulting in more rapid
drug metabolism. Clinically relevant CYP drug interactions are included in
Table 139.2.
Phase II metabolism pathways are conjugation reactions that add an
endogenous substrate to the drug molecule, resulting in a metabolite with larger
size and decreased lipophilicity. The Phase II metabolite can then be eliminated
by glomerular filtration, renal secretion, or biliary secretion. Glucuronidation,
sulfation, acetylation and amino acid conjugation reactions are the most
common Phase II metabolism pathways. Specific enzymes are associated with
each type of conjugation reaction and there are often enzyme subtypes. Drug
interactions with conjugation enzymes are not well characterized in animals and
are thought to be rare.
Species-specific differences in conjugation reactions have been identified. For
example, uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) is the enzyme
family catalyzing glucuronide conjugation with UGT1A6, 1A7, 1A9, 1A11 and

2B31 present in dogs. Cats are deficient in UGT1A6 and 1A9, which results in
decreased or alternate conjugation of some conjugation substrates including
acetaminophen and morphine.10 The lack of acetaminophen glucuronide
conjugation results in large amounts of acetaminophen undergoing Phase I
metabolism producing toxic metabolites in cats even at low (subtherapeutic)
acetaminophen doses. In contrast, the lack of morphine glucuronidation in cats
is clinically “irrelevant” as no reactive morphine metabolites are formed and
morphine is rapidly eliminated in cats by an alternate pathway (sulfate
conjugation), resulting in a similar elimination half-life in dogs and cats.
Dogs lack N-acetyltransferase enzymes and as such are deficient in forming
acetyl conjugates. Clinical effects of the deficiency include lack of N-acetyl
procainamide (NAPA) metabolite formation of procainamide, a class I
antiarrhythmic (sodium channel antagonist).11 The NAPA metabolite is a class
III antiarrhythmic (potassium channel antagonist); therefore, the
antiarrhythmic effects of procainamide in dogs are different (class I effects only)
compared to other species (class I and III antiarrhythmic effects). Sulfonamide
metabolism in most species also involves acetylation reactions, but acetylation
deficiency in dogs contributes increased risk of sulfonamide hypersensitivity
reactions due to reactive metabolite formation.12
Drug metabolism (both Phase I and Phase II) may be decreased with hepatic
disease, but the extent of decreased drug metabolism may not be proportional to
the extent of disease (both groups of enzymes occur in other tissues such as the
intestine) (chs. 269 to 271). There are little data evaluating the
pharmacokinetics or metabolism of drugs in animals with naturally occurring
liver disease; therefore, specific recommendations on dosage adjustments are
not available. If single parenteral doses or PO doses of highly bioavailable drugs
are administered, the maximum drug effect will be similar, but the duration of
effect may be markedly longer. However, multiple doses may result in greater
than expected drug accumulation due to a prolonged terminal half-life and drug
accumulation (see Half-Life, below). Low PO bioavailable drugs may result in
adverse effects even with a single dose, due to less first-pass metabolism
resulting in higher PO bioavailability (and drug concentrations) in animals with
liver disease. The best option for animals with hepatic disease would be
choosing a drug with a similar effect, but undergoing renal elimination (e.g.,
choosing atenolol instead of propranolol for beta-blockade). Another approach
would be to choose a drug with a greater safety profile, such as choosing an
opioid vs. a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug for analgesia. Therapeutic drug
monitoring (TDM) is available for some drugs and patient-specific dosage
adjustments can be made based on plasma concentrations (e.g., digoxin dosage
adjusted base on TDM), but progression of disease may result in unpredictable
changes in plasma concentrations. Adjusting dosage based on clinical response
is another option, but this option would be limited to drugs with a high
therapeutic index and in which responses can be readily monitored (e.g., oral

codeine without acetaminophen in a dog with liver impairment and
osteoarthritis).

Other metabolism enzymes are present, but contribute less commonly to drug
metabolism. Plasma esterases metabolize remifentanil. Xanthine oxidase
metabolizes a 6-mercaptopurine, an azathioprine active metabolite. Ethylene
glycol and ethanol are metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase. These enzymes

also have the potential for drug interactions (e.g., allopurinol inhibits xanthine
oxidase and high ethanol doses saturate alcohol dehydrogenase).

ELIMINATION
Elimination removes drug and metabolites from the body (Box 139.1). Some
drugs are not metabolized and instead are eliminated as unchanged drug (e.g.,
gentamicin eliminated by glomerular filtration). Some drugs are eliminated as
both intact drug and drug metabolites (e.g., renal elimination of codeine and
norcodeine in cats). Other drugs are almost completely metabolized and
eliminated primarily as metabolites (e.g., morphine glucuronide in dogs).
Renal elimination of drugs and drug metabolites can occur by glomerular
filtration and renal tubular secretion. Renal tubular reabsorption of drugs can
also occur, decreasing elimination as drug is reabsorbed from the renal tubules
and back into the systemic circulation. Renal elimination can be highly efficient,
since approximately 25% of cardiac output goes to the kidneys. Glomerular
filtration is a method of ultrafiltration in which proteins and cells are retained in
the vasculature while a portion of the plasma fluid enters the urine. Therefore,
protein-bound drugs tend to be retained in the vasculature, resulting in slow
elimination of some protein-bound drugs by glomerular filtration. For example,
cefovecin is >95% bound to plasma proteins and persists for weeks after a single
dose. Glomerular filtration is not saturable, and increases in dose or drug
concentration result in proportional increases in renal elimination by
glomerular filtration. Glomerular filtration is dependent on renal blood pressure
and plasma oncotic pressure. Therefore, renal hypotension may decrease
glomerular filtration and drug elimination or conversely hypoproteinemia may
increase renal drug elimination by glomerular filtration.

Drugs may also be actively eliminated in the urine in the renal tubules by
transporters. Weak acid (organic anion transporters; OAT) and weak base
transporters (organic cation transporters; OCT) are most associated with renal
secretion but other transporters such as the p-gp pump are also present.
Transporters are subject to saturation and competition with the classic example
of probenecid (a weak acid) competing with penicillin G (a weak acid) secretion,
resulting in decreased penicillin elimination and prolonged dosing intervals.
Drugs and metabolites can also undergo active renal tubular reabsorption and
diffusion from the tubules back into the plasma, with a net effect of decreasing
drug elimination. Similar to active renal tubular secretion, active tubular
reabsorption can be saturated and competition for reabsorption can occur,
decreasing reabsorption. Renal tubular reabsorption that occurs by diffusion
undergoes similar principles as any drug movement by diffusion. The rate of
diffusion could be decreased (enhancing elimination) by increasing urine flow
through fluid diuresis or altering the urine pH. For example, phenobarbital is a
weak acid; therefore, alkalinizing the urine results in phenobarbital ionization
decreasing reabsorption in the renal tubules and significantly increasing
phenobarbital elimination in dogs (ion trapping) in overdose cases.13 Urinary
acidification (for drugs or toxins that are weak bases) and urinary alkalinization
(for drugs or toxins that are weak acids) are strategies to help enhance
elimination of drugs and toxins that undergo passive renal tubular reabsorption.
Drugs or diseases that result in decreased renal function are expected to result
in near-proportional decreases in renal drug elimination. For example, the renal
elimination of amikacin is proportional to changes in glomerular filtration rate
and decreased amikacin elimination (monitored through TDM) occurs sooner
than changes in urine specific gravity or azotemia. The best strategies for drug
choices in an animal with renal dysfunction are to choose a drug eliminated by
hepatic metabolism (e.g., marbofloxacin instead of enrofloxacin) or choosing a
drug with a higher therapeutic index (e.g., amoxicillin with clavulanate instead
of enrofloxacin).
Biliary secretion occurs through active transporters including OAT and OCT
as well as neutral and heavy metal transporters, p-gp and other active
transporters. Drugs and metabolites eliminated by biliary secretion tend to be
larger molecules, including some drugs (e.g., doxycycline) and drug metabolites.
Once secreted through the bile into the intestine, the drugs and drug metabolites

can be eliminated in the feces. However, there are situations in which drugconjugate (Phase II) metabolites secreted in bile are deconjugated by intestinal
flora, resulting in liberation of free drug which has the potential for reabsorption
(i.e., enterohepatic recycling). Enterohepatic recycling is the rationale for
multiple doses of activated charcoal following some drug or toxin exposures.
The activated charcoal can bind the drug conjugates and deconjugated drug,
preventing reabsorption and enhancing elimination.
Other mechanisms of drug elimination occur. Respiratory elimination of most
inhalant anesthetics occurs through exhaled air. Some drug elimination can
occur in milk through lactation, but in companion animals this is not typically a
substantial route of elimination. However, drug elimination in the milk can
result in clinically relevant drug exposure to nursing animals. Rifampin can be
eliminated in tears, which is a clinically irrelevant elimination route, but can
produce red discoloration of tears that may alarm clients.

PHARMACOKINETIC PARAMETERS
Pharmacokinetic parameters are often determined from studies using a small
number of healthy animals, often of the same breed and typically young adults.
For example, the pharmacokinetics of oral gabapentin are described with 6
healthy Greyhound dogs aged 1.5-3 years.1 The means and ranges are then
reported. These studies typically described pharmacokinetics very well in that
specific group of animals (e.g., young, healthy Greyhounds), but may not
describe the range or variability in pharmacokinetics seen in all clinical patients
due to differences in ages, breeds, health, etc. Therefore, extrapolation from a
small study to a specific patient should be done with the understanding that
every animal is not an “average” animal. Population pharmacokinetic studies are
being performed more commonly in veterinary species in which large numbers
of animals are included of various breeds, ages and health statuses. The purpose
is to better describe the variability in a population that more accurately
represents the target population to be treated. Additionally, as described in the
preceding section, numerous factors could alter the pharmacokinetics in a
clinical patient including drug interactions and disease states.

HALF-LIFE
The half-life most commonly refers to the terminal half-life, which is the half-life
of the terminal portion of a plasma-time profile. The terminal half-life describes
the amount of time it takes for plasma concentrations to decrease by half (50%).
The terminal half-life may be the elimination half-life (the amount of time it
takes to eliminate 50% of drug), but may be affected by other factors such as
slow absorption (i.e., extended-release formulations).

The terminal half-life has many clinical applications. The obvious utility is to
estimate how long drug exposure will persist after administration. The terminal
portion of the plasma versus time curve most often decreases in logarithmic
decay, in which a fixed portion of drug concentration is decreased per unit time.
This is the reason many plasma profiles are presented with a logarithmic drug
concentration scale. For example, the plasma concentrations of morphine in
dogs and cats decrease by approximately one-half every hour. Based on these
assumptions, after 5 half-lives (or 5 hours in this case) plasma concentrations
will decrease by ∼97% (Table 139.3).
The terminal half-life is used for other clinical situations. For example, the
duration of a dose of 0.5 mg/kg IM morphine in dogs is about 4 hours. If the
dose is doubled to 1 mg/kg IM, then the duration of effect is increased by 1 halflife (1 hour in the case of morphine) since the extra amount will be eliminated in
1 half-life. Doubling the dose does not double the duration of effect, but typically
extends it by 1 half-life. However, doubling the dose does double the CMAX (see
below) and may markedly increase adverse effects such as morphine-induced
sedation. As another example, a dog that ingested a bottle of meloxicam in the
morning is brought to you in the evening. How long do you need to monitor for
signs of meloxicam toxicosis? Meloxicam has a terminal half-life ∼24 hours in
dogs; therefore, in 5 days (120 hours) the plasma concentration will decrease by
∼97% from the time of presentation and in 7 days, the plasma concentration will
decrease by ∼99%. Therefore, you may recommend hospitalization and fluid
therapy for 5-7 days to minimize renal adverse effects.
The terminal half-life is also an important parameter to predict the amount of
time it takes to reach steady state plasma concentrations with multiple doses or
drug infusions (Table 139.3). If the second dose is administered prior to
complete drug elimination from the first dose, then there will be some
accumulation from the first to the second dose on the plasma drug
concentrations until steady state plasma concentrations are reached. Steady
state occurs when no further accumulation in drug concentration occurs with
continued dosing; the amount of drug administered during a dosing interval
equals the amount of drug eliminated in the dosing interval and the plasma drug
concentration plateaus (Figure 139.2). The time to reach steady state can be
predicted knowing the terminal half-life with 97% of steady state plasma
concentrations achieved in 5 half-lives (Table 139.3). For example, meloxicam
with a 24 hour half-life will achieve ∼97% of the steady state plasma
concentration in 5 half-lives, or 120 hours (5 days).
The extent of drug accumulation can also be estimated knowing the terminal
half-life and dosing interval (Table 139.4, Figure 139.2). If the dosing
interval is much shorter than the half-life, extensive accumulation can occur
since the subsequent dose is administered prior to elimination of the first dose.
If the dosing interval equals the half-life, then a 2-fold increase in plasma
concentrations between the first dose and steady state plasma concentrations is
predicted. If the dosing interval is 5 times (or greater than) the terminal half-

life, then minimal accumulation (<5%) will occur between the first dose and
steady state plasma concentrations as the majority of the previous dose will be
eliminated prior to the administration of the subsequent dose.
The fluctuation between peak and trough plasma concentrations can also be
predicted by assessing the dosing interval and half-life. An IV constant rate
infusion (CRI) has essentially no fluctuation in plasma concentrations because
the dosing interval is infinitesimally smaller than the half-life for any drug.
However, as the dosing interval gets closer to, and then exceeds, the terminal
half-life, the fluctuations between peak and trough concentration will increase
(Table 139.4). Large fluctuations in peak and trough concentrations may be
desirable (e.g., gentamicin to reduce risk of nephrotoxicosis) or minimal
fluctuations may be desirable (e.g., morphine infusion to maintain analgesia, but
minimize dose-dependent effects such as sedation).

CLEARANCE
The plasma clearance is a measurement of the ability of the animal to remove
drug from the plasma through metabolism or elimination. Plasma clearance is
the sum of hepatic, renal and other mechanisms of metabolism and elimination.
Plasma clearance predicts the steady state plasma concentrations (or average
plasma concentrations) for a given dose rate with the following equation: {Dose
Rate = Plasma Clearance × Average Plasma concentration}. Therefore, if the
plasma clearance is known, the dose rate needed to achieve a targeted mean (or
steady state) plasma concentration can be calculated. Many published
pharmacokinetic studies report the clearance for veterinary species. For
example, the published mean plasma clearance of IV ceftriaxone in dogs is 3.61
mL/kg/min.14 An infusion rate of 1.73 mg/kg/hr will achieve an 8 mcg/mL
mean (steady state) plasma concentration (

Video 139.1).

It is important to remember that the time to reach steady state is still
predicted by the terminal half-life (0.9 hours for ceftriaxone) and it would take
approximately 4.5 hours (5 × half-life) to reach steady state plasma
concentrations with an IV CRI of ceftriaxone. It is also important to note that

the specific animal treated may not have the “average” clearance and as such the
dose may need to be adjusted based on other factors such as renal dysfunction,
fluid diuresis and individual variability in drug clearance. If a drug is
administered by a route other than IV, then the bioavailability (F) must be
included in the equation as follows: {Dose rate = (plasma clearance × average
plasma concentration)/F}.

VOLUME OF DISTRIBUTION
The volume of distribution is a measure of the dilution of a drug into the body
after IV administration. There are numerous ways to calculate and express
volumes of distribution, but they are beyond the scope of this chapter. The
primary utility of the volume of distribution is to calculate the dose needed to
achieve a targeted plasma concentration with the following equation: {Dose =
volume of distribution × plasma concentration}.
Loading doses are used to immediately achieve an effective plasma drug
concentration. For example, ceftriaxone has a mean volume of distribution of
277 mL/kg. If you desire to immediately achieve a plasma ceftriaxone
concentration of 8 mcg/mL (you do not want to wait 4.5 hours to reach steady
state), you may administer a loading dose (2.2 mg/kg IV) to immediately
achieve 8 mcg/mL, and then start the IV CRI to maintain 8 mcg/mL (Video
139.2)

.

Maximum Plasma Concentration and Time to
Maximum Plasma Concentration
The maximum plasma concentration (CMAX) is the highest (peak) plasma
concentration achieved after drug administration following extravascular
administration (Figure 139.3). The CMAX is often correlated with drug toxicity
(e.g., propofol-induced cardiac depression) or efficacy in concentrationdependent drugs (e.g., aminoglycoside antimicrobial effects). Concentrationdependent drugs are drugs in which the effect is best predicted by the peak
(CMAX) concentration. Other drugs, time-dependent drugs, may be correlated
with maintaining minimum plasma concentrations (e.g., opioids) or achieving a
targeted area under the curve. The CMAX for most drugs is directly proportional
to the dose (e.g., doubling the dose doubles the CMAX, halving the dose halves
the CMAX), but there are some exceptions; for example, gabapentin has less than
proportional increases in CMAX with dose increases due to saturation of active
transporters in the intestine.1 The time of the CMAX is abbreviated TMAX. The

TMAX is typically unchanged by dose (e.g., if the dose is doubled, the TMAX is
unchanged), but there are some exceptions.

For a drug with a half-life of 24 hours administered every 6 hours (a dosing
interval to half-life ratio of 1:4) a 6.29 fold accumulation is predicted between
the first dose and steady state. Conversely, a drug dosage with a dosing
interval:half-life of 5:1 will have minimal drug accumulation between the first
dose and steady state plasma concentrations as most of the drug will be
eliminated prior to the next dose being administered. Drugs administered as a
constant rate infusion (CRI) will have no fluctuations in plasma drug
concentrations, but as the dosing interval increases, the fluctuations in peak and
trough concentrations increase with a 32 fold difference between peak and
trough concentrations if the dosing interval:half-life is 5:1.

AREA UNDER THE CURVE
The area under the curve (AUC) is a measure of total drug exposure and it
encompasses both the plasma concentrations and the length of time the plasma
concentrations persist (Figure 139.3). The AUC is often correlated with
efficacy (e.g., fluoroquinolone clinical cures) or toxicity (e.g., aminoglycosideinduced renal failure). The AUC for most drugs is directly proportional to dose
(e.g., doubling the dose doubles the AUC). Decreased elimination due to disease
or drug interactions results in directly proportional effects on AUC (e.g., when
the half-life of gentamicin doubles due to renal insufficiency, then the AUC
doubles). Similarly, increased elimination results in directly proportional
decreases in AUC (when the half-life of phenobarbital is halved due to CYP
induction, then the AUC is halved).

GENERIC AND COMPOUNDED DRUGS
Generic drugs are approved by the appropriate regulatory agency and must have
the same drug and drug content as the pioneer product, be bioequivalent, be
manufactured in inspected facilities and demonstrate stability in the dosage

form. However, the inactive ingredients can be different (e.g., different
flavorings).
Bioequivalence studies are pharmacokinetic studies in which the CMAX and
AUC from two (or more) different formulations are assessed as the pivotal
parameters to determine if the formulations are expected to produce near
equivalent results in a patient. The assumption is that similar CMAX and AUC
will produce a similar peak and total drug exposure over time and subsequently
similar efficacy and safety. There are specific statistical parameters that must be
met for bioequivalence studies.
Veterinary compounding is the practice of using FDA (in the USA)-approved
drugs to make a formulation or strength that is not currently available for a
specific patient. Compounding from bulk ingredients or active pharmaceutical
ingredients (API) is not considered as legitimate veterinary drug compounding
by the FDA. Compounding from API is considered drug manufacturing and is
illegal in the USA. Compounding just to decrease cost is not considered a
legitimate reason for choosing a compounded formulation when an approved
formulation is available.15 In contrast to generic drugs, compounded drugs are
not required to contain the same drug content, drug form, or have stability and
bioequivalence data. In the USA, the state boards of pharmacy have the primary
regulatory authority over compounding pharmacies. Since compounded drugs
do not undergo bioequivalence assessment, there should be no expectation of
similar safety, adverse effects and efficacy as an approved drug. Numerous
instances of poor quality of compounded drugs have been reported in the
literature and through surveillance programs.16 For example, random testing of
compounded drugs (human and veterinary) between 2006-2020 by the
Missouri State Board of Pharmacy found 13-25% of tested drugs failed to have
the correct drug content (i.e., 1 out of every 4-6 compounded drugs failed). The
range of content in the failing drugs was as low as 3% and as high as 225% of the
stated content.17 The use of compounded drugs in lieu of available FDAapproved drugs increases the risk of adverse effects, ranging from the lack of
efficacy to toxicosis. If adverse effects (including lack of effect) occur with a
compounded drug, it could be due to true drug effects (e.g., drug intolerance or
true lack of efficacy) or poor compounding practice (e.g., wrong amount of drug
in the dosage). Therefore, clinical decisions cannot be made with a compounded
product on assumptions of appropriate dosing since the true dose administered
is unknown. Client education is critical if compounded drugs are used, so the
clients are aware of the added risks of compounded drugs. The American
Veterinary Medical Association has a Veterinary Compounding Policy with
further details on legitimate compounding practices.15
