INTRODUCTION
Antimicrobial therapy is performed either for a primary condition, or
perhaps more often, to treat infections that are secondary to another
problem. Based on surveys, skin/soft-tissue infections and urinary
tract infections are the conditions most often treated with antibiotics
in dogs and cats. Others include respiratory infections, blood-borne
infections, and post-surgical infections. Because of the emergence of
antimicrobial drug resistance, veterinarians are encouraged to use
antimicrobial agents prudently, and to follow appropriate
antimicrobial stewardship principles (ch. 7), which have been
developed by several organizations, including the American College

of Veterinary Internal Medicine (acvim.org) and the American
Veterinary Medical Association (avma.org). The most up-to-date
versions are available on the websites for these organizations.
This chapter will discuss the essential principles of effective and
prudent antimicrobial therapy in order to optimize treatment and
decrease risks from resistant organisms.

EMPIRICAL ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY
Every veterinarian should ask simple and basic questions before
starting antimicrobial therapy. These include: the activity of the drug
against the typical strains (wild-type strains) of the presumed
organism causing the infection, the ability of the drug to reach the
site of the infection (penetration issues), local factors that may affect
the drug activity (pus, or pH effects, for example), dose regimen, and
drug safety.
Most of the time, veterinarians will start antimicrobial treatment
before a culture and susceptibility test is obtained. In order to begin
this treatment, veterinarians should have confidence that their
empirical selection will produce the desired results. The first step is
to consider the bacteria that are likely at the site of infection. This is
accomplished by considering the most common commensal bacteria,
opportunistic bacteria, and those most likely to invade the tissue. For
example, Staphylococcus pseudintermedius is the most common
isolate from the skin of dogs, Escherichia coli is the most common
urinary tract isolate in dogs and cats, and the respiratory tract can be
infected with a mixed population that can include P asteurella
multocida (cats) and Staphylococcus spp., Streptococcus spp.,
Escherichia coli and Bordetella bronchiseptica (dogs).1 A
presumptive diagnosis can be based on tissue site and cytologic
examination of infected material. Based on these assumptions, initial
empirical treatment can begin with—but not be limited to—
antibiotics listed in Table 140.1. A more detailed guide to empirical
antibiotic selection can be made by consulting the recommendations
from the International Society of Companion Animal Infectious
Diseases (ISCAID; www.ISCAID.org). The ISCAID has published

guidelines for treatment of respiratory, skin, and urinary tract
infections in small animals.2-4
The susceptibility pattern of many organisms is predictable.
Treatment for wild-type strains of the most common pathogens from
dogs and cats can be initiated with suggested antibiotics listed in
Table 140.1. A wild-type strain is defined as an isolate with no
phenotypically detectable mechanisms of acquired resistance, and
without reduced susceptibility to the antimicrobial agent.5
Conversely, non-wild-type strains are those isolates with presumed
or known mechanisms of acquired resistance and reduced
susceptibility for the antimicrobial agent. Wild-type strains may
include bacteria that have inherent resistance to antimicrobials. For
example, wild-type anaerobic bacteria are inherently resistant to
aminoglycosides by virtue of a lack of an oxygen-dependent
mechanism of drug entry to the bacteria. Gram-negative bacteria of
the order Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas aeruginosa are
inherently resistant to macrolide antibiotics.
Empirical treatment of common infections in animals listed in
Table 140.1 can be accomplished by selecting the antimicrobial
agent with a high likelihood of success for the suspected clinical
infection. Dosage regimens are provide in other sources.6

SELECTION OF ANTIBIOTICS FOR
INFECTIONS NOT RESPONDING TO
EMPIRICAL THERAPY
If the initially chosen antibiotic is not effective, or if antimicrobial
resistance is anticipated, treatment should be guided by a culture
and antimicrobial susceptibility test (AST). For Pseudomonas
aeruginosa, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus, or Enterococcus
spp., a susceptibility test is always advised because these organisms
can have unpredictable susceptibility. A susceptibility test is
particularly important for bacteria of the order Enterobacterales (for
example, E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis) because
acquired resistance is common after recent exposure to antibiotics.

SUSCEPTIBILITY TESTING
Culture and AST will provide the best guidance for drug selection
when susceptibility is not known, or if the seriousness of the
infection warrants an accurate selection.
When a susceptibility test is performed, the laboratory must use
the standards for testing and interpretation available from the
Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI).7 Guidance on the
interpretation of these tests is available in a report from CLSI.5

The most common test used by commercial laboratories is to
directly measure the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) of an
organism with an antimicrobial dilution test. Zone inhibition (also
known as the Kirby-Bauer test) also is performed but provides only
qualitative information. The MIC dilution test is performed by
inoculating the wells of a plate with the bacterial culture and tested
against dilutions of antibiotics. The test is usually performed in
modern laboratories using high-throughput plates and automated
devices. Antibiotic drug concentrations are arranged in serial
dilutions, with each concentration doubled from lowest to highest in
a range. Concentrations are always listed in mcg/mL. For example, if
one were to start at a concentration of 256 mcg/mL, the MIC dilution
series would be as follows: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.12,
0.06 mcg/mL, etc. (Log2 dilutions). If, for example, bacterial growth
occurs at a dilution of 0.5 mcg/mL for a specific drug, but not at 1
mcg/mL and above, the MIC is reported as 1 mcg/mL. The lower the
MIC value, the more susceptible the isolate is to that drug because a
low concentration was capable to inhibit growth. The MIC dilution
test is only semi-quantitative because there are gaps between each
dilution. Realistically, the true MIC lies somewhere between these
values, but the MIC is recorded as the lowest value where growth was
inhibited. Frequently this is expressed as MIC50 or MIC90, which is
the MIC that inhibits 50% or 90% of the bacteria, respectively.

Interpretation of Susceptibility Tests
Resistance and susceptibility are determined by comparing the
bacterial isolate’s MIC to the drug’s breakpoint. The breakpoints
define 3 interpretive categories referred to as “SIR,” which
designates S, susceptible; I, intermediate; or R, resistant. If the MIC
for the bacterial isolate falls in the susceptible category, there is a
greater likelihood of successful treatment (cure) than if the isolate
were classified as resistant. It does not assure success; drug failure is
still possible owing to other drug or patient factors (for example,
immune status, immaturity, or severe illness that compromises the
action of antibacterial drugs), and interactions. If the MIC is in the
resistant category, bacteriologic failure is more likely because of
specific resistance mechanisms or inadequate drug concentrations in

the patient. However, a patient with a robust immune response may
sometimes eradicate the infection even when the isolate falls in the
category of “resistant” based on the susceptibility test result.
The intermediate category is intended as a buffer zone between
susceptible and resistant strains. This category reflects the possibility
of error when an isolate has an MIC that borders between susceptible
and resistant. The intermediate category allows for inherent
variability in test methods, which prevents small, uncontrolled
technical factors from causing major discrepancies in interpretation.
If the MIC value is in the intermediate category, therapy with this
drug at the usual standard dosage is discouraged because there is a
good likelihood that drug concentrations may be inadequate for a
cure. However, successful therapy is possible when drug
concentrates at certain sites—in urine, or as the result of topical
therapy, for example—or at high dosages if the clinician is able to
safely increase the dosage above the minimum labeled dosage. A new
category called “susceptible dose-dependent” (SDD) has replaced the
intermediate category for some drugs (e.g., fluoroquinolones). This
category implies that the organism may be susceptible if high doses
are administered.
MIC data should not be used in isolation. By coupling the MIC
from a laboratory report with CLSI breakpoints and other important
information such as the virulence of the bacteria and the
pharmacologic characteristics of the antibiotics being considered, the
clinician can make a more informed selection of an antibacterial
drug.

TISSUE PENETRATION OF ANTIBIOTICS
The susceptibility test interpretation and pharmacokineticpharmacodynamic (PK-PD) criteria are based on plasma/serum
concentrations of the antibiotic. Tissue-specific interpretations are
not provided in susceptibility test reports to account for differences
in drug distribution among tissues. There is an exception for isolates
from the urine for a few drugs—amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate,
first-generation cephalosporins, and cefovecin. For these exceptions,
the breakpoints for urine isolates are higher than isolates from other

infected sites to account for the high concentration of the drugs in
the urine.
A frequent mistake in MIC interpretation is to compare the MIC
with published tissue concentrations derived from whole-tissue
homogenized samples. Tissue concentration data are often published
by pharmaceutical companies in their product information. These
concentrations may be misleading because they may either
underestimate or overestimate (depending on the drug’s affinity for
intracellular sites) the true drug concentration at the site of infection.
For most tissues, antibiotic drug concentrations in the serum or
plasma approximate the drug concentration in the extracellular
space (interstitial fluid). This occurs because there is no barrier that
impedes drug diffusion from the vascular compartment to
extracellular tissue fluid.8 Clinicians should not make the mistake of
categorizing antibiotics with properties of “good penetration” or
“poor penetration.” Pores (fenestrations) or microchannels in the
endothelium of capillaries are large enough to allow drug molecules
to pass through unless the drug is restricted by protein binding in the
blood. Tissues lacking pores or channels may inhibit penetration of
some drugs, shown as penetration barriers in Figure 140.1.
If adequate drug concentrations can be achieved in plasma, there
is no barrier in the tissue to prevent drug diffusion to the site of
infection as long as the tissue has an adequate blood supply. Drug
diffusion into an abscess or granulation tissue is sometimes a
problem because in these conditions, drug penetration relies on
simple diffusion and the site of infection lacks adequate blood
supply. In an abscess, there is no physical barrier to diffusion, but
low drug concentrations can occur because of a poor blood supply.

FIGURE 140.1 Antimicrobial agent passing from
the blood to the interstitial compartment and across
barriers to reach other tissues. Unbound drugs in
plasma pass readily to the interstitial space, which is
the site of action for most antimicrobial drugs. For
tissues that have a barrier, the drug must be
sufficiently lipophilic to pass across the barrier
membrane.

FIGURE 140.2 Plasma concentration vs. time
profile illustrating the principal pharmacokineticpharmacodynamic (PK-PD) relationships for
antimicrobial therapy. AUC, Area under the curve;
CMAX, peak concentration; MIC, minimal inhibitory
concentration.

TISSUE BARRIERS
In some tissues there is a barrier to drug diffusion, usually caused by
tight junctions on capillaries or a continuous basement membrane.
In these instances, a drug must be sufficiently lipid-soluble, or be
actively carried across the membrane, in order to reach effective
concentrations in tissues. These tissues include: the central nervous
system, eye, and prostate (Figure 140.1). A functional membrane
pump (p-glycoprotein) also contributes to the barrier. There also is a
barrier between plasma and bronchial epithelium (blood-alveolar
barrier). This limits the concentration of some drugs in the bronchial
secretions and epithelial lining fluid of the airways, unless the barrier
is disrupted by disease. Such a disruption often occurs in the
treatment of pneumonia. With lung infections, the drug

concentrations in extracellular fluids can diffuse to pneumonic areas
of the lung because the barrier is disrupted.9 If the blood-bronchus
barrier is intact, it is difficult to predict the extent of penetration for
veterinary antimicrobials. Macrolide antibiotics (e.g., azithromycin)
and tetracyclines can concentrate in these fluids, but their spectrum
of activity is limited.

URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS (ch. 307)
For uncomplicated urinary tract infections, high urine antibacterial
drug concentrations may be sufficient to achieve a cure.10,11
However, this assumption does not hold up when treating a
complicated infection, an infection in a patient with dilute urine
(e.g., chronic kidney disease) or when other structures are involved
such as the layers of the bladder mucosa, kidney, or prostate. In
these cases, high urine concentrations alone are not sufficient.
Rather, it is the tissue concentration—which is correlated to the
plasma concentration—that will be predictive of a bacteriologic cure.

PHARMACOKINETICPHARMACODYNAMIC (PK-PD)
PRINCIPLES
The use of exposure-relationships and PK-PD principles to evaluate
antimicrobial agents is important for dosage and dose interval
selection (ch. 139). Antibiotics are evaluated for whether their
activity is time-dependent or concentration-dependent. Bactericidal
versus bacteriostatic properties are no longer considered clinically
relevant. For a drug that is concentration-dependent, it is the
exposure measured by the area-under-the-curve (AUC) in relation to
the MIC (AUC:MIC ratio) that predicts antimicrobial efficacy. For a
drug that is time-dependent, it is the time above the MIC (T>MIC)
that predicts efficacy.
The clinical effects of drugs that are considered protein-synthesis
inhibiting agents—aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, macrolides,
clindamycin, and chloramphenicol—are best measured by total

exposure, or AUC/MIC. The time-dependent drugs are those that act
on the cell wall: beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins,
and carbapenems) and glycopeptides (vancomycin) (Figure 140.2).
The index for the optimum AUC:MIC ratio is defined for each class
of drugs, as is the optimum T>MIC for time-dependent drugs. These
values are used to design dosage regimens, determine the
susceptibility testing breakpoints, and evaluate factors that can affect
these concentrations, and therefore, clinical outcome.12
The reference point for measurement of AUC:MIC or T>MIC
parameters is the plasma/serum drug concentration. It is preferred
to use the protein unbound fraction (free drug concentration) to
differentiate total drug concentrations from the unbound,
pharmacologically active concentrations.13 The unbound drug
concentration in plasma is theoretically in equilibrium with the
unbound concentration in tissue fluid (Figure 140.1). If the PK-PD
index does not consider the unbound fraction, it can overestimate
the drug’s activity.

OPTIMIZING DOSAGE REGIMENS WITH
PK-PD PRINCIPLES
For a concentration-dependent drug, dosage regimens are designed
to administer the highest dose safely possible to produce exposure
(measured by AUC) above the MIC during a 24-hour dose interval
(AUC:MIC ratio). For most drugs in this category, this can be
accomplished with once-daily dosing. Therefore, fluoroquinolones
and aminoglycosides are administered as a single dose, once daily,
regardless of the elimination rate (half-life). Some drugs are
administered more frequently during the day if adverse effects limit
the size of the dose, or if bacterial inhibition requires long exposure
times. Tetracyclines, clindamycin, and chloramphenicol are
administered more frequently during the day to maintain the
AUC:MIC optimum exposure throughout the dose interval.
The beta-lactam antibiotics, such as penicillins, potentiated
aminopenicillins (e.g., amoxicillin plus clavulanate, piperacillintazobactam), and cephalosporins act more slowly; therefore, the
concentration should be kept above the MIC as long as possible

during the dosing interval (T>MIC) for the optimal bactericidal
effect. To maintain this relationship, drugs with short half-lives may
require administration 3 times daily (e.g., injectable cephalosporins
and penicillins), or twice daily for highly susceptible bacteria with
low MIC values (cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate). Drugs with
long half-lives can be administered less frequently (cefovecin,
cefpodoxime). Animals without other comorbidities can be treated
with drug concentrations that are above the MIC for 40-50% of the
dose interval, but critically ill and immunosuppressed animals may
require longer exposure. For these patients, a constant-rate infusion
(ch. 77) can be used for maintaining continuous exposure
throughout the treatment.

Antifungal and antiviral drugs are administered to dogs and cats to
treat both primary and secondary infections. Antifungal drugs are
used for treating serious systemic fungal diseases as well as skin
infections caused by dermatophytes and yeasts. Some animals are at
a greater risk of fungal infections because they are
immunosuppressed or receiving cancer drugs, radiation therapy, or
prolonged courses of corticosteroids. Antiviral drugs have a more
limited role in small animal veterinary medicine. There are some
agents that improve the clinical course of feline herpesvirus
infections (FHV-1; ch. 205), but other viral infections, such as feline
immunodeficiency virus (FIV; ch. 198), feline leukemia virus (FeLV;
ch. 199), or feline infectious peritonitis (FIP; ch. 200), respond
poorly or incompletely to antiviral agents.
Unfortunately, there are few drugs approved for these indications
in animals. Therefore, veterinarians have used drugs labeled for
human use, compounded drugs, and sometimes experimental drugs,

to manage these infections. Because there are few veterinary-specific
products available, we rely on published evidence of efficacy and
guidance on safety and dosing. Fortunately, there have been many
advances in the last 15 years that have provided much of this needed
information.
Compared to antibacterial drugs (ch. 140), the relationships
between plasma drug concentration and clinical effectiveness has not
been well established for antifungal and antiviral drugs. Some
guidance on the pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PK-PD)
criteria for antifungal drugs is available for human infections.1,2
Relationships between clinical outcome and plasma drug
concentrations are not available for veterinary uses of these agents,
but it is assumed that similar relationships exist. Likewise, compared
to antibacterial drugs, susceptibility testing is not routinely
performed on isolated pathogens for antifungal or antiviral agents.
Standards are available for testing and reporting antifungal drug
susceptibility from the Clinical and Laboratory Standards
Institute,3,4 and for some limited viruses,5 but these are rarely used
in veterinary medicine.

ANTIFUNGAL DRUGS
DRUGS FOR DERMATOPHYTE INFECTIONS
Isolated dermatophyte lesions caused by Microsporum spp., and
Trichophyton spp. in dogs and cats can be treated with topical
products (Table 141.1). Topical ointments, creams, or solutions can
be applied to the skin without concerns for systemic effects unless a
large amount is consumed by licking. Systemic treatment options
have consisted of griseofulvin (Fulvicin), the azole antifungal agents,
and terbinafine. Dosages for these drugs are provided in another
reference.6 Included with the dermatophyte infections is the yeast
infection caused by Malassezia pachydermatis. These infections
most often affect the external ear, but also can occur on the skin.

DRUGS FOR SYSTEMIC FUNGAL
INFECTIONS
The most serious diseases treated with antifungal agents are the
systemic mycoses. These may include the filamentous fungi such as
Aspergillus spp. (chs. 210 and 211), Fusarium spp., and Penicillium
spp. (ch. 211), and opportunistic fungi such as Histoplasma
capsulatum (ch. 209), Blastomyces dermatitidis (ch. 209),
Coccidioides immitis (ch. 208), Cryptococcus neoformans (ch.
207), and Candida spp. (ch. 211).

AMPHOTERICIN B

Amphotericin B (Fungizone) is a polyene macrolide antibiotic with
antifungal activity. It has been a valuable drug for the treatment of
serious systemic fungal infections. Amphotericin B is active against
Blastomyces dermatitidis, Histoplasma, Cryptococcus,
Coccidioides, Candida, and Aspergillus. Amphotericin also has
activity against Leishmania (ch. 197). It is the most active of all the
antifungal agents but it has important disadvantages. It must be
administered intravenously. It is associated with a high incidence of
adverse effects, which requires careful administration and patient
monitoring.
Kidney injury is the most severe dose-limiting adverse effect and
the cause for discontinuing therapy or limiting dosages. Early
reversible nephrotoxicosis is seen with each daily dose, but
permanent nephrotoxicosis is related to the total cumulative dose.
Risk can be minimized by following administration guidelines, pretreating patients with intravenous (IV) fluid therapy and assessing
renal function throughout treatment. It may become necessary to
abandon therapy with amphotericin if there is persistent azotemia.
Other adverse effects that may be observed include vomiting,
tremors, increased body temperature, and anorexia. These effects
may be associated with each daily treatment and are somewhat
alleviated with pre-medication of antihistamine drugs, nonsteroidal
anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and antiemetics.

Liposomal Formulations
To overcome some of the problems associated with the conventional
form of amphotericin B, newer formulations composed of lipid
complexes have been used in some veterinary patients. These have
the advantage of less toxicity, which allows for higher doses. These
formulations are used often in people, but are more expensive than
the conventional formulation; therefore, the use has been more
limited in veterinary medicine. Lower risk of toxicosis is attributed to
a selective transfer of the lipid complex amphotericin B, releasing the
drug directly to the fungal cell membrane and sparing mammalian
cell membranes. Reduced drug concentrations in the kidneys, and
diminished release of inflammatory cytokines from the amphotericin
lipid complex compared to the conventional formulation, also may
prevent adverse reactions.

AZOLE ANTIFUNGAL DRUGS
Azoles overcome some of the problems of amphotericin B because
they are administered orally and generally do not produce toxicosis,
which is a problem with amphotericin B. The disadvantage is that
they slowly inhibit the synthesis of fungal cell membranes and
require long treatment protocols. These agents are highly lipophilic,
which means they accumulate in the skin and other tissues, but they
are less soluble. Poor solubility produces low oral absorption unless
the medication is administered with food to stimulate stomach acid
and provide lipids for dissolution. These drugs are subject to drug
interactions that diminish oral absorption. If antacids, histamine H2 blocking drugs (e.g., famotidine), or proton pump inhibitors (e.g.,
omeprazole) are administered, oral absorption is diminished. These
drugs are not good candidates for compounding because
manipulation affects oral solubility.7,8

Ketoconazole
Ketoconazole is the oldest of this group of antifungal azole drugs
administered systemically to animals. Ketoconazole has a wide
spectrum of activity that includes yeast (e.g., Malassezia
pachydermatis), systemic fungi, and dermatophytes. Although
ketoconazole is seldom used in people because of adverse effects and
drug interactions, it remains an important antifungal agent for
animals because of its low cost and familiarity.
Ketoconazole commonly causes adverse effects in animals.
Nausea, anorexia, and vomiting are the most common signs
observed. They are usually dose-related and may be diminished by
decreasing the dosage, dividing the total dose into smaller doses, and
administering each dose with food. Ketoconazole inhibits the
synthesis of steroid hormones (via inhibition of the cytochrome P450 enzymes), most notably cortisol and testosterone. Although this
may be a side-effect of therapy, it has been exploited for the
temporary management of hyperadrenocorticism in dogs and as an
anti-androgen treatment. Hepatic enzyme activities may become
elevated with therapy (especially alkaline phosphatase and alanine
aminotransferase), and hepatotoxicosis has been associated with
ketoconazole therapy. This reaction is most likely an idiosyncratic

reaction (unpredictable), but hepatotoxicosis appears more likely
with high dosages.
Ketoconazole is one of the most potent inhibitors of hepatic and
intestinal microsomal enzymes (cytochrome P-450 enzymes). It may
inhibit metabolism and elimination of a variety of other drugs. It also
is an inhibitor of the multi-drug resistance (MDR) membrane pump
also known as p-glycoprotein (p-gp), which is involved in drug
penetration across the intestine, blood-brain barrier, and other
tissues. For example, when ketoconazole is administered with
cyclosporine, the cyclosporine concentrations are increased in dogs
by 2-3 fold.

Itraconazole
Itraconazole is an azole of the triazole group. Triazoles and
imidazoles have similar antifungal mechanism of action, but triazoles
lack affinity for some of the cytochrome P-450 enzymes in animals,
which results in fewer endocrine effects. Itraconazole is one of the
most widely used triazoles. It has been used successfully to treat both
systemic and cutaneous fungal infections in animals. It is
considerably more potent than ketoconazole (5 to 100 times more
active) and is associated with fewer side-effects.
The commercial formulation (Sporanox) is available in capsules
and oral liquid solution. Itraconazole is insoluble and is not absorbed
well unless administered as the commercial formulation.
Bioequivalence studies in dogs have shown that compounded
formulations are not sufficiently absorbed in dogs or cats.7,8 The oral
solution is also available in a veterinary formulation (Itrafungol),
which is identical in composition to the human oral solution. This
product is approved for cats, but may be used in dogs.9
The long half-life in cats, and persistence in skin, allow once a day
or once-every-other-day dosing. The commercial formulation
(Itrafungol) can be administered on alternate weeks for treatment of
dermatophytes in cats. In dogs, it is used for a variety of fungal
infections, including blastomycosis, other systemic fungi,
dermatophytes, and Malassezia pachydermatis dermatitis.
Itraconazole is better tolerated in dogs and cats than ketoconazole,
but adverse reactions are still are possible. Since most adverse effects

are dose-related, lowering the dosage in animals is advised if adverse
effects are observed. Hepatopathy is not as common as for
ketoconazole, but elevations in liver enzyme activities and hepatic
injury have been reported in dogs. Anorexia and vomiting also may
occur as a complication of treatment, especially with high dosages
and high serum concentrations. Some cytochrome P-450 enzyme
and p-gp inhibition occurs and itraconazole may increase
concentrations of cyclosporine, digoxin, cisapride, and possibly other
drugs when used concurrently.

Fluconazole
Fluconazole is better tolerated than the other azoles, more soluble,
and better absorbed orally, but it is not as active against many fungi.
Fluconazole is less active than itraconazole against dermatophytes,
Blastomyces (ch. 209), and Histoplasma (ch. 209), but has good
activity against Coccidioides spp. (ch. 208) and Cryptococcus
neoformans (ch. 207), and has been used successfully to treat dogs
and cats with those infections. Its use in dogs has included treatment
for dermatophytes and yeast infections, as well as some systemic
fungi. Fluconazole is more water-soluble than the other azoles, and
therefore has different pharmacokinetic characteristics than
ketoconazole and itraconazole. The oral absorption can be variable
among animals, but it is not affected by other factors (diet and
antacid medications) as much as itraconazole.

Newer Azole Antifungals Used Less Frequently
Voriconazole (Vfend), one of the newer azole drugs, is a triazole like
itraconazole and fluconazole. It has become an important drug for
humans, especially to treat disseminated aspergillosis. Voriconazole
is similar in structure to fluconazole, but has much better activity
against several species of molds, including Aspergillus spp. and
Fusarium spp. (ch. 211). Its use in animals has been limited at this
time because ocular and neurotoxicosis have been reported in cats,
and the half-life is short in dogs.10,11
Posaconazole (Noxafil) is also one of the newer azole antifungal
drugs. It is similar to itraconazole, but with a wider spectrum of
activity. It is used primarily in people for treating Aspergillus and

Candida infections (chs. 210, 211), but also is active against
dermatophytes, Histoplasma capsulatum (ch. 209), Blastomyces
dermatitidis (ch. 209), Coccidioides immitis (ch. 208), and
Cryptococcus neoformans (ch. 207). The difference in activity
compared to other azoles is the additional activity against Mucorales
(formerly called Zygomycetes) such as Mucor and Rhizopus. This
may be one of the most promising new drugs for dogs and cats. The
long half-life in dogs allows for dosing once every 2-3 days, and the
oral suspension produces effective concentrations in cats.12,13
Adverse effects have been rare, based on anecdotal accounts of use in
these animals.

ANTIVIRAL DRUGS
The administration of systemic antiviral drugs has been very limited
in veterinary medicine. The use of antiviral agents has been primarily
in the realm of ophthalmology, particularly for treating feline
herpesviral ocular infections. These treatments usually employ
topical ointments. Systemic treatment of viral diseases in dogs and
cats has not been thoroughly evaluated, pharmacokinetic
information is incomplete, and dosing protocols are mostly
anecdotal. Treatment of viral diseases in dogs and cats primarily
relies on supportive care and prevention and treatment of secondary
bacterial infections. Antiviral chemotherapy does not eliminate the
virus in infected dogs and cats.
For some diseases, such as FeLV (ch. 199), immunomodulators
have been used such as acemannan, interferon omega, bacterins, and
other products purported to act as “immune stimulants,” with little
documented evidence of efficacy. Unfortunately, what constitutes
“immunomodulation” or “immune stimulation” is not well-defined.
There is some evidence that interferon omega may improve survival
in cats infected with FeLV, but this product is not available in the
United States and other evidence is lacking. For some diseases,
attempts at using human antiviral drugs have resulted in failure or
toxicosis.

FELINE RETROVIRUSES

Management of cats with FIV (ch. 198) or FeLV (ch. 199)
represents one of the frustrating areas in which antiviral drugs have
been investigated. There are no drugs that will eliminate these
viruses from infected cats, and few controlled studies on
effectiveness of most agents. In 2020, the American Association of
Feline Practitioners (AAFP) published its guidelines for management
of retroviral infections in cats.14 One of its conclusions is that “few
large long-term controlled studies in naturally infected cats have
shown long-lasting benefits of using antiviral drugs. Drugs available
to treat retrovirus-infected cats are limited and tend to show lower
efficacy in feline patients compared with human patients. Many of
these drugs require impractical long-term use, are costly, and often
come with mild to severe toxic side effects that limit their utility.”
Several drugs have been investigated but few are promising.
Zidovudine (AZT) has been investigated more than other agents.
Other drugs have in vitro activity against these viruses, but have
either not been investigated sufficiently in vivo, have failed
treatment, or have produced adverse effects that discourage use for
clinical patients. AZT has activity in vitro against both FeLV and FIV
by inhibiting replication of the virus. AZT is a nucleoside analog that
blocks reverse transcriptase of retroviruses. In clinical studies in cats
with FIV at dosages of 5-10 mg/kg q12h, SC or PO, it had clinical
benefit, improved cats’ quality of life, and decreased viral load.
However, in cats with FeLV, it produced no statistically significant
improvement and at high dosages it suppressed the bone marrow.

FELINE HERPESVIRUS-1
One disease for which systemic treatment with antiviral drugs has
been justified is the treatment of FHV-1 infections (ch. 205). The
drugs examined for their efficacy have been those used in people to
treat human herpes simplex type-1 virus infection. Some drugs have
been investigated, such as acyclovir, valacyclovir, and ribavirin, but
these have either been ineffective, toxic to cats, or both. Penciclovir
has shown to have good in vitro activity against FHV-1, but is not
well absorbed when administered orally. However, the prodrug of
penciclovir is famciclovir. It is converted to the active drug by
deacetylation in the intestine and liver to produce the active drug.

Administration of the prodrug substantially improves bioavailability,
but conversion to the active drug is less efficient in cats than in
people, which requires higher dosages. Once absorbed, penciclovir is
converted in a step-wise process to the triphosphate, which inhibits
viral DNA polymerase and hence viral replication.
The optimal dose of famciclovir in cats has been a source of
debate. The available tablet sizes for people are 125, 250, and 500
mg. A dosage of 62.5 mg per cat (one-half of a 125 mg tablet) has not
been consistently effective. Higher dosages of 125 mg per cat, every
8-12 hours, are now recommended based on clinical observations,15
but some experts have recommended higher dosages of 90 mg/kg
based on pharmacokinetic studies and infections in experimental
cats.16,17 The compounded oral suspension of famciclovir has not
been effective.

FELINE INFECTIOUS PERITONITIS
There are no approved drugs that are effective for treating FIP in cats
(ch. 200). However, there are new experimental drugs that show
promise.18,19 These new small molecules (GS-441524 and GC376)
have undergone tests for treating cats with FIP, but neither of these
drugs is yet available. Published studies show promising
effectiveness for treatment of cats with FIP. These molecules include
a protease inhibitor (GC376) and a nucleoside analog (GS-441524)
capable of inhibiting RNA virus replication, which is similar to
remdesivir that is used to treat the human coronavirus (SARS-CoV2).

Chapter 142: Antiparasitic Drugs
Byron L. Blagburn, and Lindsay A. Starkey

A C RO N YM
ML macrocyclic lactone
First and foremost, selection of the appropriate parasiticide is dependent on an
accurate diagnosis.1,2 Intestinal parasites and those that are found in the lungs,
hepatobiliary system and other organs that open to or communicate with the
gastrointestinal tract usually pass stages that are recovered from feces. These
parasites are usually confirmed by properly conducted fecal examination (ch.
80).1 Given the spectrum of parasites in companion animals, and the complexity
of the parasiticide market, the selection of antiparasitic products can be
difficult.3,4 The goals of parasiticide therapy are to reduce or eliminate signs of
disease and to remove the causative parasite(s). Antiparasitic agents must be
safe, effective, and convenient to use.5 Additional considerations are spectrum of
activity (types of parasites that are eliminated), formulation, sex and age of the
target animal, other concurrent health problems, pregnancy and nursing,
product approval or off-label use, ease of acquiring the parasiticide, and other
current parasite control strategies such as heartworm prevention and flea and
tick control. Current prevention strategies (heartworms, intestinal parasites)
rely less on an initial diagnosis than on the historical risk of parasitic infection.
Available products are intended to provide protection against major internal
parasites while improving compliance.5

TARGET ANIMAL AND FORMULATION,
SPECTRUM OF ACTIVITY, PREVENTION
AND/OR TREATMENT
Foremost in our considerations of which parasiticide to select is whether it is
label-approved for the target parasite, or if its efficacy is supported by legitimate
published research data.5 The spectrum of activity, dosage, and route of

administration of antiparasitic drugs are usually developed and approved with
specific hosts in mind. Using a product extra-label in a host or using in an
alternative species could result in a shorter or longer duration of activity, lack of
efficacy, or toxicosis.
Combining more than one active ingredient in a product usually increases the
spectrum of activity against internal parasites and may add external parasites to
the label. When heartworm prevention is needed, the spectrum of available
products changes further. We must also consider the use of antiparasitic drugs
that have not gained regulatory approval but are often used safely and effectively
against problem parasites (Table 142.1). Examples are clindamycin,
metronidazole, secnidazole, ponazuril and ronidazole, just to mention a few.5
Another consideration is whether the goal is to eliminate existing parasites or
to prevent additional infections, or both. These are important points because
concentrations of the active ingredient(s) often will determine the level of
efficacy achieved and whether efficacy is against mature or immature stages. The
difference between antiparasitics with therapeutic effects and those with
preventive effects is often one of dosage and frequency of administration.
Therapeutic products that are administered to eliminate established infections
are often administered once or twice at a higher dosage. Preventive products are
usually administered at longer intervals (e.g., monthly or every 6 or 12 months).
Some parasiticides are both therapeutic and preventive at the same dosage, but
this is usually a unique situation involving treatment of one parasite and
prevention of another. Examples are the products that eliminate adult intestinal
parasites while preventing heartworm infections.

EFFECTIVENESS
Efficacy of parasiticides is a must when removal of target parasites and
elimination of disease are the goals. To reach the market, approved parasiticides
must be effective enough to eliminate the majority of the target parasites.
Regulatory approval usually requires the removal of 90% of the parasites from
treated animals compared to non-treated controls.6 Heartworm preventives are
the only exception. Heartworm preventive products must be 100% effective after
either experimental or natural infection (ch. 237). Interestingly, melarsomine
dihydrochloride, the only approved heartworm adulticide, must achieve a high
level of efficacy (usually >90%) but is not required to be 100% effective. Many
parasiticides that are not approved for specific parasites are used successfully
based on either published data or testimony that supports their efficacies. The
authors strongly recommend that approved parasiticides are used when
possible. Antiparasitic drugs that are not approved should be researched
thoroughly and used in a manner consistent with available published data.

RESISTANCE TO ANTIPARASITIC DRUGS

Resistance to antiparasitic drugs has been documented for important small
animal parasites.7-12 Many view the development of resistance as an indication
that subsequent use of these drugs will provide little or no benefit in preventing
parasitic disease. Although this may be true for some parasites of livestock and
horses, it has not proven true for companion animal parasites. In the majority of
cases, antiparasitic drugs remain effective and beneficial to companion animals;
however, parasiticide resistance has been identified for some field strains of
heartworm, hookworms in canines, Dipylidium caninum tapeworms, and
Giardia spp.
When approved, all the heartworm preventive products were 100% efficacious
in laboratory and field studies at killing 3rd and 4th stage Dirofilaria immitis
larvae. Over the past decade, lack of efficacy reports have continued to surface
relating to the failure of macrocyclic lactone (ML) heartworm prevention
products; many of these reports may involve a failure of compliance, but
documented ML-resistant isolates of heartworm continue to occasionally be
isolated from infected animals, and product failures have been documented in
experimental and field studies against all four of the available ML molecules.7
Even though the occasional product failure may occur as these products can no
longer be expected to protect 100% of treated individuals in the face of a MLresistant isolate, continued advocacy for the year-round use of heartworm
preventives is paramount in protecting the vast majority of dogs and cats.

Unless otherwise indicated, treatment consists of using only one drug at a time.
#

This product is labeled for this parasite in countries outside of the U.S.
Another parasite exhibiting drug-resistance is the canine hookworm,
Ancylostoma caninum. Some isolates of this parasite have been shown to
survive treatments with the three labeled drug classes historically considered
effective at treating this parasite: pyrantel, fenbendazole/febantel, and the MLbased heartworm preventive products. Greyhounds are over-represented among
the animals infected; however, any breed can potentially be infected with
multidrug resistant hookworms. Researchers at the University of Georgia have

created a useful algorithm for detecting and managing affected dogs that focuses
on performing a fecal egg count reduction test with the post-treatment fecal
sample collected and evaluated at 10-14 days as well as treatment with all three
drug classes simultaneously (either oral pyrantel pamoate [5 mg/kg]/febantel
[25 mg/kg]/praziquantel [5 mg/kg] + topical moxidectin [2.5 mg/kg], or oral
fenbendazole [50 mg/kg daily for 3 days] + oral pyrantel pamoate [5 mg/kg] +
topical moxidectin [2.5 mg/kg]).8 Should the aforementioned regimen not result
in successful treatment, the extra-label use of emodepside (1 mg/kg PO) may be
pursued with caution.8
Recently, Dipylidium caninum, the flea tapeworm, has been shown to be
resistant to the isoquinolone drugs praziquantel and epsiprantel, even when
used at elevated dosages and durations.9 Optional therapies include
nitroscanate (50 mg/kg once PO), compounded pyrantel pamoate (5
mg/kg)/praziquantel (5 mg/kg)/oxantel pamoate (20 mg/kg once PO), or
nitazoxanide (100 mg/kg once PO). However, it is not known if these therapies
are successful or if infections and proglottid shedding spontaneously cease, as
the lifespan of this parasite has not been well-characterized.9,10
Although there have not been any studies confirming drug-resistant Giardia
spp. isolated from veterinary species, as there have been in human medicine,
anecdotal cases continue to emerge. The two primary drug classes selected for
treatment of giardiasis in dogs and cats, the 5-nitroimidazoles (e.g.,
metronidazole) and benzimidazoles (e.g., albendazole), have both been shown to
be resistant in human studies.11 Alternative therapies with drugs like
nitazoxanide or secnidazole have been shown effective.12,13
There are several things that can be done to deter the development of drug
resistance. First, use approved products at their label doses and according to
their approved regimens. Underdosing and use of products at treatment
intervals that are too frequent may lead to resistance development. Always
monitor the efficacy of antiparasitic drugs by performing post-treatment tests,
or at the very least, annual tests. Avoid the use of off-label products unless
sufficient research supports that treatments are effective at eliminating the
parasite. If a product appears to lose its efficacy, retreat with a product from a
different chemical group. The most important aspect of resistance management
is to monitor the effectiveness of antiparasitic drugs by regular fecal
examination or other appropriate tests.

Anti-inflammatory drugs are commonly administered to dogs and cats as a key
strategy to decrease inflammation, hyperthermia, and pain. Anti-inflammatory
drugs most often refer to two families of pharmaceuticals: non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and glucocorticoids. This chapter discusses
NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, and other anti-inflammatory strategies.

INFLAMMATION IN DOGS AND CATS
Inflammation is a ubiquitous response to tissue injury, secondary to infection,
neoplasia, burns, trauma, immune-mediated disease, and other causes.
Inflammation can be acute or chronic. Acute inflammation is empirically
characterized by redness, heat, edema, and pain (ch. 6). It is associated with
increased blood flow and vascular permeability. Clinically, while chronic
inflammation has a pathophysiologic mechanism similar to acute inflammation,
it includes the presence of macrophages, monocytes, and lymphocytes and the
proliferation of blood vessels and connective tissue. In joints, for example,
chronic inflammation appears both more difficult to detect (because it is less
intense) and more challenging to treat (because fibrosis and chronic pain cannot
be eliminated with short-term management steps) than acute inflammation.
Inflammation can be focal, affecting any organ, or can be systemic. The systemic
expression of inflammation includes the synthesis of acute phase proteins, fever
(ch. 16), hypotension (ch. 121), leukocytosis (ch. 58), and cachexia (ch. 151).

Biochemically, inflammation is mediated by soluble polypeptides known as
cytokines that promote chemoattraction and cellular adhesion.1 Inflammation is
also promoted by metabolites of arachidonic acid from cellular phospholipids:
prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and lipoxins, by coagulation, by complement
activation, and by nitric oxide.

ANTI-INFLAMMATORY STRATEGIES
The fundamental anti-inflammatory strategy in dogs and cats is the
administration of NSAIDs or glucocorticoids.
In dogs, NSAIDs are approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration
(FDA) to relieve pain and inflammation associated with surgery or osteoarthritis
(OA) but are used in practice to manage inflammation and pain from many
other sources (ch. 6). The NSAIDs that are currently approved by the FDA for
use in dogs and cats are listed in Table 143.1.
NSAIDs inhibit the production of prostaglandins from arachidonic acid in cell
membranes by blocking the cyclooxygenase (COX) enzyme (Figure 143.1).

Several isoforms of COX have been described, primarily COX-1 and COX-2. In
simple terms, the COX-1 isoform has been described as physiologic or
constitutive and the COX-2 isoform was initially described as pathologic or
inducible in response to pre-inflammatory factors and other stimuli. However,
the demarcation between constitutive and inducible COX isoforms has been
questioned.2 Glucocorticoids inhibit both COX and lipoxygenase (LOX)
enzymes. Since both COX and LOX contribute to inflammation, glucocorticoids
have a strong anti-inflammatory effect.
The safety, toxicity, and efficacy of NSAIDs in dogs and cats have been
reviewed.3-6 NSAIDs are safe overall. However, in dogs and cats, their use is
associated with side-effects. The reported frequency of adverse drug events is
approximately 3%.5 The most common side-effects are gastrointestinal, hepatic,
and renal. Adverse events are more likely when patients are dehydrated,
hypotensive, or have impaired renal or liver function.7 Adverse events also are
more likely and possibly more severe when patients receiving an NSAID are
overdosed or receive a second NSAID or glucocorticoids.8,9 At the time of this
writing, it is unclear whether any specific FDA-approved NSAID has a lower rate
of side-effects than any other FDA-approved NSAID. Similar to NSAIDs,
glucocorticoids are associated with gastrointestinal ulceration or erosion in
dogs.10
Several NSAIDs have been approved for both oral or parenteral
administration. In one experimental study of 18 Beagle dogs comparing drug
exposure after a single dose of carprofen, concentrations at steady state were
bioequivalent but peak plasma concentrations were higher and were reached
earlier (0.5 to 3 hours) after oral administration compared to subcutaneous
injection (1.5 to 8 hours), respectively.11
NSAIDs that are not FDA-approved are sometimes used for specific purposes.
For example, piroxicam is used for the management of transitional cell
carcinoma (TCC) (ch. 330). In one clinical trial of piroxicam (0.3 mg/kg PO
q24h) monotherapy for TCC of the urinary bladder in dogs, complete or partial
remission was achieved in 19% of dogs and 91% of owners reported
improvement in quality of life regardless of tumor remission.12 Other NSAIDs,
such as carprofen, also decrease the viability of cancer cells.13 It is unclear from
the literature, however, how the efficacy and safety of piroxicam compare to
other NSAIDs when used for managing neoplasia.
Glucocorticoids used in dogs include triamcinolone (FDA approved in 1987),
prednisolone (approved in 1991), betamethasone valerate (approved in 1993),
dexamethasone (approved in 2003). A more detailed list appears in Table
143.2. Clinically, the main use of glucocorticoids is immunosuppressive
(enteropathies, rhinitis, immune-mediated joint disease, myositis; ch. 144) and
hormone replacement (hypoadrenocorticism [ch. 296], critical illness-related
corticosteroid insufficiency). Glucocorticoids, however, are also used for

preventing or treating acute and chronic inflammation. Glucocorticoids are used
for managing several neurologic (chs. 242 and 250), dermatologic (ch. 178),
ophthalmic, orthopedic (ch. 177), and metabolic conditions.
NSAIDs have been shown in several prospective randomized clinical trials to
alleviate the clinical signs resulting from OA.3,4 One systematic review,
published in 2007, concluded that a high level of comfort supported the claimed
efficacy of meloxicam to alleviate the clinical signs of OA and a moderate
comfort supporting carprofen and etodolac.4 Another systematic review,
published in 2009, concluded that there was a high level of comfort supporting
the claimed efficacy of carprofen, firocoxib, and meloxicam and a moderate level
of comfort supporting etodolac. Even if the number of clinical trials varies
among NSAIDs, it is fair to assume, based on the published literature, that all
FDA-approved NSAIDs constitute effective anti-inflammatory therapies and
reduce pain in dogs and cats.

CLINICAL USE OF ANTI-INFLAMMATORY
MEDICATIONS
SHORT-TERM NSAID THERAPY: PERIOPERATIVE USE
The most common context for short-term use of NSAIDs is likely the
perioperative period relating to orthopedic or soft tissue surgery. For that
purpose, NSAIDs are effective at decreasing perioperative pain and are safe
when given to well-hydrated patients with normal blood pressure and renal
function.7 NSAIDs typically are used in this context in conjunction with other
pain medications, such as local anesthetics, opiates, and alpha-2 adrenergic
agonists (ch. 6).

LONG-TERM NSAID THERAPY:
OSTEOARTHRITIS
The most common long-term use of NSAIDs is for the management of OA in
dogs and cats. A large epidemiologic study of dogs in the United Kingdom (n =
455,557) identified an annual period prevalence of appendicular OA of 2.5%.14
NSAIDs are given to achieve several physiologic purposes in OA, which may
also apply to the use of NSAIDs in managing inflammation of other body
systems: to decrease inflammation (e.g., synovitis, joint effusion, early
disruption of cartilage metabolism, subchondral bone inflammation),15 to
decrease peripheral (periarticular, regional) sensory sensitization,16 and to
decrease central sensitization.17

Clinically, NSAID use in young dogs with early OA is both effective and safe.
The reduction of clinical signs is most often rapid, occurring within a day of the
onset of therapy, and is often complete in dogs that experience joint pain and
inflammation but do not experience a severe loss of muscle mass or joint
motion. Information regarding the optimal duration of therapy in dogs treated
with NSAIDs at an early stage is lacking. In early OA, several factors influence
the decision to discontinue NSAID therapy. These include the therapeutic
principle derived from human medicine to use NSAIDs at the lowest effective
dosage for the shortest effective duration, and the risk of adverse events suggest
that the duration of therapy during early OA should be short—1 to 2 weeks, for
example. Practically, the duration of administration is often proportional to the
response to therapy. In patients with rapid resolution of clinical signs, therapy is
often limited to a few weeks. In patients without rapid resolution, therapy can
last several months, during which an effort is made to develop an effective
multimodal medical therapy (ch. 6), optimize body condition (chs. 72, 145, and
150), facilitate daily activities (ch. 226), and develop a tailored exercise
program. The decision to end NSAID therapy should consider whether the
disorder being treated persists; for example, most forms of OA in dogs persist
over time and may lead to undetected chronic pain.
In middle-aged dogs, OA becomes more impactful. Dogs can have difficulties
in their daily activities, such as being unwilling to climb stairs or jump up or
being less willing to go on walks or play. These signs are generally due to local
disease amplification (increased pain due to peripheral secondary sensitization)
and to loss of strength and joint motion secondary to the chronicity of OA. The
need for NSAID therapy increases in dogs with functional signs of OA relative to
younger dogs: NSAIDs will likely be needed for a period of 4 weeks or more,
together with supportive measures (e.g., flooring that provides traction).
In older dogs, the consequences of OA are more complex and generalized.
Chronic pain, combined with the loss of strength resulting from decreased
activity, can be so severe that dogs lose the ability to walk. At that stage, OA may
lead to euthanasia.18 Because they provide predictable pain relief, NSAIDs must
be considered in older dogs with severe signs of OA. Also, since the disease is
chronic, therapy is likely to be needed for several months. However, older dogs
are at higher risk of chronic kidney and liver disease, potentially increasing the
risk of adverse event. It is therefore recommended to evaluate renal and liver
function at the onset of therapy and monitor dogs for adverse events. Alternative
oral or injectable medications such as amantadine (an NMDA receptor
antagonist), gabapentin (a GABA analogue), tramadol (a synthetic opiate
analogue and serotoninergic), and polysulfated glycosaminoglycans are used to
manage signs of OA in older dogs. However, their evidence of efficacy is limited
to a few clinical trials for dogs with chronic OA.19
OA is common in cats. Cats metabolize NSAIDs differently from the way dogs
do and, therefore, NSAID use differs among dogs and cats. NSAIDs such as
meloxicam and robenacoxib are used to manage signs of OA in cats.20 It is

unclear whether the long-term use of NSAIDs in cats is safe. The FDA currently
requires a boxed warning for the use of meloxicam; however, a recent review
article and a retrospective study considered the use of meloxicam and
robenacoxib in cats with chronic renal disease to be relatively safe.21,22

CHANGING NSAIDs
If the clinical response to an NSAID is less than anticipated, a change of NSAID
may be considered because NSAIDs differ in their mode of action. A positive
response to a change in NSAID has been observed in clinical trials.19 A washout
period of 5 to 7 days has been recommended.7,23 Some recommend a longer
washout period of 10 to 14 days after aspirin administration because of the
presence of aspirin-triggered lipoxins and potential irreversible inhibition of
platelet function. That duration allows full elimination of the first NSAID and
gastrointestinal inflammation to subside via epithelial cell turnover and other
mechanisms.

ADVERSE EFFECTS OF NSAIDs
When mild adverse events such as vomiting or diarrhea occur, NSAID
administration is discontinued. Hepatic enzyme activities and renal values are
measured and, when abnormal, liver and kidney status can be evaluated further
via measurements of serum bile acids and urine protein excretion, respectively.
Dogs whose liver dysfunction is limited to alkaline phosphatase elevation are
considered candidates for future NSAID administration. However, hepatic
disease may place dogs at risk of future gastrointestinal adverse events. In dogs
with chronic kidney disease (ch. 301), the COX-2 isoenzyme is overexpressed
and its inhibition via NSAID is expected to negatively impact renal function.24

GLUCOCORTICOIDS AS ANTIINFLAMMATORIES
Glucocorticoids remain in use to manage the symptoms of OA in humans,
particularly at a low dosage and with a short treatment duration.25,26 In dogs
and cats, glucocorticoids have been used for alleviating the signs of OA.
Evidence comparing the clinical response between glucocorticoids and NSAIDs
is lacking. Since glucocorticoids also carry a risk of gastrointestinal side-effects
(ch. 224)10 and since their long-term administration leads to common systemic
changes, the use of glucocorticoids to manage OA in dogs appears to be
decreasing. Also, whereas the presence of NSAIDs in joints with OA does not

appear to influence the rate of cartilage breakdown, the use of glucocorticoid
does appear to accelerate cartilage breakdown.26

ANTI-NERVE GROWTH FACTOR
MONOCLONAL ANTIBODIES
The management of chronic OA pain in dogs and cats by use of anti-nerve
growth factor monoclonal antibodies (anti-NGF mAb) has been discussed.27
Although not strictly aimed at reducing inflammation, NGF has a role in
nociceptive sensitization and, as such, it has been compared to prostaglandin E2.
Several anti-NGF mAbs for dogs and cats are in development. One (frunevetmab
injection) appeared effective in a randomized clinical trial and received FDA
approval for use in cats in 2022 as a monthly subcutaneous injection.28

Most currently available immunosuppressive drugs target the adaptive
arm of the immune system. Although antibody-based therapies are
becoming more widely used in humans, most immunosuppressives used
in dogs and cats are still small molecules that fall into the categories of 1)
glucocorticoids, 2) antiproliferatives, or 3) calcineurin inhibitors (Table
144.1). Characteristics of commonly used agents from these classes are
discussed below. For monitoring and adverse events associated with
immunosuppressive drugs, see ch. 169. For use of immunosuppressive
drugs in specific diseases, see chs. 174-179.

GLUCOCORTICOIDS
MECHANISM
Many of the effects of glucocorticoids (GCs) are mediated through a
cytosolic receptor that translocates to the nucleus after ligand binding
and influences gene transcription. Notable genomic actions of GCs that
contribute to immunosuppression include 1) interference with activatorprotein 1 (AP-1) and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of
activated B-cells (NFκB), which regulate the production of proinflammatory cytokines, cytokine receptors, chemotactic proteins, and
adhesion molecules, 2) inhibition of other transcription factors regulating
genes that code for inflammatory cytokines (e.g., Interleukin [IL]-2), 3)
promotion of lymphocyte apoptosis through upregulation of proteins
from the Bcl-2 family, and 4) induction of annexin (lipocortin) I, which
inhibits phospholipase A2 and eicosanoid generation. The consequences
of these actions are decreased signaling, cytokine production, survival,
and effector function in T- and B-lymphocytes and dendritic cells,
reduced neutrophil extravasation and mast cell degranulation,
diminished function of stromal fibroblasts and other resident
mesenchymal cells, and shifting of macrophages toward an antiinflammatory rather than a pro-inflammatory phenotype. GCs also have
nongenomic actions that include intercalation into immune cell
membranes and disruption of calcium and sodium cycling, inhibition of
lymphocyte-specific protein tyrosine kinase (which initiates T-cell
receptor signaling) via membrane-bound GC receptors, and release of Src
kinase from the inactive GC receptor, resulting in reduced arachidonic
acid generation.1,2 These typically take effect in minutes to hours, rather
than hours to days as for the genomic actions.

PHARMACOKINETICS/PHARMACODYNAM
ICS

GCs are lipid-soluble and typically have rapid oral absorption (1-2 h),
high oral bioavailability, wide tissue distribution, and relatively short
half-lives (0.5-4 h). In dogs, oral prednisone is efficiently converted to
prednisolone by hepatic 11-betahydroxysteroid dehydrogenase and
inactive metabolites are excreted in the urine.3 In cats, prednisolone area
under the curve (AUC) is 4 times greater after oral prednisolone than oral
prednisone, indicating either reduced absorption or reduced hepatic
biotransformation of prednisone. Obese cats have twice the prednisolone
AUC of lean cats, suggesting that not as much of the drug distributes into
fat as might be expected, and dosing should be based on lean body
weight.4
The duration of biological effect of GCs varies with the individual GC
and formulation. In general, GCs with higher binding affinity for the
receptor have greater potency and duration of effect.2 Relative potencies
of dexamethasone, methylprednisolone, and prednisone relative to
cortisol are 25, 5, and 4, respectively, and biological half-lives are 36-72
hours for dexamethasone and 12-36 hours for the other steroids listed.5
For injectable steroids, esterification with a fatty acid (e.g., acetate) slows
absorption and prolongs duration of action, whereas formulation as a
water-soluble salt (e.g., sodium phosphate) increases the rate of
absorption from intramuscular or subcutaneous sites. Budesonide, which
is poorly bioavailable due to high hepatic first-pass metabolism,
accumulates in epithelial cells after local delivery and is stored as an
inactive fatty acid ester. This is gradually hydrolyzed to release the active
form, which has a high affinity for local intracellular GC receptors
(leading to higher local than systemic activity) and is in equilibrium with
budesonide in plasma.5,6
The magnitude of GC effect is dose-dependent and is related to the
degree of GC receptor saturation, which approaches 100% as
immunosuppressive doses are reached in humans.2 Cats are anecdotally
less sensitive to the effects of GCs; this may be related to fewer, loweraffinity GC receptors, at least in the liver and skin.7

ADVERSE EFFECTS
Potential adverse effects of GCs are familiar to most clinicians and are
related to activation of GC receptors in tissues other than those of the
immune system. They include polyuria/polydipsia, polyphagia, excessive

panting, behavior changes (lethargy, aggression), muscle atrophy and
weakness, connective tissue degeneration (leading to curled pinnae in
cats, and ligament rupture in cats and dogs), dermal atrophy, poor wound
healing, calcinosis cutis, gastrointestinal disturbances or ulceration,
hepatomegaly and elevated liver enzymes, changes to the hemogram
(neutrophilia, lymphopenia, eosinopenia, monocytosis), low serum
thyroxine concentration, proteinuria, systemic hypertension, adrenal
atrophy, insulin resistance (ch. 224), and fluid retention (with potential
unmasking of diabetes and/or heart disease, particularly in cats). GCinduced diabetes in dogs is rare but has been reported.8 Fluid retention
may be related to mineralocorticoid activity, which is more significant for
hydrocortisone than for synthetic GCs, and least significant for
dexamethasone1,5; hyperglycemia-associated fluid shifts also have been
implicated in cats.9

ANTIPROLIFERATIVES
AZATHIOPRINE
Mechanism
Azathioprine (AZA) is a prodrug for 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP), which is
metabolized by the purine salvage enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine
phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) and subsequently a variety of
kinases to form thioguanine nucleotides (TGNs). TGNs are incorporated
into DNA and, to a lesser extent, RNA. Incorporation is cytotoxic via
triggering of DNA damage-related cell cycle checkpoints. TGNs also
promote apoptosis in activated T-cells by binding to Rac-1, a cell cycleregulating G protein. This results in reduced proliferation of actively
dividing T- and B-lymphocytes.10

Pharmacokinetics/Pharmacodynamics
Minimal data regarding the pharmacokinetics of AZA in dogs and cats are
available. However, administration of oral 6-MP in dogs led to
accumulation until stable trough concentrations were reached after
approximately 2 weeks. After the drug was discontinued, these
concentrations persisted for 3-6 weeks, suggesting regeneration from an
intracellular depot.11 Consistent with this, radioactivity from radiolabeled
AZA redistributed into plasma after initial rapid uptake into blood cells in

dogs.12 6-MP is inactivated by xanthine oxidase and thiopurine
methyltransferase (TPMT) to thiouric acid and 6-methylmercaptopurine,
respectively, and these and other inactive metabolites are eliminated in
the urine.12 In humans, AZA has a delayed onset of action (weeks to
months), which may be related to time necessary for inactive TGN-bound
Rac-1 to accumulate intracellularly, and/or may reflect a greater impact
on memory T-cells than on initial differentiation into effector cells.10 A
lag time of anywhere from 2-6 weeks is also commonly expected in dogs,
based on mechanism of action and studies in humans and mice,13,14
although this is difficult to confirm as it is rarely used as a sole agent, and
occasional more rapid responses have been reported.15 Efficacy in
humans correlates with tissue (e.g., erythrocyte) TGN concentrations
rather than with serum concentrations of AZA or 6-MP.10

Adverse Effects
The primary adverse effects of AZA are myelosuppression and
hepatotoxicosis (chs. 321 and 269, respectively). Myelosuppression
(progressive neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, or pancytopenia) has been
reported in dogs receiving 2 mg/kg/day of AZA for 3-13 weeks.16-18
Hepatotoxicosis may be dose-dependent (as it has been demonstrated at
high dosages of AZA in experimental dogs) or idiosyncratic, and it is
thought to result from formation of 6-methylmercaptopurine (6-MMP)
and nucleotide metabolites, with subsequent oxidative injury and
mitochondrial damage. It is exacerbated by glutathione depletion in
experimental settings.18 Frequencies of occurrence for myelosuppression
and hepatotoxicosis (subclinical increases in serum alanine
aminotransferase and/or alkaline phosphatase activity) in dogs in
retrospective studies were 8% and 15%, respectively, within the first 2
months of therapy. In most cases, these effects are reversible within 1-8
weeks of dosage reduction or drug discontinuation, but neutropenia may
be persistent.16,18 In humans, individuals with low TPMT activity are
more susceptible to myelosuppression because less of the active drug is
metabolized to 6-MMP, and a greater proportion of cytotoxic TGN is
formed. In people with high TPMT activity, risk of hepatotoxicosis is
greater, and the clinical effect is diminished because of rapid
inactivation.10 Cats are much more susceptible to AZA-induced
myelosuppression and have significantly lower erythrocyte TPMT activity

than dogs or humans.19 However, TPMT activity does not correlate with
likelihood of myelosuppression in individual dogs.17 Administration of
allopurinol with AZA can result in increased TGN concentrations due to
xanthine oxidase inhibition and shunting of 6-MP toward TPMT.10
Pancreatitis and predisposition to neoplasia are known adverse effects
of AZA in humans (with pancreatitis possibly being due to decreased
pancreatic perfusion).10,20 Pancreatitis has also been reported in dogs
receiving AZA but causation has not been as clearly established.20

MYCOPHENOLATE
Mechanism
Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is an orally bioavailable prodrug for
mycophenolic acid (MPA). MPA noncompetitively, reversibly inhibits
inosine 5′ monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), which catalyzes a
rate-limiting step in the synthesis of guanine ribo- and
deoxyribonucleotides. Of the two isoforms of IMPDH, MPA more
potently inhibits type II, found in activated lymphocytes; proliferating
lymphocytes also lack nucleoside salvage pathways and are dependent on
de novo synthesis. Therefore, guanine depletion by MPA leads to
impaired proliferation of B and T cells, reducing cytotoxic activity and
antibody production. Other actions that may be of benefit in immunemediated disease include induction of T-lymphocyte apoptosis,
suppression of dendritic cell maturation, monocyte recruitment, nitric
oxide (NO) synthesis, and reduction of fibrosis.21

Pharmacokinetics/Pharmacodynamics
In both dogs and cats, MMF is rapidly absorbed, highly protein-bound,
and metabolized in the liver to form glucuronide and/or glucoside
derivatives that are excreted in the urine.21,22 In dogs, bioavailability is
relatively high (50-90%), the drug undergoes enterohepatic recirculation,
and the half-life is 3-9 hours (with significant variation in both half-life
and extent of absorption among individuals).21 In cats, plasma
concentrations are also highly variable and the drug and metabolites are
nondetectable by 12 hours after oral administration of either 10 or 15
mg/kg of MMF twice a day for up to 1 week.23 The onset of action of
mycophenolate appears to be more rapid than that of AZA; dogs given IV

MMF for generalized myasthenia gravis (MG, ch. 253) showed signs of
clinical remission within 48 hours, and in dogs with immune-mediated
thrombocytopenia (ITP, ch. 175), platelet counts increased within 2-6
days of starting therapy with MMF as a sole agent.21

Adverse Effects
The most common adverse effect of MMF in humans and dogs is
gastrointestinal upset (vomiting, diarrhea, inappetence). This is dosedependent and is generally considered reversible, but with greater
exposure (e.g., 15 mg/kg every 8 hours, or >30 mg/kg in a laboratory
setting) necrotizing enterocolitis has been reported in dogs. Proposed
mechanisms for gastrointestinal toxicosis include interference with
proliferation of enterocytes (which, like lymphocytes, have a relative
dependence on de novo purine synthesis), cytokine release stimulated by
the acyl glucuronide metabolite, local irritation by the mofetil ester, or
disruption of normal flora related to the antibiotic effects of MMF.21 In a
study of laboratory cats given oral MMF, all 3 cats receiving 15 mg/kg
orally every 8 hours developed diarrhea or anorexia necessitating drug
discontinuation.23 A starting dosage of 10 mg/kg every 12 hours may be
less likely to lead to adverse reactions and has been reported to be
clinically effective in both dogs and cats.21,24 Mycophenolate-induced
myelosuppression, hepatopathy and pancreatitis have been reported in
humans, and the latter two were suspected in a cat receiving compounded
mycophenolate.21,25

LEFLUNOMIDE
Mechanism
Leflunomide is a prodrug that is metabolized in the plasma, liver and
intestinal mucosa to teriflunomide (A77 1726, also approved as an
immunosuppressive in humans). Teriflunomide inhibits dihydro-orotate
dehydrogenase, a key enzyme in de novo synthesis of pyrimidines, and
thereby reduces lymphocyte proliferation. It may also be antiproliferative
through reduction of CD25 expression (which renders lymphocytes less
responsive to IL-2), have anti-inflammatory activity via inhibition of
Janus kinase (JAK)1, JAK2, nuclear factor kappa beta (NFkB), and
cyclooxygenase 2 (COX-2), and increase generation of regulatory T-cells
by induction of Foxp3 expression.26,27

Pharmacokinetics/Pharmacodynamics
Leflunomide is well-absorbed, with a bioavailability of approximately 80100% in dogs and 100% in cats based on teriflunomide concentration
(since leflunomide rapidly becomes nondetectable in plasma as it is
converted to teriflunomide).28-31 Teriflunomide is eliminated in the urine
and bile in dogs.29 The half-life of teriflunomide in humans is 15-17 days
(possibly due to enterohepatic recirculation),27 but in dogs it is much
shorter (21-25 hours) after a single oral dose, and steady state is expected
in 4-5 days.30 In cats, the half-life is approximately 2.5 days.31 In
humans, teriflunomide concentrations after leflunomide administration
are dose-proportional, and concentrations >16 mcg/mL are associated
with a greater likelihood of therapeutic success.28 In dogs, good clinical
responses have been reported with a median dosage of 1.9 mg/kg/d;
however, teriflunomide concentrations do not seem to correlate well with
either leflunomide dosage (r = 0.26) or clinical response, as the mean
plasma concentration for dogs with controlled disease was significantly
lower (30 ± 15 mcg/mL) than that for uncontrolled dogs (52 ± 39
mcg/mL).32

Adverse Effects
Adverse effects of leflunomide reported in dogs in a clinical setting
include diarrhea and lethargy (3% of dogs, within 1 week of starting
leflunomide), unexplained hemorrhage (ecchymosis, hematochezia,
and/or hematuria in 3% of dogs, 6-20 weeks after starting leflunomide),
mild thrombocytopenia (6% of dogs) and liver enzyme elevation (6% of
dogs). Both of the latter occurred within 2 weeks of starting leflunomide,
and all adverse effects were reversible with dose reduction or
discontinuation. The median leflunomide dosage in dogs with adverse
events (2.9 mg/kg/d) was significantly higher than the dosage in dogs
without adverse events (1.6 mg/kg/d). In other studies, dosages of 3-4
mg/kg/d caused lethargy, blood dyscrasias, elevated liver enzymes,
and/or anorexia in dogs.33,34 In cats, occasional vomiting was noted with
2 mg/kg of leflunomide every other day for up to 6 doses, after two
consecutive daily doses of 2 mg/kg.31

CALCINEURIN INHIBITORS

CYCLOSPORINE
Mechanism
Cyclosporine A is one of a series of cyclic polypeptides of fungal origin
whose primary mechanism of action is inhibition of calcineurin.
Calcineurin is activated by binding of antigen to T-lymphocyte CD3
receptors. In the absence of cyclosporine, calcineurin dephosphorylates
the nuclear factor of activated T-cells (NFAT), allowing this transcription
factor to translocate to the nucleus and upregulate genes coding for IL-2,
IL-4, tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha, and interferon (IFN)-gamma.
When cyclosporine is present (as a complex with intracellular proteins
called cyclophilins), it binds to calcineurin and prevents NFAT
translocation and cytokine gene transcription. Because IL-2 is
instrumental in initiating proliferation and clonal expansion of T-cells,
this leads to reduction in both helper and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte number
and function.35

Pharmacokinetics/Pharmacodynamics
Cyclosporine is lipophilic and requires micronization for consistent oral
absorption. Maximum plasma concentration is achieved 2 hours after oral
administration, and the drug is widely distributed and achieves high
concentrations in erythrocytes (>50% of absorbed drug). In humans, Pglycoprotein efflux from enterocytes affects the extent of absorption.
Although this was not the case in a small study of normal and Pglycoprotein-deficient dogs,35 one dog with the MDR-1 mutation was
found to have higher than expected cyclosporine concentrations.36
Cyclosporine is extensively metabolized via the cytochrome P450 system
and excreted primarily in bile. The half-life in dogs is 7-10 hours, but is
highly variable (1-150 h) depending on breed, concurrent medications,
and other factors. Drug interactions with other P450 inhibitors or
inducers can occur (ch. 139) and the interaction that is best recognized
in veterinary medicine is slower metabolism when given with azoles
(enabling a 50-75% dose reduction when the drug is given with
ketoconazole or fluconazole). A list of other potential interactions can be
found in Reference 35. Cyclosporine is typically expected to exert a
clinical effect within 24-48 hours of starting therapy. A dosage of 10
mg/kg q12h was found to reliably induce immunosuppression in all dogs
in one study,37 but some dogs are significantly immunosuppressed even

at 5 mg/kg q24h or less.36 Monitoring and individualization of therapy
are discussed in depth in ch. 169.

Adverse Effects
Gastrointestinal upset occurs in up to 30% of dogs receiving cyclosporine
at dosages of 5-10 mg/kg/day. Secondary infection may be more common
with cyclosporine than with other immunosuppressive agents in
environments with opportunistic fungi.38 Cutaneous papillomatosis
secondary to immunosuppression, other dermatologic side effects, and
reversible gingival hyperplasia (Figure 258.3) have also been reported.
Cats on long-term cyclosporine after renal transplantation were 6 times
more likely to develop malignant neoplasia than were control cats.39
