Chapter 145: Nutritional
Assessment
Kathryn E. Michel

A C RO N YM
BCS body condition score
Whether to maintain optimum health or as part of a treatment
regimen for a diseased state, good nutrition is essential to maximize
the quality and quantity of life in all animals. The purpose of
nutritionally assessing a patient is to allow the clinician to answer the
question, “Is intervention for this patient necessary?” and to aid the
clinician in selecting the most appropriate nutritional intervention
for that patient. This simple and rapid process involves evaluating
both subjective and objective information regarding the patient, the
patient’s diet and the patient’s feeding management and
environment.1,2 In addition to aiding in the selection of a suitable
diet and feeding management for the patient, nutritional assessment
will also help the clinician to advise the client on their feeding
practices as well as anticipate potential problems or complications
and to devise strategies to avoid or monitor such developments.

PATIENT ASSESSMENT (ch. 72)
In addition to signalment (including life stage and neuter status) and
any previous or ongoing medical conditions (including medications),
evaluation of body condition is a chief consideration in the
assessment of the patient. There are some sophisticated techniques

currently being used in human patients or in a research setting (e.g.,
multiple-frequency bioelectrical impedance, dual-energy
radiographic absorptiometry [DEXA]) that have not been sufficiently
validated in companion animals as well as several that have been
investigated in companion animals (ultrasonographic or computed
tomography epaxial muscle measurements) but do not lend
themselves to a clinical setting because of logistic considerations or
expense.3-5 Body condition scoring (BCS; see inside covers; ch. 72),
although subjective, is simple to learn, requires no special
equipment, and has been shown to be repeatable and consistent
among multiple observers (

Video 72.1).6 The BCS systems that

have been published for companion animals are principally based on
characterization of body silhouette and palpation of body fat (ch. 3).
These systems are useful, particularly for identification of patients
that have an overweight body condition; however, they may
misclassify some malnourished patients. It is important to recognize
that catabolism of lean body tissue can occur very rapidly and may
account for a disproportionate amount of the body mass lost in sick
patients. Although the purpose of adipose tissue is to serve as an
energy reserve, no analogous reserve of endogenous protein exists.
Because all endogenous protein is serving some function, continuous
catabolism will eventually have deleterious consequences for the
patient. Therefore, the process of body condition assessment should
include not only the standard evaluation of body silhouette and
evaluation of adipose tissue as an assessment of energy reserves but
also a separate evaluation of muscle mass (i.e., a muscle condition
score) as a subjective means of assessing lean tissue status (inside
covers; ch. 72). This can be accomplished by palpation of skeletal
muscle over the axial skeleton and other bony prominences (
Video 72.2, ch. 151).7
Other aspects of the physical examination of a patient that should
be taken into consideration include haircoat quality and skin
condition (ch. 12), dental abnormalities or disease (ch. 258),
evidence of peripheral edema or ascites (which may indicate
hypoproteinemia; chs. 30 and 21, respectively), and clinical signs

that may indicate specific micronutrient deficiencies such as neck
ventroflexion (chs. 3, 14;

Video 68.1) or tetany (ch. 23).

TAKING A DIET HISTORY
The more information that is available about the patient’s diet and
feeding management, the better the clinician will be able to assess
the adequacy of nutrient intake, the suitability of feeding practices,
and the urgency for nutritional intervention. At the core of a dietary
history is the careful gathering of information that will give an
accurate picture of the foods that the patient consumes. Ideally, the
person who is most responsible for feeding the patient should be
questioned; however, it is important to find out who else resides in
the household or has regular contact with the patient, including
other pets. The patient’s caregiver should be questioned about all
foods that the patient receives (Box 145.1) and asked whether the
information reflects what is typical for this pet, whether changes
have occurred, and if so, when they happened.
In addition to particulars about the patient’s diet, the history
should also include information regarding appetite, feeding
management, documented or perceived changes in body weight or
condition, level of physical activity, and occurrence of any
gastrointestinal (GI) signs. Again, the patient’s caregiver should be
queried as to whether the information reflects what is typical for this
pet or whether (and if so, when) changes have occurred. Although it
is often the case that a pet owner cannot precisely recount an exact
weight change, he or she may have an impression of the period of
time over which the change occurred. Rapid weight loss and
deterioration in body condition, particularly if associated with
muscle wasting, suggests a greater degree of metabolic derangement
or reduction in food intake (or both) and greater potential for
significant malnutrition than a more gradual loss of weight.
Box 1 4 5 .1 I nfo rmatio n t o Be Inc lu de d in a D ie t
H is t o ry

• Commercial pet foods (specific type
[brand/formulation/flavor]and daily portion; dry foods should
be weighed or measured with an 8-oz [250 mL] measuring cup;
canned foods should be measured by can size and portion used)
• Commercial treats (brand, size, and frequency of use)
• Table foods or scraps (detailed information about type of food,
portion size, and frequency of use)
• Treats for chewing (e.g., rawhide, pig’s ears; size and frequency

• Dietary supplements (brand and daily portion)
• Foods used for medication of the patient (type of food, portion

• Pet’s access to garbage
• Pet’s ability to scavenge or roam
• Timing, location, and method of feeding and storage of food
Whether assessing a pet in an outpatient wellness visit or a patient
with ongoing significant illness, the opportunity should not be
missed to communicate to the patient’s caregiver what they are doing
right (ch. 1) as well as recommending any indicated modifications to
the patient’s feeding regimen.

SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS
REGARDING ASSISTED FEEDING
No definitive tests are available for establishing a patient’s
nutritional status. However, based on the information gathered from
the patient’s medical (ch. 2) and dietary history (above) and physical
examination (ch. 3), the clinician should be able to classify broadly
the patient as being well nourished, mildly malnourished, or severely
malnourished. The decision to intervene with some nutritional
support has to balance the anticipated benefits with the potential
risks and costs of the proposed intervention. Therefore, the intent of
nutritional assessment should not simply be to diagnose inadequate
food intake or malnutrition, but rather to identify patients that are at

risk of a poor outcome as a result of their compromised nutritional
status. Investigations of human patients have found an increased
risk of morbidity and mortality associated with various objective
markers of nutritional status, including hypoalbuminemia,
lymphopenia, and attenuated delayed hypersensitivity reactivity.
Other investigators have found that clinical assessment of patients
based on a carefully performed history and physical examination, as
described previously, has a predictive value similar to that of
objective markers of nutritional status such as serum albumin
concentration.8 Furthermore, investigations of the effect of
nutritional support on improving clinical outcome suggest that the
most significantly malnourished patients are the most likely to show
benefit from nutritional support.
There has been only limited investigation of the prognostic value
of nutritional assessment in veterinary patients; however, an
association between weight loss and/or low BCS and survival has
been found in studies of feline patients with different conditions,
including chronic kidney disease (ch. 301), cancer (chs. 163, 331),
and heart failure (chs. 157, 229, 234).9-11 Serum albumin
concentration at the time of admission to the hospital has been
shown to correlate with risk of poor clinical outcome in critically ill
dogs, and elevation of serum creatine kinase activity has been found
to be associated with anorexia in feline patients.12,13 To date, there
have been few investigations of the prognostic value of subjective
nutritional assessments and the impact of nutritional support on
clinical outcome in companion animals; however, it is not
unreasonable to expect results to be similar to those found in human
patients. Therefore, it is recommended that patients assessed to be
significantly malnourished on presentation or that are at risk of
becoming significantly malnourished in the course of their illness
due to decreased food intake, malassimilation of diet, or metabolic
derangement should be considered candidates for assisted feeding.

MONITORING NUTRITIONAL
INTERVENTIONS

Once a dietary recommendation has been made, the patient should
be reassessed after an appropriate interval of time. The actual timing
of reassessment depends on the severity of the patient’s illness and
the type of nutritional intervention it has received. One should
determine whether the prescribed recommendations are being
followed, if problems with diet acceptance or tolerance are seen, if
the desired outcomes have been achieved, or if any adverse events
associated with the diet or feeding management have occurred. A
thorough nutritional assessment at the outset will often identify
potential problems or complications and thereby determine what
parameters should be monitored in the patient. At the least, body
weight and condition should be reassessed regularly to ascertain that
the patient is maintaining, gaining, or losing weight appropriately.

Chapter 146: Neonatal and
Pediatric Nutrition
Cecilia Villaverde

A C RO N YM S
BCS body condition score
BW body weight
DHA docosahexaenoic acid
ME metabolizable energy
RER resting energy requirement

Nutrition and feeding are critical during the growth period to
ensure animals achieve their body weight (BW) and size determined
by their genetic potential, without nutrient imbalances.

NUTRIENT NEEDS
Dogs and cats require around 40 essential nutrients, including
protein and amino acids, fat and fatty acids, vitamins, and minerals.
Puppies and kittens have different nutrient requirements than
adults, both quantitatively and qualitatively,1 including protein,
calcium, and phosphorus (required for new tissue formation) and
docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). This long chain polyunsaturated

omega-3 fatty acid is essential for growing animals due to its role in
retinal and neural development2,3 and it can increase learning
performance in puppies.2,4 While calcium requirements are
relatively higher in puppies than adults, large- and giant-breed dogs
are also susceptible to excess.5 Nutrient deficiencies or excesses are
rare in puppies and kittens fed life-stage-appropriate commercial
diets from reputable manufacturers but can be seen with improperly
formulated home-prepared diets (ch. 167) and can have lifelong
consequences. Nutrient excesses with implications in skeletal health
(calcium, vitamin D, vitamin A) can be seen in growing pets given
vitamin/mineral supplements (ch. 162).

ENERGY NEEDS
Growing animals have higher energy requirements (on a metabolic
weight basis) than adults, especially during the first 4 months of life.1
Growing dogs and cats that are inactive, that belong to specific
obesity-prone breeds, or that have been neutered can have lower
energy requirements than average and may be prone to overweight.6
Energy requirements expressed as kilocalories of metabolizable
energy (ME) per day for puppies can be estimated at 3 times the
resting energy requirement (RER, 70 × BW(kg)0.75) from weaning to
4 months of age and 2 × RER for the rest of the growth period. For
cats, the average daily energy requirement is estimated at 2.5 × RER
for the whole growth period.7 The growth period can be considered
to extend to when an animal reaches mature BW and size and its
growth plates have closed (cats and small- and medium-breed dogs,
12 months; large- and giant-breed dogs, 18-24 months). These
energy requirement formulas are just a crude estimate and
individual needs might vary. Therefore, the daily calorie provision
will need to be adjusted individually.

FEEDING GROWING ANIMALS
FEEDING THE NEWBORN

Nutrition in newborns plays a key role in survival.8 Nursing is the
main source of nutrition. Colostrum (the secretion from the
mammary gland during the first few days of lactation) provides
nutrients, energy, and passive immunity, and newborns must receive
it within the first 24-48 hours after birth.9 Adequate nutrition of the
mothers is critical for milk production; their diet must be
nutritionally complete, formulated for reproduction or all life stages,
and with an energy density of at least 4 kilocalories ME per gram (on
a dry matter basis). This is especially important in large-breed dogs
with large litters, where intake can be volume-limited. While some
puppy foods can also be indicated for lactation, this is not always the
case; some large-breed puppy diets can have a relatively reduced
energy density. Both food and water must be always available. Signs
like restlessness, continuous vocalization, and failure to grow at an
adequate rate signal a maternal health problem, a failure to suckle,
or inadequate milk production. The BW of the young should be
recorded every 24-48 hours. For the first 4 months of life, puppies
should grow 2-4 g/kg of adult BW/day and kittens should grow 10-15
g per day (average of 100 g per week).10,11
Maternal milk is enough as a sole source of nutrients only until
weeks 3-4 after birth and solid food should be introduced at that
time (earlier for larger breeds and large litters). The food can be the
same as the mother’s, either dry (as a gruel with water, 1:1
volume/volume) or wet. Canned or dry (gruel) puppy/kitten food is
also a good choice. Some brands have specific weaning products that
are nutritionally adequate and have a good texture. For large breeds,
using a large-breed puppy diet is indicated to ensure an adequate
mineral balance. Shallow plates are useful, so the animals will step
on the food and lick their paws. The paws and the mouth (never the
nose) can be smeared with the gruel to encourage eating as well.
Solid food should be introduced slowly and gradually until it is the
sole source of nutrition by the time of weaning at weeks 7-9.

Rearing Orphan Puppies and Kittens
Newborns that are orphaned, unable to suckle, or whose mother
cannot produce enough milk due to disease or too large a litter size
can be completely or partially hand reared. The mother not only

provides nutrition but also warmth, humidity, elimination,
sanitation, and security. All of this should be provided as well.10-12
The best way to feed orphans is a foster mother; if this is not
possible, milk replacers will be necessary, using either commercial
products or home-prepared recipes.9,11 The latter are not ideal13 and
should be reserved for emergencies, although commercial products
are not without problems. A study14 described a high nutrient
variability in canine milk replacers available in the US (some had
deficiencies in amino acids, calcium and DHA, and some were quite
low in energy density compared to the 1.4 kcal/mL of canine milk).
One European study15 also found issues with nutrient excesses of
calcium and vitamin D in canine milk replacers, which could be a
risk for fast-growing, large-breed puppies. It is important to choose a
product with at least 1 kcal/mL (reconstituted) and to carefully select
the manufacturing company, asking them about their nutritional
expertise.16 Energy requirements of newborn puppies and kittens are
estimated at 20-25 kcal/100 g BW.1 Dividing this by the energy
density of the milk replacer will yield the volume per day to provide,
divided over several meals per day every 2-4 hours. Stomach capacity
can be assumed to be 4 mL/100 g of BW. It is recommended to start
slower (50% of energy requirements) the first day to ensure a safer
transition. Lower intakes (or formula dilution) are also indicated in
cases of diarrhea. Adjustments every 48 hours will be necessary to
achieve the desired rate of weight gain. Water requirements are
estimated to be 180 mL/kg/day and additional water should be
provided if the milk replacer is not enough. Strong, vital animals can
be bottle fed (

Video 146.1), whereas weak newborns should be

tube fed with a 5 to 8 French feeding tube, placing them with the
head held high to prevent aspiration (

Video 146.2). Formula

should be warmed up to body temperature before use. After feedings,
the perineum must be massaged with a warm wet cloth or cotton to
stimulate elimination. Solid food should be introduced at week 3 as a
gruel (puppy/kitten canned or dry food as a gruel, can be mixed with
water or with the milk replacer).

FROM WEANING TO ADULTHOOD
Growing animals require a complete and balanced diet formulated
for this life stage (and for all life stages) from a reputable
manufacturer. Large- and giant-breed puppies should be fed growth
diets specifically formulated for these body sizes of breed, since these
puppies have an immature calcium regulation system and are
susceptible to excess.5 The maximum dietary calcium for these
puppies17 is 4.5 g/1000 kcal of ME (2.5% dry matter basis).
Nutritional supplements, especially those providing minerals, should
not be a routine part of the feeding regimen.
Free feeding is only indicated for small- and medium-sized
puppies and kittens that show an adequate rate of weight gain and a
lean body condition score (BCS, ch. 72). Portion-controlled feeding
is recommended for all other animals: large-breed dogs, obesityprone breeds, animals unable to maintain a lean BCS, and neutered
animals. One study18 found that Labrador Retrievers kept at a BCS
of 4/9 (compared to 6-7/9; see textbook’s inside covers for BCS
charts) from weaning into adulthood and maturity lived longer and
chronic diseases appeared at later age. Another study found that fast
growth rates were associated with obesity later in life.19 Large-breed
dogs need specific feeding care20 to prevent overfeeding (excess
energy supply). A fast growth rate in these breeds can predispose to
developmental orthopedic disease and osteoarthritis later (ch. 162),
in addition to obesity (ch. 150). These dogs should always be fed in
a portion-controlled manner and the daily allowance adjusted to
achieve a lean BCS of 4/9 and a moderate rate of growth. Size- or
breed-specific growth charts19 can be used to monitor this. Largebreed puppy diets, besides being complete for growth and having
controlled calcium concentrations, might be lower in energy density
compared to regular puppy foods in some cases, to facilitate a slow
rate of growth. The common recommendation to feed adult foods to
large- and giant-breed puppies to prevent orthopedic issues is
incorrect and can result in deficiencies. Moreover, depending on the
adult diet of choice, it could even provide more calcium and energy
than assumed, given the high variability in nutritional composition
of maintenance diets. The growth food should be fed until the animal

has reached its mature BW and size and the growth plates have
closed (12 months for small and medium sized dogs and cats; 18-24
months for large and giant breed dogs).

REASSESSMENT
A complete nutritional evaluation (ch. 145) each visit and BW and
BCS every 2 weeks during the fast growth phase (first 6 months) is
important; weight and BCS can be assessed every 3-4 weeks
afterwards. The BW must be plotted and compared to growth
curves19 and BCS should be kept in the ideal range. Pet caretakers
should be taught how to perform BCS (ch. 72

, Video 72.1) and

what a healthy lean puppy/kitten should look like. Adjustments in
the calorie allowance can be made by 10% increments or decrements
to achieve growth rate and BCS goals. Switching to a growth diet
with lower energy density can help keep hungry puppies or kittens
more sated. Blood work is not a sensitive or specific measure of the
nutritional status and both serum biochemistry results (such as
calcium, phosphorus, albumin, liver enzymes, lipids) and complete
blood cell count results can be affected by age in both puppies and
kittens; altered values compared to adult reference ranges should not
be misconstrued as indicative of malnutrition.

OVERVIEW
Data from 2021-2022 indicate that 69.0 million households in the United States had pet dogs.1 Many
pet owners are making pet food choices they believe are in the best interest of their dog. In a survey of
pet owners, 53% reported giving equal and 44% more priority to buying healthy food for their pets
compared to themselves.2 This same survey reported that health and nutrition were the most important
pet food characteristic for cat and dog owners. Across a range of studies, common factors that influence
pet food purchasing decisions range from the ingredients, quality, cost, company reputation, veterinary
recommendation, and ease of purchasing.2-4
Quality nutrition should begin when dogs are young and healthy, not just considered after an illness is
identified. “Young adult healthy dogs” can be defined as a group ranging in age from about 1 to 7 years,
depending on breed and size. A complete nutrition assessment should be performed on every dog at
every visit with a goal of preventative nutrition (ch. 145). Nutritional goals during early adulthood
should include optimizing health, disease prevention, increasing performance, and enhancing longevity.

UNIQUE NUTRITIONAL PHYSIOLOGY
DOGS AS OMNIVORES
Dogs are members of the order Carnivora. The word carnivore describes both the taxonomic group and
its feeding behavior. The order Carnivora includes true carnivores such as those in the family Felidae
and herbivores, such as the panda, in the family Ailuropodinae. The dog is in the Carnivora family, but
its metabolism and nutritional needs approach those of omnivores. Unlike true carnivores, dogs have
the capability to synthesize taurine, arachidonic acid, and vitamin A from their metabolic precursors in
plants: cystine, linoleic acid, and beta-carotene, respectively.
Although dogs do not have a nutritional requirement for carbohydrates, domesticated dogs are
adapted to thrive on a starch-rich diet. Genes that play a role in starch digestion—pancreatic amylase
(AMY2B), maltase-glucoamylase (MGAM), and the sodium/glucose cotransporter (SGLT1)—
demonstrate changes in expression and activity that favor starch digestion in dogs when compared to
wolves.5 The ability to handle a starch-rich diet may have some breed variability, as demonstrated by a

wide variation in AMY2B activity amongst dog breeds.6 Like true carnivores, however, dogs possess
metabolic characteristics such as an obligation to conjugate bile acids with taurine and an inability to
synthesize vitamin D. Dogs are not simply omnivores, but have developed their own metabolism and
nutritional requirements as they evolved.

PROTEIN AND AMINO ACIDS
The crude protein requirement represents the dog’s nitrogen requirement. Crude protein is defined as
the quantity of nitrogen times 6.25. Protein requirements for healthy dogs have been determined using
nitrogen balance and endogenous nitrogen excretion. The National Research Council (NRC)
requirement for crude protein in adult dogs is 2.62 g/kg body weight (BW)0.75 or 20 g per 1000 kcal and
recommended allowance is 3.82 g/kg BW0.75 or 25 g per 1000 kcal.7 Minimum protein
recommendations by the Association of American Feed Control Officials (AAFCO; 45 g per 1000 kcal)
are, in part, based on this information and account for changes in processing that can alter protein
digestibility or bioavailability.8 The NRC and AAFCO also set minimum recommendations for amino
acids. After the amino acid requirement is met, additional protein is deaminated by the liver. The
estimated percentage gram per 1000 kcal to define low-, moderate-, and high-protein diet when
comparing commercial pet foods for a dog is provided in Table 147.1.
Taurine is a conditionally essential amino acid in the dog. Daily taurine turnover in the dog is the
result of fecal excretion of taurine conjugated to bile acids. Dogs can synthesize taurine from the sulfur
amino acids methionine and cysteine; however, if the daily taurine loss is greater than the synthesis of
taurine, then taurine becomes a conditionally essential nutrient. Dietary factors (e.g., low protein, high
fiber) and breed (e.g., Golden Retrievers, Newfoundlands) have been shown to influence the blood
taurine concentrations of dogs.9-11

ESSENTIAL FATTY ACIDS
The polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) linoleic acid (18:2n-6) is an essential fatty acid (EFA) because
dogs lack enzymes to synthesize this fatty acid de novo. Various sources of plant oils (e.g., corn) and
some animal fats (e.g., poultry versus beef) are rich with linoleic acid. The EFA canine requirement is
greatest for linoleic acid, a deficiency of which results in hyperkeratosis, water loss through the skin, and
testicular degeneration. Linoleic acid is incorporated into sphingolipids in the epidermis of the skin,
aiding with barrier function and to help maintain skin and coat quality. Dogs, unlike cats, can desaturate
and elongate linoleic acid to form arachidonic acid (20:4n-6).
Alpha-linolenic acid (18:3n-3) is also an EFA but may not be required in the diet of a healthy adult
dog, unlike a growing or reproducing dog. Other EFAs, eicosapentaenoic acid (20:5n-3) and
docosahexaenoic acid (22:6n-3), are also not required in the diet of adult dogs; however, higher dosages
of these fatty acids may have a therapeutic effect due to their anti-inflammatory properties.
Fats provide over twice the calories as protein and carbohydrate; therefore, dog food containing high
levels of fat will have increased calorie density. The estimated percentage gram per 1000 kcal to define
low, moderate, and high fat diets when comparing commercial pet foods for a dog is provided in Table
147.1.

FIBER (CH. 165)
While dogs do not have specific nutritional requirements for carbohydrates or fiber, fiber can be added
to dog diets to optimize health through various functions, such as promotion of satiety or maintenance
of stool quality. Fiber is a poor source of energy; therefore, its inclusion in pet food will decrease energy
density and be useful when feeding animals prone to overweight or obesity (ch. 150). Fiber content is
expressed on pet food labels as maximum percentage of crude fiber, which reflects the percentage of
cellulose (insoluble fiber) in the diet. Total dietary fiber more accurately reflects the fiber content of a
pet food by including both soluble and insoluble fibers, except for certain types of fiber.

VITAMINS AND MINERALS
Adult dogs require the same minerals and vitamins as those that are essential for growing puppies (ch.
146). Our knowledge of these requirements for adult maintenance is sometimes based on our knowledge
of requirements during growth and these requirements are less precise than requirements established
for growing puppies. Vitamin and mineral requirements are published by the NRC and the
bioavailability of minerals must be considered when formulating diets.
Dogs must consume vitamin D as they cannot synthesize it using ultraviolet light due to a lack of
dermal concentrations of 7-dehydrocholesterol. The requirement for vitamin E, an antioxidant, is a
function of total PUFA content in a diet (i.e., higher levels of vitamin E are required with higher levels of
dietary PUFAs). Canine vitamin K requirements are largely met through intestinal synthesis, making
dietary supplementation less critical. Choline, although partially synthesized in the liver, is considered
an essential vitamin because it supplies labile methyl groups. Deficiency in methyl groups results in
accumulation of fat in the liver. Vitamin C is not essential in dog diets as de novo synthesis occurs from
glucose via the glucuronic acid pathway. There is insufficient evidence to indicate that a healthy pet dog
benefits from additional dietary vitamin C. L-carnitine (a vitamin-like substance), while non-essential,
may benefit certain individuals in certain breeds of dogs with a limited capacity to synthesize this
nutrient (e.g., Boxers).

MEETING ENERGY REQUIREMENTS
Maintenance energy requirements (MERs) and resting energy requirements (RERs) of adult dogs can be
estimated using formulas relating MERs to BW (Box 147.1). Because adult dogs have about a 50-fold
range in BW, and because MERs per unit of BW decrease with BW, formulas generally include some
power function of BW (e.g., BW raised to three-fourths power). RER, 70 kcal/BW0.75, represents the
energy needs of a normally-fed animal at rest in a thermoneutral environment.
Various life stage factors can be applied to the RER depending on the activity level and neuter status
of an adult dog. Typically, RER × 1.4-1.6 is used to determine adult MERs based on ideal BW in a

neutered dog. The NRC recommends MER predictive equations of 95.0 kcal/kg BW0.75 (1.36 × RER) for
inactive dogs and 130 kcal/kg BW0.75 (1.85 × RER) for active and kenneled dogs. Several studies have
suggested more precise predictive MER calculations for client-owned adult dogs.12–16 Meta-analysis of
the MER of adult dogs demonstrated average MERs of 142.8 ± 55.3 kcal/kg BW0.75/day with a suggested
allometric equation of 81.5 kcal/kg BW0.93/day.12 The energy requirements of adult dogs in this metaanalysis were impacted by husbandry (highest in racing dogs, then working/hunting dogs, and least in
pet and kenneled dogs) and neuter status (decreased in neutered animals versus sexually intact) with no
effect of sex. The recommended equation for determining the MER of pet dogs is 62.5 kcal/kg
BW0.97/day.12
Large variation exists in the prediction interval of MER; therefore, formulas should be used only as
starting points when determining MER and dogs should be fed to an ideal body condition. A complete
diet history together with following the dog’s weight and body condition score (BCS; ch. 72) over time
will help practitioners accurately determine an individual’s MER (ch. 145). These equations can be
useful clinically to estimate energy requirements, particularly when a complete diet history is not
available to estimate energy intake. This includes calculations to estimate energy requirements for
enteral or parenteral nutrition or making recommendations for either BW loss or gain.

DETERMINING THE OPTIMAL CANINE DIET
SELECTING A COMMERCIAL DIET
Commercial pet food should be complete and balanced, safe, and appropriate for the dog’s life stage. The
nutrition adequacy statement on a pet food label specifies if a diet is complete and balanced (versus for
intermittent or supplemental feeding), for what life stage (growth, gestation/lactation, adult
maintenance, or all life stages), and by what method nutritional adequacy is determined (formulation or
feeding trial). Diets formulated to meet AAFCO requirements meet specific nutrient requirements based
on either a calculated nutrient profile or analysis of the finished product. If a diet formulated to meet
AAFCO requirements is chosen by a pet owner, determination of nutrients by analysis of the finished
product is recommended. Diets formulated to be complete and balanced and demonstrated to be fully

adequate in adult dogs through feeding trials are ideal when selecting a product. Diets designated for all
life stages are typically higher in fat and more calorie-dense, as they are also intended for growing and
reproducing animals. Therefore, not all adult dogs should be fed this type of diet, especially not if they
are overweight or prone to obesity.
Evaluating the quality of pet food is a challenge. Unfortunately, the pet food label tells the consumer
very little about product safety and quality. Recommending pet foods “approved” by AAFCO is incorrect
because this organization does not regulate, test, approve or certify pet foods. The quality of pet food is
better reflected in the nutrient profile, digestibility, bioavailability of nutrients, safety surrounding the
manufacture of the product, and the nutritional knowledge and skill of the pet food company and
manufacture. The World Small Animal Veterinary Association (WSAVA) has released a list of
questions/guidelines to help consumers and veterinarians select commercial pet food.17 While these
questions are not the panacea for pet food quality, they are a good place to start beyond what is provided
on the pet food label.

UNCONVENTIONAL DIET STRATEGIES AND
CONTROVERSIES (CH. 167)
Unconventional diet strategies, including home-prepared, raw- meat-based, and vegan/vegetarian diets,
may be selected by pet owners for a variety of reasons often related to perceived health benefits. Pet
owner motivations may also vary by diet type. A survey of pet owners found of those feeding a raw meatbased diet, only 9% consulted with a veterinarian prior to feeding this type of diet and most did not trust
veterinary advice in general or with respect to nutrition.18 Pet owners who were themselves vegan
expressed concern regarding meat-based diets for pets with regards to farm animal welfare (74%), farm
animal rights (76%) and the environment (65%).19 Understanding and acknowledging why a pet owner
has chosen a specific diet for their pet can aid in communication with clients about alternative diet
choices.

PREVENTIVE NUTRITION
A nutritional assessment, including assessment of the animal, diet, and feeding management should be
completed prior to making dietary recommendations (ch. 145). Diet selection, calculation of energy
requirements, feeding amounts, and feeding methods should be determined.
While we expect young adult dogs to be relatively healthy, obesity and periodontal disease commonly
begin during this life stage.20,21 Prevention of excess BW is one of the most important nutritional
interventions to promote health and wellbeing. Excess BW can significantly impact both the life span
and the development of chronic diseases in dogs (ch. 150). Labrador Retrievers fed 25% less than agematched pairs had a median life span of 13 years while dogs fed 25% more had a median life span of 11.2
years.22 Dogs fed more were overweight, not obese, with a mean (9-point scale) BCS of 6.7 ± 0.19
compared to the feed-restricted dogs with a mean BCS 4.6 ± 0.19. Advising owners to feed measured
meals using standard measuring devices (8 oz [250 mL] measuring cup) or by weight (grams) rather
than ad libitum feeding is recommended to aid in the prevention of overweight and obesity. In a study
evaluating 3 different measuring devices at 3 different volumes (1/4, 1/2, and 1 cup), individual accuracy
of dry extruded dog food ranged from approximately 48-152%.23 Inaccuracy also increased with smaller
feeding volumes. Measuring food by weight, rather than volume, is recommended as a method to
improve feeding accuracy and avoid overfeeding.

OVERVIEW
Cats have unique metabolic and nutritional needs, many of which
reflect evolutionary adaptations to a carnivorous diet, which lessened
the selection pressure to maintain energetically expensive pathways
for nutrient synthesis.1 However, there is much controversy
regarding the “ideal” diet in order to achieve optimal longevity and
health in pet cats, with little evidence to support any particular
feeding style. A focus on disease prevention has led to an emphasis
on obesity prevention as well as the adoption of feeding management
strategies designed to accommodate the needs of specific households
and of individual cats.

UNIQUE NUTRITIONAL PHYSIOLOGY
OF THE HEALTHY ADULT CAT
PROTEIN AND SPECIFIC AMINO ACIDS
Cats have higher dietary protein requirements as compared with
dogs, despite similar amino acid needs. Although cats can adapt
protein oxidation to manage excess intake, there is limited ability to
conserve nitrogen if protein intake is too low.2 The reliance on
glucogenic amino acids as a source of energy may influence the high
protein requirement of carnivorous mammals with relatively large,
glucose-consuming brains.3 Cats also require dietary taurine and
arginine due to low enzyme activities in those synthetic pathways.

VITAMINS
Essential vitamins in cat diets include vitamin D, vitamin A, and
niacin. Unlike other species capable of synthesizing vitamin D when
the precursor, 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin, is exposed to UV light, a
dietary source of vitamin D is essential for cats because their
physiology shunts 7-dehydrocholesterol for metabolism to
cholesterol.4 Similarly, cats have a dietary requirement for niacin
despite possessing all its necessary synthetic enzymes. The picolinic
carboxylase enzyme activity in cats degrades an intermediate in the
pathway that would lead to niacin synthesis. Cats also have low
efficiency for beta carotene (the plant-based precursor) conversion to
vitamin A, and the retinol form of vitamin A is required.5

CARBOHYDRATES (FIBER, STARCH,
AND SUGAR)
Due to their natural history, it has been theorized that cats are
inflexible with regard to the digestion, absorption, and metabolism
of dietary carbohydrate. Although specific saccharides, starches, and
fibers are not considered nutritionally essential, fiber is a beneficial,
but often overlooked, component of feline diets (ch. 165). Digestible

carbohydrates are often included in the diets of both dogs and cats as
an energy source that allows a decrease in protein content, which is a
critical consideration given the importance of pet food sustainability.
It has been well documented that cats are able to digest and absorb
sugar and starch despite their carnivorous nature. Although simple
sugars are not a component of cat diets, cats produce several
intestinal disaccharidases, and pancreatic amylase secretion is
sufficient to enable efficient digestion of ground or cooked starch at
concentrations similar to amounts in commercially available diets.6,7
Once absorbed, glucose must be phosphorylated by gluco- or
hexokinase prior to entering one of several metabolic pathways,
including glycolysis. Cats only produce hepatic hexokinase rather
than glucokinase or fructokinase. Interestingly, cats have higher
activities of not just hexokinase but of several other glycolytic as well
as gluconeogenic enzymes when compared with dogs.8,9 Further,
insulin response and adaptive enzymatic activity appear to be
adequate compensation for the lack of glucokinase under conditions
of both typical and supraphysiologic carbohydrate intakes in cats.
Overall, there is a lack of evidence that consumption of carbohydrate
results in adverse effects when supplied in the moderate
concentrations typical of commercial pet foods.

DETERMINING THE OPTIMAL FELINE
DIET
OVERVIEW
The known nutritional needs of cats are summarized by the National
Research Council as “minimal requirements” or “adequate intakes”
depending on available data, “recommended allowances,” and for
some nutrients, “safe upper limits.” In addition, minimum and, in
some instances, maximum concentrations of nutrients for use in
commercial cat foods are suggested by the Association of American
Feed Control Officials (AAFCO). These Cat Food Nutrient Profiles,
guidance for product labeling, and other aspects of pet food
manufacturing and marketing as defined in the AAFCO Model
Regulations for Pet Food are adopted by many authorities in the

United States, as well as in Canada, Costa Rica, and Puerto Rico.
However, exact quantitative information regarding the optimal
intake of both micro- and macronutrients for adult cats remains
unknown. Many guidelines are extrapolated from data generated
using growing kittens, or represent minimal intakes that prevent
defined deficiency syndromes rather than characterizing the ideal
diet for longevity or other, more global, health parameters.

THE FERAL CAT MODEL
Defining the optimal intake of any nutrient in order to maximize
both quality and quantity of life is a challenge. The utility of
preference studies is thus far limited due to the lack of relevant
measurable outcomes. Analyses of natural diets may also have
limited utility, given the known poor health and short lifespan of
free-roaming cats. The estimated nutritional profile of free-roaming
domestic cats has been reported,10,11 but the life expectancy and
general health status of most free-roaming cats differs markedly
from that desired by most pet owners. Regardless, avoidance of
feeding practices associated with known problems can help promote
health and longevity in the pet cat population.

FEEDING MANAGEMENT OF CATS
AVOIDING OBESITY, EFFECT OF NEUTERING
The most common nutritionally-related disease in pet cats is obesity
(ch. 150). Although dietary carbohydrate and the use of dry cat
foods have been blamed for increasing obesity risk in cats, the
concept has not been supported by epidemiological data or
prospective research.12-15 Rather, dietary fat has clearly been shown
to promote overeating that leads to weight gain, likely due to the
increased energy density compared to carbohydrate and protein.14,15
Obesity in cats is associated with diabetes mellitus (ch. 292),
constipation (chs. 51, 263), orthopedic disease (ch. 31), urinary
tract disease (ch. 311), hepatic lipidosis (ch. 274), skin disease, and
other negative health issues.12,16,17 Of course, neutering is an

important risk factor for obesity in cats. As the majority of pet cats
have a known risk factor (neuter status) for a disease that is likely to
result in potentially significant morbidity (obesity and related
disease), feeding management strategies aimed at prevention are
indicated.
The relationships among food intake, body weight (BW) and
condition, and energy expenditure after neutering are complex (ch.
150). It seems clear that cats fed ad libitum after neutering are most
likely to gain weight.18-21 Free access to food results in greater BW
and body fat gain after neutering in both male and female cats, as
compared with cats that have restricted access to food.22,23 In
addition, greater weight gain and body fat accumulation is seen after
neutering when cats are fed energy-dense diets.14,15 As such,
unrestricted access to food should be actively discouraged for most
cats and energy-dense (i.e., high fat) foods should be used with
caution.
It has been demonstrated that BW gain can be avoided after
neutering provided that food intake is actively limited, although it
seems clear that some cats need fairly severe restriction to maintain
pre-neutering BW.19,24 This underscores the role of food intake and
feeding management in cats after neutering. It also supports an
individualized approach to determining the necessary amount of
restriction. Some cats need a reduction of 30% or more of their preneutering dietary intake.23 Although using diets high in moisture or
fiber may be effective in limiting food intake, more active restrictions
on food consumption are probably needed.25,26 Further, given the
marked reduction in voluntary activity in queens after neutering, it is
possible that encouraging increased activity may help offset the effect
of neutering.23 Thus, less severe food restrictions are required of
active cats. In any case, portion-controlled feeding is recommended
and regular monitoring of BW and body condition may be needed to
enable adequate and timely adjustments (ch. 72). Weight loss is
difficult to achieve and regaining lost weight is always a concern, so
the focus should be on prevention.

MAINTENANCE REQUIREMENTS
Daily energy maintenance requirements of cats can be highly
variable among individuals, which may be explained by many
factors. The National Research Council provides different equations
for lean versus overweight adult cats which both use metabolic,
rather than absolute, BW:

Many clinical nutritionists use a simpler equation based on a
neuter/activity status factor applied to the resting energy
requirement (RER) at the current weight:

where RER = 70 × (current weight in kg)0.75. Regardless, any
equation used should be seen as a starting point and
recommendations for individuals require reassessment and
adjustments as needed to maintain an ideal body condition.

CHOOSING A COMMERCIAL DIET
There are many options for commercial diets for healthy cats,
encompassing a wide range of prices, marketing approaches,
availability, ingredients, and nutritional profiles. This can be a
benefit in that there are products to meet the needs and preferences
of most cats as well as most owner financial limitations and any
philosophical inclinations. However, the wide range of choices can
also be overwhelming, confusing and, at times, misleading. The most
important information is the nutritional adequacy statement
required on pet food labels in localities that follow AAFCO Model
Regulations for Pet Food.
The nutritional adequacy statement on the label should specify
whether there is a complete and balanced claim versus “for
intermittent or supplemental feeding only.” If balanced, it should
state the intended use of the food (species and life stage). The label
should also disclose how claims are substantiated (passed feeding
tests or formulated to contain nutrient concentrations as specified by
AAFCO). Neither method of adequacy substantiation is perfect;
however, many nutritionists favor the animal feeding test method as
it at least partially accounts for nutrient digestibility and
bioavailability and provides proof of adequacy by direct testing
in vivo. Ideally, commercial pet foods are formulated to meet the
AAFCO nutrient profiles by laboratory analysis (not just by
calculation) as well as being subjected to and passing appropriate
animal feeding tests.

OWNER EDUCATION
Underestimation of obesity or a general unawareness of body
condition is common among cat owners and can contribute to the
development of obesity (ch. 150). One study identified owner

underestimation of cat body condition as a main variable influencing
feline obesity.13 Owners should be counseled on appropriate body
condition for their pet and encouraged to perform regular home
body condition scoring (ch. 72). Determination of energy needs
should be based on prior intake if known; however, the degree of
restriction necessary to avoid weight gain is variable, which
underscores the importance of monitoring and adjustment.
Free feeding is common for cats and, while convenient for many
owners, it may contribute to overeating. Free feeding is practiced by
many cat owners, regardless of their pet’s body condition. Some cats
successfully regulate their food intake to maintain an ideal BW while
others tend to overeat and become overweight or obese. In multi-cat
households, individual, portion-controlled meal feeding can be an
effective, albeit not as convenient, method for ensuring appropriate
food intake and body condition. Microchip feeders and other tools
including food toys can be used to help provide environmental
enrichment as well as control food intake.
Collection of diet history information should be done at every
veterinary visit and should include not only the main diet used but
also amounts and types of any treats and supplements. Monitoring of
the pet’s body condition score and BW (ch. 72), accompanied by any
necessary adjustment in the amount and type of food fed, is a critical
component in providing recommendations that meet the needs of
individual pets. This process starts with a veterinary assessment (ch.
145) and should be maintained by both the owner and the veterinary
team.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Nutrition for Healthy Adult Cats
Cats have specific nutritional needs that reflect their carnivorous
nature. For example, cats do not make vitamin D in the skin when
exposed to sunlight like people do. Also, cats need specific amino
acids (arginine and taurine) in addition to the 9 essential amino
acids people need. Cats evolved on a high-protein diet, and have a
higher requirement compared to other animals like dogs or people.
There are other special needs too, so it is important to feed a diet
specifically designed for cats.

Cats also have a reputation for being finicky, which may be related
to the fact that many cats, especially those that live indoors, have low
energy requirements and do not need to eat much food to maintain
their weight. Additionally, cats develop fixed preferences for flavors
and textures, and exposure to a variety of foods is recommended.
Finally, cats are quick to lose their appetites when they are sick.
When a cat stops eating for whatever reason, there is a risk of
developing a serious liver problem (hepatic lipidosis), so it is
important to seek veterinary attention in order to find and address
the lack of appetite quickly.
Most cats will do well eating any one of the various types of food.
Typically, the most convenient and economical type of cat food is dry
kibble, but other options are available as well. If you want to use a
homemade diet, there are ways to carefully provide a balanced diet,
but it takes time and effort, and will cost more than feeding most
commercial foods. Consult a board-certified veterinary nutritionist
for guidance if you want to pursue a homemade diet for your cat.
Regardless of diet choice, use wide, shallow bowls for food and water
since cats do not like having their sensitive whiskers compressed by
the sides of deep and narrow bowls. Quiet, low activity areas are
ideal for feeding cats, so remove children or other pets, and avoid
using noisy appliances such as the blender or vacuum during
mealtime.
The most common nutritional problem in cats is obesity, and it
can have serious health consequences. Studies have reported that up
to 28-63% of cats are overweight or obese. Overweight cats are more
likely to suffer from many problems, including diabetes mellitus,
constipation, orthopedic disease, urinary tract disease, liver disease,
and skin disease. Ideally, young cats should be fed to maintain an
ideal body weight throughout the growth period and into adulthood,
especially after spaying or neutering when weight gain often occurs.
It is much easier, and better for their health, to prevent obesity
rather than having to address it once it becomes a problem. It is
important to remember that different foods can vary widely in the
amount of calories they provide. In addition, many cats gain too
much weight if allowed free access to food; in those cases, meal
feeding of controlled amounts is critical, not free-choice feeding.
Every pet should be fed as an individual, and a cat’s family members
or caretakers need to monitor their cats regularly to ensure an ideal

body condition. “Body condition” refers to whether the body weight
is appropriate, too low, or too high for a cat, and a cat should be fed
more or less depending on weight changes in order to have an ideal
body condition. Maintaining an appropriate weight helps to ensure a
long, healthy life. Consider using microchip feeders and food toys to
help control your cat’s intake and make mealtimes more interesting.
Treats of human foods or commercial products are fine provided
that the total amount of calories remains below 10% of the total daily
intake. The calorie content of commercial treats can be found on the
bag or by contacting the manufacturer. Do not use foods that can be
dangerous, such as grapes, raisins, chocolate, garlic, onions, and
artificial sweeteners. Many plants are also potentially harmful to
cats, especially lilies, so be sure to avoid access to potentially toxic
potted plants and bouquets.
Jennifer A. Larsen (Davis, California)

Chapter 149: Nutrition in
Healthy Senior Cats and Dogs
Cecilia Villaverde

A C RO N YM S
BCS body condition score
MCS muscle condition score
MCT medium chain triglyceride
MER maintenance energy requirements
PUFA polyunsaturated fatty acid
Geriatric cats and dogs are an important percentage of the pet
population in the US.1 Older cats can be classified2 as “mature adult”
from 7 to 10 years of age and “senior” from 11 onwards. For dogs, size
affects lifespan, with smaller breeds living longer than larger
breeds.3 It has been suggested4 that pets should be considered
geriatric when they are in the last 25% of the predicted life span for
their species and breed. An individualized assessment,5 where aging
“milestones” such as joint disease and muscle atrophy are recorded,
can be a more accurate measure of aging rather than a cut-off age.
Aging is a continuum and individuals vary greatly as to their aging
process, so any age classification should only be taken as a guide.

NUTRIENT- AND ENERGY-RELATED
CHANGES ASSOCIATED WITH AGING

Nutrient and energy utilization can be affected by age,1 due to
alterations in gastrointestinal structure and function. While older
dogs seem to have similar digestion capacities6 compared to young
adults despite described anatomical and microbiotic changes,
macronutrient (protein and fat) digestibility can be reduced in some
geriatric cats.7 As for energy, there is a lack of data and requirements
are highly variable but, on average, canine maintenance energy
requirements (MER; the energy needed to maintain a stable weight)
appear to decrease with age.8 This can contribute to obesity risk.
Mature cats have decreased energy requirements compared to
adults, but older senior cats tend to have increased energy
requirements,9 which can, in part, be related to the lower
digestibility of fat and protein in some individuals and can contribute
to undesired weight loss. Protein requirements can increase with
aging in both dogs10 and cats,11 but existing data are not enough to
support separate dietary recommendations for this age group. Also,
lean body mass tends to decrease (sarcopenia) in older dogs12 and
cats13 (ch. 151). As for other essential nutrients, such as fatty acids,
vitamins, and minerals, there are not enough conclusive data to
know if their requirements can be affected by old age. At this time,
scientific14 and regulatory institutions do not have specific
requirements described for senior pets, and they are considered the
same as adults due to both the lack of data and the high variability on
the aging process among individuals. Aging changes not related to
nutrient utilization but which can respond to nutrient modification
include brain aging, joint degeneration, and alterations in the
immune system.5,15,16Aging can also result in a change in feeding
patterns and feed intake, sometimes associated with pain secondary
to oral or joint problems or to cognitive disorders. Moreover, it has
been described in aged people that their sense of taste and smell is
altered, which could also happen in veterinary senior patients.

CAN NUTRITION SLOW DOWN OR
MODIFY THE EFFECTS OF AGING?

Controlled energy intake can influence quality and quantity of life.
Maintaining a lean body condition score (BCS; ch. 72 and textbook’s
inside covers) during a dog’s lifetime has been associated with a
longer lifespan and a delay in the appearance of chronic disease,
including osteoarthritis.17 In cats, an elevated BCS (>7/9) is
associated with a variety of diseases,18 in cats of all ages. Therefore,
weight management is considered an important part of preventative
medicine. Shorter survival has been associated with BCS <5 (on a 9point scale).19 Having a slightly high BCS (6/9) might be acceptable
in older cats.
The effect of antioxidant supplementation on the rate of
progression of signs of aging is unknown. Studies on proprietary
“cocktails” of antioxidants alone or with other substances (like
prebiotic fiber and essential fatty acids) show potential positive
effects on muscle mass loss attenuation20 and cognitive
dysfunction21; however, there is a lack of standardized doseresponse studies to make a specific recommendation currently.
Other nutrients of interest due to their effects on cognition are longchain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) from fish oil and
medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs). The data regarding their effects
on canine and feline brain aging are still preliminary. In one study,
middle-aged cats fed a blend of fish oil, B vitamins, antioxidants and
arginine performed better in cognitive tests than did control cats, but
it is impossible to separate the effects of the different nutrients.22
Long-chain omega-3 PUFAs have also been proposed to help reduce
clinical signs of joint disease, which are common in aged dogs and
cats. As for MCT, there are preliminary data in dogs23 showing that
an MCT mixture (mainly caprylic acid) can help manage mild
cognitive dysfunction; the authors propose that the ketone bodies
obtained from metabolism of MCTs provide alternative sources of
fuel to the aged brain, which has a reduced glucose oxidation
capacity. The use of prebiotic fiber to affect intestinal microbiota and
the immune system is potentially interesting, but data are still
lacking.

FEEDING PLAN
The goals of feeding geriatric pets are to provide energy and
nutrients, slow down changes associated with aging, promote
wellbeing, and promote longevity, while keeping a stable weight and
a good BCS and muscle condition score (MCS). The feeding plan
includes what, how much, and how to feed, and must be decided
after performing a nutritional assessment (ch. 145).

NUTRITIONAL EVALUATION OF THE
SENIOR PET
The nutritional assessment must be performed at each senior patient
visit to customize the feeding plan, given how dogs and cats can age
differently. Particularly for aged patients,5 it is important to focus on
assessing BCS and MCS, energy intake, and feeding behavior.
Equally important are ensuring the diet is complete and balanced
and assessing if there are any age-associated alterations that
potentially could be addressed with adequate dietary management,
such as degenerative joint disease (ch. 226), cognitive alterations,
and changes in appetite. If the assessment does not identify any
malnutrition risk factors, changes to the feeding plan might not be
necessary. However, if risk factors are present, the feeding plan will
have to vary accordingly.

HOW MUCH TO FEED: ENERGY
REQUIREMENTS
The food allowance depends on the MER. Ideally, MER can be
determined from the current energy intake with a good diet history
in patients with a stable weight (ch. 145). This is not always
possible, for example, in pets fed ad libitum or with varied diets. In
these cases, MER can be estimated using formulas15,24 but the
associated error can be as high as 50%24; therefore, monitoring and
adjusting the energy allowance is necessary. If there is a history of

weight loss or the patient has a low BCS, MER should be increased
by 10-20%. If this does not result in weight gain, or the patient will
not eat enough, diagnostic tests will be necessary to investigate a
medical cause of the problem. Patients that are overweight and
otherwise healthy should be considered for a weight loss plan (ch.
150).
The daily allowance is calculated by dividing MER by the energy
density of the diet of choice. Label recommendations on food
allowance can be used directly, without MER calculation, but the
same error as the formulas applies. It is recommended that the main
diet provide at least 90% of the daily calories, with a maximum of
10% for unbalanced items (such as treats, table scraps, or
supplements). Frequent reassessment and readjustment of the daily
allowance is necessary. Senior dogs and cats should be weighed at
least once a month using the same scale, and the food allowance
increased or decreased by 10% to achieve weight stability and an
ideal BCS.

FEEDING METHOD
For overweight (or prone to overweight) patients, portion control is
the best approach. Diet form will also affect the decision, since only
dry food can be safely left out all day. Portion control might be
required even when weight gain is desired, as when feeding wet food
only or in multi-pet households, where animals have different
nutritional needs. Food can be offered in one or in multiple feedings
per day. In thin patients, where an increase in energy intake is
indicated, options include free feeding, increasing the volume of each
meal, adding one more meal to the schedule, and choosing a more
energy-dense diet. The latter is especially useful in patients whose
intake is volume-limited. Warming the food or using flavor
enhancers such as home-prepared broth can help increase the appeal
of the meal. Including environmental enrichment strategies for
feeding (such as hiding food, using food dispenser toys, etc.), can
help reduce boredom and provide stimulation (ch. 311).

WHAT TO FEED: DIET CHOICE

The diet must be nutritionally complete for maintenance and be
palatable. Commercial diets marketed as senior/mature/geriatric
have no commonalities because there is no regulatory definition of
what a senior diet is; therefore, their nutritional composition varies
widely25,26 and reflects the philosophy of each manufacturing
company. For this reason, a blanket recommendation to “feed a
senior diet” when a dog or cat reaches a certain age is not useful or
precise enough advice. Assessment of the current diet is important to
establish the baseline. A healthy, lean patient doing well on its
current complete adult diet will not necessarily require a diet change
as it ages. Overweight patients will benefit from therapeutic nutrientfortified weight loss diets and a weight loss plan while obese prone
individuals can be switched to a diet with moderate energy density
(ch. 150). Some senior and light diets can be considered in this case,
but the energy density of the product of choice must be compared to
the current diet, to ensure the change is made in the right direction.
For thin patients, weight gain can be promoted using diets with
higher energy density than the current one (such as kitten/puppy
diets, convalescence or performance type diets, or a variety of overthe-counter adult/senior diets).
Regarding nutrient composition, protein is a controversial issue,
since there is the mistaken impression that senior pets should eat
moderate protein diets to protect kidney function. However, protein
requirements of healthy senior pets are at least as high as those of
adults and protein moderation/restriction provides no apparent
benefit. It is particularly important to avoid this in healthy patients
showing some degree of muscle mass loss (ch. 151). At the same
time, there is no evidence that high-protein diets are helpful in
preventing sarcopenia, and the focus must be on avoiding marginal
protein intakes. Protein is also an important driver for palatability,
which is particularly important in thin patients struggling to
maintain a healthy weight. Both senior and adult diets from
reputable manufacturers meet protein requirements for adults, even
if the range is very wide.25,26 If patients have a disease that requires
protein moderation, they will benefit from therapeutic diets for that
specific problem.
For older dogs showing mild signs of canine cognitive dysfunction
associated with brain aging (ch. 244), there are over-the-counter

(and therapeutic) diets with cocktails of nutrients like antioxidants,
MCT, and PUFAs (e.g., omega-3 fatty acids). Their efficacy might
vary, but these should be formulated to be complete and balanced,
and if so, it is safe to try them.
There are various supplements marketed towards the elderly pet
population, and those should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis
(Box 149.1).

KEY POINTS
The feeding plan of aging dogs and cats must be tailored to each
patient after a careful nutritional evaluation, since individual
variation precludes generic recommendations. Senior pets should be
fed a complete and balanced diet for maintenance from a reputable
manufacturer (with specific modifications depending on each case),
fed in sufficient amounts to maintain an ideal weight and a lean BCS.
Weight management from weaning onwards is the best-known
strategy to ensure a healthy geriatric pet. Diet can play a role in the
multimodal management of conditions that cause pain, discomfort,
and alterations in cognition. There are many commercial diets
(marketed for both adult and senior pets) that can be used, with
different energy density, nutrient profiles, ingredients, processing,
and texture to accommodate for needs and preferences.
BOX 1 4 9 .1 Su p p le me nts fo r Ge riatric Pe ts
There are many supplements and nutraceuticals marketed towards
older patients, including joint products, pre- and probiotics,
antioxidants, multivitamins, and oils (such as fish, coconut). These
can be a useful tool, but supplements are loosely regulated, and
many lack data on efficacy and safety.27,28 Potential risks of
supplements include:
• Provision of unaccounted calories: for example, oil supplements
(blends, fish, coconut) provide approximately 40 kcal per
teaspoon (5 mL).

• Nutrient toxicity and diet imbalance: some nutrients, if provided
in excess, can cause health problems,15 such as vitamin D
(which can be provided in supplements alone, in multivitamins,
or in some fish oils).
• Quality control issues: supplements and nutraceuticals can be
contaminated with undesirable substances. They might also not
contain the amounts of the active nutrients stated on the label.
• Other: They can be costly and provide uncontrolled antigens.
Sometimes they are the wrong product for the patient (for
example, not all medium-chain triglycerides [MCTs] have the
same fatty acid composition).
What to do when using a supplement:
• Read the literature to decide if the patient could benefit from
such a product.
• Carefully assess their claims. The manufacturer should be
contacted for details on both their quality control measures and
their research on safety and efficacy. Choose a well-researched
product if there are different options on the market.
• When using caloric supplements, ensure they do not provide,
together with other unbalanced items, more than 10% of the
daily calorie intake.
• Pay special attention to nutrients that can be toxic (like vitamins
A and D), considering they will be provided by both the diet and
the supplement. Overall, generic multivitamins are unlikely to
be of benefit and can be a risk.
• Consider choosing a diet from a reputable manufacturer that
already includes the nutrients of interest for each situation.

Chapter 150: Obesity
Juan José Ramos-Plá

Obesity is a disorder that is characterized by a positive energy
balance in which more calories are ingested than spent. If this
tendency is maintained for an extended period of time, the energy
excess accumulates in the form of subcutaneous and perivisceral fat,
increasing the patient’s weight and volume and negatively affecting
its health. Numerous studies link obesity with a predisposition or
worsening of respiratory, orthopedic, endocrine, oncologic,
metabolic and cardiovascular disorders in dogs and cats. A patient is
considered overweight if the excess weight is 10-20% over ideal and
obese if it exceeds 20%.1

EPIDEMIOLOGY
Obesity is the most frequently encountered nutritional disorder of
small animals in industrialized countries, reaching a prevalence, in
some countries, of up to 59% in dogs and 63% in cats.2 These results
should be interpreted with caution, as there is great variability
among countries, ways of measuring the body condition score (BCS;
ch. 72), patient populations in reported studies, number of clinics
participating in each study, patients’ living conditions, and
perceptions of participating veterinarians.

RISK FACTORS
Many factors influence the positive energy balance in a patient
(Table 150.1). Some are intrinsic to the animal and others (the vast
majority) are the result of interactions with humans.3

FACTORS LINKED TO THE ANIMAL
Breed is an influential factor in obesity in dogs and cats. In dogs, the
Golden Retriever, Labrador Retriever and Pug have shown a greater
tendency to be overweight, partially exacerbated by breed selection
criteria that can predispose to obesity. In Labrador Retrievers and
Flat-Coated Retrievers, a deletion mutation of proopiomelanocortin
(POMC), which is strongly associated with weight, adiposity, an

increased appetite, and behavioral changes, has been proven.4 In the
cat, crossbreeds have a higher tendency to be overweight and obese,
although some studies indicate that pure breeds such as the British
Shorthair, Maine Coon and Norwegian Forest Cat have higher BCSs.5
Sex influences overweight in the feline species, affecting males to a
greater extent. In the canine species, however, although
epidemiologically there are more overweight females, a metaanalysis has not been able to show that sex affects energy
consumption.6 The prevalence of obesity increases with age in both
species due to the decrease in both physical activity and basal
metabolic rate. Middle-aged dogs and cats are more prone to being
overweight/obese, with the incidence decreasing after 10-12 years of
age.7,8 On the other hand, there is a clear link between neutering and
obesity. Both dogs and cats are more likely to be overweight/obese if
they are neutered, and more so in males than females in the feline
species.9 The lack of sex hormones induces a lower resting energy
expenditure, less physical activity and a lack of appetite suppression,
contributing to an increase in BCS.7,8

FACTORS LINKED TO THE OWNER
The type of diet and way of feeding have a direct impact on BCS.
High-fat and low-carbohydrate diets increase the amount of body fat
in dogs and cats.10,11 Cats fed ad libitum consume more food and
their weight is higher after neutering compared to before.12 Despite
this, there are studies in cats indicating that ad libitum feeding is a
risk factor for obesity, while others indicate that eating twice a day is
more predisposing to obesity than ad libitum feeding. Regarding
dogs, studies are inconclusive. Some studies indicate that dogs are at
higher risk to become obese when fed once a day, others when dogs
receive several meals a day, and others when dogs are fed either one
or three-plus portion(s). Dogs eating homemade food and those
receiving excessive “treats” or table scraps are more likely to be
obese.13 Cats fed dry food are more likely to be overweight/obese,
possibly due to free choice feeding and to dry food’s higher energy

density. Physical activity strongly influences BCS, as dogs that can
exercise freely tend to have better body condition than those that do
not (ch. 226).14 Cats living outdoors or outdoors with restricted
access to indoors are less likely to be overweight or obese than those
living indoors. But the type of owner probably has the greatest
influence on a pet’s BCS. Owners who are obese, who have little
interest in a balanced diet, who buy low-quality or lower-cost food,
with lower income and older age, tend to have more overweight or
obese dogs.15 In cats, there was no correlation between owner age
and cat overweight, but owning one or two cats predisposes to
obesity, while cats living with a dog are less likely to be obese. Cats
apparently begging for food frequently are more than three times as
likely to be overweight or obese, due to owner’s misinterpretation of
cat behavior and the use of food as a reward. On the other hand,
owners who feed cats following the pet-food companies’ feeding
instructions are more likely to have overweight or obese cats than
those who determine the amount of food based on the cat’s appetite.5
