PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF OBESITY
An animal’s daily caloric balance depends on both intrinsic factors,
such as the metabolic energy consumption rate (at rest and during
activity) or its digestion efficiency, and on external factors, such as
the amount and intensity of the activity performed by the animal and
factors affecting the assimilation of nutrients. Obesity occurs in a
patient when calories ingested exceed expended calories over an
extended period of time. Historically, the maintenance of a constant
weight in adults throughout life has been explained by two theories:
glucostatic and lipostatic. The glucostatic theory postulated that
hunger was controlled by glucose homeostasis and hormones that
regulate it (insulin, amylin, and glucagon-like peptide 1 [GLP-1] in
particular), stimulating or inhibiting the hunger centers in the brain.
This theory has been progressively replaced by the lipostatic theory,
postulating that blood levels of fatty acids determine the release of
the different gastrointestinal hormones that stimulate or inhibit
appetite. Both theories are probably valid when interpreted together
and influenced by other factors.16 Control of food intake and energy

expenditure are regulated by the interaction of several hormonal
mechanisms in the central nervous system, digestive system, and
adipose tissue.

CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (CNS)
At a central level, appetite regulation depends primarily on the
arcuate nucleus (nucleus arcuatus), located in the hypothalamus. In
the arcuate nucleus, there are two main types of neurons controlling
appetite and energy expenditure: those expressing neuropeptide Y
(NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AGRP), both with orexigenic
activity, and those expressing proopiomelanocortin/cocaine
amphetamine-related transcript (POMC-CART), which decrease
appetite. Different peripheral signals coming from the digestive
system and fat tissue are integrated in this neuronal circuit, resulting
in a control of food intake and energy expenditure.17 Activation of
mechanoreceptors secondary to gastric distension inhibits further
food intake via a neural reflex arc.

DIGESTIVE SYSTEM
The hormonal circuit in the CNS receives hormonal stimuli from the
digestive system, mainly ghrelin, cholecystokinin, peptide YY (PYY;
peptide tyrosine-tyrosine) and GLP-1. Ghrelin is synthesized in the
oxyntic neuroendocrine cells of the gastric fundus, being the only
orexigenic hormone produced by the digestive system (ch. 261). In
healthy individuals, it helps to regulate feeding behavior and energy
metabolism. During fasting, serum ghrelin concentration increases,
stimulating hypothalamic NPY-AGRP neurons and increasing
appetite in dogs and cats. When the animal eats and the stomach fills
with food, ghrelin secretion decreases.18 Cholecystokinin is secreted
by small intestinal I-cells and it reaches a peak blood concentration
15 minutes after eating, increasing satiety and decreasing food
intake. Research in humans shows that it also has other effects on
the digestive system, such as stimulation of gallbladder secretion,
delayed gastric emptying, and pancreatic enzyme secretion.19

Peptide YY is produced and secreted by L cells of the distal jejunum
and ileum. Upon release, it stimulates POMC-CART neurons and
inhibits NPY-AGRP, decreasing appetite in both humans and rodents
for up to 12 hours. Its concentrations are low on an empty stomach
and rise rapidly after eating, with reaching a maximum at 1-2 hours.
It is released in greater amounts after fat ingestion than after
carbohydrate or protein, at equal calorie intake.20 GLP-1 is another
incretin secreted by intestinal L cells in response to food intake and
its concentration decreases on an empty stomach. In humans,
rodents, and dogs, it stimulates POMC-CART neurons and inhibits
NPY-AGRP. It has a satiating effect, increases insulin sensitivity, and
promotes weight loss.21

ADIPOSE TISSUE
Healthy animals in the wild maintain a more or less constant weight
throughout their lives, although the internal mechanism by which
this happens was unknown. Traditionally, fat tissue was considered
only an energy reservoir to be used in times of food shortage. But this
all changed in 1994 when it was discovered that fat tissue, in addition
to storing energy, also secretes hormones called adipokines.22 The
first to be discovered was leptin, although more than 100 different
adipokines, including proteins, peptides and cytokines, have been
discovered since then. The most widely studied both in dogs and cats
are leptin, adiponectin, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNFalpha).
Leptin is a hormone secreted mainly in adipocytes. It stimulates
the anorexigenic POMC-CART neurons of the arcuate nucleus and it
correlates with the degree of obesity in dogs and cats. It controls
body weight (BW) by decreasing appetite and increasing energy
expenditure, improving cellular glucose uptake and decreasing
peripheral fat.23 In humans, it also has carcinogenic and proinflammatory effects.24,25 Blood leptin concentrations increase in
dogs and cats as the amount of body fat increases and decrease when
they lose weight.2,26,27 However, in obese patients, high serum leptin
concentrations do not inhibit appetite, and this energy control

maladjustment leads to fat deposition and, therefore, weight gain.28
Adiponectin is produced almost exclusively in mature adipocytes. It
increases insulin sensitivity and decreases blood glucose levels, has
an anti-inflammatory effect, and decreases triglycerides both in liver
and muscle. It is also cardioprotective due to its vasodilator effect. In
cats and obese men, its blood concentration is decreased, increasing
when the patient loses weight.29 This decrease in circulating values
may influence the presence of cardiac disorders and insulin
resistance observed in obese patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus
(DM2). In dogs, the relationship between obesity and adiponectin
blood concentrations is more controversial.28,30
Obesity is a disease that is considered a chronic state of low-grade
inflammation, as obese patients have areas of adipocyte necrosis and
inflammatory cell infiltration. This inflammation is due, among
other reasons, to the local release of TNF-alpha and systemic release
of interleukin-6 (IL-6) in the fat tissue.31 The concentrations of both
cytokines are elevated in the obese and decrease when they undergo
weight loss programs.3 TNF-alpha promotes insulin resistance at
both central (hypothalamus) and peripheral (adipocyte) levels, being
involved, in addition to inflammatory processes, in other disorders
such as DM2.31 The hyperleptinemia present in obese individuals
stimulates the production of TNF-alpha which, in turn, inhibits the
concentration of adiponectin, preventing its anti-inflammatory
action.32

PATHOLOGIC CONSEQUENCES OF
OBESITY
Obesity has a negative impact on quality of life and life expectancy in
small animals and is associated with various health problems such as
certain endocrine disorders, osteoarthritis, renal disease and
urolithiasis, neoplasms and cardiovascular disease.33

ENDOCRINE DISORDERS

DM2 is a disease that is closely linked to obesity, mainly in cats (ch.
292). In canine patients, obesity influences glycemic control by
inducing insulin resistance, although this does not lead to DM2 (ch.
291). Overweight dogs have higher basal insulinemia and insulin
sensitivity in dogs with a good BCS is 58% higher than in overweight
dogs.34 However, obese cats may exhibit insulin resistance and are
almost 4 times more likely to develop DM2 than normal weight cats.
Increased blood leptin and decreased adiponectin concentrations,
both primarily secreted by fat tissue, influence glucose metabolism
and increase insulin resistance. Weight gain is a common clinical
sign of hypothyroidism. Hypothyroid dogs have increased serum
leptin and insulin concentrations (ch. 285). However, adiponectin is
increased (unlike in other endocrine disorders), suggesting a
resistance to adiponectin that favors hyperlipidemia, insulin
resistance, and obesity.35 Obesity is also associated with
hyperlipidemia, characterized by abnormal increase of cholesterol
and triglyceride serum levels in obese dogs and cats compared to
those that are not overweight (ch. 156). These plasma alterations
are associated with pancreatitis, liver disease, atherosclerosis and
insulin resistance in dogs and with DM2 in cats.36,37 (For more
information, see ch. 155.)

ORTHOPEDIC DISORDERS
The link between overweight/obesity and orthopedic disease is well
established in humans. Studies in dogs, although more sparse, show
that BW reduction alone results in a significant decrease in lameness
in obese patients with hip and/or elbow osteoarthritis. This seems
logical, since increased BCS will lead to a greater load on the limbs.38
Further, dogs with higher BCS do have higher blood concentrations
of inflammatory mediators such as IL-6 and monocyte chemotactic
protein-1, which can have a negative impact on the joints. The
likelihood of cranial cruciate ligament rupture in obese dogs is 4
times higher than in non-overweight dogs. In one study, the severity
(but not the frequency) of elbow osteoarthritis in the Labrador
Retriever group receiving a calorie-restricted diet was lower than in
those receiving a normal calorie diet and, in addition, they developed

radiographic evidence of hip dysplasia later.39 Obese/overweight
cats are 2.9 times more likely to have lameness.

KIDNEY DISEASE AND LOW URINARY
TRACT DISEASE
In cats with chronic kidney disease (CKD; ch. 301), weight loss and
low BW are negatively associated with survival time.40 However, the
link between obesity and CKD in cats remains unproven so far.
Recent studies did not demonstrate differences in certain biomarkers
of kidney disease (creatinine, symmetric dimethylarginine) in
obese/overweight cats compared to cats with normal BCS.41 In
addition, obesity in the cat may be linked to DM2, so an association
between obesity and CKD may be altered by other factors such as
hyperglycemia. Regarding dogs, it is unclear whether obesity is an
obvious risk factor for developing CKD, but studies in obese
individuals have shown that urine protein to creatinine ratio, urine
albumin to creatinine ratio, and serum creatinine concentration
decrease after weight loss. Using techniques such as contrast
enhanced ultrasound, disturbances in renal perfusion have been
detected in obese dogs in which there was no evidence of
hyperfiltration nor increases in renal function biomarker
concentrations.42 Numerous studies link feline lower urinary tract
disease (FLUTD; ch. 311) to overweight in cats, but the
pathophysiological mechanism is not known. It has been speculated
that overweight cats are less active, urinate and drink less, and may
be stress eaters, which increases their obesity. In addition,
overweight may induce fat accumulation around the urethra and
penis, compressing these structures and increasing dysuria.
However, other studies have found no link between FLUTD and
BCS.43 In dogs, one study linked BCS to a higher frequency of
infection in the obese and another to a higher frequency of calcium
oxalate stones, although in the latter there was no difference between
the proportion of overweight cases in both groups.44 (For more
information, see chs. 158 and 159.)

NEOPLASIA
Obese individuals have high blood levels of leptin, which has an
angiogenic, anti-apoptotic and mitosis-stimulating effect, and low
levels of adiponectin, which has an opposite effect. Obesity is
considered a pro-inflammatory state, being associated with elevated
blood levels of adipokines such as TNF-alpha and IL-6. Chronic
inflammation leads to tumor development and macrophage
accumulation in the mammary gland in obese humans and rodents.
Furthermore, in obese or overweight patients, lower adiponectin
concentration and increased number of macrophages are associated
with a poorer clinical prognosis, higher tumor histological grade, and
invasion of the lymphatic system. However, studies linking obesity
and cancer in dogs and cats are less conclusive. Macrophage
infiltration of tumors is higher in overweight or obese dogs than in
lean ones. A high BCS is a risk factor in inflammatory breast
carcinomas in the dog, stimulating its progression and the presence
of metastases.45 But in one study in dogs, obesity/overweight at the
time of diagnosis of lymphoma or osteosarcoma did not negatively
affect disease progression or patient survival. Furthermore, weight
gain during treatment to dogs with both types of cancer was
associated with increased survival time.46 In the cat, few studies link
BCS and neoplasms. In a study with 57 patients with cancer, cats
whose BCS was >5/9 lived longer than those whose BCS was <5/9,
and cats in remission had higher BCS that those not in remission.47
(For more information, see ch. 163.)

CARDIOVASCULAR DISORDERS
The influence of overweight on heart disease in dogs and cats is
controversial. Elevated leptin concentrations present in the obese
may contribute to the development of a catabolic state, inducing
cardiac cachexia (chs. 151, 157). In addition, obese dogs exhibit
cardiac changes such as an increased ratio of interventricular septal
thickness in diastole to ventricular internal dimension in diastole, a
decreased ratio of early and late maximal left ventricular inflow
velocities and an increased left ventricular fractional shortening and

ejection fraction.48 Similarly, a 10% weight gain in the dog increases
heart rate, cardiac output and blood pressure.49 However,
overweight in dogs is not associated with reduced patient survival
(the “obesity paradox,” described below). The direct association
between overweight/obesity and congestive heart failure (CHF) and
coronary heart disease in dogs and cats remains unclear.
Despite the fact that obesity predisposes to certain diseases, the
“paradox of obesity” indicates that, once some diseases have been
diagnosed, it is not always advisable to lose too much weight, if any.
In fact, it has been shown that dogs and cats with heart failure, renal
disease, and certain neoplastic diseases and with moderate
overweight survive longer than lean ones.50,51 Some possible
explanations for this fact are the presence of neuroendocrine
protective factors secreted by the fatty tissue or that overweight or
obese patients have, in addition to an excess of fatty tissue, also more
lean body mass, which gives them a greater reserve in catabolic
diseases such as CHF. (For more information, see ch. 157.)

ASSESSMENT AND TREATMENT
There is evidence that most veterinarians do not routinely integrate
assessment of patient body condition into pet consultations, leading
many owners to have insufficient information about their pet’s
potential overweight/obesity. Making owners understand that their
pet is overweight/obese often requires an investment of time by the
veterinarian or nurses to explain it in a careful but firm manner.52
Treatment of obesity requires proper and careful planning and
monitoring by the veterinary team, but also, as a first step, an
acceptance of the problem by the owner. In the experience of most
veterinarians, it is the latter that is often the major stumbling block,
since quite often owners do not realize or accept their pet’s
obesity/overweight, or do not recognize it as a problem.
Consequently, owners’ awareness, adherence to goals, and their
commitment to cooperate should be considered essential to any
effective plan regarding weight loss. Initial assessment of the patient
and client, the design and establishment of a weight loss program,
and proper monitoring of the process and maintenance of goals in

over the long term are the three main stages to consider in any
weight loss program.

INITIAL ASSESSMENT
The veterinarian’s evaluation needs to take both the patient and the
client into consideration.

Patient Assessment
Assessment of body condition, including ideal body weight (IBW),
BCS, and muscle condition score (MCS)

(chs. 72 and 145, Video

150.1, textbook’s inside covers), should be carried out and explained
to the client using tables, charts or brochures. This will allow the
veterinary team to have a reference starting point to design the
weight loss program and monitor fat loss, ideally without a change in
MCS. In addition, it is important to perform blood and imaging tests
that allow the veterinarian to know the physical condition of the
patient and possible limitations to the treatment (orthopedic,
cardiac, endocrine diseases, etc.; ch. 226).53 The prospect of a
healthier and longer life is also persuasive and should be discussed
with the owner. Detailed information should be obtained regarding
breed, sex, age, neutering status, current weight, physical activity,
feeding routines, type of diet, treats, number of daily meals, meal
schedule, bowl size, size and how food portions are measured, etc.54

Client Assessment
Understanding the pet-owner relationship is essential for treatment
to be successful (ch. 1). Attachment to a pet can be both positive and
negative: in some cases, the owner may be willing to do whatever is
necessary for the pet to lose weight and feel better, whereas in others
this attachment may foster obesity-inducing behaviors in the owner,
such as overfeeding or giving excessive treats. It is important to
explain that losing weight in a controlled manner is not detrimental
to the pet; in fact, failing to lose weight can have negative
consequences. It has been shown that weight loss reduces pain and

increases vitality and quality of life.55 It is also necessary to consider
other aspects of the pet’s owner and environment, such as economic
status, age, whether the owner is overweight, how many people live
in the household and the number of times the pet is walked, duration
of walks, as all these can influence the success of treatment.56

ESTABLISHMENT OF A WEIGHT LOSS
PROGRAM
Treatment should be focused on decreasing calorie intake and
increasing calorie expenditure. With all the information collected
when obtaining the history and performing the patient assessment,
the veterinary team will get an idea of the composition and total
amount of calories ingested by the animal, including food, treats, and
table scraps (ch. 145). Information about family members (how
many, who feeds and walks the pet, etc.) and about other pets that
may live in the household should also be obtained.57 Once all the
patient information has been collected and the physical examination
has been performed, the BCS and IBW should be determined. This is
easily achieved by visually and palpably assessing the amount of
body fat in different areas on the patient’s body (ch. 72). The next
step is to calculate the amount of calories to be administered to
target weight reduction. This is achieved by calculating the resting
energy requirement (RER; chs. 147, 148) with the following
formula: RER = 70 × IBWkg0.75. For patients between 2 and 25 kg,
the linear equation RER = 30 + IBWkg × 70 can be used, but this will
overestimate the caloric needs for larger patients.53 Alternatively,
RERs can be calculated using the formulae 63±10.2 kcal/IBW0.75 for
dogs (<42.6 kcal/IBW0.75 is not recommended) and 52±4.9
kcal/IBW0.711 for cats (<42.2 kcal/IBW0.711 is not
recommended).58,59 Using these calculated amounts of calories, it is
recommend to start with the RER based on the ideal weight and
reassess every 2-4 weeks, increasing or decreasing the amount of

food according to the result.60 Once the amount of calories to be
ingested has been calculated, and following the instructions on the
diet manufacturer’s label, the next step is to calculate the serving size
to be administered. To do so, bowls, measuring cups, or kitchen
scales can be used. The latter are more accurate and are
recommended, especially in cats or small dogs.61 If a scale is not
available, a graded plastic container such as those used for urine
collection can be used. A “fill line” can be marked in the container so
the owner can provide a more accurate amount of food.

Nutritional Management
A weight loss program does not necessarily mean eating less, but
rather eating differently. Providing smaller quantities of the same old
food does not only decrease caloric intake, but also the amount of
essential nutrients. Commercially available weight loss diets are an
excellent choice, since they reduce the amount of calories, modify the
sensation of satiety and minimize the likelihood of undesired
nutritional deficiencies. If it is not possible to provide a commercial
diet, either because the owner is unwilling or the patient does not
accept/tolerate it, it is advised to consult a veterinary nutritionist, so
a tailored and balanced weight loss diet can be formulated. The
National Research Council recommends a daily protein amount of
4.96 g/BW (kg)0.67 in cats and 3.28 g/BW (kg)0.75 in dogs.62 High
protein (103 g/1000 kcal metabolisable energy [ME]) and high fiber
(60 g/1000 kcal ME) weight loss diets in dogs result in a greater
percentage of weight loss than diets with only high protein or high
crude fiber. Lower digestibility of high protein-high fiber diets helps
to decrease food’s caloric density and these diets have a greater
satiating effect.63 Diets should also be high in moisture (as with
typical canned food) and low in fat, both of which allow higher
volumes of food to be fed with lower caloric density. In cats, it may
be worth using weight loss diets that are low in carbohydrate rather
than high fiber diets. Low carbohydrate diets result in a change in
the pattern of energy intake, stimulating the use of hepatic ketone
bodies as a source of energy. This results in lower blood glucose

levels, which is of great interest in the management of feline
overweight and DM2 (ch. 292).64
The owner initially decides on whether to feed a dry or wet diet,
although the final decision about which one to use relies on the
patient (the best diet is useless if the animal does not eat it). The
owner can carry out “test trials” at home and decide which diet the
pet eats best. Low-carbohydrate, dry, weight loss diets are more
calorically dense than high-fiber diets and accurate dosing can be a
problem in small dogs and cats.65 For this reason, especially in cats,
using a wet diet is preferred, as it increases satiety, decreases energy
density and accelerates weight loss.66 If dry diets are used in cats,
low-calorie, high-protein, possibly high-fiber, reduced-fat diets are
preferable to low-carbohydrate diets because the latter have high
levels of fat.65 Transition to the new weight loss diet should be
gradual. A reasonable recommendation is to replace 10-15% of the
old food with the new diet daily, completing the transition in 6-8
days in dogs and up to 2 weeks in cats. Faster changes may induce
gastrointestinal disturbances in dogs and food aversion in cats, with
prolonged anorexia and risk of hepatic lipidosis. In addition,
distributing the total daily food allotment into several small meals
minimizes the behavior of begging for food (appeases owner anxiety
about food restriction), increasing the energy consumed during
digestion (meal-induced thermogenesis). Weight loss should not
exceed 2% per week in dogs and cats, except in patients with
comorbidities, in which a maximum of 0.5% is recommended.53
Some clients, especially dog owners, are accustomed to giving treats
as part of their relationship with the pet (play, training, etc.).
Maintaining the use of treats during the weight loss diet can help the
owner to be more committed with the weight loss plan, but the
veterinary team must provide detailed information about which
treats can be given and how often, being sure that their caloric
contribution does not exceed 10% of the daily total amount.

Physical Exercise
Since sedentary lifestyles are a risk factor for obesity, any weight loss
plan should include, in addition to restricting caloric intake,

increasing energy expenditure. Combining diet and exercise
improves cardiovascular performance and decreases the adverse
effects of being overweight (such as hypertension, decreased cardiac
function, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemias) in human patients.67
Physically active dogs and cats are less likely to be overweight/obese
(ch. 226). As the owner’s perspective directly influences the amount
of exercise of the pet, having a dog engage in exercise or physical
activity together with the owner is positive for the weight loss
program since it improves interaction with the pet, maintains lean
body mass, and increases energy expenditure. Longer leash walks,
swimming, underwater treadmill therapy (ch. 256), jogging, and the
use of feeding toys can be effective in dogs.68 Interactive toys, such
as ropes, feathers or objects with treats rewards are useful in cats
involved in weight loss programs. Weight loss programs including
both physical exercise and diet are recommended since, unlike dietonly weight loss programs, they preserve lean body mass.69
Measurement of energy expenditure during exercise in small animals
is almost undocumented. In dogs, one study reported an expenditure
of 1.1 kcal/kg/km at a pace of 10-10.5 min/km, so approximate
duration and intensity of exercise walks can be calculated and
entered into the weight loss program.70 Initially, 30-60 minutes of
daily exercise can be set, but length, endurance, intensity and type of
exercise will be tailored depending on patient’s age, physical
condition, owner’s availability, BCS and patient’s possible comorbidities. Management of coexisting obesity and mobility issues in
the same animal is discussed in ch. 226.

MONITORING WEIGHT LOSS AND
PREVENTING WEIGHT REGAIN
After starting the weight loss plan, the owner should be contacted by
phone once or twice during the first week to be sure that no concerns
have arisen. Recheck visits are recommended every 2 weeks for the
first month and once monthly for the next 4-6 months. The patient’s
weight should be recorded, and owner’s concerns heard and
addressed, in addition to carrying out a physical exam and

reevaluating the BCS at every visit. Weight records can be drawn in
graph form so that the owner can easily see the progress (if any).
Every 2 weeks, depending on the change in weight, the amount of
food to be given can be readjusted. Owners should weigh the pet at
home once a week and record the weight. Achieving optimal or
desired weight usually takes up to 4-6 months in dogs and cats, but
can be extended to a year or more.71 Once the target weight is
achieved, the work is not over since almost half of patients regain
weight as a “rebound” effect. Several studies have shown that, after
weight loss, patients have a decrease in energy expenditure (up to
19% in cats and 10% in dogs), so that less energy intake is needed to
maintain the achieved weight. Owners should be aware of this effect
once the ideal weight has been reached, to avoid weight regain or
abandonment of the program in the medium to long term. These
patients should be maintained on calorie-restricted weight
management diets for prolonged periods of time, perhaps lifelong, to
avoid the risk of weight regain. After achieving a target weight,
patients should be re-evaluated every 2-3 months during the first
year to ensure that the program is properly followed and weight
maintained.

Chapter 151: Cachexia and
Sarcopenia
Lisa M. Freeman

A C RO N YM S
AAFCO Association of American Feed Control Officials

CHF congestive heart failure
CKD chronic kidney disease
DHA docosahexaenoic acid
SARMs selective androgen receptor modulators
TNF tumor necrosis factor
Cachexia and sarcopenia occur in a variety of chronic diseases and
aging, respectively. Although cachexia has been recognized in people
for over 2000 years, there is burgeoning interest because of the
relatively recent findings of its negative effects on morbidity and
mortality. This is spurring development of new drugs and other
treatments to combat cachexia and sarcopenia in people. Veterinary
patients will benefit from this research, but greater awareness of
these syndromes among the veterinary healthcare team and more
research in dogs and cats are needed.

CACHEXIA
Cachexia is a loss of muscle which occurs commonly in people and
companion animals with a variety of chronic diseases, including

congestive heart failure (CHF; ch. 229), cancer (ch. 163), chronic
liver disease (chs. 270 and 271), hyperthyroidism (ch. 287),
diabetes mellitus (chs. 291 and 292), and chronic kidney disease
(CKD; ch. 301), as well as in acute illness and injury (ch. 164).1
Cachexia and sarcopenia change animals’ normal metabolism such
that they lose primarily muscle, rather than fat. In healthy animals
that lose weight, fat is the primary tissue lost and muscle is
preserved. The inflammatory mediators elaborated in disease states,
however, cause an animal to lose muscle mass, rather than fat.1
This loss of muscle has direct and deleterious effects on strength,
immune function, wound healing, and survival.1-4 In addition, many
of the effects of cachexia, such as weakness, reduced food intake or
altered eating patterns, weight loss, and perceived poor quality of
life, are major contributing factors to an owner’s decision of
euthanasia.5 As a result, cachexia may be even more deleterious for
dogs and cats than for humans because of the option for euthanasia
in companion animals. These important clinical implications
underscore the importance of early identification and effective
treatment.

SPECIFIC FORMS OF CACHEXIA
The hallmark of all forms of cachexia is a loss of muscle which can be
readily assessed using the muscle condition score (ch. 72 and inside
cover). Although the basic concepts of cachexia are consistent across
different diseases, some details on cachexia associated with common
diseases are noted below.

Cardiac Cachexia
While low body condition score (BCS) is uncommon (only 5-14%) at
the time of diagnosis of CHF in dogs and cats, cachexia in this
population is very common, occurring in 42-48% of cats and 48-69%
of dogs (Table 151.1; chs. 157, 229).3,4,6,7 Cardiac cachexia
typically is recognized only after CHF has developed, but can occur
in dogs with advanced ACVIM stage B heart disease. Cachexia is
often recognized more easily in dogs than in cats, but, as noted

above, it occurs at high rates in both species. Dogs with right-sided
CHF have more advanced muscle loss compared to dogs with leftsided CHF.6
Two recent studies—one in dogs with CHF and one in cats with
CHF—showed that the presence of cachexia was associated with
shorter survival times.3,4 This emphasizes the importance of
heightened awareness of the likelihood of cachexia in animals with
CHF, preventing it as much as possible, and addressing it at its
earliest stages when present.
Whereas obesity is a risk factor for development of heart disease in
people, obesity actually may confer a protective effect once CHF is
present—this is known as the obesity paradox, and it occurs in
people, dogs, and cats with CHF.4,8,9 The benefit of obesity in CHF is
likely due to having more muscle, rather than to the obesity per se,
given the adverse effects of cachexia. With obesity, there is usually an
increased amount of muscle, which can provide a greater reserve
during the catabolic state of CHF. However, cachexia is possible even
in overweight and obese patients (see below), so muscle condition
score should be assessed in all patients. Human studies suggest that
muscle loss in the presence of obesity (“sarcopenic obesity”) is
associated with even more detrimental effects than cachexia alone.10

Cancer Cachexia
As in CHF, low BCS is uncommon in dogs and cats with cancer (46%); obesity is actually more common (Table 151.1; ch. 163).11-14
However, many animals with cancer have cachexia (35% of dogs and
91% of cats; Table 151.1).11,13 Results of one study showed that cats
with low BCS had a significantly shorter survival time compared to
those with a BCS ≥5.13 However, no published studies have reported
on the relationship between cachexia and survival in dogs or cats
with cancer.

Renal Cachexia
Prevalence rates for cachexia in dogs and cats with CKD have not
been published, but subjectively are very common (ch. 301). Studies

have evaluated the prevalence of low BCS in CKD patients: 18% of
dogs and between 36-81% of cats were reported to be thin (Table
151.1; ch. 301).15-20 One retrospective study in dogs with CKD
showed that underweight dogs had a significantly shorter survival
time compared to ideal or overweight dogs.15 Finally, two studies in
cats showed that low body weight was associated with shorter
survival times.20,21 Studies are needed to assess the prevalence of
cachexia and the relationship between cachexia and survival time in
dogs and cats with CKD.

Cachexia in Hyperthyroidism
Although most clinicians think of cats with hyperthyroidism as being
thin, the prevalence of low BCS in one study of cats with
hyperthyroidism was only 35% (Table 151.1; ch. 287).22 However,
the prevalence of cachexia in this same population was 77% (Table
151.1).22 This is consistent with other diseases where cachexia is
much more common than thin BCS, and relying on a thin BCS for
diagnosis of cachexia will dramatically underestimate the number of
cases with cachexia.

SARCOPENIA
Sarcopenia, like cachexia, is characterized by a loss of muscle, but
unlike cachexia, sarcopenia is a syndrome that occurs during aging in
the absence of disease. In people, sarcopenia begins around 30 years
of age and progresses over time. The loss of muscle in sarcopenia
often is accompanied by an increase in fat mass so the total weight
may not change (or may even increase), thus masking the
sarcopenia. Inflammation, increased autophagy, reduced physical
activity, decreased concentrations of growth hormone and
testosterone, changes in type II muscle fibers, mitochondrial
dysfunction, microvascular changes, and decreased protein synthesis
all contribute to sarcopenia.23,24 Like cachexia, sarcopenia is
associated with increased morbidity and mortality in people.24
Sarcopenia also occurs in dogs and cats during aging.23,25 It is
important to note that cachexia and sarcopenia can occur
concurrently in an animal—i.e., an elderly cat with CKD may have

muscle loss due to both sarcopenia (from aging) and cachexia
(secondary to CKD).

DIAGNOSIS OF CACHEXIA AND
SARCOPENIA
It is important to be aware that cachexia and sarcopenia are
processes and not just end-stage syndromes that many people think
of when they hear the word “cachexia.” A standard nutritional
assessment (ch. 145) includes body weight, BCS, muscle condition
score, and diet history, and can readily identify cachexia.

BODY WEIGHT
Weighing patients (and recording it in the medical record) at every
visit allows the clinician to monitor trends in body weight, rather
than waiting for a significant loss of weight to occur. Weight loss is
common in aging and chronic diseases: 40-56% of dogs and cats with
CHF,3,4,9,26 42-82% of cats with CKD,16-21,27 and 54% of dogs with
cancer11 had lost weight at the time of diagnosis. Weight loss in
chronic diseases can occur early in the disease. For example, studies
have shown that cats with CKD lost a median of 9-11% of their body
weight in the year prior to diagnosis, and that the weight loss begins
up to 3 years prior to diagnosis.21,27 After diagnosis, weight loss
becomes even more common: more than 50% of dogs with
lymphoma and osteosarcoma and 67% of cats with CHF lost weight
after their diagnosis.4,14 Therefore, frequent monitoring of body
weight in dogs and cats is important, particularly as they age. For
cats and smaller dogs, encouraging owners to have a digital baby or
pet scale or a postal scale at home for regular weigh-ins can be
valuable for early detection of weight loss.

BODY CONDITION SCORE

Despite the importance of monitoring body weight and BCS (ch. 72
and textbook’s inside covers), it is important not to rely solely on
weight loss or a thin BCS to diagnose cachexia and sarcopenia.
Waiting until weight loss occurs prevents an early diagnosis
especially in sarcopenia and certain types of cachexia where weight
loss may be masked by accumulation of fluid or fat. Similarly, one
should not only look for cachexia in thin animals as muscle loss can
occur in normal weight and even obese animals. Except in cats with
CKD, most patients with chronic diseases are not thin at the time of
diagnosis. Between 4-12% of dogs and cats with CHF or cancer have
a low BCS (<4/9) at the time of diagnosis (Table 151.1). More
importantly, muscle loss can occur even in overweight or obese
animals. In a recent study of 269 dogs with CHF, 83% of dogs with
thin BCS had cachexia, as one would expect.3 What was more
surprising was that 57% of ideal weight dogs and 30% of overweight
dogs had cachexia.3 Similar findings of cachexia occurring
commonly in ideal and even overweight patients were seen in cats
with CHF.4 Therefore, if one waits for the classical image of a thin,
severely muscle wasted patient before diagnosing cachexia, it will
delay diagnosis and make intervention less likely to be successful.

MUSCLE CONDITION SCORE
To recognize cachexia and sarcopenia in their earliest stages, when
intervention is more likely to be successful, muscle condition score
must be consistently assessed in every patient at every visit in
addition to body weight and BCS (ch. 72). BCS and muscle condition
score differ in that the BCS assesses fat stores, while the muscle
condition score specifically evaluates muscle mass.28 Evaluation of
muscle mass includes visual examination and palpation of the head,
scapulae, epaxial muscles over the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae,
and pelvic bones (chs. 3 and 72, and textbook’s inside covers). BCSs
and muscle condition scores are not directly related because an
animal can be obese but still have substantial muscle loss (or
conversely, be very thin but have a normal muscle condition score).
Palpation is required for accurately assessing BCS and muscle
condition score.

Cachexia should be anticipated in animals with chronic diseases
such as CHF, CKD, chronic liver disease, and cancer, as well as in
acutely ill or injured animals in which muscle loss can develop
quickly. Muscle loss also is likely to occur in aging, even in healthy
individuals. Therefore, body weight, BCS, and muscle condition
score should be assessed at every visit in geriatric cats and dogs. In
addition to body weight, BCS, and muscle condition score, a
complete diet history should be obtained at every visit as part of a
standard nutritional assessment because this can identify factors that
may contribute to muscle loss, such as a nutritionally unbalanced
diet or insufficient protein or calorie intake (see below and ch. 145).
Moderate to severe cachexia is not difficult to identify clinically
from a muscle condition score in a dog with CHF or a cat with CKD.
Identification of cachexia can be more difficult when it is mild unless
clinicians are in the habit of assessing muscle condition score in all
patients. However, detecting cachexia and sarcopenia when they are
mild offers more opportunities for successful intervention.
Therefore, in addition to raising awareness among clinicians and
developing consistent patterns of assessment of muscle condition
score, clinically applicable techniques are needed to identify muscle
loss at an early stage.
Some of the currently used research tools, such as dual-energy xray absorptiometry and bioelectrical impedance, have limitations for
measurement of muscle in animals with chronic illnesses due to
assumptions inherent in their methodology and software. Computed
tomography is an excellent method for identifying quantitative and
qualitative changes in muscle but requires general anesthesia or
sedation.25,29 Ultrasound is an excellent method for quantification
of muscle loss, and techniques specific to dogs and cats have been
developed.30-31 Our group has validated two ultrasound techniques,
the Vertebral Epaxial Muscle Score (VEMS) and the Forelimb
Epaxial Muscle Score (FLEMS), to more accurately quantify muscle
in healthy, aging, and ill dogs and cats with cachexia and
sarcopenia.30-33 These methods can be used for earlier detection of
cachexia and sarcopenia in dogs, as well as for quantitative outcome
measures in studies of potential treatments for these conditions in
dogs and cats.

MECHANISMS OF CACHEXIA
Factors contributing to the pathogenesis of cachexia include
decreased energy intake, alterations in metabolism due to
inflammation, decreased nutrient absorption, and increased energy
requirements. The latter two usually play a minor role in most
diseases associated with cachexia.

DECREASED ENERGY INTAKE
An important problem in many forms of cachexia is a decreased
energy (calorie) intake. Reduced food intake or altered patterns of
food intake are common in dogs and cats with the chronic diseases
associated with cachexia (e.g., CKD, CHF).6,34,35 For example,
appetite issues are present in 34-84% of dogs and cats with heart
disease (ch. 157),5,34,35 and in 21-92% of cats with CKD (ch.
158).16-20,27,36 These alterations in food intake may be secondary to
fatigue, nausea, or medication side-effects, but increased levels of
inflammatory mediators play a major role.1 Control of food intake is
a complex system, which includes numerous anorexigenic or satiety
signals (e.g., adiponectin, serotonin, insulin) and orexigenic signals
(e.g., ghrelin, neuropeptide Y, agouti-related protein).1,37 For
example, an imbalance between orexigenic and anorexigenic
hormones or a resistance to orexigenic signals can negatively affect
appetite. Inflammatory mediators, such as the cytokines, tumor
necrosis factor-alpha (TNF) and interleukin-1-beta (IL-1), play an
important role in this dysregulation and may provide targets for
treatment to increase food intake.1 In people, food intake is not only
affected by the many orexigenic and anorexigenic factors but also by
physiological factors, such as social situation, memory, time of day,
fatigue, and depression. The role of these factors in dogs and cats is
unknown but such factors could be involved because dogs and cats
appear to develop aversions to certain foods, particularly when sick,
and this can contribute to decreased food intake.
However, as important as adequate calorie intake is, reduced food
intake alone cannot cause cachexia because, as previously noted, a

healthy animal with insufficient calorie intake would lose primarily
fat so alterations in metabolism must also be present to cause muscle
loss in these conditions.

INFLAMMATION-INDUCED METABOLIC
ALTERATIONS
Although decreased energy intake and, to a lesser degree, decreased
nutrient absorption and increased energy requirements, can cause a
net calorie deficit which contributes to cachexia and sarcopenia, the
major cause in their pathogenesis is the activation of inflammatory
mediators. TNF was initially thought to be the major cause of
cachexia, and cachexia research throughout the 1990s focused on
TNF and other inflammatory mediators (e.g., IL-1, interleukin-6, and
a variety of others). Catecholamines and neurohormones (e.g., reninangiotensin-aldosterone system, epinephrine, glucocorticoids) also
can contribute to muscle catabolism.2 However, there are multiple
metabolic alterations involved that trigger the muscle loss. A detailed
discussion of the many inflammatory mediators and signaling
pathways is beyond the scope of this chapter but a number of
excellent reviews are available.2,38,39 At the core of the muscle loss
in cachexia and sarcopenia is an imbalance between decreased
protein synthesis and increased protein catabolism, resulting in a net
loss of lean tissue. The three major pathways of protein degradation
—ubiquitin-proteasome system, apoptosis, and autophagy—can
contribute to cachexia.
One example of a pathway that is altered as a result of the
inflammation in cachexia and contributing to muscle loss is the
myostatin signaling pathway. A myokine, myostatin, is a protein
produced by skeletal myocytes that negatively regulates muscle
mass, keeping muscle size in check. In healthy people, exercise
decreases myostatin concentrations, allowing muscles to increase in
size. Several myostatin mutations have been described in various
species in which enlarged musculature is present (e.g., doublemuscled cattle breeds, “bully” Whippets).40,41 However,
inflammatory mediators activate myostatin expression, which can

contribute to muscle catabolism.1,2,38,39 This is just one example and
there are numerous other signaling pathways triggered by
inflammatory mediators that contribute to muscle catabolism and
cachexia.
Although increased protein catabolism is a major contributor to
cachexia and sarcopenia, decreased protein synthesis also plays a
role in the net loss of lean tissue. For example, levels of insulin-like
growth factor (IGF-1), which stimulates protein synthesis, decline
with age and can be blunted due to inflammatory mediators
associated with chronic diseases. Several signaling pathways that
normally stimulate protein synthesis are impacted in aging and
chronic disease, contributing to loss of muscle mass.2,38,39

POTENTIAL INTERVENTIONs FOR
CACHEXIA AND SARCOPENIA
The complex mechanisms for cachexia and sarcopenia offer multiple
opportunities for targeting muscle loss. There has been great interest
from pharmaceutical and other industries in recent years in
developing effective treatments for cachexia and sarcopenia in
people but, thus far, there have been no successes. Few of these
interventions have been studied in companion animals, but the
enhanced interest in these syndromes in people will likely lead to the
development of products that will benefit both humans and
companion animals.
Although many single agents and approaches have been tested for
the treatment of cachexia and sarcopenia, it is becoming clear that a
multimodal approach is likely needed. In order for an effective
treatment, it is ideal to address the three different components
contributing to cachexia and sarcopenia in a multimodal approach:
1) reducing inflammation and other causes of catabolism, 2)
increasing anabolism, and 3) ensuring adequate substrate (i.e.,
calories, protein, and other nutrients). It is important to recognize
that this is above and beyond optimal treatment for any underlying
diseases.

REDUCING INFLAMMATION AND
OTHER CAUSES OF CATABOLISM
Specific anti-cytokine agents (e.g., soluble TNF receptors, TNF
antibodies, IL-1 converting enzyme inhibitors) have thus far not been
successful in human clinical trials for cachexia and sarcopenia. The
effects of blocking TNF or other inflammatory cytokines in dogs and
cats with naturally-occurring disease are unknown, but this approach
using available human investigational drugs is limited given the
species-specific nature of these antibodies. Many other agents with
anti-inflammatory effects, such as thalidomide and pentoxifylline,
have also been evaluated as possible drugs for people with various
forms of cachexia but none has been approved for use in people with
cachexia.
Although specific anti-cytokine agents have not been successful
thus far in people with various forms of cachexia, omega-3 (n-3)
polyunsaturated fatty acids are a non-specific approach to reducing
inflammatory cytokines and eicosanoids. Studies have shown that
omega-3 fatty acid supplementation reduced muscle loss in dogs
with CHF6 and increased body weight in people with CHF.43 The
results of omega-3 fatty acid supplementation in humans with cancer
cachexia have been variable, which may be due to their modest antiinflammatory effect, inadequate dose, or inadequate substrate, as
well as fish oil’s lack of anabolic effects.
Because of its effects on muscle, neurohormonal blockade may
provide benefits in some diseases associated with cachexia in
addition to their cardiovascular effects. For example, certain betablockers have been shown to decrease protein oxidation and to
reduce cardiac cachexia in people.2

INCREASING ANABOLISM
Muscle mass can be increased through enhanced anabolism. Exercise
provides an anabolic stimulus, particularly resistance training, which
increases protein synthesis and muscle mass. Another anabolic agent
is testosterone, but its adverse effects limit its use in cachexia and
sarcopenia. Non-steroidal selective androgen receptor modulators

(SARMs) are being developed which have anabolic activity primarily
in muscle and bone, with minimal androgenic effects in other tissues,
thus reducing side-effects. Human clinical trials of SARMs for cancer
cachexia have not been successful thus far but warrant further
research.
Although growth hormone treatment has not been overwhelmingly
successful for treating cachexia and has important adverse effects,
some promising results have been seen with IGF-1, which mediates
many of growth hormone’s anabolic effects on muscle.
Administration of IGF-1 through various approaches, including gene
or stem therapy, has not advanced in testing but ghrelin can
stimulate production of growth hormone and IGF-1. Thus, it may
have potential anabolic effects (see below).
Because of myostatin’s role in controlling muscle size, blocking
myostatin may have beneficial anabolic effects. There are several
approaches to blocking myostatin, including myostatin antibodies or
myostatin receptor antibodies or decoys. A decoy myostatin receptor
was tested in a small, open-label pilot study of dogs with cardiac
cachexia and some dogs showed improvement in muscle condition
score.44 Thus far, myostatin inhibitors have not been successful in
human clinical trials of cachexia, but further research on this drug
class is warranted.

ENSURING ADEQUATE SUBSTRATE
Appetite stimulants can improve food intake but it is unclear
whether increasing appetite alone will reverse or even minimize the
deleterious effects of cachexia. Unless inflammatory mediators are
reduced and anabolism is stimulated, weight gain is likely to be
composed of fat and not muscle, and gain of fat does not appear to
have beneficial effects in people with cachexia. However, appetite
stimulation may provide benefit for dogs and cats, even without gain
of muscle, if increased appetite is viewed by the owner as improving
the animal’s quality of life (and thus, reducing the likelihood of
euthanasia).5 As part of a multimodal approach, appetite stimulants
can help to provide adequate calories to support the antiinflammatory and anabolic agents in preventing or treating cachexia.

COMBINATION APPROACHES
The complex and redundant mechanisms of cachexia and sarcopenia
make it unlikely that there will be a single agent treatment that will
result in complete prevention or reversal of cachexia and sarcopenia.
It would be ideal to find a drug that targets multiple pathways or a
combination of therapies that address all three components (i.e.,
anti-inflammatory, anabolic, and adequate substrate). For example,
multi-modal treatments including anti-inflammatory agents,
exercise, and nutritional supplementation have been successfully
used in people with cardiac cachexia.45
Another example of addressing multiple pathways is ghrelin.
Ghrelin is an orexigenic hormone secreted primarily by the stomach
in response to fasting. Ghrelin increases food intake, which provides
the necessary calories, protein, and other nutrients for maintaining
weight and muscle. It also stimulates growth hormone and IGF-1
secretion which provide an anabolic effect. In addition, ghrelin has
multi-systemic effects and stimulates neuropeptide Y and agoutirelated protein, decreases expression of proopiomelanocortin,
stimulates gastric motility, and has anti-cytokine and antiinflammatory effects.46 Ghrelin itself has a short half-life, which
limits its use, but ghrelin agonists with longer half-lives have been
developed. One ghrelin agonist, capromorelin, is approved for use in
dogs as an appetite stimulant (Entyce)47 and for weight loss in cats
with CKD (Elura).48 A related drug, anamorelin, has gone through
extensive research in humans for cancer cachexia and while it
increased muscle mass in Phase III clinical trials, it did not reach the
other primary endpoint of improved muscle function; therefore, it
was not approved in the United States for cachexia.49 However,
anamorelin is now in clinical trials for weight loss and/or anorexia in
humans with non-small cell lung cancer, as well as a variety of other
human disease conditions.50 Whether ghrelin agonists may have
benefits on muscle mass in dogs and cats with cachexia and
sarcopenia is unknown but additional research is warranted.
Given the recent attention on cachexia and sarcopenia and their
deleterious effects, many other compounds are being investigated,
including ones that address the three key aspects inflammation,

anabolism, and substrate. One example is S-pindolol, which was
identified through screening for its specific effects: it is a beta-1
receptor blocker (anti-catabolic effects), partial beta-2 receptor
agonist (anabolic effects), and a 5-HT1A antagonist (appetite
stimulatory effects).51 This drug successfully completed a Phase II
study in human patients with cancer and is currently in a Phase IIb
study.51

PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS FOR THE
NON-PHARMACOLOGIC
INTERVENTIONS
Until effective pharmacologic interventions for treating cachexia and
sarcopenia are available for dogs and cats, these important
syndromes still can be managed in a number of ways. These other
aspects of therapy also will continue to be important since, in
addition to reducing catabolism and increasing anabolism, it is
critical to provide adequate substrate (i.e., calories, protein, and
other nutrients) to support the first two actions. Anabolic agents, for
example, will not be effective if there are insufficient calories and
protein with which to build muscle. Therefore, careful attention to
the nutritional aspects of treatment of cachexia and sarcopenia is
critical for success. In addition, early diagnosis provides the best
opportunity for successful treatment of cachexia and sarcopenia.

NUTRITION
Optimizing medical treatment for the underlying disease in animals
with chronic conditions commonly associated with cachexia (e.g.,
CKD [chs. 158, 301], CHF [chs. 157, 228, 229], cancer [ch. 163]) is
of primary importance. Physical factors (e.g., dental disease, back or
joint pain) or environmental factors (e.g., multipet households) that
can negatively affect food intake also must be investigated and
addressed.

A nutritional assessment should be performed in every patient at
every visit, including a diet history, body weight, BCS, and muscle
condition score (ch. 145).28 The diet history includes not just the
pet food (or homemade diet), but also treats, table foods, rawhides or
other chews (e.g., bully sticks, pig ears), dental products, and foods
used to administer medications. Diet history forms are available to
help capture all the necessary information
(https://wsava.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/DietHistory-Form.pdf). This information can help to determine
whether the pet is getting sufficient calories. If unsure of a patient’s
calorie requirements, calorie calculators for cats and dogs are
available (www.petnutritionalliance.org).
If owners are feeding a homemade diet, it is almost always
nutritionally unbalanced (sometimes severely so) unless a Board
Certified Veterinary Nutritionist formulated the diet and the owner is
carefully following the recipe. If a pet food label states that the diet is
“for intermittent or supplemental use,” it is not nutritionally
complete and balanced. This phrase is acceptable for therapeutic
diets that are designed to help manage diseases and are used under a
veterinarian’s supervision, but over-the-counter diets should always
be complete and balanced if they are a main component of the diet,
rather than just an occasional treat.
The diet history also may reveal that the diet is unbalanced not
because the animal is eating an unbalanced diet, but due to intake of
a large proportion of calories from treats, rawhides, or table food. In
this situation, even if the main diet is well-balanced, the other foods
may be fed in a large enough proportion that the overall diet is
unbalanced, which can contribute to weight and muscle loss as well
as not being optimal for the underlying disease.
It is important to assess not just the brand of food being fed, but
also the specific product and flavor because it may reveal factors that
can contribute to cachexia or sarcopenia (or that are not optimal for
the underlying disease). For example, animals with CHF should not
be fed a renal or otherwise reduced-protein diet unless glomerular
disease or advanced concurrent CKD are present. Providing at least
the Association of American Feed Control Officials (AAFCO)
minimum for protein (4.5 g/100 kcal for dogs and 6.5 g/100 kcal for
cats)52 is important, although higher dietary protein levels may be

desirable if muscle loss is present or likely to occur. Senior diets are
highly variable in terms of their protein content,53,54 so the
individual product (and flavor) must be investigated to ensure it is
appropriate for an individual patient. Commercial pet foods also vary
widely in calorie density—there are dog and cat foods available on
the market now that are >500 kcal/cup or <250 kcal/cup. Therefore,
it is important to ensure that undesired weight and muscle loss are
not simply the result of an owner switching to a lower calorie density
food. Even certain adult maintenance or senior diets with protein
levels at or just above the AAFCO minimums may not have enough
protein, especially if patients have cachexia or sarcopenia (or are
likely to develop it). In complicated cases, especially those with
concurrent diseases, consider referring the patient to a Board
Certified Veterinary Nutritionist (www.vetspecialists.com or
http://www.esvcn.eu/college).
It is also important to determine whether pets are receiving any
dietary supplements. Animals with diseases are more likely than
healthy pets to be receiving supplements,34,35,55 but owners typically
do not volunteer this information unless specifically asked. Dietary
supplements may contribute to muscle loss by reducing appetite or
by interacting with medications used to treat the underlying disease,
thus decreasing their efficacy or increasing the adverse effects of the
medications.

ADDRESSING CHANGES IN APPETITE
Appetite can be a challenging issue in animals with cachexia and
sarcopenia. Complete loss of appetite (anorexia; ch. 17) may not be
present but owners commonly note changes in appetite, such as
reductions in food intake (hyporexia), or altered food preferences or
“cyclical” appetite (dysrexia). Client communication (ch. 1) is
important to address decreased or altered food intake
(https://vetnutrition.tufts.edu/2019/01/pickiness-fortherapeutic-diets/). Owners who are prepared for changes in
appetite appear better able to deal with these changes effectively.
Optimal treatment of the underlying disease and treating nausea
(ch. 48), when present, are critical to avoiding weight and muscle

loss. Drugs that improve food intake are now available: Mirtazapine
(Mirataz – transdermal medication for the management of weight
loss in cats) or capromorelin (Entyce appetite-stimulant in dogs and
Elura for the management of weight loss in cats). With any appetitestimulating drug, it is important to carefully monitor body weight,
BCS, muscle condition score, and food intake to ensure adequate
calorie intake. Owners (and veterinarians) often are comforted by
some food intake, even if it is not sufficient to maintain weight or is
not comprised of an optimal nutritional profile (e.g., a cat with CKD
that will only eat meat or a high-phosphorus commercial food). In
animals that continue to lose weight and muscle, a feeding tube
should be considered (ch. 81). Early tube placement typically has a
better outcome than waiting until the animal is in end-stage disease
with severe weight and muscle loss.
Also, appetite stimulants may be beneficial not just in ensuring
adequate calorie intake but also adequate intake of an optimal diet.
Many cats with CKD, for example, are not eating an optimal diet due
to dysrexia. In a study of more than 1000 owners of cats with CKD,
49% of cats were not eating a therapeutic renal diet as any part of
their diet and 51% of owners reported feeding an over-the-counter
diet for all or part of their cats’ diets.36 Similar findings of
suboptimal diets have been found in patients with cardiac
disease.34,35 Therefore, appetite stimulants may be beneficial in
animals with chronic diseases and dysrexia to help ensure they are
eating an optimal diet. Appetite-stimulating drugs that increase IGF1 (e.g., capromorelin) may also have direct anabolic effect on muscle
although this requires research in dogs and cats.

OMEGA-3 FATTY ACIDS
Omega-3 fatty acids, either from a highly enriched diet or through
supplements, may have a number of benefits in animals with
cachexia and sarcopenia. Omega-3 fatty acids reduce inflammatory
cytokines and eicosanoids. As a result, omega-3 fatty acids have been
shown to decrease the muscle loss in dogs with CHF and, in some
animals, to improve appetite.6

The author currently recommends a dosage of fish oil to provide
40 mg/kg eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and 25 mg/kg
docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) for animals with CHF. Specific dosages
have been recommended for other conditions, although these
dosages are not specifically aimed at addressing cachexia.56 Unless
the diet is one of a few specially designed therapeutic diets (or
certain over-the-counter diets), supplementation will be necessary to
achieve this omega-3 fatty acid dosage. When recommending a
supplement, it is important to know the exact amount of EPA and
DHA in the specific fish oil brand because supplements vary widely.
Fish oil supplements with independent quality control testing should
be used and they should always contain vitamin E as an antioxidant,
but other nutrients should be excluded to avoid toxicoses. Cod liver
oil should not be used to provide omega-3 fatty acids at this high
dose because it contains high concentrations of vitamins A and D
that can result in intoxication at this dose. Flaxseed oil or other
plant-based omega-3 fatty acids also should be avoided because of
metabolic differences that make them inefficient (in dogs) or
ineffective (in cats) sources of omega-3 fatty acids for these species.

EXERCISE
Exercise has been an effective method for helping to maintain
muscle mass in people with cachexia and sarcopenia. Both aerobic
and resistance exercise are beneficial for minimizing cachexia and
sarcopenia in people, although resistance exercise appears to be most
useful. Exercise may be more challenging in some of the diseases
associated with cachexia in dogs (e.g., CHF) and particularly in cats,
but exercise such as walking may provide an effective treatment for
muscle loss in some diseases and in helping to prevent sarcopenia in
aging animals (chs. 226 and 256).

INTRODUCTION
Nutrition has many direct beneficial effects on different components
of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract and therefore plays a fundamental
role in the management of different GI diseases. This chapter focuses
on the specific nutritional strategies for acute gastroenteritis, GI
adverse reaction to food, chronic enteropathy, intestinal
lymphangiectasia, and feline constipation.

ACUTE GASTROENTERITIS
PATHOGENESIS
Acute gastroenteritis is a common presentation in veterinary practice
(chs. 48, 49, 262, and 263). There are several causes, such as
infectious, inflammatory, toxic, and dietary factors, although the
etiology is rarely confirmed. Management is aimed at treating the
underlying cause if identified, as well as supportive care and
nutritional therapy once the animal is rehydrated and stabilized.
Animals with acute gastroenteritis may present with hyporexia or
anorexia (ch. 17). The absence of nutrients within the GI tract can
lead to atrophy of the small intestine, suppressed crypt cell
proliferation, marked decrease in GI-associated lymphoid tissue and
function, decreased transport of glutamine and arginine, increased
intestinal permeability and risk of bacterial translocation and sepsis,
and enhanced pro-inflammatory cytokine production. Conversely,
nutrients within the GI tract stimulate intestinal mass and function,
and are an important stimulus for intestinal mucosal growth, repair,
and integrity. Enteral feeding with as little as 10% of resting energy
requirement (RER) to piglets resulted in significantly greater jejunal
lactase and sucrase activities, taller villi, and deeper crypts versus
findings in piglets fed nil per os.1 Therefore, food should not be
withheld from animals with acute gastroenteritis and instead
prioritized once they have been appropriately rehydrated and
stabilized. Indeed, a prospective, randomized controlled clinical trial
showed that early enteral nutrition of dogs with severe parvoviral
enteritis was associated with more rapid clinical improvement
compared with withholding food during the early stages of disease.2
Also, as a significantly higher survival rate was achieved in dogs and
cats receiving enteral nutrition with parenteral nutrition compared
to parenteral nutrition alone,3 enteral feeding should be prioritized
whenever possible over parenteral nutrition in these cases.

NUTRITIONAL STRATEGIES
Enteral feeding in dogs and cats with GI disease can be initiated with
a commercial therapeutic diet or a home-prepared diet utilizing

different nutritional strategies. Although studies are lacking to
determine the ideal dietary composition for animals with acute
gastroenteritis, nutritional strategies that may be beneficial include
increased digestibility, low fat, and high dietary fiber. In addition,
the use of probiotics may help in cases of acute gastroenteritis.

Increased Digestibility
Digestibility refers to the extent to which food or macronutrients
present in food is digested and absorbed by the GI tract and is
usually expressed as a percentage. However, the digestibility of a diet
or its ingredients is not a constant value, as digestibility is influenced
by many factors. These factors are related to the ingredients,
processing (for example, heat processing generally increases the
digestibility of starch but decreases the digestibility of protein),
animal factors, such as breed (for example, larger breed dogs
typically display lower digestibility of food compared to smaller
breed dogs4), age (for example, approximately 20% of cats older than
12 years of age have decreased protein digestibility5), GI health,
physiological status, and the amount of food fed. Although there are
currently no standard criteria for the definition of a highly digestible
diet, diets with a total digestibility of at least 80% and macronutrient
digestibility of at least 90% are considered to meet this definition.

FIGURE 152.1 Classification system used in

food.
Commercial therapeutic GI diets are generally classified as highly
digestible. Acute gastroenteritis may compromise the digestion and
absorption of nutrients; therefore, diets with high digestibility can be
advantageous in these cases. Additionally, diets with high
digestibility produce fewer residues in the GI tract, which can help to
prevent overloading of the gut, as well as help to alleviate any
osmotic diarrhea.

Low Dietary Fat
Diets high in fat may have adverse effects on the GI tract, including
delayed gastric emptying and adverse effects on the microbiota,

permeability, and the mucosal immune response in susceptible
individuals. Therefore, as a reduction in dietary fat may help to
hasten gastric transit, this strategy may be beneficial in those
animals with acute gastroenteritis that is resulting in nausea,
regurgitation, or vomiting. Animals with acute gastroenteritis may
experience reduced fat digestion and absorption, resulting in excess
dietary fat passing into the colon. This may result in dysbiosis, as
well as secretory diarrhea, so reducing the dietary fat in these cases
may help to reduce or alleviate these effects. Therefore, a low-fat diet
should be considered in those animals with acute gastroenteritis with
clinical signs that are likely to benefit from this strategy.

High Dietary Fiber (ch. 165)
Dietary fibers are plant-based carbohydrates that cannot be digested
by mammalian enzymes. Dietary fiber has many beneficial effects on
the GI tract, including modification of gastric emptying,
normalization of intestinal motility, optimizing intestinal mucosal
barrier function, anti-inflammatory effects via generation of shortchain fatty acids, buffering of toxins, binding of excess water,
supporting the growth of beneficial bacteria, and altering the
viscosity of the ingesta. Diets high in fiber may be beneficial for those
cases with large intestinal signs. However, not all animals with large
intestinal signs will respond to a high-fiber strategy. Thus, trial-anderror with this approach is needed and should be used for those cases
with large intestinal signs that do not respond to a highly digestible
diet, and especially before the use of empirical antimicrobials.

Probiotics
Several studies of probiotics in dogs and cats with acute
gastroenteritis have shown beneficial effects, such as significantly
reducing episodes or duration of diarrhea, and improving stool
consistency.6-12 However, the effects are likely strain-specific, and
larger-scale studies assessing the efficacy and safety of each,
particularly in immunocompromised animals, are needed.

FEEDING PLAN AND MONITORING

Once the animal is stabilized and rehydrated (chs. 119, 120), food
should be offered as soon as possible, starting with 25% of the
calculated RER (70 × BW (kg)0.75) divided into multiple meals to aid
gastric emptying and intestinal motility. Although dogs suffering
from hemorrhagic gastroenteritis after a short adaptation period
tolerated enteral feeding, vomiting was a severe adverse effect in the
initial phase.13 Therefore, if the animal does not tolerate enteral
feeding initially, food should be withheld for as short a time as
possible and then offered again at a reduced amount of 10-15% of
RER. If 25% of RER is well tolerated, then this can slowly be
increased by 25% increments daily until full RER is reached on day
4. A slow increase over 4 days will help to prevent overloading of the
GI tract and exacerbation of signs, as well as allow assessment of
tolerance. Animals should not be fed greater than the daily RER in
hospital, to prevent complications associated with over-feeding.
Once the GI signs have fully resolved, the regular diet can be
reintroduced slowly over the next 7 to 10 days.
Monitoring body weight, hydration status and GI signs should be
performed at least daily during hospitalization. The prognosis for full
recovery in most cases of acute gastroenteritis is very good. Further
diagnostic investigations are required if the GI signs become chronic.

GASTROINTESTINAL ADVERSE
REACTION TO FOOD (CH. 166)
PATHOGENESIS
Gastrointestinal adverse reaction to food (GI-ARF) describes a
number of conditions, which can be grouped according to their
etiology (Figure 152.1). Collectively, the non immune-mediated
causes are referred to as dietary intolerance, whereas the immunemediated causes are termed food allergy or food hypersensitivity. A
comprehensive diet history (ch. 145) may help to diagnose toxic and
some dietary intolerance cases. However, the diagnosis of food
allergy is currently more challenging, as there are no laboratory tests
commercially available that allow for a definitive diagnosis. Thus, the
current gold standard diagnostic test remains an exclusion

(elimination) diet trial with provocation testing. However,
provocation testing is commonly not performed due to low owner
compliance and hence a definitive diagnosis of food allergy remains
tentative in most cases. It is important to note that some types of
food intolerance may also relapse with provocation testing, making it
harder to distinguish those from cases of relapse due to food allergy.

NUTRITIONAL STRATEGIES
Commercial therapeutic hydrolyzed and novel protein diets, as well
as a home-cooked diet utilizing novel ingredients can be used for the
diagnosis and treatment of suspected food allergy.

Hydrolyzed Diet
Hydrolyzed diets are used in the management of food allergy; the
proteins are considered small enough to avoid a type 1 IgE-mediated
hypersensitivity reaction, as their small size precludes cross-linking
of 2 IgE antibody receptors on a mast cell. Although the type of
aberrant immune response is unknown in dogs and cats with GI food
allergy, hydrolyzed diets are used for diagnosing and treating this
condition. However, one study showed that a significant proportion
(21%) of dogs sensitized to the intact protein still reacted adversely to
the hydrolyzed diet.14 Therefore, persistent GI signs may be
anticipated with these diets, particularly in animals with a non IgEmediated cause for their food allergy. If the GI signs fail to respond
to a hydrolyzed diet, then a commercial therapeutic or homeprepared limited-ingredient novel protein diet should be trialed.

Commercial Therapeutic Limited-Ingredient Novel
Protein Diet
Novel protein diets are used in food allergy because the animal has
not been sensitized to the proteins, as they have not been previously
fed. However, the animal may become hypersensitized to these novel
antigens over time and therefore, a change to other novel ingredients
may be required to control the GI signs. A comprehensive antigen
exposure list compiled from the ingredients of all current and

previously fed diets is required to determine which ingredients
would be truly novel for the animal. Over-the-counter novel protein
diets should be avoided due to the concern for contamination with
commonly fed antigens.

Home-Prepared Limited-Ingredient Novel Protein
Diet
In some cases, the animal may be allergic to an antigen that
developed or was unmasked during the commercialization process of
the dry or canned pet food. Therefore, these animals may be unable
to tolerate any commercial pet foods, whether over-the-counter or
therapeutic. In these cases, a positive response to a home-prepared
diet can be used for diagnosis and management.

FEEDING PLAN AND REASSESSMENT
For those cases of suspected GI food allergy, a strict diet trial should
be performed for at least 8 to 12 weeks. After this time, a provocation
challenge with the original diet or single ingredients would be
needed to confirm the diagnosis of food allergy. Unfortunately, this is
not frequently performed and therefore, the diagnosis remains
tentative in most cases.

CHRONIC ENTEROPATHY
PATHOGENESIS
Food-responsive enteropathy (FRE) is a subcategory of chronic
enteropathy (CE). It encompasses a group of idiopathic diseases that
result in chronic GI signs that are responsive to diet alone. Although
the etiology of CE is unknown, it is hypothesized to involve the
interplay of 4 key components: genetic susceptibility, environmental
risk factor, intestinal dysbiosis, and altered GI mucosal immune
response. About two-thirds of dogs presenting with CE in a
secondary to tertiary referral population have FRE.15 Humans with
inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) are able to attain remission with
diet alone, due to the beneficial effects of diet on intestinal

microbiota, mucosal immune response, gene expression, GI
permeability and motility, and mucosal healing. Cases of GI food
allergy and intolerance may present similarly to those with foodresponsive CE, making it hard to distinguish between the three.
Therefore, studies assessing diet in dogs and cats with CE may have
also included those with GI food allergy or intolerance.

NUTRITIONAL STRATEGIES
As the etiology of FRE is unknown, dogs and cats may respond to
different dietary strategies, often necessitating trials with multiple
therapeutic diets. Studies have shown that most dogs and cats with
CE that respond to dietary therapy alone, respond quickly, e.g.,
within 1-2 weeks.16-19

Commercial Therapeutic GI Diet
Studies have proven the efficacy of commercial therapeutic GI diets
in cats with idiopathic chronic GI signs.20,21 The high digestibility of
these diets likely explains their efficacy, as less protein may present
intact to an immune system that may be dysregulated in CE.
However, for dogs with CE, diets with high digestibility alone may be
unlikely to provide sustained remission, as one study showed that
although a therapeutic GI diet was able to induce remission, these
dogs were less likely to remain free of clinical signs at subsequent
rechecks when compared to dogs managed with a hydrolyzed diet.22

Commercial Therapeutic Hydrolyzed Diet
Hydrolyzed diets have been used successfully in the management of
CE in dogs and cats,15,17,22-25 with some studies reporting a response
in two-thirds of animals.22,24,26 These diets employ several
strategies that may be beneficial for CE (Table 152.1).

Commercial Therapeutic Limited-Ingredient Novel
Protein Diet
Studies have shown that nearly 50% of cats and 60% of dogs with
chronic GI signs responded to a novel protein diet,19,27 with 1 study
documenting no difference in response rate between hydrolyzed and
limited ingredient novel protein diets for dogs with CE.15 Some

therapeutic limited-ingredient novel protein diets may have higher
total dietary fiber and therefore may be beneficial in those cases with
large intestinal signs, especially if a highly digestible diet failed to
improve the signs. As 1 study showed the presence of other common
food antigens in over the counter novel protein diets, these diets
should be avoided for the management of CE.28

Commercial Therapeutic High Fiber Diet (ch. 165)
High fiber diets may be effective for dogs and cats with large
intestinal signs29-33 (Table 152.2).
