Commercial Therapeutic Low Fat Diet
As well as leading to secretory diarrhea and dysbiosis, high fat diets
can increase mRNA expression of innate immune receptors,
nucleotide oligomerisation domain (NOD) 2 and toll-like receptor
(TLR) 5 in rodent models of IBD.34 These 2 receptors have been
implicated in the pathogenesis of canine CE.35-38 Therefore, those
dogs with a dysregulated mucosal immune response due to these
receptors may benefit from a low fat diet; however, studies are
needed to definitively assess this. Dietary fat did not seem to affect
the outcome of cats with chronic diarrhea39; therefore, dietary fat
may be less of a concern in cats with CE.

Therapeutic Complete and Balanced HomePrepared Diet
Certain emulsifiers and preservatives have been shown to have
negative effects on the intestinal microbiota and GI mucosal immune
system in rodent gene knockout models of IBD. Therefore, there may
be a subset of canine and feline CE cases that, due to their underlying
genetic susceptibility, may not be able to tolerate commercial foods
and require a home-prepared diet. Home-prepared diets
incorporating novel ingredients, low fat or high fiber can be used in
these cases. These diets must be formulated under the guidance of a
board-certified veterinary nutritionist to ensure that they are
complete and balanced for long-term feeding.

Probiotics
Two studies assessing the effect of a synbiotic containing
Enterococcus faecium in dogs with food-responsive CE failed to
show a difference in clinical efficacy, histology scores, expression of
intestinal genes, and fecal microbiota richness and density compared
to the placebo group.18,40 However, 2 studies assessing the effect of
VSL#3/Visbiome showed an increase in regulatory T-cell markers
and upregulated expression of tight junction proteins in dogs with
CE compared to standard treatment.41,42 Also, Saccharomyces
boulardii significantly improved clinical activity index, fecal
consistency and frequency, and body condition in dogs with CE
compared to placebo.43

FEEDING PLAN AND MONITORING
Transition to the new diet should be performed slowly over 7 to 10
days and the diet should be fed exclusively, in order to allow
assessment of the chosen dietary strategy. Feeding multiple small
meals throughout the day will help to prevent overloading of the GI
tract. Most dogs and cats with CE can be transitioned back to their
original diet without showing signs of relapse. In one study, 21% of
dogs and in another study, 29% of cats with GI signs relapsed
following challenge.16,19 The relapsed cases may have been food
allergic, as at this time it is not possible to distinguish GI food
allergy, dietary intolerance or food-responsive CE.
Regular monitoring of appetite, activity, body weight, body
condition, and GI signs will help to assess the effectiveness of the
diet (Figure 152.2). Serial measurement of the clinical activity
index will help to provide a more objective measure of treatment
response. Studies have shown a clinical response to diet in dogs and
cats with CE within or at 2 weeks of feeding.16-19

INTESTINAL LYMPHANGIECTASIA
PATHOGENESIS

Intestinal lymphangiectasia (IL) may be primary or secondary (ch.
262). Therapeutic strategies involve treatment of any underlying
cause, reduced fat intake, and decrease in intestinal inflammation.

NUTRITIONAL STRATEGIES
Low Fat
Low fat diets are recommended for IL, as they decrease chylomicron
production. In turn, this decreases lymph flow and pressure, and
therefore may prevent lacteal dilation, rupture and leakage. As longchain triglycerides may have proinflammatory effects and may cause
lipogranulomas, decreasing fat intake may be beneficial in IL.
Although glucocorticoids may also be used in IL to decrease
intestinal inflammation, one small retrospective study in Yorkshire
Terriers with IL showed that some dogs could respond satisfactorily
in the short-term to a low fat diet alone.44 In addition, another study
documented that dietary fat restriction could be used as an effective
treatment in dogs with IL that were unresponsive to prednisolone or
experienced a relapse with dosage reduction.45
Although there is no consensus for the definition of low fat,
veterinary nutritionists generally consider <20% fat on a
metabolizable energy basis to be suitably low. Several commercial
therapeutic diets meet this criterion, such as Royal Canin Veterinary
Diet Canine GI Low Fat, Hill’s Prescription Diet Canine i/d Low Fat,
and Purina Pro Plan Veterinary Diets EN Gastroenteric Low Fat
Canine. If an ultra-low fat diet is required, then consultation with a
board-certified veterinary nutritionist is recommended for
formulation of a home-prepared diet.

Medium-Chain Triglycerides
Supplementation with medium-chain triglycerides (MCT) is used in
people with IL, as MCT are directly absorbed into the portal vein.
However, in dogs, MCT are absorbed into the lymphatic system and
therefore may not help to reduce lymph flow.46 In an animal model
of ileitis, MCT modulated intestinal inflammation and caused less

damage than long chain triglycerides47; therefore, their use may help
to reduce inflammation in canine IL.

FEEDING PLAN AND MONITORING
A slow transition to the low fat diet should be performed over 7 to 10
days. If a commercial therapeutic low fat diet does not help to
improve GI signs or biochemical parameters, then an ultra-low fat
home-prepared diet formulated by a board-certified veterinary
nutritionist should be considered. Appetite, activity, body weight,
body condition, muscle condition, GI signs, and serum albumin,
globulin, and cholesterol concentrations should be assessed
regularly.

FELINE CONSTIPATION
PATHOGENESIS
Constipation is a common clinical problem in cats (ch. 263). It can
lead to obstipation, necessitating medical intervention.

NUTRITIONAL STRATEGIES
Dietary recommendations vary depending on the extent of colonic
motility remaining.

High Digestibility
In cats with obstipation, the motility patterns of the large intestine
are completely absent. Therefore, a commercial therapeutic GI diet
with high digestibility (low residue) and high caloric density should
be fed to markedly reduce fecal output. Diets with increased fiber
and supplements containing fiber should be avoided in obstipated
cats; such diets could worsen clinical signs because colonic motility
has been abolished in these cats.

High Fiber (ch. 165)
For those cats presenting with constipation that have some level of
colonic motility remaining, insoluble or a mix of insoluble and
soluble fiber may help to improve their signs. Insoluble fibers
provide fecal bulk, which helps to improve colonic motility by

causing distension of the colon. Soluble fibers are generally
fermentable in the large intestine, resulting in the production of
short-chain fatty acids. Short-chain fatty acids have several beneficial
effects on the colonocytes and colonic motility, as well as increasing
fecal water content. Psyllium is a soluble fiber with low
fermentability that can form a gel when mixed with water. One
uncontrolled trial in cats with constipation showed that a
commercial psyllium-enriched dry diet was able to improve stool
quality and clinical outcome in >80% of cats within a week of
starting the diet.48

FEEDING PLAN AND MONITORING
Cats with obstipation should have cleansing enemas (ch. 108), and
mechanical removal of impacted feces if needed, before dietary
changes are introduced. Cats with constipation should be wellhydrated (ch. 120) before a diet with high fiber is started. Feeding
multiple small meals throughout the day should be encouraged, as
this may help to improve colonic motility and reduce the amount of
ingesta entering the colon each time. A tailored weight loss program
should be considered for overweight cats (ch. 150). Ensuring
adequate hydration following discharge from the hospital is
important.

Chapter 153: Nutritional
Management of Exocrine
Pancreatic Disease
Caroline Mansfield

A C RO N YM S
CCK cholecystokinin
EPI exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
MCT medium-chain triglyceride
RER resting energy requirements
The exocrine pancreas has many physiologic functions, including
aiding in digestion of proteins, fats, and carbohydrates via secretion
of inert zymogen granules into the duodenum that are activated by
enterokinase (ch. 276). In addition, the pancreas secretes
bicarbonate to neutralize gastric contents (chyme) entering the
duodenum, intrinsic factor to promote absorption of vitamin B12 in
the distal small intestine, and bacteriostatic factors. The digestive
functions of the exocrine pancreas are mediated by the autonomic
nervous system, gastrin, cholecystokinin (CCK), secretin, and
vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). The main dietary stimulants for
CCK secretion (which occurs during the intestinal phase of
pancreatic stimulation) in dogs are fatty acids, amino acids and
proteins, whilst in cats they are long-chain triglycerides and intact
proteins. With disease that impacts the exocrine pancreas, nutrition

is considered a cornerstone of management despite a paucity of
targeted research studies in companion animals.

ACUTE PANCREATITIS
The management of acute pancreatitis in both dogs (ch. 277) and
cats (ch. 278) has undergone a paradigm shift in the past 20 years,
mirroring human gastroenterology. Early enteral feeding is now
recognized as the gold standard.1,2 The approach to feeding
hospitalized dogs and cats with assisted nutrition is discussed in ch.
164 (Critical Care Nutrition), ch. 81 (feeding tube placement
techniques), and ch. 146 (Neonatal and Pediatric Nutrition). In
brief, the main goals of nutritional management in acute pancreatitis
are to feed via the gut early, provide only resting energy
requirements [RER] (gradually increasing to reach RER) and to
avoid complications such as aspiration pneumonia. The benefits of
enteral nutrition in acute pancreatitis are multiple, and they include
reduction of intestinal permeability, inflammatory markers,
improved morbidity (reduced hospitalization times and severity
levels), and in some human studies, reduced mortality.1,2 Studies in
dogs and cats have not been extensive enough to show survival
benefits for early enteral nutrition, but they do show that it is well
tolerated and early enteral nutrition is now widely accepted as
standard practice in the management of acute pancreatitis.2-4
Milder cases of acute pancreatitis may not require interventional
enteral nutrition. However, many animals that require
hospitalization are markedly anorectic (and moribund), and so will
require some type of feeding assistance. Forced feeding should be
avoided to prevent development of food aversion. The use of
nasoesophageal, esophageal or in some cases gastric feeding tubes is
preferred, with jejunal feeding considered unnecessary and
associated with a high rate of complications. Guides to calculating
energy requirements (ch. 145) and insertion of feeding tubes (ch.
81) are discussed in these other parts of the textbook. The choice of
food for this period of hospitalization is not well established for dogs
or cats. Some clinicians advocate for use of low-fat diets when
possible (particularly if animals are lipemic during the episode);

however, to date there is no evidence this is necessary, and it is
considered unlikely that additional pancreatic stimulation will occur
with, or be detrimental to, feeding of standard veterinary
convalescent diets during this period. In some severely affected
animals that are unable to tolerate enteral feeding (e.g., due to
bleeding disorder preventing tube insertion), total or partial
parenteral nutrition may be necessary until enteral feeding is
possible (ch. 164).

AT-HOME CARE
In dogs, acute pancreatitis has been associated with ingestion of
table scraps, unusual items, and garbage (ch. 277).5 In addition,
consumption of high-fat/low-protein diets (such as urolith
dissolution diets) and the presence of pre-existing hyperlipidemia
may be associated with development of the disease. In these
instances, avoidance or treatment of the triggering factors may
prevent recurrence of clinical pancreatitis. Following recovery from
the acute episode of pancreatitis, the approach to maintenance
feeding is not well established. It is highly dependent on the
individual animal, whether there is pre-existing/concurrent disease
or hyperlipidemia, and whether there has been a previous episode.
An algorithm for deciding the type of maintenance feeding is shown
in Figure 153.1. Due to the requirement for low-fat diets to be <15%
on a metabolizable energy basis, many raw meat or grain-free diets
are not suitable and so specifically formulated commercial products
should be fed.1 Alternatively, a homemade diet formulated by a
veterinary nutritionist could be used. Careful attention should be
paid to avoid feeding fatty snacks and treats, particularly meat-based
snacks or chews.
In cats, an association between diet and development of acute
pancreatitis is rare (ch. 278). Maintenance dietary therapy is rarely
necessary, but if needed, feeding of highly digestible diets
(“gastrointestinal” therapeutic diets) may be of benefit.

CHRONIC PANCREATITIS

Chronic pancreatitis has several different etiologies and often occurs
with co-morbidities in both dogs (ch. 277) and cats (chs. 225,
278). Diet is less of an inciting factor for chronic pancreatitis than
acute pancreatitis in both dogs and cats, although hyperlipidemia
may be a contributing factor in both species (ch. 156). Often,
nutritional management of those co-morbidities will take priority
over specific nutritional management of pancreatitis. If specific
nutritional management of chronic pancreatitis is considered
necessary, then feeding of a low-fat diet is generally considered the
best initial option. However, each individual animal’s nutritional
requirements and dietary history need to be carefully evaluated.
Supportive treatment such as appetite stimulants or anti-emetics
may be required to assist animals to eat voluntarily (ch. 17).

transitioning to a maintenance diet following
hospitalization for acute pancreatitis in dogs. For the

determine on a % ME basis). ME, Metabolizable

EXOCRINE PANCREATIC
INSUFFICIENCY (EPI)
Dogs with EPI typically have poor body condition as well as
steatorrhea and polyphagia (ch. 279). The main goal of treatment is
to achieve an increase in body condition score, rather than resolution
of all clinical signs.6 This is generally achieved by supplementation
with exogenous pancreatic enzymes, rather than with diet. There has
been little experimental or clinical evidence to support the use of one
type of diet over another in the management of EPI, and
retrospective studies show highly individualized responses.6,7

Correction of micronutrient deficiencies, particularly cobalamin and
fat-soluble vitamins, is essential to optimize clinical outcome.
Experimentally, results of different dietary fat contents for
treatment of EPI are highly variable. In some, severe fat restriction
may worsen lipase activity (thereby reducing fat assimilation) or
conversely improve fat assimilation, whereas in other studies fat
supplementation will increase fat absorption.7 In one study assessing
the efficacy of hydrolyzed diets (which had a 34% fat content), dogs
had a positive response. Although this may be due to concurrent
inflammatory enteropathy, it highlights the fact that fat content does
not need to be restricted.8 Another nutritional intervention that has
been studied is supplementation with medium chain triglycerides
(MCTs), as MCTs are thought to be absorbed via the portal
circulation (instead of lymphatic vessels; ch. 152). However,
palatability issues arise with MCT supplementation and no clinical
advantage has been detected in managing EPI, so currently no
supplementation is considered necessary.6 A flow-plan for
approaching diet management in dogs with EPI is shown in Figure
153.2, highlighting the individual nature of the disease. Cats with
EPI are less studied than are dogs, as the condition is rare in cats;
however, the dietary approach is similar.

Chapter 154: Nutritional
Management of
Hepatobiliary Diseases
Vincent C. Biourge

A C RO N YM S
AA amino acid
BCAA branched-chain amino acids
dw dry weight
FHL feline hepatic lipidosis
HE hepatic encephalopathy
PSS portosystemic shunt
Being at the junction between the portal and systemic venous
circulation, the liver plays a major role in the digestion, metabolism,
and storage of most nutrients.1,2 Decompensated liver function will
therefore be associated with malnutrition and major metabolic
abnormalities.2,3 Fortunately the liver has tremendous functional
reserves and an amazing capacity to regenerate.1,2 In human and
veterinary medicine, nutrition is a key factor in the management of
patients with hepatic disease.2,4,5 This is especially true in feline
hepatic lipidosis, copper storage disease, and portosystemic shunts
(PSSs).3,6-8

GENERAL NUTRITIONAL
CONSIDERATIONS IN PATIENTS WITH
LIVER DISEASE
The objectives of the dietary management of liver disease are to
correct and/or prevent malnutrition, to minimize hepatic
parenchymal damage, and to support hepatocellular regeneration, as
well as to prevent or minimize complications associated with liver
dysfunction.2,3,5 Severe weight loss (ch. 18), muscle wasting (ch.
151), and hypoalbuminemia (ch. 60), which are all markers of
malnutrition, have been described in dogs and cats with liver
disease.2,3 They are associated with anorexia (ch. 17), nausea, and
vomiting (ch. 48) in addition to impaired nutrient digestion and
absorption. Patients with liver disease should therefore be assessed
for malnutrition (ch. 145).
Although there are many forms of liver diseases (chs. 267-275),
veterinary therapeutic liver diets are formulated similarly, with low
levels of protein and copper and high levels of fat.9 Hepatic diets
mainly have been designed for the management of hepatic
encephalopathy (HE) and copper toxicosis. Therefore, although they
are compatible with other forms of liver disease, different nutritional
profiles might better fulfill the dietary requirements of patients with
other liver ailments.
To fulfill its role and benefit the patient, the diet must be eaten.
Poor intake and anorexia are common in patients suffering from
hepatic diseases. Nausea and vomiting are complicating factors as
they induce food aversion. Patients refusing to eat and at risk of
malnutrition should be tube fed (chs. 81 and 164). In cats with
hepatic lipidosis (ch. 274), this is the only treatment.2,3

ENERGY REQUIREMENTS
The diet must provide enough calories to maintain energy balance
and minimize protein catabolism. In common with many diseases of
pets, energy requirements have not been established for patients
with hepatobiliary diseases. When patients have little or no activity,

as when they are hospitalized, it is recommended to provide the daily
resting energy requirement of 70 kcal/kg0.75 for both dogs and cats
(chs. 145 and 164). With normal levels of activity, the recommended
daily energy allowance is 95-110 kcal/kg0.75 for dogs and 50-60
kcal/kg for cats.10 Initially the goal is to maintain weight, and in
patients with poor intake and anorexia, energy allowance should be
increased very gradually (e.g., from 25-50% to 75-100% of the
calories) over 4-7 days to let the digestive tract and the animal’s
metabolism adapt to the diet.3
It is now well established that patients with hepatobiliary diseases
digest and assimilate high levels of lipids in their diets (30-50% of
their calories as fat).3,6,7 Dietary fat not only increases the energy
density of the diet, it is also an important palatability factor.
Moreover, with low or no food intake and with weight loss, the
animal’s metabolism is geared towards lipid oxidation as a source of
energy, thus facilitating adaptation to a high-fat diet.11,12
In contrast, glucose intolerance is common in anorexic patients,
especially cats, as fasting depresses glucose metabolism and insulin
secretion.12 On refeeding, primarily with tube feeding, carbohydrate
should represent <45% of calories for dogs and <35% for cats,
especially simple sugars such as those found in clinical liquid diets.
Most human liquid diets have levels above these and should be
avoided. The liver plays an important role in glucose homeostasis by
storing and releasing glucose, and it is responsible for
gluconeogenesis.2 Because of its large functional reserves, the
hepatic parenchyma can cope until late in the disease process, but in
order to avoid overwhelming the remaining hepatocytes at later
disease stages, it is indicated to divide daily food intake into three or
more meals.

PROTEIN
Adequate protein and calorie intakes are essential to maintain
nitrogen balance and promote liver regeneration. Protein
requirements of patients with hepatic disease have not been

determined.2,5 It is generally accepted that they are at least as high
as those of healthy individuals.2,5
Commercially available hepatic therapeutic diets have been
formulated with levels of proteins close to or slightly above those
found in renal diets (dogs, 35-45 g/Mcal; cats, 60-70 g/Mcal). Those
levels are often considered to be low, but they are well above the
National Research Council Recommended Allowance for adult dogs
(25 g/Mcal) and cats (50 g/Mcal).10 Some of those diets have been
fed for prolonged periods to Labrador Retrievers with copper storage
disease, as well as to dogs with PSS, with no sign of protein
deficiency such as poor haircoat, muscle wasting and
hypoalbuminemia.6-8,13 HE associated with PSS and end-stage liver
failure is the main driver for protein restriction. It is this author’s
recommendation to feed such patients hepatic diets and, if indicated,
progressively increase protein content to moderate levels (dog 50-55
g/Mcal and cats 70-75 g/Mcal) whilst monitoring for signs of
intolerance. Those moderate levels should also be considered from
the outset in patients with PSS that are not suffering from HE.14
Most other patients with liver disease will tolerate levels up to 55-65
g/Mcal in dogs and 75-110 g/Mcal in cats. Feeding protein in excess
of requirements might be counterproductive, however. Excess amino
acids (AAs) will be catabolized to produce energy, and the liver is the
only organ involved in AA catabolism and the detoxification of its
main by-product, ammonia, into urea.2
Higher levels of protein can be achieved by prescribing diets with
sources of highly digestible proteins such as hydrolyzed proteinbased diets, low-residue/intestinal diets, or recovery diets.
Homemade recipes formulated by a veterinary nutritionist will also
fulfill those needs. In cats with hepatic lipidosis, a high-protein
recovery diet (>80 g/Mcal) is a must (see below).3
Tolerance to protein is greatly affected by its source. Earlier
studies in canine models of PSS found that dogs fed a commercial,
animal protein-based pet food showed severe clinical signs and
survived only a few months, whereas those fed a soy isolate- (purified
soy protein-) based diet did not show clinical signs during a 1-year
follow-up.15,16 A commercial soy isolate-based diet was associated

with lower plasma ammonia concentrations than an animal proteinbased one with similar nutritional composition in dogs with PSS.7 In
both humans and dogs, proteins such as soy isolate and casein have
been recommended for patients with liver disease. Their very high
digestibility, which minimizes protein colonic fermentation; their
low content of non-protein nitrogen (nucleotides, bioamines, etc.);
and their fiber content (soy), would explain in part those benefits.3
New sources of highly digestible proteins low in non-protein
nitrogen, such as wheat gluten and highly hydrolyzed animal
proteins, could similarly benefit patients with liver disease.
Patients with liver disease show a decrease in plasma
concentrations of branched-chain AAs (BCAA) and an increase in
aromatic AAs.17 It has been suggested that correcting the BCAA:AA
ratio could affect clinical signs of HE. Studies in humans and animal
models have not supported this hypothesis.2

DIETARY FIBERS (ch. 165)
Dietary fibers are the part of plant materials that cannot be digested
by intestinal enzymes. They are usually divided into two families.10
The insoluble fibers, mostly cellulose and hemicellulose, are poorly
fermentable. By increasing the bulk of the intestinal content, they
promote transit and the turnover of colonic content. Soluble fibers,
such as beta-glucans, pectins, gums, and resistant starches, are
highly fermentable. They will alter the microbiota, trap ammonia in
the colon, and enhance fecal nitrogen elimination.10,18 Like
lactulose, they promote chyme acidification and reduce enteric
ammonia production.3,18 Although it has not been proven, all of
these properties mean that moderate amounts (15-30 g/Mcal) of
total dietary fibers (insoluble and soluble) could be beneficial in
managing patients with liver disease, especially patients with HE.

MINERALS AND TRACE ELEMENTS

Requirements for most minerals and trace elements in patients with
liver disease have not been established; therefore, it is assumed that
they are at least those of healthy dogs or cats.10 Sodium restriction
(0.15-0.2 g Na/Mcal) has been recommended in patients with ascites
and portal hypertension. These represent a small fraction of patients
with liver disease, but this level of restriction will fulfill the dietary
requirements of healthy and affected animals alike. Hypokalemia is
common in liver disease,2 secondary to inadequate intake, vomiting,
and diarrhea. If the diet fails to maintain normokalemia, potassium
should be supplemented in the diet or given with fluids.
Dietary copper is a very important nutrient in the management of
patients with liver disease, especially copper-associated hepatitis (see
below). Zinc deficiency is prevalent in humans with liver disease and
inadequate intake will promote deficiency.19 Zinc interferes with
copper absorption and is supplemented in hepatic diets for this
reason (see below). Manganese concentrations are elevated in the
blood and brain of humans with advanced liver disease and PSS.14
Brain lesions and clinical signs compatible with HE have been
associated with manganese accumulation in the brain.14 Similar
observations have been made in the dog.20 Further research is
warranted to determine a dietary manganese recommendation for
dogs with PSS.

VITAMINS
Vitamin deficiencies are common in patients with liver disease. This
is explained by poor intake, malabsorption, reduced storage, and
metabolic defects.2 Vitamin B deficiencies are assumed to be present
in dogs and cats.3,18 As vitamin B requirements are linked to energy
intake, it is especially important to provide them upon refeeding and
it has been suggested that liver diets should provide at least twice the
healthy requirements.3,18 Vitamin C is produced from glucose in the
liver of dogs and cats10 and has been found in lower levels than
normal in dogs with hepatic insufficiency.16 Therefore, vitamin C

supplementation is recommended in liver diets. Vitamin K stores can
be rapidly depleted with depressed intake and microbiome
disruption.3,18 If bleeding times are prolonged, parenteral
administration of vitamin K1 (0.5-1 mg/kg SQ) is recommended.

ANTIOXIDANTS
Inflammation as well as copper and iron accumulation induce the
release of large amounts of free radicals.9 Vitamin E, which is
membrane-bound, and vitamin C, which is present in the cytoplasm,
fight those reactive compounds synergistically and should be present
in the diet at levels well above requirements.18
The antioxidant system also includes glutathione and enzymes that
require trace elements (manganese, zinc, selenium, and copper).
Their requirements are fulfilled with a complete and balanced diet.10
Finally, taurine, carotenoids, and flavanols are naturally occurring
compounds that can contribute to the antioxidant system and can be
added to the diet.
S-adenosylmethionine—a precursor of glutathione—and silymarin
have antioxidant properties and have been recommended in the
management of liver disease.5 They are available as dietary
supplements.

NUTRITIONAL MANAGEMENT OF
FELINE HEPATIC LIPIDOSIS
Nutritional support is the primary consideration in the management
of feline hepatic lipidosis (FHL; ch. 274).3 The prognosis is directly
related to the ability of the clinician to intensively meet the patient’s
energy and nutrients requirements via tube feeding. Many diets have
been used successfully in FHL. Their specific characteristics are to be
highly digestible, and high in fat (>50 g/Mcal) and protein (>80
g/Mcal), in addition to being complete and balanced feline diets. The
choice of the diet will depend on the feeding tube chosen (ch. 81).

Nasogastric tubes will require liquid diets. The larger bore
esophageal and gastric tubes will allow slurry to pass through. Cats
with FHL are likely to have fasted for several weeks before
presentation.21 Therefore, food should be reintroduced very
progressively over 4-7 days. The goal is to feed 70 × kg0.75 kcal/day at
the end of this period. These cats often look worse during the first
week of tube feeding than at presentation, and clinicians should not
get discouraged too early. Tube feeding is the only treatment that will
reverse hepatic lipidosis and those cats must be fed.3

NUTRITIONAL MANAGEMENT OF
COPPER-ASSOCIATED HEPATITIS
Hepatic copper accumulation resulting from a hereditary defect of its
biliary excretion has been demonstrated in several canine breeds
(ch. 270). Differences exist in causal genes and inheritance
patterns.22 Cirrhosis is also a common cause of hepatic copper
accumulation in dogs but to a lesser degree, while cholestasis would
be a minor factor.9 A third cause would be excessive intake of
bioavailable copper.9 The National Research Council and the
Association of American Feed Control Officials do not report a safe
upper limit for copper, owing to a lack of data. More research is
necessary to assess safe intake.9,10 It is likely to be breed- and
animal-dependent. In this author’s experience, some dogs with
hereditary copper storage disease will accumulate hepatic copper
when fed a diet with 1.3 mg Cu/Mcal,8 whereas colony dogs fed
lifelong up to 10 mg Cu/Mcal have not shown any clinical signs of
liver disease.
Aside from the general nutritional considerations described above,
the dietary management of copper hepatitis consists of feeding a diet
low in copper and supplemented with zinc.9,22 Zinc reduces copper
absorption by stimulating the synthesis of metallothionein in
enterocytes.6 It also has benefits with respect to membrane
stabilization, free radical scavenging, and fibrosis.18 In a study of

affected Labrador Retrievers, 1.2 mg Cu and 25.5 mg Zn/Mcal
reduced hepatic copper below the normal threshold (400 mg/kg dry
weight [dw]) in most dogs.6 Addition of 200-250 mg Zn twice daily
before meals (14-18 times the amounts found in the daily food
ration) failed to show any benefit.6 A level of around 1.2 mg/Mcal Cu
means that dietary copper is only coming from the raw materials and
that no copper salt (e.g., copper sulfate) has been added to the recipe.
Because of these complexities, if an owner elects to feed a homemade
diet, it is highly recommended that they request the help of a
veterinary nutritionist.
In a patient with a hepatic copper concentration <800 mg/kg dw,
a low copper diet alone will restore normal copper levels.8 For
concentrations higher than this, a combination of a copper chelator
and low-copper diet is indicated.22 Affected dogs do not all respond
similarly,8 but a low-copper diet is still beneficial as it can delay
treatment with D-penicillamine, which can cause significant sideeffects.8
There is evidence of a lesser degree of copper accumulation in
patients with chronic inflammatory liver diseases, and a reduction of
copper and increase of zinc intake are also recommended for them.9
Information concerning hepatic copper accumulation in cats and its
management is scarce, but it suggests that copper restriction could
be beneficial.23
In conclusion, nutrition is a significant part of the management of
dogs and cats with hepatobiliary diseases. Diets must be adapted to
the type and degree of liver disease and the response of the patient.
Tube feeding must be considered when dietary intake is too low, and
in cases of FHL.

Chapter 155: Nutritional
Management of Endocrine
and Metabolic Diseases
Jennifer A. Larsen

A C RO N YM S

DM diabetes mellitus

T3 triiodothyronine
T4 thyroxine
TDF total dietary fiber

Successful management of many endocrine diseases may be
facilitated with appropriate nutritional strategies. Most important is
diabetes mellitus (DM; chs. 291 and 292) and, to a lesser extent,
feline hyperthyroidism (ch. 287). Hypothyroidism (chs. 285 and
286) and hyperadrenocorticism (chs. 293 and 294), while treated
medically, often require consideration of nutritional management for
appetite control, weight loss, and controlling secondary
hyperlipidemia (ch. 156).

NUTRITIONAL MANAGEMENT OF
DIABETES MELLITUS (DM)
OVERVIEW
Nutritional management of DM in both dogs and cats includes
consideration of dietary factors such as fat and fiber content, energy
density, and palatability, as well as addressing any concurrent
disease. Concurrent or historical pancreatitis should be considered,
especially in dogs (ch. 277). In both species, identifying and
addressing potential underlying causes of insulin resistance,
especially obesity (ch. 150), is critical. The goal of nutritional
therapy for DM is to help improve glycemic control in conjunction
with insulin therapy and management of other medical problems or
other individual factors. Consideration of the individualized
nutritional assessment (body weight, body condition score [ch. 72],
appetite, diet history, etc.) is warranted in order to implement a
customized and effective nutritional management plan (ch. 145).

NUTRITIONAL BACKGROUND FOR
DOGS WITH DM
The insulin requirement in dogs with DM (ch. 291) is largely
determined by dietary factors such as meal timing, meal size, and the
rate of glucose absorption from the intestine. Consistent timing is an
important aspect of the feeding schedule. Ideally, the same amount
of the same diet is fed at the same time every day. Two smaller
meals, coordinated with twice-a-day insulin injections, are preferable
to one large daily meal, to minimize wide fluctuations in blood
glucose. A minority of dogs with DM may prefer consuming food in
small amounts throughout the day. In these pets, consumption of a
significant portion of the daily energy requirement (up to 50%) at the
time of insulin administration should be encouraged, to provide
adequate concentrations of glucose for the administered insulin. Diet
palatability is important to ensure adequate and consistent intake of
energy and other essential nutrients.

NUTRITIONAL BACKGROUND FOR
CATS WITH DM
Unlike dogs, cats with DM (ch. 292) do not appear to require strict
control of meals, perhaps due to their longer gastric emptying times
and absorption of dietary carbohydrates.1,2 For example, diets
containing various starch sources at concentrations similar to those
found in commercially available feline diets (∼35% dry matter) had
only a minor impact on postprandial glucose and insulin responses
in healthy cats; maximum plasma glucose concentrations were 68-93
mg/dL (3.8-5.2 mmol/L) several hours after eating.3 The largest
differences between dogs and cats in response to feeding were noted
with diets containing cornstarch, where peak blood glucose
concentration for dogs was 92 mg/dL (5.1 mmol/L) 15 minutes after
eating, while cats reached a similar peak value of 93 mg/dL (5.2
mmol/L) after 7.2 hours.3,4 These findings are consistent with data
demonstrating that feline glycemic responses to commercial dry
diets are not only prolonged (intestinal absorption occurred over 1012 hours), but are also not associated with dietary carbohydrate
concentration or carbohydrate digestibility.5

CONTROLLING POSTPRANDIAL
HYPERGLYCEMIA IN DIABETIC DOGS
AND CATS
Introduction
Diet composition characteristics, such as increased fiber and the use
of lower amounts of carbohydrate, can reduce the magnitude of
postprandial hyperglycemia in dogs and cats with DM. Both factors
probably contribute to the lower “glycemic index” of some foods,
with those higher in fiber and/or lower in starch having lower
glycemic indices. Other strategies to prolong gastric emptying time,
such as increased amounts of fat, might be contraindicated in DM
due to obesity or to abnormal lipid metabolism and resultant dietary
fat intolerance (e.g., pancreatitis or hyperlipidemia).

Dietary Fiber
Fiber is not considered nutritionally essential for dogs or cats, but
can be used to achieve satisfactory and consistent stool quality,
promote satiety, decrease energy density of food, achieve a prebiotic
effect (e.g., fermentation by the intestinal microbiota to produce
short-chain fatty acids), or to modulate gastric emptying and
nutrient absorption (ch. 165).
Various methodologies are utilized to quantitate different fiber
fractions within food. Currently, the quantity of crude fiber (CF) is
the standard for reporting fiber content of pet foods. This method
quantifies some (cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin), but not all
insoluble fiber, and soluble fiber is not assessed. In contrast, the total
dietary fiber (TDF) method simulates enzymatic digestion within the
gastrointestinal (GI) tract, captures more insoluble fiber than the CF
method, and allows for quantification of soluble plus insoluble fiber.
Since CF is a poor measure of the true fiber concentration in
commercial pet foods, there are significant challenges in comparing
products based on fiber type and concentration, and both energy
content and carbohydrate concentration may be significantly
overestimated.6-8
There are few data describing the impact of dietary fiber on
managing feline DM. One randomized crossover study investigating
the role of insoluble fiber in the treatment of DM in cats
demonstrated improved glycemic control in 12/16 consuming a diet
high in fiber (61 g TDF/Mcal) and in 4/16 cats who consumed a diet
low in fiber (11 g TDF/Mcal) but higher in starch.9 Another study
assessing the efficacy of glipizide included unequal groups of cats
consuming commercial diets that varied in fiber content (16 fed a
high-fiber diet and 4 a low-fiber diet); cats eating each diet
responded to the treatment but the response rate could not be
compared due to the study design.10 The optimal concentration and
type of dietary fiber for nutritional management of cats with DM
remains unknown.
Insoluble fiber, in particular, appears to be beneficial in dogs with
DM, although soluble fiber may have a role as well. One study
showed lower mean 24-hour and postprandial blood glucose
concentrations when dogs were fed a high fiber diet (mostly

insoluble; 56 g TDF/Mcal) compared to baseline values.11 There is
evidence that diets high in insoluble fiber (73 g TDF/Mcal), when
compared to high-soluble-fiber (56 g TDF/Mcal) diets, are beneficial
in managing canine DM, being associated with lower mean glucose
concentrations, lower maximum blood glucose concentrations and
lower areas under the blood glucose curve.12 However, when fiber
types were compared in feeding studies of dogs with experimental
DM, diets high in either insoluble (cellulose; 70 g TDF/Mcal) or
soluble fiber (pectin; 55 g TDF/Mcal) resulted in lower blood glucose
concentrations when compared with a lower fiber diet (24 g
TDF/Mcal). There was no difference between groups fed the high
fiber diets.13 With regard to the efficacy of moderate fiber
concentrations, no benefit for dogs with DM was noted with diets
containing 18-20 g TDF/Mcal when compared with modestly-low
fiber diets containing 14 g TDF/Mcal (mostly insoluble).14 In
summary, if a higher fiber strategy is desired, it appears that the
concentration should exceed 55 g TDF/Mcal from an insoluble or
mixed fiber source to provide a beneficial effect.

FELINE DIABETES MELLITUS
Background
There is little scientific evidence to support the promotion of specific
dietary strategies for cats with DM (ch. 292). Almost all diets used
in studies of cats with DM had carbohydrate and fiber content
determined based on inaccurate calculations using CF, which would
overestimate carbohydrate content.7 Further, no studies comparing
diets for cats with DM have controlled for ingredients, fiber type,
fiber concentration, carbohydrate source, or for other
macronutrients (fat and protein). As such, these studies do not
provide definitive information on the effect of any particular nutrient
on managing feline DM. Of course, dietary factors other than
carbohydrate concentration and source have a role in treating cats
with DM, including fiber; as such, a focus on only one dietary aspect
is inappropriate.

Carbohydrate
Definitions of what constitutes a “low carbohydrate” diet are
subjective, and in the absence of data from cats with DM fed
controlled diets with graded concentrations of carbohydrate,
information to guide determinations of the optimal amounts is also
lacking. In addition, the inaccurate calculation of carbohydrate
concentrations using CF values may result in needless and incorrect
elimination of potentially beneficial dietary options.7 Feline diets
marketed as “low carbohydrate” tend to be high in fat and have high
energy density, which is not ideal for overweight cats with DM. This
may be somewhat ameliorated by the use of higher moisture
(canned) diets due to the higher volume that can be fed.

Diet Comparisons
Limited data examining the effect of diet on the control of naturallyoccurring DM in cats have been published. To our knowledge, only
four studies have investigated comparisons of two or more diets in
cats with DM, and each one reported improvement or remission of
DM for more than one dietary group.9,10,15,16 Two of these studies
demonstrated that most cats benefited from consuming a higherfiber diet, although statistical analysis of response rates was not
possible in one study.9,10 A third study found improvement when the
cats were fed a lower carbohydrate, lower fiber, higher fat diet.15 The
fourth study found no difference in improvement rates between DM
cats fed lower carbohydrate diets and those fed “maintenance” diets;
this study also reported a median body weight gain in both diet
groups.16 Overall, it appears that improvement or resolution of the
diabetic state may be more likely in cats who were obese and who
lost body fat, regardless of diet. Further investigation into why some
cats achieve remission while some do not, regardless of diet, is
necessary to understand the underlying physiology and identify
potential targets for dietary and medical therapy.

AN INDIVIDUALIZED APPROACH TO
NUTRITIONAL MANAGEMENT OF
DIABETES MELLITUS (DM)
For both dogs and cats, appropriate dietary management of DM
depends, in part, on individual factors: comorbidities, body weight,
body and muscle condition score, weight trends, diet palatability,
food acceptance, exercise, and treats. Due to the positive effects of
energy restriction and maintenance of a lean body condition on
insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance, lean body condition should
be a goal for every patient (chs. 72, 291, 292). Diets that are highly
energy dense and high in fat are not appropriate for achieving a lean
condition in an overweight pet. Conversely, a lower-energy-density,
high fiber diet is not ideal for a thin diabetic. However, in the
absence of the need to address concurrent issues, a diet change may
not be necessary if the meal schedule is appropriate and the diet
balanced. The optimal approach to feeding dogs and cats with DM
should be customized to the individual.

NUTRITIONAL MANAGEMENT OF
INSULINOMA
OVERVIEW
Insulinoma is a tumor that commonly causes clinical signs
attributable to hypoglycemia, including seizures (Video 61.3),
collapse, and weakness (Videos 61.1, 61.2) among others (chs. 61,
289). Although clinical trials assessing the efficacy of dietary
modification on signs, prognosis, and other outcomes in dogs with
insulinoma have not been reported, nutritional strategies can be
successfully employed for varying time periods. The goals of
nutritional management of dogs with insulinoma include avoidance
of prolonged periods of fasting and minimizing large variations in
blood glucose concentrations. Feeding management strategies and
specific dietary profiles may help achieve these goals through

modifying peripheral, hepatic, and normal pancreatic metabolism of
nutrients.

FEEDING MANAGEMENT AND
NUTRITIONAL PROFILE
Dietary factors such as meal timing, meal size, and meal frequency
are important to ensure a steady and low to moderate absorption of
glucose from the intestine. Feeding several small meals each day,
including a last one at bedtime, is indicated. In addition, controlling
the amount of digestible carbohydrate (sugars and starches) will
contribute to this effect. Dietary simple sugars may stimulate
secretion of profound amounts of tumor-derived insulin and must be
avoided.
Moderate fat and protein intake (20-35% of dietary energy for
each macronutrient) will help slow stomach emptying and GI transit,
but attention to the dietary energy density as well as the total daily
amount fed is indicated to prevent unwanted weight gain secondary
to the anabolic effect of hyperinsulinemia. Fiber, especially soluble
fiber, also slows GI transit and promotes a more viscous chyme from
which absorption of glucose is slowed or reduced. Veterinary
therapeutic diets formulated for canine DM incorporate many of
these strategies and remain a good option for dogs with insulinoma.

NUTRITIONAL MANAGEMENT OF
FELINE HYPERTHYROIDISM
Thyroid hormone is integral for growth, development, and
metabolism (chs. 287, 288). Selenium and iodine are among the
nutrients required for normal thyroid function. Selenoproteins such
as type I iodothyronine 5′-deiodinase, which converts T4 (thyroxine)
to T3 (triiodothyronine), are impacted by the dietary supply of
selenium. As in other mammals, cats fed diets low in selenium have
increased circulating T4 and decreased T3 concentrations, as well as
low serum concentrations of selenium and glutathione peroxidase

(another selenoprotein).17 Despite the variability in selenium
concentrations in pet foods, deficiencies in cats consuming
commercial food are either rare or not recognized.18 Likewise,
selenium toxicosis is not described, and studies have shown that cats
appear to increase urinary excretion in order to regulate selenium
homeostasis at high intakes.19,20
Iodine is necessary for synthesis of thyroid hormones T3 and T4.
Like selenium, the concentration of iodine in pet foods is highly
variable.21-23 There has been speculation that variability and/or
extremes in iodine intake may contribute to the pathogenesis of
hyperthyroidism (ch. 287). One report found that serum free T4
concentrations in 10 cats were not affected by chronic and stable
intake of high or low (21 vs. 0.11 mg/kg dry matter) iodinecontaining diets over a period of 5 months.24 However, alternating
intake levels every 2 weeks over a 12-week period in 2 groups of 8
cats resulted in a significant inverse relationship between iodine
intake and serum free T4 concentration.25
Reduction in iodine intake has been a target for dietary
modifications aimed at controlling hyperthyroidism in cats, as
dietary deficiency in other species reliably results in hypothyroidism.
There are limited data on the effect of iodine deficiency in cats. One
study reported thyroid gland hyperplasia but lack of other clinical
abnormalities in kittens fed a diet low in iodine for several weeks
(0.45 mg/kg dry matter).26 Another study showed no clinical signs of
deficiency nor any impact on thyroid hormone concentrations
despite achieving a negative iodine balance in adult cats over a
period of 9 months (0.46 mg/kg dry matter).27 The dietary iodine
requirement for hyperthyroid cats is unknown; however, low-iodine
diets have been explored as a strategy to reduce the synthesis of
thyroid hormone in hyperthyroid cats. There are data supporting
successful use of dietary iodine restriction as a treatment for cats
with hyperthyroidism, mostly using the wet and dry formulas of an
iodine-restricted (0.2 mg/kg dry matter) veterinary therapeutic diet
formulated for this purpose. Although not all studies are controlled,
masked, or prospective, in aggregate the evidence supports that most

cats will achieve euthyroidism without negative health outcomes.2831

While definitive treatment of hyperthyroidism with radioactive
iodine therapy or surgical thyroidectomy is still preferred, dietary
therapy is an alternative for cats who are not suitable candidates for
those procedures. Dietary therapy is also an alternative when use of
antithyroid medication is not an option. Due to the need for strict
and consistent control of the amount of dietary iodine consumed,
issues potentially impacting compliance should be considered.
Iodine intake from treats, access to other foods, hunting, and some
supplements must be avoided. Therefore, dietary therapy may work
best for indoor-only, single cat households or for owners who can
control intake of individual cats in multi-cat homes.
