CLIENT INFORMATION
Nutritional Management of Diabetes Mellitus
Diabetes mellitus (DM) is an endocrine (hormonal) disorder
characterized by absolute or relative lack of insulin. In dogs, genetic
as well as environmental influences have been implicated. The
primary cause of DM may include pancreatitis, pancreatic islet
hypoplasia (loss of pancreatic cells for making insulin), and
degeneration of pancreatic tissue, leading to insulin dependence.
Remission, meaning the spontaneous disappearance of diabetes, is
uncommon. In cats, type 2 DM appears to be more common, which
generally requires treatment with insulin. Regardless, identifying
and addressing potential underlying causes of insulin resistance,
especially obesity, remains essential in cats, and remission is
possible.
Individualized treatment and care of dogs and cats with DM is
ideal in order to meet their specific needs. If weight loss is needed,
that should be pursued using a veterinary therapeutic diet
formulated for treatment of obesity. This will help ensure that all

essential nutrients are still provided in adequate concentrations even
when calories are restricted. Achieving an ideal body weight is
important to help promote good regulation or even remission (in the
case of cats); additionally, many chronic diseases are improved or
even prevented by avoiding excess body weight. Likewise, addressing
any other diseases your pet may have is also important. Some dogs
with DM have had pancreatitis, for example, in which case a low-fat
diet is important. While diet can play an important role in the
treatment of DM, a change in diet may not be necessary if your dog
or cat with DM is otherwise healthy and is of an ideal body weight,
depending on the current diet. In some cases, your pet’s DM may be
easier to treat long-term with a high fiber diet. Speak to your
veterinarian regarding your pet’s current diet and whether a switch
might benefit your pet specifically.
Jennifer A. Larsen (Davis, California)

Chapter 156: Nutritional and
Medical Considerations in
Hyperlipidemia
Panagiotis G. Xenoulis, and Jürgen Zentek

A C RO N YM S
5-ALA 5-aminolevulinic acid
LDL low-density lipoprotein
LPL lipoprotein lipase
VLDL very-low-density lipoprotein

INTRODUCTION
Hyperlipidemia is a common condition in dogs but is less common in
cats. In contrast to human beings, hyperlipidemia traditionally has
been considered a fairly benign condition in cats and dogs, and
clinical experience with and research regarding hyperlipidemia has
been limited in these species. In the last decade, several studies in
both humans and dogs have associated specific forms of
hyperlipidemia with a much wider range of diseases than previously
thought. Therefore, canine hyperlipidemia is emerging as an
important clinical condition that requires a systematic diagnostic
approach and appropriate treatment. In cats, disorders of lipid
metabolism are considered less common than in dogs and the related

bibliography is sparse. Therefore, the clinical importance of
hyperlipidemia is largely unknown in this species.

CAUSES OF HYPERLIPIDEMIA
SECONDARY HYPERLIPIDEMIA
A list of the most important causes of canine and feline
hyperlipidemia is shown in Chapter 63 (Table 63.1). Postprandial
hyperlipidemia is physiologic and it typically resolves within 7-12
hours after a meal. Therefore, determination of serum lipid
concentrations should always follow a fast of at least 12 hours,
although evidence in dogs suggests that food might need to be
withheld >12 hours when assessing fasting concentrations of serum
triglycerides.1
Persistent fasting hyperlipidemia can be either primary (typically
due to an inborn inherited error in lipid metabolism) or secondary to
other diseases or drug administration. Secondary hyperlipidemia is
the most common form of hyperlipidemia in dogs and cats. Most
often, secondary canine hyperlipidemia (hypertriglyceridemia
and/or hypercholesterolemia) is the result of an endocrine disorder,
such as hypothyroidism (ch. 285), diabetes mellitus (ch. 291), or
hyperadrenocorticism (ch. 293).2-9 In cats, secondary
hyperlipidemia is also often the result of an endocrine disorder,
diabetes mellitus being the most common and important (ch.
292).10,11
Although the pathogenesis is multifactorial, hypoinsulinemia likely
plays an important role, as it leads to decreased lipoprotein lipase
(LPL) activity and increased activity of the hormone-sensitive lipase.
In turn, this leads to accumulation of chylomicrons and very-lowdensity lipoproteins (VLDLs) in the circulation. Hyperlipidemia may
resolve with successful management of diabetes but it may persist
despite treatment. Hypothyroidism and hyperadrenocorticism are
also commonly associated with hyperlipidemia, especially in dogs.
Thyroid hormone deficiency in hypothyroidism and cortisol excess in
hyperadrenocorticism lead to decreased LPL and increased
hormone-sensitive lipase activity, which lead to
hypercholesterolemia and/or hypertriglyceridemia. Hyperlipidemia

typically resolves with successful management of the primary
disorder, although it may persist despite treatment, especially with
hyperadrenocorticism.
Hyperlipidemia (hypertriglyceridemia and/or
hypercholesterolemia) has also been associated with naturally
occurring pancreatitis in dogs (ch. 277).2,3,12,13 However, data from
experimental studies suggest that hyperlipidemia is not a feature of
experimentally induced pancreatitis in dogs.14-16 In addition, results
of a recent study in dogs with naturally occurring pancreatitis
indicate that when concurrent diseases (e.g., diabetes mellitus,
hypothyroidism) and the use of certain drugs that can cause
hyperlipidemia are excluded, hypertriglyceridemia and
hypercholesterolemia occur infrequently (18% and 24%,
respectively) as a possible result of pancreatitis and are typically
mild.17 Therefore, fasting hyperlipidemia (especially when severe) in
dogs with pancreatitis likely reflects concurrent primary
hyperlipidemia or hyperlipidemia secondary to other causes (e.g., an
endocrine disease), and warrants further diagnostic investigation. No
association between hyperlipidemia and pancreatitis has been
confidently identified in cats (ch. 278). Experimentally induced
pancreatitis led to hypercholesterolemia in cats18 but convincing
clinical evidence is lacking.
Another important cause of secondary hyperlipidemia in dogs and
cats is obesity (ch. 150).19-21 In one study, obese cats had increased
plasma concentrations of triglycerides and non-esterified fatty acids
compared to lean cats.22 Increased plasma triglycerides were the
result of dramatic increases (500% on average) in VLDL
triglycerides.22 The mechanism by which obese animals accumulate
triglycerides in their VLDL molecules is likely related to decreases in
LPL activity, which has been demonstrated in recent studies.
Other possible causes of hyperlipidemia in dogs and/or cats
include protein-losing nephropathy (nephrotic syndrome; ch. 302),
cholestasis (chs. 272 and 273), high-fat diets (dogs), hepatic
lipidosis (cats; ch. 274) and possibly other conditions (e.g.,
infections, inflammation, neoplasia, congestive heart failure).23,24
Administration of certain drugs, mainly glucocorticoids and

estrogens (such as megestrol acetate) can induce marked
hyperlipidemia. Other drugs reported to cause hyperlipidemia in
dogs (such as phenobarbital, potassium bromide, and progestagens)
may also cause hyperlipidemia in cats.25

PRIMARY HYPERLIPIDEMIA
Primary lipid abnormalities in dogs are usually, but not always,
associated with certain breeds (ch. 63). Depending on the breed, the
prevalence of a primary lipid abnormality can vary widely. Also, the
geographic region of the canine population tested seems to play an
important role due to genetic differences. Primary hyperlipidemia is
very common in Miniature Schnauzers in the United States (>30% of
Miniature Schnauzers affected in 1 study).26-28 Miniature
Schnauzers from Japan have also been described with this
condition,29 but based on anecdotal evidence, hyperlipidemia does
not appear to be as common in this breed in Europe. Primary
hyperlipidemia in the Miniature Schnauzer is typically characterized
by hypertriglyceridemia resulting from an abnormal accumulation of
VLDL or a combination of VLDL and chylomicrons.27,30 Although
hypercholesterolemia may also be present, it is not found in all
affected dogs and is always present in association with
hypertriglyceridemia.27,28,30 Hyperlipidemia in Miniature
Schnauzers is an age-related condition and both its prevalence and
severity increase with age.28 The cause of primary hyperlipidemia in
Miniature Schnauzers is currently unknown.31
Primary hyperlipidemia (mainly hypercholesterolemia but in some
cases with concurrent hypertriglyceridemia) has also been reported
in Shetland Sheepdogs.29,32,33 Primary hyperlipidemia with
hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia has also been
reported in Beagles.34 Primary hypercholesterolemia without
hypertriglyceridemia has been described in Briards and a family of
rough-coated Collies from the United Kingdom.35,36 In addition,
primary hypercholesterolemia has been reported anecdotally in
Doberman Pinschers and Rottweilers.

Primary lipid abnormalities are uncommon in cats. Inherited
hyperchylomicronemia leading to hypertriglyceridemia was first
described in 1983 in an 8-month old kitten.37 Subsequent mating of
this cat yielded a colony of cats that had variable increases in serum
triglyceride and cholesterol concentrations as a result of massive
increases in serum chylomicron and VLDL concentrations.37-39 In
addition to this colony of cats, sporadic case reports since the early
1980s have documented several individual cats or families of cats
with hyperlipidemia.40-43 Although these cats historically were
classified as having inherited hyperchylomicronemia (i.e., the
condition described in the colony cats), this might not be the case
because the LPL-gene mutation described in the research colony cats
was not found. Furthermore, the clinical presentation of these cases
differed from that of the colony cats because kittens with
spontaenous hyperlipidemia are usually presented at a younger age
(3 to 8 weeks) and the clinical course of the disease is transient,
meaning that the cats recover and are clinically and biochemically
normal during the first months of age. Common phenotypic
characteristics include variable increases in serum triglyceride and
cholesterol concentrations as a result of massive increases in serum
chylomicron and VLDL concentrations. Burmese cats have been
reported to commonly have a familial form of lipoprotein
metabolism disorder.44,45 Although some of these cats can have mild
to moderate fasting hypertriglyceridemia, many cats have normal
fasting serum triglyceride concentrations and their lipid disorder is
identified only after a fatty meal challenge produces marked postprandial hypertriglyceridemia and delayed clearance of serum
triglycerides. About half of the randomly selected healthy Burmese
cats in a study from Australia were affected by this condition.44 It is
thought to most likely reflect an inborn error of lipid metabolism
resulting in increased VLDL concentrations, while chylomicron
concentrations typically are normal.44,45 Burmese cats with this
condition typically are young, clinically healthy adults, while some
cats may present with lipid aqueous as an ocular manifestation.

CLINICAL CONSEQUENCES OF
HYPERLIPIDEMIA IN DOGS AND CATS
Hyperlipidemia per se does not appear to lead to any clinical signs.
However, many animals with hyperlipidemia develop diseases as a
result of hyperlipidemia and clinical signs develop as a result of those
diseases.

PANCREATITIS
Hyperlipidemia, and more specifically hypertriglyceridemia, has long
been suspected as a risk factor for canine pancreatitis (ch.
277).12,13,23 Also, the high prevalence of pancreatitis in Miniature
Schnauzers has been attributed to the fact that dogs of this breed
commonly develop primary hypertriglyceridemia.46 Two recent
clinical studies provided evidence that hypertriglyceridemia,
especially severe hypertriglyceridemia, is a risk factor for pancreatitis
in Miniature Schnauzers.47,48 In one of those studies, Miniature
Schnauzers that developed pancreatitis were 5 times more likely to
have hypertriglyceridemia before the development of pancreatitis
than dogs of the same breed that did not develop pancreatitis.47
Pancreatitis and diabetes mellitus often co-exist in cats, although it is
not clear whether the former triggers the latter or vice-versa.49
Based on evidence from humans and dogs, it has been hypothesized
that diabetes-associated hyperlipidemia may trigger pancreatitis in
cats. However, experimentally-induced hyperlipidemia in healthy
cats did not lead to any biochemical or histopathological evidence of
pancreatitis, although study limitations may have hindered such an
association.50

INSULIN RESISTANCE
Serum triglyceride concentrations are considered to be one of the
major determinants of insulin resistance in both humans and animal
models.51 Evidence of insulin resistance has been documented in

Miniature Schnauzers with primary hypertriglyceridemia.52 In one
study, almost 30% of Miniature Schnauzers with primary
hypertriglyceridemia had evidence of insulin resistance as
determined by serum insulin concentration.53 This might have an
implication regarding glycemic control in dogs with
hypertriglyceridemia and concurrent diabetes mellitus. The
association between hyperlipidemia, insulin resistance, and type 2
diabetes is not clear in cats. A study of 25 cats with naturally
occurring hypertriglyceridemia demonstrated significantly increased
serum insulin and decreased serum adiponectin concentrations in
these cats compared to 117 healthy control cats, indicating insulin
resistance.54 In another study, experimentally induced severe
hyperlipidemia (mean serum triglyceride concentration: 2,984 ±
1,526 mg/dL [33.7 ± 17.2 mmol/L]) was found to induce insulin
resistance, as assessed by glucose clamps.55 In contrast, in a previous
study, lipid infusion for 10 days did not affect insulin sensitivity in
cats.56 Overall, there is some evidence that both naturally occurring
and experimentally induced hyperlipidemia in cats might be
associated with insulin resistance as is the case in humans and dogs.

HEPATOBILIARY DISEASE
Clinical studies and anecdotal observations suggest that two
hepatobiliary disorders are associated with hypertriglyceridemia in
dogs: diffuse vacuolar hepatopathy (ch. 274) and gallbladder
mucocele (ch. 273).23 Hyperlipidemia-associated vacuolar
hepatopathy, characterized by hepatocellular accumulation of
triglycerides and glycogen, has been anecdotally reported and
associated with primary hyperlipidemia in dogs.23 In one study,
primary hypertriglyceridemia was found to be associated with
increased serum hepatic enzyme activities in clinically healthy
Miniature Schnauzers, presumably due to hyperlipidemia-associated
vacuolar hepatopathy.57 In that study, 60% and 45% of the
Miniature Schnauzers with serum triglyceride concentrations ≥4.52
mmol/L (≥400 mg/dL) had increased serum alkaline phosphatase

and alanine aminotransferase activities, respectively. Gallbladder
mucoceles commonly have been reported in dog breeds that are
predisposed to primary hyperlipidemia (e.g., Miniature Schnauzers
and Shetland Sheepdogs).33 In pathology studies in cats with
primary hyperchylomicronemia, histopathologic examination of the
liver revealed hepatic xanthomata and vacuolar hepatopathy
characterized by hepatocellular and Kupffer cell accumulation of
triglycerides.58,59 Severe hepatic lipid accumulation has been
identified in kittens with transient primary hyperlipidemia.41 The
clinical importance of these findings remains unknown.

ATHEROSCLEROSIS
Although dogs appear to be resistant to atherosclerosis due to their
lipoprotein composition and metabolism, they have been reported to
develop atherosclerosis in both experimental and clinical studies.6063
Spontaneous atherosclerosis has been reported in dogs mainly in
association with secondary hypercholesterolemia due to
endocrinopathies. In one study, 60% of 30 dogs with atherosclerosis
had hypothyroidism and 20% had diabetes mellitus.62 Cats appear to
be resistant to atherosclerosis. No gross or microscopic evidence of
atherosclerotic changes was found in cats with primary
hyperchylomicronemia.58,59

OCULAR DISEASE
Several ocular manifestations of hyperlipidemia, such as lipemia
retinalis, lipemic aqueous, and lipid keratopathy, have been reported
in dogs (ch. 13).64 Several ocular manifestations of hyperlipidemia
have been described in cats, including lipemia retinalis, lipemic
aqueous, and lipid keratopathy.44,45,64,65

XANTHOMATOSIS

Xanthomas are benign granulomatous lesions that are believed to
result from disrupted lipid metabolism and transport (ch. 12).
Formation of single or, more commonly, multiple xanthomas has
been reported commonly in the skin and internal organs (liver,
spleen, kidneys, adrenal glands, intestine, mesentery, etc.) in cats
with primary hyperchylomicronemia and may also be seen in cats
with uncontrolled severe secondary hyperlipidemia.58,59,66

PROTEINURIA AND GLOMERULAR
LIPIDOSIS
Hypertriglyceridemia in Miniature Schnauzers has been associated
with proteinuria, glomerular lipidosis and glomerular lipid
thromboemboli (ch. 302).67-69 The clinical importance and longterm consequences of findings are unknown and warrant further
investigation.

NEUROLOGIC DISEASE
Seizures, ischemic strokes, and other neurologic signs have been
reported to potentially occur as a result of severe hyperlipidemia in
dogs and may also be seen in cats (ch. 243).70-72 Cats with severe
primary hyperchylomicronemia have been reported to develop
severe peripheral neuropathy, most commonly encountered as
hindlimb paralysis.59,73

CLINICAL SYNDROME OF TRANSIENT
HYPERLIPIDEMIA IN KITTENS
Several cases of transient hyperlipidemia have been described in
young kittens.40-43 Affected kittens are usually 3-8 weeks old and
they appear heathy prior to developing clinical signs. Affected kittens
become lethargic, weak, anorexic and dyspneic, and typically
collapse and die within 48 hours if left untreated.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH TO DOGS AND
CATS WITH HYPERLIPIDEMIA
Hyperlipidemia typically is diagnosed by measurement of fasting
serum triglyceride and/or cholesterol concentrations. In some dogs
and in Burmese cats, clinically important lipid disorders as
determined by oral fat tolerance tests can exist with normal serum
triglyceride concentrations.44,45 The general diagnostic approach
when evaluating dogs and cats with hyperlipidemia is presented in
ch. 63. After hyperlipidemia has been diagnosed, the next step is to
determine whether the patient has a primary or a secondary lipid
disorder. If hyperlipidemia is secondary, the condition causing
hyperlipidemia should be diagnosed and treated. Thus, specific
diagnostic investigations should be performed to diagnose or rule out
specific diseases that can cause secondary hyperlipidemia (ch. 63,
Table 63.1). If secondary hyperlipidemia is excluded, a tentative
diagnosis of a primary lipid disorder can be made.
A detailed history (ch. 2) should be obtained and physical
examination (ch. 3) performed first. This is crucial because dogs and
cats with secondary hyperlipidemia typically show clinical signs of
the primary disease (e.g., obesity, polyuria and polydipsia in animals
with diabetes mellitus), which can help prioritize the selection of
diagnostic tests and lead the way towards an appropriate diagnostic
plan. Dogs and cats with primary hyperlipidemia may not have
clinical signs and hyperlipidemia may be diagnosed during routine
blood testing. Animals with hyperlipidemia should have at least a
complete blood count, serum biochemistry panel, and urinalysis
performed. Additional tests may be needed depending on the
suspected underlying condition. The selection of tests to be
performed is based on information from the history and physical
examination and is tailored to each individual case. A more general
and wide selection of tests might be necessary for patients that have
vague or no clinical signs. One possible exception is the Miniature
Schnauzer, in which primary hyperlipidemia is common. A detailed
diagnostic investigation of hyperlipidemia might not be necessary in
this breed in the absence of clinical signs suggesting an underlying
cause.

TREATMENT OF HYPERLIPIDEMIA
Treatment of secondary hyperlipidemia relies on the successful
treatment of the underlying disorder, after which hyperlipidemia
usually resolves. Resolution of secondary hyperlipidemia after
treatment of the cause should always be confirmed by laboratory
testing (typically 4-6 weeks after initiation of treatment of the
primary disease and periodically thereafter). If hyperlipidemia has
not resolved, another underlying cause, alternative or additional
therapy, or concurrent primary hyperlipidemia should be
considered.
Treatment of primary or persistent secondary
hypertriglyceridemia is clinically important. It has been traditionally
recommended that hypertriglyceridemia should be treated only
when exceeding 500 mg/dL (5.7 mmol/L). However, recent studies
have shown that insulin resistance, hepatobiliary disease, and
possibly other complications of hypertriglyceridemia can exist even
with serum triglyceride concentrations below 500 mg/dL (5.7
mmol/L). Therefore, treatment should be considered even in
patients with less severe hypertriglyceridemia to keep serum
triglyceride concentrations as low as possible and lower the risk for
complications.
In most cases, treatment should initially be pursued with dietary
management, while drug therapy can be initiated later if deemed
necessary. Although the management of hypercholesterolemia seems
to be of less clinical importance than that of hypertriglyceridemia in
dogs and cats and there are no studies evaluating the need for
treatment of hypercholesterolemia in these species, severe
hypercholesterolemia may be treated at least with dietary
management.

DIETARY MANAGEMENT
Low-Fat Diets
Typically, the first step in the management of primary or persistent
secondary hyperlipidemia is dietary modification. The most
commonly used and likely most effective dietary option for
hyperlipidemia in dogs and cats is feeding a low-fat diet. Dogs and

cats with persistent primary hyperlipidemia should be offered a lowfat diet throughout their lives, while animals with transient primary
or persistent secondary hyperlipidemia should be offered low-fat
diets on the basis of repeated testing and effectiveness of control of
the primary disease. Kittens with transient hyperlipidemia respond
very well to low-fat diets and they only need these diets for a few
weeks until they recover from this condition.40-42
Many commercially available diets are labeled as low-fat but their
fat content can vary widely. It needs to be pointed out that the
percentage of fat content of the diet (commonly listed on food labels)
does not reliably reflect the amount of fat the animal is consuming
because a certain percentage of fat that is ingested is not absorbed
and metabolized. Therefore, fat content should be assessed on a
metabolizable energy basis. The authors generally recommend diets
that contain less than 25 g of total fat per 1,000 kcal (metabolizable
energy). In a recent study, Miniature Schnauzers with primary
hyperlipidemia were fed the Royal Canin Gastrointestinal Low Fat
diet for 8 weeks.74 The fat content of the study diet was 18.6 g of fat
per 1000 kcal. By the end of the treatment period, there was a
significant reduction in both serum triglyceride and cholesterol
concentrations. Serum cholesterol concentrations returned to
normal in all dogs, while serum triglyceride concentrations returned
to normal in about 30% of dogs. However, all dogs that had serum
triglyceride concentrations >500 mg/dL (>5.7 mmol/L) at the
beginning of the study had serum triglyceride concentrations <500
mg/dL (<5.7 mmol/L) by the end of the trial.
Home-made low-fat diets have not been systematically evaluated
for the management of hyperlipidemia in dogs and cats. If such diets
are used, care should be taken to make sure that they are balanced,
especially when intended for long-term feeding, and that the
minimum nutrient requirements are met for all nutrients, including
essential fatty acids. Some of these diets (e.g., rice and boiled lean
turkey breast without the skin) may have an even lower fat content
(<18 g/1000 kcal) than some commercially available low-fat diets
and may be more effective in lowering serum lipid concentrations.
Treats and table scraps should be avoided unless they are low in fat.
In some dogs and cats, additional dietary modifications may be
used if low-fat diets are not effective. These include the following:

Dietary Fiber
Other options in the dietary management of dogs and cats with
abnormal serum lipid concentrations include the addition of dietary
fiber (ch. 165). Complex carbohydrates seem to have a positive
effect in clinical disorders of lipid metabolism. Although explicit
studies in these species are lacking, it might be useful, based on
experience in humans and other animals, to achieve a reduction in
blood lipid levels via inclusion of dietary fiber. Sources of fiber can be
soluble and insoluble. While insoluble fibers such as cellulose have a
typical bulk effect, soluble fibers can, depending on their character,
lead to a change in the viscosity of the digesta. Furthermore, they can
influence the composition and metabolic activity of the intestinal
microbiota. Metabolic problems such as overweight, diabetes
mellitus, insulin resistance, and hyperlipidemia, can be influenced by
the use of fiber. There is ample need for research in this area to
determine the optimal dosage at which fiber should be included in a
diet for dogs with such conditions. While veterinary diets have a
large market share, individual recipes can be helpful in many cases.
Pet owners can modify the amount of fiber or even the fat content
relatively easily.

Omega-3 Fatty Acids
Polyunsaturated fatty acids of the n-3 series (omega-3 fatty acids;
eicosapentaenoic acid [EPA], and docosahexaenoic acid [DHA]) exist
abundantly in marine fish. Omega-3 fatty acid supplementation has
been shown to lower serum triglyceride concentrations in
experimental animals and in humans, including cases of primary
hypertriglyceridemia. Specifically, omega-3 fatty acids have been
shown to reduce serum triglyceride concentrations by up to 50%
when used at high dosages in humans with hypertriglyceridemia.75
The mechanisms of the lipid-lowering action of omega-3 fatty acids
are complex and include regulation of several transcription factors
that lead to reduced lipogenesis, increased beta-oxidation, and
activation of LPL.75,76 In a study of healthy dogs, fish-oil
supplementation led to a significant reduction of serum triglyceride
concentrations, suggesting that this supplement may be helpful in
the treatment of canine hypertriglyceridemia.77 No major side-

effects have been observed in humans or in dogs receiving omega-3
fatty acids. However, studies evaluating the efficacy and safety of
omega-3 fatty acid supplementation in dogs or cats with
hyperlipidemia are lacking. A “fishy” odor is often noted in dogs
receiving high doses of omega-3 fatty acids and it might be
unacceptable for some owners (ch. 33). Omega-3 fatty acids may be
used in dogs and cats at dosages ranging from 200 mg/kg to 300
mg/kg, PO, once a day, and their effect on serum triglyceride
concentrations is dose-dependent. Their lipid-lowering effect
typically requires dosages at the high end of the recommended
dosage range for dogs. An upper daily limit of 4 to 5 grams might be
recommended.

Niacin (Nicotinic Acid)
Niacin is a form of vitamin B3 that has been used successfully for the
treatment of hyperlipidemia in humans for many years.78 When
used in pharmacological dosages, niacin is a broad-spectrum lipidmodifying drug. In humans, it reduces both low-density lipoprotein
(LDL)-cholesterol and serum triglyceride concentrations.76 The
mechanism of action of niacin is complex and incompletely
understood but it includes inhibition of hormone-sensitive lipase
activity and the enzyme diacylglycerol acyltransferase; both of these
actions eventually lead to reduced triglyceride biosynthesis.76
Clinical trials regarding the efficacy and safety of niacin in dogs and
cats with primary hypertriglyceridemia are lacking and clinical
experience is limited. In some dogs, niacin reduced serum
triglyceride concentrations for several months without causing any
side-effects.79As is often the case in humans, niacin administration
in dogs and cats may be associated with adverse effects such as
erythema and pruritus, which may require discontinuation of
therapy. Long-term risk for myotoxicosis and hepatotoxicosis may
also exist.76 Niacin may be administered to dogs and cats at a dosage
of 50 to 100 mg/day. Both the therapeutic and side-effects of niacin
are dose-dependent, and it is therefore recommended that niacin be
started at a low dosage and slowly titrated upward (every 4 weeks)
based on the results of follow-up serum cholesterol and triglyceride

concentrations. It should be used with caution in diabetic patients
because it can increase blood glucose concentration, especially when
used at higher dosages. Serum liver enzyme activities should be
monitored with long-term use of niacin.

Chitosan
Chitosan is a natural compound derived from the polysaccharide
chitin. It appears to bind to negatively charged lipids in animal trials,
hence reducing gastrointestinal lipid uptake and lowering serum
cholesterol. Some human trials have suggested that chitosan may
decrease body weight and serum lipids, while other studies have
found no effect on clinical outcomes. One study has evaluated the use
of chitosan (3 g/cat once a day) in a small number of cats with
induced hyperlipidemia.80 Chitosan was found to be effective in
reducing both serum triglyceride and cholesterol concentrations,
although concentrations did not seem to normalize in some of the
cats. The efficacy of chitosan was compared to that of atorvastatin in
that study, and chitosan was found to be less efficacious. No sideeffects were noted.

5-Aminolevulinic Acid
5-Aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) is a natural delta-amino acid that has
been hypothesized to improve lipid and glucose metabolism in obese
mice. In a recent study, 5-ALA was used in 5 Miniature Schnauzer
dogs with severe hypertriglyceridemia and was found to significantly
improve (but not normalize) serum triglyceride concentrations.
Further studies are needed to evaluate the use of 5-ALA as a
treatment for dogs with hyperlipidemia.

Summary and Monitoring
Not all dietary options should necessarily be tried before
pharmacologic management is initiated. Serum lipid concentrations
should be re-evaluated every 3-4 weeks after any dietary
modification. If additional reduction of serum triglyceride
concentration is desired, additional dietary modifications or
pharmacologic treatment should be considered.

PHARMACOLOGIC MANAGEMENT
Some animals with primary hyperlipidemia may not sufficiently
respond to dietary modification, or faster and more predictable
lowering of serum lipid concentrations may be required. In these
cases, pharmacologic treatment may be required. No studies have
evaluated the efficacy and safety of most lipid-lowering drugs in dogs
and cats, and therefore, evidence-based recommendations cannot be
made. Drugs that are more commonly used in the management of
hyperlipidemia are shown in Table 156.1.

Fibrates (Fibric Acid Derivatives)
Fibrates are weak agonists of peroxisome proliferator-activated
receptor-alpha (PPAR-alpha), a nuclear transcription factor that
regulates lipid and lipoprotein synthesis and catabolism.81 Fibrates
suppress fatty acid synthesis, stimulate fatty acid oxidation, activate
LPL, and noncompetitively inhibit diacylglycerol acyl transferase 2,
the enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of diglycerides to
triglycerides. These effects lead to an overall reduction in serum
triglyceride concentration.75,76 In humans, fibrates typically reduce
serum triglyceride concentrations by 25% to 50%.75,76 Fibrate use in
humans is associated with a low incidence of myotoxicosis and of
increases in serum liver enzyme activities. Gemfibrozil is one of the
most commonly used fibrates in humans, and it also has been used
anecdotally in dogs and cats with hypertriglyceridemia. In dogs, it
can be administered at 10 mg/kg PO q12h. No side-effects have been
observed in dogs, although no studies have evaluated its safety in this
species. In the authors’ experience, similar to what has been reported
in humans,82 many canine patients with primary hyperlipidemia do
not respond well to treatment with gemfibrozil. Bezafibrate, another
fibric acid derivative, may be both more effective and associated with
fewer adverse effects in the treatment of humans and dogs with
hyperlipidemia.82 Bezafibrate has been evaluated for the treatment
of hyperlipidemia of various causes (both primary and secondary) in
dogs and was found to be highly effective in reducing serum
triglyceride and cholesterol concentrations.83 In that study,

bezafibrate was used at a dosage of 4-10 mg/kg q 24 h for 30 days.
Normalization of serum triglyceride and cholesterol concentrations
was achieved in 91% and 68% of cases, respectively. No side-effects
were observed. In a more recent study, fenofibrate (10 mg/kg, q24h)
was also evaluated in the treatment of severe hypertriglyceridemia in
dogs (both primary and secondary) and was found to be highly
effective, leading to normalization of serum triglyceride
concentrations in 86% of dogs.84 In that study, normalization of
serum cholesterol concentrations occurred in only about 50% of
dogs.84 No significant adverse effects were reported. No studies have
evaluated the safety and efficacy of fibrates in cats and clinical
experience has been extremely limited. In this species, gemfibrozil
may be administered at 10 mg/kg PO q12h, while bezafibrate may be
administered at 4-10 mg/kg q24h. Periodic testing of serum
triglyceride concentration and liver enzyme activities is
recommended.

Statins
Statins are among the most potent and commonly used lipidlowering drugs and they constitute first-line therapy for the
treatment of hypercholesterolemia in humans.76 They are reversible
inhibitors of the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase, which is the ratelimiting step for cholesterol biosynthesis. Therefore, statins are
mainly cholesterol-lowering drugs (in humans they specifically lower
LDL-cholesterol) with less potent effects on triglyceride
metabolism.76 This makes them less than ideal for cases with
hypertriglyceridemia as the main lipid abnormality.81 Statins have
been associated with myopathy, rhabdomyolysis, and
hepatotoxicosis in humans. In a recent study, the pharmacokinetics
of simvastatin were described in healthy Beagle dogs.85 However,
this drug has not been tested in dogs with hyperlipidemia. In a study
of 7 cats with experimentally-induced hyperlipidemia through
feeding of cholesterol powder, atorvastatin, a commonly used statin
in humans, given at a dosage of 5 mg/kg, was effective in
significantly reducing (and possibly normalizing) both serum
triglyceride and cholesterol concentrations compared to controls.80

The drug was well tolerated and all cats were clinically healthy at the
end of the 2-month study, although liver function and pathologic
changes were not evaluated. The number of cats was small in this
study and the hyperlipidemia was experimentally induced and
relatively mild. Therefore, strong conclusions cannot be drawn but
this study suggests that atorvastatin may have a use in the
management of some cases of feline hyperlipidemia, even when
hypertriglyceridemia is present. In animals in which statins are used,
serum hepatic enzyme activities should be periodically monitored for
potential hepatotoxicosis. In humans, concurrent administration of
statins and fibrates (especially gemfibrozil) is not recommended,
because the latter has been shown to affect the pharmacokinetics of
statins, leading to increased risk for toxicosis.81 However, other
fibrates (e.g., bezafibrate) appear to be safer and better tolerated
than gemfibrozil when combined with statins.76,81

Chapter 157: Nutritional
Management of Heart
Disease
Lisa M. Freeman, and John E. Rush
