Nutrition is an integral part of medical therapy for dogs and cats
with heart disease. While recognized in veterinary medicine for more
than 50 years, the role of nutrition in heart disease has expanded and
has been refined. In the 1960s, the main nutritional
recommendations for dogs with heart disease were to feed a lowsodium diet (for all stages of heart disease), to feed a restricted
protein diet, and to provide supplemental B vitamins.1 Few changes
to these recommendations were made until the 1970s, when mention
of cardiac cachexia appeared in veterinary medicine2 and when the
question of how early to institute sodium restriction was raised in the
1980s.3 It was also in the late 1980s that the discovery of the
relationship between taurine deficiency and feline dilated
cardiomyopathy (DCM) was published.4 Now, research is beginning
to show that nutrition may be able to modulate heart disease, either
by slowing progression, minimizing the number of medications
required, improving quality of life or, in rare cases, actually
improving or reversing the disease. Therefore, the optimal care of
patients with heart disease should include attention to the diet.
The main goals of nutrition for patients with heart disease are to
maintain optimal body composition, to avoid nutritional deficiencies
and excesses, and to take advantage of the potential benefits of
pharmacologic doses of certain nutrients.

MAINTENANCE OF OPTIMAL BODY
COMPOSITION
A key goal for the optimal management of heart disease is to
maintain ideal body composition, because body weight, body
condition, and muscle mass can significantly impact health,
especially in animals with heart disease.

CACHEXIA
Cardiac cachexia is the muscle loss commonly seen in patients with
congestive heart failure (CHF) (ch. 151). Cachexia occurs in 42-48%

of cats with heart disease and in 48-69% of dogs with heart disease.59
The weight loss that occurs in animals with CHF is unlike that seen
in a healthy dog or cat that loses weight. In a healthy animal
receiving insufficient calories to meet requirements, metabolic
adaptations allow fat to be used as the primary fuel source, thus
preserving lean body mass. Conversely, the primary fuel source in
animals with CHF is amino acids from muscle; therefore, these
animals quickly catabolize lean body mass. Thus, the distinguishing
feature of cachexia is a loss of lean body mass, which has direct and
deleterious effects on strength, immune function, and survival.6,8,9
Cardiac cachexia is often mistakenly viewed as an end-stage
syndrome manifested by an emaciated dog or cat. In fact, cachexia is
a progressive process of muscle loss that can be very subtle initially
and can even occur in an obese animal. Recognizing the process of
cachexia at an early stage provides better opportunities to manage it
effectively.
The loss of lean body mass in cardiac cachexia is a multifactorial
process caused by decreases/alterations in food intake, increased
energy requirements, and metabolic alterations.6 Animals with CHF
can have anorexia (complete lack of food intake), hyporexia (reduced
food intake), or dysrexia (alterations in eating patterns and food
preferences).10 Reduced food intake, particularly hyporexia and
dysrexia, are common in dogs and cats with clinically significant
heart disease.6,11,12 These alterations in food intake may be
secondary to weakness or medication side-effects.6 However,
inflammatory mediators, such as the cytokines tumor necrosis
factor-alpha (TNF) and interleukin-1-beta (IL-1) are primary
mediators of cachexia.6 These inflammatory cytokines can reduce
appetite, increase energy requirements, and increase catabolism of
lean body mass. TNF and IL-1 also cause cardiac myocyte
hypertrophy and fibrosis and have negative inotropic effects.
Cardiac cachexia is typically recognized only after CHF has
developed. It is most often seen in DCM or right-sided CHF and,
while it is more often recognized in dogs than in cats, prevalence
rates are similar in the two species.8,9 It is ideal to identify cachexia
at its earliest and mildest stages (i.e., mild muscle loss), when there

is more opportunity to reverse it or at least prevent it from
worsening. Therefore, muscle condition score (along with body
weight and body condition score [BCS], which assesses an animal’s
fat stores—chs. 3, 72, and 145, and inside covers) should be assessed
at every visit for every animal with heart disease.13,14 Loss of muscle
can usually be recognized first in the epaxial muscles, although loss
in other muscle groups (e.g., gluteal, scapular, temporal) also can be
readily identified as muscle loss progresses. Temporal muscle loss is
more variable and may be severe in some dogs and almost nonexistent in others. The muscle condition score is best categorized as
normal, mild muscle loss, moderate muscle loss, or severe muscle
loss (ch. 72, textbook’s inside covers), rather than using a numerical
score.14
Nutritional considerations for cardiac cachexia should include
management of altered food intake, if present. Nutritional
modulation of cytokine production also may be helpful. One method
of decreasing the production and effects of cytokines is omega-3 (n3) polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation (see below).
Supplementation of fish oil, which is high in omega-3 fatty acids, can
decrease cytokine production in dogs with CHF and has some
benefits for cachexia.6 In some but not all dogs with CHF-induced
hyporexia or dysrexia, fish oil supplementation can have mild
benefits for food intake.6 In addition, omega-3 fatty acid intake has
been associated with longer survival in one retrospective study of
dogs with CHF.15 Appetite stimulants, such as capromorelin (Entyce
for dogs, Elura for cats; Elanco, Greenfield, IN) or mirtazapine
(Mirataz transdermal ointment for cats; Dechra, Overland Park, KS),
can be beneficial for maintaining adequate and more consistent food
intake in animals with hyporexia or dysrexia, and can help to ensure
pets with heart disease are fed optimal diets (see below), rather than
whatever the owner can get a dysrexic animal to eat. Capromorelin,
through its stimulation of insulin-like growth factor-1, also might
have beneficial effects on muscle mass.

OBESITY

Overweight (i.e., over ideal body weight) and obesity (i.e., more than
20% over ideal body weight) are common in the pet population and
can have detrimental effects on health (ch. 150). Therefore,
maintaining an optimal body weight and BCS (ch. 72) should be a
goal for healthy dogs and cats and for those with subclinical heart
disease. Optimal body weight and growth in early life may be even
more important in cats. Cats with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
(HCM) are skeletally larger (i.e., larger heads, vertebrae, and longer
humeri), are heavier at diagnosis, and are heavier at an early age
compared to cats without HCM (ch. 234).16-19 In one study, Maine
Coon cats with HCM also had a significantly higher BCS than those
without HCM.19 This suggests that early growth and/or obesity
might play a role in cats with a genetic risk for HCM and increase the
phenotypic expressivity in individual animals. Cats (and dogs)
should be kept at an ideal BCS of 4-5/9 throughout growth and
adulthood.
While there are clear benefits of maintaining an ideal (4-5/9) BCS
in healthy animals, what constitutes ideal BCS in animals with CHF
requires more research. However, this is an important consideration
because overweight and obesity are common in animals with CHF. In
two recent studies, 37% of dogs and 49% of cats with CHF were
overweight (in fact, only 5% of dogs and 12% of cats were thin in
those studies).8,9 Although obesity has some theoretical physiologic
effects which could be detrimental in CHF, numerous studies in
people with CHF have shown that obesity actually is associated with
a longer survival time; this is called the “obesity paradox” and is
likely related more to muscle mass, which is often higher in
overweight people, than to any direct benefits of excess adipose
tissue.20 In cats, one study showed that overweight but not obese
body condition was associated with longer survival time.21 However,
in a recent study of 125 cats with CHF, being overweight was not
associated with survival.9 In dogs with CHF, being overweight or
underweight was associated with shorter survival times.8 While
additional research is needed, human and veterinary research
suggest that careful attention to body weight, BCS, muscle loss, and
food intake is important in animals with heart disease.

A common mistake is to assume that cachexia only occurs in thin
animals. In recent studies, muscle loss was common even in
overweight and obese animals: cachexia was present in 30% of
overweight dogs with CHF (and 57% of ideal weight dogs) and 18% of
overweight cats with CHF (53% of ideal weight cats).8,9 Therefore,
monitoring of body weight, BCS, and muscle condition score at every
visit is important.14 The authors aim for a BCS of 4-5/9 for healthy
animals and those with asymptomatic heart disease. For animals
with CHF, a higher BCS, (6-7/9) is preferred by the authors, while
avoiding weight gain to achieve this goal since weight gain in the face
of CHF is likely to be primarily fat and, therefore, not beneficial. A
BCS >7/9 may still have detrimental effects so obesity should be
avoided. The authors typically will not try to initiate a weight loss
plan in dogs or cats after the onset of CHF (unless obesity is severe
and adversely affecting quality of life), since the loss of weight will be
primarily due to loss of muscle.

BODY WEIGHT
It is important to weigh animals with heart disease at every visit.
Even though few animals are thin at the time of diagnosis, and many
are overweight, 42-45% of dogs and cats had lost at least 5% of their
body weight in the 6-12 months prior to diagnosis of CHF.8,9 In
addition to the muscle loss previously noted, weight loss becomes
even more of an issue after the diagnosis of CHF. In one study, 67%
of cats lost weight after the diagnosis of CHF.9 The weight loss has
been associated with mortality: in one study of dogs with CHF, dogs
that lost weight after the diagnosis had a significantly shorter
survival time than those that gained or maintained weight.15

MODULATION OF SPECIFIC NUTRIENTS
Nutritional deficiencies once were a relatively common cause of
DCM in people and probably animals. In cats, taurine deficiency was
a common cause of heart disease until as recently as the late 1980s.
Identifiable nutritional deficiencies are now uncommon in dogs and

cats unless owners are feeding homemade, vegetarian, or otherwise
nutritionally unbalanced diets (ch. 167). However, deficiencies can
be present and they play a role in the etiology of some heart diseases,
especially as homemade and other unconventional diets become
more popular. Nutritional deficiencies also may develop secondary to
heart disease or its treatment. A new area of nutritional research is
that of nutritional pharmacology, the concept that supplementation
of certain nutrients may provide benefits above and beyond their
known nutritional effects. Therefore, providing higher levels of
certain nutrients may be recommended for some animals with heart
disease.

PROTEIN AND TAURINE
Protein
Protein restriction should be avoided in dogs and cats with heart
disease because these patients are predisposed to loss of muscle
mass. Diets that are low in protein should not be recommended for
patients with heart disease unless proteinuria or severe renal disease
is present (even in those cases, the authors try to avoid low protein
diets and make adjustments for the individual patient so that protein
is restricted as little as possible). Therefore, cardiac diets that are low
in protein, diets designed for renal disease, and many “senior” diets
should be avoided, and a good quality nutritionally balanced food
providing at least the canine (4.5 g/100 kcal) and feline (6.5 g/100
kcal) minimum protein levels according to the Association of
American Feed Control Officials (AAFCO) is recommended.22
Higher protein levels are often desirable depending on the individual
patient, especially in animals with CHF or cachexia.

Taurine
Taurine is an amino acid found in high levels in the myocardium.
Taurine is an essential nutrient for cats and must be provided in
their diets, as opposed to most other species that can synthesize
adequate amounts endogenously. Taurine deficiency in cats is
associated with a variety of health issues, including DCM and retinal
degeneration. What is unusual about taurine deficiency-induced

DCM in cats is that it is reversible. If cats with taurine deficiencyinduced DCM survive the first few weeks, their hearts typically
undergo dramatic improvement, and they often do not require longterm cardiac medications. Since the increase in AAFCO minimums
for taurine after the landmark publication documenting this
association in 1987,4 the incidence of DCM in cats has decreased
dramatically. A small number of cats still develop DCM (ch. 234),
but few are associated with taurine deficiency. However, taurine
deficiency should still be considered as a differential diagnosis in all
cats with DCM. A dietary history should be elicited from owners (ch.
145) to determine whether the cat has been fed a poor-quality,
homemade, vegetarian/vegan, or otherwise unbalanced diet (ch.
167). Plasma and whole blood taurine concentrations should be
measured, and treatment with taurine (125 to 250 mg PO q12h)
should begin concurrently with medical therapy. If the taurine
concentration is found to be normal, taurine supplementation can be
discontinued. However, some benefits may still be derived from
taurine’s other effects (see below).
Unlike cats, dogs are thought to be able to synthesize adequate
amounts of taurine, which is not considered essential in canine diets,
as long as they contain adequate methionine and cysteine. Most dogs
with DCM do not have taurine deficiency, but low taurine
concentrations have been found in some dogs with the disorder.23-32
The most common breeds in which DCM has been reported to be
associated with taurine deficiency are the Cocker Spaniel and Golden
Retriever, but other reported breeds include Labrador Retrievers,
Portuguese Water Dogs, Saint Bernards, English Setters, and
Newfoundlands (ch. 233).23-32
In the minority of dogs with DCM that have taurine deficiency, diet
may play some role as very-low-protein, lamb and rice, certain grainfree diets, and some high-fiber diets have been associated with
taurine deficiency, as have been diets low in methionine.25-28,33-37
Taurine deficiency was associated with DCM in a study of 24 Golden
Retrievers with DCM eating non-traditional diets, but the exact role
of diet remains unknown.32 Taurine deficiency also may be the result
of increased renal or fecal loss of taurine, higher requirements, or
other metabolic defects present in certain breeds.28,30,34-37 A recent

study in Golden Retrievers suggests that this breed may have a
slightly higher reference range for taurine than commonly used
reference ranges.38
In some dogs with DCM that have low circulating taurine
concentrations, taurine supplementation can be beneficial, although
the response is usually not as dramatic as the response to repletion
in cats with taurine-deficient DCM. One small prospective study
showed that Cocker Spaniels supplemented with taurine and
carnitine had clinical and echocardiographic improvements.39 It is
not known whether the response would be similar with either taurine
or carnitine alone. A retrospective study of 12 dogs with taurine
deficiency and DCM documented improved cardiac contractility after
taurine supplementation.27 In a study of 9 Portuguese Water Dog
puppies, plasma taurine was low in all puppies tested, and DCM was
diagnosed in 8 puppies.25 Taurine supplementation was instituted in
6 of the puppies, which significantly increased circulating taurine
concentrations and cardiac function.25 In one study of Beagles fed a
low-taurine, very-low-protein diet for 48 months, one dog developed
DCM but showed significant improvement in cardiac contractility
after supplementation of taurine.33 In a retrospective study of
English Cocker Spaniels in the United Kingdom, 13/16 dogs between
2008-2018 in which taurine was measured had low taurine
concentrations and, while echocardiographic improvements were
noted in the dogs following taurine supplementation, improvements
were also noted in the dogs with normal taurine concentrations.31
Finally, in a recent study of Golden Retrievers with DCM and taurine
deficiency associated with non-traditional diets, there was a
significant improvement in echocardiographic measurements after
taurine supplementation and, in most dogs, diet change.32
Until the role of taurine in canine DCM with respect to different
breeds and different diets is better defined, the authors believe
measurement of plasma and whole blood taurine concentrations is
justified in all dogs with DCM, and measurement is strongly
encouraged if dogs are the breeds that appear to be predisposed to
taurine deficiency or if dogs are eating a non-traditional, lamb meal
and rice, low-protein, vegetarian/vegan, or high-fiber diet.

Supplementation with taurine (250 to 1000 mg PO q12h) is
recommended in dogs with documented taurine deficiency, although
the exact dosage required for repletion is not known. As with any
dietary supplement, it is important to recommend supplementation
of taurine brands with evidence of independent quality control
testing (see below). If taurine concentrations are not measured, it
seems reasonable to administer taurine to dogs with DCM as it is a
safe supplement (assuming a brand with good quality control is
used), and taurine may have some potential benefits above and
beyond correction of a deficiency (e.g., positive inotropic and
antioxidant effects).

FAT
Fat provides calories and increases the palatability of pet foods but it
also can significantly affect immunologic, inflammatory, and
hemodynamic parameters. The omega-3 fatty acids,
eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), are
long-chain fatty acids in which the first double bond is at the position
of the third carbon from the methyl end (vs. the omega-6 PUFAs,
namely linoleic, gamma-linolenic, and arachidonic, in which the first
double bond is at the sixth carbon).40 This minor chemical
difference conveys different structural and functional characteristics
to the fatty acids. Plasma membranes normally contain very low
concentrations of omega-3 fatty acids, but levels can be increased by
a food enriched in omega-3 fatty acids or a supplement. Dogs with
CHF have been shown to have plasma fatty acid abnormalities,
including decreased concentrations of EPA and DHA compared to
normal dogs.5 In one study of dogs with DCM and CHF, fish oil
supplementation normalized these plasma fatty acid abnormalities.5
Another potential benefit of omega-3 fatty acid supplementation is
that breakdown products of the omega-3 fatty acids (3- and 5-series
eicosanoids) are, in general, less potent inflammatory mediators
than eicosanoids derived from omega-6 fatty acids (2- and 4-series
eicosanoids). This decreases the production of cytokines and other
inflammatory mediators, which may minimize cachexia.5,40 Finally,
omega-3 fatty acids have antiarrhythmic effects in humans and dogs,

including one study in Boxers with ventricular arrhythmias (ch.
233).41 The authors currently recommend a dosage of 40 mg/kg
EPA and 25 mg/kg DHA PO q24h for dogs and cats with
reduced/altered food intake or cachexia. This dosage also can be
used as an adjunct to medical therapy for arrhythmias. Finally, the
authors discuss the possible benefits of omega-3 fatty acid
supplementation with all owners of dogs or cats with CHF, advising
that there may be some benefit to supplementation in all cases of
CHF unless they are contraindicated (e.g., coagulopathies, certain
gastrointestinal disorders). While some specially designed veterinary
diets have high levels of omega-3 fatty acids, most commercial diets
do not achieve this level of omega-3 fatty acids, so supplementation
is usually necessary. The amount of EPA and DHA in individual fish
oil supplements varies widely, so it is important to know the exact
amount in the brand of supplement recommended. The most
common formulation of fish oil, however, is 1-g capsules that contain
approximately 180 mg EPA and 120 mg DHA and can be purchased
over the counter at most human pharmacies or health food stores. At
this concentration, fish oil can be administered at a dose of one
capsule per 10 pounds (4.5 kg) of body weight to achieve the authors’
recommended EPA and DHA dosage. However, for medium- to
large-size dogs, more concentrated forms of fish oil are usually
preferred to avoid the need to administer so many capsules. Fish oil
supplements should contain vitamin E as an antioxidant, but other
nutrients should not be included to avoid toxicosis. Cod liver oil and
flaxseed oil should not be used as sources of omega-3 fatty acids. As
with any dietary supplement, it is important to recommend only fish
oil supplements with independent quality control testing (see below).
Fish oil has a very strong flavor so if owners are unable to pill the pet
without using food and the animal does not like the taste, fish oil
should be discontinued as it can cause food (and medication)
aversions.
In addition to modifying inflammation, the type of dietary fat may
also provide benefit in terms of myocardial energy metabolism.
Before birth, glucose is the heart’s primary fuel but, after birth, most
of the adenosine triphosphate (ATP) generated in the heart is from
fatty acid metabolism. In heart disease—even in its early stages—the
generation of ATP from fatty acid oxidation is impaired and glucose

again becomes the major fuel for the heart. This switch in cardiac
metabolism limits energy generation in the heart and may contribute
to progression of disease. The metabolic shift that occurs in heart
disease and, particularly in heart failure, however, also allows the
heart to begin to utilize ketones for energy.42 In addition to being an
additional energy source for the heart in heart failure, ketones may
also have other beneficial effects on endothelial function, oxidative
stress, inflammation, and cardiac remodeling.42 Other types of fat,
such as medium-chain triglycerides, may provide another possible
source of energy for the heart in heart disease since their transport
into the mitochondria is carnitine-independent.
Two small studies have evaluated diets modified in fat content in
dogs with subclinical (American College of Veterinary Internal
Medicine [ACVIM] stage B) degenerative mitral valve disease
(DMVD). A 1-month study of a reduced-sodium diet enriched with
omega-3 fatty acids (as well as antioxidants, taurine, carnitine, and
arginine) showed that client-owned dogs eating the study diet had
larger reductions in maximal left atrial dimension and left
ventricular internal dimension in diastole compared to dogs eating
the control diet.43 A 6-month study of a reduced-sodium diet
enriched with medium-chain triglycerides (as well as omega-3 fatty
acids, vitamin E, taurine, lysine, methionine, and magnesium)
showed that dogs in a colony eating the study diet had a larger
reduction in the ratio of the left atrium to aortic diameters compared
to dogs eating the control diet.44 Additional research is needed to
confirm these findings in larger populations and to determine
whether modifications of dietary fat types and other nutrients can
alter progression of disease, survival, or quality of life in dogs with
heart disease.

MINERALS
Sodium
Recommendations regarding the degree of dietary sodium restriction
and when sodium restriction should be initiated continue to evolve
for dogs and cats with heart disease. Studies in the 1960s showed

that very–low-sodium diets could help to control fluid accumulation
in dogs with CHF.1 Authors in the 1960s and 1970s recommended
changing animals to a severely sodium restricted diet when a heart
murmur was first detected, even before clinical signs were present.
However, sodium restriction in subclinical heart disease (and even in
CHF) can activate the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system; much
additional research is needed on the optimal timing and degree of
sodium restriction in dogs and cats with heart disease. Because of
lack of documented benefits and potential adverse effects of severe
sodium restriction in subclinical disease, the authors recommend
only mild sodium restriction (<100 mg/100 kcal) in subclinical heart
disease (ACVIM, stages A and B). However, this is an opportune time
to begin educating the owner about sodium coming from the
animal’s overall diet—the pet food, treats, table food, and how
medications are administered—as it is generally much easier to
institute dietary modifications at this earlier stage, before the animal
develops clinical signs of CHF (ch. 229). Most owners are unaware
of the sodium content of pet foods and human foods and need very
specific instructions regarding appropriate foods and acceptable lowsalt treats (https://heartsmart.vet.tufts.edu/).
When CHF first arises (ACVIM stage C), additional sodium
restriction is recommended (<80 mg sodium/100 kcal). This can be
achieved with a veterinary diet designed for animals with heart
disease (although cardiac diets with low protein levels should be
avoided) or with certain other veterinary diets (which may be
designed for other disease) or even some over-the-counter diets. The
content of sodium and other nutrients, such as protein, potassium,
and magnesium, can be found by consulting manufacturers’ product
guides, by calling the manufacturers, or from reputable websites
(e.g., https://heartsmart.vet.tufts.edu/). Caution is indicated
with “senior diets,” which often are reduced in protein, as this is not
recommended for animals with heart disease. Senior diets also vary
tremendously in sodium content (and content of other nutrients). In
one study of 37 commercial diets marketed for senior dogs, the
sodium content ranged from 33-412 mg/100 kcal.45 Similarly, diets
designed for animals with renal disease are usually not
recommended, even though they might be low in sodium content,
because of the protein restriction (unless proteinuria or advanced

renal disease is present). As CHF becomes more severe, more
sodium restriction may allow lower dosages of diuretics to be used to
control clinical signs.46 There currently are no commercial
veterinary diets marketed specifically for cats with heart disease in
the United States, but several veterinary and over-the-counter diets
are reduced in sodium and may meet an individual cat’s nutritional
needs. This information can be found in manufacturers’ product
guides, by calling manufacturers, or from reputable websites that
compile this information (one list of some products is available at
https://heartsmart.vet.tufts.edu/). In addition to sodium from
the pet food, all sources of dietary sodium must be considered (see
below).

Potassium
Hypokalemia (ch. 68) causes muscle weakness and potentiates
arrhythmogenesis. In addition, Class I antiarrhythmic drugs (e.g.,
mexiletine, lidocaine) are relatively ineffective in the face of
hypokalemia. Hypokalemia can be precipitated using loop diuretics
(e.g., furosemide, torsemide), thiazide diuretics (e.g.,
hydrochlorothiazide), or inadequate dietary intake (often associated
with anorexia or hyporexia). Hypokalemia is most common when
animals are receiving high diuretic doses or multiple diuretics.
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors cause renal
potassium sparing, which can result in increased serum potassium
and, therefore, some animals develop hyperkalemia. Spironolactone,
now recommended for dogs with ACVIM stage C CHF, is an
aldosterone antagonist and a potassium-sparing diuretic. While
animals receiving ACE inhibitors or spironolactone can develop
hyperkalemia, hyperkalemia severe enough to affect appetite or
clinical status is a less common occurrence, unless dogs are eating a
diet that contains high levels of potassium or are receiving a
potassium supplement. A serum potassium concentration between
5.5-6.0 mEq/L (5.5-6.0 mmol/L) warrants more detailed assessment
of the diet for high sources of potassium and more frequent
monitoring. Potassium concentrations >6.0 mEq/L (>6.0 mmol/L)
likely require intervention (e.g., medication adjustment, potassium
binders, and/or further reduction in dietary potassium
concentrations).

Commercial diets vary widely in potassium concentrations.
Commercial reduced-sodium diets range from <150 to >300 mg
potassium/100 kcal, with an AAFCO minimum of 150 mg/100 kcal
for dogs and for cats. If hyperkalemia is present in an animal with
heart disease, a diet with a lower potassium content should be
selected. Conversely, if an animal is hypokalemic, a diet higher in
potassium or oral potassium supplementation is indicated. Dietary
potassium information can be obtained by contacting manufacturers
or reviewing reputable websites that compile this information (e.g.,
https://heartsmart.vet.tufts.edu/).

Magnesium
Magnesium (ch. 68) plays an important role in normal cardiac
function. Alterations in magnesium homeostasis can occur in people
and dogs and can have deleterious effects in a variety of
cardiovascular conditions including hypertension, coronary artery
disease, CHF, and cardiac arrhythmias. Some cardiac drugs,
including loop diuretics, are associated with magnesium depletion.
Therefore, animals with CHF have the potential to develop
hypomagnesemia.47 Hypomagnesemia can increase the risk of
arrhythmias, decrease cardiac contractility, cause muscle weakness,
contribute to renal potassium loss, and can potentiate the adverse
effects of certain cardiac medications.
Hypomagnesemia has not been well-studied in animals with heart
disease, but hypomagnesemia can be difficult to measure since
serum magnesium concentrations are a poor indicator of total body
stores. Therefore, normal serum magnesium does not necessarily
mean there are adequate total body stores. Ionized magnesium levels
are thought to be a better reflection of total body magnesium.
However, it still can be useful to routinely measure serum
magnesium concentration, especially in animals with arrhythmias or
those on large doses of diuretics.
Like potassium, magnesium concentrations vary widely in
commercial pet foods. Commercial reduced-sodium diets for dogs
can contain between 10 and 50 mg magnesium/100 kcal (AAFCO
minimum of 15 mg/100 kcal for dogs and 10 mg/100 kcal for cats). A
diet high in magnesium would be indicated for an animal with a low
serum magnesium concentration. In some animals with low serum

magnesium concentrations, diet adjustment alone will not correct
the problem and oral supplementation will be required.

VITAMINS
B Vitamins
Thiamine deficiency (ch. 14) is known to be a cause of
cardiomyopathy in people and to occur in human patients with heart
failure,48 but there has been little investigation into the role of B
vitamins as a cause of heart disease in dogs and cats. However,
reduced food intake and urinary loss of water-soluble vitamins
secondary to diuretics could contribute to low B vitamin
concentrations in patients with CHF. Research suggests that
vitamins B6, B12, and folate may be significantly lower in cats with
cardiomyopathy than in healthy controls, an effect that appeared to
be unrelated to diet or furosemide use.49,50 Animals with heart
disease (at least those receiving diuretics) may have higher B vitamin
requirements. Routine supplementation of B vitamins in animals
with heart disease on good quality commercial diet is likely
unnecessary; however, empirical supplementation may be
considered in animals on high dosages of diuretics, especially those
with anorexia or hyporexia, or in animals on an unbalanced diet.

OTHER NUTRIENTS
Carnitine
L-carnitine is concentrated in skeletal and cardiac muscle and is
critical for fatty acid metabolism and energy production. Carnitine
deficiency is associated with primary myocardial disease in a number
of species, and has been described in a family of Boxer dogs.51
Anecdotal reports exist regarding the efficacy of L-carnitine in canine
DCM, but no blinded prospective monotherapy studies have been
done so its role in DCM remains unclear. Even if carnitine deficiency
is not the inciting cause of DCM, L-carnitine supplementation could
be beneficial by improving myocardial energy production. A study of

rapid pacing–induced CHF in dogs showed that myocardial
concentrations decreased in normal dogs after the onset of CHF52;
however, effects of supplementation in dogs that do not have a
primary deficiency are unknown. There are few side-effects of Lcarnitine supplementation except for mild gastrointestinal issues in
some animals. The authors currently discuss the option of Lcarnitine supplementation (50 to 100 mg/kg PO q8h) with owners of
dogs with DCM. As with other dietary supplements, quality control
varies widely,53 so specific brands of L-carnitine supplement should
be recommended.

Antioxidants
Much attention has been given to antioxidants for their potential role
in the prevention and treatment of human heart diseases. Reactive
oxygen species are a byproduct of oxygen metabolism for which the
body normally compensates through the production of endogenous
antioxidants. An imbalance between oxidant production and
antioxidant protection, however, could increase the risk for heart
disease or contribute to progression. Antioxidants are produced
endogenously but also can be supplied exogenously. The major
antioxidants include enzymatic antioxidants (e.g., superoxide
dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase) and oxidant quenchers
(e.g., vitamin C, vitamin E, glutathione, and beta-carotene). In dogs
with heart disease, there have been conflicting results on oxidants
and antioxidants. Early studies of oxidative stress and antioxidants
in heart disease showed that in dogs with CHF due to either DCM or
DMVD, there is an imbalance between increased oxidant production
and reduced antioxidant protection, particularly as the disease
becomes more severe and particularly for the fat-soluble vitamins
(e.g., vitamin E).54,55 Two subsequent studies did not show a
significant difference in oxidative stress (although, in one, a measure
of oxidative stress decreased significantly in dogs with DMVD after
treatment with atorvastatin). Results of recent studies on antioxidant
results also have been variable, with some showing reduced
antioxidant capacity, some showing no difference, and others
showing increased antioxidants.56-62 It is challenging to compare
study results due to differences in methodology (e.g., breeds, form of

heart disease, measures and methodology for assessment of
antioxidants and oxidative stress, etc.). Therefore, more research is
needed on the potential role of oxidative stress in the pathogenesis
and progression of heart disease in dogs. Only one study has
assessed antioxidants and oxidative stress in cats with heart
disease.63 Cats with HCM had lower concentrations of superoxide
dismutase but no significant differences in total antioxidant capacity,
glutathione peroxidase, or malondialdehyde (a measure of lipid
peroxidation).63
Despite the variable and conflicting results, supplemental
antioxidants are included in many commercial veterinary diets. In
one study of dogs with ACVIM stage B DMVD, a cardiac diet
enriched with antioxidants increased circulating antioxidant
concentrations and reduced measures of oxidation.43 However,
potential clinical benefits of antioxidant supplementation require
additional study.

Coenzyme Q10
Coenzyme Q10 is a cofactor in a number of energy-producing
reactions but it also has antioxidant properties. Some studies in
people with CHF due to DCM suggest a beneficial effect of this
supplement. Possible reasons for the purported benefits of
supplementation include correction of a deficiency, improved
myocardial metabolic efficiency, or increased antioxidant protection.
Although coenzyme Q10 supplementation has anecdotally been
reported to be beneficial in dogs with DCM, there is limited
information from experimentally-induced models and naturallyoccurring heart disease that support efficacy of this product. One
study of experimentally-induced CHF in dogs showed that neither
serum nor myocardial coenzyme Q10 concentrations were reduced
after the development of CHF.64 Additionally, coenzyme Q10
supplementation increased serum, but not myocardial,
concentrations.64 In dogs with a variety of naturally-occurring
acquired heart diseases of different stages, plasma concentrations of
coenzyme Q10 were not significantly different compared to healthy
controls and did not differ based on severity of disease.65 As in the

induced canine model, myocardial concentrations were significantly
lower in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels with CHF (ACVIM stage C)
compared to either Cavalier King Charles Spaniels in stage B or
healthy control dogs of other breeds.66
An often-recommended dosage of coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) in
dogs is 30 mg PO q12h, although up to 90 mg PO q12h has been
recommended for large dogs. However, the dose depends not only on
dog size but also on the form of coenzyme Q10. The most common
supplemental form is ubiquinone (the oxidized form) which may be
better absorbed with meals. The reduced form, ubiquinol, is thought
to have greater bioavailability and is the active form, at least in
humans. The optimal dosage of ubiquinol for dogs is unknown. One
study in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels with DMVD showed that 3
weeks of supplementation with coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone; 100
mg/dog) was not associated with changes in echocardiographic
measurements or cardiac biomarkers.67 Further research is needed
in dogs and cats with different forms of heart disease, especially
DCM, and with different forms and dosages of coenzyme Q10.

OTHER RELEVANT DIET/NUTRITIONAL
ISSUES
DIET-ASSOCIATED DCM
In July 2018, the United States Food and Drug Administration
(FDA) released an initial alert on its investigation of a potential
connection between diet and DCM in pets eating diets containing a
high proportion of peas, lentils, other pulses, or potatoes, many of
which were labeled as grain-free. This initial communication was
followed by three additional updates.68-71 What differentiates these
diet-associated DCM cases from typical primary (genetic) DCM
occurring in certain breeds, such as Doberman Pinschers and Great
Danes, is that diet-associated DCM can occur in any breed (including
breeds predisposed to primary DCM) and they have improvements
in cardiac function or even reversal of heart disease after a diet
change.32,72-76 Additionally, if the diet is changed, these dogs have a

longer survival time than do dogs with primary DCM.73,75 As of
November 2022, 1380 canine cases of DCM had been reported to the
FDA.76 Very few dogs with diet-associated DCM (except one study of
Golden Retrievers) have had low taurine concentrations (in fact,
many are high), so the exact role of taurine remains unclear.32,72-75
Although the cause of diet-associated DCM in dogs is currently
unknown, it is thought to be due to a deficiency or, more likely,
toxicity resulting from diets high in pulses. It is also possible that the
cause might be a combination of these nutritional factors, along with
yet unknown genetic or metabolic factors. 77-79
Not only have grain-free and high-pulse diets (often called “nontraditional diets” [ch. 167]) been associated with DCM, but they also
have been associated with earlier, subclinical abnormalities in
cardiac size and function that improve after diet change.74,80 Even
in apparently healthy dogs eating non-traditional diets, studies have
shown larger left ventricular diameter, lower contractility, higher
circulating cardiac troponin I concentrations, and more ventricular
premature complexes.81-83 While studies have shown that longer
duration eating non-traditional diets was associated with more
advanced disease and shorter survival time,74,75 at least one study in
healthy dogs showed a significant increase in left ventricular size
after only 3 months of eating a high-pulse diet.84 These results
suggest that DCM may represent end-stage damage to the heart, with
more subtle, subclinical changes occurring initially.
The majority of cases reported to the FDA have been dogs, but, as
of July 2020, more than 20 cats with suspected diet-associated DCM
were also reported.70,76 One small retrospective study showed that
cats with DCM eating high-pulse diets that changed diet had a
significantly longer survival time than those that did not change
diet.85 Grain-free diets and diets high in pulses have become
extremely popular for cats, as well as dogs, so further investigation in
cats is warranted. Until then, diet-associated DCM should be
considered in cats with DCM eating high-pulse diets (or
unconventional diets, such as vegan, vegetarian, or homemade diets
in which taurine deficiency can still occur [ch.167]).

At this point, specific ingredient(s) and the etiology of the current
diet-associated DCM problem remain unknown, but pulses (i.e.,
peas, lentils, chickpeas, dry beans) appear most likely at the heart of
diet-associated DCM.77 It is impossible to determine the presence or
absence of pulses in diets based only on the diet’s name or whether it
contains grains since many grain-inclusive diets now contain pulses.
Therefore, the diet’s full ingredient list must be reviewed. If the diet
contains pulses in the top 10 ingredients (or multiple pulses
anywhere on the list), it might put some pets at risk for DCM.
Although potatoes and sweet potatoes are also common in many of
the reported diets, their role remains unclear. If DCM (or earlier
changes, such as reduced systolic function, left ventricular
enlargement, or unexplained arrhythmia) is diagnosed in a dog or cat
eating a high-pulse diet, the authors recommend changing the diet to
one without pulses or potatoes/sweet potatoes (and with an
appropriate nutritional profile for the individual patient). If clinical
signs or significant systolic dysfunction or cardiac enlargement are
present, cardiac medications are indicated (chs. 233 and 234).
Despite the low prevalence of taurine deficiency in dogs with dietassociated DCM, until more is known, the authors recommend
measuring plasma and whole blood taurine concentrations in dogs
with DCM/systolic dysfunction if financially feasible (or
supplementing taurine if cost is prohibitive; see above).
Improvement of the heart can take months to years and, unless
changes are detected early, most dogs’ hearts do not reverse
completely. Therefore, it is important not to taper or discontinue
cardiac medications too quickly. Also, sudden death is common so
careful monitoring and treating arrhythmias proactively is
important. More research is needed but this issue has emphasized
the importance of the nutritional assessment, particularly the diet
history, in all patients (ch. 145).

PRACTICAL ASPECTS OF FEEDING THE
PATIENT WITH HEART DISEASE
There is not a single “best” diet for managing heart disease. It is
important to match the nutritional needs of an individual patient to

the diet or diets that best suit those needs. Patients with heart
disease vary in terms of their clinical signs, laboratory parameters,
and food preferences, and these all affect diet selection. Concurrent
diseases, which were present in more than half of dogs and cats with
heart disease, also influence diet choice (ch. 223).11,12 For example,
the optimal diet for a cat with HCM alone is very different from that
of a cat with HCM and chronic kidney disease or feline lower urinary
tract disease (ch. 223). Laboratory results, such as the presence of
moderate to severe azotemia, or alterations in potassium or
magnesium, also can affect selection of optimal diet(s). Therefore,
the same diet will not be ideal for all animals with heart disease. For
example, a different diet will be appropriate for a small breed dog
with DMVD and well-controlled CHF, with normal laboratory values,
a BCS=7/9, and no muscle loss than for another dog with the same
disease but with more advanced CHF, with a BCS=4/9 and moderate
muscle loss, dysrexia, hyperkalemia, and hypoalbuminemia. It is also
important to take the animals’ and owners’ preferences into
consideration (e.g., canned vs dry, brand, type, veterinary diet vs
over-the-counter) to increase the likelihood for good compliance and
successful outcome.
Performing a nutritional assessment on every patient at every visit
can optimize nutritional and medical management (ch. 145). The
nutritional assessment helps to identify whether the current diet
could be contributing to the heart disease (e.g., in a dog with DCM
eating a non-traditional or vegan diet or a cat with CHF eating a diet
very high in sodium), if the current diet is optimized for managing
the heart disease, and what the animal’s and owner’s preferences are.
In addition, the nutritional assessment identifies all components of
the animal’s diet that will need to be addressed in making a
nutritional plan. Nutritional screening includes a diet history, body
weight, BCS (ch. 72), muscle condition score, and the knowledge of
other medical conditions that also require nutritional modification
(e.g., gastrointestinal disease, feline lower urinary tract disease,
chronic kidney disease).13,14 Diet history (ch. 145) should be
assessed at every visit as this can identify factors that are
contributing to the cardiac disease, clinical signs, or muscle loss (e.g.,
high sodium intake, inadequate calorie or protein intake,
nutritionally unbalanced diet) or that need to be modified in order to

optimize the overall care of the patient. General diet history forms
are available14 or one specifically designed for animals with heart
disease can be used (E-Box 157.1). The diet history includes the
main pet food being provided (or the home-prepared diet recipe
being used, if any), but also treats, table food, dietary supplements,
rawhides, dental chews, and foods used for medication
administration.

W it h H e ar t D is e as e

From Smith FWK Jr, Tilley LP, Oyama MA, et al. Manual of Canine
and Feline Cardiology. 5th ed. Elsevier; 2016; reprinted with
permission.
Based on the nutritional assessment, diets can be matched to the
individual patient. In the United States, there currently are three
commercial veterinary diets that are specifically designed for animals
with heart disease. Specific characteristics of these foods vary, but
they are moderately to severely sodium-restricted, generally contain
increased levels of B vitamins, and vary widely in their protein

content; ensuring adequate protein intake is critical. Some cardiac
diets also may include increased levels of taurine, carnitine,
antioxidants, or omega-3 fatty acids. There also are many veterinary
diets designed for other diseases or even over-the-counter diets that
may have the desirable nutritional profile (examples can be obtained
from individual manufacturers or on some websites: e.g.,
https://heartsmart.vet.tufts.edu/). Above all, the diet must be
palatable enough that the animal will willingly eat it. The authors
typically determine several diets that would be appropriate for an
individual animal. These diets are offered as choices for the owner
and the pet. Having dietary choices is particularly beneficial for
patients with moderate to severe CHF, in which dysrexia is present
and a cyclical or selective loss of appetite is common. A starting goal
for calorie recommendations in animals with CHF is 1.0-1.2 × resting
energy requirements (ch. 145), but adjustment is necessary to
maintain ideal body weight, BCS, and muscle condition score. All
diet recommendations should also include discussion of treats, table
food, and foods used for medication administration (Box 157.2).13
As mentioned earlier, changes in food intake and eating patterns
are a common problem in animals with CHF and can contribute to
cachexia (ch. 151). Another important problem with reduced or
altered food intake is that it may affect survival by influencing an
owner’s decision to euthanize the pet. In one study of owners of dogs
euthanized for CHF, reduced appetite was one of the most common
contributing factors to the euthanasia decision.86 Anorexia,
hyporexia, and dysrexia become more common as heart disease
becomes more advanced. Sudden changes in appetite often herald a
change in CHF control or a need to change medications, but
fluctuation in appetite does happen even when CHF is well
controlled. Owners of dogs and cats with CHF often report a variable
or cyclical appetite, where the animal will eat one food well for a few
days and then refuses it but will eat a different food well. This
dysrexia is common in animals with moderate to advanced CHF. The
authors find it beneficial to warn owners of animals with CHF of
hyporexia and dysrexia and to provide multiple appropriate diet
options for the owner to feed (e.g., they can feed one diet for several
days until the animal no longer has interest for that food and then
switch to a different food; animals will often be willing to eat the

original food again, so owners can use a “rotation” of foods to keep
the pet eating). It is important to advise the owner that if the animal
also is acting lethargic, is tachypneic, won’t eat any foods or if it has
been eating very well and then suddenly stops eating, this usually
indicates the need for reassessment and adjustment of medications.
Recommendations for managing reduced or altered food intake are
listed in Box 157.3. In animals with an acute episode of CHF, it is
important to avoid changing the diet until the patient is stabilized.
Once the animal is home and stabilized on medications, a gradual
change to a new diet can be made. Forced dietary changes when the
animal is sick or starting new medications may induce food aversions
and should be avoided. As previously mentioned, appetite stimulants
(e.g., capromorelin, mirtazapine) can be helpful to minimize issues
with food intake.

Foods commonly used to administer your pet’s pills can provide a
large amount of additional salt to your pet’s diet, which is not
recommended. Preferable ways to give medications include:
• Have your veterinarian show you how to give medications
without using food
• Use a “pill popper” or “pill gun”
• Insert medications into one of the following foods:
Dogs or Cats
• Low-sodium canned pet food
• Home-cooked meat such as chicken or hamburger (made
without salt); not lunch meats or rotisserie chicken
• Canned whipped cream (e.g., Reddi Wip)
• Whipped cream cheese; find a brand with less than 80 mg
sodium per 100 calories
• Mini marshmallows

• Greenies Pill Pockets (Caution: Not all similar products from
other companies are low in sodium.)
• Dog Pill Pockets: peanut butter, hickory, or cheese flavors
• Cat Pill Pockets: tuna or salmon flavors are recommended
• Avoid chicken flavor and grain-free duck and pea flavor which
are higher in sodium
• Try to use the smallest size possible and as few as possible to
avoid excessive sodium
Dogs
• Soft fruit, such as banana, orange, melon, or strawberries (avoid
grapes)
• Peanut butter (only if labeled as “no salt added” or “unsalted”)
For up-to-date lists of low-sodium foods, see the HeartSmart
treats list: https://heartsmart.vet.tufts.edu/forms/

• Assess the patient for optimal medical control of heart failure
(ch. 229).
• Assess the patient for side effects of medications (e.g.,
dehydration, azotemia, hyperkalemia, drug toxicosis).
• Feed more frequent but smaller meals.
• Provide multiple diet options so owners can rotate foods if
hyporexia or dysrexia occurs.
• Warm the food to body temperature (for cats). Try different
temperatures of food for dogs—they may prefer it warmed, at
room temperature, or even cold.
• Feed the animal from a different type of dish (e.g., a new food
dish or a human dinner plate).
• Feed in a different location in the house (or feed outside for a
change of scenery).

• Flavor enhancers
• Add homemade chicken, beef, or fish broth made without salt
or seasoning to the food (even low-sodium store-bought
broths are too high in sodium).
• Add a small amount (1-2 teaspoons [5-10 mL]) of cooked
meat (hamburger, chicken, or fish) to the food. Be sure to
instruct the owner not to use any prepared foods, such as
rotisserie chicken, lunch meats, or canned meats or fish due
to their high sodium content.
• Cats typically prefer meat or fish as a palatability enhancer.
Meat or fish also may enhance food intake in dogs, but some
dogs prefer sweet flavors as a palatability enhancer (e.g.,
maple syrup, applesauce, sugar, fruit-flavored yogurt).
• Supplement fish oil, which is high in omega-3 fatty acids, to
reduce inflammatory cytokines. This may have modest benefits
for appetite. However, if the pet does not like the taste and the
owner cannot administer the capsule without food, fish oil
should be avoided.
• Consider an appetite stimulant drug (i.e., capromorelin in dogs,
capromorelin or mirtazapine in cats).
In many cases, desired nutrient modifications can be achieved
through diet alone. However, supplementation of certain nutrients
may be desirable if they are either not in a particular diet or not at
high enough levels to achieve the desired effect. It is important to be
aware that dietary supplements currently do not require proof of
safety, efficacy, or quality control to be marketed. Therefore,
veterinarians should consider recommending specific brands of
dietary supplements that bear the logo of the United States
Pharmacopeia Dietary Supplement Verification Program
(https://www.quality-supplements.org/), which tests human
dietary supplements for ingredients, concentrations, dissolvability,
and contaminants. Another good resource is Consumerlab.com,
which performs independent testing of dietary supplements
(primarily human supplements but also some pet products).
In addition to finding one or more diets that have the desired
nutritional properties and palatability, it also is important to devise

an overall dietary plan that meets the owner’s expectations. This
includes finding a diet that the owner perceives the pet to enjoy,
providing acceptable treats, and devising a satisfactory method for
administering medications. In one study, > 90% of dogs with heart
disease received treats and these treats are often high in sodium.11
Fewer cats (33%) receive regular treats but this additional source of
nutrients also should be addressed with cat owners.12 In addition,
the majority of people administering medications to their dogs use
foods as a way to administer the medication,11,12 so appropriate
methods of medication administration should be provided to owners
(see Box 157.2). Only 34% of cat owners use foods to administer
medications,12 but because of the difficulty of this activity in cats,
special care should be taken to ensure that the cat owner can be
successful and adherent in medication administration. Including
information regarding all sources of food from pet food, treats, table
food, and medication administration in the overall diet plan is
important to achieve success with nutritional modification.

OVERVIEW—CHRONIC KIDNEY
DISEASE
Special nutritional management is indicated in patients with renal
insufficiency due to chronic kidney disease (CKD). CKD is a
prolonged process marked by irreversible loss of kidney function,
usually without an identifiable cause, and associated with high
morbidity and mortality (ch. 301). A pathological sequence of
events occurs, with the development of secondary

hyperparathyroidism triggered by increased circulating
concentrations of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). This is
followed by a reduction of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 and calcium
levels, thereby increasing parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion,
which leads to the complex of chronic kidney disease–mineral bone
disorder (CKD-MBD). An appropriate dietetic intervention can help
to slow the progressive decline of renal function or may even
temporarily stabilize it. The nutrient supply should be tailored to
meet a patient’s specific requirements in a way that reduces the
kidney workload, as well as slowing the progression of the disease
and compensating for increased renal nutrient losses. Therapeutic
intervention is most successful when initiated early, whereas
treatment of animals that have, or are approaching, end-stage kidney
disease is mostly limited to palliative or supportive care. As the
impact of dietary treatment on a patient’s life expectancy and quality
is highly significant, such treatment should be implemented no later
than when the initial signs of impaired renal efficiency are
diagnosed. Clinical signs and changes in laboratory parameters occur
only after about two-thirds of the nephrons are non-functional.1 This
is due to the kidneys’ substantial functional reserve, and that they
can compensate for sizeable losses of functional tissue through
hypertrophy of viable nephrons. Therefore, animals with an
increased risk of developing CKD should be monitored at regular
intervals. An animal that appears completely healthy in a clinical
examination may have already suffered a significant, yet undetected
loss of kidney function. The development of newer and better early
detection methods, such as measurement of symmetric
dimethylarginine (SDMA) concentrations, to identify impaired renal
health and reduced organ efficacy is a high priority; nevertheless, it
is obvious that an unascertainable, but significant proportion of the
cat and dog population suffers specific and progressive degrees of
CKD. Therefore, a balanced feeding regime to minimize strain to the
kidneys should already be considered in those animals at risk of
developing clinically apparent CKD.
The progressive deterioration of kidney function in patients with
CKD leads to a decreasing ability to excrete various substances
within the urine, such as phosphorus (Figure 158.1). Serum
phosphorus concentrations in the fasted animal remain within

normal ranges until the disease has advanced to a certain stage,
rendering compensatory mechanisms increasingly insufficient.
Hyperphosphatemia and consequently increasing concentrations of
PTH and FGF23 are associated with increased death risk.2 Hence,
high dietary phosphorus intake may worsen hyperparathyroidism
and renal osteodystrophy, especially in patients with CKD. It may
also promote metastatic calcification of the kidneys and vascular
system, the latter increasing cardiovascular events. In addition to
limiting the total amount of dietary phosphorus, its type (“organic”
versus inorganic), source (plant versus animal origin) and other
dietary factors are important considerations. Phosphorus from
plants and animal tissues including bone and cartilage is commonly
defined as “organic.” Phosphorus from phosphate salts such as
sodium and potassium phosphate is considered an inorganic form.
Several of these phosphate salts are highly soluble in water and
acidic solutions,3 which is a precondition for the absorption from the
gastrointestinal tract.4 The apparent digestibility of highly soluble
phosphorus (soluble after 1 minute in water) from NaH2PO4,
KH2PO4, Ca(H2PO4)2 and CaHPO4 amounted to 94.1±7.9% in dogs
in one study, while organic phosphorus from poultry meal and
bovine meat and bone meal had an apparent digestibility of only
21.2±5.9%.5 Serum phosphorus concentrations peaked 3 hours after
ingestion of these soluble phosphorus sources and did not return to
preprandial levels 7 hours postprandially, while excessive intake of
organic phosphorus caused no such effect.6 Hence, knowledge about
the total phosphorus concentration in a diet does not correspond to
assumptions on the quantities absorbed. This is relevant to the
feeding of dogs and cats in general, but especially for canine and
feline CKD patients as complete diets can contain considerable
amounts of highly soluble phosphates. Inorganic phosphate additives
in food and feed processing are used for various reasons, e.g., to
preserve, enhance flavor, retain water, improve color, emulsify,
texturize, buffer, and as an acidulant agent. In plants, especially
some grains and legumes, phosphorus is present in the form of
phytate, which has a reduced bioavailability in monogastric species.
Other dietary factors such as base excess, concentrations of other

minerals (e.g., potassium, sodium, magnesium)—especially calcium
and therefore the Ca:P ratio—influence the absorption and
homeostasis of phosphorus.6,7 Hence, evaluation of total phosphorus
intake alone may not suffice in predicting the actual phosphorus
burden on the animal. High intake of highly soluble inorganic
phosphate can disrupt the phosphorus and calcium homeostasis in
dogs6 and affect renal health indicators in cats.8 Conversely, feeding
excessive amounts of phosphorus from organic sources had no effect
on phosphorus homeostasis and renal health indicators in both
species.

PREVALENCE
CKD leading to uremia is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in
cats and dogs (ch. 301). The prevalence of CKD increases with the
age of the animal, probably due to an increasing chance to develop
irreversible lesions and therefore increasing the likelihood of
progression. The condition has also been increasingly diagnosed over

the past 3 decades in both cats and dogs.9-11 The same holds true in
human medicine.12 This may be partly explained by the increasing
improvement in diagnostic methodology, but also by the increasing
stress levels on renal health. The underlying reasons for such
alterations are mostly unknown; therefore, a retrospective
verification of the cause is seldom possible, which limits the
opportunity to prove the hypothesis of increased burden on renal
health. For dogs and cats, the estimates of prevalence vary widely
depending on the source population, case inclusion criteria and
screening methods. Values from 0.0513 to 3.74%14 are reported for
the canine population. For cats, literature data indicates an even
higher prevalence.11,15

RISK FACTORS FOR DEVELOPMENT OF
CKD
Retrospective verification of underlying reasons for acute or chronic
kidney injury resulting in clinically apparent CKD is generally
impossible. The longer an individual lives, the higher the probability
that incidents of renal injury, and therefore loss of functional
parenchyma occurs; the risk to develop CKD therefore increases with
age. Alongside the well-established causes for renal damage such as
ischemic or nephrotoxic injuries due to anesthesia, infections,
certain drugs, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, fever, sepsis, trauma,
etc., dietary level of protein and phosphorus also is discussed. In
contrast to an assumed potential disadvantage of high dietary
protein intake causing increased kidney strain, it has been
demonstrated that a higher protein supply increased gentamicin
clearance and reduced its nephrotoxicity.16 The authors of this study
hypothesized that in this situation, the beneficial effects of high
protein intake are associated with increased glomerular filtration.
Singer17 described an increasing perfusion rate and glomerular
filtration rate in mammalian species both after acute and chronic
increases in protein intake. Similarly, Böswald and coworkers18
evaluated the protein and phosphorus intake of canine and feline

CKD patients and age-matched healthy controls in a retrospective
study and found no differences between the protein intake of
patients and healthy animals.

NUTRITIONAL FACTORS
ENERGY
Decreases in appetite and thus body weight may be the initial signs
of renal function loss, even months and years before diagnosis.19
Although nonspecific, these signs indicate that a checkup and regular
monitoring of the animal is advisable. Keeping in mind that the
success of an intervention is greatest when the degree of damage to
the organ is still low, the diet should be evaluated and optimized
early. Primarily, a sufficient supply not only of energy, but also of
protein, must be ensured to prevent body weight loss that is
associated with shorter survival. A series of measures should be tried
in case of inappetence (chs. 17, 151). High energy density, i.e., more
calories per unit dry matter, is advantageous in a diet as smaller
amounts have to be ingested to meet energy requirements. Dividing
daily rations into smaller portions to be fed at multiple meals might
increase feed intake. Unfed amounts of food should be removed from
the bowl after about 30 minutes, especially in case of fresh or moist
foods and higher temperature. Some patients increase their food
intake when motivated, e.g., by hand feeding, or when the diet is
heated at ∼30°-35°C. In order to avoid further weight loss, patients
should be motivated and sufficient energy consumption boosted also
by use of appropriate medication and use of individually preferred
feedstuffs or snacks mixed into the daily ration whenever needed.
Water should be offered at any time to help avoid dehydration.

PROTEIN
If a reduction of dietary protein is necessary in a patient with CKD,
this has to be evaluated carefully and individually as a deficient
supply can be detrimental. Reducing an excessive protein supply
might be appropriate in case of considerably increased blood urea
nitrogen (BUN) concentrations in the fasted patient, but an intake

below maintenance requirements should be considered only if the
benefit of protein restriction, i.e., control of hyperammonemia,
outweighs possible negative consequences such as loss of lean body
mass and reduced appetite. Especially in cases of reduced feed
intake, sufficient protein digestibility and quality (e.g., amino acid
pattern) becomes more important. In dogs, maintenance protein
requirements are lower than in cats and consequently the percentage
of essential amino acids in food must be high. In cats, the supply
with nitrogen or crude protein is even more important. To maintain
nitrogen balance, cats need comparably higher amounts of protein
due to their reduced ability to downregulate nitrogen-catabolic
enzymes and therefore protein catabolism. The need for a certain
amount of protein is also due to the fact that protein, especially from
animal sources, enhances palatability in carnivorous species. The
dietary protein level should be adjusted individually to avoid
excessive intake but also to provide a supply high enough to prevent
a negative nitrogen balance with resulting loss of lean body mass and
decreasing plasma protein concentration. Furthermore, protein
intake affects organ perfusion and might help to maintain kidney
function. A dietary intervention must aim to ensure a sufficient level
of albumin and total serum protein whilst limiting the increase of
BUN above the reference range by restricting protein intake. In
patients with fasted BUN levels persisting above the reference range,
the commonly excessive amounts of protein delivered by compound
foods should be slowly reduced, in the beginning to the
recommended allowance of about 6.3 g protein/100 kcal in cats and
4.5 g in dogs.20 The goals of maintaining lean body mass on one
hand and reducing the potential adverse effects on the progression of
protein-losing nephropathy on the other, are controversial and may
indeed be conflicting. A compromise based on the patient’s
individual situation should be sought. To a certain extent, a
limitation of protein intake can be achieved by increasing the fat
content of the diet, which in turn increases the energy density.
Adding a fat source rich in omega-3 fatty acids such as fish oil can be
advantageous due to its renoprotective properties. Adding
fermentable fiber such as pectin (ch. 165) should also be considered,
aiming at nitrogen trapping, i.e., reduced NH3 reabsorption from the

gut and increased fecal excretion of nitrogenous wastes by increased
bacterial growth.

PHOSPHORUS
Even though it is a well-established fact that monitoring of serum
phosphorus concentration is mandatory when animals are growing
older and especially in suspected and diagnosed CKD patients, the
increasing knowledge over the past decades about regulation and
importance of phosphorus homeostasis has highlighted this element.
Multiple hormones (PTH, vitamin D3, FGF23) and organs (kidney,
bone, parathyroid gland, intestine) are involved in this complex
regulatory cascade (chs. 69 and 283). For the body it is crucial to
normalize hyperphosphatemia because it could otherwise lead to
metastatic calcification and increased progression of CKD.21
Phosphorus-induced renal injury is partly mediated through
calcium-phosphate deposition in the organ, which is probably
initiated by local inflammation. In vitro studies in human aortic
smooth muscle cells incubated in a phosphorus medium
demonstrated an increased expression of pro-inflammatory
mediators, as well as an increase in reactive oxygen/nitrogen
species.22 The degree of kidney calcification is related to phosphate
excreted per functional unit rather than plasma phosphate
concentrations alone.23 With progressively reduced renal functional
mass, the concentration of phosphorus per nephron, and therefore
its nephrotoxicity, increases significantly. Both—high intake of
bioavailable phosphorus and a reduced percentage of functioning
renal tissue—increase the potentially harmful amount of phosphorus
that has to be handled by each nephron.
Reported adverse effects of phosphorus range from cytotoxic
impacts to tumor growth, mammalian aging, cardiovascular
disorders, reduced mineral content of bone, and metastatic
calcification, with the resultant effect of compromised survival.24
Features of phosphate toxicosis may appear in
normophosphatemia24; phosphate loading in early CKD results in
renal damage and a more rapid decrease in renal function due to

renal tubular injury. Furthermore, even in the general human
population, high-normal serum phosphate concentrations are
associated with mortality.25,26 In human medicine, it is known that
healthy individuals with serum phosphorus levels in the top quartile
of the normal range have an increased risk of developing CKD.27
Therefore, oral phosphorus intake should be limited in early CKD
and probably even in healthy individuals and as yet undiagnosed
CKD patients. High phosphate intake increases the phosphate
burden and the resulting phosphaturia, which produces secondary
kidney damage by inducing tubular injury and interstitial fibrosis.
Furthermore, it was demonstrated that human subjects with high
serum phosphate concentrations had a higher risk for developing
kidney disease.26 In a recent study, serum phosphorus levels were
the only significant outcome predictors in cats with acute and
chronic renal disease.28
When evaluating the serum phosphorus concentrations, it is
necessary to determine serum calcium concentrations also, and to
calculate the important parameter, calcium-phosphorus product (Ca
× P). This shows the probability of hydroxyapatite crystals forming,
i.e., that metastatic calcification of soft tissue is likely to occur. For
this reason, a serum Ca × P product of ≥55 mg2/dL2 should be
avoided.29 Calcification of the paws in feline and canine CKD
patients has been associated with Ca × P product >70 mg2/dL.2 (30)
Further, serum Ca × P >77 mg2/dL2 is a negative prognostic marker
for dogs with CKD.31 Consequently, this parameter has been
correlated to the staging system according to the International Renal
Interest Society (IRIS) in dogs.32 It is important to note that vascular
mineralization can be suppressed by reducing serum phosphate
levels, even in the presence of extremely high serum calcium and
1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels, as demonstrated in mice.33,34 This
indicates that reducing the phosphorus burden should be the key
therapeutic priority in CKD patients for minimizing the risk of
developing vascular mineralization and disease progression.35
Because other features of the diet such as concentration of other
major minerals may amplify the effects of high phosphorus intake, a

narrow or even inverse Ca:P ratio (i.e., <∼1.3/1), low potassium, and
low magnesium should be avoided.

PRACTICAL FEEDING
If a patient’s serum phosphorus concentration is in the upper
quartile of the reference range for a prolonged time, measures have
to be taken, i.e., phosphorus intake has to be evaluated and adjusted.
This holds true even before the diagnosis of CKD is made, and
therefore in the (apparently) healthy population. When a complete
compound feed is used, it should not contain soluble inorganic
phosphates, which are readily absorbed. If no specific information on
usage of phosphate additives in a specific diet is available, the total
phosphorus concentration should not exceed the recommended daily
allowances36 (RDAs; 75 mg/100 kcal metabolizable energy (ME) in
dogs and 64 mg/100 kcal ME in cats; valid for healthy animals). In
homemade diets, no mineral supplements containing such
phosphate salts should be used. The recommended phosphorus
supply at maintenance level is expressed as an amount per energy
unit or kg of body weight and is based on the average amount of
inevitable endogenous losses of this element and its digestibility or
availability. Nutrient concentrations of compound foods on the
market very often significantly exceed the RDA for most
nutrients,37,38 and in the case of phosphorus, it is often derived
mostly from inorganic phosphorus sources. Moreover, current
recommendations for phosphorus36 are defined for healthy animals
with a normal capacity to excrete this element. A first step should be
to avoid excessive intake and to supply nutrients at maintenance
levels or slightly below. When CKD progresses, the diet should be
adapted individually, based on results of laboratory tests. The use of
a “renal protective” diet that minimizes or avoids highly soluble
inorganic phosphate salts should therefore be considered from IRIS
stage 1 onwards. Further reduction of dietary phosphorus is
necessary when the patient develops hyperphosphatemia,
independent of the stage. This is important also because increasing
FGF23 concentrations are held responsible for direct cardiovascular
effects, amplifying the risk for hypertension. Concerning dietary

protein, an adaptation should be made in proteinuric patients,
independent of the IRIS stage. In all non-proteinuric patients, the
protein intake should ensure a nitrogen balance and sufficient
perfusion of the kidneys provided no conflicting issues exist. In other
words, in proteinuric patients, the protein intake should be at or
somewhat below the RDA provided the caloric intake is normal. This
equates to a protein intake with sufficient concentration of essential
amino acids of about 3.6-4.5 g protein/100 kcal ME in dogs and of 56.3 g protein/100 kcal ME in cats.
Consultation with a board-certified veterinary nutritionist to
advise on an individually adapted diet based on the patient’s most
recent diagnostic values by applying ration calculation is preferable.
