Chapter 159: Nutritional
Management of Lower
Urinary Tract Disease
Yann Queau

A C RO N YM S
CaOx calcium oxalate
FIC feline idiopathic cystitis
IC idiopathic cystitis
LUTD lower urinary tract disease
RSS relative supersaturation
USG urine specific gravity
UTI urinary tract infection

Lower urinary tract disease (LUTD) refers to a variety of disorders
characterized by dysuria, stranguria, pollakiuria, hematuria, periuria
and sometimes urethral obstruction. Leading causes include
idiopathic cystitis (IC; two-thirds of cases; ch. 311) and urolithiasis
(ch. 309) in cats, and bacterial cystitis (ch. 307) followed by
urolithiasis (ch. 308) in dogs.
Determining the etiology (or the lack thereof in the case of IC) of
LUTD is crucial for successful nutritional management. Dietary
history (ch. 145), information on the patient’s environment,

potential comorbidities or metabolic disorders, and quantitative
analysis of the stone(s) when present, are essential to guide and
optimize dietary treatment.

UROLITHIASIS
Uroliths are polycrystalline structures that form under certain
conditions, affecting concentrations of crystalloids, inhibitors or
promoters of crystallization, and pH. Relative supersaturation (RSS)
is a risk index of crystallization in humans and companion animals.1
To calculate RSS, urine pH and the concentrations of 10 solutes from
a representative urine sample are entered in a computer algorithm.
RSS defines three levels of urine saturation: undersaturation (crystal
dissolution), metastable supersaturation (neither crystal formation
nor dissolution) and labile supersaturation (spontaneous crystal
formation and growth). Another risk index has been developed in
humans (Bonn risk index) and dogs and cats (calcium oxalate [CaOx]
titration test2) for CaOx, to take into account organic promoters and
inhibitors of crystallization. Both are well correlated with RSS. To
date those risk indices are not available in the clinical setting. Urine
specific gravity (USG), urine pH and microscopic evaluation can be
readily performed as indirect and imperfect ways of assessing risk of
crystal formation. Maintaining USG <1.030 in cats and <1.020 in
dogs is often recommended in animals at risk.3

GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS:
STIMULATING DIURESIS
Urine dilution is the paramount strategy for the prevention and/or
dissolution of all types of uroliths. Increased diuresis lowers RSS and
stimulates more frequent urination, decreasing the time for crystal
aggregation. Using wet diets (dietary moisture >70%, cans, pouches,
trays) is an effective way to enhance water intake and diuresis in
dogs and cats.4,5 Adding some wet diet as a portion of a dry diet does
not bring total moisture to a sufficient level to promote urine
dilution. However, warm water can be poured onto kibble: adding 1.5

cups (355 mL) of water to 1 cup (237 mL) of kibble yields
approximately 80% moisture. Acceptance of such diet typically
requires progressive habituation but can be successful in dogs and
cats (Video 159.1

). Palatable liquids offered in addition to tap

water can also increase total water intake and urine volume in both
species.
When feeding exclusively a wet diet is not possible, sodium
chloride supplementation of dry diets is an alternative to promote
urine dilution. In a large number of studies, cats and dogs had
greater water intake and urine volume, and in most cases lower USG
when fed dry commercial diets with sodium contents >2.5 g/1000
kcal.5 The use of high dietary sodium is subject to controversy. Based
on human studies, concerns have been raised regarding renal and
cardiac functions, and blood pressure. However, the vast majority of
short (up to 12 weeks) and long (up to 24 months) studies have
found no effect of a higher sodium intake on renal and cardiac
functions, nor on systemic blood pressure.5 The challenge of
managing concurrent renal disease and cardiac disease in the same
patient is discussed in ch. 223.

SPECIFIC CONSIDERATIONS
ACCORDING TO STONE TYPE
Most stones occur as pure uroliths, whereas 5-15% occur as
compound or mixed uroliths. For the latter, dietary prevention
should target the inner part of the calculus (nidus), which formed
first and facilitated the precipitation of the second mineral.
Nutritional strategies are similar for uroliths in the upper or the
lower urinary tract, but medical and surgical treatment options may
differ (ch. 117).

Struvite
Struvite crystals are composed of magnesium, ammonium, and
phosphate. They can form in sterile urine (most feline cases; ch.
309), or secondary to a urinary tract infection (UTI) with urease-

producing bacteria in dogs (ch. 308). Bacterial urease hydrolyzes
urea into ammonia, increasing urine pH, which overcomes the
acidifying effect of the diet. Therefore, the goals of dietary
management for struvite uroliths depend on the species: prevention
and dissolution in cats, dissolution in dogs. The target is a struvite
RSS <1 for undersaturation and [1-2.5] for metastable
supersaturation.1
High dietary levels of phosphorus and magnesium increase their
urinary excretion and the risk of struvite formation in cats.6
However, urine dilution and pH are more important determinants of
struvite formation.7 Urine dilution is effective to obtain a low struvite
RSS, but so is an acidic urine pH <6.5.5 In alkaline urine, phosphate
is in its trivalent state (PO43−), making it readily available to form
struvite crystals (NH4MgPO4·6H2O). When urine is acidified,
protonation of phosphate (HPO42−, H2PO4− or H3PO4) decreases its
availability. The acidification potential of a diet depends on its
ingredients and the balance between acidifiers (e.g., methionine,
calcium or sodium sulfate, calcium or ammonium chloride) or
alkalizers (e.g., calcium or sodium carbonate, potassium citrate).
Consumption of small meals throughout the day rather than one or
two large meals blunts the postprandial alkaline tide (an increase in
circulating HCO3− concentration after a meal, associated with
secretion of H+ into the gastric lumen; ch. 261) and is associated
with more acidic urine production and less struvite crystalluria.8 The
target urine pH to manage struvite urolithiasis is generally 6.0 to 6.5
(at least for dry diets), to help obtain an RSS <2.5.5 Excessive chronic
acidification increases urinary potassium excretion and can lead to
body potassium depletion if dietary potassium is too low. It could
also promote bone demineralization, although this effect is not
supported by studies in cats.9,10
When struvite uroliths are suspected, medical dissolution is
indicated before surgical removal, except in uncontrollable UTI.3 Dry
and canned veterinary commercial diets with controlled amounts of

precursors, acidifying and/or diuretic properties, successfully
dissolved naturally occurring struvite uroliths in feline studies11-13
(ch. 309). Average dissolution times varied (range 6-141 days), and
dissolution failures were due to stones other than struvite. In dogs,
dissolution can take up to 3 months, and protocols must be
accompanied by appropriate antibiotic therapy14,15 (ch. 308).

Calcium Oxalate
CaOx uroliths are not amenable to medical dissolution. The goal of
dietary management is to reduce the risk of recurrence after stone
removal or prevent further growth when it is not possible (e.g.,
nephroliths). A CaOx RSS of 1-12 corresponds to urine in the
metastable supersaturation zone.
Increasing water intake through dietary moisture or dietary
sodium lowers CaOx RSS in healthy and stone-forming animals in
the majority of studies.5 A concern raised with high sodium diets is
the increased urinary calcium excretion through the inhibition of
renal tubular absorption of calcium.16,17 However, due to concurrent
urine dilution, urine calcium concentration is either unchanged4,16
or decreased.17 The urine concentrations of solutes such as oxalate
can decrease, thus lowering CaOx RSS.4,16,17
The role of dietary precursors in the mechanism of CaOx
formation is poorly understood (chs. 308 and 309). In a
retrospective study, higher dietary moisture, protein, sodium, and
potassium were associated with a lower risk of CaOx in cats.6 In dogs
fed dry and canned diets, the risk of CaOx was higher for diets with
the lowest levels of protein, sodium, potassium, calcium, phosphorus
and magnesium.18,19 Until the underlying pathophysiologic
mechanisms in stone-forming animals, and in particular the role of
hypercalciuria, are further elucidated, the dietary prevention of CaOx
aims at reducing urinary concentrations of calcium and oxalate. High
calcium levels increase its absorption and urinary excretion, which
lead to higher RSS.20 However, calcium absorption is also affected
by dietary phosphorus, magnesium, oxalate and vitamin D. The
effect of dietary oxalate (contained in ingredients such as beets,

beans, potatoes, and leafy vegetables) on its urinary excretion is
variable.20,21 Oxalate absorption is also affected by dietary calcium
and intestinal oxalate-degrading bacteria. In addition, urinary
oxalate excretion is influenced by endogenous production via the
metabolism of some sugars (glucose, fructose), amino acids
(hydroxyproline, glycine, serine) or vitamin C. Deficiency in vitamin
B6 (pyridoxine) leads to increased endogenous production and
urinary excretion of oxalate. However, it is very unlikely, and large
supplementation does not decrease oxaluria.22 In humans, high
animal protein diets are associated with metabolic acidosis and
hypercalciuria and are considered a risk factor for CaOx. Conversely
in dogs and cats, high dietary protein appears to be protective
against CaOx,6,18,19 and leads to increased urine volumes.23 In cats,
one study found slightly higher CaOx RSS with increasing dietary
protein (35-57% dry matter) in dry diets24 but not in wet diets.23
Increasing protein was not associated with a consistent increase in
calcium excretion or a decrease in urinary pH in either study.23,24
The effect of urine pH on the risk of CaOx remains controversial.
The increasing prevalence of CaOx stones has been hypothesized to
be associated with the general acidification of pet foods in the 1980s
and 1990s. Retrospective epidemiological studies have found the
urine acidifying potential of diet (pH <6.25) to be associated with an
increased risk of CaOx in cats6 but not in dogs.18,19 Chronic
metabolic acidosis is believed to promote release of calcium and
phosphate from bone and calciuria—although this has been an
inconsistent finding9,25—and to decrease urinary citrate, an inhibitor
of CaOx crystallization. Retrospective data on short-term feeding
trials do not show a correlation between urine pH and CaOx RSS in
cats.5 Controlled prospective studies have yielded conflicting results,
showing either higher RSS despite similar ionized calcium and
calciuria10 or no difference in RSS.26 Potassium citrate (75 mg/kg
PO q12-24h) is recommended to decrease the risk of CaOx by
alkalinizing urine and increasing citraturia,3 but the optimal dosage
and clinical benefit remain to be determined in controlled studies.

Several veterinary diets include various strategies for the
management of CaOx (e.g., high dietary sodium, addition of
potassium citrate, etc.). Feline diets are typically acidifying to avoid
the concurrent risk of struvite formation. Canned diets exclusively
should be attempted first if possible to maximize urine dilution.3
Studies evaluating the efficacy of those diets to limit recurrence in
stone forming animals are scarce. One feline study showed no
difference of recurrence at 2 years between diets that differed in
calcium and magnesium contents and in urinary pH potential.27 In a
retrospective study, stone-forming dogs fed a high sodium, acidifying
diet (dry or canned) had lower recurrence of oxalate stones on
diagnostic imaging over time than did a group of dogs fed any other
diet.28 Data suggest that despite diet modification, the recurrence
rate in animals with CaOx is high: 33% at 2 years in cats27 and up to
57% at 3 years in dogs.29 If CaOx nephroliths are present with
concurrent kidney disease (ch. 301), a diet formulated for renal
disease is indicated (ch. 158).

Calcium Phosphate
When calcium phosphate uroliths occur as a minor component of
CaOx or struvite stones, the management should be directed towards
the original urolith (nidus). Pure calcium phosphate stones are
associated with metabolic disorders leading to hypercalciuria (e.g.,
hypercalcemia, hyperparathyroidism) and/or alkaline urine pH (e.g.,
renal tubular acidosis). These uroliths are not amenable to medical
dissolution. Treating the underlying cause should be the first step to
reduce the risk of recurrence. The diet should promote urine
dilution, contain a controlled amount of calcium, phosphorus and
vitamin D, and induce a moderately acid urine pH. Commercial diets
marketed for the management of CaOx stones are typically
formulated to achieve those goals, except for some variation
regarding acidification potential of canine diets.

Urate
Dietary management of urate uroliths focuses primarily on
preventing recurrent episodes in susceptible dogs (SLC2A9

mutation, portosystemic shunt) and cats. Medical dissolution has
only been reported in Dalmatians and not in dogs with uncorrected
shunts or in cats.3 As for other uroliths, urine dilution by promoting
water intake should be the first step. Urinary urate results from the
catabolism of endogenous or dietary purines (ch. 267). Decreasing
the purine content of the diet by lowering its protein content or by
selecting protein sources low in purines (plant source, egg white)
helps control urinary urate concentrations.30 Urate crystals are
slightly less soluble in acidic urine; therefore, the diet should not
promote acidic urine.
In dogs, a few commercial diets that are low in purine
concentrations have been evaluated for their effect on urinary urate
excretion and/or stone recurrence in dogs with the SLC2A9
mutation.30-32 Allopurinol (15 mg/kg PO q12h), which inhibits the
conversion of hypoxanthine to uric acid, can be administered to dogs
in conjunction with purine restricted diets to decrease urate
excretion.3 In animals with uncorrected portosystemic shunts and
hepatic encephalopathy, a diet designed for liver disease may be
advised (ch. 154). Properly formulated homemade diets with lowpurine protein sources and sufficient moisture content are also an
option. No dietary study has been conducted in cats, but diets
designed for renal or liver disease are recommended owing to their
protein limitation.

Xanthine
Xanthine uroliths usually occur secondary to allopurinol use in dogs
fed diets high in purines but can also occur spontaneously (ch.
308). No medical dissolution has been reported. Preventing
recurrence of xanthine stones relies on adjustment of allopurinol
dosage and a similar but strict dietary strategy as for urate uroliths.

Cystine
For cystine stones, dietary treatment should be aimed at dissolution
and prevention of recurrence. Again, promoting water intake and
urine dilution is of paramount importance. Urinary cystine excretion
can be modulated by dietary protein intake, and more specifically the

sulfur amino acids methionine and cystine (cysteine). Therefore,
feeding a diet containing amounts of these essential amino acids
close to their minimum requirements is recommended. Most plant
protein sources have lower amounts of sulfur-containing amino acids
than do animal proteins. The solubility of cystine is highly dependent
on pH, with higher solubility for pH >7.5.3 Medical treatment with 2mercaptopropionylglycine (2-MPG) has been successfully used in
dogs3 (ch. 308). In cystinuric dogs, carnitinuria and taurine
deficiency have been found33 and taurine and carnitine are advised
to prevent dilated cardiomyopathy, especially if such dogs are fed
diets restricted in their precursor methionine.

Silica
Silica uroliths are uncommon in dogs and cats, and medical
dissolution has never been reported. For prevention, emphasis
should be put on urine dilution. Preventing pica, avoiding diets high
in high silica plant ingredients (e.g., brown rice or soybean hulls),
and offering bottled water in areas where soil content is high in
silica, are recommended. Canned diets, aside from promoting
diuresis, are typically lower in vegetable ingredients. The effect of
urine pH on the solubility of silica is unknown.

FELINE IDIOPATHIC CYSTITIS
Feline idiopathic cystitis (FIC) is currently believed to result from
abnormal activation of the stress response system (ch. 311). Most
episodes of FIC are self-limiting within 2-7 days. Therapy is aimed at
preventing recurrence: multimodal approach with environmental
enrichment, limitation of social stressors, and improved litterbox
management. Diet is part of this multimodal approach. Based on
limited evidence, wet diets have been recommended for their effect
on diuresis, as diluted urine might be less irritant.34 Oral
glycosaminoglycans have been tested, with no apparent benefit.35 A
commercial diet decreased the incidence rate of some LUTD signs
compared to a control diet differing in several nutrients, although
there was no difference in the proportion of relapsing cats over a 1-

year period.36 The various proportions of dry and wet forms of test
and control diets in those studies, and the multiple nutritional
differences, prevent a firm conclusion from being reached on the
importance of specific nutrients. As stress is a component of FIC,
dietary compounds with anxiolytic effects (tryptophan as a precursor
of serotonin, and alpha-casozepine, which binds to gammaaminobutyric acid receptors) may be useful,37,38 but controlled
studies in cats with FIC are lacking.

URINARY TRACT INFECTION
The role of diet in the prevention and treatment of bacterial UTI (ch.
307) has not been well studied in companion animals and remains
unsettled in humans. Higher urine concentration and osmolality are
hypothesized to be protective against bacterial growth due to the
effects of urea, sodium, and other antimicrobial peptides. In vitro
data suggest greater growth of Escherichia coli in canine urine when
it is more dilute.39 However, low USG has been inconsistently
associated with clinical UTI or subclinical bacteriuria in
epidemiological studies in dogs and cats. Increased water intake and
urine production may help flush out urinary bacteria, and it
decreases cystitis recurrence in women.40 In vitro, bacterial growth
was higher with acidic urine pH in dogs.39 Those results are difficult
to extrapolate because of the important variation of urine pH over
the course of the day, especially with meal feeding.41 No prospective,
controlled study exists to support the recommendation of a target
urine pH to prevent UTI in dogs and cats, nor to maximize the
efficacy of antimicrobials in urine.
Cranberries contain proanthocyanidins, which can inhibit the
adherence of E. coli P-fimbriae to uroepithelium. A randomized trial
did not show any benefit of cranberry supplementation on
bacteriuria or positive culture in dogs.42 In humans, the efficacy of
cranberry supplementation depends on its form, dose, and the target
population. Further studies are needed in companion animals.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Nutritional Management of Urolithiasis
Your dog or your cat has been diagnosed with urinary stones. Diet is
extremely important to manage this condition. It can help dissolving
some types of stones and can reduce the risk of forming stones again.

Struvite Stones (Also Called “Magnesium
Ammonium Phosphate”)
• Your animal has bladder stones. Struvite are suspected and
dissolution attempted:
Adhere strictly to the diet that has been prescribed by your
veterinarian. Not all diets have the same potential to dissolve struvite
stones. Dissolution diets have been specifically formulated and
tested to induce acid urine pH, limit the amount of struvite forming
compounds in the urine, and to dilute urine. Such diets have been
shown to effectively dissolve pure struvite stones: the time required
varies from several days to several weeks depending on the number
and size of stones.
In dogs, it is very important to adhere to the antibiotic treatment.
Struvite stones form because of urinary infection with specific
bacteria. If this infection is not treated, diet alone will not work. A
follow-up consultation with your veterinarian is necessary to ensure
that the dissolution protocol is effective, as sometimes, struvite is
mixed with other stone types, preventing full dissolution.
• Your animal has formed struvite stones, and they have been
removed:
Several diets, including prescription diets, are formulated to
reduce the risk of struvite stone formation. They typically induce acid
urine pH, contain controlled levels of specific minerals (such as
magnesium and phosphorus) to limit the amount of struvite forming
compounds in the urine, and may also dilute the urine.
In dogs, specific diets are not necessary to prevent struvite stone
formation. Struvite form because of a urinary infection with specific

bacteria, which cannot be prevented by the diet.

Calcium Oxalate Stones
Calcium oxalate stones form in urine when concentration of calcium
and/or oxalate is too high. They cannot be dissolved, but diet can
help reduce the risk of formation.
The most important thing is to encourage your animal to drink
important amounts of water, to induce urine dilution (see below).
Some prescription diets are formulated specifically to limit the
excretion of calcium and oxalate in the urine, by controlling dietary
levels and/or dilute urine.

Urate or Xanthine Stones
Urate or xanthine stones form when they are not sufficiently
converted to other more soluble compounds by your animal. It is
therefore important to limit the amount of ingredients that contain
precursors of urate and xanthine (called “purines”). Ingredients such
as vegetables typically contain less purine than meat. Some
prescription diets are formulated specifically to be low in purine. If it
has been prescribed to your animal, it is important to only feed this
diet.
Encouraging your animal to drink to obtain dilute urine is also
very important (see below).

Cystine Stones
In some dogs with genetic abnormality, cystine can leak into the
urine (a condition called “cystinuria”) and form stones due to its low
solubility. Limiting the precursors of cystine in the diet (the two
amino acids methionine and cystine) is important. However, your
animal still needs a minimum quantity of those amino acids in the
diet to avoid deficiencies. Some prescription diets are formulated
with controlled amounts of methionine and cystine and
supplemented with other compounds (such as taurine or carnitine),
which can also be low in dogs with cystinuria.
Encouraging your animal to drink to obtain dilute urine is also
very important (see below).

How to Get Your Animal to Drink Enough Water to
Dilute Its Urine?
There are several ways to ensure that your dog or your cat drink
water in excess of their minimum need, which leads to increased
urination and urine dilution. This can be achieved by feeding canned
food exclusively. Some dry foods are also formulated with salt to
promote drinking, which has been proven safe in dogs and cats
(unless heart disease or kidney disease is present). In dogs, drinking
water can also be poured onto kibbles in significant amounts to
achieve a “soup” consistency (2 cups of water per cup of kibbles).
Mixing dry with canned food is not enough for urine dilution, unless
specifically recommended by your veterinarian. Always ensure that
your animal has access to clean and fresh water.

Can You Give Treats to Your Animal?
Treats should not exceed 10% of the daily calories to avoid
unbalancing the main diet, or negate the effects of this diet in the
management of urinary stones. Some treats may be inappropriate for
some types of stones, because of their effect on urine pH, or because
they contain inappropriate ingredients or nutrients. Always follow
your veterinarian’s advice for appropriate treats.

What Should You Monitor in Your Animal?
• Any signs of difficult and/or painful urination, accompanied
sometimes by vocalization
• Dribbling urine (instead of a continuous stream)
• Urination in inappropriate locations (e.g., outside the litterbox,
inside the house)
• Urine with abnormal color: red, brown
If any of those signs recur, please consult your veterinarian
rapidly. They can be caused by stones that have formed again, but
also by other causes which must be investigated.
Yann Queau (Aimargues, France)

Nutrition has a fundamental role in the prevention and
management of several dermatologic disorders.1-3 This chapter will
discuss the following three distinct areas: (1) food allergy (cutaneous
adverse food reaction); (2) nutritional deficiencies; and (3)
nutritional supplementation for the management of skin diseases.

FOOD ALLERGIES1,4-13

The development of hypersensitivity to one or more food ingredients
in the diet can cause skin or gastrointestinal (ch. 262) disorders or
both (ch. 166).9,10 Pruritus is the most frequently observed
presenting dermatologic sign, which can be accompanied by
subsequent self-inflicted lesions (e.g., alopecia, excoriation,
erythema). Allergic otitis externa is a common feature of food
hypersensitivity in dogs and sometimes is the only clinical
manifestation. Food allergy can mimic other allergic conditions such
as atopic dermatitis or flea allergy dermatitis, and the clinical picture
can be complicated further by the presence of these disorders
concurrently, as well as with secondary pyoderma or M alassezia
dermatitis. In cats, food hypersensitivity can present as self-inflicted
symmetrical alopecia, excoriations (particularly involving the head
and neck), miliary dermatitis, and eosinophilic plaques.6,10

DIAGNOSIS OF FOOD
HYPERSENSITIVITY
Currently, an elimination (i.e., restriction) diet followed by
provocation trials remains the gold standard for diagnosing skinmanifesting food allergies in dogs and cats.7,12,14 Other tests such as
intradermal skin testing with food antigens, skin patch testing,
measuring serum food-specific immunoglobulin E, as well as direct‐
to‐consumer hair and saliva test for pet allergies are not reliable in
dogs and cats because of their low sensitivity and/or specificity for
the diagnosis of food allergy.7,13
Before considering initiating an elimination diet trial, it is of
utmost importance to first exclude ectoparasites (e.g., fleas, lice,
Sarcoptes, Cheyletiella, Otodectes; see textbook’s inside covers) and
bacterial and yeast infections as potential causes of pruritus. Usually,
the food trial is conducted only if residual pruritus persists after
parasitic and infectious causes of pruritus have been excluded or
controlled.

Feeding the Elimination Diet

The elimination diet consists of feeding dietary components to which
the animal has not previously been exposed. The length of the trial is
usually up to 8 weeks.4 This can be accomplished either with a
home-prepared diet or a commercial diet.

Home-Prepared Elimination Diets
Home-prepared elimination diets, which typically contain a single
novel meat source and a single novel starch source, have long been
considered the “gold standard” for diagnosing a food allergy.
The food ingredients chosen for the elimination diet trial should be
based on the known past exposure of the patient to various foods,
avoiding dietary protein and carbohydrate sources to which the
patient has been exposed. Because ingested animal proteins often are
incriminated as the offending allergen and because of possible crossreactivity among various meat sources, lentils, kidney beans, or other
legumes could be a more suitable protein source for home-cooked
diet trials in dogs. Conversely, only a novel animal meat source is
sometimes used in cats. Usually, it is not recommended to add
supplements (e.g., essential fatty acid [EFA], vitamins, minerals)
during the elimination trial since they could be potential sources of
allergens (e.g., fish oil, gelatin capsule), and because of the fixed
duration of the trial. Home-cooked diets, although incomplete and
unbalanced, can be used safely for the diagnostic phase in most
otherwise healthy adult pets.

Commercial Hypoallergenic Elimination Diets
Commercial hypoallergenic elimination diets contain either a
hydrolyzed or “novel” (i.e., restricted) ingredients. They offer
convenience and are guaranteed to be nutritionally complete and
balanced. However, they are not always as reliable as home-prepared
elimination diets. This may be due to presence of processing agents,
storage mites, only partially hydrolyzed proteins, and/or crosscontamination in processing plants with proteins and carbohydrates
not even listed on the pet food label.8,11
The trial diet should be introduced gradually over a few days. No
other food sources should be given (no treats, bones, table scraps,
flavored medications, toothpaste, or toys; no glucosamine, vitamins,

omega-3 EFAs, or other supplements; no access to other pet food if
in a multipet household, etc.). Extensive client education is essential
for client compliance to avoid failure of dietary trials.
Improvement of clinical signs usually is observed within 4 weeks
but may take up to 12 weeks for complete resolution in some cats
(e.g., those with eosinophilic plaques).

Dietary Provocation Test (Oral Food Challenge)
If resolution or a substantial decrease in pruritus level is observed
during the course of the elimination diet trial, the patient must be
rechallenged with all the original dietary components at the end of
the trial to confirm the diagnosis of food hypersensitivity. This is to
ensure that improvement over this length of time was not only
coincidental (e.g., change of season, concurrent new treatments).
Recurrence of pruritus within 2 weeks (as early as 15 minutes postingestion, and usually within 1 week) should occur in cases of food
hypersensitivity.12 The diagnosis of food hypersensitivity is
confirmed if pruritus relapses upon challenge with the original diet
and subsides again on re-introduction of the elimination diet.

Identifying the Offending Dietary Ingredients
Normally, this is done once the patient is fed a suitable commercial
hypoallergenic diet and the pruritus is in remission. One food
ingredient which is most likely to be the cause of food
hypersensitivity (e.g., beef, chicken, dairy products, wheat, lamb,
fish) is introduced and given for a period of 2 weeks or until pruritus
is noted.5,12 If the patient eats this food item for 2 weeks with no
adverse effect, he/she is not allergic to that ingredient and should be
able to consume it without a problem. However, if the patient
develops clinical signs on a challenge food item, the owner should
avoid giving that food item in the future. The patient should then be
fed only with the suitable commercial hypoallergenic diet until the
signs have resolved before repeating this process with other
suspected ingredients.

LONG-TERM MANAGEMENT OF FOOD
HYPERSENSITIVITY
Long-term nutritional management of food hypersensitivity usually
relies on feeding the allergic patient with a diet that is palatable,
complete and balanced, and that does not contain the offending
allergen(s). This is usually accomplished by feeding a commercial
“hypoallergenic diet” tolerated by the patient. Occasionally, once the
offending food item(s) is/are identified, it is possible to feed a
standard commercial diet that the patient tolerates. Home-cooked
diets generally are not recommended for long-term maintenance
because they are inconvenient for many owners and need to be
supplemented to be complete and balanced. If a home-cooked diet is
chosen (because of unavailability of a suitable commercial diet or
owner’s preference) it is essential that the diet be properly balanced
(ch. 167).

PROGNOSIS OF FOOD
HYPERSENSITIVITY
The prognosis for animals with food hypersensitivity is generally
very good if it is possible to achieve strict avoidance of the food
item(s) to which the patient has been shown to be allergic. If there is
recurrence or recrudescence of pruritus on a maintenance
hypoallergenic diet, one must consider lack of long-term compliance,
change in the commercial diet formulation, recent sensitization to
the novel food item, or a possible recurrence of a bacterial or yeast
skin infection or ectoparasite infestation. Conversely, spontaneous
resolution of food hypersensitivity is possible, but it is not known
how commonly, or when, it might occur.

NUTRITIONAL DEFICIENCIES
The skin is a large organ with high nutritional requirements and diet
is crucial in providing nutrients to maintain epidermal integrity and
optimize skin healing. Many systemic nutrient deficiencies (e.g.,

protein, EFAs, zinc, vitamin A, vitamin B) can be associated with
dermatopathies1,3,14; however, most produce a similar range of
dermatologic clinical signs that can become evident only after
feeding a deficient diet for several months (ch. 12). Signs usually are
nonspecific and include excessive scaling, erythema, alopecia or poor
hair growth, and greasy skin, which can be accompanied by
secondary pyoderma and pruritus.
Dermatologic conditions that occur as a result of nutritional
deficiencies currently are rare in developed countries because most
dogs and cats are fed complete and balanced commercial diets that
meet their nutritional needs. Nonetheless, prolonged or
inappropriate storage of the diet (e.g., fatty acid [FA] oxidation) and
inappropriate over-supplementation (e.g., zinc deficiency following
excessive calcium supplementation) can be responsible for
nutritional deficiencies. In addition, with the recent trend of feeding
unconventional diets (e.g., raw, home-cooked, grain-free or
vegetarian diets), it is likely that dermatoses associated with
incomplete and unbalanced diets will emerge (ch. 167). When
nutritional deficiency is suspected, it is usually recommended to
change the diet to one that is well formulated and has been stored
properly rather than to attempt to correct a deficiency by adding FAs
and vitamins.
Despite the feeding of an adequate diet, nutritional deficiencies
occasionally can arise in animals with chronic gastrointestinal
disease (e.g., maldigestion and malabsorption; ch. 262), metabolic
disease (e.g., superficial necrolytic dermatitis), and genetic factors
(e.g., impaired zinc absorption in Siberian Huskies and Alaskan
Malamutes).
There are two syndromes of zinc-responsive dermatosis in the dog
(chs. 12 and 262).1,2,14 Syndrome I predominantly is seen in Arctic
breeds, and syndrome II is seen in rapidly growing puppies, often fed
poor-quality dog food. Both syndromes present with adherent
scaling around the mouth, chin, eyes, pinnae, and foot pads. Dogs
with syndrome I require oral zinc supplementation (together with
dietary correction, where appropriate), while dogs with syndrome II
require a better diet.
Superficial necrolytic dermatitis (also called metabolic epidermal
necrolysis, necrolytic migratory erythema, and hepatocutaneous

syndrome; chs. 12 and 274) is a rare disease seen in older dogs in
which nutritional deficiencies (e.g., hypoaminoacidemia and possibly
deficiency in EFA and zinc) are associated with systemic metabolic
disturbances often resulting from hepatic disease.1-3,15 Palliative
nutritional management (e.g., feeding of egg yolks, zinc, and EFA
supplements) or intravenous amino acid infusions can be of some
benefit.2,16

NUTRITIONAL SUPPLEMENTATION
FOR THE MANAGEMENT OF SKIN
DISEASES
Nutritional supplements given at supraphysiologic levels have been
recommended for the management of several skin diseases.1-3,17
Much interest has been paid to the therapeutic value of EFA in the
management of canine atopic dermatitis. High levels of omega-3 (n3) FA typically are used for controlling inflammation, and omega-6
(n-6) FA to promote a healthy epidermal barrier. Although there is
some evidence that supplements containing n-3 FA and diets
enriched with n-3 FA do provide some clinical benefits in the
management of atopic dermatitis,18 the magnitude of these benefits
still is poorly documented. It is still unknown if alpha-linolenic acid
(ALA, from flaxseeds) is as useful as eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA)
and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), both found mainly in cold-water
fish (ch. 151). Typically, supplementation with EPA 40-50 mg/kg
PO q24h is recommended. It may take 8-12 weeks to observe a
reduction in pruritus (varying from 0 to 40%).
Major pet food companies have formulated prescription diets for
the management of canine skin diseases, particularly for atopic
dermatitis. Various micronutrients or cofactors are added in addition
to high levels of n-3 FA to support the epidermal barrier and immune
function. However, their benefits are largely anecdotal, and
controlled studies are needed to support these claims. Of note,
canine diets specifically formulated to improve joint health and
mobility often contain more n-3 FA than those designed for skin

health, although the main source of n-3 FA in these diets is usually
ALA from flaxseeds.
The oral administration of an ultra-micronized
palmitoylethanolamide (PEA-um), a naturally occurring bioactive
lipid, appears to be effective and safe in reducing pruritus in dogs
with moderate atopic dermatitis.19
Supplementation with n-3 FA,20 PEA-um,19 zinc21 and/or vitamin
D22 and/or vitamin E23 might be of some value in atopic dogs in an
attempt to reduce the maintenance dosage of antipruritic drugs such
as glucocorticoid or cyclosporine.
Supplements containing n-3 and n-6 FAs (or diets enriched with
n-3 and n-6 FAs) also could be of some benefit to dogs with
symmetric lupoid onychodystrophy (symmetric lupoid onychitis; ch.
178).24
Supraphysiologic doses of natural vitamin A (800-1,000
IU/kg/day), in lieu of the more expensive synthetic retinoids (e.g.,
isotretinoin, acitretin), are recommended for the treatment of some
cornification disorders such as sebaceous adenitis, ichthyosis, and
comedones in hairless canine breeds, as well as in actinic dermatitis,
infundibular keratinizing acanthomas, epitheliotropic T-cell
lymphoma, and squamous cell carcinoma. Supraphysiologic doses of
niacinamide (vitamin B3), usually in combination with tetracycline
(or doxycycline) or vitamin E, are used for their antiinflammatory
and immunostimulatory effects in several immune-mediated skin
disorders (e.g., discoid lupus erythematosus, lupoid
onychodystrophy, dermatomyositis) with variable effects (ch. 178).
Supraphysiologic doses of zinc are required in Siberian Huskies and
Alaskan Malamutes suffering from zinc-responsive dermatosis
syndrome I.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Diagnosis and Management of Food Allergy
The development of an allergy to one or more food ingredients in
the diet can occur in dogs and cats, which then produces symptoms
like skin problems, gastrointestinal signs (like vomiting and/or

diarrhea), or both. Itchiness (pruritus) is the most frequently
observed presenting dermatologic symptom, which can be
accompanied by subsequent self-inflicted lesions (e.g., hair loss, skin
redness, crusts (scab), and sores). Food allergy, when it produces
these symptoms, can mimic other skin conditions such as flea
allergic dermatitis, nonseasonal environmental allergies, skin
infections and skin parasites.
The only reliable way to confirm or eliminate food allergy as the
cause of the symptoms is to perform an elimination diet trial, which
involves exclusively feeding a specific home-cooked or a commercial
hypoallergenic diet, usually for a period of up to 8 weeks, based on
avoiding ingredients previously fed. If an animal is allergic to a
particular food ingredient, then completely avoiding it for several
weeks should be met with significant improvement in itchiness and
other symptoms. No other foods of any kind can be fed during this
period, because even one bite of a food that contains an ingredient a
pet is allergic to can set off the symptoms for days or weeks. Before
considering initiating an elimination diet trial, it is of utmost
importance to first identify and eliminate any skin parasites (e.g.,
fleas, lice, mites) and bacterial and yeast infections as potential
causes of itchiness. These are common problems and they are
relatively easier to control and eliminate. Usually, the food trial is
conducted only if a significant amount of itchiness persists after
parasitic and infectious causes of pruritus have been excluded or
controlled (e.g., flea allergic dermatitis).
Home-cooked elimination diets are more reliable than commercial
hypoallergenic diets. They consist of feeding a novel protein source
and a novel carbohydrate (starch) source for up to 8 weeks.
Sometimes only a novel protein (meat) source is used in cats. The
food ingredients chosen for the elimination diet trial should be based
on your pet’s known past exposure to various foods, avoiding dietary
protein and carbohydrate sources to which he or she has been
previously exposed. It is usually not recommended to add
supplements (e.g., essential fatty acids, vitamins, minerals) during
the elimination trial period because they can be potential sources of
allergens. Home-cooked diets often are not nutritionally complete or
balanced for long-term use, but they can be used safely for the 8
week diagnostic phase of the feeding trial in most otherwise healthy
adult pets. Consultation with your veterinarian and/or a veterinary

dermatologist or nutritionist is necessary. Commercial
hypoallergenic diets containing a hydrolyzed or a novel protein
source sold by veterinarians offer convenience and they are
guaranteed to be nutritionally complete and balanced. However, they
are not as reliable as home-cooked elimination diet (up to 25%
failure rate) because of the possible presence of processing agents,
storage mites, only partially hydrolyzed proteins, and/or crosscontamination in processing plants with proteins and carbohydrates
not even listed on the pet food label. During the food trial, no other
food sources should be given (no treats, bones, table scraps, chew
toys with flavoring, glucosamine, vitamins, omega 3 supplements,
oral flavored heartworm preventatives, flavored toothpaste, etc.). A
positive response to the feeding trial is visible as an improvement of
symptoms, usually within 3 to 4 weeks but occasionally taking up to
10 to 12 weeks for complete resolution in some cases.
If there is no resolution or significant reduction of itchiness and
scratching after 8 weeks, your pet can return to the previous diet and
your veterinarian might then suggest investigating for the presence
of environmental allergy. If, by the end of the 8 week elimination diet
trial, a resolution or a significant reduction of itchiness and
scratching is observed, your pet must then be rechallenged with all
the original dietary components to confirm the diagnosis of food
allergy. This is to ensure that improvement over this length of time
was not simply coincidental (e.g., change of season, concurrent new
treatments), as occurs often. Recurrence of itchiness and scratching
within 2 weeks is expected, and confirmatory, with food allergy. The
diagnosis is confirmed only if this recurrence occurs upon challenge
with the original diet and subsides again on re-introduction of the
elimination diet. The long-term plan for confirmed food allergy cases
is to find a suitable commercial hypoallergenic diet that keeps the
your pet asymptomatic. If a home-cooked diet is chosen (because of
unavailability of a suitable commercial diet or your preference) it is
essential that the diet be properly nutritionally balanced.
Manon Paradis (St-Hyacinthe, Québec, Canada)

Only recently has the importance of diet on central nervous system
(CNS) structure and function in health and disease and its interplay
with the gut microbiota been scrutinized. A deficiency of certain
nutrients can lead to CNS impairment and accelerate brain aging. On
the other hand, the abundance of specific nutrients can improve CNS
function and prevent neural damage. In this chapter, dietary
management strategies will be discussed to help counteract
neurologic and cognitive disorders.

GLUCOSE AND FAT METABOLISM IN
THE BRAIN1-5
Brain tissue consumes a large amount of energy in proportion to its
volume, largely for sustaining its membrane potentials (adenosine
triphosphate [ATP]-dependent sodium potassium pump),
transporters such as neurotransmitter transporters, synaptic activity,
and cell homeostasis of neurons. In a fed state, the brain derives
most of its energy from oxygen-dependent metabolism of glucose,
which provides a substrate for ATP. The brain has no glucose storage
capacities but requires 20-25% of body glucose consumption and is
therefore dependent on a constant glucose supply.3,4 During
exercise, blood lactate is increased and can be metabolized by the
brain to provide energy; however, its contribution to brain energy
requirements is small. On the other hand, ketones, e.g., betahydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate, resulting from triglyceride
metabolism, provide an important alternative brain energy source,
especially in periods of starvation where they provide up to 60% of
the requirement.Triglycerides are esters derived from glycerol and
three fatty acid (FA) carbon chains. The attributes of fats are due to
the carbon chain length and the degree of hydrogen saturation.
Fewer hydrogen atoms means more double carbon chain bonds,
resulting in mono- (one double bond) or polyunsaturated fatty acids
(PUFAs). Long chain fatty acids (LCFAs) have 16 to 22 carbons,
medium chain triglycerides (MCTs) have 6 to 12 carbons, and short
chain FAs have <6 carbons. LCFAs are oxidized by beta-oxidation to
form acetyl-coenzyme A (CoA), which is further oxidized by the
tricarboxylic acid (TCA, citric acid, Krebs) cycle. If the TCA cycle is
challenged, e.g., due to low amounts of intermediates such as
oxaloacetate, acetyl-CoA is used instead to synthesize ketones. The
brain has a limited ability to utilise LCFAs; LCFAs do not readily
pass the blood brain barrier and neuronal mitochondria lack
enzymatic capacity for beta-oxidation. Unlike LCFAs, medium chain
fatty acids (MCFAs) have a higher ketogenic yield, can pass the blood
brain barrier more freely, and are oxidized in brain astrocytes,
providing a glucose-sparing effect and an alternative energy
source.1,2 The most important MCFA for brain metabolism and
function are octanoic acid (8C; caprylic acid) and decanoic acid (C10;

capric acid). In the brain, certain decanoic FAs can also directly
inhibit alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid
(AMPA)-type glutamate receptors and the mTORC1 (mechanistic
target of rapamycin complex 1) signalling pathway.2

ENERGY METABOLISM IN THE AGING
BRAIN
The brain’s high metabolic rate makes it susceptible and intolerant to
disruptions in energy supply. This is aggravated by aging, which
causes a decline in mitochondrial function and glucose.3,4 Regional
and overall brain glucose metabolism can be reduced by as much as
25% in dogs by 6 years of age.3 Glucose hypometabolism and
mitochondrial dysfunction can be present prior to any measurable
cognitive dysfunction and has been associated with an increase of
oxygen free radicals and oxidative stress.

COGNITIVE DYSFUNCTION
With a rising number of elderly dogs and cats, the effective
management of these patients is increasingly important in daily
veterinary practice. One-third of a dog’s life is in the senior part of
life. Like in cats, 1 out of 3 dogs aged 11-12 years and 2 out of 3 dogs
aged 15-16 years show clinical signs of cognitive dysfunction
syndrome (CDS).6 The most commonly seen behavioral changes in
pets include spatial or temporal disorientation, altered interaction
with family members and animal companions, changes in sleep-wake
cycles, housesoiling, vocalization (cats) and anxiety, all leading to a
reduced quality of life for the pet and its owner (DISHAA in dogs:
Disorientation, social Interaction, changes in the Sleep-wake cycle,
Housesoiling, learning and memory, Activity, Anxiety; VISHDAAL
in cats: Vocalisation, alterations in Interactions [e.g., increased
affection], changes in the Sleep-wake cycle, Housesoiling,
Disorientation, alterations in Activity levels, Anxiety, and Learning
and memory).1,7 Clinical signs of CDS can be aggravated by dental
disease, (osteoarthritic) pain, systemic illnesses, or other behavioral
problems, which need to be considered in its diagnosis and
management.The antemortem diagnosis is based on clinical signs
and ideally advanced brain imaging (ch. 112) which can reveal brain
atrophy (widening of sulci, ventriculomegaly) and evidence of past
vascular accidents (ch. 243). Compromised cerebral blood flow and
chronic free radical damage are thought to play a major role in the
pathophysiologic mechanism of CDS. Studies looking at the brains of
geriatric cats and dogs with CDS revealed a decrease in cerebral
vascular blood flow, microhemorrhages or infarcts of periventricular
vessels, and arteriosclerosis.1,3,4 Accompanied by an age-related
decrease in cardiac output, systemic hypertension, or anemia, these
mechanisms lead to hypoxia. Due to the high oxygen demand of
neurons, the brain is especially susceptible to hypoxic damage. Due
to the high oxygen demand of neurons, the brain is especially
susceptible to hypoxic damage, resulting in the generation of reactive
oxygen species. Aging mitochondria become less efficient in
producing energy and need readily available energy sources, such as
ketone bodies, to counteract increases in reactive oxygen species. In
contrast to Alzheimer disease in people, the role of the formation of

amyloid beta-plaques and Tau fibrils in CDS has not been
established in dogs and cats.
There are no commercially available dietary management options
for the treatment of cats with CDS. It has been shown that dogs fed a
commercial diet appropriate for lifestage, body condition, and size
are about three times less likely to develop CDS later in life.1 In dogs
with CDS, a diet containing MCTs as an alternative energy source to
glucose has been promising for reversing clinical signs. MCT
enriched diets have been shown to improve the cognitive function of
aged dogs. A diet including a brain protection blend containing
arginine, antioxidants (vitamins C and E, and selenium), B vitamins,
and fish oil as a source of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and
eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) also improved clinical signs of CDS.1,4 A
similar improvement in cognitive function and clinical signs of CDS
was seen in dogs fed a diet supplemented with FAs, antioxidants
(vitamins C and E, beta-carotene, selenium, flavonoids, carotenoids),
and mitochondrial cofactors (DL-alpha-lipoic acid and Lcarnitine).1 Table 161.1 shows a summary of proposed nutritional
solutions that address risk factors for brain atrophy and CDS in
dogs.1,3,4

EPILEPSY
Epilepsy is defined by recurrent seizure activity (ch. 247). During
the high brain activity that occurs during a seizure, affected brain
regions have a high glucose consumption. More interestingly, in
between seizures epileptogenic brain tissue, whether
morphologically altered or not, can appear hypometabolic with a
reduction in glucose consumption.2 The extent of the
“hypometabolic” state of the brain regions can be greater with an
increase in seizure frequency and severity, indicating that a change
in local energy metabolism can be associated with seizure generation
and propagation and drug resistance.
The interictal hypometabolic state of epileptogenic brain regions
and their energy deficit is in contrast to the higher need of energy the
altered brain region requires. The epileptic foci are not dormant

interictally, and they require more energy. This is confirmed by
electroencephalographic studies, which show frequent interictal
spike activity. The lack of energy that is a consequence of altered and
reduced glycolysis might result in changes in cell membrane
potentials and glutamate transporter and synaptic activity, resulting
in lowering of the seizure threshold and potentially causing
comorbidities, such as anxiety and cognitive deficits.2 This highlights
the need for treatment strategies to improve brain energy
metabolism and supply of alternative energy carriers.
In addition, altered mitochondrial function plays a critical role in
epilepsy.2 Physiologically, pyruvate enters the mitochondria where
pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) converts it to acetyl-CoA, which
enters the TCA cycle. Carbons derived from glucose not only provide
the intermediates for the TCA cycle but also act as precursors for the
biosynthesis of lipids, amino acids and neurotransmitters, which are
important for brain physiology and structure. This system can be
altered in epilepsy resulting in an altered energy supply as well as
failure of repair after a seizure.
As glucose metabolism is disrupted with epilepsy, ketones provide
a good alternative energy source, which is independent of PDH
activity. As aforementioned, ketones readily cross the blood brain
barrier and can be metabolized effectively in the brain. The classical
LCFA-based ketogenic diet, in which fat provides three-quarter of
the energy requirement, has been used successfully for the treatment
of drug-resistant epilepsy in children. However, a classical LCFA
based ketogenic diet failed in dogs with epilepsy. First, dogs are more
resistant to nutritionally induced ketosis. The peripheral utilisation
of ketones is more efficient in dogs compared to humans. Second,
despite seeing some trends of seizure reduction in drug resistant
canine epilepsy patients in a high-fat diet study, dogs have the risk of
developing pancreatitis when they eat such diets.2,5 A safer and more
effective ketone-producing diet is enriched with MCTs. Several MCT
efficacy studies in dogs with idiopathic epilepsy have been performed
and they have shown that ∼20-50% of dogs with antiseizure drug
resistant epilepsy respond adequately, with a >50% reduction in
seizure frequency.2 In some dogs, the comorbidities of anxiety and
cognitive impairment also improve.

Several other dietary considerations should be considered when
managing dogs with epilepsy. These considerations include dietary
macronutrient distribution, body composition, serum trace nutrient
concentrations, PUFA supplementation, dietary chloride intake, the
possible role of food allergies, and the risk of pancreatitis secondary
to a high-fat diet and phenobarbital or potassium bromide
treatment. The role of gluten hypersensitivity has not been
established for epilepsy but needs to be considered in certain
movement disorders such as paroxysmal dyskinesia (ch. 41).8

Several nutrients have an effect on bone metabolism. Furthermore, the skeleton serves as the main
reservoir for calcium and phosphorus, which can be mobilized if there is a systemic shortage. Therefore,
nutrition-related skeletal disorders are linked to calcium and phosphorus metabolism. Obesity (ch.
150) and osteoarthritis (chs. 226 and 256) are also nutrition-related disorders that affect the
musculoskeletal system, and they are discussed elsewhere. The relation between nutrition and inherited
disorders such as hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia, osteochondritis dissecans, and hypertrophic
osteodystrophy is debated and will not be discussed in this chapter.

INTRODUCTION
CALCIUM METABOLISM
Calcium is an important macronutrient for the skeleton, but also for maintaining several other functions
such as cellular, contractive, and enzymatic processes. As a result, plasma calcium is tightly controlled
by a complex homeostatic mechanism involving fluxes of calcium between the extracellular fluid and
kidney, bone, and gut. Three major hormones—parathyroid hormone (PTH), calcitonin (CT), and 1,25dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol)—regulate the influx and efflux of calcium (ch. 69).1
If a drop in plasma calcium level occurs, PTH is secreted with the aim to restore the plasma calcium
level (ch. 283). PTH acts on the bone to release calcium and phosphorus. Furthermore, PTH enhances
reabsorption of calcium and phosphorus from the glomerular filtrate. To prevent calcium-phosphorus
deposits from forming, PTH also stimulates active renal excretion of phosphorus. Lastly, vitamin D is
activated to calcitriol under the influence of PTH by the activation of 1-alpha-hydroxylase in the kidney.
This aims to enhance uptake of calcium and phosphorus within the gastrointestinal tract. To prevent an
ongoing process, calcitriol inhibits PTH secretion.2,3
By contrast, a high plasma calcium level triggers the release of CT by the thyroid gland. CT acts on the
bone by retraction of the ruffled border of osteoclasts, thus preventing them from resorbing bone.
Instead, CT stimulates mineralization of bone in order to restore a normal plasma calcium level.
Furthermore, CT facilitates transportation of calcium to cell organelles, and enhances glomerular
calcium excretion.4 Phosphorus regulation is closely tied to calcium regulation, and phosphorus is also
mainly stored in the skeleton. If the plasma phosphorus level is high, fibroblast growth factor-23 (FGF23) is released, which stimulates inactivation of vitamin D by 24-hydroxylase (reducing gastrointestinal
uptake of calcium and phosphorus), and stimulates PTH secretion (promoting renal phosphorus

excretion). An imbalanced/inverse dietary calcium-to-phosphorus ratio (should be between 1:1 and 1.6:1
in growing large breed dogs) stimulates extra secretion of PTH, which worsens osteopenia, especially
when overall calcium intake is low.

VITAMIN D METABOLISM
Vitamin D plays an important role in calcium and phosphorus metabolism. However, its main function
is in bone remodeling and growth. In contrast to people and many other species, dogs and cats lack
sufficient capacity to synthesize vitamin D in the skin under the influence of sunlight and thus depend
on dietary intake. Dietary vitamin D is converted in the liver to 25-vitamin D, which is often used as an
indicator for vitamin D status. 25-Vitamin D can be converted into the most active metabolite, calcitriol,
by 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which is predominantly present in the kidney. Calcitriol stimulates reabsorption
of calcium and phosphorus from the glomerular filtrate, enhances uptake of calcium and phosphorus
from the gastrointestinal tract, and stimulates osteoblastic and osteoclastic activity. The latter releases
calcium and phosphorus from inactive bone and stimulates mineralization of osteoid and bone to which
more pressure is applied, thus using the released calcium and phosphorus. If calcitriol is not needed, or
is not produced in sufficient amounts, 24,25 vitamin D is formed by 24-hydroxylase, which is present in
multiple tissues. 24,25 vitamin D stimulates mineralization of bone. Calcitriol can also be inactivated by
24-hydroxylase into 1,24,25 vitamin D, which can then be excreted by the urine.

YOUNG VERSUS ADULT
Dietary imbalances in calcium, phosphorus, and vitamin D can result in skeletal problems, especially in
young growing animals, as they have a much higher rate of bone turnover compared to adults. In adult
animals, bone metabolism and calcium and phosphorus turnover is much lower; therefore, adults have
lower requirements for calcium and phosphorus, and the dietary calcium-to-phosphorus ratio is not
important as long as sufficient calcium and phosphorus are supplied.

CLINICAL PRESENTATION
Clinicians can be confronted with (especially young) osteopenic animals with multiple fractures. This
can be caused by nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism (NSHP, dietary calcium deficiency), rickets
(vitamin D deficiency), all-meat syndrome (combination of calcium deficiency and an inverse dietary
calcium-to-phosphorus ratio), renal secondary hyperparathyroidism (RSHP), osteogenesis imperfecta (a
hereditary disease caused by defective or deficient collagen production and marked by extreme
brittleness of the long bones), or mucopolysaccharidoses (ch. 244, Table 244.4). The latter is a group
of metabolic disorders caused by the absence or malfunction of lysosomal enzymes needed to break
down molecules called glycosaminoglycans (GAGs, formerly called mucopolysaccharides), which are
long chains of sugars/carbohydrates that occur within the cells that help build bone, cartilage, tendons,
cornea, skin and connective tissue, and are also found in synovial fluid. To distinguish between these
possible causes, careful review of case information and diagnostic testing are warranted (Table 162.1).
Osteogenesis imperfecta is characterized by extremely thin bony cortices and low mineralization of bone
in the absence of blood work abnormalities.5 The skeletal deformities in mucopolysaccharidoses are
characterized by shortened bones, thickened bones, bones that are abnormally shaped, and bones with
articular erosions.6
To further distinguish between the different nutrition-related skeletal disorders, a thorough dietary
history should be obtained (ch. 145). Nutritional assessment should be performed to determine if
nutrition-related risk factors are present, followed by an extended evaluation which includes comparison
of the nutrient composition of the diet with the nutrient requirements as defined by National Research
Council (NRC) (2006),7 Association of American Feed Control Officials (AAFCO) (2018),8 and
Fédération européenne de l’industrie des aliments pour animaux familiers (European Petfood Industry
Federation) (FEDIAF) (2020).9 The feeding amount should be appropriate, to prevent excessive weight
gain (ch. 150), which also implies excessive intake of nutrients. Treatment often consists of transition to
a complete and balanced diet for the appropriate life stage. Target levels of important nutrients for the
skeleton are demonstrated in Table 162.2.

SPECIFIC NUTRITIONAL-RELATED SKELETAL DISORDERS
NUTRITIONAL SECONDARY HYPERPARATHYROIDISM
Nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism occurs when chronic insufficient calcium intake or
absorption results in continuous PTH secretion.
If increased calcium absorption in the intestine is insufficient to meet daily requirements, calcium will
be resorbed at the endosteal surface of the diaphyses and in the areas of cancellous bone. Excessive
osteoclasia and pathologic fractures of growing bone are the results of long-term hyperparathyroidism.
Mineralization of osteoid and cartilage will be undisturbed, resulting in normal-width growth plates.10,11

Clinical and Radiographic Examination
Although animals of any age can be affected, most animals with nutritional secondary
hyperparathyroidism are young individuals eating foods deficient in calcium.12 For example, animals fed
improperly formulated homemade foods or all-meat diets may receive insufficient calcium and/or
excessive phosphorus. Clinical signs may include reluctance to move and play, lameness, uncoordinated
gait, sternal recumbency, loose teeth, and painful mastication.
Blood calcium concentrations are generally within normal limits, although such values can,
uncommonly, be decreased. Increases in serum PTH and calcitriol concentrations can be detected3,11
(Table 162.1). Radiographs may reveal thin cortices, wide medullary cavities, folding (greenstick)
fractures, normal width of growth plates with relatively white metaphyseal borders, as well as
compression fractures of cancellous bone of epiphyses and vertebrae10,11 (Figure 162.1).

Treatment
Correction of the diet includes utilizing a commercially available, complete and balanced dog or cat food.
The absolute amount of calcium in the food is more important than the dietary calcium-phosphorus
ratio in young growing dogs.7,13,14 Improved mineralization of the skeleton should be evident in 3 to 4
weeks, because almost 100% of the ingested calcium will be resorbed due to the PTH-induced high
calcitriol levels.2 During this time it is important to prevent more pathologic fractures, especially of the
vertebrae, by reduced handling and consistent cage rest, as the skeleton is too weak for bandages, splints
or implants. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs should be prescribed for proper pain management.
Supplementing calcium as calcium carbonate or calcium lactate (and not calcium phosphate or bone
meal) at 50 mg Ca/kg body weight (BW) may accelerate osteoid mineralization, but correcting the diet is
usually sufficient. Corrective osteotomies can be planned, if necessary, after the skeleton is normally
mineralized. Even pets with compression fractures of the vertebral column may have a full recovery.

RICKETS
Since dogs and cats are not capable of synthesizing vitamin D under the influence of ultraviolet B light,
they require a source of this essential vitamin (hormone) in their food.3,10 Vitamin D is absorbed in the
small intestine by bile salt–dependent passive diffusion. It is then transported to the liver, where it is
hydroxylated into 25-hydroxyvitamin D.3 A second hydroxylation takes place in the kidney, either to
24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D or to calcitriol.3 Both metabolites are necessary for osteoid and cartilage
mineralization.3 Rickets is characterized by defective mineralization of newly formed bone and cartilage
as well as metaphyseal thickening.10,15

Rickets is the term used to describe hypovitaminosis D in young animals; in adults it is referred to as
osteomalacia. Hypovitaminosis D arises most commonly from inadequate intake of vitamin D, but
rickets lesions can also occur secondary to decreased phosphorus intake or by an abnormal dietary
calcium-to-phosphorus ratio.16-18 Additionally, rickets can occur despite normal vitamin D intake if
intake of calcium is excessive at an early age (∼3 weeks of life). This causes hypercalcemia, secondary
hypoparathyroidism, and tertiary decreased calcitriol formation.11,17

Clinical and Radiographic Examination
A thorough dietary history is critical. Since commercial pet foods contain 2 to 10 times the AAFCO
minimum recommended amounts of vitamin D, rickets is generally only seen in animals fed improperly
formulated homemade foods such as un-supplemented strict vegetarian foods (ch. 167). It can also
occur in animals with biliary atresia or inborn errors of vitamin D metabolism.19-23 Radiographs
demonstrate thin long bone cortices and extremely thickened growth plates. Increased growth plate
width is a strong indicator of rickets. Despite hyperparathyroidism, plasma calcium and phosphorus can
be normal or low-normal. A diagnosis of vitamin D deficiency can be made by measuring circulating
levels of vitamin D metabolites. In rickets, circulating levels of calcitriol will be decreased, whereas in
nutritional or renal secondary hypoparathyroidism calcitriol will be increased (Table 162.1).3,19

FIGURE 162.2 Renal secondary hyperparathyroidism. Lateral radiograph
from a 6-year-old Cavalier King Charles Spaniel dog with International Renal
Interest Society (IRIS) stage 3 kidney disease. There is profound osteopenia,
notably of the dental alveolar bone, and soft-tissue proliferation in the jaws
consistent with fibrous osteodystrophy. Courtesy Dr. L. L. van Stee, DECVS.

FIGURE 162.3 Radiograph of a 9-year-old cat with hypervitaminosis A. Note
the new bone formation on the thoracic vertebrae and sternum.

Treatment
Transition to a nutritionally balanced commercial dog or cat food is generally sufficient to resolve
rickets. Mineralization of bone cortices, callus, and growth plates will occur within 3 weeks. If the dog or
cat fails to respond to a balanced diet, vitamin D therapy can be recommended. Supplementation with
25-vitamin D at 2.3 mcg/kg body weight0.75 (which is about 700 IU for a 15 kg dog per day) PO q24h for
2 weeks is the preferred option, as 25-vitamin D supplementation has been proven to be more successful
compared to supplementation of non-hydroxylated vitamin D.24

ALL-MEAT SYNDROME
All-meat syndrome is characterized by low dietary intake of calcium and vitamin D, combined with an
inverse dietary calcium-to-phosphorus ratio. This results in severe nutritional secondary
hyperparathyroidism. The relative excess of phosphorus reduces the ionized calcium concentration in
serum via mass action equilibrium, resulting in hypersecretion of PTH. Because there is also limited
vitamin D intake, calcitriol levels may remain low/normal, resulting in a failure to enhance uptake of
calcium in the gastrointestinal tract, and reduced negative feedback on PTH production. Clinical signs
and radiographic signs are a combination of nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism and rickets.
Treatment consists of feeding a nutritionally balanced commercial dog or cat food. Mineralization of
bone cortices, callus, and growth plates will usually occur within 3 weeks.25

RENAL SECONDARY HYPERPARATHYOIDISM
The kidney plays an important role in calcium metabolism. In patients with renal disease, less calcium
will be re-absorbed from the glomerular filtrate, and it will therefore be excreted in the urine. As a

consequence, plasma calcium levels decrease, triggering an increase in PTH secretion. PTH will try to
exert its effects, but activation of vitamin D to calcitriol and increasing renal phosphorus excretion will
not be very effective. Decreased calcitriol levels, combined with increased PTH levels and decreased
renal phosphorus excretion, will result in mobilization of calcium and phosphorus from the bone. This
will increase both plasma calcium and plasma phosphorus levels. As a consequence, FGF-23 will be
released, which ultimately results in fibrous osteodystrophy, also known as rubber jaw (

Video 162.1)

(Figures 162.2 and 162.3).26 Increased plasma levels of both calcium and phosphorus may also result
in exceeding the solubility product, with formation of calcium-phosphate deposits in different organs,
including the kidney, thereby worsening renal disease. Because active phosphorus excretion is impaired,
and high phosphorus levels are detrimental for renal health, kidney diets have a low phosphorus
content, combined with a normal to high calcium content (ch. 158).

ENOSTOSIS (= PANOSTEITIS = GROWTH PAIN)
High calcium intake in young dogs leads to hyperplasia of CT-producing cells in the thyroid gland. This
results in reduced osteoclastic activity, which can last even months after an episode of high calcium
intake.27 In immature dogs, a large blood supply to the metaphyseal area (bordering the growth plates)
exists. This network of arterioles receives blood from branches of the periosteal vasculature and the
medullary arteries. The latter enter the bone mainly in the nutrient foramen. The direction of efferent
blood flow is through the diaphyseal cortex and it runs through rigid bone canals. For the widening of
these canals in the growing bone, osteoclastic activity is necessary. Due to hypercalcitoninism, the canals
cannot be widened, resulting in edema. This edema may also be present underneath the periosteum and
thus makes the periosteum painful in response to pressure or muscle activity. So far, no other causes
than high calcium intake have been demonstrated.28

Clinical and Radiographic Examination
Panosteitis is mainly seen in medium and large-breed dogs (especially German Shepherd Dogs), starting
at 6 months of age. A sudden onset of shifting lameness is common, with dogs showing a painful
reaction to deep palpation of the long bones. Radiographs or computed tomography scans demonstrate
a blurring of the trabecular pattern and well-defined subperiosteal cortical thickening can be noted.

Treatment
Because the disease is self-limiting and is not diagnosed in dogs >22 months of age, treatment is limited
to administration of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and adaptation of the diet. Dietary
treatment consists of a reduced Ca intake by feeding a diet that is close to the minimum Ca
requirements, and by feeding an amount of food that is necessary to maintain ideal body condition.

HYPERVITAMINOSIS A
Vitamin A is needed for terminal differentiation and normal function of osteoblasts and osteoclasts.
High vitamin A intake in young animals inhibits chondrogenesis in growth plates and inhibits collagen
synthesis in osteoblasts in most species, causing “hyena disease” (so named because the conformation
and gait of calves with hypervitaminosis A have been compared to those of a hyena) due to premature
closure of the growth plates. Because cats are unable to excrete large amounts of retinol and retinylesters in the urine, cats are more susceptible to hypervitaminosis A. In older cats, hypervitaminosis A
has been described as a cause of osteoarthritis.29

Clinical and Radiographic Examination
Most cases reporting hypervitaminosis A in cats are due to consumption of large amounts of (pork or
beef) liver.30 In contrast to other species, hypervitaminosis A in cats is characterized by new bone
formation without osteolysis, starting at the points of insertion of ligaments, muscles and joint capsules,
finally causing ankyloses in vertebrae and large joints which is clearly visible on radiographs. This
results in pain, stiffness, and sometimes lameness. Elevated plasma and liver retinol concentrations

supports the diagnosis, as well as characteristic portal-portal bridges, liver fibrosis and swollen hepatic
stellate cells seen in liver biopsies.31

Treatment
The ankyloses are irreversible so dietary treatment aims at prevention of further ankyloses by feeding a
low vitamin A diet for several weeks followed by a complete and balanced diet for long-term feeding.
Supportive treatment consists of administration of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

CARPAL LAXITY SYNDROME (CLS)
CLS describes either hypo-extension, hyperextension, or hyperflexion of the carpal joint. Although the
clinical presentation can make the clinician suspect a skeletal disorder, it is a disorder of the tendons. It
is mostly diagnosed in male medium- to giant-breed dogs at the age of 10 weeks (mostly 6-12 weeks).32
Feeding of a deficient diet and/or excessive food intake are thought to be the cause of CLS, as this results
in rapid weight gain before adequate bone development; this occurs in combination with weakness of
the ligaments due to decreased collagen synthesis. This decreased collagen synthesis can be caused by
copper deficiency, as copper is incorporated in lysyl-oxidase, which is needed for collagen synthesis.33
CLS is treated by adjusting the diet to a complete and balanced puppy food being fed in amounts to
prevent rapid weight gain, as well as exercise on traction surfaces (sand, grass, or carpeting), and
swimming, providing good muscle traction.34 In severe cases, bandage, splints, tenotomy and/or
arthrodesis are indicated. Usually, CLS is self-limiting.
