CANCER-ASSOCIATED MALNUTRITION:
CANCER CACHEXIA
“

Cancer cachexia” is the complex form of protein-calorie
malnutrition classically associated with the tumor-bearing state (ch.
151). It is common in people and also is described in cats and dogs.
Cancer cachexia is defined in people as a multifactorial syndrome
characterized by loss of >5% of current body weight, or loss of >2%
in cases where there is pre-existing depletion. Affected individuals
have loss of skeletal muscle mass, often with concurrent loss of fat
stores. Underlying causative metabolic defects have been identified,
although decreased food intake as well as functional abnormalities

interfering with food digestion or absorption frequently play
contributory roles. Progressive development of cachexia occurs
through stages, from pre-cachexia to cachexia to refractory cachexia,
with each stage defined by the degree of depletion of lean body mass
and energy stores combined with the severity of ongoing weight
loss.1
Cancer cachexia is important because it has an independent and
negative impact on prognosis. People and animals with cancer and
concurrent weight loss have increased morbidity and mortality, and
poor quality of life. Depletion of lean body mass leads to decreased
muscle mass and to weakness. Essential cardiovascular,
gastrointestinal, respiratory, and immune functions are lost. Altered
body composition can change drug pharmacokinetics and
pharmacodynamics, increasing treatment-related toxicosis and
compromising a patient’s ability to tolerate intensive therapy.
Regardless of species, individuals with cancer-associated weight loss
have shorter survival compared to weight stable patients with
otherwise identical disease.2-7
Cancer cachexia is best conceptualized as a paraneoplastic
syndrome (ch. 331) where energy metabolism is altered by a tumorrelated systemic inflammatory response: ultimately, consumed
calories are used inefficiently and weight loss results.2,8 Thus, one of
the hallmarks of cancer cachexia is that it cannot be reversed by a
simple increase in food intake. Various cytokines including tumor
necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) are
implicated in underlying pathophysiologic mechanisms, and
distinctive biochemical changes such as glucose intolerance,
hyperlactatemia, and increased lipolysis are seen in affected
individuals.8 Surveys suggest that the prevalence of weight loss in
cats and dogs with cancer is at least 50%, although the proportion of
clinically significantly affected dogs appears less than what is
reported in people.6,7,9,10 Some metabolic changes typical of cancer
cachexia are documented in dogs with cancer,11,12 but clear causeand-effect links between such changes, weight loss, and clinical
outcome remain unproven. For instance, the most common cause of

hyperlactatemia in tumor-bearing dogs is hypoperfusion, not cancer
cachexia.13

CANCER-ASSOCIATED MALNUTRITION:
OBESITY
Despite the traditional correlation between weight loss and cancer, a
relationship between obesity (ch. 150) and cancer is now widely
recognized. Obese people are predisposed to develop cancers
including lymphoma and tumors of the esophagus, colon,
endometrium, and breast.14 Obesity-associated increases in the
synthesis of factors such as insulin-like growth factor-1, estrogen,
and leptin are believed to promote malignant transformation by
stimulating cellular proliferation, as well as through disruption of
cellular differentiation and apoptosis. The systemic inflammatory
response that occurs with obesity also might result in an
environment that is permissive for the induction and progression of
tumor.15-17 Only a few studies have examined the relationship
between obesity and cancer in cats or dogs,18 but based on published
surveys, at least 20-30% of dogs with cancer are likely to be
overweight or obese.9,10 While this does not prove a cause-and-effect
relationship, links between tumor development and obesity as well
as historical fat intake have been demonstrated among female dogs
with mammary carcinoma.19
Obesity has a complex impact on cancer prognosis. Obese people
are more difficult to diagnose and treat than their normal-weight
counterparts,16 and similar effects are likely in cats and dogs.
Diagnoses tend to be made later in the course of disease: physical
examinations are difficult to perform, and the accuracy of diagnostic
tests such as ultrasonography is compromised. The metabolism of
chemotherapeutics can be significantly altered by obesity, and
precise dosing is challenging.20 Radiotherapy is more difficult to
deliver because of increased mobility of skin and abdominal viscera,
and obscured bony landmarks. Finally, obesity increases the

likelihood of some types of surgical complications.21 Some studies
show that overweight people with cancer have shorter survival times;
however, other studies reveal that moderate obesity confers a
paradoxical survival advantage, presumably because of increased
energy reserves.22,23

FEEDING CATS AND DOGS WITH
CANCER: GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS
So-called “cancer diets” are often recommended for cats and dogs
with neoplastic disease. Most of these diets share two main features:
they are high in fat, and low in carbohydrate. One justification for
this is that animals with cancer are generally assumed to be at risk
for weight loss, which could be addressed by a high fat, energy dense
diet; a second is that many tumor cells prefer to generate energy
through glycolysis instead of using fat derived fuels.24 Theoretically,
then, a high-fat, low-carbohydrate cancer diet preferentially supplies
usable energy to an animal with increased needs at the same time as
it limits the energy available to their tumor.

FIGURE 163.1 Clinical decision tree outlining the
nutritional management of cats and dogs with
cancer. Full nutritional assessment as well as
objective evaluation of the animal’s cancer-related
quality of life and prognosis must be repeated at
regular intervals to ensure that optimal choices are
made throughout the course of disease.
Although high fat cancer diets may be appropriate in many cases,
it is important to recognize that a diet change is not indicated for
every cat or dog with cancer. When a good quality, well-tolerated diet
is already being fed and the animal is in optimal body condition (ch.
72 and textbook’s inside covers), it is often reasonable to continue
feeding the current ration. Diet changes will be contraindicated in
many animals eating prescription foods for the management of preexisting conditions such as kidney disease, pancreatitis, or food
allergies. Furthermore, high fat cancer diets may be
counterproductive in animals that are already obese at the time of
their cancer diagnosis. Careful nutritional assessment (ch. 145) is
the best way to determine whether an individual cat or dog with
cancer might benefit from a diet change (chs. 149 and 151). This

process involves the systematic collection of clinical data evaluating
individual nutritional status which are integrated into routine
patient evaluation and used to make precise nutritional
recommendations. A diet change is indicated if nutritional
assessment reveals evidence of disease caused by suboptimal
nutrition, or disease where nutrition may be used as adjunct therapy.
If the decision is made to change the diet of a cat or dog with
cancer, the best choice is a good quality commercial ration made by a
reputable manufacturer. Over-the-counter products should have
clear label claims confirming appropriate testing to prove nutritional
adequacy (chs. 147-149, 167). Prescription products might not have
a label statement of nutritional adequacy, but rations intended for
long-term use typically undergo nutritional adequacy testing and this
information should be available from the manufacturer. If a homecooked recipe is followed, it must also be complete and balanced,
including added vitamins and minerals. Once a specific diet has been
selected, a target level of intake is calculated. In a self-supportive cat
or dog in the home environment, this is based on the maintenance
energy requirement (MER). Many different equations can be used
for calculating MER (chs. 145, 147, and 148), but each yields an
estimate of the calories of metabolizable energy needed for daily
maintenance in an individual. The new food is introduced gradually,
especially if it is high in fat. Once the target intake is reached, body
weight and condition score are followed through repeated nutritional
assessment (ch. 72), moving food intake up or down as indicated to
maintain optimal condition (Figure 163.1).
Cancer diets and prescription critical care diets often are enriched
with nutrients potentially required in greater quantities by animals
with cancer, including omega-3 (n-3) fatty acids, arginine,
glutamine, and antioxidants; countless over the counter supplements
are promoted for use in cats and dogs with cancer as well.
Unfortunately, few studies have objectively evaluated the clinical
benefit of such products, so indications as well as contraindications
must be considered on a case-by-case basis. Ideally, before any
nutritional supplement is administered to a cat or dog with cancer,
there should be a clear mechanism by which the product will work;
there should be a limited risk of negative interactions with ongoing
cancer therapy; there should be objective data supporting the shortand long-term safety of the product for cats and/or dogs; and, there

should be some means of ascertaining that the product is of good
quality, with consistent concentration and bioavailability of the
active ingredient and lack of contamination.
A common issue in this area involves the use of antioxidants
during cancer treatment. Antioxidant supplementation for people
receiving cancer therapy is controversial, because the efficacy of both
radiation and chemotherapy is often dependent on oxidative damage
and free radical generation; high antioxidant intake could
theoretically limit this injury, thereby decreasing the effectiveness of
therapy.25 Unfortunately, there are no well-designed veterinary
studies that provide clear guidance on the use of antioxidants in cats
and dogs during cancer treatment. Furthermore, it is often
challenging to determine what the precise antioxidant content of
various proprietary and over-the-counter supplements might be.
Based on these considerations and extrapolating from guidelines for
people, the author currently recommends that all nutritional
supplements containing antioxidants be stopped prior to radiation or
chemotherapy. Administration can be resumed 7 days after
completion of ablative dose radiotherapy (i.e., stereotactic
fractionation), and usually within 28 days of finishing a course of
chemotherapy. Because of the central and protracted role played by
indirect oxidative damage after sublethal dose radiotherapy (i.e.,
conventional fractionation), supplementation might reasonably be
paused not only during therapy, but for weeks or months thereafter.
More study in this area is needed.

FEEDING MANAGEMENT OF WEIGHTLOSING CATS AND DOGS WITH
CANCER
Gradual introduction of an energy-dense diet providing 40-60% of
calories as fat should be considered for cats and dogs with cancerassociated weight loss, as well as animals at risk for future weight
loss. Unless contraindicated by kidney (ch. 158) or liver (ch. 154)
disease, this is usually accompanied by an ample or increased
protein intake (from 30-50% of calories) to protect existing lean
body mass and meet the potentially increased needs of illness (ch.

151). In general, commercial rations fitting the desired profile
include performance rations, puppy and kitten foods, and
prescription critical care diets. MER is calculated as previously
described to determine initial food intake, although feeding an
increment above MER at the animal’s current body weight may be
needed to prevent or reverse weight loss; once again, a trial-anderror process with repeated nutritional assessment is used to
eventually identify optimal intake.
Additional strategies beyond simple diet change can be used to
manage cancer-associated weight loss in cats and dogs with
neoplastic disease. Supplementation with n-3 fatty acids is often
recommended, although results in people with cancer are
inconsistent: decreased synthesis of pro-inflammatory cytokines and
stabilized body condition are reported in some but not all
studies.26,27 Analogous changes in cell membrane fatty acid
composition are seen in dogs with increased dietary intake of n-3
fatty acids, which impacts cell membrane eicosanoid production and
alters synthesis of cytokines such as interleukin-1, TNF-alpha and IL6.28 Decreased systemic inflammation could in turn have beneficial
effects on clinical outcome,29 although this has yet to be proven
definitively. Fewer data are available regarding the use of n-3 fatty
acids in cats but regardless, the optimal dosage and scheduling to
manage cancer-associated weight loss is unknown in either species.
Pharmacologic appetite stimulation is another approach that can
be practical and cost-effective in cases where voluntary food intake is
inadequate (ch. 17). Although progestational agents such as
megestrol acetate are often prescribed to treat cancer and cancertreatment related anorexia in people,30 their use is infrequently
reported in cats and dogs. Benzodiazepine derivatives and the
serotonin antagonist cyproheptadine historically have been used in
small animals; more recently, the tetracyclic antidepressant
mirtazapine and the ghrelin receptor agonist capromorelin have
shown promise. No matter which appetite stimulant is chosen,
however, careful monitoring of actual food intake is essential:
clinicians must avoid postponing feeding tube placement while they
await a response to pharmacologic appetite stimulation that does not
materialize.

The most intensive nutritional treatment for animals with cancer
that are unable to maintain themselves through voluntary food
intake is assisted feeding, which usually involves feeding tube
placement (ch. 81). Parenteral feeding (ch. 164) may be considered
in some cases where intestinal tract dysfunction is severe but
increased complications, marginal improvement in nutritional
status, and trends toward decreased survival are seen in
intravenously fed people with cancer.31 This may be related at least
in part to the compromised gut function and immunity that occurs
during parenteral feeding, and a combination of parenteral and
enteral feeding should be used whenever possible to minimize these
potential complications.
Although assisted feeding provides clear clinical benefit for many
cats and dogs with cancer, it also can pose an ethical challenge.
When an animal’s quality of life is severely compromised and their
long-term prognosis is very poor, careful assessment of the expected
advantage of assisted feeding is always indicated. Studies in people
with terminal cancer show that assisted feeding likely will not
improve nutritional or functional status when the expected survival
time is very short.32 A frank discussion with the pet owner regarding
the realistic value of assisted feeding is an essential part of the
decision-making process.

FEEDING MANAGEMENT OF OBESE
CATS AND DOGS WITH CANCER
The health risks associated with obesity in normal cats and dogs are
well documented (ch. 150).18 However, the potential benefit of
weight loss in an obese animal with cancer must be carefully
assessed, especially when the prognosis associated with the
underlying neoplastic disease is poor. Weight loss programs can be
stressful, labor intensive, and expensive, so the expected cancerassociated survival time must be long enough to justify the effort
needed for weight loss.
The food intake for healthy weight loss in cats and dogs is usually
calculated based on MER at the animal’s estimated ideal body
weight, which is then decreased by an increment of 20-40% (chs.

149, 150). A more conservative decrease is likely appropriate for
many animals with cancer, and consideration should be given to
stopping weight loss at a more overweight body condition than
would normally be accepted. Weight loss is contraindicated during
critical illness, regardless of the severity of obesity. It is also arguable
whether weight loss should be attempted during active anticancer
therapy, even when the animal appears clinically stable. Excessive
loss of lean body mass during purposeful weight loss could
contribute to clinically important complications including loss of
muscle and muscle function, reduced performance scores,
immunosuppression, and increased risk of cancer therapy-related
toxicoses. Weight loss may also make monitoring more difficult,
especially in cats: stabilization or reversal of weight loss can be a
valuable surrogate marker of remission status in this species.6

CLIENT INFORMATION
Nutritional Management of Cancer
FEEDING YOUR PET WITH CANCER
The families and caretakers of cats and dogs with cancer often
want to include nutrition and nutritional supplements as part of the
overall treatment plan for their pet. However, huge amounts of
information—and misinformation—on this topic are available from
many sources, and it can be difficult to impossible to separate
legitimate science from marketing hype or unsupported personal
opinion. This handout provides information on two common topics:
cancer diets and supplements. Note: pet owners should always

consult the veterinarian in charge of their pet’s cancer
therapy before the diet is changed or supplements are
added.
CANCER DIETS
Many so-called “cancer diets” are promoted for cats and dogs with
cancer. Most of these diets are high in fat and low in carbohydrate.
They are recommended because animals with cancer are assumed to
be at risk for weight loss, and also because cancer cells seem to prefer
carbohydrate as an energy source. So, a high fat “cancer diet”
theoretically supplies concentrated energy to the patient to maintain
body weight while limiting energy available to the cancer cells.
It is important to realize that many cats and dogs with cancer will
not benefit from a high fat diet. There is no reason to change the diet
of a cat or dog with cancer that is already doing well and eating a
good quality, well tolerated food. Diet changes are not advised for
animals already eating prescription foods that help manage preexisting conditions such as kidney disease or food allergies. High fat
diets can even be harmful for cats and dogs with cancer that are
already overweight, because they promote further weight gain with
all its associated health risks.
High fat diets are most appropriate for cats and dogs with cancer
that have already lost weight, and they are sometimes considered
when there is a real risk of future weight loss as well. If a switch is
made, a good quality, complete and balanced food made by a
reputable manufacturer is always the best choice. The new high fat
diet should be introduced slowly and in gradual increments over a
period of up to several weeks, in order to allow the pet’s intestinal
tract time to adapt. Otherwise, gastroenteritis with vomiting and
diarrhea may result.
NUTRITIONAL SUPPLEMENTS
Innumerable nutritional supplements and nutraceuticals are
promoted for use in cats and dogs with cancer. While it is not
possible to discuss every one of these here, it is possible to provide a
framework that can be used to make safe choices for a pet with
cancer. In the end, before any sort of supplement is started, there
should be reasonable answers to four basic questions. First, has the
product really been proven to work? Second, will it interfere with the
benefits of radiation or chemotherapy being used to treat the
underlying cancer? Third, is it safe? And finally, is the product of

good quality? To answer the first question, the active compound or
compounds should be specifically identified and there should be
proof of benefit, ideally from independent clinical trials done in cats
and dogs. Pet owners must be cautious in accepting testimonial
“evidence” as a substitute for clinical trials: this can be unreliable
and biased, and it is easily manipulated. For the second question,
research is needed to confirm that the supplement will not interfere
with the effectiveness of therapies being used to treat the pet’s
cancer. For example, a common potential interaction involves high
antioxidant intake that might limit the ability of radiation or
chemotherapy to kill cancer cells through oxidative damage. To
answer the third question, data from controlled studies investigating
the safety and lack of toxicity of the product in cats or dogs (not mice
or people) is needed. And finally, for the fourth question there
should be testing that shows the product being used contains a
consistent amount of the active ingredient(s) and is free of
contamination.
Glenna E. Mauldin (Austin, Texas; Calgary, Alberta, Canada)

OVERVIEW
Metabolic responses to illness or injury place critically ill animals at
high risk for malnutrition and its deleterious effects. These problems
include alterations in energy metabolism, compromised immune
function, decreased wound healing, and probably a negative impact
on overall survival.1-4 Whereas healthy animals primarily lose fat
when they do not receive adequate calories (simple starvation), sick
or traumatized patients catabolize lean body mass when they are not
provided with sufficient calories (stressed starvation; ch. 151).

Inadequate calorie intake is a common problem in critically ill
animals due to anorexia, an inability to eat or tolerate feedings (e.g.,
vomiting), or decreased absorptive capabilities.1,4
Because malnutrition may occur quickly, it is important to provide
nutritional support by either enteral or parenteral means if oral
intake is not adequate. The goals of nutritional support are either to
prevent or treat malnutrition. Although unproven in dogs and cats, it
is logical to assume that treatment or prevention of malnutrition
decreases morbidity and mortality.1,2,4,5 Whenever possible, oral
nutritional support (enteral) should be used because it is safest, most
convenient, most physiologically sound, and least expensive (chs. 81
and 146-149). Although enteral nutrition is preferred in critically ill
animals, parenteral nutrition (PN) is an established method of
providing nutritional support to patients whose gastrointestinal (GI)
tracts cannot tolerate enteral feedings.2,3,5-11
Although the use of PN support has become more common, there
remains a perception that this is technically difficult, associated with
complications, and limited to university hospitals and referral
centers. In reality, PN support can be adopted in many practice
settings. Moreover, complications can be significantly reduced with
proper management techniques. The goals of this chapter are to
outline the identification process of dogs and cats most likely to
benefit from PN, to review the process of formulating, implementing,
and monitoring parenteral nutritional support, and to discuss how
PN can be incorporated into various practice situations.

GOALS OF NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT
The goals of nutritional support are to provide for the animal’s
ongoing needs, prevent or correct deficiencies or imbalances,
minimize metabolic derangements, and prevent further catabolism
of lean body tissues. Restoration of optimal body condition should
not necessarily be the goal of nutritional support in the acute stages
of diseases. In severely undernourished dogs and cats, nutritional
support is directed towards preservation of lean body tissue and
organ function, rather than complete reversal of malnutrition, which
is accomplished during convalescence. The ultimate goal of

nutritional support is to provide the necessary nutrients and calories
until the dog or cat voluntarily consumes an adequate amount of
food in its own environment.

THE NUTRITIONAL PLAN
The formulation of a nutritional plan involves firstly a nutritional
assessment (ch. 145). In the context of critically ill animals, risk
factors that predispose them to malnutrition include anorexia for
longer than 3 days, serious underlying disease (e.g., severe trauma,
sepsis, peritonitis, pancreatitis, GI surgery), or significant protein
losses (e.g., protein-losing enteropathy, protein-losing nephropathy,
draining wounds, burns).
Providing nutrition to critically ill animals via a functional
digestive system is the preferred route. Therefore, care should be
taken to determine whether enteral feedings would be tolerated.
Even if only small amounts of enteral nutrition would be tolerated,
this route of feeding should be used and the patient supplemented
with PN only as necessary. The placement of enteral feeding devices
is described in ch. 81.
The first steps of instituting nutritional support include
reestablishing proper hydration status, correction of electrolyte or
acid-base disturbances, and achieving hemodynamic stability.
Commencing nutritional support before such abnormalities are
addressed can increase complication risk and, in some cases, further
compromise the animal. Implementation of the nutritional plan
should be gradual, with a goal of reaching the target level of nutrient
delivery in 48-72 hours being appropriate.

CALCULATING NUTRITIONAL
REQUIREMENTS
Ideally, nutritional support should provide ample substrates for
gluconeogenesis, protein synthesis, and energy necessary to
maintain homeostasis. The clinician must ensure that enough
calories are being provided to sustain critical physiologic processes
(e.g., immune function [ch. 168], wound repair, cell division and

cell growth). The resting energy requirement (RER) is the number of
calories required per day for maintaining homeostasis at rest in a
thermoneutral environment while the animal is in a postabsorptive
state.12 While there are several formulas proposed to calculate the
RER (chs. 147 and 148), a widely used allometric formula that can
be applied to both dogs and cats regardless of body weight is RER (in
kcal/day) = 70 × (body weight in kg)0.75. For animals weighing
between 2 and 30 kg, a formula that provides reasonable estimation
of the RER is RER (in kcal/day) = 30 × (body weight in kg) + 70.
Despite the convention of multiplying the RER by an illness factor
between 1.0 and 2.0 to account for increases in metabolism
associated with different diseases and injuries, less emphasis is now
placed on such subjective and extrapolated factors.5 The current
recommendation is to use more conservative energy estimates (i.e.,
start with the animal’s RER) to avoid overfeeding. Overfeeding can
result in metabolic and GI complications, hepatic dysfunction, and
increased carbon dioxide production.7,12 Using “illness factors” in
calculating energy requirements for cats has been strongly associated
with the development of hyperglycemia.13
As the preservation of lean body mass is a primary goal of
nutritional support, close monitoring of body weight, fluid
distribution, response or tolerance to feedings, and changes in the
underlying condition should dictate whether to increase the calories
in the nutritional plan. Typically, if an animal continues to lose
weight on nutritional support, the calories provided should be
increased by 25% and the plan reassessed in a few days. Additional
adjustments to the nutritional plan might also include the addition
or restriction of electrolytes such as magnesium and potassium as
dictated by serial serum biochemical profiles.

NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT
A major advantage of enteral over PN is superior maintenance of
intestinal structure and function. The presence of nutrients within
the intestinal lumen elicits trophic effects that mediate mucosal cell
proliferation. It has also been proposed that a lack of enteral

nutrition contributes to impairment of mucosal barrier function,
allowing for translocation of intestinal bacteria or endotoxins leading
to sepsis and a systemic inflammatory response.
However, in animals unable to tolerate enteral feedings, e.g., those
that are vomiting, regurgitating, or unable to protect their airway, PN
should be considered. Inability to tolerate enteral feedings is the only
major indication for PN support. Although obtaining enteral access
in critically ill animals can be difficult, every effort must be made to
ensure that a functional GI tract is not bypassed. A review of enteral
feeding devices is provided in ch. 81.

PARENTERAL NUTRITION
The terminology used for describing the use of PN in veterinary
patients has evolved and it is worth reviewing the current
terminology. Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) was previously defined
as the provision of all of the patient’s protein, calorie, and
micronutrient requirements intravenously, whereas partial
parenteral nutrition (PPN) was defined as the provision of only a
part of this requirement (typically 40-70% of the energy
requirement).5 More recently, there has been a shift away from
describing PN in terms of “meeting energy and nutrient
requirements” as they remain largely unknown in animals; recent
recommendations emphasize categorizing PN by the mode of
delivery. PN delivered into a central vein (ch. 75) is described as
“central PN” (CPN) and PN delivered into a peripheral vein is
described as “peripheral PN” (PPN).14 The lower osmolarity of PPN
solutions, as compared to CPN solutions, is achieved by diluting the
solution (ideally to less than 800 mOsm/L), which decreases the
caloric and protein density but makes it suitable for administration
via peripheral veins.

COMPONENTS OF PARENTERAL
NUTRITION
PN is formulated as a mixture of carbohydrate (dextrose), amino
acids, and, usually, fat (lipid). Carbohydrate, in the form of dextrose
(typically 5% or 50%), may have benefits in addition to acting as a
fuel substrate. These potential benefits include stimulation of insulin
secretion, reduction of muscle protein catabolism, and inhibition of
hepatic glucose output, which may spare muscle protein from being
catabolized for gluconeogenesis. However, administration of
dextrose or supplementation of maintenance fluids with dextrose as
the sole source of calories, in most cases, does not amount to
adequate nutritional support and should be discouraged. For
example, a 5% dextrose infusion provides only 170 kcal per liter, and
would provide <25% of the RER for a dog or cat at maintenance fluid
rates. Dextrose infusions are more appropriate for the treatment of
hypoglycemia (ch. 61) rather than for nutritional support.
Crystalline amino acid solutions are an essential component of PN.
The importance of amino acids relates to maintenance of positive
nitrogen balance and repletion of lean body tissue. This may be vital
as critically ill dogs and cats begin to recover from illness.
Supplementation of amino acids may support protein synthesis and
spare tissue proteins from being catabolized via gluconeogenesis.8
The most commonly used amino acid solution (Travasol, Clintec
Nutrition) contains most of the essential amino acids for dogs and
cats. The exception is taurine. However, as PN is typically not used
for more than 10 days, the lack of taurine does not usually become a
problem.

Amino acid solutions are available in concentrations from 4-10%,
but the most commonly used is 8.5%. They are available with and
without electrolytes. Animals with normal serum electrolyte
concentrations typically receive amino acid solutions with
electrolytes, whereas those with electrolyte disturbances may benefit
from amino acid solutions without electrolytes.
Lipid emulsions are the calorically dense component of PN and a
source of essential fatty acids. They are isotonic and are available in
10-20% solutions (Intralipid, Clintec Nutrition). These commercial
lipid emulsions are made primarily of soybean and safflower oils
(ch. 132). They predominantly provide long-chain polyunsaturated
fatty acids including linoleic, oleic, palmitic, and stearic acids. These
solutions are emulsified with egg yolk phospholipids and the tonicity
is adjusted with glycerol. The emulsified fat particles are comparable
in size to chylomicrons and are removed from the circulation via
peripheral lipoprotein lipase. According to guidelines provided by
the American Society of Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition, people
with serum triglycerides >400 mg/dL (>4.5 mmol/L) should have
the lipid proportion in PN markedly reduced or eliminated.15,16
Although specific data regarding the maximal safe level of lipid
administration in dogs and cats are not available, it would seem
prudent to maintain normal serum triglyceride concentrations.
Daily vitamin recommendations for dogs and cats receiving PN are
extrapolated from established oral nutritional requirements.5
Multivitamin preparations intended for intravenous (IV)
administration provide a convenient and practical means for
supplementation and can be added to PN solutions. The addition of
other parenteral medications to PN admixtures is also possible;
however, their compatibility must first be verified. Drugs that are
known to be compatible and sometimes added to PN include
heparin, insulin, potassium chloride, and metoclopramide. While the
addition of insulin to PN is often required in people receiving PN, the
hyperglycemia seen in dogs and cats receiving PN does not usually
require insulin administration. However, diabetic pets require
adjustments to their insulin regimen. Although there is a described
veterinary protocol for the addition of insulin directly to PN, it is
often easiest to manage diabetics receiving PN with subcutaneous
injections of insulin.2,5

PARENTERAL NUTRITION
COMPOUNDING
Based on the nutritional assessment and plan, PN can be formulated
according to the worksheets found in Boxes 164.1 and 164.2. For
CPN (Box 164.1), the first step is the calculation of the patient’s
RER. Protein requirements (grams of protein required per day) are
then calculated, taking into consideration factors such as excessive
GI, renal, or cutaneous protein loss, or severe hepatic or renal
disease (where a reduced protein level might be warranted).
Although some recommendations meet all energy requirements with
only dextrose and lipids, the protocol listed accounts for energy also
provided from amino acids in the calculations and subtracts the
calories provided by amino acids from the daily RER to estimate the
total nonprotein calories required. Nonprotein calories are then
usually provided as a 50:50 mixture of lipids and dextrose. This
50:50 ratio can be adjusted in cases of persistent hyperglycemia or
hypertriglyceridemia (e.g., a higher proportion of calories from lipid
in an animal with hyperglycemia). The calories provided from each
component (amino acids, lipids, and dextrose) are then divided by
their respective caloric densities, and the exact amounts of each
component are added to the PN bags in an aseptic fashion. The
amount of CPN delivered will often provide less than the daily fluid
requirement, and additional fluid can either be added to the PN bag
at the time of compounding or be provided as a separate infusion
(ch. 120).

For formulation of PPN, Box 164.2 provides a step-by-step
protocol in which animals of various size can receive 70% of their
RER and approximately meet their daily maintenance fluid
requirement. In extremely small animals (≤3 kg), the amount of PPN
will exceed the maintenance fluid requirement and increase the risk
for fluid overload, so volume adjustments are necessary. Also, in
animals requiring conservative fluid administration (e.g., congestive
heart failure), these calculations for PPN may provide excessive fluid
volumes. This formulation has been designed so that the proportion
of each PN component is dependent on animal weight such that a
smaller animal (3-5 kg) will receive proportionally more calories
from lipids, compared to a large dog (>30 kg), which would receive
more calories in the form of carbohydrates. This allows the resulting
formulation to approximate the daily fluid requirement.

Compounding of PN should be done aseptically under a laminar
flow hood using a semiautomated, closed-system, PN compounder.
Regulations implemented by the United States Pharmacopeia in
2004 require strict adherence to sterile compounding of PN
solutions.17 Given these strict conditions, it has become easier to
have a local human hospital or a human home health care company
(e.g., Coram CVS Specialty Infusion Services) compound PN
solutions according to protocols outlines in Boxes 164.1 and 164.2
and have the solution delivered to the practice within hours.
Alternatively, commercial ready-to-use preparations of dextrose,
amino acids, and lipids are available for IV use (Table 164.1), and
clinical experience with such products have been recently
published.17,18 While these ready-to-use preparations are
convenient, they provide only 30-50% of caloric requirements when
administered at maintenance fluid rates and as a result should only
be used for interim nutritional support or to supplement low-dose
enteral feedings.17,18 In practices that do not have access to
compounded PN, the use of ready-to-use PN solutions may be a
viable option for provision of nutritional support. Some of these
products are available as segregated chambers and the solutions are
mixed before use by squeezing the bag and breaking the internal
seals, yielding an admixture of amino acids, dextrose and lipids
(Video 164.1

).

PARENTERAL NUTRITION
ADMINISTRATION
The administration of any PN requires a dedicated, aseptically placed
catheter, used solely for PN administration. Most critically ill dogs
and cats that receive PN require placement of a new or additional
catheter, because PN should not be administered through previously
existing catheters placed for reasons other than PN. Long catheters
composed of silicone, polyurethane, or tetrafluoroethylene are
recommended for use with any type of PN to reduce the risk of
thrombophlebitis.3,5 Multilumen catheters are often recommended
for CPN administration and can remain in place for long time
periods. Such catheters can be used for blood sampling,
administration of additional fluids, and IV medication
administration, and they negate the need for separate catheters
placed at other sites.5
The high osmolarity of CPN solutions (often >1200 mOsm/L)
requires administration through a central venous (e.g., jugular)
catheter (ch. 75), while PPN solutions can be administered through
either a jugular or a peripheral venous catheter. The concern with
administering fluids high in osmolarity has been the risk of
thrombophlebitis, although this side-effect has not been
demonstrated in dogs or cats.
Because of the metabolic derangements associated with critical
illness, PN should be instituted gradually over 48 hours. It is
recommended that CPN be started at 50% of RER on day 1 and
increased to the targeted amount by the second day. In this manner,
serum electrolyte, glucose, acid-base status, total fluid requirements,
and other parameters can be monitored as CPN is administered. In

most cases, PPN can be started without a gradual increase. It is also
important to adjust the rates of other fluids being administered
concurrently. For both CPN and PPN, the animal’s catheter and
infusion lines must be handled aseptically at all times to reduce the
risk of PN-related infection (ch. 75).
PN should be delivered as continuous rate infusions over 24 hours
via fluid infusion pumps. Inadvertent delivery of massive amounts of
PN can result if administration is not properly regulated. Once a bag
of PN is set up for administration, it should not be disconnected even
for walks or diagnostic procedures. The drip regulator can be
decreased to an extremely slow rate and can accompany the animal if
it needs to be moved. Administration of PN through an in-line filter
(Air Eliminating Filter, Clintec Nutrition Division) is recommended
and is attached at the time of setup. This set up process is performed
daily with each new bag of PN. Each bag should only hold 1 day’s
worth of PN, and the accompanying fluid administration sets and inline filter are changed at the same time using aseptic technique. If
using ready-made PN solutions, the recommendation is that the bag
be in use only for 24 hours, and any solution remaining after 24
hours is discarded. However, there are no studies confirming if this
is necessary. Discontinuation of PN should be done when the animal
resumes consuming an adequate amount of calories or at least 50%
of RER. Whereas CPN should be gradually discontinued over a 6- to
12-hour period, PPN can be discontinued abruptly.

COMPLICATIONS
As with any therapy intended for critically ill animals, complications
can occur. Complications associated with PN can include mechanical
complications of the catheter and lines, thrombophlebitis, metabolic
abnormalities, and sepsis. Mechanical complications such as
inadvertent catheter removal, catheter occlusion, and line
disconnection or breakage are probably not inherently related to PN
and are likely no more common than in any dog or cat with an IV
catheter. Metabolic complications are much more likely to be related
to PN and include hyperglycemia, hypertriglyceridemia,
hyperbilirubinemia, increased alkaline phosphatase activity,
azotemia, electrolyte shifts, and

hyperammonemia.2,5,6,10,11,13,14,17,18 The more commonly
encountered complications, namely hyperglycemia and
hypertriglyceridemia, are usually transient and can be effectively
managed without serious consequences. However, one study
demonstrated higher mortality rates in cats that developed
hyperglycemia within the first 24 hours of PN.11 Decreasing the
infusion rate for 12-24 hours is often effective, although sometimes
reformulation of PN is required. Animals with biochemical changes
subsequent to initiation of PN should have more frequent laboratory
parameter evaluations.
Septic complications (ch. 128), including catheter-site infection
with and without systemic sepsis, have been reported in dogs and
cats receiving PN. This complication is uncommon, ranging from 312% in dogs and cats receiving PN.2,6,10,11,17 Septic complications
can be minimized by strict adherence to established protocols and
careful attention to early signs of problems relating to catheter care
(ch. 186). Any catheter suspected of causing fever, increase in white
blood cell count, or other sign compatible with infection should be
removed and cultured.

MONITORING
Given the potential for complications, monitoring of dogs and cats
receiving PN is a vital part of nutritional support and should be
similar to that for any critically ill animal. Careful daily monitoring of
the catheter site is recommended to detect problems early (e.g.,
inflammation or malposition). Catheters should be evaluated for
patency and bandages changed daily. At a minimum, body weight,
body temperature, respiratory rate, catheter site, and serum glucose
should be evaluated daily. All blood tubes should be inspected for
visible lipemia. Monitoring of other parameters (e.g., electrolytes,
acid-base status, complete blood count, biochemical profile) may
also be indicated. Persistent hyperglycemia, hypertriglyceridemia, or
signs of encephalopathy should prompt reevaluation and may
necessitate decreasing rate of infusion or reformulation of PN and
serial evaluation of blood work.

SUMMARY
With the growing recognition that nutritional support is an integral
part of the therapeutic regimen of critically ill animals, it is becoming
increasingly important for veterinarians to be able to initiate enteral
or parenteral nutritional support in their practice or to refer these
cases to facilities capable of providing such therapy when necessary.
Proper identification of dogs and cats most likely to benefit from
nutritional support and the ability to formulate, administer, and
monitor nutritional interventions are key factors in ensuring the
successful implementation of critical care nutrition.

Fiber includes a vast array of heterogeneous compounds, including
naturally derived and synthetic, differing in chemical composition, size,
structure, and behavior but unified by indigestibility. Fiber participates in
complex interactions within the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) to produce local
and systemic effects via gut microbiota-dependent and independent routes
to influence gut motility, digestion, physiology, the immune system, and
metabolic function. Type and amount of fiber, food matrix, and diet
composition interact with individual variations in digestion, microbiome,
and physiology to determine its ultimate effect. Fiber is important in health
maintenance and disease prevention, possibly affecting GIT transit time,
satiety or food intake, glycemic response, bile acid and cholesterol use, gut

microbiome, and fecal volume. Therapeutic applications include GIT issues
(chs. 48-52, 260, 262, 263), obesity (ch. 150), diabetes mellitus (chs.
291, 292), and hyperlipidemia (ch. 156).

DIETARY FIBER
Initially referring only to indigestible components of plant cell walls,
including naturally associated non-carbohydrate structures such as lignin,
the definition of dietary fiber (DF) has been revised multiple times and now
includes other carbohydrates escaping digestion by intestinal enzymes,
including non-digestible oligosaccharides (NDO) and resistant starch (RS).
Due to changing definitions and analyses, RS and NDO may be referenced
separately from DF in the literature.1 Animal “fiber” (indigestible
substances such as bone, fur/feathers, and connective tissues) may
functionally overlap somewhat with plant-derived fiber; however, more
work is needed to understand this and it is currently outside the scope of
this definition.2
Fiber has commonly been differentiated by molecular weight and
solubility because they are more easily analyzed, although other aspects,
such as viscosity and fermentability, are more relevant to physiologic effect
and behavior in the GIT.3 General correlations between molecular weight,
solubility, and function have been made historically, but are not always
reliable.

MOLECULAR WEIGHT
High molecular weight DF (HMWDF) includes fiber with degree of
polymerization (DP) ≥10, while low molecular weight DF (LMWDF)
includes soluble NDO (DP of 3-9),4 many of which are considered prebiotic fibers. Many natural fibers are mixed molecular weight, e.g., inulin,
found in fruits and vegetables or purified from sources such as chicory
(Figure 165.1).

SOLUBILITY
The ability to disperse in water results from chemical structure and
interactions with surrounding molecules. General trends have been drawn
between solubility, water absorption, and effects in the GIT; however,
chemical analysis and actual behavior in GIT do not correlate perfectly.6,7

Chemical modification can also affect solubility and activity. Insoluble DF
(IDF), typically obtained from plant cell walls (e.g., cellulose,
hemicelluloses, lignin), are generally non-viscous and less fermentable. IDF
primarily adds bulk, which can dilute calories and increase food volume
and fecal output. Associated gastric distention may trigger other effects.
Coarsely ground IDF promotes laxation by physically stimulating colonic
motility and secretion of water and mucus to soften stool; longer fiber
length also increases water-holding capacity compared to smaller particles.
Finely ground IDF may actually be constipating.8 IDF is useful in
therapeutic diets for weight management (ch. 150), constipation (chs. 51,
152, and 263), hairball control,9 and possibly diabetes mellitus (chs. 291
and 292).10,11 It is also used to create the “brushing” matrix in some dental
diets. Drawbacks to its use can include altered nutrient digestibility,12
which must be accounted for in dietary formulations. Some pet owners may
also perceive larger bowel movements negatively. Soluble DF (SDF) can
help dilute calories and add bulk; however, its effects in the GIT and on
stool output are more complicated due to variations in viscosity and
fermentability. RS may act as IDF in the upper GIT and be useful in
glycemic control or weight loss, but RS is typically moderately to highly
fermentable, so effects in the lower GIT will diverge from most other IDF.

FIGURE 165.1 Dietary fiber classification based on
molecular weight or degree of polymerization (DP) and
solubility. Total dietary fiber by the Prosky method (AOAC
985.29) captures high molecular weight dietary fiber
(HMWDF) but excludes low molecular weight dietary
fiber (LMWDF). Some resistant starch (RS) is captured as
part of insoluble dietary fiber (IDF) measurements.5

VISCOSITY
The ability to render digesta more resistant to flow depends on fiber’s
molecular weight, chemical structure, solubility, and concentration.6 Highly
viscous fibers even form gel-like substances at sufficient concentrations.
Viscous fibers are soluble, but not all soluble fibers are viscous (e.g.,
LMWDF/NDO). Viscosity can be modified by local GIT conditions (e.g., pH,
ions), form ingested (purified vs. whole food), and meal composition.
Chemical modification of fiber also alters viscosity (e.g., guar gum vs.
partially hydrolyzed guar gum; Figure 165.1).

Viscosity alters flow and mechanical mixing of digesta, changing its
interface with the GIT, which alters nutrient diffusion, digestion, and
absorption.13,14 Increased viscosity slows gastric emptying and small
intestinal transit.12 Viscous fibers, therefore, are used to increase satiety,
decrease food intake, and modulate post-prandial glycemic responses.10 If
the fiber retains enough structure through the colon, its water-holding and
gelling capacity can normalize stool, useful in both constipation and
diarrhea. Potential drawbacks may include excessive interference with
digestion or absorption. Delayed gastric emptying may also worsen
disorders like dyspepsia, especially if the fiber is also fermentable, which
can relax the lower esophageal sphincter.15

FERMENTABILITY
Some fibers can be fermented by gut microbiota to varying degrees in the
lower intestine, which may impact gut microbial composition or metabolite
production.16 Fibers selectively utilized by host microorganisms to confer a
health benefit are designated pre-biotic. By providing an alternative
substrate, fermentation of proteins and other substances linked to negative
health outcomes may be spared.17 Fermentation of fiber may produce
lactate, gases (e.g., methane), and the short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs)
acetate, propionate, and butyrate.
The majority of propionate is utilized by hepatocytes, while acetate is the
main SCFA to reach peripheral tissues.18,19 Propionate may reduce lipids in
blood and liver or enhance insulin sensitivity in some species.20 In cats, it
may spare amino acids from gluconeogenesis.21 Butyrate is the preferred
energy source of colonocytes and is important in maintaining the anaerobic
environment. By stimulating proliferation of both colonocytes and
enterocytes, it enhances mucosal weight, surface area, brush border
enzymes, and functional capacity, including absorption of water and
electrolytes.13 SCFAs also alter gene expression and signal transduction,
variably activating receptors in multiple tissues,21 and may also affect
appetite and food intake by acting centrally21 or stimulating release of
glucagon-like peptide-1, peptide YY, and/or leptin.18-20
Collectively, SCFAs are important in maintenance of health and response
to disease. They are important immune modulators, with a vital role in
mucosal immunity and tolerance, increase colonic blood flow, and help

maintain intestinal barrier function and local environment.20 SCFAs acidify
luminal pH, potentially inhibiting growth of pathogens6,13 and/or creating
ammonia or nitrogen traps. Diets lacking in fermentable fibers may
increase the risk of colitis20 and obesity, decrease microbiota diversity1 or
impair intestinal healing; therefore, inclusion is recommended in GIT
recovery diets.22 Fermentable fibers have broad therapeutic applications,
with potential effects on glycemic control, lipolysis, satiety and energy
intake, immune response or tolerance, and gut health or function.18-20,23
The role of SCFAs is complex, likely with interspecies differences; therefore,
much remains to be learned. SCFAs can also become disruptive at high
concentrations,20 and accumulation exerts an osmotic effect.14 Overactive
fermentation increases flatulence, abdominal distension, and fecal
frequency, with reduced fecal quality.24
IDF, excluding RS, is typically slowly to non-fermentable. Most soluble
fibers are fermentable. As fibers are fermented, associated fecal bulk
decreases, although microbial mass may increase. Rapidly fermented fibers
are utilized more extensively in the ileum and/or proximal colon, quickly
producing more gases and SCFAs,1 while mixed fiber sources or blends
moderate fermentation.

OTHER
Additional effects of fiber are quite varied. For example, specific fiber
structures directly bind to receptors on intestinal epithelial or immune cells
(e.g., toll-like receptors), interact with regulatory molecules such as AMPactivated protein kinase (AMPK),25 or provide alternative adhesion sites for
microbes.13 Fibers may favorably alter exposure to certain compounds
and/or protect the mucosa from toxins, carcinogens, or other irritants.
Some fibers bind mineral ions, particularly cations (e.g., calcium and
zinc). Non-purified fibers can also introduce other compounds (e.g., phytic
acids, polyphenols) that affect mineral bioavailability differently than do
purified fibers. Fiber has the potential to sequester minerals, which can
then be released for absorption in the colon or lost with excretion, so the
effects on mineral bioavailability are not uniform across fiber types or
concentrations. IDF (e.g., cellulose) appears to decrease digestibility of
minerals and increase excretion in some studies,26 but have little effect in
others, while SCFAs may enhance absorption of calcium and magnesium.

Mineral bioavailability, whether it is impaired, enhanced, or minimally
affected,12,23 must be accounted for in pet food formulations.
Fibers may impede bile acid function and/or interfere with enterohepatic
recycling.8 Interference with bile acids can be used therapeutically to
reduce fat digestion (e.g., for obesity or hyperlipidemia), deplete cholesterol
stores, or treat bile-acid-induced diarrhea (chs. 272, 273). Both viscous
and fermentable fibers are associated with increased excretion of bile acids;
however, natural mixed fibers sources typically higher in IDF (e.g., wheat
bran) have also been associated. It becomes detrimental when loss of bilesalt–associated taurine exceeds endogenous synthesis. Increased loss also
can occur if fermentation over-shortens GIT transit or increases gut
microbial consumption of taurine.
In general, greater amounts of less fermentable fiber (e.g., IDF) decrease
total diet dry matter digestibility, so highly digestible diets contain less IDF.
Fiber has variable effects on protein digestibility and other nutrient
bioavailability,12,27 although total tract digestibility is unreliable due to
confounding effects of microbial changes related to fermentation.
Alterations in diet digestibility have potential for therapeutic application,
e.g., obesity or glycemic control, provided appropriate compensatory
dietary fortifications occur (e.g., minerals, taurine, protein). The antinutritive effects can be detrimental in other circumstances (e.g., growth,
exocrine pancreatic insufficiency). Safe upper limits for inclusion in pet
foods have been set for some fibers14; however, given the complexity of
interactions and the use of newer fiber sources, research and diet trials are
needed. Fiber effects on digestibility, mineral absorption, and bile acids are
not uniform and can become problematic, so it must be accounted for in
food formulations.

QUANTIFYING DIETARY FIBER AND PET
FOOD
The ability to identify and quantify fiber facilitates comparisons and guides
dietary recommendations; however, analytical quantification is sometimes
discordant with physiologic effect.4 Although the expectation may be that
“total” DF values represent all fiber in a food, the reality is that “total DF”
(TDF) measurements are limited by analytical methods. The “Prosky
method” has long been the gold standard for measuring TDF; however, this
method cannot capture LMWDF or all RS.4 Although specific fiber types
may be measured separately, these cannot simply be added to TDF without

double-counting some fiber. Newer methodology more comprehensively
measures TDF, capturing both LMWDF and HMWDF with increased RS.
Unfortunately, these methods are not yet uniformly adopted due to
increased cost, technical expertise, and decreased availability. TDF by
Prosky method remains the most common reported measure, so it is
important to be aware of the fiber excluded.
The pet food industry has been very slow to adopt any TDF methodology;
most pet foods only provide crude fiber (CF) as per required guaranteed
analysis. An outdated method from the 1800s,28 CF only recovers the IDF
cellulose, along with variable fractions of lignin and hemicellulose, and
possibly some connective tissue. CF is not predictive of DF content, does
not correlate with other methods, and no substantial conclusions can be
reached using this measure. Fiber analyses for forage (e.g., acid or neutral
detergent fibers) are inadequate for pet food.29
Importantly, fiber measurements impact assessment of digestible starch.
Any underestimation in DF overestimates digestible starch. This is
supported by studies in pet food where predicted digestible starch was too
high with CF but more realistic with TDF (Prosky method),29 although even
this overestimates starch in some pet foods compared to methods that
include NDO.29-32 In short, total fiber is not yet routinely quantified in pet
food, which presents major limitations.
Some pet food companies voluntarily measure TDF, most often for
selected therapeutic diets. This may be reported on a dry matter or energy
basis (g/1000 kilocalories). High quality pet foods should be able to provide
nutrients per calorie, as are often provided in product guides for
therapeutic diets, on some company websites, or by request. Use of TDF,
IDF and SDF (g/1000 kcal) allows comparison between diets and
prediction of individual intake regardless of variations in diet moisture or
energy. Ingredient lists are not reliable for accurately gauging fiber intake,
with several drawbacks: amounts are not provided, RS is not predicted,
natural sources of fiber (e.g., fruit pomaces, beet pulp) provide variable
TDF,33 and not all fibers are obvious from ingredient lists. Fiber in pet food
can be provided as part of more complex whole ingredients or added from
semi-purified sources (e.g., fruit pomaces, beet pulp) or purified sources
(e.g., fructooligosaccharides [FOS]).
Traditional fiber sources in pet food include cellulose and beet pulp.
Cellulose is insoluble, non-viscous, and poorly fermentable. Beet pulp, a
natural mixed fiber source (∼80:20 IDF:SDF) providing a mixture of
viscous and non-viscous fibers of moderate fermentability, has desirable
effects on fecal quality and output.17 A drawback is its variability in fiber

content, composition and quality, so blends of purified fibers sources have
been evaluated and incorporated into some pet foods. Large amounts of
highly viscous, fermentable fibers (e.g., 8.5-9.5% TDF) are generally
unsuitable for cat food and more likely to result in diarrhea and decreased
protein digestibility.23 More moderately fermentable fibers and/or lower
concentrations are preferred. Low levels of NDO (0.5-2%) do not appear to
decrease digestibility of pet food.23,27,33

CLINICAL UTILITY
Misconceptions regarding the utility of fiber in canine and feline diets have
persisted, but even the natural diet of wolves can contain a substantial
amount of plant matter34 and both dogs and cats are able to ferment
diverse plant fibers.23,35 DF supplied via high quality pet foods is often the
preferred way to incorporate large amounts of fiber into pet diets for both
palatability and to ensure diets remain balanced, although supplementing
fiber to a base diet is desired is some cases. Incorporating fiber and diet
transitions should be gradual and incremental to avoid negative sideeffects, allowing gut microbial adaption and monitoring for signs of
intolerance.
Review of a pet’s diet history and tolerance to DF, in conjunction with
TDF, IDF and SDF concentrations, is useful in predicting the type of change
in DF intake that may be helpful, particularly when combined with
knowledge of fibers’ potential benefits and drawbacks. Individual variation
in response to or tolerance for the differing DFs is possible, however;
therefore, use is still often a matter of trial and error. Standardizing doses
for supplementing fiber to a base diet is further limited by the substantial
variations in fiber that already exist between different diets. For example,
many dogs with chronic idiopathic large bowel diarrhea benefit from
adding psyllium husk to their diet (ch. 263) but, in one study, effective
dosages ranged anywhere from 0.31 to 4.9 g/kg (median 1.33 g/kg).36
Psyllium seed husk is essentially a mixed fiber source, while providing
mostly soluble, viscous, moderately to slowly fermentable fiber that forms
mucilaginous gels in water.37 It is more slowly fermented compared to most
SDF, shifting fermentation distally. In addition to increasing viscosity and
slowing transit, psyllium also normalizes feces, increases SCFAs, promotes
peristalsis, and binds certain toxins. Psyllium can improve stool
consistency, reduce urgency and frequency in cases of chronic diarrhea, and
also soften stool and increase frequency to improve output and prevent

constipation.37-39 Psyllium fiber is, therefore, often a first choice to trial
and has also been incorporated into some commercial therapeutic diets. If
it is being added as a supplement, it should be given with every meal and
the dose titrated to the individual.
If supplementation with psyllium is unsuccessful or contraindicated,
other fiber supplements are available. The type of supplement that is
chosen will depend on the desired effect (Table 165.1) and expected purity
and quality. Supplementation with purified fermentable or “prebiotic” fiber
types such as inulin or FOS may be trialed; however, given their more rapid
fermentability, doses should likely be a fraction of expected psyllium doses
and gradually titrated to give time for microbial adaptation. Wheat dextrin
should potentially be avoided in some animals as portions are easily
degraded to sugars and may increase post-prandial blood glucose.8 In
people, it can also decrease stool moisture and be constipating. Coarse
wheat bran (primarily IDF) or cellulose may be used for providing bulk to
food or feces. Some products provide mixtures of several fibers or
individual supplements may be combined for blended effect (e.g.,
combining FOS or inulin with an IDF to moderate fermentability).
Although natural sources of fiber (e.g., flaxseed, pumpkin) are popular and
more palatable, they are also likely to provide other nutrients and energy as
well, so care must be taken to avoid adding excess calories and unbalancing
a diet. If benefits are noted with use of whole foods, it may be difficult to
disentangle the effect of fiber from nutraceutical benefits related to other
plant-derived compounds. Although pumpkin contains mixed fibers,
including rapidly fermentable pectins, provided TDF per unit is relatively
low (∼6-7 grams TDF per cup; 0.4-0.5 g/tbsp, U.S. Department of
Agriculture [USDA] food database), compared to purified fiber
supplements. Its traditional benefits may relate to co-administration of
other bioactive compounds and/or that only relatively small amounts of
highly fermentable fiber are needed.17,40

Chapter 166: Adverse
Reactions to Foods: Allergies
Versus Intolerance
Jason W. Gagné

A C RO N YM S
AFR adverse food reaction
CAFR cutaneous adverse food reaction
GI gastrointestinal
OTC over-the-counter
An adverse food reaction (AFR) is an aberrant response to a
component of the diet and encompasses both terms food intolerance
and food allergy. Both disorders may clinically manifest as
dermatologic and/or gastrointestinal (GI) signs. Food intolerance
encompasses pharmacologic and metabolic reactions, food
poisoning/intoxication, and food idiosyncrasy; it is believed to have
no immunologic basis. Food allergy is a term reserved for those with
clinical signs due to an immune-mediated reaction to a food antigen.
Recently, the term cutaneous adverse food reaction (CAFR) has been
used to describe signs associated with the skin (Figure 166.1).
The prevalence of AFR in dogs and cats varies from source to
source. A recent critically appraised topic has stated a prevalence of
CAFR of 1-2% of dogs presenting to their veterinarian for any
diagnosis, and 0-24% for those with skin disease.1 The prevalence of
CAFR in cats is 0.2% of those presenting to a university hospital, or

3-6% for those with skin disease.1 The prevalence of CAFR does
increase when accounting for those with pruritus and those with
allergic skin disease. It is not unusual for those with atopic
dermatitis to also experience AFRs. The prevalence of concurrent
cutaneous and GI signs in dogs with AFR is believed to be anywhere
from 6-44%.2,3 This wide range is likely to decrease as the profession
becomes more attuned to those examining dermatologic signs
recording GI signs and vice-versa.
A more accurate prevalence of AFR is hindered from being
achieved due to differences in location of studies, method of
diagnosis, referral vs primary care center reporting, and low sample
size in studies. Therefore, there is a need for additional research on
this topic.

FOOD INTOLERANCE
Food intolerance has a non-immunologic etiology and may occur on
a first exposure to a food, “food additive or substance.”
Pharmacologic and metabolic reactions include an array of
compounds. This category includes vasoactive and biogenic amines
such as histamine found in scombroid fish (mackerel, tuna,
skipjack), which may cause an adverse reaction within minutes of
ingestion. The concentration of histidine available for bacterial
conversion to histamine to cause such reactions in unspoiled
commercial pet food is low.4 Therefore, reactions are more prevalent
in raw and spoiled homemade fish diets. The maldigestion with
secondary malabsorption that causes an osmotic diarrhea (e.g.,
lactose intolerance) is an example of a metabolic adverse reaction.5,6
Undigested lactose is rapidly fermented by small intestinal and
colonic bacteria creating short chain fatty acids and resulting in
borborygmus, gas, abdominal discomfort, and diarrhea.
Food poisoning/intoxication reactions occur in response to
ingestion of food containing toxins or microbial contamination.
Methylxanthines found in chocolate are a classic example as
documented in dogs.7 Strains and toxins of bacteria known to
contaminate food and cause acute enteritis in dogs and cats include

Salmonella, Campylobacter, and Clostridium spp. in addition to
Escherichia coli (ch. 195).
The term food idiosyncrasy is used to describe an abnormal
response to food additives and substances such as gelling agents,
gums, emulsifiers, preservatives, colors, and humectants. While they
have all been implicated as a cause of GI disorders of dogs and cats,
minimal evidence exists.8

FOOD ALLERGENS
While incompletely understood, food allergy is an AFR with an
immunologic basis in response to ingestion/absorption of a dietary
antigen, usually a dietary protein. A compromise in digestion
(breakdown of antigenic factors of a protein), the intestinal epithelial
barrier, and/or oral tolerance may lead to development of food
allergy. It is worth noting that the role of the gut associated lymphoid
tissue (GALT) is to distinguish “self” from “non-self,” to eliminate
what is foreign to the body, and to protect components of “self.” All
dietary antigens are foreign, which speaks to the remarkable ability
of the GALT to create an oral tolerance to nutrients, while removing
pathogens.
Food allergy may involve the well-understood IgE-mediated (type
I hypersensitivity) sensitization and stimulation reactions that occur
within minutes of ingesting the dietary antigen, but may also involve
non-IgE-mediated (type III and/or IV hypersensitivity) reactions
that are less understood, and include immune complex formation
and cell-mediated delayed responses. This may explain why a low
number of dogs and cats experience a flare-up of signs on the first
day after a food challenge (ch. 160).
Most food allergens that elicit an immune response in humans are
water-soluble glycoproteins with molecular weights between 10-70
kDa, which are relatively stable to heat, pH, and digestive enzymes.9
In dogs, all recognized allergenic proteins have weighed ≥20
kDa,10,11 and the most common food allergens are beef, dairy
products, and chicken. In cats, the most common food allergens are
beef, fish, and chicken.12 This reflects the most fed ingredients in
commercial pet food.

CLINICAL FEATURES
DERMATOLOGIC RESPONSES IN DOGS
There are no sex predilections for cutaneous disease due to AFR in
dogs.13-16 The age at which clinical signs have been reported ranges
from 4 months to 14 years,17 with initial signs reported in those prior
to 6 months of age or less than 1 year of age in 22% and 38% of cases,
respectively.18 Conflicting information exists regarding breed
predispositions.
Presentation of dogs with AFR occurs on a nonseasonal basis and
may be indistinguishable from atopic dermatitis (ch. 160). Clinical
signs include erythema, otitis externa, secondary lesions due to selftrauma, and variable degrees of pruritus that may be generalized or
localized to the face, pinnae, perineal, axillary, inguinal, ventral
abdominal and paw regions.13,15,19,20 While pruritus is the most
common sign, otitis externa is commonly observed, and may be the
only sign. Secondary bacterial/yeast infections, papules, pustules,
crusts, epidermal collarettes, and seborrhea may also be observed.1316
Chronic changes may include hyperpigmentation, lichenification,
and alopecia.

FIGURE 166.1 Classification of adverse reactions
to food. IgE, Immunoglobulin E. Adapted from
Guilford WG. Adverse reactions to food. In: Guilford
WG, Center SA, Strombeck DR, eds. Strombeck’s
Small Animal Gastroenterology . Philadelphia: WB
Saunders; 1996:436-450; Roudebush P, Guilford

MS, Thatcher CD, Remillard RL, et al, eds. Small
Animal Clinical Nutrition . Topeka, KS: Mark
Morris Institute; 2000:431-453; Verlinden A, Hesta
M, Millet S, et al. Food allergy in dogs and cats: a
review. Crit Rev Food Sci Nutr . 2006;46(3):259273.
Uncommon clinical signs that have been reported include urticaria
(hives) characterized by wheals,21 erythema multiforme (ch. 178),22
vasculitis (ch. 181),23 and anaphylaxis (ch. 129). Angioedema, a
localized form, is characterized by edematous swellings of the lips,
face, eyelids, ears, conjunctivae, and/or tongue, with or without
pruritus. Angioedema may also result from drugs, vaccines,
infections, atopic dermatitis, and blood transfusions.

DERMATOLOGIC RESPONSES IN CATS

There are no sex predilections for cutaneous disease due to AFR in
cats. The age at which clinical signs have been reported ranges from
3 months to 15 years, with 50% of cats experiencing initial signs by
the age of 3 years in one study.24
Clinical signs include nonseasonal, localized or generalized
pruritus in 100% of cats with food allergy.20,25 Pruritus is primarily
localized to the head, neck, and ears (which may lead to severe selftrauma), but may spread to the limbs, ventral abdomen, and inguinal
region. Self-induced alopecia, as well as exfoliative, exudative, and
miliary dermatitis and secondary scaling dermatoses have been
reported. Otitis externa, eosinophilic plaques, ulcers, and
granulomas may also develop. Urticaria, angioedema, and
conjunctivitis may occur.25,26 See Figure 166.2, A-F for
dermatologic clinical manifestations of canine and feline CAFR.

GASTROINTESTINAL RESPONSES IN
DOGS AND CATS
There are no sex or age predilections for GI disease due to AFR in
dogs or cats. Clinical signs may include vomiting, borborygmus,
flatulence, weight loss, intermittent manifestations consistent with
abdominal pain, and diarrhea (increased frequency, volume, and
loosened consistency).14,16,26-28 Diarrhea and vomiting are more
frequently reported signs, with a higher prevalence of diarrhea in
dogs, and vomiting in cats.29
AFRs are included in a vast array of differential diagnoses for GI
disease since they can occur in every segment of the GI tract and may
present as acute or chronic. Acute onset of signs due to AFR is likely
food intolerance rather than food allergy.
Food-responsive enteropathy (FRE) is a type of chronic
enteropathy (ch. 262). In a recent short communication that looked
at the long-term outcome of 203 cases of dogs with chronic
enteropathy, 64% of dogs were classified as having FRE, making it
the most common canine enteropathy.30
Inflammatory bowel disease involves a complex interplay between
host genetics, immune status, and the GI microbiota (ch. 262). Diet

influences quantity, diversity, and metabolic activity of the
microbiota.31 While we cannot be certain, it is possible that a
dysbiosis of the GI microbiota may occur in patients with AFR, which
may contribute to development of inflammatory bowel disease
(IBD). Since IBD is a chronic cluster of enteropathies,
histopathologic findings do not correlate well to those that are foodresponsive or other treatment, and our limited knowledge of the GI
microbiome makes it difficult to draw any conclusions currently.

PRURITIC THRESHOLD
The concept of the pruritic threshold is that each individual dog or
cat has a different tolerable level; once that level is reached, pruritus
develops. The stimuli that cause one to reach or exceed their
threshold include (but are not limited to) ectoparasites, atopic
dermatitis, and diet. Regarding ectoparasites and atopic dermatitis,
these stimuli may not be present (or may be pharmacologically
controlled) at certain times of the year, and therefore may lower the
allergen load to threshold for an individual. This would allow a dog
or cat to tolerate a food to which they might be allergic or intolerant
without experiencing the clinical manifestation of pruritus. This
situation would result in food allergy appearing to be seasonal in
nature.
It is not uncommon to observe multiple allergens affecting the
same patient. In dogs, 20-30% of food allergy cases have skin disease
including atopic dermatitis and flea allergy.11,17,18,26 The
combination of diseases may hinder the diagnosis of food allergy.
This highlights the importance of diet and dietary history as a means
of reducing allergen load, to avoid exceeding the pruritic threshold.
