INTRODUCTION AND
CONSIDERATIONS BEFORE STARTING
IMMUNOSUPPRESSIVE THERAPY
Despite years of research, immune-mediated (IM) disorders, and
immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA) in particular, continue
to cause significant morbidity and mortality in dogs and cats.1-4 This
chapter will focus more on IM blood disorders. As well, ch. 144
describes immunosuppressive drug pharmacology in detail. Once a
diagnosis is made for an IM disorder, clinical management involves
initiation of immunosuppressive therapy. This is hopefully achieved
with one or more medications, each with its own positive and
negative traits. With each patient, it would be ideal to complete all
testing prior to initiation of therapy, including adequate testing to
arrive at the correct diagnosis as well as appropriately looking for
any secondary triggers/diseases as deemed appropriate. This could
include imaging and appropriate testing to screen for possible
cancer/lymphoma before starting glucocorticoid therapy, based on
the likelihood of cancer in the individual patient, because once
treatment with glucocorticoids is started, making the diagnosis of
lymphoma can be challenging.1,4,5 In addition, appropriate testing
for infectious diseases based on signalment, environment, travel
history (ch. 9), physical exam findings (ch. 3), and minimum
database are indicated to ensure immunosuppressive therapy is not
contraindicated.1
IM disorders cause clinical disease through multiple avenues, with
immune dysfunction being central to the pathologic process and
supporting the rationale for immunosuppressive therapy. Goals of
immunosuppressive therapy for IM disorders include achieving
disease remission followed by implementing a controlled taper of
medications while maintaining disease remission. Once starting
immunosuppressive therapy, next considerations are which drug or
drugs to choose, and whether to start with one drug or a combination
of drugs. Despite all of the research and studies surrounding
immunosuppressive medications in small animals, appropriate
controlled randomized prospective clinical trials designed to identify
the best drug or combination of drugs to treat IM disorders are

lacking. No combination of drugs has been shown to be more
effective than sole glucocorticoid therapy5 and no second agent
beyond glucocorticoid therapy has been shown to be superior to
another.5 Many advocate to not use three medications unless
absolutely necessary, as there are no studies demonstrating evidence
that three medications induce remission more efficiently, but using
three immunosuppressive medications will increase the risk of
adverse effects including secondary infections (ch. 227).5-8
Glucocorticoid therapy is a mainstay of initial immunosuppressive
therapy because of its wide availability, cost advantage to the client,
rapid onset of action, and overall effectiveness in suppressing the
immune system (ch. 144).4,5,9-13 However, glucocorticoid therapy
does not come without possible significant side-effects, especially in
dogs, and in particular large-breed dogs,5,11,12 with the side-effects
this author hears most about being severe polyuria and polydipsia (to
the point of urinary incontinence), muscle wasting and weakness,
panting, and behavior changes. These clinical effects make
glucocorticoids less than ideal for long-term use at higher dosages.

STRATEGIES WHEN ADDING A SECOND
IMMUNOSUPPRESSIVE AGENT
Although the benefit has not been established, considerations for a
secondary immunosuppressive medication beyond glucocorticoid
therapy alone are (1) when the IM disease is severe and lifethreatening, (2) when the patient does not satisfactorily attain
disease remission with single-agent glucocorticoid therapy, or (3)
when the side-effects of sole glucocorticoid therapy are severe or are
expected to be severe based on previous treatment.5,9 Examples
could include the IMHA patient that is refractory to glucocorticoid
therapy alone and is needing ongoing transfusions, or a case in which
disease remission is initially achieved on sole glucocorticoid therapy
but a relapse of disease occurs during the tapering process. In dogs
with IM disorders, and especially IM blood disorders, this author
advocates for initially using glucocorticoid therapy in addition to a
second immunosuppressive medication with the aim of limiting

glucocorticoid side-effects. In cats, because they often tolerate
glucocorticoid therapy so well, and because the other
immunosuppressive medications can be contraindicated or hard to
get right sizes for cats, they are often started out on glucocorticoid
therapy alone.14
The commonly used secondary immunosuppressive medications
in dogs for IM blood disorders are often considered to be
cyclosporine A (CsA), mycophenolate, azathioprine, and
leflunomide.5,6 Which one a clinician ultimately chooses likely stems
from factors such as expert opinion, available studies in the
literature, cost, possible adverse effects, mechanism of action,
clinician experience, and availability. Availability and drug selection
can be affected by the drug choices stocked in a clinic, human
pharmacy stock, drug shortages, compounding availability/needs,
and the ability to obtain an appropriate dosage based on available
tablet sizes. Because of the similar mechanism of action,
recommendations are to not use azathioprine and mycophenolate
together.5,9 This author likes to use CsA in addition to glucocorticoid
therapy for dogs because of no known bone marrow suppressive
effects, and having significantly more experience using this drug that
the others in clinical patients.

STRATEGIES ONCE STARTING
IMMUNOSUPPRESSIVE THERAPY
Once the decision is made to start immunosuppressive therapy, first
and foremost it is essential to make sure to start at appropriate drug
dosages. Individual drug information, including appropriate starting
dosages for each drug, is discussed in ch. 144. This would also
include using the modified or ultramicronized preparation of CsA
and not the Sandimmune preparation, to allow for more consistent
and predictable absorption.15
A second strategy is to not assume therapy has failed until there
has been enough time for the drug(s) to work. While there is no gold
standard as to the right amount of time, glucocorticoid therapy is
often thought to take days up to 1 week to produce a response.5 This

would only apply to IM blood disorders in which the marrow was not
the target. Based on research and clinical experience, this author
uses up to 1 week as the appropriate time to see a response with
CsA.15,16 Mycophenolate, azathioprine, and leflunomide seem to be
more variable, and are thought to take longer to take effect, often
between 1-2 weeks or longer.10,11,17-19 In clinical patients, this could
mean waiting up to 1 week or longer (depending on the drugs used)
before adjusting an immunosuppressive protocol, provided
appropriate initial dosages of the drug(s) are being used. However, if
using glucocorticoid therapy alone, considerations for escalation of
therapy earlier than 7 days may be needed depending on the severity
of disease. According to the current American College of Veterinary
Internal Medicine consensus statement for treatment of canine
IMHA, a second immunosuppressive medication should be
considered if the packed cell volume (PCV) does not remain stable,
meaning if there is an absolute decrease of greater than or equal to
5% within 24 hours during the first 7 days of treatment with sole
glucocorticoid therapy.5 There are no concrete guidelines, and often
clinical judgment is needed for the individual patient.
A third strategy is to use therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) when
available. The goal of TDM is to improve patient outcomes by
guiding drug dosage adjustments in the individual patient based on
either (1) measurement of blood concentrations (pharmacokinetic
[PK] monitoring, or “what the body does to the drug”) or (2)
measurement of the effects of the drug on the target cells in the body
(PD monitoring, or “what the drug does to the body”).
Immunosuppressive drugs for which TDM is currently routinely
available are CsA and leflunomide (PK monitoring only) therapy,
although others may become routinely available in the future.5,15 PK
monitoring involves the collection of samples (and often includes
considerations for peak and trough samples) during the dosing
interval to ensure blood concentrations are adequate for treatment of
the disease. PD monitoring involves collecting samples to assess the
effect of CsA on the target cell, which is the T cell. The only
veterinary lab in North America currently running the CsA PD assay
is Mississippi State University College of Veterinary Medicine, and
only in dogs, where they assess the ability of the T cell to produce

interleukin-2 (IL-2), although the lab is not currently accepting
samples. In dogs with significant suppression by CsA therapy, T cells
produce minimal to no IL-2 when activated. In dogs with minimal to
no immune suppression by CsA therapy, the T cells can produce a
significant amount of IL-2 when activated. Extensive investigations
into the PD evaluation of CsA in dogs, including prospective
controlled studies in research dogs, clinical studies in canine
patients, as well as validation of the assay, have gone into the
development of this clinical assay for use in dogs.15,16,20-24 Since this
assay was first offered to practitioners, thousands of samples from
dogs have been analyzed, with results returned to the veterinarian
explaining the level of immune suppression achieved with the
current CsA therapy and considerations for optimizing therapy in the
individual patient. When using PK monitoring of CsA and
leflunomide, recommendations are to consult with the lab running
the assay to identify the best samples to be collected, for interpreting
the blood concentrations, and how to then adjust therapy best in the
individual patient.
PD monitoring of CsA has shown an enormous variation in the
amount of immune suppression achieved in both normal dogs and
individual canine patients being treated with a standard
immunosuppressive starting dosage of CsA. Because of this extensive
variation in immune suppression, with some dogs attaining
significant suppression and others attaining very little suppression,
one dosage does not fit all for achieving systemic immune
suppression, and TDM would ideally be used to optimize therapy.
This author uses CsA PD monitoring, when available, in dogs with
acute and life-threatening diseases in the following instances: (1)
after the first week of therapy to ensure the CsA is achieving an
appropriate amount of immune suppression (and giving confidence
in hopefully allowing continued disease remission with the first dose
reduction of glucocorticoid therapy), (2) if a poor clinical response is
occurring despite CsA therapy, (3) with dosage reductions in later
stages of therapy if there is a concern about a relapse or a relapse has
occurred, and (4) when a secondary infection has unexpectedly
developed to assess whether the CsA therapy is causing massive
immune suppression (ch. 227). Dogs not responding to CsA therapy
with documented significant suppression of T-cell function would

suggest the need for alternate management strategies, while dogs
with inadequate suppression of T-cell suppression would suggest the
need to increase the CsA dosage. A recent case report described the
development of a secondary infection in a dog being treated for
IMHA while receiving a relatively low dosage of CsA (3.1 mg/kg PO
q12h). PD monitoring unexpectedly demonstrated significant
immune suppression, highlighting the need for individualized
immunosuppressive drug monitoring, especially in patients not
responding to standard immunosuppressive therapy or in patients
with secondary infections at low dosages.20

TAPERING OF IMMUNOSUPPRESSIVE
MEDICATIONS
Strategies for appropriately monitoring specific IM diseases are
covered in the specific disease chapters (chs. 174-179). In general,
for severe IM disorders, such as IMHA and immune-mediated
thrombocytopenia (ITP), immunosuppressive therapy is initiated
and continued until a positive response to the disease is attained
(and ideally disease remission achieved), with regular and frequent
monitoring until this positive clinical response is seen. Then, fulldose immunosuppressive therapy is continued for an additional
period of time while the disease is stable and in remission, with an
improvement in the majority of measures of disease, which is often
between 2 and 4 weeks.5,11 While the frequency of monitoring will
depend on the disease being treated, the drugs being used, and how
well the patient is doing at home, rechecks would ideally occur at
least weekly to ensure the disease is remaining in remission and no
adverse effects are occurring. Then, a controlled taper of medications
occurs over time, with recommendations to only taper one
immunosuppressive drug at a time. If sole glucocorticoid therapy is
used, the first dosage reduction is recommended to be approximately
25%.4,5,11 If a second immunosuppressive medication is being used
to help alleviate the side-effects of glucocorticoid therapy, the second
immunosuppressive medication is kept at full dosage so that the first
taper is the glucocorticoid therapy, with consideration for a greater a
reduction of the glucocorticoid dosage (between 25-50%) compared

to the reduction recommended for single agent glucocorticoid
therapy.5
Then a controlled taper of medications continues over time, by
reducing the dosage of one drug at a time (by approximately 25%)
every 2-4 weeks, provided the disease remains stable with a
continued improvement in measures of disease activity.4,5 With IM
blood disorders, during the initial treatment period, this author often
schedules a recheck 1 week after each dose reduction (as an example:
a simple PCV and total protein measurement for IMHA patients) to
ensure a relapse has not taken place, and then another recheck
before the next dosage reduction to ensure it is safe to move forward
with the taper. At a minimum, rechecks should occur before any
dosage reductions to ensure a continued response to therapy.5 This
process often takes 4-6 months or longer. Alternatively, if the
glucocorticoid has been tapered and discontinued, and the patient is
still on a second immunosuppressive agent, instead of tapering this
medication over time, another possible recommendation is to
continue this second medication for an additional 4-8 weeks and
then stop the second medication without tapering.5 Again, the
overall goal is to adjust therapy over time in a controlled fashion to
find the lowest dosage(s) of medications that allow continued disease
remission.

RESPONDING TO DISEASE RELAPSE
If a relapse of disease occurs during immunosuppressive therapy,
considerations for adjustments in therapy will depend on how far
along the patient is in the tapering process as well as how severe the
disease is at the time of the relapse. If the relapse occurs when the
patient is receiving high-dose sole glucocorticoid therapy, a second
immunosuppressive medication should be started.5 If the relapse
occurs when the patient is receiving two immunosuppressive
medications at full dosages, TDM should be considered if available.5
If the relapse occurs during the tapering process, and results in mild
disease, suggestions are to return to the last dosage of drugs which
were allowing disease remission (just before the last dosage

reduction in the taper).5,11 If the relapse occurs during the tapering
process, and results in severe and fulminant disease, treatment at
full dosages of immunosuppressive medications initially used to
achieve disease remission should occur.5,11 After a relapse and once
disease remission is re-attained, suggestions are to perform the
tapering of medications more gradually, with times between dosage
adjustments at least doubled in length as previously recommended.5
If continued relapses occur, re-investigation for a possible secondary
trigger/disease which was not apparent in the initial investigation
should be considered. If none can be identified, this may be a patient
that needs lifelong immunosuppressive therapy. If this is a patient
with IMHA or ITP, and relapses occur and ongoing
immunosuppressive therapy is needed to attain disease remission, a
splenectomy may be considered to hopefully allow for continued
tapering of medications and continued disease remission.5,11,25

MONITORING FOR ADVERSE EFFECTS
Appropriate monitoring while patients are receiving
immunosuppressive medications is warranted to ensure adverse
effects do not develop. Adverse effects are covered in greater detail in
ch. 144, and depending on the drug, monitoring with appropriate
bloodwork may be needed to assess for possible bone marrow
suppression and liver toxicosis (chs. 134, 138, 321). Ideally,
baseline blood work (complete blood count [CBC], biochemistry
panel) is obtained prior to starting therapy for comparison purposes
later during therapy. Due to the side-effect profiles of specific drugs,
mycophenolate is often not used in patients with pre-existing
gastrointestinal (GI) disease and azathioprine is often not used in
patients with pre-existing liver disease, as it may be hard to
differentiate abnormalities caused by disease from drug side-effects.
As well, when using glucocorticoid therapy, consideration of risk
versus benefit will need to take place for the individual patient when
dealing with advanced concurrent heart disease or diabetes mellitus
(ch. 224).
When using azathioprine in dogs, recommendations are to
perform a CBC and measure liver enzyme activities every 2 weeks

during the first 2 months of treatment, and then every 1-2 months
until discontinuing therapy.5 Chronic use of azathioprine can
sometimes cause a mild to moderate poorly regenerative anemia,
which should not be confused with severe myelosuppression or
treatment failure.5
When using CsA in dogs, recommendations are to measure liver
enzyme activities every 2-3 months because of the risk of
hepatotoxicosis in dogs (chs. 65, 269).5 One advantage of CsA is
that it has not been shown to be myelosuppressive, and therefore
monitoring of CBCs is not warranted.5,15 Other significant possible
side-effects seen with CsA are GI. Strategies to help with GI sideeffects during CsA therapy can include administering the capsules
frozen, administering CsA with a concurrent antiemetic as needed, or
administering CsA with food.
When using mycophenolate in dogs, recommendations are to
evaluate a CBC every 2-3 weeks for the first month of treatment, and
then every 2-3 months thereafter.
When using leflunomide in dogs, recommendations are to evaluate
a CBC and liver enzyme activities every 2 weeks for the first 2
months, and then every 1-2 months until discontinuing therapy.
If myelosuppression is documented during therapy, the causative
drug should be discontinued.5 If the patient is not showing clinical
signs due to the myelosuppression and the neutrophil count is
greater than 1000 cells/mcL, antibiotics do not have to be
administered unless other risk factors for infection are present (ch.
321).5 If the neutrophil count is less than 1000 cells/mcL in and
there are no clinical signs due to the myelosuppression, prophylactic
antibiotics are indicated.5 In neutropenic patients showing
associated clinical signs (e.g., fever), antibiotics are indicated, as well
as more intensive treatments and monitoring as indicated by the
individual patient.5 During the time of documented neutropenia,
close observation of the patient will be needed for the possible
development of sepsis (ch. 128).
Additionally, recommendations are to be vigilant for the
development of a possible secondary infection, which can occur in
any patient receiving immunosuppressive medications.26-31 Signs of

the patient being unwell, not eating, or a change in clinical signs
(such as lower urinary tract signs or development of skin disease)
should prompt an evaluation for a secondary infection. If one is
present, appropriate testing and treatment can then be instituted. As
well, a risk versus benefit decision will need to be made as to if and
how to modify the treatment regime, with no one single option being
best but instead depending on the individual case. Often, the
decision depends on multiple factors, including the severity and
nature of the infection, the severity and stage of the IM disorder, as
well as the drugs and dosages being used for immune suppression. If
the patient is receiving CsA therapy and a fungal infection develops,
discontinuation of this drug ahead of others seems prudent based on
the association of CsA therapy and fungal infections.30,31 The
clinician should also consider an emerging infection as the possible
secondary trigger for the IM disease that may not have been
apparent on the initial investigation. In this author’s opinion,
patients at risk for secondary infections include those receiving three
immunosuppressive medications and those in which TDM has
deemed them at an increased risk based on significant immune
suppression. More information on infections in patients requiring
immunosuppression can be found in ch. 227.

Laboratory hemostasis testing is divided into preanalytical,
analytical (the test), and postanalytical (interpretation) phases. The
preanalytical phase covers all aspects of preparation of the patient,
collection of the sample, processing, storage, labeling, and
submission. Hemostasis testing requires stringent attention to detail,
particularly during the preanalytical phase, due to variation in
interpretation associated with hematocrit, hemolysis, choice of
anticoagulant, and fill volume (anticoagulant to whole-blood ratios).
Preanalytical errors have accounted for up to 75% of total lab errors
in human laboratories, mostly from interfering substances in the
sample.1 Interpretative hemostasis services can assist with all three
phases2 (Table 170.1; Figure 170.1). Common preanalytical
mistakes include inappropriate choice of anticoagulant (e.g., using
ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid [EDTA] instead of citrate), incorrect
ratio of anticoagulant to blood, cooling or heating of samples,
delayed laboratory transport, and inappropriate centrifugation
speeds. These factors can impact interpretation significantly, leading
to inappropriate therapeutic decisions. Machine learning accurately
identified clotted samples in one study and may be useful to decrease
preanalytical errors in the future.3

HISTORY AND PHYSICAL EXAM
A comprehensive history (ch. 2) includes previous bleeding episodes
(e.g., ear or tail docking, spay or castration, declawing, loss of
deciduous teeth, estrus), anatomical distribution of bleeding, and
whether bleeding was spontaneous or provoked (e.g., injury) and
immediate or delayed. Signalment, breed, age at first episode, travel
history (ch. 9), and current medication or toxin exposure (ch. 132)
should be recorded. Although both congenital and acquired bleeding
disorders can cause bleeding anywhere, acquired disorders typically
appear later in life with no history of bleeding during previous
surgeries (e.g., spay, castration). Congenital bleeding disorders often
manifest early in life (e.g., spay, declawing).4 In patients at risk for
thrombosis, essential aspects of the history include predisposing
diseases (e.g., hyperadrenocorticism [chs. 293, 294], protein-losing
nephropathy [ch. 302], immune-mediated hemolytic anemia

[IMHA, ch. 174]), current medications or toxin exposure, and recent
interventional procedures (e.g., intravenous catheter placement [ch.
75]).5
A thorough physical examination (ch. 3) includes evaluation of
the skin, eyes, joints, mucous membranes, urine, and feces for
evidence of bleeding (ch. 124). Disorders affecting platelets and the
endothelium include thrombocytopenia (chs. 59, 175),
thrombocytopathia, von Willebrand disease (vWD, ch. 175), and
vasculitis (ch. 181). Thrombocytopenia can lead to petechiation if the
platelet count is <20,000/mcL, while thrombocytopathia, vWD, and
vasculitis more often cause mucosal surface bleeding and bruising
(ch. 29).6,7 Coagulation factor deficiencies or disorders result in
ecchymoses, hematomas, and/or muscle, joint, or body cavity
bleeding (ch. 171).4 In animals at risk for thrombosis, a thorough
evaluation of perfusion (e.g., palpation of pulses, extremity
temperature, mentation, urine output) and oxygenation are
essential. Ultrasound evaluation of suspected areas (e.g., distal aorta,
femoral vessels, etc.), may help diagnose peripheral
thromboembolism (ch. 238). Evaluation for pulmonary
thromboembolism may reveal an oxygen deficit (tachypnea, pulse
oximetry and low PaO2, increased alveolar-arterial gradient) with
normal or mild changes on thoracic radiographs (e.g., minimal
pleural effusion, loss of definition of the pulmonary artery,
hyperlucent lung regions).

SAMPLE COLLECTION AND STORAGE
METHODS
Ideally, all specimens should be collected prior to therapeutic
interventions. Elimination or minimization of preanalytical errors in
collection and storage will optimize interpretability. Communicating
with the laboratory regarding aspects that may affect the test (e.g.,
hemolysis, icterus, ingestion of a fatty meal) is important. The
preanalytical phase has been reviewed for veterinary medicine.8,9
Venipuncture technique, tube/additive selection, and storage are
particularly important. Direct venipuncture into a vacuum tube is

preferred as this approach results in less hemolysis than needle and
syringe collection.10 Results for prothrombin time (PT), activated
partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), and fibrinogen for dogs agree
clinically between the two collection methods.11 If using a central line
for collection, flushing with heparinized saline followed by removal
of at least 3 mL of blood from the catheter before specimen collection
will minimize contamination with heparin, saline, or other fluids.11
The clearance blood may be returned to the patient but will have
undergone some degree of contact activation. Immediately following
filling, tubes should be inverted 4-6 times.12 The preferred
anticoagulant for complete blood count (CBC) and platelet count is
potassium ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (K+EDTA), a chelating
agent that binds calcium.13 Sodium citrate (3.2%, 1:9 ratio citrate to
blood) is the anticoagulant of choice for most coagulation assays.14

TESTS OF PLATELETS AND THE
VASCULAR WALL
PLATELET COUNT
Thrombocytopenia may be due to decreased platelet production,
destruction, loss, or sequestration (ch. 59). Sources of error in
automated counts include cells (i.e., microspherocytes, cell
fragments) of similar size being counted as platelets, giant platelets
being counted as other cells, and agglutination.15 Manual platelet
estimates can be performed by evaluation of a peripheral blood
smear using EDTA-anticoagulated blood or fresh samples. An
estimate of the count is obtained by multiplying 15 × 103/mcL by the
average number of platelets counted from at least 5 oil-immersion
fields.

BUCCAL MUCOSAL BLEEDING TIME
(BMBT)
The BMBT should only be performed on a patient with a normal
platelet count and coagulation panel (ch. 79).

CUTICLE BLEEDING TIME (CBT)
The CBT test is unpredictable, unreliable, and painful; it is not
recommended in veterinary patients.

PLATELET FUNCTION TESTING
Options for detection of thrombocytopathia include impedance
whole blood platelet aggregometry (WBA), plasma-based light
transmission aggregometry, flow cytometry, and a commercially
available platelet function analyzer (PFA-100). There are also
adaptations to thromboelastography/ometry (TE) for testing of
thrombocytopathia. Platelet count affects TE results and TE cannot

discriminate which changes are from thrombocytopenia versus
thrombocytopathia; therefore, its use should be limited to patients
with a normal platelet count. Aggregometry techniques, due to cost
and requirements for trained personnel, have classically been used
for research, but a rapid, automated multiple electrode aggregometry
technique (Multiplate) has been developed for WBA with potential
for clinical use.16 Flow cytometry, used for quantifying receptors and
platelet activation markers on the platelet surface, gives a
comprehensive characterization of the platelet phenotype. Imaging
flow cytometry and mass cytometry are promising new flow
cytometric developments to identify subpopulations.17 The PFA-100
measures time to cessation of whole blood flow (closing time)
through a central aperture under high shear conditions. The
membrane is coated with collagen and either epinephrine or
adenosine-5′-diphosphate (ADP). The collagen/ADP cartridge has a
higher sensitivity for canine platelets.18 Whole blood is collected in
sodium citrate and held at room temperature prior to processing.
The PFA-100 is easy to use and gives accurate and rapid results that
are reproducible. Platelet aggregation is dependent on platelet
number and function, as well as functional vWF.15 Results can also
be affected by holding time, anticoagulants, hematocrit and
medications.15,19 Use is limited in patients with anemia and/or
thrombocytopenia and the PFA-100 is no longer recommended by
the International Society for Thrombosis and Hemostasis for
humans for these reasons.17 The PFA-100 is used as a screening test
to detect abnormalities of platelet function but is not specific for any
particular disease. A normal PFA-100 closing time result generally
rules out a severe platelet function defect or severe vWD, but milder
forms of these diseases may still be present. The test had a 95.7%
sensitivity and 100% specificity in dogs using the collagen/ADP
cartridge in one report.20 Microfluidics uses whole blood to assess
platelet adhesion, aggregation and thrombus formation under flow
via bright field fluorescence microscopy. With the recent addition of
cultured endothelial cells within microfluidic devices, the assessment
of platelet-endothelial interactions is now possible and will likely
advance the field of platelet function testing to new levels.17

VON WILLEBRAND FACTOR/VON
WILLEBRAND DISEASE
vWD is covered in ch. 175.

TESTS OF COAGULATION
PROTHROMBIN TIME (PT)
The PT evaluates the tissue factor pathway (extrinsic; FVII) and the
common pathway (FX, FV, prothrombin, fibrinogen; ch. 171).
Citrated plasma is added to CaCl2 and tissue factor in a lipid
membrane (thromboplastin); the PT is the time until formation of
the first fibrin strands. A prolonged PT (with a normal aPTT)
indicates FVII deficiency. Heparin does not generally prolong the PT
due to the inclusion of heparin antagonists in commercial PT
reagents. Due to the short half-life of FVII, PT prolongation in
vitamin K deficiency initially is due to FVII deficiency (not associated
with bleeding); then, clinical bleeding occurs with development of
prothrombin deficiency. In an evaluation of a direct oral
anticoagulant (DOAC; e.g., rivaroxaban) in dogs, PT was very
strongly correlated with rivaroxaban-specific anti-Xa activity and PT
correlation was stronger than aPTT, rapid TEG
(thromboelastography/ometry, TE), and thrombin generation.21
However, due to variability in PT reagents, results cannot be
extrapolated to all centers and anti-Xa activity is still the gold
standard for monitoring of DOACs.

ACTIVATED PARTIAL
THROMBOPLASTIN TIME (aPTT)
The aPTT evaluates the contact pathway (prekallikrein, FXII, FXI);
intrinsic pathway (FVIII, FIX); and the common pathway (FX, FV,
prothrombin, fibrinogen) (ch. 171). The only coagulation factors that

do not impact the aPTT are FVII and FXIII.15 Citrated plasma is
incubated with a contact activator (e.g., celite, kaolin) and lipids to
allow for the generation of FXIIa and FXIa, then recalcified to allow
for downstream coagulation steps.

ACTIVATED CLOTTING TIME (ACT)
The ACT is a simple, rapid, inexpensive test that is similar to the
aPTT (evaluating all factors except FVII and FXIII) except that it
uses whole blood. The tube contains a contact activator, and the
platelets in the blood sample provide the lipid surface; note that
therefore, the ACT can be prolonged with severe thrombocytopenia
even when the coagulation cascade is intact.22 The ACT can screen
for rodenticide intoxication, hemophilia, hepatopathy-associated
coagulopathies, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).23
The original ACT tubes (Becton Dickinson) are no longer available.
The newer MAX-ACT tube (Helena Laboratories, Beaumont, TX)
was designed for use in an automated system. It contains 3 FXII
activators (celine, kaolin, glass beads) and a magnet. A manual
version of the test (using the tubes alone) has been validated using
blood from healthy dogs and cats. The MAX-ACT tube needs to be
filled immediately after direct venipuncture (needle and syringe)
with 0.5 mL of whole blood, gently tapped to mix the sample without
inversion, and placed in a 37°C bath for 30 seconds, then rotated
every 5-10 seconds. Visible clot formation is the endpoint. The
sensitivity and specificity and validation of its use in animals with
clinical bleeding have not been reported. Reported normal values are
66 (range: 55-85) seconds for cats and 71 (range: 55-80) seconds for
dogs.22

FACTOR LEVELS
Concentrations of individual coagulation factors can be measured
using specialized modifications of the PT or aPTT. These tests
usually only are available in specialized veterinary laboratories.
Factor testing is required to confirm a suspicion of FXII deficiency,

or hemophilia A (FVIII deficiency), B (FIX deficiency), or C (FXI
deficiency), in a patient with a normal PT but prolonged aPTT (ch.
171).23 The laboratory should be contacted prior to phlebotomy to
discuss appropriate sample preparation and testing.

TESTS OF FIBRINOGEN AND
FIBRINOLYSIS
FIBRINOGEN
Fibrinogen defects can be qualitative (dysfibrinogenemia) or
quantitative (hypo- or afibrinogenemia) and either acquired
(consumption, decreased hepatic synthesis, or inhibitory antibodies)
or congenital. In addition to its role in coagulation, fibrinogen is a
strong acute phase reactant in dogs, with increases
(hyperfibrinogenemia) occurring during inflammation and
infection.24 The most common assay for detection of fibrinogen
activity is the Clauss method, which is coagulation-assay–based. Low
fibrinogen activity measured by this method can indicate either
hypofibrinogenemia or dysfibrinogenemia. With this method, false
decreases can occur due to the presence of anticoagulants, elevations
in fibrin(ogen) degradation product (FDP) concentrations,
hypoalbuminemia, factor XIII deficiency, or amyloidosis.25

THROMBIN TIME (TT)
The TT is the time from recalcification until formation of the first
fibrin strands after the addition of thrombin and it indicates
fibrinogen concentration and/or function. As with the Clauss
method, TT results can be increased due to the presence of
anticoagulants, elevations in FDPs, hypoalbuminemia, factor XIII
deficiency, and amyloidosis.25 Similar to the Clauss method, other
factors may falsely prolong the TT.

FIBRIN[OGEN] DEGRADATION
PRODUCTS (FDPs)
FDPs are created when plasmin lyses fibrinogen, soluble fibrin
monomers, insoluble fibrin, and/or cross-linked fibrin (ch. 171). The
presence of excess FDPs merely indicates plasmin activity; FDPs are
not specific for cross-linked fibrin degradation. FDP concentrations
can be increased in a variety of disorders, such as DIC (ch. 171),
anticoagulant rodenticide intoxication (ch. 138), hepatic disease
(chs. 266, 267), thrombosis (chs. 219, 238), IMHA (ch. 174),
neoplasia (ch. 331), pancreatitis (ch. 277), gastric dilation-volvulus
(ch. 261), and heatstroke (ch. 130).

D-DIMER
D-dimers are a form of FDP that can only be generated from crosslinked fibrin. Most available assays are immunologic, with no crossreactivity with fibrinogen or fibrin monomer fragments.26 Increased
D-dimer concentrations indicate thrombin generation, fibrin
formation, cross-linking by FXIIIa, and plasmin activity. Because Ddimers have a short half-life, their presence indicates recent (∼5
hours) fibrinolysis.26 Increased D-dimer concentrations have been
reported in dogs with IMHA, liver and renal disease, heart failure,
neoplasia, internal hemorrhage, and after surgery.27 Not all
commercially available assays designed for human samples crossreact with animal D-dimers.

ANTITHROMBIN (AT) ASSAY
AT (formerly antithrombin III) is a member of the serine protease
inhibitor (serpin) family. It is an important inhibitor of multiple
coagulation enzymes, the most clinically relevant of which are
thrombin and FXa. The inhibitory action of AT requires the binding
of sulfated proteoglycans (either endothelial cell surface-associated
heparans or pharmacologically delivered heparins).28 Plasma levels
of AT can be evaluated via a chromogenic functional assay that

measures the in vitro ability of AT (provided by the patient sample)
to inhibit bovine FXa in the presence of added heparin (both
provided by the assay kit). Because many animal AT molecules
inhibit bovine FXa with different potency than does human FXa, the
degree of inhibition is tested against a standard of pooled normal
plasma from the species being tested. The results are then reported
as a percentage of normal.29 AT deficiency is a known risk factor for
development of thrombosis. Deficiency can occur due to decreased
hepatic production, consumption associated with coagulation
activation, or renal or enteric loss.30,31

INDICATORS OF GLOBAL HEMOSTATIC
POTENTIAL AND IN VIVO HEMOSTASIS
Research on the contribution of cells (e.g., platelets, red blood cells)
to in vivo coagulation highlights the deficiencies of standard
coagulation tests, which are performed on platelet-poor plasma
(PPP) and may only assess 5% of total clot formation. The following
is a general overview of assays that have shown promise in the
evaluation of global hemostatic potential and prothrombotic states.

THROMBOELASTOGRAPHY/OMETRY
(TE)
Viscoelastic coagulation analyzers, using whole blood, provide an
assessment of coagulation, from the beginning of clot formation
through fibrinolysis. Although a significant improvement over
previously existing methods, this technology only assesses one aspect
of Virchow’s triad (i.e., endothelium and flow are not assessed). In
veterinary medicine, clinical use of viscoelastic technology has been
reported in dogs, cats, foals, and horses.32-40 There are, however,
substantial limitations to their use, including erroneous data in
animals with altered red cell mass.41,42

Current point-of-care viscoelastic tests, including the Sonoclot,
TEG and ROTEM devices, have been reviewed.43 A new addition, the
VCM Vet™, uses fresh whole blood, no activators (depends on
contact activation), and is handheld. Reference intervals have been
established for healthy dogs and cats but information on diseased
animals currently is lacking.44,45 The use of the Sonoclot has been
reported mostly for equine blood. TEG and ROTEM have been
reported in both research and clinical settings with blood from small
animals (Figure 170.2). TE results are not dependent solely on
generation of coagulation enzymes but also are impacted by the
platelets, red cell mass, and fibrinogen. Abnormalities in these
parameters can lead to misinterpretation of TE results.41,42
Specifically, samples with a higher hematocrit (erythrocytosis)
display relatively hypocoagulable tracings while samples with lower
hematocrit (anemia) display hypercoagulable tracings.40,41,46 This is
likely due to a fixed volume in the cup resulting in relatively more
fibrinogen with lower red cell mass and relatively less fibrinogen
with higher red cell mass. Interpretation of TE, especially in anemic
states (e.g., IMHA, hemoabdomen, DIC), may be difficult. As with
the PT and aPTT, results obtained with TE depend on the activators
added to the whole blood sample. The handling conditions applied to
the sample can also impact the results obtained; for example, in
dogs, longer holding times lead to activation of the contact pathway,
and this, or addition of incorrect amounts of tissue factor, or lack of
use of a contact activator, can produce results that are erroneous or
irrelevant to a patient in vivo. Attempts have been made to improve
standardization.47

CALIBRATED AUTOMATED
THROMBOGRAM (CAT)
Thrombin is the central enzyme in hemostasis and thrombosis, but
the majority of thrombin is produced after formation of the fibrin
clot.48 The CAT assay evaluates the ability to generate thrombin in
real time in vitro in response to specific stimuli. It can be used with
platelet-poor plasma (PPP) or platelet-rich plasma (PRP). CAT

sensitively evaluates the contributions of all clotting factors except
fibrinogen and FXIII and is sensitive to anticoagulant drugs and
direct thrombin inhibitors.49 Contributions of vWF,
hypofibrinogenemia, thrombocytopenia, and antiplatelet drugs can
be evaluated using PRP.50 CAT results have been reported in
hypercoagulable states in animals and had good correlation with
rivaroxaban-specific anti-Xa activity in a study in dogs.21,51,52 Newer
versions use whole blood to incorporate the contribution of cells and
may represent a more physiologically relevant option in the future.53

THROMBIN-ANTITHROMBIN (TAT)
ELISA
The half-life of thrombin is extremely short in vivo, as it is rapidly
inhibited by AT. Consequently, it is not possible to measure the
concentration of thrombin directly in plasma. Rather, the
concentration of the stable TAT complex is an indirect indicator of
thrombin generation in vivo. TAT was found to be 97% sensitive for
DIC in humans.54 The commercially available enzyme-linked
immunosorbant assay (ELISA) does cross-react with canine, feline,
and equine TAT. An increase in TAT complexes has been reported in
Cushing’s syndrome, malignant neoplasms, and
blastomycosis.51,55,56 The multi–well plate design and cost generally
necessitate batch processing of samples, making this assay
impractical for routine clinical use.

Chapter 171: Hyper- and
Hypocoagulable States
Shauna L. Blois

The hemostatic system is responsible for controlling hemorrhage
while maintaining adequate blood flow. Platelets and plasma
coagulation proteins work simultaneously in response to vascular
injury and trauma, ultimately generating a thrombin-based blood
clot (Figure 171.1). Anticoagulant proteins keep this system in
balance by preventing spontaneous generation of clots and
eventually lysing formed clots at vascular injury sites.1
Quantitative and qualitative abnormalities in the coagulation
process can lead to hemostatic derangements. Hypercoagulability is
often attributed to one or more abnormalities in Virchow’s triad:
increased coagulability (increased activity of platelets or

procoagulant factors; deficiencies of anticoagulant factors, or
inhibited fibrinolysis), vascular stasis, and disruption or activation of
vascular endothelium. Thrombosis refers to a blood clot (thrombus)
in a blood vessel occluding blood flow; when a blood clot is dislodged
from its origin and travels to a distant site in the circulation, this is
referred to as thromboembolism (chs. 219 and 238).
Hypocoagulability can be secondary to decreased platelet or
procoagulant activity, or excessive fibrinolysis. Such conditions can
lead to clinical signs of hemorrhage. (Box 171.1)

HEMOSTATIC TESTING
Tests of primary hemostasis include measurement of platelet count
and function, and mucosal bleeding times (chs. 79, 170, and 175).
Activated clotting time (ACT) and coagulation profiles consisting of
prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time
(aPTT), and sometimes fibrinogen levels, are commonly used to
assess the secondary hemostatic system (ch. 170). Prolongation of
the PT indicates decreased in vitro activity of the extrinsic (factor
VII) and common (factors I, II, V, and X) pathways, whereas
prolongation of the aPTT and/or ACT indicates decreased activity of
the intrinsic (VIII, IX, XI, XII) and common pathways (Figure
171.2). Coagulation times are prolonged when the activity of one or
more coagulation factors is reduced to <30-50%. PT and aPTT are
considered insensitive for detecting hypercoagulability.
Measurement of individual clotting factor levels might be indicated
in selected patients to rule out factor deficiency (ch. 170). Low
fibrinogen concentrations can occur secondary to consumption in
disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) as well as in synthetic
liver failure. Fibrinogen is an acute phase reactant and high
concentrations are common in systemic inflammation. D-dimers are
a breakdown product of cross-linked fibrin and concentrations can
be elevated in states of thrombosis and/or fibrinolysis. While
elevated D-dimer concentrations can be observed in DIC and other
states of thrombosis, they are not specific for hypercoagulability and
thrombosis.
Viscoelastic tests of hemostasis (thromboelastography, TEG;
rotational thromboelastometry, ROTEM) are whole blood assays that

depict clot formation from onset, throughout the process to
fibrinolysis (ch. 170). Viscoelastic testing is more likely to correlate
with clinical bleeding risk compared to conventional coagulation
testing.2 While viscoelastic testing can identify hypercoagulability,
results have not been predictive of thrombosis in dogs.3 Results of
viscoelastic testing can be confounded by several factors including
low hematocrit, which causes a hypercoagulable artifact.4

ACQUIRED HYPERCOAGULABLE
STATES
Common comorbid conditions in dogs with thrombotic conditions
include protein-losing nephropathy (PLN, ch. 302), protein-losing
enteropathy, liver disease, corticosteroid administration, neoplasia,
endocrinopathy, and inflammatory conditions such as immunemediated diseases (ch. 174), sepsis (ch. 128) and pancreatitis (chs.
277 and 278).5-8 Aortic thromboembolism secondary to
hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the most common feline
thromboembolic disorder (ch. 238).

IMMUNE-MEDIATED HEMOLYTIC
ANEMIA
Dogs with immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA) are prone to
both venous and arterial thrombi and thromboemboli, although
pulmonary thromboembolism appears to be most common (ch.
174). The mortality rate of dogs with IMHA can be up to 80%. Most
deaths occur shortly after diagnosis and up to half of the deaths are
attributed to thromboembolism of major organs even when
thromboprophylaxis is administered. The mechanisms of
hypercoagulability in IMHA patients are likely multifactorial and
include increased platelet reactivity; increased tissue factor
expression on platelets, monocytes and endothelial cells; exposure of
red blood cell membrane phosphatidylserine; circulating
procoagulant microparticles; and imbalanced procoagulant and

anticoagulant factor levels.9-11 IMHA creates a systemic
inflammatory state in patients, providing further procoagulant
stimuli.

PROTEIN-LOSING DISORDERS
Glomerular disease, and subsequent PLN, is the most common
chronic kidney disease in dogs and it can also occur in cats (ch.
302). While loss of antithrombin through the damaged glomerulus
is suspected to contribute to the hypercoagulability of PLN patients,
other likely mechanisms include increased platelet reactivity,
hyperfibrinogenemia, and decrease in fibrinolysis.12,13 There is a
high prevalence of hypercoagulability among dogs with PLN based
on TEG findings, and PLN is a reported cause of venous and arterial
thrombotic disease in dogs.12,14 Hypoalbuminemia is a marker of
thromboembolic risk in people with PLN, but it has not been
associated with an increased risk of hypercoagulability in dogs with
PLN.13-15

FIGURE 171.1 The cell-based model of
coagulation. Initiation (1): Exposure of tissue
factor (TF) is the primary initiator of coagulation.
Factor VIIa binds to the exposed TF to form a TFfactor VIIa complex. Reactions on the cell surface
lead to small amounts of thrombin (factor II)
generation. Small amounts of factor IXa diffuse away
from the cell surface to activate more platelets or
other cells. Amplification (2): The small amount of
thrombin generated on the TF-bearing cell surface
binds to thrombin receptors (TR) on the surface
of platelets. Platelet activation is also facilitated by
von Willebrand factor (vWF) and exposed
collagen in the subendothelial matrix. Upon
thrombin binding, platelets undergo morphologic
change and release granule contents to further
amplify coagulation. Thrombin from the initiation
stage activates factor XI and factor V on the platelet
surface and liberates vWF from factor VIII to further
stimulate platelet activation and aggregation.

Propagation (3): Activated platelets expose ligands
to facilitate platelet-platelet interactions and
aggregation. Phosphatidylserine is expressed on the
surfaces of activated platelets, providing a surface to
support the assembly of coagulation factors from the
initiation and amplification phases. Factor XIa
activates factor IX; factor IXa binds to factor VIIIa to
form the tenase complex, leading to activation of
factor X. On the platelet surface, factor Xa complexes
with factor Va, generating a burst of thrombin and
converting fibrinogen to fibrin. Fibrin
polymerization then forms an insoluble fibrin clot.
Roman numerals refer to coagulation factors; “a”
denotes activated factor.

Dogs with chronic inflammatory enteropathy with or without
protein-losing enteropathy also demonstrate hypercoagulability as
measured by TEG.16 Thromboembolic complications have been
reported in dogs with PLE, although the incidence appears relatively
low.17

NEOPLASIA
Coagulation abnormalities are frequently identified in patients with
neoplasia (ch. 331). Hemostatic changes vary between types of
neoplasia, but the majority of patients show hypercoagulable
tendencies.18,19 Increased soluble or cellular expression of tissue
factor is thought to be an essential mechanism of hypercoagulability
in patients with neoplasia. Other possible factors causing
hypercoagulability include platelet hyperactivity, systemic
inflammatory reaction, tumor disruption of vascular endothelium,
concurrent drug therapy (e.g., glucocorticoids, cytotoxic drugs), and
development of DIC.20

Viscoelastic evidence of hypocoagulability has been documented in
some patients with neoplasia. The presence of metastatic disease and
a more severe stage of disease were associated with
hypocoagulability in some studies.21,22 Cancer patients with
hypocoagulability commonly demonstrate thrombocytopenia and
prolonged coagulation times. DIC is common in cancer patients and
is a possible explanation for hypocoagulable tendencies in this
patient population.23

FIGURE 171.2 The classic coagulation cascade
model is useful for describing the components of
coagulation evaluated by the activated clotting time
(ACT), activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT
), prothrombin time (PT), and thrombin clotting
time (TCT) tests. Roman numerals refer to
coagulation factors. APLT, Activated platelets; Ca2+,
calcium ions; HMK, high-molecular-weight

ENDOCRINOPATHIES
Endocrine diseases, particularly hyperadrenocorticism (ch. 293),
are associated with hypercoagulability and thrombotic diseases in
dogs. Exogenous glucocorticoid therapy has also been associated
with hypercoagulability and thrombosis in dogs. The mechanism of

hypercoagulability in dogs with endogenous or exogenous
glucocorticoid excess is unknown, but contributing factors could
include atherosclerosis, increase in platelet activity, imbalanced
hemostatic factor activity, and diminished fibrinolysis.24,25
Thrombosis has been reported in a small proportion of dogs with
hypothyroidism (ch. 285) and diabetes mellitus, although many
patients had comorbidities that could have led to thrombosis.

INFLAMMATION AND SEPSIS
Inflammatory diseases including acute pancreatitis, sepsis, systemic
inflammatory response syndrome, trauma, and immune-mediated
disease have been associated with hypercoagulability and thrombosis
in dogs (ch. 128).26 Inflammation and hemostasis are closely linked
processes in the body, and inflammation can induce coagulation via
several mechanisms. Pro-inflammatory cytokines, endotoxin, and
other inflammatory mediators can stimulate platelet production and
reactivity.27 Inflammatory cytokines and other mediators increase
tissue factor expression on endothelial cells and monocytes,
initiating the coagulation cascade via the tissue factor pathway.
Anticoagulant activity and fibrinolysis are diminished in
inflammatory states.28,29 Presence of neutrophil extracellular traps
in inflammatory conditions can promote clot formation and delay
fibrinolysis.30 Some inflammatory conditions can result in a
consumptive coagulopathy and DIC, leading to hypocoagulability.

ANTIPLATELET, ANTICOAGULANT,
ANDTHROMBOLYTIC THERAPY
Thromboprophylaxis should be instituted in patients with IMHA and
PLN unless specific contraindications such as marked
thrombocytopenia (platelet count <30,000/mcL) are detected, and
should be considered in other patients where hypercoagulability or
other thrombosis risk factors have been detected.31-33 The most
effective methods to prophylactically treat patients at risk of

thromboembolic disease are not well defined, and likely vary
depending on the underlying mechanisms. Clopidogrel has shown
superior efficacy in platelet inhibition compared to low-dose
aspirin.34 Low molecular weight heparin, unfractionated heparin,
and direct oral factor Xa inhibitors (e.g., rivaroxaban) have
anticoagulant activity in dogs and cats but large, prospective and
randomized studies investigating efficacy in clinically diseased
patients are lacking.31 Multimodal therapy is likely needed to
successfully treat patients with severe vascular occlusion secondary
to thromboembolic disease. Anti-platelet and anticoagulant
therapies do not dissolve existing thrombi but are used to decrease
thrombogenesis. In some cases, thrombolytic therapy is indicated
but risks include hemorrhage, reperfusion injury, and embolism.
Endovascular stents can be used in some cases of vascular occlusion
(chs. 113, 115, 118).35

ACQUIRED HYPOCOAGULABLE STATES
VITAMIN K DEFICIENCY
Vitamin K deficiency is one the most common acquired
coagulopathies in small animals and is usually caused by ingestion of
vitamin K antagonist rodenticides (ch. 138). Less common causes
include decreased vitamin K synthesis from the intestinal
microbiota, decreased vitamin K absorption, and severe cholestasis.
Vitamin K is an important cofactor in production and activation of
the vitamin K–dependent coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X and
anticoagulant proteins C and S. Reduced vitamin K is essential for
carboxylation of the glutamic acid residues of these coagulation
factors. Anticoagulant rodenticides antagonize vitamin K epoxide
reductase, causing rapid depletion of the vitamin K–dependent
coagulation factors (Figure 171.3).36 Factors II, VII, IX, and X have
relatively short half-lives (42, 6.2, 13.9, and 16.5 hours, respectively)
and gradually decline over 36-72 hours following intoxication.
Clinical signs of bleeding are typically observed 3-5 days after
ingestion of anticoagulant rodenticide. Because factor VII has the
shortest half-life, PT will be prolonged within 36 to 72 hours of

ingestion, followed by prolongation of aPTT and ACT.37 Proteins
induced by vitamin K absence/antagonism (PIVKA) levels will
increase 12-24 hours after ingestion; these are not specific for
anticoagulant rodenticide intoxication.

FIGURE 171.3 Vitamin K epoxidase cycle
illustrating the carboxylation of clotting factors and
the site of warfarin inhibition.
Vitamin K antagonism is treated with vitamin K1 supplementation
and supportive care (chs. 124, 138). PT typically normalizes 14-36
hours after starting vitamin K1 therapy. PT should be rechecked 3648 hours after discontinuing vitamin K1 therapy to ensure
normalization of coagulation tests and sufficient treatment
duration.37

HEPATIC DISEASE
The liver has a central role in hemostasis, being responsible for
synthesizing and clearing most pro- and anticoagulant factors and
regulators of fibrinolysis. Liver disease can alter coagulation factors,
cause endothelial activation, and lead to vitamin K deficiency. Most
patients with liver insufficiency have a parallel decline in pro- and
anticoagulant proteins, resulting in a relatively balanced hemostatic
system in vivo in initial disease stages. Prolonged PT and aPTT, and
decreased fibrinogen levels, are commonly detected in patients with
liver disease, but clinical bleeding is usually associated with only
fulminant or end-stage liver failure38,39; an exception is that
gastrointestinal (GI) ulceration can be observed in dogs with hepatic
disease and lead to GI blood loss in the absence of coagulopathy.
Routine coagulation profiles are likely inadequate in characterizing
hemostatic abnormalities in liver disease.
Given the complex and multiple effects that liver disease has on
hemostasis, thrombosis and/or bleeding can be consequences.
Hepatic diseases are common underlying conditions in dogs and cats
diagnosed with portal vein thrombosis, although other risk factors
for thrombosis including glucocorticoid therapy are present in many
of these patients. Dogs with hepatopathies have variable findings on
viscoelastic testing (ch. 170). Dogs with chronic hepatopathies,
portosystemic shunts, and extrahepatic biliary duct obstruction are
generally normo- to hypercoagulable based on viscoelastic testing.
Advanced chronic hepatopathies can cause hypocoagulability.40-42
Viscoelastic testing shows that most dogs with acute hepatopathy are
normo- or hypocoagulable.43 Vitamin-K replete cats with cholestatic
disease are typically hyper- or normocoagulable, although
hypocoagulability and hyperfibrinolysis can be observed in cats with
synthetic failure.44 Changes in primary hemostasis are not well
described in liver disease, although thrombocytopenia and
thrombocytopathia have been reported in some liver diseases.

DISSEMINATED INTRAVASCULAR
COAGULATION

DIC is a systemic activation of coagulation and impairment of
anticoagulants and endogenous fibrinolysis, leading to non-localized
intravascular fibrin deposition, thrombosis, and organ dysfunction.
DIC is a consumptive coagulopathy that can result from many
systemic diseases including widespread inflammation, sepsis, and
neoplasia. Tissue factor is a primary mediator of DIC.
Proinflammatory cytokines and endotoxins induce tissue factor
expression and release. High concentrations of tissue factor can be
found on circulating monocytes, endothelial cells, neoplastic cells,
microparticles, and other sources.45 Once in circulation, tissue factor
forms a complex with activated factor VII, a potent stimulus for
thrombin formation. Excess circulating thrombin cleaves fibrinogen,
leaving behind multiple fibrin clots and leading to microvascular and
macrovascular thrombosis. Coagulation inhibitors are consumed in
DIC, further promoting coagulation. As clots form, platelets become
entrapped, resulting in thrombocytopenia. Simultaneously, excess
circulating thrombin results in the conversion of plasminogen to
plasmin, leading to fibrinolysis. Fibrinolysis results in excess
amounts of fibrinogen degradation products, which have
anticoagulant properties, possibly contributing to hemorrhage.
Excess plasmin also activates the complement and kinin systems,
leading to clinical signs such as shock, hypotension, and increased
vascular permeability.46
Patients with DIC can display consequences of widespread
thrombosis of the microvasculature as well as increased bleeding
tendencies, either sequentially or concurrently. During the initial
(non-overt, or compensated) stages of DIC, patients are in a
hypercoagulable phase. However, procoagulant factors progressively
become consumed, leading to a hypocoagulable (overt, or
uncompensated) phase. Prolonged coagulation times accompanied
by clinical signs of bleeding might be apparent in the hypocoagulable
phase. Patients in acute fulminant DIC present with bleeding;
however, in more chronic forms, patients may only show signs
related to the underlying disorder.
Typical laboratory findings of DIC patients include
thrombocytopenia, prolongation of PT and aPTT, elevation of
fibrinolysis markers (D-dimers), hypofibrinogenemia, decreased
antithrombin, and signs of red blood cell fragmentation on the blood

smear (ch. 57). No single diagnostic test has high sensitivity or
specificity for diagnosis of DIC. Diagnostic algorithms combining
multiple hemostatic parameters have been developed in people and
likely have utility in veterinary patients.47 Viscoelastic testing can be
used for distinguishing between the various stages of DIC in dogs.
The prognosis for DIC varies depending on the underlying
disorder but is considered poor regardless. Mortality appears to be
higher in dogs with hypocoagulability and multiple hemostatic
laboratory abnormalities.47,48

ACQUIRED ANTICOAGULANTS
Coagulation inhibitors are antibodies (usually IgG) that bind to and
inhibit activity of coagulation factor or cause increased coagulation
factor clearance. Acquired anticoagulants are rare in veterinary
patients and can develop secondary to immune-mediated disease,
multiple blood transfusions, stem cell transplantation, and
neoplasia. Anti-phospholipid protein antibody (i.e., lupus
anticoagulant) inhibits the interaction between coagulation proteins
and cell membranes, causing prolongation of coagulation times such
as aPTT. Paradoxically, the presence of anti-phospholipid protein
antibodies is clinically associated with thrombosis. Clinical signs
related to acquired anticoagulants may be absent or can include
signs of hemorrhage. Coagulation times (PT, aPTT) are abnormal
depending on which factor(s) is/are affected. A plasma mixing test
can be used to support a diagnosis of acquired anticoagulant, and
confirmatory testing with specific assays can be performed (e.g.,
Bethesda assay for quantification of factor inhibitor).49

GENERAL TREATMENT OF ACQUIRED
HYPOCOAGULABILITY
Therapy to address the underlying disorder for hypocoagulability is
recommended when possible. Vitamin K1 therapy is recommended in
anticoagulant rodenticide intoxication cases (ch. 138), and in liver
dysfunction causing coagulopathy. An initial dose of 2.5 to 5 mg/kg

SC or PO, followed 6-12 hours later with maintenance therapy (2.5 to
5 mg/kg PO, split into 2-3 doses per day) can be given and long-term
duration is guided by PT rechecks. Cats with liver disease can be
given doses of 0.5 to 1.5 mg/kg SC every 12 hours. Intravenous
vitamin K1 administration has been associated with anaphylaxis.
Vitamin K3 therapy is not recommended due to slower onset of
action and possible Heinz body formation.
Plasma transfusions can temporarily replenish coagulation factors
(ch. 124). Coagulation times are not sensitive predictors for risk of
hemorrhage, and viscoelastic testing might be useful in determining
if a patient would benefit from plasma transfusion and at what
dosage. Plasma is usually administered as an initial dose of 10-20
mL/kg IV in dogs.50 Lower dosages (e.g., 6 mL/kg) are
recommended in cats.51 Fresh frozen plasma contains all coagulation
factors and plasma proteins, including the labile coagulation factors
(V and VIII). Cryoprecipitate primarily contains factors VIII, XIII,
von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, and fibronectin, at approximately
50-80% of the levels as fresh frozen plasma but in a smaller volume.
Cryoprecipitate-poor plasma has sufficient quantities of most
coagulation factors except for those contained in cryoprecipitate.52
Coagulation factor stability generally declines in plasma products
over prolonged storage. Factors V and VIII significantly diminish
after 1 year of storage in human plasma products, although stability
in dogs likely exceeds this timeframe.53 Either fresh frozen or stored
plasma is suitable for replacement of vitamin K-dependent factors,
as well as for treatment of most other factor deficiencies.
Therapeutic recommendations to address consequences of DIC are
controversial. Heparin therapy is commonly used in the
hypercoagulable phase of DIC, but optimal dosing protocols are not
known.54 Heparin is an indirect anticoagulant, exerting most of its
effect through potentiation of AT activity, which can be diminished
in states of DIC. Heparin therapy should be avoided in veterinary
patients with DIC and evidence of bleeding. Prophylactic plasma
transfusion does not show a consistent benefit in humans with DIC,
and thus plasma transfusions are usually recommended only in
veterinary DIC patients with clinical signs of bleeding.55

HEREDITARY HYPOCOAGULABLE
STATES
SCOTT SYNDROME
While Scott syndrome is a defect of procoagulant activity on the
platelet surface, this disorder manifests as a coagulopathy because
the platelet surface cannot support plasma coagulation protein
activity.56 Further details can be found in ch. 175.

HYPERFIBRINOLYSIS
The fibrinolytic system regulates hemostasis and is activated
alongside coagulation. Hyperfibrinolysis prematurely degrades fibrin
clots, leading to hemorrhage. Hyperfibrinolysis can occur secondary
to other disorders including trauma, DIC, and liver disease. Delayed
hemorrhage has been observed in Greyhounds following trauma or
surgery. While the disorder is not fully characterized, it is suspected
to be due to hyperfibrinolysis.57
The diagnosis of hyperfibrinolysis is challenging. Increased levels
of fibrin degradation products and D-dimers are suggestive of, but
not specific for, hyperfibrinolysis. Increased fibrinolysis can be
detected by viscoelastic testing, but the test appears to lack
specificity and sensitivity. Peri-operative treatment of Greyhounds
with anti-fibrinolytic drugs (e.g., aminocaproic acid 500 mg per 30
kg dog PO q8h, beginning postoperatively the evening of surgery)
mitigates post-operative hemorrhage.58

HEREDITARY FACTOR DEFICIENCIES
Single or combined factor deficiencies produce variable clinical signs
ranging from subclinical to severe bleeding tendencies. Depending
on the factor(s) deficient, prolongation of PT and/or aPTT is
observed. Measurement of individual coagulation factor activity is
required for a definitive diagnosis. Genetic testing is also available
for some inherited coagulation disorders.

Hemophilia A and B
Hemophilia A and B are deficiencies in factors VIII and IX,
respectively. Hemophilia A is more common than hemophilia B and
both forms have been documented in dogs and cats. Maine Coon cats
are suspected to have an inherited deficiency in factor I and IX.59
Hemophilia A and B are autosomal X-linked recessive traits;
therefore, males are most commonly affected. Various genetic
mutations are responsible for hemophilia A or B. In some cases,
hemophilia within a pedigree can be traced to the original index
animal while other cases are suspected to arise from de novo
mutations.60 Lack of factor VIII or IX inhibits formation of the
tenase complex, hindering downstream thrombin generation and
blood clot formation. Accordingly, hemorrhage is the principal
clinical sign associated with hemophilia A and B and it can manifest
as prolonged bleeding after trauma or surgery, subcutaneous or
intramuscular hematomas, mucosal bleeding (ch. 29), and lameness
due to hemarthrosis.
Hemophilia A or B is suspected in patients with a bleeding
diathesis (i.e., tendency to bleed) and prolonged aPTT or ACT, with a
concurrent normal PT. Measurement of coagulation factor activity
(FVIII:C or FIX:C) is required to definitively diagnose these
conditions. Normal factor activity levels are 50-150%. Hemophilia is
considered mild when the measured factor level is approximately 620%; moderate and marked hemophilia can be defined when factor
levels are approximately 2-5% and <2%, respectively.61 Severity of
factor deficiency correlates with clinical signs in affected people,
although additional variables such as function of other hemostatic
proteins, patient physical condition, and concurrent illness play a
role. Occurrence of spontaneous bleeding episodes was not
significantly different between dogs with mild, moderate, and severe
hemophilia A in one study.62
Depending on the severity of hemorrhage episodes, plasma
transfusion can be used to replace deficient factors and alleviate
short-term bleeding. While injection of desmopressin temporarily
increases circulating factor VIII in people, the same does not appear
to be true in dogs.63 Prophylactic transfusion might be warranted in
patients with hemophilia prior to performing invasive procedures.

Prognosis for dogs and cats with hemophilia appears variable.
Severely affected animals likely die at birth. The prognosis did not
correlate with the degree of factor deficiency in dogs with hemophilia
A in one study.62 Following repeated transfusion, the patient can
develop inhibitors to the deficient factor (i.e., factor VIII or IX
inhibitors), leading to higher transfusion requirements on
subsequent transfusion.64-66 Pedigree analysis and factor activity
levels should be examined in breeding groups that have given rise to
individuals with hemophilia. Factor levels are often low-normal in
carrier females and can overlap with those of clear females, making it
difficult to determine carrier status based on factor analysis alone.
Lack of clinical signs in carrier or mildly affected animals can lead to
propagation of the condition through a pedigree.

Other Inherited Coagulation Factor Deficiencies
Hereditary fibrinogen (factor I) disorders include complete or partial
lack of fibrinogen (afibrinogenemia and hypofibrinogenemia,
respectively) as well as qualitative defects in fibrinogen
(dysfibrinogenemia).60 Disorders of fibrinogen appear to be
uncommon in dogs and cats.67-70 Depending on the severity of the
disorder, hemorrhage might occur spontaneously or after trauma or
surgery. Fibrinogen defects can be suspected when PT, aPTT, ACT,
and thrombin clotting time are prolonged; quantitative fibrinogen
disorders will have a concurrently decreased fibrinogen
concentration. Patients with dysfibrinogenemia typically have
normal to low fibrinogen concentrations and low functional
fibrinogen activity (e.g., Clauss test; ch. 170).67 Due to the
uncommon nature of hereditary fibrinogen disorders, more common
causes of low fibrinogen concentrations such as DIC or liver disease
should be ruled out prior to pursuing this diagnosis.
Feline factor XII deficiency (Hageman trait) is a common
hereditary trait in domestic cats.71 Cats with factor XII deficiency
demonstrate prolonged aPTT and ACT, but hemorrhage or other
clinical signs do not result from this deficiency as in vivo clot
formation is primarily dependent on factor VII and tissue factor
activation. Concurrent hemophilia A or B has been reported in cats

with factor XII deficiency and can give rise to clinical signs of
hemorrhage.72
Other inherited factor deficiencies resulting in hemorrhage have
been described. Coagulation panel abnormalities and clinical signs
depend on the factor(s) affected and severity of the deficiency.
Congenital deficiency of the vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors
causes combined factor deficiencies (factors II, VII, IX, and X;
anticoagulant proteins C, S, and Z). Congenital vitamin K-dependent
coagulation factor deficiency has been reported in Devon Rex cats
and is responsive to vitamin K1 supplementation. Reports of single
factor deficiencies exist in cats and dogs.

TREATMENT OF INHERITED
COAGULOPATHIES
Single or combined factor deficiencies can be treated using a plasma
product transfusion to temporarily replenish the deficient factor(s)
during episodes of hemorrhage (ch. 124). Plasma dosages are
similar to those outlined above for acquired coagulopathies. Fresh
frozen plasma can be used for most factor deficiencies, including
hemophilia A. Stored plasma has diminished levels of factors V and
VIII but can be used to treat other factor deficiencies.
Cryoprecipitate is suitable for transfusing smaller plasma volumes
rich in factors I, VIII, and XIII; cryosupernatant is lacking in those
factors but can be used to treat other deficiencies. Factor XII
deficiency does not require treatment as it does not result in clinical
signs.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Acquired Hyper- and Hypocoagulable Syndromes
The body uses a finely balanced system called hemostasis to
prevent blood loss. Normally, blood circulates through the body in
blood vessels. Upon injury to the vessels, bleeding or hemorrhage
can result. The hemostatic system is made up of many components.

Platelets and coagulation factors work together to form blood clots at
the site of injury. Over time, other factors work to dissolve these
blood clots as the blood vessel injury heals.
Many conditions and diseases can disrupt normal hemostasis.
Factors that decrease platelet or coagulation factor activity can result
in decreased ability to form blood clots, resulting in haemorrhage.
Additionally, if blood clots are dissolved too rapidly, hemorrhage
could also result. In contrast, increased platelet or coagulation factor
activity can lead to excessive blood clot formation. Inappropriate
blood clot formation can block normal blood flow in blood vessels.
This is referred to as thrombosis.
Common conditions that cause hypercoagulability, and increased
risk of thrombosis include:
• Immune-mediated hemolytic anemia
• Serious inflammation (e.g., trauma, pancreatitis)
• Widespread bacterial infection (“sepsis”)
• Heart disease (cats)
• Kidney disease
• Gastrointestinal disease
• Cancer
• Endocrine diseases (especially Cushing’s disease or
hyperadrenocorticism)
• Disseminated intravascular coagulation
Common conditions that cause hypocoagulability, or increased
risk of haemorrhage include:
• Rat poison ingestion (anticoagulant rodenticide)
• Advanced liver disease
• Cancer
• Disseminated intravascular coagulation
Specific blood clotting tests may be performed to better identify
the abnormality in the hemostasis system. These tests might include
coagulation profiles (prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin
times), thromboelastography or thromboelastometry, and other
specialized tests. Specific identification of thrombosis can be difficult
to detect with diagnostic tests.

Treatment for abnormal hemostasis is first directed at the
underlying disorder, if possible. When patients have conditions
resulting in hypocoagulability, treatments may also include plasma
transfusions (to temporarily replace coagulation factors) and vitamin
K1 therapy (to support coagulation factor production). Treatment of
thrombosis can include medications to decrease activity of platelets
(e.g., clopidogrel) or clotting factors (e.g., heparin, rivaroxaban).
Treatment aimed at dissolving the clot may also be recommended.
Shauna L. Blois (Guelph, Ontario, Canada)

Sarah Winzelberg Olson
