Anemia (ch. 57) is defined as hematocrit (Hct), hemoglobin
concentration ([Hb]), or red blood cell (RBC) count below the
laboratory’s reference range. In veterinary medicine, Hct is most
frequently used for making a diagnosis of anemia. Multiple factors
influence the frequency of diagnosis of anemia, including defining
anemia as one, two, or all three of these parameters outside the
reference range; the demographics of the patient populations
studied; and whether primary care or referral center populations are
evaluated. Despite these distinctions, anemia remains a common
clinical problem in veterinary medicine, occurring in approximately
4% of all feline patients and in as many as 31% of canine patients >8
years of age.1,2
Nonregenerative anemia is the most common form of anemia seen
in the cat and dog.1,3,4 Caution should be used when making a
diagnosis of anemia in a cat since Hct, [Hb], and RBC count decrease
approximately 25% in cats during general anesthesia.5 In dogs, the
Hct, [Hb], and RBC count results depend on the blood vessel
sampled. Arterial blood samples give lower values than venous
samples and a spurious diagnosis of nonregenerative anemia could
be made if arterial samples are compared to venous sample reference
intervals.6
Nonregenerative anemia can also be described as anemia with
reticulocytopenia because the hallmark of nonregenerative anemia is
a reticulocyte count <60,000/mcL in dogs or <50,000/mcL in cats,
although these values vary based on method of reticulocyte
enumeration.7 Automated reticulocyte counts have a smaller
coefficient of variation and are more reproducible than manual
ones.8,9 Once hypoxemia occurs, 3-7 days are required for
production of reticulocytes; thus, blood loss anemia and hemolytic
anemia initially may appear nonregenerative. Consequently, anemia
in some patients may not be immediately classifiable as regenerative
or nonregenerative. Surrogate measures of regeneration, including
mean corpuscular volume (MCV), mean corpuscular hemoglobin
(MCH), mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC), and
RBC distribution width, are not reliable indicators of regeneration in
either dogs or cats.1,9,10 Observation of polychromasia provides a

better estimation of regeneration than do RBC indices in dogs.9,11
Feline reticulocytes occur in at least two forms: punctate and
aggregate (ch. 57). Aggregate reticulocytes are believed to be most
important for assessing the response to anemia and they represent
those counted using automated hematology analyzers. The
reticulocyte production index (RPI), correcting the magnitude of
reticulocytosis for the severity of the anemia, has both high
sensitivity and high specificity for manual and automated
reticulocyte counting in cats but not in dogs.12,13
Some automated hematology analyzers have the capacity to
measure reticulocyte indices, including those similar to MCV and
MCH reported for mature RBCs. Low reticulocyte hemoglobin
content (CHr or CHretic), reticulocyte hemoglobin equivalent (RETHe) and reticulocyte mean corpuscular volume (rMCV or MCVretic)
have been associated with hematologic and biochemical markers of
iron deficiency.14,15 Reticulocyte indices may prove useful in the
diagnosis of iron deficiency prior to the development of microcytosis
and hypochromia.16 However, changes in reticulocyte indices are not
specific for iron deficiency and can also be found in other causes of
microcytosis such as portosystemic shunts and breed-associated
microcytosis.17
An understanding of the pathophysiologic mechanism of
nonregenerative anemia, an extensive list of differential diagnoses,
and a comprehensive diagnostic plan are required to identify the
cause of, and successfully manage patients with, nonregenerative
anemia (Table 172.118-21). Determining the cause of
nonregenerative anemia is critical to optimal patient management
and outcome, as anemia is an important prognostic variable. In dogs
with the nonregenerative variant of immune-mediated hemolytic
anemia (IMHA [ch. 174]), Leishmania infantum infection (ch.
197), or lymphoma (ch. 322), anemia predicts outcome.22-24
Severely anemic cats are less likely to be discharged from the
hospital and if anemia is due to chronic kidney disease (ch. 301),
cats with anemia have a shorter survival than those without.25

CLINICAL SIGNS AND PHYSICAL EXAM
FINDINGS
Clinical signs of anemia are vague in both dogs and cats and are
attributable to decreased oxygen delivery to tissues. Physical
examination reveals findings such as pallor (ch. 25), weakness (ch.
23), and depression (chs. 10 and 44). Physical examination may also
identify physiologic mechanisms compensating for decreased oxygen
delivery such as tachycardia and tachypnea. In some cases, a heart
murmur or gallop sound may be identified (ch. 38). Thorough
physical examination (ch. 3) can frequently identify findings
attributable to the underlying disease process responsible for anemia
including icterus (ch. 28), lymphadenopathy and cranial
organomegaly. Patients may be pyrexic or hypothermic (chs. 16,
130). Histories reported by caretakers are frequently non-specific
and may include lethargy, decreased appetite, weight loss, pica
(more common in cats), respiratory signs, exercise intolerance,
collapse episodes, or recent administration of drugs, such as
phenobarbital, estrogens or chloramphenicol (ch. 138).26,27

PATHOGENESIS
Many systemic illnesses result in nonregenerative anemia (Table
172.1), and its pathogenesis is complex and multifactorial (Figure
172.1). Pathogenetic mechanisms typically are separated into two
categories: decreased erythrocyte lifespan and decreased or
ineffective erythropoiesis.

DECREASED ERYTHROCYTE LIFESPAN
The lifespan of a normal RBC is 100 days in a healthy dog and 72
days in a healthy cat.28 During this time, the RBC is responsible for
oxygen delivery to tissues and it requires maintenance of cellular
features of deformability in order to optimize its performance. As the
RBC ages, numerous biochemical, immunologic, and mechanical
changes impair its ability to recover from various insults. The
accumulation of such injuries triggers the removal of a senescent
RBC from circulation by the reticuloendothelial system (RES),
primarily by mononuclear phagocytic cells within the spleen, liver
and lymph nodes. RBC oxidative stress is caused by both endogenous
hemoglobin autoxidation and exogenous oxidants that can result in
cellular aging and functional impairment. The result is a shortened
erythrocyte lifespan due to removal by the RES.29 Oxidative stress,
mechanical stress, complement-induced injury, rearrangement of
membrane phospholipids, contact with cationic proteins released
from activated neutrophils, Heinz body formation, and hemotropic
parasites all alter cytoplasmic viscosity. This change results in
impaired deformability, targeting the RBCs for early removal from
circulation.30 Similarly, hereditary erythrocyte defects such as
membrane protein abnormalities, erythrocyte enzyme deficiencies,
hemoglobinopathies and increased osmotic fragility lead to
shortened erythrocyte lifespan. Excessive activation of the RES, as
seen with certain immune-mediated, infectious, inflammatory, and
paraneoplastic conditions, can also stimulate early removal of RBCs
from circulation. In general, disorders resulting in decreased RBC
lifespan cause regenerative anemia in dogs and cats, but they can
also be contributing factors in cases of nonregenerative anemia.

DECREASED AND INEFFECTIVE
ERYTHROPOIESIS
Erythropoiesis can be decreased due to an absolute or a relative lack
of erythropoietin or it can be ineffective secondary to decreased
marrow response to erythropoietin. Erythropoietin is produced
primarily by the kidney in the peritubular interstitial cells of the

inner renal cortex and outer medulla. Renal hypoxia is the main
driving factor stimulating erythropoietin synthesis. Renal hypoxia
leads to an inhibition of hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1)
degradation, allowing HIF-1 to bind to hypoxia-response elements of
oxygen-regulated genes, leading to an increased production of
erythropoietin.31 Erythropoietin production is decreased in both
acute and chronic causes of kidney disease, and chronic kidney
disease is known to be a common cause of nonregenerative anemia
(ch. 301).31 The most important extrarenal production site of
erythropoietin is the liver, with additional limited production in sites
including the brain, vascular endothelial cells, lung, uterus, testis,
and various solid tumors.31-33 However, erythropoietin synthesis
from extrarenal tissues cannot be adequately induced to compensate
when there is decreased renal production.33 Hypoxemia does not
increase hepatic production of erythropoietin; however, other causes
of liver injury can lead to increased erythropoietin production from
the liver.31
Ineffective erythropoiesis can be secondary to absolute deficiencies
in nutrients crucial to hemoglobin biosynthesis and RBC maturation
or due to a number of different cytokine abnormalities seen in
various states of inflammation, commonly designated anemia of
chronic disease or anemia of inflammation. Inflammatory cytokines,
such as interleukin (IL)-1, IL-6, tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha,
and interferon-gamma, reduce the production of endogenous
erythropoietin in the face of hypoxia and suppress the erythroid
progenitor response to erythropoietin.34 IL-6, in particular,
increases the production of hepcidin, an acute phase protein
produced by the liver that is responsible for iron homeostasis,
resulting in a systemic state of relative iron deficiency. Increased
hepcidin levels can also occur secondary to decreased renal clearance
and mutations in hepcidin suppressors.34 Elevated hepcidin levels
result in increased cellular internalization and degradation of
ferroportin, an integral enterocyte membrane protein responsible for
the movement of iron out of the enterocyte and into circulation. The
net effect of hepcidin elevation on ferroportin is iron trapping within
enterocytes, sequestering iron from systemic utilization.

Additionally, hepcidin prevents the release of iron stores from
macrophages and hepatocytes and blocks luminal intestinal iron
absorption. This leads to low blood iron levels and relative systemic
iron deficiency. Iron deficiency, whether absolute or secondary to
elevations in hepcidin, impairs hemoglobin biosynthesis and causes
a blunted erythropoietin response due to reduced erythropoietin
sensitivity of progenitor cells in the bone marrow. Copper deficiency
is associated with a functional iron deficiency due to decreased
hemoglobin synthesis and there is evidence to support that
iatrogenic, congenital, and nutritional copper deficiencies are an
uncommon cause of ineffective erythropoiesis and nonregenerative
anemia in the dog.21 Deficiencies of vitamin B12 inhibit purine and
thymidylate syntheses, impairing DNA synthesis within
erythroblasts and causing erythroblast apoptosis.35 In humans,
pernicious anemia is caused by inadequate gastric parietal cell-origin
intrinsic factor, a cofactor that enables ileal vitamin B12 absorption
from food. By contrast, in dogs and cats, lack of intrinsic factor
leading to hypocobalaminemia is not a recognized cause of anemia.
Hypocobalaminemia due to hereditary selective cobalamin
malabsorption is a cause of nonregenerative anemia in the dog, and
when it occurs, it is often erythroblastic.19 While folate deficiency is
similarly associated with ineffective erythropoiesis in humans, there
is a paucity of documentation in the veterinary body of literature
regarding folate deficiency and anemia. Only one case report is
identified where two cats fed a commercial vegan diet were
diagnosed with severe hypofolatemia and mild nonregenerative
anemia, which resolved with folate supplementation.20
Hypoalbuminemia and elevations in parathyroid hormone, ferritin,
and transferrin saturation significantly impair the erythropoietic
response and can result in ineffective erythropoiesis.36 Aluminum
intoxication, secondary to chronic high doses of aluminum hydroxide
or other toxic exposure, can result in ineffective erythropoiesis due to
interference with erythroid precursor iron utilization and shortened
erythrocyte lifespan resulting from morphologic changes to RBCs.37
Reports of anemia secondary to aluminum accumulation are limited
in veterinary medicine, but are well-documented in human and

rodent populations.37-39 In humans, the use of angiotensinconverting enzyme inhibitors can lead to anemia, although this drug
adverse effect has not been observed in dogs or cats. The
mechanisms by which this anemia is mediated are not fully
elucidated; reduced erythropoietin release as well as ineffective
erythropoiesis due to direct drug effects on erythrocyte precursors
are suspected.40,41
Differentiating iron-deficiency anemia from anemia of
inflammation can be difficult and, in some cases, both conditions
may be driving factors; however, differentiation is essential for
selecting the appropriate treatment. Evaluating a variety of iron
indices can help distinguish if a component of iron restriction is
contributing to the anemia, which helps to guide therapeutic
recommendations. Serum iron levels are low in both iron-deficiency
anemia and anemia of inflammation, and can also be low in dogs
with portosystemic shunts.42 Ferritin, the soluble storage form of
iron in tissues, is a positive acute-phase protein and in health is a
representative measure of total body iron stores. Ferritin levels are
classically decreased in iron-deficiency anemia and increased in
anemia of inflammation. However, ferritin can also be increased in
acute hepatopathies or hepatic necrosis due to upregulated
production as an acute phase protein or increased release from
damaged hepatocytes.17 Transferrin is the main protein in blood that
binds and transports iron. In veterinary medicine, transferrin is
measured indirectly and reported as total iron binding capacity
(TIBC). Transferrin is a negative acute-phase protein. Although TIBC
levels are typically normal to increased in cases of iron deficiency,
concurrent inflammation can hinder interpretation due to the
downregulation of transferrin levels and may result in normal TIBC
with acute inflammation and low TIBC with chronic inflammation.
Elevations in transferrin can also be seen with chronic liver disease
or an iron overload state.43 Iron saturation percentages (serum
iron/TIBC) <20% can be suggestive of iron deficiency.43 Because
conventional evaluation of MCV and MCHC for microcytosis and
hypochromasia are insensitive markers of iron deficiency,
reticulocyte indices are better indicators of iron status.16

Reticulocyte indices have been evaluated in different causes of
anemia. While changes in these indices are not specific to dogs with
iron deficiency, a decreased reticulocyte [Hb] (≤26 g/dL), CHretic
(≤20.1 pg), RET-He (<20.9 pg) and increased percentage of
reticulocytes with low reticulocyte [Hb] (≥74.2%) and low CHretic
(≥50.7%) is suspicious for iron-deficient anemia in dogs.15,17 The
RPI in cats (Ret% × [Hct/37])/([−0.05] × Hct + 3.25), with a cutoff
of 0.35 for manual counting and 0.59 for automated counting, has a
high sensitivity and specificity for predicting regenerative status.13

IDENTIFYING THE UNDERLYING
CAUSE OF NONREGENERATIVE
ANEMIAS
The differential diagnosis list (Table 172.1) for causes of
nonregenerative anemia is extensive. Differential diagnoses should
be prioritized based on patient signalment, history, and presentation.
Uncommon causes of nonregenerative anemia should be considered
in certain cases. Using an algorithm to guide diagnostic
recommendations will help to minimize unnecessary testing while
simultaneously maximizing the chances of obtaining a diagnosis
(Figure 172.2). It is important to keep in mind that up to one-third
of dogs and over 50% of cats with IMHA may be nonregenerative at
the time of diagnosis (ch. 174).27,44

Anemia of Inflammation
Anemia of inflammation, also referred to as anemia of chronic
disease, is a common cause of nonregenerative anemia in cats and
dogs and is a diagnosis of exclusion. Due to the effects of various
cytokines, inflammation from many different systemic conditions
leads to iron sequestration within the RES and functionally restricted
erythropoiesis. Additional mechanisms contribute to restricted
erythropoiesis (see Pathogenesis, above). This results in a mild to
moderate nonregenerative anemia, typically with low serum iron
levels and increased tissue iron stores.43,45 In humans, systemic

inflammatory states encompass a broad clinical spectrum and are
induced by a number of chronic diseases including infections,
autoimmune conditions, malignancies, kidney disease, pancreatitis,
and diabetes mellitus.34 Additionally, cardiac disease, trauma,
critical illness, postoperative recovery, and aging are included in this
broad definition.34 In dogs and cats, similar inflammatory states are
also identified secondary to these conditions and others including
additional endocrine diseases, hepatic disease, and gastrointestinal
disease45 (Table 172.1).

patient with nonregenerative anemia. ACTH,

Bone Marrow Failure as a Cause of Nonregenerative
Anemia

Multiple bone marrow disorders can produce a nonregenerative
anemia (Table 172.1). These include primary medullary disorders:
pure red cell aplasia, which may be a more severe form of
nonregenerative IMHA (ch. 174), and bone marrow disorders (ch.
176), such as aplastic anemia/pancytopenia, primary
myelodysplastic syndromes, primary myeloproliferative disorders,
primary dysmyelopoiesis, and primary myelophthisis. Some
publications have tried to differentiate nonregenerative IMHA from
precursor-targeted immune-mediated anemia (PIMA). There is
substantial overlap between these conditions and not enough data to
determine if these are distinctly separate diagnoses or if they
represent different parts of one spectrum of disease attributed to
immune-mediated destruction of erythroid precursors.46 Secondary
or extramedullary causes of bone marrow failure induce
nonregenerative anemia as well, but because these disorders have an
extramedullary etiology, treatment targets the primary disorder.
Myelophthisis, both primary and secondary, may result in
nonregenerative anemia. For more information on tumors causing
myelophthisis, see chs. 322, 327 and 328. Pyruvate kinase
deficiency (ch. 174) and estrogen toxicosis (ch. 138) can lead to
secondary myelofibrosis. Phenobarbital administration and copper
deficiency can result in secondary dysmyelopoiesis. Secondary
myelodysplastic syndromes occur in humans as a result of cytotoxic
drug therapy or radiation exposure. Their occurrence has not been
documented in veterinary patients. For further classification of
primary and secondary medullary disorders, see ch. 176.

Pure Red Cell Aplasia Versus Aplastic Anemia
Pure red cell aplasia is an acquired syndrome that arises secondary
to systemic disease such as feline leukemia virus in cats and
parvovirus in dogs, or occurs as a primary idiopathic hematologic
disorder with a presumptive immune-mediated pathogenesis.47,48 It
can also occur secondary to the formation of anti-erythropoietin
antibodies from the use of erythropoietin-stimulating agents (ESAs;
see below).49 It is characterized by a normocytic, normochromic,
nonregenerative anemia in the absence of other cytopenias. Bone
marrow cytologic evaluation and biopsy demonstrate erythroid

hypoplasia or aplasia with normal to increased granulopoiesis and
megakaryopoiesis.47
In comparison, aplastic anemia is characterized by
nonregenerative anemia in the presence of other cytopenias
(bicytopenia or pancytopenia) where bone marrow cytologic
evaluation and biopsy reveal a marked reduction in, or absence of,
normal hematopoietic tissue of all lineages, which is replaced by
fat.50 Aplastic anemia can occur secondary to toxins, infection,
adverse pharmacotherapeutic effects or can be idiopathic with an
immune-mediated etiology (ch. 176).51

DIAGNOSIS
The diagnosis of bone marrow failure requires bone marrow
aspiration to assess cell morphology and a bone marrow core biopsy
to assess cellularity (ch. 84). When no other cause of a
nonregenerative anemia can be identified, bone marrow testing is
often the final diagnostic step (Figure 172.2). Most primary
medullary disorders carry a poor prognosis, in part because
identification of the underlying molecular defect is lacking in
veterinary patients and because, as the least common cause of
nonregenerative anemia, their rarity hampers identification of
optimal treatment. The prognosis in the subset of patients with
nonregenerative IMHA is fair, with the majority of cases responding
to medications and 43% survival at 12 months (ch. 174).46 These
patients typically required prolonged periods of therapy to achieve
remission and while medications can be tapered or removed in some
patients, many will relapse. Additionally, anemia secondary to
immune targeting of RBC precursors may remain nonregenerative
until the patient is adequately immunosuppressed.

THERAPEUTIC OPTIONS
Treatments for nonregenerative anemia include supportive therapy
when needed and identification and treatment of the underlying
cause. If patients have clinical signs of anemia, transfusion with

packed RBCs or whole blood may be indicated (ch. 124). When the
anemia is severe, therapeutic options may include supplementation
of RBC building blocks such as iron and cobalamin as well as
targeted use of ESAs until the bone marrow recovers. For specific
treatments of underlying causes of extramedullary causes of
nonregenerative anemia, see chs. 198 and 199. For regenerative
anemia, see chs. 57 and 174. For pancytopenia, see ch. 176. For
further information on immunosuppressive medications, see chs.
144, 169, and 227.

SUPPORTIVE THERAPY
Transfusion (ch. 124)
Although nonregenerative anemia is more common than
regenerative anemia, review of the indications for RBC transfusion in
the dog shows transfusion for bone marrow failure is much less
common than for blood loss or hemolytic anemia.52 Because of the
high frequency of chronic kidney disease in cats, transfusion for
nonregenerative anemia is more common than in the dog.53 The low
rate of RBC transfusion for nonregenerative anemia reflects the
moderate degree of anemia present in this condition, its slow onset,
adequate compensatory mechanisms, and poor prognosis. Certain
patients with nonregenerative anemia may receive multiple RBC
transfusions, increasing the importance of blood typing and
crossmatching prior to transfusion.54

SPECIFIC THERAPIES
Iron Supplementation
Iron can be supplemented parenterally or enterally, with parenteral
administration being preferable given more reliable absorption.
Additionally, in cases of iron deficiency, parenteral supplementation
results in a faster resolution when reticulocyte indices are
evaluated.16 Oral supplementation, however, is the least expensive
form of supplementation and is also considered the safest. In dogs

receiving iron supplementation, CHretic and MCVretic may be more
sensitive to identifying a response in iron body stores.16
• Oral Supplementation: Ferrous sulfate is the most common of
the oral supplements, with varied dosing reported in the
veterinary literature. The recommended dosage is 100-300
mg/dog PO q24h (20-60 mg of elemental iron) or 50-100
mg/cat PO q24h (10-20 mg of elemental iron). Side-effects
with the recommended dosages can include gastrointestinal
upset, which is typically mild. Other oral supplements such as
ferrous gluconate and ferrous fumarate are available and used
for human supplementation. There is less information
published regarding dosing of these forms in veterinary
medicine; however, anecdotal information targets the same
amount of elemental iron as that with ferrous sulfate
administration. A suggested dosing for ferrous gluconate is
16.25 mg/kg/day in cats.55
• Parenteral Supplementation: Iron dextran is the most
common parenteral iron supplement in veterinary medicine.
The recommended dosage is 10-20 mg/kg in dogs (maximum
dose 300 mg) and 10 mg/kg in cats given as needed.
Intramuscular administration is recommended, due to an
increased risk of anaphylactic reaction when it is given
intravenously. Newer agents without the dextran moiety, such
as iron gluconate and iron sucrose, are associated with a lower
rate of anaphylactic reactions in humans and can be
administered intravenously as well as intramuscularly. One of
the newest of the iron-carbohydrate compounds is ferric
carboxymaltose, designed to mimic physiologic ferritin.56
However, data on the use of these newer parenteral iron
supplements and intravenous administration are lacking in
veterinary populations.57

Erythropoiesis-Stimulating Agents (ESAs)
The use of recombinant human ESAs may be considered in the
treatment of nonregenerative anemia. Dogs with a nonregenerative
anemia lacking features of primary myelodysplasia respond to the

use of ESAs and tend to have a prolonged survival in comparison to
dogs with primary myelodysplasia, who typically do not respond to
standard therapies.58 However, ESAs have also been used with
positive response in a case of myelodysplastic syndrome with
erythroid predominance in a dog.59 In humans, ESAs are in wide
clinical use and are the most commonly used therapy for anemias
secondary to myelodysplastic syndromes, despite not being approved
by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for this specific use.60 In
dogs with secondary myelofibrosis, the use of ESAs in conjunction
with other therapies is associated with a prolonged survival.18 In
humans, these agents are also used to address relative erythropoietin
deficiency, as is seen with multiple myeloma and non-Hodgkin’s
lymphoma.61
Several recombinant human erythropoietin products are available
on the market, including epoetin alfa, epoetin beta, and darbepoetin
alfa. Significant homology (>80%) between human erythropoietin
and canine and feline erythropoietin allows recombinant human
products to bind to and interact with erythropoietin receptors in
dogs and cats.62 The choice of which agent to use should be based on
numerous factors, including immunogenicity and cost. Antierythropoetin antibodies resulting in pure red cell aplasia are
reported in up to 25-30% of dogs and cats treated with epoetin and
6-8% of dogs and cats treated with darbepoetin.49,63 This
complication can occur months to years after starting therapy, with a
median of 14.5 weeks reported in cats.64 Antibodies persist for
months and patients become transfusion-dependent, with weekly
transfusions necessary in some cases (ch. 124).63 If pure red cell
aplasia develops, the ESA should be discontinued and many
clinicians start immunosuppressive therapy (ch. 169), although an
ideal immunosuppressive protocol has not been established in
humans or in animals.63 Because of possible side-effects, ESA
therapy should only be instituted when the patient is clinically
affected by the anemia and other methods of addressing the anemia
are not successful or are unlikely to produce a sustained response.

Therapy is started in most patients when a moderate to severe
anemia is present (packed cell volume [PCV] ≤20%); however, the
threshold for starting treatment also depends on the cause of the
anemia. For darbepoetin, the recommended dosage in cats is 1
mcg/kg SQ once weekly until the target PCV is attained, and then the
frequency is decreased to every 2-3 weeks with further adjustments
to maintain a PCV of 25-35%. For dogs, the recommended dosage is
0.5-0.8 mcg/kg SQ once weekly initially, with subsequent reductions
in dosing interval up to q 21 days to maintain PCV >30%.49 For
epoetin, the recommended dosage in dogs and cats is 100 units/kg
SQ 3 times weekly with reduction to twice weekly maintenance
therapy once target PCV is attained. Concurrent monthly parenteral
iron supplementation with ESAs is recommended.

TREATMENT OF MEDULLARY CAUSES
OF NONREGENERATIVE ANEMIA
Evidence-based treatments for nonregenerative anemia stemming
from primary medullary disease are lacking in veterinary medicine.
Single case reports and case series predominate in the literature and
because multiple classification schemes exist for bone marrow
diseases, comparison of treatment outcomes is difficult.

Glucocorticoids
If treatment of medullary causes of nonregenerative anemia is
pursued, nearly all patients receive initial treatment with
immunosuppressive doses of glucocorticoids (ch. 169). Many dogs
with pure red cell aplasia, the nonregenerative variant of IMHA or
PIMA respond to glucocorticoids as single-agent therapy or in
combination with other immunosuppressive medications with
resolution of anemia.26,46,50 In other bone marrow disorders,
response is more variable.

Cyclophosphamide
Although most dogs with pure red cell aplasia and some with
nonregenerative IMHA respond to glucocorticoid

immunosuppression alone, some dogs appear to require additional
immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide 50 mg/m2 PO q24h × 4
days, repeated weekly.26,48 Cyclophosphamide is not currently
recommended for the treatment of regenerative immune-mediated
hemolytic anemia (ch. 174).

Azathioprine
Azathioprine (2 mg/kg PO q24h × 5 days, then q48h) has been
described for the treatment of pure red cell aplasia and for
nonregenerative IMHA in dogs.26,46 Many protocols for various
diseases recommend dosing azathioprine daily for 1-4 weeks prior to
reducing the frequency. The use of azathioprine is not recommended
in feline patients and a safe dosage has not been determined for cats.

Cyclosporine
In humans, cyclosporine coupled with other immunosuppressive
agents can induce remission in patients with pure red cell aplasia,
aplastic anemia, and certain myelodysplastic syndromes. While
evidence for the use of cyclosporine in veterinary patients with
myelodysplastic syndromes is lacking, the use of cyclosporine as a
second agent for immunosuppression has been reported for dogs
with nonregenerative IMHA at dosages of 4-12 mg/kg PO q24h (ch.
174).46,65 Cyclosporine is also used as adjunctive therapy to treat
pure red cell aplasia in cats with median dosages of 10 mg/kg PO
q24h required to achieve clinical remission.47 Modified versions of
cyclosporine are typically preferred due to higher and more
predictable bioavailability in veterinary patients (chs. 144, 169).

Mycophenolate Mofetil
Mycophenolate mofetil has also been used in conjunction with
glucocorticoids for dogs with aplastic anemia, myelodysplastic
syndromes and nonregenerative IMHA (ch. 169). Dosages of 10-15
mg/kg PO q12h have been used.51,65

Other Cytotoxic Agents
Cytarabine and combination chemotherapy have been used with
variable success to treat myelodysplastic syndromes in cats with
feline leukemia virus infection (ch. 199).66

Vitamin K2
Menatetrenone, a vitamin K2 analog, ameliorates cytopenias by
promoting cellular differentiation in vivo and apoptosis of immature
blasts in human myelodysplastic syndromes. A preliminary report
indicated menatetrenone 2 mg/kg was beneficial in feline
myelodysplastic syndromes and it has been also used in dogs with
myelodysplastic syndromes and nonregenerative IMHA at a median
dosage of 1.4 mg/kg/day (range, 0.7-2.1 mg/kg/day).65,67

NEW DIRECTIONS IN THERAPY
Attempts at management of nonregenerative anemia of
inflammation using iron and ESAs have been ineffective for some
patients and may carry risks. These limitations are driving the search
for cutting-edge therapies to target the hepcidin-ferroportin axis,
including inhibiting hepcidin function with direct hepcidin
antagonists, preventing hepcidin transcription with hepcidin
production inhibitors (including IL-6 pathway inhibitors and
vitamin D), and promoting ferroportin resistance to hepcidin action
with ferroportin agonists/stabilizers.68 Prolyl hydroxylase enzyme
inhibitors promote endogenous erythropoietin production by
reducing hepcidin levels and stabilizing hypoxia-inducible factors.
Preliminary results of toxicologic and pharmacokinetic studies with
canine models for some of these compounds are encouraging and
warrant further investigation.69 A novel erythroid maturation agent,
luspatercept-aamt, regulates late-stage erythropoiesis and is labelled
for use in humans with specific myelodysplastic syndromes. As the
use of these agents is explored further for humans and their efficacy
and safety profiles are established, these novel therapies will be
considered in veterinary patients to expand our armament of options
for long-term management of these challenging cases.

Erythrocytosis is an increase in red blood cells (RBCs) that is
recognized by elevations in packed cell volume (PCV), hematocrit
(HCT), hemoglobin (Hb) concentration, or RBC count (ch. 57).
Although the terms erythrocytosis and polycythemia are often used
interchangeably, erythrocytosis is the more appropriate term since
polycythemia is a multilineage hypercellularity of RBCs, leukocytes,
and platelets, which is not often observed in veterinary patients.
Erythrocytosis can occur due to reduced plasma volume, termed
relative erythrocytosis (RE), or due to true expansion of the RBC
mass, termed absolute erythrocytosis (AE). AE can then be classified
as primary or secondary. In primary erythrocytosis (PE),
erythropoiesis proceeds independently of erythropoietin (EPO). In
secondary erythrocytosis (SE), EPO production is increased,
driving increased RBC production. Increased EPO production can
either be physiologically appropriate, where EPO is produced in
response to hypoxemia, or physiologically inappropriate, where
excess EPO is produced in the absence of hypoxemia.

NORMAL ERYTHROPOIESIS
RBC production is regulated by renal oxygenation and EPO in a
feedback loop.1 As RBCs are responsible for oxygen transport to
tissues, reduction in RBCs is detected by renal oxygen sensors. Renal
hypoxia leads to generation and stabilization of hypoxia-inducible
factors, which in turn incite EPO transcription in renal cortical
interstitial fibroblasts.2,3 Reduced renal oxygen delivery from
anemia, hypoxemia, or decreased renal blood flow stimulates EPO
production; adequate renal oxygen delivery decreases EPO
production.1
EPO binds to EPO receptors on bone marrow RBC precursors,
stimulating their proliferation and differentiation into RBCs.1,4 EPO
receptor engagement triggers a signaling cascade involving Janus 2
tyrosine kinase (JAK2), a detail that is key to understanding the
pathogenesis of PE.3 Other hormones such as cortisol, thyroxine,
and growth hormone also facilitate erythropoiesis.5-8

MECHANISMS OF RELATIVE
ERYTHROCYTOSIS
RE occurs when plasma water is lost without concurrent loss of
RBCs, as occurs with dehydration, usually associated with vomiting,
diarrhea, or primary polyuria.4 Anxiety or excitement-induced
splenic contraction in dogs or horses can cause transient
catecholamine-mediated RE.4

MECHANISMS OF PRIMARY
ERYTHROCYTOSIS
In PE, RBC production is independent of EPO levels and EPO
production is suppressed by adequate renal oxygen delivery. PE can
be congenital or acquired, but only acquired PE is described in
veterinary patients. Acquired PE in people is caused by a mutation in
the RBC progenitor cells that results in increased RBC mass, usually
due to a myeloproliferative neoplasm.9 The best characterized one is
polycythemia vera (PV) in which a mutation, usually in JAK2
(V617F), leads to increased RBC production independent of EPO and
a variable increase in platelet and myeloid cells.3 One dog with
acquired PE has been described with JAK2 mutations, including
V617F.10 PE in companion animals may not be the same as human
PV since most cats and dogs with PE lack the splenomegaly,
leukocytosis, and thrombocytosis seen with the human disease.4,11

MECHANISMS OF SECONDARY
ERYTHROCYTOSIS
APPROPRIATE SECONDARY ERYTHROCYTOSIS
In appropriate SE, chronic hypoxemia drives increased EPO
production.1 The resulting increase in RBC mass expands the blood
oxygen carrying capacity to improve tissue oxygenation.4 Common

causes of hypoxemia leading to SE are cardiopulmonary disease,
especially congenital heart defects with right-to-left shunting of
blood like reverse patent ductus arteriosus (rPDA) and tetralogy of
Fallot1,12-14 (ch. 231). Chronic pulmonary diseases (ch. 217) less
commonly result in severe erythrocytosis (Table 173.1).15,16 Highaltitude–associated hypoxemia can cause erythrocytosis, but it is
usually not associated with clinical signs.1,9 Congenital
methemoglobinemia secondary to methemoglobin reductase
deficiency can also cause SE in dogs and cats17,18 (ch. 174).

INAPPROPRIATE SECONDARY
ERYTHROCYTOSIS
Inappropriate SE occurs when there is elevated circulating EPO in
the absence of hypoxemia.4 Increased EPO production is the result
of reduced renal blood flow leading to renal hypoxia or inappropriate
EPO production by neoplastic cells.9,26,28 Renal tumors are the most
commonly associated with overproduction of EPO, but others have
been reported (Table 173.1).20,30-33,35-38 Since renal hypoxia
drives EPO production, non-neoplastic renal disease like infection
can also cause SE19,20 (ch. 304). Mild inappropriate SE can occur
with endocrinopathies from non-EPO hormone stimulation of
erythropoiesis (Table 173.1).4

CLINICAL PRESENTATION OF
ERYTHROCYTOSIS
SIGNALMENT AND CLINICAL SIGNS
PE usually occurs in middle-aged to older dogs and cats, without sex
predilection, though some case series document an increased
frequency of male cats with PE.11,17,41,42 The signalment of animals
with SE varies with the cause. AE results in hyperviscosity and

hypervolemia, which are responsible for the majority of clinical
signs. Hyperviscosity causes impaired microcirculation, local tissue
hypoxia, and capillary distention, potential vessel rupture, and
sometimes thrombosis.1,43 Neurologic signs, especially seizures (ch.
45), altered mentation (ch. 44), and twitching (ch. 42), are
common manifestations of the resultant central nervous system
hypoxia; they can also result from thromboembolism or
bleeding.1,11,42
The polyuria and polydipsia that are common in patients with
erythrocytosis may be due to hyperviscosity and subsequent
hypervolemia impeding vasopressin release33 (ch. 53).
Erythrocytosis-associated vomiting and diarrhea may be the
sequelae of reduced gastrointestinal perfusion. Thrombotic
outcomes, though a common cause of morbidity/mortality in human
PV, have been rarely reported in dogs with PE and SE42,44-46 (chs.
171 and 219). While signs of dogs and cats with SE are similar to
those with PE, animals with SE may also show signs referable to
their underlying disease.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION FINDINGS
Patients with PE often have tortuous scleral and retinal vessels11,47
(ch. 13). Neurologic deficits including blindness and ataxia are often
appreciated (ch. 241).11 Human PV patients commonly have
splenomegaly (ch. 182) which is rare in dogs but has been described
in cats with PE.43,47

Cyanotic mucous membranes are suggestive of SE caused by
disorders such as congenital heart disease with right-to-left shunting
or severe respiratory disease1 (ch. 27). In contrast, animals with
rPDA may have differential cyanosis affecting only caudal body
parts, hind limb weakness, and they often lack a heart murmur (ch.
231).1,21 Animals with hereditary methemoglobinemia have brown
mucous membranes, while PE and all other SE patients have notably
hyperemic mucous membranes.1

CLINICOPATHOLOGIC
ABNORMALITIES
Hypoglycemia may accompany erythrocytosis (ch. 61) due to
increased erythrocyte consumption of glucose in vivo or in vitro.4
Furthermore, glucometers can report falsely low glucose measures
with erythrocytosis due to the mechanism by which they convert
whole blood glucose measurements to equivalent plasma glucose
readings, which assumes a normal HCT.45 Cats with PE may have
increased creatine kinase (ch. 66), likely due to ischemic
myopathy.11

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP FOR
ERYTHROCYTOSIS
Before pursuing an extensive diagnostic workup for AE, RE should
be excluded based on physical examination, lab work (at a minimum
PCV, total solids, renal values and urine specific gravity to assess for
other indicators of dehydration; ideally complete blood count, serum
biochemistry profile, urinalysis), and RE resolution with
rehydration. Similarly, breed-specific reference intervals for RBC
indices should be reviewed, as several breeds of dogs (notably sight
hounds) and cats (Norwegian Forest Cat, Siberian, Holy Birman)
have HCTs that exceed those of the general population.48-49a To
avoid missing a diagnosis of erythrocytosis, RBC count should be

considered the most reliable indicator of RBC mass. Microcytosis
may accompany erythrocytosis, which may lower the HCT and mask
erythrocytosis.50

EVALUATION FOR CAUSES OF
SECONDARY ERYTHROCYTOSIS
When AE is confirmed, history, physical examination, and diagnostic
testing should focus on distinguishing PE from SE. A diagnosis of PE
is mostly one of exclusion; thus, hypoxemia (appropriate SE) and
conditions associated with inappropriate EPO production
(inappropriate SE) must first be ruled out. Testing should follow an
organized scheme, focusing on the respiratory, cardiovascular, and
renal systems as well as searching for neoplastic causes of
erythrocytosis (Figure 173.1). Arterial blood gas measurement (or
pulse oximetry if arterial blood gas evaluation is unavailable) should
be performed (ch. 74). Partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) <80 mm
Hg and Hb oxygen saturation (SaO2) <95% are consistent with
hypoxemia or tissue hypoxia, respectively, and suggest a
physiologically appropriate SE. In these cases, cardiac and
pulmonary evaluation by thoracic radiographs, echocardiography,
and contrast echocardiography/echoaortography should be pursued.
Contrast echoaortography with agitated saline contrast (bubble
study) is an ideal diagnostic for detection of right-to-left shunts51
(chs. 97 and 231). It should be noted that compensatory right
ventricular hypertrophy (RVH) can be observed in PE due to
hyperviscosity but is mild in contrast to RVH associated with SE.11,17
Blood gas evaluation will also enable a diagnosis of
methemoglobinemia.
If hypoxemia is excluded, further workup for inappropriate EPO
production should include a minimum database (complete blood
count, serum biochemistry profile, urinalysis) and imaging.
Azotemia or hematuria might suggest a renal disease as the SE
trigger. Diagnostics for endocrinopathies such as
hyperadrenocorticism (ch. 293) and hyperthyroidism (ch. 287)
should be pursued in cases with mild RBC elevations and consistent

clinical signs and lab work results. Computed tomography or
abdominal ultrasound can evaluate for masses and renal lesions that
could be sources of EPO.

UTILITY OF ERYTHROPOIETIN
MEASUREMENT
Several limitations impact EPO testing in veterinary medicine. First,
the use of an EPO assay validated for the species being tested is
imperative but is not readily available. Second, overlap between the
EPO levels in normal animals with those in PE and SE means EPO
values must be cautiously interpreted.17,41 Dogs and cats with SE can
have low or normal EPO values, but elevated levels of EPO are
strongly suggestive of a diagnosis of SE (i.e., it is a specific, but not
sensitive, test).17,41

MUTATION TESTING AND BONE
MARROW EVALUATION
Confirmation of a JAK2 mutation is integral to the diagnosis of PV in
humans.52 Testing for the V617F JAK2 mutation in dogs (through
North Carolina State University) confirms a diagnosis of PV (only 1
of 5 tested dogs with PE had the mutation; a negative test does not
exclude a PE diagnosis).10 Genetic testing is not currently available
for cats with suspected PE. Bone marrow assessment (ch. 84)
demonstrates nonspecific erythroid hyperplasia in both PE and SE,
so the procedure is not warranted unless there is clinical suspicion
for a myeloproliferative neoplasm.

MANAGEMENT
The approach to an AE depends on its underlying cause but the
overall aim is to reduce hyperviscosity and related clinical signs. This
is typically accomplished via phlebotomy, cytoreductive therapy, or a

combination thereof. Treatment of inappropriate SE should focus on
the underlying cause, such as removing EPO-producing tumors or
treating with chemotherapy or radiation therapy, which can resolve
the erythrocytosis.25,26,29,35 Pre-operative phlebotomy might be
useful in stabilizing the patient.4 Treatment of the underlying cause
may not be possible with appropriate SE and attempts to reduce RBC
mass may exacerbate tissue hypoxia.53 A HCT minimizing clinical
signs of hypoxia and hyperviscosity should be targeted,22 although
some prefer to use owner-perceived recurrence of clinical signs to
establish the interval between treatments.53 SE dogs with rPDA have
been managed with phlebotomy, hydroxyurea (HU), or a
combination thereof.22,53

PHLEBOTOMY
Therapeutic phlebotomy is the mainstay of controlling RBC mass in
PE or in SE where the underlying cause cannot be corrected. Serial
phlebotomies of 10-20 mL/kg with or without crystalloid fluid
replacement are performed until clinical signs are resolved.1,54
Target HCT in people with PV is <45%, but at least in cats, target
PCV <50% may be unnecessary to control signs.11,46 Phlebotomy
intervals average 6.5 weeks, but can be much longer in some
patients.11 Iron deficiency, sedation risk (if needed), cost, and patient
compliance may make repeated phlebotomies infeasible.11
Hirudotherapy, or medicinal leeching, a natural form of phlebotomy,
has been successfully used to treat primary PE in cats.11,55 Each
leech removes 5-10 mL of blood per feeding followed by oozing of the
same volume for 24-48 hours after detachment.56 Pain and
secondary infections can result.11,55,56

erythrocytosis. EPO, Erythropoietin; Hb,
hemoglobin; HCT, hematocrit; JAK2, Janus kinase
2; Minimum database, complete blood count, serum
biochemistry profile and urinalysis; RBC, red blood
cell count.

CYTOREDUCTIVE THERAPY
In most cases, only if phlebotomy is required too frequently or not
well-tolerated should cytoreductive therapy with HU be considered.
HU inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, inhibiting DNA synthesis and
thus cellular proliferation.57 Empiric dosing strategies in the
literature include: 50 mg/kg PO q48h; 30 mg/kg PO q24h × 7 days
followed by 15 mg/kg PO q24-48h.22,42,43,47 Alternate dosing

schedules for cats have been reported with lower daily doses; feline
dosages should remain under 100 mg/kg and that dose should not be
given more than every 5 days.11
Because HU blocks recycling of methemoglobin to Hb,
methemoglobinemia can result.11 Other potential side-effects of HU
include reversible bone marrow suppression, Heinz bodies (cats),
macrocytosis, alopecia, and nail sloughing.11,22,58 Adverse effects are
responsive to dosage reduction and are less common with every
other day therapy.11,22

JANUS-ASSOCIATED KINASE
INHIBITORS
Ruxolitinib, an inhibitor of JAK1 and JAK2, is utilized in human PV
patients that are HU-resistant or -intolerant, but due to uncertainty
regarding long-term effects, it is not recommended as a first-line
therapy.46 Oclacitinib, or Apoquel, though developed as a JAK1
inhibitor, has some inhibitory activity against JAK2 in ex vivo
enzyme systems and might have utility in managing veterinary PE,
especially those with documented JAK2 mutations.59 Rigorous
genetic and therapeutic studies are required to confirm this would be
an appropriate therapeutic.

ALTERNATIVE THERAPIES
Feline Hb sensitivity to oxidative damage has been exploited
therapeutically. One cat with PE was managed with onion powder
mixed into the food for at least 15 months, purportedly via causing
mild hemolysis despite absence of Heinz bodies.60 Although an
interesting approach, induced hemolysis has the potential to cause
pigmentary nephropathy and could be detrimental. Pentoxifylline
may aid in management of PE or SE by improving RBC flexibility
and microcirculatory perfusion.61

PROGNOSIS
In veterinary patients, the risk of progression to myelofibrosis and
leukemia, which shortens the lifespan of human PV patients, is
unknown. Leukemic transformation was suspected in one cat with
PE.11 A recent feline PE case series reported survival times of over 17
months with the only two non-survivors living over 4.5 years.11 The
majority of these cats had perceived good quality of life.11 Reported
canine survival times with PE range from 1 year to 33 months with
treatment with phlebotomy, HU, or both.42,43,54 The prognosis for
SE depends on the underlying cause.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Erythrocytosis
Definition and Clinical Signs (“Symptoms”)
You pet has been diagnosed with erythrocytosis, which means that
they have an excess of red blood cells in their blood. Having too
many red blood cells can make your pet feel unwell because it makes
their blood too thick (viscous). Your pet may show signs of increased
thirst and urination, abnormal behavior, weakness, seizures,
vomiting, and diarrhea related to the high number of red blood cells.
Erythrocytosis can be a primary disease of the bone marrow—the
organ that produces blood cells—or secondary to heart, lung, or
kidney disease, or different types of cancer.

Excessive Red Blood Cell Production When Oxygen
Is Low
The most important function of red blood cells is to carry oxygen
throughout the body. When a dog or cat does not have enough
oxygen in their bloodstream they are considered to have hypoxemia.
The kidneys detect hypoxemia and respond to it by producing a
hormone called erythropoietin which stimulates the bone marrow to
make more red blood cells. As a result of increased levels of this

hormone, the body increases how fast it makes red blood cells which
allows it to increase oxygen delivery to body tissues.
The lungs and heart are the key organs that bring oxygen into the
body and deliver it around the body, respectively. If the heart or
lungs are very diseased, the body becomes depleted of oxygen. This
oxygen depletion will stimulate the body to make more red blood
cells. After oxygen depletion is present for some time, the dog or cat
develops an increased red blood cell count, or erythrocytosis (called
secondary appropriate erythrocytosis).

Excessive Red Blood Cell Production When Oxygen
Is Normal
Erythrocytosis can also occur with normal oxygen levels. This can be
due to erythropoietin being inappropriately overproduced by
diseased kidneys, cancers of the kidney, or less commonly, other
types of cancer. This is called secondary inappropriate
erythrocytosis.
Another form of erythrocytosis, called primary erythrocytosis,
occurs with normal blood oxygen levels and normal erythropoietin
levels. In primary erythrocytosis, the bone marrow inappropriately
makes an increased amount of red blood cells without any hormonal
stimulation. This is similar to a disease in people called polycythemia
vera.

Diagnostic Testing for Pets With Erythrocytosis
Since there are so many different causes of erythrocytosis, your
veterinarian will likely need to perform a wide variety of tests in a
stepwise manner to identify the underlying cause. They will first
measure blood oxygen levels to help determine if your pet has
erythrocytosis secondary to low blood oxygen. If low oxygen levels
are present, your pet will be evaluated for diseases of the heart and
lungs with chest x-rays and a heart ultrasound. If oxygen levels are
normal, your pet will be evaluated with x-rays, ultrasound and
maybe even a CT scan for kidney disease or cancer that could be
making excess erythropoietin. Your veterinarian may also measure
the levels of erythropoietin in your pet’s blood. However, this
hormone assay is a specialized test that is not always available for
dogs and cats. Diagnosis of primary erythrocytosis involves ruling

out all other causes of increased red blood cells and, if possible,
confirming normal or low erythropoietin levels.

Treatment and Prognosis
If your dog or cat is showing signs of illness from erythrocytosis, the
simplest and quickest treatment is to remove red blood cells from
them just like would occur with a blood donation. This process is
called phlebotomy. If the erythrocytosis is caused by heart, lung or
kidney disease or cancer, successful treatment of the disease can
resolve the erythrocytosis. If the underlying disease cannot be
treated or the diagnosis is primary erythrocytosis, then your dog or
cat may require intermittent phlebotomy to control their clinical
signs by keeping their blood from being too viscous. If phlebotomy is
required more often than every 4-6 weeks or is difficult because your
pet’s blood is very viscous, your dog will likely be prescribed a
medication to reduce red cell production. The most common
medication used is hydroxyurea. Hydroxyurea is a chemotherapy
drug that must be monitored with bloodwork, but the side effects are
typically minimal. Usually, in cases of primary erythrocytosis,
phlebotomy, hydroxyurea, or the two treatments combined, can
result in good quality of life for several years. The outcome for dogs
and cats with erythrocytosis secondary to an underlying disease like
heart disease, lung disease, or cancer, depends on the prognosis for
that causative disease.
Dana Nicole LeVine (Auburn, Alabama) and Ann
Hohenhaus (New York, New York)

ANEMIAS DUE TO HEMOLYSIS
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Hemolytic anemias are caused by an accelerated erythrocyte (red
blood cell [RBC]) destruction and decrease of the normal RBC life
span (dog: 100-120 days, cat: 70-75 days) due to an intrinsic (e.g.,
erythroenzymopathy) or extrinsic (e.g., antibody formation against
the RBC membrane) defect. Hemolytic anemias are usually
regenerative, and extramedullary hematopoiesis in the spleen and
liver may occur. Hemolysis can be extravascular or intravascular.
Extravascular hemolysis is the predominant form and refers to
phagocytosis of RBCs by the mononuclear phagocytic system of the
spleen, liver, and bone marrow. Damaged (as well as physiologically
senescent) RBCs are first sequestered, then phagocytosed, and finally
degraded. Hemoglobin (Hb) is degraded to bilirubin, iron, and
amino acids. Depending on the extent of hemolysis,
hyperbilirubinemia and bilirubinuria may result, although serum
bilirubin may be normal in the case of slow chronic hemolytic
anemia (especially in cats). Less commonly, RBCs are lysed in the
blood vessels (intravascular hemolysis) as a result of membrane

damage or cellular fragmentation (resulting in hemoglobinemia and
hemoglobinuria). Renal damage caused by Hb is very rare in small
animals.1 The pathophysiological classification of hemolytic anemias
is presented in Table 174.1.

Clinical Presentation
Clinical signs depend on the severity and rate of hemolysis,
complications, and the underlying disease. Mild and chronic cases
show no or only mild, nonspecific signs. Severe hemolytic anemias
are associated with sudden weakness, collapse, and signs of shock. In
addition to the typical signs of anemia, icterus (with plasma bilirubin
concentration >1.5-2 mg/dL [>26-34 micromol/L]) and pigmenturia
(hemoglobinuria or/and bilirubinuria), fever, hepato- and
splenomegaly, and tachypnea may be present.

Laboratory Findings
Usually, hemolytic anemias are regenerative (polychromasia,
reticulocytosis [dog >60,000/mcL, cat >40,000/mcL], increased
numbers of nucleated RBCs, macrocytosis), although they may be
nonregenerative during the acute phase, i.e., approximately the first
3 days. Cats have 2 types of reticulocytes: punctate (2-10 granules)
and aggregated reticulocytes. The aggregated reticulocytes
correspond to canine reticulocytes (ch. 57). Aggregated reticulocytes
become punctate reticulocytes after about 12 hours, and the latter
circulate over a period of 2-3 weeks and therefore do not allow any
assessment regarding the current activity of erythropoiesis.2
Punctate reticulocytes can also be found in healthy non-anemic cats.
Aggregated reticulocytes represent polychromatophilic RBCs on
blood smears. Hyperbilirubinemia may be present in all forms of
hemolysis; hepatopathy or internal hemorrhage should be
considered as differential diagnoses. Plasma protein concentrations
are usually normal or elevated. The osmotic fragility of the RBCs is
generally increased, regardless of the cause.3-6

IMMUNE-MEDIATED HEMOLYTIC
ANEMIA (IMHA)
IMHA is the most common form of hemolytic anemia. In IMHA,
antibodies to the patient’s own RBCs shorten RBC life span. The
antibodies result from immune dysregulation or cross-reactivity and
can be directed against normal (non-associative, primary, or
cryptogenic IMHA, autoimmune hemolytic anemia) or altered RBC
membranes (associative [secondary] IMHA with comorbidities).
Non-associative IMHA occurs in dogs of all ages (median age 5-7
years), but is more common in certain breeds, e.g., Cocker Spaniels,
Irish Setters, Dachshunds, Poodles, Springer Spaniels, Bearded
Collies, Old English Sheepdogs, and is somewhat more common in
female dogs.7-19 A sex or breed predisposition has not been reported
in cats; in one study, 12 of 19 cats were <3 years of age.20 Nonassociative IMHA is diagnosed by excluding possible underlying
causes (diagnosis of exclusion). Genetic factors (breed) and triggers
(estrus, stress) may play a role.21 In associative IMHA, a stimulus for
antibody production or a comorbidity is present. Possible causes of
secondary IMHA are listed in Table 174.1.11,12,18,22-30 IMHA can
also occur in the context of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) (ch.
179). In about one-third of dogs, IMHA is accompanied by immunemediated thrombocytopenia (ITP) (so-called Evans’ syndrome; ch.
175).11
