Pathophysiology
The following mechanisms can be involved in the immune-mediated
destruction of RBCs: a) autoagglutinins (IgM or IgG in high levels;
agglutinate RBCs in 0.9% saline), b) hemolysins (IgM, IgG), and c)
so-called incomplete warm antibodies (IgG, less frequently IgM,
complement), which agglutinate only after the addition of Coombs’
reagent (most common). The antibodies adhere to RBCs and cause
binding and activation of complement. Extensive complement
activation causes the formation of transmembrane channels
(membrane attack complex) in the RBC membrane and, rarely,
intravascular hemolysis. Intravascular hemolysis may result in ghost
cells, which are empty RBC shells. Lower levels of RBC-bound
complement cause extravascular hemolysis through the
mononuclear phagocytic system, predominantly in the spleen, but
also in the liver and bone marrow.21 IgG-loaded RBCs can also be
destroyed without complement activation, as tissue macrophages
express receptors that recognize the Fc portion of the IgG molecule.
As a result, RBCs can be phagocytosed either completely or only
parts of the membrane (spherocyte formation) can be phagocytized.
Since macrophages do not exhibit receptors for the Fc portion of IgM
antibodies, the destruction of IgM-loaded RBCs is mediated by

complement.31 In addition to the warm antibodies that react at 37°C,
so-called cold antibodies (reaction at 4°C) are rarely detected.21,31

Clinical Presentation
Clinical signs vary depending on the antibody class involved and the
severity of the hemolysis. The signs of anemia may be accompanied
by anorexia, pigmenturia (very rare in cats), jaundice, occasionally
vomiting, diarrhea, fever, splenomegaly, rarely hepatomegaly, and
possibly signs of the underlying disease. Cats may also show pica
(e.g., eating cat litter) and perhaps even signs of a secondary
cardiomyopathy (due to chronic anemia).20,32 Serious complications
in dogs include thromboembolism (chs. 219 and 238) and
disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) (ch. 171). Thrombus
formation is promoted by vascular endothelial damage, stasis of
blood flow (predisposing factors can include intravenous (IV)
catheters, for example) and hypercoagulability, i.e., Virchow’s
triad.33 Depending on the location of the thrombus, sudden dyspnea,
cough, cyanosis, painful abdomen, ascites, and neurological signs
may occur.19,33,34 With cold antibodies (very rare), cyanosis and
necrosis of the extremities can occur without anemia during the cold
season.31

Laboratory Findings
Anemia is usually moderate to severe and mildly to markedly
regenerative but can be non-regenerative in up to 30% of dogs (in
cats up to 50%) at initial presentation.19,20 Possible causes for the
lack of a regenerative response include pre-regenerative anemia,
antibody formation against RBC precursor cells, and reduced
erythropoiesis due to inflammation.35 These cases can be
diagnostically difficult. In some dogs, there is evidence of ironrestricted erythropoiesis (functional iron deficiency, inflammationmediated iron sequestration).36
The following are typical findings, although it must be
remembered that they do not occur in all cases and do not serve to

distinguish associative from non-associative IMHA: a) RBC
agglutination is common in dogs and cats with IMHA. The saline
agglutination test (SAT) is performed by mixing 1 drop of RBCs with
4 drops of 0.9% saline (

Video 174.1). In most patients with

IMHA (dogs, 78-100%; cats, 65-100%), RBC agglutination with a
positive SAT occurs.14,17,19,20 Macroscopic agglutination could be
caused by immunoglobulins (IgM, IgG), cold agglutinates, and
plasma components (e.g., patients with hyperproteinemia and
increased fibrinogen concentration). For confirmation of persistent
agglutination (caused by IgG and IgM, not rouleaux formation or
nonspecific binding of plasma proteins), the RBCs are washed 3
times in 0.9% saline at 21-37°C (

Videos 174.2, 174.3).

Persistence of agglutination after washing is rare in the absence of
IMHA (4-10% in dogs and 21% in cats) and is almost pathognomonic
for IMHA11,14,15,20; b) marked spherocytosis (in a fresh pretransfusion blood sample37) occurs in about two-thirds of dogs with
IMHA.11,14,19 Greater than 5 spherocytes/100× oil immersion field is
supportive of a diagnosis of IMHA (ch. 57).38 However, 3-4
spherocytes/100× oil immersion field are also consistent with IMHA
if no other cause for hemolysis is present.12 In high numbers,
spherocytes are almost always pathognomonic for IMHA. In cats,
spherocytes are difficult to identify due to the lack of central pallor;
c) a positive direct Coombs test (direct antiglobulin test [DAT],
usually performed on microtiter plates) detects RBC-bound
antibodies or complement (if there is no persistent
autoagglutination).21 Sensitivity and specificity are 61-82% and 94100%, respectively, in dogs, and 82% and 95-100%, respectively, in
cats.20,24,39-42 Various commercial in-clinic tests such as
immunochromatography or gel test show a good correlation with the
microtiter method.41 False negative test results can occur due to
technical errors, low antibody concentrations, unfavorable antigenantibody ratio, or pre-treatment with glucocorticoids. However, even
after a few days of immunosuppressive therapy, the DAT can still be

positive.11 If the DAT is negative, the diagnosis should be thoroughly
reconsidered. If possible, the samples for DAT should be collected
before any RBCs are transfused. Flow cytometry has also been used
to detect erythrocyte-bound antibodies, but has not (yet) replaced
the DAT.42 False-positive flow cytometry results are possible (8% of
non-anemic dogs).43
In addition to the standard hematocrit (Hct) determination with
automated blood counting devices, the spun packed cell volume
(PCV) must also be assessed, as machine-calculated and manually
determined values can differ significantly in the case of RBC
agglutination. Dogs often show a marked leukocytosis (white blood
cell [WBC] counts up to 100 × 109/L) with or without a left shift,
sometimes with toxic changes in neutrophils, and monocytosis. The
high WBC counts may indicate a “cytokine storm” due to severe
inflammation and necrosis. Thrombocytopenia may occur if IMHA is
complicated by DIC or in the presence of Evans’ syndrome. Moderate
to severe hyperbilirubinemia and bilirubinuria are common in dogs,
but in chronic and well-compensated cases, plasma bilirubin may be
only mildly elevated, especially in cats. Hemoglobinemia and -uria
are indicative of intravascular hemolysis (rare in cats). Serum liver
enzyme activities are often elevated, which may be due to hypoxia
and hepatocellular necrosis caused by severe anemia. Concentrations
of acute phase proteins such as C-reactive protein (CRP) are usually
severely increased in dogs.13 Marked hypokalemia may result from
renal tubular acidosis.44 The antinuclear antibody (ANA) test is
rarely positive (indicative for SLE; ch. 179). Changes in coagulation
tests (prothrombin time [PT], activated partial thromboplastin time
[aPTT], antithrombin, D-dimer concentrations,
thromboelastography) initially or during progression are suggestive
of hypercoagulability (50%) and DIC (51-80% of dogs), respectively
(ch. 171).14,33,45 Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS;
ch. 128) and organ failure are common complication in dogs, but
rare in cats.20,33,46,47

Confirming the Diagnosis

In both human and veterinary medicine, there is no gold standard
test for the diagnosis of IMHA.12 The diagnosis is based on history,
typical clinical and laboratory findings, and exclusion of other
diseases or causative factors in non-associative IMHA. The presence
of ≥2 signs of immune-mediated destruction of RBCs (spherocytes
[dogs], agglutination of RBCs [without washing], positive DAT/flow
cytometry or persistent agglutination) and ≥1 sign of hemolysis
(hyperbilirubinemia, hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, ghost cells)
is diagnostic for IMHA. The presence of 1 sign of immune-mediated
RBC destruction and ≥1 sign of hemolysis is also suggestive if no
other reason for the anemia can be identified.12 Further
investigations to detect possible underlying causes include urinalysis
and urine culture, screening of blood smears (e.g., for Babesia, blasts
[ch. 57]), serologic titers/polymerase chain reaction test (Table
174.1), radiography and ultrasound examinations (e.g., exclusion of
neoplasia, zinc-containing foreign bodies), and, if necessary, fineneedle aspiration of enlarged lymph nodes or organs (chs. 85, 88),
ophthalmic (including retinal) examination (ch. 13), possibly an
ANA test if SLE is suspected (ch. 179) or platelet-bound antibody
test if Evans’ syndrome is assumed (which is rare in cats).

Therapy
Treatment can be divided into 3 phases:

Induction of Remission
In associative IMHA, the underlying disease must be treated, all nonessential drugs should be discontinued, and drugs that are essential
for survival should be replaced by others if possible. Initially PCV
measurement once or twice daily may be indicated, as the PCV may
drop rapidly and a transfusion might be required. The decision for a
blood transfusion (ch. 124) depends on the clinical signs, the
severity of anemia (PCV in dogs approximately <15-18%, cats <1215%), how rapid the onset of anemia is, and an elevated blood lactate
concentration. RBC products should be as fresh as possible (not
older than 7-10 days) as transfusion of blood that has been stored for
longer periods is associated with a higher mortality rate.48 Blood
substitutes can be administered if available. Infusions are indicated

for rehydration and prevention of complications such as DIC (ch.
171) and thromboembolism (chs. 219, 238). Plasma transfusions
are not routinely recommended except in cases with DIC and
bleeding tendency.49 In cats with a critically low PCV, fluid
resuscitation/fluid therapy should only be administered after blood
transfusion because further lowering of PCV can lead to
decompensation and death. Antibiotic administration is
recommended if vector-borne disease is suspected (ch. 183) or
myelosuppression is documented (ch. 321).

Dogs
Prednisolone 1 mg/kg PO q12h or 50-60 mg/m2/day is given in dogs
>25 kg (or starting with short-acting water-soluble
methylprednisolone [e.g., sodium succinate, Solu-Medrol] 10 mg/kg
IV once, then change to oral treatment). Alternatively, if oral therapy
is not possible, dexamethasone (initially 0.2-0.4 mg/kg IV q24h) can
be administered (ch. 144). Up to 2-3 weeks may pass before a
response to treatment occurs (i.e., the Hct remains stable or rises).
Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) (8-10 [-12] mg/kg PO q12h) inhibits
purine synthesis in B and T lymphocytes and thus their proliferation,
similar to azathioprine, but is not myelotoxic or hepatotoxic (ch.
169). Thromboprophylaxis (chs. 219, 238) is indicated in all dogs
during the initial phase of treatment (except in the presence of
thrombocytopenia <30,000/mcL).49 Since venous thrombi are the
primary cause of thrombosis (composed predominantly of fibrin),
the administration of anticoagulants such as heparin (unfractionated
or low molecular weight heparin [LMWH]) or rivaroxaban (factor X
inhibitor, 1-2 mg/kg PO q24h) is indicated.49,50 Dosage
recommendations for unfractionated heparin are approximately 150300 U/kg SC q6h or 100 U/kg IV bolus followed by 900 U/kg
q24h.49 LMWHs such as dalteparin or enoxaparin are preferred in
human medicine because they have a more predictable
pharmacokinetic profile and lead to fewer complications. In
veterinary medicine insufficient evidence is available with regard to
the choice and dose of anticoagulant in IMHA. Suggested starting
dosages are dalteparin 150-175 U/kg SC q8h or enoxaparin 0.8-1
mg/kg SC q6-8h. Individual dosage adjustment (if available using

factor X measurement) is recommended.49 As dogs with IMHA have
increased platelet activity, antiplatelet drugs (preferably clopidogrel
[initially 10 mg/kg, then 1-4 mg/kg PO q24h], or if not available
acetylsalicylic acid [0.5 mg/kg PO q24h]) should be
administered.45,49,51 Thromboprophylaxis could be discontinued
when the dog is in remission (Hct and inflammatory markers [e.g.,
CRP] in the normal range) and no other risk factors exist.49

Cats
Prednisolone may be administered, initially 1.5-2 mg/kg PO q12h for
about 3 days (or starting with short acting, water-soluble
methylprednisolone 10 mg/kg IV once, then changing to oral
treatment), then reducing to prednisolone 1 mg/kg PO q12h.

Maintenance Therapy and Prevention of
Relapses/Complications
Dogs
After the first 1-2 weeks, if the PCV is stable, the prednisolone dosage
can be carefully reduced. Depending on the patient’s evidence of
stability or improvement (a stable PCV [>30% for 2 weeks],
reduction of RBC agglutination and the number of spherocytes,
decreasing bilirubin values), the prednisolone dosage can be
carefully reduced by approximately 25% every 3 weeks. If a second
immunosuppressant is administered in combination (ch. 169), the
prednisolone dosage may be reduced by 25%, and the dosage of the
second immunosuppressant may also be gradually reduced every 3-4
weeks. When there are moderate to severe side-effects of
prednisolone (e.g., a gastrointestinal [GI] ulcer is suspected) the
dosage has to be reduced approximately 50-75% while the dosage of
the second drug remains unchanged. In the majority of cases after an
expected duration of 6-8 months of treatment, prednisolone and the
additional immunosuppressant may be discontinued if no relapse
has occurred. After discontinuation of drugs, the patient should be
monitored (physical examination, complete blood count [CBC]) for
at least 4 weeks. Beyond this time, the owner should be aware of

clinical signs.49 When prednisolone is given at high dosages, the
authors prefer to also administer proton pump inhibitors (e.g.,
omeprazole 1 mg/kg PO q12h) and antacids (e.g., sucralfate 20-30
mg/kg PO q12h) because of the risk of ulcers and GI bleeding.
Urinalysis may be performed every 8-12 weeks because of an
increased risk of urinary tract infection. In severe cases (e.g.,
intravascular hemolysis, dependent on blood transfusion after 7 days
of treatment), autoagglutination, and/or poor response or severe
side-effects of prednisolone, one of the following cytostatic drugs
may be used additionally (chs. 144 and 169): cyclosporine (initially
5 mg/kg PO q12h), MMF (8-10 [-12] mg/kg PO q12h), azathioprine
(initially 2 mg/kg [50 mg/m2] PO q24h; after 2-3 weeks, reduced to
2 mg/kg q48h). Another alternative is leflunomide (2 mg/kg PO
q24h). Due to the myelosuppressive effect of cytostatic drugs,
neutrophil and platelet counts should be checked every 1-2 weeks.
Liposomal clodronate (leads to macrophage depletion, inhibition of
clearance of opsonized cells), complement inhibitor (human
recombinant C1-esterase inhibitor) and the use of plasmapheresis
may be promising, although there are currently not enough data
available.52-54 Human immunoglobulins (0.5-1 g/kg once IV) can be
administered in non-responders, but routine use is not
recommended.49 In refractory cases, splenectomy may be considered
but is considered controversial.49,55

Cats
Monitoring and the dosage reduction protocol are similar to those
described for dogs. In severe cases with a poor response to
prednisolone, non-regenerative IMHA, recurrences, a high risk of
severe glucocorticoid side-effects (e.g., overweight cats, diabetic cats,
cats with heart disease), or development of glucocorticoid sideeffects, chlorambucil (initially 0.2 mg/kg PO q24h, then 0.1 mg/kg
PO q24h), cyclosporine (initially 7 mg/kg PO q24h), MMF (initially
5-10 mg/kg PO q12h) or leflunomide (initially 2 mg/kg PO q24h)
may be administered additionally (ch. 224).

Management of Relapses (Dogs and Cats)

If there is a decrease of the PCV and an increase in the WBC count,
GI bleeding and infectious diseases must be carefully ruled out. GI
bleeding results in melena, occult blood in feces and an elevation of
blood urea nitrogen without an elevation in creatinine. The
cornerstone of therapy will again be prednisolone at an increased
dosage, but in combination with another immunosuppressive drug
(ch. 169). In the cat with relapse, dexamethasone 0.15-0.25 mg/kg
PO q24h is an alternative to prednisolone. In the case of a mild
decrease in PCV, the dosages should be increased carefully; in the
case of a severe decrease in PCV, the initial dosage should be given.
Recurrences can be accompanied by resistance to therapy. Therefore,
the dosage of the drugs should be tapered very carefully, or the
patient should be kept on a very low maintenance dose for life.

Prognosis
In dogs and cats with associative IMHA, the prognosis is favorable if
the underlying diseases can be successfully treated and
immunosuppressive medication can be discontinued. The prognosis
is poor in non-associative IMHA, with fatality rates of 24-52% in
dogs.7,9,10,14 In dogs, findings such as autoagglutination,
intravascular hemolysis, persistently low reticulocyte counts,
leukocytosis, left shift, thrombocytopenia, high serum bilirubin and
urea concentrations, elevated liver enzyme activities,
hypoalbuminemia, hyperlactatemia, and prolonged PT/aPTT are
negative prognostic markers with regard to short-term
survival.7,14,16,56 Due to complications such as thromboembolism
and DIC, most IMHA-associated mortality occurs within the first 1-2
weeks after diagnosis; thereafter, prognosis improves significantly
and a 6-month overall survival rate of 73% has been reported.7
Because of a high tendency to relapse (up to 33%), dogs may require
lifelong medication. Relapses are possible after several months or
years. In a long-term evaluation of 61 dogs, relapses occurred in
22.9% after 94-3972 days (median 517 days).18 Data on mortality
rates in cats with non-associative IMHA range from 23.5-38%, and
older age and high serum bilirubin concentrations are negative

prognostic factors.17,20 In cats, the recurrence rate was 31% (up to
40 weeks after diagnosis) in one study.20

HEMOLYTIC ANEMIA DUE TO
ALLOANTIBODIES
Pathogenesis
In contrast to autoimmune antibodies, allo(iso)antibodies are not
directed against the patient’s own but against foreign RBCs, e.g., in
incompatible blood transfusions. Since cats, unlike dogs, have
clinically relevant naturally occurring antibodies against the other
blood groups, neonatal isoerythrolysis (NI) occurs in cats. When
kittens with blood type A or AB (new designation C) receive colostral
anti-A antibodies from a type B queen during the first 16 hours of
life, NI may develop.57 In dogs, sensitization of breeding females by
DEA-1 incompatible transfusions should be avoided, as these
antibodies can be excreted in the colostrum and absorbed by puppies
during the first days of life.58

Clinical Presentation
The severity of clinical signs is dependent on the amount of colostral
antibodies ingested. Peracute death is possible during the first days
of life. In the acute course, kittens show weakness, weight loss and,
as a result of intravascular hemolysis, anemia, hemoglobinemia,
hemoglobinuria, hyperbilirubinemia and bilirubinuria. Some kittens
develop subclinical disease and tail tip and toe necrosis due to
ischemia.

Therapy and Prevention
Type A kittens born to type B queens should be separated from the
mother at least during the first 16 hours after birth and fed milk
replacer or, if available, by a blood type A foster cat. If the kittens are
already anemic, they should be transfused with type B packed RBCs
(free of anti-A antibodies) because they have already absorbed anti-A

antibodies with the colostrum.59 To prevent NI, blood typing of the
parents and mating of type B females with type B males are
recommended.

HEMOLYTIC ANEMIA DUE TO
INFECTIONS
Pathogenesis
Blood parasites and various other infectious agents (Table 174.1)
can directly damage RBCs or cause hemolytic anemia (associative
IMHA) immunologically (ch. 227).

Clinical Signs, Diagnosis, and Therapy
See disease-specific chapters: Bartonellosis (ch. 191), Ehrlichiosis,
Anaplasmosis, Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, and Neorickettsia
(ch. 193), Hemotropic Mycoplasmas (ch. 194), Systemic Protozoal
Diseases (ch. 197), Feline Immunodeficiency Virus Infection (ch.
198), Feline Leukemia Virus Infection (ch. 199), Coronavirus (ch.
200), and Heartworm Disease in Dogs and Cats (ch. 237).

HEREDITARY ERYTHROCYTE DEFECTS
Various hereditary RBC defects can cause severe RBC malfunction
and premature destruction, may be associated with systemic illness
(e.g., lethargy, fever, cardiovascular signs) or merely represent
hematological peculiarities (such as microcytosis in the Akita).
Hereditary RBC defects have been classified into 4 groups: 1)
hemoglobinopathies (not documented in dogs and cats), 2)
erythroenzymopathies, 3) membrane abnormalities, and 4)
production and maturation defects (Table 174.1).
Erythroenzymopathies and some membrane abnormalities
(increased osmotic fragility, spectrin deficiency, stomatocytosis,
spherocytosis) may result in hemolysis.

Erythroenzymopathies

Pyruvate Kinase (PK) Deficiency in Cats
This is a commonly-described blood disorder in cats. In a study
evaluating 502 blood samples from Somali and Abyssinian cats in
Germany (n=328) and other European countries (n=174) 7.4% of
cats were affected.60 The genetic defect was first described in the
Abyssinian and Somali breeds and since then also in European or
Domestic Shorthair cats, Bengals, Singapura, Maine Coon, and
Norwegian Forest cats.60,61 There are different PK isoenzymes in
RBCs: the M2 isoenzyme is present in RBC precursors, including
reticulocytes, while the R isoenzyme is found in mature RBCs; the
latter is absent in affected cats.62 Since PK catalyzes adenosine
triphosphate (ATP)-producing steps in glycolysis, PK deficiency
results in a shortened RBC lifespan due to energy deprivation.62 The
consequence of PK deficiency is chronic hemolysis, and the clinical
signs can vary. As early as a few months of age, (intermittent) signs
of anemia and inappetence, diarrhea, weight loss, and eating of cat
litter may be seen.60 Sudden death, e.g., during routine procedures
such as spaying/neutering or parturition, is possible. Hemolytic
crises (e.g., due to stress) with icterus and fever may occur, or the
hemolysis may be compensated and subclinical. In 11 of 25 affected
cats, the owner did not notice any signs of disease up to a median age
of 4.4 years (range, 0.8-7.8 years). Therefore, affected cats may be
used for breeding for many years.60 Splenomegaly with
extramedullary hematopoiesis is common. Hct may be normal to
severely decreased, and anemia is usually regenerative. In 25 affected
cats in one study, the Hct ranged from 13-44% (median 29%) with
reticulocyte counts of 5000-936,000/mcL (median 98,000/mcL).60
The osmotic fragility of the RBCs is normal or only slightly increased.
Other laboratory findings that are variably present include
lymphocytosis (54%), hyperbilirubinemia (53%), hyperglobulinemia
(53%), and mildly elevated liver enzyme activities (46%). The total
PK activity is reduced; for diagnostic purposes a DNA test is available
to detect homozygous-affected and heterozygous carrier cats.31
There is no specific therapy; therefore, breeding measures are
important. In severe anemia, blood transfusions can be lifesaving
(ch. 124). To prevent hemolytic crises, stressful situations (e.g.,

breeding, cat shows) should be avoided. Cats are often treated with
prednisolone because immune-mediated anemia is suspected. The
effect of prednisolone therapy may be related to its membranestabilizing effect and inhibition of the mononuclear phagocytic
system in the spleen. In severe cases, splenectomy may be
considered, which may lead to a temporary stabilization of the Hct.
Six of 25 cats in one study died at an age of 1.3-11.3 years (median
4.1) presumably due to PK deficiency.60

Pyruvate Kinase (PK) Deficiency in Dogs
The gene defect has been detected in the Basenji, Beagles, West
Highland White Terrier, Dachshund, and other breeds.31,63 Dogs
may develop clinical signs at a young age (pale mucous membranes,
exercise intolerance, tachycardia), but sometimes clinical signs are
not noticed by the owner.64 Usually the anemia is severe, with a
marked reticulocytosis. Progressive myelofibrosis (possibly due to
permanently elevated erythropoietin concentrations), and
osteosclerosis of the bone marrow (pathomechanism unknown)
develop at approximately 1 year of age. Furthermore, dogs may
develop hepatic failure (hemosiderosis secondary to hepatic iron
overload). PK activity is reduced in affected dogs, but may be normal
or even elevated because M2 isoenzyme reticulocyte activity (which
persists in dogs, contrary to cats) may also be measured. Diagnosis is
confirmed by a DNA test. Affected dogs usually die at the age of 1-8
years due to bone marrow and/or liver failure.62

Phosphofructokinase (PFK) Deficiency
Phosphofructokinase (PFK) deficiency has been described in the
English Springer Spaniel, Cocker Spaniel, Wachtelhund, Whippet,
and in mixed breeds.62,65 In affected dogs, PFK of the RBCs and
muscle cells is deficient. The PFK-deficient RBCs contain a low
intraerythrocytic 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) concentration
due to lower production, and therefore, they have a high Hb-oxygen
affinity. The low intraerythrocytic 2,3-DPG concentration results in
increased alkaline fragility. Typical features include chronic
hemolysis with hemolytic crises triggered by exertion, panting,

barking, and/or heat (hyperventilation-induced alkalosis), with
severe anemia, pigmenturia, and intermittent myopathy causing
muscle weakness and cramps. The Hct may be normal or severely
decreased, and the reticulocyte count is always severely increased. A
DNA test can be used to identify affected and carriers.62 Avoidance
of stress and supportive treatment in hemolytic crises (e.g., fluid
therapy, blood transfusion) are recommended.

Cytochrome b5 Reductase Deficiency
Normally, about 3% of heme iron is unable to bind and transport
oxygen because it has been oxidized from the ferrous (Fe2+) to the
ferric (Fe3+ = methemoglobin [Met-Hb]) state. The cytochrome b5
reductase (Met-Hb reductase) reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+, keeping the MetHb concentration in the blood <1%. A hereditary deficiency of this
enzyme occurs in dogs and cats and results in Met-Hb
accumulation.62 Hereditary cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency has
been recognized in Chihuahua, Borzoi, English Setter, Corgi,
Pomeranian, and Poodle mixed breed dogs and in Domestic
Shorthair cats.62 Often, affected animals have no clinical signs.
Mucous membranes appear cyanotic at a Met-Hb level of ≥10%.
Clinical signs occur at a Met-Hb level of ≥40%, and ataxia, lethargy,
dyspnea, stupor, and coma may occur when the level exceeds 60%.31
In hereditary deficiency, the Met-Hb content varied from 13-41% in
dogs and 44-52% in cats.62 When the Met-Hb concentration in blood
exceeds 10% of the total Hb, the blood remains brown when applied
to a filter paper, whereas normal venous blood turns red. Increased
amounts of Met-Hb are detectable spectrophotometrically. The Hct
is normal or slightly increased.62 A definitive diagnosis is based on
the measurement of RBCs Met-Hb reductase activity. Depending on
clinical signs, treatment can include antioxidants, fluid therapy and
administration of blood products. Hereditary cytochrome b5
reductase deficiency usually does not require treatment.62

Membrane Abnormalities

In dogs elliptocytosis, stomatocytosis (Alaskan Malamute,
Schnauzer), spectrin deficiency (Golden Retriever), potassium-rich
RBCs (Akita/Shiba Inu, Shar Pei, other East Asian breeds), familial
microcytosis (Akita/Shiba Inu), and familial macrocytosis (Poodle)
have been described (ch. 57).5,66,67 Examination of the RBC
proteome revealed an altered protein spectrum similar to human
hereditary spherocytosis in a Jack Russell Terrier with hemolysis,
spherocytosis and reticulocytosis.68

Increased Osmotic Fragility (OF) of Erythrocytes
Increased OF of erythrocytes has been described in Abyssinian and
Somali cats, European Shorthair cats, one Siamese cat and one
Ocicat.4,69 A RBC membrane defect is suggested.4 The age at which
clinical signs of anemia were first apparent ranged in 18 cats from 6
months to 5 years.4 In addition to intervals without clinical signs and
normal Hct values, severe hemolytic crises may occur. Most often,
the Hct is between 15% and 25%, but it can be as low as 5%. The
anemia is characterized by macrocytosis (52-85 fL) and mild to
moderate reticulocytosis. RBCs of these cats may lyse in vitro when
stored in a refrigerator for 1 day and are more fragile in hypotonic
(and often even in physiological) saline compared to those of healthy
cats. The mean erythrocyte OF has ranged from 0.66 to 0.78% (in
healthy cats: 0.48-0.58%). The OF assay is a rough index of
erythrocyte surface-to-volume ratio. For performing the OF test,
RBCs are placed in a hypotonic solution and water is drawn
osmotically in the RBCs, resulting in cell swelling. Macroscopic
agglutination of the RBCs is detectable in approximately 50% of the
cats.4 Hyperglobulinemia, lymphocytosis, mild hyperbilirubinemia
and high liver enzyme activities also are common findings.
Splenomegaly is common.4 In hemolytic crises, blood transfusions
can be lifesaving (ch. 124). Immunosuppressive prednisolone
therapy is often used initially because immune-mediated disease is
suspected or difficult to rule out. Splenectomy may be considered
and seems to lead to a temporary improvement in osmotic
resistance. Ten of 18 affected cats died or were euthanized during
hemolytic episodes in one study.4

HEMOLYTIC ANEMIAS CAUSED BY
CHEMICALS, DRUGS, DIETARY
INGREDIENTS OR ADDITIVES (HEINZ
BODY ANEMIA,
METHEMOGLOBINEMIA)
Pathogenesis
Toxins, drugs, and dietary ingredients or additives can directly
damage RBCs, e.g., by oxidative metabolites that directly alter lipid
solubility, membrane permeability, and Hb (Table 174.1) (ch. 138).
The consequences are: 1) oxidation of heme iron and thus,
methemoglobinemia, 2) oxidative denaturation of Hb and Heinz
body and/or eccentrocyte formation, 3) membrane damage with
reduced RBC deformability and ion transport disorders.

Heinz Body Anemia/Methemoglobinemia
In contrast to other species, the Hb of cats is more susceptible to
oxidation and denaturation because it contains 8-10 free reactive
sulfhydryl groups per Hb molecule (in other species there are only 24). Glutathione, a thiol protector, is unstable in feline RBCs and
reservoirs are rapidly depleted. In addition, dissociation of Hb
tetramers to dimers occurs 10 times faster in cats than in other
species. The changes in globin chains and oxidative membrane
damage result in binding and “cluster” formation of denatured,
precipitated Hb at the membrane. Met-Hb formation often occurs
concurrently with or precedes Heinz body development. Unlike dogs,
cats have relatively large openings in the sinusoidal walls of the
spleen (non-sinusoidal structure). The feline spleen therefore has an
impaired ability to remove Heinz body-containing RBCs from
circulation and Heinz bodies can be present in up to 5% of RBCs
even in healthy cats.2 RBCs containing Heinz bodies are less
deformable and are prematurely removed from circulation by
intravascular lysis or phagocytosis.70 Development of anemia
depends on the rate and quantity of Heinz body formation and the
extent of RBC membrane damage.

Eccentrocytes (hemighosts) are formed as a result of oxidative
damage to the RBC membrane and cytoskeleton. They represent the
dominant marker of oxidative stress of RBCs in dogs. Eccentrocytes
are characterized by shifting of Hb to one side of the cell, leaving a
clear eccentric zone, and they are formed by adhesion of opposing
faces of the RBC membranes.71 For different causes of oxidative
damage to RBCs, see Table 174.1.71-76

Clinical Signs
In patients with Heinz body anemia and/or methemoglobinemia,
clinical signs depend on the type and amount of exposure. Signs such
as ataxia, lethargy, cyanosis, dyspnea, stupor, and coma are not
expected until Met-Hb levels exceed approximately 60%.31 Oxidative
injury due to acetaminophen (paracetamol) intoxication in cats is
associated with lethargy, cyanosis, edema of the head, dyspnea, and
vomiting 2-4 hours after ingestion (ch. 138). Methemoglobinemia
can be expected after 2-4 hours, and hemolytic anemia after 2-3
days. Doses as low as 10 mg/kg may cause clinical signs in cats. In
dogs, acetaminophen intoxication (expected at a high dose of 200
mg/kg) causes clinical signs similar to those seen in cats.77 Zinc
intoxication may cause GI signs like vomiting and diarrhea due to
pancreatitis and to acute kidney injury and uremia.

Diagnosis of Heinz Body Anemia and
Methemoglobinemia
Brown discoloration of unpigmented mucous membranes/blood may
suggest chemical (toxin)-induced methemoglobinemia. In blood
smears stained with new methylene blue (or brilliant cresyl blue),
Heinz bodies can be detected. Heinz body percentage is estimated on
1000 RBCs. The presence of ghost cells indicates hemolysis. In
addition, eccentrocytes may be seen in the blood smear, especially in
dogs. The diagnosis of zinc intoxication can be strongly suspected
radiographically (coins) and confirmed by measuring zinc
concentrations in plasma (ch. 138).

Therapy of Heinz Body Anemia and/or
Methemoglobinemia
In addition to treatment of the triggering cause (e.g., endoscopic
extraction of coins), supportive treatment such as fluid therapy and,
if necessary, blood transfusion, is recommended (ch. 124).
Antioxidants such as N-acetylcysteine (initially 140 mg/kg IV, then
70 mg/kg IV q6h) or S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe, 20-40 mg/kg PO
q12h 1 h before feeding) are administered.72,78 The prognosis is
usually favorable after elimination of the causative factors and if the
patient responds to treatment during the acute stage.

HEMOLYSIS DUE TO “TRAUMATIC”
ERYTHROCYTE DAMAGE
Pathogenesis
Mechanical RBC damage and hemolysis usually occur as additional
factors exacerbating a preexisting anemia. Microangiopathic
hemolytic anemia results from capillary endothelial damage and
fibrin strand formation in vasculitis (ch. 181), DIC (ch. 171), in the
capillary area of tumors (e.g., hemangiosarcoma; ch. 325), and in
liver disease; these disorders fragment the RBCs and lead to
schistocytosis and intravascular and extravascular hemolysis.
Intravascular hemolysis also occurs in association with splenic
torsion (ch. 182), which is particularly prevalent in large dog breeds
such as Great Danes.79 RBCs can be damaged mechanically and by
toxins. A hemolytic-uremic syndrome characterized by acute kidney
injury, thrombocytopenia, thrombosis, and microangiopathic
hemolysis has been described in dogs.80 For other causes, see Table
174.1.79-81

Diagnosis
The diagnosis is made by identification of a triggering factor and
detection of schistocytes, which, however, also occur in numerous
other anemias (e.g., iron deficiency anemia, zinc intoxication).

Therapy
Treatment depends on the underlying disease.

HYPOPHOSPHATEMIA-INDUCED
HEMOLYSIS
Pathogenesis
Severe hypophosphatemia has been associated with acute treatment
of diabetes mellitus (ketoacidosis [ch. 290]), inadequate feeding
after prolonged fasting (refeeding syndrome), and oral
administration of phosphate binders.

Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis
Phosphate values <0.8 mmol/L (<2.5 mg/dL) may result in
hemolysis, myopathy, and cardiac and neurologic dysfunction.82
Hemoglobinemia and hyperbilirubinemia can lead to laboratory
errors.83 Hemolysis is thought to be due to a deficiency of ATP, DPG,
and reduced glutathione, which decreases RBC deformability,
increases OF, and makes RBCs susceptible to oxidative damage.

Therapy
In anorectic and vomiting patients, phosphate is administered
intravenously as a constant-rate infusion (0.01-0.03 mg/kg/h).
Potential complications include hypocalcemia, kidney injury, and
dystrophic soft-tissue calcification. Oral administration of
commercial phosphate products (if available) is preferred for mild
hypophosphatemia; prophylactic phosphate supplementation should
be considered during in-hospital management of complicated
diabetes mellitus.

ANEMIAS DUE TO BLOOD LOSS
PERACUTE AND ACUTE BLOOD LOSS ANEMIA

Pathogenesis
Rapid blood loss of >20-30% of the circulating blood volume (the
latter being 8-10% of body weight) results in cardiovascular signs.
Blood loss may result from trauma, vascular rupture in ulcers or
tumors, or spontaneous bleeding in coagulation disorders. In
peracute blood loss, clinical signs can vary. Minor bleeding may lead
to compensated hypovolemic shock, while severe bleeding causes
life-threatening shock (ch. 121). The Hct may remain normal
initially due to splenic contraction (in the dog) and until interstitial
fluid shifts or therapeutic volume substitution occur. Thus, the initial
oligemia does not progress to anemia until approximately 4-12 h
after the onset of blood loss. In cases of bleeding into the abdominal
and thoracic cavities, about half of the blood can be reabsorbed
within 24 h via autotransfusion.

Clinical Presentation
Clinical manifestations include signs of hypovolemia, and, after a few
hours, anemia can be detected. If bleeding occurs internally, mild
icterus may be seen after about 1-2 days. If bleeding occurs in the
thorax or abdomen, dyspnea and an abdominal fluid wave may
occur, respectively.

Laboratory Findings
A decrease in Hct and plasma proteins is detectable approximately 412 h after the onset of bleeding. In the first 3 days after the initial
hemorrhage, the anemia is normocytic-normochromic and nonregenerative. Thereafter, it becomes macrocytic, hypochromic, and
regenerative. Although platelets are being consumed, this does not
result in clinically significant thrombocytopenia; during recovery,
reactive thrombocytosis occurs. When visceral bleeding (or in
tumors) occurs, there may be an increase in plasma and urinary
bilirubin. Other laboratory findings depend on the cause of bleeding
(e.g., prolonged clotting times in anticoagulant rodenticide
poisoning).

Diagnosis

The diagnosis of acute external blood loss is usually straightforward
from the history and physical examination. The diagnosis of bleeding
into tissues, tumors, or body cavities may be more challenging.
Radiographic and ultrasound examinations of the thorax and
abdomen are helpful (ch. 73). Repeated PCV and plasma protein
measurements are necessary for assessment of the blood loss. If the
cause of bleeding is not obvious, coagulation testing (primary and
secondary hemostasis; ch. 170) should be performed before the
administration of blood products.

Therapy
In addition to preventing further blood loss, infusion therapy should
be performed in case of (per-) acute blood loss; one-quarter of the
blood volume (full blood volume being: dog, 80-90 mL/kg; cat, 5060 mL/kg) is administered as a large bolus over 15-30 minutes (ch.
124). After reassessment the bolus can be repeated. Plasma
substitutes may be helpful if there is failure to respond to infusion
therapy (ch. 120). Alternatively, low-volume resuscitation can be
considered, using the smallest volume of fluid to restore
intravascular volume, minimizing fluid extravasation and the
probability of disrupting blood clots.84 Blood transfusion is indicated
if blood loss is severe (>30 mL/kg) or if the Hct drops rapidly to <
approximately 20-25% (depending on the patient’s general condition
or if anesthesia/surgery is deemed necessary, respectively). In
addition, the underlying cause must be treated.

ANEMIA DUE TO CHRONIC BLOOD
LOSS (IRON DEFICIENCY ANEMIA)
Pathogenesis
Chronic external blood loss initially leads to increased erythropoiesis
and, after depletion of iron stores, to iron deficiency because
approximately 1 mg of iron is lost per 2 mL of blood and GI iron
absorption is limited. Absorption of iron occurs only as Fe2+ in the
duodenum, and iron is transported in the blood bound to transferrin,
which is normally 20-60% saturated with iron. Intestinal iron

absorption and the release of iron into plasma are regulated by the
acute-phase protein hepcidin. Hepcidin production in the liver is
inhibited by hypoxia/anemia and iron deficiency. Hepcidin
concentration is elevated by inflammatory cytokines leading to
decreased absorption of iron in the intestine, iron sequestration
within macrophages, and low circulating iron concentrations,
resulting in a functional iron deficiency (ch. 172).85 Total body iron
amounts to 20-40 mg/kg body weight, which is distributed to: Hb,
65%; myoglobin/enzymes, 3%; storage pool in liver, spleen, bone
marrow (soluble ferritin, insoluble hemosiderin), 30%; and “labile
pool,” 2%.86 Physiologic iron losses in small animals amount to <1
mg/day. In nucleated RBCs, DNA synthesis and mitosis cease as
soon as the intracellular Hb concentration rises above a critical
concentration. Inhibition of Hb synthesis in iron deficiency leads to
delayed nuclear degeneration and additional dividing of RBC
precursors (formation of microcytic, hypochromic RBCs).
Progressive iron loss initially leads to increased bone marrow
activity, and only results in decreased activity in far advanced
cases.86

Causes of Iron Deficiency Anemia
The major causes for chronic blood loss include GI bleeding (ulcers,
e.g., after administration of glucocorticoids and nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs [NSAIDs], frequently bleeding tumors, rarely
severe endoparasite infestation [hookworms, whipworms], chronic
inflammatory bowel disease), massive flea or lice infestation in
young animals, uterine bleeding, and bleeding tumors outside the GI
tract.87 Thrombocytopenia and thrombopathies or coagulopathies
also occasionally can lead to chronic blood loss. Prostatic, urinary
tract, or renal bleeding rarely are the sole cause of chronic blood-loss
anemia. Frequent blood collections for diagnostic purposes
especially in small breeds and in cats or blood donations for
transfusions may lead to iron deficiency. In one study, dogs with
advanced-stage chronic kidney disease had occult GI bleeding
leading to iron deficiency.88 Rare causes include nutritional

abnormalities in young animals (limited ability to store iron) or
malabsorption (e.g., in chronic inflammatory bowel disease).

Clinical Presentation
Despite severe anemia, clinical signs are often mild if the body has
time to adapt. Clinical signs may occur when the Hct falls below a
critical range of about 12-15% or if there are stressful situations.
Severe iron deficiency, in addition to anemia, can lead to weakness,
behavioral changes, skin and claw changes, and occasionally pica
(eating unusual substances such as soil or feces). Clinical signs such
as melena and/or hematochezia from GI ulceration after NSAID
administration, hematuria, endo- or ectoparasites, and the history
provide valuable information about the cause of bleeding. Occult
blood loss is usually localized to the GI tract.

Laboratory Findings
Anemia is often severe. Initially, it is markedly regenerative, but in
advanced cases the anemia is poorly or non-regenerative. In one
study, anemia was severe (Hct <20%) in 9/15 dogs, moderate (Hct =
20-29%) in 4 dogs and mild (Hct >30%) in 2 dogs and in all except
for one dog regenerative. In 10 of 15 dogs, reticulocyte counts were
>100,000/mcL.87 Initially, anisocytosis is present with a still-normal
mean corpuscular volume (MCV) but increased RBC distribution
width (RDW); i.e., the decrease in MCV precedes the decrease in
mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration. In advanced cases,
iron-deficiency anemias are microcytic-hypochromic (other causes of
a low MCV: portosystemic shunt, anemia of inflammatory disease,
dyserythropoiesis, physiological in certain breeds, e.g., Akita/Shiba
Inu, Chow Chow).85 Measurement of reticulocyte indices (reduced
reticulocyte hemoglobin content [CHretic], Hb content of
reticulocytes, and average size of reticulocytes [MCVretic]) may be
helpful in diagnosing early-phase iron deficiency anemia.89 Since
reticulocytes circulate for a short time compared to mature RBCs, Hb
content is an early parameter of iron deficiency. However, these
indices may also be altered in inflammation and portosystemic
shunting.90 Blood smear findings in 8 dogs with iron deficiency

anemia included hypochromasia (8), knizocytes (= triconcave RBCs,
8), elliptocytes (8), polychromasia (6), schistocytes (6), anisocytosis
(5), target cells (3), and keratocytes (3) (ch. 57, Figure 57.2).87
Fragmented RBCs (schistocytes) occur because iron-deficient RBCs
are stiffer and less deformable, presumably because of oxidative
membrane damage. Reactive thrombocytosis is present in
approximately 50% of the canine patients.87 Plasma protein
concentration is decreased or in the lower reference range. Serum
iron concentration is decreased, and total iron binding capacity
(measured indirectly as transferrin) is usually in the reference range
but may be increased. Iron saturation (serum iron : total iron
binding capacity) is decreased (<20%, normal: 20-60%).85 Serum
ferritin is decreased or in the lower reference range, but it can also be
increased in inflammation as an acute phase protein. Bone marrow
examination of an affected dog reveals the absence of iron storage
and erythroid bone marrow hyperplasia with late maturation block.
Cats store no hemosiderin in the macrophages of the bone marrow.
Therefore, lack of staining on cytologic and histologic bone marrow
samples with Prussian blue is not diagnostic of iron deficiency in this
species.85 Occult blood in feces can be detected, for example, with
the Hemoccult test (guaiac-based test). False positive (after feeding
meat or due to peroxidase or catalase activity in vegetables) and false
negative results may occur.91 Fecal parasitologic examination (ch.
80), e.g., for hookworms or whipworms, should be performed.

Diagnosis
The diagnosis is based on identification of a source of bleeding,
laboratory test results, and exclusion of other causes of anemia.
Occasionally, detection of GI bleeding can be difficult and may
require further procedures such as ultrasonography, endoscopy, and
possibly exploratory laparotomy.

Therapy
Treatment addresses the underlying cause (e.g., with anthelmintics,
flea control, discontinuation of drugs such as NSAIDs, proton pump
inhibitors for ulcers, surgery for tumors). In case of a very low Hct

(<12-15%), blood transfusion should be performed, which is also the
best source of iron (ch. 124). Iron replacement is administered as
Fe2+ sulfate (5 mg/kg elemental iron PO distributed in 2 doses [ch.
172]), and is continued for weeks after the normalization of
hematological parameters.92 In cases of malabsorption or severe GI
side effects with this treatment, iron dextran 10 mg/kg IM,
maximum 100 mg/dog, may be given initially as a single dose but the
injection can be very painful and there is a risk of anaphylaxis.

Prognosis
The response to treatment is expected to be good if the cause can be
eliminated. In a study of 15 dogs with iron deficiency anemia, 4 dogs
had a survival time >1 year, 5 dogs survived >1-3 months, and 6 dogs
were euthanized after the diagnosis of an unresectable tumor.87
Replenishment of iron stores requires several weeks.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Immune-Mediated Hemolytic Anemia (IMHA)
Immune-mediated anemia is a blood disorder that involves selfdirected damage of an individual’s own red blood cells. This is a
condition that affects dogs more than cats, and the fundamental
disorder is incorrect interpretation by the immune system of the
normal red blood cells as foreign. The resulting rupture of red blood
cells, hemolysis, leads to anemia that can be life-threatening, and
possibly blood clots that also can be severe.
The symptoms caused by IMHA are generally vague and may be
mild or intense: lethargy, sluggishness, a decrease in appetite, and
failure to thrive are the most common. The ruptured red blood cells
may lead to a pigment circulating in the blood stream that is then
found in urine, producing a dark, discolored urine. The gums, moist
edges of the eyes (conjunctivae), and unpigmented areas of skin may
appear unusually pale, and possibly yellow (icteric, jaundiced). Left
untreated, IMHA can produce such a profound anemia, or such
severe blood clot formation, that vital functions are threatened and a
dog can die of this disease.
Assessing whether a dog has IMHA or not requires blood tests.
Anemia can be detected on routine testing, and since there are many
possible causes of anemia in dogs, the diagnosis of IMHA is usually
one of exclusion. That is, the diagnosis of IMHA is made once other
possibilities have been ruled out by process of elimination.
Therefore, diagnostic imaging like x-rays and abdominal ultrasound
are commonly used, and advanced blood tests may be necessary as
well. These may even identify an inciting trigger that is causing the
IMHA as a secondary phenomenon, such as certain cancers.

However, most cases of IMHA are idiopathic, meaning they occur
spontaneously and without an identifiable cause.
When IMHA is confirmed in a dog, the treatment mainly requires
reducing the overexuberant immune system’s attack on the dog’s
own red blood cells. This requires medications that are usually given
orally, and often need to be given for many, many months to reach a
stable state. When this is successful, the medications can be tapered
and ultimately stopped.
Dogs that have severe, sudden IMHA often require hospitalization
and intensive care. Severe anemia may require one or more blood
transfusions. Administration of blood thinners to reduce the risk of
blood clot formation can be very important. Immunemodulating/immunosuppressive drugs may need to be given by
injection in patients who are too ill to receive medications orally.
Often, a dog with IMHA spends at least the first 2 or 3 days in the
hospital to receive intensive care and to undergo tests that attempt to
pinpoint whether there is an underlying cause of the IMHA and to
define whether permanent damage has occurred as a result of IMHA.
IMHA is a disease that can recur. This means that follow-ups and
adjusting medications after discharge from intensive care is
important, and is tailored to each dog. It is common for rechecks to
be more frequent initially and for decisions on treatment to be
modified based on the results of blood test rechecks at those visits.
IMHA is a disease that can respond very well to treatment in some
dogs, and very little or not at all in others. Therefore, it is possible
that some dogs who have recurrent episodes of hemolysis, meaning
flareups of IMHA despite medications, may reach a point where
treatment is no longer considered reasonable to pursue and
euthanasia is considered. While this can happen at any point in the
illness, the initial period of hospitalization, and the first several
weeks that follow discharge, are the times of greatest vulnerability, as
would be the time around any relapses or occurrences. IMHA is not
known to be a painful disorder, so ongoing treatment and
monitoring are humane and can lead to a normal quality of life in
dogs that respond optimally.
Christiane Weingart (Berlin, Germany) and Barbara
Kohn (Berlin, Germany)

PRIMARY HEMOSTASIS
OVERVIEW
Platelets play a critical role in the initiation, regulation, and localization of
hemostasis. The term primary hemostasis refers to the interactions
among platelets, von Willebrand factor (VWF), and the vessel wall that
culminate in the formation of a platelet plug. These reactions begin with
platelets contacting a damaged vessel wall, VWF-mediated adhesion, and
proceed through platelet activation, degranulation, aggregation and
conclude with development of platelet-dependent procoagulant activity
and clot retraction.

PLATELET PHYSIOLOGY
Megakaryocytic precursor cells in the bone marrow are programmed,
through the action of transcription factors and thrombopoietin, to form
platelet-specific organelles and to express platelet cell surface proteins. In
the final stages of megakaryocyte maturation, large pseudopodia develop
and stretch to form thin proplatelet processes. The processes elongate as
platelet organelles move individually over microtubules to the end of the
proplatelet, where nascent platelets accumulate. The growing proplatelets
branch and form constrictions along their length, giving them a beaded
appearance. The entire megakaryocyte is converted into a mass of
proplatelets that break away from the megakaryocyte body and fragment
into individual platelets. The platelets are released from the marrow and
circulate in the vascular compartment as quiescent, non-adhesive, smooth
disks that act as sentinel cells scanning for sites of vessel damage.
Approximately 100 billion platelets are released each day to maintain a
peripheral platelet count of 200 million to 500 million cells per milliliter
of blood. Platelets have a lifespan of 6 to 10 days in circulation.
Injury to a vessel wall triggers platelet activation within nanoseconds.
Platelets rapidly transform into adhesive, spiny spheres capable of
recognizing and binding to exposed subendothelial matrix components.
Binding initiates cell-signaling pathways, which then mediate granule
secretion. Granule contents include adenine nucleotides, calcium,
serotonin, and adhesive proteins such as fibrinogen, VWF, fibronectin,
and P-selectin.1 Secreted compounds accumulate locally, interact with
their respective cell surface receptors, and recruit additional platelets to

the site of injury. Large-order platelet aggregates then bridge the zone of
vascular damage to form a hemostatic plug. Thrombin cleavage of
fibrinogen strengthens the platelet plug as a fibrin-platelet meshwork
develops.
A subset of collagen and thrombin-activated platelets externalizes
phosphatidylserine (PS) and releases PS-rich microparticles, which act as
scaffolding for assembly of tenase and prothrombinase complexes.
Expression of platelet procoagulant activity (PCA) greatly amplifies local
thrombin and fibrin generation. Contraction of platelet cytoskeletal
proteins linked to platelet integrin receptors results in consolidation and
subsequent retraction of the growing clot.
Platelet activation requires simultaneous engagement of the platelet
membrane surface receptors (Figure 175.1). Species differences in
response to platelet stimuli may reflect differences in cell signaling
pathways, receptor density and/or subclasses for specific ligands.
Endothelial cell-derived endoperoxides prostacyclin (prostaglandin I2
[PGI2]), prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), and prostaglandin D2 (PGD2) serve as
antagonist ligands that react with their respective platelet receptors to
dampen platelet reactivity.2
Platelet integrins and nonintegrin glycoprotein receptors play a critical
role in adhesion (platelet–subendothelial matrix interactions) and
aggregation (platelet-platelet association). The alpha-IIb-beta-3 complex
(GPIIb/IIIa) is the most abundant platelet integrin and it functions as the
activation-dependent receptor for fibrinogen, fibronectin, and VWF.
Binding of fibrinogen to this receptor is essential for aggregation and clot
retraction.3 Platelet adhesion to collagen and collagen-induced signaling
are supported by collagen’s interaction with the integrin receptor alpha-2beta-1 (GPIaIIa) and interaction of collagen with platelet GPVI.
Surface receptors, coupled to G proteins, span platelet membranes and
transmit signals induced by agonist binding. In platelets, Gq serves as the
link for most agonists and is coupled to phospholipase C, which in turn
generates diacylglycerol and inositol triphosphate, leading to calcium
release from the endoplasmic reticulum, protein kinase C and myosin
light chain kinase activation, and phosphorylation of platelet-signaling
proteins. During activation, phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid
from membrane phospholipids. Cyclooxygenase and thromboxane
synthetase convert arachidonic acid to the potent agonist thromboxane A2
(Figure 175.1).

PLATELET–VON WILLEBRAND FACTOR
INTERACTION
Subendothelial collagen fibrils and bound VWF are exposed after vascular
endothelial injury. The affinity and strength of the VWF-collagen bond is
proportional to VWF multimer size. Collagen-bound VWF displays a
conformational change that allows it to interact with the platelet
GPIb/V/IX complex. As platelet GPIb contacts and engages with VWF,
platelets slowly roll and become activated by interaction with collagen
fibrils. VWF then binds to GPIIb/IIIa receptors exposed on the surface of
activated platelets. Adhesion and aggregation at high shear rates depend
on this VWF binding to activate platelet GPIIb/IIIa.

FIGURE 175.1 Major signaling mechanisms involved

CLINICAL PRESENTATION OF PRIMARY
HEMOSTATIC DISORDERS
Surface bleeding is a hallmark feature of primary hemostatic disorders.
Petechiae, ecchymoses (ch. 29) and epistaxis (ch. 36) are most
commonly observed with severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count
<30,000/mcL) but may also be noted with a thrombopathia (ch. 59) or
vasculopathy (ch. 123). Von Willebrand disease (VWD) rarely causes
petechiae, although ecchymoses may be observed in some dogs with VWD
following trauma or surgical procedures. Mucosal surface bleeding (e.g.,
epistaxis, melena, hematuria) may be severe and can lead to blood loss
anemia requiring transfusion therapy (ch. 124). Life-threatening
bleeding into the central nervous system or lungs may occur.4,5 Although
cavity bleeding is more commonly associated with disorders of secondary
hemostasis (i.e., coagulopathy; ch. 171), hematomas, hemothorax,
hemoperitoneum, and hemarthrosis have been reported in dogs with
primary hemostatic disorders.4,6-8 Excessive bleeding following surgery
or trauma might be the first indication of a hereditary bleeding disorder,
including primary hemostatic defects, coagulopathy (e.g., hemophilia), or
excessive fibrinolysis. Repeated episodes of surface bleeding or similar
bleeding in related individuals should prompt evaluation for a hereditary
primary hemostatic disorder.

IMMUNE THROMBOCYTOPENIA
DEFINITIONS/PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Primary Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP)

ITP is a complex disorder characterized by both platelet destruction and
impaired megakaryocyte and platelet production that result from a
combination of humoral and cell-mediated attacks on platelets
peripherally and megakaryocytes in the bone marrow.9 Primary ITP is an
autoimmune disease directed against platelets. Antibodies directed
against epitopes on platelet GPIIb/IIIa, the fibrinogen receptor, have
been identified in dogs with primary ITP.10 In addition, a novel canine
model of primary ITP has been developed using a murine monoclonal
antibody, 2F9, against canine GPIIb that causes profound, dosedependent, thrombocytopenia.11 An excellent review of the
immunopathogenesis of ITP is available.9 A pilot study documented a
reduction in regulatory T (Treg) cells, which play an important role in
self-tolerance and regulation of immune responses, in dogs with primary
ITP, suggesting that loss of Tregs might be causally associated with the
onset of ITP in dogs.12

Secondary Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP)
Secondary ITP develops as a result of an antigenic stimulus, typically
from a drug, infectious disease, or neoplasia, leading to antibody
production. A retrospective, case-control study of 48 dogs with
presumptive primary ITP failed to find an association between recent
vaccination (within 42 days) and onset of ITP.13 Any drug has the
potential to cause secondary ITP, but antibiotics, including sulfonamides
and cephalosporins, are most common.14-16 When a medication is
administered for the first time, approximately 5 to 7 days of exposure is
typically required to produce sensitization and onset of
thrombocytopenia, though subsequent re-exposure to the same drug
could result in a rapid thrombocytopenia relapse due to the indefinite
persistence of antibodies.17 Infectious agents that have been associated
with development of antiplatelet antibodies in dogs include: Anaplasma
spp. (ch. 193),6,18,19 Babesia spp. (ch. 197),4,6 Ehrlichia spp. (ch.
197),4,6,18 Emmonsia spp.,18 Leptospira spp. (ch. 192),4,6 and
Leishmania infantum (ch. 197).6,20 This suggests that the
thrombocytopenia noted with these conditions might be due in part to
secondary ITP. Neoplasia can be associated with thrombocytopenia
through several mechanisms (e.g., increased platelet consumption
secondary to a bleeding tumor or disseminated intravascular coagulation

[DIC], splenic sequestration, decreased platelet production due to
myelophthisis), in addition to secondary ITP. Neoplastic disorders in
which antiplatelet antibodies have been documented include lymphoma
(ch. 322),4,6,18 hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325),4 mast cell tumor (ch.
327),18 disseminated carcinoma,18 histiocytic sarcoma (ch. 328),6 and
concurrent apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma and acute
megakaryocytic leukemia.18 Inflammatory diseases, including chronic
hepatitis (ch. 270), pancreatitis (ch. 277), and systemic inflammatory
response syndrome (SIRS, ch. 128), have also been associated with
antiplatelet antibodies in thrombocytopenic dogs.6 Severe
thrombocytopenia has been reported in 2 dogs following massive bee
envenomation, but it is unclear whether the venom triggered a type II
hypersensitivity reaction (i.e., secondary ITP) or its main components,
melittin and phospholipase A2, had direct toxic effects resulting in platelet
apoptosis.21,22

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
Thrombocytopenia is a common laboratory abnormality noted in dogs
and cats and it may be spurious due to traumatic venipuncture. If there is
no evidence of bleeding, one should repeat a platelet count on a fresh
blood sample and evaluate the blood smear for evidence of platelet
clumps (ch. 59). In a retrospective study of 871 dogs with
thrombocytopenia (defined as platelet count <150,000/mcL), primary
ITP accounted for only 5.6% of the cases, while thrombocytopenia was
attributed to neoplasia and infectious/inflammatory disease in 28 and
35% of the dogs, respectively.7 However, ITP is considered the most
common cause of severe thrombocytopenia in dogs.
The diagnosis of primary ITP is always presumptive and is based on
exclusion of known causes of thrombocytopenia and underlying diseases.
This necessitates a complete medical history (ch. 2), physical
examination (ch. 3), and diagnostic evaluation that may include imaging
and infectious disease screening (ch. 59). The physical examination of
dogs with primary ITP frequently reveals evidence of surface bleeding
(petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis; chs. 29, 36) and, potentially, pallor
(ch. 25), splenomegaly (ch. 182), and fever (ch. 16).4 The severity of
bleeding can vary greatly amongst dogs with ITP, potentially due to
variable thrombocytopenia-induced endothelial changes.23 In a canine

ITP model, a significant decrease in the number of pinocytotic vesicles,
which can be used for repair of damaged endothelial cells, was observed
in thrombocytopenic endothelium.23 Severe thrombocytopenia
(≤30,000/mcL) is typical4,6,7,13,24 and might be the only laboratory
abnormality noted. In a prospective study of 34 dogs with primary ITP,
the median platelet count was 9500/mcL (range 0-40,000/mcL).5
Platelet count does not consistently predict bleeding risk or mortality.5
Therefore, a bleeding assessment tool, DOGiBAT, was developed to
standardize quantification of bleeding in dogs with ITP, with a total score
based on severity of bleeding (0 – none; 1 – mild; 2 – severe) at 9
anatomic sites.5 DOGiBAT score and platelet count were inversely
correlated, and DOGiBAT score, but not platelet count, directly correlated
with transfusion requirements and hospitalization duration.5 In clinical
practice, the diagnosis of primary ITP is typically based on the finding of
severe thrombocytopenia, exclusion of underlying disease, and a response
to immunosuppressive therapy (see below).
Documentation of antiplatelet antibodies further supports a diagnosis
of ITP. A flow cytometric assay to detect platelet-bound antibody (also
referred to as platelet-associated immunoglobulin [PAIg]) is a variably
sensitive (29.4-100% for direct PAIgG)18,25 and nonspecific tool for the
diagnosis of primary ITP.4,6,7,18,25 Other platelet parameters, including
mean platelet volume (MPV), mean platelet component (MPC),
plateletcrit, and reticulated platelets, have been evaluated in dogs with
primary ITP but are unlikely to aid in making a diagnosis.6,24,25

TREATMENT AND OUTCOME
Immunosuppression
Removal of the offending drug or treatment of the underlying disease is
essential for resolution of thrombocytopenia in dogs with secondary ITP.
Concurrent immunosuppressive therapy may be necessary in some dogs,
though it is generally recommended to treat any underlying infectious
disease first and reserve immunosuppression for those dogs not
responding to antimicrobial therapy. Glucocorticoids are the mainstay of
treatment for primary ITP (chs. 144, 169, and 227). Vincristine and
human intravenous immunoglobulin (hIVIG) have been documented to
shorten the duration of severe thrombocytopenia in dogs with primary

ITP compared to prednisone alone.26,27 A subsequent clinical trial
comparing the effect of single dose hIVIG (0.5 g/kg) with vincristine
(0.02 mg/kg) on platelet recovery time in dogs with primary ITP receiving
concurrent corticosteroid therapy determined that there was no
difference between the treatment groups.28 It was concluded that
vincristine should be the first-line adjunctive treatment for the acute
management of canine primary ITP because of its lower cost and ease of
administration as compared with hIVIG.28 Although vincristine, at a
single dose of 0.02 mg/kg IV, is generally well tolerated by dogs with
primary ITP, there are potential complications, including perivascular
sloughing if extravasation occurs. Furthermore, in a retrospective study of
127 dogs that received vincristine for presumptive ITP, neutropenia was
observed in 19 dogs, 14 of which received cyclosporine concurrently,
between 2 to 14 days (median, 5 days) after vincristine administration.29
Cyclosporine administration was associated with development of
neutropenia (odds ratio 12.97) in dogs receiving vincristine, possibly due
to effects of cyclosporine on vincristine metabolism.29 Since the majority
of dogs with primary ITP respond to glucocorticoids alone within 7
days,26,27 adjunctive treatment with a second immunosuppressive agent
may not always be necessary.
The duration of treatment for dogs with primary ITP varies, but many
dogs are managed with tapering dosages of immunosuppressive drugs
over 4 to 6 months while monitoring for relapse.30 Serial monitoring of
antiplatelet antibodies in dogs with primary ITP demonstrated that
persistence of antibodies was not associated with response to treatment,
but recurrence of antibodies was associated with relapse of disease.18

Immunomodulation
Beyond administration of vincristine and hIVIG for management of acute
and severe thrombocytopenia, there are no prospective, controlled studies
documenting efficacy of adjunctive immunomodulatory agents in
treatment of dogs with primary ITP. Retrospective studies and case series
of canine primary ITP report the use of azathioprine,4,13,18,29,30
cyclosporine,4,18,29-31 mycophenolate mofetil,18,29-31 and
leflunomide18,29 in combination with corticosteroids (with or without
vincristine) (ch. 169). It is not possible to make conclusions regarding
their efficacy, however. There is a case report describing treatment with

mycophenolate mofetil (median dosage 8.5 mg/kg PO q12h) as a single
agent in 5 dogs with presumptive primary ITP in which corticosteroids
were considered contraindicated due to chronic nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug administration.32 All 5 dogs achieved a complete
remission and no evidence of relapse during a median follow-up time of
16 months (range 5 to 32 months).32

Transfusion Therapy
In addition to immunosuppressive therapy, blood transfusions (ch. 124)
might be required in dogs with ITP and severe mucosal surface bleeding.
In such cases, packed red blood cell (PRBC) transfusions are indicated to
provide additional oxygen-carrying support. Platelet transfusions are
uncommonly administered to dogs with ITP due to the belief that
transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed following administration.
However, in dogs with ITP experiencing uncontrolled or life-threatening
bleeding (e.g., suspected bleeding into the brain or lungs), platelet
transfusions may provide short-term hemostasis despite a negligible
increase in platelet count post-transfusion. In clinical practice, fresh
whole blood is the most readily available platelet source. Lyophilized
(StablePlate Rx, BodeVet) and cryopreserved canine platelets have been
administered to thrombocytopenic dogs, the majority of which were
diagnosed with ITP.33 While the efficacy of the platelet transfusions was
not evaluated, the administration of the commercially available platelet
products was associated with low adverse reaction rates.33

Prognosis
Dogs with primary ITP have a good prognosis with appropriate treatment
and supportive care. In one retrospective study of 67 dogs, 60 dogs
(89.6%) survived to hospital discharge, and 58 dogs (86.6%) achieved
remission, defined as platelet count >150,000/mcL.30 Of 45 dogs that
met the inclusion requirements for evaluation of relapse rate, 14 dogs
(31%) relapsed between 15 to 1239 days (median 79 days) from the time of
diagnosis, with 11 dogs relapsing within 1 year from presentation.30 Oneyear mortality rate from all causes was 19.4% and that from presumed
primary ITP was 11.9%.30 In a retrospective study comparing short-term
outcome in dogs with primary ITP and amegakaryocytic
thrombocytopenia having adequate and less than adequate numbers of
megakaryocytes, respectively, on bone marrow histopathologic or

cytologic evaluation, 29 of 34 dogs (85%) with ITP and 1 of 7 dogs (14%)
with amegakaryocyte thrombocytopenia survived to hospital discharge,
suggesting that the latter group has a poor prognosis.34

CONCURRENT ITP AND IMHA IN DOGS
Dogs with ITP infrequently have sequential or concurrent immunemediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA), a condition referred to as Evans’
syndrome in humans (ch. 174). Two retrospective studies have reported
on the outcome of dogs with concurrent IMHA and severe
thrombocytopenia, with differing conclusions. Twenty one dogs with
concurrent IMHA and severe thrombocytopenia (defined as
<50,000/mcL) were identified and 16 (76%) died or were euthanized
within 30 days of hospital admission, leading to a conclusion that
concurrent IMHA and severe thrombocytopenia is associated with a poor
outcome.35 In contrast, 12 dogs with concurrent IMHA and severe
thrombocytopenia (defined as platelet count ≤15,000/mcL) had a
mortality rate of 25%, similar to that reported for dogs with ITP or IMHA
alone, suggesting that dogs with concurrent IMHA and ITP do not have a
worse prognosis.36 A potential explanation for differences in these 2
studies is the greater likelihood of excluding dogs with DIC, known to
have a poor prognosis, with the more stringent definition of severe
thrombocytopenia in the latter study.36

FELINE IMMUNE THROMBOCYTOPENIA
Primary ITP is diagnosed rarely in cats. In a retrospective study of 194
thrombocytopenic cats, 6 cats (3%) were diagnosed with presumptive
primary ITP and had a mean platelet count of 19,000/mcL (range 540,000/mcL).37 In a study evaluating PAIg by flow cytometry in 49
thrombocytopenic cats, 19 cats were positive for antiplatelet antibodies,
but only 2 cats were diagnosed with presumptive primary ITP.38 The
other 17 cats were diagnosed with secondary ITP, with underlying
conditions including viral infections (feline leukemia virus, feline
immunodeficiency virus, and feline infectious peritonitis), inflammatory
disease (fat necrosis), and neoplasia (lymphoma).38 Two case series
described primary ITP in 5 and 4 cats during 8- and 5-year periods,

respectively.39,40 Surface bleeding in cats with primary ITP is similar to
that in dogs, including petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, gingival
bleeding, and hematuria.39,40
Based on the reported 13 cats with primary ITP in the 2 case series, the
mortality rate was 15% and 11 cats survived to hospital discharge.39,40
While glucocorticoids are the mainstay of treatment of primary ITP in
dogs, oral prednisolone was deemed to be effective in only 5 of 9 cats in
the 2 case series.39,40 Other immunosuppressive agents administered to
these cats included dexamethasone, cyclosporine, and chlorambucil,
though there are insufficient cases to comment on efficacy.39,40 In the
series with 4 cats, each had a chronic course with frequent relapses noted
and long-term immunosuppressive therapy was required for 3 cats that
survived to hospital discharge.40

VON WILLEBRAND DISEASE
HEREDITARY CANINE VON WILLEBRAND
DISEASE
Definition and Classification
VWD is a platelet adhesion disorder resulting from quantitative (types 1
and 3 VWD) or qualitative (type 2 VWD) deficiencies of plasma VWF.
Canine VWD is classified according to the concentration and multimeric
structure of plasma VWF, as well as clinical severity. Type 1 VWD is
characterized by a low plasma VWF concentration, a full array of VWF
multimers, and mild to moderate bleeding tendencies. In type 2 VWD,
there is a variable reduction in plasma VWF concentration but an absence
of the high molecular weight VWF multimers, causing moderate to severe
bleeding tendencies. Type 3 VWD is characterized by a complete absence
of plasma VWF, resulting in a severe bleeding tendency.

Diagnostic Evaluation
Screening Tests
Mucosal surface bleeding or excessive bleeding following surgery or
trauma in a dog with a normal platelet count, prothrombin time (PT), and
activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) should prompt evaluation
for VWD. A screening test that can be performed in clinical practice is a

buccal mucosal bleeding time (BMBT) test (ch.79), with an abnormal
result being specific for primary hemostatic disorders.41 A prolonged
BMBT (>4 minutes) in a dog with a platelet count >100,000/mcL and
packed cell volume (PCV) >30% is suggestive of VWD, thrombopathia, or,
rarely, a vasculopathy (ch. 181). Because VWD is much more common in
the dog than are intrinsic platelet function defects, measurement of
plasma VWF antigen (VWF:Ag) concentration is recommended before
platelet function testing. The Platelet Function Analyzer (PFA-100,
Siemens) (ch. 170) is sensitive in identifying dogs with type 1 VWD
having plasma VWF:Ag concentrations <35%.42,43

Quantitative VWF Assay
The laboratory diagnosis of VWD is most often based on measurement of
plasma VWF:Ag concentration by an enzyme-linked immunosorbent
assay (ELISA). The Comparative Coagulation Section of the Animal
Health Diagnostic Center at Cornell University is the most widely used
laboratory in the United States for VWD testing. Results are reported as %
VWF:Ag compared to a pooled canine plasma standard of 100%: normal
range = 70-180%, borderline (indeterminate) range = 50-69%, and
abnormal range = 0-49%. Ill dogs, particularly those with severe
inflammatory disease, such as sepsis, could have an increase in plasma
VWF:Ag concentration.44 Plasma VWF:Ag concentration also increases
during pregnancy and peaks at parturition in both normal dogs and dogs
with type 1 VWD.45 Therefore, screening for VWD (via measurement of
plasma VWF:Ag concentration) should not be performed during illness or
pregnancy.

DNA Testing
DNA tests are commercially available for canine breeds for which the
causative mutations (or what is believed to be the causative mutation) for
VWD have been identified (Table 175.1).46-50 The mode of inheritance
for type 2 and type 3 VWD is autosomal recessive. In canine type 1 VWD,
evidence for autosomal dominant51,52 or recessive46,53 modes of
inheritance has been reported. Since the plasma VWF:Ag concentration of
heterozygous carriers for type 2 and type 3 VWD can overlap with the low
end of the reference range, DNA testing will more reliably detect carriers
and, therefore, be of use to breeders trying to eliminate VWD from their
lines.49

Qualitative VWF Assays
While measurement of plasma VWF:Ag concentration can be used to
detect type 1 or type 3 VWD, the diagnosis of type 2 VWD requires
documenting an absence of the high molecular weight multimers of VWF
through a functional VWF assay or analysis of the size distribution of
multimers. Since the latter is complex, an ELISA measuring plasma
VWF:collagen-binding activity (CBA) is often used to diagnose type 2
VWD.54

Summary
In practical terms, the first step in a diagnostic evaluation for VWD in a
dog that is actively bleeding would be a screening BMBT. Submission of
pre-treatment plasma to a reference laboratory for measurement of VWF :
Ag concentration is recommended to confirm the diagnosis, regardless of
the BMBT since thrombopathia and vasculopathy can also cause a
prolonged BMBT, and a normal BMBT does not completely rule out a
diagnosis of VWD (i.e., it is not 100% sensitive).

Treatment
Management of VWD is aimed towards controlling spontaneous (e.g.,
epistaxis, hematuria) or trauma-/surgery-induced bleeding. While dogs
with type 2 and type 3 VWD inevitably have a severe bleeding tendency,
the phenotype among dogs with type 1 VWD is variable, with some dogs
having marked reductions in plasma VWF:Ag concentration but no
apparent bleeding tendency.55 Therefore, the need for prophylactic
treatment, particularly with blood component therapy, should be assessed
on a case by case basis.

Desmopressin
Desmopressin acetate (1-deamino-8-D-arginine vasopressin [DDAVP])
has been used to control bleeding in dogs with VWD. While
administration of DDAVP to humans with type 1 VWD and clinically
normal individuals typically results in a 2- to 5-fold increase in plasma
VWF:Ag concentration, the effect of DDAVP is less dramatic in dogs. One
hour following administration of DDAVP (1 mcg/kg SC) to 16 Doberman
Pinschers with type 1 VWD, mean plasma VWF concentration increased
from 10% (baseline) to 17%.56 Despite the modest increase in plasma
VWF:Ag concentration, however, DDAVP resulted in improved

hemostatic function as assessed by the PFA-100 and shortening of the
BMBT.43
DDAVP is available as a sterile solution (4 mcg/mL) for IV
administration and a nasal spray (100 mcg/mL) that can be administered
SC to dogs. The nasal spray preparation is used more frequently in dogs
with VWD due to its lower cost, and a recommended dosage is 1 mcg/kg
SC administered not more than once daily due to the risk of water
retention and hyponatremia, as well as tachyphylaxis, i.e., a failure to
elicit VWF release with repeated administration. DDAVP should be
administered 30 minutes prior to surgery when used prophylactically to
prevent excessive bleeding in dogs with VWD.
