Blood Component Therapy
Blood products containing VWF include fresh whole blood, fresh frozen
plasma (FFP), and cryoprecipitate (CRYO), the latter representing the
blood component of choice to treat bleeding in dogs with VWD. CRYO is
prepared from FFP and contains a concentrated amount of VWF, FVIII,
fibrinogen, fibronectin, and FXIII (ch. 171).
Guidelines for blood component therapy in the management of
bleeding in dogs with VWD include administration of CRYO at a dosage of
1 unit/10 kg (1 unit defined as CRYO prepared from 200-250 mL FFP) or
FFP at a dosage of 10-15 mL/kg (ch. 124).57 Due to the short half-life of
plasma VWF (∼12 hours), CRYO or FFP transfusions may need to be
administered every 8-12 hours to control severe bleeding. Blood type- and

crossmatch-compatible PRBCs should be available when dogs with VWD
are undergoing surgery, even when DDAVP and CRYO are administered
prophylactically, in the event of excessive blood loss.

ACQUIRED VON WILLEBRAND
SYNDROME
In people, acquired von Willebrand syndrome (AVWS) is a rare bleeding
disorder characterized by structural or functional alterations in VWF
caused by lymphoproliferative, myeloproliferative, cardiovascular,
autoimmune, or other disorders.58
Although not reported to cause bleeding in Cavalier King Charles
Spaniels or other dogs, AVWS secondary to myxomatous mitral valve
disease (ch. 232) and subaortic stenosis (ch. 231) has been documented,
with a decrease in plasma VWF:Ag concentration and a loss of the high
molecular weight VWF multimers.59 There is a report of possible AVWS
secondary to angiostrongylosis (ch. 217) in a young Golden Retriever
with cerebral and conjunctival hemorrhage.60 In a prospective study
evaluating primary hemostatic function in dogs with acute kidney injury,
the VWF Ag : CBA ratio was significantly higher in dogs with kidney
injury (2.2) compared to healthy control dogs (1.1), suggesting an
acquired type 2 VWD phenotype, though association with clinical
bleeding was not determined.61 AVWS should be considered in cases with
new-onset bleeding whenever laboratory findings suggest VWD,
particularly in the presence of conditions similar to those reported in
humans with AVWS.

FELINE VON WILLEBRAND DISEASE
There are only 2 reported cases of VWD in cats, both diagnosed with type
3 VWD.62,63 Although VWD appears to be an uncommon disorder in cats,
it should be considered as a differential diagnosis in cats with a bleeding
tendency in the absence of severe thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy. As
with dogs, a diagnosis of VWD in cats can be confirmed by measurement
of plasma VWF:Ag concentration.

PLATELET FUNCTION DISORDERS
HEREDITARY PLATELET DYSFUNCTION
Hereditary thrombopathia, or intrinsic platelet dysfunction, is a
potentially underrecognized cause of spontaneous and postsurgical/trauma bleeding. Several inherited platelet function defects have
been identified in dogs and cats (Table 175.2).64-76 Excellent reviews of
the clinical features and molecular characterization of these inherited
platelet disorders are available.77,78

Platelet Procoagulant Deficiency (Scott Syndrome)
Platelet procoagulant deficiency, also known as Scott syndrome, is an
autosomal recessive disorder identified in German Shepherds.69 Platelets
from dogs with Scott syndrome have decreased prothrombinase
activity.67 Diminished platelet procoagulant activity (PCA) causes
insufficient thrombin generation to support fibrin clot maturation and
stabilization, resulting in a bleeding tendency. Reported hemorrhagic
events include post-surgical bleeding, epistaxis, and soft-tissue
hemorrhage.68 Affected dogs do not develop spontaneous petechiae and
ecchymoses, suggesting that PCA is not required to maintain general
capillary integrity but is needed for maintenance of the nasal cavity
arterial microvasculature, as evidenced by the profound epistaxis
requiring local embolization in some affected dogs.68 A simple flow
cytometric assay, based on the inability of canine Scott syndrome platelets
to externalize PS when stimulated, and DNA testing for the recently
identified mutation causing Scott syndrome in German Shepherds, are
available at Cornell University.69

FIGURE 175.2 Diagnostic algorithm for primary
hemostatic defects. aPTT, Activated partial
thromboplastin time; BMBT, buccal mucosal bleeding
time; N, normal; PFA-100, platelet function analyzer100; PT, prothrombin time; VWD, von Willebrand
disease; VWF:Ag, von Willebrand factor antigen
concentration.

P2Y12 Receptor Disorder
A novel P2Y12 receptor gene mutation, a 3 base-pair (CTC) deletion
predicted to eliminate serine 173 (173Sdel) from the second loop of the
extracellular domain of this ADP receptor, has been identified across 5
generations in a family of Greater Swiss Mountain dogs and is associated
with postoperative hemorrhage.70 Spontaneous bleeding is absent to mild
in affected dogs; however, severe and life-threatening bleeding requiring
platelet transfusions has been observed following ovariohysterectomy in
dogs homozygous, as well as heterozygous, for the P2Y12 mutation.70,71
The prevalence of the mutant allele in the Greater Swiss Mountain Dog
breed is reported to be about 50%, including heterozygous and
homozygous affected dogs (Peter Christopherson, personal
communication, March 31, 2021).

Bernard-Soulier Syndrome
Bernard-Soulier syndrome (BSS), characterized by
macrothrombocytopenia and impaired platelet adhesion due to lack of a
functional platelet membrane VWF receptor complex, GP1b-IX-V, was
recently diagnosed in Cocker Spaniels with a mild to severe bleeding
phenotype.75 A large deletion was identified in the GP9 gene, resulting in
a frameshift and premature stop codon.75 Affected dogs were homozygous
for this variant genotype whereas it was not identified in control Cocker
spaniels, suggesting that it is causative for the BSS phenotype.75

ACQUIRED PLATELET DYSFUNCTION
Platelet function defects have been documented in association with
various systemic disorders, including renal disease,61,79 hepatobiliary
disease,80,81 and paraproteinemia.82,83 The mechanisms underlying
acquired thrombopathias are not well defined and are likely
multifactorial. Anemia can be a contributing factor to a bleeding
tendency, potentially due to altered rheological properties of the blood
limiting contact of platelets with the vessel wall, as well as a decreased
source of ADP (from fewer RBCs) to activate platelets.84 Many drugs
(e.g., hydroxyethyl starch,85,86 nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs,8789
cephalosporins90,91) have been documented to have an adverse effect
on platelet function in vitro, though the clinical significance is unclear.
Two drugs that are frequently administered for their anti-platelet activity
to patients predisposed to thromboembolic complications include aspirin,
an irreversible inhibitor of cyclooxygenase, and clopidogrel, a platelet
P2Y12 ADP receptor antagonist (chs. 174, 219, and 238).

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
The classic clinical presentation for many hereditary thrombopathias
includes spontaneous bleeding in the form of petechiae, ecchymoses, and
mucosal surface bleeding, and excessive bleeding following trauma or
surgery. This bleeding history, in conjunction with a normal platelet
count, PT, aPTT, and plasma VWF:Ag concentration, should prompt
diagnostic evaluation for a thrombopathia (Figure 175.2). As for VWD, a
BMBT test and PFA-100 can be performed as screening tests for a

thrombopathia. For dogs of a breed with a known mutation for a
thrombopathia, the diagnosis can be confirmed by DNA testing (Table
175.2). Special platelet function testing for dogs and cats suspected to
have a hereditary thrombopathia includes platelet aggregation studies,
measurement of ATP release, flow cytometry to evaluate the presence of
platelet membrane glycoproteins and activation-specific changes, and
electron microscopy. Platelet function tests require meticulously collected
and fresh blood samples, making remote platelet function testing difficult.
However, blood samples can be shipped overnight to the Comparative
Coagulation Section at Cornell University for flow cytometric testing for
platelet procoagulant deficiency and evaluation of the platelet fibrinogen
receptor.

TREATMENT
Dogs and cats with hereditary thrombopathias experiencing severe (e.g.,
hemoabdomen resulting in anemia following an ovariohysterectomy) or
life-threatening bleeding (e.g., pulmonary hemorrhage) require platelet
transfusions to control bleeding. Prophylactic platelet transfusions should
be considered in patients undergoing surgery with a known bleeding
tendency and documented thrombopathia. Options for platelet
transfusions include fresh whole blood, fresh platelet-rich plasma
(PRP)/platelet concentrate (PC), and cryopreserved PRP/PC (ch. 124).
Canine cryopreserved platelets have been administered to dogs with Scott
syndrome prophylactically prior to neutering, as well as in the
management of nonsurgical hemorrhage, mainly epistaxis, with apparent
efficacy.68 Since thawed canine cryopreserved platelets have been
documented to externalize PS, it has been hypothesized that
cryopreserved platelets may provide an advantage to fresh platelets in
promoting thrombin generation in dogs with Scott syndrome.68

CLIENT INFORMATION
Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP)
Platelets are essential for maintaining blood vessel integrity and
promoting clot formation at a site of blood vessel injury. A normal platelet
count for a dog or cat is approximately 200,000-400,000/mcL. A
decrease in platelet number is referred to as thrombocytopenia, and if it
is significant, it places a dog at risk for spontaneous bleeding. Many

disease processes can cause varying degrees of thrombocytopenia,
including infectious diseases, cancer, and destruction by the immune
system. The latter is referred to as immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), and
it is the most common cause of severe thrombocytopenia in dogs (ITP
occurs rarely in cats). ITP can be a primary autoimmune disorder in
which the dog makes antibodies against its own platelets for no
identifiable reason, or ITP can develop secondary to a medication,
underlying infectious disease, or cancer.

CLINICAL SIGNS (SYMPTOMS)
Dogs and cats with ITP frequently develop pinpoint hemorrhage
(petechia) on the gums (gingiva) and the inner surface of the ear (pinna)
and larger areas of bruising (ecchymosis), most easily noticed on the
sparsely haired portion of the abdomen. Bleeding from the nose and
gingiva may be noted, as well as blood in the urine or feces (black-colored
stool indicates the presence of digested blood). Some dogs and cats with
ITP lose a large amount of blood, particularly into the gastrointestinal
tract, resulting in anemia that could be severe enough to warrant a blood
transfusion.

DIAGNOSIS
The diagnosis of primary ITP is one of exclusion, meaning underlying
diseases must be ruled out and the diagnosis of ITP is reached by process
of elimination. Therefore, the veterinarian might recommend testing for
vector-borne diseases (e.g., ehrlichiosis or babesiosis) or imaging (chest
radiographs [X-rays] and abdominal ultrasound) to look for cancer. The
diagnosis of primary ITP is based on the finding of severe
thrombocytopenia (platelet count <30,000/mcL) and the absence of any
detectable underlying disease.

TREATMENT
For dogs and cats with secondary ITP, withdrawal of certain medications
if they are considered likely to be causing the thrombocytopenia (e.g.,
trimethoprim-sulfa), or treatment of an underlying infectious disease,
may be all that is necessary to resolve the thrombocytopenia. For dogs
and cats with primary ITP, the mainstay of treatment is
immunosuppression with glucocorticoid medications such as prednisone
or dexamethasone. Other drugs which may be administered in-hospital
include vincristine and human intravenous immunoglobulin. If the
platelet count does not improve within 1-2 weeks or the patient develops

severe adverse effects from the prednisone, then other oral
immunosuppressive medications may be prescribed. Most dogs and cats
with primary ITP are treated with tapering dosages of prednisone for 4-6
months. A platelet count is typically checked approximately 1 week after
each dose reduction to make sure that the platelet count remains within
the reference range.
Some dogs and cats with ITP will develop a severe blood loss anemia
and require a red blood cell transfusion. If the patient experiences lifethreatening bleeding (e.g., bleeding into the lungs), platelet transfusions
may be necessary to control bleeding.

PROGNOSIS (OUTLOOK FOR LONG-TERM HEALTH)
Dogs and cats with primary ITP have a good prognosis with appropriate
treatment and supportive care, with an estimated 75-95% of patients
surviving to hospital discharge. Relapse of ITP is possible at any point,
however, within weeks to years of initial diagnosis. Relapse requires
additional treatment, and is reported to occur in approximately 25-30% of
dogs; the relapse rate may be higher in cats.
Mary Beth Callan (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania) and James
L. Catalfamo (Ithaca, New York)

CLIENT INFORMATION
Von Willebrand Disease
Platelets are essential for maintaining blood vessel integrity and
promoting clot formation at a site of blood vessel injury. Platelets require
the presence of a protein, von Willebrand factor (VWF), to function
efficiently. Without them, the blood cannot clot properly and bleeding can
continue even with minor injuries. Von Willebrand disease (VWD), the
most common hereditary bleeding disorder in dogs, is a result of a
deficiency of plasma VWF.

CLINICAL SIGNS (“SYMPTOMS”)
Dogs with VWD frequently experience excessive bleeding after surgery or
trauma. Affected dogs may also develop spontaneous bleeding from the
nose, urinary tract, or gastrointestinal tract. Much less commonly, dogs
with VWD can have serious neurologic effects when bleeding occurs
around, or into, the brain or spinal cord.

DIAGNOSIS
Blood tests (a platelet count and coagulation screening assays) will be
performed first to look for disorders other than VWD that may be
associated with a bleeding tendency. These are performed first because
they usually have a shorter turnaround time. If these results are normal,
then evaluation for VWD should be pursued. An in-office screening test
that can be performed is a buccal mucosal bleeding time (BMBT). A
prolonged BMBT (>4 minutes) is suggestive of VWD or a platelet function
defect (thrombopathia), whereas a normal result makes these unlikely.
Definitive diagnosis requires measurement of plasma VWF concentration
in a blood sample. Normal dogs have a plasma VWF concentration
ranging from 70-180%, and affected dogs have levels less than 50%,
though bleeding is typically not likely if the plasma VWF concentration is
greater than 30%. DNA testing for VWD is available for many breeds for
which a disease-causing mutation has been identified; such tests can help
to identify carriers (dogs that do not experience abnormal bleeding but
that can transmit VWD to offspring through a mutant allele that the test
detects).

TREATMENT
Immediate management of excessive bleeding that can be performed in
the veterinary hospital includes administration of a medication
(desmopressin, also called DDAVP) and blood component therapy
(meaning giving a dog a blood or plasma transfusion). Cryoprecipitate, a
concentrated form of VWF, is the blood product of choice for treating a
dog that is bleeding significantly. If cryoprecipitate is not available, a
veterinarian may administer fresh frozen plasma to help temporarily
increase the dog’s plasma VWF concentration. If neither cryoprecipitate
nor fresh frozen plasma is available, fresh whole blood can be given.
Twice daily transfusions of these blood components may be necessary to
control severe bleeding.
For dogs with a known bleeding tendency and a prior diagnosis of VWD
who need to undergo surgery, prophylactic (pre-emptive) administration
of DDAVP and cryoprecipitate or fresh frozen plasma should be
considered as important precautionary measures to help minimize the
risk of bleeding. In addition, compatible packed red blood cells should be
available for transfusion in the event of excessive bleeding.

PROGNOSIS (OUTLOOK FOR LONG-TERM HEALTH)

There is a variable bleeding tendency among dogs with VWD, so the
diagnosis of VWD indicates an increased risk that varies in severity from
dog to dog. Some dogs will bleed excessively only following surgery or
trauma, while others may experience intermittent spontaneous bleeding
even during day-to-day activities. In most cases, bleeding can be
controlled with transfusion of blood products. Some dogs with the most
severe forms of VWD will require intensive transfusion support, such as
3-4 units of cryoprecipitate twice daily for 2-3 days for a Doberman
Pinscher with severe bleeding.
Mary Beth Callan (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania) and James
L. Catalfamo (Ithaca, New York)

CLIENT INFORMATION
Thrombopathia
Platelets are essential for maintaining blood vessel integrity and
promoting clot formation at a site of blood vessel injury. A platelet
function defect, or thrombopathia, is a type of blood disorder that makes
dogs more likely to bleed spontaneously or to bleed excessively following
surgery or trauma. Thrombopathia sometimes can occur as part of an
underlying disease process like severe kidney disease, but more often
thrombopathias that cause a severe bleeding tendency are transmitted
genetically (inherited) from parent dog to offspring.

CLINICAL SIGNS (SYMPTOMS)
Dogs and cats with a hereditary thrombopathia may first show a bleeding
tendency when they lose their baby teeth (deciduous teeth) and bleed
excessively from their gums, or when they develop excessive bleeding
following a spay or castration. In addition, pinpoint hemorrhage
(petechia) may be visible on the gums (gingiva) and the inner surface of
the ear (pinna), while larger areas of bruising (ecchymosis) may be
observed on the sparsely haired portion of the abdomen. Bleeding from
the nose, as well as blood in the urine or feces (black-colored stool
indicating the presence of digested blood), may also be noted.

DIAGNOSIS
If thrombopathia is considered a reasonable possibility because of
unexplained instances of bleeding, a panel of blood tests (hemostatic
screening tests) including assays to rule out von Willebrand disease

(VWD) should be performed first. If these results are normal, then a
diagnosis of thrombopathia is suspect. Next, an initial screening test that
is often performed in the veterinarian’s office is a buccal mucosal bleeding
time (BMBT). A prolonged BMBT (>4 minutes for a dog, >2 minutes for a
cat) in a patient with a normal platelet count and normal plasma von
Willebrand factor concentration is suggestive of a thrombopathia. DNA
testing for thrombopathia is confirmatory and is available for the
following breeds and platelet disorders:
• Glanzmann thrombasthenia – Great Pyrénées and Otterhound
• P2Y12 receptor disorder – Greater Swiss Mountain Dog
• CalDAG-GEFI thrombopathia – Basset Hound, Spitz, Landseer
• Leukocyte adhesion deficiency-III – German Shepherd
• Platelet procoagulant deficiency (Scott syndrome) – German
Shepherd
• Cyclic hematopoiesis – Gray Collie
For dogs (or cats) of other breeds with a suspected thrombopathia,
special tests of platelet function can be performed at a few veterinary
schools.

TREATMENT
Dogs and cats with hereditary thrombopathias experiencing severe
bleeding require platelet transfusions in a veterinary hospital to control
bleeding. Options for platelet transfusions include fresh whole blood,
fresh platelet-rich plasma/concentrate, and cryopreserved platelet-rich
plasma/concentrate. In addition, pre-emptive (“prophylactic”) platelet
transfusions should be considered as a precaution in patients with a
known bleeding tendency and documented thrombopathia who are about
to undergo surgery.

PROGNOSIS (OUTLOOK FOR LONG-TERM HEALTH)
There is a variable bleeding tendency among dogs with hereditary
thrombopathias. Some dogs will bleed excessively only following surgery
or trauma, while others may experience intermittent spontaneous
bleeding. In most cases the bleeding can be controlled with platelet
transfusions at a veterinary hospital, though some dogs will require
intensive transfusion support (e.g., 3-4 units of platelet concentrate daily
for a few days for a Greater Swiss Mountain Dog experiencing severe
bleeding following surgery).

IMMUNE-MEDIATED NEUTROPENIA

CLINICAL PRESENTATION
Immune-mediated neutropenia (IMN) in dogs and cats may occur in
tandem with other immune-mediated disorders, including immunemediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA) (ch. 174), immune-mediated
thrombocytopenia (ITP) (ch. 175), and polyarthritis (ch. 177).1-3
Patients may present with clinical signs relating to severe
neutropenia, including lethargy, persistent fever,
recurrent/persistent skin infections or abscesses, lymphadenopathy
due to reactive hyperplasia, gastrointestinal signs (vomiting,
diarrhea, inappetence) and/or coughing, or patients may be
subclinically affected. The presence of concurrent immune-mediated
disorders such as IMHA can also affect clinical presentation. A
diagnosis of IMN should exclude other causes of neutropenia
including acute or overwhelming peripheral demand (e.g., sepsis or
endotoxemia [ch. 128]); decreased production due to 1) hemic
neoplasia or other causes of myelophthisis [ch. 322], 2) viral or
fungal infection, or 3) drug-induced marrow injury (ch. 138);
vector-borne diseases (chs. 9, 193); feline chronic idiopathic
neutropenia; and sequestration due to splenomegaly (ch. 182).4
Careful evaluation of patients for clinical evidence of sepsis (e.g.,
fever, brick red mucous membranes if hyperdynamic; pale mucous
membranes, hypothermia, cold extremities if hypodynamic) is
necessary.5 As with other immune-mediated hematologic diseases,
IMN can be idiopathic (primary/autoimmune) or secondary to
causes such as drug administration causing type II hypersensitivity.
IMN along with thrombocytopenia and anemia caused by
cephalosporin administration was experimentally proven in dogs,
and potential associations with phenobarbital, primidone,
ivermectin, and methimazole administration are reported in canine
and feline IMN.4,6,7 One dog with glucocorticoid-deficient
hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296) was diagnosed with IMN and
thrombocytopenia.5 Idiopathic IMN was the least common cause of
neutropenia in one study (ch. 58) but is likely underdiagnosed.3
Younger age is reportedly a risk factor for dogs to develop IMN, with
a median age at diagnosis of 5 years (range, 1-12 years) reported in

one study, and a four-fold increased risk of disease in dogs under 4
years of age reported in another.8,9

HEMATOLOGIC ABNORMALITIES
Absolute neutrophil counts in IMN were significantly lower than in
other neutropenic disorders of dogs.9 A cut-off value of 1500
neutrophils/mcL repeatable in at least 2 sequential complete blood
counts was used for defining IMN in one study.8 In the same study,
neutrophil counts were <500/mcL in 60% of dogs, and <1000/mcL
in 91%. Band neutrophil counts are often low or zero in IMN. A
degenerative left shift with immature neutrophilic cells (Figure
176.1, C-D) outnumbering segmented neutrophils was considered
evidence of overwhelming peripheral demand rather than support
for IMN8; note that substantial neutrophil toxic changes (Figure
176.1, E-F) often accompany degenerative left shifts in small
animals and also are seen with overwhelming demand. Bone marrow
findings (ch. 84) can vary, as different stages of neutrophil
maturation are subject to immune attack. Myeloid hyperplasia in
bone marrow was shown in 23/35 affected dogs, with myeloid
hypoplasia seen in another 10 dogs.8 A “left shift” in myeloid
maturation (decreased late-stage neutrophilic cells) is reported often
in bone marrow evaluation,8,10 and immune attack against myeloid
precursors has been demonstrated via immunofluorescence assay
(IFA) for canine IgG and C3.4

DEFINITIVE DIAGNOSIS
Methods to positively diagnose IMN require species-specific
antibodies and specific expertise. The use of neutrophil antigenspecific antibodies is not currently established in veterinary
medicine. Flow cytometric methods can be used for direct and
indirect detection of anti-neutrophil antibodies, but they cannot
differentiate between primary and secondary IMN. Flow cytometry is
considered variably sensitive in dogs; the sensitivity of direct flow

cytometry using patient neutrophils can be impaired by severe
neutropenia and by cell fragility, degranulation and agglutination.
Fresh patient blood is needed for direct testing. Indirect flow
cytometry or leukoagglutination using patient serum and donor
neutrophils avoids some sensitivity issues and can be performed on
banked patient serum samples with variable to high sensitivity but
unknown specificity reported.8,11,12 Leukoagglutination and IFA
were not considered sensitive for IMN in a study of neutropenic
cats.13 As a positive diagnosis of IMN is often not achieved, a
presumptive diagnosis is common and it requires elimination of
other potential causes of neutropenia as listed above, along with
response to therapy.

TREATMENT
Immunosuppression is indicated for treatment of IMN, and a rapid
response to immunosuppressive therapy is considered necessary to
confirm the diagnosis.1 In cases of secondary IMN, treatment or
withdrawal of the suspected underlying cause is indicated.
Corticosteroids are the mainstay of IMN treatment (ch. 144).
Adjunctive therapy with azathioprine or cyclosporine is common in
treating IMN (ch. 169), and can be started at the time of diagnosis
or reserved for refractory cases or those in which adverse effects of
high-dose corticosteroids are unacceptable. As azathioprine can have
myelosuppressive effects, its use might be delayed until an initial
clinical and/or neutrophil response is seen, to avoid confusion.1
Alternately, cyclosporine can be used as initial adjunct therapy.
Medication tapering strategies and time course vary (e.g., from 1-6
months in one study8); 17 of 27 (63%) dogs at 6 months and 12 of 19
(63%) of dogs at 1 year after initiation of therapy required continued
corticosteroid treatment to maintain neutrophil concentration.8
Relapse is common; 34% of dogs became neutropenic during or after
medication taper, and 4 of 5 dogs had episodes of relapse despite
addition of adjunct therapy (considered refractory cases).8

PANCYTOPENIA
Pancytopenia is defined as a combination of non-regenerative
anemia (chs. 57, 172), neutropenia (ch. 58) and thrombocytopenia
(chs. 59, 175). Pancytopenia can occur due to multiple concurrent
disorders (e.g., sepsis with increased platelet consumption and
anemia of inflammatory disease), or to impairment of bone marrow
production and release of mature blood cells. Lymphopenia is
variable with pancytopenia due to acquired bone marrow diseases,
but can be seen in pancytopenic patients due to a concurrent cortisol
stress response.
Differentials for pancytopenia due to bone marrow disease are
generally based on findings in bone marrow evaluation, and are
listed in Box 176.1.14-23 Note that the terms “aplastic anemia” and
“aplastic pancytopenia” are often used to describe hypocellular or
acellular bone marrow conditions resulting in pancytopenia; marrow
cellularity in this context does not include neoplastic cells.

MYELONECROSIS AND
MYELOFIBROSIS
Myelonecrosis and/or myelofibrosis are often seen concurrently with
bone marrow disorders as listed in Box 176.1. Primary
myelofibrosis is a rare, clonal myeloproliferative disease resulting in
progressive ablation of marrow space due to fibrosis; extramedullary
hematopoiesis can be marked. Confirmation of primary
myelofibrosis in human patients relies on molecular genetic testing.
Presumptive primary myelofibrosis has been reported in both dogs
and cats. However, the occurrence of suspected primary
myelofibrosis in all domestic animals is extremely rare,24 and most
cases of myelofibrosis are likely secondary (non-clonal). In dogs,
pyruvate kinase deficiency is the most frequently reported cause of
secondary myelofibrosis (ch. 174). Other causes reported in small
animals are high-dose recombinant human erythropoietin (EPO),
feline leukemia virus (FeLV) infection (ch. 199), bone marrow
necrosis, infections, and drugs/toxicoses.25 Myelonecrosis can
associated with myelofibrosis and/or marrow ischemia due to

various underlying bone marrow disorders, including IMHA, sepsis
(ch. 128), hemic neoplasia infiltrating bone marrow (ch. 322), and
drugs/medications.

MYELODYSPLASIA
Primary Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS)
True primary MDS are clonal (neoplastic) disorders arising from
mutations in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. Testing for
clonality to confirm primary MDS is not available for dogs and cats,
and the differentiation between primary MDS and secondary
dysmyelopoiesis therefore can be difficult.26 A combination of
consistent history, clinical signs and accurate categorization of
hematopathologic abnormalities is needed for diagnosis.27
Nonregenerative anemia is a necessary feature in primary MDS of
both dogs and cats (ch. 172). Feline retroviruses, particularly FeLV,
can cause MDS and dysmyelopoiesis (ch. 199); a clonal origin to
FeLV-associated myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukemia is
proven.28 Primary MDS is rare in dogs and a clonal origin has not
been proven.29 Morphologic changes in blood or bone marrow that
suggest primary MDS instead of secondary dysmyelopoiesis include
higher numbers of immature precursors, dysplastic cells, and/or
megaloblastic erythroid precursors (Figure 176.1, G-J).
Additionally, a history of drug/toxin exposure or concurrent disease
may support secondary dysmyelopoiesis instead of primary MDS.
Primary MDS is similar to chronic myeloid leukemia: both feature
anemia or multiple cytopenias and normal/hypercellular bone

marrow. Marrow blast cells comprise less than 20% of nucleated
cells (a few veterinary references cite a cutoff of 30%30) in both
disorders. A key difference is the lack of increased myeloid cells
(predominantly mature) in circulation of patients with primary MDS.
Modified versions of the French-American-British (FAB) working
group scheme for classification of MDS in human medicine are often
used in small animal medicine.27 The following is one modified-FAB
scheme for classification of primary MDS in small animals.29 Note
that the 2016 revision to the World Health Organization (WHO)
classification of human myeloid neoplasms includes reclassification
of MDS subtypes,31 but published veterinary classification schemes
do not currently reflect this revision.

MDS–Excess Blasts (MDS-EB)
MDS-EB is likely the most common MDS in dogs and is associated
with more severe clinical signs and a poor prognosis at
presentation.32 Neutropenia, thrombocytopenia and
nonregenerative anemia are associated with MDS-EB. Increased
myeloblasts (up to 20%; note that >20% myeloblasts is considered
diagnostic for acute myeloid leukemia per WHO classification but
>30% erythroblasts in marrow is required to diagnose erythroid
leukemia33) and dysplasia of all three cell lines are found in bone
marrow. Dysplastic changes include asynchronous maturation in all
cell lines, hypersegmented granulocytes, dispersed megakaryocyte
nuclei, and erythroid dysplasia as described below for MDSrefractory cytopenia. The prognosis for dogs with MDS-EB is worse
than that for other forms of MDS.34 MDS-EB is reported in cats from
1 to 17 years old.35 Cats with MDS-EB comprise between 31-65% of
all cats with primary MDS if cats with secondary dysmyelopoiesis are
excluded.35 In one study, 6 of 13 cats with MDS-EB tested positive
for FeLV infection. Other studies found higher percentages of FeLVpositivity; discrepant results may be due to decreasing FeLV
prevalence and/or differing prevalence between geographic regions.
As for dogs, the prognosis for cats with MDS-EB tends to be worse

and the risk of developing acute myeloid leukemia higher than with
other forms of feline MDS.

MDS–Refractory Cytopenia (MDS-RC)
MDS-RC tends to occur in older dogs and it has an insidious onset of
clinical signs due to progressively worsening nonregenerative
anemia. Other cytopenias, including neutropenia, can occur but are
uncommon. Bone marrow may be hypercellular due to erythroid
hyperplasia, or normocellular. Erythroid dysplasia including
nuclear:cytoplasmic asynchrony, binucleation, and nuclear
fragmentation is a characteristic finding.32 Rubriblasts may be
increased (up 30% of all nucleated bone marrow cells). Descriptions
of MDS-RC in cats often include cytopenias and dysplastic changes
in multiple blood cell lineages; it is proposed that such cases
represent MDS-RCMD (see below) rather than MDS-RC in this
classification scheme.

MDS–Refractory Cytopenia With Multilineage
Dysplasia (MDS-RCMD)
MDS-RCMD is defined as dysplasia in at least 2 cell lineages in bone
marrow, similar to MDS-EB but without a substantial increase in
myeloblasts (<5% myeloblasts for MDS-RCMD). MDS characterized
by refractory anemia with sideroblastic differentiation can be
included in this category, as dysplasia occurs in multiple lineages.29
In cats, experimental infection with FeLV produced hematologic
disease resembling MDS-RCMD, with cytopenias and dysplasia in
multiple cell lines.36 Several cats with sideroblastic forms of MDSRCMD are reported. Note that the updated WHO classification for
MDS in human patients combines all forms of MDS with ring
sideroblasts into a single category regardless of the presence or
absence of multilineage dysplasia, based on recent genetic
information.31

Secondary Myelodysplastic Syndromes
Secondary MDS in humans are clonal disorders. Mutations are
induced by chemotherapeutic agents, toxin exposure, and/or

radiation therapy. Dysmegakaryopoiesis and myeloproliferative
disorders following radiation are reported in dogs, suggesting these
syndromes may occur in small animals as well.

SECONDARY DYSMYELOPOIESIS
The most common diseases associated with secondary
dysmyelopoiesis, a non-clonal disorder, in dogs are ITP (ch. 175)
and IMHA (ch. 174), pure red cell aplasia (ch. 174), and lymphoma
(ch. 322).29 Other causes include drugs/medications (e.g.,
chemotherapeutic agents, chloramphenicol, estrogens, and
phenobarbital37 [ch. 138]), endogenous overproduction of
estrogens, heavy metal toxicosis, iron deficiency, adenocarcinoma,
and leishmaniasis (ch. 197). Diseases associated with secondary
dysmyelopoiesis in cats include IMHA and ITP, pure red cell aplasia,
lymphoma, glomerulonephritis (ch. 302), feline infectious
peritonitis (ch. 200) and feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV)
infection (ch. 198). Dysplasia can affect one or multiple blood cell
lineages, often depending on the underlying etiology. For example,
sideroblastic forms of disease are associated with inflammatory
disorders and myelofibrosis.29 Bone marrow cytology alone can be
insufficient to distinguish primary MDS from secondary
dysmyelopoiesis. Lower percentages of dysplastic cells and/or
normal blast cell percentages may suggest secondary
dysmyelopoiesis, but exceptions may include recovery from sepsis or
toxic bone marrow injury. Differentiation of primary MDS vs.
secondary dysmyelopoiesis may instead rely on history or clinical
evidence to support potential underlying cause(s) of
dysmyelopoiesis.

TREATMENT OF PANCYTOPENIC
DISORDERS
If possible, elimination or withdrawal of the underlying cause (e.g.,
medications, infectious causes, neoplastic disorders) is indicated.
Cytotoxic treatment agents for dogs and cats with MDS or suspected

immune-mediated pancytopenic disorders have included
cyclophosphamide, cytosine arabinoside, prednisone, cyclosporine,
daunorubicin, vincristine, hydroxycarbamide, and cytarabine (chs.
169 and 172).38 Additional therapeutic options regardless of the
underlying cause of pancytopenia include transfusion if indicated
(ch. 124), and stimulation of blood cell production via exogenous
growth factors (e.g., EPO, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor [GCSF]) and/or receptor agonists.23,39,40

PARANEOPLASTIC LEUKOCYTOSIS
Neoplastic processes can cause a secondary, non-neoplastic increase
in production of specific mature leukocyte subtypes. Paraneoplastic
neutrophilia and eosinophilia are infrequently recognized in small
animals. Paraneoplastic leukocytosis resulting in mature
neutrophilia is most often associated with carcinoma (e.g., squamous
cell,41 renal,42 or pulmonary43 carcinoma) or rectal polyps.44 These
tumors can cause increased production of G-CSF and/or
granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor.42,43 Note that
tumors can cause substantial neutrophilia due to inflammation, and
paraneoplastic leukocytosis is considered an uncommon or rare
cause of neoplasia-associated neutrophilia by comparison.
Paraneoplastic eosinophilia is most often associated with T-cell
lymphoma45 and mast cell neoplasia.46 A possible association with
leiomyosarcoma is also reported (ch. 324).47 See ch. 331 for
additional information on paraneoplastic syndromes.

INFECTIOUS DISEASES CAUSING
CYTOPENIAS OR OTHER LEUKOCYTE
ABNORMALITIES
PARVOVIRUS INFECTION
Canine and feline parvoviral infections (ch. 201) cause bone marrow
injury and leukopenia. Neutropenia occurs in some but not all cases

of severe canine parvovirus infection; leukopenia has been reported
in less than half of infected dogs on presentation.48 Neutropenic
dogs may have marked evidence of left shift and/or neutrophil toxic
change in blood smears (Figure 176.1, C-F and ch. 58); 92% of
clinically ill dogs and 84% of cats with parvoviral infection had
acellular bone marrow on evaluation.49 Survival is strongly predicted
by a patient’s ability to maintain total leukocyte counts >4500/mcL
and lymphocyte counts >1000/mcL.50

DISTEMPER AND PARAMYXOVIRUS
INFECTION
Canine distemper virus (ch. 204) infects numerous tissues and cells,
including lymphoid and other hematopoietic cells.
Immunosuppression occurs early in infection due to viral-mediated
lysis of lymphocytes; grossly enlarged lymph nodes and thymic
atrophy develop. Secondary lymph node follicles are microscopically
absent. Lymphopenia can occur, and cytoplasmic (rarely nuclear)
viral inclusions may be seen in white blood cells in peripheral blood
smears (Figure 176.1, K) in early infection.51 Immunosuppression
can be prolonged in some dogs and may exacerbate viral replication
and spreading.

FELINE LEUKEMIA VIRUS (FeLV)
INFECTION
Bone marrow suppression is a frequent clinical syndrome associated
with FeLV infection (ch. 199 and above section on Myelodysplastic
Syndromes). Erythroid precursors are most commonly affected, but
suppression of hematopoiesis can occur in all cell lineages.
Neutropenia is reported in approximately 50% of cats presenting
with FeLV-related illness.52 Cyclic hematopoiesis has also been
reported in infected cats. Cats with myelodysplasia and myelofibrosis
are frequently FeLV-positive. Myelophthisis due to myelofibrosis

and/or other causes, particularly hemic neoplasia, can contribute to
decreased leukocyte production.

FELINE IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS
(FIV) INFECTION
Acute FIV infection (ch. 198) may trigger mild leukocyte
abnormalities. No differences were found between FIV-infected and
non-infected cats in the occurrence of peripheral leukocyte
abnormalities in one study.53 In another, FIV infection increased the
odds ratio of neutropenia.54 Panlymphopenia can occur in acute
infection.55 Viral strain is an important factor: severe neutropenia
with lymphocytosis of granular lymphocytes was seen during acute
experimental infection with FIV-CPGammar.56 Chronic infection is
associated with decreased CD4+:CD8+ T-cell ratios and
development of secondary neoplastic and inflammatory disorders.55

RICKETTSIAL INFECTIONS
In dogs, the rickettsial agents most often associated with leukocyte
abnormalities are Ehrlichia canis, Ehrlichia chaffeensis, Ehrlichia
ewingii, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Neorickettsia helminthoeca,
Neorickettsia risticii and Rickettsia rickettsii (ch. 193). Natural
and/or experimental infections with E. canis, A. phagocytophilum or
N. risticii causing clinical signs are reported in cats. Acutely, E. canis
infection can cause neutropenia and/or total leukopenia; bacterial
morulae can be found in lymphocytes, monocytes and macrophages
in smears of peripheral blood/buffy coat, bone marrow and lymph
node specimens.57 Severe chronic infection causes pancytopenia and
marked panhypocellularity of bone marrow. E. chaffeensis is another
agent of canine monocytic ehrlichiosis in North America, but
hematologic abnormalities are milder and chronic pancytopenia is
absent. E. ewingii and A. phagocytophilum cause granulocytic
ehrlichiosis and granulocytic anaplasmosis, respectively.
Lymphopenia, neutropenia, eosinopenia, monocytosis and/or total

leukopenia are noted in A. phagocytophilum infection. Morulae of
either bacterium can be seen in peripheral blood neutrophils
(Figure 176.1, L). Neutrophilic polyarthritis can develop in both
infections; morulae may also be found in synovial fluid neutrophils.
Neither infection causes chronic pancytopenia. Acute infection with
N. helminthoeca, the causative agent of “salmon poisoning disease”
in dogs, causes lymphopenia; peripheral and internal lymph nodes
are enlarged due to lymphoid reactivity and histiocytic inflammation.
Organisms can be found within macrophages in lymph node cytology
smears stained with Giemsa stain, and vary from irregular inclusions
to morulae (Figure 176.1, M).58 Rickettsia rickettsii natural
infection of dogs has been characterized by leukocytosis
accompanied by toxic granulation of neutrophils (note that initial
leukopenia progressing to leukocytosis was reported in experimental
infection).59,60

BARTONELLA INFECTIONS
Bartonella infections of dogs (ch. 191) can induce granulomatous
inflammation of lymph nodes, heart, liver, and/or other localized
sites or systemic inflammation. Neutrophilic leukocytosis,
monocytosis and eosinophilia occur in Bartonella vinsonii-infected
dogs. Persistent eosinophilia is seen in some Bartonella-infected cats
(ch. 191); neutrophilia can occur with inflammation. Lymphoid
hyperplasia in lymph nodes and spleen are noted in infected cats,
along with pyogranulomatous inflammation in organs.

MYCOBACTERIAL INFECTIONS
Mycobacterial infections in dogs and cats (ch. 188) can induce focal
or multifocal pyogranulomas or can become disseminated.
Depending on the degree of inflammation and dissemination of
lesions, non-specific hematologic abnormalities such as mature
neutrophilia and monocytosis may occur, or hematologic evaluation
may be unremarkable. Cytologic and histopathologic evaluation of
lesions is often helpful in diagnosis. Acid-fast stains are required to

identify mycobacteria, as routine stains “negatively stain” organisms
within macrophages (Figure 176.1, N).

FUNGAL INFECTIONS
Fungal infections of dogs and cats can cause neutrophilia and
monocytosis as well as pyogranulomatous inflammation in tissues
(chs. 207, 208, 209, 210, and 211). Some fungal infections, e.g.
Pneumocystis jirovecii (P. carinii) (Figure 176.1, O), are associated
with underlying immunodeficiency. Other fungal pathogens
commonly found in macrophages in tissue specimens include
Sporothrix schenckii (Figure 176.1, P), Histoplasma capsulatum,
Blastomyces dermatitidis, and Cryptococcus spp.

PROTOZOAL INFECTIONS
Protozoal infections (ch. 197) can elicit systemic leukocyte
abnormalities, especially neutrophilia and eosinophilia. Many
protozoa infect leukocytes and can be found on cytologic
examination of tissue aspirates, and rarely in peripheral blood
smears. Intracellular tachyzoites of Neospora caninum or
Toxoplasma gondii may be seen in monocytes or macrophages in
samples including airway lavage fluid. Cytauxzoon felis schizonts
may be found in macrophages in tissue aspirate smears and/or at the
feathered edge of blood smears (merozoites may be seen in red blood
cells in blood smears); pancytopenia can occur in acute infection.
Leishmania amastigotes are found in macrophages in lymph node
and bone marrow aspirates and draining wound imprints (Figure
176.1, Q). Marked neutrophilia and monoclonal gammopathy are
reported in dogs. Cytologic examination can be insensitive for
detection of Leishmania organisms in infected cats. Hepatozoon spp.
infections often cause substantial neutrophilia and monocytosis in
infected dogs; organisms can be seen in blood and tissue leukocytes
(Figure 176.1, R).

Chapter 177: ImmuneMediated Polyarthritis and
Other Polyarthropathies
Michael Stone

A C RO N YM S

IMPA immune-mediated polyarthropathy
NSAID nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug

SLE systemic lupus erythematosus

Polyarthropathies are characterized by neutrophilic inflammation
of multiple joints. Clinical signs are lameness, stiffness, and/or
reluctance to walk, and some patients show signs of systemic illness
(ch. 31). The diagnostic evaluation can identify an etiologic agent or
other inciting cause, which then warrants specific treatment. A
diagnosis of idiopathic, immune-mediated polyarthropathy (IMPA)
is made by excluding the presence of known causes of joint

inflammation, and a good response is expected with
immunosuppressive treatment of IMPA.
Polyarthritis is defined as neutrophilic inflammation of two or
more joints. Polyarthritis may be divided into infectious, reactive,
and primary (idiopathic immune-mediated) etiologies. Primary
IMPA is subdivided further into erosive and non-erosive forms (Box
177.1).

GENERAL DIAGNOSTIC OVERVIEW
TYPICAL FEATURES OF IDIOPATHIC,
IMMUNE-MEDIATED POLYARTHRITIS
• Involvement of multiple joints, especially if there has been no
response to anti-rickettsial treatment. Degenerative
arthropathies (such as degenerative joint disease or
osteochondritis dissecans) are differentiated by mononuclear
inflammation of synovial fluid (chs. 32 and 71).
• Fever of unknown origin (ch. 16).
• Neutrophilic inflammation in synovial fluid, if only one joint
was evaluated (ch. 71). Differentiation of mono- from
polyarthropathies is sometimes difficult by physical
examination alone. Unless a monoarthropathy is obviously
present (e.g., previous joint surgery or penetrating injury),
analysis of synovial fluid from multiple joints is recommended
(ch. 87).

Typical Features of Septic (Bacterial) Arthritis
• Swelling and pain in a joint that has undergone surgery.
• Swelling and pain in a single, large joint (elbow, shoulder,
stifle, or hip). Degenerative joint disease predisposes joints to
bacterial arthritis from hematogenous spread. Fever, marked
pain, and systemic illness suggest infection rather than
exacerbation of degenerative joint disease. In contrast,
immune-mediated polyarthropathies typically affect multiple,
smaller, and distal joints.

• Lameness in a patient with a history of immunosuppressive
therapy, such as with corticosteroids or cyclosporine.
• Lameness in a patient with history of chronic bacterial
infection, most frequently of urinary tract or skin origin.

Exclusion of Infectious Agents From the List of
Probable Etiologies
• Tick-borne agents (such as Borrelia burgdorferi, Anaplasma
phagocytophilum, Rickettsia rickettsii and Ehrlichia canis;
chs. 187 and 193) are most easily excluded with trial therapy
using doxycycline or minocycline. Response to anti-rickettsial
treatment occurs within 72 hours. Measurement of serologic
titers could be helpful, but clinical signs of disease can occur
before the development of serum antibodies and therefore,
test results can be negative in acutely infected dogs. A.
phagocytophilum, R. rickettsia, or E. canis infection cannot
be excluded by a single negative serologic result.
• Dogs with a single swollen and painful joint should be most
carefully evaluated for an infectious etiology. Prior surgery
greatly increases the likelihood of a bacterial etiology. The
sensitivity of bacterial culture of synovial fluid is low; synovial
fluid is best subcultured in blood culture medium prior to
laboratory submission.1 Concurrent cultures of blood and
urine should be obtained in cases of suspected hematogenous
origin (ch. 184).
