• Dogs with systemic infections (such as bacterial endocarditis
[ch. 232], deep pyoderma, fungal disease [chs. 208, 209,
211], or leishmaniasis [ch. 197]) can develop a secondary
IMPA. In these cases, synovial fluid culture often is negative,
despite an infectious etiology. Evaluation of patients with
polyarthropathy can include serologic testing, thoracic
radiographs, echocardiography, abdominal ultrasonography,
and/or skeletal radiographs.
• Unusual organisms occasionally are identified as the cause of
arthritis. Culture of joint fluid might include evaluation for
aerobic, anaerobic, mycoplasmal, fungal and L-form agents.
• Bacterial culture of synovial fluid rarely is positive when
multiple joints are involved. However, in some patients, one
joint is obviously swollen and involvement of other joints is
uncertain. In these cases, centesis of multiple joints is
warranted (ch. 87) and fluid from the most obviously affected
joint is submitted for culture.
• Locally endemic diseases are considered when making a
differential diagnosis list. Systemic fungal diseases are
considered in, or after travel to, endemic areas, for example
(chs. 9, 208, 209). Serologic titers, microbial cultures in a
specialized laboratory, and/or molecular assays could be
useful.

INFECTIOUS POLYARTHROPATHIES
TICK-BORNE/RICKETTSIAL
In endemic areas, vector-borne infectious disease is a common cause
of inflammatory polyarthritis. B. burgdorferi (ch. 187), A.
phagocytophilum, R. rickettsii, E. canis, Ehrlichia ewingii, and
Ehrlichia chaffeensis (ch. 193) all have been implicated. In areas
where tick-borne diseases are endemic, arthrocentesis rarely is
indicated in a dog or cat with multiple swollen joints until there has
been failure to respond to a 3-5 day course of doxycycline or
minocycline.

LEISHMANIASIS
Leishmaniasis is a chronic systemic disease caused by a protozoal
parasite found mainly in South America, Africa, India, and the
Mediterranean (ch. 197).2 In the United States, visceral disease has
been reported in American Foxhounds. Clinical abnormalities
develop 3 months to 7 years after infection and typically consist of
inappetence, weight loss, muscle atrophy, and cutaneous lesions.
Polyarthritis causing lameness and exercise intolerance is common
and joint radiographs can reveal erosive changes. The diagnosis is
made when the organisms are identified cytologically, or by serologic
or molecular diagnostic testing.

BACTERIAL
Large joints such as the stifle, hip, shoulder, or elbow are affected
most frequently, but any joint can be involved (chs. 31 and 32).3-5
Most non-surgical joint infections develop from hematogenous
spread but only rarely does bacterial disease simultaneously involve
multiple joints. The most common agents are Gram-positive aerobes.
When non-surgical bacterial arthritis is suspected, blood (ch. 184)
and urine (chs. 71, 98) should be collected for culture and if positive,
additional imaging (echocardiography [ch. 97], abdominal

ultrasonography) performed. See “Polyarthropathies Occurring
Secondary to Distant Immunogenic Stimulus (“Reactive”),” below.

MYCOPLASMA
There are isolated veterinary reports of polyarthritis associated with
Mycoplasma species: M. gatae and M. felis have been isolated from
cats and M. spumans from dogs. Synovial fluid analysis reveals nondegenerate neutrophils. Routine aerobic and anaerobic cultures of
joint fluid are negative, and the diagnosis requires isolation in special
mycoplasma medium. Polymerase chain reaction assays can be more
sensitive than culture for detection of Mycoplasma species.
Doxycycline and fluoroquinolones are active against most
Mycoplasma isolates.6

BACTERIAL L-FORM–ASSOCIATED
ARTHRITIS
A rare syndrome of subcutaneous abscesses with associated
polyarthritis has been described in dogs and cats with L-forms of
bacteria suspected as the cause. An L-form is a mutant bacterium
that has lost its cell wall. Affected cats have swollen, painful joints,
and fever. Fistulating subcutaneous wounds can develop over the
affected joints. Cultures for aerobic, anaerobic, mycoplasmal, and
fungal organisms are negative, and specific L-form media must be
used for growing the organism. L-form bacteria are difficult to
recognize with a light microscope, but can be identified on electron
microscopy. Treatment with doxycycline or a fluoroquinolone should
be effective.7

FUNGAL
Systemic fungal diseases (blastomycosis [ch. 209], histoplasmosis
[ch. 209], coccidioidomycosis [ch. 208]) can be associated with
direct joint involvement. Reactive, immunologically mediated,

culture-negative polyarthritis also can occur, and probably is more
common than direct involvement of the joint.

VIRAL
Both calicivirus infections (ch. 205) and attenuated liver calicivirus
vaccines (ch. 185) have been associated with transient polyarthritis
in kittens 5-7 days following their first vaccination.8 Clinical signs
include lameness, stiffness, and fever, with spontaneous
improvement in 2-4 days. Synovial fluid analysis reveals a
mononuclear pleocytosis.9

POLYARTHROPATHIES OCCURRING
SECONDARY TO DISTANT
IMMUNOGENIC STIMULUS
(“REACTIVE”)
Animals with reactive polyarthritis can have vague or few clinical
signs referable to their underlying disease and be presented only
when joint inflammation makes them reluctant to walk.10 It is
important to perform a thorough physical examination of animals
with polyarthritis (

Video 177.1), to obtain a complete drug and

travel history (ch. 9), and to evaluate for evidence of systemic
illness. Screening tests (complete blood count [CBC] with manual
differential count, serum biochemical profile, serologic testing for
endemic infectious diseases, urinalysis, thoracic radiographs, and
abdominal ultrasound) often are performed to screen for an
underlying cause of polyarthritis.

NON-JOINT INFECTIOUS FOCUS
(BACTERIAL, FUNGAL, PROTOZOAL,
OTHER)

Patients with infection in sites distant from the joints can develop a
secondary IMPA. Endocarditis (ch. 232), discospondylitis (ch.
250), pyometra, bacterial pyoderma/cellulitis, foreign body
abscesses, prostatitis (ch. 314), pyelonephritis (ch. 304),
pneumonia (ch. 217), or actinomycosis (ch. 188) can represent a
source of chronic inflammation, leading to circulation of immune
complexes that are deposited into the synovium. Even though the
underlying inflammatory disease is infectious, synovial fluid cultures
will be negative. In some cases, such as those with a positive urine
culture, it can be difficult to determine whether the infection
represents the origin of hematogenous bacterial spread, the inciting
source of inflammation, or incidental disease. The low sensitivity of
synovial fluid cultures for the detection of infection contributes to
this confusion. Heartworm disease (ch. 237), chronic otitis, and
severe gingivostomatitis (ch. 258) represent common conundrums.

NONJOINT, INFLAMMATORY,
NONINFECTIOUS FOCUS (IMMUNEMEDIATED SKIN DISEASE,
INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE,
AND CHRONIC HEPATITIS)
This form of reactive arthritis originates with non-infectious
antigenic stimuli distant to the joints. In some cases, these diseases
may qualify the patient’s disease to be categorized as systemic lupus
erythematosus (SLE) (ch. 179). It can be difficult to establish
whether an inflammatory focus is the primary problem and causing a
secondary reactive arthropathy, or if both represent manifestations
of a single disease process (i.e., SLE).

DRUGS AND VACCINATION
Polyarthritis can develop after the administration of any medication
but is most commonly reported with antibiotics. Polyarthropathy has
been described after administration of sulfonamides, vaccines,

human albumin, penicillin, cephalexin, lincomycin, erythromycin,
phenobarbital, and erythropoietin, although not all are welldescribed. With sulfonamides, signs of polyarthritis develop 5-20
days after drug exposure and can be associated with fever,
thrombocytopenia, hepatopathy, and skin or oral lesions. Doberman
Pinschers appear to be predisposed. Improvement occurs within 7
days of drug cessation.11
Vaccination represents a potential cause of polyarthritis (ch. 185);
onset within 30 days of vaccine administration is suspicious.
Whether vaccination itself represents a risk, or whether immune
stimulation triggers the disorder in a patient with a genetic
predisposition, remains difficult to determine.12 Vaccine-triggered,
immune-mediated disease can be self-limiting and could respond
more favorably than spontaneously arising disease. Dogs with
vaccine-induced polyarthropathy have been reported to recover in 12 days without immunosuppressive drug therapy.13
In 7 healthy dogs given human albumin, 6 developed signs
consistent with immune-complex disease (5 of 7 developed
lameness).14 Signs developed 5 to 13 days after administration of
human albumin, and in surviving dogs, resolved after 2 to 37 days.

DISTANT NEOPLASIA
Polyarthropathy has been associated with carcinomas of tonsillar,
mammary, pancreatic and renal origin; seminoma; Sertoli cell
tumor; a splenic hyperplastic nodule; and leiomyoma. It can be
unclear if the cancer is causing polyarthropathy or if it represents a
coexisting condition. In cases where neoplasia is the inciting cause,
resolution of the neoplastic condition (for example, by surgical
removal) would be expected to eliminate polyarthropathy and
associated lameness. In many cases, joint pain is responsive to
immunosuppressive therapy, even if the primary neoplasm remains
untreated.

PRIMARY IMMUNE-MEDIATED
POLYARTHROPATHIES
NONEROSIVE PRIMARY IMMUNE-MEDIATED
POLYARTHROPATHY (IMPA)
Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (ch. 179)
SLE is defined as an immune-mediated polysystemic disorder, often
associated with a positive antinuclear antibody titer. The most
common manifestation of SLE is polyarthropathy. Diagnostic testing
reveals additional, immune-mediated manifestations that can
include proteinuria, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and
immune-mediated skin disease, and/or mucocutaneous or oral
ulcerations (ch. 178). Treatment of polyarthropathy associated with
SLE is the same as for idiopathic IMPA; however, additional
attention is given to monitoring for development and/or progression
of systemic disease manifestations.

Breed-Associated
Shar-Pei
Shar-Pei dogs can experience short (12- to 48-hour) recurrent bouts
of fever, accompanied by inflammation of joints (especially the
hocks, i.e., swollen hock syndrome). This disorder also is known as
familial Shar-Pei fever (FSF). Episodes typically are more frequent
during the first years of life and become less frequent with age.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) administration seems
helpful during episodes. The major constituent of the thickened skin
of Shar-Peis is hyaluronic acid (HA), and HA is overexpressed in
Shar-Peis compared with other canine breeds. The extent of
hyaluronanosis varies among individual Shar-Peis, although almost
all are affected. The administration of corticosteroids decreases
cutaneous mucinosis in Shar-Peis, perhaps by decreasing expression
of hyaluronan synthase.15 The role that excessive HA in Shar-Peis
plays in FSF needs to be investigated further. Shar-Pei dogs affected
with FSF are at risk of developing reactive systemic AA amyloidosis
and subsequent kidney or liver failure. Treatment of FSF-affected

Shar-Peis with colchicine (0.025-0.03 mg/kg [maximum dose: 0.6
mg/dog] PO q12h) has been recommended. The benefit of long-term
colchicine, corticosteroid, or other immunosuppressant
administration, however, remains to be published.

Akita
One report has described 8 Akita puppies (<8 months old) with
severe polyarthropathy.16 Only 2 of 8 were responsive to
antimicrobial and immunosuppressive therapy. Affected patients
were traced back to a common ancestor and this syndrome does not
appear to be widespread.

Idiopathic Immune-Mediated Polyarthritis (IMPA)
Once infectious agents and degenerative disease have been excluded,
an idiopathic, immune-mediated etiology is presumed.10,17-20 The
cause is felt to be an immune-system dyscrasia, either targeting the
joint directly or involving circulating immune complex (Arthus type
III) disease. Immunosuppression is associated with rapid clinical
response, and avoidance of medication-related side-effects is
paramount.

Signalment
Idiopathic immune-mediated polyarthritis is most commonly
diagnosed in 3- to 7-year-old dogs, although patients have been
diagnosed from 6 months to 12 years of age. There is no sex
predilection and all breeds can be affected. IMPA is rare in cats;
reported cases are young to middle-aged.

Physical Signs
Most cases present with a stiff gait and reluctance to stand and/or
walk (

Video 23.2). Anorexia, weight loss, and peripheral

lymphadenopathy can be present. Fever is reported in one-half of
affected patients. Joint swelling and pain often are detected, but in
some cases, these abnormalities are subtle (ch. 32). The carpal and
tarsal joints are preferentially affected. Polyarthritis can occur

concurrently with meningitis, polymyopathy, dermatopathy,
hepatopathy, gastroenteropathy, or as a paraneoplastic syndrome,
and physical findings can reflect concurrent disease. IMPA is a
common cause of fever of unknown origin (ch. 16) and the diagnosis
cannot be excluded by physical examination findings alone.21
Differential diagnoses include tick-borne/rickettsial disease,
hematogenous infectious processes (bacterial, fungal, protozoal),
meningitis, polymyositis, panosteitis, hypertrophic osteodystrophy,
degenerative joint disease, congenital lesions (i.e., elbow dysplasia,
osteochondritis dissecans lesions), and trauma.

Diagnostic Testing
In juvenile dogs, it is important to palpate the diaphysis and
metaphysis of long bones to differentiate polyarthritis (no signs of
pain expected from deep palpation at these locations) from
panosteitis or hypertrophic osteodystrophy (chs. 31 and 162). The
oral mucosa should be evaluated for ulceration (suggesting immunemediated disease [ch. 178], particularly SLE [ch. 179]) and the neck
palpated and manipulated for signs of resistance or pain consistent
with meningitis (chs. 242, 250). Auscultation can reveal a cardiac
murmur (chs. 38 and 232) suggestive of bacterial endocarditis. All
joints are evaluated for swelling, pain, range of motion and
instability. The carpi and tarsi are preferentially affected and should
receive special attention: palpation for evidence of joint effusion, and
gentle but firm hyperflexion for signs of pain are indicated (
Video 177.1). In the general dog population, stifle lameness
commonly is associated with cruciate ligament tear, rather than
polyarthritis, and careful evaluation must be performed to avoid
misdiagnosis.
Laboratory testing includes a CBC with manual differential,
platelet count, serum biochemical profile, and urinalysis. Mild
nonregenerative anemia and mild leukocytosis are common. The
presence of thrombocytopenia suggests tick-borne disease or
concurrent immune-mediated thrombocytopenia rather than
idiopathic disease. Marked elevations of liver enzyme activities can
prompt additional evaluation (bile acids, ultrasonography, and
possibly histopathologic examination of a liver biopsy specimen) to

assess for hepatopathy as a distant immunogenic stimulus.
Proteinuria should prompt evaluation of urinary protein/creatinine
ratio (ch. 302) and systemic blood pressure (ch. 91).
The need for imaging is evaluated on an individual basis. Thoracic
radiographs, joint radiographs, and abdominal ultrasonography are
most useful for patients with advanced age, joint instability, and/or
abnormalities on CBC, serum biochemistry profile, or urinalysis.
Joint radiographs are clearly indicated in non-responsive cases or in
those with joint instability; however, in most cases, at least at the
time of initial diagnosis, results are usually uninformative.22 Erosive
arthropathy, if it were present, might not be radiographically visible
at the time of initial evaluation and only be detected with repeated
assessment (Figure 177.1).
Antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor (RF) serologic titers
may be evaluated (ch. 179) (see “Erosive Immune-Mediated
Polyarthropathies,” below). Titers for tick-borne diseases may be
performed to help determine the cause of polyarthritis; however, in
areas where these diseases are endemic, a course of anti-rickettsial
antibiotics (doxycycline or minocycline) is always recommended.
Because signs of illness can precede development of serum
antibodies, acute rickettsial disease cannot be excluded based on
negative serum titers. Conversely, in endemic areas, subclinical
(“asymptomatic”) seroconversion to tick-borne agents is common.
Most practically, failure to respond to a 3-5 day course of appropriate
antibiotic therapy excludes the diagnosis of rickettsial disease.

FIGURE 177.1 A, Dorsoplantar radiograph of a
canine tarsal joint, demonstrating extensive
subchondral bone destruction, and moderate
periarticular soft-tissue swelling. These findings are
consistent with the diagnosis of erosive arthritis. B,
Normal canine tarsal joint for comparison.
Arthrocentesis is fundamental to the diagnosis of inflammatory
joint disorders. The technique is described in ch. 87. At least four
joints (for example, both carpi and both tarsi) are routinely sampled,
regardless of physical examination findings. Abnormal synovial fluid
can be detected in the absence of either pain or joint swelling. It is
common to obtain <0.2 mL of synovial fluid and in many cases only
slides for cytologic evaluation can be prepared. Larger volumes allow

culture and/or nucleated cell counts; however, slide preparation is
sufficient for diagnostic purposes in most cases.

Interpretation of Synovial Fluid Cytology
Degenerative joint disease, trauma, and previous ligament injury are
associated with mononuclear inflammation (<10% neutrophils in
synovial fluid) whereas immune-mediated and infectious diseases
are associated with >10% neutrophils (ch. 71). Blood contamination
alters the differential cell count and makes the interpretation of
inflammation less certain. In the presence of marked blood
contamination, cytologic results from additional joints, along with
comparison to peripheral blood counts, must be utilized.

Treatment (Dogs)
Corticosteroids (prednisone, prednisolone; ch. 144) are highly
effective. Prednisone 1-2 mg/kg PO q24h is started initially; lower
dosages can be effective in less severe cases. High dosages are
administered until the disease is in complete remission, defined as
resolution of clinical signs as well as laboratory changes (anemia,
thrombocytopenia, and/or proteinuria) that were present initially.
After remission is attained, the dosage is tapered, generally by 50%,
approximately every 4 weeks. Prior to each dosage decrease,
reevaluation is performed and if signs of disease are absent (on
physical examination and laboratory evaluation), the dosage is
halved again. The prednisone dosage is decreased monthly by 50%
until the animal either relapses or medication is discontinued. The
recommended minimum duration of therapy is 4 months.
Polyarthritis temporally related to vaccination or drug
administration may not require as long a duration of therapy.
Combination immunosuppressive therapy with the addition of
mycophenolate mofetil often is more effective, and produces fewer
adverse effects, than corticosteroid therapy alone because the initial
dosage of prednisone is lower in combination therapy than in
monotherapy and it is tapered more quickly (ch. 169). Prednisone (1
mg/kg PO q12-24h) and mycophenolate (10 mg/kg PO q12h) are
administered in combination. The dosage of prednisone is tapered
25-50% every 2 weeks while mycophenolate is continued at the same
dosage. The goal is to discontinue corticosteroids completely and

maintain remission with mycophenolate alone. If, after 2 months,
remission is maintained on mycophenolate alone, the dosage is
decreased by 50%, and after 2 months at the decreased dose,
mycophenolate is discontinued. Animals that relapse after
discontinuation of mycophenolate are reinduced with a short course
of prednisone; mycophenolate is then continued for life at 10 mg/kg
q12-24h. Side-effects of mycophenolate are generally mild (diarrhea)
and hematologic side-effects are uncommon.
Inability to control the signs of IMPA using mycophenolate
monotherapy may prompt a change of therapy or therapeutic drug
monitoring (ch. 169). If mycophenolate is discontinued, either
leflunomide (2-3 mg/kg PO q24h) or cyclosporine (5 mg/kg q12h)
can be administered together with corticosteroids. Corticosteroids
are again tapered, with the goal of complete discontinuation. If good
control is maintained for several months on leflunomide alone, the
dosage may be gradually tapered (2-3 mg/kg PO q48h × 3 months,
then q72h × 3 months, and then discontinued). If good control is
maintained for several months on cyclosporine alone, the dosage
may be gradually tapered (5 mg/kg q24h × 3 months, then 5 mg/kg
q48 h × 3 months, and then discontinued). Relapses are treated with
a short course of corticosteroids and the dosage of
immunosuppressant that previously maintained remission. Sideeffects of leflunomide or cyclosporine generally are mild (anorexia,
lethargy, vomiting); however, CBCs and serum biochemical profiles
should be monitored.23,24
Patients receiving NSAIDs (carprofen, meloxicam, deracoxib, etc.)
when IMPA is diagnosed require special attention. When combined
with NSAIDs, corticosteroids are associated with a prohibitively high
risk of gastrointestinal ulceration. Therefore, the two should never be
coadministered. For any transition from NSAIDs to corticosteroids,
NSAIDs should be discontinued with a 7-day “washout” period prior
to corticosteroid administration. Administration of mycophenolate,
leflunomide, or cyclosporine may begin during this washout period
and alternative pain medications (acetaminophen [dogs only],
amantadine, gabapentin) started (ch. 6). After 7 days,
corticosteroids may be added if there is a lack of response to initial
therapy.

Lack of response or initial response but inability to taper
corticosteroids may prompt consultation with an internal medicine
specialist. Alternative immunosuppressants may include
azathioprine, chlorambucil, or cyclophosphamide.

Treatment (Cats)
Some cats do not respond to prednisone and an alternate
corticosteroid (prednisolone, methylprednisolone, triamcinolone, or
dexamethasone) needs to be substituted. Chlorambucil may be
administered along with corticosteroids for cats that require
additional immunosuppression. Chlorambucil is dosed at 15 mg/m2
PO q24h (often 4 mg/cat/day) for 4 days, and the 4-day treatment is
repeated every 3 weeks. Alternatively, 2 mg chlorambucil (total dose
per cat) may be administered every 2 to 3 days. Potential side-effects
can include anorexia and bone marrow suppression. In cats, the
dosage of chlorambucil should be tapered before the prednisolone is
tapered. Treatment with methotrexate and leflunomide also have
been described (see “Rheumatoid Arthritis,” below).

Follow-up
The need for and timing of reevaluation are dependent on the clinical
response of the patient, requirement for monitoring of concurrent
disease, laboratory abnormalities, and avoidance of drug-related
side-effects. Since the expected response of idiopathic IMPA cases is
good with corticosteroid administration, a lack of response to
corticosteroids within 7 days should prompt reevaluation. This
should include reconsideration of the diagnosis, assessment of the
dosage and proper administration of drugs, and consideration of
possible drug-related side-effects.
Previous laboratory abnormalities (anemia, thrombocytopenia, or
proteinuria) should be monitored. Rapid resolution of
thrombocytopenia, gradual resolution of anemia (most commonly
due to anemia of chronic disease with resolution over several weeks)
and either slow resolution (months) or stability of proteinuria are
expected. Administration of corticosteroids is associated with
proteinuria (mean urine protein to creatinine ratio in healthy dogs
increases from 0.29 ± 0.10 without corticosteroids to a maximum of

1.27 ± 1.02 after 28 days of prednisone 2.2 mg/kg PO q12h)25 and
this effect must be considered. Progressive proteinuria can suggest
glomerular injury, and standard treatment for glomerular disease
can be warranted in such cases. The skin and urinary tract should be
monitored for infection.
Repeated/serial arthrocentesis is not routinely recommended;
instead, patients are monitored by clinical evaluation. In selected
cases with joint instability or concurrent degenerative change,
repeated synovial fluid analysis could be needed to determine if
lameness is due to inadequate control of immune-mediated disease.
C-reactive protein cannot be recommended as a serologic marker of
clinical response.26

Prognosis
A rapid response to immunosuppressant therapy is expected in most
cases (90%). Some patients respond promptly and can be tapered off
medication completely. Many others will respond but require some
dosage of immunosuppressant to avoid relapse. Some (10%) fail to
respond and suffer continued lameness along with progressive joint
damage. Many patients suffer side-effects related to corticosteroid
therapy, especially when long-term administration is needed. Many
dogs are euthanized due to these effects and an important goal is
avoidance of medication-related harm. Weight gain is a serious
problem; many owners are unaware of it and body condition should
be carefully monitored (chs. 72 and 145). One successful strategy to
decrease glucocorticoid-induced adverse effects is the use of an
additional immunosuppressive agent, as described above and in ch.
169. Administration of mycophenolate, cyclosporine, or leflunomide
is—for most patients—safer than long-term corticosteroid
monotherapy.

EROSIVE IMMUNE-MEDIATED
POLYARTHROPATHIES
Erosive arthritis is distinguished by the presence of radiographically
visible subchondral bone lysis (Figure 177.1). Destruction of

supportive joint ligaments leads to joint instability and luxation.

Breed-Associated
A severely erosive polyarthritis has been described in young
Greyhounds.27 A single case suggested Mycoplasma spumans as the
causative agent; however, Mycoplasma was not isolated from two
additional Greyhounds. The true cause is unknown and the
prognosis is guarded to poor. Ten Border Collies with trapped
neutrophil syndrome have been described in Australia, New Zealand,
Japan, Israel, and recently, the United States.28 Affected dogs
develop failure to thrive, fever, gastrointestinal signs, lameness, joint
swelling, and neutropenia before 4 months of age. Neutropenia is
typically mild to moderate. The early radiographic findings of
trapped neutrophil syndrome include metaphyseal lucencies
surrounded by sclerosis in the distal femur, tibia, radius and/or ulna
and with time, erosive joint lesions appear. Differentiation from
hypertrophic osteodystrophy may be challenging before joint erosion
is seen. The diagnosis of trapped neutrophil syndrome can be
confirmed by commercially available testing for the BPS13B gene
mutation. Treatment is supportive and nonspecific. The prognosis is
guarded.

Feline Periosteal Proliferative Arthritis
Erosive joint disease in cats includes two syndromes: one showing
marked periosteal new bone formation (periosteal proliferative
form), and another showing minimal periosteal new bone formation
(rheumatoid arthritis).29 Treatment is as for rheumatoid arthritis
(see below).

Rheumatoid Arthritis
In dogs and cats, rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a rare disorder
characterized by inflammation, articular cartilage loss, erosion of
periarticular bone, and joint deformation. Many patients have a
positive RF serologic test result. The cause of RA is unknown and the
prognosis guarded. Many patients become severely disabled despite
treatment.

RA is suspected by the presence of radiographically visible erosive
lesions and/or joint instability. The age at diagnosis in dogs averages
5 years. Approximately one-third of cases exhibit fever, lethargy
and/or inappetence in addition to lameness.30,31 Most dogs
demonstrate joint pain, decreased range of motion, and palpable
evidence of joint effusion (ch. 32). Joint deformation suggests
erosive disease, although ligament laxity may also occur in
nonerosive cases.32 Although by definition RA is a disease that
involves the joints, other body systems also can be affected.
Feline RA is very rare. Gradual onset of stiffness with swollen and
painful joints is typical. Radiographically, erosive polyarthritis in the
cat has been separated into one group with primarily bone lysis (RA)
and another with marked periosteal proliferation adjacent to joints
(periosteal proliferative polyarthritis). It is unclear if these diseases
are separate entities or if they represent different manifestations of
the same disease process.
RF is a collective term for autoantibodies against IgG. These
antibodies are thought to play a role in opsonization and elimination
of immune complexes. Serum RF levels can be elevated in any
inflammatory disease, and the utility of the test is limited by lack of
specificity for RA. Approximately 70% of dogs with clinically
diagnosed RA are positive for RF; therefore, its absence does not
exclude the diagnosis. The concentration of RF, if present, can be
useful to follow the course of disease: a decrease in RF
concentrations can be associated with effective therapy and an
increase with relapse of disease.

Diagnosis
Diagnostic testing includes a CBC with manual differential, platelet
count, serum biochemical profile, urinalysis, radiographs of the
thorax and of affected joints, and synovial fluid analysis (chs. 71,
87). Cats may be tested for feline leukemia virus and feline
immunodeficiency virus. Radiographic findings include loss of bone
at the epiphyses, narrowing of joint spaces, and irregular joint
margins. Erosive mono- or oligoarthropathies prompt synovial fluid
culture for bacteria, Mycoplasma spp., and if possible, L-form
bacteria. Most cases initially are treated with antibiotics pending

results of culture. Doxycycline, minocycline, or a fluoroquinolone is
the drug of choice.

Treatment
Immunosuppression is the mainstay of therapy for immunemediated erosive arthritis. Prednisone and mycophenolate, as
described above for treatment of IMPA, are recommended for dogs.
Treatment of cats with methotrexate 7.5 mg PO once a week (q 7
days) and leflunomide 10 mg PO q24h has been described with
marked improvement in 7 of 12 treated cats.33 When clinical
improvement occurred, the dosage was decreased to 2.5 mg
methotrexate once a week and 10 mg leflunomide every 3-4 days
(twice a week). Serious signs of toxicosis were not noted.
Drugs used in humans with RA include the interleukin-1
antagonist anakinra and the tumor necrosis factor-alpha inhibitors
infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumab pegol, golimumab, and
etanercept. There are no published reports of their use in dogs with
RA. Adalimumab was used in 2 dogs with dermatopathy.34

Prognosis
RA is a relentlessly progressive disorder and most patients
experience joint deterioration over time. Small dogs can fare
reasonably well despite obvious joint deformation; larger dogs less
well. Pain medications (acetaminophen [dogs only], gabapentin,
amantadine) often are needed (chs. 6 and 256). Surgical procedures
occasionally can be used for improving joint stability and pain;
synovectomy, arthroplasty, joint replacement, and/or arthrodesis
can be beneficial in selected patients.35 Monitoring for side-effects of
immunosuppressive medications (ch. 227) as well as systemic
manifestations of immune-mediated disease is suggested.

Immune-mediated skin diseases result from a broad spectrum of
aberrant immune responses that damage the skin and/or skin
adnexae. Most of these diseases are rare to very rare. Indeed, based
on reported data, immune-mediated skin diseases (excluding
hypersensitivity) account for <5% of all canine and feline
dermatoses.1,2 Because of their rarity, they often present a diagnostic
challenge for clinicians. Depending on the pathogenesis, these
diseases can present with a variety of skin lesions, including
pustules, vesicles, erosions, papules, nodules, or even draining tracts.
Diagnosis is often dependent on histopathologic features and,
therefore, proper lesion selection for a biopsy (ch. 83) is a key step
in the diagnostic process. Secondary bacterial infection is common
and should be resolved prior to skin biopsy, whenever possible. The
proper biopsy site depends on the lesion type and suspected etiology
based on the relevant list of differential diagnoses—key examples are
i) an entire pustule or vesicle, ii) the margin between intact and
eroded skin, iii) the center of alopecia, iv) the center of atrophy and
scarring and v) the excision of an entire papule/nodule. Four to five
biopsy specimens should be collected whenever possible. This
chapter provides an overview of selected immune-mediated
dermatoses and, at the end, a summary of treatment principles.

IMMUNE-MEDIATED SKIN DISEASES
ASSOCIATED WITH PUSTULES,
SUPERFICIAL EROSIONS, AND CRUSTS
PEMPHIGUS FOLIACEUS (PF)
This is the most common autoimmune skin disease of dogs and
cats.3 It is caused by autoantibodies that disrupt desmosomal
adhesion between keratinocytes and induce keratinocyte

acantholysis and subcorneal pustules. Desmocollin-1 is a major
target autoantigen in canine PF, which in cats remains unknown.4
The majority of affected dogs and cats are middle-aged (5-6 years).3,5
The primary, and diagnostically most valuable, skin lesion is the
subcorneal pustule, but, because of its fragility, superficial erosions
and crusts are the most common lesion types found in dogs and cats.
The face, particularly the nasal planum, dorsal muzzle, periocular
areas, and the concave pinnae are often affected (Figure 178.1).
Symmetrical lesion distribution is typical. Pawpad involvement is
frequent, and helpful when trying to distinguish PF from other
similar-appearing diseases such as impetigo and superficial pustular
dermatophytosis. More than half of PF-affected dogs and cats will
exhibit a more generalized phenotype, with lesions on the trunk. In
insecticide-triggered PF, a clinical entity described recently in
association with flea preventatives such as Promeris Duo, Certifect
and Vectra 3D, the initial lesion is always present at the application
site. In most of these dogs, lesions may become generalized and
mimic naturally occurring PF.6-8 Lethargy, anorexia, and even fever
can be seen in up to 50% of affected dogs and cats.
The pustule is the best lesion type for cytologic evaluation or
biopsy, whenever PF is suspected. As it is not always present, crusted
areas overlying active erosions with exudation can be biopsied
instead. Neutrophilic or mixed neutrophilic and eosinophilic
subcorneal pustules with acantholysis are the hallmark of this
disease. However, acantholysis is not specific for PF and can be
detected in pyoderma (e.g., impetigo) or pustular dermatophytosis.
Therefore, the diagnosis of PF is based on the combination of: i) skin
lesion type and distribution, ii) exclusion of infectious causes, and iii)
supportive cytologic/histopathologic findings.

IMMUNE-MEDIATED SKIN DISEASES
ASSOCIATED WITH VESICLES/BULLAE
AND DEEP EROSIONS
PEMPHIGUS VULGARIS (PV)

This is a very rare autoimmune blistering skin disease of dogs and
cats caused by antibody-mediated targeting of desmoglein 3, a key
deep epidermal adhesion protein.9 As a response, deep suprabasal
acantholysis leads to vesicle formation, which rapidly progresses to
deep erosions and ulcers. In contrast to PF, PV usually affects both
mucosae and haired skin, and is associated with anorexia, lethargy,
fever and/or halitosis in most affected individuals. Histopathologic
evaluation of an intact vesicle or of a sample collected from the
margin of eroded and intact skin is necessary to differentiate this
disease from paraneoplastic pemphigus, autoimmune subepidermal
blistering skin diseases (AISBDs), erythema multiforme (EM), some
presentations of vasculitis (ch. 181), idiopathic lymphoplasmacytic
stomatitis (ch. 258), or some ulcerative viral diseases such as feline
calicivirus and herpesvirus-1 (ch. 205).

PARANEOPLASTIC PEMPHIGUS (PNP)
This is a very rare paraneoplastic skin disease resembling PV and
EM, likely because both pathomechanisms, i.e., suprabasal
acantholysis and single-cell apoptosis at multiple epidermal levels,
have been discovered to play a role in lesion development. Dogs and
cats affected with PNP show acute and rapidly progressive erosive
mucosal and haired skin lesions as well as extracutaneous signs such
as lethargy, anorexia, weight loss, fever and signs attributable to the
underlying neoplasia. Histopathologic examination of a sample
collected from the margin of eroded and intact skin/mucosa is
necessary to confirm the diagnosis of PNP and rule out resembling
diseases such as PV, AISBDs and EM. Management of PNP requires
identification and elimination of the primary neoplasm. Other
paraneoplastic syndromes are discussed in ch. 331.

FIGURE 178.1 Canine and feline pemphigus
foliaceus. Characteristic skin lesions consist of
pustules, erosions and crusts involving the nasal
planum and dorsal nose (A, B, E), concave pinnae
(C) and pawpads (D, G). In cats, the area of the

nipple (F) and claw folds (H) are frequently
affected.

AUTOIMMUNE SUBEPIDERMAL
BLISTERING SKIN DISEASES (AISBDs)
These disorders are recognized rarely in dogs and, even more rarely,
in cats. The three most common diseases are mucous membrane
pemphigoid (MMP),10 epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA)11 and
bullous pemphigoid (BP).12 The common pathomechanism is the
autoimmune attack on structural proteins on the dermo-epidermal
junction, which leads to dermo-epidermal separation, and formation
of tense vesicles/bullae. These lesions rapidly progress to deep
erosions and ulcers.
Biopsies of either intact vesicles/bullae and/or from the margin of
intact and eroded skin are suitable for histopathologic examination,
which is necessary to confirm the diagnosis of AISBD and exclude
relevant differential diagnoses such as mucocutaneous lupus
erythematosus (MCLE), PV, PNP, EM, some presentations of
vasculitis (ch. 181), idiopathic lymphoplasmacytic stomatitis (ch.
258), or some ulcerative viral diseases such as feline calicivirus and
herpesvirus-1 (ch. 205). Histopathologic evaluation, however, is
unable to reliably differentiate between the specific diseases.
Unfortunately, the ability to identify the specific AISBD in veterinary
medicine is further limited by the lack of commercially-available
immunological testing (e.g., direct immunofluorescence [IF],
indirect IF on salt-split mucosa, antigen-specific enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assay).13 Therefore, differentiation of these diseases
relies heavily on clinical information, especially on lesion
distribution and signalment.
Mucous membrane pemphigoid is a chronic AISBD with lesions
affecting exclusively mucosae and/or mucocutaneous junctions
(Figure 178.2). Haired skin lesions, if present, are usually very
minor and often located on the concave pinnae.10 Systemic signs are
usually not observed.

EBA is a severe blistering skin disease with a relatively acute onset,
and lesions affect both mucosae/mucocutaneous junctions as well as
haired skin. Pawpad sloughing is frequent (Figure 178.2), and
patients often suffer with fever, lethargy, anorexia, and pain; the
latter is usually associated with the mucosal and pawpad sloughing.
Unlike other blistering skin diseases, EBA is often seen in relatively
young dogs and Great Danes are over-represented.11
In contrast, the diagnosis of BP is usually made in older adult dogs
with haired skin involvement, with or without very mild mucosal
lesions. Systemic signs usually are not observed, though some dogs
may have a decreased appetite and lethargy.

IMMUNE-MEDIATED SKIN DISEASES
ASSOCIATED WITH
DYSPIGMENTATION AND SCARRING,
WITH OR WITHOUT EROSIONS
This category includes cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE), which
is covered in ch. 179.

IMMUNE-MEDIATED SKIN DISEASES
ASSOCIATED WITH PRIMARY
EROSIONS
ERYTHEMA MULTIFORME (EM), STEVENSJOHNSON SYNDROME (SJS) AND TOXIC
EPIDERMAL NECROLYSIS (TEN)
These are immune-mediated, epidermal necrotizing diseases
characterized by lymphocyte-mediated cytotoxic attack on
keratinocytes, causing a deep erosive dermatitis that spares the
dermis. In people, EM is triggered by infection with herpes simplex
virus or mycoplasma, while SJS and TEN are separate entities that
are mostly considered to be drug reactions. In veterinary medicine,

such a distinction has not been made yet, possibly because of the lack
of typical target lesions in EM and the lack of knowledge about the
pathogenesis of EM (reviewed in 14). EM minor and major have been
described in both dogs and cats. In many cases, a drug reaction was
considered to be the trigger, although EM-type lesions were
described in a cat and dog with thymoma.15 An infectious trigger has
yet to be confirmed. Animals with EM usually present with
erythematous to purpuric macules and papules that often acquire
central clearing (i.e., targetoid lesions). Erythroderma in EM cases
does not exceed 50% of the body surface area (BSA). The
erythematous skin often becomes eroded and/or crusty, but the
epidermal detachment does not exceed 10% of BSA in both EM
minor and major. It is the number of affected mucosae that dictates
the diagnosis of EM minor (0-1 mucosa) or EM major (>1 mucosa).
Mucosa-exclusive involvement has been seen in some animals (i.e.,
“oral EM”). Systemic signs are usually not observed in EM minor,
but animals described as having EM major are often systemically ill
(lethargy, anorexia, depression).14,16

FIGURE 178.2 Canine mucous membrane
pemphigoid (MMP) and epidermolysis bullosa
acquisita (EBA). Characteristic skin lesions consist of
deep erosions and ulcers on hard palate and anus
(MMP) and typical pawpad sloughing often seen in
dogs with EBA. Photos courtesy Dr. H.L. Tham, case
material NCSU [MMP].

FIGURE 178.3 Toxic epidermal necrolysis in a
dog. Painful, generalized, patchy to diffuse
erythroderma (>70% of body surface area) with deep
erosions and ulcers (>50% of body surface area
detached) affecting the haired skin. No mucosal
involvement was observed in this patient.
SJS, TEN, and SJS/TEN overlap and are severe, often lifethreatening drug reactions with a sudden onset and rapid
progression of skin lesions and systemic signs. The most commonly
associated drugs include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
(NSAIDs) (e.g., carprofen) (ch. 143), antibiotics (ch. 140) (e.g.,
sulphonamides, amoxicillin, cephalosporins, penicillin),
phenobarbital and others.17-19 The distinction between the 3 types is
solely based on the percentage of BSA with epidermal detachment:
SJS <10%, TEN >30%, SJS/TEN overlap 10-30%. Mucosal
involvement is variable. In contrast to EM, the BSA with
erythroderma in SJS exceeds 50%. The calculation of the percentage
of BSA can be estimated by using a diagram designed for animals
with thermal injuries (the “rule of 9”).20 Early lesions are
characterized by patchy to diffuse and very painful erythroderma to
purpura, which rapidly progresses to deep erosions (Figure 178.3).
Gentle pressure with a gloved finger will slough the epithelium in
areas of erythroderma. Haired skin exhibits the most severe lesions,
while mucosal involvement is not seen in every case. Corneal
sloughing has been reported in one animal.21 Systemic signs such as
severe depression, anorexia, pain, hyperthermia or hypothermia are
observed early in the disease course and progress with time. These
diseases present true dermatological emergencies with a high

mortality rate. The mortality is mostly due to secondary
complications such as sepsis (ch. 128), acute kidney injury (ch.
300), hypoalbuminemia (ch. 60), dehydration, and organ
hypoperfusion leading to multi-organ failure (TEN>SJS).
Additionally, animals with epidermal sloughing have disruptions in
thermoregulation and, therefore, should be kept in warmer rooms to
prevent hypothermia. The diagnosis is based on the clinical picture
and histopathologic evaluation. In cases of EM, histopathologic
examination is necessary to rule out similar-appearing diseases such
as PV, PNP, AISBDs, MCLE, vesicular CLE (VCLE), herpesvirus
dermatitis, calicivirus, idiopathic lymphoplasmacytic stomatitis,
sterile neutrophilic dermatitis (Sweet’s syndrome), canine acute
eosinophilic dermatitis and edema (CAEDE), and others. In SJS and
TEN, rapid confirmation of a diagnosis and initiation of proper
treatment are critically important. Therefore, a presumptive
diagnosis based on the acute onset of characteristic skin lesions
accompanied by severe systemic signs is usually made promptly by a
trained dermatologist, to allow immediate initiation of treatment.
Samples for histopathologic evaluation are collected from
erythematous skin or from a margin between eroded and intact
skin/mucosa to confirm the diagnosis. Stat frozen-section histologic
examination may be considered in cases in which the clinical
diagnosis cannot be confidently established. Histopathologic features
do not reliably distinguish EM from SJS or TEN, and differentiation
is dependent on clinical assessment and % BSA affected.

IMMUNE-MEDIATED SKIN DISEASES
ASSOCIATED WITH PRIMARY
DEPIGMENTATION WITH OR WITHOUT
EPIDERMAL INJURY
UVEODERMATOLOGICAL SYNDROME (UDS)
This is a disease recognized in dogs that resembles Vogt-KoyanagiHarada (VKH) syndrome in people (reviewed in 22). Lymphocytemediated attack of melanocytes leads to a cutaneous and/or mucosal
depigmentation, sometimes accompanied by leukotrichia. Erosions,

ulcers, and crusts in depigmented areas are fairly common, which
are most prominent on the muzzle, lips and eyelids (Figure 178.4).
Uveitis frequently precedes the skin lesions. During the active
disease state, dogs are often lethargic and have a reduced appetite.
Neurological signs such as a head tilt and a cranial nerve II deficit
have been reported also (ch. 241). Young adult Akitas, Samoyeds,
and Siberian Huskies are susceptible to this disease and males are
reported twice as commonly as females. Other breeds have been
described to suffer with this disease.22 Confirmation of the diagnosis
is fairly straightforward when both skin and uveitis are present. In
cases with skin lesions only, histopathologic assessment is needed to
rule out relevant differential diagnoses such as vitiligo, PV, facial
discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE), MCLE, AISBDs, EM, and
epitheliotropic lymphoma. In these cases, biopsy should be collected
from erythematous, newly depigmenting skin/mucosa and/or from
the margin between erosion and intact skin.

IMMUNE-MEDIATED SKIN DISEASES
ASSOCIATED WITH PRIMARY
ALOPECIA WITH OR WITHOUT
EXCESSIVE SCALING AND FOLLICULAR
CASTING
There are several diseases in which inflammation targets either hair
follicles or sebaceous glands and leads to alopecia, with or without
scaling and follicular casting. These include, for example, alopecia
areata, pseudopelade, granulomatous mural folliculitis, thymoma,
and non-thymoma-associated exfoliative dermatitis and sebaceous
adenitis.23-28 The etiology of most of these diseases remains
unknown, although some conditions have been associated with a
drug reaction (e.g., granulomatous mural folliculitis in a cat treated
with methimazole)29 or cancer (thymoma-associated exfoliative
dermatitis in cats, alopecia areata and testicular neoplasia).26,30
Clinical signs and exclusion of more common hair follicle-targeting
diseases such as demodicosis, dermatophytosis, bacterial folliculitis,

or endocrinopathies should be made before performing a skin
biopsy. Histopathologic confirmation is required to establish the
diagnosis and multiple punch biopsies that are at least 8 mm in
diameter should be collected from fully developed alopecia with or
without scaling.

FIGURE 178.4 Uveodermatological syndrome in a
cross-breed dog. Depigmentation affecting the nasal
planum, eyelids and lips with a loss of epidermal
architecture (atrophy) and deep erosions/ulcers.
Note the ocular changes caused by chronic uveitis.

IMMUNE-MEDIATED SKIN DISEASES
ASSOCIATED WITH NAIL LOSS
SYMMETRIC LUPOID ONYCHITIS (SLO)
This is an immune-mediated disease recognized in dogs in which a
lymphocyte-mediated attack on the nail bed epithelium is suspected.
As a result, affected dogs manifest nail pain (onychalgia) and
sloughing (onychomadesis; Figure 178.5, A). Regrown nails are
short, misshapen, dry, soft/brittle, and crumbly. Although the initial
nail loss may affect one to a few nails, very rapidly, the majority of
nails become affected, which is a useful diagnostic clue. Indeed, in an
overall healthy dog with nail loss affecting the majority of its digits,
and without other skin issues, a diagnosis of SLO can be made
clinically, without any additional tests. If histopathologic evaluation
is considered, a biopsy containing the nail bed region of the affected

nail is required. Therefore, many veterinarians will elect to amputate
a dewclaw, if dewclaws are affected. Relevant differential diagnoses
for dogs with a single to few sloughed nails during early disease
include injury and infection (fungal, bacterial). Many breeds have
been diagnosed with SLO, although Gordon Setters and German
Shepherds appear to be predisposed.

OTHER IMMUNE-MEDIATED SKIN
DISEASES WITH SYSTEMIC SIGNS
JUVENILE CELLULITIS (JC)
This is an uncommon granulomatous skin disease of puppies (often 3
weeks to 5 months of age; occasionally adult dogs can be affected) of
unknown etiology.31 Genetic predisposition and vaccine reactions
are thought to play a role. Golden and Labrador Retrievers,
Dachshunds, Gordon Setters, Cocker Spaniels and, recently,
Goldendoodles and Labradoodles, are some of the more frequently
affected breeds. Puppies with JC may present with prodromal signs
such as fever, lethargy, depression, anorexia and severe
lymphadenopathy (submandibular) prior to developing skin lesions.
Early cutaneous signs include swelling of the muzzle, lips, eyelid, and
pinnae, which rapidly progress to painful, erythematous to
hemorrhagic papules, pustules, ulcers, and draining tracts (Figure
178.5, B). Other mucocutaneous junctions may be involved (e.g.,
anus, perigenital). In some puppies, lesions of sterile nodular
dermatitis and panniculitis can occur concurrently (see below).
Lameness, arthritis, spinal epidural abscesses, and paresis have been
described in rare cases.31-34 The diagnosis is usually made based on
typical clinical presentation and sterile pyogranulomatous
inflammation on cytologic evaluation from intact hemorrhagic
papules or recently developed ulcers. Differential diagnoses in dogs
with milder lesions, or those without lymphadenopathy, include deep
pyoderma, demodicosis, and eosinophilic furunculosis. Older
ulcerated lesions should be checked for secondary pyoderma, which
can complicate the treatment process and delay recovery.

STERILE NODULAR DERMATITIS AND
PANNICULITIS (SNDP)
This is an uncommon syndrome of unknown etiology recognized in
juvenile and adult dogs of various breeds, although Dachshunds,
Golden and Labrador Retrievers, Boxers, Collies, and Miniature
Poodles are more frequently affected (reviewed in 35).
Dermatological signs include deep dermal and/or subcutaneous,
variably firm papules and nodules, which are most often on the trunk
and proximal limbs. The overlying skin can appear normal or exhibit
erythema (Figure 178.5, C). Lytic necrosis causes these lesions to
ulcerate and drain an oily, hemopurulent exudate (Figure 178.5,
D). These lesions are variably painful (mild to severe), and affected
dogs may or may not exhibit systemic signs such as fever, lethargy,
anorexia, and lameness. Some dogs may exhibit lesions on their
eyelids and muzzle, which are similar to those seen in JC (see above).
Relevant differential diagnoses include infectious panniculitis
(Mycobacterium, Nocardia, Actinomyces, fungi, oomycetes, algae),
foreign body, reactive histiocytosis, and pancreatic panniculitis. The
diagnosis is confirmed by a combination of clinical and laboratory
findings and microscopic evaluation of the nodules. Fine needle
aspiration cytology of nodules should be performed, as should
excisional biopsy of nodules for histopathologic evaluation, including
special staining for infectious agents, and for tissue culture and/or
polymerase chain reaction.

FIGURE 178.5 Immune-mediated skin diseases.

CANINE ACUTE EOSINOPHILIC
DERMATITIS WITH EDEMA (WELLSLIKE SYNDROME) (CAEDE)
This is a rare inflammatory disease of dogs. The majority of affected
dogs have a history of recent, or concurrent, gastrointestinal (GI)
disease. The etiology remains unknown; adverse drug reaction has
been hypothesized, but not confirmed.36,37 Cutaneous signs include
an acute onset of maculopapular erythroderma (Figure 178.5, E),
which can coalesce into larger and more diffuse plaques. Because of
the prominent edema, some lesions may not fully blanch on diascopy
(

Video 12.1). Pruritus is usually not a feature, and the majority of

dogs do not exhibit obvious systemic signs (beyond those associated
with the GI issues). Laboratory findings are inconsistent, with
hypoalbuminemia being the most common finding. Peripheral blood
eosinophilia is not a common finding. The diagnosis is made based
on a combination of history and clinical signs. Histopathologic
evaluation of erythematous papules/plaques collected from the
center of these lesions (not a margin) confirms eosinophilic
dermatitis with edema, and rules out similar-appearing diseases
such as urticaria, sterile neutrophilic dermatitis, toxic shock
syndrome, urticarial vasculitis, sterile pustular erythroderma of
Miniature Schnauzers, and EM.

STERILE NEUTROPHILIC DERMATITIS
(SWEET’S-LIKE SYNDROME) (SLS)
This is a very rare inflammatory disorder recognized in dogs. An
adverse drug reaction (NSAIDs were implemented in several
previously published cases) has been suggested as a possible
trigger.37,38 Cutaneous lesions overlap with those described in
CAEDE, although formation of pustules appears to be more specific
to SLS. These dogs, in contrast to those with CAEDE, exhibit more
severe systemic signs including fever, anorexia, lethargy, depression,
polyarthritis, peripheral lymphadenopathy, and/or pneumonia and
have frequent abnormalities on their complete blood count and
biochemistry profiles (e.g., neutrophilia, lymphopenia,
thrombocytopenia, elevated liver enzymes, hypoalbuminemia).
Histopathologic examination of erythematous papules/plaques from
the center of the lesions, together with a thorough clinical
assessment, is necessary to rule out resembling diseases such as toxic
shock syndrome, CAEDE, urticarial vasculitis, and EM. These
clinical, laboratory, and histological features closely overlap those of
a condition called sterile pustular erythroderma of Miniature
Schnauzers (Figure 178.5, F). This disease is suspected to be a
form of adverse drug reaction. Interestingly, due to the onset of the
condition shortly (within 2 days) after bathing, shampoo application
has been implicated as one of the triggers.39
Both SLS and sterile pustular erythroderma of Miniature
Schnauzers have a higher risk of mortality; therefore, rapid
recognition and treatment initiation (including supportive care) are
critical.

IMMUNE-MEDIATED SKIN DISEASES:
TREATMENT PRINCIPLES
In veterinary medicine, systemic immunosuppression is the
cornerstone of management of currently recognized immunemediated skin diseases. Because most of these diseases are rare,
treatment guidelines are non-existent and the evidence of efficacy of

various treatment regimens remains limited to case reports and
small, often retrospective, case series. Treatment selection should be
tailored to the patient and should consider the patient’s general
health status and individual risk for developing treatment-associated
side-effects. The goal of the initial treatment phase is to achieve
rapid disease control and disease remission. This initial step is often
accomplished by using broadly and rapidly acting drugs such as
glucocorticoids (ch. 144) at standard immunosuppressive dosages
or with high-dose pulse therapy.40 Because of the high risk of sideeffects associated with long-term use of glucocorticoids, and because
many immune-mediated skin diseases require long-term
management, non-steroidal immunosuppressive drugs are often
started during this initial phase or shortly after (e.g., azathioprine,
mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, colchicine,
doxycycline/niacinamide, etc.) (ch. 169).
As soon as no new lesions have formed for at least 2 weeks and the
majority of old lesions (>80%) have healed, a tapering of the drug
dosages can be started. Glucocorticoids are usually the first drug to
be tapered (25-50% of their original dosages every 2-4 weeks). In
most immune-mediated skin diseases, the goal is to transition onto a
non-steroidal drug within the first 3 months and, ideally, discontinue
glucocorticoids or reduce their dosage to the minimal necessary dose
(e.g., <0.5 mg/kg 2-3× weekly), if possible. Once this is achieved and
the disease remains in remission, a tapering of the non-steroidal
drug dosage can be initiated. The goal is to find an effective
maintenance strategy with the lowest necessary dosage and/or the
fewest drugs. All patients on immunosuppressive therapy should be
regularly monitored to ensure the disease is well-controlled, and the
patient is not experiencing significant adverse effects associated with
the treatment. Eventually, in patients treated for at least 8-12
months, and in which the disease remains in remission on minimal
maintenance treatment, an attempt to discontinue the
immunosuppressive drug(s) should be made.
Veterinary dermatologists use a variety of immunosuppressive
drugs to maintain disease remission. Treatment strategies are often
similar between the diseases listed in this chapter. Certain drugs or
regimens are sometimes used for particular diseases. For example, a
high-dose glucocorticoid pulse therapy is often used during the

initial phase in canine PF and PV for its potential non-genomic
effects on keratinocyte adhesion.40 Mucous membrane pemphigoid,
PB, facial DLE, and MCLE, after the initial phase with oral
glucocorticoids, are often well-maintained only with doxycycline or
minocycline (e.g., 2-5 mg/kg PO q12-24h, usually beginning with
q12h) and niacinamide (250 mg/dog if <10 kg or 500 mg/dog if >10
kg, coadministered PO with doxycycline) with or without
intermittent topical glucocorticoids or tacrolimus. Colchicine is a
drug of choice in human EBA, and it has been shown to be effective
in canine EBA. In this disease, colchicine can be used as
monotherapy, or concurrently with other immunosuppressants to
reduce their dosages. Potential drug interactions, however, need to
be considered, and colchicine should not be used together with oral
cyclosporine, which is a frequently used drug for many immunemediated skin diseases. Indeed, cyclosporine has been shown to be
effective in a variety of diseases including facial and generalized
DLE, MCLE, VCLE, EM, SJS, TEN, alopecia areata, pseudopelade,
sebaceous adenitis, non-thymoma-associated exfoliative dermatitis,
and UDS. Therefore, cyclosporine is often use as a first-line nonsteroidal treatment for these diseases. Because of its delayed efficacy,
it is often combined with glucocorticoids during the first several
weeks. In diseases in which severe systemic signs are present (e.g.,
SJS, TEN, SLS, sterile pustular erythroderma of Schnauzers)
supportive treatment is as important as the immunosuppressive
therapy and its quality often dictates the chances of survival. Finally,
some of the diseases mentioned in this chapter will require only
short-term immunosuppression, and once the disease is in
remission, they can be discontinued rapidly. Examples of such
diseases are JC and CAEDE in which a 2- to 4-week course of
predniso(lo)ne started at 2 mg/kg/day is sufficient to induce
complete resolution of the disease.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by a broad
spectrum of clinical signs related to immune-mediated dysfunction of the kidney, skin, joints, blood, and
other organs. The cause of SLE is unknown, but the immunological hallmark of SLE is the production of
arrays of autoantibodies against intracellular antigens, such as antinuclear antibodies (ANAs).

PATHOGENESIS
The pathogenesis of human SLE is complex and our understanding of it is constantly evolving. Several
factors have been linked to its development and expression, including genetic, hormonal, and
environmental influences.1 It has been postulated that immune activation in canine and feline SLE
resembles SLE in humans; however, further investigations regarding the pathophysiology of SLE in
veterinary patients are needed. Both innate and adaptive immune systems play a role in the
pathogenesis of human SLE. One of the key concepts in the pathogenesis of SLE is an imbalance
between cellular waste (such as apoptotic cells) and the disposal of apoptotic material.1,2 The resulting
persistent apoptotic debris stimulates an innate inflammatory response by activating nucleic acid
recognition receptors, such as toll-like receptors, intracytoplasmic RNA sensors and DNA sensors.
Activation of nucleic acid recognition receptors upregulates the type I interferon (IFN) production,
which promotes B-lymphocyte differentiation, loss of tolerance, and autoantibody production.1,2

GENETICS OF SLE
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified more than 100 genes or genomic loci that are
robustly associated with human SLE.3 Although heterogeneity across populations was observed, GWAS
studies identified three main SLE-associated pathways: lymphocyte signaling, IFN signaling pathways
involving nucleic acid-sensing or the production and response to IFNs, and clearance of immune

complexes and other waste.3 In dogs with SLE, there is also a genetic predisposition and experimental
colonies of dogs with SLE have been established in the past.4-7 SLE in a breeding colony of dogs has
been associated with the allele DLA A7, a specific allotype of the fourth component of complement, and
decreased serum IgA.7 Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retrievers (NSDTRs) are affected by an SLE-related
immune-mediated rheumatic disease (IMRD) characterized by non-erosive polyarthritis (ch. 177) and
elevated ANA titers in some patients.8 A recent GWAS study in NSDTRs revealed the association of 11
genes (WFDC3, HOMER2, VRK1, PTPN3, WHAMM, BANK1, AP3B2, DAPP1, LAMTOR3, DDIT4L and
PPP3CA) with IMRD disease sub-phenotypes; most of the gene regions are related to T-cell activation.8

ENVIRONMENTAL RISK FACTORS AND SLE
Studies of SLE in monozygotic twins only show a concordance rate of 11-57%, suggesting that
environmental factors influence the pathogenesis of SLE.9 However, knowledge gaps remain regarding
potential mechanisms by which environmental factors contribute to SLE development.3 Ultraviolet (UV)
light has long been recognized as a contributor to human SLE through activation of keratinocytes,
increased keratinocyte apoptosis and upregulation of type I IFN; UV light-induced disease flares have
also been observed in dogs.10 Women comprise 90% of most human SLE cohorts, suggesting the
influence of hormones estrogen and prolactin11; sex predilection has not been identified in the dog or
cat. Several drugs may induce SLE-like disease in humans; clinical signs resolve within a few weeks after
discontinuation of the offending drug. Some drugs such as procainamide work as inhibitors of DNA
methylation3,12; DNA methylation regulates gene expression by serving as a platform for repressive
protein binding. Other drugs like propranolol are converted by UV light into a proinflammatory aryl
hydrocarbon receptor ligand, possibly explaining its association with lupus-like disease.13 In dogs and
cats, drug-induced SLE-like disease is rare. Propylthiouracil-induced elevations in ANA titers have
occurred with hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia in a cat14 and hydralazine has been associated
with the development of positive ANA titer in the dog.15

INFECTIOUS AGENTS AND SLE
Infections have been implicated in SLE for many years. However, no infectious agents have been
identified that cause SLE. Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus are considered to be SLE triggers in
humans.16 Feline leukemia virus (FeLV; ch. 199) and feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV; ch. 198) can
induce SLE-like disease in cats, and serum ANA can occur early in FeLV infection.17

CLINICAL FINDINGS
SLE is a clinically highly diverse autoimmune disease because it can affect almost any organ and patients
can display a broad spectrum of manifestations. As in the human disease counterpart, canine and feline
SLE is a chronic disease with successive development of clinical signs and in some patients alternating
periods of remission and relapse. Previously reported clinical signs of canine and feline SLE are
summarized in Table 179.1.18-29 However, most of these studies were retrospective and were
performed in the 1980s and 1990s; newer prospective series of well-characterized canine and feline SLE
cases are lacking. Major clinical signs of SLE in dogs and cats include polyarthritis (ch. 177), fever (ch.
16), renal disorders (ch. 302), and dermatologic lesions (ch. 178), although hematologic signs (chs.
174 and 175) and other clinical manifestations are also possible.18-29
Lameness due to nonerosive polyarthropathy is the major presenting sign in most patients; smaller
joints (carpi, tarsi, elbows, stifles) are affected most frequently (ch. 177). Dogs and cats can show the
gradual onset of generalized stiffness and involved joints may be swollen and painful. Synovial fluid
analysis (ch. 87) reveals neutrophilic inflammation and occasional lupus erythematosus (LE) cells can
be observed. An LE cell is recognized as a neutrophil that contains phagocytized nuclear material.

Histopathologic assessment of the synovial membrane reveals hypertrophy and hyperplasia of lining
cells, and a mixed cellular infiltrate with mononuclear cells predominating.
Vasculitis (ch. 181) is also common. Fever is present in a high proportion of dogs and cats, most
commonly intermittent and cyclical, but sometimes also persistent.
Renal involvement is present in some 50% of cases and can range from a subclinical to a progressive
and life-threatening complication. Glomerular lesions are indicated by proteinuria (>0.5 g/L); biopsies
usually reveal mesangial and/or endothelial hypertrophy, proliferative and/or membranous
glomerulonephritis, immune complexes deposition and sclerotic changes.

Skin lesions encountered in LE (ch. 178) are divided into those with characteristic microscopic
changes of lymphocyte-rich interface dermatitis with basal keratinocyte damage (i.e., “lupus-specific”
skin diseases = cutaneous LE or CLE) and those without such microscopic pattern (i.e., “LE-nonspecific”
skin diseases). The cutaneous manifestations of canine SLE are highly variable and include erythema,
erosions to ulcers, scaling, crusting, depigmentation, alopecia and occasionally scarring. Lesions can
develop in the skin, mucocutaneous junctions, and oral cavity; the face (lips, nasal planum), ear tips,
distal legs are frequently affected and symmetry of skin lesions is sometimes present. In some cases,
buccal ulcers and pruritic, generalized seborrheic dermatitis are observed. Multifocal subcutaneous
draining nodules over the trunk, histologically consistent with lupus panniculitis, are seen in rare cases.
The cutaneous lesions in feline SLE include erythema, ulceration, crusts, and depigmentation of the
face, ears, and paws. Histopathologic evaluation reveals a lichenoid, largely lymphoid infiltration of the
dermo-epidermal junction with basal keratinocyte damage; leukocytoclastic vasculitis may be observed
in some cases. Two variants of canine CLE (generalized discoid LE, exfoliative CLE), in which initially
only skin disease is present in the absence of ANA, have shown progression to develop SLE-like
symptoms and positive ANA titers.30
Hemolytic anemia (ch. 174) is a moderately common finding in canine SLE; approximately half of
patients with SLE have an immune-mediated reaction with hemolysis, positive direct Coombs tests or
autoagglutination whereas the remaining half have anemia of chronic disease (ch. 172). Mild
thrombocytopenia is noted in some patients, although severe thrombocytopenia (ch. 175) can also
occur. Neurological abnormalities are rarely recorded; however, psychological and behavioral
abnormalities are occasionally documented (ch. 11). Polymyositis has been suspected in several dogs
∗

and cats, and polyneuropathies (ch. 252) characterized by hyperesthesia, convulsions, and/or
noticeable behavioral changes are noted in few cases.

DIAGNOSIS
A diagnosis of SLE requires a combination of history, clinical signs, physical examination findings, and
laboratory and/or pathologic studies. Human SLE classification recently has been updated by the
American College of Rheumatology (ACR) with new criteria utilizing a positive ANA test (1:80) as an
entry criterion for classifying patients as having SLE.31 As the new SLE criteria fail to classify some early
or potential SLE patients in different phases of disease development (e.g., ANA-negative patients), the
terms “incomplete SLE,” “probable SLE” and “potential SLE” have been used for human patients with
some SLE signs and symptoms that don’t meet the ACR classification for diagnosable SLE.31 Although
the SLE classification criteria were not developed and should not be used for diagnostic purposes, many
clinicians rely on them to aid in the diagnosis of human SLE.
Human SLE classification criteria have been historically modified to apply to veterinary patients
(Table 179.2).24,32-36 Currently proposed criteria for the definition of SLE in veterinary patients
include at least two separate manifestations of multisystemic autoimmune disease along with a positive
serum ANA titer, without any evidence of an underlying disease or recognized trigger factors (e.g.,
infectious diseases, drug or vaccine administration). Interestingly, only rarely do veterinary patients
satisfy the SLE criteria and “probable” or “potential” SLE clinical cases are more frequently documented
in practice.
In veterinary patients, underlying trigger factors or disease processes need to be excluded as the
primary drivers for all multisystemic immune-mediated diseases demonstrating the features of SLE.
Infectious organisms in some geographic regions (e.g. leishmaniosis, arthropod-borne diseases) may
lead to multisystemic diseases that clinically mimic some features of SLE. Dogs with leishmaniosis (ch.
197) can present with combinations of fever, lymphadenopathy, skin disease, polyarthritis, immunemediated anemia or thrombocytopenia, protein-losing nephropathy and high ANA titers.36 In tickinfested areas (e.g., tick-borne diseases [chs. 9, 193], Bartonella [ch. 191]),37 a course of doxycycline
(10 mg/kg PO q24h, up to 1 week) may be considered prior to conclude the presence of immunemediated disease. Cats should be tested for FeLV (ch. 199) and FIV (ch. 198), as both diseases can
cause some clinical signs of SLE and positive ANA titers.17 Ruling out infectious causes of clinical signs
will require a combination of cytology, serology, and real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
Although rare, drugs and vaccine administrations historically have been connected to SLE development
in veterinary patients (see above), and such drugs should be discontinued (and replaced with equivalent
alternatives if necessary) in dogs or cats showing SLE signs. Vaccine-associated immune-mediated
disease in the dog (i.e., ischemic dermatopathy, dermatomyositis; ch. 12) with skin lesions, occasionally
severe muscle involvement, and a positive ANA titer, is widely recognized,38 but the development of
complete clinical features of SLE is rarely observed.

Diagnostic testing of suspected SLE patients should include a complete blood count (CBC), serum
biochemistry profile, urinalysis, imaging, cytologic evaluation of synovial fluid (chs. 71 and 87),
histopathologic examination of the skin (ch. 83) and/or kidney (ch. 302), and serum ANA titer.
Immunodiagnostic investigations may include Coombs testing; screening for platelet autoantibodies and
rheumatoid factor; coagulation testing for antiphospholipid antibodies; and testing for serum
immunoglobulin, complement, circulating immune complex concentrations and endocrine
autoantibodies (e.g., antithyroglobulin) (Table 179.2). Histopathologic findings can provide important
information to support a diagnosis of SLE. In SLE patients with skin disease and oral ulcers,
histopathological examination can reveal an interface dermatitis with vacuolar change of the basal
keratinocytes in the epidermis. When obtaining the skin biopsy, care should be taken to avoid the center
of ulcers and erosions since an intact epidermis is necessary to substantiate the diagnosis (ch. 83). Skin
biopsies of affected areas at the margins of ulcers and erosions yield the most useful diagnostic results.
Oral biopsy specimens also need to follow the above-mentioned collection guidelines for ulcers and
erosions to achieve diagnostic value.

SPECIFIC TESTING
Antinuclear Antibody Test (ANA)
Antinuclear antibodies are a collection of autoantibodies that target proteins within the nucleus of the
cell (nuclear material, DNA and histones). A diagnosis of SLE in the dog requires the presence of
elevated serum ANA titers; titers are a quantitative measure of the amount of antibody, expressed as the
number of dilutions a sample can undergo and still demonstrate detectable antibody binding. Indirect
immunofluorescence (IIF) with human epithelial laryngeal carcinoma type 2 (HEp-2) cells is considered
by the ACR to be the gold standard for detecting ANAs in human SLE, and nuclear staining pattern
recognition (i.e., homogenous, speckled, membranous) is helpful for clinical correlation of specific ANA
subtypes.31 There is no universally accepted protocol for ANA testing used by veterinary diagnostic
laboratories; mouse and rat liver, and HeLa, Vero or HEp-2 cells monolayers are utilized as substrates.
The reported titer cut-off for a diagnosis of SLE and the sensitivity of the test vary between laboratories,
based on the substrate employed and subjective interpretation of the individual reading the results. It is
important to emphasize that serum ANA may be present in healthy dogs (low prevalence) and dogs with
chronic inflammatory, infectious (e.g., tick-borne diseases, Bartonella),37 or neoplastic diseases, or
immune-mediated diseases other than SLE.39 ANA-negative SLE cases have been described in human
and veterinary patients.1,5,22,24 For these reasons, a single ANA result does not have a single
interpretation and its clinical significance should be considered within the patient’s context. ANAs
positivity against several autoantigens (e.g., anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm) is clinically valuable for the diagnosis
of SLE in humans. Still, variable results are observed in canine SLE and further research is needed to
elucidate the clinical meaning of various autoantigens in canine SLE.

MANAGEMENT
Because SLE is photoaggravated through UV light activation of type I IFN in the skin, owners should be
advised to keep affected dogs out of direct sunlight. Medical therapy of dogs and cats with SLE requires
the use of immunosuppressive doses of glucocorticoids (ch. 144) and, depending upon the perceived
severity of the clinical presentation, additional immunosuppressants (e.g., azathioprine, cyclosporine,
chlorambucil, mycophenolate mofetil) (ch. 169). There have been no extensive controlled trials
comparing outcomes for different immunosuppressive protocols employed in canine and feline SLE. Full
doses are administered until SLE is in complete remission and then immunosuppressants are slowly
tapered. Any relapses of SLE will require further therapy cycles, and sometimes, lifelong low-dose
maintenance therapy is required to control clinical signs. Oral glucocorticoids prednisone or
prednisolone at 1 to 2 mg/kg/day are commonly initiated for SLE therapy in dogs; cats should be treated
with an alternate steroid to prednisone, like prednisolone or dexamethasone. Adjunct
immunosuppressive therapy (ch. 169) can include azathioprine (dogs; 2.2 mg/kg PO), cyclosporine
(dogs and cats; 5 mg/kg PO q12-24h), mycophenolate mofetil (dogs and cats; 10 to 20 mg/kg IV or PO
q12-24h) or chlorambucil (cats; 2 mg PO every 48-72h). Potential side-effects (ch. 169) of azathioprine
and chlorambucil include anorexia and bone marrow suppression; azathioprine also can cause acute
liver injury and is not recommended for use in cats. Oral mycophenolate mofetil can induce hemorrhagic
diarrhea as a side-effect. In a single controlled study, good results were reported with the combined use
of prednisone (1-2 mg/kg PO q24h) with the anthelminthic and immunomodulatory drug levamisole (2
to 5 mg/kg, max 150 mg, PO every 48 h); levamisole was able to sustain SLE remission after prednisone
was discontinued compared to a group of dogs that only received prednisone.19 Despite this, the use of
levamisole in dogs requires careful consideration due to the severe side-effects associated with this drug
(e.g., agranulocytosis, excited behavior, vomiting, bradycardia).40 Oral hydroxychloroquine, an
antimalarial drug recommended for all human patients with SLE,41 has been successfully utilized for
canine CLE therapy (5-10 mg/kg PO q24h) in conjunction with other immunosuppressive agents,30 but
not SLE, and therefore warrants further investigations in dogs and cats with SLE. Oral Janus kinase
(JAK) inhibitors are currently under investigation for human SLE41 and CLE treatment. Oral oclacitinib,
a JAK inhibitor approved for use in canine dermatology,42 reversed the lesions of canine CLE patients
(0.6 mg/kg PO q12h) by the author (unpublished data), but has not been used for canine or feline SLE
patients.
Routine follow-up evaluation should include CBC, serum biochemistry profile, urinalysis, and serum
ANA every 1 to 3 months until complete resolution of SLE-associated signs (i.e., resolution of all
clinicopathological abnormalities associated with SLE, meaning resolution of clinical signs and
laboratory abnormalities) and then as needed during maintenance therapy. Renal function should be
monitored for life in all patients suspected of having SLE. The ANA titer may persist at a low level during
clinical remission in some patients.
