Canine and feline immunodeficiency is generally divided into the
two categories of primary and secondary immunodeficiency. Primary
immunodeficiency refers to inherited immunodeficiency syndromes
with a known or suspected genetic etiology. Secondary
immunodeficiency refers to immunodeficiency associated with drug
therapy, infectious disease or neoplasia. Primary and secondary
immunodeficiencies are discussed here. Secondary
immunodeficiencies associated with specific infectious diseases or
drug therapies are found elsewhere in the text.

CLINICAL PRESENTATION
Diagnosing immunodeficiency can be difficult because the initial
clinical presentation is often vague. The history is usually one of
younger animals presenting with recurrent infections from the same
or similar pathogens (ch. 183). In general, repeated infection with
pyogenic bacteria is caused by one or more defects in phagocytic cell
function, complement function, or antibody production. Recurrent
viral infection suggests defects in adaptive immunity, such as poor T
cell function. Further, recurrent fungal infection of skin and mucous
membranes suggests defects in T cell function and/or defects in
antibody production.1 For the purposes of this chapter, innate
immunity refers to components of the immune response that are
antigen-nonspecific, including cells such as neutrophils and
macrophages and complement components. Adaptive immunity
refers to antigen-specific immunity mediated by T cells, B cells,
and/or plasma cells. Pedersen listed characteristic features of
immunodeficiency that are a useful starting point: infections caused
by microorganisms that are normally not pathogenic, unusually
severe or persistent infections that are typically mild and selflimiting in healthy patients, an inordinate number of different
infections in the same animal, recurrence of infections that occurred
in a subclinical (or mild) form earlier in life, and infections that are
unexplainably difficult to treat.2

INNATE IMMUNE SYSTEM DEFECTS
LEUKOCYTE ADHESION DEFICIENCY (LAD)

Leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD) has been reported in dogs and
cats. Dogs with LAD generally present in the first year of life with
vague clinical signs including decreased appetite and activity,
depression and fever. Following the human categorization of LAD, 2
of the 3 human subtypes are recognized in dogs (LAD1 and LAD3).
LAD1 is the partial or complete absence of CD18. In mammalian
species, CD18, a beta-2 integrin, is highly conserved and forms a
heterodimer with CD11a, b, or c.3 Canine neutrophils and monocytes
typically express the CD18/CD11b heterodimer (also known as Mac1) most abundantly, while other leukocyte subsets express other
CD18/CD11 heterodimers.3 Therefore, dogs deficient in CD18 will
not form the heterodimer, leading to decreased or absent surface
expression on neutrophils and monocytes. The CD18/CD11b
heterodimer mediates strong adhesion and extravasation at
endothelial sites (Figure 180.1). This heterodimer is also a
complement receptor and in affected animals, phagocytosis of
opsonized material is poor.
LAD1 was first reported in Irish Setters and at least one mixed
breed dog as an autosomal recessive trait (ITGB2 gene mutation).4,5
Affected dogs typically die within the first or second year of life from
severe infection. LAD1 was also reported in a mixed breed Domestic
Shorthair cat with a different ITGB2 mutation.6 LAD1 of
undetermined genetic origin is also recognized in mixed breed dogs;
however, the CD18 deficiency may be incomplete, with somewhat
less severe clinical signs.7 Flow cytometry demonstrating the
complete or partial absence of neutrophil CD18 and CD11b, in
combination with a typical clinical history, is usually diagnostic. A
genetic test for the mutation in Irish Setters is also available. In
research settings, LAD1 has been treated successfully using viral
vector gene therapy.8
LAD2 is caused by decreased or absent CD15 expression and has
yet to be reported in dogs or cats.
LAD3 in dogs is characterized by normal CD18 and CD11
expression but affected dogs a defect in the FERMT3 (also known as
KINDLIN3) gene.9 This defect leads to poor beta-1, 2, and 3 integrin
function and was reported in a German Shepherd Dog and a mixed

breed dog. Affected dogs exhibit poor platelet aggregation and poor
neutrophil function. Similar to LAD1, recurrent infections occur in
young animals; however, bleeding from thrombocytopathia can be
the predominant clinical sign.10

CYCLICAL NEUTROPENIA
Cyclical neutropenia, also known as gray collie syndrome or cyclic
hematopoiesis, was first recognized in Collies in the late 1950s. The
disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in
the AP3B1 gene, which causes defects in lysosomal membrane
protein trafficking.11 Affected dogs have a gray haircoat and reduced
skin pigmentation due to melanocyte dysfunction associated with the
mutation.12 There is a cyclical neutropenia and thrombocytopenia
occurring about every 10-14 days, as well as functional defects in
neutrophil elastase and myeloperoxidase. Affected animals begin to
show clinical signs associated with infection soon after maternal
antibody wanes. Dogs typically have recurrent respiratory and
gastrointestinal infections along with a constellation of signs
including gingivitis, arthralgia and lymphadenopathy.12 Affected
dogs rarely live past 3 years of age. Treatment with recombinant
granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF) helps resolve
neutropenic episodes but does not cure these dogs. Likewise, gene
therapy using a lentiviral vector to deliver G-CSF is partially
successful, but to date, is only available in an experimental setting.13

CANINE TRAPPED NEUTROPHIL
SYNDROME
Canine trapped neutrophil syndrome, similar to Cohen syndrome in
people, is an autosomal recessive disorder in Border Collies caused
by mutations in the VPS13B gene, which lead to abnormal vesicular
and protein trafficking within the cell.14 Affected dogs have profound
accumulation of neutrophils in the bone marrow but very few in the
peripheral circulation, which explains the name of the condition.

Severely affected dogs may have craniofacial developmental
abnormalities and stunted growth compared to littermates.14 Like
cyclical neutropenia, infections occur in young animals following the
waning of maternal antibody; however, infections seem to be more
severe and affected dogs rarely live past 6 to 12 months.15

CHÉDIAK-HIGASHI SYNDROME
Chédiak-Higashi syndrome is an autosomal recessive neutrophil
defect of blue smoke Persian cats.16 A defect in the lysosomal
trafficking regulator gene LYST leads to abnormally large secretory
granules that rupture spontaneously, causing tissue damage.
Neutrophils from affected cats have poor chemotaxis and reduced
killing, while lymphocytes and natural killer cells also exhibit poor
cytotoxic function.12,17 Further, affected cats also exhibit
thrombocyte dysfunction. Clinically, affected Persian cats present
with recurrent infections. G-CSF therapy is reported to help boost
neutrophil activity and function.18

PELGER-HUËT (PH) ANOMALY
Pelger-Huët (PH) anomaly is an inherited neutrophil defect found in
purebred and mixed breed dogs and cats.12,19,20 It is usually
discovered on routine blood smear evaluation with neutrophils
exhibiting hyposegmented nuclei (sometimes mistaken for band
neutrophils). The degree of neutrophil dysfunction in these animals
is generally considered subclinical. One of the earliest reports in a
research colony of inbred foxhounds demonstrated somewhat
decreased neutrophil function as well as decreased humoral immune
function.19 Further, they reported that the anomaly was associated
with a lower percentage of weaned pups from litters of affected dams
when compared to litters from outbred dams. However, it is
uncertain if the anomaly alone was responsible for reduced litter
size, or as a result of overall reduced hybrid vigor from inbreeding.19

BIRMAN CAT GRANULATION ANOMALY
Birman cat granulation anomaly is an inherited autosomal recessive
trait resulting in prominent eosinophilic granules within
neutrophils.21 Like the PH anomaly, the degree of neutrophil
function is most likely subclinical. A similar anomaly was reported in
2 Siamese cats suggesting that purebred lineages related to Birmans
may also carry the trait.22

DOBERMAN PINSCHER NEUTROPHIL
DYSFUNCTION
Doberman Pinscher neutrophil dysfunction was reported in a group
of closely related dogs. Phagocytosis was normal; however, the
neutrophils exhibited decreased bactericidal activity associated with
alterations in granule function.23 The dogs exhibited an array of
clinical signs including dull haircoats, neutrophilia, and
bronchopneumonia. Adaptive immune function in these dogs
appeared intact.

WEIMARANER NEUTROPHIL
DYSFUNCTION
Weimaraner neutrophil dysfunction has been reported sporadically
in the breed and may occur in conjunction with defects in IgM and
IgG production.24,25 Further, Weimaraner dogs are among the
breeds reported for IgA deficiency (discussed below). Collectively,
this spectrum of immune deficits suggests a complex, multifactorial
immune dysfunction syndrome in the breed. Clinical signs include
fever, diarrhea, pneumonia, skin infections and osteomyelitis.
Further complicating diagnosis, an important consideration is that
autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease is also reported for the
breed and the presenting complaints and clinical signs are often
similar (fever, inappetence, lethargy). However, Weimaraner dogs

with autoinflammatory and/or autoimmune disease consistently
demonstrate sterile inflammatory lesions.26

GRANULOCYTE COLONY-STIMULATING
FACTOR (G-CSF) DEFICIENCY
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) deficiency was
reported in a single Rottweiler with a history of fever, polyarthritis
and recurrent infection.27 The dog had persistent neutropenia and
hyperglobulinemia. Bone marrow cytology demonstrated a decreased
myeloid to erythroid ratio and incomplete granulocytic maturation.

COMPLEMENT COMPONENT (C3)
DEFICIENCY
Complement component (C3) deficiency was reported in a colony of
Brittany Spaniels as an inherited, autosomal recessive trait. Affected
dogs exhibited increased bacterial infections including pneumonia,
sepsis, and pyometra. The lack of C3 results in poor opsonization,
leading to impaired phagocytosis, particularly of extracellular
pathogens.28

CANINE GRANULOCYTOPATHY
SYNDROME IN IRISH SETTER DOGS
Canine granulocytopathy syndrome in Irish Setter dogs, seemingly
distinct from LAD discussed above, was first reported in a single
male dog who was used for establishing a research colony.29 The
trait was determined to be inherited in an autosomal recessive
fashion. Neutrophils from affected dogs had impaired bactericidal
function associated with defects in glucose metabolism.29

ADAPTIVE IMMUNE SYSTEM DEFECTS
IgA DEFICIENCY
IgA deficiency is probably the most commonly reported immune
deficiency in the dog and is also the most difficult to definitively
diagnose. The deficiency has been reported in many different
purebred dogs, including Shar-Peis, Beagles, Cocker Spaniels,
Dalmatians, Akitas, and others, as well as in mixed breed dogs.12
Further, IgA deficiency as the most prominent component of
multifactorial immune dysfunction has been reported in German
Shepherd Dogs, Irish Wolfhounds, Rottweilers, Weimaraners,
Dachshunds, and Bull Terriers (Table 180.1).12
It is important to note that patients with IgA deficiency exhibit
clinical signs similar to those of dogs with neutrophil defects. Clinical
signs in dogs with IgA deficiency are often associated with infections
at mucosal surfaces and the skin including pyoderma, otitis,
demodicosis, bronchitis, pneumonia, and enteritis with
gastrointestinal dysbiosis. The most severe clinical manifestations
seem to predominate in younger animals, but young adults and older
adult dogs are also affected.30
Dimeric IgA is produced and secreted by plasma cells at mucosal
surfaces, where it acts locally to bind pathogens (Figure 180.2).1
Serum IgA is a combination of mucosally derived IgA and
monomeric IgA produced by cells of the bone marrow and spleen.
Further, mammalian species differ in their IgA coding regions, IgA
structure, transport, and function; therefore, extrapolation of data
from laboratory animal models or humans to dogs and cats should
be approached with caution.
When considering evaluation of a canine patient with potential IgA
deficiency, serum IgA concentrations should not be utilized as the
sole diagnostic criterion. The most directly relevant measure of IgA is
at mucosal surfaces; therefore, when available, mucosally derived
IgA (feces or saliva) should be measured in tandem with serum
IgA.30,31 Because concentrations can vary, sampling serum and
mucosally derived IgA at two or more time points is recommended.
Persistently decreased concentrations of either serum or mucosal
IgA, in the face of appropriate clinical signs in a predisposed breed,

is suspicious, while decreased concentrations of both serum and
mucosal IgA at multiple time points is strongly indicative. Further
complicating diagnosis, it is likely that IgA quality may differ
between breeds, meaning that even if IgA concentrations are normal
in the serum and at mucosal surfaces, the IgA may not effectively
bind pathogens. Finally, commercially available assessment of fecal
or salivary IgA is not widely accessible; however, canine-specific IgA
enzyme-linked immunosorbant assay kits are available from multiple
manufacturers with at least one that can be used for serum and saliva
(Bethyl Laboratories, Inc., Montgomery, TX, Steiner JM: Personal
communication, April 1, 2021).

COMMON VARIABLE
IMMUNODEFICIENCY (CVID)
Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) is consistently
documented in dogs with Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly known as
P. carinii) pneumonia. Interestingly, juvenile demodicosis is also
noted in some dogs subsequently diagnosed with CVID. First
reported in Miniature Dachshunds, CVID has been reported in
Cavalier King Charles Spaniels (CKCSs), other purebred dogs and
mixed breed dogs.12,32,33 Analogous to CVID in people, affected dogs
typically exhibit impaired T cell function along with decreased
concentrations of serum IgG and IgA. Most dogs also have low IgM
concentrations, with the exception being the CKCS, which can have
increased IgM.32,33

T CELL DEFICIENCY
T cell deficiency resulting from thymic aplasia has been documented
rarely in Birman kittens. Affected kittens were hairless and exhibited
thymic aplasia caused by a loss of function mutation in the FOXN1
gene.34 Similar FOXN1 mutations cause hypotrichosis and thymic
aplasia in mice, rats and people (“nude” syndrome).12

AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE SEVERE
COMBINED IMMUNODEFICIENCY
(SCID) IN JACK RUSSELL TERRIERS
Autosomal recessive severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) in
Jack Russell Terriers is caused by a defect in the DNA-dependent
protein kinase catalytic subunit (DNA-PKcs). First described in 2
litters of Jack Russell Terrier puppies, this defect prevents
completion of V(D)J recombination events essential for functional Tcell receptor (TCR) and B-cell receptor (BCR) development.35
Unable to display fully functional TCRs or BCRs, puppies exhibit a
complete lack of lymphocyte development which manifests clinically

as severe lymphopenia, profound lymphoid tissue hypoplasia,
agammaglobulinemia, and death.

X-LINKED SCID
X-linked SCID is reported in Basset Hounds and Cardigan Welsh
Corgis. Basset Hounds have a deletional mutation while Cardigan
Welsh Corgis have an insertional mutation, both of which cause a
dysfunctional interleukin-2 receptor gamma protein (IL-2Rgamma).35 The IL-2R is composed of 3 signaling chains: alpha, beta,
and gamma. Following ligation of the alpha subunit by IL-2, the 3
signaling chains rapidly cluster at the cell surface to initiate the IL-2
signaling cascade. Without the gamma subunit, the intracellular
signal is defective and the downstream intracellular events are
absent. Lacking the proper IL-2 signals, T cell maturation in the
thymus is defective. Further, IL-2 signals are needed for efficient B
cell maturation, including immunoglobulin class switching;
therefore, affected dogs also exhibit poor antibody production.1 The
resulting T cell and B cell deficiency causes marked lymphoid
hypoplasia. Affected pups begin to develop clinical signs as maternal
antibody wanes and eventually die from opportunistic infection.

POORLY CHARACTERIZED IMMUNE
SYSTEM DEFECTS
INFECTION WITH PROTOTHECA SPECIES
Infection with Prototheca species is sporadically reported in dogs
(ch. 263).36 Common clinical signs include bloody diarrhea, acute
blindness and progressive neurologic defects caused by disseminated
protothecosis. Boxers and Collies are overrepresented in case reports
of the disease, suggesting one or more underlying immune defects.
In humans, disseminated protothecosis is associated with neutrophil
defects, suggesting the same is likely for dogs.

INCREASED OCCURRENCE AND
SEVERITY OF PARVOVIRUS INFECTION
Increased occurrence and severity of parvovirus infection (ch. 201)
in Doberman Pinschers, German Shepherd, and Rottweiler dogs is
suspected based upon early epidemiologic surveys, anecdotal
evidence, and the occurrence of other immune deficiencies for these
breeds.12,37,38

DISSEMINATED FUNGAL DISEASE IN
GERMAN SHEPHERD DOGS
Disseminated fungal disease (Aspergillus sp. and others; ch. 211) in
German Shepherd Dogs is likely a result of multifactorial immune
dysfunction including IgA deficiency/dysfunction, T cell dysfunction,
and perhaps innate immune dysfunction.39 Female, middle-aged
German Shepherd Dogs appear to be at increased risk for this
disease.40 Clinical signs result from infections of the central nervous
system, eyes, lungs, and bone and include central and peripheral
neurologic signs, ocular lesions, cough, dyspnea, pain and lameness,
while response to antifungal therapy inversely correlates with the
disease severity.40

FIGURE 180.2 Origin and function of
immunoglobulin A in the gastrointestinal tract. A,
Plasma cells in the lamina propria of the mucosal
epithelium secrete IgA as a monomer. B, Monomeric
IgA is rapidly polymerized into dimeric IgA by the J
chain (red coil) which then binds the polymeric
immunoglobulin receptor (pIgR, green coil) at the
basal surface of mucosal epithelium. Next, the pIgR
facilitates transcytosis of dimeric IgA. C, A small
piece of the pIgR, known as the secretory component
(green sphere), remains attached to the dimeric IgA.
The secretory component facilitates binding to the
mucous layer and protects the dimer from
degradation by gut enzymes. Illustrations by A.
Harvey and J. Fogle.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Immunodeficiencies
Your veterinarian has diagnosed what they think could be an
immunodeficiency in your pet. Below are some common questions
that pet owners have regarding immunodeficiency.

CAN I CATCH IMMUNODEFICIENCY FROM MY
PET?
No, immunodeficiency diseases in pets do not spread to humans.

WHAT DOES IMMUNODEFICIENCY MEAN?
White blood cells in the body are important for fighting infection
from germs that cause disease, like viruses and bacteria. There are

different types of white blood cells and they share the job of fighting
infection. When your veterinarian suspects an immunodeficiency,
this means that one or more of the different types of white blood cells
are not working properly.

HOW DO I KNOW IF MY PET HAS AN
IMMUNODEFICIENCY?
Immunodeficiency is usually diagnosed in young animals less than 2
years of age but is sometimes seen in older animals. The first clues
that your pet might have immunodeficiency are that a puppy or
kitten has infections and fever over and over again that often need
treatments like antibiotics to clear up. Many times these infections
occur on the skin, in the ears, in airways, or even in the intestine.
Symptoms include a fever, poor appetite, reduced activity, inflamed
areas of skin, and sometimes nasal discharge (pus or other liquid
coming from the nostrils), coughing or diarrhea. Immunodeficiency
can be difficult to diagnose and your veterinarian may need to
perform repeated testing including complete blood counts, known as
“CBCs”, and different types of specialized tests that examine white
blood cell functions. Also, your veterinarian may need to identify the
specific type of infection to help with diagnosis and therapy.

IS THERE A CURE FOR IMMUNE DEFICIENCY IN
MY PET?
Unfortunately, most of these immunodeficiency diseases are
inherited, genetic diseases and there is not a cure. Experimental
cures include gene therapy and bone marrow transplantation but
these are not currently available for pets. Your veterinarian can help
manage the symptoms of disease for months or even years.
Unfortunately, most pets with immunodeficiency eventually die from
complications associated with infection.
Jonathan Fogle (Raleigh, North Carolina)

Chapter 181: Vasculitides
James Swann

A C RO N YM S
ANCA anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibodies
CRGV cutaneous and renal glomerular vasculopathy
IMHA immune-mediated hemolytic anemia
IMV immune-mediated vasculitis
SLE systemic lupus erythematosus
Vasculitis refers to inflammation of the blood vessel wall, which may
occur with intravascular or endotheliotropic pathogens, localized
inflammation that damages nearby blood vessels as a bystander
effect, or with immune dysregulation that causes damage in vessel
walls. Vasculitis syndromes are encountered uncommonly in cats
and dogs but may be underdiagnosed owing to a requirement for
histopathologic evaluation for a definitive diagnosis.

PHYSIOLOGY
All blood vessels are lined by endothelium on their luminal surfaces,
with endothelial cells forming an essential interface between blood
and tissues by producing factors that modulate blood flow, by
preventing thrombosis, and by controlling egress of leukocytes from
the blood.1 In arteries and arterioles, endothelial cells form the
tunica intima, which is surrounded by a tunica media composed of
vascular smooth muscle and elastin fibers. Around this, the tunica
adventitia forms a layer of connective tissue containing vessels and

nerves. The tunica media is innervated by neurons of the
sympathetic nervous system, which cause constriction of vascular
smooth muscle to alter blood flow and pressure. The walls of veins
and venules are composed of similar layers, but the tunica media
contains fewer muscle and elastin fibers, whereas capillaries are
composed only of a single layer of endothelium supported by
mesenchymal pericytes.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Inflammation of the vessel wall disturbs its normal functions,
resulting in leakage of fluid and proteins or frank hemorrhage into
surrounding tissue. Inflammatory lesions may interrupt blood flow,
and exposure of subendothelial tissue factor also creates a
thrombogenic surface upon which platelets and coagulation factors
may assemble to produce thrombi (chs. 172 and 175). Together, this
predisposes to ischemia and infarction of areas supplied by inflamed
vessels.
Vasculitis may be caused by pathogens such as Rickettsia rickettsii
(ch. 193) that infect endothelial cells, resulting in necrosis or
destruction by the immune response. Infectious agents may also
cause physical trauma to vessel walls, as occurs with Dirofilaria
immitis (ch. 237) and Angiostrongylus vasorum (ch. 217) in
pulmonary arteries. Alternatively, vasculitis may occur as a
consequence of localized tissue inflammation, where accumulation of
inflammatory cells and mediators causes inadvertent damage to
nearby blood vessels; this immunopathologic process has been
described in dogs with abscesses, mastitis, and diskospondylitis2
(ch. 250).
Immune-mediated vasculitis (IMV) also occurs in small animals
and may be attributable to deposition of immune complexes,
activation of T cell responses, or production of autoantibodies.3,4
Immune complexes are structures composed of soluble antigen
bound by antibodies, which may be deposited in vessel walls to cause
recruitment of leukocytes, activation of complement, and local tissue
damage. Human IMV may be associated with production of antineutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibodies (ANCA) specific for the

neutrophil proteins myeloperoxidase and proteinase 3, with the
resulting clinical syndromes described as ANCA-associated
vasculitides.5 Similar ANCA have been detected in Beagles with
polyarteritis of unknown etiology in research studies,6 suggesting
ANCA-associated vasculitis could occur in small animals. However,
serum concentrations of ANCA are also increased in some dogs with
chronic enteropathies (ch. 262)7,8 and immune-mediated hemolytic
anemia (IMHA, ch. 174)9 that have no clinical features of vasculitis,
suggesting they may act as non-specific markers of inflammation.
Hyperthyroid cats treated with propylthiouracil also developed antimyeloperoxidase antibodies, but this was associated with systemic
immune-mediated disease and not cutaneous vasculitis (ch. 179).10
In many cases of IMV in dogs and cats, aberrant immune
responses may be precipitated by exposure to drugs, vaccines, or
insect bites, or by concurrent infections or neoplasia (Table 181.1):
in previous studies, ∼75% of dogs with any type of vasculitis and
∼50% of those with cutaneous vasculitis had a concurrent problem
that could have been causative.2,11 Primary IMV syndromes are rare
in dogs and cats, with the most common being idiopathic cutaneous
vasculitis, which chiefly affects small vessels in the dermis. Previous
reports have described distinct cutaneous vasculitis syndromes in
Jack Russell Terriers,12 German Shepherd Dogs,13 and juvenile
Chinese Shar-Peis,14 but it remains unclear whether these breeds are
predisposed to the disease or whether the syndrome occurred only in
some kindreds. Other vasculitis syndromes with no known
underlying cause in small animals include steroid-responsive
meningitis arteritis (SRMA, ch. 242), proliferative arteritis of the
nasal philtrum in Giant Schnauzers and Saint Bernards,15 nasal
planum vasculitis in Scottish Terriers,16 pulmonary arteritis,17 and
several forms of vasculitis affecting central nervous system
vessels.2,18-21 Cutaneous and renal glomerular vasculopathy (CRGV),
which was first described in Greyhounds in the United States in the
1980s and more recently as an emerging disease across the United
Kingdom, is attributable to formation of microscopic intravascular

thrombi, particularly in dermal and glomerular vessels.22 Affected
vessels also frequently show evidence of inflammatory damage,
suggesting the initiating event could be vasculitis that disrupts the
anti-thrombotic endothelial surface. However, it remains unclear
whether CRGV is a form of IMV or a response to an as-yet
undetected toxin or infectious pathogen.
Clinical features of systemic vasculitis are encountered
occasionally in dogs with other immune-mediated diseases, such as
IMHA or polyarthritis (ch. 177), producing a syndrome resembling
human systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE, ch. 179).

PATHOLOGY

Vasculitis is recognized when there is infiltration of the vessel wall by
leukocytes, resulting in necrosis of endothelial cells and/or smooth
muscle myocytes. Histologically, necrosis of cells in the vascular wall
results in accumulation of eosinophilic hyaline, fibrillar, or nonstructured material, which is called fibrinoid change or necrosis. This
finding is useful because, in localized inflammatory responses, it may
be difficult to determine whether leukocytes are accumulating in the
wall or only migrating into surrounding tissue; the presence of
fibrinoid change indicates the vessel wall is being damaged. In some
cases, the nuclei of neutrophils in the vessel wall appear to fragment,
presumably as they undergo apoptosis or necroptosis, leading to a
histological description of “leukocytoclastic vasculitis.” However, this
does not appear to be associated with any particular clinical
phenotype in people or animals. Depending on its underlying cause,
vasculitis is often focused on particular types of vessel, leading to
pathological descriptions of small, medium, or large vessel vasculitis.
Vasculitis may be further classified according to the types of cells
infiltrating the vessel wall, with the most common patterns being
neutrophilic infiltrates in the dermis, and less commonly
lymphoplasmacytic, eosinophilic, or granulomatous.11 The
significance of these distinct types of inflammatory infiltrate is
unclear and might only reflect differences in the temporal
progression of lesions, though there has been speculation that cases
with neutrophilic infiltrates were less responsive to pentoxifylline.11

HISTORY AND PHYSICAL
EXAMINATION
Vasculitis is often associated with an underlying cause that produces
other signs of illness or clinicopathologic abnormalities in affected
dogs and cats. Animals with vasculitis are often systemically unwell
and have clinical evidence of acute phase responses, including fever,
lethargy, and decreased appetite. Vasculitis may rarely cause splenic
infarction, splenic vein thrombosis, or splenomegaly as a nonspecific reaction to systemic inflammation.23 Clinically, vasculitis
should be suspected in animals with edematous swelling (ch. 30) or
intracavitary effusions (chs. 21, 220) that cannot be explained by

other problems. Because vasculitis is often associated with local
inflammatory responses, the affected area may appear erythematous
or warm, which is unusual for edema attributable to changes in
oncotic pressure.
In addition to edema, cutaneous vasculitis frequently causes areas
of purpura attributable to hemorrhage, and these lesions may be
distinguished from erythema because they do not blanch when a
glass slide is pressed against the skin

(Video 12.1). Formation of

thrombi in dermal vessels often leads to ischemia, infarction, and
well-demarcated, painful ulceration. Ulcers may occur in poorly
vascularized regions (such as the tips of the pinnae, the nasal
planum, the digital pads, or tail), in the mouth, or over the flanks or
limbs.24 In more severe cases, large areas of skin may become
ulcerated or even slough.14 Dogs with vasculitis of the nasal planum
may have severe ulceration in this region, sometimes causing
considerable hemorrhage if arterial walls are eroded. Animals with
CRGV typically have one or more cutaneous, ulcerated lesions, often
on the limbs, at the time of presentation; this is often followed by a
rapid onset of azotemia and oligoanuric acute kidney injury within
the following 48 hours.

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
A definitive diagnosis of vasculitis can be made only by
histopathological evaluation of tissue sections, which limits the
ability to detect syndromes affecting internal organs if biopsy is not
possible. Histological features of cutaneous vasculitis also change
rapidly with time, meaning that vasculitis lesions may be missed
depending on when the case is presented for evaluation.
Animals with systemic vasculitis will often have anemia (ch. 57)
and thrombocytopenia (ch. 59),25 which are attributed to
concurrent antibody responses or microvascular damage as cells pass
through inflamed vessels. In such cases, additional tests should be
undertaken for evidence of underlying immune-mediated diseases
such as IMHA (ch. 174), immune thrombocytopenia (ch. 175), or
SLE (ch. 179).

Where vasculitis is suspected clinically or diagnosed histologically,
investigations should be undertaken to detect any underlying cause.
This may include questioning of the owner about exposure to toxins
or drugs (ch. 132), testing for infectious pathogens according to
local conditions and travel history (ch. 9), and imaging of the thorax
and abdomen to exclude inflammatory foci or neoplasia. A diet trial
with a novel protein or hypoallergenic diet may be considered in
animals with cutaneous vasculitis because some cases have been
associated with dietary hypersensitivity (ch. 160).

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES
Development of localized peripheral edema or intracavitary
effusions, which often herald the development of vasculitis, may
occur with hypoproteinemia, cardiac disease, vascular
malformations, or obstruction to lymphatic drainage (ch. 30). In
such cases, physical examination and evaluation of serum
biochemistry results should distinguish these possibilities. Problems
with vascular or lymphatic flow may also be evaluated further by
computed tomography angiography or lymphangiography (ch. 239).
Signs suggestive of cutaneous vasculitis, such as ulceration or
crusting lesions on the skin, pinnae, digital pads, or nasal planum
may also occur with traumatic wounds, exposure to caustic
chemicals or thermal injury, or other immune-mediated skin
diseases, such as pemphigus vulgaris. Similarly, arteritis of the nasal
philtrum may produce similar clinical signs to nasal lupus or
uveodermatologic syndrome in dogs (ch. 178).

THERAPIES
Treatment should be directed at any underlying cause of vasculitis.
In those cases with suspected IMV where no underlying cause can be
found, treatment with an immunosuppressive dosage of prednisone
or prednisolone is indicated (starting at 2 mg/kg or 40 mg/m2 in
dogs or 4 mg/kg in cats) (ch. 144). In some cases, additional
immunosuppressive drugs, such as azathioprine, cyclosporine,
chlorambucil, or mycophenolate mofetil, may be warranted if

glucocorticoids are insufficient or to limit glucocorticoid-associated
adverse effects (ch. 169).
Animals with vasculitis frequently have been treated with
pentoxifylline (15 mg/kg PO q8-12h in dogs and cats26), which is a
methylxanthine derivative reported to decrease leukocyte chemotaxis
and degranulation, inhibit production of the pro-inflammatory
cytokine tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha, and decrease blood
viscosity. Additionally, dogs with cutaneous vasculitis have been
treated with a combination of oxytetracycline and niacinamide (ch.
178), which is purported to have various immunomodulatory effects.
Whereas all these effects could be helpful in principle, there is no
published evidence to indicate how efficacious these medications will
be for treatment of cutaneous or systemic vasculitis.

PROGNOSIS
The long-term prognosis for animals with vasculitis depends on its
underlying cause. In those with infectious agents, clinical and
pathological features of vasculitis will usually resolve or improve
with appropriate treatment. Similarly, presumed immune-complex
vasculitis in dogs with other immune-mediated diseases will often
resolve with conventional immunosuppressive treatment. Dogs with
idiopathic cutaneous vasculitis may be cured or managed with good
quality of life with appropriate immunomodulatory treatment (see
above), but the prognosis is much poorer for those with systemic
IMV or vasculitis affecting central nervous system vessels, which is
usually progressive and terminal.

The spleen has always been an organ of mystery and curiosity, and throughout the ages
many roles and functions have been ascribed to it—including the site of production of black
bile (the cardinal humor of melancholy), a filter of the liver, an inhibitor of the running
capacity of horses and men, and it has been held simultaneously as “seat of conflicting
emotions such as joy, anger, spite, whim, malice and impetuosity, among others.”1 As time
has passed we have become more learned regarding this majestic structure, as has our
ability to intervene when it is diseased. While we are more advanced in our techniques
than the late 2nd century Chinese physician Hua Tuo’s use of wine and hemp preparations
in performing a partial splenectomy,2 we still have leagues of travel left in our mastery of
the humble spleen. The diagnosis of splenic disease often requires a multimodal approach
via clinical history (ch. 2), physical examination (ch. 3), imaging, and often tissue
sampling (ch. 85). As there are no specific clinical signs or laboratory tests to assess
function and dysfunction, evaluation for splenic abnormalities must be a considered part
of any patient workup and may be missed if not considered. This chapter will detail
information about nonmalignant and selected malignant splenic masses and nodules,
causes of splenomegaly (benign, infectious, inflammatory), splenic torsion, splenic
thrombosis and miscellaneous clinically relevant entities.

STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION

GENERAL FEATURES
The spleen is a large, flattened, elongate lymphoid organ suspended by the gastrosplenic
ligament within the left cranial region of the abdomen, the structure of which allows
intimate contact between blood and lymphocytes.3,4 Roles of the spleen include mounting
immunological responses to antigens, removal of aged or defective blood cells from
circulation, blood filtration including elimination of foreign particles and infectious agents,
acting as a reservoir of blood, and hematopoiesis in the fetus and in some disease states of
the adult.3-6 The spleen can mount a strong response to blood borne pathogens.
Splenectomy can lead to an increased susceptibility to infectious diseases, including
hemotropic mycoplasmosis (formerly hemobartonellosis; ch. 194), eperythrozoonosis,
and babesiosis (ch. 197).7,8

TYPES OF SPLEENS
The spleens of different species of animals can be classified in two ways: by 1) blood flow
and 2) ratio of lymphoid tissue to smooth muscle trabeculae. When classifying by blood
flow, “sinusoidal” spleens are characterized by emptying of the post-capillary blood into
venous sinusoids (as in dogs). In “non-sinusoidal spleens” as seen in cats, venous sinusoids
are absent or poorly developed,9 and the blood is drained via pulpous veins with a wall
structure that is highly different from that of venous sinusoids.9-11 Sinusoidal spleens,
therefore, have access to larger amounts of blood for release into the circulation during an
emergency situation.5,9,12 The spleen of the dog is able to store one-third of the dog’s blood
volume during sleep, replaced upon waking.4,10,13 When classifying by amount of
lymphoid tissue, “defensive type” spleens (as in rabbits and humans) have large amounts
of lymphoid tissue and relatively little smooth muscle in the capsule and trabeculae,
whereas “storage type” spleens (as in the dog and cat) have large amounts of smooth
muscle and trabeculae.4,5,14

PREVALENCE OF SPLENIC DISEASE
The prevalence of splenic disease historically has been difficult to estimate as most
descriptive studies are based on pathology submissions—which may not represent a
natural population, as “normal” spleens are typically not removed for biopsy nor sampled.
As such, their contribution to systemic disease in the absence of gross abnormalities can be
challenging to ascertain, as surgical biopsy studies may skew for surgical diseases, and
autopsy-based studies may have a bias for incidental findings. Focal lesions or
splenomegaly can indicate clinically significant disease—but not always, so the finding of
splenic abnormalities can pose a clinical conundrum. Splenic lesions accounted for 1-3% of
cases in two large surveys of canine surgical accessions from diagnostic laboratories.15,16
In these surveys, the most commonly reported splenic lesions were benign nodules
(predominantly hyperplastic nodules and splenic hematomas) (19-24%), with a higher
incidence of hyperplastic nodules (48%) in one study of a colony of dogs that were exposed
to strontium/radium over their lifetime.15
It is important to note that dogs with splenic masses or nodules without
hemoperitoneum most frequently comprise benign processes (70% in one study),17 and

that benign nodular hyperplasia of the spleen is a very common incidental lesion of aged
dogs. An internal review by one of this chapter’s authors of 500 complete canine
postmortem examinations (examination of all organs) from the authors’ institution found
benign nodular hyperplasia in approximately 18% of cases.
It has been previously reported that two-thirds of dogs with splenomegaly or splenic
mass lesions have neoplasia, and that two-thirds of those with splenic neoplasia have
hemangiosarcoma (HSA; ch. 325) (the double “two-thirds rule”); however, this rule is
subject to considerable refinement.18-20 HSA is the most commonly reported neoplasm of
the spleen, with a prevalence ranging from 9-74%15,17,21-23 Most descriptive studies
evaluate the prevalence of splenic masses removed surgically. The prevalence of
malignancy in splenic masses can vary from 30-58%,17,21,23 meaning that nonmalignant
masses comprise a significant proportion of splenic masses in dogs. Splenic hemorrhage is
the most common cause of nontraumatic hemoabdomen (74-90% of dogs).24,25
Hemoabdomen has been shown to be more strongly associated with malignancy in
multiple studies,19,21,22 with no correlation between hemoabdomen at the time of
diagnosis of splenomegaly and malignancy in one study in small breed dogs.18 In three
retrospective studies, acute, nontraumatic hemoperitoneum was more likely to be caused
by malignancy in 68% (41/60) to 87% (67/77) of patients.18,24-26 Similarly, nontraumatic
splenic rupture was attributed to malignancies in 67% (97/145) to 76% (54/71) of canine
cases.18,27 In addition to hemoperitoneum, older age, breed size, larger body weight, lower
splenic mass to volume ratio, lower mean splenic weight, presence of thoracic metastasis,
anemia, and thrombocytopenia have been shown to be associated with malignancy at the
time of diagnosis.17,19,20,27,28 Patient size may be a contributing factor, as smaller dogs
(<27.8 kg) are significantly less likely to be diagnosed with HSA,22,23 and amongst smaller
breed dogs, nodular lesions have been overreported in Miniature Schnauzers, Dachshunds,
and Beagles.22

CLINICAL SIGNS
Clinical signs of splenic disease can be vague and non-specific and may relate to
manifestations of systemic disease with splenic involvement. Lethargy, inappetence,
vomiting, anorexia, weight loss, and weakness/collapse may be present at the time of
examination, reported by the owner, or both.29 Active intra-abdominal bleeding may
manifest with pallor, tachycardia, tachypnea, weak femoral pulses, and the presence of a
fluid wave on palpation (

Video 182.1). Concurrent cardiac arrhythmias (ch. 230) may

present as lethargy, collapse (ch. 40), or malaise. Of note, profound polyuria/polydipsia
(ch. 53) can be observed with acute splenic disease (such as torsion, acute congestion, or
secondary hemoabdomen). The mechanism is unknown but may be due to a psychogenic
polydipsia component due to abdominal pain or distension of splenic stretch receptors,
and acute splenic disease and should be on the differential list when these signs are
reported.29,30

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH

Like many other conditions, the diagnostic approach for splenic disease should begin with
a detailed physical examination (ch. 3) and clinical history (ch. 2). Splenomegaly can
often be appreciated on deep palpation of a non-turgid abdomen and may be aided by
positioning the patient on their hind limbs to allow abdominal viscera to fall caudally.
Generalized splenomegaly may be obvious, especially if the organ is firm, and large masses
may similarly be palpable or suspected when present. Breed variability in spleen size and
relative location should be taken into consideration during examination: German
Shepherd Dogs may have normally large spleens and Greyhounds, Cocker Spaniels, and
Miniature Schnauzers may normally have a more caudally-oriented spleen.29 Given less
variation in the size of normal spleens in cats, splenomegaly may be easier to appreciate. If
there is concern for hemoabdomen, ballottement for a fluid wave should be performed (
Videos 21.1, 182.1). Of note, splenomegaly may also be present but not appreciated on
examination in many cases.
After physical examination, imaging for confirmation or screening for abnormalities is
recommended. Radiographs and ultrasound as first or second-tier diagnostics are
commonly utilized, while advanced imaging such as computed tomography (CT) or
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may be reserved for evaluation of the spleen in
conjunction with other organ systems/systemic disease when screening for metastatic
disease, or for surgical planning purposes.

CLINICAL PATHOLOGY
There are no clinicopathologic findings that are pathognomonic for splenic disease.
Anemia may be present and non-regenerative in the case of anemia of inflammatory
disease, of which the spleen may be the primary or secondary cause (ch. 172).
Regenerative anemias may be seen secondary to loss in the case of ruptured or bleeding
splenic masses, or with immune-mediated conditions, in which the spleen may play an
etiopathological role (ch. 174). Nucleated red blood cells (nRBCs)—often seen in the face
of a regenerative anemia—can also be present with altered or abnormal splenic function.31
Howell-Jolly bodies may be present in mammals with decreased splenic function or after
splenectomy.32 Red blood cell morphologies that may be seen with splenic disease include
acanthocytes, elliptocytes, schistocytes, and spherocytes (ch. 57).32 In a study of 100
splenectomized dogs, those with anemia, nRBCs, abnormal RBC morphology, or splenic
rupture prior to surgery had a greater chance of having splenic neoplasia.19
Post-splenectomy patients will experience transient thrombocytosis and leukocytosis,33
sometimes marked, owing to increased thrombopoiesis and increased blood
concentrations of thrombopoietin,32 which resolves after weeks. Additionally,
splenectomized patients will not have the normal physiologic erythrocytosis observed as a
result of splenic contraction.32

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
Survey radiographs of the abdomen are helpful in initial assessment of the spleen,
especially to help discern its size and to screen for large masses or associated abdominal
effusion. However, given the dynamic nature—including breed-related “normals” for size
and location—there are limitations to this diagnostic test. The proximal extremity (head) of

the spleen is relatively fixed in the left craniodorsal aspect of the abdomen due to
attachment of the gastrosplenic ligament. The distal extremity (tail), however, can be
positioned variably due to lack of attachment. On ventrodorsal views, the head is typically
seen as a triangular soft tissue opacity caudolateral to the gastric fundus and craniolateral
to the left kidney.34 On lateral views, the triangular soft tissue opacity of the head of the
spleen is located dorsally, caudal to the stomach, and the tail is typically immediately
caudal and slightly ventral to the pylorus or liver.34 The feline spleen is thinner and
smaller in comparison and typically less variable in size and position.34
Signs of generalized splenomegaly include thickened, rounded, blunted margins,
displacement of local structures, and sometimes a folded appearance.34 Splenic torsion
(Figure 182.1, A-C) with resultant occlusion of venous (and ultimately arterial) drainage
will lead to not just diffuse splenomegaly but often an atypical position, with caudal and
dorsal displacement. Radiographs are helpful in identifying emphysematous splenic
changes which may occur secondary to torsion and ischemia or rarely with splenic
abscess.34,35 Splenic masses can result in local displacement of viscera based on size and
location: body or distal (tail) splenic masses may appear as a ventral abdominal mass or
cause caudal displacement of the jejunum on the lateral view, while on ventrodorsal views
they may appear midline or just lateral to midline.34 Masses of the proximal spleen (head)
may displace the stomach cranially with local displacement of intestine, and possible
caudal displacement of the left kidney.34 Smaller masses or nodules, especially if noncapsule-deforming, will not be seen radiographically. Peritoneal effusion may be present
with both benign and malignant processes. Mineralization within the spleen may be seen
with dystrophic calcification of neoplasia, hematomas, granulomas, abscesses or siderotic
plaques.34
Due to its relative low cost, non-invasiveness, ubiquity, and plethora of information
provided, ultrasound remains the imaging diagnostic most commonly utilized for
evaluating the spleen. This modality offers information on appearance (echotexture, size,
contour, blood flow) of both the organ itself, as well as lesions within it, which make it
valuable in aiding clinical decision making. While excellent at describing lesions and
changes within the splenic parenchyma, it is of importance to note that there are few
pathognomonic patterns which can diagnose neoplastic conditions definitively and
cytologic evaluation or biopsy are usually required.36-38 The ultrasound appearance of
common splenic lesions can be found in Tables 182.1 and 182.2.
Based on position and breed/species, the head of the spleen may need to be imaged
through the abdominal retrocostal or left intercostal approach,38 and the tail may extend
to the level of the bladder. As such, full examination of the organ may require an approach
tailored to the patient’s anatomy. Splenic size is hard to evaluate subjectively in dogs but in
cats there is more general uniformity, with a mean thickness reported to be 8.2 mm (SD 1.4
mm) and width 26.7 mm (SD 4.4 mm) on transverse images.39 In obese cats, the spleen
can be displaced significantly dorsally.
Splenic venous thrombosis can be identified by solid echogenic material within the
lumen of a normally anechoic vessel. Thrombi may be clinically inconsequential if there is
sufficient flow around the thrombus or if there is sufficient collateral circulation.38
Spontaneous contrast visualized in the large splenic vessels may suggest red cell
aggregation either due to hypercoagulable states (ch. 171)40 or low shear rates seen with
low flow velocity.41

Gas inclusions within splenic parenchyma are uncommonly seen; they can occur with
infection involving gas-producing bacteria or abscessation.35 Dystrophic mineralization or
mineralized neoplasia will appear as strongly hyperechoic areas with strong distal acoustic
shadowing.38
CT can be a valuable aid in the assessment of the spleen. In addition to providing
information about structural characteristics, this modality allows for evaluation of vascular
and perfusion studies. While general anesthesia is required for most evaluations,
abdominal CT may be utilized with sedated or critically ill patients, and may detect lesions
more readily than ultrasound in dogs >25 kg.42 Normal perfusion patterns of contrast
studies have been described and should be taken into account when used.43 Contrast
evaluation of splenic tumors can be helpful in the assessment of focal splenic masses as
both pre-contrast and post-contrast attenuation patterns may help discriminate malignant
from benign processes.44,45 Phase contrast CT is helpful for evaluation of perfusion
characteristics, but has not proven reliable for differentiating benign from malignant
lesions.46
There are currently few MRI studies to recommend its use for abdominal imaging. One
pilot study of 8 dogs with splenic lesions was able to accurately differentiate malignancy
from non-malignancy47; however, this modality is not currently commonly used for
abdominal imaging.

SAMPLING OF THE SPLEEN
FINE-NEEDLE ASPIRATION AND CYTOLOGY
Fine-needle aspiration with cytologic evaluation of samples may aid in obtaining a
definitive diagnosis without further, more invasive intervention. However, it may be of
limited diagnostic value with the exception of some situations, including metastatic
neoplasia, diffuse lymphoma and extramedullary hematopoiesis (EMH).16,48 The clinician
should keep in mind that infiltrative (diffusely disseminated) round cell neoplasia
(lymphoma, mast cell tumor [MCT], plasma cell tumor) is more likely to exfoliate and yield
a diagnosis compared to mesenchymal origin tumors.49,50 The aspiration of discrete
nodules cannot reliably discern between hematoma, hemangioma, HSA and nodular
hyperplasia and as such, caution should be used in interpreting results.51 Aspiration of
blood-filled or cystic structures is often of low informational yield.

One of the largest limitations of cytology is that a negative/normal result can carry a
poor negative predictive value (51%),50 which may be attributable to errors in sampling or
requiring tissue architecture for characterization of a lesion in question (e.g., for nodular
lymphoma, including marginal zone lymphoma). Positive aspirates for neoplasia generally
carry a high specificity and positive predictive value (97% in one study).50 Cytologic
diagnosis of splenic lymphomas carries a low sensitivity.50 Agreement between cytologic
and histologic evaluations of canine splenic lesions has been reported to range from 38100%, although some of those comparisons were reported before there was widespread
acceptance of nodular splenic lymphomas, which can be misinterpreted as reactive
lymphoid hyperplasia on cytologic evaluation.49-53 Although cytologic examination has
shown high agreement with histologic examination for MCT, undifferentiated round cell
tumors, HSA and carcinoma, in most cases, cytology is not a reliable substitute for
histopathology in the definitive diagnosis of splenic tumors.50 In short, while needle
aspiration may answer the question “is this neoplastic?”, histopathologic evaluation is
better to definitively diagnose malignant neoplasia, and assess benign disorders of growth,

vascular disturbances, and necrosis.51 When multiple nodules are present within the
spleen, aspiration may be a reasonable initial diagnostic test given a higher association
with malignancy.52,54 If peritoneal effusion is present, cytologic evaluation of the effusion
(chs. 71, 86) is indicated before direct sampling of the spleen.55
Aspiration largely is considered safe, with a low rate of complications associated with
hemorrhage.53 Owing to the presence of a capsule, hemorrhage associated with aspiration
during states of thrombocytopenia/thrombocytopathia may be lower compared to
aspiration of the liver. Of note, the spleen of any cat with concern for plasma cell neoplasia
should be evaluated for plasmacytosis (even in a normal-sized organ) given a high
incidence of visceral organ infiltration; the possible benefit of diagnostic sampling has to
be weighed against the possible drawback of bleeding tendency due to thrombopathia in
cats with paraproteinemia.56 If ultrasonography is used, contamination of the skin, slides,
and needles with ultrasound gel should be avoided, as this material can interfere with
microscopic evaluation.55,57
Both aspiration (with the application of suction via syringe) and non-aspiration (using a
“pin-cushion” technique with just a needle) have been described and at least one paper
suggests that a non-aspiration method is superior in order to reduce blood contamination
and increase cellularity (chs. 85, 88).58,59 Significant thrombocytopenia or recent
treatment with anticoagulants or thromboprophylactics may be relative contraindications
for aspiration.

BIOPSY AND HISTOPATHOLOGY
While total splenectomies are undertaken cautiously in human medicine due to concerns
for sepsis (overwhelming post-splenectomy infection [OPSI]), these sequelae are not
identified in veterinary medicine.60 As such, when splenic lesions are observed, especially
if there are multiple nodules or regional abnormalities, total splenectomy is often the
intervention of choice. However, partial splenectomy in veterinary medicine has been
described, especially in context of non-ruptured splenic lesions,61 and may be considered.
Needle core biopsy of the spleen as a viable diagnostic in characterizing focal lesions has
been reported to be safe53,62 but in one author’s experience it is uncommonly pursued and
not often clinically helpful. Non-surgical biopsy may be helpful in cases where patient
comorbidity abounds or in patients with pre-existing infectious disease where splenectomy
may increase risk of relapse.7,8,63
After splenectomy, the accuracy of the pathologic diagnosis relies upon adequate
sampling of the splenic lesions. Ideally, 5-10 wedge samples should be obtained from each
mass, focusing on the viable tissue at the junction between the mass and surrounding
spleen, which has the highest probability of providing diagnostic information.64,65 Tissue
from the center of the mass typically comprises hemorrhagic and necrotic tissue, and
therefore, should be avoided. A general rule is to sample firm, white to tan tissue rather
than friable red tissue,65 as these regions have a higher likelihood of containing cells and
not hemorrhage/hematoma or necrosis. Shiny regions may also indicate a higher
likelihood of viability as opposed to dull, necrotic areas. If adequate sections of this
junction are evaluated and a cause has not been identified, sampling of additional tissue
may be warranted.

SPLENOMEGALY
Causes of splenomegaly are summarized in Table 182.3.

SPLENIC NODULES
Despite different sources of origin, nodules can be similar with regards to clinical
presentation, imaging findings, and morphology.65 This significant morphologic overlap
can pose challenges to clinicians, radiologists, and pathologists alike.

HEMORRHAGIC SPLENIC NODULES
Hematomas of the spleen occur due to disruption of the splenic parenchyma that results in
altered blood flow and accumulation of blood.4,65 The splenic artery enters the splenic
hilus as trabecular arteries.3,4,9 These arteries branch further to become the central
arteries which are peripheralized by lymphoid tissue (periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths
[PALS])3,4,9 and merge directly with the marginal sinus that surrounds the splenic
lymphoid follicles. Distortion of the marginal zone and thus marginal sinus due to pooling
of blood within and surrounding hyperplastic nodules is hypothesized to interfere with
drainage and may play a role in hematoma formation.4,15 In the cat, the marginal sinus is
not as well developed as it is in the dog. This may explain why dogs have a higher tendency
for splenic hematoma formation (more frequent nodular hyperplasia and well developed
marginal sinuses).
Splenic hematoma formation can occur with benign nodular hyperplasia, neoplasia
(such as HSA), or trauma, or it can be idiopathic.65 Lymphoid nodular hyperplasia is one
of the most commonly reported causes of splenic hematoma, with ranges of 30-60%.15,6567

If numerous lymphoid nodules are observed within or adjacent to the hematoma, the
pathologist should surmise that lymphoid nodular hyperplasia is the underlying cause.65
Lymphoid nodules were observed in 27% of 100 cases of splenic hematoma but were not
observed in any of 120 cases of splenic HSA in one series.65,66 HSA is the most common
malignancy associated with hematoma formation in dogs.15 Less frequent causes of splenic
hematoma include splenic amyloidosis (chs. 269 and 302) and infection. Distension of the
splenic capsule from large hematomas along with separation from the blood supply can
predispose to rupture, hemoabdomen, and potentially repeated rupture with formation of
adhesions.65 Hemoabdomen is reported in 20-30% of canine splenic hematomas.65,66,68
Diagnostic investigations of splenic masses with large hematoma formation are
predominantly focused on ruling out a malignant process. Most frequently, the entire
spleen is removed surgically and submitted for histopathologic evaluation. Samples from
hematomas should be obtained as described above (see Sampling of the Spleen). Splenic
hematomas are common in the dog but are rare in other domestic animals. Ages of affected
dogs range from 3 to 16 years of age with no sex predilection. When adjusting for breed
popularity, German Shepherd Dogs and Standard Poodles have been reported to be
predisposed.65,66,68 When evaluating hematomas microscopically, proliferative stromal
cells or neovascularization in chronic hematomas may have histomorphologic overlap
(appear microscopically similar) to HSA.65,68

SPLENIC INFARCTION
Splenic infarction can be seen with or without splenic torsion. The splenic vein is a branch
of the portal vein that can easily be imaged via ultrasound examination.69 Infarcted
parenchyma will cause the affected tissue to appear hypoechoic to anechoic, with a sharp

demarcation of perfused versus devitalized parenchyma and may or may not distort the
capsular contour.38 Poor contrast uptake is expected after injection in affected areas.
Splenic vein thrombosis (Figure 182.2, A;

Video 182.2) is the most common disease

of the splenic vein, typically caused by abnormalities in one or more components of
Virchow’s triad (endothelial injury, blood stasis, hypercoagulability; ch. 171). Etiologies
for thrombosis (chs. 219, 238) include neoplasia, corticosteroid excess (chs. 293, 294),
immune-mediated disorders (chs. 174-179), endocrinopathy (e.g., diabetes mellitus [chs.
291, 292]), coagulopathies (ch. 171), splenic enlargement/hematoma, cardiac (ch. 238),
liver and renal disease (ch. 302), sepsis (ch. 128) and vasculitis (ch. 181Chapter
219Chapter 238).69-71 In one study, neoplasia was the most common condition
associated with splenic vein thrombosis in dogs, with lymphoma as the most common
neoplasm.69,72 Splenic vein thrombosis is typically caused by chronic conditions with slow
progression and may not produce clinical signs (can be an incidental finding); however,
rare cases with an acute presentation have been reported.69 Dogs with splenic infarction
may have a higher mortality rate in the post-operative period.70
Infarcts commonly occur in the peripheral, subcapsular regions in which the sinusoidal
areas have poor perfusion and venous return.4 Acute infarctions are characterized by
raised, dark red parenchyma (Figure 182.2, B) which, if large enough, can be identified
with imaging. Grossly, acute splenic infarcts can be difficult to distinguish from incomplete
capsular contraction.4 Over time, breakdown of blood and subsequent fibrosis results in
changes of size, shape and color of these lesions (Figure 182.2, C and D ).

NEOPLASIA
SELECTED MALIGNANT TUMORS (HEMORRHAGIC AND NONHEMORRHAGIC)
HSA, the most common malignancy of the canine spleen, is discussed in ch. 325.
Malignant neoplasia may cause hemorrhagic or non-hemorrhagic nodules in the spleen. It
is virtually impossible to grossly differentiate between benign and malignant processes
when a large hemorrhagic nodule is present.15

Stromal Sarcoma
Knowledge of the cellular components of the spleen is an important part of understanding
the disease processes of this complex organ, particularly for neoplastic processes. The
outer fibromuscular splenic capsule and trabecular extensions comprise predominantly
smooth muscle with interwoven fibers to allow for capsular expansion and contraction.3-5,9
Within the splenic parenchyma, there are two major intermingling compartments: the
hematogenous red pulp and the lymphoid white pulp, separated by the marginal zone.5
The red pulp consists primarily of loose tissue (red pulp vascular spaces) supported by
stromal cells (reticular cells, fibroblasts and myocytes), permeated by arterioles and
capillaries.3,4 Splenic stromal sarcoma is a diagnosis of exclusion, representing a
malignancy from the stromal mesenchyme of the spleen. This term includes neoplasms
previously designated as non-angiomatous, non-lymphomatous spindle cell sarcomas.65,73
Histiocytic neoplasms are no longer included in this category65 but should be ruled out in
cases of splenic mesenchymal spindle cell tumors as they can exhibit spindle cell
morphology.74 Histiocytic diseases are discussed in ch. 328.
Splenic stromal sarcomas can arise from various cell types, the most common of which
are fibrocytes (fibrosarcoma) and smooth muscle cells (leiomyosarcoma).73 However,
multipotential stem cells can give rise to other tumor types, including liposarcoma,
myxosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, or mesenchymoma
(ch. 324).65,73 When a distinct cell of origin cannot be found, these neoplasms are
classified as undifferentiated stromal sarcomas.65 Differentiation between these subtypes
is of uncertain prognostic significance, as some investigators found considerable overlap
within neoplastic groups when using immunohistochemistry in an attempt to distinguish
fibrosarcomas, leiomyosarcomas and undifferentiated sarcomas.73 Immunohistochemical
identification of muscle tissue-associated cytoskeletal proteins in tumors that were

classified as non-myogenic in origin may indicate the possibility of a common histogenesis
from smooth muscle trabeculae, vascular smooth muscle or myofibroblasts.73 The
mesenchymoma represents a rare neoplasm in which two or more distinct differentiated
cell phenotypes are found in the same neoplasm.65,73 In one study, dogs with splenic
mesenchymomas were found to have a statistically significantly longer median survival
compared to dogs with other stromal sarcomas (12 months versus 3 months).73
Most splenic stromal sarcomas carry a guarded prognosis, with post-splenectomy
survival times reported to be similar to HSA; however, these reports included histiocytic
sarcoma.65,73 Longer survival times have been reported with a single nodule as compared
to dogs with identified metastasis.65,75 Mitotic count (number of mitoses within a
determined area, [typically 2.37 mm2 for most modern microscopes with an ocular field
number (FN) of 22])76 has been correlated with outcome for non-angiomatous, nonlymphomatous primary mesenchymal neoplasms of the spleen.73 In that study, a mitotic
count of 9 represented a cutoff between survival times; however, the mitotic counts were
performed with a high power field diameter of 0.5 mm (corresponding to an ocular FN of
20) and histiocytic sarcomas were not excluded.73 Benign tumors arising from the splenic
stroma are rare.65,73

Formerly Splenic Fibrohistiocytic Nodules (SFHN)
The umbrella term “splenic fibrohistiocytic nodule” (SFHN) is no longer considered an
appropriate term to categorize this heterogeneous and complex group of diseases.77 SFHN
has morphologic overlap with both benign and malignant proliferative processes, including
nodular hyperplasia (complex and lymphoid, formerly encompassed within grades I and II
SFHN) as well as nodular or diffuse lymphoma, stromal and histiocytic sarcoma which
should be carefully categorized.65,67,77 In the original study, dogs with grade III SFHN had
a 1 year survival rate of 32%, while those with grades I-II SFHN had a 1 year survival of
87%.67,77 However, SFHN was described before the commercial availability of
immunohistochemical means to classify histiocytic sarcoma and before marginal zone
lymphoma was described in dogs.67,77

Metastatic Neoplasia
Metastatic neoplasia represents an uncommon cause of splenic lesions in dogs and cats
(range of 1-6% of splenic lesions)15,57,65 Although the spleen is considered to be an organ
that filters blood, the lack of afferent lymphatic vessels may account for the paucity of
metastatic lesions in this organ. Types of metastatic neoplasia include sarcomas (ch. 324),
carcinomas, neuroendocrine tumors, hematogenous processes including leukemias (ch.
322), disseminated lymphoma (

Video 182.3, ch. 322), plasma cell neoplasia (ch.

322), histiocytic sarcoma (ch. 328), and visceral MCT (ch. 327).65

BENIGN PROLIFERATIONS
NODULAR HYPERPLASIA

Benign splenic nodules are common in dogs, and they can become complicated by
hematoma formation, rupture and hemoabdomen.65 Nodular hyperplasia refers to a
benign proliferative process in any organ derived from the cells which normally reside in
that organ. In the spleen, there are four major types of benign nodular hyperplasia,
designated by the predominating cell type with no difference in biological behavior
between the following categories: 1) lymphoid, 2) splenic stromal, 3) hematopoietic, and 4)
complex.65 Lymphoid nodular hyperplasia is the most common.67,77,78 In any given
splenic nodule, variable combinations of these four categories can make classification
challenging, but precise classification has no prognostic significance. The biggest challenge
for the pathologist is to rule out the possibility of malignancy with representative sections.
Differentiation of small, well-differentiated stromal sarcomas from complex nodular
hyperplasia can be difficult in some situations.65 These benign lesions also need to be
differentiated from marginal zone lymphoma and mantle cell lymphoma, two relatively
recently described types of indolent lymphoma for which evaluation of the nodular
architecture is an important part of classification.78-82 See ch. 322 for more information
about hematopoietic tumors.
Splenic myelolipomas (Figure 182.1, D and E;

Video 182.4) are benign

proliferations which comprise a combination of well-differentiated adipocytes and
hematopoietic cells. They are a common incidental finding and are easily identified, being
strongly hyperechoic, along the mesenteric border of the spleen or within the parenchyma,
often tracking along vessels, and non-cavitated83 (Figure 182.1 D,). It is uncertain
whether these masses represent a neoplastic, metaplastic, or hamartomatous process.65
These masses can be small or large, and are typically incidental,65 although one author has
observed a case of splenic myelolipoma resulting in fatal hemoabdomen.

SPLENOMEGALY WITHOUT NODULES:
NONNEOPLASTIC CAUSES
Hemolytic Anemia
Erythrophagocytosis (phagocytosis of red blood cells by macrophages) in the spleen is
increased with hemolytic anemia, including immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (ch.
174). Inherited erythrocyte defects such as osmotic fragility and pyruvate kinase deficiency
may lead to diffuse splenomegaly in both dogs and cats84,85 (ch. 174). Macrophages of the
spleen reside within the red pulp vascular spaces, splenic cords, and (in the dog) around
the sinusoid endothelium.4 The venous sinusoids are lined by a discontinuous
endothelium through which erythrocytes squeeze and empty into splenic venules, the
splenic vein, and ultimately the portal vein.3,4 Defective cells are less pliable and cannot
bend into the narrow slits of the basement membrane; thus, they are entrapped and
removed by macrophages. Phagocytosis of the entire erythrocyte or removal of portions of
the erythrocyte membrane or cytoplasm is encompassed in a term called “pitting” and is
performed predominantly by perisinusoidal macrophages.4 This process can be
physiologic or pathologic. In the feline spleen, pitting also takes place, but it is a
comparatively slow or less efficient process that is performed by macrophages of the red
pulp cords. Acute hemolysis will result in a more congested enlarged spleen, and chronic
hemolysis will result in a more meaty (cell infiltrated) enlarged spleen.4 A heightened need
for phagocytosis, resulting in increased numbers of macrophages throughout the splenic
cords and red pulp vascular spaces, can also occur with other causes including
hematogenous infections (e.g., prolonged bacteremia, hemoparasites).4

Torsion
Twisting of the spleen around the gastrosplenic ligament results in venous occlusion with
severe congestion, which may progress to arterial occlusion and splenic infarction4
(Figure 182.1, A-C). Splenic torsions often cause vague clinical signs including lethargy,

vomiting, and anorexia.30 German Shepherd Dogs, Great Danes, and English Bulldogs are
overrepresented in descriptive studies.30,86 Palpable splenomegaly should be a consistent
finding. Previous episodes of gastric dilation and volvulus (GDV) have been posited as a
risk factor for subsequent splenic torsion,30 but a larger and more recent study did not
show that previous splenectomy was associated with increased incidence of subsequent
GDV.87 Torsion associated with the presence of accessory splenic tissue and torsion
around the uterine horn of a pregnant bitch have been reported.88,89
Radiographs consistently demonstrate splenomegaly with variably poor abdominal
detail.30,86 On ultrasound, torsions are commonly described with spleens being markedly
enlarged with mottled and “lacy” parenchyma, along with abnormal positioning of the
organ34,90 (

Videos 182.5 and 182.6). The appearance of a hyperechoic hilar

perivenous triangle has been significantly associated with torsion, in comparison to
infarction without torsion.90 CT changes associated with splenic torsion include an
enlarged, rounded, or folded organ with a minimal difference in median parenchymal
attenuation (1.15 Hounsfield unit) pre- and post-contrast91 (

Video 182.7). A “whirl

sign” alongside a strongly hyperattenuating center on pre-contrast images may also be
present (Figure 182.1 B, ).91 The treatment for splenic torsion is surgical splenectomy,
which generally carries a favorable short- and long-term prognosis.30,86 Severe (21-23
k/mcL) thrombocytopenia has been described in 2 dogs with splenic torsion, which
resolved after surgery.92

INFECTIOUS/INFLAMMATORY DISEASES
Splenitis, or inflammatory splenomegaly, is usually secondary to primary or systemic
infection. Causes of splenitis are listed in Box 182.1.

HYPERSPLENISM
Hypersplenism refers to a decrease in red cells, white cells, and platelets in the blood due
to increased destruction by or sequestration within an enlarged spleen. In veterinary
medicine, hypersplenism is defined not just by the presence of splenomegaly but is
histologically distinctive due to the presence of diffuse hematopoiesis (myeloid
metaplasia), vascular thrombosis with splenic infarction, and a reactive and proliferative
cellular reticular meshwork containing excess macrophages.93 The macrophage presence
can range from reactive histiocytosis with excessive erythrophagocytosis in the bone
marrow and spleen to overtly malignant histiocytic neoplasia.93 In a study of 65 cases of
hypersplenism diagnosed via splenectomy, erythrophagocytosis was present in 92% of
cases.93 Total bilirubin was elevated in 30% of cases, and Coombs testing was only positive
in 21% of the 14 dogs tested93; 70% of dogs died in the 1-year post-operative interval,
either spontaneously or via euthanasia as a result of their splenic disease. The presence of
giant cells was reported to be a histologic feature indicative of a poor prognosis.93
Treatment for hypersplenism is directed at secondary causes, if identified and possible.
Splenectomy is the most common intervention when a secondary cause cannot be treated

or none is identified. Non-surgical therapies—including the injection of ethanolamine
oleate into the spleen and the use of high-intensity focused ultrasound to target and
destroy parenchyma—have been described experimentally but are not available in
practice.94

POLYCLONAL B-CELL LYMPHOCYTOSIS IN ENGLISH
BULLDOGS (PBLEB)
PBLEB is a newly-recognized syndrome which is initially nonneoplastic but is
hypothesized to have the potential for malignant transformation95 (

Video 182.8). In a

study of 84 cases of patients with CD21+ lymphocytosis, 70% had polyclonal or restricted
polyclonal immunoglobulin gene rearrangements, and splenomegaly or splenic masses
were detected in 57% of cases.95 Hyperglobulinemia was a common feature (65%). The
median age of dogs was 6.8 years and males were overrepresented (74%).95 Splenectomy
was pursued in a subset of cases, more due to discomfort than hematologic indicators of
hypersplenism, and histologic evaluation in 4 cases demonstrated lymphoid follicular
hyperplasia of variable severity consisting predominantly of heterogeneous B-cells.95

EXTRAMEDULLARY HEMATOPOIESIS (EMH)
EMH is defined as the development of sites of hematopoiesis outside the bone marrow.55
Immature myeloid, erythroid and platelet precursors can be seen at low levels within the
spleen of healthy animals.55 However, abundant EMH resulting in splenomegaly can be
caused by numerous, diverse processes.55 EMH of clinical significance can be found with
inflammatory disease, acute and chronic hemolytic anemia and/or thrombocytopenia,
hemorrhage, myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative disorders.55,59 Less common
causes include recovery from chemotherapy or intoxications, or in association with
neoplastic processes.55

MISCELLANEOUS
SIDEROTIC PLAQUES

Splenic siderotic plaques are also called hemosiderotic nodules or Gamna-Gandy bodies
and are focal accumulations of blood and blood breakdown products (hemosiderin,
hematoidin) with mineral (calcium) and fibrous connective tissue. Aspiration of these
plaques reveals numerous macrophages containing blue-green to black (hemosiderin) or
golden yellow (hematoidin) granular material.59 These plaques are most commonly
observed along the edges of the capsule but can also be observed within the trabeculae.65
These plaques are grossly firm to hard, raised, and range from white to yellow or brown.
Chronic hemorrhage is the presumed cause of the formation of these nodules. In one
study, siderotic plaques were not specifically associated with splenic hematoma as
compared to splenic HSA.65,66

CHORISTOMA (ACCESSORY SPLEEN) (FIGURE 182.2,
H-J)/SPLENOSIS
Heterotopic spleens can be characterized either as accessory spleen, which is congenitally
duplicated splenic tissue, or as splenosis, which is splenic tissue that was autotransplanted
via surgery, splenic trauma or rupture.96 Ectopic or accessory splenic tissue is one of the
most common congenital anomalies in animals and humans.97,98 Ectopic splenic tissue
can be found anywhere in the abdomen; however, the left limb of the pancreas is a
common location in both humans and domestic animals (sometimes called intrapancreatic
accessory spleens). These are benign, incidental findings and must not be misinterpreted
as metastases when observed with diagnostic imaging or gross evaluation (laparotomy,
necropsy).97,99 Accessory spleen usually is a single structure, and on ultrasound it has a
homogeneous echotexture that is the same as the echotexture of the spleen itself;
conversely, metastases typically have a heterogeneous echotexture, sometimes with a
hypoechoic rim with either homogeneous or heterogeneous inner parenchyma (“target
lesion”). Differential diagnoses for the gross lesion include a lymph node draining
hemorrhage, hematoma, hemangioma, HSA, or any other vascularized tumor.

SPLENOSYSTEMIC SHUNT (FIGURE 182.2, E-G)
Splenosystemic shunts have been reported to occur in the left and mid-abdominal cavity of
cats; they are defined as an anomalous vessel arising from the splenic vein and connecting
to the left renal vein or adjacent caudal vena cava. A description of these shunts in cats
found predominantly single shunts (90% of 33 cases) and that spayed females were
overrepresented (91%).100 The authors hypothesized that these shunts may be acquired
secondary to past or present portal hypertension, or that they are congenital and of
unknown clinical significance. In that study, 42% of 33 cats had clinicopathologic or
histopathologic evidence of hepatopathy. Given the sex predisposition, a possible
consideration is that adhesions from ovariohysterectomy may influence vascular
communication between the splenic and ovarian veins.100 This anomaly can also be
recognized on plain radiographs and is known as the “spaghetti sign,” typically observed
caudal to the spleen and lateral to the left kidney.101 This finding is reported to be more
readily identifiable on ventrodorsal projections (18/18 cases) as opposed to lateral views
(4/18 cases).101

SMALL SPLEENS
Reduced splenic size can be caused by contraction of the smooth muscle
capsule/trabeculae, trauma, cachexia, developmental abnormalities (e.g., hypoplasia
caused by immunodeficiencies), aging changes (lymphoid atrophy) or radiation.4
