CLIENT INFORMATION
Diseases of the Spleen
The spleen is a non-vital organ, which means it is not essential for life and can be removed
through surgery if necessary. In dogs and cats, as in humans, it lies on the left side of the
abdominal cavity. Its normal size and position can vary greatly based on breed of dog. The
function of the spleen is involved in both red and white blood cell function. In dogs, the
spleen acts as a reservoir for mature red blood cells which normally rest outside of
circulation but can be moved into the bloodstream quickly in case of hemorrhage. In
addition, the spleen can make new red blood cells (alongside the bone marrow which does
most of this job), remove old red blood cells from circulation, and remove red blood cells if
they are infected or tagged for removal from the immune system. The spleen also is a
lymphoid organ (like a big lymph node) which helps to filter the circulatory system and
provide immunologic function in training antibody-producing lymphocytes which are
important in fighting against bacteria, viruses, and parasites.
Patients with splenic disease can have symptoms that include lethargy, poor or absent
appetite, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, collapse, pale gums, or increased thirst and
urination. Alongside a physical examination, bloodwork and imaging (such as x-rays or
ultrasound) are commonly used for helping to diagnose splenic disease in dogs and cats.
Tumors of the spleen are the most common cause for splenectomy (surgical removal of the
spleen). These tumors can include both hemangiosarcomas (common) and hemangiomas
(rare), both of which arise from blood vessels within the spleen and present a high risk of

rupturing and causing bleeding into the abdominal cavity (hemoabdomen). A spontaneous
rupture can cause a dog to become lethargic very quickly and show pale gums, high heart
rate, and weakness and collapse due to bleeding into the abdomen. Hemangiosarcomas are
malignant tumors which means they have a high likelihood of spreading to other organs,
including the heart and lungs, and removal of the spleen alone may not be curative.
Hemangiomas are more locally invasive (stay with the spleen) but can still present a risk
for rupture. The ability to know exactly which type of tumor is affecting a particular
animal’s spleen requires processing the splenic tissue by a laboratory (typically takes 48-72
hours), so the decision of whether or not to proceed to surgery in a dog with a ruptured
splenic mass usually needs to be made before knowing for sure whether the splenic mass is
cancerous or not. Other types of masses or tumors can develop within the spleen, including
benign local growth of tissue (lymphoid hyperplasia), a blood bruise (hematoma), or fatty
tissue (myelolipoma). Because these can look very similar to cancer on x-rays and
ultrasound, it can be a complicated decision as to whether to monitor the changes, take a
small biopsy, or remove the entire organ. The spleen can also require removal if it loses
blood supply (commonly seen with gastric dilatation-volvulus, also called GDV or bloat) or
if it twists on itself (splenic torsion) or becomes damaged with trauma. Dogs and cats can
live without spleens; some may have difficulty fighting infections in the future but the
majority of patients can live a normal life without this organ.
Taryn A. Donovan (New York, New York) and Dennis J. Slade (New York,
New York)

ACCURATE DIAGNOSIS
THE CHALLENGE

Infectious diseases, many with zoonotic implications, are common
causes of morbidity and mortality in dogs and cats. The
consequences of overlooking infection are almost always significant
and sometimes fatal. Inappropriately attributing clinical problems to
infection can be equally detrimental due to progression of an
unrecognized disease or adverse effects from unwarranted
treatment. Accurately diagnosing infection requires appropriate
clinical reasoning. The problem-oriented approach is a useful
analytical clinical reasoning method (Box 183.1). Considering case
context is key to recognizing relevant differentials regardless of the
clinical reasoning method (Figure 183.1).

SIGNALMENT, ENVIRONMENT,
HISTORY, PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
(CHS. 2 AND 3)
Age is a risk factor for certain infections due to a lack of immunity in
young dogs, cumulative exposure risk in older dogs, and lengthy
incubation or prepatent periods for some pathogens. For example,
parvovirus infection (ch. 201) is more likely in a puppy and
heartworm infection (ch. 237) is more likely in an adult dog. Neuter
status and sex can also affect exposure risk. Sexually transmitted
diseases may be more likely in animals used for breeding, and male
dogs may be used more often for certain activities like hunting. Some
breeds are genetically predisposed to infectious diseases, such as
German Shepherd Dogs and disseminated aspergillosis (ch. 211).
The “occupation” of certain breeds may also increase risk. For
example, hunting breeds or kenneled dogs such as racing
Greyhounds are at higher risk for tick-transmitted diseases (chs.
187, 193). Some Babesia species (ch. 197) and hemotropic
mycoplasmas (ch. 194) may be transmitted by biting or vertically,
which may contribute to both occupational and breed risk. For cats,
housing (e.g., cattery, shelter or home), whether they have outdoor
access, and their FeLV/FIV status are important to note (chs. 198,
199).
For both dogs and cats, geographic locale and travel history
provide important case context that can raise the index of suspicion

for certain infectious diseases (ch. 9). Answers to questions about
coughing, sneezing, vomiting, diarrhea, polyuria/polydipsia
(PU/PD), and changes in drinking and urination can help identify
affected body systems. Specific history about dates and types of
vaccinations given is more valuable than noting “current on
vaccinations.” Documenting heartworm testing and the type of
heartworm prevention (and compliance with administration) has
importance beyond determining the likelihood of heartworm as a
differential; e.g., Trichuris vulpis infestation as a cause for large
bowel diarrhea or nasal mites as a cause for sneezing are less likely if
the preventative is milbemycin oxime. Flea and tick exposure
increase the likelihood of many infectious diseases. Use of flea and
tick preventatives and the specific products used should be
considered, since there are differences in efficacy for repelling or
killing ticks and preventing transmission of specific pathogens (see
textbook’s inside covers). A complete list of medications and
responses should include nutraceuticals, immunomodulators,
immunosuppressives, and antimicrobials. Subtle findings on
respiratory and cardiac auscultation (ch. 38), ophthalmic
examination (ch. 13), palpation of joints (ch. 32), lymph nodes (ch.
3), and abdomen (spleen) and observation of gait (ch. 31) are
particularly useful in localizing infections and ultimately making a
diagnosis.

Anemia: Anemia is localized to regenerative and nonregenerative. Regenerative anemia is further localized to
hemorrhage or hemolysis. Hemolysis is further localized to

oxidative damage, enzymatic deficiencies, physical damage,
metabolic).
Thrombocytopenia: Decreased production, sequestration
(vasculitis or splenomegaly), consumption (hemorrhage, DIC),

Neutropenia: Margination, increased demand, decreased

LABORATORY TESTING
Complete Blood Count (CBC; chs. 57, 58, and 59)
Either leukopenia or leukocytosis may occur during infection.
Neutrophils are arguably the main harbingers for bacterial and other
infections. Neutrophilia, with or without a left shift and toxic
changes, signals clinicians to look at the case context and consider
specific infectious diseases as differentials, or take a body systems
approach to localize where infection might be hiding. However,
neutrophilia is not specific for infection, as inflammatory conditions,
such as immune-mediated and hemolytic anemia can be associated

with dramatically increased neutrophil counts. Profound
neutrophilia is also a hallmark for some infections, such as
Hepatozoon americanum. Monocytosis is common with neutrophilia
and may be associated with infections that cause pyogranulomatous
inflammation. The neutrophilia and monocytosis of infection can be
difficult to differentiate from a “stress” leukogram: neutrophilia,
lymphopenia, monocytosis, and eosinopenia. Identifying band
neutrophils and/or toxic changes are not specific for infection vs
non-infectious inflammation.

Lymphocytosis
Although often overlooked, lymphocytosis can be a helpful clue that
certain infections are present. Many infections cause lymphocytosis
due to chronic antigenic stimulation, although some acute infections
may also cause lymphocytosis. Lymphocytosis in dogs can suggest
the presence of specific vector-borne diseases including ehrlichiosis
(ch. 193), babesiosis (ch. 197), hepatozoonosis (ch. 197),
leishmaniosis (ch. 197), trypanosomiasis (ch. 197), Anaplasma
platys (ch. 193), and Rangelia spp.1-8 There are also isolated
reports of lymphocytosis in dogs with fungal and parasitic
infections.9,10 Lymphocytosis and hyperglobulinemia, which can be
monoclonal or polyclonal (ch. 60), can be associated with
ehrlichiosis.1-3,11 Dogs with ehrlichiosis may have “atypical”
lymphocytes on CBC or noted in liver, spleen, and/or lymph node
aspirate or biopsy results.11,12 Bone marrow plasmacytosis may
occur, and clonal rearrangement of abnormal lymphocytes consistent
with lymphoid neoplasia has been described.11,13 These striking
effects on lymphocytes and antibody production suggest that
ehrlichiosis be considered when lymphoreticular neoplasia is
suspected. Lymphocytosis, bone marrow plasmacytosis,
hyperglobulinemia, and polyclonal and monoclonal gammopathies
have also been described in dogs with leishmaniosis (ch. 197).
Non-neoplastic lymphocytosis due to polyclonal expansion of B-cell
or heterogenous (both T and B cell) lymphocyte expansion due to
infection is common in cats.14 Lymphocytosis has been documented
in association with protozoal (ch. 197), hemotropic Mycoplasma

(ch. 194), Bartonella spp. (ch. 191), Aelurostrongylus abstrusus,
FeLV (ch. 199), and FIV (ch. 198) infections, and during the
recovery phase of experimental feline herpesvirus infection (ch.
205).15-21 Large granular lymphocytosis has been associated with
FIV infection concurrent with marked neutropenia.22

Eosinophilia, Basophilia
Parasitic infections should always be considered in the diagnostic
assessment of pets with eosinophilia. Fungal infections, pythiosis,
and protozoal infections, such as toxoplasmosis and babesiosis, are
also sometimes associated with eosinophilia (ch. 197). Basophilia is
relatively rare and usually accompanied by eosinophilia from similar
causes including allergy (ch. 129), drug reaction (ch. 178), certain
neoplasms, and parasitic infections. Basophilia has been noted in
specific infections, including heartworm disease (ch. 237) and some
protozoal infections. Tick infestations have also been rarely
associated with basophilia.

Neutropenia, Lymphopenia, Pancytopenia
Neutropenia may signal serious systemic infection or sepsis (ch.
128); however, transient neutropenia is common in the acute phase
of many vector-borne and other infections. Lymphopenia may occur
with different stages of many infections. Pancytopenia (ch. 176) is
associated with several infections, such as parvovirus (ch. 201),
panleukopenia (ch. 201), ehrlichiosis (ch. 193), histoplasmosis (ch.
209), and leishmaniosis (ch. 197).

Thrombocytopenia (chs. 59 and 175)
Thrombocytopenia can be suspected on a blood smear but should be
confirmed with a platelet count. Artifactual thrombocytopenia is
common with automated thrombocyte counts and should be verified
(chs. 58, 175). Infection, a common cause of thrombocytopenia in
both dogs and cats, can induce thrombocytopenia by any one, or a
combination of mechanisms that is used for localizing (categorizing)
it from a diagnostic standpoint. For example, Ehrlichia may cause
thrombocytopenia via immune-mediated destruction, sequestration
(due to vasculitis and splenomegaly), and/or by affecting bone
marrow production. Presenting case context can aid in identifying
infection as a cause of thrombocytopenia. For example, in the
context of a puppy with pancytopenia and diarrhea, it is consistent
with parvovirus infection (ch. 201). In a dog with acute kidney
injury (AKI), leptospirosis may be a top differential (ch. 192).
Thrombocytopenia is common in sepsis (ch. 128) and endocarditis
(ch. 232), either of which usually is suspected based on additional
clinical and laboratory findings. Infection that induces
thrombocytopenia can be clinically identical to primary immune
thrombocytopenia (ITP; ch. 175), usually treated with
immunosuppressive drugs that are often contraindicated in infection
(ch. 227). Platelet-bound antibodies and thrombocytopenia have
been documented in dogs with rickettsioses, ehrlichiosis,

anaplasmoses (ch. 193), babesiosis (ch. 197), dirofilariasis (ch.
237), and leishmaniosis (ch. 197). Vector-borne disease is an
important consideration in dogs with suspected ITP. Presumptive
ITP has also been described in a dog with Angiostrongylus vasorum
(ch. 217) and several other infections.23 American College of
Veterinary Internal Medicine (ACVIM) consensus recommendations
for infectious disease screening for dogs and cats with ITP will be
available in the near future (L Kidd personal communication).
Thrombocytopenia is associated with many infections in cats as
well, including viral (FeLV [ch. 199], FIV [ch. 198], feline
infectious peritonitis [FIP, ch. 200]), and vector-borne infections.
The presence of thrombocytopenia (verified with a blood smear)
warrants careful consideration of infectious disease as a differential
diagnosis.

Anemia (ch. 57)
Infections can cause non-regenerative anemia due to iron
sequestration or deficiency, proinflammatory cytokine production, or
direct bone marrow effects. Blood loss anemia can occur with
gastrointestinal (GI) infections or agents that cause
thrombocytopenia, thrombocytopathia, or coagulopathies.
Extravascular and intravascular hemolysis can occur from oxidative
and direct membrane damage by erythroparasites and some
infections can trigger immune-mediated hemolysis (Box 183.1).
ACVIM consensus recommendations for infectious disease screening
in patients with immune-mediated hemolytic anemia are available
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30806491/).

Blood Smears (ch. 57)
Blood smear evaluation is important to help discriminate
regenerative from non-regenerative anemias, to search for evidence
of hemolysis or other morphologic changes that provide diagnostic
clues, and to verify thrombocytopenia. In addition, toxic changes in
neutrophils, inclusions in circulating cells, and/or extracellular
organisms can also be detected (ch. 176).

Serum Chemistry Profile

Hyperbilirubinemia (chs. 28 and 272)
Serum biochemical abnormalities such as azotemia or increases in
liver enzyme activities help localize infection to affected body
systems. For hyperbilirubinemia, in addition to considering
infectious causes of hemolysis, cholestasis or severe hepatic
insufficiency, it is noteworthy that pathogen-associated molecular
patterns and proinflammatory cytokines produced during sepsis can
cause hyperbilirubinemia and may serve as an important clue that
sepsis is present (ch. 128).

Hypoglycemia, Hyponatremia,
Hypocholesterolemia, Hypoalbuminemia (chs. 61,
67, 63, 60)
Serious systemic bacterial infections and sepsis are important
differentials for hypoglycemia. Infection with microbes such as
Babesia spp. can also cause hypoglycemia. Other serum chemistry
abnormalities including hyponatremia, hypocholesterolemia, and
hypoalbuminemia can be more subtle indicators of serious infection,
e.g., hyponatremia in dogs has been associated with Rocky Mountain
spotted fever (ch. 193) and leptospirosis (ch. 192), possibly due to
third space loss from vasculitis and associated antidiuretic hormone
release. Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia have been reported in dogs
with Trichuris infections (ch. 263). Hypocholesterolemia (ch. 63)
serves as a prognostic indicator in septic dogs.24 It has also been
reported in dogs with severe babesiosis. Hypoalbuminemia (ch. 60)
can result from loss associated with GI tract infection or glomerular
damage. Hypoalbuminemia can also occur during severe infections
that cause vasculitis and third space loss, or severe inflammatory
responses that result in decreased hepatic production.

Hyperglobulinemia (ch. 60)
Hyperglobulinemia can be relative (dehydration) or absolute.
Increases in beta and gamma globulins can be monoclonal or
polyclonal. Polyclonal gammopathies are usually caused by chronic
antigenic stimulation and associated with many of the infections that
cause lymphocytosis and/or proteinuria, including ehrlichiosis (ch.

193), babesiosis, leishmaniosis, trypanosomiasis, and
schistosomiasis.25-29 Hyperglobulinemia also occurs in cats with FIV
infection, FIP, and bartonellosis.30-32 Nocardiosis, actinomycosis
and some fungal infections in dogs and cats are also associated with
hyperglobulinemia.33-36 Monoclonal gammopathies are usually
associated with immunoglobulin production from a single clone of
neoplastic lymphocytes. Rarely, some infectious diseases (e.g.,
canine monocytic ehrlichiosis, leishmaniosis, and bartonellosis) are
associated with a monoclonal gammopathy in dogs.37-39

Hypercalcemia (chs. 69 and 283)
Hypercalcemia can be associated with infections that cause
pyogranulomatous inflammation. These include fungal infections
such as aspergillosis, coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis,
blastomycosis, and oomycete infections (pythiosis). Hypercalcemia is
also common in dogs with Heterobilharzia americana infection.29
Nocardiosis in cats and mycobacterial infection have also been
associated with hypercalcemia.

Urinalysis (UA, ch. 70) and Proteinuria (ch. 302)
Presence of pyuria and visualization of bacteria with compatible
clinical signs of upper or lower urinary tract disease can indicate
clinically significant urinary tract infection (UTI). Infection can
cause prerenal, renal, and postrenal proteinuria. Light chain
proteinuria has been associated with ehrlichiosis, babesiosis, and
leishmaniosis. Proteinuria associated with AKI and leptospirosis is a
classic example of tubular proteinuria. Glomerular proteinuria has
been documented in dogs with leishmaniosis, heartworm disease,
babesiosis, ehrlichiosis, Lyme disease, bartonellosis, anaplasmosis,
pyometra, and coccidioidomycosis. Postrenal proteinuria can result
from infection anywhere distal to and including the renal pelvis.

Patterns

Systematically assessing individual problems on the CBC and serum
biochemistry profile for evidence of possible viral, bacterial
(including atypical bacterial), protozoal, fungal/algal and parasitic
etologies is helpful. Recognizing when organisms are differentials for
more than one problem allows one to consider infection when more
established pattern recognition would drive the clinician to other
differentials. For example, in addition to lymphoreticular neoplasia,
the problems of lymphocytosis, hyperglobulinemia and proteinuria
with or without thrombocytopenia should make vector-borne and
fungal infections come to mind as differentials. Similarly, the pattern
of hyperglobulinemia and hypercalcemia should prompt
consideration of fungal and protozoal infections and schistosomiasis.
Certain infections cause many of the same serum biochemical
abnormalities (hypoglycemia, hypoalbuminemia, hyponatremia and
hyperkalemia) as hypoadrenocorticism. In addition to using
analytical reasoning, machine learning is a promising new frontier in
pattern recognition for diagnosing infections and other diseases.

Testing for Immune-Mediated Disease (ch. 179)
Tests for antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and/or
perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibodies can be
positive in infection, particularly with vector-borne diseases.
Therefore, “immune-panels” are of questionable value before
infectious agents are ruled out.

SPECIFIC DIAGNOSTIC TESTS FOR
INFECTION
Testing for Infection (Figure 183.2; ch. 184)
Diagnostic testing for infection can be challenging. Even the most
sensitive tests can be negative in the face of infection, and a positive
test does not necessarily mean that an organism is causing the
presenting abnormalities. Sound clinical reasoning is the key to
knowing when repeat testing or empiric treatment is justified when
an infection is strongly suspected based on case context, but testing
was negative. It also ensures a positive result likely means the

organism is indeed causing the problems that prompted the testing.
Diagnostic tests for infection can be broadly divided into those that
directly demonstrate active infection and those that indirectly
document infection. Culture, cytology, polymerase chain reaction
(PCR), and assays designed to detect antigens using enzyme linked
immunosorbent assay (ELISA) or immunofluorescence assay (IFA),
are direct tests. Detecting antibodies using ELISA or IFA are
examples of indirect means of documenting infection.
A positive direct test usually means that the organism is present,
while a positive antibody test generally signals exposure. Active
infection can be differentiated from previous exposure using
serologic titers to document seroconversion on acute and
convalescent samples. In addition to previous exposure in the
absence of active infection, depending on the specific pathogen, a
positive antibody test can sometimes result from serologic crossreactivity to pathogenic or non-pathogenic agents. Even if a test that
directly demonstrates an organism is positive, it is important to
consider whether the organism is responsible for the clinical
abnormalities. If not, or if they don’t resolve with appropriate
treatment, coinfecting or alternative agents should be suspected, and
the diagnosis revisited.

FIGURE 183.2 Theoretical results of polymerase
chain reaction (PCR) and serologic testing during the
acute and chronic phases of infection for a typical
vector-borne organism that infects monocytes and
circulates in peripheral blood in high numbers
acutely and in low numbers intermittently during the
chronic phase of infection. Combining PCR with
serologic titers and repeat testing increases
sensitivity. (From Kidd L. Optimal vector-borne
disease screening in dogs using both serology-based
and polymerase chain reaction-based diagnostic
panels. Vet Clin North Am Small Anim Pract.
2019;49(4):703-718.)
Both direct and indirect testing can also be negative in the face of
active infection. Even extremely sensitive direct tests such as PCR
will be negative if the organism is not present in the sample.
Antibody tests may be negative if testing is performed before they are
produced (usually 2-4 weeks post exposure), or in young or immunecompromised patients. Furthermore, the absence of antibody
formation appears to be common for some agents like Bartonella in
dogs. Principles of PCR and serologic testing are illustrated in
Figure 183.1 and described in detail elsewhere.40

DIAGNOSIS OF INFECTIOUS DISEASE IS
A MULTIFACTORIAL PROCESS
INTEGRATING INFORMATION
Diagnosing infectious diseases is not confined to the laboratory but
can be made in some scenarios exclusively on clinical examination.
In most situations, however, clinical findings are integrated with
laboratory and other test results. It is critical that the diagnosis of an
infectious disease be accurate and, if possible, made quickly. In
addition to guiding treatment in an individual pet, in veterinary
medicine the diagnosis is often used to guide management of a large
number of animals. An accurate diagnosis relies on an
understanding of the organisms that frequently cause the infectious
disease suspected, including their prevalence and epidemiology.

PRINCIPLES OF DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
AND INTENT OF USE
The principles of diagnostic testing are generally simple and some
infectious diseases are so distinctive as to be identified clinically.
Pathogens responsible for most cases of a particular clinical
syndrome (e.g. pyoderma or urinary tract infection [UTI]) are
adequately predictable that testing is waived and treatment is
initiated empirically. Conversely, some pathogens are ubiquitous and
can cause disease in many body systems and/or cause a wide
spectrum of clinical signs. When predicting an organism causing an
infection, veterinary clinical microbiologists and the microbiology
laboratory play key roles in the diagnostic process. Clinicians who
engage with their clinical microbiologist can gain unique
perspectives useful in developing an appropriate differential
diagnosis and the tests best suited to confirm a diagnosis.1 Escalating
rates of antimicrobial resistance among common pathogens mean
that organism isolation, identification, and susceptibility testing are
essential (ch. 7).
The “purpose of a test” or “intent of use,” should be considered.2 Is
a test being used to diagnose, screen, evaluate risk, prognose, or to

determine treatment? Put another way, is the test being used to rulein an infectious agent as a cause of illness in an individual
(diagnostic test) or to rule-out infection (screening test)? The
introduction of in-clinic point-of-care (POC) assays has led,
unintentionally, to those definitions being blurred. Quality control
programs are essential for POC assays (as in the laboratory) to
ensure accuracy of test results. A rapid POC test for parvovirus
diagnosis in a puppy with diarrhea is not a screening test, because
the assumption is that the puppy has parvovirus infection and the
test is used to rule-in that diagnosis (ch. 201). Conversely, testing
cats for feline leukemia virus (FeLV) can have 2 purposes:
diagnosing a cat with clinical signs (rule-in) or to show the cat is free
of the virus (rule-out). While >3% of cats in the United States are
FeLV or feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) positive, it also means
the majority of cats are negative (chs. 198 and 199). Geographical
prevalence can impact rates.3 Therefore, the purpose when screening
healthy cats is to rule out FeLV. A confirmatory test is generally
(should be) performed when the results of a true screening test are
non-negative, e.g., a non-negative rapid slide agglutination test
(RSAT) for Brucella spp., which should be confirmed by a more
specific 2-mercaptoethanol rapid slide agglutination test (2MERSAT) or agar gel immunodiffusion assay using cytoplasmic antigen
(AGIDcpa) test (ch. 189).4

TEST DEVELOPMENT
Defined Attributes and Performance
Characteristics
During test development and validation, laboratories consider
purpose, optimal specimen type, the measurand (what is being
measured or detected), the type of result desired (qualitative or
quantitative), and ease of interpreting results. The basic attributes
and considerations used by laboratories to design and implement
diagnostic tests in a clinical microbiology laboratory are well
defined.5 The performance characteristics of a laboratory test for the
diagnosis of an infectious disease are accuracy, sensitivity (analytic

and diagnostic), specificity (analytic and diagnostic), reproducibility,
positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV)
(ch. 5).

Definitions
Diagnostic accuracy is the overall ability of a test to both rule in and
rule out an analyte or specific disease. Analytical sensitivity measures
the smallest quantity of an analyte that can be detected and is more
appropriately called the limit of detection (LOD). Analytical
specificity is the ability of a test to detect only the analyte that it was
designed to measure, with no cross reactivity. Diagnostic (or clinical)
sensitivity is a measure of the test’s ability to accurately detect a
specific disease. Diagnostic specificity is a measure of the test’s
ability to accurately identify all non-infected animals.5 The highest
test sensitivity is desired when a disease is serious and treatable and
when false-positive test results will not lead to serious clinical issues.
The highest specificity is desired when the disease is serious but not
treatable or when false-positive results might cause serious clinical
or economic concerns. The PPV is the probability that an animal
testing positive is truly positive. The NPV is the probability that an
animal that tests negative is truly negative. Reproducibility,
“precision,” measures the extent to which replicate tests agree. The
term reproducibility is most often used when referring to qualitative
assays while precision is used for quantitative assays.

CLINICAL MICROBIOLOGY
METHODS AND INTERPRETATIONS
Clinical microbiology has been described as a science of
interpretation and judgment that is becoming increasingly more
complex.1 Organism detection methodologies are evolving rapidly. In
addition to conventional tests, e.g., staining, culture, and serology,
proteomics and molecular diagnostics are more commonly offered by
veterinary diagnostic laboratories. Interpretation of results is always
dependent on the quality of the specimen submitted for analysis.
Accurate diagnosis of microbial infections requires proper sample

selection, collection, and preservation. The “tenets of specimen
management” have been well defined by the Infectious Diseases
Society of America.1 Veterinarians and veterinary diagnostic
laboratories should be held to the same standards. Poor quality
specimens should be rejected. Laboratories should not report
everything that grows as this can lead to inappropriate therapy.
Specimens (urine, tissue, aspirate, fluids) are preferred over swabs of
a specimen. Specimens should be collected prior to administration of
antimicrobials where possible. Clinical information should always be
included with the submission because this allows the laboratory to
determine if an appropriate test has been selected. Additional
submission details should always be available from the diagnostic
laboratory as requirements may vary on specimen labelling, the
metadata that accompanies the specimen, and details of the clinical
history that may be relevant to the diagnosis.

24-HOUR FACILITIES, LAG-TIMES,
EMPIRIC TREATMENT?
It has been argued in human medicine that a 24-hour hospital
clinical microbiology service is essential, especially for critically ill
patients.6 However, 24-hour veterinary microbiology services are not
practical. Many veterinarians use centralized veterinary reference
laboratories and the turnaround time (TAT) from specimen
submission to result may be prolonged due to shipping. The time to
result should not influence treatment decisions. However, the
unavailability of rapid test results or their cost may be barriers to
testing over empiric therapy.7 There is clear need for developing POC
diagnostic tests to avoid these dilemmas. As with laboratory tests all
POC testing must be properly quality controlled to guarantee test
accuracy and interpretation.8

DIAGNOSTIC METHODS

ORGANISM-DETECTION VS ANTIBODYDETECTION TESTING
In most situations, organism detection tests are most appropriate. In
chronic persistent infectious diseases or acute diseases associated
with an early rise in antibody titer that can be captured using acute
and convalescent serology testing, then antibody detection tests may
be preferable. Sometimes a combination of organism-detection tests
and antibody-detection tests is required.

MICROSCOPIC EXAMINATION
Cytology
Clinical microbiology laboratories have key roles in diagnosing
infectious diseases. Some conditions require use of specialized
laboratories. Clinical pathologists are usually involved in preliminary
identification of bacteria, fungi, or parasites. Many diseases are
identified on cytologic evaluation of fluid specimens, e.g., urine (ch.
70), respiratory endotracheal or transtracheal lavage fluid (ch. 93),
or cerebrospinal fluid (ch. 109). The cytologic evaluation of
aspirates (chs. 71, 85, 88), blood smears (ch. 57) and fecal smears
(ch. 80) can quickly yield information that leads to presumptive
diagnoses that are later confirmed in the clinical microbiology
laboratory, the parasitology laboratory, or the immunology/serology
laboratory.

Preparation and Stains
Microorganisms can be observed on stained smears prepared from
fluid specimens following centrifugation at 2000 g for 5 minutes,
prior to staining with Wright Giemsa, Diff-Quik, Gram’s stain, or
acid-fast stains. Acid fast stains rely on mycobacteria retaining
certain dyes after washing with an acid-alcohol decolorizer (hence,
“acid fast”), unlike most other bacteria. Carbolfuchsin stains
mycobacteria red in both the Ziehl-Neelsen and Kinyoun stains. The
Ziehl-Neelsen stain requires a heating step and has been replaced in
many laboratories by the Kinyoun stain, a “cold” acid-fast stain. It is
important to prepare multiple smears for the clinical pathology

laboratory as many different stains are often applied. The organism
morphology observed during the cytologic evaluation can provide
preliminary information useful for guiding empiric therapy or may
indicate alternative testing (bacteriologic culture, fecal float, a
serologic immunoassay, or a specific nucleic acid amplification test
[NAAT]) be performed to confirm any observation.

Common Diagnoses and Stains Utilized
The presence of intracytoplasmic acid-fast bacteria in macrophages
or neutrophils from respiratory secretions or tissue aspirates can be
diagnostic for infections caused by Mycobacterium spp. Nocardia
spp. and Actinomyces spp. have similar morphologies in smears
stained with Diff-Quik (filamentous rods) and the Gram’s stain
(Gram-positive filamentous rods) but can be differentiated using an
acid-fast stain, because Nocardia are acid fast positive (termed
partially acid fast).
Babesia (ch. 197), Anaplasma spp. (ch. 193 and Figure 176.1),
Ehrlichia spp. (ch. 193), and hemoplasmas (ch. 194) can be
observed in thin blood smears stained with Wright Giemsa or DiffQuik. The fungal pathogens Cryptococcus spp. (ch. 207),
Histoplasma spp. and Blastomyces spp. (ch. 209) can be visualized
using cytology stains, as can some of the filamentous fungi.
Cryptosporidium can be identified in fecal smears using an acid-fast
stain. The characteristic “gull wing” morphology of Campylobacter
species can be observed on a fecal smear stained with Gram’s stain,
although observation of these organisms on a stained slide cannot be
used as a definitive diagnosis of campylobacteriosis in an animal
with diarrhea. A fecal culture or a NAAT should be performed to
confirm the diagnosis of Campylobacter spp., infection. Failure to
observe any of these microorganisms does NOT indicate that
infection has been ruled out.

Value and Limitations
In the microbiology laboratory, it is of value to determine whether
any organism(s) is Gram-positive or Gram-negative. The Gram’s
stain is a simple first-line diagnostic tool that can provide results in
minutes, but they require expertise for interpretation. Such rapid

results can often guide appropriate targeted therapy,9 e.g., Gramnegative bacilli in urine sediment or Gram-positive cocci from a
pustule of a dog with superficial pyoderma is often all that is needed
to initiate therapy without guessing, while the culture results are
pending. Microscopy is useful when an organism is seen, but it must
be regarded as a complex test which should be performed by trained
individuals. It is easy to misinterpret Gram’s stain results. The issue
of sensitivity should be considered when sampling directly from a
specimen. In one multicenter assessment of Gram’s stain error rates
on 6115 specimens (between 976-1864 specimens/site), 5% of results
were discrepant from culture.10 Of the discrepant results, 58% were
from specimens with no organism reported on Gram’s stain but
significant growth in culture; 42% of discrepant results had
organisms reported by Gram’s stain but not recovered in culture
(Table 184.1).

BACTERIAL CULTURE
Submissions
Bacterial culture for diagnostic purposes should always be performed
in laboratories that meet standards for biosafety level-2
containment, have trained microbiology technologists, have
reference strains for quality control testing, use standard protocols,
and have appropriate facilities for infectious waste disposal.11,12 The
entire case history should be provided to the laboratory with the
specimen, especially relevant when pathogens with special culture
requirements are suspected, e.g., Actinomyces, Nocardia, or
Mycobacterium spp. Fastidious organisms may require special
media or prolonged incubation times and/or rapid transport to the
laboratory to preserve the organisms. Special transport media may
be required for some suspected organisms.

Turn Around Times
A major barrier to culturing is the time required to grow an organism
and perform antimicrobial susceptibility testing. For aerobic and
anaerobic cultures, specimens are plated to various non-differential,
differential, selective, or chromogenic agars and evaluated for
growth. Aerobic organisms require oxygen for growth and typically
grow on agar plates overnight (18-24 hours) but some

(Corynebacterium urealyticum from canine and feline urine) may
take up to 48 hrs.13,14 Anaerobic organisms, such as Clostridium
spp. and Bacteroides spp., do not have a requirement for oxygen
during growth and typically require 48 hrs or longer to grow in an
environment depleted of oxygen. Most laboratories hold anaerobic
cultures for 5-7 days before calling results negative.15 Facultative
anaerobes can switch metabolism and grow in the presence or
absence of oxygen; e.g., Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus. Many
fastidious organisms require temperature and/or atmospheric
modification to optimize growth, e.g., Campylobacter jejuni, a
microaerophilic bacterial species that requires 5% O2 and 10% CO2
to minimize damage from oxygen-related products for which
microbiology laboratories use special gas generating packs. In
addition to the atmospheric requirements, C. jejuni is thermophilic,
preferring growth temperature of 42°C.16 Some specimens may be
pre-enriched in non-selective or selective broth media for 24-48
hours before being sub-cultured to agar plates. All such “bestpractices” can prolong time required for adequate growth or to call
the result negative.

Organism Identification Systems, Matrix Assisted
Laser Desorption Ionization–Time of Flight Mass
Spectroscopy (MALDI-TOFms)
Once growth is observed, organisms are most often identified via
biochemical testing. Commercial identification systems are available
and perform well for common aerobic bacteria.17 Technologies
enable microorganism identification (i.e., bacteria, yeast,
mycobacteria) in minutes. Procedures exist for sampling directly
from a positive fluid media (i.e., blood culture) to MALDI-TOFms,
shortening time for organism identification.18 The utility of MALDITOFms is likely to expand (see below). Detection of specific
antibiotic resistance genes will provide this information earlier.19
Other semi-automated systems for organism identification, e.g.,
Vitek II, Phoenix, Microscan, and Sensititre, differentiate among
organisms based on biochemical/carbohydrate organism profiles

with varying times required for organism identification. Overall,
these have longer TATs (hours/day) than with MALDI-TOFms.
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing is also often performed in
conjunction with identification by these systems using a brothmicrodilution method.20 Alternatives to broth microdilution are
Kirby Bauer disk diffusion or the use of antibiotic gradient strips
(i.e., E-test) as described by the Clinical and Laboratory Standards
Institute (CLSI).20
Clinical microbiology has been transformed with the development
of better stains, better microscopes, and more novel media for
organism recovery and growth. Lagier and colleagues published an
excellent review on media used in microbiology laboratories.21 In
particular, use of chromogenic agar allows specific isolation of some
pathogens and/or presumptive identification based on color
reactions specific for a target pathogen. Often used for methicillin
resistant Staphylococcus aureus, extended spectrum beta-lactamase,
or carbapenemase-producing Gram-negative bacilli, Chromogenic
agar is also used to differentiate key urinary tract pathogens.

BLOOD CULTURES
Definitions, Indications
In human medicine, blood is the single most important specimen
processed for culture in clinical microbiology laboratories. In
veterinary medicine, submission of blood cultures from dogs and
cats is rare. One must distinguish bacteremia (presence of bacteria in
the bloodstream) from sepsis (the body’s extreme response to
infection, including the presence of bacteria in blood and other body
spaces). In humans, sepsis is associated with 30-50% mortality rates
and, in dogs, 20-68%.22 In septic cats, mortality is as high as 40%.23
Sepsis is a medical emergency requiring accurate and rapid diagnosis
to ensure optimal antimicrobial therapy. This is even more critical if
sepsis is likely due to multi-drug resistant bacteria following the
failure of initial empiric antimicrobial therapy. Aside from the
clinical diagnosis of sepsis, blood cultures are indicated to isolate and

identify any pathogen(s) and determine susceptibility/resistance to
antimicrobial agents.24

Protocol and Volumes in Humans
When possible, blood for culture should be obtained prior to giving
antimicrobial therapy. Prior to inoculating any blood culture bottle,
the bottle tops should be disinfected with 70% isopropyl alcohol or
ethyl alcohol to reduce risk of bottle contamination during
inoculation. Separate collections for aerobic and anaerobic culture
are generally necessary and blood should be inoculated into those
specific blood culture bottles. Multiple collections (depending on
disease severity) from different venipuncture sites may be collected
over 24 hours in order to enhance the chance of organism recovery.
The volume of blood to be inoculated into each blood culture bottle
varies and is dependent on animal size. Recommendations for the
volume of blood cultured varies. Some recommend 1 mL/bottle from
cats and small dogs and 2-3 mL from large dogs. Others recommend
targeting 10 mL from large dogs. Similar volumes from larger
animals such as livestock are generally acceptable.25 Smaller
volumes might be necessary from exotic animals. In humans, the
larger the volume of blood sampled, the higher the rate of detecting
blood stream infections.26 In one study, blood cultures from 345
humans with sepsis, severe sepsis, or septic shock,27 the blood
culture mass (grams determined by weighing bottles) was a
significant predictor of positivity, e.g., for each additional 1 mL of
blood collected there was a 1% increase in positivity (odds ratio was
similar for blood volume). A study on collecting from pediatric
patients indicated that the volumes were considered adequate based
on patient weight and divided into 2 blood culture bottles (1 set) for 1
and 3 mL collections and 4 bottles (2 sets) for 6-40 mL collections:
<3.9 kg: 1 mL; 4-7.9 kg: 3 mL; 8-13.9 kg: 6 mL; 14-18.9 kg: 12 mL;
19-25.9 kg: 16 mL; 26-39.9 kg: 20 mL; 40-53.9 kg: 32 mL; and >54
kg: 40 mL.28 Rates of contamination were higher with lower blood
volumes.

Protocol and Volume in Dogs and Cats

Given the vast weight range of dogs and cats, either adult-drawbottles (higher blood volume, i.e., 8-10 mL) or pediatric-draw-bottles
(1-5 mL) might be most appropriate. If a fungemia or
mycobacteremia is suspected, special blood culture bottles (i.e.,
MycoF lytic, 1-5 mL) can be used; however, Candida species grow
well in routine blood culture bottles. If antimicrobial agents have
been given prior to blood culture collection, resin-containing blood
culture bottles are available. Resin neutralizes antibiotics, thereby
optimizing recovery of microorganisms. Other normally “sterile”
body fluids might be best processed by inoculation into a blood
culture bottle; particularly for specimens that might be delayed in
transit to the laboratory and organism viability is a concern. In such
circumstances, a separate specimen aliquot needs to be available for
cytologic evaluation as necessary. Dumoulin and colleagues
investigated blood culture medium enrichment of synovial fluid from
horses and found use of an automated Bactec 9050 system superior
to other methods.29 Effluents from human patients on continuous
ambulatory peritoneal dialysis are often inoculated at the bedside
into blood culture bottles and then shipped to the laboratory.30

Manual vs Automated Technology
Blood culture processing methods that are more manual include
Septi-Chek Signal Blood Culture System and the Isolator (Lysis
centrifugation) Blood Culture System. The major disadvantage of
non-automated blood culture systems is delayed identification of a
positive culture, as continuous reading is not done and sub-culture
might be required, further delaying TAT. The primary advantage of
manual systems is that they will be preferred by laboratories where
blood cultures are infrequently processed. A study reported on the
recovery of pathogenic aerobic bacteria from blood cultures from 90
septicemic neonatal calves using the automated BACTEC 9240
system.31 Pathogenic organisms recovered included E. coli, betahemolytic Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella spp.,
and Corynebacterium spp. Importantly, 70/89 (78.7%) positive
cultures were detected in the first 24 hrs, 14/89 (15.7%) on day 2,
and 5/89 (5.6%) on day 3, indicating early detection. Conventional
methods take longer, are time consuming, and have increased risks

for contamination if subculturing is required.32 The Bacti-Alert
VIRTUO system, the latest innovation in blood culture systems,
offers similar organism recovery rates to other systems but as of yet
has not been evaluated with specimens from dogs or cats.33 The
incidence of bacteremia and bacteruria in febrile neutropenia was
studied in 55 dogs.34 The overall incidence of bacteremia was 12.3%
and Gram-positive organisms predominated, some with
antimicrobial resistance profiles. This study demonstrated the
importance of blood cultures in a vulnerable population.

MATRIX-ASSISTED LASER
DESORPTION IONIZATION TIME-OFFLIGHT (MALDI-TOF)
MALDI-TOFms has revolutionized bacterial/yeast identification in
clinical microbiology laboratories.35 Identification is based on
ionizing the target organism with a laser and detecting the resultant
proteins. Smaller particles travel faster than larger particles (time of
flight). A spectrogram of the protein profile is constructed and
compared to bacteria in annotated databases that continue to
expand. The time from picking an isolated colony from an agar plate
to organism identification is between 15-20 minutes in most
laboratories but can be a little longer based on workflow, with sameday reporting possible. In a report evaluating MALDI-TOFms for
identification of bacteria in a veterinary diagnostic laboratory, 95.3%
of 620 isolates agreed with the phenotypic/biochemical test
identification for species level and 100% at the genus/species level.36
For a further 107 anaerobes and 234 aerobes, a comparison of
MALDI-TOF/biochemical tests to 16S ribosomal sequencing, as the
gold standard, showed that agreement was between 93 and 100%,
depending on the comparison being made. It was concluded that
MALDI-TOF was a rapid and reliable method to identify bacteria
isolated from animals. Another study reported that MALDI-TOFms
was excellent for identifying and differentiating animal
mycoplasmas, combining convenience, speed, and precision, with

low running costs.37 The Study Group for Veterinary Microbiology of
the European Society for Clinical Microbiology and Infectious
Diseases have recommended the use of MALDI-TOF for organism
identification and suggest that veterinary practitioners should select
a veterinary diagnostic laboratory that is using state-of the art
methods, to ensure accurate identification of pathogens.38

IMMUNOASSAYS
Definitions
Serology is the measurement of antibodies or antigens for diagnostic
purposes, a term most often used for detecting antibodies in
serum.39 Different classes of antibodies can be detected, most
commonly IgG or IgM, and the methods used to detect antibodies
can also be used to detect antigens. Assays that measure antigenantibody interactions for diagnostic purposes are most broadly
referred to as immunoassays, measuring the presence or
concentration of an analyte in solution using antibody or antigen
capture.

Assays Used and Antibody Titer Interpretation
A variety of immunoassays exist; some of the most common include
RSATs, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs), agar gel
immunodiffusion tests (AGIDs or gel ID tests), immunofluorescent
antibody (IFA) tests, and Western blotting. ELISA and IFA provide
quantitative results, expressed as optical density units (ODs) or titers
(e.g., 1:800, or reciprocal titer = 800). The titer is defined as the
reciprocal of the last dilution in a series that gives a positive test
result; the higher the number, the higher the antibody concentration.
Exposure to an infectious agent results in a rise in antibody titer over
time. The first antibody class produced by plasma cells is IgM,
followed by IgG. When exposure to a pathogen occurs for the first
time, there is a lag phase of 5 to 7 days before IgM antibodies can be
detected in the blood (primary antibody response). The antibody
titer increases, and if the infectious agent is cleared, there is a
progressive decline in the titer over weeks to months. The speed and

magnitude by which the antibody titer rises depends on host factors
and the infectious agent. Serologic diagnosis of infectious diseases
relies on an understanding of the timing of the antibody response in
relation to development of clinical signs for different infectious
diseases.

Antigen Assays
Available antigen assays used on serum or plasma from dogs or cats
include Dirofilaria immitis (ch. 237), Cryptococcus spp. (ch. 207),
Blastomyces spp. (ch. 209), Histoplasma spp. (ch. 209),
Aspergillus spp. (ch. 211), and FeLV (ch. 199). Parvovirus (ch.
201), Cryptosporidium parvum (ch. 196), and Giardia spp. (ch.
196) antigen detection procedures are available for use with feces.
The Blastomyces, Histoplasma and Aspergillus antigen assays have
been shown to have clinical utility when applied to urine.40

MOLECULAR DIAGNOSTIC TESTS,
POLYMERASE CHAIN REACTION (PCR)
PCR assays can detect very low copy numbers of DNA or RNA in a
clinical specimen and amplify them many thousand-fold using
sequence-specific oligonucleotides, heat stable DNA polymerase, and
thermal cycling. The detection of RNA requires the enzyme reverse
transcriptase (RT) to convert the RNA into DNA: RT-PCR assays. In
conventional (endpoint) PCR, detection and quantification of the
nucleic acid is performed at the end of the reaction after the last PCR
cycle and involves gel electrophoresis and image analysis. In realtime quantitative PCR (qPCR), PCR product is measured at each
cycle. By monitoring reactions during the exponential amplification
phase of the reaction, the initial quantity of the target can be
determined with precision. In qPCR, DNA amount is measured after
each cycle via fluorescent dyes that produce a fluorescent signal that
is in direct proportion to the number of PCR product amplicons that
are amplified.
PCR assays have long been available, but there are challenges. The
biggest challenge is undoubtedly that the same organisms can infect
multiple animal species. Thus, development and validation of

veterinary assays are highly complex. PCR tests are generally
performed at reference laboratories because their high-complexity
requires trained and skilled analysts.
The purpose of a PCR test is rapid, accurate pathogen detection.
Tests can be designed to detect organisms at the level of the genus or
the species with high specificity. Genus-level tests are common for
organisms considered to be true pathogens regardless of the species,
e.g., Salmonella spp. and Leptospira spp. Similarly, species-specific
assays can be designed for organisms that may be host specific or
host specialists such Mycoplasma felis or organisms from large
genera that have a species that is a specific, or more common,
pathogen of animals such as Bordetella bronchiseptica.41,42 A
variety of amplification technologies have been developed that allow
multiple organisms to be detected in the same qPCR, the most widely
used method in diagnostic laboratories.17 Internal amplification
controls are generally incorporated into the assay to eliminate false
negative test results due to the presence of inhibitors.
Excluding inhibitors and poor assay design, the accuracy of
molecular diagnostic tests depends on appropriate specimen
selection, collection, and transportation to the laboratory. Specimen
transport and storage can affect specimen integrity and falsenegative results can occur if specimen degradation occurs during
transport. A knowledge of the disease process (acute versus chronic)
is important, and in some cases, time is a critical factor to ensure an
accurate diagnosis. It is always recommended that clinical specimens
be collected before administration of antimicrobials but that is not
critical for molecular diagnostics.

NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING
(NGS)
NGS, also known as high throughput, massively-parallel or deep
sequencing, allows DNA from clinical specimens to be sequenced
directly.43 There are a variety of technologies and methodologies to
identify microorganisms using NGS. The first NGS method was
known as pyrosequencing and gained popularity for producing whole
genome sequences from individual bacteria as well as for sequencing

16S rRNA genes for microbiome analyses.44 In the past 15 years or
so, there has been ongoing expansion of methods, developments in
instrumentation and bioinformatics, and improvements in the
quality, quantity, and cost of sequence data. Two general strategies
are used in clinical microbiology to identify microorganisms using
NGS.45
Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is generally performed on pure
cultures of organisms that are known or unknown. WGS of an
organism that has been cultured can provide detailed information
used for the simultaneous identification, strain typing, and
prediction of antimicrobial resistance genes. WGS has proven
particularly useful for epidemiological and surveillance studies.46 In
addition to identification of an unknown organism, WGS can also
provide information regarding known, or putative, virulence factors
and can detect antimicrobial resistance mechanisms. WGS has
become important in veterinary medicine for the surveillance and
typing of zoonotic disease pathogens, particularly those that may be
transmitted via animal derived food.47 In recent years, the U.S. Food
and Drug Administration Veterinary Laboratory Investigation and
Response Network (FDA VetLIRN) has been conducting WGS
surveillance on common bacteria, such as Staphylococcus
pseudintermedius, isolated from dogs and cats.48
Targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) allows identification
of a particular microorganism, or microbial sequence of interest, in a
clinical specimen using an enrichment, or selection, process prior to
NGS.45 There are a variety of enrichment methods, the most
common uses PCR to amplify a specific gene from the pathogen of
interest. This approach allows detection of organisms in complex
specimens, such as feces.49 It also has the advantage that it can
selectively amplify organisms that may be present in a specimen in
very small numbers.50
Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) allows
unbiased detection of all microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi
and parasites), antimicrobial resistance genes, and virulence genes
directly from a clinical specimen.51-54 mNGS has been called a
“culture-independent game changer” but it is not without

detractors.51,55-57 There is still a long way to go to develop these
technologies for use in veterinary diagnostic laboratories. The
validation of any NGS test is incredibly complex and while they show
great potential for use in some situations, such as the detection of
pathogens in difficult to diagnose patients, there are still laboratory
workflow issues to refine, inadequate data analysis protocols for
veterinary medicine, and it is possible that there may be regulatory
hurdles to overcome as the technology develops.58 The potential of
these tests to detect uncommon, unknown, or co-infecting pathogens
is an advantage over current diagnostic test methodologies but it will
likely be some time (5-10 years) before these technologies will be
available in veterinary, or medical, diagnostic laboratories.53,56

DIAGNOSTIC STEWARDSHIP AND
ANTIMICROBIAL STEWARDSHIP (CH.
7)
Infectious disease diagnostics have evolved due to advances in
chemistry, immunology, molecular biology, engineering, automation,
and nucleic acid amplification. It is now theoretically possible to
determine the specific etiology of an infectious disease in a clinic,
specialty hospital, and soon in a patient’s home. Automation and
specific syndromic “panels” can identify pathogens from a wide
variety of specimen types such as feces and respiratory secretions.17
Increasingly, as new types of assays become available, the diagnosis
and understanding of veterinary infectious diseases may rely on the
application of multiple different types of tests. We are reminded that
clinicians seek 3 basic truths from the laboratory, “(i) whether the
patient is infected, (ii) if so, with what, and (iii) what will treat it?”59
It has been stated clearly: “The weapons of choice in clinical
microbiology are culture, antimicrobial susceptibility, qPCR, and
serology. This is not because clinical microbiologists are antiquated –
we have rapidly adopted syndromic multiplex testing in the last few
years – but rather because these methods answer the questions that
clinical microbiologists are asked to answer in a validated, cost-

effective, and actionable manner.”56 In many cases, it is necessary to
begin broad spectrum empiric therapy once a specimen has been
collected and submitted to the lab, and for that reason there is an
obvious need to decrease the test TAT and provide accurate results
quickly. Rapid immunoassays and molecular diagnostic tests can
help to achieve that, but they must be implemented properly. New
technologies show great promise, and it is hoped that as they are
adopted by veterinary diagnostic laboratories and in clinics, this will
lead to better patient care. Diagnostic stewardship is minimally
defined as, selecting the right test, for the right patient, to generate
clinically relevant results to optimize patient care.59 The process of
designing and implementing a diagnostic test is complicated, and
diagnostic stewardship is best achieved using a multi-disciplinary
approach. One test does not fit all clinical settings. Centralization of
veterinary diagnostic reference laboratories will allow for more
complex diagnostic tests to be offered, but, as always, that will be at
the expense of TAT. The implementation of rapid POC molecular
diagnostic tests in clinics require appropriately trained staff,
development of diagnostic algorithms and clinical use guidelines,
and reasonable cost for an individual test. Diagnostic stewardship
and antimicrobial stewardship (the right antimicrobial, for the right
patient, at the right dose) are intertwined.59 Results from rapid
diagnostic assays are only useful if there is a plan to inform the
clinician once a test result is available. Decision support strategies
must then be available to the clinician that cover everything from the
interpretation of the positive or negative test result, to ensuring that
antimicrobials are selected or modified accordingly. Frequent
exchanges between clinicians and laboratory diagnosticians are
encouraged to ensure that the context and clinical relevance of the
organism detected remains the driving force of better medicine.

Tribute to Michael J. Day
This chapter is dedicated to the memory of Michael J. Day, who worked
tirelessly to transform companion animal vaccination practice around the
world and to advocate the vital importance of companion animals within
One Health. Professor Day was a member of the WSAVA Vaccination
Guidelines Group since 2004, and at the time of his death he was their
Chair. His scientific contributions to veterinary medicine throughout the
world were enormous. The body of work he left us with is an incredible and
a truly remarkable legacy for the profession. Michael was modest, kind,
generous, and polite. He was an inspiration to many people around the
world. His passion for history, art, travel, and wine equaled his love for
veterinary science. He will be sorely missed but never forgotten.

INTRODUCTION
Vaccination is an important and fundamental part of veterinary practice.
Recently, there has been a shift away from the concepts that pets be
vaccinated yearly with boosters that contain as many antigenic
components as possible and that similar vaccination protocols be applied
to every dog and cat. Vaccination should be delivered as one part of a
preventive annual health check visit, and protocols should be based on the
requirements of that pet after assessing risk factors based on lifestyle,
geographic area of residence, age, and previous vaccination history.
Vaccination should not only be carried out to protect the individual pet but
also to protect the population through development of “herd immunity.”
The herd immunity concept suggests that the more vaccinated individuals
there are in a community, the more difficult it will be to introduce and
spread that infectious agent. Herd immunity related to the use of core
vaccines that provide a long (many years) duration of immunity (DOI) is
highly dependent on the percentage of vaccinated animals in the
population and not on the number of vaccinations that each pet receives
annually.

TYPES OF VACCINES
Modified Live Vaccines (MLV) and Inactivated
Vaccines

MLVs contain live but attenuated whole organisms capable of infecting and
replicating within cells, establishing a low-level transient infection,
stimulating a strong immune response without causing overt disease. They
are generally more immunogenic, should require fewer doses to achieve
the desired response, and may generate a consistent and lasting immune
response (for many years, if not for life) after a single dose, without the
need for revaccination.1-3 Inactivated vaccines contain antigenically intact
microorganisms not capable of infecting or replicating, but able to
stimulate an immune response. They usually produce less potent immune
responses, may not produce adequate mucosal or cellular immunity, and
generally require multiple doses and an adjuvant to stimulate an adequate
immune response. Most inactivated vaccines require at least 2 initial doses
to immunize, regardless of a dog’s or cat’s age. The first dose generally
primes the immune response and the second provides the protective
immune response. Inactivated vaccines usually have a shorter DOI when
compared to MLVs and require frequent administrations (i.e., boosting) to
maintain immunologic protection and memory. Rabies vaccine is an
exception; it is highly immunogenic, inducing protective immunity with a
single dose.1-3

Subunit, Recombinant Vectored, and DNA Vaccines
Subunit vaccines are based on antigenic components of microorganisms
that have been purified from cultures or produced by recombinant DNA
techniques (gene cloning). Since those vaccines tend to be less
immunogenic, they usually require adjuvants and have a shorter DOI.1-3 In
recombinant vectored vaccines one or more genes that encode
antigens can be cloned directly into a vector (e.g., attenuated canarypox
virus). The virus replicates in the host and expresses the introduced (or
cloned) antigens. These vaccines are extremely safe; the virus vector is
nonpathogenic and they induce both humoral and cellular immune
responses usually without need for an adjuvant.1-3 DNA vaccines are
produced using similar technology as in recombinant vectored vaccines.
Genes encoding a specific protein antigen of interest are isolated and
spliced into a bacterial plasmid, which is inoculated into the recipient
animal as a vaccine. DNA vaccines are not currently available for use in
dogs and cats but there is a canine melanoma vaccine labeled for
therapeutic use.1-3

CORE VACCINES, NON-CORE VACCINES,
AND NOT RECOMMENDED VACCINES
To reduce unnecessary administration of antigens to dogs and cats,
vaccines can be classified as core, non-core, and not recommended. A core
vaccine is one which every dog or cat, no matter where or how they live,
should receive because it protects that animal against infectious disease
which may be lethal or cause high morbidity. Rabies vaccine is considered
core since it should be given to all dogs and cats in any country in which
the disease is endemic, even without mandating legislation. In contrast, the
decision to administer a non-core vaccine should be based on geographic
prevalence of that infection, the lifestyle of the pet (e.g., indoor vs. outdoor,
frequency and location of travel, solitary home cat or within a multi-cat
household), and the risk for that animal to become infected. A third
category, of not recommended, is used for vaccines that do not have
sufficient scientific evidence base to justify their use.4

MATERNALLY DERIVED IMMUNITY AND
IMMUNIZATION
Maternally derived antibodies (MDA) provide important protection for
puppies and kittens in their first weeks of life, but they also interfere with
their ability to mount a protective immune response to most core vaccines.
Serum MDA inhibits immunoglobulin (Ig)G production within the neonate
and prevents vaccine antigens from stimulating an immune response.4,5 In
most puppies and kittens, MDA decline at about 8-12 weeks to a level
where a response to vaccination is possible. During the period when MDA
are insufficient to provide complete immunologic protection but able to
block endogenous immune responses, the “window of susceptibility,” a
puppy or a kitten can become infected. It is not possible to predict when
this “window” occurs, as the amount of MDA transferred varies between
and within litters. As it is impossible to predict the exact moment of MDA
loss, initial core MLVs usually require administration of multiple doses.
These are not booster doses. They are given to trigger a primary immune
response as soon as possible after the MDA has dropped.3,4,6 The presence
of MDA can also interfere with the immune response to inactivated
vaccines but not commonly after 6-9 weeks of age.3,7,8 If at the time of the
administration of the first dose there is still enough MDA to block the

immune response, immune priming will not occur and the second dose will
not be able to immunize.4

CORE VACCINES FOR DOGS (CHS. 200-204)
OVERVIEW
Core vaccines for dogs include those that protect against canine distemper
virus (CDV), canine adenovirus (CAV-2), and canine parvovirus (CPV-2
and its variants). For any dog in an endemic country, rabies vaccine is also
considered core4,8-10 (Table 185.1). See textbook’s inside covers for
protocol table.

PUPPIES
Core vaccination should start at 6-8 weeks of age with subsequent doses
given every 2-4 weeks until 16 weeks or older.4,8 The 2-week interval is
recommended for dogs in environments likely to be heavily contaminated,
such as shelters or breeding kennels.4 Therefore, the number of primary
vaccinations will be determined by the age at which the first vaccination is
given and the interval between vaccinations. In the absence of MDA, a
single dose of core MLV vaccine provides adequate and robust immunity.
The most important dose is administered at 16 weeks of age or older, when
almost all puppies should have lost MDA and are able to respond to the
vaccine.4,11,12 Even with the administration of the last dose of vaccine at 16
weeks of age a small percentage of dogs may not respond adequately.3,4,8
High-titer MLV CPV-2 (either alone or combined with CDV) vaccines may
be given from 4 weeks of age and have been used as a strategy to reduce the
window of susceptibility.11,13 Moreover, a CDV canarypox vector
recombinant vaccine, that can overcome the interference of maternal
antibodies in puppies and appears to immunize puppies about 2-4 weeks
earlier than MLV vaccines, is available in some countries.4,8 Since there
are no guarantees that every puppy will have a rapid active immune
response to these vaccines, puppies should be vaccinated every 2 to 4
weeks with CDV, CAV-2, and CPV-2 vaccines, up to 16 weeks of age.3,4,8
After an initial series of core vaccinations, it has been recommended to
administer another set of core vaccines at 12 months of age. The purpose of
this vaccine is not to “boost” the immune response, but to ensure the
development of a protective immune response in any dog ​that may not

have responded to the primary core vaccines. However, a puppy that fails
to respond to any of the core primary vaccinations will be unprotected until
it receives this vaccine at 12 months of age. For this reason, the World
Small Animal Veterinary Association (WSAVA) Vaccination Guidelines
Group (VGG) suggests that veterinarians try to reduce this possible period
of susceptibility by moving the time for administering this vaccine from 52
to 26 weeks of age or any time between 26 and 52 weeks of age.4 In
endemic areas puppies must also be vaccinated against rabies. The global
recommendation is to give the first vaccine no earlier than 12 weeks of age
with a second vaccine given 1 year later.4,11,12

ADULT DOGS
Dogs that responded to vaccination with core vaccines containing MLV
maintain solid immunity (immunologic memory) for several years in the
absence of any repeat vaccination. Therefore, after vaccination at 6
months, subsequent revaccination should be administered at 3-year
intervals.4 Canine core MLV vaccines can induce a protective immune
response lasting as long as 9 years for some components and sometimes
lifelong protection.14-17 An adult dog (or puppy over 26 weeks of age) with
an unknown vaccination history requires only a single dose of core MLV
vaccine to generate a protective immune response.4,10 Rabies vaccines can
carry a 1-year or a 3-year licensed DOI. Revaccination should be based on
DOI and local laws.4,9

NON-CORE VACCINES FOR DOGS
The most widely used vaccines for dogs that have been designated noncore are those against Bordetella bronchiseptica, CAV-2, canine
parainfluenza virus (CPiV), and leptospirosis.4,9 Other non-core vaccines
with more restricted geographic availability include those against Borrelia
burgdorferi, canine influenza virus (CIV), and Leishmania infantum4,9,10
(Table 185.1). There is a vaccine against rattlesnake venom available in
the United States (USA); however, efficacy and recommended doses are
based on studies conducted on mice.3,9

RESPIRATORY TRACT PATHOGEN
VACCINES (CHS. 203-205)
Vaccines against respiratory tract pathogens will not prevent clinical
disease but may reduce its severity. CPiV, B. bronchiseptica, and CAV-2
vaccines are available in different combinations of 3 antigens, as parenteral
(subunit B. bronchiseptica; inactivated B. bronchiseptica; MLV CPiV),
intranasal (IN; attenuated B. bronchiseptica with or without CPiV, and
CAV-2), and oral (attenuated B. bronchiseptica with or without CPiV)
formulations. IN and oral vaccines may be given as a single dose to
puppies, as early as 3-4 or 8 weeks of age (depending on the manufacturer)
for IN, and 8 weeks of age for oral vaccines.4,9 Parenteral vaccines are
given as 2 injections 2-4 weeks apart starting at 6-8 weeks of age.4,9
Parenterally administered CPiV and B. bronchiseptica vaccines may not
provide a level of protection that is comparable to mucosal vaccines, and
there is evidence that suggests that the IN route provides superior clinical
outcomes.18 Transient cough, sneezing, ocular or nasal discharge may
occur in a small percentage of dogs vaccinated with IN or oral
vaccines.4,9,18,19 Adult dogs that have never been vaccinated should receive
2 doses of parenteral vaccine or 1 dose of IN or oral vaccine to generate a
protective immune response.4 Revaccination should be annual.4,20
Vaccines against CIV infection are licensed only in the USA and are
available for H3N8 or H3N2 canine influenza, or as a bivalent vaccine
offering protection against both strains. Vaccination may not prevent
infection but may reduce the severity and duration of clinical signs;
however, infected dogs may still transiently shed virulent virus. The CIV
vaccine contains inactivated virus and is administered to puppies from 6
weeks of age with a second dose 2-4 weeks later and then annual
revaccination.3,4,9

LEPTOSPIROSIS (CH. 192)
Leptospirosis is a highly prevalent severe disease with potential zoonotic
implications in many parts of the world. Depending on geographic region,
this vaccine may be regarded as core.4,10 Vaccination can start at 8 weeks
of age, with a second dose given 2-4 weeks later. Adult dogs that had never
been vaccinated should also receive 2 doses.4,9 Annual vaccination is
suggested since leptospirosis vaccines have been shown to protect for at

least 12 months.4 The traditional canine Leptospira spp. vaccine
containing serogroups Canicola and Icterohaemorrhagiae are available in
many countries. Newer quadrivalent vaccines that also contain the
serovars Grippotyphosa, Pomona, Bratislava, and/or Australis are
increasingly available in countries where dogs vaccinated against Canicola
and Icterohaemorrhagiae are continuing to develop disease.4,21-23 In most
countries there is incomplete understanding of infecting dog serovars.
Studies rarely include isolation, making it difficult to determine which
serovars should be included to protect dogs.21

CANINE VISCERAL LEISHMANIOSIS (CVL)
(CHS. 196 AND 197)
No vaccine against CVL confers sterile immunity; however, vaccination can
prevent clinical signs or decrease their intensity in some dogs, but do not
consistently prevent infection.24-27 Thus, vaccinated dogs can act as
reservoirs for L. infantum.25-27 Vaccines against CVL are an additional tool
to protect exposed dogs that already make regular use of topical
insecticides (such as collars) as protection. There are 3 vaccines
commercially available; one with recombinant protein A2 of L. donovani
and saponin; one with purified excreted-secreted proteins (LiESP) of L.
infantum and saponin; and one with a recombinant protein (Protein Q)
without adjuvant.25-27 Vaccination protocols depend on the vaccine used.
One should follow the manufacturer’s recommendations.

B. BURGDORFERI VACCINES (ch. 187)
B. burgdorferi vaccines are controversial. In Lyme endemic areas the
prevention of tick-borne diseases in general is necessary, usually via use of
ectoparasiticides and routine inspection of dogs for ticks. These strategies
help prevent Lyme borreliosis. No Lyme vaccine can provide complete
protection, efficacies are uncertain, and it is unknown if any provide
protection against Lyme nephritis, the most severe form of the disease.2832
Depending on the region, several bacterins (monovalent, bivalent, and
trivalent) and subunit vaccines (a recombinant non-adjuvanted lipidated
OspA subunit, and a subunit vaccine consisting of OspA and an OspC
chimeritope) are available for the prevention of Lyme borreliosis in dogs.32

A systematic review of the efficacy of B. burgdorferi vaccination in dogs in
North America suggests that dogs vaccinated have less chance of
developing clinical signs than unvaccinated dogs.32 For most vaccines,
primary immunization is based on 2 initial doses, given 2-4 weeks apart,
regardless of the dog’s age, starting as early as 9-12 weeks of age,4,9
followed by annual revaccination, preferably before the beginning of tick
season (spring).4,8,11

NOT RECOMMENDED VACCINES FOR DOGS
Vaccines against canine enteric coronavirus (CCoV), Giardia duodenalis,
and dermatophytosis are not recommended. There is little evidence that
CCoV is a primary pathogen that leads to intestinal disease in adult dogs,
in puppies the diarrhea associated with infection is mild, and infection
usually occurs in puppies <6 weeks of age, making vaccination at 6-12
weeks of age too late to prevent most disease.4,10,33 Moreover, protection
against CCoV is dependent on the presence of intestinal secretory IgA.
Dogs vaccinated parenterally do not appear to develop a protective
intestinal IgA antibody response.34 There is no evidence that available
vaccines protect against mutant pathogenic forms of the virus (pantropic
strain) that occasionally emerge.4,10,33 Canine Giardia vaccines have been
removed from most global markets but persist in some Latin American
countries. Giardia duodenalis infection is non-life threatening, responds to
therapy, is rarely zoonotic, and there is no convincing evidence that the
vaccine can prevent elimination of oocysts (ch. 196).35 Vaccines do not
prevent infection and vaccinated dogs can develop clinical signs.10 While
there is a commercially available inactivated vaccine to prevent
dermatophytosis in dogs in some countries, there are few efficacy studies
and these vaccines do not protect against challenge infection.4,10,36

CORE VACCINES FOR CATS (CHS. 198-202,
205, AND 206)
OVERVIEW
The core vaccines for cats include feline panleukopenia virus (FPV), feline
herpesvirus-1 (FHV-1), feline calicivirus (FCV), and rabies in endemic

countries (Table 185.2).4 Core vaccines for cats are often available as a
combination of three MLV pathogens, inactivated adjuvanted or nonadjuvanted antigens, and in some countries, an IN MLV combination
(FHV-1 and FCV with or without FPV). The 2 respiratory tract components
(FHV-1 and FCV) are sometimes formulated as a multi-pathogen
parenteral vaccine. In general, MLV parenteral vaccines induce the best
protective response to all 3 components.4,37 Inactivated vaccines should be
preferably selected for use in retrovirus-infected cats or pregnant queens
(ch. 201).4,5 IN vaccines provide faster protection, important for high-risk
cats, but they may cause transient respiratory signs.5 See textbook’s inside
covers for protocol table.

KITTENS
The same considerations related to MDA in puppies apply to kittens.
However, a few studies suggest that persistence of MDA in kittens may be
longer than in puppies, as long as 17-20 weeks of age.38,39 Vaccination
should start at 6-8 weeks, with subsequent doses given every 2-4 weeks
until at least 16 weeks4 or from 16-20 weeks.5 The 2-week interval should
be used in environments likely to be heavily contaminated, such as shelters
or breeding catteries. As for dogs, the vaccine that was usually given at 12
months of age should be administered at 6 months of age.4,5
