ADULT CATS
Unlike FPV vaccines which induce a long-lasting complete protection,
FHV-1 and FCV vaccines can reduce clinical signs, but do not provide
complete protection. Several FPV vaccines now have a licensed minimum
DOI of 3 years. Therefore, when available product range allows, current
recommendations are for triennial revaccination of adult cats against
FPV.4,5 The recommendations for revaccination of adult cats against FHV1 and FCV are more variable. Revaccination against respiratory virus
should be determined by the risk of exposure of the individual cat. A lowrisk cat (i.e., a solitary indoor animal that does not visit catteries) might
safely be vaccinated triennially, while a high-risk cat (i.e., an indooroutdoor cat or a cat within a multi-cat household or regularly visiting
catteries) should be given an annual vaccine against upper respiratory

virus components.4,40 Some studies have demonstrated that FPV, FHV-1,
and FCV vaccines provide protection for a minimum of 3 years, with a
demonstrated minimum DOI of 7.5 years for an inactivated vaccine.41-43
An adult cat brought to a veterinarian for initial vaccination should receive
2 parenteral doses, even with MLV vaccines, because of the limited
immune response to the FHV-1 and FCV components of the vaccine.4
Adult cats should receive just 1 dose if an IN vaccine is used; annual
revaccination is required.5 Inactivated rabies vaccines are available for cats
as for dogs and a vectored (canarypox) recombinant rabies vaccine is also
available. Kittens should receive a single dose at 12 weeks of age, with
revaccination 12 months later; then repeat annually or every 3 years if
using a vaccine licensed for this interval.4,5,40

NON-CORE VACCINES FOR CATS
FELINE LEUKEMIA VIRUS (FeLV)
While the WSAVA VGG4 and the European Advisory Board on Cat
Diseases (ABCD)40,44 classify the FeLV vaccine as non-core, the American
Association of Feline Practitioners (AAFP) considers it core for cats <1 year
old.5,45 A range of FeLV vaccines are available, including adjuvanted
inactivated whole virus and subunit vaccines, and a recombinant virusvectored (canarypox) non-adjuvanted product. They provide protection
against progressive infection and FeLV-associated diseases but do not
protect against all outcomes of FeLV infection.4,45 In general, these
vaccines may be administered to kittens from 8 weeks of age with a second
vaccine given 3-4 weeks later.4,5 The WSAVA VGG and ABCD guidelines
recommend a single dose 1 year after the final kitten dose, then
revaccination not more often than every 2-3 years for cats at risk of
exposure.4,40 The AAFP recommends annual revaccination for cats at high
risk of exposure.5 Cats of uncertain FeLV status should be tested prior to
vaccination and vaccinated only if antigen-negative (and preferably also
provirus-negative).4,40

FELINE IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS (FIV)

The FIV vaccine is either classified as non-core40,41 or not recommended
(Table 185.2; ch. 198).4 The FIV vaccine was not licensed in Europe. In
2017, it was taken off the market in the USA and Canada. It is
commercially available in Australia and New Zealand. Although the
efficacy of the vaccine against FIV heterologous subtype B was suggested in
a field study,46 there has been debate as to whether the subtypes of virus
contained within the vaccine (A and D) effectively cross-protect against
other subtypes dominating in different geographic areas. A field study
demonstrated a protective rate of 56% in vaccinated cats,47 and a 2020
study conducted in New Zealand showed lack of vaccine-induced
protection against field FIVs.48 The introduction of the FIV vaccine has
complicated diagnosis since vaccination results in the production of
antibodies which cannot be readily differentiated from those produced in
response to natural infection. However, 2 point-of-care FIV antibody test
kits can help to discern the true FIV infection status of cats at the time of
annual booster.49 The vaccine is an inactivated adjuvanted product that
may be given to kittens from 8 weeks of age with 2 further injections each
2-3 weeks apart, a 12-month injection and then an annual booster for adult
cats deemed at being of sustained risk.4

CHLAMYDIA FELIS (C. felis)
Vaccines against C. felis provide incomplete protection. It may be used in
multi-cat groups when there is a previous history of C. felis infection.
Attenuated and inactivated adjuvanted parenteral C. felis vaccines are
available. These may be used in kittens from 8-9 weeks of age with a
second dose 2-4 weeks later, and an annual booster for adult cats at
constant risk of exposure. Adult cats not previously vaccinated need 2
doses to induce immunity.4,5

BORDETELLA BRONCHISEPTICA
The B. bronchiseptica vaccine might be considered for cats in high-risk
situations, for example, cats kept in large colonies. The vaccine is an
attenuated IN product that may be used as a single dose in kittens over 4
weeks of age, with an annual booster for adult animals at sustained risk of
exposure.4,5

NOT RECOMMENDED VACCINES FOR CATS
Vaccines against feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) and dermatophytosis
are not recommended for cats.4,5,50 There is insufficient evidence that the
FIP vaccine induces clinically relevant protection.4,5,33 Only cats known to
be feline coronavirus antibody-negative at the time of vaccination are likely
to develop some level of protection. This vaccine is labeled for
administration from 16 weeks of age, but most kittens become infected
with coronaviruses well before this age.4,5 Moreover, this vaccine contains
a serotype II strain of FIP virus that does not induce cross-reactive
protection to serotype I, which is the strain that predominates in America
and Europe.33 A monovalent (Microsporum canis) and a multipathogen
(Microsporum and Trichophyton species) inactivated product are licensed
for the prevention and treatment of dermatophytosis in cats in some
countries; however, there is little evidence to support their use for
prevention of infection.10,36,50

VACCINATION IN SHELTERS
Animal shelters usually have a random source population without known
vaccination histories, a high population turnover, and a high risk of
infectious diseases—an environment where eradication of infectious
disease cannot be attained. For this reason, vaccination protocols in
shelters are different from those used for individual care in a practice.
Many guidelines and recommendations for vaccines to be used in dogs and
cats in a shelter were published and those interested are referred to these
published articles and guidelines.4,5,51

SEROLOGIC TESTING
The commercial availability of point-of-care kits that demonstrate whether
an animal has serologic evidence of protection has advanced vaccinology
for companion animals. Tests should be validated independently, and their
performance compared with gold standard tests. The kits are simple to use
and provide rapid results (protection or not) within 20-30 minutes. For
CDV, CPV-2, CAV and FPV the presence of serum antibody provides an
extremely strong correlation with protective immunity. However, the
absence of detectable antibody is not predictive of susceptibility.4,16,52 For

FHV-1, protection is better correlated to the cellular immune response. For
FCV, protection is better correlated to local mucosal immune response.4
For puppies, these tests can be used to determine whether protection
exists, and they can be used to identify vaccination failure or non-response.
A puppy can be tested 2-4 weeks after the last dose of the initial series
(typically at 20 weeks). Seropositivity at this stage indicates that it has
made an endogenous immune response to vaccine as there can be no MDA
remaining. A puppy that is seronegative at 20 weeks should be
revaccinated (perhaps with an alternative product) and then tested again 2
weeks later. A positive result indicates protection. A second negative result
may indicate that the pup is either a “low responder” or a “nonresponder.”4,16 Knowing that triennial revaccination still reflects only the
minimum DOI, some practitioners now elect serologic testing every 3 years
rather than routinely revaccinating an adult dog.4 Dogs that are
seropositive (or cats seropositive for FPV) are not revaccinated with core
vaccines as these are not required. Where this approach is used, the testing
interval is reduced to annually for senior animals to ensure that
immunosenescence (aging of the immune system) is not an issue.53
Another valuable application of in-house serology has been in the
management of infectious disease outbreaks in shelters.4
Finally, if a dog or a cat had a potentially life-threatening adverse
reaction and there is a suspicion that vaccination might have been the
trigger, such animals should be subject to rigorous benefit-risk analysis
before revaccination is considered. For dog core vaccine antigens, this
decision is now facilitated with the application of in-house serology. A dog
with serum antibody to CDV, CAV, and CPV-2 does not require
revaccination with MLV core vaccines and whether additional non-core
vaccines should be administered should be carefully considered based on
lifestyle assessment.4

ADVERSE EVENTS FOLLOWING
VACCINATION
A wide range of adverse consequences of vaccination have been observed
in dogs and cats. Some “adverse event” simply indicates that the vaccine
has stimulated immune and inflammatory pathways as part of generating
the protective immune response, such as mild and transient pyrexia,
lethargy, anorexia, and regional lymphadenopathy. However, more serious
and lethal reactions can occur, such as type I (immediate) hypersensitivity

reactions (e.g., urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis), the potential to trigger
life-threatening autoimmune disease (e.g., immune-mediated hemolytic
anemia [IMHA], thrombocytopenia [IMTP], polyneuritis, and
polyarthritis), or feline injection site sarcoma (FISS).4,6,54,55 The site of
administration of vaccines should be considered carefully in cats and
include locations at which surgery would likely lead to a complete cure,
avoiding the interscapular region because complete tumor resection there
is almost impossible.4,6,56 Recommended injection sites include the skin of
the lateral abdomen,4 the distal thoracic and pelvic limbs,4,6,56 and the
tail.57 Vaccines in cats should be given as often as necessary but as
infrequently as possible. Vaccines should be brought to room temperature
prior to administration.4 Non-adjuvanted, MLVs or recombinant vaccines
are recommended over adjuvanted vaccines, if available and proven
equally effective.4,6,56 The largest epidemiologic investigations suggest
between 30 and 50 adverse reactions (mostly mild and transient) for every
10,000 vaccinations (0.3-0.5%) given in practice.58,59,60 The risk of
contracting life-threatening infectious disease far outweighs the risk of
adverse events.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Companion Animal Vaccination
Vaccination is considered a medical procedure that should be personalized
to the individual animal, and not all vaccinated dogs and cats must receive
a similar annual combination of vaccines. For this reason, dog and cat
vaccines are categorized as core (essential; for every animal), non-core
(optional; for some animals only) and not recommended (without
sufficient scientific evidence to justify their use). The core vaccines for dogs
are those against canine distemper virus (CDV), canine parvovirus (CPV),
and canine adenovirus (CAV) (the latter causes a disease known as canine
infectious hepatitis). The core vaccines for cats are those against feline
panleukopenia virus (FPV) (that causes feline panleukopenia), and for
upper respiratory tract disease pathogens such as feline calicivirus (FCV)
and feline herpesvirus (FHV). In endemic countries, rabies is also a core
vaccine for both dogs and cats. Non-core vaccines should be used only after
making an appropriate analysis based on an animal’s risk of exposure, and
for dogs include those against leptospirosis, respiratory tract pathogens
(i.e., parainfluenza virus, Bordetella bronchiseptica, and canine influenza
virus), Lyme borreliosis, and leishmaniosis. Non-core vaccines for cats are
those against feline leukemia virus, and upper respiratory tract disease
caused by Chlamydia felis and B. bronchiseptica. The feline
immunodeficiency virus vaccine is variably classified as non-core or not
recommended and is not available in many countries. The current advice
for puppies and kittens is for core vaccination starting from 6-8 weeks of
age, with subsequent doses given every 2-4 weeks, with the last injection
given at 16 weeks of age or older. An integral part of this protocol is
another dose given at 6 months. Newborn pups and kittens receive
maternal antibodies by taking in the “first milk” (or colostrum) from the
mother. However, although essential for survival, the presence of
maternal-derived antibodies (MDA) also can prevent that young animal
from mounting an immune response to a vaccine. These MDA have a finite
life span and only when the MDA level is low is that young pup or kitten

able to generate its own immune response to a vaccine. Since it is
impossible to know the exact time when this will occur, and a few pups and
kittens can maintain MDA until 16 or even 20 weeks of age, the last
vaccination dose should be given at 6 months.
In vaccines that contain “modified live virus” (MLV) the infectious
agents replicate in the animal; however, since they are “weakened” they are
not able to cause disease, but can induce a long duration of immunity
(DOI), ranging from years up to the lifetime of that animal. On the other
side, “inactivated” (or killed) vaccines provide a shorter DOI. For the core
puppy MLV vaccines (CDV, CPV, CAV), after the dose given at 6 months of
age, the revaccination should be done not more often than every 3 years.
This is the same for MLV FPV vaccines. Vaccines that protect against FCV
and FHV infections should be given annually or every 3 years depending
on the risk of infection. Non-core vaccines for dogs and cats induce
immunity only for months rather than years or may simply reduce the
clinical signs of disease rather than preventing the actual infection and
must be given more frequently (annually) in adult animals to maintain
protection.
In recent years, simple test kits have become available for in-clinic or
point-of-care use that demonstrate whether an individual animal has
serological evidence of protection in the form of antibodies. These test kits
can now inform if dogs or cats are still protected from previous vaccination
or need to be revaccinated, particularly for CDV, CPV, CAV (dogs) and FPV
(cats) vaccines, instead of simply vaccinating them every 3 years.
Mary Marcondes (Araçatuba, São Paulo, Brazil)

CHAPTER 186: HospitalAssociated (Nosocomial)
Infections
J. Scott Weese

AC RO N YM S
EMR electronic medical record
HAI hospital-associated infection
MRSA methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
SSI surgical site infection

REVIEW
HUMAN HOSPITALS
Hospitals, by their nature, are high-risk sites for acquiring infectious diseases.
Large numbers of patients and personnel, patients at increased risk of shedding
pathogens, and patients with varying degrees of infection susceptibility, raise the
risk of individuals encountering an infectious agent and developing clinical or
subclinical infection. Hospital-associated (nosocomial) infections are an inherent
risk of hospitalization and a risk for every pet and person in contact with patients
or the hospital environment. The realistic goal is to reduce (not necessarily
eliminate) hospital-associated infections (HAIs). To accomplish this, first requires
an understanding that infections are occurring and why.
In human medicine, HAIs have a profound impact on morbidity, mortality and
healthcare costs. On any given day, it is estimated that 1 in 31 patients
hospitalized in the U.S. have an HAI
(https://www.cdc.gov/hai/data/index.html) and HAIs may play a role in
one-third of unexpected deaths of hospitalized patients.1 Overall, HAIs were
estimated in 2002 to have caused 1.7 million infections, 99,000 associated deaths,
and $28-32 billion dollars in healthcare costs

(https://www.ahrq.gov/professionals/quality-patient-safety/patientsafety-resources/resources/hais/index.html).

VETERINARY HOSPITALS
Less is known about HAIs in veterinary patients. The relative impact is likely
much less compared to humans because veterinary patients tend to be less
compromised, have shorter lengths of stay, and are in smaller facilities. Yet, HAIs
undoubtedly have an impact. Reports are largely confined to sporadic case reports
and outbreak reports, involving a diverse range of bacterial and viral pathogens
such as methicillin-resistant staphylococci, Salmonella, canine influenza virus,
canine parainfluenza virus, canine papillomavirus, and dermatophytes (chs. 7, 9,
195, 203, 204).2-6 HAIs also include important syndromes such as surgical site
infections (SSIs), infections of invasive devices, respiratory disease, diarrhea, and
various opportunistic infections of patients compromised by treatments or
disease. Most data have been focused on SSIs as a common and readily
identifiable HAI, but the impacts of HAIs on veterinary patient
morbidity/mortality, medical costs, and clinic operations are poorly understood.

OUTBREAKS VS ENDEMIC DISEASE
It is generally accepted that the main burden of HAIs is endemic disease.
Outbreaks receive the majority of the attention but may compromise only a small
(but highly evident) fraction of HAIs. In a survey of veterinary teaching hospitals,
82% reported having identified an outbreak within the past 5 years, with 45%
reporting more than one.7 Less common but endemic incidents presumably have
a greater impact on the health of patients than high profile outbreaks, but are
rarely reported. Further, some HAIs are not readily apparent and can be missed,
even with good surveillance. For example, hospital-based transmission of many
multidrug resistant bacteria can occur in the absence of clinical disease at the
time of acquisition, but create a risk for subsequent development of disease or
transmission to other animals (including people). Identification of delayed-onset
HAIs such as this is difficult and rarely attempted. Yet, they are an increasing
concern in veterinary medicine from both animal and human health perspectives,
as hospitalization and treatments (particularly antimicrobial therapy) are clearly
identified risk factors for shedding multidrug resistant bacteria (chs. 7, 140).8,9

ZOONOTIC DISEASES
HAIs can also include human infections. As with infections of pets, the scope of
the problem is poorly understood and is limited to sporadic case reports. Lack of
communication, lack of specific diagnoses, and privacy concerns tend to limit
understanding of zoonotic infections of personnel. Yet, in a survey of veterinary

teaching hospitals, 50% of facilities reported knowing of zoonotic infections at
their facility within the past 2 years.7 Myriad zoonotic risks exist and most reports
are associated with large animal patients (e.g., salmonellosis, cryptosporidiosis,
methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus [MRSA]). However, similar risks are
present to some degree in small animal hospitals, along with exposure to other
pathogens ranging from likely common and mild (e.g., dermatophytosis) to rare
but potentially devastating (e.g., plague).10,11 As multidrug resistant bacteria
become more common in veterinary patients and many of those are the same as
cause disease in people (e.g., MRSA, extended spectrum beta-lactamase
producing Enterobacterales), zoonotic threats will likely increase (ch. 7).

IDENTIFICATION OF HOSPITAL-ASSOCIATED
INFECTIONS
SURVEILLANCE OVERVIEW
General principles of infection control are the cornerstone of any infection control
program. Good understanding of local HAI challenges is needed to modify,
monitor, and re-assess practices and to understand the scope of HAIs in a facility.
This requires some form of surveillance. There are no standard approaches to
surveillance in veterinary hospitals, but general concepts can be considered
anywhere. A variety of factors must be considered when designing a surveillance
program, including the goals of surveillance, local disease risks, risk aversion,
availability of personnel, and expertise. Full time, specifically trained personnel
are not required for an effective surveillance program, but some degree of
dedicated effort by people with basic expertise, tools, and support is needed.
Surveillance programs can range from highly structured formal programs with
integrated reporting and active surveillance approaches to ad hoc passive
approaches relying on readily available clinical information. While a fairly basic
surveillance program may be adequate for some facilities, some form of formal
surveillance program should be present as part of an overall infection control
program.

PASSIVE SURVEILLANCE
Definition and Value
Passive surveillance is a practical, efficient and cost-effective tool that can (and
should) be implemented in every veterinary clinic. It involves using data already
available through normal clinic activities, such as medical record information and
laboratory results. Passive surveillance represents an easy approach to obtaining
data but is also subject to the greatest variability in data quality and biases. Wellcollected passive surveillance data can provide useful information about endemic
rates for certain disease, antimicrobial susceptibility patterns and trends, and

changes in disease patterns. Passive surveillance can also identify important
incident events, such as identification of an unusual or particularly concerning
pathogen or disease, or a situation where a single report would lead to a specific
intervention (e.g., selected multidrug resistant bacteria, canine influenza, plague,
canine parvovirus) (chs. 201, 203).
The value of passive surveillance data is dependent on the data collection
system. Progress in electronic medical record (EMR) systems can greatly facilitate
passive surveillance, with the ultimate goal being the ability to automatically
generate reports about specific issues (e.g., SSI rate, antimicrobial susceptibility
patterns, antimicrobial use) and create automatic alerts for certain diseases or
thresholds (e.g., fever of unknown origin, SSI, targeted high impact diseases). The
current reality is that most EMR systems are not well designed for such practices
and data entry can be suboptimal. However, improvements in EMR systems with
incorporation of surveillance ability, use of standardized field codes (e.g., SSI)
and integration of patient and laboratory (e.g., culture) data are underway.
Ultimately, machine learning and artificial intelligence offer great promise for
providing better quality, data, classification, and recognition of important events.
Regardless of improvements in EMR systems, as with any aspect of surveillance,
simply collecting data is of no use if no one analyses it or if there is no plan for
using the results. Therefore, passive surveillance must be an organized, structured
activity with clear objectives and methods, tied into the overall goal-based
infection control program.

Strategies for Immediate Implementation of Passive
Surveillance
Based on limitations in active surveillance, passive surveillance remains the focus
in veterinary hospitals. While technological advances will improve the depth and
quality of data, any clinic can implement some form of effective passive
surveillance immediately. For example, monitoring SSI rates, either involving
overall procedures or, ideally, overall rates plus specific rates for common or
high-risk procedures should be straight forward. Critical limits for specific
hazards can be established, with a pre-determined plan of action should limits be
exceeded.

Use of Antibiograms
Another passive surveillance activity that can be useful or misused involves
collection and analysis of routine culture and susceptibility testing results
(antibiograms). Antibiograms can be useful patient management and
antimicrobial stewardship tools, but can also be relatively useless or even
misleading. Having data about bacterial species isolated from various sites and
their susceptibility patterns can aid in selection of empirical therapy when culture
is not possible or while culture results are pending. The data allows for more
targeted antimicrobial selection if the typical susceptibility pattern can be
reasonably inferred based on the patient and disease. Antibiograms are useful

when the patient likely reflects the population from which culture and
susceptibility data were obtained. A major consideration is the patient population
tested. If culture and susceptibility testing is focused on patients with severe or
refractory disease, or patients that have been previously treated with an
antimicrobial, there will be a bias toward an increased apparent antimicrobial
resistance rate. For example, urine culture is not performed on most patients with
bacterial cystitis, but is more often done on patients with recurrent disease or
those that failed empirical treatment. Therefore, resistance data poorly reflect the
average patient and probably profoundly overestimate the likelihood of
antimicrobial resistance. Similarly, hospital-associated pathogen trends may not
accurately reflect patients with similar diseases that originated in the community.
Antibiogram data can be useful to understand current patterns and changes, but
their use for guiding treatment must be based on the likelihood that those data
reflect the specific patient.

ACTIVE SURVEILLANCE
Active surveillance is more involved and expensive. It involves specific efforts to
gather data that would not otherwise be available through normal practices.
Therefore, it inherently adds time, effort, and cost, but it can provide the highest
quality data. Active surveillance is widely used in human hospitals, particularly
screening of admitted patients for carriage of multidrug resistant pathogens such
as MRSA.12 This type of approach is rarely indicated in veterinary hospitals and is
typically reserved for large facilities with increased infection control threats and
personnel available to direct such testing, or during a specific outbreak
investigation. Even then, it is rarely used in small animal hospitals, as opposed to
equine hospitals where routine screening for Salmonella shedding is common.
Potential applications include screening of patients for infection or colonization
with specific pathogens, either as a routine measure for all or a subset of patients
(e.g., screening selected orthopedic cases for methicillin-resistant S.
pseudintermedius colonization13) or a targeted response to an identified problem
(e.g., infectious respiratory disease testing when a group of coughing patients is
identified). Active surveillance measures such as this can identify risks that might
influence routine practices, help understand the epidemiology of selected high
consequence pathogens and/or lead to specific actions in positive patients (e.g.,
isolation). It can be done as an ongoing tool or used as a short-term measure to
provide some baseline information about endemic rates or investigate a potential
problem. The latter is most relevant to small animal practices, where the cost and
effort for active surveillance can perhaps be best justified for uncommon timelimited investigations in response to an apparent problem or concern. As with
other aspects of surveillance, active surveillance must be performed using an
organized, pre-determined program designed to fulfill specific objectives, with
associated plans for analysis of data and use of results.

SYNDROMIC SURVEILLANCE
Syndromic surveillance involves the analysis of certain clinical signs that may be
indicators of an infectious disease (e.g., cough, fever, diarrhea). It is done with the
recognition that there can be various causes of any given syndrome, both
infectious and non-infectious, but that individuals with those signs are at greater
risk of having an infectious agent of concern. This type of surveillance does not
indicate which disease is present or even confirm that an infectious disease is the
cause of the syndrome, but it provides readily accessible data to act as an easy or
early warning and lead to specific investigation. Therefore, syndromic
surveillance has a lack of specificity and limitations, but can be useful for
surveillance and control.
Syndromic monitoring can be performed by all personnel including non-clinical
personnel, such as front office staff. Syndromic surveillance is designed to easily
and rapidly identify potential problems and facilitate early interventions unless or
until a non-infectious cause is identified, e.g., acute onset of cough might be a
targeted syndrome and front office staff would flag each new patient presented for
this concern. The patient could then be admitted directly to an isolation area or
examination room, and clinical personnel would know to use enhanced infection
control practices. If a non-infectious cause is identified, precautions can be
relaxed. By its broad nature, syndromic surveillance is not highly specific and
non-infectious animals will be managed with unnecessary precaution. However,
considering the minor implications of over-identifying potentially infectious cases
versus the potential problems with failing to identify an infectious case, lack of
specificity is acceptable. Syndromic surveillance can also be used to detect
complications that develop during hospitalization. Because signs such as cough,
fever, or diarrhea are obvious and can be easily detected and recorded, syndromic
surveillance can be a practical tool to detect infections or early stages of an
outbreak. Syndromic surveillance is only a means to identify problems for further
investigation, and any potential problems must be investigated further through
other means.

ENVIRONMENTAL SURVEILLANCE
Environmental surveillance, while commonly used, is often used improperly. It is
a minimally useful surveillance measure. Hospital environments are not sterile
and it is expected that many potential pathogens, including various multidrug
resistant pathogens, are present in any veterinary hospital.14-16 Neither the
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention nor the American Animal Hospital
Association recommends routine environmental culture. However, environmental
culture is sometimes the first response by veterinary clinics in response to a
perceived nosocomial infection. Sampling from environmental surfaces,
inanimate objects, or the air is not efficient. A specific objective and organized
approach with a pre-determined action plan are needed to avoid wasting time and
resources. Routine cleaning and disinfection practices are designed to reduce the

environmental burden. Greater emphasis should be placed on higher risk items or
areas, but the goal is not a sterile environment. Therefore, identification of
bacteria in general hospital environmental sites is not particularly useful and
environmental surveillance is best reserved for rare situations where there is a
plausible role of the environment in disease, where a logical sampling and testing
plan is available and where there is a plan to act on the results.

PREVENTION AND CONTROL of HOSPITALASSOCIATED INFECTIONS
REASONABLE GOALS
Absolute prevention of HAIs is not realistic. The nature of hospitalization and risk
factors inherently present in many hospitalized patients (e.g., wounds, invasive
devices, immunological impacts of drugs or disease) mean that opportunistic
infection risk is ever-present. A “zero HAI rate” is aspirational but not practical.
However, there are many “preventive fractions” of HAIs. In humans, it has been
estimated that 20-70% of HAIs (35-55% is realistic) could be prevented with
common practical measures.17 While far from a 0% HAI rate, moderate rate
reductions would save thousands of lives and billions of healthcare dollars.
Similar estimates are not available for veterinary hospitals but it is reasonable to
assume that a substantial percentage of HAIs are preventable using practical,
cost-effective, basic infection control practices.

INFECTION CONTROL PROGRAMS FOR EVERY
FACILITY
Development and application of an infection control program is beyond the scope
of this chapter. However, every facility should have some form of infection control
program, ideally coordinated by a specific individual. Resources tend to be
limited. Support of administration and senior or influential clinicians is
important. Time must be dedicated to required activities along with some
resource allocation. Common problems with infection control programs include

failure to document programs, poor training, poor communication, lack of
support from administration, unwillingness to allocate time or money until an
outbreak is present, and lack of sustained interest as infection control programs
are successful and limit evident HAIs. Good references are now available to assist
in the design and implementation of an infection control program, and facilitate
development of an effective program with limited expertise or resource
requirement (Table 186.1).

CONCLUSION
Infection control is an important and often overlooked component of good
veterinary practice. Undoubtedly, HAIs occur in every veterinary practice,
regardless of type or size. The relative incidence and risk of infection may vary
between practices but all practices need to be aware of the risks and implement
basic infection control measures to detect, prevent and control HAIs and zoonotic
infections. As the awareness of HAIs and zoonotic infections increases and more
infection control resources have become available, it is reasonable to assume that
the expectations for veterinary hospitals to implement more active and formal
infection control practices have increased in parallel.

INTRODUCTION
Lyme disease (borreliosis, LD) is the most common tick-borne disease in people in North America.
Many dogs and cats are exposed, become chronic carriers, and have persistently high antibody titers, yet
only a small fraction become ill. Comprehensive reviews1-6 show that controversy still exists regarding
diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of canine LD.

THE AGENT, THE TICK, AND THE BIRDS, MICE, AND DEER
There are 52 known Borrelia spp. including 21 in the LD group (Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato) and 29
in the tick-borne relapsing fever (TBRF) group. The main causes of LD are B. burgdorferi sensu stricto
(Bb) in North America and Bb, Borrelia afzelii and Borrelia garinii in Eurasia. Borrelia spp. DNA in
ticks in 20 million-year-old “amber”7 and Bb DNA in the 5300-year-old “Tyrolean Iceman”8 prove the
disease is not new, but it was named after a cluster of affected children in Lyme, CT (U.S.) in 1976.9
Maternal activism led to work by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and Dr. Allen Steere.
Willy Burgdorfer was studying ticks from Shelter Island, NY for Rickettsia rickettsii but found many
Ixodes scapularis ticks carried spirochetes.2 Serologic testing in affected people proved exposure and
associated disease with those spirochetes. Experimental models in laboratory animals and dogs
confirmed this association. The organisms and the disease have been studied extensively, including

genomic sequencing. Dozens of strains of Bb exist, based on OspC antigen genotypes, with variable host
and tissue tropisms.1,3,10,11
There is transstadial, but not transovarial, transmission of Bb in ticks. In the typical 2-year life cycle of
Ixodes, eggs hatch outdoors in the summer, and larvae then feed on birds, mice, and small mammals
that recently acquired Bb from infected nymphs which fed on them the previous spring. Transmission of
Bb occurs in mice no later than 53 hours after tick attachment,1,3,4 the time required for OspA (the outer
surface protein A which attaches to the tick’s midgut) to be down-regulated, allowing Bb to detach and
enter the host. By this time OspC and other antigens are expressed more than OspA and antigens
expressed by Bb within the tick or when cultivated in vitro. Tick larvae pick up Bb in summer from their
first host, emerge as infected nymphs the next spring, transmitting Bb to birds, small mammals, dogs,
deer, people, and other animal species. The nymphs feed, molt, and emerge the next autumn,
transmitting Bb to their third hosts, often larger mammals, as adult ticks quest on higher brush.
The geographical range of Bb-infected ticks has expanded due to the movement of migratory birds.
Most LD in people in the U.S. occurs in 15 New England, mid-Atlantic, and Upper Midwestern states:
ME>VT>PA>NH>RI>DE>MA>NJ>CT>WI>WV>MN>MD>NY>VA.12 Results for Lyme-seropositive
[Lyme(+)] dogs are similar, extending into eastern and midwestern Canada.13-18 In some areas before
prevention was broadly used, 70-90% of healthy dogs were Lyme(+).2-3 High seropositivity exists in
wolves in MN (76%) and coyotes in PA (65%).19,20
Besides Bb, Ixodes ticks can transmit the human pathogens B. mayonii (in the LD group), TBRF
group agents Borrelia miyamotoi (Bm) and Borrelia davisii, Anaplasma phagocytophilum (ch. 193),
Ehrlichia muris, Babesia microti (ch. 197), Bartonella spp. (ch. 191), Powassan (tick-borne
encephalitis) virus (ch. 9), and possibly more agents. Coinfections can occur and be missed, e.g., with
Bm. In a Connecticut study, 35% of Ixodes ticks were positive for Bb and 6% for Bm.21 In people, Bm can
cause neurologic and flu-like signs.1,3,22,23 In southern NY, Bm-seropositivity was found in 1% of
healthy people, 3.2% of LD patients, and 21% of those with a flu-like illness in late spring/summer.23
Pathogenic Borrelia spp. are spiral-shaped motile Gram-negative spirochetes, transmitted by Ixodes
ticks which infect host mammals and birds, and migrate interstitially from the tick bite site, hiding out
extracellularly with collagen and fibroblasts. Possible recurrent signs can be due to evasion of the host’s
immune system by recombination of DNA cassettes, producing antigenic variation,4 antigenic
peptidoglycan cellular remnants,24 or a cystic dormant form of Bb in a hostile environment.2,4,25 Bb
does not generally circulate in blood or body fluids. This is in contrast to the human pathogen B.
mayonii, as well as the TBRF pathogens (Bm from Ixodes ticks, and Borrelia hermsii (Bh) and Borrelia
turicatae (Bt) from Ornithodoros soft argasid ticks, which only feed for 15-90 minutes). The TBRF
organisms can be seen in peripheral blood smears with Wright-Giemsa stain. Blood for TBRF culture
(Barbour Stoenner Kelly medium) or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis is best collected before
initiating antibiotics. TBRF has been seen in sick dogs in TX and FL (Bt) and WA (Bh), and in sick dogs
and cats in Israel (Borrelia persica) and Spain (Borrelia hispanica).1,3,26-31 Antibodies to Bt cross-react
with tests for Bb antibodies by whole cell indirect fluorescent antibody (IFA), VetScan, and AccuPlex4,
but not with C6 tests.31

COMPARING HUMAN, CANINE, AND FELINE LYME DISEASE
In Europeans, it was known for many years that a post-tick bite rash or neurologic illness responded to
penicillin. In the U.S., the expanding rash at the tick bite site is more often accompanied by flu-like signs
(headache, fever, myalgia/arthralgia) and later, swollen painful oligoarthritis in a joint near the tick bite
site. Subsequent neuroborreliosis, cardiac, and chronic skin manifestations may also occur.1-4 An
experimental tick bite model of canine LD has been well studied.1-4 When infected New England ticks
were placed on 6- to 12-week-old puppies, no acute illness occurred, but after 2-5 months a self-limiting
illness was seen (i.e., 4 days of fever, hyporexia, and lameness with nonseptic neutrophilic joint
inflammation in the limb closest to tick bite sites), possibly with a few recurrent episodes in the same or
different limb every 2 weeks. A group of 13- to 26-week-old puppies showed only 2 days of this selflimiting illness with fewer recurrences. Older puppies or adult dogs showed no signs of illness even
when followed for more than a year, yet all the experimental dogs showed carrier status and persistently

high antibody titers. Histologic changes included subclinical synovitis, suppurative/nonsuppurative
dermatitis, and lymphoplasmacytic periarteritis/perineuritis.
The experimentally infected dogs often had coinfections from tick exposure (35-45% with A.
phagocytophilum, or rarely Babesia microti).2,4 Carrier status for Bb for more than a year after tick
exposure was documented by culture or PCR test results on skin biopsies of tick bite sites. Antibiotics
cleared carrier status in most, but 10-15% of the dogs remained carriers despite receiving 1 month of
high-dose doxycycline (10 mg/kg PO q12h), amoxicillin (20 mg/kg PO q8h), azithromycin (25 mg/kg PO
q24h), or ceftriaxone (25 mg/kg IV q24h).1,2 Carriers in the experimental model remained non-clinical
but persistently Lyme(+) (the magnitude of titers did not correlate with illness). None developed Lyme
nephritis; some exhibited lameness after abrupt glucocorticoid withdrawal, but coinfections or trauma
could have played a role.1,2
Cats appear more resistant to illness from spirochetal infections; Lyme(+) cats are not more likely to
show illness,1 but cats with suggestive clinical signs were more likely to be Lyme(+) than healthy cats.32
Myocarditis is a rare manifestation of LD in cats as in dogs.1,3,33,34 Screening for coinfections
(bartonellosis [ch. 191], anaplasmosis [ch. 193], feline leukemia virus [ch. 199], feline
immunodeficiency virus [ch. 198]) is recommended. Experimentally, tick-exposed cats had
polyarthritis and pulmonary, lymphoid, and central nervous system inflammation at necropsy.3

CLINICAL SIGNS OF CANINE LYME DISEASE
LYME ARTHRITIS (LA)
As in the experimental model, Lyme(+) status in the field, no matter how high the titer, does not predict
illness in dogs.1 Cutaneous rash, neurologic, and cardiac signs of LD rarely or never occur.1-4 Original
New England reports showed <5% of Lyme(+) dogs had a history of lameness, even when followed for
20 months; the same percentage of seronegative dogs had similar signs.2 Even fewer Lyme(+) cats show
signs. One study showed that 40% of LA diagnoses are incorrect.1 It is estimated that <3% of Lyme(+)
dogs have signs due to LA. Clinical signs attributed to LD include oligo- or polyarthritis with painful,
hot, swollen joint(s), joint effusion, local lymphadenopathy, fever, and hyporexia (ch. 32). The
differential diagnosis list is extensive: tick-borne arthritis (ch. 193), immune-mediated polyarthritis
(ch. 177), lupus erythematosus (ch. 179), rheumatoid arthritis (ch. 177), bacterial endocarditis (ch.
232), septic arthritis (chs. 31, 177), degenerative joint disease (chs. 31, 177), joint ligament rupture,
intervertebral disc disease (ch. 250), trauma, panosteitis (ch. 162), osteomyelitis (ch. 31),
polymyositis, neoplasia (ch. 326), or immobility due to cardiopulmonary, metabolic, or neurologic
disease.1-4 Many dogs in Lyme endemic areas have coinfections with Anaplasma, and coinfected dogs
could be more likely to show clinical signs.1 Cytopenia suggests coinfection. Synovial fluid cytologic
evaluation (ch. 71) from arthrocentesis (ch. 87) shows neutrophilic inflammation, and sometimes A.
phagocytophilum morulae (Figure 176.1). Radiographs may reveal nonerosive arthritis and soft tissue
swelling. Signs are typically self-limiting or they resolve within 1-2 days of antimicrobial treatment;
treatment for 1 month is recommended.1 Doxycycline or minocycline usually is chosen because of the
possible presence of susceptible copathogens (Anaplasma, Ehrlichia, Rickettsia, Bartonella,
Mycoplasma spp.) and for anti-inflammatory and anti-arthritic properties. Bb is also sensitive to
amoxicillin, erythromycin, azithromycin, cefovecin, and ceftriaxone.1,3

LYME NEPHRITIS (LN)
Less than 2% of Lyme(+) dogs develop LN,35 a protein-losing nephropathy (PLN, ch. 302) associated
with immune-complex glomerulonephritis (ICGN) and Lyme-specific antigen-antibody complex
deposition in renal glomeruli.1,3,36 Lyme(+) dogs appear at higher risk for chronic kidney disease (CKD)
(ch. 301).37 Dogs with proteinuria are more likely to be seropositive.38 Although Bernese Mountain
dogs have higher risk for seropositivity and for CKD, no causal association was found.39 Labrador and
Golden Retrievers appear at higher risk for LN, but proteinuria was not found to be associated with

Lyme(+) status in retrievers in one study.1 It is unknown why so many dogs with high titers and
presumably high concentrations of circulating immune complexes do not develop LN (host genetics,
immune factors, or Bb strain differences are proposed). In people, certain genetic haplotypes are
predisposed to developing immune-mediated disease triggered by Lyme antigens (HLA-DR4).1,2
It is difficult to study LN in the absence of an experimental model. Perhaps some retrievers are
genetically predisposed to having glomerulopathy due to a podocytopathy or immune-dysregulation. It
is unknown if Lyme-specific immune complexes are primary (causative) or passively trapped in alreadyabnormal glomeruli. Elution studies on necropsy-obtained kidneys showed a variety of Lyme antigenantibody complexes, but no such studies on clinical cases have been published. There are no validated
Lyme-specific stains to use on renal biopsies for immunohistochemical documentation. Thus, LN is
diagnosed presumptively in Lyme(+) dogs with PLN. Clinical signs can be occult (proteinuria, ch. 70),
or dramatic, e.g., thromboembolism causing neurologic deficits (ch. 243), pelvic limb paresis/paralysis
(ch. 238), or respiratory distress (ch. 219); hypertensive damage causing blindness or cerebrovascular
accidents (ch. 236); or the nephrotic syndrome with edema or effusions (ch. 302), even before signs of
uremia (anorexia, vomiting) are seen. Polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD) is a late sign, signaling secondary
tubular damage. Dogs with primary glomerular disease may have azotemia without isosthenuria, e.g.,
with urine specific gravities of 1.020-1.030. The differential diagnosis includes leptospirosis (ch. 192)
and causes of PLN (infectious, immune-mediated, genetic, toxic, vascular, neoplastic, and amyloidosis;
ch. 302).1-3,35
In the original description of LN, only 30% of affected dogs had a history of lameness.1 Clinical
manifestations of PLN can include hypertension, thromboembolic events, edema, effusions, and
eventually signs of uremia such as anorexia, weight loss, vomiting, and/or PU/PD. Laboratory changes
are those seen with PLN such as proteinuria, cylindruria, hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia,
anemia, and thrombocytopenia (consumptive or due to coinfection). Secondary to severe glomerular
disease and tubular damage, some dogs have an active sediment, glucosuria, and isosthenuria. Since
leptospirosis can cause tubular changes, hypoalbuminemia, and/or azotemia, Lyme seropositivity may
be coincidental.1,3
Original reports of histopathologic changes in severely affected dogs showed a triad of ICGN, tubular
necrosis/regeneration, and interstitial nephritis,1,35 but early or milder forms likely exist without
tubular changes. Original reports included 30% of dogs with prior Lyme vaccine history; it is unknown if
vaccine was given after exposure or was non-protective, or whether Lyme vaccine antigens could cause
sensitization to or aggravation of ICGN.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTS FOR LYME EXPOSURE
The site of the tick bite is rarely known. Bb migrates interstitially, does not circulate in blood, and is
rarely found in synovial or other bodily fluids. Therefore, diagnostic tests to document exposure do not
rely on cultures or PCR testing but rather on serologic testing for antibodies directed against Bb
antigens. Older tests, such as whole cell IFA or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), showed
cross-reactions with other spirochetes as well as vaccinal antigens. Western immunoblotting helps to
show banding patterns that change over time due to antigenic variation shown by Bb in the host during
the carrier state but cross-reactions may occur. IgM and IgG titers are not helpful in dogs due to the long
incubation time before illness (2-5 months), so that dogs are unlikely to present ill during IgM+/IgG−
status. Antigenic variation can induce new IgM peaks during the carrier phase, so IgM+/IgG+ status
does not necessarily prove recent exposure.
The SNAP 4DxPlus (IDEXX Laboratories, Portland, ME) cage-side test provides a qualitative result
for heartworm antigen, and antibodies against Ehrlichia canis, E. chaffeensis, E. ewingii, A.
phagocytophilum, A. platys, and against the Lyme C6 peptide antigen. The C6 peptide antigen is a
recombinant replica of the constant region of antigen VlsE, which is only expressed by Bb when it is in
the host. It is not found in the tick, in Bb cultivation in vitro, nor in any Lyme vaccines.40 Thus, C6
peptide antibodies are specific for natural exposure. The SNAP 4DxPlus test uses no species-specific
reagents, so it can be used off-label on cats for antibodies to Bb as well as to Anaplasma spp.; validation
of the assay for this purpose is under investigation.
The Lyme C6 Quant test (IDEXX) provides quantitative results. The magnitude of any Lyme titer does
not predict illness and is not a cause for treatment in nonclinical nonproteinuric dogs.1-3,5 In treated

dogs, the sensitive qualitative SNAP 4DxPlus test likely remains positive for years, even with a low C6
Quant level. The latter has been shown to wane after treatment1 so that a post-treatment baseline test
(3-6 months after treatment) may be useful for later comparisons. If signs of illness suggest LD relapse
or reinfection, but the C6 Quant level is similar to the post-treatment baseline, the signs are probably
not attributable to LD and retreatment is not indicated.
The Accuplex4 (Antech) test gives qualitative results for heartworm antigen, and antibodies against E.
canis, A. phagocytophilum, and Lyme C6 antigens. A prior AccuPlex4 assay utilized an algorithm that
interpreted the magnitude and relationship of antibodies to OspA, OspC, OspF, p39, and SLP. OspA
(p31) is an antigen found in all Lyme vaccines. It is sometimes also expressed in the host and can be
found in non-vaccinated people with chronic non-antibiotic responsive LD, which has an immunemediated pathogenesis.1,4 Antibody titers to OspC rise 2-3 weeks after natural exposure and decline 3-5
months later if re-exposure does not occur; bacterin vaccines aim to induce OspC antibodies. Titers to
OspF rise 6-8 weeks after exposure, persist long-term, but possibly wane with treatment.3 Antibodies to
p39 are detectable in 88% of naturally exposed dogs vs. 47% of vaccinates.4 The SLP peptide is
proprietary. According to Antech Laboratories and studies done at Colorado State University, the
AccuPlex4 test may have detected antibodies 1 week earlier for Lyme and Anaplasma when compared to
the SNAP 4Dx test. However, another study found the AccuPlex4 test was not as repeatable, specific, or
sensitive as the SNAP 4DxPlus test for Lyme and Anaplasma antibody testing.1,3 Other tests include the
Multiplex (Cornell University Animal Health Diagnostic Center) test, which provides quantitative titer
results for OspA, OspC, and OspF. The VetScan FLEX4 and VetScan Canine Lyme Rapid qualitative
cage-side tests (Abaxis, distributed by Zoetis) is a test for antibodies against VlsE, OspC, and flagellin
(which might cross-react with other bacterial flagellins). In a comparison study regarding Bb antibodies,
the sensitivity of the VetScan test was only 41%, compared with 96% for the SNAP 4Dx Plus Test.41
Differentiation of vaccinal from natural-exposure antibodies and early from late infection might not
be straightforward. Although OspA antibodies are seen mostly in vaccinates and OspC antibodies are
seen mostly in non-vaccinates, both types of antibodies can appear in either vaccinates or nonvaccinates. OspC and OspF antibodies may provide clues regarding when a dog was last exposed to these
Lyme antigens, but not when it was first exposed. Whether an infection (exposure) is early or late might
not be clinically useful information in the dog.
Whenever a dog shows evidence of natural exposure, whether healthy or sick, at least three important
repercussions are apparent: (1) the dog should be screened for renal proteinuria: early treatment of LN if
indicated; (2) the dog has been exposed to ticks and wildlife, so testing for coinfection exposure or signs
might be indicated (e.g., for anaplasmosis, babesiosis, bartonellosis, ehrlichiosis, Rocky Mountain
spotted fever, leptospirosis, other Borrelia spp., etc.); and (3) the dog needs better tick control. Lyme(+)
dogs are sentinels, indicating that the owners live in an area where ticks are carrying LD.42 Owners are
usually grateful when their veterinarians provide education about tick-borne diseases, tick control,
landscaping, and public health issues. Veterinarians can also warn people not to wait for the rash or
illness before calling their physician when they find an engorged tick on themselves. For people living in
a Lyme endemic area, taking 1 day’s dose of doxycycline within 72 hours of removal of an engorged
Ixodes tick has been helpful in preventing LD.1,2

TREATMENT OF LYME ARTHRITIS AND LYME NEPHRITIS
(TABLE 187.1)
TREATMENT OF NONCLINICAL, NONPROTEINURIC DOGS
There is debate about whether to treat nonclinical nonproteinuric dogs that have positive Lyme
titers.1,2,5 The Lyme titer magnitude is neither predictive of, nor even associated with, illness, and
treatment for these dogs is not recommended. All Lyme(+) dogs should be screened and monitored
several times a year for proteinuria (frequency and duration are unknown). Treatment has not been
shown to prevent future illness.

TREATMENT OF CANINE LYME ARTHRITIS

Experimentally, LA is self-limiting; therefore, need for treatment is questionable. Clinically, however,
dogs with suspected LA usually are treated with doxycycline (5-10 mg/kg PO q12h for 4 weeks; the best
protocol is unknown) or minocycline because of common coinfections (e.g., anaplasmosis). Clinical signs
generally improve dramatically within 1-2 days of starting therapy; if not, other diagnoses should be
entertained, such as immune-mediated polyarthritis, which responds to glucocorticoids (ch. 177). Most
LD cases will be cleared of carrier status with 1 month of antibiotics. Lyme C6 Quant (IDEXX) levels are
helpful for comparisons (0 and 3- to 6-month post-treatment) since a ≥50% decline commonly is seen if
the level was >100 originally, and if proper tick control has been used to prevent re-exposure. The 6month post-treatment level may then be used as a new baseline, which may be helpful for future
reference should the dog show new signs of LD, to indicate whether reinfection or relapse warrants
retreatment. Qualitative C6 Lyme tests are likely to remain positive for years, even after treatment and
are not an indication of carrier status or need for retreatment. OspF antibodies might also wane after
treatment, but whole cell IFA or ELISA antibodies do not wane as markedly as C6 peptide antibodies.1-3
The antibodies may be due to immune memory and not necessarily due to ongoing carrier status.

TREATMENT OF CANINE LYME NEPHRITIS
Without an experimental model for LN, the best treatment protocol is speculative. The duration of
antimicrobial treatment usually is prolonged (3-6 months or until the Lyme C6 Quant level has waned)
because in 10-15% of dogs, the organism might not be cleared with only 1 month’s treatment. Standard
treatment for PLN1-3,43 is indicated (ch. 302). Monitoring is recommended every 1-2 weeks when dogs
are showing moderate clinical signs, or less frequently in stable patients. Monitoring and management
are based on blood pressures, average urine protein/creatinine ratio results on a mixture of equal
aliquots of 3 daily samples, hematocrit, and serum albumin, globulin, creatinine, blood urea nitrogen,
phosphorus, calcium, Na, and K. The prognosis is guarded for azotemic, vomiting, and anorexic dogs.
Dogs identified earlier, before they present with signs of uremia, can respond to standard treatments for
PLN.
Since LN is associated with ICGN, immunosuppressive therapy could be warranted.1-3,43 Ruling out
differential diagnoses and documentation of ICGN by renal biopsy are recommended before
immunosuppressive treatment is initiated. Renal biopsies should ideally be sent to the International
Veterinary Renal Pathology Service for examination by thin section light microscopy, special stains,
immunofluorescence, and transmission electron microscopy; however, there are no validated stains to
prove if immune complexes are Borrelia-specific. If clinical signs of disease are rapidly progressive,
immunosuppressive therapy could be warranted even without biopsy confirmation of ICGN.
Mycophenolate (ch. 169) is chosen often, but it may cause gastrointestinal adverse effects. Other
protocols include pulse glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, azathioprine, or cyclosporine
(ch. 144).

PREVENTION OF LYME DISEASE IN DOGS
TICK CONTROL
Since there are many tick-borne diseases in Lyme-endemic areas, tick control is warranted whether or
not Lyme vaccines are used. Tick control/prevention entails landscaping, avoiding tick habitats, tick
removal (Video 187.1

), and use of tick control products if the ambient temperature is ≥40°F (≥4°

Celsius). Although Lyme transmission does not generally occur until 2-4 days after tick attachment,
products which only kill ticks after 24 hours of attachment (e.g., fipronil) are not preferred because
other tick-borne agents can be transmitted more rapidly. Therefore, products that prevent tick
attachment or that kill ticks soon after attachment are advocated, e.g., topicals containing permethrin
(e.g., K9 Advantix II [Bayer], monthly), pyrethroid collars (e.g., Seresto [Bayer]), amitraz collars (e.g.,
Preventic [Virbac]), or the oral (chewable) isoxazoline compounds that kill ticks early after feeding (e.g.,
NexGard [Boehringer Ingelheim], Simparica [Zoetis], or Bravecto [Merck]). Sarolaner (Simparica)
showed tick killing efficacy of 68% (8 h), 98% (12 h), and 99% (24 h).44 See textbook’s inside covers for
information on spectrum of activity of antiparastic drugs.

LYME VACCINES
Several bacterins, a recombinant non-adjuvanted lipidated OspA subunit vaccine, and a chimeric
recombinant vaccine (crLyme, Zoetis, which includes OspC material from 7 strains of Bb) are available.1
All the vaccines induce production of OspA antibodies, to kill Bb within the tick as it feeds. The lipidated
subunit OspA vaccine may induce higher anti-OspA titers than non-lipidated vaccines.45 Bacterins also
claim induction of OspC antibodies as well as other antibodies which can kill Bb organisms that are

transmitted to the host. However, the diversity of OspC genotypes, lack of immunogenicity for conserved
domains, and low OspC vaccinal antibody production are problematic for bacterin efficacy against
various strains.10,11,45-50 The crLyme vaccinal antibodies reacted with 25 different recombinant OspC
variants.47 Duration of immunity (DOI) is still a concern; although the crLyme vaccine holds a 15-month
license, almost half the dogs studied were unprotected at 15 months.1
Lyme vaccines are controversial51 because (1) current tick control products work well and are needed
anyway to prevent other tick-borne diseases in Lyme endemic areas; (2) LA occurs in only <5% of dogs
exposed to Bb; (3) LA is self-limiting or easily treatable with antibiotics; (4) Lyme vaccines are less
effective, with shorter DOI and more post-vaccinal events, than other vaccines used (ch. 185)1-3,6; (5)
vaccination can give a false sense of security; (6) Lyme vaccines have not been shown to prevent LN; (7)
Lyme vaccines can interfere with some diagnostic test result interpretations; and (8) the rare serious
forms of LD are probably immune-mediated; it is unknown if Lyme vaccinal antigens could sensitize or
aggravate illness in genetically predisposed individuals.1,6 In animal models and genetically predisposed
people, OspA is inflammatory, sensitizing, and induces a marked TH1 response. High anti-OspA
antibody levels are associated with chronic non-responsive post-Lyme immune-mediated disease, and
Lyme antigens including OspA were found in immune-complex deposits in dogs with suspected LN.1-4,6
Proponents of Lyme vaccination point out that tick control compliance is not ideal, and that vaccination
can help reduce the risk of illness.1-3,6,52

CLIENT INFORMATION
Lyme Disease
Lyme disease is the most common tick-borne disease in the USA, with 95% of human cases reported in
just 15 New England, Mid-Atlantic, and Upper Midwestern states. It is caused by the bacterium Borrelia
burgdorferi, and transmitted by an Ixodes tick bite after 2-3 days of tick attachment. These “deer ticks”
live in outdoor greenery and feed on birds, mice, small mammals, deer, dogs, people, etc. Migrating
birds bring infected ticks to new habitats. Lyme disease is not contagious between infected animals and
people without a tick bite. An individual tick only feeds on one host each season. Nymphal ticks are
mostly active in the spring; adult ticks are active in the fall. Sometimes dogs, and rarely cats, show
illness due to Lyme disease.

In some areas up to 70-90% of healthy dogs are Lyme-seropositive (“Lyme-positive,” “Lyme[+]”) for
antibodies, which confirms natural exposure to the spirochete, but less than 5% of Lyme(+) dogs get sick
with Lyme disease. Based on experimental studies, young puppies (6-12 weeks old) appear to be more
sensitive, with a self-limiting illness consisting of 4 days of fever, decreased appetite, and limping
occurring 2-5 months after the tick bite. Older puppies (13-26 weeks old) have a shorter, 2-day illness,
and adult dogs show none of these symptoms in an experimental setting. Therefore, being Lyme(+), no
matter how high the titer, does not predict illness in dogs. Rash, neurologic, and cardiac signs of Lyme
disease, so commonly described in people with Lyme disease, rarely or never occur in dogs. “Lyme
nephritis,” with Lyme-specific immune-complex deposits in the kidneys, is a form of kidney damage that
has been associated with Lyme disease in dogs. Labrador and Golden Retrievers appear predisposed, but
even among Lyme(+) retrievers, fewer than 2% develop these kidney effects. The earliest warning of
Lyme nephritis is protein in the urine (proteinuria). All Lyme(+) dogs should be screened and
monitored through urine samples over time for proteinuria, even if previously treated for Lyme disease,
since treatment may not prevent the development of Lyme nephritis.
The decision to treat an asymptomatic, nonproteinuric, Lyme(+) dog is controversial: giving
treatment (antibiotics) could prevent the development of symptoms of Lyme disease, but in dogs,
treatment has not been shown to prevent Lyme-related illness and overtreatment should be avoided. For
treated dogs, pre- and then 3 to 6 month post-treatment blood testing for C6 Quant results are helpful
for a new baseline and comparisons if future signs of illness occur (other Lyme test results often remain
positive for years despite treatment). By the time a dog shows Lyme arthritis or proteinuria due to Lyme
disease, it should be Lyme(+). Dogs with Lyme arthritis are treated with antibiotics for 1 month but
improve markedly within 1-2 days (if not, consider another cause). Doxycycline or minocycline are often
chosen due to their antiarthritic and anti-inflammatory properties and ability to treat some coinfections.
Lyme nephritis often is treated for a longer period of time, and additional medications and renal diet
frequently are used for improving kidney function in these cases.
Since so many healthy dogs are Lyme(+), when a Lyme(+) dog is sick, it is difficult to know if Lyme
disease is the cause of illness or if the positive test result is just a coincidence. Being Lyme(+) is an
important marker for tick and wildlife exposure; coinfections causing similar symptoms include
leptospirosis, anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis, babesiosis, bartonellosis, other forms of borreliosis, and Rocky
Mountain spotted fever. Diagnostic tests for infectious and non-infectious causes for lameness, fever, or
protein-losing nephropathy can include blood and urine tests, blood pressure measurements, joint taps,
imaging (radiographs, ultrasound), and perhaps kidney biopsy, to plan the best management protocol.
Lyme vaccinations are controversial, but excellent tick control products (e.g., topicals, collars, oral
chewables), are available and recommended year-round for all dogs living in Lyme endemic areas, to
prevent exposure to Lyme disease as well as other tick-borne diseases.
Meryl P. Littman (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania)

MYCOBACTERIAL INFECTIONS
OVERVIEW
Mycobacteria are mostly intracellular, aerobic, acid-fast, non-spore-forming, nonmotile bacilli. They are generally saprophytic and non-pathogenic; however, several
species are considered primary or opportunistic pathogens. While mycobacterial
infections are being diagnosed more frequently in companion animals, the prevalence
is likely still underestimated due to non-specific signs, a low index of suspicion, and
difficulties in clinical diagnosis.1 Mycobacteria have been classified based on their
clinical presentations in affected people (Mycobacterium tuberculosis [MTB] vs
mycobacterium other than tuberculosis [MOTT]) or their physical and biochemical
properties (Runyon classifications). In companion animals, mycobacterial species are

now generally divided into infections caused by slowly-growing mycobacteria (SGM)
and those caused by rapidly-growing mycobacteria (RGM).

ETIOLOGY
Members of the MTB complex are obligate SGM, known to cause disease in humans
and animals, and which display specific host predilections. Feline tuberculosis has
been caused by infection with Mycobacterium bovis, Mycobacterium microti, and
rarely M. tuberculosis. Canine tuberculosis is less common, associated with infection
by M. tuberculosis or M. bovis. A single case of M. microti tuberculosis has been
reported in a dog with abdominal disease.2 Saprophytic SGM and RGM infections
typically arise from opportunistic infection with environmental species (Table 188.1).
The leproid mycobacteria are SGM which cannot be cultured readily on standard
mycobacterial media and have therefore not been completely characterised. Molecular
diagnostic techniques have allowed elucidation of the identity of these organisms.

EPIDEMIOLOGY
Tuberculous Mycobacteria
Domestic cattle are the primary reservoir of M. bovis, although other wildlife species
have been proposed as vectors of infection.3 Both cats and dogs are considered to be
“spill-over” hosts with cats appearing more susceptible. Infection is believed to occur
primarily through ingestion of infected prey. Small outbreaks have been reported in
groups of cats, purportedly associated with feeding of commercial raw food diets (ch.
167).4,5 Feline tuberculosis is generally identified in areas where M. bovis or M.
microti are endemic although occasional infections have been detected in unlikely
locales, possibly from anthroponosis.6,7 There are a small number of reports of M.
bovis outbreaks in cats housed in close proximity, due to either direct transmission
between individuals, nosocomial spread, or exposure to the same source of infection.811
A recent outbreak of M. bovis infection in a foxhound kennel provided the first
suggestion of dog-to-dog transmission.12
