Humans are the reservoir host of M. tuberculosis and infection of companion
animals is generally considered to result from close contact with infected humans.13-16

Canine tuberculosis is considered rare. Transmission to dogs living in high-risk
environments has been demonstrated, although the incidence of clinical infection is
low.17 The field vole is the maintenance host of M. microti in Great Britain. Hunting
and catching rodents is a risk factor for M. microti infection in cats and
immunosuppression may result in reactivation of latent infections.18

Saprophytic Mycobacteria
Infection by members of the Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare complex (MAC) is
the most common SGM implicated in feline and canine systemic infections. The SGM
cause opportunistic infections usually in young and immunosuppressed animals (chs.
180, 227), although disseminated disease has been reported in apparently
immunocompetent adults. Miniature schnauzer and basset hound dogs; and Somali,
Siamese, and Abyssinian cats are overrepresented in reports of MAC infections,
suggesting a hereditary immune dysfunction in these breeds. A CARD9 variant gene
has recently been identified in miniature schnauzers with MAC infections. The
intracellular CARD9 signalling pathway is integral in the innate immune response to
mycobacteria. Dogs homozygous for this mutation always develop systemic disease
following M. avium infection.19 Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis has
been isolated from the gastrointestinal (GI) tract of dogs with chronic enteropathies
although its significance remains unclear (ch. 257).20 Unlike other SGM,
Mycobacterium ulcerans produces mycolactone, a macrolide toxin believed to cause
distinct “Buruli ulcers.” Infection is most common in Australia, Africa, Papua New
Guinea, Sri Lanka and Latin America.21
Feline leprosy has been reported in Australia, the Pacific coast of Canada, the United
Kingdom, Europe, the United States (US), Japan, and New Zealand. Some specific
causative agents have restricted geographic ranges (ch. 9).22 Mycobacterium
lepraemurium is globally distributed and the most commonly identified cause of feline
leprosy. It is likely a saprophytic organism adapted to a rodent host. Infection is most
common in young male cats with rodent contact.23,24 “Candidatus Mycobacterium
lepraefelis” has been isolated from cats with feline leprosy in Australia and New
Zealand. Metabolic studies of this organism indicate that it is an obligate pathogen
with an intracellular niche, although a reservoir host has not been identified.25
“Candidatus Mycobacterium tarwinense,” only identified in southeastern Australia, is
likely an environmental saprophyte. Cats infected with “Candidatus Mycobacterium
lepraefelis,” and “Candidatus Mycobacterium tarwinense” tend to have an age
distribution reflecting that of the general population.22,25 Cats in this cohort
inconsistently have immunosuppressive comorbidities (ch. 180).
Canine leproid granuloma syndrome (CLGS) is a relatively common mycobacterial
dermatopathy in Australia and Brazil; it is less frequently diagnosed in the US, New
Zealand, and Europe (ch. 9). Transmission of infection by insect vectors in dogs is
suggested by geographic distribution, anatomical location of lesions, conformation of
and similar living conditions in affected breeds.26 CLGS has a predilection for largebreed short-haired dogs, with Boxer dogs being over-represented.26 Clusters of disease
have been identified in foxhounds housed together in New Zealand. Similar clusters

have been less well described in Australia and the US.27 Outbreaks may be due to
environmental factors (e.g., hunting) or a hereditary predisposition or
immunodeficiency in foxhounds.27
Infection with the RGM results in subcutaneous (SQ) and cutaneous infections in
cats. It is less common in dogs. Infection presumably follows inoculation during
fighting or trauma. Affected animals are often immunocompetent and obese. Female
cats are over-represented. Sporadic cases of pulmonary and disseminated infections
with Mycobacterium fortuitum, Mycobacterium thermoresistibile, and
Mycobacterium smegmatis have been reported.28-32

PATHOGENESIS
The portal of entry of mycobacteria into the host appears to be responsible for the
initial manifestation of disease and for the anatomical location of the primary lesion(s)
of the skin, GI or respiratory tracts. Due to the chronicity of disease and potential for
hematogenous dissemination, the primary site of infection may not be identifiable at
the time of diagnosis.

HISTORY AND CLINICAL SIGNS
The SGM cause local and systemic granulomatous disease in dogs and cats. The most
common signs in cats are SQ masses, often with draining tracts and regional
lymphadenomegaly. Cats may also show systemic signs that include lethargy, anorexia,
weight loss, respiratory distress and pyrexia. Ocular and neurological lesions may
occur as a component of systemic disease. The clinical signs of mycobacterial infection
in dogs are generally nonspecific or reflect the site of infection. Commonly, signs are
chronic and include lethargy, anorexia and weight loss, cough, dyspnea, vomiting, and
diarrhea. Other intermittently reported signs include neurological dysfunction, ocular
lesions, cutaneous lesions, epistaxis, polyuria/polydipsia, and lameness. Dogs can be
pyrexic and in poor body condition at the time of examination.
“Leproid” granulomas in cats caused by fastidious SGM may be single or multiple
cutaneous to SQ nodules with or without ulceration on the head and limbs but can be
identified anywhere on the body. Cats with “Candidatus M. tarwinense” infection
typically have one to two nodules on the head.22 Infection with “Candidatus M.
lepraefelis” and M. lepraemurium tend to result in multiple lesions or disseminated
disease, likely associated with hematogenous spread.23,25
CLGS most commonly appears as firm, non-painful, well-circumscribed dermal to
SQ nodules on haired skin. The head and dorsolateral pinnae are most commonly
affected. Papules, plaques, and masses have also been described with lesions also on
the face and limbs. Nodules have variable surface ulcerations and exudations that are
usually more extensive over larger or protuberant lesions.
The RGM have a predilection for adipose tissue in cats and infections most
commonly result in a panniculitis of the ventral abdomen and inguinal area. The
infected tissue is firm with thickening of the SQ tissue with multiple draining tracts.
Although respiratory infections and systemic spread are rare, affected cats may be

pyrexic, inappetent and lethargic. Most often, however, infected cats appear
systemically well.

DIAGNOSIS
Initial diagnosis is based on clinical suspicion, geographical location and identification
of acid-fast bacilli (AFB) within tissue samples (chs. 83, 85). Acid-fast staining of
tissues obtained from animals infected with MAC and other SGM often reveals a
greater number of organisms than tuberculous infections. Cytological and histological
examination of lesions from RGM infection often reveals granulomatous inflammation
without visible infectious organisms. Traditionally, confirmation of mycobacteriosis
has relied on culture, but SGM growth may take 4 to 12 weeks and requires specialised
media. Fastidious species cannot be cultured. RGM can often be grown readily on
routine culture medium, although molecular diagnostics may be required for definitive
diagnosis.
Clinicopathologic and diagnostic imaging findings are generally non-specific, but
may reflect the location or severity of infection. Differentiation among species within
the SGM and RGM groups cannot be based on clinical findings. Diagnostic imaging
studies of cats with systemic infection commonly reveals thoracic abnormalities with
diffuse pulmonary lesions and lymphadenomegaly.33,34 Large discrete pulmonary
tuberculomas, typical in human infections, are rare in cats.35 A commercially available
highly sensitive feline interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) has been validated for
detecting MTB complex infections in cats.36 The IGRA and other serological tests were
used when investigating an M. bovis outbreak in dogs, but results were inconsistent.12
A rapid definitive diagnosis may be obtained by amplification and sequencing of the
16S rRNA gene, 16-23S rRNA gene internal transcribed spacer region (ITS) and/or
hsp65 gene, amongst others. Identification via matrix-assisted laser
desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF) analysis is also
becoming more available (ch. 184).

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
The zoonotic potential of the infecting mycobacterial species must be considered prior
to treating a pet. Owners must be advised of the potential risk their pet may present to
human family members. Most mycobacterial infections in North America are not
zoonotic, but MTB infections in endemic areas, including Great Britain and Europe,
are associated with greater risk of spread to humans.
Cats diagnosed with SGM infection caused by MTB and MAC have a guarded
prognosis. Although many cats initially respond to various antimicrobials,
inappropriate drug selection and/or insufficient duration of treatment often results in
recurrence of disease followed by systemic spread.37 Successful treatment involves
long-term antimicrobial therapy. Surgical excision of discrete localized cutaneous
lesions may be beneficial when complete removal is possible. The SGM, particularly
members of the MAC, have greater innate resistance and variable antimicrobial
susceptibilities, and susceptibility testing should be performed where possible. Cats
should be treated for 3 months with a combination of rifampicin, a fluoroquinolone

(preferably pradofloxacin), and clarithromycin or azithromycin; followed by 3 to 4
months of rifampicin and either the fluoroquinolone or macrolide (Table 188.2).
Although the inclusion of rifampicin is indicated in the treatment of all MTB and MAC
infections due to its action against non-replicating intracellular mycobacteria, its
clinical use is limited by its potential hepatoxicity and GI effects. Treatment should be
continued for 2 months beyond resolution of clinical and radiographic signs.35
Dogs with systemic SGM infection have a grave prognosis with many euthanised
near the time of diagnosis. Rapid progression of disease despite treatment with
antimicrobials to which the isolate is sensitive in vitro has been reported.38
Although spontaneous remission is occasionally reported in cats with M.
lepraemurium infection, immediate treatment of cutaneous feline leproid granuloma
is recommended as the condition is generally progressive.23,39 The majority of cats
infected with M. lepraemurium respond favorably with appropriate therapy, even with
disseminated cutaneous disease.23 About one-third of cats with “Candidatus M.
tarwinense” have persistent localized and non-fatal infection despite treatment.22 Cats
with “Candidatus M. lepraefelis” infection carry a more guarded prognosis with only
one-third of cases resolving with treatment. Unlike other leproid infections in
companion animals, some cats develop progressive systemic signs resulting in death or
euthanasia despite treatment.25
Treatment of CLGS may not be required, as spontaneous remission has frequently
been reported.26,40 Refractory lesions should be treated with surgical resection and
long-term dual antimicrobial therapy (Table 188.2).24,40,41 CLGS generally has an
excellent prognosis, although persistent lesions may become disfiguring.27 Treatment
of granulomatous panniculitis associated with RGM infection in cats is most successful
with preoperative and perioperative antimicrobials (gentamicin), potentially followed
by radical surgical debulking, and single or combination antimicrobial therapy based
on susceptibility testing.42,43 The overall prognosis is geographically variable with
some organisms having high reported rates of disease recurrence.42

PUBLIC HEALTH CONSIDERATIONS
There are occasional reports of transmission of M. tuberculosis and M. bovis from pets
to close-contact humans. The zoonotic potential of infected animals is of increasing
concern, particularly for immunocompromised owners.8 Care should also be taken in
handling patients and specimens in veterinary hospitals when tuberculosis is a
differential diagnosis. Infection of veterinary personnel with M. tuberculosis was
reported following necropsy of an infected dog from which the organism was
aerosolised.44

ACTINOMYCOSIS
ETIOLOGY

Actinomyces spp. are facultatively anaerobic or microaerophilic Gram-positive,
irregularly-staining branching filamentous bacteria that are non-acid fast, nonsporing, and non-motile. These opportunistic pathogens are commensals of the
mucous membranes, particularly within the oral cavity. Several Actinomyces species
have been isolated from infected tissues in dogs and cats; however, identification is
often only to a genus level (Table 188.1).

EPIDEMIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS
Actinomycosis results from introduction of the organism from commensal sites into
body tissues, e.g., foreign body migration; in the oral cavity secondary to chronic
gingivitis and periodontal disease; inoculation via bite wounds or plant-material; or
aspiration of oropharyngeal material. Infection usually develops in immunocompetent
dogs and cats although it has been reported with concomitant immunosuppressive
diseases and neoplasia (chs. 180, 227).
Young male large-breed dogs kept outside are overrepresented in reports of
actinomycosis. Hunting and working animals are the most often affected, particularly
with soft-tissue abscesses and pyothorax. Although there is more variability in
signalment, young male cats are more likely to be affected, probably as a result of
increased aggressive interactions.
Actinomycosis is typically characterized by pyogranulomatous lesions containing
microcolonies of bacterial and host cells surrounded by macrophages, neutrophils and
plasma cells. Subacute and chronic infections result in the formation of granulation
tissue, extensive fibrosis and draining tracts. Exudates and effusions are often
malodourous and may contain macroscopic aggregates of bacteria and hyaline
commonly referred to as “sulfur granules.”

HISTORY AND CLINICAL SIGNS
Actinomycosis in dogs is most commonly associated with periodontal disease or with
SQ or soft tissue abscesses and pleuritis/pneumonia secondary to penetration or
inhalation of contaminated plant material. Central nervous system, ocular, peritoneal,
cardiac, and orthopedic implant infections have also been reported. Immune-mediated
polyarthropathy has been reported in a dog secondary to actinomycosis.45 Most
infected cats have pyothorax (ch. 220) following aspiration of oral flora. Other
reported signs include nasofacial infections, intra-abdominal and GI granulomas,
intracranial/spinal empyema, and cholecystitis.

DIAGNOSIS

A provisional diagnosis of actinomycosis may be based on identifying non-acid-fast
filamentous organisms on cytological examination of fluid or tissue samples stained
using a modified Ziehl-Neelsen (Kinyoun) method. While culture has traditionally
been used for isolation and identification, 16S rRNA gene sequencing of clinical
specimens is preferred.

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
The combination of surgery and antimicrobial therapy is superior to medical therapy
alone in resolving most actinomycotic infections in dogs and cats. Thoracotomy and
debridement are recommended in dogs with pyothorax but cats typically only require
thoracic drainage and antimicrobials (ch. 220).46,47 Actinomyces spp. are typically
responsive to long-term (weeks to months) penicillins in high doses or a range of other
antimicrobials (Table 188.2). The prognosis for animals with SQ and soft-issue
infections, and for cats with pyothorax is generally good when treated appropriately.
However, the reported survival in dogs with thoracic disease is variable and all
reported cases of CNS actinomycosis have been fatal.

NOCARDIOSIS
ETIOLOGY
The genus Nocardia consists of Gram-positive, variably acid-fast, catalase-positive,
non-motile aerobic bacteria that form filaments which may break into bacillary and
coccal forms. They are saprophytic soil organisms, ubiquitous in the environment, in
contrast to the commensal nature of Actinomyces spp., which are not soil organisms.
Nocardia spp. reported to be pathogenic in dogs and cats are listed in Table 188.1.

EPIDEMIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS
Infections in dogs and cats occur following inhalation of aerosolized organisms or
inoculation via puncture wounds or invasive medical procedures. In
immunocompetent animals, especially cats, infection most commonly causes skin
lesions. Disseminated disease, often involving the CNS and thorax, has been reported
more commonly in young and immunosuppressed dogs but can also occur in cats on
immunosuppressive drug therapy (ch. 180). Nocardia spp. have also been isolated
from animals with osteomyelitis, cystitis, and hepatitis.

HISTORY AND CLINICAL SIGNS
Cutaneous and SQ lesions may develop into superficial abscesses or more indurated
masses (mycetomas) involving the extremities, inguinal area or neck, with or without
local spread and lymph node involvement. Superficial lesions are often associated with
the development of draining tracts and sinuses. Thoracic disease may manifest as
pneumonia (ch. 217) or pyothorax (ch. 220), resulting in signs of dyspnea,
tachypnea, lethargy, weight loss, and fever. Many of these signs are nonspecific, with

similar findings often identified in peritoneal and disseminated nocardiosis or in other
systemic infections.

DIAGNOSIS
A presumptive diagnosis of nocardiosis may be based on microscopic examination of
clinical specimens. Organisms appear as Gram-positive, thin filamentous organisms
within a background of lymphocytes and macrophages. Uptake of acid-fast stains by
these organisms can increase suspicion for nocardiosis. However, this reaction is
unreliable in direct clinical specimens, and may be dependent on the growth media
used and age in culture samples.
Nocardia spp. can be grown on most culture media, although extended incubation
periods may be required. Due to the increasing number of recognized species and
differences in pathogenic traits and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns between
Nocardia spp., molecular methods, most commonly 16S rRNA gene sequencing or
MALDI-TOF analysis have become the methods of choice for accurate and rapid
bacterial identification (ch. 184). However, these methods may be insufficiently
sensitive to discriminate between some Nocardia spp.48

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Like actinomycosis, treatment of nocardiosis relies on appropriate antimicrobial
therapy; in some cases debridement and drainage of the lesion may also be required.
Most Nocardia spp. are susceptible to sulfonamide antibiotics, which have historically
formed the basis of medical therapy. Sulfonamides, however, may not be well tolerated
and some species of Nocardia are resistant.49,50 A range of other antimicrobials have
been shown to be efficacious with multiagent protocols advocated for treatment of
persistent or disseminated infections (Table 188.2). Prolonged therapy of 6-12
months based on culture and susceptibility testing is required in the majority of cases
to achieve optimal results.
Pets with disseminated disease, particularly with CNS involvement, generally carry a
grave prognosis. While animals with superficial disease may initially respond to
treatment, many are euthanised due to deterioration despite treatment or due to
disease recurrence. Higher rates of disease resolution are reported in medically
immunosuppressed dogs in which immunosuppressive medications can be
discontinued concurrent to appropriate tissue debridement and antimicrobial
administration (ch. 227).51

CLIENT INFORMATION
Mycobacterial Infections in Dogs and Cats
WHAT IS MYCOBACTERIOSIS?
Mycobacteriosis is an infectious disease caused by a group of bacteria known as
mycobacteria. Several different types of mycobacteria can cause infection in dogs and
cats and may be primary pathogens (carried by other infected animals and/or humans)
or opportunistic pathogens (environmental bacteria that cause disease in susceptible
animals).
Mycobacteriosis can occur in two forms in dogs and cats based on the species of
bacteria:
• Tuberculous mycobacteriosis
• Saprophytic mycobacteriosis (including leproid syndromes)
Cats are generally more susceptible to mycobacteriosis than are dogs.
WHAT ARE THE CLINICAL SIGNS OF MYCOBACTERIOSIS?
The clinical signs of the different forms of mycobacteriosis are often overlapping, often
depending on the route of infection rather than the bacterial species.
• Skin lesions - skin infections may develop after bite wounds or injuries. These
may appear as small nodules or non-healing wounds, often on the limbs, head
or ears. Spread of disease or enlargement of the local lymph nodes may result
in new swelling and nodules developing over time. In some cases, infection can
spread to the lungs and other internal organs.
• Panniculitis - diffuse infection of the subcutaneous fat in cats, usually on the
abdomen. This presents as firm swelling under the skin of the abdomen
associated with draining, non-healing wounds.
• Lung infections - occur following inhalation of the bacteria or spread from
another site. Clinical signs include cough and difficulty breathing.
• Systemic disease - widespread infections can occur in dogs and cats following
ingestion or inhalation of the bacteria or spread from other sites. Clinical signs
include depression, weight loss, decreased appetite, vomiting, diarrhea,
breathing difficulty and seizures.
HOW IS MYCOBACTERIOSIS DIAGNOSED?
A diagnosis of mycobacteriosis requires a piece of infected tissue to be collected. This is
then examined for evidence of tissue changes consistent with the disease. Definitive
diagnosis requires culture or molecular identification (DNA typing) of the organism.

Blood tests, radiographs and ultrasound may need to be performed to determine the
extent of infection and prior to commencing treatment.
HOW IS MYCOBACTERIOSIS TREATED IN DOGS AND CATS?
With or without surgery, medical treatment is imperative and involves administration
of two or three types of antibiotics for a prolonged period (at least 3-6 months).
Sometimes, the infected tissue may need to be removed surgically.
WHAT IS THE PROGNOSIS?
The outlook for improvement and recovery (prognosis) depends on the infecting
organism, the site of infection and the severity of infection. While skin infections,
particularly in dogs, can be cured with appropriate treatment, they often recur. Lung
and systemic infections have a grave prognosis and are usually fatal.
WHAT IS THE RISK TO HUMANS?
Although infection of humans living with affected pets is rare, tuberculous
mycobacteriosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium bovis can
spread to humans, causing tuberculosis. Young, old and immunocompromised people
are at particular risk. Saprophytic infection in humans can occur following
environmental exposure. Bite wounds from dogs and cats may facilitate the spread of
infection. The organisms causing the leproid syndromes are not known to be infectious
to humans.
Joanna Whitney (Sydney, Australia) and Carolyn O’Brien (Parkville, Victoria,
Australia)

CHAPTER 189: Brucellosis
Bronwyn Crane

A C RO N YM S
AGID agar gel immunodiffusion
CFU colony forming units
ELISA enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
LFIA lateral flow immunoassay
LPS lipopolysaccharide
2-ME 2-mercaptoethanol
PCR polymerase chain reaction
RSAT rapid slide agglutination test
TAT tube agglutination test

DESCRIPTION
Brucella spp. are intracellular, host-adapted bacteria. They are
highly transmissible within their host species and possess the ability
to cross-infect other non-host species, including humans. Brucella
canis was first identified and linked to abortions in beagle colonies in
1966-68.1-4 Brucella abortus, Brucella melitensis, and Brucella suis
are host-adapted to cattle, small ruminants, and swine, respectively,
yet infections by each of these organisms have been documented in
dogs. Brucella canis is a small, Gram-negative, aerobic, coccobacillus

with rough, colonial morphology. This “rough” colonial morphology
is the feature that characterizes both B. canis and Brucella ovis as
rough Brucella strains. In contrast, most other Brucella species (B.
abortus, B. melitensis, and B. suis) appear smooth in culture due to
the mucoid “O” polysaccharide side chain of their lipopolysaccharide
(LPS). Rough Brucella strains lack this mucoid “O” side chain, which
is also an important immunogenic antigen and the basis for
screening tests identifying infections with these strains.

ZOONOTIC CONCERNS
It is estimated that there are 500,000 new human cases of
brucellosis annually.5 The greatest concern for humans is infection
by smooth Brucella strains. B. canis infections are less commonly
documented in humans and are considered to be of low zoonotic
potential. However, it is likely that human B. canis infections are
underreported due to the non-specific flu-like symptoms it causes in
addition to a low degree of suspicion from medical doctors.
Furthermore, most screening tests in humans only identify infection
by smooth Brucella strains. B. canis infection in people can result in
prolonged, intermittent fevers and lymphadenopathy, which may or
may not respond to antimicrobial therapy. Individuals at greatest
risk are children, the elderly, pregnant women, and the
immunocompromised.6 The greatest prevalence of human infection
is found in the Middle East, Africa, Asia, and Latin America.7 Since
there is no vaccine for humans and treatment is challenging, the
most effective way to control disease in humans is through the
prevention of disease in animals.8

DISTRIBUTION AND PREVALENCE
B. canis has a global distribution. Continued propagation of B. canis
exists where there are reproductively intact free roaming dog
populations. B. canis can easily enter shelters from the stray dog
population. Geographically, the greatest seroprevalence (>20%) has
been found in regions of Brazil, Asia, and Eastern Europe (ch. 9).7

Areas with moderate seroprevalence (6-20%) include the
southeastern USA, Latin America, and Africa while most of Europe,
Canada, and the northeastern and western USA have a
seroprevalence <6%.7 A large serological survey of mostly freeroaming, intact dogs from regions of South Dakota estimated a
prevalence of 29.4%9 while a survey of shelter dogs in Mississippi
estimated a prevalence of 7.4%.10
Serological surveys show that B. canis infects dogs of any age,
those neutered or intact, and mixed or pure breeds. One report found
that while the greatest number of diagnostic submissions was from
intact and breeding animals compared to neutered animals, the
greatest proportion of positive test results was from neutered
animals (spayed 33% vs. 9% intact females and castrated 28% vs. 8%
intact males).11 Another large serological survey of stray, mostly
intact (96%) animals found that a higher proportion of intact
animals was positive (6.9% vs. 2.8%) but this difference was not
significant (p=0.07).9 In one study, young (1-6 years), mixed breed
animals were more likely to be seropositive than older purebred
animals.11
The significance of smooth Brucella strains (B. abortus, B.
melitensis, B. suis) in canine infections is under consideration. One
study found that some dogs in contact with feral swine from different
regions of Georgia, USA, were infected with B. suis (n=9).12 A
serological survey in the southeastern USA of hog hunting,
companion, and shelter dogs found that 3.5% (3/84) had detectable
antibodies to smooth Brucella strains,13 Meanwhile, a survey of
Mississippi shelter dogs found that 0% (0/571) dogs had detectable
antibodies to smooth Brucella strains,10 while in Iran, herding dogs
on ruminant farms had an overall seroprevalence of 24.3% (42/173)
for Brucella melitensis.14 These findings highlight the potential for
dogs to harbor non-B. canis Brucella species, increasing the risk of
human exposure.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND
TRANSMISSION
B. canis can be shed in milk, vaginal discharges, semen, and urine.
The route of entry is through mucous membranes; primarily
oronasal and venereal. Transplacental infection can occur in
pregnant bitches. Aborted fetuses are highly contaminated (>500
infective doses/mL).15 Following abortion, the highly contaminated
vaginal discharges may persist for 4-6 weeks. Apparently healthy
pups born to an infected dam may have been infected in utero or
may become infected in the perinatal period through contact with
vaginal discharge or ingestion of milk. An infective oral dose is 106
colony forming units (CFU) while an infective conjunctival dose is
104 CFU.5 From the mucous membranes, B. canis becomes
phagocytosed by monocytes and neutrophils and enters the
bloodstream. After an initial period of bacteremia, the organism
demonstrates tropism for the lymphoendoreticular and reproductive
systems. Infection then persists for 5 years or more with intermittent
bacteremia and shedding.

CLINICAL PRESENTATION
Canine brucellosis has a high infectivity rate and a low mortality rate,
with the greatest mortality in fetal and neonatal loss. Fever is
uncommon due to the lack of LPS, which normally causes endotoxin
release. Reproductive failures and abortions are the most common
clinical signs. Brucellosis is also associated with chronic, nonspecific
conditions including lymphadenomegaly, diskospondylitis (ch.
250), osteomyelitis (ch. 31), polyarthritis (ch. 177),
meningoencephalitis (ch. 242), pyogranulomatous dermatitis (ch.
12), and ocular lesions (ch. 13). More vague and subtle signs include
exercise intolerance, poor hair coat, and lethargy, but in the majority
of infected animals, no clinical signs are reported. Intact males with
B. canis can develop orchitis, epididymitis, scrotal edema, scrotal
dermatitis, testicular atrophy, and poor semen quality.
Display of estrus and breeding are not affected by infection with B.
canis. Bitches exposed to B. canis up to 20 days after conception

usually experience early embryonic death and resorption, often
diagnosed as conception failure. If infection occurs later in
pregnancy, abortion occurs around day 45 to 59 of gestation. Aborted
fetuses are often partially autolyzed with subcutaneous edema,
hemorrhage, and congestion. Other fetal lesions can include
bronchopneumonia, lymphadenitis, hepatitis, multifocal renal
hemorrhage, and myocarditis.5 A chronically infected bitch may
abort 2 or 3 consecutive litters and then have a normal litter.

DIAGNOSIS
AVAILABLE TESTS
Canine brucellosis is a diagnostician’s dilemma. Clinicians must have
a solid understanding of the progression and pathogenesis of
brucellosis, which can guide appropriate test selection and specimen
collection timing. Diagnosis often requires more than one test, and
repeated testing may be needed to confirm a true negative or positive
result. When a sensitive test is positive, it should be followed by a
more specific confirmatory test. Negative screening tests should
ideally be followed by a second test after 8-12 weeks.
Diagnostic options include direct identification of the organism
through polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or culture of blood, semen,
urine, or vaginal discharge; or identification of antibodies through
serologic tests (ch. 184). Serologic testing options include the rapid
slide agglutination test (RSAT), the RSAT with addition of 2mercaptoethanol (2-ME), agar gel immunodiffusion (AGID),
microagglutination tests (MAT), complement fixation tests (CFTs),
tube agglutination tests (TATs), lateral flow immunoassays (LFIAs),
and several enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) tests using
different antigens.

TEST SENSITIVITY, SPECIFICITY, AND
TIMING
Serologic tests vary significantly in their sensitivity and specificity
and may crossreact with other common bacterial antigens. The

timeline of infection also influences the accuracy of diagnostic tests
as both recently infected and chronically infected dogs may test
seronegative. It takes 3-12 weeks after infection for antibody
development. Bacteremia develops usually 1-4 weeks post-infection
and persists for 6-64 months. Blood, semen, vaginal swabs, urine,
and milk can all be tested for the presence of Brucella. B. canis
shedding in semen is highest during weeks 3-11 and decreases after
week 12.16 Chronically infected dogs present the greatest diagnostic
challenge. After 4-5 years, the organism can still be found in lymph
nodes, spleen, liver, or reproductive tissue and may recrudesce at
any time; during this time, direct identification methods, such as
PCR and culture, will have lower sensitivity. Seropositive dogs may
also become seronegative over time and then intermittently
seropositive again.
The RSAT is a sensitive screening test after week 12 of infection,
but it is not specific and positive results can occur when antibodies to
Staphylococcus spp., Streptococcus spp., Bordetella spp.,
Pseudomonas spp., Moraxella spp., and other Gram-negative
bacteria are present. The RSAT is rapid, commercially available, and
can be performed in clinic. The addition of 2-ME improves the
specificity of the RSAT. The TAT is also a sensitive but not specific
serologic test that provides quantitative results. A promising
screening test is the LFIA: an initial study showed a sensitivity and
specificity of 98.6% and 100%, respectively, in a format that is quick
and easy to use in the field.17 Positive results with the RSAT, MERSAT, LFIA, or TAT should be confirmed with a more specific test,
such as AGID, ELISA, or PCR. The sensitivity of AGID or ELISA
depends on the antigen used. Tests using cell wall antigens tend to
crossreact with other bacteria and result in more false positives than
those using cytoplasmic antigens.
B. canis PCR testing is most frequently performed on blood,
semen, or vaginal swabs but can be used to identify organism in
milk, urine, or aborted fetuses. The presence of any amount of B.
canis, whether viable or not, is of epidemiological significance and
indicates infection even when infections are subclinical. In one study,
PCR could detect 3.9 femtograms of bacterial DNA in semen,
equivalent to two bacterial cells, amongst 444.9 nanograms of host
DNA.16 Semen and vaginal swab PCR tests were more sensitive than

both the 2ME-RSAT and semen/vaginal culture, and had similar
performance to blood PCR, indicating that these could be useful
confirmatory tests in suspect dogs testing negative by blood PCR or
culture.16,18

TURNAROUND TIME AND COST
Other considerations in the selection of tests are turnaround time
and price. Culture is definitive but requires time (7 days), may lack
sensitivity, and has the potential to expose laboratory personnel to a
potentially hazardous zoonotic pathogen. Screening a kennel or large
group of animals can quickly become cost prohibitive, especially for a
shelter where this type of testing is most often needed.

TREATMENT
Identification of a positive B. canis case is reportable to authorities in
some US states. Due to the lack of effective treatment options, risk of
recrudescence, and exposure of other animals and humans,
euthanasia is often recommended. When treatment is attempted it
requires the use of combination drug therapy for prolonged periods,
and repeated courses of treatment, and is still often unsuccessful.
Dogs undergoing antibiotic treatment should be spayed or neutered
and isolated from other dogs for the foreseeable future. The owners
must be informed of the zoonotic risks, especially to children and
immunocompromised people. Treatment protocols with some
reported success include a 3-month course of doxycycline,
gentamicin, and rifampin19; or monotherapy with enrofloxacin.20
Dogs should be tested following treatment and re-tested every 4-6
months.19 Animal care attendants in contact with fluid or tissues
from an aborting bitch should strive for strict hygiene precautions as
this discharge is highly infective to both humans and other dogs.
Brucella spp. are short lived outside the host and sensitive to most
common disinfectants. Any positive diagnosis should result in
quarantine of the entire kennel for at least 3 months. A breeding
kennel should stop all breeding and sales of puppies. Monthly tests

should be performed on all remaining dogs and positive dogs
removed as they are detected.

PREVENTION
Reducing the global prevalence of B. canis will require efforts on
multiple levels. At a local level, breeding kennels and shelters should
focus on testing and quarantining new arrivals. Animals should be
tested upon arrival and after at least 8 weeks, prior to introduction to
the rest of the kennel. Routine screening of all breeding animals in a
kennel should take place every 6 months. Education of the public,
clients, physicians, and veterinarians to increase awareness and
suspicion of brucellosis will improve disease recognition. An
increased regulatory focus including mandatory testing of imported
animals and a requirement to report positive cases to authorities
would help prevent importation of disease and reduce spread. Lastly,
continued research and development of diagnostic tests and vaccines
will be key aspects of disease control or potential eradication in the
future.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Brucellosis
What Is Canine Brucellosis?
Brucella canis is a bacterium which causes reproductive losses in
both the stud dog and the bitch resulting in infertility and abortions.
Neutered animals and puppies can also be infected but may show no
signs or a very low-grade non-specific illness, such as back pain, poor
haircoat, and lack of energy. Once infected, an animal remains
infected for months to years and is highly contagious. Treatment is
very difficult because of the way this bacterium hides inside the
animal’s cells.
Is Brucella canis a Concern for Humans?
Yes. Besides the serious reproductive losses that may occur, one of
the greatest concerns with this bacterium is that it can also spread to
humans, causing intermittent fevers for long periods of time.
Immunocompromised people, pregnant women, and children are at
the greatest risk of acquiring the infection. For this reason, Brucella
cases must be reported to the USDA in many US states and positive
kennels would have mandatory quarantine and follow up. If you have
been in contact with a dog diagnosed with B. canis, you should
contact your healthcare provider and arrange for testing.
How Do Dogs Become Infected With B. canis?
B. canis is transmitted between dogs through nose to nose contact,
contact with infected urine, consumption of infected milk, breeding
with infected semen, and contact with the discharge from an
aborting bitch. The discharge from an aborting bitch has the highest

levels of infective doses. Once an animal is infected, the bacteria
enter the blood cells and move to organ systems where it can avoid
the immune system. If the animal is reproductively intact, they will
continue to shed B. canis through their semen or vaginal secretions.
Infected females will often conceive normally but then abort later in
pregnancy. Surviving puppies are often infected and contagious, even
when they appear normal and healthy.
How Is B. canis Diagnosed?
One of the biggest challenges with Brucella is in the diagnosis of the
disease. Shedding of the bacterium and the production of antibodies
against it will rise and fall over time because of its ability to hide
from the immune system. Veterinarians will typically need to use
more than one test over a time period to diagnose an animal as either
negative or positive. Any dog with reproductive losses should be
tested.
How Can We Prevent B. canis Infections and Reduce Risk
of an Outbreak?
The proportion of dogs infected with Brucella is regionally varied.
The greatest infection rates are in stray dog populations in subtropical and tropical areas, but outbreaks have been documented
worldwide. Breeding kennels are at the greatest risk for losses if B.
canis is introduced and should adopt a routine screening protocol to
prevent an outbreak. Animal shelters are also at risk when they bring
in free-roaming, intact dogs and should have a test and quarantine
protocol to prevent transmission.
Unrestricted international movement of breeding dogs and
importation/adoption of stray dogs from highly infected regions,
coupled with the complicated course of infection and the strategic
testing needed to declare an animal brucellosis free, make
controlling and eliminating B. canis a very difficult challenge for
veterinarians and regulatory bodies.
Bronwyn Crane (Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, Canada)

CHAPTER 190: Tetanus and
Botulism
Simon R. Platt

A C RO N YM S
CNS central nervous system
SNARE soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive-factor attachment
receptor

Clostridial organisms are Gram-positive, anaerobic spore-forming
bacteria found ubiquitously in the environment. Neurotoxins
produced by the bacteria are responsible for both tetanus
(manifested as spastic paralysis) and botulism (manifested as flaccid
paralysis) in humans and domestic animals. The basic underlying
mechanism of action of these zinc metalloprotease toxins is
inhibition of neurotransmitter release in both diseases, despite the
dramatically different clinical signs observed.1,2

TETANUS
ETIOLOGY
Tetanus is caused by the actions of neurotoxins formed in the body
by Clostridium tetani, a motile, Gram-positive, non-encapsulated,
anaerobic, spore-forming rod-shaped bacterium. The toxin is

produced during vegetative growth of the organism in a suitable
environment.3,4 The organism’s resistant spores are ubiquitous, with
a natural habitat in moist, fertile soil; however, they can survive
indefinitely in dusty indoor environments.2

PATHOGENESIS
Tetanus develops when spores are introduced into wounds or via
penetrating injuries. Most cases develop after skin wounds; but
infection can follow teething, dental fractures, nailbed infections,
parturition, or surgeries such as ovariohysterectomy.5-7
Occasionally, no obvious wound can be found.8 Under anaerobic
conditions found in necrotic or infected tissue, the tetanus bacillus
secretes two exotoxins: tetanospasmin and tetanolysin. Tetanolysin
is capable of locally damaging otherwise viable tissue surrounding
the infected area and optimizing the conditions for bacterial
multiplication.3 Tetanospasmin leads to the clinical syndrome of
tetanus.9,10 Tetanospasmin binds to the membranes of the local
motor nerve terminals. If toxin load is high, some toxin may enter
the bloodstream and to bind to nerve terminals throughout the body,
even entering the central nervous system (CNS) through an intact
blood-brain barrier. The toxin then is internalized and rapidly
transported intraaxonally and in a retrograde fashion to the cell
body.2,3 Transport occurs first in motor and later in sensory and
autonomic nerves. Further retrograde intraneural transport occurs
with toxin spreading to the brainstem in a bilateral fashion, up the
spinal cord.
The light chain component of the toxin becomes activated after
internalization into inhibitory neurons; at this stage the toxin is no
longer accessible for neutralization by antitoxin.10 It prevents
neurotransmitter release by cleaving and inactivating
synaptobrevin.11 Synaptobrevin is a member of the SNARE (soluble
N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive-factor attachment receptor) protein
family, a highly conserved group of proteins essential for docking

and fusion of neurotransmitter vesicles with the presynaptic
membrane (Figure 190.1).1,9-12
The toxin predominantly affects inhibitory interneurons,
preventing release of glycine and gamma-aminobutyric acid
(GABA).3 Interneurons inhibiting alpha-motor neurons are first
affected, and the motor neurons lose inhibitory control. Disinhibited
autonomic discharge leads to disturbances in autonomic control,
with sympathetic overactivity and excessive plasma catecholamine
levels. Neuronal binding of toxin is thought to be irreversible.
Recovery requires the growth of new nerve terminals, which explains
the long duration of tetanus.

CLINICAL SIGNS
History and Initial Signs
Tetanus most commonly affects young large breed dogs, is rare in
cats, and has been reported to be more common in the winter in
Europe.13 Clinical signs can take up to 3 weeks to become apparent
from the onset of infection, although most cases exhibit signs within
5 to 12 days.5,7,8 The clinical signs initially can be localized or
generalized, with the former more common in cats. Only a few cats
with tetanus have been documented in the literature; most had
localized clinical signs.14-18 A study of 38 dogs with tetanus revealed
that ocular and facial changes were the most common initial signs.5
Localized signs begin proximal to the site of introduction of the
infection and can include focal muscle rigidity, entire limb rigidity,
and facial muscle spasms; cats may be more likely to experience
carpal flexion, whereas dogs exhibit extension.14,15 Signs may
progress with more extensive muscle involvement.19 Generalized
signs include a stiff gait affecting all limbs, increased muscle tone,
dyspnea, an elevated tail and a “sawhorse stance.” The animal may
become uncomfortable standing with such excessive muscle activity.
At least 50% of dogs progress in a median of 4 days (range 0-14 days)
to recumbency with severe muscle spasms.5,7,8

Lockjaw and Other Progressive Signs
Involvement of the head can lead to spasms of the masticatory and
pharyngeal muscles, causing trismus (lockjaw) and dysphagia.
Trismus is not pathognomic for tetanus. Tetanus must be
distinguished from other causes, which include temporomandibular
joint disease or subluxation, masticatory myositis and retrobulbar
abscess.20 Trismus can be exacerbated functionally by increased
salivation, increased bronchial secretions, and increased respiratory
rate resulting from involvement of the parasympathetic and somatic
cranial nerve nuclei. Regurgitation and gastroesophageal reflux can
result rarely from esophageal hiatal hernia and megaesophagus,
which may lead to aspiration pneumonia.21 Excessive contraction of
the facial muscles causes erect ears and a wrinkled forehead (Figure
190.2) and gives the animal a characteristic sneering of the lips
known as risus sardonicus (sardonic grin) (Figure 190.3; Video
190.1)

. Dogs and cats can exhibit protrusion of the third eyelid

and enophthalmos caused by hypertonus of the extraocular muscles
and retraction of the globe.2 Severe progression of signs can cause
recumbency, opisthotonus, seizure-like activity, respiratory
paralysis, and central respiratory arrest, potentially causing death if
not rapidly recognized and managed. Death is seen in up to 50% of
dogs.5,7,8

FIGURE 190.1 A, Schematic view of a mammalian
motor neuron and inhibitory interneuron. The sites
of action of tetanus toxin (TeNT) and botulinum
toxin (BoNT) are highlighted. B, The cellular
mechanism of the two clostridial neurotoxins are
illustrated; both TeNT and BoNT follow a 4-step
mechanism to enter and inhibit neurons: membrane
binding (1), internalization (2), translocation (3) and
intracellular action (4). SNAP-25, Synaptosomalassociated protein of 25 kDa; VAMP, vesicleassociated membrane protein.

Autonomic Nervous System Signs
It is possible to see an effect on the autonomic system evidenced by
episodes of bradycardia and tachycardia, hypertension, marked
vasoconstriction, and fever.7 In the mild generalized cases,
autonomic involvement may be manifested by dysuria and urinary
retention, constipation, and gaseous gastrointestinal distention.

Classification
A tetanus severity classification system has been proposed in dogs:5
class I: only facial signs; class II: generalized rigidity or dysphagia,
with or without class I signs; class III: class I or II signs and
recumbency or seizures; and class IV: class I, II, or III signs and
autonomic dysfunction.5 Survival rate decreases with severity class.

DIAGNOSIS
Routine Testing
History and clinical signs are usually sufficient to make a
presumptive diagnosis of tetanus. Differential diagnoses should
include immune-mediated polymyositis, strychnine intoxication (ch.
133), spinal trauma (ch. 251), hypocalcemia (chs. 69, 284), or
meningoencephalitis (ch. 242). A complete blood count may suggest
an infectious process from a wound, whereas serum biochemistry
(with the exception of muscle enzymes) and cerebrospinal fluid
analysis findings are normal.2 Muscle enzymes may increase with
tetanus because of the persistent muscle spasticity; high activities of
serum creatine kinase (1599-18,405 U/L [reference range 61-394
U/L]) have been documented in more than 50% of dogs.8
Radiographs may be helpful to identify involvement of the
esophagus, diaphragm, and secondary changes in the lungs resulting
from aspiration pneumonia.

FIGURE 190.2 A 3-year-old Bull Terrier with
tetanus. Note how the ears are drawn together and
the dog’s “brow” is furrowed.

FIGURE 190.3 A Labrador Retriever with tetanus,
illustrating the effect of the toxins on the muscles of
facial expression creating the classical risus
sardonicus appearance.

Electrodiagnostics
Electrodiagnostics results in tetanus are nonspecific. They consist of
prolonged electric discharges after needle insertion on
electromyography (ch. 111).18 There is subsequent persistence of
“doublet” motor unit discharges, which are double discharges of the
same motor unit at short intervals. Often, simultaneous activity of
agonist and antagonist muscles are noted.18 Nerve conduction
velocities are normal,22 and F waves have been reported to be
abnormal.18

Culture
Attempts to isolate C. tetani from wounds often fail because of the
low concentration of organisms and the requirement for strict

anaerobic culture conditions at 37°C for at least 2 weeks.2 A Gram
stain of a smear from an open wound may identify Gram-positive
rods and dark-staining spheric endospores, but the morphology of
the bacterium is nonspecific.2

TREATMENT
General Requirements
Intensive nursing care is essential for successful treatment of dogs
and cats with tetanus. The pet should be isolated in a dark and quiet
environment, with cotton wool placed in the external ear canals
(Figure 190.4). Minimal handling is optimal, and treatments
should be coordinated to occur together at set times through the day.
Pressure sores or decubital ulcers should be prevented with
appropriate soft or padded bedding and frequent turning.

Need for Gastrostomy or Tracheostomy Tubes
Gastrostomy tubes may help prevent complications associated with
nasogastric tube feeding, particularly the stress associated with an
indwelling intranasal tube (ch. 81). Gastrostomy- or
gastrojejunostomy-assisted tube feeding can also reduce risk of
aspiration pneumonia. If airway obstruction develops because of
laryngeal spasm or a buildup of saliva or tracheal secretions,
intubation and mechanical ventilation may be necessary. In such
cases, a tracheostomy is suggested to decrease the need for
continuous anesthesia (ch. 94).

FIGURE 190.4 Intensive care treatment of
tetanus patients often requires respiratory support;
in this patient intranasal oxygen and a tracheostomy
were necessary. Supportive therapy includes
reducing the environmental stimulation which can
be accomplished by placing cotton wool balls in the
external ear canals as can be seen in this dog, and
even using sleep masks.

Antitoxin
Antitoxin only neutralizes toxin not bound to the CNS. Therefore the
timing of administration in relation to the onset of the disease is
essential to its effectiveness.23 There has been no significant benefit
in survival, severity of clinical signs, or duration of clinical signs

shown in dogs treated with antitoxin.7 Benefit of early antitoxin
administration on progression of clinical signs (i.e., worsening
tetanus severity classification) or mortality rate has not been
demonstrated.5 The recommended equine antitoxin dose for dogs
and cats is 100 to 1000 U/kg (maximum 20,000 U/kg) IV, SC, or
IM.2 To reduce the risk of anaphylaxis, a test dose (0.1-0.2 mL of
1:10,000 solution) should be administered intradermally 15-30
minutes prior, with a wheal at the site of injection indicating that an
anaphylactic reaction may develop. Epinephrine (0.1 mL/kg IV of the
1:10,000 dilution), glucocorticoids, and an antihistamine (e.g.,
diphenhydramine) should be readily available in case of an adverse
reaction.

Removing the Source of Infection
Parenteral antimicrobials are essential to kill vegetative C. tetani
organisms and thereby reduce the amount of circulating toxin.
However, metronidazole (7-10 mg/kg PO or IV q8-12h for 10 days)
has been shown superior to the classically advocated penicillin G in
clinical tetanus because it achieves bactericidal therapeutic
concentrations in anaerobic tissues.2 Other options include
clindamycin (10 mg/kg PO, IV, or IM q8-12h) or doxycycline (5-10
mg/kg PO or IV q12h).2 Flushing the wound with hydrogen peroxide
which inhibits anaerobic organisms has been suggested, although it
may impair wound healing.2

Control of Rigidity and Spasms
Prevention of unnecessary stimulation is mandatory, but the
mainstay of treatment is sedation with a benzodiazepine. Diazepam
(0.5-1 mg/kg PO q8h in dogs [maximum 10 mg], 0.25-0.5 mg/kg in
cats [maximum 5 mg, caution with oral diazepam in cats because of
hepatotoxicity], or a continuous IV infusion of 0.1-1 mg/kg/hr in
dogs and cats or clorazepate (0.5-1 mg/kg PO q8h in dogs; 0.2-0.5
mg/kg PO q12-24h in cats) can be used. As an alternative,
midazolam can be used as a continuous IV infusion (0.2-0.5
mg/kg/hr). Additional sedation can be provided with anticonvulsant

therapy, particularly phenobarbital (1-4 mg/kg PO or IV q12h or IM
q6h). Phenothiazines may be highly effective in controlling the
hyperexcitable state; chlorpromazine (0.1-0.5 mg/kg IM, IV, or PO
q6-12h) is the drug of choice, although acepromazine (0.005-0.05
mg/kg IV q2h as needed [maximum 3 mg in any dog]) is a useful
substitute.

Treating Severe Signs
With severe signs, such as tonic-clonic seizure activity, generalized
body stiffness, and opisthotonus, an IV propofol infusion may be
necessary. Cardiovascular parameters should be monitored closely
and careful consideration should be given to intubation and positivepressure ventilation. Recently, the use of magnesium sulfate
(MgSO4) infusions or supraphysiologic magnesium therapy has been
documented as a potential adjunct therapy in the management of
dogs with tetanus.24,25 A dose of 70 mg/kg over 30 minutes followed
by an initial constant rate infusion of 100 mg/kg/day has been
recommended (ch. 77). Oral magnesium aspartate (12 mg/kg q12h)
can be continued for 14 days once this is feasible.25

Prognosis
Recovery in dogs with tetanus depends on thorough support while
new axonal terminals form, as continued improvement may take
place over 3 to 5 months.5,7,8 Most dogs that recover show some
improvement within 5 to 12 days, although the presence of
autonomic abnormalities is a poor prognostic indicator.5,7 The
estimated mortality rate is as high as 50%.24 Mortality is likely
related to the severity of clinical signs; in one study, all dogs with
class I or II clinical signs survived but only 58% of dogs with class III
or IV signs survived.5 Cats are reported to recover well from localized
tetanus with some residual deficits remaining for months.14-17
Abnormal “dream enactment” clinically consistent with REM sleep
behavior disorder has been seen in up to half of recovering dogs.26
Twitching, running, and vocalization during sleep as new behaviors

were seen within 2 weeks of recovery in some dogs and were not
controlled by antiepileptic medications. In many cases the disorder
spontaneously resolved within 6 months.26

BOTULISM
ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS
Botulinum toxin is usually produced by C. botulinum, a
heterogeneous group of Gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming,
rod bacteria distributed in soil worldwide. Seven antigenically
distinct types of toxin are described (A, B, C1, D, E, F and G),27 with
the majority of canine and feline cases caused by type C toxin.27-32
Although other mechanisms have been purported, botulism most
commonly occurs following ingestion of preformed toxin in rancid
food or carrion.27,29-32 The spores formed by these bacteria, which
are highly resistant to severe environmental conditions, will
germinate in anaerobic conditions such as those provided by rotting
carcasses of dead animals. Lysis of the spore is necessary for the
release of the inactive progenitor toxin complex, which becomes
active within the alkaline environment of the intestinal tract. The
toxin is released into and absorbed from the small intestine by
endocytosis. Toxin then enters the lymphatic system and the
bloodstream. The botulism toxin heavy chain then binds rapidly and
with extremely high affinity to presynaptic peripheral nerve
terminals, where it is internalized by endosomes. The toxin then
modifies SNARE proteins required for exocytosis of acetylcholine at
the neuromuscular junction (Figure 190.1).9,10,27,33,34 Action of
the toxin is prolonged and functional recovery depends on sprouting
new axon terminals and reformation of neuromuscular endplates.35

CLINICAL PRESENTATION
Botulism is characterized by an afebrile, acute-onset, progressive
flaccid paresis, with additional involvement of the autonomic
nervous system.25,29,30 Clinical signs typically develop within 12

hours of toxin ingestion.27-32 Some animals may quickly progress to
tetraplegia (Video 190.2)

while others only exhibit a mild

ascending weakness, predominantly affecting the pelvic limbs.
Consistent with a lower motor neuron lesion, reflexes and muscle
tone are decreased to absent (ch. 241). Cranial nerve deficits (e.g.,
facial nerve paralysis, depressed gag reflex, decreased jaw tone,
reduced vocalization and megaesophagus), are common in severely
affected animals but sensory function, including pain perception,
and level of consciousness are unaffected. Cholinergic signs may be
seen which include alterations of heart rate (increased or decreased),
pupil changes (mydriasis with depressed pupillary light reflexes),
keratoconjunctivitis sicca, urinary retention and constipation.27-32
In severe cases, the respiratory musculature may be affected, with
decreased abdominal tone and primary diaphragmatic respiration.
The diaphragm is more resistant to botulism toxin and is only
affected in severe cases.27 Death may result from paralysis of the
respiratory muscles or secondary to aspiration pneumonia and
complications resulting from prolonged recumbency.

DIAGNOSIS
Diagnosis of botulism is primarily based on the history and
suggestive clinical presentation. Due to the dietary origin of the
toxin, multiple cases may occur within one group of animals with a
history of carrion exposure (Video 190.3)

.27-32 The results of

routine investigation (including complete blood count, serum
biochemistry profile, urinalysis, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis) are
usually normal or reflect secondary complications of recumbency
and paralysis. Conscious thoracic radiographs should be performed
to assess for evidence of megaesophagus and secondary aspiration
pneumonia. Definitive diagnosis is based on the demonstration of
botulinum toxin early in the course of the disease, either in blood or
intestinal contents.36
The typical electrodiagnostic feature of botulism is marked
reduction in compound motor action potential amplitude during

motor nerve conduction in the presence of normal nerve conduction
velocity with no evidence of temporal dispersion of the compound
motor action potential (ch. 111).30,37-41 Repetitive nerve stimulation
at low frequency rates (3Hz) may produce a small decrement in
compound motor action potentials.

TREATMENT
Supportive care is the mainstay of treating botulism. Bladder
management is important, as recumbent animals will tend to retain
urine and may develop retention cystitis. All recumbent patients
should be maintained on soft bedding and turned frequently in order
to avoid the development of pressure sores. Physical therapy
(massage and passive range of joint movement) will also help to
maintain joint movement (ch. 256). The animals should also be kept
clean in order to avoid urine scald and contamination of any
pressure sores with fecal material.
Antitoxin is only effective in limiting the severity of the clinical
signs if administered early in the disease course and will not reverse
established weakness or paralysis. If type C antitoxin is available,
then anaphylaxis and other hypersensitivity reactions are possible; a
small subcutaneous or intradermal test dose should therefore first be
administered.

PROGNOSIS
Animals with botulism have the potential for complete recovery with
no long-term deficits if they can be supported through the period of
flaccid paralysis and if secondary complications are avoided. Most
dogs will recover within 2 to 3 weeks (Video 190.4)

. Despite

apparent full recovery, muscle weakness may still be present for up
to a year after recovery.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Tetanus
WHAT CAUSES TETANUS?
Tetanus is caused by the actions of bacteria called Clostridium
tetani. The organism lives as resilient spores in moist, fertile soil;
however, they can survive indefinitely in dusty indoor environments.
Tetanus develops when these spores are introduced into wounds
or via penetrating injuries. Most cases develop after skin wounds, but
infection can follow teething, dental fractures, nailbed infections, or
surgeries such as neutering if the incision becomes infected.
Occasionally, no obvious wound can be found and it is presumed to
have healed. Once in the wound, the tetanus bacteria releases toxins
which attach to nerves in the area and then spreads rapidly around
the nervous system. The main function of the nerves that the toxin
predominantly affects is to calm all other nerves down; when they
don’t work, the other nerves become very excitable and over-active.
The attached toxin is thought to be irreversible and recovery requires
the growth of new nerve terminals, which explains the long duration
of tetanus.
WHAT ARE THE CLINICAL SIGNS (SYMPTOMS)?
Tetanus most commonly affects young large breed dogs and is rare in
cats. Clinical signs can take up to 3 weeks to become apparent from
the onset of infection, although most cases exhibit symptoms within
5 to 12 days. The clinical signs initially can be localized or
generalized, with the former more common in cats. Localized signs
can include focal muscle or leg limb stiffness and this may progress
to involve other areas of the body. Generalized signs include stiff

front and back limbs, an elevated tail and a “sawhorse stance,”
although the animal may become uncomfortable standing. At least
50% of dogs progress rapidly to be unable to stand.
Involvement of the head can lead to spasms of the jaw and throat
muscles, causing a condition called lockjaw and swallowing
difficulties. Involvement of muscles of the face causes erect ears and
a wrinkled forehead and gives the animal a characteristic sneering of
the lips. Severe worsening can cause recumbency, seizure-like
activity, and potentially breathing problems.
HOW IS TETANUS DIAGNOSED?
Your animal’s symptoms are usually sufficient to make a
presumptive diagnosis of tetanus.
HOW IS TETANUS TREATED?
A lot of nursing care is essential for successful treatment of patients
with tetanus. The dog or cat should be isolated in a dark and quiet
environment, with cotton wool balls placed in the ears and kept
comfortable on a soft padded bed. Assistance with feeding and
drinking may be necessary and sometimes requires a special tube to
be placed.
An antitoxin can neutralize any toxin that is still in the
bloodstream although it is not as successful as we would like and it
carries some risk. Antibiotics are essential to kill any bacteria that
are still in the body and any obvious wounds should be thoroughly
cleaned. Some animals will need to be sedated and treated with
muscle relaxants due to the severity of signs.
Most dogs that recover show some improvement within 5 to 12
days, although the disease can be fatal. Abnormal “dream
enactment” can be seen in up to half of recovering dogs which can
have twitching, running, and vocalization during sleep. These
abnormalities can resolve within 6 months.
Simon R. Platt (Athens, Georgia)

CLIENT INFORMATION
Botulism

WHAT CAUSES BOTULISM?
Botulism is caused by a bacteria called Clostridium botulinum which
makes a toxin in rancid food or rotten carcasses of dead animals.
When the toxin is eaten, it is spread around the body in the
bloodstream. The botulism toxin then binds rapidly to nerves mainly
responsible for making muscles move.
WHAT ARE THE CLINICAL SIGNS OF BOTULISM?
Botulism causes dogs to become weak in all 4 limbs within 12 hours
following ingestion of the toxin. It is exceptionally rare in cats. The
legs are considered very “floppy” with no real tone detectable. Some
animals will have a drooping face with a weak jaw and throat. In
severe cases the respiratory muscles may be affected and cause
death.
HOW IS BOTULISM DIAGNOSED?
Diagnosis of botulism is primarily based on the clinical signs and
what happened leading up to them, such as whether there is a
possibility of eating a dead animal recently.
HOW IS BOTULISM TREATED?
Nursing care represents the mainstay of treatment in botulism.
Bladder management is important as recumbent animals will tend to
retain urine and may develop a bladder infection. All recumbent
patients should be maintained on soft bedding in order to avoid the
development of pressure sores and turned frequently. Physical
therapy (massage and passive range of joint movement) will also
help to maintain joint movement. Animals should also be kept clean
in order to avoid urine scald and contamination of any pressure sores
with faecal material.
Antitoxin is only effective in limiting the severity of the clinical
signs if administered early in the disease course and will not reverse
established weakness or paralysis. Animals with botulism have the
potential for complete recovery with no long-term deficits if they can
be supported through the period of weakness and secondary
complications can be avoided. Most dogs will recover within 2 to 3
weeks. Despite apparent full recovery, muscle weakness may still be
present for up to a year after recovery.

Simon R. Platt (Athens, Georgia)

CHAPTER 191: Bartonellosis
Pedro Paulo V.P. Diniz

A C RO N YM S
EDTA ethylenediamenetetraacetic acid
PCR polymerase chain reaction

ETIOLOGY
Bartonella species are Gram-negative bacteria transmitted by bloodsucking arthropods and are capable of infecting many domestic and
wild animals. Most Bartonella species are adapted to a primary
mammalian host where persistent bacteremia may occur without
clinical signs. Cats are the natural reservoirs for Bartonella henselae,
and likely the reservoir for Bartonella clarridgeiae and Bartonella
koehlerae. Dogs are the reservoir for Bartonella vinsonii subsp.
berkhoffii and Bartonella rochalimae. When Bartonella infects an
immunocompromised or incidental host, clinical manifestations are
more frequent.
More than 14 species of Bartonella have been described in dogs or
cats, with most of them also capable of infecting humans.1 In
addition, genetic variants have been reported, including four distinct
genotypes of B. vinsonii subsp. berkhoffii (I-IV), as well as two
serotypes of B. henselae (I and II).1-3 Hosts can be infected with two
or more Bartonella species or strains.4,5 This chapter will focus on B.

henselae and B. vinsonii subsp. berkhoffii as they are the most
frequent species infecting dogs and cats. Clinical manifestations are
not distinguishable among Bartonella species, subspecies, or strains,
with infective endocarditis (ch. 232) being the most diagnosed
condition in dogs and cats.

TRANSMISSION AND RISK FACTORS
Cat fleas (Ctenocephalides felis) are the main vectors of Bartonella
in companion animals, with B. henselae multiplying in the digestive
system of the cat flea and surviving several days in flea feces.6
Several other Bartonella species have been detected in cat fleas by
molecular methods. Bartonella DNA has been detected in Pulex fleas
but their role in natural infection is unclear.3 The role of ticks in the
natural transmission of Bartonella species in dogs and cats is likely,
but not yet confirmed. Indirect evidence from epidemiological and
in-vitro studies suggests that ticks such as Ixodes ricinus and
Rhipicephalus sanguineus may transmit Bartonella spp. among
dogs and cats.7,8 Blood transfusions are also considered a risk factor
for transmission to companion animals and humans.9-11 Other risk
factors for dog exposure to Bartonella species include living in rural
environments, multi-dog households, and outdoor access.1,12
Cats and rodents may also serve as reservoirs for Bartonella
transmission to dogs by sharing infected fleas. Wildlife reservoirs
may play a significant role in the ecology of Bartonella species.
Coyotes, foxes, raccoons, and other mammals can be infected with
the same species of Bartonella detected in dogs and humans.13
Circumstantial case-based evidence also suggests that cats may
transmit Bartonella species to dogs via scratches or bites, as they do
to humans. However, no transmission was detected when infected
cats cohabited with uninfected cats in a flea-free environment.14
Transmission does not occur between bacteremic female and male
cats during mating, or to kittens of infected queens during gestation
or in the neonatal period in flea-free environments.15 Therefore, cat
fleas remain the most relevant risk factor for Bartonella infection.

EPIDEMIOLOGY
Bartonella species have been described on all continents except
Antarctica. Tropical areas tend to have a higher prevalence than
subtropical, but prevalence of infection in dogs and cats varies widely
among regions and countries. Detection of Bartonella infection is
generally more frequent in cats than in dogs, perhaps because cats
can develop higher levels of bacteremia. Overall, the prevalence of
infection in domestic cats ranges from 5-40% and in domestic dogs
1-20% depending upon the diagnostic method used.16-18 Dogs and
cats are commonly subclinically infected with Bartonella spp., with
18-20% of clinically healthy dogs infected with B. henselae or B.
vinsonii subsp. berkhoffii.19,20 Current serologic methods do not
reliably identify active infection with Bartonella spp., with at least
50% of seropositive dogs or cats being negative by molecular
methods.21 Conversely, serologic tests may underestimate the real
prevalence of Bartonella spp. infection in dogs because over half of
infected dogs do not mount a detectable antibody response.1 Younger
cats appear more likely to be bacteremic and older cats to be
seropositive. A similar trend has not been described in dogs.

PATHOGENESIS
Bartonella species are inoculated following a bite or scratch as well
as excreted in the feces of the vector. They primarily invade
endothelial cells to establish persistent infection and are seeded into
the bloodstream at about 5-day intervals. Bacteria invade and
replicate in mature red blood cells without causing hemolysis to
facilitate their acquisition by the vector.22 Experimentally infected
cats maintained relapsing B. henselae or B. clarridgeiae bacteremia
for as long as 454 days.23 Bartonella species disseminate throughout
the body. Disease can occur in a single organ or multiple organs.
Chronic subclinical Bartonella infection may recrudesce after
infection with other vector-borne organisms.24 Signs and lesions
may be associated with 5 intrinsically related mechanisms:
intravascular infection, host immune-mediated response,

pyogranulomatous lesions, lymphatic infection, and abnormal
vascular proliferation (Table 191.1). Due to genetic diversity,
heterologous protection against reinfection is uncommon. Cats
infected with B. henselae 16S rRNA type II were susceptible to
infection with type I.25 Similarly, maternal antibodies against one
strain of B. henselae did not protect kittens from infection with a
different strain.26 Genetic variation makes vaccine development
difficult but is useful in epidemiologic studies.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS AND
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
CANINE BARTONELLOSIS
Heart (chs. 233, 234)
Endocarditis is the most recognized consequence of Bartonella
infection, frequently affecting the aortic valve and causing congestive
heart failure (Figure 191.1; ch. 232).27-33 About 19-28% of dogs
with infective endocarditis have Bartonella infection, with a higher
risk of death when compared to other bacteria. Frequent findings on
physical examination include a heart murmur (89%; chs. 38, 232),
lameness (43%; ch. 177), respiratory abnormalities (28%; ch. 37),
and weakness/collapse (17%; ch. 23). Fever (ch. 16) is common, but
not as frequent in endocarditis caused by Bartonella spp. as with
other bacteria. Endocarditis predisposes to septic thromboembolic
disease (chs. 232, 238), which can cause lameness, recumbency,
anisocoria, obtundation, and other neurologic signs. Cardiac
arrhythmias (ch. 230), secondary to myocarditis (ch. 233), can be
detected in dogs lacking echocardiographic evidence of
endocarditis.32-34 Clinicians should always consider Bartonella
infection in the differential diagnosis of infective endocarditis, as
early therapy may increase survival.
Other Affected Organs
Since other organs may be affected by Bartonella infection, clinical
signs can vary greatly (Table 191.1). In one study, the most common

clinical signs in 47 sick dogs confirmed to be infected with
Bartonella spp. were: fever (40%), lethargy (40%), weight loss
(34%), anorexia (32%), lymphadenopathy (30%), diarrhea (23%),
neurological signs (21%), heart murmurs (21%), respiratory signs
(21%), polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD) (21%), lameness (19%),
vomiting (15%), and splenomegaly (13%).35 Weight loss occurred
more frequently in sick dogs infected with Bartonella spp. than in
dogs suspected to have other vector-borne diseases.36 These signs
are nonspecific and of limited help in distinguishing Bartonella
infection from other causes of vector-borne disease in dogs;
therefore, other vector-borne pathogens should always be ruled out
in any dog suspected to have Bartonella infection.

FELINE BARTONELLOSIS
Clinical signs are much less common in cats than in dogs,
presumably due to bacterial and host adaptations. The most
frequently reported signs or syndromes are fever, lymphadenopathy,
lethargy, uveitis, endocarditis, myocarditis, pyogranulomatous
disease, and reproductive failure (fetal reabsorption and
stillbirth).31,37-40 Endomyocarditis (ch. 234) has been rarely
reported in cats infected with B. vinsonii subsp. berkhoffii or B.
koehlerae.41 Osteomyelitis of the thoracic limb of a cat infected with
B. vinsonii subsp. berkhoffii was described.42 Neurologic signs
(nystagmus, body tremors, focal motor seizures, exaggerated
response to stimuli, behavior changes) were also reported in a few
cats after experimental infection.23 Other signs and syndromes have
been described in cats naturally infected with Bartonella species;
however, the large number of cats bacteremic for these pathogens in
the absence of clinical signs makes it difficult to associate infection
with disease.

DIAGNOSIS
OVERVIEW
The diagnosis of bartonellosis requires a careful and systematic
approach because infected dogs or cats may be apparently healthy or
present nonspecific signs. Unfortunately, positive culture or
polymerase chain reaction (PCR) results do not indicate disease
causation. Consequently, the clinician relies on piecing together
findings from history, physical examination, laboratory, imaging,
and specific diagnostic techniques (Figure 191.2). With lifethreatening illnesses such as endocarditis, myocarditis, and
neurologic disease, the presence of Bartonella spp. should be
investigated while the patient is presumptively treated with specific
antibiotics to improve chances of survival. In all cases of suspected
bartonellosis, other possible causes of disease must be investigated.
An extensive workup should be performed to rule out fungal disease
(chs. 207-211), bacterial (including mycobacterial; ch. 188)
infections, parasites, and neoplastic, genetic, degenerative, or

immune-mediated disorders. Of note, if immunosuppressive therapy
is necessary to address a suspected immune-mediated disease (ch.
227), the clinician should try to rule out concomitant Bartonella
infection, because immunosuppression may facilitate the
development of endocarditis or other Bartonella-related syndrome,
with poor outcome.30,43,44

LABORATORY ABNORMALITIES
Frequently, infected dogs and cats have no hematologic
abnormalities. When present, abnormalities are usually mild and
nonspecific. In one study, the most common laboratory findings
among 47 sick dogs confirmed to be infected with Bartonella species
were: proteinuria (40%), anemia (38%), leukocytosis (36%),
thrombocytopenia (34%), increased serum liver enzyme activities
(32%), hyperbilirubinemia (30%), hyperglobulinemia (26%),
hypoglobulinemia (23%), azotemia (21%), monocytosis (17%),
abnormal coagulation panel (prothrombin time/partial
thromboplastin time; 13%), leukopenia (11%), and lymphocytosis
(11%).35,36 In dogs with Bartonella endocarditis, myocarditis, or
cardiac arrhythmias, other common hematologic and biochemistry
abnormalities include eosinophilia and neutrophilia (rarely
accompanied by left shift).29 In cats, anemia, eosinophilia, mature
neutrophilia, and thrombocytopenia are the most frequently
reported laboratory abnormalities.37,38 Hyperglobulinemia has been
reported in natural infection in cats, but not from experimental
studies.45 Cats with unexplained hyperglobulinemia, particularly
polyclonal gammopathies (ch. 60), should be evaluated for
Bartonella with culture and PCR.

ELECTROCARDIOGRAPHY (CH. 96)
Cardiac arrhythmias (ch. 230) are detected in 9-60% of dogs
infected with Bartonella species. For both dogs (ch. 233) and cats
(ch. 234), arrhythmias are more frequent in endocarditis or
myocarditis, characterized by sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation,
intermittent ventricular premature complexes, ventricular
tachycardia, or third-degree atrioventricular block.29,31,46,47

Bartonella infection.46,48
