MICROSCOPY
Examining blood smears for intraerythrocytic Bartonella spp. is not
effective when using conventional staining methods. This is due to
the small size of the organism, staining characteristics, and the
presence of intermittent bacteremia. Bartonella spp. can be
visualized in tissue specimens stained with modified silver stains
(e.g., Warthin-Starry or Dieterle’s) but other pathogens can also stain
and cannot be differentiated from Bartonella spp. based on
morphology alone.49

SPECIFIC TECHNIQUES
Molecular Diagnostic Methods
Whenever bartonellosis is suspected, clinical specimens
(ethylenediamenetetraacetic acid [EDTA]-anticoagulated whole
blood, serum, plasma, tissues, etc.) should always be collected and
stored at −20°C before antibiotic therapy. Antimicrobials rapidly
decrease the chance of detecting Bartonella spp. Tissue specimens
and non-blood fluids (effusion, synovial fluid, etc.) from affected
organs should be preferentially tested by culture and PCR, as they
may provide better clinical sensitivity than blood samples due to the
cyclic nature of bacteremia.50,51 Molecular diagnostic tests such as
PCR assays are highly sensitive and specific and have a faster
turnaround time than culture. PCR has the added benefit of allowing
the identification of the species and/or strain of Bartonella following
sequencing of the PCR product. The diagnostic value of PCR assays
depends upon the host and the type of specimen tested. Dogs with
Bartonella endocarditis and infected cats generally maintain high
levels of bacteremia; therefore, PCR of EDTA-blood samples often
detects the organism. For other syndromes, dogs generally maintain
very low levels of Bartonella bacteremia (<1 to 10 organisms/mcL),1
that can be below the PCR assay detection limit. Thus, in cases other
than endocarditis, canine blood samples may not be the optimal
diagnostic clinical specimen. Clinicians should keep in mind that, as
for any other blood-borne pathogen, a single negative PCR result
from a blood sample does not rule out infection.

Serologic Methods
High Bartonella serologic titers (>1:512) support a diagnosis of
Bartonella endocarditis.33 However, with other local or systemic
diseases, serology alone is of limited diagnostic value; it
overestimates infection in cats and underestimates infection in
dogs.5,36,38,52 In cats, a negative serologic result indicates a lower
risk of being infected, due to a high negative predictive value.16,17
Species-specific serologic assays for antibodies to various Bartonella
species, genotypes, and serotypes are available but some degree of
cross-reactivity may occur in dogs.16 Conversely, the canine antibody
response was both species-specific and genotype or serotypespecific.53 Therefore, an animal infected with a specific Bartonella
type may not mount a detectable antibody response to other bacterial
types under the same species, which may explain some of the
discrepancies between serologic titers and culture/PCR results.

Culture Methods
Isolation in solid culture media, which may take 4-8 weeks, is the
gold standard for microbiologic detection of Bartonella spp.
However, some wild types of Bartonella do not adapt to laboratory

conditions. As cats generally develop higher levels of bacteremia,
blood culture is indicated for ill cats whose history and clinical
presentation suggest Bartonella infection, but culture should not
replace more sensitive diagnostic methods. On the other hand, blood
cultures from sick dogs generally yield no isolates, unless significant
bacteremia (endocarditis, for example) is present. Often, PCRpositive samples fail to yield cultivable isolates and can only be
characterized based on DNA amplification and sequencing.
A combined approach using enrichment culture coupled with DNA
amplification and sequencing (so-called “enrichment PCR” or
“Bartonella alpha-Proteobacteria growth medium [BAPGM] ePCR”)
is available in the United States∗ 54 to increase the number and
variety of organisms before PCR detection and solid media isolation.
This is one of the most successful diagnostic techniques available,
capable of detecting more infected dogs, cats, or humans than a
single PCR assay from blood.36,55-58 However, similar to serologic
testing and PCR assays, negative results do not rule out infection. In
humans, higher clinical sensitivity was reported when blood samples
were drawn on 3 separate days for a week (so-called “triple draw”)
because of relapsing bacteremia.57 A similar approach may be
considered in dogs and cats suspected to have bartonellosis.

TREATMENT
OVERVIEW
The optimal antimicrobial protocol for the treatment of Bartonella
infections in cats, dogs, or people is yet unknown. While some
antibiotics are effective in vitro, clinical efficacy varies. A growing
body of evidence suggests that the use of antimicrobial monotherapy

cannot adequately prevent Bartonella growth.59 Current
recommendations are based upon limited case series, experimental
studies, clinical experience, and data extrapolated from the human
literature.

CANINE BARTONELLOSIS
Antibiotics
Antibiotic therapy should be reserved for dogs suspected of having
bartonellosis, while apparently healthy dogs with a positive PCR or
culture result should be monitored but not treated. Monotherapy
with doxycycline or azithromycin is no longer recommended because
of treatment failures and risk of rapidly developing antimicrobial
resistance. Long-term therapy with a combination of two antibiotics
with different modes of action, one achieving high plasma
concentrations and the other achieving high intracellular
concentrations is recommended until other antibiotics or antibiotic
combinations are proven more effective (Table 191.2).

Duration of Treatment
The duration of antibiotic therapy required to eliminate Bartonella
species in a chronically infected dog is not known. In general,
antibiotic therapy should be continued for at least 2 weeks after
resolution of clinical signs, but no less than 4-6 weeks depending on
the antibiotic combination. Several months of antibiotic treatment
may be required.60 Frequent monitoring of clinical status, laboratory
abnormalities, and repeated serologic and enrichment PCR tests are
recommended to determine treatment duration. Effective
antimicrobial therapy is supported with antibody titers decreasing
after weeks to several months. Monitoring bacteremia by enrichment
PCR 2 and 6 weeks after completion of antibiotic therapy may also be
used to infer whether microbial cure has been attained. However, it
is unclear if true elimination of the pathogen can be achieved with
any antibiotic regimen.

Timing the Second Antibiotic
If the patient is reasonably stable, the second antibiotic should be
started five to seven days after the first antibiotic, to decrease the risk
of a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.61 The reaction, characterized by

lethargy, fever, and vomiting (signs similar to bacterial sepsis), tends
to occur within the first week after starting antibiotics. It is caused by
the rapid death of bacteria due to adequate intracellular and
intravascular drug concentrations, followed by release of endotoxins
that trigger the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (ch.
128). Clinicians should avoid interrupting antimicrobial therapy or
switching antibiotics based on a suspected adverse drug reaction in
such cases. A short-term course of glucocorticoids at antiinflammatory dosages such as prednisone (dogs: 0.5-1 mg/kg PO
once daily) or prednisolone (cats: 1-2 mg/kg PO once daily) can be
used to alleviate these signs (ch. 227).

FELINE BARTONELLOSIS
Antibiotic treatment of infected but apparently healthy cats is not
recommended, due to risk of rapidly developing antimicrobial
resistance.62 According to panels of specialists in human and
veterinary medicine, there is no general indication for testing or
treating healthy cats for Bartonella infection.63,64 Similar to dogs,
no antibiotic regimen has proven effective in controlled studies with
long-term follow-up in cats. Therefore, current recommendations for
treatment of sick cats suspected to have bartonellosis include the use
of two antibiotics with different mechanisms of action, prolonged
treatment periods, and frequent monitoring (Table 191.3). Serum
antibody titers typically decrease rapidly (3-6 months) and remain
below detection limits in animals responding to treatment.1,38 A
third-generation fluoroquinolone (pradofloxacin) has demonstrated
better antimicrobial activity against human and feline Bartonella
isolates than enrofloxacin.65 While single antibiotic therapy with
pradofloxacin or doxycycline has been described in cats,66,67 it is
unknown if monotherapy eliminates Bartonella infection or
temporarily suppresses bacteremia. Azithromycin should not be used
alone, as resistance may develop quickly.62

PREVENTION
There are no available vaccines to prevent Bartonella spp. infection
in dogs, cats, or humans. Prevention of infection is based on vector
control. Veterinarians should educate clients about the importance of
year-around ectoparasite control for dogs and cats to prevent the
transmission of Bartonella species, as well as other vector-borne
pathogens.63,68

PUBLIC HEALTH CONSIDERATIONS

In people, Bartonella species are an important potential cause of
fever of unknown origin, endocarditis, and encephalitis. The most
recognized manifestation of Bartonella infection in humans is cat
scratch disease, a syndrome characterized by a cutaneous papule or
pustule associated with regional lymphadenopathy ipsilateral to the
inoculation site (Figure 191.5).69,70 Veterinarians and other
professionals with frequent exposure to animals and blood-sucking
arthropods should consider bartonellosis an occupational
hazard56,68,71,72 and take appropriate precautions, including:
wearing personal protective equipment when handling animals
infested with fleas, flea feces, and specimens from sick animals;
avoiding needle-stick injuries; and avoiding animal bites and
scratches.68,71,73 Feline practitioners should utilize feline-friendly
handling practices.63 Direct transmission of Bartonella spp. from
dogs to humans through bites or scratches has not yet been
documented, but dogs should not be allowed to lick open human
wounds, as Bartonella DNA was detected in dog saliva.74,75
Veterinary professionals play an important role in public health
education about the disease and the steps towards minimizing or
eliminating exposure.68 The recommendations to prevent exposure
to Bartonella spp. from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the
Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the Human
Immunodeficiency Virus Medicine Association (HIVMA) of the
Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) include:64
• Immunocompromised individuals should consider the
potential risks of cat ownership.
• Patients who want cats should acquire animals that are older
than 1 year of age and in good health.
• Cats should be acquired from a known environment, have a
documented health history, and be free of fleas.
• Stray cats and cats with flea infestation should be avoided.
• Declawing is not advised but individuals should avoid rough
play with cats.
• Patients should avoid contact with flea feces (i.e., flea dirt), and
any cat-associated wound should be washed promptly with

soap and water.
• Care of cats should include a comprehensive, ongoing fleacontrol program under the supervision of a veterinarian.
• No evidence indicates any benefits to cats or their owners from
routine culture or serologic testing of the pet for Bartonella
infection or from antibiotic treatment of healthy, serologically
positive cats.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Bartonellosis
WHAT IS BARTONELLOSIS?
Bartonellosis is a disease caused by small bacteria called Bartonella,
which are found worldwide. Bartonella can infect dogs, cats, other
animals, and humans. It is mainly transmitted by fleas, and probably
by ticks. Pets with fleas or ticks and with outdoor access have a
higher risk. Bartonella can cause a long-term infection with little
sign of disease until weeks or months later. An uncommon but fatal
manifestation is inflammation of the heart muscle (myocarditis) or
heart valves (endocarditis).
WHAT ARE THE SYMPTOMS OF BARTONELLOSIS?

In dogs, the most common clinical signs are:
• Fever and depression
• Lack of appetite and weight loss
• Swollen lymph nodes
• Increase in urination and thirst
• Cough and difficulty breathing
• “Potbelly” or abdominal swelling
• Swelling and stiffness of joints
• Reddened and sensitive eyes
• Unusual nose bleeds
• Mental confusion, seizures
Cats generally do not show any signs. Some of the findings
suggestive of bartonellosis in sick cats are:
• Fever and depression
• Swollen lymph nodes
• Muscle pain and tremors
• Pregnancy loss and stillbirth
• Inflammation of the eye (uveitis)
• Behavior changes and seizures
Humans should consult their physician if the following symptoms
are seen a week to months after a tick/flea bite or a cat scratch:
• Red, infected spots and sore lymph nodes
• Fatigue (tiredness) and muscle or abdominal pain
• Fever, chills, aching joints, night sweats, shortness of breath
• Headaches, seizures, memory loss, or numbness of hands and
feet
WHAT TESTS ARE NEEDED?
Many tests may be needed to find Bartonella infection in a sick
animal. Repeated testing may be needed as well. A combination of
blood culture and detection of Bartonella DNA is the most sensitive
but may take weeks for results to be obtained. Healthy dogs and cats
should not be tested for Bartonella, as they may carry the organism
and do not require treatment.

WHAT TREATMENT IS NEEDED?
Only dogs and cats with consistent signs and Bartonella infection
confirmed by laboratory testing should receive treatment. Sometimes
treatment needs to last for weeks, and different antibiotics may be
used. Early interruption of therapy increases the risk of multiantibiotic resistance. Tests are needed to confirm that the infection is
gone. Sometimes the bacteria cannot be cleared. During the first
week of treatment, some dogs have a temporary loss of appetite,
fever, and may become lethargic. This can be a reaction to the
bacteria dying and not a drug reaction. Consult with your
veterinarian when any signs occur. Dogs with damaged hearts may
need hospital care.
WHAT IS THE PROGNOSIS?
Depending on how much damage the bacteria has caused and how it
responds to antibiotics, the long-term outlook for health varies from
good to grave. Dogs with heart valve injury have a very poor chance
of recovery.
WHAT CAN BE DONE TO PREVENT BARTONELLOSIS?
For Dogs and Cats: The best way to prevent infection in
companion animals is by avoiding scratches, fleas, ticks, and other
biting insects. Use good flea and tick preventive products all year
round. Currently, there are no available vaccines against Bartonella
infection for dogs, cats, or humans.
Humans: Infected cats can transmit Bartonella to humans by
bites or scratches, but it is unknown if dogs can do the same. Any
bite or scratch wound should be cleaned thoroughly and checked by
a healthcare provider. Do not remove ticks or fleas with bare hands
and avoid letting a pet lick the face or skin wounds of humans, since
Bartonella has been detected in dog and cat saliva. Contact with
stray animals should be avoided. These recommendations are
particularly important for young kids and immunocompromised
patients, such as people who are undergoing chemotherapy, on
immunosuppressive drugs, or with AIDS.
Pedro Paulo V. P. Diniz (Pomona, California)

ETIOLOGY
Leptospirosis is a zoonotic disease of worldwide distribution
affecting most mammalian species.1 It is caused by spirochetes of the
genus Leptospira. Leptospires are thin, elongated, highly motile,
helically coiled organisms which can be differentiated from other
spirochetes by their distinct hooked ends.2 Leptospires have Gramnegative staining properties but phenotypic features of both Gram-

negative and Gram-positive bacteria. The taxonomy of the genus
Leptospira is fairly confusing as serologic and genotypic typing are
often used in parallel. Serologic classification is based on differences
in the carbohydrate component of leptospiral lipopolysaccharide.2
Antigenically related serovars are grouped into serogroups. Over 250
pathogenic serovars have been identified belonging to 24
serogroups.3 Based on comparative genomic analysis, it has been
proposed that the genus Leptospira be divided into 4 subclades,
called P1 (pathogenic), P2 (intermediates), and S1 and S2
(saprophytic).4 Serologic and genotypic classification do not always
concur, in that serovars of one serogroup may belong to different
genomic species. The accepted nomenclature is the name of the
genus, followed by species name, serovar, and then strain (if
appropriate). Genus and species are italicized, with the serovar name
not italicized and with an upper case first letter (e.g., Leptospira
interrogans serovar Australis).

EPIDEMIOLOGY
Leptospires are maintained in the environment by chronically
infected reservoir hosts, which harbor leptospires in their renal
tubules and shed organisms in urine. Small rodents are considered
the most important reservoir hosts but it is likely that a large
spectrum of animals, including dogs, cats, and humans can act as
reservoir hosts.5-7 Hosts become infected either by direct contact
with mucous membranes or broken skin with urine from infected
animals, or indirectly, via contact with contaminated soil or surface
water (Figure 192.1). In contrast to reservoir hosts, which do not
exhibit clinical signs of illness, incidental hosts can develop acute,
severe and potentially lethal disease. Acute infections in dogs were
commonly associated with production of antibodies to the
serogroups Canicola and Icterohaemorrhagiae, but it is now clear
that dogs can be infected with serovars belonging to a wide range of
serogroups, including, but not restricted to Australis, Grippotyphosa,
Pomona, Autumnalis, and Sejroe.8-11

Leptospirosis is seasonal, with peak incidence during warmer
months with links to rainfall or flooding.12 Thus, seasonal patterns of
leptospirosis are dependent on the regional climate.13 Dogs with
access to outdoor water sources and/or exposed to wildlife have a
higher risk of infection.14 Males, herding dogs, hounds, working
dogs, and mixed breeds have been reported to be at increased risk in
the USA.15 While males and younger animals are significantly more
likely to test positive to leptospirosis compared to the general dog
population in some studies,16,17 other studies did not confirm any
sex, age, or breed predispositions.18,19 Veterinarians therefore
should suspect leptospirosis in any dog with suggestive clinical signs
regardless of signalment and lifestyle.

PATHOGENIC MECHANISMS OF
LEPTOSPIROSIS
LEPTOSPIREMIA AND TISSUE INVASION
After entering the host, pathogenic leptospires quickly establish
systemic infection via hematogenous spread. Unlike bloodstream
infections with other Gram-negative bacteria, leptospires do not
cause fulminant septic disease shortly after infection. This has been
attributed to the low endotoxic potential of leptospiral
lipopolysaccharide.20,21 During the initial phase, leptospires evade
host immune responses by binding inhibitors of complement
activation on their surfaces.20,22 Leptospiremia continues until the
host mounts an effective acquired immune response, which clears
the organism from bloodstream and most tissues. Thereafter,
leptospires can persist in “immune-privileged” sites, such as the eye
and renal tubules.23 Leptospirosis is a multi-systemic disease,
primarily affecting the kidneys and liver. Many organs can be
infected, however, including lungs, spleen, endothelial cells,
uvea/retina, skeletal and heart muscles, meninges, pancreas, and the
genital tract. The exact mechanisms by which pathogenic leptospires
cause organ dysfunction and tissue damage are not known. While

vasculitis can be a feature, most human and animal studies have not
consistently identified vasculitis as a primary cause of tissue
damage.24 In a recent study, plasma soluble intercellular adhesion
molecule 1 (sICAM-1), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF),
and angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2), markers of endothelial activation
(sICAM-1) or dysfunction (VEGF; Ang-2), were significantly
increased in dogs with leptospirosis compared to healthy dogs. The
markers did not, however, discriminate between dogs with acute
kidney injury (AKI) secondary to leptospirosis and those with AKI
due to other causes (ch. 300).25

SPECIFIC ORGAN INJURY
The Kidneys
During the acute phase of infection, the predominant renal lesions
are those of an acute interstitial nephritis, with tubular cell necrosis,
apoptosis and regeneration (chs. 300, 302, and 303).26,27 Tubular
lesions are assumed to be caused by direct effects of the organisms
because they are generally associated with their presence.
Leptospiral outer membrane components induce cell damage and
inflammation in tubular epithelial cells in vitro.28 Glomerular
structural and functional abnormalities have been described in both
dogs and experimental animals with leptospirosis.29 Leptospires can
cause a specific hypokalemic non-oliguric form of AKI due to
inhibition of the tubular Na+-K+ ATPase (ch. 68).30 Hyposthenuria
can occur due to an acquired vasopressin resistance of the inner
medullary collection ducts (chs. 53, 282).31

FIGURE 192.1 Transmission cycle of pathogenic
Leptospira spp. Pathogenic leptospires are
maintained in the environment by wild or domestic
reservoir hosts. Incidental hosts become infected
either via direct contact with reservoir hosts or
contaminated soil and surface water. The role of
dogs and cats as reservoir hosts requires further
study.

The Liver
Hepatic lesions described in humans and animals with leptospirosis
include cholestatic hepatitis (with complete or partial liver-plate
disruption; ch. 269), hepatocellular necrosis, binucleation of
hepatocytes, periportal edema with inflammatory cell infiltration,
and proliferation of Kupffer cells along sinusoidal linings.26,27
Hyperbilirubinemia is not correlated with hepatocellular necrosis in
humans.32 Hyperbilirubinemia coincided with the invasion of
hepatic intercellular junctions by migrating leptospires and
subsequent disruption of bile canaliculi in experimentally infected
hamsters.31 In humans, both icteric (more severe and rapidly
progressive) and non-icteric forms of leptospirosis have been
described.33,32 A serum bilirubin of ≥10 μmol/L (≥171 micromol/L;
reference range 0.5-4.0 μmol/L [8.6-68 micromol/L]) was

associated with death or euthanasia in a cohort of 254 dogs with
acute leptospirosis.16

The Lungs
The leptospiral pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome (LPHS) has been
increasingly recognized in humans, dogs, and other species,
becoming a major cause of mortality.16,34 LPHS lung tissue shows
various degrees of intra-alveolar hemorrhage without a marked
inflammatory cell infiltrate or vasculitis (Figure 192.2) (ch. 217).34
Intra-alveolar edema, fibrin, and hyaline membranes, characteristic
of disorders with diffuse alveolar damage such as acute respiratory
distress syndrome (ARDS), can be present, but are not predominant
features.34,35 Few leptospires are observed in affected lung tissue in
immunocompetent hosts and they do not co-localize with the
pulmonary lesions observed.27 Several hypotheses, including
coagulopathies, systemic inflammation, immune-mediated damage,
and direct leptospiral effects, are currently under investigation. It is
likely that the pathogenic mechanisms of LPHS are multifactorial,
with both host and pathogen-related factors playing a role.24 It has
been suggested that introduction of clones with enhanced virulence
might be a contributing factor to the recent emergence of LPHS.3
However, evidence linking seroconversion to a specific serogroup or
serovar with particular clinical manifestations in either humans or
animals is weak.36,37

DIAGNOSIS
CLINICAL FINDINGS IN ACUTE
LEPTOSPIROSIS
The clinical signs of leptospirosis are non specific and usually relate
to renal failure (ch. 300) and/or hepatic injury (ch. 269). The most
common signs in dogs are anorexia, vomiting, lethargy, abdominal
pain, diarrhea, jaundice, dehydration, stiffness, musculoskeletal
pain, fever or hypothermia, dyspnea and tachypnea, weakness and

weight loss.16,29,38-46 Polyuria and polydipsia (PU/PD) are common,
caused by tubular dysfunction or decreased responsiveness of the
inner medullary connecting duct to antidiuretic hormone. Oliguria or
anuria were present in about 30% of dogs with acute leptospirosis in
a referral population.16 In a recent study in a cohort of 298 dogs with
acute leptospirosis from Switzerland, predominant clinical signs
related to disease of the renal (99.6%), hepatic (26%) and pulmonary
(76.7%) systems. Signs consistent with disseminated intravascular
coagulation (DIC) were present in 18.2% of dogs16 (ch. 171). This
study reflects the recent emergence of LPHS as a common
complication in acute canine leptospirosis in some areas in the
world. Isolated hepatic involvement was uncommon in this cohort
but has been described in 14% of dogs diagnosed with acute
leptospirosis by others.46 Other clinical abnormalities include
ventricular tachyarrhythmias (ch. 230), abdominal pain due to
intussusception (ch. 126),47 ocular signs (ch. 13),48 and skin
calcifications (ch. 12).49 In contrast to large animal species,
reproductive disorders in dogs in relation with leptospiral infection
appear to be rare.50

FIGURE 192.2 Lung tissue from a dog affected by
leptospiral pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome.
Extensive intra-alveolar hemorrhage is present in the
absence of significant inflammatory cell infiltrates
(H&E, 400 ×).

CLINICAL FINDINGS IN CHRONIC
LEPTOSPIROSIS
The role of chronic leptospiral infection as a cause of chronic kidney
disease (CKD) in cats and dogs is not fully understood (ch. 301).
Progression of tubulointerstitial nephritis to tubular atrophy and
renal fibrosis has been described in dogs infected with serovar
Canicola and rats infected with serovar Icterohaemorrhagiae.51,52 In
a recent study, cats with kidney disease (acute and chronic) were
more likely to have antibodies against Leptospira spp. and to shed
pathogenic leptospires in their urine than cats without kidney

disease.6 Amplification of leptospiral DNA from liver biopsies of
dogs with chronic hepatitis was unrewarding.53 However, smaller
case series suggest that leptospiral infections can cause chronic
granulomatous hepatitis54-56 (ch. 270). Silver staining,
immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence, fluorescence in situ
hybridization (FISH) or real-time polymerase chain reaction (RTPCR) are used to investigate the presence of Leptospira spp. in liver
tissues of suspected cases.

COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT (CBC),
SERUM BIOCHEMISTRY, URINALYSIS
(UA)
Mild to moderate anemia is present in about half of dogs with
leptospirosis. Anemia can be due to blood loss via the respiratory or
gastrointestinal (GI) tracts or reflect anemia of inflammatory
disease. Hemolysis due to the effect of leptospiral toxins on
erythrocytic membranes appears to be less common in dogs than in
cattle.57 Neutrophilic leukocytosis with a left shift, lymphopenia, and
monocytosis are often present. Mild to severe thrombocytopenia is
common in dogs and can be caused by platelet or endothelial
activation, immune-mediated destruction, or splenic
sequestration.58,59 Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine
concentrations are increased in most dogs, either initially or later in
the course of disease. Hepatic injury as evidenced by increases in the
activity of serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate
aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and
hyperbilirubinemia, almost exclusively occur in conjunction with
azotemia.16 Increases in serum activity of ALP and total bilirubin are
more frequent than increases in serum ALT activity. Electrolyte
abnormalities, such as hypo- and hyperkalemia, hyper- and
hypophosphatemia, hyponatremia, and hypochloremia, are common
in canine leptospirosis and usually parallel the degree of renal and GI
dysfunction. Hypokalemia can occur due to renal and/or GI losses

plus K wasting due to leptospirosis-induced inhibition of Na+-K+ATPase.30
Hemostatic disorders in dogs with leptospirosis vary widely in
severity and are multifactorial in origin. Hypocoagulable conditions
from DIC, failure of coagulation factor synthesis, thrombocytopenia,
thrombocytopathy, and hypercoagulable states associated with
inflammation and renal disease can occur (ch. 171).60 Isosthenuria
is seen in the majority of dogs with leptospirosis, but hyposthenuria
has also been described.29,37,39,42 Glucosuria, hematuria, pyuria and
granular casts can be present (ch. 303). Proteinuria is common and
can be due to glomerular and/or tubular dysfunction.29,61 The width
of leptospires is below the resolution of light microscopy and so
organisms are not typically visible by routine urinary sediment
examination.

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
Radiographic and CT changes in dogs with LPHS have been
described. Early pulmonary changes on radiographs appear in the
caudodorsal parts of the lung fields and range from a mild interstitial
to severe reticulonodular patterns with focal alveolar infiltrates.62
Mild mediastinal and/or pleural effusion can be present.63 The most
common abdominal ultrasound (US) findings include renal cortical
hyperechogenicity, renomegaly, mild pyelectasia, a medullary band
of hyperechogenicity, and mild perirenal fluid accumulation.64,65
Other findings include hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites,
enlargement and hypoechogenicity of the pancreas, thickening of the
gastric and (rarely) intestinal walls, and mild lymphadenomegaly.

CONFIRMING A DIAGNOSIS
Overview
Leptospirosis is a zoonotic disease. Confirmation of a clinical
suspicion of leptospirosis in dogs and cats is important from a public

health perspective. Due to their slow growth and specific growth
requirements, culturing leptospires is difficult. It requires up to 6
months and is not routinely performed by diagnostic laboratories.
Darkfield microscopy to identify intact leptospires in urine (Video
192.1)

has poor sensitivity and specificity, even when performed

on fresh urine. Testing for anti-leptospiral antibodies via the
microscopic agglutination test (MAT) or enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
to detect leptospiral DNA, are currently the most useful diagnostic
tools available for practitioners.

Serologic Testing: Microscopic Agglutination Test
(MAT)
Despite marked limitations, the MAT remains the gold standard test
for confirming acute leptospirosis. The MAT is based on determining
the ability of serial dilutions of patient serum to agglutinate live
leptospiral serovars in vitro. MAT reactivity to a serovar suggests
exposure to a serovar belonging to the corresponding serogroup, but
not necessarily to the serovar tested. The panel of serovars should
ideally be based on antibody prevalence data in the relevant
geographic location, as failure to include the infecting serogroup can
lead to false negative results. MAT results are strongly dependent on
the quality control in the laboratory. There is considerable interlaboratory variability.66 Practitioners are therefore encouraged to
utilize a laboratory that adheres to a proficiency scheme.67 The MAT
has marked limitations with regards to sensitivity, specificity and
repeatability, especially if single titers are interpreted.66,68 Infected
dogs can be antibody-negative in the acute phase of disease due to
the normal delay in appearance of serum antibodies. On the other
hand, non-infected dogs vaccinated with bi- or quadrivalent whole
cell anti-leptospiral vaccines, can have post-vaccinal titers of 1:6400
or higher to both vaccinal and non-vaccinal serovars.69,70 While the
majority of vaccinated dogs have been shown to become antibodynegative by week 15 post-vaccination, vaccinal titers can persist for
12 months in a small percentage of dogs.70

Dogs with consistent clinical signs, vaccinated with a bivalent
vaccine against Canicola and Icterohaemorrhagiae, and a single titer
≥1:800 for 1 or more serogroup(s), are likely to have leptospirosis.
However, it is best to confirm a recent infection by MAT-testing
paired samples, collected 1 or 2 weeks apart. This greatly increases
the sensitivity of the MAT.66,68 Obtaining a sample for a follow-up
titer at the time of hospital discharge can be practical. A fourfold or
greater rise in MAT is highly suggestive of leptospirosis or when a
dog, initially antibody-negative, exhibits a convalescent titer ≥800 to
1 or multiple serovars (Figure 192.3).

FIGURE 192.3 Suggested algorithm for
confirmatory testing in dogs suspected to have
leptospirosis. The interpretation of microscopic
agglutination test (MAT) titers can be particularly
difficult in recently vaccinated dogs, because in these
dogs vaccinal titers cannot be reliably distinguished
from acute infection. In dogs which have received
early antibiotic treatment, a rise in titer can be
blunted due to early eradication of the pathogen.
PCR, Polymerase chain reaction.

Serologic Testing: Point of Care (PoC) Enzyme
Linked Immunosorbent (ELISA) and Lateral Flow

Assays
Detection of anti-leptospiral IgM and/or IgG via ELISA or lateral
flow assay can support early clinical decision making. Several
patient-side assays are commercially available that provide results
within minutes, but suffer the same limitations as the MAT with
regard to the possible absence of antibodies in early infection or their
presence due to recent vaccination.71-74 Initially antibody- negative
animals with a clinical suspicion of leptospirosis should be retested
within a few days. It is advised to use these tests in conjunction with
paired MAT titers.

Serologic Testing: PCR and Molecular Typing
PCR assays for detection of leptospiral DNA can be performed on
blood, urine, or tissue specimens. In experimentally infected dogs,
leptospiral DNA can be found in blood during the first week of
infection and thereafter in urine.75 Because the exact time of
infection is typically unknown in naturally infected dogs, PCR testing
should be performed on both blood and urine, ideally prior to
antibiotic administration. The stability of leptospiral DNA in canine
blood and urine has not systematically been examined. Clinicians are
encouraged to follow their laboratory’s guidelines regarding sample
collection, storage, and shipment. Several PCR assays for diagnosis
of canine leptospirosis have been described, most of them targeting
the lipL32 gene specific for pathogenic Leptospira spp.5,75,76 or 23S
rDNA.77 These PCRs provide no information on the infecting
serovar. However, molecular typing methods have been developed
including multi-locus sequence typing (MLST) and multiple loci
variable-number tandem repeat analysis (MLVA).78,79 These
methods can be applied directly to biological samples without prior
culture and allow for rapid identification of the infecting serovar.
While serovar identification is not crucial to guide treatment
decisions, the knowledge of regionally prevalent serovars is
necessary to select pertinent serovars for inclusion in anti-leptospiral
vaccines.
Diagnostic performance of all PCR assays is not equivalent. PCR
assays validated for human clinical specimens, probably used by

some veterinary diagnostic laboratories, might not perform similarly
when applied to dog specimens.80,81 PCR can be used in conjunction
with MAT in recently vaccinated dogs because previous vaccination
does not lead to positive results.82 In dogs with consistent clinical
signs, a positive PCR on whole blood is suggestive of leptospirosis. A
negative PCR, however, does not exclude the disease.

TREATMENT
Effective treatment of canine leptospirosis consists of appropriate
antimicrobial therapy and supportive care for the different organ
systems involved as outlined elsewhere (chs. 217, 269, 300).
Leptospires are susceptible to a wide range of antibiotics in vitro but
the capacity of antibiotics to completely eradicate infection, in
particular renal carriage in vivo, varies.83 Penicillin and its
derivatives have been shown to reduce leptospiremia but fail to
reliably clear the organisms from the kidney.23,84,85 Doxycycline has
been shown to clear leptospires from blood and organs including
kidneys in rodent models84 and is currently recommended for dogs
with leptospirosis (oral: 5 mg/kg q12h or 10 mg/kg q24h) for 14
days. Unfortunately, doxycycline is not often well-tolerated in the
early treatment of acute leptospirosis due to GI side-effects. In these
dogs, initial therapy with an IV penicillin derivative (e.g., penicillin
G, ampicillin, amoxicillin) is recommended until doxycycline can be
used. Macrolide antibiotics such as azithromycin and thirdgeneration cephalosporins have been assessed in animal models and
have been proposed as alternative treatment in humans who cannot
tolerate doxycycline treatment.85-87
Treatment of LPHS is largely supportive. Radiographic screening
is recommended even in the absence of respiratory signs in order to
detect early lesions and implement precautionary measures that
include avoidance of stress, overhydration, or hypervolemia and
control of systemic hypertension (ch. 236). Depending on the
severity of pulmonary hemorrhage, oxygen therapy and in severe
cases, mechanical ventilation may be required (ch. 123). Based on
the hypothesis of an immune-mediated mechanism of LPHS, the

efficiency of immunomodulatory treatments has been assessed.
Results of small and often not well controlled clinical trials in
humans suggest that immunosuppressive treatment with
methylprednisolone,88 dexamethasone alone or in combination with
desmopressin,89 or plasmapheresis,90 can improve survival in
patients with LPHS. It is not known if immunosuppression is an
effective treatment for LPHS in dogs.
After initial stabilization, renal recovery can continue for several
months. A follow-up study of dogs with leptospirosis indicated that
approximately 50% of the dogs surviving the acute phase of the
disease had impaired renal function more than a year after hospital
discharge.91 Long-term monitoring of renal function is therefore
strongly recommended (ch. 301).
Concurrent infection of other dogs that reside in the same
household can occur, probably following infection from the same
environmental source. Treatment of dogs living with dogs diagnosed
with leptospirosis with doxycycline for 2 weeks is therefore currently
recommended.

LEPTOSPIROSIS IN CATS
Cats can become infected with leptospires, and can shed leptospires
in urine, but clinical signs of acute disease are rare.6,91-97 In
experimentally and naturally infected cats, interstitial nephritis is the
most consistent histopathological finding.92,95,98,99 Cats with kidney
disease (acute and chronic) were more likely to have serum
antibodies against Leptospira spp. and to shed pathogenic
leptospires in their urine.6 The role of healthy cats as reservoir hosts
as well as the role of leptospirosis as a clinical disease in cats
deserves further study.

PREVENTION VIA VACCINATION
Bivalent whole cell vaccines including serovars belonging to
serogroups Canicola and Icterohaemorrhagiae have been available in

Europe since the 1960s.92 These bivalent vaccines confer only partial
or no immunity to heterologous serogroups such as Australis,
Grippotyphosa and Pomona, which have been shown to cause acute
disease in dogs.8 Quadrivalent vaccines that contain not only
serogroups Canicola and Icterohaemorrhagiae, but also
Grippotyphosa and Pomona have been available in USA since 2001.
New vaccines containing serovars to three (Icterohaemorrhagiae,
Canicola, and Grippotyphosa), or four (Icterohaemorrhagiae,
Canicola, Grippotyphosa, and Bratislava) serogroups have been
developed in Europe to increase the spectrum of protection (ch.
185). In a recent case-control study including 469 dogs with AKI
from Switzerland, vaccination with a quadrivalent anti-leptospiral
vaccine which included serogroups Icterohaemorrhagiae, Canicola,
Grippotyphosa and Australis was associated with significantly lower
odds to be diagnosed with leptospirosis.93

PUBLIC HEALTH CONSIDERATIONS
Leptospirosis is a zoonotic disease and humans are at increased risk
of infection if they perform activities that involve animal contact,
such as hunting, abattoir work, dairy farming and veterinary
practice.33 Recreational activities, such as swimming, canoeing,
fishing, potholing, and caving, are also associated with a significant
risk of exposure due to intense contact with water or soil.94,95 Dogto-human transmission of leptospirosis has been suggested by
several authors.96,97 Based on the detection of leptospiral DNA in
canine and feline urine it is likely that both contribute to the
maintenance of pathogenic leptospires in the environment. No antileptospiral antibodies were detected in 13 owners exposed to dogs
with confirmed acute leptospirosis and 78 staff members of a
teaching hospital with a very high leptospirosis caseload.98 However,
the exact risk of exposure of humans by infected dogs and cats is
unknown. Appropriate precautions should be taken when handling
dogs suspected to have leptospirosis. Owners should be informed
that their dog likely contracted leptospirosis through direct or
indirect contact with wild or farm animals, which could represent an

ongoing risk for humans and animals. Owners should be instructed
to wash hands after handling their pet and to wear gloves when
cleaning up urine spills until the course of antimicrobial drug
therapy is completed. Routine household disinfectants should be
used to clean urine spills, and dogs should be taken outside to
urinate in places that are not intensely frequented by humans and
other animals.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Leptospirosis
WHAT IS LEPTOSPIROSIS?
Leptospirosis is a disease caused by infection with pathogenic spiral
bacteria of the genus Leptospira. Transmission of the disease can
occur via direct contact with urine from infected animals, or
indirectly via contaminated soil and surface water. All mammalian
species including humans, domestic and wildlife animals can become
infected; there is evidence that reptiles and amphibians can also
become infected. Leptospirosis is a seasonal disease, with a higher
risk of infection during the warm and humid part of the year, when
conditions for survival of the organism in the environment are
favorable. Larger outbreaks in humans are often linked to flooding.
WHAT ARE THE SYMPTOMS OF LEPTOSPIROSIS?
Infection of dogs with pathogenic leptospires can lead to a wide
range of clinical manifestations from a short febrile illness, to severe
and potentially life-threatening disease characterised by acute renal

failure, hepatic injury and bleeding tendencies. Breathing difficulties
due to bleeding into the lungs can also occur.
Common clinical signs of infection in dogs are:
• Fever
• Loss of appetite
• Vomiting and diarrhea
• Stiff gait, Muscle pain
• Weakness and lethargy
• Decreased (or rarely increased) urine production
• Jaundice
• Discolored urine
• Malodorous breath
• Breathing difficulties
• Bleeding tendencies
• Conjunctivitis
HOW IS LEPTOSPIROSIS DIAGNOSED?
If clinical signs are suggestive of leptospirosis, tests are required to
confirm the diagnosis. These tests either rely on the detection of
leptospiral DNA in blood, urine or tissues or detection of antibodies
against pathogenic Leptospira in blood. Tests relying on the
detection of antibodies in blood may yield negative results in early
infection, when the dog’s immune system has not had time to
produce high concentrations of antibodies. Therefore, testing of a
second blood sample typically taken 1-2 weeks later is necessary to
confirm the diagnosis. Confirmation of a diagnosis of leptospirosis in
dogs is important because of the potential risk of infection of humans
from the same source.
HOW IS LEPTOSPIROSIS TREATED?
If a dog is suspected to have leptospirosis, early antibiotic therapy
may clear the organism from the body and limit the severity of the
damage to the kidneys and liver. In many cases intensive supportive
treatment is required in order to help restore fluid balance and organ
function. Dogs with severe kidney failure may require hemodialysis
treatment until kidney function has improved.
WHAT IS THE PROGNOSIS?

The long-term outlook for health in animals with leptospirosis
depends on the severity of organ damage, the occurrence of
complications and the level of care that can be provided. While
typically the mortality rates of leptospirosis are cited to be around
20%, mortality rates can be as high as 70% if severe complications,
such as bleeding into the lungs, occur. Many dogs will be discharged
from the hospital with moderate impairment of their kidney
function, but in many of them renal function with continue to
improve over the following weeks to months.
WHAT CAN BE DONE TO PREVENT LEPTOSPIROSIS?
Annual vaccination with anti-leptospiral vaccines is an important
preventative measure. Vaccination can occasionally cause mild
reactions (fever, decreased appetite, allergic reactions), but the
benefit of protecting against this potentially life-threatening
infection outweighs the risks of adverse effects.
Leptospirosis is considered the most common infectious disease
transmitted from animals to humans worldwide. Most affected
people in developed countries acquire infection not from dogs, but
from recreational activities involving water, or occupational activities
that involve contact with fresh water, wildlife (especially rodents), or
large domestic animal reservoir hosts. Manifestation of the disease in
humans varies from mild flu-like symptoms with fever to signs of
severe liver, brain, kidney, and lung damage. Owners of infected dogs
should be aware of the risk of transmission and should consult their
physician about the need to take particular precautions. Good
hygiene when handling infected animals and potentially
contaminated soil and water can minimize the risk of transmission.
Simone Schuller (Bern, Switzerland)

OVERVIEW: THE ANAPLASMATACEAE
AND RICKETTSIACEAE FAMILIES
The primary causes of canine ehrlichiosis are the intracellular Gramnegative bacteria Ehrlichia canis, Ehrlichia ewingii, and Ehrlichia
chaffeensis, belonging to the family Anaplasmataceae. Other bacteria
within this family are Anaplasma platys and Anaplasma
phagocytophilum, which cause canine thrombocytic and
granulocytic anaplasmosis, respectively, and Neorickettsia
helminthoeca, the agent of salmon poisoning disease (SPD).
Rickettsia rickettsii, the cause of Rocky Mountain spotted fever
(RMSF), and other spotted fever group (SFG) rickettsiae belong to
the family Rickettsiaceae. The families Rickettsiaceae and
Anaplasmataceae are related through the order Rickettsiales (Table
193.1).
These organisms are transmitted to dogs and cats by arthropod or
trematode vectors (Table 193.2), are maintained in nature through
infection of wildlife reservoir hosts, and can be transmitted by blood
transfusion. Their geographic distribution is restricted to that of
their vectors and intermediate hosts. Several of these pathogens
cause human disease. Dogs, therefore, serve as potential sentinels for
human infection and precautions should be taken to prevent
transmission while handling engorged ticks, blood, and tissue from
dogs with suspected infections. Because of shared arthropod vectors
and/or concurrent exposure to multiple vector ticks, coinfections
with more than one of these pathogens (as well as other vector-borne
pathogens) can occur and may complicate the clinical picture.
Severity of clinical signs depends on the size of the inoculum, host
immunity, and pathogen strain virulence.

EHRLICHIOSIS
EHRLICHIA CANIS

Etiology and Epidemiology
Ehrlichia canis causes canine monocytic ehrlichiosis (CME), a
disease of dogs exposed to ticks worldwide. The organism infects
circulating monocytes and, within its cytoplasm, forms morulae
(Latin for “mulberry”; a cluster of bacteria). Ehrlichia canis is
transmitted by Rhipicephalus sanguineus ticks. Infection has been
reported in dogs from Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas (ch.
9). In the United States (USA), it is diagnosed most frequently in
southern states. However, dogs with chronic subclinical infections
can be transported to nonendemic regions before developing the
condition. Ticks acquire infection by feeding as larvae or nymphs on
infected dogs. Jackals, foxes, and possibly coyotes may also act as
reservoir hosts. The organism is transmitted transstadially but not
transovarially within the tick. No age, breed, or sex predilection for
CME has been clearly documented.
Clinical Signs
Acute Phase
The course of CME is divided into acute and chronic phases,
although discrete phases are not always clinically distinguishable.
Transmission can occur within hours of tick attachment and acute
signs of disease occur 8 to 20 days later. Common vague signs
include lethargy (ch. 10), fever (ch. 16), inappetence (ch. 17), and
weight loss (ch. 18). Replication of the organism in
reticuloendothelial tissues is associated with generalized
lymphadenomegaly and splenomegaly (ch. 182). Ocular and nasal
discharge (ch. 35), peripheral edema (ch. 30), and less commonly,
petechial and ecchymotic hemorrhages (ch. 29) are observed.
Neurologic signs, likely caused by meningeal inflammation or
hemorrhage, include twitching, ataxia, seizures, vestibular signs,
hyperesthesia, and cranial nerve deficits (ch. 242).
Thrombocytopenia (ch. 59) and sometimes mild leukopenia (ch.
58) and anemia (ch. 57) occur 1 to 4 weeks after infection (ch. 176).
Transient proteinuria, which resolves within 6 weeks of infection,
has been reported.1,2 Dogs may recover from the acute phase after 2
to 4 weeks without treatment.

Subclinical Phase
After the acute phase, some dogs remain subclinically infected for
months to years. They may have mild persistent thrombocytopenia.
Organisms may sequester within the spleen and evade host immune
systems through antigenic variation.3
Chronic Phase
“Chronic ehrlichiosis” ranges in severity from mild to lifethreatening, with signs that include lethargy, inappetence, bleeding
tendencies, pallor, fever, weight loss, lymphadenomegaly,
splenomegaly, anterior uveitis (ch. 13), retinal hemorrhage, retinal
detachment, polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD, ch. 53), and edema
(Figure 193.1). Bleeding tendencies are the result of
thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction.4 Cutaneous and
mucosal petechial or ecchymotic hemorrhages, epistaxis, melena,
hematochezia, hematuria, and prolonged bleeding from
venipuncture sites have been reported (ch. 171). Polymyositis may
develop, with muscle atrophy and tetraparesis (ch. 23).5 Secondary
opportunistic infections, including viral papillomatosis, protozoal
infections, and bacteriuria, also occur, although mechanisms of

immune suppression and persistence of E. canis have not yet been
elucidated (Figure 193.2).6
Pancytopenia on a complete blood count (CBC) caused by
hypoplasia of all bone marrow cells typifies the severe chronic form
of ehrlichiosis (ch. 176). Thrombocytopenia and nonregenerative
anemia are common. Moderate to marked granular lymphocytosis
(≤17,000/mcL) and bone marrow plasmacytosis may occur. Some
dogs have a monoclonal gammopathy, similar to that seen with
lymphocytic leukemia or multiple myeloma (ch. 60). Dogs with
well-differentiated lymphocytosis or an otherwise unexplained
monoclonal gammopathy should be tested for E. canis infection.7
Serum chemistry abnormalities include hypoalbuminemia,
hyperglobulinemia, and increased serum alanine aminotransferase
(ALT) and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activities. The
hyperglobulinemia is usually a polyclonal gammopathy. A proteinlosing nephropathy may develop as a result of an immune-complex
glomerulonephritis, possibly associated with azotemia (ch. 302).
Dogs with central nervous system (CNS) involvement may have
increased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein concentrations and cell
counts8 (ch. 109).

Diagnosis

Overview
Detection of morulae within monocytes is diagnostic but not
sensitive for diagnosing monocytic ehrlichiosis. The morulae of E.
canis and E. chaffeensis cannot be discriminated cytologically. In
one study, morulae were found in 2 of 19 dogs with chronic
monocytic ehrlichiosis.9 Diagnosis of ehrlichiosis is usually
confirmed with serology, using indirect fluorescent antibody (IFA) or
enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (ch. 184). Antibodies,
not detected until 7 to 28 days after initial infection, may cause dogs
with acute ehrlichiosis to have negative test results. Retesting should
be performed after 2 to 3 weeks to demonstrate seroconversion. A
positive serum antibody titer for E. canis may occur with previous
exposure. Serology results must be interpreted in the context of the
clinical signs and results of testing for other conditions. Dogs with
chronic E. canis infection in association with clinical signs of disease
typically have extremely high IFA titers, sometimes >1:600,000.
Antibodies may persist despite treatment, suggesting persistence of
the organism.9 Test results do not correlate with severity of
hyperglobulinemia or disease. Serologic cross-reactivity to other
Ehrlichia species occurs, including E. ewingii and particularly E.
chaffeensis. Cross-reactivity to Anaplasma phagocytophilum
antigens can occur but is minor.

ELISA Assays
A variety of ELISA assays detect antibodies to E. canis. A point-ofcare (POC) lateral flow ELISA device detects canine heartworm
antigen and antibodies to E. canis, E. ewingii, Borrelia burgdorferi,
and A. phagocytophilum in serum, plasma, or whole blood (SNAP
4Dx Plus, IDEXX Laboratories, Westbrook, ME) (ch. 184). This test
includes recombinant surface proteins of E. canis and E. ewingii.
Since antigens of E. canis and E. ewingii are combined in a single
spot, a positive result reflects either seroreactivity to E. canis, E.
ewingii, or both. The sensitivity of this assay for detection of
antibodies to E. canis was 97.8% and its specificity 92.3%.10 Other
POC ELISA assays detect E. canis antibodies. One laboratory-based
ELISA assay detects antibodies to E. canis, B. burgdorferi, A.
phagocytophilum and Dirofilaria immitis (Accuplex, Antech

Laboratories). Dogs identified as having E. canis seroreactivity when
screened with ELISA assays that also detect heartworm antigen
should undergo a thorough physical examination (PE), plus a CBC,
chemistry panel, and urinalysis to evaluate for thrombocytopenia,
hyperglobulinemia, and proteinuria. Treating seroreactive clinically
healthy dogs is controversial, since it does not change survival and
has the potential to lead to antimicrobial resistance or adverse effects
of drug therapy (ch. 7).

FIGURE 193.2 Secondary viral papillomatosis in a
dog naturally infected with Ehrlichia canis. Image
courtesy University of California, Davis, Internal
Medicine Service.

Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)
PCR assays are widely available for identifying E. canis infection as
part of “vector-borne pathogen” panels offered by veterinary
diagnostic laboratories (ch. 184). Assay results must be interpreted
in context of history, clinical signs, and serologic assay results. E.

canis DNA can be detected using PCR on blood, lymph node
aspirates, splenic aspirates, or bone marrow. However, sensitivity of
PCR from bone marrow samples can be as low as 25%.9 Thus, PCR
alone is not suitable for screening potential blood donors for
infection but may be useful for confirming infection in the first week
of illness, when serologic assays are often negative.

Treatment
The recommended treatment for CME is doxycycline (10 mg/kg PO
q24h) for 28 days.7 Shorter periods of treatment (e.g., 16 days) may
be effective for dogs with acute CME.11 Most dogs show clinical
improvement within 24 to 48 hours, but those with severe chronic
disease may not respond to therapy or their “cytopenias” may require
several months to resolve. Platelet counts generally improve and
normalize within 2 weeks of therapy. Following therapy, titers may
decline and become negative over 6 to 9 months, but some retain
high titers for years. Treatment for such dogs should be based on
resolution of platelet counts and decreases in hyperglobulinemia.
Hyperglobulinemia may take months to resolve after treatment.
Platelet counts should be reassessed 1 and 3 months after
discontinuing therapy because of potential for relapse or reinfection.
Other illnesses should be considered when dogs fail to respond.
Drugs used with variable success include chloramphenicol,
imidocarb dipropionate, and enrofloxacin.7 Members of the E. canis
genogroup appear to have intrinsic gyrase-mediated resistance to
fluoroquinolones.12 While enrofloxacin therapy may lead to clinical
improvement, it is not recommended. The efficacy of imidocarb
dipropionate is controversial. Intravenous (IV) fluids or blood
products may benefit dogs that are dehydrated or anemic,
respectively (chs. 120 and 124). Use of darbepoetin or granulocyte
colony-stimulating factor could be considered for dogs with severe
chronic ehrlichiosis.13 If thrombocytopenia fails to respond to
doxycycline administration, adding a short course (up to a week) of
immunosuppressive doses of glucocorticoids may be beneficial (ch.
144).

Prevention and Public Health
Significance
Prevention of CME relies on tick control with careful searching for
and prompt removal of attached ticks (ch. 187, Video

187.1).

DNA of an E. canis–like organism has been detected in people with
clinical signs of monocytic ehrlichiosis.14 Appropriate precautions
are indicated when handling engorged ticks, blood, or tissue
specimens from infected dogs.

EHRLICHIA EWINGII
Ehrlichia ewingii has caused granulocytic ehrlichiosis in people and
dogs in North America and, possibly, dogs from Brazil and
Cameroon (ch. 9).15,16 Infection has been mostly identified in the
south-central and southeastern areas of the USA, where exposure is
widespread and E. ewingii is the predominant cause of canine
ehrlichiosis. Like E. chaffeensis, E. ewingii is transmitted primarily
by Amblyomma americanum ticks from the expanding reservoir of
white-tailed deer, likely contributing to the emergence of these
pathogens. Like A. phagocytophilum, E. ewingii infects and forms
morulae within granulocytes. Infection causes fever, headache, and
cytopenias in people. Dogs may be subclinically affected or may
exhibit lethargy (ch. 10), anorexia (ch. 17), vomiting (ch. 48),
diarrhea (ch. 49), fever (ch. 16), a neutrophilic polyarthritis (chs.
32, 177), or neurologic signs (chs. 14, 242). Persistent subclinical E.
ewingii infection lasting more than a year has been reported in
laboratory and naturally-infected dogs, supporting their possible
status as a reservoir.17 Laboratory abnormalities include anemia (ch.
57), mild leukopenia or leukocytosis (ch. 58), thrombocytopenia
(ch. 59), hyperglobulinemia (ch. 60), and increased serum ALP
activities (ch. 65).
Ehrlichia ewingii has yet to be cultivated. Antibodies to E. ewingii
can be detected using a POC lateral flow ELISA device (SNAP 4Dx
Plus, IDEXX Laboratories, Westbrook, ME) with a sensitivity and
specificity for detection of E. ewingii antibodies, as compared with a

plate ELISA, of 96.5% and 93.9%, respectively.10 Granulocytic
morulae are commonly detected in blood smears and synovial fluid
from affected dogs. Ehrlichia ewingii–specific PCR assays provide
the only method for confirming infection. Treatment with
doxycycline for 2 to 4 weeks results in rapid clinical improvement
and may be sufficient to eliminate infection.

OTHER EHRLICHIA SPECIES
Ehrlichia chaffeensis causes human monocytic ehrlichiosis in North
America, characterized by fever, headache, myalgia,
thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and increased liver enzyme activities.
In the USA, human monocytic ehrlichiosis occurs primarily in the
south-central, southeastern and mid-Atlantic states; the areas
inhabited by A. americanum and their white-tailed deer reservoir.
Experimental infection of dogs with E. chaffeensis results in
subclinical infection or prolonged fever, mild anemia, leukopenia,
and/or thrombocytopenia.18 Naturally infected dogs can have
lymphadenopathy and/or epistaxis.19 Dogs maintain high antibody
titers and are PCR-positive for months after infection, supporting
their role as a reservoir.18 As with E. canis infection, diagnosis of E.
chaffeensis infection may be made using acute and convalescent
serology or PCR. Serologic cross-reactivity can occur with other
Ehrlichia species (ch. 184). Although clinical improvement occurs
following doxycycline therapy, doxycycline may not completely
eliminate infection.19 Treatment for a minimum of 28 days is
suggested. Other Ehrlichia species detected include Ehrlichia muris
subsp. eauclairensis in dogs from the upper Midwest,20 Panola
Mountain Ehrlichia in a dog from North Carolina,21 and an Ehrlichia
ruminantium–like organism in dogs from South Africa.22
Importance of these infections is unknown.

ANAPLASMOSIS

ANAPLASMA PHAGOCYTOPHILUM
Etiology and Epidemiology
Anaplasma phagocytophilum is the cause of canine granulocytic
ehrlichiosis, infects various domestic and wildlife host species and is
an important emerging pathogen in people worldwide. Clinical
infections have been documented in dogs, horses, cats, and people.
In Europe, infections also occur in domestic ruminants (sheep,
cattle, goat). Different strains of A. phagocytophilum exist
worldwide and these differ in their host tropism and virulence.
Anaplasma phagocytophilum forms morulae in neutrophils and less
frequently in eosinophils (Figure 193.3). Anaplasma
phagocytophilum is spread by several Ixodid tick species and is
transmitted only transstadially within ticks (Table 193.2). Ticks
must be attached for 24 to 48 hours for transmission. Ixodes
scapularis is the vector in the upper midwestern and northeastern
USA and southeastern Canada. Ixodes pacificus is a vector on the
west coast of North America. In Europe and the United Kingdom, the
vector is Ixodes ricinus. Ticks (commonly Ixodes persulcatus)
infected with A. phagocytophilum infection have been detected in
Asia and Russia.23 Ticks with molecular evidence of A.
phagocytophilum have been noted in the Middle East, South Africa,
and South America (ch. 9). Small mammals, including mice,
woodrats, chipmunks, voles, shrews, and deer, serve as reservoir
hosts for A. phagocytophilum. Because B. burgdorferi is transmitted
by the same Ixodid ticks, coinfections are frequently detected and
together, their pathogenicity is enhanced (ch. 187). In the upper
midwest and northeastern USA, infection is most common from
spring to early summer and in the fall. Labrador and Golden
Retrievers account for half of reported cases, possibly reflecting their
popularity for outdoor activities.24 The median age of infected dogs
in one study was 8 years, although dogs of all ages are at risk.24
Clinical Signs
Infection is subclinical in many dogs. When seen, signs occur after
an incubation period of 1 to 2 weeks and often are nonspecific: fever
(ch. 16), lethargy (ch. 10), inappetence (ch. 17), scleral injection,
lameness (ch. 31), stiffness, and reluctance to move (ch. 31). An

infrequent soft nonproductive cough (ch. 34) may be noted. Mild
lymphadenomegaly, splenomegaly (ch. 182), and/or neutrophilic
polyarthritis (ch. 177) may occur. Less common signs include
PU/PD, vomiting, diarrhea, CNS signs (abnormal placing reactions),
and cervical pain.24,25 Infection appears to be self-limiting in dogs
since chronic disease (>30 days) has not been described.
Thrombocytopenia (ch. 59) is documented in >80% of infected
dogs. Less common abnormalities include lymphopenia,
eosinopenia, or mild nonregenerative anemia. Serum chemistries
may reveal hypoalbuminemia and mild to moderately increased
activities of serum ALT and ALP.

FIGURE 193.3 Anaplasma phagocytophilum
morula within a neutrophil from a dog with
granulocytic anaplasmosis. Image courtesy
University of California, Davis, Internal Medicine
Service.
Diagnosis and Treatment
The finding of morulae within neutrophils in an endemic area is
highly suggestive of infection with A. phagocytophilum, although
their morulae cannot be distinguished from those of E. ewingii
(Figure 193.1). Morulae, when present, are found in 7 to 37% of
circulating neutrophils.24 Diagnosis can also be accomplished using
acute and convalescent phase serology using IFA or ELISA assays. A
POC lateral flow ELISA device (SNAP 4Dx Plus, IDEXX
Laboratories, Westbrook, ME) can also be used to detect antibodies
to A. phagocytophilum, with a reported sensitivity of 92% and

specificity of 89% when compared with IFA.26 However, many
acutely ill dogs with granulocytic anaplasmosis have negative
serologic test results because they have not had sufficient time for an
antibody response when first brought to a veterinarian. Further,
positive titers may reflect previous subclinical exposure (within 8 to
10 months) so demonstration of a fourfold rise in titer is required.
With all current serologic assays, serologic cross-reactivity with other
Anaplasma species, especially A. platys and possibly other Ehrlichia
species, can occur. PCR on whole blood (usually as part of a panel
designed to simultaneously test for multiple vector-borne pathogens)
can be used to identify infection in acutely ill dogs and allows A.
phagocytophilum to be distinguished from E. ewingii when morulae
are seen in granulocytes. The treatment of choice for granulocytic
anaplasmosis is a 2-week course of doxycycline (5 mg/kg PO q12h).
Most dogs show rapid improvement, with signs abating within 12-48
hours. Prevention relies on tick control.
Public Health Significance
Anaplasma phagocytophilum causes human granulocytic
anaplasmosis, a febrile disease that resembles the disease in dogs.
Death is rare but can be a result of complications due to secondary
infections. Dogs are an important sentinel for human infection and
may be a source of infection by bringing infected ticks into contact
with humans. Precautions should be taken when handling blood or
tissue from infected dogs, or during tick removal.

ANAPLASMA PLATYS
Anaplasma platys, the cause of canine thrombocytic anaplasmosis,
is yet to be cultured. Rhipicephalus sanguineus is the likely vector,
although attempts to transmit infection using this tick were
unsuccessful.27 The organism has been reported from South
America, Australia, Asia, Africa, Europe, and North America (ch. 9).
Thrombocytopenia occurs after an incubation period of 1 to 2 weeks
and then normalizes within days. Morulae within platelets may be
seen in blood smears shortly after infection and in megakaryocytes
within bone marrow aspirates.28 The majority of infections reported

in the USA have been mild or subclinical. Cases from Europe and
South America have had more severe clinical manifestations,
including fever, splenomegaly, and hemorrhage. However,
coinfection with other tick-borne pathogens may have contributed to
clinical signs. Diagnosis is based on visualization of morulae within
platelets together with acute and convalescent phase serology.
Because of cross-reactions with A. phagocytophilum, serology is not
specific for A. platys. Anaplasma platys–specific PCR assays have
been developed. Treatment of canine thrombocytic anaplasmosis is
as for granulocytic anaplasmosis. Persistent human infection with A.
platys has been documented.29 The extent to which A. platys can
cause disease in humans is unknown.

NEORICKETTSIOSES
NEORICKETTSIA HELMINTHOECA (SALMON
POISONING DISEASE [SPD])
Etiology and Epidemiology
Neorickettsia helminthoeca causes SPD, a condition diagnosed from
the western slopes of the Cascade Mountains of northern California
to southern Vancouver Island, Canada (ch. 9). Disease may occur
elsewhere following transportation of infected fish for feeding or in
dogs that travel to a site containing infected fish. A similar disease
has been noted in Brazilian dogs.30 The vector of SPD is
Nanophyetus salmincola, a fluke that harbors the organism
throughout its life cycle. Fluke eggs transform into miracidia, which
infect small snails, Oxytrema silicula, that live in both fresh and
brackish stream water. Cercariae leave the snail and penetrate a fish,
most commonly a salmonid fish, although certain nonsalmonid fish
can also be infected. Hatchery-reared fish can be infected. The
cercariae transform into metacercariae, usually within the kidneys
but also in the muscle and other tissues. Fish may retain the
infection for several years. Dogs become infected with the rickettsia
after ingesting parasitized fish. Following ingestion, the
metacercariae transform into adult flukes. Labrador Retrievers and
intact male dogs are overrepresented, but dogs of either sex and of

any age or breed may be affected.30 Foxes, coyotes, and captive bears
may become infected.31 Domestic cats are not susceptible to SPD,
but the flukes mature to adults within their intestines. SPD may also
be acquired after ingesting adult flukes (potentially following
coprophagy), infected snails, or fluke eggs.32
Clinical Signs
After maturation, flukes attach within the intestinal tract.
Neorickettsia helminthoeca infects and replicates within cells of the
mononuclear-phagocyte system. Rapid dissemination of the
organism to the lymph nodes, spleen, liver, lungs, and brain occurs.
After an incubation period of 5-33 days, early clinical observations
include anorexia (ch. 17) and fever as high as 42°C (107.6°F) (ch.
16). Later signs include lethargy (ch. 10), weight loss (ch. 18),
vomiting (ch. 48), diarrhea (ch. 49) with or without blood (ch.
50), and mild to severe lymphadenomegaly. Rarely, vomiting and
diarrhea are absent. The presence of adult flukes may contribute to
the gastrointestinal signs. Dogs lacking peripheral
lymphadenomegaly often have abdominal lymphadenomegaly on
ultrasound examination. Associated laboratory abnormalities include
neutrophilia, sometimes a mild to moderate left shift, lymphopenia,
and monocytosis. Thrombocytopenia occurs in about 90% of affected
dogs and may be as low as 16,000/mcL. Serum chemistry
abnormalities include hyponatremia, hypokalemia, increased liver
enzyme activities, and hypoalbuminemia, which can be profound and
sometimes accompanied by hypocholesterolemia and
hypoglobulinemia.30
Diagnosis
Diagnosis of SPD may be inferred by finding characteristic
trematode eggs in the feces using sedimentation or sugar flotation
(Figure 193.1) (ch. 80). Eggs appear 5 to 8 days after infected fish
ingestion. A combination of fecal sedimentation and centrifugal
flotation increases the sensitivity for detection of fluke ova. In one
study, 93% of dogs with SPD tested positive for N. salmincola ova
using a combination of fecal flotation and fecal sedimentation.30 The
finding of fluke ova on fecal examination may not be diagnostic of

SPD, as dogs may be infected with trematodes that do not harbor the
rickettsia, and ova may be shed for months after recovery.
Nevertheless, N. salmincola ova were detected in only 0.2% of over
1800 fecal flotations in dogs seen at a teaching hospital in an
endemic area, and all positive test results were in dogs suspected to
have SPD. Thus, specificity of fecal flotation is high.30 Neorickettsiae
may also be visible using cytologic examination of lymph node
aspirates (Figure 193.4), together with moderate to marked
histiocytic inflammation and lymphocytic-plasmacytic reactivity (ch.
88). Organisms may appear as granular to amorphous material
filling infected cells, best visualized using Giemsa stain. PCR-based
assays can also be used on lymphoid tissue to identify infection.30
Treatment and Prevention
The treatment of choice is doxycycline. Parenteral administration of
a tetracycline may be necessary in vomiting dogs. In addition,
supportive therapy using fluids, blood products, and antiemetics may
be necessary. Praziquantel should also be administered to treat the
helminth infection (ch. 142). Prevention involves feeding only
thoroughly cooked fish. Freezing fish for 24 hours also effectively
destroys the metacercariae and rickettsiae.

FIGURE 193.4 Neorickettsia helminthoeca within
macrophages in a lymph node aspirate from a dog
with salmon poisoning disease. Image courtesy
