Service.

NEORICKETTSIA RISTICII
Neorickettsia risticii is the cause of Potomac horse fever. The life
cycle of this organism likely involves the trematode vector,
Acanthatrium oregonense.33 The fluke miracidia infect aquatic
snails (Juga spp.) and parasitize caddisflies. Horses may become

infected following accidental ingestion of infected caddisflies
containing metacercariae. Neorickettsia risticii has been identified
using culture and PCR in dogs with signs mimicking ehrlichiosis
from the western and southwestern USA.34 The dogs were
seroreactive to N. risticii antigens using IFA. Further studies are
required to determine the significance of this organism in dogs and
cats.

TICK-BORNE RICKETTSIOSES
GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS
Rickettsia rickettsii, the cause of Rocky Mountain spotted fever
(RMSF), belongs to the Rickettsiaceae, a family that contains a
number of pathogenic and nonpathogenic Rickettsia species. Many
novel species have been characterized with molecular methods.
Clinical signs in humans infected with rickettsias include fever,
lymphadenopathy, headache, eschar formation (tissue slough), and
rash. Formation of an eschar at the inoculation site does not usually
occur in RMSF. The ability of novel Rickettsia species to cause
disease in dogs and cats, and the role of dogs and cats as reservoirs,
require further study. Tick-borne SFG rickettsiae cause disease after
infecting vascular endothelial cells and increasing microvascular
permeability.35 Organisms inhibit apoptosis, favoring rickettsial
growth. Widespread endothelial injury is associated with production
of proinflammatory cytokines and activation of the coagulation
cascade without disseminated intravascular coagulation.35

ROCKY MOUNTAIN SPOTTED FEVER
(RMSF)
Etiology and Epidemiology
RMSF is a severe, life-threatening illness of humans and dogs caused
by Rickettsia rickettsii , most commonly diagnosed in south-central
and south-eastern USA (ch. 9). It also occurs in Central America and
parts of South America (Brazilian spotted fever). Approximately

2000 cases of RMSF are reported annually in people in the
USA.36 Rickettsia rickettsii is transmitted primarily by Dermacentor
ticks in North America, although transmission by R. sanguineus
occurs in Arizona.37 The American dog tick (Dermacentor
variabilis) is the primary vector in the south-eastern states, and the
Rocky Mountain wood tick (Dermacentor andersoni) transmits the
rickettsia in the Rocky Mountain region and Canada (Table 193.2).
Rhipicephalus sanguineus and Amblyomma spp. ticks have been
implicated as vectors in Central and South America,
respectively.38,39 It is transmitted transstadially and transovarially
within ticks. Uninfected larvae and nymphs can become infected
when they feed on wild mammals, such as ground squirrels. In the
USA, most cases occur between March and October. In humans, the
highest incidence has been reported in Caucasian males <10 years
and 40-64 years of age.38 Most cases originate from rural or wooded
areas. Exposure to dogs is a risk factor.40,41 The disease occurs
sporadically, but may cluster in small geographic regions. Rarely,
familial clusters occur, sometimes including the family dog.42 A
history of a tick bite is present in <70% of infected people and is even
less common in dogs.43

Pathogenesis and Clinical Signs
Following tick attachment, a reactivation period of 4 to 24 hours is
necessary before transmission occurs. Disease in humans and dogs
requires incubation periods of 2 to 14 days (mean: 7). Common
nonspecific signs include fever (ch. 16), lethargy (ch. 10), anorexia
(ch. 17), and lymphadenopathy. Extreme headaches may occur early
in the course of human illness and can be accompanied by myalgia,
vomiting, anorexia, and abdominal pain.38 Early RMSF is often
misdiagnosed as a viral illness in humans.38 About 60-70% of
infected people, within 2 weeks of the tick bite, have the
characteristic triad of rash, fever, and headache. The rash initially
appears as small macules on the wrists and ankles and spreads to
involve the arms, legs, and trunk, eventually becoming
maculopapular with central petechiae.38 Dogs may develop edema

and erythema of extremities, including the lips, muzzle, scrotum,
penile sheath, pinnae and, rarely, the ventral abdomen (ch. 30).43
Continued tissue damage may lead to necrosis and gangrene,
requiring amputation in some. Stiffness and reluctance to walk may
be apparent. Ocular manifestations include conjunctivitis,
mucopurulent ocular discharge, scleral injection, uveitis, hyphema,
iridal and retinal hemorrhage, and retinal edema (ch. 13).44
Petechial and ecchymotic hemorrhages have been noted (ch. 29).
Epistaxis, melena, and hematuria may occur in severely affected dogs
(ch. 171). Neurologic signs (ataxia, tremors, vestibular signs,
hyperesthesia, opisthotonus, seizures) have been reported in up to
80% of dogs with RMSF (chs. 14, 242).39,43 Other signs include
respiratory distress and cough due to pulmonary edema, cardiac
arrhythmias due to myocarditis, hepatomegaly, icterus, and acute
kidney injury (ch. 300). Death can result from progressive
neurologic signs, acute oliguric renal failure, or cardiovascular
collapse and shock. Death is reported in 2-10% of humans, although
a study from Mexico reported a mortality rate of 22% in children.41
The median time from onset of illness to death is only 8 days,
making early recognition and treatment crucial. Laboratory
abnormalities include leukocytosis, sometimes with a left shift,
anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Serum chemistry abnormalities may
include increased liver enzyme activities and creatine kinase
concentrations, hypoalbuminemia, and electrolyte disturbances. In
severe cases, azotemia and hyperbilirubinemia are noted.
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis may reveal increases in protein
concentrations (usually <100 mg/dL), neutrophil and mononuclear
cell counts (chs. 109, 242).39 Neutrophilic polyarthritis has been
documented using synovial fluid analysis (chs. 31, 71, and 177).
Thoracic radiography may reveal an interstitial pulmonary pattern.

Diagnosis
Antibody detection using microimmunofluorescence is the serologic
reference method, but ELISA assays are also used (ch. 184). Wide
antigenic cross-reactions exist among pathogenic and nonpathogenic
SFG rickettsiae. Thus, positive titers are not specific for R. rickettsii

infection. Because antibodies are generally not detectable until 7 to
10 days after disease onset, a fourfold rise in IgG titer using acute
and convalescent phase sera is necessary to confirm recent infection.
A single titer exceeding 1:1024 is also considered diagnostic of recent
infection, if associated with clinical signs. Given the acute nature of
RMSF, serology is of limited usefulness for early diagnosis.
Direct immunofluorescence or immunoperoxidase staining of
infected tissues, including biopsies of affected skin, can be used to
detect R. rickettsii antigen in tissue early in the course of disease or
at necropsy, with a specificity and sensitivity of about 75%.45-47 PCR
assays for R. rickettsii can be used on blood or tissue. The number of
circulating rickettsiae is generally low with poor PCR sensitivity.48,49
Use of PCR together with immunohistochemistry on skin biopsy
specimens in acute disease improves laboratory confirmation of
RMSF (ch. 83). Real-time PCR assays that differentiate between
SFG rickettsiae that infect dogs are available. Rickettsia rickettsii has
been classified as a biosafety level-3 agent, and cultivation requires
special facilities and is not routine. Laboratory-acquired infections
have been reported.

Treatment
Doxycycline, recommended for RMSF, causes rapid (12-24 h) clinical
response. Other tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, and
fluoroquinolones are effective.50,51 Treatment should be continued
for at least 7 days. Parenteral antimicrobial drug therapy may be
needed if vomiting or neurologic signs are present. Treatment delays
have been correlated with more severe disease and increased
mortality in humans. Treatment should not be delayed while
awaiting results of diagnostic testing. Other supportive therapy may
be required for dogs in shock, including IV fluids and blood products
(ch. 120). Care may be required to avoid pulmonary or cerebral
edema if giving IV crystalloids. Residual neurologic signs, renal
insufficiency or cutaneous scarring may persist despite treatment,
especially if treatment is delayed.

Prevention

Natural infection is followed by development of solid immunity.
Reinfection has not been documented in naturally infected dogs.
Prevention relies on tick control (see above). Prophylactic antibiotic
administration is not indicated to prevent RMSF after a tick bite, as
this only appears to delay onset of illness.38

Public Health Aspects
Dogs are important sentinels for human infection with R. rickettsii.
Recognition of the disease in dogs has contributed to prompt
diagnosis and treatment of RMSF in humans interacting with those
dogs. Veterinarians that manage dogs with RMSF should educate
their clients about their potential for infection and should contact
human health care providers should humans become ill in
association with canine disease. Dogs may carry unattached infected
ticks, which may subsequently attach to people. People may become
infected through improper removal of attached ticks from their dogs.
Guidelines for safe removal of ticks have been published (Video 187.1
) (https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/removing_a_tick.html).52
Ticks should be lifted from the skin using fine forceps. Gloves should
be worn. Hands should be washed with soap and water after
removal. The skin should be thoroughly examined for attached ticks
after these activities.

FELINE RICKETTSIAL DISEASE
Cats are rarely infected with rickettsial agents. The DNA of E. canis–
like organisms has been detected in cats from North America,
Europe, and South America. One of three North American cats
showed signs of polyarthritis, two had cytopenias, none was
seroreactive in an IFA assay using E. canis antigens.53 Ehrlichia-like
morulae have been identified in mononuclear cells in cats from the
USA, Kenya, France, Brazil, and Thailand. Clinical signs have
included fever, lethargy, anorexia, pallor, and splenomegaly,
although some had coinfections with hemoplasmas or retroviruses.
The most consistent laboratory abnormalities in infected cats have
been nonregenerative anemia and hyperglobulinemia. Many infected

cats respond rapidly to treatment with doxycycline. Cats infected
with monocytic ehrlichiae should be treated with doxycycline at 10
mg/kg PO q24h for a minimum of 28 days.7
Several case series of cats with suspected or proven A.
phagocytophilum infection have been described from Europe and
the USA, with diagnosis based on cytologic evaluation of morulae
within circulating granulocytes with or without PCR confirmation.54
Clinical abnormalities included lethargy, anorexia, fever, pallor,
epistaxis, hyperesthesia, lameness, lymphadenopathy,
hepatomegaly, ataxia, vomiting, and thrombocytopenia. Signs in cats
infected with A. phagocytophilum resolve following treatment with
doxycycline.55

INTRODUCTION TO THE HEMOPLASMA
SPECIES
The hemotropic mycoplasmas (hemoplasmas) are small (0.3-1
micrometers) wall-less bacteria that live on the surface of the
erythrocyte (red blood cell) membrane (Figure 194.1). They infect a
variety of hosts worldwide (ch. 9) including cats, dogs, rodents, pigs,
cattle, horses, bats and beetles. Humans have been infected with
novel hemoplasma species,1,2 as well as species that may have
originated in cats3 or dogs,4,5 raising the possibility of zoonotic
infections.

Initially the hemoplasmas, then members of the genus
Haemobartonella, were classified as rickettsial organisms, but gene
(mainly 16S rRNA-based) sequencing analysis and phylogenetic
studies resulted in their reclassification within the genus
Mycoplasma. Though similarities between the hemoplasmas and
mycoplasmas are recognized, such as the absence of a cell wall and
small (including genome) size, hemoplasmas’ niche environment in
blood differs from that for Mycoplasma species, which commonly
colonize mucosal surfaces of respiratory and urogenital tracts. It has
been proposed that hemoplasmas should reside in the family
Mycoplasmataceae but in a separate genus from Mycoplasma
species.6
Five main characterised hemoplasma species infect cats and dogs
with varying pathogenicity (Table 194.1); Mycoplasma haemofelis,
‘Candidatus Mycoplasma haemominutum’ and ‘Candidatus
Mycoplasma turicensis’ in cats and Mycoplasma haemocanis and
‘Candidatus Mycoplasma haematoparvum’ in dogs. Additionally, ‘Ca.
M. turicensis,’7 ‘Ca. M. haemominutum,’7-9 and a species similar to
the latter,10 have also been detected occasionally in dogs, as has the
ovine Mycoplasma ovis,11 the bovine ‘Candidatus Mycoplasma
haemobos’12-14 and the porcine Mycoplasma suis.15 A ‘Ca. M.
haematoparvum’-like organism has also been reported in 2 studies
on cats.16,17 The clinical importance of these additional hemoplasma
species in dogs and cats remains unclear.

PREVALENCE AND RISK FACTORS FOR
INFECTION
VARYING PREVALENCES
Prevalence studies for feline and canine hemoplasma species,
performed worldwide, have had varied results (Table 194.1). The
cats and dogs sampled in these studies have varied enormously, from
healthy to anemic patients or retrovirus-infected cats, and from
client-owned indoor only cats to outdoor feral cats or fighting dogs.
These factors contribute to the variation in reported prevalence as

well as the different risk factors identified for infection. Additionally,
geographic variation in prevalence exists. Different polymerase chain
reaction (PCR) methods, with likely differing sensitivities and
specificities, also likely contribute to the variation.

FELINE HEMOPLASMAS
‘Ca. M. haemominutum’ is the most common species (Table 194.1);
with infection prevalences ranging from 4.4-46.7% (median 15.5%) of
cats. Reported prevalences for M. haemofelis range from 0.4-27.0%
(median 5.1%) and for ‘Ca. M. turicensis’ from 0-26.0% (median
1.9%). Variable numbers of cats infected with more than one
hemoplasma species were also reported in different studies. ‘Ca. M.
turicensis’ infected cats are often co-infected with another
hemoplasma species, particularly ‘Ca. M. haemominutum.’

FIGURE 194.1 Scanning electron
photomicrography showing Mycoplasma haemofelis
as a rounded organism within an indentation on the
surface of erythrocytes in an infected cat (×1000).
In many studies, feline hemoplasma (especially ‘Ca. M.
haemominutum’) infections were more common in male, older, nonpedigree cats with outdoor access. Some studies have shown
associations between hemoplasma infection and positive retroviral
status (particularly feline immunodeficiency virus [FIV]) and
between hemoplasma infection and anemia or being unhealthy.

CANINE HEMOPLASMAS
Reported hemoplasma prevalences in dogs also vary widely in
different studies (Table 194.1); generally M. haemocanis is more
prevalent, ranging from 0-48.6% (median 6.9%) but occasionally

‘Ca. M. haematoparvum’ is more common, with 0-33.3% of dogs
infected (median 1.5%). Geographic variation is marked, possibly due
to the presence of the proposed canine hemoplasma tick vector
Rhipicephalus sanguineus.18,19 Ticks are often identified as risk
factors for canine hemoplasma infection. In contrast to cats, age and
sex are less commonly associated with infection. Fighting dogs have
been associated with hemoplasma infection. Associations may exist
between canine hemoplasma infections and vector borne
infections,20 particularly Babesia spp. (notably Babesia vulpes and
Babesia gibsoni; ch. 197).21-23

PATHOGENESIS OF INFECTION
FELINE HEMOPLASMAS
M. haemofelis is the most pathogenic hemoplasma species in cats.
Untreated cats that die from M. haemofelis infection need not be
immunocompromised or splenectomized.
Acute infection often results in severe hemolytic anemia (usually
extravascular), but some have only mild anemia (chs. 57, 174). In
experimental studies, clinical signs typically occur around 2-34 days
after infection, with anemia lasting from 18-30 days. Onset of anemia
is usually followed by a significant regenerative response with
reticulocytosis. Chronic infection is not usually associated with
significant anemia. Experimental studies have demonstrated that the
numbers of M. haemofelis blood organisms can fluctuate in brief
time periods, especially in the first few weeks of infection. Antigenic
variation, to evade host immune systems, may explain these
fluctuations:24 a large portion (62%) of the M. haemofelis genome
encodes a set of uncharacterized hypothetical proteins arranged in
series of paralogous repeats which could mediate differing
expression of hemoplasma surface proteins over time. Young cats
may be more susceptible to severe clinical disease from M.
haemofelis infection. As discussed, not all studies demonstrate
association between anemia and M. haemofelis infection, maybe
because these studies often include chronically M. haemofelisinfected cats without clinical signs.

IMHA, Immune-mediated hemolytic anemia.
Some species have the status Candidatus, which is the name used for
newly described organisms for which genetic sequence data are
available but which cannot be phenotypically characterised to meet
the needs of the International Code of Nomenclature of Bacteria60
due to the inability to grow them in vitro. The species Mycoplasma
haemofelis and Mycoplasma haemocanis do not have the
Candidatus status, even though they cannot yet be grown in vitro,
because they represent the renamed previously existing
Haemobartonella felis and Haemobartonella canis species,
respectively. Bacterial nomenclature forbids the ‘demotion’ of any
bacterial species, including during renaming.
Persistent autoagglutination or positive Coombs’ test results,
indicating presence of erythrocyte-bound antibodies, have been seen
in anemic cats with acute M. haemofelis infection.25 However,
antibodies appeared only after anemia had developed, suggesting
that erythrocyte-bound antibodies may be due to hemoplasmainduced hemolysis rather than initiating it. Further, antibodies
disappear with antibiotic and supportive treatment, without need for
glucocorticoid treatment.25 Nevertheless, M. haemofelis infection
remains an important potential cause of immune-mediated
hemolytic anemia (IMHA) in cats (ch. 174).26 Osmotic fragility and
reduced erythrocyte lifespan have also been reported with M.
haemofelis infection.
Although acute ‘Ca. M. haemominutum’ infection is associated
with decreases in erythrocytes,25 anemia is not common except in
cats with concurrent diseases or infections, e.g., lymphoma or feline
leukemia virus (FeLV) infection.27,28 The pathogenicity of this

organism does not appear to be increased in splenectomized cats.29
‘Ca. M. haemominutum’ infection has been associated with
development of myeloproliferative diseases in cats with experimental
FeLV infection.28 Since anemia has been reported in association with
‘Ca. M. haemominutum’ infection without concurrent disease or
infection,30 infection alone may cause anemia in cats.
‘Ca. M. turicensis’ infection has caused anemia31 or mild
erythrocyte parameter decreases in some experimental studies.25
Anemia is uncommon. Immunosuppression or concurrent diseases
may be involved in the pathogenesis.32 Determining the
pathogenicity of ‘Ca. M. turicensis’ in naturally infected cats has been
difficult in epidemiological studies as cats are often co-infected with
other hemoplasma species.

CANINE HEMOPLASMAS
Studies regarding the pathogenicity of canine hemoplasmas are
sparse. Hemoplasma infection only causes hemolytic anemia in
splenectomized or immunocompromised dogs.33-36 Latent M.
haemocanis infections can be reactivated following splenectomy.
Some infected dogs have evidence of erythrocyte-bound antibodies
with positive Coombs’ tests.37 Nevertheless, little evidence exists for
canine hemoplasmas being a major cause of IMHA.26

OVERALL PATHOGENESIS
The pathogenicity of different hemoplasma species varies. Not all
studies show an association between infection and anemia. M.
haemofelis and M. haemocanis (splenectomized dogs), are most
likely to be associated with clinical signs during acute infection,
whereas ‘Ca. M. haemominutum,’ ‘Ca. M. turicensis’ and ‘Ca. M.
haematoparvum’ are not generally associated with clinical signs
unless concurrent disease or immunosuppression is present. Health

status and transmission route of infection may determine the
outcome of hemoplasma infection with any species.

CARRIER STATUS
Long-term feline hemoplasma carrier state, without clinical signs,
can occur, particularly with ‘Ca. M. haemominutum.’38,39 Many M.
haemofelis–infected cats and some with ‘Ca. M. turicensis’ naturally
clear infection from peripheral blood within a few months of acute
infection. However, general statements regarding long-term carrier
status cannot be made since great variation exists. Variations likely
reflect different host-organism interactions and different
hemoplasma species. Carrier cats often have subclinical infections
and, uncommonly, reactivation of infection and clinical disease can
occur.30 Little work has been done regarding the time course of
carrier status with canine hemoplasmas, but subclinical carrier dogs
infected with ‘Ca. M. haematoparvum’ and M. haemocanis are
thought to exist.19

TRANSMISSION
The natural route of transmission of hemoplasma infection to cats
and dogs has not yet been determined. Different routes may
predominate for different hemoplasma species.
Canine and feline hemoplasma DNA has been found in fleas, ticks,
and mosquitoes. However, the DNA found in potential vectors could
just reflect their hematophagous activity on infected hosts. The cat
flea, Ctenocephalides felis, has been implicated in transmission of
feline hemoplasma, but only transient M. haemofelis infection
without clinical signs has been reported in cats experimentally
infected via the hematophagous activity of fleas.40 Transmission of
M. haemocanis by the brown dog tick, Rhipicephalus sanguineus,
has been suggested but remains unconfirmed.20,41
The association between hemoplasma infection and male sex
and/or retrovirus status (particularly FIV) seen in some studies
could suggest that cat fights are involved in transmission of infection.

Studies suggest subcutaneous inoculation of ‘Ca. M. turicensis’containing blood resulted in infection, whereas the same inoculation
method using ‘Ca. M. turicensis’-containing saliva did not.42 This
suggests that hemoplasma transmission by social contact (e.g., saliva
via mutual grooming) is less likely than via aggressive interaction
(e.g., blood transmission during a cat bite incident), as inferred with
rodent hemoplasmas.43 Further, high prevalence of hemoplasma
infection has been reported in fighting dogs, supporting blood as a
transmission route.44,45 Vertical transmission has been strongly
suggested for M. haemocanis but has not been definitively shown for
feline hemoplasmas.46 Blood transfusion is another route of
transmission. Blood donors should be screened for hemoplasma (ch.
124).

CLINICAL SIGNS AND LABORATORY
ABNORMALITIES
In pathogenic infections, common clinical signs of hemoplasmosis
are lethargy (ch. 10), pallor (

Video 194.1; ch. 25) and weakness

(ch. 23). Inappetence, dehydration, weight loss (ch. 18) and
intermittent fever (ch. 16) are also reported. Splenomegaly may be
evident with feline hemoplasmosis (ch. 182). This is not common in
dogs with clinical hemoplasmosis because most clinically affected
animals have been previously splenectomized (e.g., for tumor
removal). Animals with severe anemia may have tachycardia,
tachypnea (ch. 37), weak or bounding femoral pulses (ch. 39), and
cardiac murmurs (ch. 38). Icterus is rare, despite the severe anemia.
Moribund cats may be hypothermic.
Pathogenic hemoplasma infection typically causes a regenerative
macrocytic hypochromic anemia (ch. 57), although pronounced
reticulocytosis is not always evident. Normoblasts may be present.
Positive Coombs’ test results, particularly with cold agglutinins, and
persistent autoagglutination have been reported in acute
hemoplasmosis (ch. 174). Hyperproteinemia and
hyperbilirubinemia are occasionally seen. Hypoxic liver damage may

increase alanine aminotransferase activity (chs. 65, 269).
Retrovirus testing may be positive in cats (chs. 198, 199).

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES
Hemoplasmosis should be considered as a differential diagnosis in
cats or dogs with regenerative anemia and possibly associated fever.
Other diagnoses to consider are primary IMHA (ch. 174), secondary
IMHA (e.g. secondary to drugs, neoplasia, infections),
cytauxzoonosis (cats, ch. 197), retroviral infection (cats; chs. 198,
199), babesiosis (ch. 197), Heinz body associated hemolysis (cats,
ch. 138), hypophosphatemia and inherited erythrocyte disorders
such as pyruvate kinase deficiency (ch. 174).

DIAGNOSIS
CYTOLOGY
Cytologic examination of blood smears may show hemoplasmas on
erythrocyte surfaces (Figure 194.2), occasionally in chains,
especially with M. haemocanis (Figure 194.3). Cytology, however,
has poor sensitivity (0-37.5%) and specificity for diagnosis. Huge
numbers of organisms are needed before they can be visualized. Also,
cytology cannot differentiate hemoplasma species.14,15,38,47-50 ‘Ca.
M. turicensis’ has never been visualized cytologically,51 probably due
to the low numbers of organisms seen in the blood with this
infection.25 Specificity can also be an issue for cytological diagnosis
of hemoplasma infection as the untrained eye can fail to distinguish
stain precipitate, Howell-Jolly bodies, and basophilic stippling from
hemoplasma organisms. Careful staining with filtered Romanowskytype solutions (e.g., Wright Giemsa or Diff-Quik) is essential. With
board certified clinical pathologists, specificity is 84-98%.38,47-49
Finding epicellular organisms on the surface of erythrocytes together
with clinical signs of hemoplasmosis supports the diagnosis, but PCR
testing is required for confirmation.

FIGURE 194.2 Mycoplasma haemofelis
organisms (arrows) on the surface of erythrocytes in
a Romanowsky stained blood smear. Cytology is,
however, an insensitive method for diagnosing
hemoplasma infections and cannot differentiate
between hemoplasma species; the polymerase chain
reaction is the diagnostic method of choice for
hemoplasma infection.

POLYMERASE CHAIN REACTION (PCR)
ASSAYS

PCR is the preferred method for diagnosis, with excellent specificity
and sensitivity in good laboratories. This testing usually requires a
few days because samples need to be delivered for analysis. Often
PCRs are duplexed with a host housekeeping gene (such as the 28S
rRNA gene) PCR assay52 to prevent false negative results for
hemoplasma infection occurring due to the failure of DNA extraction,
the presence of PCR inhibitors or PCR setup errors. Quantitative
PCR (qPCR) assays allow quantification of hemoplasma DNA in the
patient’s blood, providing an ability to monitor the course of
hemoplasma infection and evaluate response to treatment, e.g., a
decrease in the level of hemoplasma DNA in the blood following
institution of effective antibiotic treatment. The fluctuations in blood
organism numbers that can occur during M. haemofelis infection
should be considered when interpreting qPCR results, as decreases in
organism number cannot always be deemed a consequence of
effective antibiotic treatment. When a positive PCR result is obtained
for hemoplasma infection, as healthy carrier cats exist, the result
must always be interpreted in the context of clinical signs,
clinicopathological results, and any concurrent disease or
immunosuppression. Pathogenicity of the agent detected should also
be considered when deciding whether a positive result represents the
cause of disease. In-house PCR is not available, although a point-ofcare machine that uses isothermal non-quantitative amplification of
DNA to diagnose M. haemofelis infection has recently been
described.53 This method requires in-house extraction of DNA from
blood and technique markedly influences sensitivity, precluding
current routine recommendation of this method.

SEROLOGY
Serological assays to detect antibodies to feline hemoplasma proteins
are not commercially available. Studies have suggested that serologic
testing may be able to differentiate acute from chronic M. haemofelis
infection54 and be more sensitive than PCR in detecting exposure to
‘Ca. M. turicensis.’55

TREATMENT
ANTIBIOTICS
Antibiotic treatment (Table 194.2) is indicated for cats and dogs
with clinical signs and clinicopathological abnormalities consistent
with clinical hemoplasmosis. Doxycycline is recommended as firstline therapy typically for 2-4 weeks, with clinical improvement
occurring within 2-3 days of effective treatment. If this is the first
episode of hemoplasmosis due to M. haemofelis or M. haemocanis
infection in a patient that exhibits a rapid and favorable clinical
response to treatment, 2 weeks of doxycycline may be adequate with
no further monitoring. However, if the situation is complex, e.g.,
repeated episode, concurrent disease (ch. 227), and/or clinical signs
do not improve within 3 days, blood organism numbers can be
monitored by qPCR to ensure they are decreasing with therapy.
Repeat hematology profiles are also helpful to assess response to
treatment.

The varied doses stated are due to differences in licensed dosages in
different countries and those used in published studies to document
efficacy.
Fluoroquinolones can be used as second-line agents if there has
been inadequate response to doxycycline. Marbofloxacin and
pradofloxacin are both active against M. haemofelis. Enrofloxacin is
also effective but diffuse retinal degeneration and acute blindness
have been reported following its use in cats. Although this adverse
side-effect is rare, great caution must be exercised with enrofloxacin
use in cats. Azithromycin was not effective in one study of cats
infected with M. haemofelis and/or ‘Ca. M. haemominutum.’ In one

M. haemocanis case report,35 oxytetracycline followed by
enrofloxacin did not markedly reduce organism numbers, although
clinical signs did improve.
Although marbofloxacin treatment results in a marked sustained
fall in blood M. haemofelis organisms in cats,56 it only results in a
temporary fall of ‘Ca. M. haemominutum’ organism numbers.57
Similarly, ‘Ca. M. haemominutum’ infection was not as effectively
treated by doxycycline as M. haemofelis infection,29 and PCR
positive results for ‘Ca. M. haemominutum’ infection have been
reported in cats following either enrofloxacin or doxycycline
treatment.17 Little work has been done on the response of M.
haemocanis, ‘Ca. M. haematoparvum’ or ‘Ca. M. turicensis’ to
antibiotic treatment, but one report described a successful response
of ‘Ca. M. turicensis’ to doxycycline.58
Clearance of hemoplasma infection would help ensure reactivation
of latent infections cannot occur. However, reactivation of infection
is thought to be uncommon and, until recently, a protocol for
clearance of infection had not been identified, making it very difficult
to warrant longer treatment courses. A treatment protocol of 4 weeks
of doxycycline followed by 2 weeks of marbofloxacin has been
suggested to clear chronic M. haemofelis infection for any cat that
remains positive by qPCR (as determined by repeated testing on
multiple occasions) after doxycycline treatment (Table 194.2).59
Treatment breaks of up to 4 weeks between the courses of
doxycycline and marbofloxacin did not influence outcome. This may
be of value to use in cats with M. haemofelis infection that have had
particularly severe disease and/or reactivation of infection. However,
given concerns related to antimicrobial stewardship (ch. 7), such
protocols should be reserved for cats with PCR-proven M. haemofelis
persistent infection and anemia.

SUPPORTIVE TREATMENT
Affected dogs and cats may also require supportive treatment with
nutrition (ch. 164), crystalloids (ch. 120), or blood transfusions
(packed erythrocytes) (ch. 124).

IMMUNOSUPPRESSIVE TREATMENT
Immunosuppressive glucocorticoid treatment to suppress IMHA is
not recommended because antibiotic treatment and supportive care
alone are usually adequate, even in animals with erythrocyte-bound
antibodies.25 Glucocorticoids can cause hemoplasma infection
reactivation and in one case negative M. haemocanis PCR results
were only obtained once prednisolone for presumed IMHA was
stopped.36 Additional information is provided in chs. 144 and 227.

PREVENTION
As the natural route of transmission of hemoplasma infection is not
known, it is hard to reliably prevent infection. Blood donors should
be screened for hemoplasma infection by PCR to help prevent
inadvertent transmission from subclinical carrier cats or dogs.
Indoor housing may prevent transmission to cats compared to being
outdoors, although behavioral welfare implications must be
considered before adopting in cats used to going outside. Since there
is potential vector transmission by ticks, and possibly fleas,
preventative ectoparasite treatment is recommended for animals at
risk for these vectors.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Hemotropic Mycoplasmas (Hemoplasmosis)
WHAT IS HEMOPLASMOSIS?
Hemoplasmosis is a disease, usually associated with anemia, which
can result following infection with one of the hemoplasma species in
both cats and dogs. Hemoplasma species are very small bacteria that
attach to the surface of red blood cells, causing their breakdown in a
process called hemolysis. The disease is more common in cats and
hemoplasmosis has a worldwide distribution. The hemoplasma
species most associated with disease are Mycoplasma haemofelis in
cats and Mycoplasma haemocanis in dogs, during acute infection,
although M. haemocanis usually only causes disease in dogs that no
longer have a spleen. Other hemoplasma species exist that are less
harmful unless the dog or cat has another disease or infection (e.g.,
feline immunodeficiency virus infection in cats) or is receiving drugs
that can affect the immune system (e.g., chemotherapy for cancer).
WHAT ARE THE CLINICAL SIGNS OF HEMOPLASMOSIS?
Common clinical signs seen with hemoplasma infections that are
associated with disease are pale mucous membranes, tiredness,
weakness, and sometimes a faster breathing rate. Animals may also
have a reduced appetite, loss of weight, dehydration and/or a fever.
WHICH TESTS ARE NEEDED FOR DIAGNOSIS?
Hemoplasmosis is likely to be suspected following the diagnosis of
anaemia (reduced red blood cells) after blood sampling a dog or cat
with the above clinical signs. Although hemoplasma organisms may
be visible on the surface of red blood cells on blood smears prepared
by your veterinarian, this is rare and so diagnosis is usually
performed by sending a blood sample to a laboratory for polymerase
chain reaction (PCR) testing, which is very reliable and allows
identification of the infecting hemoplasma species. Since both dogs
and cats can carry infections with hemoplasma species without
outward clinical signs (e.g., those infected with a less harmful
hemoplasma species or during chronic M. haemofelis infection), it is
important for the veterinarian to decide, following diagnosis,

whether the infection is truly responsible for the animal’s clinical
signs.
WHAT TREATMENT IS GIVEN?
Two weeks of antibiotic treatment with doxycycline is usually
effective in treating the anemia associated with hemoplasmosis.
Alternative antibiotics include fluoroquinolones (e.g., marbofloxacin,
pradofloxacin) if doxycycline treatment is inadequate. Supportive
care to correct dehydration and ensure animals eat is also important.
In severe cases a blood transfusion may be required.
HOW ARE HEMOPLASMAS TRANSMITTED?
We are not sure, and different transmission routes may work for
different hemoplasma species. Cat bites and fighting between cats
have been implicated and fleas and ticks may act as vectors. Vertical
transmission from mothers to offspring may occur. Blood
transfusions can transmit infection too if the donor is infected with
haemoplasma species.
WHAT IS THE PROGNOSIS?
With early antibiotic treatment, most infected animals can make a
full recovery. Some animals remain carriers of infection following
treatment, so an awareness that the disease may return is important
although in reality this is probably uncommon.
Séverine Tasker (Solihull, United Kingdom)

With “fecal enteric panel” options offered by diagnostic
laboratories, selecting appropriate tests, interpreting results, and
making treatment decisions can be challenging. Detection of
potentially pathogenic bacteria in pets with acute or chronic diarrhea
may be incidental. Often pets require no specific treatment because
most bacterial infections are self-limiting and co-infections or
secondary infections are common. However, severe clinical signs
with sepsis and extra-gastrointestinal (GI) infections can develop,
especially in immunocompromised or immature dogs and cats,
warranting the use of antimicrobials in addition to supportive
therapy.

DIAGNOSTIC AND TREATMENT
APPROACH (Figure 195.1)
Clinical signs of bacterial enteritis, physical examination (PE)
findings (ch. 2), and minimum database results are nonspecific.
Diagnosis relies on pathogen confirmation after ruling out other
disorders. Complete blood count and routine serum chemistry
results can be unremarkable or show neutrophilia (with or without
left shift), evidence of dehydration (increased hematocrit and total
solids, prerenal azotemia), a variety of electrolyte changes (e.g.,
hypo- or hyperkalemia), mildly elevated liver enzyme activities
(reactive hepatopathy), regenerative anemia in some animals with
blood loss, and reduced total solids. Other findings can suggest
extra-GI disease (e.g., cholecystitis with associated
hyperbilirubinemia [ch. 272]). Patients with sepsis (ch. 128) can
show neutropenia and hypoglycemia, and some may develop
abnormalities in coagulation testing with disseminated intravascular
coagulation (DIC).
Diagnostic imaging is recommended, especially in dogs or cats
with more severe or extra-GI signs, to rule out obstruction, detect
peritonitis, or identify neoplastic changes, etc. Ultrasonography
complements radiology and allows a more detailed examination to be
performed. In bacterial enteritis, abdominal lymphadenomegaly,
abnormal motility, and thickening of the intestinal mucosa with less
well-defined layering are common. Supportive therapy and dietary
modifications resolve signs in most pets with mild to moderate signs

(ch. 152). The prognosis for uncomplicated bacterial enteritis is
generally excellent.
Most enteropathogens have zoonotic potential. Clients should be
educated about hygiene measures and risks of interacting with
immature, shelter, and diarrheic animals, as well as the risks of
feeding raw meat. People at greater risk of serious illness include
infants/young children, pregnant women, the elderly, and the
immunocompromised. Feeding a “raw-meat-and-bones-diet”
(RMBD) is a risk factor for infecting dogs and cats with
enteropathogenic bacteria, with potential for increased fecal
shedding, enteritis, extra-GI infections, and fatal bacteremia (ch.
167).1-3

CAMPYLOBACTER SPP.
DESCRIPTION AND TRANSMISSION
Campylobacter spp. are Gram-negative rods (0.2-0.8 microns wide
by 0.5-5 microns long) that occur singly, in pairs, or in chains as long
spirals. Over 30 different species and subspecies have been
confirmed and in many animals Campylobacter organisms are
commensals of the intestinal tract. Colonization prevalences of 087% for dogs and 0-75% for cats have been reported, worst in
immature and intensively housed animals. Campylobacter spp. are
transmitted via the direct or indirect fecal-oral route. They survive
for weeks in feces. In dogs, the Campylobacter species most
frequently isolated from fecal samples are Campylobacter
upsaliensis, Campylobacter jejuni, and Campylobacter helveticus;
and in cats, C. helveticus, C. upsaliensis, and C. jejuni.4,5
Intermittent excretion and co-infections with parvovirus,
coronavirus, circovirus, endoparasites, Clostridium spp., and others
have been described.5,6

PATHOGENESIS
Pathogenicity involves motility, adhesiveness, invasiveness, toxin
production, multidrug resistance, and stress response genes. These

organisms adhere to epithelial cells throughout the intestinal tract
facilitated by flagella and adhesins. They multiply, invade, and
excrete toxins (e.g., cytolethal distending toxin [CDT]) that induce
mucosal damage and inflammatory responses that cause diarrhea.7
Although some studies failed to detect a significantly increased
prevalence of Campylobacter spp. in animals with signs of diarrhea
as compared to healthy animals, other studies confirmed a higher
prevalence.5 In addition, a wider species range and higher
concentration of Campylobacter spp. was detected in dogs with
diarrhea via direct fecal quantitative polymerase chain reaction
(qPCR).8 Experimental infections cause mild enteritis. Colony dog
outbreaks of Campylobacter spp. enterocolitis have been reported.9

CLINICAL SIGNS
Infection is usually subclinical, but immature animals and those with
predisposing factors (e.g., co-infections or concurrent disease) are
more prone to developing overt clinical signs.4 Infected dogs and
cats usually have mild to moderate diarrhea (watery or with blood or
mucus; chs. 49, 50), tenesmus (ch. 51), lethargy (ch. 10),
dehydration, anorexia (ch. 17), and less frequently fever, vomiting,
and signs of abdominal pain. Extra-GI conditions have been
described, including cholangiohepatitis, cholecystitis, reproductive
issues, and neurological disorders.4,5 Campylobacter spp. may also
play a role in chronic enteric disease. In humans, an association with
inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has been confirmed, but whether
the bacteria are causative or simply present as a result of dysbiosis
and intestinal inflammation remains to be elucidated.10 In cats with
neutrophilic IBD, significantly higher numbers of Campylobacter
coli were demonstrated retrospectively by applying fluorescence in
situ hybridization (FISH) to endoscopic biopsy specimens and
comparing results with those from cats that had lymphoplasmacytic
IBD (ch. 262).11

DIAGNOSIS

The organism is detected in fecal or other specimens (e.g., bile) by
microaerobic bacterial culture at 37°C. Specialized agar (modified
charcoal cefoperazone deoxycholate) is needed for routine isolation
of the most common campylobacters. Other media or conditions are
required for some of the “emerging species” that are gaining clinical
importance such as C. upsaliensis, Campylobacter concisus and
Campylobacter rectus. Identification is performed by matrixassisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass
spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) on cultures (ch. 184).
Internationally accepted criteria for antimicrobial susceptibility
testing of veterinary Campylobacter spp. are lacking. Direct
polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on fecal specimens from dogs and
cats can also be performed (as genus-level PCR or with subspecies
determination) and improves sensitivity and accuracy depending on
methodology and the range of species tested.

TREATMENT
Treatment with erythromycin (10-15 mg/kg PO q8h), tylosin (6-16
mg/kg PO q12h), azithromycin (5-10 mg/kg PO q24h), or
enrofloxacin (5 mg/kg PO q24h) for 5-7 days has been recommended
where indicated (chs. 140 and 262).4,12 Campylobacteriosis has
major zoonotic potential. Poultry is the most common source of
human infection, usually via consumption of contaminated food.10
Confirmed identical subtypes of Campylobacter spp. in pets and
humans with campylobacteriosis have been reported. Contact with
immature and diarrheic pets is a significant risk factor for C. jejuni
and C. coli infection, with children and infants at the highest risk for
developing clinical signs.13

SALMONELLA SPP.
The genus Salmonella belongs to the Enterobacterales and contains
two species: Salmonella enterica causing the majority of infections
in mammals with six subspecies, and Salmonella bongori.
Salmonella enterica organisms are facultative anaerobic, motile,

Gram-negative rods with a large range of different serotypes, further
divided into bioserotypes based on their O, K, or H major antigenic
determinants. Salmonellae are ubiquitous and associated with GI or
systemic signs in a range of animal species. The organism is resistant
and can survive in dry feces for several months. Infection of dogs and
cats occurs in unclean environments by the fecal-oral route, by
consuming raw or undercooked food, feeding contaminated dry diets
or treats, drinking contaminated water, or fomite exposure.14
RMBDs have been important sources of Salmonella (ch. 167).1,3
Similar prevalences have been detected in dogs and cats with and
without clinical signs. Strain-type, dose, and host-related factors
(concomitant diseases, host-immune status) determine severity of
signs.4,15 In healthy pet dogs and cats the S. enterica prevalence is
generally low: 0-3.6% in dogs;4,16 0-4% in cats;17 0-3.8% and 0-8.6%
in diarrheic dogs and cats, respectively.4,16 Juveniles, sheltered pets,
stray dogs, and working dogs have higher prevalences of
colonization18-20 and of co-infections (e.g., canine parvovirus [ch.
201]).19

PATHOGENESIS
Pathogenicity of different strains of Salmonella serotypes varies, and
they possess several virulence and resistance genes. Adhesins
facilitate interaction between Salmonella spp. and M-cells in the
Peyer’s patches and intestinal epithelial cells. This is followed by
invasion, replication, toxin production, and an inflammatory
response resulting in secretory diarrhea. Salmonella spp. can persist
in enterocytes and phagocytic cells of lymph nodes, liver, and spleen.
Immunosuppression, co-infections, and stress can cause reactivation
with clinical illness and fecal shedding. Fecal shedding often persists
for 3 to 6 weeks after resolution of diarrhea.21

CLINICAL SIGNS

The majority of Salmonella spp. infections do not cause clinical
signs. Some dogs and cats develop acute self-limiting disease with
malaise (ch. 10), anorexia (ch. 17), fever (ch. 16), vomiting (ch.
48), signs of abdominal pain, and watery-to-mucoid (sometimes
hemorrhagic, ch. 50) diarrhea (ch. 49). Chronic enteritis has also
been documented.14,15,21 Eleven percent of Greyhounds fed RMBD
had subclinical Salmonella spp. infections, but 76% had clinical
enteritis with strains genetically related to those recovered from the
RMBD (ch. 167).18 Dogs in a kennel outbreak exhibited fever,
vomiting, lethargy, inappetence, diarrhea, dysentery, arthritis, and
several puppy deaths.2 Salmonellosis, described in closed colony
cats, caused lethargy, anorexia, vomiting, and hemorrhagic
diarrhea.15 Endotoxemia (ch. 128) and bacteremia, potentially
causing DIC (ch. 171), can develop with or without GI signs,
especially in young and immunocompromised animals. Extra-GI
infections involving the biliary tract, spleen, kidneys, heart, uterus,
meninges, joints, and lungs have been reported.3,14,21

DIAGNOSIS
Bacterial isolation of Salmonella spp. can be done on fecal or other
specimens, and requires selective enrichment followed by culture
onto MacConkey, XLD, or brilliant green agar. Biochemical testing
and MALDI-TOF MS are used for further identification (ch. 184),
but serotyping is not routinely performed by commercial
laboratories. Molecular testing by PCR can be performed, ideally
after overnight enrichment, and is more sensitive than culture.4,14
Due to intermittent shedding and low sensitivity of cultures, PCR or
multiple cultures on specimens should be collected at 2-3 week
intervals until 3 consecutive negative results are obtained.4

TREATMENT
Inappropriate antimicrobial treatment should be avoided because
this may alter commensal flora, promote the carrier state, and

enhance development of antimicrobial resistance (chs. 7, 140).
Salmonella organisms can acquire transferable plasmid-mediated
resistance, especially to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline,
streptomycin, and sulphonamides.15,20,22 Multidrug resistance was
found in 43% of household dog and cat isolates.22 Antimicrobial
susceptibility results should be considered whenever specific
treatment is indicated. Antimicrobials with good phagocytic cell
penetration are preferred, e.g., trimethoprim-sulfonamides (15
mg/kg PO q12h) or enrofloxacin (5 mg/kg PO q24h). Salmonellosis
is a common foodborne disease in humans. Contact with pets, pet
foods, and pet treats are confirmed risk factors for human
salmonellosis.23

CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE
Clostridioides (reclassified former Clostridium) difficile is a
ubiquitous, anaerobic, Gram-positive, spore-forming bacillus. Spores
are highly resistant to different environmental conditions and most
disinfectants. C. difficile colonizes the intestinal tract of humans and
animals, causes nosocomial infections, antimicrobial associated
pseudomembranous colitis in humans, and diarrhea in food animals,
horses, and companion animals.24,25 Infection usually occurs via the
fecal-oral route and from contaminated environments. Dogs have
been shown to be subclinical carriers or can have self-limiting small
bowel, large bowel, or diffuse enteritis or severe hemorrhagic
diarrhea.4,7

PATHOGENESIS
Clinical signs may develop following intestinal overgrowth of
toxigenic C. difficile. Enteritis can be induced from the production of
exotoxins A and B (encoded by genes tcdA and tcdB) and the binary
toxin CDT expressed by some strains. Associations between toxigenic
C. difficile infection (CDI) and clinical signs have been confirmed,
including a hospital outbreak in dogs and cats.26 However, most

infections are subclinical or the organism acts as a secondary
pathogen.4,24 Prevalences as high as 58% and 21% have been
reported in healthy dogs and cats, respectively, with higher rates in
juveniles and in veterinary hospitals.4 Feline clostridiosis is not well
documented but GI pneumatosis linked to toxin-producing C.
difficile with multifocal necrotizing hemorrhagic enterotyphlocolitis
has been documented.27

DIAGNOSIS
Anaerobic fecal culture of C. difficile requiring broth enrichment and
selective media, and antigen (glutamate dehydrogenase)
immunoassay testing, have high sensitivities. Since toxigenic strains
cannot be discriminated from the non-toxic, only negative results to
rule out clostridiosis are useful.12 PCR identification of clostridia
combined with detecting fecal toxin A and B genes (tcdA and tcdB) is
recommended.4 Human immunoassays for detection of toxins A and
B have not been validated in dogs and cats and are of limited use.

TREATMENT
Supportive therapy including probiotics and dietary modification is
advised (chs. 152, 262, and 263). Current antimicrobial therapy
should be discontinued, if possible. Fecal microbiota transplant (ch.
106) is relatively novel for dogs but was superior to metronidazole
treatment, as indicated from fecal scores and dysbiosis index (DI)
changes in dogs with acute diarrhea.28 Metronidazole (10-15 mg/kg
PO q12h) can be administered to dogs and cats with CDI where
indicated4 but antimicrobial resistance has been described in 21% of
C. difficile isolates from dogs29 and dog-specific antimicrobial
susceptibility breakpoints are not available. Identical ribotypes and
toxigenic strains that cause human CDI are detected in pets, and
although the zoonotic risk is minimal, pets should be considered a
potential source of community-acquired human CDI.25

CLOSTRIDIUM PERFRINGENS
Clostridium perfringens is an anaerobic, Gram-positive, sporeforming bacillus with 7 toxinotypes (A to G) based on major toxin
genes (alpha, beta, epsilon, iota, CPE and NetB). Toxinotypes are
able to express several toxins linked with pathogenicity, e.g., C.
perfringens enterotoxin (CPE).4,30 The organisms are ubiquitous in
soil and commensal in intestinal tracts of vertebrates. C. perfringens
has been cultured in as many as 84% and 91% of fecal specimens
from healthy and diarrheic pet dogs, respectively.30,31
Enterotoxigenic C. perfringens type A is most common, causes food
poisoning and diarrhea in humans, and acute or chronic small and
large bowel disease in dogs with mild self-limiting signs to
potentially fatal hemorrhagic diarrhea (ch. 262).4

PATHOGENESIS
Increased enterotoxin production following sporulation of
commensal enterotoxigenic strains can be triggered by diet change,
antimicrobial therapy, co-infections, or concomitant disease, and
may result in enteritis. However, investigations on the association of
toxin production and presence of toxin encoding genes with clinical
signs in dogs have shown variable results. A significant association
was noted in dogs with diarrhea and detection of the cpe gene by
PCR and/or CPE by ELISA.31,32 Quantitative PCR for the cpa gene
was shown to be useful in confirming an association between toxin
production and clinical signs, with a cut off of >300,000 copies
considered significant.33 Fecal microbiota investigations may further
elucidate the role of Clostridia and their toxins in dysbiosis resulting
from or causing acute or chronic enteritis.32 The term ‘acute
hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome’ (AHDS, ch. 262) was proposed for
dogs with acute bloody diarrhea and vomiting where other
differentials were ruled out. C. perfringens, identified by bacterial
culture and immunohistochemistry on small intestinal biopsies, was
considered the primary pathogen in dogs with AHDS.34 Novel sporeforming netE and netF toxin encoding genes were detected via real-

time PCR in fecal C. perfringens type A organisms from dogs with
AHDS.35 In cats, an association between C. perfringens toxin genes
and clinical signs has not been confirmed. Shelter cats commonly
had C. perfringens cpa gene detected by real-time PCR (50% and
42% in the diarrheic and healthy cats, respectively). Also, 49% of cats
with GI signs in multi-cat households tested positive.36 A case of
feline intestinal pneumatosis was linked to C. perfringens and
Escherichia coli infection.37

DIAGNOSIS
C. perfringens detection alone has no diagnostic value in dogs or cats
with enteritis, but is confirmatory when combined with positive toxin
(gene) testing results.4 Fecal enterotoxin (CPE) human
immunoassays lack specificity and sensitivity and should be
combined with molecular methods to detect and quantify toxin
genes. Direct fecal PCR testing to detect toxin genes cpa, cpe, netE,
and netF is available. As these genes can also be present in the feces
of healthy dogs and dogs with diarrhea due to other causes, diagnosis
should not be based on their mere identification.35

TREATMENT
Supportive therapy of C. perfringens-associated enteritis is generally
sufficient (ch. 152). Probiotic therapy may hasten intestinal
microbiome recovery. Antimicrobial therapy is reserved for the
severely ill, e.g., AHDS with signs of sepsis (ch. 128).38
Antimicrobial treatment options include metronidazole (10-15
mg/kg PO q12h), tylosin (6-16 mg/kg PO q12h), and ampicillin (1020 mg/kg PO or IV q8h),12 but resistance has been described and
veterinary breakpoints are lacking (chs. 7, 140).

ESCHERICHIA COLI

E. coli are facultative anaerobic, Gram-negative, pleomorphic rods
belonging to the order Enterobacterales. Their serologic
classification is based on surface antigens O, H, and K. Most strains
can be cultured from the enteric microbiota of healthy animals, but
may act as opportunistic pathogens resulting in enteritis and extraGI disease in the presence of virulence factors and/or immunity
impairment. Pathogenic E. coli are categorized into pathotypes
depending on characteristic virulence factors and mechanisms.4,7

PATHOGENESIS
Pathotypes described in healthy animals and those with acute or
chronic GI disease include enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC),
enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC), and enterohemorrhagic E. coli
(EHEC). EHEC include verocytotoxin-producing E. coli (VTEC),
necrotoxigenic E. coli (NTEC), enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC),
enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC) and adherent-invasive E. coli
(AIEC).4,39 Transmission occurs via the fecal-oral route, and from
contaminated environments, food, and/or water. Prevalences of E.
coli pathotypes in healthy and diarrheic dogs and cats vary. A VTEC
prevalence of 12.3% was reported in cats, but without association
with clinical signs.40 E. coli was cultured from the feces of 60 of 61
tested shelter kittens with and without diarrhea. Using direct qPCR
for the E. coli eae gene, 42% kittens were atypical enteropathogenic
E. coli (aEPEC) positive, with larger aEPEC loads in diarrheic
kittens, those with more severe disease, and increased mortality in
positive kittens.41 More dogs with signs of acute or chronic diarrhea
excreted EPEC and VTEC compared to healthy kennelled and
household dogs. However, E. coli was not suspected as the primary
cause of their diarrhea.39 Granulomatous colitis has been associated
with AIEC infection and was first described in Boxer dogs.42 It
typically results in large intestinal diarrhea, hematochezia, anorexia,
and weight loss (ch. 263).42

DIAGNOSIS
Bacterial culture on selective media, e.g., MacConkey agar, is
followed by phenotypic, MALDI-TOF MS, and antimicrobial
susceptibility testing (ch. 184). Typing of pathogenic E. coli strains
is not routinely performed because they require specialized bioassays
and molecular tests.7 A presumed diagnosis of AIEC-associated
granulomatous colitis can be made on endoscopic biopsy;
histopathologic findings include severe mucosal ulceration and
infiltration of the lamina propria and submucosa with periodic acid‐
Schiff (PAS)–positive-staining macrophages. Application of FISH on
histopathologic samples, and bacterial culture of fresh colonic
biopsies, are advised for confirmation and management decisions.42

TREATMENT
Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for AIEC-associated
granulomatous colitis and long-term remission can be achieved in
most dogs with enrofloxacin treatment (5 mg/kg PO q12h for 6-8
weeks).43 Other types of E. coli enteritis should only receive
antibiotics when there are severe clinical signs, systemic disease, or
immunosuppression (chs. 180, 227), and treatment should be based
on susceptibility results (ch. 140). Within-household sharing of E.
coli strains has been confirmed via DNA fingerprinting analysis of E.
coli isolates from dogs and humans44 and pet owners had almost 7
times the risk for colonization with extended spectrum betalactamase-producing (ESBL) E. coli versus non-pet owners,
suggesting zoonotic risk.45

YERSINIA SPP. AND OTHER
ENTEROPATHOGENS
Yersinia enterocolitica is a motile Gram-negative facultative
anaerobic bacterial species that belongs to the Enterobacterales.
Infection is usually subclinical but signs of enteritis and extra-GI

infections (myocardium, liver) have been described in dogs and cats.
Ingestion of contaminated pork and other meat products has been
suggested as a source.46 Infection is usually self-limiting;
antimicrobial therapy if needed is based on susceptibility testing. Y.
enterocolitica is an important human foodborne pathogen and
contact with pets may represent a risk factor for human infection,
with dogs and cats shedding pathogenic bioserotypes.47 Tyzzer’s
disease (caused by Clostridium piliforme) is rare in dogs and cats
and typically causes hepatitis, enterocolitis, and myocarditis after
ingestion of sporulated forms from wild rodent or rabbit feces.
Patients typically are immature or immunosuppressed, with an acute
and often fatal clinical course. Diagnosis is based on special staining
and PCR on histopathologic specimens, and fecal PCR
assay.48 Clostridium sordellii has recently been described in a dog
with rapidly fatal hemorrhagic and necrotizing GI
disease.49 Anaerobiospirillum spp., anaerobic Gram-negative spiral
shaped rods, have been described in cats with acute GI signs with
systemic progression and collapse, and ileocolitis on necropsy. The
organism can be isolated in feces from healthy dogs and cats, and
prevalence may be underestimated due to unique culture
requirements. In humans Anaerobiospirillum spp. infection is
associated with diarrhea and bacteremia.7

HOSPITAL INFECTION CONTROL
Should hospitalization be needed, consideration should be given to
housing dogs and cats with bacterial enteritis in an isolation ward
with barrier precautions, where contaminated waste can be disposed
immediately and dogs are walked in a separate area. Thorough
handwashing with bactericidal soap and hot water is recommended
after contact with the isolation area and with pets excreting
enteropathogenic bacteria. Alcohol-based hand sanitizer disinfection
alone is insufficient as C. difficile spores are alcohol-resistant.
Routine kennel cleaning and disinfection protocols using potassium
peroxymonosulfate or accelerated hydrogen peroxide are effective in
the environmental control of most enteropathogens. Household

bleach (diluted 1:10 with water) applied after thorough cleaning to
remove organic debris is superior in C. difficile outbreak situations;
surfaces should be scrubbed, left for 10 minutes, rinsed and air dried.
Management and prevention of hospital-acquired infections are
discussed in ch. 186.

CLIENT INFORMATION
“My Pet Has Bacterial Enteritis”
WHAT IS BACTERIAL ENTERITIS?
Bacterial enteritis is caused by abnormal proliferation of bacteria in
the intestine of your dog or cat resulting in inflammation and
diarrhea, and sometimes also other clinical signs. Most of these
bacteria are also present in healthy dogs and cats, but testing or
treatment of healthy animals is generally not recommended.
Examples of bacteria that can cause enteritis include Salmonella,
Campylobacter, and Clostridium.
WHAT ARE THE CLINICAL SIGNS OF BACTERIAL
ENTERITIS IN A DOG OR CAT?
Your pet has diarrhea and passes loose stools (feces), often with
increased volume or increased frequency of defecation. Some pets
can be less active, have less appetite, lose weight and vomit as well.
Diarrhea results in dehydration with loss of water, fluids, and
electrolytes. In some patients the infection can invade the rest of the
body causing severe illness.
HOW DID MY PET CATCH THE BACTERIA CAUSING
DIARRHEA?
A common route of infection is swallowing bacteria that are in the
environment (from contamination with feces, e.g., in kennels, parks).
Pets can also be infected via direct contact with other dogs and cats,
eating contaminated foods (especially raw meat diets) and treats,
and drinking unpasteurized milk or contaminated water.
CAN I ALSO BECOME ILL?
Yes; most bacteria causing enteritis in pets are “zoonotic” (meaning
they can infect humans) and people can get infected when handling
animals, disposing of stools and cleaning litter trays, through contact
with contaminated items in the environment (e.g., toys, soil), and
handling food/treats for dogs and cats. Especially infants, young
children, pregnant women, the immunocompromised, and elderly
people are at risk becoming ill. However, the risk is minor when
applying good household hygiene.

HOW IS BACTERIAL ENTERITIS DIAGNOSED?
Bacterial enteritis is relatively uncommon and your veterinarian will
first recommend performing diagnostic tests to rule out other causes
of diarrhea (e.g., parasites). You may be required to collect several
stool samples of your pet for analysis. Usually clinical signs are mild
but in some cases the bacteria may cause severe illness. Pets that are
showing more severe signs also need blood sample analysis and
diagnostic imaging (radiographs, ultrasound) and bacterial culture of
fluids like blood or bile may be needed. A diagnosis with
confirmation of the bacteria can be established via culture of stool
samples, and/or “genetic code” testing (polymerase chain reaction
[PCR]) for bacteria or their toxins.
HOW IS BACTERIAL ENTERITIS TREATED?
Bacterial enteritis most commonly gets better without antibiotic
treatment. Antibiotic treatment could cause side effects, affect the
normal bacterial population in the intestine, and cause antibiotic
resistance which is a risk not only to pets but also to humans. You
will be recommended to monitor your pet closely at home and feed
small quantities of a bland diet (e.g., cooked chicken and boiled rice),
ensure fluid intake, restrict exercise, avoid contact with other
animals, and to administer supportive treatment. In cases with
severe illness, specific antibiotic treatment and hospitalization may
be required. In some dogs and cats it will be advised to place them in
an isolation ward to avoid spreading the bacteria into the
environment and to other pets and humans.
WHAT IS THE PROGNOSIS FOR MY DOG OR CAT?
If your pet has mild or moderate signs of enteritis the prognosis to
make a full recovery is excellent. Some animals remain carriers of the
bacteria that were thought to cause the symptoms, but further
treatment is not needed if your pet is back to normal. If your pet is
not better or does not improve within a few days, in case of any
deterioration, and if new symptoms (e.g., fever, blood in stool) or
side effects to treatments are observed, please contact your
veterinarian.
To prevent re-infection of your pet and infection of other animals
and humans, control of contamination with stools and during food

preparation is very important. Routine household infection control
measures consist of regular handwashing (and especially after
handling your pet and disposing of stools) with soap and hot water,
washing surfaces of food preparation, pet bowls and utensils, and
litter trays with soap and hot water, rinse and dry thoroughly. Wash
and dry your pet’s bedding at high heat. Pick up and dispose of pet
stools immediately. Special advice for you specifically and for the
environment of your pet can vary and should be discussed with your
veterinary clinic.
Els Acke (Kornwestheim, Germany)

The protozoan parasites that most frequently infect the gastrointestinal tract in dogs and cats are:
• Coccidians: Besnoitia spp., Cryptosporidium spp., Cyclospora cayetanensis, Cystoisospora
spp., Hammondia spp., Neospora caninum, Sarcocystis spp., and Toxoplasma gondii
(Figure 196.1)
• Flagellates: Giardia spp. (Figure 196.2), Tritrichomonas foetus (blagburni), and
Pentatrichomonas hominis
• Ciliate: Balantidium coli
• Amoeba: Entamoeba histolytica

TRANSMISSION
The route of transmission for all enteric protozoa is fecal-oral except for C. cayetanensis, the path of
transmission of which in cats and dogs is unknown. Coccidian parasites have similar direct life cycles,
with infection occurring after the ingestion of sporulated oocysts from the environment. Oocysts
undergo asexual and sexual replication in host enterocytes, and unsporulated oocysts are shed in the
feces. The sporulation time is variable and depends on the type of parasite and on environmental
conditions. Cryptosporidium spp. and Sarcocystis spp., in contrast, are excreted as sporulated oocysts
that are immediately infectious. In addition, Cryptosporidium spp. have an autoinfection cycle
characterized by rupture of oocysts in the intestines prior to excretion. The life cycle of C. cayetanensis
is not fully characterized but apparently requires a single human host to complete the entire life cycle.
Noninfective C. cayetanensis oocysts are passed in feces and sporulate in the environment.
Giardia spp. are transmitted by direct ingestion of cysts from feces or by indirect contamination of
food or water. The cyst is the resistant stage primarily responsible for transmission. Giardia spp.
trophozoites constitute the active, motile form found in the intestinal tract; in dogs trophozoites are
found from the duodenum to the ileum, while in cats they predominate in the jejunum and ileum.
Giardia spp. trophozoites are susceptible to inactivation by many environmental conditions, and are
usually not responsible for spread among animals. Members of the order Trichomonadida do not form
cysts. T. foetus and Pentatrichomonas hominis trophozoites are detected in cats and dogs, with infection
occurring in the large intestine and ileum. Tritrichomonas blagburni was a proposed name to
differentiate the T. foetus “cattle genotype” and the T. foetus “feline genotype.” Several studies reported
significant genetic differences between both genotypes; however, cross transmission experiments are
considered insufficient. At the moment, many researchers considered that changing the name of feline
genotype may be premature.1

Trichomonads undergo an asexual cycle, in which trophozoites multiply by binary division, and
transmission occurs by ingestion of trophozoites directly.1 For E. histolytica and B. coli, the cyst is the
infectious stage. After ingestion of cysts, excystation occurs in the small intestine and trophozoites
migrate to the large intestine; these later multiply by binary fission and produce cysts. Dogs only pass
fragile E. histolytica trophozoites in feces. In contrast, humans excrete infectious cysts.
Infection with enteric protozoa can also occur by ingestion of prey species that harbor
Cryptosporidium spp., Giardia spp., E. histolytica, and B. coli in their intestines. Dogs can become
infected with Neospora caninum after ingestion of contaminated tissues including placental material,
heart muscle, liver, brain, and skeletal muscle.2 Infection with Cystoisospora spp., Giardia spp., and
other enteric pathogens can also occur following ingestion of paratenic hosts such as flies, cockroaches,
or dung beetles that have ingested sporulated oocysts.3,4
Most coccidian oocysts are highly resistant to environmental degradation, and excretion of parasite
oocysts/cysts is variable among parasite species. Cryptosporidium spp. oocysts can be excreted by the
host months after infection. Giardia spp. cysts may survive in the environment for months but are
susceptible to desiccation and are greatly reduced in numbers by freeze-thawing. T. foetus trophozoites
can survive in moist feces for 7 days at room temperature (23-24°C).5 Prepatent and patent periods are
variable and depend on the parasite species (Table 196.1).
Enteric protozoa have worldwide distribution; Giardia duodenalis, Cryptosporidium spp.,
Cystoisospora spp., T. gondii, and N. caninum, are common parasites of cats and dogs. B. coli can
occasionally infect humans and dogs, but infection has not been reported in cats. E. histolytica is not
common in cats or dogs; however, one study reported that in Pakistan, 9% (27 of 300) of dog fecal
specimens tested positive for E. histolytica by microscopic examination.6
Risk factors for excretion of protozoan parasites include crowding in environments such as shelters or
pet shops, and unsanitary conditions. Living in the same household with a cat that is excreting
Cryptosporidium oocysts and Giardia cysts, contact with livestock, and drinking untreated water are
considered risks for excretion of Cryptosporidium oocysts.7-10 Feeding cats and dogs processed foods
may lessen the chance for exposure since Cryptosporidium DNA was amplified from some raw meat
diets.11 Younger, immunosuppressed animals and those living in crowded conditions are at the highest
risk of showing signs of clinical disease after infection with Giardia cysts.9,10,12 Dogs frequenting dog
parks are more likely to be positive for Giardia spp. than socially active dogs that do not visit dog
parks13,14; however, there is no association between positive Giardia tests and having diarrhea. In
addition, genotyping of Giardia isolates from dogs attending dog parks has revealed host-specific
genotypes. Cats are infected with T. foetus more commonly than dogs; infections are most common in
young, purebred animals, and are not common in feral cats.1 Concurrent infections with other enteric
pathogens are frequently observed in cats with T. foetus.15 Infections are more common in catteries with
a history of individuals with recurrent diarrhea, and co-infections with Cystoisospora spp. and Giardia
spp. can increase the potential for clinical disease. The relative hardiness of T. foetus trophozoites in the
environment combined with overcrowded conditions in catteries can increase the transmission of T.
foetus through feline self- and mutual grooming as well as fecal contamination.5

FIGURE 196.1 Cystoisospora felis (hashtag), Toxoplasma gondii sporulated
oocysts (asterisks), and Cryptosporidium spp. oocysts (white circle). Courtesy
Dr. Michael Lappin.

FIGURE 196.2 Giardia spp. cysts.

PATHOGENESIS
The pathogenic mechanisms of disease for each of the enteric protozoans mentioned are not completely
understood. The enteric protozoan parasites described here undergo replication in the epithelium of
host intestinal cells; however, some of these parasites rarely cause diarrhea.
Cystoisospora spp. developmental stages occur in the enterocytes or in the cells within the lamina
propria of the villus. Some dogs and cats that excrete Cystoisospora spp. oocysts can show no signs.
Clinical disease associated with Cystoisospora spp. infection occurs after the lysis of infected cells, and is
most common in young, debilitated, and immunosuppressed animals. The pathogenesis of Giardia spp.
and Cryptosporidium spp. infections is considered to be multifactorial with a combination of intestinal
malabsorption and hypersecretion as the leading mechanisms associated with development of
diarrhea.16 After infection, Cryptosporidium sporozoites attach to the intestinal epithelium between the
cell membrane and the cell cytoplasm; this extracytoplasmic location may explain their resistance to
pharmacotherapy.17 Cryptosporidium is intracellular but can be considered minimally invasive, because
it does not penetrate into deeper mucosal layers. However, in immunosuppressed individuals, infection
can spread to the epithelial cells of the biliary tract, pancreatic duct, stomach, esophagus, and
respiratory tract.18 Tritrichomonas spp. are located within the superficial mucus and in contact with the
surface epithelium of the cecum and colon. Trichomonads generate disease by several mechanisms, such
as disruption of the mucosal microenvironment, adhesion, and degradation of the mucosal barrier
induction of epithelial apoptosis, and evasion of the host immune system.19 It is unclear if
trichomonosis could be a multifactorial disease, associated with other, coinfecting enteric pathogens and

affected by host-related factors.1,19 B. coli inhabits the colon as either a commensal or as an invasive
parasite; B. coli cysts are passed in the feces and constitute the infective form. The reason why
commensal B. coli becomes invasive is not clear, but co-infections with specific colonic bacteria and
Trichuris vulpis may be considered risk factors.20 If infection occurs, B. coli multiplies by binary fission
or conjugation and encystment starts in the colon or rectum.21 E. histolytica trophozoites attach to host
cells and secrete enzymes that disrupt intracellular connections. The host immune response can
exacerbate the clinical signs.
