CLINICAL SIGNS
The most frequent clinical signs exhibited by cats and dogs infected with Cystoisospora spp. include
diarrhea, weight loss, and dehydration. Animals that are severely affected may manifest anorexia,
vomiting, and depression, and death is a potential outcome. T. gondii replicates in intestinal cells and
clinical illness may result from lysis of these cells. However, only 10-20% of experimentally infected cats
developed diarrhea after being inoculated with T. gondii tissue cysts.22 In one study, T. gondii
enteroepithelial stages were detected in two cats with lymphocytic-plasmacytic enteritis, one with
clinical signs and the other showing serological evidence of active toxoplasmosis.23 Cryptosporidium
spp. have been detected in dogs and cats with and without gastrointestinal signs of disease. Clinical signs
include diarrhea, usually small bowel, characterized by high volume, low frequency stools and
significant weight loss. Fresh blood, tenesmus and discomfort are reported in some chronic cases.24-27
The majority of the published cases of dogs and cats with diarrhea and Cryptosporidium spp. infection
have been immunosuppressed, had preexisting disease of the intestine, coinfections, or chronic

diarrhea.28-32 Cryptosporidium spp. oocysts have been detected in cats and dogs with and without
diarrhea co-infected with other enteric pathogens, thus it is difficult to determine if Cryptosporidium
spp. were the primary cause of the observed clinical signs.32-40 Non-infectious diseases associated with
cryptosporidiosis in cats include lymphoma and inflammatory bowel disease.28,41
Most dogs and cats that excrete G. duodenalis show no clinical signs. Clinical signs of giardiasis are
acute or chronic small- or large-bowel diarrhea and weight loss. Diarrhea is usually mucoid, pale, and
soft, and has a strong odor; steatorrhea may be also present. Giardia is not usually enteroinvasive, so
blood in the stool is uncommon, unless other coinfecting pathogens are present. Feline trichomonas
infections are characterized by episodes of waxing and waning large bowel diarrhea.42-43 The severity of
clinical signs varies, ranging from none to intractable diarrhea.1,43 Feces from affected animals are semiformed, and can contain mucus and fresh blood; straining or tenesmus may be observed.42 Since T.
foetus infection only affects the large intestine, most infected cats have good body conditions.1,31,41
Some infected kittens develop fecal incontinence and swelling of the anal region. Infections with E.
histolytica are usually subclinical but can also be associated with ulcerative colitis. B. coli and E.
histolytica cause hemorrhagic large-bowel diarrhea that can be indistinguishable from the diarrhea
cause by trichuriasis.

DIAGNOSIS
The Companion Animal Parasite Council (CAPC) guidelines suggest that cats and dogs with diarrhea
should be tested by direct smear, fecal flotation by centrifugation (ch. 80), and with a specific fecal
enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).44
Giardia spp. and Tritrichomonas trophozoites can be observed in a small specimen of fresh diarrhea
when mixed with a drop of 0.9% saline solution and then placed on a microscope slide with a coverslip
(ch. 80;

Video 196.1). In cats, care should be used in differentiating motile trophozoites of Giardia

versus Tritrichomonas, as both can be visualized in diarrheic feces. The active falling leaf motion of
Giardia spp. trophozoites can be observed at 100× magnification. In contrast, Trichomonads are teardrop shaped, have an undulating membrane, and exhibit vigorous motility. At 400× magnification,
structural characteristics can be observed. If it is difficult to distinguish Tritrichomonas from Giardia
trophozoites based on light microscopic morphology, a Giardia ELISA test can be performed to
distinguish them.1 Preparing a wet mount is a relatively simple way to diagnose tritrichomoniasis, but
the sensitivity of this test is very low (≤14%).1 Wet mounts can also be used to identify B. coli and E.
histolytica trophozoites, with special dyes included to facilitate identification.
The use of microscopic examination after centrifugal fecal flotation allows for the detection of cysts of
most enteric protozoa (ch. 80). The flotation solutions used to detect enteric protozoa from cats and
dogs are zinc sulfate and Sheather’s sugar. For the diagnosis of Giardia spp., zinc sulfate is considered
the flotation solution of choice because it is the least likely medium to distort or destroy the cysts.45,46
Because of the intermittent pattern of cysts excretion by canine and feline hosts, it is recommended that
at least three specimens be examined over a period of about 1 week before ruling out the presence of
Giardia.47,48 Another factor to consider is that in general, dogs and cats do not excrete large numbers of
Giardia cysts.49,50 T. gondii, N. caninum, and Hammondia oocysts cannot be distinguished by
microscopic examination but they can be differentiated by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays.51-53
A commercially available direct immunofluorescent assay (FA) test that detects Giardia cysts and
Cryptosporidium oocysts has been used in cats and dogs. The direct FA method is higher in sensitivity
and specificity than fecal flotation, Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast stain, and ELISA test when applied to dog
and cat specimens.54-57 Commercial ELISA assays are available for detecting Giardia spp. antigens in
feces. Since antigen excretion can continue for several weeks even after resolution of diarrhea in dogs,
CAPC recommends that commercial fecal ELISA tests should only be used in animals with diarrhea, and
not to assess patient response of treatment after resolution of diarrhea.44
Several PCR assays have been designed to amplify enteric protozoal DNA in feces, each reporting
different sensitivities and specificities depending on whether the objective was screening or diagnosis.52-

54,58-67 In the case of Giardia spp., the amplification of more than one gene can be used to determine

the presence of host-specific or zoonotic assemblages.66 False negative PCR results may result from the
presence of PCR inhibitors in feces.14 In the case of diagnosis of T. foetus, PCR is considered the most
sensitive test.1 However, PCR results can be influenced by the way the fecal specimen is collected, as well
as by antimicrobial therapy. If repeated wet mount examinations render negative results for
trichomonads, feces may be cultured using commercially available pouches.1 The specimen must contain
live organisms to generate positive results from fecal culture. Fecal cultures should be performed inhouse to avoid the risk of organism die-off during shipment to a diagnostic laboratory.1 The organisms
can be later observed under 20× and 40× magnification under the microscope.

TREATMENT (CH. 142)
Some enteric protozoans including Giardia spp., Cryptosporidium spp., and Cystoisospora spp.
regularly dwell in the intestines of healthy animals, so they can be detected in animals without diarrhea.
The main goal of treatment is to resolve diarrhea, and it has become controversial to treat clinically
normal animals that test positive for Cryptosporidium spp., Giardia spp., and Cystoisospora spp. but
that do not have diarrhea. Certain situations, such as co-infection by other pathogens or
immunosuppression, can trigger excretion of parasites which can then be detected in diarrheic
specimens, so it is difficult to determine if these parasites are primary or secondary pathogens.
Therefore, animals with enteric protozoal infections that do not respond to therapy should be evaluated
for other causes of disease.
If small-bowel diarrhea is the primary sign of infection, highly digestible bland diets are indicated (ch.
152). When the primary sign is large-bowel diarrhea, high-fiber diets are recommended. Feeding a highfiber, highly digestible, hypoallergenic diet combined with a probiotic mixture has been shown to resolve
clinical signs of large-bowel diarrhea.68 The administration of probiotics alone contributes to resolution
diarrhea in some cases.68-70
Effective treatments for B. coli and E. histolytica infections in cats and dogs are not clearly
established. A recent article showed that 9 dogs receiving a combination of metronidazole (20 mg/kg IV)
and nalidixic acid (5 mg/kg PO) for 5 days had reduced severity of clinical signs of E. histolytica
infection.6
Giardia spp. infections can be treated with metronidazole, fenbendazole or nitazoxanide. CAPC does
not recommend treating Giardia-positive animals that do not have diarrhea.44 Although controversial,
metronidazole is usually prescribed if clinical findings suggest concurrent Clostridium perfringens
overgrowth. CAPC recommends 10 to 25 mg/kg twice daily PO for 5 to 8 days if administered as
monotherapy. If metronidazole is administered concurrently with fenbendazole, CAPC recommends 25
mg/kg twice a day orally for 5 days.44 Central nervous system toxicosis after long-term therapy or acute
toxicosis associated with high doses of metronidazole have been reported in some dogs and cats.71,72
Fenbendazole can be prescribed for treatment of giardiasis especially when concurrent infection with
cestodes or nematodes is suspected. CAPC recommends 50 mg/kg once daily PO for 3 to 5 days if
administered as monotherapy.44 If administered in combination with metronidazole (25 mg/kg twice a
day orally), CAPC recommends that fenbendazole be given at 50 mg/kg once daily orally for 5 days. A
combination of febantel, pyrantel pamoate and praziquantel is labeled for the treatment of giardiasis in
dogs in some countries outside the United States.71,73 The label dose given for 3 consecutive days is
generally effective. Fenbendazole does not appear to adversely impact the composition of the fecal
microbiome.74 Secnidazole 30 mg/kg PO in a single dose has been demonstrated to resolve diarrhea and
eliminate Giardia cysts shed in naturally infected cats, but 1 cat developed increased serum liver enzyme
activity.75 In a different study, secnidazole 30 mg/kg PO was shown to be effective at eliminating
diarrhea in adult shelter dogs, with a single dose or two doses showing different efficacy in the
elimination of diarrhea. A 90% reduction of Giardia cysts shedding (9/10 puppies) was achieved within
22 days after the administration of two doses of secnidazole (30 mg/kg, 2 weeks apart).76
Nitazoxanide (NTZ) was administered to G. duodenalis–Cryptosporidium spp. coinfected cats and
dogs. In one study, diarrhea resolved following administration of NTZ at 10-25 mg/kg PO every 12 hours

for at least 5 days.77,78 But since NTZ is a gastrointestinal irritant, it frequently causes vomiting and is
not effective in the absence of an appropriate immune response.79 Another study showed that after G.
duodenalis–infected dogs were treated with different dosages on days 0 and 14, in dogs that received a
single dose of 75 mg/kg or 150 mg/kg PO a reduction in cyst excretion was observed.80
Auranofin, a gold-containing drug that was approved by the FDA in 1985 for the treatment of
rheumatoid arthritis, has shown anti-protozoan and Gram-positive antibacterial activity as well as
efficacy against Cryptosporidium parvum, similar to NTZ.81 Auranofin was administered (in dosages
ranging from 0.3 mg/kg to a maximum of 6 mg/day once daily PO for 5 days) to shelter dogs with
diarrhea caused by Giardia spp. infections alone and Giardia spp. and Cryptosporidium coinfections.82
These dogs became negative and produced normal stools 5-10 days post-treatment82 Other drugs such
as furazolidone, quinacrine and paromomycin have also been used to treat giardiasis.44,83,84
Many compounds including tylosin, paromomycin, NTZ, and azithromycin with antiCryptosporidium activity have been evaluated in humans and companion animals, but none consistently
controlled clinical signs of disease or eliminated infection. Azithromycin has been administered at 10
mg/kg PO per day for a minimum of 10 days for the treatment of cryptosporidiosis, with variable
response.83 The ideal duration of therapy is unknown but frequently several weeks of therapy are
required for diarrhea to resolve completely. Paromomycin can cause mild gastrointestinal adverse
effects. When paromomycin was administered in one study to naturally and experimentally infected
Cryptosporidium-positive cats, oocyst excretion decreased to below the detectable limits of the assays
used, but it was unclear whether or not infection was truly eliminated.85,86 Paromomycin should not be
administered to patients with bloody diarrhea because it can be absorbed systemically, resulting in renal
toxicosis and ototoxicosis. When cats infected with Tritrichomonas were treated with paromomycin, 4
out of 32 cats developed acute kidney injury (ch. 300) and 3 of those 4 cats became deaf.87 The severity
of cryptosporidiosis is influenced by the immune status of the host; cryptosporidiosis is more severe in
children and individuals with immune disorders that affect T cells. Since no drug is completely effective
in eliminating the infection, addressing the underlying causes of immunosuppression is highly beneficial
and the mainstay for management of severe infections. In human medicine, the use of drugs in
combination (azithromycin and paromomycin; azithromycin, paromomycin and NTZ) shows a
significant reduction in oocyst excretion and improvement of clinical signs in some patients.88,89
Several drugs are available for the treatment of Cystoisospora spp. infections in cats and dogs (Table
196.2). Sulfadimethoxine is the only drug approved for treatment of coccidiosis.
Trimethoprim/sulfonamide combinations, sulfadimethoxine, furazolidone, and amprolium are used
most commonly but with variable success (Table 196.2). Among the newer drugs, ponazuril (50 mg/kg
PO single dose) has been demonstrated to be effective and safe for the treatment of coccidiosis in kittens
and puppies. Another study reported that best results in eliminating the infection were obtained
following a 3-day protocol (50 mg/kg PO q24h).90
The drug of choice for the treatment of trichomoniasis is ronidazole.91 The recommended dose is 30
mg/kg PO for 14 days.92 Ronidazole can also be effective for the treatment of canine giardiasis.
However, ronidazole is the only currently recognized treatment for T. foetus (blagburni), so it should
not be used for treatment of Giardia spp. infections unless co-infection exists. Neurotoxicosis has been
reported in cats after administration of ronidazole.93 After the administration of ronidazole, the
consistency of the feces improves in a few days and generally normalizes after 2 weeks of treatment.
Efficacy of the treatment should be assessed by PCR. If diarrhea persists and a PCR is negative, other
infectious and noninfectious causes of diarrhea should be suspected. If PCR remains positive, then
Tritrichomonas infection is still present. In PCR-positive cats the following explanations for failure to
clear Tritrichomonas should be considered: the dose of ronidazole administered was insufficient, the
duration of the therapy was insufficient, the patient was reinfected by another, there is a subclinical
carrier in the household, or the infection is with a strain of Tritrichomonas that is resistant to
ronidazole.

PUBLIC HEALTH
G. duodenalis, Cryptosporidium spp., T. gondii, E. histolytica, and B. coli are all potentially zoonotic.
Humans generally acquire Cryptosporidium spp. and G. duodenalis infections by drinking
contaminated water during recreation, or by direct contact with infected cattle. The majority of
Cryptosporidium spp. are host adapted and have a narrow spectrum of natural hosts. Cats and dogs are
usually infected with the mainly host-specific C. canis and C. felis, and humans are usually infected with
C. hominis and C. parvum. Cryptosporidium canis or C. felis DNA is rarely amplified from human feces.
The majority of Giardia spp. infections in humans and animals are caused by G. duodenalis.94 Based on
molecular characterization studies, G. duodenalis is a species complex composed of eight different
assemblages (labeled A-H). Some of these assemblages are host-specific, but others can be harbored by
several species and may be considered potentially zoonotic.95 Dogs are most commonly infected by hostspecific assemblages C and D, and cats harbor host-specific assemblage F. Cats and dogs also harbor
zoonotic assemblages A-I, A-II, B-III, and B-IV.96 The risk of acquiring Cryptosporidium spp. and
Giardia spp. infection from pets is low. However, cats and dogs can harbor zoonotic pathogens and
when they have diarrhea, care should be taken with clean-up because of the potential risk of zoonotic
transmission. B. coli and E. histolytica infections are uncommon in cats and dogs, so the likelihood of
zoonotic infection from them is low. Despite the low risk of humans acquiring these enteric protozoan
pathogens, immunosuppressed individuals are advised to avoid contact with animal feces.

Protozoal pathogens that disseminate widely in the bodies of cats
and dogs belong to the family Apicomplexa. These protozoa are
intracellular parasites of vertebrate hosts with cellular tropism
varying from blood cells (including erythrocytes and leukocytes) as
well as epithelial and connective tissues.

BABESIA
PATHOGENESIS
The genus Babesia encompasses a group of intracellular pathogens
capable of infecting human, dog, cat, horse, and wild mammalian
erythrocytes. Like other apicomplexan parasites, Babesia spp.
undergo a complex lifecycle with both sexual and asexual
reproductive phases. Sexual reproduction occurs in the definitive
host (generally Ixodidae ticks) and asexual reproduction occurs in
mammalian hosts. Inoculation of the parasite occurs primarily via
tick bite: the parasite is injected by the tick into the host interstitium.
The parasite then migrates into the vascular space where it invades
erythrocytes and undergoes schizogony or binary fission to form
clones. Babesia can also be transmitted via blood transfusion and
direct inoculation during fighting between infected animals.
Intravascular and extravascular hemolysis can occur due to
parasitemia. Clinical signs depend on the species infecting the
animal, the host immune response, and co-existing diseases. Dogs
infected but subclinical are common and may be a reservoir of
infection.

LARGE BABESIA SPECIES
Prior to availability of molecular methods, Babesia organisms in
dogs were classified by size and morphology, resulting in broad
categories of “large” and “small” Babesia species. The most common
large (2.4 × 5 micrometers) Babesia species belong to the Babesia
canis species complex, previously recognized as 3 subspecies of B.
canis, but now subdivided into their own species: B. canis, Babesia
vogeli, and Babesia rossi.1 Geographic distribution of these species
is constrained by their definitive host (i.e., tick vectors). B. canis is
found throughout Europe and into Asia (ch. 9); it is transmitted by
Dermacentor ticks. Babesia vogeli, identified in the Americas,
southern Europe, and Africa, is transmitted by Rhipicephalus
sanguineus ticks. This species causes the least disease. The
prevalence of B. canis infection in dogs in the US has ranged from 460%, and is higher in adults, kenneled dogs, and greyhounds.

Babesia rossi is limited to sub-Saharan Africa and is transmitted by
Haemaphysalis leachi and Haemaphysalis elliptica ticks.

SMALL BABESIA SPECIES
The small (1-2.5 micrometers) species include Babesia gibsoni,
Babesia conradae, and Babesia vulpes. The epidemiology of small
Babesia species is less understood and their transmission often
occurs via non-tick vectors. B. gibsoni was first recognized in Asia
and is vectored by the Haemaphysalis tick. In the US, this tick is
rare; transmission is more likely via direct transmission during dog
fights, vertical transmission, or blood transfusion. Babesia were
identified with polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in up to 55% of
kenneled dogs and pet Pit Bull Terriers in Alabama, but not
identified in other breeds surveyed.2 B. conradae was initially called
the “California isolate” and was misidentified as B. gibsoni. It has
been detected in dogs in California and other southern US states and
has been associated with coyote fighting.3-5

CLINICAL SIGNS
Clinical signs of Babesia infection range from subclinical to
fulminant. Dogs with B. vogeli infection may have no signs of illness
unless immunosuppressed due to chemotherapy or splenectomy.
Dogs with B. canis, B. rossi, B. conradae, and B. gibsoni infection
typically are evaluated for illness caused by parasitemia.2,3,6,7 These
dogs might have anemia and fever. Pallor and hypotensive shock
with tachycardia and tachypnea may be present on physical
examination (PE) in peracutely and acutely affected dogs. Icterus
and splenomegaly may be evident, and petechiae may occur in
animals with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC, ch. 171)
or immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (ITP, ch. 175). In severe B.
rossi or B. canis infections, increased erythrocyte adherence may
cause neurologic signs, rhabdomyolysis, and/or acute kidney injury
(AKI, ch. 300).6 Kidney damage may result from immune-mediated
glomerulonephritis (ch. 302) or hypoxia. After recovery from acute

infection, the immune system can fail to eliminate infection and dogs
can become chronic carriers.

ROUTINE DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
Most dogs infected with B. vogeli in the US are subclinical
carriers.8 B. gibsoni infection causes regenerative anemia, apparent
2-3 weeks after infection, and the packed cell volume (PCV) may
normalize over a period of 2-3 months (ch. 57). Severe
thrombocytopenia can occur early in the disease and mild
thrombocytopenia can persist for months (chs. 59, 175).9
Neutropenia has been reported in dogs infected with B. conradae
(chs. 58, 176).3 A Coombs’ test may be positive. Serum chemistry
abnormalities include hypoalbuminemia and increased serum liver
enzyme activities.2,6 Hyperbilirubinemia is common in dogs infected
with B. canis, B. rossi, and B. gibsoni.6,9

DEFINITIVE DIAGNOSIS
Definitive diagnosis rests on visualization of the organism in
erythrocytes using cytologic examination after staining with Wright’s
or Giemsa stains (Figure 197.1), or via molecular techniques.
Genus-wide PCR assays and those specific for detection of B. canis,
B. conradae, B. gibsoni, B. vulpes, or B. vogeli are commercially
available and are the most sensitive and specific methods for
diagnosing infection. Sequencing of DNA that is amplified using
genus-wide assays is required to identify infection with unnamed
Babesia species.10,11 After the initial episode of parasitemia,
organisms can be difficult or impossible to find via cytology.9 Dogs
infected with B. conradae have recovered and had disease
recrudescence, with worse parasitemia. Serologic testing to detect
anti-Babesia antibodies uses indirect fluorescent antibody (IFA) or
enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) testing. Recent
infection can be documented via rising antibody titers over 2-3
weeks. Current tests are designed to detect antibodies to B. vogeli

and B. gibsoni, and because only limited cross reactivity occurs
among species, they are not reliable for detecting antibodies to B.
conradae.

TREATMENT
Treatment with azithromycin (10 mg/kg PO q24h) and atovaquone
(13.3 mg/kg PO q8h) for 10 days has led to remission in dogs
infected with B. conradae, B. gibsoni, or B. vulpes, though relapses
occur.4,12,13 Imidocarb (IM or SQ; 5-6.6 mg/kg, twice, 14 days apart,
or 7.5 mg/kg, once) has been used to treat infections with B. vogeli,
B. canis, or B. rossi.14,15 Diminazene aceturate (3.5 mg/kg, IM, once)
has also been used in treating dogs with B. rossi infection, as well as
dogs with relapsing B. gibsoni infection and suspected resistance to
atovaquone (in combination with clindamycin 25 mg/kg PO q12h).16
Even when treated, dogs can remain persistently infected. Therefore,
anti-Babesia therapy should be reserved for dogs with clinical
disease, as treatment has been associated with selection of
antimicrobial-resistant strains.17 Some dogs develop a state of
premunition, becoming subclinical carriers and unlikely to
recrudesce without immunosuppression (such as splenectomy or
cancer chemotherapy).

CYTAUXZOON
DESCRIPTION, PATHOGENESIS
Cytauxzoonosis is a tick-borne protozoan disease of domestic cats,
caused primarily by Cytauxzoon felis. In the US, it has been reported
from the southeast, mid-Atlantic and Midwest locations.18,19 Disease
usually occurs in outdoor cats between May and September. In the
US, Amblyomma americanum is the primary tick vector.20,21
Reservoir hosts include the North American bobcat, which appears
to be subclinically infected, and potentially domestic cats that
recover following acute infection.22,23

Cytauxzoon infection develops in two phases. During the
schizogonous phase in the mammalian host, the organism infects
mononuclear cells in the spleen, lung, liver, and lymph nodes. There,
it replicates by binary fission, forming large, distinct nucleated
schizonts. Infected cells line vascular beds, causing vascular
occlusion. The infected mononuclear cells then rupture, releasing
organisms into the blood or tissues. This phase usually results in
shock, DIC, and a rapidly fatal illness. The intra-erythrocytic phase
occurs 1-3 days after merozoites appear in macrophages. This phase
is associated with hemolytic anemia and intra-erythrocytic
piroplasms (chs. 57, 174). The prevalence of the intra-erythrocytic
phase has been reported in up to 78% of free-ranging bobcats and
between 6 and 28% of domestic cats in endemic areas in the US.19,22

CLINICAL SIGNS AND ROUTINE
LABORATORY RESULTS
Cytauxzoonosis is a peracute and rapidly fatal disease in most
infected domestic cats; ∼90% of untreated cats die following
infection. Prognostic factors associated with survival are
unclear.24,25 Clinical signs include anorexia and lethargy. On PE,
cats are typically febrile although some are hypothermic.
Dehydration, icterus, and/or pale mucous membranes are common.
Affected cats tend to be pancytopenic (ch. 176) with
hyperbilirubinemia, increased liver enzyme activities, and
hypoalbuminemia; hyperglycemia may be seen.18 Due to
consumption of coagulation factors, cats can be coagulopathic with
significantly prolonged clotting times (ch. 170).

FIGURE 197.1 A, Blood smear from a dog

and Dr. Andrew Burton (B).)

DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT
Diagnosis requires either organism identification using cytologic
examination or PCR. Serologic testing to detect antibodies is not
typically helpful due to its short incubation period.26 Approximately
60% of cats treated with combination therapy of atovaquone and
azithromycin survived, compared to 26% of cats treated with
imidocarb dipropionate.27 Cats with cytauxzoonosis are often
critically ill and require intensive care (IV fluids [ch. 120],
nutritional support [ch. 164]) as well as antiprotozoal medications.

LEISHMANIA
DESCRIPTION

More than 30 species of Leishmania cause disease in humans and
dogs across the Americas, Europe, Asia, and Africa. Leishmaniosis is
an important disease of public health concern, particularly in
geographic areas where poor sanitation and inadequate vector
control result in pets serving as a reservoir for human infection.28
Leishmaniosis is a reportable disease in the US. Treatment is
controversial as it is rarely curative and might be associated with
selection for antiprotozoal drug resistance.29,30

PATHOGENESIS
Most dogs diagnosed with visceral leishmaniosis in North America
were infected on another continent. Infected dogs are introduced
every year from endemic regions in Europe and Latin America (ch.
9). Visceral disease has been described in US dogs with no history of
travel.31 Though there are competent sandfly vectors in North
America, the prevalence of this disease is considerably lower in the
US than in endemic regions.28 Transmission by blood transfusion
has been described.32
Visceral and focal cutaneous leishmaniosis have been described in
dogs. In the Old World, Phlebotomus sand flies act as the vector; in
the New World, Lutzomyia sand flies act as primary vectors.29 The
regional distribution of disease depends on the regional distribution
of the specific vectors involved. Leishmania transitions between two
forms: the promastigote and the amastigote. Promastigotes are
infectious to dogs and humans while amastigotes are the form that
infects the sand fly vector during feeding on the mammalian host.
Promastigotes are inoculated into the skin when the sand fly feeds.
The promastigotes are then engulfed by macrophages and transform
into intracellular amastigotes which replicate and cause the
macrophages to rupture and release amastigotes that then infect
other macrophages. If the host immune response fails to control the
infection, amastigotes disseminate via regional lymphatics and the
blood to infect the entire reticuloendothelial system. Amastigotes
ingested by a female sand fly during feeding convert back into
promastigotes in the sand fly gut, and replication of promastigotes

within the sand fly completes the life cycle.33 Dogs that mount strong
T-cell–mediated immune responses can eliminate the infection,
whereas those that mount weak cell-mediated immune responses
and marked, nonprotective humoral (IgG) immune responses
develop clinical disease.34 Others can remain subclinically infected
and disease can reactivate later in life.35

CLINICAL SIGNS AND ROUTINE
DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
The most common clinical signs in dogs are cutaneous lesions
characterized by alopecia, scaling, and nodules or papules (Figure
197.2) that develop long before signs of systemic disease, despite the
presence of disseminated infection. Systemic signs include fever,
muscle wasting, splenomegaly, secondary immune-mediated
polyarthritis (ch. 177), anterior uveitis (ch. 13), glomerulonephritis
(ch. 302), and hematologic abnormalities such as nonregenerative
anemia (ch. 172) and lymphopenia.35,36 Leishmaniosis can induce
either a mono- or polyclonal gammopathy (ch. 60).37

DEFINITIVE DIAGNOSIS
Diagnosis of leishmaniosis can be achieved via direct identification of
the organism in tissues using histopathologic or cytologic
examination. However, molecular detection using PCR is preferred
due to its excellent sensitivity.38 Serologic testing to detect antiLeishmania antibodies can pose diagnostic challenges in endemic
areas as many dogs will remain seropositive despite clearance of
infection.

TREATMENT
Treatment can be challenging since most dogs do not clear the
infection. Some can relapse or, in endemic areas, become reinfected.

Many treatments are not available in the US. Dual therapy with
allopurinol and meglumine (a pentavalent antimonial) is the
treatment of choice. Most dogs require weeks to months of treatment
before clinical improvement is evident. Clinical trials have shown
that both miltefosine, an FDA approved drug for human
leishmaniasis, and artesunate, an FDA approved drug for malaria,
could be reasonable treatment options for canine Leishmania
infections.39,40

HEPATOZOON
DESCRIPTION
Two species of Hepatozoon cause disease in dogs.41 In Europe, Asia,
Africa, and South America, Hepatozoon canis is vectored by the
brown dog tick (Rhipicephalus sanguineus) (ch. 9). In the US,
Hepatozoon americanum is vectored by the Gulf coast tick
(Amblyomma maculatum).42 Sporozoites, found within tick vectors,
are the infectious stage for dogs. Dogs are infected by ingestion of
infected ticks or by ingestion of infected mammalian prey.42 Cats are
rarely infected. When a dog ingests an infected tick, sporozoites are
released from the tick’s gut, invade mononuclear cells, and spread
systemically. In H. americanum infections, the organism spreads
preferentially to skeletal muscle where it encysts between myocytes.

FIGURE 197.2 Image of a 7-year-old male terrier
mixed breed dog with leishmaniosis imported from
France to the US 2 years prior to presentation. Note
the ulcerative and exudative crusting lesions across
the nasal planum at the mucocutaneous junction.

CLINICAL SIGNS AND ROUTINE
DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
Infection results in a wasting disease characterized by fever,
apparent pain or lameness, and mucopurulent ocular discharge.
Clinicopathologic testing often reveals a nonregenerative anemia,

marked leukocytosis, hypoglycemia, hypoalbuminemia, and
increased activity of serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP). Cytologic
evaluation of blood smears is insensitive for diagnosing
hepatozoonosis because there tends to be low levels of parasitemia in
circulating granulocytes. Once encysted in muscle,
pyogranulomatous myositis develops.43 In some dogs, persistent
infection is associated with glomerulonephritis. Osteoproliferative
lesions are common in dogs infected with H. americanum; they are
most common in the proximal appendicular skeleton, but can extend
to distal tibia, fibula, radius, and ulna. The axial skeleton is less
commonly affected.44 Radiographs can reveal profound periosteal
proliferation particularly at sites of muscle attachment.

DIAGNOSIS
ELISA assays that detect antibodies to both H. americanum and H.
canis are available, sensitive and specific for diagnosing
hepatozoonosis in dogs.45 The application of PCR assays to whole
blood and buffy coat specimens allows detection of Hepatozoon spp.
and differentiation between H. americanum and H. canis. PCR
assays have been shown to be more sensitive than cytologic
evaluation of blood smears for detection of Hepatozoon.46,47

TREATMENT
Treatment of hepatozoonosis is difficult. Even long-term
administration of anti-protozoal drugs such as potentiated
sulfonamides, clindamycin, and pyrimethamine have been
associated with relapsing infections. In one study, long-term
administration of decoquinate (10-20 mg/kg PO q12h) achieved
prolonged remission.48 Supportive care including administration of
NSAIDs can be helpful in ameliorating clinical signs. Spontaneous
remissions have been documented, but the reason for this outcome
in dogs is unclear.

TOXOPLASMA
DESCRIPTION AND PATHOGENESIS
Toxoplasma gondii, an obligate intracellular coccidian parasite in
the family Apicomplexa, is one of the most prevalent parasites
infecting warm-blooded vertebrates. Cats are the definitive host, and
the parasite depends on cats to complete its life cycle, undergo sexual
reproduction and pass infectious oocysts via feces into their
environment.49 There are three life stages of Toxoplasma. The first
is sporozoites, which develop in oocysts after 1 to 5 days of exposure
to oxygen and appropriate environmental temperature and humidity.
Tachyzoites develop after extraintestinal infection, disseminate in
blood or lymph during active infection and replicate rapidly
intracellularly until the cell is destroyed.49 Bradyzoites are the slowly
dividing, persistent, tissue stage that form in the extraintestinal
tissues of infected hosts as immune responses attenuate tachyzoite
replication. Tissue cysts can occur in the central nervous system
(CNS), muscles, and visceral organs.
Infection of warm-blooded vertebrates occurs after ingestion of
any of the 3 life stages of the organism or transplacentally via
tachyzoite spread during pregnancy.50 There are rare reports of
Toxoplasma transmission during transfusion or transplantation of
organs.51 Most cats are not coprophagic, and therefore are typically
infected by ingesting T. gondii tachy- or bradyzoites resulting from
ingestion of prey. Following enteroepithelial infection, oocysts can be
shed in feces from 3-21 days. Sporulated oocysts can survive in the
environment for months to years and are resistant to most
disinfectants. Bradyzoites may persist in tissues for the life of the
host. About 30-40% of cats and 20% of dogs in the US are
seropositive and presumed infected.

CLINICAL SIGNS
Clinical disease during the gastrointestinal (GI) phase of infection is
rare. Detection of T. gondii oocysts in feces has been rare in studies
of naturally exposed cats with diarrhea. Most clinical signs result

from systemic dissemination following extraintestinal infection that
develops from overwhelming intracellular replication of tachyzoites.
Disease can be severe, potentially resulting in death in dogs and cats.
Liver, lungs, CNS, pancreas, and/or eye, are commonly involved
(Figure 197.3).
Immune deficiency secondary to viral infection or immunesuppressive therapy can lead to fatal toxoplasmosis. Retroviral
infection in cats does not seem to increase risk of disease
reactivation.52-54 Common clinical findings in cats with
disseminated toxoplasmosis include lethargy, anorexia, and fever
followed by hypothermia, peritoneal effusion, icterus, and tachypnea
or cough.55
In dogs, respiratory, GI, or neuromuscular infection resulting in
respiratory signs (such as cough or tachypnea), vomiting, diarrhea,
fever, cutaneous disease, and icterus are most common, occurring
most frequently in immune-suppressed dogs, such as those with
canine distemper virus infection or those receiving cyclosporine for
control of immune-mediated disease (chs. 144 and 204). Neurologic
signs depend on primary lesion location and can range from ataxia,
seizures, tremors, and cranial nerve deficits, to paresis and paralysis.
Dogs with myositis can be weak, be stiff-gaited or have muscle
wasting. Rapid progression to tetraparesis and paralysis with lower
motor neuron dysfunction can occur.
Depending on geographic region, some dogs suspected of
neuromuscular toxoplasmosis may have neosporosis (see below).
Myocardial infection can result in ventricular arrhythmias in some
infected dogs. Cough, tachypnea, vomiting, or diarrhea can occur in
dogs with polysystemic disease. Chorioretinitis, anterior uveitis,
iridocyclitis, and optic neuritis occur in some dogs but are less
common than in cats. Keratitis due to T. gondii infection has also
been reported.
Chronic toxoplasmosis occurs in some dogs and cats. Toxoplasma
gondii infection can cause anterior or posterior uveitis in cats
(Figure 197.3, A), fever, muscle hyperesthesia, weight loss,
anorexia, seizures, ataxia, icterus, diarrhea, cutaneous disease, and
pancreatitis.

ROUTINE DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
Toxoplasmosis can cause a variety of clinicopathologic and
radiographic abnormalities, but none are pathognomonic.
Nonregenerative anemia, neutrophilic leukocytosis or neutropenia,
lymphocytosis, monocytosis, eosinophilia, proteinuria, bilirubinuria,
hyperglobulinemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and increases in serum
creatine kinase, alanine aminotransferase, ALP, and lipase activities
occur in some animals.55 Pulmonary toxoplasmosis typically causes
diffuse interstitial to alveolar patterns or pleural effusion (Figure
197.3, B). Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein concentrations and cell
counts are often increased (ch. 109).56 The predominant white
blood cells (WBCs) in CSF are small mononuclear cells, but
neutrophils also are commonly found. In cats with neurologic signs,
CSF findings can resemble those found in feline infectious
peritonitis.

FIGURE 197.3 Images from a 13-year-old male

DIAGNOSIS
A diagnosis of toxoplasmosis can be strongly suspected if tachyzoites
are demonstrated within a clinical specimen (recognizing that they
may not be distinguishable from those of Neospora caninum);
however, bradyzoites or tachyzoites are rarely detected in tissues,

effusions, bronchoalveolar lavage fluids, aqueous humor, or CSF.
Detection of 10 × 12 micrometer oocysts in feces (ch. 80) in cats
with diarrhea suggests intestinal phase infection (cats with systemic
disease usually do not shed oocysts) but is not definitive, because
Besnoitia and Hammondia infections of cats produce
morphologically similar oocysts.
Toxoplasma gondii–specific antibodies (dogs or cats), antigens
(cats), immune complexes (cats), and DNA (dogs or cats) can be
detected in the blood of normal animals, as well as in those with
clinical signs of disease. It is not possible, therefore, to make a
diagnosis of clinical toxoplasmosis based on these tests. A single high
(>1:64) IgM titer or a fourfold change in serum IgG in an animal
with consistent clinical signs and a clinical response to
antimicrobials with known activity against Toxoplasma can help
establish a clinical diagnosis. Because bradyzoites persist in tissues
after initial infection, most animals will be antibody-positive for life;
therefore, repeating serum antibody titers after clinical disease has
resolved is of little use unless being used to confirm suspicion of
recent infection. The combination of aqueous humor or CSF T.
gondii–specific antibody detection and organism DNA detection by
PCR is most accurate for diagnosing ocular or CNS toxoplasmosis in
cats (Diagnostic Laboratory, College of Veterinary Medicine and
Biomedical Sciences, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO).57

TREATMENT
Clindamycin hydrochloride, trimethoprim-sulfonamide
combination, or azithromycin have been successful in treating
clinical toxoplasmosis.58 Pyrimethamine combined with sulfa drugs
is effective for the treatment of human toxoplasmosis but commonly
results in toxicosis in cats. Cats or dogs with uveitis should be treated
with topical, oral, or parenteral glucocorticoids to avoid secondary
glaucoma and/or lens luxation that can be irreversible. Optimal
treatment duration for clinical toxoplasmosis in dogs or cats is
unknown but generally is recommended for at least 4 weeks.

ZOONOTIC RISK
Risk of human infection by T. gondii is greater from consumption of
contaminated food or environmental exposure than from direct
exposure to domestic cats.59 In many parts of the world,
seroreactivity to T. gondii is similar in humans to that in cats.60-62
Regardless, it is sensible for those at greatest risk for toxoplasmosis
(e.g., seronegative women of childbearing age or
immunocompromised individuals) to receive information about
toxoplasmosis and how to prevent infection (see client handout).

NEOSPORA
DESCRIPTION
N. caninum is an apicomplexan protozoal parasite first identified as
distinct from Toxoplasma in 1988.63,64 Similar to T. gondii, the
sexual cycle is completed in the GI tract (albeit in dogs) and results
in the shedding of oocysts in feces. Sporozoites develop in oocysts
within 24 hours of passage. Tachyzoites (rapidly dividing stage) and
tissue cysts containing hundreds of bradyzoites (slowly dividing
stage) are the other two life stages that develop following infection.
Transplacental infection has been well documented; females giving
birth to infected offspring can repeat transplacental infection during
subsequent pregnancies. Naturally occurring infections have been
reported in dogs, cattle, sheep, goats, horses, and deer. Prevalence is
estimated to be 17% worldwide (range from 2% to >50%) with higher
proportions found in rural and farm dogs.65,66 Similarly, the
prevalence in cattle on farms with dogs is much higher than in cattle
on farms without dogs. Although organism replication occurs in
many tissues, clinical illness primarily reflects neuromuscular
infection in dogs. Although encephalomyelitis and myositis develop
in experimentally infected kittens and some naturally exposed cats
are seropositive for N. caninum antibodies, clinical disease in
naturally infected cats has not been reported. Canine neosporosis has
been reported in many countries around the world.

CLINICAL SIGNS
Several clinical syndromes associated with neosporosis have been
described in dogs. The most severe infections are in congenitally
infected puppies that can develop ascending paralysis with
hyperextension of the pelvic limbs and muscle atrophy. This can lead
to generalized weakness that can result in dysphagia and death.
Polymyositis and multifocal CNS disease can occur alone or in
combination. Clinical signs can be evident soon after birth or may be
delayed for several weeks. Neonatal death is common. Although
disease tends to be most severe in congenitally infected puppies,
dogs as old as 15 years have been clinically affected. Most dogs are
infected post-natally.65 In some dogs, myocarditis, ulcerative
dermatitis, pneumonia, CNS disease, and hepatitis occur. Dogs
treated with immunosuppressive drugs can reactivate subclinical
infections or develop severe clinical illness if exposed to N. caninum
for the first time. Dogs with CNS neosporosis generally have
multifocal disease, which can affect the cerebellum, cerebral cortex,
and brainstem.67

ROUTINE DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
As with toxoplasmosis, there are no specific hematologic or
biochemical findings specific to neosporosis, but increased serum
creatine kinase and aspartate transaminase activities are common in
dogs with myositis. Nonregenerative anemia can also occur. CSF
abnormalities include moderately to markedly increased protein
concentrations and a mild to marked mononuclear pleocytosis.67
Interstitial and alveolar patterns can be noted on thoracic
radiographs. Demonstration of tachyzoites in CSF or tissues supports
the diagnosis, although tachyzoites are rarely identified on cytologic
examination of CSF, dermatologic lesions, or bronchoalveolar lavage.
Dogs with CNS neosporosis usually have multifocal disease on
magnetic resonance imaging. N. caninum tissue cysts have a wall
thickness greater than 1 micrometer (greater than T. gondii cysts
that are <1 micrometer). The organism can be differentiated from T.
gondii by electron microscopy, immunohistochemistry, or PCR.

Molecular techniques have also been used to show that different
strains of N. caninum exist and might account for variability of
clinical signs of disease.

DIAGNOSIS
A presumptive diagnosis of neosporosis can be made by combining
appropriate clinical signs and positive serologic titers with the
exclusion of other causes associated with similar clinical syndromes,
particularly T. gondii. Immunoglobulin G antibody titers ≥1:200
have been detected in most dogs with neosporosis and minimal
serologic cross-reactivity with T. gondii occurs when measured by
IFA testing.64 Antibodies to N. caninum can also be detected in CSF
of some affected dogs.

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis for dogs with severe neurologic involvement is
guarded. Some have survived after treatment with trimethoprimsulfadiazine combined with pyrimethamine; sequential treatment
with clindamycin hydrochloride, trimethoprim-sulfadiazine, and
pyrimethamine; or clindamycin alone. Although improvement has
been associated with clindamycin treatment, it does not appear to
clear infection.68 Newer drugs like artemisone have shown
promising results in vitro and should be evaluated in vivo in dogs.69
Glucocorticoids or other immune-suppressive drugs may predispose
to more severe infection.

ZOONOTIC CONCERNS
N. caninum antibodies have been detected in people, including those
with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and neurologic
disease. However, there is no other evidence of zoonotic spread as
neither organism nor parasite DNA has been isolated from human
specimens.70 Overall, the zoonotic link is unclear, but it seems

prudent to avoid ingesting canine feces or undercooked meat. There
has been an epidemiologic link between dogs and cattle; therefore,
efforts should be made to lessen dog fecal contamination of livestock
feed, and dogs should not be allowed to ingest bovine placentas or
venison. Bitches that whelp clinically affected puppies should be
spayed as pregnancy leads to reactivation of infection and
development of clinical neosporosis in their litters.71,72

CLIENT INFORMATION
Risk of Toxoplasmosis in People
Toxoplasmosis is associated with various forms of disease in people
that are most severe in the fetus and immune-suppressed
individuals. Risk factors associated with Toxoplasma gondii
infection in humans in the United States include eating undercooked
meat as well as exposure to oocysts (the infectious particles) found in
cat litter boxes. Thus, at-risk people should also avoid exposure to
feline feces that are >24 hours old by cleaning the litter box daily,
washing hands or wearing gloves while gardening or otherwise
coming in contact with soil, and washing (or cooking) produce well
before it is eaten.
Although owning a pet cat has occasionally been associated with
acquiring toxoplasmosis, touching individual cats is not a common
way to acquire toxoplasmosis as cats generally shed oocysts only for
days to several weeks after primary inoculation and repeat shedding
is very rare. Furthermore, cats are fastidious groomers and tend not
to allow feces to remain on their coats for long enough to allow to
oocysts the opportunity to dry out and become infectious.

Unfortunately there is no blood test that accurately predicts when
a cat will shed T. gondii oocysts. Cats that have antibodies to T.
gondii are unlikely to shed oocysts, but a cat that lacks antibodies to
T. gondii may shed oocysts if it becomes infected. Risk of infection in
cats can be reduced by keeping cats indoors and feeding cooked or
commercial diets. If you are concerned that you have toxoplasmosis,
are immunocompromised or considering pregnancy, you should seek
counseling and medical advice from your doctor.
Jonathan David Dear (Davis, California)

OVERVIEW

Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) infection is common among
domestic cats worldwide. Transmission occurs primarily during
aggressive territorial encounters. Infection with FIV is lifelong.
Although the immunological consequences of FIV infection in cats
mirror many of those seen in human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)infected humans, the clinical manifestations of most FIV infections
are mild or absent. Cats that die from FIV-associated diseases have
no pathognomonic signs, which makes assigning clinical relevance to
FIV infection in an individual cat challenging. Diagnostic
investigation of ill, FIV-infected cats with clinical signs frequently
reveals treatable problems. Screening diagnostic tests detect
circulating antibodies to the virus. Depending on the circumstances,
additional serologic or molecular testing can assist in determining a
cat’s true infection status. Confinement of uninfected cats is the most
effective way to prevent transmission. FIV presents no known
zoonotic risk.

ETIOLOGY AND EPIDEMIOLOGY
Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV), family Retroviridae, subfamily
Orthoretrovirinae, genus Lentivirus, describes a large group of
closely related viruses that are endemic in domestic and wild cats, as
well as spotted hyenas.1 FIV of the domestic cat is classified into
distinct subtypes or clades (currently designated A to E) based on
sequence diversity (up to 26%) of the variable region of the env gene.
The true genetic diversity of FIV at the population level is likely
higher due to the frequent occurrence of recombination.2,3 Virus
diversity has implications for the design and interpretation of
molecular diagnostic tests as well as the efficacy of FIV vaccines (ch.
185).
Antibodies to FIV are found in domestic cat populations across the
globe. Seroprevalence varies from <2.5% to >14%,4 depending on the
region and the population tested. Risk factors for FIV infection
include age, sex, environment, breed, and health status; adult, male,
free-roaming, crossbred, and sick cats are at increased risk.5 The
average age of FIV-infected cats is 5 to 6 years.6 FIV is transmitted

by direct inoculation of saliva or blood during fighting.7 Other routes
of transmission are of minor epidemiological significance. Horizontal
transmission of FIV between cats in stable households is rare, in
sharp contrast to the major feline retroviral pathogen, feline
leukemia virus (FeLV) (ch. 199), which spreads rapidly between
housemates.6 Vertical or perinatal transmission of naturally acquired
FIV is documented infrequently, but primary infection of the queen
during pregnancy may increase risk of maternal transmission.8
Natural sexual transmission of FIV is not documented, but the virus
can be recovered from semen.9
In veterinary hospitals, no additional biosecurity precautions over
and above those for any feline patient are necessary for dealing with
FIV-infected cats. Virus shed in secretions is rapidly inactivated in
dry conditions; routine cleaning and disinfection procedures to
prevent the spread of feline herpesvirus 1 (FHV-1) (ch. 205), feline
calicivirus (FCV) (ch. 205), and feline panleukopenia virus (FPV)
(ch. 201) effectively eliminate any residual risk of environmental
contamination. Nosocomial transmission of FIV infection is virtually
impossible unless there is parenteral inoculation of contaminated
blood or saliva from an FIV-infected cat. Cats used as blood donors
must be free from FIV infection since iatrogenic transmission by this
route is inevitable.10 Cats should not be housed in isolation facilities
on the basis of FIV status alone, since this places potentially
immunosuppressed cats at risk of exposure to other infectious
diseases.
FIV presents no known zoonotic risk. However,
immunosuppressed humans, e.g., transplant recipients, should
minimize contact with FIV-infected cats or observe meticulous
hygiene precautions to avoid possible exposure to shared
opportunistic pathogens.

PATHOGENESIS
FIV infection can be broadly considered to progress in three stages: a
transient primary stage, a chronic subclinical stage, and a terminal
stage (Figure 198.1). In contrast to HIV, where without

antiretroviral treatment patients progress through predictable, wellcharacterized clinical stages to the terminal acquired
immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) stage, the consequences of FIV
infection are less predictable.11,12 A majority of FIV-infected cats
remain free from significant disease and have a normal life
expectancy.11

CLINICAL SIGNS
All FIV-infected cats are at risk of developing immune dysfunction,
which can manifest as immune deficiency or immune-mediated
disease. Healthy FIV-infected cats should be carefully examined and
even minor problems fully assessed. Immune dysfunction can be
seen clinically as atypical and refractory bacterial, viral, or parasitic
infections. Respiratory infections, bacterial pyoderma, generalized
demodicosis, mycobacterial infection, disseminated cowpox,
pulmonary cryptococcosis, and lungworm infections are reported.
Persistent cytopenias, particularly neutropenia or lymphopenia, are
described in advanced FIV infection (chs. 172, 175, and 180).13 FIV
infection has been linked to feline chronic gingivostomatitis (FCGS),
a painful and debilitating condition that can severely impact quality
of life (Figure 198.2).14 Risk of lymphoma is increased in FIVinfected cats by 5- to 6-fold.15 This increased risk is small in
comparison to the 60-fold increase in risk of lymphoma associated
with FeLV infection. FIV-associated lymphomas are typically highgrade, extranodal, B-cell tumors, similar to HIV-associated diffuse
large B-cell lymphoma (Figure 198.3).

FIGURE 198.1 Course of feline immunodeficiency
virus (FIV) infection. During the acute stage, plasma
virus load increases. An adaptive immune response
suppresses viremia within approximately 8 weeks.
The chronic stage follows, lasting for several years
and is characterized by relatively low viral load, and
progressive decline of CD4+ T lymphocytes. In a
minority of FIV-infected cats, an immunodeficiencylike syndrome (terminal stage) develops, which can
last for several weeks and ends with euthanasia on
humane grounds or death. CTL, Cytotoxic T
lymphocytes; PVL, plasma viral load; p24, viral
capsid protein.

FIGURE 198.2 Gingivostomatitis with marked
involvement of the fauces. Courtesy Matthew
Oxford.
Severe unexplained weight loss (ch. 18) can occur in the terminal
stage of FIV infection. This presentation resembles “wasting
syndrome,” an AIDS-defining condition in HIV infection, indicating
weight loss of 10% or more over 30 days with no identifiable cause
other than HIV infection. FIV-associated neuropathology has been
studied extensively as an experimental model for neurodegenerative
diseases in HIV infection.16 The incidence of neurological signs
accompanying natural FIV infection is unknown.

DIAGNOSIS
CATS THAT SHOULD BE TESTED
FIV-infected cats should be identified to optimize individual health
care and to prevent new infections. Ideally, the current retrovirus
status of all cats should be known. Priorities for FIV-testing include
free-roaming cats, ill cats, cats with fight wounds, blood donors,

adult cats being rehomed, kittens born to FIV-infected queens, and
any cat prior to FIV vaccination.17

TESTING OVERVIEW
Determining the true FIV infection status of an individual cat may
involve repeat testing. Advising owners of this possibility at the
outset can be helpful for maintaining confidence. Commercial FIV
tests detect either anti-FIV antibodies by immunoassays or viral
nucleic acid by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (ch. 184). Other
serologic assays, including immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) assays
and Western blotting, have limited availability, are technically
demanding, and are subject to interoperator interpretation
variability. Western blotting appears to be less sensitive than
enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) in some
laboratories.18 Virus isolation from peripheral blood mononuclear
cells is not commercially available.
Serologic assays are the first line for testing. Point-of-care (POC)
tests, utilizing bidirectional-flow ELISA or lateral flow
immunochromatography technologies, and diagnostic laboratorybased ELISA assays have high sensitivities and specificities for
antibody detection.17 In cats over 6 months of age that have not been
vaccinated against FIV, anti-FIV antibodies are a marker for FIV
infection.

FIV, Feline immunodeficiency virus; PCR, polymerase chain
reaction.
Molecular tests target DNA provirus and some also detect viral
RNA in plasma. PCR is not indicated as a screening test for FIV. It is
recommended as an adjunct to serology to determine the true FIV
status of cats in certain circumstances. For PCR, diagnostic
sensitivity is 5-15% lower than serologic testing, and specificities
comparable with those for serologic testing are reported.19 Sequence
variability among isolates and low virus load may contribute to lower
sensitivity of PCR than serologic testing for FIV detection.

INTERPRETING FIV SEROLOGY
FIV serologic test results need to be interpreted in the context of the
case to guide whether repeat serologic testing or PCR is indicated,
and the timing of any repeat testing. The time to seroconversion
following natural infection is variable.20 In a seronegative cat where
recent exposure cannot be ruled out, the cat should ideally be
isolated from other cats and retested after 60 days. Some cats in the
terminal stage of FIV infection have impaired antibody production
and test seronegative. These cats often have high plasma viral
loads.21 If terminal FIV infection is suspected, a negative serologic
result should be followed by PCR (Table 198.1). Considerations
when interpreting positive serologic test results for an individual cat
are shown in Table 198.2.

Cats at Low Risk of Infection
False positive tests results are more common in cats at low risk of
infection, such as young, purebred, indoor cats. In this group the
positive predictive value of the test is reduced because the prevalence
of FIV in a low-risk population is close to the expected frequency of
false positives.

Maternal FIV Antibodies
Antibodies absorbed by kittens from colostrum of infected (or
vaccinated) queens may result in positive FIV serologic test results in
uninfected kittens. Maternally derived anti-FIV antibodies can
persist for months. Young cats with positive serologic test results
should be retested after 6 months.

Prior Vaccination Against FIV
An inactivated, whole virus FIV vaccine is still commercially
available in some regions, including Australia and New Zealand. If
prior vaccination against FIV is documented or if it cannot be ruled
out, then selection of the POC test for FIV is important because
vaccine-induced antibodies are detected in some circumstances. The
SNAP Combo FeLV Ag/FIV Ab Test (IDEXX Laboratories, Inc.,
Westbrook, Maine, USA) has high (94-100%) sensitivity and
specificity for detection of anti-FIV antibodies, but does not readily
distinguish between the antibody response induced by vaccination
and that induced by natural infection. Two other POC assays,
WITNESS FeLV‐FIV Test Kit (Zoetis, Inc., Florham Park, NJ, USA)
and Anigen Rapid FIV Ab/FeLV Ag Test Kit (Bionote, Inc.,
Hwaseong‐shi, South Korea) can be used to distinguish FIV-infected
cats from cats administered an annual FIV booster vaccination with
100% specificity.22 However, even these two POC tests may give
positive results in FIV-uninfected cats that have recently received a
primary FIV vaccination course. The reliability of a negative
serologic test result is unchanged by a history of vaccination.

PROGNOSIS
Long-term survival in FIV-infected cats is comparable with that in
uninfected cats. There is no justification for the euthanasia of healthy
cats on the basis of FIV status. Even though the negative effect of FIV
infection on survival is minor or nonexistent when groups of cats are
studied, the effect of FIV on morbidity is potentially underestimated.
It is incumbent upon clinicians to maintain an index of suspicion for

subtle consequences of immune dysfunction in every FIV-infected
cat.

MANAGEMENT
Comprehensive international guidelines for the management of FIVinfected cats from the American Association of Feline Practitioners
and the European Advisory Board on Cat Diseases (ABCD) are
available online.17,23,24

REGULAR AND PREVENTIVE
HEALTHCARE
Since FIV-infected cats are the source of new infections, they should
be prevented from contacting uninfected cats. This means confining
FIV-infected cats indoors or in an enclosure, singly or with other
FIV-infected cats. Overcrowded housing conditions should be
avoided because environmental stress can have a significant impact
on disease progression in FIV-positive cats.12 When a cat from a
multicat household is identified as FIV-infected, all cats in the house
should be tested and infected and uninfected cats should be housed
separately. Owners should be advised that FIV can spread between
cats in the household, although this risk appears to be small in
stable, small, closed households.
Annual or semiannual veterinary check-ups for FIV-infected cats
can facilitate early detection of emerging health problems. Whether
booster vaccinations for core pathogens FPV, FCV, and FHV-1 are
safe or efficacious in FIV-infected cats, given the potential for
immunosuppression, has been clarified by recent ABCD
guidelines.24 Core booster vaccinations for FIV-infected cats kept
indoors are not recommended unless indicated by FPV serology.
Where potential exposure to FPV (ch. 201), FCV (ch. 205), or FHV1 (ch. 205) has occurred, inactivated vaccines are recommended for
FIV-infected cats (ch. 185). Advice on the importance of
ectoparasites and endoparasite control (see textbook’s inside covers),

dental prophylaxis (ch. 258), and a balanced diet (ch. 148) should
be given to owners.

SICK FIV-INFECTED CATS
Management of Clinical Signs
In the absence of reliable surrogate markers for disease progression,
the prognosis for an individual FIV-infected cat should be
determined without regard to its FIV status. Many sick FIV-infected
cats have treatable diseases. Knowing that a cat is FIV- infected is
not a reason to curtail the investigation but instead will inform the
list of differentials and help guide the diagnostic investigation and
treatment selection.
Where antibiotics are indicated, selection should ideally be based
on the results of susceptibility testing. Bactericidal antibiotics are
preferred and extended or repeat courses may be required. Clinicians
should be vigilant for drug reactions; severe drug-induced
neutropenia following griseofulvin administration has been reported
in FIV-infected cats.25 Use of glucocorticoids is counterintuitive in
immunosuppressed cats, but may be indicated to treat inflammatory
or immune-mediated conditions (ch. 227). Glucocorticoids should
be used judiciously, only where specifically indicated, and patients
should be monitored closely.
Severe or persistent cytopenias in FIV-infected cats should be
investigated for treatable underlying causes since cytopenias are
common in sick cats regardless of their FIV status (ch. 176).11,26
There is no treatment for FIV-associated neutropenia. Anemia
occurs with FIV infection, although less commonly than neutropenia.
Although studies in FIV-infected cats have not been reported,
darbepoetin could be considered (off-label) in moderately or severely
anemic FIV-infected cats.27
Management of FIV-associated wasting involves investigation for
treatable diseases including enteropathies (ch. 262) and exocrine
pancreatic insufficiency (ch. 279), supportive care, nutritional
support (ch. 151) and appetite stimulation (ch. 17). In cats with
lymphoma there is no evidence that FIV infection per se is a negative

prognostic indicator for response to multiagent chemotherapy,
although data are limited.28

Immune Modulation
Before embarking on a treatment with immunomodulators, the
owners’ expectations should be carefully managed. The small chance
of improving clinical signs should be balanced against potential risks
and costs. Interferons such as feline interferon-omega are effective
against FIV in vitro.24 Although improvements in clinical
parameters are reported using recombinant feline interferon-omega
(rFeIFN-omega,Virbagen Omega, Virbac), and oral recombinant
human interferon alpha (rHuIFN-alpha),29 convincing clinical
evidence that the use of immune modulators has a positive effect on
the health or survival of FIV-infected cats is lacking. Nonspecific
immune stimulation may even be contraindicated as it risks
unintended outcomes, including increased virus replication and
progression of the disease.24

Antiviral Therapies
As for immune modulators, management of owner expectations for
antiviral therapy is important at the outset.
In contrast to HIV infection, the use of antiretroviral therapies for
FIV infection is limited by their toxicity and poor efficacy. Most
inhibitors of HIV protease are not active against FIV protease and
data on potential inhibitors of FIV integrase are limited to their
in vitro activity.30 Several nucleoside analogues inhibit FIV reverse
transcriptase, including zidovudine (AZT, 3′-azido-3′deoxythymidine), lamivudine (3TC, 2′,3′-dideoxy-3′-thiacytidine)
and adefovir (PMEA, 9-[2-(phosphonomethoxy)ethyl]adenine).
Improvements in clinical scores, virus load, and CD4 counts are
reported in some studies but adverse effects, including anemia,
neutropenia, and gastrointestinal signs, are common and can be
severe. Monitoring weekly complete blood counts for the first month
of treatment and then monthly is advised. Treatment is not
recommended for cats with myelosuppressive diseases. AZT should
be discontinued if the hematocrit drops below 20%, after which

anemia usually resolves in a few days. AZT-resistant FIV mutants
can develop as early as 6 months from initiation of treatment.30
Plerixafor (AMD3100), a selective CXCR4 antagonist, has been
evaluated in client-owned, FIV-infected cats. A prospective, placebocontrolled, double-blind trial showed mild reductions in proviral
load, minimal adverse effects, and no emergence of resistance over a
6-week period, but without improvement in clinical or immunologic
variables.30

PREVENTION
The most effective method of preventing FIV infection is to confine
uninfected cats. Free-roaming cats are at high risk of FIV infection,
as well as being an important source of new infections. Confining
owned FIV-infected cats is also advised to prevent new infections.
Providing an enriched environment that prevents roaming is
effective not only in reducing infectious disease risk, but also in
preventing trauma, straying and hunting.
An inactivated whole virus FIV vaccine (Fel-O-Vax FIV,
Boehringer Ingelheim) was discontinued in the USA and Canada in
2015 and has never been available in Europe. The FIV vaccine is
considered “non-core” by the World Small Animal Veterinary
Association (WSAVA [2016]; ch. 185 and textbook’s inside
covers).31 In regions where it remains available the FIV vaccine
could be considered for cats at high risk of infection, such as outdoor
cats involved in territorial aggression, although recent studies
suggest that the FIV vaccine confers only limited protection in the
field.32,33

CLIENT INFORMATION
Feline Immunodeficiency Virus Infection
SUMMARY
Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) is a common viral infection of
cats worldwide. The virus is spread by biting. Although any cat can
become infected, FIV is more common in intact (not neutered) male
cats that are involved in territorial fights. Most FIV-infected cats
have a normal life-expectancy although some cats can become sick
from the virus. Humans or other animals cannot catch FIV from
infected cats.
HOW DO CATS CATCH FIV?
FIV is spread during serious territorial cat fights when saliva from an
infected cat is “injected” into another cat through a bite wound.
Adult, male, outdoor cats that are not neutered, are at greatest risk of
infection. It is rare for FIV to be passed from infected queens to their
kittens or between cats that live together in small, stable groups.
HOW DOES FIV-INFECTION AFFECT A CAT’S HEALTH?
The outcome of FIV infection is variable between cats. Most FIVinfected cats remain healthy for years and they may never get sick
from the virus. In other cats, FIV can predispose to chronic
problems, like inflammation in the mouth. Over time, FIV can affect
the immune system and increase susceptibility to infections. This
means that your veterinarian might need to prescribe longer courses
of treatment, or they may need to run tests for unusual diseases. In a
few cats, usually many years after becoming infected, FIV can
contribute to development of life-threatening diseases such as severe
muscle wasting or cancer.

HOW CAN I FIND OUT IF MY CAT HAS FIV?
If your cat becomes ill at any time during its life or goes outside and
gets involved in fights with other cats, your veterinarian may suggest
testing for FIV. If you are introducing a new cat to the existing
household, it is always a good idea to test it for FIV as well as feline
leukemia virus (another retrovirus) infection. Testing usually
involves a collection of a blood sample that is checked for antibodies
to FIV. Depending on the circumstances, your veterinarian may
recommend additional or repeat testing to confirm the result.
WHAT SPECIAL CARE DO HEALTHY FIV-INFECTED CATS
NEED?
There are no treatments that can eliminate the virus from the cat’s
body. However, many FIV-infected cats can stay in good health and
have a normal life span. There is no justification for the euthanasia of
a healthy FIV-positive cat. Your veterinarian will advise on optimal
care such as regular annual or bi-annual dental and health checks,
blood tests, vaccinations, and parasite control. FIV-infected cats
should be fed high quality commercial maintenance diets, unless
your cat has a concurrent disease which requires a special diet
formulation. All FIV-infected cats should ideally be confined indoors
and neutered to reduce the risk of territorial fights and spreading the
virus to other cats. FIV-infected cats tend to do well in stable, stress
free households. If you are planning to confine cats indoors or in an
enclosure, you can find helpful information on providing
environmental enrichment for your cats online (e.g.,
https://indoorpet.osu.edu/cats). Healthy FIV-infected cats do
not need to take antiviral medications. Use of any dietary
supplements or immune stimulants, unless advised by your
veterinarian, is discouraged.
WILL MY FIV-INFECTED CAT GET SICK?
If you adopt a healthy adult FIV-infected cat, there is a good chance
that it will be unaffected by the virus for many years, or even for its
whole lifetime. If your FIV-infected cat gets sick, it is important to
remember that FIV-infected cats are at risk from the same problems
that can affect any cat and many of these problems are treatable. In

some cats, usually only many years after becoming infected, FIV can
causes serious, terminal diseases.
Julia Beatty (City University of Hong Kong) and Paweł M.
Bęczkowski (City University of Hong Kong)

DEFINITIONS AND PREVALENCE
Feline leukemia virus (FeLV) is a retrovirus that affects domestic cats
worldwide. FeLV infection is associated with a variety of illnesses,
including neoplasia, bone marrow suppression, and
immunodeficiency. FeLV prevalence (usually determined by FeLV
antigenemia) is reported between 2.3% to 3.3% in the United States,
0% to 15.6% in Europe, 3.0% to 28.4% in South America, and 0% to
24.5% in Asia and Australia/New Zealand.1 The prevalence of FeLV
infection is higher in cats with specific risk factors (Table 199.1)
and in sick cats, e.g., up to 15% of certain diseases are associated with
FeLV,2 including lymphoma,3 cutaneous abscesses, bite wounds,4

and chronic gingivostomatitis.5 In a pan-European prevalence study
using FeLV RNA to assess cats for FeLV antigenemia in >6000 saliva
samples from 32 countries, the FeLV prevalence was 2.3%. There
was a high variability among countries, with a very low prevalence
(0-1%) in the northern European countries Denmark, Finland,
Norway, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. In western European
countries (The Netherlands, Germany, Austria, France, Belgium, and
Luxemburg) the prevalence was 0-1.3%. A higher prevalence of 4.58.8% was identified in southern European countries that included
Croatia, Italy, and Portugal.6 Generally, prevalence has decreased for
decades subsequent to widespread test and removal or separation
programs and common use of FeLV vaccines;2,7,8 however, in many
regions prevalence is still high or has not decreased any further,9-11
thereby demanding continuous awareness and vaccination of at-risk
cats (ch. 185).

PATHOGENESIS
VIRUS REPLICATION
The genomic RNA of the retrovirus FeLV is reverse transcribed into
DNA within infected cells. The DNA copies are then inserted into the
host genome (provirus). Thus, division of infected cells will result in
daughter cells that also contain the provirus. The viral genome
encodes for the major proteins: group-specific antigens (gag),
reverse transcriptase (pol), and envelope (env). One of the gag
proteins, p27, is abundant in the plasma of persistently infected cats
and is the basis for diagnostic point-of-care tests (PoCTs) (ch. 184).
The env protein defines the virus subgroup with different
pathogenicity (i.e., FeLV-A, -B, -C) and is important for inducing
immunity.1

OUTCOMES OF INFECTION
“Balance of Power”

There are 4 potential outcomes of FeLV infection that depend on the
balance of power between the virus and the cat’s immune system:
progressive (least favorable for the cat), regressive, abortive (most
favorable for the cat), and the probably rarely occurring focal
(atypical) infection (Box 199.1).12-16 Outcomes are determined by
certain risk factors (Table 199.1). Although the majority of cats
follows one of the 4 outcomes within a few months of infection,
varying and discrepant FeLV test results can be observed during this
early phase of infection. This is a time during which the interplay
between the cat’s immune system and the virus is at its peak and the
host-virus balance has not yet been definitively set.14,16
Even later after infection, the host-virus balance is not fixed (Box
199.1) and the advantage can swing to either cat or virus and, in
turn, change the course of FeLV infection. Examples are cats that
have been positive for soluble p27 antigen for a long period of time
(which would be classified as progressive infection) and then
suddenly become antigen-negative.17 On the other hand, in some
regressively infected cats, FeLV infection might be reactivated any
time after infection, although this occurs more frequently during
early infection.18 These observations demonstrate that FeLV
infection outcome is not fixed, and the course of infection is
determined by balance of power between immune system and virus,
not only during initial infection, but life-long in some cats (Box
199.1).

Early Infection
After mucosal or cutaneous exposure to FeLV, the virus replicates in
local lymphoid tissues. From there, infected cells carry the virus to
other target tissues, such as thymus, spleen, and lymph nodes. About
3 weeks after infection, bone marrow cells can become infected
(mainly in progressively infected cats that lack sufficient immunity
against FeLV), producing infected neutrophils and platelets that
circulate in the blood and carry the virus to salivary glands and
mucosal glandular epithelium, the sites that will eventually secrete
most of FeLV responsible for horizontal transmission. FeLV genetic
material is usually detectable within 1 week (viral RNA) to 2 weeks
(proviral DNA) of infection. In most cats, antigenemia (presence of

viral proteins in the blood) correlates with viremia (presence of
infectious virus that can be cultured from the blood), although some
cats have discordant findings.19,20

Four Potential Outcomes
Infected cats can either remain viremic and antigenemic (progressive
infection) or remain in or revert to an aviremic state (regressive
infection with or without transient viremia) in which neither antigen
nor culturable virus is detected but in which FeLV proviral DNA can
still be identified.12,21 Regressive and progressive infections can thus
be distinguished by repeated testing for soluble p27 antigen in
peripheral blood (Figure 199.1).22 They also can be distinguished
by their provirus load later (a few weeks to months) in the course of
infection.12,18,21 However, during early infection, cats undergoing
progressive or regressive infections have similar proviral and viral
RNA loads.23 Moreover, soluble p27 antigen loads can indicate
likelihood of infection outcome a few weeks after infection.21,24
Antigen loads were also suggested as a prognostic marker. Among
progressively infected cats, apparently healthy cats had lower soluble
p27 antigen loads than did cats with FeLV-associated diseases18 and
in shelter cats tested at intake, high antigen as well as high provirus
loads were associated with shorter survival.25 Cats with abortive
infection are negative in all direct virus detection methods (such as
tests for soluble p27 antigen and proviral DNA) and anti-FeLV
antibodies are the only sign of abortive infection.12,13
