Progressive Infection
The percentage of cats that will develop progressive FeLV infection
varies, and it is most often determined by risk factors (Table 199.1)
and infection pressure. There is about a 3% chance of progressive
infection after a single contact with a FeLV-shedding cat and a 30%
chance when a cat lives with a shedding cat for several weeks.26 The
virus has the upper hand in cats with progressive infection (Box
199.1). These cats continuously shed virus, frequently succumb to
FeLV-associated diseases within a few years, and have a decreased
life expectancy.8,27-29 In a long-term follow-up study on
experimentally FeLV-infected cats, progressively infected cats lived
an average (median) of 3.1 years (range from 0.6 to 6.5 years).18 Cats
with progressive infection have ineffective FeLV-specific immunity,
allowing extensive virus replication in the bone marrow, spread to
many tissues, and shedding of the virus.18,21,30

Regressive Infection
In regressive infection, an effective immune response can keep the
virus in check so that no, or only very limited, viral replication takes
place prior to or at the time of bone marrow infection (Box 199.1).
Between 1% and 11% of cats were found to be regressively infected. In
these cats, soluble p27 antigen is sometimes detectable in peripheral
blood within 2 to 3 weeks after virus exposure but the antigen
becomes undetectable 2 to 8 weeks later or, in rare cases, even after

many months.14,21,31,32 Cats with regressive infection have
persistent integration of FeLV DNA in their genome. Complete
clearance of FeLV provirus has not been detected in cats with
regressive infection, even up to 12 years after exposure.18 However,
FeLV provirus levels can fall under the detection limit of molecular
assays. Regressively infected cats only rarely develop FeLVassociated diseases such as lymphoma or bone marrow disorders.3336
In these cats, the provirus itself can disturb cellular mechanisms
(leading to bone marrow suppression) or act as an oncogenic
substance causing tumor development without necessity of
replicating virus. Even though viral shedding does not occur, it is
possible for cats with regressive infection to transmit FeLV following
blood and tissue donation since proviral DNA can be infectious.37
The regressive state can convert to a progressive state, called
“reactivation” (Box 199.1). This is more likely to occur soon after
exposure to FeLV, but also has been described in cats that were
antigen-negative for many years.38

Abortive Infection
Abortively infected cats have efficient immunity against FeLV and
neither provirus integration nor viral replication occurs (Box 199.1).
It is unclear how common abortive infection occurs naturally, but its
frequency might be under estimated.14,31

Focal Infection
In cats with focal (i.e., atypical) infection, the immune system keeps
FeLV in check and virus replication is sequestered in tissues e.g.,
spleen, lymph nodes, small intestine, mammary glands (Box 199.1).
Soluble p27 antigen can be released at times into the peripheral
blood, but no infected cells are detectable. This can result in
discordant or alternating test results and diagnostic difficulties. Cats
with focal FeLV infection are probably rare and not a major
epidemiological concern, but this infection outcome can lead to
confusing FeLV test results.14,16,39

It is important to realize that infection outcome is not fixed at all
times—it depends on the balance between the immune system of
the cat and the virus, which can tip under certain circumstances.
For example, immunosuppression for any reason can favor the
virus, whereby a regressive infection can be reactivated or a focal
infection can become systemic. On the other hand, if the cat gains
the upper hand, a progressive infection can be overcome even late
after exposure. Vaccine-induced immunity leads to a situation that
is more beneficial for the cat (e.g., regressive or ideally abortive
infection).

TRANSMISSION
Generally, only antigenemic cats (thus progressively or some
regressively infected cats in early infection) transmit the virus to
other cats. In these cats, infectious virus is found in multiple body
fluids with highest concentrations found in saliva, but also in milk,
nasal secretions, feces, and urine.40-42 FeLV is mostly transmitted
horizontally via the oronasal route. Intimate contact between cats is
ideal for transmission, such as mutual grooming and sharing of food,
water, and litter pans. Transmission can also occur through biting,
fighting, mating, intrauterine, or via milk from infected queens to
kittens. Indirect transmission through FeLV-containing feces is
possible but infected cats will only develop abortive infection.13,41
Blood transfusions (ch. 124) are another mode of transmission from
either progressively or regressively infected cats. Every blood donor

cat should be screened for both antigen and proviral DNA.37
Susceptibility to FeLV is much higher for kittens than for adults.
Kittens develop progressive infection more frequently. Adult cats can
be infected, but their risk of developing progressive infection is much
lower, and if infected they develop regressive infection.

DISEASE CONDITIONS ASSOCIATED
WITH FeLV
PREVALENCE OF CLINICAL SIGNS
Although infected cats can be clinically healthy for many years, a
variety of disease conditions is associated with FeLV infection,
including bone marrow disorders (mainly anemia), neoplasia
(mainly lymphoma), and immunosuppression leading to increased
susceptibility to secondary infections.7,43,44 It is rarely possible to
determine whether a disease is a consequence of FeLV infection or
an independent event. In one study of 3712 progressively FeLVinfected cats presented for veterinary care, 29% had no clinical
signs.45 In a study of 8756 progressively FeLV-infected ill cats seen
at teaching hospitals, anemia (18%), respiratory infections (11%),
lymphoma (10%), myeloproliferative diseases (6%), stomatitis (5%),
leukopenia (3%), hemoplasmosis (3%), lymphadenopathy (3%), and
uveitis (2%) were identified.7

BONE MARROW DISORDERS
Bone marrow suppression (ch. 176), especially anemia (ch. 57), is
the most common clinical syndrome associated with FeLV
infection.28 The virus infects both hematopoietic stem cells and bone
marrow stromal cells responsible for a supportive environment.
Progressive infection with active viral replication is usually required
for bone marrow suppression, while regressive infection is only
rarely associated with myelosuppression.34,36 The most common
FeLV-induced bone marrow suppression is pure red cell aplasia, a

severe non-regenerative anemia with marked depletion and
maturation arrest of erythroid precursors (ch. 172). The cats have a
characteristic finding of a lack of reticulocytes but a high mean
corpuscular volume. An immune-mediated mechanism can be
involved in FeLV-associated hemolytic anemia but also in nonregenerative cytopenias, and some of these cats respond favorably to
glucocorticoid treatment (ch. 174). In addition to the direct bone
marrow suppressive effects of FeLV, non-regenerative cytopenias can
also be a consequence of secondary effects of the virus, such as bone
marrow infiltration with neoplastic cells (e.g., lymphoma).

NEOPLASIA
The most common tumors associated with FeLV infection are
lymphomas, which are mostly caused by progressive FeLV infection
and only rarely by regressive infection.3,35,36 Progressively infected
cats have about a 60-fold increased risk of developing lymphoma
compared to non-infected cats (ch. 322). Lymphoma affects up to
25% of cats with progressive FeLV infection and, usually, large
amounts of FeLV RNA can be detected with in situ hybridization in
these lymphomas.46 As the prevalence of FeLV has decreased, so has
the incidence of FeLV-associated lymphoma.3,47 Mediastinal
lymphomas are still commonly associated with FeLV infection, while
other lymphomas, e.g., multicentric, spinal, renal, and ocular, are
rare; intestinal lymphomas are almost never associated with FeLV
infection.3 The most important mechanism by which FeLV causes
malignancy is by insertion of the FeLV genome into the cellular
genome near a cellular oncogene or a tumor suppressor gene. This
results in activation and overexpression or disruption of these genes,
which leads to uncontrolled proliferation of these cells (clone). FeLV
can also incorporate the oncogene to form a recombinant virus
containing cellular oncogene sequences that are then rearranged and
activated; these new recombinant viruses (e.g., FeLV-B) are then
oncogenic when entering cells.

IMMUNOSUPPRESSION

Diseases associated with FeLV-associated immunosuppression
account for many of the clinical signs in progressively FeLV-infected
cats (ch. 180). Thymic atrophy and depletion of lymph node
paracortical zones are common, particularly in kittens. Neutropenia
and lymphopenia can exacerbate immunosuppression. Several
immune function tests can be abnormal in FeLV-infected cats,
including poor response to T-cell mitogens, prolonged allograft
rejection, reduced immunoglobulin production, depressed
neutrophil function, complement depletion, cytokine dysregulation,
and poor responses to vaccination. There are many reports of FeLVinfected cats having concurrent bacterial, viral, protozoal, and fungal
infections. However, few studies prove that these cats have higher
rates of infection than non-FeLV-infected cats or that they have less
favorable response to treatment. In shelter cats, upper respiratory
tract infection (ch. 205) was the most common comorbidity in
progressively FeLV-infected cats (16%) at the time of admission but
this prevalence was not significantly different from that in FeLVuninfected cats (20%).22 While FeLV commonly suppresses immune
function, it should not be assumed that all concurrent infections are
a result of FeLV infection.44

MISCELLANEOUS DISORDERS
Transient generalized lymphadenopathy has been observed in young
FeLV-infected cats. Reproductive failures are associated with
abortion caused by endometritis or transplacental infection of
fetuses. A “panleukopenia-like syndrome” of FeLV can mimic feline
parvovirus infection, characterized by panleukopenia, crypt necrosis,
and high mortality. Some of these cats were coinfected with
parvovirus, explaining those clinical signs (ch. 201). Chronic
gingivostomatitis, although more common in cats infected with
feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV), can also be associated with
FeLV infection (ch. 198),5 although not all studies agree.48-50 Most
FeLV-associated neuropathies are associated with lymphoma in the
brain or spinal cord or secondary infections, such as cryptococcosis,
toxoplasmosis, feline infectious peritonitis, encephalitozoonosis, or
listeriosis. In cats without morphologic changes, direct neurotoxic

effects of FeLV might be responsible for some signs, e.g., anisocoria,
mydriasis, central blindness, Horner’s syndrome, or urinary
incontinence.51 A polypeptide of the FeLV envelope (especially in
FeLV-C) was found to cause dose-dependent neurotoxicosis and
alterations in intracellular calcium ion concentrations, neuronal
survival, and neurite outgrowth.52,53 FeLV can lead to disruption of
intracellular thiamine uptake by blocking a putative thiamine
receptor (THTR1, receptor of FeLV-A) which might contribute to the
neuropathogenesis.54

DIAGNOSIS
INDICATION FOR FeLV TESTING
The FeLV status of every cat should be known because the diagnosis
of FeLV infection is important in healthy as well as sick cats.1
Identification and segregation of infected cats are considered the
most effective methods for preventing transmission. Cats should be
tested when newly acquired, ill, about to be vaccinated against FeLV,
or believed to have been exposed to potentially infected cats.39
Kittens can be tested at any time as passively acquired maternal
antibodies do not interfere with testing for viral antigen. Vaccination
against FeLV also does not interfere with testing.

POINT-OF-CARE TESTING (PoCT)
PoCTs for soluble p27 antigen (such as enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assays [ELISA] or other immunochromatographic
tests) are generally highly reliable for detecting progressive FeLV
infection (ch. 184). Plate-based ELISA performed in commercial
laboratories detecting soluble p27 antigen are not superior to
PoCT.55-59 PoCTs use serum, plasma, or whole blood. In some
studies, results were more often false positive on whole blood.22
Thus, use of plasma or serum might be preferred despite its testing
being more time-consuming. Tests for soluble p27 antigen become

positive by 3-6 weeks after exposure,19,21 but might take
considerably longer in some cats.16,17 If the results of soluble p27
antigen testing are negative but recent exposure cannot be ruled out,
testing should be repeated ≥6 weeks after the last potential exposure
(Figure 199.1). Follow-up testing to confirm positive results is
recommended, especially in low-risk areas and in apparently healthy
cats in which the predictive value of a positive test is low.59,60 On the
other hand, negative test results are highly reliable (negative
predictive value 94% to ∼100%).

CONFIRMATION OF POSITIVE PoCT
RESULTS
The preferred method for confirming a positive PoCT result is
polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for detection of FeLV provirus (ch.
184). PCR should be performed in reliable specialized laboratories.
With few exceptions (i.e., focal infection), cats that test soluble
antigen-positive are also provirus-positive. If PCR is not readily
available, testing for soluble p27 antigen can be repeated, preferably
by using a PoCT from a different manufacturer.55,61 PCR is used to
detect FeLV provirus (the viral DNA integrated into the cat’s
genome) and is necessary to detect regressive FeLV infection), while
reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) (in which
a reverse transcription step is required first) detects FeLV genomic
RNA and thus, replicating virus. Both assays are positive earlier in
infection than antigen tests (Box 199.1). RT-PCR on saliva can be
used to detect viral RNA if blood collection is not possible, as viral
RNA in saliva correlates well with antigenemia.40 Test results are
highly sensitive and thus, can be used to test cat colonies for absence
of virus shedders by pooling samples into one test.62
IFAs detect intracellular p27 antigen within infected blood cells
(neutrophils and platelets) following bone marrow infection. IFA is
only positive in antigenemic cats but does not become positive
during the first 3 weeks of infection. Therefore, IFA is not
recommended as a screening test. Moreover, false positive and

negative results occur and the reliability of the result highly depends
on experienced personnel.

ANTIBODY TESTING
Although not commercially available in many countries, testing for
anti-FeLV antibodies is the only way to detect abortive infection and
cats immune to new infection (Box 199.1). Detection of antibodies
to the FeLV envelope (SU) by ELISA correlates with the presence of
neutralizing antibodies as well as with infection outcome and has
been suggested as a useful addition for FeLV diagnostic testing.30,63
A recombinant preparation of the FeLV transmembrane protein
p15E proved highly effective for the detection of anti-FeLV
antibodies and holds promise for recognizing all FeLV-exposed
cats.64 The first routine diagnostic p15E PoCT is available
commercially in Europe; however, there is not yet sufficient data on
whether this test reliably detects cats with abortive FeLV infection
under field conditions.

PREVENTION
SEGREGATION AND DISINFECTION
The control of FeLV is facilitated by its short survival outside of the
host (up to 48 hrs under moist conditions) and because it is readily
inactivated by detergents, heating, drying, or disinfectants.
Transmission among cats usually requires direct contact and can be
prevented in homes, veterinary clinics, and animal shelters by
segregation and effective disinfection.39

VACCINES
Adjuvanted inactivated whole virus, recombinant antigen, and nonadjuvanted canarypox-vectored FeLV vaccines are commercially
available (ch. 185). Vaccine efficacy studies are difficult to compare
because they have used differing methodologies. Further, vaccine

formulations vary, probably influencing the immune response.63
Several recent comparative studies had contradictory conclusions,
and some were criticized for their study designs (e.g., induction of
immunosuppression either inadvertently by contamination of the
FeLV challenge virus with feline parvovirus or deliberately using
immunosuppressive drugs to reach a strong viral challenge).65-69
While it is difficult to compare efficacy, non-adjuvanted vaccines
cause less inflammation at the injection site70 and thus, might be
less commonly associated with feline injection-site sarcoma
formation (ch. 324).71 While FeLV vaccination significantly reduces
the risk of progressive infection and thus, of FeLV-associated disease
and shortened life expectancy, it does not prevent provirus
integration after exposure (regressive infection).72
FeLV vaccines are considered non-core; they are recommended
only for cats at risk of exposure (e.g., cats permitted outdoors) (ch.
185). Still, in regions with high prevalence, every kitten should be
vaccinated because their future lifestyle might pose a risk. FeLV
vaccine-induced duration of immunity appears to persist for at least
2 years.73,74 Due to the long duration of immunity and lower
susceptibility of adult cats to develop progressive FeLV infection, a
booster immunization every 3 years is considered sufficient in cats
older than 2 years. Protection is not 100%, and it is not safe to cohouse progressively infected with uninfected cats even if the latter
are vaccinated. Cats should be tested for infection before FeLV
vaccination because administration of FeLV vaccines to infected cats
has no benefit.18

MANAGEMENT AND TREATMENT
FeLV-infected cats should be confined indoors to contain the spread
and to protect affected cats from infectious agents carried by other
animals.39 Specific management measures for multi-cat households
with FeLV infection as well as for individual FeLV-infected cats
should be considered (Box 199.2). Vaccination programs to prevent
common infectious diseases should be maintained. Some cats

infected with FeLV might not adequately respond to vaccination, and
thus, protecting those cats from exposure to other pathogens is
important. Although it has been recommended that FeLV-infected
cats should receive inactivated vaccines and not modified-live virus
(MLV) vaccines (when available), little evidence indicates that such
cats are at increased risk of adverse effects through MLV
vaccines.1,75
Prompt and accurate identification of FeLV-associated as well as
secondary diseases is important to allow early therapeutic
intervention and a more successful outcome (Box 199.2). Many
FeLV-infected cats respond as well as their uninfected counterparts
to appropriate treatment and therapy of secondary infections.
Although antiviral drugs and drugs aimed at modulating the immune
system have commonly been used in FeLV-infected cats, only a few
large well-controlled studies have been conducted in naturally
infected cats and most of them have shown no effect of the antiviral
drugs or immunomodulators that were used.76

Management of Multi-Cat Households With Progressively
FeLV-Infected Cats
• FeLV is mainly transmitted through social contact, but also
through biting and fighting.
• If progressively FeLV-infected cats live in a household with FeLV
antigen-negative cats, many of these other cats might already
have been exposed and developed abortive or regressive
infections. These cats are likely immune to new infection.
• The risk of new infections in cats with pre-existing long-term
exposure to FeLV-infected cats is low. If they eventually become
antigen-positive, this is more likely caused by reactivation of a
regressive FeLV infection than by transmission from the other
cats in the household. However, transmission cannot be totally
excluded and thus, the only 100% safe prevention is to separate
infected and uninfected cats.
• If owners refuse to separate housemates, the uninfected cats
should receive FeLV vaccination to enhance their natural level

of immunity. However, owners should be informed that
vaccination does not provide complete protection in these high
exposure environments.
Management of Individual Progressively FeLV-Infected
Cats
• Progressively FeLV-infected cats should be kept indoors to avoid
spread to other cats and exposure of the cat to infectious agents
carried by other animals.
• “Routine vaccination programs” should be maintained in cats
with progressive FeLV infection. They might not be able to
mount an adequate immune response to vaccines and
protection might not be comparable to that in a healthy cat.
Therefore, testing for the immune response (e.g., antibody
testing after feline panleukopenia virus vaccination) and
protecting against exposure should be considered.
• Progressively FeLV-infected cats should have health care visits at
the veterinarian at least every 6 months in order to promptly
detect changes in their health status. A complete blood count
should be performed every 6 months, and a biochemistry profile
and urinalysis performed every 12 months.
• Intact male and female cats should be neutered to reduce stress
associated with estrus and mating behavior and the desire to
roam outside the house and interact aggressively.
• Surgery is generally well tolerated, but perioperative antibiotic
administration should be used.
• Cats with progressive FeLV infection can be housed in the same
ward as other hospitalized patients, but in individual cages.
They should not be placed in a “contagious ward” with cats
suffering from other infections.
• If progressively FeLV-infected cats are sick, prompt
identification of the secondary illness is essential to allow early
therapeutic intervention.
• Most cats with progressive FeLV infection respond as well as
uninfected cats to appropriate medications, although a longer
and more intensive course of therapy (e.g., antibiotics) might be
necessary.

• Glucocorticoids, other immunosuppressive, or myelosuppressive
drugs should generally be avoided in progressively and
regressively infected cats and only be prescribed if there is a
clear indication.
Treatment Recommendations for Individual Cats With
Progressive FeLV Infection
If no clinical signs and laboratory changes are present
• Keep cats strictly indoors; no treatment is indicated
If clinical signs or laboratory changes are present
• Always look for underlying diseases first (FeLV itself might not
be responsible for the clinical signs, e.g., secondary infections
could be present)
• Treat underlying diseases
Treatment of FeLV-Infected Cats With Lymphoma
• Use chemotherapeutic drug protocols (e.g., COP protocol
including cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and prednisone)
• Inform owners about the more guarded prognosis
Treatment of FeLV-Infected Cats With Anemia
• Give blood transfusions if anemia is severe
• Look for underlying diseases causing the anemia
• Treat underlying diseases
• If underlying diseases have been ruled out, consider
glucocorticoids in both regenerative and non-regenerative
anemia (because anemia in FeLV-infected cats can have an
immune-mediated origin)
Treatment of FeLV-Infected Cats With Neurological Signs
• Look for underlying diseases causing the neurological signs (e.g.,
lymphoma)

• Treat underlying diseases
• If no underlying disease is present (and the neurological signs
are assumed to be indeed caused by FeLV) treat with zidovudine
(5 mg/kg PO q12h)
Treatment of FeLV-Infected Cat With Recurring
Infections
• Treat recurring infections proactively (e.g., antibiotics)
• Consider treatment with feline interferon-omega (106 IU/kg SQ
q24h) and/or treatment with raltegravir (10-25 mg/kg PO q12h)

CLIENT INFORMATION
Your Cat Has Been Diagnosed With Progressive
Feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) Infection
GENERAL INFORMATION ABOUT FeLV
• FeLV is a retrovirus. This means the virus inserts copies of its
genetic material into that of the host cell it has infected. The
host cell then handles FeLV as part of its own genome.
• FeLV is present almost throughout the entire world’s domestic
cat population but geographic differences in prevalence exist.
FeLV is spread both vertically (from an infected queen to her
kittens) and horizontally (from cat to cat). Transmission of

infection mainly occurs through social contact but also
through biting and fighting.
• If not defeated by the cat’s immune system, FeLV can cause
variable clinical signs, including tumors, immune suppression,
and blood disorders, such as anemia. Diseases secondary to
immune suppression account for many clinical signs in FeLVinfected cats, and it is important to know that many of these
conditions are treatable.
• The median survival time of progressively FeLV-infected cats is
approximately 3 years. However, with proper care, a FeLVinfected indoor-only cat can live much longer with good
quality of life. A decision for treatment or euthanasia should
never be based solely on the presence of an FeLV infection.
MANAGEMENT OF FeLV IN MULTICAT-HOUSEHOLDS
• All cats in a household in which a cat with progressive FeLV
infection has been identified, should be tested by the
veterinarian to determine their FeLV status. If FeLV antigenpositive and antigen-negative cats are identified in the same
household, the best method of avoiding spread is separating
the antigen-positive cats and preventing them from
interacting with housemates.
• FeLV cannot survive for long outside the host. Surfaces
contaminated with an infected cat’s saliva, blood, urine, feces,
or other secretions can be disinfected by cleaning thoroughly
with soap and warm water, followed by drying.
• If segregation is not possible, uninfected cats should receive
FeLV vaccination to enhance their natural level of immunity.
However, vaccination does not provide complete protection in
high-exposure situations with FeLV-shedding cats.
MANAGEMENT AND HEALTH CARE IN INDIVIDUAL
CATS WITH PROGRESSIVE FELV INFECTION
• FeLV-infected cats should be kept strictly indoors to avoid
spread to other cats and exposure of the cat to infectious
agents carried by other animals.

• New uninfected cats should not be introduced in a household
with a progressively FeLV-infected cat, because the new cat is
at risk for contracting the infection, even with vaccination. The
stress of a newcomer might also adversely affect the
progressively FeLV-infected cat.
• Progressively FeLV-infected cats should be taken to the
veterinarian at least every 6 months in order to promptly
detect changes in health status. A complete blood count
should be performed every 6 months, a biochemistry profile
and urinalysis once a year.
• “Routine vaccination programs” against common pathogens
should be maintained. FeLV-infected cats might not able to
mount an adequate immune response to vaccines and
protection might not be comparable to that in a healthy cat.
Therefore, testing for the immune response after vaccination
(e.g., through testing for antibodies against feline
panleukopenia virus) can be considered. In addition,
protection from exposure to sick cats is essential.
• Intact male and female FeLV-infected cats should be neutered
to reduce stress associated with estrus and mating behavior
and the desire to roam outside the house and interact
aggressively. Surgery is generally well tolerated, but
perioperative antibiotics should be used.
• If progressively FeLV-infected cats appear sick, they should be
taken to the veterinarian immediately to allow early
therapeutic intervention.
• Most cats with progressive FeLV infection respond as well as
uninfected cats to appropriate medications, although a longer
and more aggressive course of therapy might be needed.
Katrin Hartmann (Munich, Bavaria, Germany) and Regina
Hofmann-Lehmann (Zurich, Switzerland)

FELINE CORONAVIRUS
FELINE ENTERIC CORONAVIRUS (FECV) VERSUS
FELINE INFECTIOUS PERITONITIS VIRUS (FIPV)
The Dichotomy of Diseases Caused by Feline Coronavirus
(FCoV)
FCoV is a pathogen of wild and domestic cats and is endemic in multi-cat
environments, e.g., catteries and shelters.1 Most cats exposed to FCoV
develop mild or subclinical enteritis; however, a small subset experiences
progression to a systemic and usually lethal immune-mediated disease
known as feline infectious peritonitis (FIP). This dichotomy in disease
severity has resulted in classifying FCoV infections into one of two
biotypes: FECV and FIPV. The term biotype refers to a virus infection
associated with a distinct clinical outcome: FECV is proposed to cause
mild self-limiting enteritis while FIPV causes systemic inflammation and
death. The preponderance of evidence suggests that FIPVs arise from
FECVs by mutations that occur spontaneously within each affected cat
and a mix of host and viral factors that dictate whether FIPVs will arise
and what form the disease will take.
The emergence of FIP in cats was documented in necropsy records
from Angell Memorial Animal Hospital (Boston, MA, USA) from the late
1950s and was first described in 1963.2 It appears to have emerged in the
United States and spread worldwide by the mid-1970s.3 The origins of
FCoV are less clear, but coronaviruses are well known for their ability to
cross species boundaries and FIPV emerged in approximately the same
time frame as its closest relatives: transmissible gastroenteritis virus
(TGEV) of swine (in the 1940s) and canine enteric coronavirus (CCoV) of
dogs (in the 1970s) (Figure 200.1).

Serotypes of FCoV
Two distinct serotypes of FCoV have been identified, separated by the
antigenic and genetic properties of their viral spike (S) protein (Figure
200.2).4,5 S is a crucial mediator of infection responsible for both
receptor binding and membrane fusion. Feline coronavirus serotype 1
(FCoV-1) and feline coronavirus serotype 2 (FCoV-2) have evolutionarily
distinct S proteins that, in many ways, make them behave like different
viruses.6 FCoV-1 is more prevalent clinically, grows poorly in cell culture,
and is less studied. FCoV-2 is easily propagated in cell culture but
accounts for a smaller proportion of natural infections. Aminopeptidase
N (APN) has been identified as the receptor for FCoV-2 while FCoV-1
uses a different, unidentified receptor.7 FCoV-1 S contains a notable
insertion of a proteolytic cleavage site (S1/S2) that plays an important
role in infection. FCoV-2 viruses lack this insertion.8 Despite differences,
the clinical outcome of infection appears to be the same: both FCoV-1 and
FCoV-2 can result in FECV or FIPV in an infected cat. Superinfection, or
simultaneous infection with more than one serotype, is possible but
poorly documented.

PATHOGENESIS AND CLINICAL SIGNS OF
FECV
FECV replicates within the intestinal epithelium. Most cats are
subclinically infected, but some have signs of fever, anorexia, and mild
diarrhea.9,10 FECV is ubiquitous among cats in multi-cat environments
such as catteries and shelters. Within 24 hours of infection, FCoV can be
detected in the tonsils and small intestine.11 It then spreads
systemically.12 Monocyte-associated viremia is common,13-15 with virus
shed in the feces and transmitted by the oronasal route. Primary infection
can last several months. Some cats clear the virus, but many continue to
shed at low levels for up to 2 years.4,16 Colonic columnar epithelial cells
appear to serve as a reservoir for persistent infection and shedding.12
Immunity is not long-lasting and reinfection may occur.17 Despite the
term “enteric,” FECV can be detected in all major organs, including the
central nervous system, for up to 80 days post-infection with no clinical
signs.12 It is suspected that mesenteric lymph nodes and tissue

macrophages also serve as virus reservoirs. Like other coronaviruses,
FCoV can survive 1 to 2 days on surfaces. Anecdotally, it has been
reported to remain viable as long as 7 weeks in dried feces. This finding is
reported in previous reviews and textbooks and is based on data collected
in a laboratory setting; however, the longevity of FCoV in natural
environments is likely to be much shorter. Like other enveloped viruses,
FCoV is highly susceptible to destruction by detergents, disinfectants,
prolonged exposure to UV light, or desiccation (ch. 186).

PATHOGENESIS AND CLINICAL SIGNS OF
FIPV
Pathogenesis
In approximately 5% of FCoV infections, the virus gains an ability to
replicate robustly within blood monocytes and tissue macrophages,
resulting in FIP—an immune-mediated disease associated with activation
of monocytes, macrophages, and endothelial cells. Naturally occurring
FIPVs are thought to arise independently and to be largely nontransmissible; however, cats can be experimentally infected through
oronasal exposure and, while transmission data are limited, have been
shown to shed virus in nasal secretions.18 FIP has a predilection for
kittens and young cats, but animals of any age can succumb. It may strike
more than one animal in a household and has been known to devastate
shelters and catteries.

Early Clinical Characteristics
Early clinical signs are nonspecific

(Video 6.4): fever, lethargy,

anorexia, and weight loss. Laboratory test results often reveal a
nonregenerative anemia, neutrophilia with a left shift, and lymphopenia
due to cytokine mediated depletion of cluster of differentiation (CD)8+
and CD4+ T-cells.19,20 Hyperbilirubinemia, increased serum aspartate
aminotransferase (AST) activities, and decreased albumin : globulin
ratios are common.21 The characteristic lesion of FIP is granulomatous
phlebitis (ch. 181).22

Development of FIP
Individual immune responses play an important role in determining
which cats develop FIP. Resistance is linked to strong cellular mediated
immunity (CMI) driven by cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) that target
virus infected cells.23 Additionally, it is associated with the development
of a T helper (Th)1-mediated interferon (IFN)-gamma driven cellular
immune response.24,25 In susceptible cats, productive infection of
monocytes and macrophages triggers a tumor necrosis factor (TNF)alpha response that quickly becomes dysregulated.26 FIPV infection
triggers up-regulation of inflammatory pathways leading to the

production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin
(IL)-1beta and IL-6.27,28 Enhanced expression of the integrin adhesion
molecules CD18 and CD11a facilitates emigration of FIPV-infected
monocytes into tissues, resulting in the formation of granulomatous
lesions.29 Monocyte and macrophage derived vascular endothelial
growth factor (VEGF) and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) also
contribute to increased vascular permeability.30 The outcome is systemic
vasculitis and immune-mediated tissue destruction, organ failure, and
death.

“Wet” FIP
In cats that mount a predominantly Th2 mediated humoral immune
response, the disease is characterized by development of a protein-rich
effusion in the thoracic and/or abdominal body cavities (ch. 71).31 This
rapidly progressive form of the disease is known as “wet” (or effusive)
FIP. The time from diagnosis to death can be as short as a few days. This
is due in part to a phenomenon known as antibody-dependent
enhancement (ADE) of infection, in which antibodies against FCoV
opsonize the virus and allow it to enter monocytes and macrophages by a
specialized receptor that recognizes the invading pathogens.32 Uptake via
this pathway leads to rapid infection and the development of more
fulminant disease.33 This is an uncommon method of viral entry that is
best documented in human cases of dengue.34

“Dry” FIP
Cats that develop the non-effusive, or “dry” form of FIP, have a mixed
Th1/Th2 response that prolongs the clinical course of infection but is
ineffective in completely clearing the virus. While the immune response
is adequate to eliminate virus from the visceral organs, it fails to
effectively penetrate the blood-brain barrier, leading to development of
lesions within the eyes and brain.35 These lesions include uveitis, or
inflammation of the pigmented structures of the eye. Uveitis can produce
clinical manifestations that include a darkening of the iris, abnormal
pupil shape, and deposition of keratic precipitates (a mixture of
inflammatory cells, fibrin, and pigment) on the corneal endothelium.36
Within the brain, inflammation is typically centered around the ventricles
and can result in ataxia, tremors, and seizures (ch. 242). Granulomatous

lesions are classically associated with non-effusive FIP but are less
pervasive than the pyogranulomatous lesions that characterizes effusive
FIP. The course of non-effusive FIP is more protracted and cats may live
for months before eventually succumbing to the disease. In the terminal
stages of illness, cats with non-effusive FIP may develop effusion.

TRANSITION FROM FECV TO FIPV
Internal Mutation Hypothesis vs Circulating Strain
Hypothesis
There are two theories regarding the development of FIP. The most
widely supported is the internal mutation hypothesis37 suggesting every
case of FIP arises uniquely from mutation of FECV within the affected
cat. An important supposition of the internal mutation hypothesis is that
FIP is not readily transmissible, making infection of monocytes and
macrophages an evolutionary dead-end for the virus. The second theory
is the circulating strain hypothesis,38 that presumes both FECV and FIPV
are actively circulating among cats and development of FIP depends on
the variant to which it is exposed. This theory has the advantage of
explaining FIP outbreaks, common in catteries and shelters. The 2
theories need not be mutually exclusive and it is plausible that some
strains of FECV are more likely to transition to FIPV than others.
Increasing evidence suggests that multiple mutations are associated with
the transition from FECV to FIPV and it is logical to suppose that if a
given FECV strain already possesses one or more of the predisposing
mutations, the switch to FIPV is increasingly likely.

S Protein and Other Viral Factors
Increasing lines of evidence suggest that multiple viral factors are
associated with the transition from FECV to FIPV. The exact
combination(s) of mutations that enhance pathogenicity has yet to be
defined but appear to involve open reading frames (ORFs) termed 3c and
7b and the S surface protein.39 Coronaviruses have large genomes—the
largest of any in all known RNA viruses. Despite some ability to
proofread, this expansive genomic template combines with an errorprone RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) and a well-documented
propensity for recombination. The result is a high rate of genetic change.

Closely related, but inherently variable viral progeny are referred to as
quasi-species and with FCoV infection, the analogy of a host being
exposed to a “quasi-species cloud” may be helpful. It illustrates and
explains that many closely related viral variants can coexist within one
host. This natural variation makes identifying single nucleotide
polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with the transition from FECV to FIPV
analogous to finding the proverbial “needle in the haystack.” Early
studies identified deletions in ORF3c and changes in ORF7b genes in cats
with FIPV but not FECV.40 ORF7 appears essential for replication in
monocytes and macrophages41 and may function as a type I IFN
antagonist,42 while ORF3 is suspected to play a supportive role in the
replication of FECV within the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.43 Changes in
the S gene may predict FIP. S is the logical home for factors that enhance
infection of monocytes and macrophages, as it is responsible for both
receptor binding and membrane fusion, two principal drivers of
infection.
The S protein has two functional units: the S1 domain responsible for
receptor binding and the S2 domain which mediates membrane fusion
(Figure 200.2). Two SNPs in the S2 domain at amino acid positions
1058 and 1060 were first proposed to be discriminatory for FIP,44 but
were demonstrated to be indicative of systemic spread of FCoV, but not
FIP itself.45 An alternative to SNPs (markers of genetic change) are
amino acid substitutions (markers of functional change), e.g., an
important exposed structural loop at the boundary of the S1 and S2
domains known as the S1/S2 cleavage site. This cleavage site functions as
a “pathogenicity switch” in influenza and Newcastle disease viruses. It is
involved in interactions with host proteases, e.g., furin that primes the
virus for fusion with host cell membranes. Sequence changes that
correspond to amino acid substitutions in the S1/S2 cleavage site are
associated with the development of FIP,46 likely in combination with
other mutations within spike. One hypothesis is that by selecting for
amino acids that favor macrophage-specific proteases (versus the
ubiquitous enzyme furin), the virus gains the ability to initiate more
productive infection of these cells, a critical step in the transition to FIP.
To complicate matters, many genetic permutations (not one single SNP)
have the potential to lead to amino acid substitutions which change the
character of the S1/S2 site. The complex nature of identifying viral
markers associated with the development of FIP, has to date, stymied the
development of reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-

PCR) and sequencing-based tests to discriminate between FECV and
FIPV.

Host Factors
A cat’s immune response plays a critical role in determining the
development of FIP and the form of disease the virus will take (see FIPV
pathogenesis). Experimentally, coinfection with feline immunodeficiency
virus (ch. 198), but not feline leukemia virus (FeLV, ch. 199), is a risk
factor for FIP,47,48 suggesting that population-specific factors may have
roles, e.g., genetics and husbandry. Cats <2 years of age make up the

majority of cases.49 Identified risk factors vary in studies. There is
general agreement that pedigreed male cats are more likely to develop
FIP50 and that there is a genetic susceptibility to FIP: a cat with a close
relative that succumbs to FIP is more likely to develop the disease. About
33% of cats are resistant to FIP,51 associated with SNPs in the IFNgamma gene,52 but likely impacted by many genetic factors.53

Environmental Factors
Overcrowded conditions create stress and increase the likelihood of
coinfection, either of which may result in immunosuppression and failure
to control coronavirus replication. Further, overcrowding increases the
viral load in the environment, making FIP a notable problem in catteries
and shelters. Stray cat populations tend to have lower prevalence of
FCoV, likely because they have no communal spaces for defecation and
there is decreased contact between individuals. Seropositivity in stray
cats ranges from 7-15% but increases to nearly 100% when they are
introduced into shelters.54,55

FCoV DIAGNOSIS
Diagnosis by Exclusion
Diagnosis of FIP can be challenging. Cats may be evaluated for effusive,
non-effusive, or a combination of forms. Although young cats (<2 years)
make up most cases, older animals may also be affected. Diagnoses are
based on a high index of suspicion but usually remain presumptive
(Figure 200.3). As such, FIP is often considered a diagnosis of
exclusion. When confirmation is achieved, it is typically through testing
at necropsy. This adds another layer to the challenge of diagnosing FIP as
clients (and veterinarians) often struggle to accept a grave prognosis for a
young animal without definitive antemortem testing.

Histology and Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
The gold standard for FIP diagnosis is IHC of tissues that reveal
granulomatous lesions containing FCoV antigen. Improving RNA-based
in situ hybridization (ISH) techniques are expected to improve yield
(Figure 200.4). IHC of multiple tissues (liver, spleen, small intestine,
omentum, mesenteric lymph node) is recommended since tissue

distribution of antigen varies. Any (pyo-)granulomatous lesions should
be sampled. Surgical biopsy is not always feasible as many cats
undergoing work-up for FIP are poor candidates for general anesthesia.
Less invasive techniques, e.g., fine-needle aspirate (FNA) and tissue core
biopsy have low sensitivity, presumptively due to variability in antigen
distribution.56,57

Serology/Antigen Detection
Serologic titers are a common method of documenting FCoV exposure
but there is little association between results and clinical outcomes: cats
with both high and low titers can develop FIP. Since the serology of FECV
is indistinguishable from FIPV, antibody/antigen-based testing has been
hindered (ch. 184). Any cat with antibodies to FCoV is at risk for
developing FIP. Negative results must be interpreted in context of the
history and clinical signs. Antibody/antigen complexes in cats with FIP
can lead to false-negative results; 10% of the serologic test results on cats
with confirmed FIP were falsely negative.58 Importantly, prevalence of
FCoV increases with number of cats housed together. FCoV is almost
invariably found in environments with ≥6 cats. Negative serum antibody
tests must be interpreted in context of a cat’s history when used to
exclude a diagnosis of FIP.

Rivalta Test
The Rivalta test was first described in 1895 to help differentiate exudates
from transudates in humans. The test is inexpensive, fast, and easy.
About 8 mL of distilled water is mixed in a tube with one drop of acetic
acid. Then a drop of effusion is gently placed on top of this solution. If a
precipitate forms on the surface or floats to the bottom the result is
considered “positive” and if the effusion dissipates into the clear solution,
the result is “negative.” Inconclusive results occur when a distinct
precipitate fails to form but the solution becomes slightly cloudy. Positive
tests may be obtained with various exudative diseases, e.g., lymphoma
and bacterial pleuritis/peritonitis.58 The Rivalta test can be used cageside to classify an effusion and to assess the likelihood of FIP (
Video
200.1).59 Further fluid analysis including total protein, cellularity, and
microscopic evaluation of cell type should be performed (ch. 71).

Fluid Analysis, Cytology, Immunostaining

FIP effusions are considered exudative variants: high protein, low
cellularity, with vacuolated neutrophils and macrophages on microscopic
examination (ch. 71).60 Immunostaining macrophages within effusion
specimens was thought highly specific for FIP but subsequent research
has demonstrated lack of specificity, with false positives caused by
nonspecific binding to macrophage by specific proteins or FECV-related
viremia.61 False-negative results and reduced sensitivity of
immunostaining are related to the number of macrophages in specimens,
degradation of specimens during storage, and competitive binding with
circulating anti-FCoV antibodies.62 Testing can also be performed on
cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and aqueous humor from cats suspected of
having dry FIP, with similar limitations.

RT-PCR
Most RT-PCR tests target conserved regions of the viral genome and
amplify both FECV and FIPV (ch. 184). FCoV shedding can be detected
by RT-PCR of feces; however, the utility of this testing is limited by
intermittent shedding, high rates of reinfection, and polymerase chain
reaction (PCR) inhibitors present within feces. Some breeders routinely
test fecal specimens to identify chronic shedders. Higher antibody titers
are associated with increased fecal shedding, but the most reliable way to
quantitate shedding is through serial RT-PCR testing.63 It was initially
thought that amplification of FCoV RNA from blood, effusion, CSF, or
any tissue outside of the GI tract was a marker for FIPV but it has since
been shown that FECV can be found outside the GI tract in otherwise
healthy cats or in cats with other systemic diseases, although typically at
lower levels than in cats with FIPV. Cats with high copy numbers of FCoV
RNA in extra-GI tissues (effusion, CSF, FNA specimens) are more likely
to have FIP, which is the basis for the RT-PCR test offered by Auburn
University. Submitting specimens from multiple sites helps decrease the
possibility of false negative results, but only tissue IHC has been
demonstrated to be definitive. IDEXX’s FIPVirus Real PCR test detects
mutations in the S protein at nucleotide positions 1058 and 1060. These
have been associated with systemic spread but are not specific to FIP.
This test is run in parallel with RT-PCR to detect the 7b gene.

TREATMENT OF FIPV

Palliative Therapies
Without antiviral treatment, the prognosis for a cat with FIP is grave.
Palliative therapies are aimed at controlling clinical signs and reducing
systemic inflammation. These may include use of anti-inflammatory
drugs (typically prednisolone; ch. 144), fluid support (ch. 120), and
therapeutic abdominocentesis (ch. 86) or thoracocentesis (ch. 92).
Progression of disease can be rapid, and in this case, euthanasia should
be recommended to the cat owner.

Antivirals: Nucleoside Inhibitors
The most promising new drug is a nucleoside analog developed by Gilead
Sciences, GS-441524. It is a bioactive metabolite of remdesivir, a COVID19 treatment approved for emergency use by the U.S. Food and Drug
Administration (FDA). Nucleoside analogs mimic their natural
counterparts. They are recognized by the viral polymerase and
incorporated into nascent RNA strands, leading to premature
termination of transcription. The initial clinical trial of GS-441524
reported recovery in 25 of 31 (84%) naturally infected cats. Of the
recovered cats, owners reported a return to “near normal” within 2 weeks
of treatment. Fever resolved within the first 12-36 hours, accompanied by
a return in appetite. Effusions were reported to resolve over 10-14 days.
Relapse occurred in 8 cats and was successfully treated with a second
course of treatment in 5. The most common adverse effect was the
development of skin lesions at the injection site. The optimal dosing
regimen reported was 4 mg/kg SQ q24h for 12 weeks.64 Early data
suggest that higher dosages (8-10 mg/kg) may be required for treating
non-effusive FIP.65 At the time of publication, GS-441524 is not FDAapproved and cannot be purchased legally from a regulated source in the
United States, but is becoming available through respective regulatory
agencies of other countries. A study of unlicensed home GS-441524-like
therapy indicates it can be an effective treatment for FIP. Complications
related to the daily injections are common.66 Oral formulations are now
available,66a as is an alternative replication inhibitor (molnupiravir),
which has a distinct inhibitory mechanism through ambiguous basepairing (or mutagenesis) and distinct safety concerns due to its mode of
action.66b Off-label use of remdesivir for treatment of FIP has also been
described, but (at the time of writing) is expensive and not widely
available.

Antivirals: Protease Inhibitors
The cysteine protease inhibitor GC376 is an antiviral drug with promise.
It is related to nirmatrel/ritonavir (Paxlovid), a drug approved for
treatment of COVID-19 in humans. During viral assembly, coronavirus
proteins are cleaved by the virally encoded protein 3C-like (3CL)
protease, an essential function inhibited by GC376.67 In an initial trial,
19/20 cats with naturally occurring wet FIP had an initial response to
GC376 and 7 remained in remission.68 This compound is under
development as a treatment for FIP.

Antiviral Combination Therapies
In people, protease inhibitors are commonly combined with nucleoside
analogs, with superior outcomes. When using a single therapy, there is
greater potential for antiviral resistance. The most successful antiviral
treatments in human medicine involve combination therapies targeting
different aspects of viral replication. Studies into drugs that might be
suitable for combination FIPV therapy are currently underway.68a

Antivirals: Prophylaxis
The prophylactic use of an oral GS-441524-based antiviral treatment
(Mutian X) in multi-cat environments stopped FCoV shedding.69 While
there is a precedent for pre-exposure prophylaxis in people at high risk of
contracting HIV, it is important to point out that this type of medication
(e.g., Truvada) is a combination antiviral therapy. Widespread
prophylactic use of monotherapies against FCoV is to be strongly
discouraged due to increased risk of generating antimicrobial-resistant
viruses.

PREVENTION
Controlling FCoV is challenging and largely impractical due to its
endemic circulation among communally housed cats.22 In shelters and
catteries, regular disinfection of litterboxes and food bowls can help
reduce the number of infectious viral particles in the environment but
will not eliminate FCoV.22 Although a vaccine is commercially available,
the American Association of Feline Practitioners/American Animal
Hospital Association does not recommend it due to limited efficacy (ch.

185). This intranasal vaccine is a temperature-sensitive mutant of a type
2 virus. ADE of FIP has made development of more effective vaccines
challenging.70 Catteries seeking to minimize FIP are encouraged to
eliminate overcrowding, actively manage litter boxes and litter dust,
breed a minimum number of litters, and restrict breeding to adults that
have not previously produced kittens that have died of FIP.22

CANINE ENTERIC CORONAVIRUSES
(CCoV)
INCIDENCE; CLASSIC VERSUS PANTROPIC CCoV
CCoV infection is common in dogs, particularly those housed in group
environments, e.g., kennels, shelters, and breeding facilities.71,72 CCoV
was first reported in 1971 during an outbreak of GI disease in military
dogs in Germany.73 Its emergence began about 5 years before canine
parvovirus (CPV, ch. 201), a better-known cause of canine GI disease.
CCoV was previously understood to cause mild diarrheal disease in young
dogs74 with severe disease limited to dogs coinfected by other viral
pathogens, e.g., CPV. In 2005, a more virulent and multisystemic CCoV
variant associated with severe (often fatal) disease in the absence of
coinfection was reported,75 leading to classifying CCoV into two biotypes:
classical CCoV and pantropic CCoV.
The high degree of recombination between coronaviruses challenges
categorization attempts. CCoV is closely related to FCoV of cats. Like
FCoV, there are two distinct serotypes: CCoV-1 and CCoV-2,
differentiated by their S proteins.76 Serotype 1 CCoVs and FCoVs appear
to have evolved from a common ancestral virus, while the serotype 2
CCoV and FCoV lineages are hypothesized to have arisen from multiple
recombination events with an unidentified genetic source. CCoV-2
viruses can be further characterized into subgroups 2a and 2b with CCoV2b expressing an S protein that is the result of recombination event
between CCoV-2a and TGEV. The pantropic biotype has been primarily
associated with the CCoV-2a genotype.

PATHOGENESIS AND CLINICAL SIGNS

CCoV is thought to be transmitted by the fecal-oral route. CCoV typically
replicates within mature epithelial cells along the sides and tips of GI
villi. Infected enterocytes degenerate and eventually die, leading to villus
atrophy and attenuation. The epithelium that lines intestinal crypts is
spared from infection and responds with an increase in mitotic activity,
increasing the population of immature enterocytes. These cellular
changes translate into the clinical signs of diarrhea and dehydration in
CCoV-infected dogs. Rarely, infection is fatal, particularly in puppies
coinfected with CPV. CPV targets epithelial crypts and the combination
infection leads to complete destruction of the GI epithelium.77 Severity of
clinical signs is associated with age when infected, level and type of
pathogen exposure, and degree of maternal transfer of immunity.
An increasing number of reports of highly virulent CCoVs have also
been documented in puppies without apparent coinfections. In pantropic
CCoV, infection causes systemic illness with various clinical signs similar
to CPV infection, e.g., high fever, hemorrhagic gastroenteritis, and
lymphopenia.78,79 Some features of pantropic CCoV infection are similar
to severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) in humans and FIP in cats:
pulmonary alveolar damage, fibrinous exudation, and macrophage
involvement.80 Despite virus similarities, FIP is much more common
after FCoV infection in cats as compared with pantropic CCoV infection
of dogs.

DIAGNOSIS
Achieving a definitive diagnosis is difficult. The gold standard is
postmortem identification of viral antigen in tissue sections using
immunofluorescence or immunostaining. CCoV-1 viruses, like their
FCoV-1 counterparts, grow poorly in cell culture. Diagnosis through virus
isolation is limited to CCoV-2 strains. The most useful antemortem tests
involve RT-PCR.81 As with FECV and FIPV, there is no molecular test to
differentiate pantropic CCoV from classical CCoV.

PREVENTION AND TREATMENT
Inactivated and modified-live virus vaccines are commercially available,
designed to prevent CCoV infection. The vaccines are safe but do not
provide complete protection; they reduce but do not eliminate CCoV

replication in the GI tract (ch. 185).82 History of natural infection with
classical CCoV is not protective against challenge with more virulent
pantropic strains.83 Treatment of CCoV mirrors that of CPV (ch. 201):
maintenance of fluid and electrolyte balance, nutritional support,
treatment of secondary bacterial infections, and general supportive care.
There are no available antiviral drugs for treatment of CCoV infections.

CANINE RESPIRATORY CORONAVIRUS
(CRCoV)
CRCoV was first identified in 2003 and linked to canine infectious
respiratory disease complex (CIRD) or “kennel cough” (ch. 203). As its
name suggests, it is respiratory-transmitted and is in a different genus
(betacoronavirus) from CCoV and FCoV (alphacoronavirus). CRCoV is
closely related to bovine coronavirus and a human “common-cold”
coronavirus OC43. It likely shares a common receptor with these viruses
but is distinct from equine coronavirus (ECoV) (Figure 200.1). CRCoV
is widespread globally, especially in animal shelters, and is believed to be
highly infectious via aerosols. Diagnosis is via PCR from respiratory swab
specimens or by acute and convalescent serologic testing in conjunction
with compatible clinical signs. Virus isolation is possible, but not typically
achieved as the virus is challenging to culture. There are no vaccines for
CRCoV. CCoV vaccines are not expected to be protective. The association
of CRCoV with CIRD has been an active area of investigation, and with
the advent of COVID-19, its role in the etiology of respiratory infections
in dogs deserves further attention.84

SEVERE ACUTE RESPIRATORY
SYNDROME CORONAVIRUS-2
In early 2020, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARSCoV-2) emerged as a novel zoonotic coronavirus, causing a devastating
global pandemic. This virus is most likely from a bat species, with an
initial outbreak in Wuhan, China in late 2019. The virus was
subsequently shown to be highly transmissible. It uses angiotensin
converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) as a receptor. Early work implicated cats as
a potential host for SARS-CoV-2 based on the high degree of similarity

between human and feline ACE2 at the virus binding interface.85
However, the first reported infection of pets by SARS-CoV-2 occurred in
dogs, which have a more divergent receptor binding interface. The first 2
dogs diagnosed in March of 2020 were in Hong Kong. The dogs had been
in contact with SARS-CoV-2 positive owners. The dogs tested positive
from nasal and oral swabs but remained subclinical during their
isolation. Despite 1 elderly dog dying shortly afterwards, this was not
attributed to the SARS-CoV-2 infection (although no necropsy was
performed). Subsequently other dogs have tested positive for SARS-CoV2 and have been implicated in SARS-CoV-2 emergence, but to date
evidence is lacking for dogs being a significant public health or veterinary
concern in relation to SARS-CoV-2.
In contrast, cats have become more established as hosts for SARS-CoV2. Following reported cases in Hong Kong and Belgium during March
2020, the most notable early natural infection was at the Bronx Zoo in
New York City. In April, 4 tigers and 3 lions developed mild respiratory
signs as a result of transmission of infection from their handlers, with
SARS-CoV-2 detected by PCR and sequencing.86 Subsequently, infection
of both domestic and non-domestic cats has become relatively common
where owners and handlers are SARS-CoV-2 positive. Clinically, SARSCoV-2 infection in cats has been considered to be mainly subclinical, with
some animals showing mild respiratory signs.87 However, some cats may
show more severe respiratory distress and additional signs, possibly
connected to underlying feline hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM).88
An increased incidence of canine and feline myocarditis linked to the
surge of the B.1.1.7 (Alpha) variant in the UK was also reported at a
veterinary hospital. More studies in this area are clearly warranted, as are
possible links between coronavirus infections in cats and multisystem
inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C), a rare outcome of SARSCoV-2 infection.
Studies in laboratory animals have also been key to understanding
SARS-CoV-2 infection in cats and dogs—with early studies reporting poor
replication in dogs, whereas cats were highly susceptible to infection by
the airborne route. Subsequently, mild respiratory signs or subclinical
infection, viral shedding, cat-cat transmission and the development of a
robust neutralizing antibody response was confirmed in cats. More recent
studies have shown that long term immunity exists following re-infection
of cats, but that cats may develop long-term sequelae, including
persistence of inflammation and other lung lesions.89 In summary, and

as with SARS-CoV in 2003, cats in particular may hold important clues to
the pathogenesis and immune responses induced by SARS-CoV-2.

Andrew L. Leisewitz

ETIOLOGY AND EPIDEMIOLOGY
Canine and feline parvoviruses are a common cause of high
morbidity and mortality among dogs and cats worldwide. Members
of the parvovirus genus infect a wide range of mammalian hosts but

do show host specificity. Canine parvovirus (CPV) and feline
panleukopenia virus (FPV) are the two important parvoviruses of
dogs and cats, respectively. They are classified according to the hosts
from which they have been isolated. Both CPV and FPV are
considered to be host range variants among the feline parvoviruses,
and cats are capable of carrying and shedding CPV.1 The genetic
sequences of CPV and FPV differ by only around 2% and they are
antigenically similar. CPV can infect multiple host species. In areas
where dogs and wildlife interface this impacts transmission ecology
and the protection of wild species.
CPV is a simple, small, non-enveloped, single stranded DNA virus
with a genome size of around 5000 base pairs. Capsid proteins are
the key structures determining host specificity and antigenicity. The
host range of CPV and FPV differs and is determined by less than 10
amino acid differences in the capsid protein. The virus makes use of
the transferrin receptor to gain entry into cells. The polymorphisms
in this receptor are responsible for host specificity. There is evidence
that viral pathogenicity is related to phylogeny.2 FPV replicates in
feline-derived cell lines in vitro and in vivo but not in canine cell
lines. CPV on the other hand replicates in feline and canine cell lines
in culture and in dogs in vivo. FPV is able to replicate to a limited
extent in dogs but without causing illness. Since it infects dog
thymus and bone marrow, it is not able to spread among dogs. The
first CPV discovered in 1967 was called the minute virus of canines
(later called CPV-1). It is no longer considered clinically important.
CPV-2 was discovered in dogs in 1978 in the United States and,
within months, was responsible for a devastating global pandemic.
The virus is now well established worldwide and is probably the
single most common infectious disease of dogs with a high morbidity
and mortality. This virus has subsequently mutated into CPV2a,
CPV2b and then to CPV2c; CPV2c was first identified in Italy in
2000 but is now reported worldwide. CPV2a and CPV2b are capable
of infecting cats and causing a clinical illness indistinguishable from
panleukopenia but this is uncommon.3 There are occasional reports
of multiple diarrhea-associated viral co-infections in dogs, e.g.,
canine distemper virus (CDV, ch. 204), rotavirus, kobuvirus, and
bufavirus.

CPV and FPV are transmitted by the fecal-oral route, and fomite
transmission is also efficient. Diseased dogs can excrete large
quantities of virus in their stools (up to 109 median tissue culture
infectious dose [TCID50] per gram of feces). Parvoviral enteritis
caseload has been directly correlated with wind speeds and inversely
to humidity.4 There is also evidence for seasonality of CPV infections
in Canada,5 and the incidence of FPV infections in North America is
correlated to a peak in the susceptible kitten population.6 There is
evidence that certain breeds are more susceptible to infection with
Rottweilers, American Pit Bull Terriers, Doberman Pinschers,
English Springer Spaniels, and German Shepherd Dogs being at
increased risk. The risk for development of CPV gastrointestinal (GI)
inflammation was higher in purebreds compared to mixed-breed
puppies in one study.7 There is no published evidence of breed
susceptibility among cats.
Because immunity is conferred by antibody, maternally-derived
titers effectively protect neonates. Approximately 90% of maternallyderived antibody is from colostrum. This antibody has a half-life of
around 10 days. Susceptibility increases as maternal immunity
wanes at around 12-14 weeks of age. Vaccination is highly protective
in preventing infection. During periods where there is an abundant
supply of susceptible animals (such as puppies and kittens that lack
maternal antibody), disease incidence increases. Introduction of
infected animals into shelter environments may also result in
explosive outbreaks. Other factors that contribute to infection
include GI parasites, overcrowding, and unsanitary and stressful
environmental conditions. Both CPV and FPV are extremely stable in
the environment, which makes indirect transmission important and
environmental decontamination difficult. Care should be taken in
veterinary clinics where unvaccinated or inadequately vaccinated
puppies are likely to come into contact with contaminated surfaces.
Dogs with CPV enteritis that are admitted to hospital for treatment
should be kept isolated from the hospital population. Flies may also
play an important role in the spread of the infection among dogs.8

PATHOGENESIS
The pathogenesis of CPV and FPV infections are similar. The virus is
unable to induce mitosis in the cells it infects and hence it relies on
the rapidly multiplying cells of the body for its success. The virus
thus shows a tropism for cells of the thymus, bone marrow, spleen,
and crypt cells of the GI epithelium. Stress factors, in particular
parasitic and other nonspecific factors such as weaning, may
predispose dogs to infection by increasing mucosal cell activity. FPV
lesions have been documented to be enhanced by co-infections with
feline leukemia virus (ch. 199),9 Clostridium piliforme (chs. 195,
262),10 and feline coronavirus (ch. 200).11

FIGURE 201.1 German Shepherd Dog puppy with
canine parvovirus infection. The dog is moribund
(A) and in hypovolemic shock with hemorrhagic
diarrhea (B) and pale dry mucous membranes (C).

Following oral infection, CPV and FPV disseminate to regional
lymph nodes of the pharynx and the tonsils. In an experimental
study in dogs, fecal shedding was present from day 3 following oral
infection, peaked on days 3 and 4, and was greatly reduced by day 7.
Shedding may occur for a day or 2 before clinical signs are apparent.
The incubation period varies from around 4 days (under
experimental conditions) to the more typical 1 to 2 weeks usually
seen under natural conditions. Following infection of lymphoid
tissues of the upper GI tract (including the tongue), a cell-free
viremia ensues (chs. 260, 262). Under experimental conditions this
lasts from 1 to 5 days post-infection, serum antibodies appear on day
5, and they peak from day 7 onwards. Thymic and lymphoid tissue
infection leads to thymic atrophy, lymphoid depletion, lymphopenia,
and immunosuppression. Viral antigen is detectable in the
proliferative zone of the GI crypt epithelium from day 4. Very little
antigen remains in either the lymphoid tissues or GI epithelium from
day 7 onwards. Subclinical infection is probably common, especially
in older immune-competent animals.

CLINICAL SIGNS
The earliest clinical signs include fever, lethargy, and inappetence,
followed by diarrhea and vomiting. This is true for CPV infections
and most infections with FPV. Initially, small bowel diarrhea with a
fetid odor is typical. Melena and then hematochezia may follow (ch.
50), suggesting mixed small and large bowel involvement (Figure
201.1 and ch. 49). Vomiting (ch. 48) usually increases in frequency
and can become severe and frequent with little more than foam
produced. Ascarids may be observed in the vomitus. In peracute
feline panleukopenia, young cats can die within 12 hours of showing
lethargy due to profound septic shock, dehydration, and
hypothermia. Vomiting and diarrhea are far less common in cats
infected with FPV.
Bone marrow infection may lead to marrow necrosis in both dogs
and cats (ch. 176). This contributes to leukopenia and may also
contribute to anemia (chs. 57, 58). Leukopenia, not
thrombocytopenia, is typically present by the time hemorrhagic
diarrhea and vomiting appear.12 An increased concentration of

granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) has been documented
in dogs with CPV and this likely to be a response to the
neutropenia.13 Neutropenia is partially explained by the
overwhelming demand for neutrophils in the gut. The
immunosuppression associated with CPV infection increases
susceptibility to acute secondary infections. The most common of
these are bacterial bloodstream infections which manifest clinically
as endotoxic shock (chs. 121, 128). On recovery, some puppies have
been reported to develop skin necrosis (Figure 201.2, ch. 181),
bacterial polyarthritis (ch. 177), and/or discospondylitis (Figure
201.3, ch. 250).14 Immunosuppression should be managed by
strictly enforced barrier nursing practices (Figure 201.4). Puppies
with other contagious infectious diseases, especially CDV, should not
be kept in the same ward or cared for by individuals simultaneously
caring for dogs with CPV infection (ch. 204). CDV is an important
differential diagnosis for CPV-like signs and mixed infections with
CDV and CPV can occur.

FIGURE 201.2 A young Basset Hound puppy that
recovered from parvoviral diarrhea complicated by
secondary Salmonella bacteremia. The bacteremia
resulted in ear-tip skin necrosis, probably due to
micro-embolization of the peripheral vasculature.

FIGURE 201.3 A 12-week-old Labrador crossbreed puppy was treated for parvovirus infection and
discharged from hospital. It returned 3 days later
with spinal pain. Radiographs showed a collapsed
lumbar 4-5 disc space with mild subluxation (A).
Follow up radiographs taken 2 weeks later showed
findings typical of discospondylitis with subluxation
(B), as well as a new cervical vertebral lesion (not
shown). Images courtesy R. Kirberger.
Viral infection of the gut leads to crypt necrosis and collapse of
intestinal villi, with loss of the normal GI barrier function. This has

serious consequences as elements of the gut content can no longer be
kept out of the bloodstream.15 Escherichia coli was recovered from
the lungs and liver of 90% of 98 CPV-infected puppies.16 GI
hemorrhage may be significant, resulting in melena, hematochezia,
and anemia (which may be masked by dehydration). Concurrent
hookworm infestations may cause further blood loss and are known
to aggravate parvovirus enteritis. Concurrent giardiasis and/or
coccidiosis may also occur (chs. 196, 262).

FIGURE 201.4 The isolation ward of the
Onderstepoort Veterinary Academic Hospital where
dogs with parvovirus are treated. The highly
contagious nature of the disease necessitates barrier
nursing. The resistant nature of the virus requires
that the facility be easily disinfected.
Devastating life-threatening fluid and electrolyte losses,
exacerbated by lack of oral intake, are caused by the vomiting and

diarrhea21a (chs. 119-121). In addition to dehydration, the most
common electrolyte concern is hypokalemia (ch. 68). The
dehydration would be classified as isotonic or hypotonic (due to
hypertonic fluid loss) and results in dry mucous membranes,
increased skin turgor, increased capillary refill time, tachycardia,
hypotension, collapse, and reduced urine production (chs. 120 and
121). The acid-base disturbances that occur are complex and heavily
influenced by chloride, free water, and albumin concentrations.
Severely affected animals tend to demonstrate hypochloremic
alkalosis, whereas mildly affected puppies have a hyperchloremic
acidosis. The strong ion model proposed by Stewart provides better
insights into pathological mechanisms than the traditional
Henderson-Hasselbalch model.17
Coagulation abnormalities were also documented in 9 dogs with
CPV infection (ch. 170). These dogs had a high prevalence of clinical
thrombosis or phlebitis (chs. 181, 238) and laboratory evidence of
decreased antithrombin activity, prolonged activated partial
thromboplastin time, increased maximum amplitude in their
thromboelastograms, and increased fibrinogen concentrations (ch.
171). The dogs demonstrated hypercoagulability without
disseminated intravascular coagulopathy.12 Clinically obvious
petechiation or hemorrhage from sites other than the gut are not a
feature of CPV infections.
FPV causes cerebellar hypoplasia in kittens exposed to the virus in
utero or in the early neonatal period (Video 201.1

). The virus

destroys Purkinje cells and granule precursor cells in the developing
cerebellum (ch. 244). Pathologic changes vary from mild cerebellar
disease to severe hydranencephaly, hydrocephalus, and
porencephaly. Less seriously affected animals may make acceptable
pets as the disease is non-progressive. Clinical signs also vary widely
and may be multifocal depending on the areas of the brain affected
and the degree to which they are affected. Seizure activity is possible
with cerebral involvement.
Early in the CPV-2 disease pandemic, when dogs were not
vaccinated and dams transferred no maternal antibodies to their
pups, very young (<8 weeks of age) pups or pups in utero became
infected. At that time, myocardial infections were more common.

Myocardial disease due to CPV is now considered rare, although it
still occurs in isolated unvaccinated populations (ch. 233).18
However, evidence of myocarditis and myocardial fibrosis associated
with CPV-2 in dogs has been shown by in situ hybridization, despite
the dogs being vaccinated.19 Cardiac signs sometimes occurred in the
absence of obvious enteric disease. A wide range of cardiac signs
have been described, from peracute congestive failure to more
chronic failure becoming evident only months after infection.
However, other molecular studies in search of CPV DNA in heart
muscle from dogs with myocarditis or dilated cardiomyopathy have
not yielded positive results. Using molecular methods, FPV was
identified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in 10 of 31 cats with
cardiomyopathy but in none of the 17 controls in one study,
suggesting a possible role of viral infection in the pathogenesis of
feline cardiomyopathy (ch. 234).20
The most common causes of death in acute CPV and FPV
infections are bacteremia, endotoxemia, and shock (Figure 201.1).
Endotoxins and the subsequent inflammatory cascade they initiate
correlate with disease severity and outcome (ch. 128).21 One study
showed that 22% of the intravenous (IV) catheter tips used for fluid
infusion were colonized with bacteria (ch. 186). Most of the
organisms involved were Gram-negative GI-associated bacteria.
Hypoglycemia, a common finding, is likely due to the young age of
most affected dogs and their concomitant anorexia. The
hypermetabolic state associated with endotoxic shock increases the
chance of hypoglycemia and is the most likely cause of seizures in
puppies with CPV infection.

DIAGNOSIS
The diagnosis of parvoviral disease is usually based on combining a
cluster of findings that includes the typical signalment (young and
un- or inadequately vaccinated), classic owner concerns of lethargy,
anorexia, vomiting and diarrhea (which may be hemorrhagic),
typical clinical findings of pyrexia, dehydration, fluid and gas-filled
intestinal loops (which may be painful), and leukopenia. In many
resource-deprived settings (where the greatest disease burden

occurs) no further tests are performed and a presumptive diagnosis
is made.
The next step in diagnosis, a fecal parvovirus antigen enzymelinked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), can confirm the disease (chs.
183, 184). These tests are widely used, detect all CPV variants, are
specific, but can lack sensitivity.22 False positives may occur
following vaccination with attenuated live CPV vaccines due to the
shedding of vaccine virus for 4-8 days afterward (up to 28 days in
one study).23 Indeed, the vaccine strain can be transmitted among
dogs, but is shed in the absence of clinical signs. A similar
phenomenon can occur after FPV vaccination. Fecal viral shedding is
transient and fecal antibodies can bind the virus, making it
undetectable by assay reagents. Serum antibody testing is seldom
used. ELISA assays that are semiquantitative for anti-CPV 2
antibodies are more often used to determine the need for vaccination
rather than for diagnosis, because of widespread exposure and
vaccination. Fecal electron microscopy, although useful, is seldom
used due to limited availability. PCR assays are available, but
subclinical shedding of low quantities of virus make it difficult to
determine the significance of a positive test result. PCR may be
useful if an ELISA assay is negative in an animal with suggestive
clinical signs. Feline panleukopenia is diagnosed from signalment,
clinical signs, and the same point-of-care (POC) fecal ELISA tests
used for detecting CPV. The same testing limitations apply to
detection of FPV as for CPV. Fecal flotation and direct smears (ch.
80) for evidence of concurrent parasitic infections should be routine
in all dogs and cats with suspected CPV or FPV infection.
