intraperitoneal (IP) route.

CLINICAL MANAGEMENT
HOME MANAGEMENT
There is no specific antiviral treatment available for canine and feline
parvovirus infections and hence supportive care is the mainstay of
therapy. In-patient care is cost prohibitive for many clients and this
is a frequent reason for euthanasia. A single owner may have an
entire litter of puppies become sick and the financial burden often
dictates practical best-practice home-based care. Although inpatient
care is generally superior to outpatient care, the outcome of dogs
treated with a simple outpatient protocol was not significantly
different from those treated as inpatients.24 Large numbers of
infected dogs can be successfully treated in a welfare setting with
practical, easily applied treatment.25 Outpatient care includes daily

SQ or intraperitoneal (IP) fluids (KCl can be added to IP fluids;
Figure 201.5), parenteral antibiotics (ampicillin or cefovecin),
maropitant (occasionally metoclopramide for home administration
may be added), fenbendazole PO (for 5 days), an oral rehydration
mixture for home administration, and a high-energy liquid diet to be
dosed by the owner at home. Daily revisits are scheduled until
recovery. In severely affected dogs (in shock) or when owners can
afford more advanced treatment, cases are admitted to a facility that
can provide isolation and barrier nursing.

IN-HOSPITAL CARE
Overview
Intensive treatment with crystalloid fluids, synthetic and natural
colloids, correction of hypoglycemia and any electrolyte
disturbances, a combination of antimicrobials, antiemetics,
analgesics, enteral nutritional support, and anthelmintics usually
form the basis of in-hospital care (chs. 119, 120, 121). Fluid therapy
to treat dehydration, re-establish effective circulating blood volume,
as well as correct electrolyte and acid-base disturbances is the
mainstay of managing more severely affected puppies and kittens
(chs. 120 and 121). Fluid therapy in these pets can be complex due
to changing fluid, acid-base, electrolyte, and glucose status. Close
monitoring of the physical examination, electrolyte, and acid-base
status is critical for success. The preferred route for fluid
administration is IV, but intraosseous administration may be
necessary in pets in dire need of fluids where IV access is not
possible due to severe dehydration and patient size (ch. 76). IV
catheters should be replaced q72h.

Fluids and Electrolytes
The initial fluid of choice is a balanced electrolyte solution isotonic to
blood (i.e., lactated Ringer’s solution). The initial rate of fluid
administration will depend on the condition of the animal. IV fluid
boluses may be necessary for treatment of shock (chs. 120 and 121).
Fluid deficits should be replaced as soon as possible (within 1 to 6
hours of initial examination). Once perfusion is restored, the fluid

administration rate should be adjusted to a maintenance rate plus
estimated ongoing losses. Hypokalemia is common and KCl should
be added to the IV fluids until potassium concentrations have
normalized (chs. 68, 290). Hypoglycemia is also common
(especially in smaller dogs) and in severe cases a 25% dextrose bolus
can be given (chs. 61, 289). Following the correction of
hypoglycemia, the IV fluid may be supplemented with glucose to
create a 2.5 to 5% solution to maintain normoglycemia until appetite
returns.

Managing Oncotic Pressure and Anemia
Hypoalbuminemia (ch. 60) is common due to GI losses. Colloid
oncotic pressure may require support with a synthetic colloid such as
hetastarch if albumin drops below 2.0 g/dL (20 g/L) or if there is
obvious third-space fluid loss (chs. 120 and 121). The role of blood
products in the treatment of CPV is controversial. Animals with
anemia secondary to hemorrhagic diarrhea, bone marrow failure, or
concurrent endoparasitism should be transfused with packed red
blood cells or whole blood (ch. 124). Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)
transfusion has been recommended in the treatment of CPV enteritis
for its ability to provide oncotic components (albumin),
immunoglobulin, and serum protease inhibitors, which may help to
neutralize circulating virus and control the systemic inflammatory
response associated with this disease (ch. 128). However, FFP
infusion has been shown to be a poor means of supporting colloid
oncotic pressure due to the large volumes that are often required.26
A study evaluating the effects of IV hyperimmune plasma found that
markers of shock improved, but the study was insufficiently powered
to evaluate the effect on hospital stay or mortality.27

Nutrition
Puppies receiving early enteral nutrition via a nasoesophageal tube,
when compared with puppies that received nil per os until vomiting
ceased, showed earlier clinical improvement, significant weight gain,
and improved GI barrier function, which could limit bacterial or
endotoxin translocation (chs. 81, 146; Video 201.2

). In some

cases of severe ileus, gastric distension can be relieved through
suctioning gas and excess stomach contents. Caution is advised
because excessive suctioning can worsen fluid, electrolyte, and
caloric deficiencies. Once vomiting has ceased, treatment for
endoparasites should be initiated.

Antiemetics
Antiemetics are indicated in managing CPV. Commonly used
antiemetics for CPV enteritis include metoclopramide,
prochlorperazine, ondansetron, cisapride, and maropitant (ch. 48).
Metoclopramide, ondansetron and maropitant appear to be equally
effective.28 With intractable vomiting, combination therapy and
administering these drugs via constant rate infusion (CRI) may be
more effective than monotherapy or bolus administration. In a
retrospective study, antiemetics did not completely control vomiting,
and puppies receiving them required longer hospitalization. A causeand-effect conclusion could not be drawn.29

Antibiotics, Parasitacides, and Other Therapies
Treatment with IV, broad-spectrum, bactericidal antibiotics is
warranted in puppies with CPV enteritis due to the disruption of
their GI barrier and severe leukopenia (ch. 140). A combination of a
beta-lactam (ampicillin, 20 mg/kg IV q8h) with an aminoglycoside
(e.g., amikacin, 20 mg/kg IV, IM, or SQ every 24 h for a maximum of
5 days once proper hydration has been established) provides
effective coverage. Although some authors have expressed concern
about the use of a nephrotoxic antibiotic in dogs with parvoviral
enteritis, renal failure has never been observed by the author despite
regularly using aminoglycosides. A short course of parenteral
fluoroquinolone such as enrofloxacin is an alternative for Gramnegative coverage and is unlikely to cause clinically significant
cartilage damage when used in this manner. Metronidazole (15-20
mg/kg PO q12h for up to 10 days) or, preferably, fenbendazole (50
mg/kg PO q24h for 5 days) is indicated in cases where motile
protozoa are found on fecal wet preparation (chs. 142, 196).
Several studies have shown recombinant interferons to
significantly ameliorate severe enteritis caused by CPV and reduce

mortality, although these are not widely available. One study
concluded that recombinant canine G-CSF increased circulating
white cell counts but its effect on outcome was unclear. Suitable
analgesics for abdominal pain, which may be severe, include
buprenorphine, fentanyl, and in some cases a lidocaine-ketamine
combination CRI (ch. 6). Several other adjunctive agents have been
investigated, including recombinant human G-CSF (rhG-CSF) and
recombinant bactericidal/permeability-increasing protein (rBPI21),
but neither demonstrated benefit. Oseltamivir, an antiviral drug that
inhibits neuraminidase of influenza viruses, was also found be of
minimal benefit.30 Enteric dysbiosis is a feature of CPV (ch. 260).31
Fecal microbiota transplantation has resulted in faster resolution of
diarrhea (ch. 106).32

Monitoring
Close monitoring allows treatment adjustments and crucial
assessment of progression (ch. 119). Clinical data (including a full
physical examination) to specifically assess hydration (body weights
are helpful), frequency of vomiting and defecation, abdominal
palpation (to assess for development of intussusception), and
assessment of levels of pain are standard care. Under normal
circumstances the following laboratory data should be monitored at
least daily (and in some cases more frequently): hematocrit, total
serum solids (or total serum protein and albumin); serum
electrolytes (Na, K, Cl) and blood glucose.

PROGNOSIS
The survival rate for dogs infected with CPV enteritis ranges from
around 10% for untreated puppies to >90% with aggressive inhospital treatment. Thus, prognosis depends in part, on an owner’s
financial limitations. Despite this, as noted above, outpatient-based
treatments and welfare/shelter based treatment protocols have
shown encouraging survival data at a significantly reduced cost.24,25
The earlier that intensive treatment is initiated in the disease course,
the better the outcome. Various hematological variables have been

associated with prognosis, including leukopenia, lymphopenia,
monocytopenia and neutropenia (ch. 180).7,33 The presence of a
systemic inflammatory response syndrome at the time of admission
was also a negative indicator (ch. 128).7 Other factors that have
been correlated with outcome include season of year, purebred
nature, body weight, vomiting, hypercoagulability,
hypercortisolemia, hypothyroxinemia, hypoalbuminemia, elevated
C-reactive protein, increased tumor necrosis factor,
hypocholesterolemia, and hypocitrullinemia. A more flexible method
of modeling that yielded a sensitive and specific prediction of disease
outcome combined concentrations of plasma antithrombin, serum
aspartate aminotransferase, serum lipase, plus counts of monocytes
and lymphocytes.34 Dogs that survive infection appear to be at
increased risk of developing chronic GI disease.35

PREVENTION
Live attenuated and inactivated vaccines for canine and feline
parvovirus infection are widely available and are considered “core” in
any vaccination program for both dogs and cats (ch. 185). Immunity
is antibody-dependent and sterile. Immunity following natural
infection is probably lifelong. It is not recommended to vaccinate
pregnant animals with the attenuated live vaccine as vaccine virus
has the potential to cause disease in the fetus; however, in shelter
situations it may outweigh the risk of a shelter outbreak. Inactivated
vaccines require more time to provide protection, which translates to
a much longer period of susceptibility early in life. By far the most
common cause for vaccine failure remains vaccine neutralization by
maternally derived antibodies. Traditional vaccination programs
start at 4-6 weeks, with additional vaccination 1 and 2 months later.
The final vaccination should be given no earlier than 14-16 weeks of
age (ch. 185). Where problems exist in breeding establishments,
vaccination programs could commence earlier in an attempt to
protect puppies that lack adequate maternal antibody, and
vaccinations can be repeated every 2 weeks in an attempt to reduce
the window of vulnerability. A high titer modified live virus vaccine
can provide protection for pups vaccinated as early as 4 weeks of

age.36 The frequency of boosting through life is contentious but it is
generally accepted that a booster should be given at a year of age and
then every 3 years thereafter. Some concern has been raised about
the ability of available CPV-2 strain vaccines to protect against CPV2c. Challenge studies using dogs vaccinated with CPV-2 have
however demonstrated good protection against CPV-2c.37
The highly contagious and very resistant nature of canine and
feline parvoviruses make barrier nursing of infected animals and
very stringent disinfection protocols (such as using 0.75%
hypochlorite or potassium peroxymonosulfate) crucial to preventing
transmission. Because soil/organic matter cannot be disinfected,
only vaccinated animals should be allowed onto potentially
contaminated natural surfaces.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Canine and Feline Parvovirus
WHAT IS PARVOVIRUS?
This is one of the most common and serious viruses that puppies and
kittens can contract. Viruses are much smaller than bacteria and they
cannot cause disease unless they infect a living and multiplying cell
in dog or cat. Parvoviruses are particularly small and attack the
rapidly dividing cells of the body, which include the cells that line the
intestine, the bone marrow, and cells of the immune system.
Infection of the fetus can also cause very serious birth defects or
death.
WHICH ANIMALS ARE AT RISK?
The disease affects mostly puppies and kittens, especially under
about 4 months of age. Female dogs and cats that have been
vaccinated provide antibodies to their young through their milk;
these antibodies are absorbed within the first day after birth. These
antibodies protect puppies and kittens for the first few weeks of life
but after that they are fully susceptible. The antibodies provided by
the mother in her milk prevent vaccinations from being effective.
There is a window during which time the antibodies a puppy or
kitten absorb from their mother are no longer sufficient to protect it
from infection but are sufficient to prevent a vaccine from being
effective. This is known as “the window of vulnerability” and is the
reason why vaccination programs comprise 3 injections about a
month apart starting at 4-6 weeks of age. The very last vaccine given
(usually at 14-18 weeks of age) is the one that is most likely to be
protective as there will be no antibodies from the mother left in the
puppy or kitten’s system to destroy the vaccine by this point. The
most common reason for vaccine failure is only partial completion of
the vaccination series. Puppies and kittens catch the disease from
other infected animals, from people who have had contact with
infected animals, or from an environment that has been

contaminated by infected animals. Parvovirus is very hardy and can
survive for many months in soil and on surfaces. Household bleach
diluted 1:30 and left on a surface for 30 minutes is an effective
decontaminating agent. Steam cleaning is also effective. Hygiene and
limiting contact with other animals until after the vaccination
program is complete is strongly recommended. About 10 days after
the last vaccination, a puppy or kitten will be immune.
HOW WOULD I KNOW MY PUPPY OR KITTEN HAS
PARVOVIRUS INFECTION?
The first sign is usually lethargy and a loss of appetite. This is
followed a day or two later by vomiting and diarrhea. The diarrhea
may well become bloody. Once this stage is reached the animal
becomes very dehydrated and is unable to stand. The incubation
period between exposure and showing signs of disease ranges from 4
days to about 2 weeks.
WHAT CAN BE DONE ABOUT THE DISEASE ONCE MY
ANIMAL HAS IT?
Most puppies or kittens that contract parvovirus infections will die if
they are not properly treated. If you suspect your puppy or kitten has
the disease, the earlier you seek the help of a veterinarian, the better
the chances of recovery. Early initiation of aggressive treatment may
save expenses later. Unfortunately, because of the serious nature of
the disease, many affected puppies and kittens require
hospitalization and treatment with intravenous fluids, antibiotics,
and other medications. Home treatment may not be rewarding
because often almost everything given by mouth may be vomited
back up.
HOW CAN I PREVENT MY ANIMALS FROM GETTING THE
INFECTION?
Proper vaccination is absolutely crucial. In addition to this,
preventing contact with other infected dogs or kittens and
contaminated environments is important until about 10 days after
the vaccination program is complete.

MY PUPPY OR KITTEN HAD PARVOVIRUS AND IS NOW
BEING DISCHARGED FROM THE HOSPITAL. WHAT
SHOULD I KNOW ABOUT HOW TO CARE FOR IT NOW?
By the time your puppy or kitten is discharged from hospital it is
unlikely to still be shedding virus in its stool. It may, however, still be
carrying virus on its fur coat, so thorough bathing is recommended
before it has contact with other puppies or kittens in its home
environment. Dogs and cats that are fully vaccinated are not going to
be in danger from exposure to your returning puppy or kitten. Any
medication you may have been provided by your veterinarian must
be completed. Nutrition is very important to assist in recovery. Your
animal will most likely have lost weight in hospital and feeding a diet
appropriate for a recovering intestine for a few weeks after discharge
will aid recovery. This should gradually be switched to an age
appropriate diet. It is suggested that the animal’s weight be
monitored and that an age and breed appropriate weight should be
achieved within a few months of discharge. There are very unlikely to
be any long term effects from the disease. Puppies and kittens that
recover usually do so completely. Recovered animals are also
normally completely immune and will not contact parvovirus again
in their life time.
Andrew L. Leisewitz (Auburn, Alabama)

THE GLOBAL BURDEN OF RABIES
OVERVIEW
“Rabies” often invokes keen attention and/or powerful fear among
veterinarians, pet owners, caregivers of domestic and wild animals,
and the public. Rabies continues to have the highest mortality rate of
any known infectious agent. In contrast to Ebola and Lassa fever,
which are 50-90% lethal, rabies is still virtually 100% fatal. There has
only been one well-documented human survivor of clinical rabies.
The global burden of human and animal rabies continues through
transmission among domestic dogs mainly in Asia and Africa and
many wildlife hosts around the world. Rabies is a viral zoonosis
transmitted through the bite of a rabid animal.

CONTROLLING TRANSMISSION:
HUMANS, DOG-TO-DOG, AND
WILDLIFE ANIMALS

The most important threat of exposure to humans and domestic
animals in Europe and North America was significantly reduced
several decades ago through extinction of canine rabies virus
variants, which are perpetuated dog-to-dog. The last known case of
dog-to-dog transmitted rabies in Mexico was in 2015. In 2019, the
World Health Organization declared Mexico free from human rabies
transmitted by dogs. This was achieved through coordinated,
methodical, population-based vaccination of dogs against rabies, as
well as control of stray dog populations. These techniques, applied
globally, could push remaining canine rabies virus variants to
extinction, if sufficient effort and resources were applied in a
cooperative manner.
While the incidence of human rabies decreased over the past 50+
years due to fewer exposures and better prophylactic biologics, an
increase in wildlife rabies was detected, in part due to enhanced
surveillance among wildlife reservoir species and in part because
infections have increased. The 1970s and 80s brought an intensified
epizootic among skunks and the 1990s saw the raccoon rabies virus
variant spread from the southeastern USA to the northeast and into
Canada (ch. 9). Awareness of rabies in insectivorous bats
(throughout North America) enhanced their surveillance. Improved
canine rabies control over the past 2 decades has taken place in
Central America. Overall, there has been a decline in animal rabies in
North America from over 20,000 animal diagnoses/year a decade
ago to about 10,000 per year currently. About 85% of cases occur in
the U.S. (Figure 202.1). These downward trends demonstrate the
recent success in canine rabies control in Mexico and
implementation of oral rabies vaccination of red foxes in Canada.
The continuing enzootic in the United States and more recently in
Canada is due to spread of raccoon rabies. Despite the historic
extinction of canine rabies virus variants in much of North America,
many rabies virus variants have been identified in wildlife, which
constitutes an ever-present risk of exposure (Figure 202.2). The
4000-5000 animal rabies cases diagnosed every year represent a
subset of all naturally occurring cases (Figure 202.3).

CAUSE AND EPIDEMIOLOGY
GENUS LYSSAVIRUS, FAMILY
RHABDOVIRIDAE
Rabies viruses are relatively fragile. Dried saliva or contaminated
tissue is no longer infectious. The envelope bilayer of virions is
readily disrupted by common disinfectants, also rendering the
material non-infectious. The term rabies describes an acute fatal
disease of the nervous system caused by viruses in the genus
Lyssavirus, family Rhabdoviridae, which are bullet-shaped
enveloped viruses with a negative-sense single-stranded genome. In
addition to the Type Member “rabies viruses,” the Lyssavirus genus
has 6 well-described and 4 newly described members. The rabiesrelated Lyssaviruses include Lagos bat, Mokoka, Duvenhage,
European bat Lyssaviruses 1 and 2, Australian bat Lyssavirus, and
Eurasia bat viruses (West Caucasian, Irkut, Aravan, Khujand bat

Lyssaviruses). The species of animals in which these viruses are
perpetuated are restricted to the orders Chiroptera (bats) and
Carnivora (carnivores). Mammals are variably susceptible to rabies.
Rabies does not occur in amphibians, reptiles, birds, or
invertebrates.
While the USA, Canada, and Mexico are free of dog-to-dog
transmission of canine rabies virus variants, rabies is occasionally
reported in unvaccinated dogs infected by a wildlife source. Rabies
may occur in dogs imported from countries where dog-to-dog
transmission still occurs (ch. 9).

SKUNKS, RACOONS, BATS, AND FOXES
IN NORTH AMERICA
Rabies viruses in North America are the wildlife species perpetuated
through animal-to-animal transmission within a single reservoir
species (Figure 202.2). The epizootiology of “spillover” to other
species is influenced by the ecology of the reservoir species and
mixing susceptible wild and domestic mammalian hosts. Rabies is
transmitted primarily among skunks or raccoons in 4 major North
American areas: the raccoon rabies virus variant from Florida
through Maine into Ontario and New Brunswick, Canada, extending
westward to the Appalachians and Ohio; two distinct skunkassociated viruses termed North-Central and South-Central skunk
rabies virus variants in the midwestern USA; a skunk rabies virus
variant in southern California; and a recently emerged rabies virus
variant associated with Big Brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus) but now
transmitted among skunks in the Flagstaff, Arizona area. Smaller
geographic areas are affected by rabies virus variants associated with
grey foxes (Texas, southern Arizona) and an occasional coyote/dog
rabies virus variant from Mexico in Texas. In Alaska and Canada, a
variant of the rabies virus in arctic foxes is an ever-present risk.
Throughout Puerto Rico, a rabies variant is present in the mongoose.
Superimposed and extending beyond these terrestrial sources of
wildlife rabies throughout North America are numerous rabies virus
variants associated with various species of insectivorous bats.

FIGURE 202.3 Concepts in rabies case
occurrence, detected cases, and estimated human
exposures.

CATS AND OTHER RABIES SOURCES
Among domestic animals in the USA, 3 times more cats are
diagnosed as having rabies than dogs (Figure 202.4).1 The
explanations for this several-decade trend include cats being less
likely than dogs to be vaccinated, more likely to roam and interact
with wildlife, and outdoors more often at night with a greater
likelihood of exposure to skunks, raccoons, and bats. Rarely,
encounters occur within homes. Occasionally, livestock develop
rabies, posing a substantial public health risk if animals are in
contact with the public, e.g., petting zoos, competitions/sales, or in
raw products. Wildlife displays also have risk for exposure to
indigenous sources of rabies. To be safe, one must exclude these
sources and consider extralabel use of animal rabies vaccines.

TRANSMISSION

Cat and Dog Diagnoses vs. Vaccination Status in
the United States
The predominant and natural route for rabies virus transmission is
via bite wounds.2 In a survey of 21 US states, a total of 264 rabid
dogs and 840 rabid cats were identified; 13 (4.9%) rabid dogs and 22
(2.6%) rabid cats had a history of rabies vaccination. Of these, 2 dogs
and 3 cats were classified as currently vaccinated. Overall, 6 animals
(1 dog and 5 cats) had a history of receiving 2 doses of rabies vaccine
in their lifetime, including 2 cats that were classified as currently
vaccinated. These results demonstrate that rabies is uncommon in
vaccinated dogs and cats but can occur. Rabies should be included in
the differential diagnosis for any dog or cat with clinical signs
compatible with rabies, regardless of vaccination history.
Surveillance is imperative for documenting and identifying trends
related to vaccination failures.

Contact Transmission of Infection
Contact transfer of rabies by either animate or inanimate objects
does not cause infection. Over 100 years ago, transmission of rabies
was demonstrated experimentally through intentional contacttransfer of saliva from a rabid animal to another animal by
“painting” freshly collected saliva on an open wound. Thus, in
addition to transmission via direct bite by a rabid animal,
contaminating an open bleeding wound with infectious material such
as saliva or tissue from a rabid animal that contains nervous system
components, is clear exposure to rabies. Documented inadvertent
nosocomial transmission has followed corneal, organ, and/or
vascular transplantations from people with unrecognized rabies who
are dying. Diagnosis of rabies in recipients leads to the source.
Contaminating the eyes with infectious material can cause rabies.
Oral exposure or ingestion of infected material is a small but
potential risk of exposure, e.g., predation on a rabid animal with
penetration of the predator’s oral mucous membranes with shards of
contaminated bone. The virus is inactivated by the acidic stomach
environment.

FIGURE 202.4 Most common rabid domestic
animals, United States, 1990-2018.

Aerosol Transmission
The natural history of rabies virus transmission does not rely upon
aerosolization, but some natural and artificially created aerosols pose
potent risks of infection, e.g., 2 laboratory workers were accidentally
infected due to experimental manipulation of virus-laden material
that became aerosolized. Natural conditions that allow aerosolization
of live rabies viruses are stringent and occur rarely, e.g., in caves
occupied by a natural reservoir species, such as the Mexican freetailed bat (Tadarida brasiliensis) who live in highly dense colonies.
Under these conditions, active manifestation of rabies may only
occur in a small percentage of bats (∼0.5-5% of apparently healthy
bats), but in a population of several million this rate of infection
causes virus-laden droplet secretions to descend from roosting bats
on the ceilings and walls of caves. People, e.g., spelunkers or bat
biologists, entering such caves risk rabies exposure via rabid bat
bites and/or via inhalation or contamination of mucous membranes
or open wounds. People entering bat-infested caves should wear
personal protective equipment (e.g., respiratory and eye protection,

gloves and other clothing to protect skin surfaces) and have preexposure rabies immunization.

Defining “Exposure” to Rabies
In general, a known bite from or direct contact with a potential or
proven-rabid animal is considered an exposure to rabies. For people,
contact with infectious material on intact skin is not considered
“exposure to rabies,” nor is touching or petting a rabid animal.2
Assessing exposure risk after a pet contacts a wild animal or other
suspect- or proven-rabid animal is difficult. Close contact of a pet or
other animal with a suspected or proven-rabid animal is usually
considered a potential exposure by local or state public health
professionals. Authority for making such a determination varies by
jurisdiction. Other, less clear but still risky, scenarios may include: 1)
an animal returns from unsupervised activity with a wound
compatible with a bite; 2) an animal returns from unsupervised
activity smelling of skunk (especially in a skunk or raccoon rabies
enzootic area); 3) sounds of animals fighting are overheard by the
owner and they suspect that their pet was involved; and, 4) a dead
animal (especially a high-risk species such as a raccoon, skunk, or
bat) is found in the vicinity of their pet. Even cats maintained
indoors are at risk for exposure if a bat or other wild animal enters
the home or if they escape from the home. Pet owners should be
encouraged to routinely examine their animals for wounds,
especially following any unsupervised activity outdoors. If a wound is
discovered, the animal should be brought to a veterinarian for
medical assessment and appropriate management.

Response to Rabies Exposure in Vaccinated Animals
If a currently vaccinated animal is determined to be potentially
exposed to rabies, the Compendium of Animal Rabies Control
recommends giving a booster rabies vaccination as soon as possible
and then observing for 45 days (ch. 185).3 The observation period
may vary according to locale and is imposed as a precaution. If a
rabies exposure occurs to a currently vaccinated animal, and it is
recognized in a timely manner with local wound cleansing and a
vaccine booster, the chance of vaccine failure is minimized. If

vaccination failure occurs, the manifestation of clinical signs of
rabies would have the highest likelihood of occurring within a 45-day
observation period.

Response to Rabies Exposure in Unvaccinated
Animals
If an animal is potentially exposed to rabies while unvaccinated or
outdated on its vaccination status, the recommendation is
euthanasia. If an owner refuses to follow this recommendation, a
quarantine of 6 months is imposed because this is the duration of
risk for developing rabies. The level and conditions of quarantine are
determined by local or state authorities but is typically in the home.
Based on a 2015 study,4 an update of the Compendium of Animal
Rabies Control will likely include another option for managing
rabies-exposed dogs and cats overdue for booster vaccination:
immediate wound cleansing, giving a rabies booster, and establishing
a baseline serum rabies neutralizing antibody titer. A blood sample
should be collected within 5-7 days of the booster vaccination. In that
study, a robust anamnestic response was observed in all animals,
regardless of time since the previous rabies vaccination. Thus,
vaccination after potential exposure could avert unnecessary
euthanasia of many dogs and cats while also maintaining protection
of humans from a rabid pet.

CLINICAL SIGNS
Within the reservoir host of a particular virus variant, rabies
infection can cause dramatic behaviors that likely favor transmission
via contact, e.g., infection may change vocalization by an adult that
mimics the call of a juvenile, attracting predators of the same or
different species and providing a chance for transmission. Early
clinical signs of rabies are nonspecific: lethargy, inappetence,
diarrhea, and/or vomiting. There is no waxing and waning of clinical
signs; rather, there is daily, if not hourly, irrevocable deterioration.
Other early-onset changes in behavior may also be seen, including
episodes of mild or dramatic abnormalities, e.g., an animal may
become abnormally reclusive or attention-seeking and it may

unpredictably and intermittently attack animate (humans or other
animals), inanimate, or unseen objects (e.g., humans report
hallucinatory episodes; animals may appear to be “snapping at
flies”).
Since rabies is neurotropic, irritation or paresthesia at the site of
initial exposure may occur even if the wound has healed. The
combination of increased saliva production and a decreased ability to
swallow could profoundly contaminate the mouth, chin, and thoracic
limbs with infectious saliva. Cranial nerve involvement can be focal
and unilateral, with anisocoria, facial or tongue paresis, and altered
phonation. As infection progresses, unpredictable episodes of
attempts to bite may be invoked by auditory, visual, or tactile stimuli
with aggression to the point of self-mutilation. In the end stage, most
animals become profoundly moribund.

PATHOGENESIS
EXPOSURE TO A HIGHLY UNPREDICTABLE
NEUROTROPIC VIRUS
After exposure to rabies, the probability of infection depends upon
the host, host species, rabies virus variant, virus dose delivered, and
route. Multiple deep bite wounds to the head and face delivered by a
proven rabid animal are more likely to cause infection than is a
superficial wound in a distal extremity (Figure 202.5). Regardless,
an exposed rabies-naïve animal is at risk for developing rabies for
about 6 months. There is no reliable method for determining if an
animal has been exposed to a rabid animal or the probability of
infection.
Rabies virus is highly neurotropic with no viremia or shedding via
urine or the GI tract. Progression of a viral infection from local
neurons at the initial site to the central nervous system (CNS) is
unpredictable, with a variable incubation period. In general,
infection is inversely related to viral dose and severity of exposure.
Most infected animals develop clinical signs within several weeks to
several months. Experimental and field data support a 6-month
quarantine (or euthanasia to prevent the development of rabies) for

exposed, unvaccinated or vaccinated but outdated, domestic animals.
Once signs develop, the clinical period usually lasts days, not weeks.

FIGURE 202.5 Pathogenesis implications for
incubation period versus viral shedding.
There may be limited viral replication locally but once virus
reaches the CNS, infection usually spreads quickly through
numerous neuronal tracts. After infection of the brain, rabies virus
then spreads centrifugally from the CNS through the nerve supply to
major organ systems. Large numbers of virus are produced in the
salivary glands with large amounts of virus in saliva. Profound
neuronal dysfunction occurs and, even with assisted preservation of
an airway and ventilation, may manifest as autonomic instability and
death.

10-DAY OBSERVATION PERIOD
Traditional pathogenesis studies have been conducted in dogs, cats,
and ferrets. Data from these studies together with decades of
epidemiologic observations support the 10-day observation period.
Therefore, if a healthy dog, cat, or ferret bites or otherwise
potentially exposes an animal to rabies, the animal that bit should be
observed for 10 days, regardless of its vaccination status. If the
animal remains alive and well during this 10-day period, there are no
virologic or epidemiologic data suggesting risk of rabies
transmission. If there was risk of viral shedding and transmission,
the animal would have manifested signs of clinical rabies (sometimes
including acute death) during the observation period. If the biting
animal develops clinical illness compatible with rabies, it should be

humanely euthanized. If the biting animal dies or is euthanized for
any reason during the 10-day period, the brain should be tested for
rabies as soon as possible. This determines the need for
postexposure prophylaxis for any exposed person, as well as
management of exposed animals.
If individuals of other species bite or otherwise potentially expose
a human, transmission risk is based on local transmission patterns,
circumstances, severity of exposure, and other related factors. Local
and state public health authorities may allow extrapolation of data
on which the 10-day observation is based to domestic livestock and
exotic hooved stock and can impose a 30-day observation period. If
the animals remain well, the potentially exposed person does not
need to undergo postexposure prophylaxis. The animal may still
develop rabies in the future from a prior exposure, but was not
infectious at the time of the potential exposure to the human.

DIAGNOSIS
The direct fluorescent antibody (dFA) test is the gold standard for
rabies diagnosis (ch. 184). A definitive result is obtained through
necropsy of fresh brain material consisting of brainstem and
cerebellum full cross-section, as required by the National Standard
Protocol for diagnosis of rabies
(https://www.cdc.gov/rabies/diagnosis/animalshumans.html) (accessed July 1, 2021). Historically, the diagnosis
of rabies was made with special silver-based staining (i.e., Seller’s
stain) for the detection of Negri bodies when applied to formalinfixed brain material prepared for routine histopathologic
examination. Although a specialized immunohistochemical test for
rabies may be performed at reference laboratories, the more
sensitive gold standard dFA test requires fresh brain tissue. When
laboratory testing for rabies is necessary, fixation of brain with
formalin should be avoided since it causes significant delays in
obtaining a definitive diagnosis. This is highly undesirable as it may
result in initiation of human rabies postexposure prophylaxis with
commensurate costs and risk of adverse events associated with
unnecessary medical intervention.

TREATMENT
There is no recognized treatment for rabies. Once clinical signs are
present, the disease is ultimately fatal with extremely rare
exceptions.

PREVENTION
DOMESTIC ANIMALS
The Compendium of Animal Rabies Control3 is the guiding
document on animal rabies control in the United States. Preexposure
vaccination of domestic animals, with booster vaccination if exposed,
is an effective method of disease prevention (ch. 185). Although no
vaccine is 100% effective, rabies vaccines are licensed after
demonstrating animal protection of a vaccinated group against a
lethal rabies virus challenge. The greatest risk of rabies in a
vaccinated animal occurs: (1) when the vaccine coverage period has
expired; (2) when the animal is young and has received only one
vaccination; (3) when a severe exposure has occurred; and (4) when
a potential exposure is not recognized and no primary wound care or
postexposure booster vaccination is sought by the owner. Rabies is
prevented in most exposed animals current on vaccination if a
booster vaccination is given and wound care includes flushing the
wound site with copious quantities of fluid (which alone reduces
probability of a productive infection). As a precaution, the animal
should also be confined and observed for 45 days.

WILDLIFE
Prevention of rabies in wildlife is conceptually achievable through
oral vaccination.5 The greatest successes in rabies control have been
achieved in red foxes of Europe and Canada. The practicality of this
approach is dependent upon: 1) the ease of vaccinating a species
using the oral route; 2) population densities; 3) ecologic
characteristics, e.g., family groups with dominant animals,
interfering with equal vaccine distribution; and 4) accessibility of the

target population to efficient bait distribution methods and
constraints near high human population densities. Novel biologics
are often required for these approaches. Veterinarians may be
consulted when domestic animals contact or consume baits
distributed free-choice for oral wildlife vaccination. It is ideal for
veterinarians to be familiar with wildlife vaccination projects and
associated biologics as they may pose risk of infection and adverse
events in uniquely susceptible humans and domestic animals.6,7

POST-EXPOSURE RABIES
PROPHYLAXIS OF RABIES-NAÏVE
HUMANS
Postexposure prophylaxis of rabies-naïve humans is almost 100%
successful when managed promptly and appropriately. Management
consists of prompt wound cleansing, infiltration of rabies immune
globulin of human (or equine) origin, and five IM vaccine doses on
days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28. This approach, which has been successful in
experimentally infected dogs, might be feasible for naïve-exposed
animals.8 In practicality however, the global supply of human rabies
biologics is limited, contributing to lack of availability and
sometimes prohibitive cost in some countries. An estimated 55,000
people, mainly in Asia and Africa, die yearly from this preventable
disease. Although these biologics can be used effectively to prevent
development of rabies in exposed domestic animals in the U.S. when
owners may have neglected to vaccinate their animals, it is better to
educate people and advocate for preexposure vaccination of animals.
This would make biologics increasingly available for human rabies
prevention, especially in regions of the world with continuing
unnecessary human mortality.

PRE-EXPOSURE RABIES VACCINATION
FOR HUMANS

The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices2 recommends
preexposure rabies vaccination for persons at high-risk for potential
rabies exposure, e.g., veterinarians and their staff, animal handlers,
and some laboratory workers. Pre-exposure vaccination may be
considered for people in frequent contact with rabies virus or
potentially rabid bats, raccoons, skunks, cats, dogs, or other species.
People in the “frequent-risk group” should have serum samples
tested for rabies virus neutralizing antibody every 2 years. If the titer
is less than complete neutralization at a 1:5 serum dilution by the
rapid fluorescent focus inhibition test, the person should receive a
single vaccine booster dose. If a vaccinated person is later exposed to
rabies, they are considered “immunologically primed” against rabies
and require postexposure prophylaxis consisting of booster
vaccinations on days 0 and 3.

RABIES AND TRAVEL
The risk of animal movement introducing rabies to an uninfected
area has occurred repeatedly (ch. 9). Despite the extinction of dogto-dog types of rabies viruses through enforcement of stray dog
control measures and mandatory vaccination, the risk of
reintroduction of related variants remains real and is a compelling
reason for continuing to require vaccination of domestic animals,
especially dogs. Even though vaccination of an individual animal
simplifies management in the event of an exposure to endogenous
wildlife rabies virus variants, required vaccination of the population
provides a measure of biosecurity against potential introduction of
exogenous canine rabies virus variants. Moving young dogs infected
with rabies to the U.S. from Puerto Rico, Thailand, India, Iraq and,
most recently Azerbaijan, demonstrates this continuing risk.1,9 Risk
of disease translocation can be mitigated through carefully crafted
requirements for animal identification, vaccination, serologic
monitoring, and advanced planning for a risk-reducing waiting or
quarantine periods. The most critical component of risk mitigation is
education of animal owners and other members of the public as to
the importance of these requirements for the prevention of rabies in

domestic animals and the prevention of human exposure to rabies
from domestic pets and livestock.

COOPERATION REQUIRED OF
MULTIPLE CONSTITUENCIES
Like many zoonoses and other emerging infections, rabies control
and prevention require the cooperation of animal control personnel,
law enforcement, environmental conservation or natural resource
agency personnel, veterinarians, diagnosticians, public health
professionals, physicians, and others. Responsibilities start locally
and on the state level. Rules and regulations pertinent to rabies
control may exist under the purview of public health, agriculture, or,
less commonly, wildlife agencies. With most rabies cases now in a
range of wildlife species, animal control officers in some localities
have been trained and authorized to deal with situations involving a
variety of domestic and wildlife species, not just dogs, or dogs and
cats. Most diagnostic, educational, epidemiologic, and rabies control
and prevention responsibilities are borne by public health agencies.
Close coordination between multiple local, state, and federal entities
is necessary for updating regulations and remaining prepared for
disease emergence or reintroduction, unintentional or intentional.
This requires improved comprehensive prevention and preparedness
strategies.
The need for an accessible, interactive, real-time, geographic
information systems–based tool is critical for timely understanding
disease occurrence, planning interactions, and assessing prevention
strategies. This could be a powerful tool for spatiotemporal analysis
of land-use, interactions with rabies, other diseases, and
environmental conditions. Diligent attention and dedicated effort
will be required to maintain and indeed, even advance, emerging and
zoonotic disease control. Rabies is a tangible “best-practices”
template of the major advances made in the last 75 years.

INTRODUCTION AND DEFINITIONS
The canine infectious respiratory disease complex (CIRDC) is
composed of multiple bacterial and viral agents that can acutely
result in cough (ch. 9). Depending on the causative agent, an
infected dog may also exhibit other signs of respiratory inflammatory
disease, e.g., sneezing and nasal discharge (ch. 35) and/or ocular
inflammatory disease, e.g., conjunctivitis and ocular discharge. The

canine infectious respiratory disease (CIRD) clinical syndrome
associated with CIRDC has long been known as “kennel cough”
and/or “canine infectious tracheobronchitis.” Many of the causative
agents and resultant disease are most common in dogs boarded or
housed in shelters, favoring transmission and development of
disease from co-infections and other cofactors, e.g., stress. Dogs
housed in animal shelters generally have the highest prevalence rates
for CIRDC agents.1 Each of the agents in the CIRDC has been grown
or amplified from healthy dogs as well as those showing signs of
CIRD, making it difficult to associate a positive CIRDC agent test
result to the cause of illness in individual cases.2

CAUSES
BACTERIA
The most common bacterial agents in the CIRDC are Bordetella
bronchiseptica, Mycoplasma cynos, and Streptococcus equi
subspecies zooepidemicus.3-7 Additional information is needed to
further determine whether bacteria such as M. canis or other
Streptococcus spp. can be primary pathogens.8 A number of
bacteria, such as Pasteurella spp. and Staphylococcus spp., that
colonize the upper respiratory tract of normal dogs can overgrow and
be associated with inflammation in some dogs with viral pathogens
as the primary cause of disease.2

VIRUSES
The most common viral agents in the CIRDC are canine adenovirus
2, canine respiratory coronavirus, canine distemper virus, canine
herpesvirus, canine influenza viruses, canine parainfluenza virus,
and canine pneumovirus (chs. 9, 200, and 204-206).9-19 The most
common canine influenza viruses that infect dogs are H3N8 and
H3N2.19,20 The H3N8 virus infecting dogs in the United States
originated from horses, and may now be extinct in the USA.21 Dogs

in many countries including the United States can develop clinical
signs of CIRD after exposure to H3N2 (ch. 217).17,20 While severe
acute respiratory coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) is primarily a disease
of people, some dogs housed with infected individuals have
developed mild respiratory or gastrointestinal (GI) signs.22 Thus,
SARS-CoV-2 should be on the differential list for dogs with acute
CIRD signs that had close contact, within the previous 2 weeks, to a
person with COVID-19 (ch. 200). Use of next generation sequencing
and metagenomics has been used to identify other viral agents that
may be components of the CIRDC.23,24 Co-infections with multiple
respiratory pathogens are common in dogs and may play a role in
developing CIRD and may partially determine the severity of
disease.8,13,25 The primary agents detected in dogs with signs of
CIRD can vary by the region, by the facility, and even by the year.
Thus, when multiple cases are identified within days to weeks, a
thorough assessment of multiple dogs is required to identify the
likely primary cause and institute containment measures.26

CLINICAL FINDINGS
HISTORY
Most dogs with CIRD are evaluated for an acute onset of cough (ch.
34). The cough can sound dry or moist (

Videos 203.1, 203.2)

and affected dogs often make a hacking sound at the termination of
each coughing episode. This “terminal retch” is sometimes mistaken
as vomiting. The owner sometimes reports swallowing at the end of
the cough and affected dogs can expectorate foamy material. While
these signs are common in patients with CIRD, they also occur with
many other respiratory disorders (i.e., the signs are nonspecific).
Dogs evaluated for signs associated with CIRD often have a history of
exposure to other dogs, e.g., trips to a dog park, boarding facility, or
animal shelter. However, dogs with signs of CIRD may not have been
exposed to a clinically ill dog as CIRDC agents are carried by healthy
dogs.1,27 The incubation period varies by the organism, usually
ranging from 2 to 14 days. Since there is overlap in the incubation

periods for different agents, timing the onset of signs is of little help
in determining the agent. Dogs with Streptococcus equi subsp.
zooepidemicus infection often live in rural areas and have access to
horses. While vaccines can lessen the severity of CIRD (ch. 185),
vaccinated dogs remain susceptible and vaccines are not available for
all CIRDC agents.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (PE)
Most dogs with cough induced by an agent in the CIRDC have a
normal appetite, attitude, and exercise tolerance. Some develop
fever, inappetence, lethargy, and/or dehydration. Fever may be more
common in dogs that develop pneumonia (ch. 217). Careful thoracic
auscultation is recommended in all dogs with signs of CIRD. While
pneumonia can develop in any dog infected with any CIRDC agent,
the most common causes are Streptococcus equi subsp.
zooepidemicus and B. bronchiseptica.6,7 Viral and bacterial
coinfections are common in dogs with clinical and radiographic
evidence of pneumonia (Figure 203.1).14 Depending on the
causative agent, sneezing and/or serous-to-mucopurulent nasal
discharge may be present (ch. 35). Serous to mucopurulent ocular
discharge and conjunctivitis may also be noted. Canine herpesvirus
infection may be common in dogs with sneezing and conjunctivitis as
primary manifestations of disease.18 Hemoptysis and epistaxis can
develop if the coughing or sneezing are violent and protracted (ch.
36). Hemoptysis may be most common in intensively housed shelter
dogs with current pneumonia, particularly if infected by H3N2
influenza virus or Streptococcus equi subsp. zooepidemicus. Puppies
that develop clinical signs of CIRDC from canine distemper virus
infection before completing their primary vaccine series can develop
chorioretinitis, central nervous system disease, enamel hypoplasia,
and hyperkeratosis of the footpads or planum nasale. Puppies with
canine distemper virus infection also frequently have diarrhea as
well as respiratory disease (ch. 204).

DIAGNOSIS

HISTORY, PE, COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT
(CBC), SERUM BIOCHEMISTRIES, RADIOLOGY
The history and clinical findings are often sufficient to suggest the
CIRDC. Whether to perform a thorough diagnostic workup depends
on severity of illness, whether dog populations are affected, and
whether pneumonia is suspected. CBCs can be normal or show
nonspecific evidence of neutrophilic inflammation, particularly if
pneumonia is present (ch. 217). Serum biochemical panel
abnormalities, if present, are nonspecific. Thoracic radiographs can
be normal, show a bronchiolar–interstitial pattern, or show an
alveolar pattern consistent with pneumonia (Figure 203.1).
Cytologic examination of mucopurulent ocular or nasal discharges
can be performed but rarely have findings that prove causation and
are no longer recommended to aid in determining antibiotic
choices.2

SPECIFIC TESTING (CH. 184)
Many veterinary laboratories now offer assay panels that amplify the
nucleic acids of CIRDC agents as well as B. bronchiseptica, M. cynos,
and S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus, canine adenovirus 2, canine
distemper virus, canine respiratory coronavirus, canine
parainfluenza virus, canine influenza viruses, canine herpesvirus,
and canine pneumovirus. Culture can also be used to confirm
infection by the bacterial agents B. bronchiseptica, M. cynos, and S.
equi subsp. zooepidemicus. However, Mycoplasma spp. are
fastidious, susceptible to degradation during transport, and most
commercial laboratories do not report antimicrobial susceptibility
for Mycoplasma spp. Some laboratories perform molecular
diagnostic assays first and if DNA of B. bronchiseptica or S. equi
subsp. zooepidemicus are amplified and, if a second swab was
submitted, a bacterial culture and antimicrobial susceptibility will be
performed. Bacterial culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing
of airway washings are ideal for dogs with pneumonia to allow for
optimizing the antibiotic treatment plan.2

Nucleic acids of each CIRDC agent can be amplified using
molecular methods from both healthy and diseased dogs.1,27 Dogs
recently vaccinated with products containing modified live strains of
CIRDC agents can test positive in molecular assays.28 Thus, positive
results in these assays do not necessarily prove disease causation.2 In
addition, molecular assay results may be falsely negative by the time
dogs are examined since viral shedding rates tend to peak very early
in disease. Thus, molecular diagnostic panels are generally not
recommended for individual pet dogs with mild signs of CIRDC.2
However, if the CIRDC is suspected in dog populations, e.g., those in
shelters, breeding kennels, boarding facilities, or multiple dog
households, such assays may be indicated, particularly if there is
poor response to therapy or severe clinical disease. Specimens from
respiratory or ocular discharges should be collected from multiple
affected dogs and assayed individually to increase sensitivity and
positive predictive value. If there are fatalities, necropsy should be
performed and both molecular assays and bacterial culture and
antimicrobial sensitivity should be completed on respiratory tissues.
Infection with S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus should be suspected in
dogs with acute hemorrhagic pneumonia or sudden death.6

FIGURE 203.1 Lateral (A) and ventrodorsal (B)
radiographs from a dog with pneumonia from
Bordetella bronchiseptica infection. Alveolar
pulmonary infiltrates are apparent, especially in the
cranioventral lung fields.
Since molecular diagnostic assay results can be falsely negative
due to rapid cessation of viral shedding for some agents, serological
test results may be needed to help determine causation in some
CIRDC outbreaks. When a CIRDC outbreak is suspected, sera should
be collected from a subset of affected dogs at the time of initial
clinical signs and again 2 to 3 weeks later for testing for specific
antibodies. Detection of rising titers against a specific agent or agents
may support those organisms as the cause of the outbreak.

TREATMENT
GUIDELINES FOR THE MAJORITY OF DOGS
Most dogs with CIRDC are infected with a virus and most with
clinical signs of CIRD, including those with mucopurulent nasal
discharge, maintain normal appetite and attitude, and the illness
naturally resolves. The International Society for Companion Animal
Infectious Diseases (ISCAID) Working Group recommended that

antimicrobial therapy be considered within the 10-day observation
period only if fever, lethargy, or inappetence are present.2 Other
management strategies, e.g., using a harness rather than a collar,
feeding soft foods if hyporexia exists, enforcing exercise restriction,
and use of cough suppressants (if there is no evidence of pneumonia)
are usually effective, particularly if viral causes are believed likely.
Antiviral therapies are not generally attempted in dogs with CIRD
but research is needed to determine whether immune modulators,
e.g., toll-like receptor agonists, could shorten duration of illness.18

FIRST-LINE ANTIBIOTICS
If bacterial CIRDC is suspected in a dog, 16 of 17 ISCAID Working
Group and outside reviewers recommended doxycycline (5 mg/kg
PO q12h or 10 mg/kg PO q24h) empirically for 7-10 days as the firstline antimicrobial option.2 Doxycycline is also recommended if
waiting for culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing on airway
washings from dogs with suspected community acquired pneumonia
but with no evidence of sepsis. Doxycycline is well tolerated by dogs,
can be safely given to puppies ≥4 weeks of age, and growth of B.
bronchiseptica and Mycoplasma spp. are typically inhibited in vitro.
Since there are no established “breakpoints” for these organisms
(ch. 140), a result cannot definitively claim “susceptible” or
“resistant,” hence explaining the controversy in the ISCAID
guidelines.
Amoxicillin-clavulanate (11 mg/kg PO q12h) was the alternate drug
recommended for B. bronchiseptica infection.2 This antibiotic is
usually effective for the treatment of S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus
infection as well as many bacterial agents that may cause illness
secondary to primary viral diseases such as Pasteurella spp.,
Staphylococcus spp., anaerobes, and other Streptococcus spp.
Amoxicillin (22 mg/kg PO q12h) is usually adequate for treating
Pasteurella spp. and Streptococcus spp. infections. Oral antibiotics
are generally only required for 7-10 days.2

INHALATIONAL THERAPIES,
FLUOROQUINOLONES, AZITHROMYCIN
Inhalational aminoglycoside therapy (ch. 90) has been anecdotally
mentioned as beneficial for the management of dogs with B.
bronchiseptica-associated CIRDC. If clinical signs of CIRDC do not
resolve within 7-10 days, a more extensive diagnostic workup should
be considered prior to employing other drugs, e.g., fluoroquinolones
or azithromycin. If pneumonia with evidence of bacteremia or sepsis
is identified, the ISCAID Working Group recommends a combination
of enrofloxacin (5-20 mg/kg, SQ or IM) combined with parenterally
administered clindamycin (10 mg/kg, SQ) or a beta lactam while
waiting for culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing on airway
washings.2 When culture and antimicrobial susceptibility test results
return, the longer term treatment plan with appropriate oral
antibiotics can be instituted.

DURATION
The optimal duration of antibiotic treatment for dogs with suspected
community acquired pneumonia is unknown. The ISCAID Working
Group recommends re-evaluating dogs after 10-14 days of therapy to
determine need for longer treatment.2 Clinical disease associated
with CIRDC agents is usually self-limiting or quickly responsive to
antimicrobial therapy. Thus, primary or repeated diagnostic tests are
rarely needed unless pneumonia is suspected. Bacterial culture or
molecular assays are not recommended after successful treatment of
dogs with the CIRDC. Radiographic improvement lags behind
clinical responses in dogs with pneumonia.

PREVENTION
HOSPITAL BIOSECURITY (CH. 186)
Dogs with an acute cough and other characteristic signs and history
supporting CIRDC should be evaluated outside veterinary clinics, if
possible, to determine severity of illness. If an affected dog is alert,

active, afebrile, eating, and has no evidence of pneumonia on
thoracic auscultation, treating the dog as an outpatient should be
considered to decrease risk to other hospitalized dogs. If an affected
dog is ill, isolation areas should be used. A designated outer garment
and face mask should be worn while attending to that dog and
isolation-room-specific equipment should be used. If radiographs are
needed, they should be performed at the end of the day if possible,
the dog should be transported to the room on a gurney and kept on
surfaces that can be disinfected, and the room closed to other dogs
until cleaning and disinfection can be completed. Each time the dog
is handled, hands and other exposed skin should be washed carefully
prior to working with other dogs or cats. Dogs with active signs of
CIRDC should not be allowed contact with other dogs or cats. While
most of the CIRDC agents only infect dogs, B. bronchisepticaassociated illness occurs in cats, likely from contact with infected
dogs.29

VACCINATION
In some countries, vaccines are available for canine adenovirus 2,
canine distemper virus, canine influenza H3N2, canine influenza
H3N8, canine parainfluenza virus, and B. bronchiseptica
(www.wsava.org; ch. 185; see textbook’s inside covers).30 The
immunity induced by vaccination against CIRDC agents does not
prevent colonization and shedding of the organisms and clinical
signs of disease can develop in vaccinated dogs. However, morbidity
is generally decreased in vaccinated dogs when exposed to the
pathogens. The current canine influenza vaccines against H3N8 and
H3N2 are unlikely to provide protection to other canine influenza
viruses. While the canine influenza virus vaccines are inactivated, a
recent study in experimentally infected dogs showed that the clinical
signs of H3N2 infection were greatly diminished when the dogs were
challenged 7 days after the administration of 1 dose of vaccine.31
These results suggest that there is potential clinical benefit to
vaccinating healthy, in-contact dogs during suspected canine
influenza outbreaks.

Modified live vaccines containing adenovirus 2, B. bronchiseptica,
and canine parainfluenza virus for intranasal administration are
available in different combinations in some countries. Recently,
attenuated B. bronchiseptica vaccines for oral administration have
also been introduced. Oral delivery of vaccines can be easy in most
dogs, induces immunity that is comparable to intranasal
administration on a 7-day challenge, and can have a duration of
immunity of greater than 1 year.32,33

PUBLIC HEALTH RISKS
In general, dogs infected by the most common agents in the CIRDC
are not a danger to family members or veterinary health care
providers. However, B. bronchiseptica has been associated with
infection of immunocompromised people.34,35 Streptococcus equi
subsp. zooepidemicus is generally host-species-specific, but has also
been isolated from a dog and its handler.36 The 2 most common
influenza viruses reported in dogs (H3N2 and H3N8) are not
believed to infect people.19 However, similar influenza A viruses
could mutate to infect humans and small companion animals.
Zoonotic transmission was suspected in a veterinarian who
apparently acquired H7N2 infection while helping manage an
outbreak in cats in a New York City animal shelter.37 To date, all
SARS-CoV-2 infections of dogs are thought to have been acquired
from an infected human (reverse zoonosis; ch. 200).22 Based on
one experimental infection study in dogs, SARS-CoV-2 could not be
isolated from infected dogs suggesting that low numbers of viral
particles were shed and shedding was likely of short duration.38 Use
of personal protective equipment as described in the prevention
section and good hygiene should minimize these rare risks. However,
if an immune compromised owner is in the home, they should not
directly handle the dog until the clinical signs resolve. If an immune
compromised veterinary health care provider needs to be in direct
contact with a dog with active signs of CIRDC, wearing a well-fitted
N95 face mask should lessen any risk.
