INTRODUCTION
ETIOLOGY, SUSCEPTIBLE ANIMALS
Canine distemper virus (CDV), an enveloped RNA virus of the family
Paramyxoviridae and genus Morbillivirus, has existed for centuries,

with documentation as early as 1730. It is predated only by other
infamous members of the genus: Rinderpest and human measles.1
Evidence from historical accounts, dog teeth dating back to the preColumbian era, and gene sequencing suggest that the human measles
virus may be CDV’s parent virus.1 CDV has a large host range
including all members of the Canidae family. Dogs, ferrets, coyotes,
skunks, and raccoons are the most common animals susceptible to
CDV seen in practice or shelters. Many other host species are
susceptible but zoonotic transmission of CDV has not been
demonstrated. The term “distemper” or “feline distemper” in
reference to feline panleukopenia virus infection (ch. 201) can
create confusion, because CDV does not infect nor cause disease in
cats. Animal care workers are encouraged to only use the term
distemper in relation to CDV infection. However, CDV does cause
disease in large felids (e.g., lions, tigers).2,3

A CAUSE OF MORBIDITY AND
MORTALITY
Largely preventable through immunization, CDV is a significant
cause of morbidity and mortality in dogs primarily because of limited
access to vaccination in many areas. Strides have been made in
preventing illness, managing outbreaks, and in treating animals in
shelters, rescue organizations, and communities without resorting to
depopulation. If shelters or communities have CDV-related illnesses,
life-saving solutions can often be found. Providing treatment and
resolving outbreaks with little loss of life can build trust and bring
organizations and communities together to develop preventive
practices for the future.

CLINICAL SIGNS
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
The incubation period, depending on virus strain and host immune
status, ranges from <1 week up to 6 weeks post-infection (PI). The

longer incubation periods are not common. Experience suggests that
clinical signs usually become apparent within 2 weeks PI. Clinical
signs of CDV infection result from both virus-induced
immunosuppression and direct actions of the virus on epithelial cells
of the respiratory tract, gastrointestinal (GI) tract, and skin. Viral
effects may progress to the nervous system. CDV initially infects and
destroys lymphocytes and mononuclear cells, causing significant
immunosuppression by binding to signaling leukocyte activation
molecule (SLAM) receptors.4 Over about 14 days, CDV can cause
serious disease by binding to the nectin-4 receptor, allowing the
virus to infect epithelial cells in multiple systems as well as neuronal
cells.5 A receptor expressed in glial cells facilitates infection of
astrocytes.6

DIFFICULTY IN CLINICALLY
RECOGNIZING CDV
There is significant variation in disease course, clinical signs, and
severity of illness in CDV-infected dogs. Infection may be inapparent,
mild, or severe and fatal. Subclinical infections have not been of
great concern in transmission or outbreak management. Since signs
are nonspecific in individual animals, mild (and even severe) disease
is frequently mistaken for more common and less problematic
illnesses, especially in regions where CDV is less common. In
populations, CDV may cause acute outbreaks of characteristic illness
with high morbidity and mortality. Most confusing, shelters can
struggle with mild, smoldering CDV-associated illnesses, despite
vaccination. CDV can resemble more benign respiratory illness, and
thus go unrecognized for long periods of time (chs. 203, 212).

BIPHASIC CLINICAL SIGNS
CDV infections have been described as biphasic, with earliest signs of
infection developing days after exposure as a febrile response
coinciding with onset of immunosuppression. The earliest
recognized clinical signs of CDV infection are nonspecific malaise

and respiratory disease (chs. 34, 35, 37). Early mucopurulent
ocular discharge, blepharospasm, and conjunctivitis are common.
These signs, early in the first to third week PI, can be difficult to
distinguish from those of more benign diseases. CDV should be
included in the differential diagnosis of dogs with these signs.
Because of immunosuppression, respiratory disease associated with
secondary bacterial invasion can result in pneumonia (ch. 217) and
death. Immunosuppression may also contribute to other
opportunistic infections (ch. 180).

GI, DERMATOLOGIC, AND
OPHTHALMIC SIGNS
Early vague signs may be followed by or occur with vomiting and/or
diarrhea (chs. 48, 49). GI signs can include tenesmus and bloody
feces; intussusception is an uncommon complication. In some, GI
signs predominate. Dramatic muscle wasting can occur rapidly with
or without anorexia and should raise suspicion for CDV (chs. 18,
151). Without timely and proper medical support and intervention,
severe dehydration and multiorgan failure can occur. Skin disease,
pustules, or a measles-like rash, may be seen in a very small
percentage of infected dogs (ch. 12). Digital and/or nasal
hyperkeratosis are more chronic signs, often associated with varying
neurologic signs. Distemper was once known as “hardpad disease,” a
reference to digital hyperkeratosis. Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (“dry
eye”), which may cause corneal ulceration with or without
perforation, was first described by Dr. Henri Carré, in what may have
been one of the earliest descriptions of distemper in 1905. Secondary
to retinal degeneration and necrosis, retinal lesions are grey-pink
densities on fundoscopic examination. PI, these lesions can be
identified as hyper-reflective areas that suggest previous infection
with CDV (ch. 13). Optic neuritis, sudden blindness, and retinal
detachment can occur but are rarely reported.

NEUROLOGIC SIGNS (CHS. 14, 41, 242)

Clinical signs of neurologic disease may develop concurrently with
other signs, in the absence of other signs, or rarely >1-3 weeks after
resolution of other systemic signs. Neurologic signs may range from
subtle twitching (

Videos 41.1, 41.2) to severe seizures. Often,

dogs develop neurologic signs early in the course of infection.
Development of encephalopathy and seizure activity may occur later,
after recovery from other signs, but in the author’s experience, this
has been quite rare, and typically follows a history of no vaccination.
Neurologic disease results from viral invasion of neurologic tissue.
Neurologic signs are characterized by salivation and chewing
movements (petit mal, “chewing gum” seizures) and seizures that
may become more frequent and severe (grand mal). While central
nervous system signs are a poor prognostic indicator, some dogs
recover. Prognosis worsens with increased severity of neurologic
signs. Clinical signs can resolve in some, while others may have
neurologic signs that persist but do not progress (e.g., persistent
myoclonus; ch. 41).

SUSPECTING CDV IN A POPULATION
Several clinical signs should increase suspicion for CDV in a
population, e.g., increased frequency of respiratory illnesses even if
mild; increased severity of respiratory illness; development of
neurologic disease in any dog populations, but especially puppies
(either in a shelter or rescue or after release); vaccination practices
that do not ensure ALL dogs are vaccinated immediately on intake;
management practices that favor transmission by allowing
potentially infected dogs to remain in the general population or to
have contact with healthy susceptible animals soon after intake; and
shelter and/or community history of problems with CDV either in
the present community or a source shelter if transport is occurring.

BIOTYPES AND EPIDEMIOLOGY
BIOTYPE VS SEROTYPE

Several CDV biotypes exist that can cause different clinical
expressions of disease. Although there are multiple biotypes, there is
only one CDV serotype (antigenic type). Thus, the modified-live virus
(MLV) vaccines produced in the late 1950s and early 1960s remain
highly effective in limiting infection and preventing disease.
Outbreaks and disease are due to gaps in vaccination rather than
emergence of new biotypes able to evade the immune response
induced by vaccination. In communities where vaccination is
common, disease caused by CDV is rare because vaccinated dogs are
immune to infection and disease. Even in outbreak settings, dogs
with protective antibody titers do not develop clinical signs or shed
virus.

INCIDENCE
CDV-induced disease remains common or sporadic in regions where
vaccination is not routine and in environments such as shelters
where infected dogs or wildlife may be introduced exposing
unvaccinated or recently vaccinated dogs. This also occurs in
communities where CDV is rarely seen in private practice.
Regardless, lapses in vaccination correlate well with development of
disease.

TRANSMISSION
CDV is a labile, enveloped virus. While fomite or environmental
transmission of CDV is possible, the virus is easily inactivated by
most disinfectants and does not remain viable for more than a few
hours to a few days, depending on ambient temperature and other
conditions. Direct transmission from an infected to a susceptible dog
is the most likely source of infection, making recognition and
separation of animals with infectious respiratory disease especially
important. CDV may be shed into any body secretion or excretion,
depending on the stage of infection. In communities where
unvaccinated dogs roam freely, risk of exposure increases. This
highlights the need for and importance of community vaccination
campaigns. While dogs are the primary host for CDV, and dog-to-dog

transmission is the most likely source of infection, local wildlife
populations (e.g., raccoons, foxes, coyotes, and wolves) may act as
reservoirs for infection. Raccoons were a significant source of
infection in several investigations and at least one major CDV
outbreak in shelter dogs. Exposures occurred when both species
were collected and placed into the same animal control vehicles.

PREVENTION VIA VACCINATION
SUSCEPTIBILITY
Infection in susceptible species depends primarily on immune status
and infectious dose. Any susceptible animal can become infected
regardless of age. Animals that have been immunized by previous
infection or vaccination are protected from infection. MLV vaccines
for CDV rapidly induce strong protective immune responses (ch.
185). While vaccination has dramatically reduced the size of
vulnerable dog populations, many factors (e.g., cost, language
barriers, distance to care) may limit access. Communities without
access to vaccination still struggle with endemic or sporadic
infections and community outbreaks. CDV titers from dogs entering
shelters throughout the US have shown wide variation region to
region. About 50% ± 20% of dogs were antibody negative for CDV at
the time of intake in one study,7 suggesting that those dogs had
never been vaccinated nor naturally infected, were susceptible to
infection, and had a high probability of becoming infected if exposed
before or in close proximity to vaccination.
Providing ready access to vaccination is likely the most important
means of reducing CDV-associated infection in a community.
Implementing access to care programs in order to increase
vaccination rates for dogs, especially those that may not receive
regular veterinary care, is essential for increasing overall population
immunity (ch. 185). Increasing access to vaccination for animal
shelters and rescue groups is also critical for prevention. Many
shelters (even governmental agencies entrusted to provide care) are
not funded to vaccinate all animals on intake. In some, legal barriers
prevent shelters from vaccinating on intake despite the fact that
Guidelines for Standards of Care in Animal Shelters (2010)8 and

American Animal Hospital Association guidelines9 both clearly state
that vaccination on intake is essential to protect animal health.

EARLY BENEFIT OF VACCINATION
Vaccination provides very early partial protection from development
of severe clinical illness and neurologic disease (ch. 185). Most dogs
exposed to CDV only 1 hour after vaccination develop only mild to
moderate signs of illness, unlike the unvaccinated.10 However,
mildly infected dogs still pose a significant risk of transmission. In
this situation, CDV often goes unrecognized until an unvaccinated
dog or a puppy that was not effectively immunized develops more
fulminant disease. The American Animal Hospital Association
publishes vaccination guidance for both individually owned dogs and
shelter dogs.9 As with other infectious diseases, interference from
maternally derived antibody (MDA) can hinder effective
immunization of puppies <20 weeks of age. While many puppies will
not have sufficient MDA to interfere and will be effectively
immunized by the initial vaccine in the series, it can never be certain
which puppies may not be effectively immunized. Revaccination at
regular intervals until puppies have cleared MDA is crucial.

ENVIRONMENT
Vaccination alone will never be sufficient if the incidence of disease
and exposure risk are high. Vaccination programs must work in
concert with management plans that decrease infectious dose and
risk of exposure, especially for puppies who may remain susceptible
even after vaccination. The best management plan for susceptible
adults and juvenile animals is to create low-risk environments for
housing and care.

PREGNANT DOGS IN SHELTERS OR
OTHER AT-RISK ENVIRONMENTS

While a susceptible pregnant female can be at risk for vaccinationinduced disease in unborn puppies, risk of distemper in an
unvaccinated, susceptible female entering a shelter environment
could be high. If one tries to protect fetuses from adverse effects of
vaccination, both mother and puppies could be lost to CDV.
Theoretically, the safest CDV vaccine for pregnant dogs is the
canarypox rCDV vaccine, which does not infect fetuses in
immunologically naïve (CDV antibody-negative) dogs. Regardless of
vaccine type used (recombinant or MLV), replication of vaccine virus
in pregnant dogs that have antibody will be limited, protecting
fetuses from vaccine-induced disease (ch. 185).

DIAGNOSIS
VIRUS ISOLATION (VI)
Isolating the wild type (virulent) virus has been difficult. The virus
does not readily replicate in tissue culture cells, either primary cells
or cell lines. In the early 2000s, a highly sensitive technique was
developed for isolation of virulent distemper virus by utilizing Vero
cells expressing the dog SLAM receptor (Vero-DST cells).4 With this
technique, cytopathic effect (CPE) is visible as early as 24 hours postinoculation, and most wells have complete CPE visible within 48-72
hours (personal observations). No additional CPE is apparent past
48 hours post-inoculation, making this a very efficient method for
viral isolation.

FLUORESCENT ANTIBODY (FA),
REVERSE TRANSCRIPTASE
POLYMERASE CHAIN REACTION (RTPCR), AND HISTOLOGY
FA tests have been developed for detection of CDV in tissue sections
and other sources (e.g., conjunctival swab, rectal mucosa swab,
leukocytes, etc.).11 RT-PCR is now the most widely used diagnostic
test, largely replacing FA tests due to increased sensitivity,

specificity, and ease of performance. RT-PCR may be used on
specimens collected antemortem or at necropsy. At necropsy,
multiple tissue specimens can be collected for testing by RT-PCR,
FA, or immunohistochemistry (IHC). Histologic tissue changes and
presence of viral inclusion bodies in cells are diagnostic for CDV
infection.12-14
Since CDV is shed in all body secretions/excretions during acute
systemic disease, a variety of specimens can be tested using RT-PCR.
Nasal, deep pharyngeal, and conjunctival swab specimens are
commonly collected (ch. 184). Conjunctival swabs tend to yield the
least amount of virus and are poorly tolerated. A simple nasal swab
specimen (rather than a deep nasal swab requiring sedation) is
preferred. Blood samples may also be positive (ch. 176, Figure
176.1). Careful control of cross-contamination is especially
important since sensitivity is so high and false positives are possible
from sampling contamination.
Positive RT-PCR results are an excellent indicator that distemper
is possible, but detection of viral RNA does not prove presence of
viable, virulent, or infectious virus. Many dogs cease shedding
detectable virus within a month, but some test positive on RT-PCR
for prolonged periods. This creates welfare risks from separation,
prolonged shelter stays, and uncertainty regarding when clinically
recovered dogs can be considered safe and non-infectious. In the
closely related human measles virus, people are considered noninfectious 4 days after the appearance of the stereotypical
maculopapular rash that occurs 10-14 days PI. This directive is made
based on epidemiological information even though some may
continue shedding viral RNA based on RT-PCR testing.15,16 Just as
with human measles patients, dogs infected with CDV may shed
viable virus for a much shorter time than they excrete viral RNA as
detected by RT-PCR. Following experimental CDV infection in 12
dogs, viral RNA could be RT-PCR detected to the end of the testing
period (20 days).17

VIRUS ISOLATION (VI) ON VERO-DST
CELLS VS. RT-PCR

In one study, agreement between VI on Vero-DST cells and RT-PCR
were poor throughout the testing period except on the peak day of
viral RNA load in individual dogs, when it was good. The peak in
shedding as detected using quantitative RT-PCR was associated with
the onset of clinical signs in all dogs. In this study, and the author’s
experiences, VI was not positive for longer than 14 to 16 days with a
mean duration of 1.3 days for nasal swabs and 2.2 days for rectal
swabs.17
Isolation of CDV in Vero-DST cells appears to have high sensitivity
in studies of dogs with naturally acquired infections (author’s
personal observations). The absence of live virus in cell culture
suggests that viable virus is no longer present, in contrast to RTPCR, which does not differentiate between viable and non-viable
virus. Because VI is not usually available in clinical settings, further
study is needed to identify a safe time frame for release of dogs from
isolation in the absence of serial testing for shedding, as is the case
for measles or COVID-19 in humans. This would shorten quarantine
or isolation times, allowing puppies to be socialized and adult dogs to
have a better quality of life. For animal shelters, defining a clear time
when dogs are no longer infectious would be a critical tool for
outbreak management that could save thousands of dollars as well as
many lives.
Specimens from recently vaccinated animals may also test positive
because vaccine virus replicates in the same cell types as the wildtype virus. RT-PCR assays do not discriminate vaccine virus from
wild-type virus. It is not known how long after vaccination an
individual animal can remain positive, what exact quantitative or
semi-quantitative level would be seen, or how commonly positive
results occur after vaccination. Nevertheless, quantitative or semiquantitative RT-PCR assays may also help to differentiate among
mild infections, animals shedding large quantities of virus, and
vaccine virus. Positives may be reported as either a cycle threshold
value (CT) or an estimated viral load. When a CT value is reported,
results near the number of cycles of polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
used for amplification (typically 40) suggest a low viral load. Some
laboratories provide a cut-off value likely to differentiate wild-type
infection from vaccination. However, mild infections, early
infections, or resolving infections can have low viral loads or high

CTs. Interpretation is needed to evaluate the results in conjunction
with clinical signs, dates of vaccination, and timing of possible
exposure.

SEROLOGY
Serologic tests that measure IgM (early in infection) vs. IgG (later in
infection) have been used but are not reliable in the field or in
shelters where dogs are vaccinated at entry.18 Acute and
convalescent testing takes weeks to perform making diagnosis based
on rising titers retrospective. Rising titers also develop in recently
vaccinated dogs. IHC, FA, and PCR provide information more
rapidly. In contrast to its relatively limited value in rapidly
diagnosing disease in individual dogs, serologic testing is valuable
for determination of the immunologic status of dogs who may have
been exposed to infection or are evaluated during a distemper
outbreak.

POPULATION DIAGNOSIS
Diagnostic testing for an individual animal or population problem,
such as a new arrival with signs consistent with distemper, a
population with endemic levels of disease, or an outbreak of
distemper should be a priority. Evaluating specimens collected from
multiple dogs using RT-PCR is recommended if risk factors
(including population-level “clinical signs” mentioned above) are
present. Multiple (at least 10, or a sizeable proportion of affected
dogs) with varying stages of clinical illness should be tested,
including acutely affected dogs and dogs with a longer history of
illness. Positive RT-PCR results should be carefully interpreted,
considering both the reported viral load, the clinical manifestations
of illness in the population as a whole, and the individual animal’s
history including vaccination date, intake date, and severity of
clinical signs (ch. 184). Additional diagnostics may be necessary as
part of that evaluation process. If animals have died or are
euthanized, necropsy should be performed to confirm the diagnosis
and identify comorbidities or other possible etiologies.

TREATMENT
GENERAL SUPPORTIVE CARE
When treatment is being considered, risk of contagion to other
animals, prognosis, and welfare of the individual animal should be
assessed. Treatment of dogs with distemper focuses on supportive
care, e.g., nursing, fluid and electrolyte replacement (chs. 119 and
120), nutrition (ch. 164), and treatment or prevention of secondary
bacterial infection (ch. 186). Administration of B vitamins may have
value. Antiemetics (ch. 48) should be given when dogs exhibit
vomiting. Some dogs are unable or unwilling to eat and require other
forms of nutritional support (chs. 81 and 164). Dogs that have not
developed neurologic disease have the best prognosis for recovery.
Prognosis becomes guarded to grave for dogs that develop neurologic
signs (ch. 242). Mild neurologic signs, such as myoclonus, may be
more manageable, but neurologic disease is often progressive and
irreversible. In the author’s experience, treatment for all but minor
neurologic signs, e.g., anticonvulsant therapy, may diminish clinical
signs but outcomes are rarely good and welfare concerns often arise.

ANTIBIOTICS (CHS. 7, 140, AND 217)
Use of broad spectrum bactericidal antibiotics is essential when
treating respiratory disease associated with distemper. Viral
pneumonia is often accompanied by secondary bacterial infections
due to CDV-induced immunosuppression. Bacteria associated with
primary or secondary pneumonias include Bordetella
bronchiseptica, Streptococcus spp., Pasteurella multocida,
Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus spp., and mycoplasmas (ch. 217).
Secondary infections may have antibiotic sensitivities different from
those most commonly used in shelters to treat suspected primary
Bordetella or mycoplasma infections. With significant GI signs,
antibiotics must be administered parenterally (ch. 262).

OUTBREAK RESPONSE

Distemper outbreaks in shelters, rescues, and other facilities are
managed through a combination of diagnostic testing, risk
assessment, treatment, and separation of affected animals. Managing
flow of animals through a facility or area is needed to establish a
clean break.19 Proactive recognition, risk assessment, and
management of cases are essential to avoid outbreaks or stop
infections from continuing to spread within the shelter and the
community. Community outbreaks or ongoing endemic disease in a
community are best understood as a clinical sign of inadequate
access to care and vaccination. Provision of treatment for sick
animals and supporting owners through ready access to vaccination
is the best strategy.
When responding to an outbreak in an animal shelter or other
population, all dogs, without exception, must be vaccinated prior to
or within minutes of entry. All incoming dogs should be placed into
clean, disinfected kennels. Housing for incoming dogs should ideally
be located at least 25 feet (8 meters) away from moderate to highrisk dogs (based on titers, exposure history or clinical signs; see
below) and from other introduced dogs that have clinical signs of
disease; ideally this would be a separate building or a separate ward,
but a separate set of runs can be used with clearly identified barriers
that separate at-risk and clean areas. Separate staff and supplies
should be used for new incoming dogs versus exposed/at-risk dogs.
Unexposed dogs should be handled before sick or high-risk dogs.
Dogs designated as low-risk based on serologic test results can be
housed with new incoming dogs if necessary.
Because many dogs may be immune to infection as determined
using serologic assessment, it may not be necessary to treat all
exposed dogs as potentially infectious or “at-risk.” When antibody
titer testing is not available to assess risk, dogs can be assigned to
risk groups based on vaccination dates and likelihood of exposure.
However, this method may mean that many immune dogs will be
categorized as high-risk unless a known start date can be identified
for possible exposure or excellent management practices were in
place to prevent transmission. While antibody testing may be costly,
it may outweigh the expense of keeping animals in care longer and
has a negative impact on response and care capacity.

While assigning an animal to a risk group does not predict
outcome for that animal with certainty, defining the level of risk for
individual animals and subgroups can guide informed decisions.
Risk assessment can be used to clear animals for rescue or adoption
and help guide efforts to create isolation and separation.
Importantly, establishing risk categories for exposed animals limits
the number of dogs subjected to quarantine, isolation, or special
rescue which often turns an apparently unmanageable situation into
a manageable one.
If high-risk dogs must remain in a population, they should be
separated from other dogs, especially recently admitted dogs,
recently vaccinated dogs, and all puppies under 20 weeks of age. It
has been recommended that these dogs should be held for a
quarantine period of at least 4 to 6 weeks to ensure that they are not
incubating the disease. In many cases this long holding time is
impossible; it also creates welfare concerns or runs the risk of
contributing to more disease in shelters due to crowding. Instead,
assessment of titers and RT-PCR results is recommended. A positive
titer paired with a negative RT-PCR provides good evidence that a
dog is immune, and these results can be obtained well before a 4- to
6-week quarantine period has elapsed.
Outbreaks within a population or a shelter can be controlled with
careful attention to the measures described above. Disease may
continue to occur, but should be limited to dogs infected prior to
entering the shelter. Providing pet caregivers outreach and access to
vaccination can help reduce CDV in the community. If timely
preventive management practices are put into place as part of the
outbreak response, disease transmission from these cases can be
controlled and future outbreaks avoided. When organizations cannot
create effective separation, slow, or stop intake, or create a clean
break, outbreaks may continue, affecting many animals and the
resources of the organization and community.

Respiratory Infections
Elena Contreras

FHV-1 feline herpesvirus-1
FURI feline upper respiratory infection

VS-FCV virulent systemic feline calicivirus

ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS
Feline upper respiratory infection (FURI) refers to a multifactorial
disease complex that includes one or more viral and/or bacterial
pathogens that can produce mild to severe nasal, ocular, and
systemic clinical signs. It is thought that primary viral infections,
typically feline herpesvirus-1 (FHV-1) and feline calicivirus (FCV),
incite cellular damage in the respiratory, oral, or ocular tissues,
decrease respiratory immune function, and increase susceptibility to
bacterial infections. FURI is widespread within most feline
populations. It is more commonly found in cats housed within multicat environments such as animal shelters or catteries and in
crowded, stressful, and/or unhygienic environments.

Incubation periods for the pathogens involved are typically a few
days, ranging between 2-10 days. Transmission is mainly through
direct contact with oronasal or ocular secretions shed by acutely
infected cats; some sneezed macrodroplets can reach up to 2 meters,
although some of the organisms are unstable when aerosolized in
regular respiratory secretions.1,2 Some transmission can occur
through fomites. Infections usually persist for less than 10 days, but
severe cases can lead to mortality, namely in young kittens, geriatric
debilitated cats, or immune compromised cats.3

PATHOGENS
Feline Herpesvirus-1
FHV-1 is one of the most ubiquitous viruses in the cat population
whether a cat is clinically normal or ill. FHV-1, a member of the
Alphaherpesvirinae subfamily, is a double-stranded DNA virus
contained within a capsid in a glycoprotein-lipid envelope; it is a
mucosal pathogen characterized by rapid spread between cells, acute
cytolysis, and latent infections within the sensory ganglia of the
host.2 Infection occurs preferentially through the oronasal,
respiratory, and conjunctival mucosa and corneal epithelial cells.4
With prolonged clinical disease, mucosal erosion in the nasal
passages may result in nasal cartilage and bone exposure, leading to
osteolytic damage in the nasal turbinates. This damage could be
permanent, and subsequent remodeling and an immune-mediated
inflammatory component might contribute to chronic inflammatory
changes.5 FHV-1 has a glycoprotein-lipid envelope that renders it
fragile in the external outside environment, and it is easily
inactivated by common disinfectants.
Intermittent shedding of FHV-1 can occur throughout life, and
most cats are persistent carriers. The trigeminal ganglia are the main
site of viral latency; the virus might also reside in the cornea.4,6
Reactivation and shedding can occur due to other concurrent
disease, glucocorticoid use, or after stressful events. The nasal

turbinates are among the first viral replication sites during
reactivation.7

Feline Calicivirus
FCV is also ubiquitous within feline populations with and without
FURI. FCV, a member of the Caliciviridae family and Vesivirus
genus, is a single-stranded non-enveloped RNA virus that lacks
proofreading ability and therefore has a high mutation rate and
many isolates. FCV mainly replicates in oral and respiratory tissues.
The infected cells undergo apoptosis; outwardly, vesicles in the
tissues and epithelial cells ulcerate and rupture, inducing epithelial
necrosis and neutrophil infiltration around the lesion’s periphery.8
Persistence in the environment has been reported from several
days to several weeks depending on the environmental conditions
and disinfection procedures. Chronic carrier states may also occur
and are thought to be related to viral antigenic changes occurring in
the cat, resulting in isolates that allow escape from the host immune
response.9 It is thought that few cats are persistent shedders, and
rather some cats are exposed to reinfection or coinfection because
there are a large number of isolates and weak antigenic crossprotection.10

Bacteria
The main bacterial pathogens implicated in FURI are Gram-negative
and include Mycoplasma felis, Chlamydia felis, and Bordetella
bronchiseptica. Although Mycoplasma spp. are normal commensal
organisms in the upper respiratory tract of cats, M. felis might have a
role as a secondary or even primary pathogen in FURI or
conjunctivitis.11 M. felis is found in the conjunctival and respiratory
mucous membranes in cats. M. felis is thought to proliferate in cats
exposed to unhygienic conditions, overcrowding, concurrent
bacterial or viral infections, immunosuppression, or other stressors.
C. felis is an obligate intracellular bacterium that infects and
replicates in epithelial cells of the conjunctiva and is spread mostly
through ocular secretions; shedding can persist for 60 days after
infection. B. bronchiseptica is an aerobic bacterial species that can

colonize the respiratory tract and can persist in the environment for
10 days; shedding from infected cats can occur intermittently for
more than a month. Infection is more likely to be associated with
crowded and contaminated environments, poor hygiene, grouphousing, and contact with dogs.12

Emerging Pathogens
Emerging viral and bacterial pathogens have been associated with
FURI in rare outbreaks and occurrences. There was an outbreak of a
low pathogenic avian influenza A subtype H7N2 virus that affected
cats in a New York shelter in late 2016; this caused mostly mild
illness.13 There have also been reports of other influenza A subtypes
affecting individual cats.14 On the other hand, Streptococcus equi
subsp. zooepidemicus and Streptococcus canis (ch. 203) have been
found in association with severe FURIs progressing to lower
respiratory disease, severe morbidity, and sometimes mortality;
outbreaks have occurred in overcrowded, unsanitary catteries,
shelters, and sanctuaries.15 Other secondary bacterial pathogens
include Staphylococcus spp., Pasteurella multocida, and other
Mycoplasma and Streptococcus spp (ch. 217).16

RISK FACTORS
Risk factors for FURI in owned cats include the winter season, recent
antibiotic therapy, age of less than 1 year, intact reproductive status,
and residence in either a multi-cat household or a household with
dogs.3,17 Stress might also contribute to an increased risk of FURI.
FHV-1 infection is reactivated after stressful events such as changing
housing types; reactivation typically occurs between 4-11 days after
the stressful events.7 Cats in multi-cat households, those with
chronic gingivostomatitis (chs. 198, 258), and younger cats are
more likely to shed FCV. In the shelter environment, risk factors for
FURI can include the above as well as high population density,
overcrowding, multiple cats of different ages and backgrounds, small
living enclosures, multiple housing changes, increased length of stay,

hygiene and air quality issues, as well as high exposure to multiple
pathogens in large quantities (Figure 205.1, A and B ).11,18

CLINICAL SIGNS
Clinical signs of FURI can range from very mild to very severe and
depend on the pathogen(s) involved, pathogenicity of strains,
infective dose, number of coinfections, nutrition, environmental
conditions including ventilation and crowding, and individual
differences including immune function, stress, vaccination status,
and prior exposure. Sneezing is the most common clinical sign in
FURI17,19 (ch. 35; Video 205.1)

. Other common clinical signs

are serous, serosanguineous, mucoid, purulent, or mucopurulent
nasal discharge, nasal congestion with stertorous breathing, ocular
discharge, chemosis, blepharospasm, or conjunctivitis. Thick,
mucopurulent or hemorrhagic discharge is more commonly seen in
cases that have components of chronic inflammation, bacterial
infection, and/or prolonged viral infection; this may also be
accompanied by fever (ch. 16), oral or nasal ulceration, dyspnea,
and inappetence due to malaise and inability to smell.17,20,21
Signs of FHV-1 infection include sneezing, serous to mucoid nasal
discharge, nasal congestion, stertorous breathing, and fever. If
cytolysis is severe enough and clinical signs result in continued
irritation, ulceration on the lips or nares can also occur. Ocular
clinical signs of FHV-1 infection include conjunctivitis with
hyperemia and chemosis, and serous ocular discharge that can
progress to mucoid ocular discharge by day 5 to 7 of infection
(Figure 205.2).22 If cytolysis is severe enough in the mucosal
surfaces of the conjunctiva, discharge can become sanguineous.
FHV-1 is also a common cause of corneal ulceration, and stromal
keratitis can occur with dendritic corneal ulceration, which is the
only pathognomonic clinical sign of FHV-1 infection (Figure
205.3)6,23 (ch. 13). The uncomplicated typical clinical course of
disease can last 10-21 days.21 Adults with recrudescent disease may

have milder signs consisting of conjunctivitis, epiphora, and mild
sneezing.19
Oral ulceration is one of the characteristic lesions of FCV infection
(Figure 205.4)24; however, oral ulceration can also occur with
other diseases. Fever, conjunctivitis, nasal discharge, sneezing, and
other upper respiratory clinical signs similar to those seen with FHV1 infection, are also common with FCV infection. However,
respiratory disease is not always present when infection is induced
during experimental challenge with FCV nor in all suspect cases.25
Therefore, although FCV is mostly a respiratory and oral pathogen,
various clinical signs including acute lameness, severe systemic
disease associated with the highly virulent systemic strain (VS-FCV),
and chronic lymphoplasmacytic gingivitis stomatitis and ulcerative
stomatitis, have been attributed to FCV infection.26

C. felis mostly causes ocular clinical signs including conjunctivitis,
chemosis, hyperemia, blepharospasm, and serous to mucopurulent
ocular discharge; nasal discharge may also occur (ch. 13).27 Clinical
signs of M. felis infection also include conjunctivitis, hyperemia,
sneezing, serous to mucopurulent ocular discharge as well as nasal
involvement with mucopurulent nasal discharge, nasal congestion,

and stertorous breathing (Figure 205.5).28 FURI clinical signs that
can be attributable, in part, to B. bronchiseptica infection include
sneezing, serous to mucopurulent ocular or nasal discharge,
conjunctivitis, fever, and cough. Uncomplicated cases can resolve
within 10 days.12

FIGURE 205.3 Dendritic corneal ulceration
stained with topical fluorescein dye. (Courtesy
Professor Sheila Crispin. From Gould D. Feline
herpesvirus-1: ocular manifestations, diagnosis and
treatment options. J Feline Med Surg. 2011;13:336,
Figure 2.)
Some clinical signs might be more common with one pathogen
versus another, although this does not preclude the multifactorial
disease process and concomitant infections that might be present.
Lameness and oral ulceration are more common with FCV. Corneal
dendritic ulcers are associated with FHV-1. Conjunctivitis without
concurrent nasal clinical signs might be indicative of C. felis. Cough

can be associated with B. bronchiseptica, although it could also be
related to other infections progressing to the lower respiratory tract.

DIAGNOSIS
Accurate identification of the cause of FURI typically cannot be
determined in individual cats in uncomplicated cases. Coinfections
with multiple pathogens are common, and clinical signs attributable
to the pathogens overlap. Diagnostic testing via molecular methods
can be unrewarding and misleading, as detection of organisms does
not necessarily correlate with the cause of a cat’s illness with FURI
(ch. 184). Clinically healthy animals shed pathogens and can be
carriers, and vaccination interference can also occur. Inadequate
sample handling procedures, variable assay detection thresholds,
genetic variants, and pathogens shed in low or undetectable numbers
might lead to false negatives.29,30 Most cats have resolution of
clinical signs without need for diagnosis of the specific pathogens
involved, and testing in acute, uncomplicated single cases is not
recommended.16,20

Mycoplasma spp., Streptococcus canis, and
Haemophilus spp. Note the mucopurulent,
sanguineous to hemorrhagic nasal discharge that
could be attributed to multiple organisms or
processes.
Diagnostic tests might be used if clinical signs are severe and
persistent, resistant to empirical treatment, or in outbreak situations
in shelters or catteries in which further diagnostic evaluation would
alter treatment and management strategies.20 Assays available for
viral diagnosis include virus isolation, indirect fluorescent antibody
testing, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and polymerase chain
reaction (PCR) using oropharyngeal or conjunctival swabs to obtain
samples.30 Assays available for bacterial species include cell culture
from conjunctival or oropharyngeal swabs, cytologic evaluation of

conjunctival smears, serum antibodies, and PCR on conjunctival
swabs, scrapes, or biopsies. Nasal secretions should not be utilized
for culture.16 The use of FURI PCR panels is most helpful for testing
multiple cats in an outbreak situation in an attempt to determine
causation16 (ch. 184). Diagnostic testing including necropsy should
be used, however, in cases of mortality after FURI such as in cases of
suspected VS-FCV.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES
In complicated or unresolving cases of FURI, differential diagnoses
should be considered (Table 205.1; ch. 213). A diagnosis of
idiopathic feline chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) instead of FURI might
be considered if an adult afebrile cat has had clinical signs despite
treatment for 4 or more weeks (Figure 205.5). Etiology is very
likely multifactorial, although early and unresolving FURI has been
implicated as a precipitating factor in some cats.

PREVENTION, MANAGEMENT, AND
TREATMENT
Supportive care with attention to fluid restoration, food intake,
nutrition, and a reduction of stress are important in all management
plans, and this might be all that is necessary in uncomplicated cases
(Figure 205.2). Due to potential blockage of nasal passages and
loss of smell, oral pain due to ulceration, or general malaise and
inappetence, appetite stimulants such as transdermal or oral
mirtazapine or cyproheptadine can be used (chs. 17, 151). In
complicated or unresolving cases in which other differential
diagnoses are being considered, an esophageal feeding tube might be
necessary (ch. 81). Nasal and ocular discharge should be gently
cleaned, and nebulization and airway humidification can also be
considered. Some clinicians also anecdotally recommend gentle
human infant-formulated nasal saline flushes twice per day to clear
the nasal passages of debris.

Limiting the number of cats in multi-cat environments and
providing large and diverse enclosures in catteries or shelters may
reduce FURI rates in these environments.31 Lessening stress in
shelter cats can decrease signs of FURI and shedding.32 Feline
pheromone fractions may be used as a stress-reducing modality;
pheromone usage has reduced sneezing in cats with FHV-1 infection
when exposed to stressful housing configurations.19
Antimicrobial treatment should be reserved for cases in which the
cat’s clinical course is not resolving, worsening, and accompanied by
fever, hyporexia, and lethargy. Although purulent nasal or ocular
discharge may increase suspicion of bacterial infection, viral
infections can also recruit large numbers of neutrophils, decrease
normal secretions, and thus result in purulent discharge.21 FURI also
typically includes a viral component, thus if bacterial pathogens are
not responsible for clinical illness, antibiotics are unnecessary.
Furthermore, aversive handling for treatment or forceful medication
administration could induce undue stress leading to further
exacerbation of recrudescence of FURI. There is growing evidence
that systemic antibiotics adversely disrupt the normal flora of cats,
and antibiotic resistance is also increasing (ch. 7).16
If supportive care does not resolve clinical signs or if there are
signs of fever, lethargy, malaise, nasal congestion, purulent ocular or
nasal discharge, and hyporexia, the first antibiotic of choice is
doxycycline orally at 10 mg/kg once per day for 7-10 days; it should
be coated with a lubricating substance and/or followed by or
administered in conjunction with liquid or food. B. bronchiseptica,
C. felis, and Mycoplasma spp. are typically susceptible to
doxycycline.16 When doxycycline is compounded into a liquid
solution, that solution typically becomes ineffective after 7-10 days;
this should be considered when dispensing the medication. If
treatment is unrewarding, other antimicrobials as discussed in the
International Society for Companion Animal Infectious Diseases’
antimicrobial use guidelines for respiratory diseases16 or antivirals
as discussed below can be considered (ch. 140).

Extralabel antiviral therapies for FHV-1 should also be reserved for
cases in which the cat’s clinical course is not resolving, is worsening,
and includes fever, lethargy, malaise, and hyporexia or inappetence.
Famciclovir, an orally administered prodrug of penciclovir, is
sometimes used for the treatment of severe acute infections of FHV1. A suggested starting dosage is 90 mg/kg orally every 8-12 hours
for 7 days.33,34 There are currently no safe antiviral medications for
FCV infection in cats.
Purulent ocular discharge does not always require antimicrobial
ophthalmic treatments, as FHV-1 can also result in purulent
discharge due to neutrophil proliferation and diminished tear
production, and the stress of treatment might outweigh benefits.
Topical ophthalmic antimicrobials should be used in cats with
corneal ulceration, and they might be used if ocular clinical signs are
severe and are affecting vision or compromising future vision.21
Topical ocular anti-viral drugs have also been used for treatment
of FHV-1 infections; however, if only serous discharge or epiphora
are present, administration of ocular medications is not
recommended. The underlying cause of recrudescence should

instead be investigated. Anti-viral ophthalmic medications include
idoxuridine, trifluridine, and cidofovir, although idoxuridine and
trifluridine necessitate frequent application and are also not well
tolerated by cats.34
Another approach in the treatment of FURI has been to upregulate
non-specific immune responses. The administration of probiotics
(ch. 168), nutraceuticals, or a liposome toll-like receptor complex
has been associated with positive outcomes.22,35 Innate cellmediated immunity (CMI) has the potential to be enhanced by
intranasal (IN) vaccination, potentially targeting nonspecific
pathogens not included in the vaccine.36,37 Use of modified live
FHV-1- and FCV-containing IN vaccines in cats with FURI has been
associated with control or treatment of clinical signs, suggesting the
possibility of immune modulation and induction of nonspecific
cross-protection against multiple pathogens. Other adjunctive
therapies and preventives with mixed results have included L-lysine
and feline or human recombinant interferon.38,39

DISINFECTION
FURI is primarily spread by direct contact between cats; however,
some of the pathogens can persist on fomites. Cleaning and
disinfection should be performed with products that eliminate the
most environmentally resistant of the pathogens, FCV, while also
being mindful of necessary contact times. Solid, dry surfaces such as
food bowls should also be disinfected. Surfaces that are
contaminated with dirt or bodily fluids should first be cleaned with a
detergent. Although a 1:32 dilution of 5.25% sodium hypochlorite
(household bleach) is effective against FCV, bleach is corrosive,
inactivated by sunlight, and ineffective in the presence of most
organic materials. Accelerated hydrogen peroxide compounds,
oxidizing agents, are effective against FCV and are a preferred
alternative due to their relative safety, short contact time, and ability
to maintain efficacy in the presence of some organic material. In
multi-cat environments, proper, clean, good ventilation with an
appropriate number of air exchanges is also necessary to reduce risk

of URI, and air quality within the cat’s microenvironment should
also be considered.14

OUTCOME AND PROGNOSIS
Many or most cats have likely been exposed to FURI pathogens such
as FCV or FHV-1, respectively, and are healthy carriers. It is
therefore unnecessary to relegate cats suspected or diagnosed with
FCV, FHV-1, or FURI to single-cat households. Most cases of
uncomplicated FURI have a very good prognosis. Morbidity can be
severe in the debilitated, immune-compromised, or very young, but
with supportive care and treatment, prognosis is also usually good.
Comorbidities, stress, crowded and unsanitary environments,
antibiotic resistance, and highly pathogenic variants contribute to
poorer prognoses.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Feline Upper Respiratory Infections
WHAT IS FURI?
Feline upper respiratory infections (FURIs) are very common in cats,
similar to “colds” being common in the human population. FURI is
typically caused by one or more viruses and/or bacteria. The 2 most
common viral offenders are feline herpesvirus-1 (FHV-1), a
widespread, ubiquitous virus in the feline population to which most
cats have been exposed and feline calicivirus (FCV), while the 3 most
commonly implicated bacteria are Mycoplasma spp., Chlamydia
spp., and Bordetella spp. Cats can carry any of these pathogens with
them either throughout their lives or intermittently.
Cats are usually vaccinated for both FHV-1 and FCV in their
regular vaccination series (FHV-1 may also be referred to as feline
viral rhinotracheitis [FVR] virus in the vaccine; the combined

vaccine is often referred to as FVRCP – FVR-caliciviruspanleukopenia). Vaccination for FHV-1 and FCV only helps to
decrease severity of illness in your cat and does not prevent infection.
SYMPTOMS
These can range from mild and of little clinical importance, to very
severe especially in the very young, old, or immune compromised.
Signs include sneezing, audible nasal congestion, nasal discharge
that can be watery and clear or thick and discolored, tearing,
squinting eyes with discharge, and swollen eyelids. In more severe
cases, these signs can be accompanied by fever, lethargy, lack of
appetite, and the ocular or nasal discharge can become bloody or
very thick and green. The signs can last from a few days to a few
weeks or more in severe cases.
SPREAD AND RECURRENCE
FURI is typically spread by direct contact between cats, but it can
also be carried on contaminated objects. After a cat is exposed to the
virus or bacteria, it will usually take several days before signs are
seen, if at all.
Many cats may have been infected early in life and then harbor the
pathogens for life. STRESS can and will contribute to FURI and a
reactivation of FHV-1 several days after the stressful event(s). ANY
changes in the cat’s environment, including entering a new home,
moving, boarding, surgery, new cats or animals entering or leaving
the home, changes in routine or caregiver, sleep deprivation,
temperature extremes, other illness, or any perceived or real stress,
can contribute to stress and thus FURI resurgence.
WHEN TO VISIT YOUR VETERINARIAN
Occasional sneezing or a mildly tearing eye with watery discharge
not affecting eyesight or quality of life is rarely a problem warranting
treatment, akin to humans not seeking medical care for similar
symptoms. However, if signs are severe and include thick, mucoid,
yellow, green, or bloody ocular or nasal discharge, lethargy, or loss of
appetite, veterinary care should be sought.
Treatment might or might not include medications including
antibiotics (for bacteria) or antivirals (for severe viral infections) or

other supportive care measures such as nutritional supplements or
treatments instilled into the nose. Disinfection of the environment,
good sanitary measures, clean air quality, and a feline-friendly
environment with a minimization of stress are also important in the
management of FURI.
If your cat or kitten does not improve within 1-2 weeks with the
treatment that your veterinarian prescribed, your veterinarian might
evaluate your cat for the many other less common causes of signs
similar to FURI.
Elena Contreras (Brookville, New York)

OVERVIEW
Members of at least 15 viral families that have the potential to infect
cats have been identified. The focus of this chapter is the emerging
viruses whose impact on feline health is under investigation. Viral

discovery can be driven by the investigation of a novel disease that
has an infectious epidemiology, and in those cases, the establishment
of causality can rely on fulfilment of established postulates (e.g.,
Koch, Fredricks and Relman). However, over the last decade the rate
at which viruses are being discovered exceeds our understanding of
their clinical relevance. Metagenomics has shown unique virus
communities, or viromes, colonizing the skin, mucosal surfaces,
respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts and blood of clinically normal
animals. These viruses include “normal flora,” whose relationship
with the host has evolved over millennia, resulting in a host-virus
détente. While they may be clinically innocuous in most animals,
such persistent infections can also modify host physiology and
immune function, and in individual cases can cause disease.
Sporadic disease can occur, sometimes years after initial infection. A
high prevalence of infection in the general population can make
disease association hard to identify and impossible to rule out.
Cofactors such as immune dysfunction, host genetic background or
coinfections may be required for manifestation of disease, and one
virus species may be linked to a range of pathological sequelae.
Establishing causality relies on evaluating accumulating evidence
from multiple investigations. The prize for characterizing new viral
pathogens is the prospect of improved patient outcomes through
specific treatment and even disease prevention through viral control
measures (ch. 185). This chapter considers several viruses, most
newly discovered, where there are data addressing their link to
disease.

FELINE HEPADNAVIRUS
Domestic cat hepadnavirus (DCH), a naturally-occurring hepatitis Blike virus infecting cats, was discovered in Australia in 2018.1
Infection with DCH appears to be widespread and common with 6.512.4% of cats testing positive for virus DNA in whole blood or
serum.2-5 DCH is a member of the Orthohepadnavirus genus, other
members of which cause severe liver disease in their hosts. For
example, chronic infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV), a
hepadnavirus of humans, causes an estimated 880,000 deaths

annually from chronic hepatitis and hepatocellular carcinoma.6
Mounting evidence links DCH infection to liver disease in cats (ch.
271). An international, multicenter study detected DCH in biopsies
from 43% (6/14) of chronic hepatitis cases, and 28% (8/29) of
hepatocellular carcinomas, whereas feline cholangitis (n = 6), biliary
carcinoma (n = 18) and normal liver (n = 15) biopsies all tested
negative for DCH.3 Furthermore, in DCH-associated cases, the
histologic features and the viral distribution using in situ
hybridization were strikingly similar to those seen with HBVassociated disease. Risk factors for DCH detection include retrovirus
infection (chs. 198, 199) and increased activity of serum alanine
aminotransferase.4,5
Zoonotic transmission of DCH is extremely unlikely since
hepadnaviruses infect only one or a few closely-related hosts.
However, cross-species transmission of DCH to wild felids, many of
which are critically endangered, may be a concern. The potential for
disease is greater in a non-adapted host. Research addressing the
epidemiology of DCH and the natural history of infection is needed
to understand the threat, if any, that DCH poses to feline health
globally.

FELINE MORBILLIVIRUS
A putative association between a novel feline morbillivirus, FeMV,
and tubulointerstitial nephritis, a major cause of death in cats,
generated immediate interest in the novel virus but evidence of any
association is incomplete and is conflicting (ch. 301).7 FeMV was
discovered in 2012 in cats in Hong Kong,8 and infection has since
been detected in domestic and some wild felids worldwide by
reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (urine and blood)
and serologically.7 Genetic diversity and recombination are common
among viral isolates. One study of 38 cats identified a significant
association between the severity of renal lesions and the detection of
FeMV by immunohistochemistry.9,10 Conflicting evidence comes
from a study of 36 cats with active renal inflammation identified at
routine necropsy, 6 of which were azotemic, where none had FeMV

detectable by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (Pesavento, personal
communication) and from 80 cats in the UK, where neither
molecular detection of FeMV nor serologic detection of anti-FeMV
antibodies was significantly associated with renal disease as defined
by azotemia.11 This leaves open the possibility that, if FeMV infection
contributes to kidney disease in cats, it might be one of multiple
potential renal insults and/or pathogens.

FELINE GAMMAHERPESVIRUS
The discovery of Felis catus gammaherpesvirus 1 (FcaGHV1) in
2014,12 was driven by the clinical observation that feline
immunodeficiency virus (FIV) infection (ch. 198) confers an
increased risk of high-grade B-cell lymphoma in cats, and that
similar cancers arising in HIV-infected humans are often causallylinked to gammaherpesviruses (GHVs) that infect humans, namely
Epstein-Barr virus and Kaposi’s sarcoma-associated herpesvirus.
GHVs infecting non-domestic Felidae have been identified in the
puma (Puma concolor, PcoGHV1), African lion (Panthera leo,
PleoGHV1), bobcat (Lynx rufus, LruGHV1 and 2) and ocelot
(Leopardus pardalis, LpaGHV1).13
FcaGHV1 infection is widely endemic. The prevalence of FcaGHV1
viremia is <6% to 23.6%.14-16 Serologic evidence suggests that the
true FcaGHV1 infection rate could be at least double that indicated
by molecular studies.17 Adult, male, entire (sexually intact) cats are
most likely to be viremic and coinfections with FIV (ch. 198), feline
leukemia virus (FeLV) (ch. 199) or hemoplasmas (ch. 194) are
identified as risk factors.18
Fortunately, for a virus that is highly prevalent, most, if not all,
FcaGHV1 infections are expected to be subclinical. GHV infections in
other species are clinically latent except in certain circumstances. For
example, where cell-mediated immunity is compromised, GHVs can
cause lymphoproliferative and neoplastic disorders. Despite the
rationale for its discovery, there is yet no evidence of a role for
FcaGHV1 in feline lymphoma.15,19 Ruling out an occasional
pathogenic role for FcaGHV1 will be difficult. Even if FcaGHV1

contributes to disease in only a minority of infections, the total
number of affected cats could be sizable because the virus is highly
prevalent in many populations. Species-jumping from a well-adapted
primary host to a poorly adapted but closely related host is another
circumstance when GHVs can cause disease. Cross-species infectivity
has been identified for LruGHV1, which can infect pumas, and
FcaGHV1 has been detected in Tsushima leopard cats (Prionailurus
bengalensis euptilurus) in Japan, but no pathologic sequelae have
been described.20 FcaGHV1 is not known or suspected to infect
humans. The host range of individual GHVs is typically limited to
one or a small number of closely related species.

OTHER GAMMAHERPESVIRUSES
The bovine gammaherpesvirus, BHV4, has a wide host range but the
prevalence and pathogenic potential of feline BHV4 infections is
controversial. Early studies supporting a role for BHV4 in upper
respiratory tract and lower urinary tract disease have not been
replicated, and molecular epidemiological studies report divergent
results. In a 2015 study, none of 101 cats from California, Colorado
and Florida tested PCR positive for BHV4.21

RUSTRELA VIRUS AND BORNA
DISEASE VIRUS
Rustrela virus (RusV; Rubivirus strelense, genus Rubivirus), a
relative of rubella virus in humans, has been identified as the
probable cause of most cases of “staggering disease” in domestic cats
(chs. 41, 255).22 “Staggering disease” is a clinical syndrome
associated with a non-suppurative meningoencephalitis that has
been reported since the 1970’s. Signs are variable, progressive, and
include hind limb ataxia and behavioural changes. A viral cause for
“staggering disease” has been suspected from the histological picture
and geographic clustering to a few countries including Sweden,
Germany and Austria. In a 2023 study, RusV RNA and antigen were
detected in brain tissue from a well-curated group of affected cats,

but not in unaffected control cats.22 Wood mice (Apodemus
sylvaticus) are implicated as a reservoir host for RusV. Serologic
studies of RusV in cats are expected to follow.
Borna disease virus (BDV), a neutrotropic virus causing sporadic
disease in a wide host range, has previously been suspected to cause
some cases of “staggering disease.” Neurologic disease was
reproduced in rats experimentally infected with BDV that had been
isolated from cats with presumed Borna-associated disease.23
However, up to 20% of clinically normal cats have serological
evidence of exposure to BDV, and BDV was not detected in the
“staggering disease” case series described above.

ADDITIONAL FELINE PARVOVIRUSES
(BOCAVIRUS, CHAPPARVOVIRUS,
KOBUVIRUS)
OVERVIEW
The well-studied and clinically impactful protoparvoviruses canine
parvovirus 2 (CPV-2) and feline panleukopenia virus are covered in
depth in a devoted chapter (ch. 201), but there is much less known
about disease(s) associated with other viruses in the rapidly growing
family Parvoviridae. A recent phylogenetic reshuffling was required
to account for dozens of new parvoviruses largely revealed by
metagenomics. Currently, Parvoviridae comprise two subfamilies
(Parvovirinae and Desnoviriniae), the former containing seven
genera known to infect mammals, including humans (Amdo-, Copi-,
Boca-, Ave-, Dependo-, and Erythrovirus).

FELINE BOCAVIRUS
Feline bocaviruses are classified in 3 genotypes.24,25 Bocaviruses
have been associated with diarrheal and respiratory illnesses in
humans and other mammals, but pathogenic potential in cats
remains unknown. Feline bocavirus 1 (FBoV1) was first recognized in
a survey of cats in Hong Kong where it was detected in the blood,

feces, respiratory and urinary tract of presumed normal animals.24
Detection rate for FBoV1 in one study was 7% (9/128).26 FBoV2 and
FBoV3 were discovered, also by metagenomics, as part of the fecal
virome in shelter cats from Portugal.24 FBoV2 is phylogenetically
related to FBoV1 (∼60% identity), but divergent enough to be
categorized as a distinct species.25
An association between bocavirus infection and diarrhea has been
postulated but unproven, largely because bocavirus DNA is detected
in feces, along with other viruses, during outbreaks of diarrhea, and
also from cats without diarrhea.25 In one study, 5 parvoviruses,
including 2 that were novel, along with viruses from at least three
other viral families, were identified in cats from a single shelter
diarrhea outbreak. Nonetheless, most reports indicate that FBoVs
are detected more frequently in cats with diarrhea compared with
healthy cats, which is one of the driving reasons that molecular
diagnostic strategies have shifted to multiplex (simultaneous)
detection of multiple pathogens (ch. 184). It is possible that, in the
cases of diarrhea or respiratory disease, replication of bocaviruses is
triggered by cell damage/repair, and that these viruses contribute to
disease only as part of a polymicrobial landscape. Research based on
CPV-2 has long demonstrated viral replication limited to dividing
host cells, but human bocavirus 1 (HBoV1) replicates in terminally
differentiated airway epithelial cells.27 The significance of detection
of FBoV1 in respiratory specimens has not yet been determined.

FELINE CHAPPARVOVIRUS (FELINE
FECHAVIRUS)
A new feline parvovirus was detected during investigation of an
outbreak of diarrhea and vomiting in shelter-housed cats in British
Columbia, Canada.28 The pattern of transfer among three shelters
suggested an infectious cause, but less than 50% of the samples
contained detectable virus. At this point, there are no studies that
have investigated the prevalence of feline chapparvovirus in the
general population, and patterns of shedding and transmission are

also unknown. A related parvovirus in mice (mouse kidney
parvovirus) is associated with chronic kidney inflammation, but no
virus has ever been convincingly associated with chronic kidney
disease (CKD) in cats.

FELINE ASTROVIRUS
Astroviruses form part of the enteric virome of cats but their role in
disease, if any, is uncertain. Astroviruses are genetically diverse and
infect a broad range of mammals and birds. In humans, astroviruses
are an important cause of gastroenteritis, especially in children, and
central nervous system complications have been reported.29 Feline
astroviruses (FAstV-1 to 4) cluster into two genetically distinct
groups.30 Experimental astrovirus infection induced diarrhea in
specific-pathogen-free cats,31 but field studies reveal no consistent
association between feline astrovirus detection and clinical signs.
Whether feline astrovirus can act as a pathogen or copathogen in
some circumstances, perhaps potentiating signs induced by known
enteric pathogens such as FPV, requires further investigation.

FELINE FOAMY VIRUS
Feline foamy virus (FFV) is a retrovirus in the spumavirus subfamily
that derives its name from the characteristic appearance of its
cytopathic effect in culture caused by vacuolization and
multinucleate giant-cell formation. FFV infection is common, with
seroprevalence exceeding 50% in many studies,32 but in contrast to
pathogenic retroviruses, FeLV and FIV, a convincing case has yet to
be made that FFV infection has any clinical consequences. A role for
FFV in CKD has been mooted and experimental infection is
associated with mild renal ultrastructural changes and
histopathological changes in other tissues compared with control
cats,33 but epidemiological or other data to support a role for FFV in
CKD, or any other disease or syndrome, are lacking. FFV and other
spumaviruses show potential to be used as vaccines or gene therapy
vectors.
