CHAPTER 207:
Cryptococcosis
Krystle L. Reagan

A C RO N YM S
CNS central nervous system
CSF cerebrospinal fluid
CT computed tomography
CALAS cryptococcal antigen latex agglutination system
MRI magnetic resonance imaging
PCR polymerase chain reaction
POC point-of-care
T2W T2-weighted

Cryptococcosis is a systemic fungal infection found worldwide that
affects various mammalian species, including dogs and cats. It is
considered an emerging pathogen in some geographic locations, such
as the Pacific Northwest of the United States (US) and is the most
common systemic mycosis affecting cats. Direct animal to animal or
zoonotic transmission has not been reported. The infection, acquired
from the environment, initially involves the upper respiratory tract
where it may or may not result in clinical signs of rhinitis. It can
disseminate to other organs, including the central nervous system
(CNS), eyes, and skin.

ETIOLOGY, EPIDEMIOLOGY,
PATHOGENESIS
Cryptococcus is a dimorphic fungus that exists in a filamentous form
in the environment and as an encapsulated budding yeast in the
host. Over 37 species of Cryptococcus have been identified, but
organisms in the Cryptococcus neoformans species complex and
Cryptococcus gattii species complex are responsible for most
infections of dogs, cats, and people. Species within the C.
neoformans complex have a worldwide distribution and are the most
commonly isolated organism from dogs with cryptococcosis and
from immunocompromised people.1,2 The organisms in the
environment can be found in organic material contaminated with
pigeon droppings. Species in the C. gattii complex are associated
with leaf litter of eucalyptus and other tree species and are endemic
in Australia, New Zealand, Southeast Asia, and western North
America. Organisms in the C. gattii complex are emerging pathogens
of immunocompetent people, accounting for 50% of dog and cat
infections in Western Australia and nearly all infected cats in
California.3,4
Cryptococcus organisms had been divided into five serotypes (A,
B, C, D, and AD) based on antibody response to capsular
polysaccharides. Advances in molecular characterization of
Cryptococcus spp. have resulted in the characterization of molecular
types within the C. neoformans and C. gattii species complexes.
These molecular types are increasingly recognized as having unique
clinical features and epidemiology. Separate species designations
have been proposed but not fully accepted. The molecular types
described include VNI and VNII (C. neoformans), VNIII (C.
neoformans x C. deneoformans hybrid), VNIV (C. deneoformans),
VGI (C. gattii sensu stricto), VGII (C. deuterogattii), VGIII (C.
bacillisporus), VGIV (C. tetragattii), and a VGIII/VGIV hybrid (C.
decagattii).5
Cryptococcus spp. are dimorphic fungi that exist in a filamentous
form in the environment and as an encapsulated yeast (3.5-7
micrometer in diameter with a 1-20 micrometer thick capsule) in the
host. Desiccated yeast cells or basidiospores in the environment are

inhaled and are primarily deposited into the upper respiratory tract
in dogs and cats. This initial colonization or infection will result in
cryptococcal rhinitis in some dogs and cats, but no clinical signs will
be appreciated in some exposed individuals.6 In some cases, the
yeast will undergo hematogenous dissemination to other organs such
as the CNS, eyes, lymph nodes, and skin and establish a
disseminated infection.
The polysaccharide capsule is an important virulence factor that
inhibits phagocytosis, depletes complement, and inhibits the cellmediated immune response by shifting the host adaptive immune
response from a Th1 to a Th2 type response.7-9 Organisms can also
evade the host cell-mediated immune system by altering the cell
membrane composition and structure.10 In people, concurrent
infection with human immunodeficiency virus is a risk factor for
developing cryptococcosis, indicating that the cell-mediated immune
system is essential in preventing disease. Cryptococcosis in dogs and
cats, however, is usually diagnosed in seemingly immunocompetent
individuals; nevertheless, cats concurrently infected with feline
leukemia virus (ch. 199) or feline immunodeficiency virus (ch. 198)
may have more severe clinical signs or be slower to respond to
treatment.1,11,12

CLINICAL SIGNS
OVERVIEW
The clinical presentation of cryptococcosis varies based on host
immunity, molecular type of the infecting organism, and inoculum
dose. Some exposures result in transient colonization or self-limiting
infections.6,13 Clinical signs can develop between 2 months and 1
year after exposure.14,15 Cats are more commonly affected than
dogs.1

CATS

The most commonly infected breeds in Australia include Siamese,
Birman, and Ragdoll cats, but this has not been noted in the US.1,16
No sex or age predilection has been observed. Clinical presentation
in cats typically consists of a chronic, progressive upper respiratory
tract infection with sneezing and mucopurulent to hemorrhagic nasal
discharge (ch. 35).1,11,16 About half of cats with nasal involvement
also have a firm swelling or proliferative ulcerated cutaneous lesions
over the bridge of the nose (Figure 207.1). Cutaneous or
subcutaneous nodules that ulcerate and drain are noted in about half
of cats. Ocular involvement characterized by chorioretinitis and optic
neuritis is observed in up to one-third of cats and is strongly
associated with CNS involvement (ch. 242). Neurologic signs, due to
extension of local nasal disease or hematogenous spread, are
observed in about 20% of infected cats. Neurologic signs correlate
with the anatomic location of infection and may include seizures,
mentation change, circling, ataxia, and cranial nerve deficits (Video
207.1)

. Less commonly, lower respiratory signs (e.g., tachypnea)

due to pleural effusion or lameness due to osteomyelitis have been
reported.

FIGURE 207.1 An ulcerated nasal lesion in a cat
diagnosed with nasal cryptococcosis in northern
California. Figure courtesy Dr. Elizabeth Lee.

DOGS
In Australia, cryptococcosis infection is overrepresented in German
Shepherd Dogs, Doberman Pinschers, and Great Danes. In the US,
American Cocker Spaniel dogs appear to be at a higher risk.1,3,17,18
Most dogs diagnosed with cryptococcosis are <4 years of age and are
more likely than cats to have disseminated disease. 80% of infected
dogs have multiple organ systems involved.1 Non-specific clinical
signs such as lethargy, weight loss, and decreased appetite
predominate in dogs with cryptococcosis. Up to 75% of dogs exhibit
neurologic signs that correlate to the infected location within the
CNS and may include seizures, ataxia, and blindness (ch. 242).
Other clinical signs may include upper respiratory tract signs such as
sneezing and nasal discharge (ch. 35), ulcerated skin lesions,
lymphadenomegaly, GI signs, ocular signs associated with
granulomatous chorioretinitis (Figure 207.2), or lameness
associated with osteomyelitis.18-20 Lower respiratory involvement is
only rarely clinically observed, but more than half of dogs had
evidence of subclinical disease recognized at necropsy.1

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
CLINICOPATHOLOGIC FINDINGS
Routine Testing
Complete blood count, serum chemistry panel, and urinalysis
findings are generally within normal limits. A mild leukocytosis
characterized by a mature neutrophilia, monocytosis, and
eosinophilia may be noted. A mild nonregenerative anemia of
chronic disease may also be present. In some cases, cryptococcal
yeast organisms may be observed on urine sediment examination or
urine culture.

FIGURE 207.2 Ocular abnormalities in a 4-yearold male castrated Doberman Pinscher diagnosed
with nasal and central nervous system
cryptococcosis. Evidence of granulomatous
chorioretinitis (arrows) was noted on dilated fundic
examination. Image courtesy Dr. Kelly Knickelbein,
University of California-Davis.
Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF)
In dogs and cats with CNS involvement, CSF may have elevated
protein and leukocyte concentrations (chs. 109, 242).21 Cytologic
evaluation may reveal mononuclear and neutrophilic inflammation.

Cryptococcal organisms are observed in up to 90% of infected dogs.
CSF collection can result in acute increases in intracranial pressure
leading to clinical decompensation; this procedure should not be
pursued unless a diagnosis cannot be achieved with less invasive
methodologies.

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
Pulmonary cryptococcosis is rare, but if it is present, thoracic
radiographs may reveal an interstitial to alveolar pattern or nodular
infiltrates. Occasionally, pleural effusion or tracheobronchial
lymphadenomegaly may be noted. Computed tomography (CT) of
the nasal cavity in animals with cryptococcal rhinitis may be
suggestive of a soft tissue mass with evidence of rhinosinusitis and
lysis of the nasal bones or cribriform plate.1 Magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) in dogs and cats with CNS involvement is more
sensitive for detection of cryptococcomas than is CT. Typical MRI
findings include contrast-enhancing mass lesions that are T2weighted (T2W) hyperintense and T1-weighted hypointense and may
have evidence of edema with surrounding T2 hyperintensity (Video
207.1)

.7,21 Occasionally, lesions are observed that appear to be

fluid-filled on T2W images, but with greater T1W intensity than
expected for acellular fluid.

ORGANISM SPECIFIC DIAGNOSTICS
Cytology, Histology
The standard for diagnosing cryptococcosis is the cytologic or
histologic identification of Cryptococcus yeasts. Cytology specimens
can be obtained from nasal swabs, impression smears of ulcerated
cutaneous lesions, aspirates of mass lesions, cavitary effusions, or
bodily fluids (chs. 71, 83, and 85). New methylene blue,
Romanowsky, and Gram stains are adequate to identify cryptococcal
organisms, i.e., a stained cell surrounded by a non-staining capsule
(Figure 207.3). The yeast may appear as narrow-based budding.
Cytologic examination is 50-75% sensitive for the detection of

organisms, but a negative test cannot rule out the diagnosis.1 India
ink stain can highlight unstained cryptococcal yeasts against a dark
background; however, care must be used with this technique as
organisms can be easily confused with lymphocytes or fat droplets.7

FIGURE 207.3 Impression smear specimen
demonstrating the appearance of stained
cryptococcal yeast organisms surrounded by a large,
non-staining capsule. (100× magnification) Image
courtesy Demitria M. Vasilatis, University of
California, Davis.

Culture
Fungal culture of specimens obtained from tissue specimens,
exudative lesions, CSF, or urine can reveal growth in 2-10 days.
Cryptococcus spp. grow readily on Sabouraud’s dextrose agar, which
allows for subsequent species identification and antifungal

susceptibility testing. Subclinical colonization occurs in the nasal
cavity of some animals; therefore, a diagnosis of cryptococcosis
should not rely upon a culture of the nasal cavity alone.

Cryptococcal Antigen Latex Agglutination System
(CALAS)
CALAS, also termed latex cryptococcal antigen test (LCAT), is a
quantitative serologic test that detects Cryptococcus polysaccharide
capsular antigens. It is widely utilized as a noninvasive method to
support a diagnosis of cryptococcosis and to monitor treatment
response. This assay detects antigens from all species in the C.
neoformans and C. gattii complexes and can be used on both serum
and CSF specimens. The CALAS is highly sensitive (95-100%) and
specific (100%) for diagnosing cryptococcosis in cats, although
sensitivity may be slightly lower in dogs in the US.22,23 Prior to
performing the CALAS, specimens should be treated with pronase to
decrease likelihood of false-positive test results.7 Subclinical
colonization in cats may be responsible for false positive CALAS
results, with titers up to 1:200. Therefore, the diagnosis should be
confirmed with cytologic or histopathologic examination of
specimens if a titer of less than 1:200 is obtained.1 False-negative
test results may be observed more frequently in dogs than cats,
especially when there is localized ocular, CNS, or cutaneous lesions.1
CALAS titers in animals with cryptococcosis can range from 1:2 to
>1:524,000. Pre-treatment CALAS titers correlate with disease
severity but not mortality.12,22 A decrease in CALAS titers during
treatment is associated with a better prognosis, but the titer decrease
often lags behind clinical improvement. There is considerable
variability in CALAS titers among laboratories, so a single laboratory
should be utilized to compare antigen titers during treatment.

Point-of-Care (POC) Assays
POC cryptococcal antigen detection assays are commercially
available. An immunochromatographic lateral flow assay (CrAg;
IMMY Diagnostics, Norman, OK) is widely used as the screening test
of choice in people suspected of having cryptococcosis. This assay

has been validated in cats and dogs with a sensitivity of 92-100% and
specificity of 81-93% when compared to the CALAS.24 One study
noted that animals receiving treatment for cryptococcosis sometimes
had positive CrAg results when the CALAS had become negative.
This may indicate the CrAg may be more sensitive during treatment
monitoring, but the impact on patient outcome and rates of relapse
require further study. Another POC assay (CryptoPS, Biosynex,
Strasbourg, France) is a semiquantitative, cassette-based assay that
has a sensitivity of 80% and specificity of 95% in dogs and cats when
compared to the CALAS.24

Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)
Molecular detection of Cryptococcus DNA using real-time PCR is
offered by some veterinary diagnostic laboratories but is not typically
necessary for diagnosis. Positive PCR results must be interpreted
with caution because subclinical nasal colonization can occur, and
Cryptococcus DNA has been detected from small intestinal contents
from healthy dogs.25

TREATMENT
OVERVIEW
Treatment of cryptococcosis requires long-term antifungal
administration and supportive care tailored to the individual patient
(ch. 141). Recommendations for the treatment of dogs and cats have
been extrapolated from studies performed in humans and clinical
experience. Amphotericin B is the most effective anticryptococcal
drug in vitro and the primary therapy for people with cryptococcosis.
Azoles, e.g. fluconazole and itraconazole, are also efficacious as
monotherapy or in conjunction with amphotericin B, with only rare
reports of antifungal resistance reported.26,27

DISSEMINATED DISEASE OR CNS
INVOLVEMENT

In dogs and cats with disseminated disease or CNS involvement,
using amphotericin B for 4 weeks is recommended. Despite
amphotericin B having poor ocular and CNS distribution in health,
animals with cryptococcal meningitis have disruptions in the blood
brain barrier allowing drug penetration (ch. 141). Lipid-complexed
amphotericin B is less nephrotoxic but not more efficacious than
deoxycholate preparations, and higher dosages may be tolerated. 5flucytosine (250 mg/cat PO q8h) is synergistic with amphotericin B,
and this drug combination is the optimal treatment for
cryptococcosis in cats. However, 5-flucytosine may be challenging to
obtain or cost-prohibitive and cannot be used as a sole agent due to
the rapid development of resistance.28 5-flucytosine is not
recommended for dogs because it induces toxic epidermal necrolysis
within two weeks of starting therapy. In situations where 5flucytosine is not available or recommended, fluconazole can be used
in combination with amphotericin B. After the 4 weeks of induction
treatment, azole monotherapy is continued as outlined below (Video
207.1)

.

LOCALIZED NASAL INFECTION IN CATS
(FLUCONAZOLE AND OTHER AZOLES)
Cats with localized nasal disease can sometimes be managed with
azole therapy alone, but azole monotherapy is not recommended in
immunocompromised animals or those suspected of having
disseminated disease. Fluconazole (10 mg/kg PO q12h or 50 mg/cat
PO q12h) has good ocular and CNS drug penetration, limited adverse
effects, and is the initial azole treatment of choice.16 However, in the
authors’ institution, some cats fail to completely respond to
fluconazole, and antigen titers remain high. In some of these cats,
treatment with itraconazole (5-10 mg/kg PO q24h [capsules] or 3-5
mg/kg PO q24h [oral solution]) improves outcomes. Itraconazole
has less penetration into the CNS than does fluconazole, but it has
still been shown to treat cryptococcal meningitis successfully.29
Newer azole antifungal drugs, voriconazole and posaconazole, have
activity against Cryptococcus (ch. 141), but further studies are

needed to determine their role in the treatment of dogs and cats with
cryptococcosis. Voriconazole, when used at dosages used for humans
or dogs, is toxic in cats due to impaired hepatic metabolism.30
Terbinafine (10 mg/kg PO q24h) has been used in combination with
azole antifungals with some anecdotal improvement, but no
controlled trials have been reported.21 Surgical intervention can be
considered in animals with large cryptococcomas to improve drug
penetration but may not be necessary, as many respond favorably to
antifungal therapy without surgery.

LONG-TERM TREATMENT AND
FOLLOW-UP
During initial treatment with antifungal medications, a marked
inflammatory response may be noted in association with fungal dieoff. Worsening clinical signs, including neurologic status, in the first
4 days of therapy is not a negative prognostic indicator if supportive
care can maintain stability.21 Initial monthly monitoring of physical
examination, liver enzyme activities, and latex agglutination antigen
titer is recommended. A 4-fold decrease in CALAS titer in the first 2
months of therapy indicates a positive response to treatment.
Treatment duration for cats ranges from 2 to 12 months with a
median of 4 months, but is longer for dogs.16
Persistently elevated antigen titers should prompt investigation
into the medication formulation (ensuring it is not a compounded
formulation), therapeutic drug monitoring, or an alternate antifungal
therapy. Treatment should be continued for 2 months beyond the
clinical resolution of disease and the first negative CALAS. A recheck
examination and latex agglutination antigen titer should be
performed every 3-6 months for 2 years after discontinuation of
antifungal therapy to monitor for early relapse of disease. Relapse of
disease typically occurs within the first 2 years after discontinuing
antifungal medications, but can be observed up to 10 years later.16
Successful treatment of cryptococcosis is observed in 75% of cats:
50% and 84% in cats with and without CNS involvement,

respectively.16 Dogs have a more guarded prognosis, with 50%
successfully treated in one study.1

CLIENT INFORMATION
Cryptococcosis
Cryptococcosis is the most common systemic fungal disease
diagnosed in cats, but it can also be diagnosed in dogs, people, and
other animals. This infection is diagnosed worldwide, but some
geographic locations such as the Pacific Northwest of the United
States have emerged as hotspots. Animals become infected by
inhaling the fungus Cryptococcus neoformans or Cryptococcus
gattii from the environment. The fungal organisms grow in damp,
rich soil and are associated with pigeon droppings and tree litter.
Infections spreading between animals or from animals to people
have not been reported; rather, animals and people can become
infected from similar locations in the environment.
CLINICAL SIGNS
In cats, the most common infection site is the nasal passages, leading
to nasal discharge, sneezing, and possibly swelling of the nose and
face. The infection can also spread to other areas of the body,
including the eyes, brain, spinal cord, skin, or other internal organs.
Signs that may be present include blindness, seizures, skin masses,
decreased appetite, or weight loss.
DIAGNOSIS
Diagnosis of cryptococcosis can be made by visualizing the fungus
organisms through a microscope from samples of affected tissues,
such as a nasal swab or biopsy of a skin lesion. A blood test is also
available called the cryptococcal latex agglutination test. This test
helps diagnose cryptococcosis and monitor the response to
treatment. Other diagnostic tests may be recommended, such as xrays, a magnetic resonance image (MRI) or computed tomography

(CT) scan, or blood work to check organ function. These tests help
determine which body parts are affected by the infection.
TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
The treatment recommended is based on the location and extent of
the disease in your pet. Oral antifungal medications are used for mild
to moderate infections, and injectable medications are used for more
severe infections. Supportive care, including intravenous (IV) fluids
and anti-inflammatory drugs, are used on a case-by-case basis.
Medications often need to be continued for at least 6-9 months but
may be required for years in some animals. Regular rechecks with
your veterinarian are necessary to determine your pet’s response to
the therapy and determine if any changes should be made. The
prognosis for recovery depends on the severity and extent of the
disease when diagnosed. Over half of cats and dogs positively
respond to treatment and can be successfully taken off of antifungal
therapy. However, close monitoring should take place after
medications are stopped, as relapses can occur.
Krystle L. Reagan (Davis, California)

CHAPTER 208:
Coccidioidomycosis
Jane E. Sykes

A C RO N YM S
CNS central nervous system
GI gastrointestinal

ETIOLOGY AND EPIDEMIOLOGY
Coccidioidomycosis is a disease caused by soil-borne fungi belonging
to the genus Coccidioides. In the environment, Coccidioides exists as
a mycelium and in tissues, the organism exists as spherules. A
mycelium is a chain of barrel-shaped arthroconidia (or
arthrospores). The arthroconidia remain in the soil for long periods,
ultimately fragment, become aerosolized, and are inhaled by animal
hosts. This can lead to a localized pulmonary disease (pulmonary
coccidioidomycosis) or serious multisystemic disease (disseminated
coccidioidomycosis) if there is inadequate immune response.
Coccidioides spp. are distributed in the soil of semi-arid to arid
regions that are in low elevations above sea level with hot summers.
Coccidioides spp. are found in the southwestern and western USA,
eastern Washington state, Mexico, and parts of Central and South
America. In the USA, highly endemic regions include the south-

central valley of California (“Valley Fever”) and Arizona, especially
the greater Tucson and Phoenix areas.1 Infections have also been
reported in non-endemic areas in dogs and humans that have a
history of travel to endemic regions. Two species of Coccidioides
have been identified, C. posadasii and C. immitis, which appear to
cause similar clinical manifestations and have similar antifungal
drug susceptibilities.2 Coccidioides immitis is found in the central
valley of California and New Mexico; C. posadasii is in New Mexico
and elsewhere.3
Infection of animals and humans often follows a cycle of moist
conditions, a dry period, then soil disruption, such as may occur with
heavy rainfall, earthquakes, dust storms, prolonged droughts, or
construction.4-6 Dogs of either sex, any breed, or age may be
affected, although young adult dogs are at greatest risk.7-9
Weimaraners, Dalmatians, Hungarian Vizslas, Norfolk Terriers, and
Greyhounds appear to be predisposed.9 Risk factors for infection in
dogs from Arizona included being housed outdoors during the day,
roaming an area >1 acre, and walking in the desert.10 Among dogs
seen at the University of California, risk factors were digging
behavior (which increased risk 6.7-fold) and a history of travel to or
residence in the central valley of California or Arizona (which
increased risk 4.4-fold).9 Latent infections can occur in dogs and
reactivate following treatment of other conditions with
glucocorticoids or chemotherapeutic agents (chs. 144, 169, 227,
321). Relapse can also occur with immunosuppressive drug
treatment in dogs that have previously recovered from
coccidioidomycosis. Coccidioidomycosis occurs less commonly in
cats, with most reports coming from Arizona.11,12

PATHOGENESIS
Following inhalation, arthroconidia are phagocytosed by alveolar
macrophages and enlarge into a spherule (8-100 microns in
diameter; Figure 208.1). Hundreds of endospores (3-5 microns in
diameter) develop within each spherule and are released when the

mature spherule ruptures. This is associated with a
pyogranulomatous to granulomatous inflammatory response.
Surviving endospores then enlarge into new spherules. In hosts
unable to mount an effective immune response, endospores
disseminate to lymph nodes in the respiratory tract and elsewhere.
Inoculation coccidioidomycosis with a focal cutaneous lesion has
been described rarely.13

CLINICAL FEATURES
COMMON GENERAL SIGNS
Most infections in endemic areas are subclinical.14 Development of
clinical signs often follows a subacute to chronic course, with mild
systemic signs such as intermittent fever (range, 103-106°F [39.441.1°C], but typically low-grade), lethargy, inappetence, and weight
loss.7,15 Many dogs otherwise appear healthy with only brief periods
of inappetence.7 Signs may be present for months to years before
dogs are brought to a veterinarian.8 Signs of respiratory tract
involvement include a harsh cough, increased respiratory effort,
tachypnea and/or exercise intolerance.8,15 Rarely, diffuse fungal
pneumonia follows a fulminant course (ch. 217).

SIGNS OF DISSEMINATION
Sites of dissemination include bone, the central nervous system
(CNS), skin, peripheral lymph nodes, and the pericardium.8,16 Less
commonly, joints, eyes, testes, gastrointestinal (GI) tract, prostate,
liver, spleen, and urinary systems are affected.7 Sometimes
dissemination to only one site is detected. Evidence of past or
current pulmonary involvement may be absent.7 Bone involvement
may be manifest as nonspecific pain, lameness, and/or one or more
firm swellings associated with the appendicular or axial skeleton (ch.
31). Dogs with skin involvement may have ulcerated skin lesions that
drain serosanguineous fluid, or subcutaneous mass lesions.7

Neurologic signs resulting from fungal meningoencephalitis include
obtundation, blindness, nystagmus, absent menace reflex, ataxia,
postural reaction deficits, pacing, circling, cervical pain, tetraparesis,
and seizures (ch. 242).8,17,18 Ocular manifestations include
chorioretinitis, uveitis, and endophthalmitis (ch. 13).8,19,20
Although uncommon, liver or GI infection can lead to signs.7
Pericarditis may lead to signs of right-sided heart failure with ascites
and pleural effusion (ch. 235).7 Approximately 50% of cats with
coccidioidomycosis have skin lesions.11,12 Respiratory signs were
present in approximately one-third of affected cats, and lameness,
ocular abnormalities, and neurologic signs have been observed in
approximately 20% of cats.

specimen from the tarsus of a Dalmatian with

DIAGNOSIS (FIGURE 208.2)
HISTORY, PHYSICAL EXAMINATION,
LABORATORY RESULTS
Early diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis requires a high index of
suspicion based on consistent clinical findings and a history of travel
to or residence in an endemic region. Digging behavior or exposure
to disturbed soil should increase suspicion. The diagnosis is usually
confirmed with cytologic examination of aspirates or body fluids (ch.
85), serologic tests that detect antibodies to Coccidioides spp.,

histologic evaluation of biopsy specimens (Figure 208.1), or fungal
culture (ch. 184).
Laboratory testing of most affected dogs reveals mild nonregenerative anemia, mild neutrophilia, and hypoalbuminemia.8,21
About half of affected dogs and cats are hyperglobulinemic.8,11,12
Proteinuria, detected in 60% of dogs, can be severe (urine protein to
creatinine ratios as high as 9.5, reference range <0.5).22 Some dogs
have renal lesions typical of immune-complex glomerulonephritis at
necropsy; fewer had pyogranulomatous nephritis with intralesional
spherules (chs. 301, 302).22 Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis (ch.
109) in dogs with CNS involvement can reveal an increase in protein
concentration (generally <300 mg/dL [<3 g/L]; reference range <25
mg/dL [<0.25 g/L]), and increases in nucleated cell counts (usually
<50 cells/mcL; reference range <2 cells/mcL).8 The differential cell
count may show mixed or neutrophilic pleocytosis.

IMAGING
The most common radiographic finding in dogs with pulmonary
coccidioidomycosis is hilar lymphadenomegaly with mild to
moderate pulmonary interstitial infiltrates (Figure 208.3).8
Nodular interstitial, interstitial-alveolar, bronchointerstitial
infiltrates, and/or sternal lymphadenomegaly may also be
present.8,15 Dogs with pericarditis may have cardiomegaly and
pleural effusion, with hepatomegaly and decreased abdominal detail
(ch. 235).21 Thoracic computed tomography (CT) findings include
contrast-enhancing miliary nodular pulmonary lesions; single or
multifocal masses; tracheobronchial, sternal, or mediastinal
lymphadenopathy; focal regions of alveolar or peribronchial
infiltrates; lobar consolidation; pleural or mediastinal thickening and
rarely pleural effusion. Radiographs of affected bones reveal local
periosteal proliferation as well as osteolysis and soft-tissue swelling
(Figure 208.4).7,11 Echocardiography in dogs with pericarditis may
reveal thickening and mass lesions of the pericardium, pericardial
and pleural effusion, and evidence of cardiac tamponade (chs. 97

and 235).21 Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain in dogs
with CNS coccidioidomycosis may show focal hyperintense lesions
on T2-weighted images, isointense on T1-weighted images, and
possible contrast enhancement. Other findings include ventricular
dilation and/or evidence of meningeal enhancement. Lesions
characterized by bilaterally symmetric T2 hyperintensity throughout
both frontal lobes, caudate nuclei, and rostral internal capsule were
reported in 13 dogs from Arizona, 8 of which were Schnauzer breeds,
suggesting a possible breed predisposition.23

CYTOLOGY AND MICROBIOLOGICAL
TESTING
Cytology
Cytologic examination of tissue aspirates (chs. 83, 85, and 88) or
respiratory lavage specimens (ch. 93) usually reveal granulomatous
or pyogranulomatous inflammation. Less commonly, spherules are
visualized as deeply basophilic structures 8-70 microns in diameter
(Figure 208.5).

Microbiological Assay Tests
Serologic assays that detect antibodies to Coccidioides spp. are
valuable because cytologic and histologic examinations of specimens
are not sensitive for detecting the organism. Most laboratories screen
specimens with qualitative gel immunodiffusion assays for IgG or
IgM antibodies. Detection of IgM (tube precipitin) or IgG
(complement fixating) antibodies is reported, depending on the
antigen preparation used (ch. 184). In dogs, IgM is detectable
within 2 to 5 weeks of infection, and IgG appears after 8-12 weeks.16
Quantification of an IgG antibody response can then be performed
with quantitative immunodiffusion.14 False negative results are rare
in dogs with coccidioidomycosis from California but have been
described in dogs from Arizona.8,21,24,25 Antibody titers typically
range from 1:2 to 1:256; with a median of 1:32.8 Dogs with active

infection may have titers as low as 1:2 while healthy dogs in
hyperendemic Arizona areas have had titers as high as 1:16.14
Positive titers of 1:16 or lower should always be interpreted in the
context of other clinicopathologic results. In hyperendemic areas,
additional tests should be employed for diagnosis confirmation. A
serologic assay for Coccidioides antigen in urine has unacceptably
low sensitivity (≤20%) and is not recommended.26 A point-of-care
lateral flow assay (sona Coccidioides, IMMY, Norman, OK) has
demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity when compared with
gel immunodiffusion in both northern California and Arizona, and
may be a useful initial test for infection in dogs from endemic
regions; further validation is required.27,28

Culture
Coccidioides spp. can be isolated from clinical specimens on routine
fungal media. However, culturing Coccidioides spp. is a health
hazard for laboratory personnel and should only be performed in
suitably equipped locations. The laboratory should be warned of the
suspicion for a dimorphic fungal infection.

TREATMENT
GENERAL
Treatment generally consists of a combination of prolonged
antifungal drug therapy (ch. 141), supportive care, and in some
cases, surgery. Animals with pulmonary coccidioidomycosis may
respond well to monotherapy with fluconazole (5-10 mg/kg PO q12h)
or itraconazole (5 mg/kg PO q24h). Itraconazole is preferred for
animals with bone involvement and may be effective in dogs that fail
to respond to treatment with fluconazole, because it has greater
activity than fluconazole. Treatment with deoxycholate amphotericin
B or lipid-complexed amphotericin B is recommended either alone
or in combination with an azole antifungal for dogs with refractory or
disseminated disease (chs. 141 and 209). Voriconazole and
posaconazole have been used to treat refractory coccidioidomycosis
in people,1 and with excellent CNS penetration, could be considered

for treatment of refractory meningoencephalitis in dogs, if finances
permit its use.

ORGAN-SPECIFIC
Dogs with persistent osteomyelitis may require amputation for
infection control. Enucleation may be required in dogs with
endophthalmitis. Coccidioides pericarditis has been successfully
managed after subtotal pericardiectomy, epicardial excision, and
antifungal drug therapy. Perioperative mortality rate was reported as
24%.21 Dogs with pulmonary coccidioidomycosis may require oxygen
supplementation (ch. 123), drainage of thoracic effusions (ch. 92),
nutritional support (chs. 81 and 164), anti-inflammatory drugs (ch.
143), and intravenous fluid therapy (ch. 120). Concurrent
glucocorticoids and anti-seizure medications may be necessary in
dogs with CNS coccidioidomycosis (chs. 45, 227, 242, 247).
Topical prednisolone acetate solution and anti-glaucoma agents may
be required for dogs with ocular lesions.

FIGURE 208.4 Osteomyelitis caused by
Coccidioides spp. in a Shih-Tzu dog. There is a
predominantly lytic lesion of the left ilium (arrow).

FIGURE 208.5 Cytologic appearance of a
Coccidioides spp. spherule. A refractile spherule wall
is appreciated (arrow) surrounded by
pyogranulomatous inflammation. Endospores are
visualized within the spherule as granular material.

PROGNOSIS
Treatment duration ranges from 6 months to many years. In some
dogs, lifelong treatment is needed. In both dogs and cats, IgG titers
decrease with successful treatment, which should be continued until
lesions resolve and titers ≤1:2. Dogs with localized pulmonary
infection have the best prognosis.

PUBLIC HEALTH ASPECTS
Coccidioidomycosis is a serious infection in people. Individuals
involved in construction, agriculture, and excavation are at high risk

in endemic areas.1 African Americans, Filipinos, people with
acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), and women in the
third trimester of pregnancy are at risk for disseminated disease
(about 0.5% of infected people).
Dogs have been used as a sentinel for human exposure to
environmental sources of Coccidioides spp.29 Direct transmission as
a result of contact between infected pets and humans has not been
reported. However, inoculation coccidioidomycosis may follow bites
from animals with disseminated infections or after injury with a
contaminated instrument. If accidental inoculation occurs, people
should seek immediate medical attention. Prolonged fluconazole
prophylaxis is generally recommended with monitoring of
Coccidioides serologic titers and liver function tests. Necropsies
should be performed without delay with suitable protective clothing,
and the carcasses of animals that die from coccidioidomycosis should
immediately be incinerated, because conversion of the organism to a
mycelial form can occur after death. For the same reason, burial is
not recommended because of the potential for contamination of the
environment. Prophylaxis is also indicated after accidental
laboratory exposure.30

CLIENT INFORMATION
Coccidioidomycosis
• Coccidioidomycosis (“cocci” [pronounced ‘coxy’] or “Valley
Fever”) is a potentially life-threatening disease caused by a
fungus found in the soil. Valley Fever can occur in many
different mammals as well as humans. Animals acquire
infection when they inhale the fungus, which is found in soil.
It is not transmitted from one animal to another.
• The fungus lives in parts of the world where the soil is dry and
the summers are hot. In the United States, high-risk regions
are the south-central valley of California (but also north of Los
Angeles closer to the coast), and Arizona (especially Phoenix
and Tucson). The fungus can also be found in parts of Texas,
Nevada, and eastern Washington state as well as Mexico and
parts of Central and South America.
• Dogs are at highest risk for infection and disease in dogs can be
a sign that humans in the area are also being exposed.
Coccidioidomycosis is uncommon in cats, and most often seen
in Arizona. Risk factors for dogs include being a young adult
dog, and certain breeds (Dalmatians, Hungarian Viszlas,

Weimaraners, Norfolk Terriers, and Greyhounds) are
predisposed. Digging behavior also increases a dog’s risk of
contracting the disease. Soil disruption in the area (such as
due to construction or excavation, or following dust storms or
earthquakes) may also predispose animals and humans to
infection.
• Many animals and humans become infected, clear the
infection, and never show any signs of illness. In other
animals, the fungus multiplies slowly in the lungs, leading to
signs such as cough, decreased exercise tolerance, and
difficulty breathing. These signs can take weeks, months, or
even years after infection to become evident. In some dogs, the
fungus spreads (disseminates) further to infect other sites of
the body, including bones, the skin, brain, eye, heart, and less
commonly, other sites such as the liver, kidneys, and
gastrointestinal tract. This usually indicates a poor immune
response to the fungus. Dissemination occurs in
approximately 0.5% of infected humans, and African
Americans, Filipinos, AIDS patients, and women in the third
trimester of pregnancy are at risk for disseminated disease.
• Treatment involves an extended course of antifungal drugs
such as itraconazole or fluconazole. The duration of treatment
is usually at least 6 months and sometimes for life if disease is
disseminated. Treated animals must be re-evaluated on a
regular basis by a veterinarian in order to ensure toxicity from
these drugs is not occurring (as they have the potential to
cause liver function abnormalities). Initially, blood tests of
liver function should be performed on a monthly basis during
treatment. Compounded formulations of these drugs should
never be used.
• Dogs with severe disease may also require treatment with an
injectable drug known as amphotericin B. This is given in
hospital on a Monday-Wednesday-Friday basis together with
fluids, typically for at least the first month of treatment.
Amphotericin B can cause kidney failure and so careful
monitoring of kidney function by serial blood testing before
each treatment is needed.
• Once an animal has recovered from coccidioidomycosis,
treatment with steroids (like prednisone) or other

immunosuppressive drugs should be avoided if possible as it
may trigger a relapse.
• The decision to discontinue treatment is based on resolution of
clinical signs and monitoring blood tests (an antibody titer) to
the fungus. Ideally the titer should be 1:2 or lower before
treatment is stopped.
Jane E. Sykes (Davis, California)

and Histoplasmosis

ETIOLOGY
Blastomycosis is an invasive fungal infection caused by the cryptogenic
species Blastomyces dermatitidis and Blastomyces gilchristii, along with
Blastomyces helicus which causes “atypical” blastomycosis.
Histoplasmosis, also an enzootic invasive fungal infection, is caused by
Histoplasma capsulatum, which traditionally has been grouped into
serovars based on geographic location, host species, disease
manifestations, and yeast size. More recently, phylogenetic analysis has
shown at least 5 species worldwide with 2 cryptogenic species in the U.S.1
Proposed names for the species in the U.S. are Histoplasma

mississippiense (formerly NAm1) and Histoplasma ohioense (formerly
NAm2). Little is known regarding the clinical importance of the infecting
species and few cases caused by B. helicus have been reported.2 Except
where noted, this discussion collectively focuses on disease caused by
Blastomyces spp. or Histoplasma spp.
Blastomyces and Histoplasma are thermally dimorphic, existing as
sexually reproducing molds in the environment (<30°C [<86°F]) and
budding yeast within the body (>33°C [>91.4°F]). They are not
contagious; infection is primarily due to environmental exposure via
inhalation of aerosolized spores (conidia). Blastomyces grows,
sporulates, and aerosolizes best in moist, acidic, sandy soil enriched with
decaying plant matter exposed to wet followed by dry conditions.3 This
ecological niche is most often found in close proximity to waterways
(river, stream, lake).4,5 The ecological niche for Histoplasma is a soil rich
in nitrogen, with adequate moisture, often contaminated with bird or bat
droppings. Like Blastomyces, there is evidence that wet followed by dry
conditions are conducive to growth, sporulation, and aerosolization of
spores.

EPIDEMIOLOGY
While blastomycosis and histoplasmosis are sporadic, case clusters
appear in hyperenzootic areas. Blastomycosis is enzootic to a large area of
eastern North America. The highest prevalence in the U.S. is in the Great
Lakes (and St. Lawrence River) and midwestern regions, followed by the
mid-Atlantic, southeastern, and south central regions. In Canada, it is
most commonly diagnosed in provinces bordering the Great Lakes and in
Saskatchewan.6 In contrast, the small number of reported cases due to B.
helicus have been from Colorado, Montana, and California.2
Histoplasmosis is found worldwide. In the U.S., there is overlap with
the enzootic regions of blastomycosis. The highest prevalence of
histoplasmosis is on the western edge of its enzootic region (KS, OK, TX),
followed by the midwestern, southern, and southeastern U.S.
Blastomycosis is much more common in dogs than in cats. Animals of
any age or breed and that never leave home can be infected. Dogs at
greatest risk for blastomycosis have extensive outdoor exposure, are 2-5
years of age, weigh 20-30 kg, are sporting or working breeds, and live
near an area with fungal growth/sporulation (<400-500 meters [<1/41/3 mile] from waterways). Disease tends to occur in seasons when

outdoor activity is most likely (late spring to early fall).5-9 Male
predilection has been inconsistent in multiple studies.7,10-12
Histoplasmosis is more common in cats than blastomycosis is; about
one-third of affected cats live exclusively indoors, suggesting
Histoplasma is found in the home. The mean age of affected animals is 7
years for cats and 3 years for dogs.13-18 There is no consistent breed or
sex predilection.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Infection is a poorly understood interaction of inoculum size (number of
inhaled conidia), fungal pathogenicity, and host immune response. In
contrast to humans, infected dogs and cats are seemingly healthy at the
time of infection without obvious immunosuppression. With an
appropriate immune response, infection is eliminated with
transient/mild or subclinical disease.19 The protective immune response
involves recognition of fungal antigens (mannose-like structures and
beta-glucan) by innate pattern recognition receptors (Dectin-2, Dectin-3,
and Mannose receptor) driving an adaptive T-helper 1 (Th 1) and Th17
immune response.20 With inadequate immune responses, yeast persists
and causes organ dysfunction by stimulating chronic pyogranulomatous
inflammation. Disease can remain localized to the lung or disseminate via
lymphatics or hematogenously to essentially any organ in the body.

DIAGNOSIS
OVERVIEW
Anatomic Sites
The frequency of anatomic site involvement is shown in Figure 209.1.
Localized disease can occur in any organ, but disseminated disease is
most common. Multi-systemic inflammatory disease or fever
unresponsive to antibiotics should raise the suspicion for an invasive
fungal infection.

Blastomycosis
The respiratory tract (ch. 217) is affected in ≥90% of dogs with
blastomycosis while mammary tissue, nasal cavity, myocardium, and
urogenital systems are less often infected.21-23 Testicular involvement
was reported in 17% of intact male dogs.21 While less common, tissue
distribution of blastomycosis in cats was similar to dogs except that
central nervous system (CNS) involvement was relatively more common
(∼40%).24,25
Histoplasmosis
Disseminated disease was diagnosed in about 75% of cats and 60% of
dogs with histoplasmosis.13,16,18,26,27 Localized disease more often
involves the lung in cats (20%) and the gastrointestinal (GI) tract in dogs
(33%).13,16,18,26 In one study, 82% of cats (45/55) had ocular
involvement.27a Urogenital, nasal cavity, and cardiac involvement are
rare in both cats and dogs with histoplasmosis.13,16

CLINICAL SIGNS AND PHYSICAL
EXAMINATION
General
Vague clinical signs are common in dogs and cats infected with either
histoplasmosis or blastomycosis, including lethargy, fever, anorexia, and
weight loss. Respiratory signs include cough, exercise intolerance,
tachypnea, dyspnea, and abnormal lung sounds. Only about 10% of cats
and dogs with histoplasmosis exhibit cough even though about 50% have
respiratory involvement.13,18,27-29 Cough (ch. 34) is more common in
dogs with blastomycosis, being reported in >60%.9 Uncommonly, signs
of nasal or nasopharyngeal involvement occur, including stertor,
sneezing, epistaxis, nasal discharge, and facial deformity. Blastomycotic
rhinitis can extend into the CNS or orbit.30,31 CNS involvement can cause
multifocal or localized signs (chs. 241, 242).

Eyes

Ocular examination, including fundoscopy, should be performed in all
dogs and cats with suspected or proven fungal infections (ch. 13). Ocular
involvement can manifest as conjunctival hyperemia, scleral injection,
corneal opacity, ocular discharge, blindness, periocular swelling,
buphthalmia, exophthalmia, and blepharospasm. Retinal detachment,
chorioretinitis, anterior uveitis, and secondary glaucoma can occur
(Figure 209.2). With blastomycosis, the posterior and anterior
segments are often involved, but less commonly disease is isolated to 1
segment.32 With histoplasmosis, the posterior segment is most often
affected. Periocular involvement may be more common with
blastomycosis, whereas it is estimated to occur in 4% of cats with
histoplasmosis.33

Skin
Skin lesions can be found anywhere on the body and include cutaneous
and subcutaneous (SQ) nodules or masses often with ulceration and
draining tracts (ch. 12). In dogs, cutaneous lesions are more common
with blastomycosis. In cats, head and neck lesions are commonly seen
with histoplasmosis. Mucocutaneous lesions around the eyes and mouth
can be erythematous, ulcerated, and crusting, mimicking eosinophilic
plaques. Oral lesions can be ulcerated, slightly raised, or mass-like,
mimicking stomatitis/glossitis from other causes, or neoplasia.

FIGURE 209.2 A, Chorioretinitis of the tapetal
fundus in a cat with disseminated histoplasmosis. Note
the multiple areas of hyporeflectivity. B, Chorioretinitis
in a cat with histoplasmosis. The lesions of the nontapetal fundus are often grayish in color. C, Retinal
granuloma of the non-tapetal fundus in a dog with

blood vessel congestion, iridial swelling, and aqueous

Photos C and E courtesy Dr. Rachel Allbaugh.

Bone and Joint
Bone and joint involvement causes pain, lameness, and joint effusion
(ch. 31). These issues occur in about 20% of cats with histoplasmosis,
making it the most common cause of polyarthritis in enzootic
areas.16,18,27,29 About 50% of cats have multiple affected sites, but
carpi/tarsi and adjacent distal metaphyses are most common (Figure
209.3).34 Swelling, draining tracts, and ulceration of the overlying soft
tissues might accompany skeletal lesions. In dogs, bone/joint
involvement is more common with blastomycosis than with
histoplasmosis.

Lymph Nodes and Abdominal Viscera
Peripheral lymphadenomegaly is relatively common with both
blastomycosis and histoplasmosis. Abdominal organomegaly is palpable
in about 25% of cats and dogs with histoplasmosis.13,16 Large-bowel
diarrhea is reported in about 50% of dogs with histoplasmosis (ch.
263).13 GI histoplasmosis can also manifest as proctitis. GI involvement
is less common in cats with histoplasmosis and rare in dogs with
blastomycosis.

FIGURE 209.3 A, Bone involvement in a cat with
histoplasmosis. The distal radius and ulna are affected
with the lesion being primarily osteolytic (arrows). B,
Bone and joint involvement in a cat with histoplasmosis.
Proximal metatarsal and tarsal bones are affected
(arrows). The lesion is a mix of osteolysis and
osteoproduction.

CBC, SERUM BIOCHEMISTRY, AND
BIOMARKERS FOR INFLAMMATORY
BOWEL DISEASE (IBD)
Complete blood count (CBC) changes are generally nonspecific and
consistent with inflammation: neutrophilic leukocytosis (with or without
a left shift) and monocytosis.13,16,21,35 Occasionally, histoplasmosis is
associated with severe lymphocytosis (>15,000/mcL). Approximately
50% of dogs and cats with histoplasmosis are anemic, due to

inflammatory disease and/or bone marrow involvement.13,16 Mild to
moderate thrombocytopenia is common (13-48%).13,14,16,29 Due to bone
marrow infection in cats with histoplasmosis, 15% have leukopenia and
an equal percentage have leukocytosis, often with concurrent anemia or
thrombocytopenia. Common serum biochemistry changes include
hypoalbuminemia (negative acute phase protein and malnutrition) and
hyperglobulinemia (chronic inflammation).13,16,21,35 Hyperbilirubinemia
is found in approximately 50% of animals with histoplasmosis, often
accompanied by increased liver enzyme activity.13,16 Dogs with GI
histoplasmosis can have increases in serum biomarkers for IBD (antiporin IgA, anti-calprotectin IgA, anti-gliadin IgA).35a Due to the overlap
of clinical findings, GI histoplasmosis should be ruled out in enzootic
areas before initiating immunosuppressive treatment for IBD (chs. 262,
263).

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
Thoracic Radiographs
Findings on thoracic radiographs are highly variable and can be diffuse or
focal with any lung pattern (Figure 209.4). Mixed patterns are common
and can mimic feline bronchial disease, bacterial pneumonia (lobar
alveolar disease), primary or metastatic neoplasia (mass-like, large
nodules or lymphadenomegaly), heartworm pneumonitis (unstructured
interstitial, patchy alveolar, mixed), eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy
(unstructured interstitial, patchy alveolar, mixed), and other infectious
pneumonias. The “classic” diffuse interstitial pattern is only seen in about
50% of dogs and cats with pulmonary blastomycosis or
histoplasmosis.12,13,21,23,36 Other findings can include tracheobronchial
or sternal lymph node enlargement.12,13,21,36 Pleural effusion is
uncommon (7-12% of animals).12,21,23,36 Pneumothorax and
pneumomediastinum are rare, although one study reported that 16% of
dogs with pulmonary blastomycosis developed bullae.36

Brain and Spinal Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) –
Blastomycosis

Findings are consistent with fungal granuloma(s), meningoencephalitis,
ventriculitis, and myelitis (ch. 242).30,31,37 Lesions are typically hypoor isointense on T1-weighted sequences, hyperintense on T2-weighted
sequences, and contrast-enhancing.31,37 Granulomas can appear as 1 or
multiple intra- or extra-axial mass-like lesions with perilesional
edema.30,37 These can be an extension from fungal rhinitis. Meningitis is
seen as contrast enhancement of the meninges.30,31 Ventriculitis causes
dilation and periventricular/ependymal hyperintensity. Myelitis can
cause intramedullary mass-like lesion(s), ill-defined parenchymal
hyperintensity, and syringomyelia.31 Spinal disease can also be caused by
an extradural compressive fungal granuloma.38

Abdominal Ultrasonography (US) – Histoplasmosis
Findings on abdominal US examination in dogs and cats with
histoplasmosis overlap with other infiltrative diseases, e.g., neoplasia.
Scant to large volumes of free abdominal fluid are often present.28,39 The
liver may appear enlarged with variable changes to echotexture and
echogenicity.28 Splenic changes include splenomegaly, mottled
echotexture, and hypoechogenicity.17 These findings should raise
suspicion for disseminated histoplasmosis, especially in cats. Mesenteric
lymphadenopathy is common.39,40 GI tract changes most often include
circumferential increased wall thickness and a loss of normal layering,
changes indistinguishable from GI lymphoma or other infiltrative bowel
diseases39 (Figure 209.5). The descending colon and rectum are most
often involved.

DEFINITIVE DIAGNOSIS (FIGURE 209.6)
Cytopathology and Histopathology
Diagnosis can be confirmed by identification of yeast in tissue or body
fluid specimens (chs. 71 and 85). Specimen collection methods that carry
higher risk (lung aspirate) or require general anesthesia (bronchoalveolar
lavage [BAL, ch. 93]) should generally be reserved for dogs and cats
testing negative on non-invasive biomarkers (see below). For
blastomycosis, specimens with the highest diagnostic yield include

peripheral lymph node fine-needle aspirates (ch. 88) and swabs or
impressions of skin lesions (ch. 83).21,35 Rectal scrapings can assist with
cytologic confirmation of histoplasmosis in dogs (Figure 262.15).13
Other specimens that often yield yeasts include spleen, liver, bone
marrow, and blood smears (chs. 84 and 85). Yeasts can be missed on
histopathologic preparations using routine hematoxylin & eosin stains.
Special stains (Grocott methenamine silver [GMS] or periodic acid-Schiff
[PAS]) can aid histopathologic identification.
Blastomyces yeasts are primarily found extracellularly and are typically
surrounded by dense pyogranulomatous or suppurative inflammation.
Epithelioid and multinucleated giant cells are commonly found.41 Yeasts
are 8-15 micrometers in diameter with a thick, double-refractile wall and
single broad-based budding (Figure 209.7). In contrast, B. helicus
yeasts are variably sized and relatively smaller (average diameter of 4-5
micrometers) with multiple broad-based buds which form chains in
hyphal-like arrangements.2

FIGURE 209.6 Diagnostic and treatment algorithm
for animals with suspect blastomycosis or
histoplasmosis. EIA, Enzyme immunoassay.

FIGURE 209.7 Blastomyces yeasts (arrow) seen in a
cytologic specimen. Yeasts have thick, double-refractile
walls with broad-based budding. They are similar in size
to a neutrophil (arrowhead) and found primarily
extracellularly, densely surrounded by neutrophils and
macrophages. (Romanowsky-type stain.) Photo courtesy
Dr. Jim Meinkoth.
Histoplasma yeasts are 2-6 micrometers in diameter with a thin clear
rim and eccentrically placed crescent shaped nuclei. Nuclei are basophilic
staining with Romanowsky type stains (Wright’s or Diff-Quik).
Organisms are most often found in clusters within macrophages along
with pyogranulomatous inflammation (Figure 209.8).
Hemophagocytosis is common in specimens collected from
hemolymphatic tissues and should invoke a thorough search for
organisms.42 During antifungal treatment, yeasts become progressively
pyknotic, followed by decreasing stain uptake, finally disappearing
leaving clear vacuoles within macrophages.43

Fungal Culture
Isolation of Blastomyces or Histoplasma from tissue specimens or body
fluids, along with evidence of inflammation, confirms infection. Fungal
culture is rarely used clinically, primarily because it can take up to 30
days for a positive result, it can be a health hazard to laboratory

personnel, and its diagnostic sensitivity is low (12-67%).21,35,44
Susceptibility testing is not usually required because antifungal drug
resistance is rare.

Molecular Diagnostics
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests designed to detect Blastomyces
and Histoplasma DNA are commercially available, but their diagnostic
performance remains unknown (ch. 184). These might be most useful
when specimen volumes are small (e.g., cerebrospinal, joint, lung lavage,
or aqueous fluid specimens), and testing for multiple pathogens is
required. Genetic testing is required for differentiation of cryptogenic
species, although there is no clinical indication for this currently.

FIGURE 209.8 Histoplasma yeasts seen in a
cytologic specimen. Yeast are mostly found in clusters
within macrophages. The dark staining crescent shaped
nucleus is eccentrically placed and there is a thin clear
halo. (Romanowsky-type stain.) Photo courtesy Dr. Jim
Meinkoth.

Fungal Antigens
Tests detecting soluble fungal antigen (galactomannan [GM]) and
antifungal antibodies are commercially available and are laboratoryspecific (Tables 209.1 and 209.2). Fungal GM can be detected in body
fluids including urine, serum, cerebrospinal fluid and BAL fluid (ch.
184). Antigen testing likely has a lower sensitivity in pets with single
organ disease, e.g., false negative results are common with disease of the
GI tract, eyes, or bone/joints.34,45-47 As compared with serum, antigen
concentrations are generally higher in urine. As such, antigen detection
in urine is the biomarker with the highest overall diagnostic sensitivity.
Testing serum might be appropriate, since 5% of pets with blastomycosis
or histoplasmosis have detectable antigen in serum but not urine. A

positive antigen test suggests a fungal infection, but there is crossreactivity between some pathogenic fungi. As such, the diagnostic
specificity depends on the prevalence of other enzootic invasive fungal
infections. This is most important with Histoplasma and Blastomyces as
their cross-reactivity is high and there is considerable overlap of enzootic
regions. Lesser cross-reactivity is found with Coccidioides spp.,
Sporothrix spp., and Aspergillus spp. There is no cross-reactivity with
Cryptococcus spp.

Antifungal Antibodies
Antifungal immunodiffusion (ID) or enzyme immunoassay (EIA)
antibody tests are commercially available (ch. 184). EIA for antibodies
to the recombinant Blastomyces adhesin-1 repeat antigen (MiraVista
Laboratories, Indianapolis, IN) is preferred. It has higher diagnostic
sensitivity, while maintaining acceptable specificity.48 Indications for
antibody testing include suspect blastomycosis or histoplasmosis cases
with negative antigen testing. Moreover, antibody testing can help
differentiate between fungal species that cross-react on antigen assays
(blastomycosis vs. histoplasmosis).

TREATMENT
ANTIFUNGAL DRUGS (CH. 141)
Itraconazole, Fluconazole
Recommended antifungal drug dosages can be found in Table 209.3.
Additional information can be found in ch. 141. Often, the clinical
condition of dogs and cats worsens initially after starting antifungal drug
therapy, perhaps due to inflammation associated with dying fungal
organisms. This period generally resolves within a few days to a week.
Additional supportive care is often required during this time. Antifungal
treatment duration should be at least 6 months, though for disseminated
disease, a duration of more than 1 year is often required. Retrospective
studies have failed to clearly demonstrate superiority of either
itraconazole or fluconazole.13,16,22,28 Itraconazole remains the drug of
choice for mild or moderate (not immediately life-threatening) disease
because Blastomyces and Histoplasma are more susceptible to
itraconazole (lower minimum inhibitory concentrations). Moreover,
acquired resistance has only been demonstrated with fluconazole. There
is high animal-to-animal variability in itraconazole absorption, and
adverse effects (hepatoxicosis and ulcerative skin lesions, Figure 209.9)
are related to toxic blood drug concentrations.11,55 Drug monitoring
should be used to guide individualized dosing. Fluconazole is a
reasonable alternative when itraconazole is not well tolerated. It is
unclear if fluconazole is more effective than itraconazole for ocular, CNS,
or prostate/testicular involvement.
Amphotericin B
Amphotericin B is the drug of choice for severe, life-threatening disease
because it is fungicidal and reaches therapeutic drug concentrations very
quickly. Even dosages well below the recommended maximal cumulative
dose can be beneficial. Lipid or liposomal formulations are preferred due
to decreased nephrotoxicosis. SQ administration protocols of the original
(deoxycholate) formulation have been published, might be less expensive,
but can be associated with SQ abscesses.56 Amphotericin B should be
followed by azole therapy.

FIGURE 209.9 Ulcerative skin lesions on the neck of
a dog due to itraconazole-induced vasculitis. These are
related to toxic itraconazole blood concentrations.
Voriconazole, Posaconazole, Terbinafine

Voriconazole and posaconazole are used for salvage therapy, defined as
progressive disease after 2-3 months of treatment with itraconazole.
Terbinafine (30-40 mg/kg/day) in addition to azole treatment might also
be considered as a less expensive salvage therapy option, but there is little
information regarding its use for invasive fungal infections in dogs or
cats.

GLUCOCORTICOIDS
Retrospective studies have failed to demonstrate a survival benefit of
glucocorticoids.9,13,16,57 A short course of glucocorticoids should be
considered with ocular or CNS involvement, severe respiratory disease,
or anytime amphotericin B is administered. In addition, glucocorticoids
should be considered with persistent tracheobronchial lymphadenopathy,
which can cause a chronic cough in dogs, even after all other signs of
disease have resolved. In general, glucocorticoids should be administered
at anti-inflammatory doses (0.25-1 mg/kg/day prednisolone or
equivalent), concurrently with antifungal drug, for as short of duration as
possible (chs. 143, 227).

SUPPLEMENTAL THERAPIES
Disease and thus individualized treatment is highly variable from animal
to animal. Oxygen supplementation is often indicated (ch. 123). Animals
should be closely examined and monitored for pain. Bone/joint
involvement is exceptionally painful and multi-modal analgesia is
indicated (ch. 6). Blood transfusion(s) might be required for anemia (ch.
124). Uveitis and secondary glaucoma should be treated intensively (ch.
13). If there is no chance to salvage vision, enucleation should be
considered. With testicular involvement, neutering should be considered,
once the patient is sufficiently stable for general anesthesia. Systemic
hypertension, bradycardia, and deteriorating neurologic status are
suggestive of intracranial hypertension, which should be treated with
glucocorticoids and mannitol or hypertonic saline (ch. 125). An
esophagostomy or gastrostomy feeding tube can augment nutritional
support and simplify antifungal medication administration (ch. 81).

TREATMENT MONITORING AND SAFELY
DISCONTINUING TREATMENT
Disease relapse, after discontinuation of antifungal drug, is reported in
approximately 20% of dogs with blastomycosis and 20-40% of cats and
dogs with histoplasmosis.11,13,21,22,26,28,58 A treatment duration that is
too short increases the chance for relapse, while a duration that is
excessively long increases cost and chance for drug adverse effects. The
following criteria should be met before discontinuing antifungal
treatment: 1) minimum of 6 months treatment duration, 2) treatment for
1 month past resolution of clinical signs and physical examination
abnormalities, 3) resolution or minimal static disease on thoracic
radiographs (or other imaging studies), and 4) negative or very low
antigen concentration in urine (Figure 209.6). Repeat physical
examinations, including fundic examinations (ch. 13), are vital. New or
active retinal lesions suggest progressive or ongoing disease, even when
all other findings suggest remission. New skin lesions due to azole
toxicosis can be easily confused with progressive disease. Therapeutic
drug monitoring and repeated cytologic examination for viable yeasts are
informative. Repeat thoracic radiographs, abdominal US examination, or
other imaging studies every 3 months should also be considered.
Residual focal unstructured interstitial lung disease can persist after
remission and is likely due to pulmonary scarring.50
Urine antigen testing every 3 months during treatment, then annually
thereafter, is recommended. An increase in antigen concentration during,
or after, treatment is suggestive of progressive disease or relapse,
respectively.50,53 In cats, antifungal treatment should continue until no
antigen is detected in urine.53 In dogs, discontinuation can be considered
with very low antigen concentration in urine (≤0.4 ng/mL) documented
on 2 consecutive rechecks, if all other criteria for remission have been
met.

PROGNOSIS
Reported survival rates for blastomycosis and histoplasmosis are 8790%, 75%, and 65-69% to hospital discharge, 1-2 months and 6 months
after diagnosis, respectively.9,13,16 Negative prognostic indicators for
both diseases include CNS involvement and more severe respiratory

disease.9,11,13,16 A need for oxygen supplementation, the presence of
abnormal lung sounds, dyspnea, and a greater percentage of total lung or
primary lung lobe affected (not specific lung pattern) on thoracic
radiographs are negative prognostic indicators.9,13,16 For histoplasmosis,
indicators of bone marrow and liver involvement are also negative
prognosticators.13,16 Examples include cytopenias, fungemia, and
hyperbilirubinemia. Antigen concentration in urine at the time of
diagnosis is prognostic in dogs with blastomycosis.9 In one study, all
dogs with antigen concentration <5.0 ng/mL were alive at 6 months,
compared with only 59% with ≥5.0 ng/mL. A retrospective study in cats
with histoplasmosis failed to demonstrate any prognostic value of antigen
concentration in urine at the time of diagnosis.59

CLIENT INFORMATION
Blastomycosis and Histoplasmosis
Blastomycosis and histoplasmosis are fungal infections affecting
primarily dogs and cats. Within the U.S. and Canada, most infections
occur east of the Rocky Mountains, but infections can occur sporadically
anywhere. Infection ranges from life-threatening to mild and can affect
any organ, commonly including the lung, eyes, skin, lymph nodes,
gastrointestinal tract, and bones/joints. Clinical signs can be vague
(decreased appetite, decreased activity level, weight loss, and fever) or

more specific (lameness, skin lesions, vision loss, trouble breathing,
coughing, or diarrhea).
These infections are not contagious to other animals or humans but
occur when a dog or cat inhales spores from the environment. Living next
to a body of water (river, stream, lake) is a risk factor for blastomycosis.
Exposure to soil contaminated with bird or bat feces is a risk factor for
histoplasmosis. Surprisingly, even cats that never leave the house are at
risk, suggesting that these fungi can be found within the home. Other
animals and humans sharing the same environment might also be
exposed, and it is common for multiple pets from the same household to
become infected over time. If other animals are showing signs of illness,
or if you have concerns, it is important to talk with your veterinarian.
Early diagnosis can help with a successful treatment outcome. If you have
concerns for yourself, or other people in the household, you should talk
with your physician.
Treatment includes antifungal medication. This might be given orally
at home or intravenously in the hospital, depending on the severity of
illness. Other treatments might also be recommended based on the
severity of illness and the location of infection within the body.
Treatment duration is for at least 6 months and generally longer. It is
important to give the antifungal medications as prescribed as this
provides the best chance for a full recovery. Many animals get worse over
the first few weeks before starting to get better. Improvements are slow
initially, but most animals are noticeably improved at 1 month and even
better at 2 months. All medications have potential side-effects, and this is
true for antifungal medications. Close monitoring for medication sideeffects and for response during treatment is vital. This requires veterinary
visits for repeat physical examinations, blood work, and potentially other
testing.
Blastomycosis and histoplasmosis are difficult to completely clear and
return of the infection (relapse) after stopping antifungal medication
happens in approximately 1 out of 5 animals. After treatment, it is
important to continue to watch for sign of illness and talk with your
veterinarian if you have any concerns. Repeat veterinary visits including
physical examination, and potentially other testing, are also important to
help detect a relapse early. Like the initial infection, relapses are treated
with antifungal medication.
Andrew Hanzlicek (Indianapolis, Indiana)

ETIOLOGY AND EPIDEMIOLOGY
DESCRIPTION

The genus Aspergillus, comprised of ∼450 species, is subdivided into
6 subgenera, 27 sections and 87 series.1 These aerobic ubiquitous
saprophytic fungi grow in organic soil matter, produce abundant
conidia that become airborne after disturbance, and circulate in
indoor and outdoor air. Healthy individuals inhale conidia daily, but
disease only occurs when immune defenses are overwhelmed (after
inhalation of a massive environmental burden of conidia) or from
primary or secondary dysfunction of the immune system.2 Fungal
rhinosinusitis (FRS), the most common focal form of aspergillosis in
dogs and cats, is usually noninvasive when confined to the nasal
cavity and sinuses (sinonasal aspergillosis [SNA]). FRS involving the
orbit (sino-orbital aspergillosis [SOA]) is invasive and occurs almost
exclusively in cats.

EPIDEMIOLOGY
Etiology
SNA, usually caused by Aspergillus fumigatus (subgenus Fumigati),
occurs worldwide. Aspergillus niger complex, Aspergillus flavus,
and Aspergillus nidulans occasionally cause infection in dogs.3
Cryptic species of A. fumigatus (e.g., Aspergillus lentulus), with high
genetic and morphologic similarity, also cause SNA in cats.4 SOA is
caused by cryptic species of Aspergillus viridinutans in subgenus
Fumigati, especially Aspergillus felis and Aspergillus udagawae.5-7

Signalment
Dog breeds overrepresented for SNA include dolichocephalic large
breeds (e.g., Golden/Labrador Retrievers, German/Belgian Shepherd
Dogs, Rottweilers, Malamutes and Rough/Border Collies), as well as
Bull Terriers, Staffordshire Terriers and Miniature Schnauzers.8-15
Brachycephalic pure-breed cats are overrepresented for FRS,
including Persians and related breeds (Himalayans,
Exotic/Scottish/British Shorthairs and Ragdolls).16 The median age
at diagnosis is 5 to 7 years, but animals of any age can be affected.

There is slight male predisposition in dogs but not in cats. Systemic
immunodeficiency rarely results in SNA in dogs. In cats with FRS,
feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV, ch. 198) and feline leukemia
virus (FeLV, ch. 199) test results are usually negative, but diabetes
mellitus may be a risk factor (ch. 292).4 Local sinonasal cavity
disease (e.g., facial trauma, nasal neoplasia, plant foreign bodies) is
occasionally identified in dogs and cats with SNA.

PATHOGENESIS
SINONASAL ASPERGILLOSIS (SNA)
Inhaled conidia that are not trapped and removed by mucociliary
defenses germinate in favorable temperatures and humidity to form
plaques of hyphae that adhere to sinonasal mucosa. Canine SNA and
most cases of feline SNA are noninvasive, i.e., hyphae do not invade
the sinonasal epithelium. Aspergillus conidia are coated with
hydrophobin proteins that facilitate mucosal adherence and mask
pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) from recognition
by pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) on innate immune cells.2
Dendritic cells express different families of PRRs that recognize
different exposed fungal epitopes, especially after germination. PRRs
include the C-type lectin receptors (e.g., dectin-1 and -2 that
recognize beta-1-3 glucan and galactomannan, respectively), toll-like
receptors, NOD-like receptors and pentraxin 3. The NADPH oxidase
complex, another important innate host defense mechanism, is
activated by PRRs that (i) generate reactive oxygen species, which
facilitate neutrophil-mediated hyphal damage and monocyte or
macrophage dependent phagocytosis; and (ii) facilitates the
formation of neutrophil extracellular traps, where neutrophils
release their DNA to form traps coated with antimicrobial peptides.2
After PAMP recognition, PRRs mediate phagocytosis and,
depending on the cytokines they produce, induce differentiation of
naïve CD4+ T cells into specific T helper cells (Th1, Th2, Th9 and
Th17 cells), cytotoxic lymphocytes, regulatory (Treg), and type 1
regulatory T cells (Tr1).17 Which Th cell responses are optimal for
defense against Aspergillus is unclear. Absence of Th1 or Th17 cells

increases susceptibility to invasive fungal infection. Cytokine
profiling of dogs with SNA is consistent with a Th1 response and
upregulation of interleukin-10, which may limit local tissue
destruction but paradoxically could impede clearance of infection.1820

There is also evidence of a Th17-driven uncontrolled
inflammatory response in canine SNA that could counteract host
efforts to clear infection through Th1-directed immunity.21
In dogs and most infected cats, SNA hyphae do not invade tissue
or bone. The nasal turbinate and paranasal bone lysis are associated
with the inflammatory response to infection.22 Also, Aspergillus
synthesises enzymes (e.g., protease, phospholipase) and toxic
secondary metabolites, which can cause tissue destruction.23

SINO-ORBITAL ASPERGILLOSIS (SOA)
SOA infections can extend from the sinonasal cavity to the orbit,
causing lysis of orbital and/or frontal sinus bones.24 Hyphae first
invade sinonasal mucosa, then form lobulated retrobulbar
granulomas that displace the globe dorsolaterally, and can expand
ventrally into the caudal oral cavity (ch. 13).25 Eventually, invasion
of the ipsilateral optic nerve, optic chiasm, and/or central nervous
system occurs. Hematogenous dissemination is rare.26
