CLINICAL FEATURES
SINONASAL ASPERGILLOSIS (SNA)
SNA is characterized by chronic serous to mucopurulent nasal
discharge, sneezing, reverse sneezing or stertor, crusting or
ulceration of the nasal planum, and/or mild mandibular
lymphadenomegaly. In severe disease, nasal discharge may be
bilateral with intermittent epistaxis. Dogs are usually afebrile and
cats are variably febrile. In dogs, other signs include hyperkeratosis
or depigmentation of the nasal planum (Figure 210.1), evidence of
muzzle pain exhibited as pawing at the face or detected on palpation,
lethargy, and inappetence. Rarely, seizures (ch. 45) can occur in
dogs after cribriform plate erosion and meningeal inflammation.

SINO-ORBITAL ASPERGILLOSIS (SOA)
SOA is usually characterized by unilateral exophthalmos with
prolapse and inflammation of the nictating membrane. Central
corneal ulceration, blepharospasm, and/or conjunctival discharge
are common (Figure 210.1). Nasal signs may be subtle or not
present but mentioned on history. The opened mouth should be
assessed for swelling in the pterygopalatine fossa adjacent the last
molar tooth (ch. 258). This area can ulcerate, exposing a white to
yellow orbital granuloma or a purulent discharge (Figure 210.1).
Hard palate ulceration can occur. Fungal invasion of the maxillary
subcutaneous tissues can cause mild to severe facial swellings that
may also ulcerate. Fever and mandibular lymphadenomegaly may be
present. In advanced disease, vision loss occurs from severe
ulcerative keratitis or infiltration of the optic nerve and/or optic
chiasm.25,27,28 Exophthalmos can become bilateral and seizures or
hyperesthesia may occur.25,29

DIAGNOSIS
ROUTINE LABORATORY ASSESSMENT

Routine testing results are either unremarkable or show non-specific
changes. The mild to marked serum hyperglobulinemia in pets with
SOA are the exception.25,27 Serologic titers for Aspergillus-specific
IgG are not reliable as a stand-alone test despite excellent specificity,
since the sensitivity is variable.16,30,31 Definitive diagnosis requires
cytological or histological detection of fungal hyphae in plaques
attached to the sinonasal mucosa (SNA), or detection of hyphae
invading sinonasal mucosa or paranasal tissues (SOA) (chs. 83, 85,
184).

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
Sinonasal Aspergillosis
Computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
scans (ch. 112) should be performed before rhinoscopy (ch. 89) to
prevent imaging artefacts from iatrogenic hemorrhage. Common
findings in SNA include mild to severe cavitated nasal turbinate lysis,
increased nasal cavity or intra-sinus soft-tissue opacity due to fluid
accumulation or fungal plaques, a thickened rim of mucosa adjacent
the nasal bones, maxillary recess and/or frontal bone, frontal bone
hyperostosis, and mandibular or retropharyngeal lymph node
enlargement9,10,24,32 (Figure 210.2). Lysis of the cribriform plate,
palatine, orbital and frontal bones may also be present.

Sino-orbital Aspergillosis
CT and MRI findings in SOA usually include a ventromedial orbital
mass and mild to severe sinonasal cavity changes similar to SNA but
may include a mass effect. On CT, orbital fungal granulomas show
heterogeneous contrast enhancement with lobulated
hypoattenuating foci and peripheral rim enhancement.24,29,33
Paranasal maxillary soft-tissue involvement is common (Figure
210.2). Retrobulbar masses are T1- and T2-hyperintense on MRI,
with heterogeneous contrast enhancement.

ENDOSCOPY
Nasopharyngoscopy is performed first using a flexible endoscope and
is most useful in cats to identify choanal and nasopharyngeal fungal
plaques or granulomas (ch. 89). Antegrade rigid rhinoscopy is then
performed to evaluate the nasal cavity (chs. 89, 213). In dogs, a
small flexible endoscope can be used to also enter the frontal sinuses
via the nasofrontal opening. If unsuccessful, sinus trephination or
sinusotomy may be required for endoscopic diagnosis in cases where
imaging findings suggest sinus involvement alone. Typical
endoscopic findings include a cavernous nasal cavity from turbinate
destruction, mucopurulent secretions, and fungal colonies/plaques
adherent to the mucosa (Video 210.1

). Colony color depends on

the species and amount of sporulation. Colonies of A. fumigatus are
initially white then grey-green after sporulation (Figure 210.2).

CYTOLOGY AND HISTOLOGY
Sinonasal Aspergillosis (SNA)
In dogs, cytologic examination of endoscopic brush specimens from
suspected nasal lesions or of squash preparations of biopsied plaques
correctly identified fungal hyphae in 93 and 100% of cases,
respectively, while hyphae were identified in only 20% of cases using
blind nasal swabs.12 Histopathologic examination of biopsy
specimens has high sensitivity for diagnosis if fungal plaques are
sampled but misdiagnosis can occur if only mucosa without adherent
fungal plaques, non-fungal exudates or necrotic debris are sampled.
Characteristic findings in SNA are mats of branching, septate fungal
hyphae attached to nasal or sinus mucosa or within luminal
exudates, in a background of lymphoplasmacytic and/or neutrophilic
inflammation.

FIGURE 210.2 Sinonasal fungal plaques attached
to the nasal mucosa in a dog (A) and cat (C) with
sinonasal aspergillosis caused by Aspergillus
fumigatus. B, Close-up view of A, Fungal colonies
are white before sporulation and grey-green after
sporulation. Sagittal bone-window CT of a dog with
unilateral left sinonasal aspergillosis, showing
normal structure of the turbinates and frontal sinus
on the right side (D), turbinate lysis and thickened
mucosa, including a thickened rim of soft tissue in
the left frontal sinus (E).

Sino-orbital Aspergillosis (SOA)
Fungal hyphae can usually be detected on cytologic examination of
fine-needle aspirates (FNA) or histopathologic evaluation of orbital
masses biopsied via the oral cavity or guided by CT or ultrasound
(chs. 83, 85). Misdiagnosis may occur if only the periphery of
masses is biopsied since hyphae are confined to central necrotic foci,
surrounded by zones of pleomorphic inflammatory cells (e.g.,
neutrophils, eosinophils, macrophages, lymphocytes).25,27,29 There
may be invasion of periglobar tissues, e.g., nictitating membrane,

eyelid, optic nerve and optic chiasm.25,27,34 Mycotic invasion of
sinus or nasal mucosa may also be evident. Histological submissions
should include requests for fungal stains (e.g., Grocott’s
methenamine silver or periodic acid-Schiff). In cases where fungal
hyphae are observed but fungal culture was negative or not
requested, panfungal polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of DNA
extracted from formalin-fixed tissues can be performed for
identification (ch. 184).35

FUNGAL CULTURE AND
IDENTIFICATION
Typically, fungi that cause SNA or SOA are readily grown on routine
laboratory media (e.g., malt extract agar or Sabouraud’s dextrose
agar; incubated at 37°C) with visible growth within 4 days.36 In one
study, the sensitivity of fungal culture for diagnosis of canine SNA
was 88% for fungal plaques, 75% for nasal mucosal biopsies from the
distal nasal cavity, and 19% for blind nasal swab specimens. The
specificity of all three methods was 100%.36 Identification of
Aspergillus species using macroscopic and microscopic
morphological features is inaccurate. Definitive identification
requires molecular panfungal PCR assays using DNA extracts of
cultured isolates and amplification of a region of the ribosomal DNA
gene complex. For some species a second identification target is
necessary (e.g., beta-tubulin).1 Matrix-assisted laser desorption
ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry (ch. 184)
is an alternative method for identifying Aspergillus isolates but is
limited by strain availability in commercial libraries.

TREATMENTS AND PROGNOSES
CANINE SINONASAL ASPERGILLOSIS
Mechanical Debridement

Prior to topical application of an antifungal imidazole, mechanical
debridement of all visible fungal plaques using endoscopic biopsy
forceps and copious saline irrigation is required (Video 210.2

). If

plaques within the frontal sinuses cannot be debrided via antegrade
rhinoscopy, frontal sinus trephination or sinusotomy and curettage
is indicated. Among dogs treated with topical antifungal azole
infusions, complete debridement of fungal plaques is associated with
a higher first treatment success rate compared to partial
debridement.15
Topical Treatment Protocols
There have been numerous protocols for topical administration of
antifungal imidazoles after fungal plaque debridement. Inevitable
refinements have minimized the invasiveness, reduced overall
anaesthesia time, and optimized contact of the drug with nasal cavity
and sinus mucosa without sacrificing overall treatment
success.8,11,13,14,30,37,38 Drug formulations used include solutions of
clotrimazole (1%) or enilconazole (1 or 2%) and creams (1%
clotrimazole or bifonazole).
One retrospective study compared two minimally invasive
enilconazole infusion protocols.15 A group of 24 dogs was treated
using a 1-hour infusion of 2% enilconazole via an infusion catheter
placed in the affected sinus (endoscopically) or caudal nasal cavity
(blindly), with 90° rotation of the dog every 15 minutes to maximize
drug contact, followed by instillation of 1% bifonazole cream into the
sinus(es). A second group of 24 dogs was treated with a 2%
enilconazole infusion for 15 minutes without rotation or bifonazole
cream administration. The simplified protocol was quicker (median
92 minutes compared to 201 minutes) and overall treatment success
was 96% for both groups. Other studies describe sinonasal
administration of 1% clotrimazole cream (via endoscopic guidance or
trephination) after fungal plaque debridement with overall successes
of 94 and 100%, respectively.13,39 In one of these, sinus irrigation
and clotrimazole infusion was performed using a minimally invasive
endoscopic approach to place a rigid urinary catheter over a

guidewire (“Seldinger technique”) in the frontal sinus, replacing the
need for trephination of endoscopically inaccessible sinuses.13
Topical Treatment Complications
Since it can cause severe mucosal edema and airway obstruction, use
of propylene glycol in topical imidazole preparations is
contraindicated. This side-effect is avoided by using polyethylene
glycol (PEG).40 Enilconazole has occasionally been associated with
mucosal hypertrophy (“blebs”) or intranasal strictures.41 In dogs
with lysis of the cribriform plate or floor of a frontal sinus, direct
contact with a topical imidazole drug or its hyperosmolar carrier
(e.g., PEG) could cause seizures or death. The frequency of this
complication is unknown. Treatment with 1% clotrimazole solution
and/or cream, or 1% enilconazole solution has been performed in
small numbers of dogs with such defects without
complications.11,13,14,38 The most common and least worrisome
complication in a retrospective case series of SNA treated dogs using
sinus trephination, debridement, and topical 1% clotrimazole cream
was swelling at the trephination site.39
Topical Treatment Response
Therapeutic efficacy can only be determined by repeat endoscopic
evaluation, usually within 2 to 4 weeks of treatment (Video 210.2
). CT is unreliable since bony changes are persistent. Serial
serological monitoring is not useful, since antibodies persist for
months to years after cure.42 The recommendation, if any fungal
plaques are visualized at recheck, is repeat debridement and topical
azole infusion followed by endoscopic evaluation 2 to 4 weeks later.
First treatment success using this protocol has ranged from 17-68%,
with a median of two treatments required for cure, and overall
success rates of 94-100%.13,15,39
Systemic Antifungal Therapy
Systemic antifungals, including triazoles (itraconazole, posaconazole
or voriconazole) and/or terbinafine have been used as alternative

therapies in some dogs with cribriform plate defects,43 dogs that
have failed topical imidazole therapy,44 or as an adjunct to topical
treatment (ch. 141).15,39 All azole antifungals block synthesis of
ergosterol, a critical component of the fungal cell wall, through
inhibition of 14-alpha-demethylase. Systemic antifungals are not
recommended as an initial or sole therapy. Use of these drugs should
not replace endoscopic plaque debridement. Whether additional
systemic antifungal drug treatment improves outcome versus topical
therapy alone is unknown. Fluconazole is not recommended for
treatment of SNA because it has minimal activity against molds.
Since the target of therapy in SNA is superficial sinonasal fungal
plaques, much higher drug concentrations can be achieved using
topical therapy than systemic therapy. Although azole resistance is
increasing among environmental and human clinical isolates of A.
fumigatus in association with use of agricultural fungicides, it
appears uncommon in canine SNA.45
Long Term Prognosis
In one study, 3/27 dogs (11%) had confirmed relapse or reinfection, 2
to 36 months after cure with topical 1% or 2% enilconazole
infusions.8 In two other studies, 3 of 15 (20%) and 5 of 38 (13%) dogs
cured after debridement and 1% clotrimazole infusions were
diagnosed with recurrent SNA 5 to 30 months later.39,42 Persistent
serous or mucopurulent nasal discharge is common after mycological
cure, with 52% of dogs affected in one study. It is usually caused by
severe turbinate destruction with recurrent bacterial rhinosinusitis.8

FELINE FUNGAL RHINOSINUSITIS
Treatment of feline SNA is similar to dogs: endoscopic debridement
and topical imidazole infusion.25,28,46,47 Since frontal sinuses
cannot be entered via antegrade rhinoscopy, if involved, trephination
or sinusotomy and curettage is indicated. Imidazole solutions may be
better tolerated than depot cream preparations, since the latter can
cause nasal obstruction and cats are reluctant to open-mouth

breathe. Occasionally, feline SNA can be invasive when caused by
cryptic species such as A. felis.25 If fungal hyphae are identified
invading mucosa on histologic examination of nasal biopsies, adjunct
systemic treatment, as for cats with SOA, is recommended.4 Overall,
the prognosis for feline SNA appears similar to canine SNA, but data
are limited.
Cats with SOA require prolonged treatment (≥6 months) with
systemic antifungal drugs. The prognosis for cure of SOA with
treatment is guarded to poor. Comprehensive orbital debridement
with enucleation has not improved outcomes.25 Antifungal
susceptibility testing is indicated, since intrinsic resistance is
common among cryptic Aspergillus species. Empirical therapy can
be commenced with posaconazole and terbinafine.4 Itraconazole is
not recommended since causative agents (e.g., A. felis) typically have
low minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of posaconazole,
whereas MICs of itraconazole and voriconazole are often high.48
Also, voriconazole has been associated with severe adverse effects in
cats (e.g., paraplegia, blindness, anorexia).25,29,49 Posaconazole is
well tolerated and hepatotoxicosis is uncommon.25,50 Therapeutic
drug monitoring of trough plasma posaconazole concentrations can
be useful to determine whether MICs are being reached.26
Amphotericin B (AMB) has been used successfully in susceptible
isolates, usually in combination with posaconazole, or with
posaconazole and terbinafine.25,34 Since MICs of AMB for infecting
Aspergillus species are variable, empirical therapy is not
recommended. Caspofungin, a fungistatic echinocandin, inhibits
synthesis of the essential fungal cell wall component beta-(1,3)-D
glucan and it has also been used successfully with posaconazole or
posaconazole/terbinafine.25,51 It is well-tolerated after intravenous
administration.52

ETIOLOGY
Disseminated opportunistic fungal infections such as aspergillosis,
penicilliosis, and infections due to fungi such as Rasamsonia,
Paecilomyces, and Scedosporium are uncommon diseases of dogs
and are rare in cats. However, when such infections occur, they can

be severe, difficult to treat, and carry grave prognoses. Medically
important fungal organisms are generally part of the Ascomycota or
Basidiomycota phyla, although some species within the
Mucoromycota phylum have been diagnosed in people. Ascomycota
comprise the largest phylum of fungi and derive their name from
ascus, referring to a sac-like structure, in which spores are produced
and stored. The ascomycetes include Aspergillus, Candida, and
dimorphic fungi such as Histoplasma (ch. 209), Blastomyces (ch.
209), and Coccidioides (ch. 208).
Disseminated invasive aspergillosis (DIA) refers to a multisystemic
infection of various Aspergillus species (typically Aspergillus
deflectus, Aspergillus terreus, Aspergillus fumigatus or Aspergillus
niger) in the Circumdati subgenus and is the most often diagnosed
and best characterized systemic opportunistic fungal infection in
dogs. DIA can result in a variety of clinical signs depending on the
site of infection. Typical body sites include the brain, eye, vertebrae,
intervertebral discs, kidneys, liver, spleen, and lymph nodes. Less
common sites include lung, long bones, and pancreas. Rasamsonia
spp., a genus within the Trichocomaceae family, and part of the
Eurotiales order to which Aspergillus also belongs, has been
identified as an opportunistic mold. Disease caused by this pathogen
has clinical characteristics similar to those of Aspergillus
infections.1-3 Talaromyces and Scedosporium spp. have also been
reported to result in osteomyelitis (ch. 31) and polyarthritis (chs.
32, 177) in dogs.4-6

EPIDEMIOLOGY
Most opportunistic fungal infections are caused by saprotrophic
molds (fungi which primarily feed on decaying organic matter) that
animals encounter in their environments. Infectious propagules (like
conidia for Aspergillus spp.) can be inhaled and deposited in alveoli
where they are either cleared by innate host immunity or germinate
and disseminate via the circulatory system to distant sites. Less
often, organisms might enter the animal’s body via the skin, or
gastrointestinal (GI) tract.7

Fungal organisms have evolved several features that allow them to
invade and persist in mammalian hosts, e.g., many fungi that cause
opportunistic infections exhibit thermotolerance—the ability to
survive and reproduce at body temperature, generally above 98.6°F
(37°C). This temperature is beyond the normal range of
environmental fungi, which have mostly adapted to temperatures
between 12° and 30°C (54°F to 86°F). Invasive fungal organisms also
have developed the ability to penetrate or circumvent host barriers,
evade the host immune system, and utilize host tissue as food. In
some instances, traits that permit host invasion also contribute to
virulence—for example, secretion of lipases and phospholipase by
Aspergillus spp. allows for tissue destruction and permits growth.
Despite the plethora of identified fungal organisms, few have been
shown to cause disease in humans or veterinary patients.
A. deflectus and A. terreus are most often implicated in DIA, as
opposed to sinonasal or sino-orbital disease in dogs or cats where A.
fumigatus and A. felis are typically diagnosed (ch. 210). Genetic
susceptibility linked to an uncharacterized immunodeficiency (ch.
180) likely plays a role in the development of DIA in breeds such as
the German Shepherd Dog and Rhodesian Ridgeback, which are at
increased risk of infection.8,9 Similarly, several case reports describe
other opportunistic mold infections in German Shepherd Dogs.13,10,11 Disseminated aspergillosis is rare in cats and has typically
been associated with immunosuppression due to chemotherapy (ch.
321) or concurrent viral infection (chs. 198, 199). Invasion and
distant spread of A. felis has been described in a single cat with sinoorbital disease.12 Following dissemination to distant body sites,
pathogen recognition occurs due to toll-like receptor-2 expression by
tissue macrophages and dendritic cells. These cells promote a Thelper 1 response leading to production of inflammatory cytokines,
e.g., interleukin (IL)-18, IL-12, tumor necrosis factor-alpha, or
interferon-gamma, and recruitment of neutrophils and
macrophages. Animals that mount a predominantly T-helper 2
response appear to develop progressive disease (ch. 210).
Disseminated aspergillosis and opportunistic fungal infections
occur primarily in animals with known or suspected immune
compromise. Though studies have suggested breed predilection,

genetic traits conveying susceptibility to these infections have not
been identified. Dogs treated with immunosuppressive drugs (cancer
chemotherapy or immunomodulatory medications such as
glucocorticoids or cyclosporine) also appear to be at higher risk of
disease. Disease can occur in any age, although in predisposed
breeds it is often recognized in young adult animals (ch. 180). One
study supported a female predisposition.9

CLINICAL SIGNS
Clinical signs caused by DIA or opportunistic fungal infections are
diverse and vary depending on the site(s) of infection. Most animals
exhibit lethargy and anorexia. Other signs include fever;
polyuria/polydipsia (with renal involvement); neurologic signs such
as altered mentation, proprioceptive ataxia, seizures, or vestibular
signs (with brain or spinal cord involvement); or, rarely, respiratory
signs when bronchopulmonary involvement is present. Ophthalmic
changes resulting from uveitis or chorioretinitis sometimes precede
apparent systemic illness and should prompt investigation of fungal
infection (ch. 13).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Physical examination abnormalities reflect the anatomic location of
infection. Fever is reported in about 25% of affected dogs.1,9 Other
common findings include apparent pain, lameness, vestibular signs,
and lymphadenopathy. Occasionally dogs have decreased lung
sounds due to pleural effusion or have increased bronchovesicular
sounds. Ophthalmic examination findings can vary from mild to
severe including anterior uveitis (e.g., flare, keratic precipitates),
chorioretinitis (hypo- or hyperreflective tapetal lesions, retinal
separation), optic neuritis, or panophthalmitis (Figure 211.1; ch.
13).

DIAGNOSIS

COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT (CBC)
The CBC of dogs with DIA or other mold infections typically reveals
changes consistent with systemic inflammation, including mild to
marked neutrophilia and occasionally toxic changes or left shift.
Some dogs develop anemia (typically normocytic, normochromic
nonregenerative) or have a peripheral monocytosis. None of these
findings is specific for the diagnosis of DIA.

SERUM BIOCHEMISTRIES
Hyperglobulinemia with or without hypoalbuminemia, a nonspecific
change of chronic inflammation, can be identified in dogs with DIA
or other systemic mold infections. Dogs with fungal pyelonephritis
can be azotemic and those with abdominal visceral disease can have
mild to moderately increased liver enzyme activities. Hypercalcemia
has been reported rarely in dogs with systemic mold infections. Creactive protein has been shown to help discriminate between
invasive fungal infections and other causes of pyrexia in people but
data in dogs are lacking.13-15

URINALYSIS
Urine testing might be normal or could reflect fungal pyelonephritis
with isosthenuria, proteinuria, pyuria, hematuria, and, rarely,
evidence of funguria on sediment examination.

MICROBIOLOGIC TESTING
Detection of fungal pathogens in an anatomic site that is normally
considered sterile remains the gold standard for diagnosis. This can
occur via either fungal microbiologic culture of clinical specimens or
microscopic identification of fungal structures followed by molecular
identification (chs. 85, 86, 88). Fine-needle aspirate (FNA)
specimens of affected lymph nodes, liver, spleen, effusion fluid,
vertebral bodies, other bony lesions, or urine can be submitted for
fungal culture (typically using inhibitory mold agar [IMA]; chs. 85
and 88). Urine culture is positive for fungal growth in about 50% of
dogs with DIA. Samples for blood culture can be collected and
incubated on IMA to detect fungemia (ch. 184).

Because of the morphologic similarities between Aspergillus
species and other genera of invasive molds, polymerase chain
reaction (PCR) sequencing is necessary to identify isolates.
Antifungal susceptibility testing can be performed by specialized
laboratories. Although clinical breakpoints for antifungal drugs have
not been established in companion animals, susceptibility test results
can be used to indicate likely susceptible or resistant drugs. In
humans, matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight
mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) is used to identify fungal
species from fungal culture material (ch. 184). The sensitivity of this
technique is limited by the number of mold strains included in
commercial MS libraries and challenges associated with lysis of
fungal pathogens. MALDI-TOF MS requires further study in
veterinary medicine.16

SEROLOGIC ASSAYS
Antigen testing for galactomannan, a component of fungal cell walls,
can be employed for diagnosis of many systemic fungal infections.
Aspergillus galactomannan enzyme immunoassay (EIA) can be
performed on both urine and serum specimens (Platelia, Bio-Rad
Laboratories, Hercules, CA). Use of serum is reported to have slightly
higher sensitivity (92%) than urine and both have a high specificity
(93%) for diagnosis of DIA. Low-level false positive results have been
reported in animals undergoing treatment with products or
medications derived from Aspergillus or other fungi (e.g., probiotics,
penicillin, crystalloid fluids with buffers derived from fungal
culture).17-19 Infection with other mold or dimorphic fungi are more
likely to result in high-level false positives due to antigenic
crossreactivity.1,19 Gel immunodiffusion tests that are commercially
available for detection of antibodies to A. fumigatus lack sensitivity
for diagnosis of DIA.9 A serologic assay that detects beta-D-glucan
(Glucatell, Associates of Cape Cod, East Falmouth, MA) has been
marketed for use in early detection of invasive fungal infections but
data validating its use in dogs and cats are not available.

CYTOLOGY AND HISTOPATHOLOGY
Aspergillus spp. grow in tissues as thin walled, septate, branching
hyphae that are approximately 5 micrometers in diameter (Figure
211.2). Fungal elements can be found in aspirates of infected lymph
nodes, spleen, kidney, liver, or vertebral endplates (chs. 85 and 88).
Occasionally they can be identified in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid
(ch. 93), effusions (ch. 71), or urine. The sensitivity of cytologic
evaluation for detection of fungal elements is variable; absence of
detectable fungal elements does not rule out infection. The presence
of aleuriospores (laterally branching spherical vesicles) suggests the
presence of A. terreus. However, identification using fungal culture
+/– PCR-sequencing is required for confirmation of the species
involved.
Within tissues, pyogranulomas form in the presence of fungal
hyphae and are often identified in both kidneys, spleen, the axial and
appendicular skeleton, heart, brain, spinal cord, and lymph nodes.
Microscopically, these lesions are characterized by a predominance
of neutrophils with variable numbers of macrophages that may form
sheets of multinucleated giant cells, and central, coalescing areas of
necrosis containing fungal hyphae (chs. 85, 88). Fungal elements
can appear refractile when stained with hematoxylin and eosin and
are more easily identifiable with silver stains such as Grocott’s
methenamine silver or with periodic acid-Schiff.7

MOLECULAR TESTING
Although real-time PCR assays have been developed and applied for
the diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis in humans, their diagnostic
accuracy is variable. These assays have not been routinely used to
diagnose DIA in dogs or cats. PCR-sequencing can be used to identify
organisms to the species level, and is offered by some specialized
laboratories.

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING

Thoracic radiographs in dogs with DIA or Rasamsonia spp.
infections can reveal enlarged tracheobronchial and/or sternal
lymph nodes, cranial mediastinal masses, pleural effusion, and/or
pulmonary alveolar infiltrates. Spinal radiographs reveal evidence of
discospondylitis in approximately half of dogs diagnosed with DIA
(Figure 211.1).1,9 Productive and lytic changes suggestive of
osteomyelitis may be present in either the axial or appendicular
skeleton.
Abdominal ultrasound abnormalities in dogs with DIA are most
often detected in the kidneys, spleen, and abdominal lymph nodes.
Renal abnormalities include changes suggestive of pyelonephritis
such as papillary blunting, pyelectasia, and echogenic pelvic debris.
Splenic abnormalities include hypoechoic nodules or granulomas,
splenomegaly, or evidence of infarction. Abdominal lymph nodes
tend to be enlarged and/or hypoechoic. Magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) in dogs with DIA that has spread to the brain can reveal
multifocal lesions that are hypo- to isointense, and enhance with
contrast on T1-weighted images and hyperintense or heterogamous
on T2-weighted images, although dogs with necropsy-confirmed
brain disease can have normal MRI scans.20

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
The prognosis for dogs with DIA and other opportunistic mold
infections is typically grave, because most dogs have advanced
disease at the time of initial diagnosis along with compromised
immune function. Most dogs in case series describing outcomes have
died or been euthanized because of their disease.1,7 In one study of
30 dogs, nearly two-thirds of the dogs were euthanized within 1 week
of diagnosis and survival times for dogs receiving antifungal
treatments ranged from 2 days to 25 months.9 A study evaluating the
utility of posaconazole in 10 dogs with DIA reported a median
survival time of 241 days with all but 1 dog succumbing to its
infection before manuscript preparation.21 Dogs with a history of
immunosuppressive drug therapy (chs. 144, 169, 227) tend to have
longer survival times if disease is diagnosed before widespread

dissemination and the immunosuppressive drug therapy can be
discontinued.

PUBLIC HEALTH CONSIDERATIONS

Dogs with DIA do not shed infectious propagules. Aspergillus species
are saprophytic, opportunist molds, and are considered shared
environmental pathogens. Disease in dogs is not considered to be
zoonotic.

The goal of the approach to the respiratory patient is to obtain a
specific diagnosis by the least invasive means possible. With
respiratory disease, this approach involves first verifying that the
constellation of historical and presenting clinical signs is consistent
with respiratory disease or dysfunction, localizing the dysfunction to
a specific region or regions within the respiratory system, and
specifying the nature of dysfunction at that site. Once respiratory
disease has been verified and localized, the tools used to specify the
exact nature of respiratory disease often become more invasive (e.g.,
diagnostic respiratory sampling) and expensive (e.g., advanced
imaging, endoscopy). It is therefore critical that clinicians be able to
effectively verify and localize respiratory disease non-invasively in
order to facilitate the development of an efficient diagnostic plan and
maximize the likelihood of a successful therapeutic plan.

HISTORY AND SIGNALMENT
The diagnostic approach to the respiratory patient begins in the
exam room. Knowledge of breed- and age-specific conditions will
often help to streamline the localization process. The patient
signalment alone may lead clinicians to re-prioritize the differential
list. Juvenile, immunocompromised (ch. 180), or unvaccinated (ch.
185) patients are more likely to present with clinical signs consistent
with canine (ch. 203) or feline (ch. 205) infectious respiratory
disease. Disorders known or suspected to have a heritable or genetic
etiology will often be breed-specific (e.g., chronic pulmonary fibrosis
in the West Highland White Terrier [ch. 217], congenital laryngeal
malformation of Norwich Terriers [ch. 214], asthma in Siamese and
Havana Brown cats [ch. 215]).1-3 Patient conformation may also
lend clues to the origin of respiratory disorders. Thickened and
elongated soft palate, stenotic nares, tracheal hypoplasia, and other
conformational alterations may contribute to airway obstruction in
brachycephalic dogs (ch. 213),4,5 while dolichocephalic dogs are
overrepresented among dogs with nasal tumors (ch. 213) and nasal
aspergillosis (ch. 210).6,7 Clinicians should strive to obtain a

complete and detailed patient history (ch. 2), including knowledge
of when the patient was last normal, the rate of progression of
clinical signs, and patterns of clinical signs observed with the patient
in its normal environment. The clinician’s ability to demonstrate
clinical signs that may be unfamiliar to clients (e.g.,

Video 212.1)

may also help to localize the source and nature of respiratory
dysfunction. History of exposure to other animals (e.g., shelter
setting, boarding facility) increases likelihood of contagious causes of
respiratory signs. Questions should be crafted to not only localize
respiratory dysfunction, but also to verify that the respiratory system
is the source of the dysfunction (e.g., coughing vs. retching in cats),
or to confirm that clinical signs previously attributed to other organ
systems are actually respiratory in origin (e.g., vomiting vs. posttussive retching in dogs). Detailed, mechanistic descriptions of
symptoms (perceived by the owner) and clinical signs (observed by
the clinician) referable to the respiratory system are covered
elsewhere in the text (chs. 27, 34, 35, and 37). A brief introduction
to these symptoms and signs is included below.

HISTORICAL FINDINGS SUGGESTIVE
OF RESPIRATORY DISEASE
Sneezing (ch. 35)
Sneezing is an involuntary, expiratory reflex following irritation of
the nasal mucosa. The sneezing reflex is a protective mechanism that
can be difficult to stifle or overcome. With sneezing, the event is
expiratory, and the head usually moves sharply downward during the
event. This can help clients differentiate between sneezing and
reverse sneezing (below). Sneezing is primarily an acute response
and will often decrease or stop completely in cases of chronic or
progressive nasal cavity disease, obstruction, or irritation.

Reverse Sneezing (ch. 35)
Reverse sneezing is a voluntary or involuntary inspiratory process,
involving paroxysms or series of strong, abrupt inspiratory efforts
(snorts). Reverse sneezing is a response to obstruction or irritation of

the nasopharynx. The patient is often standing, and in some cases
walking, with the neck extended, the head tilted backward, lips
pulled backward, and nostrils flared. These postural efforts result in
elongation of the nasopharynx, and maximal widening of the
nasopharyngeal meatus. Paroxysms may last anywhere from a few
seconds to a few minutes. These events frequently occur at night or
while the patient is at rest, due to the passive narrowing of the
nasopharynx. Although these paroxysms are not typically associated
with respiratory distress, they can be quite alarming to unfamiliar or
unprepared clients (Videos 212.1, 213.7

).

Nasal Discharge (ch. 35)
Nasal discharge is the result of an increase in fluid secretions in the
nasal cavity, a change in the quality or viscoelastic properties of nasal
secretions, an impairment of nasal mucociliary clearance, or a
combination of several or all of these conditions. When it is visible,
nasal discharge should be characterized by its appearance and
consistency (mucoid, serous, hemorrhagic, etc.), as this will help to
localize the source of the discharge, or to identify the mechanical
reason for the discharge. It is important to note that nasal discharge
may not always be obvious. Cats, as well as some dogs, can be
fastidious groomers, and may remove overt nasal discharge before
owners are aware of its presence. In these cases, the nasal planum
may become ulcerated or hyperkeratotic, and the haired skin
surrounding the nasal planum may become alopecic as a result of the
repeated trauma from licking or pawing at the nose to clear the
discharge. Also, it is important to remember that normal mucociliary
clearance in the nasal airways moves secretions from the nasal cavity
caudally toward the nasopharyngeal meatus. As a result, nasal
discharge may initially be directed toward the larynx, resulting in an
upper airway-localizing cough (see below). Overt nasal discharge
from the nostrils will not become apparent until the amount or
character of the secretions exceeds the nasal mucociliary clearance
capacity, or until the mucociliary clearance apparatus has been
sufficiently damaged or impaired (e.g., Bordetella, Mycoplasma or
parainfluenza virus infections, squamous metaplasia).8,9 Nasal

discharge may also be a manifestation of non-respiratory disease
(e.g., esophagopharyngeal reflux).10

Open-Mouth/Postural Breathing (ch. 37)
Postural changes reflect attempts to decrease airway resistance by
increasing airway cross-sectional area.11 In dogs, open-mouthed
breathing is a common response to upper airway obstruction (
Video 37.1), while in cats, open-mouthed breathing is rare, and
suggests that the ventilatory reserve capacity of the respiratory
system is approaching exhaustion (

Video 37.4). An animal’s

spontaneous extension of the head and neck minimizes bending in
the trachea and pharynx. Similarly, flaring the nostrils and opening
the mouth minimize inspiratory resistance at the inlet. Animals may
also minimize extraneous (non-respiratory) activity and eliminate
actions that exacerbate airway narrowing (swallowing, vocalizing).

Audible Respiratory Sounds
Respiratory noises that are audible to clients without the aid of a
stethoscope are almost always due to airway obstruction and are
usually of upper airway origin (nasal cavity, nasopharynx, oral cavity,
larynx, extrathoracic trachea). Since stress and sympathetic tone
associated with the hospital visit may facilitate airway opening, it is
not uncommon for respiratory noises that are present at home to be
absent in the exam room. Owners should be asked to describe
whether noises are continuous (stridor) or discontinuous (stertor),
constant (fixed obstructions) or intermittent (dynamic or episodic
obstructions), and if intermittent, what events precipitate the noise
(exercise, sleep, etc.). Having owners provide video recordings of
respiratory noises can be very helpful both in characterizing the
sound and evaluating the patient’s posture during the event. While
the determination of the phase of respiration during which the noise
occurs is extremely valuable information, it can be very difficult for
clients to reliably make this type of assessment.

Cough (ch. 34)

Cough is a defense mechanism that protects the lower airways. It can
be triggered by inhalation of noxious substances or irritants, or by
the accumulation of retained substances in the large and small
airways. The sound of a cough originates from the larynx as a result
of the acute expulsion of intrapulmonary air through a narrowed
glottis. However, cough may be triggered by irritation or stimulation
of any portion of the tracheobronchial tree, or by laryngeal irritation.
Dogs and cats with irritation or stimulation originating from
different regions of the tracheobronchial tree may exhibit subtle
differences in the quality of their coughing, and these differences can
be very helpful in localizing the site and nature of the stimulus.
Cough originating in the alveoli or small airways
(bronchopneumonia, chronic bronchitis) is usually preceded by a
deep inspiration. Paroxysms may start quietly and grow louder as
tracheobronchial secretions are moved up to the central airways
(crescendo). These coughs may be productive or nonproductive, and
are frequently followed by a post-tussive retch, or swallowing of
raised secretions.
Cough originating in the central airways (trachea, mainstem
bronchi) is often associated with a “goose honk” sound in dogs
(Video 215.1

), as air is forcefully expelled through segments of

narrowed or collapsed airways.12 Paroxysms of tracheal coughing are
often “non-progressive,” in which each cough sounds like the
preceding one, triggers the subsequent one, and as a result, may be
quite prolonged.
A type of cough may also be elicited with stimulation of the larynx,
trachea, and bronchi by post-nasal drainage of nasal secretions or
oral cavity contents. With laryngeal origin coughing, the stimulus is
often abrupt and unanticipated, resulting in reflex laryngospasm,
and thus preventing deep inspiration prior to the start of the cough.
This cough is typically more of a rapid-fire cough that may be weak
or ineffective due to the small volume of air expelled. This cough may
also be followed by voluntary efforts to clear the upper airways
(gagging). Technically, this mechanism is referred to as an
expiratory reflex or “huff” rather than a cough reflex, but it is often
included in descriptions with other forms of cough.13,14

Cough can also be induced by airway narrowing during expiration
secondary to dynamic small airway disease (chronic bronchitis [dogs
and cats], asthma [cats]), tracheal collapse (primarily dogs), or
restrictive lung diseases (chs. 215, 217). This latter type of cough is
typically triggered at higher tidal flows and may only be noticed
during exercise in early stages of disease, but may become more
noticeable as cardiopulmonary reserves are diminished. Pleural
space disease can theoretically cause airway narrowing secondary to
lung compression (ch. 220). However, it is likely that cough in
patients with pleural disease is caused by pleural effusion impacting
the adjacent lung parenchyma. Similarly, cardiomegaly has also been
cited as a potential cause of cough by causing bronchial compression,
particularly in dogs.15 The role of cardiomegaly in cough is
controversial, as it is unclear whether bronchial compression in these
cases is the result of cardiac enlargement or intrinsic
tracheobronchial disease (chs. 215, 229).
Cough afferent nerves may also originate in locations outside of
the lower airways, including the nose, nasopharynx, paranasal
sinuses, ear canals, diaphragm, and pericardium.16 The exact role of
cough afferents in these locations in companion animals is not
entirely known; however, their presence suggests that
extrapulmonary sites may also be important sources of cough.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION OF THE
RESPIRATORY PATIENT
The physical examination is the next step in both verifying and
localizing respiratory disease (ch. 3). Respiratory signs may be due
entirely or in part to intrinsic respiratory disease or may represent
respiratory manifestations of dysfunction in other organ systems
(e.g., gastrointestinal, central nervous system [CNS], cardiovascular,
hematologic, adrenal, thyroidal). In addition, the stress associated
with a non-respiratory illness may unmask occult respiratory
disease, particularly in cats. For these reasons, it is always important
to perform a complete physical exam whenever patient stability
allows.

OBSERVATION
Examination of the respiratory patient should begin with detailed
observation of the patient at rest whenever possible. With stable
patients, this can occur simultaneously while obtaining a history
from the owner. Patients can be removed from their carriers or
unsecured from leashes in the exam room in order to allow them to
wander within a confined space. Respiratory rate, respiratory effort,
respiratory noises, and breathing pattern and posture can all be
assessed during this time. For the patient presenting in respiratory
distress, it is still prudent to obtain at least a cursory assessment of
respiratory pattern and posture prior to handling the patient (chs.
37, 119).

Breathing Pattern (ch. 37)
During normal respiration, the chest wall and abdominal wall move
out together during inspiration and move in together during
expiration. This coordinated movement allows maximal expansion of
the lungs with minimal effort during inspiration, with diaphragmatic
contraction, passive relaxation of the muscles of respiration, and
elastic recoil of the lungs to provide expiration.17 Normal ratios of
inspiratory time : expiratory time during tidal breathing are from
∼1:1 to 1:2. Some animals at rest may exhibit a pronounced pause at
the end of expiration during which no chest or abdominal wall
movements are detectable as CO2 accumulates to trigger the next
breath.
An increase in respiratory workload may result in an alteration in
the patient’s breathing pattern. These alterations are usually
strategies to minimize the work of breathing and will vary as a result
of the nature of the increased respiratory burden. A general
algorithm for the evaluation of breathing patterns is displayed in
Figure 212.1.
Airway obstruction results in an increase in airway resistance, or
an increase in the pressure necessary to generate air flow. The
increase in respiratory effort can exacerbate airway collapse and
worsen airflow obstruction. Extrathoracic obstructions (e.g.,
laryngeal tumors, laryngeal paralysis [ch. 214], nasal or

nasopharyngeal obstruction [ch. 213]) are typically associated with
an increase in inspiratory effort and inspiratory noise, while
intrathoracic obstructions (small airway disease, mucus plugging,
intrathoracic tracheal collapse) are associated with an increase in
expiratory effort and expiratory noise (

Video 215.2). A common

compensatory strategy for patients experiencing airway obstruction
is to decrease the velocity of airflow, thus minimizing the propensity
of the airways to collapse. This results in slow, deep respirations,
often with prolongation of the inspiratory phase in the case of
extrathoracic (upper airway) obstructions, and expiratory phase
prolongation with intrathoracic obstructions.

FIGURE 212.1 General algorithm for the
evaluation of breathing patterns in dogs and cats.
This algorithm is intended to provide general
guidelines toward the assessment of respiratory
patterns. Exceptions to this algorithmic approach
exist. ARDS, Adult respiratory distress syndrome.

Restrictive lung disease results in a decrease in lung compliance,
or the change in lung volume associated with a measured increase in
airway pressure. Patients with conditions associated with restrictive
breathing patterns (bronchopneumonia, pulmonary fibrosis [ch.
217], pleural space disease [ch. 220]) will require higher airway
pressures to fully expand their lungs. Because the increase in
workload is associated with lung expansion, patients with restrictive
lung diseases or pleural space disease may compensate by decreasing
tidal volumes and increasing respiratory rates, resulting in rapid,
shallow breathing.
Obstructive and restrictive conditions each increase the work of
breathing. With time, an increase in the work of breathing can result
in respiratory muscle fatigue, resulting in a paradoxical breathing
pattern (

Video 37.3). As respiratory muscles fail, the negative

intrathoracic pressure generated during inspiration will tend to suck
the chest wall in. In addition, diaphragmatic fatigue or
diaphragmatic paralysis can lead to recruitment of the abdominal
muscles, causing outward movement of the abdominal wall during
expiration. These chest and abdominal wall movements oppose those
seen with normal respiration and can be indicative of severe or longstanding respiratory dysfunction. In dyspneic dogs and cats,
paradoxical breathing has been strongly correlated with the presence
of pleural space diseases.18 The presence of this clinical sign in
emergent companion animal patients can help to prompt
implementation of appropriate emergency diagnostic (e.g., thoracic
ultrasound, ch. 73) and therapeutic (e.g., thoracocentesis, ch. 92)
procedures. If the pleural space is unremarkable, airway obstruction
should be strongly considered.

Breathing Posture
Patients experiencing significant respiratory compromise may adopt
a posture that helps maximize the efficiency of breathing. These
adaptations help to decrease airway resistance by increasing airway
cross-sectional area and facilitating chest wall expansion. While this
can be observed as a result of many causes of cardiorespiratory
dysfunction, postural variation in respiratory effort (orthopnea) is
commonly associated with congestive heart failure. Extending the

head and neck reduces redundancy and obstruction in the pharynx.
Flaring the nostrils opens the nasal valve (ostium internum).
Breathing through an open mouth bypasses nasal and
nasopharyngeal resistance altogether. This often represents
significant loss of cardiopulmonary reserves in cats, who often
maintain nasal breathing even in the face of severe airway
obstruction. Patients may adopt a seated posture, or prefer to remain
sternal, with the elbows abducted; cats often crouch with head
extended (

Video 37.4). Patients may also minimize extraneous

activity, and eliminate actions that exacerbate airway narrowing
(swallowing, vocalizing).

RESPIRATORY SYSTEM EXAMINATION
In many cases, the physical examination of the respiratory system
serves to confirm what the medical history and observation suggest
(ch. 3). However, in other cases, historical signs may be vague, and
overt signs of respiratory dysfunction may be subtle or absent. A
thorough examination of the respiratory system includes a nasal
exam (muzzle, head, eyes, dental arcade, hard palate, nasal airflow),
oral exam, cervical exam including palpation of the larynx and
trachea, thoracic compression, and thorough thoracic auscultation,
including auscultation over the thoracic inlet.
Examination of the nasal cavity largely entails visual inspection
and palpation of the muzzle, head, eyes, and hard palate for
conformation, symmetry, and defects. The external nares and rostral
aspect of the nasal passages can be visually inspected for mucous
membrane color and for the presence and character of any nasal
discharge. Each side of the nasal cavity should be evaluated for
patency and airflow. Nasal airway patency can be assessed using
several methods, including holding cotton or gauze in front of each
nostril to detect air movement (

Video 36.2), or by placing a

refrigerated glass slide in front of the nose during nasal breathing
and watching for the appearance of condensation from each nostril.
A stethoscope can also be used to assess nasal air flow by gently
occluding one nostril while placing the stethoscope diaphragm in

front of the other and listening for air movement. The hard palate
and upper dental arcade should be inspected and palpated, as
invasive nasal disease may extend into the oral cavity, and dental
disease (e.g., tooth root abscesses) may have nasal manifestations (
Video 213.12). Careful palpation and retropulsion of the eyes
should be performed to assess symmetry, as invasive nasal tumors or
destructive mycotic rhinitis may extent into the orbit.
The oral cavity should be inspected for mucous membrane color,
capillary refill time, and hydration. The tonsils, tongue, sublingual
area, and hard palate should be examined for defects or lesions that
may cause airway obstruction. Pharyngeal function can be assessed
by testing for the presence of a gag reflex.
Cervical examination should include observation and careful
palpation of the trachea, larynx, mandibular and retropharyngeal
lymph nodes, and the thoracic inlet. Cough can often be elicited in
dogs with tracheobronchial disease through gentle palpation of the
cervical trachea (

Video 34.5). The character of this cough (e.g.,

solitary vs. paroxysmal, dry vs. productive) can aid the clinician in
localizing the nature of disease. Patients with airway obstruction may
exhibit cranial lung lobe herniation (CLLH), in which the cranial
aspects of the left and right cranial lung lobes herniate through the
thoracic inlet during cough or increased expiratory efforts. This can
be observed during physical exam as an episodic bulging or swelling
at the thoracic inlet that varies with phase of respiration or that
occurs during an elicited cough (

Video 212.2). CLLH is strongly

correlated with dynamic intrathoracic airway collapse19 but can also
occur secondary to other forms of fixed or dynamic collapse (e.g.,
brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome).
Physical examination of the upper respiratory tract should also
include an otoscopic examination, and a complete ophthalmic
examination, including gentle retropulsion of the eyes to assess
symmetry, as invasive nasal tumors or destructive mycotic rhinitis
may extend into the orbit, and inspection of the fundus to investigate
for signs of systemic or infectious diseases that may have nasal and
ophthalmic manifestations (e.g., fungal infection, systemic
hypertension).

Physical exam findings referable to the upper airway include
stertor, stridor, and decreased or absent nasal airflow (

Video

37.1). Stertor is a discontinuous, low-pitched fluttering sound that
usually originates from the nasopharyngeal meatus. It is typically
associated with inspiratory dysfunction, but may also be present
during both phases of respiration. Because of the tendency of the
nasopharyngeal meatus to narrow during rest, stertor may be more
pronounced at night. Stridor is a continuous, high-pitched
inspiratory sound, usually produced as a result of narrowing of the
larynx or extrathoracic trachea. In contrast to stertor, stridorous
respiratory noise may be absent at rest, but exacerbated by high
airway flows (exercise, panting, etc.).
Physical exam findings referable to the lower airways include
adventitious sounds (wheezes, crackles) as well as changes in the
character of normal bronchovesicular sounds. Normal inspiratory
flow reaches peak velocity near the end of inspiration, while normal
expiratory flow reaches peak velocity near the beginning of the
expiratory phase. For this reason, thoracic auscultation of normal air
flow is typically loudest at end inspiration and early expiration.
Normal bronchovesicular sounds detected via auscultation are
primarily generated by laminar flow through the larger central
airways, and are filtered by the alveoli, pleural space, and chest wall.
Changes in the volume (increased or decreased) or pattern of
bronchovesicular sounds can be an early indicator of respiratory
disease, even in the absence of adventitious lung sounds. Increased
detection of bronchovesicular sounds can occur as a result of
increased respiratory effort or pulmonary edema of any cause.
Decreases in bronchovesicular sounds can be the result of shallow
breaths, an obese animal, or structural alterations in the pulmonary
interstitium, alveoli, or pleural space.
Adventitious respiratory sounds indicate the presence of an
abnormality. Wheezes are continuous, musical sounds associated
with intrathoracic airway narrowing, and are usually associated with
expiratory dysfunction. High-pitched wheezes can be detected with
narrowing of the lower airways or small airways, while low-pitched
wheezes may indicate larger airway narrowing. Crackles (or rales)
are discontinuous, “popping” sounds that are primarily audible
during inspiration, representing an equilibration of pressures

between two regions of an obstructed airway. Fine crackles are
typically alveolar or bronchiolar in origin and are typically loudest
near the end of inspiration. Loud, moist crackles usually are the
result of air flow through airway secretions in central airways, and
are typically detected throughout inspiration, and may also be
present during expiration. Pulmonary fibrosis typically results in
coarse, loud crackles. The thoracic location of adventitious lung
sounds can help the clinician prioritize differential diagnosis lists.
Fine crackles with a cranioventral distribution in a dog would be
consistent with bronchopneumonia, while a perihilar distribution of
the same lung sounds would be expected in a dog with left-sided
congestive heart failure.
A decrease or absence of respiratory sounds can occur as a result
of the accumulation of air, fluid, or viscera within the pleural space.
Patients with pleural space disorders may exhibit a shallow, rapid
(restrictive) breathing pattern. The location of the loss of breath
sounds should provide clues as to the nature of the pleural space
disorder. Loss of respiratory sounds ventrally is consistent with a
fluid accumulation (e.g., blood, pus, transudate, chylous effusion;
chs. 71, 220), while loss of breath sounds dorsally is most
consistent with a pneumothorax. Most pleural space disorders in
dogs and cats are bilateral as a result of an incomplete mediastinum.
However, tissue accumulations (e.g., mesothelioma) or visceral
herniations may result in asymmetry of auscultation findings.
In many cases, respiratory noises or clinical signs that are present
at home may not be present in the exam room. The tremendous
reserve capacity of the cardiopulmonary system may necessitate the
use of provocative testing during a physical exam. Detection of
cardiopulmonary abnormalities may be enhanced by inducing a
“sigh” during auscultation (close the mouth and partially obstruct
the nostrils for 4-5 breaths), by triggering a cough with gentle
tracheal palpation, or with light or moderate exercise. Having owners
record abnormalities at home can also help clinicians to accurately
verify and localize respiratory disease prior to the implementation of
more invasive and expensive diagnostic testing.

DIAGNOSTIC TECHNIQUES

The selection of appropriate diagnostic tests in the patient with
respiratory disease will be dependent upon the patient’s history,
signalment, physical examination results, and the differential
diagnoses for that patient. Screening tests including complete blood
count, serum chemistry profiles and urinalysis are important initial
tests because they are minimally invasive and can help to narrow or
prioritize the differential list for the patient’s symptoms, while also
facilitating the selection of more advanced diagnostics where
indicated. Erythrocytosis may occur as a result of chronic hypoxemia
and subsequent tissue hypoxia. Neutrophilic leukocytosis is a
common finding in patients with respiratory infection. Patients with
bronchopneumonia (ch. 217) may present with either a leukocytosis
or a transient leukopenia during the acute stage of disease. A
peripheral eosinophilia is a common finding in dogs with
eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy (ch. 215) and is occasionally
observed in patients with parasitic lung disease (ch. 217), fungal
diseases (ch. 209), and in cats with asthma (ch. 215). A
lymphocytosis in a young patient with respiratory disease and fever
can be suggestive of a viral etiology. Hypercalcemia in a patient with
respiratory signs may be suggestive of a neoplastic or fungal etiology.
Hematologic and biochemical profiles also provide an evaluation
of non-respiratory illnesses that may either directly impact the
respiratory system (e.g., severe metabolic acidosis, pancreatitis,
hyperadrenocorticism) or may unmask occult respiratory disease. An
inflammatory leukogram and hypoalbuminemia in a systemically ill
patient with respiratory distress can be consistent with acute
respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS, ch. 123). Severe
hypoalbuminemia can lead to third spacing of transudate in the
pleural and peritoneal cavities, leading to an increase in respiratory
effort. Thrombocytopenia (ch. 59), thrombocytopathia (ch. 171),
coagulopathy (ch. 171), and systemic hypertension (ch. 236) can all
result in pulmonary hemorrhage (ch. 217), hemorrhagic effusions
(chs. 71, 220), or epistaxis (ch. 36).
Serologic, urine antigen, fecal, and polymerase chain reaction
(PCR) tests can be employed in patients suspected of having an
infectious or parasitic cause of their respiratory symptoms. Factors
that may be suggestive of an infectious etiology include age,
geographical location and travel history, lifestyle (e.g., outdoor vs.
indoor cats), the presence of comorbid non-respiratory symptoms, or

a “herd” health scenario (e.g., multiple affected puppies within a
litter, multiple patients from the same boarding facility or shelter, a
cat affected after introduction of a new kitten in a household).
Testing for heartworm disease (Dirofilaria immitis) should be
routinely considered in a coughing dog, and may warrant
consideration in cats exhibiting coughing or signs of intrathoracic
airway obstruction (see ch. 237 for details of heartworm testing
recommendations in dogs and cats). Recurrent airway infections or
respiratory infection with opportunistic pathogens should prompt an
investigation into possible causes of immunodeficiency (ch. 180).
For example, diagnosis of refractory or recurrent nasal
cryptococcosis in a cat (ch. 207) may warrant testing for retrovirus
infection (chs. 198, 199), while recurrent rhinitis,
tracheobronchitis, and pneumonia in a young dog may prompt an
investigation for primary ciliary dyskinesia or heritable
immunoglobulin deficiencies (ch. 180).20-22 Unfortunately,
traditional fecal exams (ch. 80) are not sensitive for most
respiratory parasites as they are shed inconsistently through the
stool.
The method and timing of sample collection are important factors
to consider when screening for infectious or parasitic causes of
respiratory disease with laboratory testing, particularly for PCR
testing. Mucosal swabs collected for PCR should be obtained using
polyester-tipped swabs, as residues found in cotton-tipped or
calcium alginate swabs may inhibit PCR assays. PCR testing requires
the presence of the pathogen or pathogen genome in the submitted
sample. Collection of superficial mucosal samples may yield false
negative results in cases of infection with viral (e.g., canine
respiratory coronavirus) or facultative intracellular bacterial (e.g.,
Mycoplasma cynos) pathogens. In many cases, pathogen shedding
may cease prior to the resolution of clinical symptoms (e.g., canine
influenza virus). As a result, PCR testing after the organism has been
cleared may yield a false negative result. In all cases, steps should be
taken to ensure that the timing and method of sample collection are
appropriate for the differentials being considered. A list of common
bacterial, fungal, viral, and protozoal pathogens for which testing
with PCR is available is listed in Box 212.1.

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING OF THE
RESPIRATORY SYSTEM
In veterinary medicine, the investigation of suspected respiratory
disease relies extensively on diagnostic imaging of the upper airways
(nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea), lower airways (bronchi,
bronchioles), pulmonary parenchyma (vasculature, interstitium,
alveoli), and non-respiratory structures (heart, spine, ribs, sternum,
abdomen, etc.). Among the imaging modalities available, thoracic
radiography is utilized most commonly. Alternative imaging
modalities can provide additional levels of detail and dimension to
still imaging (computed tomography [CT], magnetic resonance
imaging [MRI]), provide assessment of dynamic airways in real-time
(fluoroscopy, ultrasonography), or provide assessments of regional
lung function (nuclear imaging). All diagnostic imaging studies
should be performed prior to more invasive procedures (rhinoscopy,
nasal biopsies, bronchoalveolar lavage, etc.), so that iatrogenic
hemorrhage and disruption of normal anatomic structures do not
affect the diagnostic utility of imaging studies.

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING OF THE UPPER
RESPIRATORY TRACT
Anatomically, the upper airway extends from the tip of the nose to
the thoracic inlet. In veterinary medicine, the investigation of clinical
signs and respiratory noises suspected to localize to the upper
airways relies extensively on diagnostic imaging of the upper airways
(nasal cavity, pharynx, and larynx), and related non-respiratory
structures (skull, dental arcade, bony orbits, lymph nodes, salivary
glands). Because much of this region lies within the confines of the
skull (nasal cavity, nasopharynx), or is surrounded by overlapping
soft tissue structures (larynx, cervical trachea), advanced imaging
techniques are often required to confirm abnormalities in upper

airway function or structure (ch. 213). Because of the importance of
patient positioning and the intolerance for motion artifact, all upper
airway diagnostic imaging studies should be performed under heavy
sedation (e.g., lateral cervical radiography) or general anesthesia.

Radiography
Nasal radiographs can be helpful in localization and characterization
of intranasal disease. Nasal and sinus radiographs, however, rarely
identify a specific cause for nasal disease (an exception would be a
radiopaque foreign body). Benefits of nasal radiographs include the
ability to detect asymmetry, bony destruction, and soft tissue opacity
in the nasal cavity and surrounding structures. High quality nasal
radiographs can also be obtained with minimal cost and technical
complexity, and without the need for specialized equipment. Nasal
radiographs should include a minimum of two orthogonal views.
Standard views include dorsoventral, open-mouth ventrodorsal
(occlusal), and lateral. Specialized views (oblique lateral view, skyline
view) can be extremely valuable in detecting frontal sinus and
auditory bulla involvement. Dental radiographs can provide detailed
information about the involvement of the maxillary dental arcade
and tooth roots (ch. 258) in the pathogenesis of nasal disease.
A disadvantage of nasal radiographs is that they lack the sensitivity
and level of detail obtained with cross-sectional imaging techniques.
The complexity of the canine and feline skull can make detection of
early or subtle nasal lesions difficult. While not technically
challenging, patient positioning is an extremely important factor in
determining the diagnostic utility of nasal radiographs. Poor patient
positioning can result in nondiagnostic images, or possibly result in a
misdiagnosis.
Radiography of the pharynx, larynx, and cervical trachea is
indicated in the face of respiratory symptoms localizing to that
region (e.g., stridor, gagging, ineffective coughing, change or loss of
voice). A lateral skull or neck radiograph alone is often adequate for
assessment of the respiratory structures in this region. The specific
area of interest should be centered in the image in order to minimize
the degree of parallax when viewing symmetrical paired structures
(e.g., auditory bulla, arytenoids cartilages). Patient positioning is
critical in evaluating lateral skull or neck radiographs, as even the

slightest obliquity can make interpretation very difficult. Images
centered over the larynx are most useful in the assessment of
laryngeal stridor, while images centered over the mid-cervical region
are preferred in the assessment of suspected cervical tracheal
collapse. The investigation of suspected cervical or thoracic inlet
tracheal collapse should also include both inspiratory and expiratory
lateral views in order to document dynamic collapse (when
fluoroscopic or tracheoscopic evaluation is not available).
Survey thoracic radiographs are important diagnostic tests in the
localization of lower airway, parenchymal, and pleural space
conditions. It is important to obtain at least two orthogonal views of
the thorax (one lateral and a ventrodorsal or dorsoventral projection)
to better identify and localize thoracic lesions. However, studies that
include both laterals as well as an orthogonal view are ideal, as the
dependent lung lobes on lateral views will collapse as a result of
compression from the heart and diaphragm, as well as decreased
thoracic wall movement during the respiratory cycle.23 Furthermore,
there may be cases in which both a ventrodorsal (e.g., accessory lobe
disease) and a dorsoventral (e.g., caudal lobar pulmonary vascular
enlargement) view may be indicated. Positioning and technique are
particularly important for proper evaluation and interpretation of
both intrathoracic (lungs, heart, mediastinal contents) and
extrathoracic (ribs, spine, sternebrae) structures, as any or all of
these may contribute to respiratory clinical signs or dysfunction.
Care should be taken to ensure that the forelimbs are pulled cranially
to minimize superimposition over the cranial thorax. The views
should be collimated to include the entirety of the pulmonary fields,
the cranial abdomen, and the thoracic inlet. Thoracic structures will
have inherent movement due to respiratory motion and the cardiac
cycle, so the length of exposure for thoracic imaging should be kept
as short as possible while still providing adequate contrast.
Pulmonary radiographic abnormalities can be typically classified
into interstitial patterns, bronchial patterns, and alveolar patterns.
Interstitial pulmonary patterns can be further characterized as
unstructured or structured (nodular). Unstructured interstitial
patterns result in a generalized increase in background opacity of the
pulmonary parenchyma, and a decreased distinction of the
pulmonary vasculature. Common causes of a diffuse interstitial

pattern include viral or hematogenous pneumonias, pulmonary
edema (cardiogenic and noncardiogenic), neoplastic infiltration (e.g.,
pulmonary lymphoma), and pneumonitis secondary to systemic
diseases (e.g., uremic pneumonitis). The appearance of an
unstructured interstitial pattern may also be artifactual in nature, as
a result of poor radiographic technique, hypoventilation, or as a
variant of normal in an obese patient.24 Structured or nodular
interstitial patterns appear as discrete or coalescing soft tissue
nodules within the pulmonary fields. A nodular lesion larger than 2
cm within the pulmonary parenchyma is generally referred to as a
pulmonary mass. Nodular lesions may be solitary or multiple within
a given patient, and may either appear as solid or cavitary lesions.
These distinctions in the size, appearance, and number of nodular
interstitial lesions may help to narrow the differential list for a
particular patient. A list of causes of the various types of nodular
interstitial lesions appears in Table 212.1.
An alveolar pulmonary pattern occurs when the air within the
alveoli is replaced with soft tissue or fluid, resulting in an overall
increased opacity of the lung tissue. Pulmonary edema, hemorrhage,
and inflammatory or neoplastic exudates are examples of materials
that can replace alveolar air resulting in an alveolar pattern.
Atelectasis, or the loss of alveolar air with resulting alveolar collapse,
can also cause an alveolar pattern, which usually also results in a
mediastinal shift toward the side of the atelectasis. Rarely, solid
tumors can result in an alveolar pattern, either by replacing alveolar
air or by causing bronchial obstruction resulting in atelectasis. The
radiographic hallmarks of an alveolar pattern include the presence of
air bronchograms, a lobar sign, and soft-tissue silhouetting (border
effacement) between the affected lung and the diaphragm, heart, or
vasculature. Common causes of an alveolar pattern include
bronchopneumonia, pulmonary edema (cardiogenic or noncardiogenic), hemorrhage, and atelectasis. Less common but
important differentials for an alveolar pattern include severe
inflammatory airway disease (e.g., eosinophilic
bronchopneumopathy), pulmonary thromboembolism, and
neoplasia.

Bronchial pulmonary patterns occur when the bronchial walls
become thickened, or when the immediate peribronchial space
becomes infiltrated with cells or fluid. Radiographically, the
thickened bronchi appear as rings of soft tissue density with air
opacity in the center (“donuts”), or parallel radiopaque lines (“tram
lines”). In addition to thickening of the bronchial walls, there are also
other consequences of bronchial disease that may cause changes in
thoracic radiographs, including bronchiectasis, cranial or middle
lung lobe atelectasis, and hyperlucent lung fields due to air trapping
and pulmonary hyperinflation. Common differentials for a bronchial
radiographic pattern in dogs and cats include allergic airway disease
(feline asthma, canine eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy), parasitic
bronchitis/pneumonitis, and chronic bronchitis.
The radiographic appearance or distribution of the same
conditions may differ between dogs and cats. The typical
radiographic appearance of left-sided congestive heart failure in dogs

is a perihilar interstitial or alveolar pattern, while the same condition
in cats may exhibit more of a patchy pulmonary distribution.
Similarly, the typical radiographic appearance of bronchopneumonia
in dogs is a cranioventral distribution of an alveolar pattern, while
cats with bronchopneumonia more often exhibit a multifocal or
patchy, asymmetrical alveolar pattern.
The accumulation of fluid (air, blood, chylous effusion,
inflammatory or neoplastic exudates, transudates) within the pleural
space can inhibit lung expansion, leading to respiratory difficulty,
hypoxemia due to hypoventilation, and respiratory distress,
particularly if the fluid accumulation is large or occurs rapidly (ch.
220). The presence of clinically significant pleural fluid can be
detected with routine thoracic radiographs. Approximately 100 mL
of liquid must be present within the pleural space of a medium-size
dog before pleural fluid is apparent radiographically.25 Smaller
volumes or localized accumulations may require additional imaging
modalities (CT, ultrasound) to facilitate detection. Radiographic
signs indicative of free pleural liquid include the appearance of
pleural fissure lines between lung lobes, retraction of lung lobes away
from the chest wall, rounding of the edges of dependent lung lobes,
and obfuscation of the diaphragmatic and cardiac silhouettes.
Accumulation of air or other gases within the pleural space
(pneumothorax) can also result in significant respiratory distress and
dysfunction. Air can accumulate within the pleural space from
rupture of lung tissue, from within the mediastinum, or from outside
of the body through the chest wall. The most common radiographic
appearance of pneumothorax is the retraction of lung lobes away
from the thoracic wall on the lateral views.26 Pneumothorax also
causes secondary lung collapse or atelectasis, resulting in an
apparent increase in lung opacity. Collapse of the dependent lung
lobes on lateral views allows the heart to descend into the dependent
hemithorax, resulting in a separation of the heart and the sternum
(“floating heart”). Removal of pleural fluid or air via thoracocentesis
(ch. 92) prior to diagnostic imaging may be required for patient
stabilization and can also improve the radiographic assessment of
the lungs, heart, diaphragm, and mediastinum.

Computed Tomography (CT)

Historically limited in availability, CT is now routinely available in
most veterinary referral practices and is becoming a more available
and affordable option in general practice. Historically, CT scanning
in companion animal patients required general anesthesia. However,
newer CT scanners with 32- or 64-row detectors can acquire a
complete series of images within a few seconds. As a result, CT
scanning can now be performed in critically ill or unstable patients
without anesthesia.27,28 Furthermore, the use of CT without
anesthesia allows for evaluation of the anatomic position of upper
airway structures without the presence or interference of an
endotracheal tube.29 It should be noted that general anesthesia for
CT scanning does confer some diagnostic advantages, including
reduction of motion artifact from spontaneous ventilation and
allowing for comparison of full inspiratory and expiratory images,
providing significant advantage in assessment of lower airway and
lung parenchymal disease.30
CT provides a detailed, three-dimensional (3-D) view of the nasal
cavity, nasopharynx, and sinuses (Figure 212.2). Because of the
higher sensitivity and resolution of CT, it is considered the test of
choice for evaluation of nasal disease where available. Images
obtained with this modality are superior for the detection of early
nasal lesions, and for determining the extent of invasive nasal
disease (e.g., extension into cribriform plate, orbital involvement).
While rhinoscopy and nasal radiography are insensitive in
distinguishing non-infectious rhinitis from neoplasia and/or mycotic
rhinitis, the addition of CT provides valuable detail of characteristics
that can be strongly suggestive of one of the more aggressive
processes. CT is particularly sensitive in detecting changes in bony
and cartilaginous structures associated with the nasal cavity. CT
alone provides no better distinction of soft-tissue structures versus
fluid than nasal radiographs. However, the addition of intravenous
contrast causes enhancement of vascular structures and perfused
tissues in CT images that can further aid in the delineation of the
margins of invasive nasal tumors, and can be used to distinguish
between fluid or mucus accumulation and soft tissue structures.
Measurements and 3-D reconstructions of CT images can be used to
guide subsequent nasal biopsies, and are used in planning of surgical
approaches and radiation therapy protocols (ch. 213).

One of the major advantages of thoracic CT is the enhanced ability
to detect and localize subtle pulmonary, mediastinal, and thoracic
wall lesions that may contribute to respiratory signs. While the same
5 radiographic opacities (gas, fat, soft tissue, mineral, and metal)
detected in radiographs are also used in CT interpretations, CT not
only provides better contrast between adjacent opacities (e.g.,
between air-filled lungs and airway or chest wall), it also has higher
sensitivity to changes in density within a given opacity. CT is more
sensitive than radiography for the detection of pulmonary nodules.
The limit of detection for pulmonary nodules with radiography is
reported to approach 7-9 mm, while CT can reliably detect nodules
as small as 1 mm,31,32 which makes thoracic CT a preferred method
for lung evaluation when staging results may alter treatment
recommendations.
While CT findings cannot confirm a diagnosis, in some
circumstances, a constellation of specific CT findings can be strongly
correlated with a histologic diagnosis. In human diagnostic imaging,
there exists a set of CT criteria that allow a “reasonably accurate”
diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) with a reduced need
for lung biopsy.33 Similarly, the findings of ground glass opacities,
parenchymal bands, honeycombing, peribronchovascular interstitial
thickening, and traction bronchiectasis, with a predominantly
subpleural distribution of these lesions, would be very strongly
suggestive of canine idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (ch. 217).
Furthermore, the relative severity of these findings on CT may be
correlated with pulmonary functional abnormalities and disease
severity.34,35
The 3-D nature of CT and the ability to obtain thin slices through
respiratory structures also contribute to enhanced localization and
resolution in the lower airways and alveoli. This level of detail makes
CT useful not only in the detection of respiratory abnormalities but
provides a means for the quantification of morphologic pulmonary
lesions. Measurements of airway caliber and bronchial wall thickness
relative to adjacent pulmonary arteries can be used to quantify
bronchial wall alterations in chronic bronchitis and
bronchiectasis.36,37 Thin slice CT images through the pulmonary
airways can be reformatted into virtual bronchoscopic images that

can be used to guide bronchoscopic or surgical intervention.38 The
3-D localization of pulmonary lesions also facilitates the collection of
CT-guided, percutaneous fine-needle aspirates and needle biopsies
of chest wall, pleural, and pulmonary lesions in dogs and cats.39
