Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides resolution of soft tissue
structures greater than that obtained with radiography and CT. It is
superior to radiography in the detection of subtle soft tissue lesions,

including early neoplasms and fungal granulomas, and can be used
to readily distinguish between soft tissue structures and accumulated
fluid or mucus.40,41 MRI performs similarly to CT in the assessment
of chronic nasal disease and nasal neoplasia,42 and may be useful in
differentiating among different types of nasal tumors.40 A limitation
of MRI is that, compared to CT, it is relatively insensitive in detecting
bony or cartilaginous changes in the skull surrounding the nasal
cavity.
Due to technical and practical limitations, MRI is not well-suited
for pulmonary imaging. Most MRI sequences are affected by patient
motion, so regions with inherent motion such as the lower
respiratory system are not suited to standard MRI techniques.
Additionally, gas has very little signal on MRI, so gas-filled regions
like the lungs tend to image poorly on MRI compared to CT.23

Fluoroscopy
Fluoroscopy allows for real-time imaging of dynamic structures in
the upper and lower respiratory tract. Fluoroscopic studies allow for
visualization of the respiratory tract both at rest and during clinical
signs (e.g., coughing), or during or immediately after possible
triggering events (e.g., swallowing, running). Because fluoroscopic
studies of the upper airways can be performed during eating and
drinking of food or liquid mixed with contrast material (swallowing
studies), this imaging modality is most useful in the assessment of
aerodigestive disorders, where the transfer of ingesta across the
pharynx may lead to respiratory symptoms.43 Examples include
documenting nasopharyngeal reflux in patients exhibiting postprandial sneezing or nasal discharge, or documenting
esophagopharyngeal reflux and aspiration as a potential cause of
recurrent bronchopneumonia (ch. 221).
Fluoroscopy is very useful in the detection of dynamic tracheal and
bronchial disease. Fluoroscopy is more sensitive than inspiratory and
expiratory radiography in detecting dynamic collapse of the pharynx,
trachea, carina, and lobar bronchi, and is more accurate in
estimating the magnitude and location of airway collapse.44 Tracheal
and/or bronchial collapse secondary to tracheobronchomalacia can

be evaluated with fluoroscopy during tidal breathing as well as
during an elicited cough (

Video 212.2). Coughing paroxysms can

be elicited with gentle palpation of the cervical trachea. If cough
cannot be easily elicited, then intrathoracic pressure can transiently
be increased by briefly covering the mouth and nose during
expiration. Fluoroscopy also allows the evaluation of the
contribution of cardiomegaly or cardiac movement to intrathoracic
airway collapse.45 Tracheal stents can be placed under fluoroscopic
guidance, and fluoroscopy can be used as a follow-up procedure to
monitor stent function.

Ultrasonography
Because almost all of the generated sound waves are reflected at soft
tissue/air and bone/air interfaces, ultrasound is of limited utility in
the evaluation of mural or intraluminal masses in the upper airway.
However, ultrasonography of the upper respiratory tract can be
beneficial in evaluation of extraluminal masses surrounding or
impinging on the airway. Ultrasound can be useful in determining
both the origin (e.g., thyroid, laryngeal, lymph node) and the nature
(e.g., fluid-filled, solid) of mass lesions around the upper airway.
Ultrasound has also been evaluated as a diagnostic tool for laryngeal
paralysis and tracheal collapse.46,47 In both cases, while ultrasound
is sensitive in documenting morphologic abnormalities consistent
with tracheal collapse and laryngeal paralysis, it is insensitive in
documenting the presence of co-morbidities (e.g., laryngeal collapse,
bronchial collapse) that are important when considering therapeutic
interventions, necessitating the use of additional diagnostic
approaches prior to therapy.
Ultrasound can be used to identify and characterize chest wall and
pleural abnormalities that may impact respiratory function,
including chest wall masses, pleural masses, and pleural fluid.
Ultrasound can be helpful in identifying and characterizing
peripheral lung lesions, including peripheral pulmonary masses,
lung consolidation, atelectasis, and abscesses.48 Ultrasound
guidance can facilitate collection of fine-needle aspirates of
peripheral fluid and solid mass lesions, and can help obtain

percutaneous biopsy samples from peripheral lung, pleural, and
chest wall lesions.49
Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) techniques are cageside or
tableside ultrasound examination protocols. Thoracic POCUS
techniques leverage the limitations of conventional ultrasound
imaging in normal lung and pleural space to screen for pathologic
accumulations of fluid within the pleural space or lesions in the lung
parenchyma. Thoracic Focused Assessment with Sonography for
Trauma (TFAST) is a standardized, limited ultrasound examination
that focuses on the identification and localization of fluid within the
pleural and pericardial spaces. Similarly, Vet BLUE (Bedside Lung
Ultrasound Examination) is a standardized, 9-point ultrasound
examination of the lung designed to screen for pulmonary
parenchymal changes.50,51 In the acute setting, these techniques can
be used to guide patient stabilization efforts, and can offer
preliminary information that can assist in estimate and prognosis
communications with pet owners. Serial POCUS examinations can be
used intermittently to monitor chronic conditions in hospitalized
patients or on an out-patient basis. The reader is directed to ch. 73
for a more extensive coverage of respiratory POCUS techniques in
small animals.

Nuclear Imaging
Nuclear scintigraphy is performed by administering a radionuclide
tagged to a pharmaceutical agent to the patient, and detecting the
radioactive decay as the radionuclide is delivered to the region of
interest. The radionuclide is usually technetium 99m (99mTc), and
the pharmaceutical agent is selected to ensure that the radionuclide
is biologically delivered to the region of interest. Intratracheal or
intranasal deposition of 99mTc has also been used in the assessment
of mucociliary transport in dogs and cats.52,53 For lung parenchymal
disease, radionuclides can be delivered intravenously to provide an
assessment of regional pulmonary perfusion, or can be delivered via
nebulization to assess regional lung ventilation.
Perfusion scans can be used in patients suspected of having
pulmonary thromboembolic disease (PTE, ch. 219). In areas where

nuclear imaging is available, pulmonary vascular scintigraphy
provides a more sensitive and specific method for detection and
localization of PTE than pulmonary angiography.54 However,
because of the cumbersome nature of the test and the requirement
for isolation of potentially critically ill patients, selective pulmonary
angiography is more commonly used for the evaluation of PTE in
companion animal medicine. Combination of simultaneous
ventilation and perfusion scans (V/Q scan) enables the calculation of
regional ventilation-to-perfusion ratios, which can be used to localize
areas of low V/Q within diffuse lung disease. V/Q scans can provide
important information regarding regional lung function prior to
interventional procedures such as lung biopsy or surgical lung
lobectomy, as well as an assessment of the response to therapy. The
primary limitation of nuclear imaging is poor spatial resolution, so
the functional aspects of nuclear imaging are usually combined with
other imaging modalities (e.g., CT) when planning intervention or
monitoring responses to respiratory therapy. From a practical
standpoint, the specialized infrastructural, regulatory, and safety
requirements have largely limited this modality to academic
institutions for research purposes.

ENDOSCOPIC EXAMINATION OF THE
RESPIRATORY TRACT
Endoscopy provides direct visualization of the lumen of the proximal
portions of the respiratory tract. In companion animals, endoscopic
techniques can be used for inspection of the oral cavity, oropharynx,
nasal cavity and nasopharynx, larynx, trachea, and the first several
generations of the bronchial tree, and can also facilitate diagnostic
sampling procedures from the respiratory tract. The indications and
details of these procedures are covered elsewhere in this text (chs.
89 and 93).

DIAGNOSTIC SAMPLING OF THE
RESPIRATORY TRACT

Due to the lack of specificity of physical examination, historical,
radiographic and hematological findings, and because of the
difficulty in performing pulmonary function testing in companion
animal medicine, it is often necessary to collect fluid or tissue
samples directly from the respiratory tract for cytological,
microbiological, or histopathological evaluation. Diagnostic
specimens can be obtained from the nasal airways by swabbing,
brushing, flushing, and closed biopsying. Bronchoalveolar lavage
(ch. 93), endotracheal wash (ch. 93), and transtracheal wash (ch.
93) are techniques used to collect fluid samples from the lower
airways, while a variety of endoscopic, surgical, and thoracoscopic
techniques are available for collection of tissue samples from the
lower respiratory tract. The indications and general techniques for
these procedures are covered in detail elsewhere in this text (chs. 89,
92, and 93).

ARTERIAL BLOOD GAS ANALYSIS
Arterial blood gas analysis is considered the gold standard for
evaluating the gas exchange function of the lung. Oxygenation and
ventilation can both be assessed with arterial blood gas analysis.
Arterial blood samples can be collected from the dorsal pedal
(metatarsal), femoral, coccygeal, sublingual, and aural arteries in
dogs, although the dorsal pedal and femoral are most commonly
used. The dorsal pedal and femoral arteries are typically used for
arterial blood sampling in cats. Arterial blood samples should be
collected in heparinized syringes, and should be capped immediately
after collection to prevent gases dissolved in the plasma from
equilibrating with ambient air.
Arterial blood gas sampling provides accurate measurements of
the partial pressures of oxygen (PaO2) and carbon dioxide (PaCO2) in
arterial blood. Pulmonary oxygenation is assessed by evaluating the
PaO2. Hypoxemia is defined as a PaO2 less than 80 mm Hg.
Differentials for hypoxemia include a low partial pressure of inspired
oxygen (low PiO2), alveolar hypoventilation, ventilation-perfusion
inequality (due to pulmonary disease), right-to-left shunt, and
diffusion impairment (interstitial disease, emphysema). Arterial

blood gas analysis also provides a method for estimating the alveolar
partial pressure of oxygen (PAO2) by using the alveolar gas equation:

where FiO2 = the fraction of inspired oxygen, PB = barometric
pressure in mm Hg, PH2O = water vapor pressure (at body
temperature) in mm Hg, PaCO2 = partial pressure of carbon dioxide
in arterial blood, and RQ = respiratory quotient (ratio of oxygen
consumed and carbon dioxide produced during metabolism of mixed
metabolic fuels; normally 0.8).
The difference between the estimated alveolar partial pressure of
oxygen and the measured arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PAO2 −
PaO2), also referred to as the A-a gradient, is normally <15 mm Hg
in patients breathing room air. Calculation of the A-a gradient
provides a method for quantifying gas exchange dysfunction, and
also provides a means of differentiating among the causes of
hypoxemia. Hypoxemia associated with an elevated A-a gradient is
due to ventilation-perfusion inequality, diffusion barrier, or right-toleft shunt. Hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient is either due to a
low PiO2 (e.g., breathing at altitude) or alveolar hypoventilation, and
suggests that gas exchange function of the lung is normal.
Alveolar ventilation refers to the delivery of CO2 out of the
alveolus. Alveolar ventilation is assessed on an arterial blood gas by
the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood (PaCO2). As
alveolar ventilation is impaired, alveolar (and arterial) CO2 is
retained, and PaCO2 rises above normal (hypoventilation). Common
causes of hypoventilation include central nervous system depression,
airway obstruction, pleural space disease, thoracic wall
abnormalities, and anesthesia. Hypoventilation also occurs as a
compensatory response to a metabolic alkalosis. As alveolar
ventilation increases, CO2 excretion via the lungs increases, and

PaCO2 decreases (hyperventilation). Common causes of
hyperventilation include hypoxemia, central nervous system
stimulation, pain, and excitement. Alveolar hyperventilation can also
occur as a compensatory response to a primary metabolic acidosis.

SUMMARY
The goal of the diagnostic approach to the patient with respiratory
disease is to confirm a specific diagnosis by the least invasive means
possible. The diagnostic plan selected will be dependent upon the
history, signalment, and physical examination findings. An
understanding of the pathophysiology underlying clinical signs and
symptoms will allow the clinician to verify that the clinical signs are
consistent with respiratory disease, to effectively localize the disorder
to a region or regions of the respiratory tract, and to select an
appropriate diagnostic plan for the patient. As more expensive and
invasive diagnostic tests gain consideration, the clinician must be
able to effectively select the appropriate tests for the patient, perform
the tests in the proper sequence, and balance the benefits of each test
with the cost, risk, and potential for confounding or inconclusive
results. As new diagnostic tests emerge and current technologies
evolve, the selection of a rational diagnostic plan requires that the
clinician maintain awareness of the availability and clinical utility of
respiratory diagnostic testing options.

The nose, sinuses, and nasopharynx are central regions in the relatively
young specialty of ear, nose, and throat (ENT) diseases in small animals.
ENT specialization in small animal medicine has become visible only in
about the last 10 years and has become more and more present since
then. Today, it is possible to reliably diagnose and even rediscover
diseases in the ENT field that were largely hidden just a few years ago.
Two outstanding technical innovations have made this possible: crosssectional imaging diagnostics—primarily computed tomography (CT)—
and modern explorative and interventional endoscopy. Additionally,
these two technical innovations have opened up new worlds in the
therapeutic spectrum, the exploration of which is not finished yet.
Interventional endoscopy, in particular, avoids the large, traumatic,
surgical approaches to the head. Instead, the hidden “cavities” in the
head can be reached through the natural orifices of the body. There, it is

even possible to intervene therapeutically under direct, magnifying
visualization.

NOSE
The nasal airways of the dog and cat are both anatomically and
physiologically impressively complex structures. They provide a portal
through which air can stream to three different locations, each serving a
distinct, vital function: (1) intranasally, the ventral nasal concha (concha
nasalis ventralis), for thermoregulation as well as conditioning of air; (2)
intranasally, the ethmoidal conchae (conchae ethmoidales) for olfaction;
and (3) via the caudal nasal-pharyngeal passageways, to the pulmonary
alveoli for gas exchange. Intranasally, however, they are not only simple
passageways but intricate branches of the nasal conchae providing two
huge, functionally different surface areas, serving as active organs of
thermal homeostasis and olfaction.
Each nasal cavity is composed of 4 main functional segments (Figure
213.1). The nasal airway communicates with the paranasal sinuses and
connects caudally to the nasopharyngeal airway. Although the nasal part
of the upper airway has a parallel oral passageway, dogs and cats breathe
predominantly through the nose. The importance of nasal breathing is
often severely underestimated: human noses fulfill two crucial tasks—
respiration and olfaction. Dogs’ and cats’ noses fulfill a third, vital
function—that of thermoregulation.

ANATOMY AND FUNCTIONAL
CONSIDERATIONS OF THE NASALPHARYNGEAL AIRWAY
The nasal-pharyngeal airway can be partitioned into 4 functional
segments between the nares and the intrapharyngeal ostium. This can
be useful both for understanding flow-relevant disorders as well as for a
systematic endoscopic examination or systematic interpretation of crosssectional images. Functional segments of the nose are (1) the nasal
entrance, (2) the respiratory chamber, (3) the olfactory
chamber, and (4) the nasal exit (Figure 231.1). A rostral-to-caudal
overview of the nasal-pharyngeal passageways can be viewed as a CT
study (

Video 213.1) and via anterior rhinoscopy (Video 213.2).

The nasal airway begins with the naris, the visible rostral opening
plane of a short passageway through the nasal vestibule (vestibulum
nasi). It is shaped like a comma, with a vertical broad head and a smaller
curved tail that rotates horizontally and laterally (Figure 213.2). The
nasal vestibule is primarily responsible for distributing the inspired
and expired air and has the highest airway resistance of the upper
airways. Unlike in humans, the canine and feline nasal vestibule is not
empty. It is filled nearly entirely by a voluminous bulb, evolved from the
fusion of the cranial termination of the alar fold (plica alaris) with the
internal part of the nasal wing (ala nasi). It is the most mobile portion of
the nasal entrance (

Video 213.3). The muscle-lined part of the

nasopharynx also actively expands, in synchrony with lateral abduction of
the bulb (Figure 213.2;

Video 213.3). The nasolacrimal duct that

carries lacrimal secretions from the eye opens into the vestibule by an
orifice located rostro-medially to the vestibular bulb (

Video 213.4).

The nasal cavities are separated by the nasal septum. A medial
septal wall, a lateral wall, a roof, and a floor define each nasal passage of
the main nasal chamber. Each nasal cavity is, at least in the rostral part,
divided into 4 air passages: the dorsal, middle, ventral, and common
nasal meatuses. Understanding and differentiating the nasal meatuses
as air passages becomes most obvious in the region caudal to the
vestibule and cranial to the branching of the ventral concha. Here, the socalled 5-folds-view1 clearly explains the relation of the nasal folds with
the nasal meatuses. Moving further caudally, the alar fold branches
widely into the ventral conchae, nearly filling the cross-sectional area of
the nasal cavity and eliminating the contour of all meatuses except for the
dorsal meatus (Figure 213.3). Functionally, the dorsal meatus, located
above the straight fold, turns out to be a bypass for odorant-bearing
inspired air around the complicated structure of the ventral concha
during sniffing for olfaction (Figure 213.1).2,3
Two types of conchae dominate in the nasal cavity; in the middle part
is the huge ventral concha, formerly called the maxilloturbinate
because of its attachment to the maxilla. The caudodorsal part of the
nasal cavity is filled with turbinates that are attached to the cribriform
plate of the ethmoid and therefore called ethmoidal conchae. The two
conchae differ in function: the ventral concha performs the respiratory

functions of thermoregulation and air conditioning and the ethmoidal
conchae have an olfactory function.2,4

FIGURE 213.1 Functional segments of the nasalpharyngeal airway. 1, Nasal entrance: distribution
and regulation of in- and exhaled air. 2, Respiratory
chamber: thermoregulation and conditioning of
inhaled air. 3, Olfactory chamber (with dorsal
meatus): olfaction, the dorsal nasal meatus serves as
bypass during sniffing. Nasal exit (4 & 5). 4,
Nasopharyngeal meatus: connection to
nasopharyngeal airway. 5, Nasopharynx: functional
occlusion during swallowing. Dorsal partition of
Waldeyer’s tonsillar ring and connection to middle ear.
La, Larynx; SF, frontal sinus; SS, sphenoid
sinus.
The nasal exit is formed by the nasopharyngeal meatus,
beginning with a wing of the vomer that crosses dorsally from medial to
lateral and ends caudally with the choanae (Figure 213.4). This
meatus is very delicately constructed: behind the large diameter of the
nasal cavity, the “outlet” is located as a comparatively tiny tube at the
bottom. In small dogs, this is only 1 to 3 mm high (Figure 213.5). This

hole can very easily be obstructed. Dogs and cats can usually compensate
for the functional loss of one opening as, for example, when a tumor is
expanding into the nasopharyngeal meatus. However, as soon as the
contralateral meatus shows the first signs of obstruction as well, nasal
respiration is severely impaired, and clinical signs start becoming
obvious.
Airway mucus plays a vital role in maintaining respiratory
homeostasis. It provides the first line of defense against airborne irritants
in the nasal cavity, and is essential in the mucociliary process, ensuring
that few foreign particles reach the lungs. Not only does its thick
consistency trap foreign particles, but its protein constitution also
contains bactericidal enzymes, thereby reducing the risk of infection.5

THERMOREGULATION IN THE DOG
The lateral nasal gland, more commonly called Steno’s gland,6 is the
largest of the nasal glands. The gland is located submucosally against the
medial wall of the maxilla within the maxillary recess. The functional
significance of the lateral nasal gland is that it is part of the
thermoregulatory system in the dog.7,8 While humans sweat to
evacuate heat from the body, dogs cannot sweat; they pant. But contrary
to common beliefs, dogs do not cool primarily using the surface of
the tongue. Studies have shown that panting dogs inspire through the
nose and expire through the mouth, and this begs quite a different
understanding of why dogs pant.7 The inspired air flows through the
richly vascularized spiral lamellae of the ventral nasal concha. In order
for cooling by evaporation to occur, water is required. The excretory duct
of the lateral nasal gland extends rostrally and opens laterally into the
nasal vestibule (

Video 213.5). Here, the secretion drips into the

gutter-like channel of the antrum of the middle nasal meatus and runs
caudally, driven by the inspired air. Where the plica alaris branches into
the ventral nasal concha, the liquid drips onto the broad ventral concha
and is distributed across the whole surface of this concha by the inspired
air. The liquid can then evaporate rapidly in the strong airflow, producing
cooling by evaporation (

Video 213.6). Reduction of nasal airflow or

thermoregulatory active surface of the ventral concha or both can lead to

serious heat susceptibility, as, for example, in brachycephalic animals
(Figure 213.6).

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS OF NASAL
DISEASE
Clinical signs of nasal disease can vary; they are, however, rarely specific
for the particular underlying cause. Even systemic diseases like bleeding
disorders can cause nasal clinical signs. A thorough medical history can
best be obtained by asking the owner structured questions (chs. 2 and
35).

Sneezing and Reverse Sneezing
Sneezing is a protective reflex. It manifests as an explosive burst of
expiratory airflow that is able to dislodge and expel foreign particles from

the nasal cavities (

Videos 35.4, 35.5). Any cause of nasal mucosal

irritation or nasal discharge is a differential diagnosis for sneezing (ch.
35). Reverse sneezing is defined as a mechanosensitive aspiration
reflex. In spite of the fact that reverse sneezing is not associated with
obstructive dyspnea, dogs may appear to owners as if they are having
extreme air hunger and being close to asphyxia. A wide spectrum of
disorders can cause reverse sneezing, from relatively harmless
abnormalities, such as certain foreign bodies, to very serious disorders,
such as nasal or nasopharyngeal tumors. If frequency, duration, and
intensity of reverse sneezing seem unusual, posterior rhinoscopy should
be recommended (ch. 89) (

Video 213.7).

Nasal Discharge
In contrast to humans, mucopurulent nasal discharge in dogs is
generally not a clinical sign of a transient and self-terminating
rhinosinusitis! Often, owners assume that their pet has a head cold,
that the nasal discharge will resolve spontaneously, and they tolerate
mucopurulent or purulent nasal discharge for a while. However, usually
mucopurulent nasal discharge in dogs has a serious underlying
cause (Table 213.1), that requires intensive and timely diagnostic
testing (Box 213.1) (chs. 35 and 36).
Given the prevalence of nasal cancer in dogs and cats (Table 213.1) as
a cause of nasal discharge, owners can readily understand the importance
of examining their pet under anesthesia for obtaining an accurate
diagnosis. Given the usually short survival time of animals with untreated
nasal tumor, the urgency of advanced diagnostics also can be made very
clear. A combination of endoscopic and computed tomographic
examination, supported by biopsy, is the most useful diagnostic
method.9,10
A positive bacterial culture of a dog or cat’s nasal discharge does not
provide a diagnosis for the primary nasal disease process. Primary
bacterial rhinitis is extremely rare in dogs. Bacterial growth is
almost always secondary. Even the healthy nasal and pharyngeal cavities
are colonized by a large number of bacterial species.11 However, the
finding of a positive culture can be interpreted incorrectly as justification
for initiating antibiotic therapy. Almost always, the nasal discharge then
decreases temporarily, while the underlying disease remains untreated.
Therefore, antibiotic therapy for dogs and cats with nasal discharge in the

absence of a definitive diagnosis is contraindicated because it can lead to
a dramatic worsening of the disease process, e.g., in patients with
sinonasal aspergillosis (ch. 210).

Keep in Mind
• There is no “head cold” in dogs!
• In about one-third of patients, it is a sinonasal malignancy.
• Neither quality, nor laterality, nor duration or bacterial culture of
nasal discharge confirms a diagnosis of nasal disease and none of
this information can replace subsequent advanced diagnostics.
• Positive bacterial culture of the nasal discharge does not provide a
diagnosis for the primary nasal disease process.
• Primary bacterial rhinitis is extremely rare in dogs.
Dos
• In most cases, extended examinations under anesthesia are
indicated, and ideally promptly.
• A combination of endoscopic and computed tomographic
examination is the most useful diagnostic method.
• In case of suspected tumor, a biopsy is mandatory.
• Only endoscopically guided tissue biopsies allow targeted
sampling of suspicious tissue.
• Advanced diagnostics should be performed promptly, since
about one-third of the animals have tumor disease with a short
survival time and relatively late onset of symptoms.
Don’ts
• Antibiotic therapy without a definitive diagnosis is
contraindicated.
• None of the main causes of nasal discharge listed in Table 213.1
could be cured by antibiotic therapy—for some it may even lead to
dramatic exacerbation.

• Focusing on a primarily bacterial cause almost always means a loss
of valuable time.
• Blind nasal biopsies may produce a high rate of false-negative

In brachycephalic dogs, the prevalence of OND appears to be higher
(57%) than in normocephalic dogs, probably because of the malformed
dental arch.10

Airflow Obstruction
Knowing the unique importance of nasal breathing for dogs and cats, one
can conceive of the consequences of nasal airway obstruction. The nose is
provided with such a reserve capacity that a 50% loss of function,
meaning the obstruction of 1 of the 2 nasal cavities, may be tolerated at
rest.12,13 During resting respiration, the nasal cavity accounts for nearly
80% of inspiratory resistance and about 74% of expiratory resistance in
dogs.14 Dogs attempt to complete inspiration through the nose, even
against a high anatomic nasal resistance. Dogs with partial bilateral nasal
obstruction have shown other systemic effects, such as a considerable
loss of body weight.13 Taking this into account and considering the

meaning of nasal thermoregulation, the dog, and probably the cat as well,
should be considered obligatory nose breathers.
Obstruction of the nasal-pharyngeal airway, either as a consequence of
a permanent stenosing process or due to intermittent collapse of the
nasopharyngeal airway, can lead to severe sleeping problems and
subsequent day sleepiness (ch. 244). Owners of affected dogs often
report that the dogs attempt to sleep in a sitting position (

Video

213.34) and experience sleeping pauses of variable length, regularly
interrupted by waking up and gasping for breath.15 This corresponds
quite well to the problem of obstructive sleep apnea in humans16 (see
Brachycephalic Syndrome).

EXAMINATION OF THE NOSE
The diagnostic approach to nasal disease can be challenging. Medical
history and physical examination of the awake patient alone rarely
provide a definitive diagnosis.17 Further means of diagnosis usually
require general anesthesia of the patient. However, a well-planned
combination of clinical examination, diagnostic imaging and endoscopy,
optionally with tissue biopsies, can be a highly successful approach to
establish a diagnosis in over 90% of dogs18 and cats.19

Physical Examination
A thorough medical history is followed by an examination of the external
nose. The symmetry or deformity of the face and the external nose, the
size of the nares, possibly the mobility of the alae nasi (

Video 213.3),

the pigmentation of the planum nasale, the patency of air flow in each
nostril, intraoral abnormalities (ch. 258), and the presence of nasal
discharge are all important features of the external nasal physical
examination (ch. 3). Expiratory puffing of the cheeks might also be
visible, indicating a complete obstruction of the nasal-pharyngeal airway
(

Video 213.8). Stertor or nasal stridor indicates partially obstructed

airway segments within the nasopharynx or the nose, respectively.
However detailed the medical history is that was obtained, and
however thorough the clinical examination of the patient was, in the vast
majority of cases with suspected nasal or nasopharyngeal disease, this

will neither provide a reliable diagnosis nor allow specific treatment in
the awake patient.18,20 It is advisable to communicate this to the owner
early on (ch. 1). Even in the anesthetized patient, many important
structures are more or less hidden behind bony walls inside the skull,
being neither visible nor palpable. Advanced diagnostic tools are often
indispensable to establish a definitive diagnosis.10,18,21,22

Special Diagnostic Procedures
Once the decision has been made for an extended examination under
anesthesia, careful planning is required: which special diagnostic
procedures are available and should be used within the timeframe of
anesthesia, and in which order. The owner should be advised that in
some cases, combining different special examinations might be a better
option to the conventional—and usually preferred—stepwise diagnostic
evaluation. The likelihood of establishing a diagnosis of a specific nasal
disease relies on a combination of techniques, including radiographic
examination (cross-sectional preferred), rhinoscopy (rigid preferred),
cytologic/histopathologic assessment of biopsy samples (endoscopically
guided preferred, and mandatory for suspected tumor) and bacterial
culture only if indicated (for example, in an attempt to establish a
diagnosis of idiopathic rhinitis by exclusion).19,20 The final choice of
diagnostic modalities further depends both on the availability of technical
equipment and on the preferences and means of the owner.

Radiography, CT, and MRI
For many decades, plain film nasal radiographs were a key diagnostic
method in nasal disease. Today, CT and magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) provide significant, additional information and greater diagnostic
sensitivity. However, questions of availability and cost may still be a
limitation. Both CT and MRI allow excellent evaluation of the structures
within the lumen and the tissues adjacent to the nasal cavities, the
nasopharynx, and the paranasal sinuses. Depending on their physical
working principle, the depiction of bone, air and soft tissue is different.
Nasal CT is a powerful tool, and it greatly enhances the ability to establish
an accurate, definitive diagnosis of nasal disease in dogs (

Video

213.1). It provides an accurate assessment of the extent of nasal disease
and readily identifies areas of the nose to examine via rhinoscopy, as well
as suspicious regions to target for biopsy.21 For a comparison of imaging

techniques for dogs with nasal disease, see Table 213.2 and Figure
213.7.17

Rhinoscopy (ch. 89)
Modern, rigid videoendoscopy allows a unique visualization of intranasal
conditions. The immediate differentiation of pathological fluids (mucus,
blood, pus) and effective differentiation between physiological changes of
the nasal mucosa and abnormalities such as rhinitis, foreign bodies,
fungal plaques, cysts, necrosis and tumor-suspected tissue, makes
rhinoscopy the central and indispensable diagnostic method for nasal
diseases (

Videos 213.2, 213.9, 213.10, 213.11, and 213.17).

Rhinotomy
In the past, without today’s possibilities of modern endoscopic
equipment (especially rigid rhinoscopy) and knowledge of intranasal
explorative rhinoscopy, rhinotomy could be a helpful diagnostic tool in
certain cases of nasal disease. However, there is no longer a real
indication for exploratory rhinotomy. Together with modern crosssectional imaging techniques, anterior and posterior rhinoscopy provide
adequate diagnostic coverage (Box 213.2).

DISEASES OF THE NOSE
Stenoses and Obstructions of Nasal Passageways
Hereditary malformations due to excessive breeding selection for
morphological extremes (miniaturization, exaggerated brachycephaly)
can cause obstructions on all three segmental levels—the nasal entrance,
the nasal cavity itself and the nasal exit (Figure 213.5; see Diseases of
the Nasopharynx).

Stenoses of the Nasal Entrance
Injuries of the nasal entrance due to trauma (bite wounds, car accidents,
gunshot injury), chronic ulcerative inflammation (e.g., long-lasting
sinonasal aspergillosis) or surgery at the nasal entrance using excessive
thermal energy (high-frequency surgery, electrocautery, surgical lasers)
can lead to constrictive and stenosing wound healing (Figure 213.8).
Surgical therapy can be challenging due to a high tendency for restenosis.
BOX 2 1 3 . 2 R h inos c op y — F acts and Myt hs

Anterior Rhinoscopy
• Rigid endoscopes are preferable for explorative and interventional
endoscopy.
• 2.7 mm diameter and 0° viewing angle are universally applicable.
• For small dogs and cats a diameter of 1.9 mm is appropriate.
• 30° endoscopes provide an angled view but are more likely to cause
mucosal injury and bleeding than 0° optics.
• If mucus, blood, or pus obstructs vision, suction under visual
control is more effective than irrigation (

Video 213.12).

• Rigid and flexible suction tubes can be used alongside the endoscope.
• Interventional rhinoscopy has enormous potential for both
diagnostic and therapeutic measures.
• Modern endoscopic intervention can replace almost all conventional
open surgery in the nose, sinuses, and nasopharynx.
• With proper equipment and scoping technique,
rhinoscopic exploration can be performed without
bleeding and without the need for nasal irrigation—
regardless of patient size.
Posterior Rhinoscopy
• 120° rigid endoscopes provide excellent image quality and can be
used on all dogs and cats.
• Intervention is possible using curved instruments alongside the
endoscope or simultaneously via the anterior approach.
See

Videos 213.2, 213.9, 213.10, 213.11, and 213.17.

Stenoses of the Nasal Cavity
Causes of intranasal obstruction can be any kind of benign or malignant
mass, including neoplasms, expanding granulation tissue induced by
chronic inflammation, and intranasal cysts of varying origin. Foreign
bodies frequently lodge in the nasal cavity. They rarely obstruct the
intranasal airway due to their size but they do induce inflammation and
purulent discharge, which can lead to complete obstruction of the
affected nasal cavity. Oronasal defects and other diseases causing

purulent rhinitis can lead to intranasal obstruction via the same
pathomechanism (

Video 213.12) (ch. 258). Deviations of the nasal

septum are described in small dog breeds and particularly in
brachycephalic dogs.1,23,24 They are also described in cats.25 In principle,
there should be no rise in intranasal airway resistance over the length of
the nasal cavity as long as the smallest intranasal cross-sectional area is
larger than the cross-sectional area of the nasal entrance (nasal vestibule)
and exit (nasopharyngeal duct).

Stenoses of the Nasal Exit
Because of functional considerations, the stenoses of both the
nasopharyngeal meatus and the nasopharynx are described together (see
Diseases of the Nasopharynx). Treatment is described in ch. 114.

Nasal Foreign Bodies
Various materials have been found lodged in the nasal cavity, mostly
parts of plants or other foreign material. They can enter the nose either
anteriorly by being inhaled via the nares or posteriorly during swallowing
or regurgitation into the nasopharynx or nasal cavity, respectively. If not
immediately expelled by sneezing or removed by reverse sneezing, they
cause direct trauma and irritation of the nasal mucosa. Depending on the
amount of time a foreign body remains lodged and its size and location,
chronic irritation, inflammation, and local tissue destruction may occur.
Nasal foreign bodies often result in an acute onset of sneezing and facial
pawing (

Video 35.5), but they can remain in place for a long period of

time, resulting in chronic nasal discharge. Removal techniques for
nasal foreign bodies vary. In simple cases, the foreign body is
endoscopically detected “at first sight” and can be grabbed with a
small forceps that is introduced alongside a rigid endoscope (
Video 213.13). In any case, a thorough systematic endoscopic exploration
of the nasal cavity is indicated.

Oronasal and Oronasopharyngeal Communications (ch.
258)
Congenital or acquired communications between the oral cavity and the
nose, or oropharynx and nasopharynx, allow food and fluids to enter the
nasal-pharyngeal passageways. Solid particles, if not expelled by the
sneezing reflex or removed by reverse sneezing, can cause pronounced
inflammatory reactions of the nasal-pharyngeal mucosa. Secondary
bacterial infection is common and sometimes even fungal growth can be
observed. Congenital deformities are clefts of the lip and palate.
Palatal defects usually affect the midline; however, lateral clefts can be
seen in the soft palate as well (

Video 213.14). Although the exact

cause of clefting is unknown, it is commonly agreed to be multifactorial
with a hereditary component. A variety of problems can be associated
with facial clefting. Nursing is the major problem of neonates (ch. 146).
Due to the close embryologic, anatomic and physiologic connections of
the nasopharynx and the middle ear, soft palate clefts, especially the
lateral ones, are likely to affect the auditory tube and the middle ear.26-

28

Acquired oronasal communications result from trauma of car
accidents or due to high-rise trauma (cats). Acquired oronasopharyngeal
defects can be the result of oral stick lacerations or complications after
palatal surgery.

Rhinitis
Idiopathic Rhinitis
Idiopathic (lymphoplasmacytic) rhinitis (IR) is a frustrating disease—the
etiology is unclear, the diagnosis difficult to make, the treatment options
often unsatisfactory, and the prognosis for cure unfavorable.
It is one of the most common forms of chronic, non-infectious rhinitis
in dogs and cats and was diagnosed in about 30% of dogs with nasal
discharge.10,18,19,29 It affects predominantly middle-aged, larger dogs,
males and females alike, and normocephalic dogs more often than
brachycephalic. Although there is no known cause and no definite
triggers, infectious, allergic, and immune-mediated mechanisms are
suspected.22,29-34 The clinical signs are often indistinguishable from
those of other nasal diseases, although nasal or facial deformity does not
occur. It is an important differential diagnosis for chronic nasal discharge
in dogs and cats (ch. 35). Nasal discharge is the most common clinical
complaint and may be unilateral or bilateral and of variable quality.
Other signs may include sneezing, reverse sneezing, cough, nasal stridor,
and respiratory problems. There is usually little or no disturbance of the
patient’s general condition and vital signs.10,29,30,35 The diagnosis is a
diagnosis of exclusion. Advanced diagnostics on the anesthetized
patient using CT, endoscopy, bacteriological, mycological, and
histopathological examinations are required to rule out other causes of
nasal discharge.9,10,36 Treatment can be extremely frustrating and
often yields little or only temporary success.9,30 There is no commonly
accepted therapy protocol; therapy has to be individualized for each
patient and frequently readjusted. Secretolytic medications, supportive
care, long-term administration of antibiotics with immunomodulatory
activity, in combination with corticosteroids or nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, desensitization and immunosuppression have all
been described.29,31,34,37,38
Clinical signs may recur even after successful therapy. If left untreated,
idiopathic rhinitis shows a progressive character and may lead to further

severe sequelae in the upper and lower respiratory tract.34

Fungal Rhinitis
See ch. 210.

Bacterial Rhinitis
Primary bacterial rhinitis is uncommon in both dogs and cats. In dogs,
bacterial rhinitis occurs most commonly as a sequela to the presence of a
foreign body or as a consequence of gross anatomic changes resulting
from prior mycotic disease, trauma, or irradiation.39 In such cases,
antibiotics may temporarily improve clinical signs, giving a false
impression of therapeutic success.

Allergic Rhinitis
Allergic rhinitis is either an unusual or an underdiagnosed condition
in small animals. There are sporadic reports of rhinitis of presumptive
allergic basis in the dog and cat. Such animals present with oculonasal
discharge, sneezing, nose rubbing or head shaking, and significant
numbers of eosinophils can be demonstrated in nasal exudate or nasal
lavage fluid and infiltrating the nasal mucosa on tissue biopsy.30,40

Viral Rhinitis
Viral upper airway infections in cats and canine distemper are discussed
in chs. 205 and 204, respectively.

Parasitic Rhinitis
Parasites that can cause clinical signs of rhinitis are potentially zoonotic
pathogens.41 The most common parasites are Pneumonyssoides
caninum; Capillaria species, such as Eucoleus boehmi (Capillaria
boehmi); and Linguatula serrata. Most infections are subclinical or
associated with mild clinical signs such as head shaking, pawing at the
nose, chronic nasal discharge, sneezing, reverse sneezing, or evidence of
an impaired sense of smell. The diagnosis is made using rhinoscopy to
visualize the adult parasites, or by identifying the eggs of Linguatula or
Capillaria on fecal samples (ch. 80). The success of antiparasitic therapy
is somewhat controversial. In general, after treatment with an
appropriate antiparasitic agent, the prognosis is good.42-47

Sinonasal Malignancies
Malignant sinonasal tumors are an insidious disease. Clinical signs
appear late, often seem harmless initially, and are often indistinguishable
from those of other nasal diseases. Advanced diagnostic evaluations are
necessary, a cure is rarely possible, and the long-term prognosis is
usually poor.
Nasal and paranasal sinus tumors are common neoplasms in dogs and
they often represent a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge due to being
confined to the nasal cavities.48 Although they constitute only about 2%
of all canine tumors, the prevalence is as high as 10% in oncology clinics
and sinonasal tumors are among the third most common indications for
treatment in radiation centers.49,50 Approximately one-third of all
dogs9,10,18,22,33 and 40% of cats19,51-53 with nasal discharge have nasal
neoplasia. Eighty to 90% of nasal masses are malignant. They are
primarily locally invasive; metastasis is uncommon, and when it occurs, it
does so late in the course of the disease. In dogs, two-thirds of nasal
tumors are carcinomas, most commonly adenocarcinomas. One-third are
sarcomas, most commonly chondrosarcomas (

Video 213.16),

fibrosarcomas, osteosarcomas and undifferentiated/anaplastic
sarcomas.54-57 Hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325), mast cell tumor (ch. 327),
and transmissible venereal tumor (ch. 330) are rare nasal tumors in
dogs. Nasal tumors occur mostly in middle-aged and old dogs, but dogs
of all ages can be affected. The etiology is unknown. In cats, lymphoma
(ch. 322) and adenocarcinoma are the most common tumors of the
nasal cavity.19,58,59

Clinical Signs
Common clinical signs are sneezing and stertor (ch. 35), nasal
discharge, epistaxis (ch. 36), and reduced nasal airflow.55,60,61 Signs
may be intermittent at first and progress from unilateral to bilateral.
With an initial unilateral nasal obstruction, breathing problems may not
become apparent to the owner until the mass has grown through a
nasopharyngeal meatus and extends behind the septum into the
contralateral meatus (Figure 213.9). Breathing problems may then first
become obvious during sleep. Cases with advanced disease may also
present with facial deformity and neurological signs.62,63 Tumors of the

nasal cavity may invade into the ipsilateral frontal sinus or at least
obstruct the flow of mucus from the sinus.58

Differential Diagnosis

Differential diagnoses include oronasal defect, idiopathic rhinitis,
sinonasal aspergillosis and intranasal foreign bodies.9,10,18,33 Most nasal
diseases share similar clinical signs—initially often considered harmless.

Diagnosis
A reliable diagnosis can only be obtained after advanced examinations
under anesthesia. Usually, a computed tomographic scan is followed
by endoscopically guided biopsies of suspicious tissues.
Histopathological examination of tissue samples is of central importance
and indispensable. In particular, biopsy technique is often responsible for
success or failure and misdiagnosis. The traditionally accepted
techniques of blind biopsy are responsible for a high number of
misdiagnoses. Many neoplasms are initially erroneously diagnosed as
inflammatory disease.55,64 Therefore, it is crucial that an appropriate
biopsy technique ensure that the actual tumor tissue is sampled and not
peritumoral, inflammatory tissue or portions of regular conchae. This
requires sampling under direct endoscopic view of the intranasal
tissue.38 In addition, blind biopsies often result in unnecessary tissue
damage and hemorrhage because malignant tumors of the nose are often
surrounded by larger vessels and located in the area of the ethmoidal
conchae, directly adjacent to the cribriform plate and the delicate
structures of the nasal exit. With the rigid endoscopic equipment
available today, endoscopically guided biopsies should be considered the
new standard (Box 213.3).
BOX 2 1 3 . 3 A dv antage s o f Endos cop ic all y Gu id e d
Biop s y in S u s p e c te d Sinonas al Tu mors
Sampling of suspicious tissue under direct endoscopic visual guidance
can ensure with a high degree of probability that:
• a sample is taken that actually contains representative tissue
• the risk of misdiagnosis by mistakenly sampling peritumoral tissue is
minimized
• the risk of accidental injury to large vessels and bleeding
complications is minimized
• structures whose integrity ensures a functioning nasal passage are
not injured, thus avoiding adhesions and obstructions

• perforations of the septum are avoided in cases of congenital or
tumor mass-induced deviation

Therapy
The overall median survival in 139 dogs with untreated nasal carcinomas
was 3.1 months.65 However, regardless of the therapy chosen—
irradiation, chemotherapy, or surgical tumor ablation—a complete cure
of sinonasal tumors is rarely possible. Usually, only a prolongation of
survival time can be achieved.

Radiation Therapy (RT)
A tumor prescription of 42-54 Gy in 10-15 fractions is considered the
most effective means of achieving local control of canine sinonasal
tumors, with median survival ranging from 8 to 19.7 months.66-73 As in
humans, dose to tumor within the nasal cavity is limited by the tolerance
of the eyes and brain. Although increased sparing of normal tissue occurs
with modern radiation techniques and protocols for canine sinonasal
tumors, there is little improvement in tumor control or long-term
survival.66 Regardless of the protocol pursued (definitive or palliative;
stereotactic or not), median survival times have not improved. Control of
sinonasal tumors by RT appears to be limited because most local failures
and residual disease occur in the main area of the original tumor mass,
i.e., within the irradiation field, and most dogs ultimately die from local
disease progression.74

Chemotherapy
Chemotherapy as a sole therapy for nasal tumors is not recommended.
Several studies describe combinations with RT as adjuvant therapy.
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are currently in focus and further interesting
findings are expected.75,76 In recent years electrochemotherapy has also
been described.77-81

Surgical Therapy
In humans, the gold standard of treatment for sinonasal tumors is
resection of the tumor mass followed by radiotherapy. Endoscopic
surgery is gaining more and more importance.82,83 In dogs, the initial

failures of open surgical treatment of nasal tumors led to widespread
rejection of surgical therapy.84,85 Since then, RT has appeared to be the
only accepted therapeutic procedure for nasal tumors in dogs. However,
there are recent developments of modified, endonasal endoscopic tumor
ablation. The removal of the tumor is performed through the natural
nasal orifice exclusively under continuous endoscopic control (

Video

213.16).86 This makes it possible to remove all visible tumor areas, to
spare essential intranasal structures and, if necessary, to restore a
functional nasal-pharyngeal airway by appropriate techniques. It shows
alternative ways of a predominantly palliative therapy, which can help to
reverse limitations on the patient’s quality of life starting with the very
first treatment. Other advantages include a low surgical complication
rate, extensive removal of the main tumor mass, and absence of sideeffects of RT or chemotherapy.

Future Perspectives
It seems that survival times cannot be significantly increased any further
using current RT techniques.66 Therefore, a first future focus in the
treatment of sinonasal tumors should be directed additionally towards a
significantly improved early detection of the disease. Canine
patients with a nasal tumor can be expected to have an extremely short
survival time after the time of diagnosis if the diagnosis is made late in
the course of disease, as it often is currently. Therefore, it seems
particularly important to make this diagnosis at the earliest possible
time. However, many animals with nasal tumors are evaluated and
treated based on a presumptive diagnosis of an inflammatory or
infectious cause, often for several months, before a final, correct
diagnosis is made in a referral clinic.
The second future focus should be directed towards a
reconsideration of the entire available spectrum of therapeutic
means and their possible combinations. The standard human
medicine approach should also be considered and initial interventional
targeted surgical debulking of tumor tissue, alone or in combination,
should be given due consideration.82,83

Non-Malignant Nasal Masses

Non-malignant nasal masses are uncommon. Benign tumors, e.g.,
angioleiomyomas87 (

Video 213.15), angiofibromas,88 other

miscellaneous tissues, e.g., hamartoma89-92; intranasal cysts; and
inflammatory granulation tissue can expand intranasally. They can
obstruct the nasal passageways completely (

Video 213.18).

NASOPHARYNX
ANATOMY AND FUNCTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS
The nasal portion of the pharynx extends from the choanae to the
intrapharyngeal ostium (Figure 213.1). While the lumen of the rostral
part is completely bound and protected against compression or collapse
by bony structures (hard palate, vomer, and palatine bones), the middle
part is only dorsally (skull base) and laterally (hamuli of the pterygoid)
protected by a bony boundary, and the lumen of the caudal part only
dorsally (skull base). The non-bony walls are formed by palatopharyngeal
muscles, and therefore are susceptible to compression from outside or
collapse due to negative intraluminal pressure. Nearly all the muscles of
the pharynx and the soft palate serve as constrictors, protecting the nasal
airways from aspiration of food or fluids during swallowing. Only a few
(stylopharyngeus and tensor veli palatini muscles) keep the lumen of the
soft part of the nasopharynx open.93,94 The muscle-lined part of the
nasopharynx dilates actively and in synchrony with the abduction of the
nasal wings (

Video 213.3). Pathological collapsibility of the

nasopharynx is a major problem in brachycephalic animals and will be
discussed below. Functionally, the nasopharynx is important for
breathing and swallowing. During swallowing, the pharynx closes
completely, whereas it must be open during nasal breathing. Because of
these antagonistic tasks, collapsibility of the pharyngeal wall is precisely
regulated by complicated neuromuscular mechanisms.95 However, in
dogs, the functional separation of respiratory and feeding activities might
be lost. There is evidence that dogs cannot breathe during lapping or
mastication, and it is suggested that this might be due to specializations
of the soft palate and epiglottis in order to enable thermal panting.96

Connection Between the Nasopharynx and the Middle
Ear
There is an important and complex connection between the
nasopharynx and the middle ear. Embryologically, the lumen of the
middle ear is an extension of the pharynx. The auditory tube (Eustachian
tube) connects the middle ear cavity with the nasopharynx. Opening and
closing functions of the Eustachian tube are both physiologically and
pathologically important. Normal opening of the Eustachian tube
equalizes atmospheric pressure in the middle ear; closing of the
Eustachian tube protects the middle ear from nasopharyngeal secretions.
Mucociliary clearance drains mucus away from the middle ear into the
nasopharynx, thus preventing infection from ascending to the middle ear.
Usually, the Eustachian tube is closed; it opens during actions such as
swallowing, yawning, or sneezing, and thereby permits equalization of
middle ear and atmospheric pressures. Only the tensor veli palatini
muscle induces active dilation/opening of the tube during each act of
swallowing.97,98 (

Video 213.19)

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS OF
NASOPHARYNGEAL DISEASE
Clinical signs of nasopharyngeal disorders can vary considerably because
the nasopharynx is directly connected to three different systems: rostrally
to the respiratory system of the nose, caudally to the oropharynx and
thereby to the intersection of the respiratory pathway and the digestive
system, and dorsolaterally via the Eustachian tube to the middle ear.
Accordingly, clinical signs can be of a respiratory, digestive, or
otological/neurological nature, or a mixture thereof. Typical signs are
difficult, noisy, and in particular stertorous breathing; reverse sneezing;
nasal discharge; expiratory cheek puff (indicating complete obstruction
of the nasal-pharyngeal airway) (

Video 213.8); retching; and

vestibular signs when together with Eustachian tube dysfunction.
The lumen of the nasopharynx can either be too small (up to totally
obstructed), or “too open” because the closing mechanisms fail during
feeding and drinking (velopharyngeal insufficiency). Breathing problems
predominate if the nasopharyngeal lumen is obstructed (polyp, tumor,
stenosis, brachycephalic malformation, dynamic collapse). If

nasopharyngeal closure is incomplete due to congenital or acquired
palatal defects (cleft palate, palatal fistulas after stick-induced wounds, or
complications after palatal surgery), nasal discharge, digestive and/or
middle ear problems dominate the clinical picture. In such situations,
and similar to oronasal communications, food and fluids are pressed into
the lumen of the nasopharynx during swallowing and, from there, into
the nasal cavities, causing local foreign body reactions and nasal
discharge.

EXAMINATION OF THE NASOPHARYNX
In the conscious dog, physical examination of the nasopharynx is more or
less impossible. With the exception of fluoroscopy for swallowing studies
(chs. 47, 221, 259), decisive diagnostic procedures for this area require
general anesthesia. Initially, the soft palate is inspected orally. Digital
palpation starts rostrally between the pterygoid boundaries and advances
caudally. Advanced diagnostic tools like endoscopy and/or crosssectional imaging are often indispensable to establish a definitive
diagnosis.

Endoscopy
Endoscopic examination is the key diagnostic tool for the
nasopharynx (chs. 89 and 107). It can be performed with both rigid and
flexible endoscopes, depending on the examiner’s preference. Endoscopic
access is possible from both directions. In dogs and cats, nasopharyngeal
access is usually obtained caudally/posteriorly through the oral cavity
(rigid, 120°, 4 mm, or flexible) (

Video 213.17) and in most dogs also

rostrally/anteriorly through one of the nasal cavities (rigid, 0° [or 30°],
2.7 or 1.9 mm) (

Video 213.2). The anatomic landmarks that

should be recognized are listed in Videos 213.2 and 213.17. Even minor
manipulations within the nasopharynx are very irritating and can
provoke strong reactions, particularly in cats. A potent analgesic
component should be part of the anesthetic regimen. The instillation of a
local anesthetic is usually helpful.

Computed Tomography

If a nasopharyngeal mass is palpable or endoscopically visible, or an
association with a lesion of the middle ear is suspected, a CT examination
is highly recommended. CT gives information on the extension of a mass
and on possible relations to the tympanic bulla. Wrong positioning
during CT examination can obscure certain lesions. Recommendations
on how to position patients with suspected nasal-pharyngeal disease for
CT examination are listed in

Video 213.1.

DISEASES OF THE NASOPHARYNX
Because of functional considerations, stenoses of the nasopharyngeal
meatus (as part of the nose) and of the nasopharynx are described
together. Obstruction can occur as a congenital malformation or
secondary to a foreign body, obstructive wound healing after local
inflammation with mucosal ulceration, or an expanding mass.

Stenosis and Obstruction of the Nasopharyngeal Meatus
The nasopharyngeal duct can be obstructed at one or more of three
levels: (1) the most rostral point, which is underneath the wing of the
vomer; (2) the tubular canal itself; and (3) the bilateral caudal openings
of the meatus, the choanae (Figure 213.4).

Hereditary Malformations
Ongoing breeding for exaggerated miniaturization seems to disrupt the
anatomical balance between bony boundary and the size of the soft
tissues. In toy breeds like the Chihuahua, Pomeranian, and Shi Tzu, the
vomerine alae can be too large in relation to the lumen, leaving a
passageway of only 1 mm or less (Figure 213.5).

Obstruction of the Lumen
Various disorders can lead to an isolated obstruction within one or both
lumina of the nasopharyngeal meatus. Examples of non-malignant
conditions are trauma to the skull base, rhinoliths99 and hamartoma
(Figure 213.10). Choanal atresia is rarely reported in dogs and
cats.100,101 It results from an embryological resorption failure of the
oronasal membrane that occludes the nasopharyngeal meatuses
unilaterally or bilaterally. The defect can be bony, membranous, or a

mixture of both.102 It is probably very difficult to differentiate between
true choanal atresia and obstructing scar tissue resulting from ulceration
of mucosal tissue at this location (foreign body, regurgitation into the
nasopharynx, infection) (

Video 213.20).

Stenosis and Obstruction of the Nasopharynx
Nasopharyngeal stenosis can occur as a congenital anomaly comparable
to choanal atresia or as a consequence of constrictive wound healing
resulting from an inflammatory condition, surgery, or trauma. In
addition, the lumen can be obstructed by intra- or extraluminal
expanding lesions. Intraluminal reasons can be inflammatory polyps or
foreign bodies. Examples of extraluminal reasons include expanding
lesions from the middle ear like extravasating infections causing
inflammation and swelling of the peribullar tissue, or other spaceoccupying lesions like cholesteatoma,103 intrapalatal masses, or
subepithelial cysts104-106 (Figure 213.11).

Treatment of Nasopharyngeal Stenosis
Various methods of treatment have been reported, including surgical
mucosal advancement107 and balloon dilatation (ch. 114).104,108 The
need for repeated interventions and the occurrence of complications have
been reported for all of these techniques—the greatest problem being the
recurrence of the stenosis. A promising treatment in cats and dogs with
soft tissue stenoses seems to be the use of a removable silicone stent.109
For cats, the investigators described a very simple technique for opening
the stenosis and preventing re-stenosis with an equally simple technique,
leaving no foreign material inside the patient. Potentially serious
complications such as palatal erosions and oronasal fistulas resulting
from permanent stenting can thus be avoided.110 However, even with
temporary stenting, the function of the auditory tube should be kept in
mind. Any occlusion of the nasopharyngeal openings of the Eustachian
tube leads immediately to a secondary secretory otitis media.

Malignant and Non-malignant Nasopharyngeal Masses
Nasopharyngeal Neoplasia

Lymphoma and adenocarcinoma are the most common nasal tumors in
cats. 10% were found to be isolated tumors of the nasopharynx; a further
8% involved both nasopharyngeal and nasal tissue.106,111

Nasopharyngeal Inflammatory Polyps
Nasopharyngeal inflammatory polyps are non-neoplastic masses,
developing either from inflamed mucosa of the middle ear or the auditory
tube. The cause of inflammatory polyps is unknown, and chronic
inflammation, ascending pharyngeal infection, congenital origin, and
association with feline calicivirus have all been implicated.112 They
usually occur in younger cats. Polyps either extend through the auditory
tube into the nasopharynx (nasopharyngeal polyp) or from the bulla
tympanica through the eardrum into the external ear canal (aural polyp).
When polyps grow within the lumen of the nasopharynx, respiratory
signs increase gradually, starting with occasional stertor and possibly
leading to a complete obstruction of the nasopharyngeal airway. At this
stage, expiratory cheek puff or open-mouth breathing and nasal
discharge (even mucopurulent when secondary bacterial infection) can be
seen. Owners report increasing breathing problems and restlessness,
especially during sleep or attempts to fall asleep. When the polyp grows
in size within the tympanic bulla, Horner’s syndrome and vestibular signs
can be seen (ch. 248). When expanding from the tympanic bulla through
the eardrum into the external ear canal, they cause signs of otitis externa
with otorrhea and head shaking. Large aural polyps can be visible as a
mass in the external ear canal. Direct visualization of many feline
nasopharyngeal polyps is possible during an anesthetized transoral exam
with a spay hook to retract the soft palate rostrally and a dental mirror.
However, CT is an excellent imaging tool for the supportive diagnosis of
nasopharyngeal polyps in cats and it can identify concurrent middle ear
disease, which is present in a majority of cases. Nasopharyngeal polyps
are treated by slow traction avulsion. After that, mucus or pus inside the
Eustachian tube should be removed with a curved suction pipe attached
under videoscopic control to the usually dilated opening of the auditory
tube (

Video 213.21) (ch. 82). The tympanic bulla should be

examined, ideally with CT or endoscopically. All remnants of polyp tissue
within the tympanic bulla should be carefully removed by otoendoscopic
intervention. The recurrence rate of inflammatory polyps seems to be
lower when the patient is treated with corticosteroids.113

Nasopharyngeal Cysts
Nasopharyngeal cysts of varying origins and locations can obstruct the
cranial nasopharynx and even totally obliterate the lumen. The causes of
cyst formation are not fully understood; possible congenital reasons are
(1) a pharyngeal bursa of Luschka,114 (2) a Thornwaldt’s cyst114-116 or (3)
a cyst of Rathke’s pouch.114,117 Acquired conditions can be retention cysts
of the seromucinous glands.114

Nasopharyngeal Foreign Bodies
Foreign bodies usually enter the nasopharynx caudally/posteriorly and
lodge in the middle or rostral segment. Predominant clinical signs are

reverse sneezing (

Video 213.7, ch. 35), and seldom nasal discharge.

In cats, often a blade of grass is hooked with its rough surface to the
mucosa. Posterior rhinoscopy (ch. 89) allows a fast and reliable
diagnosis. Extraction of foreign bodies from the rostral nasopharynx can
be challenging. A curved forceps is used under endoscopic control (
Video 213.22). Foreign bodies remaining undiscovered for a longer time
may cause inflammation and serious tissue damage with subsequent
nasopharyngeal stenosis.

Nasopharyngeal Closing Failure
Congenital palatal defects result when the two palatine shelves fail to
fuse during fetal development.118 Acquired defects of the soft palate
can result after stick-wounds or palatal surgery (ch. 258).

PARANASAL SINUSES
ANATOMY AND FUNCTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS
The reason for the presence of the paranasal sinuses has been a
controversial subject for 1800 years, since the time of Galen, 130-201
A.D.119 Among many other theories, the following have been discussed
for both humans and animals: absorbing shock applied to the head for
protection of sensory organs, thermally insulating the nervous centers,
and lightening the bones of the skull for maintenance of proper balance
of the head.120 In human medicine, the discovery that paranasal sinuses
produce nitric oxide (NO) has altered the traditional explanations of
sinus physiology.121 Endogenous NO is continually synthesized in the
respiratory epithelium and plays a key role in the physiological regulation
of airway functions. NO is upregulated and has diverse roles as a
modulator of ciliary function, neurotransmission, bronchodilation,
vasodilatation, platelet aggregation and immune function.122,123 Even its
potential benefits against COVID-19 infection are discussed.124,125
The frontal sinus, the sphenoid sinus and the maxillary recess are all
lined with mucosa and are connected to the middle nasal meatus. In
dogs, the frontal sinus is divided into three different parts (lateral,
medial, and rostral) and connects to the nasal cavity through a

nasofrontal opening. Ectoturbinates, covered with olfactory mucosa, can
extend into the frontal sinus. In brachycephalic animals, the frontal sinus
can either be much reduced in size or even absent altogether. A small
sphenoid sinus is largely occupied by endoturbinate IV. The lumen of
the maxillary recess is usually empty. The lateral nasal gland lies
submucosally against the medial wall of the maxilla within the maxillary
recess. In the cat, there is only one frontal sinus on each side, the
maxillary recess is small, and there is a large sphenoid sinus that extends
caudally from the nasal cavity into the sphenoid bone, ventrally to the
brain.93,126

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS OF
PARANASAL SINUSOIDAL DISEASE
Sinusoidal disorders may be primary and confined to the paranasal
sinuses, may simultaneously affect the nasal cavity and sinuses, or may
be secondary to drainage obstruction of mucus due to nasal disease.
Common clinical signs are nasal discharge of varying character and
consistency (ch. 35). Smaller amounts of discharge may remain
undiscovered as they can be swallowed. Severe cases may be associated
with visible loss of symmetry or deformity of the face.

EXAMINATION OF THE PARANASAL
SINUSES
The paranasal sinuses are not accessible for clinical examination in the
awake patient. Diagnosis requires general anesthesia, diagnostic imaging,
and endoscopy with tissue biopsies if indicated. Due to their
caudal/posterior location and subtle presenting signs, isolated sinusoidal
lesions have often been missed in the past and were reported as rare
occurrences. However, with the availability of endoscopy, CT, and MRI,
diseases of the paranasal sinuses are now more frequently diagnosed.127
Studies determining the value of rhinoscopy, radiography, and CT of the
head for evaluation of canine nasal and paranasal diseases show that
rhinoscopy and rhinoscopy combined with CT contribute significantly to
obtaining a diagnosis20 (

Videos 213.23, 213.24, and 213.25).

DISEASES OF THE PARANASAL SINUSES
The best studied and most commonly described diseases are those
affecting the frontal sinus: aspergillosis, tumors, idiopathic rhinitis,
and cysts. For the sphenoid sinus, tumors and cysts have been
described and for the maxillary recess, aspergillosis and tumors have
been described. Sinonasal malignancies and idiopathic rhinitis can
involve the paranasal sinuses (see above).

Sinonasal Aspergillosis
The best known sinonasal disease is the infection of nasal and sinusoidal
cavities with Aspergillus spp. Usually, the frontal sinus is affected but
large fungal masses can fill the maxillary recess as well (

Videos 210.1,

210.2, 213.26) (ch. 210).

Cysts of the Paranasal Sinuses
Cysts of the paranasal sinuses are usually mucous retention cysts. They
can be appreciated on routine cross-sectional examinations and are often
subclinical. The major concern lies in differentiating them from
malignant diseases. The mucous retention cyst is found within the
sphenoid sinus infrequently in brachycephalic and miniature breeds and
seems to be comparable to similar cysts in humans128 (

Video

213.27).

BRACHYCEPHALIC SYNDROME
Brachycephaly is an intentionally-bred hereditary disease in dogs and
cats. To emphasize certain characteristic malformations of the head, this
genetic defect has been selected for centuries. From the very beginning of
pedigree dog breeding, there has been a greatly exaggerated selection for
this trait, with very negative consequences for animal welfare.
Brachycephalic syndrome is an early-onset, lifelong, ultimately
deteriorating, and debilitating syndrome characterized predominantly by
respiratory impairment.15,129,130 However, far beyond the original term
brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome, referring solely to
obstructed airways, today almost all organ systems are known to
be affected by breeding-related malformations with a high impact

on animal welfare: airway obstructions (Box 213.4), skull,131-134
ophthalmic disorders,135-137 ear disorders,138-142 brain disorders,143
spinal disease,144-146 oral/dental disorders,147 gastrointestinal
disorders,148-151 reproductive disorders,152,153 orthopedic disorders,154157
and skin disorders.158,160 This multiplicity of disorders is probably
more aptly defined by the term brachycephalic syndrome.

Many popular dog breeds are affected, e.g., Bulldog breeds, Pug, and
Boston Terrier. Popular brachycephalic cat breeds are Persian, Exotic
Shorthair, Scottish Folds and Himalayan. Especially in smaller dog
breeds, adult animals show typical characteristics of young animals
addressing the baby scheme in many owners.161 In larger
brachycephalic breeds in the Middle Ages, the short muzzle and powerful
bite were intended to ensure that the dogs could breathe freely when they
set and held wild boars or bears on the big game hunt. Later, these
physically strong and extremely powerful dogs were abused in a cruel
blood sport called bull baiting, which was only banned at the beginning
of the 19th century. These tasks demanded a maximum of exercise
tolerance. Today, most brachycephalic dog breeds are described first
and foremost as suffering from pronounced exercise intolerance due
to impaired breathing.
The reason for this dramatic development is an exaggerated
breeding for a snub-nosed appearance. The shift from functional to
esthetic selection pressure, according to written breeding standards of
various kennel clubs, has malformed the entire upper respiratory tract in
these breeds, leading to a series of consecutive airway stenoses. A head
conformation that is demanded to be “round” (breeding-standard Pug) or

“square” (breeding-standard Bulldog breeds) is per se incompatible with
healthy, functional upper airways. However, a pervading acceptance of
airway disorders as “normal for the breed” may constrain reforms
intended to improve the welfare of affected breeds by “blinding”
breeders, owners, and even veterinarians to the welfare impacts of these
disorders.15,162-164 The fact that brachycephaly is a purely humanly
created disorder with massive consequences on quality of life must raise
the question of whether these animals should be bred any
longer.15,129,130,163

PATHOANATOMY AND FUNCTIONAL
CONSEQUENCES OF A MULTILEVEL
OBSTRUCTION
Originally, the typical cause of respiratory distress was seen as being
threefold: stenotic nares, an elongated soft palate and, in some dogs,
everted laryngeal ventricles (laryngoceles). However, ongoing excessive
selection for brachycephaly clearly has changed and deformed the entire
upper respiratory tract. Box 213.4 lists both well-known and previously
less well-recognized anatomical constrictions in the upper airways.

Stenosis at the Nasal Entrance
The stenosis of the canine nasal entrance seems to be influenced by three
different factors: a first and well-described stenosis is the visible opening
plane into the nasal vestibule. The naris is compressed to a small slit
(Figure 213.12;

Video 213.28). A second stenosis is hidden behind

the first stenosis and usually invisible from the outside (Figure 213.12;
Video 213.29). Finally, as third stenotic factor, there is the
immobility of the bulb. This functional restriction further reinforces the
anatomical stenosis165-169 (

Video 213.3). In cats, the stenosis of the

nasal entrance is the clinically most relevant malformation.

Stenosis Inside the Nasal Cavity and the Nasal Outlet
Various mechanisms contribute to brachycephalic intranasal airway
obstruction. First, the nasal cavity itself is far too small for the given

contents (Figure 213.6).24,93 Second, the conchae of brachycephalic
dogs are macroscopically1,24,170 and
microscopically171 malformed and grow aberrantly into airconducting spaces as rostral and caudal aberrant turbinates (RAT and
CAT, respectively),1,172 obstructing their lumina and causing a rise in
intranasal airway resistance173,174 (Figures 213.3 and 213.13). Third,
intranasal mucosal contact points contribute to the elevation of
intranasal airway resistance170 (Figure 213.13;

Video 213.29).

Failure to address intranasal obstruction might be an explanation for the
lack of therapeutic success after conventional surgery for the
brachycephalic syndrome.

FIGURE 213.12 Stenoses of nares and nasal
vestibule. Videoscopic and CT images of the nasal
entrance in (A) a healthy normocephalic dog (German
Shepherd) and (B) a French Bulldog. A1, Normal width

Videos 213.28 and 213.29)

Pharyngeal Obstruction—the “Meat-in-the-Box” Model

Several factors contribute to the obstruction of the nasopharynx in a very
complex mechanism. In general, this can be described as an anatomical
imbalance of the upper airway with too much soft tissue for a given
maxillomandibular enclosure size.165,168,175-179 A mechanical model, the
“Meat-in-the-Box” model, can provide a better understanding of its
functional importance95,180 (Figure 213.14). The craniofacial
malformation in brachycephalic dogs gives rise to a series of factors that
either constrict the lumen of the nasopharynx or cause it to
collapse1,147,177,178,181-185 (Box 213.5; Figure 213.15 and Figure
213.16;

Video 213.30).

All the factors mentioned in Box 213.5 cause constriction of the
nasopharynx due to compression from the outside. However, there are
also factors that cause functional collapse of the tube due to
negative pressure in the airways during inspiration. If collapse occurs
rhythmically, the tube walls clap together, producing a typical noise:
snoring. If there is an elevated, pathological negative pressure in the
pharynx, the causative stenosis must be located rostrally, in the nose.
This is where the typical stenoses in brachycephalic dogs occur: (a)
stenosis of the outer nares, (b) stenosis of the nasal vestibule and (c)
stenosis of the intranasal airways due to hypertrophic and dysplastic
conchae. Mathematically, halving the radius of the airways raises
resistance 16-fold. In brachycephalic animals, particularly strong
negative pressure has to be generated in the thorax to overcome the
resistance produced by the complex nasal stenoses. This results in a
typical clinical sign of this situation, which is visibly labored breathing.
This strong negative pressure causes the tube of soft tissue that forms the
nasopharynx to collapse (ch. 221).

Larynx
Malformations of the brachycephalic larynx can be very pronounced and
have serious clinical consequences (ch. 214). Both the laryngeal skeleton
and intralaryngeal structures may be affected, individually or together.
Each leads to a clinically relevant reduction in the size of the rima
glottidis, thereby increasing the resistance to airflow through the
larynx186 (Box 213.4).

Malformation of the Laryngeal Skeleton

There are indications that the “collapse” of the skeleton might have
different causes. Pugs clearly suffer from a substantial loss of cartilage
rigidity—both in larynx and trachea—while in Bulldog breeds, the
cartilages of larynx and trachea have a firm consistency,187 even in
animals with a history of longstanding, severely obstructed breathing.

Malformation of Internal Laryngeal Structures
Such malformations include everted lateral ventricles and the vocal folds.
The vocal folds are often excessively thick and have lost their typical
slim structure, also contributing to the narrowing of the rima glottidis.
Everted ventricles rather seem to be a herniation of tissue alongside
the caudal border of the ventricularis muscle and can therefore be
regarded as “laryngoceles” (

Video 213.31). Malformation of

internal laryngeal structures seems to occur independently from the
stability of the laryngeal skeleton (

Videos 213.32 and 213.33).185
