Vocal Fold Contact Granulomas
An additional problem can be the formation of vocal fold contact
granulomas188 (Figure 213.17). Laryngeal overstress causes continuous
microtrauma and direct damage to the tissue covering the vocal process
of the arytenoids, leading to the formation of vocal fold contact
granulomas. The mechanical trauma can be aggravated by regular
contact of the glottis with gastric acids due to regurgitation and
laryngopharyngeal reflux (ch. 221).189

Trachea
Tracheal hypoplasia is a congenital abnormality commonly seen in
Bulldog breeds in which the ends of the tracheal rings are apposed or
overlap, resulting in a narrow but rigid and mostly round tracheal lumen
(ch. 215). In Pugs, the tracheal lumen can also be narrow but contrary to
Bulldogs, and comparable to the laryngeal problem, this is a result of a
weak cartilage skeleton with flattened tracheal rings and a widened
dorsal membrane that may bulge into the tracheal lumen.185,190,191

• Shortening of the skull, especially of the upper and lower jaw,
makes the overall box smaller. As the tissue inside the box is not
reduced by the same proportion, narrowing occurs and less space is
available for the tube inside the box (Figure 213.15).
• Over-long soft palate: The additional length of the velum per se
does not reduce the lumen of the nasopharynx anatomically.
However, the airtight attachment to the epiglottic surface separates
the oropharyngeal from the nasopharyngeal airway. This enhances
the negative pressure in the nasopharynx during inspiration, thus
increasing its collapsibility (

Video 213.30) (Figure 213.15).

• Over-thick soft palate: The thickness of the soft palate in
brachycephalic dogs can be many times over that of normocephalic
breeds of the same or of larger size (Figure 213.15). The increased
thickness of the soft palate seems not to be muscle hypertrophy, but
due to increased stroma and increased proportions of salivary tissue
while muscle mass was reduced (Figure 213.15).

(Figure 213.14).

tissue stored in the box further narrows the tube (Figure 213.16).

regarded as additional tissue mass. Both are pressed out of the
oropharynx against the soft palate, forcing it dorsally into the
nasopharynx. This causes compression, and possibly even complete
obstruction, of the tube especially when the jaw is closed (Figure
213.16).

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS OF
BRACHYCEPHALIC MALFORMATIONS

Brachycephalic dogs show signs of nasal, pharyngeal, and laryngeal
stridor, expressed as inspiratory dyspnea (ch. 37), loud snoring/stertor
accompanied by gagging and possibly coughing. Episodes of severe
dyspnea can occur with cyanosis, syncope (ch. 40) and collapse, and
even sudden death. Gastrointestinal signs are dysphagia (chs. 47 and
259), regurgitation (ch. 48), and vomiting (ch. 48). Acute signs of
respiratory distress may be seen more frequently if the patient is obese or
in stressful situations like high ambient temperatures, excitement or
exercise. Brachycephaly can have a severe impact upon the welfare of
dogs, compromising their ability to exercise, play, eat, and sleep.15 In a
structured questionnaire, owners of Pugs and French Bulldogs that
needed surgical therapy described how they perceived frequency and
severity of their dogs’ impairments. In addition to the well-known clinical
signs, they reported exercise intolerance (95%): 75% could go for a walk
for at most 10-30 minutes in summer and only 30% of those dogs had
recovered afterwards within 15 minutes. Restrictions became obvious
above 19 °C (66 °F) ambient temperature. Owners reported that 68% of
the dogs had sleeping problems: nearly 30% showed signs of sleep apnea
or tried to sleep in a sitting position (

Video 213.34). Seventy-seven

percent of the French Bulldogs had experienced problems with feeding.15

EXAMINATION OF BRACHYCEPHALIC
ANIMALS
History and Physical Examination
Initial evaluation involves taking a history of clinical signs, along with an
assessment of the degree of respiratory compromise (ch. 2). Depending
on the stress level of the dog and the ambient temperature, clinical signs
may or may not be clearly visible during examination. A structured
questionnaire is recommended to obtain comprehensive and comparable
information, and to reveal the true extent of compromise. However, it is
also known that owners of brachycephalic dogs assess respiratory signs as
“normal for the breed.”192 Dog owners have reported a high frequency
and severity of respiratory signs but have not perceived them as
problems.163 Therefore, the clinician should obtain the history by asking
questions that use objective criteria, such as time needed for recovery and
questions about activities that could easily be observed by a dog

owner.15 Physical examination (ch. 3) includes the assessment of the
size of the nares with particular attention paid to the width of the vertical
slit (Figure 213.12). Laryngeal, tracheal, and thoracic auscultation helps
to determine the location and assess the quality of respiratory noise. In
addition, respiratory rate, mucous membrane color, and characteristics
of respiratory noise can help to determine severity.

describes a soft, collapsible tube that runs through a box
with rigid outer walls. The box is filled with soft material
(meat) that surrounds the tube. The tube corresponds to
the nasopharynx; the framing outer box is the base of

the box and around the tube is soft tissue in varying

connective tissue, tonsils). Since the tube has no rigid
wall of its own, like the trachea does, for example, it is
collapsible. Posterior endoscopic view and CT images of

(Poodle) and (B, D) a French Bulldog. 1, Soft palate; 2,
tongue. The red dotted line indicates the “box”

surrounding the “meat.” The more “meat” is in the box,

SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
The first concerns about respiratory problems in these breeds were raised
within the veterinary profession in the 1930s and new surgical techniques
were developed to correct the problems.166,193,194 Various techniques
have been recommended to enlarge the stenotic nares, to shorten
the elongated soft palate and to resect everted laryngeal

ventricles. Surgical techniques have remained amazingly unchanged
since then.
Today, a more complex and comprehensive approach simultaneously
addresses both the well-known and the more recently described
obstructions by use of multi-level surgery. The principle of this
approach is the aim to treat all serial, multiple airway stenoses at the
same time. Novel aspects are (a) the more radical opening of the nasal
entrance than is possible with the common “wedge technique” by
performing an ala-vestibuloplasty, and (b) the interventional endoscopic
resection of malformed obstructing turbinates using diode laser light
(laser-assisted turbinectomy [LATE]) to establish intranasal airway
patency. These procedures are combined with (c) bilateral tonsillotomy,
(d) staphylectomy in combination with palatal volume reduction, and (e)
microlaryngoscopic laser ablation of everted laryngeal ventricles.170,184
Such surgery reduced the clinical signs associated with brachycephaly in
all dogs in 1 study.194 There was a reduction in life-threatening events by
90%. The prevalence of sleeping problems decreased from 55% to 3%,
and the occurrence of abnormal breathing sounds declined by 50%.
There was a marked improvement in exercise tolerance but only a modest
improvement in heat tolerance.195 Another study, using noninvasive
whole-body barometric plethysmography, shows that multilevel surgery
leads to better outcomes than traditional airway surgery.196

NON-SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
Non-surgical management might involve one or more of several
tasks, including medical management, emergency treatment of acute
respiratory distress, and client education. Non-surgical management
cannot replace surgical treatment.

Medical Management
The vast majority of brachycephalic dogs with some degree of respiratory
distress have been treated, at some time or other, with corticosteroids,
often in combination with an antibiotic. However, there seems to be no
evidence to indicate benefit or efficacy of these medications.192

Emergency Treatment

The first therapeutic goal in acute respiratory distress due to upper
airway obstruction is sedation and the prevention of hyperthermia and
noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (ch. 123).197-199 This is achieved by
pharmacological means in combination with non-pharmacological
measures to prevent overexcitement. In addition to its desired
tranquilizing effects, advantages of acepromazine in this context are
centrally and peripherally mediated hypothermia.200 Nonpharmacological means, especially for hospitalized animals, are to take
them out from a box or kennel into a cool and quiet environment.
Bulldogs in particular can be intolerant of being confined in small spaces
and a narrow oxygen cage can cause a life-threatening situation for such
animals. A considerable number of patients in this stressful situation
simply do not want to be left alone and their frantic behavior can
dramatically worsen respiratory distress. An easy and fast technique to
treat or prevent hyperthermia (ch. 130) is to moisten the dog’s hair coat,
ideally not only with wet compresses, but by pouring water over the
animal until the coat is wet through to the skin.
Client education should begin before the decision is made to get a
new dog. Clients should be thoroughly educated that brachycephalic dogs
are likely to suffer from respiratory and other problems throughout their
lives (Figure 213.18); that puppies usually breathe normally and clinical
signs mostly develop after the age of 6 months; and that the assurance
the parents were “free-breathing” should be regarded with caution.
Owners of brachycephalic breeds should be educated about the specific
features of thermoregulation in dogs and its impairment in
brachycephalic animals in particular. Using the “meat-in-the-box” model,
the way obesity worsens upper airway obstruction can be explained to the
owner, as well as the importance of keeping the dog lean to help reduce
respiratory problems, at least to some degree.

LP laryngeal paralysis

The larynx is the collection of cartilages surrounding the rima
glottidis that is responsible for control of airflow during respiration.
The functions of the larynx are to regulate airflow, protect the lower
airway from aspiration during swallowing, and control phonation.
Diseases most commonly affecting the larynx include laryngeal
paralysis, laryngeal collapse, laryngeal stenosis, and laryngeal
masses. Each of these conditions results in some degree of upper
airway obstruction. Dogs and cats typically are brought to the
veterinarian because of respiratory stridor, voice change, coughing,
or gagging (chs. 34, 37, and 47).

CANINE LARYNGEAL PARALYSIS
ETIOLOGY

Laryngeal paralysis (LP) is a common respiratory disorder that can
occur uni- or bilaterally and that primarily affects older (> 9 years)
large- and giant-breed dogs. A congenital form occurs in certain
breeds such as Bouviers des Flandres, Siberian Huskies, Bull
Terriers, and White-Coated German Shepherd Dogs.1,2 An
autosomal dominant trait has been documented in Bouviers des
Flandres, resulting in Wallerian degeneration of the recurrent
laryngeal nerves and abnormalities of the nucleus ambiguus.3 An
RAPGEF6 variant has been documented as a major genetic risk
factor for early-onset LP in miniature Bull Terriers.4 Although the
mode of inheritance has not been established, a hereditary
predisposition also has been identified in Siberian Husky dogs,
Alaskan Malamutes, and crosses of those 2 breeds.5,6 One study of
25 Alaskan huskies with congenital LP found that most affected dogs
had blue eyes, white facial markings, and oral mucosal tags.7
Pedigree analysis was suggestive of an autosomal recessive mode of
inheritance. Degenerative and inflammatory polyneuropathies also
have been documented in 7 young Siberian Huskies, raising the
suspicion of a hereditary disorder.8 LP-polyneuropathy complexes
have been described in Dalmatians, Rottweilers, Leonberger dogs,
Saint Bernards, Pyrenean Mountain Dogs, and American
Staffordshire Terriers.9-13 A missense variant in the CNTNAP1 gene
is associated with LP-polyneuropathy in Leonberger dogs and Saint
Bernards.14
For the more frequently encountered acquired LP, the Labrador
Retriever is the most common breed reported; Golden Retrievers,
Saint Bernards, Newfoundlands, Irish Setters, and Brittany Spaniels
also are overrepresented.15 Acquired LP is caused by damage to the
recurrent laryngeal nerve or intrinsic laryngeal muscles most often
attributed to polyneuropathy, polymyopathy, spontaneous or
iatrogenic trauma, or intrathoracic or extrathoracic masses, although
many other causes have been proposed (Box 214.1). In many dogs,
the cause remains undetermined, and these cases are traditionally
classified as idiopathic. However, it has been shown that many dogs
thought to have idiopathic acquired LP develop systemic neurologic
signs within 1 year following diagnosis of LP, which is consistent with

progressive generalized neuropathy.16 Abnormalities in the results of
electrodiagnostic tests and histopathologic analysis of nerve and
muscle biopsy specimens reflecting generalized polyneuropathy have
been documented in a small number of dogs with acquired LP.17
Therefore, it has been proposed that dogs previously believed to have
idiopathic LP may in fact have a progressive generalized
polyneuropathy; LP is then one of the early clinical signs of this
condition.18-19 The abbreviation GOLPP (geriatric-onset LP
polyneuropathy, ch. 252) has been proposed as a more accurate
term for dogs with acquired LP where other causes have been ruled
out.20

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
With LP, the arytenoid cartilages, and consequently the vocal folds,
remain in a paramedian position during inspiration. This failure to
fully abduct creates upper airway obstruction on inspiration. Dogs
typically present with noisy inspiratory respiration (stridor) and
exercise intolerance. Early clinical signs include voice change and
mild coughing and gagging. Severe airway obstruction results in
respiratory distress, cyanosis, and collapse. Dogs may also have signs
of dysphagia (ch. 47). The rate of progression of clinical signs is
highly variable, and dogs may have clinical signs for several months
to years before the onset of respiratory distress. Often, clinical signs
are worsened by heavy exercise or increasing environmental
temperature or humidity, which results in an acute exacerbation of a
chronic condition. As respiratory rate increases, the mucosa covering
the arytenoids obstructing airflow may become inflamed and
edematous, which leads to further airway obstruction. A vicious
circle ensues that, if left unaddressed, may become life-threatening
(chs. 37, 123).

DIAGNOSIS
Routine diagnostic evaluation for dogs thought to have LP includes
physical examination (ch. 3), orthopedic (ch. 31) and neurologic

(ch. 241) examinations, complete blood count, biochemical profile,
urinalysis, thyroid function screening, thoracic radiographs, and
laryngeal examination. Dogs with LP are at risk of aspiration
pneumonia both before and after surgery. Therefore, thoracic
radiographs are a necessary part of the diagnostic workup in dogs
suspected to have laryngeal dysfunction, to rule out not only
aspiration pneumonia, but also overt megaesophagus,
noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and concurrent cardiac or lower
airway abnormalities (Figure 214.1).
For dogs that present with dysphagia or vomiting, positive contrast
esophagography or a videofluoroscopic swallow study could be
considered to rule out esophageal dysfunction that may not be
apparent on survey thoracic radiographs (ch. 259). Severe
progressive esophageal dysfunction has been reported in a set of
dogs with idiopathic LP and likely reflects the proposed generalized
progressive polyneuropathy.16 Acquiring information from
esophagography should be weighed against the potential added risk
of aspiration.

Hypothyroidism (ch. 285) occurs concurrently in up to 30% of
dogs with acquired LP, although a direct causal link has not been
established.15,21 Regardless, thyroid function screening is performed
routinely in the workup for LP. Thyroid supplementation should be
instituted if indicated, although this does not seem to improve
clinical signs associated with LP.

Laryngeal Examination
A definitive diagnosis of LP requires examination of the larynx in
order to document lack of arytenoid abduction during inspiration.
This can be accomplished by direct visualization of the larynx with a
simple laryngoscope (Video 214.1

), oral video-endoscopic

laryngoscopy, transnasal laryngoscopy (TNL), ultrasound
(echolaryngography), or computed tomography (CT). Laryngoscopy,
regardless of method, can be confounding because false-positive
results are common due to the influence of anesthetic agents and
sedatives on laryngeal function

(Video 214.1).

Echolaryngography and TNL avoid the need for heavy sedation and
general anesthesia, but neither of these methods has been shown to
be superior to traditional oral laryngeal examination for establishing
a definitive diagnosis.22

A systematic review of the influence of anesthetic drugs on
laryngeal motion23 identified that thiopental administered IV to
effect was believed to be the best choice to allow assessment of
laryngeal function. However, thiopental is no longer manufactured.
Propofol is now used most often, even though significant respiratory
depression often occurs with this drug; apnea is related to dosage,
speed of injection, and use of concurrent premedications.
Methohexital, a barbiturate derivative, has effects on laryngeal
function that are similar to those of propofol but has been associated
with adverse events such as tachycardia and seizure-like activity.24
While ketamine preserves laryngeal function better than thiopental
does in people, one study found no benefit for laryngeal examination
when combining propofol and ketamine in dogs; no dosage reduction
in propofol was achieved and respiratory depression was more
marked.25 Alfaxalone (2-4 mg/kg IV) can be used as an alternative to
propofol.26 While alfaxalone still causes respiratory depression,
apnea has been shown to be less likely when compared to propofol.27
In one direct comparison of propofol versus alfaxalone induction for
laryngeal examination in healthy dogs, the addition of
premedications (acepromazine and butorphanol) improved the
quality of the laryngeal examination regardless of the induction
agent.28 This study did not recommend the use of propofol or
alfaxalone alone for the evaluation of arytenoid motion. This is in
contrast to an unpublished study that showed alfaxalone alone
resulted in the best respiratory function and quality of examination
when compared to propofol alone and alfaxalone or propofol used
with premedications. In another study, normal dogs were induced
with either alfaxalone or propofol, followed by face-mask
administration of isoflurane for ≥20 minutes. Laryngeal function (%
change in rima glottidis surface area) was greater after 20 and 40
minutes of isoflurane inhalation by mask than at induction.29

FIGURE 214.1 Lateral thoracic radiograph of a
dog with laryngeal paralysis with megaesophagus
and an alveolar pattern in the right middle lung lobe.
Note the dramatically gas-dilated esophagus and the
subtle alveolar infiltrate of the lung overlying the
cardiac silhouette.
Laryngeal motion is key in establishing a laryngoscopic diagnosis
of LP. Mechanical stimulation (e.g., toe pinch) can stimulate
arytenoid motion during laryngoscopy. However, doxapram is
superior to mechanical stimulation to stimulate arytenoid motion.30
Doxapram HCl (1 mg/kg IV) has been advocated for routine use
during laryngoscopy to increase respiratory depth and improve
intrinsic laryngeal motion thereby improving the ability to determine
normal versus abnormal function. Low-dose (0.55 mg/kg) and highdose (2.2 mg/kg) doxapram or 90 seconds of inhalation of carbon
dioxide in oxygen were all found to be effective respiratory
stimulants in healthy dogs, but hypertension and tachycardia were
observed in some dogs receiving doxapram.31

LP should not be diagnosed based solely on the lack of arytenoid
movement; inflammation and swelling of the laryngeal cartilages
may also be apparent. The diagnosis may be challenging when there
is paradoxical movement of the arytenoids. In this scenario, the
arytenoid cartilages move inward during inspiration due to negative
intraglottic pressure that is created by breathing against the glottic
obstruction. The cartilages then passively return to their original
position during the expiratory phase, which can be misinterpreted as
adequate arytenoid movement. This error can be avoided by having
an assistant state the phase of respiration during laryngoscopy to
help in distinguishing normal from paradoxical motion.

TREATMENT
For dogs that are presented in acute respiratory distress, initial
treatment is directed at improving ventilation, reducing laryngeal
edema, and minimizing stress. A typical treatment regimen involves
oxygen supplementation and administration of short-acting
corticosteroids and sedatives (Box 214.2). If the patient is
hyperthermic, appropriate cooling procedures should be instituted.
If respiratory distress persists, intubation or a temporary
tracheostomy (chs. 94, 123) should be considered. However, the
use of a temporary tracheostomy tube preoperatively in dogs with LP
has been shown to be a negative prognostic indicator following
surgery.15 The presence of a tube within the tracheal lumen causes
epithelial erosion, submucosal inflammation, and inhibition of the
mucociliary apparatus from the level of the tracheostomy to the
bifurcation. Mucus production dramatically increases and the tube
must be suctioned at very frequent intervals to prevent clogging (ch.
94). The large majority (86%) of dogs with temporary
tracheostomies experience any of 16 types of complications (clinical
and incidental).32 The most significant and frequent complications,
occurring in 21-26% of dogs, are airway obstruction, tube
dislodgement, aspiration pneumonia, and stoma swelling.
Translaryngeal percutaneous arytenoid lateralization is under
investigation as an alternative to temporary tracheostomy for dogs in
severe respiratory distress from LP.33,34 With this technique, a

mattress suture is placed through one arytenoid cartilage via an oral
approach and exited through the skin ventral to the jugular vein.
The goal of conservative management of dogs with LP is to
improve quality of life through environmental changes, reduction of
daily exercise (ch. 226), owner education, weight loss (ch. 150),
and consideration of anti-inflammatory drugs to minimize laryngeal
swelling. Unfortunately, this medical treatment path is often
insufficient for long-term management of bilateral LP. Doxepin, a
tricyclic antidepressant, has been reported anecdotally to improve
clinical signs but this finding was not supported in a double-blinded,
randomized, placebo-controlled trial.35 For dogs with concurrent
hypothyroidism (ch. 285), thyroid supplementation should be
instituted, but doing so rarely improves the clinical signs of LP. Dogs
with unilateral laryngeal paresis or paralysis are not surgical
candidates, but dogs with bilateral paralysis frequently are.
Surgical intervention is indicated in dogs severely affected (quality
of life, clinical signs) by bilateral LP. Numerous techniques have
been described to treat LP. Unilateral arytenoid lateralization is the
current technique of choice for most surgeons (Figure 214.2), but
various types of partial laryngectomy (bilateral vocal fold resection,
partial arytenoidectomy) are also performed. Bilateral arytenoid
lateralization is not recommended as it results in unacceptable
morbidity.15 Other techniques include castellated laryngofissure,
reinnervation of the laryngeal musculature, and permanent
tracheostomy. Castellated laryngofissure is performed rarely because
of the technical difficulty and inconsistent outcomes. Reinnervation
does not provide immediate clinical relief, so it is not a practical
treatment option in dogs. A silicone laryngeal stent has been
successfully used in 7 dogs with LP and is a potentially promising
noninvasive alternative for temporary or permanent relief of stridor;
stent migration and cough are known complications.36 Permanent
tracheostomy is considered a salvage procedure for dogs most at risk
of aspiration pneumonia, but it is associated with a high rate of
major and minor complications and requires diligent postoperative
and long-term care. In 21 dogs with permanent tracheostomies, 50%
had major complications, 20% required revision surgery, and 26%
died acutely at home, most likely from airway obstruction.37 In

another study of 69 dogs receiving permanent tracheostomies, major
complications occurred in 61%, including aspiration pneumonia,
skinfold occlusion, and stoma stenosis.38 Revision surgery was
performed in 35% of dogs. An overall median survival time of 1825
days was documented, but older dogs, dogs with tracheal collapse, or
dogs receiving corticosteroids had shorter survival times.

COMPLICATIONS AND OUTCOME
Factors significantly associated with a higher risk of developing
complications and a negative effect on long-term outcome include
progression of generalized neurologic signs, preoperative aspiration
pneumonia, development of esophageal dysfunction, temporary
tracheostomy placement, and concurrent neoplastic disease. One
study found that 10 of 32 dogs with idiopathic LP had neurologic
signs at the time of enrollment, but all dogs had neurologic signs by 1
year.16 In a separate study, dogs with neurologic comorbidities were
at a greater risk for developing complications following surgical
correction of LP.39 Aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217) is the most
common complication in dogs surgically treated for LP; it occurs in
10-21% of dogs undergoing unilateral arytenoid lateralization.15,40,41
Although aspiration pneumonia is most likely in the first few weeks
following surgery, it has been recognized that these dogs are at
permanent risk of this complication. The most recent retrospective

study identifying risk factors for the development of aspiration
pneumonia found that preexisting pneumonia was not associated
with an increased risk for development of aspiration pneumonia
after surgery.42 In the same study, postoperative megaesophagus
and postoperative administration of opioid analgesics prior to
discharge were significant risk factors for development of aspiration
pneumonia.42

FIGURE 214.2 Postoperative view of the larynx of
a 12-year-old Labrador Retriever following left
unilateral arytenoid lateralization. The asymmetry of
the larynx is visible, with greater, fixed abduction of

the patient’s left arytenoid due to the procedure. This
increases the diameter of the rima glottidis.
The use of gastrointestinal motility modifiers has been suggested
to reduce the risk of postoperative aspiration pneumonia.
Metoclopramide and cisapride each increases lower esophageal
sphincter (LES) tone. Metoclopramide has also been shown to
reduce gastroesophageal reflux under anesthesia in normal dogs;
however, a prospective multicenter clinical trial in dogs with LP
undergoing unilateral arytenoid lateralization found that
perioperative administration of metoclopramide did not affect the
incidence of aspiration pneumonia in the short-term postoperative
period.43 In a separate study, cisapride significantly increased LES
pressure in normal dogs while metoclopramide and placebo did
not.44
Despite the potential for complications, unilateral arytenoid
lateralization usually results in less respiratory distress and stridor,
and improved exercise tolerance. Owner satisfaction with this
procedure has been reported as excellent, with the majority of
owners believing that the quality of the dog’s life was improved
dramatically.15,45

FELINE LARYNGEAL PARALYSIS
Laryngeal disease is uncommon in cats, but significant respiratory
stress can result when it occurs. In a review of laryngeal diseases in
cats, LP constituted 40% of cases.46 Clinical presentation is similar
to that in dogs in that it occurs most often in middle-aged to older
cats (mean 9-14 years), and both unilateral and bilateral conditions
have been documented. Significant unilateral dysfunction and
resultant clinical signs have been reported in 10-57% of cases with a
majority of these being left-sided, which is similar to reports in
humans and horses.46-48

ETIOLOGY AND DIAGNOSIS

The cause of LP in cats often remains undetermined. Several cases
have been associated with trauma, neoplastic invasion, and
iatrogenic damage (e.g., post-thyroidectomy). Neoplastic infiltration
can lead to fixed laryngeal obstruction with both inspiratory and
expiratory dyspnea and noise, and this should always be considered
in the differential diagnosis of LP in the cat. For assessment of
laryngeal function, alfaxalone has been evaluated compared to
propofol and midazolam/ketamine for effect on laryngeal function in
normal cats (Box 214.3).49 All three protocols provided similar
conditions to evaluate laryngeal motion, although subjective
arytenoid movement was present in all cats only when alfaxalone was
used. This may allow for improved functional evaluation of the
larynx in a clinical setting. In addition to traditional laryngoscopy
(direct or endoscopic), the use of echolaryngography has been
described for diagnosis of LP in cats.46,50

TREATMENT
Both conservative and surgical treatments are described in cats.
Conservative management of cats with LP consists of weight loss and
minimizing excitement and vigorous exercise. Reported survival
times in 7 cats treated conservatively for LP ranged from 120-2520
days with a median survival of 811 days.46 Unlike dogs, however, cats
with even unilateral LP can have marked clinical signs and might
require surgical intervention. Successful surgical treatment primarily
using unilateral arytenoid lateralization has been described in
several small studies of cats with LP.46-48

LARYNGEAL COLLAPSE
Laryngeal collapse is a consequence of chronic upper airway
obstruction, most often associated with brachycephalic obstructive
airway syndrome (BOAS; ch. 213). However, laryngeal collapse can
occur alone, or be associated with LP, nasal and nasopharyngeal
obstruction, or trauma in both brachycephalic and mesaticephalic
breeds. Concurrent LP and laryngeal collapse have been reported in

a small set of nonbrachycephalic small-breed dogs.51 Norwich
Terriers can be afflicted with a genetic disorder of the larynx
consisting of excessive supraglottic tissue, laryngeal collapse, everted
laryngeal saccules, and narrowed laryngeal openings.52 Most
affected Norwich Terriers have normal nares and soft palates, but
rhinomanometry has demonstrated that the skulls of Norwich
Terriers have measurements consistent with both brachycephaly and
mesaticephaly.53

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND DIAGNOSIS
Chronic upper airway obstruction causes increased airway resistance
and increased negative intraglottic luminal pressure. Over time, this
results in laryngeal collapse due to cartilage fatigue and
degeneration. However, early onset of laryngeal collapse has been
reported in brachycephalic dogs as young as 4.5 months of age.54

There are three stages of severity for laryngeal collapse. Stage 1 is
the eversion of the laryngeal saccules into the glottis, which is
present in 50-60% of dogs with BOAS (Videos 213.31, 213.32)

.

In stage 2, the cuneiform processes of the arytenoid cartilages lose
rigidity and they collapse into the laryngeal lumen. In addition, the
aryepiglottic folds also collapse ventromedially (Figure 214.3). The
most advanced phase of laryngeal collapse is stage 3, in which the
corniculate process of each arytenoid cartilage fatigues and then
collapses toward midline, resulting in complete laryngeal collapse.
The diagnosis (Video 213.33) is established via direct visualization
during a laryngeal exam, as described above

(Video 214.1).

TREATMENT
The early stage of laryngeal collapse is still amenable to surgical
treatment. Resection of the everted laryngeal saccules is relatively
simple as each saccule is grasped with Allis tissue forceps and then
sharply transected with Metzenbaum scissors. However, one study
has shown that sacculectomy may increase postoperative morbidity
following surgery for BOAS.55 Options for treatment of advanced
stages of laryngeal collapse are limited. Underlying components of
BOAS should be addressed (ch. 213) and the degree of improvement
assessed. Dogs with stage 2 and 3 laryngeal collapse benefit
markedly from removal of everted laryngeal saccules in addition to
surgical correction of elongated soft palate and stenotic nares.56
Unilateral arytenoid laryngoplasty (cricoarytenoid lateralization
combined with thyroarytenoid caudolateralization) has been
reported to produce reasonable long-term outcomes in a small
number of brachycephalic dogs with laryngeal collapse, but this
technique should be used with caution as the opposite cartilage may
continue to collapse medially.57 Permanent tracheostomy is the
recommended treatment when dogs do not respond to other medical
or surgical treatment, although many owners consider this an
unacceptable option due to the high risk of complications
(mentioned previously) and degree of maintenance required.

FIGURE 214.3 Intra-oral view of Stage 2 laryngeal
collapse in an 8-year-old Pug; note complete collapse
of cuneiform processes into laryngeal lumen.

LARYNGEAL STENOSIS
Acquired laryngeal stenosis most commonly occurs as a complication
from bilateral ventriculocordectomy, although other causes include
traumatic tracheal intubation and foreign body or caustic trauma.
The most common clinical sign associated with laryngeal stenosis is
exercise intolerance, but inspiratory stridor and respiratory distress
occur as well. Ventriculocordectomy performed through an oral
approach can lead to laryngeal webbing from formation of scar tissue
(cicatrix) as the mucosal defects are left to heal by second intention.
This procedure is most commonly performed for devocalization
(debarking). The American Veterinary Medical Association opposes
devocalization except as a final alternative to euthanasia after
behavioral modification to correct excessive vocalization has failed

and after discussion of potential complications from the procedure
with the owner.58
Ventriculocordectomy as a treatment for LP is best performed
through a ventral laryngotomy incision so that the mucosa on each
side can be closed primarily, decreasing the risk of scar formation; a
similar procedure is performed to treat laryngeal stenosis.59 A
temporary soft silicone intraluminal stent (keel stent) can be inserted
through the thyroid cartilage to separate the healing mucosal
surfaces but is often not necessary except in small dogs.60
Regardless, laryngeal web resection with mucosal apposition has
been reported to have a good to excellent outcome.61

LARYNGEAL MASSES
NEOPLASTIC
Though uncommon, numerous types of tumors of the larynx have
been reported. In the dog, these include rhabdomyosarcoma
(oncocytoma), squamous cell carcinoma (Figure 214.4),
adenocarcinoma, osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, chondroma,
myxochondroma, lipoma, fibrosarcoma, undifferentiated carcinoma,
extramedullary plasmacytoma, and mast cell tumor.62 Squamous
cell carcinoma and lymphoma are the most common tumors of the
larynx in the cat, but adenocarcinoma and other poorly differentiated
round cell tumors have been reported.63

FIGURE 214.4 Intra-oral view of a 10-year-old
Labrador Retriever with laryngeal squamous cell
carcinoma of the right arytenoid cartilage.
Small lesions may be removed by mucosal resection or partial
laryngectomy through an oral approach or ventral laryngotomy.
Excision of cartilaginous tumors (e.g., chondroma or
chondrosarcoma) can be performed with reasonable success.
Extensive surgical intervention involves complete laryngectomy with
permanent tracheostomy but has been reported only in isolated
cases. Radioresponsive tumors may be treated with radiation
therapy. Otherwise, most treatment is palliative, consisting of airflow
bypass of the laryngeal area through a permanent tracheostomy.
The prognosis for laryngeal tumors is guarded as most cases are
quite advanced at the time of diagnosis. Treatment of 4 cats with
laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma with tube tracheostomy alone
resulted in a median survival of only 3 days, and chemotherapeutic
treatment of 5 cats with laryngeal masses resulted in a median
survival of 141 days.64 Two cats with laryngeal lymphoma were
treated with chemotherapy, resulting in survival times of 60 and

1440 days.63 In this same study, 1 cat with laryngeal squamous cell
carcinoma treated with prednisolone survived 180 days. Permanent
tracheostomy in 5 cats with laryngeal carcinoma documented
survival at home from 2-281 days with 2 cats dying from
tracheostomy site occlusion and 3 cats euthanized because of disease
progression.65

INFLAMMATORY
Inflammatory laryngeal disease is an uncommon nonneoplastic
condition of the arytenoid cartilages reported in both dogs and cats.
It can be granulomatous, lymphocytic-plasmacytic, or eosinophilic in
nature. Severe cases can result in laryngeal stenosis and significant
upper airway obstruction. Biopsy of the laryngeal mass is crucial to
differentiate these disorders from neoplasia, although it is still
possible that inflammatory changes may represent a secondary
response to underlying neoplasia. Treatment of inflammatory
laryngeal disease is palliative and consists of debulking of the mass,
corticosteroid therapy, or permanent tracheostomy. Permanent
tracheostomy has been associated with a higher mortality rate in cats
with inflammatory laryngeal disease than in cats undergoing
permanent tracheostomy for any other reason.

CYSTIC
Benign laryngeal cysts also have been described in isolated canine
and feline cases. Cysts are typically epithelial in origin and stem from
the ventral aspect of the larynx. Surgical removal is usually curative.
Some cysts are very large and can significantly obstruct airflow.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Laryngeal Paralysis
This is a condition commonly seen in old large-breed dogs that is
thought to be due to a peripheral neuropathy (degeneration of
nerves) or specific damage to the nerve supply of the larynx. This
nerve damage makes it difficult to impossible for dogs to fully open
the larynx when breathing in, resulting in noisy breathing, exercise
intolerance, and distress. This can be a dangerous condition

especially when dogs get overheated. Since the larynx cannot open,
when dogs breathe harder it causes the larynx to swell, making the
condition markedly worse. If this occurs, emergency medical
attention needs to be sought immediately.
When a dog is evaluated for laryngeal paralysis by a veterinarian
the following are commonly performed: physical examination,
orthopedic and neurologic examination, complete blood work, chest
radiographs, thyroid hormone testing (for low thyroid levels), and a
sedated laryngeal examination.
Surgery is recommended when the dog’s quality of life is
dramatically affected and there are no concerning findings on
evaluation that would significantly increase the risk of surgical
complications.
The surgical procedure of choice is a unilateral arytenoid
lateralization, or “tie-back.” A tie-back procedure pulls one side of
the larynx open enough such that the dog can breathe easier and be
more active. The most serious complication from this procedure is
aspiration pneumonia, which may occur in 10-20% of dogs.
However, long-term outcome has been reported to be good to
excellent for improved quality of life.
Catriona MacPhail (Fort Collins, Colorado)

TRACHEAL DISEASES
Most tracheal disorders can involve both intra- and extrathoracic
segments of the trachea. Noninfectious tracheal diseases are
common and include dorsal tracheal membrane flaccidity, tracheal
collapse, tracheal injury/laceration, posttraumatic stenosis, foreign
body, intratracheal tumor, and tracheal avulsion (cat).
Tracheitis refers to an inflammation of the epithelial lining of the
trachea, which can be infectious or noninfectious. When dogs
develop tracheitis, it is often a part of the canine infectious
respiratory disease complex (CIRDC; ch. 203). Tracheitis can also
be secondary to prolonged barking, or disease of the oropharynx,
esophagus, or even the stomach (aerodigestive disorders; ch. 221)
(see Figure 215.4). In cats, tracheitis is most often associated with
infectious feline respiratory disease (ch. 205). Tracheitis in cats
does not always induce a significant cough, as it does in dogs.
Tracheal compromise can also result from extratracheal diseases,
such as extreme cardiac enlargement, mediastinal enlargement
(hematopoietic neoplasia [ch. 322], or megaesophagus [ch. 259]),
or space-occupying masses, which can cause deviation of the trachea
and possibly affect the shape or lumen of the trachea (Figures
215.1, 215.2).

TRACHEAL COLLAPSE (DOGS)
Tracheal collapse, also referred to as collapsing trachea and canine
tracheal collapse syndrome, is a very common disorder encountered
in middle-aged to older toy or miniature breeds. The “goose honk”
sound of the cough is characteristic (Video 215.1)

Etiology and Pathophysiology

.

The cause of primary tracheal collapse syndrome is complex and is
best regarded as multifactorial.1 The traditionally considered form of
dynamic mechanical collapse can be caused by a combination of
progressive malacia of the tracheal cartilages and laxity of the
trachealis muscle, resulting primarily in dorsoventral collapse,
possibly associated with malacic airways (or bronchial collapse). In a
different form, dorsoventral narrowing gives the trachea a W-shaped
cross-section due to malformation of the tracheal rings. This is
referred to as tracheal malformation. It is a more static form of
narrowing of the tracheal lumen that is distinct from, or occurs in
addition to, dynamic narrowing caused by invagination of the
trachealis muscle during respiration.
In the traditional form, clinical disease occurs when 2 factors exist
concurrently: a primary cartilage abnormality that results in intrinsic
weakness of the tracheal rings, and secondary factors capable of
initiating progression to the point of causing clinical signs. Softening
of cartilage rings seems to be due to a reduction of
glycosaminoglycan and chondroitin sulfate content, which leads to a
decreased ability to maintain functional rigidity, further leading to a
weakness and flattening of the tracheal rings.2,3 Potential triggering
factors include obesity, cardiomegaly, inhalation of irritants and
allergens, periodontal disease, respiratory infections, and recent
endotracheal intubation.4 The dynamic changes of tracheal collapse
may be confined to either the cervical or the thoracic region of the
trachea, or both can be affected; frequently, the changes are more
pronounced at the cervicothoracic junction. Dorsoventral flattening
of the tracheal cartilaginous rings causes a stretch of the dorsal
tracheal membrane, which becomes inflamed and pendulous. Thus,
it can prolapse into the tracheal lumen as soon as extraluminal
pressure exceeds intraluminal pressure, further reducing the
diameter of the tracheal lumen.5 Inside the thorax, during
inspiration, the redundant dorsal membrane is aspirated
by/subjected to negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration
and may excessively enlarge the tracheal lumen, as seen on lateral
radiographs (Figure 215.3). The syndrome is perpetuated by the
cycle of chronic inflammation of the tracheal mucosa, which
exacerbates—and in turn, is exacerbated by—the cough. In dogs with

tracheal collapse, concurrent bronchomalacia is frequently
encountered and does not appear to be related to airway
inflammation.6 Pulmonary hypertension (PH) can develop in dogs
with tracheal collapse and bronchomalacia (ch. 218).7-9

Clinical Presentation
Primary tracheal collapse is commonly seen in middle-aged to older
miniature, toy, and small breed dogs. Overrepresented breeds
include the Yorkshire Terrier, Pomeranian, Pug, Poodle, Maltese,
and Chihuahua.5,9
Clinical signs include chronic cough in all cases (ch. 34), mild to
severe panting, exercise intolerance, and varying degree of
respiratory distress (ch. 37) as well as a varying degree of cyanosis
in advanced cases (ch. 27). A prolonged clinical history is common.
The cough is harsh, often followed by a terminal retch; it is often
described as “honking/goose honk”10 and is precipitated by activity,
excitement, tracheal pressure (such as that caused by pulling on a
leash) or drinking. This characteristic cough can be elicited easily by
palpation of the trachea. Collapse of the cervical trachea can
sometimes be appreciated as a flattening of the tracheal rings on
cervical palpation. In some cases, a cough is not audible as such and
owners only report inspiratory-expiratory stertor, sometimes
described as a pig-grunt- or -growl-like sound (Video 215.2)

. In

severe cases, the cough or stertor almost never stops, leading to
muscular fatigue and exhaustion of the animal. In rare cases,
excitement can lead to cyanosis because of complete obstruction,
vagally mediated syncope, or PH,7,8 especially when concomitant
bronchomalacia is present.

FIGURE 215.1 Lateral thoracic radiograph of a
middle-aged mixed-breed dog showing the presence
of a large mediastinal mass, causing marked ventral
deviation of the trachea.

FIGURE 215.2 Endoscopy of the trachea in a dog
with severe respiratory distress and cyanosis. Note
the extreme reduction and altered shape of the
tracheal lumen, caused by a huge mediastinal mass.
During thoracic auscultation, crackles on both inspiration and
expiration can be appreciated in dogs with small airway collapse,
and/or concurrent bronchitis. A thorough cardiac auscultation is
recommended (ch. 38), since a heart murmur associated with mitral
regurgitation can be heard (ch. 232); indeed, concurrent
myxomatous/degenerative mitral valve disease is a common finding
in the same population affected by tracheal collapse; i.e. older, smallbreed dogs. However, the role of cardiomegaly and specifically left
atrial enlargement in airway collapse by airway compression remains
unclear, with evidence of airway inflammation as the likely cause of
cough in dogs that had both left atrial enlargement and airway
collapse in one study.11 Hepatomegaly is common in dogs with

tracheal collapse and could be a reflection of obesity, although
hepatic dysfunction has been reported in dogs with tracheal
collapse.12 Bronchial collapse/bronchomalacia is common in dogs
with tracheal collapse.13

Diagnosis
The diagnosis of tracheal collapse is strongly suspected based on
signalment, history of cough, and physical examination findings.5
Additional diagnostic evaluation (radiography, fluoroscopy [ch.
212], tracheal ultrasound,14 echocardiography [ch. 97],
bronchoscopy [ch. 93] and pulmonary function testing15) can be
used for confirming the extent and severity of the tracheal collapse,
and the presence of concomitant or complicating diseases such as
bronchomalacia, PH, cardiomegaly, or lower airway diseases.
Imaging is required to obtain adequate measurements prior to
placement of any tracheal stent (ch. 114).
Radiographic examination of animals with collapsed trachea can
use both still and motion studies. The most useful radiographic
examinations include lateral projections over the thoracic inlet, and a
tangential (craniocaudal) projection of the thoracic inlet (in this
skyline projection, the collapsed trachea is seen as an oval, “C” or
crescent shape). Because of the relationship of collapse to the
respiratory cycle, fluoroscopic investigation may be more sensitive
than radiographs (ch. 212).9
On lateral radiographs, a redundant dorsal tracheal membrane
that invaginates into the tracheal lumen can be seen as a soft-tissue
opacity along the dorsal aspect of the caudal cervical tracheal lumen.
This radiographic appearance can be seen in both small- and largebreed dogs as a consequence of coughing, and must be differentiated
from a superimposed esophagus. Therefore, lateral radiographs
made during both the maximal inspiratory and maximal expiratory
phases of the respiratory cycle are needed to demonstrate dynamic
collapse. Indeed, collapse of the cervical tracheal segment occurs in
inspiration because of the decreased pressure within the trachea
whereas the thoracic portion tends to collapse during the expiration
phase as a consequence of increased intrathoracic pressure. These

dynamic changes are best viewed in real time using image-intensified
fluoroscopy (Video 215.3)

. Radiography and fluoroscopy are

complementary imaging techniques; confirming the presence or
absence of tracheal or bronchial collapse can require multiple
imaging modalities as well as bronchoscopy.16 Cervical lung lobe
herniation (CLLH), or protrusion of lung parenchyma beyond the
musculoskeletal entrance of the thorax, is a frequent concurrent
finding identified by fluoroscopy (ch. 212;

Video 212.2).17-19

Although rarely needed to confirm the diagnosis, tracheoscopy can
reveal a decreased dorsoventral diameter due to flattening of the
cartilaginous rings with a pendulous dorsal membrane, potentially
leading to complete obstruction of the tracheal lumen (Figure
215.4). Tracheobronchoscopy (Videos 215.4 and 215.5;

ch. 93)

is advised in all cases since it is very helpful in determining the
degree of severity of the tracheal and especially bronchial collapse, as
well as in assessing concomitant airway disease including secondary
infection. Those findings should be properly addressed and taken
into account for prognostic purposes before stent placement can be
considered, although the presence of mainstem bronchial collapse at
the time of stent placement might lack significant association with
outcome.20

Management
In animals with marked respiratory difficulty, oxygen
supplementation can be delivered (ch. 123), and sedation and
antitussive agents are needed. Butorphanol (0.05-0.2 mg/kg q4-6h)
and/or acepromazine (0.01-0.1 mg/kg) can be injected SC, and
prednisolone sodium succinate (15-30 mg/kg slow IV bolus) can be
administered to decrease acute inflammation.
Long-term treatment may involve multimodal medical therapy or
mechanical stenting. Medical therapy is the cornerstone of treatment
for collapsing trachea-associated coughing (Video 215.1)

.

Severely-affected dogs with clinical signs caused by dynamic tracheal
obstruction (severe inspiratory-expiratory tracheal stertor,

obstructive dyspnea [Video 215.2])

may benefit from placement

of a stent (ch.114).21 For all, decreasing factors that promote cough
and tracheal mucosal inflammation is key. Weight reduction in the
obese animal is essential (ch. 150). Likewise, neck collars should be
replaced by harnesses. Removing the dog from respiratory irritants
such as noxious gases, smoke and dust is common sense. It is also
important to detect and treat other diseases, like chronic airway
disease, cardiac disease, and hyperadrenocorticism.

FIGURE 215.3 Lateral thoracic radiographs of an
8-year-old Yorkshire Terrier during (A) peak
inspiration and (B) peak expiration, showing the
dramatic change in tracheal diameter that can occur
during the respiratory cycle in animals with
collapsing trachea. This illustrates the importance of
obtaining inspiratory and expiratory views. C,
Collapsing trachea observed at the thoracic inlet in a
dog with moderate rotation of the trachea. As a
result of the rotation, the trachea appears wide in
this lateral projection, rather than collapsed.
Medical therapy typically includes antitussives, sedativeantihistamines, low dose corticosteroids, and may also include use of
bronchodilators or a short course of antimicrobials for secondary
infection. Oral agents such as hydrocodone (0.22 mg/kg PO q12h) or
butorphanol (0.55 mg/kg PO q12h) can control cough. A very low
dose of steroids orally (prednisone 0.2 mg/kg daily for 1 to 2 weeks,

at 3-month intervals, for instance), or by inhalation (fluticasone, one
120 mcg puff q12h [ch. 90]), often in combination with a sedativeantihistamine, can reduce mucosal inflammation. Oversedation must
be avoided since mobility is important to avoid gaining weight and
promote clearance of tracheal secretions. Bronchodilators
(methylxanthines or beta-agonists) might allow reduction in smaller
airway spasm, reducing intrathoracic pressures and thus reducing
the tendency of the larger airways to collapse.

Prognosis
Most dogs improve with an individualized treatment plan, but the
condition is generally progressive. Recent studies suggest improved
long-term prognosis with the use of tracheal stents, although this
treatment is certainly susceptible to important complications.21

TRACHEOBRONCHIAL FISTULA
Tracheo- or bronchoesophageal fistula is a rare disease in dogs. It is
discussed in ch. 259.

OBSTRUCTIVE AND/OR TRAUMATIC
TRACHEAL DISEASES
Etiology
Tracheal Obstruction
Tracheal obstruction may be caused by collapsed or malformed
tracheal rings (above), stenosis subsequent to injuries, foreign
bodies, neoplasia, granulomas, external compression, or a
complication of tracheostomy.22

Tracheal Injuries
Tracheal injuries range from small lacerations to tracheal avulsions
and can be caused by intraluminal or external trauma. Intraluminal
trauma is mostly associated with endotracheal intubation, while the

most common forms of external trauma involve dog bites or
automobile accidents.

FIGURE 215.4 Tracheal abnormalities in dogs,
endoscopic views. A, Tracheitis with prolapsed and
irritated dorsal membrane; B, tracheal hypoplasia in
an English Bulldog; grade 1 (C) and grade 3 (D)
tracheal collapse.
In cats, a well-reported problem of intraluminal trauma concerns
stenosis after necrosis/rupture following endotracheal intubation23
(Video 215.6;
Figure 215.5). Delayed stenosis can occur after

intrathoracic tracheal (or bronchial) rupture caused by blunt trauma
to the neck or thorax24 (Video 215.7).

These problems have been

reported rarely in dogs.

Tracheal Foreign Bodies
Generally, when a foreign body enters the trachea, it is small enough
to pass into a bronchus (Video 215.8

). Once lodged in a

bronchus it can cause bacterial bronchopneumonia that is responsive
to antibiotics but recurrent. When the foreign bodies are too large,
they usually lodge at the carina and cause airway obstruction that
can be life threatening (Figure 215.6). Reported cases of tracheal
foreign bodies in dogs and cats are rare but have involved mineral
oil, hair, bullets, bones, plant material, toys, etc.22

Intratracheal Tumors
Intratracheal tumors are uncommon in dogs and cats. In young dogs,
osteochondroma is more likely while in older dogs or in cats, many
other tumor types can be found (e.g., mast cell tumor, lymphoma,
squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, osteosarcoma,
extramedullary plasmacytoma, leiomyoma, fibrosarcoma).22,25

Tracheal Granulomas
Tracheal granulomas can be a complication after intraluminal stent
placement in dogs with tracheal collapse and can result in a severe
reduction of the tracheal lumen (ch. 114). Tracheal parasitic
granulomas can be caused by lungworms (Filaroides [Oslerus]
osleri) in dogs and tracheal cuterebrosis in cats.

Clinical Presentation
Tracheal obstruction or injury can cause inspiratory stridor with a
prolonged inspiratory phase followed by a variable expiratory phase,
coughing, inspiratory stridor, exercise intolerance, gagging,
exertional distress, fever, change in bark, intermittent cyanosis or
collapse, and open-mouth breathing in cats.22 Tracheal tears

characteristically result in subcutaneous emphysema over the
cervical and thoracic areas due to air escaping from the trachea into
the subcutaneous tissue. Typically, subcutaneous emphysema is
palpable as crepitations in the subcutis. Pneumomediastinum can
occur rarely; in a recent study, endotracheal intubation with positive
pressure ventilation was the most common cause of
pneumomediastinum, followed by trauma, and tracheal foreign
bodies.26
After tracheal avulsion injury, the airway lumen is thought to be
maintained by either intact tracheal adventitia or by thickening of
mediastinal tissue leading to the development of a pseudoairway.24
Stenosis of the lumen then occurs at both ends of the injury.
Therefore, clinical signs such as inspiratory distress and tracheal
stridor are delayed and are due to tracheal obstruction.24 Tracheal
foreign bodies cause an acute onset of clinical signs.

Diagnosis and Management
The diagnosis of tracheal injury or obstruction is usually made by
thoracic radiography and/or tracheoscopy (Videos 215.6-215.8)

.

Minor tracheal tears may heal without intervention. Surgical
management may be necessary for more substantial injury or for
tumors, with anastomosis repair if necessary. The prognosis can still
be good even with substantial tracheal injuries.24

endotracheal intubations in a cat, endoscopic view.
The rupture has been repaired with suture.

FIGURE 215.6 Foreign body obstructing a cat’s
trachea, endoscopic view. The stone was dislodged

INFECTIOUS
TRACHEITIS/TRACHEOBRONCHITIS
Canine infectious respiratory disease complex (CIRDC), formerly
known as “kennel cough,” is commonly seen in young dogs,
especially in boarding kennels or after time spent in animal shelters.
This contagious disease is described in detail in ch. 203.

BRONCHIAL DISEASES
BRONCHIAL DISEASES—PRIMARY
Chronic Bronchitis in Dogs
Definition, Overview
Chronic bronchitis (CB) is an incurable disease of insidious onset,
characterized by chronic and persistent cough, and related to chronic
inflammation of the airways unassociated with any identified specific
primary cause. It is a syndrome more than a true diagnosis.27
Therefore, in dogs, it is also called nonspecific/aspecific chronic
bronchitis.
CB in dogs is defined when 3 diagnostic criteria are fulfilled: (1) ≥2
months of coughing; (2) evidence of mucus hypersecretion and (3)
exclusion of other chronic cardiopulmonary diseases (e.g., congestive
heart failure, chronic infectious bronchopneumonia, pulmonary
neoplasia, eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy [EBP]) as the sole
cause of cough. Such cardiorespiratory diseases (e.g., congestive
heart failure, airway collapse) may coexist and complicate the
diagnosis and treatment of CB. In humans, the functional sequela of
CB is chronic airway obstruction, referred to as chronic obstructive
pulmonary disease (COPD), and subsequent emphysema. This
mechanism appears to be less frequently observed in dogs, although
the diagnosis of COPD relies on documentation of airflow
obstruction by pulmonary function tests that are not widely available
in veterinary medicine. Dogs with severe and longstanding CB can
exhibit either bronchiectasis (dilation and destruction of the walls of
the bronchi) or bronchomalacia (airway collapse during expiration
and cough) or both combined.

Etiology, Epidemiology, and Risk Factors
By definition, primary causes of CB are poorly understood. The
major difficulty is that the disease is detectable only in its advanced
stages, since it has an insidious onset and protracted pathogenesis.
Therefore, the diagnostic work up is based on exclusion of possible
specific causes, which can be frustrating for both the clinician and
the owner. Clinicopathological findings are variable and

inconclusive. Nonspecific CB is mostly diagnosed in middle-aged to
old smaller breeds of dogs, but it can also occur in larger breeds.
Many dogs with CB are overweight and have periodontitis and dental
tartar, which could be potential risk factors.
In humans, the most important risk factors include smoke
exposure, atmospheric pollution, and infection. The same factors
could impact development of CB in dogs. Moreover, in dogs,
chronic/previous infection with CIRDC pathogens (e.g., Bordetella
bronchiseptica) or canine distemper virus, with parasites leading to
eosinophilic CB, or presence of other diseases like tracheal collapse
or chronic cardiac disease, are all potential causes leading to
development of CB. Exposure to environmental tobacco has not been
confirmed as a risk factor.28
In people, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is generally
considered among the most common etiologies of chronic cough.
Indeed, cough management guidelines published by numerous
respiratory societies worldwide recommend evaluation and
treatment of GERD as an integral component of the
diagnostic/therapeutic algorithm for the management of chronic
cough. Silent aspiration occurs in over half of healthy humans during
sleep without clinical consequence29 so it is reasonable to suspect
that healthy dogs could have silent aspiration without clinical
respiratory disease (ch. 221).30,31 Indeed, GERD has been shown to
be common in healthy dogs in a study using nuclear scintigraphy to
document reflux32 while GERD and microaspiration of gastric juice
reflux aspiration have been documented in specific breeds (such as
healthy West Highland White Terriers) using detection of bile acids
in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF).31 Aerodigestive disorders
causing cough in dogs are probably underdiagnosed due to poor
clinical recognition and diagnostic limitations.33
Videofluoroscopic swallow studies (VFSS) and detection of bile
acids in the BALF have been used for confirming the contribution of
GERD and microaspiration/occult aerodigestive disorders in dogs
presenting for cough without gastrointestinal (GI) signs,33,34
including cases of CB.35 Another finding supporting the occurrence
of repetitive microaspiration is the heterogeneity and alterations of

the lung microbiota in dogs with CB, believed to result from
increased colonization of the lower airways during compromised
airway function.35

Pathophysiology
CB results in inflammatory changes within the bronchial mucosa,
including increased mucus production. Bronchial wall thickening
and possible progressive bronchomalacia contribute to airflow
obstruction and further worsen inflammation, which induces cough;
the cough, in turn, triggers further inflammation.

Clinical Presentation
Middle-aged to older dogs of smaller breeds are more often affected.
The disease is more common in obese and overweight animals (ch.
150) and the presence of dental tartar is frequently recognized. A
persistent, sonorous cough often followed by a terminal retch, and
without any identified cause, is generally the chief (and often only)
client concern.

Diagnosis
Chronic cough related to specific causes should be ruled out,
specifically including tracheal collapse, lung fibrosis (ch. 217), EBP,
parasitic lung diseases (ch. 217), airway or lung tumors (ch. 217),
and mitral valve disease (ch. 232). Diagnostic tests are performed to
rule out other causes of chronic cough. Results of a complete blood
count are usually normal. If detected, peripheral eosinophilia points
instead towards pulmonary eosinophilia or parasite infection. Other
laboratory testing that should be considered includes heartworm
antigen testing (ch. 237), fecal analysis for both eggs and lungworm
larva (ch. 80), and evaluation of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic
peptide (NT-proBNP) as a biomarker for left atrial
enlargement/congestive heart failure (ch. 229) or PH (ch. 218).
Elevated NT-proBNP concentrations should prompt further
evaluation by echocardiography (chs. 73, 97).36 Thoracic
radiographs show bronchial wall thickening or a generalized increase
in airway-oriented interstitial opacity or both. Thoracic radiographs
are also useful to exclude other conditions that cause cough, such as

congestive heart failure, lung masses, or interstitial lung disease.
Fluoroscopy is useful for evaluating the airways for collapse (ch.
212). Ultrasound is not particularly useful in bronchitis.37
Computed tomography (CT), which is widely used in people with
airway diseases, is growing in popularity for identification of canine
bronchial disease. CT scanning usually requires brief general
anesthesia, so is commonly combined with evaluation of laryngeal
function (ch. 214), bronchoscopy (ch. 93), and collection of airway
cytologic samples in dogs suspected of having CB.38,39
Bronchoscopic findings are variable but can include irregular
mucosal surfaces with a loss of the normally glistening appearance, a
granular and roughened aspect, and sometimes signs of partial
bronchial collapse. However, similar significant findings have been
reported in aging healthy dogs, together with some degree of
bronchiectasis,40 and therefore such findings must be interpretated
with caution. The presence of excessive thickened and sticky mucus
in the airways is also consistent with CB.
Cytologic evaluation of BALF typically reveals excessive mucus
with possible hyperplasia of epithelial cells, and increased numbers
of neutrophils, goblet cells, and macrophages.41 Analysis of
bronchial brushings might be a more sensitive indicator of airway
inflammation than cytologic examination of BAL, showing greater
percentages of leukocytes and neutrophils.41 As with peripheral
eosinophilia, airway eosinophilic inflammation suggests EBP or
parasitic infection (e.g., heartworm disease, Angiostrongylus or
Crenosoma infection).42-45
Echocardiography (ch. 97) helps to diagnose mitral valve disease
that might be concurrent with CB or might be an alternative
explanation for cough. It can also detect evidence of PH, which can
occur secondary to chronic tracheobronchial disease.
As mentioned, VFSS allows identification of dogs with occult
aerodigestive disorders.34

Management and Monitoring
The bronchial alterations are not readily reversible, if at all.
Therefore, treatment won’t cure the disease but ideally will prevent

or slow disease progression. Therapy is based on an assessment of
the nature and severity of the individual animal’s problems, and
relies on client education. Treatment goals for dogs with CB include
avoiding exacerbating factors, reducing inflammation, limiting
cough, and improving stamina.
Any environmental pollutants should be eliminated. Owners
should be advised not to smoke indoors and to limit exposure of dogs
to airborne irritants, including perfumes.
Control of body weight is very important. Obesity (ch. 150) should
be treated comprehensively because it markedly worsens cough and
limits activity. Furthermore, obesity impairs lung function and
increases airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR).46,47 Weight loss
induces a significant improvement of cardiopulmonary function.47
In fact, weight loss alone can cause major improvement in clinical
signs without any additional drug. A harness should be used in place
of a collar, and episodes of excessive barking should be curtailed with
appropriate behavioral modification.
Control of infection and dental hygiene are advocated (ch. 258)
since bacteria from dental tartar may be inhaled into the lower
airways, especially during panting.
Glucocorticoids are the mainstay of treatment of CB because they
reduce mucus hypersecretion and mucosal bronchial wall thickening
as well as reducing airway inflammation, which reduces cough.
Glucocorticoids can be administered orally or via inhalation.
Prednisone is the most commonly used glucocorticoid and is
administered at 0.5-1 mg/kg PO q24h initially and then tapered to
the lowest effective dosage that controls clinical signs. Alternate-day
therapy is preferred to allow normalization of the hypothalamicpituitary axis and to limit clinical signs associated with use of
exogenous glucocorticoids.
Inhaled glucocorticoids have been used widely in people and are
used with growing frequency in dogs with CB, since avoidance of
systemic steroid effects can improve quality of life. One study
demonstrated the benefits of therapy with fluticasone, delivered via a
spacer chamber and face mask designed especially for dogs (e.g.,
AeroDawg; ch. 90).48 Bronchodilators (beta-2 agonists,
theophylline) are frequently used, although their effectiveness in the
treatment of CB has not been well-investigated.

Antibiotics are warranted in dogs with an acute exacerbation of CB
and a reasonable suspicion of infection. Doxycycline and macrolides
(azithromycin) are good choices for dogs with CB because these
drugs have anti-inflammatory properties as well as antimicrobial
effects.27 Fluoroquinolones also have good tissue penetration but
concurrent administration of fluoroquinolones with theophylline can
result in theophylline toxicosis.49
When coughing is exhausting to dog and owner despite antiinflammatory therapy, cough suppressants can be helpful. Over-thecounter cough suppressants are rarely effective in dogs, whereas
narcotic cough suppressants are most effective. In some countries,
oral preparations containing opioids have become less and less easily
available. In countries where no oral preparation of butorphanol can
be prescribed, a couple of drops of injectable solution deposited on
the tongue can be effective but neither the necessary dosage, nor the
dosage-effect relationship, have been studied (Table 215.1). In
human medicine, gabapentin has shown efficacy for controlling
cough related to hyperactive cough reflex sensitivity,50 but no
studies are available in dogs. Since neurogenic pathways mediated by
tachykinins that bind neurokinin (NK)-1 receptors may induce cough
and airway inflammation, the effect of maropitant, an NK-1 receptor
antagonist, has been investigated in small dogs with CB. While
maropitant may have antitussive properties, it is unsuitable as a sole
drug for the treatment of CB since it has no effect on airway
inflammation.51

Idiopathic Eosinophilic Bronchopneumopathy in
Dogs
Etiology, Pathophysiology
Canine idiopathic eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy (EBP) is a
disease characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of the pulmonary
and bronchial mucosa, considered to be manifestations of
immunological hypersensitivity. The associated terminology is
somewhat confusing since EBP is also called idiopathic eosinophilic
lung disease (ELD), where ELD encompasses eosinophilic bronchitis
(EB) and eosinophilic bronchopneumonia, subgroups based on the
findings of thoracic imaging.52 ELD also has been categorized on the
basis of radiographic, bronchoscopic, and BALF analysis into EB,
EBP and eosinophilic granuloma (EG).53 However EG is also
reported as eosinophilic pulmonary granulomatosis (EPG), defined
as a variant of eosinophilic disease characterized by granulomatous
masses. It is discussed in ch. 217.

Although the etiology of EBP is unknown, the association of
eosinophilic infiltration and predominance of CD4+ T-cells suggests
a dominant T helper 2 immune response mounted in the lower
airways.54 Suspected and known causes of pulmonary
hypersensitivities in humans and animals include fungi, molds,
drugs, bacteria, and parasites. In many cases, no underlying cause is
found. The role of inhaled allergens in EBP is still unclear. EBP is
mostly diagnosed in young dogs. Siberian Huskies and Malamutes
are predominantly affected but many other breeds are susceptible. In
a study assessing detection rates of Mycoplasma canis (M. canis), M.
cynos and Bordetella bronchiseptica in dogs with EBP and CB
compared with healthy dogs, higher B. bronchiseptica loads were
only present in dogs with EBP and high clinical score, indicating a
possible relationship between B. bronchiseptica infection or load and
EBP.55

Clinical Presentation
Unless the disease is associated with concomitant bacterial
bronchopneumonia, the patient’s overall condition is generally good.
Clinical signs consistently include coughing, gagging, and retching.
In acute cases, gagging and retching are sometimes the main
concern, extending the differential diagnosis to GI disorders.
Respiratory distress is a very frequent sign, and about half of affected
dogs have nasal discharge.

FIGURE 215.7 Eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy
in a 3-year-old Husky dog. This left lateral thoracic
radiograph shows a severe bronchointerstitial
pattern with peribronchial infiltration. Courtesy G.
Bolen.

Diagnosis
Elements that lead to a diagnosis of EBP include signalment and
history (breed, young age, previous response to corticosteroids),
clinical signs, radiographic and bronchoscopic findings, blood
eosinophilia, tissue eosinophilic infiltration as demonstrated by
cytological or histopathological examinations, response to adequate
treatment, and exclusion of other disorders. The most common
radiographic finding is a moderate to severe bronchointerstitial
pattern (Figure 215.7). Computed tomographic findings associated
with EBP are variable and heterogeneous, and include marked to
moderate bronchial wall thickening, plugging of the bronchial lumen
by mucus/debris, bronchiectasis, presence of pulmonary nodules

and lymphadenopathy.56 Typical macroscopic findings on
bronchoscopy include the presence of abundant yellow-green mucus
or mucopurulent material (Video 215.9)

, severe thickening of the

mucosa with an irregular or polypoid surface (Video 215.10)

and,

in some cases, partial airway closure during expiration (Video 215.11)
. Peripheral blood eosinophilia is observed frequently (∼60%).
BALF or a brush cytologic specimen always demonstrates a marked
eosinophilic component (Figure 215.8); usually, >50% of the
inflammatory cells are eosinophils. In most cases, eosinophilic
infiltration of the bronchial mucosa can be observed in biopsies.
Elevated BALF levels of procollagen type III amino terminal
propeptide (PIIINP), a protein used as a marker of collagen type III
synthesis, occur in dogs with EBP, possibly due to secondary
fibrosis.57

Differential Diagnosis
Parasitic diseases are the major differential diagnosis to be excluded
in these cases. Several parasites, like Strongyloides spp., Ascaris
spp., Toxocara canis, or Ancylostoma spp. (ch. 217) can lead to
eosinophilic pneumonia in humans and probably in dogs as well;
respiratory signs are only mild and GI signs usually predominate.
In the dog, occult heartworm disease caused by Dirofilaria
immitis can cause eosinophilic pneumonitis (ch. 237). Migration of
Angiostrongylus vasorum larvae through pulmonary parenchyma
may also result in eosinophilic pneumonia in dogs (Video 215.12)
. A. vasorum infection (i.e., French heartworm disease) is an
emerging disease, with reported increase in both distribution and
incidence in the United Kingdom, Europe, South Africa and Atlantic
Canada (ch. 217). The worm is spread through ingestion of
intermediate hosts, including slugs and snails. The main clinical
signs include respiratory signs, coagulopathies and neurological
abnormalities.58 Early diagnosis is required since angiostrongylosis
can be fatal if left untreated. In cases with respiratory clinical signs,

pulmonary changes can already be suggestive and include moderate
to severe bronchointerstitial or alveolointerstitial changes, often
more severe in peripheral and/or caudodorsal areas (Figure 215.9).
The diagnosis is made by Baermann fecal flotation; a point-of-care
antigen test is available in Europe,59 and A. vasorum DNA can be
detected by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in BALF60 (ch. 217).

FIGURE 215.8 Cytological preparation
(bronchoalveolar lavage cytospin) from a dog with
eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy, showing 47%
eosinophils (arrow). Total cell count was 7000
cells/mcL.

FIGURE 215.9 Angiostrongylosis in a dog. Left
lateral thoracic radiograph shows a generalized
bronchointerstitial pattern with air bronchograms
indicating a severe alveolar pattern at the periphery
of the caudal lung lobes. A faint pleural fissure line
between the left cranial and the caudal lobes could
indicate mild pleural effusion. Enlarged pulmonary
