Other bronchopulmonary parasites, like Eucoleus aerophilus
(formerly Capillaria aerophila), Filaroides (Oslerus) osleri,
Filaroides hirthi, Crenosoma vulpis (Video 215.13)

or

Paragonimus kellicotti, are also implicated in the influx of
eosinophils in the airways (F. osleri) or lungs (other parasites) in
dogs, and can mimic EBP. A higher frequency of bronchial disease
due to infection by Crenosoma vulpis is also emerging in Europe.61

FIGURE 215.10 L1 Angiostrongylus larva seen on
cytological examination of a cytocentrifuged MayGrünwald-Giemsa-stained smear of bronchoalveolar
lavage fluid.
A thorough search for parasites should be completed using fecal
examination (zinc sulfate centrifugation-flotation and especially
Baermann sedimentation procedure; ch. 80) (Figure 215.10) or
even BALF analysis (ch. 93). A single negative fecal examination is
not conclusive so such exams should be repeated, or alternatively,
the animal may be given appropriate anthelmintic drugs.

Management
The response of eosinophilic airway disease to corticosteroid therapy
is generally very good, independent of radiographic findings,
although achievement of total cure is not always obtained.
Prednisolone is initiated at a dosage of 0.5-1 mg/kg q12h PO × 1
week, then q24h × 1 week, then q48h × 1 week, followed by gradual
decrease until the lowest dosage that maintains clinical response is
attained. Since chronic oral steroid therapy has limitations (side-

effects, contraindication with certain comorbidities [ch. 224]),
inhaled steroid therapy (IST) has been increasingly used (ch.
90).48,62 However, it seems that treatment of EBP with long-term
IST alone may be insufficient and that sustained long-term IST may
induce inhibition of the pituitary–adrenal axis.62 Other drugs with
immunomodulatory effect have been proposed, but no trial results
are available to date.

Prognosis
Relapse often occurs within weeks to months after drug
discontinuation although clinical signs remain fully resolved in some
dogs after discontinuation.52,54,62

Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia
Etiology and Pathophysiology
Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), previously referred to as immotile
cilia syndrome, results from a heterogeneous group of inherited
defects that cause ciliary dysmotility. These are mostly associated
with ultrastructural abnormalities, and clinically they cause
recurrent upper and lower airway bacterial infections. In dogs as in
humans, uncoordinated and ineffective ciliary function results in
ineffective clearance of airway mucus. In turn, this results in chronic
mucus plugging and inflammation of nasal cavities and airways as
well as infection. The dysfunction of the monocilia of the embryonic
node may also lead to randomization of situs (left-right body
symmetry) and transposition of the thoracic and/or the abdominal
organs in 50% of cases.13 Kartagener’s syndrome represents a triad
that consists of bronchiectasis, complete left-right transposition of
viscera (situs inversus) and chronic rhinosinusitis. This syndrome
has been reported in humans and in dogs with PCD. PCD is a rare
disease that has been reported in many dog breeds.63-66
This genetic disease is usually inherited in an autosomal recessive
mode. In dogs, a mutation has been identified in Old English
Sheepdogs66 and in Malamutes.67 A genetic test is now currently

available for breeding purposes in those breeds, but not yet in other
breeds where other defects occur. Most cases in dogs are reported
from a single animal, but sometimes littermates are affected or
different cases occur within the same breed.64,65,68 The disorder is
extremely rare in cats.

Clinical Presentation
Clinical signs include chronic respiratory abnormalities such as
rhinosinusitis, bronchitis, bronchopneumonia, and bronchiectasis.
Although respiratory system signs are most common, signs can
reflect dysfunctional ciliated epithelia or microtubules in other
tissues, such as otitis media, infertility, asthenoteratospermia in
males, hydrocephalus, and renal fibrosis or dilation of renal tubules.
Respiratory signs typically begin at an early age in a purebred
vaccinated dog; however, some dogs only begin to show signs at
several months to several years of age. Hallmark clinical features,
e.g., recurrent bilateral mucopurulent nasal discharge and recurrent,
antibiotic-responsive bronchitis or bronchopneumonia since birth,
should alert the clinician to include PCD in the differential diagnosis.

Diagnosis
Confirmation of a diagnosis of PCD requires both in vivo and in vitro
functional and ultrastructural analysis of cilia. However, finding the
hallmark clinical features in combination with situs inversus is
strongly suggestive, as could be sperm evaluation or other tests
demonstrating signs associated with microtubular defects. In vitro
functional analysis of cilia in dogs suspected of having PCD utilized
scintigraphy as the diagnostic tool to evaluate mucociliary clearance.
In vivo functional analysis in PCD consistently demonstrates an
uncoordinated or a dyskinetic ciliary beat. In the Old English
Sheepdog, a Taqman assay with excellent sensitivity and specificity
has allowed study of the prevalence of the mutation within the breed;
the mutated allele was found both in European and in American Old
English Sheepdogs.68 This genetic test also allowed removal of silent
carriers from breeding programs, as occurs in the Malamute.67

Differential Diagnosis
Other causes of recurrent bacterial infection of the upper and lower
airways should be investigated. Immune deficiency (ch. 180),
pathogens resistant to chosen antimicrobial drugs (ch. 203),
bronchial foreign bodies (above), and other causes are important
differential diagnoses for PCD. In Irish Wolfhounds a
rhinitis/bronchopneumonia syndrome causing transient to
persistent mucoid or mucopurulent nasal discharge, cough, and
dyspnea from an early age has been described; so far PCD has not yet
been identified as its cause.69

Management
Even though PCD is not a curable disorder, it can frequently be
managed for some years. A key element in successful management is
the judicious use of effective antibiotics over time (ch. 7). Moreover,
good systemic and local hydration together with daily coupage and
vigorous exercise will help to clear mucus from the airways (ch. 90).

Prognosis
Once the diagnosis is established, the long-term prognosis is poor
because despite adequate management, the disease generally
progresses over time and the response to treatment decreases.

Bronchial Mineralization, Broncholithiasis
Bronchial mineralization is rarely encountered. It can occur
secondary to any chronic inflammatory or infectious condition.
Bronchial mineralization may in fact be totally unassociated with
clinical evidence of dysfunction. Peribronchial mucous glands may
mineralize in normal cats, appearing as multifocal mineralized
opacities.70,71

BRONCHIAL DISEASES—SECONDARY
Bronchiectasis
Introduction

Bronchiectasis is defined as an abnormal and permanent dilatation
and distortion of subsegmental airways, resulting from chronic
airway inflammation that damages elastic components of the bronchi
leading to bronchial wall destruction and impaired clearance of
respiratory secretions.72 It is considered a unique disease entity
although several congenital or acquired conditions that lead to a
cycle of chronic airway infection and inflammation may result in
bronchiectatic changes. In dogs, bronchiectatic changes can be
associated with bronchomalacic changes (Video 215.14)

.

Etiology, Pathophysiology
In dogs and cats, focal bronchiectasis can result from foreign body
aspiration and/or bronchial obstruction.73 Diffuse bronchiectasis
often occurs subsequent to acquired diseases (ch. 217)28,73,74
including aspiration or inhalation injury, chronic infectious
bronchopneumonia75 (including parasitic76,77 and Irish Wolfhounds
with recurrent bacterial pneumonia75), chronic infection with
Bordetella bronchiseptica or with Pneumocystis carinii in dogs with
immune deficiency, EBP (bronchiectasis identified on CT in 60% of
affected dogs),56 CB, West Highland White Terriers with idiopathic
pulmonary fibrosis,78 and possibly, allergic bronchopulmonary
aspergillosis (a rare cause of localized cavitary bronchiectasis).74 In
cats, chronic bronchial inflammatory disease has been suggested as
the most common disease associated with bronchiectasis, especially
CB, neoplasia, and bronchopneumonia,79 and has been recently
described in a case of diffuse feline fibrotic lung disease.80 Affected
airways are usually partially obstructed by purulent or viscid
exudates since the dilation greatly interferes with normal airway
clearance. Dysfunction of mucociliary clearance, in turn, allows
pooling of mucus, exudates and microbes, and secondary infection
stimulates a host inflammatory response, creating a vicious circle of
further damage to the airway wall and predisposition to recurrent
bronchopulmonary infections (Figure 215.11).

Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis
In dogs, bronchiectasis is more common in dogs >7 years of age, with
a predilection for the American Cocker Spaniel, Miniature Poodle,
Siberian Husky and English Springer Spaniel.73 Clinical signs likely
reflect the underlying disease process, and generally include
coughing (most common), gagging, tachypnea, dyspnea, and
occasionally fever.73
Bronchiectasis can be detected by thoracic radiography, high
resolution computed tomography (HRCT) or bronchoscopy (Videos
215.14 and 215.15)

. Radiographic and bronchoscopic

characteristics of bronchiectasis in dogs have been described.73
Bronchoscopy is not considered the gold standard, but it is helpful to
recognize/visualize bronchiectatic lesions, and more importantly to
enable collection of samples for identification and potential
treatment of possible underlying diseases. Bronchoscopic evaluation
identifies mucopurulent plugs in the dilated airways as well as rough,
hyperemic bronchial wall linings. In people, survey thoracic
radiographs are not considered a very sensitive technique for
evaluation of bronchiectatic changes. HRCT has been described as
the noninvasive gold standard for diagnosing bronchiectasis.
Primary CT features of bronchiectasis in people include bronchial
dilation, lack of peripheral bronchial tapering, and identification of
distinct airways within 1 cm of the pleural surface. Secondary
features of bronchiectasis include bronchial wall thickening, mucus
plugging in the bronchial lumen, and peripheral air trapping as
reflected by measurable reduced pulmonary density in affected
regions.81 The most widely used CT criterion for quantifying
abnormal bronchial dilation is the bronchoarterial ratio (BA, ratio of
the cross-sectional bronchial luminal diameter to accompanying
pulmonary artery diameter) >1.81 However, healthy dogs can have a
bronchoarterial ratio up to 2.0.82 In dogs with bronchiectasis
diagnosed via bronchoscopy and/or histopathologic assessment of
tissue samples, the most common CT characteristics of
bronchiectasis are dilatation, a lack of peripheral airway tapering,
and lobar consolidation.83

FIGURE 215.11 Vicious circle hypothesis in
bronchiectasis. Host-mediated inflammatory
response to foreign material and bacteria in the
airway causes tissue damage, resulting in
bronchiectasis, which contributes to abnormal
mucus clearance and further bacterial colonization.
Given the lack of studies comparing CT and bronchoscopic
features of bronchiectasis in dogs, the sensitivity of a bronchoscopic
diagnosis of bronchiectasis is questionable. Age affects such findings:
bronchiectasis has been described as a normal endoscopic finding in
old Beagle dogs, and this finding does not seem to be associated with
an increased neutrophilic content of the BALF.40 Such age-related
differences should be considered when interpreting bronchoscopic
findings in old dogs with respiratory disease.
Culture and sensitivity of BALF for aerobic and anaerobic bacteria
are suggested because this is likely to be helpful in treating the
patient. In dogs, no conclusion regarding the frequency of
distribution of individual bacterial species in bronchiectasis could be
drawn.73
Cytologic evaluation of BALF typically identifies neutrophilia,
eosinophilia if secondary to an allergic cause or a parasitic infection,
and squamous metaplasia of the epithelial cells. PCR on BALF may

identify Bordetella spp., Mycoplasma spp. or Aspergillus spp., since
allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis might be a cause of localized
cavitary bronchiectasis,74 as described in people.

Management
The goal of therapy is to control clinical signs, and treat or even
prevent bacterial infections. In human medicine, inhaled therapies,
including antimicrobials and mucoactive drugs (e.g., mucolytics and
hyperosmolar agents) form the backbone of treatments. Macrolide
antibiotics have anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory
properties (without suppression of the immune system) in addition
to antibacterial activity, but equivalent studies in dogs or cats with
bronchiectasis are lacking. At present, there are no definitive data to
support the routine use of glucocorticoids, even in inhaled form,
unless the patient suffers from coexisting asthma/EBP.

Prognosis
Addressing the primary underlying pathological process is vital to
slow the progressive destruction of bronchial walls. Despite
substantial clinical abnormalities, dogs with bronchiectasis may
survive for years.72,73 Surgical resection of lung lobes with focal
bronchiectasis may be curative.

Bronchomalacia
Overview and Etiology
Bronchomalacia (BM) is characterized by weakness of the wall of
principal or smaller bronchi leading to collapse of the bronchial wall.
In humans, BM is described in children but no disease clearly
parallels the syndrome in dogs. In dogs, BM has been increasingly
recognized, mainly in aged dogs.5,6,11,84-86 The etiology is unclear.
Based on endoscopy, BM can be classified as diffuse or localized, and
static, dynamic, or both.84 While static BM is common in
brachycephalic dogs,85 dynamic BM, based on bronchoscopic
examination (Video 215.14)

, most frequently occurs in

association with some degree of tracheal collapse—either primary or
secondarily induced—and is called tracheobronchomalacia. BM can
involve only the bronchi,6 which shows that dynamic BM can occur
as an isolated clinical entity. It is then either associated with
bronchial infection and/or inflammation84 or not. Indeed, the role of
airway inflammation or infection in BM cannot be confirmed in
many cases.6,84-86 Furthermore, the role of cardiomegaly in the
disorder has been investigated but no association between left atrial
enlargement and airway collapse could be identified.11

Clinical Presentation
Since BM is frequently associated with tracheal collapse, Poodles and
Yorkshire Terriers, especially if overweight or obese, are most
commonly affected.6,84,86 Many brachycephalic dogs show static
BM.85 Other breeds (mostly older, small dogs) can be affected as
well.
Clinical signs include chronic cough in the vast majority of the
cases. In many of them, signs of airway obstruction such as
wheezing, intermittent or continuous respiratory distress, cyanosis,
difficulty in clearing secretions, and possible recurrent bronchitis
and pneumonia occur. Pulmonary crackles (ch. 212) can be heard
on lung auscultation.84

Diagnosis
Multiple imaging modalities and bronchoscopy (ch. 93) might be
required for confirmation of BM.4,5 Radiography is less sensitive
than bronchoscopy for detecting airway collapse.4,6 Radiography and
fluoroscopy are complementary, both being useful for documenting
bronchial collapse in dogs.16 Thoracic CT scans are of great
interest,39 but due to the dynamic nature of airway collapse, paired
inspiratory-expiratory scans are needed, which should be performed
in anesthetized and intubated dogs with ventilator-assisted breathholds. Assigning pathologic significance to airway collapse is
challenging in view of the substantial bronchial collapsibility that has

been described in healthy animals87,88 and grading systems to assess
the magnitude of the collapse are needed.
Bronchoscopy seems essential because it allows visualisation of the
airways during the breathing cycle, severity of the lesions, and
localization of the segments affected. In the author’s opinion, severe
cases of dynamic BM, showing pronounced bronchial collapse during
expiration, also exhibit signs of bronchiectasis during the inspiratory
phase. Analysis of BALF is warranted and can reveal underlying
infectious or inflammatory diseases requiring specific therapy. Blood
gas analysis often confirms impaired oxygenation, with mild
hypoxemia and increased alveolar-arterial difference for O2 (ch.
212).89 Echocardiography is also advised to detect PH, since PH has
been described in dogs with BM7 and should be recognized and
treated accordingly (ch. 218).8,90,91

Treatment and Outcome
Treatment is nonspecific and supportive, and should be based on
clinical findings in each case. Like in dogs with tracheal collapse,
long-term therapy mainly aims to decrease factors that can promote
BM. Measures include strict weight control (ch. 150), use of a
harness, removing the dog from respiratory irritants, and dealing
with comorbid conditions such as inflammation, infection, PH, or
concomitant mitral valve disease.
Studies investigating how dogs with BM respond to treatment are
lacking. In the author’s experience, static and localized BM in
brachycephalic dogs does not require therapy. Some dogs with more
diffuse dynamic BM respond reasonably well to close monitoring,
but BM may be associated with a poor prognosis in some dogs with
intractable cough and/or worsening signs of airway obstruction.

Feline Lower Airway Disease (FLAD)
Cough is an infrequent clinical sign in cats compared to dogs (Videos
215.16 and 215.17)

. Furthermore, in cats, cough is fairly specific

for tracheobronchial disease since cough of cardiac origin is rare.
Feline lower airway disease is a term encompassing all bronchial

diseases, including inflammatory and noninflammatory bronchial
diseases. Inflammatory bronchial diseases are by far more common.
Feline inflammatory bronchial disease (feline asthma or CB) is
characterized by inflammation of the lower airways without an
identifiable cause. It is recognized clinically by various combinations
of cough, wheeze, abnormal increase in respiratory effort with
activity, and respiratory distress. These signs are attributable to
airway obstruction caused by bronchial inflammation.
Many confusing terms are found in the literature, such as CB,
allergic bronchitis, EB, and bronchial asthma. Differentiating
asthmatic bronchitis from non-asthmatic bronchitis is still
challenging.
Whether feline asthma and CB are truly separate entities or two
facets of the same disease remains uncertain.92,93 According to some
authors, feline asthma and CB should be considered two distinct
diseases.94 Differences in etiology, thoracic radiographic findings,
bronchoalveolar eosinophil/neutrophil percentages, serum allergenspecific IgE testing and response to airway responsiveness testing
have been investigated but no clear-cut discriminatory test exists.95101
Categorization is based on eosinophil and neutrophil percentages
in BALF. Several articles report values for cell types in feline
BALF,101,102 but since specific reference ranges have not been
established,98 both eosinophil and neutrophil thresholds for defining
asthma and CB are arbitrarily assigned.96,97 Due to this lack of
consensus regarding how feline asthma is defined, most published
studies fail to discriminate between spontaneous feline asthma and
feline CB. Therefore, information on both diseases is presented here
in a single section titled “Feline Inflammatory Bronchial Disease.”
This is followed by a brief differential diagnosis for feline bronchial
diseases of noninflammatory origin. Differentiating feline
inflammatory bronchial disease from noninflammatory chronic
lower airway diseases is necessary because of differences in
pathogenesis, treatments, and prognosis.99 Therefore, differential
diagnosis with feline bronchial diseases of noninflammatory origin
will be addressed.

Feline Inflammatory Bronchial Disease
Pathogenesis and Pathophysiology
According to some authors,93,98,99 asthma and CB in cats should be
considered two distinct syndromes. CB is thought to arise due to a
previous insult that has permanently damaged the airway, leading to
clinicopathological features that are similar to those of asthma.
Feline asthma is thought to be allergic,93 although at present, it is
not clear whether an allergic form can be differentiated from a
chronic disease of other origin. In humans, asthma is mediated by an
allergic response after exposure to inhaled allergens. This induces
stimulation of a T helper 2 response, leading to the secretion of an
array of cytokines that drive the immune response that causes
pathological changes in the airways. In human asthma, clinical signs
are related to 3 hallmark features: 1) reversible airway inflammation,
2) consequent obstruction/airflow limitation, 3) linked to AHR, and
also to smooth muscle hypertrophy, excessive mucus production and
accumulation, and bronchial wall edema.103 Those changes are
sometimes reversible. However, chronic inflammation can lead to
severe lower airway obstruction that causes lung hyperinflation,
because cats are unable to exhale completely past the narrowed
airways, resulting in air trapping. Lung hyperinflation may lead to
permanent changes, as evidenced by progressive airway remodelling
including bronchiectasis, fibrosis, or emphysema.

Clinical Presentation
Although middle-aged females (2-8 years) seem to be more
frequently presented, cats of any age (usually begins in young or
middle age) and either sex can be affected.92,104-107 Some studies
report an increased frequency in Siamese cats,104,106 but this could
be affected by regional feline breed distributions. Clinical signs vary
in severity but include cough with or without increased breathing
effort.93,98 Clinical signs are often chronic or slowly progressive. In
some cats, signs go unnoticed by the owner for long periods of time.
In others, complaints include vomiting or hairballs, driving the
clinical examination toward a GI work-up and/or treatment. Mildly

affected cats may only have occasional, brief episodes of cough
separated by long periods without clinical signs, while in moderately
or severely affected cases, cough occurs daily and cats may have a
decreased quality of life due to breathing discomfort. Cats with
severe exacerbations (“asthmatic crisis,” “status asthmaticus”) may
present acutely with open-mouth breathing, respiratory distress, and
cyanosis. Exacerbation may occur in association with exposure to
potential allergens or irritants, such as aerosol sprays, cigarette
smoke, environmental dust, or after stress or exercise, including
stress-related visits to the vet!

Diagnosis
Cats experiencing an asthmatic crisis should be manipulated
minimally (ch. 37). Auscultation can reveal decreased heart sounds
due to extreme lung hyperinflation. Cats should be stabilized as soon
as possible (below and ch. 123). In less severe or chronic cases,
physical examination findings are variable. The physical examination
can be normal at rest or may include positive tracheal reflex,
presence of tachypnea or obstructive expiratory dyspnea while
auscultation may be unremarkable or reveal wheezes during the
expiratory phase, or more rarely crackles. Cardiac function is not
impaired unless there is a concomitant disease. At this stage,
additional testing is required. In particular, different species of
lungworms (Aelurostrongylus abstrusus and Troglostrongylus
species) and heartworms (specifically heartworm [Dirofilaria
immitis]-associated respiratory disease; HWD [ch. 237]) can induce
overlapping clinicopathologic features.108,109 In view of the apparent
geographical expansion of feline lungworms and heartworms,110-112
they are probably underrecognized and represent a challenging
differential diagnosis with feline asthma.

Imaging
Routine thoracic radiographs can be unremarkable in some affected
cats. The classic pattern includes a bronchointerstitial pattern and
evidence of bronchial wall thickening (doughnuts or railroad tracks);
air trapping may also be evident (increased lucency and flattening of
the diaphragm), as well as sometimes right middle lung lobe

atelectasis.106,113 In many cases, radiographic findings are not
specific enough to confirm the diagnosis. Thoracic CT is a more
sensitive means of detecting bronchial wall thickening and
bronchiectasis114 than are plain radiographs. In cats, CT can be
performed using a plexiglass chamber (the VetMousetrap), allowing
acquisition of images without chemical restraint.115 This can be of
great benefit in cats that are unable to tolerate any stress.

Blood Testing
No finding is specific for FLAD. Approximately 20% of affected cats
have peripheral eosinophilia,104-106 which is not correlated with the
degree of airway eosinophilia. A stress leukogram can be observed,
as well as nonspecific hyperglobulinemia in 14-50% of cases. A
heartworm antibody/antigen test can be used to investigate
heartworm-associated respiratory disease108; qPCR tools can
identify different species of lungworms (A. abstrusus and
Troglostrongylus species) and should be used whenever possible.118
Serum specific IgE directed against aeroallergens has been found
in some cats with eosinophilic airway inflammation, but the number
of affected cats with positive results does not differ from controls.119
A strong correlation has been found between the identification of
allergic-specific IgE and cats with asthma, and the majority of these
cats were polysensitized. However, large numbers of allergens with
positive IgE reactivity or magnitude of IgE reactivity were not
significantly associated with clinical severity or airway
eosinophilia.100

Fecal Analyses
Fecal examination (ch. 80) is recommended in an attempt to rule
out/detect a parasitic origin for the eosinophilic infiltration (such as
A. abstrusus [using a Baermann test] or Toxocara cati [by fecal
flotation]).

Bronchoscopy and Bronchoalveolar Lavage Fluid
(BALF) Analysis (ch. 93)

In cats, bronchoscopy is considered less safe than in dogs, mainly
due to the small size of the airways and the higher airway
responsiveness of the cat120 compared to the dog. The procedure is
more hazardous in a cat with respiratory distress. Bronchoscopy is
not highly specific; it can reveal the presence of moderate to large
amount of mucoid or viscous material and airway mucosal
hyperemia (Video 215.16)

.

Cytological examination of airway (BAL) or endotracheal wash
(ETW) samples generally provides evidence of airway inflammation,
with increased numbers of eosinophils and/or neutrophils.117
Although up to 15% eosinophils can be found in fluids from healthy
cats, the number of eosinophils and neutrophils in BALF correlates
with disease severity, both in cats with spontaneous disease102 and
experimentally. Feline asthmatic disease clearly is primarily
characterized by a predominance of eosinophils in the BALF, but
definitive cutoffs are lacking. Inflammatory infiltrates have been
described as being predominantly eosinophilic when BALF contains
>20% eosinophils and neutrophils % within reference limits, or
>50% eosinophils; as predominantly neutrophilic when BALF
contains >7% neutrophils with eosinophil % within reference limits
or >50% neutrophils; and mixed when concurrent increases in both
eosinophil and neutrophil percentages or absolute numbers are
found.123 On the other hand, many studies mention that eosinophilic
infiltration relates to the presence of >17% eosinophils while CB
relates to the presence of >7% neutrophils in the BALF, with cats
with >17% eosinophils and >7% neutrophils being grouped with
asthmatic cats.98 Such definitions are even less useful as soon as the
cat was previously treated with any kind of glucocorticoid therapy,
which induces a decrease in the eosinophilic content. Another study
has confirmed that a BALF eosinophil percentage of <5% can be
expected in healthy feline airways, and that there is good correlation
between the findings (in particular the relative concentration of
eosinophils) in BALF and in tissue in feline asthma.123
Although some findings on bronchoscopic examination (e.g.,
bronchiectasis) can appear more frequently in cats infected with A.
abstrusus, and although larvae may be observed in the BALF in rare

cats, bronchial alterations and cytological findings in
aelurostrongylosis are not specific and there is an overlap with those
of other feline airway diseases.109 Troglostrongylus spp. can also
cause a similar clinical picture.110 Then, samples of BAL and ETW
fluid may be submitted for culture or PCR testing for parasitic
organisms, and also for bacterial and mycoplasmal cultures since
Mycoplasma infection can cause lower respiratory tract infection in
cats92,124,125 and might be associated with feline bronchial
disease.93,125 Mycoplasma spp. can also be detected in the BALF of
sick cats without respiratory signs and might represent commensals
of the lower respiratory tract of cats.125
Concentrations of several inflammatory biomarkers (such as
cytokines involved in the allergic response, e.g., interleukin-4,
interferon-gamma and tumor necrosis factor-alpha) have been
measured in BALF from cats with bronchial disease in an attempt to
differentiate asthma and CB, but the study failed to detect any
difference, even compared with control cats.95 The concentration of
endothelin-1 (ET1) in BALF is lower in normal cats compared to
those with experimentally induced asthma; therefore, BALF-ET1
might be a potential diagnostic biomarker for asthma.126 Potential
biomarkers might also be assessed by a non-invasive method of
exhaled breath condensate collection127,128 and hydrogen peroxide
has been suggested as a potential non-invasive biomarker.129

Pulmonary Function Tests
An important clinical feature of asthma is airflow limitation that is at
least partially reversible with bronchodilators. In human medicine,
pulmonary function testing is commonly used in the diagnosis and
monitoring of therapeutic response in patients with asthma or CB. In
cats, spirometry is inadequate since it requires patient compliance to
exhale forcefully through a mouthpiece. However, some noninvasive
tests have been developed, such as tidal breathing flow volume loops
(TBFVL) using a tight fitting face mask,102,116 barometric wholebody plethysmography (BWBP),121,130 or a combination of TBFVL

and BWBP131 and forced expiratory flow-volume curves using a
thoracic compression technique.132 BWBP can be used for
estimating basal functional parameters as well as AHR, usually
quantified by calculating the concentration of bronchoconstrictor
agent that can induce a 300% increase of basal enhanced pause.
TBFVL and BWBP have been used in clinical case series97,116,130,132
and in airway responsiveness testing96,97,133,134
During TBFVL, the presence of airflow limitation is affected by the
overall extent of granulocyte infiltration while most BWBP studies
provide evidence of a correlation between airway eosinophilic
inflammation and plethysmographic measures of
bronchoconstriction and airway responsiveness. This suggests that
BWBP associated with airway responsiveness testing may offer a new
method for identifying cats with inflammatory lower airway disease,
and possibly for monitoring disease progression or response to
therapy.

Differential Diagnosis
The differential diagnosis for feline inflammatory bronchial disease
mainly includes feline bronchial disease of noninflammatory origin
and pulmonary parenchymal diseases, including infectious
pneumonia/bronchopneumonia (bacterial, viral, parasitic,
protozoal),122,135-137 which are uncommon but probably
underdiagnosed; airway foreign bodies; neoplasia (ch. 217); pleural
effusion (ch. 220); and rare diseases such as “feline pulmonary
fibrosis”138,139 and “endogenous lipidic pneumonia”140 (ch. 217).
The parasitic diseases (A. abstrusus, Troglostrongylus brevior,
Eucoleus aerophilus, Dirofilaria immitis with Wolbachia [ch.
237],141,142 Toxocara cati [ch. 262]), can cause similar clinical
findings including eosinophilic airway inflammation; therefore,
empirical therapy is justified in endemic regions.

Management/Treatment and Monitoring
Acute Respiratory Distress

In cats with severe acute respiratory distress, stress should be
minimized and an oxygen-enriched environment should be provided
(ch. 123). Parenteral therapy with bronchodilators (beta-2 agonists,
e.g., terbutaline 0.01 mg /kg IV, IM or SC) and rapidly acting
corticosteroid (e.g., dexamethasone 0.25-0.5 mg/kg IV or IM) should
be administered promptly.107 Inhaled bronchodilators can be used,
although respiratory distress limits the amount of drug that reaches
the bronchi. These treatments aim to quickly reduce
bronchoconstriction. If a cat fails to respond, spontaneous
pneumothorax needs to be considered and investigated, as
emergency thoracocentesis could be life-saving (ch. 92). Indeed,
asthma is the most common cause of spontaneous pneumothorax in
cats (25%)143 and asthma-associated pneumothorax can carry a good
short-term prognosis.143

Chronic Presentations
Most retrospective studies in cats with lower airway diseases have
documented a beneficial response to oral or parenteral
glucocorticoids and/or bronchodilators.102,104,105 Classic therapy for
chronic forms of FLAD includes the use of long-term, oral
corticosteroid (e.g., prednisolone, 1-2 mg/kg PO q12h for 1-2 weeks,
followed by gradual tapering of the dose) which remains a consistent,
reliable and effective treatment to date. It has been suggested that
oral propentofylline, a methylxanthine derivative with
bronchodilating actions, might carry an additive benefit when
administered with prednisolone compared to monotherapy with
prednisolone.144
Currently, there are few easy measurable parameters to closely
monitor response to therapy. Therefore, in practice, treatment
monitoring generally relies on assessing improvement of clinical
signs. Both airway eosinophilia and AHR are considered hallmarks
of the disease and are potentially interesting parameters to monitor
during treatment. However, a study showed that even in cats with a
good clinical response to therapy and resolution of clinical signs,
BALF evidence of inflammation was persistent. Repeat analysis of
BALF for resolution of inflammation may be a preferred monitoring

tool.145 BWBP and pseudo-TBFVL also are noninvasive means of
evaluating lung function in conscious, spontaneously breathing cats;
both have also been proven useful to monitor the response to
treatment in experimental models and spontaneous
cases.96,97,132,146
The use of inhaled medication using a face mask and spacing
chamber, first described by Padrid147 has become commonplace148
(ch. 90). Medications given by inhalation offer the advantage of
high drug concentrations within the airways while attenuating
systemic side-effects. Inhaled corticosteroids (e.g., fluticasone
propionate), utilized essentially as chronic therapy, and
bronchodilators (e.g., albuterol), used to palliate an acute
exacerbation of clinical signs, are the most commonly used. Their use
was first developed experimentally.150-152 Several clinical studies
have evaluated the response to nebulized therapy in feline patients.
One of them showed that with inhaled budesonide 400 mcg q12h,
clinical signs and BWBP both improved, and other treatment could
be withdrawn in 47% of cats.133 The same study showed an absence
of corticosteroid-induced side-effects but hypothalamic-pituitaryadrenal axis suppression in 20% of cats.
In another study, one group of cats was treated with inhaled
fluticasone propionate (Flixotide, GlaxoSmithKline, 2 puffs, 250
mcg/puff) q12h.97 Despite a significant improvement in clinical
scores, and apparent resolution of clinical signs in some cats, BWBP
values did not change significantly by first recheck; this provides
further evidence that overt clinical resolution may precede recovery
of normal airway function. This result does not appear to be due to
insufficient dosage of nebulized fluticasone. Indeed, a study
involving a feline asthma model showed that inhaled fluticasone
dosages of 44 mcg and 220 mcg had identical effects152; therefore,
the lower dosage should be considered for the management of cats
with naturally occurring inflammatory bronchial disease. As only
oral prednisolone is capable of eliminating the late-phase asthmatic
reaction,150 a combination of both oral and inhaled
glucocorticosteroid medication can be started, followed by a single
inhaled therapy in the follow up period.

Bronchodilators, such as inhaled albuterol (salbutamol), are very
useful to quickly alleviate clinical signs. However, as they fail to
control airway inflammation, they should not be used alone (for
monotherapy). They should be used with caution due to possible
adverse effects, including tachycardia, central nervous system
stimulation, tremors and hypokalemia. Chronic daily racemic
albuterol administration has been associated with increased severity
of airway inflammation in an experimental model of feline
asthma.153
Cats with FLAD can benefit from other treatments. Weight loss
should be encouraged in obese cats (ch. 150). A recent study
compared pulmonary function variables between obese and nonobese cats via BWBP.154 Although obesity failed to demonstrate a
significant increase in bronchoconstriction index variable as
previously reported in humans and dogs, significant impaired
pulmonary function was confirmed. Saline nebulization and oral and
nebulized mucolytics or phytotherapeutic agents have not been
proven beneficial and should be administered with great caution, if
at all. In cats, any nebulized substance can potentially trigger a
bronchospastic reaction and/or bring on extra stress, all having a
negative impact in the cat with FLAD. In a feline model of chronic
allergic asthma, the effects of allogenic, adipose-derived
mesenchymal stem cells were documented.155 There were no
differences between treatment groups or within groups over time
with respect to airway eosinophilia, AHR, or immunologic assays;
however, airway remodeling, as assessed by CT findings, was
significantly limited in stem cell-treated animals compared to
placebo-treated ones.

Prognosis
Feline bronchial disease is associated with substantial morbidity and
even mortality in cats. Although most cats are well controlled with
oral or nebulized therapy or both, they generally required lifelong
treatment. Importantly, unchecked airway inflammation can lead to
irreversible remodeling resulting in a decline in lung function. In
chronic cases when remodeling has taken place, alleviation of clinical
signs can become challenging. Although data documenting

prognostic factors in feline bronchial disease are lacking, severe
clinical signs and failure to respond to glucocorticoid treatment
would be considered unfavorable characteristics.

Chapter 216: Small Airway
Diseases
Carol Reinero

A C RO N YM
CT computed tomography

OVERVIEW
DEFINITION AND CLASSIFICATION
Small airway diseases, also called bronchiolar disorders, represent
specific diseases involving pathological changes of small airways <2
mm in diameter lacking cartilage. These unique anatomic units are
interposed between the upstream larger airways (conducting
airways) and the downstream pulmonary acini (gas-exchange units)
and can serve as the primary targets for a variety of different insults.
In cats and dogs, there are no pathognomonic clinical signs or
cytologic findings (e.g., from lung fine-needle aspirates or airway
lavage) for bronchiolar disorders. Due to their small size, small
airways are not visible on thoracic radiographs or even computed
tomographic (CT) scans of healthy individuals. While diseased
bronchioles can be appreciated on CT scans and while pathologists
can microscopically visualize disease involvement of the small
airways, historically there has been a lack of crosstalk between
veterinary clinicians, radiologists and pathologists. Collectively, all
these factors have contributed to a lack of recognition of small airway
diseases as distinct clinical entities.

Recently, a classification scheme was proposed for bronchiolar
disorders in cats with the caveat that as understanding of small
airway diseases improved that further refinement of the scheme
would be needed.1 The proposed classification split small airway
disorders into three categories: (1) primary bronchiolar disorders,
(2) secondary bronchiolar disorders from extension of large airway
disease, and (3) secondary bronchiolar disorders as a component of
interstitial lung diseases (ILDs).1 This classification was modeled
after a human scheme2 with the intent to group historical findings,
clinical features, CT findings, and histopathologic findings into
discrete syndromes that may have similar etiologies, clinical courses,
and treatments.
Unlike in cats, there has been no proposed classification for
bronchiolar disorders in dogs, with only sporadic case reports and
small case series suggesting that pet dogs also develop lesions
associated with their small airways.3-7 Experimentally, bronchiolar
disease could also be induced in dogs although the clinical
syndromes resulting from these exposures were classified as
parenchymal disease (pneumonia and interstitial lung disease).8,9

ETIOLOGY
Inciting causes of bronchiolar disorders in people vary and include
environmental exposures, infection, drugs, chronic aspiration,
neoplasia, or immune-mediated disease. Dogs and cats share the
environment with humans and are susceptible to many of the same
triggers, including particulate matter in air pollution. Dogs in
polluted outdoor environments have been reported to sustain injury
to their bronchioles.10 Mineral dust airway disease from inhaled
inorganic dusts has been described in a cat.1 Exposure to various
environmental chemicals, gases, smoke and other inhaled
particulates as a cause for bronchiolar disorders still needs
investigation in veterinary medicine and underscores the need for a
thorough history from owners about potential exposures. The role of
some of the other aforementioned causes in inducing small airway

disease in cats has been reviewed recently1 and many if not all of
these are likely to affect canine small airways.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Bronchiolar disease can lead to an obstructive or a restrictive
phenotype. These disorders can be acute or chronic in nature.
Inflammatory (infectious or noninfectious), fibrotic and neoplastic
processes can lead to small airway disorders when bronchioles <2
mm in diameter are affected. Fibrosis is considered a sequel to injury
and inflammation such that in the end stage of disease, the
underlying inflammatory response may be missed. If histologic
evaluation is used for characterizing the microscopic features of the
lesions, it is critical to examine multiple areas of the lung to assess
for early lesions, patchy lesions, and subtle lesions. The extent of
disease (i.e., number of small airways involved, severity of airway
occlusion or luminal narrowing, and involvement of upstream large
airways or downstream gas exchange units) contributes to the type
and severity of clinical signs.

CLINICAL PRESENTATION
It is important to understand that there is/are no pathognomonic
clinical sign(s) in dogs or cats with small airway disease. Bronchiolar
disorders must thus remain on the differential list for many
respiratory signs. As we are still learning more about these
syndromes, it will be critical to thoroughly investigate potential
underlying exposures in the environment by taking a comprehensive
history and to combine that with findings on physical examination,
and ultimately a more sophisticated set of diagnostics.

HISTORY
Historical questions (ch. 2) should start with an understanding of
the environment of the dog or cat. Does the cat live outdoors,
indoors, or both? Is the setting rural, suburban, or urban and what is
known about environmental air quality in those regions? Is there

exposure to smoke (cigarette, incense, fireplace, wood-burning stove,
wildfire smoke) or vapor (e.g., e-cigarettes, which may emit nicotine,
formaldehyde, acetone, heavy metals, and volatile organic
compounds)? Is there use of plug-in or canned air fresheners or
other fragrances or essential oils? Is there a possibility the house
might have radon or mold? Has there been recent construction or
renovations in the home, including use of paint or solvents? Which
cleaning products are used? Is there exposure to pesticides,
herbicides, or heavy metals? For cats, what type of cat litter is used?
It will take further study in large numbers of dogs and cats to
determine if any of these are direct triggers of small airway
inflammation, fibrosis, or both. Knowledge of exposures also plays a
role in treatment to promote a healthy respiratory tract whether or
not environmental substances directly or indirectly promote
inflammation and tissue injury.
Along with environmental exposures, it would be helpful to
question owners about any other systemic signs of illness that might
point toward an underlying infectious, immune-mediated, or
neoplastic disorder. Other respiratory clinical signs, including an
association with drinking or eating (that could indicate the potential
for repetitive macro- or micro-aspiration; ch. 221) should be
identified. Owners should be asked about administration of any
drugs (prescribed or over-the-counter), nutraceuticals, homeopathic
remedies, and any other alternative medical therapies. Finally,
owners should be questioned about the onset of signs (subacute,
acute, or insidious) and if disease is static or progressive over time.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (CH. 3)
In the author’s experience, dogs and cats with bronchiolar disease
have been described to have a range of clinical signs including cough
(ch. 34), wheeze, tachypnea, increased expiratory effort, mixed
inspiratory/expiratory effort (ch. 37), exercise intolerance, syncope
(ch. 40), and cyanosis (ch. 27), and the presence of these should be
recorded. There should be an attempt to elicit cough with gentle
tracheal pressure (

Videos 3.11, 34.5). Evidence of systemic signs

of illness, such as poor body condition or documented unintentional

weight loss (ch. 18), and fever (ch. 16), should be noted, and a
fundic examination should be performed (ch. 13). Careful attention
should be paid to cardiopulmonary auscultation (ch. 3). Cardiac
murmurs (ch. 38) or arrhythmias (ch. 230) may suggest comorbid
cardiac disease. Wheezes, crackles and increased bronchovesicular
sounds may be heard (ch. 212).

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
The most common disease mimics depend on whether the disease
process is localized to the small airways alone, or if it involves the
large airways, pulmonary acini, or all three anatomic regions. Many
of the disorders isolated to the small airways (especially
constrictive/obliterative bronchiolitis) present as an obstructive
airway disorder, including patients having increased expiratory effort
and air trapping noted on radiography. In cats, asthma would be the
top differential. If large and small airways are involved in tandem,
cough frequently predominates as the main clinical sign (ch. 34)
and any cause of cough (i.e., respiratory, cardiac, aerodigestive)
should be considered as a differential until a more comprehensive
diagnostic evaluation can be performed. If small airways and the
parenchyma are affected, or if the large and small airways and the
parenchyma are affected, the disease may present as a restrictive
lung disease. Top differentials would include infection, neoplasia and
interstitial lung diseases. These are only a few general guidelines for
determining likely differentials, but it is important to remember that
the small airway disorders are very diverse, and our understanding
of them is still in its infancy.

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
In general, the diagnostic evaluation of a dog or cat with respiratory
signs should start with localizing disease to the likely anatomic
regions of the respiratory tract (ch. 212). The clinical signs
associated with small airway disease resemble those causing
intrathoracic airway and parenchymal disease. While thoracic
radiographs are often the initial diagnostic test to be performed, they

are incapable of detecting bronchiolar disease. This may be one
reason why cats “diagnosed” with asthma or chronic bronchitis
frequently have unremarkable thoracic radiographs: these cats may
instead have primary bronchiolar disease. Thoracic radiographic
lung patterns may suggest the predominant region of disease with a
bronchial pattern reflecting large airway disease and interstitial and
alveolar patterns reflecting pulmonary parenchymal disease.
Regardless of lung pattern, and even with unremarkable thoracic
radiographs, small airway disease must always remain a differential
diagnosis.
Ancillary diagnostics including complete blood count, infectious
disease testing, pulse oximetry or arterial blood gas (as sole
diagnostics or in tandem with a 6-minute walk test in dogs), lung
ultrasound, respiratory fluoroscopy, and videofluoroscopic swallow
study (

Videos 221.1, 259.2, 259.3) can be considered prior to

diagnostics requiring anesthesia (ch. 212). Additionally, screening
other regions of the body for infectious disease involvement or a
primary neoplasm can be performed.
The author strongly advocates anesthetized CT scans in lieu of
awake or sedated CT scans as the latter are usually compromised by
motion artifact, variable inflation and poor detail of CT lung patterns
required to better identify and characterize small airway disease. The
most optimal thoracic CT study would employ ventilator-assisted
paired inspiratory and expiratory breath-holds to help detect
evidence of dynamic changes.11 Patients with small airway disease
can have direct and indirect CT signs. Direct CT signs of bronchiolar
disease include tree-in-bud pattern (nodular opacities connected to
branching linear opacities), bronchiolectasis (dilation; Figure
216.1) and peribronchiolar ground-glass opacity or consolidation.1
Indirect CT signs of bronchiolar disease include mosaic attenuation
secondary to air trapping (requiring paired inspiratory and
expiratory breath-hold series) or, rarely, mosaic perfusion.1 Aside
from providing evidence of small airway disease, thoracic CTs can
demonstrate abnormalities associated with the upstream larger
airways and the downstream pulmonary parenchyma. If other
regions of the respiratory tract demonstrate abnormalities, it might

indicate either a secondary bronchiolar disorder or the presence of
unrelated comorbid disease.
Thoracic CT studies are one of two tests to definitively diagnose
small airway disease, but additional diagnostics are required to
determine the underlying cause. Cytologic evaluation of airway
lavage (ch. 93) or pulmonary fine-needle aspiration are most helpful
when identifying the presence of infectious organisms or neoplastic
cells; otherwise, cytologic evidence of inflammation is non-specific
and can be appreciated with many types of large airway, small airway
and parenchymal disease. The other diagnostic test to definitively
diagnose small airway disease is histopathologic evaluation of a
tissue sample. Lack of routine antemortem lung biopsies has
hampered our recognition and understanding of small airway
disorders. Histopathologic evaluation has the potential to most fully
characterize the type, extent and severity of lesions, but expertise in
respiratory pathology is likely to be required until these are more
commonly understood disorders.

TREATMENT
Currently, there is insufficient knowledge of bronchiolar disorders to
know how to best treat these diseases. In general, treatment can be
divided into three categories: (1) strategies to promote respiratory
health, (2) addressing comorbid respiratory and cardiovascular
conditions and (3) specific therapy to target the primary disease
process.

Strategies to promote respiratory health include providing good
airway quality, prophylactic measures against respiratory pathogens,
and achieving/maintaining an ideal body weight (ch. 72). Improving
airway quality includes removal of any identified harmful inhaled
substance(s) and other irritating triggers of cough. Promoting good
air quality includes removal of inhaled irritants or other damaging
inhaled substances, and airway humidification. In indoor
environments, high efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters are
effective at removing airborne particulates. Airway humidification is
a general strategy employed to assist mucociliary function.
Mucociliary clearance is the primary clearance mechanism for
conducting (i.e., larger) airways and if associated with subsequent
cough, can help with alveolar filling disorders and thus may be
helpful for secondary bronchiolar disorders. However, as small
airways lack ciliated epithelial cells, airway humidification is less
likely to be helpful in primary bronchiolar disorders. Regular

chemoprophylaxis for respiratory parasites (e.g., Dirofilaria; ch.
237) and vaccination against contagious respiratory pathogens (chs.
185, 203) should be considered to protect patients against
preventable disorders in patients with pre-existing bronchiolar
disease. As obesity negatively impacts respiratory function, weight
loss should be considered in overweight animals (ch. 150).
After a thorough diagnostic evaluation has identified comorbid
respiratory (chs. 213-215 and 217) and cardiovascular (chs. 231235 and 237) conditions, and the patient has been evaluated for
pulmonary hypertension (ch. 218), a comprehensive therapeutic
plan should be developed to address each disorder.
There are no studies in dogs or cats describing treatment of
primary small airway diseases. Targeted therapy to address the
specific type of bronchiolar disorder is the ideal approach; however,
unless infection or neoplasia is identified in the diagnostic
evaluation, definitive understanding of the type of bronchiolar
disorder will rely on histopathologic evaluation of the lung. As lung
biopsy is an expensive and invasive diagnostic, it is uncommonly
performed, and a specific treatment plan cannot be developed.
Without knowledge of the underlying etiology, it seems reasonable to
comprehensively attempt to identify an underlying infectious process
or neoplasia and treat directly. If infection or neoplasia is not
identified, if general strategies to promote respiratory health along
with addressing comorbid conditions do not result in acceptable
control of clinical signs, and if the owners have declined lung biopsy,
an empiric trial of glucocorticoids (0.5-2 mg/kg/day prednisolone
[cats] or prednisone [dogs]) can be tried. Close attention must be
paid to worsening of clinical signs, especially when using higher
dosages of glucocorticoids. The optimal dosage and duration of
glucocorticoid therapy is unknown.

PROGNOSIS
There are insufficient studies of small airway disease in dogs and cats
to be able to provide prognostic information and the following
statements are based on the author’s experience. Small airway
disease in association with large airway disease in dogs and cats
tends to have the best response to glucocorticoids and a good overall

prognosis. Infectious causes of bronchiolar disease, if identified and
treated effectively in a timely fashion, may similarly have a good
prognosis. Small airway disease in association with substantial
pulmonary parenchymal disease (especially if there are thoracic CT
changes compatible with fibrosis, if the patient has pulmonary
hypertension and if clinical signs are severe), has a guarded to grave
prognosis. Finally, small airway disease associated with air trapping
that is unresponsive to glucocorticoids, and in cats unresponsive to
bronchodilators, may indicate constrictive/obliterative bronchiolitis,
which carries a grave prognosis.

The structure of the pulmonary parenchyma permits the primary
function of the lung:gas exchange. The lung consists of millions of
alveolar airspaces, each bathed by a dense network of capillaries.
Fine, lacey, supporting interstitial tissues are interposed between the
epithelial lining of the alveoli and the surrounding vascular
endothelium of the capillary network; these interstitial tissues
contain the slightly larger pulmonary arterioles and veins.
Parenchymal disease includes disease focused on the alveoli,
pulmonary microvasculature, or the interstitial tissues while
excluding disease of the large (ch. 215) and small (ch. 216) airways
and the pleural space (ch. 220).

MANIFESTATIONS OF PULMONARY
PARENCHYMAL DISEASE
Pulmonary parenchymal disorders cause a variety of clinical signs
related either to respiratory dysfunction or to systemic disease.
Clinical signs and physical examination abnormalities in animals
with pulmonary disease are similar to those found in animals with
airway, mediastinal, or pleural space disease (ch. 212). Additionally,
nonrespiratory diseases (e.g., neuromuscular disease [chs. 252,
253], anemia [ch. 57], acidosis [ch. 128]) can cause signs that
mimic respiratory disease. Recently, we have come to understand
that pulmonary (and airway) disease can be intimately tied to
gastrointestinal (GI) disorders, a combination referred to as
aerodigestive disorders (ch. 221). Common respiratory

manifestations of pulmonary parenchymal disease include cough
(ch. 34), exercise intolerance, tachypnea (ch. 37), excessive
panting, and increased respiratory effort or respiratory distress (ch.
37). Often, respiratory distress caused by pulmonary parenchymal
disease results in mixed inspiratory and expiratory effort. This
contrasts with the predominantly inspiratory effort observed in
animals with upper airway obstruction (

Video 37.1) or pleural

space disease (ch. 220) or the expiratory effort observed in animals
with lower airway disorders (

Video 37.2). Certain interstitial

lung diseases that limit pulmonary compliance offer exceptions to
this general rule, in that they are associated with a predominantly
inspiratory effort. Less common manifestations of pulmonary
parenchymal disease include hemoptysis (ch. 36), collapse or
syncope (ch. 40), and cyanosis (ch. 27). Animals with marked
respiratory compromise may demonstrate minimal clinical evidence
of respiratory disease. This is especially true in cats, for whom the
first sign of lung disease might be death.
Physical examination of animals with pulmonary disease can be
unremarkable. Weight loss, fever, lymphadenomegaly, and distal
limb swelling from hypertrophic osteopathy are a few of the many
potential systemic manifestations of pulmonary diseases.
Abnormalities in respiratory rate or effort, cyanosis, increased or
decreased bronchovesicular sounds, and/or adventitial sounds (i.e.,
crackles and wheezes) on auscultation are possible. Examination of
the patient with respiratory disease is described in detail in chs. 3,
37, and 212.

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION OF
PULMONARY PARENCHYMAL DISEASE
Diagnostic testing for pulmonary disease involves a combination of
modalities. Routine blood, urine, and fecal tests can provide
diagnostic clues but rarely confirm a specific lung disease (Box
217.1). Tests to assess oxygenation, confirm suspected infectious
disease, or assess biomarkers (e.g., natriuretic peptides; ch. 229) are
often indicated. Nearly always, diagnostic imaging is necessary both

to rule out alternative or complicating diagnosis (e.g., cardiomegaly,
tracheal collapse, diaphragmatic hernia) and to narrow the list of
differential diagnosis for lung disease.
The presence, location, and intensity of abnormal radiographic
patterns provide information to guide the differential diagnosis and
diagnostic plans (Box 217.2). Lung disease sufficient to cause
respiratory signs occasionally occurs in the absence of radiographic
change in the pulmonary parenchyma. For example, radiographic
changes can lag behind acute development of respiratory signs in
animals with aspiration pneumonia, acute respiratory distress
syndrome (ARDS), or pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE; ch. 219).
However, when thoracic imaging studies fail to demonstrate
abnormalities, additional consideration should be given to
conditions that can mimic respiratory disease, such as anemia, pain,
or acidosis.
Computed tomography (CT) and ultrasound are also used to image
the lungs of pet animals. CT offers advantages over standard thoracic
radiography, including increased sensitivity for the detection of small
lesions such as metastasis, a truer three-dimensional image of the
thoracic cavity and its contents, minimization of summation artifact,
and the ability to view images in axial, coronal, or sagittal planes.1
The best thoracic CT images require anesthesia and, ideally,
controlled ventilation to allow for comparison of images acquired
during inspiration and expiration. For many years, pulmonary
ultrasound was used primarily for evaluation of consolidated lung
tissue or vascular patency (e.g., lung lobe torsion [LLT]) or to guide
needle aspirates. In recent years, point-of-care thoracic ultrasound
has become a crucial tool for emergent evaluation of animals with
respiratory distress. It can quickly help differentiate lung disease
from pleural space disease or heart failure (chs. 73 and 123)

For many animals with lung disease, diagnosis requires invasive
testing (ch. 212). Bronchoscopy plus airway lavage for culture,
cytologic analysis, or special testing is often employed (ch. 93).
Fine-needle lung aspirates are simple to perform and provide good to
excellent diagnostic yield from consolidated or mass lesions or in the
presence of heavy cellular infiltrates. Lung biopsy, although used

infrequently, can at times not only provide a diagnosis but serve as a
treatment modality when a diseased lobe is removed.

SPECIFIC PULMONARY DISORDERS
PULMONARY PARASITES
Parasitic pulmonary disease is caused by both lungworms and nonlungworms. Some intestinal worms, especially Toxocara
(roundworms) but also Ancylostoma (hookworms), undergo
pulmonary migration before reaching their final destination in the
intestine (ch. 262). Usually, pulmonary migration causes few (if
any) respiratory signs. However, massive larval migration can result
in verminous pneumonia. Such profound infections typically occur in
juveniles who may present with cough and tachypnea. Often, a
complete blood count (CBC) is omitted but eosinophilia would be
expected. Fecal flotation (ch. 80) can be negative because larval
migration occurs before the mature worms have reached the
intestine. Empiric treatment is reasonable if pulmonary migration is
suspected as a cause of cough. An anthelmintic (e.g., pyrantel
pamoate 5 mg/kg PO; ch. 142) should be administered at least
twice, 2 weeks apart. Fortunately, most animals require no further
treatment. A short course of an anti-inflammatory dosage of
glucocorticoid can ameliorate severe cough but should not be used
before ruling out other causes of infectious pneumonia.

In contrast to intestinal worms that migrate through the lungs, for
lungworms the final destination is the respiratory tract.2,3 These
parasites can reside primarily in the pulmonary parenchyma, in the
airways, or both. Parasitic lung disease easily can be confused with
other conditions such as bronchopneumonia, eosinophilic
pneumonia (EP), asthma, pulmonary granulomatosis, or even
pulmonary neoplasia. Unfortunately, intermittent fecal shedding of
parasite ova or larvae after expectoration means that fecal
examination is an insensitive diagnostic method. For this reason,
therapeutic trials often are employed when lungworms are
suspected. Fenbendazole (50 mg/kg PO q24h for 10-14 days) or
ivermectin usually is used.2 Ivermectin must be used with caution in
Collies and other breeds with a high prevalence of the MDR-1
(ABCB1) mutation.

PULMONARY PARENCHYMAL
PARASITES
Paragonimus kellicotti
This trematode lung fluke can infect dogs and cats. Found
worldwide, in the United States lung flukes are endemic in the Great
Lakes region, the Midwest, and the South. Pets are infected after
eating crayfish. The parasite migrates from the intestine into the
peritoneum, across the diaphragm, and into the pleural space. Soon
thereafter, immature flukes invade the subpleural tissues, where they
cause eosinophilic and neutrophilic inflammation.4 Often, the
parasites form bullae and cysts within the pulmonary parenchyma.
Mature flukes have access through a series of communicating
“tunnels” to the bronchioles, allowing ova to be coughed up and
swallowed before fecal shedding.
Animals infected with P. kellicotti are usually well but can present
with cough or even respiratory distress.5 Rupture of cavitary
pulmonary lesions can lead to hemoptysis or pneumothorax.5 Often,
the diagnosis is suspected when animals with respiratory signs have
concurrent eosinophilia or is based on radiographic findings.6

Radiographic lesions, not identified uniformly, can include nodular
or cystic lesions or bullae, especially involving the right caudal lung
lobe.4,6 Serial CT scans from experimentally infected dogs initially
identified pleural effusion and a subpleural ground-glass appearance
along with linear opacities. After 1 month, persistent peribronchial
nodules, bronchial dilation, and cavitary changes were observed.7
Ova can be demonstrated from airway lavage fluid or, using
sedimentation, in feces.4
In addition to fenbendazole, praziquantel (25 mg/kg PO q8h for 3
days) has been used for treatment of P. kellicotti.6 Pneumothorax
that results in respiratory embarrassment requires specific therapy
(i.e., thoracocentesis; chs. 92 and 123).

Filaroides
Filaroides spp. are relatively uncommon pulmonary parasites of
dogs. Adult nematodes of both Filaroides hirthi and Filaroides
milksi (also known as Andersonstrongylus milksi) species reside in
the alveolar spaces and terminal bronchioles; differentiation of these
very similar parasites from each other is not necessary.8 The
ovoviviparous parasite is transmitted directly via the fecal-oral route,
allowing transmission between an infected dam and her pups or
between infected and uninfected pups. Repeat infection
(autoinfection) of the host with larvae before they even leave the host
also is possible and increases the potential for “superinfections.”9
Dogs can remain healthy while parasitized or can develop severe or
even fatal disease. Severe disease is especially likely in young, smallbreed dogs, immunosuppressed dogs, or dogs with
superinfections.8,10
Clinical signs can include cough and respiratory distress. Diffuse
bronchointerstitial and alveolar infiltrates result from
granulomatous inflammation in reaction to the dead or dying worms.
Zinc sulfate centrifugation fecal flotation is used for identifying
larvae but lacks sensitivity due to intermittent shedding (a common
feature of most lungworm infections). Recognition of ova and/or
larvae via airway lavage is an alternative method of diagnosis. A
variety of anthelmintic treatments has been employed, but

fenbendazole (25-50 mg/kg PO q24h for 10-14 days) or ivermectin
(0.4 mg/kg SC for dogs lacking MDR-1 mutation, repeated in 1 week)
is used most often.2,11 An inflammatory reaction to dying worms can
worsen disease severity shortly after treatment, a complication that
can be ameliorated by a short course of corticosteroids (e.g.,
predniso[lo]ne 0.5-1 mg/kg PO q24h for 3-7 days).10

OTHER PARASITES OF RELEVANCE TO
THE LUNG
Dirofilaria immitis
D. immitis is responsible for heartworm disease, an important cause
of pulmonary and cardiac disease in dogs and cats from temperate
climates throughout the world. The host-parasite interaction, clinical
consequences, diagnosis, and treatment of D. immitis differ greatly
between dogs and cats, but efficacious prophylactic mediations are
available for use in both (ch. 237).

Angiostrongylus vasorum
Infection with this metastrongylid parasite of canids occurs in
Europe, Asia, and Africa, as well as in an endemic focus in
Newfoundland, Canada. It has been dubbed “French heartworm”
because, like D. immitis, the mature parasites reside in the
pulmonary artery, right heart, and pulmonary arterioles. Dogs are
infected after consuming infected intermediate (i.e., mollusk) or
paratenic (e.g., frog) hosts; L3 larvae are liberated into the intestine
before eventually making their way to the pulmonary vasculature.
Ova from the mature worms are carried to the pulmonary capillaries,
where they hatch. The L1 larvae then migrate into the alveoli. After
gaining entrance to the airways, the larvae can be coughed up and
swallowed. Inflammatory and immune responses to the parasites
contribute to clinical disease.12
Infected dogs can appear healthy or have a range of clinical signs,
including death. The predominant syndromes associated with
infection are respiratory disease or a bleeding diathesis. The most

common findings are chronic cough and general unthriftiness.
Severe pulmonary hypertension (ch. 218) with resultant cor
pulmonale and syncope are reported, as is pneumothorax.13
Spontaneous bleeding, which can occur without respiratory signs,
may be due to a consumptive coagulopathy (ch. 171).14-16
Additionally, neurologic and ocular signs are reported.17,18
Diagnosis follows clinical suspicion or screening of healthy dogs
from endemic regions. Associated laboratory findings can include
anemia, eosinophilia, thrombocytopenia, abnormalities of
coagulation times, and hypercalcemia.14,19 Thoracic radiographs can
show any combination of bronchial, interstitial, and/or peripheral
alveolar lung patterns but the classic vascular changes associated
with heartworm disease caused by D. immitis are absent. A groundglass opacity, consolidation, and mosaic attenuation are common on
thoracic CT as are nodules in the pleural and subpleural regions.20
In a recent study, the finding of small hypoechoic subpleural nodules
on thoracic ultrasound was 100% sensitive and 92% specific for
infection.21 A definitive diagnosis requires identification of parasites
via sensitive and specific point-of-care antigen testing, Baermann
fecal examination, or testing of airway lavage by cytologic evaluation
or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing.22,23
Several effective prophylaxis regimens are available, and
appropriate treatment of dogs that do become infected is generally
associated with a good prognosis.23-26 Treatment options include
fenbendazole (25-50 mg/kg PO q24h for 10-20 days), ivermectin
(0.2 mg/kg SC each week for two doses), milbemycin oxime (0.5
mg/kg PO each week for 4 weeks), or imidacloprid 10%
moxidectin/2.5% spot-on solution.2,23 Despite recovery of most dogs
after treatment, post-treatment reactions including dyspnea, ascites,
and sudden death have been observed.

Airway Parasites
Several airway parasites result in respiratory signs indistinguishable
from those caused by pulmonary and pulmonary vascular parasites.
Among these are Aelurostrongylus abstrusus (feline lungworms),

Crenosoma vulpis (canine airway nematodes), Troglostrongylus
spp. (metastrongyloid nematodes of feline airways), Oslerus osleri
and Eucoleus aerophilus (nematodes of airways in both dogs and
cats).

PNEUMONIA
The lungs have a limited ability to respond to injury regardless of
cause. Historically, the term pneumonia has been used to describe
lung injury and inflammation due to many causes. In human
medicine, there has been a recent proposal that pneumonia be
defined as an infection of the lung parenchyma by one or more
pathogens, but excluding viral bronchiolitis.27 Lung injury due to
aspiration of liquids or solids (i.e., aspiration pneumonia) may or
may not have an infectious component.

BACTERIAL PNEUMONIA
Bacterial pneumonia encompasses a wide spectrum of disease, from
acute to chronic, unilobar or multilobar, clinically silent infection to
fatal infection. There are multiple potential routes of pulmonary
exposure to potentially pathogenic bacteria. Bacteria can be inhaled
or aspirated into the lung (including nosocomial infection related to
ventilatory support28 [ch. 186]), they can reach the lung through
direct extension from the pleural space or intrathoracic structures, or
they can gain access to the lung hematogenously.29 Most bacteria
that cause pneumonia are secondary pathogens and only cause
disease when allowed the opportunity (e.g., in association with viral
respiratory damage, immune suppression, aspiration). About onethird of pneumonia cases are caused by multiple bacterial species,
and as many as 20% may involve anaerobic pathogens.29-35 The
bacteria most commonly implicated include streptococci, enteric
pathogens (e.g., Escherichia coli, Klebsiella), Pasteurella spp.,
coagulase-positive staphylococci, Mycoplasma spp., and Bordetella
bronchiseptica.29-36 It is unusual for healthy adult pets, especially
cats, to develop bacterial pneumonia. With the exception of

infections caused by primary bacterial respiratory pathogens (e.g.,
Bordetella bronchiseptica), most animals with bacterial pneumonia
have been compromised in some fashion. The diagnosis of bacterial
pneumonia should prompt the clinician to search for a predisposing
cause.

Presentation
Dogs develop bacterial pneumonia more often than do cats.29 Many
pets with bacterial pneumonia have a predisposing factor for
infection, including extremes of age, debilitation,
immunocompromise, or preexisting respiratory disease (Box
217.3). Occasionally, bacterial pneumonia is accompanied by only
minor clinical signs or physical examination abnormalities,
especially when it is regionally limited to involve a single lung lobe.
Commonly, clinical signs include cough (often soft and productive,
ch. 34), nasal discharge (ch. 35), exercise intolerance, or
respiratory distress (ch. 37). Anorexia and lethargy also are
commonplace. Fever (ch. 16) is inconsistent at best, and
normothermia does not rule out bacterial pneumonia. Loss of body
condition, tachypnea, increased (or when consolidation is present,
decreased) bronchovesicular lung sounds, inspiratory crackles,
wheeze, sinus arrhythmia, and cyanosis may be identified.

Diagnostic Evaluation
Diagnostic screening tests for animals with suspected bacterial
pneumonia include thoracic radiographs, CBC, and arterial blood gas
or pulse oximetry measurement. Ideally, a serum biochemical
profile, urinalysis, and fecal examination also are performed because
they provide potentially valuable information regarding the animal’s
overall health and sometimes provide clues as to the presence of a
systemic disease that might predispose to development of
pneumonia. Neutrophilia (± left shift), lymphopenia, and mild
anemia are inconsistent but common findings on CBC. Hypoxemia is
common but depends on severity of functional lung impairment. The
classic radiographic appearance of bacterial pneumonia is an
alveolar pulmonary pattern with a predominantly ventral
distribution. Sometimes, only a single lung lobe is involved,

particularly following foreign body inhalation or aspiration.
Dorsocaudal involvement may predominate after hematogenous
bacterial exposure, and all lung fields can be involved in cases of
severe pneumonia. In less severe pneumonia or early in the disease
course, only an interstitial pattern might be identified. Occasionally,
complications such as abscessation, pleural effusion, or
pneumothorax are identified concurrently.

Sepsis/bacteremia
A specific diagnosis of bacterial pneumonia is confirmed by
identification of pulmonary sepsis. Airway lavage provides material
for cytologic examination, as well as culture and susceptibility (C/S)
testing. Antimicrobial decisions made in the absence of C/S data
often lead to inappropriate treatment with either resistance to
therapy or overly aggressive therapy, while bacterial C/S allow for
identification of the safest, most economical, and correctly targeted
antimicrobial drugs.32 Appropriate samples can be obtained via
bronchoalveolar, endotracheal, or transtracheal lavage (chs. 93 and
212).35,37 In severe bacterial pneumonia, foreign body pneumonia,
aspiration pneumonia, or when areas of pulmonary consolidation are
present, samples should be inoculated into appropriate transport
media to allow anaerobic as well as routine aerobic culture.29,38
Because some Mycoplasma spp. can be primary bacterial pathogens
but are difficult to culture using routine methods, specific
Mycoplasma PCR can be considered as well.39 It must be recognized
that prior antibiotic therapy, incorrect sample handling, or infection
with fastidious organisms can result in a negative culture result even
in the face of bacterial pneumonia. Blood culture (ch. 184) has been
suggested as a less invasive alternative to airway lavage.40 Although
specific, blood culture is insensitive for the purpose.41 Discordant
results between airway cytologic evaluation and C/S can occur.37
Therefore, the diagnosis of bacterial pneumonia must be based on
integration of all clinical and radiographic findings, ideally in
conjunction with cytologically demonstrated neutrophilic airway
inflammation and intracellular bacteria in addition to a positive
bacterial culture.

Treatment and Prognosis
Bacterial pneumonia should be treated with antimicrobial drugs.
Initial empiric therapy can be informed by published guidance from
the International Society of Companion Animal Infectious Diseases
(ISCAID) as well as clues such as cytologic and staining

characteristics of microbes, prior antibiotic use, and other cues (e.g.,
pneumonia in puppies is often due to B. bronchiseptica).40
Adjustments can be made later based on clinical response and C/S
results. For severely affected or unstable animals, initial therapy
must include antimicrobials with Gram-positive, Gram-negative,
aerobic and anaerobic efficacy. Most often, this approach involves
combination therapy (e.g., fluoroquinolone combined with ampicillin
or clindamycin) administered parenterally (Box 217.4). Animals
with mild to moderate disease may be treated initially with orally
administered antimicrobials with a more limited spectrum of activity
(Box 217.4). Although many antimicrobials (including beta-lactam
drugs) do not readily penetrate the airway’s blood-bronchus barrier,
this is less of a concern with pneumonia, which is a parenchymal
tissue infection rather than an airway infection. While aerosolized
antimicrobials might have benefit in the treatment of certain animals
with bacterial pneumonia (especially bordetellosis), aerosol delivery
is not routinely recommended and should be considered an adjuvant
therapy and not a replacement for systemic antimicrobials.40,42
Historically in veterinary medicine, antimicrobials were prescribed
for a minimum of 3 to 4 weeks. This is in extreme excess compared
to the duration of therapy recommended for treatment of pneumonia
in humans.43 The ISCAID guidelines for respiratory infections
suggest reevaluation of animals 10-14 days after treatment has
begun, with antimicrobial use extended, altered, or halted on the
basis of clinical response.40 While more studies are warranted, this
approach is gaining evidence-based support in animals.44,45
