Dogs with severe bacterial pneumonia often are hypoxemic.
Ideally, PaO2 is determined via arterial blood gas analysis (chs. 74
and 212) but SpO2 can be used as a rough correlate. In animals with
acute hypoxemia, oxygen supplementation should be provided when
PaO2 is <80 mm Hg or SpO2 is <94%. The most practical means of
delivery include oxygen cages or placement of nasal cannula
(standard or high flow humidified oxygen delivery; ch. 123).46,47
Persistent hypoxemia or continued marked respiratory effort despite
oxygen supplementation indicates the need for mechanical
ventilation.

Fluid therapy is indicated for the treatment of animals with severe
bacterial pneumonia (ch. 120). Dehydration is common in weak,
depressed, anorectic, febrile, and tachypneic animals. In addition to
systemic effects, dehydration impairs mucociliary respiratory
defenses. Airway mucus functions to trap bacteria and inhaled
particulates. The respiratory epithelial cilia propel entrapped
particulates craniad to the oropharynx, where they can be expelled
through coughing or swallowing. The mucus itself is made of two
layers—the watery sol layer through which the cilia move and the
overlying gel layer that traps the particulates. If the sol layer becomes
dehydrated, the cilia themselves become entrapped in the gel layer,
effectively inhibiting the mucociliary escalator. Crystalloid fluids
should be provided at a rate to attain and maintain hydration. Overly
aggressive fluid therapy can lead to iatrogenic pulmonary edema and
worsen respiratory compromise. Nebulization of sterile saline (ch.
90) can enhance mucus fluidity and more effective mucociliary
function, although this benefit has not been documented in pets (
Video 217.1). Use of isotonic and hypertonic saline are described,
often given alternately with each nebulization session.
Cough (ch. 34) is encouraged in animals with bacterial
pneumonia, and cough suppressants are contraindicated. Coupage
(i.e., thoracic physical therapy) is a simple technique of thoracic
percussion that aids mobilization of airway secretions and
encourages cough (

Video 217.2). Other techniques that do not

require patient cooperation and can be adapted for dogs and cats
include prolonged slow expiration and assisted cough (

Video

217.3). A recent prospective study of dogs hospitalized with airway
fluid accumulation documented improved oxygenation and reduced
need for oxygen supplementation when these techniques were
applied.48 When physical techniques are used, they should follow
saline nebulization. Animals should be encouraged to move and
recumbent animals should be repositioned frequently to aid in
mobilization of respiratory secretions.
Additional therapeutic considerations for animals with pneumonia
include bronchodilators, mucolytics, and nutritional and supportive
care. Bronchodilators are not used routinely for the treatment of

bacterial pneumonia. Either inhaled albuterol (salbutamol) or oral
methylxanthine bronchodilators (e.g., theophylline) are considered
in animals that remain hypoxemic despite supplemental oxygen
administration, when there is concurrent bronchoconstriction
(especially likely in cats), or prior to administration of inhalant drug
therapy. Bacterial pneumonia can result in the production of copious
quantities of thick, tenacious mucus. Theoretically, liquefaction of
mucus can result in more effective mucociliary clearance. Simple
maintenance of systemic hydration and airway humidification
typically are adequate, but mucolytic drugs sometimes are
advocated. The mucolytic N-acetylcysteine (NAC) reduces viscosity
by breaking mucin disulfide bonds, but unfortunately nebulization of
NAC causes bronchoconstriction.49 Oral administration of NAC has
not been investigated in pets with naturally occurring pneumonia but
in other species has demonstrated utility in the treatment of airway
disease associated with excessive mucus secretion.50 The author has
used oral NAC in animals with excessive mucus accumulation at a
dosage of 125 mg up to 600 mg PO q8-12h, to seemingly good effect.
Animals with pneumonia might be reluctant to eat, and nutritional
support must not be neglected.
Lung lobectomy occasionally is indicated for treatment when
pneumonia fails to resolve with appropriate antimicrobial therapy.5153
Residual infection in a single lobe can be related to an underlying
physical problem such as a bronchial foreign body, abscess, or
tumor. Removal of the lobe can result in cure in such cases.
Occasionally, failure to respond to appropriate antimicrobial therapy
is the result of an incorrect diagnosis. Any lung tissue removed
surgically should be submitted both for tissue culture and for
histopathologic analysis.
The prognosis for pneumonia (bacterial or other pathogens)
depends on factors including the overall health and immunologic
competence of the animal, disease severity at diagnosis, virulence
and antimicrobial susceptibility of the pathogen, and institution of
appropriate treatment. Attempts to tease out specific prognostic
indicators are difficult with a disease as heterogenous as pneumonia,
but the number of lung lobes involved, proportion of band
neutrophils on CBC, need for mechanical ventilation, and correct

choice of antimicrobials are among the factors that impact
survival.31,32,54-57

UNIQUE PATHOGENS CAUSING
BACTERIAL PNEUMONIA
Bordetella bronchiseptica
B. bronchiseptica is a primary respiratory pathogen. Essentially, it
creates its own opportunity to cause infection via secretion of
exotoxins that result in dysfunction of the mucociliary escalator.58
Bordetellosis is contagious; both dogs and cats are susceptible but
disease is more common in dogs.59,60 Infection usually results in
tracheobronchitis but can cause severe pneumonia in
immunocompromised or young animals. In a retrospective study of
community-acquired pneumonia in dogs <1 year of age, B.
bronchiseptica accounted for nearly half of all cases.31 These
infections can be difficult to eliminate despite the use of
antimicrobials with demonstrated in vitro susceptibility. Pneumonia
has been demonstrated in Bordetella-infected puppies treated with
amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate even though Bordetella’s
susceptibility to these antimicrobials had been shown in vitro.31 The
addition of nebulized aminoglycosides (ch. 90) to systemic
antimicrobials was recently demonstrated to be associated with
improvement in dogs with chronic Bordetella infection.42

Streptococcus equi subspecies zooepidemicus
Streptococcus equi subspecies zooepidemicus can cause necrotizing
hemorrhagic pneumonia in dogs and has been recognized to affect
cats also.61,62 Unlike other causes of contagious canine infectious
respiratory disease complex (ch. 203), illness rapidly can become
life-threatening.63-65 The pathogen is particularly likely to cause
severe and even fatal hemorrhagic pneumonia in kenneled dogs,
including those in shelters and research colonies. Dogs dying acutely,

or with evidence of pneumonia, in a kennel setting should undergo
necropsy with bacterial culture to confirm infection.

Mycoplasma species
Mycoplasma species, fastidious microbes that lack a cell wall,
include pathogenic (e.g., Mycoplasma pneumoniae in humans) and
commensal organisms. As many as 15 different species of
Mycoplasma have been isolated from dogs, and many have been
isolated from cats as well.66 However, because these organisms are
difficult to grow and difficult to speciate, their exact role in canine
and feline respiratory disease is not well defined.39
Mycoplasma species are found commonly in the upper airways
and occasionally in the lower airways of healthy dogs and cats.67 In a
study of 93 dogs with bacterial pneumonia specifically tested for
mycoplasmas, Mycoplasma species were recovered from only 7 dogs
as the sole bacterium but from 58 dogs with additional nonMycoplasma bacteria.68 This, combined with a favorable clinical
outcome even when antimicrobial therapy was not directed at
Mycoplasma spp., suggests that Mycoplasma bacteria usually were
opportunists. Experimental inoculation of some mycoplasmas causes
pneumonia, and naturally occurring pneumonia in both dogs and
cats occasionally has been attributed to Mycoplasma spp.39,67,69
Recently, a systemic review and meta-analysis confirmed a
significant association between M. cynos and lower respiratory
disease but could not confirm such an association for any other
Mycoplasma species.39
Special culture or PCR testing must be requested to identify
Mycoplasma spp., with greater sensitivity for PCR
(81.8%).39,70 Mycoplasma spp. usually respond well to macrolides,
tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, and fluoroquinolone antimicrobials
but do not respond to antimicrobials that interfere with cell-wall
synthesis (e.g., beta-lactams), which this genus lacks.

Mycobacterial Pneumonia

Cats and dogs occasionally are diagnosed with mycobacterial
pneumonia. Both tuberculosis (i.e., Mycobacterium tuberculosis,
Mycobacterium bovis, Mycobacterium microti) and
nontuberculosis-type (e.g., Mycobacterium avium complex,
Mycobacterium fortuitum) infections cause pneumonia in pets (ch.
188).71-74 Pneumonia can occur as the primary manifestation of
infection or as a component of disseminated infection. Pneumonia
due to mycobacteria often is granulomatous, and radiographs can
demonstrate lymphadenomegaly and pleural effusion in addition to
interstitial to alveolar pulmonary infiltrates. Mixed pulmonary
patterns are common, frequently including bronchial, alveolar,
nodular structured interstitial, or unstructured interstitial
components.74 Organisms are found in low numbers, if at all, in
samples retrieved by bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) or aspiration of
lung or lymph nodes. Because they do not take up routinely used
stains, these acid-fast inclusions show up as negatively staining
(“empty”) rods on routine cytologic examination. Both culture and
PCR have been used for confirming the presence of mycobacterial
species from dogs and cats, but tuberculosis-type mycobacteria are
notoriously slow-growing.71 M. tuberculosis primarily is a human
pathogen; when identified in dogs, it is considered a reverse
zoonosis.71 With such cases, the local health department should be
contacted and owners of infected pets should be instructed to contact
their physician. Both tuberculosis and nontuberculosis mycobacterial
infections require prolonged, multiple drug treatment regimens to
achieve control (ch. 188).

Yersinia pestis Pneumonia (Plague)
Practitioners in the midwestern and far-western United States,
especially New Mexico and Colorado, must consider plague as a
differential diagnosis in any cat or dog with pneumonia. Although
infection is relatively rare, its importance relates to zoonotic
potential. While relatively resistant compared to cats, dogs may
succumb to plague pneumonia and can transmit disease to
humans.75-78 Domestic cats, a more common source of zoonosis
through contact or inhalation of aerosolized droplets, have a

mortality rate from plague that approaches 50%.79,80 Rodents are
the natural reservoir of the Gram-negative coccobacillus Yersinia
pestis. Pets can be infected either by ingestion of bacteremic rodents
or rabbits, or via infected fleas. Most commonly, cats that consume
infected rodents develop suppurative lymphadenitis (buboes)
initially in the submandibular and cervical nodes. This bubonic form
can develop into either a septicemic or secondary pneumonic form
that poses a severe risk to exposed people. In endemic regions, any
cat with pneumonia should be strictly isolated and handled with
extreme caution; caution is also warranted for dogs. Cytologic
examination of exudate or lymph node aspirates typically reveals
bipolar, safety-pin-shaped Gram-negative rods. The Centers for
Disease Control and Prevention should be contacted if the diagnosis
is suspected; confirmation relies on fluorescent antibody testing,
culture, or rising antibody titer. Pending diagnosis, patients should
be treated for fleas and antimicrobials begun immediately.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, chloramphenicol, and
tetracyclines all have been used for the treatment of Y. pestis.

VIRAL PNEUMONIA
As opposed to bacterial respiratory infection, viral respiratory
disease is caused predominantly by primary pathogens and is usually
contagious (Box 217.5). Some viral pathogens that cause
pneumonia target the respiratory tract specifically (e.g., influenza),
whereas other viruses are polysystemic (e.g., distemper virus [ch.
204], feline infectious peritonitis [FIP, ch. 200]). Feline retroviral
diseases (chs. 198, 199) lead to immunosuppression and secondary
infectious but non-viral pneumonia. Many of the primary viral
pneumonia pathogens are part of canine infectious respiratory
disease complex (CIRDC; ch. 203) or causes of feline upper
respiratory infections (ch. 205). Effective vaccines (ch. 185)
minimize morbidity associated with many potential causes of viral
pneumonia. There is no single simple test with which to confirm viral
pneumonia. Often, infection is merely presumed, although
specifically targeted serologic or PCR tests (panels or single tests)
can confirm some infections.

In many respects, bacterial and viral pneumonia are similar. In
fact, much of the mortality associated with viral pneumonia results
from opportunistic bacterial infections. Because there are few
specific antiviral therapies, and little evidence to support the use of
these medications when they do exist, treatment of viral pneumonia
is largely supportive. Animals suspected of having viral pneumonia
should be isolated to reduce contagion. Additional information on
viruses relevant to the respiratory health of dogs and cats can be
found in chs. 203-206.

Influenza Virus
Since a 2004 outbreak of H3N8 influenza virus in a kennel of racing
Greyhound dogs, several other influenza type A viruses have been
recognized to cause sporadic or experimental infection in pets.81-83
Most have not resulted in sustained transmission within the species
for which infection is newly recognized. However, H3N2 influenza,
like H3N8, has developed the ability to spread readily from dog-todog, resulting in epidemics in Asia and the United States
(https://www.vet.cornell.edu/animal-health-diagnosticcenter/veterinary-support/disease-information/canineinfluenza-h3n2-updates, accessed July 12, 2021). Influenza
viruses are RNA viruses adept at mutation.82 The H3N8 canine virus
apparently originated as an equine influenza virus, while H3N2
seems to be of avian origin. For both of these highly contagious
viruses, an acute onset of cough, fever, and lethargy are typical.
Morbidity is marked but mortality is uncommon. When fatalities
occur, they often are related to opportunistic bacterial pneumonia. It
does not appear that canine influenza (i.e., H3N8, H3N2) are
zoonotic, but the possibility of multiple reassortment events means
that veterinarians must remain vigilant to this possibility. Although
specific anti-influenza drugs are available commercially, their use is
not encouraged. These costly drugs have not been evaluated in
canine influenza and as labeled for human influenza, they must be
administered within 48 hours of illness and result in only minor
reductions in disease duration and severity. Inactivated canine
influenza vaccines are available for at-risk dogs.

Cats are susceptible to natural and experimental infection with
several types of influenza A, including those that cause seasonal
influenza in people.82,84,85 Humans can transmit influenza to pet
cats, and cats are suspected to have been a source of avian influenza
virus infection in exposed humans.82,86 While seasonal influenza
causes mild illness, cats infected with virulent avian influenza H5N1
may develop fatal illness.85,87 Veterinarians should be vigilant for
possible influenza virus infection in pets both because of the
resultant illness in the examined animal, and also because of the
potential for contagion and zoonosis.

Coronavirus
There are several types of pathogenic coronaviruses. In cats,
mutations of the alphacorona feline enteric coronavirus result in FIP.
The dry form of FIP can cause granulomatous pneumonia (ch. 200).
In late 2019, human infections with the betacoronavirus SARS-CoV2 were recognized, soon developing into a worldwide pandemic.
Shortly thereafter, serologic and molecular evidence of feline

infection with SARS-CoV-2 was documented.88,89 As with human
infection, infected cats might remain healthy or develop respiratory
illness.90 Infected cats are competent to transmit the virus to other
cats,91 but as of this writing there is no evidence that cats play an
important role in zoonotic disease transmission.89 Nevertheless, the
owners of cats with acute onset of cough or signs of pneumonia
should be questioned about respiratory illness in people with close
contact to the cat and precautions should be used in handling such
cats. Gloves, medical masks or respirators, and face shields are
appropriate, particularly if aerosol generating procedures such as
intubation or airway lavage are performed. At this time, testing of
cats for SARS-CoV-2 is regulated by local rules.

PROTOZOAL PNEUMONIA
Protozoal pneumonia is not common. Of the protozoal causes of
pneumonia, toxoplasmosis is the most frequently encountered. Cats
are the reservoir host for Toxoplasma gondii and often are infected
without displaying clinical illness. When illness does occur, it can
involve the GI tract, the central nervous system, the abdominal
viscera, heart, eyes, or the respiratory tract (ch. 197).92 Serologic
identification of specific IgM supports active disease but both falsepositive and false-negative tests occur. Occasionally, T. gondii
tachyzoites are identified in airway lavage from animals with
pneumonia.93,94 Rapid response to treatment with potentiated
sulfonamides or clindamycin is expected, but recurrence is possible.

MYCOTIC PNEUMONIA
A variety of systemic fungi (especially Blastomyces dermatitidis [ch.
209], Histoplasma capsulatum [ch. 209], and Coccidioides
immitis [ch. 208]) can cause mycotic pneumonia in dogs and cats.
Progressive lower respiratory disease can be the primary
manifestation, but extrathoracic manifestations including weight loss
and lymphadenopathy also are common. Radiographic changes

associated with mycotic pneumonia often include nodular or miliary
nodular interstitial lung patterns and hilar lymphadenopathy.
Treatment is expensive and potentially toxic; therefore, a definitive
rather than a presumptive diagnosis is important. Because
interstitial mycotic infections do not result in early exfoliation of
fungal elements into the airways, airway lavage is not a sensitive
diagnostic technique. Diagnosis often is confirmed from other sites
(e.g., lymph node aspirates, impression smears of dermal lesions) or
via a sensitive and specific fungal antigen test typically performed on
urine samples.
Pneumocystis carinii (also known as Pneumocystis jirovecii)
originally was classified as a protozoon but now is considered a
fungus. Although this widely distributed saprophyte is not highly
virulent, in immunocompromised hosts it can result in severe
morbidity with high mortality. Infection has been described in
several small-breed dogs with presumed immunocompromise.95-98
Several immunodeficiencies have been documented in affected dog
breeds, including common variable immunodeficiency (Dachshunds,
Pomeranians), IgG deficiency (Cavalier King Charles Spaniels), and
CD40 ligand deficiency (Shih Tzu) (ch.180).95,97,99,100 Most
infected dogs are young, and most are presented for veterinary
attention due to progressive lower respiratory signs. Although there
are no unique physical, radiographic, or laboratory signs, absence of
fever despite severe pneumonia is a clue to this infection.99 The
diagnosis is complicated because the pathogens are not recovered
easily by airway lavage. The sensitivity of airway lavage is improved
through special stains (e.g., Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver) or
the use of molecular methods.101,102 Potentiated sulfonamides
appear to be the most effective therapy when administered early in
the disease course. Although Pneumocystis pneumonia is important
in immunocompromised people (e.g., during human
immunodeficiency virus infection), dogs are not thought to harbor
the same strain of Pneumocystis and thus should pose little zoonotic
risk.103

ASPIRATION PNEUMONIA

Aspiration pneumonitis/pneumonia result from inhalation of
material into the lower respiratory tract. Often, the aspirated
material consists of stomach contents with or without solid
particulate matter. Iatrogenic aspiration can occur as a result of
forced feedings, oral administration of substances such as barium or
mineral oil, or induction of emesis. Aspiration pneumonia
apparently is less common in cats than dogs, perhaps because the
strong laryngospasm reflex of cats provides better airway
protection.104 Depending on the volume of material aspirated, as
well as the physical properties of the material (e.g., pH, bacterial
contamination, particulate volume and size), the result can range
from minimal to fulminant pulmonary edema, necrosis, and
hemorrhage. Irritating chemicals (including stomach acid) result in
chemical pneumonitis, while aspiration of larger volumes of a more
benign fluid can result in drowning. Aspiration of polyethylene glycol
bowel-cleansing solutions can be especially harmful as these
substances draw interstitial fluid into the lungs.105,106 Aspiration of
large particulates can result in acute airway obstruction and
postobstructive pneumonia. Aspirated oral secretions contain a wide
variety of organisms that could cause infectious pneumonia;
however, stomach content has a low bacterial burden due to the
acidic gastric pH.107 Nevertheless, the damage done to the
respiratory tract by acid or irritants predisposes to opportunistic
bacterial infection. Aspiration injury occurs in phases beginning with
an acute airway response, followed by lung inflammation, and often
culminating in opportunistic infection.107

Presentation and Diagnostic Evaluation
Multiple conditions predispose to aspiration (Box 217.6).107 Many
of these conditions are found in hospitalized animals, so aspiration
(usually unwitnessed) should be considered in any hospitalized
animal with a new onset of lower respiratory signs. In retrospective
studies, fewer than half of dogs with aspiration pneumonia were
febrile while an even smaller proportion of cats had an increased
temperature and some cats with aspiration pneumonia were
hypothermic at presentation.36,54,104,108 Panting and tachypnea
were common but inconsistent findings in dogs, and most had cough
and either harsh/loud, adventitial, or diminished lung sounds on
auscultation.54,108 Nonspecific signs of illness (e.g., anorexia,
vomiting, lethargy) were more common than respiratory signs in
cats. For cats with aspiration pneumonia, 60% had abnormal lung
sounds but cough was noted in only ~20% and increased respiratory
effort in even fewer cats.36,104 Leukocytosis, with or without a left
shift, is a common but inconsistent finding in both
species.36,54,104,108 The classic radiographic appearance of
aspiration pneumonia is that of a patchy or focal alveolar infiltrate
(Figure 217.1) but one-quarter of affected dogs in a retrospective
study demonstrated a predominantly interstitial pattern.108
Radiographic changes can lag behind aspiration because fluid
accumulation lags behind chemical lung injury. Radiographs should
include both lateral views. The left lateral view is especially
important to improve recognition of an alveolar pattern in the right

middle lung lobe, a lobe that is largely silhouetted against the cardiac
shadow. Because aspiration of liquids is gravity-dependent, the most
commonly affected lung lobes are the right middle, right cranial, and
caudal portion of the left cranial; however, the lobe affected depends
on the position of the animal at the time of aspiration.54,104,108,109
Airway lavage (ch. 93) can be used diagnostically when there is no
clear history of aspiration nor any known predisposition to
aspiration. Neutrophilic inflammation is expected, and lipid-laden
macrophages or debris (e.g., foodstuffs) can be identified.
Polymicrobial and anaerobic infections are common delayed
complications of aspiration. Biomarkers have been examined to
distinguish aspiration from bacterial pneumonia, with limited
success.107,110

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment of aspiration largely is supportive. Efforts should be made
to prevent aspiration when possible, ideally via correction of
predisposing factors (Box 217.6). Animals should be fasted prior to
anesthesia and insufflated endotracheal cuffs used when
appropriate. For animals with dysphagia or megaesophagus,
adjustment of consistency of food and viscosity of water (e.g., using
Thick-It) may be beneficial (ch. 259). Feeding pets with
megaesophagus from elevated bowls and keeping the pet upright
after feeding are common practices, but efficacy of these techniques
to prevent aspiration is unknown. For animals with frequent
regurgitation due to megaesophagus not responsive to other
treatments, the placement of a gastrostomy tube can facilitate
feeding while minimizing risk of aspiration (ch. 81). Administration
of H2 receptor antagonists or proton pump inhibitors increases the
pH of stomach content and could lessen chemical lung injury due to
aspiration but might also increase gastric bacterial content.111
Prokinetic drugs promote gastric emptying and tighten the lower
esophageal sphincter, which might diminish the risk of aspiration of
gastric content.112 Unfortunately, neither morbidity nor mortality is
decreased in humans given prokinetic or acid-reducing drugs. In
studies reported to date, neither the prokinetic drug metoclopramide
nor cisapride were demonstrated to reduce the likelihood of

aspiration shortly after surgical arytenoid lateralization in
dogs.113,114 When aspiration is witnessed (for instance, during
anesthesia), physical clearing of the airways may be attempted.
Airway lavage also has been used therapeutically to “rinse” irritating
substances from the airways.105,106 Following known aspiration,
baseline thoracic radiographs should be obtained and oxygenation
monitored.109 If dyspnea occurs after aspiration, bronchodilators
could ameliorate acute bronchospasm. Oxygen supplementation
should be employed and adjusted as needed (ch. 123); overly
aggressive oxygen supplementation could worsen oxidative lung
injury associated with chemical pneumonitis, however. Nebulization
and physiotherapy are often used in animals with aspiration
pneumonia (ch. 90;

Videos 217.1, 217.2, 217.3). Secondary

bacterial infection requires treatment with appropriate
antimicrobials but not all aspiration results in bacterial infection.
Antimicrobial use is ideally guided by airway lavage cytologic
evaluation and C/S, both to choose an effective treatment option and
to avoid overuse of antimicrobials when they are not actually
required.

The prognosis for recovery cannot be predicted by severity of
radiographic changes alone.56,104 The prognosis may be worse for
animals with more than a single involved lung lobe,54 and slightly
more than one-third of dogs and one-half of cats demonstrate
radiographic evidence for involvement of two or more lobes.54,104
Nonetheless, in published studies, approximately 80% of dogs and
cats survived to discharge.54,56,104

PULMONARY EDEMA AND ACUTE
RESPIRATORY DISTRESS SYNDROME
Pulmonary edema is not a disease but is a consequence of disease. As
a result of increased hydrostatic pressure, decreased oncotic
pressure, impaired lymphatic drainage, or increased vascular
permeability (ch. 30), fluid accumulates in the interstitium and then

the alveoli at a rate faster than it can be reabsorbed. Fluid
accumulation in the alveolar space leads to ventilation-perfusion
mismatching and hypoxemia. Fortunately, the lungs are relatively
resistant to edema formation compared with other tissues.
Pulmonary edema is described as either “cardiogenic” or
“noncardiogenic.” Differentiation is crucial because the conditions
are treated differently. Cardiogenic edema, which follows increased
venous pulmonary hydrostatic pressure associated with left-sided
heart failure, is treated via diuretic administration, afterload
reduction, and any therapy aimed at the cause of congestive heart
failure. Cardiogenic pulmonary edema and its treatment are
discussed in detail in ch. 229. This section focuses on
noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.
It is useful to have a basic understanding of microvascular fluid
movement in the lung.115 In health, minute quantities of fluid and
solutes leak from gaps between the capillary endothelial cells and
enter the interstitial space. Tight junctions between alveolar
epithelial cells prevent the fluid from entering the alveoli. Instead,
interstitial fluid moves into the peribronchovascular space, where it
is removed by lymphatics and returned to the circulation. In
congestive heart failure or intravascular volume overload, increased
microvascular hydrostatic pressure leads to increased transvascular
fluid filtration and pulmonary edema. Because capillary endothelial
permeability is unchanged, this edema fluid contains little protein.
On the other hand, most noncardiogenic pulmonary edema occurs
when vascular permeability increases as a result of lung injury. In
contrast to cardiogenic edema, noncardiogenic edema fluid is
relatively rich in protein. The protein-rich fluid modifies oncotic
pressure gradients, which further alters fluid flux. In both
cardiogenic and noncardiogenic edema, accumulation of alveolar
fluid, combined with decreased lung compliance and airway
compression resulting from edema, all act to increase pulmonary
vascular resistance. Hypoxemia is the consequence of ventilationperfusion mismatching resulting from each of these factors.
Spontaneous removal of alveolar fluid depends on active transport of
sodium and chloride from the luminal surface through the epithelial
cell and across the basolateral membrane. Water movement
passively follows salt movement. Because fluid removal requires

active salt transport across the epithelium, injury to the epithelial
cells not only leads to edema formation but impedes the lung’s ability
to resolve edema. As a result of these mechanisms of causation and
resolution, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema is more refractory to
treatment than is cardiogenic edema.

There are myriad potential causes of noncardiogenic pulmonary
edema (Box 217.7). Severe hypoalbuminemia (<1.5 g/dL [<15 g/L])
is correlated with diminished vascular colloid oncotic pressure.
Although hypoalbuminemia can contribute to pulmonary edema,
pulmonary lymphatics are very efficient at fluid removal from the
interstitial space. Therefore, animals with low oncotic pressure are
far more likely to be presented for ascites, peripheral edema, or even
pleural effusion than for pulmonary edema. Nevertheless,

hypoalbuminemia will potentiate pulmonary edema in the face of
vascular permeability changes, the overzealous administration of
crystalloid fluids, or pre-existing heart disease.116 Similarly, although
lymphatic drainage is an important key to normal interstitial fluid
balance, impairment of thoracic lymphatic drainage (e.g., granuloma
or neoplasia, lymphangitis) is more likely to result in chylous
effusion than in pulmonary edema. Electrical shock or acute insult to
the central nervous system can lead to a unique neurogenic form of
noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. Although the mechanisms
causing neurogenic edema are incompletely understood, both
intense pulmonary vasoconstriction (and resultant increased
pulmonary hydrostatic pressure) and an inflammatory mechanism
are hypothesized to increase pulmonary capillary permeability.117
Noncardiogenic edema most commonly is related to (direct or
indirect) pulmonary epithelial injury. Acute pulmonary
inflammation and edema from a variety of initial insults resulting in
respiratory compromise may be termed the acute respiratory distress
syndrome (ARDS).118-120 These insults to the lung can be direct
(e.g., pneumonia, aspiration, smoke inhalation) or indirect (e.g.,
pancreatitis, uremia, sepsis).119-121 A genetic mutation has been
identified in Dalmatian dogs that results in disordered bronchiolar
epithelium with resultant familial ARDS.122
The most recent working veterinary definitions related to ARDS
were developed in 2007 and are no longer in line with the more
recent definitions developed for use in humans.118 For humans, a
consensus panel developed a set of definitions related to ARDS
known as the “Berlin Definition.”123 In this new system of
nomenclature, the term “acute lung injury” has been discarded;
ARDS itself is now characterized as mild, moderate, or severe, and
specific diagnostic criteria for ARDS have been developed. By these
criteria, ARDS is defined as having a characteristic time of onset
(within 1 week of the inciting event or onset/worsening of respiratory
signs), thoracic radiographic and/or CT findings (bilateral opacities
beyond those expected with effusions, atelectasis, or mass lesions),
and noncardiogenic origin (exclusion of heart disease of sufficient
severity to cause cardiogenic pulmonary edema).123 ARDS is

characterized as mild (PaO2/FiO2 = 200 to 300 mm Hg with positive
end-expiratory pressure [PEEP] or continuous positive airway
pressure ≥5 cm H2O), moderate (PaO2/FiO2 = 100 to 200 mm Hg
with PEEP ≥5 cm H2O), or severe (PaO2/FiO2 = <100 mm Hg with
PEEP ≥5 cm H2O), and these categories of severity have predictive
value in regards to outcome of lung injury in humans.121,123

PRESENTATION
Regardless of cause, the clinical presentation of animals with
noncardiogenic pulmonary edema is similar. Clinical signs can follow
rapidly or can be delayed for as much as 72 hours after the inciting
insult. The severity of signs depends on the degree of pulmonary
injury and amount of fluid accumulation; early signs include exercise
intolerance and tachypnea. A moist cough (ch. 34) can produce
frothy foam. Respiratory distress (ch. 37) and an aversion to lateral
or dorsal recumbency can be observed, and animals can demonstrate
cyanosis (ch. 27) and/or hemoptysis (ch. 36). Harsh, loud
bronchovesicular sounds are expected, and inspiratory and/or endexpiratory crackles ausculted. Occasionally, lung sounds are quiet
when edema is severe. Animals with cardiogenic edema often have
an audible heart murmur, but these findings are also possible in
animals with noncardiogenic edema; therefore, the absence of a
murmur is strongly suggestive of a noncardiogenic mechanism, but
the presence of a murmur is nonspecific. Sinus tachycardia is
common in animals with cardiogenic edema, whereas vagal
stimulation associated with lung disease often causes respiratory
sinus arrhythmia in noncardiogenic edema. Other abnormalities on
physical examination can be associated with the underlying disease
process (e.g., fever, pain).

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
Because animals with pulmonary edema are fragile, thorough
diagnostic investigation must follow medical stabilization (see
treatment, later). Abnormalities on CBC, serum biochemical profile,

and urinalysis depend almost entirely on the underlying disease
process. Likewise, radiographic changes vary, depending on both the
underlying condition and the degree of edema. An unstructured
interstitial and/or peribronchial radiographic pattern that progresses
with severity of edema produces an alveolar pattern; patchy
infiltrates are common in ARDS. The caudodorsal lung fields often
are the most severely affected, but depending on the source of lung
injury, the predominant location may be elsewhere (e.g., edema
associated with aspiration would be most severe in the affected
lobes). Cardiomegaly (especially left atrial enlargement) or
pulmonary venous engorgement suggests cardiogenic rather than
noncardiogenic edema. Thoracic ultrasound is expected to
demonstrate numerous B lines (ch. 73). Hypoxemia is expected, and
typically the alveolar to arterial oxygen gradient is increased as a
result of ventilation-perfusion mismatching (ch. 212).

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Treatment of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema should include
measures to address the underlying disorder but it might be
impossible to correct the instigating cause (e.g., electrocution) or
doing so might require time (e.g., pancreatitis). Treatment must
address hypoxemia. When respiratory distress is apparent, or if PaO2
is <80 mm Hg or the SpO2 is <94%, supplemental oxygen should be
provided in the least stressful manner possible (ch. 123). Because
animals with hypoxemia often are distressed, judicious use of
sedatives (e.g., butorphanol, morphine sulfate, or acepromazine IV)
could be warranted. Caution must be used because sedatives can
depress respiration. Animals in respiratory distress should be
allowed to position themselves for comfort, but if recumbent, they
should be either supported in a sternal position or placed with the
more severely affected lung in the dependent position. Animals with
ARDS often have critical respiratory compromise; if stabilization is
not possible with less invasive measures, intubation and ventilatory
support might be required.119,120 Positive pressure ventilation (PPV)
should be considered if initial therapy is unable to maintain SpO2

≥90%, PaO2 ≥60 mm Hg, and PaCO2 <60 mm Hg; PPV also can be
indicated to relieve sustained respiratory effort, which might result
in respiratory muscle fatigue.
Diuretic administration is more effective in the resolution of
cardiogenic or intravascular volume overload-associated edema than
noncardiogenic edema. Neurogenic pulmonary edema results from
both increased hydrostatic pressure and vascular permeability
changes. Therefore, diuretics such as furosemide could be of some
benefit in this condition. Neurogenic pulmonary edema usually
resolves without specific treatment, assuming that neurologic and
respiratory function can be preserved for 48 to 72 hours after the
initiating insult.117 Alpha-adrenergic blockade and dobutamine have
been suggested to be of benefit in the treatment of neurogenic
pulmonary edema. Drugs that result in cerebral vasodilation should
be avoided. Noncardiogenic edema that results from or is
exacerbated by hypoalbuminemia can be addressed with colloidal
support. Synthetic colloids such as hydroxyethyl starch have largely
fallen out of favor.124,125 Plasma transfusion is impractical to
replenish colloid oncotic pressure due to both the large associated
fluid volume required and the high costs of massive plasma
transfusion. Instead, albumin transfusion should be considered in
animals with pulmonary edema resulting from decreased colloid
oncotic pressure. Due to adverse effects of xenoalbumin transfusion,
use of canine albumin for dogs is ideal (chs. 123, 124).124-126 As an
additional complication of colloid administration, any increase in
pulmonary vascular permeability can lead to colloid leakage into the
alveolar space. This may in turn actually worsen noncardiogenic
pulmonary edema. The balance between these limitations and the
benefits of treatment must be considered on a case-by-case basis.
Medical treatment of ARDS, like the medical treatment of the
systemic inflammatory response syndrome (ch. 128) that often
accompanies ARDS, is complex. A variety of drugs that inhibit
inflammation, alter production of cytokines or enzymes, or act in any
of a dozen other ways has been used in the treatment of ARDS with
variable (usually minor) success. Intravenous fluid administration
could be required for the appropriate treatment of the underlying
disease processes (e.g., uremia), but it must be used judiciously to

avoid worsening edema via increased pulmonary hydrostatic
pressure. Conversely, reduction of hydrostatic pressure via
furosemide, which may also cause bronchodilation and improve
lymphatic flow, can be considered in well-hydrated animals but will
not have the profound effects often observed by resolution of
cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Despite the fact that mechanical
ventilation can actually exacerbate functional and structural lung
alterations, it often is necessary in the treatment of humans with
ARDS.121 The same could be true in animals.119,120 The treatment of
ARDS largely is dependent on supporting oxygenation and treating
the underlying disease while allowing the lungs to heal themselves,
but the prognosis for ARDS is guarded to grave.119-121

LUNG CANCER
Both primary respiratory neoplasia and metastasis of nonrespiratory
cancers occur in the lung. Differentiating less-common primary lung
tumors from the more common metastatic variety is important
because the diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of primary lung
tumors differ from those of metastatic cancer. Animals with lung
cancer can be presented due to cough (ch. 34), hemoptysis (ch. 36),
or other signs of respiratory dysfunction. Often, lung cancers are
identified radiographically in animals without respiratory signs
during evaluation for nonspecific signs such as weight loss or
extrathoracic neoplasia. Occasionally, animals with lung tumors are
presented for investigation of paraneoplastic conditions such as
hypertrophic osteopathy (ch. 331).

METASTATIC AND SPECIAL LUNG
CANCERS
The pulmonary vascular bed receives the entire output of the right
ventricle during each cardiac cycle. The blood passes through
numerous small-diameter, well-oxygenated capillary beds, making
the lung an ideal location for metastasis. The “seed and soil”
hypothesis describes detached tumor cells as seeds that can only

flourish in suitable soil (tissue).127 Besides simple mechanics, the
lung might be targeted specifically by certain tumors as a preferential
site of metastasis. Cancer metastasis is complex; cancer cells must
detach from the primary tumor, gain access into blood or lymph
vessels to be carried to distant sites, migrate from the vessels into the
tissues, adhere and then grow in the new site (ch. 316).127 Virtually
any neoplasm may metastasize to the lungs, but several that are
particularly likely to do so include hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325),
osteosarcoma (ch. 326), oral and nail bed melanoma (chs. 258,
323), histiocytic sarcoma (ch. 328), thyroid carcinoma (ch. 288),
and mammary carcinoma (ch. 329).128

Presentation and Diagnostic Evaluation
Often, animals with metastatic lung cancer have few respiratory
signs despite a large tumor burden with pulmonary metastasis
identified via screening thoracic radiographs. Radiographic
screening should include a combination of images obtained in dorsal,
ventral, right lateral and left lateral recumbencies, because the mild
atelectasis that occurs in the dependent lung can obscure
identification of tumors. The radiographic appearance of metastatic
cancer varies widely, typically with few to many interstitial nodules
of varying size distributed throughout the lungs. However,
metastasis can appear as a single nodule, an interstitial or alveolar
lung pattern, a miliary interstitial pattern, or even as multiple cysts (
Video 217.4). Thoracic CT is a more sensitive means of imaging
small tumors, but the need for anesthesia or sedation, equipment,
and financial resources prevent CT scan from serving as a routine
screening test.129,130 Because there is no pathognomonic
radiographic appearance of pulmonary metastasis, animals should
not be condemned based on thoracic radiographs alone when a
primary tumor has not been definitively identified. Instead, the
neoplastic nature of lung disease should be confirmed or refuted via
aspirate, lavage, or biopsy techniques (ch. 212).

Treatment and Prognosis

Unfortunately, with few exceptions, the prognosis is poor for
treatment of metastatic lung cancer. Growth of metastasis for some
tumors (e.g., thyroid carcinoma, anal sac adenocarcinoma) is slow,
minimizing impact of pulmonary metastasis on overall survival.
Treatment with tyrosine kinase inhibitors has benefit in certain
metastatic tumors.131,132 Radioiodine treatment has the potential to
treat both primary tumor and metastatic disease for animals with
thyroid carcinoma (chs. 287, 288).133 In those cases where only a
single or few pulmonary nodules is/are present, surgical resection
via thoracoscopy or thoracotomy (± adjunctive chemotherapy) may
be an option.134-136 Metastasectomy particularly can be useful in
cases where metastasis occurs long after treatment of the primary
tumor and is confined to one lung lobe.137 Inhalant therapies with
chemotherapy drugs, immunologic molecules (i.e., liposomal
interleukin-2), and gene therapy resulting in production of
immunogenic molecules have been described but are not yet readily
availible.138-140

Pulmonary Lymphoma
Lymphoma can affect the lungs either in conjunction with lymphoid
and solid organs or, rarely, without additional tumor burden.
Interstitial, alveolar, and mixed pulmonary infiltrative patterns are
observed on thoracic radiographs with or without concurrent hilar
and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Fine needle aspiration (FNA),
BAL (ch. 93), or lung biopsy may be used for confirming isolated
pulmonary lymphoma. A more complete discussion of lymphoma
and its treatment can be found in ch. 322.

Pulmonary Lymphomatoid Granulomatosis
Lymphomatoid granulomatosis (LG) is a rare lymphoproliferative
cancer in which atypical lymphoid cells infiltrate around and destroy
blood vessels. The condition has been reported more commonly in
dogs than in cats.141-143 In humans, LG is regarded as a low-grade
precursor to T-cell lymphoma. Immunophenotyping has
demonstrated the presence of T-cell markers and sometimes B-cell

markers in dogs and cats.141-143 Although pulmonary involvement is
reported most often, other sites including lymph nodes, abdominal
organs, eyes, and the dermis can be involved. Thoracic radiographs
typically demonstrate pulmonary masses and/or lobar consolidation.
Interstitial and alveolar infiltrates also are common, as is
tracheobronchial lymphadenopathy. Pulmonary biopsy is required to
achieve a diagnosis because the unique relationship between the
granulomatous lymphoid infiltrates and the vasculature (not the
airways) defines the disease. Utility of the less-invasive tests is
largely to rule out more common causes for pulmonary
consolidation. Supportive care might be necessary for hypoxemic
animals, but definitive treatment relies on chemotherapy. Protocols
used for treatment are identical to those used for treating lymphoma
(ch. 322). Treatment often results in durable remission, but
recurrence or development of lymphoma in other organ systems can
occur months to years later.

Histiocytic Sarcoma
Histiocytic sarcoma (malignant histiocytosis) is one of several
histiocytic diseases that occur more commonly in dogs than cats (ch.
328). The condition was first recognized in Bernese Mountain Dogs,
a breed for which a genetic basis with a polygenic mode of
inheritance is suspected.144 Flat-Coated Retrievers, Golden
Retrievers, Miniature Schnauzers, Pembroke Corgis, and Rottweilers
are among overrepresented breeds. As with lymphoma, histiocytic
sarcoma can affect any combination of organs, including the bone
marrow, central nervous system, abdominal viscera, and lungs;
primary pulmonary histiocytic sarcoma can radiographically mimic
more indolent primary carcinoma.144-147 Atypical histiocytic cells (a
mononuclear cell lineage) accumulate within the affected organs,
resulting in dysfunction. Clinical presentation often involves
nonspecific signs such as lethargy and anorexia; cough and/or
dyspnea are common.148,149 When pulmonary involvement exists,
radiographs can demonstrate thoracic lymphadenopathy
(tracheobronchial and sternal nodes, especially); pulmonary nodules
(often quite large, and most often found in the right middle lung
lobe) or an interstitial infiltrate; and sometimes pleural

effusion.145,146,150 On CT scan, most masses are mildly to
moderately contrast-enhancing and heterogeneous, poorly
marginated, and bronchocentric.150 Intrathoracic metastatic disease
to lymph nodes or other lung lobes can occur.145,150 Diagnosis
usually is based on histopathologic or cytologic assessment of
involved tissue or suggestive clinical findings and supportive bone
marrow cytologic features. To date, chemotherapeutic regimens have
been largely ineffective and the prognosis remains guarded to grave
for disseminated disease (ch. 328). However, the prognosis is better
for dogs with primary pulmonary histiocytic sarcoma, with a median
survival of 374 days for dogs treated with surgery and
chemotherapy.145
Another histiocytic lung disease, feline pulmonary Langerhans cell
histiocytosis, was described in 7 cats diagnosed at necropsy.144,151 All
were older adults with progressive respiratory failure and a
radiographic diffuse bronchointerstitial pattern with miliary to
nodular opacities.

PRIMARY LUNG CANCER
Primary lung cancer is uncommon in dogs and even less common in
cats. A relationship between accumulation of inhaled dust and
primary lung cancers has been proposed, but no definitive link to
living with smokers or an urban environment has been confirmed in
pets.152,153 Adenocarcinomas predominate, with other tumors
morphologically classified as carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma,
or anaplastic carcinoma.154-157 Recently, primary histiocytic sarcoma
has become a key differential diagnosis.147 Primary mesenchymal
lung tumors are rare.

Presentation
Most primary lung tumors are identified in older animals. Affected
animals can be brought to veterinary attention due to weight loss,
lethargy, and diminished appetite with or without concurrent
respiratory signs. Just over half of dogs with primary pulmonary

neoplasia are presented for evaluation of a chronic, nonproductive
cough.152,155,158Although other respiratory signs can occur as well
(e.g., tachypnea, hemoptysis), as many as one-third of dogs with
primary lung tumors display no respiratory clinical signs.155,158
Similarly, respiratory signs often are absent in cats with primary lung
tumors; only 20-40% of cats with primary lung tumors present with
dyspnea.154,159 Animals with primary pulmonary neoplasia can be
presented for evaluation of lameness due to either paraneoplastic
hypertrophic osteopathy or, in cats, metastasis to the phalanges
(lung-digit syndrome).152,160 Other presentations might include
edema of the head and neck (chs. 30, 239), ascites resulting from
tumor obstruction of lymphatic or venous flow (ch. 21), vomiting
(ch. 48) or diarrhea (ch. 49), or respiratory distress due to pleural
effusion or pneumothorax (ch. 220).

Diagnostic Evaluation
Although any radiographic pattern is possible in animals with
primary lung cancer, rare or solitary parenchymal masses often are
observed.156,159,161 Non-histiocytic solitary nodular tumors are
identified most frequently in the caudal lung lobes (
Video
217.4).156,159 On CT scan, primary lung tumors often are wellcircumscribed, bronchocentric masses with internal air
bronchograms; up to one-quarter of these tumors demonstrate
metastasis at the time of diagnosis.161 The radiographic pattern
cannot be considered pathognomonic and the differential diagnosis
for solitary or multifocal pulmonary nodules must be considered
(Box 217.8).
The diagnosis must be confirmed by microscopic examination of
cells for criteria of malignancy. Samples obtained by BAL or tracheal
lavage (ch. 93) help identify or rule out nonneoplastic disease and
rarely demonstrate cells with neoplastic morphology. Radiographic
localization of nodules can be used for estimating needle placement
for FNA, or aspirates may be obtained with fluoroscopic or CT
guidance.162,163 Nonaerated solid masses located near the edge of

the lung are most amenable to ultrasound-guided needle aspiration,
but there is a minimal risk of needle-tract seeding.164 Percutaneous
lung biopsy should be obtained only with imaging guidance due to
the risk of complications (i.e., pneumothorax, hemothorax).163
Although good correlation has been found between the diagnosis
obtained by FNA and percutaneous biopsy, results of FNA are less
likely to provide a conclusive diagnosis.163,165 Other lung biopsy
techniques include thoracoscopy, keyhole biopsy, and limited or full
thoracotomy.166-168 Depending on tumor size and location, these
techniques also offer the opportunity to completely excise the lung
tumor.

Because metastasis greatly affects prognosis, tumor staging should
be attempted before lung lobectomy. Efforts must be made to
identify distant tumors because single lung nodules can be either
metastatic or primary tumor. Thorough physical examination
(including prostate, mammary glands, and long bones; ch. 3), as
well as abdominal imaging, are indicated. Ideally, thoracic CT should
be performed prior to any planned surgical intervention to identify
small masses in other lung lobes that might otherwise be missed.
Canine primary lung tumors typically appear radiographically as a
well-circumscribed solitary mass in the periphery of a caudal lung
lobe, but up to one-third of primary lung tumors affect multiple
lobes.154,156,158,161 CT also improves the ability to detect
involvement of tracheobronchial lymph nodes, impacting the
prognosis.161,169

Treatment and Prognosis
Excision is the treatment of choice for primary lung tumors confined
to one lobe. Because lymph node involvement negatively impacts
prognosis, even normal-sized nodes should be sampled and
examined histologically.155,169,170 Favorable prognostic findings
include complete tumor removal, the presence of a single tumor
without metastasis, a lack of clinical signs referable to the lung
tumor, lower histologic grade or more well-differentiated tumor,
peripherally located tumor, and absence of pleural
effusion.154,155,170,171 Postoperative survival times vary widely but
can be up to 2 years, which can represent a normal life expectancy in
geriatric patients. In a recent study of radiotherapy for unresectable
pulmonary adenocarcinoma, treatment allowed reduction in tumor
size sufficient to allow surgical resection in 7/9 dogs.172 Damage to
intrathoracic structures and constant movement of the target
associated with respiration have limited the use of traditional
radiation therapy in the treatment of lung tumors, but intensitymodulated radiation therapy could offer effective treatment.173 Large
reports of traditional chemotherapy for the treatment of primary
lung tumors in dogs and cats are not available. A subset of lung
cancers in people is responsive to targeted chemotherapy based on

the presence of activated oncogenes including EGFR and HER2.
Recently, the presence of these potential genetic targets has been
investigated in dogs and cats but response to therapy aimed at these
targets is not yet known.152,174 Intracavitary chemotherapy
occasionally has been utilized to good effect in dogs with malignant
pleural effusion, carcinomatosis, or mesothelioma (ch. 220).175,176
Several reports document the potential utility of inhalational
chemotherapy or biologic response modifiers in the treatment of
metastatic or primary lung cancer.140,177,178

INTERSTITIAL LUNG DISEASE
Interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) are a heterogeneous group of
noninfectious, nonmalignant respiratory disorders that require
integration of clinical findings (including a thorough history as well
as imaging and clinicopathologic testing) and histopathologic
examination of lung tissue for diagnosis.179,180 Because lung biopsy
is rarely obtained in pet animals, ILDs, which account for ∼20% of
lung disease in humans, are likely underrecognized in dogs and cats.
The pulmonary interstitium is the space between the basement
membrane of the alveolar epithelial cells and the capillary
endothelial cells but disorders in the distalmost airways, vasculature,
and lymphatics of the lung parenchyma can be included as ILDs.180
For that reason, ILDs are also known as diffuse parenchymal lung
diseases. There are limited ways the lung can respond to injury
regardless of cause; the ILDs are characterized by inflammation,
fibrosis, and/or abnormal accumulations of protein or lipid that
restrict effective lung volume and diminish pulmonary compliance.
Recently, a classification scheme for ILD of dogs and cats has been
proposed, based on similar schemata for ILDs in people (Figure
217.2). The three major groupings include idiopathic interstitial
pneumonias (IIPs), ILDs secondary to a known cause, and
miscellaneous ILDs. Many ILDs have been recognized in dogs and
cats. Most are described only as single case reports, small case series,
or as experimentally induced disease; the reader is referred to other
sources for an excellent overview of ILD.180,182 Those ILDs that are

encountered more often include idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF),
EP, and lipid pneumonia.

IDIOPATHIC PULMONARY FIBROSIS
Pulmonary fibrosis can occur as a reaction to lung injury of
essentially any cause, or as a primary disease process of unknown
etiology (i.e., IPF).182,183 Further, IPF includes familial and sporadic
forms. It is important to understand that finding fibrosis on lung
biopsy is not sufficient to diagnose IPF. Instead, that diagnosis relies
on a multidisciplinary approach involving the treating veterinarian
as well as veterinarians with expertise in imaging and pathology after
a concerted effort to rule out potential explanations for fibrotic lung
change. This said, pulmonary fibrosis without an identifiable cause
presumed to be similar to IPF in people has been recognized in both
dogs and cats. In cats, the condition shares the histologic features of
usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), which characterizes IPF in
humans.184,185 These features include interstitial fibrosis, fibroblast
and myofibroblast proliferation, enlarged airspaces lined by
prominent epithelium (so-called honeycombing), and relatively mild
inflammatory changes. The lungs are heterogeneously affected, with
areas of normal lung admixed with diseased tissue. Lesions from
dogs with presumed familial IPF contain some histopathologic
features of UIP, but even more so those of another common type of
human interstitial pneumonia known as “nonspecific interstitial
pneumonia.”186 In dogs but not cats, there is a very strong breed
predisposition to IPF. The vast majority of dogs with IPF are West
Highland White Terriers.186-189 This strongly suggests a genetic
component to the disorder but no candidate gene has yet been
identified. It is likely that genetically susceptible individual dogs
experience an abnormal response to repetitive alveolar injury. In
recent years, there have been multiple studies aimed at identification
of genetic underpinnings, triggers, and aberrant
inflammatory/reparative responses for familial canine IPF (CIPF)
but as of yet the disease remains idiopathic.186-192 In addition to the
West Highland White Terrier, a similar fibrotic lung disease has been

occasionally described in other terrier breeds (Staffordshire Bull
Terriers, Bull Terriers, Cairn Terriers, and Scottish Terriers) and in a
cohort of Pekingese dogs from Hong Kong; it is not clear if these too
are a familial CIPF.186,193
