Presentation
Pulmonary fibrosis causes manifestations of restrictive lung disease.
Canine IPF is generally recognized in older dogs (mean age 9-13
years) and manifests first as exercise intolerance and/or cough with
eventual progression to tachypnea, dyspnea

(Video 37.2), and/or

syncope.186,187 As opposed to dogs, cats of any age can have IPF.
Because cats are adept at hiding clinical signs of lung disease, they
can present with what appears to be a very acute onset of respiratory
distress or even sudden death rather than with cough or insidious
increase in respiratory effort.185,194 Adventitial lung sounds
commonly are identified in animals with IPF. In dogs especially,
prominent inspiratory crackles are typical, and in contrast to
cardiogenic pulmonary edema, patients with mild or moderate IPF
often have crackles that are readily apparent and widespread despite
a normal or minimally increased respiratory effort. A systolic heart
murmur of tricuspid regurgitation can be noted, especially in dogs
that have pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale. Cyanosis is a
common finding in dogs (but not cats) with IPF late in the disease
process. There are no specific changes on routine blood or urine
testing suggestive of IPF, but in the later stages of disease,
hypoxemia might result in erythrocytosis and/or increased serum
alkaline phosphatase activity. Pulse oximetry, arterial blood gas
analysis, and 6-minute walk tests (dogs) are often abnormal but are
limited to supporting respiratory dysfunction. Non-invasive (e.g.,
serologic titers, breath and blood biomarkers) and minimally
invasive diagnostics (e.g., bronchoscopy, BAL with culture and
cytologic evaluation) are helpful to rule out alternative explanations
for respiratory disease but cannot confirm IPF.186,187
Imaging studies can be supportive but not confirmatory for
pulmonary fibrosis in pets. Radiographic lung patterns in cats with
IPF are nonspecific, while dogs often demonstrate
bronchointerstitial infiltrates and right-sided heart enlargement.185187
The absence of an alveolar pattern in a dog with loud crackles on
auscultation can suggest pulmonary fibrosis. Characteristic findings
on thoracic CT in people allow diagnosis of IPF without lung biopsy
but findings in pets are not as specific. The most common pulmonary

CT findings in CIPF include ground-glass appearance, mosaic
attenuation, and reticular pattern.186,187,195 In cats, reticular
patterns, areas of increased attenuation, consolidation or masses,
and traction bronchiectasis are described.194,196 Echocardiography
(ch. 97) should be performed both to rule out primary heart disease
and to assess for pulmonary hypertension, a common but treatable
complication of CIPF (ch. 218). Histologic examination of lung
tissue is mandatory to confirm fibrosis, but only the totality of
findings can result in a diagnosis of IPF.

Treatment and Prognosis
Pulmonary fibrosis is irreversible, so emphasis is given to alleviation
of clinical signs and supportive care. The drugs (e.g., pirfenidone,
nintedanib) used for slowing progression of IPF in humans are
untested and too expensive for use in pet animals. Because cough can
be a prominent component of the disease in dogs, pharmacologic
suppression of cough can improve the quality of life. Control of
pulmonary hypertension, when present, can also improve the quality
of life. Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors sildenafil (e.g., sildenafil 0.5-1
mg/kg PO q8h) or tadalafil (2 mg/kg PO q24h) can be used for this
purpose in CIPF.186,187,197-199 There are anecdotal reports of
improvement in response to glucocorticoids or bronchodilators. The
long-term prognosis for IPF is poor; however, dogs with pulmonary
hypertension who respond well to treatment and/or dogs whose
owners are content with calmer pets can live a length and quality of
life that approach normal for the dog’s age. In other dogs, the
diagnosis comes only towards the end of life or disease progression is
rapid.186,187 Less is known regarding treatment of cats. Most
reported cats are either euthanized or succumb quickly, but some
long-term responses have been reported.

EOSINOPHILIC PNEUMONIA
Many names have been used to describe eosinophilic diseases of the
terminal bronchioles, alveoli, and pulmonary blood vessels in dogs
and cats (chs. 215 and 216). Variably called eosinophilic pneumonia

(EP), pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia/eosinophils,
eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy (EBP), pulmonary
hypersensitivity, eosinophilic granulomatous pneumonia, pulmonary
eosinophilic granulomatosis, hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES),
and eosinophilic pneumonitis, there is little agreement on
classification of eosinophilic lung disorders.182,200 In humans, EP
can be broadly categorized as being of either determined or
undetermined origin and either acute or chronic. Recently, a
proposed scheme adapted from human medicine has sought to
categorize eosinophilic lung disease in dogs considering anatomic
location of disease.182 This would classify eosinophilic bronchitis as
confined to the airways, EBP as affecting airways and pulmonary
parenchyma, and EP as affecting the pulmonary parenchyma.
Further, chronic EP would include more severe subtypes of
eosinophilic pulmonary granulomatosis (EPG) and HES. HES is
often a systemic disorder impacting tissues in addition to the lung,
and will not be further discussed here.201 Determinate causes of EP
include parasitic (especially D. immitis and various lungworms),
fungal, or other infectious agents, allergic response, drug
administration, and toxin exposure.
Although reactive eosinophilic airway disease (i.e., asthma) is
more common in cats, EP of undetermined origin is more common
in dogs. EBP is a well-reported but idiopathic condition of young to
middle-aged dogs with a slight female predominance (ch. 215).202204

A predisposition has been reported in Siberian Husky, Alaskan
Malamute, Labrador Retriever, and Rottweiler breeds, but any can
be affected.202,204-206 Dogs typically present for cough with or
without gagging, retching, respiratory effort, or nasal discharge.
About half of affected dogs demonstrate peripheral eosinophilia.
Radiographs typically demonstrate a bronchial or bronchointerstitial
pattern most pronounced in the caudodorsal lungs, sometimes with
alveolar infiltrates, and often with bronchiectasis.202,203,207,208 In
fact, eosinophilic pulmonary disorders are among the most common
diseases associated with bronchiectasis in dogs.206 On bronchoscopy
(ch. 93), copious yellow-green mucus and bronchiectasis are often
visible. BAL fluid from dogs with EP demonstrates increased

cellularity (>200 to 400 cells/mcL) with a marked increase in
eosinophil percentage. Lavage fluid from dogs with suspected EP
should be examined carefully for the presence of neoplastic cells
(e.g., mast cells, lymphoma), fungal elements, or pulmonary
parasites and should be cultured. Parasitic infections should be ruled
out through repeated fecal testing (i.e., Baermann sedimentation and
zinc sulfate centrifugation-flotation [ch. 80]) and/or deworming
(ch. 142), as well as heartworm antigen testing (ch. 237).
Treatment consists of oral corticosteroids (0.5-2 mg/kg
predniso[lo]ne q24h, tapered to effect) or inhaled steroids (ch.
90).209 Response to treatment is often rapid but relapse is not
uncommon.202-204,206 If eosinophilic inflammation is left
unresolved, bronchiectasis can worsen and predispose to subsequent
infection.
EPG, which is characterized by nodules and masses of eosinophils
and other inflammatory cells in a fibrous matrix, has been
uncommonly reported in dogs.210 EPG differs from the description
of other authors of eosinophilic granuloma (EG), wherein airways
are plugged by masses of eosinophils.203 Cough, exercise
intolerance, and increased respiratory effort are typical of EPG, as
are peripheral eosinophilia and basophilia. Affected dogs are usually
young adults, which can help steer away from lung cancer, the
primary imaging differential diagnosis. Unlike EBP or EG, the
prognosis is guarded to poor.210

LIPID PNEUMONIA
Lipid pneumonia results from an inflammatory response to globules
of lipid in the alveolar airspaces.211,212 Exogenous lipid pneumonia
follows aspiration of lipid—for instance, after the aspiration of
mineral oil or petroleum-based products used for treating
constipation or hairballs.213 Endogenous lipid pneumonia (EnLP) is
unassociated with aspiration. Although uncommon, EnLP has been
reported in both cats and dogs.211,214,215 Pneumocyte injury
associated with obstructive pulmonary disease, including diseases

related to pulmonary neoplasia, has been associated with
EnLP.214,215 Pneumocyte injury leads to cellular degeneration with
release of cholesterol and overproduction of cholesterol-rich
surfactant.211 Lipids then are phagocytosed by pulmonary
macrophages; these foamy macrophages accumulate in the alveoli.
Endogenous lipid also is involved in the pathogenesis of certain
infectious pneumonias, such as atypical mycobacterial pneumonia in
cats.216
EnLP is rare enough that no comprehensive statements can be
made regarding presentation or therapy. In a series of 24 cats with
EnLP diagnosed at necropsy, ages ranged from 1-15 years with a
median age of 8.4 years.211 Fewer than half had respiratory signs,
and none had lipemia. Because animals with EnLP often have
additional lung disease (e.g., heartworm disease, neoplasia), it is
difficult to determine which imaging lesions are related to EnLP and
which to concurrent disease.211,215 BAL (ch. 93) and lung FNA in
animals with EnLP can be suggestive of concurrent respiratory
disease and/or demonstrate foamy, lipid-filled macrophages with
positive staining for fats (e.g., Oil Red O).215,217 Because alcohol
fixatives can remove lipid, air-dried specimens are preferred.
Necropsy most often has been used for achieving the diagnosis of
EnLP in veterinary patients.126,211,215 When a specific concurrent
lung disease is identified in animals with EnLP, that disease should
be addressed directly. In humans, idiopathic EnLP may respond to
corticosteroids.

MISCELLANEOUS LUNG DISEASES
LUNG LOBE TORSION (LLT)
LLT is uncommon in dogs and rare in cats.218,219 The lobe usually
rotates on the long axis, resulting in occlusion of both the bronchus
and pulmonary vasculature at the hilus. Because the muscular
pulmonary artery continues to allow the passage of small amounts of
blood while the thin-walled pulmonary vein collapses completely, the
affected lobe becomes congested and consolidated. Eventually, fluid

leaves the lobe surface and enters the pleural space, resulting in
effusion (ch. 220). Although torsion results in pleural effusion,
effusion might also predispose to torsion. Torsion can occur
spontaneously or can be associated with other disease processes,
including neoplasia or trauma.218,219

PRESENTATION
Although torsion can occur in any breed, Pugs and sighthounds
(especially Afghan Hounds) are overrepresented.218,220-224 Most
affected dogs are young to middle-aged and the condition has been
reported in a number of puppies.218,221-224 Although duration of
clinical signs is usually <1 week, there are many reports of animals
with signs present for several months prior to diagnosis. Vague signs
of illness (e.g., anorexia, lethargy, vomiting) are very common, with
most affected having at least some respiratory signs. These include
increased respiratory effort and rate, cough, hemoptysis, exercise
intolerance, and collapse. Common physical abnormalities include
tachypnea or panting, dyspnea, fever, diminished or loud
bronchovesicular lung sounds, and muffled heart sounds. Cyanosis,
tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill time, and poor or bounding
pulses sometimes are identified.

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
Peripheral neutrophilia (with or without left shift) is common, along
with a variety of other nonspecific abnormalities on CBC and serum
biochemistry profile.218,220,221 Thoracic radiographs usually reveal
pleural effusion; if so, they should be repeated after thoracocentesis
(ch. 92) to facilitate recognition of lung lobe consolidation.
Abnormal positioning of the bronchus is inconsistently identified,
and a narrowed proximal bronchus can be seen. When identified, a
vesicular gas pattern (small, scattered bubbles) in the affected lobe is
strongly suggestive of torsion.218,220,221 Thoracic CT (with or
without reconstructed “virtual bronchoscopy”) is more sensitive and
specific than are radiographs for detection of LLT, because it does

not rely on secondary changes (e.g., lung lobe consolidation) to
suggest the diagnosis and is not obscured by pleural effusion.220
Ultrasonography can be suggestive, with a recent description of a
hypoechoic band around the periphery of the affected lung as being
highly suggestive of torsion.223 Though seldom necessary,
bronchoscopy (ch. 93) can confirm LLT.218 Evaluation of pleural
effusion often reveals a blood-tinged modified transudate with high
numbers of neutrophils and lymphocytes, but chylous effusion
occurs in some affected dogs and cats (ch. 71).218-221,225 Chylous
effusions often are identified in Afghan Hounds both with and
without LLT, making it especially unclear in this breed if effusion
leads to torsion, torsion leads to effusion, or some of each
occurs.226,227 Reactive mesothelial cells frequently are identified but
seldom indicate mesothelioma. Bacterial culture of resected lung
tissue is recommended because of possible infection of necrotic
tissue, but more often than not, no growth is identified.220,221,228

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Once LLT is recognized, removal of the affected lobe is the only
appropriate treatment. Torsion can occur in any lobe(s), but in Pugs
the left cranial lobe is most affected while the right middle lobe is
more likely to torse in large-breed dogs.218,222
Most dogs recover fully after surgery, with a worse prognosis for
secondary torsion or in large dogs.218-222 In a recent study,
increased APPLEfast score and depressed mentation were correlated
with reduced odds of survival.221 Postoperative morbidity including
pneumothorax, persistent or new chylous effusion, and torsion of
additional lung lobes has been reported in a proportion of animals
surviving surgery.218-222

PHYSICAL LUNG INJURY

Physical injury to the lungs may range from minor to profound, and
from subclinical to fatal. The most common means of injury include
blunt thoracic trauma, drowning, and smoke inhalation. These
conditions seldom pose a diagnostic dilemma because historical
circumstances and concurrent wounds typically make the cause of
injury apparent.

THORACIC TRAUMA
Automotive injury and fight wounds are the most common causes of
thoracic trauma in small animals. Regardless of the specific cause,
trauma can result in serious concurrent injury including hemorrhage
and shock. Thorough examination of the entire patient is warranted
not only because additional injuries directly affect therapy, but
because the discovery of serious coincident injury (e.g., spinal injury,
bladder rupture) can have a substantial impact on extent of
treatment, prognosis, and the owner’s decision as to whether to
embark on treatment (ch. 119). Trauma can result in airway rupture
(ch. 123), rib fracture, lung laceration, flail chest (ch. 220),
diaphragmatic hernia (ch. 222), pneumothorax (ch. 220), and/or
pulmonary contusion, any of which can result in tachypnea and
respiratory distress.
Pulmonary contusion results from bleeding into the interstitium
and alveoli. Occasionally, contusion occurs as the result of a bleeding
disorder rather than thoracic trauma. Respiratory distress occurs as
a result of ventilation-perfusion mismatching due to flooding of
alveoli with blood. Crushing lung injury, airway and chest wall
injury, and pain often worsen respiratory distress. Although crackles
and/or diminished bronchovesicular sounds can be heard, their
presence does not confirm contusion and their absence does not rule
it out. Hemoptysis (ch. 36) is uncommon following thoracic trauma
but does suggest pulmonary hemorrhage when present.229 Thoracic
radiographs allow evaluation of extrapulmonary structures (e.g.,
ribs, diaphragm, pleural space) and the pulmonary parenchyma.
Intrapulmonary hemorrhage can be evident as interstitial and/or
alveolar radiographic lung patterns, and these radiographic changes
can be delayed by up to 24 hours. Thoracic focused assessment with
sonography for trauma, triage, and tracking (FAST) ultrasound

allows detection of B lines and sometimes identifies air or blood
(fluid) in the pleural space (ch. 73). When available, CT scan
provides earlier, more accurate information regarding consequences
of injury.230,231 Electrocardiographic monitoring can demonstrate
premature ventricular complexes as a result of traumatic myocarditis
after substantial thoracic trauma (ch. 230).
Animals presenting with tachypnea or respiratory distress after
thoracic trauma should receive immediate supplemental oxygen
during all diagnostic procedures (ch. 123). Many animals with
pulmonary contusions have mild to moderate lung injury and
respond well to supplemental oxygen and supportive care. High-flow
oxygen may be required, but when hypoxemia and/or dyspnea
persists, intubation and mechanical ventilation are required.47,232
Specific treatment of traumatic pulmonary contusion is not
possible, but therapy for concurrent traumatic injury and its
complications (e.g., shock, hypovolemia) is vital. In animals with
contusion due to bite wounds, surgical exploration of the wound and
thoracic cavity can improve outcome.233 When pulmonary
contusions are due to a bleeding disorder rather than trauma,
specific treatment is indicated (ch. 171). Antimicrobial drugs are not
indicated for pulmonary contusion in the absence of other
indications for such therapy (e.g., penetrating trauma). Fluid therapy
should be carefully monitored to avoid pulmonary edema and
worsened lung function. Complications such as cavitary lung lesions
or abscessation occur rarely, and most animals that survive the first
several hours to a day after pulmonary contusion recover
completely.231,234 The prognosis worsens when pulmonary
compromise is sufficient to require mechanical ventilation and is
worse in smaller animals than in larger animals.232

DROWNING
Drowning occurs when submersion or immersion in liquid causes a
primary respiratory impairment. All drowning (fatal or not) involves
aspiration of liquid. Although older literature referred to
laryngospasm during or after submersion as “dry drowning,” this

phenomenon is now believed to be very rare and inappropriately
described as drowning. The pathophysiology of drowning differs
somewhat when hypotonic fresh water is aspirated as compared with
hypertonic salt water. Regardless of minor differences in systemic
and pulmonary vascular volumes and electrolyte alterations, the
most important immediate consequences of either type of drowning
relate to hypoxemia.235,236 Alveoli filling with fluid, diluted and
dysfunctional surfactant allowing alveolar collapse, and
intrapulmonary vascular shunting all result in ventilation-perfusion
mismatching and subsequent hypoxemia. Diminished pulmonary
compliance and pulmonary inflammation resulting in
noncardiogenic pulmonary edema due to ARDS further contribute to
hypoxemia. Hypoxemia leads to lactic acidosis, and hypercapnia due
to pulmonary compromise can result in respiratory and metabolic
acidosis. Pulmonary injury can be worsened by aspiration of
chemicals or pathogens in the water.236
Drowning is far more common in dogs than cats, probably because
cats are less likely to enter water.237 Because dogs often are strong
swimmers, drowning occurs most often when circumstances prevent
their egress from water (e.g., a swimming pool with steep sides and
no steps, falling into an ice-covered pond, strong currents), when
medical circumstances prevent their normal airway protective
reflexes from working appropriately (e.g., laryngeal paralysis), or
when they lose consciousness while swimming (e.g., seizure).237 A
larger-than-expected proportion of dogs presented for near
drowning is young (age <4 months). Typically, drowning victims are
presented for care following rescue from the water. Common
presentations include respiratory arrest, respiratory distress, cough,
altered mental status, or loss of consciousness. Circulatory shock
(ch. 121) and hypothermia (ch.130) often are identified
concurrently. Thoracic auscultation can reveal either diminished
bronchovesicular sounds or a combination of crackles and wheezes.
Assessment of oxygenation and acid-base status should be
conducted, ideally via arterial blood gas analysis (chs. 74 and 212).
Radiographs typically demonstrate a diffuse interstitial to alveolar
pattern, but as with pulmonary contusion, radiographic changes can
underestimate the severity of lung injury because changes often

progress following rescue due to development of ARDS. The
radiographic appearance of “sand bronchograms” (radiopaque
material in the airways) is a poor prognostic indicator. Other poor
prognostic indicators include the need for cardiopulmonary
resuscitation or mechanical ventilation, and acidosis. Level of
consciousness at admission was not associated with outcome in a
retrospective review of freshwater drowning, with full recovery
occurring even in some animals presenting in a coma.237
Supplemental oxygen should be administered immediately (ch. 123)
but hypoxemia might persist. If the animal is unable to maintain
PaO2 >60 mm Hg with an FIO2 >50%, mechanical ventilation should
be initiated.57,236 Even animals who remain normoxemic following
rescue can develop ARDS and should therefore be observed for at
least 24 hours. Hypothermic animals should be warmed, and shock
directly addressed. There can be a difficult balance between fluid
administration to address shock and overhydration in the face of
lung injury. Continuous hemodynamic monitoring is indicated, and
inotropic support could be necessary. Severe acidosis (pH <7.1) or
electrolyte imbalances require treatment. Despite the potential
occurrence of bacterial pneumonia after drowning, prophylactic
antibiotics have not been shown to reduce the risk in humans or
animals.57,236-238 If evidence of bacterial pneumonia develops later,
cytologic evaluation and culture of airway lavage fluid should guide
the choice of antimicrobials. Corticosteroids are not indicated.236

SMOKE INHALATION
Despite the frequency with which house fires occur, there is limited
information on smoke inhalation injury in pet animals.239-242
Smoke inhalation does not always follow every exposure to fire, but
when inhalation occurs, often it results in serious respiratory injury.
Upper airway obstruction related to bronchospasm and laryngeal
swelling can result from thermal and chemical injury; such
obstruction typically peaks within the first 24 hours.240 Inhalation of
soot and noxious gases released through combustion of household
components (e.g., hydrogen cyanide, ammonia, aldehydes, acrolein),

inflammation of airways and airspaces, systemic inflammatory
mediators, inactivation of surfactant, reflex bronchoconstriction,
atelectasis, airway edema, and ARDS all can contribute to lung injury
in this context (chs. 123, 128).239-242 Carbon monoxide and
cyanide exposure further compromise oxygen delivery and utilization
by tissues (ch. 137). Exfoliation of dying epithelial cells and soot can
result in delayed airway obstruction even days after the event,
meaning that respiratory compromise from smoke inhalation
remains dynamic for up to a week after the inciting event.243 As a
further concern, impaired local and systemic defense mechanisms
markedly predispose to secondary bacterial pneumonia.
Animals rescued from fire can be presented for care in a state that
ranges from apparent good health to severe injury. Common clinical
findings include the scent of smoke on the haircoat, cough and gag,
hyperemic mucous membranes, tachypnea, increased respiratory
effort, harsh bronchovesicular or adventitial lung sounds, upper
airway noise, nasal discharge, and burns or lacerations.240,241,242
Additionally, neurologic abnormalities can be identified (e.g., ataxia,
stupor) as a result of CNS hypoxia, or such abnormalities can occur
days later due to leukoencephalomalacia.244 Oxygenation ideally is
measured via arterial blood gas analysis (chs. 74 and 212). Because
these patients usually are being provided supplemental oxygen,
assessment of PaO2:FIO2 ratio is more useful than simple assessment
of PaO2; a ratio <300 signifies marked respiratory compromise. Only
dissolved oxygen is measured via blood gas analysis, so it must be
remembered that tissue hypoxia may be profound in animals with
carbon monoxide intoxication despite a normal PaO2. Although
carbon monoxide interferes with hemoglobin-oxygen saturation,
pulse oximetry cannot distinguish oxyhemoglobin from
carboxyhemoglobin. Thus, oximetry can provide an overestimation
of the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity in carbon monoxide
intoxication cases.245 If available, a cooximeter can be used for
measuring carboxyhemoglobin concentration. On thoracic
radiographs, dogs frequently demonstrate an alveolar pulmonary

pattern, whereas interstitial and alveolar patterns have been
identified nearly equally in smoke-exposed cats.239,242
Supplemental oxygen should be administered at least until initial
assessment is complete; administration of oxygen (ideally beginning
at rescue) can result in rapid clinical improvement (ch. 123).239
Supplemental oxygen is useful for treatment of hypoxemia and also
facilitates the pulmonary elimination of carbon monoxide. The role
of hyperbaric oxygen therapy remains controversial and has limited
availability for most veterinarians.241 Persistent hypoxemia in the
face of supplemental oxygen delivery could indicate the need for
mechanical ventilation. Occasionally, upper airway swelling requires
either intubation or tracheostomy (chs. 94 and 123). Crystalloid
fluid therapy is required for animals presenting with burns or in
shock but excessive fluid therapy could contribute to respiratory
edema.241 Prophylactic antimicrobial therapy has no proven benefit
in humans with smoke inhalation injury. Corticosteroids were not
effective in a clinical study using a dog model and are neither proven
effective nor routinely used in humans with smoke inhalation.245,246
Other therapies sometimes employed to treat animals with smoke
inhalation include bronchodilators, saline nebulization and coupage,
ocular lubricants, and treatment of concurrent burns (including
analgesia, ch. 6). Because ARDS can develop and worsen after initial
smoke exposure, monitoring through the first 24 hours is suggested
even when animals appear well. Improvement in respiratory status
during the first day after rescue is a positive prognostic indicator,
while worsening respiratory status, the presence of concurrent
burns, and the need for mechanical ventilation all are negative
prognostic indicators.239,242

ATELECTASIS
Pulmonary atelectasis is simply noninflated or underinflated lung
and not a lung disease. The term can be used for describing newborn
lungs that have not yet inflated, lungs that have collapsed as a result
of mechanical compression (including compression associated with
recumbency), areas of alveolar collapse resulting from alveolar

filling, or areas of alveolar collapse resulting from airway obstruction
with resorption of trapped air.

CAVITARY LUNG LESIONS
Cavitary lung lesions can vary in size, shape, wall thickness, number,
location, and content. There is a multitude of potential causes for
cystic (wall <3 mm thickness) or cavitary (wall ≥3 mm thickness)
lung lesions (Box 217.9).1,247 A few specific causes are addressed
next.

ABSCESSES
Pulmonary abscessation is an uncommon diagnosis in dogs and cats.
An abscess can predominantly be air-filled or can have a nodular
soft-tissue radiographic appearance due to fluid accumulation. A
fluid line can be visible when both air and fluid are present,
specifically on horizontal-beam projections. Typically, abscesses
occur in areas of otherwise diseased lung (e.g., pneumonic regions,
bronchiectasis) and have a thick wall or capsule with an irregular
inner margin.248,249 In humans, lung abscess formation especially is
likely as a sequela of aspiration pneumonia with secondary bacterial
infection, or when there is obstruction of distal airways as a result of
malignancy, inflammation, foreign material, or inspissated mucus
plugging.250 Respiratory signs or signs of systemic infection can be
identified in animals with pulmonary abscesses; evidence of
hypertrophic osteopathy also can be noted.248,249,251,252 When only
a single lung lobe is involved, surgical excision is preferred to
antimicrobial therapy alone. The excised lung can be cultured and
examined histologically. Sometimes, an underlying cause of
abscessation such as foreign material or neoplasia is identified.52,253
Surgical lobectomy also minimizes the risk of pneumothorax and
pyothorax due to abscess rupture.251 When surgery is not possible,
antimicrobial therapy ideally is guided by C/S results, but acquiring
a specimen carries possible risks: rupture of an abscess during

needle aspiration could lead to pyothorax and/or pneumothorax (ch.
220), while airway lavage might result in pneumothorax due to
rupture of an air-filled abscess pocket.

PULMONARY BLEBS, BULLAE, AND
EMPHYSEMA
Blebs and Bullae
Bullae are air pockets within the pulmonary parenchyma; they result
from destruction of alveolar walls with confluence of adjacent alveoli
and are not lined by epithelium as are pulmonary cysts. Bullae have
been classified into several subtypes depending on size and
connectivity with surrounding tissue. Bullae can be large or small
and can occur near the lung surface or deep within the parenchyma.
Pulmonary blebs are accumulations of air formed when air that has
escaped from the lung becomes trapped immediately underneath the
visceral pleura; blebs always are found on the lung surface. Bullae
formation very often is idiopathic, but it can result from lung damage
due to parasitic, neoplastic, infectious, or other disease conditions in
either dogs or cats. Bullae can be related to congenital disease
including bronchopulmonary dysplasia.254,255 Idiopathic bullae
occur predominantly in otherwise healthy deep-chested or largebreed, middle-aged dogs. While bullae can be an incidental imaging
finding, idiopathic bullae usually are discovered as a consequence of
rupture with resultant spontaneous pneumothorax. Unfortunately,
thoracic radiography is insensitive (<5 to 50% detection) for bullae
and blebs.256,257 CT scanning, ideally in both sternal and dorsal
recumbency, improves detection (up to 75%) but still is
imperfect.256,258 Once significant pneumothorax has occurred,
partial lung lobectomy to remove affected lung tissue is
recommended whenever possible.257,259 Additional information on
spontaneous pneumothorax can be found in ch. 220.

Emphysema
Emphysema is any lung condition marked by distention and eventual
rupture of alveoli with resultant loss of pulmonary elasticity and lung
function. In humans, emphysema most commonly is found in
conjunction with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and
often is a consequence of long-term exposure to cigarette smoke or
pollution. This form of emphysema is exceedingly rare in pet
animals. However, lobar emphysema has been reported in a number
of young dogs and very rarely in cats.260-262 Unlike emphysema of
adult humans, congenital lobar emphysema is a condition wherein a
lung lobe becomes overexpanded. The condition can be idiopathic or
may result from bronchial obstruction, defect, or compression. The
enlarged, emphysematous lobe causes compression of the more
normal lobes, and increased alveolar pressure in the affected lobe
results in progressive emphysema with development of blebs and/or
bullae. Radiographic findings usually include lobar hyperinflation
with pulmonary blood vessels extending to the lobe margin,
contralateral mediastinal shift, caudal displacement of the
diaphragm (unilateral or bilateral), thoracic cavity enlargement,
atelectasis of unaffected lobes, and possibly pneumothorax,

pneumomediastinum, and/or subcutaneous emphysema.260-262
While thoracic CT is now the preferred imaging modality,
comparison of inspiratory and expiratory thoracic radiographs can
be useful because the emphysematous lung will not deflate on
expiration. Typically, only a single lobe is affected, allowing for
successful surgical removal.

DEFINITIONS AND TERMINOLOGY
In veterinary medicine, as in humans, pulmonary hypertension (PH) is an increasingly recognized,
clinically important finding. It is a hemodynamic condition defined by abnormally increased pressure
within the pulmonary circulation. In humans, PH has been defined by a mean pulmonary arterial
pressure (PAP) ≥25 mm Hg at rest as measured by right heart catheterization (RHC).1 More recently, an
evidence-based cutoff of a mean PAP >20 mm Hg has been offered.2 Documenting an elevated PAP does
not define an underlying disease or pathologic process; doing so requires further characterization. There
are several hemodynamic causes of PH and the clinical management of each differs considerably from
the others. Causes of PH include: 1) increased pulmonary blood flow/increased cardiac output, 2)
increased pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), 3) increased pulmonary venous pressure, or 4) some
combination thereof (Table 218.1). PH secondary to increased PVR without increased pulmonary
venous pressure is called precapillary PH. PH secondary to increased pulmonary venous pressure is
called postcapillary PH. Postcapillary PH most commonly results from left heart disease that causes left
atrial (LA) hypertension. Chronic postcapillary PH associated with severe left heart disease can cause
pulmonary artery (PA) vasoconstriction, remodeling, and pulmonary vascular disease, thereby
increasing PVR. Thus, postcapillary PH can occur alone, i.e., isolated postcapillary PH (IpcPH), or can
be associated with increased PVR, i.e., combined postcapillary and precapillary PH (CpcPH).
Hemodynamic characterization and the definitive diagnosis of PH are performed by RHC, which
includes measurement of PAP (systolic, diastolic, and mean), PA wedge pressure (a surrogate for
pulmonary venous pressure and LA pressure), and assessment of cardiac output. PVR is calculated as:

(mean PAP – PA wedge pressure) / cardiac output. Although such measurements provide a diagnostic
gold standard, they are not practical for veterinary outpatients.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
The mechanism of PH depends on the underlying cause but some common themes exist.3–5 Sustained
increases in mean PAP are either initially caused by, or eventually result in, increased PVR secondary to
PA vasoconstriction and adverse remodeling of the pulmonary vasculature (also called pulmonary
vascular disease). The latter, also known as pulmonary vascular disease, can result from left-to-right
shunting lesions that reverse (Eisenmenger physiology) or chronic postcapillary PH secondary to severe
left heart disease (CpcPH). Vasoconstriction can result from endothelial cell dysfunction (impaired
endothelial-dependent vasodilation), hypoxia, or both. Endothelial cell dysfunction also causes reduced
anticoagulant properties and promotes thrombosis.4 Adverse vascular remodeling includes obstructive
lesions characterized by accumulation of vascular cells in the PA wall (smooth muscle cells, endothelial
cells, fibroblasts, etc.), exaggerated perivascular inflammation, and loss/destruction of precapillary
arteries. Postcapillary pulmonary venous vasculature also undergoes adverse remodeling to variable
degrees.4 This is particularly apparent in PH secondary to left heart disease.5
Increased PAP contributes to increased right ventricular (RV) afterload, which triggers RV
hypertrophy. Compensatory hypertrophy initially enables the RV to adapt or become “coupled” to the
PA load. Stroke volume, RV systolic function, and filling pressures remain normal (adapted). However,
the RV is not well-suited to sustained and progressive pressure overloads. Progressive RV hypertrophy,
reduced stroke volume, systolic dysfunction, and elevated RV filling pressure follow. The RV becomes
“maladapted” and “uncoupled” to the increased vascular load.6 Clinically, these manifest as exercise
intolerance, exertional syncope (ch. 40), breathing difficulty (ch. 37), or signs of increased systemic
venous pressure and congestive heart failure (CHF; ch. 229).

CLINICAL AND ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIC ASSESSMENT
ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIC SIGNS OF PH AND ESTIMATES OF PULMONARY
ARTERIAL PRESSURE
RHC is rarely performed in veterinary medicine. Veterinarians are heavily reliant on echocardiography
and other supportive clinical findings to make a presumptive diagnosis of PH. Echocardiography should
be viewed as a clinical tool to help determine the probability a patient has PH, not a definitive diagnostic
test for the presence and severity of PH. Echocardiography is also heavily involved in the presumptive
hemodynamic characterization, clinical classification, and management of PH. Recommendations for
the echocardiographic assessment of PH in dogs have been published by an American College of
Veterinary Internal Medicine (ACVIM) consensus panel.7 These were influenced by available human
echocardiographic guidelines8-10 and considered the limitations of Doppler echocardiography, notably
the potential for inaccuracy11,12 and imprecision13,14 to estimate PAP in individual dogs.

Combinations of the mechanisms of PH are possible.
The echocardiographic probability assessment of PH includes the conventional method of using
Doppler echocardiography to estimate systolic PAP noninvasively by interrogating tricuspid
regurgitation velocity (TRV) and importantly, it also advocates for evaluating for numerous
∗

echocardiographic signs of PH (Fig. 218.1;

Video 218.1). The latter involves observing structural or

functional changes that commonly result from PH at 3 important anatomic sites: 1) the ventricles, 2) the
PA, and 3) the right atrium/caudal vena cava. Once an RV outflow tract obstruction is excluded,
quantitating peak TRV using continuous wave Doppler permits an estimate of systolic PAP (Note: mean
PAP can be estimated from peak early pulmonary regurgitation jet velocity, if present). This assumes
tricuspid regurgitation is present, which is common even in healthy dogs. Peak TRV is frequently
converted to a pressure gradient using the simplified Bernoulli equation (pressure gradient [mm Hg] = 4
× velocity [m/s]2) and often categorized as follows: mild PH, 30-50 mm Hg; moderate PH, 50-75 mm
Hg; and severe PH, >75 mm Hg (ch. 97). Although there is some potential value of these categories,
they are empirical and potentially misleading. Several factors influence TRV aside from PAP and PVR,
such as RV systolic function. Assessment of the severity of PH is ideally based on a multifactorial
approach that includes a combination of TRV, the degree and number of echocardiographic signs of PH,
and clinical signs (Fig. 218.2). Clinically significant PH is unlikely unless the patient has clinical signs
and an intermediate or high probability of PH is apparent.7 Methods describing the Doppler
examination and assessment of cardiac size and function are described in ch. 97.

CLINICAL CLASSIFICATION
Once an animal is deemed to have sufficient evidence of PH, determining the underlying disease causing
the PH can help the clinician optimize clinical management. Diseases causing PH are classified into 6
groups: PH secondary to 1) pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), 2) left heart disease, 3) respiratory
disease/hypoxia, 4) pulmonary thrombotic or thromboembolic disease (PT/PTE), 5) parasitic disease
(heartworm or Angiostrongylus), and 6) multifactorial or unclear mechanisms (Figure 218.2, Table
218.2).7 Diseases are intended to be grouped according to shared features of clinical presentation,
hemodynamic characterization, pathophysiologic mechanism, and treatment strategies. Detailed
algorithms to aid diagnostic evaluations for dogs with an intermediate or high probability of PH are
presented in the ACVIM guidelines.7 Often, definitively determining the cause of PH, particularly if not
readily apparent on echocardiography, is challenging. Proving causation (vs. association) also can be
difficult. Invasive and impractical diagnostics might be required for a definitive diagnosis (e.g., lung
biopsy) of some diseases, and the benefit of having a definitive diagnosis must always be weighed
against the risks of obtaining it. An echocardiographic examination performed by a skilled and
knowledgeable operator and as thorough of a diagnostic evaluation as possible tailored to the clinical
context and client’s resources should be considered standard of care.

USING ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY FOR HEMODYNAMIC
CHARACTERIZATION AND CLINICAL CLASSIFICATION OF
PH
In veterinary medicine, echocardiography is also relied upon to provide a presumptive hemodynamic
characterization of PH. The presence or absence of unequivocal echocardiographic LA enlargement
represents an important finding. Enlargement of the LA serves as a crude but reliable surrogate for
chronic LA and pulmonary venous hypertension. Thus, in a patient with PH, unequivocal LA

enlargement is highly suggestive of postcapillary PH and lack of LA enlargement is highly suggestive of
precapillary PH. In other words, lack of LA enlargement essentially rules out postcapillary PH and rules
in precapillary PH regardless of left heart disease status. One rare exception would be an animal with
acute postcapillary PH, e.g., rupture of a chorda tendinea in a dog with myxomatous mitral valve disease
(MMVD) without LA enlargement. Determining if a patient has IpcPH versus CpcPH is challenging
without RHC (a common conundrum in dogs with MMVD). Both should have sufficient evidence of
postcapillary PH, e.g., at least an intermediate probability of PH based on unequivocal LA enlargement.
However, dogs with CpcPH likely have higher TRV (higher estimated systolic PAP) and more severe
right heart remodeling (2D echo signs of PH) due to the increased PVR and heightened RV afterload.
Echocardiography also aids the clinical classification of PH. It represents the clinical gold standard to
diagnose cardiac shunts (Group 1d1) and all left heart diseases (Group 2). It can also identify a
pulmonary thrombus (Group 4), a compressive/obstructive mass/lesion (Group 6), or intravascular
parasite(s) (Group 5) near the pulmonary trunk or proximal branch PAs.

CLINICAL FINDINGS
Clinical findings associated with PH largely reflect the underlying disease causing the PH. There are no
clinical signs specific to PH and the absence of clinical signs does not rule out PH. Syncope (ch. 40),
particularly following exertion or activity, breathing abnormalities (ch. 37), cough (ch. 34), abdominal
distension (ch. 21; right-sided CHF), and exercise intolerance are among the most common clinical
signs reported in dogs diagnosed with PH.15–18 Physical examination (ch. 3) might reveal abnormal
respiratory sounds, tachypnea, dyspnea, cyanotic or pale mucous membranes, or jugular venous
distension or pulsation (Videos 229.1, 237.3

). A prominent or split second heart sound might be

apparent on cardiac auscultation (ch. 38). A systolic murmur over the mitral region due to MMVD,
tricuspid region, or both are common. Loud right apical systolic murmurs have been shown to be highly
suggestive of PH in dogs with MMVD.19

In general, assessment for PH should be considered when the aforementioned findings are
encountered and physical examination, bloodwork, and thoracic imaging fail to provide a likely
explanation. Another consideration might be a dog with respiratory disease or MMVD that has
refractory clinical signs. Both have a high prevalence of clinically significant PH.20-22 A relatively
common clinical scenario where assessment for PH is warranted is a dog that has experienced syncope
(ch. 40) that is not associated with a brady- or tachyarrhythmia, severe heart disease/failure, or severe
hematologic derangements. Unexplained abdominal effusion (high-protein/“modified” transudate; ch.
71) coupled with a dilated caudal vena cava should also warrant an echocardiographic examination to
assess the probability of PH. Right-sided CHF secondary to PH is a likely explanation in this scenario,
particularly in older, smaller dogs.

MANAGEMENT
Clinical management of PH should involve treatment of the underlying disease, if possible. It might also
involve PH-specific treatment, i.e., therapy specifically intended to decrease PVR or limit pulmonary
vascular disease. These treatments target one of 3 pathways: 1) prostacyclin, 2) endothelin, and 3) nitric

oxide.23 PH-specific treatment is not indicated for all causes of PH. In veterinary medicine, the use of
PH-specific therapy is largely confined to phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (PDE5i’s). Treatment is based
on the presumed hemodynamic characterization via echocardiographic findings and whether
precapillary PH is considered a significant component driving the increased PAP; the presence of clinical
signs; and clinical classification (Table 218.2). Numerous clinical scenarios and treatment
recommendations on when and when not to use PH-specific therapy are presented elsewhere.7 Oxygen
supplementation in animals with acute, severe dyspnea; heartworm prevention; exercise restriction; and
avoiding air travel and high altitudes are sensible general recommendations. In humans, beneficial
effects of PH-specific therapies have mostly been demonstrated for Group 1 PH (PAH), whereas clinical
trials for Group 2 (PH secondary to left heart disease) and Group 3 (chronic lung disease/hypoxia) have
failed to demonstrate a clear benefit.24-26

PH-specific therapy is rarely indicated in the absence of clinical signs.

Administration of PDE5i warrants particular caution. See text.
The PDE5i’s target the nitric oxide pathway and inhibit degradation of cyclic guanosine
monophosphate (cGMP). Subsequent accumulation of cGMP promotes relaxation of vascular smooth
muscle cells via nitric oxide and limits PA smooth muscle proliferation.23 The PDE5i’s are generally
effective at decreasing PVR and might help delay adverse remodeling of the PAs. These drugs are also
thought to increase myocardial cGMP and might enhance myocardial function and limit hypertrophy.27
Sildenafil (1-4 mg/kg PO q8h) is a highly selective PDE5i and typically represents first-line therapy
when a PA vasodilator is indicated. Studies in dogs have suggested a clinical benefit.16,28-32 A PDE5A
gene polymorphism has been identified in dogs33 and might limit effectiveness of sildenafil in some

dogs with PH.28 Sildenafil should be administered every 8 hours given its short half-life.34 Tadalafil (2
mg/kg PO q24h) represents a convenient alternative given its longer half-life. A randomized doubleblinded pilot study comparing sildenafil and tadalafil in dogs with PH, showed tadalafil was non-inferior
to sildenafil.32
Additional PH-specific treatment strategies are common in humans (prostacyclin analogs, endothelin
antagonists) but are impractical for veterinary patients. Alternative largely anecdotal therapies in dogs
include calcium channel blockers to augment PA vasodilation, phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitors
(pimobendan, milrinone) for RV inotropic support and potential PA vasodilatory activity, tyrosine
kinase inhibitors (toceranib, imatinib) to limit growth factor-mediated PA vasoconstriction, or Larginine, an amino acid nitric oxide precursor. Some also consider antithrombotic therapy given it
seems to be a common pathophysiologic theme of most causes of PH, not just for Group 4. All of these
strategies represent unproven, adjunct therapies considered on a case-by-case basis, and potentially for
refractory PH.
Empirical use of PDE5i therapy without an echocardiographic examination is discouraged. Also, these
drugs should be avoided or used with particular caution in cases where increased PVR is not considered
the dominant or only cause of PH. This includes patients with postcapillary PH (Group 2 PH) and cases
with left-to-right or low-velocity/bidirectional cardiac shunting lesions (Group 1d1 PH; congenital
cardiac shunts are a subgroup of Group 1 PH). Use of PDE5i’s has no known justification in patients with
IpcPH or with high-velocity left-to-right cardiac shunting defects, where significantly increased PVR is
very unlikely. Further, in patients with CpcPH or low-velocity/bidirectional cardiac shunts, PDE5i’s
might acutely increase RV cardiac output (via PA vasodilation) and enhance venous return to the LA.
This could increase LA, pulmonary venous, and pulmonary capillary pressure culminating in pulmonary
edema and acute clinical decompensation. Predicting vascular responsiveness to a PDE5i in this
situation is difficult or impossible. Thus, if a PDE5i is used (typically only in cases with refractory clinical
signs; see ACVIM guidelines7) conservative dosages should be considered (e.g., sildenafil 0.5 mg/kg PO
q8h) and close monitoring of breathing rate and effort is recommended.

PROGNOSIS AND MONITORING
The prognosis for patients with PH is variable and strongly linked to the cause and severity of the
underlying disease(s) causing the PH. It might be reversible in some cases but is likely to worsen
survival in most cases. PH worsens the prognosis of dogs with MMVD21 and respiratory
disease/hypoxemia.20,31 In a population of dogs with acquired and irreversible PH that excluded
heartworm disease and cardiac shunts, echocardiographic right atrial area and RV systolic dysfunction
(quantitated with tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion), and right-sided CHF were independently
associated with a worse outcome.18
Monitoring response to PH-specific therapy should be tailored to the individual patient. Clinical
response to therapy is most important and typically involves reassessment of adverse clinical findings,
notably improved exercise capacity and perceived quality of life.29 The utility of performing repeat
echocardiographic examinations for all cases of PH is unknown. Improvement in echocardiographic
variables (e.g., TRV and estimated PAP) is not always documented following administration of PDE5i.29
However, lack of improvement in echocardiographic variables should not necessarily prompt
adjustments of PH-specific therapy (e.g., dosage escalation) provided the clinical response is otherwise
positive.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Pulmonary Hypertension
Pulmonary hypertension is a condition in which blood pressure is elevated in the lungs. It can lead to
reduced exercise capacity, breathing abnormalities, fainting/collapse following exercise/activity, heart
dysfunction, and even heart failure (usually manifest as fluid accumulation in the abdomen). Pulmonary
hypertension is challenging to definitively diagnose in dogs and cats. It primarily relies on ultrasound of
the heart to help make a presumptive diagnosis. Pulmonary hypertension is not a disease in and of itself.
It can occur secondary to a broad array of medical conditions. It is particularly common in animals

affected with chronic lung disease and heart disease and complicates clinical management. Treatment of
pulmonary hypertension includes determining and treating the underlying disease/cause, if possible. It
might also involve a medication that is intended to dilate blood vessels in the lungs (sildenafil or
tadalafil). Unless the underlying cause of pulmonary hypertension can be determined and corrected, it is
likely to worsen the patient’s prognosis.
Lance C. Visser (Fort Collins, Colorado)

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE) is a collective term for
obstruction of the pulmonary arterial system by either a locally

formed thrombus (primary pulmonary thrombus) or a thrombus
formed elsewhere in the vascular system that translocates to the
pulmonary arterial system (pulmonary embolism). When the
pulmonary vasculature is occluded, neurogenic flexes, humoral
factors, and alveolar hypoxia induce reflex vasoconstriction that
increases pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR).1-3 Subsequently,
pulmonary arterial hypertension and increased right ventricular
(RV) afterload develop. As the embolic burden increases, RV
afterload also increases, inducing RV dilation and hypokinesis.4
With continued progression, the interventricular septum shifts
toward the left, which impairs left ventricular (LV) filling and
diastolic distensibility, a phenomenon known as ventricular
interdependence. Cardiac output (CO) is subsequently compromised,
leading to forward heart failure. With progressive pulmonary arterial
hypertension, backward (congestive) heart failure subsequently
develops.

PREDISPOSING FACTORS
A myriad of diseases and conditions can predispose cats and dogs to
PTE, including trauma (ch. 119), dirofilariasis (ch. 237), indwelling
intravenous catheters (ch. 75), surgery, neoplasia (ch. 331),
immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (ch. 174), protein-losing
nephropathy (ch. 302), protein-losing enteropathy (ch. 262),
hyperadrenocorticism (ch. 293), and sepsis (ch. 128).5-17 Studies
indicate the majority of dogs and nearly half of cats with PTE have
more than one predisposing condition.5,6,10 We do not know the true
incidence of PTE in cats and dogs.

CLINICAL PRESENTATION
Clinical signs depend on the magnitude of PTE and a patient’s
pulmonary physiologic reserve. Signs of acute PTE are nonspecific
and include visible anxiety, tachycardia, tachypnea, and dyspnea.
Other signs may include coughing, cyanosis, hemoptysis, and dull
mentation; sudden death is possible. Auscultation in eupneic

patients may be unremarkable. In those with dyspnea, increased
bronchovesicular sounds or muffled cardiopulmonary sounds are
common (ch. 212). Reduced capillary refill time, mucous membrane
pallor, hypotension, and hypokinetic peripheral pulses may be
appreciated when left-sided heart failure is present (ch. 229).
Jugular venous distension (Videos 229.1, 237.3) and ascites (
Videos 21.1, 21.2) may be present in patients with right-sided heart
failure. Other clinical signs relate to underlying disorders that led to
PTE.

DIAGNOSIS
Diagnosing PTE is challenging (Figure 219.1). A combination of
clinical signs and physical examination findings in patients with
predisposing factors may raise the suspicion of PTE. A prediction
model in dogs has been developed but not yet validated.18 In
veterinary medicine, many patients are treated for PTE based on
compatible patient history and clinical signs instead of documenting
the presence of a clot in the pulmonary vasculature.
Initial testing often includes arterial blood gas analysis, thoracic
radiography, point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS, ch. 73), and
echocardiography (ch. 97). Arterial blood gas analyses in PTE
patients generally show hypoxemia, hypocapnia, and increased
alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen tension gradients (ch. 212). Arterial
blood gas analysis results may raise suspicion for PTE, but
abnormalities are non-specific. Most cats and dogs with PTE have
abnormal thoracic radiographs.10 Documented radiographic changes
include focal or diffuse interstitial and/or alveolar infiltrates;
regional oligemia, uneven vessel diameter, lobar artery or vein
attenuation, pleural effusion, and right-sided cardiomegaly have also
been described.19 Some patients with PTE have normal thoracic
radiographs.
Veterinary lung POCUS protocols have been published to visualize
pulmonary parenchymal consolidation (ch. 73).20 The shred sign is
a static sonographic sign of lung consolidation. Consolidated lung
tissue appears as a subpleural hypoechoic region with an irregular

(shredded) deep border (fractal line) abutting normally aerated lung.
The wedge sign, a subset of the shred sign, in the perihilar and
caudodorsal regions is supportive of but not diagnostic for PTE.20
With the exception of direct thrombus visualization (Figure 239.7,
Video 219.1

), echocardiographic findings are not specific for

PTE, thus limiting the utility of this imaging modality. Veterinary
echocardiographic studies are justified to rule out other disease
processes like cardiomyopathy, endocarditis, and pericardial
tamponade.
A minimum database of a complete blood count (CBC), serum
biochemical profile, and urinalysis is recommended to screen for
abnormalities that aid in the identification of conditions that
predispose patients to the development of PTE.21 Traditional
coagulation profiles have minimal diagnostic utility due to lack
sensitivity or specificity for PTE and are of questionable diagnostic
utility.5,22 An antithrombin concentration <60% was associated with
a moderate risk of thrombosis while a level <30% was associated
with an immediate risk in 1 study in dogs.23 Thromboelastography
and rotational thromboelastometry (ch. 170) may be used as an
overall assessment of hypercoagulability, but results lack specificity
for PTE. The utility of D-dimers for the diagnosis of thrombosis in
cats and dogs has been investigated (ch. 171).18,24-26 Elevated Ddimer concentrations are not specific for PTE, as increased levels
may be associated with other disease processes. In contrast, normal
D-dimers have a high negative predictive value, making a diagnosis
of PTE unlikely. Myocardial injury induced by PTE may increase
cardiac troponin I (cTnI) levels, but elevations are not specific given
the numerous other conditions associated with cTnI elevations.27,28

FIGURE 219.1 Diagnostic algorithm for
pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE) in cats and
dogs. A-a, Alveolar-arteriolar; CTPA, computed
tomography pulmonary angiography; IMHA,
immune-mediated hemolytic anemia; IV,
intravenous; PLN, protein-losing nephropathy;
POCUS, point-of-care ultrasonography.
Advanced diagnostic imaging is indicated for patients with a
compatible patient history and clinical signs, predisposing factors,
and elevated D-dimer concentrations. Computed tomography
pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the current diagnostic standard.
PTE is identified as partial or complete intraluminal filling defects or
abrupt cut-off of the pulmonary arteries after contrast injection.
Detailed interpretation of CTPA images is demanding because of
resolution limits for detecting smaller clots. Dual-energy computed

tomography and computer assisted diagnosis techniques allow for
improved detection of small pulmonary emboli.

TREATMENT
Therapies for patients with PTE have three goals: thrombolysis,
prophylaxis, and stabilizing measures to enhance pulmonary
function.

THROMBOLYSIS
The goals of thrombolysis are to augment RV function, improve
hemodynamics, ameliorate neurohormonal activation, and reduce
likelihood of recurrence. Thrombolytic drugs accelerate clot
fibrinolysis via administration of plasminogen activators. Tissue
plasminogen activator (tPA) may be administered systemically or via
catheter-directed techniques. Alteplase has been used successfully in
an experimental model of canine PTE.29 The dosing protocol in dogs
is to administer a 0.2 mg/kg IV bolus followed by 0.7 mg/kg IV over
30 minutes, and subsequently 0.5 mg/kg IV over 60 minutes (total
dose: 1.4 mg/kg over 90 minutes). For cats, the dosing protocol is to
administer a 0.75 mg total IV bolus followed by 2.5 mg total IV over
30 minutes, and subsequently 1.75 mg total over 60 minutes (total
dose: 5 mg over 90 minutes). Given the risk of hemorrhage,
ischemia/reperfusion injury and cost, tPA is not commonly used
although use is justifiable in those with hemodynamically unstable
PTE that can be monitored exquisitely.

PROPHYLAXIS
Future recurrence of PTE can best be prevented by eliminating the
inciting cause. Therefore, identification and control of predisposing
factors should occur to the fullest feasible extent. Regarding
thromboprophylaxis, anticoagulants and antiplatelet medications
prevent progression of an existing thrombus and reduce recurrence
(Table 219.1). The American College of Veterinary Emergency and
Critical Care Consensus on the Rational Use of Antithrombotics in
Veterinary Critical Care guidelines suggest anticoagulants may be
more effective for venous thromboembolism while antiplatelet drugs
may be more effective for prevention of arterial thromboembolism.30
However, there is evidence of efficacy of both antithrombotic classes
in the treatment of both venous and arterial thromboembolic
conditions.31
The most commonly used anticoagulants are unfractionated
heparin (UFH) and low molecular weight heparins (LMWHs; e.g.,
dalteparin, enoxaparin). Recent consensus guidelines on the use of
antithrombotics in veterinary medicine recommend the use of
LMWHs over UFH.30 Patients receiving UFH are typically serially
monitored using activated partial thromboblastin time (aPTT) or
anti-factor Xa levels, while those receiving LMWHs are chiefly
monitored using the latter. Common therapeutic goals are an aPTT
that is prolonged to 1.5-2.5 times baseline and an anti-factor Xa
target of 0.35-0.7 U/mL.
Clopidogrel and aspirin are common antiplatelet agents (ch.
238).32 The former has been shown to be superior to the latter for
prevention of feline arterial thromboembolism.33 Rivaroxaban, a

direct factor Xa antagonist, has been used for successfully treating
both systemic and pulmonary thrombosis in dogs.34 In veterinary
medicine, prescription of LMWHs and direct factor Xa antagonists
may not be feasible due to financial limitations of pet owners.
Commonly used drugs and associated dosages are summarized in
Table 219.1.

STABILIZING MEASURES
Dyspneic and hypoxemic patients should be provided supplemental
oxygen via the least stressful method (ch. 123). Intubation and
positive pressure ventilation may be indicated in those that fail to
respond adequately to oxygen supplementation. If mechanical
ventilation is needed, low tidal volume strategies should be used in
order to minimize reduction in PVR from ventilation-induced
increase in intrathoracic pressure. Similarly, positive end expiratory
pressure should be limited to prevent exacerbation of RV
dysfunction. Intravenous fluid therapy should be used cautiously and
guided by RV filling assessed via echocardiography.35 Hypotension
may be improved with norepinephrine (0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min IV
constant rate infusion [CRI]) through enhancement of preload and
afterload.36
Increased PVR is secondary to pulmonary vasoconstriction
induced by vasoactive mediators like serotonin and thromboxane, so
induction of pulmonary vasodilation is a rational intervention to
reduce PVR and improve hemodynamics. Nitric oxide (NO) has been
shown to decrease mean pulmonary arterial pressure and PVR, as
well as attenuate decrease in CO in an experimental model of canine
PTE.37 However, use of NO may be cost-prohibitive. Experimental
canine PTE studies showed sildenafil-induced pulmonary arterial
vasodilation to attenuate pulmonary hypertension.38 Thus,
administration of sildenafil (0.5-1 mg/kg PO q8h; may increase up to
3 mg/kg PO q8h based on clinical signs) may be appropriate for PTE
patients with documented pulmonary hypertension. Aminophylline
(3-11 mg/kg IV or IM q6-12h) reduced PVR in an experimental

canine model of pulmonary hypertension and may be a consideration
for PTE patients with pulmonary hypertension.39

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis for PTE in cats and dogs is largely unknown. One
canine study of naturally occurring PTE documented a 14% hospital
discharge rate.40 Similar studies have not yet been completed in cats.
The prognosis for PTE is suspected to vary depending on underlying
cause, as well as thrombus size and location, with massive,
hemodynamically unstable PTE patients likely having a very poor
prognosis.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Pulmonary Thromboembolism
A thrombus is a blood clot. Blood clots may form in one part of the
body and subsequently travel through blood vessels to another body
part where they can become trapped; such movement is called
embolization. The lungs are part of the pulmonary system. A blood
clot that forms outside of the lungs and then becomes trapped in
their blood supply is called a pulmonary thromboembolism. A
pulmonary thromboembolism is a true emergency and may rapidly
cause death due to disruption of blood flow through the lungs.
Altered lung blood flow rapidly causes heart dysfunction and
negatively impacts oxygen delivery to organs of the body.
A classic clinical sign of pulmonary thromboembolism in cats and
dogs is sudden onset of difficulty breathing. Affected pets often
breathe rapidly and cough, occasionally coughing up blood. Their
gums may appear blue/grey/purple (called cyanosis), and weakness,
exercise intolerance, and fainting/collapse are common. Sudden
death is possible.
A pet having trouble breathing should be evaluated by a
veterinarian as quickly as possible. The veterinary team will work
quickly to try to stabilize your pet’s breathing and will recommend
tests and treatments to figure out what caused the pulmonary
thromboembolism and to make your pet feel better, respectively.
Several factors predispose a pet to developing a pulmonary
thromboembolism, including an intravenous catheter, surgery,
inflammatory conditions (e.g., pancreatitis), cancers, infections,
immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA), and protein-losing
nephropathy (PLN).

Tests that may be recommended are:
• Arterial blood gas – a minimally invasive, necessary blood test
to determine the degree to which oxygen delivery to organs
has been compromised.
• Chest radiography (x-rays) – a non-invasive imaging test that
allows a veterinarian to look for other causes that could be
causing a pet’s breathing difficulty.
• Heart and lung ultrasonography – a non-invasive bedside
imaging test that may identify changes in the lungs consistent
with pulmonary thromboembolism and helps rule out other
diseases that could be causing a pet’s clinical signs;
occasionally, a blood clot can be directly seen in the major
artery going to the lungs.
• D-dimers – a test that involves a routine blood sample to
evaluate a specific product of the blood clotting process.
• Computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) – a
special type of CT scan (CAT scan) that is performed under
sedation to visualize a pulmonary thromboembolism in the
blood vessels of the lungs.
Many patients are treated for pulmonary thromboembolism based
on compatible patient history and clinical signs instead of
documenting the presence of a clot in the pulmonary vasculature.
Therapies that may benefit pets with pulmonary thromboembolism
are supplemental oxygen, thrombolytics (drugs that break-up
existing clots), and antithrombotics (medications to prevent a clot
from growing bigger and to reduce the formation of new clot).
The prognosis for cats and dogs with pulmonary
thromboembolism is guarded to poor. Factors that influence
outcome are the underlying cause of the thromboembolism and
timeliness of veterinary intervention, as well as the size and location
of the blood clot.
Christopher G. Byers (Omaha, Nebraska)
