ANATOMY
The pleural space is defined as the area or potential space between
the lungs and the chest wall. Normally there is no free air present in
this space and only a very small amount (1-5 mL) of fluid, which is
undetectable on radiographs or ultrasound. The pleural cavity is
lined by the visceral and parietal pleura, which cover the lungs and
the thoracic wall, respectively. In small animals, the two
hemithoraces are incompletely separated, which results in pleural
effusions being generally equally divided between the right and left
side; this is in contrast to people and other larger animals, like
horses. Interestingly, bison also have an incomplete mediastinum;
this is thought to have contributed to the decimation of the species

by hunting, as a unilateral shot or arrow could result in tension
pneumothorax and death.1 Longstanding effusions may result in the
formation of fibrous adhesions, which may result in loss of
communication between the right and the left side of the thorax in
dogs and cats.

PHYSIOLOGY
Adequate lung function depends on adequate oxygenation and
ventilation, which in turn depends on lung mechanics and the ease of
lung expansion. The normal intrathoracic pressure is
subatmospheric, with an average pressure of –5 cm H2O (–3.7 mm
Hg). A negative intrathoracic pressure in conjunction with surfactant
acts to keep the lungs inflated, which reduces the work of breathing.
The first breath taken after birth is a momentous occasion as the
lung have previously been filled with fluid.2
Pleural space disease affects lung function by creating a restrictive
defect that decreases total lung capacity (TLC) and functional
residual capacity (FRC).3 In advanced cases, there will be increasing
ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Left untreated, severe pleural
effusion/pneumothorax will result in decreased cardiac output and
ultimately cardiac arrest.3 This phenomenon is more common with
pneumothorax, where tension pneumothorax may arise quickly, in
contrast to pleural effusions, which tend to develop more slowly
(Figure 220.1).
As pleural effusion or pneumothorax forms, there is gradual
collapse of the lung parenchyma, and also an increase in
intrathoracic pressure. In the presence of marked effusion or
pneumothorax, the intrapleural pressure is positive. While typically
it is assumed that removal of isolated pleural effusion will result in
immediate improvement in lung function, this is not always the case.
In people, two separate categories of non-recruitable lung associated
with pleural effusion are recognized.4 The first is termed lung
entrapment, which develops in association with active pleural
inflammation or neoplasia. Active formation of pleural effusion is
responsible for collapse of the lung parenchyma, and therefore,

thoracocentesis can be expected to be beneficial. The second is
termed trapped lung, wherein the lung is tightly constricted by
overlying visceral pleura and cannot adequately re-expand, even in
the presence of negative intrathoracic pressure.4 Trapped lung is a
result of immature fibrin and overlying inflammation leading to
thickening and constriction of the visceral pleural and thickening of
the parietal pleura over time. These changes mean that
thoracocentesis is less likely to resolve clinical signs. Trapped lung
has been evaluated much less in dogs and cats than it has in people,
but it can explain the development of thoracocentesis-associated
pneumothorax (see below). Lung entrapment likely is more common
in veterinary patients, as most effusions are associated with more
active inflammation,5 although an association is recognized between
chylothorax and fibrosing/constrictive pleuritis causing trapped lung
in cats with chylothorax.6,7 Varying degrees of lung entrapment,
trapped lung, or both, can be expected to exist in dogs and cats with
pleural effusion, depending on the nature, duration, and rate of
formation of the effusion.

FIGURE 220.1 A dorsoventral thoracic
radiograph of a dog that developed a tension
pneumothorax shortly after chemotherapy induction
for lymphoma. The dashed arrow highlights the
collapsed lung, while the solid arrow shows the
pneumothorax.
In contrast to removal of chronic pleural effusions in patients with
trapped lung, removal of air in pneumothorax results in rapid
improvement in ventilatory mechanics, provided there is no ongoing
air leak or concurrent pulmonary disease.

CLINICAL OVERVIEW
Clinical signs of pleural space disease include tachypnea, reluctance
to lie in lateral recumbency, or overt difficulty breathing with
classically rapid/shallow breathing considered the most common
manifestation (Video 220.1)

. Some animals have marked

abdominal effort. Physical examination findings may include
respiratory distress, use of accessory respiratory muscles, and
muffled heart/lung sounds. Paradoxic breathing (Video 37.3

) is

strongly associated with pleural effusion in dogs and cats.8,9
Occasionally, lung sounds may seem normal. It may be possible to
percuss a ventral hyporesonance (i.e., dullness due to pleural
effusion) or dorsal hyperresonance (due to pneumothorax). In cats,
moderate- to large-volume pleural effusion can increase the central
venous pressure (mean, 4.5 cm H2O; range, 0-7 cm H2O), so that
jugular distension may not always reflect a cardiac cause of
effusion.10 Other clinical findings of pleural space disease may reflect
the underlying disease process (e.g., gallop heart sound [ch. 38],
noncompressible cranial thorax with large cranial mediastinal
masses in cats [ch. 212], evidence of trauma).
Identification of pleural effusion should be considered an
important clinical finding, but not a final diagnosis. The etiologies of
pleural effusion are described below. Pneumothorax can be due to
traumatic, spontaneous or iatrogenic causes, with the prognosis
reflecting the underlying cause. Space-occupying lesions, such as
diaphragmatic hernia or neoplastic masses, may cause clinical signs
that are indistinguishable from those of pleural effusion. Overall, the
prognosis for a patient with pleural effusion is guarded, although
many cases respond well to therapy (e.g., thoracocentesis), at least in
the short term. The long-term prognosis depends on the inciting
cause and its response to treatment.

PLEURAL EFFUSION
DIAGNOSIS

A diagnosis of pleural effusion can be made through either
thoracocentesis or diagnostic imaging. Radiographs classically have
been the most commonly used imaging technique to identify pleural
effusion, but ultrasonography is widely used in emergency and
general practices (ch. 73). Computed tomography (CT) and
magnetic resonance imaging can demonstrate pleural effusions, but
are not practical to be used as the initial diagnostic imaging
modality.
Radiographic signs of pleural effusion include diffusely decreased
intrathoracic detail (“white out”), scalloping of the ventral (lateral
projection) and lateral (dorsoventral [DV] projection) lung borders,
fissure lines between lung lobes, and an obscured cardiac silhouette
(Figure 220.2). A DV radiograph is preferred for confirming the
presence of pleural effusion with minimal stress on the patient,
particularly in cats and in dogs with barrel-shaped thoracic
conformations. Chronic pleural effusions may result in the
radiographic appearance of “rounded” lung margins representing
pleural fibrosis and likely trapped lung (Figure 220.3).
Radiographic changes can be suggestive of etiology. For example, in 1
study of cats with pleural effusion, cardiomegaly was 86% sensitive
and 87% specific for congestive heart failure (CHF) as the cause of
pleural effusion.11 On ultrasonography, pleural effusion is recognized
as an anechoic area between the thoracic wall and the lung (
Video 73.11).

THORACOCENTESIS
Therapy of pleural effusion is directed at both improving respiratory
status by removing fluid/air and at identifying and treating the
underlying cause. Thoracocentesis is performed by clipping and
aseptically preparing an area between the 7th and 9th rib at
approximately the costochondral junction (Videos 220.2 and 220.3)
. The procedure is described in detail in ch. 92. Volumes of fluid
and air retrieved should be recorded; in general, 5-30 mL/kg are
required to improve ventilatory mechanics. However, a smaller
amount may be useful for diagnostic purposes (ch. 71). As much

effusion should be removed as is possible, keeping in mind that
trapped lung may reduce the volume that lung parenchyma is able to
re-expand. The presence of fibrin or loculated effusion may make
thoracocentesis more challenging by occluding the catheter or
needle. If thoracocentesis is unsuccessful, the presence of effusion
should be re-confirmed, ideally with ultrasound. If the fluid is
present, a longer needle may be required to reach the thoracic cavity
or a different location can be attempted.

FIGURE 220.2 Thoracic radiographs from a cat
with pleural effusion due to hypertrophic
cardiomyopathy (congestive heart failure), lateral
and dorsoventral projections. On both views, the
cranial thorax has a uniform soft-tissue/fluid opacity
without airway markings, consistent with pleural
effusion, and the caudal lung lobes are likewise
surrounded by a fluid opacity and rounded,
suggesting chronicity. Dorsal displacement of the
carina is consistent with cardiomegaly.

FIGURE 220.3 A thoracic radiograph from a cat
with chylous effusion. Note the rounded lung
borders, which would lead to concern about the
possibility of an iatrogenic pneumothorax associated
with thoracocentesis.
Complications of thoracocentesis are uncommon. The most
significant complication is iatrogenic pneumothorax, which may
occur from either damage to thickened/fibrotic visceral pleural and
lung parenchyma or from marked drops in pleural pressure, which
result in the formation of spontaneous tears in the lung/pleura and
subsequent creation of a pulmonary-pleural fistula due to trapped
lung.4 Small volume iatrogenic pneumothorax may resolve without
treatment, but large or ongoing leaks may require placement of a
thoracostomy tube or even surgery. Other potential complications
include hemorrhage if a great vessel or the heart is inadvertently
punctured or leakage of infected pleural effusion or neoplastic fluid
subcutaneously.

Pleural pressure determinations are often recommended in people
with pleural effusion, and may be performed easily in animals as
well.12 Pleural pressure may be monitored during thoracocentesis for
pleural effusion or pneumothorax or continuously if a thoracostomy
tube is in place. Additionally, pleural manometry can confirm that
the needle or catheter is still in the pleural space following repositioning, patient movement, or apparent completion of the
procedure, which is perhaps the most useful insight that may be
gained in animals.

Fluid Analysis (ch. 71)
Fluid analysis should be performed to help characterize the effusion.
The gross appearance of the fluid may be purulent, chylous (milky),
hemorrhagic, serous or serosanguineous, or icteric. Most effusions
are serous or serosanguineous. Pleural effusion associated with
pyothorax may be associated with a foul odor (anaerobic bacteria) as
well as appearing purulent (Figure 220.4). Fluid may be
characterized as a low-protein (formerly “pure”) transudate, highprotein (formerly “modified”) transudate, or exudate based on the
protein level and cell count (ch. 71). After assessing the gross
appearance, protein level, and cell counts, the cytological assessment
of the effusion is often very helpful in reaching a final diagnosis.
Cytological findings can include the presence of neoplastic cells
(carcinoma, lymphoma), small lymphocytes, neutrophils, bacteria or
fungi, red blood cells, macrophages and/or mesothelial cells.6 In
longstanding effusions, mesothelial cells may assume bizarre
cytological appearances, which may make distinction from neoplastic
cells difficult.13

FIGURE 220.4 Thoracocentesis from a cat with
pyothorax, confirming purulent material.
Biochemical assessment of pleural effusion is useful in some cases.
In human medicine, Light’s criteria are widely applied to pleural
effusion, and have been described in cats.14 Light’s criteria evaluate
the ratio of effusion protein to serum protein, as well as lactate
dehydrogenase (LDH) concentrations. Exudates have higher ratios
(>0.5) and higher concentrations of LDH.7 In people, biochemical
analysis of pleural effusion is more commonly pursued than in dogs
and cats. Biochemical properties of pleural effusion include glucose,

amylase, pH, creatinine, cholesterol, triglycerides and variety of
other substances.15,16 In people, pleural fluid amylase has been used
to confirm esophageal perforation, but dogs and cats do not produce
salivary amylase.10 Biochemical analysis of pleural effusion in dogs
and cats has been limited although recently there has been increased
interest.15,16 Glucose levels do not routinely identify sepsis as they do
in abdominal effusion. NT pro-BNP concentration in pleural effusion
is high in cats with CHF.18 High effusion triglyceride concentration
can be used for identifying an effusion as chylous. It may be that
further studies of biochemical properties of pleural effusion will add
useful information to individual case evaluation.

Identification of Organisms
Bacterial culture and sensitivity testing is warranted in cases with
suspected infection or with evidence of neutrophilic inflammation.
Recurrent thoracocentesis could predispose a patient to iatrogenic
infections. Bacterial culture is most frequently used for evaluating for
aerobic organisms, although pyothorax is often due to mixed
infections that include anaerobic organisms. Anaerobic bacterial
cultures may be hard to perform, and limited sensitivity data may be
gained. In some cases, in vitro culture may identify only a more
robust, easily cultured pathogen. More fastidious organisms may
require a special media and a dedicated microbiological laboratory.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing is also very useful for
identification of infectious organisms, and may be pursued,
especially for more atypical pleural space infections (e.g., Bartonella
[ch. 191]).19

FURTHER DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
Other diagnostic testing in patients with pleural effusion should be
guided by signalment, physical examination and results of fluid
analysis. Routine laboratory testing, including a complete blood
count, serum biochemistry profile and urinalysis are advised to look
for systemic disease. Thyroid testing in cats (ch. 287) and

heartworm testing of dogs and cats (ch. 237) in endemic areas are
also recommended.20,21
Thoracic radiographs after removal of the pleural effusion are
often useful to evaluate for mass lesions, diaphragmatic hernia, or an
enlarged cardiac silhouette. Echocardiography (ch. 97) is essential
to look for evidence of right-sided heart disease (dogs, cats), leftsided heart disease (cats), or pericardial effusion. Thoracic
ultrasound may be useful to evaluate and biopsy mass lesions and to
evaluate the integrity of the diaphragm (ch. 222). CT is also helpful
to investigate the underlying cause of the effusion. Exploratory
thoracotomy or thoracoscopy may be used for more completely
evaluating the chest and obtaining biopsies.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS OF
PLEURAL EFFUSIONS
In cats, pleural effusion is associated with heart disease (41%),
neoplasia (26%), pyothorax (15%), idiopathic chylothorax (6%),
trauma (4%), and feline infectious peritonitis (3%).22
Low-protein transudates (formerly called pure transudates) are
the type of pleural effusion most often noted in animals with chronic
protein-losing nephropathy (ch. 302) or enteropathy (ch. 262),
other causes of hypoalbuminemia, or overzealous parenteral fluid
administration. Macroscopically, the effusion looks similar to water
and microscopically it is relatively acellular. Yorkshire Terriers with
lymphangiectasia appear particularly likely to develop pleural
effusions.
High-protein transudates (formerly called modified transudates)
are the most common type of pleural effusion observed in dogs and
cats. Common causes include CHF (ch. 229), pericardial
disease/cardiac tamponade (ch. 235), lung lobe torsion (ch. 217),
and neoplasia (e.g., ch. 322).
Exudates can be caused by penetrating trauma, esophageal
rupture (ch. 259), ruptured abscess (ch. 217), or foreign body
(pyothorax), and feline infectious peritonitis (ch. 200).

SELECT PLEURAL EFFUSIONS
Pyothorax 23-26
Affected animals often have systemic signs of sepsis (e.g., lethargy,
fever [ch. 16], leukocytosis or leukopenia [ch. 58]). Cytologic
evaluation of infectious effusions may demonstrate degenerative
neutrophils, and possibly intra- and extracellular pathogens.
Infections may be aerobic or anaerobic. Anaerobic infections may be
particularly foul-smelling, although deliberate assessment of odor
should be avoided due to zoonotic risk. In cats, bite wounds were
long considered to be the most frequent source of infection, but
recent work has identified parapneumonic extension (aspiration of
organisms) from upper respiratory tract infection as more
common.27 In dogs, bite wounds and penetrating foreign bodies
(sticks/plant awns) are frequently responsible. Occasionally, pleural
effusions are identified secondarily to bacterial pneumonias (i.e.,
parapneumonic effusions), but these are rare in contrast to people
and horses. Other less common infectious causes of effusion include
Bartonella (ch. 191), Mycobacterium (ch. 188), Toxoplasma (ch.
197), and viral infections (ch. 205). PCR testing is particularly
useful in atypical infections.
Therapy for pyothorax involves drainage (usually via chest tube)
and antibiotics based on culture and sensitivity, with coverage for
presumed anaerobic pathogens even if anaerobic culture was not
performed (ch. 140). Some animals, particularly dogs, may require
surgical intervention for resection and drainage of affected
tissues.25,26 The prognosis for pyothorax is frequently good if the pet
does not present in a moribund condition and comprehensive
treatment can be provided. Pyothorax is one of the few effusions that
can be cured.

Hemothorax
Hemothorax can result from bleeding disorders such as
anticoagulant rodenticide intoxication (e.g., brodifacoum; ch. 138),
trauma, lung lobe torsion, or neoplasia.28 In hemothorax, the packed
cell volume of the effusion is >20%, or more than 50% of the

patient’s peripheral hematocrit. Clinical signs of hemothorax more
commonly reflect hypovolemia than the presence of pleural effusion.
In dogs with anemia and pleural effusion, it is prudent to check
coagulation status prior to thoracocentesis in order to exclude
coagulopathy although in recent years the frequency of anticoagulant
rodenticide intoxication has decreased. Therapy of hemothorax
depends on the underlying cause and may include blood transfusion
(type depends on presence of coagulopathy (plasma) and anemia
(packed red blood cells, whole blood)), vitamin K therapy, surgery or
rest (ch. 124). Autotransfusion may be considered except in cases of
malignancy. Rib tumors may result in hemothorax, with resection
required to control hemorrhage. Small-volume traumatic or
intoxication-induced hemothoraces that are not affecting ventilation
may be left alone to re-absorb.

Chylothorax
Cats (mean age 6.3 years; range, 0.5-14 years)29 and dogs (mean age
4 years; range, 1.5-12 years)22 can develop chylous pleural effusion,
termed chylothorax. The most frequent presenting concern is rapid
and/or labored breathing (78% of cats,29 79% of dogs30);
interestingly, 4/37 (11%) of cats in 1 series had cough as the only
historical finding.29 15/37 affected cats (41%) and 24/39 affected
dogs (62%) have been described as having muffled heart sounds on
auscultation of the ventral thorax.29,30 Both increased and decreased
bronchovesicular sounds have been reported, presumably depending
on the region of the thorax being ausculted.
No clinicopathologic finding is specific for chylothorax. A
hypoadrenocorticism-like profile (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia) has
been documented in dogs with chylothorax.31 Radiographic findings
have been described above (Figure 220.3), and rounding of lung
lobes to suggest chronic, fibrosing pleuritis is associated with
chylothorax in cats.6,7
Grossly, chylous effusion appears milky white or pinkish. It has a
high triglyceride content: mean in cats, 1464 mg/dL (16.5 mmol/L)
(range, 303-4670 mg/dL [3.4-52.87 mmol/L], versus mean 84
mg/dL (1.0 mmol/L) (range, 28-210 mg/dL [0.3-2.4 mmol/L]) in

serum29 and median in dogs, 877 mg/dL (9.9 mmol/L) (range, 1582750 mg/dL [1.8-31.1 mmol/L], versus median 73 mg/dL (0.8
mmol/L) (range, 35-544 mg/dL [0.4-6.2 mmol/L]) in serum.22 The
predominant cell type is small lymphocytes. These characteristics are
the basis for the diagnosis of chylothorax.
There are many potential causes of chylothorax, with idiopathic
disease accounting for about 50% of cases. The pathophysiologic
mechanism involves extravasation of chyle from the thoracic duct on
its course from the cisterna chyli in the abdomen to its insertion in
the cranial vena cava in the cranial thorax. Physical disruption of the
thoracic duct (spontaneous leakage or rupture, iatrogenic
laceration), high intraductal hydrostatic pressure (heartworm
disease, other disorders of the right heart, pericardial disease
including fibrosing/constrictive pericarditis induced by chylothorax
itself) or both, are implicated. Evaluation of a patient with chylous
effusion includes a careful search for an underlying cause, such as
cardiac disease, cranial vena cava thrombus or mass (ch. 239), lung
lobe torsion (ch. 217), heartworm disease (ch. 237), or neoplasia,
notably cranial mediastinal masses (ch. 322); these are implicated
in a minority of cases of chylothorax, but finding them offers the
possibility of addressing the inciting cause. Postoperative
chylothorax has been described.32 Idiopathic effusion is associated
with dilation of the lymphatics (lymphangiectasia), but the
mechanism of this remains elusive.
If a specific cause is found, therapy may be directed against that.
In idiopathic effusion, medical treatment (e.g., low fat diet, rutin,
octreotide) is seldom effective and surgical intervention is often
preferred. The various surgical techniques for palliating chylous
effusion have been reviewed.33,34 No therapy is universally
successful, and cure rates hover around 50-70%. Missed ducts
during thoracic duct ligation, and the existence of collaterals that
become patent after thoracic duct ligation are possible explanations
for persistence of chylothorax post-operatively.35 In a study of 15
cats with chylothorax, the median survival time after thoracic duct
ligation plus subphrenic pericardectomy was 774 days (range, 32844 days).36 In dogs, 50% of chylothorax patients that undergo
thoracoscopic thoracic duct ligation and pericardectomy are alive at

a median of 43 months post-operatively.22 The best surgical outcome
appears to be associated with a meticulous and experienced
surgeon.22 Without surgery, palliation can be provided with periodic
thoracocenteses, with the interval between centeses varying from one
to many weeks depending on rate of reaccumulation of effusion and
respiratory comfort.

Mesothelioma
Mesothelioma, a neoplasm arising directly from mesothelial cells,
affects the pleura (79%), pericardium (64%), and peritoneum (7%) in
dogs.37 It is rare in cats.38 The cause of mesothelioma is unknown;
exposure to asbestos has been significantly associated with
intrathoracic mesothelioma in dogs.39,40 Transformation over time
from idiopathic benign inflammation to mesothelioma has been
documented in dogs.41 Chronic body cavity effusions that
accumulate slowly (often, over periods of weeks to months initially)
are common.37,41
Macroscopically, affected pleura shows varying degrees of
thickening. Cytologic examination is rarely diagnostic, although a
block preparation technique involving immunohistochemistry has
been described.42 The diagnosis requires histologic analysis of a
pleural biopsy sample,43 typically obtained via thoracotomy or
thoracoscopy.
Treatment has been administered systemically and via
intracavitary (IC) infusion using an indwelling subcutaneous pleural
port.37 Reported protocols in dogs include 5-fluorouracil 150-200
mg/m2 IC q 2 weeks or weekly × 4 weeks then q 2 weeks until either
progressive disease occurs or effusion does not recur37 or
carboplatin 250-300 mg/m2 IV or IC q 3 weeks × 6 doses or until
disease progression occurs.37 In a feline case report of suspected
pleural mesothelioma, IC carboplatin (180 mg/m2) administered
twice, 6 weeks apart, reduced the frequency of thoracocentesis and
led to a survival of 4 months.44

The prognosis for dogs and cats with mesothelioma is guarded in
the short term, and poor long-term. In 1 study of 34 dogs with
mesothelioma, the median survival time was 195 days (95% CI 53324) and the 1-year survival rate was 22%.37

Idiopathic and Miscellaneous Effusions
In some dogs and cats, despite a concerted effort, no specific cause is
identified for the pleural effusion. Pancreatitis, immune-mediated
diseases, chronic diaphragmatic hernia, pulmonary
thromboembolism and recent abdominal or thoracic surgeries have
been associated with pleural effusion.45-47 If none of these is
present, analysis of effusion triglyceride concentration is indicated,
to identify effusions that are biochemically chylous without being
visibly opaque. If this is negative, treatment is directed at
ameliorating clinical signs, often through periodic thoracocentesis.
Implantation of pleural ports has been successful in some dogs.48,49
A search for atypical infections is warranted before therapy for
suspected immune-mediated disease with immunosuppressive
agents (ch. 144).

CHRONIC EFFUSIONS
Chronic pleural effusions may occur secondary to a wide variety of
diseases, but are most commonly seen with idiopathic effusions,
chylothorax, CHF, and mesothelioma. Survival times with chronic
effusions depends on the underlying disease, as well as the patient
and pet owner characteristics. Some dogs with chronic effusions may
be managed for months to years with intermittent thoracocentesis,
particularly if their quality of life is otherwise good, there is limited
formation of adhesions, and the owner has emotional and financial
resources for chronic disease management. Importantly, animals
with chronic effusions are much more likely to develop a
pneumothorax following thoracocentesis and may develop infected
fluid, even with aseptic technique.
Pneumothorax is also a common iatrogenic complication of
thoracocentesis in animals with chronic pleural effusion resulting in

thickening of the pleura and possibly trapped lung. This may be a
devastating complication as the pleura is unlikely to heal
spontaneously. Pleural ports may be placed to permit
thoracocentesis without the risk of inadvertent laceration of the
pleura.48 In larger dogs, the size (20 g) of the Huber needle may
result in long times required to drain the chest. Additionally,
iatrogenic infections may occur, particularly if drained by lay
individuals that have not been properly trained.

PNEUMOTHORAX
Pneumothorax is defined as free air in the pleural space.50 It can be
characterized as traumatic, spontaneous, or iatrogenic, as well as
open or closed. A tension pneumothorax is a pneumothorax severe
enough to affect cardiac output and if not promptly evacuated will
result in the death of the patient. A tension pneumothorax can result
from any type of pneumothorax, although it is almost always closed.

TRAUMATIC
Traumatic pneumothorax results from injury to the thorax; it is
divided into open where there is an open wound connecting the chest
cavity and the outside air (Video 220.4)

, and closed where air

leak is from damaged lung parenchyma. Trauma is thought to be the
most common cause of pneumothorax in small animals. Traumatic
wounds can be blunt (e.g., hit by car) or penetrating (e.g., bite
wounds). The type and extent of treatment of traumatic
pneumothorax is selected based on the severity of the clinical signs.
As animals with pneumothorax often also have pulmonary
contusions (ch. 217) or rib fractures (ch. 222), it is occasionally
hard to determine the contribution of pneumothorax to respiratory
distress. Confirmation of traumatic pneumothorax may be made
through diagnostic thoracocentesis, thoracic radiographs, or
ultrasonography. A negative diagnostic thoracocentesis may be truly
negative, or may reflect an inadequate length of needle/catheter or
pocketing of the air. Point of care ultrasound is popular as a

diagnostic test for pneumothorax (ch. 73). Loss of the “glide sign” (
Video 220.5) is a hallmark finding of pneumothorax, although
generally on ultrasound, accurate determination of pneumothorax is
more challenging than effusions.51 Treatment of traumatic
pneumothorax depends on the severity of the pneumothorax and the
mechanism of the development of pneumothorax (blunt versus
penetrating trauma). Most blunt traumatic pneumothoraces will heal
rapidly (1-4 days) with supportive care and rarely require surgery to
control air leak. Traumatized lung lobes will rapidly heal if the
underlying parenchyma and pleura are normal due to the high tissue
thromboplastin content of lung tissue. The prognosis for a blunt
traumatic pneumothorax is good with the majority of cases requiring
only a short hospital stay. It is important to evaluate the patient fully
for other wounds, as injuries such as vertebral fractures may be
present and these can impact decision-making as much as, or more
than, the pneumothorax.
Penetrating wounds often require surgery, as bite wounds may
bring fur and debris into the chest cavity. Specifically, in bite
wounds, the clinician should recall that the site of the skin puncture
wound may be far removed (several centimeters) from the site of
penetration into the thorax. Occasionally, dogs and cats with thoracic
trauma have a flail chest, which is defined as the presence of two or
more fractures in 3 or more adjacent ribs. A flail segment is
physiologically important because it moves paradoxically during
ventilation and is invariably associated with a severe underlying
pulmonary contusion. Historical references suggest that surgical
stabilization of the rib fractures is warranted, but more recent
evidence suggests that this is not necessary, and analgesia and time
are sufficient. If the thorax of a patient with flail chest is being
explored for treatment of other injuries anyway (e.g., bite wounds),
rib fractures can be surgically stabilized. Flail chest should be
distinguished from intercostal muscle tears (

Video 220.6); both

involve paradoxical inward movement of segments of thoracic wall
on inspiration, but with intercostal tears, rib fractures are absent.

SPONTANEOUS PNEUMOTHORAX IS A
PNEUMOTHORAX WITHOUT
ASSOCIATED TRAUMA52
Spontaneous pneumothorax is termed primary if there is no
underlying lung disease, and secondary if it is due to recognizable
lung disease. Spontaneous pneumothorax is more common in dogs,
where pneumothorax is due to the rupture of blebs or bulla, than it is
in cats. Northern dog breeds such as Huskies are overrepresented,
and more recently the overrepresentation of Golden Retrievers has
been reported.52 Clinical signs include restlessness, respiratory
distress, and tachypnea. It is important to distinguish if
pneumothorax is truly spontaneous or if it could be unobserved
traumatic pneumothorax, because the approach to management of
affected dogs is very different. Spontaneous pneumothorax in dogs is
considered a surgical disease, with prompt surgical intervention
associated with a higher cure rate and shorter duration of
hospitalization.53 In cats, it is less clear if surgery should be pursued
immediately because the incidence of spontaneous pneumothorax is
far lower in cats than it is in dogs.54 Surgical exploration is typically
via a median sternotomy, permitting exploration of both
hemithoraces. In some cases, despite an open surgical approach, it
has been difficult to identify the source of the air leak; higher
ventilation pressure (e.g., to 25 cm H2O) may help. Pre-operative
diagnostics should include 3-view thoracic radiographs, and baseline
laboratory testing. Other testing, such as echocardiography (ch. 97),
abdominal ultrasonography, heartworm (ch. 237) or lungworm (ch.
217) testing or CT (Figure 220.5), is at the discretion of the
attending clinician. The vast majority of dogs with spontaneous
pneumothorax managed surgically have a good outcome. It is not
clear that routine CT scanning is helpful for surgical planning or
identification of the lesion. In the author’s practice, CT is only
performed if there is an atypical signalment and is not required for
surgery.
Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax may also be seen in both
dogs and cats. It develops without trauma but rather is due to pre-

existing lung disease. It has been reported in dogs secondary to
neoplasia (ch. 217), pulmonary thromboembolism (ch. 219), and
rarely to pneumonia (ch. 217). In cats, the most likely cause is
thought to be asthma/airway disease (ch. 215) or heartworm disease
(ch. 237). Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax characterized by a
small volume of air may be treated conservatively (medically)
whereas large volumes or cases associated with a mass lesion should
be treated surgically. The prognosis for spontaneous pneumothorax
is good in dogs, unless it is associated with a tumor. In cats it is less
clear, but it appears the prognosis is reflective of the underlying
condition.36

FIGURE 220.5 A computed tomography image of
from a dog with a spontaneous pneumothorax. The
asterisk indicates free air in the pleural space.

Iatrogenic pneumothorax is a pneumothorax associated with
veterinary care. It may be created out of necessity, such as with a
thoracotomy, which will be self-limiting, but may also develop
following thoracocentesis of a pet with a chronic effusion or in
association with intermittent positive pressure ventilation. This is an
under-appreciated category, and the unfortunate truth is “if you tap
enough chests you will eventually cause a pneumothorax”!
Pneumothorax develops in these pets due to damage to the pleural
tissues covering the lung. In normal pets, the pleura is thin, and will
seal rapidly if punctured. However, if there is a thickened pleura due
to ongoing effusion (classically chylous), then there is a much greater
chance of damaging the pleura, which will not be self-sealing.
Chronic effusions can be either identified clinically from the medical
history, or suspected if the lungs appear rounded on radiographs
(Figure 220.3). The trapped lung is at particular risk for iatrogenic
pneumothorax.

ADDITIONAL TREATMENT
MODALITIES
Treatment options for pneumothorax are listed in Box 220.1.
Additional options are described below.

Autologous Blood Patch
A blood “patch” or pleurodesis refers to the instillation of autologous
naïve fresh whole blood into the pleural space in an attempt to stop
air leak from the pulmonary parenchyma. Debate exists as to the
mechanism by which this is successful; most likely coagulated blood
“plugs” the site of air leak rather than producing a true pleurodesis.
This concept is supported by the rapid resolution reported in many
studies, typically with minimal to no complications. The major
benefits are that it is painless, inexpensive, easy to perform, and that
the patient’s blood is readily available.55,56 An allogenic blood patch
technique also has been described.55
The most common complication of blood patching seen in people
is pyothorax. Iatrogenic tension pneumothorax due to blood clotting

in the thoracostomy tube is also possible. To limit these
complications, the blood must always be collected from the patient in
a sterile fashion, transferred immediately through the largest bore
thoracic catheter possible, and then the catheter must be flushed
with 10 mL sterile saline.

Thoracostomy Tubes
Thoracostomy tubes may be required for the management of pleural
space disease in cases with 1) large-volume effusion that is reforming quickly, 2) cases of infectious effusion, 3) large volume
pneumothorax or 4) postoperatively. The technique for placement
and maintenance is described in ch. 92. Red rubber catheters have
been used as chest tubes, but more commonly, either a trocar-style
catheter or small-bore catheter (e.g., MILA Internationala) is placed.
Continuous suction units may be applied to help with fluid and air
removal (Video 220.7

), but are uncommonly used in cases of

pleural effusion. With any thoracostomy tube, it is important to
recall that due to kinking or malpositioning, a large volume of
pleural effusion or pleural air may be present and if clinical signs
suggest distress, diagnostic imaging or thoracocentesis should be
considered even if no air or fluid can be aspirated from the tube. In
the author’s experience, this is particularly common after a
thoracotomy when the chest tube has been surprisingly
unproductive.
BOX 2 2 0.1 T h e rap e u t ic Op t io ns fo r Tre atme nt
o f Pne u motho rax
The recommendations for management of pneumothorax are based
on the cause, with simple supportive care being adequate in some
cases, while other cases benefit from more intensive medical or
surgical therapy. Options include:
a. Observation - This technique is appropriate for animals with
small-volume pneumothoraces detected radiographically,
which are due to a known underlying cause and when patients
are not showing clinical signs or evidence of progression.

Small volumes of air will be reabsorbed across the pleural
space over a period of a few days to a week. Animals with
pneumothorax should not be left unobserved if at all possible
for 24-36 hours, during which time ongoing clinical
improvement is expected.
b. Supplemental oxygen (ch. 123) - Oxygen therapy has been
proposed as a method to hasten the recovery of
pneumothorax. The rationale is that if the patient was
breathing room air at the time the pneumothorax developed,
the major component of the pneumothorax is nitrogen gas
(78%), and oxygen is only 21%. Thus, if supplemental oxygen
is provided, the relative partial pressure of nitrogen decreases
in the surrounding tissues, and this permits nitrogen to be
reabsorbed more quickly. However, while this is true in
principle, in clinical practice, if a pneumothorax is causing
clinical signs, it should be evacuated using any of the various
options available to the clinician.
c. Needle thoracocentesis (ch. 92) - This is a good first-line
approach for most cases of pneumothorax. Since the
mediastinum in most dogs and cats is not intact,
pneumothorax is unlikely to be confined to one side. Caveats
include making sure the needle is long enough to reach the
pleural space, and recognition that if there is a large volume of
air, needle thoracocentesis may need to give way to
thoracostomy tube placement. Classically, needle
thoracocentesis for removal of air is performed more dorsally
on the chest wall (standing animal) or the nondependent side
(laterally recumbent animal); however, in severe cases, air can
be retrieved from virtually any location on the chest surface.
d. Small bore chest tube (SBCT) - SBCTs have been introduced in
recent years as modifications of jugular catheters.a These
catheters (6.3 Fr [14 gauge]) are placed using a modified
Seldinger technique, and may easily be placed and secured in
an awake patient. They are proving particularly popular in
patients with moderately large volume pneumothoraces, and
appear more comfortable than standard large-bore chest
tubes or intermittent thoracocentesis. SBCTs are less effective

when continuous suction is required, as the negative pressure
(15-25 cm H2O) appears to collapse the tube (ch. 92).
e. Large bore chest tube (LBCT) - LBCTs (20-36 Fr) are also
placed for management of larger volume pneumothoraces, or
when continuous suction is chosen as a therapeutic modality
(Video 220.7

). LBCTs are typically placed under general

anesthesia in all but the most severely affected patients,
although occasional clinicians prefer to place them awake with
local anesthetics. Similar to LBCT, thoracic radiographs
should be performed after placement of a chest tube.
f. Thoracotomy - In severe cases of ongoing pneumothorax, or in
the case of spontaneous pneumothorax in dogs, exploratory
thoracotomy may be pursued to resect diseased lung and to
explore the chest cavity for evidence of other disorders.
KEY POINT: The presence of a chest tube does not exclude
clinically significant pleural space disease. If there is any doubt as
to the patency of the chest tube, and a patient is showing
respiratory difficulty, a new tube should be placed or needle
thoracocentesis performed.
a

MILA chest tube. MILA International, Erlanger, KY.

BOX 2 2 0.2 S u mmary o f Ple u ral Effu s io n
1) Detection of pleural effusion should prompt a thorough search
for the underlying cause.
2) Many cases of pleural effusion can be palliated successfully but
true cure is unlikely except with infection, trauma or
anticoagulant intoxication.
3) Iatrogenic air leak may occur as a result of thoracocentesis,
particularly in chronic effusions.

4) Cytologic evaluation of withdrawn fluid is warranted with
every thoracocentesis, even “repeat offenders.”
Both large and small bore thoracostomy tubes alone can cause
inflammation and a small amount of pleural fluid (<2
mL/kg/day).57,58 Tubes should be removed when no longer
productive after confirmation that effusion or pneumothorax has
resolved, and the patient should be closely monitored.

SUMMARY (BOX 220.2)
Pleural effusion and pneumothorax are relatively common
conditions in dogs and cats. Removal of the effusion or air usually
results in rapid improvement. A search for the underlying cause
should follow stabilization. Some conditions are curable while others
may require ongoing management.

Aerodigestive disorders reflect the complex interrelationship
between swallowing and respiration.1 In people, gastroesophageal
reflux disease (GERD) is a frequent source of acute and chronic
pulmonary disease, with a prevalence of 50% in patients with chronic
cough, asthma, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
(COPD).2,3 Aerodigestive diseases represent a diagnostic challenge
because many patients present in the absence of clinical signs of
alimentary disease.4 This makes clinical recognition of the
relationship between the alimentary and respiratory tracts critically
important. Uncontrolled reflux in people has been demonstrated to
lead to progression of respiratory disease, exacerbations of clinical
signs, increased patient morbidity, and increased treatment costs.5
Importantly, the treatment of GERD and extra-esophageal reflux
disease has been demonstrated to reduce the frequency of disease
exacerbations and slow the rate of decline in lung function in people
with COPD.6
Although aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217) is the best recognized
example of aerodigestive disease in dogs, the scope of possible
conditions associated with aspiration and reflux is far greater.7
Animal models, clinical case reports, and case series have
demonstrated bronchoconstriction, laryngeal dysfunction, and
micro-aspiration in response to experimental or naturally occurring
reflux (Table 221.1).7 Further, a recent study found that 80% of
dogs presenting exclusively for cough had evidence of swallow
dysfunction on a free-feeding videofluoroscopic swallow study
(VFSS), indicating that, as in people, aerodigestive diseases in dogs
likely represents an important and underrecognized clinical
population.8 A case series in dogs treated for gastrointestinal (GI)
tract disease prior to brachycephalic airway surgery found a
decreased complication rate and improved prognosis.9 A recent
publication showed that respiratory signs in dogs improved with
treatment exclusively for concurrent upper digestive tract
abnormalities.10 This suggests that dogs with respiratory disease,
like people, may respond to interventions targeting the GI tract.

AIRWAY PROTECTIVE MECHANISMS
As many as 50% of normal people have been demonstrated to
aspirate in their sleep, the pathologic consequences of which are
mitigated by robust airway protective mechanisms. These include
respiration/swallow coordination “gate keeping,” as well as basal and
response mechanisms.11,12

GATE-KEEPING
Gate-keeping refers to the centrally-mediated coordination of
swallow and respiration. In health, breathing is a regular function
that may be interrupted by conscious or unconscious (i.e., reflexive)
swallows. Swallowing and breathing are under the regulation of
central pattern generators in the brainstem: the swallow central
pattern generator (swCPG) and respiratory central pattern generator
(rCPG), respectively. Communication between the swCPG and rCPG
coordinates swallowing and breathing such that swallowing is
initiated preferentially during specific phases of the respiratory cycle,
and corresponds with the generation of swallow-apnea, and a
“swallow breath” occurring just prior to the onset of swallow.12,13
Timing of swallow varies with species. In humans, swallows are
initiated following expiration and are also followed by expiration.12
This is different in dogs, where in both anesthetized and in awake,
spontaneously swallowing dogs, >90% of swallows are initiated
during the inspiratory phase.14 The changes in the timing of the
swallow may reflect differences in the position of the larynx with
recumbency as has been demonstrated in studies in adult people.15
Importantly, alterations in breath-swallow coordination have been
implicated in the elderly and in patients with dysphagia, two
populations at increased risk of aspiration.12,13
Another means of airway protection during swallowing is swallowapnea. Studies in small and large animal models have documented a
drop in airflow corresponding with pharyngeal swallow. This occurs
because of laryngeal adduction and restriction of diaphragmatic
contraction. Multiple swallows in series prolong swallow apnea. This

may increase risk of aspiration in patients with existing respiratory
disease as they are less tolerant of apneic periods.

BASAL MECHANISMS
Basal mechanisms are barriers to aspiration independent of
stimulation. In gastroesophageal reflux, refluxate must cross 2 highpressure zones to reach the pharynx: the lower esophageal sphincter
(LES) and upper esophageal sphincter (UES). The LES is a highpressure zone comprised, in part, of a band of circular smooth or
striated muscle fibers. In humans and dogs, this is a band of smooth
muscle.16 The basal pressure of the LES in non-anesthetized dogs
ranges from 14 to 45 mm Hg (median 30 mm Hg) and is reduced in
patients under anesthesia.17 The UES is a barrier between the
proximal esophagus and the pharynx, comprised predominantly of
the cricopharyngeus muscle. The role of the UES is to accommodate
an anterograde swallowed bolus while preventing retrograde
esophago-pharyngeal reflux, which could lead to aspiration. The
esophagus itself can contain refluxate until it can be cleared, without
allowing it to escape to the pharynx. The pharynx, like the
esophagus, can contain a certain volume before it triggers a swallow
or overflows into the airways. Within the airways and lungs,
mucociliary clearance and innate immunity represent additional
basal barriers to aspiration associated respiratory syndromes
(AARS).13

RESPONSE MECHANISMS
Unlike basal mechanisms, response mechanisms become active in
response to mechanical or chemical stimulation. These can be
divided into 4 categories:

Volume Clearing
Reflexes that clear volume from the pharynx and esophagus include
the reflexive pharyngeal swallow (RPS) and secondary esophageal
peristalsis.18 The RPS acts as a major airway protective mechanism
by removing debris and residue from the entrance to the respiratory
tract.18 These swallows also play a significant role in airway
protection during sleep in cases of nocturnal reflux. Secondary
peristalsis refers to peristalsis activated by distention. This occurs in
response to retained volume within the esophagus following primary

peristalsis or in response to refluxed materials from the stomach
(ch. 47).

Upper Esophageal Sphincter Pressure
The UES maintains a high-pressure zone between the esophagus and
pharynx that relaxes in response to a pharyngeal swallow and
eructation. The magnitude of UES pressure is variable in response to
level of arousal; the degree, location, and rate of esophageal
distention; the type of distending material (gas vs. liquid, acidic vs.
non-acidic); and body orientation.19 In response to slow esophageal
dilation (e.g., liquid refluxate), the UES responds by increasing tone
(esophago-UES reflex).20 Rapid esophageal gas distention, however,
results in UES relaxation to allow gas passage (i.e.,
eructation/belch).21 The contractile reflex varies with arousal and is
nearly abolished during deep sleep.19 The pharyngo-UES contractile
reflex occurs in response to mechanical pharyngeal stimulation.22 It
is presumed that activation of this reflex prevents further leakage of
gastric contents into the pharynx. This reflex response is nearly
always followed by RPS. The laryngo-UES contractile reflex describes
increases in basal UES tone in response to laryngeal stimulation.

Laryngeal Closure
Reflexes that induce laryngeal closure include the esophagolaryngeal closure reflex, pharyngo-laryngeal adduction reflex, and
laryngeal adductor reflex. Studies in both animal models and people
have documented reflexive adduction of the larynx in response to
abrupt esophageal distention, and pharyngeal and laryngeal
stimulation. These serve as a protective mechanism against
aspiration by decreasing the diameter of the glottal opening of the
larynx during swallowing. Unlike the esophago-UES reflex, abrupt
esophageal distention triggers laryngeal closure regardless of
location. Small animal experimental models have demonstrated
suppression of this response with increased anesthetic depth,
suggesting that diminished laryngeal reflexes may result in increased
risk of aspiration during sedation and anesthesia.23

Particulate Clearing
The most easily recognized and evaluated airway protective
mechanisms are cough and throat clear (TC) (ch. 34). Cough and TC
play an important protective role that facilitates clearance of
particulate matter, irritants, debris, and/or fluid from the respiratory
tract. Cough, when excessive, may also become harmful to the
airways and negatively impact the quality of life for both dog and
client.24 This highlights the need to balance targeted therapy,
allowing adequate airway protection while not allowing cough to
become detrimental. Cough can be subdivided into 3 phases: an
inhalation phase, a pressurization phase, and an expulsion phase
that forcefully ejects air against a closed glottis. A TC lacks an
inhalation phase but otherwise serves a similar role. Both cough and
TC are stimulated by chemical or mechanical stimuli.25 Cough is
triggered by stimulation of the pharynx, larynx, trachea, carina, and
bronchi while TC is typically associated with stimulation of the
pharynx, larynx, and cervical trachea only.24

ASPIRATION AND RESPIRATORY
INFLAMMATION
In people, the inhalation of low pH gastric fluid, digestive enzymes,
and/or particulate material leads to sterile aspiration pneumonitis,
which may or may not develop a secondary bacterial complication
(aspiration pneumonia) (ch. 217).26 These are considered separate
conditions and treatment with antibiotics is reserved for those with
confirmed bacterial infection. This distinction is rarely made in
veterinary medicine and may contribute to antimicrobial overuse in
veterinary patients (ch. 7).
The response to acid entry into the respiratory tract is biphasic.
The initial inflammatory response is caused by direct damage to the
respiratory epithelium, followed 4-6 hours later by neutrophilic
inflammation. Like acid, digestive enzymes also play a role in
respiratory inflammation. Pepsin is active in an acidic environment.
Deactivation begins at a pH of 6.8 and it becomes irreversibly
deactivated at pH 7.5. In humans and animal models, pepsin-

sensitive receptors have been demonstrated in laryngeal tissue. After
binding, pepsin is taken up into endocytic vesicles where the pH is
approximately 5. At this pH, pepsin that is not irreversibly denatured
may become re-activated at up to 40% of its maximal activity,
leading to tissue injury.27 Bile acids have been documented in
bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) in human patients with AARS
and in dogs with pulmonary fibrosis.28
Small non-acidified gastric particles (SNAPs) also induce
inflammation. In small animal models, tracheal instillation of small
(<10 micron) particles leads to neutrophilic inflammation after 4-6
hours. A lack of pulmonary edema distinguishes SNAP-induced
inflammation from inflammation secondary to aspiration of acid.
Importantly, the combination of acidic aspiration and SNAP
aspiration appears to have a synergistic effect on inflammation.29

RISK FACTORS FOR ASPIRATION
Increased risk for developing AARS in dogs has been demonstrated
for decreased consciousness, body position during anesthetic
recovery, duration of anesthesia, vomiting and regurgitation,
seizures, cranial nerve deficits and the presence of megaesophagus
(ME).30 The most common underlying disorders in one study
included esophageal disease (39.8%), vomiting (38.6%), neurologic
disease (27.3%), laryngeal disease (18.2%), and post-anesthetic
aspiration (13.6%). Of those with esophageal disease, ME was
identified in 71.4% of dogs; the remaining dogs were diagnosed with
non-ME esophageal dysmotility, hiatal hernia, and an unknown
disorder in 17.1%, 2.8%, and 8.6% of dogs, respectively.30 Though
they focus specifically on aspiration pneumonia, these studies
highlight the role of alimentary disease, particularly esophageal
disease, in the development of AARS.

RECOGNIZED ASPIRATION-RELATED
RESPIRATORY SYNDROMES IN DOGS

The ultimate prevalence of aerodigestive disease in dogs is currently
unknown, though evidence suggests that they are common.8 As dogs
are susceptible to many of the same conditions as people, a similar
spectrum of disorders should be expected. An extensive review has
been performed previously.7 A brief overview of aspiration
associated respiratory syndromes reported in dogs and in people is
presented in Table 221.1.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTING FOR
AERODIGESTIVE DISORDERS
Thoracic radiographs are often considered the first-line diagnostic
test for patients presenting with evidence of respiratory disease.
Though widely available, radiographs are poorly sensitive for
aerodigestive disease where signs are elicited by extra-thoracic
stimulation or caused by dynamic and/or intermittent disease. In a
recent study evaluating dogs presenting exclusively for cough, 9/11
dogs with normal thoracic radiographs had evidence of aerodigestive
disease on VFSS.8 Computed tomography (CT) is helpful for
evaluation of static lesions including masses and foreign bodies, as
well as a thorough evaluation of AARS (e.g., aspiration bronchiolitis
and bronchiectasis). CT is considered the most sensitive diagnostic
modality for the identification of bronchiectasis and inhaled foreign
bodies. Survey radiography and a single breathing phase CT are both
limited, however, in that they can only reliably detect static anatomic
and obstructive changes. Inspiratory and expiratory breath-holding
CT may help detect dynamic changes to the airways; however, these
cannot assess swallow dysfunction.
Videofluoroscopic swallowing studies are considered the criterion
standard for the evaluation of dysphagia in dogs (Figures 221.1 and
221.2; ch. 259).31-33 This modality is available at many specialty
referral centers. Examples of VFSS depicting both normal and
abnormal swallowing are shown as Videos
Videos

221.1 and 221.2, and

47.1, 47.2, and 47.3. An advantage of VFSS is that is

allows real-time imaging over a period of time and is an excellent
means of detecting subtle, segmental, and dynamic motility
disorders that result in, or may underlie, aerodigestive disease (ch.
47).8 Reflux and sliding hiatal hernias may also be detected by VFSS
(chs. 259 and 261). A recent study demonstrated VFSS were
superior to radiographs for the detection of sliding hiatal hernias.34
Reflux is often detected by VFSS even in normal dogs, and
dysfunction is determined by severity and degree of margination
rather than its presence or absence (e.g., extra-esophageal reflux;
Figure 221.2). Respiratory fluoroscopy may be performed alone or
in combination with VFSS. If combined with a VFSS, it is
recommended that respiratory fluoroscopy be performed first so that
airways and associated structures are not masked by contrast in the
esophagus. Respiratory fluoroscopy is particularly recommended
where dynamic architectural changes to the larynx, trachea, and
mainstem bronchi are suspected. For some cases, sedated respiratory
fluoroscopic examinations should be considered, as in the case of
suspected obstructive sleep apnea.

Endoscopy in the form of laryngoscopy (ch. 214), esophagoscopy
(ch. 107), choanal examination (chs. 89 and 213), and
bronchoscopy with BALF culture (e.g., aerobic, anaerobic, and
mycoplasma) and cytologic evaluation (ch. 93) are important
diagnostics for patients with many kinds of aerodigestive disorders.
A laryngeal function examination should also be considered even in
animals without stridor or apparent respiratory distress (Video 214.1
). Common cranial nerve innervation between the pharynx,

larynx and proximal esophagus makes it especially important in
patients with dysphagia localized to these areas (ch. 241).
Other less commonly considered diagnostic options include
nuclear scintigraphy and assays of protein biomarkers. Nuclear
scintigraphy has recently been used for measuring reflux and
cumulative small volume aspiration in dogs.35 Biomarkers have been
used reliably to provide evidence of reflux and aspiration in human
patients.36 Though not used routinely in veterinary medicine, a
recent study demonstrated GI-specific proteins in oropharyngeal
swabs from dogs with cough, likely suggesting aerodigestive disease
in this population.28

THE MEDIASTINUM
ANATOMY
The mediastinum is a true space created by pleural reflections, and it
lies between the right and left pleural cavities.1 It is located primarily
on the midline of the thorax, although it deviates slightly to the left to
accommodate extension of the right cranial and accessory lung lobes.
The mediastinum contains and encloses the heart, trachea,
esophagus, thymus, thoracic lymph nodes, thoracic duct, vagus
nerves, aorta, cranial and caudal venae cavae, and all other vessels

that enter or leave the heart. The mediastinal space extends dorsally
to the longus colli ventral to the thoracic spine, and ventrally to the
sternum, and from thoracic inlet to diaphragm. It is not a closed
space; it communicates with the cervical soft tissues via the thoracic
inlet, and with the retroperitoneal space via the aortic hiatus.
Therefore, disease in any of these compartments can spread to the
others. For example, subcutaneous emphysema in the cervical soft
tissues can extend into the mediastinum, creating a
pneumomediastinum, and from there into the retroperitoneal space.
The mediastinum is separate from the pleural space, but mediastinal
fenestrations allow pleural air and fluid to communicate between
pleural cavities. The mediastinum is divided into 5 compartments:
cranioventral, craniodorsal, middle, caudoventral, and caudodorsal.
Three sets of lymph nodes are located within the mediastinum, but
they are not typically visualized unless enlarged.2,3 The cranial
mediastinal lymph nodes are located along the cranial vena cava, just
ventral to the trachea, and cranial to the heart. They vary in number,
and receive afferent lymphatics from the trachea, esophagus, heart,
pericardium, and pleura, as well as muscles of the neck, thorax, and
abdomen; scapulae; last six cervical vertebrae; thoracic vertebrae;
ribs; thyroid; thymus; and mediastinum. The tracheobronchial
(hilar) lymph nodes are paired, with one pair located inside the
bifurcation of the principal bronchi (carina), just dorsal to the left
atrium. They are located slightly more cranially in the cat compared
to the dog. Additional tracheobronchial nodes are located lateral to
the carina. These nodes receive afferent lymphatics from the lungs
and bronchi. The sternal lymph nodes lie along the ventral aspect of
the cranial mediastinum, just dorsal to the second and third
sternebrae. The feline sternal lymph nodes are located slightly more
caudally on the sternum compared to those of the dog. Sternal lymph
nodes receive afferents from the diaphragm, pericardium, ventral
thoracic and abdominal walls and peritoneal cavity.

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
The mediastinum is not easily accessible for clinical evaluation due
to its location within the thorax, and there are no blood tests that are
specific for mediastinal disease. On physical exam, a large cranial

mediastinal mass can be suspected, particularly in cats, if the cranial
thorax is noncompliant during gentle compression. Loss of normal
breath sounds on auscultation also can suggest a mass lesion;
pneumothorax (ch. 220) is an important differential diagnosis.
Imaging of the mediastinum (radiology, ultrasound [US], computed
tomography [CT], magnetic resonance imaging [MRI], or nuclear
medicine) is essential for noninvasive evaluation.

Survey Radiography
The mediastinum is seen as a soft-tissue opacity only in the cranial
thorax, ventral to the trachea. This opacity is created by border
effacement of several mediastinal structures, including esophagus,
cranial vena cava, left subclavian artery, brachiocephalic trunk, and
cranial mediastinal lymph nodes. These structures are seen
individually only when air is present in the mediastinum to act as a
negative contrast medium (Figure 222.1). On the ventrodorsal
(VD) or dorsoventral (DV) view, the mediastinum is superimposed
over the spine, and should be no more than twice the spinal
thickness, although fat deposits in the mediastinum can cause
thickening. Thickening due to fat should result in smooth straight
margins. In young animals, the thymus may be visualized as a
triangular, sail-shaped soft tissue opaque structure in the
cranioventral aspect of the mediastinum, just to the left of midline,
and cranial to the heart.

FIGURE 222.1 Pneumomediastinum. Lateral
thoracic radiograph of a 6-year-old mixed breed dog
presented after being hit by a car. Free air in the
mediastinum outlines anatomic structures not
normally seen, including cranial vena cava (vc),
esophagus (E), inner and outer aspects of the
tracheal wall, brachiocephalic trunk (bt), left
subclavian artery (sa), and azygos vein (a).
Survey radiography is ideal as the first step for localizing
mediastinal disease, and can assess size, shape, opacity, and position
of abnormalities. In general, mediastinal lesions include mediastinal
shift, pneumomediastinum, and increased size and/or opacity of the
mediastinum (mediastinal mass).
A mediastinal shift occurs when there is a decrease in volume of
one or more lung lobes on one side. The mediastinum shifts towards
the affected side to compensate for the loss of volume. The heart is
the largest organ in the mediastinum, and a deviation to one side (on

a properly positioned VD or DV view) is indicative of a mediastinal
shift. The diaphragm on the affected side also can shift cranially to
compensate. Alternatively, the mediastinum shifts towards the
normal hemithorax when the opposite side has increased in volume
secondary to a large volume of unilateral pleural effusion or a very
large pulmonary mass.
Increased mediastinal size may be due to a mediastinal mass,
esophageal enlargement, or fluid in the mediastinum. These diseases
are manifested radiographically as diffuse or focal enlargement of the
mediastinum. Diffuse soft-tissue widening on VD/DV views can be
caused by the accumulation of fluid secondary to inflammation or
hemorrhage. Focal mediastinal widening is usually the result of a
mass lesion. Masses in the cranial mediastinum are most common,
and if large enough, can result in border effacement of the cranial
margin of the heart, dorsal displacement of the trachea and caudal
displacement of the carina (normally located at the sixth intercostal
space) and heart. Cranial widening of the mediastinum on VD/DV
views is present. Middle mediastinal masses are most commonly
enlarged hilar lymph nodes. These create a mass effect at the base of
the heart, with ventral deviation of the carina and principal bronchi
(lateral view), and lateral deviation of the principal bronchi (DV/VD
view). Caudal mediastinal masses may be due to esophageal disease,
abscess, granuloma, or tumor.

Ultrasonography
US of the thoracic cavity is limited in its efficacy for imaging the
normal mediastinum, as air in adjacent lung lobes prevents
transmission of the sound waves. However, sonographic evaluation
may provide useful information in animals with pleural effusion
(which creates a window to the mediastinum; ch. 220) or with
cranial mediastinal disease.4,5 Ultrasonography allows visualization
of most cranial mediastinal masses. Placing the transducer in a
cranial parasternal position or using the heart as an acoustic window
may be necessary for adequate evaluation of smaller masses.
Ultrasonography is especially helpful in defining the internal
architecture of masses as solid or cystic, and providing localization of
vascular structures relative to the mass. Although the US appearance
of a mass is not specific for the exact tissue of origin, US can be used

for directing needle placement for fine-needle aspirate (FNA) or
tissue core biopsy.6

Computed Tomography
CT of the thorax provides more detailed information regarding
presence, location, and extent of disease. It provides better contrast
discrimination than survey radiographs do, allowing distinction
among solid, fatty, or cystic structures.7 The cross-sectional imaging
format eliminates the issue of superimposed anatomic structures.
The ability to do multiplanar reconstruction is an additional
advantage. Contrast enhancement after intravenous administration
of an iodinated contrast agent provides added information regarding
perfusion of soft tissues and vascular anomalies.7-10 Especially in the
presence of pleural effusion, CT is superior to thoracic radiographs in
locating mass lesions to the mediastinum, determining their
character (cystic or cavitated, versus solid), and determining extent
of disease, including regional vascular invasion. This is critical
information for determining the surgical resectability of a mass.
Computed tomographic angiography is necessary to more reliably
evaluate vascular invasion. To control respiratory motion, general
anesthesia is usually necessary for thoracic CT examination.

Further Diagnostic Evaluation
Thyroid scintigraphy using technetium 99m or iodine 131 can be
used for identifying ectopic or metastatic functional thyroid tissue
within the mediastinum.11

DISEASES OF THE MEDIASTINUM
Pneumomediastinum
Pneumomediastinum is the abnormal accumulation of air within the
mediastinum and it can be caused by a variety of mechanisms.12-15
Tracheal disruption can leak air into the mediastinum, and has been
reported with cervical trauma, mechanical ventilation, transtracheal
aspiration, tracheostomy, tracheal intubation and overinflation, or

central venous catheter placement (ch. 215).13,16 General anesthesia
with endotracheal intubation and positive pressure ventilation
(possible barotrauma and tracheal rupture), followed by trauma and
tracheal foreign bodies, have been reported as the most common
causes of pneumomediastinum in cats.15,17 Similar to tracheal
trauma, esophageal or pharyngeal rupture can result in
pneumomediastinum.18,19 Subcutaneous emphysema from any
location can eventually enter the mediastinum via the cervical soft
tissues and thoracic inlet. Lung trauma or overdistension and
rupture of alveoli can result in free alveolar air dissecting along the
pulmonary interstitium and bronchovascular sheath, into the
mediastinal space (Macklin effect).20 This can occur completely
separately from lung trauma that results in pneumothorax. Severe
pulmonary lesions or preexisting respiratory disease can lead to
bronchial or alveolar rupture with subsequent
pneumomediastinum.21,22 Less commonly, air can enter the
mediastinum from gas accumulation in the retroperitoneal space. In
some cases, the cause of pneumomediastinum is not determined
(spontaneous pneumomediastinum).14,15
The presence of air in the mediastinum creates enhanced
radiographic contrast and detail, allowing visualization of individual
mediastinal structures (best seen on lateral images), including
cranial vena cava, brachiocephalic trunk and left subclavian artery,
esophagus, and azygos vein (Figure 222.1). Visualization of the
tracheal wall is enhanced due to the presence of both intraluminal
and extraluminal air. Mediastinal air can communicate with the
retroperitoneal space via the aortic hiatus, resulting in secondary
pneumoretroperitoneum. Pneumomediastinum does not occur
secondary to pneumothorax. However, a severe
pneumomediastinum has the potential to cause a secondary
pneumothorax.
While pneumomediastinum can create dramatic radiographic
changes, respiratory distress typically is absent unless concurrent
pleural or pulmonary disease is present. If pneumomediastinum
progresses to pneumothorax, tachypnea and dyspnea often are seen
(ch. 220). Animals with pneumomediastinum associated with
esophageal rupture present with signs associated with esophageal

disease, such as regurgitation, evidence of pain, and dysphagia (ch.
259). The air trapped within the mediastinum does not require
treatment and will spontaneously resolve within 2 weeks if there is
no ongoing source of air leakage.

Mediastinitis
Clinical signs associated with mediastinitis include tachypnea (likely
related to thoracic pain), dyspnea, cough, head and/or neck edema,
and regurgitation. Voice changes may occur secondary to recurrent
laryngeal nerve involvement. Physical examination may also reveal
head and/or neck edema, fever, and decreased lung sounds if
pneumothorax or pleural effusion is also present.

FIGURE 222.2 Mediastinal hemorrhage. Lateral
(A) and dorsoventral (DV) (B) thoracic radiographs
of a 5-year-old dog with mediastinal hemorrhage
secondary to rodenticide intoxication. Note the
tracheal compression due to surrounding
mediastinal hemorrhage (lateral) and widened
mediastinum (DV view).
Mediastinal inflammation is manifested radiographically as either
focal or diffuse widening of the mediastinum. Mediastinal pleural
thickening, mediastinal air and fluid, mediastinal lymph node
enlargement, and mediastinal mass lesions have been identified with

CT.23,24 Mediastinitis may result from esophageal or tracheal
perforation, deep cervical soft tissue infections extending along
fascial planes into the mediastinum, or extension of infection from
the pericardium, pulmonary parenchyma, or pleural space.25
Migrating intrathoracic grass awns have been reported as a cause of
mediastinitis.23 Chronic granulomatous mediastinitis may be caused
by fungal organisms, such as Histoplasma or Cryptococcus spp., or
bacterial organisms, such as Actinomyces or Nocardia spp.26,27
Mediastinitis has been documented secondary to spirocercosis in
dogs.28 Abscessation of the mediastinum may result from
progression of chronic infectious or neoplastic mediastinal
disorders.25 Both mediastinal abscesses and granulomas typically
appear on radiographs as mediastinal masses and thus may be
mistaken for neoplasia (Video 222.1)

.

Therapy involves resolving the underlying disorder. Esophageal
perforation may require surgical repair, and mediastinal masses may
require surgical resection and/or drainage, along with appropriate
medical therapy (antimicrobial, antineoplastic, etc., as indicated)
and supportive care.25,27,28 Mediastinitis without a mass lesion may
respond to antimicrobial therapy and supportive care alone.

Mediastinal Hemorrhage
Hemorrhage into the mediastinum usually results from either
trauma or coagulopathy.29,30 The clinical signs associated with
mediastinal hemorrhage are related to the effects of acute blood loss.
Dyspnea may occur if mediastinal hemorrhage progresses to
hemothorax, or if the trachea is compressed by surrounding
mediastinal hemorrhage. Radiographic signs include widening of the
mediastinum with soft-tissue opacity on both lateral and VD/DV
views. Tracheal diameter may be narrowed due to compression, or
tracheal wall thickening may occur due to submucosal hemorrhage
(Figure 222.2).29 Treatment, when warranted, is aimed at
resolution of the underlying cause, such as plasma and vitamin K1

therapy for anticoagulant rodenticide intoxication, along with
supportive care (ch. 138).

Mediastinal Masses
Mediastinal masses frequently are classified by location (Table
222.1).

Mediastinal Cysts
Benign cranial mediastinal cysts can originate from different
anatomic structures (parathyroid cyst, thyroglossal cyst, thymic
branchial cyst, and pleural cyst), and are identified most commonly
in older cats.31 Radiographically, they appear as focal soft-tissue
masses located in the cranioventral mediastinum, often more
caudally than other mediastinal masses (Figure 222.3). US or CT
can be used for demonstrating the fluid contents, and differentiate
these from solid mass lesions. On US exam, mediastinal cysts are
ovoid/bilobed and thin-walled, contain anechoic fluid, and usually
are accompanied by distal enhancement. Solid neoplasms, abscesses,
or granulomas may have cystic components and must be
differentiated from a simple cyst. Fine-needle aspiration with US
guidance is the diagnostic test of choice. Aspirated fluid is typically
clear, colorless, and minimally cellular. Mediastinal cysts often are
incidental findings that produce no clinical signs unless they are
large enough to compress adjacent structures such as the trachea.

Mediastinal Lymphadenopathy
Mediastinal lymph node enlargement can be caused by a variety of
diseases. Hilar (tracheobronchial) lymph nodes enlarge most
commonly secondary to lymphoma (ch. 322) or fungal pneumonia
(histoplasmosis [ch. 209], blastomycosis [ch. 209],
coccidioidomycosis [ch. 208])32 (Figure 222.4). Additional causes
include histiocytic sarcoma complex (ch. 328), metastatic
adenocarcinoma (hepatocellular, anal sac, pancreatic), mycobacterial
infections (ch. 188), eosinophilic bronchopneumopathy (ch. 215),
eosinophilic pulmonary granulomatosis (ch. 217), and
lymphomatoid granulomatosis.32-39 There does not appear to be a

correlation between the size of the tracheobronchial lymph nodes
and the type of disease. Cranial mediastinal lymph nodes receive
afferents from the head/neck (see Anatomy section, above), and may
enlarge with diseases of these areas. Lymphoma likely is the most
common cause of visible enlargement. Sternal lymphadenopathy can
be identified early on radiographs, as these nodes are relatively
isolated from other soft-tissue structures, making enlargement more
readily visible (Figure 222.4). Since these nodes receive afferent
drainage from the peritoneal cavity, enlargement should prompt
investigation of abdominal disease.
