Mediastinal Neoplasia
Mediastinal tumors can originate from any structure in the
mediastinum (lymph nodes, thymus, great vessels, trachea,
esophagus, or ectopic thyroid or parathyroid tissue) or from
extension of neoplastic lesions in adjacent tissues.40-43 Mediastinal
neoplasms may also be metastatic lesions or components of a
multicentric neoplastic process.43-45 Benign tumors have been
documented.46
Clinical signs associated with mediastinal tumors are usually
caused by compression or invasion of structures such as the great
vessels, thoracic duct, esophagus, and trachea, or are due to
associated pleural effusion (ch. 220). Signs include coughing,
dyspnea, dysphagia, regurgitation, and edema of the head, neck,
and/or forelimbs. Signs caused by peripheral nerve entrapment are
less common and include laryngeal paralysis, vocalization changes,
or Horner’s syndrome. Signs associated with multicentric disease
may reflect other sites of neoplastic involvement or may be related to
paraneoplastic syndromes (ch. 331). These signs include anorexia,
weight loss, regurgitation, vomiting, diarrhea, and
polyuria/polydipsia.
Mediastinal lymphoma originates from either lymph node or
thymic tissue in the cranial mediastinum (Figure 222.5, Video
222.2

), and is more common in the cat than the dog (ch.

322).40,42 It typically occurs in younger cats (2-4 years of age), and
they are often feline leukemia virus-positive (ch. 199).40,42,45
Mediastinal lymphoma is often associated with pleural effusion,
which may obscure radiographic visualization of the mediastinal
mass. The diagnosis of mediastinal lymphoma can usually be
confirmed by cytologic identification of neoplastic lymphocytes in

either a sample of pleural fluid (ch. 92) or a sample obtained
directly from the mediastinal mass via fine-needle aspiration or core
biopsy (

Video 222.3) (ch. 85). In dogs, mediastinal lymphoma

may be associated with hypercalcemia (ch. 331).46
Chemodectomas, which are usually aortic or carotid body tumors,
are most often identified as heart base masses (ch. 235) (Figure
222.6).
Other less common neoplastic mediastinal masses include ectopic
thyroid carcinoma, neuroendocrine carcinoma, and anaplastic
carcinoma.43 The tumor type of a mediastinal mass cannot be
determined from radiographic signs alone. However, it is critical to
identify this information, as the recommended treatment for cranial
mediastinal tumors other than lymphoma is surgical resection. CT is
invaluable in aiding in a more detailed evaluation of mass location,
morphology, involvement with adjacent vessels, and identification of
pulmonary metastasis.47

DISEASES OF THE THYMUS
The thymus extends from the thoracic inlet to the fifth rib in the dog
and the sixth rib in the cat. Dorsally, it lies next to the phrenic nerves
and cranial lung lobes. At puberty, the thymus attains its largest
absolute size, and then involutes to an extremely small size at
adulthood.48 As the thymus atrophies, it is gradually replaced by
connective tissue and fat, but remnants persist into old age.48

Thymic Hemorrhage
An uncommon disease consisting of spontaneous thymic
hemorrhage has been described in dogs and one cat.49-51 Although
not uniformly fatal, most animals documented with this syndrome
have died. Most affected animals are <2 years of age; thus, it appears
to be associated with thymic involution. Clinical signs include
lethargy, signs of thoracic pain, increased respiratory effort, and
dyspnea. Physical examination findings are attributable to acute

blood loss/hypovolemia and pleural effusion. Signs include pale
mucous membranes, prolonged capillary refill time, tachycardia,
tachypnea, and muffled lung sounds. Thoracic radiographs
demonstrate a mediastinal mass (hemorrhage, hematoma), usually
associated with pleural effusion. Treatment is supportive (ch. 119)
and involves intravascular volume support (ch. 120), blood
replacement (ch. 124), and thoracocentesis as needed (ch. 92).

Thymoma
Thymomas are well-recognized but uncommon tumors in the dog
and cat. Thymomas arise from the epithelial cells of the thymus, and
can be benign or malignant.40,41,45,52-54 This assessment appears to
be based on invasiveness and resectability rather than
histopathologic characteristics.41 Malignancy is associated with
invasiveness, vascular infiltration, and local or distant metastasis.
Radiographically, a thymoma appears as a soft-tissue opacity in the
cranioventral, or occasionally craniolateral aspect of the thorax
(within the mediastinum). Tracheal deviation or compression,
pleural effusion (ch. 220), or in some cases, paraneoplastic
megaesophagus with evidence of aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217),
can be seen. Sonographically, thymomas can appear as solid, cystic,
or both. Cytologic examination of FNA samples reveals a variable
number of mature lymphocytes, which makes cytologic
differentiation of thymoma from mediastinal lymphoma difficult.
Mast cells also are frequently identified in cytologic samples from
thymomas. Surgical or US-guided percutaneous biopsy is required
for a definitive diagnosis. Paraneoplastic syndromes (ch. 331) are
common with thymoma in both dogs and cats,52,55 notably
myasthenia gravis (ch. 253), which is often associated with
megaesophagus (ch. 259) in dogs with thymoma (Figure 222.7).52
Surgical resection is the treatment of choice for thymoma, but
recurrence and metastasis have been reported.

THE CHEST WALL AND DIAPHRAGM
ANATOMY OF THE CHEST WALL
The sternum and ribs surround and protect the thorax ventrally and
laterally. Thirteen pairs of ribs and 8 sternebrae are normal.
However, congenital abnormalities in numbers are common, and
typically of no clinical significance. The last set of ribs (13th) may be
smaller than normal, or even absent. Sternebrae may be fused or
decreased in number. Lesions involving these structures are best
evaluated on radiographs or CT scans of the thorax.

DISEASES OF THE RIBS
Rib fractures commonly are associated with trauma, and should be
carefully assessed on thoracic images taken after a traumatic
incident. Flail chest occurs when at least 2 consecutive ribs are
fractured both dorsally and ventrally, resulting in an independent

thoracic wall segment (ch. 220). This segment demonstrates
paradoxical movement with respiration, moving inward with
inspiration, and outward with expiration. Mechanical failure
secondary to chronic respiratory distress/coughing can result in
nontraumatic rib fractures in cats with chronic airway disease.56,57
These are usually the more caudal ribs (9-13), and involve the
midportion.

FIGURE 222.7 Lateral (A) and ventrodorsal (B)
thoracic radiographs of a 13-year-old dog with
thymoma and myasthenia gravis. A cranial
mediastinal mass is present, along with
megaesophagus. An alveolar lung pattern consistent
with aspiration pneumonia is noted in the caudal
subsegment of the left cranial lung lobe (∗).
Tumors involving the ribs, most commonly osteosarcoma and
chondrosarcoma (ch. 326), can create an extrapleural mass lesion,
which is a broad-based mass arising peripheral to the parietal pleura,
creating a convex margin facing the lungs. Rib tumors also may
result in a secondary pleural effusion (Figure 222.8). The ribs
should be evaluated with care in patients with pleural effusion of
unknown etiology. Other tumors, such as multiple myeloma (ch.
322), or metastatic disease, can cause lytic lesions in the ribs. CT is
an excellent imaging modality for a more detailed evaluation of the
ribs and pleural space in these cases.

DISEASES OF THE STERNUM
Pectus excavatum is a deformity of the sternum and associated costal
cartilages characterized by dorsal deviation of the sternebrae (usually
the caudal sternebrae) and a ventral to dorsal compression of the
thorax (Figure 222.9).58,59 This is most often a congenital defect,
especially in Maltese and English Bulldog breeds. Clinical signs are
dependent on the severity of the deformity, and are secondary to
compression of the heart and lungs. While many patients have no
clinical signs, others exhibit exercise intolerance, tachypnea,
cyanosis, respiratory distress, and a heart murmur. The murmur may
be functional (secondary to cardiac malposition) or may be due to a
congenital heart defect occurring concurrently with—but unrelated
to—the pectus excavatum. Clinical signs can be progressive, and in
some cases, life-threatening. A mild to severe dorsal deviation of the
caudal sternebrae with corresponding deviation of the cardiac
silhouette are the most common radiographic changes. Treatment
depends on the severity of the deformity and associated signs, and
ranges from conservative management to surgical repair.

DIAPHRAGM
Anatomy
The diaphragm is the musculotendinous partition between the
thoracic and abdominal cavities.60 The muscular portion is
composed of the pars lumbalis, attaching to the ventral aspect of the
third and fourth lumbar vertebrae (forming the left and right crura);
the pars costalis, which attaches to ribs 8-13; and the pars sternalis,
attaching to the xiphoid cartilage of the sternum.

FIGURE 222.8 Chondrosarcoma of a rib.
Dorsoventral thoracic radiograph of a 10-year-old

FIGURE 222.9 Lateral thoracic radiograph of a

Diseases
Diaphragmatic Hernia (Traumatic)
The most common disease of the diaphragm is traumatic rupture,
often secondary to vehicular trauma or falls. With rupture, varying
amounts of abdominal viscera become displaced cranial to the
diaphragm; the most frequently herniated organ in the cat is the
liver, followed by small intestine, stomach, omentum, spleen,
pancreas, and large intestine.61 A similar order of organ herniation is
present in reports in the dog (liver, small bowel, stomach, spleen,
omentum).62,63
Clinical signs of acute diaphragmatic hernia most often are related
to respiratory compromise, and include dyspnea, coughing, exercise
intolerance, or lethargy. On thoracic radiographs, herniated organs
may be visualized cranial to the diaphragm, especially if gas-filled,

such as the stomach or intestine (Figure 222.10). The displaced
liver or spleen (solid organs) may be difficult to differentiate from
pleural effusion or pulmonary consolidation. Cranial displacement of
abdominal organs, or absence of visualization in their normal
location, may be noted. Pleural effusion (ch. 220) often is present,
especially with chronic diaphragmatic hernias.63 Not all
diaphragmatic hernias are recognized immediately, likely due to
minimal clinical signs, poorly defined radiographic changes, or lack
of awareness of a traumatic incident. Clinical signs of chronic hernias
may be nonspecific, and include anorexia, lethargy, vomiting, or
weight loss. Not all patients have respiratory signs. US and CT are
beneficial as adjunct imaging modalities for the detection of
abdominal viscera cranial to the diaphragm, especially when pleural
effusion obscures visualization on thoracic radiographs.
Caval foraminal hernias have been reported in both dogs and cats,
and mimic caudal pulmonary masses.64-66 Most commonly the right
lateral liver lobe (less often right medial lobe) is herniated through
the caudal vena caval foramen, ventral to the thoracic portion of the
caudal vena cava. Varying degrees of vena cava compression by the
herniated liver lobe can occur, possibly resulting in Budd-Chiari-like
syndrome (ch. 239). It has not been determined if these hernias are
acquired or congenital, but they are often diagnosed incidentally. If
clinical signs are present, they are typically nonspecific (anorexia,
lethargy, vomiting, weight loss). Radiographically, the hernia creates
a round, soft-tissue mass, abutting the diaphragm in the
caudoventral thorax (Figure 222.11, A, B). CT is very helpful in
differentiating pulmonary mass from herniated liver lobe, as well as
assessing any degree of vena cava compression or involvement of
biliary structures (Figure 222.11, C, D).

Peritoneopericardial Diaphragmatic Hernia
Peritoneopericardial diaphragmatic hernia (PPDH) is discussed with
pericardial diseases (ch. 235).

Hiatal Hernia
Hiatal hernias (Figure 222.12) are discussed with disorders of the
esophagus (ch. 259).

OVERVIEW
A patient with concurrent heart disease and kidney disease poses a
dilemma because of intravascular volume. A normal or slightly
increased circulating blood volume is important for maintaining
glomerular filtration, but in a patient with heart disease, increasing
blood volume (such as with parenteral fluid administration) also

risks causing congestive heart failure (CHF). Conversely, a reduction
in circulating blood volume is the goal of diuretic treatment in
patients with CHF, and yet pursuing this goal in a patient with
concurrent chronic kidney disease (CKD) can decrease glomerular
filtration rate (GFR). Thus, managing a patient who has disorders of
both organ systems requires finding a balance within a range of
intravascular pressures that is narrower than would be tolerated by a
healthy individual.
The coexistence of cardiac and kidney disease in the same patient
is referred to by many names, including the cardiorenal syndrome1
and cardiovascular-renal axis (CVRA) disorders.2 The latter term is
most appropriate in veterinary internal medicine. The basic principle
of vascular over-/underload is common to humans and small
animals, and several essential pathways are shared among these
species (Figure 223.1), notably the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone
system.3 However, there are certain species-specific differences that
differentiate human and veterinary cardiac-renal comorbidities. This
makes CVRA a more accurate term for veterinary use.

CARDIORENAL SYNDROME IN
HUMANS
In humans, the definition of cardiac-renal pathophysiologic
interactions has evolved, from emphasizing an end-stage time frame
originally (“worsening renal function limiting diuresis despite
obvious clinical volume overload”4) to more of a bidirectional
interaction (“a spectrum of disorders involving both the heart and
kidneys in which acute or chronic dysfunction in 1 organ may induce
acute or chronic dysfunction in the other organ”1). This change
indicates an acknowledgment that cardiac disease may be a patient’s
predominant issue and kidney disease a less-pressing concern
(“cardiorenal”), or vice-versa (“renocardiac”). Veterinary patients are
similarly affected, with one of the two disorders usually being
clinically more severe than the other.2 However, the implication that
dysfunction in one system is independently responsible for

worsening in the other in a way that should alter treatment is not
proven in animals.
The types of diseases that cause cardiac and renal dysfunction
superficially are similar in humans and in dogs and cats. CHF and
CKD are the prototypes, respectively. However, the pathophysiologic
mechanisms are often quite different. The most common heart
disease in human adults in industrialized countries is
atherosclerosis, a chronic coronary artery-based disorder in which
dyslipidemias, inflammation, and platelet-coronary interactions play
pivotal roles.5 Although early findings offer intriguing insights into
inflammation and feline hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM),6
these mechanisms are not known to provide a therapeutic target for
any frequently-encountered heart disease of dogs or cats. The most
common cause of CKD in humans is diabetes mellitus (DM),
accounting for nearly half of all cases of end-stage kidney disease
requiring dialysis or transplant.7 While the lesions of diabetic
nephropathy are similar in cats and humans (ch. 292), the disease
burden in cats is insignificant on a population basis, likely because
the prevalence of DM in humans (estimated 10.5% of the US
population in 2021)7 is at least an order of magnitude greater than in
cats, for example (0.25-1%) (ch. 292). Another important cause of
renal dysfunction in humans is renal artery stenosis, a disorder that
is currently of little clinical importance in veterinary practice.

FIGURE 223.1 Putative pathophysiologic

Together, obesity, atherogenic dyslipidemia, elevated blood
pressure, insulin resistance and elevated blood glucose, a prothrombotic state, and a pro-inflammatory state are said to define the
metabolic syndrome, a cluster of disorders that is responsible for
rising morbidity and mortality in industrialized nations.8 The obesity
epidemic in companion animals could involve the emergence of
some of these pathologic processes, but no equivalent to the
metabolic syndrome with these components has been identified to
date as a significant clinical entity in small animal medicine.

Therefore, the concept of a narrower-than-normal range of
tolerance for hyper- or hypovolemia is common to both humans and
animals with cardiorenal disorders, but the underlying disease
mechanisms and consequences of the primary disease processes are
at best partially shared. This has important implications for optimal
treatment and prevention strategies in dogs and cats. For example,
there is rapidly growing interest in SGLT-2 inhibitors for treating
humans with coronary artery disease and diabetes9 but this class of
drugs is mechanistically more limited in its scope of applications to
dogs compared to people.

CARDIOVASCULAR-RENAL AXIS
DISORDERS IN DOGS AND CATS
In veterinary medicine, the fact that treating one organ system may
come at the expense of the function of the other in patients with both
cardiac and kidney disease has been known for many decades.
Largely, this has led to conservative (often referred to as cautious)
management of intravascular fluid volume. In practical terms,
veterinarians might reduce parenteral fluid doses when treating a
dog or cat that has CKD if that animal also has concurrent heart
disease, and might use lower dosages of diuretics when treating an
animal in CHF if that animal is azotemic. While these approaches are
logical, the optimal amount of change that should be applied, and
which patients benefit more (or less) from these changes, is
unknown.
A unifying mechanism continues to be sought that could explain
the coexistence of heart disease and kidney disease in an animal
patient, but no such common track has been identified between CKD
and any of the principal heart diseases of dogs or cats. Definitive
documentation of CHF through direct or surrogate intracardiac
pressure measurements and of renal dysfunction through
assessment of GFR10 is rarely described in veterinary publications.
Recent developments have provided intriguing new information
regarding CVRA disorders (Table 223.1). While these findings offer
additional insights on coexistent CKD and heart disease in small

animals, their immediate utility for guiding treatment and
prognostication is limited.

The current state of knowledge regarding mechanisms of CVRA
disorders in dogs clinically centers on abnormalities known to
involve both systems. The following is an abbreviated list of
abnormalities that occur with CVRA disorders, affect the CVRA, or
both.

HYPOKALEMIA
Hypokalemia is common in both heart disease and CKD. Animals
with CHF are treated with diuretics and the first choice is loop
diuretics (furosemide, torsemide). These are potassium-wasting

drugs that routinely cause hypokalemia.11,12 Hypokalemia also is
common in animals with CKD (e.g., 20-30% of cats with CKD; ch.
301) due to urinary potassium loss, decreased intake, and decreased
muscle mass as a reservoir of intracellular potassium. The
consequences of hypokalemia can be polysystemic (ch. 68). In the
heart, hypokalemia decreases K+ channel conductance, which
prolongs action potential duration. It does so heterogeneously in the
myocardium (dispersion of repolarization), which, together with
intracellular Na+ and Ca2+ effects, predisposes the heart to early
afterdepolarizations and thus, to tachyarrhythmias.12 Furthermore,
hypokalemia causes resistance to class I antiarrhythmics like
lidocaine. Therefore, hypokalemic patients are more likely to have
tachyarrhythmias that are refractory to antiarrhythmic treatment.
Hypokalemia also is associated with muscular weakness and
inappetence in cats, notably causing lethargy and neck ventroflexion
if severe (Video 68.1), and also constipation (ch. 301).

Of note,

hyperkalemia also must be avoided because of its potentially
catastrophic cardiac effects. Hyperkalemia can occur in patients with
kidney disease but usually in the context of oliguria/anuria or
urinary tract rupture. Factitious hyperkalemia (from analyzing
serum instead of plasma) occurs in dogs and cats13,14 and could
artifactually normalize a hypokalemic result; therefore, heparinized
samples (e.g., Vacutainer green-top tube) are most accurate for
determining circulating potassium concentration.

SYSTEMIC HYPERTENSION
CKD is the most common cause of systemic hypertension (e.g., 2065% prevalence in cats with CKD; ch. 236). Heart disease does not
cause systemic hypertension in animals (neither directly nor
indirectly). Thus, the heart is the victim in systemic hypertension,
not the culprit. Target organs that can be damaged in systemic
hypertension include the heart (increased afterload increases
myocardial oxygen demand and can worsen mitral valve
regurgitation) and the kidney itself (increased nephron loss).

ANEMIA
Anemia occurs commonly in CKD (ch. 301) and has been reported
in 47%, 71% and 82% of dogs with International Renal Interest
Society (IRIS) stages 2, 3, and 4 CKD, respectively.15 By reducing
oxygen delivery to myocardium, anemia can predispose to
arrhythmogenesis. Anemia also contributes to a vicious circle by
decreasing oxygen delivery to renal tissue, further decreasing
erythropoietin production. Disparate results have been encountered
regarding anemia in dogs with heart disease, with 2 studies
indicating its increasing prevalence with worsening heart disease and
its negative prognostic significance16,17 and 2 others showing a lack
of association between anemia and severity of heart disease.18,19 This
issue is confounded by hemoconcentration due to diuretics, which
could mask anemia.19

OUTCOME
In veterinary medicine, the optimal management and specific
outcome of patients with CVRA disorders are unknown. Since the
cardiac and renal components often are incurable, the assumption
can be made that dogs and cats with CVRA disorders have a poor
prognosis. This assumption represents a simplification that may or
may not serve a patient and its owner well. For example, an animal
whose family is only able or willing to provide a short course of
treatment with an expectation of cure will seldom be well served if
the patient has a CVRA disorder. Conversely, applying such a blanket
perspective to all patients can be expected to cause simple and logical
aspects of case management to be overlooked, and to lead some
animals to be euthanized prematurely. Ultimately, identifying and
correcting abnormalities that often occur with CVRA disorders
(Tables 223.2 and 223.3) can make the most of an otherwise
guarded prognosis, if this is what the animal’s owner wishes.

MANAGEMENT

In human cardiorenal syndrome, management is aimed at reversing
the primary disease processes causing cardiac disorders, renal
disorders, or both.20 The therapeutic targets (e.g., dyslipidemia and
other contributors to coronary artery disease, DM as a principal
cause of CKD) and options (e.g., end-of-life and palliative care
without euthanasia) are different from those encountered in
veterinary medicine. In the author’s experience, the focus in
veterinary medicine usually is different. A stronger emphasis is
placed on avoiding iatrogenic complications related to CVRA
disorders, such as how to best manage parenteral fluid
administration in a dog or cat that has a heart murmur, or how much
diuretic to give to a CHF patient that is azotemic. Management of
simultaneous end-stage or extremely advanced diseases in
companion animals (e.g., concurrent IRIS stage 4 CKD and
American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine [ACVIM] stage D
heart disease decompensating simultaneously in the same patient)
occurs, but it seems to draw less clinical attention than avoidance of
iatrogenic cardiorenal complications. Therefore, management
techniques and goals are difficult to translate from human to
veterinary medicine, and a great shortage of objective information
exists to guide veterinarians managing patients with CVRA
disorders. The following observations and approaches represent a
combination of existing evidence and clinical practice.

ACUTE VERSUS CHRONIC
MANAGEMENT
The time frame surrounding a patient’s clinical presentation should
guide the interventions to be applied. For example, a dog or cat with
a CVRA disorder that is in fulminant CHF and has subclinical
azotemia requires diuretic treatment, even though the azotemia is
likely to become more severe when higher dosages of diuretic are
used acutely to control CHF, e.g., 3-4 mg/kg furosemide IV PRN (ch.
229). Although subjecting the kidneys to decreased perfusion
(prerenal azotemia) can be necessary for the patient to survive the
CHF crisis, the use of such high diuretic dosages is brief; prolonged
use of high-dose diuretics should be avoided to minimize the

risk/magnitude of actual renal damage. Prolonged use of high-dose
diuretics may also lead to iatrogenic dehydration (systemic signs and
renal injury possible) and iatrogenic hypokalemia (systemic signs
and cardiac arrhythmias possible). Long-term dosages need to be
reduced based on the patient’s response, as acute management ends
and chronic management begins—typically in the first 24-36 hours.
The underlying lesion in DMVD and many other cardiac disorders in
small animal practice usually cannot be eliminated, so chronic
management of CHF involves using the least amount of diuretic that
controls or avoids cardiogenic pulmonary edema and body cavity
effusions. Thus, dietary sodium restriction (while maintaining
palatability) is logical in the chronic stage, meaning after the patient
has been discharged and is home and eating well (ch. 157). Acute
and chronic approaches often are substantially different (Tables
223.2 and 223.3).

INTRAVASCULAR FLUID VOLUME
Finding a patient’s optimal fluid balance while avoiding over- or
underhydration can be challenging. In hospital, it is appropriate to
change intravenous (IV) fluid types from sodium-rich to sodiumlimited once a dehydrated patient is euvolemic, to avoid sodium (and
therefore fluid) overload. An example is to change from lactated
Ringer’s solution or 0.9% sodium chloride IV during fluid
resuscitation to 0.45% sodium chloride with or without 2.5%
dextrose for maintenance once a patient is euvolemic21; the risk of
negative pancreatic beta-cell effects must be considered when
deciding whether to include dextrose in maintenance fluids for
cats.20a The volume to be delivered remains the same as would
otherwise be calculated based on assessment of a patient’s hydration
and fluid losses (ch. 120). Monitoring is critical, because early
detection of intravascular volume overload can lead to modifications
that avoid more serious complications. In the early stage of
iatrogenic fluid overload, fluid leaks from the vascular space into the
interstitial space. In the lungs, this interferes with gas exchange,
reflected in an increased respiratory rate. If not identified and
managed, the fluid overload can progress to leakage from the

interstitial space into the alveoli, further worsening gas exchange.
This sequence of iatrogenic problems is best avoided by careful
notation of changes in respiratory patterns. In the kidneys,
interstitial edema from volume overload increases intracapsular
pressure because each kidney is contained within an inelastic renal
capsule. This increased pressure causes a decrease in GFR, leading in
turn to decreased urine production which could exacerbate volume
overload. The cornerstones of effective assessment of intravascular
fluid volume expansion are surprisingly simple: monitoring of
respiratory rate and effort, body weight, and urine output; and
cardiac auscultation to note the onset of a gallop sound (Table
223.2). These are accessible to any veterinarian and are of great
value in optimal patient care. In critical states, they should be
assessed as often as every 1-2 hours (for respiratory rate and effort),
q 6 hours (gallop sound), and q 12 hours (body weight). Noting
trends in these parameters during a patient’s hospitalization is useful
for deciding when a patient shows evidence of excessive
intravascular volume expansion. The practice of simultaneously
administering diuretics and either subcutaneous (SQ) or IV fluids is
discouraged. While the idea of providing “renal protection” with fluid
therapy to an azotemic patient receiving diuretics is wellintentioned, the two treatments are mutually antagonistic by virtue
of administering and simultaneously removing water, sodium, and
other electrolytes. An emphasis on enteral hydration, such as placing
a nasogastric tube or using a patient’s existing esophagostomy tube
(ch. 81) to deliver a fluid complement by this route rather than IV,
has gained popularity in recent years. Anecdotal reports of the
greater safety of this route and lower risk of iatrogenic CHF in
patients with existing heart disease remain to be investigated
objectively. Home monitoring of intravascular volume status
revolves principally around having an owner assess resting
respiratory effort and rate (ch. 229).22 Doing so can provide
objective information that allows appropriate titration of treatments
(e.g., home administration of SQ fluids to a uremic cat with CKD and
concurrent ACVIM stage B2 HCM).

effusions (versus higher
diuretic dosages).

CHF, Congestive heart failure; CKD, chronic kidney disease; C&S,
culture and sensitivity; UTI, urinary tract infection.

INCITING CAUSES
In general, both adult-onset heart diseases and CKD have an
irreversible and protracted course, with preclinical stages typically
lasting months to years. Knowing whether clinical worsening is due
to deterioration of the primary problem, or to a separate event, is
important. This is because one implies permanent disease
progression whereas the other may be correctable in the moment
and avoidable in the future. For example, animals with cardiacdominant CVRA disorders often present with acute or recurrent
CHF. This can be due to worsening of the cardiac lesion, or to a
parallel disturbance such as acute sodium ingestion (treats from
well-meaning individuals, dietary indiscretion), acute tachycardia
(excitement, exercise, fear), or miscommunication around
medication schedules. These complicating factors are more likely if
the cardiac structure has not changed (e.g., similar
echocardiographic findings compared to prior to CHF) and they
seem to carry a better prognosis, since decompensation to CHF is not
caused by inherent worsening of cardiac structure. Therefore, such
inciting causes should be inquired about during collection of the
medical history. Similarly, in animals with renal-dominant CVRA
disorders, urinary tract infection (e.g., pyelonephritis; ch. 304) can
be detected and treated, leading to improved renal function.

HYPOKALEMIA
Correction of hypokalemia (ch. 68) can benefit both patients with
CVRA disorders that are cardiac-predominant and those that are
renal-predominant. Oral supplementation with potassium gluconate
(e.g., 4 mEq/cat PO q24h) significantly increases serum and muscle
potassium content in cats with CKD.23 A typical dosage for dogs is 28 mEq/dog PO q12h, based on approximate body weight and severity
of hypokalemia, and the final dosage in either species is adjusted to
achieve normokalemia, barring adverse effects such as inappetence.

While oral KCl is available in the form of salt substitutes in
supermarkets, it is not palatable to many dogs and cats and may
cause signs of nausea. Flavored or coated potassium gluconate
supplements (e.g., MicroK) are usually a better choice. For dogs or
cats that are receiving furosemide or torsemide for CHF,
spironolactone 1-2 mg/kg PO q12h can be added if there is evidence
of recurrent, mild pulmonary edema or pleural/abdominal effusion
or it can replace part of the existing diuretic dose (ch. 229). As a
potassium-sparing diuretic, it increases circulating potassium
concentration and provides a more balanced diuretic effect
(sequential nephron blockade). Finally, hypokalemia can be
improved by decreasing the dosage of furosemide or torsemide
outright if a patient with a CVRA disorder transitions to eating a
lower-sodium food; a lower dietary sodium intake means less
diuretic effect is needed, and therefore, less potassium wasting
occurs.

SYSTEMIC HYPERTENSION
The high prevalence of systemic hypertension in patients with CKD
means it should be screened for accurately and consistently in this
patient population (ch. 91). Treatment of confirmed systemic
hypertension, typically with amlodipine or an angiotensin-receptor
blocker (ch. 236), can carry benefits at both cardiac and renal levels.

DIETARY SODIUM CONTENT
Sodium content of commercially available dog and cat foods varies
by up to 20-fold. Since the purpose of diuretics is to promote
natriuresis, and dysregulated sodium homeostasis can occur in CKD,
substantial sodium ingestions should be avoided in patients with
CVRA disorders. Palatability remains paramount and various
techniques can be used for maintaining a patient’s appetite while
limiting excesses in dietary sodium content (chs. 151, 157, 158). In
general, there is no known benefit to restricting sodium content
below a maintenance diet level in patients with subclinical (ACVIM
stage B1 or B2) heart disease. Rather, peaks of sodium ingestion need

to be avoided (see above). Therapeutic diets that are formulated for
management of lower urinary tract disease may be high in sodium
content by design, to promote diuresis and thus reduce the risk of
urolith formation through dilution of urine (ch. 159). A patient who
has experienced CHF and needs a urolith prevention diet should be
transitioned on to a lower-sodium stone diet, or may require a slight
increase in diuretic dosage to offset the increased dietary sodium
content. It is important to note that the diuretic medication alone
may achieve the goal of urinary dilution. Such a patient, or any dog
or cat in this situation who has not experienced CHF, should have its
resting respiratory rate and effort monitored closely at home by its
owner.

CLIENT COMMUNICATION AND
EXPECTATIONS (CH. 1)
Like appropriate intravascular volume, client expectations regarding
patients with CVRA disorders exist on a spectrum between two
extremes. The irreversible nature of most cardiac and renal diseases
that occur concurrently means that ongoing care and follow-up are
almost certain to be needed. Therefore, a client whose perspective or
resources require a simple one-time treatment is unlikely to be
satisfied with ongoing care of a patient with a CVRA disorder.
Conversely, when a grim prognosis is assumed by an owner, whether
from personal concern or knowledge acquired from acquaintances or
online, the ability to achieve a stable and thriving state might be
overlooked. In general, a guarded prognosis and the need for
ongoing care are almost certain in the majority of CVRA cases. Still,
many principles and techniques described in this chapter involve
adjustments and practical approaches that can restore an animal’s
well-being for a period of time that can only be known when it is
undertaken.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Heart Disease and Kidney Disease
WHAT IS IT?
Animals can develop heart health problems and kidney health
problems, often with age. Treatments for heart problems may place
some strain on the kidneys, and likewise, treatments for kidney
problems may place some strain on the heart. Therefore, taking care
of an animal who has both heart and kidney problems at the same
time is a delicate balance.

WHY DOES IT MATTER?
Heart problems exist in a whole range of severity, from minor to
severe. More heart problems are minor than they are severe in dogs
and cats. Similarly, kidney problems range from minor to severe,
likewise with more of a minor degree predominating. Treatment of
either heart or kidney problems rarely involves surgery in animals.
Rather, medications are given that control symptoms and try to delay
the longer-term consequences of the heart and kidney issue. The
concern in any dog or cat with simultaneous heart and kidney
problems is to treat the greater concern enough without causing
complications for the other. For example, injectable fluids given IV
or under the skin are a common type of treatment for significant
kidney disease. In some dogs or cats who have heart disease in
addition to their kidney disease, the fluid may travel to the lungs and
cause difficult breathing. Another example is a patient with heart
problems who needs to take a diuretic medication like furosemide or
torsemide. These medications help significantly with reducing fluid
retention caused by heart disease, but in doing so, they can increase
the workload of the kidneys. Therefore, dogs and cats who have both
heart and kidney issues almost always need an individualized
medication plan and follow-up visits to adjust the treatments over

time. Compared to most other dogs and cats, they usually need to be
monitored more closely. This means both rechecks with the
veterinarian and monitoring at home.

WHAT CAN I DO ABOUT IT?
If animals have both heart problems and kidney problems, they need
to be monitored more closely at home for fluid accumulation in the
lungs. Labored breathing or persistently rapid and uncomfortable
breathing are symptoms that warrant a call or visit to the
veterinarian. Home monitoring involves a dog or cat’s family
member or caretaker counting the resting respiratory rate when the
dog or cat is resting or asleep, to be sure it remains less than 30
breaths per minute (cats) or less than 40 breaths per minute (dogs).
Any number less than this is reassuring because it means fluid
retention in the body, and especially the lungs, is unlikely. A higher
number warrants a call to the veterinarian if it is maintained for
minutes to hours and is not caused by an obvious external source like
hot weather or exercise.
Animals with kidney problems and heart problems also need to be
monitored closely at home for symptoms that might indicate
decreased kidney function. Most often, this appears as a sense of
feeling sluggish, less interested in food, and possibly showing nausea
or vomiting. Since these kinds of symptoms can worsen once they
start if they are not treated, it is worth calling or making an
appointment to see a veterinarian if these symptoms occur.

WHAT SHOULD I EXPECT?
The combination of heart disease and kidney disease is often quite
serious. Regrettably, even with treatment, it shortens the lifespan of
most dogs and cats who have it. Almost inevitably, in order to finetune treatments, veterinary rechecks will be needed on a regular
basis. Many animals have reserves in their heart and kidney
functions, and medications are intended to make the most of that
and to relieve symptoms. Even so, a best-case scenario is usually to
have a dog or cat feeling somewhat better, even if not fully back to
normal, and to see how long that can be maintained. In some
animals, despite all efforts, this is only a matter of days, whereas in
other animals, months or more can be expected. The outlook

Mellitus and Corticosteroid-Responsive
Disease
Lucy J. Davison

AC RO N YM
NSAID nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug

Corticosteroids are an important category of drugs used in veterinary medicine, with a wide range of
indications (Table 224.1) (chs. 143, 144, and 169). Diabetic dogs and cats commonly suffer from
concurrent diseases which require corticosteroid treatment; however, this situation leaves the clinician
with a dilemma. In such patients, the anticipated benefit of corticosteroid treatment must be carefully
weighed up against the potentially detrimental effects that corticosteroids may have on glycemic control,
such as profound insulin resistance. There is also the possibility that a pre-diabetic patient may become
overtly diabetic once treated with corticosteroids.

BACKGROUND
The prescription of corticosteroids for canine and feline patients is a delicate balancing act, where
indication, route of delivery and dosage must be considered and optimized for each individual patient.
For the theoretical reasons outlined in this chapter, many clinicians might, understandably, choose to
avoid corticosteroids in diabetic patients altogether, but this is not strictly necessary, and their judicious
use can be extremely helpful. For example, in some debilitating and painful conditions such as immunemediated polyarthritis (ch. 177), the inclusion of an anti-inflammatory dose of corticosteroid in the
therapeutic regimen can have a dramatic effect on improving the quality of life of the patient. In
addition, resolving active inflammation using corticosteroids in the diabetic patient can, in some cases,
actually lead to an improvement in glycemic control, when the comorbidity is antagonistic to glycemic
control. For example, in the classic feline inflammatory “triaditis” presentation of chronic pancreatitis,
inflammatory bowel disease and cholangiohepatitis (ch. 225), an anti-inflammatory dosage of
prednisolone can paradoxically help to improve insulin sensitivity in some cats, presumably by reducing
the severity of inflammation, which is a possible cause of insulin resistance. The challenge for the
clinician is to identify the lowest effective steroid dosage, the most appropriate dosing frequency, and
the least impactful route of delivery for the diabetic patient.

CORTICOSTEROIDS AND THEIR ACTIONS
Corticosteroids are synthetic analogues of the natural adrenocortical hormones (e.g., cortisol). They can
have a combination of glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activities (ch. 144).1 Glucocorticoid actions
include effects on carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism, insulin antagonism, as well as dosedependent anti-inflammatory, immunosuppressive, vasoconstrictive and antineoplastic properties.
Mineralocorticoid activity mimics naturally occurring aldosterone and its impacts on electrolyte and
water balance in the renal tubules, primarily leading to sodium and water retention, with potassium loss.

In the case of corticosteroid treatment of diabetic patients, it is often the glucocorticoid effect of insulin
antagonism that is most challenging to overcome, because of its impact on glycemic control and
appetite. Glucocorticoid activity is mediated via the glucocorticoid receptor in the cytosol, which is
widely expressed. Therefore, systemic steroid therapy affects many body systems.2 In dogs, ex vivo
studies of peripheral mononuclear cells treated with dexamethasone indicate that glucocorticoids affect
the metabolism of these important immune cells, with a notable fall in adenosine triphosphate being
detected.3 Glucocorticoids alter the expression of many anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory genes,
with the overall effect of reducing inflammatory and immune responses. Corticosteroids are therefore
the treatment of choice in many immune-mediated and inflammatory conditions (ch. 169).4 In addition
to their effects on the immune system, corticosteroids also affect metabolism, with a net effect of raising
blood glucose,5,6 which is undesirable in diabetic patients. Glucocorticoids stimulate gluconeogenesis in
the liver by increasing the expression of the enzymes involved in generating glucose from amino acids
and glycerol.5,7 They also promote lipolysis, amino acid mobilisation from tissues, and they antagonise
insulin, inhibiting the uptake of glucose into tissues. In a healthy animal, the reduction in peripheral
insulin sensitivity can be compensated for by an increase in beta cell function, but hyperglycemia occurs
if this compensation is not fully effective.2

CORTICOSTEROID COMPOUNDS
Corticosteroid compounds have variable glucocorticoid to mineralocorticoid activity ratios, side-effects,
potencies, and durations of action (Table 224.2), ranging from predominantly glucocorticoid effects to
predominantly mineralocorticoid effects.7-9 In addition to parenteral formulations, a number of topical
(eye, ear, skin) and inhaled preparations also contain glucocorticoid at anti-inflammatory dosages. Since
corticosteroids are generally metabolized by the hepatic p450 system, topical application bypasses the
liver and its first-pass effect, minimizing dosages required and associated side-effects.7 Other steroid
preparations include budesonide—a glucocorticoid designed for humans with Crohn’s disease which
undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism (therefore having a local effect in the intestine, but
not systemically),10 which may be used to limit systemic steroid side-effects in gastrointestinal disease.
Steroids such as fluticasone and budesonide may also be used in an inhaled form for respiratory disease
(chs. 90, 215).11 Systemic effects have been demonstrated in cats12 and in humans treated with inhaled
steroids, which can have a negative impact on glycemic control13,14; however, in practice, topical and
inhaled steroids appear to be minimally disruptive to glycemic control in dogs and cats.

One of the most commonly used corticosteroids in veterinary medicine is prednisolone, because of its
high glucocorticoid to mineralocorticoid activity ratio. Prednisone is activated to prednisolone in the
liver. It is less well absorbed orally and less well activated in cats,15 so prednisolone is preferred in this
species. Dexamethasone has a similar glucocorticoid to mineralocorticoid ratio to that of prednisolone
but is more potent.8,9 It is available in an injectable formulation and has a longer duration of activity.
Cortisone and hydrocortisone are the least potent glucocorticoids, although their higher
mineralocorticoid activity can benefit patients with hypoadrenocorticism. The most commonly used
mineralocorticoid drug is fludrocortisone, which is prescribed orally in cases of hypoadrenocorticism.
Although high dosages may result in signs of glucocorticoid excess, including hyperglycemia, this sideeffect is rare. The other major side-effect of mineralocorticoid drugs such as fludrocortisone and
desoxycorticosterone pivalate (which does not have any glucocorticoid activity) is potassium wasting.
Therefore, it is important that plasma electrolyte concentrations be monitored during therapy, especially
in diabetic patients where insulin may also reduce circulating potassium concentrations.

CORTICOSTEROID THERAPY AND POTENTIAL SIDEEFFECTS IN CANINE AND FELINE DIABETIC PATIENTS
A key difference between diabetes in dogs (ch. 291) and cats (ch. 292) is that feline patients can enter
diabetic remission, especially if good glycemic control and optimal body weight can be achieved,
whereas remission is an unlikely scenario in dogs. Therefore, it is common sense, where possible, to
avoid the use of steroids in cats that have been previously diabetic but have entered remission, since
diabetes may recur. Similarly, it may also be wise to avoid corticosteroid therapy, where possible, in
non-diabetic cats with known feline diabetes risk factors—especially obesity, since they may already be
pre-diabetic.16 Dogs receiving corticosteroid therapy also have an increased risk of diabetes, so it is

prudent to avoid corticosteroid therapy in dogs with known diabetes risk factors such as chronic
pancreatitis or high-risk breeds such as the Samoyed.17

SIDE-EFFECTS OF STEROID THERAPY
The main concern of any clinician when prescribing corticosteroids is that the side-effects may be more
detrimental than the disease being treated. This is a valid concern, as corticosteroids have a known
range of potential side-effects, even in otherwise healthy patients. The risk of side-effects increases with
dosage and duration of treatment but it is important to note that they are highly variable between
individual patients receiving similar doses.4 This may be due to variability in the number or activity of
glucocorticoid receptors. Some patients immediately become polyphagic, polyuric and polydipsic,
develop hair thinning, and lose significant muscle mass, whereas others show very limited side-effects.
Dogs appear to suffer more steroid side-effects than cats do, and cats appear more tolerant of higher
dosages, although the risk of diabetes being induced by corticosteroids may be higher in cats. It is also
likely that very young and very old patients may be more susceptible to steroid side-effects. Certain
medications may also interact with glucocorticoids, e.g., ketoconazole (may decrease glucocorticoid
metabolism), digoxin (may result in hypokalaemia if given with prednisolone) and thus concurrent
treatment with additional medications may increase the risk of detrimental effects of corticosteroid
therapy. With long-term glucocorticoid use, especially at high dosages, dogs and cats may develop the
classic clinical signs of (iatrogenic) hyperadrenocorticism such as abdominal enlargement, muscle
wasting, polyphagia, bilaterally symmetrical alopecia, polyuria, and polydipsia (chs. 293 and 294).
Other potential corticosteroid side-effects, in addition to insulin resistance-induced hyperglycemia, may
include osteoporosis, destabilisation of cardiovascular disease,18 systemic hypertension, muscle wasting,
proteinuria, a hypercoagulable state, and increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections.19
Significant plasma lipidome alterations are another consequence of glucocorticoid exposure in dogs,
with these changes becoming more severe with long-term exposure.20

SIDE-EFFECTS OF STEROID THERAPY IN DIABETIC
PATIENTS
Clearly all the steroid side-effects discussed above are undesirable in diabetic patients, especially insulin
resistance. Indeed, there is the potential for certain steroid side-effects to be more common or severe in
diabetic patients, especially where there is insulin resistance present already, for several reasons. First,
the majority of diabetic dogs21 and cats22 are middle-aged or older, so they are more likely to have preexisting conditions, e.g., renal or cardiac disease that may be exacerbated by steroid therapy. Second,
there is considerable overlap in the clinical signs of diabetes and the side-effects of steroid therapy (e.g.,
polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, dyslipidemia, steroid hepatopathy), so additive effects, where a
particular clinical sign like polyphagia is exacerbated by steroid treatment, may be seen. Third, diabetic
patients are already at increased risk of infection21,23 due to persistent hyperglycemia, so the addition of
steroids may exacerbate this, allowing infection to develop or progress, with a consequent further
detrimental effect on glycemic control. Although some effects of initiating corticosteroid treatment may
be predictable and dose-dependent, the response of the diabetic patient depends on a range of individual
factors4 including the presence of pre-existing insulin resistance syndromes (e.g., acromegaly in cats;
diestrus in dogs), the presence of infection, the presence of inflammatory disease, and the level of
glycemic control currently being achieved in the patient at the time the treatment is started.
Corticosteroid-induced insulin resistance without adequate adjustment of insulin therapy may have
catastrophic consequences, including the development of diabetic ketoacidosis or non-ketotic
hyperosmolar syndrome (ch. 290). Conversely, overzealous increases in insulin dosage because of
anticipated insulin resistance due to corticosteroid treatment may lead to dangerous hypoglycemic
episodes, so this must also be avoided.

DECISION-MAKING IN TREATING CORTICOSTEROIDRESPONSIVE DISEASE IN DIABETIC PATIENTS
The decision to use corticosteroid-based medications in diabetic patients is a challenging one and risks
must be weighed against benefits (Figure 224.1). Corticosteroids are preferred to other drugs in many
allergic, inflammatory and autoimmune conditions because of their effectiveness and rapid action,4 but
if a suitable alternative is available, then this should always be considered in diabetic patients (Table
224.1). There are some situations, however, where there is no alternative to steroid therapy. For
example, in cortisol deficiency associated with hypoadrenocorticism, a daily physiologic replacement
dose of corticosteroid is a necessary requirement whether the patient is diabetic or not.24 Steroids are
also used commonly in diabetic patients in some referral scenarios associated with management of
diabetes-causing syndromes. For example, in cats with hypersomatotropism and diabetes,
hydrocortisone is used routinely following hypophysectomy, to prevent iatrogenic
hypoadrenocorticism.25 Following pituitary radiotherapy for hypersomatotropism, corticosteroids have
also been used to limit the risk of localized swelling and to reduce risk of hypoglycemia as insulin
requirements fall. If corticosteroids cannot be avoided, then where possible, topical or local (e.g.,
inhaled) therapy may be preferable if appropriate, since this may limit systemic side-effects.

FIGURE 224.1 Use of corticosteroids in diabetic patients. IMHA, Immunemediated hemolytic anemia; NSAID, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug.

Steroid Treatment of Human Patients and Impact on Glycemic Control

Guidelines have existed since 1998 for steroid treatment of common steroid-responsive diseases such as
asthma, inflammatory bowel disease or autoimmune diseases in type 1 and type 2 human diabetic
patients,26 but no similar guidelines exist in veterinary medicine. The American Diabetes Association
and the European Association for the Study of Diabetes emphasize the requirement for close monitoring
and treatment targets which are individualized to each patient.27 While pre-emptive treatments to
stabilize blood glucose are tailored to the pharmacodynamics of the glucocorticoid being given,28,29
there is no consensus on best practice.30 There are likely to be species-specific differences between dogs,
cats, and humans, but it is still beneficial to review the broad principles behind the human guidelines. In
human studies, the effects of dexamethasone administration on blood glucose occur within a few hours
of steroid exposure and are dose-dependent, with high-dose therapy increasing insulin resistance
(characterized by depressed peripheral utilisation of glucose and impaired glucose transport31) in
patients with both pre-existing and new-onset diabetes.32 Human patients receiving steroid therapy
more than once daily tend to suffer from hyperglycemia throughout the day. Conversely, those receiving
prednisolone only once daily, in the morning, usually experience hyperglycemia only in the afternoon
and evening,26 with peak plasma prednisolone levels at 2-3 hours after intake returning to baseline
within 12 hours.33 Adaptation in beta cell function to dexamethasone-induced insulin resistance is
lacking in humans with low inherent insulin sensitivity34,35 and although dexamethasone-induced
hyperinsulinemia is usually accompanied by normoglycemia at rest, the dynamic dysregulation of
glucose homeostasis by steroids is emphasized by the presence of post-prandial hyperglycemia36 in
some steroid-treated individuals. This effect of poor compensation can also be seen in obese rodent
models37 and may be relevant to the use of corticosteroids in obese cats. Such cats are already likely to
have low insulin sensitivity and may therefore be at high risk of steroid-induced hyperglycemia and
diabetes.38
One steroid-responsive disease encountered in human diabetic patients is ulcerative colitis, which
serves as a good example to illustrate an individualized approach to steroid treatment in diabetic
patients. This involves assessment of the diabetes itself, as well as assessing the risks and benefits of
steroid therapy in the concurrent disease being managed. In ulcerative colitis, treatment is based mainly
on the activity and location of disease,39,40 and in severe cases, if the patient has concurrent diabetes
that is well-controlled, corticosteroids are the treatment of choice. Instigation of corticosteroid
treatment requires close monitoring of blood glucose, evaluation for potential sepsis and ketoacidosis, as
well as careful electrolyte control. However, in some ulcerative colitis patients with very unstable
diabetes mellitus, the risk of steroid treatment is considered too high and alternative drugs are used
such as cyclosporine or monoclonal antibody therapy.41 In more moderate ulcerative colitis with
concurrent diabetes, to avoid systemic steroids, topical or oral mesalazine and topical steroids such as
beclomethasone are recommended.

Evidence for Corticosteroid Impact on Glycemic Control in Cats
In one experimental study evaluating the effect of immunosuppressive steroid treatment on healthy cats,
significant increases in serum albumin, glucose, triglycerides and cholesterol were identified after 56
days of therapy.42 In a similar study, investigating the diabetogenic potential of prednisolone and
dexamethasone, 14 healthy cats received either daily prednisolone (4.4 mg/kg) or dexamethasone (0.55
mg/kg) for 56 days, followed by evaluation of urine glucose and serum fructosamine and glucose
tolerance. At the end of the study, several cats were glycosuric and fructosamine concentrations were
elevated, with a trend towards dexamethasone having a more marked impact on blood glucose than
prednisolone at the equipotent dose.6 In a separate study, healthy cats were treated with
methylprednisolone by injection, resulting in a substantial increase in serum glucose concentration at 3
to 6 days after administration. Importantly, variables only returned to baseline 16-24 days after
treatment,43,44 with response kinetics varying between individuals.

Evidence for Corticosteroid Impact on Glycemic Control in Dogs

In healthy dogs, methylprednisolone treatment significantly enhances gluconeogenesis and
hyperglycemia induced by norepinephrine. This effect is most marked if the glucocorticoid was given at
for at least 2 consecutive days prior to the epinephrine challenge, suggesting de novo synthesis of
gluconeogenic enzymes as well as more immediate effects.5 While there are also two case reports of dogs
being made transiently diabetic with prednisolone therapy,45,46 once diabetic, most dogs are likely to
remain diabetic, even if steroids are withdrawn. Topical dexamethasone applications (dermal and otic)
have been associated with an exaggerated rise in insulin in Beagles, despite normal serum glucose
levels47; upon drug withdrawal, it may take 1 week for insulin secretion to return to baseline. Similarly,
in atopic dogs treated with prednisolone, serum insulin concentration can increase even though serum
fructosamine and glucose concentrations do not; this emphasizes the need for functioning, reactive beta
cells to maintain euglycemia.48 Finally, in an experimental model of canine diabetes, glucose tolerance
and insulin sensitivity fall following 60 minutes of cortisol treatment, emphasizing the immediate
impact of steroid treatment on glycemic control.49

USE OF CORTICOSTEROIDS IN DIABETIC DOGS AND CATS
In managing comorbidities, the optimal approach to treating combined disorders is not always the same
as the sum of optimal treatments for the two disorders when being managed separately.29 There is also a
key difference between canine and feline diabetes to consider, namely the question of insulin sensitivity
and secretion, with diabetic dogs usually having no remaining functional beta cells while diabetic cats
have the important requirement to preserve or even enhance any remaining beta cell function.38 In
some situations, where acute, life-threatening disease such as anaphylaxis occurs, the use of steroids
must take priority over the potential impact on the management of diabetes.4 However, in other chronic
conditions such as immune-mediated disease or neoplasia, consideration can be given to the use of
alternative immunosuppressive drugs4 or chemotherapeutic or antineoplastic drugs (Table 224.1).
Alternative drugs may be used alone or in combination with a lower dosage of steroid to minimize the
impact on glycemic control. Alternatively, locally-acting steroid preparations or “first-pass metabolism”
preparations (e.g., inhaled fluticasone or budesonide in respiratory disease,11,12 oral budesonide
inflammatory bowel disease10) may achieve disease remission in some inflammatory conditions with
less pronounced side-effects. Of note, however, some of the alternative non-steroid immunosuppressive
drugs (ch. 169) may also have an impact on glycemic control or pancreatic function. For example,
cyclosporine, a commonly-used immunosuppressant, can result in raised glucose and fructosamine
concentrations in dogs because of its negative effect on insulin secretion.50 Arguably, while cyclosporine
could thus precipitate diabetes in dogs with impaired glucose tolerance,51-53 it is unlikely to significantly
impact dogs that are already diabetic as they have no functional islets. Similarly, the
immunosuppressant azathioprine54 (which is not recommended for cats) has been linked to the
development of pancreatitis in dogs, a disease which is likely to complicate glycemic control further.
Indeed, the relationship between corticosteroid treatment and pancreatitis is complex and not well
characterized in either dogs or cats, although the disease is commonly associated with diabetes in both
species.55 Some clinicians have successfully used anti-inflammatory dosages of prednisolone to treat
chronic pancreatitis in cats,56 while there is ex vivo experimental evidence to suggest that
corticosteroids may actually have a detrimental effect on pancreas function in dogs.57 Another option
when using corticosteroids in diabetic patients, particularly cats, may be to consider the use of oral
hypoglycemic drugs58 or insulin sensitizers such as pioglitazone,59 which appear to hold some promise
in obese cats.

CLINICAL CASE DECISION-MAKING SCENARIO EXAMPLES
TOPICAL STEROIDS

In the case of a diabetic dog, well controlled on porcine insulin, with unilateral chronic superficial
keratitis and no corneal ulcer, the advantages of topical steroid therapy are clear. Eye drops will treat
painful keratitis successfully, will remove a superficial focus of inflammation, and will prevent
progression of a disease that could eventually impact vision. Theoretically, topical steroids may still be
systemically absorbed and affect glycemic control, so depending on severity of disease, topical
nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) could be a viable replacement. If steroids are
considered clinically necessary then, based on experience, topical dexamethasone appears to be least
likely to be systemically absorbed, whereas prednisolone acetate drops are more likely to be absorbed.
This is an interesting personal observation, since in a recent study, an ophthalmic preparation of
prednisolone acetate was not shown to cause any differential effect on diabetes regulation in diabetic
dogs compared to a topical NSAID treatment (diclofenac sodium).60 The shortest course of topical
steroid treatment to control the condition would be recommended (maximum 10-14 days), with the
owner monitoring clinical diabetes signs, such as 24-hour water intake, to ensure diabetes is not
becoming less well controlled. Typically, most patients receiving a short course of topical steroids will
not require an insulin dosage adjustment.

SEASONAL ORAL STEROIDS
In another example, the clinician may consider steroids for treatment of a diabetic dog with a seasonal
allergy causing severe pruritus. It is important to find an individual solution for this type of patient, as
the allergy is likely to be a recurring issue. There may be particular pressure on the veterinarian to
prescribe steroids if they have previously been used successfully, and especially if there are budgetary
constraints preventing the use of alternative therapy such as cyclosporine, oclacitinib, or a
desensitization programme. In this scenario, a daily anti-inflammatory dose of prednisolone (0.1-0.2
mg/kg) might be justified by improved welfare of the patient—for example, by reducing pruritus and risk
of secondary pyoderma, which could affect glycemic control. However, this must be balanced with the
risk of insulin resistance and the negative impact on glycemic control, as well as the potential for
increased risk of bacterial infection (e.g., skin or urinary tract). In particular, if the patient has a history
of relatively stable diabetes, use of steroids is less concerning than in a patient with unstable diabetes or
a history of complications such a diabetic ketoacidosis. It is also important to ensure that other methods
to limit the severity of seasonal allergic skin disease are in place, e.g., reduced exposure to known
allergens, administration of essential fatty acid supplements, ensuring effective ectoparasite control, and
ensuring there are no dietary or home environmental triggers. An antihistamine could also be trialled,
ideally beginning before the expected onset of the allergy, and topical steroid therapy may also be
suitable in some cases. However, if an oral route is chosen, the lowest effective dose of prednisolone
should be used (0.2-0.5 mg/kg) and blood glucose monitored to determine the effect of prednisolone on
insulin sensitivity in this individual patient. Continuous glucose monitors, such as the Freestyle Libre,
can be an effective way of monitoring trends in glycemic control after steroid treatment is started (ch.
78). Individual responses to steroids are highly variable, so any insulin adjustment must be made
cautiously, and based on blood glucose evaluation. Consideration should also be given to daily steroid
treatment rather than every other day—as might be favoured in non-diabetic patients, so that the daily
routine in the diabetic patient is consistent. While the canine diurnal rhythm of steroid secretion61 and
the potential exposure to allergens in the daytime would support steroid dosing in the morning for this
type of patient, for some diabetic patients an evening steroid dose has a less detrimental impact on
glycemic control, as some patients tend to eat less overnight. Based on experience, typical insulin dose
changes required during administration of a short course (up to 10 days) of an oral anti-inflammatory
dose of prednisolone (up to 0.5 mg/kg) once daily are remarkably small. Requirements usually stay
within 10% of the original insulin dosage, and typically range from an increase of 0 to 1 unit twice daily
in cats, and an increase of 0 to 4 units twice daily in dogs. In contrast, higher, immunosuppressive
dosages of prednisolone (2 mg/kg) used in autoimmune disease are much more likely to increase insulin
requirements, which may rise by as much as 20% per injection with long-term steroid use.

INHALED STEROIDS
Chronic inflammatory airway disease in diabetic patients represents another challenge for the
veterinarian. While antitussives and bronchodilators can help to control clinical signs, and drugs such as

doxycycline can treat additional complications such as Mycoplasma infection, they will not address the
underlying inflammatory response (ch. 215). In many dogs with chronic bronchitis and in cats with
asthma, inhaled steroids (e.g., fluticasone; ch. 90) can be very effective, with minimal clinically
apparent systemic impact and only rarely requiring a change of insulin dose. For this reason, where
possible, it is recommended to begin with inhaled steroids and avoid systemic steroid treatment where
possible. Clinical experience suggests that a twice daily inhaled steroid treatment works well alongside
twice daily insulin injections, although it may take up to 4 weeks to see the maximum benefit. In a
diabetic dog or cat with severe disease, and where coughing is having a significant impact on quality of
life, a short course (5-10 days) of oral prednisolone at a dosage of 0.5 mg/kg or less may be required to
gain initial control of clinical signs, before transitioning to inhaled steroids over a 7-10 day period. This
oral treatment phase will require closer monitoring of clinical signs and blood glucose, potentially by
continuous glucose monitoring (ch. 78). Particular care should be taken in patients with a history of
diabetic ketoacidosis. In some cases, a temporary increase in insulin may be needed, as described above,
which can be gradually returned to the original insulin dosage during the transition from oral to inhaled
steroids. As an alternative to corticosteroids, cyclosporine has been used successfully in some feline
asthma cases,62 and anecdotally has proven beneficial in some dogs with chronic bronchitis.

DEVELOPMENT OF DIABETES DURING STEROID
TREATMENT
Another situation in which the clinician must confront the use of steroids in diabetic patients is where a
patient already receiving steroids becomes diabetic. For example, in a feline patient being treated with
prednisolone for inflammatory bowel disease, diabetes may develop as a side-effect of treatment. This is
not unusual: in a recent study of 143 diabetic cats treated at a tertiary referral centre, 14 were found to
have received prednisolone therapy prior to diagnosis, with 12 cats becoming diabetic within 3 months
of beginning their steroid treatment.63 At this point, the veterinarian is faced with several choices,
ranging from tapering and discontinuation of prednisolone in order to pursue diabetes remission, or
accepting and managing the diabetes, recognizing that it is a consequence of the prednisolone treatment
needed to control the clinical signs of inflammatory bowel disease. While it may not be impossible to
attain diabetes remission in a cat with inflammatory bowel disease, it will likely be much more
challenging than in a cat not requiring treatment for this condition. The decision made about whether to
continue steroids in this scenario will depend on factors including the current steroid dosage, the
severity and duration of clinical signs of inflammatory bowel disease and their impact on patient quality
of life, and the presence of other diabetes risk factors that could be addressed in another way (e.g.,
obesity [ch. 150]). Possible options in this case could include steroid-sparing strategies such as
introduction of an alternative immunosuppressant (e.g., cyclosporine or chlorambucil; ch. 169) or use
of a drug with potential immunomodulatory action such as metronidazole alongside a lower dosage of
prednisolone. A steroid such as budesonide, with its extensive first-pass effect and consequently limited
systemic absorption, may also be effective in cases where inflammation is limited to the gastrointestinal
tract, but convincing large scale data on its effectiveness in veterinary species are lacking.64 Diabetes
remission may still be achieved even in cats who have been diabetic for 6 months or longer, so it is
recommended that a steady approach be taken to steroid withdrawal when diabetes develops during
steroid therapy in a cat. The clinician should focus on maintaining control of gastrointestinal clinical
signs, rather than reducing steroids so rapidly that a relapse occurs. This will also enable gradual
reduction of insulin therapy, if appropriate, based on blood glucose monitoring, and will minimize the
risk of hypoglycemia if the cat does enter remission. While hypoallergenic diets may also help to reduce
the need for steroids, diets formulated for gastrointestinal disease are not usually reduced in
carbohydrate, which would be optimal for diabetes management in cats, so the diet must be selected
carefully (ch. 155).

SUMMARY OF IMPORTANT POINTS WHEN ADMINISTERING
STEROID TREATMENT TO DIABETIC PATIENTS
1. Oral or parenteral corticosteroids should only be used where a firm diagnosis has been reached
and only under careful supervision. The lowest effective dosage should be used, for the

minimum period possible, avoiding the use of long acting (depot) preparations.
2. The patient should be assessed for the risk of steroid-related exacerbation of disease by
considering their age, other comorbidities (especially infection and insulin resistance
syndromes [ch.227]), other drug treatments (e.g., NSAIDs) and the condition being treated.
3. The type and dosage of glucocorticoid should be selected carefully and used for informing initial
adjustments to the insulin regimen,28 with shorter acting and topical preparations being
preferable.
4. Despite possible adrenal suppression, once-daily steroid protocols may be preferable to every
other day protocols for the purposes of maintaining glycemic control. Many veterinarians
recommend dosing feline patients with steroid in the evening and canine patients in the
morning to minimize adrenal suppression. In patients receiving twice daily insulin,
administering the steroid with the evening dose of insulin may minimize issues of postprandial
hyperglycemia since less food is generally consumed overnight than during the day.
5. For long-term steroid use, the insulin dosage is likely to require titration to suit the needs of the
individual. In addition, once steroid therapy is tapered, careful adjustments in insulin dosage
must be made to avoid hypoglycemia. Continuous glucose monitoring (ch. 78) may help with
this.
6. Close monitoring of the patient is necessary. For low-dose steroid therapy in a stable diabetic
animal, home glucose or urine monitoring to avoid profound hyperglycemia or ketosis may be
appropriate, but for more severe disease or in previously unstable diabetic patients, monitoring
in a hospital environment may be necessary.
7. Where very high dosages of steroid are required and the patient has a poor appetite, pancreatitis
or infection, consideration should be given to switching to a short-acting soluble insulin
preparation during the initial phase of steroid therapy so that this can be titrated more
accurately according to blood glucose and appetite.
8. It is useful to provide the owner of the pet receiving treatment with a steroid information sheet
(an example accompanies this chapter online) to advise them about adverse effects and to
ensure that treatment is tapered rather than stopped abruptly.
