CLIENT INFORMATION
Oral Corticosteroid Therapy
Your pet has been prescribed the following corticosteroid treatment:
MEDICATION NAME:
INITIAL DOSE:
EXPECTED DURATION OF TREATMENT:
TO TREAT THE FOLLOWING CONDITION:
Please note the following extremely important points about corticosteroid treatment. If
your pet has to attend an emergency clinic or is going into a boarding kennel or cattery, please provide
them with a copy of this information.
1. It is very important that corticosteroid treatment is not stopped suddenly as this can
have serious consequences for the health of your pet. This is particularly important with
higher dosages or after more than 2 weeks of treatment. Your veterinarian can discuss a plan
for gradual reduction in dosage with you when appropriate. In the meantime, please make sure
you do not run out of medication.
2. When administering this medication, please make sure you give the correct amount at the
same time of day and try not to miss any doses. If you do miss a dose and it is close to the
time of the next dose, do not give a double dose.
3. Corticosteroid treatment can cause noticeable secondary effects including increased thirst,
increased hunger, panting, muscle wasting and lethargy. These are more prominent in dogs
than in cats. It is important that your pet have access to fresh water at all times and be
able to urinate frequently while receiving corticosteroids. There is no need to offer more
food than usual unless you have been advised otherwise by your veterinarian. In the longer
term, corticosteroids may have other side-effects, including thinning of the hair coat, high
blood pressure or a swollen abdomen. More rarely, some animals can develop blood-related
disorders such as blood loss into the intestine, bruising or blood clots. Not all animals show
obvious side-effects but if you are concerned about your pet, please contact your
veterinarian to discuss treatment rather than discontinuing corticosteroid therapy
suddenly.
4. Corticosteroid treatment can make some dogs and cats more susceptible to infections so it
is best to avoid situations where your pet might be exposed to infectious disease (such as
parvovirus).
5. Please make sure that your veterinarian knows about all other medications that your pet is
receiving including tablets, liquids, eye drops, ear drops, ointments and inhalers. Certain

types of medication (e.g., nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [NSAIDs]) are
incompatible with corticosteroids and giving both could be very dangerous.
Corticosteroids may sometimes make other medical conditions worse (e.g., high blood
pressure, heart disease) so please discuss this with your veterinarian in advance and contact
him/her if you notice any deterioration in your pet’s health while on treatment.
6. In some cases, high-dose corticosteroid therapy can increase the risk of diabetes
(high blood sugar). If your pet currently has diabetes, has had diabetes in the past, has a history
of pancreatitis, or is overweight, then there is an increased risk that corticosteroid therapy will
cause problems with blood glucose. In this situation, your veterinarian is likely to recommend
more regular checks of urine glucose or blood glucose. Please be aware that many of the signs
of uncontrolled diabetes are similar to the side-effects of corticosteroids (e.g., increased thirst),
so please contact your veterinarian if your pet appears unwell, is less keen to eat,
or you are concerned in any way.
7. If your pet is already diabetic and receiving insulin treatment, closer monitoring will be
required during corticosteroid therapy, because corticosteroids can counteract the effect of
the insulin. Please follow any specific instructions given to you by your veterinarian regarding
adjustment of insulin therapy and contact the veterinary hospital if you have any queries.
8. This corticosteroid medication has been prescribed for a particular condition for your pet only.
Please do not administer any of the corticosteroid medication to any other pets in
the household even if they appear to have similar signs or symptoms. If you have any
medication remaining once treatment for this condition has been stopped, then please return it
to the veterinary hospital.

Chapter 225: Feline Triaditis
Jonathan Andrew Lidbury

AC RO N YM S
ALT alanine aminotransferase
GI gastrointestinal
IBD inflammatory bowel disease

INTRODUCTION
Feline triaditis is the term used for describing concurrent inflammation of the
small intestine, pancreas, and liver.1-3 This syndrome is somewhat ill-defined
but it encompasses a range of intestinal, pancreatic, and hepatobiliary diseases,
including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), pancreatitis, and cholangitis (Box
225.1). The clinical signs and laboratory findings for the diseases comprising
triaditis overlap and biopsy of all 3 organs is needed for a definitive diagnosis.
Some cats have involvement of 2 of these organs but not the third (e.g., IBD
with concurrent pancreatitis). Cats may also present with disease of 1 organ
dominating the clinical picture but with histologically-confirmed inflammation
of other organs that may or may not be clinically relevant.

PREVALENCE
The reported prevalence of triaditis varies greatly depending on the population
of cats studied.4-7 For example, in a retrospective study of 54 cats with
cholangitis, 26% had pancreatitis, 46% had IBD, and 17% had triaditis.5 The
authors found that interstitial nephritis was a common comorbidity and
suggested that feline triaditis is part of a wider multisystemic process that they
termed “feline inflammatory syndrome.” However, it should be noted that

interstitial nephritis is a common postmortem finding in cats. In 300 cats with
suspected small bowel signs, IBD and gastrointestinal (GI) small cell lymphoma
were common but concurrent hepatic or pancreatic lesions were not.6 In a
prospective study, IBD with cholangitis was noted to occur in 22% of 27 cats
with GI signs, IBD with pancreatitis in 4%, and triaditis in 30%. However, some
combination of histopathological changes of 2 or more of these organs was also
found in 55% of 11 overtly healthy cats undergoing ovariohysterectomy.
Interestingly, none of the cats in this control group had inflammation of all 3
organs.7 Some controversy exists as what are the “normal” histological features
of each of these organs.8 It is possible that the misclassification of histological
variations as being “abnormal” may have increased the apparent prevalence of
triaditis in the veterinary literature. The only safe conclusion to make is that
cats can have combinations of intestinal disease, pancreatic disease, and
inflammatory liver disease.

ETIOPATHOGENESIS
IBD is caused by a loss of mucosal immune tolerance due to a combination of
genetic and environmental (i.e., dietary or microbial) factors.9 This results in
cellular infiltrates in the intestine that are usually lymphoplasmacytic in nature
and architectural changes such a villous stunting, villous fusion, or fibrosis (ch.
262).10
While infectious agents, trauma, certain drugs, and possibly autoimmune
disease are occasionally recognized as causing pancreatitis in cats, an
underlying cause is not identified in most cases (ch. 278).11 Enteric bacteria
were visualized in the pancreata of some of cats with pancreatitis.12 However,
the clinical significance of this finding is unknown.
Bacteria (most commonly Escherichia coli or other enteric bacteria) can
often be cultured from the bile of cats with neutrophilic cholangitis and these
patients usually respond to antimicrobial therapy (ch. 272).13 The route by
which these enteric bacteria reach the liver is controversial. Traditionally, it was
thought that they ascended the biliary tract. However, the location of bacteria
in a more recent study suggested that they are more likely to reach the liver by
translocation across the intestinal wall or via the portal circulation.14
Lymphocytic cholangitis is caused by a loss of immune tolerance resulting in
the targeting of bile ducts by the adaptive immune response (ch. 271).15 The
mechanisms behind this have not been precisely determined.

Several models that may explain the interplay between pancreatitis, IBD, and
cholangitis have been proposed.1 In one of these, which could explain the
development of acute pancreatitis and neutrophilic cholangitis, enteritis leads
to dysbiosis and increased intestinal permeability. This results in
hematogenous seeding of bacteria to the liver and/or pancreas. The
aforementioned studies that demonstrated enteric bacteria in the livers14 and
pancreata12 of cats support this. Alternatively, increased intra-abdominal
pressure due to vomiting could cause reflux of duodenal contents into the
pancreaticobiliary duct system, allowing enteric bacteria to reach the liver
and/or pancreas. In another model, the development of acute pancreatitis is the
initial event. In turn, this leads to acute enteritis and/or cholangitis, possibly
due to the close anatomical relationship among these 3 organs. The enteritis
then leads to bacterial translocation to the pancreas and/or liver. In an
experimentally-induced feline acute pancreatitis model, seeding of the
pancreas, liver, and gallbladder with enterically translocated E. coli was shown

to occur, supporting this hypothesis.16-18 In a third model, which could explain
the development of chronic pancreatitis and lymphocytic cholangitis, loss of
immune tolerance originating in the small intestine secondarily affected the
liver and/or pancreas.1 One potential mechanism is due to aberrant homing of
T lymphocytes from the small intestine, as has been shown to occur in humans
with primary sclerosing cholangitis.19 Alternatively, microbiota-derived or
host-derived molecules in the portal circulation may stimulate an immune
response in the liver and/or pancreas.20 IBD could also be associated with the
development of autoantibodies against hepatic and/or pancreatic proteins,
possibly due to molecular mimicry between host and microbial proteins. Such
autoantibodies have been described in humans with autoimmune
pancreatitis.21,22

CLINICAL FINDINGS
There is a paucity of data on the clinical presentation of cats with triaditis but it
is likely that any age, breed, or sex of cat may be affected. In a prospective
study, cats with triaditis were significantly older than those with IBD,
cholangitis, or the combination of IBD and cholangitis.7
As triaditis is a syndrome that encompasses several disease processes, it is
not surprising that its clinical features are very variable (Table 225.1).
Common historical observations in cats with triaditis include decreased
appetite, lethargy, vomiting, diarrhea, weight loss, and icterus.2 In a study of 8
cats with triaditis, the most common clinical signs were vomiting (88%),
anorexia (63%), and polyphagia (37%).7
Possible physical examination findings include poor body condition,
thickened bowel loops, signs of abdominal pain associated with pancreatitis or
cholangitis, abdominal distension due to ascites, and icterus.2,3

DIAGNOSIS
LABORATORY TESTING
Triaditis and its components cannot be diagnosed with laboratory testing alone
(Table 225.1). In 8 cats with triaditis, the most common biochemical
abnormalities finding was increased alanine aminotransferase (ALT) activity
while the most common hematological changes were anemia, neutrophilia, and
lymphocytosis.7

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
Triaditis (and its components) cannot be definitely diagnosed with abdominal
imaging but ultrasound findings may be suggestive (Table 225.1).23-26 The
absence of ultrasound findings does not rule these conditions out.

PERCUTANEOUS CHOLECYSTOCENTESIS
Diagnostic percutaneous cholecystocentesis is performed using ultrasound
guidance in heavily sedated or anesthetized cats (ch. 272).27 Cytologically
confirmed septic suppurative inflammation and bacterial growth are diagnostic
for neutrophilic cholangitis.28 The most commonly isolated bacteria are E. coli,
Enterococcus spp., and Streptococcus spp.29-32

HISTOLOGIC ASSESSMENT
A definitive diagnosis of triaditis requires histological documentation of
inflammation of the small intestine, pancreas, and liver. This necessitates
laparotomy or laparoscopic liver and pancreatic biopsies followed by intestinal
biopsy through a small abdominal incision. Bleeding risk assessment should be
performed prior to liver biopsy and in icteric cats vitamin K (0.5-1.5 mg/kg SQ
q12h for 3 doses) is often administered to reduce the risk of hemorrhage.33
Pancreatitis is often cited as a concern following pancreatic biopsy, but studies
have shown that this procedure can be performed safely using careful
technique.34 Samples of liver and bile should be submitted for aerobic and
anaerobic bacterial culture.
The histological features of IBD include morphological (architectural)
changes and inflammatory infiltrates (ch. 262). The morphological changes
are more meaningful and can include villous stunting, epithelial injury, crypt
distension, lacteal dilation, and mucosal fibrosis. The inflammatory infiltrates
are most commonly lymphoplasmacytic, but eosinophilic, neutrophilic, or
mixed infiltrates can also occur.10 The clinical importance of minimal or mild
inflammatory infiltrates, especially when they are lymphoplasmacytic, is
questionable.8,10 Furthermore, it can be difficult to distinguish severe
lymphoplasmacytic enteritis from GI small cell lymphoma.35
Chronic pancreatitis, characterized by a monocytic infiltrate and varying
degrees of fibrosis, is the form of pancreatitis that is most commonly observed
in cats with triaditis (ch. 278). However, acute pancreatitis, characterized by a
neutrophilic infiltrate, pancreatic necrosis, and pancreatic edema, can also
occur.3,7,11,36 It is important to note that because of the heterogeneous

distribution of pancreatic lesions, their absence based on evaluation of a single
biopsy specimen does not rule out pancreatic disease.3,36

DGGR, 1,2-o-dilauryl-rac-glycero glutaric acid-(6’-methylresorufin) ester; EPI,
exocrine pancreatic insufficiency; fPLI, feline pancreas-specific lipase; fTLI,
feline trypsin-like immunoreactivity; IBD, inflammatory bowel disease; LC,
lymphocytic cholangitis; NC, neutrophilic cholangitis.
Acute neutrophilic cholangitis is characterized by an infiltrate of neutrophils
and edema centered around the bile ducts (ch. 272). In chronic neutrophilic
cholangitis, the inflammatory infiltrate is mixed with neutrophils, lymphocytes,
and plasma cells, with biliary hyperplasia, biliary epithelial degeneration, and
varying degrees of fibrosis (ch. 272).28 Lymphocytic cholangitis is
characterized by infiltration of lymphocytes in the portal region, with bile duct
proliferation, bile duct epithelial degeneration, bile duct loss, and varying
degrees of fibrosis.28

CHALLENGES IN DIAGNOSING TRIADITIS
There are several unique challenges when diagnosing feline triaditis syndrome.
Financial or patient-related constraints may mean that biopsy of all 3 organs is
not performed. In this situation a presumptive diagnosis of triaditis (or its
components) may have to be made based on clinical findings, laboratory
testing, and diagnostic imaging findings. When this is the case, cats may be
treated empirically and if they don’t respond, the presumptive diagnosis should
be re-evaluated. Prior therapy can have a confounding effect on subsequent
diagnostic tests (e.g., prior antimicrobial therapy may lead to negative bacterial
culture results). Even when it is possible to biopsy the pancreas, liver, and
intestinal tract, interpretation of histopathological findings is not always
straightforward. For example, many veterinary pathologists do not recognize
triaditis as a distinct disease entity and therefore this syndrome is uncommonly
mentioned in their reports. More importantly, the clinical relevance of mild
histological changes (e.g., mild lymphoplasmacytic enteritis) is uncertain and
this must be taken into consideration. It is essential to consider all the available
information as one component disease may dominate the clinical picture and if
so, this should be prioritized when formulating a therapeutic plan.

MANAGEMENT
SUPPORTIVE CARE AND NUTRITION

An individualized fluid therapy plan should be made by considering the cat’s
maintenance needs, current deficits, ongoing losses, and its ability to tolerate
intravenous fluids (ch. 120).37 Electrolyte abnormalities, such as hypokalemia
(ch. 68) or hypophosphatemia (ch. 69), must also be addressed promptly.
Some cats actively vomit or show signs of nausea, so antiemetics are frequently
indicated. Maropitant is a neurokinin-1 (NK1) receptor antagonist that is a
potent antiemetic that also has analgesic effects38 (1 mg/kg SQ/IV/PO q24h).
Ondansetron (0.2-0.5 mg/kg IV/PO, q24-48h; if given PO, doses should be
towards the high end of the dosage range and shorter end of the interdose
interval39) is a serotonin-3 (5HT3) receptor antagonist antiemetic drug. Cats
with triaditis may experience abdominal pain (ch. 6). Buprenorphine (0.010.03 mg/kg sublingual/IV/SQ q8-12h) is a partial mu opiate receptor agonist
that can be administered sublingually to cats by owners.
Appetite stimulants, such as mirtazapine (1.875-3.75 mg/cat PO q24h or 1.5
inches [∼2 mg] transdermally q24h40), can also be used as a short-term
measure. Enteral feeding is preferred to parenteral feeding and placement of a
feeding tube is often indicated (ch. 81). Withholding food from cats with
pancreatitis is no longer recommended and early enteral nutrition is believed to
be beneficial (ch. 278).41 The optimal diet to feed cats with pancreatitis is not
currently known but fat restriction has not been proven to be beneficial and the
author often feeds a commercial diet marketed for intestinal disease. Up to 50%
of cats with chronic enteropathy will respond to dietary intervention (ch. 152).
Therefore, a diet trial with a novel protein or hydrolyzed antigen diet should
ideally be performed in cats with chronic enteropathies.9,42
There is a rationale behind administering antioxidant medications, such as Sadenosyl methionine (20 mg/kg PO q24h on an empty stomach), silymarin (10
mg/kg of silymarin complexed with phosphatidylcholine PO q24h), or vitamin
E (alpha-tocopherol, 15 IU/kg PO q24h), to cats with cholangitis. These
mediations have not been proven to improve outcomes in cats with
inflammatory liver disease but are generally well-tolerated.43,44 However,
essential supportive medications and those that treat the cat’s underlying
disease process(es) should be prioritized.

TREATING THE COMPONENT DISEASES
Prednisolone is the typical treatment for cats with IBD (1-2 mg/kg PO per day,
tapered to the lowest effective dose) (ch. 262). Sometimes chlorambucil (2 mg
per cat PO q48-72h; several other protocols have also been described) is used
as adjunctive treatment in cats that either incompletely respond to

prednisolone or don’t tolerate effective doses of prednisolone (chs. 144, 169,
224).9
Treatment for pancreatitis in cats (ch. 278) is comprised mainly of the
supportive and nutritional measures discussed above. Antimicrobials are not
routinely recommended for the treatment of pancreatitis in cats. Antimicrobials
are indicated when there an infected pancreatic fluid accumulation (most are
sterile), when there is concurrent aspiration pneumonia, or if sepsis is
suspected.11 In a recent consensus statement on feline pancreatitis, several
panel members felt that the use of prednisolone could help reduce
inflammation and prevent fibrosis in cats with chronic pancreatitis.
Hyperglycemia is a potential side-effect and panel members could not reach a
consensus on whether an anti-inflammatory or an immunosuppressive dosage
should be used initially.11 Cyclosporine or another immunomodulatory agent
could be considered if prednisolone is not tolerated, but evidence of their
efficacy for treating this disease is lacking.
Antimicrobial agents are the primary treatment for cats with neutrophilic
cholangitis (ch. 272). Ideally, these drugs are selected based on the results of
culture and susceptibility testing of bile and/or liver samples. Empirical
antimicrobial therapy is usually started pending culture results or if there is no
bacterial growth and neutrophilic cholangitis is confirmed or highly suspected.
The antimicrobial(s) chosen should be effective against enteric bacteria and
have good biliary penetration. Reasonable choices include potentiated
penicillin alone, enrofloxacin (5 mg/kg PO q24h) with concurrent potentiated
penicillin or clindamycin, or pradofloxacin alone (7.5 mg/kg PO q24h).
Treatment is typically continued for 4-6 weeks.
Immunomodulation with prednisolone is the primary treatment for cats with
lymphocytic cholangitis (ch. 271). In a retrospective study, prednisolonetreated cats had a median survival time of >800 days.45 In cats that fail to
respond completely or that have unacceptable glucocorticoid side-effects, the
addition of chlorambucil may be helpful. It is not known if the addition of
ursodeoxycholic acid (10-15 mg/kg PO q24h) to prednisolone treatment is
beneficial. However, cats treated with prednisolone monotherapy have survived
longer than those treated with ursodeoxycholic acid monotherapy.45

CONSIDERATIONS WHEN MAKING A
TREATMENT PLAN
When make a therapeutic plan, possible interactions between medications
should be considered (e.g., cats receiving mirtazapine and the analgesic agent
tramadol are at increased risk of serotonin syndrome). The risk of the
medication indicated for one condition making another condition worse should
also be carefully thought about. For example, for a cat with IBD that also has

(or is suspected to have) neutrophilic cholangitis, immunosuppressive doses of
prednisolone could lead to a worsening of signs or even sepsis (ch. 227). In
this scenario, it would be ideal to treat with an appropriate antimicrobial before
starting prednisolone. In other cases, the presence of a comorbid condition
does not alter therapy. For example, for a cat with IBD and suspected
pancreatitis that does not need immediate supportive care, therapy for IBD
(i.e., prednisolone and an elimination diet) takes precedence.
The potential for the presence (or development of) comorbid conditions
should also be considered when monitoring response to treatment. For
example, a cat that has recently been treated for neutrophilic cholangitis and
starts to vomit could be found to have an increasing serum ALT activity. In this
scenario, it is possible that the deterioration is due to a recurrence of
neutrophilic cholangitis but it would also be possible that the patient developed
either acute pancreatitis or a chronic enteropathy.

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis for cats with combinations of IBD, pancreatitis, and cholangitis
has not been well described. Overall, it should be considered to be very
variable; some may not survive initial hospitalization whereas others respond
well to treatment. The literature provides some evidence that cats with more
than 1 of the component diseases have a worse prognosis. For example, cats
with cholangitis that had concurrent conditions, including IBD and
pancreatitis, had a lower survival rate than those without46 and cats with
triaditis had more severe histological inflammation than those with
inflammation in only 1 or 2 organs.7

CLIENT INFORMATION
Feline Triaditis
BACKGROUND
Triaditis is the term used to describe simultaneous inflammation of the small
intestine, pancreas, and liver in cats. Rather than being a single disease, feline
triaditis is a syndrome that encompasses a range of small intestinal, pancreatic,
and liver diseases. Because of this cats can be affected in a number of different
ways. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD; chronic inflammation of the intestine
without an identifiable underlying cause), pancreatitis (inflammation of the
pancreas), and cholangitis (inflammation centered around the bile ducts in the
liver) are the common components of triaditis. Some cats have involvement of 2
of these organs but not the third (e.g., IBD and pancreatitis in the absence of
cholangitis). It is not known exactly how often cats are affected by triaditis but
it is reasonably common for cats with cholangitis to also have IBD and/or
pancreatitis and for cats with pancreatitis to also have cholangitis and/or IBD.
When cats are diagnosed with IBD, pancreatitis, or cholangitis, it is important
to consider if they could also have the other components of triaditis.

UNDERLYING CAUSES
As triaditis encompasses several different diseases there are many factors that
may contribute to its development.
IBD in cats is caused by the immune system abnormally reacting to the
contents of the intestine (components of the diet and/or members of the
community of microbes that normally inhabit the intestine). This leads to
inflammation and structural changes in the intestinal wall, resulting in an
impaired ability to absorb nutrients.
While infectious agents, physical damage due to traumatic events, certain
drugs, or possibly an abnormal immune response are occasionally recognized
as causing pancreatitis in cats, an underlying cause is not identified in most
cases even with thorough diagnostic testing.
The 2 most common forms of cholangitis in cats are neutrophilic cholangitis
and lymphocytic cholangitis. Neutrophilic cholangitis is caused by a bacterial
infection of the bile and liver (often with species of bacteria normally found in
the intestine). Lymphocytic cholangitis is caused by an abnormal immune
reaction targeting bile ducts in the liver. The reason why this occurs is not
known.
Several theories that may explain why cats develop combinations of IBD,
pancreatitis, and cholangitis have been proposed. Firstly, it has been shown
that cats with intestinal disease often have an imbalance of the bacteria that
inhabit their intestine. These bacteria could cross the damaged intestinal wall
into the blood stream and reach the pancreas and/or liver. The bacteria could
then cause pancreatitis and/or cholangitis. Alternatively, the bacteria could

travel from the small intestine up the pancreatic and common bile ducts into
the pancreas and/or liver. In more chronic cases it is possible that the abnormal
immune response to the intestinal contents that leads to IBD could progress to
also target the pancreas and/or bile ducts in the liver.

CLINICAL SIGNS (SYMPTOMS)
Cats of any age, sex, or breed can be affected by triaditis (and its components)
but this syndrome may be more common in older cats. The clinical signs
(symptoms) experienced by cats with triaditis are very variable but include:
decreased appetite, decreased activity levels, vomiting, weight loss, diarrhea, or
occasionally yellow tinged gums and whites of the eyes (jaundice, also called
icterus). When your veterinarian examines your cat they may find evidence of
weight loss, thickened intestinal loops, evidence of abdominal pain, distension
of the abdomen, or jaundice. Note that these are nonspecific findings (if found,
these features are not automatically related to triaditis); therefore, they are one
piece of information that raises or lowers a veterinarian’s suspicion of triaditis.

DIAGNOSIS
Blood tests are an important part of the diagnostic workup of cats with
unintended weight loss and chronic gastrointestinal signs. There are also some
common blood test abnormalities seen in cats with triaditis (and its
components) including: increased liver enzyme activities, increased globulins (a
type of protein), increased bilirubin (the yellow pigment that causes jaundice),
mild to moderately decreased red blood cell levels (anemia), and increased
white blood cell counts. However, many of these abnormalities can also be
caused by other diseases and their absence does not rule out triaditis.
Therefore, blood tests are helpful but cannot fully diagnose triaditis in cats.
Pancreas-specific lipase is a digestive enzyme that leaks from the pancreas
when it is inflamed. Therefore, increased blood levels are suggestive of
pancreatitis. Your vet may also measure blood levels of 2 types of B vitamins
(cobalamin and folate) to assess how well they are being absorbed from the
small intestine.
Abdominal ultrasound is a diagnostic imaging test that is widely available,
non-invasive, and can usually be performed on non-sedated or mildly sedated
cats. Triaditis (and its components) cannot be fully diagnosed with an
abdominal ultrasound scan but the findings may be suggestive of this syndrome
(and its components). For example, cats with IBD often have thickened small
intestinal walls and cats with cholangitis may have dilated bile ducts. The
absence of such ultrasound abnormalities does not rule out triaditis. Abdominal
ultrasound can also be used by your vet to allow them to collect samples of the
liver and bile with a fine needle (about the size of the type they use for a routine
vaccination). This is done in heavily sedated or anesthetized cats and can help
make a diagnosis of liver disease. As the needle used is so narrow the risk of
bleeding is low and cats typically recover very quickly. The samples collected

are evaluated under a microscope and are also used to identify any bacteria that
are present in the bile. This procedure can allow the diagnosis of neutrophilic
cholangitis. Sometimes the results are not definitive though.
To fully diagnose triaditis (or its components), biopsy of the small intestine,
pancreas, and liver is performed. This requires either a traditional open
abdominal surgery or a key-hole (laparoscopic) surgery performed under
general anesthesia. You veterinarian will assess your cat’s suitability for these
procedures and talk to you about the potential risks and benefits beforehand.
Cats typically recover well from these surgeries but may need to be hospitalized
briefly afterwards. Interpreting the microscopic findings of small intestinal,
pancreatic, and liver biopsy can be challenging. For example, it is hard to know
how much importance to place on mild changes of these organs and it can be
very hard/impossible to differentiate IBD from a cancer called gastrointestinal
small cell lymphoma.
If it is not possible to perform biopsy, your veterinarian will try to use the less
invasive tests described above to make a tentative diagnosis. If your cat fails to
respond to a treatment plan based on this, biopsy can be reconsidered.
However, it is important to note that sometimes prior treatments can make it
harder to make an accurate diagnosis when biopsy is performed.

TREATMENT
Cats with triaditis and its components may require hospitalization and
supportive care, especially if they are very sick. Intravenous fluids (an IV drip)
help correct and prevent dehydration and can be lifesaving. Antiemetic drugs
can help reduce vomiting and nausea. Some cats with triaditis may experience
abdominal pain and so pain killing drugs might be necessary. Cats that don’t
eat for more than 2 or 3 days are at risk of developing a serious disease called
feline hepatic lipidosis (characterized by a fatty liver). Therefore, if your cat is
not voluntarily eating enough your veterinarian may recommend an appetite
stimulant or even placing a feeding tube. Force feeding cats by syringing food
into their mouth can lead to inhalation of food with resultant pneumonia and
long-term aversion to food. Cats typically tolerate feeding tubes very well, they
can be used by cat owners to provide nutrition at home, and they can be
removed at a later time when the cat starts eating again. Feline patients that
have not eaten for several days should be slowly reintroduced to food. You
veterinarian may recommend a therapeutic (prescription) diet depending upon
the components of triaditis that your cat has and what the main symptoms are.
Antioxidant nutritional supplements (e.g., S-adenosyl methionine, milk
thistle derived products, and vitamin E) are theoretically beneficial to cats with
liver disease and rarely have side effects and so are often recommended. Other
essential supportive medications and those that treat the cat’s underlying
disease processes should be prioritized though. If your cat is hard to pill, talk to
your veterinarian about which mediations are the most important to give.

The main treatment for cats with IBD is the anti-inflammatory drug
prednisolone (a corticosteroid). Possible side-effects of prednisolone in cats
include increased appetite, increased thirst and urination, thinning of the skin,
and occasionally diabetes. This drug is typically started at a higher initial dose
to get the inflammation under control and then the dose is slowly reduced over
time to minimize the side effects. It is important not to suddenly stop giving
prednisolone or other corticosteroids to a cat as this can lead to an acute
corticosteroid deficiency, which could make them very sick. It is also very
important not to give non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, such as aspirin,
meloxicam (Metacam) or carprofen (Rimadyl), at the same time (this can lead
to severe gastric ulcers). Some cats require long-term treatment and sometimes
a second immunosuppressive drug is also given. Cats with chronic
gastrointestinal disease may respond to a “hypoallergenic” prescription diet
and so your veterinarian may recommend you feed one of these for several
weeks to see if your cat responds positively. When performing a diet trial it is
essential that you do not feed any other food or treats and that you let your
veterinarian know if you cat will not eat the trial diet.
The main treatments for pancreatitis in cats are the supportive medications
described above and providing adequate nutrition. Most cats with pancreatitis
do not require treatment with antibiotics. However, they may be indicated in
patients that have or may have a secondary infection, such as pneumonia, or in
cats that also have a bacterial infection of their liver or gall bladder. Some cats
with chronic pancreatitis that do not respond to other treatments seem to
respond to prednisolone or other anti-inflammatory drugs. However, these
medications have not been conclusively shown to be beneficial in this situation
and should be use cautiously.
The main treatment for cats with neutrophilic cholangitis is antibiotics
therapy. The choice of antibiotics is ideally based on testing of the liver and/or
bile. Antibiotics are usually given for at least 4-6 weeks. The cat is carefully
monitored before and after treatment. Prednisolone (see above) is the main
treatment for lymphocytic cholangitis in cats.
Sometimes the combination of diseases in cats with triaditis can present a
challenge. For example, for a cat with IBD that also has neutrophilic cholangitis
the prednisolone that is indicated to treat their IBD could weaken the immune
response to the bacterial infection causing their neutrophilic cholangitis.
Careful planning can help diminish these issues. In the aforementioned
scenario this would entail being aware that there is more than one disease
process and then prioritizing them by initially treating the neutrophilic
cholangitis with an appropriate antibiotic for a period of time to control the
infection before starting treatment with prednisolone.

PROGNOSIS (OUTLOOK)
The outlook for cats with triaditis is very variable. Some cats can have acute
life-threatening illness but some of these will go on to make a full recovery with

treatment. Others have a more insidious chronic illness that waxes and wanes
or is slowly progressive and it may not be possible to completely cure them, but
long-term control of their clinical signs may be achieved. The is some evidence
that having more than one of the individual components of triaditis leads to a
slightly worse outlook, but again every case is different.
Jonathan Andrew Lidbury (College Station, Texas)

Chapter 226: Obesity and
Immobility
Ross H. Palmer

A C RO N YM S
BCS body condition score
BW body weight
NGF nerve growth factor
NSAID nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug
OA osteoarthritis
RER resting energy requirement
TrkA tropomyosin receptor kinase A

THE PROBLEM
The combination of obesity and immobility robs dogs and cats of
their quality of life and often, ultimately, leads to agonizing family
decisions for pet euthanasia. Immobility may result from any
combination of osteoarthritis (OA), poor fitness, pain, muscular
weakness, and neurologic dysfunction, all of which are worsened by
obesity. Immobility itself also reduces an obese patient’s ability to
lose excess weight through physical exercise. The pairing of
immobility and obesity thus creates a management quandary that
occurs frequently in practice.

Both pet obesity and OA are on the rise in the United States and
elsewhere.1,2 Unfortunately, obesity contributes to the development
of OA and its symptoms of pain and immobility. In the Labrador
lifespan study, caloric intake was inextricably linked to the onset and
symptoms of OA and it shortened median lifespan.3 This landmark
study used a “paired-feeding” design in which 6-week-old Labrador
puppies from each of 7 litters were paired based upon body weight
(BW) and sex and randomly assigned into either “control-fed” or
“limited-fed” groups. Control group dogs were initially fed ad libitum
(later reduced to 62.1 kcal/kg of ideal BW at ∼3 years of age) and
paired littermates in the study group were fed the same ration but
limited to 75% of the amount consumed by each pair-mate. Housing
and all other environmental factors were identical; only the quantity
of food (caloric intake) differed between groups. Not surprisingly,
dogs with 25% restricted caloric intake weighed less (26% less on
average) and had lower body condition scores (BCSs) through life.
These same calorie-restricted dogs had a decreased incidence,
delayed onset, and reduced clinical signs, of OA. For instance, multijoint OA was only present in 10% of calorie-restricted dogs at 8 years
of age, but was exceedingly common (77%) in dogs fed the same diet
without caloric restriction.4 Additionally, the median lifespan of the
control group (no caloric restriction) was 1.8 year shorter than the
calorie-restricted group; the leading cause of death was euthanasia
prompted by the inability to satisfactorily manage the immobility
and pain caused by OA.
While advancing age is the primary causal risk factor for OA in
cats, a recent study demonstrated that obesity, among other factors,
may predispose cats to developing owner-reported immobility
associated with degenerative joint disease.5

THE SOLUTION
Effective treatment of patients suffering from comorbid obesity and
immobility requires a focus upon correcting the obesity problem.
Certainly, there are other aspects of treatment of immobility that
must be directed toward the primary source of pain, reduced
muscular strength, and neurologic dysfunction, but attaining a lean

body conformation is the foundational strategy to treatment of
comorbid obesity and immobility.
Most veterinarians have the knowledge necessary to effectively
manage the comorbidities of obesity and immobility; rather, it seems
more the lack of awareness of the gravity of the obesity problem and
the relative disbelief that we possess the power to effectively prevent
and manage this “dreaded duo” that explains our profession’s
relative impotence to do so.

OBESITY PREVENTION
Development of healthy feeding habits early in a pet’s life is
preferable to altering established habits that have contributed to
obesity and, then, to immobility. Additionally, pet owners tend to be
more receptive to veterinary counseling directed at helping them to
attain their lifestyle and life quality goals for their pet than they are
to veterinary communications that may be perceived as judgment,
blaming or shaming (ch. 1). Further, pet owner preventative
education can focus on development of healthy family lifestyle habits
in which physical activity and playful interaction are the primary
means for bonding, with a de-emphasis on the role of food and treats
for that purpose. Awareness of the positive impact of maintaining a
lean body conformation (BCS 4-5/9) upon pet life quality and
lifespan can serve as positive motivator for early adherence
(compliance) and ongoing positive reinforcement from the
veterinary team can support long-term client adherence. Veterinary
teams’ communication with their clients is complex and can
profoundly affect pet owner adherence to wellness- and treatmentrecommendations,6,7 yet there is surprisingly little peer-reviewed
evidence as it relates to effective nutritional counseling. Thus, the
above observations are based on the author’s private practice and
academic clinical experience as well as synthesis of other authors’
published recommendations.8,9

OBESITY TREATMENT

In contrast to obesity prevention, several barriers to effective
treatment may need to be overcome (ch. 150). Pet owners are often
unaware that their pet is overweight and therefore, they can be
reluctant to accept a treatment plan.8 Additionally, pet owners often
need to be educated about the adverse impacts of obesity, but this
conversation risks the perception of veterinarian judgment if
sufficient emphasis is not placed on the realistic goal of restoring pet
health and well-being. Entrenched pet behaviors such as begging and
pet owner attitudes about food as a source of demonstrating love for
their pet can also be challenging to overcome.

Patient Assessment
Subjective assessment using a 9-point BCS is commonly practiced for
the purposes of detecting overweight or obese states (ch. 72 and
textbook’s inside covers). This may be complemented by a subjective
muscle condition score (MCS; textbook’s inside covers). A target BW
can be estimated by assuming that each BCS point above 5
represents 10% BW excess (ch. 150). For example, a 45 kg dog with
BCS = 8 is estimated to weigh the target weight × 130%. Thus, the
target weight is estimated as follows: 45 kg/130% = 34.6 kg.

Pet Owner Engagement, Support and
Encouragement
Effective communication with the pet owner about nutritional plan
rationale, goals and strategy is vital to successful implementation
(ch. 1). Alignment of the plan with owner outcome goals that include
specific mobility and lifestyle milestones is important. For instance,
the pet owner may wish for the pet to be able to go on neighborhood
walks of a defined length or be able to regain the ability to ascend
stairs; these can be critical milestones to engage the pet owner, to
measure treatment success and to serve as sources of celebration and
motivation when attained. A non-judgmental approach to obtaining
a dietary history will help the veterinary team to identify barriers to
success that are of concern to the pet owner. For example, there are
several reasons why a veterinarian’s edict to “eliminate all treats”
may not be feasible. Instead, incorporating ways to include those
treats as part of the total daily nutritional account may be more

effective. Multi-pet household feeding practices may have to be
modified or require use of microchip-activated feeding systems
(example: Sure Petcare Surefeed selective automatic pet feeder).10
Effective implementation often requires ongoing pet owner support
and encouragement along with nutritional plan adaptations as serial
patient monitoring is performed.

Developing, Implementing, and Monitoring a
Nutritional Plan
Ad libitum feeding is not appropriate for management of obesity
since excessive caloric intake is the root cause. The nutritional plan is
based upon the patient assessment (ch. 145) and awareness of
household impediments to weight loss to be addressed. Additionally,
the plan should take into account all of the patient’s conditions
including any combination of endocrine, gastrointestinal, renal,
hepatic, cardiopulmonary and other conditions. Especially in such
complex scenarios, consultation with a board-certified veterinary
nutritionist is advised.
Resting energy requirement (RER) is the daily caloric requirement
for a patient and is typically expressed as kilocalories per day. The
estimated daily RER for a patient can be calculated as 70 kcal/kg0.75
(example: RER for a 10 kg dog can be calculated as 70 kcal × 100.75 =
394 kcal / day). In order to promote caloric restriction, the initial
daily energy goal can be calculated as 100% of the RER for the target
weight in dogs. Some prefer to start at 80% of RER for the target
weight in cats. Regardless of the calculated initial daily energy goal,
serial monitoring at 2- to 4-week intervals is required to measure the
rate of weight loss and make adjustments to the plan as needed. The
ideal rate of weight loss is 1-2% of BW per week for dogs and 0.5-2%
of BW per week in cats. It is common when starting a weight loss
plan to discover the rate of weight loss is less than ideal. In this
instance, exploration into the home history to identify unaccountedfor calories is warranted. If the nutritional plan is being
appropriately administered at home but is failing to achieve the
desired rate of weight loss, the daily caloric consumption is reduced
to 80-90% of the original recommendation. In the rare event of

weight loss that is too rapid, the daily caloric consumption is raised
to 120% of the original recommendation.
Simply reducing the feeding volume of the normal ration is seldom
appropriate for obese animals, as this practice reduces the daily
consumption of important macronutrients such as protein, fatty
acids, vitamins and minerals along with the caloric reduction.
Meeting or exceeding protein requirements is important for
maintaining lean muscle mass during weight loss. Similarly, overthe-counter “weight management” or “light” diets are often
insufficiently balanced for such strict weight loss programs.
Commercially prepared veterinary prescription weight loss diets tend
to offer the advantage of being appropriately balanced as well as
being high in insoluble fiber (which promotes satiety) and can reduce
stressful food begging behaviors. Though some pet owners may
object to the apparent expense of commercial weight loss diets, these
foods are often a cost savings when the cost of monitoring and
managing the source of patient immobility is considered. Additional
measures to address food begging may include increased feeding
frequency and use of food puzzles can help to address those
behaviors (ch. 150). Finally, pet owners can be educated that what
may be perceived as food begging is actually a more general
attention begging such that taking time to play with their pet may be
equally or even more effective that giving a treat with regard to
serving the pet’s core need.
Total elimination of daily treats is not achievable in many
households because treats may be used for conveying love for the
pet, for training purposes, or to administer medications. The caloric
consumption associated with these treats should be accounted for in
the nutritional plan and should not exceed 10% of the daily caloric
consumption. The caloric density of common treats such as
vegetables, fruits, eggs, etc., has been reported elsewhere.9,11 One
strategy is to use a pre-determined portion of the normal daily ration
as treats to avoid nutritional imbalance issues.
After an initial challenge to adjust the nutritional plan, the desired
rate of weight loss is frequently attained. The pet owner often
requires encouragement at this stage because improved patient
mobility is often not noted until 10% weight loss or more has been
achieved. At this early stage, pet owners might question the value of

their efforts, and reminders of the therapeutic goals of improved life
quality can be a necessary reminder. Pets predictably show improved
mobility, activity, energy and comfort as the successful weight loss
plan progresses and owners tend to be encouraged at this stage.
Some owners of very obese pets require continued incentive and
encouragement as they are satisfied with the improvement seen
when BCS drops from 8/9 to 7/9, for example. These owners can be
encouraged that the best is yet to come. The Labrador Retriever
lifespan study suggested that the benefit of an extended lifespan
(presumably related to reduced immobility and pain) was most
evident upon attaining a BCS of 5/9. Client counseling may also be
needed if the initial target weight is attained, but the pet still has a
BCS >5/9. Once the ideal BW and BCS are attained, the daily caloric
consumption may need to be increased 10-20% to prevent continued
weight loss. Continued serial monitoring of BW and BCS is advised
to ensure that rebound weight gain does not occur because the pet
may maintain a lower-than-average daily energy requirement.

Developing a Physical Rehabilitation and Lifestyle
Plan
Nutritional management combined with an exercise plan is likely to
be more effective than dietary management alone, especially in
regard to preserving lean muscle mass.12,13 This program can be
designed as a progressive training period directed at pet owners’
specific mobility and lifestyle goals for their pet. For instance, if the
goal is to be able to complete neighborhood walks of defined length,
the plan can focus on identified current impediments (lack of
cardiovascular fitness, muscular weakness, obesity, pain, etc.) Much
like training for a marathon, the program should include progressive
steps toward the ultimate goal. Working in collaboration with a
certified canine rehabilitation practitioner, when possible, is often
very helpful in this regard (ch. 256). In-clinic physical rehabilitation
and therapeutic exercise, combined with training the pet owner to be
able to perform at-home therapies, is most likely to be successful.
Some pet owners may be more willing to exercise for the health
benefit of their pets than they are for themselves, and this is one
subject of various One Health initiatives.14 The veterinary team

should champion and support the pet owner through the initial
stages of the program because it often takes 3-6 weeks of
comprehensive nutritional and physical rehabilitation management
before discernible improvements in patient activity, mobility and
weight loss are seen. Once attained, however, this observable
increase in enthusiasm for activity often serves as the tipping point
within the program. In the author’s opinion, photo and video
documentation of these cases can serve as powerful motivator to
engage subsequent pet-owning families to start such a program and
as well as to maintain long-term adherence.

IMMOBILITY MANAGEMENT
When considering the comorbid conditions of obesity and
immobility, effective management of the obesity component often
has profoundly positive impacts upon restoring mobility.
Nonetheless, therapies targeted at specific underlying diseases such
OA and neurologic diseases are often indicated. With OA, for
instance, pain control may be essential in order to achieve the
moderately active lifestyle and physical rehabilitation plan needed to
optimize the weight loss plan (ch. 6). OA is often the result of an
inciting event such as joint instability; examples include cranial
cruciate ligament disease and juvenile stages of canine hip dysplasia
characterized by hip joint hyperlaxity. In such instances, while often
not 100% curative, surgical management of the instability mitigates
the progression of OA and is usually indicated. In addition to surgical
management, lifelong support of joint health combined with
appropriate analgesic strategies are indicated.

Pain Control
Relief of pain is central to the restoration of life quality (and,
therefore, life quantity) for pets afflicted by obesity and immobility
(ch. 6). Control of inflammation and pain has primarily focused
upon the role of prostaglandin E2 for many years (ch. 143). Beyond
cyclooxygenase-inhibiting nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
(NSAIDs) and, more recently, a prostaglandin receptor antagonist,
grapiprant, treatment options for inflammation and pain are limited.

It is important, however, to recognize that pain and inflammation
are mediated through several other potent signaling proteins such as
nerve growth factor (NGF) that represent novel therapeutic targets.15
NGF, released from chondrocytes and synovial lining cells
(fibroblasts and macrophages), circulates in increased amounts in
osteoarthritic joints. NGF, through binding to tropomyosin receptor
kinase A (TrkA) on primary afferent (sensory) nerve endings,
induces both functional and phenotypic alterations responsible for
pronociceptive effects. NGF also stimulates the release of
inflammatory mediators through binding to TrkA receptors on mast
cells and other immune cells. Binding of free NGF circulating in the
synovial fluid of osteoarthritic joints via administration of speciesspecific, anti-NGF monoclonal antibodies shows promise as a novel
therapy for OA pain in humans, dogs, and cats (ch. 143). Other
treatment modalities in the evolving field of biomedicine include
plasmid therapy. Plasmids, which are extrachromosomal DNA
molecules that are often of supercoiled circular topology, can be used
for altering cellular functions including the reduction of chronic
inflammation. Improved plasmid manufacturing efficiencies and
scalability are making this field increasingly accessible and initial
safety and efficacy study in dogs appears promising.16
Non-systemic OA therapy using a novel radioisotope (tin-117m) in
homogeneous colloid suspension via intra-articular injection is also
encouraging as a novel therapy for up to 1 year of relief of OA pain in
dogs.17 The tin-117m microparticle remains within the joint space
and emits low-energy conversion electrons with a 0.3 mm range of
activity. This is said to provide targeted therapy without systemic
side-effects. Circulating inflammatory macrophages and
synoviocytes selectively engulf the microparticles and undergo
apoptosis by the conversion electron activity. Limited penetration of
tin-117m has preserved the integrity and functionality of nonsynovial tissues such as bone, cartilage, tendons and ligaments in
healthy dogs. Ultimately, the microparticles decay to inert tin, but
the effects are said to last up to 1 year.

Joint Health Support

Polysulfated glycosaminoglycans (PSGAGs) are semisynthetic
products that stimulate collagen synthesis and inhibit its breakdown.
There is weak evidence of efficacy at reducing clinical signs based on
clinical trials. As with many veterinary studies, the inability to
discern strong evidence of efficacy may have resulted from low
patient numbers and/or outcome measures that fail to effectively
discriminate between varying levels of patient mobility and function.
Nutraceuticals are products derived from food sources, often with
purported but unsubstantiated health benefits. Pragmatically, it is
important to realize nutraceuticals are classified as dietary
supplements in the United States by the Food and Drug
Administration and, as such, are not subject to the same stringent
regulatory guidelines as pharmaceuticals. Thus, veterinarians should
consider efficacy and quality control data when advising such
supplements. Evidence of efficacy could include improvement in
clinical signs, but evidence of joint health preservation may also be of
value. High quality supplementation with chondroitin
sulfate/glucosamine/avocado soybean unsaponifiable ingredients
may be of value over the long term. Additionally, there is a growing
body of evidence that undenatured type II collagen (UC-II) offers
pain relief comparable to NSAID therapy.18

SUMMARY
The “dreaded duo” of obesity and immobility needlessly robs
millions of pets of life quality and, as a result, of life quantity. In
reality, these comorbid conditions are almost entirely preventable.
Further, they are often readily treated and the cornerstone to that
treatment is effective weight loss through a comprehensively
managed program that typically combines both nutritional and
lifestyle/therapeutic exercise plans. While many veterinarians are
knowledgeable enough to know that these comorbidities can be
effectively managed, many seem reluctant to fully engage the effort.
Perhaps this stems from the belief that the pet owner is not
sufficiently motivated or the lack of inner conviction that such
management applied to their patient will have sufficient impact to
warrant the effort expended. The author simply notes that there is
little that is more satisfying than being able to restore life quality to

an obese pet whose well-being has been robbed by immobility. The
ability to give a life back to such a pet (and often its owner) stems
from the ability to see the potential of “the lean dog within” and to
believe that the principles described in this chapter will predictably
achieve satisfying results.
