Chapter 227: Concurrent
Infection and Immune
Suppression
Andrew L. Leisewitz

A C RO N YM S
CDV canine distemper virus
CNS central nervous system
IHA immune-mediated hemolytic anemia
ITP immune-mediated thrombocytopenia
IV intravenous
UTI urinary tract infection

INTRODUCTION
An animal’s body contains all that is required to sustain microbial
life and as such it is an ideal environment in which microbes can
flourish. Despite this, we survive and thrive in the face of this
constant onslaught and this survival depends on a very complex,
highly regulated and multifaceted set of defense systems. This
defense allows coexistence with normal microbial organisms that are
required in health (such as the gut and skin microbiota) while at the
same time fending off invasion from pathogens.
When a host’s own defenses turn against self, autoimmune
disease-mediated self-destruction results (ch. 169). This is fairly

common, probably affecting about 5% of animals.1 The cornerstone
of treating these immune-mediated conditions are drugs that
generally cause quite indiscriminate suppression of the immune
system (ch. 144). This opens the host up to the danger of a new or
reactivation of a dormant infection. Examples include urinary tract
infections (UTIs) in dogs on long-term glucocorticoids (ch. 307) or
cats with relapsing herpesvirus-associated upper respiratory tract
disease (ch. 205). Some infections may actually themselves trigger
autoimmunity. Canine babesiosis (ch. 197) is a well-known trigger
for immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (ch. 174), with multiple
species of this parasite having been described as triggers.2
For microorganisms to survive in the host, they have been
pressured to evolve means of subverting the host defenses and in
some cases, this can result in dangerous host-wide
immunosuppression. Again, this exposes the host to microbial
invasion. In this vein, canine ehrlichiosis (ch. 193) and distemper
virus infection (ch. 204) are frequently associated with dangerous
secondary infections.
Clinicians will frequently insert medical devices (such as catheters)
into patients and this compromises what is usually a robust physical
defense barrier, making the host vulnerable to infection.
Although rare, there are immune deficiency diseases that occur as
a result of genetic abnormalities that directly compromise
components of the immune system and these can result in life
threatening infection early in life (ch. 180). An example would be
cyclic hematopoiesis in gray Collies in which a genetic mutation
results in neutrophil malfunction and life-threatening pyogenic
infections.
Some infections (such as Pneumocystis jirovecii) are seen only in
immunocompromised patients. As such, awareness of unusual
pathogens should alert the clinician to immunosuppression.
There are occasions when a host’s immune response to an
invading pathogen can be so exuberant that it is unfocussed,
excessive, and even dysfunctional, resulting in life-threatening
collateral organ damage and concurrent immune suppression. The
classic examples here are blood-borne infections as seen with
bacterial sepsis or severe babesiosis.

WHEN NECESSARY
IMMUNOSUPPRESSION ASSOCIATES
WITH INFECTION
TREATING AUTOIMMUNITIES IN THE FACE
OFINFECTION OR WHEN TREATING
AUTOIMMUNITIES RESULTS IN INFECTION
There are numerous situations in which a clinician will be faced with
the dilemma of a patient requiring immunosuppressive treatment
while harboring an infection or a patient that develops an infection
while on the immunosuppressive regime. These situations are very
varied and as such, a strict algorithmic approach cannot be followed.
Rather, sound clinical judgment will be required to balance the need
for treatment adjustments.
The cornerstone of treatment in the management of autoimmunity
is drug-induced immunosuppression3 (ch. 169). These treatment
modalities may result in new infections (such as high levels of
glucocorticoids in cats resulting in dermatophyte infections),4
unmask occult infection (such as upper respiratory herpesviral
reactivation in stressed cats)5 or aggravate existing low-grade
infections (as can be seen with inappropriate immunosuppression in
dogs suffering from atopy).6 There are numerous case reports of
animals that developed opportunistic infections when
immunosuppressed with various drugs, most commonly
prednisolone and cyclosporine used alone or together.7 Such
infections include Nocardia spp., Neospora spp. and
papillomavirus,8-13 as well as opportunistic fungal infections.14-21
Because of the role infections play in triggering autoimmunity,
clinicians should be aware that poor response to
immunosuppression may be associated with a flare-up of an
infectious agent that could perpetuate the autoimmune
inflammation.
The most common reason for pet owners seeking veterinary care is
dermatological disease and the most common skin disease is allergyinduced pruritus (ch. 160). If the allergen cannot be identified and

specifically avoided (as may be the case with a food allergen), lifelong
immune modulation becomes necessary. Although allergen-specific
immunotherapy is available, many practitioners prefer to use an
immunosuppressive drug. This has been a very rapidly growing area
of drug development and increasingly targeted treatments with fewer
side-effects have become available (such as oclacitinib and
lokivetmab). However, the newer treatments are expensive and
glucocorticoids (usually prednisolone or prednisone) are still widely
used because they are very cheap and also effective (ch. 144). The
side-effects of glucocorticoids are numerous and serious, however,
and include indiscriminate immunosuppression and metabolic
derangements. Cyclosporine, which is safer than glucocorticoids in
the long term, has been available in a veterinary-specific formulation
for decades and is used most commonly to manage atopic disease in
both dogs and cats. There have been several studies that have
reported on infectious complications of long-term steroid and/or
cyclosporine use for the control of allergic skin disease. Lower UTI is
a well-known complication (ch. 307). One-third of cyclosporinetreated dogs had at least one positive urine culture during
treatment.22 Cyclosporine (often used in feline dermatology
practice) may also play a role in toxoplasmosis infection in cats (ch.
197).23 Just under a fifth of dogs receiving long-term corticosteroid
treatment developed culture-positive UTIs.24 The same is not true
for oclacitinib.25 Neither prednisolone or cyclosporine appears to
increase the incidence of UTIs in cats.26
Some of the most commonly managed autoimmunities in the small
animal veterinary domain are hematological and include immunemediated hemolytic anemia (IHA; ch. 174) and immune-mediated
thrombocytopenia (ITP; ch. 175). In some parts of the world,
primary IHA and ITP (no diagnosable trigger) are more common
than secondary IHA or ITP (commonly triggered by an infectious
agent). Usually, irrespective of whether these diseases are caused by
an infection or occur as a primary disease, immunosuppression is
required. The suppression of primary autoimmunity may result in a
new infection or the reactivation of a dormant infection.
Antimicrobial therapy will be required together with immune

suppression in cases of secondary autoimmunity where the trigger is
an infectious agent.
Examples of clinical presentations where the clinician is faced with
this conundrum can include:
1. A dog receiving glucocorticoid monotherapy for IHA develops a
clinical lower UTI. In this scenario, one can try to taper the
steroid dose as quickly as the hematological response to
immune suppression will allow, while introducing a
bactericidal antibiotic for a week to 10 days (or until several
days past cytological cure). Reculturing the urine after
completion of the antibiotic treatment would be
recommended, to prove bacteriological cure. The danger of
leaving a dog on long-term immunosuppression with a clinical
UTI is the possibility that the infection will ascend and result
in pyelonephritis (ch. 304).27 Suppression of hemolysis
would, however, remain the therapeutic priority. Should
infection become life-threatening, the intensity of antibiotic
treatment should be increased (to include 4 quadrant drugs
preferably administered parenterally).
2. A cat is being treated with cyclosporine for recurring
eosinophilic granulomas on its lips (ch. 258) and an upper
respiratory tract infection develops characterized by epiphora,
sneezing and a serous nasal discharge (ch. 205). Reactivation
of a herpesvirus infection seems most likely. As long as the
respiratory disease remains mild and the cat continues to eat
and drink and show normal habitus, treatment adjustment is
probably not indicated. Should the cat’s respiratory signs
worsen, however, it would be necessary to withdraw the
cyclosporine and provide supportive treatment (which may
include an antiviral medication). It would be important to
remember that >50% of cats will maintain good control of
their allergic skin disease on alternate day (or less)
cyclosporine treatment and as such, once disease is controlled,
attempts should be made to reduce drug frequency to the
lowest possible controlling dosage. Treatable triggers for the
eosinophilic granuloma (such as food allergy or flea bite
hypersensitivity, ch. 160) must be rigorously investigated and
controlled. Therapeutic monitoring of cyclosporine blood

levels is not recommended by dermatologists in the
management of allergic skin disease; however, there is interest
in the therapeutic monitoring of the immunosuppressive
effects on T cells when monitoring cyclosporine use in the
treatment of other immune-mediated diseases (ch. 169).28
3. A 2-year-old Rhodesian Ridgeback is treated with high dosages
of prednisolone orally for steroid-responsive meningitisarteritis (ch. 242). The dog had neurological deficits in its
hind limbs and had developed a non-healing ulcer over the
dorsum of one of its carpi from dragging that paw. Initial
response to treatment is good but then the dog suddenly
becomes weak and febrile, and deteriorates rapidly. A
significant infection is suspected, with the ulcer providing a
portal of entry. Although no murmur is ausculted, a vegetation
is discovered on a mitral valve leaflet (ch. 232).
Immunosuppression, while providing rapid and obvious relief
to the central nervous system (CNS) inflammation, had
precipitated life-threatening sepsis (ch. 128). The endocarditis
was most likely chronic and, being subclinical, was missed on
physical examination. The presence of a non-healing ulcer
should have alerted the clinician to the possibility of
bacteremia and endocarditis before potent
immunosuppression was initiated. This is a difficult scenario
to manage but immediate withdrawal of the prednisolone and
the initiation of a high dose intravenous (IV) broad spectrum
antibiotic is warranted (after collection of samples for bacterial
culture and sensitivity). Very cautious reintroduction of
immunosuppression could be considered together with longterm oral antibiotics following stabilization.
4. A 4-year-old male Great Dane is diagnosed with acquired
(autoimmune) myasthenia gravis (ch. 253).
Anticholinesterase therapy is associated with an unacceptable
level of cholinergic side-effects but the dog does well on
glucocorticoid-induced immunosuppression. As is common
with this disease, the dog develops aspiration pneumonia (ch.
217) as a result of megaesophagus and weakness in the
muscles of deglutition. Fever, depression, and a high serum Creactive protein concentration confirm the radiographic

findings of pneumonia. The conflicted situation of the absolute
need for glucocorticoid-induced immunosuppression to try to
prevent further aspiration in the face of acute septic
pneumonia poses a unique challenge and the need to balance
treatment priorities. The addition of non-steroid drugs that are
more selective in targeting lymphocytes and less suppressive of
the innate immune system (azathioprine, mycophenolate
mofetil, cyclosporine; ch. 169) should be considered in
addition to a lowered glucocorticoid dosage. If possible, a
percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube (ch. 81) should be
placed in an attempt to bypass the upper gastrointestinal tract
and make the use of enteral drugs possible. However, there are
substantial risks associated with anesthesia in a patient like
this and risk/benefit should be carefully considered and
discussed with the owner. Empirical antibiotic use will be
necessary as it is unlikely that a sample from the lower airways
will be available and culture and sensitivity data would take
too long to generate to be useful immediately. Antibiotics that
have the potential to worsen neuromuscular transmission
should be avoided (aminoglycosides, ampicillin, ciprofloxacin,
erythromycin, imipenem). Parenteral use of high-dose
antibiotic combinations would be advised initially (such as
amoxicillin/clavulanate and enrofloxacin). Good supportive
nursing care and monitoring the trend in acetylcholinesterase
antibody levels can be a helpful way of establishing the
response to immunosuppression.

WHEN INFECTION CAUSES
AUTOIMMUNITY
Idiopathic autoimmunity develops in the absence of any identifiable
trigger—and this is termed primary autoimmunity. A secondary
autoimmunity develops when a known trigger is involved in the
pathogenesis. Infection is an increasingly recognized trigger to
autoimmune diseases.29 There are many mechanisms whereby
infections can trigger autoimmunity including immune dysregulation
and loss of immune tolerance. Many factors play a role in

predisposing certain individuals to infection-induced autoimmunity
including genetic predisposition, epigenetic phenomena, or a
microenvironmental milieu favoring infection.30-35 Circulating
immune-complex deposition may also activate immune cells through
receptor engagement or may deliver immunoglobulin bound host
nucleic acid to toll-like receptors during some infections.36
Infectious agents may also damage target cells in such a way as to
expose otherwise invisible epitopes.30
An infectious trigger of red cell destruction in IHA has specifically
been proposed37 and more than 20 different infections have been
associated with the pathogenesis of this autoimmunity.38 ITP (ch.
175) has also been associated with Angiostrongylus (ch.
217),39 Leishmania (ch. 197),40 Ehrlichia (ch. 193),41 and Babesia
(ch. 197)42 infections. In humans, Helicobacter has been associated
with ITP and Mycoplasma with IHA.43,44 A recent veterinary
example of a non-hematological immune-mediated disease that is
infection-associated is histiocytic ulcerative colitis of Boxer dogs.
Work has shown it to be the result of an infection with an invasive E.
coli. The disease is antibiotic-responsive (ch. 263).45

WHEN INFECTION CAUSES
IMMUNOSUPPRESSION
There are several important and common infectious diseases of
companion animals that cause immunosuppression. They may result
in significant secondary infection that will require antimicrobial
treatment. Feline retroviruses (chs. 198, 199) are a classic example
in the cat. Parvovirus infection in puppies (ch. 201) is strongly
immunosuppressive and causes severe gut barrier disruption,
predisposing to sepsis. Puppies also are not old enough to have
developed immunity to many infectious agents and are thus at far
greater risk of infection. This cluster of vulnerabilities results in
septicemia (usually with Gram-negative bacteria of enteric origin) as
well as occasional infections at IV catheter sites and joints. Upper

airway defenses are compromised by nasal aspergillosis (ch. 210)
that disrupts normal nasal turbinates and Bordetella bronchiseptica
organisms paralyze respiratory cilia function (chs. 203, 215).
Anaplasma phagocytophilum resides within the neutrophil and
compromises this crucial immune cell’s function (ch. 193). Canine
distemper virus (CDV, ch. 204) causes immunosuppression by
inducing both a T- and a B-cell lymphopenia; bacterial pneumonia is
a common consequence (ch. 217). Other infections identified in
CDV infected dogs include those caused by Toxoplasma (ch. 197),
Salmonella (ch. 195), and Nocardia (ch. 188). Generalized
demodicosis has also been mentioned.
The type of secondary infections that may take advantage of
infection-induced immunosuppression depends on the immune
mechanism that the primary infection compromises. Viral infections
that compromise cell-mediated immunity predispose to infection
with opportunistic agents such as Toxoplasma gondii,
Mycobacterium spp., and Nocardia spp. Reactivation of dormant
feline respiratory viruses (such as herpesvirus) may also occur.
Where barrier function is compromised, opportunistic pyogenic
bacteria frequently become problematic.

WHEN IMMUNOSUPPRESSION IN THE
FACE OF INFECTION IS HELPFUL
There is convincing evidence that people suffering from a range of
infectious diseases (bacterial meningitis, tuberculous pericarditis,
typhoid, pneumocystis and viral pneumonia) show increased survival
if treated with corticosteroids. There are also many diseases in which
corticosteroids reduce clinical signs and enhance patient comfort and
do not alter outcome. Very few infectious diseases (notably viral
hepatitis and cerebral malaria) have been shown to have a worse
outcome on corticosteroids.46 Most of these infectious diseases do
not affect small animals and there is little evidence beyond a few case
reports and specialist opinion that corticosteroids actually improve
disease outcome in any small animal infection. The use of a
glucocorticoid in the treatment of an infection could seem
counterintuitive (why use a potentially immunosuppressive drug in

an animal with an infection?). Although this may be true in the
management of most infections, it is clearly not true in all cases. A
recent and classic human example is the use of dexamethasone in the
management of COVID pneumonia.47 Benefits include suppression
of harmful inflammation, alleviation of pain and discomfort and
suppression of secondary immune-mediated disease.
Many veterinarians use glucocorticoids at anti-inflammatory
dosages for short periods of time to relieve the irritation caused by
infectious agents that cause acute upper airway infections in dogs
(canine infectious respiratory disease, so called “kennel cough” [ch.
203]). Fungal pneumonia caused by blastomycosis and
histoplasmosis may actually worsen in the immediate post-treatment
period as the fungus dies, liberating proinflammatory components of
the organism (ch. 209). Glucocorticoids may assist in relieving
this.48 In an uncontrolled study in dogs with blastomycosis treated
with an antifungal drug and either nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories
or glucocorticoids, no difference was noted in the outcome between
the two treatment groups.49 A retrospective study of dogs with
chronic histoplasmosis-induced coughing due to hilar
lymphadenopathy showed that there was a quicker clinical response
in cases treated with glucocorticoids.50
Infections of the CNS (chs. 242, 250) often will be more injurious
to the host because of inflammation than because of a direct effect of
the organism itself. There are no controlled studies to demonstrate
the benefit of glucocorticoids in animals with CNS infections and
inflammation but there is anecdotal and case report evidence in
small animals and clear evidence in people. If glucocorticoids are
being considered, it is important to ensure that all diagnostic
samples have been collected (for culture, cytologic analysis, titers,
polymerase chain reaction) before treatment is commenced.
Hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia are commonly
associated with blood-borne infections such as Babesia spp.,
Ehrlichia spp., other rickettsias, and hemoplasmas (chs. 193 and
194). The addition of glucocorticoids to the treatment protocols for
these infections is common, as they reduce the immune-mediated
cytopenias often associated with infection. Despite the fact that
controlled studies have never been done, glucocorticoids are often

suggested as part of the management protocol for cats with feline
infectious peritonitis (ch. 200).51
There is a long-running debate around the use of glucocorticoids
in the treatment of sepsis in people and animals. A dysregulated
immune response is a significant contributor to morbidity and
mortality in this multiorgan disease (ch. 128). This has been
associated with a syndrome of relative adrenal insufficiency, which
some argue requires glucocorticoid support. Often these patients are
immunosuppressed while at the same time presenting with a
hyperinflammatory systemic milieu. There has been recent interest
in the role various antibiotics (especially macrolides) may play, not
because of their antimicrobial effect but for their role in stimulating
the repair of damaged tissues as well as assisting metabolic
reprogramming to restore immune homeostasis in sepsis.52
If glucocorticoids are used as part of the management protocol of
an animal that has an infectious disease, the steroid of choice should
be a short-acting oral or IV formulation with a low relative potency
(such as prednisolone, prednisone, prednisolone sodium succinate or
methylprednisolone sodium succinate) (chs. 144, 224).
Dexamethasone is less ideal as a first choice. Depo formulations
should never be used in this context. As is usual with glucocorticoid
use, the lowest dosage and shortest course necessary is best. A typical
prednisolone dose should not usually exceed 1 mg/kg/day unless
there is life-threatening autoimmune disease present, in which case
significantly higher doses may be required. The obvious concern
when using glucocorticoids in the management protocol for an
infectious disease is the possibility for immunosuppression-induced
infection flare-up or the development of additional infections.
However, clinical experience seems to suggest that this is not a
common occurrence. With some difficult-to-confirm infectious
diseases (such as bacterial endocarditis and Bartonella spp.),
glucocorticoids may in fact aid the clinician in recovering the
microorganism and facilitate confirming the diagnosis.
Helpful guidelines regarding the use of glucocorticoids in
infectious disease have been published and some of these include53:
• Diagnose the infection before initiating steroid treatment.
• Only use steroids with or after employing anti-infective drugs.

• Think critically about the justification for steroid use in each
case.
• Monitor patients for progressive infection, as steroids will
reduce inflammation and may make progressive infection less
obvious.

IMMUNE DYSREGULATION IN
CRITICAL ILLNESS
Sepsis is common in the human hospital population and despite
valiant efforts, little progress has been made in reducing the
mortality in this subset of patients. Although sepsis is less common
in small animal veterinary practice, severe and life-threatening
inflammatory disease is a common cause for dogs and cats to be
admitted to a hospital for intensive care (ch. 128). Sepsis is
characterized by a state of hyperinflammation early in the disease
process and this is typified by what has been termed a “cytokine
storm.”53-56 Early death is probably caused by an overwhelming,
unregulated inflammatory response while later death is associated
with persistent immunosuppression and recurrent infection and
organ failures.57 There is growing evidence that these two phases of
sepsis are not distinct, with immune suppression following
hyperinflammation, but these phases may in fact run concurrently.
There is an interest in this immune dysregulation as a therapeutic
target. It has been shown that sepsis impairs delayed type IV
hypersensitivity to antigens against which patients have been
vaccinated. Autopsy studies have shown apoptosis-induced collapse
of lymphocyte populations. Cytokine production is also severely
impaired later in sepsis. These findings are all clearly deleterious and
expose a patient to an elevated risk to recovery.
Numerous drug interventions have been trialed in an attempt to
alter the poor prognosis. These have included many immune
modulators such as glucocorticoids, synthetic antagonists of toll-like
receptors, statins, antiendotoxins, anti-cytokines, antioxidants, and
nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories. None of these interventions has
succeeded in altering outcome. One group of drugs that has shown
promise in numerous trials is macrolide antibiotics. They have

shown potent and wide-ranging immunomodulatory potential
beyond just an antibiotic effect and an effect in altering the immune
response of hyperinflammation or suppression.58 Independent of
their antimicrobial effect, macrolides modulate key pathways and
mechanisms involved in immune dysregulation, improving survival
and reducing inflammation-induced tissue damage in animal models
and in human randomized controlled trials.58

WHEN HOST GENETICS RESULT IN
IMMUNOSUPPRESSION
Primary immunodeficiency states in dogs and cats are rare genetic
deficiencies in a component of host defense (cells or proteins of
innate or acquired systems or a barrier compromise) (ch. 180).
Many of these diseases have been genetically characterized and some
can be tested for. Examples include Pneumocystis pneumonia in the
Miniature Dachshund (ch. 217), systemic aspergillosis in the
German Shepherd Dog (ch. 211), a breed propensity in Rottweilers
and Doberman Pinschers for parvovirus infection (ch. 201) and a
predisposition to systemic avian mycobacteriosis (ch. 188),
toxoplasmosis, and neosporosis (ch. 197) in Basset Hounds and
Miniature Schnauzers. Shar-Peis are prone to myxedematous skin
disease with an immunodeficiency that predisposes to pyoderma
(chs. 177, 181).
There are some clinical features that should alert the clinician to
the possibility of a genetic cause of immune deficiency. These include
recurrent, protracted or chronic infections; infections with
opportunistic organisms that are not usually associated with disease;
severe or atypical manifestations of disease; delayed, incomplete or
no response to antimicrobial treatment; and adverse events following
the use of a modified live virus vaccine.
Genetic defects may affect the innate or acquired limbs of the
immune system or the various body barriers (such as the skin).
Innate deficiencies result in compromised phagocytic cells
(neutrophils, monocytes) and complement proteins. These usually
result in pyogenic or chronic granulomatous infections of the skin,
respiratory tract and oral cavity. Overwhelming sepsis may also

result. Chronic relapsing or persistent infections predispose to
amyloidosis, vasculitis and the complications of immune complex
deposition. Diseases of the acquired immune system compromise Band T-lymphocyte functions and thus affect antibody and cytokine
production. These deficiencies may also result in pyogenic infections
but in addition may predispose to viral and fungal infections and
infections with intracellular bacteria.

MANAGING ORGAN REJECTION IN
POST-TRANSPLANT PATIENTS
Feline renal transplant surgery is performed in a few centers around
the world. Recipients are on life-long immunosuppression (usually
with glucocorticoids and cyclosporine) and as such are prone to
develop postoperative infections. In the largest study to date (169
cats) to evaluate post-transplant infection, infection was the second
most common reason for death (organ rejection being the most
common), accounting for 14% of the mortalities. Most infections
occurred within 2.5 months of the surgery and cats that became
diabetic following surgery were more likely to develop infections.
Infection is thus an important cause of morbidity with this
procedure.59
Acquired deficiencies develop in animals with a previously intact
immune system that becomes transiently or permanently
dysfunctional because of an underlying disease condition, exposure
to a drug, infectious agent or medical device. These have been
discussed above. Clinicians sometimes fail to recognize the danger of
introduced medical devices and the infection risks posed by these
(ch. 186). Perhaps the most common examples would be urinary
(ch. 98) and IV (chs. 74, 75) catheters. The longer these devices are
in place, the greater the chance of infection and this is especially true
in dogs that are already immunosuppressed (as is the case in puppies
with parvovirus infection). Prevention of catheter-induced UTI
through prophylactic antibiotic use is not advised (ch. 7).

The heart has two fundamental mechanical functions that are
essential for operation of the circulatory system. One is to eject
enough blood into the aorta and pulmonary arteries with sufficient
force to meet the perfusion requirements of the metabolizing tissues.
The other is to receive blood from the pulmonary and systemic veins
in a manner that provides adequate drainage of the pulmonary and
systemic capillary beds and maintains an appropriate distribution of
the circulating blood pool. Mean arterial pressure in the systemic
arterial tree approximates 90-100 mm Hg in healthy dogs and cats,
ensuring adequate distribution of blood through the multitude of
vascular beds in this high-resistance circuit. Mean arterial pressure
in the low-resistance pulmonary circuit averages around 20 mm Hg.
Cardiac failure can be defined as the pathophysiologic state
wherein the heart is impaired in its ability to eject or receive blood,

and this impairment becomes severe enough to overwhelm the
compensatory mechanisms of the cardiovascular system.1 Heart
disease is defined as the presence of any cardiac finding outside the
accepted limits of normality, including a cardiac murmur caused by
any structural heart lesion (ch. 38); an abnormal cardiac rhythm on
electrocardiogram (ECG; chs. 96, 230); or reduced contractility
noted on echocardiogram (chs. 73, 97, 233, 234). The presence of
identifiable heart disease does not inherently imply that heart failure
is currently present or will ever manifest as a clinical problem. Heart
failure is present when abnormal cardiac function results in either
the retention of sodium and water and elevated venous and capillary
pressures (congestive heart failure or backward failure) or
inadequate cardiac output (low-output heart failure or forward
failure).
Heart failure (ch. 229) can result from functional impairment of
the myocardium (chs. 233 and 234), heart valves (ch. 232), or
pericardium (ch. 235), or as a consequence of increased resistance
to ejection (chs. 218, 231, and 236). Myocardial failure is defined as
a decrease in myocardial contractility and is not synonymous with
heart failure. Although myocardial failure is common in patients
with heart failure, some patients suffer heart failure even though
myocardial function is preserved. Relevant examples include
patients that experience massive pulmonary thromboembolism (ch.
219), acute valvular insufficiency (ch. 232), or cardiac tamponade
(ch. 235). It is helpful for the practicing clinician to be mindful that
normal circulatory function is dependent on the overall functional
integrity of the heart, the vascular bed, and the blood, together with
its regular mass of circulating red blood cells.2 Signs of circulatory
compromise develop with serious disruptions of any one of these
components of this integrated system. Thus, although all patients
with heart failure evidence signs of circulatory compromise, the
converse is not necessarily true.

PATHOGENESIS
Heart failure is a progressive disorder that begins with an initial
insult or event that perturbs myocyte or myocardial function. It is

clinically helpful to characterize patients with heart failure based on
the main or most obvious functional consequences of their
underlying disease (Box 228.1). Accordingly, some patients develop
signs of heart failure primarily as a consequence of impaired cardiac
filling due to restrictive pericardial diseases (ch. 235), mitral and
tricuspid valvular stenoses (ch. 231), cor triatriatum (ch. 231), or
primary myocardial disorders that reduce ventricular compliance,
including hypertrophic (HCM) and restrictive (RCM)
cardiomyopathy (chs. 233 and 234). Patients that develop heart
failure from these diseases are often appropriately described as
suffering from diastolic heart failure due to the primary effect of
reduced diastolic filling. The concept of ventricular compliance is
best explained by a graphic display of the ventricle’s end-diastolic
pressure-volume relationship, the slope of which defines compliance
at any given level of preload (Figure 228.1).3 Distensibility is
closely related to compliance and refers to the pressure that is
required to fill the ventricle to a specified volume. Given the same
end-diastolic volume, end-diastolic pressure will be higher if the
ventricle is stiffer (less distensible and less compliant) than normal.
In other patients, heart failure results from afterload that is
increased to such a degree that it impedes ventricular ejection.
Examples include aortic or pulmonic stenosis (ch. 231), acute
pulmonary thromboembolism (ch. 219), and chronic systemic (ch.
236) or pulmonary (ch. 218) hypertension. Afterload represents the
sum of all those forces that oppose the ejection of blood from the
ventricle into the circulation and is often expressed as the systolic
tension or wall stress experienced by the ventricles during the period
of ejection.4 Afterload is determined mainly by the peripheral
(systemic) vascular resistance, the physical properties (compliance)
of the arterial tree, and the volume of blood in the ventricle at the
onset of systole.
Volume overload, whether the result of a left-to-right shunt or
valvular insufficiency, is a commonly encountered cause of heart
failure, wherein ventricular systolic performance is impaired due to
the combined influence of misdirected blood flow and a progressive
decline in myocardial contractility. Conversely, patients with primary
myocardial failure, including dilated (DCM) and ischemic
cardiomyopathy, secondarily develop volume overload due to

decreased contractility and altered chamber geometry. Inasmuch as
the diastolic and systolic functions of the heart are interrelated, both
tend to be compromised concurrently in animals with many heart
diseases. It is nonetheless clinically useful to distinguish those
patients with reduced systolic pump function from those with
compromised diastolic function and normal or nearly normal systolic
function.
Cardiac arrhythmias and conduction disturbances may exert
adverse effects on systolic or diastolic function depending on the type
and duration of the rhythm disturbance (ch. 230). In some clinical
situations, it can be quite difficult to determine if a specific
arrhythmia is the cause of the observed functional deficit or an
unfortunate complication of pre-existing heart disease. Patients with
severe chronic anemia, arteriovenous fistulas, or hyperthyroidism
may experience signs of heart failure even though their cardiac
output equals or exceeds that of normal animals, a disorder termed
high-output heart failure.5 In these circumstances, cardiac output
after the onset of heart failure is always less than it was prior to the
onset of heart failure, indicating that the heart can no longer meet
the increased blood flow requirements imposed by the underlying
disorder.

Regardless of the inciting abnormality, many patients with heart
disease show no clinical signs for a period of time, likely due to the
activation of a number of compensatory mechanisms. Ultimately,
sustained activation of these neurohormonal and cytokine
compensatory mechanisms leads to end organ changes and cardiac
remodeling, and thus precipitate the progression of heart failure.2
