Spironolactone
Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic that inhibits aldosterone
receptors. Benefits demonstrated in human patients with heart failure13 imply an
action independent of its diuretic effect. This agent therefore should be regarded
more broadly as an aldosterone receptor antagonist. Two studies have confirmed
its effectiveness in the management of dogs with CHF caused by MMVD14,15
leading to its frequent administration to dogs with heart failure.
Spironolactone has been administered for its diuretic effect, and other putative
benefits, in cats with heart disease and heart failure. A small randomized trial
conducted in cats with heart failure suggested an improved outcome in cats
receiving spironolactone in addition to other heart failure medications,16 but the

interpretation of the results was confounded by differences in disease severity in
the two treatment groups. Possible cutaneous adverse drug reactions17 have not
been observed in other studies.16 Available evidence suggests that spironolactone
may be of benefit in cats with heart failure, but limited data prevent stronger
conclusions.
In dogs, the effective dosage of spironolactone is 2 mg/kg PO q24h.18 In
contrast to furosemide, there is little evidence that improved control of clinical
signs will be obtained by higher dosages or more frequent administration.
Spironolactone does not have sufficient natriuretic potency to be used as the
sole diuretic in patients requiring medical management of signs of congestion.19 It
should be regarded as an agent to be administered alongside other diuretics,
particularly loop diuretics, to potentiate their effect. Additionally, aldosterone
receptor blockade is thought to block detrimental effects on the vasculature and
decrease cardiac remodeling.

Thiazide Diuretics
Thiazide diuretics represent another class of diuretic widely used in human
patients, particularly those with systemic hypertension. They are also used in
canine heart failure patients, especially where congestive signs are refractory to
furosemide and spironolactone. Thiazides predominantly act by inhibition of
sodium reuptake in the distal convoluted tubule; therefore, when used with a loop
diuretic and a potassium-sparing diuretic, thiazides produce “sequential nephron
blockade,” resulting in greater diuresis through inhibiting sodium reabsorption at
numerous sites in the nephron (Figure 229.3). Hydrochlorothiazide (e.g., 0.5-2
mg/kg PO q12-24h) is a commonly used thiazide diuretic.

Complications of Diuretic Treatment
There are numerous possible complications and side-effects of diuretic
administration that warrant the careful monitoring of patients receiving them
chronically. The most obvious “side-effect” of diuretics is polyuria and polydipsia.
Owners should always be warned that this is an expected effect of their pet’s
treatment.
All of the most commonly observed complications are direct consequences of
the drugs’ mechanisms of action and the patient’s adaptation to their
administration. These include volume depletion and reduction in cardiac output,
and electrolyte abnormalities.

Volume Depletion and Reduction in Cardiac Output
The intended effect of diuretic administration is a reduction in circulating fluid
volume. The goal is to reduce volume sufficiently to relieve congestive signs while
allowing maintenance of adequate perfusion. If the circulating fluid volume is
reduced excessively, or the patient is especially dependent on a high ventricular
filling pressure to maintain adequate cardiac output (notably in patients with

diastolic dysfunction, e.g., cats with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy [HCM]) then
there could be a fall in cardiac output and perfusion may be compromised. This
can manifest in a number of ways, including hypotension or azotemia. If these
signs develop after diuresis, it may be necessary to consider one or both of the
following:
• Reducing the intensity of diuretic treatment
• Introducing a more balanced heart failure treatment regimen that
counteracts the drop in cardiac output by other means, e.g., vasodilation
or the administration of inotropic drugs.
One common misapprehension is that a patient showing these signs is
“dehydrated” and will therefore benefit from IV fluid administration. Heart failure
—as explained above—is a problem of inappropriate fluid distribution. In a patient
with a normal heart, IV fluid administration is likely to improve cardiac output,
thereby improving signs of low cardiac output and poor perfusion. In a patient
with heart failure, particularly one with active congestion, there is already more
than enough fluid in the venous circulation; the problem is that the heart is unable
to adequately transfer that fluid into the arterial circulation. Adding more fluid
into the venous circulation is likely to worsen signs of congestion and is unlikely to
improve signs of poor perfusion. In human patients, IV fluid therapy during acute
decompensated heart failure worsens outcome.20 IV fluid therapy is usually
contraindicated in CHF.

Electrolyte Abnormalities
Electrolyte abnormalities commonly occur with diuretic treatment. The normal
physiologic response to increased sodium and water loss is stimulation of
homeostatic mechanisms that retain sodium and water, notably the RAAS and
also vasopressin release (ch. 228). One of the effects of stimulation of these
homeostatic mechanisms is altered electrolyte handling. Increased aldosterone
activity favors sodium retention and potassium loss in the distal nephron,
commonly leading to hypokalemia. Hypokalemia is less likely in patients
concurrently receiving treatments that counteract the RAAS.21 Widespread use of
angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs; see below) and spironolactone,
in addition to loop diuretics, means that hypokalemia is seen less frequently than
previously. Hypokalemia is now most likely to be encountered during the
emergency stabilization of patients that receive large doses of furosemide, might
not yet have been started on other agents and may have reduced intake due to
inappetence.
Severe, advanced heart disease and vigorous diuretic treatment can stimulate
vasopressin release. The resultant retention of free water can be associated with
hyponatremia.21 In human studies, the presence of hyponatremia in heart failure
patients is associated with a worse prognosis.22

Within the first 10-14 days of diuretic administration, a patient will adapt to the
increased sodium and water loss and reach a new steady state whereby increased
sodium loss has been balanced by more vigorous sodium retention.8,23 In this
new steady state, sodium intake will equal sodium loss, but crucially this will have
been achieved following a reduction in the patient’s circulating fluid volume. This
lower circulating fluid volume will be maintained, and signs of congestion remain
controlled, as long as the patient continues to receive (and respond to) the same
diuretic dosage, the sodium intake is consistent, and the heart disease does not
worsen significantly. The patient is most likely to develop complications of
diuretic treatment during the period in which this new equilibrium develops, i.e.,
in the 10-14 days following introduction or modification of a diuretic regimen.
Given the frequency with which abnormalities of volume homeostasis,
perfusion, and blood electrolyte concentrations occur in patients receiving
diuretics, it is good practice to evaluate indicators of renal function and blood
electrolyte concentrations before and after the initiation or substantial
modification of diuretic treatment. Re-checking serum urea, creatinine, sodium,
potassium and chloride concentrations 10-14 days after initiation or alteration of a
diuretic regimen allows early detection of abnormalities and necessary treatment
adjustments to be made.
For hospitalized patients with acute heart failure receiving intensive heart
failure therapy and frequent dosage adjustments, it is prudent to check serum
electrolyte concentrations and indicators of renal function regularly: ideally at
least once in every 24 hour period and more frequently in patients experiencing
complications.

Venodilators
Venodilators are agents that dilate the systemic veins. Many vasodilators act on
both veins and arteries and are described as “balanced” vasodilators (see below).
Some vasodilators act predominantly on veins and therefore primarily reduce
preload. By dilating veins, these agents increase the volume of the capacitance
vessels within the circulation, decreasing venous pressures, reducing the pressure
at which blood returns to the heart and reducing capillary hydrostatic pressures—
thus tending to reduce signs of congestion (Figure 229.2, D). Venodilators
reduce preload in a way that is complementary with diuretics: diuretics reduce the
volume of blood in the veins and venodilators increase the venous capacity to hold
that volume of blood at relatively lower pressures. The class of vasodilators that
acts predominantly on the veins is nitrate vasodilators and the most frequently
administered agent to veterinary patients is nitroglycerin (glyceryl trinitrate).
Some nitrate vasodilators, particularly nitroprusside, have effects on afterload and
preload (see balanced vasodilators, below).
Venodilators tend to be administered in situations where preload reduction is
required acutely, e.g., in the management of patients with severe heart failureinduced dyspnea requiring emergency management. Nitroglycerin typically is
administered as an ointment, requiring percutaneous absorption to be effective.
The method of administration and rapid development of tachyphylaxis (tolerance

and rapid loss of efficacy) limit the use of nitroglycerin to short periods of
administration in hospitalized patients.
There is some limited evidence of favorable effects of nitrate vasodilators in
human patients in the acute setting.24 Long-term, controlled studies of these
agents have not been conducted in veterinary patients. In anesthetized normal
dogs, splenic volume—and therefore, by inference, capacitance vessel volume—
increases in response to transdermal nitroglycerin administration,25 but orally
administered isosorbide dinitrate is not associated with a redistribution of blood
volume between body cavities,26 implying it may not be an effective venodilator in
dogs.

DRUGS USED IN THE TREATMENT OF HEART
FAILURE: DRUGS THAT DECREASE
AFTERLOAD
CHF is brought about by the chronic stimulation of several homeostatic
mechanisms responding to a perceived drop in pressure within the arterial
circulation (ch. 228). Many systems stimulated in heart failure—including the
sympathetic nervous system, the RAAS and the vasopressin system—result in
increased systemic vascular resistance. This aims to restore blood pressure to a
more normal level. Although initially beneficial, chronic vasoconstriction has a
detrimental effect on cardiac function. Increased vascular resistance either
impairs cardiac output or increases cardiac work needed to maintain adequate
cardiac output. Increased cardiac work increases myocardial oxygen consumption
and, if chronically increased, leads to further deterioration in cardiac function. In
patients with MMVD, systemic arterial constriction resists the ejection of blood
from the left ventricle into the aorta and favors the backward flow of blood
through the incompetent valve into the left atrium. Conversely, reduction of
resistance to ejection into the aorta (through reduced systemic vascular
resistance) favors blood leaving the ventricle this way, reducing the magnitude of
the regurgitant jet. If the resistance to ejection is reduced, it is also possible that a
similar cardiac output can be maintained with a lower ventricular preload—thus,
agents that reduce systemic vascular resistance may indirectly reduce preload.
The hypothetical advantages of arterial vasodilators are easy to understand:
they should lead to an improvement in cardiac output or alternatively the
maintenance of the same cardiac output but with reduced myocardial work
(Figure 229.2, E). These advantages translated into clinical benefits in
groundbreaking human studies.27,28
Various classes of drugs that are administered to heart failure patients act either
entirely or partly through a vasodilator effect, including the nitrates, ACEIs,
pimobendan, and calcium channel blockers. Previously, hydralazine29 and
prazosin were used for this purpose, but their use has fallen out of favor as
evidence to support the use of other agents has strengthened.

A potential disadvantage of vasodilator administration is that reducing vascular
resistance in a patient with already impaired cardiac function could cause signs of
hypotension such as syncope (ch. 40), weakness, and hypoperfusion. Patients
with certain underlying cardiac diseases, particularly outflow tract obstructions
and disorders of diastolic dysfunction (e.g., HCM), might be less able to increase
cardiac output following afterload reduction, and are therefore at greater risk of
the development of these complications. Despite these valid concerns, the wide
variety of benefits, beyond simple reduction in vascular resistance, associated with
administration of agents such as ACEIs, means that in practice they are frequently
given to patients with such underlying diseases. In such cases, more cautious
introduction and careful monitoring are warranted.

Nitroprusside
Nitroprusside is a rapidly acting, intravenously administered nitrate vasodilator
with a balanced effect, meaning that it reduces preload through venodilation and
afterload through arteriodilation. It is rapidly-acting with profound effects and
requires careful administration by IV constant rate infusion. In an intensive care
unit, where blood pressure can be carefully monitored (ch. 91), it can be a very
useful adjunct to other treatments in the acute management of a patient requiring
intensive preload and afterload reduction. Administration of nitroprusside in the
primary care setting is probably not safely practicable. Nitroprusside must be
protected from light during infusion. As with nitroglycerin, above, patients rapidly
become refractory to nitroprusside, which limits its value for chronic
administration. In human patients it has been shown that nitroprusside is
metabolized to cyanide, which limits the duration of its use.

Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors (ACEIs)
As a class, the ACEIs have been one of the most widely used types of agent in the
management of veterinary patients with heart failure. There are numerous agents
with similar pharmacodynamic effects; these include enalapril, benazepril,
ramipril and imidapril. The effectiveness of ACEIs for the treatment of canine
patients with heart failure was established in several studies in the 1990s.30,31
Since then, ACEIs have become a standard part of chronic therapy for most
patients with heart failure.
Evidence for the effectiveness of ACEI in the treatment of feline heart failure
patients is less well established. Due to their theoretical (rather than proven)
benefits, they are frequently given to cats with heart failure. One study’s
preliminary results suggested that ACEIs were superior to beta-blockers in the
treatment of heart failure secondary to feline myocardial disease.32 However, a
more recent prospective, blinded clinical trial failed to demonstrate a clear benefit
of ACEI administration to cats with heart disease, including cats in heart failure.33
Through the inhibition of angiotensin converting enzyme, ACEIs bring about
vasodilation and inhibit fluid retention (ch. 228). Their interference in the RAAS
is particularly beneficial in patients that are also receiving diuretics. The

complementary effect of the two types of agents is frequently used as an argument
for their routine co-administration. Generally ACEIs have been administered to
most patients with heart failure that require chronic diuresis unless
contraindicated. In practice this means that many dogs and cats receiving therapy
for heart failure will receive an ACEI. The dosages of some of these agents are
outlined in Box 229.2.
ACEIs are not particularly profound vasodilators, and their benefits are
associated more with chronic than acute administration. For this reason, their use
is more likely to constitute part of a chronic treatment regimen than to be initiated
in the acute heart failure setting.
Much controversy has surrounded whether ACEIs have a beneficial effect in
preclinical heart disease. Three prospective placebo-controlled studies in dogs
with preclinical mitral valve disease34-36 failed to conclusively demonstrate a
prolongation of the time to onset of heart failure. A retrospective study in dogs
with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM)37 suggested that benazepril could be
associated with improved outcome, but a prospective placebo-controlled study of
these agents has yet to be undertaken in the preclinical stage of this disease. No
conclusive evidence currently supports their use in the preclinical stages of feline
myocardial disease (ch. 234).
Evidence from clinical trials supports the use of ACEI in most canine patients
with signs of heart failure requiring chronic diuretic administration. Recently,
however there has been controversy regarding the continued necessity for ACE
inhibition in patients with MMVD if they are also receiving pimobendan.38 This
debate has not yet been concluded and many cardiologists continue to
recommend ACEI administration in this setting.
The evidence for the benefit of ACEI in feline heart failure patients is weaker33;
a recent consensus statement on the treatment of cats with myocardial disease39
did not strongly recommend their use in heart failure, although they continue to
be used by some cardiologists.

Pimobendan
Pimobendan is described as an “inodilator”: an agent with both inotropic and
vasodilatory effects. It is impossible to separate these two effects and therefore
somewhat artificial to consider the drug as either an “inotrope” or a “vasodilator.”
Further description of the mechanism of action of, and indications for, this drug
are found below under Drugs Used in the Treatment of Heart Failure: Drugs That
Enhance Systolic Function.

Calcium Channel Blockers
As a class, the calcium channel blockers have numerous and varied cardiac
electrophysiological and vascular effects. The calcium channel blocker most
widely administered to veterinary patients for its vasodilator effect is amlodipine.

It is most frequently used as an antihypertensive agent in cats with systemic
hypertension (ch. 236). Its marked effects as an arteriodilator have led some to
advocate its use as a vasodilator in dogs with heart failure. Arteriodilators may be
of particular benefit when that heart failure is secondary to MMVD, for reasons
outlined above. Experimental studies have shown a reduction in left atrial
pressure in dogs with mitral regurgitation associated with the administration of
amlodipine, which suggests a pathophysiological rationale for its administration
in dogs with heart failure secondary to this condition40; however, a prospective
study of the effect of this drug on clinically meaningful outcomes in dogs (or cats)
with heart failure has yet to be published.
Therefore, amlodipine could be considered for administration to dogs with
heart failure, particularly when secondary to mitral regurgitation, but should
probably be given as a second or third-line vasodilator to normo- or hypertensive
patients that are already receiving pimobendan and ACEI and have refractory
signs of heart failure despite receiving such treatment.

Diltiazem
Diltiazem is also a calcium channel blocker that has been advocated for use in
canine and feline patients with heart failure. In dogs, it is widely used as an
antiarrhythmic (ch. 230) and in cats as a possible positive lusitrope (see below
and ch. 234).

Pulmonary Vasodilators
The vasodilators described above act either predominantly or exclusively on the
systemic arterial vasculature. Some agents act principally or partially on the
pulmonary circulation and they are discussed in detail in ch. 218. In patients with
right-sided heart failure, clinical signs can be improved by reducing pulmonary
vascular resistance. For example, sildenafil is advocated for administration to
dogs in the later stages of MMVD where right-sided heart failure develops
secondary to pulmonary hypertension (ch. 232); it has been documented to
reduce pulmonary artery pressures and improve exercise tolerance and quality of
life.41 Pimobendan may also have pulmonary vasodilatory properties in addition
to its systemic vasodilating effects and could therefore also be effective in
controlling clinical signs of right-sided heart failure in dogs with more advanced
MMVD.

DRUGS USED IN THE TREATMENT OF HEART
FAILURE: DRUGS THAT ENHANCE SYSTOLIC
FUNCTION
One of the primary determinants of a patient’s cardiac output is myocardial
contractility. If myocardial contractility is physiologically or pharmacologically

enhanced, a greater cardiac output will be achieved with the same cardiac filling
pressure (preload), or the same cardiac output can be achieved with lower cardiac
filling pressures. Drugs that enhance contractility therefore have the capacity to
increase cardiac output or indirectly decrease preload by allowing patients to
sustain a similar cardiac output at lower filling pressures (Figure 229.2, F).
Myocardial contractility is frequently impaired in patients with heart failure.
Impaired contractility can be the primary abnormality causing a patient to have
heart failure, e.g., in patients with DCM, or may be secondarily impaired due to
chronic changes in load imposed upon the heart by other conditions such as
MMVD or hypertension. Enhancement of cardiac contractility can improve the
clinical signs of many patients with heart failure. Patients with signs of forward
failure are particularly likely to benefit from improved cardiac output. Indirect
reduction of preload can also improve signs of congestion.
Positive inotropes can be administered in the hospitalized patient that has acute
onset heart failure (or an acute exacerbation of chronic heart failure) or may be
chronically administered to patients being managed at home. The positive
inotropic agent most commonly administered to heart failure patients in the acute
setting is dobutamine. The positive inotropic agent most commonly administered
chronically is pimobendan. Other positive inotropic agents used in canine patients
include digoxin and milrinone. The former is still frequently administered to dogs
but principally for its parasympathomimetic effects in dogs with supraventricular
arrhythmias (ch. 230). The latter, a phosphodiesterase inhibitor, is not used
commonly.

Dobutamine
Dobutamine is a sympathomimetic agent that acts primarily through stimulation
of beta-1 receptors. It enhances contractility and the rate at which the
myocardium relaxes; i.e., it has both positive inotropic and lusitropic effects. It
must be administered by constant rate IV infusion and so can only be
administered to hospitalized patients. There is a very marked dose-response
relationship and higher dosages are more likely to be associated with side-effects
such as induction of arrhythmias. For these reasons, it is an agent that is most
safely administered in an intensive care setting where accurate dosing and careful
monitoring can be ensured.
Dobutamine is most likely to be indicated in patients with acute signs of heart
failure complicated by either hypotension or primary failure of myocardial
contractility (e.g., DCM). It is also of value as a “rescue” agent in the treatment of
patients with an acute crisis that are already receiving chronic treatment for heart
failure of any cause, e.g., dogs with MMVD presenting with signs of heart failure
that are refractory to oral medication.
Due to the restrictions on dobutamine’s use imposed by the method of
administration, it is inevitable that it will be given for short periods of time—at
most a few days—and it should therefore be regarded as a bridge to the
development of an effective chronic treatment regimen.

Pimobendan
Pimobendan is a widely used agent with both positive inotropic and vasodilatory
properties. These are brought about by calcium sensitization and
phosphodiesterase inhibition. Since these effects are inseparable, it is impossible
to determine which of pimobendan’s effects are brought about through which
mechanism and broadly regarding the drug as an “inodilator” is probably most
helpful. Due to effects outlined above, these inodilatory effects will enhance
cardiac output through reduced systemic vascular resistance and improved
myocardial contractility. It is argued that these combined effects overcome some
of the disadvantages of purely inotropic agents, enabling cardiac output to be
improved without a substantial increase in myocardial work, due to the
simultaneous reduction in afterload.
These hypothetical benefits of pimobendan are supported by a wealth of data
from prospective randomized clinical trials demonstrating improved outcomes in
dogs with heart failure secondary to both myocardial and valvular heart
diseases.42-44
Pimobendan is indicated for chronic administration to all dogs with heart
failure secondary to MMVD or DCM, the most common acquired causes of canine
heart failure. Although evidence for a benefit in canine patients with heart failure
secondary to other causes is less strong, it can be regarded as indicated in most
canine patients unless medical treatment is not appropriate (e.g., in dogs with
pericardial effusion causing cardiac tamponade) or where its administration is
contraindicated (e.g., in dogs with a ventricular outflow tract obstruction).
Pimobendan is administered orally; an IV preparation is available in Europe for
use in the emergency setting.
It is more difficult to formulate a pathophysiological rationale for the benefits of
an inodilator in cats with HCM, since the underlying disease process is not
conventionally believed to be associated with impaired contractility (ch. 234). A
recent prospective randomized study failed to show a clear benefit of pimobendan
in cats with heart failure secondary to myocardial disease.45 A sub-analysis
suggested that there may be a less favorable response to pimobendan therapy in
cats with heart failure and ventricular outflow obstruction, but the study was not
of sufficient size to draw robust conclusions in this respect. The findings of this
trial were contrary to previously published retrospective studies.46-48
Pimobendan may therefore be administered to some cats with heart failure,
particularly those without left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. It is usually
administered to cats in addition to a diuretic. It is particularly indicated in those
presenting with signs of poor cardiac output (forward failure) in conjunction with
signs of congestion and in those already refractory to the more conventional
treatment with a diuretic with or without an ACEI. The need to determine whether
a cat has ventricular outflow obstruction prior to the administration of
pimobendan significantly limits its ability to be used in patients that have not
undergone an echocardiographic examination.

DRUGS USED IN THE TREATMENT OF HEART
FAILURE: DRUGS THAT INHIBIT INOTROPIC
FUNCTION
Beta-Blockade
Some patients with heart disease can have clinical signs precipitated by increased
sympathetic stimulation, which increases cardiac contractility and heart rate. This
is particularly thought to be the case in cats with HCM with outflow tract
obstruction, where increased contractility can worsen the outflow tract
obstruction and increased heart rate may further impair already compromised
diastolic ventricular filling. It has been argued that there could be a benefit of
administering drugs that reduce contractility and limit or prevent tachycardia to
these patients—particularly drugs that inhibit increased contractility associated
with sympathetic stimulation. For many years, cardiologists advocated the use of
beta-blockers such as atenolol for cats with HCM, particularly those with dynamic
left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. More recently, studies suggest a possible
detrimental effect of beta-blockers on outcome in cats with heart failure secondary
to myocardial disease32 and a neutral effect of atenolol on the outcome of cats
with preclinical myocardial disease.49 The use of beta-blockers in cats with
myocardial disease is therefore now falling out of favor.
Studies have evaluated the effect of beta-blockade in dogs with DCM50 and
MMVD.51,52 The rationale for these studies was based on the extrapolation of
favorable outcomes associated with beta-blocker administration in human heart
failure patients. None of these studies demonstrated clear improvement in clinical
status, however, nor improvement in a clinically meaningful outcome, such as
survival. Currently, there is insufficient evidence to advocate their administration
to dogs with preclinical cardiac disease, and some evidence to suggest that their
administration to dogs with overt clinical evidence of heart failure is
contraindicated.
The only remaining uncontroversial indication for beta-blocker administration
to canine and feline patients with heart failure is due to their effects on cardiac
rate and rhythm in patients where pathologic tachyarrhythmias are contributing
to their clinical signs (ch. 230).

DRUGS USED IN THE TREATMENT OF HEART
FAILURE: DRUGS THAT IMPROVE CARDIAC
FILLING
In order to maintain a normal cardiac output at normal intracardiac filling
pressures, the heart must be able to fill normally between contractions. This
requires normal myocardial relaxation and a compliant myocardium. Cardiac

filling can be impaired in many ways: there could be inadequate time for the heart
to fill if the heart rate is excessive, the myocardium might be excessively stiff due
to fibrosis or hypertrophy, and normal physiological mechanisms that reduce wall
tension at the onset of diastole (principally mechanisms that lead to a reduction in
intracellular calcium concentrations) might be impaired.
Heart failure therapy can directly or indirectly influence cardiac filling.
Indirectly, interventions that reduce heart rate and improve oxygenation improve
myocardial diastolic function. “Positive lusitropic” agents directly improve
myocardial relaxation (Figure 229.2, G). Part of the rationale underlying
diltiazem administration to cats with HCM was its positive lusitropic effect. Only
weak evidence of a benefit of administering diltiazem to cats with HCM exists53
and no placebo-controlled studies have demonstrated that long-term diltiazem
administration is associated with an improved outcome in cats with HCM. As
such, diltiazem treatment of feline HCM is no longer widely advocated.

DRUGS USED IN THE TREATMENT OF HEART
FAILURE: DRUGS THAT OPTIMIZE CARDIAC
RATE AND RHYTHM
Patients with heart failure often have abnormalities of cardiac rate and rhythm.
Cardiac output is the product of heart rate and stroke volume (ch. 228).
Bradyarrhythmias compromise cardiac output due to the reduction in heart rate.
Tachyarrhythmias compromise output due to a reduction in stroke volume, due to
reduced time available for diastolic filling. Some tachyarrhythmias also cause loss
of atrioventricular synchrony and/or abnormalities of the sequence of activation
of the ventricular myocardium, both of which can further impair stroke volume. A
well-recognized example of the impact of the impairment of cardiac function
secondary to an arrhythmia is that of a patient with previously stable advanced
preclinical (stage B2) heart disease that develops acute-onset heart failure
associated with the onset of atrial fibrillation.
Patients with signs of heart failure directly attributable to a cardiac arrhythmia,
e.g., rapid persistent supraventricular tachycardia or bradyarrhythmias like thirddegree atrioventricular block, can improve substantially if the arrhythmia is
controlled. Restoration of synchronous atrial and ventricular activation,
secondary to abolition of ventricular arrhythmias, is also likely to improve output
when such arrhythmias are present. In patients where signs of heart failure are
exacerbated by a concurrent arrhythmia, although the arrhythmia may not be the
primary cause of the signs, appropriate management of that arrhythmia should be
an additional treatment goal (ch. 230).
Restoration of a more normal heart rate, by either a reduction or an increase in
the heart rate as appropriate, is likely to improve cardiac output. However, it
should be borne in mind that many patients with heart failure will have a
moderately elevated heart rate and sinus tachycardia. In these patients it is often
beneficial, during an acute episode of heart failure, to have a heart rate higher

than would be expected in a normal dog. Reduction of heart rate in these patients
should be achieved by better control of signs of heart failure rather than by direct
administration of negatively chronotropic (heart-rate–reducing) agents such as
beta-blockers.

MONITORING AND ADJUSTMENT OF HEART
FAILURE THERAPY
The two main purposes of monitoring patients receiving heart failure therapy are
to establish whether the initial aims of treatment have been achieved, and whether
any adverse treatment reactions have developed (Figure 229.4). Complications
of diuretic treatment—specifically, their detection and management—are outlined
above in the section on diuretics.
The success of therapy will be demonstrated by resolution of the clinical signs
and/or diagnostic findings that necessitated treatment introduction. If a patient
required treatment because of pleural effusion leading to dyspnea, then successful
treatment would be evident as resolution of the pleural effusion and restoration of
a more normal respiratory rate and effort. Similarly, if the main indication for
treatment was dyspnea confirmed radiographically to be secondary to pulmonary
edema, successful treatment would be apparent as restoration of normal
respiratory rate and effort in conjunction with radiographic resolution of the
pulmonary edema.
In a patient hospitalized for the initial management of CHF, successful
treatment ideally would result in an improvement in respiratory rate and effort
within the first few hours of treatment. Radiographically detectable improvement
of pulmonary edema usually lags behind any improvement in clinical signs and
may take longer to achieve, perhaps 24-48 hours. If clinical indications of CHF,
such as respiratory rate, are not improving, there is probably little point in reradiographing a patient unless there is doubt over the initial diagnosis of
cardiogenic pulmonary edema and alternative explanations for the patient’s signs
are being sought. The purpose of repeating radiographs therefore is often to
confirm and document improvement in the signs of CHF in a patient already
showing clinical evidence of improvement. Certain cardiologists do not routinely
repeat radiographs when a patient’s clinical response to treatment is proceeding
as expected.
In patients that present with clinical signs of poor perfusion, resolution of those
signs is likely to indicate successful treatment. If a patient was hypotensive on
presentation, then an improvement in blood pressure would be an indication of a
favorable response to treatment. Evidence of improved perfusion can be indicated
by a patient having warmer extremities and/or improving azotemia in patients
with cardiac disease that present with prerenal azotemia.

MONITORING OF RESTING RESPIRATORY
RATE
One of the most effective means of chronically monitoring the successful
resolution of clinical signs of CHF is owner measurement of home resting
respiratory rate. In dogs receiving treatment for CHF, a resting respiratory rate of
<40 breaths per minute is strongly associated with adequate CHF control.54
Similar values are also valid to guide the adequacy of heart failure control in cats:
normal cats and cats with subclinical heart disease rarely have respiratory rates
higher than 30 breaths per minute.55 Similarly, when heart failure is wellcontrolled (or before it has occurred), owners can be encouraged to obtain a brief
video clip of their pet sleeping and breathing comfortably at home, and to keep it
as an objective baseline of respiratory effort and rate for comparative purposes in
the future.
Most owners can measure their pet’s resting respiratory rate and there is a
range of smartphone apps available to facilitate this. Owners can be given, or can
themselves establish, ranges of respiratory rates that represent good control of
CHF, and values which would be a cause for concern. In an individual patient,
after a period of monitoring, owners can develop a good idea of their own pet’s
normal range for resting respiratory rate. Owners can then alert their veterinarian
if their pet’s respiratory rate increases. Some owners can even be given
instructions as to how to titrate their pet’s diuretic dosage according to the
respiratory rate; this approach is particularly useful in unstable patients that
require frequent adjustment of heart failure therapy, or feline patients that get
very stressed when visiting the veterinary hospital.

ADJUSTMENT OF CHRONIC HOME THERAPY
The intensity of a patient’s heart failure therapy may be increased or decreased.
An intensification of treatment is usually indicated because of poor control of
heart failure signs. Although most patients respond well to the introduction of
heart failure therapy, in almost all cases clinical signs of heart failure redevelop
after a variable period. In the QUEST study, which followed a population of dogs
with ACVIM stage C MMVD, it was common for heart failure therapy to require
adjustment and most dogs that had adjustments required treatment modification
within the first 3 months of treatment.56
The treatment change needed is usually indicated by the type of clinical signs
the patient is showing. The most frequent treatment adjustment is intensification
of diuretic treatment due to the redevelopment of congestive signs (e.g.,
tachypnea or dyspnea). In such cases, furosemide dosages can be increased until

the patient’s clinical signs are refractory to treatment despite doses of up to 4
mg/kg PO q8h. As has been explained above, this often then necessitates the
administration of additional diuretics or the substitution of torsemide instead of
furosemide.
Occasionally, after a prolonged period of clinical stability, it may be possible to
consider reduction of a patient’s diuretic dose, particularly if, where appropriate,
sodium consumption has been reduced. This can be done with a sequential
reduction in the dosage administered. Every time the diuretic dosage or frequency
is changed, the patient should be monitored for a change in respiratory rate. If the
respiratory rate remains stable despite the reduction in the diuretic dose, then
further dose reduction can be attempted until the lowest dose that continues to
adequately control the clinical signs is found.
If a patient redevelops clinical signs of poor cardiac output, then intensification
of therapy aimed at improving cardiac output could be required. Depending on
the patient’s underlying disease, this may require modification of the dosage of
drugs already being administered (such as optimization of the pimobendan dose)
or improved control of a patient’s arrhythmia (ch. 230).

OUTCOME OF HEART FAILURE THERAPY
Most canine and feline patients can enjoy many months, and in some cases more
than a year, of good quality life with successful pharmacological management of
their heart failure. Unfortunately, it remains the case that the most common
outcome following the development of heart failure is for the patient, despite
treatment, to eventually succumb to their heart disease. Studies in dogs42,57 and
cats58 with heart disease and heart failure show that most patients with heart
failure die of their heart disease within 1 year of diagnosis. For dogs with DCM the
median survival time is <6 months (ch. 233).57
It is a realistic and laudable aim of therapy to relieve patients’ clinical signs and
prolong their life where that life remains of a good quality. It should also be the
responsibility of the veterinarian to counsel the owner of the patient about the
likelihood of the pet’s death and a realistic time frame in which this will probably
occur. Although initially hearing about this guarded prognosis can be difficult and
distressing for owners, many then feel better prepared for the death of their pet
when it eventually occurs. Eventually, despite the best therapy, patients will
almost invariably succumb to their heart disease. Prioritizing a patient’s welfare
when providing end of life care is also of great importance during this phase of
their disease.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Heart Failure: Clinical Management
DIURETICS

What Are Diuretics?
Diuretics are a type of medication that is often prescribed for the treatment of
conditions that result in the retention of fluid—they are sometimes referred to as
“water pills.” Diuretics increase the amount that a patient will urinate and in this
way help them to eliminate excessive fluid that they have retained. Diuretics are
most often prescribed to animals in an effort to control signs of heart failure.
Heart failure occurs when a disease of the heart has resulted in the retention of
fluid, often in or around the lungs. The retained fluid causes animals to breathe
more rapidly and with more effort.

How Will I Know if the Treatment Is Working?
Successful diuretic treatment for heart failure results in a reduction in the
breathing rate; breathing effort should return to normal. One of the best ways you
can monitor the effectiveness of treatment is to measure your pet’s respiratory
rate. This can be done by counting the number of breaths your pet takes in 30
seconds and multiplying by two. One breath is one full in and out movement of
the chest wall. Measurement is best done when your pet is resting and should
ideally be done daily at approximately the same time of day. Keep a diary of the
values you obtain; this will help to build up a picture of how well the diuretics are
working. If the diuretics are working well, the respiratory rate will consistently be
below 40 breaths per minute. If the respiratory rate exceeds this value, or
suddenly increases (even without exceeding 40 breaths per minute), this may be
an indication that signs of heart failure are recurring and you should contact your
veterinarian. Smartphone apps are available that can help you measure
respiratory rate and monitor trends in the values you obtain.

What Effect Will Diuretics Have on My Pet?
An expected effect of diuretics is that they will lead to an increase in the amount
that your pet drinks and urinates. You should ensure that your pet has a plentiful
supply of fresh water and is given the opportunity to urinate frequently. Your pet
may want to go to the toilet more often; if they are not given the opportunity to do
so there is a risk that they may go to the toilet in the house.

Can the Medication Have Side-Effects?
Side-effects can happen with any medication. In the case of diuretics, an expected
effect is the increase in drinking and urination mentioned above. In some
patients, diuretics may change the levels of certain salts in the blood (electrolytes)
and have an effect on the function of the kidneys. These changes can be detected
with blood tests and your veterinarian may recommend that blood tests are taken
after a few days to weeks of treatment.
In some patients, an excessive loss of fluid may cause low blood pressure and
make them feel weak and lethargic. If signs of weakness or lethargy develop in
your pet while they are receiving diuretics, contact your veterinarian.

How Long Should I Give the Medication?
When diuretics are prescribed, it is usually necessary for them to be given
indefinitely in order to prevent the recurrence of signs of heart failure. Carefully
follow your veterinarian’s instructions with respect to the dosage and frequency of
administration. Do not suddenly stop administering them unless you have been
told to do so. Always ensure you have an adequate supply of medication to avoid
running out.

Is There Anything Else I Should Know?
Diuretics are less likely to be effective and higher doses may be necessary if your
pet has a high salt content in their diet. It may prove more difficult to control their
heart failure if the amount of salt in their diet varies a lot from day to day. Try to
feed a diet with at most a modest salt content and avoid salty treats. For further
advice on appropriate nutrition for patients with heart failure, consult your
veterinarian.
Adrian Boswood (Hatfield, Hertfordshire, United Kingdom) and
Melanie Hezzell (Bristol, United Kingdom)

GENERATION OF THE NORMAL
ELECTROCARDIOGRAM
Knowledge of the generation of the normal electrocardiogram (ECG) is
essential before being able to comprehend arrhythmogenesis. Coordinated
electrical activation of the heart depends upon the interplay of a complex
apparatus of impulse formation, conduction, and distribution to the
contractile myocardium. Impulse generation normally begins in the
sinoatrial node (SAN), the dominant cardiac pacemaker, and propagates
through the atria to the atrioventricular node (AVN). After more slowly
conducting through the AVN, the impulse rapidly propagates through the
His-Purkinje system (HPS) to the ventricular myocardium, triggering
coordinated ventricular contraction.1 The various cardiac regions are
distinguished electrically by specific action potential (APo) morphology
and duration as a result of regionally distinct collections of ionic currents.
APos in various cardiomyocytes and the currents underlying various
phases of the APo in different cardiac cells are shown in Figure 230.1.
As the primary pacemaker of the heart, the SAN is no longer considered
compact and discrete, but is now known to be a more diffuse, elaborate,
anatomically and electrophysiologically heterogenous cellular collection.
It is a crescent-shaped, subepicardial structure located along the crista
terminalis (CT) in the right atrium (RA) with an extensive paranodal
area.2 SAN APos are distinctly different from those of working atrial
myocytes, exhibiting diastolic (phase 4) depolarization, a relatively
depolarized diastolic membrane potential, and a slow upstroke driven
primarily by L-type calcium (Ca2+) current (ICa-L), rather than the fast
sodium (Na+) current (INa) responsible for the upstroke in atrial and
ventricular myocytes.3 There are two main hypotheses for the mechanism
underlying SAN diastolic depolarization, and it is likely the tight

integration of the two that forms the overall pacemaker clock.4,5 The first
mechanism is the membrane or voltage clock, referring to time and
voltage-dependent membrane ion channels underlying pacemaking
activity. These membrane channels include decay of outward-rectifying
potassium (K) currents (IKr and IKs) and the activation of multiple inward
currents, principally the funny current (If; a mixed Na+ and K+ current),
but also ICa-L and ICa-T.3 The calcium clock is the second hypothesis for
mechanisms responsible for SAN diastolic depolarization. Spontaneous,
rhythmic Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via the ryanodine
receptor in SAN cells activates the Na+-Ca2+ exchange current (INa-Ca) in
the forward mode, generating a net inward current that causes late
diastolic depolarization to increase exponentially.3-5 SAN cells are heavily
regulated by autonomic inputs, which determine the rate of phase 4
depolarization by phosphorylation-dependent gradation of the speed at
which the calcium clock cycles. This allows quick adaption of the heart
rate (HR) to the needs of the organism.2 Sinus arrhythmia, which is a
normal rhythm in the dog but typically only seen in the resting cat on
Holter monitoring at home, is complexly mediated by alterations in
parasympathetic tone on both SAN cells and the pathways leading from
the SAN to the atria (see below).6,7
It is important to remember that the SAN is a long, banana-shaped
structure located along the epicardial groove of the sulcus terminalis, with
cells at its cranial portion depolarizing at a higher frequency (generating
faster HRs) than slower depolarizing cells at its tail.4,8,9 SAN cells are
electrically insulated from surrounding atrial myocytes, apart from a small
number of preferential exit pathways that allow transmission of SAN
impulses to the atrial myocardium. This electrical insulation is critical to
protect SAN cells from being hyperpolarized by the much larger atrial
myocardial “sink,” while restricting impulse delivery to the branching
myofibers of the sinoatrial conduction pathways. This slows conduction
from the SAN to allow sufficient time to build up the charge needed to
depolarize the atria.9,10 The surface ECG is only able to record electrical
activity from large myocardial masses, namely the atria and ventricles.
SAN and AVN activities are not recordable from the body surface. Figure
230.2 shows normal sinus arrhythmia in a dog with intracardiac
recordings in the atria, AVN region, and right ventricle.

Once the impulse leaves the SAN, it excites the atrial myocardium via 25 (in the dog) sinoatrial conduction pathways.9 Left atrial (LA) activation
preferentially occurs over Bachmann’s bundle, a bundle of parallel aligned
myocardial bands that pass from the cranial vena cava across the
interatrial groove and to the LA appendage.11 Atrial and ventricular APos
are distinctly different, which, coupled with the anatomy of the atria, can
help explain differences in arrhythmias arising from these chambers and
their response to antiarrhythmic (AA) drugs. The atrial resting membrane
potential (RMP) is more depolarized than the ventricular RMP due to a 56 fold decrease in the density of the inward rectifier K+ current (IK1) in
atrial versus ventricular myocytes.12 IK1 is the major current determining
RMP. Maximal APo upstroke velocity in atrial myocytes is less than that of
ventricular myocytes. Differences in INa and the more depolarized RMP of
atrial cells account for this difference.13 Delayed rectifier K+ currents
contribute to repolarization and differ in atrial and ventricular myocytes.
The ultrarapid delayed rectifier K+ current (IKur) is present only in atrial
cells and is a major contributor to atrial repolarization.14 In atrial
myocytes, IKr and IKs have small densities and are unable to fully activate
due to the relatively negative membrane voltage in the plateau phase. This
is in contrast to the ventricles, in which IKr and IKs are the major
repolarizing currents. The atrial-selective nature of IKur makes it an
attractive target for AA drug development for use in atrial
tachyarrhythmias.13 The net result of these ionic differences between
atrial and ventricular myocytes results in a triangular-shaped atrial APo
versus the spike-and-dome shape of the ventricular APo (Figure
230.1).15 Electrical heterogeneities exist in different regions of the atria,
including between the left and right atria, due to differences in densities
and biophysical properties of respective ionic currents in these regions.
Excitation of the atrial myocardium produces the P wave on the surface
ECG, which normally has a rounded morphology of low amplitude due to
the smaller size of the atria (smaller amount of current per unit time).

The PQ segment represents the total duration of atrioventricular (AV)
conduction and should be isoelectric. The AV junction lies within the
triangle of Koch, a low RA region bordered by the septal leaflet of the
tricuspid valve (TV), os of the coronary sinus (CS), and tendon of Todaro
(Figure 230.3).16 Atrial cells communicate with the compact AVN only
through 1) transitional cells located in the anterior and middle portions of
the triangle of Koch and 2) cells of inferior nodal extensions (INE) located
in the inferior and middle portions of Koch’s triangle (Figure
230.3).16,17 Transitional cells express intermediate levels of connexins
(Cx 40 and 43) with intermediate to high conductive properties, while INE
cells express low levels of these.18 Transitional and His bundle (HB) cells
express high levels of Nav 1.5, responsible for INa and fast APo upstroke,
while the compact AVN and INE cells express high levels of Cav 1.3,
responsible for ICa-L and slow APo upstroke.16,17 INE cells also express
high HCN4 levels, responsible for If and underlying spontaneous
depolarization within the AV junction.19 The compact AVN is the upper
portion of the AVN with cells having less negative RMPs, smaller APo
amplitudes, and slower APo upstrokes. The lower nodal bundle is the
lower portion of the AVN that connects to the rightward INE and has cells

that are functionally intermediate between the compact AVN and HB.17
Abundant expression of both fast sodium channels and connexin proteins
in HB cells enable rapid conduction of the electrical impulse once it
reaches this structure. Experimental data suggest there may be two
functionally dissociated axes of the AV conduction system: 1) the fast
pathway: transitional cells—compact AV node—HB; 2) the slow pathway:
atrial cells/transitional cells—rightward INE—lower nodal bundle—HB.20
This finding explains both the anatomical basis for atrioventricular node
reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) and raises the potential of clinically
modulating the ventricular response rate to atrial arrhythmias.

From the HB, the electrical impulse enters the left and right bundle
branches. The left bundle branch divides quickly into 2 fascicles (anterior
and posterior), allowing the mass of left ventricular (LV) myocardium to
be quickly activated from 2 areas. This trifascicular system depolarizes the
dense subendocardial Purkinje fiber network in a precise sequence so that
contraction moves from the apex in a twisting motion to the base of the
heart, minimizing the energy requirement for ejection of blood into the
outflow tracts.21 The large mass of ventricular myocardium, combined
with its fast-response APos, results in a rapid slope of the QRS complex.
The larger mass of the LV myocardium determines the normal mean

electrical axis of the QRS complex. Repolarization of the ventricles occurs
over a much longer period of time than depolarization, thus explaining the
rounded shape and decreased slope of the T wave compared to the QRS.20

GENERAL APPROACH TO ARRHYTHMIAS
When examining the ECG, several methodical steps are helpful in
appropriately identifying the rhythm present. Interpretation, however,
can only be as accurate as the quality of the data obtained. Several aspects
of ECG acquisition can be optimized to aid determination of the
arrhythmia present. First, the ECG should be run ideally at both 25
mm/sec and 50 mm/sec in the typical dog and cat. This will be helpful in
1) determination of intervals, which is better at 50 mm/sec, and 2)
recognizing low dV/dt signals (such as P waves originating outside the
sinus node, known as P’ waves) at the 25 mm/sec paper speed. In
addition, arrhythmia interpretation is enhanced the more leads that are
recorded. Whereas P’ waves may be isoelectric in one lead and thus
overlooked, they could be visible in other leads. Precordial leads are also
better at detecting low amplitude atrial activity than are the limb leads.
Finally, increasing the ECG gain (particularly in cats, in which 20 mm/mV
should be standard) can aid in detection of low amplitude deflections.
A stepwise approach should be followed in the initial evaluation of any
ECG. The first question to be answered is the overall HR: is it too fast, too
slow, or within reference ranges? Normal HRs vary according to the
species and age of the animal being examined (see below, and ch. 96).
Next, is the rhythm regular or irregular? This refers to whether the R-R
interval is constant or not, respectively. Dogs commonly have an irregular
heart rhythm (sinus arrhythmia), which is normal in this species with high
vagal tone. Cats normally only have regular rhythms in the clinical setting;
any irregular rhythm is considered abnormal in this species. 22 If the
rhythm is irregular, is there a pattern or cyclical rhythm to the
irregularity? In other words, is the rhythm regularly irregular or
irregularly irregular? Third, do the QRS complexes appear normal in
morphology or abnormal in terms of duration and axis? An abnormal QRS
morphology is seen when part or all of the ventricle is activated by cell-tocell conduction rather than entirely over the HPS. Fourth, the relationship
between P waves and QRS complexes should be evaluated. Is there a QRS
following each P wave and an identifiable P wave preceding each QRS
complex? Finally, P wave morphology and timing should be assessed. Is
the P wave axis normal (positive in the inferior and left precordial leads)?

What is P wave timing in relation to the QRS: 1) within the TQ segment at
a normal PQ (PR) interval? 2) within the TQ segment at a prolonged PQ
(PR) interval? 3) within the ST segment?

Arrhythmias are initially divided into tachyarrhythmias (three or more
consecutive complexes occurring at a rate >160 bpm for dogs and >220
bpm for cats) or bradyarrhythmias (HRs <70 bpm for dogs and <140 bpm
for cats). Note that these rates must be assessed in relation to several
factors: breed, age, temperament, and environmental factors impacting
autonomic tone. For example, a nervous small breed dog with an HR of 75
bpm is bradycardic relative to its degree of sympathetic tone. Similarly, an
unmedicated, nervous cat in a veterinary clinic with an HR of 144 bpm is
bradycardic relative to its autonomic tone. Finally, a relaxed, large breed
dog with an HR of 150 bpm is tachycardic relative to its presumed
predominance of vagal tone.

TACHYARRHYTHMIAS
The first major differentiator in correctly diagnosing tachyarrhythmias is
the QRS width. Narrow (QRS) complex tachyarrhythmias (NCTs) have a
normal QRS duration for that species (≤60 msec for dogs and ≤40 msec
for cats), while wide (QRS) complex tachyarrhythmias (WCTs) have QRS
durations beyond these ranges. The drugs commonly used to treat
tachyarrhythmias are listed in Table 230.1.

NARROW COMPLEX
TACHYARRHYTHMIAS
These rhythms include three main categories: 1) those that are confined to
the atria: sinus tachycardia (STach), atrial tachycardia (AT), atrial flutter
(AFL), atrial fibrillation (AF), 2) those that arise from the AV junction:
focal junctional tachycardia (FJT), AVNRT, 3) those that incorporate a
large reentrant circuit involving the atrium, ventricle, accessory
atrioventricular pathway (AP), and typically the normal conduction
system: orthodromic atrioventricular reciprocating tachycardia
(OAVRT).23 The signalment of dogs with frequent or sustained NCTs
depends upon the underlying rhythm. Dogs with persistent or permanent
AF tend to have severe underlying congenital (ch. 231) or acquired (e.g.,
myxomatous/degenerative mitral valve disease [ch. 232], dilated
cardiomyopathy [ch. 233]) heart disease or be giant breed dogs. AF is a
common type of NCT in dogs seen in first-line veterinary practice. AF can,

however, also be paroxysmal in dogs with rapid AP-mediated tachycardia.
Dogs and cats presenting with AP-mediated tachycardias or focal atrial
tachycardias (FATs) are typically young to middle-aged, although dogs as
old as 10 years have presented with these rhythms.24-28 Clinical signs are
often subtle and unrecognized by owners. Easily and more rapidly
identifiable signs are generally noticed only when a sufficiently rapid
rhythm is sustained for prolonged period. Frequent nonsustained NCTs or
slower sustained NCTs can result in myocardial damage but be difficult
for owners to detect outwardly. Common clinical signs in 130 NCT dogs
presented for radiofrequency catheter ablation (RFCA) of either OAVRT
or FAT have included: intermittent lethargy (71%), hyporexia (60%),
vomiting (40%), head bobbing/body pulsing (37%), tachypnea/labored
breathing (25%), syncope (12%), and abdominal distention (11%). It is
important to note the frequency of gastrointestinal signs in these young
dogs, as many were originally presumed to have dietary indiscretion or
gastrointestinal foreign bodies due to their signalment and lack of
awareness of tachyarrhythmias as a differential diagnosis for these signs.
Congestive heart failure (CHF) in these same 130 NCT dogs included: 14%
with left-sided CHF only, 11% with right-sided CHF only, and 11% with
biventricular CHF.

Stepwise Approach to ECG Evaluation of NCTs
Careful evaluation of the surface ECG will aid in the diagnosis of the
underlying mechanism of an NCT. AF is recognized by the absence of
discrete P waves, presence of fibrillatory (f) waves, and irregularly
irregular R-R intervals due to variation in AVN conduction of fibrillatory
(f) waves.29 If AF is excluded, 3 ECG findings should be carefully
evaluated to help narrow the diagnosis of an NCT: 1) P:QRS ratio, 2) P
wave timing relative to the QRS complex in those with a 1:1 P:QRS ratio,
3) P wave morphology.

A. P:QRS Ratio
1. NCTs with a P:QRS ratio >1 include AT and AFL. Very rarely, in
humans, AVNRT can have 2:1 AV block at the level of the HB,
thereby resulting in more retrograde atrial than antegrade
ventricular depolarizations. AVNRT has not been documented to
date in dogs and cats. OAVRT is mediated by an AP with a large
reentrant circuit that involves atrial myocardium, antegrade AVNHPS, ventricular myocardium, and retrograde AP.23 Thus, there

cannot be more atrial than ventricular depolarizations (or vice
versa) in this rhythm.
2. NCTs with a P:QRS ratio = 1 include STach, OAVRT, AVNRT, AT,
and FJT.
3. NCTs with a P:QRS ratio <1 are quite rare and include sinus or
atrial rhythms with simultaneous conduction over fast and slow
AVN pathways, AVNRT or FJT with retrograde block to the atria,
and high septal ventricular tachycardias (VTs).30

B. R-P Interval in NCTs With 1:1 P:QRS Ratios
1. P wave buried in the QRS complex (and thus not visible) can occur
in AT with long AVN conduction and AVNRT (slow-fast variety). It
is important to remember that P’ waves may not be visible in all
leads, so one may erroneously assume they are not visible if only
one or a few leads are recorded. P’ waves are typically of low
amplitude also, so that baseline artifact may obscure them.
2. Short R-P interval NCTs with visible P waves within the ST segment
or T wave of the preceding QRS complex (RP interval < PR interval)
include OAVRT, AVNRT (slow-slow), AT, and FJT. This can also be
seen in STach with prolonged AVN conduction relative to sinus
cycle length (CL).
3. Long R-P interval NCTs with P waves visible within the T-QRS
segment (RP > PR) include STach, AT, OAVRT using a slow,
decrementally-conducting AP, and AVNRT (uncommon fast-slow
variety).

C. P Wave Morphology
1. P waves that are negative in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF) indicate
initial activation of the lower portion of the atria, including the AV
valve annuli, coronary sinus (CS) os, inferior portion of the CT, and
inferior portion of the atrial septum. The majority of canine cases of
OAVRT fall into this category. Other differentials include AVNRT
and AT arising from these atrial locations. Investigations into novel
placement of the precordial leads may aid in localizing P wave
origin in dogs (and cats).31
2. P waves that are positive in the inferior leads generally denote atrial
activation from high to low, including origins in the superior CT
(including the SAN), cranial vena cava, RA appendage, cranial
portion of the tricuspid annulus, LA appendage, and upper

pulmonary veins. Leads I, II, and the precordial leads can help to
narrow the site of origin.31a STach and ATs account for nearly all of
these NCTs; however, OAVRT with an AP inserting along the
cranial portions of the AV valves, may also have this axis.23,32
With this framework, we will examine specific categories of NCTs and
their treatment in more detail below.

Sinus Tachycardia (STach)
This refers to SAN discharge that is faster than the normal range for a
given species (ch. 96). STach is a physiologic response to sympathetic
activation and parasympathetic withdrawal. Triggers can include anxiety,
fear, pain, exercise, decreased cardiac output or oxygen delivery to the
tissues, and sympathomimetic or anticholinergic medications.33 The P
wave morphology is consistent with a sinus origin (positive in I, II, III,
aVF; negative in aVR and aVL). Sometimes it is nearly impossible to
distinguish between a high RA or right upper pulmonary vein tachycardia
and STach based on P wave morphology; however, clinical history and
ECG findings, such as abrupt onset and offset, and a rate higher than the
physiologic range of STach, would support an AT.34 Vagal maneuvers
(such as breath-holding or carotid sinus massage) can gradually slow
STach in some patients, with a gradual increase in the tachycardia rate
upon maneuver termination. This does not differ, however, from the
response of many FATs to vagal maneuvers.35 Treatment of STach is
focused on addressing the underlying cause, as the rhythm is secondary to
an inciting factor. Examples include minimizing pain and excitement/fear,
addressing blood loss, volume contraction, or anemia, and improving
forward cardiac output. In the case of CHF, medications are used to
improve forward cardiac output and congestive signs (ch. 229), with
improvement in STach resulting from these measures. In an animal with
significant structural heart disease, it is important to educate owners on
avoidance of situations known to provoke STach. The increased HR
decreases diastolic filling time and myocardial perfusion, while increasing
myocardial oxygen consumption.36 Benefits of pharmacologically slowing
the sinus rate via beta-blockers, digitalis, or ivabradine (If blocker) have
been demonstrated in human CHF patients.36-39 Small, predominantly
retrospective studies in dogs and cats with various forms of heart disease
prior to the onset of clinical signs have not demonstrated a benefit to HR

modulation through beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, or If
blockers.40-43 Large scale, prospective, future studies are necessary to
accurately assess the potential benefits and risks of rate modulating drugs
in our pet population.

Focal Atrial Tachycardia (FAT)
Organized ATs are broadly caused by either focal or macroreentrant (see
later) mechanisms. “Focal” signifies that the site of origin is a small area
as mapped by a 4-mm-tip catheter, from which atrial activation spreads
centrifugally.44 Macroreentrant atrial tachycardia (MRAT), on the other
hand, is defined by atrial activation that can be recorded over the entire
tachycardia cycle length (TCL) as the wavefront rotates around a large
central obstacle that is either anatomic or functional.45 FATs can be
caused by 1 of 3 mechanisms: abnormal automaticity, triggered activity, or
microreentry.44 Spontaneous phase 4 depolarization in non-SAN atrial
cells underlies abnormal automaticity. These automatic rhythms cannot
be induced or terminated by programmed electrical stimulation. There
also tends to be a “warm-up” or gradual increase in rate over the first
several complexes and a “cool down” or gradual decrease in rate over the
last several complexes prior to termination.46 Triggered activity results
from delayed afterdepolarizations, which are low amplitude
transmembrane oscillations occurring at the end of the APo and caused by
calcium entry into the cell from a “leaky” ryanodine receptor.47 If the
membrane voltage oscillations reach threshold potential, then a
regenerative APo can occur and FAT result. Triggered activity FAT can
typically be initiated and terminated by programmed electrical
stimulation. Microreentrant FATs can also typically be initiated and
terminated by pacing maneuvers, and have high frequency, low amplitude
electrograms in their small zone of slow conduction. These 3 mechanisms,
however, can be difficult to distinguish from one another, even with
electrophysiologic (EP) testing, as there is significant overlap in their
characteristics.
FATs are incessant, or present for at least 50% of the time, in up to 25%
of human focal ATs, and we have found this to be similar in dogs
presented for RFCA. Such incessant tachyarrhythmias are highly
associated with the development of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy
(TICM), secondary myocardial dysfunction that is clinically difficult to
distinguish from idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM, ch. 233).48

TICM relates to both the rapidity and the frequency of a given
tachyarrhythmia. Time to onset of ventricular dysfunction also is
dependent on other factors, including underlying structural heart disease
and patient age.49 Data from several studies and individual case reports
have shown that rhythm control results in significant improvement of
ventricular systolic function and resolution of clinical signs of CHF (Video
230.1

).24,50,51 FATs may also precipitate other atrial arrhythmias,

particularly AF or AFL, if the focal atrial rate is particularly rapid and
secondary atrial remodeling occurs (Wright KN, unpublished manuscript
2021).28,45,46

FIGURE 230.4 Focal atrial tachycardia (FAT)
displayed on 4 surface electrocardiogram (ECG) leads
and 8 representative intracardiac dipoles. A
duodecapolar catheter is positioned along the crista
terminalis (CT) in the right atrium. A decapolar catheter
lies within the coronary sinus (CS), and a quadripolar

(AVN)-His bundle region (His). The FAT has earliest
activation high along the crista terminalis (CT 10). Atrial
depolarization (A’) spreads from the focus to the
remainder of the atrial tissue, such that the time
difference in atrial activation (high right atrium to low
left atrium) is small (less than 50% of the atrial cycle
length). Initially, 2-to-1 AVN block is present, that then
resolves for 3 complexes before occurring for a single
complex. A’, Intracardiac atrial depolarization (during
atrial tachycardia in this figure); H, His bundle
depolarization; P’, atrial depolarization represented on

represented on the surface ECG; V’, intracardiac
ventricular depolarization. Sweep speed is 100 mm/sec.
FATs do not occur uniformly throughout the atria, but rather arise from
characteristic anatomic locations based on human EP studies. RA sites
predominate (over 60%), with the CT accounting for nearly one-third of
all FATs and the tricuspid annulus accounting for another 22%.52 The

CT’s propensity to be a site of FAT origin is thought to be due to two
factors. First, the distribution of the SAN complex, and thus the presence
of automatic tissue, occurs along the long axis of the CT. Second, there is
marked anisotropic conduction due to poor transverse cell coupling along
the CT. This would prevent neighboring cells from electrotonically
suppressing abnormal automaticity. Two-thirds of all LA FATs arise from
the pulmonary venous ostia. When examining the distribution at the two
veterinary referral centers performing the majority of canine ablations, a
similar distribution of FAT foci is seen (Wright KN, unpublished
manuscript, 2021).28 Sixty percent of canine FATs arose from the RA,
with the CT being the most common location (36% of the total), and the
pulmonary veins accounting for 89% of the LA FATs.
Dogs with electrophysiologically-proven FAT are more commonly male
(71%), have a median age of 44 months (range, 5-152 months), and have
no particular breed predilection (no breed made over 11% of this
population). ECG findings that support FAT include NCT with discrete P
waves having an isoelectric sequence between them and tachycardia
continuation in the presence of AV block (Figure 230.4; Video 230.2
).44 The atrial CL tends to be similar in an individual dog, but varies
widely between dogs (172-328 msec), while the ventricular CL in the
unmedicated state has been 191-344 msec. Depending upon the interplay
between the atrial rate and antegrade AVN conduction, FAT may be a
short RP or long RP NCT during periods of 1:1 AVN conduction. In FAT
cases with particularly rapid atrial rates or the presence of intraatrial
conduction disturbances, there may be the loss of an isoelectric baseline. P
wave morphology depends on the anatomic location of the atrial focus and
the conformation of the thorax (which determines the cardiothoracic
orientation). The surface ECG algorithms developed for localization of the
atrial focus in humans, therefore, have not proven as uniformly useful in
dogs and cats. It is important to note that the diagnosis of FAT can only be
definitively established during an EP study.
FATs are frequently unresponsive to pharmacologic therapy; hence
RFCA has become the primary treatment in humans with FAT that is
frequent or symptomatic.35,52 This is an option for dogs at certain centers,
but this technology is not adaptable to cats at this time. If the ventricular
rate is too rapid, it can be acutely slowed using a negative dromotrope
such as intravenous diltiazem (0.125 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes, can be
repeated up to a cumulative dose of 0.375 mg/kg).53 Rarely will FAT itself
terminate with a calcium channel blocker, and if it does, triggered activity
is the likely mechanism. Other acute therapies for hemodynamically

unstable animals include IV Nexterone (amiodarone without
preservatives) at 3-5 mg/kg IV over 15 minutes in dogs.53 If successful in
terminating the FAT, a constant rate intravenous infusion can be used
subsequently, at 0.014 mg/kg/min for 6-8 hours and then 0.007
mg/kg/min for up to 18 more hours. Synchronized direct current
cardioversion (DCCV) also can successfully terminate nonautomatic FATs.
Chronic pharmacotherapy focuses on a 2-pronged approach to suppress
the atrial focus and slow AVN conduction to the ventricles. Drugs used to
suppress the atrial focus include class IC agents (e.g., propafenone, 5-8
mg/kg PO q8h of the nonsustained release formulation in dogs, dose not
established in cats; preferred over flecainide due to similar properties but
less negative inotropy) and class III agents (sotalol, 1-3 mg/kg PO q12h in
dogs and cats and amiodarone, 15 mg/kg PO q24h for 7-10 days, then 10
mg/kg PO q24h for 7-10 days, then 5-8 mg/kg PO q24h long term in
dogs).53 The authors have used oral amiodarone successfully in cats with
refractory arrhythmias but its dosage has not been experimentally
established. Negative dromotropes that are commonly used include
diltiazem (1-2 mg/kg PO q8h of the nonsustained release preparations,
dogs and cats), digoxin (0.003-0.007 mg/kg PO q12h [based on lean body
weight] in a normokalemic dog with normal renal function and 0.0312 mg
total PO q24-48h in a normokalemic cat with normal renal function,
noting that digoxin is rarely used in cats), and atenolol (0.5-1 mg/kg PO
q12h, dogs and cats).53

(MRAT) recorded during electrophysiologic study. Three

Macroreentrant Atrial Tachycardia/Atrial Flutter
MRAT is a reentrant activation around a large central obstacle (often
several centimeters in diameter) that requires a zone of slow conduction
and area of unidirectional conduction block.45 The atria lend themselves
to these criteria via their anatomy, including the pulmonary venous ostia,
AV valve annuli, and CT. The central obstacle itself can be fixed,

functional, or a combination of both. The nomenclature associated with
MRATs has evolved over the years. Importantly, classification of MRATs
based on the 12-lead ECG has been abandoned, as it has become apparent
that the underlying mechanism, as defined by EP mapping techniques,
does not correlate well with the surface ECG patterns.45,54 MRATs are
now divided into 2 groups according to whether the cavotricuspid isthmus
(CTI) is critical to the reentrant circuit. CTI-dependent MRATs include
clockwise and counterclockwise AFL, double loop reentry, and intraisthmus reentry. Non-CTI MRATs include upper loop reentry, perimitral
macroreentry, pulmonary vein macroreentry, and left septal
macroreentry. Typical AFL is a term that is now reserved for CTIdependent MRAT proven at EP study to have its activation wavefront
rotating clockwise or counterclockwise around the tricuspid annulus and
using the CTI as an essential central obstacle. Atypical AFL is a confusing
term that is no longer used.
MRATs typically occur in patients with structural heart disease (Figure
230.5). These ATs are typically persistent (Video 230.3

). The ECG

alone is often inadequate to distinguish MRAT from FAT, and definitive
diagnosis requires intracardiac mapping. The P wave morphology of a
spectrum of LA and RA MRATs is highly variable, often due to the
presence of congenital or acquired abnormalities that can result in
deviated atrial activation vectors and low amplitude P waves.55 Despite
these significant limitations, certain ECG findings can be helpful.
Variation in the TCL of more than 15%, however, has been suggested to be
a marker of focal AT (versus MRAT) in human patients. Lead V1,
particularly if positioned at the costochondral junction of the first
intercostal space, can be helpful in distinguishing RA versus LA origin. LA
MRAT circuits frequently generate low amplitude P waves that may only
be visible in V1.56 In the absence of significant atrial scarring, most
MRATs lack an isoelectric baseline between atrial depolarizations at
standard ECG speeds. MRATs have been noted to occur in dogs with APs
following a prolonged episode of OAVRT (Figure 230.6). All clinical
MRAT circuits that have been mapped to date in dogs have been confined
to the RA (Wright KN, unpublished manuscript, 2021).27,57 The ATs
observed in cats with structural heart disease surely include MRATs, but
these have not been studied via electrophysiologic study (EPS) to confirm
their mechanism.

FIGURE 230.6 Macroreentrant atrial tachycardia
(MRAT) occurred following sustained orthodromic
atrioventricular reciprocating tachycardia (OAVRT).
Three surface electrocardiogram (ECG) leads are
displayed, as well as 5 intracardiac dipoles, and a femoral
arterial pressure tracing. This MRAT had the
characteristics of typical atrial flutter with high-grade
second-degree atrioventricular (AV) block. Note the
number of flutter waves (F on the surface ECG, A’ on the
intracardiac recordings) that are not conducted to the

placed in the coronary sinus; HIS, quadripolar catheter
