RVa, right ventricular apical dipole.
The pharmacologic treatment of MRAT is similar to that of FAT. Acute
therapy is directed at slowing the ventricular rate (IV diltiazem or less
commonly IV esmolol) or using synchronized DCCV to terminate the
reentrant rhythm. A comparison of intravenous negative dromotropic
agents (drugs that slow AVN conduction) in healthy dogs showed that
esmolol was a significantly less effective negative dromotrope than
diltiazem and caused a severe drop in LV contractility measurements at
dosages required to prolong AVN conduction.58 Class IC AA agents, such
as propafenone, depress conduction velocity within the circuit and widen
the excitable gap. This can slow the atrial rate, but paradoxically increase
the ventricular rate, as AVN conduction improves with the increased time
between atrial wavefronts.35 For this reason, it is critical to combine them
with a negative dromotrope, such as diltiazem. Class III agents (sotalol,

amiodarone) have a weaker effect on conduction velocity and more
profound effect on prolonging atrial repolarization than do the class IC
drugs. This combination of effects could abolish the excitable gap and
make these the drugs of choice in MRATs.35 Long-term pharmacologic
control of MRATs is notoriously difficult in human, and likely veterinary,
patients.

Atrial Fibrillation
AF is one of the most recognizable rhythms on thoracic auscultation and
the surface ECG. It is also the arrhythmia which has received much recent
attention amongst cardiologists, due to the morbidity and mortality
associated with it in both humans and companion animals. It is the most
common arrhythmia identified in dogs, with a prevalence of 0.1-0.43% in
dogs presenting to a veterinary clinic and increasing to 6.27-10.5% in dogs
with clinical heart disease.59-61 AF has been classified as paroxysmal,
persistent, or permanent based on duration and response to
cardioversion. Paroxysmal AF is characterized by self-terminating
episodes, with most ending within 24 hours, but some lasting up to 7
days.62 Paroxysmal AF has been identified in dogs on Holter
monitoring,63 at EP study for other tachyarrhythmias, and it may occur
perioperatively in dogs (particularly large breed dogs) receiving opiate
drugs. In this context, AF may be vagally-mediated (see below) and
typically self-terminates in 2-3 days. It is likely underrecognized in our pet
population due to their inability to bring intermittent palpitations to their
owners’ attention. Persistent AF lasts longer than 7 days and includes
episodes that are terminated by direct current or pharmacologic
cardioversion. In permanent AF, cardioversion has failed or AF has been
sustained for more than 1 year with unsuccessful attempts to restore sinus
rhythm.62 The vast majority of identified dogs and cats with AF fall into
the persistent or permanent categories. As DCCV is attempted in few
veterinary patients, the distinction between these two categories becomes
obscured. “Lone” or “idiopathic” AF has variable definitions, but is
commonly used to refer to AF patients who have no other clinical or
echocardiographic evidence of cardiopulmonary disease. Ongoing
advances in the study of AF, however, have uncovered numerous diverse
pathogenic mechanisms related to lone AF. Electrophysiologists are
abandoning this category, therefore, as it no longer has mechanistic or
clinical utility.64

There are two populations predisposed to AF in dogs and cats: 1) those
with severe underlying structural heart disease resulting in severe atrial
dilation, 2) giant breed dogs with AF in the absence of significant
identifiable structural heart disease. Irish Wolfhounds (IWs), as the
prototypical breed with AF, have a prevalence rate of 8.9-12% in North
America, increasing to 28% if only IWs over 8 years old are included.65,66
AF and DCM both occur commonly in giant breeds (ch. 233), and each
one may occur independent of the other or they may occur together. A
dominant mode of inheritance has been found in the IW breed.66 AF is
considerably less common in cats, likely due to their small atrial size
compared to medium to large breed dogs and humans. Studies of cats
with AF have confirmed that cats with this arrhythmia usually have severe
structural heart disease leading to atrial enlargement.67,67a AF occurrence
is also associated with APs, presumably through OAVRT-induced changes
in atrial vulnerability, from altered atrial refractoriness, repetitive atrial
firing, and increased intra-atrial conduction delay. Ablation of the AP is
associated with elimination or marked reduction of AF in these
patients.24,68

FIGURE 230.7 Three surface electrocardiogram
(ECG) channels and 13 intracardiac dipole channels are
displayed during acute onset of atrial fibrillation at
electrophysiologic study of a focal atrial tachycardia.
Note the rapid, disorganized atrial activity on the
intracardiac dipoles and the low amplitude fibrillatory (f)
waves on the surface ECG leads. More discrete atrial
depolarizations are seen in some dipoles (such as the
ablation catheter dipole ABL) than in other dipoles (Halo
2-4 and 7-10). The majority of the fibrillatory impulses
are not conducted through the AV node to the ventricles,
thus accounting for the slower ventricular rate. Abl,
Quadripolar catheter placed in the high right atrial
region; CS, decapolar catheter placed within the
coronary sinus; Halo, duodecapolar catheter placed from
the cranial vena cava to the caudal vena cava; HIS,
quadripolar catheter placed in the AV nodal-His bundle
region.
The pathogenesis of AF is complex, multifactorial, variable between
patients, and incompletely understood. A combination of triggering
factors and maintenance factors are at play in a given individual. Potential
mechanisms underlying AF include single and multiple sources. Single
sources include automatic foci, mother waves, fixed rotors, and moving
rotors, while AF arising from multiple sources includes multiple
simultaneous foci, unstable circuits, multiple wavelets, and a combination
of a focus/multiple wavelets.69 Triggering foci have been identified within
venous structures that join the atrium, particularly the pulmonary veins.
Discontinuous myocardial fibers separated by fibrous tissues in these
structures can promote reentry, automaticity, and triggered activity.70

Other triggers include OAVRT, FAT, MRAT, bradycardia/SAN
dysfunction, and acute atrial stretch.71 The role of the autonomic nervous
system (ANS) in the initiation of AF is unclear. There is a distinct entity,
known as vagally-mediated AF, that has been identified in certain human
and canine cases.70,72 The recognition of this unique form of AF is
important, because of the potential to treat with anticholinergic drugs and
avoid drugs such as digitalis that enhance vagal tone. The majority of AF
patients, however, do not appear to have ANS abnormalities. Maintenance
of AF commonly requires the combination of electrical and structural
atrial remodeling, explaining why it is typically found in the setting of
other cardiac disease. Atrial remodeling includes atrial dilation, patchy
fibrosis, increased dispersion of refractoriness, and conduction
abnormalities. Even in the patients with apparently structurally normal
hearts, occult abnormalities can be observed that parallel early atrial
remodeling and contribute to the AF substrate, suggesting that AF in these
patients represents an arrhythmic manifestation of fibrotic atrial
myopathy.73 AF itself produces atrial architectural alterations that further
contribute to atrial remodeling, mechanical dysfunction, and the
perpetuation of AF.74 This explains why electrical or pharmacologic
cardioversion becomes less successful the longer AF has been present.
The key auscultatory findings in dogs and cats with AF include an
irregularly irregular rhythm and often tachycardia, particularly in animals
with underlying structural heart disease. Pulse deficits are present on the
most closely-coupled ventricular complexes. Other physical examination
findings, such as the presence and characteristics of a heart murmur,
gallop sound, and pulmonary abnormalities, depend upon any underlying
structural cardiopulmonary disease. Distinctive ECG findings in AF
include the absence of identifiable P waves. Instead, there is a rapidly
undulating baseline due to fibrillatory or f waves, which are not visible in
all patients, particularly cats and small dogs (Figure 230.7) The intervals
between QRS complexes are irregularly irregular (without pattern) and
generally rapid in the unmedicated state (Videos 230.4, 230.5

),

except in giant breed dogs with “idiopathic” AF. QRS complexes are
narrow except in cases of a preexisting or functional conduction system
defect.
Treatment of AF in companion animals generally focuses on controlling
the ventricular response rate; however, electrical cardioversion is
attempted in some animals (Video 230.5

).75 The overall success rate

of electrical cardioversion is inversely linked to AF duration and atrial
size.75 Catheter ablation of AF is performed in certain human patients,
and the linear lesions created depend upon the substrate in an individual
patient.71 Negative dromotropes slow conduction of the fibrillatory
impulses from the atria to the ventricles. As with other atrial
tachyarrhythmias previously discussed, the most commonly used drugs in
this category are diltiazem, digoxin, and atenolol. The goal is to achieve an
average daily ventricular rate of <125 bpm in dogs.75a As cats do not
generally tolerate Holters well, the authors aim for ventricular rate on an
in-hospital ECG of < 200 bpm. Certain dogs with presumed “idiopathic”
AF have an acceptable ventricular rate and require no medication. In the
majority of dogs and cats with AF and structural heart disease, however,
medications are needed to slow an unacceptably high ventricular rate.
Diltiazem is typically the first drug used in either the standard release
formulation at 1-2 mg/kg PO q8h (dogs and cats) or sustained release
formulation at 1-4 mg/kg PO q12h in dogs and 30-45 mg total dose PO
q12-24h in cats. The sustained release preparations have a higher
incidence of gastrointestinal side-effects in cats.75b If adequate ventricular
rate control is not achieved with diltiazem alone (and it often is not), then
digoxin is commonly added at 0.003-0.007 mg/kg PO q12h in dogs (not
typically used in cats). Atenolol is used less commonly by the authors,
except in select canine cases when beta-blockade is helpful (such as
subaortic stenosis or hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy) and no
active congestive heart failure is present. Restricting vigorous activity in
dogs with AF and a rapid ventricular response is also important. The
adequacy of the therapeutic response is best evaluated by Holter
monitoring, but if that is not possible, an owner can send multiple ECG
recordings at various times over several days using an Alive Cor device.
Pharmacologic cardioversion is rarely attempted in dogs and cats and
not usually successful in long-standing AF. Its highest success in human
AF patients comes when initiated within 7 days of AF onset and using
drugs such as IV ibutilide and oral dofetilide, which have not been used in
veterinary patients. The class IC agents (propafenone, flecainide) also
successfully cardiovert over 50% of recent-onset AF, while amiodarone is
successful in only about 25% of cases. Amiodarone is the agent of choice,
however, for maintaining sinus rhythm following successful electrical or
pharmacologic cardioversion.71

Orthodromic Atrioventricular Reciprocating
Tachycardia
OAVRT is an underrecognized cause of NCT in companion animals. It is
most frequently diagnosed in young to middle-aged dogs and cats, with a
median age of 2.1 years in North American dogs with EPS-confirmed APs.
Males are overrepresented, accounting for 67% of dogs with EPSconfirmed APs. As a single breed, Labrador Retrievers comprise 45% of
dogs with confirmed APs, suggesting a genetic predisposition in this
breed. APs have been identified, however, in 28 dog breeds (Wright KN,
unpublished manuscript, 2021).24 TICM is a common finding in dogs with
OAVRT. Cats have also been identified with ECG findings of an AP. These
have not been confirmed at EPS due to technical limitations in the
cardiovascular anatomy-to-instrumentation size in this species.
APs are anomalous bypass tracts typically composed of working
myocardial cells.76 Such APs can form the retrograde limb of a
macroreentrant circuit involving the atrial myocardium, AVN-HPS as the
antegrade limb, and ventricular myocardium. This results in a regular,
NCT known as OAVRT. If the AP is capable of antegrade conduction, an
ECG recorded during sinus rhythm may demonstrate ventricular
preexcitation (VPE), characterized by a short PR interval and slurred
upstroke to the QRS, known as a delta wave. The degree of VPE visible
during sinus rhythm depends upon: 1) AVN and HPS conduction time, 2)
conduction time of the sinus impulse to the AP, and 3) conduction time
through the AP.76 VPE may be present consistently in sinus rhythm
(manifest APs) or only intermittently. Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
(WPW) is the combination of VPE during sinus rhythm and periods of
symptomatic tachyarrhythmia. An AP only capable of retrograde
conduction is known as a concealed AP, and the ECG during sinus rhythm
will have a normal PR interval and QRS complex. Even in patients with
WPW, the QRS complex during OAVRT is narrow because the AVN
conducts the electrical impulse antegrade from atrium to ventricle, while
the AP conducts the impulse retrograde from the ventricle to the atrium.
ECG findings during OAVRT include an NCT, often with visible
retrograde P waves within the ST segment. The likelihood of identifying
retrograde P waves is enhanced the more ECG leads that are recorded
(Figure 230.8; Video 230.6

). The only time that OAVRT presents as

a wide complex tachycardia (WCT) is when a preexisting or functional
interventricular conduction delay is present (see later). Median
documented OAVRT TCL prior to AA medications in 120 dogs with

documented APs was 180 msec (range, 140-240 msec), corresponding to
HRs of 250-428 bpm. The RP interval was shorter than the PR interval in
all dogs except one, which had a decrementally conducting AP. P’ waves
within the ST segment or T wave of sinus complexes occurred
intermittently in over 75% of dogs, having a fixed RP interval equal to RP
measured during OAVRT (Figure 230.9). Retrograde P waves generally
were visualized best in the caudal (inferior) limb leads (II, aVF, or III), but
in approximately 20% of dogs the cranial (superior) limb leads provided
the best visualization of the P’ onset. Forty-five percent of dogs exhibited
VPE at some time during sinus rhythm. Of these dogs with VPE, 48% were
manifest, whereas 42% had intermittent VPE (Figure 230.10). It is
important to recognize that the PR interval and QRS duration can be
within reference ranges, yet VPE still be present. This depends upon AP
location and relative conduction properties of the AP and AVN-HPS.
Acute treatment of OAVRT centers around terminating the
tachyarrhythmia with intravenous AA drugs or synchronized DCCV. Vagal
maneuvers are rarely effective, but could be tried briefly. Lidocaine has
proven to be an effective agent in terminating OAVRT in a majority of
dogs with blockade occurring in the retrograde AP.25 This is likely due to
the similarities between AP cardiomyocytes and those of the ventricular
myocardium.77 Lidocaine is administered in dogs as a 2 mg/kg IV bolus
over 20-30 seconds. If no cardioversion occurs after 2 minutes and no
adverse effects develop, 2 mg/kg IV boluses are repeated, to a total
cumulative dose of 8 mg/kg.25 If the lidocaine bolus is successful in
cardioverting OAVRT to sinus rhythm, it can be followed by an
intravenous constant rate infusion (CRI) of 25-75 mcg/kg/min. A protocol
has not been developed for cats with OAVRT. This species is much more
sensitive to lidocaine’s adverse effects. Lower doses of 0.25-0.75 mg/kg
have been successfully administered slowly IV, followed by infusion at
rates of 10-20 mcg/kg/min. Intravenous diltiazem has also been
successful in terminating OAVRT, by slowing AVN conduction and
inducing second-degree AV block, rather than affecting the AP.
Intravenous diltiazem is administered 0.125-0.35 mg/kg slowly IV over 3
minutes and can be followed by a 0.125-0.35 mg/kg/hr CRI if needed for
recurrent OAVRT. Finally, Nexterone, at the dosages listed previously, can
acutely terminate OAVRT, primarily through its effects on the AP, but also
through some modest effects on the AVN.
Chronic therapy for OAVRT can be either pharmacologic or catheterbased. RFCA has been shown to be a highly effective cure for OAVRT,
through ablation of the AP itself (Video 230.7

).24,26 Resolution of

TICM occurs within 1-6 months of successful RFCA in nearly all dogs.
Pharmacologic therapy centers on attacking the two limbs of the circuit:
the retrograde AP and the antegrade AVN. Drugs that may block
conduction through the AP include class IA (procainamide), class IB
(mexiletine), class IC (propafenone, flecainide), and class III (sotalol,
amiodarone). Mexiletine is typically dosed at 4-8 mg/kg PO q8h in dogs.
Mexiletine has been rarely used in cats, due to their increased
susceptibility to side-effects, with dosing of 1-2 mg/kg PO q12h. Drugs
that slow conduction through the AVN include calcium channel blockers
(class IV), beta-blockers (class II), and digoxin. A combination of drugs
from these two groups is generally used; however, sotalol and amiodarone
may be effective as single agents, as they themselves are drugs combining
negative dromotropism and prolongation of the AP refractory period.

Focal Junctional Tachycardia
The rarest of the NCTs discussed, FJT is a tachycardia arising in the AV
junction and has also been called junctional ectopic tachycardia and HB
tachycardia.78 In people, this tachyarrhythmia is divided into categories
according to its etiology. The identified forms include congenital,
postoperative, paroxysmal, and secondary to digitalis toxicosis. FJT may
be caused by enhanced automaticity or abnormal automaticity of either
low in the AVN or high in the HPS or by triggered activity. Congenital FJT
is usually rapid and incessant, resulting in hemodynamic compromise or
TICM. FJT presenting after 6 months of age in humans tends to follow a
more benign course and is often exacerbated by sympathetic
stimulation.78 We have identified FJT in several young dogs. It has been
suggested to be more common in mature Labrador Retrievers, in
association with isorhythmic AV dissociation.79 Its ECG characteristics
can be variable, depending upon whether it is paroxysmal or incessant
and whether retrograde AV nodal conduction is present. An example of
FJT is shown in Figure 230.11. Incessant FJT with 1:1 AVN conduction
will present as an incessant NCT with short RP’ interval that must be
differentiated from OAVRT and AVNRT. By contrast, paroxysmal FJT
without retrograde AVN conduction will show an irregular NCT with
intermittent sinus captures. FJT is often unresponsive to pharmacologic
therapy; however, the drug most successful in its management is
amiodarone. Calcium channel blockers may be successful in slowing FJT
caused by abnormal automaticity in the AV junction. The risk of AV block
with RFCA is higher than in the other NCTs. For this reason, cryoablation
is preferred in human patients.80

WIDE COMPLEX TACHYARRHYTHMIAS
ECG Appearance/Differential Diagnoses
WCTs in companion animals are most commonly due to VT, with a
smaller percentage due to one of the mechanisms of NCT but conducting
aberrantly to the ventricles (NCT-A). This aberrancy can be functional
(developing due to the rapid HR), preexisting (due to damage to one of the
bundle branches), or rarely due to anterograde AP conduction. It can be
very challenging to differentiate VT (Figure 230.12, A) from NCT-A
(Figure 230.12, B), but certain criteria can be helpful. The most helpful
distinction is the presence of AV dissociation in VT versus NCT-A.23 The

difficulty is that P waves are often impossible to identify within the setting
of a WCT. Capture or fusion complexes are also helpful in diagnosing VT.
A capture beat occurs when an ideally timed supraventricular impulse
exclusively depolarizes the ventricles, resulting in a single QRS
morphology/duration matching that of the patient’s sinus rhythm.81 A
fusion complex occurs when ventricular depolarization wavefronts
emanating from supraventricular and ventricular sources collide and
create a hybrid QRS complex that shares ventricular depolarization
characteristics of both the VT and sinus rhythm. In humans, NCT-A
produces QRS configurations in V1-2 and V6 typical of a right (RBBB) or
left bundle branch block (LBBB) pattern, while VT only rarely does.81
Work remains to be done in companion animals to establish normal
precordial patterns in different thoracic conformations, thus making
identification of true RBBB and LBBB more accurate. Multiform or
polymorphic WCTs are highly likely to be VT. Comparison of WCT to a
baseline ECG is valuable, as preexisting bundle branch block may be
apparent (Figure 230.12, C). Ventricular flutter is a term that has been
applied to a rapid VT having a sinusoidal QRS configuration that prevents
clear identification of the QRS morphology. Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is
a pulseless, fatal rhythm characterized by lack of coordinated ventricular
contraction and high frequency disorganized excitation causing
undulation of the ECG baseline (Figure 230.13).

Underlying Causes
Extracardiac and primary cardiac disorders can predispose to ventricular
premature complexes (VPCs)/VT. Several dog breeds have genetic
predispositions to VT and more are being discovered. Boxers and English
Bulldogs are predisposed to arrhythmogenic right ventricular
cardiomyopathy (ARVC), an adult-onset inherited disease which can lead
to sudden death82,83 (ch. 233) (Video 230.8

). A deletion in the

striatin gene has been identified as at least one underlying cause of ARVC
in the Boxer breed.82 An autosomal dominant trait in the Doberman
Pinscher, involving mutations in PDK4 or TTN (titin) genes, to date,
results in a unique DCM associated with often severe VT (ch. 233).84,85
Breeds which have been identified with inherited juvenile VA include
German Shepherds, Rhodesian Ridgebacks, and Leonbergers. Cats with
primary cardiac causes of VA commonly have one of the
cardiomyopathies, including ARVC (which is rare in cats).86 Extracardiac

causes of VA include splenic disease, gastric dilation with/without
volvulus, trauma, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, systemic inflammatory
response, pheochromocytoma, thyrotoxicosis, autonomic imbalance due
to intracranial disease, hypoxemia, acid-base imbalance, and adverse
effects of drugs (including several AA agents). In some of these situations,
an accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR) may be seen. A gradual
transition back and forth between sinus rhythm and AIVR, which is a
spontaneous ventricular rhythm that occurs at a rate of 40-160 bpm,
commonly occurs. The patient is not generally hemodynamically
compromised by this rhythm, so it is important to differentiate AIVR from
true VT. AA therapy is not generally required for AIVR; rather, the
underlying extracardiac cause is addressed.

Clinical Signs
Clinical signs most commonly observed with sustained WCTs include
weakness, lethargy, syncope, hyporexia, and vomiting. Sudden cardiac
death may be the first and only sign observed.

FIGURE 230.13 Representative surface 12-lead
electrocardiograms of various forms of ventricular

Clinical Arrhythmology and Electrophysiology. 3rd ed.

Therapy

The decision of when to treat VAs is a complicated one. It depends on
multiple factors, including an animal’s structural heart disease and
hemodynamic tolerance of the rhythm. Single VPCs, AIVRs, and VAs with
both mild complexity and rate <200 bpm do not generally require AA
therapy; however, very frequent, single VPCs are now being recognized as
a cause of cardiomyopathy in some people.86a At the other end of the
spectrum, VF always requires immediate treatment (defibrillation) or
death will ensue within minutes. Sustained runs of rapid VT (>200 bpm)
are a medical emergency, as they can degenerate rapidly into VF.
Nonsustained rapid ventricular runs (≥3 consecutive VPCs occurring
during <30 seconds) are generally considered to warrant AA drug therapy,
although there is a dearth of evidence to demonstrate a survival benefit.
Emergent/acute treatment of sustained, rapid VT centers around DCCV
or select intravenous AA drugs. These AA drugs are also used in
emergently treating frequent, rapid, nonsustained WCT. Such drugs
include those that block sodium or potassium channels, beta-blockers,
and magnesium sulfate. Lidocaine is a first-line drug for VT, with dosing
as discussed under OAVRT. Procainamide is often the second-line
parenteral agent used, at 6-8 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes in dogs and 1-2
mg/kg IV over 5 minutes in cats, although the authors are moving more
commonly to Nexterone as a second-line agent in dogs. We have also used
Nexterone successfully in cats with VT at 2-3 mg/kg IV over 15 minutes,
but more data are needed in this species. Procainamide infusions at 20-40
mcg/kg/min in dogs and 10-20 mcg/kg/min in cats can be used if
cardioversion occurs after a “bolus.”53 Magnesium sulfate is the first-line
AA treatment for torsades de pointes and has been used with variable
success to treat drug-refractory VT or arrhythmias in patients with known
hypomagnesemia.86b It is administered slowly IV at 30 mg/kg (equivalent
to 0.243 mEq/kg) over 5 to 10 minutes.53 Identification and correction of
underlying contributing factors is important. Hypokalemia,
hypomagnesemia, hypoxia, blood loss, gastric malpositioning, sepsis, and
a systemic inflammatory response, for example, should be identified and
addressed, while simultaneously treating the VT.
Oral AA therapy of VT in dogs and cats centers around similar channel
and receptor blockade as described in acute management. Sotalol is one of
the most commonly used AA drugs for VT in both dogs and cats at dosages
of 1-3 mg/kg PO q12h. Mexiletine, often in combination with sotalol or
other AA drugs, is the class IB agent of choice in dogs, but is rarely used in
cats due to side-effects. Propafenone and flecainide are effective class IC
agents for VAs, with their potent sodium channel blocking ability.

Concern has arisen in human medicine regarding the use of these agents
in the face of structural heart disease; however, this has only been proven
for human patients with prior myocardial infarction.87 Whether these
class IC AAs increase mortality in patients with nonischemic
cardiomyopathy is not known. Recent studies have shown their benefit in
ARVC patients and those with VPC-induced cardiomyopathy.88,89
Amiodarone is also an effective ventricular AA agent, given its
combination blockade of sodium channels, rapid and slow delayed
rectifying potassium channels, and beta-1 adrenergic receptors. It opposes
EP heterogeneity, which underlies some severe VAs. The efficacy of
amiodarone exceeds that of other AA compounds, including sotalol, in
human patients with severe VAs.90 Furthermore, the incidence of
torsades de pointes with amiodarone is much lower than expected from its
class III effects. A retrospective study of dogs with severe ventricular or
supraventricular tachyarrhythmias concluded that amiodarone resulted in
an improvement in the severity of the tachyarrhythmia and clinical signs
in 26 of 28 dogs.91 A major drawback is that amiodarone is associated
with a host of multisystemic, potentially serious adverse effects that do
not occur with sotalol. A retrospective evaluation of the use of amiodarone
in Doberman Pinschers with severe ventricular tachyarrhythmias
documented adverse effects in 30% of the 20 patients studied.92 These
adverse effects included vomiting, anorexia, hepatopathies, and
thrombocytopenia, and were more common with higher maintenance
dosages. The authors will typically monitor serum biochemistry panels,
total thyroxine, and thyroid stimulating hormone concentrations every 34 months, and complete blood counts every 6 months, in animals
receiving amiodarone. RFCA can be helpful in certain cases, specifically in
dogs having probable idiopathic monomorphic VT.

BRADYARRHYTHMIAS
Bradyarrhythmias are first broadly divided into disorders of impulse
formation and disorders of impulse conduction. Subsidiary pacemakers
contained within the AV junctional region and Purkinje fibers can
spontaneously depolarize, an important physiological redundancy to
prevent asystole. Chronic activation or failure of the subsidiary
pacemakers to discharge can lead to clinical signs which may include
weakness, lethargy, exercise intolerance, CHF, syncope, and sudden
cardiac death. Orally administered therapy can be considered in certain

situations if there is concurrent parasympathetic influence; however,
pacemaker implantation is often necessary to alleviate clinical signs.

SINUS BRADYCARDIA
Sinus bradycardia is an excessively slow, regular heart rhythm that
originates from the sinus node. In dogs and cats, this is commonly defined
when the HR is <70 bpm and <140 bpm respectively, in a clinical setting.
On ECG, there is a regular, but prolonged interval between QRS
complexes, with a P wave preceding each QRS complex and a QRS
complex following each P wave (Figure 230.14). There are multiple
patient variables to consider when identifying a sinus bradycardia,
including temperament, age and breed, to name a few.93 In both cats and
dogs, it is normal to have a slower HR when resting or sleeping, but when
there is adequate sympathetic stimulation, such as in a clinical setting, a
bradycardia should not be present. While generally due to high levels of
resting vagal tone, whether physiologic or pathologic (gastrointestinal,
respiratory, ocular and neurologic diseases), other considerations can
include hypothyroidism, hypothermia, and medications (opioids, betablockers, calcium channel blockers, alpha-2 agonists, sedatives). If there is
concern for underlying intrinsic sinus node disease, an atropine response
test can be performed which will remove vagal influence on the SA node
(0.04 mg/kg atropine IV, ECG q 1 minute for the first 5 minutes, then at
10 and 15 minutes). This bradyarrhythmia rarely leads to clinical signs
and treatment is targeted at removing the underlying cause if necessary. If
the bradycardia is thought to be relevant to the patient’s status, either
sympathomimetic or parasympatholytic therapies can be considered:
theophylline sustained-release formulation (10 mg/kg PO q12h),
terbutaline (0.1-0.2 mg/kg q8-12h, dogs), propantheline bromide (0.5-1
mg/kg PO q8h), or hyoscyamine sulfate (0.003-0.006 mg/kg PO q8h).

ATRIOVENTRICULAR BLOCK
Atrioventricular block (AVB) is one of the most widely recognized
disorders of impulse conduction resulting in a delay or termination of an
SAN or atrial impulse as it travels through the AVN, HB, and bundle
branches.94 While the AVN does limit rapid impulse transmission to the
ventricles when a supraventricular tachyarrhythmia occurs (physiologic
AV block), disease of the AVN can impair the transmission of normal
impulses and result in a significant bradyarrhythmia and clinical signs. AV

blocks are subdivided into first-, second-, and third-degree, with seconddegree being further subdivided into Mobitz Types I and II. These
arrhythmias can be transient or persistent and progression is possible
depending on the underlying etiology.
First-degree AVB is classified as a delay in conduction causing a
prolongation of the P-Q interval noted on an ECG. In dogs and cats, this is
diagnosed when the P-Q interval is greater than 120 ms and 80 ms
respectively, with an associated QRS complex following each P wave
(Figure 230.15). Primary structural causes include degeneration
(fibrosis), infectious, inflammatory and infiltrative diseases of the
conduction system; other causes include elevated vagal tone, injectable
and inhalant anesthetics, medications including AAs, and hyperkalemia.
First-degree AVB does not cause clinical signs; therefore, therapy is not
necessary. In certain irreversible situations, such as degenerative valve
disease, the authors have observed that progression towards second and
third-degree AVB can occur.
Second-degree AVB occurs when there is an intermittent disruption in
AVN conduction resulting in an isolated P wave noted on ECG with no
corresponding QRS complex. The severity of this arrhythmia can vary
from occasional block of a single P wave to a high-grade block that can
ultimately result in clinical signs. When the block occurs rarely and not on
consecutive QRS complexes, second-degree AVB is further subdivided
into Mobitz Types I and II. Mobitz type I (also known as Wenckebach) is
characterized by a progressive lengthening of the P-Q interval until a
block occurs (Figure 230.16).95,96 Mobitz type I characteristically
involves only the AV node, is considered non-pathologic and clinical
sequelae are not expected. Additionally, this physiologic block can be
considered normal in young puppies, especially between 8-11 weeks of age
when resting.97 In contrast to Mobitz type I, Mobitz type II typically has a
relatively fixed P-Q interval prior to interrupted conduction through the
AV node (Figure 230.17). Mobitz type II, is most often associated with
structural cardiac disease, often involves the infranodal conduction
system rather than the compact AV node, and can progress toward a more
significant bradyarrhythmia, such as high-grade second-degree or thirddegree AVB.

High-grade second-degree AVB is characterized by multiple nonconducted P waves that result in a significant bradycardia. The number of
P waves is counted in relation to the number of associated conducted
complexes. For example, if there are three P waves but only one conducted
QRS complex, it is considered 3:1 conduction. While there is no consensus
for the definition of high-grade second-degree AVB, it has been suggested
that in dogs there should be an AV conduction of at least 3:1 and a
reasonable atrial rate of <200 bpm.98 Certain breeds such as Chow
Chows, Cocker Spaniels and Labrador Retrievers have a higher
predisposition for high-grade second-degree AVB. Clinical signs of highgrade second-degree AVB include lethargy, weakness, exercise
intolerance, syncope, ascites, and respiratory-related clinical signs
including coughing and dyspnea. The latter signs are generally due to the
presence of concurrent severe structural heart disease with CHF
exacerbation by a chronic bradyarrhythmia.Third-degree AVB is a

complete disruption of AV nodal conduction and synchronization leading
to subsidiary pacemaker activation to maintain cardiac output (Video
230.9

). On ECG, there are multiple P waves occurring at a regular

interval with no associated QRS complexes (Figure 230.18). Ventricular
depolarization is the result of spontaneous depolarization from either the
AV junctional region or Purkinje fibers resulting in a clinically significant
bradyarrhythmia. AV junctional escape rates in dogs tend to be between
35-65 bpm, whereas ventricular (Purkinje) escape rates are between 2040 bpm. In the absence of concurrent bundle branch disease, the AV
junctional escape beats are usually narrow and can more closely resemble
the normal QRS complex. The ventricular subsidiary pacemaker results in
a wider QRS complex, relying on cell-to-cell conduction. On ECG, thirddegree AVB for feline patients is similar to dogs, although the P to P
interval is generally closer to a feline sinus discharge rate of
approximately 200 bpm. In a retrospective study of 21 cats with thirddegree AVB, 90% of cats have a narrow escape complex suggesting a
higher level of block within the AV node vs. block within the HB or below
(which would lead to escape within the Purkinje system and a widened
QRS complex).99
While it is possible that patients with third-degree AVB have no clinical
manifestations of cardiac disease, referral to a tertiary location is
commonplace due to the uncharacteristically slow HR noted on physical
examination. Similar to high-grade second-degree AV block, patients with
third-degree AV block can experience lethargy, weakness, exercise
intolerance, coughing, dyspnea, syncope (

Videos 40.1, 40.4), and

ascites. Occasionally, gastrointestinal changes including vomiting,
diarrhea and decreased appetite are noted.6 Cats with high-grade seconddegree and third-degree AVB may present with respiratory signs, syncope,
and seizure-like episodes attributed to compromised cerebral perfusion (
Video 40.2; Figure 230.19).99,100 Importantly, one retrospective
study noted approximately one-third of cats with third-degree AVB
present with no clinical signs, attributed to the fact that the escape rates
are generally higher (80-140 bpm) and compatible with a cat’s typical
sedentary lifestyle.99
For both second-degree and third-degree AVB, degeneration (fibrosis)
of the AV junctional area is considered the most likely structural cause.
Myocarditic changes resulting from traumatic, immune mediated,
infectious, toxic, and infiltrative (neoplastic) insults have been

described.101-108 While exceedingly rare, a congenital defect resulting in
stenosis of the HB has also been reported in a Pug.109 Species differences
exist and causes in cats include structural cardiac changes
(cardiomyopathies and infiltrative disease), inflammatory/infectious
(myocarditis), and systemic diseases (hyperthyroidism). Reversibility of
second- and third-degree AVB is possible if associated with high vagal
tone, intoxication, electrolyte abnormalities, anesthesia, and negative
chronotropic medications. Historically, third-degree AVB was thought to
be sustained, but a recent retrospective study showed that in
approximately 12% of dogs, there can be regression to a less severe form of
AVB.110 In this same study, however, second-degree AVB progressed to
third-degree AVB in approximately 61% of patients. Regression to seconddegree AVB or conducted sinus rhythm from third-degree AVB can also
occur in cats.

For both feline and canine patients, the approach to AVB diagnosis and
treatment is similar. If a clinically significant bradyarrhythmia is detected
on physical exam, all reversible causes should be ruled out initially. This
includes full systemic evaluation with complete blood count and serum
biochemistry profile, blood pressure (ch. 91), echocardiography (ch. 97),
and thoracic radiography. Additionally, troponin I levels can be performed
for assessment of myocardial damage/inflammation, and if found to be
elevated, infectious disease screening should follow. Initially, an atropine
response test is performed to remove vagal influence on the AV node (see
Sinus Bradycardia, above). In most advanced AV block cases, the atropine
response test is unrewarding, with minimal to no improvement in the
escape rate. Oral therapy can be attempted but is unlikely to help in
patients with high-grade second- and third-degree AV block. Ultimately in
most patients, to decrease clinical signs and the risk of sudden death, the
treatment of choice is permanent pacemaker implantation (

Video

230.10).
Overall, the prognosis of AVB is variable, with first-degree and
subclinical second-degree AVB generally considered good. In dogs with
high-grade second-degree and third-degree AVB, however, a slower
ventricular rate was paradoxically associated with a better long-term

prognosis in one study.98 In this same study, high-grade second-degree
AVB was associated with a guarded prognosis and a higher risk of sudden
death (approximately 40%). In feline patients with third-degree AVB, the
median survival was 386 days, with no change in outcome if CHF was
present or not.99

PERSISTENT ATRIAL STANDSTILL
Persistent atrial standstill (PAS) is a bradyarrhythmia caused by the
progressive loss of atrial electrical and mechanical activity corresponding
with a lack of P waves on ECG. The resultant rhythm relies on subsidiary
pacemakers to cause ventricular depolarization. On ECG in dogs, this is
seen as a nodal escape rhythm (HR between 35-65 bpm) with no
detectable P waves (Figure 230.20). In contrast to this, transient atrial
standstill, most often associated with hyperkalemia, can be driven by the
sinus node if the internodal tracts remain functional. The resulting
rhythm is termed a sinoventricular rhythm. While PAS is a rare
arrhythmia, it is typically encountered in dogs with an atrial myopathy
causing progressive loss of the atrial myocardium with myocardial
necrosis and replacement fibrosis.111,112 Although the name implies a
primary atrial disease, occasionally extension into the ventricular
myocardium can occur. Less commonly, myocarditis has been associated
with the development of atrial standstill. Various breeds have been
reported with this arrhythmia, but there is a breed predilection in English
Springer Spaniels and Labrador Retrievers.112,113 This condition has been
rarely reported in cats.114
Since PAS causes a significant bradyarrhythmia and concurrent
structural chamber enlargement, the most common clinical signs are
associated with syncope and CHF (cough, dyspnea, ascites).112,113
Treatment is aimed at controlling CHF with oral therapy (ch. 229) and
chronotropic support with permanent pacemaker implantation. With
pacemaker implantation, the reported median survival time in dogs is 866
days.113

spayed female Miniature Schnauzer with sick sinus

SINUS NODAL DISEASE/SICK SINUS
SYNDROME
Sinus nodal disease/dysfunction (SND) is a bradyarrhythmia caused by a
failure of impulse formation from the SAN. Although this has been used
interchangeably with the term sick sinus syndrome (SSS), the latter is
considered when clinical signs such as weakness, exercise intolerance and
syncope are present.115,116 SND/SSS can manifest with different ECG
abnormalities such as inappropriate sinus bradyarrhythmia, sinus arrest,
and tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome. Furthermore, concurrent
conduction abnormalities such as AVB and failure of subsidiary

pacemaker discharge are often present increasing the likelihood of patient
symptomology.
For patients with SND/SSS, intermittent sinus arrest is present in
approximately 80% of cases.117 Sinus arrest is defined as a pause in a
sinus rhythm longer than 2 regular sinus R to R intervals (Figure
230.21). In this same study, 21% of dogs displayed evidence of
tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome on Holter. The mean longest duration
of sinus arrest in the clinic was 2.5 seconds, but on Holter increased to 7.3
seconds in duration. When clinical signs are present, syncope was
documented to occur in approximately 95% of cases with multiple daily
episodes possible. Older females are predisposed, with Cocker Spaniels,
West Highland White Terriers and Miniature Schnauzers being
overrepresented.117-120 This condition is thought to arise from a
degeneration/depletion of SAN cells with an increase in fibrous and fibrofatty replacement impacting SAN communication with the atria.117,120
Autonomic influence on SAN tissue can further contribute to the ECG
abnormalities with SND/SSS and may be responsive to vagolytics. When
comparing SSS to SND, however, SSS is more likely to have an insufficient
response to atropine (approximately 30% of cases).117
Various therapeutic options have been considered in SSS patients,
including the use of oral medications and pacemaker implantation. Oral
positive chronotropic therapy has included the use of theophylline,
terbutaline, propantheline bromide, and hyoscyamine sulfate as
monotherapy or dual therapy (sympathomimetic/vagolytic) at the dosages
listed under the Sinus Bradycardia section. Of these, the authors prefer
hyoscyamine (0.003-0.006 mg/kg PO q8h). In a slight majority of cases,
oral treatment can improve or control short-term clinical signs and act as
a bridge until pacemaker implantation can be performed. For patients
with persistent syncopal episodes, tachyarrhythmias that require
treatment and/or structural cardiac disease that has resulted in CHF, the
treatment of choice is permanent pacemaker implantation. It does not
appear, however, that pacemaker implantation will prolong survival time
when compared to oral therapy, but will improve clinical signs.117 Median
survival for both SSS and SND is approximately 18 months with a median
age of death of 14 years.117 Unlike high-grade second-degree and thirddegree AVB, patients with SSS/SND do not have a higher risk of sudden
cardiac death.

THERAPEUTIC OPTIONS FOR
BRADYARRHYTHMIAS
As previously discussed, bradyarrhythmias, when severe, can result in
clinical signs of weakness, lethargy, or syncope; exacerbate or cause CHF;
and occasionally cause sudden cardiac death. Prescribed oral therapy can
include the use of sympathomimetics (theophylline most commonly)
and/or anticholinergics (hyoscyamine sulfate is most readily available).
Permanent pacemaker implantation, however, is considered a standard
procedure for chronic chronotropic support with the ultimate goal of
decreasing or eliminating clinical signs.
Permanent pacemaker implantation has been used for years in both
dogs and cats for second-degree AVB, third-degree AVB, SSS, atrial
standstill, and vasovagal syncope when clinical signs are present (Video
230.10

).94,99,108,114,116,117,121-127 Multiple large retrospective studies

have shown the majority of patients who receive pacemaker implantation
tend to require it due to third-degree AVB. For both transvenous and
epicardial pacemaker implantation, the main components are the
hermetically sealed pulse generator (housing the lithium-iodide battery)
and lead(s). There are many different options to consider, including but
not limited to: unipolar vs. bipolar, single vs. dual chamber, and passive
vs. active fixation. Additionally, the pacemaker generator can be
programed in different modes (delineated by a three letter code; Table
230.2) with various output and sensing adjustments.

Deciding which pacemaker to utilize is ultimately dependent on the
clinician and available resources for device implantation. Prior to
permanent pacemaker implantation, it is common to perform temporary
transvenous pacemaker placement under light sedation or transthoracic
pacing under heavy sedation for chronotropic support. Epicardial pacing
is generally favored in patients of small body size, and in those with a
higher risk of endocarditis (neck pyoderma, immunosuppressive therapy,
etc.), hypercoagulability, or other comorbidities that would necessitate
simultaneous thoracic or abdominal surgeries.127,128 Epicardial
implantation is most often performed through the transdiaphragmatic
approach with pulse generator implantation into the lateral abdominal

wall.127-129 One or two leads are then sutured onto the cardiac apex via a
steroid-eluting epicardial button. Other surgical methods for epicardial
lead placement include either a thoracotomy or minimally invasive
transxiphoid approach.130 In contrast, a transvenous approach involves
fluoroscopically guiding a single or dual leads into the right heart via
access from the right jugular vein. If a single lead is used, it is most
commonly a passive or active fixation lead placed in the right ventricular
apex. When AV nodal conduction is intact, atrial-based pacing can be
considered in sinus node diseased patients.119 To maintain AV synchrony,
dual chamber pacing is an option (1 lead is placed in the ventricle and 1 in
the atrium) and more closely mimics the normal activation of the cardiac
electrical sequence when compared to a single ventricular lead.
Additionally, there has been documented improvement in chamber
dimensions, hemodynamics, and neurohormonal profiles with AV
synchronization, although as expected, there are longer associated
procedural times.131 Over time, technological advancements have allowed
for a single VDD lead to be used in patients with AV block to maintain AV
synchrony.125,132,133 This is accomplished with the use of a floating atrial
electrode to detect atrial activity, causing a triggered ventricular
depolarization.
Possible complications can arise with pacemaker implantation and
should be thoroughly discussed with the client. In a large retrospective
study of transvenous pacemaker implantation in 154 dogs, 55% of patients
experienced some degree of pacemaker-related complications and 33% of
patients experienced a major, life-threating complication.122 Other
retrospective studies have been performed and did not conclude a similar
frequency of complications (Table 230.3). Rarely reported complications
of transvenous pacemaker implantation include: tricuspid valve
stenosis,134-136 intracardiac thrombosis,124 right ventricular outflow tract
obstruction,137 caval obstruction/stenosis,138-141 cardiac
perforation,124,142 and pacemaker twitch (
Video 230.11). Major
complications occur in 25% of dogs undergoing epicardial pacemaker
implantation. While dislodgment of the lead(s) is the most commonly
reported complication of pacemaker implantation (endo- or epicardial),
other complications include loss of capture, ventricular tachyarrhythmias,
and bilateral tension pneumothorax.124,126,127,131 Considering the
treatment options to manage clinically significant bradyarrhythmias,
permanent pacemaker implantation is commonly performed with

improvement or resolution of clinical signs and in certain cases, improves
survival.

INTRODUCTION
The term congenital heart disease (CHD) encompasses a large
number of morphologic and functional abnormalities of the heart
and contiguous blood vessels that are present at birth. These
malformations generally arise from some altered or arrested
development of the embryonic heart triggered by genetic or
environmental factors. The severity of CHD can range from trivial to
life-threatening, and clinical signs might manifest anytime from the
neonatal period to relatively late in life. Although some types of CHD
are well-tolerated, severe functional consequences can occur with
others. These consequences can include congestive heart failure
(CHF; ch. 229), hypoxemia, cardiac arrhythmia (ch. 230), or
sudden cardiac death. This chapter provides an overview of CHD in
dogs and cats along with principles of diagnosis and management of
commonly encountered defects. The reader is also referred to ch.
239 which addresses some forms of venous vascular anomalies, to
ch. 259 for additional consideration about the diagnosis and
management of esophageal obstruction caused by vascular ring
malformations, and to ch. 115, which addresses cardiovascular
interventional therapies.
In most cases, successful management of CHD begins with the
prompt recognition of a cardiac disorder by the family veterinarian,
followed by referral to a cardiologist for detailed evaluation. In most

situations, a definitive diagnosis of CHD can be attained
noninvasively following a complete echocardiographic examination
(ch. 97). However, precise definition of some complex forms of CHD
—as well as certain vascular malformations—can demand advanced
imaging techniques. The prognosis for any CHD relates to the type
and severity of the underlying malformation. Some forms of CHD
require no treatment and carry a favorable prognosis. Other defects
are amenable to definitive therapy or to some form of palliative
treatment.

ETIOLOGY
Congenital cardiac malformations can be caused by genetic or
environmental factors, and in most cases a single causative agent
cannot be conclusively identified. The potential interaction of
toxicologic, nutritional, infectious, and genetic factors makes it
difficult to determine a definitive cause. The observation that certain
congenital defects display a species or breed predilection1-4 strongly
suggests a heritable basis in many cases (Table 231.1). This
hypothesis has been demonstrated for several specific defects in
certain canine breeds.1,5-11 Several studies indicate a simple
Mendelian basis for transmission, supporting the concept that
identifiable genetic factors contribute to development of the
embryonic heart and relate to specific types of CHD. Other genes can
demonstrate additive or modifying effects and produce a discrete
phenotype once a Mendelian trait has been inherited including
variability in the penetrance and expression of that characteristic.1216

The complexity and uncertainty surrounding the exact mode of
inheritance of many cardiac defects hamper the counseling of owners
who want to use individual dogs for breeding. Although cardiologists
often attempt to identify CHD in breeding dogs during screening
clinics, these efforts are confounded by the limited sensitivity and
specificity of available diagnostic studies. Certainly, a normal
physical examination (ch. 3) does not equate with genetic normalcy.
Moreover, many soft murmurs are difficult to interpret,17-19 and
echocardiographic screenings often yield equivocal findings in the
absence of true, gold-standard criteria for the diagnosis of mild
disease. Even with careful attention to pedigree and the results of
breeding trials, it can be very difficult to influence the overall
prevalence of a specific defect in the larger population. Progress in
this regard hinges on the development of economical genetic tests
that can detect the presence of the genetic mutations responsible for
specific malformations.

The situation in cats is even more complicated and there are no
detailed genetic studies of cats with CHD. Several possible breed
predispositions have been reported, such as tricuspid valve dysplasia
(TVD) and atrial septal defect (ASD) in the Chartreux cat,20,21 and
older reports link endocardial fibroelastosis (EFE) and supravalvular
mitral stenosis to Siamese cats.

PREVALENCE
The prevalence of CHD in dogs has been reported to be between
0.46% and 0.85% of referral hospital admissions.22-24 In a shelter
population, a prevalence of CHD of 0.13% in 76,301 mixed-breed
dogs has been reported.25 The most common cardiac malformations

in dogs have been largely unchanged over time.2-4,23-28 Patent
ductus arteriosus (PDA), subaortic stenosis (SAS), and pulmonic
stenosis (PS) have topped the list of most surveys (Table 231.2).29
The shifting popularity of some dog breeds over time certainly
influences the regional prevalence of a particular defect.
Surveys of CHD in cats30-36 have indicated a prevalence of 0.020.1% of hospital admissions and 1.95-2.9% (adults)32-34 or 3.5%
(kittens)31 of necropsies. A study of 57,025 mixed-breed cats from a
shelter population reported an overall prevalence of 0.14%.25
Proportions of specific cardiac malformations vary across surveys,
which might represent sampling methods or true geographical
differences.37 The most commonly diagnosed feline congenital heart
defects are listed in Table 231.3. Some surveys have shown a male
predilection. In a retrospective of mixed-breed shelter cats,25
ventricular septal defect (VSD) (21%) and SAS or valvular AS (17%)
were the most common feline CHD diagnoses. Obstructions across
the span of the right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) also were
relatively common in this population.

CLASSIFICATION
While several schemes have been devised to classify CHD, the
standard in human pediatrics today is for a sequential segmental
analysis that models the heart as three major segments: atria,
ventricles, and great arteries. The relationships between these
segments—atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial—are also critical to
the scheme. In segmental analysis, the atria and ventricles are not
defined by their venous, arterial, or other connections, but by their
morphology. The position (situs) of each atrium is also relevant to
the classification system. This approach is especially appealing for
complex CHD.38,39 An example of this scheme applied to cats has
been published.37
Older and simpler organizational schemes are still relevant to
veterinary medicine, and these include classifying lesions as
anomalies of the cardiac valves; obstructions to ventricular outflow;

and defects allowing left-to-right, right-to-left, or bidirectional
shunting. Other types of malformations can involve the cardiac
position or situs (as with cordis ectopia and situs inversus)37; defects
or cysts affecting the pericardium (ch. 235) and a number of
vascular anomalies involving or connecting to the heart (ch. 239).

CLINICAL APPROACH
While assembling the history (ch. 2), it is important to note the
species and breed, as many congenital diseases have a suspected or
proven genetic basis, and most canine cardiac malformations show
breed predilections (Table 231.1). Whenever possible, the health
records of the sire, dam, and any siblings should be reviewed. The
clinical diagnosis of CHD is usually stimulated not by clinical signs
but by the identification of a cardiac murmur during a routine
examination or health clinic. Most young animals with CHD are not
manifesting overt clinical signs when first examined. Even those
dogs and cats with hemodynamically severe regurgitant, obstructive,
or shunting defects seem completely normal to many owners,
especially during the first 6-12 months of life. The clinician should
not necessarily conclude from an unremarkable history that the
underlying defect is mild. A useful rule-of-thumb is that when a dog
or cat with CHD does exhibit clinical signs of heart disease, the
patient is at high risk of death unless some therapy can be instituted
relatively soon.
There are no specific historical features or clinical signs of CHD.
When respiratory signs such as tachypnea are attributed to heart
disease, the possibility of underlying CHD should at least be
entertained, especially in younger animals. The author has evaluated
many patients in which clinical signs of CHD manifested during
middle age or even later in life. Sometimes an arrhythmia, such as
ventricular tachycardia or atrial fibrillation (ch. 230), will
supervene and incite syncope (ch. 40) or CHF (ch. 229). Clinical
signs of significant CHD can include exercise intolerance, exertional
collapse or syncope, sudden cardiac death, or clinical signs of CHF.
The occasional cat is presented for arterial thromboembolism (ch.

238), especially when there is left atrial (LA) dilatation secondary to
obstruction of the mitral valve inlet.40
