PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
A cardiac murmur is a hallmark feature of CHD (ch. 38); however,
many heart murmurs are missed in clinical practice. Intractability,
panting and purring, rapid heart rates, cardiac rotation, and closelyspaced auscultatory areas typical of puppies and cats pose challenges
to auscultation. Additionally, a failure to auscult over the left,
craniodorsal cardiac base (for PDA) and over the tricuspid valve area
(for tricuspid regurgitation) are common examination errors. Soft
murmurs are common in puppies and in kittens, and in most
instances are benign (functional) in origin.17,19,41-43 Unfortunately,
there are no specific auscultatory findings distinguishing a functional
murmur from that associated with mild CHD. The systolic murmur
that is soft, brief, and musical or vibratory is more likely to represent
a functional (innocent) murmur, but these characteristics are not
absolute. Even murmurs that come and go can be associated with
malformations, as with mitral valve dysplasia (MVD) with dynamic
left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. Especially
problematic is the diagnosis of trivial-to-mild SAS and AS in dogs,
especially in breeds prone to those diseases. There are simply no gold
standards for the diagnosis of clinically insignificant, but potentially
heritable conditions (see below). In contrast, a moderate to loud
systolic murmur or a murmur with a palpable thrill will be indicative
of CHD in a young animal. These should be promptly investigated by
Doppler echocardiography, remembering that the intensity of a
murmur can but might not correlate with the severity of the lesion.
Most healthy puppies and kittens with faint or soft murmurs—
especially those not intended for breeding—can reasonably be
followed with repeated physical examination during the vaccine
sequence. Physiologic reasons for murmurs, such as fever, infections,
and anemia,44 should be excluded. Many functional murmurs fade
during the first 4 months of life, but those murmurs that increase in
intensity or duration, especially in larger-breed dogs prone to SAS or
TVD, should be further evaluated with echocardiography (ch. 97). A
client should probably be offered echocardiography for their pet
when a soft murmur persists. Early detection of CHD allows
definitive treatment when applicable. Accepting that most people
quickly develop a bond with their pets, the early detection of CHD is

valuable to that pet owner who is willing to accept a healthy
replacement for one affected by a cardiac malformation.
Murmur intensity and duration do correlate with the severity of
some lesions, especially with SAS and PS.45 Conversely, a murmur
can be inconspicuous in some cases of serious CHD. In theory, a
large VSD might produce only a soft murmur due to equilibration of
ventricular pressures, but practically, most cases have at least a
moderately loud murmur unless there is concurrent pulmonary
hypertension. In the setting of severe pulmonary hypertension, as
with reversed PDA, murmurs can be completely absent and only a
tympanic or split second heart sound identified in some cases.
Secondary erythrocytosis in right-to-left shunting also reduces the
likelihood of turbulence associated with murmurs. The murmur
associated with severe atrioventricular (AV) valve dysplasia can be
faint, especially in the setting of pure AV valve stenosis.
Ancillary physical examination findings are sometimes useful in
the differential diagnosis and clinical assessment. Palpation for a
ventricular heave (a prominent apical impulse indicating ventricular
enlargement) or a precordial thrill (indicating the palpable
expression of turbulent blood flow over the point of maximal
intensity of a loud cardiac murmur) can be instructive regarding the
underlying lesion. Arterial and venous pulses can also offer insight
about the underlying defect (ch. 39); however, the rapid heart rates
and small sizes of many patients diminish the sensitivity and
specificity of physical diagnosis, especially for inexperienced
examiners. A prominent jugular venous pulse or jugular venous
distension (

Videos 229.1, 237.3) indicates an abnormality of the

right side of the heart, as can occur with TVD or PS.
The finding of cyanosis (ch. 27) in a young animal, especially in
the absence of dyspnea or overt pulmonary disease, should strongly
signal consideration for “cyanotic heart disease.” The term “cyanotic
congenital heart disease” is used for categorizing those congenital
defects causing admixture of venous and arterial blood, such as
tetralogy of Fallot (ToF). Right-to-left shunting refers to situations
wherein desaturated blood flows into the systemic arteries allowing
admixture of desaturated and oxygenated blood, leading to
hypoxemia. This can occur as a result of defects such as transposition

of the great vessels or a combination of a communicating defect
connecting the 2 sides of the circulation and some mechanism
elevating pressures on the right side as with ToF. Reversed (i.e.,
right-to-left) shunting has been observed with PDA,
aorticopulmonary window, VSD, ASD, and PS or TVD with patent
foramen ovale (PFO). Differential cyanosis is typical of reversed
PDA.

PHYSIOLOGY OF RIGHT-TO-LEFT
SHUNTING
The term Eisenmenger’s syndrome (Eisenmenger’s physiology) is
invoked to describe those circumstances wherein increased
pulmonary vascular resistance (pulmonary hypertension; ch. 218)
causes reversal of a left-to-right shunt and causes cyanotic heart
disease.46-48 The factors underlying the development of
Eisenmenger’s syndrome are most likely related to shear stresses
caused by the high flow rates in the pulmonary vasculature and
proliferative changes within the vessel wall.46,48-51 Eisenmenger’s
syndrome usually develops rapidly in affected dogs and almost
always before 6 months of age. Development of pulmonary vascular
disease in cats can be more gradual. Pulmonary arterial intimal
thickening, medial hypertrophy, and plexiform lesions of dogs and
cats with Eisenmenger’s physiology are similar to those of humans.52
In some cases, a component of increased pulmonary vascular
resistance is related to arterial vasoconstriction. These patients can
respond clinically to phosphodiesterase V inhibitors such as
sildenafil that function as pulmonary vasodilators (ch. 218),
whereas plexiform lesions are generally considered irreversible.
Surgical closure of the shunt usually is contraindicated because it
would force the right ventricle (RV) to work against a tremendous
pulmonary resistance, resulting in outcomes that can include RV
failure, circulatory collapse, and death.
Systemic responses to arterial hypoxemia include an increase in
red blood cell mass in an attempt to improve systemic oxygen
delivery. Renal hypoxia incites erythropoietin release and induces
secondary erythrocytosis (chs. 57, 173). As packed cell volume

(PCV) increases, the high viscosity of the blood predisposes patients
to thrombosis and microvascular complications.46,49 This
hyperviscosity syndrome, which typically occurs once the PCV
exceeds 68%, is the primary cause of morbidity and mortality in
affected animals rather than CHF, which is rare with Eisenmenger’s
syndrome. Clinical manifestations include cyanosis that is usually
unaccompanied by dyspnea and is not oxygen-responsive, weakness,
hemostatic deficiencies, renal dysfunction, metabolic acidosis, iron
deficiency, cerebrovascular events, syncope, and seizures.53-56
The direction of blood flow across shunting lesions depends on the
relative resistances of the systemic and pulmonary circulations.
Exercise promotes systemic arteriolar vasodilation and decreases
systemic resistance, thereby increasing the magnitude of right-to-left
shunting and prompting potentially severe exercise intolerance. In
cases of RV hypertrophy and VSD, tachycardia or elevated
sympathetic tone can increase the magnitude of right-to-left
shunting by exacerbation of dynamic infundibular obstruction and
increased resistance to RV ejection.57 Nonspecific beta-adrenergic
blocking drugs are sometimes used to blunt or prevent this
phenomenon, particularly in patients with ToF.55,58 Beta-blockers
also tend to limit exercise intensity, offering another explanation for
their efficacy in some patients. Anemia, absolute or relative, reduces
the ratio of systemic to pulmonary resistance when pulmonary
resistance is fixed.54 By this mechanism, overzealous phlebotomy
can increase the severity of arterial hypoxemia as it decreases the
oxygen carrying capacity of blood.
Right-to-left shunting leads to compensatory increases in nutritive
systemic blood flow to the lung via the bronchial arteries. These
systemic collateral vessels are easily recognized on angiograms.
Paradoxical embolization can occur with right-to-left shunting,
because venous blood clots “paradoxically” cause arterial
embolization instead of being trapped in the pulmonary vasculature.
This risk warrants particular vigilance around intravenous catheters
in patients with Eisenmenger’s syndrome.

DIAGNOSTIC STUDIES

The diagnostic workup in the patient with suspected CHD centers
today on echocardiography with Doppler studies (ch. 97).
Additional examinations including radiographs, electrocardiograms
(ECGs), and clinical laboratory tests can be contributory, but rarely
definitive, in terms of a diagnosis. Advanced imaging such as
computed tomography (CT) with contrast (CT angiography) or
magnetic resonance angiography is most useful for the diagnosis of
complex CHD or vascular anomalies. Cardiac catheterization with
angiography30,59-63 (Figure 231.1) is still a gold-standard method
for diagnosis. Its use in veterinary patients with CHD now centers
mainly around catheter-delivered therapies (ch. 115).

FIGURE 231.1 Intracardiac pressure tracing from
a 1-year-old mixed-breed dog obtained during
catheterization of the right heart and pulmonary
artery (PA). The PA pressures are normal. There is a
systolic pressure gradient between the right ventricle
(RV, 100 mm Hg) and PA (25 mm Hg) of 75 mm Hg,
indicating the presence of an obstruction to RV
outflow (in this case, valvular pulmonic stenosis
[PS]). There is also a small diastolic pressure
gradient between the PA and RV, which is caused by
the diastolic closure of the pulmonic valve, and is a
normal finding. The electrocardiogram displays a
deep S wave, which is often found in animals with PS
and secondary RV hypertrophy.

Thoracic Radiographs
Thoracic radiographs should be obtained in all cases with respiratory
signs. In addition to showing changes indicating CHF, radiographs

can also help stage severity of disease, especially in volume-overload
states caused by AV valve malformation or left-to-right shunts.64-67
Key features include identification of specific chamber enlargements,
dilation of the great vessels, and pulmonary circulation. However,
concentric ventricular hypertrophy will be underestimated by
radiography, and might only be recognized by apex elevation for the
RV or mild cardiac elongation for the left ventricle (LV). Dilation of
the main pulmonary artery is suggestive of PS, left-to-right shunt, or
pulmonary hypertension. Dilation of the aorta is observed with SAS,
aortopathies,68 and PDA. Increased pulmonary vascularity is
compatible with a significant left-to-right shunt, whereas scant
vascular markings are often found with right-to-left shunts or with
pulmonary hypertension.
In the absence of a cardiac arrhythmia, the value of the multiplelead ECG (ch. 96) recording is lower in the era of Doppler
echocardiography. A normal ECG does not exclude a diagnosis of
CHD. Nevertheless, the ECG can often identify evidence of moderate
to severe atrial or ventricular enlargement or conduction
disturbances that might be suggestive of one or more specific
disorders.69,70 As examples, increased R wave voltages in caudal and
left precordial leads are typical of PDA, a right axis deviation is
common with moderate to severe PS, and splintered QRS complexes
are reported with TVD.71 The frequent finding of a cranial frontal
mean electrical axis often limits the value of the standard limb leads
in cats. Importantly, the principal indication for an ECG in CHD is
the identification of arrhythmias or evidence of myocardial ischemia
that might indicate a more advanced disease state. An ambulatory
(Holter) ECG can be useful to detect exercise-induced arrhythmias or
ischemia that might prompt treatment (ch. 96). It should be noted
that some heart rhythm disorders should be considered a form of
CHD, notably accessory pathways associated with ventricular preexcitation and re-entrant supraventricular tachycardias (ch. 230).
Aside from a PCV, routine laboratory tests are of limited utility
except in cases complicated by CHF, arterial thromboembolism, or
other comorbidities. Hypoxemia can be verified by pulse oximetry or
arterial blood gas analysis, but these tests are rarely needed.

Echocardiography
Echocardiography with Doppler studies has largely supplanted
cardiac catheterization and angiography for the diagnosis and
assessment of most congenital heart lesions.72,73 This diagnostic
modality is described in detail in ch. 97. Saline contrast
echocardiography is indicated for identifying, or ruling out, right-toleft shunting.
The major outcomes of the echocardiographic study in CHD can be
summarized as follows: 1) identifying morphologic lesions such as
septal defects, PDA, valvular malformations, and outflow tract
obstructions using 2D and 3D imaging; 2) characterizing secondary
responses such as dilation of cardiac chambers and great vessels and
identifying myocardial hypertrophy using 2D, 3D, and M-mode
studies; 3) delineating abnormal blood flow such as shunts and
valvular dysfunction using color- and spectral-Doppler methods; 4)
quantifying systolic and diastolic ventricular function using multiple
modalities; and 5) assessing pressures, flow, and resistances using
mostly Doppler methods. These detailed evaluations generally
require an examiner with specialty training because many
evaluations have to be modified during the examination based on
contemporary findings. Transesophageal echocardiography is also
highly relevant to CHD, not only for the diagnosis of some lesions,
but also for guidance during interventional catheterization
procedures (ch. 115).74

PATENT DUCTUS ARTERIOSUS
The ductus arteriosus develops from the embryonic left sixth aortic
arch. In utero, this vital structure shunts transplacentallyoxygenated blood from the pulmonary artery through the descending
aorta, thereby diverting the majority of the RV output away from the
nonfunctional fetal lungs. Following parturition and the onset of
breathing, pulmonary vascular resistance falls, flow in the ductus
reverses to become left-to-right, and the resulting rise in arterial
oxygen tension inhibits local prostaglandin release. These processes
lead to constriction of vascular smooth muscle in the wall of the
ductus arteriosus, causing its functional closure. While the ductus

arteriosus may be probe-patent in puppies <4 days of age, it is
usually closed securely by 7-10 days after birth.75,76 Persistence of an
open ductus arteriosus beyond the early neonatal period is called
PDA and is the first or second most commonly diagnosed congenital
cardiac defect in dogs, depending on the survey (Table 231.2). Cats
are also affected (Table 231.3) but much less commonly than
dogs.77,78

PATHOGENESIS
The normal fetal ductal wall contains loosely branching,
circumferential smooth muscle fibers throughout its length, whereas
in prenatal puppies bred to have a high probability of PDA, varying
portions of the ductal wall are comprised of elastic fibers only.79,80
The increased prevalence of PDA in specific breeds (Table 231.1)
indicates that genetic factors are likely involved in its pathogenesis. A
mixed-breed, Poodle line of dogs with hereditary PDA has been
extensively investigated, and a polygenic pattern of inheritance has
been suggested.81 Increasing genetic liability to PDA results in
“extension of the noncontractile wall structure of the aorta to an
increasing segment of the ductus arteriosus, progressively impairing
its capacity to undergo physiologic closure.”2 In humans,
abnormalities in the genes that interfere with the remodeling of
vascular smooth muscle cells of the ductal media, the putative cause
of PDA, have been identified.82 It is likely that similar genetic defects
might be operational in the vascular smooth muscle of dogs with
PDA.

FIGURE 231.2 Macroscopic anatomy of patent
ductus arteriosus (PDA). A, The left-sided view of
the heart from a 9-week-old Australian Shepherd
with a left-to-right PDA, demonstrating the anatomic
location of the ductus (D) between the descending
aorta (Ao) and main pulmonary artery (PA). The left
auricle (LAu) is enlarged. B, Cut-away view of a left-

to-right PDA in a dog. The ductus is funnel shaped,
tapering toward the PA end. C, The left-sided view of
the heart from a dog with a right-to-left shunting
PDA. Note the enlargement of the right ventricle
(RV) and right auricle (RAu). The pulmonary artery
(PA) is enlarged. D, Cut-away view of a right-to-left
shunting PDA in a dog. Note the cylindrical nature of
the ductus (D) and the fact that the anatomic
location of the ductus is distal to the aortic branches
that supply the cranial portion of the body.
In its mildest, clinically silent form, the ductus closes completely at
the pulmonary arterial end and a blind, funnel-shaped pocket in the
ventral aspect of the aorta, known as a ductus diverticulum,
develops. This type of PDA, characterized by incomplete ductal
closure (the forme fruste of the disease) can only be diagnosed by
angiography or necropsy. It indicates that the dog carries a genetic
liability for this defect.2,81 Echocardiographic diagnosis of a ductus
diverticulum has not been reported in dogs or other animals.
Increasing genetic liability results in a tapering, funnel-shaped
ductus arteriosus that remains patent after the early postnatal period
and allows blood to flow from the aorta to the pulmonary artery,
where intravascular pressures are lower (Figure 231.2, A and
B).This is the most common form of PDA observed in dogs.83,84 The
most severe, but relatively uncommon, form is the cylindrical,
nontapering ductus with persistent postnatal pulmonary
hypertension (Eisenmenger syndrome) and bidirectional or right-toleft shunting (Figure 231.2, C and D). PDA may also be identified
in animals with complex forms of CHD.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
The direction of blood flow through a PDA is determined by the
relative resistances of the pulmonary and systemic vascular beds,
and in the vast majority of cases it proceeds from left to right (i.e.,
from the aorta to the pulmonary artery). The extent of shunting is
determined by the relative pressure gradient between the systemic
and pulmonary circulation, as well as the level of resistance within

the PDA. Most often, the flow-limiting region is at the level of the
pulmonary ostium, where the ductus is at its narrowest (

Video

231.1). Flow through the PDA results in pulmonary overcirculation as
blood is shunted from the aorta to the pulmonary artery. Higher LV
stroke volume resulting from an increase in pulmonary venous
return and end-diastolic volume associated with eccentric
hypertrophy contribute to a rise in systolic aortic pressure. In
diastole, rapid run-off of blood from the aorta to the lower-pressure
pulmonary artery via the PDA causes a reduction in aortic diastolic
pressures. The resultant pressure difference between systolic and
diastolic blood pressures creates the hyperkinetic (“waterhammer”)
arterial pulse detected in dogs with substantial shunting through
their PDA. Since blood shunts continuously across the PDA during
both systole and diastole, a continuous murmur arises, and is
typically loudest near the time of the second heart sound. All
vascular structures involved in the transport of the shunted blood
enlarge to accommodate the extra volume flow, with dilation of the
proximal aorta, main pulmonary artery, and pulmonary vasculature.
Dilation of the LA and eccentric hypertrophy of the LV develop in
proportion to the volume of flow across the shunt (

Video 231.2).

This mechanism permits compensation of the volume overloaded
state for a variable period of time; if the shunt is large, however,
myocardial failure (cardiomyopathy of volume overload) develops
together with progressive elevation of LV end-diastolic pressure and
eventually, overt pulmonary edema. Because the left-to-right shunt
occurs at the level of the great vessels, the RV and right atrium (RA)
are not directly exposed to the shunted blood, and these structures
remain normal unless pulmonary hypertension develops.

FIGURE 231.3 Thoracic radiographs from a dog
with a left-to-right shunting patent ductus
arteriosus. A, Lateral projection shows left atrial
enlargement and enlarged cranial pulmonary
arteries (a) and veins (v). B, Dorsoventral projection
shows moderate cardiomegaly, a characteristic bulge
in the descending aorta and dilation of the main
pulmonary artery. The pulmonary arteries (a) and
veins (v) are prominent.
In a small percentage of canine cases, the lumen of the PDA
remains wide without tapering at the pulmonary ostium. The
absence of a restrictive ductal orifice allows aortic pressures to be
transmitted to the pulmonary circulation unimpeded, thus
preventing the normal postnatal decline in pulmonary vascular
resistance. In this circumstance, the aortic and pulmonary arterial
pressures equilibrate, the RV remains concentrically hypertrophied
after birth, and reversal of flow through the shunt can develop.
Pulmonary hypertension causing balanced or reversed (right-to-left)
shunting has developed within the first few weeks of life,81 as well as
in adulthood in conjunction with necrotizing pulmonary arteritis.52
Most dogs with reversed PDA flow exhibit diminished pulmonary
blood flow and marked concentric hypertrophy of the RV. Residual
LV enlargement can be evident on thoracic radiographs and by

echocardiography with adult-onset reversal of flow direction, and RV
hypertrophy is less pronounced than in dogs that reverse the
direction of shunting at an early age. The pathogenesis of pulmonary
hypertension is debated; histologic changes in small pulmonary
arteries include hypertrophy of the media, thickening of the intima
and reduction of lumen dimensions, and development of plexiform
lesions of the vessel wall.51,52,85 Most of these changes are
considered to be irreversible, precluding surgical correction of the
reversed PDA, except possibly in rare cases where pulmonary
hypertension is recent in onset and pulmonary arterial pressures
remain subsystemic, sometimes observed in cats with PDA and less
often in dogs.86

CLINICAL FINDINGS
PDA is the only CHD with a documented sex predisposition
(2.49/1000 in females versus 1.45/1000 in males).1 Many breed
predilections for PDA have been reported (Table 231.1). Severely
affected pups and kittens might develop stunting, poor body
condition, or tachypnea from left-sided CHF, and it is likely that
some affected animals die from heart failure prior to the first
veterinary examination. Most puppies are reported to have no
clinical signs and show normal physical development at the time of
diagnosis.

Left-to-Right Shunting PDA
A thorough physical examination usually suffices to suggest the
initial diagnosis. Often, the arterial pulses are hyperkinetic (ch. 39).
Mucous membranes are pink, or pale grey/cyanotic in patients with
severe dyspnea and hypoxemia due to severe left-sided CHF. The
precordial impulse is often exaggerated and covers a larger area
across the thoracic wall than normal because of LV enlargement. A
thrill is commonly palpated craniodorsally from the precordial
impulse, in the left axillary region. A classic continuous murmur (ch.
38) is best heard in the same location, over the craniodorsal left
heart base. It may radiate cranially to the thoracic inlet and to the

right base, where it is almost always softer.81,87,88 Frequently, only a
systolic murmur is audible over the mitral area, as a result of
radiation of the loudest portion of the continuous murmur from the
heart base, secondary mitral regurgitation, or both. In cats with PDA,
the continuous murmur may be heard best somewhat more
caudoventrally than in affected dogs and the murmur is often
confused with a pansystolic murmur (ch. 38), especially if
pulmonary hypertension is developing, making the diastolic
component softer. Differential diagnoses for a continuous heart
murmur in this location include aortopulmonary shunts, coronary
arteriovenous fistula, rupture of sinus of Valsalva aneurysm,
aorticopulmonary window, anomalous left coronary artery and other
arteriovenous shunts, although these are comparatively rare given
the high prevalence of PDA.89-92
Thoracic radiographs indicate left heart enlargement and
pulmonary overcirculation in proportion to the magnitude of the leftto-right shunt (Figure 231.3). On the dorsoventral projection, the
aortic arch, left auricle, and main pulmonary artery may be
abnormally prominent. The most specific radiographic finding is the
appearance of an aortic bulge (“ductus bump”), which is caused by
abrupt narrowing of the descending aorta just caudal to the origin of
the ductus, aneurysmal dilatation of the aorta, and/or the ductus
itself (Figure 231.3). Moderate to severe LV enlargement
sometimes causes the cardiac apex to shift to the right (common in
cats). Pulmonary edema is present following the onset of CHF.

FIGURE 231.4 Echocardiography of a dog with
left-to-right patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). A, The
right long-axis view reveals eccentric hypertrophy
(dilation) of the left ventricle (LV) and left atrium
(LA). The right ventricle (RV) and right atrium (RA)
are normal. B, View of the ductus (D) imaged from
the left heart base. The typical left-to-right ductus is
widest at the aortic (Ao, bottom right corner) end
and tapers near the main pulmonary artery (PA). C,
Color-flow Doppler imaging applied to the
echocardiographic view in B, demonstrating
turbulent left-to-right blood flow through the ductus.
D, Continuous wave Doppler tracing of the PDA jet
obtained from the left heart base demonstrating
continuous flow and a peak velocity of ∼6.0 m/s.
When the rhythm is normal, the ECG contributes little to the
overall diagnosis. Indications of LV enlargement (increased R-wave
voltages in leads II, III, aVF and in the left precordial leads, V2 and
V4) are almost always found and can be marked; widened P waves
suggesting left atrial enlargement (P mitrale) also are possible (ch.

96). An arrhythmia is the principal indication for recording an ECG,
and in dogs with long-standing PDA, atrial fibrillation, as well as
supraventricular and ventricular premature complexes, may develop
(ch. 230).
Although strongly suspected from signalment, physical
examination, and thoracic radiographs, the diagnosis of PDA can be
confirmed by a complete Doppler echocardiographic study.
Echocardiography also demonstrates the extent of secondary
changes, and allows other congenital heart malformations to be
identified, although concurrent malformations occur only in a
minority of cases. The ductus may be imaged and its size estimated
(for selection of an occlusion device; ch. 115) from the left cranial
parasternal view (Figure 231.4, B; Video 231.1

).93 Doppler

interrogation of the main pulmonary artery demonstrates highvelocity, continuous ductal flow directed towards the pulmonic valve
(Figure 231.4, C; Video 231.1

). In the typical case, the peak

velocity of this jet is at least 4.5 to 5.0 m/s and occurs at end-systole
(Figure 231.4, D). 2D and M-mode echocardiography demonstrate
secondary changes (

Video 231.2): eccentric LV hypertrophy and

dilatation of the LA, ascending aorta, and pulmonary artery (Figure
231.4), mildly increased peak LVOT velocity (1.8-2.3 m/s, but
sometimes higher) and mild secondary mitral, aortic, and pulmonic
valve insufficiency, although in some dogs moderate to severe mitral
regurgitation might be identified. Evidence of reduced LV systolic
function, such as reduced LV fractional shortening, increased Epoint to septal separation, and/or increased LV end-systolic volume,
is possible in advanced cases. Owing to increased ejection volume
and flow velocity across the LVOT with PDA, the diagnosis of
concurrent mild SAS can be difficult to achieve, and in the setting of
overt SAS, its severity might not be evident until the ductus is closed.
Transesophageal echocardiographic techniques can provide
enhanced visualization of the ductal anatomy, typically during
interventional closure of the PDA (ch. 115).74,94 Cardiac
catheterization and angiocardiography are reserved for such
interventional procedures as well; angiography is not required to

confirm a diagnosis of PDA (Video 231.3

) and is not advised

unless the Doppler echocardiographic evaluation is ambiguous or
additional congenital malformations are suspected.

Right-to-Left Shunting PDA (PDA With Pulmonary
Hypertension)
Pulmonary hypertension causing right-to-left shunting through a
PDA defines the clinical syndrome commonly referred to as a
“reversed PDA.”51,53,81,85,95-99 Right-to-left shunting is observed in
a very small minority of dogs with PDA, but the prevalence of this
phenomenon is probably underestimated and may be increased in
dogs living at altitudes >1500 meters (>5000 feet) above sea level.
Clinical signs are usually evident during the first year of life, but
some animals are not diagnosed until >3 years of age. Reported signs
include exertional fatigue, exertional and symmetrical hind limb
weakness (e.g., inappropriate sitting mid-walk), tachypnea/dyspnea,
and, more rarely, seizures. Clinical examination findings are very
different from those of the more common left-to-right PDA. Rightto-left flow through a wide PDA produces little to no turbulence and
physical examination reveals either no murmur or only a soft,
systolic murmur at the left base. The most common auscultatory
finding is an accentuated and split second heart sound. Differential
cyanosis (cyanosis of the caudal mucous membranes with pink
cranial membranes) may be observed (ch. 27), but it is often
transient and recognition may require examination after exercise.
Differential cyanosis is caused by the location of the ductus
arteriosus, which shunts right-to-left from the pulmonary artery into
the descending aorta (Figure 231.2, C and D) but spares the
proximal branches of the aorta, which provide arterial blood with a
normal oxygen content to the cranial portion of the body. Perfusion
of the kidneys with hypoxemic blood triggers elaboration of
erythropoietin and secondary erythrocytosis and hyperviscosity as
the PCV gradually increases to ≥65% (chs. 57, 173).53 Erythrocytosis
may occur during the first year of life, but often does not become
severe until 18-24 months of age. The finding of an increased PCV in
a dog with intermittent, symmetrical, exertional hindlimb weakness

should always prompt the consideration of right-to-left PDA, even
when cardiac auscultation is unremarkable.
The ECG of dogs with a reversed PDA virtually always reveals
evidence of RV hypertrophy (right axis deviation, increased S wave
amplitude in leads I, II, III, and the left precordial leads, V2 and V4;
ch. 96). Thoracic radiographs typically indicate right heart
enlargement, dilatation of the main pulmonary artery, a visible
“ductus bump” and variable appearance of the lobar and peripheral
arteries. Echocardiography demonstrates RV concentric hypertrophy
and a dilated main pulmonary artery (Figure 231.5). In some cases,
a wide and cylindrical ductus may be imaged (Figure 231.5).
Pulmonary hypertension can be verified in some cases by Doppler
interrogation of tricuspid or pulmonic insufficiency jets (Figure
231.5; ch. 218). Contrast echocardiography, nuclear scintigraphy,
oximetry, or angiography can be used to demonstrate the presence of
right-to-left shunting should Doppler interrogation prove
inadequate. Contrast echocardiography is performed by injecting airagitated saline (

Video 97.5) into a cephalic or saphenous vein,

thereby opacifying the right heart, pulmonary artery, and the
descending aorta (best observed by imaging of the abdominal aorta
dorsal to the bladder;

Video 231.4). Angiography is rarely

necessary; when performed, it can demonstrate RV hypertrophy, a
wide PDA, and tortuous pulmonary arteries with RV contrast
injections and an often extensive bronchoesophageal collateral
circulation with aortic or LV injections.

NATURAL HISTORY AND PROGNOSIS
Puppies and kittens with PDA often appear clinically unaffected by
their defect at the time of diagnosis. However, if left uncorrected,
left-to-right PDA typically leads to complications such as left-sided
CHF and death. Pulmonary artery dissection is a potential
complication of uncorrected PDA in the dog, and affected dogs are
more likely to present at an older age.100 Not correcting left-to-right
PDA has a markedly negative effect on survival in dogs (hazard ratio
= 16.9): dogs that undergo occlusion or surgical ligation of left-to-

right PDA die at a median age of 12 years, compared to 2 years of age
for untreated dogs.101 A study of untreated PDA in 14 dogs identified
that 64% died within a year of examination.102 Cats with PDA may
develop significant pulmonary hypertension from left-to-right
shunting more frequently than dogs do.77,99,103-105 Importantly,
pulmonary hypertension due to PDA can develop more slowly and
might be arrested with prompt intervention.104,105 When persistent
pulmonary hypertension in the neonate leads to right-to-left
shunting, clinical signs result from hypoxemia, erythrocytosis,
hyperviscosity, and cardiac arrhythmias. CHF almost never develops
with right-to-left shunting (in dogs and cats) but sudden death and
complications from hyperviscosity are common. A small minority of
dogs and cats will have small PDAs and can survive to maturity or
even beyond 10 years of age.106-108

CLINICAL MANAGEMENT
Correction of uncomplicated left-to-right PDA is considered to be
curative. It results in an immediate decrease in LV volume overload,
gradual reversal of LV eccentric hypertrophy over time,109 and an
excellent prognosis (see above).101 Correction may not be warranted
in older pets if the shunt volume is small and cardiomegaly is
minimal or absent. Generally, closure of PDA is an elective procedure
that should be scheduled immediately when the diagnosis is made,
and at the earliest age possible to prevent irreversible changes and
deterioration of the patient’s condition. If the patient presents in
CHF with LV myocardial failure, the patient should be stabilized for
a short period of time with medical therapy for CHF (ch. 229)
before considering anesthesia. In such cases, treatment for CHF is
often continued for several months following closure of the ductus.
In some cases with atrial fibrillation, consideration can be given to
electrocardioversion at the time of ductal closure or later; however,
chronic medical management (ch. 230) might be needed. Unlike in
human neonates, treatment with prostaglandin inhibitors is not
effective in dogs and cats, most likely because of the paucity of
smooth muscle in the ductal wall.

Closure of left-to-right PDA with concurrent pulmonary
hypertension of varying degrees of severity has been successful in
both dogs86 and cats.104,105 Some such dogs have shown clinical
benefit to pretreatment with sildenafil (1-3 mg/kg PO q8-12h), and
this should be tried for at least 3-4 weeks to gauge clinical response.
The PDA can be surgically ligated via thoracotomy or closed by
minimally-invasive transcatheter techniques using an occluding
device (ch. 115;

Video 115.7). Determining which of the 2

approaches is appropriate depends on ductal morphology (tubular
PDA favors ligation), patient size (smaller patient favors ligation),
operator experience, and owner preference. After ductal closure most
dogs experience an uneventful recovery. Although overall cardiac
size decreases after closure, in many dogs some left-sided heart
enlargement persists.110-114 Postoperative Doppler examination may
indicate a small residual shunt,88,115 although the continuous
murmur is usually absent and the clinical outcomes are good. A soft
left apical systolic murmur, usually from residual secondary mitral
regurgitation, is often heard for a variable period after ductus
ligation.87
Animals with right-to-left PDA have irreversible obstructive
pulmonary vascular disease. Morbidity and mortality are usually the
result of complications related to erythrocytosis and chronic
hypoxemia rather than CHF. Treatment of these patients consists of
exercise restriction, avoidance of stress, prevention of dehydration,
and maintenance of the PCV between 58% and 65% by periodic
phlebotomy.80 Treatment with sildenafil can also improve clinical
signs, and anecdotally, pentoxifylline may reduce clinical signs.116,117
Long-term management by these techniques is possible.118
Phlebotomy should be performed cautiously to avoid weakness or
collapse, and intravascular volume may be supported during
phlebotomy by administration of crystalloid solutions. Attempts to
reduce the red cell volume of reversed PDA cases using drug therapy
(e.g., hydroxyurea) have been reported and may be an alternative to
repeated phlebotomy.119 Activity restriction is usually advised, as
exercise-induced systemic vasodilation increases the degree of right-

to-left shunting and predisposes to hind limb paresis or collapse and
cyanosis. Closure of reversed PDA is strongly contraindicated, as it
invariably leads to late operative or early postoperative acute right
heart failure and death.

ATRIAL AND VENTRICULAR SEPTAL
DEFECTS
During cardiac embryonic development, the atria and ventricles
begin as a common chamber. The heart is subsequently partitioned
into the normal postnatal 4-chambered heart by the growth of
cardiac septa and AV valves. The atria are partitioned by a wall
formed mainly from 2 septa: the septum primum, which forms first,
and the septum secundum, which develops to the right of the septum
primum. The foramen ovale, a slit-like passageway between these
septa, permits right-to-left atrial shunting in the fetus, but
functionally and anatomically closes in the neonate once the lungs
expand and rising LA pressures press the septum primum into
apposition with the septum secundum. The major portion of the
ventricular septum forms by inward growth from the ventricular
walls. The area of AV confluence, including the upper ventricular
septum, lower atrial septum, and AV valves, is formed primarily by
growth and differentiation of the endocardial cushions. The AV
valves normally insert at different levels of the ventricular septum,
with the tricuspid valve connecting slightly apically to the mitral
valve. The resultant offset, defined as the AV septum, essentially

forms an atrial septum on the right and a ventricular septum on the
left.120

FIGURE 231.6 Macroscopic anatomy of
secundum-type atrial septal defect (ASD) in a dog.
View from the (A) left side and (B) right side
showing the ASD (∗) in the mid-atrial septal region
where the foramen ovale would exist.
Defects in the development of the embryonic ventricular septum,
the primum or secundum atrial septa, or the endocardial cushions,
can result in a VSD, an ASD, or both lesions, respectively, along with
malformations in the AV valves. Congenital septal defects are
common in both dogs and cats as isolated lesions or as components
of more complex lesions such as complete AV septal defects (AVSDs)
and ToF.21

PATHOGENESIS OF THE SEPTAL
DEFECTS
Except for the proven genetic basis of VSD in Keeshonden with
conotruncal malformations,10 there are no data on the cause(s) of
spontaneous septal defects in dogs or cats. ASDs are usually

classified based on the anatomic region of the malformation. Defects
at or near the foramen ovale are most common and are referred to as
ostium (or septum) secundum defects (Figure 231.6). Defects of
the lower atrial septum are called ostium primum defects and can
occur in isolation or as a component of partial or complete AVSD.
The rarely-observed sinus venosus ASD is most often found
dorsocranial to the fossa ovalis near the entrance of the cranial vena
cava121 and often involves the entry of a pulmonary vein into the RA.
Since the endocardial cushions are largely responsible for
partitioning the lowermost atrial septum, defects in the region
immediately adjacent to the AV valves (septum primum) have been
called “endocardial cushion defects”; however, this term is less
preferred today. A defect in this area can also involve anomalous
development of the AV valves. These can range from a “cleft” in the
septal leaflet of the mitral valve to a common AV septal leaflet that
bridges across the 2 sides of the heart. A complete AVSD
(endocardial cushion defect; common AV canal defect) consists of a
large defect of the lower atrial septum, an inlet VSD (apical to the
septal tricuspid valve leaflet), and a common (bridging) AV valve that
includes a cleft in the septal mitral leaflet. Partial and complete
AVSDs are more commonly detected in cats122,123 compared to
dogs124,125 and can cause left-sided or bilateral CHF. PFO is not a
true ASD inasmuch as the atrial septum forms normally, but the
walls bordering the foramen remain pushed apart. Most often a PFO
is due to conditions that increase RA pressure, although severe LA
dilation can also be a cause. A PFO usually achieves clinical
significance when it allows right-to-left shunting, as might occur
with severe PS124 or TVD.
Most VSDs are located within or adjacent to the membranous
portion of the upper ventricular septum, just below the aortic valve
and cranial to the septal tricuspid leaflet (Figure 231.7).125 These
are variously termed “membranous,” “perimembranous,”
“paramembranous” and “infracristal.” Membranous ventricular
septal aneurysm with or without a small, patent perimembranous
VSD has also been described by echocardiography in both dogs and
cats.126

The typical membranous VSD, when viewed from the LV, is
located just below the aortic valve, most often centered between the
right coronary and noncoronary cusps. On the RV side, the opening
is often described by its position relative to the supraventricular crest
(crista supraventricularis), the muscular ridge that separates the
inflow from the outflow tracts. Membranous defects are subcristal
(infracristal), whereas subarterial defects are located in a supracristal
position just below the pulmonic valve. Large membranous defects
can obliterate the crista and these are often associated with
additional defects such as ToF (Figure 231.7, B). The altered
geometry of the aortic root that accompanies many VSDs can result
in substantial aortic valve regurgitation. Defects in the muscular
ventricular septum are rare in dogs and cats and can be located
dorsally or apically. Inlet VSDs were mentioned previously under
AVSD.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Shunting across small (resistive or restrictive) defects depends
primarily on the size of the defect and the pressure difference
between the 2 chambers, while shunting across large (nonresistive)
defects depends primarily on the pressure differences between the
systemic and pulmonary vasculatures.125,127-129 In the absence of
other abnormalities, left heart pressures exceed those on the right
and the direction of shunting is left-to-right. With left-to-right
shunts, cardiac chambers in the circuit of the shunt enlarge to
accommodate the excess blood volume, and the pulmonary
vasculature becomes overcirculated. Large-volume left-to-right
shunts can eventually result in myocardial failure, elevated atrial and
ventricular filling pressures, and the development of overt CHF.
Right-to-left shunting occurs via a septal defect when PS, tricuspid
dysplasia, or pulmonary hypertension raises pressures on the right
side of the heart. The consequences of “reversed” shunting include
cyanosis from arterial hypoxemia, erythrocytosis, hyperviscosity, and
sudden death.

Atrial Septal Defect

Flow across an ASD occurs primarily during ventricular diastole. The
pressure difference across the defect is low and the direction and
magnitude of the shunt are determined mainly by the defect size and
relative diastolic resistance to inflow for each ventricle. Normally, the
RV is more compliant than the left and offers little resistance to
filling, causing blood to preferentially shunt from the LA into the RA
and RV. The result is dilation of the RA, eccentric hypertrophy of the
RV, and pulmonary overcirculation. The LA receives the shunted
blood from the pulmonary veins, but most of the increased
pulmonary venous return is shunted immediately into the RA,
resulting in minimal LA dilation. If considerable LA enlargement is
observed in an animal with an ASD, an AVSD with mitral
regurgitation should be suspected.

FIGURE 231.7 Macroscopic anatomy of
ventricular septal defect (VSD). A, Small resistive
VSD (arrow) in a young cat viewed from the left
ventricle (LV). The VSD is just below the level of the
aorta (Ao). A fine network of excessive moderator
bands/false tendons is an unrelated finding. B,
Large, nonresistive VSD in a young dog with
tetralogy of Fallot, viewed from the right ventricle
(RV). The large defect (white arrow) is located just
cranial to the tricuspid valve apparatus. The RV is
markedly thickened and a narrow subvalvular
fibrous ring of subvalvular pulmonic stenosis is
present (black arrow).
The flow across an ASD does not usually generate an audible heart
murmur because the low pressure gradient and low resultant flow
velocity across the defect do not produce appreciable turbulence.
When the shunted blood joins with blood entering from the vena
cava, the volume and velocity of flow through the right heart are
increased, resulting in a murmur of relative PS (common) or
tricuspid stenosis (uncommon). Delayed closure of the pulmonic
valve and early closure of the aortic valve can cause splitting of the

second heart sound.127,130 Since the volume overload affects the RV
and not the LV, large shunts culminate in the development of right
heart failure or pulmonary vascular injury with clinical signs related
to pulmonary hypertension and, if it is sufficiently severe, right-toleft shunting.

Ventricular Septal Defect
Flow across a VSD occurs primarily during ventricular systole. In the
absence of other cardiovascular defects, peak LV systolic pressure is
about five times that of the RV, and flow proceeds from the LV to the
RV. The magnitude of left-to-right shunting with small (resistive)
defects is mainly determined by the diameter of the defect and the
systolic pressure difference (gradient) between the ventricles. The
peak pressure difference across the defect can be estimated
noninvasively with Doppler echocardiography. A resistive defect with
normal RV (∼20-25 mm Hg) and LV (∼100-120 mm Hg) pressures is
expected to produce a peak jet velocity through the defect >4.5 m/s,
corresponding to a peak pressure gradient >80 mm Hg. This highvelocity flow creates a prominent systolic murmur. If the peak
velocity is lower than predicted, RV systolic pressure is most likely
increased, most often due to PS or pulmonary hypertension (from
high pulmonary flow, left heart failure, or increased vascular
resistance) and a lower-intensity murmur would be expected.
When a small VSD is located high in the membranous septum,
blood is ejected by the LV directly towards the RVOT and out the
main pulmonary artery; the right heart experiences only a modest
volume overload and right heart enlargement is minimal. Right heart
enlargement is more prominent when the VSD is large or is located
in the muscular portion of the interventricular septum (IVS). Large
shunts (pulmonary to systemic flow ratio >3:1) can overload the left
heart enough to increase LV diastolic pressures and cause signs of
left-sided CHF. Very large, nonresistive VSDs cause the pressures in
both ventricles to equilibrate, and the 2 ventricles behave as a
common pumping chamber; unless a stenotic pulmonic valve
protects the pulmonary circulation, the development of CHF or
pulmonary hypertension is unavoidable. With VSDs that affect aortic
valvular geometry, aortic regurgitation (AR) can occur because of

prolapse of the right aortic valve cusp into the VSD during diastole,
increasing LV wall stress and further predisposing to CHF.

CLINICAL FINDINGS
Atrial Septal Defect
Canine breed predispositions for ASD are presented in Table 231.1.
In cats with ASD, 1 study found an overrepresentation of domestic
shorthair, Persian, and Chartreux breeds.21 Clinical findings of the
typical left-to-right ASD include a soft, grade 2-3/6, systolic ejection
murmur over the left heart base and splitting of the second heart
sound.21,131 The murmur is often misinterpreted as one arising from
mild PS or as an innocent murmur. Cyanosis is absent unless there is
an additional defect such as PS or TVD,132 or the infrequent
complication of pulmonary hypertension, to cause right-to-left
shunting.21 Signs of right-sided CHF may be present in dogs or cats
with large defects.
The ECG may indicate RV enlargement (right axis shift, increased
S wave depth in leads I, II, III), and intraventricular conduction
disturbances, especially partial or complete right bundle branch
block, are also seen, especially with ostium primum defects or
AVSD.2,123 The latter can also exhibit a left-cranial axis deviation in
the frontal axis (ch. 96). Thoracic radiographs may show
enlargement of the right heart, main pulmonary artery, and
pulmonary hypervascularity proportional to the magnitude of the
shunt. 2D echocardiography permits direct imaging of ASD,21 but
false positive impressions of an ASD are common because of imaging
artifacts caused by beam orientation and the thinness of some
portions of the normal fossa ovalis. Doppler evidence of transatrial
shunting is more reliable and typically shows laminar or mildly
turbulent diastolic flow through the ASD (Figure 231.8; Video
231.5

) and increased RVOT and transpulmonic valvular

velocities. Doppler studies also can demonstrate associated problems
such as mitral regurgitation.133 One pitfall is confusing normal

venous return from the caudal vena cava for left-to-right atrial
shunting, as this flow enters along the atrial septum in the
parasternal long-axis view. Additionally, in short-axis imaging
planes, the atrial septum can be foreshortened, confusing the
location of a secundum ASD with that of a primum defect. Contrast
echocardiography is helpful to identify right-to-left shunting,
particularly when the defect is large or when PS or pulmonary
hypertension is suspected. (ch. 115).

FIGURE 231.8 Echocardiography of a secundumtype atrial septal defect (ASD) in a dog. A, The right
long-axis view shows the absence of a segment of the
atrial septum between the right atrium (RA) and left
atrium (LA). The RA and right ventricle (RV) are
moderately enlarged. B, Color-flow Doppler study
demonstrating low velocity left-to-right flow through
the ASD. LV, Left ventricle.

Ventricular Septal Defect
Canine breed predispositions for VSD are indicated in Table 231.1.
VSD is one of the most frequent congenital cardiac anomalies in
cats.36 No known breed predispositions have been reported,
although clinical experience suggests they are relatively common in
the Maine Coon cat. The clinical features of VSD depend on the
magnitude of the shunt and presence of complications or other
defects. Animals with a typical small, membranous VSD show no
clinical signs and they present with a harsh, holosystolic murmur

that is heard best over the right, ventral, mid- to cranial
precordium.125,134,135 In rare cases of subarterial VSD, the defect
opens just under the pulmonic valve, and the systolic murmur is
heard best at the left heart base. Splitting of the second heart sound (
Audio 38.2) can occur but is often unrecognized because of the
superimposition of the murmur on the second heart sound. If
distortion of the aortic root causes substantial AR, a blowing,
decrescendo diastolic murmur can be evident over the LV outflow
area. This results in a combination of systolic and diastolic murmurs
(“to-and-fro” murmur;

Audio 38.16) that can be readily confused

with a PDA. AR can also flow through the VSD into the RV to
produce a diastolic murmur best heard on the right hemithorax (
Audio 38.15). Systolic murmurs over the mitral or tricuspid valve
may also be detected if a VSD is part of a complete AVSD.
ECG findings in animals with a VSD are variable. With moderate
or large left-to-right shunts there is often evidence of LA or LV
enlargement, but RV conduction defects also can occur. Frontal
plane leads may demonstrate a subtle abnormality in early
ventricular septal activation, characterized by a Q wave that is wide
or contains high-frequency notching.136 Right-axis deviation in a dog
with VSD usually indicates RV hypertrophy due to PS or pulmonary
hypertension. Thoracic radiographs are very useful in assessing the
magnitude of left-to-right shunting VSDs. Pulmonary
hypervascularity and LA and LV enlargement are observed in
proportion to shunt magnitude (Figure 231.9).64 The main, lobar,
and peripheral pulmonary arteries are usually prominent. In animals
with small defects, thoracic radiographs may appear entirely normal.
With large defects, the RV may also enlarge. A large pulmonary
artery segment, small lobar pulmonary arteries and veins, and scant
peripheral pulmonary vasculature suggest the possibility of PS or
pulmonary hypertension and right-to-left shunting.
On echocardiography, LA and LV enlargements of variable degrees
are observed. With moderate to large VSDs, right heart enlargement
may also be present. Membranous VSD can be identified just below
the aortic valve (Figure 231.10) and adjacent to the cranioventral

edge of the septal tricuspid leaflet. The rare subarterial VSD is best
identified on the short-axis image at the level of the aorta that
includes the RV inlet and RV outlet into the pulmonary artery. Offangle views are often needed. The left apical 4-chamber image is best
for visualizing an AVSD. As a general rule, when the maximal
diameter of the VSD is <40% of the aortic root diameter, the lesion is
likely to be restrictive/resistive and often is well-tolerated as long as
there is no AR. Small aneurysms of membrane-like tissue may
occasionally be seen protruding into the RV from the margins of the
VSD.126 As for ASDs, Doppler studies of VSDs should be performed
to confirm the presence of the shunt, and color-flow Doppler is
particularly useful for identification of small lesions. For a
perimembranous defect, a jet of blood moving toward the transducer
can be observed in the long- or short-axis views from the right side
(Figure 231.10; Video 231.6

). The larger the VSD, the smaller

the pressure difference between the ventricles, and the lower the
velocity of blood flow through the VSD. Bidirectional or right-to-left
shunting is observed when RV systolic pressure reaches and exceeds
LV systolic pressure. Contrast echocardiography can be used for
assessing a patient for right-to-left shunting (

Video 97.5). The

region of the aortic valve should also be interrogated for AR.

Atrioventricular Septal Defect
A partial AVSD with a primum ASD and relatively normal AV
valvular function should behave like an isolated ASD. When an
AVSD includes significant AV valve malformation, there can be
substantial valvular regurgitation, including mitral regurgitation,
tricuspid regurgitation, and mitral regurgitation into the RA across
the ASD. The classic appearance of a complete AVSD on
echocardiography includes an ASD, inlet VSD, and a “floating,”
bridging AV valvular leaflet that serves both ventricles. Outcomes
can include clinical signs of CHF or of pulmonary hypertension.122

enlarged and there is rounding of the cranial border
of the heart on the lateral view. The pulmonary
arteries and veins are enlarged on the dorsoventral
view.

NATURAL HISTORY AND PROGNOSIS
The morbidity and mortality associated with ASDs and VSDs depend
on defect size and location, magnitude and direction of shunt flow,

and the presence of additional lesions. Spontaneous closure of small
VSDs often occurs in children, but this is seemingly an uncommon
occurrence in cats and dogs.126,137 Animals with uncomplicated and
small defects that result in only modest shunting (and often a loud
murmur) usually live a normal lifespan without ever developing
recognizable clinical signs. Larger shunts causing moderate to severe
cardiomegaly can lead to intractable CHF; in neonates, many such
cases may die before seeing a veterinarian. Moderate to severe AR,
an uncommon complication of VSD, presents a very substantial risk
of CHF and may shorten survival. When VSD is associated with
obstruction to RV outflow—from a double-chambered RV,
infundibular stenosis, or obstruction near the valvular level—right to
left shunting can lead to signs similar to those of ToF. It is often
difficult to predict outcome in very young animals with a VSD until
they grow closer to adult size at 6-12 months of age. Cats with severe
AVSD often develop marked cardiomegaly and biventricular CHF.
Some will succumb at an early age (<2 years), while others survive
much longer.122 Most animals that develop pulmonary hypertension
(Eisenmenger’s syndrome) have a guarded to poor long-term
prognosis, although survival beyond 7 years is possible.

FIGURE 231.11 Echocardiograms of a Samoyed
with aortic regurgitation (AR) associated with a
quadricuspid aortic valve. A, The apical 5-chamber

from the aorta (Ao) into the left ventricle (LV). B,

CLINICAL MANAGEMENT
Medical therapy, surgery, and catheter-based treatments are possible
but rarely needed for small isolated ASDs or VSDs. Patients with
CHF (unilateral or biventricular) should be treated medically as any
other patients with volume-overloaded hearts. These patients
typically have large septal defects; therefore, they are also candidates
for palliative or definitive repair, although these procedures are not
widely available to veterinary patients. Percutaneous closure, or
hybrid procedures involving thoracotomy and transmural cardiac
delivery of the device, are discussed in ch. 115. Open-heart
correction is uncommonly attempted in animals because of the
requirement for cardiopulmonary bypass or other techniques to
arrest and perfuse the heart.130,138-145 Palliative surgical treatment
of a large VSD can be considered without bypass by applying a
constrictive band around the main pulmonary artery. This technique
creates a supravalvular PS and increases the RV systolic pressure,
thereby reducing the magnitude of left-to-right shunting.146

Alternatively, systemic arterial vasodilators can be administered to
reduce systemic vascular resistance and the magnitude of left-toright shunting.147 As noted for reversed PDA, surgical correction of
animals with Eisenmenger’s syndrome should not be attempted.
Restricted physical activity is probably the most prudent and
effective strategy in such cases, and sildenafil can also improve
clinical signs. Periodic phlebotomy to maintain a PCV of 58-65% may
be useful in some patients developing extreme erythrocytosis.

VALVULAR DYSPLASIA
PULMONIC AND AORTIC VALVE
REGURGITATION

Pulmonic Regurgitation
While inconsequential pulmonic regurgitation (PR) is a common
finding in dogs and cats of all ages,148 primary congenital PR is a
very uncommon abnormality. It results from abnormal development
of valve leaflets or dilation of the pulmonary artery annulus.149 PR
causes RV volume overload and eccentric hypertrophy, and
secondary pulmonary artery enlargement.
Thoracic radiographs in severe, isolated PR usually show
enlargement of the main pulmonary artery and RV, giving the
erroneous impression of PS. Color-flow Doppler echocardiography
can document valvular structure and function and valvular
insufficiency. Treatment for congenital PR has not been described in
companion animals.

Aortic Regurgitation
Isolated congenital AR (aortic insufficiency) is a rare disorder. It is
occasionally detected in young or older dogs with idiopathic dilation
of the aorta (annuloaortic ectasia). Mild to moderate AR has also
been reported in dogs with bicuspid150 or quadricuspid aortic

valves151,152 (Figure 231.11, A and B) (Video 231.7

). AR often

accompanies SAS. It also has been observed with VSD, ToF, and
following balloon catheter dilation for SAS. The potential
mechanisms for aortic valvular insufficiency in these conditions have
been reviewed.153 The diastolic murmur caused by AR is best heard
over the left hemithorax (
Audio 38.15). In patients with
concurrent SAS, the murmur is both systolic and diastolic (to-andfro; Audio 38.16). Many dogs with mild or moderate AR do not have
an audible murmur. When AR is audible, the valvular incompetency
is generally severe, although blood pressure, direction of the
regurgitant jet, and other variables can affect murmur intensity. The
diagnosis of clinically significant AR is supported by palpation of a
hyperkinetic arterial pulse (ch. 39) resulting from the combination
of higher LV stroke volume and reduced diastolic pressures owing to
diastolic run-off into the LV. Documentation of AR and estimation of
its severity require Doppler echocardiography. Eccentric to mixed LV
hypertrophy of the LV develops in proportion to the volume of AR.
Chronic, severe AR commonly results in left-sided CHF. Definitive
repair requires cardiac bypass surgery and valve replacement. Use of
arterial vasodilators can reduce the regurgitant volume and may
delay the onset of CHF but at the risk of reducing coronary
perfusion. Medical treatment is indicated if CHF is present (ch.
229).

ATRIOVENTRICULAR VALVE
DYSPLASIA
Congenital malformations of the mitral and tricuspid valves are
reported in both cats and dogs. In cats, MVD is one of the most
common congenital anomalies (Table 231.2). Consequences of
these malformations include 1) mitral or tricuspid valve
regurgitation (most common); 2) inflow obstruction (i.e., mitral or
tricuspid valve stenosis); and 3) dynamic obstruction of the LVOT via
inappropriate, systolic displacement of the mitral valve into the
LVOT. Fixed obstruction of the LVOT has also been described from

mitral valve malformation.154 The pathophysiologic mechanisms and
clinical course of congenital mitral regurgitation are similar to those
described in acquired degenerative valvular disease in the dog (ch.
232). Ebstein’s anomaly is a congenital defect reported in dogs
related to TVD, whereby the origins of the tricuspid valve leaflets are
apically displaced into the RV.20,155,156 It may or may not be
associated with leaflet dysplasia.

FIGURE 231.12 Macroscopic anatomy of tricuspid
valve dysplasia (TVD). A, Cranial view of the heart
from a patient with severe right atrial, auricular, and
right ventricular enlargement caused by TVD. B,
Tricuspid valve from a 2-year-old Labrador with
severe TVD. The edges of the valve leaflets insert
directly into the papillary muscles and there is
conspicuous shortening or absence of the chordae
tendineae. The right atrium and right ventricle are
dilated. C, Curtainlike deformity of the tricuspid
valve from a 2-year-old Samoyed with TVD and
tricuspid stenosis. The tricuspid valve is thickened
and opaque. There are multiple large and fused
papillary muscles with short chordae tendineae.

Systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve apparatus and
dynamic LVOT obstruction in cats and dogs, long regarded solely in
association with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (chs. 233, 234),
may be caused primarily by architectural changes in the mitral valve
apparatus in some animals.

Pathogenesis
TVD is known to have a genetic basis in some breeds of dogs,8,9,157
and in Labrador Retrievers, an autosomal dominant mutation with
incomplete penetrance has been mapped to chromosome 9.9 A wide
spectrum of congenital morphologic abnormalities of the mitral and
tricuspid valves has been described, including shortening, rolling,
notching, and thickening of the valve leaflets; incomplete separation
of valve components from the ventricular or septal wall (failure of
delamination); elongation, shortening, fusion, and thickening of the
chordae tendineae; direct insertion of the valve edge into a papillary
muscle; and atrophy, hypertrophy, fusion, and malpositioning of the
papillary muscles and chordae tendineae.155,158-162 The usual
consequence of these changes is valvular insufficiency. Examples of
tricuspid and mitral valve dysplasia are shown in Figures 231.12 and
231.13. Some dogs and cats with mitral or tricuspid dysplasia have a
PFO or a concurrent ASD, resulting in right-to-left or left-to-right
shunting, depending on whether resistance to RV outflow is
markedly elevated or not, respectively.

Pathophysiology
The valvular insufficiency caused by AV valve malformations
produces volume overload and manifests as atrial dilation and
eccentric hypertrophy of the affected ventricle. When sufficiently
severe, these changes are followed by the onset of CHF. The
development of atrial fibrillation (ch. 230) is especially destabilizing
to patients with these lesions. In some cases of TVD, cyanosis is
observed as a consequence of right-to-left shunting across a PFO or
ASD. When AV valve stenosis is present and is severe, cardiac output
may be reduced so that hypotension, syncope, or collapse with
exertion can be observed. In such cases, tachycardia abbreviates

diastole and increases the transvalvular diastolic gradient further,
contributing additionally to exercise intolerance. Pulmonary
hypertension (ch. 218) and right-sided CHF frequently develop
secondary to severe mitral stenosis as a consequence of chronic
elevations in LA pressure; this is more common in cats. As a result,
some patients initially presenting with signs of left-sided CHF from
mitral stenosis can present again months later with signs of rightsided CHF.

FIGURE 231.13 Macroscopic anatomy of mitral
valve dysplasia (MVD). A, Specimen from a cat with
MVD showing a thickened and opaque mitral valve
leaflet, direct attachment of the papillary muscle to

recorded from a 1-year-old Labrador Retriever with

Clinical Findings
The increased prevalence of MVD and TVD in several breeds (Table
231.1) indicates that genetic factors are likely involved in their
pathogenesis. Mitral valve stenosis, in particular, is common in Bull
Terriers, where it often occurs together with valvular aortic
stenosis.163 Although TVD has been described in cats, it appears to
occur most commonly in large male dogs and especially in the
Labrador Retriever.164
Dogs and cats with AV valvular dysplasia can appear clinically
well. Clinical signs arise from exertional forward failure (fatigue or
collapse), or right-sided, left-sided, or biventricular CHF, pulmonary
hypertension, or right-to-left shunting. Hemoptysis can occur with

mitral stenosis. The hallmark of valvular insufficiency is a
holosystolic murmur heard best over the affected valve area (ch.
38). With marked ventricular dilation, a loud gallop may be
detected.165 A soft, late diastolic murmur and opening “snap” is
sometimes auscultated in dogs or cats with valvular stenosis, but this
finding is often absent or missed. In TVD, murmur intensity may not
always reflect the severity of disease: in severe cases, for example, a
murmur may be very soft or absent as the valve offers no resistance
to regurgitant blood flow. Jugular venous distension and pulsations
are common findings in cases of TVD (

Videos 229.1, 237.3), and

hepatomegaly and ascites are present in dogs that present with rightsided CHF. Animals with right-sided CHF often have a poor body
condition.
Splintered or notched QRS complexes are a distinctive and
common ECG finding in dogs and cats with TVD (Figure 231.14)
(ch. 96).71 Right heart enlargement patterns may also manifest. Tall
or wide P waves are observed with all types of AV valvular dysplasia,
but ventricular enlargement patterns are mainly limited to animals
with regurgitant physiology and are not observed with isolated AV
valve stenosis, except when pulmonary hypertension develops
secondary to mitral stenosis. Atrial arrhythmias, including atrial
premature complexes, atrial tachycardia, and atrial fibrillation
(Figure 231.14) are often recorded (ch. 230). The pattern of
chamber enlargement on thoracic radiographs generally reflects the
involvement of the affected valve and resulting physiologic
consequences (Figure 231.15). In cases of TVD, the degree of
cardiomegaly is often impressive, and may resemble the globoid
appearance of pericardial effusion. The possibility of valvular
stenosis should be considered whenever the atrium is markedly
dilated without enlargement of the ipsilateral ventricle.
Definitive diagnosis of AV valve malformation requires
echocardiography, which can demonstrate the primary and
secondary changes described above (Figure 231.16, A to D; Video
231.8

). With isolated AV valve stenosis, the ventricle appears

small and the atrium enlarged, and the thickened valve leaflets can
be observed to “dome” into the ventricle during diastole. Color-flow

Doppler studies in AV valve stenosis show a high-velocity jet (often
>2.0 m/sec) entering the LV or RV during early diastole (median
[range] E wave Vmax in normal dogs = 1.8 [1.4-2.5] m/s; median
[range] E wave Vmax in normal dogs = 0.7 [0.5-1.0] m/s), and a
prolonged pressure halftime (median [range] in normal dogs = 31
[10-52] msec; median [range] in dogs with mitral stenosis = 68 [50105] msec) as determined by measurement along an abnormally
shallow E-F slope.163 With MVD and dynamic LVOT obstruction,
variable degrees of concentric LV hypertrophy (Figure 231.16, A),
and high-velocity turbulent flow within the LVOT accompanied by a
posterolaterally directed jet of mitral valve insufficiency can be seen.
Continuous-wave Doppler interrogation of the LVOT in such cases
will display a dynamic and labile pressure gradient secondary to
SAM of the mitral valve (Figure 231.16, B). TVD is identified by
varying degrees of apical displacement of the tricuspid valve
insertions (Figure 231.16, C and D). In human Ebstein’s anomaly,
apical displacement with atrialization of the proximal part of the RV
is observed. However, the diagnosis of apical displacement should be
made with caution as the normal insertion point of the tricuspid
valve leaflets is slightly more apical than the normal insertion point
of the mitral valve leaflets and the reason for apical displacement is
typically an embryonic failure of the valve to delaminate from the
walls. Confirmation of Ebstein’s anomaly is best made at cardiac
catheterization, where a ventricular electrogram is recorded along
with an atrial pressure tracing within the supravalvular chamber.
This is rarely undertaken in clinical cases.

Natural History and Prognosis
The morbidity and mortality associated with mitral or tricuspid
dysplasia depend on the form and severity of valvular dysfunction,
and the presence of additional lesions. Animals with small
insufficiencies usually live a normal lifespan without ever developing
recognizable clinical signs. Large insufficiencies and/or severely
stenotic valves causing moderate to severe cardiomegaly often lead
to atrial arrhythmias and intractable CHF. These outcomes are not
invariable, however, and survival to 6 or 8 years of age is not
uncommon, especially with TVD.

Clinical Management
Surgical repair or replacement of dysplastic AV valves has been
successfully accomplished in dogs with mitral166-168 or tricuspid
dysplasia.169,170 Cardiopulmonary bypass is required for these
infrequently-performed procedures. Balloon valvuloplasty has been
described in dogs with mitral171,172 and tricuspid173,174 stenosis, and
is further discussed in ch. 115. Medical treatment for CHF is
instituted if it develops (ch. 229). In dogs with TVD and refractory
heart failure, periodic paracentesis despite concurrent medical
therapy is often needed (chs. 86 and 92). Inasmuch as tachycardia is
poorly tolerated in AV valve stenosis patients, every effort should be
made to avoid stress, restrict exercise, and manage tachyarrhythmias
if they occur (ch. 230). Animals with significant LVOT obstruction
secondary to SAM of the mitral valve, regardless of the presence or
absence of clinical signs, are commonly treated with beta-blockers
(such as atenolol), which has been reported to successfully alleviate
the dynamic LVOT obstruction.175-177

VENTRICULAR OUTFLOW
OBSTRUCTIONS

PULMONIC STENOSIS
PS is the third most common congenital heart defect in dogs and it is
occasionally recognized in cats (Table 231.2). PS usually occurs as
an isolated heart defect, but it can also be accompanied by additional
cardiac anomalies, such as TVD. Congenital outflow tract
obstructions of the right heart can develop in the subvalvular and
supravalvular regions, but primary malformation of the pulmonic
valve (dysplasia) is the most frequently observed defect in dogs in
general. Patterson and associates studied the heritability and
pathologic lesions of pulmonic valve dysplasia in the Beagle and
initially suggested a polygenic mode of transmission for this defect;
however, they did not exclude the possibility of a single gene
mechanism with variable penetrance.178

Pathology
Valvular lesions consist of varying degrees of valve thickening, leaflet
fusion, and hypoplasia of the valve annulus. While some dogs
manifest a thin, dome-shaped valve with a central orifice (Figure
231.17), many dogs have more complicated lesions resembling
atypical PS in children.49,178,179 The valve leaflets are often
thickened, misshapen, or fused (Figure 231.17). The annulus of the
pulmonic valve is hypoplastic in some dogs,180 further narrowing the
area available for RV ejection. Histologic abnormalities include
thickening of the valve spongiosa and the presence of bands of
fusiform cells in a dense collagen network. These changes are
thought to represent overproduction of normal valve elements or a
failure of conversion of the cushionlike embryonic valve primordia.
Some dogs with valve dysplasia also have a fibrous ring just below
the valve leaflets accompanying the valvular changes. In other dogs
and cats181 the obstructive lesion occurs in the infundibular region of
the RVOT. On occasion, the RVOT is partitioned from the body
(inflow region) of the RV by a well-developed, fibromuscular ridge,
resulting in an anomaly referred to as double-chambered RV or
primary infundibular stenosis.182 The distinction between

infundibular PS and double-chambered RV is not always clear,
especially in cats.181 Supravalvular PS is uncommon in most breeds,
but has been reported more frequently in the French Bulldog.180
Subvalvular PS has been associated with anomalous development of
the coronary arteries, especially in English Bulldogs and in
Boxers.183,184 In this condition, the coronary circulation is derived
from a single ostium located in the right or left aortic sinus of
Valsalva, and both left and right coronary arteries branch from a
single large coronary artery (Figure 231.18). From this location, the
anomalous coronary artery encircles the RVOT just below the
pulmonic valve (R2A malformation).184 Whether this lesion
contributes to the subvalvular component of this malformation or is
an incidental finding varies from case to case, as it has been observed
in Bulldogs without PS. Regardless, it is clinically relevant because
vigorous balloon valvuloplasty of the subvalvular lesion is
contraindicated, having been associated with coronary artery
avulsion and sudden death.
Increased resistance to systolic ejection results in concentric RV
hypertrophy, which likely begins in utero and develops in proportion
to the severity of the obstructing defect. While this compensatory
response serves to normalize ventricular wall stress, it can have
deleterious consequences on RV diastolic function as well as
myocardial oxygen supply and demand. In some dogs with PS,
secondary hypertrophy of the infundibular region of the RVOT
contributes to a mainly dynamic RVOT obstruction, particularly
evident during exercise or stress. The presence of this additional
mechanism of obstruction can complicate the clinical outcomes of
surgical valvotomy or interventional balloon valvuloplasty.
The term double-chambered RV is applied when the RV is divided
into a distal low-pressure region (the infundibulum) and a proximal
region of high pressure (the apex and inlet portion of the RV) by a
muscular or fibromuscular ridge deep in the infundibulum (Figure
231.19). Some confusion can develop between this lesion and a
subvalvular PS that is not immediately adjacent to the valve leaflets.

Pathophysiology
Obstruction to RV outflow increases resistance to ejection, causing a
proportional increase in RV systolic pressure. Concentric RV
hypertrophy develops in an attempt to normalize wall stress. During
systole, blood ejected from the RV accelerates as it traverses the
obstructive orifice. Blood flow velocity increases and becomes
turbulent distal to the obstruction, causing the typical systolic
murmur of PS (

Audio 38.11). Poststenotic dilation develops in

the main pulmonary artery as the turbulent jet of blood decelerates
and expends some of its kinetic energy against the vessel wall.
Concentric hypertrophy reduces RV diastolic compliance, impairs
ventricular filling, and often results in elevated RA pressure.
Tricuspid regurgitation from progressive ventricular dilation,
valvular dysplasia, or a combination of these factors, can contribute
to further increases in atrial pressure. As RA pressure approaches 15
mm Hg, jugular distension, ascites, pleural effusion, and other signs
of right-sided CHF develop (ch. 228). Syncope (ch. 40) secondary
to transient hypotension is presumed to develop as a consequence of
reduced cardiac output (secondary to bradycardia or worsening of a
dynamic infundibular obstruction) and in combination with
peripheral arteriolar vasodilation, especially with or in anticipation
of exercise. Stimulation of mechanoreceptors in the pressureoverloaded RV might also trigger reflex bradycardia and
vasodilation. Reduced right coronary blood flow has been
documented in some dogs with PS and may contribute to the
development of syncope due to arrhythmias, exercise intolerance,
and myocardial failure. On rare occasion of PS severe septal
hypertrophy and diminished LV size result in dynamic LVOT
obstruction.185 Other cardiac defects can affect the clinical signs and
prognosis of patients with PS. For example, PS and TVD can cause
high-velocity tricuspid regurgitation, raising RA pressure and
possibly leading to intractable right-sided CHF. A patient with PS
and ASD, PFO,124 or VSD can have right-to-left shunting and
oxygen-unresponsive cyanosis. A meticulous echocardiographic

examination, often using contrast echocardiography, is necessary to
identify most of these additional lesions (ch. 97).

FIGURE 231.17 Macroscopic anatomic specimens
from dogs with pulmonic stenosis (PS). A, Pulmonic
valve leaflets are thickened and fused with a central
