(PA). TV, Tricuspid valve.

Clinical Findings

PS is common in several breeds (Table 231.1).24,95,98,180,186 Most
dogs with PS are not showing overt clinical signs during the first year
of life when the condition is usually discovered via detection of a
heart murmur. Approximately 35% of dogs with severe disease
demonstrate clinical signs, which can include exertional fatigue,
syncope (ch. 40), or ascites (ch. 21).187 Signs of right-sided CHF,
such as ascites, are most often reported in dogs that are older (ch.
228).179 In cats with severe PS, exertional dyspnea and lethargy may
be present.188 Cyanosis (ch. 27) may be noted when PS is
complicated by right-to-left shunting across a PFO or coexisting ASD
or VSD.
The most prominent physical examination finding of PS is a
systolic ejection murmur (

Audio 38.11) that is best heard over

the left heart base and that often radiates dorsally. In some cases the
murmur is heard well on the right cranial thorax. In dogs with
concurrent severe pulmonic valvular insufficiency, the systolic
ejection murmur is accompanied by a soft decrescendo diastolic
murmur heard best just ventral to the pulmonic valve region. Less
often a systolic ejection click is detected, which presumably indicates
a fused but mobile valve. A holosystolic murmur may be noted over
the right hemithorax in dogs with tricuspid regurgitation. Largeamplitude jugular pulses may result either from a giant a wave
caused by atrial contraction into the stiff RV or from cv waves
indicating significant tricuspid regurgitation. Jugular venous
distension and prominent jugular pulses are evident in most dogs
with right heart failure and ascites (

Videos 229.1, 237.3).

Peripheral arterial pulses (ch. 39) are usually normal.
Evidence of RV enlargement is usually present on the ECG unless
the lesion is very mild (ch. 96).69,189,190 Right axis deviation, with
deep S waves in leads I, II, III, aVF, and precordial leads V2 and V4,
are common indicators of right heart enlargement. Thoracic
radiographs typically show a prominent right heart and poststenotic
dilation of the main pulmonary artery.64,95,179,191 These changes are
usually most evident on the dorsoventral view. Additional and more
variable findings include dilation of the proximal left pulmonary

artery, diminished size of the pulmonary vasculature, and
enlargement of the caudal vena cava.
Echocardiography (ch. 97) is used for confirming a diagnosis of
PS. M-mode and 2D imaging typically show concentric RV
hypertrophy in proportion with degree of stenosis,192 increased
prominence of the RV papillary muscles, deformity in the region of
the obstruction(s), narrowing of the RVOT, varying degrees of RA
enlargement, and poststenotic dilation of the main pulmonary artery
(Figure 231.20).193,194 Of the 4 cardiac valves, the pulmonic valve
is the most difficult to visualize clearly by transthoracic
echocardiography. Thus, it might be impossible to visualize the exact
location and nature of the obstruction in some dogs without
additional imaging modalities such as transesophageal
echocardiography. It is often particularly difficult to identify a
discrete subvalvular obstruction in close proximity to the pulmonic
valve. The pulmonic valve leaflets are typically thickened, often
fused, and appear to dome upwards into the pulmonary artery
during systole (Figure 231.20). The distal edges of the leaflets can
appear partially tethered to the pulmonary artery wall, creating an
hourglass appearance relative to the sinuses. This is not
supravalvular stenosis per se, but does indicate a supravalvular
component to the stenotic, dysplastic valve. In comparison, isolated
supravalvular obstruction with otherwise-normal pulmonic valves is
rare. When present, hypoplasia of the pulmonic valve annulus can
further obscure the valve’s anatomic structure and make the
selection of an optimal treatment challenging. Color-flow Doppler
echocardiography is useful in establishing the anatomic location of
the obstruction, as a region of flow acceleration changes to a
turbulent, high-velocity jet that can usually be seen emerging just
distal to the obstructive orifice (Figure 231.20). Careful inspection
of the coronary artery anatomy, especially as these vessels arise from
the aortic sinuses, can help identify cases of coronary artery
anomalies. This is particularly important with subvalvular PS in
Boxers and English Bulldogs (Figure 231.21; Video 231.9

).

Mild to moderate pulmonic valve insufficiency is also apparent in
many dogs with valvular PS.

To accurately quantify the severity of the obstruction, the peak
velocity of the blood flow jet must be recorded on a spectral Doppler
tracing acquired with the continuous-wave Doppler beam in parallel
alignment with the direction of flow (Figure 231.20) (ch. 97). The
RV systolic pressure can be estimated by adding a normal PA systolic
pressure (20-25 mm Hg) to the RV-PA pressure gradient, as PA
pressure is invariably normal in cases of isolated PS. In dogs with
both dynamic (infundibular) and fixed (valvular) stenosis, Doppler
interrogation of the outflow tract and pulmonary artery can produce
a tracing that displays the temporal and velocity relationship
between the 2 components of the stenosis. Doppler interrogation of
the right heart can also identify any coexisting tricuspid valve

insufficiency and RV systolic pressure can also be estimated using
the Bernoulli relationship and assuming the RA pressure is 0-5 mm
Hg (in dogs without CHF). This approach offers a quality control on
the estimate obtained from RVOT signal. Measuring the velocity of
this regurgitant jet is particularly helpful for assessing the severity of
the PS obstruction when it is not possible to attain proper alignment
with flow through the outflow tract. The Doppler-derived systolic
RV-PA pressure gradient has been used for dividing patients with PS
into mild (<50 mm Hg), moderate (50 to 80 mm Hg) or severe (>80
mm Hg) categories.179,195,196
Angiocardiography is often performed just before balloon
valvuloplasty (ch. 115), and it can clearly demonstrate the anatomic
location of the obstruction(s), the degree of RV hypertrophy,
presence of tricuspid regurgitation, and the poststenotic dilation of
the pulmonary artery (

Video 115.2). Coronary arteriography (or

multislice computed tomography197,198; Figure 231.18, B) should
be performed when abnormalities of the left heart or coronary
circulation are suspected. Such studies must be performed whenever
surgery or balloon valvuloplasty is contemplated in an English
Bulldog or Boxer dog. Even in breeds at lower risk for coronary
anomalies, the “follow through” levophase of the right
ventriculogram can be instructive by identifying discrete right and
left coronary arteries.

subvalvular aortic stenosis. The view of the left

circumferential ring of fibrous tissue (∗) directly

Natural History and
Prognosis
Only broad criteria exist for establishing an approximate prognosis
for dogs and cats with PS. Clinical experience indicates that most
dogs with mild and even moderate PS (Doppler derived gradient <80
mm Hg) usually live normal or nearly normal lives, especially if no
clinical signs are evident.199 This generalization does not encompass
those dogs with other complicating defects. While systolic pressure
gradients are not always predictive of clinical outcome, there appears
to be a general correlation between pressure gradient and survival.
Dogs with Doppler-derived RV-PA gradients >125 mm Hg frequently
develop secondary tricuspid regurgitation, heart failure, exertional
syncope, and/or a serious cardiac arrhythmia, e.g., atrial fibrillation
(ch. 230). When an ASD, PFO, or VSD coexists with PS, there is the
potential for right-to-left shunting. If that shunting is pronounced,
consequences include arterial hypoxemia, erythrocytosis, and serious
debilitation. Sudden death occurs in some dogs with severe PS, but
this occurrence is uncommon.

Clinical Management
Patients with uncomplicated and subclinical, mild or moderate PS
usually do not require treatment. Serial echocardiographic
examinations (ch. 97) can be performed to monitor the degree of
ventricular hypertrophy, development of secondary infundibular
stenosis, and development of tricuspid regurgitation. Exercise
restriction is usually unnecessary. Some dogs will develop more
severe obstruction over time. Dogs with severe PS and/or PS that is
associated with clinical signs are candidates for balloon valvuloplasty
(ch. 115;

Video 115.3). Data from retrospective studies suggest

that balloon valvuloplasty in dogs with severe PS is associated with
reduced clinical signs and reduced risk for cardiac-related death.199201
Intervention at a young age should be encouraged, as the

development of overt CHF substantially lessens the chance for a
successful outcome, regardless of the method of repair or palliation.
Because of a high likelihood of heritability, even mildly affected dogs
should not be bred.

AORTIC STENOSIS
Subvalvular aortic stenosis (SAS) is the most common congenital
cardiac malformation in large breed dogs4,153,202-212 Most cases of
SAS result from a fixed ridge or ring of fibrous tissue located in the
LVOT, just below the aortic valve. SAS is a problematic disorder for
several reasons. It is very difficult to diagnose in mildly affected dogs
and it is difficult to treat when it is severe. The phenomenon of
dynamic SAS is also being recognized with increasing frequency in
dogs and cats with a variety of cardiac disorders, including fixed SAS,
MVD, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and other conditions causing
hypertrophy of the interventricular septum (e.g., PS, ToF).213 Bull
Terriers are predisposed to valvular aortic stenosis, wherein the
leaflets are thickened and the aortic valve annulus is mildly
hypoplastic. Normal Boxers also demonstrate aortic annulus
diameters that are smaller than those of other breeds of dogs, and
this confounds the diagnosis of mild SAS in this breed.214 Mild AS
caused by a bicuspid valve occurs on rare occasions.150 Fixed aortic
stenosis has been described in a small number of cats,32-34,215
including 1 case of supravalvular stenosis.216

Pathology and Pathogenesis
SAS has been most extensively studied in the Newfoundland dog.
Breeding studies in this and other breeds have established a genetic
basis for the perpetuation of SAS.2,217-219 An autosomal dominant
abnormality in the PICALM gene has been associated with SAS in
Newfoundland dogs,11 although these data might require further
validation.220 An autosomal recessive mode of inheritance is
reported in the Dogue de Bordeaux.157 Thus, it is likely that SAS in

the dog can be the result of different genetic abnormalities. The
obstructive lesion of SAS is not expected to be present at birth, but
instead develops during the first 4-8 weeks of life.2,204,207,217 This
progression has particular significance relative to the identification
of cardiac murmurs in pups of breeds known to be at risk for SAS. An
aortopathy or narrow, abnormal septal-aortic angle might play a role
in the development or progression of SAS in dogs, a situation
previously reported in children.221
The lesions of SAS in Newfoundlands have been described in
postmortem studies as mild (grade 1), consisting of “small, whitish,
slightly raised nodules on the endocardial surface of the ventricular
septum immediately below the aortic valve,” which would not be
expected to be visible echocardiographically; moderate (grade 2),
consisting of a “narrow ridge of whitish, thickened endocardium”
extending partially about the LVOT; and severe (grade 3), consisting
of “a fibrous band, ridge, or collar completely encircling the LVOT
just below the aortic valve.”2,217 This ring is raised above the
endocardium, extends to—and may involve—the cranioventral leaflet
of the mitral valve and the base of the aortic valve (Figure 231.22).
The stenotic ring consists of loosely arranged reticular fibers,
mucopolysaccharide ground substance, and elastic fibers. Discrete
bundles of collagen and even cartilage are found in advanced
lesions.217 A variety of cardiac abnormalities can accompany SAS,
most notably MVD, PDA, and a host of aortic arch abnormalities.
The valvular AS lesions seen in Bull Terrier dogs, including
myxomatous degeneration and cartilaginous metaplasia of the valve
leaflets, resemble those in humans with calcific valvular stenosis.222
Most dogs with moderate or severe SAS exhibit some degree of aortic
dilation distal to the stenosis. This post-stenotic dilation can range
from trivial to severe and can extend into the arch vessels. The
degree of post-stenotic dilatation is often greater with severe
obstructions, but this relationship is variable.
In some affected dogs, the pathologic findings diverge from the
classical description. The anterior mitral valve leaflet is thickened in
apposition to a septal plaque of endocardial fibrosis where the mitral
leaflet impacts the IVS as a consequence of dynamic obstruction.223
Instead of a fibrous collar, the septum is uniformly hypertrophied or

a broad fibromuscular ridge, arising from the base of the
interventricular septum, protrudes into the LVOT. Malformed,
malpositioned, or malaligned papillary muscles, thickened chordae
tendineae, and elongated or distorted mitral leaflets contribute to the
development of obstruction.224 Mitral valve malformations are also
associated with SAS in cats, although the disorder is rare in this
species.215,225 In some cats, longer, tunnel-like obstructions have
been observed.
Concentric hypertrophy of the LV develops in dogs with valvular,
fixed, or dynamic SAS more or less in proportion to the severity of
the outflow obstruction, although the correlation between wall
thickness and the magnitude of the measured LV-aortic gradient is
often poor.226 Structural and functional abnormalities of the LV227
and coronary circulation are well-documented in dogs with
SAS.204,207 Abnormal coronary flow has also been measured in the
larger, extramural arteries with diminished baseline diastolic flow
and reversal of coronary flow during systole.95,207 Focal areas of
myocardial infarction and fibrosis are commonly observed in the
papillary muscles and subendocardium of dogs with severe SAS,
often in association with abnormal intramural coronary arteries.
Histologic changes of the intramural coronary arteries in these
locations include intimal proliferation of connective tissue and
smooth muscle, and medial degeneration. These changes are
presumably related to the high wall tension found in this condition,
and their origin may be related to the elaboration of angiotensin II or
other biochemical mediators of hypertrophy and remodeling.228-230
Moreover, these arterial lesions may be important in the genesis of
malignant ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death.

Pathophysiology
Obstruction to LV outflow causes an increase in LV systolic pressure
and concentric LV hypertrophy. Consequent to fixed obstruction, the
rate of LV ejection is delayed, causing a diminished and late-rising
arterial pulse (parvus et tardus; ch. 39). High velocity and turbulent
flow across the stenotic area produces the systolic ejection murmur
and contributes to poststenotic dilation, which usually involves the

ascending aorta, aortic arch, and brachiocephalic trunk. Left atrial
hypertrophy develops as a consequence of impaired relaxation and
reduced compliance of the hypertrophied LV. Mild AR is commonly
present, presumably because of thickening of the valve leaflets or
dilation of the ascending aorta. Damage to the aortic valvular
endothelium (jet lesions) predisposes dogs with SAS to infective
endocarditis (ch. 232).231,232 Dogs with severe SAS can develop
left-sided CHF from myocardial failure, diastolic dysfunction, mitral
regurgitation, atrial fibrillation, or a combination of these factors.
Exertional syncope and sudden death are the most commonly
reported physical manifestations of severe SAS; presumably, these
events occur as a result of myocardial ischemia and the development
of malignant ventricular arrhythmias. Congruous with this finding is
that exercise ECGs can reveal significant, labile ST-segment
depression. In some dogs, exertional collapse might be caused by
hypotension precipitated by exercise-induced increases in LV
pressure, activation of ventricular mechanoreceptors, and
inappropriate bradycardia or vasodilation.233

Clinical Findings
Congenital SAS is common in many large breeds of dogs (Table
231.1).148,234 Valvular AS is common only in Bull Terriers. The
clinical findings of SAS vary with the severity of the obstruction and
the presence of concurrent cardiac defects. Clinical findings in pups
with mild SAS are often subtle and easily overlooked. Dogs with
subclinical SAS have a soft to moderately intense ejection murmur
that can easily be confused with an innocent or functional heart
murmur.235 More sophisticated time-frequency or heart rate
turbulence analysis of soft murmurs may provide clues as to which
murmurs are associated with mild disease.236,237 Insofar as the
lesions of SAS can develop during the postnatal period, the murmur
may become increasingly prominent during the first 6 months of life.
The grading of SAS severity in a puppy should be reserved until the
dog has attained nearly full maturity, because progression from mild
to severe has been observed during this interval.217,221,238 Severely
affected dogs can present with exertional fatigue, syncope, or left-

sided CHF, but the vast majority of dogs with SAS do not show
clinical signs. In dogs with severe SAS, a common client observation
is that the affected dog is smaller than its healthy littermates. Sudden
death, without premonitory signs, is common in severely-affected
dogs aged 1-3 years.232
Recognition of severe SAS is more straightforward, as the systolic
murmur generally becomes louder and later-peaking-to-holosystolic
when the obstruction is more severe (

Audio 38.9).45,239 The

murmur of severe SAS is usually best heard at the left heart base,
recognizing that in some dogs, the systolic murmur is equally loud or
louder at the right cardiac base, presumably from radiation into the
ascending aorta. The murmur of aortic stenosis often radiates up the
carotid arteries and can be auscultated over the ventral cervical
region. Frequently the murmur projects towards the apex and can be
confused with mitral regurgitation, a deduction that is made
challenging by the varying spatial orientation of the heart in dogs
depending on their thoracic conformation. In fact, a substantial
percentage of dogs with SAS also have mitral regurgitation, but these
murmurs are usually difficult to separate given their similar timing
and overlapping areas of maximal intensity. Despite the frequent
occurrence of AR captured by Doppler echocardiography, a soft
diastolic murmur of aortic valve insufficiency is infrequently
detected, probably because the amount of aortic valvular
insufficiency is often mild. Other physical abnormalities detected in
moderately- to severely-affected dogs include a diminished and late
rising arterial pulse (ch. 39) and a prominent LV precordial impulse
arising from the hypertrophied LV.
The ECG is often normal, but may, in severe cases, indicate LV
hypertrophy (increased R wave amplitude in leads II, III, aVF, V2,
V4). Depression of the ST segment and T wave changes suggest
secondary repolarization changes or myocardial ischemia; the latter
is especially likely when ST changes are precipitated by exercise or
occur in the company of ventricular ectopy. Compared with the
resting ECG, 24-hour ambulatory (Holter) ECG recordings offer a
more sensitive method of detecting intermittent or exercise-induced
ventricular arrhythmia and ST segment changes (ch. 96). The

severity of arrhythmias detected in this fashion often corresponds to
the severity of disease.240
Thoracic radiographs can be normal or may suggest LV
hypertrophy.64,95,191 Poststenotic dilation of the horizontallyinclined ascending aorta causes loss of the cranial waist on the lateral
projection and widening of the mediastinum on the dorsoventral
radiograph in severe cases. Mild LA enlargement is common in dogs
with moderate or severe SAS but marked LA enlargement suggests
concurrent mitral regurgitation, LV failure or concurrent left-to-right
shunt. Although unnecessary nowadays for the diagnosis,
angiocardiography can delineate the site and geometry of obstruction
and secondary changes (Video 231.10

). Hemodynamic

recordings document the presence and severity of a systolic pressure
gradient across the obstruction (Figure 231.23),95,241 although this
is largely replaced by outpatient echocardiography.
Moderate to severe SAS is easily confirmed by 2D and Doppler
echocardiography (ch. 97). Typical findings include concentric LV
hypertrophy, a subvalvular obstructing lesion, reduced LV orifice
area, and poststenotic dilation of the aorta (Figure
231.24).193,194,209,242,243 In Golden Retriever puppies, a more
acute angle between the ascending aorta and IVS (aortoseptal angle)
has been associated with increased LV outflow tract velocities and
development of SAS (Figure 231.25).221 The papillary muscles and
endocardial surface of the ventricular myocardium often appear
hyperechoic in severe disease, presumably as a result of myocardial
ischemia and replacement fibrosis or calcification. Structural
changes in the mitral valve can often be appreciated and abnormal
motion of the mitral valve (SAM) is evident in those cases with
coexisting MVD and dynamic obstruction.223 Spectral Doppler
interrogation of the LVOT is used for assessing disease severity by
measuring the peak velocity of flow in the LVOT.244 Such measures
show excellent correlation with invasive measures (Figure
231.24).63 Doppler measurements can be made from a variety of
parasternal or subcostal imaging windows, although velocities
obtained from the subcostal position generally display the highest

values.245 Disease severity is most often defined as follows: mild =
LV to aortic pressure gradient [PG] < 50 mm Hg; moderate = PG
range 50-80 mm Hg; severe = PG range 80-130 mm Hg; and very
severe = PG >130 mm Hg.246 Doppler-derived pressure gradients
are affected by the amount of flow (stroke volume) crossing the
obstructive orifice and may either overestimate the severity of
obstruction if cardiac output is high (e.g., in dogs that are stressed or
excited, or affected with a PDA), or underestimate the severity if flow
is subnormal (e.g., in dogs under anesthesia or with concurrent
myocardial failure). In these cases, indexing the gradient to stroke
volume or some related measure or simple estimation of the 2dimensional orifice area may provide a better estimate of disease
severity via calculation of effective orifice area.226,243,247 Color-flow
Doppler recordings are valuable for detecting and estimating the
severity of coexisting aortic or mitral valve insufficiency, although
focusing solely on jet area is likely to result in overestimation of
severity.248

FIGURE 231.23 Intracardiac and aortic pressures
obtained via cardiac catheterization of a 2-year-old
Golden Retriever with subvalvular aortic stenosis
(SAS). The catheter is withdrawn from the left
ventricle (LV) (left, 4 beats) into the left ventricular
outflow tract (LVOT) (center, 2 beats) and into the
ascending aorta (right, 2 beats). A 100 mm Hg

the LV and LVOT, indicating the subvalvular location
of the obstruction.
Antemortem detection of the mildest forms of SAS by auscultation,
or echocardiography is often not achievable and the precise outflow
velocity at which the diagnosis of AS becomes both sensitive and
specific is controversial and undefined by any gold standard. Dogs
with subtle abnormalities (i.e., macroanatomic grade 1 lesions)
escape detection by even the most accomplished examiners. Even in
dogs with grade 2 lesions, segregation from normal dogs solely on
the basis of Doppler-derived peak LVOT velocities is problematic. An
upper limit for aortic velocity in normal dogs has been reported but
is not well established for differing breeds and examination
conditions.249 The averaged, maximum pulsed-wave aortic velocity
in the author’s laboratory for healthy dogs without any cardiac
murmur is 1.7 m/s, and this is similar to values reported in a study of
healthy dogs without cardiac murmurs in which maximal LVOT

velocities were <1.8 m/s when measured from the left apex (upper
limit of the 95% confidence interval).250 Velocities recorded using
CW Doppler from the subcostal position are minimally faster but
generally <2 m/sec in dogs without murmurs. However, LVOT
ejection velocities in excess of these values are often recorded in dogs
with soft ejection murmurs but with no 2D evidence of discrete
outflow tract obstruction. Such velocities are especially common in
breeds characterized by slightly-diminished outflow tract dimensions
(e.g., Boxers, Bull Terriers). A diagnosis of mild SAS is more secure
once averaged maximal velocity measurements exceed 2.4 m/s and
are accompanied by other findings, particularly: disturbed flow on
PW Doppler; an anatomic lesion on 2D imaging; holodiastolic AR;
and when flow velocity abruptly accelerates over a discrete region in
the LVOT. Some investigators consider an echocardiographic LV
outflow tract area indexed to body surface area <1.46 cm/m2 or
aortoseptal angle <145° as indicators of mild or developing SAS in
Golden Retriever pups.221,243 The inability to reliably detect mild
SAS is a great source of frustration when attempting to provide
genetic counseling to breeders, who are interested in reducing the
incidence of disease.

Natural History and Prognosis
Dogs with minimal LV hypertrophy, mild LVOT obstruction, and a
maximal Doppler pressure gradient <50 mm Hg are more likely to
live normal lives, whereas dogs with pressure gradients >130 mm Hg
are very likely to develop serious complications such as endocarditis
and/or CHF or experience sudden death232,246,251; the median
survival is 3 years in such cases. Complicating factors that contribute
to an adverse outcome include: progressive LV diastolic and systolic
dysfunction, mitral regurgitation, AR, aortic valve endocarditis, and
atrial fibrillation.238,252,253 Sudden death is most likely to occur
during or shortly after vigorous activity.

Clinical Management
Dogs with mild SAS are not treated other than administration of
prophylactic antibiotics during periods of anticipated bacteremia,

such as during dental procedures, surgery, or whenever a concurrent
infectious disease is suspected. This practice remains common
despite the fact that the efficacy of prophylactic antibiotics for
reducing the risk of infective endocarditis in dogs with SAS has not
been definitively established.253 A number of treatment options can
be considered for dogs with moderate to severe SAS, but most are of
uncertain value. Open resection of the obstructing lesion during
cardiopulmonary bypass can substantially and permanently reduce
the systolic pressure gradient254,255; however, an otherwise
successful procedure does not appear to substantially alter the
prevalence of sudden death.255 Other surgical procedures employed
to dilate or bypass the obstruction have either failed to achieve a
sustained reduction of the systolic pressure gradient or entail an
unacceptable risk of complications.256,257 Moreover, these remedies
are usually limited in their availability and can be prohibitively
expensive for widespread use.
Balloon dilation of SAS has been attempted in dogs as an
alternative to surgery or lifelong medical therapy (ch. 115). On
average, catheter-based balloon dilation is able to reduce the severity
of SAS obstruction in dogs by 50%258; however, this short-term
benefit is attenuated in some (and perhaps a majority) of dogs over
time,244 and balloon valvuloplasty has not been shown to improve
survival versus medical therapy with atenolol.259
The author typically recommends avoidance of prolonged vigorous
exercise, recognizing that in young and otherwise healthy dogs, even
this conservative recommendation is not always practical. Based on
clinical and pathologic evidence of myocardial ischemia, the author
also considers administration of beta-adrenergic receptor blockers to
dogs with high gradients or a history of syncope. Beta-blockers (such
as atenolol) reduce maximal heart rate, decrease myocardial oxygen
consumption, and increase the time for diastolic coronary artery
flow, thereby offering a theoretic protective benefit to the
myocardium against ischemia and the development of arrhythmias.
Moreover, dogs receiving high dosages of beta-blockers seem less
willing (or are less able) to indulge in prolonged vigorous exercise.

Despite these theoretic advantages, a retrospective study found no
survival benefit of atenolol in dogs with SAS (Figure 231.26).251

OTHER CARDIAC DEFECTS
TETRALOGY OF FALLOT
The defining anatomic features of ToF are RV outflow obstruction
due to infundibular obstruction, secondary RV hypertrophy, a
typically large perimembranous VSD, and a rightward-positioned
aorta (dextroaorta) (Figure 231.27). The pulmonic valve is often
hypoplastic in ToF and can contribute to RVOT obstruction in
addition to, or instead of, purely valvular PS. Valvular PS occurring
in combination with an isolated VSD produces similar
pathophysiology and clinical findings of ToF; however, the

infundibular septum is not malaligned, the aorta is normally
positioned, and the infundibulum of the RV is not narrowed.260 In
children, pulmonary atresia is considered the extreme variant of ToF.

Pathogenesis
ToF has been extensively studied in Keeshond breeding colonies and
is likely oligogenic in etiology.10 The pathogenesis of this
malformation likely relates to ventrocranial deviation of the
ventricular outlet septum.261 In veterinary medicine, the term
“conotruncal septal defects” has persisted. Regardless of the
terminology, a spectrum of lesions, ranging from the subclinical to
the clinically complicated, has been identified.262-266 Three grades
of severity are described in Keeshond dogs. Grade 1 conotruncal
defects include subclinical defects of the RV conal septum, including
ventricular septal aneurysm and absence of the conal papillary
muscle. Grade 2 conotruncal defects include an infundibular VSD or
PS combined with grade 1 defects. Grade 3 conotruncal defects
consist of the complete ToF.262 Extreme asymmetry in truncal
partitioning can cause only vestigial pulmonary artery development
(pulmonary atresia), with only one functional artery coming from
both ventricles (pseudotruncus arteriosus). Additional abnormalities
found in some dogs have included a dilated and tortuous ascending
aorta, hypoplasia of the supraventricular crest, and anomalies of the
aortic arch system.

Pathophysiology
As a result of RVOT obstruction and secondarily elevated RV systolic
pressure, desaturated blood shunts from the right heart through the
septal defect to mix with oxygenated blood from the LV.267,268
Pulmonary arterial blood flow and pulmonary venous return are
reduced, and the LA and LV are small and underdeveloped. The
addition of desaturated blood from the RV to the systemic side of the

circulation causes arterial hypoxemia, decreased hemoglobin oxygen
saturation, cyanosis, and secondary erythrocytosis. Systemic
collateral circulation to the lung increases via the bronchial arterial
system. These vessels supply blood to the capillaries of the
pulmonary parenchyma either directly or via anastomosing
connections with a larger pulmonary artery. A substantial portion of
this blood can participate in pulmonary gas exchange. Bidirectional
shunting across the VSD is common. In cases of pulmonary atresia,
the pulmonary blood flow will be derived from the ductus arteriosus,
bronchial arteries, or systemic collaterals. Other aspects of clinical
pathophysiology have been described above for right-to-left shunts.

Clinical Findings
ToF is common in the Keeshond, English Bulldog, and in some
families of other breeds (Table 231.1). It has also been recognized
in the cat.269 Presenting complaints and clinical signs are as
previously described for cyanotic heart disease. In most cases, the
murmur of ToF is produced by high-velocity, turbulent blood flow
through the obstructed RVOT.260 Exercise or excitement may induce
or enhance detection of peripheral cyanosis by accentuating right-toleft shunting. Radiography usually reveals a small or normal-sized
heart with rounding of the RV border, classically producing a cardiac
silhouette described as “boot-shaped” (“coeur en sabot”) on the
dorsoventral or ventrodorsal projection.270 The main pulmonary
artery is not enlarged on survey radiographs, in contrast to the usual
case of PS with intact ventricular septum. The pulmonary
vasculature is diminished. The ECG (ch. 96) typically exhibits
criteria for right heart enlargement including right axis deviation,
although left- or cranially-directed vectors may be found in some
cats.271 Echocardiographic findings (ch. 97) include RV
hypertrophy, increased RV chamber dimensions, reduced LA and LV
dimensions, a large perimembranous-outlet VSD, and RV outflow
obstruction (Figure 231.28). Echocardiographic saline contrast or
angiography can be employed to document right-to-left shunting at
the ventricular outflow level (Figure 231.29).193,272 On Doppler

studies, shunting is usually bidirectional but predominantly right-toleft and of low-velocity owing to the small pressure gradient across
the ventricles.

FIGURE 231.27 Macroscopic anatomy of tetralogy
of Fallot (ToF). A and B, The left-side view of 2 dogs
with ToF shows a large nonresistive ventricular
septal defect (VSD) located between the aorta (Ao)
and left ventricle (LV). Note the close proximity to

of an aortic valve cusp into the VSD. C, Right-side

Clinical Management
Mean survival time has been reported to be about 2 years in a case
series of dogs and cats; however, for patients with soft or no
murmurs, mean survival was just over 3 months.269 Progressive
hypoxemia, erythrocytosis and hyperviscosity, arrhythmias, and
sudden death at an early age are common. This is consistent with the
concept that marked secondary erythrocytosis and hyperviscosity,

severe PS or pulmonary atresia, or a combination of these findings
worsens the prognosis. Nevertheless, mildly affected animals or
those that have undergone a successful palliative surgical shunting
procedure have lived well into middle age, provided pulmonary
blood flow is maintained and hyperviscosity is controlled.118 Most
affected animals have severely limited exercise capacity. Unlike PS
with intact ventricular septum, CHF is an unusual outcome in ToF.
Options for treating animals with ToF include medical and surgical
approaches. Definitive correction of the defect (closing the VSD and
removing or bypassing the stenosis) can be done under
cardiopulmonary bypass, but such surgery is rarely performed in
animals.273,274 As a general rule, the stenosis should not be
completely relieved if the VSD cannot be closed because the loss of
RV pressure results in marked left-to-right shunting with subsequent
left-sided CHF.266,275 Some dogs have been treated with partial
balloon dilation of severe PS to increase pulmonary blood flow and
reduce systolic RV pressure and right-to-left shunting. This
essentially aims to create a balanced shunt across the VSD and
dextroaorta. As an alternative to definitive correction, surgical
palliation through the creation of a systemic-to-pulmonary shunt can
be quite rewarding.266,276-278 Some variant of the subclavian to
pulmonary artery shunt (Blalock-Thomas-Taussig) has been created
most often in dogs and cats. Some surgeons prefer to use a graft
instead of turning down the subclavian artery. By creating a left-toright shunt distal to the cyanotic defect, pulmonary perfusion is
increased and there is a greater contribution of oxygenated blood to
the systemic circulation. The size of the accessory shunt must be
controlled to prevent overloading of the diminutive LV and
subsequent pulmonary edema. The extent to which these shunts
remain patent over long periods of time in veterinary patients has
not been reported. Another option, if a ductus arteriosus is still
patent, is catheter-based stenting of the PDA to maintain or increase
pulmonary blood flow.
Maintenance of hydration is important. Periodic phlebotomy,
performed to maintain the PCV between 62% and 68%, produces a
satisfactory result in many cases.118 Excessive withdrawal of blood
should be avoided, and the blood volume withdrawn should be

replaced with crystalloid fluids to maintain cardiac output and tissue
oxygen delivery.54 Some children with ToF benefit from nonspecific
beta-blockade with propranolol to reduce hyperdynamic contraction
of the RV that can increase outflow obstruction; however, controlled
studies of the clinical efficacy of this treatment in animals are
lacking.55,58 Severe hypoxemic spells should be treated with cage
rest, oxygen, IV fluids, and sodium bicarbonate (if metabolic acidosis
is evident). Treatment with vasoconstrictive agents such as
phenylephrine can also help reduce the amount of right-to-left
shunting in an urgent situation. Drugs with systemic vasodilating
properties should be avoided.

ATRIAL MALFORMATIONS
Congenital heart defects affecting the atria include the previously
mentioned forms of ASD along with defects that are more complex.
These latter malformations include cor triatriatum sinister (CTS), cor
triatriatum dexter (CTD), supravalvular mitral ring, and double
outlet right atrium. As implied by the name, cor triatriatum refers to
a partitioning of the left (sinister) or right (dexter) atrium into 2
chambers, creating “3 atria.” Cor triatriatum is characterized relative
to blood flow by a proximal (usually caudal) chamber in continuity
with venous return and a distal chamber in continuity with the
atrioventricular valve. The intra-atrial membrane obstructs venous
return from the proximal chamber, leading to venous congestion
behind the affected side of the heart.

FIGURE 231.28 Echocardiogram of a Keeshond
puppy with tetralogy of Fallot. A, The right long-axis
view shows severe right ventricular concentric
hypertrophy and right atrial enlargement. B, The
right short-axis view shows severe right ventricular
concentric hypertrophy, flattening of the
interventricular septum, a small underloaded left
ventricle (LV), and hyperechogenicity of the right
ventricular subendocardium. C, The M-mode study
shows enlargement of the right ventricle (RV) as
compared with the LV. The tricuspid and mitral
valves are seen moving in the center of their
respective ventricles. There appears to be

paradoxical septal motion toward the RV during
systole. D, The right long-axis view shows the
ventricular septal defect (VSD) and rightward
(dextropositioned) displacement of the aortic root
and aorta (Ao). E, Color-flow Doppler study of an
image similar to that in D shows right-to-left
shunting of blood from the RV (1), across the VSD,
and merging with blood from the LV (2) into the Ao.
F, Continuous wave Doppler study from the left
heart base across the pulmonic valve indicates the
presence of high-velocity blood flow and pulmonic
stenosis. LA, Left atrium; RA, right atrium.
Partitioning of the LA is more often observed in cats. With CTS,
the left auricle is located distal to the obstructing membrane. A
differential diagnosis for CTS is supravalvular mitral stenosis or
supramitral ring. This is a form of mitral stenosis characterized by an
obstructive membrane between the mitral valve and the LA.40,279
The left auricle is incorporated in the proximal, high-pressure
chamber of the LA and the mitral valve can be normal or malformed.
Both of these obstructions to pulmonary venous return lead to
clinical signs of left-sided CHF. Management options are limited but
successful surgical and hybrid (surgical-catheter) procedures have
been reported.280,281 The differential diagnosis of obstructed
pulmonary venous return must also include the so-called doubleoutlet right atrium. This malformation is characterized by extreme
leftward deviation of the ventral atrial septum with insertion of the
membrane dorsolateral to the mitral valve. Pulmonary venous return
enters the LA and crosses a primum ASD into the RA, which
connects to both atrioventricular valves.282

FIGURE 231.29 Angiogram from a Keeshond with
tetralogy of Fallot. The right ventricular injection
opacifies the right ventricle, pulmonary artery, and
aorta. Contrast can be seen in the region of the
suspected ventricular septal defect (∗). The contrast
column narrows in the right ventricular outflow tract
and region of the pulmonic valve (arrow). There is a
large poststenotic dilation of the main pulmonary
artery (arrowhead). A wide and rightward-positioned
aorta can be appreciated.
CTD (persistent sinus venosus valve) occurs mainly in dogs.283
This condition involves an intra-atrial obstruction that impedes
venous return from the caudal vena cava and coronary sinus. The
distal (cranial) part of the RA includes the right auricle, which
receives cranial venous return normally. This defect can develop in
isolation or as part of a more general hypoplasia or obstruction
within the right heart. Tricuspid valvular or supravalvular

stenosis,284 hypoplastic RV, and PS have been observed in dogs with
CTD. The typical case of isolated CTD leads to post-hepatic venous
obstruction with the clinical presentation of ascites (ch. 21) being
most common. The degree of inflow obstruction varies and
presumably can worsen over time, as some cases present after 2
years of age. The absence of a murmur can lead to an erroneous
diagnosis of hepatic or intra-abdominal disease. Echocardiography is
diagnostic. Both catheter-based and surgical interventions have been
used to successfully manage CTD in dogs.

VENTRICULAR MALFORMATIONS
In addition to VSD and double-chambered RV discussed previously,
several disorders of the ventricles are reported uncommonly in dogs
and cats. The near absence of RV myocardium with replacement by
fibrous tissue and fat (similar to Uhl’s disease in humans) has been
reported in cats and perhaps 1 dog.285-287 The condition should be
considered in the differential diagnosis of RV dilation and failure.
EFE has been reported in dogs and cats27,288,289 and is believed to
be familial in some lines of Burmese and Siamese cats. The
macroscopic pathologic findings of primary EFE include LV and LA
dilatation, with severe endocardial thickening characterized grossly
by diffuse, white, opaque thickening of the luminal surface.
Obstruction or abnormalities of lymphatic drainage of the
myocardium is a suggested cause. Histologic lesions in well-studied
feline cases include diffuse hypocellular, fibroelastic thickening of
the endocardium with layering of thin, randomly organized collagen
and elastic fibers. Edema of the endocardium with dilation of
lymphatics is prominent, and there is no evidence of myocardial
inflammation or necrosis. The clinical features of EFE include early
development of left-sided or biventricular failure, generally before 6
months of age. Left ventricular and atrial dilation are evident on
radiographs, ECG, and echocardiography. Medical treatment of CHF
might prolong life, but recovery is unlikely.

Ventriculoarterial Connection Malformations

Malformations of the ventriculoarterial connection include double
outlet right ventricle (DORV), transposition of the great arteries and
persistent truncus arteriosus.
DORV describes a heterogeneous group of malformations in which
both great vessels exit from the RV. This has been reported in both
dogs and cats.290,291 A VSD provides the LV an avenue for outflow
into the great vessels. Depending on the location of the VSD in
relation of the origin of the great vessels, DORV can manifest as
either pulmonary overcirculation or as a form of cyanotic heart
disease.
In D-transposition of the great arteries, the aorta originates from
the RV and the pulmonary trunk from the LV.49,292 In the pure and
uniformly fatal extreme, 2 independent circulations coexist and the
systemic arteries never receive oxygenated blood. Survival of an
animal with D-transposition depends on the presence (or
development) of shunts between the 2 circulations to allow for
mixing of blood to prevent fatal hypoxemia. These defects are
complex, generally lethal, and most likely underdiagnosed in
animals, relative to children, since most animals probably die
undiagnosed at a very young age.
Truncus arteriosus communis is caused by failure of septation in
the fetal truncus arteriosus and is characterized by a large VSD, a
single great vessel exiting the heart, and is further classified by the
origin and number of pulmonary artery branches originating from
the truncus. The condition has been observed rarely in dogs and in
cats,293-296 and clinical signs depend largely on whether pulmonary
blood flow is increased (i.e., left-to-right shunt) or restricted (in
which case cyanosis is likely).

MALFORMATIONS OF THE GREAT
ARTERIES
Coarctation of the Aorta
Coarctation of the aorta, a shelf-like narrowing near the ductus
arteriosus, and more extreme examples of aortic obstruction such as

tubular hypoplasia or interruption of the aorta are rarely observed in
dogs and cats (2 cases are reported in English Bulldogs).297,298

Vascular Ring Anomalies
In veterinary medicine, vascular ring anomalies refer to
malformations that entrap the esophagus leading to regurgitation in
weanlings. Persistence of the right aortic arch, as opposed to the left
fourth aortic arch is the most commonly reported. Vascular ring
anomalies include this common malformation along with other total
or partial ring anomalies. These include esophageal compression
formed by retroesophageal subclavian arteries, double aortic arch, or
left aortic arch with right-sided ligamentum arteriosum.4,24,29,299303
Vascular ring anomalies are less common in cats but have been
described.92,299,302,303 These conditions are described more fully in
ch. 259.

Pulmonary Artery Anomalies
Abnormalities of the pulmonary arteries can be observed under a
number of conditions. Unilateral atresia or hypoplasia of a
pulmonary artery has been recognized in cats. An overlooked
diagnosis is that of systemic-to-pulmonary arterial vascular
malformations.92,304,305 These arteriovenous malformations are
typically multiple, and can connect the aorta, brachiocephalic artery,
or other systemic arteries to the pulmonary arterial system. The
result is volume overloading of the left side of the heart. Murmurs
are often difficult to detect but can include continuous murmurs
related to the shunts or systolic murmurs due to functional mitral
regurgitation from LV dilation and increased aortic blood flow. The
diagnosis can be suspected from color-flow Doppler imaging of the
pulmonary artery and failure to identify a typical ductus arteriosus.
CT angiography or contrast angiography is diagnostic. Management
can include surgical intervention or coil occlusion of the vascular
malformation; however, the clinician should always suspect multiple
shunts and the potential for opening of new arteriovenous
communications with the closure of others.

MYXOMATOUS MITRAL VALVE DISEASE
Myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) is a common adult-onset valvular heart disease in dogs. The
disease is characterized by progressive degeneration of the mitral valve, eventually leading to mitral
valve leakage, mitral regurgitation (MR), and later to chronic dilatation of the left atrium (LA) and left
ventricle (LV). Affected dogs have a variable progression and outcome: in some dogs, the disease
progresses to the point that they develop signs of congestive heart failure (CHF) and other
complications, whereas others can compensate for the MR for years and thereby remain clinically
healthy.

OCCURRENCE
Approximately 10% of the total dog population develops cardiac disease,1 of which MMVD accounts for
more than 75% of the cases. This makes the disease one of the most common causes for morbidity and
mortality in dogs.2 The disease occurs in other species, including humans, cats, horses, monkeys, and

pigs,3 but the prevalence of MMVD in cats is low. The disease has been reported to account for the vast
majority of the cases of CHF in dogs,4 a proportion even considerably higher in predisposed dog
breeds.2,5,6
MMVD is encountered in all dog breeds, but the prevalence is highest in small to medium-sized dogs,
such as Cavalier King Charles Spaniel (CKCS), Dachshunds, Miniature Poodles, and Yorkshire
Terriers.2,5,7,8 The prevalence of MMVD in dogs increases with age and is, at a given age, higher in
males.2,4,5,9 The disease has an unusually early onset in the CKCS breed and closely related breeds:
approximately 50% of CKCS dogs aged 6-7 years and nearly 100% of CKCS dogs aged >10 years have
been reported to be affected.5,10

UNDERLYING CAUSES AND MECHANISMS
Valve remodeling in MMVD has been well described, but the underlying causes for its development and
its progression remain poorly understood. A combination of a sire and a dam that both have an early
onset of MMVD has previously been shown to produce offspring that have, on average, an early onset of
MMVD (and CHF), whereas a combination of dogs with late onset will give offspring that manifest the
disease at an old age or never do.11,12 According to the currently leading scientific hypothesis, supported
by pedigree analyses and reports of familial transmission in both dogs and humans,11-13 MMVD is
inherited as a polygenic trait. However, the genetic architecture of the disease is hitherto inadequately
explored. Two regions (on CFA13 and 14) have been associated with early onset MMVD in the CKCS
breed,14 but these regions are unlikely to solely explain the exceptionally high prevalence of MMVD in
this breed. Recently, mutational variants near a gene (NEBL), which is exclusively expressed in the heart
and encodes a protein that is important for stabilizing and strengthening muscle fibres,15 were identified
in dogs of the CKCS breed. Two of the variants could also be linked to early disease onset in the
Dachshund breed.16 Disease associated alleles were, furthermore, shown to be associated with reduced
NEBL expression in the papillary muscles of MMVD affected dogs. Considering the pivotal role of the
papillary muscle in maintaining mitral valve geometry and integrity (see Pathophysiology, below), these
results could indicate that papillary muscle weakening could be a significant component of the
development of MMVD.
Damage to the lining of the endothelial cells covering the valve surface17 might play an important role
in the progression of MMVD. Endothelial cells are known to communicate extensively with
subendothelial cells (e.g., valvular interstitial cells [VICs]), and endothelial-damage–induced release of
vasoactive substances might lead to a transformation of subendothelial VICs from a predominantly
fibroblast phenotype into more active myofibroblast and smooth muscle cell phenotypes.18,19
Transformation of VICs has also been suggested to be initiated by serotonin (5-HT),19,20 and altered
5HT signaling might be causatively linked to MMVD: experimental animals exposed to exogenous
serotonin administration are at risk of developing similar valve lesions as those seen in MMVD-affected
valves. Furthermore, serum concentrations of 5-HT have been shown to be higher in dogs of the CKCS
breed,20,21 and higher concentrations have been shown in mitral valve and myocardial tissue from dogs
with MMVD relative to healthy dogs.22 Expression of 5-HT receptors and extracellular matrix signaling
molecules has also been shown to be altered in diseased mitral leaflets.19,23

PATHOLOGY
Myxomatous degeneration begins in the area of apposition of the leaflets and is usually most
pronounced in sections where chordae tendineae insert.4,9,17,24,25 With progression, the lesions spread
into other parts of the leaflets (Figure 232.1, A and B). The mitral valve leaflets, which are normally
thin, translucent, and soft, become thickened due to the degeneration, and typical pathological findings
vary from mild nodular thickening of the mitral valve leaflets to severe thickening and billowing. Both in
normal and in MMVD dogs, the anterior mitral leaflet has been described as having a greater length and

area compared to the posterior leaflet,26,27 which is presumably the reason MMVD lesions may appear
more prominent on the anterior leaflet.27

FIGURE 232.1 Thickened and contracted mitral valve leaflets in a
postmortem specimen of a dog that had severe myxomatous mitral valve disease
(MMVD) viewed from the lateral (A), and atrial (B) sides with left atrium (LA)
and ventricle (LV) opened. C, Histology sections of a mitral valve leaflet from a
dog with mild (upper), and severe MMVD (lower) showing marked deposition of
acid-staining glycosaminoglycans (blue color in a periodic acid-Schiff
reaction/alcian blue staining) in the spongiosa and fibrosa layers of the
leaflet. C , Courtesy Lisbeth Höjer Olsen, University of Copenhagen, Denmark.
The chordae tendineae are also commonly affected by myxomatous degeneration, which leads to
lengthening and eventually rupture in some dogs.7,9,24,25
Histopathological findings of the affected mitral valve include weakening and disturbance in the
organization of the connective tissue (Figure 232.1, C). The spongiosa component becomes unusually
prominent and the collagen fibers in the fibrosa layer are disorganized.18,28 Increased amounts of
mucopolysaccharides and glycosaminoglycans are commonly seen within affected valves.24,28,29
Furthermore, pleomorphism and a damaged lining of the endothelial cells covering the valve surface can
be observed. Regional loss of endothelial cells can lead to exposure of the underlying basement
membranes or subendothelial matrix.25
Dogs with early stage MMVD have a normal heart size, whereas dilatation of the LA and eccentric
hypertrophy of the LV (see Pathophysiology, below) develop with disease progression. Histopathological
findings in the walls of the heart chambers include changes in the composition and structure of both the
myocytes and the extracellular matrix (ECM). Myocardial fibrosis and intramyocardial arteriosclerosis,

especially in the papillary muscles, have been described in dogs with advanced stages of MMVD.30 Atrial
endocardial lesions (fibrosis) opposite the mitral orifice (i.e., “jet lesions”) might be observed in the LA.
The LA also becomes gradually more thin-walled and more vulnerable with increasing LA dilatation, and
rupture of the atrial wall, such as endomyocardial splits, ruptured pectinate muscles in the atrial
appendage, acquired atrial septal defect, and atrial tear and hemopericardium may be detected in dogs
with severe MMVD (see below, and Figure 232.2, A-D).4,31

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY (CH. 228)
Mitral Valve Function, Mitral Regurgitation, and Remodeling of the Left
Heart Chambers
The mitral valve annulus is normally characterized as “saddle-shaped” (hyperbolic paraboloid), and this
geometry confers a mechanical advantage for maintaining valve competence by providing optimal leaflet
stress.32,33 Dogs with MMVD present a more circular and less saddle-shaped mitral valve, with reduced
tenting height and area compared to healthy dogs.27 This change of the normal mitral valve geometry
leads to increased mechanical stress imposed on valvular structures and could, thereby, initiate
MMVD.19,27 Interestingly, the mitral valve in clinically healthy CKCS dogs has been shown to be
significantly flatter (e.g., reduced leaflet tenting) compared to healthy dogs from other examined
breeds,34 which potentially could be a predisposing factor for early development of MMVD in this breed.

FIGURE 232.2 Left lateral radiographs illustrating changes in cardiac size,
lung fields and vasculature as myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD)
progresses into congestive heart failure. A, Normal heart outline and size
(Vertebral Heart Score [VHS] 10.2) and unremarkable lung fields and
vasculature (stage B1). B, Mild cardiac enlargement (VHS 11.4) and normal lung
fields and vasculature (early stage B2). C, More advanced cardiac enlargement
(VHS 12.2) with tracheal elevation and more prominent vascularization, but no
signs of pulmonary edema (late stage B2). D, Severe cardiac enlargement (VHS
14.6), and evidence of pulmonary congestion and interstitial edema (stage C).
The myxomatous degeneration and altered geometry of the mitral valve apparatus also lead to atrial
displacement of the mitral valve leaflets (i.e., mitral valve prolapse) during ventricular systole,35 and
abnormal leaflet apposition. As a result, a percentage of the LV stroke volume is ejected backwards into
the LA (primary MR). Most commonly, dogs with MMVD have a laterally directed MR jet, presumably
because the anterior leaflet is longer and has a greater mobility during systole than the posterior leaflet
(as described in dogs and people),26,27,36 and hence, may prolapse more than the posterior leaflet.
However, the spatial orientation of the jet is not constant, particularly not in mild cases of MR, probably
due to changes in the shape and orientation of the mitral orifice during LV contraction.37 Primary MR of
a lesser degree does not induce any apparent change in indices of cardiac size or function. The forward
stroke volume is maintained, and the small regurgitant volume is easily accepted by the LA. With
progression of the valve lesions, the regurgitant part of the total LV stroke volume increases, but several
cardiac and non-cardiac (e.g., renal, neurohumoral, and vascular) compensatory mechanisms contribute
to maintaining the forward stroke volume.38 The extra outlet (into the low-pressure LA) for stroke
volume ejection reduces the LV afterload (the resistance to LV emptying), whereas the increased volume
load leads to an increased preload.39 The retrograde ejection of LV stroke volume starts in early systole,
leading to a short or absent isovolumetric contraction period.40 The presence of atrioventricular
dilatation exaggerates the abnormal valve apposition, leading to secondary MR.4,36 Consequently,
regurgitation begets regurgitation, and it has been estimated that more than 75% of the total LV stroke

volume may be ejected into the LA during systole in some dogs with severe MMVD.41 Elongation and
potentially rupture of the chordae tendineae can worsen MR by causing valve flail, when the edge of a
leaflet or, in severe cases, an entire leaflet, moves into the LA in systole.7
The LA allows the regurgitant volume to be absorbed within the atrial cavity, and LA expansion allows
the intra-atrial pressure to remain comparably low for a relatively long period of time. The pulmonary
vascular bed is thereby protected, and pulmonary venous congestion and edema can be postponed.42
The effect of regurgitant volume on LA pressure and volume, and consequently on the pulmonary
capillary pressure, depends on the LA size, as well as on the compliance of the LA wall, the latter being
determined by the rate of increase in regurgitant volume. In cases with slowly progressing MMVD, there
is often a drastic enlargement of the LA, resulting in late development of pulmonary congestion and
edema. Pulmonary edema is also delayed by the development of a more effective lymphatic drainage of
the pulmonary interstitium in patients with chronic pulmonary congestion.43 However, passive backtransmission of increased LV filling pressure, and therefore higher LA pressure, can subsequently lead
to development of pulmonary edema and/or pulmonary hypertension (PH) in dogs with severe MR. In
dogs with acutely increased MR, such as dogs experiencing chordae tendineae rupture, the LA is unable
to adapt to the rapid increase in LA pressure, which leads to acute development or exacerbation of
pulmonary congestion and edema.
The LV compensates for the loss of forward stroke volume (due to MR) by increasing the end-diastolic
volume. In order to accommodate the increased filling pressure (preload), the LV undergoes
compensatory responses. The volume overload triggers an unnatural growth: so-called eccentric
hypertrophy, which is characterized by chamber enlargement, but with maintained relative wall
thickness sufficient to normalize pressure in the volume-overloaded LV and maintain an adequate
forward stroke volume.44-46 Although both long- and short-axis dimensions increase in response to
chronic volume overload, the short-axis dimension increases more, which leads to a change in LV shape
from elliptical to more globular in dogs with more pronounced MMVD.47
Various compensatory mechanisms, such as eccentric hypertrophy of the LV and enhanced activity of
the neurohormonal system, are all initially considered beneficial in order to maintain sufficient cardiac
output despite MR. However, with progression of disease, these mechanisms themselves become factors
contributing to deterioration of the failing heart. Mechanical function decreases slowly, but
progressively and inexorably, even in clinically compensated patients.47-49 Although myocardial systolic
function declines with progression of disease, the cardiac remodeling process allows the LV to maintain
a relatively well-preserved forward cardiac pump function even in advanced MMVD,38,50 and an
increased pulmonary blood volume, not decreased forward stroke volume, has been shown to be the
main cause of abnormal cardiopulmonary function in dogs with MMVD.51

Tricuspid Valve Function, Tricuspid Regurgitation, and Cardiac Remodeling of
the Right Heart Chambers
The degenerative changes of the tricuspid valve apparatus are identical to those affecting the mitral
valve.31 Mild to moderate tricuspid regurgitation commonly occurs concomitantly with myxomatous
degeneration of the mitral valve, as a consequence of primary valvular degeneration of the tricuspid
valve and/or secondary to PH due to left-sided myxomatous degeneration (or other etiologies; ch.
218).52,53 Tricuspid regurgitation in the absence of concurrent obstruction of the pulmonary valve or
PH is comparably well tolerated.54 The right ventricle (RV) is, however, designed to contract against a
low-pressure artery, and it is vulnerable to increases in pressure. In addition to RV dilatation, right atrial
(RA) enlargement develops, and as a consequence of increased RA pressure, signs of right-sided CHF
may develop (see below).

CLASSIFICATION SYSTEM FOR ASSESSMENT OF DISEASE
SEVERITY (CH. 229)
The severity of MMVD should be staged for treatment decisions, risk assessment (e.g., anesthetic risk),
and for establishing prognosis. This involves a scale of classification that ranges from stages A to D

according to the American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine (ACVIM) MMVD Consensus
Statement (Table 232.1).55

CLINICAL PRESENTATION
ACVIM Stages B1 and B2
Dogs with mild to moderate MMVD (ACVIM stages B1 and B2) usually do not present any clinical signs
of disease, but exercise intolerance may be noted in some B2 dogs that are in close proximity to
developing CHF. Dogs with MMVD may present with cough, but coughing spells are, however, not
specific for heart disease (ch. 229). Coughing due to other respiratory problems, such as
tracheobronchial instability (ch. 215), are also commonly seen in middle-aged to old dogs of breeds
commonly affected by MMVD (ch. 34). Coughing in dogs with tracheobronchial instability may
potentially worsen as a consequence of MMVD and cardiomegaly (see below).

ACVIM Stage C
The first clinical signs of decompensated (unstable) CHF (ACVIM stage C; ch. 229) are usually mild and
vague, but the signs may be aggravated within days or sometimes weeks. Increased respiratory rate
(tachypnea) and effort are present when pulmonary congestion and edema have developed.56 Ownerreported sleeping (SRR) and/or resting respiratory rates (RRR) observed in the dog’s home
environment, when the dog is located in a “thermoneutral environment,” are expected to be increased
(i.e., >30 breaths/min) at repeated measurements at the onset of CHF, and again later if medications are
no longer preventing recurrence of pulmonary edema (“decompensated CHF”).56-58 A dog’s normal
panting should be differentiated from respiratory signs consistent with CHF: a pathologically increased
respiratory rate that is present even at rest and sleep, increased respiratory effort, or both. Abnormal
respiratory sounds, such as wheezes and crackles may be audible on pulmonary auscultation, and
coughing spells may be observed. Dogs in decompensated CHF are often inactive and show signs of
reduced exercise tolerance and may present with varying degrees of inappetence. Cardiac cachexia (ch.
157) may develop, although loss of body weight may be masked by concurrent fluid retention and
edema.

Left Atrial Rupture
Dogs that are severely affected with MMVD may experience a full-thickness rupture of the LA wall due
to pronounced LA enlargement (and thereby a more thin-walled structure). Left atrial rupture causes an
acute development of hemopericardium, cardiac tamponade and often sudden death. There is
sometimes a history of trauma, excitement or physical exercise preceding the atrial rupture. For dogs
surviving the initial event, clinical signs of cardiac tamponade, such as collapse, marked exercise
intolerance, or ascites, with or without signs of left-sided CHF, are to be expected. Echocardiography is
required for establishing a definitive diagnosis of LA rupture by identifying the presence of significant
pericardial effusion in combination with MMVD, but it is often difficult to visualize the actual tear on an
echocardiogram (see below and Figure 232.2, A-D).

Syncope
Dogs with pronounced MMVD can experience syncopal events (ch. 40), and the frequency of events can
vary from occasional spells to several attacks per day. The syncopal events may be associated with acute
decompensated CHF and/or arrhythmia. Syncopal events, reduced exercise tolerance (even at mild
exercise), weakness, respiratory distress and increased respiratory effort may also be seen in dogs with
PH (ch. 218), developing as a consequence of longstanding severe MMVD or due to other reasons.52,59
These dogs may also have signs of right-sided CHF that can include abdominal distention due to ascites,
hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and/or gastrointestinal signs such as diarrhea, vomiting, and anorexia.
Myxomatous lesions of the semilunar valves are comparably common but rarely result in significant
leakages associated with clinical signs.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (CH. 3)

A systolic click and/or a systolic heart murmur may be detected during auscultation of the heart, thereby
alerting the clinician to the possible presence of cardiac disease (

Audio 232.1; ch. 38). However,

lack of an audible murmur cannot rule out mild MMVD.60,61 Detection of a soft murmur over the mitral
valve area (Audio 232.2
) on the left side of the thorax in a dog of a typical breed and age is indicative
that disease severity is mild and that CHF is unlikely.62 With further disease progression, a murmur of
“harsher” and more intense quality, and longer duration (holosystolic) develops (Audios 232.3 and
232.4)

.60,63 Moderate to loud murmurs can radiate throughout the left and right sides of the thorax,

and loud heart murmurs may also be accompanied by a palpable thrill on the left thoracic surface
(cardiac apical area). An association exists between murmur intensity and severity of MMVD, but it is
imprecise: 56% of dogs with moderate (grade III/VI) murmurs and 29% of dogs with loud (grade IV/VI)
murmurs have been described to lack secondary cardiac chamber enlargement and thus would not be
candidates for treatment with any cardiac medication.62 Dogs presenting with a precordial thrill have a
higher risk of experiencing CHF and/or PH.62 Musical murmurs (whoop sounds) of high intensity may
be detected in dogs with MMVD but may not necessarily reflect the severity of MMVD (Audio 232.5
).64 Pathological TR can be characterized by a systolic murmur of variable (depending on severity of TR)
intensity.

Merging of the first heart sound (S1) with the forceful murmur of more advanced MMVD might give
an impression of increased intensity of S1 during cardiac auscultation. The intensity of S2 decreases with
increasing MMVD severity, as a consequence of reduced LV forward stroke volume.60,63 The heart rate
increases with worsening disease severity in preclinical dogs with cardiomegaly (ACVIM stage B2), and
it is usually significantly increased, with a loss of respiratory sinus arrhythmia, in dogs experiencing
acute decompensated CHF (ACVIM stage C-D) (Figure 232.3).58,65
The lung sounds and respiratory rate and effort are expected to be normal in preclinical MMVD dogs
(stages B1 and B2), but the respiratory rates are expected to be higher in the clinical setting than at home
simply due to stress or excitement.58,66 Dogs in decompensated left-sided CHF, affected by pulmonary
congestion and edema, present with tachypnea and signs of increased respiratory effort of varying
severities (Figure 232.3) (ch. 37).56,67 In dogs in left-sided CHF, the pulmonary sounds are usually
more pronounced, and crackles and wheezes may be detected. Similar abnormal sounds may also be
heard in dogs with small airway disease68 (ch. 216).
Mucous membranes are usually normal, even in dogs in acute decompensated CHF, but may
occasionally be pale, grayish, or ashen in advanced cases of CHF. Weak peripheral pulses may be noted
in dogs in CHF. Weak and variable pulses with deficits (ch. 39) can also be observed in dogs with
rhythm disturbances (ch. 230). If tamponade develops owing to pericardial hemorrhage due to a tear in
the LA wall, the femoral pulse will be weak, and jugular venous distention may be present (ch. 235;
Videos 229.1, 237.3

).

Progressed MMVD may involve the right-sided heart chambers, as a consequence of advanced
myxomatous degeneration of the tricuspid valve, PH, and/or due to development of a tachyarrhythmia,
such as atrial fibrillation. However, physical examination findings in these dogs may be
indistinguishable from MMVD dogs lacking right-sided heart involvement. A left apical systolic murmur
is present due to the MR, but a switch of the point of maximal intensity to the right side may occur with
development of PH in some dogs.52,69 A physical examination may reveal evidence of right-sided CHF,
such as jugular vein distension (

Videos 229.1, 237.3), positive hepato-jugular reflux, and abdominal

distention caused by hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and/or ascites (ch. 229).

ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIC FINDINGS
Echocardiography (ch. 97) is the method of choice for establishing a diagnosis of MMVD and for
staging the disease. It is also valuable for monitoring disease progression, identifying potential
complications, and for providing definitive information for treatment.

Mitral Valve and Left-Sided Heart Chambers
Leaflet thickening and systolic leaflet protrusion (mitral valve prolapse) of 1 or both leaflets into the
atrial side of the mitral annulus are seen in dogs with MMVD, and the valvular changes can be evaluated
using 2-dimensional (2D) (

Videos 232.1 to 232.4; Figure 232.4) and real time 3-dimensional

(RT3D) echocardiography (Video 232.16).27,33,34,70 With progression of disease, the valvular changes
become more prominent (

Videos 232.5 to 232.15; Figure 232.4). The gross pathologic changes of

the 2 leaflets (anterior and posterior) are often equally severe at postmortem examination, but the
degenerative changes commonly appear more prominent on the anterior leaflet in the right parasternal
four-chamber long axis view on the echocardiogram.71 Valve flail—when the edge of a leaflet or, in
severe cases, an entire leaflet moves into the LA in systole—may be identified (

Video 232.17; Figures

232.4, D and 232.5, E), and is indicative of a rupture of 1 or more major chordae tendineae.72
Valvular regurgitation can be detected and quantified by color-flow and spectral Doppler (Figure
232.4, A-D)37,73 (ch. 97). Color-flow Doppler echocardiography confirms the presence of a regurgitant
jet; however, trivial regurgitations in the vicinity of the mitral valve may also be detected in healthy dogs,
and should, accordingly, not be overinterpreted in dogs with normal valve morphology. The modality
can provide information regarding regurgitant jet size, width, and spatial orientation, as well as flow
convergence into the regurgitant orifice and vena contracta (VC).37,41,74,75 The ratio of regurgitant jet
area to LA area is commonly used as a qualitative or semiquantitative method to assess MR severity (
Videos 232.2, 232.4, 232.6, 232.8, 232.11, 232.13, and 232.15).73 The method is comparatively easily
performed, but findings are influenced by numerous physiologic and technical factors. Because of these
drawbacks, MMVD assessments of MR severity should not rely only on the color Doppler
echocardiogram. A small jet does rule out the presence of moderate to severe MR, but the modality may
not be effective in discriminating between moderate and severe MR.
The VC, which is defined as the narrowest central flow region of a jet that occurs at or just
downstream to the orifice of a regurgitant valve where the blood velocity is highest, can also be used
when assessing MR severity.37,75 Furthermore, MR severity in dogs with MMVD can be assessed by
measuring the effective regurgitant orifice area (EROA), which corresponds hemodynamically to the
cross‐sectional area of the VC. The EROA can either be calculated by use of color Doppler 2D
echocardiography or measured by RT3D echocardiography; the latter technique allows the regurgitant
jet to be visualized from any plane, and the EROA to be measured directly without the use of a
predefined geometric model.37
The severity of MR may also be assessed by calculating regurgitant volume and fraction, and several
echocardiographic methods have been described for this purpose.37,41,74 The calculations involve
multiple measurements, each with its own errors, which means that they will only provide estimates of
the MR. Spectral Doppler gives information on the velocity of the regurgitant jet and velocity time
tracings may help in estimating regurgitant volume. Ideally, the regurgitant flow should be aligned with
the ultrasound beam and this is often best achieved in the left apical 2- or 4-chamber views (ch. 97).76
Estimation of the systolic transmitral pressure gradient includes quantifying peak MR velocity, and then
estimating the pressure gradient between the LA and LV using the modified Bernoulli equation
(pressure gradient (mm Hg) = 4 × (MR velocity (m/sec))2. Dogs in compensated MMVD (i.e., stage B)
typically have a velocity of the regurgitant jet of 5-6 m/sec, whereas the velocity may be increased in
dogs with systemic hypertension, and decreased in dogs with significantly increased LA pressure (as in
dogs at stage C in acute fulminant CHF and/or myocardial failure) or with systemic hypotension.
Spectral Doppler may also be used to study transmitral flow during diastole. Significant MR is usually
associated with increased diastolic transmitral flow and consequently, increased diastolic filling
velocities.77,78 Furthermore, evidence of abnormal diastolic ventricular function as a consequence of
severe volume overload may be detected. The diastolic filling pressure (i.e., degree of congestion) can
also be estimated indirectly using a set of diastolic time intervals, and tissue and blood flow Doppler
echocardiographic measurements66 (ch. 97).

LA size reflects disease severity37,78,79 and it is, accordingly, an important structure to evaluate in
dogs with MMVD. LA anatomical dimensions, volume and function can be assessed subjectively or by
using an arsenal of echocardiographic methods that rely on 1-dimensional (M-mode), 2D or 3D
techniques.80-83 The most commonly used technique for this purpose is to measure the LA and aortic
diameters in the right short axis view and use the ratio between these 2 dimensions as an indicator of LA
size.80,81,84 Dogs with early signs of MMVD and only minimal to mild MR, have no echocardiographic
signs of LA enlargement. The LA dimension increases, however, with disease progression, and
pronounced LA enlargement is seen in dogs that will soon develop or that have already developed CHF (
Videos 232.9, 232.12, 232.17, 232.18, and 232.19). A LA/Ao ratio of ≥1.6 obtained in the short axis
view separates dogs in stage B1 from dogs in stage B2,55 and a ratio of ≥2.0 heralds CHF in
development, if not already present.79,85 The echocardiographic findings of cardiac size vary, however,
in dogs with acute rupture of a major chorda tendinea: depending on how far the MMVD had progressed
before the chordal rupture, some dogs with an acute increase in MR, and thereby LA pressure, can
present with less pronounced LA enlargement.

regurgitation (A), and hearts with different severities of myxomatous mitral
