Likewise, the LV anatomy, dimensions, volume, shape, and function can be assessed subjectively or by
using various echocardiographic assessment methods that rely on 1D (M-mode), 2D or 3D techniques.
(Figure 232.4, A-D).47,86,87 Normal reference ranges for LV dimensions and volumes are available for
some breeds, but measurements are usually corrected for body weight using formulas generated by
allometric scaling, and normal inter-breed reference ranges are available using this method.88-90 These
normal reference ranges appear to be valid for most breeds, but not for some sight hound breeds.89,90
Normal LV size, or a mildly enlarged LV, is usually found in dogs with mild MMVD. With progression,
the LV end-diastolic dimension and volume increase (

Videos 232.9, 232.12, and 232.17 to 232.19),

whereas the end-systolic measurements do not increase at the same rate47,91 since the LV shortens to an
almost normal end-systolic dimension in dogs with preserved LV systolic function.92 The end-systolic
dimensional and volume indices do, however, increase in dogs with more severe MMVD, which is
considered a sign of systolic dysfunction.47,49 The rate of change of LV enlargement is highest when
dogs are in close proximity to developing CHF.91 Dogs with signs of LV dilatation usually present with a
normal wall thickness, indicating the presence of volume overload and eccentric hypertrophy (see
Pathophysiology, above).
Depending on the severity of MR, normal to hyperdynamic LV contraction (hyperkinesis) can be
observed on the echocardiogram (

Videos 232.9, 232.12, and 232.17 to 232.19), even in the presence

of intrinsic myocardial dysfunction. Thus, given the fundamental pathophysiologic mechanism of MR in
dogs with MMVD, identification of systolic dysfunction using various echocardiographic indices (e.g., LV
fractional shortening [FS%], ejection fraction [EF%], and mean velocity of circumferential shortening) is
challenging.92 Dogs with moderate to severe MMVD may have an increased LV FS% and EF%, whereas,
in the same setting, values of FS% and EF% within the normal ranges may represent myocardial
failure.92 Tissue Doppler imaging (TDI) and speckle tracking techniques have also been shown to be
affected by loading conditions and sympathetic tone in a similar fashion as the more traditionally-used
echocardiographic techniques.93,94

Pulmonary Veins and Pulmonary Parenchyma
The pulmonary veins can be evaluated subjectively, and dilated veins speak in favor of pulmonary
venous congestion. The pulmonary vein diameter to pulmonary artery diameter ratio has been suggested
to quantify the degree of venous congestion, and has been reported as promising in predicting the
presence of CHF in dogs with MMVD.95
The presence and number of so called “B-lines” or “rockets” in the pulmonary parenchyma with 3 or
more lines in 1 view can be considered a sign of pulmonary edema96 (ch. 73). The method has been
reported to have similar sensitivity and specificity as thoracic radiography to identify cardiogenic
pulmonary edema.97 It has become a popular point-of-care method in emergency clinics to distinguish
dyspnea caused by fluid in the alveoli (including pulmonary edema) from respiratory distress of other
etiologies.

Tricuspid Valve and Right-Sided Heart Chambers
The 2D echocardiographic appearance of a tricuspid valve affected by myxomatous degeneration is
similar to the myxomatous lesions described in the mitral valve section. With the use of color-flow

Doppler, TR may be detected and semiquantified. The RA is, however, not as easily imaged as the LA
owing to its anatomic configuration.

FIGURE 232.5 Development of complications may occur in dogs with
myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD). A, Severe MMVD leading to atrial
tear/rupture (arrow) and (D) hemopericardium/pericardial effusion (PE)
(arrow). B, Severe MMVD leading to a partial rupture of the left atrial wall
(arrows) and (C) formation of a thrombus (arrow). E, Severe MMVD causing
rupture of a major chorda resulting in valve flail into the left atrium (LA)
(arrow). F, Severe MMVD precipitating bursts of supraventricular tachycardia
(arrow) with a rate of approximately 300/min. LV, Left ventricle.
PH is a common complication found in dogs with longstanding severe MMVD, and the severity of the
PH is typically mild to moderate.53 Multiple echocardiographic imaging modalities and methods may be
used for reaching a diagnosis of PH (ch. 218).52,53,59

ELECTROCARDIOGRAPHIC FINDINGS
Electrocardiographic findings in MMVD vary from normal tracings to marked abnormalities in rate,
rhythm, or configuration of complexes (chs. 96 and 230). Findings indicative of cardiac enlargement,
usually left-sided, may be identified in dogs with moderate to severe MMVD, but ECG is an insensitive
indicator for this purpose. Sinus tachycardia and a loss of sinus arrhythmia are common findings in dogs
in decompensated CHF but are, of course, not specific to decompensated CHF. Supraventricular
premature complexes commonly occur in MMVD dogs with cardiomegaly (stages B-D),98,99 but this
type of arrhythmia is of little hemodynamic significance in most dogs. An enlarged LA also increases the
risk for development of atrial fibrillation and supraventricular tachycardia (Figure 232.5, F).98,100
Although ventricular premature depolarizations and tachyarrhythmias occur in MMVD dogs, often at
advanced stages of the disease, supraventricular premature depolarizations and tachyarrhythmias are
far more common.98,99

RADIOGRAPHIC FINDINGS (CH. 229)

Radiographic findings in dogs with MMVD are not specific for this disease but they can indicate the
degree of left and right sided enlargement and the circulatory consequences of MMVD (Figure 232.2,
A-D). Dogs in ACVIM stage B1 MMVD are expected to have a normal heart size, normal lung fields, and
normal vascular markings on a radiographic examination, whereas dogs with more advanced MMVD
may have signs of cardiomegaly (ACVIM stages B2-D) and pulmonary congestion and edema (ACVIM
stages C, D). Radiography may to some extent be used as a surrogate for echocardiography in detecting
cardiomegaly in dogs with MMVD, but it is less sensitive and there are significant breed differences to
account for. Furthermore, radiographs are useful for characterizing the degree of pulmonary edema and
congestion and rule out potential differential diagnoses for clinical signs.

CARDIAC BIOMARKERS IN BLOOD
Concentrations of the cardiac biomarkers N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) and
cardiac troponin I (cTnI) have been reported to increase with increasing MMVD severity.101,102 Cardiac
TnI is a non-specific marker of myocardial damage; consequently, increased concentrations can be
detected in the blood for many reasons, including various extracardiac disease processes. Circulating
NT-proBNP concentration increases in response to myocardial stretch (ch. 228); therefore, it is an
indicator of cardiomegaly. Measurement of NT-proBNP has been shown to be comparably effective in
separating mild MMVD (stage B1) from moderate to severe MMVD (stages B2-D).103,104 In the
emergency setting, NT-proBNP can be useful in distinguishing increased respiratory rate and effort
caused by left-sided CHF from primary respiratory disease etiologies.104 However, dogs may present
with a combination of significant MMVD and primary respiratory disease, and the additional value of
natriuretic peptides is limited in this setting. Other drawbacks with the method include the absence of
point-of-care tests for dogs and a comparatively wide interbreed variation in NT-proBNP
concentrations.105

MANAGEMENT
Although several medications have been suggested to counteract the valvular degeneration of MMVD,
none has hitherto been shown to halt or slow the degenerative process in clinical patients. Surgical
intervention has shown promising results in case series of open-heart surgery and mitral valve
repair.106,107 However, these procedures are only offered at very few sites in the world, and only
technically and/or economically possible for very few veterinary patients today. Different implantation
devices to improve mitral valve function have been tested,108,109 but currently they are not widely used.
Managing MMVD in veterinary patients therefore mainly involves improving quality of life by
prolonging the preclinical (“asymptomatic”) period, ameliorating clinical signs (if present), and
improving survival.

Management of MMVD is presented for 2 groups of patients in this section: dogs with preclinical
MMVD (ACVIM stage B) and dogs with clinical MMVD (ACVIM stages C and D) (Table 232.1).
Management of possible complications is discussed separately. It is unusual to treat MMVD in cats and
therefore, details of drug dosages for cats are not specifically covered in this section.

Dogs With Preclinical MMVD (ACVIM Stage B1 and B2)
Dogs belonging to ACVIM stage B are a comparably heterogenous group of dogs ranging from those that
have only mild MR and a normal heart size (ACVIM stage B1) to dogs having moderate to severe MR and
significant LA and LV dilatation (ACVIM stage B2). Clinical drug trials have studied the outcome in
ACVIM stage B1 dogs, but no therapy has hitherto been shown to have beneficial effects and improve
outcome. Therefore, medical treatment is not recommended at this stage. However, medical treatment is
recommended for MMVD stage B2 dogs.

Pimobendan (ch. 229)
Pimobendan is approved for use in dogs with MMVD stage B2 in many countries, at a dosage of 0.2-0.3
mg/kg PO q12h and, according to the most recent ACVIM Consensus Statement concerning canine
MMVD,55 it is the only drug currently recommended for MMVD stage B2 in dogs. The approval and
recommendation are based upon the results from the EPIC trial, which was a large, international,
placebo-controlled, multicenter trial comparing the effect of pimobendan versus placebo in delaying the
onset of CHF in dogs in MMVD stage B2 (Figure 232.6, A).110 The study reported an improved
outcome associated with pimobendan treatment that was presumably conferred by a reduction in heart
size, which is mediated by the inotropic and vasodilatory effects of the drug (see below).79

ACE Inhibitors (ch. 229)
Historically, ACE inhibitors have been used widely in dogs with preclinical MMVD, but currently there is
no evidence that ACE inhibitor administration to dogs with stage B MMVD slows or prevents
progression of clinical signs of CHF or improves survival. Two placebo-controlled multicenter trials, the
SVEP and the VETPROOF trials,111,112 both failed to show a significant difference between the ACE
inhibitor (enalapril) and placebo treatment groups in time from onset of therapy (when the dogs were in
the preclinical stage of the disease) to development of CHF. Furthermore, a recent clinical trial could not
show a preventive effect, i.e., delay the onset of CHF, with the combination of benazepril and
spironolactone compared to placebo in ACVIM stage B2 MMVD dogs.113

Other Medications (ch. 229)
A large, prospective, placebo-controlled clinical trial investigating the preventive effect of the betablocker bisoprolol in ACVIM stage B2 MMVD dogs was terminated prematurely because of lack of
efficacy114 and currently no evidence exists confirming a beneficial effect of beta-receptor antagonists to
MMVD dogs at this stage of the disease. Arterial vasodilators, such as amlodipine, may theoretically
reduce MR severity, and consequently have been suggested to be beneficial in stage B2 MMVD. The
clinical documentation of arterial vasodilator treatment in this group of dogs is scarce,115,116 and a
potential additive effect to the vasodilating effect achieved from pimobendan has not been evaluated.

Owner Instructions (ch. 229)
Owners of dogs with preclinical MMVD should be instructed to count their dog’s respiratory rate
preferably during sleep (or deep rest) at home. Respiratory rates consistently >30 breaths/minute
warrant further investigation as this can be an indication of the development of CHF.56 Information
about other signs of CHF should also be provided to the owner. Dietary or exercise restrictions are not
indicated in ACVIM stage B1 dogs.55 Dogs in MMVD stage B usually tolerate comparably long walks at
their own pace, have a better quality of life with this type of exercise, and do better if obesity is avoided.
However, strenuous exercise and diets with high sodium content (ch. 157) should be avoided in dogs
with more advanced ACVIM stage B2 MMVD as they may promote pulmonary edema.55
Regular rechecks at 6-12 month intervals can be recommended for stage B dogs, but more frequent
rechecks are indicated in some cases.55 Dogs previously staged at ACVIM B155,110 should be re-checked
with an echocardiographic examination, particularly if the murmur intensity has increased from mild to
moderate to severe. This examination allows the clinician to note if the criteria for initiation of
pimobendan are fulfilled.55,110

Dogs With Clinical MMVD (ACVIM Stages C and D)
Considering the pathophysiology of MMVD, therapy of MMVD dogs in CHF (ACVIM stages C and D; ch.
229) should be directed toward (1) reducing venous pressures to alleviate edema and effusions, (2)
maintaining adequate cardiac output to prevent signs of weakness, lethargy, and organ hypoperfusion,
(3) reducing cardiac workload and regurgitation, and (4) reducing the negative long-term effects of
exposure to neurohormones (ch. 228).
Dogs with MMVD suspected to have developed CHF should be treated based on the nature and
severity of clinical signs rather than radiographic, echocardiographic or laboratory findings. Because the
disease often is slowly progressive from very mild to more severe forms, signs of CHF may develop over
days or weeks. Dogs with mild signs of acute left-sided decompensated CHF may often be managed on
an outpatient basis if careful instructions are provided to the owner, and if follow-up conversations with
the owner over the phone or via email, and rechecks at the clinic, are scheduled. Dogs with moderate to
severe signs of acute decompensated CHF often need intensive care, including oxygen supplementation
administered via a humidity and temperature-controlled oxygen cage or incubator, or via a nasal oxygen
cannula (ch. 123). Narcotics (such as butorphanol 0.2-0.25 mg/kg IM or IV) may be given to the dog in
order to treat anxiety associated with dyspnea. In addition to an appropriate medical treatment protocol,
as suggested below, optimal nursing care is recommended. Various diagnostic procedures may have to
wait until the dog has become more stable after medical treatment has been initiated.

Diuretic Treatment (ch. 229)
A usual course of medical treatment for a dog with mild to moderate signs of CHF includes an initial
intensive treatment with furosemide. An alternative to furosemide is torsemide (torasemide), which has
been shown in clinical trials to be non-inferior to furosemide in dogs in CHF due to MMVD (ch.
229).117,118 The dosage of either of these loop diuretics should keep the dog free from clinical signs of
CHF and should preferably be based on clinical signs rather than radiographic findings. Unnecessarily
high maintenance doses should be avoided. The maintenance dosage of diuretic (furosemide and/or
torsemide) in a MMVD stage C patient usually must be gradually increased over time to prevent clinical
signs of CHF from reoccurring. Reasons for increasing the dosage often include recurrent tachypnea and
pronounced respiratory effort caused by pulmonary edema or, less commonly, development of ascites
(ch. 229).
Spironolactone, which is an aldosterone antagonist and a potassium-sparing diuretic agent, used
alone or in combination formulation with benazepril, can be added to the loop diuretic
treatment.55,119,120 To obtain more complete blockage of the nephron, hydrochlorothiazide can be
considered for dogs receiving very high daily doses of loop diuretics and spironolactone but still showing
persistent signs of CHF (ch. 229). Mechanical treatments, such as abdominal paracentesis (ch. 86) and
thoracocentesis (ch. 92), may be required in dogs with severe ascites or pleural effusion that causes
respiratory distress and/or compromises ventilation.55 However, many MMVD cases with less severe
ascites respond to increased doses of diuretics. Even in case of centesis, the diuretic dosage should be
increased, as the effusion will re-occur without intensified medication.

Pimobendan (ch. 229)
Clinical trials have shown that pimobendan is indicated as first-line treatment in dogs with CHF caused
by MMVD, because dogs receiving pimobendan as adjunct therapy to diuretics have been shown to have
less severe signs of CHF and have a longer survival time than those receiving an ACE inhibitor and
diuretics (Figure 232.6, B).121-123 Other beneficial effects of pimobendan in treating MMVD dogs in
ACVIM stage C includes a reduction in heart rate and pulmonary transit times,124 and a reduced
tendency for retention of free water.84

Other Positive Inotropic Agents (ch. 229)
Digoxin is a comparably weak positive inotropic agent compared to pimobendan, and in dogs with
MMVD, it is currently used almost exclusively as an antiarrhythmic drug.55 For critically ill patients that
are judged to be too sick to wait for oral inotropy, dobutamine, which is a synthetic sympathomimetic
that acts via beta-1 receptors, can be administered.55 However, no clinical trial involving dobutamine
has been conducted in dogs with MMVD and its potential benefit in dogs already receiving pimobendan
has not been evaluated.

ACE Inhibitors (ch. 229)
ACE inhibitors are recommended in dogs with MMVD at ACVIM stages C and D,55 because placebocontrolled clinical trials conducted in the 1990s reported that dogs in CHF receiving an ACE inhibitor
combined with other standard therapy (including a diuretic) had less severe clinical signs, better
exercise tolerance,125,126 and lived longer than those only receiving standard therapy and no ACE
inhibitor.127-129 However, a recent clinical trial reported no apparent beneficial effect in outcome of
therapy consisting of the ACE inhibitor ramipril, furosemide, and pimobendan compared to dogs
receiving therapy consisting of furosemide and pimobendan.130

Vasodilators (ch. 229)
For patients showing severe signs of CHF despite intensive loop diuretic and pimobendan treatment, an
agent with vasodilating effects may be considered to reduce pre- and afterload further and stabilize the
CHF.

Owner Instructions
Owners should be informed about the need for regularly counting SRR (or RRR) at home (preferably
should be <30/min on repeated measurements when investigated in a calm and temperature neutral
environment)56,57,130 and for monitoring other important variables such as respiratory effort and
appetite, all of which can indicate improvement or impairment of the dog’s clinical condition. See ch.
229 for further owner instructions and recommendations for reexaminations.

Management of Other Complications Associated With MMVD
Coughing due to Left Mainstem Bronchial Compression (ch. 34)
Compression of the left mainstem bronchus may potentially occur in dogs with significant left-sided
chamber enlargement (see Clinical Signs section). The severity and duration of associated coughing
spells are variable, and mild and occasional coughing does not require daily medication. Treatment
using pimobendan and/or diuretics has the potential to reduce cardiac size, which theoretically could
improve coughing spells, but the actual clinical benefit from such treatments on frequency and severity
of coughing is currently unknown.

Development of Arrhythmia Leading to Syncopal Events
Dogs with MMVD may develop syncopal events, commonly occurring in association with exercise,
excitement, or coughing spells (ch. 40). In such dogs, a 24-hour (Holter) ECG recording may show
episodes of a rapid supraventricular rhythm (Figure 232.5, F; ch. 96) immediately followed by a
bradycardia during which the dog faints.98,99 For management of different arrythmias, see ch. 230.
Dogs with severe MMVD may also experience syncopal events as a consequence of insufficient CHF
therapy (ch. 229) and/or PH (ch. 218).

Pulmonary Hypertension and Right-Sided CHF (ch. 218)
Many patients with long-standing history of MMVD develop PH and the severity of the PH is typically
mild to moderate.53 A standard MMVD therapeutic protocol should be initiated based on the
recommendations for the different stages. If clinical signs suggestive of PH, such as right-sided CHF and
syncope with exertion, are present even in the absence of pulmonary edema, therapy for PH should be
initiated.55,59

Chordal Rupture
Chordal rupture may be suspected in all dogs with MMVD presenting with an acute, severe development
of left-sided CHF and PH (

Video 232.17; Figure 232.5, E). The most important ruptures involve

those of first order chordae that are attached to the septal leaflet. Ruptures of lower order chordae may
result in mild clinical signs or none at all.72 Patients with chordal rupture require intensive care to
stabilize the condition, which may take a longer time than when treating dogs lacking signs of chordal
rupture and thereafter adequate maintenance therapy for MMVD. The outcome is entirely dependent on
remaining mitral valve function, and medical treatment of complete flail of 1 of the leaflets is usually
futile.

Left Atrial Rupture and Cardiac Tamponade
Treatment of atrial rupture with hemopericardium (Figure 232.5, C) and cardiac tamponade is usually
futile (

Video 232.19). Immediate pericardiocentesis can be attempted (ch. 95), and pericardial fluid

should be removed to alleviate the tamponade without removing so much that further bleeding is
stimulated. If the bleeding continues after pericardiocentesis, the final option is emergency thoracotomy
with pericardiectomy and closure of the tear, but the prognosis for this procedure is poor and generally
not recommended.

PROGRESSION AND PROGNOSIS

Although a risk exists for future development of CHF, many dogs with stage B MMVD will never develop
clinical signs from the disease during their lifetime.55,111-113 Normal progression of the disease from the
detection of a soft heart murmur to end-stage disease is often a matter of years in small dogs. Some
large-breed dogs, however, appear to have a more drastic progression with more severe clinical signs
than in small dogs.55,132 The results from the EPIC trial showed that disease progression from moderate
to severe MMVD (stage B2) to CHF (stage C) can be prolonged by pimobendan treatment.110 The
variables that consistently show the highest prognostic value for disease progression from preclinical
disease/ACVIM stage B into severe disease/ACVIM stage C, or overall survival, include degree and rate
of increase in cardiac size (VHS radiographic score [Figure 232.3], LA size (LA/Ao) and LV enddiastolic dimension estimated by echocardiography). Other variables have also been shown to have
prognostic value, including age, sex, breed, heart rate, severity of valve lesions, severity of MR, diastolic
E wave velocity, and circulating concentrations of NT-proBNP and cTnI.72,78,79,101,110,111,114,123,113,133135
More than 50% of dogs that develop CHF due to MMVD do not survive more than 1 year after the
diagnosis has been established.123,130 After the onset of CHF (ACVIM stage C or D), the expected
survival time has been shown to decrease with worsening exercise tolerance, decreased appetite and
development of cardiac cachexia (ch. 151), worsened severity of mitral valve prolapse, increasing
maintenance dosage of furosemide, increasing cardiac size and severity of MR, worsening systolic
function (increased LV end-systolic dimension), and decreasing serum creatinine concentration
(indicating cardiac cachexia [ch. 151]).72,78,123,128,130 The evidence that breed affects the outcome is
currently not conclusive, but there are some indications that suggest this.123 Furthermore, the
development of a complication, such as PH, syncopal events, arrhythmia (e.g., atrial fibrillation) and
rupture of a major chorda tendinea, is associated with a worse clinical outcome.53,85,100,130 Treatment
of ACVIM stage C dogs with a diuretic in combination with pimobendan or an ACE inhibitor has been
shown to increase the survival time,123,128,129 although combining pimobendan and an ACE inhibitor
with furosemide was recently shown to not confer survival benefit in stage C MMVD dogs.130 Dogs
already receiving intensive CHF therapy (stage D dogs) that develop severe and fulminant pulmonary
edema have a poor prognosis, and euthanasia should be considered in these cases.

INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS
Infective endocarditis (IE) involves microbial colonization of the endothelial surfaces of the heart,
primarily of the heart valves and the mural endocardium, commonly resulting in proliferative or erosive
lesions of the affected cardiac structures. Major complications such as CHF and consequences of
embolization (e.g., renal dysfunction, ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, abscess formation in
multiple organs) may occur.136

OCCURRENCE
IE is a comparatively rare clinical condition with reported incidences of approximately 0.1% in dogs
based on case series from veterinary teaching hospitals.137,138 However, the true incidence is presumed
to be considerably higher. The risk of developing IE is substantially lower in cats compared to
dogs.139,140 Signalment risk factors associated with IE in dogs include male sex, belonging to a medium
or large breed, and being middle-aged.141,142 Certain congenital heart diseases, such as subaortic
stenosis143 and patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)144 have been associated with an increased risk of
developing IE in dogs, but a more recent report questions these associations.145 Dogs with MMVD have
not been shown to have a higher risk for IE, despite exposure to dental procedures and infectious
processes.145

ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS

Bacterial infection at any location that causes intermittent or persistent bacteremia can lead to IE, but
the source and location of infection may not be readily identified.146 Fungal infections of the heart
valves are uncommon, but have been reported.147,148 Foreign bodies, which were either implanted in the
cardiovascular system to correct a congenital heart defect or migrated to the heart, have been reported
to have caused IE.148,149 Acute manifestations of IE have been described to be more commonly
associated with Gram-negative bacteremia, and subacute or chronic conditions to be more commonly
associated with Gram-positive bacteremia.138,150 Bacteria described associated with IE in dogs and cats
include Staphylococcus spp. (S. aureus, S. pseudintermedius, coagulase-positive and coagulasenegative), Streptococcus spp. (S. canis, S. bovis, and beta-hemolytic), Bartonella spp., Escherichia coli,
Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae and Corynebacterium spp.138,139,146,151-153 In
some geographic locations, Bartonella spp. have been reported as a common cause for IE.138 Bartonella
infection has been suggested to occur via ticks and fleas as vectors, and concurrent seroreactivity to
Ehrlichia canis, Anaplasma phagocytophilum and Rickettsia rickettsii (ch. 193) have been reported as
common findings in dogs with IE caused by Bartonella spp.138 (ch. 191).
Depression of the immune system (ch. 180) or endothelial damage, with or without depositions of
platelet-fibrin complexes, may enable bacteria to adhere to the endocardial surface and create IE.145,154
Degradation of the structure of involved cardiac tissue progresses further due to inflammation in
combination with enzymes released from the bacteria. The bacteria may be protected from the immune
system and from antibiotics by becoming internalized within the endothelial and other cells,154 which
allows continued bacterial growth.
The consequences of IE are influenced by several factors, such as the virulence of the infective agent,
site of infection, degree of exo- or endotoxin production, formation of circulating immunocomplexes,
degree of valvular destruction and thereby the influence of vegetations on valvular function, and seeding
of septic thrombi leading to infarcted organs and metastatic infections.141,155,156 Necrosis and
destruction of the valve stroma and/or chordae tendineae may cause acute severe valvular regurgitation
and CHF, and deposition of immunocomplexes can lead to consequences such as glomerulonephritis
(ch. 302), encephalitis (ch. 242), panosteitis (chs. 31, 162), myositis, or polyarthritis (ch. 177).142
Clinical signs caused by thromboembolic complications (chs. 219, 238) have been reported in
approximately 30-40% of dogs with IE,142,145 where the lungs have been reported to be the most
common site for embolization followed by the kidneys and the distal part of the aorta.145

PATHOLOGY
The mitral and aortic valves (Figure 232.7) are considerably more commonly affected by IE compared
to the tricuspid (Figure 232.8, A-D) or the pulmonic valve, and the mitral valve is slightly more
commonly affected than the aortic.142,145,136 The mural endocardium may also be affected, particularly
in cases of aortic IE.157 The vegetative lesion (macroscopic, often cauliflower-shaped mass) is usually
covered by an intact endothelium and consists of layers of fibrin, platelets, bacteria, and blood cells.

CLINICAL PRESENTATION
In many IE patients, presenting signs might be nonspecific and represent the consequence of
complications associated with IE. Accordingly, signs vary and they occur in different combinations, such
that IE can easily be overlooked as a differential diagnosis. The case history (ch. 2), including details
about clinical signs and medical history, in combination with physical examination findings (ch. 3) can
raise the suspicion of a diagnosis of IE. Predisposing factors that may raise the suspicion of IE include a
recent history of immunosuppressive drug therapy, such as corticosteroids,141,145 infected wounds,
abscesses, chronic bacterial skin infections, non-oral surgery within 3 months, infections in the oral or
genital tract secondary to trauma to the mucosal surfaces in these body regions, and indwelling
catheters.145 Infectious endocarditis patients lacking identifiable portals of entry are challenging to
approach due to the lack of guidelines when systematically searching for the source of infection.

The majority (50-90%) of dogs with IE presents with sustained or undulant fever (ch. 16).141,142 In
some cases, absence of fever can be the result of treatment already initiated with antibiotics or
corticosteroids before the diagnosis was established. Furthermore, patients with IE of the aortic valve
have more frequently been reported to be afebrile, which potentially is attributable to Bartonella
infections because these have been shown to be associated with afebrile infections.142 Because IE may
result in thromboembolism and/or precipitation of immune complexes in several organs, affected
animals may present with nonspecific signs, such as lethargy, anorexia, respiratory abnormalities,
weakness, weight loss, abdominal pain, gastrointestinal disturbances, and neurological signs.141,142
Lameness has been reported as a common presenting sign, occurring in 30-50% of dogs with IE (chs.
31 and 32). It is suspected to be caused by immune-mediated or septic polyarthritis (ch. 177) and/or
peripheral arterial thromboembolism (ch. 238).137 Clinical signs of CHF due to significant valve
insufficiency have been reported in approximately 50% of dogs diagnosed with IE.138,150 Patients with
IE may, furthermore, present with or develop cardiac arrhythmias (ch. 230), primarily of ventricular
origin, and these may cause syncopal events or even sudden cardiac death (ch. 40).146,158

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Patients with suspected IE should have the body temperature thoroughly monitored because undulant
or persistent fever is a common finding (ch. 16).141,142 Cardiac auscultation of patients with IE may
reveal a murmur, which is usually a consequence of valve insufficiency (ch. 38).142,145 A murmur has
been reported to be present in ∼75% of canine IE cases.145 A recently-developed murmur in a patient
presenting with other typical historical and clinical signs of IE should increase the suspicion of IE. The
timing of the murmur can be systolic, diastolic or both, depending on the location of the valve
insufficiency.141,145 Vegetative IE lesions of the aortic valve often obstruct the aortic outflow tract,
leading to a systolic murmur over the aortic valve area. Severe aortic regurgitation (AR) may also (if
audible) generate a diastolic murmur. Severe AR is uncommon in the general dog population, and even
if they are incidental findings, the combination of a diastolic murmur and bounding peripheral pulse
should raise the suspicion of IE of the aortic valve. Vegetative IE of both the mitral and aortic valve can
lead to both diastolic and systolic murmurs (so called “to and fro” murmurs). A similar murmur can be
noted when a large aortic vegetative lesion partially obstructs aortic valve outflow during systole and
causes aortic valve regurgitation during diastole (

Audio 232.6).

Dogs with severe valve insufficiency may present with signs of CHF such as tachypnea and increased
respiratory effort in the case of left-sided CHF and ascites and/or pleural effusion in the case of rightsided CHF (see Physical Examination for MMVD patients, above; ch. 229). A range of other physical
findings may be present due to precipitation of immunocomplexes or septic embolization in different
organs.141,142,146

ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIC FINDINGS
Echocardiography is crucial for establishing a clinical diagnosis of IE (ch. 97). Two-dimensional
echocardiography may allow visualization of valvular vegetations (

Videos 232.20 to 232.22, and

Figures 232.7; 232.8, A; and 232.8, B) that commonly appear hyperechoic with an irregular outline.
The vegetations may move with the blood flow independently of the valve.141 Other valve damage of
different severities may be present in the form of mitral valve chordal rupture and avulsion of aortic

valve cusps. Mitral or AR may be detected using spectral or color-flow Doppler echocardiography.
Assessment of severity of MR is described in the MMVD section, above. Because moderate to severe AR
is comparatively uncommon, identification of moderate to severe AR on the color echocardiogram
should raise the suspicion of IE of that valve. The differential diagnosis for AR includes congenital aortic
stenosis (ch. 231), myxomatous lesions (usually results in only mild AR), severe systemic hypertension
(ch. 236), and bi- or quadricuspid aortic valve (comparatively uncommon congenital malformations).

ELECTROCARDIOGRAPHIC FINDINGS (CH. 230)
An arrhythmia is reported to be a comparatively common finding in cases with IE, occurring in 50-75%
of dogs with IE.141,142 Common forms of arrhythmia in IE include ventricular premature complexes and
sustained or non-sustained ventricular tachycardia. Third-degree atrioventricular block has been
reported in dogs with IE, but this finding is uncommon. Cardiac chamber dilatation in chronic IE may
result in changes to PQRS deflections, and the nature of these are dependent on the location and degree
of enlargement. However, all the mentioned ECG abnormalities are nonspecific for IE.

RADIOGRAPHIC FINDINGS
Findings on radiographs are usually not specific for IE, but they can be useful for assessing the
consequences of the condition. Left-sided cardiac enlargement may be present in cases with IE affecting
the aortic or mitral valve, particularly in cases with chronic IE. However, a comparatively large
proportion of dogs with CHF caused by aortic or mitral valve IE has been reported to present normal or
near-normal radiographic cardiac size.138 Infiltrates caused by pulmonary edema have been reported in
∼50% of dogs with IE, and this proportion was similar in dogs with IE of the mitral valve and the aortic
valve.138,142

IDENTIFICATION OF INFECTIVE MICROORGANISM
Blood Cultures
Blood cultures are important for establishing a definitive diagnosis of IE and for choosing appropriate
antimicrobial treatment, but as many as 60-70% of blood cultures have been reported to be negative in
dogs with IE.138 The absence of growth may be attributable to many factors, including “encapsulation”
of chronic infections, absence of bacteria in a vegetation, failure to grow organisms from samples, and a
high proportion of dogs receiving antimicrobial therapy prior to blood culture sampling.138 Collection
and handling of samples should be conducted aseptically (ch. 184).

Polymerase Chain Reaction and Serologic Testing
Sensitive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) methods can be used as an alternative to blood culture to
identify bacterial nucleic acid in blood, and thus, bacteremia (ch. 184). The general clinical usefulness
of PCR for the diagnosis of IE appears to be limited in small animal veterinary patients as PCR has been
reported to be no more sensitive for diagnosing bacteremia than blood culture in dogs with or without
IE.159 PCR method is widely used for diagnosing an ongoing Bartonella spp. infection, due to difficulties
associated with culturing Bartonella spp.153 Serologic testing is otherwise the method of choice to
investigate previous exposure to Bartonella spp. and to monitor the course of the disease (ch.
191).139,153

OTHER LABORATORY FINDINGS
Mild regenerative anemia (ch. 57) is found in 50-60% of cases with IE.139,141-142,145 As with anemias
found in other states of chronic inflammation, it is usually normocytic and normochromic. Leukocytosis
(ch. 58), usually characterized by neutrophilia and monocytosis (+/– left shift), has been reported in

∼80% of dogs with IE.142,145 Thrombocytopenia (ch. 59) is reported in ∼50% of IE cases.142 There are
few reports of C-reactive peptide (CRP), which is a nonspecific test for inflammatory processes, in the
veterinary literature, but concentrations are likely to be increased in cases of active IE. This is in
agreement with the authors’ experience. Likewise, although increased serum concentrations of the
cardiac-specific tests NT-proBNP and cardiac-specific troponin I (cTnI) are likely present in patients
with IE,157 these findings are not specific for IE and are caused by the consequences of IE rather than IE
itself. Increased concentrations of blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, and alkaline phosphatase, and
decreased concentrations of serum glucose and albumin/total proteins, represent other common
laboratory findings in IE.137,139,142 Urinalysis (ch. 70) may show proteinuria, hemoglobinuria,
hematuria, pyuria, and/or bacteriuria. A urine sample, preferably obtained by cystocentesis (ch. 98),
should be collected and cultured in an attempt to isolate the infective microorganism in patients with
suspected IE.

DIAGNOSIS
Although a diagnosis of IE may be suspected in many animals, a definitive diagnosis of IE includes a
pathologic examination, which is not possible in the living dog. The diagnosis of IE is often based on
identification of more than 1 major and/or minor criteria for IE. A scoring system, based on a set of
major and minor criteria and adapted from the modified Duke criteria for IE in people,156,160 has been
proposed for dogs and cats (Table 232.2)139,146 to aid in the recognition of a “possible” or “definitive”
clinical diagnosis of IE.

MANAGEMENT
Infectious endocarditis confers a guarded prognosis in dogs and cats. An early diagnosis and immediate
and intensive treatment aimed at eradicating the infective microorganism and to treat all secondary
complications are vital for a successful outcome.156 Possible complicating conditions, such as CHF (ch.
229) or kidney injury (chs. 300 and 301), suggest a worse prognosis. Such complications should be
identified as soon as possible because they may need specific attention and treatment, may affect the
antibiotic protocol decision, and may affect the prognosis.142 Outcome is also dependent on
identification and immediate intensive treatment of the primary source of infection, e.g., using surgical
drainage or debridement.156
The choice of antibiotic depends on the location of the primary source of infection, because organ
distribution and tissue penetration differ for different antibiotics (ch. 140). Geographical distribution of
antibiotic resistance is also important for antibiotic selection. The potential outcome of treatment is
dependent on an antibiotic sensitivity profile, which may be available in cases where the bacteria
involved have been successfully identified (ch. 7). While waiting for various test results, intravenous
treatment should commence using a broad-spectrum antibiotic IV, e.g., beta-lactam antibiotics, such as
amoxicillin 20 mg/kg IV q8h.146 An aminoglycoside, such as amikacin 20 mg/kg IV q24h can be
combined with beta-lactam antibiotics to obtain a more complete spectrum (ch. 140).146 However,
aminoglycosides are potentially nephrotoxic and are only recommended to be used for a limited time.
Furthermore, patients receiving aminoglycoside therapy IV should be supported with IV fluids.
Aminoglycosides should be avoided in patients with CHF because concurrent furosemide therapy can
enhance nephrotoxicity. Alternatives to aminoglycosides are enrofloxacin (5 mg/kg IV q12h [q24h in
cats]) or marbofloxacin (2 mg/kg IV q24h) for suspected Gram-negative IE, but their usefulness may be
limited at different geographical sites owing to local resistance patterns to fluoroquinolone antibiotics.
The initial treatment outlined above is similar for dogs with suspected IE caused by Bartonella spp. The
benefit of antithrombotic therapy is unknown, but such treatment may be considered (ch. 238).

Possible endocarditis: Findings consistent with IE with insufficient criteria for “definite,” but the
diagnosis is not rejected
Reject diagnosis of IE: Alternate diagnosis, or resolution of clinical signs with short-term antibiotic
therapy (<4 weeks), or no histopathologic evidence of IE.

DOGS
CATS
The veterinary criteria are adapted from the Modified Duke criteria used in human medicine for the
diagnosis of IE.160 From Palerme et al.139 based on previously published criteria with consensus of 3
or more references in the veterinary literature.
AR, Aortic regurgitation; BAPGM, Bartonella alpha-proteobacteria growth media; IE, infective
endocarditis; IV, intravenous; PCR, polymerase chain reaction; SAS, subaortic stenosis.
The clinical response to treatment should be carefully monitored to evaluate the effectiveness of
therapy. IV Intensive antibiotic treatment may be indicated for 1-2 weeks in some patients. When the
patient is eating and is hemodynamically stable, SC or PO administration may replace IV treatment. In
cases with positive culture results, treatment with appropriate antibiotics should be initiated as soon as
possible according to bacterial sensitivity results. In cases with negative culture results, the decision to
continue or cease antibiotic therapy should be based on the animal’s clinical status and response to the
initial treatment and whether or not a clinical suspicion of IE remains. The duration of appropriate
antibiotic therapy in IE has been suggested to be at least 6 weeks, but there is limited information
supporting this strategy in veterinary patients. The duration of therapy is influenced by the ability to
eliminate the inciting cause, severity of lesions, and nature of the infective agent. Repeated blood
cultures may be performed at 1-2 weeks after initiation of therapy, and at 1-2 weeks after the termination
of therapy, but this may be difficult to routinely practice in all patients for different reasons (i.e.,
negative initial blood cultures or due to financial and practical reasons). Repeated echocardiographic
examinations, blood panels, and urinalyses are recommended during and after antibiotic therapy to
monitor therapeutic response and identify possible complications.146,156,160 Repeated serologic titers
can be performed 1 month after the initiation of antibiotic therapy in animals diagnosed with IE caused
by Bartonella.146 A significant reduction in titer indicates effective treatment, whereas an increased titer
suggests ineffective treatment, indicating that a change of antibiotic may be appropriate. Repeated PCR
testing may be considered as an alternative to serologic titers. Treatment of animals in CHF and/or with
arrhythmia is outlined in chs. 229 and 230, respectively.

PROGNOSIS
Several factors have been associated with the outcome of IE in dogs and cats. A worse outcome is
associated with a late-established diagnosis and late start of therapy,156 aortic valve involvement,
valvular vegetation,138,142 infections with Gram-negative bacteria including infections with Bartonella
spp. (most commonly associated with aortic IE),150 cardiac and/or renal complications, septic
embolization and metastatic infections, thrombocytopenia,142 elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase,
hypoproteinemia/hypoalbuminemia,137 concurrent treatment with corticosteroids with or without
concurrent antibiotic treatment (ch. 227),141 treatment with inappropriate antibiotics, and premature
termination of therapy. Factors reported to indicate a more favorable prognosis include isolated mitral
valve involvement,138 infection with Gram-positive bacteria, and infections originating from the
integument, such as skin abscesses, cellulitis, or wound infections.145

PREVENTION
Invasive cardiovascular diagnostic or therapeutic procedures, e.g., pacemaker implantation, balloon
valvuloplasty, or closure of PDA or VSD, may require prophylactic antibiotic treatment 1-2 hours before
and 6 hours after the procedure.156 Amoxicillin may be the first choice, but other antibiotics, such as
clindamycin, may also be considered depending on the organ system involved in the intervention (e.g.,
skin, gastrointestinal tract, urinary system).154 Routine prophylactic antibiotic treatment of all dogs with
MMVD undergoing dental procedures is not indicated, because geriatric dogs with MMVD rarely
develop IE following these procedures.145

CLIENT INFORMATION
Myxomatous Mitral Valve Disease (MMVD)
Myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) is the most common heart disease of adult dogs. The disease
is most commonly seen in dogs of small to medium-sized breeds, such as Cavalier King Charles Spaniel
(CKCS), Dachshunds, Miniature Poodles, and Yorkshire Terriers, but dogs of any breeds can be affected.
The underlying cause of MMVD is currently not known, but the disease is, to a large extent inherited,
and accordingly developed due to the influence by various genes. It is an age-related weakening of the
valve tissue within the heart. It is also called mitral valve disease, mitral regurgitation (a broader term),
mitral valve endocardiosis (very different from endocarditis), and degenerative mitral valve disease.
Affected dogs have no signs of valve abnormalities at birth, but develop MMVD later in life. The
disease is characterized by ongoing lesions of the mitral valve, which is the valve in between the left
atrium and the left ventricle in the heart. The valve leaflets, which normally are thin, translucent and
soft, become scarred with disease worsening. The valve lesions lead to valve leakage (commonly referred
to as mitral regurgitation). The severity of valve leakage is dependent on the severity of valve lesions:
usually it is mild in the early stages, when there are no symptoms and the only abnormality is a murmur
heard with a stethoscope, but it can increase gradually over time to more severe forms.
Dogs with MMVD are asymptomatic for most of the time they have the disease. Evolution of the
disease occurs at different rates in different dogs, but dogs can usually have the disease for years without
showing any abnormal behavior or external signs, and also tolerate exercise and outdoor activities well.
Evidence of reduced exercise tolerance and weakness might be noted when the disease has reached more
severe stages, although it is important to remember that adult dogs can have other conditions, such as
degenerative joint disease, excessive body weight, and primary airway disorders, that cause similar
symptoms.
In some dogs, the valve leakage might eventually become so severe that pulmonary edema due to
congestive heart failure develops. Early signs of congestive heart failure are usually mild but may be
aggravated within days or sometimes weeks. Increased respiratory rate and effort are present when
pulmonary congestion and edema have developed. Coughing is also commonly observed, although many
unrelated causes of coughing exist in dogs too. Dogs with acute signs of congestive heart failure are often
anxious and restless during the night, unable to get comfortable, and if they previously preferred to lie
on their sides or on their backs, they may switch to preferring to lie on their bellies. Furthermore, dogs
with MMVD that has reached the point of causing congestive heart failure are often inactive and have
varying degrees of decreased appetite. Some dogs may also experience abrupt spells of fainting. In some
affected dogs, signs of right-sided CHF, such as abdominal distention caused by free fluid in the
abdomen, and/or gastrointestinal signs such as diarrhea and/or vomiting, may be present. Since these
clinical signs are nonspecific, confirmation of MMVD and especially of the presence or absence of
congestive heart failure, requires veterinary attention.
A heart murmur, detectable by a veterinarian using a stethoscope during a physical examination
(auscultation), is a prominent clinical finding in MMVD-affected dogs. The murmur originates from
vibrations primarily caused by the turbulent flow of blood leaking backwards through the degenerated
leaflets of the mitral valve up into the left atrium. Murmurs can be classified according to their intensity,
and murmurs caused by MMVD tend to gradually increase in intensity with severity of the disease; this
usually occurs gradually (months to years) and a murmur that has become louder does not automatically
indicate a severe problem. The diagnosis of MMVD can be confirmed by an ultrasound examination of
the heart. Once MMVD is detected, its progression can be monitored by ultrasound, radiography (Xrays), and physical examinations. Dogs with MMVD should regularly be examined by a veterinarian,
because even if the dog appears completely normal, the disease might have caused the heart to enlarge.
If heart enlargement is detected by ultrasound or radiographic examinations, medication with a drug
called pimobendan can significantly prolong the period before the dog shows signs of heart failure.
At home, it is useful for a dog’s family or caretaker to monitor the dog’s respiratory pattern and
sleeping (or resting) respiratory rates at home. This is best done when the dog is located in a
“thermoneutral environment,” meaning normal room temperature, and asleep or at rest. The sleeping
(and resting) respiratory rates are usually less than 30/min in dogs whose lungs are clear of fluid. If the
sleeping respiratory rate is consistently above 30/min on repeated examinations at home, a veterinarian
should be contacted as this can be an indication of fluid accumulation in the lungs (congestive heart
failure in development).
The way dogs with mild to moderate congestive heart failure are managed is centered on giving
medications daily at home. The cornerstone of treating congestive heart failure is a diuretic drug, and

drugs with other modes of action are added to the diuretic agent. Regular contacts by phone or email
should be maintained with the veterinarian when the dog is managed at home in order to monitor
therapeutic outcome and to establish a suitable maintenance dosage of diuretic. Disease evolution may
be monitored at regular rechecks. Strenuous exercise and diets with high sodium content should be
avoided in dogs with congestive heart failure due to MMVD.
Ingrid Ljungvall (Uppsala, Sweden) and Jens Häggström (Uppsala, Sweden)

Myocardial diseases are those that affect the heart muscle
(cardiomyocytes and interstitium), distinct from those primarily
affecting the valves (chs. 231 and 232), endocardium (ch. 231), or
pericardium (ch. 235). The most common myocardial diseases in
dogs are in the group of cardiomyopathies, including dilated
cardiomyopathy and arrhythmogenic right ventricular
cardiomyopathy. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, while very common
in cats (ch. 234), is rare in dogs. Other canine myocardial diseases
include myocarditis, myocardial infarction, muscular dystrophies,
and neoplasia (chs. 235 and 325).

DILATED CARDIOMYOPATHY
Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is the second most common
acquired heart disease in dogs after degenerative mitral valve
disease. DCM is classically characterized by left ventricular (LV) or
biventricular systolic dysfunction and dilatation (Figure 233.1) that
is not attributable to underlying disorders that cause abnormal
cardiac loading conditions such as volume overload states, shunts or
other congenital cardiac disease, valve disease, primary
tachyarrhythmias, or systemic hypertension.1 The importance of the
latter is recognition that ventricular dilatation and systolic
dysfunction can represent a morphologic and functional response
common to a variety of potential insults, and the identification of
these features (phenotype) alone does not automatically indicate a
diagnosis of DCM. Furthermore, while the classic phenotype is a
dilated and hypokinetic heart, DCM can manifest as a spectrum of

functional and electrical abnormalities, which often differ by breed,
including arrhythmic and intermediate phenotypes.1,2

PREVALENCE, BREED AND AGE
DISTRIBUTION
The prevalence of DCM among the general canine population is
unknown. The reported prevalence in historical canine referral
populations has been 0.5-1% (1-2 cases per 200 patients examined),3
but this may be influenced by geographic differences in breeds and
ages examined, degree of prospective screening of high-risk breeds,
and true changes in epigenetic factors over time. Large breeds are
predominantly affected and highly predisposed breeds include the
Doberman Pinscher (DP), Great Dane, Irish Wolfhound (IW),
Newfoundland, Boxer, Saint Bernard, Labrador and Golden
Retriever, while the Cocker Spaniel, Portuguese Water Dog, and Toy
Manchester Terrier are smaller affected breeds.3-9 DCM is typically
an adult-onset disease; however, juvenile forms are reported
including in the Portuguese Water Dog, DP, and Toy Manchester
Terrier.5,9,10
More is known about breed-specific prevalence. Prevalence
estimates in the DP increase from 10% in 2- to 4-year-olds to 44% in
dogs over 6 years of age, around the median age of diagnosis.11 There
are sex differences in how the disease manifests in DPs, with females
having a higher incidence of an arrhythmic phenotype and males
having LV dilatation and systolic dysfunction at an earlier age.11
Prevalence in the IW is up to 25% in large screening studies, with
earlier mean age of onset (4 years) and males more commonly
affected and at a younger age.12 Prevalence up to 36% has been
reported in the Great Dane13 and 10% in the Newfoundland.14

ETIOLOGY

DCM may have a genetic or non-genetic etiology, with the former
likely playing a role in many canine cases (Table 233.1).6,15 The
nature of genetic etiology is complex, with increasing recognition of
interplay between genetic and non-genetic factors such as lifestyle,
diet, and environment (epigenetics), potential for multiple gene
involvement (oligogenic inheritance rather than monogenic), and
variability in both penetrance (probability of manifesting the
phenotype) and expression (wide spectrum of phenotypes when
expressed).6,15 Familial DCM accounts for 30% or more of human
DCM cases, with mutations in over 50 genes identified to date. Most
encode for sarcomeric or cytoskeletal proteins leading to altered
cardiac protein structure and function.1 By comparison, the
proportion of canine DCM cases attributable to inherited genetic
mutations is unknown and specific genetic mutations identified to
date are few. Mutations in two genes (pyruvate dehydrogenase
kinase 4, a mitochondrial enzyme; and titin, a sarcomeric protein)
with autosomal dominant inheritance are associated with DCM in
the DP in North America.16 These mutations do not account for all
cases in this breed, and another unidentified locus is suggested to be
associated with DCM in European DP, highlighting the genetic
heterogeneity that exists even within a breed.17 A mutation in the
phospholamban gene (a protein regulating the calcium pump of the
sarcoplasmic reticulum) was recently identified in a family of Welsh
Springer Spaniels with highly penetrant DCM causing sudden
death.18

Non-genetic causes of DCM include nutritional, drugs or toxins,
and chronic manifestation of myocarditis. An association between
taurine deficiency and canine DCM has been described in American
and English Cocker Spaniels, Golden Retrievers, and sporadically in
other breeds.4,19-22 Taurine is a free amino acid with important roles
in bile acid conjugation, central nervous system development, and
cardiac contractility and osmoregulation, and deficiency may occur
through insufficient dietary intake or bioavailability of taurine or its
precursors, or abnormal utilization or excretion.23 Myocardial Lcarnitine deficiency was described in a small family of Boxer dogs
with DCM; however, there is little other information linking cause
and effect in this or other breeds.24 Other speculated nutritional
causes of DCM include chronic consumption of low-protein diets,
limited and novel ingredient diets, and possibly some legume-rich or

grain-free diets (ch. 157).23,25,26 The most common drug toxicosis
associated with development of a DCM phenotype in dogs is
doxorubicin (also see ch. 321).27 The incidence of cardiotoxicosis
appears to be similar to humans (<5% with the typical doses used in
veterinary medicine), though factors associated with increased risk
include higher cumulative dose, higher body weight, and breeds
already predisposed to DCM.28 Several causes of myocarditis are
known to cause a DCM phenotype in the chronic phase of infection
(see below). The above-mentioned non-genetic causes may account
for a low percentage of total DCM cases, but are worthy of
consideration as contributing factors depending on clinical
presentation and geographic area because of potentially important
differences in treatment and prognosis.

PHENOTYPES AND CLINICAL STAGES
Dogs with DCM experience a preclinical phase (occult phase) during
which there is echocardiographic or electrocardiographic evidence of
disease but clinical signs are absent as perceived by the dog’s owner.
The duration of this phase may last months to years and importantly
may be modified by treatment.29-31 Both the phenotype expressed
and the duration of the preclinical phase may vary between breeds.
Some dogs manifest arrhythmias before echocardiographic changes:
ventricular arrhythmias (VA) in DPs11,32 and Great Danes,13 and
atrial fibrillation (AF) in IWs.33,34 Alternatively, ventricular
dilatation and systolic dysfunction may often be recognized first (
Video 233.1). Intermediate forms characterized by either
ventricular dilatation or systolic dysfunction in isolation may also be
recognized and may represent very early or developing forms of
DCM (

Video 233.2).2,14 Furthermore, there are subtle but

recognized differences among breeds regarding ventricular geometry
and function in DCM. DP with DCM tend to have quite profound
systolic dysfunction, while IWs and some Newfoundlands may

exhibit more ventricular dilatation (left and right) and less severe
systolic dysfunction.12,14,33
The clinical phase of DCM is the result of progressive systolic
dysfunction, ventricular dilatation, and/or worsening arrhythmias
precipitating heart failure, syncope, and/or sudden death (
Videos 233.3 and 233.4). Heart failure may manifest as backward
failure—that is, congestive heart failure (CHF) causing fluid
congestion in the lungs (left-sided CHF) or cavitary spaces (rightsided CHF), and/or as forward heart failure, in which signs of poor
cardiac output predominate (ch. 229). Sudden death may be the
first clinical sign or may occur after the onset of CHF, and is more
common in some breeds than others. It is the first clinical sign for
25-30% of DP with DCM.32

CLINICAL PRESENTATION
Dogs with preclinical DCM are identified through active cardiac
screening programs (high-risk breeds, breeding dogs) or following
detection of a cardiac abnormality on physical examination such as a
heart murmur or arrhythmia. Many dogs in this phase will have a
normal physical examination.
In most clinical settings, dogs are presented due to the onset of
clinical signs, with respiratory signs due to left-sided CHF including
tachypnea, dyspnea, and cough being most common (ch. 37) (
Video 233.5).7,8 Other signs include those associated with forward
heart failure like weakness, exercise intolerance, and syncope, which
may predominate in some cases (ch. 40).7,8 It is common for
Newfoundlands, IWs, and dogs with AF to present with signs of right
heart failure (tachypnea/dyspnea due to pleural effusion and
ascites).35-37 Nonspecific signs including weight loss and hyporexia
may also be noted. Physical examination (ch. 3) may reveal a low
intensity heart murmur (≤ grade 3/6) over the mitral or tricuspid
area (ch. 38) and weak femoral pulses (ch. 39). In retrospective
studies, as few as 33% but as many as 76% of dogs with DCM were
reported to have heart murmurs, highlighting the potential for a

normal auscultation even in the setting of clinical disease.7,8 Other
abnormalities may include a low frequency third heart sound
(gallop), arrhythmia, increased bronchovesicular sounds or crackles
on pulmonary auscultation, diminished breath sounds with pleural
effusion, pale or cyanotic mucous membranes, hepatomegaly, or
palpable abdominal fluid wave.

DIAGNOSIS
Establishing a diagnosis of DCM necessitates a minimum of
echocardiography (ch. 97) and electrocardiography (ECG), the latter
by longer-term ambulatory recording (Holter) in some cases (ch.
96). Complementary diagnostics can include cardiac biomarkers,
whole blood or plasma taurine levels, thoracic radiography, and
genetic tests in the DP. Given the spectrum of phenotypes described
and the potential for other disorders to produce a similar phenotype
(imposters, Table 233.1), it is not surprising that diagnosis can be
challenging. In the preclinical phase, a diagnosis is not always
certain on the basis of one examination and serial examinations may
be necessary (

Video 233.2). Guidelines for the diagnosis of

canine DCM have been proposed utilizing a scoring system involving
major and minor criteria, though these have yet to be prospectively
validated.2 There are breed-specific guidelines for the DP based on
years of prospective observation.38

Echocardiography
Identification of ventricular dilatation and systolic dysfunction forms
the basis of echocardiographic diagnosis (

Videos 233.3 and

233.6). Ventricular dilatation may be identified by measuring LV
dimension, typically on a short- or long-axis motion-mode (M-mode)
image or alternatively on two-dimensional images if proper
alignment cannot be achieved (Figure 233.2, A and B). A more
sensitive means to identify LV dilatation for more experienced
sonographers is by calculation of LV volume using Simpson’s method
of discs, which involves tracing the LV endocardium on a long-axis or

apical four-chamber view and use of augmented software (Figure
233.2, C). Use of calculated LV volumes derived from linear
dimensions (e.g., Teichholz formula) should be avoided due to their
inaccuracy. Systolic function is best assessed using LV end-systolic
dimension or volume (using the techniques described above) and
calculated ejection fraction: ([LV end-diastolic volume − LV endsystolic volume] / LV end-diastolic volume) × 100%. Breed-specific,
and sometimes sex-specific, reference intervals for LV dimensions,
volumes, and systolic function indices should be used whenever
possible given the influence of breed on cardiac size.12,13,33,38 When
not available, prediction intervals derived from allometric scaling of
ventricular dimensions and volumes in large populations of varioussized dogs may be used.39-41 LV fractional shortening is a calculated
value derived from linear dimensions: ([LV end-diastolic dimension
− LV end-systolic dimension] / LV end-diastolic dimension) × 100%;
it is an unreliable index of systolic function and should not be used in
isolation.
An accurate diagnosis also requires recognition of imposters—that
is, other disorders that can produce a similar phenotype, which are
summarized in Table 233.1. An important differential for DCM
particularly in young dogs is tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy
(TICM), a condition characterized by a primary tachyarrhythmia
resulting secondarily in ventricular dilatation and systolic
dysfunction. Recognition, often involving Holter monitoring, has
important implications for treatment and prognosis, because
treatment or resolution of the tachyarrhythmia can result in reversal
of the secondary cardiac remodeling and normalization of cardiac
chamber dimensions (

Videos 230.1 and 233.7).42

Left atrial dilation may be found with more advanced disease and
in those with CHF or AF. Right ventricular (RV) and atrial dilation,
which are largely assessed subjectively but may be quantitated, are
found with biventricular disease and often with AF (

Videos

233.4 and 233.6).36 Doppler findings can include secondary mitral
regurgitation due to annulus dilation and papillary muscle
dysfunction, evidence of diastolic dysfunction (abnormal transmitral
flow patterns including impaired relaxation, pseudonormal, and

restrictive), reduced aortic velocities, and reduced myocardial tissue
velocities.8,43,44

Electrocardiography
Arrhythmias are frequently reported on ECG in dogs with clinical
DCM (89% of cases in one large retrospective study), with VA and AF
(ch. 230) being most common.7 VA are common in DPs and Great
Danes with DCM. Therefore, their presence should always raise
suspicion of the diagnosis in these breeds.13,32 AF is common in
Newfoundlands,37 in IWs with both clinical DCM (>95%) and
preclinical DCM (70%),12,35 and it is associated with future
development of the DCM phenotype in the IW when identified before
echocardiographic changes.33,34
Holter recordings (ch. 96) are useful for detecting arrhythmic
forms of DCM, seeking causes of collapse, and assessing candidacy
for and response to antiarrhythmic (AA) therapy. In DPs, the
presence of >300 premature ventricular complexes (PVCs) in 24
hours, or two subsequent recordings within a year with 50-300 PVCs
in 24 hours, is suggestive of DCM.38 Holter recording is also useful
for assessing heart rate (HR) control in AF. Holter analyses that have
been manually edited and verified by qualified personnel are
preferred over automated analyses which are often inaccurate.

Cardiac Biomarkers
Circulating cardiac biomarkers, including N-terminal pro-B-type
natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) and cardiac troponin-I (cTnI), can
be complementary tools but cannot replace echocardiography or
ECG in the diagnosis of DCM. Neither NT-proBNP nor cTnI is
specific for DCM; rather, elevated levels reflect increased myocardial
stress and stretch, and evidence of myocardial injury, respectively.
NT-proBNP has had sensitivity = 70-80% and specificity = 90% for
detecting preclinical DCM in the DP, with greater ability to detect
echocardiographic change than the arrhythmic form.45-47 High
sensitivity cTnI had sensitivity = 81% and specificity = 73% for

detecting DCM in the DP at a cut-off value of 0.113 ng/mL.48
Combining the two tests may increase detection accuracy in the
DP.47 NT-proBNP may also have utility in differentiating CHF from
primary respiratory disease in dogs presenting with respiratory signs
(ch. 229).49 This may have utility when physical exam and thoracic
radiography are ambiguous and echocardiography is not available,
but otherwise may not provide added value. It is important to note
that there can be substantive daily and weekly variability in NTproBNP values,50 as well as breed variability in normal values for
NT-proBNP, with breeds including Labradors and Newfoundlands
having higher normal values compared to other breeds.51

Taurine
Measurement of whole blood or plasma taurine is recommended in
Cocker Spaniels, Retrievers, any atypical DCM breed, or DCM cases
with a history of eating a lamb-based diet, vegetarian diet, lowprotein diet, or other non-traditional diet (ch. 157).4,19-23 Whole
blood taurine <150 nmol/mL and/or plasma taurine <40 nmol/mL
indicates significant taurine deficiency.52 Golden Retrievers may
have higher circulating taurine levels in health, necessitating
adjustment of reference values for this breed (low being <213
nmol/mL in whole blood and <63 nmol/mL in plasma).53 The
clinical importance of identification of low taurine is the implication
of at least a partial role in etiology, with the potential for
improvement with taurine supplementation and diet change.

Thoracic Radiography
Thoracic radiographs are indicated to evaluate and document
evidence of CHF (cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion,
pulmonary edema, pleural effusion; ch. 229). While cardiomegaly is
expected in advanced disease, thoracic radiographs may be relatively
insensitive to detect milder degrees of cardiac enlargement in
preclinical disease.

FIGURE 233.2 Techniques for echocardiographic
measurement of left ventricular (LV) dimensions. A,
Right parasternal short-axis two-dimensional image
at the level of the papillary muscles showing diastolic
