Diagnosis
Echocardiography is the essential diagnostic test to diagnose
pericardial effusion, and to help differentiate etiologies of pericardial
effusion. Radiographs and electrocardiograms are insensitive and
nonspecific, but may increase suspicion for pericardial disease in
some cases.

Thoracic Radiographs
Although the quintessential thoracic radiographic abnormalities of
globoid cardiomegaly with crisp cardiac margins are classic for
pericardial effusion (Figure 235.9), the reality is that radiographs
are both insensitive and nonspecific for pericardial effusion. In fact,
radiographic appearance of globoid cardiac silhouette was only
41.9% sensitive and 40% specific for the diagnosis of cardiac
tamponade and pericardial effusion in 50 dogs in one series, and was
present in approximately half of 107 dogs in another study.28,43
Cardiomegaly, defined as a vertebral heart score >10.7, also was
insensitive (sensitivity = 77.6%) and nonspecific (specificity = 47.8%)
for cardiac tamponade, likely due to rapid accumulations of small
volume pericardial effusion in acute tamponade.43 Pulmonary
hypoperfusion and diminished caudal vena caval size are common in
dogs with cardiogenic shock from acute cardiac tamponade.
Conversely, a dilated caudal vena cava, loss of abdominal detail, and
pleural effusion may be seen with more chronic cardiac tamponade,
and often are accompanied by the more classical globoid
cardiomegaly appearance. Identification of a cardiac mass on
radiographs (Figure 235.9) is insensitive but specific (100% in one
study), and was noted in 10 of 63 dogs with cardiac masses.28

Pulmonary metastases commonly occur (Figure 235.9), but
radiographs have a low detection rate: only 1/3 of necropsy- or
thoracotomy-confirmed cases with pulmonary metastases are
identified radiographically.28

FIGURE 235.10 Electrical alternans on the
electrocardiogram of a dog with severe pericardial
effusion. There is a beat-to-beat variation in QRS
amplitude due to the swinging of the heart in the
pericardial effusion, as well as dampened QRS
complexes (<1 mV). 50 mm/sec; 1 cm = 1 mV.

Tomographic Imaging
The use of multidetector computed tomography increases the
diagnostic sensitivity for detection of pulmonary metastases
compared to thoracic radiography, but does not increase the
diagnostic yield for detection of cardiac masses compared to
transthoracic echocardiography.44 Likewise, cardiac magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) does not increase diagnostic yield for
detection of cardiac masses in dogs with pericardial effusion
compared to echocardiography, but may provide descriptive
information on extent of disease, location, and tumor characteristics
if performed by specialists with extensive additional training in
cardiac MRI.45

Electrocardiography (ch. 96)

An electrocardiogram is indicated for any patient with an arrhythmia
ausculted on physical examination (chs. 3, 230), but it is not an
accurate diagnostic test for pericardial effusion. Abnormalities are
variably present, and in a series of 107 dogs included, in order of
occurrence: electrical alternans (30/107 dogs [28.0%]), sinus
tachycardia (30/107 dogs [28.0%]), dampened QRS voltage (lead II
R wave <1 mV) (26 dogs [24.3%]), and ventricular arrhythmia
(14/107 dogs [13.1%]).28 Electrical alternans is the beat-to-beat
variation in QRS amplitude caused by the heart swinging back and
forth in a large volume of pericardial effusion, and is rather specific
for pericardial effusion in dogs (Figure 235.10). Dampening of the
QRS voltages is due to pericardial effusion insulating the electrical
signal from being transmitted to the body surface, and it also may
occur with pleural effusion, obesity, large thoracic masses, or
hypothyroidism. Other less common electrocardiographic
abnormalities in dogs with pericardial effusion can include
supraventricular tachycardia (3/107 dogs [2.8%]), premature atrial
complexes (2/107 dogs [1.9%]), atrial fibrillation (2/107 dogs
[1.9%]), and ST segment changes (2/107 dog [1.9%]).28

Echocardiography (ch. 97)
Echocardiography is the essential test not only to confirm the
diagnosis of pericardial effusion on a triage-level scan, but, using
higher level scans, to provide additional information on possible
etiology of the effusion, whether pericardiocentesis is needed, and if
there is underlying structural or functional cardiac disease.
Echocardiographic detection of a cardiac mass is sensitive (82%) and
specific (100%) when performed by a cardiologist, which is similar
whether the mass involves the RA (82% and 99%, respectively) or
heart base (74% and 98%, respectively).28 Repeat echocardiographic
evaluation within weeks to months increases sensitivity (88%) for
detection of cardiac masses.28
Pericardial effusion appears as an anechoic space surrounding the
heart, within the pericardial space. The pericardium is seen external
to the anechoic fluid, and is often highlighted by the concurrent
presence of pleural effusion. Along with characteristic physical
examination findings, echocardiographic diagnosis of cardiac

tamponade is important to help define treatment strategies and
timing of pericardiocentesis. A relatively low pericardial fluid volume
can cause acute tamponade if it occurs very quickly, as may be seen
in acute hemorrhage from HSA. Conversely, in cases of slowly
accumulating pericardial effusion, there may be an extremely large
volume of pericardial effusion that ultimately causes chronic
tamponade and right heart failure. Echocardiographic evidence of
cardiac tamponade includes diastolic compression of the RA with
concave bowing of the wall inward into the RA chamber, and often
RV compression or collapse seen as an inward bowing of the RV free
wall or RV chamber obliteration in severe tamponade (E-Figure
235.11; Video 235.2

). The LV appears underloaded, with a

reduced chamber size, especially in cases of acute cardiac
tamponade. Chronic tamponade also often causes hepatic venous
distension, generalized hepatomegaly, ascites, and pleural effusion.
Pulsus paradoxus may be diagnosed echocardiographically using
pulsed wave Doppler interrogation of the aortic blood flow velocity,
which, as described above, shows a cyclical reduction in aortic blood
flow velocity during inspiration and increase in velocity during
expiration (and the converse for pulmonic blood flow velocities).

cardiac tamponade. This right parasternal long-axis
view (A) shows pericardial effusion and collapse of
the right atrial free wall (arrow) consistent with
cardiac tamponade. The right parasternal short-axis

ventricle; PE, pericardial effusion; RA, right atrium;

Careful examination of all chambers, with particular focus on the
heart base and right atrium/auricle, is needed to evaluate for cardiac
masses. Masses typically are characterized as heart base, right
atrial/auricular, or other. The reason for this characterization is that
there is a predilection of tumor types for anatomic locations in the
heart and there is a different biologic behavior for each of the
different neoplastic etiologies. For example, 88% of RA masses in a
case series were HSA, whereas heart base masses are more likely to
be neuroendocrine tumors (40%) or thyroid adenocarcinoma
(25%).28 Despite the generalization of tumor predilections for RA
and heart base, there is an overlap of tumor etiologies at each
location. For example, RA masses other than HSA include the
following (each accounting for 2.5% of cases): neuroendocrine
tumor, thyroid adenocarcinoma, mesothelioma, lymphoma, and
sarcoma.28 Similarly, heart base tumors other than neuroendocrine
tumors or thyroid adenocarcinoma include mesothelioma (20%) and
HSA (15%).28
The echocardiographic tissue characteristics of right atrial or
auricular HSA consist of an irregular, heterogeneous mass that
moves with the atrial/auricular wall, and has intratumoral
hypoechoic or cavitary spaces consistent with hemorrhage. The mass
may be localized to the right auricle, which must be visualized using
the left cranial parasternal long-axis view (Figure 235.12; Videos

235.3 and 235.4

; ch. 97), or more commonly may extend along

the RA wall and/or right AV groove (Videos 235.3 and 235.5

).

Sometimes, there are concurrent RA and heart base masses, most
likely from spread of the primary mass but rarely from two different
neoplastic causes. Sometimes, RA masses penetrate into the RA
lumen, and can obstruct venous return to the RA or impair RV filling
(Videos 235.3 and 235.5; see also ch. 115).

FIGURE 235.12 Echocardiogram of a dog with a
right atrial mass. This left cranial parasternal longaxis view shows a heterogeneous, mottled right
auricular mass (arrow) as well as pericardial effusion
(PE). Arrowhead indicates the right auricle. RA,
Right atrium.

FIGURE 235.13 Echocardiogram of a dog with a
heart base mass. This right parasternal long-axis
view shows a well-defined, homogeneous mass
(arrow) adherent to the ascending aorta, which is
characteristic of a heart base mass. Ao, Aorta; LV,

Heart base masses that are neuroendocrine tumors usually are
homogeneous, encapsulated masses growing from the ascending
aorta, adjacent to but separate from either the LA or RA (Figure
235.13; Video 235.6

). Since heart base masses comprise a

variety of neoplastic etiologies, echocardiographic characteristics
also may vary. Some heart base masses are small and easy to
overlook unless the ascending aorta is carefully examined in the right
parasternal long-axis LV outflow tract view as well as short-axis
views along the base of the heart (ch. 97). Other heart base masses
can be so large that the site of origin is challenging to determine.
Large heart base masses may externally compress the RV outflow
tract or pulmonary artery in some cases, which can be treated with
pulmonary artery stenting.46 Sometimes, heart base masses do not

cause pericardial effusion, and are diagnosed incidentally based on
suspicion of a heart base mass on radiographs or during workup of a
heart murmur.
The presence of pericardial effusion greatly facilitates the
detection of intrapericardial masses, especially cardiac HSA and
heart base tumors, because fluid forms an anechoic zone around the
RA and auricle, as well as the ascending aorta. Consequently, if the
clinical condition permits, pericardiocentesis should be deferred
until a thorough echocardiographic examination has been
completed. However, in dogs with cardiac tamponade and
cardiovascular collapse, pericardiocentesis should not be delayed as
it is a lifesaving procedure (ch. 95).
Pericardial effusion secondary to LA rupture accompanies
echocardiographic evidence of myxomatous mitral valve disease and
severe LA dilation (ch. 232). An elongated, hyperechoic thrombus
usually is visualized extending from the epicardial surface of the LA
into the pericardial space (Videos 232.18, 235.7

).

In cases where no mass is seen, the main differential diagnoses
include idiopathic pericarditis, mesothelioma, infective pericarditis,
or a mass that is too small or too remote to be imaged readily. It is
impossible to distinguish between idiopathic pericarditis and
mesothelioma by echocardiography. Diagnosis requires
histopathologic and immunohistochemical evaluation of the
pericardium to help differentiate these two diseases in dogs with
recurrent pericardial effusion that undergo pericardectomy.
Sometimes, a definitive diagnosis of mesothelioma is impossible, but
the suspicion is increased in dogs with recurrent pleural effusion
within 4 to 6 months of subtotal pericardectomy.

Pericardial Fluid Analysis
Pericardial fluid analysis with cytologic evaluation typically is
nonspecific,47 and the fluid usually is characterized as hemorrhagic.
Nevertheless, fluid analysis remains an essential diagnostic step to
diagnose infective pericarditis and certain neoplastic causes such as
lymphoma. Pericardial fluid may be characterized as hemorrhagic
(40/47 [85%]), suppurative inflammatory (6/47 [12.7%]),
pyogranulomatous inflammatory (4/47 [8.5%]), modified

transudative (2/47 [4.2%]), or chylous (1/47 [2.1%]). Cytologic
evaluation of pericardial fluid has been found to be nondiagnostic in
87-92.3% of dogs, yet was able to identify a specific neoplastic
etiology in 4.6% of 250 dogs (n = 7 round cell neoplasia, n = 3
atypical epithelioid cells, n = 1 hematopoietic neoplasia) and all cases
of infective pericarditis (n = 8; 3.1%).28,48 Therefore, despite a low
diagnostic yield, it is essential to submit pericardial fluid for analysis.
Mesothelial reactivity was identified in 25 of 47 (53.2%) dogs, and is
not typically helpful to differentiate idiopathic pericarditis from
mesothelioma. Since hyperreactive mesothelial cells may be
inadvertently mischaracterized as mesothelioma (ch. 220), the
diagnosis of mesothelioma is made by histopathologic evaluation of
the pericardium after pericardectomy or on necropsy. Among cardiac
tumors, cardiac lymphoma is unique because cytologic evaluation of
the pericardial fluid establishes the diagnosis in many cases (11/12
dogs [88%] in one case series) and the tumor may be amenable to
combination chemotherapy (ch. 322).41,45,49 Aerobic and anaerobic
culture of pericardial effusion should be submitted in cases with
gross evidence of flocculent light-colored fluid, and/or when fluid is
characterized as an exudate on fluid analysis (ch. 71). Serologic
testing for C. immitis (ch. 208) is indicated in dogs with
inflammatory pericardial effusion that live in endemic areas (ch.
208). Pericardial fluid pH has a wide overlap between neoplastic
and non-neoplastic etiologies, and its measurement is not considered
reliable.50,51 Measurement of serum cardiac troponin I (cTn-I) has
produced different results in different studies. Serum cTn-I
concentration is consistently higher in dogs with pericardial effusion
than in normal dogs, but some results identify a higher level in dogs
with HSA compared to dogs with other tumors or to non-neoplastic
disorders, whereas other results do not demonstrate such a
difference.52-54

Treatment and Prognosis
In patients with cardiac tamponade and hemodynamic compromise,
pericardiocentesis and rapid intravenous fluid resuscitation are
immediately lifesaving (ch. 95). The timing of pericardiocentesis
depends on the severity of cardiovascular compromise, and should
not be delayed if cardiogenic shock is present. In stable patients,
pericardiocentesis should be delayed if a high-level echocardiogram
is possible, then performed after the echocardiogram.
Abdominocentesis (ch. 86) ± thoracocentesis (ch. 92) may be
palliative in patients with chronic cardiac tamponade and ascites or
pleural effusion, respectively.
Approximately 50% of idiopathic pericarditis cases have recurrent
pericardial effusion, which requires subtotal pericardectomy. In
cases of recurrent pericardial effusion without an identifiable mass,
subtotal pericardectomy is necessary, and histopathologic evaluation
of the pericardium should be performed (often with special
immunohistochemical stains) for differentiation of idiopathic
pericarditis from mesothelioma. Subtotal pericardectomy is curative
for idiopathic pericarditis: dogs with idiopathic pericarditis treated
with subtotal pericardectomy never reached a median survival time
(MST) during a 3 year study (100% survival rate), yet dogs with
idiopathic pericarditis undergoing thoracoscopic pericardial window

(Video 235.8

) did much more poorly, with a disease-free interval

of 11.6 months and an MST of 13.1 months.55
Mesothelioma may be clinically suspected during thoracotomy by
the gross appearance of abnormal serosal surfaces of the pleura and
pericardium, which mandates biopsy of pleura and lymph nodes. The
MST of patients with mesothelioma undergoing subtotal
pericardectomy was 10.3 months, and not significantly different
from pericardial window (MST, 8.6 months). Intracavitary infusions
of carboplatin have been used for treatment of mesothelioma, with
sparse clinical reports published (ch. 220). A case report
documented 1 dog that was disease-free 27 months after treatment
with intrathoracic carboplatin and intravenous doxorubicin.56
Another case report documented 2 dogs with peritoneal
mesothelioma treated with intracavitary carboplatin and daily
piroxicam who lived for 8 months and >3 years, respectively.56,57
Partial pericardectomy is indicated for dogs with heart base
masses, as it relieves cardiac tamponade and is associated with a
significant prolongation of survival time (MST, 730 days with
pericardectomy versus 42 days without pericardectomy).58 In that
study of 24 dogs with aortic body tumors, only pericardectomy, and
no other treatments including chemotherapy, was found to increase
survival time.58 A second study of 25 dogs with heart base masses
treated with either pericardectomy or nonsurgical management with
pericardiocentesis ± chemotherapy or diuretics showed similar
results (MST 661 days pericardectomy vs. 129 days non-surgical).59
Other additional treatments have not been assessed for efficacy.
Three-dimensional conformal radiation therapy was performed in a
dog with histopathologically confirmed chemodectoma; there was
>50% reduction in tumor volume 25 months after therapy, and the
dog was still alive 42 months after therapy (after undergoing
pericardectomy for recurrent pericardial effusion).60
Pericardectomy is controversial for dogs with presumptive HSA,
unless it is combined with mass resection, which is rarely possible. In
one study, partial or subtotal pericardectomy in dogs with all
neoplastic causes combined resulted in disappointing MSTs of 2.7

and 3.8 months, respectively.55 In dogs with isolated right auricular
HSA, surgical resection is a feasible option, followed by
chemotherapy, yet results still remain underwhelming. In a small
study of 23 dogs with surgically resected RA or right auricular HSA,
administration of chemotherapy increased survival time (MST with
chemotherapy and surgery 175 days versus 42 days with surgery
alone).61 A retrospective study evaluating 64 dogs with presumptive
HSA (i.e., right atrial/auricular masses with a characteristic
heterogeneous appearance) treated with doxorubicin compared to 76
dogs without doxorubicin showed an extension in overall survival
time with doxorubicin treatment (116 days vs. 12 days, respectively),
yet dogs in the doxorubicin treatment group underwent more
pericardiocenteses and owners could have been more motivated to
continue therapy than those in the no-treatment group.62 Only 14%
of doxorubicin-treated dogs had a probability of surviving >6
months. Neither group underwent pericardectomy or mass resection.
Presence of metastases was not related to overall survival, but mass
size and thrombocytopenia were negative prognostic indicators.
Lastly, a retrospective study of dogs without surgical resection of
cardiac HSA that were treated with doxorubicin ± other
chemotherapeutic agents reported an MST of 139.5 days (range 2302 days), yet no control group was evaluated for comparative
purposes.63 In the author’s experience, recurrent acute hemorrhage
and cardiac tamponade is common in dogs with cardiac HSA, and
usually is lethal before the animal succumbs to metastatic disease.

Cardiac lymphoma is classified as stage V, substage b (ch. 322).
Dogs with stage III lymphoma or higher and clinical signs (substage
b) have a poor prognosis for remission and survival. In a
retrospective study of 12 dogs with cardiac lymphoma and
pericardial effusion that were treated with various combinations of
pericardiocentesis, pericardectomy, and chemotherapy, MST was 41
days. However, 3 dogs were still alive 328 days after the initial
diagnosis, suggesting that cardiac lymphoma does not always
warrant a poor prognosis.49
Subtotal pericardectomy, postoperative chest tube drainage, and
long-term (at least 6 months) antibiotic therapy is the treatment of
choice for infective pericarditis. The prognosis is good for dogs
undergoing pericardectomy and receiving long-term antibiotics.25
Long-term antifungal treatment for many months to years may be
necessary in dogs with C. immitis infections (ch. 208).
∗

CONSTRICTIVE PERICARDITIS
Constrictive pericarditis occurs when the parietal pericardium, the
visceral pericardium, or both develop(s) fibrosis, with or without
fusion of the parietal and visceral layers to each other. This process
decreases compliance and possibly intrapericardial volume (Figure
235.14; Table 235.1). The fibrotic pericardium constricts the
cardiac chambers and increases atrial and diastolic ventricular
pressures. A small volume of pericardial fluid sometimes is present—
a process called constrictive-effusive pericarditis—such that for any
mild increase in pericardial effusion volume, there is a dramatic
increase in intrapericardial pressure. The pathophysiologic
consequence of pericardial constraint is similar to chronic cardiac
tamponade. Ascites is a consistent feature, and jugular venous
distension is common.26 Pulsus paradoxus is an uncommon finding
in constrictive pericarditis, probably because the rigid, stiff
pericardium does not transmit the respiratory variations of
intrathoracic pressures to the heart as a structurally normal
pericardium would. Causes of constrictive pericarditis are unclear,
but case reports cite the following causes: previous idiopathic
pericarditis, previous infective pericarditis (especially C. immitis
infections, ch. 208), intrapericardial foreign body, osseous
metaplasia of the pericardium, or idiopathic disease.26,64,65
Medium- to large-breed dogs are most commonly affected.
In contrast to other forms of pericardial disease, echocardiography
is not sufficient to provide a definitive diagnosis of constrictive
pericarditis. Typically it shows minimal or no pericardial effusion
and no RA and RV collapse, yet there is usually evidence of hepatic
venous distension and ascites. Several echocardiographic features of
constrictive pericarditis in humans include: 1) respirophasic
interventricular septal shift (septal bounce) with beat-to-beat
diastolic septal motion abnormalities due to exaggerated ventricular
interdependence within the confines of a constrictive pericardium, 2)
reversal of hepatic venous diastolic flow during exhalation, and 3)
increased medial transmitral E’ (Table 235.1).66 In humans, the
combination of these three findings is 91% specific and 87% sensitive
for the diagnosis of constrictive pericarditis.67 Other features

reported in people but not studied clinically in animals may include
increased respiratory variation in transmitral and transtricuspid flow
velocities, and higher medial e’ velocity compared to lateral e’
velocity due to greater effect of pericardial constraint on the lateral
ventricular wall.
The diagnosis of constrictive pericarditis requires right heart
catheterization. Pericardial constriction does not limit early active
diastolic filling, but limits diastolic filling in mid-diastole as the heart
is confined by the stiff pericardium. This results in a characteristic
“dip and plateau” pressure waveform (the square root sign) when
measuring RV diastolic pressures during cardiac catheterization
(Figure 235.14). The dip portion of the pressure tracing is the
enhanced rapid early diastolic filling of the heart operating in low
volumes not limited by the pericardial constraint. The plateau occurs
once the chamber volume expands to be limited by the pericardial
constriction, which creates a rapid increase in filling pressure in midto late diastole and cessation of diastolic filling. This may be more
obvious during rapid saline intravenous infusion. A characteristic Wor M-shaped RA diastolic pressure tracing also is present in
constrictive pericarditis, where there is accentuated early diastolic
filling after ventricular systole (y descent), and a rapid decrease in
RA pressure after atrial systole (x descent) (Figure 235.14; Table
235.1).
Treatment of constrictive pericarditis requires subtotal
pericardectomy and removal of the constricting pericardium from
the underlying myocardium if possible (Figure 235.15). Overall
prognosis depends on whether the process is limited to the parietal
pericardium (better prognosis) or if it extends to the visceral
pericardium such that the pericardium is adhered to the epicardial
surface (grave prognosis). In a case series of 13 dogs, 8 dogs had
parietal pericardial constriction, 5 dogs had visceral pericardial
constriction, and parietal pericardectomy was successful in relieving
the syndrome in 6 of 10 dogs.26 Perioperative mortality was most
often due to pulmonary thromboembolism in those cases. In cases
where constrictive pericarditis is a complication of systemic C.
immitis infection, adjunctive long-term antifungal therapy is
necessary (ch. 208). In a retrospective study of 17 dogs with
constrictive pericarditis due to C. immitis infection, perioperative

mortality was high (23.5%). However, surgery was successful in
relieving clinical signs in some dogs for >2 years.64

FELINE PERICARDIAL EFFUSION
Pericardial effusion is the most common type of pericardial
abnormality in cats, and is present in approximately 6% of feline
cardiology patients.68 Most cases are mild and not caused by
pericardial disease but by elevated intracardiac filling pressures
secondary to congestive heart failure (44-75% of feline cases of
pericardial effusion) through the same pathophysiologic mechanism
as pleural effusion development in heart failure (ch. 228).69,70
Unlike dogs, cats rarely develop pericardial effusion that is severe
enough to cause cardiac tamponade or clinical signs, or require
pericardiocentesis. After congestive heart failure, neoplasia is the
second most common cause of pericardial effusion in cats (19% of 83
cases, including lymphoma, adenocarcinoma, thymoma,
chemodectoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and mesothelioma).69
Lymphoma was the most common cardiac tumor in a study of 30
cats with cardiac neoplasia (13/30 lymphoma, 12 B cell, 1 T cell; ch.
322).71 Pericardial lymphoma was diagnosed in 7 cats, 6 of which
died 7-11 days after diagnosis, and 1 cat receiving a
cyclophosphamide-doxorubicin-vincristine-prednisolone (CHOP)
protocol was alive 750 days after diagnosis with clinical remission.72
Pericarditis is also rare in cats, and was only found in 3 of 83 cats in
that case series.69 Likewise, infective pericarditis is rare in cats, and
reported causes of infection are E. coli, Staphylococcus aureus,
Enterococcus, and Actinomyces. Other uncommon causes include
feline infectious peritonitis, hypoalbuminemia, systemic infection
and inflammation, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Pericardiocentesis (ch. 95) is necessary in cats with
echocardiographic evidence of cardiac tamponade. The pericardial
fluid usually has a gross appearance similar to pleural effusion, and,
unlike in dogs, is rarely hemorrhagic. Fluid analysis (ch. 71) and
cytologic evaluation ± microbial culture should be submitted to
evaluate for infectious, neoplastic, or inflammatory etiologies.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF SYSTEMIC
HYPERTENSION
Systemic hypertension (SH) is defined as a pathologic elevation in
systemic arterial blood pressure (BP) usually recognized with sustained
elevations in systolic blood pressure (SBP). The complex neurohormonal
interactions between the kidneys, nervous system, vasculature, and heart
may lead to altered BP control (Figure 236.1).1,2 Guidelines for
identification and evaluation of SH have been devised based on the
probability of developing target-organ damage (TOD), and both
monitoring and therapeutic guidelines have been established.1-3 Feline
studies have documented a normal SBP range of 111-162 mm Hg
depending on measurement method.3 Canine studies suggest a narrower
range of 131-154 mm Hg.2 Methods for measuring BP are described in
ch. 91.
The prevalence of SH has been reported as 19.5% for cats, and in dogs
0.5-13%.2,4 Cats aged >9 years have significantly higher BP than cats
aged 3-9 years, and risk of SH also increases with age,5 whereas a slight
increase in BP (13 mm Hg/year) has been reported in dogs.6 The
association between SH and age is likely multifactorial and unclear at
this time. No relationship exists between breed and BP in cats;5 however,
certain breed variations likely exist in dogs.

TYPES OF HYPERTENSION
SH can be divided into three broad categories: secondary hypertension,
idiopathic hypertension and situational hypertension. Secondary
hypertension is induced by clinical disease or medications and is most
common. Idiopathic hypertension occurs in absence of a readily
identifiable cause. Situational hypertension is most often caused by the
“white coat” effect.

Secondary Hypertension
Obesity (ch. 150)

There is either a small or no correlation between obesity and SH in dogs.
Furthermore, SH in obese dogs is more likely related to
endocrinopathies, renal disease or cardiac disease. In cats, no studies
correlate sex, breed, and body weight with increased SH risk.2,3

Renal Disease (ch. 301)
The most common cause of SH in dogs and cats is renal disease.
Impaired renal function is noted in 60-100% of cats presenting with SH
and TOD.7-9 Whereas cats with chronic kidney disease (CKD) have a
prevalence of SH between 20-65%, the severity of CKD does not
correlate with magnitude of BP elevation or prevalence.2,10 The
pathophysiologic mechanism is multifactorial and involves systemic
renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) activation (Figure
236.2), local (tissue-specific) RAAS activation, impaired sodium (Na+)
excretion, increased intravascular volume, sympathetic stimulation,
structural arterial changes, endothelial dysfunction, reduced nitric oxide
(NO)-mediated vasodilation, increased vascular endothelin production,
and reactive oxygen species generation/oxidative stress (Figure
236.1).3,10 Excessive angiotensin II (ATII) and aldosterone (ALDO) are
directly nephrotoxic and likely contribute to fibrotic remodeling of
glomeruli.11
ATII is also locally produced in the renal parenchyma. This intrarenal
RAAS likely contributes to and maintains SH, promotes glomerular
hypertension, worsens proteinuria, and leads to oxidative damage and
renal fibrosis.7,11 Systemic RAAS concentration may not reflect
intrarenal RAAS. No consistent association between plasma ALDO or
renin concentrations, and SH and feline CKD, have been observed.3,10
However, ALDO concentrations are higher in cats with CKD, indicating
that elevated ALDO concentrations may contribute to SH. This may be
independent of RAAS, as SH did not respond to treatment with
angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) and plasma renin
activity was found to be low to normal in cats.12 Increased vascular tone
may explain the response to treatment with calcium channel blockers
(CCBs) in cats with SH.3 Therefore, systemic RAAS activation may less
be responsible for SH in feline CKD patients.
Proteinuria is an independent variable that is significantly associated
with survival in cats with CKD and with all causes of SH.8 Both

glomerular and tubular protein loss likely stimulate the production of
inflammatory mediators and cytokines, leading to glomerular
hypertension, glomerular sclerosis, and renal fibrosis.10 Glomerular
disease, independent of cause, has been associated with the development
of SH from sodium retention as well as excessive RAAS and sympathetic
activity.1 SH is more common in dogs with glomerular disease (ch. 302)
and leishmaniasis (ch. 197) than in dogs with other forms of CKD.9 SH
may also increase intraglomerular hypertension and independently
contribute to proteinuria.
SH is common in acute kidney injury (AKI; ch. 300) and with the use
of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents.13,14 Cats with AKI have a
prevalence of SH of almost 59%, and it is not related to grade of AKI or
serum creatinine concentration.15 SH is present in 75% of dogs with AKI,
56% of them severe (SBP >180 mm Hg). No association is known to exist
among AKI grade, SH, and survival to discharge.16 Iatrogenic volume
overload in patients with reduced urine output is a major contributor to
SH.

Hyperadrenocorticism (ch. 293)
SH is reported in 59-86% of all dogs with hyperadrenocorticism (HAC);
dogs with unilateral adrenal tumors have a higher prevalence.17 Severe
SH can be found in 46% of cases, and thrombocytosis may be 100%
specific and 61% sensitive in identifying these dogs.18 Increased intrinsic
mineralocorticoid activity, activation of RAAS, and glucocorticoidinduced suppression of vasodilatory mechanisms (i.e., NO) have been
suggested in people. No clear evidence of decreased NO or increased
ALDO concentrations exists in dogs. Glucocorticoids may also contribute
to SH by increasing cardiac output (CO), total peripheral resistance and
renal blood flow. Furthermore, development of glomerular dysfunction
or glomerulosclerosis and proteinuria may contribute in some patients.19
Many dogs remain hypertensive even after the diagnosis and treatment
of HAC, and some become hypertensive after treatment; therefore, it is
important to measure BP at every recheck visit.17,20

Adrenal Tumors/Hyperplasia (chs. 295 and 298)
Over 90% of cats with primary hyperaldosteronism have SH (i.e., SBP
>180 mm Hg), with SH resolving in all cats when BP is measured
following adrenalectomy.7,17 SH does not appear to be negatively
associated with survival. This is rarely seen in dogs.21
Pheochromocytomas reported in dogs and cats can result in increased
catecholamine secretion and excessive alpha- and beta-adrenergic
stimulation. This may cause sustained or paroxysmal SH. At least half of
these dogs will present SH at some point.17

Hyperthyroidism (ch. 287)
The prevalence of SH with feline hyperthyroidism varies from 5-25%.
However, studies evaluating cats with TOD such as retinopathy indicate
very few cats were hyperthyroid and severe SH in feline hyperthyroidism
seems rare.22 The pathogenesis remains poorly understood. Excessive
thyroxine causes substantial reduction in systemic vascular resistance
(SVR), decreased diastolic BP and reflexive increase in CO in people.
This triggers activation of RAAS, contributing to increased BP. Thyroid
hormones also increase catecholamine sensitivity, increasing cardiac
inotropy and chronotropy.7,17

Diabetes Mellitus (DM; chs. 291 and 292)
SH is common in human DM patients. Diabetic nephropathy is the main
factor for its development in type 1 DM, whereas a wider range of
metabolic syndrome factors (obesity, insulin resistance, hyperlipidemia)
contribute to SH in type II DM. Loss of insulin may lead to decreased
natural vasodilatory effect (NO generation), increased Na+ and water
retention, increased intracellular Ca2+ leading to increased vascular
smooth muscle contractility, proliferation of vascular smooth muscle,
and sympathetic nervous system stimulation.17
SH is recognized in 35-46% of dogs with DM. However, no
associations between hypertension, proteinuria, and retinopathy with
time of diagnosis of DM or degree of glycemic control have been found,
and SBP tends to be <160 mm Hg.23 BP does not seem to increase
significantly over time, suggesting the effect of DM on BP occurs early
on; this contrasts with previous evidence suggesting increased
prevalence with disease duration.23 In cats, SH may only occur in a very
small percentage of diabetics.17

Cardiovascular Disease, Diet (ch. 157)
SH causes cardiovascular changes in cats and dogs, but contrary to
humans, cardiac disease does not seem to produce SH.24 Excess dietary
salt has been documented to increase BP in dogs experimentally but no
evidence supports that this occurs commonly with variances in sodium
concentrations.25 No known association between high salt diets and SH
exists in cats.26

Situational Hypertension
Situational hypertension, often referred to as white-coat hypertension, is
defined as a transient increase in systemic BP in the hospital setting
compared to a non-hospital setting. Because it is considered to be a
result of transient sympathetic nervous system activation, treatment is
unlikely to be needed. External signs of nervousness, anxiety and/or
aggressive behavior during BP measurement correlate to a higher BP in
cats.5 However, cats may acclimatize faster and return to normal BP
than previously thought.27 In retired racing greyhounds, adaptation and

acclimation may not occur until after many hours or days.28 Care should
be taken to not overestimate SH due to situational hypertension, and
repeated measurements should be considered (ch. 91).

IDIOPATHIC HYPERTENSION
True idiopathic hypertension is likely quite rare in dogs. In cats, reports
indicate that the prevalence varies between 13-24%.7 However, this may
be an overrepresentation, as underlying diseases such as early CKD may
have been overlooked. When compared to a population of normotensive
non-azotemic geriatric cats, cats with SH had a significantly higher
plasma creatinine concentration (but were still nonazotemic) and lower
urine specific gravity.29 The recent development of more sensitive renal
biomarkers may change the prevalence of idiopathic hypertension in
cats.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS OF
HYPERTENSION
SH can cause both mechanical and functional alterations in the
vasculature, leading to the development of TOD.30 Independent risk
factors for TOD likely exist, including neurohormonal alterations,
metabolic or inflammatory factors, and patient factors (obesity, diet,
age). Vascular changes may transmit elevated pressures to tissue or
induce local ischemia. The most common organs affected include the
eyes, brain, kidneys, and heart.
Little information exists in animals regarding the development of TOD
and magnitude of BP elevation. The 2018 American College of Veterinary
Internal Medicine (ACVIM) Consensus Statement on SH suggests an
ideal target to minimize TOD be an SBP <140 mm Hg. An SBP ≤160 mm
Hg should be the minimum clinical goal to reduce TOD.2

OCULAR MANIFESTATIONS (CH. 13)
The most common site of TOD is the eye, with the posterior segment
most commonly affected.31 As BP exceeds retinal autoregulation, a

hypertensive choroidopathy/retinopathy leads to breakdown of the
blood-retinal barrier and altered vessel diameter, reducing
retinal/choroidal perfusion. Autoregulatory vasoconstriction with
sustained SH may result in vascular occlusion, ischemic necrosis,
increased vascular permeability and potential hemorrhage.32 The
magnitude of SH may be associated with ocular changes, but overlap
exists between hypertensive patients with and without ocular
manifestations. The mean SBP in hypertensive cats was 262 mm Hg with
ocular lesions and 221 mm Hg without in one study.33 The mean SBP in
hypertensive dogs was 197 mm Hg with ocular lesions and 189 mm Hg
without, suggesting a lower threshold for ocular injury in dogs.32 The
acuity of SH development and variations in BP, rather than simply
absolute pressure, may also contribute to ocular TOD.10
Common ocular lesions caused by SH include: partial to complete
retinal detachment, hemorrhage, multifocal edema, retinal vessel
tortuosity, retinal perivascular edema, papilledema, optic nerve atrophy,
and vitreal hemorrhage (Figure 236.3, A and B).2,32,34 Pre-retinal
hemorrhages are most commonly observed, and may be large and
obscure retinal vasculature. Punctate retinal hemorrhages, including
superficial intraretinal hemorrhages (involving the nerve fiber layer) or
deep intraretinal hemorrhages, do not obscure retinal vasculature and
are generally smaller and more subtle.35 Retinal edema and/or retinal
detachments are also a common finding. The fluid likely originates from
a hypertensive choroidopathy. Retinal edema may be localized or
generalized and may create the appearance of narrowed retinal arterioles
early. This may progress to form flattened/partial or more bullous
detachments.35 Primary retinal vascular changes are less commonly
appreciated. Focal arteriolar dilations, a consequence of ischemic
damage to the retinal arterioles documented as retinal arterial
macroaneurysms, may be seen.35 Chronic SH may cause degenerative
changes to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and retina. These may
be visualized as pigmentary changes to the retina or focal areas of retinal
degeneration (i.e., vascular attenuation, hyperreflectivity).35 Changes to
the anterior chamber occur less frequently and generally are manifested
as hyphema and/or iris hemorrhage. This finding may be more common
in dogs, with hyphema occurring in 19% of hypertensive dogs.32,35

Hypertensive retinal lesions are common in geriatric feline patients
and were reported in 16% of cats >8 years old. Ocular lesions are the
most commonly observed complication of SH in cats, although the
prevalence rate varies amongst studies from 50-100%.2,10 In a study of
dogs with AKI and SH, 16% of admitted dogs had evidence of
hypertensive retinopathy.16

VASCULAR MANIFESTATIONS
SH can cause a vasculopathy that is characterized by endothelial
dysfunction and remodeling of arteries (i.e., arteriosclerosis,
arteriosclerotic stenosis, smooth muscle hypertrophy, increased collagen
content) (Figure 236.4).36 The end result is reduced dilation capability
and reduced elasticity of the resistance vasculature. Vascular changes are
less common in dogs and cats relative to people. Recently, carotid artery
plaques were documented in 5/5 dogs in an experimental model of
chronic SH. These non-atherosclerotic plaques were characterized by
smooth muscle cells, proteoglycans, and collagen fibers and altered
carotid luminal diameter. These plaques contained few macrophages,
little lipid and had no fibrous cap or lipid core typical of atherosclerosis.
This was thought to represent a response to endothelial injury from SH
and may impair vascular relaxation and vasa recta formation.37

Animal Medical Center.
Increased aortic stiffness has been reported in people with SH. The
normal elasticity dampens pressure pulsations from LV ejection,
transforming pulsatile flow into continuous flow. Loss of elasticity
results in increased transmission of pulsatile energy toward the
periphery and potentially contributes to TOD. Alterations in aortic
stiffness occur with SH in dogs and can be measured by changes in
diameter at systole or diastole caudal to the left renal artery or cranial to

the external iliac arteries.38 Rarely, aortic dissection can occur in dogs
and cats (Figure 236.5

, Video 236.1).39

CARDIAC MANIFESTATIONS
SH can result in both functional and structural cardiac changes.
Increased wall tension (pressure overload) results in myocardial
mechanoreceptor activation, leading to increased synthesis of
myocardial proteins and associated tissue. This results in left ventricular
concentric hypertrophy (LVH). Hypertrophy occurs in an effort to
normalize wall stress and preserve LV chamber function.36,40 LV free
wall and interventricular septum thicknesses are significantly different
from age-matched controls without SH.41 LVH is non-linearly correlated
with SH in cats, with a reported prevalence of 74-85%.33 In cats, SH may
be associated with different patterns of LV changes, although concurrent
hypertrophic cardiomyopathy could explain asymmetrical LVH in cats
with SH. Concentric hypertrophy (59%), concentric and symmetric left
ventricular hypertrophy (26%), asymmetric concentric left ventricular
hypertrophy (33%) with free wall or septal predominance (23% and 10%,
respectively), eccentric left ventricular hypertrophy (13%) and localized
septal hypertrophy at the subaortic level (13%) have been reported; 15%
may have normal left ventricular geometry.33 Aortic dilation, seen
commonly in cats, correlates linearly with BP and less commonly with
aortic regurgitation or dissection.42 A heterogeneous echotexture
characterized by hyperechoic myocardial plaques, suggested to be
fibrotic zones in the subendocardial region, may be seen in cats and may
resolve with anti-hypertensive therapy.43
Structural alterations occur in 5-91.4% of dogs with spontaneously
occurring SH, depending on echocardiographic criteria.44 About 47% of
dogs have symmetric or concentric myocardial hypertrophy, but unlike
cats, other forms of LVH have not been described.45 Histologic LV
myocardial hypertrophy and LV fibrosis have been documented in dogs
with chronic SH.37 Aortic root dilation and aortic insufficiency is
estimated to occur in one-third of canine cases.45

FIGURE 236.5 Contrast-enhanced computed
tomographic scan of a dog with hypertension-induced
aortic dissection. On both the sagittal view (left) and the
coronal view (right), the dissection creates a false lumen
(F) and a true lumen (T), separated by the dissected
aortic endothelium (hypointense line;
arrowheads). Courtesy The Animal Medical Center.
SH also can induce functional cardiac alterations.46 Hypertensive
diastolic dysfunction occurs in people and animals.47,48 Diastolic
dysfunction precedes hypertrophy and fibrosis; however, it also can
contribute to functional impairment. LV relaxation is slowed but overall
LV stiffness or the rate at which LV stiffness changes with changes in
volume is not different. Additionally, increases in LV systolic and arterial
stiffness exacerbate load-dependent relaxation.47 Echocardiographic
features of diastolic dysfunction (ch. 97) can include: reversal of the
mitral valve E wave (early diastolic filling) to A wave (atrial contraction)
ratio, lengthening of isovolumetric relaxation time and alterations in
tissue Doppler imaging (ch. 234).45 Systolic dysfunction, manifested as
a reduced velocity of myocardial shortening, stress-corrected mid-wall
shortening, and longitudinal LV free wall systolic velocities and
gradients, may be observed. Some of these changes could be contributing
to fibrosis, hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction (Figure 236.6).45,47
However, ejection fraction is often normal, afterload enhancement of

systolic performance is maintained and other systolic parameters may be
increased.
Left atrial enlargement and congestive heart failure are not reported in
dogs with SH and uncommonly reported in cats with SH: 12 and 28%,
respectively.33 Remodeling of the coronary vasculature can lead to
reduced coronary blood flow reserve. However, direct coronary
remodeling is less common compared to the equivalent situation in
hypertensive humans. Changes in coronary autoregulation, response to
adenosine and blood flow distribution independent of vasculopathy have
been described in dogs.49 Additionally, reduced coronary reserve, which
can increase susceptibility to mortality when coronary arterial flow is
disrupted, is reported.50
SH can result in cardiac electrical instability. Ventricular and
supraventricular arrhythmias are described in people but are less well
characterized in small animals with SH. This could be more common in
dogs with pheochromocytoma (ch. 298), as catecholamines can
contribute independently to arrhythmogenicity.24 Additionally, SH
associated with RAAS activation is associated with a reduction in the
refractory period of myocytes and promotes both atrial and ventricular
arrhythmias.51

RENAL MANIFESTATIONS (CH. 301)
Hypertensive nephrosclerosis that is generally characterized by vascular
changes (intimal thickening/fibrosis, hyalinosis of the afferent arteriole,
occlusion of glomerular capillaries, breakdown of elastic fibers in large
arteries) and glomerular changes (replacement with collagen,
extracellular matrix deposition, capsular adhesions/scarring) can occur
with SH. These changes can result in altered renal blood flow and
development of glomerulosclerosis. Due to the common coexistence of
hypertension and kidney disease, cause and effect have been
questioned.2 Additionally, treatment of SH could mitigate vascular
changes histologically. These vascular changes could result in a
reduction in glomerular blood flow from preglomerular arterial
narrowing and resultant ischemic injury. However, glomerular
hypertension and hyperfiltration from preglomerular vasodilation also
likely occur.1 Activation of the RAAS could be a key player in the
development of hypertensive nephropathy in animals, as in people.11

Autoregulation usually maintains glomerular capillary pressure
between 60-65 mm Hg despite wide fluctuations in SBP. However,
altered autoregulation can occur with renal disease; therefore,
fluctuations in BP can have a direct effect on glomerular pressure and
changes in glomerular filtration, with decreasing and increasing BP
potentially contributing to ischemia or intraglomerular hypertension,
respectively.52 SH may also result in direct injury to the tubular cells,
inducing epithelial-mesenchymal transition and tubulointerstitial
fibrosis.53
SH is linearly associated with death and likelihood of uremic crises in
dogs with renal disease.44 Proteinuria is directly correlated with extent
of increased BP and decline in GFR in an experimental model.55 SH was
directly correlated with histopathological and laboratory evidence of
glomerular disease in leishmaniasis (ch. 197) in one study, supporting
the effect of SH on the progression of CKD.56 In cats, glomerulosclerotic
changes are slightly more common in SH patients; however, SH has not
been correlated directly with increased mortality.57 The direct
association between SH and proteinuria, an independent predictor of
renal disease progression, makes correlations between spontaneous
(especially proteinuric) kidney disease and SH difficult. Additionally,
effective BP control limits the ability to determine its independent role in
disease progression.44,57-59

CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM
MANIFESTATIONS (CH. 243)
Hypertensive encephalopathy is the most common neurologic clinical
manifestation of SH (Figure 236.7). Autoregulation normally
maintains cerebral perfusion pressure constant in response to changes in
BP via myogenic reflexive vasoconstriction or dilation. Sudden and
severe increases in arterial pressure can exceed autoregulatory

mechanisms because the arterioles are limited in their ability to
constrict. Intracerebral BP then increases and the blood-brain barrier
(BBB) is breached. The result is vascular fluid diffusion across capillary
membranes into the brain parenchyma, leading to cerebral edema,
increased intracranial pressure, and potentially neurologic deficits.60
Other factors could increase the susceptibility to hypertensive
encephalopathy from acute episodes of hypertension.
In chronic SH, the cerebral vasculature undergoes adaptations, such as
arteriolar hypertrophy, to allow for a higher autoregulatory range. These
changes in cerebral vasculature may result in loss of regulatory tone and
changes to vessel walls. A rightward shift in the range of BP needed to
maintain constant cerebral blood flow occurs. As a result, reductions in
BP may contribute to hypoperfusion and stroke.41,60 Additionally, the
cerebral vasculature is unique in that it also possesses the property of
flow-induced vasodilation. As a result of shear stress on the endothelial
cell membrane, the arachidonic acid cascade is activated and the
vasoconstrictive metabolite 20-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (20-HETE)
is produced. This mechanism is upregulated in SH and likely contributes
to adaptation.
Both vascular remodeling and vasoconstriction can induce ischemia
and lead to edema with development of hypertensive encephalopathy.41
Hypertensive encephalopathy has a predilection for white matter and
predominantly occurs within the cerebrum (parietal and occipital lobes),
although it can occur anywhere in the brain. Clinical signs include
seizures, altered mentation, blindness, vestibular or cerebellar ataxia and
pathologic nystagmus.61 Cerebellar herniation has been reported in
some patients. Additionally, SH has been shown in some models to
directly result in breakdown of the BBB via increases in ATII
concentration. This allows for the entrance of ATII into the brain, which
may increase central sympathetic outflow. This “neurogenic
hypertension” may contribute to maintenance of SH.62 SH has been
linked to both grey matter changes and white matter changes in people,
and such changes contribute to age-related degeneration and loss of
memory in executive function.63 Another factor that may contribute to
neurologic decline could include alterations in pulsatile flow within the
cerebral vasculature. The increased transmission of pulsations is due to
altered adaptation and peripheral arterial stiffness from hypertension as
well as additional factors (e.g., loss of aortic elasticity). The “pulsating
brain” or “brain is destroyed by the pulse” are areas of active research.64

This could be relevant in dogs where recent evaluation of carotid plaques
increasing stiffness and loss of aortic elasticity have been documented.37

Cognitive dysfunction (Figure 236.8; ch. 244), a neurodegenerative
condition of small animals, shares pathologic similarities to Alzheimer’s
disease in humans.65 SH is a risk factor for and contributes to
progression in Alzheimer’s disease, potentially through impaired
vascular repair mechanisms.66 Vascular dementia (VD) is a form of
dementia associated with altered blood flow to the brain. SH is a risk
factor for its development in people. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy has
been reported in geriatric cats and dogs and has been associated with VD
in people.67 Additionally, ischemic infarcts and/or hemorrhages might
be more common in patients with cerebral amyloid angiopathy when
hypertension is present. Antihypertensive therapy can slow the
progression of cognitive dysfunction and reduce the incidence of stroke
in people.68 The significance of SH in dogs and cats in the development
of VD remains unknown.
SH has been associated with spinal injury in cats (ch. 251).69
Ischemic myelopathy secondary to ventral spinal cord white matter
ischemia is seen in cats (Figure 236.9). Histopathologic vascular
changes (hyalinization, aneurysmal dilation, and/or thrombosis) may be
seen.70 Most cats present acutely, with paresis/plegia and/or cervical
ventroflexion. All spinal segments can be affected, but there is a
predilection for C1-C5 and most commonly C2 or C3.71 Intramedullary
hyperintense (T2) and isointense > hypointense (T1) lesions are seen on
MRI (ch. 112).71

EPISTAXIS (CH. 36)
Retrospective reviews of epistaxis in dogs and cats suggest a rare
occurrence in animals with SH.41,72 The association in people has been
questioned.

TREATMENT OF SYSTEMIC
HYPERTENSION
TREATMENT GOALS
The main treatment goal is to reduce TOD risk with a gradual decrease in
BP. Rapid decrease in BP is rarely recommended and should be avoided
unless in the presence of significant acute TOD and severe SH. In people
and likely animals with SH, reducing BP will lower the risk of TOD.2
Therapy should be aimed at gradually lowering BP to the normotensive
range if possible, and if not, to the prehypertensive category.
Normal perfusion of the brain, heart, and kidneys remains relatively
constant, despite normal fluctuations in BP. In the presence of SH, this
ability to autoregulate shifts upward to protect the exposed organ from
excessive pressure. This increases the susceptibility to hypoperfusion,
with a 20-25% reduction in the lower threshold for autoregulation.
Initial lowering of BP to 20% below pretreatment values has been
recommended in people but recent information may suggest that this
may not be necessary in patients with ischemic strokes.73
Categories for BP ranges and risk are reported by the ACVIM 2018
Consensus Statement:
• Normotensive: <140 mm Hg: minimal TOD risk
• Prehypertensive: 140-159 mm Hg: low TOD risk
• Hypertensive: 160-179 mm Hg: moderate TOD risk
• Severely hypertensive: >180 mm Hg: high TOD risk
Screening (and treatment when appropriate) for SH is recommended
annually from 9 years of age, as well as those with the following
considerations:
• Clinical abnormalities indicating possible hypertensive TOD
• The presence of medical conditions associated with SH
• Certain pharmacologic agents or toxin ingestions associated with
SH
• Cats >9 years of age and with possible occult disease
Investigation of secondary SH is important, as management of the
underlying disorders will likely improve BP control and outcome.
However, treatment of SH should not be delayed because a risk exists for
TOD. Reduction or recognition of situational SH is primordial in

properly identifying animals with SH to ensure safe treatment. Proper
BP measurement is also necessary (ch. 91). The presence of SH is
unlikely to be suspected clinically unless TOD is apparent; therefore,
routine monitoring of BP is recommended. The top indications for SH
treatment include evidence of TOD and also repeatable systemic BP of
>160 mm Hg with unlikely situational SH.

TREATMENT OF SH
Hypertension Treatment in Cats
First-line therapy for oral treatments of SH in cats include amlodipine
and telmisartan, and superiority of one therapy over another has not
been demonstrated. The effects of angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARBs)
for proteinuric conditions may lead to preferential use in some clinical
scenarios. However, amlodipine may be preferentially selected in
patients with severe SH (SBP >200 mm Hg). Monotherapy is
recommended to start and is usually sufficient to control SH.

Amlodipine Besylate
Amlodipine leads to a decrease of 30-70 mm Hg in cats with SH, with
60-100% of cats responding to this medication as monotherapy.11 The
typical starting oral dosage is 0.625 mg per cat q24h. In one study, cats
that required an increased dosage to achieve optimal BP control had a
higher systemic BP baseline, and cats with SH >200 mm Hg likely
require a starting dosage of 1.25 mg PO q24h.74 Little is known about the
efficacy of transdermal amlodipine.75

Telmisartan
Telmisartan has been shown to be an effective and safe anti-hypertensive
medication in cats in two recent studies, with significant and sustained
decrease in SBP in SH cats. However, both studies excluded cats with
SBP >200 mm Hg and cats with evidence of TOD. The starting dosage
varies from 1.5 mg/kg PO q12h as a loading dose for 14 days with a
subsequent reduction to 2 mg/kg q24h, or starting immediately at 2
mg/kg PO q24h.26,76 A decrease in renal function has been reported in a
small number of cats receiving telmisartan, likely due to a decrease in

GFR from efferent arteriole dilation; therefore, monitoring of renal
function is recommended.58

Hypertension Treatment in Dogs
Benazepril
RAAS inhibition with an ACEI has been suggested as the initial therapy
for dogs with SH. ACEIs also may be beneficial in addressing proteinuria
in animals with CKD (ch. 301) or protein-losing nephropathies (ch.
302).2 ACEIs are administered at dosages ranging from 0.5-2 mg/kg PO
q24h with a gradual increase in dosage based on BP rechecks. However,
ACEIs have a marginal effect on BP with an estimated 10-15% reduction
in dogs.77 Therefore, in the setting of moderate to severe subclinical SH
or of TOD, it is recommended that an ACEI be combined with another
antihypertensive drug such as amlodipine.

ACEI, Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor; ARB, angiotensinreceptor blocker; ALDO, aldosterone; ATII, angiotensin II; BP, blood
pressure; cAMP, cyclic adenine monophosphate; cGMP, cyclic guanosine
monophosphate; CO, cardiac output; CRI, constant rate infusion; HR,
heart rate; MOA, mechanism of action; NO, nitric oxide; PVR, peripheral

vascular resistance; RBCs, red blood cells; SBP, systolic blood pressure;
SH, systemic hypertension; SV, stroke volume; SVR, systemic vascular
resistance; VSM, vascular smooth muscle.
a

Unlike ACEI, ARBs allow for ATII-mediated subtype 2 binding and
evade proteolytic pathways of ACE, which may preserve beneficial effects
of ATII and provide more sustained suppression of subtype I receptormediated effects.
b

By contrast, beta-2 adrenergic receptors are located on vascular
smooth muscle and activation results in G protein-mediated
vasodilation. Beta blockers vary in their receptor selectivity and
therefore their effects.
c

Beta-blockade alone leaves catecholamine stimulation of alphareceptors unopposed, with consequent compensatory increase in SVR
and similarly, alpha-blockade alone generally results in compensatory
tachycardia.

Telmisartan
Use of ARBs in dogs with SH has not been critically evaluated. However,
recent information has suggested that with renal disease, telmisartan has
a modest effect on BP, with 59% of dogs having a reduction in SBP <160
mm Hg at day 120.78 Additionally, a study in proteinuric dogs
demonstrated that telmisartan was more effective than enalapril in
reducing SBP and proteinuria at all time points.79 Thus, telmisartan may
be an ideal first-line therapy with or without secondary therapies in dogs
with SH.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine has been recommended as a second-line therapy or in
addition to ACEI in dogs. Monotherapy with amlodipine is currently not
recommended, as preferential dilation of the afferent renal arteriole can
result in increased glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure which can
result in exacerbation of proteinuria and damage to the glomerulus.2
Hence, the recommendation is to use this medication with an ACEI.
Some clinicians have suggested that if the BP can be controlled with
amlodipine, then the effect on intraglomerular pressure is minimized.
However, amlodipine impairs renal autoregulation, thus allowing minor

changes in BP to potentially directly alter glomerular filtration and
minimize the renoprotective effects of BP control. Therefore, single agent
amlodipine is not recommended, particularly in patients with underlying
renal disease. As with cats, additional antihypertensive therapies may
need to be involved in refractory cases of SH, patients with side-effects
from ACEI therapies (e.g., gingival hyperplasia, AKI, etc.) or specific
disease processes (e.g., pheochromocytoma).
Dietary salt restriction is not recommended for BP management as
evidence regarding its efficacy is mixed and its restriction may trigger
systemic RAAS activation (ch. 157). However, an elevated sodium
content in the diet may be detrimental to pre-existing diseases and likely
should be avoided.2

Monitoring
Once therapy is instituted, a recheck physical exam and BP
measurement are recommended within 7-10 days or 1-3 days if TOD is
present, and dosage adjustments made accordingly (ch. 91).

HYPERTENSIVE EMERGENCIES
SH is rarely urgent to treat unless there are acute and significant signs of
TOD and documentation of severe hypertension (>180 mm Hg).
Regardless, the goal is a gradual decrease in SBP and the best way to
achieve this is ideally by parenteral medications as incremental BP
decrease can be finely adjusted. It has been suggested that the BP be
reduced 10% in the first hour and 15% over the next few hours, as
patients with chronic SH may have an increased risk of iatrogenic renal,
cerebral, or coronary ischemia from more rapid drops. Unfortunately,
parental antihypertensive drugs are not always available (Table 236.1).

Parenteral Medications
Sodium nitroprusside consistently reduces SBP.80,81 Gradual titration of
the dosage every 5-15 minutes is recommended to achieve the desired
effect, beginning at 1-2 mcg/kg/min IV constant rate infusion (CRI) and
not exceeding a maximum of 10 mcg/kg/min in dogs.
Labetalol recently has been studied in dogs. It has been shown to
reliably reduce systolic, diastolic, and mean arterial BP in dogs with
perioperative SH without increasing the heart rate.82 Its use in dogs for

hypertensive emergencies has yet to be critically evaluated; less is known
in cats. A dose of 0.25 mg/kg IV over 2 minutes, repeated to a total
dosage of 3.75 mg/kg, followed by an IV CRI of 25 mcg/kg/min in dogs,
have been suggested.
The use of fenoldopam, a selective dopamine 1 receptor agonist,
cannot be recommended at this time, given the paucity of information in
this population and lack of consistent effects on BP in normotensive dogs
and even less so in cats.83
Hydralazine has been shown to reliably decrease BP in dogs and cats
and may be used in hypertensive crises.2,84 Tachycardia is a potential
side-effect of this medication and it may be associated with increased
myocardial oxygen demand. Due to the rapid onset of action, oral
formulations are generally utilized at a dosage of 0.5-2 mg/kg PO q12h.
However, IV administration may be considered in dogs at loading dosage
of 0.1 mg/kg IV over 2 minutes, followed by an IV CRI of 1.5-5
mcg/kg/min. IV administration has not been studied in cats. However,
subcutaneous administration at a total 1-2.5 mg per cat dose has been
used for post-renal-transplant hypertension.85
Phentolamine has been shown to be effective in dogs and cats
experimentally.86 Its clinical usage is largely reserved for management
of intraoperative SH in dogs with pheochromocytoma but it could be
considered in other scenarios.87 The current dosage recommended in
dogs is a 0.1 mg/kg IV loading dose followed by 1-2 mcg/kg/min IV CRI.
Esmolol has a rapid onset and short duration of action (<15
minutes).88 Its use in animals has largely been anecdotal for
intraoperative hypertension in dogs with pheochromocytomas but it may
be appropriate in any tachycardic, hypertensive patient. However, beta
blockade alone can result in adrenergic crisis with unopposed alpha
stimulation and severe SH in patients with pheochromocytoma and
therefore, use in this population requires prior alpha blockade.87 It has
been dosed at 50-75 mcg/kg/min IV CRI in dogs but has been used at
higher dosages for cardiac arrhythmias.
Magnesium infusions have been used clinically for patients with
hypertensive crises, particularly in the setting of pheochromocytomas in
people.89 Magnesium infusions have multiple potential benefits,
particularly in this setting, as magnesium inhibits the release of
catecholamines, directly inhibits catecholamine receptors, and is a
calcium antagonist. It attenuates catecholamine release from noxious

stimuli (e.g., endotracheal intubation) and reduces the arrhythmias
induced by epinephrine. It also profoundly dilates arterioles, reduces
peripheral vascular resistance (afterload), and exerts minimal effect on
venous return (preload). Its use in this clinical setting in dogs has been
anecdotal and it has not been widely studied. In the authors’ experience,
it has been used at 30 mg/kg IV loading dose and 15-30 mg/kg/hr in
dogs.

Oral Medications
In addition to hydralazine, amlodipine may be appropriate for
hypertensive crises and it has been used for treating severe SH in dogs
with AKI. An initial dose of 0.25 mg/kg has been recommended, with
repeat dosing in increments of 0.25 mg/kg q1-3h until a target SBP of
140-160 mm Hg is reached or a maximal cumulative dose of 1
mg/kg/day is reached. In one study, dosage increments were postponed
for 2 hours in dogs responding to amlodipine therapy with a decrease in
SBP ≥20 mm Hg, but not reaching the target, except if potentially life‐
threatening hypertensive complications were observed. Subsequent
dosages of amlodipine were based on the cumulative 24‐hour dose
necessitated for initial control and on individual clinical response to
maintain the target SBP.13 Dosages >0.8 mg/kg may be associated with
toxicosis and the authors do not recommend the cumulative dose of 1
mg/kg/day reported.

CONCLUSION
SH often does not lead to clinical signs until TOD is apparent, which
highlights the importance to screen for SH and to determine the cause
prior to the onset of signs. TOD changes can be irreversible and lifethreatening. Treatment of SH is usually well tolerated by cats and dogs,
and should be instituted without delay once SH is documented.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Systemic Hypertension
High blood pressure is common in animals like in humans, but the
causes are usually different. In cats and dogs the most common type of
high blood pressure is secondary to medical conditions such as kidney

disease and certain endocrine diseases (for instance, Cushing’s disease).
Animals rarely show signs of elevated blood pressure until damage
occurs in certain critical organs. The most common manifestations
include the eyes (for instance, acute blindness), the nervous system
(seizures), and the kidneys (leading to severe kidney failure). This
damage may be permanent and lead to serious, life-threatening
consequences. High blood pressure causes “silent damage” because
damage occurs without you or your pet knowing it.
Therefore, your veterinarian may recommend measuring your pet’s
blood pressure yearly along with an annual exam to help screen for high
blood pressure and to catch it before it causes harm to your pet. Along
with measuring blood pressure, your veterinarian may recommend
screening for certain medical conditions that predispose your pet to high
blood pressure.
Serge Chalhoub (Calgary, Alberta, Canada) and Douglas
Palma (New York, New York)

CHAPTER 237: Heartworm
Disease in Dogs and Cats
Ashley B. Saunders

A C RO N YM S
AHS American Heartworm Society
ECG electrocardiographic

OVERVIEW
Heartworm disease is an important mosquito-borne disease caused
by the filarial nematode Dirofilaria immitis, a parasite most often
found in temperate zones throughout the world. Adult heartworms
typically reside in the host’s pulmonary arteries, causing
inflammation and endothelial damage. Some infected animals do not
have clinical signs, while others develop clinical manifestations of
heartworm disease related to the host’s immune response, worm
burden, and duration of infection.1-3 Clinical disease is most often
characterized by abnormal respiratory signs and exercise
intolerance. Dyspnea, hemoptysis, right-sided congestive heart
failure, and hemolysis with hemodynamic instability are indicators of
severe disease.

ETIOLOGY AND EPIDEMIOLOGY
Heartworm disease is caused by D. immitis, a parasitic roundworm
of the superfamily Filarioidea, transmitted by mosquito insect
vectors. The life cycle of the worm takes place in a mosquito insect
vector and in a mammalian host (Figure 237.1; Video 237.1

).

INSECT VECTOR AND TRANSMISSION
Various mosquito species located throughout the world are able to
transmit D. immitis. The mosquito species attributed most often
with D. immitis transmission to domestic dogs and cats are genera
Aedes, Ochlerotatus (formerly Aedes), Anopheles, Culex, and
Psorophora.4-11 Mosquitoes thrive in warm, humid climates
including swamps, marshlands, pastures, rice fields, slow moving
canals or streams, and any areas of flooding, and require very little
water to reproduce.7,12-14 Small amounts of water in containers and
tires, for example, can provide enough habitat for mosquitos to
reproduce and spread.7 Mosquito habitats continue to expand and
change to include any urban or rural location with adequate
temperature to support heartworm transmission. Habitats can also
be influenced by natural disasters, namely large tropical storms and
hurricanes, that lead to the reshaping of geographical areas, an
increased incidence of free-standing water, increased numbers of
mosquitoes, and the disruption of routine heartworm prevention.7,1519
While exposure to feeding mosquitoes is higher outdoors,
mosquitos can enter structures and buildings to feed on animals
indoors.
D. immitis is transmitted by female mosquitoes seeking blood
meals necessary to continue reproducing.20 Larva development
requires an average daily temperature of at least 57° F (14° C);
however, successful larval development can also occur with adequate
hourly temperatures and in urban locations with higher
temperatures or areas of microclimates that provide optimal
conditions.15,16,21,22 Additionally, some species of mosquito are able

to survive the winter.23 Mosquito feeding activity can be categorized
into diurnal (day), nocturnal (night), and crepuscular (dawn and
dusk).7 The characteristics of known mosquito species in an area can
be useful for minimizing exposure during peak activity times.
Movement of animals to and from areas with infected mosquito
vectors increases with travel, rehoming, dissemination through
rescue organizations and with natural disasters, all of which can
increase the spread of infectious disease and parasites including D.
immitis.17-19,24-32 Many of the mosquito species that transmit D.
immitis can also transmit Dirofilaria repens, a filarial nematode
primarily identified in Europe, Africa, and Asia, that does not
typically result in clinical disease but can cause cutaneous
disorders.33 Identification of D. repens in specific locations within
these regions can provide insight into potential distribution for D.
immitis.10,34

HOSTS
Dogs and cats are susceptible to infection with D. immitis. In
addition to domestic dogs and cats, D. immitis infection has been
detected in wild and captive canids (e.g., coyote, jackal, red fox, wolf)
and felids (e.g., bobcat, leopard, lion, ocelot) as well as many other
mammalian species that can serve as natural reservoir hosts or
incidental hosts including coati, ferret, horse, lemur, muskrat,
raccoon, and sea lion.35-53 For example, coyotes with D. immitis in
California are documented reservoirs of infection for domestic
dogs.54 Humans can also become infected with D. immitis, with
worms or inflammatory granulomas identified predominantly in the
lungs, mucous membranes or other aberrant locations associated
with worm migration.55-58

LIFE CYCLE OF DIROFILARIA IMMITIS
(MOSQUITO TO HOST TO MOSQUITO)

When a mosquito bites an infected animal with circulating
microfilariae (L1) and ingests the microfilariae, the microfilariae
enter via the proboscis and begin to develop within the mouth of the
mosquito. The larvae molt in the mosquito twice (L1-L2, L2-L3) over
an approximately 2-week period at which point they become
infective (Figure 237.1; Video 237.1

). The transition from L1-

L3 requires adequate temperature and humidity and benefits from
the presence of the endosymbiotic bacteria, Wolbachia.20,59-62 A
feeding mosquito infects a host by penetrating the host skin or
mucous membranes and transmitting the L3 larval stage (Figure
237.2). The L3 larvae begin to molt and migrate to the fourth larval
stage (L4) in the host tissues within 12 days of entry.63 The final molt
to the fifth larval stage (L5, immature adult) occurs 2-3 months (5070 days) after host infection, at which time immature adults enter
into the vascular system and are carried through the right heart and
to the pulmonary arteries, where they fully mature and where the
majority of the damage occurs. Mature male and female worms
measure 15-18 cm and 25-30 cm, respectively, and live for many
years (5-7 years in experimental infection in dogs).64,65 Male worms
are shorter than females and are also characterized by a corkscrewshaped tail (Figure 237.3). Microfilariae (L1) are released from the
mature female worms into the host’s circulatory system 6-9 months
after the canine host becomes infected and can live for as long as 30
months.63 The presence of circulating microfilariae (L1) in a host
provides a source of infection for biting mosquitoes to continue the
D. immitis life cycle. Microfilaria detection in dogs can be higher
during summer months when daylight is longer.66 Damage to the
host begins early in the infection process with the molt to the
immature adult (L4-L5) 2-3 months after host infection and
importantly, before an antigen test for D. immitis would detect
infection. This is the typical life cycle for D. immitis in a domestic
dog.
