The D. immitis life cycle in cats is shorter, which is attributed to
differences in host-species immune response.20,67 The period of the
life cycle within the mosquito is comparable to that of the dog. When
a mosquito transmits L3 larvae to a cat, the larvae reside and molt in
the host tissues to the fourth larval stage (L4). The final molt to the
immature adult (L5) occurs approximately 2 months after infection
and then to the mature adult in approximately 4-6 months. If mature
adult female worms are present, they are able to produce
microfilariae 7-8 months after the initial host infection. However,
while circulating microfilariae can live for many years, they are often
transient or rarely detected in cats due to immune-mediated
destruction of microfilariae.68 Additionally, cats typically have a
small number of adult worms (<6), generally fewer than dogs, and
this is attributed in part to the smaller overall size of cats.20,69 Adult
heartworms are estimated to live 2-3 years in experimentally infected
cats and possibly longer in natural infections.70-72 Similar to dogs,
inflammation and lesions in the host begin early in the infection.

GEOGRAPHIC DISTRIBUTION
D. immitis infections are reported throughout the world (ch. 9),
most often in areas with warm climates and generally in the middle
latitudes of the Earth.73 Infections are documented in North, South
and Central America, Europe, Asia, Australia, and Africa.73-79 Some
of the highest known prevalence rates are reported in the United
States, Australia, Italy, and both western and southern regions of
Spain.20,80,81 Endemic areas in the United States include the south
east, most notably the Mississippi River Delta where the Mississippi
River joins into the warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico at the
southeast coast of Louisiana; the Gulf Coast; and areas along the
Ohio and Missouri rivers (Figure 237.4).17,58,83 Heartworm
infection has been diagnosed in dogs in all 50 states in the United
States, while transmission of infection has been described in all but
Alaska.2,84 The prevalence in dogs in Canada varies, with the highest
rates reported in Ontario.24,85 In Mexico, the prevalence of infection
in dogs is ~8% (7.5-8.3%), with higher rates reported in coastal
areas.86-88 The prevalence of infection varies based on many factors.
In some highly endemic areas, the prevalence of infection can reach
100% in dogs, whereas in cats, the corresponding prevalence is often
reportedly lower than in dogs, even in endemic areas, although
detecting infection and thus assessing prevalence, remains
challenging in cats.59,89,90

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
The primary lesions of D. immitis infection occur in the host’s
pulmonary arteries and lungs. Immature and mature adult worms
are predominantly located in the pulmonary arteries. The small size
of the immature adult worms allows them to be carried via blood
flow to the lumen of the distal pulmonary arteries. As the worms
grow in diameter and length, they can be found in more proximal
locations in the pulmonary arteries, and in some cases, worms
migrate into the right ventricle, right atrium, and venae

cavae.20,91,92 Pathologic changes to the pulmonary arteries,
characterized by local damage to the intimal surface with intimal
thickening and proliferation (Figure 237.5), occur within the first
18 months and as early as even a few days after infection.92,93
Pulmonary vascular lesions develop secondary to worm-induced
damage to the vascular endothelium and activation of the host’s
immune response, resulting in inflammation, villous myointimal
proliferation and fibrosis, release of vasoactive mediators that
promote vasoconstriction, and increased vascular permeability.94,95
Activation of the immune system promotes a pathologic process that
is complicated by inflammation, platelet activation, and thrombus
formation.95 Release of platelet-derived growth factors and
endothelin-1 promotes vasoconstriction.96,97 Vascular proliferation
contributes to occlusion of the arterial lumen as do thrombi, worms
and worm fragments from parasitic embolism of dead worms that
die naturally or that are associated with administration of an
adulticide in dogs (Figure 237.6). Macroscopic changes to the
pulmonary arteries include enlargement, wall thickening, increased
tortuosity, villous proliferation and the presence of thromboembolic
material.95,98 Damage to the pulmonary arteries, reduced
pulmonary arterial blood flow, and pulmonary thromboembolism
(ch. 219) contribute to the development of pulmonary arterial
hypertension (ch. 218), a diagnosis that is more commonly made in
dogs than cats with heartworm disease.1,20,58,99,100 An increase in
pulmonary vascular permeability can result in pulmonary edema,
representing a different mechanism of developing pulmonary edema
than increased hydrostatic pressure that occurs with left-sided
congestive heart failure (ch. 217).20,101 Myocardial changes to the
right ventricle characterized by loss of myocardial collagen have been
documented early in the disease process.102,103 The increase in
pulmonary vascular resistance and development of pulmonary
hypertension result in right ventricular hypertrophy. Right atrial
enlargement occurs secondary to both increased right heart pressure
and volumetrically important tricuspid valve regurgitation, if
present. In severe disease, right-sided myocardial dysfunction and

right-sided congestive heart failure lead to ascites and less often,
pleural effusion.
The pathologic process associated with D. immitis infection also
results in damage to the lung tissue, characterized as interstitial
inflammation and hemorrhage eventually resulting in hemosiderosis
and fibrosis with and without involvement of the pleura.94 This
damage can be diffuse or localized to the caudal lung fields and it has
been associated more frequently with the right caudal lung
lobe.20,104 Infarction of lung tissue in dogs with heartworm infection
has been reported but is relatively rare; this has been attributed in
part to the collateral blood supply of the lungs in dogs.101,105,106
Resolution of lesions after adulticide treatment in dogs can occur
over time, although dogs with chronic infection and evidence of
pulmonary fibrosis may have little improvement.101,107 Immune
complexes formed in response to microfilariae, adult worms, and
Wolbachia promote systemic inflammation and damage, primarily in
the glomerulus and lungs.108-112 Glomerulonephritis is associated
with urinary protein loss (ch. 302) while the development of renal
azotemia is rare.109,113 In cats, immature and mature worms (L3-L5)
induce pulmonary and vascular inflammation (Figure 237.7) early
in the disease process (3-6 months), resulting in respiratory disease
often mistaken for allergic airway disease or asthma (ch. 215).114,115
Distinguishing heartworm infection from asthma is important
because heartworm disease can result in chronic damage to the
pulmonary arteries, heart and lungs and unlike asthma, heartworm
disease can be prevented.116

Worms can be found in places other than the pulmonary arteries
when aberrant migration occurs to ectopic locations within body
cavities and the systemic circulation. This results in identification of
worms in pleural effusion or ascites and damage to other organs
including the brain, spinal cord and eyes causing systemic arterial,
neurologic, and ophthalmic presentations.117-127 Successful surgical
removal of D. immitis worms from the femoral artery of a cat and

anterior chamber of the eye and spinal subarachnoid space in dogs
has been reported with subsequent resolution of clinical signs.125-127
The symbiotic Gram-negative bacterium, Wolbachia, has been
identified in filarial nematodes, including all developmental stages of
D. immitis.20,128-130 Wolbachia promotes worm growth and survival
but is harmful to the infected host and contributes to disease (Box
237.1). Surface proteins on Wolbachia stimulate inflammation and
have been identified in the lung, liver, and glomerulus of infected
dogs and cats and the reproductive tract of adult female
worms.20,131-133 The host immune response to Wolbachia can
develop within 2 months of D. immitis infection.133 Release of
Wolbachia from natural worm death (dog, cat), adulticide-induced
worm death (dog), and microfilaria turnover is associated with
activation of the host’s immune system and a pro-inflammatory
response.130-134 The interaction between Wolbachia and host
immune system is complex, and the collective understanding
continues to develop.

CLINICAL PRESENTATION
Dogs and cats can be infected with D. immitis without any overt
evidence of clinical disease, particularly early in the disease process.
However, over time, infected dogs and cats are more likely to develop
clinical signs of heartworm disease.

DOGS
Clinical signs in heartworm-infected dogs are most often related to
the respiratory system (e.g., cough, increased respiratory rate and
effort at rest or with activity, dyspnea, hemoptysis), and reduced
exercise ability. Characterizing the clinical signs is useful for
assessing severity of disease and to guide treatment planning.135
Hemoptysis (ch. 36) and acute respiratory distress (ch. 37) suggest
pulmonary arterial thromboembolism has occurred (ch. 219).
Identification of dark red urine (ch. 55) in a heartworm-positive dog
suggests hemoglobinuria from intracardiac worms causing red blood
cell lysis and is highly suggestive of caval syndrome (dirofilarial
hemoglobinuria) (Figure 237.8).136-139 Dark red urine can be

intermittent if the worms move from an intracardiac location back
into the pulmonary arteries; therefore, in some cases, discolored
urine (pigmenturia) is initially observed by owners.137 Syncope (ch.
40), abdominal distension from ascites (ch. 21), jugular venous
distension, and weight loss (ch. 18) are more likely as heartworm
disease progresses and serve as clinical indicators of pulmonary
hypertension (syncope) or right-sided heart failure (ascites, jugular
venous distension, weight loss).1,2,138 Exercise can worsen clinical
signs in dogs with severe pulmonary lesions and pulmonary
hypertension.2,140
Abnormal physical exam findings (ch. 3) are often indicators of
the underlying disease process in an individual case. Respiratory
abnormalities include auscultation of harsh lung sounds or
pulmonary crackles and the presence of tachypnea or dyspnea (ch.
37). A systolic murmur with a point of maximal intensity at the mid
right-thorax suggests high velocity tricuspid valve regurgitation from
pulmonary hypertension (ch. 218) or the presence of intracardiac
heartworms creating tricuspid valve regurgitation and turbulent
blood flow.137,139,141 Dogs with pulmonary hypertension also can
have a split second heart sound auscultated at the left heart base (left
axillary region) caused by delayed closure of the pulmonary valve
leaflets compared to the closure of the aortic valve leaflets (Videos
38.2, 237.2

). Arrhythmias are not commonly reported, but

supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias (ch. 230) can occur
with myocardial wall stretch and tissue damage. Indicators of rightsided heart failure and elevated right heart pressure include jugular
venous distension (Videos 229.1 and 237.3

), positive

hepatojugular reflux, hepatomegaly, and ascites. Muffled heart and
lung sounds suggest the presence of pleural effusion (ch. 220).
Indicators of caval syndrome, when worms are present in the right
side of the heart resulting in hemolysis, include a right-sided heart
murmur over the tricuspid valve, hemoglobinuria/pigmenturia, and
evidence of hemodynamic instability associated with insufficient
perfusion (e.g., lethargy, weakness, hypotension).137,139,142

CATS
Clinical signs in heartworm-infected cats are most often attributed to
the respiratory system (e.g., cough, tachypnea, dyspnea,
hemoptysis), termed heartworm-associated respiratory disease
(HARD), although sudden death may be the first sign of disease
(Box 237.2).71,115,143 Many infected cats do not develop or have

only transient clinical signs associated with an acute inflammatory
response or worm death.144 Other less commonly reported
abnormalities in cats with heartworm disease include vomiting,
weight loss, abdominal distension, ataxia, paresis, seizures and
syncope, and in some cases these are attributed to aberrant worm
migration.20,125
Abnormal physical exam findings include increased respiratory
rate and effort (ch. 37) with auscultation of harsh lung sounds.
Muffled heart and lung sounds are more likely when cats have
pleural effusion. A right-sided or sternal systolic murmur can be
auscultated with tricuspid valve regurgitation (ch. 38). Other
abnormalities can be detected with aberrant worm migration and are
specific to worm location.

DIAGNOSIS
DETECTING DIROFILARIA IMMITIS
INFECTION
The diagnosis of heartworm infection can be simple with an antigen
or antibody test or it can require multiple tests to confirm a
suspected infection. Whether there has been inadequate heartworm
prevention, a lapse in heartworm prevention, travel to an endemic
area (ch. 9), or a newly acquired animal with unknown history,
consistent annual testing provides a mechanism for detecting
heartworm infection. Identifying a heartworm infection prior to the
development of clinical signs allows for proper treatment and a plan
for prophylaxis that can limit progression of the disease process and
be beneficial for the animal.

Microfilariae
Microfilariae from multiple filarial worms have a similar appearance
to D. immitis. Identifying D. immitis is important for the diagnosis
and proper treatment of heartworm disease.20 Filarial worms other
than D. immitis can be encountered throughout the world and their
differentiation from microfilarial D. immitis is important because the
worms may have different insect vectors, routes of transmission, and
pathogenesis.145,146 For example, in North America,
Acanthocheilonema reconditum (Dipetalonema reconditum in older
literature) differs from D. immitis in that A. reconditum is
transmitted by fleas, lice and ticks, and the adult worms localize to
subcutaneous tissues.147 While the microfilariae of D. immitis are
slightly larger and have a tapered cephalic end and straight caudal
end with stationary body movement, microfilariae of A. reconditum
have a blunt cephalic end, curved caudal end and progressive body
movement.20 Identification of D. immitis microfilariae (L1) in the
host indicates the presence of adult heartworms producing the
microfilariae (Figure 237.9). Additionally, microfilariae serve as a
source of infection that can be acquired by blood-feeding mosquitoes
and transmitted to other hosts. It is important to remember that not
all infected dogs and very few infected cats will have circulating
microfilariae; therefore, the absence of microfilariae does not
indicate an animal is free from heartworm infection.68 Additionally,
the number of microfilariae identified does not directly correlate
with the severity of the infection or number of adult worms in the
host.148 Detection of microfilaria is enhanced by utilizing
concentration techniques (e.g., modified Knott test, millipore filter).

FIGURE 237.9 Slide review of peripheral blood
smear documenting a microfilaria (L1) in a dog with
Dirofilaria immitis infection and echocardiographic
identification of worms in the pulmonary arteries.
The presence of adult worms in a dog or cat without circulating
microfilariae has been designated as an “occult” infection.108
Potential reasons for an absence of microfilariae in an infected
animal include testing early in the prepatent period, all-male
infections, host immune system destruction of microfilariae, and use
of medications that kill microfilariae including macrocyclic lactonebased preventatives. The reduction in identifiable microfilariae
attributed to the use of macrocyclic lactone preventatives has led to
the perception that testing for microfilariae is low-yield, resulting in
more recent efforts to re-educate veterinarians about the value of
microfilaria testing.149 Potential reasons for detecting microfilariae
in an animal that tests negative for adult worms include the presence
of a parasite other than D. immitis that produces microfilariae (such
as A. reconditum), a puppy that acquired microfilariae

transplacentally, an animal that received microfilariae through blood
transfusion, and immune-complex binding that prevents an antigen
test from detecting adult worm antigen.149-151 Additionally,
microfilariae can be slow to clear after adulticide treatment as the
adult worms die, and can remain present in fewer numbers for >6
months after the animal has received a macrocyclic lactone
preventative (see preventative section below).20,152

Adult Heartworms
The principal method of identifying adult worms in dogs and some
cats is with a test that detects circulating antigens that arise
primarily from the uterus of the adult female worm.149,153 Antigen
tests are single- or multi-step, easy to use tests that can be performed
in house or at a reference laboratory. The tests use enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assay (ELISA) or immunochromatographic
techniques specific for dogs (e.g., at current writing, they include
HESKA Solo Step CH, IDEXX SNAP 4Dx Plus, Modern Veterinary
Therapeutics Anigen Rapid, Zoetis WITNESS, Zoetis VETSCAN
Heartworm Rapid or Flex4 Rapid, Zoetis DiroCHEK) or cats (Heska
Solo Step FH, IDEXX SNAP Feline Triple Test, Zoetis WITNESS,
Zoetis WITNESS FFH, Zoetis VETSCAN Heartworm Rapid, Zoetis
DiroCHEK). Antigen tests for D. immitis that are combined with
other tests for vector-borne diseases include the IDEXX SNAP 4DX
Plus and Zoetis VETSCAN Flex4 Rapid that test for Anaplasma
phagocytophilum, Anaplasma platys, Borrelia burgdorferi,
Ehrlichia canis, Ehrlichia ewingii (plus Ehrlichia chaffeensis with
VETSCAN Flex4) in dogs. The IDEXX SNAP Feline Triple Test and
Zoetis WITNESS FFH include tests for feline immunodeficiency
virus antibody and feline leukemia virus antigen. Current antigen
tests are highly specific and sensitive, most detecting infections with
as little as 1 female worm. Antigen tests are widely used to diagnose
heartworm infection in dogs (Figure 237.10). A positive antigen
test in a cat is indicative of an adult heartworm infection, but false
negative test results are not uncommon because of immunemediated destruction of juvenile worms or a low worm burden
consisting of an all-male infection. False negative test results can also
occur in dogs for similar reasons (all male infection, juvenile worms).

False negative or delayed positive antigen results have been
documented for 9 months in dogs when the host-antigen response is
suppressed by recent administration of a routine preventative (i.e.,
macrocyclic lactone-derived).153 Antigen-antibody complex
formation can block antigen detection, resulting in false-negative test
results.149 A method of heat treatment of samples has been
described to increase the sensitivity of detecting infection in dogs
and cats.154,155 Currently, heat treatment is performed at reference
laboratories and is not recommended for every antigen test but
would be considered if an antigen test is negative and either D.
immitis microfilariae are present or there is a clinical suspicion of
heartworm disease.149 Because of the limitations of detecting
heartworm infection solely with an antigen test in cats, additional
tests can be needed for diagnosis including antibody test for D.
immitis, thoracic radiographs, and echocardiography (Figure
237.11). When heartworm status is unknown, antigen testing in dogs
is performed at the time of examination and even if negative, again
approximately 7 months (no sooner than 6 months) later to monitor
for recent infection that would have gone undetected with the first
test. This includes a dog with an unknown heartworm prophylaxis
history or a missed dose of preventative. Testing is also currently
recommended at 9 months (no sooner than 6 months) after a dog
completes adulticide therapy with melarsomine to provide enough
time for worm death prior to retesting with an antigen test.135
Antibody tests detect antibody in the blood from the immune
response stimulated by both male and female worms in infected
animals. Antibody develops in response to larval (L3, L4) migration
in pulmonary tissue; however, the sensitivity of different tests varies,
results are often transient during the course of the infection, and
false negative results occur as the immune response wanes.90,115,156
Due to the overall challenges in detecting heartworm infection in
cats, antibody tests (i.e., Antech Fel Heartworm AB, HESKA Solo
Step FH for antibody) are one method of attempting to identify
infection. A positive antibody test indicates prior infection (detected
from any worm stage) or confirms a current infection particularly
when combined with a positive antigen test or identification of adult
worms or microfilariae. Antibody tests have not been routinely used

in dogs but have been explored in combination with other tests in an
effort to increase the potential for making a positive diagnosis in
infected dogs.157
While microfilaria and antigen testing are widely available, they do
not detect heartworm infection until specific time points in the life
cycle once the animal has been infected for a period of weeks to
months. Prior and ongoing work continues to explore other testing
methods to improve diagnostic capabilities and early detection of
heartworm infection using blood screening for microfilariae with
lens-free technology and light diffraction and the use of genetic
markers to detect early infections at the L3 and L4 larval
stages.158,159

FIGURE 237.10 Flowchart for diagnosing
heartworm disease in a dog.

CLINICAL EVALUATION AND
DIAGNOSTIC TESTS
The diagnostic evaluation of D. immitis infection includes tests to
assess the severity of the disease process or investigate the cause of
clinical signs. In some cases, testing for D. immitis infection is
prompted by abnormal diagnostic test results that suggest the
presence of heartworm disease, such as the presence of eosinophilia
and identification of microfilariae on a complete blood count or
thoracic radiographic evidence of enlarged, tortuous pulmonary
arteries and right ventricular enlargement in a coughing dog.

Thoracic Radiography
Radiographs provide non-invasive imaging of the thorax to evaluate
the heart, pulmonary arteries, and lungs. Radiographs can be normal
—typically early in the disease process—or they can show changes
that reflect lesions associated with progression of disease.
Radiographs can also appear normal despite extensive disease and
dogs can also have severe pathologic changes that are not adequately
reflected on radiographic images.20,32,160 In 200 dogs with
heartworm infection, 28 (14%) had normal thoracic radiographs, and
the most common abnormalities in the remaining dogs were
enlargement of the pulmonary trunk, right ventricle, and right
branch pulmonary artery.161 Pulmonary trunk (main pulmonary
artery) enlargement is best identified on a dorsoventral or
ventrodorsal view (Figure 237.12). The branch pulmonary arteries
can become enlarged, tortuous and in some cases blunt, tapered, or
pruned (Figure 237.12). This abrupt narrowing is attributed to
pathologic narrowing of the arterial lumen and embolism of distal
portions of the arteries.101 Abnormalities are often appreciated in the
caudal lobar arteries earlier than in the cranial lobar arteries, with
right branch changes identified more often than left branch
changes.160 Enlargement of the branch pulmonary arteries can be
assessed by comparing the artery diameter to its corresponding
pulmonary vein diameter or to the diameter of the 4th rib on a lateral
view or 9th rib on a dorsoventral view.101 As the disease progresses

and pulmonary hypertension develops, right ventricular enlargement
can be appreciated radiographically (Figure 237.12). Radiographic
changes associated with pulmonary hypertension (ch. 218) are not
unique to heartworm disease except for increased pulmonary artery
tortuosity and blunting that are more likely to indicate heartworm
disease.
The pulmonary patterns associated with heartworm disease range
from bronchial, to interstitial secondary to inflammation and
fibrosis. An alveolar pattern is an indicator of pulmonary
thromboembolism, hemorrhage, or edema (Figure 237.13).
Increased vascular permeability can result in interstitial edema,
representing a different mechanism than the pulmonary edema that
develops from increased hydrostatic pressure associated with high
filling pressures and congestive heart failure from left-sided heart
disease.101 Caudal vena cava enlargement and ascites are indicators
of elevated right heart pressure and right-sided heart failure,
respectively. In 28 dogs with heartworm disease and concurrent
right-sided congestive heart failure, radiographic abnormalities were
detected in all dogs, including pulmonary changes and enlargement
of the caudal vena cava.160 Pleural effusion is not as commonly
identified as an indicator of right-sided congestive heart
failure.101,160
Pulmonary patterns can improve with corticosteroid
administration when pneumonitis is suspected (Figure 237.14) or
worsen following administration of adulticide as worms die.160,162 In
Beagles inoculated with D. immitis larvae, pulmonary artery
enlargement was best detected on ventrodorsal views and pulmonary
parenchymal lesions were worse during the 6 months after adulticide
therapy.162 While pulmonary artery enlargement and parenchymal
lesions did improve following adulticide therapy in some dogs, they
did not resolve in the dogs with persistent infection. In other studies,
enlargement of the pulmonary trunk, pulmonary arteries, and right
ventricle persisted long-term despite successful heartworm
treatment.20,101,160

FIGURE 237.11 Flowchart for diagnosing
heartworm disease in a cat.
Radiographs can serve as an additional test to aid in the diagnosis
of heartworm disease in cats when abnormal findings support
heartworm infection; however, similarities to asthma and
Aelurostrongylus infection and discrepancies between radiographic
abnormalities or lack of abnormalities and serologic status continue
to make the diagnosis challenging.116,163 The most common
abnormalities identified in cats with heartworm disease include
pulmonary artery enlargement with tortuosity and pruning and
bronchial to interstitial pulmonary patterns (Figure 237.15).115,164
The vertebral heart size on its own is not a reliable assessment of
heart enlargement in feline heartworm disease.164

Echocardiography (ch. 97)
Echocardiography is not required nor possible in every infected
animal. The potential benefits of echocardiography include
identifying the presence and location of intracardiac heartworms,
estimating the probability of pulmonary hypertension, and

evaluating associated secondary changes to the heart, particularly in
patients showing overt clinical signs. Echocardiography may be a
useful screening tool to consider in heartworm-positive, small-breed
dogs at risk for intracardiac worm migration.20,139 Due to the
challenges with making a serologic heartworm diagnosis in cats,
echocardiography is an additional diagnostic aid (Video 237.4

),

particularly in cats with clinical signs or radiographic findings that
suggest heartworm disease.116,165 On ultrasound images, adult
heartworms look like hyperechoic parallel lines that represent the
cuticle of the worm, with a central hypoechoic area measuring
approximately 1.3 mm in diameter that represents the coelomic
cavity (Figure 237.16).68 While heartworms are most often located
within the pulmonary arteries, echocardiographic imaging is
inherently limited to the pulmonary trunk and proximal pulmonary
arteries (Figure 237.16; ch. 97) and does not provide images of the
distal pulmonary arteries due to air within the lung creating
interference. Worms can be identified in intracardiac locations
including the right atrium and ventricle and the caval veins (Figure
237.16), and in rare instances, worms are identified in an aberrant
location such as the left atrium or ventricle (Figure 237.17).
Echocardiographic estimates of worm number are not generally
reliable because worms are entangled together (Figure 237.18).168
Intracardiac worm burden in the right atrium and ventricle can be
categorized as low (estimated <5 and not filling the right atrium) or
high (filling the right atrium) (Figure 237.19; Video 237.5

)

when assessing risk of host red blood cell destruction and caval
syndrome.139 In 72 dogs with intracardiac heartworms, the majority
had a high worm burden (58 dogs, 81%) and high likelihood of
pulmonary hypertension (67 dogs, 93%) based on echocardiography,
yet only 18 (25%) had evidence of caval syndrome (i.e., anemia,
hemoglobinuria, clinical signs) and only 1 with an estimated low
worm burden had heartworm extraction performed.139

with heartworm disease. Dog 1 had a positive antigen

Heartworm disease is a recognized cause of pulmonary
hypertension (ch. 219) (Figure 237.20).169 While some of the
pathologic changes that occur in response to the worms can improve
once the worms are eliminated,162 echocardiographic changes
including evidence of pulmonary hypertension have been found to
persist for months following adulticide therapy in dogs.170,171
Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography can also be
utilized to assist with or confirm worm removal during and after a
heartworm extraction procedure in dogs and cats.172,173

Other Imaging Modalities
Pulmonary artery size, pulmonary damage, and the presence of
pulmonary embolism and pulmonary granulomas have been
evaluated with computed tomography in dogs and cats with
heartworm disease.115,127,174 Computed tomography and magnetic
resonance imaging can detect the presence of worms in the
pulmonary arteries but cannot reliably quantify the number of
worms present in experimental studies of heartworm infected
dogs.175 D. immitis worms have been identified in aberrant locations
with computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging
investigating neurologic disease in dogs and within a femoral artery
in a cat.125,127

Electrocardiography
Electrocardiographic (ECG) abnormalities reflect the presence of
right heart enlargement or myocardial damage; therefore, most ECG
abnormalities indicate the dog or cat is further along in the disease
process. In general, electrocardiography is an insensitive test for
detecting cardiac enlargement compared to thoracic radiography and
echocardiography. Right ventricular enlargement affects the ECG by
altering the QRS complex morphology to a more prominent S wave
and by moving the electrical axis from a standard position to one
that indicates right ventricular enlargement (ch. 96). When present,
ECG changes associated with right ventricular enlargement, as can
be seen on pre-operative ECG assessment for example, can prompt

further diagnostic evaluation to confirm right heart enlargement and
the presence of heartworm disease.

a dog with heartworm disease that presented on
emergency due to spontaneous, acute respiratory
distress and hemoptysis. There is a diffuse nodular to

Clinical Pathology
Evaluation of the dog or cat with heartworm disease provides
information about disease severity and informs patient-specific
treatment planning. Abnormalities on the complete blood count can
include mild non-regenerative anemia, mild mature neutrophilia,
and thrombocytopenia. Anemia and thrombocytopenia become more
severe with the development of caval syndrome. The presence of
eosinophilia and basophilia are indicators of parasitic disease.101,115
Microfilariae can be identified on a blood smear (Figure 237.9).
Abnormalities on biochemical analysis can include hyperproteinemia
(albumin and globulin) and less often azotemia as indicators of
dehydration (pre-renal). Increased liver enzyme activities, most
often alanine aminotransferase, and hyperbilirubinemia can also
develop with caval syndrome.138,139 Urinalysis abnormalities can
include proteinuria, which is associated with glomerular deposition
of immune complexes, and bilirubinuria as an indicator of red blood
cell lysis attributed to traumatic destruction from passing through
intracardiac worms (although trace bilirubinuria can be normal in
dogs because of renal conjugation of bilirubin in this species).
Elevated D-dimer concentrations have been reported in dogs,
suggesting the presence of thromboembolic complications or
coagulation abnormalities (ch. 171).176 Biomarker analysis
performed in dogs with heartworm disease have reported cardiac
troponin I, N-terminal prohormone brain natriuretic peptide and Creactive protein elevations, and in some cases elevations are
correlated to severity of disease.176,177 Ascitic fluid from right-sided
congestive heart failure is characterized as a high-protein transudate
(ch. 71). Rarely, chylous effusions have been reported with
heartworm disease.172 Co-infection with other infectious diseases
does occur, often in shelter situations which have been most
extensively reported, complicating the clinical scenario.178-182

Diagnostic Summary
In summary, the diagnostic screening test of choice for dogs is
antigen testing with microfilaria testing; thoracic radiographs and
bloodwork are indicated in positive cases, and additional evaluations

can be pursued based on results and on the physical exam. In cats,
combined antigen and antibody testing increases the chances of
detecting heartworm infection, with careful evaluation of thoracic
radiographs for evidence of heartworm disease and
echocardiography for the presence of worms when physical exam
and clinical signs suggest heartworm disease.

TREATMENT IN DOGS
The spectrum of disease is so highly variable that prior to treatment,
clinical evaluation, including physical examination and diagnostic
testing, is recommended to tailor a plan best suited for the individual
animal based on severity of disease and risk assessment. In dogs,
comprehensive treatment plans address adult worms, microfilariae,
and management of the host’s clinical heartworm disease while
considering comorbidities when present. In addition to the presence
of other systemic diseases, considerations that can play a role in the
decision-making process when planning treatment include finances
and the owner’s ability to restrict activity after adulticidal therapy.
The American Heartworm Society (AHS) guidelines categorize
clinical signs to provide context when assessing disease severity and

for treatment planning.135 Dogs without clinical signs or with cough
are considered mildly affected, and moderately affected when cough
or abnormal lung sounds and exercise intolerance are present.
Evidence of severe disease includes cough, exercise intolerance,
abnormal lung sounds, dyspnea, syncope and ascites, at which point
medical therapy is a key factor in management and options for
adulticide therapy can become more limited. Caval syndrome is
characterized by a unique set of clinical signs and treatments.

TETRACYCLINES: DOXYCYCLINE,
MINOCYCLINE
Wolbachia are susceptible to treatment with tetracyclines and a
reduction in Wolbachia burden has negative effects on D. immitis
and positive effects for the host (Box 237.1). A reduction in
Wolbachia inhibits worm growth by contributing to fewer
microfilariae, sterility of female worms, and worm death while also
reducing inflammation in the host.183 Doxycycline is an integral
component of heartworm treatment in dogs and is typically dosed at
10 mg/kg PO q12h for 1 month at the time of diagnosis of heartworm
infection. This dosage was able to clear Wolbachia more effectively
than a lower dosage of doxycycline or minocycline in experimental
infections.184 Doxycycline can be administered at a reduced dosage
(5 mg/kg PO q12h) to finish the course if it is associated with adverse
gastrointestinal signs.184 Minocycline can serve as an alternative at
the same dosage if doxycycline is not available.185

ADULTICIDE THERAPY
The goal of adulticidal therapy is to kill and clear the adult worms
while limiting injury to the host. Thromboembolism of worm
fragments is an inevitable consequence of adulticide therapy and
worm death. Factors associated with low risk of thromboembolic
complications following adulticide therapy in dogs include no clinical
signs, normal appearing thoracic radiographs, no heartworms
observed with echocardiography, no concurrent diseases, and an
owner who is able to restrict exercise.20 Factors associated with high
risk include clinical signs (cough, syncope), presence of ascites,
thoracic radiographic abnormalities consistent with heartworm
disease, heartworms observed with echocardiography, concurrent
disease, and an owner who is unable to restrict exercise.20 Treatment
in dogs is a multistep process summarized in Table 237.1.

Arsenical-Based

Adulticide therapy has historically been accomplished through use of
organoarsenical-based medications including the no longer available
thiacetarsamide and the currently approved (for dogs) melarsomine
dihydrochloride (Immiticide, Merial; Diroban, Zoetis). A single
injection of melarsomine can kill up to 90% of male worms but only
10% of female worms and it is not effective against
microfilariae.20,186,187 Therefore, adulticide protocols include
multiple injections of melarsomine to improve effectiveness. A 2phase protocol is currently recommended by the AHS that includes 3
total injections of melarsomine (2.5 mg/kg IM injection in the
epaxial muscle), also called the split or 3-dose protocol (Table
237.1).135 Specifically, a single injection is administered and after at
least 30 days, 2 additional injections are administered 24 hours
apart. 20,187 The package inserts for melarsomine dihydrochloride
(Immiticide, Merial; Diroban, Zoetis) provide a detailed description
of heartworm disease stage and recommendations for use of
melarsomine including its contraindication for use in dogs with very
severe heartworm disease and caval syndrome.188,189 Additionally,
the drug inserts provide a description of how to administer the
intramuscular injection including specific location in the epaxial
muscles and needle size. A single-phase, 2-dose protocol consisting
of the administration of a single injection followed in 24 hours by a
second injection is a described standard regimen for adulticide
therapy. When evaluating the 2 protocols, the 2-phase protocol of 3
total injections that takes place over at least 30 days is associated
with fewer complications, a higher efficacy of worms killed (98%)
and thus a higher rate of treatment success135,186,187; however, it
also requires a longer time frame for treatment, longer period of
exercise restriction and is associated with a higher cost.
Adverse effects reported after use of melarsomine typically occur
within the first few days of administration when related to the drug
itself, and within the first few weeks (average 10-13 days) when they
are related to the death of worms and pulmonary vascular
embolization.188 Administration of the drug has been associated
with local irritation, swelling or pain at the injection site, reluctance
to move, and prolonged presence of a firm nodule at the injection
site. Also reported are fever, hypersalivation, lethargy, and cough or

other heartworm infection-related respiratory signs. Rarely, paresis
and paralysis have been reported if an injection is inadvertently
made in or near the spinal cord.190 Death of worms secondary to
administration of melarsomine results in embolization to the
pulmonary arteries, which can occur without causing clinical signs or
can result in severe respiratory distress and hemoptysis. Exercise
restriction is essential to minimize this risk.20,140

Non-arsenical Based
Because of the complexities of adulticide therapy and potential for
adverse effects, alternative treatment protocols have been explored
to shorten the process or improve the options when complicated,
prolonged treatment is not possible or melarsomine is not available.
Examples include animal shelters where resources and time can be
limited, and clients with limited access to veterinary care for a
variety of reasons.191,192 The effects of ivermectin at preventative
doses (6 mcg/kg/month PO) have been studied and an ability to
clear 56% of worms at 16 months and 95% of worms at 29 months
has been shown193-195; however, Wolbachia is not addressed in this
scenario and the prolonged time to worm death is associated with
potential continued damage to the pulmonary vasculature and lungs
and an increased risk of developing caval syndrome. Therefore, a
macrocyclic lactone preventative alone as a method of adulticide
therapy is not recommended.135
Combined use of doxycycline with preventative doses of either
ivermectin or moxidectin have been shown to have adulticidal effects
and are currently recommended prior to melarsomine or in dogs that
are unable to receive melarsomine.194 When ivermectin was
combined with doxycycline, the efficacy for clearing worms was 73%
at 10 months and even higher when followed by administration of
melarsomine.196,197 Non-arsenical-based protocols include
consistent use of a monthly macrocyclic lactone preventative, namely
oral ivermectin (6 mcg/kg) or topical moxidectin (2.5 mg/kg) with
imidacloprid (10 mg/kg), plus doxycycline 10 mg/kg PO q12-24h for
1 month.191,198-200 Moxidectin and doxycycline protocols vary

slightly in research settings but have been associated with efficacy
rates of >95% by 12-18 months in most scenarios.191,198-200

SURGICAL REMOVAL (ALSO SEE CH.
115)
Removal of intracardiac worms is performed when migration of
worms into the right heart chambers results in caval syndrome
characterized by evidence of hemolysis (anemia, hemoglobinuria)
and clinical signs consistent with hemodynamic instability.20
Removal of intracardiac worms would also be considered when a
large intracardiac worm burden (Figure 237.18; Video 237.5

)

is identified with echocardiography prior to the onset of hemolysis
and clinical signs.139 Presumably, this is a fortuitous diagnosis
made prior to the development of clinical signs when the patient is a
more stable candidate for the procedure. Occasionally, only a few
worms are identified with echocardiography in the right side of the
heart (Figure 237.19; Video 237.5

), either in the absence of

clinical signs or with clinical signs attributed to pulmonary
hypertension or right heart failure and not hemolysis.139 In this case,
medical management of pulmonary hypertension and congestive
heart failure is often preferred to stabilize the patient in lieu of
surgical removal.
In preparation for surgical removal, stabilization of the patient can
be necessary to manage respiratory signs, heart failure, hemolysis,
and poor cardiac output. This should include administration of a
corticosteroid (e.g., dexamethasone sodium phosphate 0.2 mg/kg
IV) and an antihistamine (diphenhydramine 2 mg/kg IM)
approximately 1 hour before the surgical procedure, and fluid
therapy, blood products, inotropic support, oxygen supplementation
and abdominocentesis as required. Other preoperative therapies can
include a bronchodilator (albuterol sulfate inhaler) for airway signs
related to pneumonitis and heparin 75-150 IU/kg SC q8h if there is a
concern for thromboembolic complications or historical or
radiographic evidence of recent thromboembolism. Surgical removal

is performed with sedation and local block or with anesthesia via a
jugular venotomy. Ideally the procedure is performed with
fluoroscopic or echocardiographic (transthoracic, transesophageal)
guidance to avoid inadvertent damage to cardiac structures
(tricuspid valve, right atrial wall) that can occur when extraction is
performed without imaging (Figure 237.21; Video 237.6
).173,201 Multiple types of extraction devices have been utilized for
this procedure with the goal of removing intracardiac worms without
damaging the heart (Figure 237.22). These include snare catheters,
endoscopic basket retrieval devices, flexible alligator forceps, and red
rubber catheters with suture attached. Removal of worms from the
pulmonary arteries can be challenging even with some of the
extraction devices that are equipped to reach out that far. Worms can
also be located deep in peripheral pulmonary arterioles where they
cannot be readily removed. Therefore, adulticide therapy is a
component of managing heartworm disease in some dogs even after
extraction has been performed. Debulking large heartworm burdens
can be beneficial for reducing thromboembolic complications
associated with worm death.

MICROFILARIAE
The use of macrocyclic lactone preventatives results in a decrease
and eventual elimination of microfilariae. Eliminating microfilariae
removes the dog as a potential reservoir of infection for feeding
mosquitoes. Pre-treatment with a corticosteroid (e.g.,
dexamethasone 0.2 mg/kg IV) and antihistamine (diphenhydramine
2 mg/kg IM) is recommended prior to administration of the first
dose of preventatives in dogs with high microfilaria counts and when
using preventatives containing milbemycin (500 mcg/kg
preventative dose is microfilaricidal) which is associated with a more
rapid elimination of microfilariae. Clinical observation for adverse
reactions is prudent for dogs receiving their first dose of
preventative. Topical moxidectin is labeled for use in dogs with
microfilariae and has not been associated with adverse reactions that
might occur with rapid kill of microfilariae.191,202 Moxidectin,

ivermectin and selamectin are more likely to reduce and clear
microfilariae over a period of months.152

TREATMENT IN CATS
Medical management of clinical signs and surgical removal of
heartworms are the currently available treatment options.
Administration of an organoarsenical (melarsomine,
thiacetarsamide) has been evaluated in experimentally infected cats
and reported in retrospective evaluation and is not recommended
because of adverse reactions including pulmonary thromboembolism
and death.203,204 Surgical removal of heartworms is similar to dogs
but can require smaller devices to access the jugular vein, and cats
are at increased risk of hemodynamic collapse if worms tear during
removal.172,205

MEDICAL MANAGEMENT OF CLINICAL
DISEASE ATTRIBUTED TO
HEARTWORM INFECTION
RESPIRATORY SIGNS
Because of the lung damage that occurs in both dogs and cats with
heartworm infections, respiratory signs (e.g., cough, increased
respiratory effort, dyspnea, hemoptysis) are prevalent in heartworm
disease in both species. A detailed history, physical exam and
thoracic radiographs provide useful information for developing a
management plan. The anti-inflammatory effects of corticosteroids
can improve clinical and radiographic signs of pneumonitis.101
Addressing respiratory signs and pneumonitis in dogs can lead to a
more clinically stable patient prior to adulticide therapy-induced
worm death and inevitable embolization to the distal pulmonary
arteries. Therapeutic goals include reducing airway inflammation,
relieving bronchoconstriction, supplementing oxygen (ch. 123), and
addressing thromboembolic complications (ch. 219). For
pneumonitis in dogs, the AHS recommends a tapering 4-week course

of prednisone (0.5 mg/kg PO q12h × 1 week, 0.5 mg/kg PO q24h × 1
week, 0.5 mg/kg PO q48h × 2 weeks). For pneumonitis in cats, the
AHS recommends prednisolone 1 mg/kg PO q12h tapering to 0.5
mg/kg PO q48h over 4 weeks similar to dogs. If pulmonary
thromboembolism is suspected, the use of heparin or
antithrombotics or thrombolytics can be considered on an individual
basis.

PULMONARY HYPERTENSION (ALSO
SEE CH. 218)
Pulmonary hypertension is a sequela of heartworm infection-related
pulmonary artery damage and pulmonary thromboembolism.
Clinical signs that suggest pulmonary hypertension are increased
respiratory effort at rest or with exercise (ch. 37), syncope (ch. 40),
and right-sided congestive heart failure (ch. 229). Medical
management for moderate to severe, clinically overt pulmonary
hypertension includes addressing the underlying disease
contributing to pulmonary hypertension and use of specific
treatment to lower pulmonary pressures with a phosophodiesterase5 inhibitor (sildenafil 0.5-2 mg/kg PO q8h, or tadalafil 2 mg/kg PO
q24h) plus supplemental oxygen therapy if in respiratory distress
(ch. 123).169,206 While these medications can improve quality of life
in dogs with pulmonary hypertension, they typically require longterm use.206

Right-Sided Congestive Heart Failure (also see ch.
229)
The presence of ascites (ch. 21), often with concurrent muscle
wasting (ch. 151), is a strong indicator of right-sided congestive
heart failure in dogs with heartworm disease. Congestion occurs as a
result of increased hydrostatic pressure and myocardial failure.
Jugular venous distension (Video 237.3

) and hepatojugular

reflux support the presence of high right heart pressure. Medical
management can require the simultaneous use of medications to
lower pulmonary pressures with a phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitor (see
above), address fluid accumulation with diuretics (furosemide,
spironolactone), and improve ventricular myocardial function with a
positive inotrope/inodilator (pimobendan).138-140 Centesis (chs. 86
and 92) is beneficial for removing large-volume effusions instead of
relying on diuretics alone that can result in overdiuresis and reduced
cardiac output without fully resolving the effusion. The objective is to
improve forward cardiac output, perfusion, and signs of congestion.

Once right-sided congestive heart failure has occurred, similar to
pulmonary hypertension, treatments can improve quality of life but
are typically required long-term.

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis depends on the severity of the disease and clinical
signs. Heartworm infection in an animal without clinical signs or
evidence of disease on diagnostic tests is often correlated with a good
prognosis if appropriate prevention and treatment are provided.
Infected dogs that receive adulticide therapy can experience adverse
effects during treatment yet have good outcomes long term.207 Dogs
and cats with severe lung lesions associated with clinical signs,
severe pulmonary hypertension, right-sided heart failure and caval
syndrome are more likely to have a guarded to poor long-term
prognosis. However, some animals with severe disease can be
managed long-term. In caval syndrome, heartworm removal is
associated with poor outcomes in severely affected dogs; survival to
discharge is associated with a better long-term prognosis.136-139
Without heartworm removal, the prognosis for dogs with caval
syndrome is considered guarded to poor; patients already showing
clinical signs can progress to developing hemolytic anemia,
disseminated intravascular coagulation, hepatorenal dysfunction and
heart failure often resulting in death within a few days.

PREVENTION AND EDUCATION
PREVENTION

Heartworm disease is complex due to a complicated parasite life
cycle, variable clinical manifestations of the disease, and multi-step
testing and treatment protocols. Therefore, prevention of heartworm
disease with a plan for prophylaxis of parasite infection and
mosquito vector control is key for animal health and requires active
participation on the part of the veterinarian and pet owner on behalf
of the animal. Preventing exposure to biting mosquitoes is an
important component of prophylaxis. This includes vector control by
cleaning up mosquito habitats, protecting animals from being
exposed to mosquitoes by bringing them indoors when mosquitoes
are at peak activity when possible, use of screens in kennel
situations, and topical medications to prevent mosquitoes from
biting or with insecticidal properties that promote vector death and
therefore prevent transmission of microfilariae.208
Multiple macrocyclic lactone preventatives are available for dogs
and cats with topical, oral and injectable routes of administration.
Most are combination products with broader antiparasitic effects
against intestinal and ectoparasites (Table 237.2). The primary
activity of the preventatives is to interrupt the life cycle of juvenile
worms (L3, L4) with varying degrees of microfilaricide and
adulticide effects. Prevention can be initiated for puppies and kittens
at least 8 weeks of age and older. Drugs in this class include
ivermectin, milbemycin, selamectin, and moxidectin; all are safe for
all breeds at preventative dosages. Resistance and lack of efficacy are
reported, and while identifying the specific cause can be quite
complicated, failures have been associated with underdosing, missed
dosing, poor absorption and parasite susceptibility.209 Preventatives
are considered safe and effective when given as directed by the
manufacturer. However, prior to their use in an animal with
unknown microfilaria status, recommendations are to test for
antigen and microfilariae and if microfilariae are present, clinical
observation for an adverse reaction and pretreatment with a
corticosteroid and diphenhydramine should be considered prior to
the first dose of prevention.

EDUCATION

As heartworm infections continue to expand to new areas and
increase in numbers, an integral component of preventing and
treating heartworm disease includes educating students, medical
professionals and clients.210-212 This includes increasing awareness
about prophylaxis which is estimated to be prescribed to less than
half of dog owners and even fewer cat owners.135 The AHS and
Companion Animal Parasite Council continue to serve as resources
that regularly provide guidelines and updated information for
educational purposes.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Minimizing Heartworm Transmission in
Relocated Dogs

Transporting and relocating dogs is an increasingly
common practice. Whether the situation is an owned pet
accompanying emigrating or traveling caretakers, the
relocation of homeless animals for adoption, or the
movement of dogs for competition, exhibition, research or
sale, this process carries the risk of spreading infectious
diseases. This includes the transmission of Dirofilaria
immitis when infected dogs have become microfilaremic.
The following practices will minimize the risk of
heartworm transmission associated with the

transportation and relocation of dogs:
1. Test all dogs greater than 6 months of age for
microfilariae and heartworm antigen.
a. Testing should occur as close to the day of transport as
possible but no longer than 30 days prior to relocation
unless there is evidence of a negative antigen test along with
continuous administration of a preventive leading up to the
transport date.
b. If testing is not possible, assume transmission is possible
and treat according to one of the options presented in Step
3b(i). In keeping with antimicrobial stewardship practices,
it is not recommended to administer doxycycline without
confirmation of microfilaremia or antigenemia.
c. When transportation and relocation involve a change in
ownership, all diagnostic test results (along with
preventives and treatments administered where applicable)
should be made available at the time of such transfer.
2. If dogs test positive for microfilariae or antigen, reconsider
relocation at this time and begin treatment in accordance with
the American Heartworm Society (AHS) Guidelines.
a. Dogs with clinical signs attributed to heartworm infection
should not be transported.
b. Dogs that have been treated with melarsomine
dihydrochloride should not be transported until at least a 4week recovery period has elapsed so as not to exacerbate
complications that may arise as a result of stress and
physical exertion that may accompany the relocation
process.
c. The AHS recognizes that large-scale animal relocation for
adoption plays a critical role in non-lethal population
control of companion animals in the United States and
postponing or treating heartworm positive dogs may not be
feasible for many source organizations. In these
circumstances, responsible relocation (see Step 3) of
heartworm positive dogs is encouraged to decrease
reservoirs for community transmission and enhance
individual animal welfare through appropriate management
at the destination.

3. If dogs test positive and relocation cannot be postponed,
clinical decisions should be based on the dog’s heartworm
status.
a. If Mf−, Ag+:
i. Administer an approved macrocyclic lactone product.
This should prevent the pre-patent dog from becoming
microfilaria positive.1
ii. Begin doxycycline therapy.
A 4-week course of doxycycline should prevent the prepatent dog from becoming microfilaria positive.2,3
Note: It is not recommended to give the first dose of
doxycycline the day of transport in order to monitor
for adverse effects and distinguish those from
transport-related nausea and/or stress.
iii. Repeat Knott’s testing in 7 days; if negative, proceed
with relocation. If positive, repeat Knott’s testing in 7
days or proceed to Step 3b.
Two negative tests 7 days apart can provide
reasonable assurance of a lack of circulating
microfilariae and reduced risk of transmission.
b. If Mf+, Ag- OR Mf+, Ag+:
i. Apply an approved moxidectin topical product, proceed
with relocation.
A single dose of topical moxidectin prior to transport
will eliminate most microfilariae.4-6
OR
i. Administer an approved macrocyclic lactone product
along with a topical canine insecticide that is labelled to
kill and repel mosquitoes.
This will prevent infection of mosquitoes and
subsequent transmission of infective larvae during
transportation and for 1 month thereafter.7
OR
i. Administer an approved macrocyclic lactone product
along with a dose of an isoxazoline insecticidal product
at least 24 hours prior to transport.

The isoxazoline will kill mosquitoes after they feed,
preventing larval development to the infective stage;
the duration of insecticidal activity varies based on
specific product.8-10
ii. Begin doxycycline therapy.
Administration of a 4-week course of doxycycline will
render microfilariae incapable of normal development
to infective larvae in mosquitoes and subsequent
development of these larvae in dogs.11,12
Once heartworm-positive dogs have been safely
transported, heartworm treatment should be completed
according to AHS Guidelines as soon as possible.
4. If dogs test negative for microfilariae and antigen, proceed
with relocation.
a. Administer macrocyclic lactone preventive drugs to dogs
greater than 6 weeks of age prior to relocation.1
b. Repeat microfilariae and antigen testing in 6 months. If a
history of preventive administration is well-documented,
repeat testing in 12 months.1
Caring for dogs that undergo relocation is an everyday challenge
veterinarians face in today’s mobile society, and one that necessitates
the adoption of approaches to mitigate heartworm transmission.
Along with considering the recommendations in this document,
veterinarians should ensure that transportation of animals is carried
out in accordance with state and/or federal transportation
regulations, as well as professional guidelines.13,14 In the case of
organized homeless animal relocation programs, veterinarians
should work with both source and destination organizations to
establish protocols for minimizing transmission of infectious
diseases, including heartworm disease.

CHAPTER 238: Arterial
Thromboembolic Disease
Kieran Borgeat

INTRODUCTION
Arterial thromboembolism (ATE) is an important cause of morbidity
and mortality in cats. Feline ATE has a prevalence of 0.26% in cats
presenting to primary care practice, and 0.6% of those admitted to
referral centers.1,2 The majority of cases identified are associated
with heart disease, but a minority have other causes, including
neoplasia, protein-losing nephropathy or an unidentified aetiology.14

Thromboembolism is the process of vascular occlusion distant to
the site of thrombus formation. This should be differentiated from
thrombosis, where a thrombus occludes a vessel at the site of

formation. Dogs may be diagnosed with aortic thrombosis,
associated with causes of a hypercoagulable state or unknown breedspecific factors5,6; the most common associated disorders are
protein-losing nephropathy (ch. 302), neoplasia (chs. 322, 324,
and 331), and corticosteroid excess (ch. 293). Although some
theoretical models suggest that cardiomyopathy in cats is associated
with an increased risk of true arterial thrombosis in the distal aorta
because of altered flow dynamics at this site,7 the vast majority of
clinical information suggests that the heart is the site of thrombus
formation, which predisposes to ATE.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
THROMBUS FORMATION
A balance of prothrombotic and antithrombotic factors exists in
order to prevent inappropriate platelet activation in the healthy
patient. Antithrombotics produced by the endothelium include
antithrombin, prostacyclin (PGI2), and tissue plasminogen activator
(tPA).
Virchow’s triad suggests thrombus formation is promoted by stasis
of blood flow, hypercoagulability, and endothelial dysfunction (ch.
170). In cats with cardiomyopathy, these criteria could be met in a
number of ways, including enlargement and reduced contractile
function of the left atrium,1,3,4,8-12 endothelial dysfunction caused by
chronic neurohormonal activation in cardiomyopathy,13-15 and
chronic inflammatory cytokine activation.16-18

CLINICAL SYNDROME
Clinical signs of ATE result from deep tissue ischemia, induced by
both primary blockage of the arterial supply to a vascular bed and
secondary vasoconstriction of collateral vessels (promoted by
vasoactive mediators produced by the thrombus itself) (Video 238.1

). This interrupts the delivery of oxygen and essential
metabolites and impedes the removal of waste products.

PRESENTATION AND DIAGNOSIS
THE TYPICAL ATE PATIENT
Most cats with ATE present with acute-onset signs of limb
dysfunction and pain. Owners typically perceive their cat to be
previously healthy and then exhibiting signs of sudden and severe
distress. However, some cats do have a previous diagnosis of heart
disease, or reported auscultatory abnormalities which support occult
heart disease, such as a murmur, gallop sound or arrhythmia.1,2
Depending on the severity of tissue ischemia, partial motor function
may be present or affected limbs may be completely paralyzed.
Physical examination findings (ch. 3) are often specific enough to
provide a confident diagnosis of ATE without further testing,
especially where the cat exhibits the “five Ps” (Figure 238.1): pain,
pallor, pulselessness, paresis or paralysis (affecting one or more
limbs), and poikilothermia (differences in surface temperature of
body parts, i.e., cool limbs). Hypothermia is common, especially in
those with bilateral pelvic limb signs, but it is not a pre-requisite for
diagnosis. Since rectal temperature has been shown to be a reliable
predictor of survival, measurement should be prioritized at
presentation and the result used for informing an open prognostic
discussion with owners (ch. 1). Measurements <37°C (<98.6°F)
have been associated with less than 50% survival to discharge.1,2
The most common presentation with ATE is ischemic
neuromyopathy of both pelvic limbs, reported in 71-78% affected
cats.1,2 Thoracic limb involvement is less common (10-14%) and
when it occurs, it is unilateral. The reason for this is anatomical;
most caudally-directed ATE lodge at the aortic bifurcation, affecting
both pelvic limbs simultaneously (Figure 238.2). In cats, the right
and left subclavian arteries, which supply the forelimbs, branch
separately from the aorta and are therefore not simultaneously
affected by a single thrombus.

Pallor is best assessed by comparing the foot pads and claw beds of
affected limbs to those of unaffected limbs. Absence of a pulse is
more easily detected in the pelvic limbs using the femoral artery,
where the vessel is large and easily palpable even without a pulse.
Doppler methods (ch. 91) can assist in confidently comparing pulses
between the right and left forelimbs.
Pain associated with limb ischemia is severe, but tends to reduce
dramatically after the first 24 hours, so this sign may be more
variable where a delay has occurred between ATE event and
veterinary assessment.
Ancillary testing to confirm impaired tissue blood flow in affected
limbs is not usually required, but may be considered if presenting
signs or physical examination are inadequate or inconsistent. This
includes comparison of glucose,19 lactate, or arterial oxygen
concentration between normal and affected limbs, and Doppler
ultrasound of arteries supplying the limb.

phenotype.
Because of the high prevalence of cardiomyopathy, combined with
a surge in sympathetic drive (pain, fear, stress), congestive heart
failure (ch. 229) is common in cats with ATE.1-4 However,
tachypnea (ch. 37) cannot reliably be used to identify cases with
pulmonary edema because of the overlap in respiratory rate between
cats in heart failure and those that are simply painful or
metabolically compromised.1 If in doubt, an empirical dose of
furosemide (1-2 mg/kg IM or IV; IV preferred if feasible, for rapid
onset of action) may be administered in order to help stabilize the
patient.

THE UNUSUAL ATE PATIENT

Most cats present with limb ATE, but an unknown number of nonlimb ATE are likely mistaken for acute disorders of different organ
systems. If imaging confirms regional ischemia (Figure 238.3),
echocardiography should be performed to exclude a cardiogenic
ATE. In addition, clinically silent ATE events probably occur more
often than we appreciate. In one study, cats with renal infarcts were
over 4 times more likely to have hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
(HCM) than a control population.20 This suggests that overt limb
ATE is part of a larger clinical phenomenon.
Noncardiac causes of ATE are reported in up to 16% of cases.1
Protein-losing nephropathy (ch. 302), protein-losing enteropathy
(ch. 262), and hyperthyroidism (ch. 287) are reported in
association with feline ATE, as is neoplasia (chs. 171, 331).
Seemingly, the most common cause of ATE after excluding
cardiomyopathy is pulmonary neoplasia.4 It is possible that tumorassociated thrombus forms in one or more pulmonary veins adjacent
to a mass, and then embolizes to the left heart and into circulation.
Neoplastic embolism is also possible.

ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIC FINDINGS
Echocardiography (ch. 97) is an essential diagnostic test to exclude
clinically significant cardiomyopathy as a cause of ATE, and it should
be performed once the patient has been stabilized. The most
common underlying heart disease identified is an HCM phenotype
(ch. 234), but dilated, restrictive and non-specific phenotypes are all
associated with a risk of ATE,21 as are rarer congenital diseases.1
Transient myocardial thickening22 also has been anecdotally
reported to cause ATE.
