Left atrial dilation and reduced left atrial wall motion have both
been described as causes of ATE in cats (Figure 238.4).1,3,4,8-12
Spontaneous echocontrast (SEC) is a common finding, caused by
ultrasound reflecting from microaggregates of activated platelets
(Video 238.2

). This reflects blood stasis, and has been linked to

an increased risk of thrombogenic stroke in humans.23 In cats, SEC
is associated with reduced left atrial function24 and shorter survival
time (ch. 234).25,26
A cat that has characteristic clinical signs of ATE and a normal
echocardiogram or stage B1 cardiomyopathy should be considered to
have a noncardiogenic episode of ATE, and further diagnostic testing
is recommended.

TREATMENT OF ARTERIAL
THROMBOEMBOLISM
THE FIRST 6 HOURS
Analgesia (ch. 6) must always be prioritized for cats presenting with
signs of ATE, beginning with an opiate such as methadone (0.3
mg/kg IM or IV q4h; IV route preferred whenever feasible), and
potentially increasing in intensity using ketamine or fentanyl IV
constant rate infusion as required. Adjunct treatment with
gabapentin (50-100 mg/cat) may help to manage neuropathic pain
and also provides additional anxiolysis. Empirical furosemide can be
administered if heart failure is suspected, (ch. 229) but diagnostics
to further evaluate this must be carried out before longer-term
decisions regarding diuretic treatment are made. Oxygen therapy
should be provided if required, and thoracic ultrasound performed to
evaluate the possibility of pleural fluid or cardiogenic edema (ch.
73).
There are no published data to support which antithrombotic drug
protocol offers the best hope for cats with acute ATE, but there is
some evidence on which to base decision making.

Antiplatelet Drugs
A randomized, controlled trial examining secondary prevention of
ATE (in cats that were stable at 3 months after an initial ATE)
compared clopidogrel, an antiplatelet drug which inhibits activation
by binding to the adenosine diphosphate receptor, to aspirin.27 This
study demonstrated increased survival time in clopidogrel-treated
cats. In addition, one retrospective study suggested that early
antiplatelet treatment was associated with improved survival to 24
hours and 7 days post-ATE,2 so clopidogrel should be administered
as soon as oral medication administration is tolerated.

Heparins
Heparin inhibits free factor Xa and thrombin via an antithrombindependent mechanism. Although heparin is used frequently by
practitioners treating ATE, there are no clinical trials to show that
heparins improve survival in ATE. Pharmacokinetic data in cats
suggest that both unfractionated and low-molecular weight heparin
are safe to use and inhibit factor Xa, but because of rapid elimination
they should be administered at a higher dosage and more frequently
than in humans.28 Optimal dosage and frequency have not been
determined in cats. In a retrospective case series, 52 cats were
treated with dalteparin after ATE, with 43 of these receiving ongoing
injections at home.29 Only 1 cat had a bleeding event attributed to
the drug, but this individual had also recently received streptokinase.
No cats in this cohort received dalteparin more frequently than twice
daily, so—based on pharmacokinetic data—they were potentially
underdosed.

Direct Anti-Xa Agents
Direct anti-Xa drugs inhibit free and clot-bound factor Xa.
Rivaroxaban and apixaban have been evaluated in normal cats.
Rivaroxaban increased anti-Xa activity and was not associated with
any adverse effects at a dosage of 1.25 mg/cat PO q12h in one
study.30 Similarly, apixaban was effective and well-tolerated at 0.2
mg/kg,31 but dosing frequency and the effects of repeated doses are

yet to be published. As a result, rivaroxaban should be the firstchoice if an anti-Xa drug is used in cats.

Rational Antithrombotic Treatment
Clinical trials investigating the optimal first-line therapy for acute
ATE are underway. Consensus guidelines on the rational use of
antithrombotics in small animals suggest clopidogrel as a first-line
therapy for acute ATE, and no consensus regarding the addition of
heparin-based products was reached.32 However, if combination
therapy is used, clopidogrel and low-molecular weight heparin would
be first-choice. The consensus group advised against the use of
aspirin in cats with ATE because of a poor safety profile and
inconsistent results, although many cardiologists recommend
combining clopidogrel with aspirin and report almost no adverse
events. In cats with recurrence of ATE, addition of rivaroxaban to
clopidogrel oral therapy is recommended by consensus.
Warfarin is associated with severe adverse events and highintensity monitoring. Because it is difficult to use safely,4,33 it is not
recommended at any stage of ATE management.

Thrombolytic Treatments
Thrombolytic therapies may rapidly restore blood flow to ischemic
tissue. Streptokinase, urokinase, and exogenous tPA all activate
plasmin, which breaks down fibrin crosslinking and thereby reduces
thrombus strength and integrity. These drugs are used widely in
human medicine to treat patients with acute embolic stroke or STelevation myocardial infarction.
In cats with ATE, thrombolysis became controversial after two
initial studies reported a high rate of adverse events associated with
treatment. Ischemia-reperfusion injury was suspected to explain
many of the observed complications, where rapid restoration of flow
leads to the release of accumulated protons, potassium and lactate,
and the generation of reactive oxygen species from enzymes that
have been inhibited by ischemia.34 This can cause acidemia,
systemic inflammation and kidney injury, and appears more likely in
cats with prolonged limb ischemia.

Streptokinase use was described retrospectively in 46 cats with
ATE. The outcome of cats receiving streptokinase did not appear to
be better than the outcome reported for cats treated with antiplatelet
therapy alone, but dosing schedule was inconsistent and no control
group was reported.33 Overt bleeding occurred in 11/46 cats (24%)
and reperfusion injury was suspected in 16/46 cats (35%). Two
studies have reported the use of tPA for treating feline ATE. The first
was planned to prospectively include 24 cats, but enrollment was
terminated after the first 11 cats because of adverse events in every
case.35 The second, a larger but retrospective study, compared cats
treated with tPA within 6 hours of the ATE event to a control group
of cats receiving standard therapy. This did not identify higher
numbers of adverse events with tPA, perhaps because of less
prolonged tissue ischemia, but outcome was no different between
groups.36
Given the published data, it is reasonable to state that using tPA
may help manage some cats known to have presented in the early
hours after ATE, but complications are possible and outcome is no
different on a population basis than with standard antiplatelet drugs.

THE FIRST DAY
After stabilization, heart failure should be confirmed or excluded if
not done so previously (ch. 229), and pain and anxiety managed
appropriately (ch. 6). Cats should be monitored for complications in
the least invasive manner possible. Although ECG monitoring and
blood gas measurements are helpful, they will add to patient stress.
Auscultation may be a good compromise: changes in heart rate could
suggest uncontrolled pain (tachycardia) or ischemia-reperfusion
injury (bradycardia), and development of a new gallop sound (ch.
38) should trigger reassessment of heart failure status (ch. 229).
Often, cats with ATE become dehydrated because of inappetence
caused by stress, pain and metabolic derangements. Providing IV
fluid therapy may risk pulmonary edema, so judicious use of an
appetite stimulant (e.g., mirtazapine 2 mg/cat q24-48h) or
placement of a feeding tube (ch. 81) may be used for managing fluid
balance enterally. Nursing care is vital to stay abreast of patient

needs. Passive range of motion exercises may be carried out in the
affected limbs in order to try and maintain tissue flexibility and
passively distribute tissue fluid and metabolic by-products (ch.
256). Assistance will probably be needed to facilitate voiding of
urine and feces in the early stages. Comfortable bedding and
frequent turning should help to prevent exacerbation of tissue
damage associated with cage rest.

DAYS 2 TO 7
The pain associated with ATE appears to decrease substantially from
day 2 onward. Buprenorphine (0.02 mg/kg q6h) is likely to provide
adequate analgesia after the first 24 hours and cats are more likely to
eat once methadone is discontinued. Clopidogrel should be
continued, and this therapy will be lifelong in most cases. Cats that
presented with heart failure may tolerate weaning of the diuretic
dose if their condition was significantly destabilized by sympathetic
drive at presentation—this can be helpful in cats with inappetence or
dehydration.
Superficial limb tissue should be checked twice daily for evidence
of necrosis, and claw beds and pads checked for a return to normal
color. The return of a pulse is an inaccurate indicator of patient
recovery because tissue perfusion is more likely to be restored by the
development or opening of collateral circulation than the removal of
the initial arterial occlusion (Video 238.1

). If tissue necrosis is

suspected, photographs should be taken daily to ensure progression
is recognized and measures instigated to manage any dehiscence. In
extreme cases, a limb may not be viable without surgery, or
amputation may be required. Although surgery is feasible, a frank
conversation about risks and longer-term prognosis should be held
with owners of such severely affected cats and euthanasia should be
discussed.

AT-HOME CARE
Patients with ATE can be discharged when they are pain-free on oral
analgesia (gabapentin, oral buprenorphine or nonsteroidal anti-

inflammatory drug if non-azotemic), eating and able to posture for
urination/defecation. Gait is likely to be abnormal for some weeks
(Video 238.3

) or even months, dependent on the degree of tissue

damage, but this is acceptable as long as welfare is not compromised.
A physical rehabilitation program could improve limb function in the
longer term (ch. 256).
Clopidogrel therapy is lifelong, but may be relatively ineffective in
a proportion of cats because of genetic differences in metabolism
between individuals.37 Measurement of platelet function or
clopidogrel active metabolite may help identify non-responders and
decide when alterative therapy should be sought.38-40

PROGNOSIS
SHORT-TERM PROGNOSIS
At continuing education meetings, we have asked clinicians the
question “Do you recommend euthanasia for all cats with ATE at
presentation?” Data collected from 809 veterinarians (unpublished)
found that 59.7% do so. This is similar to the published figure of 61%
from general practice.2 In the same study, death rate in cats where
treatment was attempted was 30%. This suggests that veterinary
awareness of a poor prognosis has led to a self-fulfilling prophecy of
euthanasia in the majority of cases. However, ATE does cause
substantial morbidity and a relatively high risk of mortality, so cases
should be assessed based on known prognostic indicators at the
point of presentation (Box 238.1), and treatment prioritized for
those cats most likely to respond. By aiming to treat those with less
severe disease, we minimize poor welfare for the worst-affected cats.
BOX 2 38 .1 Pr ognos t ic Ind icat ors in Fe line
A r te rial T hro mb o e m b olis m ( A TE) 1 , 2
A better prognosis for cats with ATE is associated with:
• Partial limb motion

• Only one limb affected
• Early treatment with an anti-platelet drug
A worse prognosis for cats with ATE is associated with:
• Hypothermia at presentation (<37°C [98.6°F])
• Diagnosis of congestive heart failure
• Bradycardia

Longer-Term Prognosis
It is important to recognize that most studies reporting long-term
outcome of cats with ATE were published prior to the routine use of
clopidogrel as a first-line treatment. Historically, where treatment
often comprised aspirin with or without heparins, the recurrence
rate of ATE was reported at 25-47%,1,2,33 with a median survival
time of 51-117 days.1,33 When considering cats treated with
clopidogrel alone, recurrence rate remained similar, at 49%, but
median survival time (to cardiac death or recurrence) appeared
longer, at 346 days.27 One earlier study from a referral center also
reported a median survival of almost 12 months.4 It is possible that a
more up-to-date approach, with the addition of anti-Xa drugs in
persistent or recurrent cases, may yield a more favorable survival
time.
Most cats that survive ATE have severe cardiomyopathy, which
will require lifelong monitoring and treatment. The effect of this on
patient and owner quality of life should not be underestimated. The
impact of daily medication should be raised early in the dialog with
owners, in order to best manage their expectations.

PREVENTION OF ATE
Identification of at-risk cats is challenging. The single best predictor
of ATE is having a history of previous ATE. Echocardiographic
measurement of left atrial wall motion (left atrial fractional
shortening [LAFS%]; Figure 238.4, B) provides the most clinically
useful tool, where reduced LAFS% is associated with a higher risk of

ATE.9 In the absence of measuring this, increased left atrial size can
be used as a surrogate based on consensus statement guidelines for
stage B2 feline cardiomyopathy (ch. 234).21 Although the only
clinical trial data currently available focus on secondary
prevention,27 this is extrapolated for prevention of primary ATE;
administration of clopidogrel (18.75 mg/cat PO q24h) is
recommended.
Cats with very poor left atrial function (LAFS% <15%) may benefit
from the addition of pimobendan, if no clinically significant left
ventricular outflow tract obstruction is present. Several studies now
suggest that pimobendan (1.25 mg/cat PO q12h) is associated with
increased left atrial function,41-44 and is well tolerated in cats45,46
despite use being off-label.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Arterial Thromboembolism

WHAT IS ARTERIAL THROMBOEMBOLISM?
Arterial thromboembolism (ATE) in cats is a distressing and painful
event for affected cats. Many cats appear to be healthy before the
sudden onset of an event, which is most easily recognized by pain
associated with the loss of use of one or more limbs. The cause of this
syndrome is abnormal blood clot formation, which blocks the arterial
blood supply. About 75% of cats have both hindlimbs affected, and
25% have a single front leg that is affected by ATE.

WHY MIGHT MY CAT BE AFFECTED?
Arterial thromboembolism is most commonly caused by advanced
heart disease (cardiomyopathy), but other causes are possible,
including tumors, hormonal problems, and kidney or intestinal
diseases. In some cats, no obvious causative disease can be found. All
cats that show signs of an ATE should have their heart scanned by a
vet, best done by a cardiologist. This helps us to understand why they

developed an ATE, and what we can do to manage any cardiac
problems that are present.

WHAT MIGHT HAPPEN TO MY CAT?
Cats affected with ATE sadly often die or are euthanized in the first
few days. Cats with a low temperature on day 1, a slow heart rate, or
complete absence of limb movement are more likely to die because of
their disease. Vets will be able to make a basic judgement about how
well a cat will respond to treatment for ATE based on these things. If
they do respond well, cats will require up to a week in hospital, and
have to take lifelong medicine, once or twice daily.
On the first days in hospital, cats with ATE need injectable pain
relief, and those with the worst heart disease will need to receive
medicine that controls signs of heart failure (shortness of breath).
Technicians will help to make sure your cat is comfortable and can
help by providing basic physiotherapy. A drug called clopidogrel will
be prescribed to help improve the chances of your cat surviving the
ATE, possibly alongside other treatment.
Despite the best efforts of vets, some cats do not respond well to
treatment. ATE is a very difficult disease to predict in some cats,
even for experienced vets.

WHEN CAN MY CAT COME HOME?
Cats can be discharged from hospital once they can effectively use
their legs to walk and use the litter box. They may need a few days of
pain-relief medicine and all cats are likely to need lifelong treatment
with clopidogrel. Cats may take a few weeks or even months to walk
normally after an ATE, but they often feel well after a few days and
can have a fairly normal lifestyle and activity level at home. Sadly, up
to half of cats with ATE experience another episode; this may be less
severe once they are on clopidogrel, but some cats do experience the
same pain and stress as before. If you are worried about any signs of
a possible ATE at home, you must contact your local vet to discuss
your concerns further.

IS THERE A CURE FOR HEART DISEASE IN CATS?

Heart diseases in cats sadly cannot be cured at this time. The best we
can do is to help cats feel well by controlling any signs of
breathlessness and trying to reduce their risk of developing an ATE.
The average cat with heart disease can have a good quality of life on
appropriate treatment for a year or more, but some cats are not so
lucky and may live for less time.
Kieran Borgeat (Swindon, United Kingdom)

Clinical signs resulting from disorders of the peripheral veins or
lymphatics are less frequently encountered in veterinary practice.
However, diseases of these vessels should be considered in the
differential diagnosis of the dog or cat with swelling of the
extremities (including the head and neck), in patients with cavitary
effusions (chs. 21, 220, 235, 265), or in cases of unexplained edema
(ch. 30). Changes in the microcirculation that alter venous
hydrostatic or oncotic pressures, increase vascular or lymphatic
permeability, or impede venous or lymphatic drainage can underpin
such clinical signs. These disorders can be primary, including
developmental anomalies or inherited syndromes, or be secondary to

compression, inflammation, or infiltration of venous or lymphatic
vessels (Box 239.1).

PHYSIOLOGY OF SYSTEMIC VENOUS
AND LYMPHATIC FLOW
The systemic veins serve as a low-pressure, compliant reservoir for
the intravascular volume, with approximately 60% of blood volume
contained within these vessels.1 Systemic venous return is controlled
by a number of forces. These include the positive intravascular
pressures behind and the more negative intracardiac pressures
ahead of a column of venous blood; lateral forces, especially the
alternating contraction and relaxation of skeletal muscles; gravity
and posture; vascular resistance modulated by autonomic traffic,
hormones, and local vasoactive mediators; and changes in
intrathoracic pressures operative during both spontaneous
ventilation and mechanical ventilation. In health these forces drive
systemic blood back towards the right atrium, assisted by one-way
venous valves that prevent backflow (Figure 239.1).2 Dysfunction
or insufficiency of the systemic veins is common in humans and can
be related to abnormalities in the venous valves, dysfunction of
muscular pumps, venous reflux, venous dilatation, venous
thrombosis, or venous outflow obstruction.2 Similar conditions in
small animals are rarely recognized, though thrombotic conditions
do occur, particularly with indwelling central venous catheters.
Venous insufficiency and outflow obstruction can also develop
secondary to extraluminal compression or from intraluminal
narrowing, phlebitis, and thrombosis.
The lymphatic system plays a critical role in regulating body cavity
and interstitial fluid volumes. Lymphatics also assist in the removal
of inorganic material from subcutaneous tissues and the modulation
of fat absorption in the gastrointestinal tract, while contributing to
antigen transport and immune surveillance.3 Additionally, the
lymphatic system is the preferred metastatic route for many forms of
cancer. This diversity of function highlights the pivotal role played by
the lymphatic system in both health and disease.

Lymphatics originate within the interstitium as specialized
endothelial-lined capillaries transporting fluid, solutes, and
macromolecular particles back into the venous system. Fluid,
protein, cells, and macromolecular particles from the interstitial
space empty into the initial lymphatics that are composed of a series
of small lymphatic capillaries beginning blindly in the tissues. The
lymph then flows through a system of lymphatic vessels, which
progressively increase in diameter. As lymph flows centrally it passes
through at least one lymph node before emptying into larger
lymphatic trunks.4 The deep trunks unite to form two major
lymphatic vessels: the thoracic and right lymphatic ducts. The
thoracic duct drains most of the body and returns lymphatic fluid
into the venous system at the brachycephalic vein or the left
subclavian vein. The right lymphatic duct drains the right side of the
head and neck and right forelimb.
Lymphatic vessels contain many junctions in between individual
endothelial cells, which are connected to the surrounding
extracellular matrix by reticular fibers and collagen. These junctions
open when tissue hydrostatic pressure becomes elevated and the
anchoring filaments stretch, allowing fluid to move into the vessel.5
As the fluid is cleared from the interstitium, the connecting fibers
contract and the junctions between the endothelial cells close. The
opening and closing of these junctions allows them to act as inlet
valves, preventing the backflow of lymph into the interstitium. The
larger vessels of the lymphatic system have progressively fewer open
junctions, increasingly muscular walls, and frequent intralymphatic
valves that also prevent backflow of lymph. The action of external
muscular contraction along with intrinsic contractility of the
lymphatic vessels aids in the movement of lymph through the
lymphatic system and lymph nodes. While in the lymph node, the
lymph is in contact with the blood circulation and approximately half
of the fluid is drained before leaving into the larger lymphatic ducts.4
In addition to its transport function, the lymph system plays a major
role in the immunologic responses to infectious agents.3 It serves as
a filtering system to impede the spread of microorganisms and
neoplastic cells. The cellular components, in particular the

lymphocytes, are indispensable for immunologic reactions and
antibody formation.3,5

TECHNIQUES USED TO EVALUATE
VENOUS AND LYMPHATIC DISEASE
ANGIOGRAPHY
Angiography is the traditional diagnostic test for evaluating
peripheral vascular diseases due to its ability to characterize and
allow visualization of normal and abnormal vascular anatomy. A
favorable diagnostic outcome requires careful attention to three
important elements: selection of radiopaque contrast agent,
technique for vascular delivery of contrast material, and high-quality
radiographic imaging.
As discussed in ch. 115, iodine-based particles are almost
singularly used as contrast agents in the vascular system. Today,
second-(iohexol, iopamidol) and third-(iodixanol) generation
contrast agents are administered due to a greater safety profile than
first-generation agents. Factors to be considered when selecting a
contrast agent include patient safety, image quality, and cost. For
animals with renal impairment, conservative administration of
contrast agents should be employed and concurrent fluid diuresis
performed.

Venography
Venography is far easier to accomplish than lymphangiography and
is generally less challenging than arteriography owing to easier
vascular access and the lower pressures of the venous system. A
small-gauge intravenous catheter can be placed in a superficial vein
distal to the site of the suspected vascular lesion and iodinated
contrast material injected. Images are acquired during and following
the injection to evaluate anatomy and rate of venous clearance.
Venography may be used for detecting venous thrombi or vascular
invasion by a neoplasm (each appearing as a vascular filling defect),
venous stenosis (Figure 239.2; Video 239.1),

or complete

obstruction. With fluoroscopic cine imaging, venous insufficiency
can also be appreciated. The presence of prolific collateral
vasculature suggests chronic obstruction.

Lymphangiography
Lymphangiography facilitates regional assessment of the lymphatic
system. The technique of indirect lymphangiography relies on a
contrast agent, infused into tissue, to be selectively absorbed and
transported through lymphatic channels.6 Indirect
lymphangiography is now employed commonly for computed
tomographic lymphangiography, with injection of iodinated contrast
into the metatarsal pads.7 Direct lymphangiography is more
challenging (unless lymphangiectases have formed) but provides

superior results when performed successfully (Video 239.2

).

Selective lymphatic cannulation requires aseptic cut-down over the
lymphatic region of interest (note—the identification of
lymphangiectases may be facilitated by subcutaneous injection of
vital dyes [e.g., 3% Evans blue dye or 11% patent blue violet] into the
toe web or consumption of a high fat meal for intestinal lymphatics).
The lymphatic vessel is then cannulated with a 27- or 30-gauge
needle or a special lymphatic cannula.6 An iodine-containing soluble
contrast medium as discussed above is then injected slowly into the
vessel. Because water-soluble contrast media rapidly diffuse through
lymphatic walls into surrounding tissues, the radiographic detail is
blurred unless radiographs are taken shortly after contrast injection.
Alternatively, oily iodine-containing contrast agents (e.g., Lipiodol)
can be used, reducing leakage of contrast from the lymphatic vessels.
The oily contrast agents are sequestered within the lymphatics and
lymph nodes along the draining pathways; some human reports
suggest lymphangiography with this agent can even be curative for
chylous leaks.8 During lymphangiography, patency of the lymphatic
channels can be appreciated in addition to the size of regional lymph
nodes. Metastatic disease to the lymph nodes or granulomas appears
as filling defects within the contrast-filled node. Lymphangiography
can also be used for identifying the location of lymphatic leakage or
thoracic duct localization in small animals with chylous effusion.9,10

DIAGNOSTIC ULTRASOUND
Ultrasound imaging provides a direct, noninvasive technique for
assessing venous abnormalities, patency, and function.11,12
Ultrasound can aid in the diagnosis of venous thrombosis,
aneurysms, traumatic vascular disease, and compression of vascular
structures from local disease processes (Figure 239.3).
Duplex ultrasonography incorporates grayscale two-dimensional
imaging, coupled with simultaneous pulsed and color flow Doppler
techniques.11 Thrombi, foreign bodies, compression, and abnormal
vascular anatomy can be identified with two-dimensional
imaging.12,13 Color Doppler superimposed on the two-dimensional
image can further define anatomic structure and identify turbulence
associated with vascular malformation and stenotic lesions.14 Failure

of a vein to compress with pressure from the ultrasound probe is a
marker of partial or complete thrombosis.13 Ultrasound assessment
of venous flow reversal duration following Valsalva maneuvers or calf
muscle compression and release are diagnostic tests for venous
insufficiency in people, but are challenging if not impossible to adapt
to animals.15
Ultrasound is performed for lymphatic disease primarily to
evaluate for other causes of limb or head swelling; direct
visualization of lymphatic vessels by ultrasound is generally
impractical. Specialized ultrasound methods have been used in
people to image the venous entry of the thoracic duct, but these have
not been reported in dogs or cats.

LYMPHOSCINTIGRAPHY
Lymphoscintigraphy involves injection of a radioactive tracer,
monitored by a gamma camera. Lymphoscintigraphy is routinely
employed in human medicine for evaluation of lymphatic drainage
and oncologic staging,16 and has been reported in veterinary
medicine for similar purposes.17

CROSS-SECTIONAL IMAGING
Three-dimensional imaging of vascular structures requires computed
tomography angiography (CTA) or magnetic resonance angiography
(MRA). Both CTA (Figure 239.4) and MRA (Figure 239.5) have
been employed to evaluate vascular structures in animals. The
benefit of cross-sectional imaging such as CTA or MRA is the
avoidance of selective central catheterization since only peripheral
venous access is required for these techniques. While much of the
published literature on these modalities has focused on anatomic
delineation of portosystemic shunts, these methods can be used to
investigate any vascular structure. Respiratory gating, or subjecting
the animal to a breath-hold or apneic period during the scan, is
preferred to avoid movement during scan acquisition, particularly if

the abdominal or thoracic veins are being evaluated; this may not be
required for CTA of the limb vasculature.
In addition to gating or breath holding, the method of processing
and viewing images obtained during a CTA or MRA can enhance the
information gained from the study. Reconstructions in maximal
intensity projections (MIPs), minimal intensity projections, and
three-dimensional volume rendering with the ability to stack images
can improve image interpretation—particularly for vascular studies.
The MIP is a technique whereby the image viewing software creates a
single image by projecting the voxel with the highest attenuation
value on a series of images, or slab, onto a two-dimensional image.
When stacks of images are processed in this manner, the entire
course of a vessel and its relationship to surrounding structures can
be more clearly appreciated. Three-dimensional volume rendering of
a CTA allows for the full spatial relationship of the vasculature to be
realized and can greatly enhance surgical or interventional planning.
Unique to MRA, imaging techniques are available to visualize
blood clearly on the image without the administration of contrast
(Figure 239.5). Contrast agents may still be used and are preferred
for some studies (such as perfusion scans) but may not be necessary
for anatomic delineation of blood vessels.

Computed tomography (CT) lymphangiography is commonly
employed in people to evaluate lymphatic structures, and has been
applied to canine imaging (Figure 239.6), particularly for
evaluation of thoracic duct anatomy prior to surgery for idiopathic

chylothorax (Video 239.3

)9,18,19 or for evaluation of sentinel

lymph nodes in oncologic staging.20 Improved identification of
lymphatic branches and removal of superimposing anatomic
structures are two benefits seen with CT lymphangiography over
radiographic lymphangiography in dogs.9 Injection of aqueous
iodinated contrast can be performed by ultrasound guidance into the
regional (e.g., popliteal) lymph node. More recently, injection into
the subcutaneous fat of the metatarsal pad has proven successful in
both dogs and cats.7,21 One study in dogs documented improved
lymphatic flow if the distal limb is massaged after injection.22
Magnetic resonance lymphangiography is now performed in
humans,23 with preliminary work suggesting similar utility in
veterinary medicine.24

DISEASES OF VEINS
Diseases of the venous system seldom result in significant morbidity
in small animals, even though trauma, thromboembolism, edema,
local inflammation, tumor invasion, and septic processes commonly
affect veins. Many conditions, however, go unrecognized.

VENOUS THROMBOSIS
Venous thrombi form in the venous circulation under low blood flow
conditions and are composed of fibrin and erythrocytes. Venous
thrombi are understood to develop secondary to the classic
components of Virchow’s triad—flow stasis, endothelial disruption,
and a hypercoagulable state.25 Luminal implants in veins—
transvenous pacemaker leads (ch. 230), central venous catheters
(ch. 75)—are also a common cause of venous thrombosis in animals.
Venous thrombosis causes fewer overt clinical abnormalities than
arterial thrombosis and, consequently, is often undetected. Deep
venous thrombosis is a major risk factor for pulmonary embolism in
humans but is not known to be a risk factor for pulmonary

thromboembolism (PTE) in animals. Pulmonary thrombosis is an
often life-threatening complication associated with a variety of
systemic and metabolic diseases when a thrombus develops within
the pulmonary vasculature.26 A thrombus that is formed in the
peripheral veins, caval veins, or right heart may embolize to the
pulmonary arterial vasculature, resulting in PTE (ch. 219).
Development of PTE can occur in several prothrombotic disease
states including the nephrotic syndrome, hyperadrenocorticism,
immune-mediated hemolytic anemia, thrombocytosis, cardiac
disease, sepsis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, heartworm
disease, and neoplasia.27-31 Antithrombin (AT) deficiency (chs. 170,
171) may be involved in thrombogenesis in a number of these
diseases by altering intravascular blood chemistry and increasing the
risk for thrombosis. Thrombin and other clotting factors are
inhibited by AT such that even mild reduction in AT can result in
thrombosis or thromboembolism. The presence of multiple
concurrent disorders in animals with thromboembolism is common.
For example, 47% of cats with necropsy-confirmed PTE had multiple
predisposing disorders.31 Massive pulmonary thrombi may also
occur in situ and have been described primarily in the Cavalier King
Charles Spaniel32 (Figure 239.7) or in dogs or cats with heartworm
disease (ch. 237). PTE is covered in detail in ch. 219.

VENOUS VARICOSIS
Venous varicosis, a condition of tortuous and dilated veins, is rare in
dogs and cats (Figure 239.8). When detected, venous varices may
accompany arteriovenous fistulae or develop as a consequence of
chronic venous obstruction33 (Figure 239.2), with one review
categorizing 4 pathways for collateral venous flow in the setting of
caudal vena caval obstruction in dogs.34 Cutaneous phlebectasia is a
benign lesion sometimes erroneously called telangiectasis. It is
reported almost exclusively in dogs with spontaneous or iatrogenic
hyperadrenocorticism (ch. 293).35 Phlebectasia is an abnormal
dilatation, extension, or reduplication of veins or capillaries or a
combination of these changes.
Venous perforation or blunt trauma to veins is usually well
tolerated because rapid clotting results in venous occlusion and
prevents serious hemorrhage. When venous occlusion is severe,
resultant edema and cyanosis are usually temporary because of
collateral circulation. If all veins draining an area are compromised,
marked edema and necrosis can ensue. Blunt trauma has been
associated with caudal vena caval obstruction or kinking of the
intrathoracic caudal vena cava and subsequent ascites.36-38

VENOUS MALFORMATIONS
Venous malformations are often incidental findings and may occur
as duplication, interruption, transposition, or as an anomalous
connection; persistence of the left cranial vena cava (PLCVC) is
noteworthy.39-41 Dogs and cats normally have a right-sided cranial
vena cava. When the embryologic left anterior cardinal vein fails to

regress in these species, a PLCVC occurs (

Video 239.4). The

PLCVC may occur singularly or, more often, both left and right
cranial cavae are present (Figure 239.9). Buchanan described two
types of PLCVC in the dog—complete and incomplete.41 The PLCVC
enters the caudoventral aspect of the right atrium at the coronary
sinus (

Video 239.5), in contrast to the entrance of the right

cranial vena cava at the cranial aspect of the heart. The PLCVC
generally poses no clinical problem for the animal, although a case
report of an incomplete PLCVC in a Brittany Spaniel did suggest the
possibility of this structure causing megaesophagus if it is partially
atretic.42 Transpositional venous anomalies are common in animals
with transpositional arterial anomalies such as persistent right aortic
arch. Reports of pacemaker implantation and heartworm extraction
through a PLCVC can be found,43,44 although this approach is
technically more challenging than the standard route.

Additional venous anomalies have been reported. Unilateral
absence of the left external jugular vein has been described in the
cat45 and the author has observed absence of the right external
jugular vein in English Bulldogs.46 A left azygos vein is present in
some species but is typically absent in the dog and cat. If present, it is
a remnant of the left supracardinal system, which also enters the
coronary sinus. Case reports of left azygos vein have been reported in
the dog, occasionally as the sole source of caudal venous return if

concurrent with interruption of the caudal vena cava.47,48 Numerous
abnormalities of the caudal vena cava have been reported in
animals.39 The caudal vena cava may display duplication, leftward
transposition, or interruption with azygos continuation; these
malformations are sometimes associated with portosystemic shunts
(ch. 267). Most of these malformations cause no clinical signs
(unless concurrent with portocaval shunting) but might appear
during surgical exploration or diagnostic imaging studies and should
therefore be appreciated.
Venous malformations represent a challenging area of
classification in animals and fall within a spectrum of abnormalities
that in humans are anatomically categorized into capillary,
lymphatic, venous, or arteriovenous malformations.49,50 The
veterinary literature has not fully defined a categorization scheme or
standardized nomenclature for these lesions in animals,51 although a
histopathologic review of vascular tumors suggested parallels to
human schemes.52 Arteriovenous malformations are covered in
more detail in ch. 267.

FIGURE 239.9 Images from a 7-year-old female
mixed-breed dog with persistent left cranial vena
cava and pulmonary valve stenosis. Panel A shows
separate bilateral cranial venae cavae with a normal

Cystic dilation of veins may also occur; venous dilation or
aneurysm generally permits only low-velocity blood flow and small
lesions do not produce clinical signs. Expansion of the lesion may
occur, however, especially following trauma. Thrombosis can result
from sluggish blood flow, resulting in localized swelling and
tenderness. Larger lesions in dependent areas may enlarge, causing
significant vascular dilation, potentially causing changes in skin
color, dermal ulceration, and hemorrhage. Affected areas appear as a
warm, soft, compressible mass. No thrills or bruits are present due to
the low flow. Pain may result from pressure exerted on deep tissues
and nerves. The diagnosis is made using history, physical
examination, and ultrasound. Venography or cross-sectional imaging

such as CTA or MRA may be necessary to define the lesion,
particularly for intraabdominal aneurysms.53 Supportive therapy
using light, compressive wraps is sometimes helpful for acute
management. Surgical excision of affected vessels is occasionally
required, but complete resection is difficult and local recurrence is
common. Aneurysms of the external jugular, linguofacial, and
maxillary veins, as well as the cranial vena cava, have been
reported.54-56 In these cases, the lesions were considered to be
congenital vascular anomalies and not associated with an obstructive
or traumatic process. The author has recognized caudal vena caval
aneurysms in association with caudal vena caval interruption and
azygos continuation in a dog (Figure 239.10). Fifteen cases of
portal venous aneurysms were described in a CTA review of over
3000 dogs; none of the dogs of this study showed clinical signs,
though portal venous thrombosis at the site of an aneurysm was
described in 1 case.53

VENOUS FOREIGN BODIES
Embolization of severed intravascular catheter fragments is an
occasional complication of intravenous catheter placement.57-59 In
humans, reported complications of catheter embolization include
perforation of cardiac walls, endocarditis, pulmonary embolism, and
severe arrhythmias.60 Therefore, it is generally considered prudent
to remove catheter fragments. Nonsurgical, transvenous removal of
catheter fragments using loop-snare catheters, forceps, and basket
catheters has been described in animals.57,59 Whenever possible,
steps should be taken to avoid situations predisposing to catheter
fragmentation including inadequate restraint during catheter
placement, withdrawal of catheters through their placement needles
during repositioning, failure to properly secure the catheter to the
patient, inadvertent severing of catheters during bandage changes,
and the use of resterilized angiographic catheters during cardiac
catheterization.

PHLEBITIS
Phlebitis can occur from a local inflammatory process extending to
the veins or can originate from a venous intimal lesion. Common
causes of venous intimal lesions are perivenous or intravenous
injection of irritating drugs, infusion of large amounts of fluid, and
long-term placement of intravenous catheters. Infusion-related
phlebitis occurs in 3 forms: (1) chemical (injury to vein by irritating
drugs), (2) physical (trauma to the intima by catheters, needles,
hypertonicity or particulate matter in infused fluids), and (3)
microbial (infected fluids, skin, or catheter tip). Either sterile or
septic thrombophlebitis may result. Thrombophlebitis is typically
localized and is characterized by pain, swelling, and exudation
(Figure 239.11). Patients with serious illnesses or compromised
immune systems, however, may develop sepsis (ch. 128),
thromboembolic pneumonia (ch. 217), or endocarditis (ch. 232).
Phlebitis is a major cause of intimal damage leading to venous
thrombosis. The thrombosis is usually of little consequence if
localized to smaller vessels. However, emboli may be carried to the
lung and cause PTE. In most animals, thrombi carried to the lung are
rapidly lysed and cause no complications. However, when
inflammatory disease, dehydration, or circulatory failure occurs,
thrombus formation may continue in the pulmonary vessels and lead
to vascular occlusion, dyspnea, pain, and death.29 In infectious
thrombophlebitis, bacterial emboli may be carried to the lungs and
cause thromboembolic pneumonia. Spontaneous venous thrombosis
is rare, although thrombosis of the portal venous system including
the splenic veins is occasionally diagnosed in dogs (Figure
239.12).61 In the majority of cases, underlying hepatic disease or
conditions associated with a prothrombotic state (protein-losing
nephropathy, immune-mediated hemolytic anemia, or
hyperadrenocorticism) or compression (splenic torsion) are
identified.61 Clinical signs include ascites, abdominal pain, acquired
portosystemic shunting, and hypovolemic shock.61

THERAPY FOR VENOUS OBSTRUCTION

In cases of venous occlusion, clinical signs depend on the anatomic
location, extent, and duration of the obstruction. Acute obstruction
of centrally located deep systemic veins causes edema, cyanosis,
discomfort, and venous dilatation distal to the obstruction site.
Obstruction of the cranial vena cava causes edema in the neck, head,
forelimbs, and dependent portions of the cranial thorax (Figure
239.13; ch. 30). A common consequence of central venous
obstruction is pleural effusion. Common causes of cranial vena caval
obstruction include cranial mediastinal masses, indwelling central
venous catheters, and transvenous pacemaker leads.62,63 Clinical
disorders resulting in kinking, compression, neoplastic obstruction,
or thrombosis of the intrathoracic caudal vena cava have also been
reported with animals showing signs of ascites and subcutaneous
edema.37,64-66 Obstructions of the intraabdominal or pelvic venous
systems cause edema of the hindlimbs and the scrotum. Clinical
signs depend upon collateral vessel reserve and capacity of regional
lymphatics to drain interstitial and serous cavity fluid. In addition to
thrombosis, causes of venous obstruction include invasive malignant
processes and venous compression by abscesses, hematomas,
tumors, and lymphadenopathy. Several tumors have a tendency for
venous invasion, including chemodectoma (ch. 235), adrenal
tumors (chs. 293, 295) such as pheochromocytoma (ch. 298), and
hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325; Figure 239.14). Angiography may
indicate the occlusive or compressive lesion or highlight increased
collateral circulation (Figures 239.2 and 239.15). Diagnostic
ultrasonography is useful to detect masses or flow disturbances; CTA
or MRA can define the three-dimensional anatomy of the obstruction
and evaluate extraluminal causes (Figure 239.14). The prognosis
and therapy of venous obstruction depend on the primary disease.
Central venous obstruction should be treated promptly as delays in
therapy allow thrombus to organize and mature and limit a potential
response to therapy. If the duration of thrombus is known to be acute
(<1 week and optimally <48 h), lytic therapies may be considered.
Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) can be delivered systemically via
a peripheral vein, or locally via selective catheterization at the site of
thrombus. Newer devices are available that both infuse thrombolytic
and also mechanically agitate the thrombus with the ability to
aspirate debris during the procedure. In cases that fail thrombolysis,

venoplasty or venous stenting (Figure 239.15) may be considered.
Balloon venoplasty involves dilating the venous lumen while stent
implantation may provide a more durable result in the setting of
venous strictures. Further discussion on these therapies can be found
in chs. 113 and 118 and in other published reviews.67,68

DISEASES OF THE PERIPHERAL
LYMPHATICS
Lymphatic disorders can be subdivided into those of internal organs,
such as intestinal lymphangiectasia, and peripheral lymphatic
disorders. Several lymphatic diseases including lymphedema,
intestinal lymphangiectasia (ch. 262), chylothorax (ch. 220),
lymphadenitis, lymphocysts or lymphatic malformations, lymphoma
(ch. 322), lymphangioma, and lymphangiosarcoma have been
recognized in animals. Types and causes of peripheral lymphatic
disorders are summarized in Box 239.2.

INFLAMMATORY LYMPHATIC
DISORDERS (LYMPHANGITIS AND
LYMPHADENITIS)
Lymphangitis and lymphadenitis often occur secondary to local
inflammation, particularly involving the skin, mucous membranes,
and subcutaneous tissues. Lymphangitis can also result from
bacterial or fungal infection or adjacent neoplastic and inflammatory
disease. Lymphatics may be affected and occluded as they drain
inflammatory agents and their byproducts from tissue spaces. In
lymph nodes, microorganisms are phagocytized and inactivated or
killed by humoral and cellular mechanisms. During this process,
lymph nodes may become obstructed, enlarged, warm, and painful.
Affected limbs may be locally swollen and lameness can result. Fever,
anorexia, and depression are common and leukocytosis may be
present with acute, severe lymphangitis.
Lymphangitis may become chronic when associated with a
granulomatous or static lesion such as a foreign body or with
unsuccessfully treated acute inflammation. Lymphangitis has been
associated with cutaneous coccidioidomycosis in a dog and cat (ch.
208), intestinal lymphadenitis secondary to bite wounds,
sporotrichosis (ch. 9), and chronic lipogranulomatous lymphangitis
in chronic protein-losing intestinal disease (ch. 262).69-73
Persistence of inflammatory edema in cutaneous infections results in
mesenchymal cell proliferation, which in turn can cause irreversible
thickening of the skin and subcutis. The prognosis is variable,
depending on the cause and in general more favorable with early
treatment. Therapy consists of moist, warm, local compresses or
soaks, which reduce swelling and promote drainage. Intensive local
and systemic antibiotic therapy usually promotes recovery in animals
with fever and anorexia. Bacterial culture and sensitivity testing and
cytologic examination of regional lymph nodes should be performed
if acute lymphangitis fails to respond to treatment and in cases of
chronic lymphangitis. Contrast studies and surgical exploration may
be indicated if fistulous tracts or abscesses are present, or if a foreign
body is suspected.

LYMPHEDEMA
Pathologic fluid accumulation occurs in the interstitium when the
microvascular filtration rate exceeds lymphatic drainage.3 Starling’s
forces conceptualize the interplay of oncotic and hydrostatic
pressure, coupled with vascular permeability, which drive
microvascular filtration.5 In the microvascular bed, there is a net
movement of ultrafiltrate to the interstitium such that in states of
inadequate or impaired lymphatic flow, the ultrafiltrate accumulates,
leading to lymphedema. Lymphedema specifically refers to an
accumulation of fluid in the interstitial space resulting from
abnormal lymphatic drainage.4 This term should not be used for
other forms of edema, such as edema related to venous obstruction
or generalized edema related to hypoproteinemia (ch. 30). The
protein-rich fluid of lymphedema (2 to 5 g/dL [20-50 g/L]) causes a
high osmotic gradient and exacerbates fluid accumulation.74
Numerous classification schemes have been used to categorize
lymphedema. Commonly used etiologic categories of lymphedema
include overload, inadequate collection into lymphatic capillaries,
abnormal lymphatic contractility, insufficient lymphatics, lymph
node obstruction, and main lymphatic ductal defects.

FIGURE 239.14 Images from an 11-year-old
mixed breed dog with a left adrenal

Traditionally, clinical effort is undertaken to differentiate primary
versus secondary lymphedema. Primary lymphedema refers to an
abnormality of the lymphatic vessels or lymph nodes. Secondary
lymphedema refers to disease in the lymphatic vessels or lymph
nodes due to a different pathologic process. Secondary lymphedema

can occur because of neoplasia, surgery, trauma, parasites, radiation
therapy, or infection and is more common than primary
lymphedema. Distinguishing between primary and secondary
lymphedema is often difficult. A disease process involving a lymph
node can result in fibrosis and obstruction with secondary
lymphedema developing.

Primary Lymphedema
Primary lymphedema can result from three principal morphologic
and functional abnormalities: (1) abnormalities of large vessels such
as aplasia or hypoplasia of the thoracic duct and cisterna chyli, (2)
aplasia of the peripheral lymphatics or congenital valvular
incompetence, and (3) lymph node fibrosis or a deficient lymph node
size and number.75,76
Lymphedema caused by aplasia, hypoplasia, or dysplasia of
proximal lymph channels or lymph nodes occurs most often in the
hindlimbs of young dogs (Figure 239.16). The edema can be
transient, observed only during the juvenile period, or permanent.
Mild cases are restricted to the hindlimbs, whereas severe cases may
progress to whole-body edema.77,78 Although the condition is
frequently bilateral, one limb is often more swollen than the other. A
number of cases of suspected congenital lymphedema have been
reported, though nearly all represent single case reports from
decades ago.78 A small series of dogs with familial primary
lymphedema was described and studies of this family suggested an
autosomal dominant mode of inheritance, variable severity of clinical
signs, and a high rate of mortality in severely affected dogs.77,79
Reported breeds include Bulldogs, Poodles, Old English Sheepdogs,
and Labrador Retrievers, although it is not clear whether these
breeds remain at increased risk today.
The history may identify chronic limb swelling since birth or
edema appearing later in life. The swelling represents a pitting
edema (Video 3.8

) of varying magnitude that is neither warm

nor cold. The edema is not usually accompanied by lameness or pain
unless there is massive enlargement or cellulitis. Growth and activity
are usually normal but rest and limb massage do not typically reduce

the severity of edema. Regional lymph nodes, normally prominent in
growing puppies, are sometimes difficult to identify. Total plasma
protein, serum protein electrophoresis, complete blood count, and
serum biochemistry profile results are generally unremarkable. The
diagnosis of primary lymphedema is based on history (age of onset,
disease progression, affected limbs, and distribution of edema) and
clinical signs. Previous surgery, trauma, or infections should also be
noted and may support a diagnosis of secondary lymphedema.
Radiographic or CT lymphangiography may be necessary to confirm
the diagnosis in subtle cases and is helpful in determining
morphology of anomalous lymphatic systems (Figure 239.17).
The prognosis for resolution of congenital lymphedema is guarded
and depends on the etiology. Some puppies that develop hindlimb
edema during the neonatal period improve spontaneously. Puppies
with severe edema of the limbs and trunk are more likely to succumb
during the first few weeks after birth.80 Chronic lymphatic vessel
dilation leads to permanent lymphatic valvular dysfunction.
Metabolic byproducts accumulate and lead to collagen deposition
and fibrosis. Complications such as abrasions and recurrent infection
often develop. Dogs with primary lymphedema should not be used
for breeding—as noted above, test matings of dogs with congenital
lymphedema support the hypothesis of autosomal dominant
inheritance with variable expression.77

Secondary Lymphedema

Persistent lymphedema occurs only after destruction or blockage of a
considerable number of major lymph channels or several sequential
lymph nodes with their afferent or efferent lymphatics.74 Factors
that can delay or prevent edema formation include opening of
collateral vessels, rerouting of lymph flow through peripheral
lymphaticovenous anastomoses and perilymphatic routes of lymph
drainage, and increased venous fluid uptake. Secondary lymphedema
may be related to a combination of lymphatic and venous
obstruction. Inhibited venous return increases lymphatic flow by
altering Starling’s forces toward increased tissue fluid accumulation.
This overloads the lymphatic capillaries and results in the
accumulation of fluid in the interstitial space. Distal lymphatics may
become more distended, causing loss of valvar competency,
stagnation of lymph flow, mural insufficiency, and further
accumulation of proteinaceous fluid in subcutaneous tissues. Other
common etiologies include post-traumatic, post-radiation therapy,
or post-surgical interruption of lymphatics; lymph node excision;
and blockage of lymph nodes and lymph vessels by compression or
invasive neoplasms.81,82 Lymphedema resulting from local neoplasia
is usually a sign of a widely disseminated and highly invasive
malignant process.

Diagnosis of Lymphedema
Clinical signs associated with secondary lymphedema vary
depending on the underlying cause or presence of a systemic
response, and may overlap with clinical signs of systemic venous
obstruction. Accordingly, physical diagnosis (ch. 3) and appropriate
imaging should assess both systems. Lymphedema may be localized
to the periphery of an extremity or extend proximally through the
subcutaneous tissues.81 The location and severity of obstruction
determine the extent of edema formation. For example, sublumbar
or intrapelvic obstruction induces bilateral hindlimb edema and
edema of the thighs and external genitalia. Mediastinal masses and
thrombosis of the cranial vena cava induce bilateral edema of the
front limbs and tissues of the ventral thorax, neck, and head (Figure
239.13). The clinician must palpate all lymph nodes carefully for
enlargement and pain. With bilateral hindlimb edema, it is

important to perform rectal or abdominal palpation to assess
sublumbar lymph nodes. The prostate and anal region or mammary
glands and vaginal area should be carefully inspected for masses,
which can lead to obstructive intrapelvic processes (chs. 264, 329,
330). Intrapelvic masses should be suspected in all dogs with
hindlimb edema and vague signs of sublumbar pain, discomfort
during ambulation, or difficulties with defecation or urination.
Depending on the type and extent of underlying systemic illness,
limb edema may be the only detectable abnormality or may be
accompanied by fever, anorexia, and weight loss. Clinicopathologic
findings depend on the underlying primary disorder.

The diagnosis of lymphedema is based largely on history and
physical examination and is facilitated by diagnostic imaging and the
ruling out of venous obstruction. Survey radiographs should be taken

of suspect areas, which often include the pelvis or cranial thorax. In a
substantial number of cases, soft-tissue masses or destructive bony
lesions can be detected. Occasionally, the identification of subclinical
pleural effusions in cases of peripheral edema suggests a more
generalized lymphatic disorder. Ultrasonography can provide
information about soft tissue masses and readily identifies enlarged
lymph nodes and other structures, both peripherally and within the
abdomen. Duplex ultrasound imaging, as described previously,
should be used to exclude venous thrombosis or obstruction.
Lymphangiography, lymphoscintigraphy, venography, or CT may be
indicated to evaluate venous and lymphatic anatomy and luminal
integrity if the diagnosis remains unclear. Lymphangiography was
traditionally relied upon for definitive diagnosis of lymphatic
disorders; now, CT lymphangiography is more commonly employed.
In some cases, the lymphatics are hypoplastic throughout their
course. When aplastic, lymphatics suitable for cannulation and
injection of radiocontrast agent may not be found. Failure to outline
a lymph node after lymphography is not absolute proof of its
absence.6 Lymphangiographic features of primary lymphedema
include lymph node aplasia and small lymphatics that end blindly or
anastomose into collateral vessels around (instead of into) the
locations where lymph nodes would normally be found.
Differential diagnoses for dogs with edema confined to one limb
include inflammation, trauma, vascular obstruction, hemorrhage,
cellulitis, phlebitis, and AV fistula (ch. 30). Diagnostic
considerations for dogs with edema involving both forelimbs include
thrombosis or compression or invasion of the cranial cava by a
mediastinal mass. With the latter, edema usually involves the head
and neck regions, as well as the limbs. Causes of only bilateral
hindlimb edema include enlargement of sublumbar lymph nodes by
neoplastic infiltration, right-sided congestive heart failure (ch. 229),
and pericardial effusion (ch. 235), accepting that in some dogs no
cause is ever identified—in the authors’ experience, the Irish
Wolfhound appears overrepresented in cases of idiopathic
lymphedema (Figure 239.6). If all four limbs are involved, the
differential diagnoses should include hypoproteinemia (ch. 60),
congestive heart failure (ch. 229), uremia (chs. 300, 301), portal
hypertension (ch. 267), or a lymphatic neoplasm

(lymphangiosarcoma). As noted earlier, the close association of
lymphatic and venous structures can make it difficult to distinguish
between lymphatic and venous obstruction, and both can occur at
the same time. Ulceration, dermatitis, cyanosis, weeping varices, or
fat necrosis are signs of venous obstruction rather than lymph stasis.

Therapy for Lymphedema
Therapy is usually unrewarding unless the edema is due to an
underlying cause of elevated venous pressure (as opposed to true
lymphedema). In the early stages of lymphedema, medical
management is directed to maintaining the animal’s comfort and
reducing swelling. Infectious disorders require long-term
antimicrobial therapy. Some neoplastic conditions may benefit from
chemotherapy or radiation therapy. Long-term heavy bandage
application (comparable to compression stockings in people) and
physical therapy may encourage lymphatic flow and reduce
subcutaneous lymph accumulation (ch. 256).83 Local topical skin
care and intermittent antibiotic therapy are helpful in reducing the
common secondary cellulitis that develops with lymphedema. With
the exception of isolated cases, pharmacologic therapies are
generally unrewarding. The benzopyrones (e.g., rutin) are a group of
drugs that have been advocated to reduce high-protein lymphedema
by stimulating macrophages, promoting proteolysis, and enhancing
absorption of protein fragments, though proof of efficacy in the
treatment of lymphedema is lacking.84,85 Long-term diuretic
administration is considered contraindicated because reduction of
interstitial fluid will concentrate proteins in the residual interstitial
space, which may promote tissue injury.6 Surgical options may
include (1) procedures to facilitate lymph drainage from affected
limbs (lymphangioplasty, bridging procedures, shunts, omental
transposition) and (2) procedures to excise abnormal tissue. Surgical
excision of the subcutaneous edematous tissue should be staged to
limit devascularization.6 Short-term administration of antiinflammatory agents, bandaging, and physical rehabilitation may be
helpful in cases of traumatic or post-surgical lymphedema.

LYMPHATIC MALFORMATIONS
Lymphatic malformations are less well characterized than venous
malformations. As with venous and arterial malformations,
lymphatic malformations are benign, although they may have some
features in common with vascular tumors. The diagnosis of
lymphatic malformations relies on imaging (ultrasound, CT), and a
definitive diagnosis will likely require histopathologic staining.86

Lymphangioma, Lymphangiosarcoma
Lymphangiomas are benign tumors of small-caliber lymphatic
vessels that are thought to develop when primitive lymphatic sacs fail
to establish venous communication.87 As noted in the human
classification, lymphatic malformations and lymphangiomas may
represent similar conditions or a spectrum of the same disease
state.50 In a 5-year survey of 221 vascular tumors of dogs, only one
case of lymphangioma was definitively identified, suggesting these
are rare lesions.52 Lymphangiomas can be classified into three
categories based on their histologic appearance: (1) capillary
lymphangiomas, composed of a network of capillary-sized lymphatic
channels; (2) cavernous lymphangiomas, composed of dilated
lymphatics that infiltrate the surrounding tissue; and (3) cystic
hygromas, which are unilocular or multilocular, cystic masses lined
by a single layer of endothelium supported by a connective tissue
stroma and containing a straw-colored, proteinaceous (1.3-4.5 g/dL
[13-45 g/L]) fluid.88 The lesions in dogs present as large, fluctuant
masses in the subcutaneous, fascial, mediastinal, hepatic, lymph
node, and retroperitoneal spaces. Lymphangiomas have also been
diagnosed on the extremities, metacarpal pads, nasopharynx, axilla,
inguinal and mammary region, retroperitoneal space, and skin of
dogs. Clinical signs are related to the size, location, and extent of the
lymphangioma. They can exert pressure on surrounding structures
and may interfere with muscle function, breathing (compression of
the trachea), urination, or intestinal function. Lymph may ooze to
the skin surface through single or multiple fistulous tracts.
Differential diagnoses include other space-occupying masses such as

abscesses, enlarged lymph nodes, neoplasms, and congenital cysts of
nonlymphogenic origin. The prognosis can be good after appropriate
surgical excision, marsupialization, or radiation therapy.89 Risk of
recurrence is high due to inherent inability to identify distinct
boundaries.
Lymphangiosarcoma originates from lymphatic endothelial
cells.90 It is a rare malignant tumor in dogs and cats, although it is
frequently reported secondary to chronic lymphedema in humans.91
The diagnosis can be challenging by light microscopy with
hematoxylin and eosin staining, as features of the neoplasm are
shared with hemangiosarcoma. Prior reports suggest
hemangiosarcoma and lymphangiosarcoma can be distinguished by
a lack of erythrocytes in the vascular spaces of
lymphangiosarcoma.90 Newer immunohistochemical stains appear
to better characterize these neoplasms.52,90,92 A breed or sex
predisposition has not been detected, but medium to large breeds
may be at highest risk, and both young and older animals are
affected.90,93 Metastasis occurs commonly in dogs and cats,
estimated to be present in a third to half of cases at diagnosis.90,93
Clinical signs include pitting edema of the extremities (

Video

3.8), inguinal region, axilla, and head and neck.
In a report of 12 cats with lymphangiosarcoma, 9 presented with
fast-growing, noncircumscribed subcutaneous masses and the others
presented with a thoracic or abdominal mass.93 In all cats affected,
the tumor was invasive and complete surgical resection was not
possible. The presenting concerns were similar in a series of 12 dogs
with lymphangiosarcoma in which 10 of the cases were presented for
swelling of the neck, ventral abdomen, or limbs—nearly all with
serosanguineous discharge from the overlying tissue.90 Associated
chylous effusions (pleural, abdominal, subcutaneous) have been
reported. Pulmonary lymphangiosarcoma was diagnosed in one dog
presenting with a chylous thoracic effusion.94 Cytologic evaluation of
aspirates of the mass or swelling is unrewarding, with most cytologic
reports describing mild inflammation without signs of malignancy.90

Diagnosis is confirmed by obtaining a biopsy specimen.
Histologically, tumors of lymphatic endothelial origin are
characterized by a neoplastic proliferation of endothelial cells.
Immunocytochemical stains, such as prospero-related homeobox
gene 1, have been used to confirm the diagnosis in dogs and
cats.90,92,95 The prognosis with lymphangiosarcoma is guarded to
poor, with a high rate of local recurrence and metastasis. In early
reports, most animals were euthanized or died due to severe
lymphedema, pleural effusion, or distant metastases. In one case
report, lack of recurrence and absence of metastatic disease was
documented over 9 months following mass resection and
doxorubicin treatment.96 In the case series of 12 dogs,90 various
treatment strategies were employed with incomplete surgical
excision in 5 dogs having a mean survival time of 513 days,
chemotherapy alone having a survival time of 182 days in 1 dog,
prednisone alone in 1 dog having a survival time of 90 days,
combination therapy (surgery, chemotherapy, +/− radiation
therapy) having survival of 574 days in 1 dog and more than 248 days
in another. The 3 dogs that did not receive therapy had a mean
survival of 368 days. Currently, the optimal therapy for
lymphangiosarcoma in dogs and cats is unknown.

This chapter will explore the basic cells within the nervous system,
how membrane potential is determined, what contributes to the
electrochemical gradient and how that gradient is instrumental in
nerve transmission. It will also discuss the creation of an action
potential and how the anatomy of an axon is related to impulse
propagation and efficacy. Synaptic transmission including nervenerve and nerve-muscle transmission will be explored and placed in
a clinical context. Finally, an overview of the major clinically relevant
motor and sensory pathways will be explored.

BASIC STRUCTURE OF A NEURON1,2
The neuron is composed of a cell body and its axon. Within the cell
body are the nucleus and the cytoplasm that surrounds it.
Information is received by the neuron through both direct contact
with the cell body and also direct contact with dendrites. The
primary job of the dendrites is to receive incoming information from
neighboring neurons. After entering the neuron, information travels
away from the dendritic processes or cell body by way of the axon.
This information reaches the distal aspect of the axon, or axon
terminal (axon hillock) where an action potential is created. The
action potential is the way in which nerves communicate with their
surroundings. Nerve impulses are transmitted to other nerves and
muscles by way of a synapse.
There are several different types of neurons; the most common
type is the multipolar neuron (composed of a nerve cell body, its
multiple dendritic processes and an axon). Sensory neurons, motor
neurons and interneurons are types of multipolar neurons. Sensory
neurons transmit afferent impulses to the nervous system while
motor neurons transmit efferent information to muscle.
Interneurons are involved in nerve–nerve transmission.

CONCENTRATION AND
ELECTROCHEMICAL GRADIENT1,2
Intracellular and extracellular ion concentrations, the flow of these
ions, and the permeability for these ions across neuronal membranes
allow for creation of both concentration and electrochemical
gradients. The difference in concentration between three permeable
ions (Na+, K+, and Cl–) and the impermeable organic anions, located
within the intracellular space, determines this concentration
gradient. The difference in ion concentration between the neuron
and the extracellular fluid surrounding the neuron creates and
maintains the cell resting membrane potential. At rest, the
membrane potential of a neuron is –65 mV while it is –65 to –90 mV
for skeletal muscle. Sodium and chloride are higher in concentration
in the extracellular space, while potassium is in higher concentration

in the intracellular space. Inherently, the cellular membrane is more
permeable to K+ ions than Na+ ions. This difference in permeability
between ions, and inherent neuronal membrane impermeability to
negatively charged intracellular organic anions, create this negative
resting membrane potential. A further contributing factor is the
Na+/K+ ATPase pump located on the neuronal membrane. This
moves 3 Na+ ions into the extracellular space for every 2 K+ ions
pumped intracellularly, further potentiating the negative
intracellular charge with respect to the extracellular space.

ACTION POTENTIAL1,2
The abrupt change from a negative intracellular charge to a positive
intracellular charge relative to the extracellular environment is the
major force through which nerves communicate with other cells.
This abrupt change in cellular charge is referred to as an action
potential. There are 3 phases to action potential formation and
propagation: (a) resting, (b) depolarization, and (c) repolarization
(Figure 240.1). As stated previously, ion concentration and
membrane permeability, in conjunction with the neuronal Na+/K+
ATPase pump, create the resting (negative) phase of nerve
transmission. The cell membrane is said to depolarize when
permeability to sodium ions abruptly increases; these positively
charged ions make a rapid move intracellularly, increasing the cell
membrane potential to +35-40 mV. This abrupt intracellular
positivity is referred to as depolarization. Quickly thereafter, the
sodium channels on the neuron close, potassium channels open, and
there is a rapid exit of positively charged potassium ions into the
extracellular space; the result is a repolarization and a reversion of
the membrane potential back to its negative resting state.
Action potentials are propagated down an excitable membrane, as
is the case in axonal transmission. The speed at which these action
potentials travel down an axon is dependent on both the degree of
axonal myelination and the axonal diameter. Myelin is created by
oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system (CNS) and Schwann
cells in the peripheral nervous system (PNS). At its core, myelin is a
substance composed primarily of lipid. It insulates the axon—the

more myelinated the axon, the faster it conducts. Not all axons in the
nervous system are myelinated and varying degrees of myelination
allow for a diversity of axonal transmission speeds throughout the
nervous system.
Saltatory conduction refers to axonal transmission down a
myelinated axon. Ion movement between the intracellular and
extracellular spaces and depolarization occurs at regions along the
axon devoid of myelin—the nodes of Ranvier. Impulse transmission
is said to “jump” (saltare, Latin: to jump) from node to node,
resulting in speedier impulse conduction on myelinated portions of
the axon as opposed to those lacking myelin and thus lacking nodes
(Figure 240.2). Axonal diameter is also key to the speed of
transmission. The larger the axonal diameter, the less resistance
there is to ionic flow and the faster the propagation of axonal
impulses. Thus, those axons that are more heavily myelinated and
larger in diameter are faster impulse conductors.

SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION1,4,5
As stated previously, a nerve communicates with another nerve or
with muscle by way of a synapse at the axon terminal. There are 2
main types of synapses in the body: electrical and chemical (Figure
240.3). Electrical synapses allow for ion flow directly between gap
junctions that connect adjacent cells. This transmission is integral to
cardiac and smooth muscle transmission. Chemical synapses are
abundant in the CNS and PNS and involve the formation of synaptic
vesicles containing either inhibitory (gamma aminobutyric acid, also
known as GABA; or glycine) or excitatory (glutamate or
acetylcholine) neurotransmitters (Video 240.1

). These vesicles

fuse with the presynaptic neuronal membrane following an influx of
calcium into the neuron through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels. After
fusion, neurotransmitters are released into the synapse and they
bind to the postsynaptic membrane (another neuron in the CNS and
a skeletal muscle in the PNS). In the CNS, the action of the
postsynaptic neuron is either inhibitory or excitatory depending on
which type of neurotransmitter was released. In the PNS, the

neurotransmitter released is acetylcholine, and as such, always
excitatory.

FIGURE 240.1 Action potential including its 3
phases: resting, depolarization and
repolarization. From Hall JE. Guyton and Hall
Textbook of Medical Physiology. 13th ed. Elsevier;
2016:65.

Nerve-Nerve Transmission1,4-6
Excitatory neurotransmitter release into the synapse stimulates an
influx of Na+ into the postsynaptic membrane. The postsynaptic
membrane depolarizes and excitatory postsynaptic potentials
(EPSPs) are created. However, this type of depolarization is different
from that of action potential formation and depolarization of the
presynaptic membrane. EPSPs are smaller and shorter in time
duration. Thus, in order to create an action potential via excitation of

the postsynaptic membrane, either spatial or temporal summation
has to take place. Spatial summation refers to the simultaneous
arrival of EPSPs at different locations along the axon terminals,
while temporal summation refers to arrival of EPSPs at the same
location on the axon terminal but at different points in time.
Summation allows these less aggressive stimuli to create an action
potential and propagate signal along the postsynaptic membrane.
In juxtaposition, inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs) are the
result of inhibitory neurotransmitter release into the synapse.
Chloride channels on the neuron open and negatively charged
chloride ions flow into the neuronal membrane. Potassium channels
also open and positively charged potassium ions flow out of the cell,
further decreasing the membrane potential and leading to neuronal
hyperpolarization. Similar to EPSPs, IPSPs are also smaller and
shorter in duration.
The idea of EPSPs and IPSPs is clinically very relevant and integral
to the understanding of the paroxysmal burst activity and neuronal
depolarization observed in seizure generation and propagation.
Anticonvulsant therapies are effective because of alternations in
EPSP and IPSP activity. Glutamate is a major excitatory
neurotransmitter in the CNS. Glutamate’s release at the nerve-nerve
synapse causes an influx of positive ions (Na+) into the postsynaptic
neuron resulting in the generation of an EPSP. In order to halt
seizure activity and the propagation of these excitatory potentials
across the cerebral cortical neurons, IPSPs must be generated. The
influx of the negative ion, Cl–, into the postsynaptic neuronal cell
membrane results in hyperpolarization; it inhibits further neuronal
depolarization and action potential creation. Mechanistically,
anticonvulsant medications such as benzodiazepines and
barbiturates bind to receptors for the inhibitory neurotransmitter
GABA, Cl– ions enter the neuronal cells, hyperpolarization results,
and seizure propagation is halted.

myelinated axon. From Hall JE. Guyton and Hall

FIGURE 240.3 Chemical (A) and electrical (B)
