Neuromuscular Transmission1,2,4
With respect to neuromuscular transmission, acetylcholine is
released from synaptic vesicles and binds to the postsynaptic muscle.
This neurotransmitter is excitatory in nature and creates an EPSP.
This EPSP is also known as an end-plate potential or EPP. Being a
type of EPSP, the EPP is always excitatory in nature; voltage-gated
Na+ channels on the muscle membrane are stimulated, the resulting
Na+ influx into the skeletal muscle triggers an action potential, and
depolarization of the muscle membrane occurs. Depolarization
stimulates the release of stored Ca2+ from within the sarcoplasmic
reticulum into the muscle cell. This release of calcium ions, along
with the interaction between 2 muscle fiber proteins, actin and
myosin, and the breakdown of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) into
adenosine diphosphate (ADP), result in skeletal muscle contraction.
An example of this concept is observed during patella reflex testing.
The patella tendon is tapped, causing a stretch of the patellar tendon
and stimulation of the sensory neuron; thus, an action potential is
generated. This sensory impulse signals the motor or efferent neuron
located in the ventral grey matter of the spinal cord (lower motor
neuron [LMN]). An EPSP is created which results in depolarization
and contraction of the quadriceps muscle, and the stifle extends.

CLINICAL APPLICATION OF NERVE
AND MUSCLE TRANSMISSION AS IT
PERTAINS TO THE LMN SYSTEM3
The term LMN is the name for the anatomic location of efferent
nerve cell bodies within the spinal cord. The LMN cell bodies are
located in the lower or ventral half of the spinal cord grey matter.

Efferent information is carried from the nerve cell body in the
ventral horn of the spinal cord (CNS) into the PNS via ventral nerve
roots (Figure 240.4). Several nerve roots combine together to form
1 peripheral nerve. For example, the L4, L5 and L6 nerve roots
combine to form the femoral nerve, which then extends into the
periphery, innervating the hip flexor (iliopsoas) and quadriceps
muscles in the dog. When either the LMN cell body, its efferent nerve
root, or axon, is/are diseased, patients display decreased to absent
tone or paresis to paralysis of the muscles innervated by the affected
neural tissue. Similarly, if there is a reflex that can be used to assess
the integrity of a particular peripheral nerve, if diseased, the
associated reflex will be decreased or absent when tested. To
continue the example above, if either the LMN cell bodies, the
efferent nerve roots of spinal cord segments at L4-L6 or the
associated femoral nerve, are damaged in a canine patient, then the
dog will have decreased-to-absent tone in the hip flexor muscles,
along with a decreased-to-absent patellar reflex.

CLINICAL APPLICATION OF NERVE
AND MUSCLE TRANSMISSION AS IT
PERTAINS TO THE UMN SYSTEM2
(VIDEO 240.2)
The term upper motor neuron (UMN) refers to nerve cell bodies
located within the brain that are involved in movement initiation.
The cell bodies for these neurons are located above (hence “upper”
i.e., within the brain) whereas the LMN cell bodies are located below
(“lower” i.e., within the spinal cord). The major UMN pathways are
referred to as the pyramidal and extrapyramidal systems. The
corticospinal tracts are the major tracts that compose the pyramidal
system. The cell bodies for these tracts are located in the cerebral
cortex; their axons descend by way of the pyramids in the medulla of
the brainstem into the spinal cord. The rubrospinal, vestibulospinal
and reticulospinal tracts (medullary- and pontine-reticulospinal
tracts) are a few of the major tracts that compose the extrapyramidal
system. Their cell bodies are located in the brainstem (midbrain,

medulla and pons, respectively). Their axons descend from the
brainstem into the spinal cord.
The axons from the pyramidal and extrapyramidal systems
communicate with the LMN cell bodies by way of interneurons
located in the spinal cord grey matter. The end goal of the pyramidal
and extrapyramidal tracts is to initiate movement by way of flexion
and extension of the muscles innervated by the LMNs. In general
terms, the UMN often exerts an inhibitory influence on the LMNs;
thus, when the UMNs or their axons are diseased, the LMNs are
released from inhibition, and associated reflexes and muscle tone are
normal to increased on examination. Because the UMN pathways
initiate movement, disease of these neurons or their axons lead to
limb paresis or paralysis. However, in rare cases of significant spinal
cord injury and loss of spinal cord transmission, local spinal cord
circuitry can generate a phenomenon called spinal walking
(Video 240.2).

carrying information from the ventral horn of the

SENSORY SYSTEM AS IT APPLIES TO
CLINICAL NEUROLOGY
Both the UMN and the LMN are integral to movement of the body.
In addition to the motor systems, the sensory system is also an
important part of basic neurophysiology. There are 2 main groups of
pathways involved in the sensory system: the proprioceptive and the
nociceptive pathways.

Proprioception1,3
The term proprioception refers to the body’s awareness of its own
position in space. Proprioceptors are those receptors that sense
movement; they are located in the joint, tendon, muscle and inner
ear. Sensory information from the joint, tendon and muscle are
carried from the periphery via afferent axons into the dorsal root
ganglion. Within this ganglion is the cell body for this afferent axon.
The axon then moves into the dorsal portion of the grey matter of the
spinal cord (dorsal horn). Proprioceptive information is relayed up
the spinal cord by way of several pathways including: the dorsal and
ventral spinocerebellar tracts, the cuneocerebellar tract, the
cervicospinocerebellar tract, and pathways of the fasciculus gracilis
and fasciculus cuneatus. Ultimately, these tracts send sensory
information about the position of the limbs, trunk, tail, and neck in
space to the brain. When diseased, a patient can lose perception of
its limbs in space. A clinical example of this is the inability for a dog
to turn a paw flipped onto its dorsum back to a normal position
during proprioceptive testing (ch. 241;

Video 241.7).

Nociceptive Pathways1,3
Nociceptive pathways are those that carry sensory information from
noxious stimuli via afferent axons into the CNS. Nociceptors are

receptors located in the periphery; they are stimulated by thermal,
mechanical (touch, pressure and vibrational) and chemical stimuli.
The axons carrying sensory information are either poorly myelinated
or unmyelinated. From the nerve cell body in the dorsal root
ganglion by way of the afferent axon, sensory information is moved
into the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Nociceptive information
ascends in the spinal cord into the brain by way of 2 main pathways
(the spinothalamic and the spinoreticular tracts). The result is
conscious recognition of the painful stimulus. Clinically, if a
hemostat is used for compressing the digits of a limb (

Videos

241.22, 241.23) and there is no conscious recognition of said
stimulus, the patient is said to have lost pain sensation; there must
be damage to the patient’s nociceptive pathways.
Receiving and sending sensory and motor information into and
out of the nervous system is necessary for normal movement and
function. In order to determine if an animal has neurologic
dysfunction, both the sensory and motor PNS and CNS need to be
assessed. The neurologic examination, described in the next chapter,
is the test of both the PNS and CNS. It is the first step in determining
whether a patient does or does not have neurologic dysfunction or
disease.

responses.

A precise neuroanatomic diagnosis remains indispensable for generating an
appropriate differential diagnosis. In turn, the differential diagnosis allows the clinician
to select and interpret neurodiagnostic tests correctly. This chapter is meant to provide
the clinician with the basic, functional neuroanatomic information and clinical
examination skills necessary to make an accurate neuroanatomic diagnosis.1 Video clips
for this chapter demonstrate various components of the neurologic examination and
show characteristic abnormalities associated with the most common neuroanatomic
diagnoses.
The past 2 decades have been marked by a dramatic increase in the availability of
advanced neurodiagnostic testing for veterinary patients. Magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI), in particular, has enhanced our ability to diagnose complex and elusive
neurologic disorders (ch. 112). The “downside” to such advances is that clinicians have
developed a natural tendency to rely heavily (or exclusively!) on advanced imaging in
patients with neurologic disorders. Although MRI and computed tomography (CT) scans
are sensitive for the identification of abnormalities of the central and peripheral nervous
systems (CNS and PNS), both imaging modalities lack specificity and may be misleading
when interpreted outside the context of the neuroanatomic and differential diagnoses.
Despite the exceptional availability of cross-sectional imaging, the clinician’s ability to
successfully diagnose, prognosticate and treat patients with neurologic disease remains
critically reliant on the neurologic examination.

NEUROLOGIC EXAMINATION
The neurologic examination can be divided into five parts. These are evaluation of (1)
sensorium and behavior; (2) posture and gait; (3) postural reactions; (4) muscle mass,
tone, spinal reflexes, cutaneous sensation and nociception; and (5) cranial nerves (CNs).
The order in which the neurologic examination is performed is not critical, but the
clinician should develop a consistent routine for evaluating each dog or cat.

SENSORIUM AND BEHAVIOR
The owner is often the best judge of changes in a pet’s demeanor and behavior and
should be questioned carefully (chs. 1, 2, and 3). Examples of behavioral changes
include docile pets that have become aggressive (and vice versa) or pets that have
forgotten learned habits (ch. 11). Procurement of an accurate history may prove to be
critical because behavioral changes may be secondary to intracranial lesions that
otherwise have no impact on the neurologic examination.
Sensorium (mental attitude) should be assessed carefully in recumbent pets.
Recumbency may be associated with brainstem, cervical spinal cord, or diffuse
neuromuscular disorders (NMDs). Of the three localizations, only brainstem lesions

should affect the sensorium. An alteration in sensorium is typically due to a disturbance
in the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) and/or limbic system components of
the cerebrum or rostral brainstem (diencephalon). Numerous terms have been used to
describe changes in sensorium and/or behavior (chs. 11, 44, and 125).

POSTURE AND GAIT
Posture
The clinician should evaluate posture when the pet is standing and walking. The patient
should be assessed for a head tilt (e.g., vestibular disease, ch. 248); a head or body turn
(e.g., rostral brainstem or cerebral disease); neck position (e.g., lowered with cervical
spinal cord [chs. 250 and 251] or diffuse neuromuscular [ch. 253] disease); hock angle
(e.g., plantigrade with peripheral neuropathies, ch. 252); evidence of trembling (e.g.,
neuromuscular disease) and tail position (e.g., flaccid with lumbosacral disease). The
clinician also should recognize normal, breed-specific variants in posture such as sunken
tarsi in German Shepherd Dogs.
Severe intracranial lesions may lead to two separate opisthotonic postures:
decerebrate or decerebellate rigidity (ch. 44). Decerebrate rigidity is characterized by
opisthotonus with rigid extension of the neck and all four limbs, and is typically
associated with midbrain or rostral cerebellar lesions. Decerebellate rigidity results from
severe cerebellar lesions and is characterized by opisthotonus with extensor rigidity of
the limbs, but with the hips flexed.
Pleurothotonus refers to the deviation of the head and neck to one side and may be
present with mid- to rostral brainstem or cerebral lesions.

Gait
Strength and coordination are the key gait components to be evaluated. Gait should be
assessed in an area where the pet may move with or without a leash (if possible), and
always on a non-slippery surface (ch. 3). Pattern recognition of gait abnormalities is a
key component for making an accurate neuroanatomic diagnosis.

Paresis
Paresis refers to an inability to support weight or a deficiency in the ability to generate a
gait. In neurologic patients, paresis may result from a lesion in the lower motor neuron
(LMN)/neuromuscular system, the upper motor neuron (UMN) system, or both.
Animals with “LMN paresis” manifest a wide variation in their ability to support
weight. Thoracic or pelvic limbs (or both sets of limbs with diffuse LMN disease) may be
affected. A dog with a mild to moderate NMD may be ambulatory with a “short and
choppy,” stilted gait (Videos 241.1 and 241.2)

, whereas a patient with a severe NMD

can be tetraplegic. Some ambulatory pets with LMN disease advance both pelvic limbs
simultaneously; this also may occur with orthopedic and spinal cord disorders.
Animals with “UMN paresis” also may have considerable variation in their ability to
generate a gait. Depending on the location of a spinal cord or mid-to-caudal brainstem
lesion, thoracic and/or pelvic limbs may be affected with UMN signs. Ambulatory pets
with UMN paresis walk with a long-strided, spastic (stiff) gait that is typically
accompanied by general proprioceptive (GP) ataxia (Videos 241.3 and 241.4)

. The

latter occurs because the majority of the key UMN pathways (reticulospinal and
rubrospinal tracts) that function in gait generation are anatomically adjacent to GP
pathways (spinocerebellar tracts and conscious proprioceptive pathways). Spinal cord
and mid- to caudal brainstem lesions disrupt descending UMN pathways and ascending
GP pathways, resulting in varying degrees of paresis and ataxia.
Some clinicians utilize a grading scheme for spinal cord lesions to help prognosticate
and monitor treatment response. Such grading schemes evaluate the gait with respect to
strength and proprioception. Grading schemes typically are on a 0 to 5 scale but are
somewhat inconsistent; some utilize grade 0 as normal, whereas others are the opposite.
If a grading scheme is utilized, clinicians should qualify the grade with descriptors of
strength, proprioception, and nociception (in recumbent pets) to avoid confusion. For
spinal cord lesions, the degree of dysfunction has been classified using a modified
Frankel score.2,3
Grade 0: tetraplegia or paraplegia with no deep nociception
Grade 1: tetraplegia or paraplegia with no superficial nociception
Grade 2: tetraplegia or paraplegia with nociception
Grade 3: nonambulatory tetraparesis or paraparesis
Grade 4: ambulatory tetraparesis or paraparesis and GP ataxia
Grade 5: spinal hyperesthesia only or no dysfunction

Ataxia
Three clinical forms of ataxia (incoordination) exist: (1) GP ataxia, (2) vestibular ataxia,
and (3) cerebellar ataxia.
GP ataxia previously was mentioned in relation to UMN paresis because the two
typically occur simultaneously. GP ataxia results from disruption of the ascending long
tracts that relay the spatial location and the degree of muscle contraction of the limbs,
trunk, and neck. When ascending GP information fails to reach the brain, incoordination
results. This incoordination may include crossing the limbs, scuffing or dragging of the
digits, standing or landing on the dorsal aspect of the paws, and sometimes a delay in the
swing phase of the gait. Together with the UMN signs, this produces a relatively
characteristic gait that reflects both UMN paresis and GP ataxia (Videos 241.3 and 241.4)
.
Vestibular ataxia results from a loss of orientation of the head with respect to the
eyes, neck, limbs, and trunk. Pets with vestibular disease may lose their balance and
have a tendency to drift, lean, or fall in one direction (Video 241.5

). A head tilt and

abnormal nystagmus commonly accompany vestibular ataxia (Video 241.6). With
peripheral vestibular lesions, pets maintain normal strength and proprioception, but
with central vestibular lesions, UMN tetraparesis and GP deficits typically are present
(Video 241.7

).

Cerebellar ataxia is characterized by a hypermetric gait that is most apparent when
the animal initiates sudden bursts of motor activity (Video 241.8

). Cerebellar

hypermetria may be differentiated from a UMN gait by a marked overflexion of the
limbs on protraction (swing phase); occasionally, this differentiation is challenging.
Because of the close connection between cerebellum and vestibular systems, a head tilt,

loss of balance, and abnormal nystagmus may be seen with cerebellar lesions (Video
241.9

).

POSTURAL REACTIONS
Following the gait observation, postural reactions should be evaluated to identify subtle
deficits of strength and coordination. An animal’s ability to perform postural reactions
requires that all major sensory (GP) and motor (UMN and LMN) components of the
CNS and PNS be intact. Although many clinicians use postural reactions to assess
conscious proprioception (CP), this is a misnomer because all postural reactions rely on
both the motor and proprioceptive systems. Furthermore, when assessing postural
reactions, both the conscious and unconscious sensory pathways are tested; deficiencies
in these two key components of GP cannot be separated practically.1
The clinician should be cautious when interpreting postural reaction deficits because
they are not of localizing value when performed without other components of the
neurologic examination (Figure 241.1). For example, a recumbent dog or cat with a
severe and diffuse NMD or one with a severe cervical spinal cord lesion may have
delayed (to absent) postural reactions in all four limbs. Close assessment of spinal
reflexes, as well as muscle mass and tone, is necessary to differentiate between these two
localizations. Another example is that of a patient with unilateral postural reaction
deficits, which has several possible localizations including a unilateral lesion of the
prosencephalon (cerebrum and/or thalamus), brainstem, or spinal cord. Unilateral
prosencephalic lesions typically result in contralateral postural reaction deficits with a
normal gait (and potentially accompanied by a contralateral menace deficit,
contralateral sensory deficits, and changes in sensorium) (Video 241.10

). Unilateral

(caudal) brainstem or spinal cord lesions cause ipsilateral postural reaction deficits. The
presence of CN abnormalities and/or changes in sensorium may help to differentiate
between the two localizations and suggest brainstem dysfunction.
In recumbent patients, postural reaction testing may help to differentiate between
UMN and LMN tetraparesis. A dog with “pure” LMN disease that maintains some
voluntary movement should have relatively normal postural reactions (if most of the
body weight is supported) (Video 241.2

). This is because the GP system is unaffected

by pure LMN disease. Conversely, a recumbent pet with a brainstem or spinal cord
lesion will have delayed to absent postural reactions in all four limbs even when
supported (Video 241.4

).

Hopping and placing responses are the most useful postural reactions (Videos 241.11,
241.12, and 241.13)

. However, additional testing (e.g., wheelbarrowing, extensor

postural thrust) may prove useful when these responses are equivocal.

Hopping
While supporting the pelvic limbs, the dog or cat should be hopped on one thoracic limb
while the other thoracic limb is held off the ground. The animal should be moved

laterally (Video 241.11

). The clinician should observe the lateral aspect of the

thoracic limb being tested; the limb should move as soon as the shoulder is moved
laterally over the paw. Any delay, irregularity, or exaggeration in this response is
abnormal. Limb strength and coordination should be assessed by comparing responses
in contralateral limbs. Delayed hopping (symmetric or asymmetric) may occur with a
motor (UMN or LMN) or sensory (GP) lesions. Commonly, both the UMN and GP
systems (e.g., brainstem and spinal cord diseases) are affected simultaneously and the
abnormal hopping response is a reflection of both (e.g., UMN/GP deficits). Lesions in
the GP system or cerebellum may produce exaggerated responses (Video 241.12

).

Hopping responses in the pelvic limbs should be evaluated similarly. While supporting
the ventral thorax and thoracic limbs, the clinician should flex one pelvic limb fully and
push the animal laterally on the supporting limb. The pelvic limb hopping responses
should be compared with one another (not to thoracic limbs) (Video 241.12

).

Typically, pelvic limb hopping responses are more spastic (stiff) and show slightly larger
excursions than the thoracic limbs.

Paw Replacement, Tactile Placing Responses
Paw replacement responses assess whether the standing dog or cat corrects its paw
position after the clinician has flexed the paw and placed it so that weight is borne on its
dorsal surface (Video 241.13

). Normal animals quickly return their paw to the

normal anatomic position. Paw replacement responses should be performed on each
thoracic and pelvic limb individually. The clinician should support most of the pet’s
weight during the test, to focus the assessment on the animal’s perception of paw
position and not whether it has the strength to move. Although some clinicians attribute
a delay in paw replacement response to diminished CP (e.g., “CP deficit”), this is a
misinterpretation of the test for three reasons: (1) A severely paretic animal with a pure
LMN disease (e.g., myasthenia gravis) can have delayed or absent paw replacement due
to weakness, despite having no lesion in the CP system; (2) paw replacement responses
do not isolate the CP pathways from the other afferent sensory pathways (e.g.,
spinocerebellar tracts) of the PNS and CNS; and (3) rarely (and inexplicably!) some
animals without neurologic disease have delayed paw replacement responses.

FIGURE 241.1 Flowsheet for establishing a neuroanatomic
diagnosis in a patient with postural reaction deficits. GP, General
proprioceptive; LMN, lower motor neuron; UMN, upper motor
neuron.
Tactile placing responses typically are assessed in cats and small dogs. The animal
should be lifted off the ground and its thoracic limbs should be brought to the edge of a

table so that the dorsal surface of the paws makes contact (Video 241.14

). Normally,

the animal should step quickly onto the table, with the correct anatomic position. The
test should be performed on both thoracic limbs simultaneously, then individually. It
may help to cover the animal’s eyes because vision could compensate for sense of
position when the GP system is abnormal, giving an erroneous result.

Extensor Postural Thrust
Although this test is performed only occasionally, it may be helpful in patients with
subtle pelvic limb signs. The animal should be held off the ground and supported caudal
to the scapulae, lowered to the ground, and allowed to extend its pelvic limbs to support
its weight. Moving the animal forward and backward tests symmetry of pelvic limb
strength and coordination (Video 241.15

).

Hemiwalking
This postural reaction is not assessed routinely but it may be useful in large dogs. On one
side of the body, the thoracic and pelvic limbs should be held off the ground and the dog
then forced to walk forward or to the side. Healthy dogs hop smoothly on both thoracic
and pelvic limbs (Video 241.16

).

Wheelbarrowing
This postural reaction test also is performed rarely, but it may be helpful in patients with
subtle thoracic limb deficits. The pet should be supported under the abdomen so that the
pelvic limbs are held off the ground. Then the patient is walked forward on its thoracic
limbs (Video 241.17

). With this posture, vision is compromised and the animal relies

heavily on GP. With the head extended in a normal position, dogs and cats should walk
with symmetric movements of both thoracic limbs. With severe lesions, patients may
carry their head flexed with the nose oriented close to the ground for support.

MUSCLE MASS, TONE, SPINAL REFLEXES,
CUTANEOUS SENSATION, AND NOCICEPTION
Muscle mass and tone, spinal reflexes, cutaneous sensation and nociception should be
evaluated when a dog or cat is relaxed, preferably in lateral recumbency. It is helpful to
evaluate responses to noxious stimuli last, to maintain cooperation.

Muscle Mass and Tone
The head, neck, and thoracolumbar epaxial muscles should be evaluated for symmetry
and any evidence of atrophy. Each thoracic and pelvic limb should be assessed similarly,
from proximal to distal. Muscle tone should be evaluated by passive range of motion of
each limb. The degree of resistance should be assessed as normal, hypotonic, or
hypertonic/spastic. The degree of hypertonicity/spasticity may vary from mild to
marked, with the latter occasionally associated with a “clasp knife” response (“clasp

knife” refers to attempts made to flex the limb that actually increase the degree of
extension of the limb until it suddenly gives way to complete flexion without resistance).
Hypertonia or spasticity typically results from lesions in the UMN pathways (although
it also may be seen with myotonic disorders [ch. 42]) (Videos 241.18 and 241.19). The
UMN normally influences activity of the LMN to facilitate voluntary motor activity and
to maintain muscle tone, supporting the body against gravity. Lesions disrupting the
UMN pathways may “release” the LMNs from inhibition, leading to overactivity of the
facilitatory mechanism (ch. 240).
Conversely, hypotonia is associated with LMN/neuromuscular disease (Video 241.20
). The functional integrity of the complete “LMN unit” (cell body, nerve root,
peripheral nerve, neuromuscular junction [NMJ], and muscle) is necessary to produce
muscle cell contraction and to effectively maintain muscle tone. When the LMN unit is
diseased, one consequence is a loss of muscle tone. With LMN disease, denervation also
may lead to muscle cell degeneration and neurogenic atrophy may be appreciable over
time.
Tetraplegic animals should be supported in a standing position, and the clinician
should evaluate limb muscle mass and tone, as well as voluntary responses (above).
Dogs with cervical spinal cord disease may have a hypertonic trunk and limbs, and this
may be accompanied by a spastic gait with exaggerated movements.
Occasionally, the hypertonia associated with cervical spinal cord disease is so
profound that the recumbent animal, once lifted into a standing position, can briefly
maintain that position unassisted. Conversely, tetraplegic animals with diffuse
LMN/neuromuscular disease typically are hypotonic (or atonic). When the clinician
supports them in a standing position, these animals collapse if support is withdrawn. It
is critical to differentiate between UMN and LMN tetraplegia because the differential
diagnoses are markedly different, as are diagnostics, management, and treatment
recommendations.

Spinal Reflexes
Although most neurology textbooks describe numerous tendon and muscle reflexes, the
majority are of limited clinical use because they are not present in all normal small
animals. The most reliable reflexes are the patellar reflex and withdrawal-flexor reflexes.

Patellar Reflex
The most reliable tendon reflex is the patellar reflex, which is mediated by the femoral
nerve through spinal cord segments L4-L7. With the limb held in partial flexion, the
clinician should elicit this reflex by lightly tapping the patellar tendon with a plexor or
pediatric hammer (Video 241.21

). This reflex should be tested with the pet in both

lateral recumbencies. For inexplicable reasons, this reflex commonly is elicited more
easily in the limb adjacent to the floor. It is noteworthy that one or both patellar reflexes
may be absent in older dogs with no other neurologic signs.4 Responses are typically
graded as absent (0), hyporeflexive (+1), normal (+2), hyperreflexive (+3), or clonic
(+4). An absent or hyporeflexive reflex occurs when there is a disease of a portion of the

reflex arc (most commonly in the LMN unit; Video
may be present in UMN diseases (Video 241.19

241.2). Hyperreflexia or clonus
).

Withdrawal-Flexor Reflexes—Thoracic and Pelvic Limbs
Withdrawal-flexor reflexes assess the integrity of the thoracic and pelvic limb withdrawal
reflex arcs. They are elicited by applying pressure to the base of the toenail with a firm
manual pinch or with hemostats (Videos 241.22 and 241.23

). A normal response is

an immediate, strong withdrawal of the limb with complete flexion of all joints. Animals
with reduced withdrawal-flexor reflexes occasionally extend or kick the limb in response
to the noxious stimulus (Videos 241.18, 241.24, and 241.25

). Normal animals may

do this as well, but invariably also with visible evidence of pain sensation. In the thoracic
limb, the thoracodorsal, axillary, musculocutaneous, median, ulnar, and radial nerves
are responsible for flexion of the shoulder, elbow, carpus, and digits. The nerves
responsible for this reflex arise from spinal cord segments C6-T2. The specific sensory
nerve stimulated depends on the location of the noxious stimulus. The median and ulnar
nerves innervate the skin of the palmar surface of the paw. The radial nerve innervates
the dorsal surface and the cranial and lateral surfaces of the antebrachium; the ulnar and
musculocutaneous nerves innervate the caudal and medial surfaces, respectively. One
must be cautious not to overinterpret these dermatomes because there is some overlap
of the cutaneous innervation supplied by these nerves and a degree of individual patient
variation.
Deficiencies in the thoracic limb withdrawal-flexor reflex (Videos 241.2, 241.4, 241.24,
and 241.26

) suggest a C6-T2 lesion (spinal cord segments, nerve roots, brachial

plexus, peripheral nerves) or potentially a more diffuse LMN/NMD. The latter would be
accompanied by reduced pelvic limb reflexes, reduced tone, and other neuromuscular
signs. It has been suggested that dogs with C1-C5 spinal cord lesions may mislocalize to
C6-T2 because of reduced withdrawal reflexes that may be present in the thoracic
limbs.5 The explanation for this phenomenon is unclear.
In the pelvic limb, the withdrawal-flexor reflex is mediated by the sciatic nerve
through spinal cord segments L6-S1. Lesions of the motor component of the sciatic nerve
(distal to the pelvis) may result in hypotonia, paralysis, and atrophy of the flexors of the
stifle, tarsus, and digits, as well as of the extensors of the hip, tarsus, and digits. With
sciatic lesions, pelvic limb withdrawal-flexor reflexes will be reduced to absent (Video
241.25

). Dogs and cats can walk with sciatic nerve paralysis, but the tarsus is

typically “dropped,” or closer to the ground than normal, on the affected side (tibial
dysfunction) and the paw is often misplaced on the dorsal surface (peroneal
dysfunction); however, the limb can support weight if the femoral nerve is intact.
Sensory branches of the peroneal and tibial nerves innervate the dorsal and plantar
surfaces of the pelvic limb paw, respectively. The saphenous nerve (branch of the
femoral entering the spinal cord at L4-L6) innervates the medial aspect of the paw.
Therefore, animals with a severely contused sciatic nerve typically maintain sensation to
the medial aspect of the paw. If the medial surface of the paw is stimulated in a pet with
a pure sciatic injury, the animal will flex the hip because of intact innervation of the

iliopsoas muscle, but the stifle, tarsus, and digits will not flex. Therefore, both the medial
and lateral surfaces of the pelvic limb paw should be tested for the withdrawal-flexor
reflex and also for nociception.

Biceps and Triceps Reflexes
In the thoracic limb, the biceps and triceps reflexes often can be elicited in relaxed pets
that are in lateral recumbency. The clinician should place a finger on and tap the distal
ends of both biceps and brachialis muscles at the level of the elbow. A normal response is
slight flexion of the elbow. The musculocutaneous nerve mediates the biceps reflex
through spinal cord segments C6-C8. The triceps reflex is elicited by lightly tapping the
tendon of insertion of the triceps muscle proximal to the olecranon. This causes slight
extension of the elbow. The radial nerve mediates the triceps reflex through spinal cord
segments C7-T2.

Crossed Extensor Reflex
A crossed extensor reflex consists of extension of the contralateral limb when pressure is
applied to the base of a toenail during evaluation of the withdrawal-flexor reflex.
Although typically abnormal and indicative of UMN disease, normal dogs occasionally
have crossed extensor reflexes. To avoid voluntary extension of the contralateral limb as
a response to the noxious stimulus, the withdrawal-flexor reflex should be elicited with a
mild pinch while the opposite limb is observed.

Perineal Reflex
The perineal reflex is elicited by stimulation of the anus with a mild, noxious stimulus.
The anal sphincter and tail should be observed for contraction and flexion, respectively.
The perineal reflex is mediated by branches of the sacral and caudal segments of the
spinal cord through the pudendal nerve.

Cutaneous Trunci Reflex
This reflex is observed as a contraction of the cutaneous trunci muscle in response to
mild stimulation of the dorsal skin of the trunk. It can be elicited from the thoracic and
most of the lumbar region. Regional segmental spinal nerves carry sensory impulses
(Video 241.27

) into the spinal cord, where they are relayed cranially to spinal cord

segment C8. At this level, a synapse occurs on the LMNs of both lateral thoracic nerves
that innervate the cutaneous trunci muscle. This reflex may require multiple attempts to
elicit it; rarely, normal dogs and cats manifest no reflex. This reflex may be particularly
useful in diagnosing the level of a transverse thoracolumbar spinal cord lesion or for
monitoring a progressive spinal cord injury (e.g., ascending or descending
myelomalacia). Typically, the reflex is preserved for one to two vertebral bodies caudal to
the level of the spinal cord lesion.

Nociception (Pain Perception)
In recumbent animals, the clinician may apply a noxious stimulus to a digit (Video
241.28

). This generates afferent impulses that enter the spinal cord via peripheral

nerves and associated dorsal nerve roots that are relayed to bilateral tracts in the lateral

funiculi of the spinal cord. These tracts ascend the spinal cord and continue through the
medulla, pons, and midbrain to specific nuclei in the thalamus for relay to somatic
sensory areas of the cerebral cortex. A positive response is evidenced by vocalization,
turning of the head, or dilation of the pupils when the impulses reach the thalamus or
cerebrum.
Although several grading schemes for spinal cord injury differentiate between
superficial and deep pain perception, this can be extremely challenging and is not
typically necessary. However, it is critical to differentiate nociception from the
withdrawal component of the withdrawal-flexor reflex (see earlier). Animals with
transverse spinal cord lesions maintain the withdrawal reflex and limb withdrawal
without reaction should not be mistaken for intact nociception.

CRANIAL NERVES (CNs; ch. 249)
It is important to develop a systematic method for evaluation of the CNs. This
component of the neurologic examination is ideally performed with a dog or cat that is
cooperative. The clinical signs associated with CN dysfunction are summarized in Table
241.1.

Vision and Pupillary Light Responses (II, III, VII)
Menace Response
The menace response is the most reliable test for vision assessment in animals. It is a
learned response that may not be present until 10 to 12 weeks of age in puppies and
kittens; tracking of moving objects may be a helpful substitute in such young animals.
The menace response requires a functional optic nerve, optic tract (diencephalon), and
optic radiation to the occipital cortex, as well as the efferent pathway that includes the
facial neurons. A functional cerebellum also is required for the menace response.1 The
majority of the visual pathway caudal to the optic chiasm is contralateral to the eye being
tested. With one of the animal’s eyes covered, the clinician should make a menacing
gesture toward the open eye (with careful attention not to touch or stimulate the pet with
air currents!) (Video 241.29

).

A normal menace response is manifested as complete eyelid closure. Eyelid closure is
dependent on normal facial nerve innervation of the orbicularis oculi muscle. If the
menace is absent or delayed, the eyelids must be assessed for their ability to close by
eliciting the palpebral reflex (

Video 241.30). If facial paralysis is present, eyeball

retraction, elevation of the third eyelid, and head retraction may help in the assessment
of vision in the absence of eyelid closure (Video 241.31

). Alternatively, the patient’s

ability to navigate an obstacle course can be evaluated.

Pupillary Light Response
Following evaluation of the menace responses, the clinician should evaluate pupil size
and pupillary light responses (PLRs) (Video 241.32
symmetry (Video 241.33

). Pupils should be assessed for

) in ambient light and a dark room. A bright light source

should then be directed into each eye individually. Normal pets have rapid constriction
of the pupil into which the light is directed (direct PLR) and the opposite pupil also
should constrict (indirect or consensual PLR). The indirect response occurs because the
majority of the optic nerve fibers cross at the optic chiasm and again at the level of the
pretectal nucleus, stimulating the parasympathetic oculomotor nuclei bilaterally.
In addition to optic and oculomotor nerve lesions, there are several possible
localizations for PLR deficits (Table 241.2). If a direct PLR is not elicited in one eye, the
clinician should direct the light as close to that eye as possible and move the light to all
aspects of the ocular fundus. If no response is present, the clinician should swing the
light to the responsive pupil and the nonresponsive pupil should be assessed for
constriction. If nonresponse is the result of an ocular or optic nerve lesion, it will
constrict when light is directed into the contralateral eye (e.g., positive indirect PLR).
Such testing may need to be repeated multiple times to differentiate between an
ocular/optic and oculomotor nerve problem.

Palpebral Fissure and Third Eyelid Symmetry (III, V, Sympathetic
Nerves)
The clinician should observe the palpebral fissures for size and symmetry. A reduced
fissure size (ptosis) may be due to dysfunction of CN III (oculomotor) with secondary
paresis of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle, dysfunction of CN V (mandibular
branch of trigeminal nerve) with secondary atrophy of the masticatory muscles causing

enophthalmos (Video 241.34

), or sympathetic dysfunction with loss of orbitalis

smooth muscle tone. Atrophy of the masticatory muscles or sympathetic dysfunction
both may result in third eyelid elevation.

Eyeball Position and Movement (III, IV, VI)
While examining the head, the clinician should assess whether or not each eye is in a
central position within the orbit, which requires normal function of the peripheral and
central components of the vestibular system; CN III (oculomotor), IV (trochlear), and VI
(abducent); and the extraocular muscles that they innervate. Ventrolateral strabismus is
associated with CN III dysfunction, a medial strabismus with CN VI dysfunction, and
eyeball extorsion with CN IV dysfunction. CN IV dysfunction in cats causes a lateral
rotation of the dorsal aspect of the pupil, which cannot be recognized on external ocular
examination in dogs because their pupils are round. In dogs, fundic examination is
required and would show lateral deviation of the retinal vein.

Vestibular Function (VIII)
Physiologic nystagmus (oculocephalic or oculovestibular response) is evaluated by
moving the head in a horizontal plane from side to side (Video 241.35

) (ch. 248).

This stimulates CN VIII to relay impulses to the brainstem, on to the vestibular nuclei
and the medial longitudinal fasciculus, and finally to abducent and oculomotor neurons
for abduction and adduction of the eyeball, respectively.

Strabismus and nystagmus commonly are associated with dysfunction of the
vestibular system. A positional (e.g., with neck extension), ventrolateral strabismus
commonly is associated with vestibular disease. Nystagmus is an involuntary oscillation
of the eyeball (Video 241.6

). Resting (spontaneous) nystagmus is continual and

observed when the head is in any position, whereas positional nystagmus is seen only
when the head is held in certain positions. The latter often is seen in patients that have
accommodated for lesions in the vestibular system. Occasionally, positional nystagmus
can be elicited in compensated vestibular patients placed on their backs with their head
and neck extended.

Facial and Trigeminal Nerve Function (V, VII)
The clinician should evaluate the palpebral reflex by gently touching the medial and
lateral canthi of the eyes (Videos 241.30 and 241.31

). A normal response is an

immediate, complete closure of the palpebral fissure. Sensory branches (ophthalmic—
medially, maxillary—laterally) of CN V mediate the afferent arm of the palpebral reflex,
and the palpebral branch of CN VII mediates the efferent motor arm. The clinician also

should assess the symmetry of the face. A lip or ear droop (Video 241.31

) or

unilateral salivation suggests CN VII dysfunction. Occasionally, the nasal philtrum will
be deviated toward overstimulated facial muscles due to facial tetany, and this
appearance could mimic facial nerve paralysis of the contralateral side.
To evaluate the mandibular branch of CN V, the clinician should evaluate the
temporalis and masseter muscles for size and symmetry. With unilateral mandibular
nerve dysfunction (e.g., CN V sheath neoplasm), no loss of jaw function will be
appreciable but profound muscle atrophy may be present (Video 241.34

). With

bilateral mandibular nerve dysfunction (e.g., idiopathic trigeminal neuritis), the patient
may have a dropped jaw and drool excessively (Video 241.36

). Mandibular paralysis

may be accompanied by facial hypalgesia depending on the extent of involvement of the
ophthalmic and maxillary sensory nerve branches of CN V.
Trigeminal sensory function is most easily evaluated by testing nasal sensation. The
clinician should gently touch the medial aspect of the nasal mucosa with the tip of a pen
or closed hemostats (Video 241.37

). Normal patients will quickly pull their head

away (stoic patients occasionally will not object). This test evaluates two neural
pathways: the ipsilateral branch of the ophthalmic branch of CN V that innervates the
nasal mucosa and the nociceptive pathways that project to the contralateral thalamus
and somesthetic cerebral cortex. Therefore, nasal hypalgesia must be interpreted in light
of the remainder of the neurologic examination. It may indicate an ipsilateral trigeminal
nerve lesion or a contralateral prosencephalic lesion (Video 241.10

).

Tongue and Laryngeal-Pharyngeal Function (IX, X, XII)
The clinician may attempt to trigger the gag-reflex to simultaneously evaluate CN IX, X,
and XII (ch. 47). Upon opening the patient’s mouth, the tongue first should be
evaluated for atrophy and movement to assess CN XII function. Depending on patient
cooperation, the clinician then may insert a finger through the oral cavity into the
oropharynx and laryngopharynx. Occurrence of the reflex causes oropharyngeal
contraction, with expression of air (a mechanism intended to expel material in the
pharynx) that produces a typical retching sound. The muscle tone and gag can be
evaluated to assess pharyngeal branches of CN IX and X. Clinical utility of this test is
limited due to the variability in normal responses. Dysphagia (chs. 47 and 259) is a
more reliable indicator of CN IX and X dysfunction.

NEUROANATOMIC DIAGNOSIS
After performing the complete neurologic examination, the clinician should attempt to
make a neuroanatomic diagnosis to localize the lesion to one of five major regions of the
nervous system: (1) prosencephalon (cerebrum and/or thalamus); (2) mid- to caudal
brainstem (midbrain, medulla, pons); (3) cerebellum; (4) spinal cord; or (5)
LMN/neuromuscular system. Neurologic signs associated with lesions in each of these
regions are tabulated (Tables 241.3 to 241.6).
The clinician initially should attempt to reconcile all neurologic deficits with a single
lesion. If a single lesion cannot explain all signs, the neuroanatomic diagnosis is likely to

be multifocal or diffuse. After localizing the lesion to one of the five major regions of the
CNS or PNS, a more precise localization should be determined (e.g., side of lesion;
specific anatomic segments affected: C1-C5, C6-T2, etc.). As mentioned previously, an
accurate neuroanatomic diagnosis provides critical information for establishing an
appropriate differential diagnosis and for selecting and interpreting diagnostic tests.

PROSENCEPHALON
Although commonly used as an embryologic term to denote the area of brain composed
of the telencephalon (cerebral hemispheres) and diencephalon (epithalamus, thalamus,
and hypothalamus), this large region is a key for clinical establishment of a
neuroanatomic diagnosis. Because of overlap in clinical signs associated with cerebral
and thalamic disease, lesions affecting these areas cannot be reliably differentiated.
When neurologic signs suggest cerebro-thalamic (“forebrain”) disease, a prosencephalic
neuroanatomic diagnosis is made.
Animals with prosencephalic disease often have a history of generalized or partial
seizures and/or abnormal behavior (Table 241.3). Typical behavior changes include
depression (due to lesions of the ARAS), lethargy, disorientation, loss of training,
increased aggression or docility, irritability, hysterical or maniacal behavior, head
pressing, propulsive pacing or circling (Video 241.38

). Abnormalities in autonomic

and endocrine function (thirst, appetite, temperature, electrolyte and water balance) and
sleep patterns also may be present.
Although seizures, behavioral, and autonomic/neuroendocrine changes support a
prosencephalic neuroanatomic diagnosis, these abnormalities rarely help to lateralize
the lesion to one side of the cerebrum or thalamus. Animals with prosencephalic lesions
commonly manifest visual, sensory (facial/nasal hypalgesia), and postural reaction
deficits, all contralateral to the side of the lesion (Video 241.10

). Despite having

postural reaction deficits (a true “CP” deficit), animals with prosencephalic disease
typically have a normal gait (a transient gait deficit may be present with peracute lesions
such as a cerebrovascular accident [ch. 243]). The gait is normal with prosencephalic
lesions because the critical UMNs responsible for gait generation in domestic species
(rubrospinal and reticulospinal tracts) are spared, being located more caudally in the
midbrain, pons, and medulla.
An unusual phenomenon known as the adversive (hemi-neglect or hemi-inattention)
syndrome occurs sometimes with unilateral prosencephalic lesions. With this syndrome,
the pet “ignores” all sensory input perceived from its environment that is contralateral to
the prosencephalic lesion. The pet may circle propulsively or eat out of one side of a bowl
(ipsilateral to the lesion).

BRAINSTEM
The brainstem is ventral to the two cerebral hemispheres and the cerebellum. Although
anatomically the diencephalon is the rostral extent of the brainstem, it is considered part
of the prosencephalic localization (above). A neuroanatomic diagnosis of “brainstem” is
used for denoting lesions that include the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata.
Functionally, the brainstem contains the paired CN nuclei, the regulatory centers for
consciousness (ARAS) and respiration, and descending motor and ascending sensory
pathways. Thus, CN abnormalities, behavioral changes, loss of key autonomic functions,
and a loss of strength and coordination may be present with brainstem disease (Table
241.4).
The brainstem connects the cerebral hemispheres to the spinal cord via ascending
sensory (GP) and descending motor pathways (UMNs). As with C1-C5 spinal cord
lesions, UMN tetraparesis/tetraplegia and GP deficits may accompany brainstem
disease. Because of the presence of vestibular nuclei in the pons and medulla, vestibular
ataxia may be present and superimposed upon GP ataxia (Video 241.7

).

Depending on the region of the mid- to caudal brainstem affected, dysfunction of CN
III-XII may be present (Tables 241.1 and 241.4). Lesions affecting the CN in the caudal
brainstem typically cause ipsilateral postural reaction deficits because of their impact on
the UMN and GP systems. The presence of CN abnormalities and normal postural
reactions suggests a peripheral cranial neuropathy (ch. 249); however, an early or
slowly compressive brainstem lesion is possible. If there is ambiguity in postural
reaction testing, a neurodiagnostic workup should be considered.

A head tilt, vestibular ataxia, nystagmus, and strabismus are seen commonly with
vestibular disease (Videos 241.6, 241.7, and 241.9

). However, these neurologic signs

rarely help the clinician to differentiate between central and peripheral vestibular
disease. This key point, together with other features of vestibular disease, are discussed
in detail in ch. 248.

CEREBELLUM
The cerebellum functions as a regulator rather than a primary initiator of motor activity.
It coordinates movements in relation to the animal’s posture, providing synergy of
muscular activity. Cerebellar disease produces a unique dysmetria characterized by an
inability to regulate the rate, range, and force of a movement (Video 241.8

).

Although a dog or cat with cerebellar disease may be incapacitated and unable to stand,
voluntary movements should be elicited and normal strength should be apparent.

Ambulatory animals with cerebellar ataxia typically manifest “bursty” hypermetric
movements in all ranges of motion. Voluntary movements typically are delayed in onset
and, once initiated, exaggerated. When the patient walks, the limbs usually are raised
excessively and returned forcefully to the ground with each step. Muscle tone commonly
is increased, and spinal reflexes may be normal to exaggerated. Although CP is
unaffected with cerebellar disease, postural reactions typically are delayed and
exaggerated. When the head of a pet with cerebellar disease is extended and then
support is withdrawn suddenly, a rebound phenomenon may be present in which the
head drops excessively in a ventral direction.

disorders (Video 241.40

) (ch. 42). Finally, it is noteworthy that cerebellar disease

may be associated with an ipsilateral (bilateral with diffuse cerebellar disease) menace
deficit. Although the cerebellum most commonly is affected diffusely (e.g., cerebellar
hypoplasia or abiotrophy), occasionally unilateral or focal cerebellar lesions (cerebellar
infarction or neoplasm) produce ipsilateral cerebellar signs (Videos 241.9 and 241.41
).

SPINAL CORD
A spinal cord segment is defined as a portion of the spinal cord that gives rise to one pair
(left and right) of spinal nerves. There are 8 cervical, 13 thoracic, 7 lumbar, 3 sacral, and
at least 2 caudal spinal cord segments in dogs and cats. Functionally, the spinal cord can
be divided into four neuroanatomic regions: cranial cervical (C1-C5), cervico-thoracic
(C6-T2), thoracolumbar (T3-L3), and lumbosacral (L4-S3).
The LMN cell bodies for the thoracic and pelvic limbs are located within the ventral
gray matter of the cervico-thoracic (C6-T2) and lumbosacral (L4-S3) intumescences,
respectively. The ascending (sensory) and descending (motor) pathways comprise the
white matter of the spinal cord and are located more superficially. With rare exceptions,
spinal cord lesions predictably result in a sequential loss of GP, then motor and bladder
function, and then nociception. Recovery of function typically occurs in the reverse
direction.
As discussed in the gait and posture section, above, spinal cord lesions typically
produce a combination of UMN and GP deficits in the limbs caudal to the level of the
lesion (Videos 241.3 and 241.4

). If the spinal cord lesion is in the cervicothoracic or

lumbosacral intumescence, it will produce LMN signs in the corresponding thoracic or
pelvic limbs, respectively. Spinal cord lesions may produce a combination of UMN and
LMN signs in thoracic or pelvic limbs (Video 241.4

). For example, a herniated disk

at the C6-C7 intervertebral disk space may cause a long-strided thoracic limb gait (UMN
sign) but reduced thoracic limb withdrawal reflexes (LMN sign). Ambulatory patients
with C6-T2 lesions typically have a disconnected, “two-engine” gait in which the thoracic
limbs are “short and choppy” (LMN sign) and pelvic limbs are long-strided (UMN sign)
with GP ataxia1 (Video 241.42

).

Establishing a neuroanatomic diagnosis that localizes the lesion to one of the four
spinal cord segments typically is straightforward and is based upon four potential
combinations of normal, LMN, and UMN signs that may be present in the thoracic and
pelvic limbs (Tables 241.7 to 241.10; Figure 241.1 and Table 241.6). However, there
are a few clinical scenarios that may create confusion with T3-L3 spinal cord disease.
These situations are considered below.
Thoracolumbar (T3-L3) spinal cord lesions typically spare the thoracic limbs and
∗

cause a combination of UMN signs and GP deficits in the pelvic limbs (Video 241.3

).

However, peracute T3-L3 lesions may produce a marked spasticity (increased tone) in
the thoracic limbs, a phenomenon referred to as the Schiff-Sherrington syndrome. It
results from disruption of ascending inhibitory axons arising from interneurons (border
cells) located in the dorsolateral border of the ventral gray column of spinal cord
segments L1-L7.1 These ascending interneurons exert an inhibitory influence on the
LMNs of the cervicothoracic intumescence, which may be lost with peracute, transverse
T3-L3 lesions. Postural reaction testing will discriminate between a severe C1-C5 lesion
and Schiff-Sherrington syndrome. Postural reactions will be delayed in the former
because of the involvement of the UMN and GP pathways, but will be normal in the
latter despite the presence of spasticity.
A second challenging clinical scenario is associated with acute T3-L3 lesions that
produce contradictory LMN signs (reduced spinal reflexes and hypotonia) in the pelvic
limbs. This situation commonly is accompanied by Schiff-Sherrington syndrome, and
the LMN signs in the pelvic limbs have been referred to as spinal shock. It is thought to
be secondary to a transient disconnection between the descending UMNs and the LMNs
of the lumbosacral intumescence.6 Although spinal shock can persist for weeks in
humans, it generally is transient (hours to days) in dogs and cats.

PERIPHERAL NERVOUS SYSTEM
Lower Motor Neuron/Neuromuscular System
The LMN unit consists of the nerve cell body in the ventral gray matter of the CNS,
ventral nerve root, peripheral nerve, and muscle. Disease of any component of this unit
will produce LMN signs. Normal strength depends not only on functional LMN unit, but
also on effective neuromuscular transmission via acetylcholine across the NMJ. Diseases
affecting neuromuscular transmission (e.g., myasthenia gravis, tick paralysis), so-called
junctionopathies (ch. 253), may produce LMN signs that are indistinguishable from
neuropathies and myopathies.
Because NMDs may mimic one another, the neurologic examination rarely confirms
the exact component of the LMN unit that is affected. The clinician may require ancillary
tests (serum creatine kinase [ch. 66] and aspartate aminotransferase [ch. 65],
edrophonium testing, acetylcholine receptor antibody titer [ch. 253], electrodiagnostics
[ch. 111], and/or nerve and muscle biopsies [ch. 110]) to further localize the problem to
the nerve, muscle, or NMJ. The LMN unit may be affected diffusely or individual
peripheral or CNs may be affected. When CN deficits (e.g., facial paresis) are present,
these must be interpreted with other neurologic findings in order to differentiate
neuromuscular disease from a brainstem disorder.
Neuromuscular weakness is characterized by flaccidity and depressed or absent spinal
reflexes. Postural reactions typically are normal with pure NMDs (no sensory nerve
involvement) (Video 241.2

), although the patient’s weight must be well supported

during assessment or the patient may fail postural testing on account of weakness.
Ambulatory patients with pure NMDs typically have a “short and choppy” gait without

ataxia because GP is unaffected (Videos 241.1 and 241.2

). Exercise intolerance may

be the only abnormality present in some patients with NMDs.

An important exception to the classic “short and choppy” pattern of neuromuscular
disease is the pelvic limb gait associated with sciatic dysfunction in dogs and cats that
have polyneuropathies. Because sciatic dysfunction does not affect weight bearing, the
pelvic limb gait is not short-strided. Despite being a LMN problem, an exaggerated
pelvic limb gait is present in which the animal repeatedly initiates the gait from a
plantigrade position and “flings” its pelvic limbs forward (Video 241.26

). This

should not be confused with T3-L3 or cerebellar hypermetria. Hip flexion is exaggerated
due to the lack of antagonistic contraction of the caudal thigh muscles. Patients with
polyneuropathies also may have delayed postural reactions because of involvement of
the sensory nerve fibers in the peripheral neuropathy.
In some NMDs (e.g., polyneuropathies), involvement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve
may lead to a change in, or loss of, voice (dysphonia) and increased inspiratory noise
(stridor) (ch. 214). The development of megaesophagus in various NMDs may cause
regurgitation (ch. 259), often with accompanying aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217). The
NMDs also carry the risk of hypoventilation due to involvement of the respiratory
muscles. Finally, changes in muscle mass may vary from severe neurogenic atrophy (e.g.,
brachial plexus avulsion) to “pseudohypertrophy,” which accompanies myopathies (e.g.,
muscular dystrophy) (Table 241.11).

Peripheral Sensory Nerves
Sensory afferent nerve fibers run together with the LMNs within the peripheral nerves.
Sensory axons have a cell body in the dorsal nerve root ganglion or in homologous
ganglia of CNs. A cutaneous region innervated by afferent nerve fibers from a spinal or
CN is called a dermatome. Dermatomes can overlap, and the part of a dermatome
innervated by only one spinal or CN is called an autonomous zone. Diseases exclusively
affecting the sensory system are rare (e.g., sensory neuropathies,
ganglioradiculoneuritis) and they are characterized by variable sensory deficits ranging
from hypalgesia to analgesia of various body parts.

MULTIFOCAL LOCALIZATIONS AND DIFFUSE
CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM DISORDERS
With various neurologic disorders, the deficits cannot be explained by a single lesion.
For example, a Pug with necrotizing meningoencephalitis might manifest both
prosencephalic (seizures) and vestibular (head tilt, vestibular ataxia) signs. In this
scenario, a multifocal, intracranial localization is made.
Multifocal localizations are not analogous to disorders that affect the CNS diffusely, in
which the majority of the neural axis is affected. The most common neurologic sign
associated with diffuse CNS disease is a fine, whole body tremor (Video 241.40

) (ch.

42). Whole body tremors should not be confused with the brief, intention tremors of the
head, neck, or torso that may be present with cerebellar disease (Videos 241.8, 241.39)
. The differential list for a diffuse CNS localization is relatively narrow and includes
dysmyelinogenesis, diffuse meningitis (idiopathic tremor syndrome [ch. 42],
disseminated granulomatous meningoencephalomyelitis [ch. 242], infectious
meningitis) and various systemic intoxications (ch. 133).

There are many inflammatory, infectious, and degenerative (ch. 244) diseases
that produce multifocal central nervous system (CNS) signs and often
simultaneous systemic disease. Initially, some of these diseases may start with

focal CNS signs, but often progress to affect other areas. Multifocal or diffuse
involvement of the brain refers to clinical evidence that more than one functional
division of the brain is affected by a disease process (ch. 241). For example, a dog
with both forebrain and vestibular dysfunction would be considered to have
multifocal or diffuse involvement of the brain. A diffuse localization suggests a
more generalized and symmetric constellation of deficits, whereas multifocal
represents more asymmetric deficits and multiple abnormalities. There are several
implications of multifocal encephalopathy. In general, inflammatory disorders,
multifocal/metastatic neoplasia, and vascular infarction are highest on the
differential diagnosis list for dogs and cats with multifocal encephalopathy.
Patients with metabolic or toxic disorders are more likely to exhibit diffuse
encephalopathy. Although symmetric forebrain signs suggest a diffuse disease
process, these signs do not rule out focal disease. Focal disease can produce
multifocal/diffuse signs due to several mechanisms: (1) an extensive mass that
invades more than one region of the brain; (2) edema surrounding a focal mass,
producing a mass effect; (3) obstruction by a brain lesion of normal cerebrospinal
fluid (CSF) flow, leading to accumulations of ventricular CSF (e.g., obstructive
hydrocephalus associated with a caudal fossa lesion); and (4) lesions affecting one
area of the brain that has influence over a separate region of the brain (e.g.,
brainstem or thalamus and involvement of the ascending reticular activating
system).
This chapter reviews relevant clinical features of the more common
multifocal/diffuse brain disorders encountered in dogs and cats. Disorders that
commonly lead to multifocal/diffuse brain dysfunction are summarized according
to the DAMNITV (degenerative, anomalous, metabolic, neoplastic, nutritional,
inflammatory [noninfectious], infectious, toxins, trauma, vascular) scheme as
shown Box 242.1. This chapter discusses general features of inflammatory brain
diseases and the commonly recognized causes of infectious and noninfectious
encephalitis. There are few clinical features that are unique to CNS inflammatory
diseases, which poses a diagnostic dilemma for the clinician. A common
misconception is that dogs with inflammatory diseases of the CNS are systemically
ill but often such patients have no extraneural signs.1 Although the presence of
multifocal signs is considered a hallmark, two-thirds of dogs with CNS
inflammatory disease have neurologic deficits caused by a focal lesion.1

INFECTIOUS DISORDERS OF THE BRAIN
OVERVIEW
Etiology and Pathogenesis
Neuroinfectious diseases are a major cause of morbidity and mortality.
Encephalitis is defined as inflammation of the brain parenchyma with associated
neurologic dysfunction. Encephalitis may be the only neurologic manifestation of
infection, or may occur in association with meningitis, myelitis, radiculitis, or
neuritis.
Infections of the brain may result in neurologic dysfunction by producing a
mass effect (i.e., abscess) or release of toxins and inflammatory mediators. A
major cause of neurologic deficits is thought to be the secondary inflammation
induced by the infectious agent (Figure 242.1). The intense encephalitis and
meningitis are the direct result of activation of the host’s inflammatory pathways
by the microorganism or its products. When pathogens enter the CNS, they may
replicate rapidly and liberate active cell wall- or membrane-associated
components. These potent inflammatory substances can stimulate astrocytes,
microglia and cerebral capillary endothelia to produce cytokines and other
inflammatory mediators. The cytokines activate adhesion-promoting receptors on
endothelial cells and leukocytes, attracting neutrophils to these sites.
Subsequently, the leukocytes penetrate the intercellular junctions of the capillary
endothelium and release proteolytic products and oxygen free radicals. These
events result in injury to the endothelium and alter blood-brain barrier (BBB)
permeability. This leads to vasogenic and cytotoxic edema. The high protein and
cell counts increase the viscosity of the CSF, which contributes to generation of
interstitial edema. All of these inflammatory events, if they are not modulated
promptly, eventually cause alteration of CSF dynamics, brain metabolism and
cerebrovascular autoregulation. Neuronal injury and apoptosis ensue through
mediators such as reactive oxygen species, metalloproteases and excitatory amino
acids.

FIGURE 242.1 Pathophysiological cascade in infectious
encephalitis. BBB, Blood-brain barrier; CBF, cerebral blood
flow; CSF, cerebrospinal fluid.

Clinical Findings
History-taking (ch. 2) and the neurologic examination (ch. 241) for patients with
suspected infectious encephalitis should focus on several factors that are helpful in
establishing the differential diagnosis. In terms of temporal progression, viral and
bacterial encephalitis typically present acutely to subacutely, whereas chronic
presentations should prompt consideration of other microorganisms such as
fungi. Causative agents vary depending on host factors, seasonality, and exposure
to vectors and animals. Geographic region and the travel history can suggest
certain endemic organisms. Comorbidities may increase the risk of primary or
opportunistic infections. Prodromal symptoms or systemic manifestations of
infections may provide a useful clue that favors infectious rather than
noninfectious cause of encephalitis.
The neurologic examination should include assessment of level of
consciousness, mentation, seizures, signs of meningitis or increase in intracranial
pressure along with evaluation of cranial nerves and limbs for other focal
neurologic features. Animals with meningitis or encephalomyelitis may appear
systemically ill, lethargic, and reluctant to eat. Dogs and cats often have rigidity
with signs of generalized pain that seems worse in the cervical spinal region.

Hyperesthesia is elicited on palpation of the head and vertebral column. Signs of
generalized pain may be evident as if the patient is “walking on eggshells.”

Diagnosis
The diagnostic approach to a patient with infectious encephalitis should include
CSF studies (Table 242.1; ch. 109), brain imaging (ch. 112) and targeted testing
of serum and CSF (ch. 184).2 CSF analysis (ch. 109) is considered the most
useful test for CNS inflammatory disease, though pleocytosis is not always
observed, and, when present, is of variable degree.1,3,4 In some cases, organisms
can be found in CSF. Infection is still possible when no organisms are seen, and
such cases cannot be properly diagnosed using CSF findings alone.1,3 When
organisms are not found, bacterial or fungal culture or virus isolation in CSF can
be useful.5 All viral diseases must stay in the differential when mononuclear
pleocytosis is present and no other cause is found.1
Many case reports and case series reports detail CSF findings in infectious
diseases such as bacterial encephalitis,6 rabies (ch. 202),7 canine distemper (ch.
204),8 cryptococcosis (ch. 207),9 coccidioidomycosis (ch. 208),10 aspergillosis
(ch. 211),11 neosporosis (ch. 197),12-15 granulocytic ehrlichiosis (ch. 193),16
protothecosis (ch. 262),17-19 and cuterebriasis (ch. 255).20 Reviews cover the
diagnosis of several fungal diseases that may affect the CNS.21,22 In a retrospective
study of 62 cats with clinical signs of CNS disease and CSF findings indicating
inflammation, a presumptive diagnosis based on a combination of clinical signs,
clinicopathologic data and ancillary diagnostic tests was made in 63%.23 CSF
findings used alone were useful only for the diagnosis of feline infectious
peritonitis (FIP, ch. 200), cryptococcosis (ch. 207), lymphoma (ch. 322) and
trauma (ch. 246). The type of inflammatory pattern was helpful only in cats with
lymphoma, all of which had mononuclear inflammation. Mixed inflammation was
the most common pattern at 48.8% of cases, but this pattern was of little aid in
establishing an etiologic diagnosis.23
Combining CSF findings with cross-sectional imaging, histopathologic
examination of tissues, and/or other ancillary testing is often required to
determine the cause of inflammatory disorders, and sometimes a cause is not
determined.1,3,4,24 Lamb and colleagues determined that ∼25% of brain magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) studies of dogs with an inflammatory CSF revealed no
abnormalities, emphasizing that a normal brain MRI does not rule out CNS
inflammatory disease.4 An abnormal brain MRI in animals with CNS
inflammatory disease can reveal T2 and fluid attenuation inversion recovery
(FLAIR) hyperintensity, parenchymal and meningeal enhancement, and extent of
meningoencephalitis. Immunologic, microbial culture and susceptibility testing,
and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing have been useful in detecting various
infectious agents. Identification of an immune response in the CNS would suggest

infection. Defining a ratio between serum and CSF IgG responses may eliminate
interpretation of passive transfer of antibodies secondary to another disease that
compromises the BBB. The IgG index is calculated as (CSF IgG/serum IgG) ×
(serum albumin/CSF albumin); values ≥ 0.272 suggest increased intrathecal IgG
production.
