Treatment
Medical therapy is the most common form of treatment that is indicated for CNS
infectious diseases. Anticonvulsant therapy is indicated when seizures are a
clinical sign (chs. 45 and 247). Osmotherapy is administered when signs suggest
increased intracranial pressure (chs. 44, 125). In addition, short-term use of
corticosteroids may mitigate the effects of secondary inflammation. Effective
therapy for CNS infections depends on causal identification and selection of the
appropriate antimicrobial agent. Selection of the appropriate antimicrobial agent

is based on two principles: 1) it must be effective against the microorganism
without severely injuring the patient; and 2) it must be delivered to and penetrate
the BBB. The presence of efflux pumps located in the BBB makes it impossible for
some drugs to reach effective therapeutic levels within the CNS. In some cases,
surgical decompression and brain abscess or granuloma removal may be indicated
on an emergency basis.25

BACTERIAL
Etiology and Pathogenesis
Bacterial encephalitis/meningitis usually follows invasion of the bloodstream by
organisms that have colonized mucosal surfaces. Subsequently, organisms
penetrate vulnerable sites of the BBB (e.g., choroid plexus and cerebral capillaries)
and reach the subarachnoid space. The most common bacteria associated with
meningoencephalomyelitis based on isolation are Staphylococcus spp.,
Streptococcus, Klebsiella, Pasteurella spp., Actinomyces spp., Nocardia spp.,
Escherichia coli, and various anaerobic species including Peptostreptococcus,
Fusobacterium, and Bacteroides spp.6 Gram-negative infections are most
common, and single- versus multiple-organism infections are equally likely.6
Meningitis and abscess formation can result from either direct extension of an
infection (e.g., otitis interna), bite wound trauma, penetration of a foreign body, or
by hematogenous spread of infection (e.g., bacterial endocarditis). Severe head
trauma with a skull fracture, CSF rhinorrhea, or both, can lead to meningitis (ch.
246). Bacteria can be inoculated directly into the CSF by congenital dural defects
(dermal sinus or meningomyelocele), neurosurgical procedures (such as CSF
diversion shunts), penetrating wounds, or extension from a suppurative
parameningeal focus.

Clinical Findings
Dogs and cats of any age, breed or sex may develop bacterial meningoencephalitis,
but it is more common in young to middle-aged animals.6 Clinical signs of
neurologic dysfunction are often acute and rapidly progressive. Fever and cervical
spinal hyperesthesia are considered classic features of bacterial
meningoencephalitis. Common neurologic signs include altered mentation, ataxia,
cranial nerve deficits, paresis and seizures.6

Diagnosis
A definitive diagnosis is dependent on examination and culture of CSF (ch. 109).
If an increase in intracranial pressure is suspected, CSF collection may increase
risk for brain herniation. Typically, brain MRI is first performed to identify brain
edema, obstructive hydrocephalus and a mass effect suggesting herniation. The
common CSF pattern is degenerate and toxic-appearing neutrophils and an

elevated protein concentration. The presence of intracellular bacteria confirms the
diagnosis. Still, when bacterial CNS infection is present, bacteria may not be seen
cytologically on CSF and culture is often negative.6,26 Nonetheless, a retrospective
study of dogs with necropsy-confirmed bacterial meningoencephalomyelitis
indicated CSF analysis is the most consistent test for finding an abnormality and
that in combination with a thorough clinical workup, it can provide a strong index
of diagnostic suspicion.6 Another retrospective study indicated bacterial
encephalitis is highly probable based on marked CSF neutrophilic pleocytosis and
a rapidly declining clinical course.1
A complete blood count (CBC) and serum biochemistry results may indicate
sepsis. Serum biochemistry profiles were abnormal in 75% of cases, revealing
increased enzyme activities suggesting liver damage, increased glucose
concentration and electrolyte abnormalities.6 Blood and urine cultures may yield
positive results, but these are often negative in confirmed cases of bacterial
meningoencephalitis.
Brain MRI may be helpful in diagnosing mass lesions, ventriculitis or
obstructive hydrocephalus. An abscess is typically hypointense with a hypointense
capsule on T1-W contrast images, but findings can mimic neoplasia and vascular
accidents.27 The FLAIR sequence on imaging will increase the conspicuity of
ventriculitis.

Treatment
Antimicrobial therapy is the most important aspect of management and is ideally
guided by antimicrobial culture and susceptibility results (ch. 140). Since
antibacterial treatment of CNS infections should be initiated as soon as possible
and co-infections with multiple bacterial species are as common as singleorganism infections, empirical treatment with broad spectrum antibiotics or
combinations of compounds that can cross the BBB and attain adequate CNS
concentrations are rational therapeutic options.28 Recommendations for the
treatment of bacterial infections of the CNS in cats and dogs are often derived
from case reports or studies with small sample sizes, or are extrapolated from
human medicine. The best evidence for their effectiveness against bacterial
meningitis relative to all other antimicrobials approved for dogs exists for
enrofloxacin, benzylpenicillin, and ampicillin, while evidence in cats is particularly
deficient.28 However, several case reports indicate a frequent selection of broadspectrum beta-lactams, fluoroquinolones, trimethoprim-sulfadiazine,
metronidazole and clindamycin for CNS infections of dogs and cats, with varying
degrees of success.29-32 Unfortunately, a high mortality rate is associated with
brain abscesses and bacterial meningoencephalomyelitis.1,6 The key to
successfully treating dogs and cats with bacterial meningoencephalitis is early
diagnosis and rapid, intensive therapy.

FUNGAL
Etiology and Pathogenesis
There is a wide variety of fungal organisms that may invade the CNS, including
Cryptococcus (ch. 207), Coccidioides (ch. 208), Blastomyces (ch. 209),
Histoplasma (ch. 209), Aspergillus (ch. 211) and the phaeohyphomycoses.
Cryptococcus neoformans is the most common fungal organism associated with
meningoencephalitis in dogs and cats. Mycotic infections of the CNS of dogs and
cats are rare, depending on geographic location. Fungal disease is typically
contracted by dogs and cats via inhalation of fungal spores or hematogenously.
Dogs and cats with fungal meningoencephalitis are often young to middle-aged.
Young German Shepherd Dogs are overrepresented for
aspergillosis.11 Cladophialophora spp. are neurotropic, usually fatal and
infrequently reported as case reports in dogs and cats.33
CNS fungal infections in small animals frequently present as multifocal
meningoencephalomyelitis, intracranial lesions that accompany sinonasal lesions,
ventriculitis, or solitary brain or spinal cord granulomas.22 In cryptococcosis, the
organisms gain access to the CNS through the cribriform plate to the olfactory
bulb or via hematogenous routes (ch. 207). Infiltration of the arachnoid villi by
yeasts is believed to lead to impaired flow of CSF and an increase in intracranial
pressure, resulting in altered level of consciousness and acute onset of neurologic
signs. Overt neurologic signs were the first sign of illness in 57% of 21 dogs with
CNS cryptococcosis.9 Ventriculitis is well-documented in canine blastomycosis,
with hallmark obstructive hydrocephalus and rapid neurologic decline.34 Fungal
dissemination through the CSF follows hematogenous brain infection.
Coccidioidomycosis causes CNS mass granulomas that can be mistaken for
neoplastic lesions (ch. 208). Coccidioides granulomas also occur at various sites
along the neuraxis, especially the frontal lobe or spinal cord. Solitary CNS
granulomas do occur also with blastomycosis and cryptococcosis.22

Clinical Findings
CNS signs result from meningitis or meningoencephalitis and are attributed to
lesion location. With multifocal signs, forebrain and vestibular deficits are
common. In sinonasal mycosis with intracranial extension (ch. 210), seizures and
forebrain signs are typical. Neurologic signs of CNS mycosis can be acutely
progressive or can be chronic, especially with cryptococcosis. Concurrent
extraneural involvement with respiratory and ocular signs is common. With
cryptococcosis, extraneural infection occurs around the head region (eyes, nasal
and frontal sinuses). Initial infection of the pulmonary system is more typical with
coccidioidomycosis. Dissemination of coccidioidomycosis and cryptococcosis to
the CNS in dogs usually involves the cerebrum.21,35 In coccidioidomycosis, a

sudden onset of generalized tonic-clonic seizures was the most common clinical
presentation.36,37

Diagnosis
Antemortem diagnosis can be difficult and is definitively made cytologically, by
biopsy or culture of an affected organ, or by CSF analysis. CSF analysis (ch. 109)
is variable and may yield a neutrophilic, eosinophilic, mononuclear, or mixed
pleocytosis. Protein concentration is typically elevated. Antigen tests are a
mainstay in ruling in or out CNS mycosis. Serologic testing by galactomannan
enzyme immunoassay, latex agglutination, agar gel immunodiffusion, or enzymelinked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) could support the diagnosis of CNS
mycosis.11,21,22,37 Systemic abnormalities are common in dogs and cats with
fungal disease. A minimum database to include CBC, serum biochemistry profile,
urinalysis, thoracic radiographs, ocular examination and abdominal ultrasound is
essential. Nonetheless, clinicopathologic abnormalities are often nonspecific.
Ophthalmic examination may show evidence of inflammatory (e.g., uveitis,
chorioretinitis) (ch. 13). Pulmonary lesions may be identifiable radiographically
in some cases of Histoplasma, Blastomyces and Coccidioides.
Immunocompromised animals (chs. 180, 227) can develop opportunistic fungal
infections. For example, cats with suspected or confirmed fungal
meningoencephalitis should be tested for feline leukemia virus (ch. 199) and
feline immunodeficiency virus (ch. 198).
Brain MRI (ch. 112) is recommended for dogs and cats with intracranial signs
to assist in diagnosis, therapeutic decisions and prognosis. However, abnormal
MRI findings are often nonspecific and may mimic vascular and neoplastic
lesions. In coccidioidomycosis, brain MRI lesions often manifest as single contrast
enhancing granulomas; a second variation involves diffuse, bilateral, symmetrical
lesions of the caudate nuclei and frontal lobe.35,37 Most Coccidioides granulomas
are T2 hyperintense and T1 isointense to hypointense. Extra-axial and intradural
lesions are strongly contrast enhancing, whereas intracranial intra-axial and
intramedullary granulomas show poor contrast enhancement.22 MRI features of
CNS cryptococcosis in dogs and cats are variable and include solitary or multifocal
mass lesions (granuloma, pseudocyst), diffuse and patchy meningeal
enhancement, and ependymal and choroid plexus enhancement.9

Treatment
The optimal treatment and the prognosis for canine and feline fungal
meningocephalitis are poorly defined. CNS involvement is a negative prognostic
indicator for mycoses, and in neurologic cryptococcosis, altered mental status
further decreases the prognosis.9,38 Evidence in CNS fungal disease being treated
with appropriate antifungal agents is lacking. Few antifungal drugs can cross the
BBB effectively (ch. 141). The cytosine analogue flucytosine (5-fluorocytosine)
and triazoles such as itraconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole or posaconazole, can

penetrate the BBB. Voriconazole is toxic to cats. Because fluconazole penetrates
the BBB and itraconazole does not, fluconazole 5 mg/kg PO q12h is the preferred
antifungal agent for CNS fungal infection. Combination therapy with liposomal
and lipid complex amphotericin B formulations has better CNS penetration and
less nephrotoxicity. Long-term duration (months) of treatment with antifungal
drugs is indicated. Treatment response may be monitored by serial antigen
quantification, MRI and CSF analysis.22 Short-term (1-2 weeks) use of
corticosteroids (prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day) significantly increases survival.9
Corticosteroids may mitigate perilesional edema and secondary inflammation
caused by fungal die-off. In 21 dogs and 26 cats with cryptococcosis, remissions of
> 1 year occurred in 32% of treated animals.9 Of 45 dogs with coccidioidomycosis,
82% were reported to be alive >1 year after diagnosis when treated with
fluconazole.37 Surgical resection of fungal granulomas offers the benefit of
definitive diagnosis and may be indicated for alleviating mass effect. However,
lesions are often intraparenchymal and not easily accessible surgically.

VIRAL
Etiology and Pathogenesis
Often the agent, host properties, and environment play roles in the pathogenesis
of viral encephalitis. The most frequently encountered viral infections of the brain
in dogs and cats in clinical practice are canine distemper virus (CDV,
Morbillivirus; ch. 204) and FIP virus (FIP coronavirus; ch. 200), respectively.
Other, less common causes of viral meningoencephalitides include rabies virus
(Lyssavirus; ch. 202), feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV, a lentivirus; see ch.
198), canine herpesvirus, feline panleukopenia virus (parvovirus; ch. 201), feline
Borna disease virus (BDV; ch. 206), pseudorabies (porcine herpesvirus; ch. 202)
and West Nile virus (flavivirus; ch. 204). Neurotropic viral diseases include
canine distemper (ch. 204), rabies, pseudorabies (ch. 9), canine herpes, and
West Nile viruses (ch. 9).
Neurotropic viral infections have a pathologic pattern reflective of direct viral
replication characterized by neuronal destruction, perivascular cuffing of
inflammatory cells and gliosis. This pattern leads to multifocal lesions
predominating in grey matter with fewer in white matter. Macrophage infiltration
is the predominant pattern for viral granulomatous inflammation. In FIP, lesions
in the CNS are induced by virus-antibody complexes in the vasculature causing
severe complement-mediated inflammation. Pyogranulomatous masses localize in
the meninges, choroid plexus, and ependyma, where they can cause obstructive
hydrocephalus. Viral diseases also can induce vasculitis, with damage to blood
vessels leading to hemorrhage and vasospasm induced ischemia (ch. 181). Viral
leukoencephalitis is a lesion pattern whereby nonsuppurative inflammation causes
destruction of the white matter.39 In chronic distemper encephalitis, perivascular
lymphocytic infiltration and secondary inflammatory responses result in

destruction of oligodendrocytes and myelin.40 In chronic feline leukemia virus
infection, cats may develop lesions distributed in the ventromedial and
dorsolateral white matter of the spinal cord.
Viral infections usually occur in outbreaks, with organisms being transmitted by
infected animals through the fecal-oral or respiratory route. Rabies virus is
transmitted from an animal bite; the virus travels via retrograde axonal transport
into the CNS and spreads trans-synaptically. CNS dissemination of the virus
causes acute encephalomyelitis with neuronal degeneration.

Clinical Findings
Prodromal systemic signs may or may not precede neurologic signs of viral
encephalitis. The onset of neurologic signs often is acute and rapidly progressive,
but signs also may be insidious. In CDV, the presence and pattern of illness
depend on the viral strain and the age and immunocompetence of the patient (ch.
204).41-44 Three neurologic forms of CDV have been recognized: 1) acute
encephalitis in young dogs; 2) chronic encephalomyelitis in mature dogs; and 3) a
rare syndrome, “old dog encephalitis.”45 Distemper in young dogs or dogs unable
to mount an immune response typically causes neurologic signs with or without
systemic signs. Focal seizures (“chewing-gum fits”) are common in the acute
encephalitis form.42 Mature dogs are more likely to develop chronic, multifocal
encephalomyelitis with a predilection for the white matter of the brainstem and
spinal cord.42 Neurologic signs often include progressive tetraparesis and
vestibular dysfunction. Myoclonus is common and usually affects the head or
limbs (

Videos 41.1, 41.2). Myoclonus is not pathognomonic for CDV and is

occasionally associated with other encephalitides (ch. 41).46 Dogs with old dog
encephalitis typically are older and show progressive signs of dementia, ataxia,
circling and visual deficits.47
In FIP (ch. 200), neurologic signs are observed in ∼30% of cats.48-51
Neurologic signs may occur alone or with systemic disease. These multifocal signs
include abnormal mentation (

Video 6.4) and behavior, seizures, ataxia,

cranial nerve deficits and tetra- or paraparesis.50-53 Central vestibular signs are
often present (ch. 248) along with other multifocal signs.50

Diagnosis
An antemortem diagnosis of CNS viral disease is often challenging to establish.
The interpretation of molecular testing results is evaluated in conjunction with
signalment, history, clinical signs and results of other diagnostic tests such as CSF
analysis and brain MRI. A definitive diagnosis is often made through
histopathological identification of an inflammatory pattern coupled with
immunohistochemical identification of the virus. CSF analysis (ch. 109) in viral

encephalitis cases typically demonstrates mild to moderate pleocytosis (usually
lymphocytic), sometimes with elevated protein, or it can be normal. However, in
cats with acute FIP, the CSF shows a distinctive neutrophilic pleocytosis with
marked elevation in protein concentration.54 A mixed cell pleocytosis with
lymphocytes, neutrophils, and mononuclear cells predominates in chronic FIP. In
a combined retrospective and prospective study of 27 cats with postmortemdiagnosed inflammatory disease, more than 75% were diagnosed with viral or
suspected viral disease.54 FIP was the cause in half of those cases, and no specific
virus was identified for the other half.
Brain MRI findings (ch. 112) in viral encephalitis can be normal or show a
nonspecific pattern that overlaps with the noninfectious encephalitides. In dogs
with acute CDV, T2 hyperintense lesions and loss of contrast between cerebellar
grey and white matter have been described.55 T2 hyperintensity in the forebrain
may also be postictal edema attributed to seizures often present in acute CDV.
Chronic distemper encephalitis should be considered in dogs with symmetric T2
hyperintensity of the cerebral cortical grey/white matter junction, the arbor vitae
and brainstem.56 MRI is a sensitive means of detecting neurologic FIP,
particularly in combination with signalment, clinical presentation and CSF
findings. Brain MRI findings in cats with FIP commonly show meningeal and
ependymal contrast enhancement, ventriculomegaly, syringomyelia and foramen
magnum herniation.52 If herniation is evident, CSF collection is not recommended
and a presumptive diagnosis of FIP is made based on MRI findings alone.

Treatment
Viral encephalitis often is managed by supportive therapies to alleviate clinical
signs. This includes management of cerebral edema, treatment of seizures (ch.
125), and mitigation of CNS inflammation with anti-inflammatory doses of
corticosteroids. Generally, the prognosis is poor in animals with viral encephalitis.
There is potential for effective treatment regimens for FIP involving inhibition of
viral replication. An antiviral nucleoside analogue, GS441524 was evaluated in 26
cats infected with FIP for a 12-week period and 25 were long-term survivors.57
Additionally, in a case series of cats with neurologic FIP, GS441524 showed
clinical efficacy and may result in clearance and long-term resolution.58 See ch.
200 for additional information on treatment of FIP.

PROTOZOAL (CH. 197)
Etiology and Pathogenesis
Protozoal infection of the CNS causes mononuclear cell infiltrates, which suggests
an immune-mediated component to the pathogenesis of disease. Intact tissue
cysts in neural structures are not generally associated with inflammation but
ruptured tissue cysts induce granulomatous inflammation.59 CNS toxoplasmosis

is most commonly seen following reactivation of latent bradyzoites within the
brain, spinal cord and/or skeletal muscles.60 Neosporosis in adult dogs causes
meningoencephalitis and necrosis that may predominantly affect the
cerebellum.15

Clinical Findings
Dogs and cats of any age can develop protozoal infections. In toxoplasmosis, CNS
involvement occurs in most clinically affected cats.60 However, overt neurologic
signs of toxoplasmosis occur in only 10% of infections. Typical signs reflect a
multifocal localization and include behavioral changes, seizures, ataxia, vestibular
dysfunction, hyperesthesia and paresis/paralysis.23,60-62 However, solitary spaceoccupying lesions attributed to granulomas have also been reported.63,64
Puppies with neosporosis are affected more severely by inflammation of the
muscles and nerve roots of the pelvic limbs, which cause progressive paraparesis
and muscle atrophy. These signs progress to rigid pelvic limb
hyperextension.13,65,66 CNS infection by Neospora caninum in adult dogs has
been reported to cause cerebellar ataxia, paresis, vestibular dysfunction, tremors
and seizures.12-15,66,67 Neurologic examination (ch. 241) reveals multifocal or
focal cerebellar localizations.14,15

Diagnosis
An antemortem diagnosis of neosporosis or toxoplasmosis usually relies on
clinical presentation, results of serologic assays, PCR or histologic examination of
tissues. If abnormal, CSF analysis (ch. 109) reveals a mixed cell pleocytosis with
neutrophilic, lymphocytic or eosinophilic predominance (Table 242.2). The
protein concentration is moderately elevated. Tachyzoites may be detected in
CSF.12,68 Brain MRI (ch. 112) may reveal cerebellar atrophy and/or multifocal
brain lesions.14,15 Because identification of protozoal organisms within tissues and
CSF is often difficult, a presumptive diagnosis of neosporosis or toxoplasmosis can
be made by combining appropriate clinical signs of disease and positive serologic
titers (immunoglobulin [Ig]G, IgM, ELISA) or presence of antibodies in CSF with
the exclusion of other etiologies. Neospora caninum and Toxoplasma gondii can
be differentiated by electron microscopy, immunohistochemistry, and PCR.59

Treatment
Treatment is usually aimed at controlling the inflammation and preventing further
progression of clinical signs. Generally, the prognosis is guarded. Antiprotozoal
treatment mainly affects the active dividing form of the tachyzoites with little

effect on the tissue-encysted bradyzoites.69 Clindamycin (12.5 mg/kg PO q12h),
trimethoprim/sulfonamide (15 mg/kg PO q12h) with pyrimethamine (1 mg/kg PO
q24h), alone or in combination, have been used effectively to treat
neosporosis.13,65 Treatment protocols are for 4 weeks or longer.15 Treatment of
clinically affected puppies is more likely to be successful if started early before
muscle fibrosis develops.70

INFLAMMATORY, NONINFECTIOUS
DISORDERS OF THE BRAIN
Clinical signs of noninfectious CNS inflammatory disorders are frequently very
similar to those of infectious CNS diseases and even those of neoplasia. Diagnosis
in the clinic relies predominantly on MRI, CSF analysis, and serological tests
designed to rule in or rule out infectious disease. In most cases, neoplastic lesions,
which are generally focal, are easily differentiated from inflammatory disease,
which are usually multifocal. Therefore, the major diagnostic decision is between
infectious and noninfectious disease. Currently in the industrialized world,
noninfectious inflammatory diseases of the CNS, which can affect the brain, spinal
cord and/or the meninges, are much more common.71
Noninfectious inflammatory disease of the CNS can be divided into a number of
subtypes based mainly on the specific regions of the CNS that are affected and the
specific histopathologic features (Figure 242.2). These include steroidresponsive meningitis-arteritis (SRMA), eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, and
meningoencephalomyelitis of unknown origin (MUO) to include granulomatous
meningoencephalomyelitis (GME), necrotizing encephalitis (NE) and others.
SRMA, which primarily affects the spinal cord (and meninges) and eosinophilic
meningoencephalitis have fairly distinct disease signatures based on clinical
presentation, CSF abnormalities and histopathologic findings.

STEROID-RESPONSIVE MENINGITISARTERITIS (SRMA)
SRMA, also termed necrotizing vasculitis, juvenile polyarteritis syndrome,
corticosteroid-responsive meningitis/meningomyelitis, aseptic suppurative
meningitis, panarteritis and pain syndrome has been reported in Beagles, Bernese
Mountain Dogs, Boxers, German Shorthaired Pointers, Wirehaired Pointing
Griffons, Border Collies, Jack Russell Terriers, Weimaraners, Golden Retrievers
and Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retrievers, but is noted and probably occurs in
other medium to large dog breeds.72,73 Affected dogs are often young adults (6-18
months old) but may be of any age, and are usually febrile and hyperesthetic, with
cervical spinal rigidity and anorexia. Neurological deficits can be seen in the
chronic form of this disease and rarely, severe motor dysfunction may result from

spontaneous bleeding into the subarachnoid space.74,75 Some dogs with immunemediated polyarthritis may show similar clinical signs to dogs with SRMA and
have concurrent meningitis (ch. 177).76 SRMA is more thoroughly reviewed in
ch. 250.

FIGURE 242.2 Diagram of the noninfectious inflammatory
diseases of the brain.

IDIOPATHIC EOSINOPHILIC
MENINGOENCEPHALITIS
Etiology and Pathogenesis
Idiopathic eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is sporadically reported in dogs and
has a distinct disease signature based on clinical presentation, CSF eosinophilia
and histopathologic features. CSF eosinophilia (total nucleated cell count [TNCC]
>3 cells/mcL with >20% eosinophils) can occur in a variety of infectious and
noninfectious conditions.77,78 In a small case series in dogs with CSF white blood
cell counts consisting of 21-98% eosinophils, 2 dogs had protozoal infection and 6
cases remained idiopathic.77 Eosinophils have also been reported in CSF with
Angiostrongylus and Baylisascaris infection, protothecosis, CDV, rabies,
cryptococcosis and bacterial and protozoal encephalitides, though sometimes not
in large enough percentages to constitute eosinophilic pleocytosis.78 Eosinophils
in the CNS are toxic to neurons and myelinated axons.79 On histopathologic
examination, brain tissue in dogs with idiopathic eosinophilic
meningoencephalitis is characterized by leptomeninges infiltrated by eosinophils,
lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages and locally extensive areas of
parenchymal loss.

Clinical Findings
Idiopathic eosinophilic meningoencephalitis has been reported more in young,
large dogs, and Rottweilers and Golden Retrievers appear to be
overrepresented.77,79,80 Clinical signs often are acute and progressive and consist
of both brain and spinal cord dysfunctions.80-83 Commonly reported neurologic
examination findings (ch. 241) include mentation changes, central visual deficits,
seizures, central vestibular dysfunction and general proprioceptive ataxia.

Diagnosis
Idiopathic eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is diagnosed in dogs when neurologic
disease is associated with a CSF eosinophilic pleocytosis (ch. 109) and by ruling
out infectious causes. Brain MRI findings (ch. 112) in dogs with idiopathic
eosinophilic meningoencephalitis have been variable.78,81,82 Lesion distributions
are bilateral and symmetric, confined to the cerebral cortex, and affect both the
pachymeninges and leptomeninges. Dogs often have an increased proportion of
eosinophils on the CBC.77,80-82

Treatment
Many cases of idiopathic eosinophilic meningoencephalitis respond to a long-term
tapering immunosuppressive dosage regimen of corticosteroids and sometimes
combined with other immunosuppressive drugs (chs. 144, 169, 227).77,78,81 The
neurologic status of some dogs deteriorates despite therapy.78,79

MENINGOENCEPHALOMYELITIS OF
UNKNOWN ORIGIN
Etiology and Pathogenesis
The term MUO has been introduced to encompass all clinically-diagnosed (i.e.,
dependent on advanced imaging and CSF analysis) cases of non-infectious
inflammatory CNS disease.71,84,85 Thus, this includes all the specific subtypes of
non-infectious inflammatory disease that can be identified histopathologically,
including GME and NE, but it does not include diseases without evidence of overt
CNS involvement (such as SRMA). The MUOs likely have a multifactorial
pathogenesis, including genetic and immune-mediated factors.71
GME is a distinct pathologic entity in which neuropathologic lesions consist of
whorling, perivascular disseminated or focal infiltrates of mononuclear cells in the
white matter and meninges of the brain and spinal cord.86-88 It appears that in
acute progressive disease the grey and white matter are equally affected, whereas
in more chronic GME, white matter is predominantly involved.86 Multifocal

granuloma formation can predominate in the cerebellum and brainstem, with
epithelioid cells in advanced stages; tryptase-positive mast cells have been found
in the perivascular cuffs, meninges and CNS parenchyma of dogs with acute-form
GME.87,89-91 Focal lesions represent a coalescence of a large number of
perivascular lesions, which commonly involve the pontomedullary region and
cerebral white matter.92
NE is a subtype of MUO that appears histopathologically distinct from GME
because of characteristic necrotic lesions in cerebral white or grey matter.
Histologic features typical of the NEs include non-suppurative
meningoencephalitis and bilaterally asymmetric cerebral necrosis. There are two
subtypes of this category of lesion: necrotizing meningoencephalitis (NME) and
necrotizing leukoencephalitis (NLE) and these appear to have considerable
overlap in breed association and lesion distributions. The hallmark of NME is
extensive necrosis, which varies in severity from neuronal necrosis and gliosis in
the early stage to gross cavitation of parenchyma in advanced disease.93,94
Lesions, dominated by plasma cells, lymphocytes and histiocytes, commonly
involve the leptomeninges, cerebral cortex and corona radiata and subcortical
white matter. They lead to loss of demarcation between grey and white matter.94
Lesions are most common in the cerebrum but have also been identified in the
brainstem and cerebellum of Pugs and other breeds.95,96
Histopathologically, NLE is characterized by nonsuppurative leukoencephalitis
with multiple necrotizing foci affecting the white matter of the forebrain and
brainstem with subsequent cavitary necrosis and prominent reactive gemistocytic
astrogliosis.97-100 Importantly, leptomeningeal involvement usually is minimal, in
contrast to NME. Neurons within grey matter appear to be unaffected despite
parenchymal inflammation.101,102 Areas of necrosis and cavitation with NLE are
more extensive as compared to NME, although the cavitation is less prominent in
the brainstem and cerebellum.
It is thought that the spectrum of pathologic lesions for the MUOs may
represent combinations of genetic influences on the cascade of neuroinflammatory
responses.1 Different infectious agents and environmental and genetic influences
have been investigated as disease triggers but results have been
inconclusive.71,103-108 Although diagnostic markers often lack specificity to
distinguish between the subtypes of MUO, an increased expression of interferongamma in NME and interleukin-17 in GME in tissue biopsies may indicate their
potential as specific markers. These results support further investigations of these
findings in serum and CSF, both for diagnostic potential and to explore the
underlying pathogenesis.109

Clinical Findings
Clinical signs associated with GME and NE simply reflect the region of CNS
involved. Common presenting syndromes include meningoencephalitis, although

signs vary widely, even including myelopathy alone.110 Small, middle-aged female
dogs are most commonly affected by all subtypes of MUO. Although there are
some apparent breed predispositions for specific subtypes, those between GME
and NE are vague and there are no differences in age or sex predilection between
the two groups.24

Granulomatous Meningoencephalomyelitis
GME may represent up to 25% of all canine inflammatory CNS diseases.1 The
signalment of patients that develop GME is heterogeneous, as it affects many
breeds and both sexes; small, middle-aged, especially female dogs are thought to
be most at risk.24 Neurologic signs of GME are nonspecific and can localize to
forebrain or brainstem or appear as a multifocal syndrome. The clinical
presentation correlates with 3 pathological distributions: multifocal
(disseminated), focal, or ocular.86 Clinically, multifocal GME typically is
characterized by an acute onset and rapid progression of multifocal neurologic
signs. In the acute phase, dogs may have fever and exhibit paraspinal
hyperesthesia, especially localizing to the cervical region.86 In contrast, focal GME
tends to have a more insidious or slower progression of neurologic signs that may
suggest a space-occupying lesion, with differential diagnoses including
intracranial neoplasia.86 Forebrain and brainstem signs are reported most
frequently with multifocal GME, whereas forebrain signs alone are more frequent
with focal GME.86,111 The third form, ocular GME, clinically manifests with acute
signs of visual dysfunction attributable to optic neuritis and is sometimes
considered one aspect of disseminated GME (ch. 13).112,113

Necrotizing Encephalitis
The age of onset of neurologic signs of NE ranges from 6 months to 7 years of age.
Most commonly, it occurs in younger dogs, with a mean of 2.5 years.24 In general,
signs associated with NE are rapidly progressive. NME was originally reported as a
breed-specific disease in Pug dogs (Pug dog encephalitis).94,95 NME has also been
reported in the Maltese, Chihuahua, Pekingese, West Highland White Terrier,
Papillon, Shih Tzu, Coton De Tulear, Brussels Griffon and other breeds.85,96 Dogs
with NME commonly manifest forebrain signs, especially seizures, because of
lesions in the cerebral cortex.95 Other forebrain signs include lethargy, anorexia,
central blindness, circling and head-pressing.94,95 Cervical spinal hyperesthesia
may be evident depending upon the extent of leptomeningitis.94 NLE has been
described mostly in Yorkshire Terriers and in French Bulldogs with differing
clinical and topographical features.97-99,101,114 Clinically, most dogs with NLE
have presented with visual loss, seizures and central vestibular signs reflecting
forebrain and brainstem involvement.

Diagnosis
The establishment of an antemortem diagnosis currently relies on clinical
presentation indicative of CNS disease, diagnostic imaging and CSF analysis and
exclusion of other causes of meningoencephalomyelitis.71,84,85 Different groups of
biomarkers, e.g., acute phase proteins, antibodies, cytokines and neuroimaging
markers may prove useful in diagnostic investigation of dogs with MUOs.109 For
this reason, there is no specific noninvasive antemortem diagnostic test, and many
other diseases can mimic the MUOs; a definitive diagnosis of noninfectious
inflammatory CNS disease requires histopathologic evaluation of CNS tissue.
However, Granger and colleagues used a meta-analysis to formulate guidelines for
establishing a presumptive diagnosis of MUO in absence of a histopathological
diagnosis.24 In summary, most cases diagnosed with MUO have multifocal
neurologic signs, CSF mononuclear pleocytosis and T2 hyperintense lesions on
MRI. Nonetheless, the diagnostic efficiency of both CSF analysis and MR imaging
is incomplete because some cases lack abnormalities in one or other test.
Granger and colleagues also revealed considerable variability and overlap in
CSF findings (ch. 109) among the MUOs.24 In several case studies of dogs with
GME, most affected dogs had a mild to moderate lymphocytic or mixed
pleocytosis, with some having a neutrophilic predominance. Protein concentration
was variably elevated.86,111,115,116 Some dogs with focal signs had normal total
nucleated cell counts.111 In a study of 14 Pugs with NME, CSF analysis revealed a
pleocytosis of varying severity (mean, 120 cells/mcL) which was lymphocytic
(66%), mononuclear (17%) or mixed (17%), with a mean protein concentration of
88.4 mg/dL (0.884 g/L).95
Some MRI features (ch. 112) are common to the NEs and GME; however, none
is considered specific for the diagnosis of any disease process. The most common
MRI findings in GME include regions of multifocal or diffuse hyperintensity with
irregular margins on T2 and FLAIR sequences in any part of the CNS, with
variable enhancement after intravenous (IV) contrast is administered.117,118 Even
though histopathologic lesions of GME typically are distributed primarily in the
white matter, lesions on MRI are distributed throughout both grey and white
matter; a mass effect with suggestion of increased intracranial pressure also may
be observed.117,118 NME is typically associated with asymmetric, multifocal
cortical grey and white matter lesions with loss of grey/white matter demarcation,
and variable contrast enhancement. Forebrain predilection, perilesional edema,
mass effect and irregular lesion margins are common.119,120 Lesions appear T1
iso- to hypointense and T2 and FLAIR hyperintense. NLE lesions on MRI
predominantly affect the subcortical white matter and brainstem and, similar to
NME, they appear T1 hypointense and T2 and FLAIR hyperintense.102,114,120
Multifocal distribution of lesions and cavitation with mild to absent contrast
enhancement in the brainstem are highly suggestive of NLE.99,102

Antemortem brain biopsy may yield a more definite diagnosis by which to guide
treatment approaches, although such procedures are dependent upon obtaining
biopsy material from representative portions of the lesion. The diagnostic
accuracy of a brain biopsy in canine CNS inflammatory disease ranges from 74100%, based on the limited available data. Such information is highly dependent
on the population disease types from which the biopsies were obtained.121-123
Especially in dogs with presumptive inflammatory brain disease, a common
reason for nondiagnostic biopsy samples is the difficulty in identifying the ideal
target for taking the biopsy.121,123 A morbidity rate of 30% has been reported in
biopsy of 10 dogs with inflammatory brain disease.123

Treatment
Immunosuppression is central to therapeutic management of MUO, despite the
incompletely understood pathogenic mechanisms or triggers.71 Once infectious
causes have been ruled out, the primary treatment for the MUOs is with
corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive agents (ch. 169). Initial treatment
begins with patient stabilization based on severity of neurologic dysfunction
followed by maintenance therapy. If there are seizures, anticonvulsant therapy is
also required (ch. 247). Stabilization may necessitate supplementary oxygen for
hypoxemia (ch. 123), crystalloid/colloid support to maintain cerebral perfusion
and control hypotension, and osmotic therapy (e.g., mannitol, hypertonic saline)
to reduce elevated intracranial pressure (ch. 125).
The rationale of immunosuppression for autoimmune diseases is to induce
disease remission through the inhibition of inflammation and the modulation of
lymphocyte function. The ultimate goal is to achieve disease remission while
minimizing adverse effects, followed by gradual tapering to the lowest effective
dosage or eventual drug withdrawal. Corticosteroids historically have been the
first-line therapy for treatment of MUO. Often, anti-inflammatory to
immunosuppressive dosages of corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone, 0.25-0.5 mg/kg
PO daily) are initiated until review of negative test results for infectious diseases,
and then increased to immunosuppressive dosages (2-4 mg/kg PO daily) for 2-4
weeks; after that the dose is gradually reduced or tapered every 4 weeks when
clinical signs stabilize or improve. Dogs often will respond initially, but relapses
are common; thus, sustaining remission may require long-term high-dose
corticosteroids, or administration of alternative immunosuppressive agents by
which the undesirable side-effects of high-dose corticosteroid therapy can be
avoided (ch. 144).
Reported second-line immunosuppressive drug therapies for MUO include
leflunomide,124 procarbazine,125 cytosine arabinoside,126-130 lomustine,131
mycophenolate mofetil,132,133 azathioprine,134 COP (cyclophosphamide,
vincristine, prednisone)129 and cyclosporine135-139 (ch. 169). Radiation therapy
has also proven effective for focal GME lesions.111 Not uncommonly, second-line
therapies may be introduced early in the disease process in response to severe

neurologic signs or rapid neurologic deterioration. Many of these secondary
immunosuppressive agents have potential risks for myelosuppression,
hepatotoxicosis, gastrointestinal disturbances, and other drug-specific systemic
effects. Therefore, regular monitoring of CBCs and serum biochemistry profiles is
recommended.140
Selectivity for a specific immunosuppressive protocol depends on clinician
decision-making, the patient’s clinical status, and the pet owner’s financial
considerations. There is no consensus on the most effective immunosuppressive
therapy, dosages, or routes of administration. In recent years, an antimetabolite
synthetic nucleoside analogue, cytosine arabinoside, has become a mainstay of
treatment for MUO alongside corticosteroids. In accordance with guidelines from
other studies, a common protocol is daily administration of prednisone at an
immunosuppressive dose combined with cytosine arabinoside administered at 50
mg/m2 every 12 h as a subcutaneous (SC) bolus for 2 consecutive days or by IV
constant rate infusion (CRI) at 200 mg/m2 over 8 hours.126,127,130 The treatment
cycle is repeated every 3 to 4 weeks for 3 cycles. Subsequently the interval between
treatment cycles is increased by 1 week for 3 cycles at the new treatment interval.
The treatment cycles are gradually extended to every 6 weeks and beyond.
Concurrently, the dosage of prednisone is gradually tapered to low-dose
administration every other day. IV administration of cytosine arabinoside has
been described at higher dosages (up to 600 mg/m2) in severe cases of MUO.141
Advantages of a cytosine arabinoside IV CRI include providing more consistent
plasma levels, effective drug levels, and avoiding peaks and troughs. A
pharmacokinetic study in laboratory Beagles comparing SC bolus administration
versus IV infusion revealed that, based on Fick’s first law of diffusion, IV infusion
may produce a more prolonged exposure of cytosine arabinoside at cytotoxic levels
in plasma compared to the concentrations after SC administration.142 In MUOaffected dogs, the steady state achieved with cytosine arabinoside IV CRI
produced a consistent and prolonged exposure in plasma and serum, which is
likely to produce equilibrium between blood and the CNS.143 Unfortunately, the
cost of CRI administration can prohibit clients from pursuing this option, making
SC cytosine arabinoside administration of 50 mg/m2 4 times over 2 days another
viable treatment option. Advantages of SC administration are decreased stress and
vascular trauma associated with the multiple IV catheter placements required for
IV administration. This protocol is also more cost-effective and requires a much
shorter hospitalization. The pharmacokinetics of cytosine arabinoside in dogs with
MUO after a single 50 mg/m2 SC injection in dogs were similar to those that were
reported in healthy Beagles.144
Studies also have evaluated treatment of MUO dogs with cytosine arabinoside
using a combination of routes of administration. The safety and efficacy of a firstpresentation IV CRI cytosine arabinoside (200 mg/m2) administered over 24 h
followed by 2-day SC cytosine arabinoside (50 mg/m2 q12h) thereafter, compared

mortality at 3 months with historical control cases using a conventional 2-day SC
dosing regimen alone.128 The CRI regimen at first presentation produced a
survival advantage over SC cytosine arabinoside alone. Another study by the same
group did not show a significant difference in the medium- to long-term prognosis
of dogs with MUO treated with an initial cytosine arabinoside CRI and adjunctive
prednisolone protocol with or without sequential follow-up cytosine arabinoside
SC injections. However, the majority of dogs appeared to relapse shortly after
discontinuation of prednisolone.145 A pharmacokinetic study in dogs with MUO
that received first-presentation IV CRI cytosine arabinoside and subsequent
treatments following a SC cytosine arabinoside dosing protocol (50 mg/m2 q2h for
a total of 4 doses the same day) demonstrated consistent and prolonged exposure
of cytosine arabinoside in plasma.146
Treatment effect often is monitored by clinical response and resolution of
neurologic deficits, and occasionally repeated CSF analysis and MRI. Serial MRI
has been used for monitoring resolution of clinical signs or evolution of lesions in
dogs with meningoencephalitis. In a small cohort of dogs presumptively diagnosed
with MUO, Lowrie et al. suggested that a combination of MRI and CSF analysis
provided greater sensitivity for predicting relapse than one modality alone,
although an abnormal CSF analysis at the 3-month reexamination, despite normal
MRI findings, was associated with an increased risk of relapse.127 However,
discontinuing treatment before MRI lesions resolved always resulted in relapse,
suggesting that treatment can be tapered according to MRI or CSF findings.

Prognosis
Determining the prognosis based on treatment effect for recovery in dogs with
MUOs is challenging because of the difficulty in making definitive diagnoses,
disease heterogeneity, treatment variability and small sample sizes in published
reports.24 Currently, the prognosis for an individual patient is often based on
clinical experience and patient response to therapy in the early stages of the
disease and during the course of treatment. Approximately 15-30% of dogs with
MUO die shortly after diagnosis.24,111,127,147 MRI findings consisting of multiple
brain lesions, a mass effect, herniation, and sulci effacement have been identified
as risk factors predicting mortality.111,127 The presence of decreased mentation at
the time of presentation, seizures, and increased neutrophil percentage in the CSF
also have been significantly associated with death within 7 days after diagnosis.147
Typically, focal forebrain lesions give a significantly longer survival time than
those with multifocal or brainstem lesions.111 Dogs presenting with seizures due to
MUO have been found to have a significantly reduced survival time.125,148
Moreover, dogs with MUO and seizures at the early stage of the disease seem to be
at higher risk of developing postencephalitic epilepsy (ch. 247).149 A metaanalysis suggested a benefit of prednisone combined with other

immunosuppressive agents, based on median survival.24 Overall median survival
for dogs treated with corticosteroids plus a second-line immunosuppressive
protocol ranged from 240-590 days. In comparison, survival of dogs treated with
corticosteroids alone ranged from 28-357 days. Another study evaluating
corticosteroid monotherapy in 16 dogs with MUO reported a median survival of
602 days.150 Interestingly, Pugs with NE only receiving an anticonvulsant had
mean survival intervals similar to dogs with other subsets of MUO.95 Long-term
survival is guarded in dogs with spinal MUO; approximately 50% of dogs will die
or be euthanized regardless of therapy.151

Med. 2020;34:808–820.

CEREBROVASCULAR ACCIDENTS
(CVAs)

CVAs, or strokes, are rapidly developing clinical signs of focal (or
global) disturbance of brain function, lasting more than 24 hours or
leading to death, with no apparent cause other than that of vascular
origin.1-5 Cerebrovascular disease (CVD) is an abnormality of the
brain vasculature which may lead to a stroke. Transient ischemic
attacks (TIAs) are brief (<24 hours) periods of focal brain
dysfunction implicating a region of the brain supplied by one
vascular supply. They are characterized by complete return of
function but may recur. A vascular disorder in cats termed feline
ischemic encephalopathy has historically been described as an
infarction frequently localized in the area of the brain supplied by the
middle cerebral artery.6 It is likely that this is not a specific condition
and may just represent a topographic variant of CVAs in cats. Most
strokes in dogs and cats are ischemic strokes resulting from emboli
or from local thrombus formation within a blood vessel.6,7

CLINICAL PRESENTATION
The clinical signs typically reflect a focal abnormality referable to the
area of the central nervous system (CNS) affected (ch. 241). CVAs
have been documented to affect all neuroanatomic regions of the
brain.3,6 In dogs, the most commonly affected artery is the rostral
cerebellar artery, followed by the perforating arteries of the caudal
thalamus and rostral brainstem, the cerebral striate arteries, middle
cerebral artery and rostral cerebral artery.8,9 Ischemic strokes are
classified as territorial if affecting a large artery or lacunar if affecting
a small, perforating artery.10 The median age of dogs and cats
affected with presumed ischemic CVAs is 8 years and 12 years,
respectively.3,4,6,8-11

Forebrain CVA
Clinical signs include an abnormal mental status, seizures,
contralateral postural reaction deficits, transient contralateral motor
dysfunction, contralateral nasal hypalgesia and menace deficit with
ipsilateral circling.10,12,13 Seizures can be part of the acute

presentation; some dogs develop chronic epilepsy after the stroke
event.11

Thalamic and Midbrain CVA
Clinical signs include contralateral or ipsilateral postural reaction
deficits, contralateral menace deficit, ipsilateral head tilt or turn,
ipsilateral circling, vestibular ataxia, pathological nystagmus,
positional ventrolateral strabismus and anisocoria.5,12,14

Cerebellar CVA
Clinical signs include a peracute head tilt, vestibular or cerebellar
ataxia, intermittent opisthotonos, pathological nystagmus, and
ipsilateral menace deficits.2,4,9 Cerebellar CVAs are often divided
into rostral and caudal based on the blood supply of this structure.
Rostral cerebellar ischemic CVAs have specifically been documented
to result in gait abnormalities (cerebellar ataxia with or without
hypermetria or acute onset non-ambulatory with decerebellate
rigidity in some), head tilt, pathological nystagmus, decreased
menace response and hopping deficits.4 Although cats and dogs with
rostral cerebellar strokes are often severely compromised at
presentation, the short-term prognosis is excellent and rapid clinical
improvement may be observed within the first week.5 Caudal
cerebellar ischemic CVAs specifically have been documented to
result in intermittent intention tremors, vestibular ataxia, vertical
pathological nystagmus, and paradoxical vestibular syndrome.7,15

PATHOGENESIS—ISCHEMIC CVA
CVAs may result from excessive blood flow through the cerebral
vessels (hypertension; ch. 236), transmural extravasation of blood
components (vasculitis; ch. 181), thrombosis or embolization (ch.
238).2,3,6,16-21 Cavalier King Charles Spaniels and Greyhounds have
been suggested to be predisposed to CVA.12,22,23 Neuropathological
changes associated with ischemic CVAs are characterized by a pan-

necrotic infarct surrounded by peri-infarct injured neurons and
reactive microglia/macrophages and astrocytes, similar to what has
been described in humans.24
Dogs with brain infarction are frequently (55%) detected with a
comorbidity predisposing to CVA, chronic kidney disease (24%; ch.
301) and hyperadrenocorticism (18%; ch. 293) being most
commonly encountered.8 Cats documented with ischemic brain
infarcts have been affected by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (ch.
234), neoplasia (ch. 322), and hyperthyroidism (ch. 287).5
Atherosclerosis is a common cause of thromboembolic CVD in
people but is considered uncommon in dogs and is unreported in
cats; it has been documented in association with dysregulation of
lipid metabolism (e.g., hypothyroidism or primary hyperlipidemia;
ch. 156). Hypercoagulable states (such as protein-losing
nephropathy or enteropathy, hyperadrenocorticism, immunemediated hemolytic anaemia, and polycythemia vera) may result in
intramural emboli and subsequent thrombosis of cerebral blood
vessels (ch. 171).7,25 Other purported causes include bacteraemia
(e.g., sepsis [ch. 128], endocarditis [ch. 232]), neoplastic
infiltration of blood vessels, vasculitis (ch. 181) due to systemic
disease (e.g., leishmaniasis, ch. 197) or local CNS inflammation,
migrating parasites (Cuterebra larva in cats), and fibrocartilaginous
embolism (ch. 251).26-29

PATHOGENESIS—HEMORRHAGIC CVA
Hemorrhage into and around the brain can result in an associated
inflammatory reaction, creation of mass effect, and an increase in
intracranial pressure (ICP). Compression of tissue occurs primarily
during the first 6 hours following clinical onset. Elastic resistance of
the surrounding parenchyma and increasing ICP can limit
hematoma expansion. Once expansion ceases, the hematoma
organizes and resolves within days to weeks. Hematoma resolution
includes breakdown of blood products which can be damaging to
neuronal parenchyma through several mechanisms, including

proinflammatory and pro-oxidant activities, and stimulation of
excessive glutamate release.1,3,6,17
In cats with hemorrhagic brain infarcts, significant liver
dysfunction and nephritis have been identified in 100% and 25% of
cases, respectively.2 Systemic hypertension (associated with a variety
of conditions such as renal disease, hyperadrenocorticism,
hyperthyroidism, primary hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma)
can result in an increase in cerebrovascular hydrostatic forces
leading to intracranial hemorrhage and edema (ch. 236). Other
possible causes of hemorrhagic CVA include bleeding disorders (e.g.,
disseminated intravascular coagulation, thrombocytopenia; ch. 171),
neoplastic infiltration of blood vessels, vasculitis due to systemic
disease or local CNS inflammation (ch. 181), Angiostrongylus
vasorum, (lungworm detected in much of Europe and
Newfoundland, Canada; ch. 217), and arteriovenous
malformations.8,17,30,31

DIAGNOSIS
CVA should be suspected in any animal with peracute/acute onset
and non-progressive (after 24-48 hours) focal neurological deficits.
A blood pressure measurement should be undertaken to determine
whether hypertension is present (ch. 91). A fecal examination
should be performed to rule out Angiostrongylus vasorum infection
(chs. 80, 217).31 Specific coagulation testing is also commonly
performed (ch. 170). A serum biochemical panel and urinalysis to
evaluate for the presence of an underlying disease that predisposes to
hypercoagulability (such as proteinuria) should also be performed.
D-dimer concentrations within the normal reference range do not
rule out ischemic stroke in dogs.32 Thromboelastography may be
helpful (ch. 170), although results can be normal in some affected
dogs.23,32 A complete endocrine evaluation is often advised
including serum cholesterol and triglyceride levels (ch. 156).
Cerebrospinal fluid results (ch. 109) are often nonspecific, may be
normal, and should not be performed prior to advanced imaging, to
rule out a hemorrhagic disorder.

The imaging characteristics of CVA may vary depending upon the
degree of disease (e.g., ischemia versus overt hemorrhage) and the
time between the onset of clinical signs and the imaging studies
being performed.1,3,5,7,12,13,15,18,19,21,22,33

Computed Tomography (CT)
CT images (ch. 112) are frequently normal during the acute phase of
ischemia; therefore, the diagnosis of ischemic stroke relies on the
exclusion of other diseases. Early CT signs of ischemia may include:
parenchymal hypoattenuation due to vasogenic edema with welldefined margins; loss of differentiation between the grey and white
matter; subtle effacement of the cortical sulci; and a local mass
effect.1,21 CT is very sensitive for the detection of acute hemorrhage,
which appears as an increased opacity due to the hyperattenuation of
X-rays by the globin portion of blood.1

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
Conventional MRI (ch. 112) can be used for visualizing ischemic
stroke within hours of the onset of clinical signs. It can also
distinguish hemorrhagic lesions from infarction (Figure 243.1).
However, the overall sensitivity and specificity of conventional MRI
protocols for ischemic strokes shortly after injury in dogs is poor,
with focal inflammatory brain disease and some neoplastic lesions
(such as gliomas) having a similar appearance on MR images.19,34
With conventional sequences, ischemic infarction appears as a
well-demarcated lesion when compared to surrounding parenchyma.
The lesion is primarily in the grey matter and often there is evidence
of edema in the area of the cerebrovascular damage. Typically, a
wedge-shaped lesion is visible with the point of the wedge directed
centrally, corresponding to a known vascular territory. Contrast
enhancement following gadolinium administration depends on the
interval between the vascular damage and the MRI examination, the
resulting inflammatory response, and the degree of vascular
disruption (break in the blood-brain barrier).1 In most cases,
imaging studies are performed within 48 hours following the insult

due to the severity of the clinical signs and thus contrast
enhancement is uncommon.
Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and perfusion-weighted
imaging are techniques that monitor water transport in the
microenvironment at the cellular or capillary level and can be used
for more definitively diagnosing ischemia.1 Cytotoxic edema can be
detected as a diffusion impairment (a well-demarcated hyperintense
signal) within minutes using DWI. An apparent diffusion coefficient
(ADC) map is constructed to quantify the extent of restricted
diffusion observed on the DWI image. DWI has improved sensitivity
and specificity for the diagnosis of acute stroke, making it the ideal
sequence for positive identification of hyperacute stroke (Figure
243.1).35
Combining susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) or gradient
echo (GRE) imaging such as T2∗ with conventional T1-w and T2-w
images can increase both the sensitivity and specificity for
hemorrhagic strokes.1 Hemorrhage appears as hypointense (signal
void) lesions on these sequences, as hemosiderin is strongly
paramagnetic. Compared to CT, GRE is equally, if not more,
sensitive for detection of acute intracranial hemorrhage.1

TREATMENT
Therapy for CVA includes management of any predisposing factors,
treatment of secondary intracranial consequences such as
hemorrhage and edema, and maintenance of vital physiological
variables that regulate cerebral perfusion and energy metabolism
(systemic blood pressure and ventilation). These secondary
consequences often result in an increase in ICP and subsequent
decrease in cerebral blood flow (CBF). Treatment to decrease
elevated ICP may aid in restoration of CBF.

Head Position
Positioning the animal’s head elevated 30° up from horizontal helps
maximize arterial supply to, and venous drainage from, the brain, as

do appropriate fluid therapy and oxygenation, based on deviations
from normal parameters noted at initial patient assessment.

Fluid Resuscitation
The goal of fluid management is to maintain a normo- to slightly
hypervolemic state to ensure adequate cerebral perfusion pressure.
Initial resuscitation usually involves IV hypertonic saline and/or
synthetic colloids. Use of these solutions allows rapid restoration of
blood volume and pressure while limiting the volume of fluid
administered.

Osmotic Diuretics
Osmotic diuretics are very useful in the treatment of intracranial
hypertension. Mannitol has an immediate plasma-expanding effect
that reduces blood viscosity, leading to increased CBF and oxygen
delivery. This results in vasoconstriction within a few minutes,
causing an almost immediate decrease in ICP. Mannitol should be
administered as a bolus over a 15-minute period (rather than as an
infusion) in order to obtain the plasma-expanding effect; its effect on
brain edema begins after ∼15-30 minutes and lasts 2-8 hours. There
is no clinical evidence to prove the theory that mannitol is
contraindicated in the presence of intracranial hemorrhage, which
has been a frequently raised concern.

Oxygen Therapy
Oxygen supplementation is recommended for most animals (ch.
123). Supplemental oxygen should be administered initially via flowby, as oxygen cages are usually ineffective because constant
monitoring of the patient does not allow for a closed system.

Corticosteroids
High-dose corticosteroids are contraindicated for treatment of acute
ischemic brain injury.

Surgery
Treatment for a localized hematoma within the CNS might require
surgical evacuation via craniotomy depending on the size, location
and clinical signs. All attempts at medical therapy should be made
prior to considering surgery. If the underlying bleeding disorder is
still active based on continued neurologic deterioration despite
medical management aimed at decreasing ICP (see above), a
dilemma exists between the need for surgical drainage of the
hematoma and the risk of causing increased hemorrhage. Ultimately,
if the accumulation of blood within the CNS becomes lifethreatening, surgical drainage is a necessity that is undertaken in
view of the increased risk of hemorrhagic complications. Such
surgical intervention needs to be guided by imaging studies (CT or
preferably MRI), to determine if the lesion is appropriately
positioned for evacuation based on a superficial location. While it is
impossible to reverse all of the effects of the hemorrhage, decreasing
the size of an expanding hematoma, with the resultant decrease in
nervous system pressure, may improve clinical signs.

of a 9-year-old Boston Terrier with slowly
progressive and non-specific signs of forebrain
disease. A, T2W transverse image at the level of the

PROGNOSIS

The short-term prognosis for cats and dogs with ischemic CVAs if
they are neither severely affected nor impacted by critical concurrent
disease is good. The long-term prognosis in dogs is good if no
underlying disease is found.3,8,11 The long-term prognosis in cats
with CVAs is currently unknown.

CEREBRAL MICROBLEEDS
Cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) are small, well-defined, punctate,
intraparenchymal signal voids within the brain on T2∗ gradientecho or susceptibility-weighted MRI sequences, with a maximum
diameter ≤5 mm and no known history of head trauma (Figure
243.2).30,36-38 These signal voids correlate with pathologically
confirmed accumulations of blood, most frequently seen in the
cerebral cortex.
CMBs are more common in older and smaller dogs.38 These can be
incidental findings but compared to matched controls, dogs with
CMBs appear to present more frequently for vestibular syndrome
and have also been associated with a good prognosis.30 Systemic
hypertension (ch. 236), diabetes mellitus (ch. 291),
hypothyroidism (ch. 285), and hyperadrenocorticism (ch. 293) are
identified as concurrent systemic disorders in dogs with CMB.30,39
Cortical atrophy (determined by decreased interthalamic adhesion
diameter on sagittal T2W images, sulcal widening, and generalized
hydrocephalus ex vacuo) occurs more frequently in dogs with CMBs
and is not necessarily associated with signs of cognitive dysfunction
syndrome.38,40 Treatment is directed at any identified associated
causes; there is no specific treatment for CMBs.

HYPERTENSIVE ENCEPHALOPATHY
Hypertensive encephalopathy has been reported in dogs and cats
(ch. 236).39,41,42 It is associated with either an acute (>30 mm Hg
from resting level) or a sustained (>180 mm Hg) elevation in systolic
arterial blood pressure (ch. 91). The clinical signs reflect

involvement of the forebrain (ch. 241) and include seizures, altered
mentation, decreased level of consciousness and blindness.41 In
addition, signs may also relate to dysfunction of the CNS structures
of the caudal cranial fossa and include loss of consciousness,
vestibular or cerebellar ataxia, and pathological nystagmus. Clinical
signs of hypertensive encephalopathy have also been reversible
following normalization of blood pressure in dogs and cats with
hypertensive encephalopathy.42
Although the pathogenesis of hypertensive encephalopathy is not
completely understood, existing evidence indicates that the lesions
are the consequence of vasogenic and interstitial brain edema, which
occurs as a result of failed autoregulation of the cerebral
vasculature.42 Vasogenic edema typically results in an increased
signal intensity within the white matter on T2-weighted MR images
(Figure 236.7), which is most often bilaterally symmetrical and
located in the subcortical cerebral white matter. In addition, lesions
related to vasogenic edema are hyperintense on both DWI and ADC
mapping, which suggests a T2 shine through a phenomenon related
to facilitated diffusion of protons. In contrast, cytotoxic edema
results in a hyperintensity on DWI and a hypointensity on ADC
mapping. Hyperintensity of the white matter of the cerebrum has
been observed on both DWI and ADC mapping with hypertensive
encephalopathy in dogs.39,42 Treatment involves supportive care as
well as specific therapy for the hypertension and its underlying
associations, if found.

DEVELOPMENTAL BRAIN ANOMALIES

REVIEW
Brain malformations are classified as either primary if caused by genetic
abnormalities or secondary (encephaloclastic) if caused by exposure to teratogens
or other acquired insults (Table 244.1).1,2 Congenital malformations of the
brain would typically be present from birth and non-progressive. A few
exceptions, such as congenital hydrocephalus and Chiari malformation, can
manifest later in life with progressive signs. Severe malformations produce clear
changes on physical examination and brain imaging.3 Postmortem examination
may be necessary to detect more subtle defects. Brain anomalies may accompany
other defects such as cleft palate (ch. 258) or cardiac anomalies (ch. 231), which
relates them chronologically to specific periods of embryogenesis. For most
congenital malformations, treatment is nonspecific and supportive, and the
prognosis depends on the severity of the malformation and neurological deficits.
History and serologic testing can rule out toxic or infectious etiologies that could
be treatable. Genetic, vaccine and nutritional counseling may help prevent future
occurrences in breeding facilities.

NEURAL TUBE DEFECTS
The nervous system originates from a plate on the dorsal surface of the embryo,
which folds in to form the neural tube beginning in the thoracic area and
extending rostrally and caudally. Genetic defects and in utero infection, toxin, or
malnutrition can disrupt normal closure of the neural tube, typically seen at the
rostral or caudal ends of the developing nervous system. Cranial neural crest cells
are required for folding of the neural tube and become the mesenchyme of the
face and base of the calvaria.23 Defects in neural tube closure can vary in severity.
The most is a complete lack of brain development and no induction of calvaria
formation, known as anencephaly.
The calvaria develops from the axial mesoderm that is induced by the
development of the brain parenchyma.23 Typically, cranial mesodermal defects
are most apparent in midline structures. In some cases, concurrent malformation
of overlying tissues allows protrusion of meningeal (meningocele) or brain and
meningeal tissue through the defect (meningoencephalocele) (Figure
244.1).1,24,25 In dogs, the most common protrusion sites are ethmoidal and
intranasal, with worse neurologic signs from the caudally located lesion.25 Some
cranial defects can be treated surgically.26,27

DISORDERS OF FOREBRAIN INDUCTION
Disorders associated with development of the forebrain include
holoprosencephaly, arhinencephaly, and cyclopia. In holoprosencephaly, the

cerebrum and other midline structures fail to separate and there may be
incomplete formation of other midline structures. Agenesis of the corpus
callosum usually is accompanied by other defects but can be a distinct
malformation. The most common presenting clinical sign identified in
association with corpus callosum agenesis is hypodipsia/adipsia, leading to
episodes of hypernatremia.28

DISORDERS OF NEURONAL MIGRATION
Once the neural tube has formed, the various parts of the brain differentiate; this
can be disrupted by genetic or environmental influences. Neuronal migration
along radial glia within the cerebral cortex leads to the characteristic sulci and
gyri and the normal laminar arrangement of neurons within the cortex. Brain
malformations can be caused by abnormalities in neuronal migration (Table
244.1). In lissencephaly, some or all of the cortical surface is smooth (agyria)
(Figure 244.2) with thickening of the cortical laminae.3 Affected dogs can show
behavioral changes, central blindness and seizures. Other comorbidities include
hydrocephalus, supracollicular fluid accumulation and corpus callosum
hypoplasia. Polymicrogyria is a disorder of cerebrocortical development resulting
in excessive production of small gyri and often accompanied by hydrocephalus.
The occipital lobes are preferentially affected with central blindness being the
primary clinical sign (Figure 244.3).29,30
Cerebellar hypoplasia

(Video 41.6) is often seen in cats following in utero

or early neonatal infection with the feline panleukopenia virus (ch. 201) when
the rapidly multiplying cerebella granule cells are sensitive to viral damage.1,24
Cerebellar aplasia or hypoplasia can also occur as an isolated malformation, or as
part of a more generalized brain development abnormality.2 The Dandy-Walker
syndrome in dogs and cats is characterized by agenesis of the cerebellar vermis,
dilation of the fourth ventricle, and hydrocephalus.

HYDROCEPHALUS
Definitions
Hydrocephalus is broadly defined pathophysiologically as an active distension of
the ventricular system of the brain related to inadequate passage of cerebrospinal
fluid (CSF) from its point of production within the ventricular system to its point
of absorption into the systemic circulation.31 A diagnosis of hydrocephalus
indicates the presence of clinical signs of neurologic dysfunction related to the
dilated ventricles. The term “ventriculomegaly” is used for describing an
incidental imaging finding in animals with subjectively dilated lateral ventricles
and no clinical signs of dysfunction caused by the enlargement.
Current classification schemes separate hydrocephalus into intraventricular
and extraventricular obstructive hydrocephalus.31,32 Extraventricular
hydrocephalus occurs with obstruction at the level of the subarachnoid space or
arachnoid villi. The entire ventricular system and subarachnoid space dilate
when absorption of CSF from the subarachnoid space into the venous drainage is
impeded, e.g., when inflammatory or neoplastic cells infiltrate the arachnoid villi
and subarachnoid space. In intraventricular obstructive hydrocephalus, the
blockage of CSF flow through the ventricular system mainly occurs at recognized
bottlenecks: the connection between the lateral ventricle and the third ventricle
(the interventricular foramen) or most commonly, the connection between the
third and fourth ventricle (the mesencephalic aqueduct) and lateral apertures.
Atrophy or a necrotic process of surrounding brain tissue can enlarge the
ventricles. This is called compensatory hydrocephalus or hydrocephalus ex vacuo
(Figure 244.4). More rarely, fluid can accumulate outside the ventricular

system. External hydrocephalus results from CSF accumulating in the
subarachnoid space, presumably due to obstruction of flow secondary to
inflammation.33 Another common site of fluid accumulation is the
quadrigeminal cistern, between the cerebellum and cerebrum, that has been
recognized as intracranial intra-arachnoid diverticula or quadrigeminal cyst.34
This can be an incidental finding but it will produce clinical signs if it causes
excessive compression, particularly on the cerebrum and cerebellum.35,36
Brain injury from hydrocephalus is due to direct tissue compression or is
caused indirectly by damage to the vasculature.32 The intraventricular increase in
CSF pressure may eventually lead to focal destruction of the ependymal lining,
compromise of cerebral vessels, and damage to the periventricular white
matter.37-39 The resulting interstitial edema in severe cases leads to neuronal
injury and loss in the cerebral cortex.

FIGURE 244.5 A, Ultrasound can be used to image dilated
ventricles (asterisks) if an open fontanelle provides an acoustic
window. B, Otherwise magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or
computed tomography is necessary. On axial T2W MRI for the
dog in B, a rim of brain parenchyma (arrows) at the level of
the thalamus was evident. The chief concerns from the owners
were the dog’s irritability on restraint and inability to become
house-trained.

Causes of Hydrocephalus
Obstructive hydrocephalus can be congenital or acquired. Acquired
hydrocephalus usually occurs when a disease process such as neoplasia,

hemorrhage, or inflammation occludes the flow of CSF. Neoplasia can cause
compression of a segment of the ventricular system or ventricular occlusion by
drop metastasis (intradural, extramedullary spinal metastasis) that impedes CSF
flow. Congenital hydrocephalus is a common distinct entity in some small and
brachycephalic breeds of dogs and cats.40,41 It can be associated with brain
malformations (e.g., Chiari-like malformations, Dandy-Walker malformation,
polymicrogyria, lissencephaly).30,42-44 Hypotheses for development of congenital
internal hydrocephalus in predisposed breeds include inadequate development of
the mesencephalic aqueduct, immotile ependymal cilia, and malformation of the
arachnoid villi preventing normal CSF absorption.2 Neonatal infections, such as
parainfluenza virus in dogs, can result in stenosis without leaving any indications
of the etiology once the initial ependymitis has resolved.45,46 The strong breed
predilection, however, suggests a hereditary basis in many of these dogs.
Presence of a molera or fontanelle is common in many toy breeds (e.g.,
Chihuahua); however, a fontanelle does not necessarily indicate presence of
hydrocephalus. Nonetheless, in Chihuahuas persistent fontanelles are associated
with small size, syringomyelia, ventriculomegaly and craniocervical junction
overcrowding.47

Clinical

Signs (Video 244.1)

Onsets and rates of progression of clinical signs are variable in dogs and cats with
diagnosed congenital hydrocephalus, and a large retrospective study showed that
30% of dogs were >2 years of age.40 Clinical signs of hydrocephalus include
behavioral and mentation changes, ataxia, visual deficits, and seizures. Physical
features may include an enlarged and dome-shaped calvaria, fontanelle, and
persistent cranial sutures. Ventrolateral strabismus is common in congenital
hydrocephalus and is related to orbital malformation. Lateralized signs (circling)
are evident with obstruction of the intraventricular foramen causing dilation of
one lateral ventricle. Even in congenital cases, the disease may follow a waxing
and waning course. Sometimes dramatic hydrocephalus may be present and the
owners report few clinical signs other than learning deficits.48 Increased
intracranial pressure can lead to tentorial herniation, particularly in acute,
obstructive hydrocephalus.

Diagnosis
Hydrocephalus can be diagnosed with imaging studies. If a fontanelle is present,
the ventricles can often be adequately imaged with ultrasound. If not, then crosssectional imaging will be necessary to image the dilated ventricles and rule out
obstructive disease causes or another congenital anomaly (Figure 244.5).
Criteria of clinical relevance, based on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
findings of canine brains, were suggested for a supporting diagnosis of internal

hydrocephalus of a sufficient severity to be causing clinical signs.49 The
ventricle/brain index was significantly higher in dogs with clinical signs of
hydrocephalus and a threshold value of 0.6 was specified to differentiate between
internal hydrocephalus and ventriculomegaly.49,50 Other anatomic findings
indicative of clinical hydrocephalus include elevation of the corpus callosum,
flattening of the interthalamic adhesion, periventricular edema, dilation of the
olfactory recesses, effacement of the cortical sulci, attenuation of the
subarachnoid space, and disruption of the internal capsule.49

Treatment
The choice of treatment is guided by the patient’s neurologic and physical status
and age, and the underlying cause. Medical management of hydrocephalus is
largely directed at reducing intracranial pressure, CSF production, and tissue
destruction.32 Anti-seizure drugs are administered to control seizures (ch. 247).
Although efficacy is controversial, loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide), carbonic
anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide) or proton pump inhibitors (e.g.,
omeprazole) in combination with corticosteroids or corticosteroids alone may
help decrease CSF production.51 Mannitol can be administered in cases of acute
decompensation, but the benefits are transient. While medical therapy may
ameliorate the signs, hydrocephalus tends to be a progressive disease.
Surgical treatment involves either resection of the mass lesions causing the
ventricular obstruction or shunting of CSF away from the obstructed regions of
the ventricular system.52 Surgical treatment is reserved for animals with
worsening of neurologic signs that do not respond or that become refractory to
medical therapy. Contraindications include infection of shunt placement sites
and evidence that irreversible damage has already occurred. 32 Placement of a
drainage device (shunt) diverts CSF from the lateral ventricle through a one-way
ultra-low pressure valve and reservoir to another site such as the peritoneal
space, atrium of the heart or subcutaneous tissue.53,54

Prognosis
The prognosis for severe congenital hydrocephalus is usually guarded as clinical
signs are often severe at presentation. A decrease in ventricular volume and
reexpansion of brain parenchyma after ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement are
associated with improvement in clinical signs.55 In a retrospective study of 30
dogs and 6 cats with congenital hydrocephalus and ventriculoperitoneal shunt
placement, 72% had improvement of clinical signs within a median time of 4
months.53 Complications are likely to develop within the first 6 months after
surgery and most commonly include shunt obstruction along with shunt
migration from the calvaria, infection, mechanical failure, and overshunting.56
