CHIARI-LIKE MALFORMATION AND
SYRINGOHYDROMYELIA
Pathogenesis
Chiari-like malformation (CM) and syringohydromyelia (SM) occur in small
breed dogs, especially the Cavalier King Charles Spaniel (CKCS) and Brussel
Griffon.42,57-59 The terminology has been adopted from similar disorders in
humans. In dogs, CM is characterized by herniation of the cerebellar vermis and
medulla into or through the foramen magnum and indentation of the cerebellum
by the occipital bone.60 A sequela of CM is the development of SM, characterized
by formation of fluid-filled cavities within the spinal cord. This is most common
in the cervical spinal cord at C1-4 but can form in multiple locations.61 In the
CKCS, the risk of syringomyelia has been shown to be associated with increased
brachycephaly with rostrocaudal doming62 and premature closure of the sphenooccipital synchondrosis that may contribute to skull conformation and CM.63
Thus, the pathophysiologic mechanism of CM involves a mismatch between the
caudal cranial fossa volume and contained brain parenchyma, leading to

cerebellar herniation, medullary kinking, hydrocephalus, obstruction of the
dorsal craniocervical subarachnoid space, and alteration of CSF flow.64,65 In the
CKCS, there is an association between increased cerebellar volume and SM.66
There also are significant associations between medullary elevation (i.e.,
medullary kinking) and dorsal compressive atlantoaxial bands and the presence
of SM, but causal effects remain to be determined.67-69 The development of
hydrocephalus most likely is related to reduced craniospinal compliance due to
failed CSF absorption into the venous sinuses.70 In the CKCS, the inheritance of
SM secondary to CM is complex, with recently established associations with
PCDH17 (a gene that encodes for a cell adhesion protein in brain and spinal cord)
and ZWINT (a gene that is expressed in association with the onset of neuropathic
pain).71-73

Clinical Signs
The ages at onset of clinical signs vary from <1 year to mid-adult and usually are
related to the SM. These signs include thoracic and pelvic limb general
proprioceptive ataxia, postural reaction deficits, and neuropathic pain. Mild to
severe neck discomfort; excessive scratching in the region of the ear, neck, or
shoulder with a hindpaw; vocalization; and facial rubbing are common
presenting concerns for neuropathic pain.42,74-76 Postural pain (signs of pain
when being lifted or on rising and jumping) is the most common behavioral
sign.77 Size (diameter) and asymmetry of the syrinx are the strongest predictors
of pain.75,78 The mechanisms by which SM leads to neuropathic pain may involve
the anatomic distortion of the dorsal horn resulting in abnormal processing of
sensory information.76,78 Decreased expression of substance P and interleukin-6
in CSF and spinal cord tissue of CKCSs occur with SM and persistent pain;
interestingly, expression of these same mediators is increased caudal to the SM
lesion.79,80 Quantitative assessments for neuropathic pain show lower sensory
threshold values in CKCSs with SM when compared to normal dogs.81

Diagnosis
CM and SM are readily diagnosed on a midsagittal MRI on which the herniation
of the cerebellum, medullary kinking, and any concurrent hydrocephalus or
syringomyelia can be identified (Figure 244.6). Syringomyelia is seen as a T2W
hyperintensity and T1W hypointensity. Interestingly, up to 70% CKCS and 24%
Brussel Griffons with presence of CM and SM on MRI show no associated clinical
signs.82-84

Treatment

Management of SM depends on an imaging diagnosis combined with severity of
clinical signs. Dogs exhibiting pain or neurologic deficits or that show
progression of signs can be treated medically or surgically, but clinical signs can
be frustrating to treat given the variability in disease progression. Initial medical
therapy involves use of analgesics, including gabapentin for neuropathic pain
(ch. 6) and drugs to reduce CSF production. Specifically, a small, randomized
placebo-controlled trial assessing efficacy of pregabalin 13-19 mg/kg PO q12h
showed significant reductions of neuropathic pain in CKCSs with SM.85 Surgical
treatment of CM in dogs may have importance in restoring craniospinal
compliance but there is limited information regarding patient selection or other
criteria on which to base decisions. With the improved CSF dynamics after
decompressive surgery, the clinical signs may resolve but recurrence is common
and neuropathic pain may persist.86-88

DEGENERATIVE
REVIEW
Neurodegenerative brain diseases have a progressive course and are usually
diagnosed in quite young or geriatric pets. Degenerative encephalomyelopathies
can be selective, diffuse, or multifocal, affecting the neuron, axon, or myelin.
They often involve both brain and spinal cord (Table 244.2). Forebrain,
brainstem, spinal cord and/or cerebellar signs may predominate. Findings on
brain MRI may show bilateral and symmetrical selective lesions in the gray or
white matter that can have a regional or diffuse distribution. Additionally, MRI
findings of brain atrophy can also be regional or diffuse. Breed, age of onset, and
physical signs are suggestive of a diagnosis and specialized tests can provide
further evidence; however, a definitive diagnosis for many of these disorders is
made on biopsy or necropsy. Genetic mutation discoveries have enabled a better
understanding of the underlying disease-causing pathways that can provide
targeted therapeutic studies (Table 244.2).89 DNA tests assist with confirming
a diagnosis and assist dog breeders in efforts to reduce the disease incidence in
breeds. Currently, there is no curative treatment for most of the
neurodegenerative diseases. Therapeutic strategies such as somatic gene transfer
therapy, enzyme replacement therapy, heterologous cell transplantation, and
RNA silencing therapy hold promise and clinical trials on several disease models
of dogs and cats are underway.

CENTRAL MYELINOPATHY
Definition
Many of the central myelinopathies manifest with signs of spinal cord
dysfunction but also can cause encephalopathy.1,24 Some myelin disorders cause
severe destruction of the central or peripheral myelin and often lead to loss of
axons. Abnormalities involving the central nervous system (CNS) myelin can be
broadly categorized into reduced or absent myelination (hypomyelinogenesis),
abnormal myelination formation and maintenance (dysmyelination –
leukodystrophy, myelinolysis, leukoencephalomyelopathy), and
demyelination.1,24,90 These disorders should not be confused with acquired
demyelinating diseases, in which there is a breakdown and loss of previously
normal myelin; in general, these types of demyelinating diseases do not present
clinically as congenital problems. In primary demyelination, the oligodendrocytes
are damaged (e.g., virus, other inflammation, ischemia) and myelin-related
structures undergo degeneration and phagocytosis with axons remaining intact.
Nonetheless, demyelination also can be secondary to primary axonal
degenerations with loss of the myelin sheath.

Pathogenesis
In hypomyelinogenesis, numbers of oligodendrocytes are decreased or they are
unable to produce functional myelin.1 Typically, myelin throughout the CNS is
affected but peripheral nerves are spared. There is a delay in migration or
differentiation of oligodendrocyte progenitor cells causing abnormal myelin
production and CNS hypomyelination. Hypomyelinogenesis has been
documented in many breeds and the best studied is the Springer Spaniel
(“shaking pup,” shp) in which the disease is X-linked.90 Toy Fox and Rat Terriers
with congenital hypothyroidism with goiter (ch. 285) have regional CNS
hypomyelination most evident in the corpus callosum. In Rat Terriers, this is
associated with a mutation in the thyroid peroxidase gene.91

The leukodystrophies are a broadly classified group of diseases that includes
varieties of leukodystrophies, necrotizing encephalomyelopathies and
leukoencephalomyelopathies.1 Often, conditions are inherited and diagnosed in
younger animals with defective myelin production that cannot be maintained.
Myelin is initially formed but early in life a bilateral, symmetrical destruction of
myelin ensues with eventual loss of axons in some. Alexander’s disease (fibrinoid
leukodystrophy) has a sporadic occurrence in several breeds. Histopathologic
evaluation reveals myelin degeneration without vacuolation. This is replaced by
severe, widespread astrogliosis or Rosenthal fibers (astrocytic processes) in the
brain and spinal cord.
Myelinolysis is characterized by disintegration of initially normally formed
myelin. These disorders are presumed to be recessive traits and have been
described in several breeds. There is bilateral and symmetrical malacia and
cavitations that are severe in all spinal cord funiculi with tapering extension into
the brainstem. Myelin is predominantly affected whereas the axons are usually
spared.
If the type of myelin degeneration cannot be determined, a more general term
for inherited or acquired conditions, leukoencephalomyelopathy, is used. Spongy
degeneration is a nonspecific term used for denoting affected tissue vacuolation.
This is seen in disorders with separation of the myelin sheath or that involve the
neuronal cell body, as in the prion diseases (transmissible spongiform
encephalopathy [TSE]). Specific leukoencephalomyelopathies and spongy
degenerations have been documented in several breeds of dogs and cats (Table
244.2). Some lysosomal storage diseases such as globoid cell leukodystrophy
also cause vacuolar-like demyelination.92

Clinical Signs
Weakness is not a predominant feature of pure demyelinating or cerebellar
disorders. Rather, limb and whole-body tremor (ch. 42) is a feature of myelin
and cerebellar diseases. The clinical signs of syndromes (hypomyelination and
dysmyelination) are usually noticed in the first few weeks of life or as the affected
animals begin to walk. The cerebellum, dependent on fast conduction for sensory
feedback during movement, is quite sensitive to disorders affecting myelin or
information processing and even subtle deficits may cause signs. Signs consist of
action-related repetitive myoclonus. When standing or walking, affected animals
display what appears as a diffuse, coarse (large amplitude) tremor causing the
animal to “bounce up and down” in a rhythmic manner

(Videos 41.4, 41.5).

The pelvic limbs are generally more affected than the thoracic limbs. Severely
affected animals may be unable to walk and fall frequently. With sleep or
relaxation, the tremor is not present. Reflexes are normal or exaggerated. Ocular
examination may show pendular nystagmus and spontaneous saccadic
movements.

Clinical signs of dysmyelination, myelinolysis, and leukoencephalopathies are
manifested initially in the pelvic limbs most severely but reflect the anatomic
location that is most affected pathologically. Once the myelin reaches a critical
threshold of dysfunction and loss, the clinical course is often acute and
progresses rapidly, causing paraplegia and eventually affecting the thoracic
limbs. Often, postural reaction deficits occur in all limbs, with spinal reflexes
intact to increased (ch. 241). Cerebellar signs involve cerebellar ataxia, intention
tremor, and limb dysmetria. If the forebrain is affected, clinical signs can include
seizures, central blindness and cognitive dysfunction. Affected animals may have
cranial nerve dysfunction with vestibular signs. When these neurologic deficits
become severe, euthanasia is warranted.

Diagnosis
The diagnosis of CNS hypomyelination and dysmyelination is made primarily
from the spectrum of neurologic deficits and signs and the early age of onset.
Brain MRI (ch. 112) can show a distinctive widespread T2W hyperintensity in
white matter of the brain and spinal cord, indicating differential diagnoses of
toxic (i.e., bromethalin toxicosis), metabolic (e.g., globoid cell leukodystrophy)
and degenerative leukoencephalomyelopathy. Histopathologic evaluation of
tissue is the only definitive method to confirm a diagnosis. In cases with a
heritable basis, pedigree evaluation and genetic testing may be helpful (Table
244.2).

Treatment
There is no specific treatment for the central myelinopathies. The only means of
control and prevention is selective breeding. The veterinary literature commonly
reports that dogs with shaking puppy syndrome may recover completely, but
deficits may persist as mild, moderate or severe. In Springer Spaniels, males do
not show much improvement, but the carrier females are less severely affected
and improve considerably with maturation.

AXONOPATHIES
Central Axonopathy
Axonal degeneration results from disease within the neuronal cell body or within
the axon itself. Central axonopathy usually consists of bilateral and symmetrical
degeneration of the axon and myelin and affects both sensory and motor tracts of
the spinal cord, with the longest fibers being the most vulnerable.93 Lesions
appear as diffuse loss of myelinated fibers of varying severity in the cerebellar
white matter and/or in the dorsal funiculi and pyramidal tracts in the spinal cord
that extend into the brainstem. Clinical signs described as spinocerebellar ataxia
in several breeds can manifest as variations of general proprioception or
cerebellar ataxia and upper motor neuron (UMN) paresis (Table 244.2).

Histopathologic changes of neuronal fiber loss and astrogliosis are most severe in
the spinal cord and brainstem.

Central-Peripheral Axonopathy
The axonal degenerative diseases that selectively involve axons in the long tracts
of the CNS and in the nerve fibers of the peripheral nervous system (PNS) are
described as central-peripheral distal axonopathies. Segmental spinal reflex
abnormalities reflect PNS involvement. Disease with clinical signs and lesions
limited to the PNS are classified as neuropathies.94,95 Canine degenerative
myelopathy associated with mutations in the superoxide dismutase-1 gene
(SOD1) is a central-peripheral axonopathy of older aged dogs that affects many
breeds.96,97 A sensory central-peripheral axonopathy of maternal inheritance has
been described in Golden Retrievers.98 A central-peripheral axonopathy has been
reported in Birman cats.99

Neuroaxonal Dystrophy
Neuroaxonal dystrophies are primary disorders of axonal transport characterized
by swellings within the axons called spheroids. The “spheroids” may be indicative
of disordered trafficking of cytoskeletal elements which then accumulate in axons
or synaptic terminals and represent the histologic lesion characteristic of this
disease group.24 Because longer axons have to transport these elements farther,
spheroids are most prominent in the termination of the long proprioceptive
tracts in brainstem nuclei (i.e., nuclei gracilis and cuneatus). Affected animals
usually have progressive cerebellar ataxia and tetraparesis. Juvenile and fetal
onsets have been described in dogs and cats (Table 244.2).

NEURONOPATHIES
Neuronopathies include those disorders that affect the cell body. This is in
contrast to neuropathies, which are disorders that affect the peripheral processes;
the terms neuropathy and peripheral neuropathy are often used interchangeably
(ch. 252).

Spongiform Polioencephalopathies
The spongiform polioencephalopathies encompass a heterogeneous group of
diseases associated with neuronal spongiform changes at necropsy.100 In the
spongiform polioencephalopathies, vacuoles appear empty, and if intraneuronal,
they are not membrane-bound. Large intraneuronal vacuoles are seen in
relatively few diseases, including transmissible spongiform encephalopathies
(prion diseases), some metabolic encephalopathies, and a few viral infections
such as human immunodeficiency virus or rabies.101 Some reference sources

reserve the term spongiform encephalopathy for the TSEs, caused by an
enigmatic agent, the prion.1 The outbreak of the TSE bovine spongiform
encephalopathy (BSE) in England, and the subsequent recognition that this
disease may be spread to cats and humans by ingestion of meat products from
affected cows, has made these diseases of more general interest.102,103 The TSEs
are characterized by a long latency period and at necropsy, vacuolation of nerve
processes and to a lesser extent their cell bodies. Cats with feline spongiform
encephalopathy (FSE) show signs reminiscent of BSE: ataxia, behavioral changes,
and hyperesthesia to touch or sound. In cats, such lesions occur throughout the
gray matter of the brain.103 Control of BSE may decrease concerns of TSEs in
dogs and cats but future outbreaks are possible. Maintaining an index of
suspicion will permit early recognition of the disease.104

Hereditary Spongiform Polioencephalopathies
Hereditary spongiform polioencephalopathies have been recognized in several
breeds of dogs and cats (Table 244.2). The first sign recognized in affected <1year-old dogs is seizures. After a variable period, progressive ataxia, vestibular
signs, and thoracic limb muscle atrophy and rigidity develop, ultimately causing
recumbency.105-107 Alaskan Huskies, Rottweilers and Black Russian Terriers
show signs of polyneuropathy, ocular abnormalities, and neuronal
vacuolation.108-110 Symmetrical increased signal is apparent on T2W MRI in the
cerebellar, vestibular, and other brainstem nuclei. At necropsy, there is vacuolar
degeneration in the neuropil, astrocytes and myelin within the neurons of the
ventral horn of the spinal cord, cerebellum and brainstem (Figure 244.7).

Necrotizing Polioencephalomyelopathies

Because neurons have a high metabolic demand, they are particularly susceptible
to disturbances of energy metabolism. The selective involvement of gray matter
suggests a metabolic deficit that creates a dysfunction in neurons or glia. Clinical
signs of polioencephalopathies vary widely, but because neurons of the cerebral
cortex are often affected, seizures and behavior changes are common, as are
cerebellar ataxia and sensory or motor deficits. Thiamine deficiency (ch. 14) has
a propensity to involve the periventricular gray matter, lateral geniculate nuclei,
caudal colliculi and vestibular nuclei.111 Polioencephalomyelopathy that is
associated with altered mitochondrial metabolism has characteristic, bilaterally
symmetrical cavitating lesions of necrosis and spongy degenerative changes in
the neuropil of the thalamus, basal nuclei midbrain, and brainstem. These
changes are characteristic of subacute necrotizing encephalopathy, also referred
to as Leigh or Leigh-like syndrome in people. A mutation in the gene encoding a
brain thiamine transporter protein plays a role in the pathogenesis of necrotizing
encephalopathy in the Alaskan Husky and Yorkshire Terrier.112,113

Brain Neuronal Degenerations
Multisystem neuronal degeneration involves CNS axonopathy and neuronopathy
and, in some, neuropathy. This group of disorders can resemble the motor
neuron diseases.114 A diffuse multisystemic chromatolytic neuronopathy,
involving loss of Nissl bodies in motor neurons with or without neuron loss in the
spinal cord, brainstem and thalamus, has been reported in dogs.

MULTIPLE SYSTEMS DEGENERATIONS
When the cerebellum and basal ganglia are involved, these conditions are
referred to as multiple systems degenerations. The basal ganglia, such as the
caudate nucleus and substantia nigra, are important in movement and are
affected in Huntington’s and Parkinson’s disease in humans. The best
characterized syndrome of this type in animals is the disease of Kerry Blue
Terriers115-117 and Chinese Crested dogs118 called progressive neuronal
abiotrophy (PNA) by breeders. In these dogs, cerebellar ataxia begins at 8-12
weeks of age, and is followed at 6-12 months of age by degeneration of the basal
ganglia. As the basal ganglia degenerate, affected dogs have increasing difficulty
initiating movements and maintaining balance. Some exhibit “festination
locomotion” in which the dog begins to lose its balance and then runs in that
direction to keep from falling (Figure 244.8). The symmetrical degeneration of
the basal ganglia is visible on MRI as an increased T2 signal. The severe motor
difficulties associated with these conditions often lead to euthanasia by 1-2 years
of age.118

FIGURE 244.9 Mid-sagittal T2W magnetic resonance
images of a normal canine brain (A) and a brain from a dog

of the cerebellar cortex may be apparent as shrinkage and

the folia (B).

CEREBELLAR DEGENERATIONS
In dogs, cerebellar degeneration is in the hereditary ataxia subgroup, a
heterogeneous group of neurodegenerative diseases characterized clinically by
symmetrical cerebellar ataxia.119 Primary cerebellar cortical degeneration can be
subdivided further into diseases that primarily affect the Purkinje and/or
granular neurons. Numerous descriptions of different cerebellar degenerations
have been reported in purebred dogs and cats. Signs may manifest as neonatal,
juvenile, or adult onsets and are progressive. The age of onset and rate of
progression vary between breeds and individuals. When a hereditary basis has
been established, the most common mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive.
Routine laboratory testing and CSF analysis are normal and help rule out other
acquired causes. MRI can reveal atrophy of the cerebellum (Figure 244.9).120
Genetic tests for some of these disorders have been developed and enable a
definitive diagnosis (Table 244.2).119

METABOLIC ENCEPHALOPATHY
The metabolic encephalopathies, also known as inborn errors of metabolism, are
a heterogeneous group of disorders that affect essential metabolic pathways
involved in carbohydrate, amino acid, and fatty acid metabolism, and function of
lysosomes, mitochondria, and other organelles. Disease results from
accumulation of toxic intermediates or loss of the end-product of synthesis or of
energy production. Products that accumulate due to errors in intermediary

metabolism are typically small organic acids excreted in urine, causing organic
acidurias, while products of large macromolecule degradation that accumulate in
lysosomes cause lysosomal storage disorders. Many inborn errors of metabolism
affect other organs more readily than the brain.

ORGANIC ACIDURIAS
Pathogenesis
These diseases are characterized by the presence of abnormal organic acids in
urine due to errors in the metabolic pathways of carbohydrates, proteins, or fats.
While relatively few have been described in veterinary medicine, they are
common diseases in humans, and occur in purebred dogs (Table 244.3).

Clinical Signs
Often, waxing and waning, diffuse, symmetric encephalopathic signs occur in
affected neonates or the young. The earliest and most consistent signs are
localized to the forebrain and include abnormal mentation, behavior changes,
and seizures. Other neurologic signs vary with the regional distribution of lesions
and severity of metabolic disturbance. Fasting periods and diet may influence
severity of signs.

Diagnosis
Clinicopathologic abnormalities can include an increased anion gap, metabolic
acidosis, ketonuria, and hypoglycemia. Deficiencies in urea cycle enzymes result
in elevated blood ammonia concentrations with normal liver function. Ketonuria
or acidosis without a clear underlying cause like diabetes mellitus may reflect
errors in metabolism. If the error leads to the accumulation of an abnormal
metabolite, that product can sometimes be detected. For example, increases in
blood lactate and pyruvate are indicative of mitochondrial disorders.121 If blood
lactate levels are normal in an animal with metabolic acidosis, then an organic
aciduria is more likely. Identification of abnormal concentrations of certain
metabolites in urine can aid diagnostically, since metabolites may be excreted
renally in high concentrations and in sufficient quantities for assays to be
performed, even on small volumes of urine from neonates. Thus, urine should be
sent to a lab that can perform gas chromatography/mass spectroscopy to identify
other metabolites.122 Serum or CSF may be assayed for metabolites that are not
detected in urine, while other tests measure specific enzyme activity. Because
muscle also has a high metabolic demand, diseases affecting energy metabolism
may show changes on muscle biopsy (ch. 110).121 Some diseases show
characteristic bilateral and symmetric signal changes on brain MRI, often
involving gray matter such as the cerebral cortex and basal nuclei (Figure
244.10). Bilaterally symmetrical CNS lesions may either be manifestations of

selective susceptibility of cellular populations to altered metabolism or be
determined by vascular anatomy (ischemia). In some breeds, a mutation has
been identified in various genes coding for specific enzyme steps in energy
production pathways and causing organic acidurias (Table 244.3).

Treatment
Therapeutic intervention depends on an understanding of the pathway involved
and ability to activate an alternative pathway. Cellular malonic acid levels
regulate the use of carbohydrates or fatty acids as energy sources in the fed versus
fasted state, respectively. The B-vitamins are key cofactors in intermediary
metabolism and their supplementation should be considered in cases of
metabolic encephalopathy. In malonic aciduria, increased malonic acid blocks
utilization of fatty acids as an energy source. Affected Maltese dogs develop
seizures, stupor, hypoglycemia, acidosis, and ketonuria after a brief period of
anorexia.123 Frequent feedings of a high-carbohydrate, low-fat diet can eliminate
the need to rely on fatty acids as an energy source and ameliorate clinical signs.
Carnitine is an essential component of fatty acid metabolism and will be excreted
as conjugates with organic acids. This can lead to deficiency, requiring carnitine
supplementation.

Cobalamin Deficiency
Cobalamin (vitamin B12; ch. 262) is a necessary cofactor in the conversion of
methylmalonyl CoA to succinyl CoA, a significant step in the Krebs cycle. Typical

clinical signs of deficiency include altered mentation, inappetence, and seizures
associated with hyperammonemia and blood dyscrasia. Identifying high urinary
methylmalonic acid (MMA) and low serum cobalamin concentrations confirms
the diagnosis. Urea cycle dysfunction is a consequence of MMA accumulation.
Cobalamin deficiency has been associated with elevated urine MMA
concentrations and neurologic signs in cats.124 Clinical signs resolve with
parenteral administration of cyanocobalamin. Cats with gastrointestinal disease
can also develop a D-lactic acidosis, presumably due to excessive bacterial
production of the D isoform in the intestine.125 D-lactate is not detected by most
routine lactate assays, which are designed to detect the L isoform produced by
mammals; however, it is much more likely to produce an encephalopathy.

LYSOSOMAL STORAGE DISEASE
Pathogenesis
Lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs) are characterized by an accumulation of
metabolic byproducts within lysosomes, the cellular organelle responsible for the
breakdown of complex macromolecules. Lysosomes maintain an acidic pH and
catabolize sphingolipids (a major component of myelin), oligosaccharides,
mucopolysaccharides, glycoproteins, and proteins (Table 244.4). Storage
diseases are typically caused by a deficiency in a key enzyme, resulting in a failure
to break down molecules and therefore, pathological substrate accumulation.126129
Most syndromes are named for the accumulated product. Proteases are less
substrate-specific and single protease deficiencies are uncommon and less likely
to produce problems, although ceroid lipofuscinosis may be one such defect.
Some defects interfere with cells’ ability to utilize a normal enzyme. In I-cell
disease (mucolipidosis) of cats, for example, there appears to be a disorder of
trafficking enzymes into the lysosome, with multiple enzymes affected.130 How
accumulated storage products produce neurologic disease is not clear. In globoid
cell leukodystrophy, there is an accumulation of psychosine, a metabolite that is
toxic to myelin-forming oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells. In others, spheroid
formation may be related to neuronal death.126-128 Reviews of the LSDs in
animals provide additional details on individual syndromes.129,131-133

Clinical Signs

Accumulation of the storage product occurs over time and the onset of signs is
delayed with most storage diseases, despite enzyme deficiency since birth. The
age of onset and clinical severity can depend on residual enzyme function and on
systems affected, since some storage diseases affect multiple organs and others
only affect the nervous system. Cerebellar signs of dysmetria, truncal ataxia, and
nystagmus are often the first signs of storage diseases.127 In other patients, more
profound learning or mentation deficits may be the first indication of disease.
Signs often progress to UMN weakness, behavioral abnormalities, and seizures.
Some LSDs (e.g., neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis) cause forebrain and visual
dysfunction before cerebellar dysfunction.134 Peripheral nerves are involved in
some conditions such as globoid cell leukodystrophy, fucosidosis, glycogenosis
type IV, mannosidosis and Niemann-Pick disease.94,135 In some LSDs, signs of
other organ involvement may be apparent, such as visible retinal changes or
cataract formation, and bony and connective tissue abnormalities
(mucopolysaccharidoses, mucolipidosis and alpha-mannosidosis); radiographic
examination reveals dysmorphic bony malformations of the spine and/or face
(Table 162.1). Cardiac, hepatic, splenic or lymph node enlargement may
accompany the neurologic signs.

Diagnosis
The multisystemic distribution of lesions of LSDs affords the ability to obtain a
diagnosis from extraneural tissues. Storage vacuoles may be apparent in white
cells on a peripheral blood smear or, in the case of globoid cell leukodystrophy or
fucosidosis, on CSF analysis. Lymph nodes, liver, spleen or muscle can be
biopsied or aspirated to reveal storage vacuoles. With some LSDs, cross-sectional
imaging using MRI can show various hyperintensities and brain atrophy.127,132
Necropsy may be necessary to demonstrate storage product when only the
nervous system is involved. Electron microscopy can demonstrate that the
storage material is contained within lysosomes. Abnormal metabolites may be
detectable in urine with some of the storage diseases. Definitive diagnosis is
based on molecular testing for the known mutation (Table 244.4) and/or
demonstration of deficient enzyme activity in affected tissues, leukocytes, or
cultured fibroblasts.

Treatment
Supportive therapy for seizure control and behavior-altering drugs can help
ameliorate some of the signs. Many of the LSDs identified in dogs and cats
represent true orthologs of their respective human disease and serve as an
important intermediate-size model for the assessment of therapeutic
strategies.129,133 Enzyme replacement and viral vector-mediated therapies to
treat nervous system disease have been evaluated in the large animal models of

alpha-mannosidosis, globoid cell leukodystrophy, GM1 and GM2 gangliosidosis,
the mucopolysaccharidoses, and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis.129

NEURONAL CEROID LIPOFUSCINOSIS
Pathogenesis
Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (NCLs), known as Batten disease, are a subset of
LSDs in which the storage products are proteins with characteristic
autofluorescence, similar to ceroid and lipofuscin, which accumulate normally
with aging. The storage products in NCL are subunit c of mitochondrial ATP or
sphingolipid activator proteins (saposins A and D), due to deficient soluble
enzymes. Membrane proteins are located in the lysosome, endoplasmic reticulum
or synaptic vesicle-associated proteins.136

Clinical Signs
Clinical signs include progressive visual impairment (usually the first sign,
especially in dim light), decline in cognition and motor functions, seizures,
generalized brain atrophy and premature death in young to middle age. Behavior
changes become prominent with disease progression and include timidness,
hyperesthesia, confusion, and unprovoked aggression. Seizures, jaw chomping,
bruxism, and myoclonus are also reported. Proprioceptive and cerebellar ataxia
tend to be later manifestations in many breeds, although they are the most
prominent sign in American Bulldogs with cathepsin D deficiency.137

Diagnosis
Generalized brain atrophy can be seen on cross-sectional imaging in later stages
of the disease but a definitive diagnosis requires histologic recognition of
autofluorescent material in the brain or other tissues (Figure 244.11).
Mutations responsible for many of the canine NCLs have been identified and
DNA tests are available (Table 244.4).134

Treatment
Gene therapy, stem cell therapy and enzyme replacement therapy hold the
promise of restoring function to affected individuals.134 Supportive therapy for
seizure control and behavior altering drugs can help ameliorate some of the signs.

SLEEP DISORDERS
Sleep is a complex physiologic process driven by an active neurobehavioral state
maintained by the CNS. Ultimately, sleep plays an essential restorative function

for both physical and cognitive purposes and is an indispensable function for
health. Naturally occurring sleep disorders are uncommon in cats and dogs. In all
types of sleep disorders, the condition can vary from subtle to severe, but may
also indicate another underlying neurological disease. Having some familiarity
with both normal and abnormal sleep can assist in diagnosing sleep associated
abnormalities.138

NORMAL SLEEP
In mammals, the sleep-wake cycle is composed of 3 different states: wakefulness;
non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, also known as slow-wave sleep; and
rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Cycles of NREM and REM sleep occur in dogs
and cats, wherein NREM sleep lasts for ∼20 minutes and REM sleep follows for
∼10-15 minutes.139 These states are distinguished by electrophysiology and
behavioral characteristics. Electroencephalographic (EEG) activity during NREM
sleep is synchronized with a predominance of slow frequency and high amplitude
waves. In contrast, during wakefulness and REM sleep the EEG is
desynchronized with high frequency and low amplitude oscillations. Muscle
activity is high during wakefulness, reduced during NREM sleep and absent
during REM sleep, except for respiratory muscles and twitching of the face and
limbs.
The main wakefulness-promoting areas of the brain are in the ascending
reticular activating system (ARAS) and basal forebrain. Additionally, a group of
neurons located in the ventrolateral hypothalamus release hypocretins/orexins
that are involved in appetite, energy homeostasis, neuroendocrine functions, and
wake promotion. In wakefulness, the hypocretin-producing hypothalamic
neurons project onto many mesencephalic and pontine monoaminergic and
cholinergic nuclei involved in sleep and wake control. The released
hypocretinergic neuropeptides (Hcrt 1 and 2) are excitatory to both
monoaminergic and cholinergic systems, with stronger effects on monoaminergic
tone (Figure 244.12).140 The monoaminergic neurons in the locus coeruleus
release norepinephrine, while those in the dorsal raphe release serotonin and
those in the mammillary center release histamine, all of which inhibit
acetylcholine in the pontine reticular formation. Normally, the medullary
reticular formation center is activated by acetylcholine released from neurons in
the pontine reticular formation center. Thus, the dorsal pontine tegmentum
indirectly inhibits alpha motor neurons in the spinal cord through multiple
pathways that project to the medulla.

FIGURE 244.11 Mid-sagittal (A) and axial (B) magnetic
resonance images at the level of the thalamus of a long-haired
miniature Dachshund with neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis.
Note the generalized brain atrophy with increased
cerebrospinal fluid hyperintensity between the gyri (arrows) of
the cerebrum and folia (asterisk) of the cerebellum, and
ventriculomegaly. A diagnosis of neuronal ceroid
lipofuscinoses was based on the autofluorescent material
(arrows) in neurons (C). Courtesy Martin L. Katz, University
of Missouri.
During sleep, the hypocretin neurons fall silent and gamma-aminobutyric acid
(GABA) is released from neurons in the pons, inhibiting serotonergic and
noradrenergic transmission (Figure 244.12). In NREM sleep, decreased
hypocretin tone reduces monoaminergic and cholinergic activity. However, in
REM sleep, the depressed monoaminergic tone is so complete that cholinergic
systems are disinhibited. These cholinergic neurons then project to spinal cord
glycinergic inhibitory interneurons, hyperpolarizing motor neurons and resulting
in the atonia observed during REM sleep.

REM SLEEP BEHAVIOR DISORDER
While normal animals might display a degree of twitching and vocalization
during REM sleep, pathological loss of the normal inhibition of select lower
motor neuron ventral horn cells leads to violent limb movements and potentially
aggressive behavior during this phase of sleep – in other words, REM without
atonia. This abnormal and excessive manifestation of dream activity is termed
REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) and it has been described in dogs and
cats.141-143 With RBD sleep, repeated violent limb and facial movements, air
chewing or chewing the surrounding objects in the air, aggressive behavior, and
vocalizations have been described. Arousal from REM sleep is quick and
complete, with little confusion, ataxia, or dullness, which is in contrast to a
seizure. Diagnosis of RBD relies on owner descriptions of the characteristic
behaviors and examination of video and EEG recordings during the sleep events.
Apparent RBD is a common sequel to tetanus in dogs.144 Tetanospasmin binding
and its subsequent prevention of GABA release result in loss of inhibitory basal

nuclei output and inappropriate activation of motor centers with failure of
muscle atony during REM sleep. An RBD also has been reported as a key
phenotype in young adult Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retrievers with caudate
nuclei necrosis and axonal dystrophy.145 Treatment success in RBD has been
variable. Potassium bromide (44 mg/kg PO q24h) decreases the severity and
frequency of client-reported RBD events in 78% of treated dogs.142

SLEEP-DISORDERED BREATHING OR SLEEP
APNEA
Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) encompasses any breathing difficulty
occurring during sleep, ranging from partial obstructive snoring to complete
cessation of breathing.146 Brachycephalic dogs with short muzzles are
predisposed to the conformation-related respiratory disorder brachycephalic
obstructive airway syndrome or simply brachycephalic syndrome (BOAS/BS; ch.
213).147,148 The severity of sleep apnea correlates with alterations in muscles
that dilate the upper airways.149 The English Bulldog, proposed as a naturally
occurring model of SDB, has marked oxygen deprivation in REM sleep,
paradoxical breathing patterns, and can be awakened by events of apnea.150,151
Additionally, SBD has been documented in French Bulldogs, Pugs, CKCSs, and
Chihuahuas.152-154 Clinical signs reported by pet owners include waking up in
association with breath holding or in distress, with gasping or choking; low
activity levels or sleeping while sitting/standing; apneic episodes; and seeking a
specific sleeping position.152 Dogs ultimately develop hypersomnolence and
other health issues, which impact quality of life (ch. 213).153 Surgical
intervention depends on the severity of the obstructive anatomy to relieve the
obstructions; in many cases, the sleep problems resolve after BOAS/BS
surgery.152,155

NARCOLEPSY
Pathophysiology
The causes of canine narcolepsy are primary (inherited) or secondary (acquired,
sporadic).156-158 Narcolepsy is a recessive trait in Doberman Pinschers, Labrador
Retrievers and Dachshunds. In each breed, it is caused by a different variant
within the hypocretin receptor gene (HCRTR2).159,160 Loss of hypocretin
receptor function in monoaminergic neurons decreases monoaminergic tone and
produces a cholinergic–aminergic imbalance consistent with the
hypersomnolence and abnormal REM sleep in narcolepsy. Hypoactivity of

monoaminergic systems and widespread hypersensitivity to cholinergic
stimulation underlies the mechanism of cataplexy in canine narcolepsy.161
Similar to REM sleep, cataplexy is controlled by pontine cholinergic REM-on
cells and monoaminergic sites REM-off cells (Figure 244.12).162 Both increased
dopamine levels (consistently reported in the amygdala) and decreased histamine
levels in the brains of dogs with narcolepsy play roles in emotion-associated
events and excessive sleepiness.163,164

FIGURE 244.12 Hypothetical model illustrating the
influence of hypocretin, monoaminergic and cholinergic
activity in wakefulness, sleep and narcolepsy. Red and green
lines indicate inhibitory and excitatory projections,
respectively. During wakefulness, high hypocretin tone drives
high cholinergic and monoaminergic tone. During non-rapid
eye movement (NREM) sleep, decreased hypocretin tone
reduces monoaminergic and cholinergic activity. During rapid
eye movement (REM) sleep, the depressed monoaminergic
tone is so complete that cholinergic systems are disinhibited.
Note, hypocretin activity is depressed and absent during
NREM and REM sleep, respectively. During sleep, inhibitory
GABAergic projections to monoaminergic cell groups are also
likely to be critical. In canine narcolepsy, there is absence of
hypocretin cretin receptor 2 in dogs with the Hctr2 mutation.
The narcoleptic/cataplectic attacks are a result of cholinergic
supersensitivity and monoaminergic hypoactivity. 5-HT,
Serotonin; Ach, acetylcholine; DA, dopamine; GABA, gamma
aminobutyric acid; Hcrt, hypocretin; Hist, histamine; LMNs,
lower motor neurons; MRFC, medullary reticular formation
center. Modified from Hungs M, Mignot E. Hypocretin/orexin,
sleep and narcolepsy. BioEssays. 2001;23:397-408.

Secondary or acquired narcolepsy describes cases with detectable or suspected
underlying causes, such as hypothalamic neoplasms, head trauma, and
encephalitis.165-167

Clinical Signs
Narcolepsy is an episodic disorder that causes excessive daytime sleepiness and
immediate-onset REM sleep after an emotional trigger (e.g., eating, exercise,
play).168 Episodes often are associated with cataplexy – periods of acute
muscular hypotonia, which can last up to 20 minutes. Patterns on EEG during a
narcoleptic/cataplexic event resemble those during wakefulness or REM sleep. In
familial narcoleptics, the clinical signs often occur as early as 4 weeks of age, and
severity and the age of onset tends to plateau at 6 months.169 In acquired cases,
the median age is ∼2 years.165,170

Diagnosis
A diagnosis is based on clinical signs and observation of induced events with
feeding or play. It is important to rule out other episodic events like seizures or
syncope. Attacks of cataplexy can be assessed very quickly by using the foodelicited cataplexy test (FECT

, Video 244.2).162 Administration of a centrally

active acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (physostigmine salicylate; 0.025-0.1 mg/kg
IV) increases the frequency of cataplectic attacks within 15 minutes in narcoleptic
dogs but has no effect on normal dogs. This provocative test is used for milder
cases. A low starting dosage reduces adverse cholinergic effects. CSF hypocretin
levels define the pathophysiologic mechanism of the narcolepsy-cataplexy
episodes; however, it is difficult to find a laboratory that performs the assay.
Narcoleptic dogs with the HCRTR2 mutation have normal hypocretin levels in
CSF and brain, whereas levels have been found to be very low or absent in
sporadic canine narcolepsy cases.171,172 If acquired narcolepsy is suspected, the
occurrence of cataplectic episodes should prompt a thorough diagnostic work-up
to exclude the presence of other intracranial (and extracranial) disease.165 DNA
testing is recommended for familial cases.

Treatment
Although usually not progressive, narcolepsy affects the quality of life for the pet
and pet owner. Treatment of narcolepsy is aimed at reducing the frequency and
duration of cataplexy.168 Dogs with mild signs of cataplexy are treated by
avoiding the inciting cause such as limiting play or feeding separately in multiplepet households. Pharmacologic treatment through activation of the
monoaminergic systems inhibits cataplexy.162 Drugs that have been used for
treating narcolepsy in dogs fall into 3 classes. Tricyclic antidepressants include

imipramine (0.5-1 mg/kg PO q8-12h; monitor for sedation, anticholinergic
effects [tachycardia, hyperexcitability, tremor]), clomipramine (1-3 mg/kg PO
q12-24h; monitor for emesis, diarrhea, sedation, anticholinergic effects as above),
and desipramine (3 mg/kg PO q12h; monitor for same effects as above).
Serotonin/norepinephrine/dopamine reuptake inhibitors include venlafaxine
(2.5 mg/kg PO q12h; no cholinergic side-effects expected) and methylphenidate
(0.25-0.5 mg/kg PO q24h; monitor for seizures, excitement, tachycardia,
tremor). Alpha-2 adrenergic antagonists (presynapse) include yohimbine (0.045
mg/kg IV; monitor for seizures, excitement, ptyalism). For first-line therapy, the
author recommends starting with imipramine at the lowest dosage in range and
titrating up to an effective dose. When using these drugs, it is important to adjust
dosage to effect and to monitor for drug tolerance. The FECT can also be used for
assessing the efficacy of a treatment. Dogs with acquired narcolepsy will also
require treatment for the underlying disease process.

EPIDEMIOLOGY AND CLASSIFICATION OF BRAIN
NEOPLASMS
Brain tumors are a common cause of morbidity and death in middle-aged to geriatric dogs
and cats.1-6 Estimated incidences of canine and feline nervous system tumors have been
reported as 14.5 cases per 100,000 and 3.5 cases per 100,000 at risk, respectively.7,8
Intracranial neoplasms are observed in 2.0% to 4.5% of dogs and 2% of cats subjected to
necropsy.1,8-10
Classification of tumors of the nervous system bifurcates tumors into primary and
secondary origins (Table 245.1).1-4 Primary brain tumors (PBTs) arise from the
constitutive tissues of the brain such as the meninges, glia, and neurons. Secondary brain
tumors (SBTs) represent those cancers that metastasize to the brain from a distant organ
or invade nervous tissue via direct extension from a tissue adjacent to the brain, such as
may occur with nasal or calvarial tumors.4
Brain tumors are further classified using morphologic criteria modeled after World
Health Organization (WHO) criteria applied to human tumors,11 which relies on
traditional principles of histogenesis where light microscopic phenotypic features define
the various tumor types, with each tumor type putatively originating from a different
cellular lineage (Table 245.1). Brain tumors are also graded, with the grade being a
numeric score that represents the potential biologic behavior of the tumor. Tumor grades
are assigned on the basis of presence and degree of cytoarchitectural features of
malignancy, such as cellular atypia, nuclear pleomorphism, mitotic rate, microvascular
proliferation, and necrosis.11 Depending on tumor type, tumor grades may range from I to
IV. Grade I (low-grade) tumors are well differentiated, with low proliferative potential,
whereas grade IV tumors are anaplastic, mitotically active, rapidly progressive cancers.
The classification of canine gliomas has recently been revised and now utilizes a binary
grading schema, with tumors considered either low- or high-grade.12
It is important to recognize, however, that within the enclosed space of the calvarium,
even slow-growing grade I tumors with benign phenotypes will cause progressive
morbidity and the eventual death of the animal in the absence of therapy, due to the
development of uncompensated intracranial hypertension (ICH). Prospective application
of the WHO criteria in animal populations with brain tumors is ongoing to determine if
this classification system can provide clinically useful correlations between histologic
features of a tumor, its biologic behavior, and therapeutic outcomes in a manner that
exists for other veterinary cancers, such as mast cell tumors.13 As the fundamental genetic
aberrations that drive canine and feline brain tumorigenesis continue to be elucidated, it
is likely that veterinary brain tumor classification will evolve to incorporate classic

phenotypic, genotypic, and molecular information into the definition of neoplastic entities
similar to the paradigm that is currently used in humans.14

CANINE BRAIN TUMORS
Meningiomas (45%), gliomas (40%) and choroid plexus tumors (CPTs; 5%) account for
∼90% of canine PBTs encountered in clinical practice (Table 245.1).1,8,10,25 Numerous
other types of PBTs are rarely reported in dogs, including granular cell tumors, primary
central nervous system (CNS) lymphomas, primitive neuroectodermal tumors (PNETs),
gliomatosis cerebri, ependymomas, and primary CNS histiocytic sarcoma.1,2,15-20
Necropsy-based studies indicate that ∼50% of all canine intracranial tumors are SBTs,
with hemangiosarcoma (29-35%, ch. 325), pituitary tumors (11-25%, ch. 293),
lymphoma (12-20%, ch. 322), and metastatic carcinomas (11-20%) accounting for the
majority of canine SBTs.1,4,16
Brain tumors in dogs may occur at any age and in any breed, with the majority of
studies reporting no significant sex predispositions for the various tumor types.1,19-21
Most brain tumors occur in middle-aged to older dogs, with the majority of cases
described being >5 years of age. The median ages at diagnosis for dogs with meningiomas,
gliomas, and CPTs are 10.5, 8, and 5.5 years, respectively.1,2,20,21 There is a propensity for
PBTs in juvenile animals to be anaplastic tumors of neuroepithelial origin.1,22 A
significant and linear relationship was demonstrated between age and body weight and
the occurrence of PBTs, and large-breed dogs are at increased risk for developing
meningiomas and CPTs.1
Golden Retrievers, Boxers, Miniature Schnauzers, and Rat Terriers are breeds in which
intracranial meningiomas are overrepresented.1,2,10,20 Although CPTs were
overrepresented in Golden Retrievers in one study,21 this breed predisposition was not
corroborated in a later report.1 Brachycephalic breeds of dogs, such as the Boxer, Boston
Terrier, Bullmastiff, and English and French Bulldogs, are at significantly increased risk
for developing astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas (Video 245.1

).1,2 A locus on

canine chromosome (CFA) 26 is also strongly associated with glioma across multiple dog
breeds, with subsequent mapping of the region revealing single nucleotide variants in
three neighboring genes (DENR, CAMKK2, and P2RX7) that are highly associated with
glioma susceptibility.23 The CAMKK2 and P2RX7 genes have been previously recognized
as relevant to the development or progression of human cancers.23 Corgis and Shetland
Sheepdogs are predisposed to developing primary CNS histiocytic sarcoma (ch. 328).19

FELINE BRAIN TUMORS
Approximately 70% of all feline intracranial tumors are PBTs, and >50% of feline PBTs
are meningiomas.3,9,24 Other PBTs, such as gliomas, ependymomas, and CPTs, are rarely
reported in cats (Table 245.1).3,9,24,25 Lymphomas and pituitary tumors account for
∼50% and 30%, respectively, of all feline SBTs.3 The median age at diagnosis of cats with
meningioma is 11 years, while neuroepithelial tumors and lymphoma are typically seen in
cats in the 7-8 year age range.3,24,25 Neutered male, domestic shorthair cats are
predisposed to developing gliomas.25

CLINICAL SIGNS
As the majority of PBT manifest as solitary mass lesions, they are classically associated
with chronic and progressive signs of focal brain dysfunction referable to the anatomic
location of the tumor (Video 245.1

; ch. 241). In both dogs and cats, tumors involving

forebrain structures are more common than those arising in the brainstem.1-3,25,26
Seizures are the most common clinical presentation of PBTs in dogs, and occur in 50-70%
of dogs with forebrain tumors (ch. 45).2,26-28 Clinical suspicion for the presence of brain
tumor should increase in those dogs that experience a new-onset seizure after 5 years of
age, especially in breeds with known predispositions to brain tumors.27 Tumors involving
the frontal lobe, associated with falcine or subtentorial brain herniations, and

demonstrating marked contrast enhancement increase the risk for developing tumorassociated structural epilepsy in dogs.28 Dogs with PBT and seizures may have a normal
interictal neurological examination, especially when the tumors involve the rostral frontal
or olfactory lobes of the brain.27 Depressed levels of consciousness and abnormal
behaviors (Video 245.2
) are also frequently reported clinical signs associated with
canine brain tumors, and personality and behavioral changes are the most common
reported concern in cats with brain tumors, being observed in 16-67% of feline cases.3,29
The incidence of brain tumor-associated epilepsy is lower in cats than in dogs, with ∼25%
of cats with brain tumors experiencing seizures.3,24,29 Seizures are reportedly more
common in cats with gliomas (27%) and lymphomas (26%) compared to meningioma
(15%).24
In animals with tumors arising in the brainstem, central vestibular dysfunction (ch.
248) is the most common clinical manifestation.26,27 In >20% of cats with brain tumors,
chief concerns are nonspecific in nature, including lethargy and hyporexia, with owners
not observing any overt clinical signs referable to the brain.3 Nonspecific clinical concerns
are frequently reported in dogs with pituitary tumors.30

Although PBT are classically associated with focal clinical signs of brain dysfunction,
multifocal clinical signs are observed in 25-50% of PBT cases, which result from the tumor
or its secondary effects involving multiple brain regions.2,29 The most frequent reasons
PBT cause multifocal signs are: 1) a large tumor volume that expands across multiple
brain regions, 2) the induction of extensive regional vasogenic brain edema by the tumor,
and 3) tumor associated mass effect that compromises adjacent brain regions or
structures (Figure 245.1). Multiple, discrete tumor masses may also be present, which
occurs in ∼20% of cats with meningiomas, and also occasionally in canine meningiomas
and histiocytic sarcoma.3,31,32 Some uncommon PBTs, such as gliomatosis cerebri and
butterfly gliomas, are defined by diffuse brain involvement (Figure 245.1).17,33 Canine
gliomas may also manifest with multifocal or diffuse leptomeningeal spread, and gliomas
and choroid plexus carcinomas may metastasize within the CNS by a unique mechanism

termed drop metastases, in which cancer cells are exfoliated into the subarachnoid space
or CNS ventricular system with eventual distant implantation of tumor foci.21,34
Changes in mentation, seizures, and vestibular signs are also common neurologic signs
associated with SBTs, and SBTs also more commonly affect the forebrain than the
brainstem.4 However, 20-40% animals with SBT have no specific neurologic signs and
present with systemic signs that can be attributed to their tumor, such as polyuria or
polydipsia in cases with functional pituitary tumors (chs. 293, 294), or circulatory
collapse in animals with hemoabdomen or pericardial effusion associated with
hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325).4,30 SBTs that spread hematogenously often result in
multiple metastases within the brain, which can be associated with multifocal clinical
signs (Figure 245.1).
Abrupt changes in the neurological status of animals with brain tumors is frequently the
result of elevated intracranial pressure (ICP). ICH, which is a temporally sustained
elevation of ICP above physiologic reference ranges, predisposes the animal to developing
acute brain herniations (Figures 245.1 and 245.2).35-38 Clinical signs classically
associated with brain herniations include a depressed level of consciousness (ranging from
stupor to coma; ch. 44), anisocoria, reduced to absent pupillary light reflexes,
decerebrate or decerebellate rigidity, nystagmus, and alterations in cardiorespiratory rates
or patterns (Video 245.3

; ch. 241).37,38 Caudal transtentorial (CTH) and foramen

magnum (FMH) herniations are the most clinically relevant terminal manifestations of
ICH (Figure 245.1).36,37 CTH compresses the midbrain, which can cause oculomotor
nerve nucleus dysfunction, resulting in strabismus and a mydriatic pupil that is
unresponsive to light stimulation in the eye ipsilateral the side of the herniation, in
addition to changes in consciousness and body posture. Acute FMH, which is
characterized by caudal displacement of the cerebellar vermis into or through the foramen
magnum, can cause death, nystagmus, head tilt, gag reflex deficits, tongue weakness, or
alterations in respiratory rhythms. Unfortunately, the clinical examination is poorly
sensitive for the detection of ICH, as many animals have no or nonspecific signs associated
with CTH or FMH.36-38 Neurological abnormalities (ch. 241) referable to brain
herniations, such as cranial nerve deficits, abnormalities of consciousness, and body
postural abnormalities, are absent in 64-86% of dogs and cats with CTH or FMH.36-38
Animals with more than one type of brain herniation are more likely to have clinical
evidence of brainstem dysfunction.37

FIGURE 245.2 Intracranial pressure (ICP) wave recordings
obtained in dogs with brain tumors using an intraparenchymal
strain-gauge microsensor transducer.36 A, ICP tracing from a dog
with a mean, time-averaged ICP of 9.2 mm Hg, which is within

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
PBTs and SBTs are space-occupying intracranial masses that cause clinical signs of brain
disease by directly compressing or invading brain tissue.5 Tumors also induce secondary
local and regional effects in the brain, such as peritumoral edema, neuroinflammation,
obstructive hydrocephalus, alterations in neuronal and glial signaling, and intracranial
hemorrhage that can cause or contribute to the development of clinical signs.5,35,39
Ultimately, it is often disruption in ICP homeostasis that results in clinical deterioration
in animals with brain tumors. The ICP can be effectively maintained within physiologic
ranges in the early stages of tumor growth through compensatory autoregulatory
mechanisms, such as decreased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) production and shunting of CSF
into the spinal subarachnoid space.35,37 The rate of change of ICP is dependent on several
factors including tumor growth kinetics, the biophysical properties of the tumor, its
invasiveness into the adjacent brain, and the location of the tumor in the brain, and it has

been demonstrated that tumor volume is positively correlated with ICP in dogs with brain
tumors.35,36 It is possible to directly measure ICP in dogs and cats using a variety of
sensing instrumentation, and ICP monitoring can identify trends in ICP and ICH that
facilitate case management (Figure 245.2).36 However, as direct ICP monitoring is
invasive—requiring the placement of subdural, intraparenchymal, or intraventricular
catheters or leads in the brain—it is rarely performed in clinical practice. Clinicians more
often rely on indirect magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) indicators of ICH, such as the
presence of brain herniations, mass effect, and increased optic nerve sheath
diameter.36,38
For some slow-growing tumors, ICP-volume homeostatic regulatory mechanisms can
remain surprisingly intact despite sizeable tumor volumes.36 However, with progressive
increases in the volume of intracranial contents due to increases in tumor volume,
intracranial hemorrhage, or interstitial or vasogenic edema, autoregulatory mechanisms
become overwhelmed and ICH develops. ICH, and the resulting detrimental decrease in
cerebral perfusion pressure, is the common pathophysiologic denominator underlying the
acute clinical deterioration that may be observed in animals with brain tumors (Figure
245.2).37,38 Acute ICH can also trigger Cushing’s reflex in the animal, which is
characterized by an abrupt, severe elevation in systolic blood pressure, widening pulse
pressure variation, and bradycardia.

DIAGNOSIS
The signalment, history, and physical and neurologic examinations findings will
determine if intracranial neoplasia is an appropriate differential diagnosis in an individual
patient (ch. 241). A brain tumor should be considered as a differential diagnosis in any
middle-aged or older animal with a history and examination findings consistent with
acute or chronic brain dysfunction, especially if clinical signs are focal and progressive.5,27
In addition to brain tumors, differential diagnoses in dogs and cats with focal intracranial
disease include malformations (ch. 244), infectious or immune-mediated
meningoencephalitis (ch. 242), traumatic brain injury (ch. 246), and cerebrovascular
accidents (ch. 243). For those animals with clinical signs of multifocal or diffuse brain
disease, metabolic disorders (ch. 244), neurodegenerative diseases (ch. 244), and
meningoencephalitides (ch. 242) should be also considered.

LABORATORY MINIMUM DATABASE AND PREANESTHETIC SCREENING TESTS
Performance of a complete blood count, biochemical profile, and urinalysis is important to
further evaluate the general health status of animals with suspected brain tumors, as
anesthesia is recommended and necessary to obtain the diagnostics with the highest yield
(i.e., MRI scans [ch. 112], CSF analysis [ch. 109], tumor biopsy) in cases with structural
brain disease. As the populations at greatest risk for intracranial neoplasia are middleaged to older animals, the laboratory minimum database may also facilitate identification
of significant comorbidities that could impact case management.2,40
Thoracic radiographs and an abdominal ultrasound should be considered to screen for
other significant concurrent disease. Synchronous, unrelated neoplasms occur in 3-23% of

dogs with PBTs, the majority of which involve the thoracic or abdominal cavities.2,40,41
However, although abnormalities are frequently identified on thoracic radiographs and
abdominal ultrasound exams in dogs with PBT, studies suggest that the results of these
procedures uncommonly (1.3%) negatively affected the decision to pursue advanced
diagnostics that were indicated to diagnose the neurological condition of the animal.40,41
Findings from thoracic radiographic and abdominal ultrasonographic examinations have
been demonstrated to significantly alter therapeutic recommendations in 8% of brain
tumor cases.40,41

DIAGNOSTIC NEUROIMAGING (CH. 112)
Cross-sectional imaging modalities, such as computed tomography (CT) and MRI, are the
principal tools in the clinical diagnosis and management of brain tumors in veterinary
medicine.41-44 Skull radiography is rarely helpful for the diagnosis of PBT, although
radiographs can be useful when evaluating cases of SBT originating from the calvarium
(Figure 245.3). MRI is the preferred imaging modality for the evaluation of cases with
clinical signs of intracranial disease. Imaging data obtained from MRI examinations such
as the number of lesions, distribution and origin within the neuraxis (extra-axial
[extraparenchymal origin], intra-axial [intraparenchymal origin], or intraventricular) and
intrinsic signal properties of the lesion, often collectively provide characteristic patterns
that allow for the presumptive diagnosis of common PBTs and SBTs (Table 245.2).42,43
In general, the specificity of MR imaging is high (∼95%) for detecting PBT, although the
sensitivity is significantly lower (60-85%) for all types of PBT.42,46 It is crucial to
recognize that an MRI examination interpreted as normal does not exclude the possibility
of a brain tumor; diffuse tumors such lymphoma and gliomatosis cerebri are notorious for
their tendency to be associated with normal imaging studies.17
Meningiomas (Figure 245.3) are the most frequently diagnosed tumor of extra-axial
origin in dogs and cats.3,20,24,31 MRI features of meningiomas typically include a broadbase of attachment to the skull, well-defined tumor margination, and marked and often
uniform contrast enhancement (Figures 245.1, A and 245.2; Table 245.2).
Meningiomas may also contain intratumoral fluid, cysts, or mineralization, and can be
associated with a dural tail sign or calvarial hyperostosis.5,20,44 The dural tail sign is
characterized by a contrast-enhancing, linear thickening of the dura mater extending from
an adjacent extra-axial mass. However, a dural tail sign is not pathognomonic for
meningioma, nor for neoplastic diseases in general.47 Peritumoral edema is observed in
the majority of canine meningiomas (Figure 245.1, B).20,42,43 Reported sensitivities of
MRI to identify intracranial meningiomas in dogs and cats range from 60-100%, but
specific grades and histologic subtypes of meningioma cannot be distinguished using
standard MRI sequences.20,42,46,48 Histiocytic sarcomas, granular cell tumors, and
hemangioblastomas have MRI features that overlap considerably with those of
meningiomas.15,44
Gliomas (i.e., astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas) originate within the neuropil, and
thus appear as expansile intra-axial mass lesions that may displace or invade the brain
parenchyma (Figure 245.3).42-45 Gliomas can appear poorly marginated, and may or
may not demonstrate enhancement following intravenous contrast administration.42-45,49

The type and degree of contrast enhancement can be highly variable among those gliomas
that do enhance, although high-grade tumors are more likely to demonstrate contrast
enhancement.49 Classically, a pattern of ring enhancement has been associated with
gliomas (Figure 245.3), although ring enhancement is a nonspecific finding that can also
be observed in vascular and inflammatory brain diseases.46,52 It is not possible to
accurately discriminate types of gliomas or predict glioma grade using conventional CT
and MRI techniques and sequences.45,50 As the imaging features of gliomas,
cerebrovascular accidents, and inflammatory lesions can be quite similar, these categories
of intra-axial lesions are frequently misclassifed.50-52 Performing functional MRI
techniques, such as diffusion-weighted, spectroscopic, and perfusion-weighted imaging
sequences, in series with conventional MRI sequences, has shown promise in improving
the differentiation of neoplastic from non-neoplastic brain lesions.53,54
CPTs (Figure 245.3) are the most common intraventricular tumors, and these tumors
often uniformly contrast enhance or are associated with obstructive hydrocephalus.21
Choroid plexus carcinomas can be discriminated from choroid plexus papillomas if
intraventricular or subarachnoid metastatic tumor implants are identified on MRI exams.
Other intraventricular tumors that occur occasionally or rarely include meningiomas,
oligodendrogliomas, primitive neuroectodermal tumors and ependymomas.2,3,18
The imaging features of some type of SBTs, such as pituitary tumors and multilobular
osteochondrosarcomas, have been described elsewhere (Figure 245.3).55,56 The
majority of pituitary tumors are homogenously contrast-enhancing, and 40-60% of
pituitary tumors will compress the overlying brain (ch. 302). Invasive pituitary adenomas
tend to be significantly larger and have a more irregular shape than pituitary adenomas.55

CEREBROSPINAL FLUID ANALYSIS (CH. 109)
Sampling CSF in brain tumor patients with ICH carries the risk of causing clinical
deterioration. Although the incidence of serious adverse events arising from CSF
collection is low, risk must be thoroughly assessed in each case and evaluated in context of
the likelihood of obtaining a nonspecific test result.57 Diagnostic imaging examinations of
the brain should be obtained prior to the collection of CSF, to best evaluate an individual
animal’s risk for presumptive ICH and thus potential complications from CSF
collection.36
Generally, CSF analysis provides information that is complementary to the clinical
examination and diagnostic imaging results, which collectively assist the clinician with
refining the list of differential diagnosis. CSF abnormalities are extremely sensitive
indicators of intracranial disease, and the CSF is often abnormal in patients with brain
tumors.58,59 However, the severity of elevated CSF total protein concentrations and types
of pleocytosis that can be observed are highly variable and often nonspecific for neoplastic
disease or tumor type.57-59 CSF analysis assists discrimination of choroid plexus
carcinomas from papillomas, as a CSF total protein concentration >80 mg/dL (>0.8 g/L)
was exclusively associated with a carcinoma diagnosis.21 Identification of exfoliated
neoplastic cells cytologically on CSF occasionally allows for definitive diagnosis of a brain
tumor. Although neoplastic cells may be observed in the CSF from animals with any type
of brain tumor, lymphoma, histiocytic sarcoma, and CPTs are most frequently reported

(Figure 245.4).2,16,19,21 Definitive diagnoses of lymphoma, histiocytic sarcoma, or CPTs
were made cytologically from CSF in 68%, 52%, and 47%, respectively, of dogs with these
neoplasms in which CSF analysis was performed.16,19,21

ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY (EEG)
Electroencephalographic examinations have provided information that supported the
existence of a focal pathologic process within the brain in ∼67% of cases with cerebral
tumors, but no EEG patterns identified were specific for tumor type or location.60 EEG
abnormalities found in dogs with brain tumors commonly included slow-wave activity and
asymmetries in the waveform amplitudes and frequencies. EEG recordings can be helpful
in the management of brain tumor patients by confirming or excluding the presence of a
seizure disorder in animals presenting with paroxysmal events or unusual or stereotypical
behavioral abnormalities.61

TUMOR BIOPSY AND HISTOPATHOLOGY
Despite the utility and widespread clinical use of MRI for the presumptive diagnosis of
brain masses, histopathologic examination of representative tissue is required for the
definitive diagnosis and grading of brain tumors.62-64 Excisional biopsy performed during
surgical removal of the brain tumor is the most frequently employed biopsy technique
currently performed in veterinary practice, but these types of procedures historically have
been limited to patients with extra-axial, superficial forebrain or cerebellar tumors. In
cases where the brain lesion may not be amenable to surgical resection, stereotactic brain
biopsy (SBB) techniques can provide an alternative means for effectively sampling the
lesion for diagnosis.62-64
Numerous SBB techniques have been described in dogs and cats with brain tumors
including frame-based, frameless neuronavigational, and image-guided procedures,
although the vast majority of reported SBB performed in animals with naturally occurring
intracranial tumors have been frame-based (Figure 245.5).62-66 When frame-based SBB
is performed by experienced neurosurgeons, targets located throughout the brain
including deep subcortical and brainstem lesions can be accurately sampled.62-64 In dogs
with intracranial neoplasia, the diagnostic yield of frame-based SBB approaches 95%, and
serious adverse events occur in ∼5% of cases.62,64,66 Dogs with platelet counts
<185,000/mm3 or with brain tumors that display heterogeneous signal on T2W sequences
are at increased risk for developing complications after SBB.66 Rapid and accurate
intraoperative cytologic diagnosis of the tumor type is possible when performed on SBB

specimens (Figure 245.5).64 The histologic classification and grading of poorly
differentiated brain tumors can be challenging when evaluating the limited sample sizes
associated with SBB, but the diagnosis can be facilitated with additional
immunohistochemical evaluation of tumors (Figure 245.5).65,67

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
There are five approaches to the treatment of brain tumors: 1) palliative care, 2) surgical
cytoreduction, 3) radiation treatment (RT), 4) chemotherapy, and 5) investigational
therapeutics. These modalities are frequently used in various combinations. There
remains a considerable knowledge gap with respect to evidence-based data regarding
tumor type-specific therapeutic outcomes for many PBTs, as well as a lack of large and
rigorously designed trials comparing treatment modalities.5,6 Veterinary studies
evaluating the treatment of brain tumors frequently contain significant limitations such as
the inclusion of cases with no histopathologic diagnoses, small case numbers, nonuniform
treatment protocols, variable primary endpoints and survival definitions, and study
designs that do not include unbiased control groups, objective assessments of tumor
response such as imaging-based follow-up, or other quantitative outcome metrics of
therapeutic efficacy.5,6

PALLIATIVE CARE
The goals of palliative therapies are to transiently control tumor-and patient-specific
clinical signs to improve quality of life by reducing or modulating tumor-induced
mechanisms of brain injury. The types of drugs primarily used for palliative care (Table
245.3) include anticonvulsant drugs (ACDs) for tumor-associated structural epilepsy
(chs. 125 and 247), corticosteroids targeting peritumoral vasogenic edema and
neuroinflammation (ch. 143), and analgesics for signs consistent with somatic, visceral,
or neuropathic cancer pain (ch. 6).5,6,26 Despite seizures being the most common clinical
sign associated with brain tumors, optimal ACD protocols for the treatment of tumorassociated epilepsy are currently unknown.24,26-28,68 Phenobarbital, levetiracetam, and
zonisamide are popular clinical ACD choices.24,26,28,68 ACD polypharmacy protocols are
frequently required to control seizures in brain tumor patients, and dogs with brain
tumors that have experienced status epilepticus are more likely to have refractory

seizures.67 Poor seizure control is a frequent cause of euthanasia of palliatively treated
animals with brain tumors.68,69
