NSAID, Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug.
Animals that have diagnostic imaging evidence of peritumoral edema can have
profound improvements in clinical signs following the initiation of corticosteroid
treatment. However, the anti-inflammatory and euphoric effects of corticosteroids may
also benefit animals without vasogenic edema. Corticosteroid treatment may also
transiently and modestly reduce the tumor burden in some cases or provide clinical
benefit to animals with tumors causing secondary obstructive hydrocephalus.70 Polyuria,
polydipsia, polyphagia, and sedation are commonly reported adverse effects of palliative
treatment, but palliative treatments are rarely associated with significant morbidity that
necessitates discontinuation of therapy.26
Clinical signs consistent with head or neck pain are reported in up to 25% of dogs with
brain tumors.2,71 Brain tumors may cause pain by compressing or stretching the
meninges, nerve roots, or vasculature, inducing tumor-associated meningitis, neuritis, or
radiculitis, or by infiltrating the periosteum. Clinical manifestations of pain often respond
to corticosteroid treatment, and adjunctive opioid or neuropathic pain agents can be
added as required (Table 245.3).
Given the increasing clinical indications for longitudinal cross-sectional imaging in the
management of numerous diseases in veterinary medicine, it is likely that the frequency of
incidental identification of brain tumors will increase. Currently, ∼5% and 20% of canine
and feline meningiomas, respectively, are identified incidentally.2,3 In animals with small
brain tumors not causing clinical signs, watchful monitoring may also represent a
reasonable management approach. However, further characterization of the natural
disease history of specific types of brain tumors is necessary to define the optimal
indications and observation intervals for watchful monitoring.
There is a lack of robust data regarding survival times and prognostic factors associated
with palliative care of specific histologic types of brain tumors. Published data indicate an
average survival time of ∼8 weeks, with a range of 1-13 weeks, in animals with PBT treated
palliatively.3,6,26,72-73 The prognosis associated with palliative care of pituitary tumors
appears to be more favorable than PBTs, with median survival times (MSTs) of up to 51
weeks.74 Two studies have reported that dogs with several types of rostrotentorial PBT
treated palliatively had a better prognosis than those with caudotentorial tumors,26,72 but
tumor location was subsequently not found to be a significant prognostic factor in dogs
with presumptive gliomas treated palliatively.73 The occurrence of status epilepticus and
the presence of clinical signs for >16 days prior to diagnosis are negative prognostic
indicators in dogs with brain tumors.68,73

SURGERY
Surgical resection of brain tumors is associated with several advantages, including
allowing for definitive histopathologic tumor diagnosis and the expedient and effective
reduction of ICP (Figures 245.2 and 245.6). This reduction of ICP, via reducing or
eliminating the tumor burden, often leads to rapid post-operative improvement in clinical
signs (Video 245.4

). Comparisons of studies investigating the efficacy of surgical

treatment of specific types of brain tumors are complicated by numerous sources of
variability including surgeon experience, techniques utilized, combining surgery with
other therapies, and a repeated lack of inclusion of quantifiable surrogates of surgical
success, such as the extent of resection (EOR; Figure 245.6). As excision of wide tumorfree histologic margins is generally not practical in brain tumor cases, objective
evaluations of EOR are dependent on performance of post-operative MRI.75 These
imaging assessments are associated with practical limitations, including expense and
difficulties discriminating residual tumor from surgically-induced reactive changes
(Figure 245.6).75,76
Surgical resection is currently the standard of care for feline forebrain
meningiomas.3,29,77,78 These tumors are usually amenable to safe and effective surgical
removal even in the instances of large, multiple, or recurrent tumors; multiple tumor foci;
or recurrent tumor. Feline forebrain meningiomas frequently are located superficially on
the surface of the cerebrum, are well demarcated from the surrounding brain, and are not
infiltrative into the adjacent brain parenchyma. MSTs following surgical removal of feline
forebrain meningiomas are ≥2 years, with reported ranges of 23-37 months.3,29,77,78
Approximately 25% of cats develop clinical signs of recurrence within 3-69 months of
surgery.77,78

FIGURE 245.6 Transverse T2W magnetic resonance image
evaluating the extent of resection (EOR) of a surgically treated canine
meningioma. A, Preoperative image demonstrating the tumor and
associated mass effect, including attenuation of the left lateral
ventricle and caudal transtentorial herniation (CTH; arrow). B,
Immediate postoperative image illustrating improvement in the mass
effect and resolution of the CTH. Assessment of the EOR is
complicated by the presence of air (∗) and fluid (∗∗) in the
resection cavity. C, Image obtained 6 weeks postoperatively showing
remodeling of the resection cavity, resolution of all mass effect, and
gross total tumor resection.
Surgical treatment of canine meningiomas is associated with more highly variable
outcomes, due to the previously mentioned operator and technical factors, in addition to
the ability of all grades of canine meningiomas to invade brain tissue.20 The majority of
studies describing the surgical treatment of canine meningiomas has included
superficially located cerebral or cerebellar convexity tumors.79-84 Surgical treatment of
meningiomas located on the floor of the skull or in the caudal brainstem is technically
challenging and has not been frequently reported.79 When standard surgical techniques
are used, the MST for canine meningiomas is ∼9 months (range 7-14 months).81,82,84
Studies using techniques that facilitate removal of infiltrative tumor or intraoperative
visualization such as extirpation with an ultrasonic aspirator, or endoscopically assisted
resection in canine meningiomas have reported superior MSTs (16-70 months) compared
to conventional surgical methods.79,83
There are limited data available regarding the surgical treatment of other PBTs such as
gliomas, histiocytic sarcomas, and CPTs, although the existing evidence indicates that
management of these tumors types solely with surgery is associated with a poor
prognosis.19,84 Surgery on these tumors is seldom attempted as the approaches required
to access and remove intra-axial or intraventricular tumors are technically challenging. As
these tumor types are often poorly delineated and locally invasive, it is inherently more
difficult to discriminate the margins of tumor from the adjacent brain tissue.12,21
Surgery has also been shown to be effective for the management of certain types of SBT.
When performed by experienced surgeons, transsphenoidal hypophysectomy is capable of
producing rapid and long-lasting endocrine and clinical remissions in cases of canine and
feline pituitary-dependent hyperadrenocorticism (PDH; ch. 293) and feline acromegaly
(ch. 280), particularly when performed in cases without significant enlargement of the
pituitary gland.85-87 Larger trials investigating transsphenoidal hypophysectomy will be

required to define the utilitarian risk-to-benefit ratio of this procedure in animals with
pituitary macrotumors or other parasellar tumors.87 The surgical technique is associated
with a steep operator learning curve, and is currently only offered at a few veterinary
institutions in the world.86,87 SBTs of the skull, such as multilobular
osteochondrosarcoma, also can be managed surgically with good long-term outcomes
depending on the tumor grade and completeness of excision.88
Adverse events occur commonly in animals with brain tumors managed with surgery,
with 27% and 47% of dogs undergoing diagnostic intent SBB or therapeutic intent
craniotomy, respectively, experiencing a perioperative complication.66,89 A transient
deterioration in neurologic status is the most common adverse event reported following
intracranial surgery, and 92-95% of animals survive to discharge.64,89 Serious adverse
events associated with the surgical treatment of brain tumors include intracranial
hemorrhage or infarction, aspiration pneumonia, pneumocephalus, medically refractory
provoked seizures, permanent neurologic disability, electrolyte and osmotic disturbances,
and thermoregulatory dysfunction.6,62,66,89

RADIATION THERAPY
RT has long been demonstrated to be beneficial for the treatment of PBTs and SBTs when
used as a primary or adjunctive modality.74,81,90-94 In the last decade, the landscape of
RT for CNS tumors has evolved significantly in parallel with technological advances in RT
planning and delivery systems. As contemporary, linear accelerator-based RT equipment
is capable of performing stereotactic radiotherapy (SRT), there has been a clinical trend
away from traditional, coarsely fractionated RT protocols towards using SRT to treat
virtually all types of brain tumors in dogs and cats.91,93-95 SRT encompasses treatments
that involve the precision delivery of high doses of ionizing radiation to a stereotactically
defined anatomic target in a limited number (2-5) of fractions, compared to the 16-20
fractions for standard RT protocols.93-95 Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS), which is also
being performed in veterinary medicine using frame-based and frameless systems, differs
from SRT in that high-dose radiation is precision delivered during a single treatment
session (Video 245.5

).91 The advantages of SRT and SRS are improved target volume

conformity, particularly in tumors with complex shapes, and improved sparing of normal
tissues resulting in reduced risk for toxicosis.91,93 Extrapolating tumor-type-specific
outcome data from the veterinary brain tumor RT literature is confounded by a lack of
histologically diagnosed tumors in the overwhelming majority of RT studies, grouping of
heterogeneous intracranial masses in study designs, and significant variability in the RT
types and dose prescriptions used.91-95
Studies of cohorts of dogs treated with RT as a sole treatment modality for PBTs report
MSTs ranging from 7-23 months when an intent-to-treat analysis is performed that
includes all types of presumptively diagnosed masses and treatment protocols.69,90-94,96
MSTs associated with RT treatment of extra-axial masses, the majority of which were
presumed to be meningiomas based on imaging characteristic, range from 9-19
months.5,90-93 Reported MSTs for intra-axial tumors (presumptively diagnosed gliomas)
treated with RT range from 9-21 months.93,94,96 Retreatment of presumptive intracranial

gliomas with SRT upon recurrence was associated with a significant survival advantage in
dogs with presumed gliomas, as dogs treated with one course of SRT has an MST of 258
days, while those treated with >1 course of SRT had an MST of 865 days.94 RT is also
useful for canine meningiomas as adjunctive therapy, with combined surgical and RT
therapy producing MSTs of 16-30 months.92,95,96 There is currently insufficient evidence
to indicate whether SRT or fractionated treatment protocols are superior for the treatment
of canine PBTs.94,95 Compared with dogs, there is relatively little information available
regarding the irradiation of brain tumors in cats, but existing studies indicate that it can
be useful treatment for numerous tumor types.97
Compared to palliative therapy, RT is effective at reducing tumor size, improving
neurologic signs, and providing a survival benefit in dogs and cats with pituitary
tumors.74,95,98 Although surgery is preferred for definitive treatment of pituitary tumors
associated with a normal pituitary height to brain area ratio, RT can provide benefits when
other factors (e.g., large tumor size, lack of specific surgical experience) make surgery a
less attractive option.85,87 In cases of PDH treated with RT, the reported rates of
endocrine remission are variable, with some studies reporting persistent
hypercortisolinemia for up to a year after RT.74,99 Thus, continued medical management
and serial endocrine evaluations are necessary following RT treatment of PDH. Negative
prognostic indicators associated with RT treatment of pituitary masses include severe
neurologic dysfunction at presentation, presence of a functional pituitary tumor, and large
relative tumor size.74,95,99 A recent study also reported that survival times associated with
canine pituitary tumors treated with SRT were shorter than those previously observed in
dogs treated with definitive fractionated protocols.95
Adverse effects of treatment are observed in ∼10% of brain tumor cases treated with
RT.5,6 Frequently reported adverse effects include aspiration pneumonia; pulmonary
thromboembolism; acute CNS toxicosis, which often manifests as a decreased level of
consciousness; damage to at-risk organs in the treatment field causing deafness, cataract
formation, and/or keratitis; and late-onset radiation necrosis.6 The majority of RTassociated adverse events can be successfully managed with supportive therapies, and
manifestations of acute CNS toxicosis are often responsive to treatment with tapering
doses of corticosteroids.

CHEMOTHERAPY
Data evaluating the efficacy of chemotherapies for the management of brain tumors is
significantly limited by the absence of histologic tumor diagnoses in the vast majority of
reported cases, and a lack of inclusion of objective indicators evaluating chemotherapeutic
response (e.g., imaging evidence of reduction in tumor size following treatment compared
to a matched control group) in most case series that have investigated specific
chemotherapeutic drugs. Chemotherapeutics often prescribed for brain tumors are the
alkylating agents lomustine (CCNU), carmustine (BCNU) and temozolomide (TMZ), or
the antimetabolite hydroxyurea, as all of these agents can effectively penetrate the bloodbrain barrier (BBB).72,73,93 To date, there is extremely limited objective evidence
indicating that chemotherapeutic treatment significantly improves survival, clinical signs,
or quality of life in dogs and cats with histologically confirmed brain tumors, especially
when used as a monotherapy in the setting of macroscopic disease. Existing reports in

populations of dogs with presumptively diagnosed brain tumors provide contradictory
results, with one study reporting that lomustine treatment had no impact on survival
compared to palliative care, and another indicating that dogs receiving lomustine therapy
lived significantly longer (MST, 138 days) than those that received only supportive care
(MST, 35 days).72,73 At the dosages commonly prescribed, CCNU, TMZ, and hydroxyurea
treatment are well-tolerated in dogs, rarely resulting in life-threatening adverse effects
that would require discontinuation of treatment.72,73,93
Studies have demonstrated that the in vitro sensitivities of canine brain tumors to
chemotherapeutic agents, as well as mechanisms of chemoresistance, are similar to those
observed in human brain tumor cell lines.100 Therefore, it is reasonable to expect that the
inclusion of adjuvant chemotherapy in multimodality brain tumor treatment protocols in
companion animals could result in modest clinical benefits, as has been generally
observed in humans. Studies investigating adjuvant chemotherapy following irradiation of
canine brain tumors have also demonstrated mixed results. One report found no
difference in survival between groups of dogs with suspected gliomas treated with SRT
with (MST, 420 days) or without (MST, 383 days) TMZ.93 Another study, also in dogs
with presumed gliomas treated with SRT, identified a significant survival advantage for
those dogs that received adjuvant chemotherapy (MST >658 days) compared to dogs that
were only treated with SRT (MST, 230 days).94 However, only 5/21 dogs received
chemotherapy in this latter study, and 4 different chemotherapeutic agents were
administered to these 5 dogs.94

INVESTIGATIONAL THERAPEUTICS FOR BRAIN
TUMORS
Given the clinical, phenotypic, molecular, and genetic similarities that exist between
canine brain tumors and their human analogs, dogs with spontaneous intracranial tumors
are often used as unique animal models for pre-clinical discovery.5,12,70,82,101 Studies in
brain tumor bearing dogs can answer fundamental cancer drug and medical device
questions that meet critical and shared needs among stakeholders in the cancer research
and global healthcare communities.101 Translational studies of investigational therapies in
dogs with brain tumors have been performed for decades in order to provide
pharmacokinetic, mechanistic, safety, toxicity, and anti-tumor activity data in an
immunocompetent host, in order to guide and accelerate the therapeutic development
process and ultimately improve the lives of dogs and humans with brain cancer.101
Reviews of some of the techniques and studies being evaluated in dogs with brain
tumors are available.5,6,70,102,103 Major focus areas of active veterinary neuro-oncology
research programs include: 1) CNS drug delivery techniques, 2) biophysical brain tumor
ablation methods, 3) development of targeted molecular agents and nanoparticular
chemotherapeutics, 4) oncolytic viral and gene therapies, and 5) immunotherapy (IT).
Frequently, these approaches are used in combination, and several of the techniques
described below have multiple mechanistic effects that transcend these categorizations
(e.g., “armed” oncolytic viral IT).
Innovations in drug delivery to the brain that have and are being investigated in dogs
with brain tumors broadly include approaches that either bypass or permeabilize the BBB
to allow for direct intratumoral delivery of therapeutically relevant concentrations of

macromolecular drugs.5,70,102,103 BBB bypass techniques that have been used in dogs
include convection-enhanced delivery (CED) of chemotherapeutics, for direct and slow
infusion of the therapeutic agent into the brain (or tumor) tissue under pressure, and
direct intracerebral implantation of various biodegradable nanomaterial polymer drug
carriers.102-108 A primary advantage of CED is that it can saturate much larger volumes of
brain tissue.103,106 Both non-selective chemotherapy drugs, such as liposomal CPT-11,
and agents targeting tumor cell surface receptors, like epidermal growth factor receptor
(EGFR), EphA2, and IL-13RA2, have been delivered by CED in dogs with glioma.104-106 A
clinical benefit of implantable biodegradable polymer systems is the ability to manipulate
the chemistry of the polymer such that drug delivery can be tuned to occur over time, thus
exposing the brain to sustained drug concentrations for prolonged periods.107,108 The
chemotherapeutics TMZ and doxorubicin have been delivered to dogs with brain tumors
using implantable biodegradable polymers.107,108 These studies have illustrated the
feasibility and safety of using CED and implantable polymers for drug delivery to the
canine brain, and have provided preliminary evidence of efficacy of these treatment
approaches.
Numerous BBB disruption strategies, including the use of hyperosmotic agents such as
mannitol, acoustic energy (transcranial focused ultrasound), and pulsed electric fields
(electroporation), have been shown to be capable of inducing BBB disruption, and clinical
trials are ongoing.102,109-111
Technologies capable of ablating soft tissues using thermal or non-thermal mechanisms
are being investigated in canine brain tumors.109,112,113 Studies in dogs with gliomas and
meningiomas have demonstrated that irreversible electroporation (IRE) can safely and
effectively ablate these tumors.109-111 IRE is a minimally invasive, nonthermal tissueablation technique that involves the placement of small electrodes into a targeted area
with delivery of carefully selected electrical pulses. When the applied electrical field
exceeds critical tissue-specific thresholds, cells in the treatment region are permeabilized
irreversibly through the formation of nanoscale aqueous pores in the cytoplasmic
membranes, causing cellular death.109 IRE also transiently induces a penumbra of
reversible BBB disruption around the ablated region, which could be exploited for the
delivery of high-molecular-weight chemotherapeutics.109
Devices capable of performing laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) are also being
investigated for use in dogs with brain tumors.113,114 LITT requires minimally-invasive
placement of a light-guiding fiber or probe into the target lesion, with subsequent selective
ablation of that lesion resulting from heat liberated by a laser. Although other thermal
ablative techniques have been used for focal tissue ablation in the brain, such as
radiofrequency and microwave ablation, LITT has superior precision and results in
predictable volume of tissue death; this avoids collateral damage, especially when
performed with real-time MRI thermometry and morphologic guidance.113 In humans,
LITT has been effective for several neuro-oncologic indications, including the treatment of
glioma and brain metastases.113
There is a constantly growing library of therapeutic agents that target novel oncogenic
processes or biologic pathways being developed for and tested in canine brain tumors.
Some show promising anti-tumor effects in vitro or in vivo, the ability to penetrate the
BBB, or favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profiles in healthy dogs, and are currently

in early phase trials in dogs with tumors.5,70,103,115,116 In a feasibility study, bacteriallyderived minicells were packaged with doxorubicin, targeted to EGFR, and administered IV
to dogs with brain tumors. Durable and objective tumor responses were seen in 24% of
dogs, without significant toxicoses.115 Screening of a large archive of canine brain tumors
demonstrated that procaspase-3 is frequently overexpressed in commonly encountered
histologic types of canine brain tumors and their human analogs.116 Procaspase-3expressing glioma and meningioma cell lines are sensitive to apoptotic effects induced by
the compound PAC-1, a small molecule activator of procaspase-3.116 Biologically relevant
concentrations of PAC-1 occur in the brain following oral administration, and the in vitro
cytotoxic effects of PAC-1 can be synergistic and well-tolerated when it is co-administered
with other chemotherapeutics (e.g., TMZ) and RT.117
Several gene therapy and oncolytic viral therapies have and are being investigated in
dogs with brain cancer. In one gene therapy study, intratumoral injections of Toca 511, a
retroviral replicating vector (RRV) that infects cancer cells and inserts a gene for the
enzyme cytosine deaminase (CD), were administered to dogs with naturally-occurring
brain tumors.118 The premise of the study was that CD would convert administered
flucytosine to the anticancer drug 5-fluorouracil for a local antitumor effect. In this study,
tumors were resected several weeks following injection of the RRV, and the
biodistribution of the RRV was assessed using PCR.118
A diverse array of IT strategies, whose unifying goal is to introduce, stimulate, or
otherwise augment the patient’s T-cell-mediated immune response against cancer cells, is
being explored for use in the treatment of companion animal brain tumors.103,119 Both
wild type and engineered oncolytic viruses (OVs) have been delivered to dogs with brain
tumors.119,120 OVs that are used clinically either inherently selectively infect cancer cells
or are genetically modified to increase their ability to target and destroy cancer cells
specifically. Once cells are infected with OV, the virus kills the cell and also subsequently
triggers an anti-tumor immune response in the host; thus, OV therapy is frequently
considered a type of IT. The largest OV trial to date performed in dogs with gliomas, a
phase I dose-escalating trial, has not identified any serious adverse events or dose-limiting
toxicoses from intratumoral delivery of M032, a nonneurovirulent oncolytic herpes
simplex virus-1 vector genetically engineered to express interleukin-12.119 Therefore, stage
2 of the study is underway in which the M032 OV will be administered in conjunction with
the immune checkpoint inhibitor indoximod.119 Given the Zika virus’s propensity to infect
neural progenitor cells, a pilot study evaluated the safety of intrathecal delivery of wildtype Zika virus to 3 dogs with brain tumors.120 The treatment was well tolerated, and
tissues collected at necropsy showed that tumor cells, but not differentiated neurons, were
infected by the virus.120
IT approaches using tumor lysate-based vaccines have been evaluated extensively in
dogs with brain tumors over the last decade.5,6,70,102,103,121-123 This type of personalized
IT treatment involves collecting a sample of the patient’s tumor and then exposing tumor
and tumor-associated antigens derived from that tumor sample to an immune stimulant
or adjuvant in a laboratory setting.121,123 The stimulated tumor lysate is then
administered back to the patient in order to elicit adaptive immune responses through
various pathways. The safety, feasibility, and efficacy of such tumor vaccinations using
stimulated patient-derived dendritic cells and autologous tumor lysates have been

demonstrated in canine glioma and meningioma.121-123 Combinatorial delivery of an
autologous tumor lysate vaccine with immune checkpoint inhibitors also has been well
tolerated, resulting in clinically relevant anti-tumor effects. Dogs with intracranial gliomas
receiving a canine-specific CD200-directed inhibitor and autologous tumor lysate had
significantly longer MST (median, 12.7 months) compared to a historical control group
treated with only autologous tumor lysate (median, 6.4 months).123

CONCLUSIONS
Brain tumors are a common cause of intracranial disease in middle-aged to older dogs and
cats, with meningiomas and gliomas accounting for the majority of PBTs encountered in
clinical practice. Although presumptive antemortem diagnosis of a PBT can often
accurately be achieved based on the MRI characteristics of the mass lesion within the
brain, definitive diagnosis of a PBT requires histopathologic examination of representative
tissue. Standard of care therapies for canine and feline brain tumors remain largely
undefined, although the prognosis is generally poor for animals with PBT treated
palliatively. Surgery and RT are both useful treatments for improving clinical signs and
prolonging survivals in dogs and cats with PBT compared to palliative treatments, but it is
currently unknown if one of these modalities is superior to the other, or if combinations of
surgery and radiation confer significant survival benefits. Advancements in knowledge
related to therapeutic outcomes will require a change in clinical practice paradigms such
that the biopsy of individual animal tumors prior to treatment becomes the new standard
of care. This will facilitate the routine and systematic characterization of the phenotypic
and genotypic features of brain tumors, objectively defining the impacts of treatment
modalities on clinical outcomes associated with specific tumor types and grades, and the
rigorous design of clinical trials evaluating novel therapeutics.

Chapter 246: Traumatic
Brain Disease

Head trauma in dogs and cats is a common result of traumatic
injury resulting in presentation for emergent veterinary care.1 Head
trauma occurs secondary to blunt injury such as vehicular trauma
(most common), falls from heights, injuries secondary to horse kick,
gunshot, or bite wounds. Unfortunately, animals may also present
with head trauma due to human-inflicted injury. The acute
management of head trauma is reviewed in chs. 44 and 125.

HISTORY

Patients with traumatic brain injury are often presented acutely after
the event. Trauma may be witnessed by the client or others and
reported accordingly. In some cases, trauma is not witnessed but the
patient is found shortly afterward near the site of trauma, such as the
side of the road with vehicular trauma. Occasionally patients present
with no history of trauma, as seen in patients that were injured as
neonates that later present with deficits due to infection secondary to
the initial injury or neurological deficits due to chronic brain damage
such as missing brain parenchyma resulting in seizures.

NORMAL BRAIN PHYSIOLOGY
CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW
The brain is highly metabolically active, which results in a demand
for 15-20% of the cardiac output. Cerebral blood flow (CBF) is
dependent on cerebral perfusion pressure, i.e., the difference
between mean arterial pressure (MAP) and intracranial pressure
(ICP).2,3 CBF is held constant as long as the MAP is between 50-150
mm Hg.2,3 The ability to hold CBF constant is due to multiple
mechanisms that regulate cerebral vascular resistance, such as
vascular smooth muscle contraction and dilation, O2 and CO2
concentrations, and autonomic control. Vascular smooth muscle
relaxes in response to low systemic blood pressure and constricts in
response to increased pressure. Increasing arterial O2 concentration
causes vasodilation whereas increasing CO2 concentrations cause
vasoconstriction. Sympathetic and parasympathetic tone affect the
vasculature and allow for fine control over vessel dilation.2

INTRACRANIAL VOLUME
The skull is an enclosed compartment containing the brain, blood,
and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). The total volume within this
compartment is constant, as described by the Monro-Kellie
doctrine.2 When one component of this compartment, such as the

brain, increases in volume, compliance occurs by shunting blood
volume or CSF out of the skull, maintaining the same total volume
within the skull. Compliance will compensate for increased volume
and preserve balance up to a point, maintaining a normal ICP
between 5 and 12 mm Hg.2,3 After compliance compensation has
been surpassed, small increases in volume result in dramatic
increases in ICP.

TRAUMATIC INJURY
Traumatic injury to the head has devastating initial consequences
such as fractures and hemorrhage followed by a cascade of secondary
injury. As a result of these injuries, the brain loses the ability to
autoregulate blood flow and ICP, resulting in further damage.

PRIMARY INJURY
Primary injury is the damage to the brain that occurs from physical
insult to the tissue such as contusion (bruising), hemorrhage,
lacerations, depressed skull fractures, and edema. Hemorrhage
resulting in hematoma formation can occur in the epidural,
subdural, or subarachnoid spaces as well as within the ventricles or
the brain parenchyma itself (Figure 246.1). Intracranial
hemorrhage in veterinary patients most often occurs within the
parenchyma or the subarachnoid space. Skull fractures are common
in patients with head trauma (up to 89% of dogs in 1 study)
regardless of severity; in patients with severe injury, hemorrhage is
common (96% of patients with severe injury).4,5 Fractures often
occur in multiple areas of the skull, as seen in 89% of cats
undergoing computed tomography (CT) to assess severity of
trauma.6

SECONDARY INJURY
Secondary injury is a flood of physiological responses of the body to
the primary insult. The brain becomes depleted of adenosine

triphosphate and massive amounts of excitatory neurotransmitters
(primarily glutamate) are released. Brain cells become a mosh pit of
calcium and sodium influx disrupting physiologic maintenance of
intracellular volume. Increased intracellular electrolytes result in
cytotoxic edema and subsequent spontaneous cell depolarization as
well as further excitatory neurotransmitter release. Subsequent
surges of the arachidonic acid pathway, free radical formation, and
inflammatory mediators further damage the brain. Cascading injury
occurs to the brain secondary to systemic abnormalities such as
hypoventilation and hypercapnia, hypoxemia, hypotension (<40 mm
Hg MAP) and hyperglycemia.3,7 Secondary injury cascade results in
disruption of the blood brain barrier and loss of the autoregulatory
mechanisms that normally maintain CBF.

FIGURE 246.1 Transverse,T2-weightedturbo spin
echomagnetic resonance image of the canine brain at
the level of the cruciate sulcus. Hemorrhage resulting

red in the subdural (1), intraventricular (2), epidural
(3), intraparenchymal (4), or subarachnoid spaces
(5).

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF INCREASED
INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE
Primary and secondary injury can result in loss of autoregulation of
ICP and CBF, resulting in a Cushing reflex. Decreased CBF results in
damage to the brainstem vasomotor centers and decreased clearance

of brain CO2. Increases in brain CO2 raise sympathetic tone,
resulting in increased systemic blood pressure to facilitate CBF.
Systemic hypertension is detected by baroreceptors of the carotid
arteries and aorta, stimulating vagal tone and lowering heart rate.
These changes result in a clinical change in the patient’s mentation
and neurological responses. Significant changes in ICP disrupt the
normal mechanisms to maintain CBF, and the brain’s blood supply
becomes directly dependent on systemic blood pressure.2

CLINICAL SIGNS
A full review of emergent changes on physical examination is
presented in chs. 44 and 125. This chapter will focus on findings
specific to head trauma overall as well as neurological examination
findings.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Extracranial injuries are common in patients with head trauma and
include pulmonary contusion (may be delayed by 24 hours after
injury), pneumothorax, concurrent appendicular or vertebral column
fractures, and abdominal injury. Tachypnea, dyspnea or
abnormalities on thoracic auscultation are important signs of
thoracic cavity injury. A fluid wave on abdominal palpation (
Video 21.1) could indicate uroabdomen or hemoabdomen. Careful
palpation of the vertebral column and limbs for pain or physical
abnormalities are important to detect concurrent fracture (ch. 119).
Special attention is given to examination of the head. Palpation of
the calvarium to detect fractures or defects is gently performed. The
mouth is carefully evaluated for alignment of the mandible and
maxilla as well as fluidity of the jaw in opening and closing. If
possible, a light source should be used to help evaluate the palate for
bruising or swelling seen with maxillary fractures. Epistaxis may be
present if the nasal region has been fractured. Otoscopic
examination should be performed to detect hemorrhage associated
with petrous temporal bone or bulla fractures. Scleral hemorrhage

may be detected in patients with concurrent subarachnoid
hemorrhage or ocular injury. Significant injury to the frontal sinus
may result in movement of the skin overlying the sinus during
respiration

(Video 246.1).

EMERGENT NEUROLOGICAL
EXAMINATION
While the forebrain is most commonly affected in head trauma
patients, decline in brainstem reflexes and function are what
determine the prognosis for a patient’s survival. After initial
assessment at presentation, serial monitoring of the neurological
examination (ch. 241) should be performed to detect progression of
secondary injury to the brain. Although ICP monitoring is often
performed in human patients, this is not feasible in veterinary
medicine at most facilities. Therefore a scoring system has been
developed to monitor veterinary patients. This Modified Glasgow
Coma Scale (MGCS) is discussed further in ch. 44 and its
component parts and calculation are shown in ch. 125 (Video 44.2)
.8,9

MGCS Consciousness
Levels of consciousness are a reflection of cerebral function,
brainstem function, and systemic physiology such as blood pressure
or blood O2 level. Four levels of consciousness are considered when
assessing head trauma patients: comatose, stuporous,
demented/obtunded, alert. Comatose patients are not responsive to
any visual, auditory, or noxious stimuli. Stuporous patients have a
broad definition with responses to visual, auditory, or noxious
stimuli depending on the degree of stupor. Demented or obtunded
patients may not respond normally to stimuli or have intermittent
periods of staring off or altered consciousness. Patients with
obtundation secondary to forebrain injury may circle toward the side
of their forebrain injury (Video 246.2;

ch. 241).

MGCS Brainstem Reflexes
While many cranial nerve tests are assessed in routine neurological
evaluations, there are 3 of significant importance in head trauma
patients: the oculocephalic reflex, pupillary light reflex and pupil size
(ch. 241). The oculocephalic reflex elicits a physiologic nystagmus
that occurs with vertical or horizontal head movement where there is
a jerk of the eye in the direction of movement (Video 241.35). This
can be absent in patients with brainstem injury, as seen in Video
246.3.

Care should be taken to not rotate the patient if it cannot

be done safely, e.g., neck injury. Pupil size is a reflection of the
retina, optic nerves, thalamus, and brainstem. Miosis occurs with
injury to the thalamus or sympathetic innervation to the eye at any
point in its long pathway from the brainstem to the eye. Mydriasis
can be indicative of damage to the midbrain from initial injury or
secondary to transtentorial herniation.

FIGURE 246.2 A, Dog with brainstem injury
exhibiting decerebrate posture (extensor rigidity and
opisthotonos). B, Cat with brainstem injury
exhibiting decerebrate posture. C, Dog with
cerebellar injury exhibiting decerebellate posture
(patient had normal mentation).

MGCS Motor Activity
Assessment of motor activity is not challenging in ambulatory
patients who are mildly affected by their injury. One must remember
that this assessment includes posture and muscle tone in addition to
motor activity. Patients are either ambulatory, nonambulatory but
able to move, or recumbent with intermittent levels of rigidity or
decreased extensor tone. Patients with constant extensor rigidity and
opisthotonos are given low scores, and this can be seen with both
significant brainstem injury (Figure 246.2, A and B) and
cerebellar injury (Figure 246.2, C). The key difference between
these two injury states is that animals with cerebellar injury have

normal levels of consciousness. Tone remains increased in all limbs
until coma occurs, at which point motor tone will be decreased. Tone
is passively assessed by putting limbs through range of motion in
recumbent animals.

STABLE NEUROLOGICAL
EXAMINATION (CH. 241)
In patients with chronic injury, or in patients that have been
stabilized after initial assessment, a more thorough examination with
assessment of the remaining cranial nerve tests, postural reactions
and segmental reflexes, is performed. Patients may display signs of
lateralized brain injury that result in hemiattention, difficulty
walking, and altered levels of consciousness (Video 246.4

).

DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
After emergent assessment of patient status through blood and urine
testing, thoracic and abdominal imaging (radiographs, sonographic
assessment [ch. 73]), and blood pressure measurement (ch. 91),
more advanced tests are pursued to determine the extent of the
intracranial injury and next steps for patient treatment. Skull
radiographs can identify fractures, particularly those that are
displaced, but do not provide any additional information regarding
the severity of injury to the brain and whether intracranial
hemorrhage is present. Both CT and magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) provide superior detail in evaluating bony structures,
hemorrhage and brain parenchyma for extent of injury.

COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY
The advantages of CT are fast scans, high detail of bony structures,
and sensitive detection of intracranial hemorrhage (ch. 112).

Fractures may be subtle, as seen in the kitten in Figure 246.3, or
severe and comminuted as seen in the Golden Retriever in Figure
246.4. CT also has the advantage of 3-dimensional reconstructions
as seen in Figure 246.4, which allow for superior understanding of
injury extent. Intracranial hemorrhage is typically bright, or
hyperattenuating on CT (Figure 246.5), although over time as the
blood is broken down this signal fades. The main purpose of
pursuing CT in head trauma patients is to determine whether
surgical intervention is needed to decompress a fracture, evacuate an
epidural or subdural hematoma, or remove a chronic abscess.

MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING
Both MRI and CT are good modalities for identifying skull fractures
and correlate well regarding fracture detection. MRI has the
additional benefit of detailed imaging of the brain to detect edema,
hemorrhage and contusion that cannot be identified as well with CT
(Figure 246.6) (ch. 112). MRI has been shown to be correlated
with prognosis based on the findings, while CT has had variable
results depending on the scoring system used for assessment.10-12

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
When a patient presents with a history of observed trauma, not many
other differentials are considered. However, in patients where
trauma is not witnessed, differentials considered include vascular
events in middle-aged to senior patients (ch. 243) and congenital
abnormalities in juvenile patients (ch. 244). The author has also
experienced many cases where there is an observed “trauma” such as
falling off the couch, but the patient actually fell off the furniture due
to pre-existing neurologic deficits such as those seen in patients with
meningoencephalitis of unknown etiology (ch. 242).

PROGNOSIS
In mild to moderate injuries, outcome is typically good without longterm deficits or post-traumatic epilepsy. Severe injury in cats and

dogs is associated with a higher mortality rate and chance of postinjury deficits or seizures, although the overall incidence of posttraumatic seizures in dogs and cats is low.13,14 Initial neurologic
evaluation, results of blood tests, and advanced imaging findings are
associated with injury severity and outcome.
Head trauma patients have a good prognosis in the short and long
term when they have fewer deficits on initial examination and less
severe changes found on MRI. These categories have been
established as appropriate assessors of outcome based on scoring
patients with an MGCS and an MRI injury severity scale. Patients
with an MGCS of >8 have at least a 50% chance of survival, with
survival rate improving linearly with an increase in MGCS. MGCS
scores are correlated with outcome at 3 days, 1 month, and 6 months;
therefore, this score is essential to making initial determinations
regarding likely patient outcomes.8,10
If MRI is pursued in a patient, the severity of brain MRI changes
can be scored (I-IV), with higher scores associated with negative
outcomes. A midline shift on MRI, indicative of mass effect due to
edema or hemorrhage, is a negative prognostic indicator on brain
MRI in dogs.8 CT has been correlated with outcome using 1 scoring
system in dogs but not another, likely due to the inability to assess
parenchymal brain damage and inconsistencies between
methods.11,12

Chapter 247: Epilepsy
Karen R. Muñana

A C RO N YM S
ACVIM American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine
ASD antiseizure drug
IE idiopathic epilepsy
IVETF International Veterinary Epilepsy Task Force
MRI magnetic resonance imaging
Epilepsy is defined by the International League Against Epilepsy as “a disease
of the brain characterized by an enduring predisposition to generate epileptic
seizures”; this can be interpreted clinically as the presence of 2 or more
unprovoked seizures at least 24 hours apart.1 Two aspects of this definition
warrant emphasis. First, epileptic seizures are unprovoked. In other words,
they arise from a primary disorder of the brain that is characterized by
abnormal excessive and synchronous neuronal activity, resulting in the
transient clinical manifestations of motor, autonomic and/or behavioral signs.
This is in contrast to provoked seizures, also known as reactive seizures, which
result from a transient disturbance in function associated with a metabolic
disturbance or intoxication. In these instances, the brain is otherwise normal
and the condition is reversible once the disturbance is corrected. Second, to be
considered epilepsy, the unprovoked seizures must be recurrent, with the
second seizure occurring at least 24 hours after the first.1 Accordingly, a
diagnosis of epilepsy should not be made after a single seizure. The reader is
referred to ch. 45 for a more detailed discussion of seizures, including videos
that demonstrate generalized seizures (Video 45.1

), atonic seizures (Video

45.2), focal motor seizures with (Video 45.4) or without (Video 45.3)
automatisms, and focal sensory (fly-biting) seizures (Video 45.5).

CANINE EPILEPSY

Epilepsy has been reported to be the most common chronic neurological
condition in dogs,2 with an estimated prevalence in the general population of
0.62-0.75%.3,4 Canine epilepsy can be further classified according to etiology.
Idiopathic epilepsy (IE) refers to two or more unprovoked seizures for
which there is no underlying cause other than a known or presumed genetic
predisposition. It results from a functional defect within neurons. IE is
discussed in more detail below.
Structural epilepsy refers to recurrent seizures that are caused by a
congenital or acquired pathologic condition of the brain, specifically the
cerebrum. It is reported to account for 17-45% of the cases of epilepsy among
dogs in the general population.5,6 Causes for structural epilepsy include
neoplastic (ch. 245), inflammatory (ch. 242), cerebrovascular (ch. 243),
anomalous (ch. 244), and degenerative (ch. 244) conditions. Structural
epilepsy is diagnosed most frequently in older dogs. A study involving dogs
presenting to a referral hospital with an onset of recurrent seizures at ≥7 years
of age identified an underlying structural cause in 79% (169/214).7 The
prevalence of structural epilepsy increased with age, in that 71% (75/106) of
dogs 7-9 years of age had a diagnosis of structural epilepsy compared to 88%
(29/33) of dogs ≥13 years of age. In addition, a retrospective study evaluating
the relationship between magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings and age
in interictally normal epileptic dogs reported abnormal MRI findings in 27%
(8/30) of dogs greater than 6 years of age, but only in 2% (1/46) of dogs less
than 6 years of age.8
Along with age, the presence of interictal neurological deficits can be used to
support a diagnosis of structural epilepsy. Neurological examination
abnormalities (ch. 241) were identified in 90% (47/52) of dogs that were
confirmed to have structural epilepsy based on the presence of MRI
abnormalities; the sensitivity and specificity of the neurological examination
to predict findings on MRI were 77% and 91%, respectively.9 However,
epileptic seizures are often the initial, and sometimes only, presenting clinical
sign in animals with structural brain disease. Approximately one-third
(33/105) of dogs with a diagnosis of structural epilepsy were found to have a
normal interictal neurological examination in one study.10 Furthermore, a
retrospective study of dogs with histologically confirmed intracranial
neoplasia reported epileptic seizures as the initial clinical sign in 72% (31/43)
of dogs, with lesions in the frontal lobe associated with a higher risk for
seizures.11
Epilepsy of unknown cause is a term used to refer to recurrent seizures
that do not fulfill the criteria for structural epilepsy or IE. Typically, a genetic
cause is determined to be unlikely based on the dog’s age at the onset of
seizures or the presence of interictal neurological abnormalities, but a

structural cause is not identified. The term is also used in cases for which a
thorough diagnostic evaluation has not been performed to allow a diagnosis of
either structural epilepsy or IE.

IDIOPATHIC EPILEPSY IN DOGS
IE accounts for over half of all cases of epilepsy in dogs.5,6,12 Studies support a
hereditary basis for IE in numerous dog breeds, including the Australian
Shepherd Dog, Beagle, Belgian Shepherd Dog, Belgian Terveuren, Bernese
Mountain Dog, Border Collie, Border Terrier, Cavalier King Charles Spaniel,
Dalmatian, English Springer Spaniel, Finnish Spitz, Golden Retriever,
Hungarian Vizsla, Irish Wolfhound, Italian Spinone, Keeshond, Labrador
Retriever, Lagatto Romagnolo, Petit Basset Griffon Vendéen, Rhodesian
Ridgeback, Shetland Sheepdog and Standard Poodle.13 Breed-specific
epidemiological studies have reported IE prevalence rates far greater than
those found in the general dog population, from 3% in the Labrador
Retriever14 to 18% in the Irish Wolfhound,15 substantiating the hereditary
basis of IE in these breeds. IE is also recognized in mixed-breed dogs.
There are two IE syndromes of dogs for which the genetic basis has been
established: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy in the Rhodesian Ridgeback16 and
benign familial juvenile epilepsy in Lagotto Romagnolo dogs.17 However, the
genetic basis for the vast majority of canine epilepsy cases remains to be
elucidated, with evidence suggesting that most cases are polygenic in nature.
For example, six chromosomal regions have been identified as potential
markers associated with IE in Belgian Shepherd Dogs,18 and although
polymorphisms at specific genetic loci have subsequently been identified as
risk factors for the development of IE, the causative mutation remains
undetermined.19 The clinical characteristics of IE can vary among different
breeds, with distinguishing features regarding age of onset, seizure semiology
(manifestations), clinical course of disease and treatment response described
for several breeds. Details regarding these breed-specific clinical
characteristics can be found elsewhere.13
Male dogs have been reported to have a greater likelihood of developing IE
compared to female dogs,3,6,10 but studies evaluating the effect of neutering
on IE have yielded conflicting results. An association between estrus and onset
of seizures was reported in a study involving 45 intact female dogs with IE.20
A retrospective study involving a large population of dogs (n = 407) with IE
identified a significant association between neuter status and seizure severity,
with intact dogs more likely to have cluster seizures (defined as 2 or more
seizures within a 24 hour period) compared to neutered dogs.21 However, a

subsequent study designed to evaluate the association between neutering and
IE in a population of Labrador Retrievers (n=117) and Border Collies (n=57)
did not identify any association between neuter status and the occurrence of
seizure severity, noting that most dogs were neutered before the onset of
seizures.22
The International Veterinary Epilepsy Task Force (IVETF) undertook an
analysis of 2 previously published studies on canine IE10,12 to investigate the
predictive value of age at seizure onset to differentiate between IE and
structural epilepsy. The task force determined that dogs between 6 months
and 6 years of age were significantly more likely to be affected by IE than by
structural epilepsy compared to dogs under 6 months of age. This association
was no longer present when the age cut-off was set at 1 year; similarly, when
evaluating 5 years versus 6 years of age as a cutoff for the high end of the
range, 6 years was determined to be a better predictor and provided a greater
likelihood of a diagnosis of IE than structural epilepsy.23 The likelihood of a
diagnosis of IE in dogs between 6 months and 6 years has been substantiated
in a subsequent study.6

Diagnosis of Idiopathic Epilepsy
IE is an exclusion diagnosis. Since there is no general confirmatory test for the
disease, the diagnosis is made based on the age at onset of seizures, the
absence of abnormalities on physical and neurological examination, and the
exclusion of structural, metabolic and toxic etiologies in an animal with
confirmed recurrent seizures. The IVETF has recommended a tiered approach
to the diagnosis of IE in dogs, with a numerically higher tier associated with a
greater confidence in the diagnosis;23 this approach is summarized in Table
247.1.

FELINE EPILEPSY
Recurrent epileptic seizures in cats are less common compared to dogs, but
nonetheless are a frequent presenting complaint in primary care practice with
a reported prevalence of 0.16%.24 The etiological classification of recurrent
seizures in cats is similar to that in dogs, with the terms IE and structural
epilepsy utilized. However, application of the term IE to cats has been met
with controversy in the past, primarily because a genetic predisposition to
epilepsy—which is considered an important feature of the disease—has not
been documented in this species. Consequently, earlier publications often used
the term “epilepsy of unknown origin” or “epilepsy of unknown cause” rather
than IE. Currently, when applied to cats, the term IE refers to a disease
characterized by recurrent epileptic seizures in the presence of a normal
interictal physical and neurological examination, and for which an underlying
cause is not known based on the exclusion of structural, metabolic and toxic
etiologies.

FIGURE 247.1 Algorithm outlining a stepwise approach
to the medical management of a patient with epilepsy. ASD,
Antiseizure drug.
IE has been reported to be the cause of recurrent seizures in 34-57% of
cats.25-27 Although a specific range for age of onset of seizures cannot be
applied to the diagnosis of IE cats as it is in dogs, studies have demonstrated
that cats with IE are significantly more likely to have an onset of seizures
between 1 and 7 years of age.26,27 A retrospective evaluation of MRI findings
in epileptic cats with a normal interictal neurological examination found that
structural abnormalities were more likely identified in cats with an onset of
seizures at >5 years of age.28 Neoplasia was the most common diagnosis, with
congenital, inflammatory, vascular, degenerative and traumatic conditions
also described. 25,28
A specific epilepsy syndrome has been described in cats that is similar to
temporal lobe epilepsy in humans.29 Affected cats have focal seizures with
orofacial involvement, manifesting as salivation, facial twitching, lip smacking,
chewing, licking or swallowing, along with motor arrest (motionless staring)
and behavioral changes (ch. 255). Seizure can also secondarily generalize.
Changes in the hippocampus are identified with MRI or histopathologically in
many affected cats.30,31
Feline audiogenic reflex seizures is another specific epilepsy syndrome of
cats.32 This disorder is recognized most often in geriatric cats, with a reported

median age of onset of 15 years. Cats often present with myoclonic seizures
that frequently occur prior to the development of generalized tonic-clonic
seizures, and seizures are typically triggered by high frequency sounds.
Hearing impairment or deafness has been reported in half of affected cats.

PRINCIPLES OF THERAPY
Antiseizure drug (ASD) therapy remains the cornerstone of treatment for
epilepsy. Although treatment should be directed at any underlying cause
identified in the diagnostic evaluation, in such instances ASD therapy is also
recommended as concurrent therapy to address the epileptogenic condition.33
An algorithm outlining a stepwise approach to the medical management of a
patient with epilepsy is provided in Figure 247.1.

GUIDELINES FOR INITIATING TREATMENT
A decision on whether or not to initiate ASD therapy in an animal with
epilepsy should take into consideration the general health of the patient, as
well as the owner’s lifestyle, finances and comfort with the proposed treatment
plan. Recommendations on when to initiate therapy in dogs with epilepsy have
been proposed by both a consensus panel of the American College of
Veterinary Internal Medicine (ACVIM) and the IVETF that include: (1) 2 or
more seizures within a 6-month period; (2) history of cluster seizures or status
epilepticus (seizures lasting ≥5 minutes or repeated seizures with incomplete
recovery between events) or ; (3) postictal signs that are prolonged (>24
hours), severe, and/or unusual; and (4) increasing seizure frequency and/or
duration and/or deteriorating seizure severity as evaluated over 3 interictal
periods.33,34 The final decision on initiating ASD therapy should be made on a
case-by-case basis after careful consideration of these factors. A similar
approach can be used in cats.
Client education is key to the successful management of an epileptic animal,
and should be addressed before initiating therapy. The pet owner should have
a clear understanding of the goals and expectations of treatment. The owner
should realize that many animals do not become seizure-free with treatment,
and adverse effects are common with ASD therapy, such that management of
the disease involves maximizing epileptic seizure control while minimizing
adverse effects to allow for the best quality of life. Owners should also be
cautioned that it is common for animals to experience transient adverse effects
at the initiation of therapy, and that it is important to allow time (up to 2
weeks) to adjust to the medication before making any assessment regarding
tolerability. Furthermore, therapy is lifelong in most instances, and it is
imperative that the ASD be administered on a regular basis at established

treatment intervals. Animals with epilepsy require continuous care, and
adjustments to the treatment regimen are likely to be required over time.
Finally, each animal with epilepsy will respond differently to treatment, such
that an individualized approach is needed.

ANTISEIZURE DRUG SELECTION
The ASDs that are used most commonly in veterinary practice include
phenobarbital, bromide, imepitoin, levetiracetam and zonisamide. Factors to
consider when deciding which ASD to prescribe for a patient include the
mechanism of action, reported efficacy, potential for adverse effects and drug
interactions, frequency of administration, cost, and any applicable regulatory
guidelines. A 2014 systematic review of published studies reporting clinical
outcomes of ASDs used in the treatment of IE in dogs concluded that when
used as a sole ASD (monotherapy), there is good evidence for recommending
phenobarbital and imepitoin, fair evidence for recommending bromide and
levetiracetam, and insufficient evidence for recommending zonisamide.35
Similarly, an ACVIM consensus panel provided the following
recommendations for monotherapy based on analysis of available data:
phenobarbital and imepitoin received a high recommendation with the
assessment that they were likely effective, bromide received a moderate
recommendation with the assessment that it was most likely to be effective,
and levetiracetam and zonisamide received a low recommendation with the
assessment that they may not be effective.33 Although favorable results have
been reported in many of the studies describing ASD use in dogs with IE, a
lack of well-designed, blinded randomized controlled studies limits the quality
of the evidence upon which to base definitive recommendations. The safety
and tolerability of ASD use in dogs has also been systematically reviewed; it
was concluded that levetiracetam and then imepitoin are the safest ASDs,
followed by phenobarbital and bromide, with a strong level of evidence to
support the safety profile of all these drugs. The level of evidence on the safety
profile of zonisamide was judged to be weak.36
There are considerably fewer studies on the safety and efficacy of ASDs in
cats compared to the published literature on ASD use in dogs. A 2018 metaanalysis of published studies reporting on the use of ASDs in cats concluded
that based on the limited data available, phenobarbital might be considered
the first choice ASD followed by levetiracetam and imepitoin if phenobarbital
is judged to be ineffective or contraindicated.37 Levetiracetam has been
reported to potentially be superior to phenobarbital in the treatment of cats
with feline audiogenic reflex seizures.38
Clinically relevant pharmacologic properties, dosage recommendations, and
potential adverse effects for the ASDs used in dogs and cats are summarized in

Tables 247.2 and 247.3, respectively. A more extensive discussion of
treatment options for epilepsy can be found elsewhere.39

In general, therapy with a single ASD rather than a combination of drugs is
preferred in the initial medical management of epilepsy, as this avoids drugdrug interactions and provides a simpler regimen that may improve client
adherence.40 Treatment with the chosen ASD should be initiated at the low
end of the recommended maintenance dose range, and any required dosage
adjustments performed incrementally. A second drug should only be added
after treatment failure has been demonstrated with the first drug, based on
unacceptable seizure control despite drug administration at maximum dosage
or serum concentrations at the high end of the targeted range, or the presence
of unacceptable adverse effects. Considerations for the choice of the second
ASD are similar to those when initiating monotherapy, although potential
drug interactions should also be considered. In addition, a second drug with a
different mechanism of action from the first drug should be chosen whenever
possible, in order to maximize antiepileptic properties and optimize seizure
control. Typically, a second ASD is added to the treatment regimen and the
animal is maintained on both (polytherapy), rather than switching from one
ASD to another.

Monitoring Response to Therapy
Epilepsy is by nature a chronic condition, and should be managed accordingly
with repeat evaluations over time. An assessment of treatment response
depends to a large extent on accurate owner observation, and owners should
be instructed to maintain a calendar to record seizure activity and observed
adverse effects and note any deviations in drug administration. There are
several seizure diary computer platforms and applications available to assist
with this task.
The ultimate goal of therapy is seizure freedom. The IVETF has proposed
that treatment success be defined as seizure freedom for a time span exceeding
3 times the longest interseizure interval prior to treatment, and for a minimum
of 3 months.41 A timeframe is included in the definition, to account for the
temporal waxing and waning nature of epileptic seizures. It should be noted
that fewer than half of all dogs and cats with IE are able to achieve a seizurefree status with long-term ASD therapy. In acknowledgement of this and the
fact that a therapeutic intervention that does not result in seizure freedom may
still lead to a clinically meaningful reduction in seizure frequency or severity,
the IVETF has proposed that partial therapeutic success be considered a
secondary goal. Partial therapeutic success is based on the following criteria:
1) prevention of cluster seizures or status epilepticus; 2) relevant reduction of
seizure frequency (with the proposed target of less than one seizure every 3
months, but taking into consideration pretreatment seizure frequency); and 3)
reduction in seizure severity. Successful outcome is also dependent on the
tolerability of the ASD treatment regimen. Hence, the overall goal in the
medical management of a dog or cat with epilepsy is to optimize seizure
control while minimizing ASD-related adverse effects, in order to optimize
quality of life for both the pet and the caregiver.

Therapeutic Drug Monitoring
Therapeutic drug monitoring plays an important role in the assessment of
treatment response, and should routinely be performed for ASDs such as
phenobarbital and bromide that have a narrow therapeutic index and for
which a reference range has been established in veterinary medicine. Serum
ASD concentrations should be measured at the following times: 1) once steady
state has been achieved after initiation of treatment or dosage adjustment; 2)
when seizures persist despite an apparently adequate dosage, or 3) when there
are concerns about drug related toxicosis or interactions with other drugs.42
In addition, drug concentrations should be measured at 6-12 month intervals
in order to screen for any changes in drug disposition over time and aim to
maintain levels within the targeted range.
In general, it takes approximately 5 elimination half-lives for a drug to
attain steady state concentrations (ch. 139), so this should be taken into

consideration when scheduling the measurement of ASD serum
concentrations after initiating therapy or a dosage adjustment. Serum ASD
concentrations should be measured at this timepoint, even if seizures are wellcontrolled. This provides a baseline from which any adjustments to therapy
can be determined in the event that seizure frequency worsens. Additional
doses of the ASD may be given to an animal that has breakthrough seizures,
either at home as part of the acute management of seizures (see discussion
below) or by a veterinarian if the animal presents for emergency care. A
sample collected after the fact will not be reflective of serum ASD
concentrations at the onset of the seizures and will have limited value in
guiding treatment decisions.
In general, trough samples (collected immediately before the next dose) are
usually recommended, as these are most useful in decision making when there
is inadequate seizure control. However, a study involving 33 epileptic dogs
being treated with phenobarbital identified no therapeutically relevant change
in serum phenobarbital concentrations throughout a daily dosing interval in
most dogs.43 If a sample is collected at a different time point along the dosing
interval, efforts should be made to collect subsequent samples at the same
time to allow for a more accurate comparison of results over the course of
treatment. Steady state serum ASD concentrations can be used for
approximating dosage adjustments, according to the following formula:
New dosage (mg/kg) = current dosage (mg/kg) × (desired serum
concentration/measured serum concentration)
Many of the newer ASDs approved for humans that are being utilized in
veterinary patients, such as zonisamide and levetiracetam, have wide
therapeutic indices such that drug monitoring is not performed on a routine
basis as it is for phenobarbital and bromide. Furthermore, veterinary reference
ranges have not been established for many of the newer ASDs. Nonetheless, it
can be helpful to measure trough concentrations when adequate seizure
control is not achieved, to determine whether a dosage increase might be
beneficial based on the target range extrapolated from humans.

DRUG-RESISTANT EPILEPSY
The prevalence of drug-resistant epilepsy in both dogs and cats has been
reported to be approximately 30% of patients with epilepsy.44-46 Animals with
drug resistance continue to have frequent seizures (typically assessed as a
<50% reduction in pre-treatment seizure frequency) or intolerable adverse
effects despite appropriate ASD therapy. In human medicine, drug-resistant
epilepsy is defined as “a failure of adequate trials of two or more tolerated and

appropriately chosen and used antiepileptic drug schedules (whether as
monotherapies or in combination) to achieve sustained seizure freedom.”47
The IVETF has proposed a similar definition for veterinary medicine, with an
animal considered drug-resistant if seizure freedom is not achieved with two
tolerated and appropriately chosen therapeutic trials of adequate dosing and
treatment duration.41 Furthermore, it is suggested that the term drug
resistance be used in relation to a specific ASD. Based on the IVETF definition,
over half of all dogs and cats with IE are considered drug-resistant
(specifically, phenobarbital and/or bromide resistant in dogs, and
phenobarbital resistant in cats).46,48-52 The pathophysiology of drug
resistance in epilepsy remains poorly understood, but is likely multifactorial,
with genetic, disease-related and environmental factors playing a role.
Non-medical treatment options, including surgery, dietary therapy, and
neurostimulation are often recommended in humans with drug-resistant
epilepsy. In the field of neurostimulation, both vagus nerve stimulation53 and
transcranial magnetic stimulation54 have been evaluated in dogs with drugresistant IE. Medium-chain triglycerides, either included in the feed55 or as a
supplement56 have been the most extensively evaluated of the dietary
therapies (ch. 161). To date, there is a single published study on the use of
cannabidiol in dogs with drug-resistant IE.57 All of these studies of alternative
therapies in dogs have yielded promising results, but because of the limited
number of studies and low total number of dogs evaluated, there is currently
insufficient evidence on the efficacy and safety of these therapies on which to
base definitive treatment recommendations. However, research continues on
these alternative therapies for dogs with IE, and additional data obtained will
likely influence our management of epilepsy in the future.

ACUTE MANAGEMENT OF EPILEPTIC
SEIZURES IN THE HOME SETTING
A significant financial and emotional burden is placed on owners of pets with
poorly controlled epilepsy, especially if frequent veterinary visits to obtain
emergency care are required. Furthermore, the presence of cluster seizures
can negatively impact an animal’s health and quality of life. Consequently, the
successful management of an epileptic dog or cat should include
recommendations for “rescue therapy” to address the potential need for
emergency treatment of seizures in the home setting.
Benzodiazepines, in their parenteral formulations, are most commonly
prescribed to control cluster seizures at home. Rectal diazepam has been
shown to decrease the number of cluster seizure events over a 24-hour period

when used in the home setting.58 The recommended dosage of diazepam is 1
mg/kg administered rectally at the onset of seizures, given up to 3 times over a
24-hour period. The dosage should be increased to 2 mg/kg in dogs receiving
phenobarbital as a maintenance ASD, as chronic phenobarbital therapy
increases the metabolism of diazepam. Diazepam is inactivated by light and
adheres to plastic; therefore, the drug should be dispensed in the original,
tinted glass vial with instructions for the owner to draw up the required
amount in a syringe as needed (not in pre-loaded syringes). A rubber catheter
or teat cannula is placed on the syringe tip to facilitate rectal administration.
Suppository forms of the drug are available, but the pharmacokinetics of these
products have not been evaluated in dogs.
The efficacy of intranasal midazolam (0.2 mg/kg administered via an
atomizer) has been compared to rectal diazepam (1 mg/kg) for the in-hospital
treatment of status epilepticus in dogs.59 Findings from this study suggest that
intranasal midazolam may be superior to rectal diazepam in the short-term
management of emergency seizures in dogs.59 If an atomizer is not available,
midazolam can be slowly dripped into the nostrils. Care must be taken when
administering a drug intranasally to an animal either during active seizures or
in the post-ictal phase, to avoid being bitten.
The author advocates the use of additional doses of maintenance oral ASDs
in conjunction with a benzodiazepine to treat cluster seizures at home. The
owner is instructed to administer the benzodiazepine (intranasal midazolam
or rectal diazepam) during or immediately after a seizure, in order to stop the
seizure and prevent additional seizures over the short term. Once the animal
has recovered from the seizure and is able to swallow, the owner is instructed
to administer an additional dose of maintenance ASD to provide a longer-term
antiepileptic effect. This regimen can be repeated up to 3 times in a 24-hour
period, but not more frequently than every hour. If the pet’s seizures persist,
the owner is advised to seek emergency veterinary care.
Pulse therapy with immediate-release levetiracetam can also be used to treat
cluster seizures in the home setting.60 An initial dose of 60 mg/kg is
administered orally either after a seizure occurs or at the onset of pre-ictal
signs, followed by the administration of 20 mg/kg q8h until the animal has
been seizure-free for 48 hours.

OUTCOME
The prognosis for an animal with epilepsy depends on the underlying cause
and response to therapy. As one might expect, animals with IE have a better
prognosis than those with structural epilepsy.25,51 Breed-related differences in
seizure severity have been demonstrated among dogs with IE, with Border

Collies,50 Australian Shepherd Dogs,49 Boxers and German Shepherd Dogs21
reported to be more likely to suffer from cluster seizures. Furthermore, cluster
seizures and status epilepticus have been shown to negatively influence
survival in dogs with IE.51,61 However, many dogs and cats with IE can expect
a near-normal lifespan.46,51,61
Remission from epilepsy, defined as an absence of seizures for a minimum
of 1 year, has been reported in approximately 15% of dogs and 45% of cats with
IE.46,49,51,52 In such instances, questions may arise as to whether ASD
therapy can be discontinued. Although animals can undergo spontaneous
remission from epilepsy, this is difficult to differentiate from seizure freedom
due to effective ASD therapy. Consequently, any attempt to wean an animal off
of ASD must be done slowly and deliberately. Abrupt withdrawal of ASD
therapy can precipitate seizures, and seizures that recur after discontinuation
of ASD treatment may be more difficult to control.62 If ASD weaning is
attempted, the author recommends stepwise dosage reductions of
approximately 25% performed at intervals equal to the time required for the
ASD to reach steady state concentrations or every 2-4 weeks, whichever is
greater.

Vestibular disease is a common clinical problem encountered in
small animal medicine. Head tilt and nystagmus are the
hallmark/cardinal signs of vestibular disease. Distinguishing
between potential lesions located in the central versus peripheral
vestibular system is of utmost importance for planning diagnostics
and for establishing a prognosis.

FUNCTIONAL NEUROANATOMY
The vestibular system is responsible for maintaining balance as well
as head and body posture. It needs to detect acceleration,
deceleration and rotational movements and regulate muscle tone in

relation to gravitational forces and movements. For coordination of
head movements with eye position, and the body and limbs, it has
projections to the eyes (medial longitudinal fasciculus, MLF) and
spinal cord (vestibulospinal tract) in the central nervous system
(CNS) (ch. 241).
The vestibular system is a sensory system composed of a
peripheral and a central vestibular part. The peripheral
vestibular system (Figure 248.1) is composed of the vestibular
portion of the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve [CN] VIII) and
its receptors located in the inner ear. The inner ear is located within
the petrous temporal bone and is composed of the cochlea, vestibule
and semicircular canals, forming the bony labyrinth. Its internal
structure represents the membranous labyrinth containing
endolymph, and it consists of the cochlear duct, utricle, saccule, and
three semicircular canals. The semicircular canals are tubular
structures projecting from the vestibule and are oriented in the three
dimensions ending in a dilated structure, the ampulla, connected to
the vestibule. The ampullae contain sensory receptors, the cristae
ampullares, that due to their orientation can detect angular
movements of the head in every plane.
The central vestibular system is composed of four vestibular
nuclei (caudal, lateral, medial, and rostral vestibular nucleus) on
each side of the rostral part of the brainstem (dorsal part of pons and
medulla), and the flocculonodular lobes and fastigial nuclei of the
cerebellum. The cerebellum has an inhibitory effect on the vestibular
nuclei to prevent excessive extensor tone.
The receptors in the inner ear detect position and movement of the
head in space while the animal is standing or moving. The generated
impulses are propagated along the vestibular nerve to the vestibular
nuclei in the brainstem. Their axons project in the vestibulospinal
tract to synapse on interneurons in the ventral grey matter of the
spinal cord, which are facilitatory to ipsilateral extensor muscles and
inhibitory to flexor muscles. The interneurons also project to the grey
matter on the other side and are inhibitory to contralateral extensor
muscles. In a physiologic situation, with impulses from the vestibuli
of both sides, a well-balanced muscle tone is generated bilaterally.
The axons of the vestibular nuclei also project rostrally in the MLF
to synapse in the motor nuclei of the oculomotor (CN III), trochlear
(CN IV), and abducens nerve (CN VI). The MLF coordinates head

and eye movement, which is referred to as physiological nystagmus.
Some axons extend to the vomiting centre in the reticular formation
in the brainstem (which is responsible for motion sickness), some
directly ascend via the caudal cerebellar peduncle to the cerebellum,
and others to the cerebral cortex for conscious perception of position
through the thalamic nuclei. The vestibular nuclei receive some
influence from higher vestibular centres in the thalamus and from
the cerebellum.
Thalamic lesions and lesions in the extrapyramidal basal nuclei
and rostral mesencephalon may also cause central vestibular disease.
The clinical signs are believed to be caused by damage to adjacent
midbrain regions involved in vestibular function.1 A head tilt without
other signs of vestibular disease is occasionally observed with focal
cervical spinal lesions affecting the spinal muscles asymmetrically.

FIGURE 248.1 Cross-sectional anatomic diagram
of the ear of a dog. From Evans HE, de Lahunta A.
