Elsevier; 2013:732.

CLINICAL SIGNS
Clinical signs of dysfunction in the vestibular system are loss of
balance with head tilt, abnormal nystagmus, positional strabismus,
leaning, circling, falling, rolling, and ataxia—irrespective of whether
the peripheral or central part of the vestibular system is affected.
Additional signs, not directly related to the vestibular system, may
comprise abnormal mentation, other CN deficits (CN V, VII, IX, X,
XII), cerebellar signs (such as tremors or absent menace response),
Horner’s syndrome, paresis, and postural reaction deficits. As the
vestibular system has broad connections with various parts of the
nervous system, all aspects of the neurological examination are
important for lesion localization (ch. 241).

HEAD TILT
A head tilt (together with nystagmus) is the most consistent sign of a
unilateral vestibular lesion caused by ipsilateral loss of antigravity
muscle tone. It is characterized by a rotation of the head along the
longitudinal axis of the body resulting in one ear being held lower
than the other. In severe cases of head tilt, the neck can be tilted
(torticollis) (Videos 241.6, 255.3)

. An intermittent head tilt alone

may indicate otitis externa or aural irritation, not vestibular disease.
A head tilt needs to be differentiated from a head turn in which
both ears are at the same height parallel to the ground whereas the
nose is turned to one side. A head turn might be associated with a
body turn (pleurothotonus), indicating an ipsilateral forebrain
lesion, not vestibular dysfunction.
The head tilt is usually to the side of a unilateral vestibular lesion.
Patients with bilateral vestibular dysfunction may not show a head
tilt nor a spontaneous or positional nystagmus unless one side is
more affected than the other. Instead of head tilt the patients may
show wide head excursions, swinging their head from side to side,
and absence of a physiologic nystagmus.
The head tilt may be contralateral to the lesion if the lesion is in
the flocculonodular lobe or the cerebellomedullary pontine angle
(paradoxical vestibular syndrome,

Video 241.9).

NYSTAGMUS
Nystagmus is an involuntary rhythmic movement of the eyeballs
(Video 241.3

5). Physiologic nystagmus occurs in normal

individuals and can be elicited by moving the head from side to side
(oculovestibular or oculocephalic reflex). It has a slow (opposite to
direction of head movement) and a fast (same direction as head
movement) phase, described as jerk nystagmus. Its function is
necessary for the stabilization of images on the retina while the head
is moving.

Nystagmus that presents in the absence of head movements is
pathological and might be spontaneous when the head is in normal
position at rest or positional when the head is held in a different
position (e.g., dorsally or with the patient placed on its back). It is
caused by unilateral disturbance in bilateral tonic influence from the
vestibular nuclei to the motor nuclei of CN III, IV, and VI. The
nystagmus is described by the orientation of the plane in which the
eyeballs are moving as horizontal, vertical, or rotatory with the
direction described in regards to its fast phase (left or right) (Video
241.6)

. The fast phase is away from the lesion with peripheral

vestibular disease and can be toward or away from the lesion with
central vestibular disease. Identifying the type of nystagmus can help
to distinguish between a lesion in the central vs. the peripheral
vestibular system. Horizontal and rotatory nystagmus may indicate a
peripheral vestibular lesion whereas vertical nystagmus and
nystagmus with changing directions are typically associated with a
lesion in the central vestibular system. Spontaneous nystagmus
occurring at >66/minute has 95% specificity and 85% sensitivity for
a peripheral vestibular lesion.
Spontaneous nystagmus is often present in acute vestibular lesions
and may become less severe or disappear with time due to central
compensation. Vision and proprioception can also help to
compensate vestibular dysfunction.
Nystagmus with continuous oscillations of both eyeballs without a
slow and fast phase is a pendular nystagmus. It is not associated
with vestibular disease but occurs secondary to congenital
abnormalities in the visual pathway of certain cat and dog breeds
such as Siamese, Birman and Himalayan cats and Belgian Shepherd
Dogs.

VESTIBULAR ATAXIA
Vestibular ataxia is caused by loss of vestibular input to ipsilateral
limb extensor muscles leading to leaning, circling, falling and rolling
to the side of the unilateral lesion. The vestibular circling often is
small in diameter and with dysmetric steps (Videos 43.1, 241.6,

241.7, 241.9, 255.3

) as opposed to compulsive walking in circles

indicating a forebrain lesion (Videos 24.1, 241.10

); however, it is

important to clarify that size of the circling cannot, by itself, be used
for localizing lesions. Patients that can still stand may show a widebased stance and truncal sway. A recumbent patient prefers to lie on
the affected side of the body. A patient with bilateral vestibular
dysfunction adopts a crouched position and might fall to either side.
Examination of the gait may be challenging in acute/peracute
vestibular disease as the patient may not be able to stand. With time,
the ataxia gets milder and the spontaneous or positional nystagmus
may disappear.

STRABISMUS
Vestibular dysfunction mostly causes a ventral or ventrolateral
positional strabismus, in which the deviation of the eyeball can
be seen when the neck is extended or the patient placed in dorsal
recumbency. Normal eye movement remains possible as there is no
paralysis of the extraocular muscles. Positional strabismus can be
seen in the eye ipsilateral to the lesion. It does not aid in
differentiating between a peripheral or central vestibular lesion.

NAUSEA AND VOMITING
Due to the connection of the vestibular system with the reticular
formation containing the vomiting centre, patients may show various
degrees of nausea leading to vomiting associated with disequilibrium
and related to motion sickness.

HORNER’S SYNDROME AND FACIAL
NERVE PARESIS/PARALYSIS
Patients with vestibular dysfunction may show Horner’s syndrome
(ch. 249). The facial nerve (CN VII) may be affected, causing

drooping of the ear and lip and asymmetry of the face and nostrils.
The presence of Horner’s syndrome and facial nerve paralysis
suggests a peripheral vestibular lesion due to the anatomic proximity
of CN VII and the sympathetic nerve supply to the eye and the
vestibular nerve in the region of the tympanic bulla and the petrous
temporal bone. On rare occasions, Horner’s syndrome may also be
seen with central (rostral and/or caudal medullary) lesions because
of involvement of the upper motor neuron (UMN) (hypothalamotecto-tegmental) sympathetic pathway; this typically requires a
severe brainstem lesion and usually the animal is tetraplegic with
marked mentation changes.

CRANIAL NERVE DEFICITS
Along with vestibular signs, multiple other CNs such as CN V-XII
may show deficits. This is due to the close anatomical proximity of
the CNs and their nuclei in the pons and medulla oblongata. Deficits
of multiple CNs is suggestive of a central vestibular lesion.
In very rare cases, multiple CN deficits together with vestibular
disease can be seen in generalized or CN polyneuropathy (ch. 249).

CHANGE IN MENTATION
Lesions in the central vestibular system frequently involve the
reticular formation in the brainstem, altering mental status (e.g.,
depression, stupor, coma). As the change in mentation is a clear
indicator of central vestibular disease, it is crucial to differentiate it
from the profound disorientation resulting from severe
disequilibrium in a patient with peripheral vestibular disease.

PROPRIOCEPTION
Normal performance of postural reactions such as hopping and
proprioceptive placing necessitates normal function of the ascending
general proprioceptive tracts as well as descending UMN tracts.
Postural reaction deficits, particularly conscious proprioceptive
deficits (paw placing test), are the most important indicators for a

lesion in the central vestibular system. Due to the anatomic
proximity of ascending proprioceptive pathways with the vestibular
nuclei in the brainstem, patients with a central vestibular lesion
show ipsilateral postural reaction deficits (Video 241.7

).

HEARING LOSS
Due to the anatomical connection between the auditory and the
vestibular system, unilateral (temporary) hearing loss may occur in a
patient with peripheral vestibular disease.

PARESIS
Lesions in the central vestibular system can also involve the
ascending and descending motor and sensory pathways to the
ipsilateral limbs resulting in ipsilateral spastic hemiparesis and
general proprioceptive ataxia.

NEUROANATOMICAL LESION
LOCALIZATION (CH. 241)
Because differential diagnoses, diagnostic tests and prognosis are
dependent on the site of the lesion, it is crucial to define whether the
lesion is in the peripheral or central vestibular system. A thorough
history (ch. 2), with information about onset and course of the
disease, presence of concurrent signs, history of ear disease and
administration of drugs have to be recorded and a physical
examination as well as a complete and thorough neurological
examination have to be performed.

PERIPHERAL VS. CENTRAL
VESTIBULAR DISEASE

The features of peripheral and of central vestibular disease are
compared and contrasted in Table 248.1. Although it may seem
that the distinction between a peripheral vs. central vestibular lesion
might be straightforward, even in the absence of characteristic signs
of central vestibular dysfunction, a lesion in the central vestibular
system cannot be (completely) excluded.2-5

PARADOXICAL VESTIBULAR DISEASE
In rare instances, the patient can show a head tilt in the direction
opposite the side of the lesion. This paradoxical head tilt is caused by
a lesion in the caudal cerebellar peduncle, the fastigial nucleus or the
flocculonodular lobe of the cerebellum. As cerebellar projections
promote a mainly inhibitory effect on the vestibular nuclei, there is
excessive tone in the ipsilateral extensor muscles, causing the patient
to lean, and the head to tilt, away from the lesion. Usually, there is
also some evidence of cerebellar disease such as ipsilateral
hypermetria, truncal sway or (intention) tremor. The side of the
lesion in paradoxical vestibular disease can be determined by testing
proprioception, particularly paw positioning, which is reduced to
absent on the side of the lesion

(Video 241.9).

BILATERAL VESTIBULAR DISEASE
Bilateral vestibular disease is rare. When it occurs, a lesion affecting
both peripheral vestibular components is most likely. Physical
manifestations have been described above.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES
Lesion localization to the peripheral or central vestibular system (ch.
241), together with the history and general physical examination,
leads to an appropriate list of differential diagnoses (Table 248.2).
The most common vestibular diseases are neoplasia and
inflammation/infection (central) and otitis media/interna and
idiopathic/geriatric vestibular disease (peripheral).

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH IN AN
ANIMAL WITH VESTIBULAR DISEASE

The diagnostic work-up of patients with vestibular signs varies
considerably between central versus peripheral disease (Figure
248.2). In all patients, a complete blood count, biochemistry profile,
thyroid panel, urinalysis, and blood pressure evaluation (ch. 91)
should be performed. This is useful for the identification of potential
metabolic or inflammatory diseases, and also to serve as a general
health screen as most procedures for further diagnostics of vestibular
disease require general anesthesia.
Patients with peripheral vestibular disease should undergo a
thorough otoscopic examination (under sedation or anesthesia; ch.
82), and radiographs of the tympanic bullae (oblique and open
mouth views) if referral for computed tomography (CT) or magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) is not possible. If otitis media/interna is
suspected, myringotomy with fluid sampling should be performed
for cytology and bacterial culture. CT or MRI of the tympanic bullae
can be considered as they are the most sensitive tools to detect bulla
effusions or otitis interna, respectively (ch. 112). Brainstem auditory
evoked potentials (BAEP) can be performed to assess the cochlear
portion of CN VIII. In cats, a thorough pharyngeal examination
should be performed to check for inflammatory polyps (ch. 213;
Video 213.21).
Diagnostic work-up of patients with central vestibular disease
mostly requires advanced imaging of the brain, preferably with MRI
(ch. 112), and analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF; ch. 109) which
can be used for testing for infectious agents (ch. 242).6 BAEP may
be performed to evaluate the brainstem component of the auditory
pathway.
In case the clinician is in doubt about lesion localization or if the
signs of peripheral vestibular disease do not improve despite
treatment, the patient should undergo brain imaging with MRI and
CSF analysis.

PERIPHERAL VESTIBULAR DISEASES
OTITIS MEDIA/INTERNA

Otitis media/interna is the most common cause for peripheral
vestibular disease in dogs and cats (ch. 82).

NASOPHARYNGEAL POLYPS
Nasopharyngeal polyps may cause otitis media/interna due to
auditory tube obstruction by the polyp, resulting in signs of
peripheral vestibular disease (ch. 213).

CONGENITAL VESTIBULAR DISEASE
Unilateral congenital vestibular disease has been reported in various
dog breeds (German Shepherd Dog, Doberman, Smooth Haired Fox
Terrier, English Cocker Spaniel) and a few cat breeds (Siamese,
Burmese, Tonkinese). Bilateral congenital vestibular disease has
been described in Akitas and Beagles. The disease is thought to be
due to progressive loss of the sensory hair cells of the vestibular and
hearing system. A lymphocytic labyrinthitis was identified in a study
of Doberman puppies.7-9 The first clinical signs become obvious at
the age of 3-12 weeks when the animal starts to ambulate. Clinical
signs comprise a head tilt, vestibular ataxia, and circling unless the
condition is bilateral. Pathological nystagmus is usually not present.
In some animals, the vestibular signs are accompanied by deafness.
The diagnosis is reached by exclusion and with consideration of
signalment and history. There is no effective treatment but the
animals can learn to compensate through visual and proprioceptive
influences. Deafness tends to be permanent.

HYPOTHYROIDISM
Hypothyroidism has been associated with peripheral vestibular
disease10,11 (ch. 285). Affected animals are usually middle-aged to
older dogs. Vestibular signs are usually mild to moderate and can be
uni- or bilateral. Facial nerve paresis might be associated with
vestibular signs in some patients. If lethargy is present,
differentiation from obtundation indicating central vestibular

disease might be difficult. Moreover, hypothyroidism can cause
arteriosclerosis in dogs and is therefore a risk factor for vascular
accidents in the CNS.

The pathogenesis is not completely understood. The peripheral
nerve dysfunction might reflect a deficit in energy metabolism with a
disturbance in axonal transport as well as Schwann cell
dysfunction.12 Myxedematous deposits may also lead to compression
of CN VII and CN VIII in their course through the internal acoustic
meatus.

OTOTOXICOSIS
Ototoxicosis is caused by various substances and can be unilateral or
bilateral and lead to vestibular dysfunction, hearing loss or a
combination of both. Signs can develop acutely or can be delayed.
Due to the potential for ototoxicosis, certain substances should not
be introduced into the ear when the tympanic membrane is ruptured
or cannot be visualized (ch. 82).

IDIOPATHIC VESTIBULAR SYNDROME
Idiopathic vestibular syndrome is a common condition in cats and
older dogs, which explains why it is referred to as “geriatric
vestibular syndrome.” Clinical signs are acute/peracute in onset and
often quite severe. Signs reflect unilateral peripheral vestibular
dysfunction although bilateral disease is occasionally seen,
particularly in cats. Nausea and vomiting are common; signs of
central vestibular dysfunction are lacking. While it was previously
stated that facial paralysis and Horner’s syndrome are absent,13,14 a
recent study describes facial nerve involvement in idiopathic
vestibular syndrome.15
The etiology is unknown; a disturbance in endolymphatic
production, absorption and flow is assumed. However, as cats in the
northeastern USA seem to be commonly affected from spring to early
autumn, an association with Cuterebra larval migration was
hypothesized.16

The diagnosis is based on history, examination findings (ch. 241)
and exclusion of other causes of peripheral disease. Due to the
connection with endolymph production, it is advisable to check the
blood pressure (ch. 91) and to rule out diseases that can affect the
vessel wall (e.g., diabetes mellitus [chs. 291, 292], hypothyroidism
[chs. 285, 286]) or cause a hypercoagulable state (e.g., proteinlosing nephropathies [ch. 171]). Treatment consists of supportive
care such as fluid therapy and antiemetics in a patient that is
dehydrated or vomiting (ch. 48). Maropitant (neurokinin-1 receptor
antagonist) and metoclopramide (dopamine D2 receptor antagonist)
are the main treatment options for nausea and vomiting in cats and
dogs. The addition of ondansetron (5-HT3 receptor antagonist) may
provide an additional benefit in treatment of nausea.17 Physical
rehabilitation (ch. 256) with movement of the patient to provide
somatosensory feedback seems very important to stimulate CNS
compensation, neuroplastic reorganization, and correction of
vestibular deficits in vestibular lesions in general.18 Clinical signs
typically improve within 2-3 days and resolve on their own within 24 weeks. The prognosis for recovery is good. However, some patients
will have a residual head tilt.19

NEOPLASIA OF MIDDLE/INNER EAR
AND TRIGEMINAL NERVE SHEATH
TUMOR
Tumors involving the tympanic bulla or inner ear can cause
peripheral vestibular signs and occur in elderly dogs and cats.
Although rare, fibrosarcoma, chondrosarcoma and osteosarcoma of
the bulla, lymphoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and ceruminous
gland adenocarcinoma have been reported. The latter two are the
most common in dogs and most of these tumors tend to be
aggressive.20 Trigeminal nerve sheath tumor can present with
vestibular signs due to the anatomical proximity of CN V and CN
VIII (ch. 245).

CENTRAL VESTIBULAR DISEASES
CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE
Cerebrovascular accidents produce peracute-onset, nonprogressive
signs that can be attributed to a focal brain area1,21,22 (ch. 243).

INFLAMMATORY/INFECTIOUS CNS
DISEASE
Inflammatory diseases of the brain (encephalitis) and meninges
(meningoencephalitis) can affect any part of the CNS. Central
vestibular signs are common and can be seen in combination with
other neurological signs or neck pain as reflection of meningitis (ch.
242).

TRAUMA
Head trauma is most often caused by car accidents in dogs and cats.
It can cause vestibular signs due to brainstem and/or cerebellar
involvement (ch. 246).

ANOMALY
Chiari-like malformations and intracranial intra-arachnoidal
(supracollicular or quadrigeminal) cysts cause compression of the
cerebellum and/or brainstem, and cerebellar and vestibular signs
(ch. 244).

METABOLIC/TOXIC
Metronidazole Toxicosis
Metronidazole is a commonly administered antibiotic in dogs and
cats. The onset of clinical signs such as anorexia and vomiting can be
seen as soon as 3 days after treatment initiation but can also occur

with chronic treatment. Doses of 60 mg/kg/day for 3-14 days are
reported to cause toxicosis, although doses as low as 30 mg/kg/day
have been incriminated.23 Metronidazole intoxication in dogs causes
acute to subacute bilateral central vestibular signs with symmetrical
or asymmetrical generalized ataxia and a positional vertical
nystagmus. Additional signs such as hypermetria and intention
tremors indicate cerebellar involvement. Cats tend to show forebrain
disturbances such as seizures, blindness and ataxia instead of
vestibular signs.
Mechanistically, an interaction of metronidazole with gammaaminobutyric acid (GABA) receptors in cerebellum and vestibular
nuclei is presumed. The diagnosis is based on history of
metronidazole treatment and compatible clinical signs. Treatment
consists of drug discontinuation and supportive care. Diazepam
administration (0.5 mg/kg IV, then 0.5 mg/kg PO q8h for 3 days)
shortens the recovery time to 1-3 days (versus 2-3 weeks) due to its
effect on GABA receptors.

Thiamine Deficiency
Thiamine deficiency is described in ch. 14. Initial signs include
anorexia and lethargy; later vestibular signs (usually bilateral),
pupillary dilation and marked ventroflexion of the head and neck
become obvious. Diagnosis is based on history and confirmed by
MRI, and thiamine levels in blood.24 Treatment with thiamine (12.550 mg daily, IM, SC, or PO) can lead to rapid improvement of clinical
signs, although residual signs can persist.

Hypothyroidism
In dogs, hypothyroidism (ch. 285) can cause central vestibular
disease (besides peripheral vestibular disease) due to
arteriosclerosis-associated vascular accidents in the CNS.
Hyperlipidaemia can cause increased blood viscosity that results in
decreased CNS perfusion. Clinical signs of central vestibular
syndrome may not respond well to thyroid hormone
supplementation, depending on the severity of brain infarction and
degree of dysfunction.25-27

NEOPLASIA
Neoplasia that affects the brainstem or cerebellum is a common
cause of central vestibular disease. In dogs, choroid plexus papilloma
in the fourth ventricle and meningioma have a predilection site in
the caudal fossa. Moreover, nerve sheath tumour of CN V may affect
the brainstem by extension. Meningioma and lymphoma are the
most common CNS tumors in cats (ch. 245).

Neuropathies
John Henry Rossmeisl Jr.

The term cranial neuropathy refers to any condition that causes
dysfunction of a cranial nerve (CN) anywhere along its anatomic
course.1 Cranial neuropathies most often affect a single CN
(mononeuropathy), but can involve multiple CNs, or appear in
association with generalized polyneuropathies.2-5 A thorough
neurologic examination is necessary (ch. 241) to correctly localize
the level of CN dysfunction, with particular emphasis on
identification of involvement of the central or peripheral components

of the affected CN in order to best formulate differential diagnoses
and a management plan (Table 249.1).1 For example, identification
of deficits involving two or more CNs usually indicates that the lesion
involves the anatomic region in which the nerves are in close
proximity, as would be the case for signs of Horner’s syndrome (HS),
facial paresis, and peripheral vestibular dysfunction caused by
disease of the middle and inner ear.6 Common etiologies of cranial
neuropathies include degenerative, idiopathic, inflammatory,
metabolic, and neoplastic diseases.1-6 By convention, an idiopathic
cranial neuropathy is diagnosed only following exclusion of
structural and metabolic causes of disease with the propensity to
affect the dysfunctional CN, which can be challenging in the living
patient. Idiopathic mononeuropathies affect CNs more frequently
than other peripheral nerves, and many of these idiopathic cranial
neuropathic syndromes are self-limiting.2,3,5

OPTIC NERVE (CN II)—OPTIC NEURITIS
Optic neuritis is characterized by an acute onset of vision loss, which
is typically bilateral and associated with mydriatic and unresponsive
pupils (ch. 13; Video

249.1).7 Frequently, there are visible

changes in the posterior segment of the eye, such as optic disc
swelling (Figure 249.1), vascular congestion, hemorrhage, and
peripapillary neuroretinitis, although the ophthalmic examination
can be normal in cases of retrobulbar disease.7,8 If optic disc swelling
is visible, differential diagnoses include papilledema or optic nerve
edema that can accompany uveitis or glaucoma. These conditions
usually can be differentiated based on the collective findings of the
clinical examination.7 Papilledema is non-inflammatory disc edema
resulting from intracranial hypertension that does not cause acute
vision loss.
Potential etiologies of optic neuritis include infectious (e.g., canine
distemper viral [ch. 204], mycotic [chs. 207-211], and protozoal
[ch. 197]) and immune-mediated (e.g., granulomatous
meningoencephalitis) meningoencephalitides (ch. 242), and

neoplasms (ch. 245; Figure 249.1) that infiltrate or compress (e.g.,
meningioma, glioma, lymphoma, pituitary tumors) the optic nerves
or chiasm.7-10 Thus, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
examinations of the brain (chs. 112 and 242), cerebrospinal fluid
analysis (ch. 109), and serologic assays are diagnostic tests that are
recommended in cases of optic neuritis.8-10 The management of
meningoencephalitis is reviewed in ch. 242. Electroretinography
(ERG) is normal in patients with optic neuritis. In many dogs with
optic neuritis, no underlying cause is identified, the disease is
presumed to be idiopathic, and systemic therapy with
immunosuppressive dosages of prednisone is attempted (ch. 144).7
In dogs, sudden acquired retinal degeneration syndrome (SARDS) is
another cause of bilateral acute blindness associated with mydriatic
pupils.10,11 However, many dogs with SARDS will have sluggish and
incomplete pupillary light reflexes, the fundic examination is initially
normal, and the ERG will be extinguished.10,11 The prognosis for
complete visual recovery with optic neuritis is guarded to poor.7,12

OCULOMOTOR (CN III), TROCHLEAR
(CN IV), AND ABDUCENT (CN VI)
NERVES
Collectively, these nerves innervate the extraocular muscles. They
participate in ocular position and coordinated and conjugate
movement of the eyes, along with the vestibular and cervical
proprioceptive systems.13 The parasympathetic portion of CN III is
responsible for pupillary constriction. Clinical signs of dysfunction of
these nerves or their associated vestibular projections include
strabismus, abnormal physiological nystagmus due to external
ophthalmoplegia, pathological nystagmus if the lesion involves the
vestibular system, and internal ophthalmoplegia (i.e., a mydriatic

and fixed pupil) if the lesion affects the parasympathetic portion of
CN III (ch. 241).13-15 An idiopathic, non-progressive oculomotor
neuropathy has been recognized in dogs. These cases present with
unilateral internal and/or external ophthalmoplegia without other
neurologic or ophthalmic signs, and MRI findings that are limited to
enlargement or contrast enhancement of the oculomotor nerve.16
Idiopathic oculomotor neuropathy has a good prognosis as the
clinical signs may remain static or resolve without treatment.16
Cavernous sinus (CSS) and orbital fissure (OFS) syndromes are
defined by clinical dysfunction of two or more of the following CNs:
III, IV, and VI, and the ophthalmic or maxillary branches of CN
V.14,15 The axons of these CNs course in intimate anatomic
association with each other along the floor of the skull adjacent to the
CSS prior to exiting the skull through the OFS. Clinical signs
frequently observed with these syndromes include external and
internal ophthalmoplegia, reduced corneal sensitivity, neurotrophic
keratitis, and ptosis.14,15 Differentiation of CSS from OFS requires
demonstration of the anatomic level of the lesion with diagnostic
imaging. The most common causes of CSS and OFS are primary or
metastatic neoplasms, although infectious causes have been
reported, particularly in cats.14,15

TRIGEMINAL NERVE (CN V)—
TRIGEMINAL NEUROPATHY
The trigeminal nerve consists of three primary branches that provide
sensation to the face (i.e., ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular
nerves) and motor function to the muscles of mastication
(mandibular nerve) (ch. 241).1,2 Common clinical presentations of
trigeminal mononeuropathies involve mandibular motor
dysfunction; cases of isolated trigeminal sensory dysfunction are
rare.17 The first is an acute onset of a flaccid bilateral paresis of the
mandibular nerves resulting in a dropped jaw and the animal’s
inability to close the mouth (

Videos 241.36, 249.2).2 This clinical

presentation can result from disorders affecting mechanical jaw
function (e.g., temporomandibular joint fracture or avulsion),
diseases resulting in pain associated with jaw movement (e.g.,
masticatory muscle myositis [ch. 258], retrobulbar mass lesions),
and inflammatory (e.g., Neospora [ch. 197], Toxoplasma [ch. 197],
Cryptococcus [ch. 207], rabies [ch. 202]), idiopathic, or neoplastic
(e.g., hematopoietic neoplasia [ch. 322], nerve sheath tumor [NST])
trigeminal nerve lesions.2,18-20 Animals with clinical signs limited to
an acutely dropped jaw usually have disease of the peripheral
portions of the trigeminal nerve, because a bilateral lesion in the
pontine trigeminal motor nuclei would be expected to be associated
with additional and severe clinical signs of pontomedullary
syndrome, which often include central vestibular dysfunction, a
depressed level of consciousness, and/or CN VI-XII deficits.1
Idiopathic trigeminal neuritis (ITN) is the most common cause of
dropped jaw in dogs (

Video 249.2). ITN mainly impairs

masticatory muscle motor function, although trigeminal sensory
deficits can accompany ITN in ∼1/3 of dogs, and concurrent facial
nerve paralysis, masticatory muscle atrophy, or HS occasionally also
can be observed.2 Treatment includes supportive care with assisted
feeding (ch. 81). Affected dogs usually recover within 2-4 weeks.
MRI of the brain of animals with trigeminal neuropathy provides the
best, non-invasive method to differentiate etiologies of trigeminal
neuropathy (ch. 112). On MRI, both normal and abnormal
trigeminal nerves will demonstrate contrast enhancement.21 ITN
may be associated with normal nerve signal characteristics and
morphology, or diffusely enlarged and T2-hyperintense nerves.22
Another presentation of trigeminal neuropathy is an acute onset of
unilateral, and often severe, atrophy of the muscles of mastication
ipsilateral to the dysfunctional mandibular nerve. Trigeminal NSTs
are a common etiology of unilateral neurogenic masticatory muscle
atrophy (Figure 249.2).21-23 Facial hypalgesia or paresthesia,
manifesting as facial rubbing, itching, or pain, in addition to HS, also
can be seen. NSTs are locally invasive and slow to metastasize.
Treatment options for NSTs include surgical debulking,

radiotherapy, or supportive care with glucocorticoids.23 Stereotactic
radiation therapy treatment of trigeminal NST has been associated
with median survival times ranging from 1-2 years.23

FACIAL NERVE (CN VII)—FACIAL
NEUROPATHY/PARALYSIS
Facial paralysis is characterized by an acute inability to close the
palpebral fissure, a drooping of the ear and lip, and drooling on the
affected side.1 Causes of peripheral facial nerve paralysis include
otitis media-interna, iatrogenic surgical injury (e.g., bulla
osteotomy), idiopathic disease, metabolic disease (e.g.,
hypothyroidism [ch. 285]), otic neoplasms, trauma, and
sulfonamide hypersensitivity.3,6,24,25 Due to the close anatomic
relationships of the vestibulocochlear and facial nerves in both the
medulla and petrous temporal bone, vestibular signs can accompany
both peripheral and central (e.g., neoplasia [ch. 245],
meningoencephalitis [ch. 242]) etiologies of facial paralysis.6,26
Facial paresis also can be a feature of generalized neuropathies or
neuromuscular diseases, such as acute canine polyradiculoneuritis,
tick paralysis, and myasthenia gravis (ch. 253).27-29 Facial paralysis
is reported to be idiopathic in 75% of dogs and 25% of cats with facial
neuropathy.3 Approximately 60% of cases of idiopathic disease
present with unilateral signs and 40% with bilateral signs (

Video

249.3).30 Idiopathic facial paralysis is commonly associated with
various segments of facial nerve enhancement on MRI
examinations.30,31 Spontaneous recovery from idiopathic facial
nerve paralysis is possible. In dogs, contrast enhancement of the
nerve on MRI can provide prognostic information, with one study
indicating that recovery of facial nerve function is less likely to occur
or may be prolonged in cases demonstrating enhancement.31
Animals that recover usually do so within 3-8 weeks.3,31

VESTIBULOCOCHLEAR NERVE (CN
VIII)
The vestibular branch of CN VIII participates in maintenance of
balance and posture, and disorders affecting the vestibular system
are reviewed in ch. 248.1,12 Dysfunction of the cochlear branch
results in deafness that can be classified as conductive (e.g., otitis
externa/media) or sensorineural in origin.32 The most common
cause of deafness is congenital hereditary sensorineural associated
with a white coat color and the piebald and merle genes.32,33 In dogs
and cats, acquired sensorineural deafness can occur secondary to
progressive age-related cochlear degeneration (i.e., presbycusis) or
ototoxic drug therapy (e.g., aminoglycosides).32 Deafness is
diagnosed via brainstem auditory evoked response testing.32

GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL (CN IX), VAGUS,
(CN X), AND ACCESSORY (CN XI)
NERVES—DYSPHAGIA,
MEGAESOPHAGUS, AND LARYNGEAL
PARALYSIS
The glossopharyngeal, vagus, and accessory nerves are important for
function of the pharynx, larynx, and esophagus.1 In the dysphagic
patient, it is important to differentiate neurogenic prehensile
problems that imply dysfunction of the jaw (CN V), lips (CN VII)
and/or tongue (CN XII) from neurogenic deglutition problems (ch.
47). Prehensile and oropharyngeal dysphagic disorders can be
identified with a physical examination, including observation of
eating, while characterization and diagnosis of disorders of the
pharyngeal, cricopharyngeal, and/or esophageal phases of
swallowing often requires diagnostic imaging examinations including
contrast radiography or videofluoroscopy (ch. 259).34 Dysphagia
can be associated with clinical signs of gagging, coughing after

drinking or eating, pharyngeal accumulation of saliva or food, and an
abnormal gag reflex. Neurologic diseases that commonly cause
dysphagia include primary myopathies (ch. 14 and 23),
polyneuropathies (ch. 252), neuromuscular junctional disorders
(e.g., myasthenia gravis, botulism; ch. 253), and caudal brainstem
lesions (e.g., encephalitis [ch. 242] and neoplasia [ch.
245]).27,29,35,36

FIGURE 249.2 Clinical and magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) features of a trigeminal nerve sheath
tumor in a dog. A, Left unilateral atrophy of the
temporalis (white arrows) and masseter muscles,
along with ipsilateral partial Horner’s syndrome.
Transverse (B) and left parasagittal (C) postcontrast T1-weighted MRI demonstrating lobular,
contrast-enhancing extra-axial mass (short yellow
arrows) involving the trigeminal nerve resulting in

mesencephalic compression and loss of muscle mass
(B; left temporalis [white arrows]).
The esophagus is innervated by the vagus and internal branch of
the accessory nerves.1 Megaesophagus is characterized by
generalized dilation and abnormal peristalsis of the esophagus (ch.
259).37,38 Regurgitation is the primary clinical sign observed, and
secondary aspiration pneumonia is common (ch. 217).
Megaesophagus is more common in dogs than in cats, and can be
congenital or acquired, although most canine cases are acquired and
idiopathic.36 Although megaesophagus can be identified readily with
thoracic radiography, a thorough history and ancillary diagnostics
are required to establish the etiology.34 Acquired megaesophagus
can be caused by polyneuropathies (ch. 252), polymyopathies,
myasthenia gravis (ch. 253), endocrinopathies (e.g.,
hypoadrenocorticism [ch. 296], hypothyroidism [ch. 285]),
intoxications (e.g., lead, organophosphate, thallium; ch. 133), that
must be ruled out to make a diagnosis of idiopathic
megaesophagus.27,29,34,35,37-41 Treatment is directed at the
underlying cause, when present, and various assisted feeding
procedures (e.g., Bailey chair, gastrostomy tube). The prognosis
associated with megaesophagus is highly variable and dependent on
the underlying etiology (ch. 259).37-40
The larynx is innervated by branches of the vagus nerve (ch.
214).1 The recurrent laryngeal nerve innervates the abductor
muscles of the larynx. Lesions affecting the recurrent laryngeal nerve
can result in dysphonia, inspiratory stridor, and respiratory
distress.4 Congenital laryngeal paralysis has been described in
several breeds.27,42-45 Acquired laryngeal paralysis has been
associated with metabolic disease (e.g., hypothyroidism [ch. 285]),
trauma to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, neoplasia (e.g., squamous
cell carcinoma, thyroid carcinoma), intoxications (e.g., lead; ch.
133), and brainstem disease (e.g., neoplasia [ch. 245], encephalitis
[ch. 242]).27,42-45 In older, large-breed dogs, laryngeal paralysis is

often the initial clinical manifestation of a progressive, degenerative
polyneuropathy (see ch. 252).4,27,44

HORNER’S SYNDROME
HS results from lesions affecting any portion of the three-neuron
oculosympathetic pathway.5,46 Clinical signs consist of miosis,
ptosis, protrusion of the third eyelid, and enophthalmos. First order
(i.e., upper motor neuron or central) neurons originate in the rostral
brainstem, travel down the cervical spinal cord to synapse on second
order (i.e., preganglionic) neurons, which have their cell bodies in
the T1-T3 spinal segments. Second order axons course up the
vagosympathetic trunk to synapse on third order (i.e., postganglionic) neurons in the cranial cervical ganglion, which then
project to the eye and adnexa.5,47 Topical phenylephrine testing can
aid in lesion localization along this pathway (ch. 254).5 Observation
of mydriasis within 20 minutes of the application of phenylephrine
indicates a post-ganglionic lesion, whereas mydriasis occurring after
20 minutes suggests a pre-ganglionic lesion.5 HS can be caused by
degenerative, inflammatory, ischemic, metabolic, neoplastic, or
traumatic lesions at any site in the oculosympathetic pathway,
although in the majority of HS cases no etiology is found and the
condition is presumptively idiopathic.5,46 Golden Retrievers are
predisposed to developing idiopathic HS.47,48 The most recent data
indicate idiopathic HS is post-ganglionic in the majority of cases,
which contradicts results of earlier reports.47,48 Idiopathic HS is
mainly an aesthetic problem, as vision is not impaired unless the
problem is bilateral, and the condition will resolve in many dogs
within 3-4 months.47,48

CERVICAL SPONDYLOMYELOPATHY
ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS
Cervical spondylomyelopathy (CSM) is the most common disease of
the cervical vertebral column of large- and giant-breed dogs. Fifteen
names have been used to describe this disease (wobbler syndrome,
cervical vertebral instability, cervical malformation-malarticulation
syndrome, etc.) reflecting the limited understanding of the disease’s
pathogenesis.1-4
The cause of CSM remains unresolved. Genetic, congenital, body
conformation, and nutritional factors have been proposed; however,
both body conformation and nutrition do not appear to be
significant.5,6 Current evidence supports a congenital etiology with a
genetic basis.7
There are two forms of CSM. Despite some degree of overlap (25%
of affected dogs), CSM can be broadly divided into osseousassociated compression and disc-associated compression.1,8,9 Discassociated compression typically is seen in middle-aged large-breed
dogs (mostly Doberman Pinschers). It is caused by intervertebral
disc protrusion with or without hypertrophy of the dorsal
longitudinal ligament or ligamentum flavum (Figure 250.1, A). The
vast majority of these compressions affect the C5-6 and C6-7 discs.
Osseous CSM is seen predominantly in young adult, giant-breed
dogs, especially Great Danes. They have spinal cord compression
secondary to malformation and/or proliferation of the vertebral arch

(dorsally), articular processes (dorsolaterally), or articular processes
and pedicles (laterally) (Figure 250.1, B).1

CLINICAL FINDINGS
Dogs with CSM will typically present with a longstanding history of
chronic and progressive gait deficits. The main neurological
abnormality is proprioceptive ataxia leading to a “wobbly” gait (thus
the name “wobblers”), along with variable degrees of weakness.
Many dogs present with the so-called “two-engine gait”: the thoracic
limb gait appears choppy and short-strided, whereas the pelvic limb
gait is often wide-based (abducted), with a longer stride length
(Videos 241.42, 250.1)

. Postural reaction deficits (proprioceptive

positioning deficits; ch. 241) are usually seen, but may not be
evident in those with a chronic history (Video 241.4

). Spinal

reflexes in the thoracic limbs will usually reveal decreased flexor
(withdrawal) reflex with normal to increased extensor tone. The
pelvic limb reflexes will be normal to increased. Palpation of the
cervical spine may reveal signs of pain; however, cervical
hyperesthesia is not a prominent feature. Forceful manipulations of
the cervical spine are unnecessary and can lead to neurologic
decompensation.

DIAGNOSIS
Definitive diagnosis should be made using advanced imaging
(computed tomography [CT] or magnetic resonance imaging [MRI];
ch. 112) or myelography (ch. 109). Survey radiographs can be used
as a screening test to rule out other differential diagnoses and for a
presumptive diagnosis. Radiographic findings seen in the discassociated form are primarily changes in the shape of the vertebral
body, narrowing of the intervertebral disc space, and vertebral canal
stenosis. Osteoarthritic, sclerotic changes of the articular processes
are the radiographic hallmarks in osseous compressions.10
Myelography is no longer an ideal method to diagnose CSM. CT

myelography is preferred over plain CT, to better identify the exact
location of the compressive lesion(s).11 MRI is the gold standard test
and has been shown to be superior to myelography and
complementary to CT.12-14 The main advantage of MRI is that it
detects spinal cord signal changes (seen in ∼60% of dogs), allowing
precise identification of the most severely affected sites.15

TREATMENT
Ideally the natural history of a disease should be understood to
make appropriate treatment recommendations. It appears that the
disease progresses slowly in many dogs with both forms of CSM.4,1618
Broadly speaking, treatment options are medical (conservative) or
surgical. Conservative management is a viable option for many dogs,
primarily those giant-breed dogs with multiple lateralized
compressive lesions. Medical management also may be an
appropriate step initially to evaluate the improvement obtained with
it, and to give owners the opportunity to decide on surgery. The
response to medical management can be used for indirectly
evaluating the degree of reversibility of spinal cord lesions. The most
important component of medical management is exercise restriction
to minimize the dynamic component of spinal cord injury.1,19 Dogs
can be leash-walked, but free, unsupervised activity is strongly
discouraged. A body harness should be worn instead of a neck collar.
Corticosteroids appear to benefit dogs with CSM (e.g., prednisone
0.5-1 mg/kg PO q12-24h, tapering over 2-4 weeks). Proposed
mechanisms of actions for corticosteroids are reduction of vasogenic
edema, protection from glutamate toxicity, and reduction of
neuronal and oligodendroglial apoptosis.20-22 Surviving
demyelinated axons may also remyelinate with treatment. Due to the
possibility of gastrointestinal complications, omeprazole is often
used in conjunction with corticosteroid therapy, although supportive
evidence is sparse (ch. 261). Approximately 50% of dogs improve
with medical management.16,23-25 Physical therapy is commonly
recommended in addition to medical management (ch. 256).

Physical therapy can counteract the motor and proprioceptive
deficits, among several other benefits.26

FIGURE 250.1 A, Disc-associated cervical
spondylomyelopathy. Top, Ventral spinal cord and

Surgery is generally assumed to represent the treatment of choice
for most dogs with CSM.2,27 Because most affected dogs have spinal
cord compression, decompressing the spinal cord in theory provides
definitive treatment. However, it is important to consider several
factors such as severity of neurological signs, type and severity of
compressive lesion(s), response (or lack of response) to medical
management, short- and long-term expectations of the owner, and
presence of other concurrent neurological, orthopedic, systemic or
cardiac diseases that would affect the long-term outcome. This is also
one of the most controversial topics regarding this disease. More
than 30 surgical techniques have been proposed to treat CSM.27,28
They can be broadly divided into direct decompression (e.g., ventral
slot or dorsal laminectomy), indirect decompression (e.g., distraction
techniques with polymethyl methacrylate plug), and motionpreserving techniques (disc replacement).27-31 Currently no

technique is clearly superior. Approximately 70-80% of dogs
improve with surgical treatment, although many deteriorate within
months to 2-3 years after surgery.

DEGENERATIVE LUMBOSACRAL
STENOSIS
ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS
Degenerative lumbosacral stenosis (DLSS) is a common disease of
adult large-breed dogs. Several other terms have been used to
describe it, such as cauda equina syndrome, cauda equina
compression, and lumbosacral instability.32-34 These terms all
encompass a syndrome characterized by stenosis (narrowing) of the
lumbosacral region frequently caused by intervertebral disc
protrusion (Figure 250.2). The basic pathophysiologic mechanism
involves chronic progressive intervertebral disc degeneration, with
subsequent protrusion of the L7-S1 intervertebral disc into the
vertebral canal along with proliferation of the soft tissues
surrounding the cauda equina, such as hypertrophy of the
interarcuate ligament (ligamentum flavum), the joint capsule, and
epidural fibrosis.32,35,36
The specific causes for the high incidence of this degenerative
process in the lumbosacral region are unknown. A genetic basis has
been proposed in German Shepherd Dogs.37 It appears that the
presence of transitional vertebrae or sacral osteochondrosis at the
lumbosacral junction in German Shepherd Dogs as well as other
large-breed dogs is associated with development of DLSS.37-40
German Shepherd Dogs have also been shown to have vertebral
canal stenosis and a higher step between L7-S1 compared to other
breeds.37

CLINICAL SIGNS
The signs reflect compression of the spinal nerves and nerve roots at
the lumbosacral region. The main clinical sign is evidence of

lumbosacral pain. Patients have a history suggestive of pain, such as
difficulty or reluctance to sit, jump, go up stairs, and lameness.
Careful palpation of the lumbosacral area, including lordosing the
caudal spine while pressing on the lumbosacral area, elevation of the
tail, or rectal palpation, should cause signs of pain in affected dogs. It
is important to always perform a rectal examination in dogs with
these signs (ch. 3), as neoplasms in the pelvic canal can extend
dorsally, causing signs of cauda equina dysfunction.32
Gait examination of affected dogs reveals pelvic limb weakness
(without proprioceptive ataxia), and often a “stiff” gait. In some
cases, the only sign is uni- or bilateral lameness, which can be
misinterpreted as a sign of orthopedic disease. Many large dogs also
have concurrent orthopedic diseases, highlighting the importance of
a good neurologic evaluation (ch. 241) and spinal palpation.
Paraplegia or non-ambulatory paraparesis is not seen in dogs with
compression at the lumbosacral vertebral junction because there is
no spinal cord at the L7-S1 vertebral level in dogs and the femoral
nerve—the primary nerve responsible for weight support in the
pelvic limbs—is never affected. Most dogs will have deficits on
proprioceptive positioning tests of the pelvic limbs, with a decreased
flexor reflex (primarily poor hock flexion), and a normal patellar
reflex (sometimes with “pseudohyperreflexia”). In the latter stages of
the disease, patients may show urinary and/or fecal incontinence.

FIGURE 250.2 Schematic illustration of
intervertebral disc protrusion at L7-S1 compressing
the cauda equina. From Dewey CW, da Costa RC,
eds. Practical Guide to Canine and Feline
Neurology. 3rd ed. Wiley; 2015.

DIAGNOSIS
Diagnosis of DLSS is based on signalment (mostly middle-aged to
older, large-breed dogs), historical and clinical findings, and results
of imaging tests of the lumbosacral region. Radiographic
examination should always be the initial imaging test. It is rarely
diagnostic by itself, but can be used to rule out important
differentials, such as discospondylitis (see below), osseous spinal
neoplasms (ch. 326), and traumatic lesions (ch. 251). Common
radiographic findings are collapse of the intervertebral disc space,
sclerosis of the vertebral endplates, malalignment of the sacrum with
the L7 vertebra, narrowing of the cranial foramina of the sacrum,
and spondylosis.
Several procedures have been proposed to definitively diagnose
DLSS, but it is clear that CT and MRI (primarily MRI) provide the
most detailed structural information regarding the cauda equina,

including information concerning the L7-S1 intervertebral foramina
and L7 nerve roots.35,41-46 It is important to bear in mind that
clinically normal dogs (mainly older dogs) can have compression of
the lumbosacral region without associated clinical signs, and that the
degree of cauda equina compression seen on imaging does not
correlate with presence of disease or its severity.45,47 It is extremely
important to match the history and neurologic findings with
imaging. Lumbosacral compression is often observed on advanced
imaging in dogs with neurologic signs caused by other spinal
problems. This is one of the challenges associated with the diagnosis
of DLSS.48 Dynamic or kinematic MRI might improve the
correlation of imaging and clinical findings.49

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Treatment of the patient with DLSS may be non-surgical or surgical.
Treatment decisions are based primarily on severity of clinical signs,
age of the patient, and concurrent diseases (neurologic and nonneurologic). Non-surgical therapy consists of enforced rest initially
for a few weeks, followed by a period of regular short walks to
maintain muscle mass. Additionally, anti-inflammatory medication
(either nonsteroidal drugs or prednisone, not both; ch. 143),
analgesics (such as gabapentin; ch. 6), and body weight reduction in
overweight/obese patients (ch. 150) are recommended.32,36
Nonsurgical or conservative treatment is a reasonable initial option,
primarily in older patients with multiple orthopedic or systemic
diseases. In a referral population, medical treatment of DLSS was
described as being successful short- and long-term in 55% of cases;50
the success rate in the overall population appears to be higher.
Epidural corticosteroid injections are a popular therapeutic approach
in people with lumbar and lumbosacral disc herniations compressing
nerve roots and are gaining widespread use in dogs.51 A retrospective
study of fluoroscopic-guided epidural steroid injections found an
improved outcome in 79% of dogs.52

Surgical treatment is elected when the patient’s signs are severe or
refractory to medical management. Surgery usually consists of a
dorsal laminectomy over the L7-S1 interspace, often combined with
removal of hypertrophied soft tissue. Lateral extension of the
decompression (facetectomy) may be necessary depending on the
lesion. Stabilization may also be necessary in some cases. In cases of
lateralized foraminal stenosis, as opposed to vertebral canal stenosis,
foraminotomy (surgical enlargement of the foramen) may need to be
performed.53 The prognosis for functional recovery from this
disorder is generally good to excellent with surgical intervention.
Successful outcomes after surgery range from 66.7% to 95% of
cases.54-56 Surgical treatment is less successful in dogs with fecal or
urinary incontinence, with failure of resolution of incontinence
reported in 55% to 87% of cases.32,36,54-56

EXTRADURAL SYNOVIAL CYSTS
ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS
Extradural synovial cysts (ESCs, extradural intraspinal cysts) are
cysts arising from periarticular joint tissue. They can be divided into
two cyst types: synovial and ganglion cysts. Synovial cysts have a
synovial lining containing fluid, and ganglion cysts contain myxoid
material with no specific lining. These are pathological differences
that may indeed reflect different stages of the same disease.57
Considering that both types of cysts occur in close proximity with the
intervertebral joints, the term juxtafacet cysts has been coined to
encompass both cysts.57 The pathophysiologic mechanism that
causes these cysts to form is not well established. It is thought that
degeneration of the zygapophyseal joint (osteoarthritic changes)
causes protrusion of the synovial membrane through defects of the
joint capsule. This protrusion then causes the formation of a paraarticular cavity filled with synovial fluid, which leads to extradural
compressions.57,58 Other proposed mechanisms are proliferation of
pluripotent mesenchymal cells, myxoid degeneration with cyst
formation in collagen tissue, and increased production of hyaluronic

acid by fibroblasts.58 Some affected dogs with lumbosacral cysts
have transitional vertebrae, and this may be a risk factor.59

CLINICAL FINDINGS
The clinical signs of synovial cysts will reflect their location in the
vertebral column. The 2 most frequent locations are the lumbosacral
and cervical regions. Clinical signs of cervical cysts are those of a
cervical myelopathy with proprioceptive ataxia and tetraparesis,
whereas lumbosacral cysts are associated with pelvic limb lameness
or weakness, with or without pain on palpation.58,59

DIAGNOSIS
The majority of reported dogs with lumbosacral/caudal lumbar
synovial cysts are large-breed, middle-aged or older dogs (median
age, 8 years).57 Cervical synovial cysts occur in association with the
osseous form of CSM in 20% of young, giant-breed dogs with
CSM.3,60,61

FIGURE 250.3 Extradural synovial cyst in a Great
Dane with the osseous form of cervical
spondylomyelopathy (arrow).
The diagnosis of synovial cysts is best made with MRI (Figure
250.3). In human beings, MRI is reported to have a sensitivity of
90% for the diagnosis of ESC, compared with 70% with CT.62 Both
soft-tissue and bone windows have to be used to increase accuracy of
CT to detect these cysts. MRI in dogs reveals the cysts as wellcircumscribed extradural masses on one or both sides of the
vertebral canal. They are hyperintense in T2-weighted images, with
variable characteristics on T1-weighted images.59,60,63 Radiographic
changes are nonspecific and only indicate degenerative joint disease
in the affected sites. Myelographic changes may be suggestive but are
not diagnostic. Changes in the lateral projection are dorsal
extradural compression(s), and in the ventrodorsal view, uni- or
bilateral axial compressions.58 Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis

(ch. 109) typically reveals albuminocytologic dissociation but mild
mononuclear pleocytosis may also be seen.57,58

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Treatment is typically surgical. Many times this is done at the same
time as decompressive surgery (dorsal laminectomy) for CSM or
DLSS. In humans, however, many of these cysts are asymptomatic,
and in many cases may be incidental findings.64 The same may be
true for dogs. Therefore, attempting medical management with
activity restriction and anti-inflammatories is recommended
initially. Spontaneous regression of multiple lumbar and
lumbosacral ESCs was recently documented in a dog, lending
support for attempting medical management initially in many of
these cases.65 All reported cases of surgical treatment of synovial
cysts have had positive outcomes.57

SPINAL ARACHNOID DIVERTICULA
(CYSTS)
ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS
Spinal arachnoid diverticula (SAD) are focal dilations of the
subarachnoid space, which can lead to a progressive, compressive
myelopathy. These diverticula were previously called arachnoid
cysts, but this is a misnomer because they are not closed, epitheliallined cavities.57,66,67 They have also been called intra-arachnoid or
subarachnoid cysts, meningeal cysts, leptomeningeal cysts, and
pseudocysts.68-70 They appear to be recognized more frequently with
the widespread use of MRI. In people, cyst-like structures of the
meninges have been classified into three types, with type III
(intradural forms) best fitting the diverticula described in dogs,
which can then be classified as primary or secondary.57,66,71
A genetic predisposition has been described in Pugs.67 It appears
that a congenital etiology is likely in the cases seen in young dogs. Up

to 64% of dogs have concurrent diseases (e.g., intervertebral disc
disease [IVDD], vertebral malformations, myelitis) in close proximity
with the diverticulum, which might influence its development.72-74 It
has been postulated that a functional one-way valve mechanism
allows accumulation of CSF within the diverticulum and contributes
to CSF flow disturbances. This results in progressive expansion of the
defect and a dynamic pulsatile flow within the SAD.75
Two studies that reviewed 215 cases identified ∼55% occurring in
the cervical region (large-breed dogs predominating) and ∼45% in
the thoracolumbar region (small-breed dogs predominating).57,72
The most common specific sites were C2-C3, and T9 to T13. In Pugs,
SADs are regularly seen in the cervical region.67 Approximately 88%
of the diverticula appear to be located in the dorsal aspect of the
spinal cord, 8% in the ventral region, and the remainder in the
lateral or circumferential regions. SADs have occasionally been
reported in cats. So far, all reported feline SADs are considered to be
secondary to other causes.76

CLINICAL SIGNS
Clinical signs reflect the location of the myelopathy. This disease is
primarily characterized by proprioceptive ataxia with various degrees
of tetraparesis or paraparesis, without obvious spinal pain.77 Some
dogs with cervical diverticula display more severe signs in the
thoracic limbs, suggesting an intramedullary lesion. A common
feature is a severely spastic gait in the thoracic limbs, giving the
appearance of “pseudo-hypermetria.”78 Spinal hyperpathia is not a
prominent sign, but has been reported in 18.9% of dogs in a large
case series (although a good proportion of dogs had concurrent
diseases, thus making it difficult to know the exact source of pain).72
Urinary and fecal incontinence have been reported in ∼8% of dogs,
mainly with thoracolumbar diverticula.

DIAGNOSIS

Two breeds are overrepresented: Rottweilers and Pugs. French
Bulldogs are also predisposed to thoracolumbar diverticula.73
Overall, a male predisposition is clear, with a male-to-female ratio
ranging from 2:1 to 4:1 in large case series. The median age of
affected dogs is 2.5 years, (range, 2.5-13 years). Pugs tend to be
affected at an older age (median, 59 months).57,72
Myelography, CT myelography or MRI are required to diagnose
this disorder (Figure 250.4). Myelography and post-myelographic
CT demonstrate these diverticula as contrast-filled teardrop shaped
expansions of the subarachnoid space.57,68 It may also reveal a
blockage of the subarachnoid contrast column associated with a
filling defect of the subarachnoid diverticulae. MRI is generally
considered the imaging modality of choice to evaluate these
diverticulae because it also allows assessment of the spinal cord
parenchyma and detection of comorbidities, such as
syringohydromyelia, which may be secondary to the pulsatile flow
within the SAD. It is important to use MR myelogram or single-shot
turbo spin-echo sequences (heavy T2-weighted images) to facilitate
visualization of the diverticulum.79 Application of 3D-CISS
(constructive interference in steady state) MRI sequences has also
been associated with improved confidence in making a diagnosis of
SAD and provides improved anatomic detail and delineation of SAD
from concurrent disease processes.80 Differentiation between a
classical SAD and subarachnoid widening associated with
constrictive myelopathy in Pugs can be difficult. In contrast to MRI
findings in SAD, constrictive myelopathy is associated with an
irregular subarachnoid space with mixed T2W signal intensity.
Postcontrast images in Pugs with constrictive myelopathy also
commonly reveal a circumferential or focal contrast enhancement of
the meninges.81 The utility of cine balanced fast field echo (cine
bFFE) MRI sequences in measuring pulsatile flow in SAD has also
been demonstrated.75

FIGURE 250.4 Images of a Rottweiler dog with a
cervical arachnoid diverticulum. A, Sagittal T2weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). B,
Computed tomography (CT)-myelogram image. Note
that the diverticulum does not have the typical teardrop appearance on MRI (white arrowhead). CT

arrowhead) and confirmation. From Dewey CW, da
Costa RC, eds. Practical Guide to Canine and Feline
Neurology. 3rd ed. Wiley; 2015.
CSF analysis (ch. 109) is normal in the majority of cases.
Approximately 20% of dogs show albuminocytologic dissociation
and 10% can show mild mononuclear pleocytosis.57,68

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Medical management (i.e., glucocorticoid therapy) may be attempted
initially. In a few cases, the signs can be managed for long periods
and the disease appears to become stable. Surgical management is
typically the treatment of choice. Surgical techniques involve
fenestration with durotomy (with or without closure) or durectomy,
marsupialization of the diverticulum, and the placement of shunting
device.82-84 In cases where vertebral instability may be present,
stabilization is recommended.85 From the limited data available,
surgically treated patients appear to have a good prognosis.57,70
Factors associated with a better outcome are age (<3 years) and
duration of clinical signs (<4 months).70 One study reported that
82% of dogs treated surgically experienced a long-term neurological
improvement, while 3% remained stable and 16% deteriorated; with

medical management, 30% experienced a long-term neurological
improvement, while 30% remained stable and 40% deteriorated.86
Although rare, late-onset recurrence of clinical signs is possible. The
median time to recurrence of neurological signs is 20.5 months after
surgery and the reasons for these relapses include regrowth of the
SAD, herniation of the spinal cord through the laminectomy
membrane, and laminectomy membrane formation. 87 Although
surgery has been associated with good outcomes in most dogs, it has
been suggested that Pugs have a poor long-term prognosis after
surgery for thoracolumbar SAD. One study demonstrated that 85%
of these dogs experienced late onset recurrence of neurological
signs.88 It is currently unclear why Pugs have a less favorable
prognosis; it is possible that thoracolumbar SAD formation in this
breed is associated with a multifactorial etiology and variety of
pathological mechanisms.

SPONDYLOSIS DEFORMANS
ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS
Spondylosis is a very common degenerative process of the vertebral
column, with essentially no clinical significance by itself.89 It is
characterized by the formation of exostoses or bone proliferations
around the ventral (and sometimes lateral) vertebral endplate
margins, which could result in a bony bridge between adjacent
vertebrae.90 This is a non-inflammatory condition believed to be
associated with degenerative changes in the annulus fibrosus of the
intervertebral discs in an effort to stabilize the disc region.
Osteophytes vary from small spurs to bone bridges across the disc
space, leaving at least part of the ventral surface of the vertebral body
unaffected. A retrospective study of 2041 dogs found spondylosis in
367 (18.1%) of dogs.90 Spondylosis commonly affects the thoracic,
lumbar and lumbosacral regions.

CLINICAL SIGNS

It is very tempting to attribute signs of spinal cord disease such as
paresis, paralysis, or proprioceptive ataxia to spondylosis but such
association has never been documented (despite the high prevalence
of spondylosis). A study suggested that spondylosis might predispose
dogs to adjacent segment disease, making them susceptible to the
development of intervertebral disc protrusion (Hansen type II) in the
segments cranial or caudal to the fused disc spaces.91 Thus, the
presence of neurologic deficits should indicate the possibility of
concurrent neurologic diseases. The only sign reported to occur in
working dogs is a reduction of activity level secondary to the
diminished flexibility of the vertebral column.90 Nerve root
compression (leading to pain and lameness) has been documented in
dogs with diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis. It is possible that it
could also occur rarely in cases of spondylosis with severe lateralized
bony proliferation causing intervertebral foraminal stenosis.92

DIAGNOSIS
Spondylosis can be seen in adult animals of various sizes and ages,
but is more prominent in middle-aged to older, medium-to giantbreed dogs. Boxers, German Shepherd Dogs and Flat-Coated
Retrievers seem to be primarily predisposed.90,93 The diagnosis is
established based on the radiographic appearance of vertebral
osteophytes arising from the periphery of the endplate, along with
sclerotic endplates, and preservation of the central portion of the
vertebral bodies.90 It is important to differentiate spondylosis from
discospondylitis and disseminated idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis
(DISH). As previously stated, spondylosis by itself does not cause
neurological signs, so in patients with obvious neurologic signs,
further diagnostic work-up with myelography, CT, MRI (ch.112),
and CSF analysis (ch. 109) are recommended to definitively
diagnose the cause of signs.

FIGURE 250.5 Lateral radiograph of a Boxer
showing disseminated idiopathic skeletal
hyperostosis. Note that the osseous proliferation
involves the entire ventral aspect of vertebral bodies
for more than four contiguous vertebral bodies
(arrowheads). Osseous proliferation is also seen in
the dorsal aspect of the vertebral column at L3-4
(arrow).

TREATMENT
Spondylosis has no clinical significance in the vast majority of dogs,
and treatment is not necessary.89 In the cases where it can be
documented to cause nerve root compression, treatment with
analgesics such as gabapentin or surgical decompression of nerve
roots may be necessary.92

DISSEMINATED IDIOPATHIC
SKELETAL HYPEROSTOSIS (DISH)
ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS
DISH is a systemic disorder characterized by fibrocartilaginous
proliferation followed by endochondral ossification within soft
tissues of the axial and appendicular skeleton. Ossification of DISH
appears to affect an area rather than specific anatomic structures.

DISH in dogs is mostly characterized by generalized new bone
formation that appears as flowing ossification along the ventral and
lateral aspects of the vertebral column.90
Initially thought to be a rare condition, a large report described
DISH in 78/20,141 dogs (3.8%). Among these 78 dogs, 53 (67.9%)
also had spondylosis. The most common locations for DISH are T6T10 and L2-L6 vertebral regions.90

CLINICAL SIGNS
Similar to spondylosis, DISH is typically a radiographic finding with
little clinical significance. It can cause spinal stiffness and limited
performance in working dogs.90 Signs of spinal pain may be seen,
although this is probably quite uncommon. It has been shown to
cause foraminal stenosis leading to pain and pelvic limb lameness
(nerve root signature).92 As DISH can predispose dogs to adjacent
segment disease, any dog with clear neurologic deficits should be
thoroughly investigated.78

DIAGNOSIS
DISH is seen primarily in older (mean age, 8 years), large-breed
dogs, with Boxers being overrepresented. The characteristic
radiographic appearance is “flowing” ossification primarily at the
ventrolateral aspect of the vertebral column, extending for at least
four contiguous vertebrae (Figure 250.5).90,94 The osseous
proliferation does not invade the vertebral canal and as such does
not cause spinal cord compression or neurologic deficits. There may
also be ossification of the interspinous ligaments dorsally, which
might be quite extensive.95,96 It is important to differentiate DISH
from spondylosis deformans.90 Lesions of spondylosis typically
spare at least part of the ventral surfaces of adjacent vertebral bodies,
and that is the most important radiographic difference with DISH.
The signal intensity of the proliferative bone lesions is equal to
that of the vertebral bone marrow on both T1- and T2-weighted MRI

sequences. Conversely, in dogs with spondylosis, the signal from
osteophytes is hypointense compared to the bone marrow signal on
both T1- and T2-weighted images.97

TREATMENT
Similar to spondylosis, the vast majority of dogs with DISH do not
display signs secondary to the disease’s bone proliferation. If nerve
root compression is documented as the source of pain, treatment
with analgesics or surgical decompression of nerve roots may be
necessary.92

DEGENERATIVE MYELOPATHY
ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS
Degenerative myelopathy (DM) is a disease that affects primarily the
thoracolumbar spinal cord of medium- to large-breed dogs.98,99 It
has also been called canine degenerative radiculomyelopathy
(CDRM) because of nerve root involvement.100
Immunologic, inflammatory, metabolic, nutritional, oxidative
stress, excitotoxic and genetic mechanisms have been explored as
underlying the pathogenesis of DM.99,101-108 Definitive causal
evidence is lacking for most of these mechanisms. An incompletely
penetrant autosomal mode of inheritance has been proposed after
the identification of a mutation in the superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1)
gene in some affected dogs.105 It is hypothesized that neural
degeneration is caused by a “gain of toxic function” of mutant
SOD1.109 Familial DM has been reported in Boxers and Rhodesian
Ridgebacks.
DM is a primary central axonopathy restricted to the spinal cord
that begins in the thoracic spinal cord and ascends and descends
along the spinal cord. Axon and myelin degeneration of the spinal
cord occurs in all funiculi but primarily in the dorsal aspect of the
lateral funiculi and medial portion of the dorsal funiculi. Hence, the

lesion is best denoted as a segmental degeneration of the axon and
associated myelin rather than Wallerian degeneration.110,111

CLINICAL SIGNS
The clinical signs are those of chronic thoracolumbar (T3-L3)
myelopathy (

Video 250.2). Signs start with mild proprioceptive

ataxia and paraparesis, which can initially be asymmetric, that slowly
progresses, leading to more severe paresis until dogs are nonambulatory. This progression usually takes 6-12 months in largebreed dogs.98,99 Lack of spinal hyperesthesia is a typical feature and
greatly assists in the differential diagnosis with other compressive
myelopathies that occur in older large-breed dogs (such as
intervertebral disc protrusion and spinal neoplasia). Proprioceptive
deficits are commonly seen in the early disease stages. Spinal reflexes
in the pelvic limbs are typically normal to hyperreflexive. Decreased
to absent patellar reflexes are found in approximately 10%-15% of
patients. This does not necessarily indicate a lower motor neuron
(LMN) lesion; instead it may reflect selective damage to dorsal
(sensory) lumbar nerve roots in these dogs. The extensor tone is
always increased in the earlier phase of the disease, which suggests
that the patellar areflexia or hyporeflexia is a sensory, rather than
LMN disturbance. The disease progresses relentlessly, and if the
dogs are kept alive it progresses to involve the lumbar and cervical
spinal cord regions, as well as the brainstem, causing LMN deficits,
tetraparesis, and eventually dysphonia and dysphagia.
Hypoventilation as a result of respiratory muscle dysfunction results
in hypoxemia in later/terminal stages of the disease.112

DIAGNOSIS
Several large breeds of dogs can be affected with DM but German
Shepherd Dogs and Boxers are the most commonly affected breeds;
mixed-breed dogs have also been described with this disease.113 Age
of onset of neurologic signs is usually 5 years or older with a mean

age of 9 years in large dog breeds. The mean age of affected
Pembroke Welsh Corgis was 11.2 years in 1 study.104 There appears
to be a female predominance (1.6:1) for the disease in Corgis but not
in other breeds.99
The diagnosis is based primarily on the exclusion of other
myelopathies. Spinal imaging (myelogram, MRI, CT [ch. 112]) is
typically normal, but some dogs may have concurrent mild disc
protrusions. The clinician must then consider the duration of clinical
signs as well as the findings of the neurological examination to
determine the significance of these lesions. MRI is the imaging
modality of choice to ensure that all other differentials are ruled out,
including intramedullary lesions such as neoplasms.114 Recent work
has shown that dogs with DM undergoing MRI diffusion tensor
imaging had significant decreases in fractional anisotropy (FA)
within the regions of the spinal cord that had high expected lesion
load.115 Decreases in FA were most significant in dogs with severe
forms of the disease and correlated with neurological grade.
Patients with DM typically have normal CSF results, or increased
protein levels with a normal cell count (ch. 109).104 Phosphorylated
neurofilament heavy (pNF-H) concentration in CSF is elevated in all
stages of DM compared to old control dogs and is now proposed as a
promising sensitive biomarker for the diagnosis of DM.116
A DNA test based on the SOD1 mutation is commercially available.
Dogs that are homozygous for the mutation are at risk for developing
DM and will contribute one chromosome with the mutant allele to all
of their offspring. The heterozygotes are DM carriers that are
unlikely to develop clinical DM but could pass on a chromosome with
the mutant allele to half of their offspring.98 Pembroke Welsh Corgis
with DM have been demonstrated to have significantly higher
plasma levels of the microRNA miR-26b, which correlates with
disease progression. This has prompted the suggestion that this may
be a potential novel diagnostic biomarker of DM.117
Corticosteroids can be used for assisting in the differential
diagnosis of this disease. They will typically lead to improvement in
dogs with chronic compressive myelopathies (such as IVDD) but will

not benefit dogs with DM. This strategy might be useful to convince
pet owners to pursue advanced imaging.78

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
No pharmacological therapy has been shown to alter the course of
DM. Vitamin supplementation, glucocorticoid administration,
aminocaproic acid, and N-acetylcysteine have all been used, but none
of these medications showed beneficial effects.118 The only treatment
that has been shown to alter the long-term course of the disease is
physical therapy (ch. 256).119 In one retrospective study, dogs with
confirmed and suspected DM had controlled physical therapy,
including walking, passive range of motion of the pelvic limbs,
massage of pelvic limb and paraspinal muscles, and hydrotherapy.
Dogs that were treated with a more intense physical therapy regimen
had a mean survival time of 255 days, compared with dogs receiving
a moderate regimen (130 days) or no physical therapy (55 days).119
The long-term prognosis is poor, and most dogs are euthanized due
to severe pelvic limb dysfunction within 6-12 months. In the study of
Pembroke Welsh Corgis, the average time from diagnosis to death
was 1.25 years.120

INTERVERTEBRAL DISC DISEASE
(IVDD)
ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS
The intervertebral discs are interposed in every intervertebral space
(except between C1 and C2), uniting the bodies of the adjacent
vertebrae.121,122 Each intervertebral disc consists of an outer
laminated fibrous ring (annulus fibrosus) and a central, amorphous,
gelatinous center (nucleus pulposus).123 The nucleus pulposus is a
highly hydrated gelatinous mesodermal remnant of the
notochord.122 Chondrodystrophic breeds show progressive
collagenation and calcification in the nucleus pulposus and inner

parts of the annulus fibrosus at an early age.122 The annulus fibrosus
consists of bands of parallel fibers that run obliquely from one
vertebral body to the next. They provide a means for the
transmission of stresses and strains that are required by all lateral
and upward movements.123
Intervertebral disc degeneration or disease leads to extrusion or
protrusion (both termed herniation) of disc material into the spinal
canal, resulting in clinical signs due to spinal cord compression
and/or contusion.121,124 The component of either compression
and/or contusion varies with the specific type of IVDD.
The pathophysiologic mechanism of the resulting spinal cord
injury, which has been well described elsewhere,124 doesn’t always
explain the degree of associated neurological dysfunction.125 IVDD
has been traditionally classified as Hansen type I and type II.126
Type I IVDD is herniation of the nucleus pulposus through the
annular fibers and extrusion of nuclear material into the spinal
canal. It is typically associated with chondroid disc degeneration but
sometimes a hydrated nucleus pulposus extrusion can be responsible
for spinal cord dysfunction.127,128 The disc extrudes through the
dorsal annulus, causing ventral, ventrolateral or circumferential
compression of the spinal cord. Type I IVDD typically affects
chondrodystrophic breeds and has an acute onset. However, large
non-chondrodystrophic dog breeds such as the Doberman Pinscher
and Labrador Retriever may also be affected,129 particularly when
subsequent to trauma.130 Congenital vertebral malformations result
in early degeneration of adjacent intervertebral discs,131 although
clinical disc disease at these sites may not be as common as
elsewhere in the vertebral column.132 Long backs, miniaturization
and being overweight also increase the risk of type I IVDD.133
Hansen type II IVDD is annular protrusion caused by shifting of
central nuclear material and is commonly associated with late
chondroid disc degeneration.96,134 The annulus fibrosus slowly
protrudes into the vertebral canal to cause spinal cord compression.
The chronic compression can lead to focal ischemic and other

microvascular derangements of the spinal cord. Type II IVDD
usually occurs at the mobile points of the vertebral column and is
more common in older, non-chondrodystrophic breeds of dog. It is
not uncommon to identify multiple affected disc spaces.
In addition to these two classic forms, with the widespread use of
MRI, newer forms began to be recognized, such as acute
noncompressive nucleus pulposus extrusion (ANNPE, also known as
“type III” missile discs, high-velocity low volume disc extrusion),
hydrated nucleus pulposus extrusion (HNPE—formerly, intraspinal
cyst or canine discal cyst), and intradural/intramedullary
intervertebral disc extrusion (also known as traumatic disc
extrusion).135-140

FIGURE 250.6 Intervertebral disc disease. A,
Sagittal reconstructed computed tomography (CT)
scan post-myelography of the cervical spinal cord of
a dog with acute neck pain. The ventral contrast
column is thinned and dorsally deviated over the C3C4 disc space (arrow) due to a disc extrusion (type I
disease). B, The transverse CT-myelographic image
