acute hydrated nucleus pulposus extrusion.

CERVICAL DISC DISEASE
Clinical Findings

Most dogs with cervical disc disease, which accounts for 14-25% of
intervertebral disc disorders in dogs,141,142 have disc extrusion
rather than protrusion.143 Chondrodystrophoid and other small
breeds are at the greatest risk. Dachshunds, Toy Poodles and Beagles
have been documented to account for the majority of cases144;
however, large-breed dogs such as Labrador Retrievers, Dalmatians
and Doberman Pinschers can be affected with cervical disc
extrusions, accounting for up to 24% of all cases.121,143,145,146 Most
affected dogs are 4-8 years old when they present with clinical signs,
with a mean age ranging from 6.3 years to 8.6 years; it is extremely
rare for dogs <2 years of age to be affected.109-113 Males and females
are evenly affected.144 When large-breed dogs have acute or chronic
cervical disc disease, the disease might be part of CSM (see CSM,
above). Most cases of cervical disc disease in chondrodystrophoid
dogs occur in the cranial cervical spine, with 80% affecting C2-C4
spaces and 44-59% affecting C2-C3 alone141,142; however, most
large-breed dogs are affected at the C6-C7 intervertebral disc space
and most protrusions versus extrusions are more caudally
located.143,147
Approximately 45% of dogs with cervical disc extrusion will have
an acute onset of signs, with the other 55% experiencing a slower
onset of signs, whether the dogs are large non-chondrodystrophoid
or small breeds.143 The predominant clinical sign is evidence of
cervical pain, which can be seen in up to 60% of dogs with no
neurological deficits and nearly 90% of affected dogs overall.143,148
Cervical pain, evident from the animal’s posture or from palpation of
the spine and muscles of the neck, can be extreme, unremitting, and
refractory to medication, which is apparently less likely with the
newer forms, such as HNPE and ANNPE.128
The classic presentation of ANNPE is an acute myelopathy,
typically associated with trauma or strenuous exercise, which is often
severe, and strongly asymmetric in 90% of cases136,149 (an
important differential for this presentation is fibrocartilaginous
embolic myelopathy; MRI is required for differentiation; ch. 251).
In contrast, HNPE typically presents as a non-painful severe cervical

myelopathy (non-ambulatory tetraparesis is the most common sign),
usually with bilaterally symmetrical signs. It is important to
emphasize that HNPE happens most commonly in the cervical
region.
Nerve “root signature” is another frequent finding with cervical
disc disease. It occurs in 22-50% of dogs, mostly with extrusions or
protrusions.142,148 Neurological deficits may be restricted to one
thoracic limb or the animal may show hemiparesis, tetraparesis or
even tetraplegia with hypoventilation. Ambulatory tetraparesis is
seen in up to 42% of dogs and 11-22% exhibit non-ambulatory
tetraparesis.143,148,150 Tetraplegia is uncommon and has been
described in 2-7% of cases.143 Neurological deficits are more
common with lesions at C4-C5 to C6-C7 inclusive, which may reflect
the greater degree of space in the cranial vertebral canal compared to
more caudally.151 The reduction or loss of thoracic limb reflexes
usually implies a C6-T2 spinal cord lesion; however, 36% of dogs
with reduced to absent thoracic limb reflexes actually have a C1-C5
spinal cord lesion.146 Some large breed dogs with type II IVDD can
also show signs of a C6-8 myelopathy, with decreased flexor reflexes
and increased extensor tone.

Diagnosis
Survey radiographs can help to rule out discospondylitis, neoplasia,
and anatomic malformations, which may be considerations given the
clinical signs.152 Although radiographic signs such as narrowing of
the intervertebral disc space and dorsal displacement of mineralized
disc material may be highly suggestive of disc extrusion,
myelography, CT or MRI is essential for a definitive diagnosis (ch.
112).152 The overall accuracy rate for correct identification of the
site(s) of disc extrusion with radiography is 35%.152 CSF analysis
should be considered to rule out inflammatory disease (ch. 109).
Deviation of the ventral contrast column is the most common
myelographic finding of cervical disc disease; oblique views can help
with lateralized localizations.153,154 CT performed after myelography
can provide more detailed information on the localization of the

compressive lesion (Figure 250.6), particularly for lateralized discs
and intradural discs.138,155 MRI is the best method for evaluation of
the cervical spinal cord and it provides a safe and non-invasive
method for obtaining high-resolution images (Figure 250.6).156,157
This imaging modality can provide detailed information on the
structure of the intervertebral discs and spinal cord and may help
with prognosis.158,159 MRI also allows diagnosis of the newer IVDD
forms such as ANNPE and HNPE.

Treatment
Strict cage rest for 3-4 weeks is the most important aspect of a
conservative approach to cervical disc extrusion. This can be
followed by restricted and gradual incremental exercise over the next
month using a body harness rather than a collar and leash. The
protracted period of rest enables resolution of the inflammation and
stabilization of the ruptured disc by fibrosis, preventing further
herniation.121 The use of anti-inflammatory medications such as
corticosteroids or non-steroidal analgesics can be recommended for
a few days to accompany the rest (ch. 143). Analgesic medications
may be necessary in some dogs in addition or in place of the antiinflammatory medications (ch. 6). The use of acupuncture in dogs
with cervical disc disease has been described and was reported to be
associated with an initial recovery in 69% of cases.160 Muscle
relaxants such as diazepam and methocarbamol are useful
adjunctive medications in dogs with neck pain related to disc disease.
Signs of nerve root involvement such as nerve root signature, or
foraminal herniation identified on advanced imaging, may be treated
with gabapentin (10-20 mg/kg PO q8h) along with rest. Recently,
ultrasound or fluoroscopically guided paravertebral perineural
injections were reported as an option for the treatment of foraminal
extrusions with good success.161,162 Recurrence rates of 33-36% or
more have been reported with conservative approaches.160,163,164 A
study evaluating 88 dogs with conservatively managed presumptive
cervical intervertebral disc herniation found that 49% of cases had a
successful outcome, 33% recurred and 18% had therapeutic

failure.164 More chronic disease duration and more severe
neurological deficits may result in less success when managed
conservatively, as is the case with thoracolumbar disc disease.164 The
majority of dogs with HNPE present with cervical extrusions. These
dogs have an excellent prognosis for recovery with or without
surgery, even in the presence of respiratory compromise.165,166
The decision to treat surgically is often based on multiple factors.
Pertinent criteria include severity of neurological signs, chronicity,
whether the signs represent a recurrence, response to medical
treatment, systemic health of the patient, and owner finances.
Patients showing clinical signs can be divided into three groups:
group I, first episode involving neck pain only; group II, repeated
episodes of neck pain only; and group III, neck pain and concurrent
neurological deficits.121 Medical therapy can often be recommended
for group I dogs. Surgical decompression is most appropriate for
group II dogs and is necessary for group III dogs.

Prognosis
When affected dogs are treated with ventral slot decompression
alone, complete recovery is observed in up to 90% of dogs at 1 month
and 98% of dogs at 12 months following surgery.148 Long-term
follow-up (6 months to 4 years) for ventral slot decompression for
caudal cervical disc protrusion in large-breed dogs revealed only a
66% success rate, and it was concluded that dynamic compressive
lesions may need a stabilization procedure.167 The recurrence rate
following surgery for cervical disc disease has been suggested to be
∼5-10%, with a mean time to recurrence being 91 days for all
dogs.143,163 Several significant adverse events have been reported in
up to 10% of dogs undergoing ventral slot surgery, which include
deterioration in neurologic status, respiratory difficulty,
intraoperative hemorrhage and persistent pain.168 Cervical
hemilaminectomy may be needed in cases of lateralized or foraminal
disc extrusions.169

THORACOLUMBAR DISC DISEASE
Clinical Findings
Hansen type I IVDD most commonly occurs within the
thoracolumbar region of chondrodystrophic breeds. The
thoracolumbar junction (T12-T13 to L1-L2) accounts for the highest
incidence of all disc lesions.170 The incidence of thoracolumbar
IVDD progressively decreases from T12-T13 caudally. The most
common site for Hansen type I IVDD in large, nonchondrodystrophic breeds is the interspace between L1 and L2129;
however, German Shepherd Dogs particularly can be affected by
discs between T1-T5.171,172 The onset of neurological signs may be
peracute (<1 hour), acute (<24 hours) or gradual (>24 hours). Dogs
presenting with peracute or acute thoracolumbar disc extrusions
may manifest clinical signs of spinal shock or Schiff-Sherrington
postures (ch. 43).170 These indicate acute and severe spinal cord
injury but do not determine prognosis. The degree of neurological
dysfunction is variable and affects prognosis. Clinical signs vary from
only spinal hyperesthesia to paraplegia with or without pain
perception. The mean incidence of focal and ascending/descending
myelomalacia is 13.9% in dogs with acute thoracolumbar IVDD and
loss of nociception166,170,173,174; the risk of developing this condition
may be higher in certain breeds such as French Bulldogs.132 More
severe neurologic dysfunction is also not an uncommon scenario in
dogs with ANNPE. In some cases of ANNPE, the extruded nucleus
spreads along the epidural space and may completely surround or
penetrate the dura mater (Figure 250.7).175,136 Clinically
significant intervertebral disc extrusion has been reported in cats <5
years of age but is more common in middle-aged to older cats.176,177
Clinical signs due to disc disease in cats may reflect a painful
transverse myelopathy at any region of the spinal cord but the
probability of clinically significant disc extrusion seems to be higher
in the thoracolumbar and lumbar area. Onset of type I IVDD in cats
is usually acute.176

Diagnosis
The initial diagnosis of thoracolumbar IVDD is obtained from the
signalment, history and neurological examination. Survey spinal
radiography can help to determine the diagnosis and site of a
thoracolumbar disc extrusion if radiographic signs are well-defined
and consistent with neuroanatomical localization (Figure
250.7).178,179 In the thoracolumbar region, survey radiographs
typically have a reported sensitivity ranging between 51-61%.180-185
Importantly, radiographic findings can be suggestive of
thoracolumbar disc extrusion but are never diagnostic and can also
be fraught with significant interobserver variation.186 Estimates of
diagnostic accuracy of myelography for the diagnosis and site of
intervertebral disc extrusion have ranged from 72-99%.140 CT or
MRI are used alone or as an adjunct to myelography to more
completely delineate lateralization of extruded disc material and
lesion extent.140 Noncontrast CT is as diagnostic as myelography at
identifying the major site of disc herniation and has the advantage of
being a more rapid test, which can even be done under sedation and
with fewer side effects than myelography.187,188 Mineralized disc
material and acute hemorrhage can be identified in the vertebral
canal using non-contrast-enhanced CT. Acutely extruded disc
material typically is recognized as a heterogeneous hyperattenuating
extradural mass compressing the spinal cord,189,190 and chronically
extruded disc material has a more homogeneous hyperattenuating
appearance. MRI provides a more sensitive technique in recognition
of spinal cord lesions (e.g., edema and hemorrhage); furthermore,
three-dimensional delineation of spinal cord compression allows for
an accurate surgical approach and for determining the extent of
surgical decompression required (Figure 250.7).191 MRI is
considered the best method for early recognition of in situ disc
degeneration based on a decrease in signal intensity within the
nucleus pulposus on T2-weighted images and for determining
localization and extent of extruded disc material within the epidural
space.192,193 MRI has also been demonstrated to be superior for the
assessment of recurrent IVDD,194 as well as identification of ANNPE

and HNPE. MRI also assists in the characterization of imaging
features that can be important in the diagnostic evaluation and
prognostication of patients with IVDD, such as spinal cord signal
changes, epidural hemorrhage, contrast enhancement of extradural
compressive material or meninges (both important to be carefully
evaluated to avoid misdiagnosis of disc extrusions as other
conditions), as well as paravertebral muscle signal changes. MRI has
also a very important role in the identification of progressive
myelomalacia (PMM), with studies proposing guidelines for the
diagnosis of PMM.166,195,196 Recently, a serologic biomarker (pNFH) has been shown to have a high sensitivity and specificity for
identification of PMM.197

Treatment
Indications for nonsurgical treatment of thoracolumbar IVDD
include a first-time incident of spinal pain only, mild to moderate
paraparesis, and the financial constraints of the client. The latter is
the only reason for non-surgical treatment of a recumbent patient,
which should always be considered a surgical candidate. Dogs can be
managed with strict cage rest for 3-4 weeks combined with pain
relief using anti-inflammatory drugs, opioids and muscle relaxants
(ch. 6). Acupuncture also has been advocated as a treatment for pain
management. Dogs should be monitored closely for deterioration of
neurological status. If pain persists or the neurological status
worsens, surgical management is recommended. Studies have shown
that recovery rates in non-ambulatory dogs are lower and recurrence
rates higher following conservative rather than surgical treatment.
The prognosis of all clinical forms of IVDD was recently reviewed.166
Overall, 72.5% of ambulatory dogs recover with conservative
management, as opposed to 98.4% for those treated surgically. Nonambulatory paraparetic dogs have a similar recovery: 79.8% recover
with conservative management, whereas 93% recover with surgery.
Retrospective studies of conservatively managed dogs with
thoracolumbar disc IVDD have documented 30-50% recurrence
rates in dogs with minimally affected ambulatory status.170,198
Recurrence of spinal pain in dogs with thoracolumbar IVDD that are

managed conservatively usually occurs within 6 months to 1 year
from onset of the initial clinical signs.

Indications for surgical management of thoracolumbar IVDD
include spinal pain or paresis that is unresponsive to medical
therapy, recurrence or progression of clinical signs, and paraplegia
with or without intact pain perception. Once thought to be a
definitive poor prognostic indicator, absence of pain perception for
longer than 48 hours does not seem to negatively impact the
outcome any more than absence for less than 48 hours, although
decompressive surgery should be performed as early as possible.199
Surgery includes spinal cord decompression by removal of extruded
disc material. In ambulatory dogs, an increasing degree of deficits
preoperatively is significantly associated with longer recovery
times.200 Administration of corticosteroids or high-dose
methylprednisolone sodium succinate appears to not improve
outcome in dogs undergoing surgery for intervertebral disc extrusion
but instead has been associated with higher prevalence of
gastrointestinal and urinary tract complications, increased hospital
stay, and owner expense.124,198

Prognosis

Pain perception is considered the most important prognostic
indicator for a functional recovery. In general, most dogs with intact
pain perception have an excellent prognosis, particularly if treated
surgically.201 The overall recovery rate of paraplegic dogs with intact
pain perception treated surgically was 93%, compared to 56% of
these dogs treated conservatively. In contrast, the recovery of
paraplegic dogs without deep pain perception treated surgically
drops to 61% (data from 502 dogs), compared to 22.4% in those
treated conservatively.166 In general, the prognosis is poor if pain
perception does not return within 2 to 4 weeks from the time of
surgery.170,173,174 Recurrence of clinical signs after decompressive
surgery in dogs with thoracolumbar IVDD is a common clinical
entity, with reported incidence rates of 2-42%.170 The time to
recurrence is usually between 1 month and 2 years after surgery.
Recurrence of clinical signs within 1 month after surgery is likely
related to the original herniated disc space; later recurrence > 1
month after surgery is caused by a disc herniation at a site distinct
from the initial extrusion.170 Current guidelines for surgical
treatment of intervertebral disc extrusion indicate that fenestration
should be routinely performed, along with decompressive
techniques, to minimize the risk of future disc extrusions.199

ATLANTOAXIAL INSTABILITY
ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS
Atlantoaxial (AA) joint instability leads to compression and
concussion of the cervical spinal cord resulting from displacement of
the vertebrae (subluxation) into the vertebral canal202; AA
subluxation results from a ligamentous and/or osseous abnormality
between the atlas (C1) and the axis (C2).203 The axis has a
cranioventral peglike projection called the dens or odontoid process.
The dens lies within the vertebral foramen of the atlas, held down by
the transverse ligament, which prevents its movement into the spinal
canal but still allows rotational movement. The dens is also attached
to the foramen magnum by the apical ligament and to the occipital

condyles by bilateral alar ligaments. There is also a dorsal AA
ligament joining the dorsal arch of the atlas and the craniodorsal
spine of the axis.
Possible congenital or developmental anomalies of the AA joint
include dysplasia (34% of dogs), hypoplasia or aplasia (46% of dogs),
dorsal angulation, and separation of the dens, as well as absence of
the transverse ligament.204-207 Any abnormality of the dens will
predispose to instability of the AA joint; however, up to ∼24% of dogs
with AA subluxation have a normal dens.207 Small-breed dogs with
AA instability are more likely to have other craniovertebral junction
anomalies such as morphological alterations of the C2-C3
intervertebral disc, atlantooccipital overlapping,208 and incomplete
ossification of the dorsal neural arch.209,210
Small breeds of dogs including Yorkshire Terriers, Chihuahuas,
miniature Poodles, Pomeranians, and Pekingese are most often
affected by the congenital and developmental anomalies that
predispose to AA instability and potential subluxation.206,211,212
This is mainly because the dens is prone to maldevelopment in
miniature breeds due to aberrations of physeal growth plate closure.
However, AA subluxation due to congenital vertebral anomalies has
also been reported in large-breed dogs.213,214 AA subluxation due to
congenital vertebral anomalies in cats is very rare.215-217 Traumatic
AA subluxation can occur in any breed and age of dog.218 Traumatic
AA subluxation results from forceful over-flexion of the head, which
may tear the ligaments or cause a fracture of the dens or dorsal arch
of the axis.206,207

CLINICAL FINDINGS
Evidence of neck pain is the most common sign associated with AA
subluxation, being seen in most dogs with traumatic lesions and 3060% of dogs with congenital lesions.206,207,212,219 Neurological
deficits can range from mild postural reaction abnormalities (56%)
to tetraplegia (10%); overall, gait dysfunction has been reported in

up to 94% of affected dogs.207,219,220 These deficits can appear
asymmetrical in addition to appearing worse in either the pelvic
limbs or the thoracic limbs. In the rare cases which present with
tetraplegia, progression of clinical signs to a state of clinical
respiratory compromise and even arrest is possible.206

DIAGNOSIS
AA subluxation can be diagnosed from survey radiographs of the
cervical spine, although extreme care must be taken when
restraining and moving dogs in which this disease is suspected. On
lateral radiographs, an increased space and angle (>10°) can be seen
between the dorsal lamina of the atlas and the dorsal spinous process
of the axis (Figure 250.8)221; other measurements considered
useful include C1-C2 overlap, dens-to-axis length ratio, a ventral
compression index, and the clivus canal angle.202,208,222,223 The
presence and size of the dens can be evaluated most accurately on
ventrodorsal views and oblique radiographs.224 If there is no
evidence of subluxation on the lateral views, the neck can be
carefully flexed to approximately 50° to evaluate whether the space
between the dorsal lamina of the atlas and the dorsal spinous process
of the axis is affected. It is preferable to do this with fluoroscopy so
that the movement can be monitored to prevent accidental iatrogenic
subluxation; this can provide a rapid diagnosis in a conscious dog.
CT and MRI (ch. 112) can add vital information, which helps with
decision-making regarding treatment of the individual patient.225227
CT can assist with identification of dens conformation, dens or
vertebral fracture presence and surgical implant placing, especially
when using 3D-printed patient-specific drill guides.225,227-229
Three-dimensional CT reconstruction of the AA joint can add an
extra level of understanding to the diagnosis, and thus assist with
surgical decision-making.230 An MRI can provide additional
information regarding caudal fossa abnormalities, craniocervical
junction anomalies (including the presence of dorsal hypertrophic
AA ligaments which may be significantly compressive) and spinal

cord lesions such as hemorrhage or edema and syringomyelia which
all might be important for prognosis, as well as surgical decisionmaking (Figure 250.8).226,227,231,232

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Nonsurgical treatment of AA subluxation, including strict cage
confinement for 6 weeks, analgesia, and a rigid cervical brace, has
been successful in some patients; however, nonsurgical or
conservative approaches are likely to result in recurrent or
progressive clinical signs.211,233,234 The splint must immobilize the
AA junction, so the brace must come over the head rostral to the ears
and extend caudally to the level of the sternum. Complications
associated with the use of a splint and neck wrap include recurrence
of disease, corneal ulcers, migration of the splint to become
ineffective, moist dermatitis and decubital ulcers, hyperthermia,
respiratory compromise (dyspnea, aspiration), anorexia, otitis
externa and the accumulation of food between the splint and
mandible.211 A good long-term outcome has been documented in 10
of 26 (38%) cases managed conservatively.211,233,234 Dogs that are
affected for <30 days are significantly more likely to have a good
long-term outcome when managed conservatively, compared with
dogs affected >30 days.211 The goal of surgical treatment is to fuse
the AA joint permanently (Figure 250.8), accepting it will not
address any underlying parenchymal disease resulting from
associated concussion. The reported perioperative mortality rate
associated with AA fixation has been 10-30%.207,212 Age of onset
<24 months is significantly associated with greater odds of a
successful first surgery and final outcome.207 Duration ≤10 months
and lesser severity of clinical signs are significantly associated with
greater odds of a successful final outcome207; despite the guarded
prognosis for dogs with severe neurological deficits, many dogs that
are unable to walk before surgery have a good outcome.212 Whether
a dorsal or ventral procedure is performed does not seem to change
the odds of a successful outcome.207 Reduced levels of morbidity and

improved alignments can be achieved when using 3D-CT-printed
drill guides.235

CONGENITAL SPINAL COLUMN
MALFORMATIONS
Congenital malformations of the vertebrae are described in small
brachycephalic dogs, such as the French Bulldog, English Bulldog
and Pug236 and occasionally in cats.66,237,238 These defects may be
associated with structural abnormalities of the spinal cord, both of
which may arise during embryonic or fetal development. Survey
radiographs can often detect a vertebral anomaly but advanced
imaging such as MRI is necessary to evaluate for associated spinal
cord compression or concurrent disease (Figure 250.9). A modified
human radiographic classification scheme has been proposed to
assist in describing these anomalies,239,240 while the degree of
radiographically calculated spinal curvature has been shown to be
associated with the presence of neurological deficits.241,242 Threedimensional CT reconstructions can assist with a greater
understanding of the vertebral anomaly present in the individual
case (Figure 250.9).66,243

HEMIVERTEBRAE
These anomalies arise due to the failure of one sagittal half of the
vertebra to develop, possibly due to congenital absence of
vascularization. The result is a laterally wedged vertebra and scoliotic
angulation.66 Up to 9 subtypes of hemivertebrae have been
described, including ventral aplasia or “dorsal hemivertebra,” ventral
hypoplasia or “wedged vertebra” and ventral and median aplasia or
“butterfly vertebra,”236,244,245 named due to their ventrodorsal
appearance on a radiograph.66,246

French and English Bulldogs and Boston Terriers are the most
commonly affected breeds. In many breeds, it is considered to be
inherited as an autosomal recessive abnormality.247 Studies have
documented 78-94% of French Bulldogs having hemivertebrae,
identified significantly more often as incidental findings compared to
English Bulldogs and Pugs236; associated kyphosis is seen in up to
30% of neurologically normal French Bulldogs.242,248
Most affected vertebrae are located between T4-T9 but they can
exist in any location.242,244,249 Hemivertebrae are not associated
with severe canal stenosis; however, cranial thoracic vertebral canal
stenosis can be seen in affected dogs due to hypertrophy of the
vertebral laminae and articular processes.250 Spinal cord
compression results more from associated kyphosis and
subluxation.242 In addition, at the site of the anomaly it is not
uncommon to find concurrent disc herniation and/or an arachnoid
diverticulum; both could be responsible for neurological signs, which
can occur at a very young age or late into adulthood.242,249

FIGURE 250.9 A, A kyphoscoliotic thoracic
vertebral column in a 7-month-old French Bulldog is
demonstrated on this lateral radiograph; the
kyphoscoliosis is due to the vertebral malformations
present. The most severe vertebral body
abnormalities, compatible with centrum hypoplasia,
affect T10 (white arrow) and T5 (red arrow). B, A
sagittal computed tomography (CT) scan of the
thoracolumbar vertebral column of a different
French Bulldog reveals the shape of the vertebral
bodies and the way they may be affecting the
vertebral canal. The anomaly affecting L1 (arrow)
does not seem to be associated with canal stenosis.
The anomalies affecting the cranial thoracic vertebral
column (arrowhead) are associated with a significant
stenosis. C, A sagittal T2-weighted magnetic
resonance imaging of the thoracolumbar vertebral
column of a Pug dog demonstrates the effect that a
vertebral body anomaly (arrow) associated stenosis

has on the spinal cord causing compression and a
syrinx (red arrowhead) cranial to the lesion. D, A
three-dimensional reconstructed CT scan of the
vertebral column of a French Bulldog helps to
identify multiple vertebral body anomalies (arrows).
Hemivertebrae in Pugs are more likely to be associated with
clinical signs compared to hemivertebrae in other breeds.236 Pugs
also have different subtypes of hemivertebrae (i.e., wedged vertebra)
than French and English Bulldogs. The hemivertebra subtype most
commonly seen in Pugs is also more likely associated with spinal
kyphosis.251 Kyphosis >35° and step lesions between the vertebrae
are associated with a higher likelihood of neurological signs.241,244
Surgical realignment and stabilization rather than a dorsal
laminectomy alone has been advised in clinical cases, with the
prognosis being good to guarded.242,252,253 Several studies have
demonstrated good outcomes after vertebral stabilisation without
decompression.252 Partial vertebral re-alignment can be performed
when possible.254 Although surgical treatment has been associated
with good long-term outcomes, surgical stabilization of
hemivertebrae with kyphosis should be considered a technically
challenging procedure. Therefore, careful surgical planning is
necessary, and the use of 3D printed patient-specific drill guides has
been proposed to facilitate safe implant placement.255

BLOCK VERTEBRAE
This defect results from partial or total fusion of 2 vertebrae at any
point. They may be associated with angulation of the spinal column,
AA subluxation, and/or disc disease.256,257

CAUDAL ARTICULAR PROCESS
DYSPLASIA (CAD)

CAD is characterized by a complete (aplasia) or partial (hypoplasia)
absence of one or more caudal articular processes.258 This vertebral
malformation occurs commonly in neurologically normal small
brachycephalic dogs. CT studies of dogs without spinal disease reveal
that 70.4% of French Bulldogs, 84.1% of English Bulldogs and 97% of
Pugs have evidence of CAD.259,260 The caudal articular processes of
the caudal thoracic vertebrae, between T10 and T13, are most often
affected in animals with neurological signs.258,261,262 It has been
proposed that CAD can lead to low-grade and repetitive vertebral
instability, which can lead to a condition termed “constrictive
myelopathy” or “meningeal fibrosis.”81,260 This is characterized by
the formation of a dense, circumferential band of fibrotic tissue
causing intradural adhesions between the arachnoid and pia mater
and constriction of the spinal cord. Although meningeal fibrosis has
traditionally been associated with CAD, this condition has also been
reported in Pugs without concurrent vertebral anomalies,81,263 and
so could represent a multifactorial neurological syndrome or a
disease entity in itself. Meningeal fibrosis, confirmed to be
pathologically inflammatory, has been identified with concomitant
focal malacia, syringomyelia, and with spinal arachnoid diverticulum
formation in Pugs.263 The imaging modality of choice to diagnose
meningeal fibrosis and concurrent conditions such as IVDD, SAD
and syringomyelia264 is MRI (ch. 112)81; abnormalities include an
irregular subarachnoid space, multiple linear hypointense bands that
transverse from the arachnoid to the pia across the arachnoid space,
spinal cord distortion and compression, and bilateral V-shaped
ventrolateral extradural lesions.81,264 An intraparenchymal
hyperintensity is usually present at the site of spinal cord
compression.81,263 Surgical treatment consisting of vertebral
stabilization with or without additional decompression has been
associated with neurological improvement in the majority of
cases265; however, concurrent urinary or fecal incontinence is
expected to resolve in <50% of cases.265

TRANSITIONAL VERTEBRAE
Found at the junction between two structural divisions of the spinal
column (e.g., thoracolumbar and lumbosacral), transitional
vertebrae are congenital vertebral anomalies that share
characteristics of both divisions. The most common abnormality is
the presence or absence of a costa or transverse process, often
occurring subclinically and described in both dogs and cats.66
Similar to block vertebrae, these anomalies can be associated with
disc disease, which has been well described at the lumbosacral
junction in genetically predisposed German Shepherd Dogs.40,266268
Pugs are also predisposed for transitional vertebrae. Compared
to French and English Bulldogs, they have a higher prevalence of
thoracolumbar and lumbosacral transitional vertebrae.236,269
Although transitional vertebrae are only rarely associated with
clinical signs, they can complicate surgical planning and have the
potential to alter the biomechanical characteristics of the vertebral
column. This can result in acceleration of degenerative processes,
such as intervertebral disc degeneration. A specific type of
transitional vertebra has been described in Pugs, which is referred to
as homeotic transformation of C7 and is characterised by the
presence of cervical ribs on C7.270

MENINGOMYELITIS
Meningomyelitis is defined as inflammation of the spinal cord
parenchyma and surrounding meninges. It is relatively uncommon
for it to be present without encephalitis; a retrospective review of
220 dogs with inflammatory central nervous system (CNS) diseases
revealed that only 41 had focal spinal cord involvement.271 Canine
distemper virus (ch. 204) and protozoa (ch. 197) have been the
most commonly identified infectious causes, while steroidresponsive meningitis-arteritis is often the most frequently
recognized probable non-infectious inflammatory disease process.271
Rickettsiae, fungi, bacteria, helminths and meningitides of unknown
etiology (MUE; ch. 242) such as granulomatous

meningoencephalomyelitis are other reported causes of
meningomyelitis in dogs.272-278 However, in many cases the
underlying disease process remains undetermined. A review of 28
dogs with meningomyelitis revealed that MUE was the most
common diagnosis and that hound and toy breed dogs ≤3 years of
age had a 13 times higher odds of meningomyelitis compared with
other breeds.279
The clinical signs associated with meningomyelitis reflect the
region of the CNS involved and can include paraspinal hyperesthesia,
general proprioceptive ataxia, and limb paresis or paralysis.
Definitive diagnosis of inflammatory CNS disease requires
histopathologic assessment of tissue but a presumptive diagnosis can
be made using a combination of CSF analysis (ch. 109), advanced
imaging (ch. 112), and infectious disease testing (ch. 184). The
prognosis is presumed to be specific to the underlying disease
process and severity of clinical signs.279 For a more detailed
description of inflammatory CNS diseases, the reader is referred to
ch. 242.

STEROID-RESPONSIVE MENINGITISARTERITIS (SRMA)
Etiology and Pathogenesis
An immunological cause of this disease is suspected, resulting in a
vasculitis (ch. 181), although no specific trigger factors have been
identified.280,281 Notably, increased levels of CSF and serum
immunoglobulin A (IgA), induced by a Th2 immune response,
increased CSF and blood B-cell/T-cell ratios, and CSF interleukin
(IL)-6 and IL-8 levels are all thought to be compatible with immune
system stimulation.282-285 High CD11a expression on
polymorphonuclear cells appears to be an important factor in the
pathogenesis of SRMA and may be involved in the enhanced passage
of neutrophils into the subarachnoid space, leading to meningitis
and clinical signs.286 Matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-2 seems to
also be involved in the neutrophilic invasion into the subarachnoid

space.287 With chronic progression of the lesions, rupture and
hemorrhage of the weakened vasculature may be present
accompanied by thickened leptomeninges with less severe
inflammation.

Clinical Findings
SRMA, also termed necrotizing vasculitis, juvenile polyarteritis
syndrome, corticosteroid-responsive meningitis/meningomyelitis,
and aseptic suppurative meningitis, is reported in Beagles, Bernese
Mountain Dogs, Boxers, German Wirehaired and Shorthaired
Pointers, Border Collies, Jack Russell Terriers, Weimaraners, Golden
Retrievers, Wirehaired Pointing Griffons and Nova Scotia Duck
Tolling Retrievers,281,288-290 and occurs in other medium to large
dog breeds. Affected dogs are often young adults (8-18 months old)
but can be of any age, and are usually febrile and hyperesthetic, with
cervical rigidity and anorexia. Rarely, severe motor dysfunction may
result from spontaneous bleeding into the subarachnoid space,
spinal cord hematoma/hematomyelia or subconjunctival
hemorrhages.291,292 Some dogs (up to 46%) with immune-mediated
polyarthritis (ch. 177), especially Bernese Mountain Dogs, Boxers
and Akitas, may show clinical signs that are similar to those of dogs
with SRMA and have concurrent meningitis (ch. 242).293

Diagnosis
The clinical signs and signalment are useful in the initial suspicion of
this disease.294,295 A marked peripheral neutrophilia with a left shift
may be seen at the time of the clinical signs. Analysis of CSF (ch.
109) often reveals a marked neutrophilic pleocytosis and protein
elevation; cell counts >100 cells/mcL are common. CSF samples
from both the cerebellomedullary cistern and the lumbar
subarachnoid space should be analyzed when evaluating dogs with
suspected SRMA to improve diagnostic yield.296 Neutrophils are
non-degenerative, unlike bacterial meningitis. In the majority of
dogs, there are elevations of IgA levels in the CSF and the serum. IgA
CSF concentrations are significantly higher in dogs with SRMA

compared to other disease categories, with the exception of
inflammatory CNS disease, and so are considered nonspecific. The
sensitivity for IgA concentrations in serum and CSF was 91% with a
specificity of only 78% when evaluated in 311 dogs with SRMA.297 Creactive protein (CRP) is the primary major canine acute phase
protein (APP) and it is immediately responsive to both inflammation
and its resolution; other APPs include serum amyloid-A (SAA),
haptoglobin and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein.298 Serum CRP
concentration has been shown to be significantly higher in dogs with
SRMA in comparison to dogs with other neurological diseases.299 In
9 dogs with SRMA, all serum APP concentrations were above normal
and all decreased, apart from haptoglobin, in response to
corticosteroid treatment.300 Serum CRP and SAA were also found to
be consistently elevated in all patients exhibiting signs consistent
with a relapse during treatment in the presence of normal CSF and
leukogram findings. However, much like IgA, elevations of CRP are
considered nonspecific, are elevated in sepsis, and so can only be
used as a supportive diagnostic test.301 Diagnostic imaging is not
required for a diagnosis of SRMA but is useful to eliminate other
causes of cervical pain. MRI is often normal but may reveal
meningeal paramagnetic contrast enhancement; signal changes in
the cervical paraspinal musculature (T2 or short tau inversion
recovery [STIR] hyperintensity or contrast enhancement), the
perineural tissues, and around the joint spaces; and multifocal illdefined, T2-hyperintense lesions within the cervical spinal cord with
variable contrast enhancement.290,302

Treatment
The prognosis can be good if dogs are treated early and intensively
with immunosuppressive dosages of corticosteroids (ch. 144), with
up to 80% of cases having long-term remission.303,304 Most dogs
experience improvement within 48 hours of receiving
immunosuppressive dosages of corticosteroids, but relapses occur in
16-47.5% of cases, including after 2 years of age.290,305 Relapses
occur in approximately one-third of cases.306 Monitoring of CSF cell

count in dogs with this condition is a sensitive indicator of success of
treatment although serum CRP is a more useful marker with 3month serum and CSF levels predicting remission with high
sensitivity.306 In refractory cases or in patients having steroidrelated side-effects, alternative immunomodulation therapy should
be considered, such as cytosine arabinoside and azathioprine (ch.
169).307,308 Surgical decompression may be necessary in cases with
epidural hemorrhage.309

DISCOSPONDYLITIS
ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS
Discospondylitis is due to infection of the intervertebral disc and
adjacent vertebral endplates; if the infection is confined to the
vertebral body, it is called vertebral osteomyelitis or spondylitis.310
Coagulase-positive Staphylococcus spp. (S. pseudintermedius or S.
aureus) are a common etiological agent associated with canine
discospondylitis288; other less commonly identified organisms
include Streptococcus spp., Escherichia coli, Actinomyces spp. (ch.
188) and Brucella canis (ch. 189), as well as Aspergillus spp. (ch.
211). Young German Shepherd Dog bitches and Hungarian Vizslas
seem to be predisposed to aspergillosis,311,312 whereas young Basset
Hounds contract discospondylitis due to systemic tuberculosis (ch.
188).313 Hematogenous spread from distant foci of infection
(urogenital tract, skin, dental disease), penetrating wounds,
surgery,314 or plant material migration can cause direct infection of
the disc space or vertebrae, the latter of which is usually seen at the
level of L2-4 at the insertion of the diaphragmatic crus. The most
commonly affected sites are L7-S1, caudal cervical, mid-thoracic, and
thoracolumbar spine.288 The infection is usually slowly progressive
but can result in acute signs due to secondary pathological vertebral
fractures and IVDD. An association with empyema has been
documented in several dogs, which may represent an extension of

the disease and should be considered when selecting diagnostic tests
and/or when dealing with a refractory case.315-317

CLINICAL FINDINGS
Evidence of spinal pain is the most common initial clinical sign in
this disease, which is most frequently seen in large, intact, male,
young to middle-aged dogs.318 The condition is less common in toy
and chondrodystrophic dog breeds and is infrequent in cats.319 With
proliferation of inflammatory tissue, compression of neural tissue
can lead to ataxia, paresis, and occasionally paralysis, depending on
where the lesion is located. Approximately 30% of dogs have signs of
systemic illness such as fever and weight loss.

DIAGNOSIS
Hematological changes are usually not present unless there are
concurrent conditions such as endocarditis (ch. 232). Serum CRP
concentration is elevated and may be clinically more useful to screen
dogs with back pain than fever or leukocytosis alone.320
Urine sediment exam may reveal bacterial or fungal agents (ch.
70). Blood and urine cultures should be performed in all suspected
cases and are positive in up to 75% and 50% of cases, respectively
(ch. 184).288,310 Ideally these should be performed prior to
initiating antibiotic therapy. Serologic testing for brucellosis should
also be performed, especially in view of its zoonotic potential (ch.
189); this has been reported to be positive in up to 10% of cases. The
standard test for B. canis is blood culture but because bacteremia can
be intermittent, positive animals may be missed.321 Culture requires
up to 9 days, increasing the risk for exposure of laboratory personnel
if the cultures are not handled appropriately.
The definitive diagnosis is usually made with spinal radiographs
(Figure 250.10), although radiographic change may not be evident
in the first 2-4 weeks of infection.322 As this can be a multifocal
disease, the entire vertebral column should be radiographed.

Radiographic evidence of disease includes narrowing of the disc
space, accompanied by subtle irregularity of both endplates through
to gross lysis and osseous proliferation of the adjacent vertebral bone
and even fractures. Radiographs can also be used to monitor the
response to treatment or the progression of the disease,323 although
clinical progression is equally important, as radiographic change can
lag behind clinical improvement. Myelography used to be
recommended in patients with substantial neurological deficits to
rule out concurrent disc disease and subluxation affecting the neural
tissue; however, this should be reserved for when neither CT nor
MRI is available, both of which are considered more sensitive (ch.
112).322 A study of 27 dogs with discospondylitis found that
contrast-enhanced radiographs revealed only a 5% median cord
compression in the dogs that was not related to clinical signs or
outcome.324 CT can identify subtle endplate erosion and
paravertebral soft-tissue swelling more readily than radiographs do.
Post-myelogram CT clearly defines compression of the neural tissues
by infected tissues, as does MRI. Discospondylitis appears to have
increased signal intensity on T2-weighted and STIR images and
decreased signal intensity on T1-weighted images, changes also seen
in the paravertebral tissues in all cases.325,326 Contrast enhancement
was seen in the endplates of affected vertebrae in 15 of 17 (88%) of
sites in one study, as was endplate erosion and STIR hyperintense,
T2-hypointense bone marrow. MRI can also highlight the
inflammation in the surrounding muscles (Figure 250.10).

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
The initial treatment of discospondylitis consists of antibiotics
(potentiated amoxicillin or cephalexin), cage rest, and analgesics
(ch. 6). Intravenous antibiotics should be considered if severe
neurological compromise or signs of sepsis are present; otherwise,
oral antibiotics are acceptable. However quickly the patient
improves, continuation of the antibiotics for 8-16 weeks is
recommended, although one study evaluating 513 cases noted a
mean duration of treatment as 54 weeks.288,310,318 Resolution of

clinical signs, such as pain and fever, should be expected within 5
days of initiating therapy; however, complete neurological resolution
may take 2-3 months. Residual deficits may remain, but persistent
signs of pain indicate active disease, and these patients should be
treated with an additional antibiotic and considered for further
diagnostics as they may have a fungal infection or surgical lesion.
Discospondylitis associated with Aspergillus spp. has been treated
with itraconazole (5 mg/kg PO q24h), fluconazole, or voriconazole
(ch. 141), although long-term reports of success are lacking with the
belief being that chronic recurrence and progression is likely (ch.
211). Treatment for discospondylitis associated with Brucella
requires a minimum 6-week course of a combination of doxycycline
and rifampin +/– gentamicin, combined with surgical resection of
infected tissues (castration after 2 weeks of preoperative antibiotics),
considering zoonotic and recurrence risk (ch. 189).327

FIGURE 250.10 A, A lateral radiograph of the
thoracolumbar vertebral column of an adult Golden
Retriever with back pain due to discospondylitis at
L2-L3. The vertebral endplates associated with the
L2-L3 intervertebral disc space (arrow) are irregular
due to lysis and osseous proliferation. B, A sagittal
T1-weighted post-contrast magnetic resonance
imaging of the thoracolumbar vertebral column
depicted in Figure 250.10, A reveals contrast uptake
(hyperintensity) within the vertebral body and dorsal

proliferation and spread of infection into the

above the disc space.
Surgical decompression is rarely needed and should only be
considered in refractory cases or those with severe neurological

deficits that show no signs of improvement within 3-5 days. Both
internal fixation and external fixation techniques are reported.328330

The prognosis for this disease is generally good unless the etiology
is fungal, there are multiple lesions, vertebral fracture or subluxation
occurs or there is endocarditis (ch. 232); the potential for
recurrence should be considered, especially if brucellosis has been
diagnosed or an underlying immunosuppressive condition is present.

Diseases: Traumatic,
Vascular, and Neoplastic
Nick D. Jeffery

INTRODUCTION
MECHANISMS
Traumatic, vascular and neoplastic disorders at first sight have little
in common, but all cause spinal cord dysfunction primarily by
impairing blood flow. Acute impact trauma and vascular interruption

cause instantaneous compromise of blood flow that triggers a
secondary series of autodestructive events within the spinal cord,
forming a sharp contrast to the slow, progressive compression of
blood vessels and attenuation of circulation generally associated with
neoplastic lesions. Pure impact injury causes very little immediate
damage to the spinal cord; there are a few severed axons and there
may be focal hemorrhage where small blood vessels have been
ruptured, but there is little indication of the severity of the
subsequent destructive events.1 The functional consequences of
impact injury usually arise because trauma initiates a cascade of
molecular reactions that culminate in severe impairment of the
microcirculation causing cellular apoptosis and tissue necrosis over a
period of several days.2 Over time—in experimental studies up to
about 7 days3—there is progressive damage to the tissue such that
almost complete cross-sectional destruction can occur, although the
extent of damage is clearly related to the severity of the initiating
injury.4 The reasons behind this progressive damage after impact
injury (usually referred to as “contusion”) have been elucidated in
many hundreds of laboratory experiments carried out over the past
century, especially during the past 20 years, and they center on
impairment of circulation.5 This is mediated in large part by
inflammatory mediators and the resulting loss of blood flow then
leads to secondary consequences caused by lack of energy supply
(both lack of oxygen and lack of glucose). Ultimately, the
depolarization of the neurons and axons allows accumulation of
calcium as a key secondary messenger that activates many
autodestructive enzymes, notably calpains, caspases and xanthine
oxidase.2 Clearly, similar events follow from primary vascular
lesions, although these frequently have more limited spatial effects
because affected vessels are often of small diameter and have small
autonomous regions of distribution. They also differ in that external
trauma commonly is also associated with prolonged compression,
such as displaced vertebral fractures, which may further compromise
blood flow in a way that primary vascular events do not.
The mechanisms underlying the tissue destruction associated with
chronic compression of the spinal cord are less well understood
because it is much more difficult to carry out the relevant laboratory

experiments, but there is clear evidence of impaired
microcirculation.6,7 Most neoplastic lesions increasingly compress
the spinal cord over a period of weeks to months. Initially, blood flow
remains sufficient to preserve adequate spinal cord function but,
eventually, a “tipping point” is reached, at which the compression
becomes too severe to allow compensation and clinical signs then
appear rapidly.

DIAGNOSIS OF LESIONS IN THE SPINAL
CORD
The approach to all diseases of the nervous system is to first localize
the problem using the physical neurologic examination (ch. 241)
and then consider the possible causes of a lesion at that site (Video
251.1

). This must be done while bearing in mind the signalment

and history, most pertinently the speed of onset and whether there
has been progression or regression of clinical signs after initiation.
This same process localizes traumatic, vascular, and neoplastic
diseases in the spinal cord. Crucially, however, sometimes both
traumatic and neoplastic diseases can also be associated with spinal
pain without evidence of neurologic deficits. In such cases, careful
observation and gentle palpation may aid in localizing the lesion site,
although these observations can be misleading in animals that are
particularly anxious or stoic. Sometimes a more accurate assessment
can be achieved through in-clinic observation of the animal during a
period of 24 hours or even longer. It is important to be aware of the
phenomenon of “spinal shock” as a consequence of acute, severe
spinal cord injury because it can lead to depression of activity in
reflex arcs caudal to the lesion for ∼24 hours or even more.8,9 To
avoid mislocalization of the lesion, it is important to take careful note
of the cutaneous trunci (panniculus) muscle reflex (ch. 241) and
identify sites that are painful on palpation.

HISTORY (CH. 3)

Evaluation of historical features can be very helpful to inform the
index of suspicion for the specific types of lesion included in this
chapter (see below). Historical and signalment information are
recognized as crucial in reaching a neurologic diagnosis10; in human
medicine it is suspected that ∼80% of the diagnosis is derived from
history alone.11 Although signalment cannot be used as a substitute
for thorough step-wise diagnostic work-up, specific components of
this information might suggest the cause of spinal lesions and be
helpful in guiding subsequent investigations towards the most
informative diagnostic tests.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
In general, traumatic lesions may have few differential diagnoses,
depending on whether a traumatic incident was witnessed, and
typical signs of vascular lesions are also highly suggestive of that
etiology. The major differential diagnoses for spinal cord diseases
included in this chapter are lesions associated with acute or chronic
intervertebral disc herniation (ch. 250) and, for slowly progressive
disease, neurodegenerative conditions (ch. 244). The nature of the
differential diagnoses usually implies the need for imaging as the
next step in diagnosis.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
Although some spinal cord lesions may be poorly defined by imaging,
nowadays the next step in diagnosis after localization is almost
invariably some type of diagnostic imaging (ch. 112). Inflammatory
disease can be identified using cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis
(ch. 109),12 but it is rare for this to be a reasonable first diagnostic
step because of the possible associated risks (e.g., exacerbated
hemorrhage, spread of tumor cells, brain herniation in case of
increased intracranial pressure) and images are often required to aid
interpretation of the results. For instance, high CSF protein
concentration is a nonspecific finding that is commonly, but not
invariably, associated with spinal cord compression.13

Most traumatic, vascular, and neoplastic diseases require imaging
to confirm the localization and this may also strongly suggest the
etiology, although precise diagnosis is frequently dependent on
histopathological examination. Radiography and computed
tomography (CT) are excellent modalities for diagnosing lesions
affecting bone of the vertebral column but provide poor detail of the
spinal cord itself. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is preferable
for diagnosis of spinal cord lesions and can also detect ligamentous
injury but has the drawback of providing relatively poor detail of
bone imaging, plus it can be expensive and time-consuming. Given
unlimited funds, the two techniques can be regarded as
complementary but in most veterinary cases the decision between
the two depends on whether the lesion is suspected to be bony or soft
tissue (especially affecting the spinal cord) only. This decision is
usually made bearing in mind the nature of the inciting injury, (e.g.,
external trauma), the severity of the lesion, and the need to diagnose
a lesion for subsequent surgical intervention. Animals in which a
vascular lesion is suspected would normally be imaged using MRI
because such lesions are not visible using other modalities.

TREATMENT
Categories of disease in this chapter have extremely varied etiologies
and prognoses. For instance, traumatic lesions may require surgical
stabilization (e.g., unstable fracture-luxations; Figure 251.1) or,
alternatively, conservative (e.g., stable fractures) or nonspecific (e.g.,
acute non-compressive disc extrusion) supportive care, such as cage
rest. Spinal cord damage caused by primary vascular lesions is
generally not responsive to therapy by the time affected animals
arrive at the clinic because the damage has already been done.
However, this does not imply a hopeless prognosis because injury is
usually sub-complete and many animals recover function as
inflammation resolves and plastic alterations in circuitry supervene
(Video 251.2

).14 Neoplastic lesions also show extreme variability

in prognosis; some cases are hopeless with or without treatment
(e.g., disseminated metastases of hemangiosarcoma), whereas other

affected animals may be expected to live for several years (e.g.,
multiple myeloma15).

Role of Corticosteroid Therapy
A persistent controversy surrounding treatment of traumatic and
vascular spinal cord lesions is the role of corticosteroid therapy.16
For many decades, both human physicians and veterinarians used
corticosteroids, often at very high dosages, aiming to reduce the
functional and pathological consequences of acute insult to the
spinal cord. However, despite the positive effects of corticosteroids
that are sometimes reported from laboratory studies, these effects
have not been duplicated in the clinic.17 Initial reports on the use of
high-dose methylprednisolone sodium succinate in human spinal
cord injury suggested a benefit,18 but this has since been disputed
and the current consensus of opinion is that corticosteroids are not
helpful in ameliorating acute spinal cord insults.19 There is also
reason to suppose that their use might be detrimental, partly because
of the documented adverse effects of corticosteroids in head
trauma,20 and also because of the well-established effects of
corticosteroids to reduce muscle mass, cause gastrointestinal
disturbances and immunosuppress patients (ch. 143).

FIGURE 251.1 Thoracolumbar vertebral fractureluxations frequently cause instability that threatens
spinal cord integrity and often requires surgical
stabilization. A, Fracture of caudal aspect of the L1
vertebra (arrow) clearly visible using radiography
alone. B, T2-weighted sagittal magnetic resonance
imaging scan also shows the fracture (arrow) and
reveals detail of the spinal cord injury. C, Sagittal
reconstructed computed tomography (CT) scan
reveals excellent detail of a T13 vertebral fracture in
another dog. D, Corresponding transverse CT image
reveals the extent of vertebral canal compromise
associated with this “burst fracture,” probably
resulting from compression along the long axis of the

lesion did not cause neurologic deficits but was
associated with severe pain.
In contrast, corticosteroids often have a dramatic alleviating effect
on the neurologic deficits associated with (prolonged) central
nervous system (CNS) compression.16 The main reason is that they
reduce blood vessel permeability and therefore reduce accumulation
of edema in the vicinity of the compressive lesion (vasogenic
edema).21 Although this can be a helpful effect of corticosteroids
from the point of view of the owner and the affected animal it may be
detrimental for a veterinarian attempting to make a specific
diagnosis because corticosteroid effects often impede diagnostic
efforts and suggest to owners that they should delay further
investigations. Indiscriminate corticosteroid administration also
exposes animals to the risks of their adverse effects.

TRAUMATIC DISEASES
SIGNALMENT AND HISTORY
No specific signalment need be associated with traumatic injury, but
it is well-recognized that young, especially male, animals tend to be

overrepresented in affected populations. However, the history is
usually of more value in raising suspicion of traumatic lesions, often
dominating all other considerations: there is almost always an acute
onset of clinical signs and often the traumatic event has been
observed by the owner.
Animals that sustain spinal fracture-luxations occasionally, and by
exception, do not exhibit neurologic signs immediately after the
incident; rather, with time, vertebrae in the affected region may
become displaced, producing signs of neurologic deterioration, often
accompanied by pain. This seems to be particularly prevalent in
association with lesions of the upper cervical region (specifically the
atlantoaxial region), and at L7-S1, although lesions at the latter level
do not affect the spinal cord. External trauma that causes clinical
signs in association with spinal lesions is usually severe; however,
occasionally animals can develop signs of spinal cord injury
associated with what would appear to be minor trauma. For instance,
dogs that have congenital atlantoaxial subluxation may sometimes
develop clinical signs associated with the apparently trivial trauma of
knocking the head on the underside of furniture when rising from
recumbency.

PRESENTATION AND IMMEDIATE
MANAGEMENT
Vehicular impact, falls from heights, animal kicks and gunshot or
other projectile injuries are the most common causes of traumatic
lesions of the vertebral column that result in neurologic deficits.
Most affected animals have obvious neurologic deficits but some
cases may present with signs of pain alone that may be poorly
localized. Importantly, some animals may present in circulatory
shock so that neurologic examination is not immediately reliable
because poor CNS perfusion can cause temporary neurologic deficits
(ch. 119). For this reason it is imperative to re-examine affected
animals at frequent intervals to determine whether neurologic status
is changing.
When a patient first is presented at a clinic it may be tempting to
attend to neurologic injuries first, because they are often striking, but
it is important to prioritize treatment according to the “ABC”

system.22 On the other hand, it is crucial to be cognizant of the
possibility of neurologic injury, specifically fracture-luxation, and
especially in animals that have nonspecific pain, because careless
handling can lead to inadvertent further injury to the spinal cord.
Therefore, in animals that are presented recumbent after major
external trauma, it is important not to move the animal more than is
absolutely essential. For instance, it is often sensible to take
radiographs of the vertebral column at an early stage, even
sometimes prior to full neurologic examination, so as to identify sites
which might be at risk of iatrogenic injury. In animals in which a
single spinal fracture-luxation has been identified, it is essential to
consider the possibility that there could be additional lesions in the
vertebral column which may not be producing such obvious clinical
signs.23 Therefore, it is frequently prudent to obtain radiographs or,
better still, CT images, of the entire vertebral column.
Immediate management of fracture-luxation consists of
preventing additional motion at the injury site, which can be
achieved by securing the animal to a rigid board. Care must be taken
regarding use of sedatives and anesthetics because they often reduce
inherent muscle tone that can be helpful for resisting excessive bone
fragment motion.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
In general, traumatic lesions may have few differential diagnoses,
particularly if the traumatic incident was observed by the owner. On
the other hand, trauma should be considered as a possible
differential diagnosis for any animal that exhibits acute clinical signs
indicative of spinal cord injury or pain (including simply appearing
generally lethargic or depressed). The major differential diagnoses
for cases exhibiting acute onset of spinal cord neurologic deficits are
intervertebral disc herniation (ch. 250) or vascular lesions of the
spinal cord (see below). Occasionally, inflammatory disease, most
notably meningoencephalomyelitis of unknown origin (MUO, ch.
242), is associated with acute onset of clinical signs that mimic acute
spinal cord injury.24 Unfortunately, small-breed dogs that are
susceptible to acute intervertebral disc herniation can also be

affected by forms of MUO that cause acute spinal cord dysfunction
alone, reinforcing the need for obtaining a specific diagnosis. MRI
(ch. 112) and CSF analysis (ch. 109) usually distinguish between
these etiologies.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
For almost all cases in which a traumatic etiology is suspected, the
next diagnostic step is imaging (see above; ch. 112). Often it is most
convenient to commence with plain radiographs, which function best
as a “rule-in” test rather than a “rule-out” test. This is because many
traumatic lesions, even those affecting the vertebrae or, indeed, the
vertebral canal itself, may not be apparent on plain radiographs. CT
is indicated in animals in which a lesion of the skeletal structures is
still suspected, such as those exhibiting signs of severe spinal pain
despite negative radiographic findings. However, some traumatic
lesions (see below) may not be apparent even on CT images; MRI
almost invariably detects traumatic lesions within the spinal cord.

SPECIFIC DISEASES
Vertebral Fracture-Luxation 25
The most obvious possible result of external trauma is fracture or
luxation of vertebrae and indeed this is the most commonly observed
lesion. Unless such lesions affect the vertebral canal, they do not
cause clinical signs indicative of spinal cord injury (although spinal
nerves may be affected) but almost all cases exhibit signs of pain. In
most cases, subluxation results from fracture of part of a vertebra but
occasionally there can be simple subluxation resulting from
ligamentous injury alone, most notably in the cranial cervical region
(Figure 251.2).
Treatment of vertebral fracture-luxations depends largely upon the
severity of the clinical signs, an estimate of “stability” and the
location of the lesion.25 The most critical part of the evaluation is to
determine whether the “deep pain” response is intact. This provides
the most accurate prognostic information, although it is important to

be aware that animals in circulatory shock may have temporarily
dulled pain responses. Successful treatment options for spinal
fracture-luxations can vary greatly between individuals. For instance,
ambulatory animals displaying mild neurologic deficits in the pelvic
limbs associated with inherently stable fractures of the thoracic
vertebrae may well not require surgical intervention and could
recover with simple restriction of exercise while the lesion heals. In
contrast, an animal with paraplegia (but intact pain sensation)
caused by a fracture of a lumbar vertebral body would be a good
candidate for surgical stabilization. The treatment of vertebral
fracture-luxations is the subject of many previously published
reviews. Briefly, decision-making can be aided by thinking of the
vertebral column as a series of three dorsally-to-ventrally oriented
columns running sagittally through its entire length (ventral column
= ventral half of the vertebral bodies, intervertebral discs [annulus
primarily] and the ventral longitudinal ligament; middle column =
dorsal part of the vertebral bodies, dorsal annulus of the discs, and
dorsal longitudinal ligament with part of the pedicles; dorsal column
= laminae, spinous processes, articular processes and all the
associated ligaments). If two of the three columns are interrupted by
the lesion, it suggests instability, providing a strong indication for
internal fixation. The magnitude of subluxation at the injury site is
not often a good guide to prognosis because the position of the
skeletal elements during imaging may not accurately reflect the
extent of motion during the injury process.
A controversial aspect of surgery for acute fracture-luxation is its
timing, and this question has not been settled in human medicine
either. In general, it is advisable to carry out surgery as soon as
possible, because that reduces the risk of further mechanical injury
to the spinal cord and alleviates persistent compression.
Nevertheless, the urge for early surgery must not overcome the
necessity of having a patient in sufficiently stable condition to
undergo general anesthesia. Many animals that have sustained
external trauma have multiple injuries that may be more lifethreatening than their spinal injuries and require priority attention
(ch. 119). It is also imperative for spinal cord integrity that normal
blood pressure (BP) is maintained (ch. 121).
Animals that have sustained gunshot or other projectile injuries
(Figure 251.3) can be treated by surgery in a similar way to other

traumatic injuries. There are only a few, relatively specific, reasons to
remove bullets or fragments and so the requirement for surgery for
this purpose must be carefully evaluated; impingement on the spinal
cord or spinal nerve is usually a strong rationale.26 Although
penetrating traumatic spinal cord injuries are open wounds with the
potential for contamination, reviews of human patients suggest that
prolonged use of prophylactic antibiotics is not required.27

Acute Non-compressive Disc Extrusion
Occasional animals (especially dogs) that have suffered external
trauma to the vertebral column have signs of severe spinal cord
injury, yet no obvious sign of vertebral fracture-luxation. In some of
these cases, intervertebral disc space narrowing is apparent. An
additional group of dogs sustains a similar type of injury that is often
associated with highly vigorous exercise. Since the advent of
widespread access to MRI, these cases have been investigated in
more detail and many have collapsed disc spaces associated with
escape and dorsally-directed extrusion of the nucleus pulposus.28,29
Almost invariably this disc extrusion is not of a diseased nucleus
subjected to physiologic, everyday stresses (as commonly occurs in
type I disc herniation in chondrodystrophic dogs; ch. 250) but
instead concerns the escape of a normal nucleus through an annulus
that has been torn through stretching beyond its physiologic
tolerance.30 Several categories of lesion that can be distinguished by
their MRI appearance are now recognized,31 and specific types tend
to occur in specific locations in the vertebral column, but all have
similar etiology.

FIGURE 251.2 Lateral radiograph showing
atlanto-axial subluxation in a young Yorkshire
Terrier, resulting from partial tearing or stretching of
the intervertebral ligaments. There is increased
distance between the arch of the atlas and the cranial
tip of the spinous process of the axis (arrows). This
sign must be interpreted with caution because it can
also be observed to some extent in apparently
normal dogs.
The forceful extrusion of the small volume of nucleus creates a
spinal cord lesion that results from the contusive force applied by the
extruded material (Figure 251.4). The small volume is insufficient
to create permanent compression and often is not visible on MRI
scans. Clinical signs are often lateralized because the disc herniates
to one side of the midline dorsal longitudinal ligament and so the
signs can resemble those of fibrocartilaginous embolism (FCE, see
below). Post mortem examination of such cases has suggested that
the extruded nucleus may sometimes actually pass through the

spinal cord substance.32 The resultant spinal cord lesion cannot be
seen on images other than MRI.

Miscellaneous
There are several reports of inadvertent introduction of identifying
microchips into the spinal canal where they can cause injury. The
reports suggest that very small dogs might be at heightened risk of
this type of injury, which can occur immediately following
implantation33 and also following migration of properly placed
microchips.34 There are also sporadic reports of spinal cord
penetration by other foreign bodies, including sticks35 and porcupine
quills36 (Figure 251.5).

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis for traumatic lesions of the spinal cord is, of course,
dependent on the severity of injury, but is often surprisingly good.
The best currently available prognostic indicator is “deep pain”
sensation (Video 241.28

); if it is intact, most animals

(eventually) recover useful enough locomotor ability to live normal
or near-normal lives. Animals with traumatic lesions in the cervical
region almost always retain deep pain sensation—those that don’t
will usually die before they can be presented because of respiratory
compromise.37 Loss of deep pain sensation associated with fractureluxation in the thoracolumbar region suggests a prognosis that is
very guarded at best; few such cases are ever reported to have
recovered the ability to walk again. Animals with thoracolumbar
injury and intact pain sensation usually recover remarkably good
function. Injuries to the sacral spinal cord segments, usually situated
within L5 to L6 vertebrae, can be problematic because they contain
the lower motor neurons (LMNs) controlling the bladder and anus.
Dogs with lesions at this site are often ambulatory but may be in pain
and it can be difficult to fully assess continence before treatment. If

injuries destroy these motor neurons bilaterally, the animals are left
permanently incontinent.

FIGURE 251.3 Gunshot-induced vertebral
fracture. A-B, Lateral and ventrodorsal radiographs
illustrating comminuted fracture of the L1 vertebra
associated with multiple mineral-density fragments.
The probable entry and exit portals can be deduced
on the ventrodorsal view. C, Dorsal plane computed
tomography showing pathway of a projectile through
the left ilium before entering the L6 vertebra.

Recovery after serious traumatic spinal cord injury can be a very
prolonged process – animals frequently require at least 10 days to
show ANY change at all, and the full recovery may take 3 months or
more. After severe spinal cord injury, a “scar” develops within the
spinal cord itself, consisting mainly of astrocytic processes plus a
secreted proteoglycan matrix, both of which can be highly inhibitory
to axonal regeneration.38 More familiar fibroblastic scarring can also
develop in the subarachnoid space and can impair CSF flow. The end
result of such scarring may lead to accumulation of fluid within the
spinal cord, sometimes sufficiently severe to be recognized as
syringomyelia (ch. 244). These secondary lesions may give rise to
pain syndromes (ch. 6), although this is relatively uncommonly
recognized in dogs and cats, and loss of fecal continence.39

VASCULAR DISEASES
A wide range of circulatory disorders could potentially lead to spinal
cord dysfunction. For instance, any cause of systemic hypotension,
including primary heart disease (chs. 231-235) or
hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296), could potentially cause signs
consistent with spinal cord disease (ch. 121); however, other clinical
signs are likely to predominate in association with such systemic
circulatory disturbance. Measurement of peripheral arterial BP (ch.
91) is prudent in cases in which no obvious cause for spinal cord
dysfunction is apparent; a decreased BP measurement in affected
limbs, with simultaneously normal BP in unaffected limbs, suggests
peripheral thromboembolic disease rather that spinal cord disease.
In particular, the signs associated with aortic thrombosis in dogs
(ch. 238)40 may suggest spinal cord disease (although a more likely
confusion is with peripheral nerve or muscle disease [ch. 252]).
Similarly, systemic diseases that affect blood clotting, including both
hypercoagulable states such as hyperadrenocorticism and
hypocoagulable states such as thrombocytopenia might cause spinal
cord lesions and should be considered during physical examination
(ch. 171). However, most cases of spinal cord damage caused by
vascular lesions result from regionally specific diseases, which are
considered below.

FIGURE 251.4 Typical magnetic resonance
images from a dog that has incurred a traumatic
intervertebral disc herniation associated due to a fall.
