at the mid-portion of the C7 vertebral body reveals
abnormal hyperintensity within the spinal cord.

SIGNALMENT
In general, spinal cord vascular lesions are more common in middleaged to older animals. Specifically, FCE is traditionally thought to
occur more commonly in non-chondrodystrophic breeds (and
perhaps the Miniature Schnauzer is at increased risk41). In general,
the signalment is not especially suggestive of this type of lesion and
spinal infarctions have been documented in animals that are
relatively young.42 There appears to be a higher prevalence of acute
vascular lesions in the cranial cervical spinal cord of the cat43 that
might be associated with hyaline degeneration of the ventral spinal
artery, itself perhaps associated with systemic hypertension (ch.
236).44

HISTORY
Assumed embolic spinal cord lesions (those referred to as FCE) are
characterized by an instantaneous onset, during which the animal
may express signs of apparent pain. The dogma regarding the history
of these conditions is that the animal is typically at exercise and
suddenly cries out or simply collapses and is then immediately
neurologically impaired.45 By the time the animal is presented to the
veterinarian, there is usually no evidence of pain, although anxious
or stoic patients can confound this assessment. Typically, animals

that suffer embolic vascular lesions of the spinal cord are thought not
to show pain when examined an hour or more after the immediate
incident. This history, especially combined with other specific typical
signs (see below) can be so characteristic of vascular lesions that it is
almost pathognomonic. Over the course of several subsequent days
(if the animal is not presented until a few days later) there is often
gradual regression of neurologic signs.

FIGURE 251.5 Porcupine quill foreign body. A,
Axial T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging at
level of C7 intervertebral space revealing porcupine
quill entering vertebral canal through the left
intervertebral foramen (arrows) to impinge on the
spinal cord. B, Ultrasonographic image of
subcutaneous porcupine quill (arrowheads) in the
same dog, revealing the hollow center.
Rarely, animals present with a more slowly-developing vascular
lesion of the spinal cord, in which there is bleeding into the
parenchyma. The reason for bleeding is often not fully established,
although it has been associated with (congenital) vascular
malformations and arteritis. Many animals that present with these
lesions do not undergo biopsy or necropsy and so the masses are not
definitively diagnosed as hemorrhage, although the MRI appearance
is highly suggestive.

PRESENTATION
Acute ischemic myelopathy frequently has a highly stereotypical
presentation. The underlying causes can be obstruction of the
vasculature (thrombosis or embolism) or, more unusually an
assumed rupture of a (probably abnormal) blood vessel, but these
vessels are usually small and often lateralized. Therefore, the
presentation typically is of peracute onset of neurologic signs, which
are often highly lateralized. Often there is a striking mismatch
between the severity of motor and sensory deficits that is not
observed in more common causes of acute transverse myelopathy
(such as acute disc herniation). However, alternative presentations
do occur. For instance, animals in which the ventral spinal artery is
compromised show evidence of severe bilateral disease.
The typical progression after the immediate presentation is of
gradual recovery of lost function. The rapidity of recovery depends a
great deal on the precise localization and severity of the lesion.
Animals with lesions that do not affect the LMNs (C5-T2 and L4-S3
spinal cord segments) typically recover rapidly if the lesion is
insufficiently severe to cause loss of “deep pain sensation.”

Occasional animals present with extremely severe vascular lesions
and these are often those that undergo necropsy, demonstrating very
severe or widespread embolism. Animals in which the LMN regions
are affected are especially at risk of prolonged recovery or failure to
recover.
Patients with mass lesions associated with blood accumulation
within the parenchyma (hematomyelia) may present acutely or
chronically and, even when acute, the time of onset is typically over
days rather than hours.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Typical signs of vascular lesions are highly suggestive of the etiology.
Nevertheless, intervertebral disc herniation (ch. 250) and traumatic
spinal cord injury (see above) should be considered as alternative
diagnoses.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
For embolic lesions, the lack of apparent spinal pain, plus the
stereotypical lateralization, often strongly suggests their vascular
origin. Such a suspicion implies the need for MRI (ch. 112) because
it is the only modality that can reveal disease within the spinal cord
parenchyma and other imaging modalities cannot rule out this
diagnosis. Only if there is some real doubt about other diagnoses is it
worth obtaining other types of images. Similarly, MRI is essential for
diagnosis of intraparenchymal hemorrhagic lesions.

SPECIFIC DISEASES
Fibrocartilaginous Embolism
Pathogenesis
This classic lesion has been described well in veterinary literature for
many decades and can be observed in all species, including humans.
The inciting lesion is occlusion of the spinal cord arterial supply by
chondroid material that obliterates the vessel lumen. This then

causes the equivalent of a “stroke” in the spinal cord, in which the
dependent region of the spinal cord undergoes infarction and the
devitalized tissue immediately becomes non-functional and later
necrotic.46 In the hours following the initial lesion, edema may
develop within the surrounding spinal cord parenchyma, leading to
mild worsening of clinical signs.
The most controversial aspect of this lesion is the source of the
chondroid material. Many publications have aimed to explain how
the material can be derived from the intervertebral disc (nucleus)
and then end up in the arterial supply.47 It is fair to say that many of
these theories are rather far-fetched but, nonetheless, there are no
satisfactory explanations for the eventual location of the material.
One alternative explanation is that the blood vessel walls undergo
chondroid metaplasia and the material ends up detaching to
embolize a site further downstream.

Diagnosis
Fibrocartilaginous embolization is suspected in animals that express
typical clinical signs and have a lesion that is consistent with FCE on
MR images. Classic FCE lesions are small, often localized to one
quadrant of the spinal cord and are hyperintense to normal grey
matter on T2-weighted scans and iso- or hypointense on T1-weighted
scans.48 However, many lesions identified in dogs that are suspected
or proven45 to have FCE do not show this characteristic appearance.
Instead, they display large regions of hyperintensity on T2-weighted
and short tau inversion recovery MRI scans (Figure 251.6). A
definitive diagnosis relies on post mortem examination, but many
animals recover spontaneously and the diagnosis is not definitely
confirmed in most clinical cases. This means the precise nature of
the lesion in many cases remains speculative. For this reason, the
term “ischemic myelopathy” is sometimes used to more accurately
reflect the lack of precise knowledge of etiology.e.g.,50
Before the advent of widespread access to MRI, FCE was suspected
in a greater proportion of cases. Many similar cases are now shown
to result from various types of peracute intervertebral disc
herniations. Because of the nature of FCE, the signs can be quite
variable. Some, perhaps most, suspected cases have mild to

moderately severe, lateralized signs (Video 251.3

) that show

considerable improvement within a period of 48 hours or so. Other
cases can have devastating functional deficits from which
spontaneous improvement cannot occur. Since the only lesions that
are definitively diagnosed are those (unusual) cases that are found at
post mortem examination, confirmed cases may provide biased view
of the nature of the disease. No risk factors are known to exist for
FCE. It may be prudent to evaluate affected animals for hypo- and
hypercoagulable states (ch. 170), because hematomyelia and spinal
cord thrombosis, respectively, can produce clinical signs and MRI
findings that are virtually indistinguishable from those of FCE.

FIGURE 251.6 Magnetic resonance images
illustrating features of suspected fibrocartilaginous
embolization. A, Midsagittal T2-weighted image

illustrating mild parenchymal hyperintensity within
the caudal lumbar vertebrae (arrowheads). Note the

hyperintensity of the gray matter. C, Dorsal short tau

arrows).

Treatment and Prognosis
No specific treatment exists to address the disease process in FCE.
Supportive care can include physical rehabilitation (helping dogs to
walk with assistance, underwater treadmill, but not range of motion
exercises due to possible adverse effects in patients with spinal cord
disease; ch. 256) in severely affected animals, and general nursing
care as needed, such as management of incontinence. Patients with
ischemic myelopathy associated with hypercoagulability (not FCE)
should receive treatment for the inciting disorder.
The prognosis depends on the severity and location of the lesion.
On the whole, animals with FCE lesions in the T3-L3 or C1-C5
regions of the spinal cord have a good outlook as long as deep pain
sensation is intact. Loss of deep pain sensation or large lesions
affecting the spinal cord intumescences (i.e., C6-T2 or L4-S3) carry a
more guarded outlook because there is less scope for plastic
responses to ameliorate the functional deficits if those grey matter
regions have been destroyed. Lesions that affect the sacral spinal
cord can be particularly troublesome because persistent fecal and/or
urinary incontinence are common and difficult-to-manage long-term
sequelae. Similar to the prognosis for traumatic lesions, a period of
up to 3 months or more must be allowed to appreciate the full extent
of recovery.

Blood Vessel Rupture/Hematomyelia

A small number of cases have been documented in which an
apparently spontaneous hematoma develops within the substance of
the spinal cord.51 Many of these cases have been young animals and
the assumption has been that the hematoma developed because of
rupture of an anomalous vessel. Indeed, anomalous vessels have
been described within the spinal cord in some cases, supporting this
assumption. Risk factors for this condition are not known; it has
been presumed to occur more frequently during periods of raised
systemic BP but this certainly has not been documented in any
published case and no known traumatic episodes are associated with
onset. Although it would be expected that these lesions would occur
acutely, there is evidence that bleeding accumulates over a period of
several weeks. The severity of clinical signs varies considerably, but
the definitively diagnosed cases have tended to be quite severe,
although this might reflect the implicit need for diagnosis in such
cases. Recently, the underlying disease has been suspected to be
arteritis in some cases, specifically that associated with steroidresponsive meningitis-arteritis (SRMA; ch. 250).52,53
Diagnosis of this intraparenchymal lesion relies on MRI (ch. 112).
Blood accumulations in the spinal cord undergo a series of changes
in imaging characteristics over time, which can aid in identifying
how long the blood has been in place. However, these changes are
somewhat unreliable, and vary considerably depending upon the
field strength of the magnet and various other factors (e.g., precise
timing of image acquisitions54).
Small hematomas within the spinal cord are suspected fairly
frequently, but when they are associated with relatively mild clinical
signs that have arisen acutely, affected animals are often treated
conservatively. As a result, a definitive diagnosis is not achieved.
Such cases often recover uneventfully. Severely affected cases that
have large intraparenchymal masses might be considered candidates
for surgical intervention, which aims to drain the hematoma via
incision through the pia and superficial parts of the spinal cord
parenchyma.51 Anomalous blood vessels can be identified and
biopsied if present. The prognosis for surgical treatment depends
mainly on the severity of the clinical signs. On the other hand, the
prognosis following conservative treatment of dogs that have even

very large intraparenchymal hematomas can be surprisingly good
(Figure 251.7; Video 251.2

), drawing into question whether

surgery is justified unless the diagnosis is uncertain.

Extradural Hematoma
Extradural hematomas are commonly found in association with
acute disc herniations and occasionally with disorders of hemostasis.
Rarely, dogs are presented with acute or chronic progressive
neurologic signs, often associated with pain, for which the
underlying cause appears to be idiopathic hematoma.55 Surgical
decompression is associated with good to excellent prognosis. It is
important to recognize that such lesions exist because the imaging
appearance is also consistent with extradural neoplasia, which has a
far worse prognosis.

Macroscopic Vascular Anomalies
Macroscopic vascular anomalies56 are often incriminated in the
development of intraparenchymal hemorrhage but, in addition, they
can sometimes form mass lesions which can be detected on MRI
scans57 and might be candidates for surgical removal.

Systemic Disease Associated With Bleeding and
Thrombosis into the Spinal Cord
Bleeding into the spinal cord parenchyma may also arise from
systemic disease that causes hypocoagulable states (ch. 171). Most
obviously these conditions are disorders of blood clotting such as
hemophilia,58 although this is a rare cause of spinal lesions in dogs.
Other clotting disorders that can be associated with spinal
dysfunction include von Willebrand disease59 and, rarely, immunemediated thrombocytopenia (ch. 175).60
Vascular fragility associated with inflammation (vasculitis) can
also be a cause of hemorrhage into or around the spinal cord (ch.
181). Recognized causes in dogs include Angiostrongylus vasorum
infection (ch. 217),61,62 leishmaniasis (ch. 197),63 and SRMA (ch.
242).52,53 Conversely, vasculitis can also lead to spinal cord lesions
by causing thrombosis rather than hemorrhage.64

NEOPLASTIC LESIONS
SIGNALMENT
Some neoplastic lesions of the spinal cord or vertebral column have
clear breed associations. For instance, large dogs are more
susceptible to osteosarcoma (ch. 326),65 which is a common spinal
tumor.66 Golden Retrievers in the USA are thought to be at risk of
hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325),65 which is another common spinal
neoplasm. Older age (for this purpose, starting at ∼4 years old for
giant dogs) is a recognized risk factor for neoplasia in general, but it
is noteworthy that younger dogs (often ∼12 months old) can present

with an intramedullary spinal tumor, nephroblastoma67; therefore,
young age should not be used as a rule-out for neoplastic disease.
Some studies,68 but not others,67 report that nephroblastoma is
more common in German Shepherd Dogs. Lymphoma (ch. 322) is a
reasonably common spinal lesion in dogs, and in adult cats it is a
leading cause of spinal lesions.69 Metastatic lesions to the spinal
cord occur occasionally,70 and perhaps more commonly from
intracranial choroid plexus tumors,71 so it is worth considering that
possibility during the clinical examination, especially in cachectic
animals.

HISTORY
Neoplastic disease would be expected to have an insidious onset of
clinical signs, associated with the gradual enlargement of the lesion.
That is indeed a common pattern, but some animals with spinal
tumors exhibit an acute onset of clinical signs. This can arise through
two main mechanisms: 1) pathologic fracture, in which a
progressively weakened bone finally fractures and causes immediate
spinal cord injury; and 2) acute vascular injury associated with
tumor embolization or with compression and thrombosis associated
with prolonged or excessive pressure. Thus, it is important to
consider the possibility of a tumor in any older dog that has evidence
of spinal cord dysfunction, even if the onset is acute.

PRESENTATION
Most animals bearing spinal neoplasms present with a slow onset of
progressive neurologic deficits and evidence of spinal pain. However,
the cluster of clinical signs varies depending on the nature of the
tumor. Extradural neoplasia is typically painful, probably because it
distorts the spinal cord meninges or nerves, or because of damage to
skeletal elements. Lesions inside the dura have not traditionally been
thought to be associated with signs of pain until the later stages, but

some more recent data on intramedullary lesions suggest this may
not be accurate.70
The rapidity of growth is probably different for lesions located at
different spinal cord sites too, although the progression of signs can
be misleading because lesions may become very large before they are
associated with clinical signs (Figure 251.8). On the whole, clinical
signs associated with intradural lesions progress slowly, and some
animals may have clinical signs for many months or even years prior
to presentation.72 Animals that have clinical signs associated with
extradural lesions typically show rapid (days to weeks) progression.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Chronic progressive spinal cord dysfunction is most often associated
with neoplasia or chronic disc herniations (usually type II; ch. 250).
However, the differential diagnosis includes inflammatory or
infectious diseases such as discospondylitis (ch. 250) and MUO (ch.
242).73 In older animals, degenerative diseases are often a
consideration, most notably degenerative myelopathy, especially in
Corgis and German Shepherd Dogs74 (ch. 250). Congenital,75 posttraumatic or adhesion-associated syringomyelia (accumulation of
fluid within the spinal cord parenchyma; ch. 244) can produce
similar clinical signs in some cases, especially in small dogs.39 In
addition, there are many non-neoplastic masses or anomalies that
can be associated with gradually progressive spinal cord lesions and
neurologic deficits, such as dermoid sinus,e.g.,76 calcinosis
circumscripta,77 hematoma (see above), cartilaginous exostosis,e.g.,78
lipoma,79 bony proliferation associated with inborn errors of
metabolism80 and poorly-classified disorders such as
meningioangiomatosis.81 This wide differential diagnosis list,
including many benign lesions, implies the need for precise diagnosis
to avoid assumptions of a poor prognosis.
For animals that present with acute spinal cord dysfunction, the
main differential diagnosis is acute disc herniation (even in large
breed dogs) and the traumatic and vascular lesions discussed above.

Many, but not all, patients with acute spinal cord injury associated
with neoplastic lesions express signs of pain.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
As for most conditions of the CNS, after a lesion has been localized
the usual next diagnostic step is to image the affected area (ch. 112).
Frequently it is helpful to commence with radiographs, because a
reasonable proportion of affected animals will have lesions of the
skeletal elements that can be identified using this modality (Figure
251.1). However, only a proportion of spinal neoplasms will cause
sufficient bone loss or bone proliferation to be recognizable on plain
radiographs—lesions within the dura usually do not change bone
opacity and not even all epidural neoplasia is associated with bone
changes. Therefore, radiographs are a good “rule-in” but poor “ruleout” test; the next step is usually to use MRI (Figure 251.8),
because this modality detects lesions wherever they are—even those
within the spinal cord parenchyma. CT is limited to detection of
radiopaque lesions or those that cause changes in bone opacity,
which can be extremely useful for specific lesion types (Figure
251.9).

SPECIFIC DISEASES
Neoplastic disease of the spinal cord is best categorized according to
the location of the lesion in relation to the meninges surrounding the
cord. Thus the clinical (and pathologic) divisions are extradural,
intradural/extramedullary and intramedullary. Of these, the most
common are thought to be extradural66,72,82 with
intradural/extramedullary types probably being the next most
common.

C, Nerve sheath tumor (intradural-extramedullary to

(∗) was diagnosed in a dog that was ambulatory at
the time of presentation. E, Cervical meningioma
illustrating the typical “golf tee” appearance created
by the surrounding cerebrospinal fluid (arrows).

Extradural Tumors
These lesions lie within the epidural space, which is normally
occupied by fat. In line with their site of origin, neoplasms arising
here usually are tumors of bone or various types of soft tissue
sarcoma, such as osteosarcoma (ch. 326), hemangiosarcoma (ch.
325), fibrosarcoma (ch. 326), lymphoma (ch. 322), liposarcoma,

and multiple myeloma (ch. 322). Rare benign tumors in this
location include lipomas.79 Most are malignant and they often cause
secondary bone damage, leading to bone weakening and, commonly,
pathological fractures. In addition, many of these lesions are already
distributed throughout the body at the time of diagnosis; common
examples are hemangiosarcoma and osteosarcoma; more rarely mast
cell tumors can also be detected in the vertebrae or epidural space.83
Indeed, it is not uncommon to observe metastatic lesions at other
sites in the skeleton or within the lungs at the time of primary
diagnosis (Figure 251.9). Importantly, many dogs with extradural
spinal neoplasia appear to experience considerable pain, which can
aid in suspecting these types of lesions versus other tumor types
described below.

Intradural/Extramedullary Tumors
These are lesions of tissue that lines or projects through the
subarachnoid space, such as the meninges and nerve roots. Both
meningiomas (ch. 245) and nerve sheath tumors (and various
related sub-categories) tend to be slow-growing masses that may
produce clinical signs over a period of months to years.72 Nerve
sheath tumors (ch. 252) appear to be more common at spinal cord
intumescences, although this may also reflect the greater likelihood
of diagnosis at those sites because they are associated with lameness.
Meningiomas can occur at any site but appear to be particularly
common at the C1-C2 space in dogs,84 especially perhaps in Boxers.
Although both nerve sheath tumors and meningiomas are generally
regarded as relatively benign histologically, they both have a
tendency to invade locally into normal tissue and so can be difficult
to excise in their entirety. Some nerve sheath tumors appear to be
associated with neuropathic pain syndromes, including generalized
depression and behavioural change (ch. 6).72

Intramedullary Tumors
This lesion category is not commonly diagnosed.70 These tumors
arise from elements of the neuropil itself, such as glial cells (of
various types) and (rarely) the neurons themselves. Common tumor
types in this category include astrocytoma and ependymoma. They
can vary considerably in their histologic behaviour: some are wellcircumscribed by a capsule and can be excised, whereas others are
highly invasive and aggressive. Typically they have a slowly
progressive course over several months.
Nephroblastoma is an example of a neoplasm found in this
compartment, although it may also cross into the
extramedullary/intradural space. This tumor appears to develop
close to the thoracolumbar junction of juvenile dogs as a
consequence of an error during embryogenesis, in which a small
number of kidney progenitor cells are incorporated into the
developing neural tube and later become neoplastic.68 This type of
tumor often has a benign histologic phenotype but can be locally
invasive.

DIAGNOSIS OF SPINAL TUMOR TYPE
Bearing in mind the extreme variability in tumor behavior and,
therefore, prognosis, it is highly desirable to make a specific
diagnosis without traditional open surgery. Analysis of CSF (ch.
109) occasionally helps if cells exfoliate into the fluid,85 or if there is
evidence of an alternative diagnosis such as an infectious process.86
Blood and/or bone marrow aspirate analysis (ch. 84) may be helpful
in some cases, such as those with suspected multiple myeloma;13

similarly, it may be useful to obtain aspirates from enlarged lymph
nodes (ch. 88) to identify cases of multifocal lymphoma or lung
aspirates from lesions suspected to be metastases. If a mass lesion
has been identified on images, it may be possible to obtain biopsy
samples from within87 or outside88 the spinal cord parenchyma
without resorting to open surgery. Ultrasound, fluoroscopic or CTguided biopsies can be obtained using needles, core (e.g., TruCut)
biopsy tools, or Jamshidi needles, although iatrogenic trauma is an
important potential hazard. For lesions within the spinal cord, it may
be possible to place a needle into the spinal cord and obtain biopsy
through judicious aspiration.87 Such biopsies may be useful to rule
out other differential diagnoses such as fungal granulomas or benign
mass lesions.
Despite this multitude of potential methods, it can be difficult to
diagnose tumors percutaneously if they do not exfoliate easily and
most spinal tumors are suspected based on imaging findings but not
confirmed except at surgery or post mortem examination.
Investigation of diagnostic reliability suggests a great deal of
variability between readers in correctly identifying the compartment
in which intradural masses reside, implying that recommendations
for treatment may vary widely. Unfortunately, in general, extradural
masses are often assumed to be neoplastic and affected animals may
be inappropriately euthanized without undergoing further diagnostic
tests (to rule out hematoma, for instance).

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Neoplastic disease affecting the spinal cord has a very wide range of
treatments and prognoses, depending on the nature of the lesion. For
instance, meningiomas can often be surgically excised, although they
frequently regrow over a period of months to years following
incomplete excision. Nerve sheath tumors can theoretically be
excised in their entirety but, because they often are close to the

spinal cord and require large margins for total excision, this is rarely
achieved when they lie within the vertebral canal. Nevertheless, a
long-term (>12 month) disease-free interval can be achieved by
surgical resection alone. Some other neoplastic lesions have a
hopeless prognosis, such as hemangiosarcoma that is already
accompanied by metastases elsewhere in the body. Others have an
intermediate prognosis – and may occasionally be helpfully managed
by chemotherapy (e.g., multiple myeloma13). Although radiationinduced myelitis is a potentially devastating sequela to radiotherapy
directed at the spinal cord, careful planning89 can produce gratifying
outcomes.90 Radiotherapy is most notably an option for adjuvant
therapy for cases in which there is recurrence of a previously excised
tumor, or in which there has been incomplete primary
extirpation.58,91
In general the prognosis for most epidural tumors is poor, mainly
because they are often malignant and may be associated with
metastasis at the time of diagnosis. Surgical debulking can provide
rapid and effective relief of compression, which is often associated
with rapid recovery of much lost function. Unfortunately, the results,
especially for sarcomas, are often short-lived, with recurrence of
clinical signs within a few weeks to months.
Intradural/extramedullary tumors are amenable to surgical
excision and this is the major treatment modality. The outcome can
be quite gratifying for meningiomas, because they are frequently
slow growing and clinical signs can be alleviated for 12 months or
more. In contrast, nerve sheath tumors have a worse prognosis
because of the difficulty in removing the tumor in its entirety.
Intramedullary tumors often are of benign types and may even be
encapsulated, meaning that they can potentially be excised (Figure
251.10). This entails incising the spinal cord parenchyma and using
microdissection techniques, but the results can be quite
gratifying,68,75 (Video 251.4

) although recurrence of clinical

signs has been reported in some of the (very small number of) cases
reported in the veterinary literature.

ANATOMY AND CLINICAL EVALUATION
OF PERIPHERAL NERVE DISORDERS
The peripheral nervous system (PNS) includes all nerve structures
outside the central nervous system (CNS; i.e., the brain and spinal

cord). The PNS is comprised of motor nerve fibers innervating
skeletal muscle; sensory nerve fibers carrying touch, pain, and
proprioceptive position information from the skin, joints and
muscles; afferent fibers carrying special sense information (e.g.,
auditory and vestibular systems); and autonomic fibers innervating
the thoracic and abdominal viscera and other structures (e.g.,
salivary glands, irises, baroreceptors). The autonomic nervous
system is further divided into the sympathetic and parasympathetic
systems. Peripheral nerve fibers arise from the ventral horn of the
spinal cord, exiting via the ventral root (motor and sympathetic
fibers); from the dorsal root ganglion adjacent to the spinal cord,
entering the cord via the dorsal root (sensory fibers); and from the
brainstem or adjacent ganglia (motor and parasympathetic fibers),
entering or exiting in cranial nerves. Although some nerves carry
purely motor or sensory information, most nerves are comprised of a
combination of motor and sensory fibers. A neuropathy refers to
peripheral nerve disease (either spinal or cranial nerves [ch. 249])
while polyneuropathies affect multiple peripheral nerves, often in a
diffuse manner.

CLINICAL SIGNS
Most recognized peripheral nerve disorders in veterinary medicine
have a clinical presentation dominated by dysfunction of the motor
nerves, although sensory and autonomic signs are seen with some
conditions. Characteristic clinical signs include paresis, hypotonia,
muscle atrophy, and depressed or absent segmental spinal reflexes (
Video 252.1). The paresis may involve all limbs or may manifest
as paraparesis, and it often results in a short-strided gait. Dysphonia,
dysphagia (ch. 47), inspiratory stridor, laryngeal paresis (ch. 214),
megaesophagus (ch. 259), and reduced or absent gag and palpebral
reflexes may be seen due to involvement of the recurrent laryngeal,
glossopharyngeal, vagus and facial nerves (ch. 241). Disorders of the
neuromuscular junction (ch. 253) and muscle can result in many of
the same signs, and can be difficult to distinguish from peripheral
nerve disease based on clinical examination alone. Signs of sensory
dysfunction include ataxia, loss of proprioceptive positioning,

reduced or absent spinal reflexes and paresthesia or anesthesia,
potentially resulting in self-mutilation. Autonomic dysfunction may
result in vomiting or regurgitation, diarrhea, ileus, urinary retention,
incontinence, impaired lacrimation and salivation, and pupillary
dysfunction (ch. 254). These disorders may exhibit acute and
progressive—or occasionally episodic—signs, but more often display
a chronic, progressive course.

DIAGNOSTIC PLAN
A complete blood count, serum biochemical evaluation and
urinalysis are indicated to identify metabolic disorders responsible
for nerve dysfunction (e.g., diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism),
comorbid disease, and to assess the suitability of patients for general
anesthesia. Additional metabolic testing, including thyroid
evaluation (ch. 285) and serum fructosamine (chs. 291 and 292),
may also be considered. Serum creatine kinase (ch. 66), carnitine,
and pre- and post-exercise pyruvate, lactate, and blood gas
evaluation may be useful to identify certain muscle disorders.
Imaging of the thoracic and abdominal cavities is often indicated to
identify neoplastic disease. Serum titers or polymerase chain
reaction (PCR)–based testing for infectious disease (ch. 184), such
as toxoplasmosis or neosporosis (ch. 197), may also be appropriate.
More advanced diagnostic imaging (magnetic resonance imaging
[MRI] or computed tomography [CT]; ch. 112) is occasionally useful
to demonstrate neoplastic, inflammatory or other disease processes
affecting specific nerves or nerve roots, or for diseases also
displaying CNS lesions. However, these modalities typically play a
larger role in ruling out other disorders than they do ruling in a
neuropathy. Similarly, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) evaluation (ch.
109) is most useful to eliminate other disease processes, but is
occasionally abnormal in peripheral nerve disorders involving the
nerve roots or those with both CNS and PNS involvement.
The most useful diagnostic tests for peripheral nerve disorders are
electrodiagnostics (ch. 111) and histopathologic examination of
muscle and nerve biopsies (ch. 110). Electrodiagnostic testing
includes electromyography (EMG, Video 111.1

), motor and

sensory nerve conduction velocities (MNCV, SNCV; Video 111.2

),

F wave evaluation, cord dorsum potentials, H reflex evaluation,
magnetic stimulation, and brainstem auditory evoked response
(BAER).1 Together, EMG and MNCV are useful to confirm
dysfunction of the neuromuscular system, to differentiate peripheral
nerve disease from muscle disease, and to distinguish axonal disease
from demyelination. F wave evaluation allows investigation of the
proximal nerve and ventral nerve roots, while SNCV and cord
dorsum testing evaluates sensory nerves and dorsal nerve roots.
However, electrodiagnostic testing rarely allows the diagnosis of a
specific etiology. Histopathologic examinations of muscle and nerve
biopsies are helpful to confirm and further define abnormalities
detected with electrodiagnostic testing and are more likely to identify
a specific etiology.2 Specific tests for autonomic dysfunction may also
be useful to identify animals with involvement of this part of the
nervous system (ch. 254).

DEGENERATIVE NEUROPATHIES
There are several degenerative neuropathic disorders that are limited
to specific breeds of dogs and cats and thus, that appear to be
heritable in nature. These disorders are quite rare, and for a detailed
discussion, the reader is referred to more comprehensive reviews of
this topic.3,4

METABOLIC NEUROPATHIES
DIABETIC NEUROPATHY
Diabetic neuropathy is one of the most common causes of peripheral
nerve dysfunction in human patients, but appears to occur with less
frequency in veterinary medicine. Clinical signs are primarily noted
in cats (ch. 292) while overt disease is rarely recognized in dogs (ch.
291). The pathophysiologic mechanism of diabetic neuropathy has
been intensely studied, with a number of causative theories
proposed.5-7 Clinical signs include paraparesis, progressing in some

cases to tetraparesis; pelvic limb ataxia (

Video 292.2); difficulty

in jumping; reduced postural reactions and segmental spinal
reflexes; and distal muscle atrophy.6-8 A plantigrade stance is
frequently seen in cats (
Videos 14.2, 292.3). Although poorly
recognized, sensory nerve dysfunction resulting in paresthesias and
hyperesthesia likely occurs with some frequency in this disorder.7,8
Cranial nerve and autonomic signs are common in humans, but are
rarely reported in animals.7 However, subclinical nerve dysfunction
appears to occur with some frequency.9
The diagnosis is strongly suspected with demonstration of
hyperglycemia and glucosuria in an animal with consistent clinical
signs. Serum fructosamine may also be of some utility, as neuropathy
is more common in poorly regulated patients. Electrodiagnostic
testing may reveal spontaneous activity within affected muscles,
although these changes may be subtle and patchy.5,6,9 However,
consistent abnormalities are detectable in MNCV, SNCV, F wave and
cord dorsum evaluation (ch. 111), even when EMG abnormalities are
subtle or absent.8,9 These findings suggest that demyelination
predominates over axonal changes, which is supported by
histopathologic evaluation of muscle and nerve biopsies.8 Therapy is
primarily directed at control of the underlying diabetic disorder, and
improved glycemic control typically results in improvement or
resolution of signs.6 There are few reports of additional therapy in
veterinary medicine.10

HYPOTHYROID NEUROPATHY
Clinical signs of neuromuscular dysfunction frequently have been
associated with hypothyroidism in both canine and human patients
(ch. 285).6,11 The underlying mechanism of this association remains
poorly characterized but involves both peripheral nerve and muscle.
Thyroid hormone deficiency appears to lead to both axonal damage

and demyelination, based on electrophysiological studies.11 In
human patients, mononeuropathies (particularly carpal tunnel
syndrome) are common, and are attributed to mucinous deposits in
the soft-tissue structures, causing a compressive neuropathy.12 It has
been suggested that a similar process may be responsible for the
compression of cranial nerves in veterinary patients.6
Animals may present with paresis or rarely lameness involving a
single limb, two limbs or all four limbs.13,14 Cranial nerve deficits
(ch. 241), including facial paresis, vestibular signs and trigeminal
nerve dysfunction have been reported, are often unilateral, and may
affect multiple nerves (ch. 249).6,15 These signs may occur
secondary to a peripheral neuropathy, or in other cases may be
related to CNS involvement.16 An association has also been made
between hypothyroidism and both megaesophagus (ch. 259) and
laryngeal paralysis (ch. 214),14 although causal roles are tenuous
and remain to be proven.15 Affected animals may or may not have
classical clinical signs such as lethargy, weight gain, alopecia, and
seborrhea. A complete blood count and serum biochemistry profile
may show a mild nonregenerative anemia, hypercholesterolemia,
and/or an elevated creatine kinase level. The diagnosis is confirmed
by the demonstration of a reduced free and total serum thyroxine
(T4) level with an elevated thyroid stimulating hormone level (ch.
285). Analysis of CSF may show albuminocytologic dissociation (ch.
109). Electrophysiological testing shows spontaneous activity on
EMG, with reductions in MNCV and SNCV (ch. 111).13,14 BAERs
may also be abnormal.14 Muscle biopsy (ch. 110) shows type I and II
fiber atrophy consistent with neuropathic change, or a selective type
II fiber atrophy suggestive of a myopathy. Nerve biopsy may show
mixed changes characteristic of both axonal degeneration and
demyelination.4,5,14 In many cases, the diagnosis is partly based on
the administration of levothyroxine and demonstration of a clinical
response, which often begins within several days and is complete by
3-8 weeks.15 Cranial nerve deficits, megaesophagus, and laryngeal
paralysis are less likely to improve.6,14,15

PERIPHERAL NERVE TUMORS
Peripheral nerve dysfunction due to neoplasia may result from
compression of nerve tissue due to a nerve or nerve sheath tumor,
from adjacent neoplastic tissue, or may occur as a paraneoplastic
process (ch. 331).10,17-19 Nerve sheath tumors frequently display
malignant characteristics, based on histopathologic features and
their tendency to be locally invasive, growing proximally up nerves
and nerve roots.4,17,20 These tumors may occur in any small animal
patient (

Video 252.2), although they are most common in large-

breed dogs and are rare in cats.18,20 They commonly arise from the
brachial plexus. Lameness and muscle atrophy are the most common
and often the only clinical signs for extended periods of time before
additional signs such as paresis, postural reaction deficits, or
depressed reflexes occur.17,18,20,21 These tumors often eventually
invade the spinal cord, leading to ataxia, paresis, and postural
reaction deficits caudal to the site of invasion. Signs of pain may be
elicited with manipulation of the limb or with palpation of the axilla
or inguinal region.17 Horner’s syndrome (ch. 249) may be present
with involvement of the caudal brachial plexus.17,21 Trigeminal nerve
sheath tumors are the most common cranial nerve neoplasms and
typically lead to unilateral masticatory muscle atrophy (ch. 249).22
Tumors involving other cranial nerves are seen much less frequently.
Establishing a diagnosis of peripheral nerve sheath tumors can be
challenging. Occasionally, a mass may be palpated in the axilla or via
the rectum; MRI or CT may allow visualization of the tumor in many
cases (ch. 112).19,22-24 Ultrasonography can also be useful, and can
facilitate fine-needle aspiration or biopsy of identifiable mass
lesions.19,25 An EMG examination may be helpful in demonstrating
denervation potentials (ch. 111), supporting a neuropathic process
in lame patients without an obvious orthopedic cause.17 Definitive
therapy for peripheral nerve sheath tumors consists of surgical
removal of the neoplasm, which can be very difficult. Although
tumors involving distal portions of peripheral nerves may be

completely resectable, most tumors involve the brachial or lumbar
plexus and associated nerve roots.26 Surgical intervention for these
tumors typically requires amputation of the affected limb, and
definitive removal may require laminectomy with sectioning of the
nerve roots as close to the spinal cord as possible. Despite such
aggressive therapy, many tumors recur, as they have a tendency to
grow proximally and invade multiple nerve roots.17 Surgical removal
of trigeminal nerve sheath tumors has been reported.22 Other
neoplasms may compress or infiltrate peripheral nerves,19 including
lymphoma (ch. 322), which may involve single or, in many cases,
multiple nerves or nerve roots, leading to focal or multifocal signs.10

PARANEOPLASTIC NEUROPATHY
A polyneuropathy associated with cancer in a remote location has
been described in a number of dogs and a cat (ch. 331).10 This
syndrome has been reported most frequently with insulinoma (ch.
289),10,27,28 although various other tumors also have been
implicated.5,10,29 The mechanism of disease is suspected to be
primarily immune-mediated, wherein the immune system generates
a response to antigens present within the neoplasm that are shared
with the peripheral nerves.30 In patients with insulinoma,
hypoglycemia has also been suggested to have a causative role.
Sensory, motor, and autonomic neuropathies have been described in
humans, but motor signs have predominated in veterinary reports.
Although infrequently reported, electrophysiological or histological
evidence of peripheral nerve dysfunction is present in a large
proportion of animals with cancer,31,32 and this condition is likely an
underrecognized cause of weakness in these patients. The diagnosis
consists of documenting appropriate clinical signs (e.g., paresis,
hyporeflexia, muscle atrophy), electrophysiologic changes, and
muscle and nerve biopsy results in an animal with an identified
neoplasm, while eliminating other potential etiologies.
Dramatic improvement or resolution of clinical signs has been
documented after surgical excision or other therapy for the

cancer.28,29,33 As the underlying mechanism is likely immunemediated, immunomodulatory therapy has been utilized in human
patients, including corticosteroids, plasma exchange, intravenous
immunoglobulin, and other immunosuppressive drugs. Such therapy
may be ineffective in resolving the neurologic signs if neuronal
destruction has already occurred, although stabilization of signs may
be seen.30 Immunomodulatory therapy has been infrequently
reported in veterinary patients, although dramatic improvement
after corticosteroid therapy has been documented in a dog with
insulinoma.28

INFECTIOUS AND INFLAMMATORY
NEUROPATHIES
PROTOZOAL POLYRADICULONEURITIS
Both Toxoplasma gondii and Neospora caninum display a
predilection for nervous tissue, and can invade peripheral nerves,
muscle and the CNS (ch. 197). Neosporosis emerged as an
important cause of neuromuscular disease in dogs in the 1990s and
many cases of protozoal neuritis previously attributed to T. gondii
were likely caused by N. caninum.34 Clinical signs include paresis
involving one or multiple limbs, muscle atrophy, reduced muscle
tone, evidence of muscle pain, postural reaction deficits, and reduced
or absent segmental spinal reflexes.35,36 Cranial nerve signs such as
head tilt, dysphagia, and tongue paresis have occasionally been
reported.35 A classical presentation of N. caninum infection is
paraparesis in young puppies, which progressively leads to a nonambulatory state characterized by rigid extension of the pelvic limbs
associated with muscle contractures.37 These dogs are infected
transplacentally, and 25% or more of puppies from such litters may
show clinical signs.34,36 Ingestion of raw meat is a risk factor for
both T. gondii and N. caninum infection.34,36
Serological tests are available for T. gondii and N. caninum but
must be interpreted with care, as exposed animals may seroconvert

in the absence of clinical disease.38 Paired acute and convalescent
titers and evaluation of IgM levels (for T. gondii) may help in
distinguishing infected from merely exposed animals.36 However,
serum titers for N. caninum rarely exceed 1:800 in clinically
unaffected dogs.35,38 PCR tests have also been developed for these
organisms. Electromyograms (ch. 111) typically show spontaneous
activity in affected limb muscles. Analysis of CSF (ch. 109) may
show a mixed cell or nonsuppurative pleocytosis with protein
elevation if the CNS is involved.34 Muscle and nerve biopsies (ch.
110) often show evidence of inflammatory cell infiltrates and may
show protozoal organisms in some cases.39
Clindamycin remains the treatment of choice for T. gondii
infection in both dogs and cats, although other drugs, including
sulfonamides, pyrimethamine, doxycycline, and minocycline have
some efficacy (ch. 197).36 For N. caninum, therapy with
clindamycin or potentiated sulfonamide drugs, with or without
pyrimethamine, is often effective and can result in complete
resolution of signs.35,40 However, the disease progresses in some
patients despite such therapy, and significant improvement is very
unlikely if muscle contractures have occurred.

ACUTE POLYRADICULONEURITIS
Acute polyradiculoneuritis can be seen in both dogs and cats and
causes an acute, ascending, flaccid tetraparesis (

Video 252.3).

Clinical signs typically progress rapidly over 48-72 hours, although
progression may continue for up to 10 days.6,41-43 Although the
pelvic limbs are usually involved first, with subsequent involvement
of the thoracic limbs, the latter may be primarily or exclusively
involved in rare cases. Severe cases progress to involve the cranial
nerves and respiratory musculature, leading to hypoventilation.
Segmental spinal reflexes are reduced to absent (ch. 241), but
sensation remains intact, and many animals appear hyperesthetic.
This disorder was first recognized in dogs approximately 7-10 days

after contact with a raccoon and is colloquially known as coonhound
paralysis. However, identical signs are seen in animals without
raccoon exposure, and although other precipitating causes such as
vaccination or infection may be identified, in many cases the trigger
is unknown.42,43 Serological, electrophysiological and
histopathological evidence strongly suggests that this is an immunemediated disease with similarities to Guillain-Barré syndrome in
humans, resulting from shared antigens between the inciting
stimulus and peripheral nervous tissue.6,41,42,44,45

Diagnosis
The diagnosis is suspected based on characteristic clinical signs,
disease course, and potential history of an inciting cause. The main
differential diagnoses are tick paralysis, botulism, and elapid
envenomation, which are all diseases of the neuromuscular junction
(ch. 253). Electrophysiologic testing can be helpful in distinguishing
acute polyradiculoneuritis from these other diseases, showing early
onset spontaneous activity, and abnormalities on motor nerve
conduction studies and F wave evaluation (ch. 111).1,6,44 Analysis of
CSF collected from the lumbar cistern (ch. 109) may reveal
albuminocytologic dissociation.6

Treatment
Therapy is mainly supportive in nature, and most animals will
recover if given sufficient time (

Video 252.4).42,43 However,

recovery time is variable, and may take a few weeks or up to 6
months in rare cases.6,46 Patients with respiratory muscle
involvement may require mechanical ventilation.47 Despite the
immune-mediated nature of the disease, corticosteroid therapy has
not been shown to be beneficial; it worsens muscle atrophy and may
predispose patients to secondary infections.41 One study suggested
that administration of human intravenous immunoglobulin might
shorten the recovery time in dogs with acute polyradiculoneuritis,48

although this and other immunomodulatory therapies such as
plasmapheresis require further study in veterinary patients.

BRACHIAL PLEXUS NEURITIS
Brachial plexus neuritis is a rare condition, with only a few case
reports in the veterinary literature.26,49,50 Clinical signs include
lameness, paresis, muscle atrophy, depressed segmental spinal
reflexes, and sensory impairment exclusively affecting the thoracic
limbs, typically with a bilateral but asymmetric distribution.
Spontaneous activity is noted on EMG, while nerve conduction may
be normal or slightly prolonged (ch. 111). Analysis of CSF may also
be normal or may show a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and protein
elevation (ch. 109).49 Diagnostic imaging, particularly MRI, may
show thickened nerves and nerve roots suggestive of this condition,
although it may be difficult to differentiate neuritis from neoplastic
infiltration of the nerves (ch. 112).4,26,49 A response to
glucocorticoids has been noted in some cases,49,50 and spontaneous
remissions, although often protracted, have been described.4,46 The
cause of this syndrome is uncertain, but an immune-mediated
mechanism is likely.

CHRONIC INFLAMMATORY
DEMYELINATING POLYNEUROPATHY
Chronic inflammatory neuropathies characterized by demyelination
have been described in both dogs and cats using a number of terms,
including chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
(CIDP), chronic relapsing neuropathy, acquired demyelinating
neuropathy, and chronic demyelinating polyradiculoneuritis.6,51,52
Parallels have been drawn to the human disease, also termed
CIDP.52 The etiology is unknown, but is suspected to be immunemediated based on histopathologic features and a positive response
to corticosteroid administration.4,6,46,51 Clinical signs usually

develop insidiously and are slowly progressive, typically initially
involving the pelvic limbs followed by the thoracic limbs.52
Monoparesis is a less frequent initial manifestation. Some patients
display a relapsing-remitting course.52 Affected animals show
various degrees of paresis, exercise intolerance, muscle wasting,
reduced segmental spinal reflexes, and occasionally muscle tremors
(ch. 42; Video 42.16

), lameness, ventroflexion of the neck, facial

paralysis (ch. 249), dysphonia, megaesophagus (ch. 259), or
laryngeal paralysis (ch. 214) (

Video 252.5).4,52 EMG may be

normal or may show patchy spontaneous activity, but MNCV is
consistently decreased, often with evidence of conduction block (ch.
111).6,52 Demyelination is the predominant pathologic finding on
examination of nerve biopsies, with axonal degeneration seen less
frequently.4,46 Inflammatory cell infiltrates have a patchy
distribution and may not be appreciated in biopsy samples. Skeletal
muscle biopsies may show fiber size variation, consistent with
denervation.51 Many animals respond to corticosteroid
administration at immunosuppressive dosages, although this
response is incomplete in some animals.6,46,52 Additional
immunosuppressive regimens involving intravenous
immunoglobulin, plasma exchange, azathioprine, cyclophosphamide,
and other immunomodulatory drugs have been recommended for
humans but have not been well studied in veterinary patients.

SENSORY
POLYGANGLIORADICULONEURITIS
An inflammatory neuropathy preferentially affecting the sensory
nerves, nerve roots, and dorsal root ganglia has been described in
dogs of various breeds and ages.4,41,53 The cause of the condition is
unknown. Clinical signs consist of ataxia, reduced to absent
proprioception and segmental spinal reflexes (particularly the
patellar reflex), and hypalgesia of the face, trunk or limbs (ch.

241).41 Dysphagia, regurgitation, megaesophagus, anisocoria, and
self-mutilation have been reported in some cases.41,53 Acute and
chronic clinical courses have been noted, and the condition is
typically progressive. Limb muscle mass, tone and strength are
preserved, although masticatory muscle atrophy has been reported
in some cases, attributed to damage to motor fibers as they pass
through the trigeminal ganglion.4 EMG and MNCV are typically
normal, although SNCV is abnormal and may not be recordable (ch.
111).53 CSF analysis (ch. 109) is usually normal.53 Histological
changes characterized by axonal degeneration may be noted with a
nerve biopsy, although care should be taken to biopsy a sensory or
mixed function nerve.2 As the disease is inflammatory and suspected
to be immune-mediated, immunosuppressive therapy with
corticosteroids and other drugs has been attempted, but has not been
successful in reports published to date.46,53 A similar condition has
been described in a young cat.10

PERIPHERAL NERVE TRAUMA
Trauma to peripheral nerves can occur secondary to a variety of
insults, including blunt trauma, laceration, stretching or tearing
injuries, compression from fractures or swollen compartmentalized
tissue, or iatrogenic injury (e.g., injection site injury or surgical
trauma). The most common injuries are those involving the brachial
plexus secondary to a motor vehicle accident (

Video 252.6),50,54

the sciatic nerve secondary to trauma or iatrogenic injury,10,54,55 and
the caudal nerves secondary to traction injury of the tail.54,56
Femoral nerve dysfunction can also occur secondary to trauma
involving the iliopsoas muscle in dogs.10
The main clinical signs are varying degrees of paresis and disuse of
the limb or tail, impaired postural reactions and reflex function, pain
with ambulation or limb manipulation and possibly impaired
sensation (ch. 241).54 The diagnosis is usually obvious based on

history and examination. However, assessment of the severity of the
injury may be aided with EMG to document denervation or nerve
conduction studies to document the presence or absence of
conduction past the injured site (ch. 111).10,21,54 Ultrasonography,
CT or MRI may be useful in documenting nerve or muscle trauma
associated with the injury (ch. 112).10 Therapy typically centers on
supportive care and rehabilitation including passive range of motion,
massage and other physiotherapy exercises to help to maintain
muscle and joint integrity while awaiting recovery (ch. 256).
Removal of compressive bone fragments or implants is indicated, if
present. Some animals may traumatize limbs due to dragging during
ambulation or by self-mutilation, and covering the limb with a
bandage or bootie may help to avoid this complication. Other
potentially useful interventions include analgesics and medications
to modulate paresthesias (e.g., gabapentin, pregabalin) and orthotics
or braces for limb support.10 Recovery is dependent on the integrity
of the endoneurial structures as well as the distance required to reinnervate the target, as axonal regeneration occurs at a rate of ∼1-2
mm per day.54 A loss of sensation in the limb or tail distal to the
injury usually indicates a poor prognosis, although ideally 4-6 weeks
should be allowed for potential recovery. Ultimately amputation of
the limb or tail is often necessary.

TOXIC NEUROPATHIES
Several toxins, pharmaceuticals and other agents have been reported
to cause peripheral neuropathies in small animals (ch. 133),
although these are infrequently seen and documented. Such
substances include heavy metals (e.g., mercury, thallium, lead),
antibiotics (e.g., lasalocid, nitrofurantoin, salinomycin), pesticides
(e.g., organophosphates), organic solvents and chemicals (e.g.,
acrylamide, hexacarbons), vitamins (e.g., pyridoxine), and
antineoplastic drugs (e.g., vincristine, vinblastine, cisplatin).6,10,54

MISCELLANEOUS IDIOPATHIC
NEUROPATHIES
Distal denervating disease is an idiopathic canine polyneuropathy
with primarily axonal involvement that affects motor nerves in a
distal distribution and usually spontaneously improves in 4-6
weeks.10,46 Other axonopathies with a similar distal distribution, but
with chronic, unremitting courses, have also been described and
termed distal symmetrical polyneuropathy or chronic axonal
degeneration.6,10,46 Idiopathic neuropathies affecting the trigeminal,
facial, and vestibular nerves are frequently recognized.46,57-59
Whereas dysfunction of the trigeminal and vestibular nerves is
typically self-limiting with spontaneous improvement, facial nerve
paralysis often fails to improve, and requires long-term
management.57

GERIATRIC-ONSET LARYNGEAL PARALYSIS AND
POLYNEUROPATHY
Idiopathic laryngeal paralysis occurring in older dogs is likely one
manifestation of a more generalized peripheral neuropathy and has
been variously termed laryngeal paralysis-polyneuropathy complex,
late-onset laryngeal paralysis or geriatric-onset laryngeal paralysis
and polyneuropathy (GOLPP).5,60 Medium- to large-breed dogs are
most frequently identified, and Labrador Retrievers are particularly
overrepresented (ch. 214).5,10,60 Diagnosis is made by identifying
inspiratory stridor and other signs of laryngeal dysfunction in
conjunction with a laryngeal examination. Electrodiagnostic testing
and histopathologic evaluation of muscle or nerve biopsies (ch. 110)
corroborates a more generalized polyneuropathy.10,60 Treatment is
supportive and specifically involves arytenoid lateralization, which
improves breathing and quality of life but together with esophageal
dysfunction, predisposes affected dogs to aspiration.10

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
A review of neurophysiology as it relates to the development of
neurologic disease is presented earlier in this section of the textbook
(ch. 240). Disorders affecting the neuromuscular junction (NMJ)
can be classified as presynaptic or postsynaptic in nature. They
generally result from inability to release acetylcholine (ACh) from the
presynaptic terminal into the synaptic cleft, or from inability of the
postsynaptic muscle membrane to respond to ACh (Figure 253.1).

CLINICAL SIGNS
The NMJ is one of several components of the motor unit, and
patients with disease of the NMJ present with clinical signs
suggestive of diffuse lower motor neuron (LMN) disease (ch. 241).
Signs are typically symmetrical in nature, and may include acute
tetraparesis or tetraplegia, chronic static or progressive tetraparesis,
or episodic weakness that is exacerbated by activity. Signs are often
accompanied by decreased muscle tone (flaccid paresis;

Video

241.2). Patients may be unable to hold their head up due to weakness
of the cervical musculature. Sensory function and level of
consciousness are typically normal.

PRESYNAPTIC DISEASES OF THE
NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION
TICK PARALYSIS
Tick paralysis is most commonly associated with exposure to ticks of
Dermacentor sp. or Ixodes sp.1-3 Clinical signs result from a
neurotoxin produced in the salivary glands of female ticks that is
released into an animal’s circulation after the tick attaches and feeds
for several days. The proposed mechanism is interference with ACh
release from the presynaptic nerve terminal via a calcium-mediated
mechanism.4 Clinical signs are present when an engorged tick is
attached, and resolve when the offending tick is removed.

Bloodwork, diagnostic imaging, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
evaluation are typically normal. The diagnosis is usually presumptive
based on identification and removal of an engorged tick.

FIGURE 253.1 Schematic representation of the
neuromuscular junction. ACh,
Acetylcholine. Reproduced with permission from
The Ohio State University.
In North America, the genus of ticks that is most often associated
with tick paralysis is Dermacentor.4 Dogs are commonly affected,
while cats are relatively resistant. Clinical signs begin 5-9 days after
tick attachment and consist of an acute, rapidly progressive,
ascending flaccid paresis that can progress to tetraplegia over the

course of 12-72 hours.5 Segmental spinal reflexes are severely
diminished in all four limbs, and muscle tone is decreased.1 Cranial
nerve deficits are uncommon in American tick paralysis, but mild
facial and masticatory muscle weakness and dysphonia have been
reported.1 Autonomic, sensory, and sphincter abnormalities do not
occur. In severe cases, respiratory paralysis may necessitate
mechanical ventilation and death due to hypoventilation can occur.
Tick removal (Video 187.1

) yields rapid improvement in signs,

usually within hours.
In Australia, a more severe form of tick paralysis is caused by
Ixodes sp. ticks.2 Cats as well as dogs may be affected.3 Australian
tick paralysis also presents with an acute, rapidly progressive
ascending flaccid paresis. Other clinical signs such as autonomic
dysfunction (ch. 254), micturition disorders (ch. 310), and
congestive heart failure (ch. 229) due to diastolic dysfunction can
occur. Pupillary dilation is common in cats and often observed in
advanced canine cases. Affected animals may develop pulmonary
edema, aspiration pneumonia, and progressive hypoventilation.
Unilateral cranial nerve deficits and Horner’s syndrome have also
been reported.6 Unlike American tick paralysis, the clinical condition
of animals with Australian tick paralysis may continue to decline for
several days after tick removal.2,7
Tick removal (Video 187.1)

in conjunction with supportive

care is the primary treatment for both American and Australian tick
paralysis. A careful search for ticks should be performed. This may
include clipping the hair and examining the ear canals, perineum,
mouth, nasal cavities, and interdigital spaces. If a tick cannot be
found, topical acaricides may be applied (ch. 142, and textbook’s
inside covers). In Australian tick paralysis, phenoxybenzamine and
acepromazine are used for treating autonomic signs.1,2
Glucocorticoids are not routinely used for treatment, and antibiotic
therapy is not helpful.

BOTULISM
Botulism is an acute diffuse LMN disease caused by neurotoxins
produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum. Most animals
develop botulism by ingesting pre-formed botulinum neurotoxin in
spoiled or uncooked meat. Rarely, botulinum toxin may be produced
inside the body after infection with C. botulinum. This latter scenario
is referred to as toxico-infection. While 8 types of botulinum toxin
have been identified, botulinum neurotoxin type-C (BoNT-C) is most
commonly associated with disease in dogs.8-11 Naturally occurring
botulism is extremely rare in cats, but has been reported.12
Botulinum toxin blocks release of ACh at the presynaptic terminal
of skeletal muscle and cholinergic autonomic synapses by
irreversible enzymatic cleavage of soluble N-ethylmaleimidesensitive factor activating protein receptor (SNARE) proteins.
SNARE proteins are essential for docking of ACh vesicles to the
presynaptic membrane to allow release into the synaptic cleft.5,13
Impaired ACh release results in an acute onset of progressive
tetraparesis (Videos 190.2, 190.3)

accompanied by autonomic

signs such as ileus, tachy- or bradycardia, mydriasis, and urinary
retention (ch. 254). Cranial nerve deficits such as a decreased
palpebral reflex (chs. 241, 249), megaesophagus (ch. 259), and
diminished pupillary light reflexes (chs. 241, 249) are also common.
Severity and progression of clinical signs vary with the quantity of
toxin ingested, with signs occurring from hours to days after
ingestion of contaminated food.5,14
In reality, a clinical diagnosis of botulism is often presumptive
based on history and clinical examination but demonstration of
BoNT in the blood, feces, stomach contents, or food source provides
a definitive diagnosis.14 Routine bloodwork will not show
abnormalities. Electrodiagnostic testing may demonstrate
incremental increases in compound muscle action potentials (CMAP)
with stimulation at high rates10 (ch. 111).
Treatment for botulism is primarily supportive. Antibiotics are not
generally indicated but may have utility for suspected toxicoinfection or for treatment of secondary aspiration (ch. 217).

Aminoglycosides and ampicillin potentiate neuromuscular blockade
and should be avoided. Although the administration of antitoxin has
been recommended, most available products do not contain
antibodies against BoNT-C and therefore are not useful for dogs.
Antitoxin cannot bind toxin after it has entered nerve terminals, but
it can bind circulating toxin to help halt progression of disease.15 If
given, a test injection should be performed, as these products are of
equine origin, and anaphylactic reactions are possible.15 Recovery
from botulism occurs spontaneously over 1-4 weeks (Video 190.4
), and the prognosis for most animals is excellent if they can be
adequately supported.5

ELAPID SNAKE ENVENOMATION
Elapid snakes include the eastern (Micrurus fulvius) and Texas
(Micrurus tener) coral snakes in North America, the tiger (Notechis
scutatus), brown (Pseudonaja spp.) and red-bellied black snakes
(Pseudechis porphyriacus) in Australia, as well as a variety of snakes
from other continents, including cobras, kraits, and mambas.16-20
Elapid snakes have short, rigid, immovable fangs, and therefore may
not produce an obvious bite. Depending on the snake, the venom
causes either a postsynaptic nondepolarizing neuromuscular
blockade by tightly binding to the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) on
the postsynaptic membrane, or a presynaptic inhibition of ACh
release.21-23
Clinical signs occur rapidly (within hours) after envenomation and
include flaccid tetraparesis or tetraplegia, hypotonia, reduced
segmental spinal reflexes, and hypoventilation.20,22 Pelvic limb
ataxia may also be a prominent clinical sign in some cases. Cranial
nerve signs such as ptyalism, dysphagia, dysphonia, and facial
paresis or paralysis are frequently observed.16,21 Urine discoloration
due to hemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria (ch. 70) is seen in a
substantial proportion of dogs and less frequently in cats.24 This is
helpful in diagnosis, as it is not a feature of other diffuse LMN

diseases.22,24 Other clinical signs may include vomiting, depression,
hypotension, hypothermia, bleeding disorders, and ventricular
arrhythmias.17,22,24,25 A complete blood count (CBC) may reveal
anemia with spherocytosis and erythrocyte “burring.”26 The
diagnosis of elapid snake envenomation is typically presumptive
based on clinical signs and history.
Treatment is mainly supportive. Placing a pressure bandage at the
site of envenomation can reduce lymphatic circulation of venom.22
Fluid diuresis should be considered if pigmenturia is present.
Administration of snake-specific antivenin may be beneficial in
preventing or reducing the severity of clinical signs. Tiger snake and
Mexican coral snake antivenins are cross-protective against North
American coral snake venom.16,27,28 Most animals will recover in 1-2
weeks with adequate supportive care.24,26,29

POSTSYNAPTIC DISEASES OF THE
NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION
TERMINOLOGY AND MYASTHENIA GRAVIS
Historically, veterinary texts have discussed acquired and congenital
forms of myasthenia gravis (MG). However, the term congenital MG
has been recently discarded in favor of congenital myasthenic
syndrome (CMS), where MG is now reserved for conditions of
autoimmunity against the NMJ.30 This shift closely follows the
human classification of these diseases, where MG is also used only in
the context of autoimmunity.

MYASTHENIA GRAVIS
Pathophysiology
MG is an yacquired autoimmune disorder characterized by
autoantibodies produced against nicotinic AChR on the postsynaptic
muscle terminal.30-32 These autoantibodies lead to destruction of

the AChR, reduced numbers of functional receptors, and diminished
ability of the muscle to respond to ACh, resulting in skeletal muscle
weakness that is often exacerbated by activity. There is a bimodal age
distribution for MG and dogs are usually affected at <4 years of age
or >9 years of age.34 Overrepresented dog breeds include the Akita,
German Shorthaired Pointer, Chihuahua, German Shepherd Dog,
and Golden Retriever.32,35 Familial predispositions for MG have
been identified in the Newfoundland and Great Dane breeds.36,37 In
cats, Abyssinian and Somali breeds are overrepresented.38,39

Forms of Myasthenia Gravis
Generalized, focal and severe fulminant forms of the disease exist.40
The generalized form, characterized by diffuse appendicular muscle
weakness, is most common. Patients with generalized MG often have
a normal neurologic examination at rest. During a bout of activityinduced weakness, they will demonstrate a choppy, stilted gait that is
first noted in the pelvic limbs. If encouraged to continue activity,
thoracic limb involvement becomes apparent. Some animals
demonstrate a fatigable palpebral reflex, although this is not a
reliable finding. Segmental spinal reflexes are typically normal. Signs
of pharyngeal or laryngeal dysfunction such as ptyalism (due to
difficulty swallowing, ch. 46), and dysphonia are variably present.
Megaesophagus is present in 84% of dogs with generalized MG and
in 40% of cats with the condition.32,38 Ventroflexion of the neck due
to cervical muscle weakness occurs in both species but is more
common in cats.41

Clinical Presentation
Animals with fulminant MG present with a rapid onset of severe
diffuse weakness that does not improve with rest. These patients
progress quickly to nonambulatory tetraparesis and lateral
recumbency.5 Spinal reflexes (ch. 241) may be diminished.5
Frequent regurgitation associated with megaesophagus (ch. 259) is
typical, and the development of aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217) is
common. Additional signs may include respiratory muscle weakness,

and urinary retention (ch. 310). The presence of thymoma has been
associated with the development of this severe form of the disease in
both dogs and cats.30,32,38,42
Focal MG presents as weakness of an isolated muscle group or
groups, most commonly the ocular, facial, esophageal, pharyngeal, or
laryngeal muscles. Generalized appendicular weakness is not
observed. Presenting complaints are referable to the muscle groups
involved and often include regurgitation, dysphagia, dysphonia, or
strabismus.30,32,40
Several comorbid conditions have been associated with the
development of MG in veterinary patients, including thymoma or
other neoplastic processes (ch. 331), hypothyroidism (chs. 285 and
286), hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296), polymyositis, and
masticatory myositis (ch. 258).32 The prevalence of concurrent
thymoma is 3.4% in dogs and as high as 52% in cats.32,39 In
hyperthyroid cats (ch. 287), an association between MG and
initiation of methimazole treatment has also been reported in a small
cohort of animals, where the condition resolved once the medication
was discontinued.38

Diagnosis
A CBC may be normal in animals with MG, or may show evidence of
inflammation when concurrent aspiration pneumonia is present. A
serum biochemistry profile is helpful to exclude metabolic causes of
neuromuscular weakness. Thoracic radiography or computed
tomography is useful to evaluate for thymoma or other neoplasms,
and to screen for aspiration pneumonia. Abdominal ultrasound can
assist in ruling out paraneoplastic causes.
The gold standard for diagnosis of generalized MG in dogs and
cats is demonstration of anti-AChR autoantibodies in serum:
measurement of species-specific anti-AChR autoantibodies will
detect approximately 98% of canine cases.43 Positive antibody titers
are also reported in a smaller percentage of dogs with focal MG.
Antibody levels are highly variable between patients and do not
correlate with clinical severity; however, within patients, a decrease
in antibodies correlates with improvement in clinical signs and can

be followed to assess remission of disease. Antibody titers may be
falsely negative early in disease or if corticosteroids are administered
prior to measurement.30 Retesting in 1-2 months is suggested when
either scenario is suspected.30 A small number of patients may have
true seronegative MG reflective of autoantibodies directed against
other NMJ proteins. In these cases, response to anticholinesterase
therapy and electrodiagnostic repetitive nerve stimulation testing
(ch. 111) can support a diagnosis.30
Administration of the short-acting anticholinesterase drug
edrophonium has been used historically as a diagnostic tool to assess
improvements in muscle strength, gait, or the ability to swallow.34
This drug is no longer available in some countries and neostigmine
may be used in its place. Either drug inhibits acetylcholinesterase
(AChE), allowing ACh accumulation in the NMJ, thereby improving
neuromuscular transmission. Animals with MG will often show
improvement shortly after receiving these drugs. The effect lasts for
several minutes (edrophonium) to several hours (neostigmine),
followed by a return of signs. Improvement is not completely specific
to MG, as some animals with other causes of neuromuscular
weakness can show improvement and not all animals with MG will
improve.5,40 Precipitation of a cholinergic crisis is possible by
overstimulation of AChR, leading to signs such as worsened
weakness, salivation, tremors, vomiting, bradycardia,
bronchoconstriction, and respiratory distress. In the author’s
experience, these signs are more common with neostigmine than
edrophonium.5 Animals should be monitored closely after
administration of either drug, and atropine and equipment to
provide intubation and respiratory support should be available.

Treatment and Outcome
Long-term treatment for animals with MG consists of treatment via
AChE inhibitors, as well as immunosuppressive therapy to reduce
autoantibody production against the AChR. Anticholinesterase drugs
such as pyridostigmine bromide (oral) or neostigmine
(intramuscular) are the mainstays of supportive therapy and they
work by inhibiting AChE so that ACh remains within the synaptic

cleft longer.5 These medications must be carefully titrated to effect,
and neostigmine is generally used only in hospitalized animals in
acute crisis or with profound regurgitation. Both medications have a
narrow therapeutic window, and significant side-effects such as
bradycardia, hypersalivation, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle cramping,
and weakness can occur. Clinical signs associated with excessive
anticholinergic drug administration may be difficult to distinguish
from those of uncontrolled MG and careful monitoring is required at
the time of therapy initiation.
Immunosuppressive agents such as cyclosporine, mycophenolate
mofetil (MMF), and azathioprine (chs. 144 and 169) are frequently
used in the treatment of MG to reduce levels of circulating
autoantibodies.44,45 Extrapolating from the human literature, MMF
was once considered the drug of choice for canine MG; however, a
recent study comparing dogs treated with MMF and pyridostigmine
to those treated with pyridostigmine alone showed no difference in
survival time or remission rate between groups.45
Corticosteroids can also be effective in the treatment of MG, but
should be used with caution in animals with aspiration pneumonia
(ch. 227).5 Corticosteroids may potentiate muscle weakness and
exacerbate clinical signs in some patients, and a gradual increase in
corticosteroid dose is recommended to help avoid this complication.
Other strategies for immunomodulation may also be employed in
patients with MG, including therapeutic plasma exchange and
intravenous administration of immune globulin (IVIG).46,47 Neither
technique has been thoroughly evaluated for MG in a controlled
veterinary study, although their utility is supported by small case
series and efficacy in other immune-mediated diseases. A long-term
spontaneous remission rate as high as 88% has been reported for
dogs with MG; spontaneous remission is not a characteristic of feline
MG.32,39

CONGENITAL MYASTHENIC
SYNDROME

CMS has been reported in a number of pure and mixed-breed dogs,
and cats.30 A deficiency of the AChR is assumed in most breeds and
has been documented in Jack Russell Terriers, Springer Spaniels,
and Miniature Dachshunds.30,48,49 Abnormalities in ACh synthesis
or in AChE function have also been reported. CMS often affects
multiple animals in the same litter and clinical signs are usually
apparent beginning around 6-9 weeks of age. Generalized limb and
cervical muscle weakness that worsen with activity are common.
Megaesophagus is variably present. An autosomal recessive-mode of
inheritance has been demonstrated in Smooth Fox Terriers, Jack
Russell Terriers, and Gammel Dansk Honsehund (GDH) dogs.50,51
Measurement of AChR autoantibodies is not useful in diagnosis of
CMS. A definitive diagnosis is made in some cases by quantification
of AChR in a muscle biopsy. Treatment with pyridostigmine often
results in improvement; however, long-term response to
anticholinesterase therapy is variable and many reports describe
death or euthanasia of affected animals due to difficulty in
controlling clinical signs. Exceptions to this are CMS in Miniature
Dachshunds, where signs spontaneously resolved by 6 months of
age, and GDHs, which tend to remain stable with mild clinical
signs.48,51

OTHER
Although not a disease of the NMJ, exercise-induced collapse (EIC)
of Labrador Retrievers causes fatigue and flaccid para- or
tetraparesis during or after strenuous activity. Examination findings
are normal at rest. Ataxia, pelvic limb weakness, and collapse
develop in association with intense or prolonged field training,
hunting, or vigorous play (Video 253.1

). Clinical signs may

progress to involve the thoracic limbs. Recovery occurs with rest, and
most dogs are clinically normal within 30 minutes; however, severe
episodes can result in death.52-54
The condition is heritable in Labradors, associated with an
autosomal recessively inherited mutation (Arg256Leu) in the gene

encoding for the protein dynamin 1 (DNM1). DNM1 is expressed at
synaptic terminal membranes within the CNS and is important in the
recycling of synaptic vesicles during high frequency neurological
stimulation.52,55 A collapse phenotype is also recognized in
Labradors and other breeds in the absence of homozygosity for the
DNM-1 mutation.55
Dogs with DNM1-associated EIC (d-EIC) typically experience their
first episode of collapse before 2 years of age.54 Loss of the patellar
reflex is common during an episode, and dogs maintain normal
mental status.54,56 Hyperthermia and elevated plasma lactate often
develop during an episode, but are not distinct from what is observed
in normal exercising dogs.56 Serum lactate/pyruvate ratios are
normal in dogs with EIC both at rest and during exercise, and muscle
biopsies are unremarkable.56 A genetic test for the Arg256Leu
DNM1 mutation is now commercially available to assist in diagnosis.
While there is no cure for EIC, affected dogs have an excellent
prognosis if they refrain from intense physical activity known to
trigger episodes.56
