ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY
Diseases of the autonomic nervous system (ANS) can be focal (Horner’s syndrome, ch. 249) or systemic
(dysautonomia). They manifest as disordered function of organs and physiologic responses that are not
under voluntary control. Although considered part of the peripheral nervous system with both motor
and sensory components, the ANS has distinct anatomic differences from the somatic (voluntary
control) nervous system.1,2 Whereas the upper motor neuron in the somatic nervous system never leaves
the central nervous system, the axon of the preganglionic nerve of the ANS exits the central nervous
system to synapse with the postganglionic nerve in ganglia that are either close to (parasympathetic) or
distant from (sympathetic) the target organ.1,2
The preganglionic fibers of the sympathetic nervous system exit the central nervous system through
ventral roots from the first thoracic to the second lumbar spinal nerves. Preganglionic sympathetic
neurons release acetylcholine to activate postganglionic neurons, which, in turn release norepinephrine
to activate the effector organ. Peripheral vasoconstriction, mydriasis, tachycardia, increased inotropy,
and suppression of gastrointestinal motility are all consequences of increased sympathetic activity.1,2
Preganglionic fibers of the parasympathetic nervous system exit the central nervous system with
cranial nerves (CNs) III, VII, IX, and X and through the ventral roots from the second and third sacral
spinal nerves. The vagus nerve (CN X) carries the bulk of the parasympathetic fibers (∼75%), supplying
parasympathetic input to thoracic and abdominal viscera. There are four distinct, paired
parasympathetic ganglia (ciliary, pterygopalatine, mandibular, and otic) found in the head, whereas all
other parasympathetic ganglia are found in the wall of the effector organ. All remaining distinct ganglia
found throughout the body are sympathetic. Both preganglionic and postganglionic parasympathetic
neurons release acetylcholine as a neurotransmitter. An increase in parasympathetic tone can result in
bradycardia, miosis, decreased cardiac inotropy, salivation, and activation of gastrointestinal motility
and the digestive process.1,2
The enteric nervous system is also considered a component of the ANS, and although the sympathetic
and parasympathetic nervous systems regulate activity of, and receive sensory information from, the
gastrointestinal tract, the enteric nervous system can function independently. The enteric nervous
system is composed of the myenteric plexus, which is located between the circular and longitudinal
smooth muscle layers, which controls peristalsis, and the submucosal plexus, which controls fluid and
electrolyte exchange across the intestinal wall. Both plexuses are heavily ganglionated with multidirectional, coordinated transmission involving an array of neurotransmitters.2

In addition to the classic motor and sensory neuropathy (ch. 252), some polyneuropathies have been
demonstrated to have lesions of autonomic ganglia or nerves, although sometimes limited just to the
myenteric plexus. Clinical signs referable to autonomic dysfunction are infrequently reported, however,
as they are overshadowed by the motor and sensory deficits.3,4 Sporadic case reports of autonomic
ganglionitis and ganglioneuritis, with or without involvement of spinal ganglia, have been reported in
dogs and cats. These have included 2 young Siberian Huskies, only 1 of which presented for clinical signs
of autonomic dysfunction (regurgitation and vomiting); a Labrador Retriever with megacolon; and a
Persian cat with chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction.5-7 Recurrent gastric dilatation was the sole
clinical sign in a Great Dane found to have severe loss of myelinated fibers in the vagus nerve without
evidence of inflammation and skeletal muscle changes consistent with a polyneuropathy.8 Sporadic
cases of focal (e.g., pupil) or territorial (e.g., head) autonomic dysfunction can be found throughout the
literature with varied etiologies and pathological findings.9,10 Widespread autonomic failure in the
routine absence of motor and sensory dysfunction is a unique disease and is termed dysautonomia.

DYSAUTONOMIA
Dysautonomia is an idiopathic neurodegenerative disorder of dogs, cats, horses, and rabbits and can
present with a peracute to subacute disease course.11-22 Chromatolytic degeneration of neurons in
autonomic ganglia with minimal to no inflammation is the hallmark histologic finding. Similar
degenerative changes have been described in the ventral horns of the spinal cord and various brainstem
nuclei in dogs and cats with dysautonomia.12,18 Although the etiology is unknown, a toxicoinfectious
etiology is suspected.23

CLINICAL FINDINGS
The clinical signs and physical examination findings of dysautonomia in dogs and cats can be
nonspecific, such as anorexia and lethargy, or more specific to autonomic dysfunction, such as dilated
and nonresponsive pupils, and poor anal tone.11-19 Gastrointestinal dysfunction can manifest with
vomiting, regurgitation, megaesophagus, generalized ileus, focal ileus with impaction at the distal ileum,
constipation or diarrhea, and poor anal tone with fecal incontinence. A unique characteristic of vomiting
in dogs with dysautonomia is that the vomitus comes out through the nose in addition to the mouth,
likely from failure of normal laryngeal/pharyngeal function. Vomiting, regurgitation, megaesophagus,
and laryngeal/pharyngeal dysfunction predispose the patient to aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217), a grave
prognostic finding. Weight loss is often rapid and substantial.
Dry mucous membranes of the eyes, nose, and oral cavity are common. Dry eyes can contribute to
photophobia and predispose to corneal ulceration. Nasal dryness frequently results in a dry crust that
accumulates within the nostrils and can disrupt or obstruct air flow, while fewer dogs will develop a
copious, thick mucoid discharge. Xerostomia (dry mouth) often results in an overestimation of
dehydration severity by the veterinarian. Urinary tract dysfunction most commonly manifests as dysuria
(ch. 310) with urinary retention and poor urinary sphincter/urethral tone, facilitating manual
expression, although a small percentage of dogs presents with urinary retention and increased urinary
sphincter/urethral tone that impedes manual expression. Additional ocular signs can include mydriasis
with poor or absent pupillary light reflexes (chs. 241, 249), also contributing to photophobia; and an
elevated nictitans.
In most dogs with dysautonomia, heart rates range from 90 to 120 beats per minute (bpm), whereas
cats more commonly range from 120 to 150 bpm; heart rates lower than these have been reported in
both.12,17,19 Transient tachycardia (∼180 bpm) is seen in some dogs. The heart rate rarely varies more
than 1-2 bpm from the established rate, even with forced exercise. This lack of heart rate variability is a
characteristic of dysautonomia. Weakness is reported and may be due to poor cardiac output from poor
ventricular function (left ventricular [LV] % fractional shortening can fall to the single digits; chs. 97,
233) without compensatory tachycardia (
diffuse lower motor neuron paralysis.

Video 254.1).24 In some dogs, weakness is a function of a

Dogs and cats may present with varying degrees of autonomic dysfunction. Clinical signs typically
develop and rapidly progress over the course of 48 hours in dogs and cats; however, they may progress
over a longer course of time (up to 2 weeks). Dogs with subacute disease frequently present with
vomiting as the first clinical sign, which is often mistaken for intestinal obstruction due to the
combination of vomiting and a radiographic pattern indicating intestinal ileus. Many affected dogs
demonstrate mydriasis, elevated nictitans, dysuria, and poor anal tone in the days following laparotomy
for suspected foreign body. Rare dogs will have no or transient gastrointestinal signs and develop
dysuria as the predominant clinical sign. This is often diagnosed as idiopathic detrusor-urethral
dyssynergia, but these dogs are often distinguished with diminished LV systolic function on
echocardiography.
The diagnostic algorithm and recommended diagnostic testing with expected results for
dysautonomia are shown in Figure 254.1 and Table 254.1, respectively. The intradermal histamine
test, bethanechol challenge, phenylephrine or epinephrine response testing, or orthostatic blood
pressure challenge are not recommended as these can be difficult to interpret, provide little additional
information, or may result in death. If the diagnosis is supported by pharmacologic testing and neither
megaesophagus nor aspiration pneumonia is present, then supportive therapy should be considered as
survival and recovery are possible. An echocardiogram is recommended for dogs with dysautonomia to
measure LV systolic function (fractional shortening), as this directs therapy. Ventricular systolic
dysfunction has not been demonstrated in the cat.

CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (CNS) DISEASES
CONGENITAL MALFORMATIONS
Cerebellar Hypoplasia
Cerebellar hypoplasia caused by perinatal infection with the feline panleukopenia virus (FPV; ch. 201)
is the most common diffuse cerebellar disorder in cats. Exposure to FPV during the last 3 weeks of
gestation or the first 3 weeks of life may induce destruction of the dividing external germinal layer in
fetuses and cause granuloprival cerebellar hypoplasia in kittens.1,2 Fetal infections before the last 3
weeks of gestation may result in hydranencephaly.3 Vaccination with a modified-live FPV vaccine during
pregnancy is contraindicated because it may result in clinically affected kittens. Clinical signs include
cerebellar ataxia, intention tremor, menace response deficits and nystagmus (Video 255.1

). The

clinical signs usually remain stable or even improve, as some compensation is possible. There are no
specific diagnostic tests. Advanced imaging, in particular magnetic resonance imaging (MRI; ch. 112),
may reveal cerebellar atrophy. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis is usually normal. There is no
treatment, but these cats may have a good quality of life. Prevention can be achieved by vaccination of
queens before pregnancy.

Congenital Pendular Resting Nystagmus
Congenital pendular resting nystagmus is an abnormal movement of the eyes seen in various breeds of
cats including Siamese, Birman (Video 255.2

), and Persian Tiger, where some disruption of the

visual pathways that control eye movement occurs; however, there is no obvious visual impairment in
affected cats.4 In some breeds, this congenital malformation has been associated with the ChediakHigashi syndrome which is characterized by oculocutaneous albinism (ch. 180).5

INBORN ERRORS OF METABOLISM
Few are reported uniquely in cats, and these typically also affect the peripheral nervous system (Table
255.1 and ch. 244).

PRION DISEASE
Feline spongiform encephalopathy (FSE) is a prion-induced disease affecting the Felidae family.6 Cats
are believed (not proven) to contract the disease by ingestion of bovine spongiform encephalopathy
(BSE)-contaminated food. The disease presents in adult cats and is characterised by chronic progressive
clinical signs (from weeks to months), including abnormal behavior, ataxia, muscle tremors,
hypersalivation, dilated and unresponsive pupils, and hyperesthesia. The diagnosis is based on
histopathologic evaluation of brain tissue. There is no treatment, and the disease is progressive and
fatal. FSE has become increasingly rare since the BSE epidemic has declined and feeding high-risk
bovine tissues to animals is being avoided. However, this disease has a long incubation period and cases
may still occur in zoo animals and housecats.7

INFLAMMATORY AND INFECTIOUS CNS DISEASES
Viral CNS Diseases
Feline Infectious Peritonitis
Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) is the most common infectious CNS disease in cats (ch. 200).8 Up to
38% of FIP cases show neurological signs, and all three forms (effusive [wet], non-effusive [dry], and
mixed) have been associated with CNS involvement; however, the non-effusive form predominates in
this anatomic location.9,10 FIP is usually seen in pedigree cats from multi-cat environments, typically <4
years of age.9,11 The most common neurologic signs include altered mental status, menace response
deficits, vestibular syndrome, seizures, ataxia, and paresis (ch. 241). Three distinct clinical syndromes
affecting cats with neurologic FIP have been identified: central vestibular syndrome, multifocal CNS
disease, and T3-L3 myelopathy (Video 255.3

).11,12 Neurological signs can present alone or in

conjunction with systemic signs.11-13 Ophthalmic signs (iritis, anterior uveitis and keratitis; ch. 13) have
been reported in up to 53% of cases with neurologic FIP.11,12 Seizures occur in up to 25% of cats with
neurologic FIP and have been associated with a poor prognosis.14 A presumptive diagnosis (ch. 200) is
based on the cat’s signalment, history, systemic clinical signs, physical examination, complete blood
count and serum biochemistry results, abdominal ultrasound and, where indicated, analysis of the
peritoneal effusion and ophthalmic examination (ch. 13). The diagnosis is more challenging when the
cat presents solely with CNS signs. Current antemortem diagnostic tests for neurologic FIP aim to
exclude other conditions that could cause a similar clinical presentation but cannot directly confirm FIP.
MRI findings can include obstructive hydrocephalus; ventricular dilation; and periventricular,
ependymal, and meningeal contrast enhancement, reflecting the superficial and ventricular nature of the
FIP lesions in the CNS (Figure 255.1) (ch. 112).11 However, up to 37% of cats with histologically
confirmed neurologic FIP can have normal MRI results.15 CSF analysis (ch. 109) can also contribute to
the diagnosis, but the risk of CSF collection must be weighed against the potential benefits, especially if
clinical signs and/or imaging findings are suggestive of increased intracranial pressure. Characteristic
CSF findings are a marked neutrophilic to pyogranulomatous pleocytosis (nucleated cell count >100
cells/L) and an increase in protein concentration to >200 mg/dL (>2 g/L).11 This high protein
concentration can increase the viscosity of CSF, impairing its flow during collection. CSF can also be

normal, show a mild mononuclear pleocytosis, or have a normal cell count with an elevated protein
concentration. Positive CSF titers can be a useful antemortem indicator of neurological disease, but this
must be interpreted with respect to the integrity of the blood-brain barrier (ch. 242). More recently,
reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction assays for feline coronavirus (FCoV) RNA and
immunostaining of FCoV antigen in CSF samples have proven useful in supporting a diagnosis of
neurologic FIP.16,17 A definitive diagnosis requires a combination of gross and histopathological
examination with the demonstration of viral antigen in postmortem CNS samples.

The aims of treatment (ch. 200) should focus on modifying the cat’s immune response and inhibiting
viral replication. The use of corticosteroids can provide some palliative treatment; however the disease
will continue to progress and some cats with neurologic FIP may only survive for days to months from
the time of diagnosis.11 Preventive measures are discussed in ch. 200. Two recent clinical trials
evaluating the safety and efficacy of antiviral compounds in the treatment of FIP have yielded promising
results, although cats with neurologic FIP were excluded from these studies.18,19 A more recent report
described a positive response to treatment with an antiviral compound in 4 cats with naturally occurring
neurologic FIP.20 However, the medications that were studied are not yet licensed. The current
prognosis for cats with neurologic FIP is unfortunately still inevitably fatal; however, new emerging
therapeutic approaches might improve this prognosis soon.

Feline Immunodeficiency Virus
Feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV; ch. 198) is a neurotropic retrovirus that causes acquired immune
deficiency syndrome, which can result in opportunistic CNS infections and neoplasms (lymphoma, ch.
322). Neurologic signs in naturally infected cats are very uncommon.21,22 The clinical signs (insidious
onset and progressive course) include abnormal behavior, facial twitching, ataxia, seizures, sleep
disorders and intention tremors.23 Slight elevations in nucleated cells (mononuclear pleocytosis) and
total proteins have been reported in CSF (ch. 109).24 In experimentally infected cats, MRI (ch. 112)
showed cortical atrophy and mild ventricular dilation, white matter changes and increased apparent
diffusion coefficients in the white matter, gray matter, and basal nuclei.25 Positive serologic titers and a
positive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test on serum and CSF can support the diagnosis. The
treatment is focussed on managing opportunistic CNS infections. The prognosis is poor, but some cats
live without any clinical signs for many years.

FIGURE 255.2 13-year-old Domestic Shorthair cat with anisocoria due to
internal ophthalmoplegia of the left eye (dilated pupil with absent direct
pupillary light reflex with normal vision). The cat was diagnosed with feline
leukemia virus infection and had large granular lymphoma affecting heart,
kidneys and the short ciliary nerves of the left eye.

Feline Leukemia Virus
Feline leukemia virus (FeLV; ch. 199) has been associated with a chronic degenerative myelopathy in
adult and geriatric cats.26 There is no breed nor sex predilection, and the onset of clinical signs is
insidious with a slowly progressive course. The neurological signs include abnormal behavior,
vocalization, hyperesthesia, and paraparesis progressing to paraplegia with urinary incontinence.26 MRI
(brain and spinal cord) and CSF analysis are normal. Positive serologic titers and a positive PCR test on
serum and CSF can support the diagnosis. This disease is uncommon, and therefore other concomitant
diseases should be considered for FeLV-infected cats with myelopathy. The prognosis is poor and the
treatment is supportive (Figure 255.2).

Feline Borna Disease Virus
Feline staggering disease refers to meningoencephalomyelitis caused by a negative-stranded RNA virus,
Borna disease virus (BDV). It has been reported mainly in Europe but occurs also in other parts of the
world, including Asia and Australia (ch. 9).27 The probable reservoirs are birds and rodents; therefore,
young adult outdoor cats from rural areas are at increased risk. The most common neurologic signs
include an unsteady “staggering” gait (ataxia) and postural reaction deficits followed by abnormal
behavior and absent or decreased menace response. MRI findings are usually unremarkable. CSF (ch.
109) can be abnormal in 50-60% of infected cats (mononuclear pleocytosis with increased total

protein). Positive viral RNA demonstrated by reverse transcription PCR in CSF can be considered
diagnostic.28 Serologic testing is of little value, as many seropositive cats are clinically normal. A final
diagnosis requires histopathologic evaluation of tissue. The disease is progressive, and despite
supportive treatment, most affected cats die or are euthanized during the first month after the onset of
clinical signs.

Feline Panleukopenia Virus (FPV; ch. 201)
Infection by FPV can be clinical or subclinical. It usually affects young unvaccinated cats, causing
anorexia, vomiting, diarrhea and leukopenia.29 Several recent cases of FPV encephalitis have been
described.30,31 The onset of these neurologic clinical signs can be peracute with progressive
deterioration over several days, resulting in death.30-31

Parasitic CNS Disease
Gurltia Paralysans Myelopathy
Gurltia paralysans is a neurotropic metastrongylid nematode that causes chronic meningomyelitis in
domestic cats.32,33 The geographic distribution includes South America; however, a recent report of
ectopic localization (anterior chamber of the eye) in the Canary Islands (Europe) might reflect a wider
distribution.32-34 The life cycle of G. paralysans is unknown. Adult worms and eggs can be found in the
thoracolumbar and lumbosacral spinal cord parenchyma and leptomeningeal veins, causing chronic and
slowly progressive meningomyelitis (feline gurltiosis). There is no breed nor sex predilection and young
adult cats from rural or periurban areas are generally affected. Clinical signs include pelvic limb
proprioceptive ataxia, paraparesis, paraplegia, lumbosacral hyperesthesia, fecal or urinary incontinence,
tail paralysis (Video 255.4

), and/or signs of uveitis. CT-myelography and MRI (ch. 112) show

diffuse enlargement of the thoracolumbar and lumbosacral spinal cord. CSF mononuclear pleocytosis
has been reported in up to 55% of affected cats (ch. 109). An antemortem presumptive diagnosis of
feline gurltiosis is based on neurological signs, epidemiological factors, and the exclusion of other causes
of feline myelopathies. Recent studies have shown that commercial serologic test for canine
angiostrongylosis and semi-nested PCR might be helpful as a new diagnostic method for feline gurltiosis
in live domestic cats.35,36 No larvae or parasite eggs are found on fecal examination. The definitive
diagnosis is histopathological, based on detection of adult G. paralysans in the spinal cord (Figure
255.3). There is no treatment, and the prognosis is poor.

CNS DISORDERS OF UNKNOWN ORIGIN
Feline Hippocampal Necrosis
Feline hippocampal necrosis (FHN) is a neuropathological entity associated with different causes
including feline limbic encephalitis (FLE) (voltage-gated potassium channel complex (VGKC)/LGI1
antibodies–associated limbic encephalitis), neurotoxicosis, and various structural brain disorders.37-39
The hippocampus is susceptible to epileptic seizures and very epileptogenic itself; therefore,
hippocampal necrosis can be secondary to recurrent epileptic seizures as well as contributing to
epileptogenesis. Cats with FHN present with interictal behavioral changes (such as increased
vocalization, aggression, or anxiety and fear-related behaviors) and recurrent focal seizures with
orofacial automatism (e.g., hypersalivation, lip smacking, facial twitching, chewing, licking, and
swallowing) which can evolve to generalized tonic-clonic seizures.37-39 Definitive diagnosis is made
histopathologically; however, MRI (ch. 112) can identify hippocampal lesions (Figure 255.4) and help
differentiate between FLE and other causes of FHN.40 CSF analysis (ch. 109) can reveal some
abnormalities, although both CSF and MRI can be normal in the early stages of FLE. Testing CSF and
serum for LGI1 and VGKC antibodies is indicated in cats with suspected FLE, but the tests are not widely
available. Treatment consists of antiepileptic medications (in cats with FHN; ch. 247), combined with
immunosuppressive medication in cats with suspected FLE (chs. 144, 169). The prognosis depends on
the underlying etiology, but generally is considered guarded in cats with FHN. In cats with FLE

diagnosed and treated promptly with both antiepileptic and immunosuppressive therapy, the prognosis
is improved.

Slowly Progressive Lymphohistiocytic Meningoencephalomyelitis
Slowly progressive lymphohistiocytic meningoencephalomyelitis is characterized by late onset (mean
age, 9 years) and slow progression (mean, 11 months).41 There is no sex nor breed predilection and all
reported cases have been outdoor cats (active hunters living in northeast Scotland). Neurological signs
include an obtunded or disorientated mental status, spastic gait, stiff extended tail posture (Video 255.5
), decreased to absent postural reactions in all four limbs and decreased to absent menace response
bilaterally (ch. 241). MRI can show brain atrophy (ch. 112). CSF analysis was normal in one tested cat.
A definitive diagnosis is reached histopathologically.41 Suggested possible causative agents include an
infective or environmental immunogenic trigger. There is no treatment and the prognosis is poor.41
Since this condition was first reported in 2012, there have been no additional scientific publications, but
one of the authors is aware of new cases being diagnosed with this condition in Scotland.

Feline Polioencephalomyelitis
Feline polioencephalomyelitis is a subacute to chronic nonsuppurative encephalomyelitis. Pathological
changes are highly suggestive of a viral etiology and occur predominantly in the gray matter of the
medulla oblongata and spinal cord.42 Cats of any age can be affected. The disease is considered rare,
with a prevalence of 1% in cats with myelopathy. Clinical signs include ataxia, paresis, and decreased
postural reactions in all four limbs.42,43 The diagnosis is established histopathologically.42 There is no
treatment and prognosis can be favourable when neurological signs are mild and nonprogressive.43

NEUROMUSCULAR SYSTEM DISEASES
INHERITED NEUROMUSCULAR DISEASES

Inherited neuromuscular diseases are rare, slowly progressive and they predominantly affect
young kittens (Table 255.1).

ACQUIRED NEUROMUSCULAR DISEASES
Acquired neuromuscular diseases are rare in cats and are attributed to infectious agents44;
intoxications; and metabolic, immune-mediated, neoplastic, or paraneoplastic disorders, although a
definitive cause is often not identified.

Motor Polyneuropathy of Unknown Origin in Young Cats
Recurrent or progressive motor polyneuropathy has been reported to affect young cats from 3-44
months of age, mainly Bengals, but any breed and either sex can be affected.45,46 Clinical signs include
generalized weakness (recurrent or progressive), ventroflexion of the neck, palmigrade and plantigrade
posture, and decreased to absent spinal reflexes.45,46 The diagnosis is based on electrodiagnostic testing
(ch. 111) and histologic evaluation of muscle and nerve biopsies (ch. 110). Treatment is supportive, and
the prognosis varies from poor to excellent, which highlights the difference in possible etiologies.45,46

SPECIFIC PAROXYSMAL DISORDERS OF UNKNOWN ORIGIN
(MALADAPTIVE PAIN DISORDERS)
FELINE OROFACIAL PAIN SYNDROME (FOPS)
Feline orofacial pain syndrome (FOPS) is a pain disorder characterized by acute behavioral signs of oral
discomfort and tongue mutilation.47,48 Predisposing causes include conditions causing oral pain and
environmental stress. The high prevalence in Burmese cats suggests an inherited component.48
However, cats of any breed or age and either sex can be affected.47 Clinical signs include exaggerated
licking, chewing movements, and pawing at the mouth, typically to one side only (Video 255.6

). The

acute-severe form of FOPS occurs in young kittens at the time of permanent teeth eruption. It is
characterized by signs of severe and unrelenting oral pain with tongue and buccal mucosa mutilation. It
is self-limiting within a few weeks. The chronic-episodic form of FOPS occurs in adult cats with
paroxysmal, episodic signs of orofacial pain and it is often triggered by oral movements.48 In adult cats
with FOPS, periodontal disease is a predisposing factor (ch. 258) and therefore, the oral cavity should
be examined under general anaesthesia and dental radiographs taken according to the World Small
Animal Veterinary Association global dental guidelines. The neurologic examination is normal (ch.
241). The diagnosis of FOPS is based on signalment, exclusion of other causes of oral or facial pain, and
identification of contributory causes. Treatment involves analgesia (ch. 6), gabapentin, and/or
phenobarbital (ch. 247), as well as mitigating environmental stressors and treating underlying triggers
of oral pain.48 FOPS can be worsened by dental intervention; therefore, referral to a veterinary dentistry
specialist is recommended for cats with periodontal disease and FOPS.

FELINE HYPERESTHESIA SYNDROME (FHS)
Feline hyperesthesia syndrome is a poorly understood disorder characterised by episodes of contraction
of the cutaneous trunci muscle (skin rippling over the lumbar area), excessive vocalisation, and
overgrooming or self-trauma to the tail.48,49 These signs may be triggered by petting and occur when
the cat is anxious or stressed. Multiple episodes per day can occur. It may be difficult to distract an
affected cat during an episode. FHS is more common in Siamese, Burmese, Himalayan, and Abyssinian
cats, and typically clinical signs appear between 1 to 4 years of age. Diagnosis is based on exclusion of
dermatologic, spinal, and renal (e.g., nephrolith/ureterolith) disorders and assessing for environmental
stressors. In a recent case series, most of the cats were young males, with a median age of 1 year at the
onset of clinical signs.49 Clinical remission or improvement was achieved in 6/7 cats with multimodal

treatment including gabapentin and phenobarbital or topiramate.49 As for FOPS, addressing
environmental stressors and needs (see multimodal environmental modification, ch. 311) is essential
for successful management of FHS.48

CLIENT INFORMATION

Feline Cerebellar Hypoplasia (FCH) Caused by Feline Panleukopenia Virus
(FPV)
WHAT IS FELINE CEREBELLAR HYPOPLASIA?
The cerebellum is the region of the brain that plays an important role in coordination of movement and
balance. Hypoplasia means that there is underdevelopment or incomplete development. Therefore,
feline cerebellar hypoplasia (FCH), also known as spastic cat syndrome or wobbly cat syndrome, is a
disorder seen in kittens where the cerebellum has not developed properly during gestation or during the
first 3 weeks of life and it is reduced in size (see picture above).

HOW CAN THE KITTENS BE AFFECTED AND WHAT ARE THE CLINICAL
SIGNS?
Exposure to the feline panleukopenia virus (FPV) during the last 3 weeks of gestation or the first 3 weeks
of life may cause FCH. The mother cat does not necessarily have to be infected during pregnancy—
vaccination with a modified live vaccine during pregnancy or during the first 2 weeks after giving birth
can cause FCH. This is the reason modified live virus vaccines are not used during pregnancy. The
symptoms of FCH are evident when the affected kitten starts toddling around and some cats can be
more severely affected than others. Cats with FCH have balance and coordination issues (losing balance,
falling towards either side, walking with a high stepping gait and standing with the legs splayed wide).
Affected cats can also show fine tremors of the head and body when excited or when trying to perform a

movement. The tremors are not present when the cat is sleeping. The symptoms do not progress, so they
do not get worse with time. Moreover, some improvement is also possible as affected cats can
compensate over time and learn to cope with the condition. FCH is not contagious and is not painful.

HOW CAN IT BE DIAGNOSED?
There are no specific diagnostic tests currently available. The diagnosis is mainly made by the medical
history (Did the queen/mother cat show symptoms of feline panleukopenia virus infection in the last 3
weeks of pregnancy? Was she vaccinated with a modified live vaccine during the last 3 weeks of
pregnancy?), the kitten’s symptoms, and ruling out other possible causes of an uncoordinated gait. A
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan may show a small cerebellum.

WHAT IS THE TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS OF CATS WITH FCH? HOW
CAN IT BE PREVENTED?
There is no treatment to recover cerebellar function; however, some cats can have a good quality of life
with supportive care. The degree and type of supportive care depends on the severity of symptoms (i.e.,
how affected is a particular kitten, and how well can it control its movements?). Affected cats should be
kept indoors to minimise the risk of trauma (e.g., high falls and road traffic accidents), and they may
prefer walking on carpet or rugs for traction. Litter boxes with high sides can give them something to
lean against while toileting to help keep their balance. Raised food and water dishes may be also
preferable. The life expectancy is not affected by this disorder. Prevention can be achieved by
vaccination of queens before pregnancy and avoiding vaccination during pregnancy or during the first 2
weeks after giving birth.
Elsa Beltran (London, United Kingdom) and Luisa De Risio (Solihull, West Midlands, United
Kingdom; Nottingham, United Kingdom)

Chapter 256: Physical
Therapy and Rehabilitation
David Levine, and Darryl Millis

ESWT extracorporeal shockwave therapy

UWTM underwater treadmill

Physical therapy is a profession with an established scientific basis
in humans and companion animals. In providing physical therapy
and rehabilitation, the goal is to restore, maintain, and promote
optimal function, fitness, wellness, and quality of life as they relate to
movement disorders and overall health.1-7 In dogs, this may include
treating patients during their recovery from orthopedic surgical
procedures, such as fracture repair and cruciate surgery (Figure
256.1); providing rehabilitation after neurological injuries, such as
intervertebral disc disease (ch. 250) or fibrocartilaginous embolism
(ch. 251); designing and implementing weight loss programs (ch.
150); and helping to manage chronic conditions, such as
osteoarthritis, or progressive conditions, such as degenerative
myelopathy (ch. 250).8-14 A major emphasis is to prevent or

minimize the onset, clinical signs, and progression of impairments,
functional limitations, and disabilities that may result from diseases,
disorders, conditions, and injuries.
Physical therapy and rehabilitation in small animal practice has
become increasingly common and will likely continue to emerge as
an essential aspect of veterinary medicine as the scientific literature
continues to expand. In many orthopedic and neurologic conditions,
physical rehabilitation is becoming routine to enhance recovery, as in
human medicine. Wellness and preventive medicine (e.g.,
maintenance of muscle strength and function, improving
cardiorespiratory fitness, and sport-specific conditioning) is also a
growing trend in rehabilitation and sports medicine. In the human
and canine literature, rehabilitation therapy has been shown to be
effective in numerous areas related to internal medicine including
pain management, cardiorespiratory function, musculoskeletal and
neurological recovery and function, and oncology, to name a few.1524

In 2012, the American College of Veterinary Sports Medicine and
Rehabilitation (ACVSMR) was approved as a recognized veterinary
specialty under the American Veterinary Medical Association and the
American Board of Veterinary Specialties (ABVS). This college is
aimed at veterinary practitioners who specialize and excel in sports
medicine and rehabilitation. Certificate programs in canine
rehabilitation are also available, and require online and live
coursework, externships, and examination processes.
Rehabilitation is a time-intensive specialty and has traditionally
employed a collaborative approach that engages multiple professions
to maximize outcomes, including veterinarians, veterinary
technicians, physical therapists, orthotists and prosthetists,
behaviorists, trainers, and of course owners.

PHYSICAL THERAPY/REHABILITATION
EVALUATION
The physical therapy/rehabilitation process begins with a diagnosis
from the veterinarian and a careful physical therapy/rehabilitation
evaluation. This evaluation differs from a medical evaluation (ch. 3)

in that function is paramount. Range of motion, strength, gait, pain,
balance, endurance, and other functional factors are all documented,
and a plan for rehabilitation is developed, in conjunction with the
owner (Appendix 256.1). The plan of care must be unique to the
patient and should account for all premorbid and comorbid
conditions, including the severity of the conditions, the age and
disposition of the dog, the expectations for future function and
performance, the urgency of recovery, the available equipment and
technical skills of the therapist, and the financial constraints of the
owner. The plan of care is continually modified as needed, based on
frequent assessments. A qualified rehabilitation practitioner may or
may not be locally available, so exclusively home-based programs are
sometimes a necessity.
It is important to determine the expectations of the owner during
the evaluation to help determine the type and length of program
necessary to meet the goals. In most cases, owners are realistic about
expectations, especially for pets with chronic, severe conditions in
which improved mobility and pain control are desired. Occasionally,
an owner will have unrealistic goals, and it is important to discuss
the realities of the underlying condition(s) and whether the desired
objectives are likely to be achieved.

ASSESSMENT TECHNIQUES
Assessing the outcome of treatments in physical therapy and
rehabilitation is essential to determine how an animal is progressing
and to assess the effectiveness of the treatment. These techniques
should consist of objective data whenever possible because
subjectively, owners and veterinarians often believe a patient is
doing better than the data suggest. In addition, documentation of
progress is important to provide an incentive for owners to continue
rehabilitation and justify continued treatment. Numerous
measurements are useful for assessing outcomes, including the
ability to perform functional activities of daily living, gait analysis,
joint motion (goniometry), assessment of muscle mass and strength,
evaluation of body composition and weight changes (ch. 72), pain
assessment (ch. 6), assessment of activity levels, and functional
scales.25-38

COMMON INTERVENTIONS IN
PHYSICAL THERAPY/REHABILITATION
THERMOTHERAPY AND CRYOTHERAPY
Superficial heat (thermotherapy) and cold (cryotherapy) have been
used therapeutically for centuries on soft tissues and joints.
Cryotherapy is commonly used after tissue trauma, whether
accidental (sprains, strains, etc.), or intentional (surgery, intense
exercise), with the goals of decreasing inflammation, swelling, and
pain, and improving function.39-41 Heating connective tissues using
superficial heat such as hot packs and compresses typically is used
for chronic conditions, such as arthritis and other disease processes
causing stiffness, and helps to increase connective tissue
extensibility.42 Thermotherapy may also be used to decrease pain
and facilitate healing.42 Both of these treatments are easily taught to
owners and can be administered at home.

THERAPEUTIC ULTRASOUND
Therapeutic ultrasound (TUS) is primarily used as a deep heating
agent (up to 5 cm) and is used in small animal practice for heating
joints, muscles, and tendons, commonly before stretching. It is also
used for tissue healing and repair and to enhance the transdermal
administration of drugs (phonophoresis). Only two frequencies are

used in TUS (in comparison to diagnostic ultrasound): 1 MHz for
treating tissues between 3-5 cm in depth, and 3.3 MHz for treating
tissues 1-2 cm in depth.43-45

ELECTRICAL STIMULATION
Electrical stimulation (ES) is a commonly used modality in physical
therapy, and can be effective for many purposes, including increasing
muscle strength, and decreasing pain.14,46-50 These devices work by
stimulating motor nerves to cause a muscle contraction, and by
stimulating sensory nerves to help decrease pain. Many dogs tolerate
ES well, but some dogs may dislike the sensation and care must be
used when applying this modality.

THERAPEUTIC LASER
LASER is an acronym for light amplification by stimulated emission
of radiation. The concept of using light for therapeutic purposes,
called phototherapy, originated from the belief that the sun and
other sources of light have therapeutic benefits. Therapeutic lasers
have become increasingly popular in veterinary rehabilitation for a
variety of conditions. The lasers used in rehabilitation are thought to
help modulate cellular functions, a process known as
photobiomodulation (PBM). PBM has been reported to modulate
various biologic processes, such as mitochondrial respiration and
adenosine triphosphate synthesis, acceleration of wound and joint
healing, and promoting muscle regeneration.51-61 It is also
commonly used for pain control, and some studies have found it to
be an effective adjunct in the treatment of musculoskeletal pain.62
Therapeutic lasers are typically Class IIIb (5-500 mW) or Class IV
(greater than 500 mW) and possess appropriate infrared
wavelengths to penetrate to various tissue depths (Figure 256.2).

EXTRACORPOREAL SHOCKWAVE
THERAPY
Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) uses high intensity sound
waves that are transmitted through tissues and that have biological
effects on tissues, especially at soft tissue-bone interfaces. Release of
growth factors, neovascularization, and analgesia are some of the
physiologic effects demonstrated with ESWT.63 The most common
indications for ESWT include osteoarthritis, delayed union or
nonunion fractures, postoperative tibial plateau leveling osteotomy
recovery, medial shoulder instability, biceps tendinitis, and
supraspinatus tendinitis.64-66

FIGURE 256.2 Treatment of an arthritic joint
with a therapeutic laser.

RANGE OF MOTION AND STRETCHING

Range of motion and stretching exercises are extremely important to
achieve improved motion of joints after acute injury or surgery (e.g.,
cranial cruciate ligament rupture, articular fractures), or in patients
afflicted with chronic conditions (osteoarthritis) (

Video 256.1).

They are also important to help increase flexibility, prevent
adhesions between soft tissues and bones, remodel periarticular
fibrosis, and improve muscle and other soft-tissue extensibility to
help prevent further injury. Joint motion may be measured using
goniometry, which has been validated in dogs (Figure 256.3).67
These exercises can also be performed at home if the owner has been
carefully instructed.

MASSAGE
Massage has many forms and is employed by many practitioners of
various backgrounds. One common definition is that massage is the
scientific and systematic manipulation of the soft tissues of the body.
The use of massage in humans is common for relaxation, pain
control, recovery from injury, and improving flexibility,68-72 and is
becoming more accepted and commonplace in veterinary practice. In
some US states (but not all), massage therapists are licensed and
regulated, but this is not common for small animal practice.
Continuing education courses and schools that teach massage are
available.

THERAPEUTIC EXERCISE
Therapeutic exercise is likely the most common and most valuable
modality used in physical therapy and rehabilitation (

Videos

256.2 to 256.18). Therapeutic exercise is an important method to
return the animal to the optimal level of independence and
function.13,14,73,74 Some of the common goals of exercises are to
improve active range of motion, flexibility, muscle mass and muscle
strength, balance, endurance, and performance of activities of daily

living.11,74-81 Therapeutic exercise programs designed for the home
environment also provide an opportunity for owners to become
actively involved in their pet’s rehabilitation (Figures 256.4 to
256.8).

AQUATIC THERAPY
Aquatic therapy has become a very valuable component of veterinary
physical therapy and rehabilitation. Underwater treadmills
(UWTMs) and pools have become commonplace in veterinary
rehabilitation facilities (Figure 256.9) (

Video 256.19).

FIGURE 256.3 Joint angles of flexion and
extension are measured using a goniometer.

FIGURE 256.4 Standing on a balance dome (half
ball, half flat surface) or a BOSU ball may be used for
core strengthening exercises.

FIGURE 256.5 Dancing activities may also be
accomplished with assistance of a physioroll or egg
ball. The patient places the forelimbs on the roll or
ball, and the therapist slowly rolls the ball toward or
away from the patient forcing the patient to move the
hindlimbs backward or forward.

FIGURE 256.6 Tetraparesis or other conditions
causing weakness in multiple limbs. A, Use of a sling

FIGURE 256.8 Standing or walking on foam
rubber, mattresses, air mattresses, or trampolines

ability.
A major benefit of using a UWTM is buoyancy, which decreases
the load on the joints during exercise.12,14,82,83 In a study performed
on dogs, the amount of body weight borne when immersed in water
(as a percentage of body weight on dry ground) was ∼91% when the
water was at the level of the lateral malleolus of the tibia, 85% at the
level of the lateral condyle of the femur, and 38% at the level of the
greater trochanter of the femur.82 This information may be
particularly useful when treating patients with conditions such as
arthritis (Figure 256.10, A to C). The use of UWTMs is favored for
enhancing function such as gait. It also encourages joint motion in a
more normal gait pattern compared with swimming. Swimming
tends to increase flexion and overall range of motion of the limbs,
but joint extension is less compared to UWTM walking.83 Swimming
is a much more difficult activity from an endurance and
cardiovascular perspective, though, and just a minute or two can be
exhausting, especially for dogs that are in poor condition. Flotation
devices are also helpful to allow for greater buoyancy and ease of
exercise.

FIGURE 256.9 Plastic bumpers in an underwater
treadmill to prevent standing on its nonmoving
sides. From Levine D, Millis DL, Flocker J, et al.
Aquatic therapy. In: Millis DL, Levine D, eds.
Canine Rehabilitation and Physical Therapy.
Elsevier Saunders; 2014:532; with permission.
Aquatic therapy such as UWTMs and swimming comes naturally
to many canine patients, which is especially beneficial because
exercises in animal patients must be in a form that they naturally
perform or can be easily trained to do. It is also an exercise owners
can perform with their dogs at home if they have the facilities.

ASSISTIVE DEVICES IN
REHABILITATION (CARTS, SLINGS,
HARNESSES, SUPPORTS, ORTHOTICS
AND PROSTHETICS)
Numerous assistive devices are used in rehabilitation to help
improve animals’ gait and locomotor function (Figures 256.11 and
256.12). These devices range from harnesses and supports to assist

during movement, to carts and wheelchairs that may be customized
to the patient (Figure 256.13). Many of these supports help provide
an ergonomic benefit for the owner, and provide comfort and safety
for the dog.84,85 Orthotics is the evaluation, fabrication, and custom
fitting of braces, known as orthoses. Prosthetics is the evaluation,
fabrication, and custom fitting of artificial limbs, known as
prostheses (Figure 256.14). Practices offering rehabilitation
services have knowledgeable staff regarding obtaining this
equipment and training owners in proper use.

INTRODUCTION
Laboratory tests can assist in ruling in or out inciting causes of gastrointestinal (GI) diseases.
However, chronic GI disorders are often multifactorial and thus even a positive laboratory
test result requires clinical judgment and integration of all patient data including history,
signalment, and other test results. Flowcharts for the diagnostic work-up of patients with
signs of GI disease can be found in chapters on halitosis (ch. 46), ptyalism (ch. 46), gagging
and dysphagia (ch. 47), regurgitation (ch. 48), acute and chronic vomiting (ch. 48), chronic
diarrhea (ch. 49), melena (ch. 50), constipation, tenesmus, dyschezia, and fecal
incontinence (ch. 51), and flatulence (ch. 52).

LABORATORY TOOLS TO DIAGNOSE
ENTEROPATHOGENS
Fecal smears, sedimentation, and flotation allow for the detection of a multitude of
pathogenic organisms (ch. 80). However, the sensitivity is usually moderate to low due to
low pathogen burden, intermittent shedding, or operator experience. Table 257.1 shows
pathogens that may be detected by different fecal examination techniques. Table 257.2
provides an overview of laboratory diagnostic tests for common enteropathogens.

LABORATORY TOOLS TO ASSESS INTESTINAL
FUNCTION AND DISEASE
SERUM CONCENTRATIONS OF FOLATE, COBALAMIN, AND
PHOSPHORUS
Both folate and cobalamin are water-soluble B-vitamins (vitamin B9 and B12, respectively).
Folate is present in a wide variety of food sources and is mostly supplied as folate
polyglutamate, which cannot be readily absorbed. In the proximal small intestine, folate
polyglutamate is deconjugated by folate deconjugase and the resulting folate monoglutamate
is absorbed by specific folate carriers in the proximal small intestine (Figure 257.1 and
Video 257.1).

33

Serum folate concentrations can be decreased due to diffuse proximal

small intestinal mucosal infiltration, subsequent destruction of folate deconjugase and folate
carriers, and malabsorption, or increased as a result of bacterial production in a state of
intestinal dysbiosis.34
Dietary cobalamin is bound to animal-based dietary protein and cannot be absorbed
directly. In the stomach, dietary protein is digested by pepsin and HCl and cobalamin is
released. The free cobalamin is immediately bound by R-protein, which is a cobalamin
transporter protein synthesized by the gastric mucosa. In the small intestine, R-protein is
digested by pancreatic proteases and the free cobalamin is bound by intrinsic factor.
Cobalamin is absorbed in the distal small intestine, especially the ileum, through binding of
intrinsic factor to its respective receptors (Figure 257.2 and Video 257.2

).35 Severe

distal small intestinal disease can lead to destruction of cobalamin receptors in the ileum,
causing malabsorption, depletion of cobalamin body stores, and resulting in cobalamin
deficiency. In dogs and cats, the vast majority of intrinsic factor is secreted by the exocrine
pancreas and thus exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) is another important differential
diagnosis for patients with hypocobalaminemia (ch. 279). While supplementation of folate
and cobalamin is beneficial in cats and people with chronic enteropathies, it is important to
note that these vitamins are likely merely surrogate markers for generalized malabsorption.
Global metabolic derangements have been documented in humans, dogs,36 and cats 37 with
chronic enteropathies. Other micronutrient deficiencies documented in dogs and cats with
chronic enteropathy include deficiencies of inorganic phosphorus 39 are correlated with
outcome in dogs with chronic enteropathy. Also, serum phosphorus is a part of the Feline
Chronic Enteropathy Activity Index (FCEAI; ch. 262, Table 262.5).41

SERUM C-REACTIVE PROTEIN CONCENTRATION
Serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration increases in dogs with idiopathic
inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and correlates with the IBD clinical disease activity
index.42 Thus, the greatest clinical utility of this test is to monitor treatment response in dogs
with IBD. Effective dietary or medical therapy is associated with decreases in serum CRP
concentration. A variety of assays for the measurement of CRP in serum is available, but
unfortunately not all of them are reliable for the measurement of serum CRP concentrations
in dogs.

not yet routinely available.

The measurement of alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor (alpha-1 PI) concentration in feces can
aid in the diagnosis of protein-losing enteropathy (PLE; ch. 262).43 Alpha-1 proteinase
inhibitor is synthesized in the liver and has a molecular mass of approximately 60,000 Da,
which is similar to that of albumin. In patients with PLE, alpha-1 PI is lost at approximately
the same rate as albumin (Figure 257.3). Due to its inhibitory effects on proteases, alpha-1
PI is not hydrolyzed in the GI lumen and can be used as a biomarker of GI protein loss.
Alpha-1 PI can be falsely within the reference interval in dogs with GI protein loss that have
severe hypoalbuminemia and can be falsely abnormal in patients with digitally retrieved fecal
samples. The test is currently only available through the Gastrointestinal Laboratory at Texas
A&M University.

FIGURE 257.1 Folate absorption. Dietary folate enters the
gastrointestinal tract predominantly as folate polyglutamate. Folate
deconjugase, a brush border enzyme in the cranial small intestine,
deconjugates folate polyglutamate to folate monoglutamate (A).
Specific folate carriers on enterocytes located in the cranial small
intestine absorb (arrows) folate monoglutamate (B). Both the
deconjugase and folate carrier molecules are only localized in the
cranial small intestine and there is no appreciable absorption of folate
in the distal small intestine or the colon. From Suchodolski JS, Steiner
JM. Laboratory assessment of gastrointestinal function. Clin Tech
Small Anim Pract. 2003;18:208.

FIGURE 257.2 Cobalamin absorption. Dietary cobalamin is bound to
dietary protein. In the stomach, pepsin and hydrochloric acid degrade
the dietary protein, releasing cobalamin (A). The cobalamin is
immediately bound by R-protein, which is produced by the gastric
mucosa. In the duodenum, pancreatic proteinases digest the R-protein,
releasing cobalamin. Free cobalamin in the duodenum is bound by
intrinsic factor (B). In dogs and cats, intrinsic factor is mostly produced
by the exocrine pancreas. Cobalamin remains bound to intrinsic factor
during passage through the cranial small intestine (C). In the distal
small intestine, the cobalamin/intrinsic factor complexes are taken up
by specific receptors found only on enterocytes in the ileum (D); the
enterocytes process the intrinsic factor/cobalamin complex and release
cobalamin into the circulation, where a final set of binding proteins
(transcobalamins) complex the vitamin and carry it to the cells. From
Suchodolski JS, Steiner JM. Laboratory assessment of gastrointestinal
function. Clin Tech Small Anim Pract. 2003;18:207.

FIGURE 257.3 Fecal alpha1-proteinase inhibitor (PI). In patients
with disturbed mucosal integrity, plasma proteins can be lost into the
intestinal lumen. Unlike albumin, which is degraded by digestive and
bacterial proteases, alpha1-PI is resistant to proteolytic degradation and
can survive intestinal transit. Therefore, alpha1-PI can be measured in
feces using an immunoassay. From Berghoff N, Steiner JM. Laboratory
tests for the diagnosis and management of chronic canine and feline
enteropathies. Vet Clin North Am Small Anim Pract. 2011;41:321.
Calprotectin and S100A12 are markers for neutrophilic inflammation that have been shown
to be increased in concentration in both serum and feces in some dogs with IBD.44,45
Methylhistamine is a stable marker of mast cell degranulation, and increased serum and fecal
methylhistamine concentrations have been described in some dogs with IBD.46 Brominated
tyrosine is a marker of eosinophil activity and increased serum concentrations have been
described in some dogs with IBD.47 Further research will be needed before the clinical utility
of these markers can be definitively established.

BIOMARKER PANELS AND OMICS-BASED
DIAGNOSTICS
In recent years it has become clear that a single biomarker is unlikely to be able to
differentiate between different causes of GI disease with sufficient specificity for reliable
clinical routine testing. Instead, efforts are now focused on utilizing a combination of
different biomarkers and even artificial intelligence for connecting these markers for disease

prediction, diagnosis, and monitoring. At this time, none of these panels is yet being used
routinely in clinical patients.
Several studies have investigated the fecal microbiome and metabolome to identify
biomarker candidates and combinations thereof (ch. 260). A fecal dysbiosis index has been
developed to predict global intestinal dysbiosis based on the alterations of 7 different
bacterial taxa as well as the abundance of total bacteria. It differentiates dogs with chronic
enteropathy from heathy dogs with a 74% sensitivity and 95% specificity.48
A recent study validated a multitude antibody ELISA assay combining anti-OmpC IgA
(antibodies to the Escherichia coli outer membrane porin C), anti-canine calprotectin IgA
(calprotectin is a primarily neutrophil-derived protein), and anti-gliadin derived peptide IgA
(gliadin is a peptide present in gluten). While the authors report 80% sensitivity and 86%
specificity for the differentiation of dogs with IBD from dogs with other diseases causing GI
signs, results should be interpreted with great caution.49 Most dogs classified as having IBD
did not undergo biopsy collection and histopathologic evaluation. The control group
comprised dogs with extra-GI diseases, such as hypoadrenocorticism or EPI, all of which
could be easily diagnosed with other, more sensitive and specific diagnostic tests. Hence, a
true test for the diagnosis and differentiation of canine or feline chronic enteropathies needs
yet to be developed and validated.
In cats with chronic GI disease, the differentiation of IBD from low-grade intestinal T-cell
lymphoma (LGITL) is still a diagnostic enigma. Polymerase chain reaction for antigen
receptor rearrangement (PARR) testing assesses the genetic composition of T- or B-cell
receptor genes and determines whether a population is monoclonal or polyclonal. The test is
frequently used in cats with chronic enteropathy to assist in the differentiation between IBD
and LGITL.50 However, finding clonality is not specific for LGITL and clonal expansion of
lymphocytes has been found to be a sequela of chronic antigenic stimulation (e.g., in chronic
inflammation and infectious diseases) or as part of the normal aging process.51 While
clonality testing is a useful tool, results cannot be used for reclassifying cases based on the
results of PARR alone. Recently, histologically-guided mass spectrometry has been
investigated as a technique for the differentiation of feline IBD from LGITL.52 This technique
relies on molecular fingerprinting through mass spectrometry of formalin-fixed paraffinembedded biopsy specimens. While results are promising, the test needs to be further
assessed in a larger group of cats and is not currently commercially available.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Laboratory Evaluation of the Gastrointestinal Tract
Signs of gastrointestinal disease, such as diarrhea and vomiting, are very common in both
dogs and cats. There are many different causes of these clinical signs and not all pets with
such signs actually have a disease that originates in the gastrointestinal tract itself, but
instead may have a disease of another organ. Thus, it is very important to systematically
work-up each patient with clinical signs of gastrointestinal disease. Depending on the clinical
sign or the signs present this work-up will slightly vary and more specific information about
your pet will depend on this clinical presentation, but regardless of such presentation it is
crucial to remember that often times many diagnostic tests are needed in order to arrive at
the diagnosis. Each negative test result is crucial in ultimately identifying the underlying
disease process and most effectively treating your dog or cat.
One of the first steps in the work-up is to rule-out the various causes outside the
gastrointestinal tract before doing more specific diagnostic tests that aim to diagnose primary
gastrointestinal disease. Also, the goal is to do less invasive diagnostic tests before performing
more invasive diagnostic tests and to do more affordable ones before doing more expensive
ones.
There are a wide variety of laboratory tests that can help with the diagnosis of
gastrointestinal problems. One group of such tests aims at identifying infectious causes, such
as viruses, bacteria, fungi, or parasites. In general infectious organisms can be diagnosed

through different types of diagnostic tests. Some bacteria, such as Salmonella spp., a bacteria
that can lead to both vomiting and diarrhea, can be diagnosed by means of culture. Other
organisms, for example Tritrichomonas foetus, one of the most important intestinal parasites
in cats that can cause diarrhea can be diagnosed by identifying the genetic coding of the
organism in feces by a method called polymerase chain reaction. Yet other organisms, such as
Clostridium perfringens, can be diagnosed based on identifying the actual toxin in the stool
that leads to the clinical signs. Immunofluorescence, a technique where the organism is
labeled with a fluorescent dye, can be used to identify Giardia lamblia, a common parasite in
both dogs and cats.
Another group of diagnostic tests aims to evaluate the function of the gastrointestinal tract.
For example, cobalamin and folate, two water-soluble vitamins that are absorbed in the small
intestine, can be measured in a blood sample. A decrease in folate indicates a severe and longstanding disease process in the proximal small intestine, while a decrease in cobalamin
indicates a severe and long-standing disease in the distal small intestine. The concentration
of another substance, alpha1-proteinase inhibitor, can be used to evaluate a patient for
gastrointestinal protein loss. C-reactive protein is produced in response to any type of
inflammatory condition and an increased concentration in the blood of a patient with
gastrointestinal disease could be used to stage the severity of the disease. There are a number
of other markers of gastrointestinal disease, such as inflammatory markers or hormones, but
none of them are currently used routinely in the evaluation of dogs and cats with
gastrointestinal disease, but may prove useful in isolated cases.
Sina Marsilio (Davis, California)

MMM masticatory muscle myositis

This chapter raises periprocedural considerations relevant to
dentistry, oral surgery, and other procedures (e.g., gastrointestinal
endoscopy, rhinoscopy), and reviews common disorders of the oral
cavity and the salivary glands, with focus on their non-surgical
management.

PERIOPERATIVE CONSIDERATIONS
MOUTH OPENING
Prolonged wide mouth opening can reduce maxillary artery blood
flow, resulting in temporary or permanent blindness post-anesthesia
and/or other neurological deficits in cats.1 Placing rigid plastic
cylinders of appropriate lengths (e.g., needle cap shortened to 20-30
mm) between maxillary and mandibular canines avoids these
complications while enabling adequate mouth opening for dental
and oral surgical procedures.2

MANIPULATION OF ORAL AND
ADJACENT STRUCTURES
Overzealous pharyngeal packing, tongue manipulation, excessive
elevation of the alveolar mucosa on the lingual aspects of the
mandibles and other iatrogenic complications can result in oral
edema, which may exacerbate already existing tissue swelling in
patients with oral inflammation or trauma.3 Affected patients may
benefit from a single injection of dexamethasone (0.1-0.2 mg/kg IV)
at the end of the procedure. The tongue can also be wrapped with a
gauze sponge soaked with a hypertonic solution prior to extubation.

FIGURE 258.1 Dog with gingivitis and

(asterisks) in the labial and buccal mucosa that

(A). Dog with idiopathic osteomyelitis and

HYPO- AND HYPERTHERMIA
Prevention of patient hypothermia is of particular importance when
water is used for cooling dental power instruments or for rinsing

debris from the mouth.4 Conversely, hyperthermia also is a concern,
especially in cats when opiates like hydromorphone, with or without
gas anesthesia, ketamine, or a combination of these drugs is/are
being used.5 Cats with postoperative hyperthermia often respond
favorably to intravenous fluid administration, removal of blankets in
the cage, mechanical cooling methods such as a fan or ice packs, and
application of rubbing alcohol to the footpads.

ORAL BLEEDING AND HEMOSTASIS
Severe oral bleeding may be due to injury of larger blood vessels,
bleeding dyscrasias (e.g., von Willebrand disease [ch. 175]), lingual
or palatal injury, oral inflammation, soft-tissue trauma, oral
neoplasia, and jaw fracture. Intravascular volume replacement is
accomplished with crystalloids, colloids, and/or blood products (ch.
120).6 Diffuse bleeding from the nasal mucosa (e.g., after
maxillectomy or palate surgery) can be stopped by irrigation with
0.05-0.1 mL/kg (cats) or 0.1-0.2 mL/kg (dogs) of a mixture of 0.25
mL 1% phenylephrine and 50 mL 2% lidocaine,7 vessel ligation, bone
wax, fibrin sealants, and many others.

ORAL INFLAMMATION
PERIODONTAL DISEASE
Gingivitis is inflammation of the gingiva. Periodontitis is
inflammation of the gingiva, periodontal ligament, alveolar bone,
and cementum (Figure 258.1). Dental plaque causes periodontal
disease, but the host’s reaction to plaque bacteria and their toxins
also plays a role in tissue destruction (gingival recession, attachment
loss, periodontal pocketing, alveolar bone resorption, tooth mobility,
and tooth loss). Affected teeth need to be scaled and polished under
anesthesia. In addition, various periodontal therapy and surgery
options (including extraction) exist. Use of antibiotics for treatment
of periodontal disease is not recommended.8

CONTACT ULCERS AND
OSTEOMYELITIS/OSTEONECROSIS
Contact ulcers tend to be located in oral mucosa facing plaque-laden
tooth surfaces. Young adult to middle-aged Cocker Spaniels,
Labrador Retrievers, Standard Poodles, Scottish Terriers, Maltese,
and Dachshunds sometimes present with severe
osteomyelitis/osteonecrosis and adjacent cellulitis (exposed infected,
inflamed, and necrotic bone and tooth roots surrounded by
ulceronecrotic oral mucosa). This can be associated with systemic
signs, such as lethargy, fever, and unwillingness to eat or drink due
to oral pain. Some of these patients also have concurrent otitis
externa, lip fold dermatitis, and pododermatitis. Treatment involves
partial or full-mouth tooth extraction; tissue debridement; pain
control; anti-inflammatory, antiseptic, and antibiotic therapy; and
nutritional support9 (ch. 81).

GINGIVAL HYPERPLASIA
Juvenile hyperplastic gingivitis can be found in immature,
adolescent, and young adult cats that present with enlarged and
inflamed gingiva (other oral mucosae are not affected) mostly
around their maxillary and mandibular cheek teeth. Certain
medications (e.g., calcium channel blockers, cyclosporine,
phenobarbital) can also cause gingival hyperplasia. Careful
gingivectomy and gingivoplasty should be performed (including
histological examination of suspicious lesions), followed by
professional dental cleaning. The owners are encouraged to perform
daily tooth brushing with an azithromycin-containing dentifrice
(8.5%). Azithromycin can reduce the occurrence of gingival
hyperplasia in dogs.10

PYOGENIC GRANULOMA
Pyogenic granuloma is a benign ulceroproliferative lesion in cats,
resulting from the maxillary fourth premolar tooth traumatizing the

gingiva, alveolar and buccal mucosa adjacent to a present or missing
mandibular first molar tooth. Surgical excision of the mass plus
blunting or extraction of the involved tooth or teeth is the treatment
of choice.11

STOMATITIS
Stomatitis in adult cats usually manifests as inflammation of the
mucosal linings of the caudal oral cavity lateral to the palatoglossal
folds, extending rostrally into gingiva, alveolar mucosa, buccal and
labial mucosa, sublingual mucosa, and occasionally also the ventral
and dorsal tongue surface. Feline calicivirus (FCV) and feline
herpesvirus-1 (FHV-1) have been implicated (ch. 205), and recent
data suggest that fungi might play a role in the etiology and
pathogenesis of feline stomatitis.12,13 Affected cats show
inappetence; weight loss; oral, nasal, and/or ocular discharge;
regional lymphadenopathy; and signs of oral pain. In severe cases,
the inflamed oral tissues become proliferative and ulcerated, and can
bleed spontaneously. An increase in serum total protein usually is
due to elevated gamma globulin concentrations. A biopsy specimen
should be obtained to rule out neoplasia or other causes of oral
inflammation. Pain management is imperative (ch. 6). Plaque
control is achieved with dental cleaning, topical and systemic
antimicrobial therapy, and partial or full-mouth tooth extraction.14
Glucocorticoids often are required to decrease inflammation, reduce
pain, and stimulate appetite. Some cats may benefit from periodic
injections of methylprednisolone acetate (Depo-Medrol) (4 mg/kg
SC or IM). Others do well with prednisolone ointment (1 mg/kg per
0.1 mL q12-24h) that is applied to the pinna of the ears. Cyclosporine
(e.g., Neoral) may be useful (start at 2.5 mg/kg PO q12h for 6 weeks
before judging effectiveness; monitor kidney values periodically;
whole-blood cyclosporine concentrations >300 ng/mL have been
associated with significant improvement of oral inflammation).15
Clinical improvement of stomatitis also was reported with bovine
lactoferrin (250 mg PO q24h). Low-dose doxycycline (1 mg/kg PO
q24h) and interferon omega (5 MU are diluted and divided as
necessary to submucosally inject all inflamed areas; the remaining 5

MU are injected into a 100 mL bag of sodium chloride and frozen in
10 mL aliquots; the client gives 1 mL PO q24h for 100 days; the 10
mL fraction in use is refrigerated and the other aliquots are kept
frozen until needed) have also been suggested as medical treatment
options for cats with stomatitis.16 Intravenous injection of fresh,
autologous, adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells resulted in
complete clinical and histological resolution or reduction in clinical
disease severity and immune modulation in most cats with severe
refractory stomatitis.17 Laser surgery (to remove proliferative tissue
and ablate inflamed mucosa) may be used as an adjunct in patients
with refractory stomatitis not responding to extractions and medical
therapy.18

EOSINOPHILIC GRANULOMA COMPLEX
Eosinophilic granuloma complex includes several conditions of the
oral mucosa (dogs and cats) and lips and skin (cats), characterized by
an eosinophilic infiltrate on histopathological examination.19
Lesions are more common in young adult female cats and male dogs.
Suggested causes include ectoparasites and other insects,
environmental allergens, or dietary hypersensitivity. Clinical signs
depend on the location of the lesion and include dysphagia, ptyalism,
and inappetence. In cats, the condition manifests either as nodules
(speckled with small, dense white or yellowish areas) at the dorsal
and lateral tongue surfaces, hard and soft palate, palatoglossal folds,
and chin, or as well-demarcated ulcers (raised edges surrounding an
ulcerated surface) on the upper lip and philtrum (occasionally also
the lower lip). In dogs, single or multiple (often confluent) ulcerated
lesions may be present on the soft palate and lateral pharyngeal
mucosa (typically in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels), or raised,
irregular, ulcerated lesions with well-demarcated edges are located
on the lateral or ventral tongue (primarily in Siberian Huskies and
Alaskan Malamutes).20 Biopsy with histopathologic evaluation is
warranted to rule out differential diagnoses, such as squamous cell
carcinoma, lymphoma, and other skin diseases. In addition to
eliminating the underlying cause, the treatment of choice is

prednisone or prednisolone (1-2 mg/kg PO q12h initially, then
tapered to the lowest effective dosage) or periodic
methylprednisolone injections (4 mg/kg SC or IM). Amoxicillinclavulanate (14 mg/kg PO q12h) also may be attempted. Surgical
excision of affected areas is rarely recommended. Untreated lesions
can result in major soft tissue loss (upper lip) and oronasal
communication (hard palate).19

AUTOIMMUNE ORAL CONDITIONS
Autoimmune diseases causing skin lesions in dogs and cats (ch. 178)
also can affect the mucocutaneous junction areas surrounding the
mouth and the oral mucosa inside the mouth (e.g., lupus
erythematosus with autoantibody production against tissue and
nuclear proteins). Occasionally, the lesions are wholly contained
within the oral cavity, as with pemphigus vulgaris and bullous
pemphigoid with autoantibody production against specific squamous
epithelial structures, or mucous membrane pemphigoid with
autoantibody production against tissue proteins. Contrary to
stomatitis in cats and contact ulceration in dogs, the hard palate
mucosa can be affected. Biopsy of the leading edge of a lesion, when
an intact blister is not found, could be sufficient. Storing the samples
in Michel’s solution is recommended by some pathologists to
preserve tissue antigenicity at ambient temperatures.21
Bullae undergo different stages, from bleb (vesicle) formation, to
erosion, to ulceration. Vesicles are characteristic, but they may no
longer be present at the time of diagnosis and are replaced by scales,
crusts, erosions and ulcers. The causative lesion in pemphigus
vulgaris is suprabasilar (intercellular clefting) with formation of
acanthocytes. The causative lesion in bullous pemphigoid is
subepidermal without formation of acanthocytes. Laminin 5 and 6,
collagen XVII, and integrin alpha-6/beta-4 have been implicated as
autoantigens in mucous membrane pemphigoid in dogs, but only
laminin 5 has been recognized in the cat. The treatment of choice is
prednisone or prednisolone (1-2 mg/kg PO q12h initially, then
tapered to the lowest effective dosage) or periodic
methylprednisolone injections (4 mg/kg SC or IM).22

HYPERSENSITIVITY AND METABOLIC
ORAL CONDITIONS
ERYTHEMA MULTIFORME AND TOXIC
EPIDERMAL NECROLYSIS (ch. 178)
Erythema multiforme is possibly mediated by deposition of immune
complexes in the superficial capillaries of the skin and less often the
oral mucosa as a result of an infection or drug exposure.23,24 Toxic
epidermal necrolysis is characterized by full-thickness coagulative
necrosis with minimal dermal inflammation25; it is an extreme form
of drug reaction, with the animal being depressed, febrile, and
inappetent. The underlying cause must preferably be eliminated
(e.g., cessation of use of a particular drug). Anti-inflammatory,
immunosuppressive, or immunomodulating therapy is instituted
(ch. 169) together with nursing care.

UREMIA
Uremia results from retention of uremic waste products after a rapid
decline in renal function26 (ch. 301). A sharp odor of ammonia in
the breath may be noticeable, and oral ulcerations can occur,
especially at the labial and buccal mucosa, lateral margins of the
tongue, lateral lip frenula, and lip commissures. Uremic vasculitis
and thrombosis can lead to necrosis and sloughing of the mucosa. In
severe cases, this may lead to sloughing of the tip of the tongue. The
lesions are often painful, contributing to anorexia in pets with kidney
disease. Any underlying condition (e.g., leptospirosis, diabetes
mellitus, etc.; ch. 171) that can produce a hypercoagulable state may
lead to thrombi formation and subsequent sloughing of the affected
areas.27 Treatment is supportive and nonspecific, until the inciting
cause can be removed or resolved, and includes pain management
(such as buprenorphine 0.01 mg/kg q8-12h, IV), bypassing the
mouth with supplemental enteral (ch. 81) or parenteral (ch. 164)
nutrition, and use of gastric protectants (sucralfate 0.5-1 g PO q46h). Topical mouthwashes, such as a mixture of diphenhydramine,
sucralfate or aluminum and magnesium hydroxide (Maalox,

Novartis), and lidocaine may provide some local pain control.
Diluted (0.12%) chlorhexidine rinse prevents secondary infection of
necrotic areas.26

ORAL FOREIGN BODY
Penetrating foreign bodies can create deep and contaminated
wounds in the sublingual area, palatoglossal fold, soft palate,
palatine tonsil, floor of the orbit, or pharyngeal wall.28 They also can
be lodged across the hard palate between maxillary cheek teeth (e.g.,
a wooden stick), entrapped in the oral mucosa (e.g., burdock and
foxtails), or caught around the tongue and saw their way into the
lingual frenulum (e.g., a needle with thread). Affected pets show
halitosis, decreased appetite and water intake, pawing at the face,
swelling in the intermandibular or neck region, sinus tracts, drooling
of clear or blood-tinged saliva, and retching, gagging, and/or
vomiting. Ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), and magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) are more helpful than radiographs in
pinpointing a hidden foreign body’s location.6 Management requires
surgical exploration, foreign body removal, wound cleansing, and, if
appropriate, drain placement and suturing. Microbial sampling is
performed, and empirical antibiotic therapy is instituted prior to
availability of culture and sensitivity results. Intraoral wounds often
are closed to prevent entrapment of food, hair, and other debris. If
the intraoral point of entry has healed by the time the patient
presents with clinical signs, the surgical approach is chosen based on
diagnostic findings to determine the most direct and safest route for
foreign body retrieval.6
