ORAL BURNS
Electric injury usually occurs in young animals that chew on power
cords.29 Affected tissues typically include the lips, cheeks, oral

mucosa, tongue, and palate. More extensive burns also affect teeth
and bones. Life-threatening complications are related to neurogenic
pulmonary edema or smoke inhalation (ch. 217). The patient
initially is stabilized, if noncardiogenic pulmonary edema has
occurred (ch. 123), and managed conservatively (wound lavage).
Later, once necrotic tissue is evident, conservative debridement may
be initiated. Tongue necrosis may cause a large piece of tissue to
slough off. Palate necrosis can cause an oronasal defect (Figure
258.2).
Thermal burns, resulting from exposure to hot items, sometimes
are seen on the nasal plane, lips, labial mucosa, tongue, and palate.
Owners are advised not to overheat food and liquids when they
attempt to make them more palatable in patients with inappetence.
Chemical burns present as acute ulcers covered by necrotic debris
from exposure to household cleaning products, phenolic compounds,
essential oils (e.g., liquid potpourri), heavy metals (i.e., thallium), or
plant toxins (e.g., Dieffenbachia). Initial therapy for thermal or
chemical burns comprises lavage with lactated Ringer’s solution,
followed by conservative management. The haircoat of an affected
pet should be cleansed if there is suspicion that it contains residuals
of the agent responsible for a chemical burn29 (ch. 132).

MASTICATORY MUSCLE MYOSITIS
Masticatory muscle myositis (MMM) is an autoimmune disease
affecting the temporal, masseter, and medial and lateral pterygoid
muscles in dogs. Large-breed, young adult to middle-aged dogs
appear to be affected most commonly.30 An acute stage,
characterized by painful muscle swelling and/or inflammation, lasts
for 2-3 weeks and may be followed by a latent stage where the animal
is apparently healthy. This is then followed by a chronic stage,
associated with muscle atrophy, or a recurrent acute stage. Dogs with
acute MMM have a history of decreased activity, lethargy, reluctance
to eat, and signs of pain on yawning or when prehending treats and
toys. They may show fever, regional lymphadenopathy, swelling of
temporal and masseter muscles (painful on palpation),
exophthalmos, and resistance or inability to open the mouth fully.

Dogs with chronic MMM usually are bright and alert, but they show
progressive atrophy of masticatory muscles, enophthalmos, and an
inability to open the mouth fully, including under general anesthesia.
Muscle swelling/atrophy can be asymmetric.30

DIAGNOSIS
A definitive diagnosis of MMM can be made if antibodies against
type 2M fibers are identified in serum and/or immune complexes
detected in biopsied muscle samples.31 A serum type 2M fiber
antibody titer of <1:100 is considered negative (a false negative is
possible if glucocorticoid therapy is started prior to blood collection),
a titer of 1:100 is borderline, and one that is >1:100 is considered
positive. CT aids in ruling out most differentials for MMM, allows
guided fine-needle aspiration of surgically inaccessible pterygoid
muscles and shows changes in size (increase in size due to edema or
inflammation; decrease in size due to atrophy, necrosis, or fibrosis),
pre-contrast tissue hypoattenuation due to edema or heterogenous
contrast enhancement due to inflammation in affected muscles, and
regional lymphadenopathy.31 Muscle biopsies (ch. 110) are taken
from areas of temporal or masseter muscles that show most obvious
contrast enhancement on CT. A 0.5- to 1-cm diameter specimen of
muscle tissue is excised, enveloped by a dry or minimally moistened
gauze sponge, and placed into a water-tight container (e.g., a 10 mL
red top tube). The sample is kept cool and shipped overnight
(Comparative Neuromuscular Laboratory, University of California,
San Diego, USA or Institute for Animal Pathology, LudwigMaximilians-University Munich, Munich, Germany). Particular
attention should be paid to complete wound closure because
glucocorticoids will delay connective tissue healing.32

Treatment
A dexamethasone injection (0.2-0.4 mg/kg IV given once after
muscle biopsy) is helpful in the immediate reduction of
inflammation in dogs with acute MMM. The patient is discharged
with prednisone (1-2 mg/kg PO q12h), usually resulting in rapid
improvement of clinical signs in acute disease (reduction of pain and

signs of systemic illness, as well as visible improvement of mouth
opening, 1-2 days after starting glucocorticoid therapy). After 2-3
weeks, the dosage can be decreased to 1 mg/kg PO q24h for another
3-4 weeks before it is slowly tapered to the lowest effective alternateday dosage over a period of 8-12 months. Dogs unable to receive
glucocorticoids, unresponsive to glucocorticoids alone, or showing
unacceptable side-effects in response to glucocorticoids might
benefit from administration of azathioprine (1-2 mg/kg PO q24h)
(chs. 144 and 169). Follow-up examinations should take place 2
weeks and 1, 2, 6, 9, and 12 months after initiation of glucocorticoid
therapy, and once every 6 to 12 months thereafter, focusing on body
weight, degree of muscle atrophy, pain upon head palpation, and
range of opening of the mouth (which is measured with a ruler
between the incisal edges of the maxillary and mandibular incisors).
Periodic antibody titer tests are important prior to decreasing
prednisone dosage, particularly when it is very low (e.g., 0.1-0.2
mg/kg PO q48h). In dogs with a relapse, treatment should be
reinstituted at the maximum prednisone dosage and slowly tapered
to the lowest possible alternate-day effective dosage.30

SALIVARY GLAND DISEASES
SIALOCELE
Sialocele, extravasation of saliva into submucosal or subcutaneous
spaces, requires surgical treatment, and the reader is referred to
surgical textbooks for information on diagnosis and treatment.29

SIALADENITIS
Sialadenitis, inflammation of a salivary gland, can be seen in middleaged to older dogs. The zygomatic salivary gland is affected most
commonly, and the dog can present with a painful swelling in the
orbital/retrobulbar area and exophthalmos. Clinical signs include
malaise, inappetence, lymphadenopathy, fever, signs of pain on
retropulsion of the eye through the closed eyelid and upon opening
the mouth, dysphagia, and mucopurulent discharge at the opening of
the duct in the mouth. The soft palate may have an asymmetric

appearance. Sialoliths can be a contributing factor. CT or MRI
should be considered to rule out differential diagnoses. Fine-needle
aspiration and cytological evaluation of the zygomatic salivary gland
(through oral mucosa or skin) and regional lymph nodes, bacterial
culture and sensitivity testing (if infection is suspected), and threeview thoracic radiographs (if neoplasia is suspected) may be
performed. A definitive diagnosis of sialadenitis requires
histopathological evaluation of an incisional biopsy. Intraoral
drainage to alleviate mucopurulent fluid accumulation and
associated pressure causing discomfort may be attempted. Medical
treatment includes management of pain (ch. 6), if present; use of
antibiotics (ch. 140), based on culture and sensitivity testing of the
fluid/tissue aspirate; and either nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory
drugs or anti-inflammatory doses of glucocorticoids (ch. 143).33

SIALADENOSIS AND NECROTIZING
SIALADENOMETAPLASIA
Sialadenosis is a non-inflammatory enlargement of a salivary gland
without obvious cytological or histological abnormalities.
Necrotizing sialometaplasia (salivary gland necrosis or infarction) is
a painful enlargement of a salivary gland with squamous metaplasia
of the salivary gland ducts and lobules and lobular ischemic necrosis.
Sialadenosis and necrotizing sialometaplasia mostly occur in young
adult to middle-aged, small breed dogs. History and clinical signs are
less severe with sialadenosis (weight loss, reluctance to exercise,
snorting, lip smacking, nasal discharge, hypersalivation,
inappetence, depression, retching and gulping). In addition to those
signs, dogs with necrotizing sialometaplasia often show gagging,
regurgitation, chronic vomiting, coughing, tachypnea, dyspnea,
reverse sneezing, and abdominal respiratory efforts. Dogs are
sensitive on palpation of the pharyngeal region, show signs of pain
associated with opening the mouth, and are depressed, nauseated,
and anorexic. A neurogenic pathogenesis is suspected to correlate
with abnormalities of the vagus nerve, and associated conditions
include esophageal disorders (ch. 259). Similar diagnostic and
therapeutic attempts as for sialadenitis should be performed. Oral
phenobarbital administration (1-2 mg/kg PO q12h) has resulted in

dramatic improvement in some cases, providing support for a
neurogenic pathogenesis.33

NON-NEOPLASTIC JAW BONE
DISORDERS
CRANIOMANDIBULAR OSTEOPATHY
Craniomandibular osteopathy is characterized by woven bone
proliferation at the ventral and caudal aspects of the mandible,
temporomandibular joint, and the tympanic bulla bilaterally in
smaller dog breeds. A thickening of the calvarium, tentorium
cerebelli, and extremities sometimes can be observed.34 The dog
may show signs of pain, unwillingness or inability to fully open the
mouth, reluctance to eat, fever, and neurological signs. Treatment
consists of anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs or glucocorticoids),
analgesics, and nutritional support (ch. 81).

CALVARIAL HYPEROSTOSIS
Calvarial hyperostosis, primarily seen in young Bull Mastiffs, is
characterized by irregular, progressive bony proliferation and
thickening of the cortical bone of the calvarium. Clinical signs
include painful swelling of the skull, exophthalmos, fever, and
lymphadenopathy. In most cases, it is self-limiting.35

FIBROUS OSTEODYSTROPHY (CH. 162)
Fibrous osteodystrophy results from a congenital condition
associated with primary hyperparathyroidism and nutritional or
renal secondary hyperparathyroidism.36 There is generalized
osteopenia with more pronounced manifestation in the jaw bones,
causing tooth mobility, facial swelling, thickened rubbery jaws
(Video 162.1

), and an ulcerated oral mucosa (ch. 162).

Radiographs display a marked decrease in bone density, loss of
normal trabecular bone structure, and loss of lamina dura. The teeth
usually do not appear to be demineralized and rarely undergo
resorption. The prognosis is very poor, except for cases of nutritional
secondary hyperparathyroidism that may be treated by feeding an
appropriately formulated diet.

BENIGN ORAL TUMORS
PAPILLOMA
Papillomas are virally-induced, cauliflower-like whitish lesions at
mucous membranes and mucocutaneous junctions of the mouth in
dogs <1 year of age. They often resolve spontaneously in 1-3 months,
unless the patient is immunocompromised; ruling out lymphoma is
particularly important in older dogs presenting with severe oral
papillomatosis.

PERIPHERAL ONTOGENIC FIBROMA
Peripheral odontogenic fibromas are mixed odontogenic tumors
(common in dogs, rare in cats) and often are located in the gingiva
near incisor, canine, or premolar teeth.37 The ossifying type
(previously called ossifying epulis) is distinguished from the
fibromatous type (previously called fibromatous epulis) by
containing varying amounts of bone-like hard tissue within the
tumor’s soft tissue. These tumors are excised together with
extraction of the involved tooth and thorough curettage of its
alveolus. Biopsy will distinguish these tumors from gingival
hyperplasia (Figure 258.3).

FIGURE 258.3 Dog with numerous peripheral
odontogenic fibromas (A). Amlodipine-induced
gingival hyperplasia in a dog (B). Cyclosporineinduced gingival hyperplasia in a cat (C). Copyright

AMELOBLASTOMA
Ameloblastomas are epithelial odontogenic tumors. The canine
acanthomatous ameloblastoma (previously called acanthomatous
epulis) is a locally-invasive tumor causing bone lysis around tooth
roots and cystic changes. Despite this locally aggressive behavior, it
does not metastasize.37 Externally, it often has a rough, cauliflower-

like surface. It occurs most commonly in the incisor and canine tooth
area. Conventional ameloblastoma is less commonly seen in the dog.

ODONTOMA
Odontomas are not true neoplasms but, rather, a conglomerate of
disorganized, normal tissue cells. Enamel, dentin, cementum, and
small tooth-like structures can compose the mass. Lesions with
characteristics resembling normal teeth are considered compound
odontomas, whereas complex odontomas have a more disorganized
arrangement.38
Other benign oral tumors that are less common include the
cementoma, giant cell granuloma, feline inductive odontogenic
tumor, amyloid-producing odontogenic tumor, plasma cell tumor,
osteoma, and lipoma.

MALIGNANT ORAL TUMORS
MELANOMA
Malignant melanoma usually occurs in older dogs with oral
pigmentation, and it is very rare in cats (also see ch. 323).39 The
tumor itself is pigmented or nonpigmented (amelanotic), grows
rapidly, and invades bone early. The tumor surface usually is
ulcerated and foul-smelling because of necrosis caused by the lesion
outgrowing its blood supply. Typical oral locations are the gingiva,
palate, dorsal surface of the tongue, and mucosal surface of the lips
and cheeks. Regional and distant metastasis is common at the time
of diagnosis.40

SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA
Nontonsillar squamous cell carcinoma typically is a tumor of older
cats and dogs, but papillary squamous cell carcinoma also can occur
in adolescent and young adult dogs (also see ch. 323).41 The tumors
are found on the gingiva as proliferative and ulcerated lesions and
less often on the mucosa of the lips, cheeks, tongue, and sublingual
area. Bone invasion is common for gingival lesions. If occurring on

the upper jaw in cats, the tumor can be less protuberant, while bone
invasion is more severe. Use of flea collars, eating canned tuna and
canned cat food, and exposure to environmental tobacco smoke have
been identified as risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma in cats.42
The rate of metastasis to the mandibular lymph nodes can be >30%
in cats, while distant metastasis may occur late in the disease
process.43 Tonsillar and lingual squamous cell carcinomas in dogs
also are highly metastatic.

FIBROSARCOMA
Fibrosarcomas are the second most common malignant oral tumor
in cats and the third most common in dogs (also see ch. 326). They
tend to occur in young adult to middle-aged large-breed dogs and
older smaller dogs, affecting the gingiva, lip/cheek mucosa, or the
hard and soft palate. Often, they appear as a protuberant, ulcerated
lesion. They can arise from the lateral surface of the incisive bone
and maxilla, presenting a slowly enlarging, firm mass at the muzzle.
Fibrosarcomas are highly invasive. Regional and distant metastasis
are less common compared to malignant melanoma and squamous
cell carcinoma. Low-grade fibrosarcomas appear benign
histologically but are malignant biologically.44

OSTEOSARCOMA
Osteosarcoma affects the mandible and, less often, the maxilla, often
manifesting as a fleshy, ulcerative or necrotic oral mass with
extensive radiographic evidence of bone lysis rather than hard tissue
proliferation (also see ch. 326). Metastasis seems to be less common
than for limb osteosarcoma.45 A multilobular tumor of bone is a less
aggressive variant of osteosarcoma, manifesting as a hard, wellcircumscribed, less ulcerated mass on the maxilla, palate, ramus of
the mandible, zygomatic arch, or calvarium. It appears
radiographically as a combination of mineralized and nonmineralized tissue (“popcorn ball” appearance).
Peripheral nerve sheath tumors sometimes are misdiagnosed as
fibrosarcomas (also see chs. 249 and 252). They tend to grow along

major nerves (e.g., infraorbital nerve, inferior alveolar nerve, major
palatine nerve) of the face, upper and lower jaw, and palate.
Other less common, malignant oral lesions include
hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325), lymphoma (ch. 322), mast cell tumor
(ch. 327), and anaplastic or undifferentiated tumors.

APPROACH TO EVALUATING ORAL
MASSES
The TNM (tumor, node, metastasis) system aids in describing the
clinical extent (staging) of neoplastic disease through evaluation of
the primary tumor, regional lymph nodes, and distant sites of
possible metastasis (ch. 316).46 Three-view thoracic radiographs
and occasionally also an abdominal ultrasound exam, are performed
prior to placing an oral tumor patient under anesthesia, particularly
when a malignant oral lesion is suspected. Whereas metastatic
lesions <5 mm in diameter might not be visible on radiographs,
inclusion of the thorax during CT of the head (to evaluate the
primary tumor) and neck (to evaluate lymph nodes) can allow for
detection of metastatic lesions <2 mm in diameter.47 The use of size
4 dental radiographic phosphor plates is superior to standard
medical radiography in the evaluation of quality and extent of bony
lesions of the tooth-bearing jaws.
A biopsy is obtained from an area that can be included in the
definitive resection. Cytological sampling can be performed in the
awake or sedated patient. Fine-needle aspiration techniques are
useful for lesions that exfoliate well, and sampling often is performed
with a 22-gauge needle by means of a needle biopsy (“woodpecker
method”) or needle aspiration (ch. 83). Palpation of lymph nodes is
neither sensitive nor specific in detecting regional lymph node
metastasis.48 Therefore, cytological examination of lymph node
needle aspirates should be performed, which can be adequate for
diagnosing metastatic melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma, but
is less satisfactory for other oral tumors (ch. 88).
Sampling of tissue for histological evaluation requires general
anesthesia and microscopic examination of a formalin-fixed
specimen. Rongeurs are ideal for bone samples and scalpel blades for

incisional and excisional soft tissue sampling. Multiple samples
should be obtained. Hemostasis is achieved with digital pressure,
and biopsy sites of more deeply invading tumors are sutured. The
specimen is placed in 10% buffered formalin at 1 part tissue to 10
parts fixative. Parotid, mandibular, and medial and lateral
retropharyngeal lymph nodes should be preferably evaluated
histologically after excision.49 A negative lymph node biopsy,
however, does not preclude the possibility of regional metastasis,
which may occur along perineural or vascular routes, or metastasis
to other less-accessible lymph nodes. If cytological or histological
results do not match the clinical findings, a second, deeper, and
larger specimen needs to be obtained. A mucosal flap could be raised
to access deeper tissue for tumors that are covered by a layer of
variably-thick normal tissue.

OUTCOME AND CONCLUSION
Client communication is extremely important prior to embarking on
an involved oral surgical procedure (ch. 1). In general, home care in
the immediate postoperative period, long-term home oral hygiene,
and the need for periodic reexaminations should be discussed with
every client. Considering that general anesthesia usually is required
to assess lesions and perform treatment, the risk of perioperative
complications also should be discussed. Additionally, some of the
diseases discussed in this chapter require medical treatment for the
rest of the patient’s life or surgical procedures that could lead to a
change in the patient’s esthetic appearance or functionality.
A diagnosis of a malignant or locally aggressive oral tumor should
lead to an in-depth discussion about the biological behavior of the
tumor, possibility of intraoperative complications, expectations in
terms of quality of life for the pet, life expectancy after the procedure,
life expectancy if surgery is not performed, and non-surgical
treatment options (such as radiation therapy, immunotherapy,
and/or chemotherapy). Collaboration with medical and radiation
oncologists is helpful to allow the client make an informed decision
that fits the pet and its family.

NORMAL ANATOMY AND FUNCTION
The oral cavity, oropharynx, and esophagus can be thought of as a
series of expanding and contracting chambers, divided by muscular
sphincters. Propulsion of a bolus through this part of the alimentary
tract is the result of positive pressure developed behind the bolus, as
well as a vacuum or negative pressure developed in front of it. Any
disturbance in the functional or anatomical elements or coordination
of this system can result in abnormal transfer of a bolus from the oral
cavity to the stomach, resulting in swallowing impairment. The term
“dysphagia” sometimes is used for denoting a sensation (symptom)
in human medicine, and some veterinary gastroenterologists,
including the author, prefer to use the term “swallowing
impairment” instead for veterinary patients. Swallowing impairment
occurs relatively frequently in dogs and there is an extensive list of
possible causes (Box 259.1). Swallowing impairment is far less
common in cats, with the exception of structural causes of
oropharyngeal (OP) disease associated with oral tumors, ulcers, and
gingivostomatitis, and esophageal disorders associated with
esophagitis, esophageal stricture formation, and less commonly, a
sliding hiatal hernia.
The swallowing mechanism is complex, involving 31 pairs of
striated muscles and 5 cranial nerves (CNs V, VII-XI sensory and
motor fibers, and motor fibers of XII), and the swallowing center in
the reticular formation of the brainstem (ch. 241). The normal
swallowing reflex is a 4-phase process: oral preparatory, oral,
pharyngeal, and esophageal.1 The esophagus transports the bolus
from the pharynx into the stomach. The outer coat of esophageal
loose connective tissue, the adventitia, is present in the cervical
portion but is largely replaced by serosa in the thorax. In dogs, the
muscularis of the esophagus is entirely striated from the
cricopharyngeus muscle to the gastroesophageal junction, whereas in
cats, the striated muscle is replaced by smooth muscle in the distal
one-third of the esophagus. The inner esophageal wall consists of
submucosa and mucosa, divided by fenestrated muscularis mucosae,
which is more prominent in the thoracic esophagus. The submucosa
contains blood vessels, nerves, and glands. The mucosa is composed
of keratinized, stratified squamous epithelium. Innervation of the

striated muscle of the esophagus in dogs and cats is provided by
special visceral efferent neurons from the bilateral nucleus ambiguus
in the medulla oblongata. Axons are carried in the vagus and
distributed with the pharyngoesophageal and recurrent laryngeal
nerves, and the vagal trunks. The smooth muscle innervations in cats
arise from the rostral bilateral nucleus ambiguus via general visceral
efferents, and are also distributed via the branches of the bilateral
vagus nerve.

PHASES OF SWALLOWING
Oral Preparatory, Oral, and Pharyngeal Phases
The oral preparatory phase is voluntary and begins as food or liquid
enters the mouth. Mastication and lubrication of food are hallmarks
of this phase. Abnormalities are associated with dental disease,
xerostomia, and weakness of the lips (CN V, VII), tongue (CN XII),
and cheeks (CN V, VII) (ch. 249). The oral phase consists of the
muscular events responsible for movement of the bolus from the
tongue to the pharynx, and is facilitated by the tongue, jaw, and
hyoid muscle movements. The pharyngeal phase starts when the
bolus reaches the tonsils, and begins with elevation of the soft palate
to prevent the bolus from entering the nasopharynx, elevation and
forward movement of the larynx and hyoid, retroflexion of the
epiglottis, and closure of the vocal folds to close the entrance into the
larynx. This is followed by synchronized contraction of the middle

and inferior constrictor muscles of the pharynx together with
relaxation of the cricopharyngeus muscle that makes up much of the
upper esophageal sphincter (UES). This allows passage of the bolus
into the esophagus (Figure 259.1). Respiration is briefly halted
(apneic moment) during the pharyngeal phase.2
Abnormalities of the pharyngeal phase of swallowing include
pharyngeal weakness and pharyngeal obstruction. Synchrony
between constriction of the pharyngeal muscles and relaxation of the
cricopharyngeus muscle is essential to allow passage of the bolus into
the esophagus. Despite the myriad causes of OP swallowing
impairment, the pathophysiologic end results fall into 1 of 2
interrelated categories: (1) abnormalities of bolus transfer or (2)
abnormalities of airway protection (ch. 221). Abnormalities of bolus
transfer can be further grouped into those caused by (a) OP pump
failure (pharyngeal weakness); (b) OP and pharyngo-UES
asynchrony (neuropathies); and (c) pharyngeal outflow obstruction
(cricopharyngeus muscle achalasia, tumors of the pharynx, foreign
bodies).

Esophageal Phase
The esophageal phase is involuntary, beginning with relaxation of
the UES and movement of the bolus into the esophagus. Sensory
feedback likely plays a role in regulating the speed and intensity of
peristaltic waves, depending on bolus characteristics. Primary
peristalsis is triggered by the swallowing center to activate lower
motor neurons and spearhead bolus transit. Secondary peristalsis is
stimulated by mechanical distension of the esophagus and assists in
clearing residual material. Multiple rapid swallows induce a period of
latency called deglutitive inhibition that terminates with an
accentuated peristaltic contraction. Relaxation of the lower
esophageal sphincter (LES) in advance of the propagated pressures
permits food to empty into the stomach and once the bolus passes,
the LES contracts to prevent reflux of gastric contents into the
esophagus. Transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxation (TLESR)
is a vasovagal-mediated reflex that is pivotal for venting gas from the
stomach, but can also be associated with gastroesophageal reflux
(GER).

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH
HISTORY AND CLINICAL SIGNS
The diagnosis of disorders affecting the OP phase of swallowing can
be challenging. Clinical signs can include repetitive swallowing,
gagging, retching, and coughing within seconds of drinking water or
attempting to swallow food, nasal regurgitation of water or food, and
food falling from the mouth during swallowing (ch. 47), and
recurrent aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217). In contrast, the hallmark
signs of esophageal swallowing impairment include regurgitation
(solids or liquids) typically minutes to hours following ingestion of a
meal, odynophagia (painful swallowing), repeated swallowing
attempts, and excessive salivation (ch. 48). Regurgitation of food or
water is the most consistent sign of esophageal disease and must be
differentiated from the signs of OP swallowing impairment or
vomiting. Pharyngeal or esophageal disease may be part of a
systemic disease in animals manifesting signs of swallowing
impairment only, underscoring the importance of a comprehensive
systemic evaluation. The assessment of dogs and cats with signs of
pharyngeal or esophageal swallowing impairment should include a
review of signalment, medication history (notably doxycycline,
clindamycin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories), and asking about
recent anesthesia. The age of onset, whether the onset of signs was
sudden or gradual, and whether signs have been progressive should
be determined. Features of swallowing impairment (between meals
or while eating; solid food, liquids, or both; how quickly signs occur
relative to swallowing) are important, as are other clinical signs
(coughing, dysphonia, odynophagia, or evidence of polyneuropathy
[ch. 252] including weakness, painful or stiff gait, exercise
intolerance). In brachycephalic dogs in particular, the presence and
evolution of upper airway signs should be determined (ch. 213).
Physical (prefeeding assessment, ch. 3) and neurologic (ch. 241)
examinations and assessing laboratory tests are valuable before
watching swallowing and using imaging studies and endoscopic
evaluations.

SIGNALMENT

Causes of OP swallowing impairment in puppies include cleft palate
(ch. 213), cricopharyngeus muscle dysfunction, muscular dystrophy,
and pharyngeal weakness. Breeds with a hereditary predisposition or
high incidence of OP swallowing impairment include the Golden
Retriever (pharyngeal weakness; cricopharyngeal muscle
asynchrony; muscular dystrophy),3 Cocker and Springer Spaniels,
Maltese, Miniature Dachshund, Toy Poodle (cricopharyngeal muscle
dysfunction); Bouvier des Flandres, Cavalier King Charles Spaniel,
Welsh Corgi, Rottweiler, German Shorthaired Pointer (muscular
dystrophy)4; and Boxer and Newfoundland (inflammatory
myopathy). Large-breed dogs are predisposed to masticatory muscle
disorders. A familial predisposition for congenital megaesophagus
has been suggested in the Great Dane, German Shepherd Dog,
Labrador Retriever, Irish Setter, Chinese Shar-Pei, Newfoundland,
Miniature Schnauzer, and Fox Terrier breeds.5 Congenital
megaesophagus is rare in cats, although Siamese are predisposed.
Acquired idiopathic megaesophagus is more commonly recognized in
large-breed dogs.

PHYSICAL AND NEUROLOGIC
EXAMINATION
Physical examination of the animal with a swallowing impairment
includes careful examination of the oropharynx, using sedation or
anesthesia if necessary, to help rule out dental disease, foreign
bodies, cleft palate, glossal abnormalities, and OP tumors (ch. 258).
The pharynx and neck should be palpated carefully for masses,
asymmetry, or pain and the chest auscultated carefully for evidence
of aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217). Complete physical (ch. 3) and
neurologic (ch. 241) examinations may reveal evidence of a
generalized neuromuscular disorder: muscle atrophy, stiffness,
and/or decreased or absent spinal reflexes. The gag reflex does not
reliably indicate effective pharyngeal swallowing nor adequacy of
deglutitive airway protection (ch. 47).6

OBSERVATION OF EATING AND
DRINKING
Carefully observing the animal suspected of having a swallowing
impairment while it eats (kibble and canned food) and drinks is
essential. Dogs with an abnormal oral phase of swallowing typically
have difficulty with prehension or aboral transport of a bolus to the
tongue base. Dogs with OP swallowing impairment affecting the
pharyngeal phase of swallowing often have nonspecific signs:
gagging, retching, and multiple swallowing attempts before a bolus is
moved successfully into the proximal esophagus (

Video 259.1).

These pets often show an abnormal transport of a bolus from the
oropharynx to the hypopharynx or from the hypopharynx to the
proximal esophagus. Cricopharyngeal muscle dysfunction, with signs
similar to those seen with pharyngeal disorders, causes abnormal
bolus transport through the UES. Dogs with esophageal strictures or
esophagitis typically exhibit evidence of regurgitation or
odynophagia seconds to minutes following bolus swallowing,
whereas dogs with megaesophagus can exhibit evidence of
regurgitation hours following ingestion of a meal. Short video-clips
recorded by the owner can be very helpful in the appropriate
assessment of the patient.

LABORATORY TESTING
Comprehensive laboratory testing is warranted in animals with OP
or esophageal swallowing impairment. Testing should include a
complete blood count (CBC), serum chemistry panel (including
creatine kinase [CK; ch. 66] activity and electrolyte concentrations),
urinalysis, evaluation of thyroid function (ch. 285), and
acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody titer for acquired myasthenia
gravis (MG; ch. 253). Persistently elevated CK activity (2,00020,000 IU/L) could indicate generalized myositis, whereas marked
CK increases (>20,000 IU/L) are more suggestive of a necrotizing or
dystrophic myopathy. Normal CK activities do not rule out
myopathy, particularly when focal (masticatory muscle myositis
[MMM]; ch. 258) or chronic. Acquired MG is an important

neuromuscular cause of OP or esophageal swallowing impairment,
causing pharyngeal, esophageal, and/or laryngeal weakness without
clinically detectable muscle weakness in the extremities. Pharyngeal
weakness as the only clinical sign of MG has been described in 1% of
dogs with MG.7 The AChR antibody test should be performed in all
pets with acquired swallowing impairment that do not have a
structural or mechanical cause for their signs (ch. 253). However,
this test is not useful for congenital MG. Also of note, if the onset of
clinical signs is recent and the antibody titer is between 0.3-0.6
nmoL/L in dogs, retesting 4-6 weeks later may be of value, as a
significant number of dogs with acute onset of disease or early
clinical signs can have antibody titers in the “gray zone” that lag
behind the clinical signs.

the diagnostic and therapeutic considerations for the

CERVICAL AND THORACIC
RADIOGRAPHY
The pharynx of healthy animals is air-filled and easily seen on
radiographs. The size of the air-filled space can be decreased by
inflammation/edema, neoplasia, or elongation of the soft palate and
it can appear increased with pharyngeal or UES dysfunction, chronic
respiratory (inspiratory) disease, or chronic severe megaesophagus.
The normal esophagus is not visible on survey radiographs, except
after aerophagia due to excitement, nausea, respiratory distress, or
anesthesia.

VIDEOFLUOROSCOPIC SWALLOW
STUDY (VFSS)
Contrast videofluoroscopy involves real-time images of the animal
swallowing liquid barium or barium-soaked kibble (

Videos

221.1, 221.2, 259.2, 259.3) and is one of the most important
procedures for assessing the functional integrity of the swallow reflex
(Figure 259.2). VFSSs usually involve assessment of 5 swallows of
5-10 mL of 60% liquid barium or iodinated contrast or 5 swallows of
canned food and 5 swallows of kibble soaked in barium or iodinated
contrast. Videofluoroscopy is used to determine the sequence of
events that make up a swallow and to time these events in relation to
one another. Movement of certain anatomic structures can be
measured in relation to a fixed point to assess function further.
Swallowing events that occur out of sequence, at inappropriate
times, or with reduced vigor can cause significant morbidity.
VFSSs in dogs in a sitting position are significantly more likely to
result in generation of primary peristaltic waves for both liquid and
kibble boluses. Alterations in body position (sitting versus lateral
recumbency) do not appear to affect measuring pharyngeal
constriction ratios or the timing of swallowing in healthy dogs.
However, cervical esophageal transit is significantly delayed when
dogs are positioned in lateral recumbency.8
When evaluating the timing of the swallow, the starting point is
the frame in which the epiglottis closes over the larynx. Frames (1/30
second) are counted until observation of maximal pharyngeal
contraction and the opening and closing of the UES. The swallow is
considered complete when the epiglottis is observed to reopen,
usually after 5 or 6 frames (0.17-0.2 seconds) in healthy dogs.9 A
contrast videofluoroscopy method for quantifying pharyngeal
contractility in dogs has been described.10 The pharyngeal
constriction ratio is calculated by dividing the pharyngeal area at
maximum contraction by the pharyngeal area at rest. As pharyngeal
contractility diminishes, the ratio approaches 1.10 This simple
procedure provides important information regarding the strength of
pharyngeal contraction in dogs with swallowing impairment.

LARYNGOSCOPY, PHARYNGOSCOPY,
AND ESOPHAGOSCOPY
Thorough laryngeal examination (ch. 214;

Video 214.1) is

important in all animals with OP and esophageal swallowing
impairment, to rule out laryngeal paralysis or paresis associated with
a polyneuropathy (ch. 252). Geriatric large-breed dogs may develop
progressive generalized neuropathy with associated pharyngeal
weakness, OP swallowing impairment, and esophageal dysmotility.11
Pharyngoscopy and esophagoscopy (ch. 107) provide information
about these areas, but both procedures are of limited diagnostic
utility for evaluating functional disorders in anesthetized animals.
Esophagoscopy is helpful for diagnosing esophagitis, esophageal
strictures or webs (that can be missed on barium swallow studies),
and hiatal hernias.

ELECTRODIAGNOSTIC TESTING
Electromyography (EMG) and measurement of motor and sensory
nerve conduction velocities (NCVs, performed under general
anesthesia) can supply nonspecific information regarding a
myopathy or neuropathy (ch. 111) and assist in selecting the optimal
anatomic site for biopsy. Such testing should include the pharyngeal
muscles and tongue.

MUSCLE AND NERVE BIOPSIES
Muscle and nerve biopsies usually are integral to reaching a specific
diagnosis (ch. 110). Muscle biopsies should be collected early in the
course of an evaluation in animals with suspected neuromuscular
disease before fibrosis and myofiber loss is extensive but after a
negative serum AChR antibody titer has been obtained. Biopsies of
pharyngeal and cricopharyngeus muscles should be obtained in dogs
with OP swallowing impairment.12

ESOPHAGEAL MANOMETRY
Esophageal manometry allows the pressures in the esophageal
lumen and sphincters to be measured to assess neuromuscular
activity. High-resolution manometry (HRM) involves up to 36
pressure sensors13 with results displayed as a spatiotemporal plot of
esophageal pressure activity. It can be employed in awake dogs and
provides a sensitive functional assessment of the UES, esophagus,
and LES.13

ENDOLUMINAL FUNCTIONAL LUMEN
IMAGING PROBE (ENDOFLIP)
An endoluminal functional lumen imaging probe (EndoFLIP) utilizes
high-resolution impedance planimetry to analyze the cross-sectional
area and distensibility of the esophagus and esophagogastric
junction (EGJ).14 The balloon can be volumetrically distended to
measure the EGJ distensibility index and can evaluate esophageal
motility. It is increasingly utilized to evaluate EGJ outflow
obstruction or achalasia in humans and may have utility in dogs and
cats.

ESOPHAGEAL pH/IMPEDANCE
TESTING
Esophageal pH/impedance testing is used for evaluating acid and
non-acid reflux in animals with suspected GER, unexplained
esophagitis, or hiatal hernias.15,16 The catheter-free Bravo pH
Monitoring System (Medtronic) is revolutionizing esophageal pH
testing because it allows people and animals to maintain their diet
and activities during testing. While traditional transnasal pH
catheters can cause discomfort and are easily dislodged, drawbacks
of the Bravo system are that it only records esophageal pH and does
not utilize impedance technology that allows more accurate
measurement of both acid and non-acid reflux events.

DISORDERS OF THE PHARYNX
PHARYNGITIS
Anatomy, Causes, Signs
The pharynx is divided into three regions: nasopharynx, oropharynx,
and laryngopharynx (ch. 213). Clinical manifestations vary
depending on location and extent of etiology, inflammation, and
involvement of adjacent structures. Pharyngeal inflammation can
occur from foreign bodies, obstructive masses (nasopharyngeal
polyps, lymphoma, squamous cell carcinoma), infectious disease,
ingestion of caustic or irritating substances, and as an extension of
stomatitis, rhinitis, or sinusitis. The most common clinical
manifestations include dysphonia, snoring, gagging, coughing,
swallowing impairment, hyporexia, and hypersalivation. Tonsillitis is
often recognized in association with pharyngitis.

Diagnosis and Treatment
History and oral examination are usually sufficient to confirm
pharyngitis, although a comprehensive oral exam under sedation
(ch. 258) or rhinoscopy with retroflex nasopharyngoscopy (ch. 89)
may be necessary if clinical signs remain suggestive despite a normal
oral exam in the awake patient. Survey radiographs of the cervical
region might be unrewarding unless a radiopaque foreign body or
pharyngitis secondary to extrapharyngeal disease is present.
Removal or treatment of the primary cause is essential. Analgesics,
topical antimicrobial rinses, systemic antimicrobials, as well as
hydration and nutritional support are important. Nasopharyngeal
polyps in cats with normal bullae may be removed by traction
avulsion (ch. 213). Nasopharyngeal stenosis can be treated by
balloon dilation (ch. 114).

PHARYNGEAL WEAKNESS
Anatomy, Causes, Signs
OP pump failure (pharyngeal weakness) is a disruption in the
coordinated transport of food and water from the oropharynx to the

hypopharynx, or from the hypopharynx into the esophagus.
Pharyngeal weakness can occur secondary to morphologic
abnormalities (infection, inflammation, trauma, neoplasia,
obstruction of the UES [cricopharyngeus muscle achalasia]) or from
functional (neuromuscular disease) causes. Specific neuromuscular
disorders that should be considered include MG (ch. 253), muscular
dystrophy, polymyositis, hypothyroidism (ch. 285), and cranial
neuropathies (ch. 249). Clinical signs commonly include dysphonia,
gagging, swallowing impairment, repeated swallowing attempts of a
single bolus, and coughing.

Diagnosis and Treatment
Survey thoracic and cervical radiographs should be obtained in all
dogs. Then, a VFSS can demonstrate absence of aboral pharyngeal
contraction, incomplete bolus transport, and occasional
nasopharyngeal reflux of barium. Fluoroscopy is pivotal for
differentiating pharyngeal weakness from cricopharyngeus muscle
dysfunction. A systemic workup (serum CK activity, AChR antibody
titer, thyroid hormone testing, electrodiagnostics) is warranted in an
effort to rule out systemic disease and an underlying neuropathy or
myopathy. Therapy of pharyngeal weakness secondary to underlying
neuromuscular disease is mostly palliative, particularly when an
underlying cause cannot be identified, and includes enteral
nutritional support, alterations in diet and water consistency, and
feedings from an elevated position. Dogs with MG should be
managed with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., pyridostigmine,
1-3 mg/kg PO q8-12h). Glucocorticoids (e.g., 1-2 mg/kg prednisolone
or equivalent PO q12h with gradual taper over the course of 10-12
weeks depending on response) or cyclosporine (5 mg/kg PO q12-24h
for 10-12 weeks) are utilized to manage inflammatory
polymyopathies (chs. 144, 169), and thyroid replacement therapy is
warranted in animals with documented hypothyroidism (ch. 285).

DISORDERS OF THE ESOPHAGUS
CRICOPHARYNGEUS MUSCLE DYSFUNCTION

Definition and Clinical Signs
Cricopharyngeus muscle dysfunction is a congenital or acquired
neuromuscular disorder characterized by failure of the UES to relax
(achalasia) or a lack of coordination between UES relaxation and
pharyngeal contraction (asynchrony). Cricopharyngeus muscle
asynchrony is essentially a “pump problem,” whereby the weak
pharyngeal muscles are unable to propel the bolus through the UES.
The etiology of neither condition is determined, although
preliminary studies are supportive of an underlying focal
neuropathy. Affected animals demonstrate progressive swallowing
impairment (typically worse when drinking water) at the time of, or
shortly after, weaning. Clinical signs are characterized by repeated
attempts to swallow, gagging, retching, and nasal regurgitation
(Video 259.1

). The clinical signs of dogs with cricopharyngeus

muscle achalasia are indistinguishable from those of dogs with
cricopharyngeus muscle asynchrony. Physical examination may
reveal evidence of aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217).

Diagnosis and Treatment
Dogs suspected of having cricopharyngeus muscle dysfunction
should be thoroughly evaluated prior to considering surgical
intervention, to ensure that systemic disorders (myopathies,
polyneuropathies [ch. 252]) have been ruled out with AChR
antibody titers (ch. 253), serum CK activity (ch. 66), EMG (ch.
111), and muscle biopsy (ch. 110). It is essential to ensure that
aspiration pneumonia is properly managed (ch. 217).17 Radiographs
may help rule out some structural causes of swallowing impairment
(foreign body, mass); however, a VFSS is the diagnostic procedure of
choice (Video 259.2

). Many affected dogs with cricopharyngeus

muscle achalasia have a prominent cricopharyngeal “bar” visible on
videofluoroscopy that is indicative of a fibrosed cricopharyngeus
muscle (Figures 259.3 and 259.4). Static contrast radiographs may
demonstrate barium retention in the pharynx or aspiration into the
trachea; however, static studies do not allow the functional integrity
of the UES or the coordinated contraction of the pharynx and
relaxation of the UES to be evaluated.

Definitive treatment for cricopharyngeus muscle achalasia
involves surgical myotomy or myectomy of the cricopharyngeus
muscle. The cricopharyngeus and thyropharyngeal muscles are
approached by standard ventral midline with 180° rotation of the
larynx on its longitudinal axis or via a lateral approach with 90°
rotation of the larynx.18 Cricopharyngeus myotomy involves
transecting the cricopharyngeus muscle to the level of the pharyngeal
mucosa. A closed endoscopic CO2 laser cricopharyngeus myotomy is
being increasingly used in people and dogs.19
Cricopharyngeus muscle asynchrony can also be managed
successfully via myectomy, and one report documented successful
bilateral cricopharyngeus per myectomy to manage an 8-month-old
dog with cricopharyngeus muscle asynchrony after initially failing
standard unilateral cricopharyngeus myectomy.20 VFSS assessment
of dogs with cricopharyngeus muscle asynchrony frequently reveals
concurrent pharyngeal weakness, and caution should be heeded
before performing surgery in these patients because the swallowing
impairment can be exacerbated if the pharyngeal weakness is not
secondary to the obstructing UES.

FIGURE 259.5 Severe esophagitis characterized
by severe erythema, ulceration, and a granular
mucosa in a 3-year-old Labrador Retriever secondary
to gastroesophageal reflux during general anesthesia.
A less invasive procedure for the temporary resolution of
cricopharyngeus muscle achalasia involves the injection of
botulinum toxin into the cricopharyngeus muscle.21 Botulinum toxin
A blocks the presynaptic release of acetylcholine. In a dosedependent manner, it weakens contraction when injected into the
target muscle and has been successfully used in people and dogs for
the temporary management of esophageal achalasia. The toxin is

reconstituted just before injection with 0.9% sterile saline to 25
units/mL and is injected into the cricopharyngeus muscle in 3 sites
(10-15 units per site) using a transbronchial needle. The limited
duration of effect (∼3-4 months) can be used to screen dogs that
might benefit from myectomy, because animals that respond well to
the toxin should do well with surgical myectomy.
An effort to identify the optimal consistency of food and water
(adding commercial food thickeners such as “Thick-It”) for these
dogs can also be helpful. Some patients succumb to repeated bouts of
aspiration pneumonia and malnutrition. Enteral feeding via a
percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube is a viable alternative
(ch. 81); however, silent aspiration and pneumonia can still occur.
Improved clinical, functional, and fluoroscopic outcomes following
serial double-balloon dilation for cricopharyngeus muscle
dysfunction has also been described in people.22

ESOPHAGITIS
Anatomy, Cause, Clinical Signs
Esophagitis is an acute or chronic inflammatory disorder of the
esophageal mucosa that occasionally involves the underlying
submucosa and muscularis. It may result from a variety of causes,
including ingestion of caustic agents, chronic vomiting, esophageal
foreign bodies, embrittled nasoesophageal or esophagostomy feeding
tubes and GER associated with general anesthesia or hiatal hernia.
Orally administered doxycycline and clindamycin have caused “pillinduced” esophagitis, particularly in cats.23 GER during anesthesia
precedes development of benign esophageal stricture in 46-65% of
cases and represents the most common cause of high-grade
esophagitis and stricture formation in dogs.24 Relaxation of the LES
is mediated by non-adrenergic non-cholinergic pathways and has
been shown to occur with the administration of commonly utilized
injectable pre-anesthetic and inhalant anesthetic agents.25,26 In
addition, TLESRs can also cause GER during general anesthesia, and
the loss of the swallow reflex during anesthesia can precipitate
markedly prolonged acid clearance times. The prolonged exposure of

the esophageal mucosa to acid is an important cause of esophagitis
and potential stricture formation, particularly when pH is <4.0 as
the proteolytic pH range for the conversion of pepsinogen to pepsin
is between 1.5 and 3.5.27 In addition, esophagitis decreases LES tone,
which leads to increased reflux and mucosal inflammation.
Disturbances in esophageal motility may occur as a sequela of
esophagitis, regardless of cause.
The clinical signs of esophagitis are dependent on the severity of
inflammation, extent of esophageal involvement, and type of injury.
Animals with mild inflammation may exhibit no clinical signs or can
exhibit a hard swallow (ch. 11), whereas animals with moderate-tosevere esophagitis may exhibit signs of anorexia, swallowing
impairment, odynophagia, regurgitation, and hypersalivation.
Coughing may be observed with concurrent aspiration pneumonia.

Diagnosis and Treatment
Results of CBC, serum biochemistry profile, and urinalysis are
usually unremarkable, and the esophagus can either appear normal
or show evidence of fluid in the distal esophagus on thoracic
radiographs. Aspiration pneumonia may be evident in the dependent
areas of the lung (ch. 217). Segmental or diffuse esophageal
dilatation may be seen with severe mucosal inflammation. VFSS may
confirm irregular esophageal surface, esophageal dysmotility (Video
259.3

), or stricture formation. Definitive diagnosis of esophagitis

requires endoscopy and esophageal biopsy; however, presumptive
diagnosis is often made from the appearance of the esophageal
mucosa: erythema and a granular surface with areas of ulceration
and active bleeding (Figure 259.5). Mild esophagitis may have a
normal endoscopic appearance and could only be confirmed
histopathologically, but collection of a biopsy is rarely indicated.
Lesions are usually most evident in the distal esophagus, adjacent to
and including the LES.
Mild esophagitis usually resolves with minimal treatment other
than feeding smaller-sized, fat-restricted canned meals frequently to
enhance gastric emptying and minimize GER. Animals with
moderate to severe esophagitis or those exhibiting signs of

swallowing impairment, regurgitation, salivation, or anorexia should
be managed with gastric acid suppressants and prokinetics. The
benefits of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), such as omeprazole, in
people with moderate to severe GER have been documented and
several studies have shown the superior acid suppressive effects of
PPIs compared to the H2-receptor antagonists (famotidine,
ranitidine).28,29 The PPIs are administered orally or IV (1-1.5 mg/kg
q 12 h) and should be administered for 6-8 weeks if managing
erosive esophagitis, before gradually tapering the drug to avoid acidrebound hypersecretion. Sucralfate, which adheres to mucosal
defects, can be added as a suspension (0.5-1 g PO q8h) for managing
reflux esophagitis. It binds to eroded mucosa and provides effective
barrier protection against refluxed barrier contents. However, the coadministration of sucralfate with PPIs does not appear to hasten
recovery of erosive esophagitis in people, and limited esophageal
retention time may decrease effectiveness. In a study of technetiumlabeled sucralfate, the drug was retained within the esophagus for 3
hours in <50% of the patients with reflux esophagitis.30 In addition,
sucralfate deposited in a non-acidified esophagus is rapidly cleared
and poorly timed to provide protection against reflux injury.31
Prokinetic agents such as cisapride (0.5-1 mg/kg PO q8-12h) or
metoclopramide (0.2-0.4 mg/kg SC or IV bolus q8h, or 1-2
mg/kg/24 h IV constant rate infusion [CRI]) can be used to increase
LES tone and enhance gastric emptying. Cisapride is a more potent
prokinetic than metoclopramide and is more effective at reducing
GER in dogs.13 Broad-spectrum antibiotics are recommended for
animals with aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217). The duration of acidsuppressant therapy depends on the severity of the esophagitis and
clinical signs, ranging from 1-2 weeks (mild cases) to 6-8 weeks
(moderate to severe esophagitis). Combined cisapride, sucralfate
(particularly if acid-reflux), and omeprazole is effective for the
management of severe esophagitis caused by persistent vomiting,
GER, or foreign body induced trauma.

in lateral recumbency in a 2-year-old mix-breed dog
documenting a focal esophageal stricture (arrow)
secondary to severe gastroesophageal reflux.

ESOPHAGEAL STRICTURE
Definition, Anatomy, Clinical Signs
Esophageal stricture, an abnormal narrowing of the esophageal
lumen, is most commonly caused by GER during general anesthesia,
chemical injury from swallowed substances, esophageal foreign
bodies, esophageal surgery, or intraluminal or extraluminal mass
lesions (neoplasia or abscess). Cats are particularly susceptible to
doxycycline and clindamycin-associated esophagitis and subsequent
esophageal stricture.23 GER during general anesthesia has preceded
stricture in up to 65% of cases. Clinical signs are seen about 7-8 days
post-anesthesia.32 The incidence of GER in dogs during anesthesia is
16-55%, and occurs secondary to a decrease in LES tone, that can be
induced by a variety of anesthetic agents, including atropine,
morphine, acepromazine, thiopental, xylazine, and isoflurane.25,26
Damage to the muscularis layer of the esophagus is associated with
fibroblastic proliferation and contraction, leading to stricture
formation. The clinical signs, progressive regurgitation, and
swallowing impairment are related to the severity and extent of the
stricture. Early clinical signs might include a subtle “hard swallow”

for a few days, and this slight increase in effort when swallowing can
be easily missed by owners. Progressive clinical signs include
swallowing impairment, odynophagia, regurgitation, salivation,
anorexia, coughing, and weight loss.

Diagnosis
A diagnosis of esophageal stricture is often suggested by the history
and confirmed with contrast radiographs using liquid barium or
barium mixed with canned food (esophagram) or via a VFSS
(Figure 259.6). Contrast radiographs are helpful for determining
the number, location, and length of strictures (ch. 116).
Esophagoscopy (ch. 107), the definitive diagnostic procedure, is
helpful for differentiating benign from malignant strictures and
facilitates balloon-dilation.

Treatment
Mechanical dilation of the stricture (ch. 116) is best accomplished
using balloon dilation (either by single intervention or by use of an
indwelling balloon dilation esophagostomy tube [BE-tube]),
intraluminal stenting, or by bougienage. These techniques are
discussed in ch. 116. The dilation procedure is repeated 5-7 days
later in an effort to maximally dilate the stricture. Continued medical
therapy is warranted following balloon dilation or bougienage using
the same medications and dietary alterations as discussed for
esophagitis. Intraluminal stents can be used in animals that have
failed dilation attempts or those with recurrent strictures (

Video

116.1).33

Transendoscopic Triamcinolone
The transendoscopic administration of triamcinolone into the
submucosa of the stricture site using a 4-quadrant approach before
the balloon dilation procedure has been associated with a reduced
rate of re-stricture formation in people.34,35 Approximately 2.5 mg
triamcinolone per quadrant is injected using a transbronchial
aspiration needle that can be threaded down the biopsy channel of

the endoscope. The triamcinolone is generally used for the first 2-3
dilation procedures. Topical mitomycin C (5 mg of mitomycin C
using a soaked gauze sponge that is placed endoscopically at the
stricture site for approximately 5 minutes) has also been shown to be
beneficial for preventing re-stricture in people, but this has not yet
been studied in dogs or cats.36 The site is rinsed with 60 mL of water
after removing the sponge.

ESOPHAGEAL FOREIGN BODIES
Definition and Clinical Signs
Foreign bodies are a common cause of swallowing impairment in
dogs, but are less common in cats. The most common esophageal
foreign bodies in dogs are bones, fishhooks, needles, and sticks,
whereas play toys are more commonly seen in cats. Foreign bodies
typically lodge at points of minimal esophageal distension: thoracic
inlet, heart base, or at the diaphragmatic hiatus. Mucosal abrasion,
ulceration, and perforation may occur with sharp or angular objects
that are lodged intraluminally.
The severity of esophageal damage and resulting signs are
dependent on the foreign body size, shape, and edges, and the
duration of obstruction. In some cases, the owner may observe
foreign body ingestion. The onset of clinical signs is often related to
the degree of esophageal obstruction and type of foreign body
ingested. Animals with smaller foreign bodies with a smooth surface,
causing incomplete obstruction, may have had signs for days to
weeks duration, whereas complete obstruction causes acute
swallowing impairment, regurgitation, odynophagia, gagging, and
excessive salivation.

Diagnosis and Treatment
Physical examination findings (ch. 3) vary from unremarkable to
halitosis (tissue necrosis), fever, and lethargy. Bone foreign bodies
can occasionally be palpated externally if they become lodged in the
cervical esophagus. Definitive diagnosis usually requires
radiography. Radiopaque foreign bodies can be detected with survey
radiography, but identifying radiolucent foreign bodies requires an

esophagram. Survey radiographs are indispensable for detection
aspiration pneumonia or esophageal perforation (i.e.,
pneumomediastinum, emphysema, or mediastinitis; Figure 259.7).
A water-soluble positive-contrast agent (iohexol, Gastrografin
[diatrizoate]) should be used rather than barium sulfate if
esophageal perforation is suspected. Esophagoscopy can be
performed to confirm the diagnosis and assess secondary mucosal
damage (Figure 259.8).
Esophageal foreign bodies should be removed promptly because
retention increases the risk of esophageal mucosal damage,
ulceration, and perforation. Foreign bodies in the proximal
esophagus may be removed with a rigid sigmoidoscope, whereas
more distal foreign bodies beyond the reach of a rigid scope should
be removed using a flexible endoscope. Large forceps passed through
the lumen of the rigid sigmoidoscope are used to grasp the foreign
body and pull it into the lumen of the sigmoidoscope for safe
removal. Distal esophageal foreign bodies can be pushed into the
stomach for removal by gastrotomy if they cannot be removed
through the mouth. Smaller foreign bodies are best removed with a
flexible endoscope and basket, biopsy forceps, or snare retrieving
forceps. Fishhooks that are lodged in the proximal to mid-esophagus
can be dislodged with the distal end of a rigid endoscope by inserting
the open end of the scope between the shaft and hook portion and
pushing aborally. Once dislodged from the mucosa, the fish-hook can
be pulled into the lumen of the rigid endoscope for safe removal. A
flexible endoscope can be used to remove fish-hooks that are beyond
the reach of a rigid endoscope.

9-month-old Border Collie that was observed playing

Animals with esophageal necrosis or ulceration should be fasted
for 24-48 hours after foreign body removal. A gastrostomy tube (ch.
81) can be placed during foreign body removal in animals with
severe esophagitis or necrosis to temporarily bypass the esophagus
during feedings. Specific therapy for esophagitis should include
sucralfate suspensions and PPIs for 2-4 weeks following removal of
the foreign body. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are warranted in
animals with severe ulceration or small perforations. Esophagotomy
is indicated if endoscopy fails to remove the foreign body; however, it
is preferable to attempt to push the foreign body into the stomach for

removal via gastrotomy. Surgery is also indicated to repair larger
esophageal perforations.

VASCULAR RING ANOMALIES
Definitions and Prevalence
Vascular ring anomalies are congenital malformations of the major
arteries of the heart that entrap the intrathoracic esophagus and
trachea and cause esophageal obstruction. Persistent right aortic
arch (PRAA) is the most common vascular ring anomaly in dogs and
cats. It occurs when the embryonic right fourth aortic arch, rather
than the left fourth aortic arch, becomes the functional adult aorta.
Circular compression of the esophagus occurs by the aorta on the
right, the ligamentum arteriosum left dorsolaterally, the pulmonary
trunk on the left, and the heart base ventrally. There is evidence of a
hereditary basis in German Shepherd Dogs and Irish Setters.37 Other
less common vascular ring anomalies include aberrant right or left
subclavian arteries, double aortic arch, left aortic arch with right
ligamentum arteriosum, and aberrant intercostal arteries.

Clinical Signs
Affected puppies and kittens usually present for regurgitation of
solid foods at the time of weaning (ch. 48), i.e., often around 4-6
weeks of age. Weight loss with failure to thrive despite a good
appetite is common. A moist cough, dyspnea, and fever suggest
aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217). Physical examination often reveals
a thin, stunted animal that is otherwise normal. Occasionally, a
dilated esophagus can be observed or palpated in the cervical region.

Diagnosis
Vascular ring anomalies should be differentiated from other causes
of regurgitation in young animals, such as congenital
megaesophagus, esophageal foreign body, and esophageal stricture.
The signalment and an onset of regurgitation during weaning are
highly supportive of a vascular ring anomaly. Survey thoracic
radiographs usually demonstrate esophageal body dilation cranial to

the base of the heart. Focal leftward deviation of the trachea near the
cranial border of the heart in dorsoventral or ventrodorsal
radiographs is a reliable sign of PRAA in dogs (Figure 259.9).38 An
esophagram is rarely necessary, especially given the associated risk
of aspiration of barium. Vascular ring anomalies occur at the base of
the heart, whereas intraluminal strictures can occur in any segment
of the esophageal body and are more common in adult animals.

Treatment
Definitive therapy for PRAA is surgical ligation and transection of
the ligamentum arteriosum, which can be performed via a left
intercostal thoracotomy or thoracoscopically. During surgery, areas
of periesophageal fibrosis should be reduced and the strictured site
should be dilated with a balloon dilation catheter. Animals with
severe debilitation from malnutrition will require enteral nutritional
support via gastrostomy tube feedings prior to surgery (ch. 81),
which can be challenging to place in a patient with a vascular ring
anomaly. Aspiration pneumonia should be treated with broadspectrum antibiotics (ch. 217). Significant clinical improvement
usually follows corrective surgery in most patients (>90%); however,
esophageal hypomotility and regurgitation may persist, particularly
in those animals that have a delay in their surgery. Affected animals
may benefit from elevated feedings as described for idiopathic
megaesophagus. Unfortunately, no drugs improve motility of
esophageal striated muscle.

ESOPHAGEAL NEOPLASIA
Definitions and Prevalence
Tumors of the esophagus are rare, accounting for <0.5% of all
cancers in the dog and cat.39 Esophageal tumors may be primary or
metastatic. Esophageal fibrosarcoma and osteosarcoma are the most
common malignant tumors in dogs, developing from malignant
transformation of esophageal granulomas associated with Spirocerca
lupi infection.40,41 Squamous cell carcinoma is the most commonly
diagnosed primary esophageal tumor in cats. Other less commonly

reported primary esophageal tumors in the dog and cat include
leiomyo(sarco)mas, adenocarcinomas, and undifferentiated
carcinomas. Metastatic lesions (thyroid, pulmonary, and gastric
carcinomas) commonly involve the esophagus but are less frequently
associated with clinical signs of esophageal disease. Periesophageal
tumors arising from regional lymph nodes, thyroid, thymus, and
heart base cause local esophageal invasion, direct mechanical
obstruction, or both.

Clinical Signs
Clinical signs develop gradually and reflect progressive esophageal
obstruction. The most common signs include regurgitation (ch. 48),
swallowing impairment, odynophagia, ptyalism, and weight loss.
Animals with metastatic disease may have general debilitation,
anorexia, and signs of pulmonary involvement such as dyspnea and
coughing. Physical examination (ch. 3) may reveal emaciation. Some
cervical periesophageal and esophageal tumors may be palpable.

Diagnosis
Survey thoracic radiographs may be normal or may reveal
esophageal dilatation, an intraluminal mass, or evidence of a
periesophageal lesion displacing the esophagus. The lungs should be
evaluated for aspiration pneumonia and metastasis. An esophagram
usually confirms the presence of an intraluminal mass or obstructive
lesion. Esophagoscopy (ch. 107) with exfoliative cytology or mucosal
biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis of esophageal neoplasia.
Small pinch biopsies obtained via endoscopy may be superficial and
non-representative of the tumor and a double-bite technique should
be performed to maximize the diagnostic yield.

Treatment
Chemotherapy, surgical resection, and radiation therapy represent
the primary modalities for treatment of malignant esophageal
neoplasia; however, radiation therapy may be complicated by acute
and chronic injury to adjacent mediastinal structures, while surgical
resection is complicated by limited surgical exposure, tension on the
anastomosis, and the risk of stricture formation post-operatively.

Lymphoma may be managed with chemotherapy (ch. 322). Slowgrowing benign esophageal neoplasms (e.g., leiomyoma; ch. 324)
generally have a favorable prognosis with complete surgical
resection.42 Esophageal granulomas associated with S. lupi can be
managed with doramectin (200 mcg/kg SC) at 14-day intervals for 3
treatments40 or injectable doramectin solution given orally (500
mcg/kg PO q24h) for 6 weeks; this regimen is repeated for an
additional 6 weeks in dogs exhibiting any evidence of granuloma
formation detected via esophagoscopy.41

ESOPHAGEAL DIVERTICULUM
Definitions and Prevalence
Esophageal diverticula are circumscribed sacculations of the
esophageal wall that affect esophageal motility. Congenital
diverticula occur secondary to abnormalities in embryological
development that permit herniation of the esophageal mucosa
through a defect in the muscularis. Acquired diverticula are
subdivided into pulsion or traction forms. Pulsion diverticula
develop in association with increases in intraluminal pressure
secondary to obstruction (stricture or foreign body) or altered
motility.43 Traction diverticula result from periesophageal
inflammation and fibrosis with adhesions to adjacent tissue. The
development of an abscess from migration of a foreign body (e.g.,
grass awn migration) is a common cause of traction diverticula in the
western United States. The accumulation of ingesta (impaction)
within diverticula leads to esophagitis, mechanical obstruction (seen
with large diverticula), and esophageal dysmotility.

Clinical Signs
As with many esophageal disorders, signs can include regurgitation,
odynophagia, and retching. Diverticula can occasionally be an
incidental finding in animals with no associated clinical signs.
Weakening of the muscularis can occur in rare cases, resulting in
perforation of the diverticulum with leakage of food and fluid into
the mediastinum and signs of sepsis and respiratory distress.

Diagnosis
Survey thoracic radiographs may reveal an air-filled or soft-tissue
opacity adjacent to or involving the esophagus; however, contrast
radiography is necessary to differentiate an esophageal diverticulum
from a periesophageal, mediastinal, or pulmonary mass.
Esophagoscopy (ch. 107) confirms the diagnosis, although it may be
necessary to suction food and fluid to visualize the diverticulum.
Diverticula should not be confused with the normal esophageal
redundancy seen in young brachycephalic breeds, Bulldogs, and
Chinese Shar-Peis. Differentials for epiphrenic diverticula include
hiatal hernia and gastroesophageal intussusception.

Treatment
Diverticulectomy is the preferred therapy, particularly for large
diverticula that are a continuous cause of esophageal impaction.
Small diverticula in subclinical patients may be left alone or
managed medically with smaller-sized, upright feedings of a liquid or
semiliquid diet to minimize impaction of ingesta in the diverticulum.
Traction diverticula are often managed with broad-spectrum
antibiotics, whereas pulsion diverticula are treated for their specific
underlying cause (e.g., stricture, vascular ring anomaly, esophagitis).
Most cases warrant a guarded prognosis because corrective surgery
can induce stricture formation and because segmental esophageal
hypomotility may persist after surgery.

ESOPHAGEAL FISTULA
Definitions and Prevalence
An esophageal fistula is an abnormal communicating tract between
the esophagus and adjacent structures. Most esophageal fistulae
involve the lungs or airways (e.g., esophagopulmonary,
esophagotracheal, and esophagobronchial fistulae). Both congenital
and acquired fistulae have been described and both are rare in dogs
and cats.44,45 Congenital fistulae result from incomplete separation
of the tracheobronchial tree from the esophagus during
embryogenesis; Cairn Terriers appear to be overrepresented.

Acquired esophageal fistulae are usually associated with retained
esophageal foreign bodies, especially bones and grass awns that
cause esophageal perforation and leakage of esophageal contents
into adjacent tissues. Healing leads to development of a
communicating tract with resultant airway contamination from
esophageal contents. Other less common causes of esophageal
fistulae include trauma and neoplasia.

Clinical Signs
Clinical signs are primarily related to the respiratory system and
include coughing and dyspnea. Coughing after drinking is common.
Regurgitation, dysphagia, lethargy, anorexia, fever, and weight loss
are less commonly observed.

Diagnosis
Survey thoracic radiographs usually reveal a localized alveolar,
bronchial, or interstitial lung pattern or a combination of these
patterns. The right caudal and middle lung lobes in dogs and the left
caudal and accessory lobes in cats are most commonly affected.44,45
Radiopaque foreign bodies may be observed in the esophagus;
however, an esophagram is required for definitive diagnosis of
esophageal-airway communication. Use of iodinated contrast agents
should be avoided because they are hyperosmolar and chemically
irritating to the lung. Esophagoscopy or bronchoscopy are of limited
value in confirming small fistulae.

Treatment
Surgical excision of the fistula with closure of the esophageal defect
is required. Lobectomy of the affected lung may be necessary as a
result of pulmonary consolidation or foreign material in the airways.
Postoperative therapy includes administration of broad-spectrum
antibiotics (based on culture and susceptibility testing) and
esophageal rest for 48-72 hours. A good prognosis is given to animals
after successful surgery. The prognosis is guarded if severe
complications such as severe pleural effusion, pneumonia, or
pulmonary abscessation are present.

MEGAESOPHAGUS AND ESOPHAGEAL
HYPOMOTILITY
Megaesophagus, the most common cause of regurgitation in dogs, is
characterized by focal or diffuse esophageal dilation and concurrent
esophageal dysmotility. It can be congenital or acquired. The
acquired form is more common and can be idiopathic or secondary
to a recognized disease.

Congenital Megaesophagus
Congenital idiopathic megaesophagus is characterized by generalized
hypomotility and dilation of the esophagus, causing regurgitation
and failure to thrive in puppies, shortly after weaning. A familial
predisposition has been suggested in the Irish Setter, Great Dane,
German Shepherd Dog, Labrador Retriever, Chinese Shar-Pei,
Newfoundland, Miniature Schnauzer, and Fox Terrier breeds.
Congenital megaesophagus in cats is rare, but Siamese cats may be
predisposed. The pathogenesis of the congenital form is poorly
understood but may involve a defect in vagal afferent innervation of
the esophagus.46,47

Acquired Megaesophagus
Similar to congenital megaesophagus, primary acquired
megaesophagus is suspected to be caused by a defect in afferent
neural response to esophageal distension.48 Esophageal achalasia
and esophageal “achalasia-like syndrome” (reported in 60% of 23
megaesophagus cases at one academic institution)49 are primary
esophageal motility disorders. Esophageal achalasia is characterized
by lack of esophageal peristalsis and by partial or absent relaxation
of the LES, leading to a functional obstruction (

Video 221.1).

MG accounts for 25-30% of acquired secondary megaesophagus
(ASM) in dogs,50,51 and may involve the esophagus only (focal MG)
or, more commonly, involves the esophagus and peripheral muscles
(ch. 253). ASM has also been associated with hypoadrenocorticism
(ch. 296), lupus myositis (ch. 179), polymyopathies,

polyneuropathies (ch. 252), dysautonomia (ch. 254), lead
poisoning (ch. 133), and severe forms of esophagitis. Dysautonomia,
a generalized autonomic neuropathy in which megaesophagus and
esophageal hypomotility are consistent findings, is more frequently
recognized in cats and is attributed to degenerative lesions involving
autonomic ganglia.52 Other causes of segmental or diffuse
esophageal hypomotility include foreign bodies, stricture, and
vascular ring anomalies.

Clinical Signs and Diagnosis
Regurgitation is the most frequent clinical sign associated with
megaesophagus. Considerable variability exists in the frequency and
timing of regurgitation episodes after meal ingestion. Puppies with
congenital megaesophagus often begin regurgitating when weaned to
solid foods. Affected animals may suffer from malnutrition and
aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217). Additional signs depend on the
underlying cause of megaesophagus, and include muscle pain and
stiff gait (polymyositis), generalized weakness, exercise intolerance
(neuromuscular disease), and vomiting and inappetence signs (lead
toxicosis, hypoadrenocorticism).
Megaesophagus should be suspected in any animal with a history
of regurgitation (ch. 48). Survey radiographs of the neck and thorax
will be diagnostic for most cases of megaesophagus (Figure
259.10), although contrast radiography (esophagram) can be
considered if survey radiographs are equivocal to help exclude a
foreign body cause of megaesophagus or to evaluate esophageal
motility. Survey radiographs may reveal alveolar opacities consistent
with aspiration pneumonia. A CBC, serum biochemistry profile, and
urinalysis should be performed to screen for causes of ASM. An
AChR antibody titer for acquired MG should be done, even in the
absence of generalized muscle weakness, because MG can cause focal
megaesophagus in 40% of dogs (ch. 253). The test should be
repeated in 4-8 weeks in all dogs with an initial titer in the “grayzone” (0.3-0.6 nmol/L), particularly when the onset of
megaesophagus has been acute. A resting cortisol or ACTH
stimulation test should be considered to help rule out
hypoadrenocorticism. Additional diagnostic procedures that should
be based on the individual case presentation include esophagoscopy

(ch. 107), EMG and NCV (ch. 111), and muscle and nerve biopsy
(ch. 110). A clear association of ASM with hypothyroidism has not
been proven and a low total T4 concentration is more consistent with
euthyroid sick syndrome (ch. 285).

Treatment
Animals with acquired idiopathic megaesophagus need to be
differentiated from those with ASM, whose underlying disorder must
be treated (Table 259.1). Treatment of congenital and acquired
idiopathic megaesophagus associated with esophageal achalasia can
involve pharmacological or surgical strategies to treat the hypertonic
LES; however, pharmacological approaches are of limited value in
people. Sildenafil 1 mg/kg PO q12h was associated with a reduction
in the number of regurgitation episodes, increased weight gain, and
decreased esophageal diameter compared to placebo controls in a
study of puppies with congenital megaesophagus.53 Sildenafil has a
short half-life and the author recommends administering it q8h.
Prokinetic drugs, such as cisapride and metoclopramide could
exacerbate esophageal retention of food by increasing LES tone. Both
drugs are thus contraindicated for the management of
megaesophagus because they can exacerbate the “achalasia-like”
syndrome documented in affected dogs. These drugs have no effect
on esophageal striated muscle, and will likely exacerbate
regurgitation. However, cisapride may be a useful prokinetic agent in
cats with distal esophageal motility disturbances affecting the
smooth muscle component of the feline esophagus. Direct injection
of botulinum toxin into the LES of individuals with esophageal
achalasia has also shown moderate effectiveness in people and in
dogs.54 Pneumatic dilation is considered to be the most cost-effective
first-line treatment for achalasia; however, the procedure typically
needs to be repeated periodically. Surgical Heller myotomy with
partial fundoplication is a more permanent therapeutic modality,
and the procedure can be performed via laparoscopy or laparotomy.
Standard supportive care of dogs with megaesophagus include the
feeding of small, frequent meals from an elevated or upright position
(e.g., Bailey chair) to assist passage of ingesta into the stomach. Food
consistency should be varied (liquid, canned meatballs or kibble) at

first, to determine which types of food are best tolerated. Severely
malnourished animals or animals suffering repeated bouts of
aspiration pneumonia should have a temporary or permanent
gastrostomy tube placed for enteral nutritional support (ch. 81).
Gastrostomy tube feeding reduces risk of aspiration pneumonia;
however, dogs with megaesophagus can still aspirate saliva or
ingesta refluxed from the stomach into the esophagus. Intermittent
at-home suctioning of esophageal content via placement of a
fenestrated esophagostomy tube for prevention of recurrent
aspiration pneumonia is a viable consideration for dogs with a giant
sigmoid esophagus.55 Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be
considered in patients with aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217). Clients
should be counseled that recurrent pneumonia is a common problem
necessitating prompt detection and treatment for long-term success.
