Monitoring and Follow-Up
Affected animals should be reevaluated at 1- to 2-month intervals to
monitor disease progression. Thoracic radiographs should be
repeated to assess esophageal dilatation and aspiration pneumonia.
Some animals with congenital megaesophagus improve over months
with diligent supportive care. The prognosis with acquired primary
megaesophagus is generally poor. These animals usually succumb to
repeated episodes of aspiration pneumonia or are euthanized
because of their irreversible disease. Animals with ASM may respond
to treatment of the underlying cause, leading to improvement or
resolution of megaesophagus. The prognosis in dogs with
megaesophagus caused by acquired MG is favorable, with
approximately 50% of dogs responding to supportive therapy.50

FIGURE 259.11 Lateral survey thoracic
radiograph of a 5-year-old Boston Terrier with a
chronic history of regurgitation. The stomach is seen
extending through the diaphragm into the
craniodorsal thorax on this left lateral projection. It
then returned to a more normal location on
subsequent projections. These findings are highly
supportive of a sliding hiatal hernia.

HIATAL HERNIA
Definitions and Prevalence
Hiatal hernia is defined as any protrusion of abdominal contents
(most commonly a portion of stomach) through the esophageal
hiatus of the diaphragm into the thoracic cavity in the presence of an
intact phrenico-esophageal ligament. Four types of hiatal hernias
have been recognized in dogs and cats: Type I is the sliding hiatal
hernia, in which the abdominal segment of the esophagus and parts
of the stomach are displaced cranially through the esophageal hiatus.

In Type II, the paraesophageal hiatal hernia, the abdominal segment
of esophagus and LES remain in a fixed position but a portion of the
stomach herniates into the mediastinum alongside the thoracic
esophagus.56,57 Type III is a combination of Types I and II and is
characterized by the herniation of the greater curvature of the
stomach as well as the gastroesophageal junction into the thorax.
One case of a Type IV esophageal hiatal hernia has been reported in
which the liver, stomach, and small intestine were displaced into the
thorax.58 Type I sliding hiatal hernia is the most common type and
may occur as a congenital or acquired lesion in the dog and cat.
Congenital sliding hiatal hernias have been documented in
brachycephalic breeds: Chinese Shar-Pei, Chow Chow, English
Bulldog, French Bulldog, Pug, and Boston Terrier.59 Due to their
nasofacial conformation and unique respiratory anatomy, these
breeds often have an upper airway tract obstruction as part of
brachycephalic syndrome (ch. 213), which increases negative
intrathoracic pressure and causes subsequent hiatal herniation and
GER. Affected animals typically develop clinical signs of
regurgitation (ch. 48) within the first 12 months of life. An acquired
hiatal hernia may also occur in any dog or cat and may result from
sudden increases in intra-abdominal pressure secondary to trauma
(via damage to diaphragmatic nerves and muscles resulting in hiatal
laxity) or respiratory distress (caused by increased negative
intrathoracic pressure seen with intermittent airway obstruction
[e.g., laryngeal paralysis, ch. 214]). Regardless of cause, hiatal
herniation reduces LES tone and leads to GER, esophagitis, and
segmental or diffuse esophageal hypomotility.

Clinical Signs and Diagnosis
The most common clinical signs of a hiatal hernia are intermittent
regurgitation (ch. 48), vomiting (ch. 48), and hypersalivation (ch.
46), often precipitated by excitement or exercise. The persistent
reflux of gastric juice can cause secondary esophagitis and
odynophagia. Respiratory distress and coughing may occur with
severe herniation or aspiration pneumonia. Survey thoracic
radiographs should be obtained in all dogs with suspected hiatal
hernia and may reveal a caudodorsal, gas-filled, intrathoracic soft-

tissue opacity (Figure 259.11). Varying degrees of esophageal
dilatation and alveolar opacities, consistent with aspiration
pneumonia may also be observed. Survey radiographs are relatively
insensitive for diagnosing a hiatal hernia and a VFSS is more likely to
identify intermittent herniation of the stomach and can allow
assessment of esophageal motility (Figure 259.2). A normal VFSS
does not rule out a hiatal hernia because the problem occurs
intermittently and could be missed. Esophagoscopy (ch. 107) can be
used for diagnosing a sliding hiatal hernia when the apparent
separation between the squamocolumnar junction and the
diaphragmatic impression is greater than 2 cm using a retroflexion
or J-maneuver.60 Esophagoscopy is also used to look for evidence of
esophagitis. High-resolution manometry is a non-invasive tool that
can be used for diagnosing hiatal hernias in people and animals
(above).

Treatment
A sliding hiatal hernia is not always associated with clinical signs,
particularly when acquired. Medical therapy should be implemented
in animals with clinical signs of severe GER, esophagitis, and
regurgitation before considering surgical intervention. PPIs such as
omeprazole are superior acid suppressants compared to H2-receptor
antagonists and should be administered with sucralfate suspension
to afford greater mucosal cytoprotection. Of note, the administration
of the 2 drugs should be spaced out so as to avoid decreased efficacy
of either drug. Drugs that increase LES tone (cisapride or
metoclopramide) can be given with PPIs and sucralfate. Animals
failing medical management may benefit from reconstructive
surgery, especially for large congenital hiatal hernias. Normal hiatal
anatomy can be restored by diaphragmatic crural apposition,
esophagopexy, and left fundic tube gastropexy techniques.42,44
Results of laparoscopic treatment have been comparable to those of
abdominal surgery for the treatment of sliding hiatal hernia and GER
in dogs. Additionally, laparoscopy is associated with shorter
hospitalization and convalescent time. With either approach, owners
of prospective patients should be counseled that the procedure may
not be curative as some patients will continue to exhibit varying

degrees of GER. Consideration for surgical management of
brachycephalic syndrome in affected dogs with concurrent hiatal
hernia is also important because the upper airway obstruction
creates an increased negative intrathoracic pressure, which can
exacerbate herniation (ch. 213). The prognosis for most dogs
following surgical correction is favorable, although persistent
regurgitation is recognized in dogs with concurrent esophageal
motility disturbances.

GASTROESOPHAGEAL REFLUX (GER)
Definition and Clinical Signs
GER consists of movement of gastric or intestinal fluids or ingesta
into the esophagus, secondary to the loss of integrity of the
gastroesophageal barrier (Figure 259.12). The consequences of
GER include varying degrees of esophagitis, resulting from
prolonged contact of gastric acid, pepsin, trypsin, and bile salts with
the esophageal mucosa. Gastric acid alone produces mild
esophagitis; however, the combination of gastric acid with pepsin or
trypsin can cause severe esophagitis. The most common causes of
GER in dogs and cats include hiatal hernia, general anesthesiainduced reductions of LES pressure, chronic vomiting causing a
weakening of LES tone, and gastric atony or pyloric outflow
obstruction causing GER. The clinical signs of GER are similar to
those of esophagitis, and may include regurgitation, hypersalivation,
odynophagia, and anorexia. Animals that reflux into their mouth can
be seen lip-smacking, panting, or exhibiting a “hard-swallow”
immediately following these episodes (ch. 11). Nocturnal reflux
occurs more commonly in people and animals because of TLESRs
during sleep and the loss of the swallow reflex.

FIGURE 259.12 Esophagoscopy performed in a 5year-old Boston Terrier with a chronic history of
regurgitation secondary to a sliding (type I) hiatal
hernia. The reader should notice the flaccid lower
esophageal sphincter at the top of the image and
evidence of gastroesophageal reflux (foam at center
and bottom of image). The esophageal mucosa at the
9-11 o’clock position appears erythematous
secondary to esophagitis.

Diagnosis and Treatment

Diagnosis of GER is suspected based on the history (e.g., nocturnal
panting, hard-swallowing, and lip-licking), recent general anesthesia,
or a history of chronic vomiting. A VFSS may demonstrate
intermittent GER; however, the procedure is relatively insensitive for
diagnosing pathological GER in light of the intermittent nature of the
problem and the fact that mild GER can be observed in healthy
animals with normal esophageal function. Esophagoscopy (ch. 107)
is a useful procedure for documenting mucosal inflammation
associated with the GER. Esophagoscopy also facilitates the
assessment of the esophageal hiatus via a retroflexion maneuver (Jmaneuver). This procedure should be performed with the stomach
moderately distended with air so that the flap valve at the opening of
the gastroesophageal junction can be carefully evaluated. Esophageal
pH/impedance testing is useful for diagnosing acid and non-acid
reflux in people and dogs with suspected GER, unexplained
esophagitis, or hiatal hernias (above).
Medical therapy is aimed at administering acid suppressants
(PPIs), diffusion barriers (sucralfate), and prokinetic agents
(cisapride, metoclopramide). Cisapride is a superior prokinetic agent
to metoclopramide and has been documented to tighten LES tone
and enhance gastric emptying in dogs. Animals should be fed a fatrestricted diet because dietary fat delays gastric emptying and can
reduce LES pressure. In people with severe GER, anti-reflux surgery
(fundoplication) is commonly performed laparoscopically and is
aimed at reinforcing and repairing the defective barrier through
plication of the gastric fundus.61 Endoscopic anti-reflux therapies,
such as transoral incisionless fundoplication are currently being
utilized in people for the correction of minor defects of the
esophageal hiatus. However, clinical trials in dogs or cats are lacking.

The gastrointestinal (GI) microbiome contains a consortium of
bacteria, archaea, viruses, fungi, and protozoa, along with their
collective genomes, that confer vital contributions to host
metabolism, energy homeostasis, gut epithelial health, and immune
system development and response. More than 100 trillion microbial
cells inhabit the GI tract, outnumbering host cells by approximately

10-fold. Some of these microorganisms inhabit the intestines
symbiotically and form an ecological community called the gut
microbiota. Examples of these mutualistic functions provided by
resident microbiota include protection against GI pathogens,
production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that can be used as an
energy source by the host, synthesis of B vitamins and vitamin K,
xenobiotic metabolism, and biotransformation of bile acids (BAs)
which influence host health and helps to support a normal (healthy)
microbiota. In addition, various immunological mediators, including
chemokines and cytokines, secreted from intestinal epithelial cells
stimulated by the gut microbiota maintain a well-balanced
relationship between gut microbes and host immunity.
The intestinal microenvironment, including the gut microbiota
and their metabolites, is rapidly altered by diet, drugs (especially
antimicrobials), stress, and bacterial and viral pathogens. Thus, host
immunity and metabolic responses must adapt to changes in the gut
environment, including dysbiosis and pathogenic bacterial
infections. Dysbiosis and mucosal inflammation are closely
interrelated with an abundance of clinical evidence supporting their
association in chronic GI diseases such as feline triaditis (ch. 225),
inflammatory bowel disease [IBD; chs. 262 and 263]), intestinal
cancer (chs. 262 and 263), and granulomatous colitis in dogs caused
by adherent/invasive Escherichia coli (ch. 263). However, what is
not known is whether intestinal inflammation is a cause of dysbiosis,
a consequence of it, or some combination of these 2 mechanisms.

THE INTESTINAL BARRIER AND
MUCOSAL HOMEOSTASIS
The mucosal barrier constructed by intestinal epithelial cells
segregates gut microbes from the host immune system to maintain
mucosal homeostasis. This barrier is a functional entity composed of
separate but interlinked components, including physical elements
(e.g., the underlying vascular endothelium, epithelial cells, and the
mucus layer), along with a chemical layer composed of digestive
secretions, immune molecules, and cellular products (cytokines,
inflammatory mediators, and antimicrobial peptides).1 Apart from

these layers, the microbiota also contributes to barrier integrity
along with immune functions and GI motility. The intestinal
epithelium is composed of a single layer of columnar cells and
different specialized cell subtypes: enterocytes, goblet cells,
enteroendocrine cells and immune cells, including intraepithelial
lymphocytes and dendritic cells. Three types of junctional complexes
(tight junctions [TJs], adherens junctions [AJs] and desmosomes)
provide mechanical cohesion to these columnar cells and seal the
paracellular space to regulate the movement of water, ions, and small
molecules across the intestinal mucosa.2 The expression pattern of
junctional proteins is a dynamic process that is steadfastly regulated
by phosphorylation, causing both beneficial and harmful
consequences.3 For example, phosphorylation can either promote TJ
protein formation to enhance barrier function or alternatively it can
disrupt and redistribute TJ and AJ proteins to increase intestinal
permeability.
The intestinal epithelium continuously renews itself every 4-5 days
under normal homeostasis, with a more rapid pace of renewal
following damage. Regulating this process are pluripotential stem
cells that give rise to all GI epithelial cell lineages and can generate
whole intestinal crypts. At the tips of villi and along the epithelia of
the colon, mature cells undergo apoptosis and are normally shed into
the GI lumen. Intestinal stem cells that express LGR5 can
differentiate into specialized cell types, including columnar cells
(enterocytes and colonocytes), goblet cells, and enteroendocrine
cells.4 Columnar cells are the most abundant epithelial cell found in
the small and large intestines and are involved in absorption. Goblet
cells produce and secrete mucus (e.g., mucin 2), which covers the
surface of the intestinal epithelium. Mucus secretion from goblet
cells is regulated by the host sensing gut microbes, or their
metabolites, including SCFAs or Th2 cytokines such as IL-5 or IL-13.
The number of goblet cells is greatly increased in the colon where
bacterial numbers are very high. Here, the mucus layer is composed
of 2 layers: an outer, loose mucus layer inhabited by large numbers
of microbes and an inner, firm mucus layer that is devoid of
intestinal bacteria. Enterochromaffin cells secrete peptide hormones
such as cholecystokinin, glucagon-like peptide (GLP) 1 and 2, and
serotonin in response to luminal nutrients and intestinal microbiota

that affect gut immunity. Antimicrobial peptides, including alphadefensins and Reg3 proteins, and lysozyme further fortify the
antibacterial properties of the mucus compartment to protect against
microbial infection.4 Epithelial cells secrete beta-defensins in
response to sensing of microbes by their pattern recognition as either
commensal bacteria or pathogens. Secretory immunoglobulin A
(sIgA) is produced by plasma cells to mediate protection at mucosal
surfaces by binding bacteria and viruses to prevent their attachment
to or invasion of the mucosa (i.e., immune exclusion).5 Finally, the
resident bacteria contribute to mucosal homeostasis through
competitive exclusion, nutrient utilization, niche localization, and
their production of bacteriocins. Impairment of the innate immune
functions of the intestinal epithelial barrier is associated with
intestinal inflammation of chronic enteropathies, including canine
IBD6 (Figure 260.1).

THE GUT MICROBIOME IN HEALTH
Once established, the intestinal microbiota is characterized by
extreme compositional and functional diversity as well as long-term
stability. Since most beneficial gut bacteria are strict anaerobes and
are not detected by routine bacterial culture, molecular methods
using detection of the 16S ribosomal RNA gene have allowed
phylogenetic identification of non-culturable bacteria within the GI
tract. Collectively, these studies have identified 5 major phyla in feces
of healthy dogs and cats: Firmicutes, Fusobacteria, Bacteroidetes,
Proteobacteria, and Actinobacteria.7 Microbial communities vary
horizontally down the GI tract to reflect the unique
microenvironment and physiological functions of each intestinal
segment. There is a general increase in diversity and total number of
bacteria moving from the duodenum to the colon, with aerobic and
facultative anaerobic bacteria predominating in the small intestine
and anaerobes being most numerous in the colon. Within this core
gut bacterial community, many taxa belong to the phylum Firmicutes
with Clostridia being the most abundant taxa. Clostridium clusters
IV and XIVa are important producers of SCFAs and other

metabolites that are beneficial to the intestinal epithelium and host
immunity.
Another molecular method for microbial analysis uses
metagenomic shotgun sequencing, which provides information on
the functional genes as well as the bacterial species present in a
biologic sample. As both next generation and metagenomic
sequencing methods are expensive and time-consuming to perform,
more rapid results with lower costs may be realized using a
polymerase chain reaction-based assay called the dysbiosis index
(DI).8 The DI measures the abundance of 7 bacterial taxa and the
total bacterial abundance in canine feces. The DI calculates a single
number that expresses the extent of intestinal dysbiosis present: a DI
below 0 indicates a normal microbiota while a DI >2 indicates
microbiota dysbiosis. The DI can be used to assess normal versus
abnormal microbiota at a single time point or longitudinally in
response to disease progression or therapeutic intervention. Finally,
fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) allows microbes to be
visualized directly in tissues and quantified by their mucosal
location. Changes in the spatial organization (increased mucosal
association) of specific bacterial groups have been observed in dogs
and cats with IBD (ch. 262)9,10 or helicobacteriosis (ch. 261),11 in
dogs with granulomatous colitis (ch. 263),12 and also in dogs and
cats with intestinal cancer (Figure 260.2).13-15
Differences in the abundance of taxa along the GI tract result in
the production and consumption of diverse metabolites that mediate
the host-microbe symbiosis. Metabolomics, the study of metabolites,
can be performed using serum, urine, or feces to assess potential
correlations between metabolic changes within the host and
microbiome alterations. Preliminary data from healthy dogs
demonstrate that the concentration of many metabolites varies
significantly along the GI tract, either increasing or decreasing
progressively, decreasing abruptly from the ileum to the colon, or
fluctuating along the length of the GI tract.7 Common metabolic endproducts produced by the intestinal microbiota include SCFAs,
ammonia, and lactate. Also, shotgun sequencing (whole metagenome
sequencing) uses short reads of all the 16S rRNA genes present
providing functional information on the microbiome in addition to

phylogenetic characterization. Metagenomic analyses in humans
have revealed that despite phylogenetic diversity, there is significant
interpersonal overlap in functional gene families.16 These findings
suggest that an individual’s “core” microbiome is best defined by its
collective bacterial genome rather than the composition of its
structure. Finally, metagenomic analysis of the intestinal
microbiome has revealed considerable functional similarity to that in
mice and humans.17 The predominant bacterial gene categories in
the canine gut include carbohydrate metabolism (13% of sequences),
protein and amino acid metabolism (9 and 7%, respectively), cell
wall synthesis (8%), vitamin and co-factor synthesis (6%), and
nucleic acid synthesis (7%). The feline microbiome is involved in
similar physiological processes.

The composition of the GI microbiota is influenced by many
environmental factors including diet, medical interventions,
infectious disease, and probiotics. The overall dietary macronutrient
composition (e.g., carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals,
fiber, and water) would appear to be the most important factor in
determining gut microbial composition. However, data indicate that
functional gene families do not differ between dogs fed high- versus
low-fiber diets or with intestinal dysbiosis.18 Different antibiotics
(e.g., tylosin and metronidazole) have been shown to reduce
compositional richness and diversity of the healthy canine fecal

microbiota in a way that may not return fully to pre-antibiotic levels
even when the drug is discontinued (see Antibiotics for
Gastrointestinal Disorders, below).

THE GUT MICROBIOME IN
GASTROINTESTINAL DISEASE
Intestinal dysbiosis refers to an alteration of the gut microbiome
associated with both acute and chronic GI disease as well as other
conditions (Box 260.1). Dysbiosis is characterized by broad shifts in
the composition of microbes, reduced species diversity, and changes
in the relative proportion of select microbial members. Several
microbial community compositional abnormalities have been
identified in dogs and cats with various acute or chronic
enteropathies. While dysbiosis is a common feature of enteropathies,
there is not a consistent pattern of dysbiosis that is commonly
observed. However, most sequencing-based studies indicate a
reduced relative abundance of Bacteroidetes, Fusobacterium spp.,
and Firmicutes, as well as increased abundance of Proteobacteria, in
fecal samples of dogs with chronic enteropathies.19 Canine chronic
inflammatory enteropathy (CIE, also referred to as IBD) is a
common chronic intestinal disorder characterized by aberrant
immune responses associated with intestinal dysbiosis that drive
chronic intestinal inflammation. There are substantial differences in
the microbiota between dogs with IBD and healthy dogs, with dogs
with IBD showing a significantly lower alpha diversity compared
with healthy controls. Dogs with IBD show a reduced abundance of
luminal and mucosal Firmicutes and Bacteroides and an increased
abundance of Proteobacteria and Actinobacteria.20 There are only a
few studies investigating the microbiome in cats with GI disease;
however, 2 studies using FISH indicate that cats with IBD have
significant dysbiosis compared to healthy cats. In 1 study, decreased
abundances of Bifidobacterium spp. and Desulfovibrio, the latter
being a producer of toxic sulfur-containing compounds, were
observed in the feces of cats with IBD.21 Another study demonstrated
an increased abundance of mucosal Enterobacteriaceae associated

with GI signs and histopathologic lesions in cats with IBD compared
to healthy controls.10

FISH has been used in other studies to investigate the mucosal
microbiota in dogs and cats with intestinal cancer. In 1 study, dogs
with colonic adenocarcinoma had increased adherent (total bacteria,
Enterobacteriaceae, and E. coli) and invasive (Enterobacteriaceae, E.
coli, and Bacteroides spp.) bacteria in biopsy specimens when

compared to control tissues.15 Separate studies in cats demonstrated
that mucosa-invasive bacteria were more frequently observed in cats
with large cell lymphoma (82%) than in cats with small cell
lymphoma (18%),22 and that some cats with small cell lymphoma
have an increased abundance of Fusobacterium spp. associated with
intestinal inflammation and myeloid CD11b+ mucosal infiltrates.13
Along with changes in microbial composition, functional changes
in the microbiome have also been reported with canine chronic
enteropathies. In 1 study, dogs with IBD exhibited changes in their
fecal microbiome and serum metabolome as compared to healthy
controls.23 Moreover, while the IBD dogs improved clinically with
treatment, this was not accompanied by improvement in the
microbiome or serum metabolite profiles. One group of metabolites
of particular interest to host health are the SCFAs (e.g., butyrate,
acetate, and propionate). They are derived from bacterial
fermentation of complex carbohydrates and act to modulate mucosal
immune responses. SCFAs serve as an essential energy source for
colonocytes, enhance epithelial barrier function by strengthening TJs
and regulate the size and function of the regulatory T-lymphocyte
pool to protect against mucosal inflammation. A decrease in the
relative abundance of SCFA-producing bacteria has been
documented in dogs with both acute and chronic diarrhea.24
In addition to SCFA alterations, select amino acids, including
tryptophan, are reduced in patients with chronic enteropathies.
Tryptophan is an essential amino acid in dogs and serves as a
precursor for compounds, such as kynurenine, serotonin, melatonin,
and indole. Increased tryptophan catabolism limits the production
and availability of serotonin, which is an essential neurotransmitter
mediating GI secretion, motility, and pain. Tryptophan also serves as
a precursor to produce indole compounds synthesized by the gut
microbiota that enhance mucosal homeostasis. Depletion of
tryptophan occurs in dogs with protein-losing enteropathy whereas
dogs with IBD have decreased indole compounds present in their
feces.25
Intestinal dysbiosis can also trigger chronic mucosal inflammation
and BA dysmetabolism. BAs are essential for lipid digestion and they
play major roles in maintenance of mucosal homeostasis through

their anti-microbial actions. In the healthy gut, select bacteria are
required for deconjugation and dehydroxylation of primary BAs into
secondary BAs. With dysbiosis, the abundance of Clostridium
hiranonis, a bacterium associated with normal BA metabolism, is
reduced. This causes increased concentrations of primary BAs in the
colon, which are pro-inflammatory and may cause secretory diarrhea
(ch. 263).26 Taken together, these observations suggest that
dysbiosis and intestinal inflammation perturb BA metabolism and
promote colonic inflammation and GI signs.

THERAPEUTIC APPROACHES TO
DYSBIOSIS
As dysbiosis is associated with intestinal inflammation and GI
dysfunction, treatments that attempt to normalize bacterial
composition and function should be considered (Table 260.1).27
Depending on the underlying cause for dysbiosis, a single treatment
approach or combination of therapies may be attempted. Dietary
trials using a highly digestible, low-fat, and antigen-restricted diet,
especially for chronic enteropathies in dogs and cats, may reduce
host responses causing intestinal inflammation (ch. 160). Prebiotics
are selectively fermented substances, most commonly fibers, that
promote specific changes in the composition and/or function of the
microbiota. Synbiotics are a combination of prebiotics and
probiotics. Antibiotics are uncommonly required in animals with
diarrhea due to their promotion of microbial dysbiosis, antimicrobial
resistance, and treatment relapse once they are discontinued. Fecal
microbiota transplantation (FMT) is the transfer of feces from a
healthy donor to a recipient with GI disease to improve gut health
(ch. 106).

PREBIOTICS FOR GASTROINTESTINAL
DISORDERS
Prebiotics are selective food ingredients that, when fermented by
colonic bacteria, promote the growth of beneficial bacteria and their

metabolites (SCFAs). They are primarily dietary fibers, such as
psyllium, fructo-oligosaccharides, mannan oligosaccharides, and
pectin (ch. 165). Psyllium is a commonly used fermentable dietary
fiber that has water- and BA-binding properties that improve fecal
consistency, increase the intestinal mucus layer, and has beneficial
effects on cell proliferation in the intestinal tract. The available
evidence supporting use of prebiotics for canine and feline
gastroenteritis is sparse and generally associated with clinical trials
using synbiotics. One study in dogs with food-responsive
enteropathy (FRE) found a small increase in bacterial richness
(alpha diversity) in response to feeding a hydrolyzed diet paired with
a synbiotic, although no change in the microbial composition (beta
diversity) was seen.28 Another study evaluated the effect of
hydrolyzed diet with and without prebiotics and glycosaminoglycans
in dogs with IBD. Using a targeted metabolomics approach to
evaluate treatment response, dogs with IBD that received cotreatment showed altered lipid metabolism when compared to
placebo (diet alone).29 Moreover, the most impacted lipid classes
were structural components of cell membranes, including the
glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids. Study limitations included a
small sample population and the inability to statistically link
metabolic changes to improved clinical and histologic indices.

ANTIBIOTICS FOR GASTROINTESTINAL
DISORDERS
Antibiotics previously have been frequently prescribed for treatment
of acute diarrhea and select antibiotic-responsive enteropathies
(ARE), including tylosin-responsive diarrhea. The most used
antibiotics for therapy are tylosin, metronidazole, and
oxytetracycline. In many instances, these empirical therapies are
initiated without confirmation of a causal infectious agent (acute
diarrhea) or histologic confirmation of intestinal inflammation,
which may lead to unnecessary administration or overuse of
antibiotics.30 Also, a recent report indicated an incidence of only 8%
of dogs with ARE in 136 dogs with chronic diarrhea.31 Furthermore,

some patients that show improved clinical signs initially to
antibiotics will get worse during treatment and many patients will
relapse when antibiotics are discontinued.32
Antibiotics also have been shown to promote dysbiosis in healthy
dogs and cats (ch. 106, Figure 106.2). In separate reports, the
administration of oral tylosin at standard dosages to healthy dogs
was associated with increases in harmful fecal bacteria (Escherichialike organisms) in some dogs33 and the induction of dysbiosis that
persisted following tylosin withdrawal for up to 56 days.34 In healthy
dogs receiving metronidazole, microbial composition differed
significantly after 2 weeks of administration compared to baseline.35
Similarly, the administration of clindamycin to healthy cats receiving
placebo or a synbiotic resulted in marked alterations in fecal
microbiota diversity and altered metabolic profiles.36 Indiscriminate
use of antimicrobials in animals, especially those that are frequently
used in humans, risks development of antibiotic resistant strains of
bacteria, which can then be transmitted to humans (ch. 7).
However, it should be noted that there have been some studies
that reported on both safety and efficacy of tylosin in dogs with
chronic diarrhea and many veterinarians continue to use this
antibiotic. In light of above limitations further research of the use of
tylosin should be undertaken.

FECAL MICROBIOTA
TRANSPLANTATION (FMT) (CH. 106)
The efforts to restore eubiosis in dogs and cats with GI disease by
administration of FMT has been investigated only to a limited extent.
Guidelines regarding optimal donor screening and clinical
indications, as well as the method of delivery (oral vs. rectal catheter
vs. endoscopy) and frequency of administration of FMT, are
currently lacking.37 In a randomized clinical trial of puppies with
parvoviral diarrhea, FMT + standard therapy (IV fluids and
antibiotics) was associated with faster resolution of diarrhea and
shorter hospitalization time compared to standard therapy alone.38

However, a separate study failed to demonstrate the efficacy of oral
FMT as treatment for post-weaning diarrhea in research colony
puppies.39 Adult dogs with acute diarrhea showed differences in the
response of the microbiota and metabolome to treatment with FMT
(enema) or metronidazole, with metronidazole causing greater
perturbations.40 In 1 small study of dogs with acute hemorrhagic
diarrhea syndrome, a single FMT failed to improve clinical scores
and the fecal microbiomes of diseased dogs vs. controls.41
Studies defining the potential role for FMT in dogs with chronic
enteropathy, including IBD, include 2 reports (total of 17 dogs)
where severity of clinical disease improved following FMT in most
dogs.42,43 The limitations in these studies were significant and
included small sample size, lack of a standardized method of fecal
delivery, failure to include a control group, and the lack of rigorous
molecular testing for microbial populations.

PROBIOTICS AND IMMUNITY
Probiotics contain live microorganisms that, when consumed in
sufficient amounts, confer health benefits to the host.44 The
rationale for probiotics is to improve the balance of the intestinal
microbiota to a more beneficial population following disease (Box
260.2). The microbes used in probiotics include various lactic acid
bacteria, such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species,
Enterococcus faecium, or non-bacterial organisms such as the nonpathogenic yeast, Saccharomyces boulardii. Both single strain and
multi-strain products are commercially available for use in dogs and
cats. Proposed mechanisms by which probiotics improve host health
include: enhanced intestinal barrier function (e.g., upregulation of
TJ proteins, increased mucin and defensin secretion), production of
SCFAs, stimulation of sIgA production that in turn prevents
pathogen colonization, and immune modulation that promotes
tolerance to commensals while protecting against gut pathogens
(Figure 260.3).45 While probiotics usually do not colonize or only
transiently colonize, they produce beneficial metabolites as they pass
through the GI tract. The mechanism of probiotics is strain-specific,

emphasizing that different bacterial strains have individual effects on
the host. Limited studies in healthy dogs and cats suggest that
probiotics may augment some aspects of host immunity. In puppies
fed either a control diet or a control diet supplemented with E.
faecium SF68 from weaning up to 1 year of age, fecal IgA and
vaccine-induced circulating IgA/IgG were higher in the
supplemented cohort.46 E. faecium SF68 also has been shown to
enhance vaccination-induced immunity in specific-pathogen-free
kittens. There was a non-significant increase in feline herpesvirusspecific serum IgG while E. faecium was recovered from the feces in
7 of 9 kittens after vaccination.47 Healthy adult cats fed a diet
supplemented with L. acidophilus DSM13241 showed increased
numbers of eosinophils and enhanced phagocytic capacity in the
peripheral granulocyte population in response to probiotic use.48

• Different probiotic strains benefit different hosts
• One probiotic does not fit all gastrointestinal diseases
• Consider the specific clinical indication for use
• Continuous consumption is required for desired effect
• Probiotic effects are modest at best
• Generally used as a supplement to conventional treatments
• Side-effects are uncommon and transient
• Flatulence and borborygmus are most common
• Avoid using in critically ill or immunocompromised patients

PROBIOTICS IN ACUTE
GASTROINTESTINAL DISORDERS
Acute diarrheal diseases are common in dogs and cats in shelters due
to stress, diet change, and exposure to bacterial, viral, and parasitic

pathogens (ch. 49). While the use of probiotics in patients with
acute gastroenteritis has been reported, the reduced rigor of some
studies and the different sources and dosages of probiotics and
synbiotics used make comparison of individual studies difficult. In
shelter dogs (n=182) and cats (n=217) with acute uncomplicated
diarrhea, E. faecium SF68 decreased episodes of diarrhea in cats but
not in dogs, compared to the placebo group.49 In a separate study
involving 36 dogs with acute diarrhea, the time from start of
treatment to the last abnormal stool was significantly shorter (2.2-1.3
days for controls) in dogs treated with a 6-strain probiotic compared
to the placebo group.50 Another small study using Bifidobacterium
animalis strain AHC7 in dogs with acute diarrhea showed a
shortened time to resolution (mean 3.9 versus 6.6. days).51 Also, 60
dogs with acute diarrhea were treated with 3 probiotic strains of
Lactobacillus spp. or placebo and their stool consistency, general
well-being, and the numbers of specific pathogens in stool samples
were analyzed.52 Probiotic treatment normalized stool consistency
while maintaining appetite and reducing vomiting. The abundances
of Clostridium perfringens and E. faecium, which typically increase
during diarrheic episodes in dogs, were decreased in the feces of the
probiotic-treated group when compared with the placebo group.
Finally, in kittens from a shelter, E. faecium SF68 significantly
decreased the incidence of diarrhea with only 9.5% of the probiotic
group developing diarrhea compared to 60% of kittens that were not
treated with the probiotic.53
The merit of probiotics in treating infectious diseases (i.e., viral
[ch. 201], bacterial [ch. 195], parasitic/protozoal [ch. 196]) and
antibiotic-associated dysbiosis has also been investigated in dogs and
cats. A 6-week treatment with E. faecium SF68 in 20 dogs with
subclinical giardiasis failed to affect giardial cyst shedding, fecal
antigen shedding, and innate and adaptive immune responses versus
placebo.54 In dogs with parvoviral enteritis, a commercially-available
lactic-acid bacteria (LAB) consortium (8 organisms; VSL#3 “de
Simone formulation”) added to standard supportive therapy
improved clinical scores compared with standard therapy alone.55
Overall, 9 dogs (90%) in the probiotic group compared to 7 dogs

(70%) in the standard therapy group survived in this study. In this
study, total white blood cell and lymphocyte counts were increased in
all parvovirosis dogs receiving probiotics, while these parameters
remained low in the dogs that received standard therapy alone. In
canine acute hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome, the de Simone LAB
mixture reduced clinical severity and increased fecal abundance of
beneficial Faecalibacterium spp., whereas C. perfringens abundance
and enterotoxins were reduced.56 Lastly, different probiotics (E.
faecium or a LAB mixture) failed to reduce the effects of amoxicillinclavulanate57 or clindamycin36 on GI signs and fecal microbiome
characteristics in healthy cats.

probiotics. Probiotic mechanisms of action include
immune modulation, inhibition of pathogens, and/or
enhanced intestinal barrier integrity. Organic acid
production includes the generation of short-chain
fatty acids.

PROBIOTICS FOR CHRONIC
GASTROINTESTINAL DISORDERS

Various in vivo and ex vivo studies have investigated probiotic
effects in dogs and cats with chronic enteropathies. Clinical studies
have reported on the role of probiotics in dogs with FRE, tylosinresponsive diarrhea, and IBD. In separate in vivo trials involving
dogs with FRE, use of probiotics E. faecium58 or a LAB mixture (3
strains of Lactobacillus spp.) failed to improve clinical outcome or
proinflammatory intestinal cytokine patterns in dogs with FRE
compared to placebo (elimination diet).59 In dogs with tylosinresponsive diarrhea, the administration of L. rhamnosus GG did not
prolong the duration of clinical remission once the antibiotic was
discontinued.32
In canine IBD, specific probiotic therapy has resulted in
modulation of host responses and enhancement of intestinal
epithelial barrier integrity. In 1 trial, probiotic therapy with VSL#3 “de Simone formulation” was investigated in comparison to
combination drug therapy.60 Dogs treated with the probiotic showed
remission accompanied by changes in tolerogenic mucosal responses
(increased numbers of FoxP3+ and TGF-beta+ regulatory T cells)
and increased mucosal expression of the TJ protein occludin.
Another probiotic trial using FISH to investigate the mucosal
microbiota showed that remission was associated with increased
beneficial bacterial species and upregulated expression of junctional
proteins following six weeks of probiotic (de Simone LAB mixture)
therapy.61 Probiotic therapy in this study was associated with an
increased expression of the TJ proteins E-cadherin, occludin, and
zonulin in intestinal biopsy specimens. Finally, the yeast probiotic
Saccharomyces boulardii (as part of a synbiotic preparation) was
shown to improve clinical severity and stool frequency at days 45 and
60 when administered to dogs that had IBD with and without
protein-losing enteropathy (PLE).62 In the PLE subgroup, 3/3 dogs
treated with S. boulardii showed improvement in serum albumin
versus 2/3 dogs in the placebo group. There are no studies evaluating
use of probiotics or synbiotics in cats with chronic inflammatory
enteropathy (IBD).
Probiotics have also been investigated for treatment of chronic T.
foetus infection and chronic constipation in cats (ch. 263). In 1
recent study, 2 strains of enterococci (including E. faecium SF68)

were assessed ex vivo for their effect on the inhibition of T. foetus
growth, adhesion to, and cytotoxicity towards the intestinal
epithelium.63 T. foetus adhesion to an epithelial cell monolayer was
reduced with pretreatment with enterococci; however, there was no
effect of enterococci treatment on intestinal epithelial cell toxicity.
Cats with chronic constipation showed a beneficial response to a LAB
probiotic mixture (SLAB51™) in 1 small pilot trial.64 Seven cats with
constipation and 3 cats with megacolon and constipation that were
unresponsive to medical management were treated for 90 days, and
then evaluated for treatment response, fecal scores, histopathologic
lesions of colonic inflammation, and select microbiota analyses via
quantitative polymerase chain reaction. While probiotic treatment
resulted in improved fecal scores, clinical recovery, and attenuation
of mucosal inflammation compared to control cats (n = 5), these
results should be interpreted cautiously considering several study
limitations.

ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY
Dogs and cats are monogastric species with simple glandular
stomachs that serve as a food reservoir, physically break down
foodstuffs, and initiate nutrient digestion through the mixing of food
with gastric secretions, including gastric acid and proteolytic
(pepsin) and lipolytic (gastric lipase) enzymes. As gastric acid and
proteolytic enzymes do not distinguish between ingesta and the
mucosa of the host, the gastric mucosal barrier plays a critical role in
shielding the underlying mucosa from its luminal contents. These
defense mechanisms include: (1) a bicarbonate-rich, double
thickness mucus layer, (2) a single layer of highly resistant epithelial
cells that repel gastric acid and are capable of rapid repair, (3) the
local production of prostaglandins that regulate blood flow, stimulate
the secretion of mucus and bicarbonate ions, and promote epithelial
repair, and (4) a rich mucosal blood supply and immune system. The
canine and feline stomach is anatomically separated into the cardia
(small region in close association with the gastroesophageal
sphincter), fundus, body, and pyloric antrum. The stomach of cats is
slightly angled, with closer approximation of the pylorus to the
midline when compared to dogs (Figure 261.1). Similar to the
intestinal tract, the gastric wall is divided into an inner mucosal
layer, submucosa, muscularis, and an outer serosal layer. The gastric
musculature is largely comprised of an inner circular smooth muscle
layer and an outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer. The fundic

musculature predominantly aids in receptive relaxation, mediated by
vagal inhibitory fibers to transiently accommodate increasing gastric
volumes with feeding, and mixes foodstuffs following a meal.
Receptive relaxation is particularly important to dogs and cats that
are meal feeders, compared to those animals that eat small meals
throughout the day. Animals that are accustomed to small, frequent
meals may have less accommodation to rapid increases in stomach
volume and pressure. Muscular churning in the pyloric antrum
against a closed pyloric sphincter breaks large foodstuffs into
smaller, more digestible components.1 Mucosal folds are more
prominent in the gastric body and tend to run parallel towards the
pyloric antrum with a fold thickness of approximately 1-8 mm in the
dog (2-50 kg).2 These folds disappear in the pyloric antrum.
The glandular stomach is also anatomically divided into sections
that accomplish their respective functional roles. In both sections,
the long, tubular glands are found beneath the surface epithelium,
where they open as pits. The mucosa of the fundus and body
represents the acid-secreting region and contains the gastric, or
oxyntic (“acid-secreting”), glands that are populated with the acidsecreting parietal cells, as well as the pepsinogen A-secreting chief
cells, histamine-secreting enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells, and the
mucus neck cells that secrete mucus, trefoil peptides, and gastric
lipase. Parietal cells also secrete small amounts of intrinsic factor,
though most intrinsic factor in dogs and cats is secreted by
pancreatic acinar cells. Cells in the gastric glands of the fundus also
secrete the orexigenic hormone, ghrelin.3 The pyloric glandular
mucosa is non-acid secreting but nonetheless plays an important role
in acid production. Pyloric glands are populated with gastrinsecreting G cells, ECL cells, and bicarbonate and mucus cells. Gastric
acid secretion is tightly regulated by paracrine, endocrine, and neural
stimulation. Acid secretion is stimulated by three major
secretagogues: acetylcholine, released by the vagus nerve and enteric
nervous system; gastrin, released by G cells and circulated to the
fundic mucosa; and histamine, released locally predominantly by the
ECL cells. These secretagogues bind to their respective receptors on
the parietal cell and stimulate the activation of H+,K+-ATPases
(“proton pumps”). Major inhibitors of acid secretion include

somatostatin, produced by gastric and pyloric gland D cells; and
prostaglandins. Vasoactive intestinal peptide inhibits gastric acid
secretion in the dog but promotes meal-stimulated acid secretion
and pepsin activation in the cat.4 Gastric acid secretion plays an
important role in the initiation of protein and micronutrient (nonheme iron, calcium, vitamin B12) digestion and helps to inactivate
ingested microorganisms.5 The role for gastric acid in limiting
antigenic material delivered to the intestines has also been proposed.

CIRCULATION AND INNERVATION
The canine and feline stomach receives the majority of its blood
supply from the left gastric and right gastroepiploic arteries. Finer
vessels are found in the distal third of the lesser curvature and
antrum compared to the fundus and body in both the dog and cat. In
both species, the largest vascular plexus is found in the submucosa.
The cat also has a smaller vascular plexus deep to the muscularis
mucosa.6 The stomach is under autonomic control, with internal
control provided by the enteric nervous system and external
innervation from the vagus and post-ganglionic neurons originating
from sympathetic ganglia, such as the celiacomesenteric ganglion.7

MOTILITY, TRANSIT, AND pH
Gastric transit is characterized by rapid movement of liquids, slower
movement of digestible solids, and a delayed clearance of
indigestible solids that occurs during the interdigestive phase.8,9
Clearance of liquids is regulated by slow, tonic contractions that
occur in the proximal stomach and is proportional to its volume
whereas gastric emptying of digestible solids is dependent on caloric
density, moisture content, and particle size. The passage of digestible
solids is also influenced by phasic contractions propagated within the
pyloric antrum and the pressure gradient between the stomach and
duodenum. Several hormones, including but not limited to gastrin,
cholecystokinin, glucagon-like peptide 1, and peptide YY, secreted by
small intestinal enteroendocrine cells upon detection of luminal
macronutrients, act to inhibit gastric emptying whereas motilin,
secreted predominantly by duodenal and jejunal enteroendocrine
cells, acts to promote gastric emptying during the interdigestive
phase.10 While the mean mucosal gastric pH in dogs and cats is

generally 1.5-3.0, the pH can vary widely throughout the day with a
potential for spikes in pH even in the interdigestive period (Figure
261.2) or during aggressive gastric acid suppressant therapy,
making a single sampling of gastric fluid to assess adequacy of
treatment relatively meaningless.11,12

MICROBIOTA AND IMMUNE SYSTEM
The gastric microbiota is largely influenced by diet, local
environment (e.g., pH, mucus layer), and host health (e.g.,
concurrent diseases, administration of xenobiotics, etc.) (ch. 260).
Gastric bacteria predominantly belong to the phyla Proteobacteria
with Helicobacter spp. being the most commonly identified bacteria
in the stomach of dogs.13 Helicobacter spp. and potentially lacticacid producing bacteria may be identified in the feline stomach.14,15
Transient microbial populations representing microorganisms
ingested externally or elsewhere in the body (e.g., pharynx,
respiratory tract) can also be observed in the stomach.

GENERAL APPROACH TO GASTRIC
DISEASE
Vomiting is one of the most common signs of gastric disease, but it
lacks specificity (ch. 48). Vomiting can also be a confusing sign for
owners to describe accurately. Therefore, assessment of a “vomiting”
animal should begin with confirmation that the owner witnessed the
event and that the animal is in fact vomiting and not displaying
immediate food ejection (

Video 259.1), regurgitating, or even

coughing, because the terminal retch at the end of a fit of coughing
can produce mucus or foam, which some owners misinterpret as
vomiting.

FIGURE 261.3 Endoscopic removal of a gastric
trichobezoar in a cat. Mucosal ulceration can be
observed to the right of the trichobezoar.
Following confirmation of vomiting, the patient’s signalment,
history, and physical examination findings (ch. 3) should be
considered and used for determining the duration of the vomiting
and to generate a complete problem list. This information helps
prioritize which differential diagnoses are more likely and therefore
what diagnostic tests are warranted and in which order.
Standardized checklists can be used to obtain detailed historical
information, minimize medical errors, and expedite acquisition of a
full history (ch. 2).16 For example, an owner reporting frequent
grooming or vomiting hairballs in a cat that has anemia and
hypoproteinemia can increase a suspicion for ulceration secondary to
the presence of a gastric trichobezoar (Figure 261.3). The cause of
vomiting, especially when acute, is frequently identified or suspected

following acquisition of the history (e.g., foreign body ingestion or
dietary indiscretion witnessed by owner, lack of monthly
anthelmintic in a young dog) and performance of a physical exam
(e.g., palpable abdominal mass or foreign body, goiter in an unkempt
cat, linear foreign body at the base of the tongue). Examination of the
vomitus should be performed when possible to evaluate for stomach
worms, blood, or bile. Particular attention during the physical
examination should be paid to hydration status, presence of
resorptive lesions or other dental disease (ch. 258), quality of the
hair coat, presence of ascites (ch. 21), signs of abdominal pain (e.g.,
tense on abdominal palpation, hunched abdominal position (
Video 277.1), hiding behavior, or facial expression17), cutaneous
signs that might support an underlying adverse food reaction (chs.
12 and 160), and muscle and body condition scores (ch. 72).
Animals with low body or muscle condition scores are more likely to
have chronic disease or comorbidities. The physical examination of a
patient that is vomiting may include a full retinal exam, as
chorioretinitis and other retinal abnormalities increase the suspicion
for underlying infectious or neoplastic etiologies (ch. 13). A rectal
examination as well as fecal evaluation (ch. 80) should be
performed to assess fecal color and consistency. Following
acquisition of the history and physical examination, the clinician can
begin to determine the chronicity, severity, and potential cause of the
gastric disease, as further outlined below.

GASTRITIS
By definition, gastritis is an inflammatory disease of the stomach.
Many patients with clinical signs suggestive of a gastric disorder,
most commonly vomiting or gastric distension, are presumed to have
inflammation or some type of mucosal injury. However, as
infiltration of the gastric mucosa with inflammatory cells is rarely
definitively proven with evaluation of tissue samples in the acute
setting and can be minimal even with severe signs, it might be more
accurate to use the term gastropathy for these cases. Inflammation,
when present, is rarely limited to the stomach and often extends into
the small intestine. As a result, dogs and cats with gastritis are more

likely to have gastroenteritis and have additional signs beyond
vomiting including decreased appetite, diarrhea, lethargy, flatulence,
or abdominal pain.
Classification schemes for gastritis in humans, such as the Sydney
classification system for chronic gastritis,18 are utilized to streamline
terminology and approach among clinicians and researchers and
incorporate both macro- and microscopic evaluation of the stomach.
A modified Sydney system, which utilizes endoscopic and
histopathologic assessment, also has been investigated recently for
assessment of chronic gastritis in dogs.19 Guidelines for the
histopathologic evaluation of gastrointestinal (GI) inflammation,
including gastritis, have been created by the World Small Animal
Veterinary Association (WSAVA) International Gastrointestinal (IG)
Standardization Group.20 Because histopathologic evaluation is not
always performed, gastritis in dogs and cats is commonly categorized
by the duration of the clinical signs rather than histological
parameters, although the latter can be helpful in the determination
of etiology and chronicity as outlined for chronic gastritis, below.

ACUTE GASTRITIS/GASTROPATHY
Acute gastritis, defined by the presence of clinical signs for <2 weeks,
is often self-limiting and responsive to supportive care. Various
etiologies have been implicated in the development of gastritis in
dogs and cats (Table 261.1). Acute gastritis can affect a dog or cat of
any age or breed. The most common causes include foreign bodies,
dietary indiscretion (“garbage gut”) or intolerance, drugs, household
chemicals or pesticides/herbicides, plants, systemic illness, and
infectious agents. Tables of common plants and household chemicals
associated with gastritis may be found in ch. 136.21 Among drugs,
nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), antibiotics, and
chemotherapeutic agents are leading causes of gastritis in dogs and
cats. NSAIDs are both directly and indirectly injurious to the GI
epithelium as a result of being weak acids and also by inhibiting
protective prostaglandins. The majority of commercially available

NSAIDs have been associated with the development of gastric lesions
in dogs (ch. 143).22
Acute metabolic illness (e.g., acute hepatic [ch. 269] or renal [ch.
300] injury, hypoadrenocorticism [ch. 296]) or conditions causing
poor GI perfusion (e.g., hypoadrenocorticism [ch. 296], gastric
dilation-volvulus, thromboembolic disease [ch. 238], extreme
exercise) can also acutely trigger gastric inflammation or ulceration,
although most of these conditions are also accompanied by systemic
signs.
Infectious agents are more common causes of chronic gastritis and
include a variety of helminths (Physaloptera spp., Ollulanus),
oomycetes (Pythium; ch. 263), fungi (Histoplasma; ch. 209),
bacteria (Salmonella spp., Campylobacter jejuni, Helicobacter; ch.
195), and rarely, viruses (parvovirosis [ch. 201], distemper virus
[ch. 204]). In cats, heartworm infection can cause acute or chronic
vomiting and gastritis (ch. 237).23 Enteropathogenic bacteria, as
listed above, are rarely primary causes of acute gastritis except in
dogs and cats with exposure to uncooked foods, treats, or roadkill or
those with a history of hunting. As with metabolic disease, gastritis
caused by most non-parasitic infectious agents is generally
accompanied by signs of intestinal involvement (e.g., diarrhea,
hematochezia) or systemic signs, such as fever.

Clinical Findings and Diagnostic Approach
Obtaining a detailed history and performing a comprehensive
physical examination are critical to determining the best diagnostic
and therapeutic approach. Standardized checklists24 can be used for
facilitating acquisition of a complete history. Dogs and cats with
vomiting from dietary indiscretion can have rapidly resolving clinical
signs with supportive care. Animals with a history of more severe

signs such as protracted vomiting, hiding behavior, hematemesis, or
physical exam abnormalities such as dehydration, hypovolemia, or
signs of abdominal pain need a more extensive evaluation. Owners
should be questioned regarding the potential for exposure of their
pet to foreign objects including plants, trash, clothing, yarn, string,
tinsel, needles, or hair ties. A full drug history should be obtained for
any dog or cat presenting with signs of gastric disease. Intoxications
secondary to chocolate (i.e., theobromine), macadamia nuts, sago
palm, mushrooms, mycotoxins (e.g., blue-green algae, aflatoxin,
molds), and marijuana should be considered in dogs or cats
exhibiting vomiting in association with an acute onset of neurologic
abnormalities (chs. 133 and 136). Viral etiologies are rarely causes
of vomiting alone but should be suspected when there is an outbreak
of GI signs in multiple dogs or cats from the same shelter or
household or when signs are severe, particularly in young animals.
Physical exam findings (ch. 3) in animals with acute gastritis vary.
Animals can have mild clinical signs and no abnormalities on
physical examination or have severe signs accompanied by a
hunched posture, signs of abdominal pain, changes in facial
expression, dehydration, ptyalism, or signs of hypovolemia and
shock (ch. 121), including weak pulses, hypo- or hyperthermia,
tachycardia, pale mucous membranes, and prolonged capillary refill
times. Signs of cranial abdominal pain can often be appreciated on
physical examination in cases of foreign body ingestion, gastric
dilatation volvulus, concurrent pancreatitis, or GI ulceration. Linear
foreign bodies can become anchored to the base of a cat’s tongue,
and careful inspection of this area on physical examination is
recommended when possible (ch. 3). Rectal and fecal examination
(ch. 80) should be performed to evaluate for frank blood, tarry
stools, and parasites. Examination of the vomitus for the presence of
blood, bile, or parasites is also recommended. Body and muscle
condition scores (ch. 72) are expected to be normal in cases of acute
gastritis in the absence of comorbidities.25
The need for an extensive diagnostic evaluation and therapeutic
intervention depends on the severity of clinical signs and physical
examination findings (ch. 119). For dogs and cats with mild signs,
supportive care is often all that is needed. In young dogs and cats,
especially those with outdoor exposure or access to foreign objects, a

centrifugal fecal flotation (ch. 80), fecal nematode antigen testing,
and abdominal radiographs are generally recommended to evaluate
for the presence of parasitic disease or foreign material. For those
dogs and cats with concerning historical findings (e.g. hematemesis,
prolonged dysrexia, possible foreign body ingestion) or moderate to
severe physical exam abnormalities (e.g., pale mucous membranes,
signs of hypovolemia, abdominal pain, tarry or frank blood on rectal
exam), additional diagnostic workup including a complete blood
count (CBC), serum biochemical profile, urinalysis, and coagulation
panel in addition to further imaging, such as ultrasound, may be
indicated. Other diagnostic tests to be considered would be based on
the history, physical exam findings, and results of the initial workup.
When the cause of acute gastritis is undetermined, nonspecific
supportive treatment is initiated.

Treatment
For dogs and cats with mild signs, a short fasting period (<12 hours)
with supportive care, followed by introduction of oral water, is
recommended. If the animal tolerates oral water, a low-fiber, low-fat,
high-moisture commercial or home-cooked diet (e.g., white fish or
chicken and rice, low-fat cottage cheese and rice), given in small
amounts multiple times during the day, can be introduced (ch. 152).
The animal’s regular food can be slowly reintroduced over a 3- to 5day period after vomiting has ceased. Prolonged fasting (>48 hours)
is not recommended because of the positive benefits of early enteral
nutrition (EEN)26 in both dogs and cats and concerns for the
development of hepatic lipidosis in cats. If the signs are more severe,
(e.g., dehydration, continuous vomiting), the animal will need fluid
replacement with intravenous (IV) crystalloids (ch. 120). Correction
of electrolyte abnormalities such as hypokalemia (ch. 68) is often
required in patients with severe vomiting. In some patients,
empirical treatment with antiemetic drugs may be needed while
evaluating for the cause of vomiting. Antiemetics are best
administered once the veterinarian is confident that a mechanical
obstruction or intoxication (in which case emesis might be induced;
ch. 132) is not the cause of vomiting. Commercially available
antiemetics commonly used in veterinary medicine include
maropitant, serotonin antagonists, and metoclopramide, though the

efficacy of metoclopramide as an antiemetic are questionable (Table
261.2). Anthelmintic treatment is recommended especially in young
animals and those without an anthelmintic preventative history.
Diagnosis of infestation with a stomach worm (i.e., Physaloptera
spp. in dogs or Ollulanus tricuspis in cats) can be challenging and
routine, pre-emptive therapy with a broad-spectrum anthelmintic
agent that is effective in eradicating stomach worms (e.g., in dogs,
pyrantel pamoate 15 mg/kg PO repeated in 2-3 weeks; in cats,
fenbendazole 50 mg/kg PO q24h for 3 days; ch. 142, and table on
the textbook’s inside covers) is prudent before recommending more
expensive diagnostic tests because this simple treatment may
eliminate the problem. Gastric acid suppressant drugs or
cytoprotective drugs (e.g., histamine-2 receptor antagonists, proton
pump inhibitors [PPIs], sucralfate) are reserved for patients in which
gastric erosion or ulceration is suspected based on hematemesis or
melena (see below).

CHRONIC GASTRITIS
The pathogenesis of chronic gastritis in dogs and cats cannot always
be determined. In some cases, a cause, such as parasitism, neoplasia,
an infectious agent, or a metabolic disorder (e.g., uremia,
hepatopathy), can be identified. Once the more common causes are
determined to be unlikely, chronic gastritis is deemed idiopathic and
an adverse food reaction or immune-mediated condition is often
considered to be responsible. Several canine and feline breeds are at
risk for chronic gastritis (Table 261.3). Clinical signs in dogs and
cats with chronic gastritis are characterized by persistent or
intermittent vomiting of variable frequency and character and are of
>2 weeks duration. Because inflammation can impair gastric motility
and delay gastric emptying, animals with chronic gastritis can retain
food in the stomach for long periods of time. Determining the cause
of chronic gastritis may require acquisition of a mucosal tissue
sample via endoscopy or surgery, but clues can be provided as to the
possible etiology with signalment and baseline blood work. For
example, a marked eosinophilia in a young Rottweiler where
parasitism has been excluded as a possible cause raises suspicion for
eosinophilic gastroenteritis. Following collection and routine
histopathologic evaluation of mucosal biopsies, the gastritis can be
classified based on the cellular infiltrate, (i.e., lymphoplasmacytic,
eosinophilic, pyogranulomatous, suppurative, lymphoid follicular
hyperplasia, neoplastic), the presence of morphologic changes (i.e.,
hypertrophy, atrophy, mineralization, ulceration, edema, glandular
nesting, and fibrosis), and lesion severity (i.e., normal, mild,
moderate, marked, or severe). More details on histopathologic

evaluation and nomenclature can be found in publications by the
WSAVA GI Standardization Group.20

Lymphoplasmacytic and Lymphocytic Gastritis
Lymphoplasmacytic (LP) gastritis is the most common histologic
type of chronic gastritis in dogs, representing 51-100% of the
inflammatory infiltrate of chronic gastritis in dogs.19,25 Mild to
moderate LP gastritis can be observed in dogs and cats in good
health, and thus the presence of clinical signs and results of other
diagnostic findings should be considered when determining the
importance and requirement for treatment of gastric
inflammation.25,27 Lymphocytic and LP gastritis are not diagnostic
of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD; more recently also termed
chronic inflammatory enteropathy [CIE] as either can be observed
with food-responsive disease, Helicobacter spp. colonization, and

high-intensity exercise [e.g., Alaskan racing sled dogs].28 Indeed,
food-responsive disease can be associated with severe LP
gastritis.29 Helicobacter spp. are frequently identified in the
stomachs of dogs with or without both gastric inflammation and
clinical signs of disease; therefore, their role as a potential pathogen
in dogs remains unclear.30 Some researchers propose that loss of
tolerance to Helicobacter rather than pathogenicity of the organism
may be responsible for development of inflammation and clinical
signs. Helicobacter spp. colonization also is frequently present in
healthy cats; however, Helicobacter organisms have been associated
with gastric lymphoid follicles and epithelial proliferation31 as well
as gastric lymphoma in cats.32 Thus, determining whether
Helicobacter is a causative agent of inflammation in companion
animals can be difficult, but treatment is often recommended when
organisms are associated with inflammation in animals that fail
initial therapies such as dietary modification. More information is
provided in a subsequent section below. Severe LP infiltration may
be difficult to distinguish from gastric lymphoma, especially with
endoscopic biopsy specimens.27 The use of immunophenotyping may
help support a diagnosis of lymphoma.
