Eosinophilic Gastritis
According to the WSAVA IG Standardization Group, the mucosa of
the normal gastric body and gastric antrum may have 0-2 and 0-6
eosinophils/10,000 mcm2, respectively. Eosinophil counts beyond
these numbers suggest the presence of eosinophilic gastritis.
Eosinophilic gastritis is often accompanied by eosinophilic
infiltration of the small or large intestine. In the absence of adverse
food reaction or parasitic disease, eosinophilic gastritis is included
under the umbrella of idiopathic IBD.33 Dogs with eosinophilic
gastritis tend to be younger (<5 years)33 and Rottweilers are likely a
predisposed breed. Gastric infiltration is usually restricted to the
mucosa, but in some patients it extends into the muscularis and even
the serosa. Mucosal involvement can cause enlargement of the rugal
folds. The diseased mucosa can become ulcerated, leading to

bleeding or leakage of plasma proteins into the gastric lumen.
Peripheral eosinophilia is a common finding, but its severity can vary
markedly. Some dogs also have a history of either urticaria or
dermatologic changes or vomiting that may be associated with the
ingestion of a specific diet (ch. 160). Parasitic, infectious, or
neoplastic diseases (e.g., mast cell tumor; ch. 327) should be ruled
out prior to presuming that the disease is immune-mediated. The
treatment of eosinophilic gastritis usually begins with dietary
modification (e.g., hydrolyzed or limited ingredient diet) and
anthelmintic therapy (ch. 142). Several dietary trials, in which the
client feeds the diet exclusively, may be needed before clinical signs
resolve (ch. 152). Dogs and cats that fail anthelmintic and dietary
therapy may have a positive response to immunomodulatory therapy
(e.g., corticosteroids, cyclosporine; ch. 144). The pathophysiology
and management strategies for eosinophilic GI disorders has been
reviewed in detail.33 Eosinophilic gastritis, as described above, is less
common in cats, including those with eosinophilic enteritis.34
However, GI eosinophilic sclerosing fibroplasia appears to be more
common in cats and, therefore, the term “feline gastrointestinal
eosinophilic sclerosing fibroplasia” or FGESF has been coined.
Ragdoll and male cats are reportedly overrepresented. Lesions of
FGESF are often identified as solitary masses, and are characterized
by dense collagen bundles containing infiltrates of eosinophils and
mast cells with fewer neutrophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.
Frequently, masses form at the pyloric sphincter or ileocolic junction
and can be palpated on physical examination. Vomiting is the most
frequent clinical sign in affected cats (∼80%) and ∼50% have a
peripheral eosinophilia. Surgical removal with immunomodulation
provides the best chance for cure, although the disease is often too
advanced at the time of diagnosis to be completely eliminated.35,36

Hypertrophic Gastropathy/Gastritis
Chronic hypertrophic gastropathy/gastritis is a rare disorder that
appears either as diffuse, generalized mucosal hypertrophy or, more
frequently, as a localized hypertrophy of the antral mucosa that can
cause intermittent or chronic pyloric obstruction. Clinical signs of
hypertrophic gastropathy include delayed gastric emptying and

abdominal distension, vomiting, dysrexia, and lethargy. Although
vomiting is more common, some animals may regurgitate if the
abdominal distension is severe enough to overcome the pressure
differential imparted by the lower esophageal sphincter. Causative
factors that can lead to gastric mucosal hypertrophy include chronic
inflammation, foreign bodies, or long-term use (i.e., years) of PPIs.
Basenjis and Drentse Patrijshonds have a predilection for the diffuse
form, known as giant hypertrophic gastritis.37 The disease resembles
Ménétrier’s disease in humans and is characterized by diffuse gastric
mural thickening, secondary to foveolar and glandular hyperplasia
and concurrent loss of chief and parietal cells. Varying degrees of
inflammatory cell infiltration are often present. Young Drentse
Patrijshond dogs can have concurrent familial stomatocytosis and
other signs, including chronic kidney and liver disease.38 A litter of 3
Cairn Terriers that later developed gastric carcinoma has also been
described.39 Ménétrier-like disease has also been reported in a single
cat.40 In contrast to giant hypertrophic gastritis, the localized form
involving the pyloric antrum is known as hypertrophic pyloric
gastropathy and is overrepresented in young to middle-aged small
breed dogs with a possible male sex predisposition. Affected dogs
often have a fluid- or gas-filled stomach on radiographs. Contrast
radiography can be useful to confirm an outflow obstruction.
Documentation of gastric distension and increased pyloric wall
thickness as visualized with ultrasound supports the diagnosis
(Figure 261.4). Definitive diagnosis is confirmed by endoscopic or
surgical identification of enlarged mucosal folds that make pyloric
intubation difficult.41 Surgical resection of the affected area is
considered to be the treatment of choice. The disease is characterized
microscopically by pyloric antral mucosal hyperplasia with or
without concurrent muscular hypertrophy.

Atrophic Gastritis
Atrophic gastritis is characterized by atrophy of the gastric mucosa.
This disorder is rarely reported in dogs and, to the author’s
knowledge, has not been reported in cats. The presence of
inflammation tends to be minimal. The fundic mucosa is often

involved, leading to loss of gastric acid secreting function. Atrophic
gastritis is most commonly reported in the Norwegian Lundehund,
where a genetic predisposition is suspected. The cause is unknown,
but the condition occurs mainly in older dogs and may be immunemediated. Atrophic gastritis may also be a sequela to chronic biliary
reflux gastritis in dogs. The predominant presenting concern is
chronic intermittent vomiting. Achlorhydria may predispose to
bacterial overgrowth from ingested microorganisms that would
normally be destroyed by the acidic stomach contents. This can lead
to malabsorption, chronic diarrhea, and loss of body weight and
condition. An association between atrophic gastritis and gastric
carcinoma has been recognized in dogs and is thought to occur
secondary to ECL cell hyperplasia from chronic hypergastrinemia.42
The diagnosis of atrophic gastritis may be suspected based on
mucosal thinning and prominent blood vessels on endoscopic
examination (ch. 107); confirmation requires histopathologic
examination.37

Helicobacter-Associated Gastritis
Helicobacter spp. are Gram-negative, microaerophilic, curved to
spiral-shaped, motile bacteria. Helicobacter spp. are predominantly
identified in the stomach; however, they can also be found in the oral
cavity, intestine, and the hepatobiliary system.43,44 Most gastric
Helicobacter-like organisms (GHLO) found in dogs and cats are
large spiral organisms (0.5 × 5-10 microns) that cannot be
distinguished by light microscopy. To date, H. felis, H. bizzozeronii,
H. salomonis, Flexispira rappini, H. bilis, H. heilmannii sensu
stricto, H. pametensis, and H. pylori have all been identified in the
stomach of dogs or cats, with non-H. pylori species
predominating.31,45 Mixed infections with two or more Helicobacter
spp. appear to be common in dogs and cats. Several studies
demonstrated a high prevalence of GHLO in cats and dogs, with an
∼100% infection rate among laboratory animals, 50-100% among
healthy pets, and 41-100% among vomiting pets.46 Housing
conditions and age appear to play an important role, with pets living
in shelters or colonies having a higher prevalence. The mode of

transmission of Helicobacter spp. is still unclear, and both fecal-oral
and oral-oral transmission have been proposed.
In human patients, there is extensive evidence implicating H.
pylori in the pathogenesis of chronic superficial gastritis. Eradication
of H. pylori by use of antimicrobial therapy can cure gastritis in
people. Infection with Helicobacter spp. also predisposes humans to
the development of gastric cancer.
In pets with naturally acquired Helicobacter colonization,
however, the pathogenic role of this organism is still highly debated
and loss of tolerance is suspected. Obvious clinical signs of infection
are absent in the majority of infected cats and dogs, and few studies
have investigated the cellular and immunological consequences of
infection. In dogs, a mild gastritis with infiltration of the gastric
mucosa involving lymphocytes and plasma cells is most commonly
identified, but a correlation between the histopathological changes
and the occurrence of GHLOs is inconsistently identified. In some
cats with Helicobacter colonization, histopathologic findings vary
from normal gastric mucosa to mild to moderate gastritis and
lymphoid follicular hyperplasia. An association between
Helicobacter infection and gastric lymphoma in cats has been
proposed.32 Gastric inflammation can persist even with eradication
of the organism.47

Diagnosis
Serologic tests by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) or
Western blotting are assays developed for the detection of H. pylori
in people, but they provide little utility in dogs and cats where nonH. pylori spp. predominate. Amplification of Helicobacter DNA from
canine fecal samples has recently been described.48 However, with
this technique, the presence of Helicobacter DNA is not specific for
GHLOs. The definitive diagnosis for the presence of Helicobacter in
the stomach requires demonstration of the organism on mucosal
tissue samples and confirmation of the presence of Helicobacter by
culture or polymerase chain reaction. A rapid urease test
(Campylobacter-like organism [CLO] test) can be used to increase
suspicion of the organism. A mucosal tissue sample is incubated in a
broth containing urea and phenol red as a pH indicator. As the

urease breaks down urea into ammonia, the pH rises and a color
change occurs. The results can often be obtained within 1-3 hours,
but can take up to 24 hours, and the test is susceptible to a false
positive result secondary to the presence of other urease-producing
bacteria such as Escherichia coli and Proteus spp. Histopathologic
analysis relies on the visualization of Helicobacter organisms in
gastric biopsy samples. Special staining such as Warthin-Starry
silver, Giemsa, or toluidine blue will enhance the visibility of
Helicobacter-like organisms. Due to the patchy distribution of the
Helicobacter-like organisms, several biopsies from the antrum and
gastric body should be evaluated. Culture for Helicobacter spp. is
cumbersome and is the least sensitive method for diagnosing these
organisms; however, a positive culture is highly specific. Polymerase
chain reaction of DNA extracted from a biopsy specimen permits
definitive identification of the Helicobacter strain present.

Treatment
Treatment with triple therapy (amoxicillin 20 mg/kg PO q8-12h,
metronidazole 20 mg/kg PO q8-12h, and omeprazole 1 mg/kg PO
q12-24h) is reasonable in animals that fail other therapies and have
evidence of gastric inflammation in association with Helicobacterlike organisms. However, animals can have evidence of re-infection,
recrudescence with cessation of therapy, and/or persistence of
gastric inflammation.47,49

Parasitic and Infectious Gastritis
Parasitic disease is a relatively common cause of gastritis and should
be ruled out prior to performance of more invasive and expensive
diagnostic tests.

Physaloptera spp.
Physaloptera spp. are commonly identified nematodes25 with an
indirect life cycle requiring an intermediate host to develop into the
infective stage. Suitable intermediate hosts (e.g., cockroaches, field
crickets, canal crickets, or flour beetles) ingest the eggs, which have
been shed by the definitive hosts (e.g., cats, dogs). After the

intermediate hosts are ingested by either paratenic (e.g., frogs,
snakes, or mice) or definitive hosts, the adults develop and attach to
the gastroduodenal mucosa. Clinical signs of parasitic gastroenteritis
can include delayed gastric emptying, vomiting, regurgitation,
diarrhea, weight loss, melena, and lethargy.50 The diagnosis can be
difficult to obtain as centrifugal fecal flotation, especially in the case
of Physaloptera, can be falsely negative. Identification of worms in
the vomitus or endoscopic visualization of stomach worms (1-6 cm in
length, stout, cream-colored to white, straight or coiled) (Figure
261.5) appears to be most successful in the diagnosis of this
parasite, but empiric treatment with an appropriate anthelminthic
agent with cessation of clinical signs is certainly more economic (ch.
142 and table on the textbook’s inside covers).

Ollulanus tricuspis
Ollulanus tricuspis is a common gastric nematode of cats, with a
prevalence of up to 20%. It also occurs rarely in dogs. After oral
ingestion of third-stage larvae, the complete life cycle occurs within
the stomach of the host, where the parasite attaches to the gastric
mucosa. Infective larvae are vomited up and survive in the
environment for up to 15 days, where they can infect another animal.
Common clinical signs are inappetence, intermittent vomiting, and
weight loss. Cats can also harbor subclinical infections. Gastric
erosions, increased mucus production, mucosal hyperplasia, and
infiltration with inflammatory cells can be present. A diagnosis can
be achieved by examining vomited material or gastric lavage
solution. Rarely, parasites can be found histopathologically in gastric
biopsy samples. Similarly to Physaloptera, fecal flotation is rarely
diagnostic. Thus, empirical anthelmintic therapy (as outlined in
Acute Gastritis, above) is recommended as a first step therapy for
any animal presenting with chronic vomiting. Evaluation for the
presence of other parasites and infectious agents that can be
identified in the stomach of dogs or cats (e.g., Gnathostoma,
Spirocerca, Histoplasma capsulatum [ch. 209], Heterobilharzia
americana [ch. 263]) should be considered based on the animal’s
environment and travel history (ch. 9).

Pythium insidiosum
Pythium insidiosum is an oomycete that can cause both cutaneous
and GI signs in dogs (ch. 263). Most commonly, infected dogs are
young, large-breed dogs that live in tropical, subtropical, or
temperate regions (ch. 9). Pythium can infect all parts of the GI
tract, including esophagus, stomach, and small and large intestine.
With gastric infection of Pythium, vomiting, with or without signs of
delayed gastric emptying, can be an early and sole sign of disease.
However, in patients with advanced stages, dogs often have
additional clinical signs including diarrhea, weight loss, anorexia,
and palpable abdominal masses. Common laboratory findings in
affected dogs include hypoalbuminemia, hyperglobulinemia, and
eosinophilia.51 Hypercalcemia is also occasionally reported.
Circulating anti-Pythium insidiosum antibodies combined with the
identification of abdominal masses or thickening of the GI tract with

regional lymphadenopathy can be used as non-invasive tests to
support the diagnosis. A definitive diagnosis is made by detection of
dark brown branching hyphae in pyogranulomatous inflammation
from GI mucosal aspirates or biopsies stained with hematoxylineosin and Gomori methenamine silver (GMS). Dogs with
disseminated disease have a poor prognosis but rarely, especially in
those cases with single lesions, may respond to a combination of
surgery (Figure 261.6), immunotherapy, and/or antimicrobial
drugs (ch. 263).52,53 GI pythiosis is rare in cats with only a few
published case reports.

Gastric Neoplasia
With the exception of predisposed breeds (Table 261.3), gastric
neoplasms are uncommonly reported in the dog and cat.54 Gastric
carcinomas, including adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma,
and undifferentiated carcinomas, are the most common gastric
tumors in the dog. Lymphoma is the most common gastric tumor
type in the cat. Other, less commonly reported gastric tumors in dogs
and cats include mast cell tumor, leiomyoma/sarcoma,
extramedullary plasmacytoma, GI stromal tumor, fibrosarcoma, and
histocytic sarcoma (ch. 324). The clinical presentation, treatment,
and prognosis for these tumors have been reviewed.37
Gastric carcinomas are often identified at the lesser curvature or
pyloric antrum in middle-aged to older dogs, with male dogs being
overrepresented. Presenting clinical signs in dogs with gastric
carcinomas include vomiting, dysrexia, weight loss, signs of
abdominal pain, ptyalism, diarrhea, hematemesis, and melena.
Gastric carcinoma carries a poor prognosis because the tumor tends
to be diagnosed at a late stage and historically has been poorly
responsive to chemotherapy (survival time <3 months after
diagnosis). In a recent multi-institutional retrospective study,55 dogs
undergoing surgical tumor resection and receiving adjuvant
chemotherapy had an improved median survival time (∼6 months).
Although additional studies are needed to determine if there is a true
benefit to adjuvant chemotherapy in dogs with gastric carcinoma, the
current treatment of choice especially for those without distant
metastasis is surgical resection and postoperative chemotherapy. The

metastatic rate for gastric carcinoma is ∼50-90% at the time of
diagnosis.55,56 Sites of metastasis include the gastric lymph nodes,
esophagus, duodenum, spleen, liver, omentum, adrenal glands, and
lungs.
In cats with gastric lymphoma, vomiting is the most common
clinical sign but dysrexia, weight loss, and lethargy are also common
(ch. 322).57 Clinicopathologic abnormalities are generally mild and
nonspecific. Anemia and neutrophilia were observed in ∼50% of cats
with gastric lymphoma in one study.57 Feline gastric lymphoma,
where the tumor is exclusively in the stomach, has a reported median
clinical remission time and overall survival of 108 and 171 days,
respectively.57 Multi-agent chemotherapy (e.g., CHOP
[cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone], LCHOP [L-asparaginase + cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin,
vincristine, and prednisone], etc.; ch. 322) is generally
recommended, although single-agent oral chemotherapy (e.g.,
chlorambucil, prednisolone) has also been utilized in cases where IV
chemotherapy is not desired.57

Diagnostic Approach to Chronic Gastritis
As vomiting is a common sign but is not pathognomonic for gastritis,
systemic causes of chronic vomiting should be ruled out through
evaluation of history, physical examination (ch. 3) including retinal
examination (ch. 13), and blood work including a CBC, serum
biochemistry panel, urinalysis, urine sediment exam, and thyroid
hormone testing (in cats >7 years old), when appropriate. Although
much work has been directed towards identification of useful
biomarkers for the differentiation of inflammation and neoplasia in
canine and feline tumors, no biomarker is currently available to
distinguish between gastritis and gastric neoplasia. Older age, thin
body condition, markedly increased serum C-reactive protein, and
low serum folate in a susceptible canine breed (Table 261.3) should
increase the suspicion for gastric carcinoma and prompt a complete
diagnostic evaluation.58 Animals with pancreatic diseases such as
exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (ch. 279) and chronic pancreatitis
(chs. 277, 278), and hepatobiliary disease (chs. 267-275), can also

be presented for evaluation of clinical signs similar to those of
chronic gastritis. Therefore, tests to evaluate for these diseases (e.g.,
abdominal ultrasound, pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity [PLI],
bile culture, pre- and postprandial bile acids) should be considered
in the diagnostic plan of dogs and cats with supportive clinical signs
and blood work findings. Fecal testing (e.g., centrifugal fecal
flotation, fecal antigen tests; ch. 80) and anthelmintic treatment
(ch. 142) are a reasonable first-tier approach in animals with mild
signs. In dogs and cats with more severe signs, the presence of blood
work abnormalities, or those unresponsive to anthelmintic and
dietary therapy, diagnostic imaging is recommended. Ultrasound is
useful to evaluate for thickness and wall layering of the GI tract, size
of abdominal lymph nodes, presence of discrete masses or
abdominal fluid, and the echogenicity and size of the pancreas and
surrounding mesentery. Positive-contrast gastropathy may enhance
the ability to detect gastric abnormalities including gastric
hyperrugosity.2 Ultrasonographic gastric wall thickening, presumed
to be secondary to gastric edema, can also be observed in dogs with
pancreatitis or hypoalbuminemia.59,60 Cats with IBD/chronic
inflammatory enteropathy or alimentary lymphoma tend to have an
increased small intestinal wall thickness as a result of increased
thickness of the muscularis propria. Diffuse thickening of the small
intestinal muscularis layer in addition to colic lymph node
enlargement may be associated with GI lymphoma. However, it is
important to note that dogs and cats with either inflammatory or
neoplastic disease of the stomach can have an ultrasonographically
normal stomach and small intestine.57,61 If no abnormalities can be
identified on blood work or abdominal imaging, additional testing is
recommended based on the history, signalment, clinical signs, and
results of the first-tier diagnostic tests. These can include, but are not
limited to, evaluation of thoracic radiographs, baseline cortisol (ch.
296), and/or infectious disease testing (e.g., Histoplasma
capsulatum [ch. 209], Pythium insidiosum [ch. 263], Dirofilaria
immitis [cats; ch. 237], viral testing [feline leukemia virus, ch.199;
feline immunodeficiency virus, ch. 198; feline infectious peritonitis,
ch. 200]). Enteropathogen panel testing is not recommended for
evaluation of dogs and cats with chronic vomiting unless the animal
demonstrates signs of systemic illness, consumes a raw food diet or

treats, or lives in or has been recently adopted from a high-density
housing environment, such as a shelter or breeding colony. For dogs
and cats that do not respond to anthelmintic or dietary intervention
as outlined below, GI biopsies can be obtained by endoscopy or
surgery and submitted for histopathologic examination. Endoscopy
provides direct visualization and sampling of luminal and mucosal
abnormalities (ch. 107). Endoscopy can be particularly important
for evaluation of the gastric mucosa, as neoplastic lesions and
infectious agents may be missed with routine imaging and
exploratory surgery. However, surgery offers the opportunity for
acquisition of full-thickness biopsies and resection of affected areas
of the stomach as well as assessment and biopsy of other organs.

Therapeutic Approach to Chronic Gastritis
Targeted therapy directed at the underlying etiology, such as surgical
resection of a neoplasm or treatment of an infectious disease, is the
approach that is most likely to result in resolution of gastritis. In
cases of idiopathic chronic gastritis, where no underlying etiology
can be identified and infectious agents are considered unlikely,
rational treatment options include dietary management followed by
immunomodulatory therapy. Dietary management may include the
following strategies: high moisture, low residue, low-fat diets to
promote more rapid gastric emptying; limited ingredient diets (i.e., a
single protein and a single carbohydrate source), ideally to which the
animal has not yet been exposed; or a hydrolysed-protein diet to
minimize an immune reaction secondary to food hypersensitivity
(ch. 152). In most cases of food-responsive disease, mild to
moderate improvement is observed within a 2-week strict dietary
trial. In young animals, adverse food reactions (ch. 166) are a
common cause of GI signs. Thus, multiple different diet trials should
be pursued before declaring dietary management a failure.
Immunomodulatory drug therapy (ch. 144) can be considered for
those dogs and cats that do not respond to dietary management
alone, where abdominal imaging and infectious disease testing do
not reveal an obvious etiology, and where the owner has declined
acquisition of GI biopsies. Corticosteroids, in addition to their
immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory properties, have
regenerative effects on the gastric parietal cells, but can cause gastric

erosions in dogs at high dosages. Therefore, dogs receiving high-dose
steroids for a prolonged period should be monitored for gastric
bleeding. Initially, prednisone or prednisolone is given at a dosage of
1-2 mg/kg PO q12h. In larger dogs, the author does not recommend
to give more than 30 mg PO q12h. This dosage is then gradually
tapered in decremental steps of 25-30% over a period of several
weeks to months. Budesonide, a corticosteroid with high first-past
metabolism, can also be considered in order to minimize systemic
side-effects (ch. 227). Budesonide (3 mg/m2 q24h) requires
compounding and is more expensive than prednisone but is a good
option in dogs and cats where systemic effects are a concern (e.g.,
diabetic animals; ch. 224). Cyclosporine and chlorambucil are also
effective alternatives for steroid-refractory disease or where steroid
side-effects are intolerable.62,63 Additional supportive care, as
outlined for acute gastritis, can also be considered during the
diagnostic evaluation and treatment trial periods.

GASTRIC EROSION AND ULCERATION
ETIOLOGY
GI ulceration is an important cause of illness in both dogs and cats.
As clinical signs of gastric ulceration can mirror those of gastric
bleeding secondary to a platelet or coagulation disorder, assessment
of platelet count, function, and coagulation (ch. 170) are
recommended prior to evaluation of a primary cause of gastric
ulceration in the dog and cat. The most common causes of gastric
ulceration (Table 261.4) in dogs and cats are GI neoplasms,
ulcerogenic drug administration (e.g., NSAIDs, toceranib,
chemotherapeutics), and hepatic failure.64 Consideration of the
animal’s signalment helps with prioritizing the likelihood of these
causes. Younger animals are more likely to have ingested a foreign
body and middle-aged to older animals, especially in an
overrepresented breed (Table 261.3), are more likely to have gastric
neoplasia.

Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs

NSAID administration is reportedly the most common cause of
severe gastric ulceration in the dog, representing one-third of dogs
requiring packed red blood cell transfusions in one study.65 NSAIDinduced GI ulceration most commonly occurs in the gastric body and
pyloroantral regions as well as the small intestine. NSAIDs are weak
acids that can be directly injurious to the gastric and proximal
duodenal epithelium and inhibit the synthesis of protective
prostaglandins that normally aid in GI mucosal blood flow, mucus
secretion, and epithelial repair. In the lower small intestine, NSAIDs
with a carboxylic acid group (e.g., carprofen) that undergo
enterohepatic recirculation can form an acyl-glucuronide metabolite
that is also present in bile. The downstream effects of this are
repeated disruption of intestinal epithelial mitochondrial function
and impaired epithelial renewal.

Liver Disease
The pathophysiologic mechanism and prevalence of GI ulceration
and bleeding in animals with hepatic disease are uncertain. Several
mechanisms have been proposed, including development of portal
hypertension, gastric antral vascular ectasia, hypergastrinemia,
altered gastric mucosal barrier function, coagulopathy, and in the
case of intrahepatic portosystemic shunts, concurrent GI disease.66
In the author’s experience, gastric ulceration is less commonly
reported in the cat and is most commonly caused by GI neoplasia.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH
Rapid evaluation and stabilization (ch. 119) should precede or occur
alongside the diagnostic evaluation in dogs and cats with suspected
or confirmed gastric ulceration. The chronicity and severity of
bleeding can be assessed by evaluation of the history, physical exam,
and results of clinical findings including CBC and serum

biochemistry profile. Clinical signs of dogs and cats with gastric
ulceration vary depending on its duration and severity. Some
affected animals show no clinical signs, while others experience
weight loss, abdominal pain, abdominal distension, delayed gastric
emptying, ptyalism, melena, or hematemesis containing digested
(“coffee grounds”) or frank blood. Animals can also have nonspecific
signs, such as lethargy, dysorexia, and weakness. Dogs and cats with
metabolic or systemic causes of gastric ulceration or those with
NSAID intoxication can also have systemic signs, such as polyuria
and polydipsia.
Physical examination findings can include mucous membrane
pallor, abdominal pain, palpable abdominal mass or foreign object,
or signs compatible with shock or systemic illness. Rectal
examination can reveal frank or tarry stool; however, its absence
does not rule out gastric ulceration.
Normocytic, normochromic anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and
neutrophilia are the most common findings in dogs and cats with
gastroduodenal ulcerations.64,67,68 Animals with chronic GI
bleeding can have mild to moderate microcytic, hypochromic
anemia, supportive of iron deficiency. Increased serum blood urea
nitrogen to creatinine ratio (>27:1) in a well-hydrated animal not
receiving a high-protein diet increases the suspicion for upper GI
bleeding, but has a low sensitivity and warrants further evaluation.69
Fecal occult blood (FOB) tests use substrates (o-tolidine or guaiac)
that become oxidized and impart a color change in the presence of
peroxidase activity found in hemoglobin. FOB tests can detect
smaller amounts of hemoglobin than are required to induce
melena70; however, the tests can have low sensitivity and
specificity.71,72 Animals undergoing FOB testing should ideally be
fed diets devoid of meat or vegetables with high peroxidase activity
(e.g., red meat, fish, turnips, broccoli, cauliflower) several days
before testing. Diet may have less of an effect when using o-tolidine
based tests on canine fecal samples,73,74 but not feline feces.72
Survey radiography is rarely diagnostic for gastric ulceration but
can help with the identification of large masses, peritoneal fluid, or
peritoneal air. An abdominal ultrasound exam may help to confirm
the presence of a gastric mural lesion or defect, and in severe cases,

peritoneal fluid or even free gas, suggesting GI perforation.67
However, a full sonographic view of the stomach is not always
possible because of the location of the stomach and the presence of
gas or ingesta within its lumen. Therefore, ulcerative lesions can be
missed with ultrasonography. Abdominal computed tomography
(CT) reportedly has approximately the same sensitivity as does
abdominal ultrasound in dogs for the detection of non-perforating GI
ulcers (67% versus 65%, respectively).67
Video capsule endoscopy (
Video 261.1) is a minimally invasive
tool that can be used for detecting gastric and, when not retained in
the stomach, small intestinal erosive and ulcerative lesions (Figure
261.7) in fully conscious medium- to large-breed dogs when
ultrasonography is inconclusive.69,75 However, upper GI endoscopy
remains the gold standard for identification of erosive and ulcerative
lesions in the stomach (ch. 107). Additional diagnostic tests to
consider in dogs or cats with gastric ulceration and no history of
NSAID or high-dose corticosteroid administration depend on the
signalment and results of diagnostics mentioned above; they could
include fecal centrifugal flotation (ch. 80), adrenocorticotropic
hormone (ACTH) stimulation test (ch. 296), fasting serum gastrin
concentration, bile acid tolerance testing (ch. 267), infectious
disease testing (e.g., Pythium ELISA; ch. 263), or abdominal CT
angiography.

THERAPEUTIC APPROACH
The treatment of gastric ulceration, as well as its prognosis, are
dependent on its etiology and severity. Surgical removal of the
injured mucosa is generally recommended for animals with or at risk
for gastric perforation or where a neoplasm is the underlying cause
of the ulceration. PPI therapy (Box 261.1) is recommended while
determining the underlying cause of ulceration. For animals with
NSAID-induced ulceration, misoprostol, a prostaglandin E1 analog,
can be given concurrently with the PPI. The PPI therapy is generally
continued q12h for 3-4 weeks in animals with NSAID-induced
ulceration. If compliance with q12h administration is a concern,
once-daily oral esomeprazole administration appears to be effective

in some dogs based on a study in healthy Beagle dogs.76
Combination acid suppressant therapy using injectable famotidine
with PPIs is not recommended for treatment of gastric ulceration as
the addition of famotidine to PPI therapy does not provide any
additional effect on gastric pH.77 Acid suppressant therapy may not
always promote gastric mucosal healing, especially in animals with
metabolic disease (e.g., hepatic failure78) or those with ulcerative
lesions caudal to the stomach and in the proximal duodenum; thus,
monitoring for response to therapy and consideration of alternative
approaches (e.g., vasoactive drugs, lysine analogues) is
recommended when clinical signs or lab work abnormalities do not
improve with gastroprotectant drug therapy. Prophylactic use of
gastroprotectant drugs is generally not recommended (e.g., healthy
dogs receiving NSAIDs),79 unless the animal has multiple risk
factors for ulceration or bleeding. Sucralfate (0.25 g in cats to 1 g in
large dogs, as a slurry or liquid PO q6-8h) can be beneficial in
animals with particularly painful lesions, but administration must be
spaced from the administration of any PPIs. Animals with acute
gastric ulceration often benefit from a low-fiber, low-fat, highmoisture diet (ch. 152).80 Multiple small meals are recommended to
promote gastric emptying.

GASTRIC DYSMOTILITY
The mean half gastric emptying time—the time at which half of a
meal should empty into the duodenum—varies widely based on the
meal offered, the environmental conditions, method for assessment,
and the individual.81 However, by 8 hours, the majority of an
ingested meal is expected to have passed into the duodenum. Gastric
distension or vomiting >8-12 hours post-meal often prompts
evaluation for a gastric motility disorder. Disorders of gastric
motility can be divided into 2 categories: mechanical or functional.
Mechanical disruptors of gastric emptying impede the passage of
contents from the stomach into the small intestine and include
neoplasms, gastric antral polyps, torsion, pyloric stenosis, or foreign
objects. Functional, non-obstructive gastric motility disorders are
generally secondary to a stimulus external to the stomach such as
opioid administration, metabolic disease, critical illness, or
abdominal surgery (Box 261.2).82 Delayed gastric emptying in a
critically ill animal is thought to be due to reduced gastric motor tone
or excessive inhibitory neural tone whereas ileus is thought to be
secondary to uncoordinated intestinal peristalsis and inflammationinduced intestinal dilation. The mechanism of postoperative ileus is
multifactorial and involves surgical stress and inflammation,
triggering neural and hormonal inhibitory pathways. Gastric

dysmotility lengthens hospitalization time and can increase patient
morbidity and mortality.
Animals with delayed gastric emptying are often presented for
evaluation of vomiting or regurgitation, but they can display a variety
of clinical signs depending on the underlying etiology. These include
dysorexia, ptyalism, eructation, abdominal distension, signs of
abdominal pain, polydipsia, and/or pica. Physical examination (ch.
3) can be normal or can reveal abdominal distension, eructation or
regurgitation with abdominal palpation, evidence of abdominal pain,
or findings associated with an underlying structural cause, such as a
palpable abdominal mass. Often, a gastric motility disorder is
suspected based on the history and physical examination. However,
in some cases, it can be helpful to document delayed gastric
emptying.

ASSESSMENT OF GASTRIC EMPTYING
Evaluation of gastric emptying and intestinal transit may be useful in
the diagnosis of a motility disorder and to monitor response to
treatment. Assessment of gastric emptying can include evaluation of
motility during the interdigestive (“fasting”) period or postprandially after ingestion of liquid or solid phases. Assessment of
solid-phase emptying is of highest clinical importance, as gastric
motility disorders are not always detectable using the liquid phase
alone. The investigator must be mindful that physiologic parameters
such as age and body size, test meal composition, the method of
assessment, and stress of the procedure can have an effect on gastric
emptying. Methods that can be used for assessing gastric motility
include pressure transducers, nuclear scintigraphy, isotope studies
(blood or breath tests), contrast radiography, barium-impregnated
polyethylene spheres (BIPSs), ultrasound, CT, magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI), and wireless motility capsules (WMCs). Nuclear
scintigraphy utilizes a radiopharmaceutical that is firmly adhered to
a test meal and allows for good assessment of solid-phase gastric
emptying. It is the gold standard for assessment of gastric motility
because it is accurate and repeatable; however, its expense, inherent
radiation hazard, and limited availability often restrict the use of this
modality to research purposes. Contrast plain radiography or CT, or

MRI, can help detect structural disease, but dogs with solid-phase
gastric emptying disorders can have normal emptying of liquids and
the stress of restraint or sedation/anesthesia and an unfamiliar
environment may delay gastric emptying in dogs without gastric
emptying disorders. BIPSs were designed to evaluate solid-phase
gastric emptying. They are inexpensive and easy to administer;
however, their size (1.5 and 5 mm) may result in their being retained
until the interdigestive state and, as a result, they may help evaluate
interdigestive motility and structural disease but not reliably
evaluate emptying of digestible solids during the fed state.83 WMCs
can be used for evaluating indigestible solid-phase gastric emptying.
They have a similar repeatability compared to scintigraphy.
Disadvantages to the use of the WMC are the need for specialized
equipment and the inability to use them in patients weighing <15 kg.
Abdominal ultrasound is most commonly used in the clinic to assess
GI dysmotility because it is non-invasive and widely available.
Abdominal ultrasound allows for assessment of gastric contractions
and intestinal motility in real time.82,84 Abdominal ultrasound can
also be used for differentiating mechanical from functional ileus. In
functional ileus, intestinal motility is decreased or absent and
intestinal loops are mildly dilated. In contrast, with mechanical ileus,
the intestine proximal to the obstruction tends to have hypermotility
and intestinal loops show moderate to severe dilation. A single,
skilled ultrasonographer is recommended to reduce the subjectivity
of the procedure. Performing the procedure with the animal in a
standing position can minimize stress and mitigate the pyloric
antrum being obscured by gas.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH TO DELAYED
GASTRIC EMPTYING
The diagnostic approach for determination of the underlying cause of
delayed gastric emptying is based on the signalment, history, and
physical examination. Mechanical obstruction, especially in young
dogs and cats with a history of foreign object ingestion, should be
ruled out with abdominal imaging prior to exploration and treatment
for functional disorders. In older animals or those with critical
illness, blood work including CBC, serum biochemistry profile,
urinalysis, and, where appropriate, thyroid testing (dog; ch. 285)
might be considered prior to or in conjunction with abdominal
imaging. Additional testing, such as ACTH stimulation testing (ch.
296), infectious disease testing (e.g., Pythium ELISA, ch. 263), or
exploratory laparotomy can be considered based on the information
gathered during the initial evaluation.

Bilious Vomiting Syndrome
Bilious vomiting syndrome is a poorly characterized condition in
dogs that is associated with vomiting after a period of fasting (e.g.,

overnight, such that vomiting occurs in the morning) and is
unaccompanied by other clinical signs. The cause of vomiting is
unknown but is hypothesized to be due to duodenogastric refluxinduced gastric irritation as a result of poor intragastric pressure.85
Signs generally improve or resolve with feeding a late-night snack
with or without gastric acid suppressant therapy.

THERAPEUTIC APPROACH TO
DELAYED GASTRIC EMPTYING
Successful treatment of gastric motility disorders is largely
dependent on identification and direct treatment of the underlying
cause. Nonobstructive functional disorders without a known
underlying etiology or those secondary to critical illness often require
a multi-modal therapeutic approach, including prokinetic and
nutritional therapy. Avoiding iatrogenic causes of gastric dysmotility
in at-risk animals is also an important consideration. Laparoscopic
surgery with experienced surgeons can reduce postoperative ileus
compared to open abdominal surgery because of reduced bowel
manipulation and tissue trauma. In addition, administration of
drugs that delay GI transit should be avoided when possible,
especially in animals predisposed to motility disorders, such as
critically ill animals or those with metabolic diseases. These include
anti-cholinergic drugs, dopamine, and pure mu opioid agonists. Pure
mu opioids bind to opioid receptors in the GI tract and decrease
acetylcholine release, resulting in reduced GI motility. However,
epidural morphine administration improves postoperative ileus in
dogs, likely because it results in a central analgesic effect and does
not interact with peripheral gut receptors.86 Epidural morphine can
also increase parasympathetic tone via inhibition of inhibitory
sympathetic innervation. Thus, whenever possible, epidural rather
than IV morphine administration should be considered in animals
undergoing abdominal surgery.

Prokinetic Drugs

In animals with severe gastric emptying disorders, prokinetic drugs
(e.g., cisapride, erythromycin, metoclopramide) should be given
intravenously when possible. If oral administration is necessary,
liquid formulations are suggested. Cisapride is a nonselective,
serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine-4 [5-HT4]) receptor agonist.
Serotonin release from enterochromaffin cells stimulates primary
afferent neurons that synapse in the myenteric plexus and stimulate
cholinergic neurons. These initiate ascending intestinal smooth
muscle contraction and descending relaxation. Cisapride is a potent
prokinetic that helps with delayed esophageal, gastric, and intestinal
motility. Cisapride’s greatest and longest-lasting effect is on gastric
antral motility. Cisapride accelerates gastric emptying via increased
frequency, amplitude, and duration of pyloric contractions,
improved antropyloroduodenal coordination, and increased mean
distance of duodenal propagation contractions in dogs.87 The
bioavailability and half-life of cisapride in the dog are approximately
50% and 4-10 hours, respectively. A prolonged QT interval on the
electrocardiogram is a reported side-effect in people and in cats
when administered at supratherapeutic doses. These cardiovascular
effects are due to cisapride’s effect on other targets, such as the
hERG potassium channel, dopamine receptors, and 5-HT1 and 5-HT2
receptors. The 5-HT4 selective agonist mosapride has not been
associated with arrhythmogenic activity but has no effect on colonic
motility. The most common adverse effect of cisapride
administration in dogs and cats is diarrhea.
Metoclopramide hydrochloride (2-methoxy-5-chloroprocainamide) is a dopamine-2 receptor antagonist (at low dosages), 5-HT3
antagonist (at high dosages), and selective 5-HT4 agonist. Like
cisapride, metoclopramide enhances acetylcholine release at postsynaptic sites, albeit more weakly than cisapride. Metoclopramide
also antagonizes the inhibitory effect of dopamine on intestinal
transit. Dopamine decreases acetylcholine release from
postganglionic cholinergic neurons. Thus, inhibition of dopamine
results in increased acetylcholine and enhanced intestinal smooth
muscle contractions. Metoclopramide transiently increases gastric
contractions in the fasting state in the dog, but has little overall effect

on gastric emptying time or pyloric contractions in the postprandial
state. Metoclopramide does enhance antropyloroduodenal
coordination and mean distance of duodenal propagation
contractions and enhances gastric emptying in the fed state in cats.88
Metoclopramide has a short half-life, approximately 3-4 hours, and
should be administered as an IV constant rate infusion, or every 6
hours.
Erythromycin and azithromycin are macrolide antibiotics that,
when administered at low dosages, have motilin receptor agonist
activity and enhance gastric emptying in dogs and cats.88 Higher
dosages of erythromycin, such as those required for antimicrobial
activity, result in retrograde peristalsis. Chronic administration of
macrolides (>2 weeks) in humans leads to tachyphylaxis due to
downregulation of the motilin receptor. Erythromycin is metabolized
by the cytochrome P450 system.
Ranitidine, an H2-receptor antagonist, also has
acetylcholinesterase inhibitor activity, which is suggested to promote
GI motility. However, oral ranitidine has not shortened gastric
emptying times in healthy dogs.89 No published studies have
evaluated the effects of ranitidine on GI transit times in dogs or cats
with gastric motility disorders.
Mirtazapine is a presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic receptor and postsynaptic 5-HT1 and 5-HT2 antagonist. It has antiemetic, anti-nausea,
antidepressant, and appetite stimulant properties. One study in
healthy dogs suggested that high-dose mirtazapine can improve
gastric emptying.90 However, standard dosages of mirtazapine are
unlikely to result in the same effect.
Ghrelin receptor agonists, such as relamorelin accelerate gastric
emptying and intestinal transit in humans. The ghrelin receptor
agonist, capromorelin, is FDA-approved as an appetite stimulant in
dogs and cats. To the author’s knowledge, there is no published study
in which the prokinetic qualities of capromorelin in dogs or cats have
been investigated.
Lubiprostone is a selective type-2 chloride channel activator that
increases luminal chloride and fluid secretion. It is used for treating
chronic idiopathic constipation and opioid-induced constipation in
humans. A recent study in dogs suggests that lubiprostone also acts

to enhance GI motility. Oral administration of 48 micrograms of
lubiprostone resulted in accelerated post-prandial gastric emptying
and small intestinal colonic transit in healthy dogs.91
Intestinal promotility properties of NK1 antagonists have been
demonstrated for humans with functional bowel disease. However,
studies in anesthetized dogs and healthy Beagles failed to reveal a
significant reduction in gastric emptying time following maropitant
administration. 92
Compound YKP10811 is a newly developed selective 5-HT4 agonist
that experimentally improves antral contractions and accelerates
gastric emptying in dogs in a dose-dependent manner. It is not yet
commercially available but appears to be a potent treatment for
gastroparesis with few reported side-effects.93

Additional Therapies
Additional therapies that can be considered in patients with gastric
dysmotility include electrolyte and fluid replacement (ch. 120),
ambulation, targeted amino acid therapy (ch. 164), and novel
interventional therapies. Electrolyte deficiencies including
hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalcemia
can slow GI motility and should be addressed. However, care should
be taken to avoid overcorrection as hypernatremia and
hypermagnesemia have also been implicated in delaying transit time.
Judicious IV fluid administration to maintain hydration and replace
losses is recommended. Overhydration can result in gut edema and
delay GI transit and should be avoided. The level of evidence for the
prokinetic effect of ambulation is weak; even so, regular mobility in
critically ill and post-operative patients, when possible, generally is
recommended.
Other novel therapies that might promote GI motility include the
amino acids L-arginine and L-glutamate which, when administered
intragastrically, promote gastric emptying and improve gastric
accommodation in dogs.94 Intrapyloric botulinum toxin injection
resulted in improved gastric emptying in one dog and in small
observational studies in humans with idiopathic gastroparesis.

NUTRITIONAL APPROACH FOR
GASTRIC DYSMOTILITY
Many systemic conditions, such as pancreatitis (chs. 277, 278),
parvovirosis (ch. 201), and septic peritonitis (ch. 265), can be
associated with gastric dysmotility.26,95,96 The concept of “bowel
rest” is no longer recommended, as several veterinary studies have
shown that EEN is well tolerated with few complications and
improved outcomes. Instead, EEN, defined as nutrition provided
within 48 hours of hospitalization, is recommended as part of a
multimodal approach to the management of GI motility
disorders.26,95,96 EEN may benefit the patient through the following
proposed mechanisms: improved mucosal blood flow to the GI tract,
decreased intestinal bacterial translocation, stimulation of GI
motility, and secretion of GI hormones, growth factors, and
bicarbonate.
Assisted feeding tubes are commonly utilized in patients with GI
motility disorders (ch. 81). Many clinicians will measure gastric
residual volumes (GRV) to evaluate for gastric intolerance to enteral
nutrition (EN). The sole measurement of GRV as a marker of
intolerance to EN may guide some clinicians to make clinical
decisions to delay or stop EN. This practice is not recommended
based on guidelines provided by the Society of Critical Care Medicine
(SCCM) and the American Society for Parenteral and Enteral
Nutrition (ASPEN).97 Moreover, a randomized clinical trial
investigating continuous or bolus nasoenteric feeding found no
correlation between GRV and the occurrence of adverse GI events.
This suggested that termination of EN due to high GRV in the
absence of other clinical signs such as abdominal distension or pain
may not be warranted.98 Post-pyloric feeding through a nasojejunal
(NJ), esophagojejunal (EJ), gastrojejunal (GJ), or jejunal feeding
tube may be helpful for patients where gastric feeding is poorly
tolerated. Adjunctive parenteral nutrition (ch. 164) should be
considered to meet nutritional requirements in patients with severe
GI dysmotility.
The most appropriate diet for patients with GI dysmotility may be
influenced by patient size, presence of comorbidities, and diagnostic

findings from tests such as barium swallow and abdominal
ultrasound. In general, the dietary approach to patients with GI
dysmotility includes one that is high-moisture, low-fat, low-solublefiber, and highly digestible to promote more rapid GI transit,
digestion, and absorption. Regardless of the feeding method chosen,
patients with GI dysmotility require a frequent nutritional
assessment and revision of their feeding plan to ensure they are
receiving optimal nutritional support (ch. 145).

GASTRIC DILATION AND VOLVULUS
Gastric dilation and volvulus (GDV) is an acute, life-threatening
condition, predominantly affecting large- and deep, narrow-chested
dogs. GDV is characterized by distension of the stomach with gas,
and rotation of the stomach typically clockwise along the
mesenteroaxial axis. Counterclockwise rotation as well as rotation
along the organoaxial axis have been reported, though much less
commonly. If not quickly identified and corrected, GDV results in
compromised perfusion and decreased venous return, GI necrosis,
bacterial translocation, distributive and cardiogenic shock, and
death. The overall mortality rate in dogs with GDV is 36% when
including dogs that are euthanized or die prior to surgical
intervention,99 while mortality rates specifically for dogs that died
prior to surgery and those that died following surgery are 23.3-37%
and 11.3-18.3%, respectively.99-101

FIGURE 261.8 Right lateral abdominal
radiograph in a dog with gastric dilation and
volvulus (GDV). The stomach is severely distended
with gas and the pylorus is abnormally positioned in
a craniodorsal location, consistent with GDV. The
small intestine is diffusely moderately gas-distended,
likely as a result of functional ileus secondary to
GDV.
Risk factors for development of GDV include breed (e.g., Great
Dane, Standard Poodle, Irish Setter, Weimaraner, Rottweiler,
German Shepherd Dog, Retrievers), dietary habits (e.g., rapid eating,
dry food, elevated position, larger food volume), thin body condition,
older age, nervous temperament, and a family history of GDV.102,103
Previous splenectomy is variably associated with an increased risk
for the development of GDV.104
History and physical examination findings in animals with GDV
can include a distended, tympanic abdomen; ptyalism; unproductive
retching; weakness; tachypnea or dyspnea; restlessness; arrhythmias

(i.e., premature ventricular contractions, ventricular tachycardia),
and varying signs of shock (e.g., pale or brick red mucous
membranes, delayed capillary refill time, bradycardia, depression,
hypothermia, or hyperthermia; ch. 121). The distended abdomen
may not be obvious in deep-chested dogs.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH
A GDV is often suspected based on compatible signalment, history,
and physical examination findings described above. Unstable
animals should be hemodynamically stabilized before proceeding
with abdominal imaging (ch. 119).
The diagnosis is confirmed through the identification of pyloric
malposition with gastric air entrapment (“Popeye arm,” “double
bubble”) on a right lateral radiograph (Figure 261.8). Although
rare, animals with organoaxial volvulus can have a normal
positioned stomach with gastric dilatation. Thus, an abdominal
ultrasound can be helpful to confirm the diagnosis in this subset of
patients. Abdominal effusion or air may be visible radiographically
or on ultrasound in animals with hemoabdomen or gastric
perforation.
Clinicopathologic abnormalities are variable and can include
evidence of hemoconcentration, metabolic acidosis or alkalosis,
hypokalemia, and coagulation abnormalities, including those
supportive of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) (e.g.,
prolonged coagulation times, thrombocytopenia, increased Ddimers, or fibrinogen degradation products; ch. 171).
Negative prognostic indicators as assessed at admission in dogs
with GDV can include delay to intervention, persistently marked
hyperlactatemia (>6 mg/dL), acute kidney injury, gastric wall
necrosis, increased serum myoglobin concentration, and increased
serum concentrations of canine pepsinogen A (not currently
commercially available) or C-reactive protein.105-107

TREATMENT

Successful treatment of GDV necessitates rapid medical and surgical
treatment, including IV fluid therapy (ch. 120), gastric
decompression and repositioning of the stomach (ch. 105),
splenectomy if there is substantial compromise to splenic blood flow,
gastrectomy of devitalized tissues when necessary, and permanent
gastropexy to prevent recurrence. Triage (ch. 119) is first directed
towards placement of large-gauge catheters in veins cranial to the
gastric volvulus (i.e., jugular or cephalic veins), followed by intensive
fluid resuscitation with crystalloids ± hypertonic saline (ch. 121).
Gastric decompression is performed after adequate fluid
resuscitation via percutaneous trocarisation utilizing a 16- or 18gauge IV catheter or by passing a well-lubricated, orogastric tube
(ch. 107). Sedation (pure mu opioids [e.g., methadone 0.2-0.5
mg/kg IV, hydromorphone 0.05-0.02 mg/kg, or fentanyl 3.5
mcg/kg], combined with midazolam 0.1-0.5 mg/kg IV) is generally
necessary to facilitate passage of the orogastric tube. Due to patient
intolerance, risk for gastric rupture, and the risk of aspiration
pneumonia, the author prefers percutaneous trocarisation as the
primary mode of gastric decompression.
Monitoring of vital parameters, blood pressure, and electrolyte
and acid-base status should be performed as frequently as needed
based on the severity of abnormalities in the patient being presented.
Once the patient is hemodynamically stable and gastric
decompression has been performed, the patient is anesthetized for
abdominal exploratory surgery, resection of compromised tissues,
and gastropexy. Dogs undergoing surgery >3 hours post-admission
have a poorer prognosis, so rapid stabilization and surgical
intervention are indicated.101
The postoperative management of GDV patients includes
alleviating pain (ch. 6) and addressing the sequelae of poor tissue
perfusion and ischemia-reperfusion injury, including electrolyte
imbalances, ventricular arrhythmias, GI ulceration, systemic
inflammatory response syndrome, acute kidney injury, and DIC.108
Serial monitoring of lactate, especially in dogs with high blood
lactate at admission, may be helpful in determining prognosis and
monitoring response to surgery and postoperative treatment.101,109
Affected dogs should also be monitored for the development of septic

peritonitis through serial abdominal ultrasonography and evaluation
of abdominal effusion (ch. 265).

GDV PROPHYLAXIS
Gastropexy is recommended for all dogs that are being surgically
managed for GDV as well as at-risk dogs undergoing abdominal
surgery for other reasons (e.g., ovariohysterectomy, foreign object
removal, splenectomy) to minimize the risk of future volvulus. A
variety of surgical fixation approaches (i.e., endoscopic-assisted,
laparoscopic-assisted, and via laparotomy) and techniques (i.e.,
incisional, belt-loop, circumcostal) has been described. Gastropexy is
performed on the right side of the abdomen, near the last rib. There
is no “gold-standard” technique and surgeon preference and
available equipment generally guide the approach. However, the
placement of the gastropexy site is critical to minimize the risk of
complications, such as partial pyloric outflow obstruction.110
Alteration of feeding behavior, including moistening wet food,
feeding smaller volumes more frequently, avoiding feeding from a
raised position, and using feeding devices to slow eating might also
help to minimize the risk of gastric dilatation and GDV. Gastropexy
does not remove the risk of gastric dilatation and approximately 511% of dogs will have recurrent gastric dilatation following
gastropexy; thus, concurrent nutritional management in these dogs
may be critical to successful long-term outcome.111,112

FUNCTIONAL ANATOMY OF THE SMALL
INTESTINE
The small intestine (SI) is among the most complex organs in the
body. It is both the main organ responsible for absorption of
nutrients and a critical participant in host defense and immunologic
function. The macroscopic and microscopic anatomical features of
the SI are directly related to its diverse and pivotal functions. A solid
understanding of normal small intestinal anatomy and function is
crucial to appreciation of dysfunction and disease.

MACROSCOPIC ANATOMY
The SI is the longest section of the digestive tube, forming a passage from the pylorus of the stomach to
the ileocolic valve. It consists of 3 segments: the duodenum, which is a short segment that receives
secretions from the pancreas and liver, followed by the jejunum, and lastly, the ileum (Figure 262.1,
A). The duodenum is relatively fixed, while the jejunum and ileum are freely moveable.
The cross-sectional structure of the SI is composed of 4 layers. Starting in the lumen and proceeding
outwards, they are the mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, and serosa (Figure 262.1, B and C).1 These
are each recognizable on gross examination of a cut section of the intestine and are also readily
distinguishable during abdominal ultrasound.2 The mucosa features grossly visible rugae or folds, which
increase the available surface area of the SI by 3-fold compared to a simple, non-folded tube of similar
diameter. If examined closely, finger-like projections, known as villi, can be seen extending from the
luminal surface of the mucosa. These structures increase the surface area of the intestine by an
additional 10-fold. Duodenal villi are short and blunt, while the villi of the jejunum and ileum are long
and narrow. Thus, the ratio of villus length to crypt depth is nearly equal in the duodenum, whereas
villus length is much longer than crypt depth in the jejunum and ileum.3
The mesentery of the SI, also known as the great or proper mesentery, attaches the intestine to the
abdominal wall. It is continuous cranially with the mesogastrium, and caudally with the descending
mesocolon. The root of the mesentery refers to the portion of the mesentery that attaches to the aorta
and diaphragmatic crura opposite the second lumbar vertebrae. This is the thickest portion of the
mesentery containing the cranial mesenteric artery, intestinal lymphatics, and the extensive myenteric
plexus of nerves that surround the artery. The remainder of the mesentery is greatly folded and ruffled
and borders the SI extending from the duodenojejunal flexure proximally to the ileocolic junction
distally.
Blood is supplied to the SI via branches of the cranial mesenteric and celiac arteries, and subsequently
it drains into the portal vein (Figure 262.1, A). The vagus and splanchnic nerves supply autonomic
innervation to the SI.4

MICROSCOPIC ANATOMY
The 4 Layers
The components of the 4 distinct layers of the SI reflect their unique functions. The outer serosa consists
of a single layer of mesothelial cells, surrounding the intestines and forming the visceral peritoneum.
Beneath the serosa is the muscularis layer, which contains inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle
fibers that are responsible for mixing and propelling luminal contents. Components of the enteric
nervous system, responsible for coordinating contractions of these muscle layers, are also found within
the muscularis layer. Moving luminally, the submucosa houses an assorted population of cells, including
lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, eosinophils, fibroblasts, and mast cells contained in a
connective tissue matrix. The submucosa also delivers blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics to the
innermost layer, the mucosa. Of the 4 distinct layers of the SI, the mucosa is the most clinically
important as it is responsible for secretion and absorption and serves as a barrier to the luminal
contents. It is thickest in the duodenum and thinnest in the ileum. The mucosa contains the epithelium,
lamina propria, and a thin sheet of smooth muscle, the muscularis mucosa, which separates the mucosa
from the submucosa below.5
The functional unit of the SI is found in the mucosal layer and contains the villi and the underlying
crypts from which specialized epithelial cells known as enterocytes arise (Figure 262.1, C).6 Within the
crypts, epithelial stem cells divide and migrate upward (luminally). Once they reach the villus tip, they
are shed into the intestinal lumen after approximately 3 days (Figure 262.1, D). The function of the
enterocytes changes as they migrate along the villus, beginning with a mainly secretory function in the
crypt and lower villus and maturing to a mostly absorptive function in the upper part of the villus. In
addition to these functions, enterocytes form the intestinal epithelial barrier. Enterocytes represent
approximately 80% of cells in the mucosal epithelium. Differentiated enterocytes on the upper part of
the villus are tall, columnar, and contain a microscopic modification on their luminal cell membrane
known as the microvillar membrane (MVM), or brush border (Figure 262.1, E). This modification

increases the available surface area of the intestine by a factor of nearly 20 compared to the surface area
afforded by the villous projections. The MVM contains specific carrier proteins responsible for the
shuttling of nutrients across the polarized enterocyte cell membrane. To help facilitate this process,
enzymes responsible for the final stages of protein and carbohydrate digestion are found anchored in the
MVM (Figure 262.1, F). These so-called brush border enzymes are found in their highest
concentrations in the proximal SI, and they decrease in activity moving aborally through the SI.
Enterocytes are interspersed with goblet cells, which secrete a protective and lubricating mucus into
the intestinal lumen. The aboral segments of the intestines contain more goblet cells compared to the
more oral segments. Hormone-producing enteroendocrine cells (synonyms: enterochromaffin,
argentaffin, argyrophil) are also present in the mucosal surface layer.6
The lamina propria is bound by the epithelium above and muscularis mucosa below and contains
connective tissue, lymphoid tissue, immunocytes, enteric neurons, capillary beds, and central lacteals.
Blood flow to the villus is supplied by arterioles that pass to the tip of the villus and form a fenestrated
subepithelial capillary network that drains into veins. Separate arterioles supply the crypts. Central
lacteals are blind-ended permeable lymphatic capillaries lacking smooth muscle and valves. These noncontractile lymphatic capillaries drain to a network of lymphatics in the mucosal layer and a seemingly
non-connected network of lymphatics in the muscularis layer of the mucosa (Figure 262.1, D). Both of
these systems drain into the lymphatic collecting vessels near the mesenteric border of the SI, then to
regional lymph nodes, and eventually to the thoracic duct and back into the blood circulation.7-8 The
muscularis mucosa contains elastic fibers and smooth muscle cells that radiate into the lamina propria
to allow shortening and lengthening movements of the villi.

Small Intestinal Microbiome
The SI is critically dependent on a population of bacteria, protozoa, fungi, and viruses that inhabit its
lumen (ch. 260). The interaction between these resident microbes and host cells is termed the
intestinal microbiome. The largest component of the microbiome is made up of bacterial species, which
is comprised of a varied mixture of aerobic, anaerobic, and facultatively anaerobic bacteria. More than
200 species of bacteria are found in any individual animal’s SI. Each individual also appears to have a
unique bacterial microenvironment present within their gastrointestinal (GI) tract, which is typically
quite stable and relatively resistant to environmental change. Bacterial numbers increase moving from
proximal to distal in the SI and are highest in the colon. In comparison with dogs, cats appear to have a
greater total number of bacteria in the SI, as well as a larger proportion of obligate anaerobic bacteria. A
properly functioning intestinal microbiome is not just important to the health of the gut, but also to
remote sites, such as the skin and brain.3,9

Components of the Small Intestinal Immune System
The GI tract is the largest immunologic organ in the body and is a major component of the common
mucosal immune system (ch. 168). Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue in the gut is referred to as gutassociated lymphoid tissue (GALT). Specific anatomical components of the GI immune system include
organized, unencapsulated, lymphoid tissue in Peyer’s patches (PPs); diffuse lymphoid tissue scattered
throughout the lamina propria; the intestinal epithelium; and mesenteric lymph nodes. Other major
players in the GI immune system include the intestinal microbiota, maintenance of the intestinal
mucosal barrier, enterocyte secretions, leukocytes, antigen presenting cells (APCs), toll-like receptors
(TLRs) and other pattern recognition receptors, interleukins, and chemotactic cytokines.10

Intestinal Mucosal Barrier
The intestinal mucosal barrier is formed by the intestinal epithelium and is highly dependent on tight
junctions that encircle the lateral aspects between enterocytes. Tight junctions are intercellular adhesion
complexes that are crucial to epithelial integrity. They form a physical barrier against external factors
and help to control the movement of solutes and water through paracellular pathways. Studies in
rodents even suggest that intercellular bridges develop between nearby enterocytes to maintain mucosal
solidarity while effete enterocytes are shed.11 The major components of tight junction strands include
membrane proteins, such as occludin and claudins, as well as cytoplasmic scaffolding proteins, such as
zonula occludens (ZO-1), which anchors the claudins to actin filaments.12 The mucosal barrier is

enhanced by a variety of other structures and substances, many of which can be disrupted in a variety of
disease states (Box 262.1).

GI Endocrine System (ch. 297)
The GI tract is considered the largest endocrine organ in the body. The endocrine cells found within the
GI tract are collectively referred to as the enteric endocrine system. As mentioned above, the enteric
endocrine system is found diffusely throughout the SI, as single hormone-secreting cells
(enteroendocrine cells) that are scattered among the other types of mucosal epithelial cells. The apical
border of these cells is in contact with the luminal contents and secretes hormones (e.g.,
cholecystokinin, secretin) in response to changes they detect in the luminal environment. This facilitates
the processes of digestion and absorption as described below.

NORMAL FUNCTION
Overview
The basic functions of the SI occur via intricate interactions between microbes, luminal nutrients,
immune cells, neuroendocrine cells, and epithelial cells. These functions include motility, secretion of
water and electrolytes, digestion and absorption, and immunologic activity.13,14 Many of these functions
are critically affected by the intestinal microbiome.

Motility
Intestinal smooth muscle is arranged in circular and longitudinal layers, and individual smooth muscle
fibers are connected by gap junctions. Gap junctions allow the cells to be electrically coupled, which
facilitates well-coordinated contractions. There are 2 fundamental patterns of motility in the digestive
tract. Propulsive motility refers to the sequential process of food moving down the digestive tube for
eventual elimination, and the principal type of propulsion seen in the SI is peristalsis. During peristalsis,
a ring of muscle contraction appears on the oral side of the bolus of ingesta. The bolus is propelled
aborally as the ring moves and the muscle on the other side of the bolus relaxes (Figure 262.2). The
second fundamental pattern of motility is mixing. Mixing motility is required for proper digestion and
absorption. Mixing ensures foodstuffs are prepared for digestion and absorption and enhances their
contact with the intestinal epithelium where these processes will occur. Segmental contractions of the

intestine promote mixing motility (Figure 262.2). Effective mixing of luminal contents is also provided
by alternating contraction and relaxation of longitudinal muscle in the intestinal wall.
Some control of small intestinal motility emanates from the connection between the digestive system
and the central nervous system. However, motility is mainly controlled by excitatory and inhibitory
signals from the enteric nervous system, the local nervous system of the digestive tract. Specialized
mesenchymal cells known as interstitial cells of Cajal are the pacemakers of this activity. Additionally,
some GI hormones, namely motilin and gastric inhibitory peptide, influence intestinal motility.
Intestinal motility patterns are described in both the fasted and fed state. In the fasted state, 3 phases
of intestinal motility are observed that cycle approximately every 3 hours. The quiescent phase lasts
roughly 1 hour. Minor contractile activity dominates in phase 2, which occurs over 15-40 minutes. Phase
3 is characterized by short migrating motor complexes (MMCs), which occur over 4-8 minutes. Intense
contractile activity meant to sweep away undigested food, secretions, desquamated cells, bacteria, and
other substances occur during the MMC phase. These “housekeeper contractions” are induced by the
secretion of motilin. True MMCs are not recognized in the cat; rather cats have migrating spike
complexes (MSCs) that are thought to serve a similar function. However, MSCs differ from MMCs in
their frequency, intensity, and propagation and the MSC is not initiated by motilin.15
Motility in the fed state is most similar to fasted phase 2 activity and is characterized by both mixing
and propulsion as described above. The duration of motility is determined by the luminal contents, with
fiber and fat prolonging activity.16-20

Secretion of Water and Electrolytes
Large quantities of water are secreted and reabsorbed in the SI during the process of digestion. Water
secretion creates a liquid environment that helps promote contact of digestive enzymes with food
particles, allowing for their eventual absorption. The liquid environment also promotes transit of
contents along the intestinal tract.
Water moves across the mucosa via the paracellular route in response to osmotic gradients established
by 2 processes. First, the influx and digestion of foodstuffs results in an increase in luminal osmotic
pressure, which results in movement of water into the lumen. As the osmotically active molecules are
absorbed, luminal contents become less osmolar, and water can be reabsorbed. An increase in luminal
osmolarity also occurs as a consequence of the active secretion of electrolytes from the cryptal
epithelium. This process is facilitated via the critically important cyclic-AMP (cAMP)-dependent
chloride channel known as the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator. The transport of
chloride across this channel results in an electric potential that attracts sodium, pulling it across tight
junctions and into the intestinal lumen. The luminal accumulation of sodium chloride (NaCl) results in
an osmotic gradient that draws water into the lumen. Intestinal fluid balance is controlled by neurocrine
systems in the submucosal plexus. The various mediators change concentrations of calcium and cAMP
to result in the desired effects of net secretion or net absorption depending on the physiologic state.21

Digestion and Absorption
Intact dietary constituents must be hydrolyzed into monomers in order to be transported across the
villous epithelium.14 The SI provides the optimal environment for this transformation to occur.
Mechanical disruption/mixing of dietary constituents in the SI lumen allows for enzymatic hydrolysis of
polysaccharides and proteins, as well as the emulsification of fats by bile salts. Most of the necessary
enzymes are secreted by the pancreas (ch. 279), although brush border enzymes also play important
roles. Large quantities of digestive enzymes are secreted by pancreatic acinar cells in response to the
binding of cholecystokinin onto pancreatic acinar cell receptors. Cholecystokinin is secreted by duodenal
“I” enteroendocrine cells in response to the presence of luminal partially digested proteins and fats. The
optimal function of pancreatic and duodenal digestive enzymes is dependent on a suitable environment.
Most of these enzymes function best at a pH near 7.0. Secretin, a peptide hormone produced by “S”
enteroendocrine cells in the duodenal mucosa, is released in response to acidification of the duodenal
luminal environment. Secretin stimulates the pancreas to produce a fluid with a high bicarbonate
concentration that will neutralize the acidic contents of the duodenal lumen, thus creating a suitable
environment for optimal function of digestive enzymes.11

Carbohydrate
The major dietary carbohydrates are starch and glycogen. In order to be absorbed, they must be
hydrolyzed to glucose (Figure 262.3, A). Hydrolysis of amylose is performed by the enzyme pancreatic
alpha-amylase, and the products (maltose, maltotriose, and glucose) are subsequently further
hydrolyzed by particular brush border enzymes. Sucrose and lactose are hydrolyzed directly at the brush
border. The brush border enzyme lactase is most important in the nursing animal. Lactase activity
declines at weaning. The remaining marginal lactase activity declines even further in animals with SI
disease. The products of carbohydrate digestion are absorbed via active transport via specific carriers.
Absorption of glucose in the SI occurs via a sodium-dependent hexose transporter, SGLT1.

Protein
Digestion of protein is initiated in the stomach via acid denaturation and the proteolytic activity of
pepsin (Figure 262.3, B). Pancreatic proteases (i.e., trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase, and
carboxypeptidase) continue the process of protein digestion in the lumen of the SI. This results in a
mixture of di-, tri-, or oligopeptides, as well as free amino acids. Oligopeptides undergo further
hydrolysis by brush border peptidases, while the other peptides are absorbed via brush border carriers.
Free amino acids are absorbed through sodium-dependent active transport via selective carriers. Peptide
absorption occurs via facilitated diffusion. Once inside the enterocyte, the bulk of di- and tripeptides are
digested into amino acids by peptidases in the cytoplasm and then exported from the cell into the blood.

Fat
The process of fat digestion is initiated by gastric lipase secreted by gastric epithelial cells (Figure
262.3, C). Following this, mixing of fat in the stomach and SI results in the formation of small droplets
and micelles, respectively. Micelles are formed after mixing with bile and pancreatic secretions in the SI
and are approximately 1/100th of the size of the smallest fat droplet. Micelles function to solubilize
triglycerides into di- and monoglycerides and free fatty acids via pancreatic lipase. Lipase activity in the
SI lumen is dependent on a protein cofactor, colipase. Colipase is secreted by the pancreas as the
inactive procolipase. Phospholipids are hydrolyzed to lysophospholipids by activated pancreatic
phospholipase A2, and finally cholesterol esters are de-esterified by pancreatic cholesterol esterase.
Absorption of the products of fat digestion occurs largely through passive diffusion from mixed micelles
into lacteals. This process is dependent on normal pancreatic function, intestinal surface area, and
lymphatic function. Within enterocytes, these products are combined with synthesized lipoproteins to
form chylomicrons, which are passed into the lymphatics. Evidence exists that a proportion of mediumchain triglycerides may be absorbed directly into the portal blood in dogs; however, some likely is still
absorbed via lymphatics. Dietary fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are also solubilized in mixed
micelles before passive diffusion across the brush border.11

Water-Soluble Vitamins
Water-soluble vitamins are absorbed in the SI through a variety of mechanisms, including passive
diffusion, saturable facilitated transport, active and facilitated transport, carrier-mediated processes,
and/or receptor-mediated endocytosis. The absorption of vitamins B9 (folic acid) and B12 (cobalamin) is
of particular interest.
Folic acid is supplied through the diet as well as being produced by intestinal bacteria. It must be
hydrolyzed by a brush border enzyme, folate deconjugase, prior to absorption. Folate is then absorbed
via a carrier-mediated process or via passive diffusion depending on its concentration in the lumen
(Figure 262.4, A). After folate is absorbed into the enterocyte, it is methylated to form
methyltetrahydrofolate.11
