Cobalamin is bound to dietary meat-based protein in the stomach. It is released by activated
pepsinogen (i.e., pepsin) and gastric acid. Subsequently, free cobalamin is bound to R protein also
known as haptocorrin to protect it from being utilized by bacteria in the proximal SI. Pancreatic
proteases separate cobalamin from haptocorrin in the duodenum, where it is then complexed with
another binding protein, intrinsic factor (IF). IF is produced largely in the exocrine pancreas in the dog,
and to a lesser extent by the gastric mucosa. IF is produced solely in the pancreas in cats. Once bound to
IF, cobalamin travels to the ileum where it is absorbed via receptor-mediated endocytosis. (Figure
262.4, B). The specific receptor complex responsible for the absorption of cobalamin is cubam, and it is
localized in the brush border of the ileum. It is made up of 2 subunits known as amnionless (AMN) and
cubilin (CUBN). Additionally, ∼1% of dietary cobalamin is absorbed via passive diffusion throughout the
entire length of the GI tract. After absorption into enterocytes, cobalamin is separated from IF and the
receptor. Cobalamin is then passed into the portal blood where it is next bound to transcobalamin 2,
which enables it to enter tissues. Some recirculating cobalamin is extracted by hepatocytes, bound to
haptocorrin, and secreted in the bile for enterohepatic recirculation.22

Immunologic Activity of the Small Intestine (ch. 168)

The GI tract is continually bombarded by dietary, bacterial, and environmental antigens. It must
perform the crucial task of excluding toxins and mounting an immune response against possible
pathogens, all while sustaining a state of tolerance towards commensal bacteria and non-harmful dietary
and environmental antigens.10
Normal peristalsis, gastric and pancreatic secretions, proteolysis, and innate immunity provide the
first line of defense. Important components of the innate immune system of the SI include the tight
junctions of the intestinal epithelial barrier, commensal microflora, immune cell populations, defensins,
and pattern recognition receptors. Immune cell populations active in the innate response include
neutrophils, mast cells, natural killer cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and T lymphocyte subtypes,
such as intraepithelial lymphocytes. M cells are specialized modified enterocytes that sample the luminal
contents and help deliver antigen to the mucosal immune system. These cells are most abundant in PPs,
but also are found scattered throughout the SI.
Importantly, immune cells are able to recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) on
the surface of a wide variety of microbes via pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), such as TLRs and
nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD1 and NOD2) molecules. Each of these molecules plays
a different role. For example, TLR2 recognizes lipopeptides found in Gram-negative bacteria, while
TLR5 recognizes the bacterial flagella protein, flagellin, and NOD2 recognizes lipopolysaccharide. TLRs
are expressed on various cell types of the GI mucosa and they play a critical role in microbial
recognition, induction of antimicrobial genes, and the signaling of the adaptive immune response. They
are also critical to commensal bacterial recognition and tolerance in the healthy GI tract.23,24 TLRs have
a unique, but poorly understood, ability to distinguish commensal bacteria from pathogenic bacteria.
Commensal bacteria express highly conserved bacterial structure elements that are best termed
microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs). Interaction between a TLR and a MAMP or PAMP will
lead to nuclear factor-kappa-beta signaling. When the interaction is with commensal bacteria,
transcription activation is blocked, whereas when there is recognition of a PAMP from a pathogenic
bacterial species, transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines is activated, triggering the inflammatory
cascade (Figure 262.5).
The adaptive response is triggered when foreign antigen is taken up by APCs and subsequently broken
into small peptides and presented on the cell surface in association with class I or II molecules of the
major histocompatibility complex (MHC). T helper lymphocytes recognize these MHC-peptide
complexes, become activated, and subsequently activate B cells binding the same antigen. This
activation is promoted and enhanced by cytokine signaling and co-stimulatory surface molecules. After
these cells are activated, they proliferate within the lymph tissue and then are exported into the
bloodstream to circulate and survey for the original antigen encountered. These activated lymphocytes
will “home” to the tissue where the original antigen was encountered via addressins on the vascular
endothelium. The effector phase of this immune response involves immunoglobulin production and
secretion and T helper cell responses. Antigen specific cells typically are kept in check by populations of
T regulatory cells, which helps to limit damage to the normal tissue. Memory cells are preserved and
able to mount a more potent immune response upon re-exposure to the antigen.10
Most immune responses that occur in the GALT lead to tolerance. It is theorized that when the
intestinal mucosa is invaded by a toxin or pathogen, cellular damage leads to the release of inflammatory
mediators, cytokines, and chemokines, all of which are considered “danger signals.” This switches the
immune response from tolerance to active. Breakdown of normal tolerance can occur due to altered
mucosal permeability, abnormal antigen presentation, inherent immune system abnormality, or other
dysregulation of the mucosal immune system.

Role of the Intestinal Microbiome (ch. 260)
The intestinal microbiota is responsible for a number of functions critical to the maintenance of GI
health. Those functions include protection of the host from invasion by pathogenic microbes, metabolic
activities, and trophic effects on the intestinal epithelium. Commensal bacteria protect the host from
pathogens and potential pathogens via several mechanisms. First, they form a biofilm that creates a
physical barrier between the luminal contents and the intestinal epithelial microenvironment. They also
compete with pathogens for colonization sites in the SI, nutrients, and other resources. In some cases,
they secrete antimicrobial substances such as lactic acid to inhibit pathogen proliferation.25 Commensal
bacteria are also responsible for the development and early education of the mucosal immune system
and they help to develop and modulate T helper cell responses. Resident bacteria in the gut synthesize

various substances such as folate and biotin and assist in the absorption of certain nutrients, such as
calcium, magnesium, and iron. Importantly, the bacterial microbiota plays an important role in various
metabolic pathways, including the metabolism of bile acids, short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and indole.
Furthermore, glucose uptake in the SI is enhanced by the bacterial microbiota. Commensal bacteria
bestow several protective effects on the intestinal epithelium that help to maintain intestinal mucosal
barrier integrity. For example, exposure of enterocytes to bacterial ligands results in phosphorylation of
specific protein kinase C isoforms, which leads to apical tightening and sealing of tight-junction–
associated ZO-1.26 In summary, the intestinal microbiota serves a number of unique functions crucial to
intestinal health and the overall health of their host.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGIC MECHANISMS OF DISEASE
A variety of pathophysiologic mechanisms can result in SI disease and dysfunction. In many patients
afflicted with SI disorders, multiple mechanisms can be responsible for the development of disease.
Comprehension of the processes that led to dysfunction allows the clinician to recognize how
recommended interventions can be formulated in a way that best addresses the underlying disorder(s).

CONGENITAL ABNORMALITIES AND GENETIC
PREDISPOSITIONS
Congenital abnormalities of the SI are rare in dogs and cats. Reported abnormalities include
spontaneous duplications of SI segments,27,28 intestinal stenosis or atresia, non-rotation of the midgut
during embryonic development,29 and arteriovenous fistulae.30 Intestinal duplications are cyst-like
lesions that are typically discovered incidentally. Duodenal blind-ended diverticula have also been
reported and similarly may be discovered incidentally. Diverticula have also been associated with foreign
body entrapment, perforations, and bleeding.31
Genetic predispositions are suggested for a variety of SI disorders. Although breed associations are
often observed, in many cases the predisposing factors are unknown. In humans with inflammatory
bowel disease (IBD), mutations in a variety of PRRs, including NOD2 and TLR4 have been associated
with IBD.32 Similarly, a polymorphism in the TLR5 gene (G22A) was found to be significantly associated
with IBD in the German Shepherd Dog. Additionally, 2 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were
also associated with IBD in the German Shepherd Dog, but not without the TLR5 risk haplotype.33 TLR5
activation may be necessary for secretion of certain defensins; thus, a defect in the gene could result in
immune system dysfunction and disruption of the epithelial barrier, leading to the development of
inflammatory responses. Additional genetic predispositions and associated mutations (if known) are
discussed under “Small Intestinal Diseases,” below.

OVERVIEW OF IMMUNOPATHOGENESIS OF MUCOSAL
INFLAMMATION
Inflammation is a cellular and vascular response triggered by a variety of mechanisms. Its presence
reflects the loss of intestinal homeostasis. Rodent experimental models of GI inflammation have
permitted better understanding of these mechanisms. Mechanisms include loss of integrity of the
mucosal barrier, dysregulation of the mucosal immune system, and/or disruption of the endogenous
microbiota. Each of these mechanisms triggers similar chronic inflammatory responses that produce
similar histological findings.

EPITHELIAL BARRIER DISRUPTION AND INNATE
IMMUNITY HYPERRESPONSIVENESS
A variety of agents can damage the epithelial barrier, including endogenous inflammatory mediators and
luminal factors (Box 262.2). Interestingly, stress alters the permeability of enterocyte tight junctions

via the release of norepinephrine.34,35 Translocation of bacteria into the circulation can occur as a
consequence of disruption of the barrier. More commonly, damage to the epithelial barrier results in
entry of antigens and subsequent inflammatory and allergic reactions.36
Inflammatory responses in the SI may occur as a consequence of innate immunity
hyperresponsiveness. In this scenario, it is suggested that the immune system may respond to organisms
in the commensal microbiota as if they were pathogens. In humans with Crohn’s disease (CD) or
ulcerative colitis, certain intestinal TLRs have been demonstrated to be upregulated.37 It is not clear
whether this upregulation occurs as a response to persistent stimulation or is part of the underlying
pathogenesis in the development of the disease. Studies in dogs with IBD have demonstrated varied
upregulation of TLRs. Notably, specific changes may be breed-dependent, as results have differed in
mixed-breed dogs compared to some purebred dogs, notably the German Shepherd Dog. For example, in
dogs (of various breeds) with clinically severe IBD, intestinal TLR2 expression, but not TLR4 expression,
was increased compared to a control population.38 However, in German Shepherd Dogs with IBD, TLR4
expression was increased by 60-fold in the duodenum, ileum, and colon when compared to samples
from healthy control dogs. In these German Shepherd Dogs, intestinal TLR2 expression was similar to
that of healthy dogs.39

DYSBIOSIS AND BILE ACID DYSMETABOLISM
The interactions between host cells and the microbial ecosystem have a significant impact on health and
disease in dogs and cats (ch. 260).40 When the microbiome is balanced, host health is promoted.
Consequently, imbalance may be damaging. Of note is the effect of an imbalanced microbiome on
metabolic pathways. Recent investigations have demonstrated that Clostridium hiranonis may be
depleted in dogs with chronic enteropathies (CEs).41 Since C. hiranonis is the main bile acid-converting
bacterial species in the intestinal lumen of dogs, its depletion may lead to a decreased proportion of
secondary bile acids in the colon. Importantly, secondary bile acids appear to have anti-inflammatory
properties. Activation of the bile acid receptor TGR5 confers various anti-inflammatory properties in
several different disease models.42 Specifically, it has been shown to inhibit the production of tumor
necrosis factor alpha by lamina propria macrophages in humans with CD.43 Thus, depletion of
secondary bile acids as a consequence of resident microbial imbalance may have a pro-inflammatory
effect on the host. Furthermore, bile acids have beneficial roles in mucosal barrier function and mucosal
defense (Figure 262.6), so depletion and dysmetabolism may lead to increased susceptibility of the
host to mucosal barrier injury and invasion by pathogens or resident bacteria. Disturbances of the
microbiota can also lead to impaired fermentation of SCFAs, such as butyrate, acetate, and propionate

from dietary carbohydrates. These SCFAs play a role in mucosal defense, help regulate intestinal
motility, act as nutrients, and have anti-inflammatory properties. Additional microbially-derived
metabolites that can be affected by dysbiosis include indole compounds, B vitamins, and vitamin K.40
A healthy microbiome promotes tight junction formation and dysbiosis can affect the integrity of the
intestinal barrier. Disruption of the intestinal barrier can lead to translocation of toxins, pathogens, and
dietary antigens. Dysbiosis can also impair host intestinal defenses against pathogens because resident
bacteria produce antimicrobials and compete with pathogens for nutrients and receptor sites. Finally,
since the microbiota educate and modulate the immune system through various mechanisms, dysbiosis
can lead to an impaired gut immune system and aberrant inflammatory responses.

FIGURE 262.6 Role of bile acids in mucosal barrier function and mucosal
defense. Bile acids have a wide variety of effects at various levels of the small
intestine. ER, Endoplasmic reticulum; NF-kB, nuclear factor kappa B; TGF-b,
transforming growth factor beta. From Pavlidis P, Powell N, Vincent RP, et al.
Systematic review: bile acids and intestinal inflammation-luminal aggressors or
regulators of mucosal defence? Aliment Pharmacol Ther. 2015;42:802-817.
While disturbances of the microbiome are now well recognized in both acute and chronic GI disorders,
the cause-effect relationships are still under investigation. Considering the complex interactions
between the gut microbiota, host immune system/mucosal defense, and bile acid metabolism, it is
reasonable to consider that these relationships may involve a self-perpetuating cycle in patients with GI
disorders.

VILLUS AND MICROVILLAR MEMBRANE DAMAGE AND
DEFECTS
Villous atrophy occurs due to an increase in enterocyte loss or a decrease in enterocyte production. The
most notable consequence of villous atrophy is the loss of intestinal surface area for absorption of
nutrients, which leads to malabsorption. Common causes of villous atrophy include idiopathic
inflammation, dietary factors such as gluten-sensitive enteropathy, infectious agents that infect or
damage villus tips or the cryptal epithelium, cytotoxic drugs, and prolonged starvation. In cases of
enterocyte loss, a compensatory increase in crypt cell proliferation may be able to compensate for the
losses. However, the replacement cells are typically immature and thus decreased in height and
suboptimal in function when compared to their mature counterparts.44 Damage to the cryptal
epithelium as a consequence of specific infections (e.g., parvovirus) or cytotoxic drugs can cause
complete villus and crypt arrest, resulting in severe diarrhea. Surviving stem cells can regenerate, but
this process is expected to take several days.
Damage to the MVM is implied when villus injury has occurred, but microvillus damage can also
occur in the absence of overt villus injury. Significant impairment of mucosal function occurs secondary
to loss of brush border enzymes and carriers when the MVM is damaged. Enteropathogens, specifically
Escherichia coli, can cause direct damage to the MVM.45 A recent comprehensive survey of histologic
lesions in dogs with diet-responsive CE described increases in both the space between microvilli as well
as tight junction width in these dogs when compared to a control population. Intermicrovillar space and
microvillus height were decreased and increased, respectively, after 6 weeks of treatment. These data
supported the increasingly held suspicion that evaluation of architectural changes to the intestine are at
least as important as conventional histologic assessments (e.g., inflammation) in patients with chronic
GI signs.46
Functional impairment of the MVM can also occur in the absence of overt structural damage.
Disorders that can lead to maldigestion/malabsorption due to loss of key digestive enzymes are
colloquially referred to as brush border membrane diseases. Primary brush border diseases, such as
those in humans caused by deficiency of lactase or sucrose, are largely theoretical in dogs and cats.
However, defects in the ileal brush border receptor responsible for the absorption of cobalamin have
been documented in dogs. While a genetic basis for cobalamin deficiency is suspected in a variety of dog
breeds, the specific genetic defect has only been confirmed for a few breeds22,47-50 (see “Small Intestinal
Diseases,” below).

ALTERATIONS IN MOTILITY
Primary or secondary disorders of intestinal motility can result in malabsorption of nutrients and induce
diarrhea through a number of different mechanisms. For example, conditions resulting in hypomotility
or stasis of luminal contents lead to increases in bacterial fermentation, which may result in diarrhea.
Conditions that result in hypermotility impair water absorption in the SI, resulting in watery diarrhea.
While primary disorders of motility are uncommon in dogs and cats, alterations in motility may occur
secondary to a variety of other disorders and may lead to worsening of clinical signs.

LYMPHATIC ABNORMALITIES
Early studies showed that when short segments of regional lymphatics in the intestine of pigs and rats
are obstructed, segmental intestinal disease develops that is histopathologically similar to CD.51 More
recently, the ablation of lymphatics in a mouse model resulted in mucosal barrier injury, allowing for the
invasion of intestinal pathogens and subsequent intestinal inflammation.52 Thus, it is generally accepted
that changes to the intestinal lymphatic vasculature can result in disease of the SI. In humans, various
defects of intestinal lymphatics, including obstruction, remodeling, pump dysfunction, and changes in
structure and pattern, are known to result in or exacerbate several intestinal conditions.7 When the
intestinal lymphatic system fails to function properly, lymphatic clearance will be inadequate, edema
and dilated lymph vessels (intestinal lymphangiectasia [IL]) will occur, immune cells can accumulate in
the mucosa and submucosa, and inflammation-induced lymphangiogenesis (growth of new initial

lymphatics) is observed.53 Furthermore, leakage of lymph from dilated or non-functional lymphatic
vessels worsens the inflammatory reaction in the intestinal wall.
Conversely, inflammatory or neoplastic intestinal mucosal infiltrates can increase hydrostatic
lymphatic pressure, resulting in IL, which can then perpetuate the inflammatory state. Increased venous
pressure secondary to portal hypertension, cardiac tamponade, and right-sided heart failure can also
result in IL. Thus, IL can be considered a primary or secondary condition. Regardless of whether IL is
considered primary or secondary, it will frequently lead to SI dysfunction. The intestinal lymphatic
vasculature plays a role in immune system function, as the major conduit of antigens and immune cells
from the periphery. Immunological deficits noted in humans with intestinal lymphatic dysfunction
include T-cell depletion, impaired antibody function, diminished immunoglobulins, and B-cell
depletion.54 Additional functions of the lymphatic system include extracellular fluid homeostasis and fat
absorption and transport. Thus, in states of dysfunction, edema develops and absorption of dietary fat
and fat-soluble vitamins is often impaired.

NEOPLASIA
Neoplasia may result in damage and dysfunction of the SI through a variety of mechanisms.11 Tumors
that infiltrate the mucosa and cause diffuse disease, such as lymphoma, obstruct blood and lymphatic
flow, which can lead to ulceration, villous atrophy, and general enterocyte dysfunction. Solitary tumors
of the SI may be associated with bleeding, complete or partial intestinal obstruction, and/or peritonitis if
bowel wall integrity is compromised. Partial obstruction as a result of a neoplastic mass can lead to
stasis of intraluminal contents. Some distant tumors can also have an effect on the SI. For example,
cutaneous mast cell tumors (ch. 327) can promote histamine-mediated increases in gastric acid
secretion that can lead to gastric or duodenal ulceration, which in some cases may result in a perforation
of the GI wall.

CLINICAL OVERVIEW
TERMINOLOGY RELATED TO SMALL INTESTINAL DISEASE
Over recent years, there have been substantial changes in the proposed terminology utilized for diseases
of the SI in small animals, particularly in the field of CE.55 While all terminology has limitations, we
define the terminology utilized throughout this chapter below. We recognize that this terminology will
likely evolve further with time. In some places, appropriate terminology may have been edited relative to
a cited reference. This has been done to maintain consistency throughout the chapter.

Chronic Enteropathy (CE)
Chronic enteropathy is a broad term used to define the presence of GI signs of >3 weeks duration, where
extraintestinal disease, infectious etiologies, or neoplastic disease have been ruled out or are considered
unlikely. Use of the term CE does not require the need for histopathologic evidence of inflammation.
From a clinical standpoint, CE is further classified according to treatment response as food-responsive
enteropathy (FRE), antibiotic-responsive enteropathy (ARE), and immunosuppressant- or steroidresponsive enteropathy (IRE/SRE).

Food-Responsive Enteropathies (FRE)
FREs are chronic enteropathies that respond to dietary manipulation alone. Various dietary
manipulations should be attempted prior to defining an animal as non-food-responsive.

Antibiotic-Responsive Enteropathies

AREs are chronic enteropathies that respond to antimicrobial therapy. Antibiotic trials are typically
attempted after dietary manipulation (ch. 152) and, as such, the response may relate to a combination
of treatments. Antibiotic response does not typically indicate an underlying infectious etiology as it may
also be due to manipulation of the microbiome or due to anti-inflammatory effects exerted by certain
antibiotics. This subgroup of CE recently has been under scrutiny and likely should be adapted to
include the subset of animals who may respond to manipulation of the microbiome though therapeutic
methods other than antibiotic use.

Immunosuppressive/Steroid-Responsive
Enteropathies (IRE/SRE)
IRE/SRE are chronic enteropathies that respond to anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive
treatment. Steroid and immunosuppressive trials are typically attempted after dietary and food
manipulation (ch. 152) and as such the response may relate to a combination of therapies.

Chronic Inflammatory Enteropathy (CIE)
CIE refers to conditions of the intestinal tract that are characterized by the presence of GI signs of at
least 3 weeks’ duration, exclusion of neoplastic, infectious, and extra-GI causes of GI signs, and,
importantly, histologic evidence of intestinal inflammation. The term IBD is often used interchangeably
with CIE in veterinary medicine. However, use of the term IBD requires documentation of inadequate
response to appropriately designed and implemented therapeutic trials (i.e., dietary, antibacterial,
anthelmintic) and clinical response to anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive agents. Thus, the term
CIE is considered more inclusive.

Protein-Losing Enteropathies (PLEs)
PLEs are a group of GI disorders characterized by excessive loss of protein across the enteric mucosa.
Potential etiologies are numerous.

CLINICAL FEATURES OF SMALL INTESTINAL DISEASE (BOX
262.3)
Small intestinal disease is commonly associated with the presence of diarrhea. Small intestinal diarrhea
is characterized by an increase in the volume of feces produced with a normal to mildly increased
frequency and lack of urgency or tenesmus. Small intestinal disease may also result in weight loss from
malabsorption, and may be accompanied by vomiting, melena, and/or borborygmus, among other signs
(ch. 263, Table 263.1). While these features have historically been used to assist in generation of
differential diagnoses and to assist in formulating a diagnostic plan, it is important to note that many
dogs have both small and large intestinal involvement and this may alter the diagnostic or therapeutic
approach.

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION OF SMALL INTESTINAL DISEASE
It is important to consider that both GI and non-GI disorders can result in diarrhea (Box 262.4). NonGI disorders should be eliminated prior to focusing on the intestinal origin of clinical signs.

Signalment
Dogs and cats of any age or breed and either sex may be affected by acute or chronic SI disease.
However, the patient’s signalment may allow for prioritization of differential diagnoses and may assist in
determining whether a therapeutic trial is indicated. Young dogs are at greatest risk of GI parasitism,
with a recent survey of 3006 healthy dogs across the USA noting that dogs ≤12 months of age were at
greatest risk of nematode and Giardia spp. infections.56 When considering dogs with chronic GI signs,
dogs infected with Giardia spp. are younger than those affected by other disease processes.57
Additionally, when considering causes of CE, dogs with food-responsive disease are typically younger
than those with steroid/immunosuppressant or non-responsive disease.58 Particular disease syndromes
may also be most prevalent in certain populations. For example, young large breed dogs (especially
German Shepherd Dogs) appear to be at greatest risk of antibiotic-responsive diarrhea, while patients
with other signalments are considered less likely to respond to antibiotic trials.59-61

A retrospective study of 95,803 cats documented that young cats were more likely to be infected with
fecal parasites than were older cats. Approximately half of the cats in that study presented for wellness
exams and this may not reflect the patient population seen in referral practice.62 Similar to dogs, cats
with food-responsive enteropathies tend to be younger than those with immunosuppressant-responsive
enteropathies (also called feline IBD). Cats with small cell lymphoma (SCL) may also be older than those
with other causes of chronic diarrhea.63-65 Anecdotally, Siamese cats are predisposed to CE.65 However,
it is important to note that extensive overlap exists in many of these studies and signalment alone
cannot be used for diagnosing a condition.

History (ch. 2)
A complete history is required in the diagnostic approach for animals with suspected small intestinal
disease. Further details can be found in Box 262.5.

Physical Examination (ch. 3)
Physical examination findings are often nonspecific in dogs and cats with SI disease and may include
dehydration, weight loss, and loss of muscle mass. Body condition and muscle condition scores should
be reported at each visit and may help to identify progressive disease (ch. 72 and textbook’s inside
covers). The mouth should be examined for the presence of a linear foreign body (ch. 258) and a rectal
examination should be performed to confirm the presence of diarrheic stool and to examine the patient
for melena (ch. 3). Abdominal palpation may reveal signs of pain or discomfort in the cranial abdomen,
which may alert the clinician to the possibility of concurrent pancreatitis (ch. 277). Signs of diffuse
abdominal pain may be noted in patients with peritonitis or those with an intestinal foreign body.
Abdominal palpation may also reveal the presence of thickened intestinal loops, a palpable abdominal
mass, or an abdominal fluid wave (ch. 21). Skin lesions caused by pruritus may be seen in conjunction
with food hypersensitivity (ch. 160).

Routine Bloodwork, Urinalysis, and Fecal Examination
The results of a minimum database are rarely diagnostic for small intestinal disease, but they are
important in helping to rule out extraintestinal causes of disease.

Complete Blood Count (CBC)
Depending on the etiology, the CBC may reveal an elevated packed cell volume (PCV) and total protein
concentration, consistent with dehydration. Marked elevations in PCV are typically seen in dogs with
acute hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome (AHDS) or as part of a paraneoplastic process (ch. 331).
Although marked hemoconcentration is considered frequent in AHDS, a recent study reported that the
PCV only exceeded 60% in 31.4% of cases (see below).66 Anemia (ch. 57) may also be present and can
reflect 1 or more of several different etiologies, including inflammation, blood loss, or iron deficiency. A
mild, normocytic, normochromic anemia is commonly noted in dogs and cats with enteropathies due to
anemia of inflammatory disease.67 Microcytosis, decreased reticulocyte hemoglobin, and decreased
reticulocyte volume may be present in patients with iron deficiency.68 Regenerative anemia may reflect
GI blood loss. Red blood cell morphological abnormalities and anemia may also be more common in
patients with intestinal lymphoma than in those with inflammatory enteropathies.69 A stress leukogram
is commonly noted in dogs and cats with chronic enteropathies.67 Lymphopenia may also be present,
particularly in cases of IL.70 Neutrophil to lymphocyte ratios (NLRs) are high in dogs with chronic
enteropathies and may help to distinguish immunosuppressant and non-responsive enteropathies from
those with food-responsive enteropathies.71 An eosinophilia may be seen in cases of eosinophilic
enteritis (including feline GI eosinophilic sclerosing fibroplasia), fungal disease, or as part of a
paraneoplastic syndrome (ch. 331). Hypoadrenocorticism should be considered in any dog with small
bowel diarrhea, in particular in dogs that lack a stress leukogram, have a low NLR, and/or demonstrate
a lymphocytosis with eosinophilia, even in the absence of electrolyte abnormalities (ch. 296).72 Less is
known about NLRs in cats with enteropathies. Platelet counts may be decreased secondary to
consumption with a GI bleed. Thrombocytosis, an elevated platelet dry mass distribution width, and an
increased mean platelet volume have also been noted in cases of CE and may be associated with disease
severity.73,74

Serum Biochemistry Profile
Abnormalities on the serum biochemistry profile differ among various etiologies of SI disease.

PLEs are characterized by hypoalbuminemia, with a variable presence of hypoglobulinemia and
hypocholesterolemia. Also, hypoalbuminemia is a negative prognostic indicator in canine CE.75 In cats
with chronic SI disease, significant protein loss is less common than in dogs and tends to be mild in
severity.76,77 Significant hypoalbuminemia in a cat with chronic SI disease should prompt consideration
of concurrent pancreatitis or intestinal lymphoma.78,79 The albumin concentration also may be low in
animals with GI blood loss. In some cases, total protein and globulin concentrations may be elevated
secondary to dehydration or chronic inflammatory states.
Hypocalcemia may be noted in dogs and cats with SI disease and may be associated with vitamin D
status.80 Hypomagnesemia may also be noted. Hypercalcemia may occur with granulomatous disease
(e.g., schistosomiasis) or as part of a paraneoplastic syndrome.81 Hypercalcemia may also occur with
extraintestinal causes of SI diarrhea (e.g., hypoadrenocorticism).82
Mild increases in liver enzyme activities are frequently noted and likely reflect a reactive hepatopathy
secondary to portal venous transport of toxins and/or ascension of bacteria and LPS from a
compromised gut barrier. Measurement of serum total bile acids concentrations can be used for ruling
out hepatic dysfunction as a cause of hypoalbuminemia. Increased plasma ammonia concentrations
should be interpreted cautiously in animals with SI disease, as hypocobalaminemia may lead to reduced
methylmalonyl-CoA mutase activity and subsequent hyperammonemia (ch. 244), in the absence of
primary hepatic dysfunction.22,83
Animals with SI disease may also have an increased blood urea nitrogen (BUN) concentration
secondary to dehydration, protein catabolism, or GI bleeding. An increased BUN concentration is a
negative prognostic indicator in dogs with CE and has also been noted in some cats with SI disease.84
One study showed that a BUN >37 mg/dL (>13.2 mmol/L) was highly sensitive (100%), but poorly
specific (29.4%) for suggesting a diagnosis of alimentary lymphoma versus immunosuppressantresponsive enteropathy in cats.85
Hypokalemia is frequently detected in dogs and cats with SI disease and may reflect decreased uptake
or intestinal loss. Hyperkalemia may occur with third spacing, hypoadrenocorticism, in cases of severe
diarrhea (i.e., whipworm infections or salmonellosis), or from in vitro blood clotting with serum
samples.86

wall (calipers A-A) caused by chronic inflammatory enteropathy in a 3-year-old
French Bulldog.

Urinalysis
The urinalysis (ch. 70) is typically normal in dogs and cats with SI disease. However, a urine protein-tocreatinine ratio may be useful to rule out a protein-losing nephropathy (PLN; ch. 302) in patients with
hypoalbuminemia.

Standard Fecal Diagnostic Tests
Fecal flotation, fecal sedimentation, direct fecal smears/wet mounts, and targeted fecal polymerase
chain reaction (PCR), enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), and IFA testing are a critical
component of the diagnostic approach to SI disease in dogs and cats (ch. 80). Untargeted fecal PCR
panels may be of lower value and the clinical significance of abnormalities may be challenging to
determine.87 Fecal cultures are not usually indicated and may indeed be challenging to interpret.88 A
recent study comparing results of fecal culture from 3 different laboratories showed a significant
variability of results.88

Diagnostic Imaging

Radiology
Plain radiographs may be used for detecting intestinal foreign bodies, evidence of GI perforation,
decreased serosal detail, and evidence of functional ileus. While 2-view abdominal radiographs are
commonly utilized in veterinary practice, 3-view abdominal radiographs (to include the left lateral
projection) have been suggested to aid in the evaluation of potential GI obstructions.89 However, a
recent study noted no perceived or statistically significant increased diagnostic utility of 3 vs. 2
radiographic projections in dogs presenting with an acute abdomen.90 Similarly in cats, a 3-view
abdominal series may not be required for all cases, but a left lateral projection may be useful in cats with

gastric distension.91 Repeat radiographs have also been suggested to improve diagnostic yield, although
recent studies suggest their value may be more limited than previously suspected.92,93 Plain survey
radiographs are generally useful in detection of acute surgical disease, and are less helpful in cases of
chronic malabsorptive disease. Contrast studies may allow for increased detection of GI lesions on
radiographs.

Abdominal Ultrasonography
Abdominal ultrasonography is frequently used in the diagnostic approach to acute and chronic small
intestinal disease. Ultrasound can detect abnormal small intestinal wall layering and thickness (Figure
262.7) in addition to the presence of ulceration, mucosal lesions, neoplasia, ileus, foreign bodies,
abdominal effusion, intussusception, and other lesions (Figure 262.8,

Video 262.1). In cats,

ultrasonographic mucosal abnormalities have a high positive predictive value for histopathologic
abnormalities in the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum, given the presence of an appropriate test
population. Additionally, endoscopic biopsies are still of value in cats with ultrasonographic evidence of
submucosal or muscularis lesions. However, ultrasonographic evidence of jejunal lesions suggests the
need for surgical rather than endoscopic biopsies.94 Hyperechoic mucosal striations can be seen in
patients with IL (Figure 262.9) and may be more readily detected following oral corn oil
administration.95 The layers of the SI include the mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, and serosa (Figure
262.1). The mucosa and muscularis are hypoechoic. Ultrasound may also detect an inner hypoechoic
nodular layer in the cecum of cats, measuring up to 2 mm in thickness, that is thought to represent the
presence of multiple coalescing lymphoid follicles.96 Disruption of wall layering is commonly seen in
patients with neoplasia, whereas wall layering is commonly preserved in inflammatory etiologies.
Infectious etiologies may also present with intestinal wall thickening with or without loss of wall
layering, e.g., histoplasmosis (ch. 209), schistosomiasis (see below), and pythiosis (ch. 263).97-99 GI
perforation may be suspected when ultrasonographically-evident free gas is noted in the peritoneal
cavity.100 Cats with large granular lymphocyte (LGL) lymphoma often present with a localized mass
lesion on ultrasound.101 Focal lesions may also be noted in infectious etiologies and in cats with GI
eosinophilic sclerosing fibroplasia.102 GI intussusception may be recognized as multiple concentric rings
in the transverse plane (Figure 262.10; Video 262.1;

ch. 263, Figure 263.6). Ultrasound also

allows for fine-needle aspiration of abnormal tissue, which can further improve the diagnostic yield.
Despite its frequent use, abdominal ultrasonography has been questioned for the routine diagnostic
approach to animals with chronic diarrhea. In a prospective study of 87 dogs with chronic diarrhea,
ultrasound was vital or beneficial to arriving at the diagnosis in only 15% of cases.103 Additionally, in a
recent retrospective study of 269 dogs with diarrhea, abdominal ultrasound was only considered
diagnostic without the need for further diagnostic testing in 3% of cases.104 A study in cats also revealed
that one-third of cats with GI signs and hypocobalaminemia or a low normal cobalamin concentration,
suggestive of SI disease, had no SI abnormalities detected on abdominal ultrasound, suggesting only a
moderate sensitivity.105 Based on the current literature, it appears that ultrasound has value in the
diagnostic approach to acute SI disease, but its value may be more limited in patients with chronic SI
disorders and a normal ultrasound should not preclude pursuit of further diagnostic tests.

Advanced Diagnostic Imaging
In recent years, several studies have investigated the use of computed tomography (CT) in the diagnostic
approach to dogs and cats with small intestinal disease. CT has been accurate in the diagnosis of
mechanical obstructions in dogs and cats.106,107 Additionally, contrast-enhanced multi-detector CT has
been an accurate screening test for differentiating surgical from non-surgical acute abdominal
conditions in dogs (ch. 126).108 Further studies are needed to determine the value of CT in patients

with chronic enteropathies. It is likely that CT, magnetic resonance imaging, and other advanced
imaging modalities such as elastography, contrast-enhanced ultrasound, and lymphangiography will
become more frequently utilized in the coming years.

Specialized Tests—Functional

Cobalamin, Methylmalonic Acid (MMA), and
Homocysteine (HCY)
Serum cobalamin concentration is frequently measured in dogs and cats with suspected SI disease.
Hypocobalaminemia may occur secondary to SI disease because of reduced receptor expression or
receptor damage in the ileum, secondary to mucosal inflammation, but it may also occur due to bacterial
competition for dietary cobalamin in dogs with dysbiosis.109 As cobalamin-dependent metabolic
reactions occur intracellularly, serum cobalamin levels may not accurately reflect true cobalamin status.
This has led to the development of MMA and HCY assays.22 MMA concentration increases during
periods of decreased intracellular vitamin B12 availability and may be a good biomarker of cellular
cobalamin deficiency.22 HCY concentration increases during periods of intracellular cobalamin or folate
deficiency, but this marker is less reliable than the measurement of MMA concentration.110,111 The
measurement of both MMA and HCY is technologically demanding and expensive; thus, routine

measurement of either marker is currently not recommended. Hereditary cobalamin deficiency
syndromes have been reported in several breeds (Tables 262.1 and 262.2).47,50,112-115

Folate
Serum folate concentration may be measured in conjunction with cobalamin; however, its diagnostic
yield and clinical relevance appear to be lower than those of cobalamin. Serum folate concentrations
may be reduced in patients with proximal SI disease, whereas SI dysbiosis may result in increased folate
concentrations.

Alpha-1 Protease Inhibitor (PI)
Fecal alpha-1-PI has a molecular weight approximately equal to that of albumin and unlike albumin, is
resistant to proteolysis. Thus, quantification in feces may act as a surrogate marker of intestinal albumin
loss.116 Due to large day-to-day variations in fecal alpha-1-PI levels, measurement is recommended in
fecal samples from 3 consecutive days. Fecal alpha-1-PI concentration is a sensitive diagnostic marker
for excessive intestinal protein loss and it increases before the onset of hypoalbuminemia or the clinical
signs caused by hypoalbuminemia in dogs with GI protein loss.117 This test is rarely necessary for
establishing a diagnosis of PLE, as the exclusion of other differentials for hypoalbuminemia is typically
straightforward (see “Protein-Losing Enteropathy” subsection of “Syndromic Diagnostic Approach to
Patients With Small Intestinal Disease,” below), but it can be helpful in those dogs with severe
hypoalbuminemia that are not manifesting clinical signs suggestive of GI disease.

Specialized Tests—Biochemical

Serum C-reactive Protein (CRP)
Concentration
C-reactive protein (CRP) is a nonspecific, positive acute-phase protein. Serum concentrations may be
increased in dogs with SI disease. Increased serum CRP concentrations may distinguish dogs with
immunosuppressive-responsive enteropathies from those with food- or antibiotic-responsive
enteropathies.118 CRP may also be used to monitor response to treatment.118

Serum and Fecal Calprotectin (S100A08/A9
Protein Complex) and Calgranulin C
(S100A12) Concentrations
Calprotectin and calgranulin are damage-associated molecular patterns, which have predominantly been
evaluated on a research basis in dogs with CE, but have not been widely adopted for clinical use.
Calprotectin is a ligand for TLR-4, whereas calprotectin has several protein targets, including receptor
for advanced glycation end-products.119,120 Increased calprotectin levels have been shown in canine
chronic enteropathies and a canine assay has undergone pre-analytical validation for use in feline
samples, but more studies are needed to determine its value in cats.121,122 Calgranulin levels have also
been shown to be increased in dogs with chronic enteropathies.123 Fecal calprotectin and calgranulin
concentrations are also increased in dogs with acute SI disease, such as AHDS and as such elevations are
not etiology-specific.124 Calprotectin and calgranulin may also be increased in patients with disease
conditions where the GI tract is not the primary organ system affected.125,126 Calprotectin, but not
calgranulin, is affected by glucocorticoid therapy.121 Breed size, recent vaccination, and reproductive
status in female dogs may also impact interpretation of these biomarkers.127

Additional Inflammatory Biomarkers
Several additional biomarkers have been investigated, predominantly in dogs with CE. They include 3bromotyrosine, N-methylhistidine, perinuclear anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies, intestinal
alkaline phosphatase and soluble receptor for advanced glycation end-products. None of these
biomarkers has gained widespread clinical use. Further information on these biomarkers can be found
in a recent review article.123 Findings from a recent study suggest that assaying a panel of antibodies
directed against various antigens (ACA, ACNA, and AGA) would be useful to differentiate among causes
of CE in dogs.128 However, this study only showed that such a panel would be useful to differentiate
dogs with CE from healthy dogs and it should not be used as a means of characterizing the underlying
disease process nor of directing case management.

Specialized Tests—Microbiomics

Dysbiosis Index (Based on Quantitative Real
Time PCR)
The dysbiosis index (DI) is a mathematical algorithm that is comprised of the abundances of 7 key
bacterial groups and the 16S rRNA gene (an estimate of total bacteria) in the feces of dogs (ch. 260). An
elevated DI (>2) is consistent with dysbiosis, while values <0 are consistent with normobiosis.129 The DI
should ideally be interpreted in conjunction with the abundance of the individual taxa. A decrease in C.
hiranonis is commonly seen in dogs with dysbiosis and may result in decreased conversion of primary to
secondary bile acids.130

Additional Diagnostics
Additional methods to assess the microbiome include fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH; see
below and ch. 263), marker gene analysis, and metagenomics (shotgun sequencing). In addition, the
taxonomic classification of the GI microbiome and the effects of the microbiota and its metabolites may

be studied (transcriptomics and metabolomics). However, to date, none of these has been shown to be
clinically useful for the assessment of dogs or cats with SI disease.

Specialized Tests—Miscellaneous

Special Stains of Direct Fecal Smears
Fecal smears may be stained for identification of fat (Sudan stain), undigested starch granules (Lugol’s
iodine) and muscle fibers (Wright’s or Diff Quik stain), the presence of which may indicate
malabsorption due to SI disease.

Fecal Occult Blood
The fecal occult blood test can be used for detecting low-grade intestinal bleeding. This test is highly
sensitive and detects hemoglobin of any origin. Therefore, patients must be fed a meat-free diet for at
least 72 hours prior to collection of the sample to allow for accurate result interpretation.131 Different
diets likely have different effects on the interpretation of fecal occult blood testing in cats.132 Some
studies suggest that the impact of diet is less important for guaiac-based tests than for o-toluidine-based
tests.133

Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D Concentrations
Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25[OH]D) concentrations are low in dogs with CE and may indicate a
negative prognosis.80,134,135 Hypovitaminosis D is likely multifactorial in origin and is more common in
dogs with increased serum inflammatory biomarker concentrations, those with more severe clinical
disease, and those with lower alpha-tocopherol, albumin, or cholesterol concentrations.136 Serum
25(OH)D concentrations are also low in cats with inflammatory enteropathies (also called IBD) and
those with SCL.137 Studies are ongoing to determine whether vitamin D abnormalities are suitable
therapeutic targets in patients with chronic enteropathies. Hypovitaminosis D also is not specific to CE
and has been noted in patients with blastomycosis and severe forms of pancreatitis (ch. 277), which
may mimic CE clinically. Additionally, hypovitaminosis D has been noted in several non-GI disorders
such as mitral valve disease, various neoplasms, kidney disease, and, more generally, in hospitalized
patients.138

Serum Gastrin Concentrations
Serum gastrin concentrations may be evaluated in dogs and cats with GI ulceration to identify the
presence of a suspected gastrinoma (ch. 297).139 Additionally, gastrin concentrations may be measured
as part of the diagnostic approach when immunoproliferative enteropathy of the Basenji is suspected.140
Hypergastrinemia may also occur in several non-intestinal disorders and serum gastrin concentrations
may be affected by concurrent antacid therapy. Both omeprazole and famotidine can lead to dramatic
increases in serum gastrin concentrations in dogs and a 7-day drug withdrawal period is required to
return gastrin concentrations to baseline.141,142

Intestinal Permeability Testing
Intestinal permeability testing has been utilized in the research setting. These tests are based on
measuring non-carrier mediated uptake of selected markers and are considered indicators of intestinal
mucosal integrity. Two probes with different absorption pathways are often utilized to account for errors

related to non-mucosal factors such as gastric emptying rate. The cellobiose to mannitol excretion ratio
and lactulose/mannitol ratio have been used historically, but the lactulose/rhamnose ratio has also been
used. None of these sugar permeability tests is applicable for clinical patients. More recently, iohexol has
been used for permeability testing in dogs, but further studies are needed to evaluate the clinical utility
of this test.143

Immunohistochemistry and Molecular
Clonality Testing
Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and polymerase chain reaction for antigen receptor rearrangements
(PARR) may be used on histopathological samples to help distinguish mixed inflammatory populations
from more uniform neoplastic populations of cells. IHC and PARR are most often used in feline
enteropathies and a stepwise approach of histopathologic evaluation, followed by immunophenotyping
and finally clonality testing is most frequently recommended to distinguish IBD from intestinal
lymphoma.144,145A recent study noted a high frequency of abnormal IHC and PARR results in clinically
healthy cats, suggesting that, as in people, these tests have a limited specificity146; however, these results
may also reflect the inappropriate use of these diagnostic tests in a healthy study population.
Histopathology-guided mass spectrometry is also being investigated as a promising tool to differentiate
inflammatory enteropathies from SCL in cats.147 Other specialized tests that are not routinely utilized in
clinical practice include various genomic, metabolomic, and cellular biomarkers.

Endoscopy (ch. 107)
In acute SI disease, endoscopy allows for identification and removal of foreign bodies and may allow for
the detection of GI ulcerations/erosions, masses/polyps, GI parasites (
lesions. Video capsule endoscopy (

Video 262.2), and other

Video 261.1) can also be used as an alternative to standard

endoscopy for detection of GI lesions and does not require general anesthesia.148,149 Biopsies and
hitulcerations/erosions, masses/polyps, GI parasitessopathologic evaluation are rarely indicated in
patients with acute disease. In contrast, histopathologic assessment of intestinal biopsies is required for
a definitive diagnosis in patients with chronic enteropathies. Biopsy specimens can be collected via
endoscopy (ch. 107), laparoscopy, or surgery. Endoscopic biopsies are generally preferred unless the
region of interest is beyond the reach of the endoscope (i.e., jejunum) or if extraintestinal disease is
suspected to be present. Some clinicians may also prefer surgical biopsies for focal disease. Methods for
obtaining laparoscopic-assisted GI biopsies have been described and appear to have acceptable shortterm complication rates, but significant advantages over other techniques have yet to be
documented.150,151 Chronic inflammatory enteropathies are frequently associated with gross
abnormalities of the mucosa, including increased friability, granularity, and hyperemia (Figure 262.11,
A and B; Videos 262.3, 262.4

). Quantitative endoscopic scoring systems have also been developed

and are frequently used in clinical and research settings (ch. 107).152 Additional lesions may include
erosions/ulceration and evidence of bleeding (Figure 262.11, C), retained food, or mass lesions.
Multifocal white villous tips and milky-white exudation support the diagnosis of IL with a sensitivity of
68% and a specificity of 42% (Figure 262.11, D).153 Feeding of a high-fat meal may allow for increased
detection of mucosal hyperechoic speckling but the difference may not be sufficient to allow for
differentiation of animals with IL from healthy animals.154 The procedure for performing GI endoscopy,
including collection of biopsies,155 is described in detail in ch. 107.

Cytology, Histopathology and Fluorescence In-Situ Hybridization

Cytology
Cytologic evaluation of specimens may be used for identifying various infectious causes of small
intestinal disease in dogs, including Pythium insidiosum (ch. 263), Histoplasma capsulatum (ch.
209), Heterobilharzia americana (see below), and Toxoplasma gondii (chs. 196, 197) amongst others.
While histopathologic examination of biopsies is preferred for identification of intestinal inflammatory
infiltrates, cytologic evaluation of squash preps of intestinal biopsy samples may allow for increased
detection of mast cells and Helicobacter species and thus provide complementary information.156
Impression smears of intestinal biopsies may also aid in the diagnosis of neoplastic masses. Cytology
also plays a pivotal role in the diagnosis of LGL lymphoma in cats.101 Other small intestinal disorders
may be diagnosed cytologically, although the diagnostic utility is limited. Fecal cytologic evaluations can
be used for detecting increased numbers of clostridial spores, yeasts, Cryptosporidium spp., and
Campylobacter spp., which may all be associated with a primary or secondary enteritis.157

Histopathology
The definitive diagnosis of chronic SI disease often depends on histologic examination of intestinal
biopsies, though this is fraught with limitations. Histopathologic samples from animals suspected of
having chronic enteropathies should be evaluated according to the World Small Animal Veterinary
Association (WSAVA) GI Standardization Group criteria. Alternatively, biopsies may be evaluated in
accordance with a recently proposed simplified scoring system that showed improved utility in

correlating histopathologic lesions with clinical activity indices.158 Histopathologic samples are
evaluated for the presence, type, and distribution of inflammatory cell infiltrates in addition to the
presence of morphologic changes, including villous stunting, crypt dilation, lacteal dilation, and others
(Figures 262.12 and 262.13).158 One study noted that in dogs with FRE, ultrastructural lesions of the
mitochondria and brush border improved in conjunction with clinical remission, while changes in
inflammatory infiltrates only changed subtly. These findings suggested that assessment of architectural
changes is at least as important as the assessment of inflammatory infiltrates in dogs with chronic
enteropathies.46 Histopathologic evaluation may be used in conjunction with immunohistochemical
staining and molecular techniques to identify neoplastic lesions. It is important to note that several
causes of chronic SI disease may lack histopathological abnormalities and a normal biopsy does not
preclude further diagnostic investigations (Box 262.6).

Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization
FISH may be utilized to identify mucosally adherent or invasive bacteria on small intestinal biopsy
samples. FISH is frequently used in patients at high risk of mucosal compromise, e.g., patients with
lymphangiectasia, ulceration, or neutrophilic or granulomatous enteritis.159 FISH is used for detection
of specific infectious etiologies, such as Helicobacter spp. (ch. 261).160 FISH can be submitted as an
add-on test for formalin-fixed biopsy samples.

SYNDROMIC DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH TO PATIENTS WITH
SMALL INTESTINAL DISEASE
Acute Enteropathy
Acute enteropathies are characterized by clinical signs that include vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, and loss
of appetite of <14 days’ duration. However, the majority of dogs and cats presented due to acute GI
disturbances will have had a shorter history of clinical signs, as most acute GI disturbances are selflimiting and likely to resolve without significant intervention within 3-7 days. Though many cases of
acute GI distress are mild, some are life-threatening. Therefore, the most important initial step in
evaluating patients with acute GI distress is to determine whether there is concern for systemic
complications.
The distinction between mild, self-limiting disease and more serious or life-threatening disease is
based on clinical history, physical examination findings, and a thorough understanding of the possible
differentials. Patients with mild cases of self-limiting diarrhea often have a normal physical examination
with no evidence of abdominal pain detected. Evidence of mild dehydration may be detected. In such
cases, fecal examination for parasites should be performed (i.e., centrifugal fecal flotation using zinc
sulfate paired with indirect fluorescent antibody [IFA] or antigen testing for Giardia cysts and IFA for
Cryptosporidium oocysts; ch. 80). Importantly, fecal cytologic examinations are not diagnostically
useful in patients with acute enteropathies. In patients with mild signs, measuring PCV and plasma total
protein concentration can give an indication of hydration status and serve as a baseline if the patient
were to be presented again due to persistent or worsening clinical signs. Indicators of potentially lifethreatening systemic complications are shown in Box 262.7. If these signs are present, a more complete
diagnostic work-up should be pursued. If it is not clear whether the patient has mild or moderate to
severe disease, it may be best to err on the side of caution and pursue a diagnostic work-up for
potentially serious or life-threatening disease. Diagnostic tests that should be considered in patients
with evidence of moderate to severe acute enteropathy include CBC, serum biochemistry profile,
urinalysis, serum baseline cortisol (or an adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation test, if necessary; ch.
296) to exclude hypoadrenocorticism, and parvovirus testing (ch. 201), if indicated based on
vaccination status. Fecal culture and PCR testing for detecting specific enteric pathogens can be
unrewarding and misleading as it is often difficult to establish causality between the presence of a
potential enteropathogen in the feces and the clinical signs. Measurement of specific enterotoxins is
similarly unrewarding and generally not going to change case management. Thus, it is recommended to
perform fecal culture and PCR testing for detection of specific organisms only in the rare circumstance
that the pet with diarrhea is systemically ill and in contact with an

immunocompromised/immunosuppressed person. Depending on the clinical presentation, and housing
history, fecal testing for identification of Tritrichomonas foetus and serologic testing for feline leukemia
virus (FeLV, ch. 199) and feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV, ch. 198) may be justified in some cats
with acute diarrhea. Importantly, abdominal radiographs and/or ultrasound should be performed in all
cases of moderate to severe acute enteropathies for evaluation of surgical conditions, including torsion
(i.e., gastric, mesenteric, colonic), intussusception, mechanical obstruction of the SI due to foreign body
or abdominal mass, and/or peritonitis (ch. 265). If clinical signs persist beyond 14 days, but last for
fewer than 21 days, this disease is identified as a subacute enteropathy.

Chronic Enteropathy, Stable
A substantial number of dogs and cats presenting for the evaluation of GI signs lasting 3 or more weeks
will be reported to be stable otherwise. In other words, these patients maintain a normal appetite, body
weight, and energy level despite ongoing diarrhea and/or vomiting. In these patients, the diagnostic
approach may be more measured initially (Figure 262.14). A careful examination of the clinical history
is necessary, first to ensure that more serious or atypical signs are not present that would change the
subsequent recommendations. Following this, routine fecal testing is recommended (ch. 80) to exclude
intestinal parasitism as the cause of clinical signs. Consideration can then be given to the exclusion of
secondary causes of GI signs via a CBC, serum biochemistry profile, urinalysis, and screening for
hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296); however, this may not be necessary in all cases of stable dogs and cats
presenting for evaluation of chronic GI signs. In many cases, non-invasive therapeutic trials, such as
dietary trials (ch. 152), or with medications meant to support or manipulate the enteric microbiota can
be considered in favor of extensive diagnostic work-ups in stable patients with CE (for which intestinal
parasitism +/– systemic disease have been excluded).

Chronic Enteropathy, Clinically Unwell
Dogs presenting for evaluation of chronic GI signs that are experiencing lethargy, weight loss, and
changes in appetite (decrease, increase, or absence of appetite) deserve a more extensive diagnostic
work-up, such that the cause of their clinical signs ideally can be identified and subsequently addressed
rapidly (Figure 262.14). In such cases, baseline testing for exclusion of intestinal parasitism and
secondary causes of GI signs remains imperative, but if those tests fail to elucidate an obvious cause for
the patient’s presenting signs, a more thorough diagnostic work-up is necessary. Next steps to be
considered in the clinically unwell patient with CE include screening for hypoadrenocorticism (ch.
296); diagnostic imaging (e.g., abdominal radiographs, abdominal ultrasound, thoracic radiographs);
measurement of serum cobalamin, folate, pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity (PLI) activity, and trypsinlike immunoreactivity (TLI); and specific testing for miscellaneous infectious agents that may be
suspected based on signalment, history, comorbid conditions, and geographic location (ch. 9). Which
tests are selected and the order in which they are pursued will depend on the case and the rank-order of
the various differentials. If results of these tests fail to determine a specific cause and thus the diagnosis
is considered idiopathic CE, collection of intestinal biopsies with histopathologic evaluation can be
considered as a next step (ch. 107). However, in certain cases, this may be postponed in favor of
therapeutic trials. Therapeutic trials including dietary trials (ch. 152) and trials with medications aimed
to support or manipulate the enteric microbiota (ch. 260) may be successful even in clinically unwell
dogs. However, discretion will have to be applied as to the patient’s ability to accept and tolerate these
trials, and the potential need for more intensive therapy. Additionally, in clinically unwell patients a lack
of response to therapeutic trials within 2 weeks, or progression of clinical signs during the trial period
should prompt a more proactive approach rather than continued or additional therapeutic trials. If it is
determined that the patient will likely need anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive medications to
control the underlying disease, intestinal biopsy with histopathologic evaluation should be considered
prior to institution of these therapies to definitively exclude infection and neoplastic causes of chronic GI
signs. In clinical scenarios where intestinal biopsies cannot be performed, the clinician should consider
whether they have done everything possible to exclude underlying diseases in which treatment with
immunosuppressive therapy could cause harm (e.g., Histoplasma urine antigen testing in endemic
regions, ch. 209).

Protein-Losing Enteropathy
In approximately 5-10% of cases of PLE, patients will present with little to no history of GI signs;
patients may even have no clinical signs in some cases.161 More commonly, patients with PLE present
with a history of chronic, relapsing or progressive GI signs +/– clinical signs associated with
hypoalbuminemia. In all cases of suspected PLE, the first step in the diagnostic work-up involves the
exclusion of other causes of hypoalbuminemia. While panhypoproteinemia is highly supportive of the
diagnosis of PLE, dogs with PLE can be hypo-, normo-, or hyperglobulinemic. Thus, a urinalysis +/–
urine protein to creatinine ratio should be performed to rule out significant renal protein loss (chs. 70,
302). Pre- and post-prandial serum bile acid concentrations can be used for assessing hepatic function
(ch. 267). Additionally, hypoalbuminemia can occur due to third spacing of serum proteins in the
setting of vasculitis (ch. 181), pleuritis (ch. 220), or peritonitis (ch. 265), so diseases that can result in

those conditions should be considered on a case-by-case basis. Hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296) can
result in hypoproteinemia and therefore should be ruled out prior to procuring intestinal biopsies.162
Rarely, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) can result in hypoalbuminemia, particularly if the disease
has been longstanding and severe malnourishment has occurred. EPI can be excluded with a normal
fasted serum canine TLI test (ch. 279). Measurement of cobalamin and folate should be performed
concurrently to screen for deficiencies and evaluate for markers of malabsorption. Measurement of fecal
concentrations of alpha1-proteinase inhibitor, a test that can help to estimate GI albumin loss, is rarely
necessary. This test is probably most useful in patients that have concurrent renal protein loss or hepatic
dysfunction or in patients with no clinical signs of GI disease.
Once it has been established that intestinal disease is responsible for the protein loss, the goal of the
diagnostic work-up shifts to determining the underlying cause of the enteropathy. In the majority of
these cases, it is recommended that the work-up be continued until a definitive diagnosis is reached,
particularly because hypoalbuminemia is considered a negative prognostic indicator in patients with GI
disease.75 However, reports have revealed that some dogs with PLE will respond to dietary manipulation
alone. Therefore, in select cases, a dietary trial may be considered before pursuing further work-up. One
study found that dogs responding to dietary management alone had lower canine chronic enteropathy
clinical activity index (CCECAI) scores when compared to dogs that needed additional therapy.58 Thus,
clinically unwell dogs with PLE, particularly those with a poor appetite, should likely receive a complete
diagnostic work-up at the outset in order to definitively characterize their disease and maximize their
chances of response to therapy. The remaining diagnostic work-up recommended includes fecal testing
(and often broad-spectrum anthelmintic treatment [ch. 142]); routine imaging, including thoracic
radiographs, abdominal ultrasound (+/– ultrasound-guided fine needle aspirates and cytologic
analysis), +/– abdominal radiographs; screening tests for infectious diseases of interest and relevance;
specific testing for deficiencies in ionized calcium, ionized magnesium, and 25(OH)D; and ultimately,
intestinal biopsy. A definitive diagnosis of PLE ultimately depends on intestinal biopsy with
histopathologic evaluation. The choice of flexible endoscopy for collection of intestinal biopsies offers
the advantage of direct visualization of the intestinal mucosa and allows for collection of samples less
invasively and with a shortened recovery period when compared to laparotomy. Surgical biopsies may be
performed and they offer the advantage of being able to sample all sections of the intestines; however,
due to increased risk associated with surgery, endoscopy is considered the preferred method of sample
collection in patients with PLE. Collection of both duodenal and ileal samples is strongly recommended,
as disease lesions can differ between sections of the intestine.163 Common histopathologic findings in
dogs with PLE include IL, mucosal edema, various types and degrees of inflammatory infiltrates, and
dilated, cystic crypts. IL has been detected in the villus, proprial mucosa and submucosa in endoscopic
intestinal biopsies164; therefore, it is important that pathologists evaluate for lymphangiectasia in each
of these areas. If concern for bacterial adherence/invasion arises during biopsy evaluation, FISH can be
considered to evaluate for bacteria within formalin-fixed tissue.

TREATMENT PRINCIPLES AND APPLICATIONS
GENERAL TREATMENT OF NON-SPECIFIC ACUTE DIARRHEA
There are many different etiologies of acute diarrhea in dogs and cats, including dietary, infectious, and
extraintestinal etiologies (Box 262.8). In animals that are bright, alert, responsive, and well hydrated, a
thorough diagnostic investigation is often not pursued, in favor of supportive, empirical therapy. Further
diagnostic tests are often only pursued in animals that are dull, hemodynamically unstable, or have an
obvious abnormality on physical examination such as evidence of abdominal pain, a palpable abdominal
mass, or intestinal thickening or plication.
