Fluid Therapy (ch. 120)
Oral or subcutaneous fluid and electrolyte therapy may be effective for the management of mild
dehydration. However, when diarrhea is associated with significant dehydration or ongoing losses,
parenteral fluid therapy is indicated.165 The intravenous route is preferred but the intraosseous route
may be used when venous access cannot be obtained (ch. 76).

Dietary Manipulation (ch. 152)
Dietary recommendations for acute diarrhea are based on anecdotal reports, scientific theory, and
extrapolation of data from other species, with fewer studies occurring in dogs and cats. Traditionally, a
period of food withdrawal followed by slow reintroduction of a bland diet was recommended for
management of acute diarrhea; however, this theory has been challenged and is no longer routinely
utilized. Food withdrawal is now only considered in cases of severe vomiting that cannot be controlled
by antiemetic therapy.166 This change in recommendation is based on the potential detrimental effects
of food withdrawal on the GI tract, even for a short period of time. These changes include morphological
alterations, such as a decreased villous height, decreased gut barrier function, increased risk of bacterial
translocation, and reduced activity of intestinal disaccharidase enzymes.167-171 Additionally, a lack of
luminal nutrients is associated with a pro-inflammatory state characterized by increased expression of
ICAM-1 and decreased expression of various anti-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-4 and
interleukin-10, which may perpetuate GI injury.172,173 Glutamine and arginine deficiencies secondary to
food withdrawal may also result in detrimental effects.174 Thus, enteral nutrition is encouraged in cases
of acute diarrhea.
Feeding through the GI tract via small frequent meals is physiologic and is safe for most patients.175
Early enteral nutrition has been shown to be well tolerated and to result in earlier clinical improvement
and weight gain in dogs with parvoviral enteritis.170 Early enteral nutrition has also been shown to be
well tolerated and beneficial in pancreatitis and septic peritonitis.176-180 For dogs with acute nonspecific
diarrhea, a highly digestible, low-fat diet with fermentable fiber is commonly recommended (ch.

152).180 It is suspected that management of acute enteritis in cats is less dependent on dietary fat
control than in dogs, and the diets of cats with acute enteritis should not be overly fat-restricted.181
Indeed, in 1 study, a highly digestible high-fat diet had a similar efficacy to a highly digestible low-fat
diet in the management of diarrhea in cats.182

Gastrointestinal Protectants
GI protectants are frequently prescribed in the management of SI disease, including nonspecific acute
diarrhea. GI protectants include antacids, histamine type-2 receptor antagonists (H2RAs), proton pump
inhibitors (PPIs), misoprostol, and coating agents such as sucralfate and barium. Antacids (e.g., calcium
carbonate) are not recommended as they only provide short-term, partial neutralization of gastric
acid.183 Oral H2RAs are considered inferior to PPIs in the management of gastric acid secretion.184,185
Esomeprazole appears to be the most efficacious.186,187 Long-acting intramuscular omeprazole
formulations are available and may be an area of future study for use in dogs.188 Although H2RAs are
considered inferior to PPIs, when administered as a continuous rate infusion (famotidine, 1 mg/kg
loading dose followed by 8 mg/kg/day constant rate infusion [CRI]), H2RAs can achieve therapeutic
targets for gastric acid suppression in dogs.189 Famotidine CRIs also achieve gastric acid suppression
more rapidly than pantoprazole during the first 72 hours of therapy, and this should be considered when
rapid achievement of gastric acid neutralization is required.186 Intravenous administration of
famotidine has been anecdotally associated with Heinz body anemia in cats, although results of a
retrospective study revealed no evidence of hemolysis.190 Misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin E1
analogue that may be suitable for prevention of aspirin-induced GI lesions but is otherwise inferior to
PPIs and H2RAs in the management of GI ulceration and erosion.183,191 Based on data in humans,
judicious use of gastroprotectants is indicated, as they may be associated with intestinal dysbiosis, which
could lead to other complications, such as bacterial pneumonia or increased risk of nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug (NSAID)-induced epithelial injury.183,191-194 Additional data in dogs suggest that
PPIs such as omeprazole fail to protect against, and may exacerbate, epithelial injury in animals
receiving NSAIDs.195 Results of survey data suggest that GI protectants are overused at this time, and
their use should be limited to animals with GI ulceration and erosion, hepatic disease (weak evidence),
stress-related mucosal disease, and esophagitis. There is no evidence to support the use of
gastroprotectants in patients with non-erosive gastritis.183,196

Manipulation of the Gastrointestinal
Microbiota
Dietary Factors
The diet can have a marked effect on the composition of the microbiota in dogs and cats, with changes in
fat, protein, carbohydrate, and fiber all contributing to changes of the microbial populations in the GI
tract (ch. 260).

Prebiotics/Probiotics/Synbiotics
Prebiotics are products that benefit the host by promoting the growth and/or the activity of selected
bacteria in the GI tract (ch. 260). Probiotics are live microorganisms that, when administered in a
sufficient quantity, confer a health benefit to the host. Synbiotic products are a combination of

prebiotics and probiotics.197 A recent systematic review suggested that probiotics have a limited efficacy
in the prevention or treatment of acute GI disease, and did not significantly improve treatment efficacy
beyond dietary therapy in chronic GI disease in dogs.198 Despite this, individual studies have
documented beneficial effects of prebiotics, probiotics, and synbiotics. A recent randomized doubleblinded placebo-controlled clinical trial revealed that dogs achieved an acceptable fecal consistency
faster with probiotic treatment than with metronidazole or placebo treatment.199 A second study
revealed that the efficacy of nutraceuticals was similar to that of antimicrobials in the management of
acute non-hemorrhagic diarrhea.200 Probiotic treatment may also be beneficial in the management of
AHDS.201 Another study suggested that a probiotic antidiarrheal product may also accelerate resolution
of acute diarrhea in dogs and reduce the requirement for additional medical intervention.202 While data
are contradictory at this time, select probiotics may play a role in the management of acute diarrhea and
it is likely that they should be prioritized over the indiscriminate use of antimicrobials.

Antimicrobial Therapy
Antimicrobial therapy is no longer recommended in the routine management of dogs and cats with acute
gastroenteritis.203 Antibiotics are only recommended in cases with a confirmed bacterial or protozoal
infection, or in cases with suspected bacterial translocation, as in animals with leukopenia, neutrophilia
with left shift, fever, or shock, for example.203 Antibiotic therapy is frequently considered in cases of
AHDS. However, 1 study comparing the efficacy of amoxicillin clavulanic acid versus a placebo found no
significant difference in outcome, suggesting that antibiotics may not be required in dogs with AHDS in
the absence of sepsis.204 Similar findings have been noted separately with uncomplicated acute diarrhea
in dogs.205 Additionally, unnecessary antibiotic use was associated with an increase in resistant E. coli
species that persisted after treatment.205 In another study, the addition of metronidazole did not show
any superior effect over amoxicillin-clavulanic acid alone in the management of AHDS.206 In yet
another study, probiotics were shown to resolve acute diarrhea more rapidly than metronidazole
therapy.199 Antibiotic therapy may also be associated with prolonged intestinal dysbiosis (chs. 106,
260).207-209 Given the potential adverse effects of indiscriminate antimicrobial use, particularly
regarding the development of dysbiosis and antimicrobial resistance (ch. 7), they should only be
prescribed in cases with a definitive indication. Despite these concerns, metronidazole therapy has been
shown to shorten the duration of diarrhea in dogs with acute nonspecific diarrhea and is still being
utilized by some clinicians.210 Also, tylosin has been shown to be efficacious in dogs with otherwise
treatment-resistant chronic diarrhea,211 but as with metronidazole, tylosin is associated with prolonged
dysbiosis regardless of amelioration of clinical signs.208

Fecal Microbiota Transplantation (ch. 106)
Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is the transfer of feces from a healthy donor to the GI tract of a
diseased recipient, with the goal of modulating the recipient’s microbiota.212 The optimal route of
delivery is unknown, but FMT is most often achieved via enema, although alternative delivery methods,
including oral capsules and endoscopy, have all been used. FMT has been documented to result in
shorter hospitalization times and faster resolution of diarrhea in dogs with parvovirosis.213 Additionally,
FMT has been shown to result in better stool consistency and fewer alterations in the microbiome than
metronidazole therapy in dogs with acute uncomplicated diarrhea.130 FMT may also be beneficial in
dogs with chronic enteropathies and/or chronic diarrhea.214-216 Data regarding the efficacy of FMT in
cats with small intestinal disease are limited.217.

Motility and Secretion-Modifying Agents
Opioids
Opioids may be used as antidiarrheals, as they increase segmental intestinal contractions and slow GI
transit time. Potential agents include diphenoxylate and loperamide. Loperamide is a substrate drug for
the ABCB1 (MDR-1) transporter and as such, caution is indicated when treating dogs of breeds affected
by mutations of the ABCB1 transporter gene, such as Longhaired Whippets, Collies, and Australian
Shepherds, amongst others.218

Antispasmodics
While the use of antimuscarinic agents such as butylscopolamine has been suggested for the
management of acute diarrhea, they are generally not recommended. They can result in a paralyzed,
non-functional SI, which may predispose to intussusception.

Cholestyramine
Cholestyramine can be used for binding primary bile acids and thus can reduce bile acid-induced
intestinal secretions. Cholestyramine may be beneficial in animals with dysbiosis or ileal resection, and
may also be beneficial in dogs with refractory diarrhea.219

SMALL INTESTINAL DISEASES
ACUTE HEMORRHAGIC DIARRHEA SYNDROME
AHDS, formerly referred to as hemorrhagic gastroenteritis (HGE), is defined as a sudden onset of severe
hemorrhagic diarrhea with significant loss of fluid into the intestinal lumen, frequently associated with
vomiting.220 AHDS is the preferred terminology as HGE implies gastric involvement and a recent study
noted lesions only within the intestine.221 Clostridium perfringens overgrowth and toxin production is
suspected to be associated with the clinical syndrome of AHDS, and a positive fecal PCR for C.
perfringens type A strains is suggestive, but not confirmatory, of a diagnosis of AHDS.222 The role of
other bacterial species, such as Providencia alcalifaciens, in AHDS is currently undergoing further
study. A CBC, serum biochemistry profile, fecal flotation (ch. 80), and potentially a baseline serum
cortisol concentration (ch. 296), are likely also indicated in dogs presenting with acute hemorrhagic
diarrhea to rule out alternative diagnoses. Additional tests may be indicated depending on the patient’s
problem list. Treatment of AHDS is supportive, with intravenous fluid therapy given at rapid rates (if
tolerated) until the PCV is in the mid-normal range (ch. 120).220 Dogs with uncomplicated AHDS
typically show rapid improvement, i.e., within 24-48 hours. Antibiotics should be restricted to patients
with signs of severe systemic complications, evidence of systemic inflammation, those that are
neutropenic or otherwise immunosuppressed, or have a high probability of ineffective clearance of
bacteria from the liver (e.g., portosystemic shunt or liver dysfunction). Additional supportive care, such
as antiemetics, probiotics, sucralfate (for secondary esophageal injury), and analgesics, are often
prescribed. Buprenorphine (ch. 6) may lead to less gastric motility suppression than other analgesics
and may be preferred in the management of AHDS.220 Enteral nutrition is encouraged and may
improve intestinal barrier function (chs. 81, 151, 164). Some clinicians utilize hydrolyzed diets (ch.
152) to minimize development of hypersensitivity, although this theory is unproven. FMT is also being
investigated in the management of AHDS (ch. 106).223

INFECTIOUS ETIOLOGIES OF ACUTE AND CHRONIC
DIARRHEA IN DOGS AND CATS (TABLE 49.2)
Viral Infections
There are several common viruses that can result in enteritis, including canine and feline parvovirus
(ch. 201), canine and feline coronavirus (ch. 200), canine distemper virus (ch. 204), FeLV (ch. 199),
and FIV (ch. 198). Several additional viral agents have been reported in association with enteritis in
case reports or case series and further study is needed to determine the clinical significance of these
agents.

Bacterial Infections
Bacterial infections are considered uncommon causes of SI disease in dogs and cats.224 Campylobacter
spp., Salmonella spp., and certain E.coli strains may be pathogenic in dogs and cats, but may also be
isolated from healthy animals, making a causative association challenging to prove in individual
patients. These and other bacterial enteritides are discussed in ch. 195. Adherent-invasive E. coli
(AIEC) is described further in ch. 263.

Other Bacterial Agents
Rickettsial organisms, such as Neorickettsia helminthoeca (ch. 193) may cause acute SI disease as part
of a systemic illness. Yersinia spp. may cause an acute enteritis in cats and dogs (ch. 195).
Mycobacterium spp. may cause multisystemic disease in cats that involves the SI (ch. 188).
Mycobacterium avium has been reported to cause granulomatous enterocolitis; Bassett Hounds and
Miniature Schnauzers may be predisposed. Hereditary immunodeficiencies may play a role in the
reported breed predispositions (ch. 180).225

Helminth Infections
Helminth infections that can cause SI disease are summarized in Table 262.3.

Canine Schistosomiasis
Heterobilharzia americana is a trematode parasite that is the causative agent of canine schistosomiasis.
The majority of cases in the United States are from Texas and Louisiana, but it has been reported in dogs
from North Carolina and Florida, and as far north as Indiana.226 Dogs are exposed when wading or
swimming in freshwater and cercariae from infected snails penetrate their skin. The schistosomes
migrate first to the lungs, then to the liver where they mature, developing into flukes. The adults then
migrate to the mesenteric veins, where they mate and deposit eggs. These eggs migrate into the
intestinal wall, causing a granulomatous reaction and subsequent malabsorption and diarrhea. Eggs are
then shed within the feces.

Various Taenia spp. have also been reported to cause systemic disease that may have small intestinal
involvement.
Dogs with schistosomiasis typically present with signs of lethargy, anorexia, weight loss, and diarrhea
with or without hematochezia. Common laboratory abnormalities include azotemia, anemia,
hypoalbuminemia, hyperglobulinemia, and hypercalcemia. The diagnosis typically is made by
histopathologic evaluation of intestinal biopsies, identification of ova on fecal saline sedimentation
evaluation, or fecal PCR. Fecal PCR appears to be more sensitive than fecal sedimentation.227
Infection with Heterobilharzia has been treated with various high dosages of praziquantel (25 mg/kg
PO q8h for 2 days; use praziquantel for human use) in conjunction with fenbendazole (50 mg/kg PO
q24h for 10 days; repeat in 3 weeks). Treatment has resulted in complete resolution in some dogs, but
may be ineffective in others.81
∗∗

Protozoal Infections
Protozoa associated with enteritis, such as Isospora spp., Cryptosporidium spp., and Giardia spp., are
covered in chs. 196 and 263. Other protozoal infectious agents, such as Sarcocystis spp., Toxoplasma
gondii, and Neospora caninum complete the sexual phase of their life cycle in the intestinal tract of dogs
and cats, but clinical disease associated with these organisms is largely due to the tissue phase of the
disease (ch. 197).

Fungal and Algal Infections

Pythiosis
Pythium insidiosum is an oomycete that can result in GI disease (ch. 263). Infection may also cause
ulcerative nodular skin lesions. Infections are usually diagnosed in tropical, subtropical and some
temperate regions worldwide, with increased prevalence in the Gulf coast region of the United
States.228,229 Young adult dogs are most commonly affected, with Labrador Retrievers being
overrepresented. Infections are rare in cats. Patients with the GI form typically present with a chronic
history of vomiting, weight loss, or diarrhea, although acute presentations of vomiting may occur with
pyloric outflow obstruction.
The diagnosis is made cytologically, histopathologically, and/or using PCR or ELISA
assays.230 Pythium does not grow well in routine fungal culture. Surgical treatment is ideal, but lesion
location and extent of disease often make complete surgical excision impossible. Therefore, medical
therapy is often necessary following surgery. The prognosis typically has been considered to be poor,
with reports of most dogs dying within 2-3 months of the onset of clinical signs.231,232 However, a
recent study described successful outcomes in dogs treated with a combination of itraconazole,
terbinafine, and mefenoxam, with a survival time of up to 443 days reported.233 Importantly, in the
United States, mefenoxam is not regulated by the Food and Drug Administration, but is rather an
Environmental Protection Agency-regulated fungicide. Extralabel use under Animal Medicinal Drug Use
Clarification Act does not apply. This is similar to products like enilconazole. Thus, prior to its use in a
clinical patient, obtaining informed owner consent is recommended. In cases of colonic pythiosis, an
alternative protocol of prednisone, itraconazole, and terbinafine may be considered.234

FIGURE 262.15 Intramacrophagic Histoplasma capsulatum organisms
(yeast form; arrow) detected cytologically on a specimen obtained via rectal

Protothecosis
Prototheca spp. are algal organisms that may cause SI disease, although large intestinal involvement is
much more common (ch. 263).

Systemic Mycoses
Several fungal organisms may also cause clinical signs of small intestinal disease, including aspergillosis
(ch. 211), cryptococcosis (ch. 207), histoplasmosis (ch. 209), and other miscellaneous fungal
organisms. Importantly, intestinal histoplasmosis may result in hypoalbuminemia; therefore, it should
be considered a differential diagnosis in dogs with PLE who live in or have travelled to an endemic
region.159 Histoplasmosis is known to affect both the small and large intestine. Thus, in these cases,
rectal scraping with cytologic examination should be performed (Figure 262.15). Additional
diagnostics to be considered in dogs with possible histoplasmosis include thoracic radiographs,
evaluation of the fundus (ch. 13), and Histoplasma urine antigen enzyme immunoassay testing.

Candidiasis

Candida spp. may be an opportunistic invader of the GI tract. Intestinal infection is rare but may occur
as a complication of parvoviral enteritis. The diagnosis is typically made cytologically or via culture.
Nystatin can be used for treatment if the infection is limited to the GI tract.

CHRONIC ENTEROPATHIES IN DOGS
Chronic enteropathies are a group of disorders characterized by the presence of GI signs of >3 weeks’
duration. Use of the term CE implies that other causes of GI signs, including infectious, neoplastic, and
extraintestinal disorders, have been ruled out or are considered unlikely.55 Clinically, CE is often further
classified into subgroups according to response to therapy as food-responsive enteropathy (FRE) or
steroid- or immunosuppressant-responsive enteropathy (SRE/IRE). Historically another classification
of CE known as antibiotic-responsive enteropathy (ARE) describes dogs that have long-lasting
resolution of clinical signs following the institution of antibiotic therapy; however, this classification has
recently been scrutinized.61 In 1 study of 203 dogs with CE, 62% were classified with FRE, 19.2% with
SRE/IRE, and 16.2% with ARE.235 When intestinal inflammation has been documented histologically in
a dog with CE, the term chronic inflammatory enteropathy (CIE) can be applied. Histopathologic
findings do not appear to differ between the subgroups.236,237
While IBD has often been used synonymously with the term chronic enteropathy, if the term IBD is to
be used it should be restricted to a very small subsegment of cases that meet strict criteria. According to
recent guidelines, a clinical diagnosis of IBD requires: 1) chronic (>3 weeks’ duration) GI signs, 2)
histopathologic evidence of mucosal inflammation, 3) inability to document other causes of
gastroenterocolitis by thorough diagnostic evaluation, 4) inadequate response to appropriately designed
and implemented therapeutic trials (i.e., dietary, antibacterial, anthelmintic), and 5) clinical response to
anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive agents. Additionally, a diagnosis of IBD cannot be made in
the absence of these criteria based on histologic findings alone.237 Given that these strict criteria are met
in very few patients, the broader terms CE and CIE are preferred.

Etiology and Pathophysiology

Food-Responsive Enteropathy
Dogs with CE responding to dietary changes may be experiencing improvement or resolution of an
adverse food reaction (ch. 166). Adverse food reactions include food intolerance or food
hypersensitivity, although clinical differentiation of these disorders can be challenging.
Food intolerance refers to any abnormal physiologic response to food that is non-immunological in
nature.238 Potential causes include food toxicosis/poisoning, which may be related to food spoilage,
microbial contamination, nutrient excess, or the presence of a known toxic principle. Pharmacological
reactions (e.g., histamine release), metabolic reactions (e.g., carbohydrate malabsorption), dysmotility,
or physical properties of the food may also cause food intolerance. Diet-induced dysbiosis may also be a
cause or consequence of food intolerance. The diagnosis is based on clinical suspicion followed by
resolution of clinical signs with dietary alteration, and possibly documentation of contamination if a
toxic exposure is suspected.
Food allergies are defined as an immune-mediated reaction to dietary components, most commonly
the protein source (ch. 166). Mechanisms that may contribute to food allergy include inadequate
mucosal barrier function, an abnormal intestinal microbiome, abnormal dietary antigen presentation to
the immune system, and immune dysregulation. Food allergies typically affect young animals.239
Clinical signs of food allergy include non-seasonal pruritus and associated alopecia or excoriations (ch.
160).240 The most common locations of pruritic lesions include the ears, paws, and inguinal regions.241
GI clinical signs include signs of abdominal discomfort, vomiting, diarrhea, and weight loss. A summary
of possible clinical manifestations of food allergy is provided in Box 262.9. The gold standard for the
diagnosis of food allergies is resolution of clinical signs when fed an elimination diet, followed by
recurrence of clinical signs with repeat exposure; the latter is not commonly performed in clinical
practice. Food trials with elimination diets are described further in ch. 152. The optimal duration of a
food trial for resolution of GI clinical signs is unknown. Three- to 6-week trials are reported anecdotally
for GI manifestations although elimination diet trials for cutaneous adverse food reactions are advised

to be at least 8 weeks in duration.242 Some animals experience improvement in GI signs in response to a
food trial within 1-2 weeks. Several additional diagnostic methods have been investigated including
intradermal skin testing, skin patch testing, and measurement of serum IgE and IgG concentrations, but
these appear to have limited diagnostic value. It is important to note that response to dietary
manipulation is not exclusive to food allergies and many other processes can respond to a dietary trial
(Box 262.10).

Antibiotic-Responsive
Enteropathy/Intestinal Dysbiosis
ARE historically has been recognized as 1 form of CE. It is associated with intestinal dysbiosis and is
known for responding well to administration of antibiotics, and recurring when they are withdrawn.61
Oxytetracycline, metronidazole, and tylosin have been used most often for treatment of this
disorder.60,243
Dysbiosis can be defined as an alteration in the composition and/or richness of the intestinal
microbiota (ch. 160).244 Developments in molecular techniques have allowed for substantial advances
in this field over the last several years, and it is now well recognized that distinct changes in the
intestinal microbiome occur in both acute and chronic GI disease as well as in extraintestinal
disorders.245 Given that 1 possible theory for the development of inflammation in CE is related to
alterations in the microbiome, management of dysbiosis is considered a potential therapeutic target in
patients with chronic enteropathies. While dysbiosis is considered in many GI and extra-GI disorders,
one might prioritize dysbiosis as a primary differential diagnosis in patients that have recently received
antibiotics or those that received antibiotics as juveniles. Additionally, dysbiosis should be considered as
a possible primary etiology of chronic SI disease in young large-breed dogs, particularly in German
Shepherd Dogs.59 A tylosin-responsive enteropathy that may suggest dysbiosis has also been reported in
laboratory Beagles.243 Dogs with primary SI dysbiosis present with signs that are similar to those of
dogs with other CEs, including chronic or recurrent diarrhea, maldigestion/malabsorption, and weight
loss. Causes of secondary dysbiosis are listed in Box 262.11. Systemic disorders and other causes of
malabsorption (e.g., EPI [ch. 279]) should be ruled out before making a presumptive diagnosis of
primary SI dysbiosis.

Steroid- or Immunosuppressive-Responsive
Enteropathy (SRE/IRE)/Idiopathic Chronic
Enteropathy
The etiology of SRE/IRE/idiopathic inflammatory enteropathy has not been fully elucidated, but it likely
involves genetic, environmental, and microbial factors and their interaction with the immune system.
Additionally, disruption of mucosal barrier function, disturbances of the microbiome, and
polymorphisms of TLRs have all been reported in patients with chronic enteropathies. A comprehensive
review of the etiology of inflammatory enteropathies is available in review articles.246,247

Diagnosis and Management
Diagnosis of a CE requires a thorough diagnostic work up to eliminate extraintestinal causes of the
reported clinical signs as well as specific etiological causes of chronic intestinal inflammation. Readers
are referred to the section of the chapter entitled “Diagnostic Evaluation of Small Intestinal Disease” to
review information regarding the laboratory and imaging features of SI disease. Measurement of serum
TLI concentration should be considered in any patient with clinical signs of SI disease that shows weight
loss when an alternate differential diagnosis is not immediately apparent (ch. 279). Based on a recent
study showing that some dogs with hypoadrenocorticism might not have any evidence of it on a
minimum database, a baseline cortisol concentration should be measured in any patient with clinical
signs of SI disease when an alternate differential diagnosis is not immediately apparent (ch. 296).248 If
a cause for the reported clinical signs is not detected using these diagnostics and fecal examination is
negative, then sequential therapeutic trials are often pursued.
Dietary trials are often the first therapeutic trial recommended due to the high prevalence of FREs, in
addition to the possibility of long-term control of clinical signs with dietary therapy (ch. 152).58,235
Principles of dietary trials for dogs with CE include improving nutrient absorption, reduction or
restriction of exposure to antigens suspected to evoke sensitivity, and improving appetite. Multiple
dietary trials may be required, utilizing different dietary strategies. In a prospective clinical trial, 39/65
(60%) dogs with chronic diarrhea responded to a salmon and rice diet fed for 10 days.249 In a
retrospective examination of 203 cases of CE, 64% of cases were found to have FRE. Among the dogs
with FRE, elimination/novel diets (i.e., a diet with both a novel protein and a novel carbohydrate
source), hydrolyzed protein diets (i.e., diets with proteins broken down into peptides to reduce antigenic
reaction), and home-cooked diets were utilized. This study found no difference in clinical responses to
the different diets.235 In some cases, an easily digestible diet is used rather than an exclusion diet. One
positively controlled field trial compared the use of a hydrolyzed protein diet to a non-exclusion, easily
digestible diet in dogs with chronic SI enteropathies and a serum albumin >2.0 g/dL (>20 g/L). Both
groups of dogs had a good initial response to their diets; however, after a 3-year period, only 1 of 6 dogs
eating the non-exclusion diet was still in clinical remission, versus 13 of 14 dogs eating the hydrolysate
diet.250 In a recently published study, use of a single source egg protein-based food was successful in
dogs with CE.251
Diet can also result in clinical remission in refractory chronic enteropathies, in particular in dogs with
PLE.252,253 Home-cooked diets formulated by a veterinary nutritionist may offer several benefits to a
patient with CE and should thus be considered in select cases. Several conditions can improve clinically
in response to dietary manipulation (Box 262.10). Additional information regarding dietary therapies
for SI disease can be found in ch. 152. Finally, broad-spectrum anthelmintic trials are often prescribed
at the initiation of dietary trials to treat any occult parasitic infection (ch. 142).
The next therapeutic strategy should consider the possibility of dysbiosis in the patient. Considering
the effects of antibacterials on the GI microbiota and concerns for antibacterial resistance (ch. 7), there
is a growing need and interest in finding alternative treatments to modulate the intestinal microbiota.
Several therapeutic strategies have evolved to manipulate the microbiome including the use of FMT (ch.
106) and administrations of prebiotics, probiotics, or synbiotics. Large-scale studies on the use of FMT
in dogs are lacking. Probiotics have been demonstrated to be beneficial in some dogs with CE, but this

response is far less than consistent and at the current time it is not possible to identify patients that are
most likely to respond.254,255
Often the next step involves intestinal biopsy prior to an anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive
trial. Biopsies are typically reserved for patients that have a high clinical disease activity index, those
with hypoalbuminemia, those that fail to respond to initial therapeutic trials (i.e., anthelmintic, dietary,
+/– therapies to target dysbiosis) or those in which there is a strong clinical suspicion for an infectious
or neoplastic etiology. The purpose of the biopsy is to confirm the presence of inflammation in addition
to identifying alternative etiologies such as fungal disease, neoplasia, or lymphangiectasia. Biopsies also
typically identify morphologic changes of the SI mucosa. The most common histopathologic diagnosis is
lymphoplasmacytic enteritis, but when neutrophilic or granulomatous—and to a lesser degree
eosinophilic—inflammation is identified, an infectious etiology should be considered.256 Granulomatous
enteritis is associated with attaching and invasive E. coli, although this typically presents with clinical
signs of large intestinal disease. Other infectious etiologies that should be considered in neutrophilic or
granulomatous enteritis include Salmonella (ch. 195), Streptococcus, Yersinia (ch. 195), mycobacteria
(ch. 188), Histoplasma (ch. 209), or Prototheca (ch. 263).256,257 Additional diagnostic tests for such
cases may include special stains (e.g., Grocott-Gomori’s methenamine silver), culture of mucosal
biopsies, PCR assays, and FISH. Eosinophilic enteritis should prompt consideration of food allergy,
parasites, or selected infectious etiologies, such as Pythium insidiosum.233 For cases in which infectious
and neoplastic etiologies are considered unlikely, and when the collection of a biopsy is not possible due
to financial or other concerns, an immunosuppressive trial may be considered with informed owner
consent. Glucocorticoids should be utilized for anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive trials and are
likely suitable as a single agent for the management of CEs and PLEs (ch. 144). Addition of a second
immunosuppressant agent may be required in refractory cases (ch. 169).258 Some studies have shown
that select multi-strain probiotics are beneficial in the resolution of dysbiosis and inflammatory cell
infiltrates, in addition to upregulation of tight junction proteins in patients with chronic
enteropathies.254,255 Given variations in study results, probiotic formulations, and the heterogeneity of
canine chronic enteropathies, more studies are needed to draw conclusions on the use of probiotics in
dogs with chronic enteropathies.259 Dogs with hypocobalaminemia should receive oral (250 mcg if <8
kg, 500 mcg if 8-16 kg, or 1000 mcg if >16 kg, daily, for 12 weeks) or parenteral (250 mcg if <4.5 kg, 400
mcg if 4.5-9 kg, 600 mcg if 9-18 kg, 800 mcg if 18-27 kg, 1000 mcg if 27-36 kg, 1200 mcg if 36-45 kg,
1500 mcg if >45 kg, SC once weekly for 6 weeks) cobalamin supplementation. Vitamin D
supplementation may be considered, although more research is needed in this area before
recommendations can be made. Treatment options for chronic enteropathies are summarized in Box
262.12.
Finally, it is important to note that the tendency to distinguish dogs with CE as food-responsive,
steroid- or immunosuppressive-responsive, or other may diminish the complexity of a disease process
that may occur due to multifactorial etiologies. Thus, it is important to consider that some dogs will
benefit from a multimodal approach to therapy.

Clinical Activity Indices
Two predominant clinical scoring systems have been utilized for objectively assessing dogs with CEs: the
canine inflammatory bowel disease activity index (CIBDAI) and the CCECAI.75,260 The CCECAI
includes 3 additional variables that are not part of the CIBDAI. The variables assessed in each system are
shown in Table 262.4.

Prognosis
Given the heterogeneous nature of CEs in dogs, the survival time is also highly variable and likely
dependent on several prognostic factors and response to therapy. The most significant negative
prognostic factor is likely the presence of hypoalbuminemia.75 Other negative prognostic factors may
include severe clinical disease (CCECAI >8, abnormal CIBDAI), BUN >20 mg/dL (>7 mmol/L), a high
endoscopic score in the duodenum, hypocobalaminemia (<200 ng/mL), and requirement for
immunosuppressive therapy.58,84,261 Hypovitaminosis D is also a negative prognostic indicator with

PLE.135 Selected histopathologic features and the results of clonality testing may also be negative
prognostic factors in dogs with certain etiologies.262

CHRONIC ENTEROPATHIES IN CATS
CE in cats encompasses a variety of etiologies that result in GI signs of > 3 weeks’ duration in the
absence of other extraintestinal or infectious etiologies.262 Thus, a comprehensive diagnostic work-up,
to include a minimum of CBC, serum biochemistry profile, urinalysis, FeLV/FIV testing, total T4, TLI,
and fecal diagnostics (i.e., fecal smear, fecal flotation, and potentially antigen tests [ch. 80]), must be
performed to rule out infectious or extraintestinal causes prior to pursuing a diagnosis of CE. 65,263
Feline PLI, bile acid concentrations, and a fecal PCR for Tritrichomonas foetus (predominantly large
bowel signs, ch. 263) may also be considered. CE in cats is frequently subclassified into FRE, SRE/IRE,
and SCL. The term IBD is often still used synonymously with SRE/IRE in cats.76 Although these disease
subclassifications are often viewed as separate entities, it is suspected that SRE/IRE/IBD may progress
to SCL in some cats and SCL has been documented to progress to large cell lymphoma in 9.9% of
cats.264 As in dogs, the etiology of CE in cats is likely multifactorial. A recent study suggested a possible
association between alterations in the microbiome and SCL in cats, although further studies are needed
to determine whether this is a causal or consequential association.265 Clinical signs are insufficient for
differentiation of conditions, but development of weight loss, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, or
hypoproteinemia in a cat previously diagnosed with SCL should prompt consideration of transformation
to large-cell lymphoma.264 Large-cell lymphoma often has a more acute and rapid progression
compared to IRE/IBD and SCL. A clinical activity index (Feline Chronic Enteropathy Activity Index
[FCEAI]) is available for use in cats and is based on an analysis of attitude/activity, appetite, vomiting
frequency, diarrhea evaluation, weight loss, endoscopic lesions, total protein, serum alanine
aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase activities, and serum phosphorus concentration (Table
262.5). The FCEAI can be used for assessing clinical severity and monitoring treatment response in cats
with IRE/IBD and FRE.266

Diagnosis
A diagnosis of chronic enteropathies in cats is based on histopathologic evaluation of biopsies, followed
by immunophenotyping and clonality testing where indicated to differentiate IRE/IBD from intestinal
SCL.144,145 Use of these techniques increases the detection of SCL but the consequence on patient
outcome is currently unclear.267 Controversies regarding the use of molecular techniques are further
discussed in the immunohistochemical and molecular clonality testing portion of this chapter. As in the
dog, the predominant inflammatory infiltrate is most commonly lymphoplasmacytic, but neutrophilic
infiltration has been associated with campylobacteriosis in cats and should prompt consideration of an
infectious etiology.268

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment for SCL and IRE/IBD in cats is similar, but different from other differential diagnoses for SI
disease, including large cell lymphoma, LGL lymphoma, and infectious etiologies. Management of
IRE/IBD and SCL in cats typically involves use of a novel protein or hydrolyzed protein diet, in
conjunction with glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisolone). Chlorambucil is typically added in refractory
cases. Cobalamin should be supplemented in cats with a low-normal or low serum cobalamin
concentration. Less information is known about the effects of probiotics on chronic enteropathies in cats
relative to dogs. There is limited information regarding prognosis in cats with enteropathies. A recent
study noted a median survival time (MST) of 416 days in cats with SCL. The 3-year survival rate for cats
with SCL was 15% vs. 71% for those with IRE/IBD.269 For a comprehensive review of chronic
enteropathies in cats, readers are referred to a recent review article.76 Given the anatomical fusion of the
pancreatic and bile duct in a cat, cats appear to be predisposed to triaditis (ch. 225). Thus, cats with CE
should be evaluated for concurrent pancreatitis and cholangitis/cholangiohepatitis.

BREED-RELATED ENTEROPATHIES
Several breed-related disorders of the SI have been reported (Table 262.1).

Basenji Enteropathy
Basenji enteropathy is a hereditary immunoproliferative enteropathy associated with progressive,
intractable diarrhea; vomiting; weight loss; and possibly transient neurologic signs.270 Histopathologic
evaluation of intestinal biopsy specimens reveals severe lymphoplasmacytic enteritis, which can
progress to spontaneous intestinal perforation. A lymphoplasmacytic gastropathy with hyperplasia of
the parietal cells and chief cells may also be associated with the enteritis.271 Serum gastrin levels (ch.
297) are frequently increased in this condition. In contrast to many other types of PLEs, Basenji
enteropathy is associated with hyperglobulinemia and edema/ascites appears to be less common.270,271
The diagnosis and treatment are as for other forms of CE, but the prognosis is typically poor. Remission
has been achieved in rare cases.11

Familial Protein-Losing Enteropathy and Protein-Losing Nephropathy in Soft
Coated Wheaten Terriers
Soft Coated Wheaten Terriers (SCWTs) are predisposed to a familial syndrome characterized by PLE,
PLN, or both, with PLE often preceding PLN in affected dogs. The disorder is suspected to be immunemediated in origin and mutations in NPHS1 and KIRREL,272 which encode slit diaphragm proteins,
have been noted in SCWTs with PLN (ch. 302).273 Food hypersensitivity may also play a role (ch. 152).
Diagnosis is based on signalment and documentation of PLE and/or PLN. Detection of perinuclear antineutrophilic cytoplasmic autoantibodies allows for detection of the syndrome on average 2.4 years
before the onset of hypoalbuminemia.274 Treatment is similar to other chronic enteropathies, but the
prognosis is poor.

Gluten-Sensitive Enteropathy in Irish Setters
A breed-associated gluten-sensitive enteropathy has been reported in Irish Setters. Dogs are typically
young to middle-aged and the disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.275 Clinical signs
are consistent with SI disease. The condition resembles gluten sensitivity (celiac disease) in people. The
pathogenesis is suspected to be related to abnormal mucosal barrier function, which permits entry of
gluten, stimulating the immune system. Biopsies reveal villous atrophy with intraepithelial lymphocyte
infiltration. Clinical signs resolve with a gluten-free diet that should be fed long-term.276

Paroxysmal Gluten-Sensitive Dyskinesia (ch. 41)
In recent years, there has been a substantial expansion in knowledge regarding ciliary movement
disorders in dogs. While these disorders are primarily considered as a neurological disorder, some forms
may have concurrent GI and/or dermatological manifestations.

Border Terrier
Paroxysmal gluten-sensitive dyskinesia (PGSD) of the Border Terrier is characterized by episodic
dystonia, chorea (irregular, spasmodic, involuntary movements), ballism (vigorous jerking or shaking
movements), and tremors without loss of consciousness (

Video 41.15). Most dogs have their first

episode before 3 years of age. Further information relating to terminology for ciliary movement
disorders is available in the recent International Veterinary Canine Dyskinesia Task Force ECVN
Consensus Statement on terminology and classification.277 GI clinical signs of PGSD in Border Terriers
include borborygmus, vomiting, diarrhea, and flatulence. Dermatological signs may also be
present.278,279 The diagnosis of PGSD in a Border Terrier is based on history, signalment, and response
to a gluten-free diet. Anti-canine gliadin IgG and anti-canine transglutaminase-2 IgA concentrations
may also be measured and are highly specific but lack sensitivity for PGSD.280 Treatment involves strict
use of a gluten-free diet and results in clinical and serological resolution of the disease. A gluten
challenge would be needed to definitively associate gluten with the clinical signs, but this is rarely
performed.

Maltese
A recent study described a PGSD in Maltese dogs, some of which presented with clinical signs of GI
disease or skin allergy in addition to episodes of sudden dystonia affecting 1 or more limbs, the trunk,
and the head. The median age at presentation was 5.4 years. Various treatments have been attempted in
Maltese dogs with PGSD, including gluten-free diets and acetazolamide. Most dogs (6/7) treated with a
gluten-free diet had resolution of clinical signs, while acetazolamide also reduced the frequency of
episodes in treated patients (4/6).281 Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that results in
potassium excretion, diuresis, metabolic acidosis, and loss of serum bicarbonate. It is theorized to
decrease brain lactate and pyruvate levels, resulting in brain acidosis and changes in intracellular and
extracellular pH; these effects are thought to alter the membrane potential and reduce neuronal
excitation.282,283 Spontaneous resolution was also described in 21% of affected dogs in a recent study,
which may make it difficult to determine the effect of therapies on disease outcome.281

Other Breeds (

Videos 41.8-41.12, 41.14,

41.16)
Many additional breeds are predisposed to movement disorders that may have concurrent GI signs,
including a recent report in a Welsh Terrier that developed vomiting following episodes of abnormal
muscle cramping. The nausea was responsive to maropitant, while levetiracetam was utilized for the
management of the paroxysmal exertional dyskinesia.284

Shiba Dog Chronic Enteropathy
Shiba dogs are predisposed to a severe lymphoplasmacytic enteritis, characterized by severe duodenal
lesions. Villous blunting and lymphangiectasia has been prevalent on histopathologic samples. The

prognosis of this condition is poor, with an MST of 74 days.285

FELINE GASTROINTESTINAL EOSINOPHILIC SCLEROSING
FIBROPLASIA
Feline gastrointestinal eosinophilic sclerosing fibroplasia (FGESF) is an emerging inflammatory
condition of unknown etiology that has been described worldwide. Bacteria have been isolated from
lesions in 56-69% of cases but their role in the pathogenesis of the disease is unclear. Male cats and
Ragdolls appear to be predisposed and the median age of onset is ∼7 years of age, although a wide age
range has been reported.102,286 Cats with FGESF typically present with chronic vomiting, diarrhea,
weight loss, and lethargy. Physical exam or diagnostic imaging subsequently reveals an intramural
abdominal mass, although cavitated and mesenteric forms have also been reported. A peripheral
eosinophilia is commonly reported. 102,286-288 FGESF is diagnosed histopathologically. Lesions are
often firm and gritty due to the presence of mature organized collagen trabeculae. A multimodal
therapeutic approach consisting of surgical excision, prednisolone, and antibiotics is recommended
based on retrospective case analysis.102

LYMPHATIC DISORDERS
Lymphangiectasia
Intestinal lymphangiectasia (IL) is commonly diagnosed in dogs, but is considered rare in cats. It is
characterized by variable intestinal lymphatic vessel dilation, lymphangitis, and/or lymphatic
obstruction. It is largely an acquired condition, occurring as a consequence of another process that
directly alters the flow of lymph. However, several breed predispositions for IL have been described
(Table 262.6), suggesting that there may be a genetic susceptibility to disturbances of the intestinal
lymphatic vasculature.
Mechanisms known to result in IL include increased hydrostatic lymphatic pressure, which may occur
secondary to inflammatory or neoplastic intestinal mucosal infiltrates; or increased venous pressure,
which may occur secondary to cardiac tamponade, right-sided heart failure, or portal hypertension.7 In
addition to lymphatic abnormalities, histologic evaluation of biopsy samples from dogs with IL often
reveals variable degrees and types of inflammatory infiltrates, as well as other lesions, including dilated
and cystic crypts. Because leakage of lymph from dilated or nonfunctional lymphatic vessels can result in
an inflammatory reaction in the intestine, and inflammation can result in dysfunctional and dilated
lymphatics, the determination of the primary and most significant process in the patient can be
challenging.

Diagnosis
IL can be diffuse or segmental, and can affect lymphatics at the villus level as well as in the deeper parts
of the intestinal wall. Mesenteric lymphatics can also be affected.70 Abdominal ultrasound in a patient
with IL may reveal hyperechoic mucosal striations (Figure 262.9).289 An endoscopic examination may
reveal pinpoint to coalescing “white spots” (Figure 262.11, D; Video 262.3

), which have been

correlated with IL. However, these lesions are only moderately sensitive and not specific for the
diagnosis of IL. Therefore, histopathologic examination of biopsies is needed to confirm it.290 While a
definitive diagnosis of IL must be arrived at histopathologically (Figure 262.13, D), the ability to
diagnose it can be limited if the disease is segmental or confined to the deeper parts of the intestine,
particularly if biopsies are obtained endoscopically.

Treatment
The cornerstone of treatment of IL is administration of a fat-restricted diet. It is not clear what level of
fat restriction is ideal in patients with IL. Diets considered low-fat (15-22.5% metabolizable energy
[ME]) or ultra-low fat (10-15% ME; 1.1-1.5 g/100 kcal) are generally recommended. The degree of fat
restriction necessary may vary by patient. Depending on whether dogs have additional
diagnoses/histopathologic findings, such as intestinal inflammation, there may be dietary requirements
in addition to fat restriction. Additional information on the dietary management of lymphangiectasia
can be found in ch. 152. There is no evidence of an immune-mediated pathogenesis for IL in dogs.159
However, IL causes lymphangitis and lymph leakage, which is known to induce secondary enteritis.
Thus, treatment with prednisone or prednisolone is often indicated. Dosages of 0.5-1 mg/kg PO q24h, or
divided q12h are preferred; higher (immunosuppressive) dosages of steroids are discouraged in cases of
IL. Dogs with IL will invariably have additional treatment requirements common to dogs with various
etiologies of PLE (see below).

Lipogranulomatous Lymphangitis
A distinct form of intestinal lymphatic disease known as focal intestinal lipogranulomatous lymphangitis
has been reported in a small number of dogs.291,292 Cases are characterized by the presence of a smallintestinal mass (typically located in the distal jejunum or ileum), often with the involvement of the
adjacent mesentery. Histopathologic examination of the mass reveals a transmural granulomatous
inflammation with extensive lipogranulomas, mainly involving the muscularis, serosa, and mesentery
(Figure 262.16). Treatment is largely via surgical excision of the mass, with variable needs for
postoperative therapy. Treatment outcome has largely been described as good. In some of the reported
cases, dogs have required treatment with a fat-restricted diet and/or additional medications in the
postoperative period and beyond.

Crypt Disease

Lesions associated with the intestinal crypts have been reported in some dogs with chronic GI disease,
namely in dogs with PLE. Crypts are reported as dilated and filled with mucus and sloughed epithelium
(Figure 262.17). The underlying pathogenetic mechanism associated with crypt lesions is not well
understood. However, reports have described crypt lesions occurring in the absence of lymphatic lesions
or inflammatory infiltrates. This suggests that they may occur earlier in the course of the disease, or that
crypt disease may be its own disorder.293 Bacterial infection was considered as a possible underlying
etiology; however, FISH analysis for bacterial DNA in crypt lesions has been unrewarding.294 Crypt
lesions appear to be most common in the Yorkshire Terrier295 and a specific treatment has not been
determined.

PROTEIN-LOSING ENTEROPATHIES
PLE is a syndrome of excessive loss of serum proteins across the intestinal mucosa
that occurs as a consequence of a wide variety of disorders. Many of these have been
discussed in the preceding sections of this chapter. PLE occurs in cats secondary to
severe CIE or intestinal lymphoma, but is much more common in dogs.

Mechanisms
PLE occurs due to 1 or a combination of: altered lymphatic function and direct loss of
protein-rich lymph, abnormal intestinal permeability resulting in a loss of protein into
the lumen, and/or direct mucosal erosion or ulceration and leakage of protein into the
lumen. Thus, following the exclusion of other causes of hypoalbuminemia (see
“Protein-Losing Enteropathy” in “Syndromic Diagnostic Approach to Patients With
Small Intestinal Disease”, above), the diagnostic approach to cases of PLE should
consider all disorders that can result in enteric protein loss through these differing
mechanisms (Table 262.7).

Etiology and Nutritional
Management
While a wide variety of disorders can result in PLE in the dog, CIE and IL are the most
common. Of 469 dogs diagnosed with PLE, 314 (68%) were diagnosed with CIE and
214 (58%) were diagnosed with IL.159 However, difficulty can arise in the management
of PLE with histopathologic evidence of both CIE and IL. While a low-fat (15-22.5%
ME) or ultra-low fat (10-15% ME; 1.1-1.5 g/100 kcal) diet is typically recommended for
dogs with IL, a novel protein, hypoallergenic, or hydrolyzed protein diet is suggested
for dogs with CIE. In 1 study of dogs with CIE, 76% of the dogs with hypoalbuminemia

had concurrent histopathologic evidence of IL.296 Thus, this situation is not
uncommon. Dogs with CIE and concurrent IL may do well on a diet formulated for
either one of these conditions. However, some patients may require consultation with
a board-certified veterinary nutritionist to determine the optimal diet. In some cases,
home-prepared diets will be the best option, particularly if it is determined that the
dog may need a diet that is lower in fat than any commercially available diet
(approximately 20 g fat/1000 kcal) or needs a combination of a low-fat and novel
protein diet. There are more frequent reports of dietary treatment alone being
successful in dogs with PLE.297 Importantly, in 1 study, dogs responding to diet alone
had lower CCECAI scores when compared to dogs that required additional
therapies.58 Optimization of diet appears to also be important in dogs with difficult to
treat PLE. Use of an ultra-low fat diet was demonstrated to be efficacious in dogs with
IL that was refractory to prednisolone.249 Additionally, following a change in dietary
approach, some dogs with steroid-resistant PLE showed improvement in clinical signs
and serum albumin concentrations.248 Additional information on the nutritional
management of GI conditions can be found in ch. 152.

Pharmacologic Management
Glucocorticoids are still considered a mainstay of therapy in many cases. However, it is
important to remember that glucocorticoids worsen the catabolic and hypercoagulable
states associated with PLE and can have other important adverse effects. Thus, the
goal should be to target the lowest effective dosage, and because there is no evidence
for an immunopathogenetic cause of IL, anti-inflammatory dosages should be targeted
in dogs with PLE primarily due to IL. Anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive
dosages (not to exceed 2 mg/kg/day or 60 mg/dog) of predniso(lo)ne should be
considered for dogs with PLE primarily due to CIE. If the response to glucocorticoids
is inadequate, relapse occurs with tapering, or side-effects are severe, additional
immunosuppressive medications can be considered (ch. 169). Interestingly a
retrospective review found no survival benefit in PLE dogs treated with corticosteroids
and immunosuppressive agents compared to those treated with corticosteroids
alone.298 A previous study found that cyclosporine (5 mg/kg, PO q24h) was effective
in some steroid-refractory cases.254 Chlorambucil (4-6 mg/m2 q24h, PO for 7-14 days
initially, then consider a dosage reduction) has been reported to be effective in
combination with prednisolone in some dogs with PLE.299

Identification and Management of
Concurrent Abnormalities
Abnormalities common to dogs with PLE that need to be considered for treatment
regardless of the underlying cause include hypercoagulability, ionized hypocalcemia
and decreased serum 25(OH)D +/– secondary hyperparathyroidism,
hypocobalaminemia, hypofolatemia, decreased oncotic pressure, and abdominal and
thoracic effusions. Amino acid deficiencies, namely of tryptophan, have also been
described; however, the potential benefit of treatment has not yet been explored.300
Clopidogrel (2-3 mg/kg, PO q24h) can be considered for thromboprophylaxis if no
contraindications are present (ch. 171). Treatment of clinically overt hypocalcemia is
recommended with intravenous 10% calcium gluconate (ch. 284). The optimal

treatment for ionized hypocalcemia and decreased 25(OH)D is unknown in dogs.
Historically calcitriol (20-30 nanograms/kg PO q24h for 3-4 days, then 5-15
nanograms/kg PO q24h) and/or calcium carbonate (25-50 mg/kg PO q24h) have been
recommended, though the former may result in hypercalcemia and
hyperphosphatemia. A benefit of vitamin D supplementation in dogs with PLE has not
yet been established. Hypocobalaminemia should be treated in dogs with PLE; a
treatment protocol is described in the “Diagnosis and Management” section of
“Chronic Enteropathies in Dogs,” above. Consideration should also be given to
treatment of hypofolatemia, if present. Colloids are most useful for oncotic support
(ch. 120). Effusions should be carefully removed only when they are resulting in
discomfort or respiratory difficulty (chs. 86 and 92). Diuretic use is discouraged.
If a histologic diagnosis is not obtained in cases of PLE, other causes of
hypoalbuminemia should be excluded definitively. Following the confirmation of GI
protein loss, every effort should be made to ensure infectious, mechanical, and
neoplastic causes of PLE are unlikely. Treatment should then be approached as if both
IL and CIE are present.

SMALL INTESTINAL NEOPLASIA
A variety of neoplasms can arise from or otherwise affect the SI. In dogs,
adenocarcinoma, smooth muscle tumors (leiomyoma or leiomyosarcoma), and
intestinal lymphoma are most common.301 Lymphoma is the most common neoplasm
of the intestinal tract in cats, with up to 70% of cats with lymphoma presenting with
involvement of the GI tract.302 Rare neoplasms of the GI tract include neuroendocrine
tumors, schwannoma, hemangiosarcoma, fibrosarcoma, and plasma cell tumors.
There may be a slight male predisposition for intestinal tumors in dogs.303 Siamese
cats are predisposed to intestinal adenocarcinoma and lymphoma, with 1 study
reporting an 8-fold increased risk in this breed.304 Clinical signs are generally similar
to those of other chronic enteropathies. However, certain intestinal neoplasms may
result in intestinal perforation or intussusception. The diagnosis is often first
suspected based on detection of a mass on abdominal palpation and/or imaging. A
definitive diagnosis often requires cytologic evaluation or tissue sampling for
histopathologic assessment.

FIGURE 262.18 Endoscopic images of alimentary lymphoma in
the duodenum of (A) an 8-year-old Collie and (B) 6-year-old

Intestinal Lymphoma
Lymphoma of the intestine is characterized by diffuse or focal infiltration of neoplastic
lymphocytes into the epithelium or lamina propria, with variable extension into the
deeper layers of the SI and involvement of the mesenteric lymph nodes (Figure
262.18). The distribution of disease is most commonly diffuse but can also be nodular
or plaque-like. More broadly, alimentary lymphoma may also affect the esophagus,
stomach, and large intestine, as well as the liver or pancreas. Lymphoma is typically
characterized histologically as small cell (SCL) (lymphocytic lymphoma; low grade;
well differentiated) or large cell lymphoma (LCL) (lymphoblastic; high grade), which
affects the clinical presentation, recommended therapy, and prognosis.305 An in-depth
discussion of lymphoma is presented in ch. 322.

Feline Intestinal Lymphoma
Lymphoma is the most common form of neoplasia diagnosed in cats and the GI tract is
the most common location for lymphoma. Both FIV (ch. 198) and FeLV (ch. 199)
infections are risk factors for the development of lymphoma but most cats with
lymphoma test negative for both viruses.306 Interestingly, cats living in a household
with cigarette smokers have a 2.4-fold increased risk for developing lymphoma when
compared to cats living in non-smoking households, and the amount and duration of
exposure has been correlated to an increasing risk.307

Most cats with GI lymphoma are middle-aged to older, but young cats can be
affected. Cats with SCL (also called lymphocytic lymphoma) typically present with a
protracted history of slowly progressive clinical signs, including weight loss, diarrhea,
vomiting, anorexia/hyporexia, and lethargy. In contrast, cats with LCL are more likely
to present with seemingly acute and severe onset of illness. Physical examination in
either case may reveal a diffusely thickened SI, a palpable mass lesion, mesenteric
lymphadenomegaly, poor body condition, and evidence of dehydration.308
CBC abnormalities include anemia (may be non-regenerative due to chronic disease
or regenerative and associated with blood loss or oxidative damage) and neutrophilia.
Hypoalbuminemia or panhypoproteinemia in a cat with GI signs is suggestive of
intestinal lymphoma, as nonneoplastic PLE is not commonly observed in cats with
chronic inflammatory enteropathies. In 1 study of 67 cats with GI lymphoma, 50% of
cats with LCL and 49% of cats with SCL were hypoalbuminemic.309 Hepatic
lymphoma or other concurrent liver disease should be considered in cats with elevated
liver enzyme activities. Measurement of serum cobalamin and folate concentrations
should be performed to support a diagnosis of severe and longstanding SI disease and
identify deficiencies for treatment. Ultrasound findings in cats with intestinal
lymphoma may include normal or increased intestinal wall thickness, abnormal or
preserved wall layering, mesenteric lymphadenopathy, focal distinct intramural mass
lesions, and/or an intestinal intussusception (Figure 262.19). 305 A study comparing
abdominal ultrasound findings between cats with SCL and those with IBD found that
cats with lymphoma were 18 times more likely to have a thickened muscularis layer as
well as a higher percentage of both a thickened muscularis layer and mesenteric
lymphadenopathy compared to cats with IBD.310 Ultrasound-guided fine needle
aspiration and cytologic evaluation of focal masses or enlarged lymph nodes should be
considered, although sensitivity is lacking and surgical biopsies may be necessary for a
definitive diagnosis.
Some controversy exists over the recommendation for surgical vs. endoscopic
intestinal biopsies in cats suspected of having GI lymphoma. While surgical biopsies
provide the advantage of transmural samples for evaluation and the ability to biopsy
all segments of the intestine, the obvious disadvantage is in the increased invasiveness
for the patient when compared to endoscopy. Endoscopic biopsies typically are
sufficient to make a diagnosis of intestinal lymphoma if the superficial mucosal layers
are affected and the lymphoma is well-differentiated.151 If a laparotomy is performed,
biopsy samples of mesenteric lymph nodes and the liver should be obtained in
addition to duodenum, jejunum, ileum, and any mass lesions, even when gross lesions
are not present.
Histopathologic evaluation of intestinal lymphoma reveals infiltration of the mucosa
by neoplastic lymphocytes, which may extend into the submucosa and transmurally.
Infiltrates of neoplastic cells can be irregularly distributed throughout the SI and
between and among individual villi. The distinction between IBD and SCL can be
challenging based on histopathologic features alone. Since cats with lymphoma should
have monoclonal populations of B or T lymphocytes in the affected segment(s) of the
GI tract, IHC labeling of lymphocytes may help to distinguish these 2 disorders.
Reclassification from IBD to SCL, or vice versa, occurred in 15.6-26% of cases in
several studies.269,311 However, IHC results can be challenging to interpret given that

techniques vary between laboratories and labeling of tumor cells is inconsistent. In
addition, some cases of intestinal inflammation are characterized by T-cell infiltration
alone, which can cause confusion. Clonality testing by PARR can also be utilized to
distinguish SCL from IBD; however, the sensitivity and specificity of PARR are still
under investigation in veterinary medicine, with at least 1 study suggesting that,
similarly to human medicine, specificity is a concern.146 The clinical significance of
distinguishing IBD from SCL in cats is questionable as it may not affect treatment
approach or outcome. However, a clear argument can be made that further study is
required to improve our understanding of these disease processes.262

FIGURE 262.19 Abdominal ultrasound image showing loss of
wall layering in the duodenum (A) and jejunal lymphadenopathy
(B) in a 15-year-old male castrated Domestic Shorthaired cat with
histologically confirmed intestinal lymphoma. A, Area of focal loss

jejunal lymph node outlined by calipers in the longitudinal

A previous study evaluating the utility of endoscopic biopsies for the diagnosis of
IBD and SCL in cats found that 44% of SCL cases were diagnosed only in ileal samples,
while the disease was not identified in the duodenum.312 The results of this study led
to the recommendation that cats undergoing endoscopic biopsy for the diagnosis of SI
disease should have both duodenal and ileal samples collected. However, a more
recent study reported that when histologic results were integrated with IHC and
clonality testing, there was moderate agreement between upper SI and lower SI
samples, and samples from the lower SI rarely changed the diagnosis.267
For cats with focal obstructive GI lymphoma, surgical resection is recommended
with concurrent biopsy of other parts of the GI tract, liver, and mesenteric lymph
nodes. Postoperative chemotherapy is also recommended since lymphoma is a
multicentric disease. For cats with diffuse disease, chemotherapy is the mainstay of
treatment (ch. 322). The chemotherapy protocol selected will depend on the type of
lymphoma as well as patient and owner factors. Chlorambucil (2 mg/cat PO q2-3d or
as a pulse-dose protocol 20 mg/m2 PO every 2 weeks) is an alkylating agent that
targets slowly dividing lymphocytes. This makes it an appropriate therapy for SCL,
which is a slowly progressive disease. Chlorambucil is typically administered with
prednisolone for the treatment of SCL. Various dosing protocols have been described
and are well tolerated and associated with good to excellent response rates.305 Bolusdosing provides the advantage of less owner exposure to chemotherapeutic agents,
especially considering that some cats will be treated with chlorambucil for months to
years. Overall response rates of cats treated with chlorambucil and prednisolone have
been reported as 76-96%, with a median duration of clinical remission of 428-897
days.308,313,314 In 1 study, rescue therapy with cyclophosphamide was successful in
7/9 cats that developed recurrent clinical signs during treatment with chlorambucil.314
Importantly, cats with SCL can experience transformation of the disease to LCL. Thus,
development of worsening clinical signs in a cat previously in remission for SCL
should prompt consideration of this possibility.264
Cats with LCL will require more intensive chemotherapy protocols. Additionally,
comprehensive supportive care is often necessary. COP (cyclophosphamide,
vincristine, +/– L-asparaginase) or CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin,
vincristine, prednisone +/– L-asparaginase +/– methotrexate) are considered
superior to single-agent protocols or corticosteroids alone in cats with LCL. Rates of
response to chemotherapy for cats with LCL are approximately 50-75%, with an MST
of 7-9 months.304 LGL lymphoma of the intestinal tract has a worse prognosis, with 1
study reporting a response rate of only 30% and an MST of 57 days.315 Lymphoma is
generally very radiation-responsive and 5 of 8 cats with LCL treated with 10 fractions
of radiation therapy following a standard chemotherapy protocol were reported to
have long-term (range, 266-1332 days) survival.316
Additional therapy that should be considered in cats with intestinal lymphoma
include dietary modifications, cobalamin supplementation, and supportive care.
Modification of the diet to one that is highly digestible and palatable is beneficial in

many cats with GI lymphoma (ch. 152). However, in cats with concurrent intestinal
inflammation, the use of a hydrolyzed protein, hypoallergenic, or novel protein diet
should be considered. Enteral feeding may be required in cats that are anorexic or
hyporexic (ch. 81). Cobalamin supplementation is recommended even if serum
cobalamin is not measured, as hypocobalaminemia was detected in 78% of cats with
GI lymphoma in 1 study.313 At the current time, it is unknown whether cobalamin
supplementation in cats with SCL must be parenteral or whether the oral route is
equally efficacious, as has been demonstrated in cats and dogs with CIEs or EPI.
Additionally, supportive care in the form of an appetite stimulant and/or antiemetic or
antinausea agent may be necessary.

Canine Intestinal Lymphoma
Roughly 7% of canine lymphoma cases involve the alimentary tract; thus, intestinal
lymphoma is less common in dogs than in cats. Canine alimentary lymphoma may be
confined to the GI tract or may be part of multicentric lymphoma, in which case
peripheral lymph nodes and/or other organs are involved.317 Disease confined to the
GI tract may be focal or diffuse. Historically, small cell (lymphocytic) lymphoma of the
SI was considered rare in the dog, with the majority of intestinal lymphoma cases in
dogs being large cell (lymphoblastic) lymphoma. However, recent publications have
better characterized SCL in the dog, describing clinical characteristics, histologic,
immunohistochemical and molecular characteristics, treatment, and outcome in a
modest number of dogs.318,319
Dogs diagnosed with intestinal lymphoma are generally older, but it can also be seen
in young animals. Male dogs may have a higher risk of developing intestinal
lymphoma compared to female dogs. The clinical presentation of dogs with intestinal
lymphoma depends on the subtype (large cell vs. small cell lymphoma) and the
involvement of other organs and/or peripheral lymph nodes. Dogs with large cell
lymphoma of the intestine most commonly present in poor clinical condition, with a
relatively rapid deterioration of health and progressive clinical signs. The most
common clinical signs are vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, weight loss, and lethargy.320
Similarly to cats, dogs with SCL may present with more chronic, insidious signs,
indistinguishable from non-neoplastic forms of chronic SI disease. Physical
examination findings in either subtype can include poor body condition, signs of pain
on abdominal palpation, a palpable abdominal mass, thickened intestinal loops, and
ascites. If there is peripheral lymphadenopathy and/or hepatic or splenic
organomegaly, this would suggest multicentric lymphoma.305
The most common serum biochemical abnormality in dogs with intestinal
lymphoma is hypoalbuminemia. Thus, intestinal lymphoma should be considered in
cases of severe hypoalbuminemia not caused by hepatic insufficiency or urinary loss of
protein. Other biochemical abnormalities include anemia (may be nonregenerative
due to chronic disease or regenerative and associated with blood loss or oxidative
damage), neutrophilia, increased liver enzyme activities, and rarely, circulating
lymphoblasts. While relatively common in multicentric lymphoma in dogs,
hypercalcemia is rarely observed in dogs with alimentary lymphoma. Similarly to cats,

decreased serum cobalamin and/or folate concentrations have been described in cases
of intestinal lymphoma in dogs, and hypovitaminosis D can occur.320
Imaging findings are similar to those observed in cats, and fine-needle aspiration for
cytologic evaluation can be performed if focal masses or mesenteric lymphadenopathy
are observed. Some cases will require surgical biopsy for diagnosis.
In dogs with LCL, the reported overall response rate to a multidrug chemotherapy
protocol in 1 study was 56%, with an MST of 117 days. Dogs not responding to
treatment were euthanized a median of 10 days following diagnosis and dogs
presenting with diarrhea had a worse prognosis than those without.321 In contrast, the
MST for 14 dogs receiving treatment for T-cell SCL was 628 days. Most dogs were
treated with the combination of a corticosteroid and a chemotherapeutic agent, such
as chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide, and/or lomustine. This study highlighted that as
in cats, SCL in dogs is a disease process distinct from LCL and dogs with SCL that are
being treated can experience prolonged survival.319

Intestinal Adenoma and Adenocarcinoma
In dogs, intestinal adenoma and adenocarcinoma have a predilection for the large
intestine (ch. 263) over the SI. When found in the SI, canine adenocarcinoma is most
likely to be found in the duodenum. SI adenoma and adenocarcinoma are more
common in the cat than large intestine forms, and the jejunum and ileum are the most
common locations. A polypoid tumor is suggestive of an adenoma, while
adenocarcinomas are locally invasive and typically grow as plaques or annular stenotic
lesions. Adenocarcinomas can extend into the serosa and mesentery and may
metastasize to the local lymph nodes and/or peritoneal cavity. Hematogenous
metastasis may also occur.305
Affected dogs and cats are typically older (mean age: 9 years [dogs], 11 years [cats])
when diagnosed with intestinal adenocarcinoma. Siamese cats are overrepresented.304
Clinical signs may include weight loss, lethargy, anorexia or hyporexia, and vomiting
or diarrhea. Signs may occur due to partial or complete intestinal obstruction or
peritonitis if rupture of the GI tract occurs. Clinical signs suggestive of GI bleeding,
such as melena or pallor, may also be present. Anemia (regenerative due to blood loss
or nonregenerative due to development of iron deficiency) and hypoproteinemia can
also be observed, and abdominal ultrasound will typically identify a mass lesion.
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration and cytologic analysis may be helpful, but
surgical biopsies may be necessary to achieve a definitive diagnosis.
The treatment of choice for intestinal adenocarcinoma is surgical resection.
Historically, for dogs with no evidence of metastatic spread at the time of surgery,
median postoperative survival times of 15 months were reported, compared to 3
months for dogs with histologic evidence of metastasis at the time of surgery.
Following surgery, 1- and 2-year survival rates have been reported as 40.5% and
33.1%, respectively.322 In a more recent retrospective case review of 29 dogs with
histologically diagnosed and surgically treated SI adenocarcinoma, MST was 544 days
following surgery. Dogs <8 years old had significantly longer survival times when
compared to dogs ≥8 years of age. Lymph node metastasis, use of NSAIDs, or use of
adjuvant chemotherapy were not associated with a decrease or increase in survival

time.323 A retrospective study evaluating long-term outcomes in 18 cats with SI
adenocarcinoma reported MSTs of 22 vs. 365 days for cats that did not receive
treatment vs. those that underwent surgical resection, respectively. Survival times for
cats without metastatic disease at the time of surgery were 843 days, compared to 358
days in cats with documented metastasis.324

Smooth Muscle and Stromal Cell Tumors
Leiomyomas and leiomyosarcomas are uncommon nodular tumors in the dog,
typically found in the jejunum or cecum (ch. 324). Smooth muscle tumors of the GI
tract are rare in the cat and are only found in the SI. Tumors are typically located on
the antimesenteric border. It can be difficult to distinguish between a leiomyoma and a
leiomyosarcoma histologically, but this may not be clinically relevant as metastatic
spread of a leiomyosarcoma is uncommon. GI stromal tumors (GISTs; ch. 324),
which arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal, are histologically similar, but can often
be distinguished by their differing expression of CD molecules.
Clinical signs of smooth muscle and stromal tumors are similar to those of other
intestinal tumors. Paraneoplastic syndromes (ch. 331), including hypoglycemia (ch.
61) as a result of production of insulin-like growth factor-II like peptide have been
reported with smooth muscle tumors.325,326 Erythrocytosis (ch. 57) due to the
elaboration of an erythropoietin-like molecule is an additional paraneoplastic
syndrome described with leiomyosarcoma.327 Mass lesions are typically identified via
abdominal ultrasound or upper GI endoscopy. Endoscopic biopsy may be sufficient for
making a diagnosis; however, surgical biopsies may be necessary and surgical
resection is the treatment of choice for smooth muscle and stromal tumors. Smooth
muscle tumors and GISTs can typically be distinguished using IHC labeling. Most
GISTs express c-kit (CD-117), a transmembrane receptor with a tyrosine kinase
component.328 Smooth muscle tumors typically express alpha-smooth muscle actin
(SMA) but are negative for c-kit.
The prognosis for leiomyoma is excellent following surgical removal, while the
prognosis for leiomyosarcoma depends on tumor size, tumor location, mitotic index,
and IHC features. If surgical resection is complete, the prognosis is typically good,
with a reported MST of 21 months, and prolonged survival described in some cases.326
The reported MST in 53 dogs with surgically resected GIST was 18 months. Survival
times were significantly longer in dogs with GIST of the cecum compared to those with
a GIST in the SI, with overall survival times of 22 months and 6 months,
respectively.329 Individual survival times may be longer. A previous report described
the MST for dogs who survived the immediate postoperative period following surgical
resection of a GIST as 37.4 months.328 Tyrosine kinase inhibitors may be a useful
adjunct to surgery in dogs with GIST, as well as providing clinical benefits in patients
with gross disease.330
