Other Intestinal Neoplasms
Hamartomatous (dogs) and adenomatous (cats) polyps can cause vomiting,
hematemesis, melena, and iron-deficiency anemia. Intestinal melanoma and
hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325) are rare, with the latter occurring more frequently in cats
than in dogs. Fibrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, schwannoma, and carcinoid tumors also
uncommonly affect the SI. These tumors are locally invasive and cause clinical signs
that are similar to those of other intestinal tumors. Carcinoids (ch. 297) are a type of
neuroendocrine tumor with secretory granules that contain various substances,
including serotonin, gastrin, secretin, and somatostatin.331 Histiocytic sarcoma (ch.
328) can infiltrate the GI tract, causing severe clinical signs. Mast cell tumors (ch.
327) of the intestine in cats behave similarly to alimentary lymphoma but may be
accompanied by substantial fibrosis and thus described as feline sclerosing alimentary
mast cell tumors. Extramedullary plasmacytomas are rare overall and occur mainly in

the stomach and large intestine but may also be found in the SI. The presence of a
monoclonal gammopathy in a patient with an intestinal mass may increase a suspicion
for this tumor type.

MISCELLANEOUS OTHER SMALL INTESTINAL
DISORDERS
Surgical Disorders

Obstruction of the Small Intestine
Small intestinal obstruction is a common problem in small animals and can be the
result of extramural, intramural, or intraluminal lesions. Intraluminal obstructions are
most commonly caused by foreign objects, some of which can be radiolucent (e.g., corn
cobs) and therefore more difficult to identify. Intestinal neoplasia, parasites,
hematomas, granulomas, and strictures may cause intramural obstructions. Hernias,
tears in the mesentery, and congenital and acquired adhesions may entrap intestinal
loops, resulting in an extraluminal obstruction. Intussusceptions are an additional
cause of SI obstruction in small animals (Figure 262.20; Video 262.1

).

Obstructions can be classified as complete, wherein ingested nutrients are unable to
pass beyond the point of obstruction, or partial, wherein some nutrients can still pass.
Importantly, small intestinal obstructions may also be acute or chronic. The prognosis
following surgical correction depends on the cause of the obstruction, viability of the
intestine, and presence of perforations and peritonitis.

Foreign Body Obstruction
Latex nipples, followed by plastic or rubber balls, stones, and strings were the most
common foreign bodies in 174 cases of intestinal obstruction in dogs in the United
Kingdom.332 In cats, linear foreign bodies and trichobezoars (hairball obstructions)
are common.333 Linear foreign bodies can anchor in multiple places throughout the
alimentary tract, including around the base of the tongue and at the pylorus. This
anchoring leads linear foreign bodies to cause obstruction of the SI due to the plicating
and pleating of the intestine around the foreign object as peristalsis ineffectively
attempts to move the linear foreign body aborally. In more severe cases, a sawing
effect causes the linear foreign body to perforate the SI, often in more than 1 site,
which can cause peritonitis.
Young dogs and cats and large-breed dogs are overrepresented in most case series of
GI foreign body obstructions.332,333 However, any dog or cat of any breed or age can
develop a foreign body obstruction. Clinical signs vary depending on the degree of
obstruction (partial or complete), site of obstruction, and whether there is concurrent
peritonitis and/or sepsis. The most common clinical signs are vomiting, anorexia,
depression, and signs of abdominal pain. Left untreated, an intestinal obstruction will

lead to severe dehydration, and eventually, death.334,335 Nonspecific lethargy,
intermittent vomiting, weight loss +/– evidence of abdominal pain may be the only
presenting complaints in dogs with chronic partial foreign body obstructions. Diarrhea
may also be observed in patients with a chronic partial obstruction. The most common
laboratory abnormalities in 138 dogs with an intestinal obstruction were
hypochloremia (51.2%), metabolic alkalosis (45.2%), hyperlactatemia (40.5%),
hypokalemia (25%), and hyponatremia (20.5%).334
Many cases of SI obstruction can be identified on plain abdominal radiographs.
Serosal-to-serosal width of the small bowel exceeding 1.6 times the height of L5 at its
narrowest point is considered the best validated radiographic characteristic for
determining a pathologic dilation of an SI loop.336 Complete obstruction usually leads
to dilation of loops proximal to the obstruction, whereas a chronic partial obstruction
may lead to extensive dilation throughout the SI (Figure 262.21). Chronic partial
obstructions may also cause accumulation of insoluble granular, variably opaque
material in the SI. This is known as “graveling” and when this material is observed in
the SI rather than in the colon, a chronic partial obstruction should be suspected
(Figure 262.21). Linear foreign bodies produce a pleated or bunched-up appearance
of intestinal loops on radiography. Enteric gas bubbles are also common. Loss of
serosal detail and the presence of free gas on plain abdominal radiographs are strongly
associated with perforation of the GI tract, thus indicating the need for swift surgical
intervention. Peritoneal gas is frequently observed dorsally and outlining the
diaphragm cranial to the liver margin in patients with peritonitis. Contrast
radiography and abdominal ultrasound may help corroborate radiographic findings
and can distinguish among foreign body obstructions, intramural obstructions, and
intussusceptions.337

FIGURE 262.21 Chronic partial small intestinal obstruction in
a 6-year-old female spayed German Shepherd Dog with a history
of chronic diarrhea, intermittent inappetence, and
hypoalbuminemia. This left lateral radiographic projection of the
abdomen shows diffusely fluid dilated small intestines with
collections of mineralized material (“gravel sign”; arrow). Surgery
confirmed the presence of a chronic partial obstruction of the
ileum, caused by a stricture suspected to be secondary to a
previously entrapped foreign body.
The outcome in patients with simple foreign bodies is generally good following
surgical correction, with reported survival rates of 83-99%.332 The prognosis becomes
guarded in cases of intestinal perforation, particularly when multiple perforations are
present. The risk of dehiscence following enterotomy is increased in patients with
preoperative peritonitis and hypoalbuminemia.338

Intussusception
Intussusceptions are defined as telescoping of a proximal segment of bowel, or
intussusceptum into a distal segment, or intussuscipiens. The most common types of
intussusceptions are ileocolic or jejunojejunal in dogs and jejunojejunal in cats.339
Intussusceptions occur when a peristaltic wave reaches a fixed segment of bowel. Most
intussusceptions in young dogs and cats are idiopathic.340,341 Intussusceptions in

older cats and dogs may increase the suspicion for a neoplastic cause. Intussusceptions
may also occur secondary to idiopathic enteritis, viral enteritis (e.g., parvovirus),
foreign bodies, and following abdominal surgery.342 Physical examination may be
noteworthy for palpation of a “sausage-shaped” abdominal mass and/or evidence of
abdominal pain. Radiographs can reveal evidence of a mass and SI obstruction, and
abdominal ultrasound may demonstrate a double-walled structure (Figure 262.10;
Video 262.1

), which is characteristic of an intussusception. Evidence of blood flow

in the mesentery of the intussuscepted bowel (detected via color Doppler
ultrasonography) may indicate that surgical reduction of the intussusception can be
achieved.343 However, surgical resection of the affected region and end-to-end
anastomosis is necessary in many cases. A speedy return to feeding is recommended
postoperatively in order to promote the return of normal intestinal motility. Postoperative complications are not uncommon, with 1 study reporting a rate of 35%.
Reported recurrence rates range from 3-27%.341,344

Intestinal Strangulation, Volvulus,
and Perforation
When loops of bowel become entrapped in tears in the mesentery or in umbilical or
inguinal hernias, strangulation can occur. Strangulation of the SI can also occur as a
consequence of entrapment of the bowel by adhesions or around intraabdominal
lipomas. Strangulation can result in obstruction, perforation, and/or intestinal
ischemia with a subsequent risk of reperfusion injury following surgical treatment.345
Intestinal, or mesenteric, volvulus refers to a rare disorder in which the intestines
rotate around the root of the mesentery. Occlusion of the cranial mesenteric artery
subsequently occurs, resulting in ischemia of the distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum,
cecum, and ascending and proximal colon. Ischemia of this magnitude quickly results
in bowel necrosis, endotoxemia, and shock, and if not addressed rapidly, death.346
The German Shepherd Dog is the most commonly affected breed, though mesenteric
volvulus has also been reported in the Great Dane, Neapolitan Mastiff, and Labrador
Retriever, among others.347 Dogs usually present with signs of intense abdominal
pain, abdominal distension, pale mucous membranes, weakness, and tachycardia.
Abdominal radiographs typically reveal marked and diffuse gas distension of the SI.
The mortality rate typically is very high; however, 1 report has noted a 42% survival
rate (5/12 cases), with the authors postulating that this was due to prompt surgical
intervention.347
Intestinal perforation and subsequent peritonitis are commonly caused by ingestion
of foreign material or NSAID administration.348,349 Perforation is most commonly
caused by ingestion of sharp, nondigestible objects, such as needles, or delayed
diagnosis of a SI foreign body. Bone fragments are less likely to cause perforation as
they are typically softened by exposure to gastric acid. Neoplastic tumors, granulomas,
and ischemia of the bowel can also result in intestinal perforation.

Short Bowel Syndrome
When large portions of the SI (more than two-thirds) are absent after surgical
resection or, much less commonly, due to congenital anomaly, short bowel syndrome
(SBS) may occur. Due to the possibility of SBS, aggressive surgical resections of the SI
should be avoided if at all possible. However, surgical resection of large swaths of SI is
necessitated in some cases by multiple intestinal perforations (commonly with linear
foreign bodies) or severe adhesions. Some patients tolerate resection of large portions
of the SI with limited effects, while others experience severe clinical disease with less
resection.350 Resection of the ileocolic valve may be especially problematic for a
variety of reasons, including a predisposition for ascending bacterial colonization.
SBS is characterized by nutrient malabsorption and protein-calorie malnutrition,
with weight loss and diarrhea, following intestinal resection. Intensive treatment with
parenteral fluids and nutrition is recommended post-operatively in patients requiring
extensive SI resection, although limited oral feeding is also recommended in order to
provide a stimulus for intestinal adaptation. Once the patient has transitioned to oral
feedings, multiple small meals of a highly digestible, easily assimilated, fat- and fiberrestricted diet is advised. In some cases, monomeric or polymeric elemental diets are
fed. Reduction of gastric hyperacidity is recommended by administration of PPIs, and
suppression of the proliferation of intestinal microbiota is advised with oral broadspectrum antibiotics.351 Supplementation of cobalamin (see the “Diagnosis and
Management” section of “Chronic Enteropathies in Dogs,” above) is recommended if
the ileum has been resected. Additionally, some patients with SBS may require
supplementation with fat-soluble vitamins (i.e., vitamins A, D, E, and K).
Cholestyramine, a bile salt-binding resin, may improve diarrhea in patients with bile
salt malabsorption following ileal resection. Ursodeoxycholic acid has been
demonstrated to enhance intestinal absorption in a feline surgical model and to
improve the nutritional status of dogs with experimentally-induced SBS.352,353 In
animals failing to respond to these therapies, antisecretory therapies such as
loperamide and octreotide could be trialed. Some animals with SBS can undergo
adaptive hyperplasia of the SI, leading to subsequent clinical improvement, while
others fail to respond.

Motility Disorders
Ileus is defined as the lack of normal propulsive activity of the intestine due to
functional causes. Mechanical obstruction of the SI must be definitively excluded
before a diagnosis of functional ileus can be made. There is a wide variety of causes of
ileus in dogs and cats. Ileus may occur as a consequence of another condition or
process, the most common of which are abdominal surgery, opioid administration,
hypokalemia, pancreatitis, parvoviral enteritis, peritonitis, or hypothyroidism.354 Less
common causes of ileus include dysautonomia, intestinal pseudo-obstruction, and
irritable bowel syndrome-like disorders. Treatment of ileus is focused on resolution of
the underlying disease process, if possible, and nonspecific therapies to improve
intestinal motility, if necessary. Those therapies include prokinetic agents, including 5HT4 receptor agonists such as cisapride, D2 dopaminergic antagonists, such as
metoclopramide, and less commonly utilized acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and
motilin-like drugs. Further details on prokinetic drugs are shown in Table 262.8. In
humans with ileus, feeding has been demonstrated to be beneficial. Thus, providing
nutritional support to dogs and cats with ileus is recommended, barring unresolved
mechanical obstruction of the intestine.

Dysautonomia (ch. 254)
Dysautonomia (sometimes referred to as Key-Gaskell syndrome) is a disorder
originally documented in dogs and cats in the UK that has now been reported
throughout Western Europe and infrequently in the United States. It is characterized
by a generalized autonomic neuropathy that results in esophageal, gastric, and small
intestinal dilation and hypomotility, urinary bladder distension, reduced tear
production, bradycardia unresponsive to atropine, and pupillary dysfunction, among
other signs. The etiology of dysautonomia is uncertain, although unidentified dietary
neurotoxins or xenobiotics have been suspected355 and a possible association with
Clostridium botulinum neurotoxin has been described in horses and cats.356 The
diagnosis is often made based on historical and physical examination findings and
treatment is supportive. The prognosis for long-term survival historically has been
considered to be poor in both dogs and cats. In a recent retrospective review of
dysautonomia in 34 cats and 19 dogs, overall survival rates were 21% and 32% in cats
and dogs, respectively. Importantly, survival times of >2 years were observed in 6 cats

and 3 dogs, suggesting that some animals may be able to achieve good long-term
outcomes.357

FIGURE 262.22 Diffuse, severe gas distension of the
gastrointestinal tract on a lateral abdominal radiograph of a 6year-old male castrated Labrador Retriever with histologically
confirmed chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction. Full-thickness
small intestinal samples obtained at necropsy revealed

Intestinal Pseudo-Obstruction
Intestinal pseudo-obstruction is a term used for describing conditions of chronic and
typically marked intestinal dilation and dysmotility not caused by mechanical
obstruction. Various conditions resulting in intestinal pseudo-obstruction have been
described in humans, and they are commonly divided into those that are caused by
disorders of the enteric smooth muscles (myopathies) and those that affect the enteric
nervous system (neuropathies).358 These conditions can occur without explanation, or
be secondary to other underlying disorders, including infectious diseases, drug
intoxications, endocrinopathies, and generalized neuromuscular diseases, among
others. The hallmark of intestinal pseudo-obstruction is evidence of severe intestinal

dilation on abdominal imaging without mechanical obstruction (Figure 262.22). In
these cases, histopathologic evaluation of full-thickness intestinal biopsies is required
to evaluate for an underlying cause. In dogs with chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction
(CIPO), a variety of intestinal abnormalities has been described, including reduced
expression of alpha-smooth muscle actin in the tunica muscularis,359 intestinal
leiomyositis,360 atrophy and fibrosis of the tunica muscularis,361 and myenteric
plexus vacuolar degeneration.362 Intestinal pseudo-obstruction has been reported
secondary to visceral myopathy in a cat.363 CIPO has also been described as a result of
smooth muscle alpha-actin deficiency in a Bengal cat364 and enteric ganglionitis in a
Persian cat.365 Feline intestinal lymphoma has also been noted as a cause of CIPO.
There have been rare reports of long-term survival in patients with CIPO. In 1 dog,
treatment with immunosuppressive dosages of glucocorticoids was successful.366 The
Persian cat with enteric ganglionitis was successfully treated with pyridostigmine. The
prognosis is guarded to grave in the majority of cases, with 1 study of 6 dogs reporting
an MST of 19 days.360

Irritable Bowel-Like Syndromes
Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a complex disorder in humans, characterized by
recurrent GI signs and lack of histopathologic evidence of intestinal disease
(inflammatory or morphologic). Recurrent abdominal pain, colonic dysmotility, and
changes in bowel habits are common, often accompanied by abdominal distension and
bloating. The condition is considered to have a heterogenous pathogenesis in which
stress and psychological abnormalities, brain-gut interactions, and altered gut motility
are all suspected to play a role.367 A similar condition may occur in veterinary patients
(ch. 11), but it is poorly defined. IBS-like syndrome in veterinary medicine can be
loosely defined by the presence of recurrent GI signs including vomiting, diarrhea, or
constipation, and abdominal pain and/or bloating, the absence of histopathologic
abnormalities on intestinal biopsies, and the suspicion that anxiety and stress (both
mental and physical) may play a role in the disease.368 As no histopathological
abnormalities have been identified as of yet and clinical signs may relate to either the
SI or large intestine, this condition cannot be clearly attributed to dysfunction of either
the small or the large bowel.

Brush Border Disorders
Brush border enzyme deficiencies have been sparsely described in small animals.
Congenital absence of the brush border enzyme aminopeptidase N has been described
in dogs, but clinical significance is lacking as other peptidases appear to
compensate.369 Relative lactase deficiency appears to occur in some animals under
some conditions, but similarly, clinical significance is considered to be low.

Congenital/Inherited Cobalamin
Deficiency
Defective apical brush border expression of the cobalamin-IF-receptor complex results
in selective cobalamin malabsorption in the dog. The human correlate of this genetic
disorder is Imerslund-Gräsbeck syndrome (IGS). Classic clinical signs include failure
to thrive, inappetence, and diarrhea. Possible laboratory abnormalities include nonregenerative anemia (usually normocytic, normochromic), neutropenia, hypoglycemia,
hyperammonemia, and ketosis, among others.22 Inherited/congenital forms of
cobalamin deficiency are detailed in Table 262.2.47-50,113-115,370-374
Treatment of selective cobalamin malabsorption in the dog is imperative, as without
treatment, dogs will die as a result of immunodeficiency and metabolic
derangements.374,375 Successful dosing intervals for parenteral supplementation are
highly variable, ranging from once weekly to supplementation every 8 weeks. Oral
therapy has also been reported to be successful in Beagle dogs with inherited
cobalamin deficiency.376 Clinical signs returned in 1 dog with IGS being supplemented
every 4-5 months; therefore, supplementation would best be administered more
frequently than that.114 Following initiation of cobalamin supplementation, clinical
signs often improve within 24-48 hours, while hematological abnormalities may take
up to 14 days to resolve.370,377

CLIENT INFORMATION
Canine Chronic Enteropathies

WHAT ARE CHRONIC
ENTEROPATHIES?
A chronic enteropathy (CE) is a broad term that describes the
presence of clinical signs of intestinal disease for over 3-weeks
duration. This broad definition is often refined in response to
treatment trials into 1 of the 4 following diagnoses: i) foodresponsive enteropathy, ii) enteropathies response to manipulation
of the intestinal bacteria (microbiota), iii) immunosuppressive/antiinflammatory responsive enteropathy or iv) non-responsive
enteropathy. Diagnosis of CE requires the exclusion of other causes
of chronic intestinal signs including infectious diseases and systemic
disorders.

WHAT ARE THE CLINICAL
SIGNS OF A CHRONIC
ENTEROPATHY?
The most common symptom is large volumes of semiformed to
liquid feces. Some dogs will pass dark, tarry stool (melena), which is
partially digested blood. Weight loss is common and is due to
malabsorption of nutrients, but it is more severe if the animal has a
reduced appetite. Vomiting and abdominal discomfort can occur,
and there may be concurrent colitis (inflammation of the colon),
which is apparent from repeated effort and straining to defecate.

HOW ARE CHRONIC
ENTEROPATHIES
DIAGNOSED?
If your veterinarian suspects that your pet has CE they will perform a
thorough physical exam including abdominal palpation (evaluation
of the organs by touching with the fingertips through the body wall).
Diagnostic tests should include examination of stool samples for
parasites. In addition, your veterinarian could perform other tests
including routine blood tests to rule out other diseases; a trypsin-like
immunoreactivity (TLI) test for pancreatic insufficiency; a pancreatic
lipase immunoreactivity (PLI) test for pancreatitis; a blood test for 2
vitamins (folate and vitamin B12) to identify intestinal damage and
any deficiency that needs treating; X-rays of the digestive tract; and
abdominal ultrasound. Your veterinarian may then prescribe a
sequence of various medications including diet to evaluate if your
dog is responsive to food, and medications intended to treat
imbalance of your dog’s intestinal bacteria (microbiota). Biopsy
samples of the intestines may also need to be collected. These
samples can be collected by endoscopy (examination of the intestine

with a small lighted camera under general anesthesia) or via surgical
exploration of the abdomen. A biopsy allows your veterinarian to
confirm the presence of inflammation and also helps them rule out
other causes of similar clinical signs such as infectious agents or
cancer.

HOW ARE CHRONIC
ENTEROPATHIES
TREATED?
CEs are treated with dietary modification and/or administration of
oral medications (tablets or liquid suspensions) at home. Few cases
of CE can be cured, but many can be managed effectively with
medications and special foods. Your veterinarian may recommend a
special food, as pets with this condition can respond to a food that
contains ingredients they have never eaten before (an exclusion or
elimination diet). Alternatively, your veterinarian could recommend
specially developed foods composed of hydrolyzed proteins that
minimize immunologic reactions to foods. Vitamin supplements may
be indicated, and sometimes probiotics are helpful. Some individuals
with CE will require the administration of steroids and/or
immunosuppressive medications. No 2 individuals with this
condition respond exactly the same way to treatment, so a stepwise
approach to identifying the best treatment for your pet is often
pursued.

WHAT IS THE PROGNOSIS?
The prognosis with CE is variable and you should discuss the
prognosis for your particular pet with your veterinarian. You should
always follow your veterinarian’s instructions carefully when you
take your pet home. You should monitor your pet’s condition, call
your veterinarian if you have any concerns and return to the hospital
for scheduled follow-up appointments and diagnostic studies. This

allows any changes to be detected early and modifications of
treatment to be implemented quickly.
Sara Jablonski (East Lansing, Michigan) and Harry
Cridge (East Lansing, Michigan)

ANATOMY
MACROSCOPIC FEATURES
The large intestine (synonym, large bowel) is a simple tubular
structure that includes the cecum, colon, rectum, and anal canal
(Figure 263.1). It starts at the ileocolic orifice (Figure 263.2),
which functions like a valve preventing retrograde flow of colonic
contents.1 The cranial and ascending part is located close to the
duodenum and is followed by the transverse part and the descending
part, which flexes caudally and runs along the left side of the
abdominal wall until it ends in the rectum and terminal anal canal.
The rectum begins at the pelvic inlet and is located dorsal to the
urinary bladder and prostate/uterus. The colon is 30-100 cm long in
dogs and 20-40 cm long in cats, or approximately one-fifth of the
length of the entire gastrointestinal (GI) tract. The cecum is a blind
pouch situated ∼1 cm from the ileocolic orifice, communicating with
the ascending colon via the cecocolic orifice. In dogs, it is 4-15 cm
long and its shape is variable; in cats it is a consistently small, 1-4 cm
long, comma-shaped diverticulum.2,3

Vasculature and Lymphatic Drainage

The large-intestinal mesentery attaches the colon to the abdominal
wall in separate sections, divided into ascending, transverse, and
descending mesocolon and supports blood vessels, lymphatics, and
nerves. The blood supply of the large intestine is primarily via the
cranial (i.e., ileocolic, right colic, middle colic branches) and caudal
(e.g., cranial rectal branch) mesenteric arteries. Short branches
(arterial arcades) then bifurcate upon entering the intestinal wall as a
subserosal or mural arterial network. The cecum and colon are
drained by the ileocolic, middle colic, and left colic vein, which, in
turn, enter the portal vein.4 Circumferential lymphatic vessels drain
into the right, middle, and left colic lymph nodes, which drain into
the cisterna chyli, and from there into the thoracic duct, which
crosses the diaphragm, into the cranial vena cava. The rich network
of mesenteric lymphatic capillaries absorbs serous fluid from the
abdominal cavity.5,6

MICROSCOPIC FEATURES
The small and large intestine are composed of 4 layers: mucosa (i.e.,
epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosa), submucosa,
muscularis, and serosa (Figure 263.1). The mucosa of the large
intestine is characterized by a lack of villi and the presence of deep
crypts, which dip into the muscularis mucosa. Epithelial cells
generated at the base of the crypts differentiate into epithelial,
goblet, or endocrine cells during outward migration to the intestinal
lumen over a period of ∼4-7 days. The luminal surface is smooth, and
is comprised of a single layer of cells that are sealed by tight junction
proteins, including occludin, claudin, and zonulin-1. This surface is
covered by a thick mucus layer, which makes up the first layer of the
intestinal barrier.7,8 Mucus-secreting goblet cells are the second
most abundant cell type in the colonic epithelium. There are also
endocrine cells that, among many other neuropeptides, secrete
polypeptide P, insulin-like growth factors, and glucagon-like
peptides.9 Enterochromaffin (EC) cells are a specific type of
enteroendocrine cells, which synthesize and secrete 5hydroxytryptamine (serotonin, 5-HT). 5-HT stimulates motility

along the colon.10,11 Lymphocytes are sparsely distributed between
epithelial cells.12
The lamina propria, which comprises the second line of defense,
contains a large number of lymphocytes and plasma cells and lower
numbers of macrophages, eosinophils, neutrophils, and mast cells.
A thin layer of smooth muscle cells (muscularis serosae)
separating the mucosa from the submucosa, and contains nerves,
blood vessels, and lymphatics. An inner circular muscle layer is
responsible for circular contraction and an outer longitudinal muscle
layer acts synergistically with the circular layer, preventing excessive
lengthening during intestinal contractions. Interstitial cells of Cajal
act as pacemakers and transduce both inhibitory and excitatory
neural signals to myocytes.13,14 The Auerbach plexus of myenteric
ganglia is located between these layers.15 Mesothelial cells form the
serosa, the outermost layer of the GI wall, which reduces frictional
forces during digestive movements.16,17

LARGE INTESTINAL FUNCTION
The colonic lumen contains mainly food remnants, water,
electrolytes, gas, and bacteria. Approximately half of the weight of
the feces consists of bacteria. Indigestible carbohydrates (e.g., starch
and other polysaccharides) serve as nutrients for these bacteria and
fermentation results in various metabolites, such as short-chain fatty
acids (SCFAs) and gas. The pH of the colonic content is slightly more
acidic than that of the small intestine. Bicarbonate secreted into the
lumen neutralizes organic acids produced by the intestinal
microbiota.

ABSORPTION AND SECRETION OF
WATER AND ELECTROLYTES
The main function of the colon is the absorption of water and
electrolytes, mainly sodium. Water absorption follows sodium
chloride exchange in the proximal colon, and up to 90% of water can
be reabsorbed this way.18 Small bowel diarrhea can be partially
compensated for by water reabsorption in the colon. Sodium
transport in exchange for potassium is modulated by aldosterone

and therefore, potassium can be actively secreted into the colon.
Moreover, glucocorticoids are potent stimulators of electrogenic
sodium absorption in the large intestine. Potassium is also absorbed
in the colon through K+/H+ exchange transporters.19 Without an
intact mucosal barrier and normal colonic function, electrolytes and
fatty acids leak back into the lumen, creating an osmotic gradient
with water no longer being able to be absorbed.20
An active mucosal barrier is comprised of goblet and epithelial
cells in the mucosal layer. It mechanically prevents intestinal
microbiota and enterotoxins from invading the mucosa. A decreased
mucus layer may be part of the pathogenesis of chronic
enteropathies.
The colon has 4 main functions that have specific motility
patterns: slowing transit time to absorb water; mixing contents to
allow contact with the mucosa; storage of feces between defecations;
and selective onward transport of feces toward the rectum when
defecation occurs. The motility of the colon is influenced by sleep,
food intake, emotions, contents of the colon, and various
medications. Peristalsis of the colon consists of segmental
contractions with distal relaxation. Acetylcholine activates excitatory
motor neurons, while the neurotransmitters adenosine triphosphate
and nitric oxide activate inhibitory neurons, resulting in smooth
muscle relaxation. Mechanical and chemical stimuli can activate
peristalsis through EC cells, which synthesize 5-HT in response to
nutrients, SCFAs, bile salts, and mechanical stimuli that are
processed through mechanoreceptors in enteric ganglia.10,11 The
peristalsis of the colon is divided into 2 different types of
contractions: low-amplitude non-propagating contractions (mixes
ingesta and transports it over short distances, ∼9 cm) and highamplitude propagating contractions (transports over longer
distances towards the anus).21 The pacemakers of these peristaltic
waves are the interstitial cells of Cajal, which transduce both
inhibitory and excitatory neural signals to myocytes.13,14

IMMUNE SURVEILLANCE

The colonic mucosa has an enormous surface area and is constantly
exposed to a wide variety of antigens from dietary components and
microorganisms. The GI tract is one of the largest immunologic
organs in the body (ch. 168) and it must provide a tight barrier
against the invasion of pathogens, while tolerating benign microbiota
and food antigens. The GI-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) is
present throughout the entire tract and in the colon it consists of
lymph nodes, lymphoid follicles, and mucosal immune cells. In the
colonic epithelium and lymphoid follicles, so-called microfold cells
are responsible for selective endocytosis of antigens and transport to
intraepithelial macrophages and lymphocytes.22 Epithelial cells of
the colon can also present antigens to the immune system. The
dendritic cell projections constantly test the surrounding milieu in
the colon’s lumen for antigens and associate with B and T
lymphocytes. In contrast, the innate immune system (macrophages,
dendritic cells, and epithelial cells) can react to microorganisms in
the lumen utilizing toll-like receptors.12

INTESTINAL MICROBIOME (CH. 260)
Composition
The intestinal microbiome consists of a complex system of
microorganisms (i.e., bacteria, archaea, fungi, viruses) and their
genome. Each of the parts of this ecosystem contributes to the
stability of the whole and the interaction with the host. Most
research available involves the bacterial microorganisms. The term
intestinal flora is outdated and should be replaced by intestinal
microbiota. This resident microbiota is crucial in suppressing
specific pathogens, plays a major role in immune system
sensitization, can have pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory
effects on the intestinal tract, and forms important metabolites,
collectively referred to as the metabolome, that are essential for the
host. Each individual’s microbiome is unique. However, these
individual differences are minimal compared to those resulting from
interspecies differences, GI diseases, or drug administration.23-26
Dietary changes affect the microbiota mostly through major changes

in substrate and macronutrient distribution (e.g., from a commercial
to a raw meat diet).27
The number of bacteria in the intestinal tract increases as one
travels distally, with more bacteria in the large intestine. The total
bacterial count is estimated to be approximately 1012 to 1014 colonyforming units (CFU) per gram of large bowel content.24 Primarily
anaerobes are found in the colon. Most research currently involves
the fecal microbiome, as this is more readily accessible than
intraluminal content. The 4 dominant phyla of the GI tract are
Firmicutes, Fusobacteria, Bacteroidetes, and Proteobacteria, with
Firmicutes being the most important. Despite the minor differences
between individuals, the basic microbiome of each organism is
generally considered stable after the individual has reached its adult
state.24-26

Assessment of the Intestinal Microbiota
Various diagnostic tests have been used for examining the fecal
bacterial microbiota (ch. 260). Routine fecal cultures are not
suitable for evaluating the fecal bacterial composition as they are not
representative of the anaerobic microbiota and potential
enteropathogens such as Clostridioides difficile or Salmonella spp.
can be found as part of the normal microbiota in dogs. However, a
positive culture may indicate that the physiologic microbiota is
altered, and dysbiosis has enabled such pathogens to proliferate,
such as through the suppression of the protective microbiota by
antibiotics.24-26,28,29
Methods such as 16S-rRNA gene pyrosequencing have generated a
basic knowledge of the fecal microbiota, although evolution of
methods makes it impossible to uniformly compare studies over
time.26 The polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based dysbiosis index
(DI) represents a newer approach, which has been shown to be
altered in a substantial proportion of animals with inflammatory
bowel disease (IBD) or after treatment with antibiotics or proton
pump inhibitors (ch. 260).30-35 The reduction of mucosally
adhering bacteria and a decrease of the inflammatory antigenic
stimulus of the intestinal immune system only lasts during antibiotic

administration, but results in a highly disturbed microbiota, lasting
weeks to months (ch. 106). As such, antibiotics should be reserved
for patients with chronic bowel disease with inadequate response to
other treatment approaches.32,33,36 Further information on DI can
be found in chs. 260 and 262.

Intestinal Metabolites
Butyrate, the most essential SCFA for colonocyte nutrition, can be
found in the feces of all mammals. It is synthesized by intestinal
bacteria from carbohydrates and, in the dog and cat, also from
proteins, and it is converted by butyryl-CoA:acetate-CoAtransferase.37-39 Neurotransmitters, such as gamma-aminobutyric
acid and 5-HT, are partially controlled by the intestinal
microbiota.40 5-HT, which is essential for motility, secretion, and
blood flow in the intestine, is mainly produced by EC cells in the
intestinal tract but also directly by intestinal bacteria from
tryptophan. The microbiome plays a major role in the development
and maintenance of a healthy enteric nervous system, hence the term
“gut-brain axis.”
C. hiranonis is one of the bacterial species that is included in the
DI. It represents an important central component of bile acid
metabolism in dogs and is having major beneficial effects in dogs and
cats. Conversion of primary bile acids that have been secreted into
the intestinal lumen to secondary bile acids requires the microbiotaprovided 7-alpha-hydroxylase. A strong correlation between the
abundance of C. hiranonis and the concentration of secondary bile
acids in the feces has been demonstrated. Proper levels of secondary
bile acids are essential for maintaining an anti-inflammatory
environment in the intestinal tract and to help inhibit potentially
pathogenic bacteria (e.g., C. difficile). In the absence of conversion,
primary bile acids accumulate in the feces, which can lead to an
osmotic type of diarrhea, so-called “bile acid diarrhea.” Most dogs
with chronic enteropathies respond to dietary changes or steroid
administration. However, in individuals that show treatment failure,
administration of bile acid binders (e.g., cholestyramine) could help
improve clinical signs—as extrapolated from human medicine and
reported in a small case series.41,42

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION OF THE
LARGE INTESTINE
One of the first steps in the work-up of dogs and cats with diarrhea is
to determine whether the patient has large or small intestinal disease
(Table 263.1 and ch. 49 [Figure 49.1]). This is not always clearcut as some dogs have mixed bowel disease and any patient with
chronic diarrhea can develop an irritation of the anorectum. The
colorectal mucosa is very sensitive, and dogs with substantial large
intestinal disease consistently show tenesmus, frequent defecation of
small amounts of feces, and the presence of mucus and/or fresh
blood in the feces (ch. 51). In contrast, cats with large bowel disease
may have clinical signs that are less pronounced or less frequently
observed. For example, some young cats with Tritrichomonas foetus
infection only exhibit fresh blood coating otherwise normal feces.
Weight loss is more commonly seen in dogs with small intestinal
disease; however, it can sometimes be observed with severe
infiltrative diseases of the large intestine, such as lymphoma,
adenocarcinoma, invasive Escherichia coli, histoplasmosis,
protothecosis, or pythiosis.43-45

HISTORY AND PHYSICAL
EXAMINATION
Patients with large intestinal disease may be presented to their
veterinarian due to diarrhea (ch. 49), tenesmus (ch. 51), and/or
hematochezia (ch. 50). The duration of clinical signs is important.
Acute clinical signs are frequently self-limiting and usually do not
require an in-depth evaluation. Patients with diarrhea that has lasted
>10 days should be considered to have subacute diarrhea, potentially
progressing to chronic disease, and should be more systematically
evaluated. To recognize chronicity, pet owners should be specifically
questioned regarding intermittent or subtle signs, such as frequent
defecation without diarrhea or the presence of mucus coating the
feces. In patients with straining, tenesmus ani (intestinal disorders)
must be differentiated from tenesmus vesicae (urogenital disorders)
through a detailed history (e.g., presence of diarrhea, fresh blood,

and mucus coating the feces versus abnormalities of urination) and a
thorough physical examination (e.g., colon filled with excessive and
hard feces, changes on digital rectal examination versus an enlarged
urinary bladder). Patients with suspected obstructive disorders need
an immediate diagnostic work-up and treatment, independent of the
underlying disease process.

The history should include all parameters of the Canine Chronic
Enteropathy Clinical Activity Index (CCECAI) to assess severity of

the disease, help predict response to treatment (e.g., young dogs with
mild chronic large bowel diarrhea are likely to respond to diet
changes), and provide an objective method for monitoring the
clinical course (ch. 262: Table 262.2).46,47 The CCECAI includes
attitude/activity, appetite, frequency of vomiting, stool consistency,
stool frequency, and unintended weight loss as information to be
gathered from the history; additional important questions are listed
in Table 263.2. Travel history (ch. 9) and information about
previous anthelmintic treatment and fecal examinations are
important to help rule in or out infestation with parasites and
infectious agents with a specific geographic distribution (e.g.,
systemic fungal diseases, Heterobilharzia americana). Foodresponsive large intestinal disease is common; thus, pet owners must
be questioned about the current and previous diets (ch. 145).
Concurrent intestinal and dermatological signs are seen in 6-44% of
affected dogs, and pruritus in a patient with large intestinal diarrhea
may suggest a food allergy (chs. 12 and 160).48
A thorough physical examination, including a digital rectal
examination, is the first step in the diagnostic work-up (ch. 3).
Sedation or even anesthesia may be necessary in some patients in
order to complete the rectal examination. Perianal fistulas, perianal
mass lesions and rectal prolapse can be detected visually (ch. 264).
Digital examination may reveal anal sac abnormalities, anorectal
strictures, anorectal masses, pelvic canal stenosis, deviation of the
colonic lumen due to perineal hernia, and/or thickening of the
mucosa or submucosal tissues, suggestive of infiltrative infectious or
neoplastic disorders.
An increased volume of firm or hard feces in the rectum of a
patient that is straining to defecate can be detected by abdominal
palpation and/or rectal examination and is indicative of
constipation. If no intra- or extraluminal (e.g., enlarged prostate,
lymph node, abdominal mass) obstruction or deviation of the rectal
wall can be detected, then a motility disorder (e.g., hypothyroidism)
may be considered. Alternatively, the ingestion of foreign material
(e.g., bones, cat litter) is a frequent cause of impaction of the colon
and rectal ampulla and these can be diagnosed by inspecting feces
obtained during digital rectal examination.

The physical examination is often normal in patients with large
bowel signs; however, attention should be given to the presence of
fever (ch. 16; may suggest a primary enteropathogen, bacterial
translocation, intestinal/colonic perforation), signs of abdominal
pain (ch. 126; may be evidence of intestinal/colonic distention,
pancreatitis, peritonitis), abdominal masses, evidence of spinal pain
(that may be seen with discospondylitis [ch. 250] or intervertebral
disc disease [ch. 250]), and neurologic signs (ch. 241; e.g, hindlimb
weakness/paresis, evidence of autonomic neuropathy [ch. 254]).49

FURTHER DIAGNOSTIC WORK-UP
In dogs with non-obstructive large bowel disease, a fecal exam (e.g.,
fecal flotation from 3 consecutive fecal samples, antigen test for
Giardia and specific parasites; ch. 80) and a treatment trial with a
broad-spectrum anthelmintic agent (e.g., fenbendazole 50 mg/kg PO
once daily for 3-5 days; see ch. 142 and textbook’s inside covers) for
occult parasites (e.g., whipworms) should be performed. Protozoa or
parasites are not always the primary cause for the diarrhea and
might be a coincidental finding. Nevertheless, parasites lower the
threshold for diarrhea caused by other problems and typically should
be treated when found.
The choice of further diagnostics is guided by history, physical
examination findings, and the clinicians’ experience: 1) Most cases of
acute uncomplicated diarrhea (e.g., alert patient interested in food
shows no systemic signs of hypovolemia and/or inflammation) are
caused by dietary indiscretion and/or infectious diseases that are
self-limiting and do not require costly diagnostic or therapeutic
interventions. 2) In chronic uncomplicated diarrhea, a minimum
database including complete blood count (CBC), serum biochemistry
profile, and serum cobalamin and folate concentrations should be
performed to rule out extraintestinal diseases, and to assess the
involvement of the small intestinal tract (cobalamin, folate) and the
severity of the disease (e.g., hypoalbuminemia) (Table 263.3).
Although 2 or maybe even 3 consecutive dietary trials might be
necessary (ch. 160), many dogs in this group respond either to a
restricted antigen diet (i.e., novel protein source, hydrolyzed protein)
or to supplementation with fermentable fiber (e.g., inulin and

fructooligosaccharides) (ch. 165). Although some dogs show
improvement of chronic large intestinal signs during administration
of antimicrobials, routine empiric trials with antibiotics are
discouraged due to the negative influence on the normal intestinal
microbiota and the potential for development of resistant bacterial
strains. 3) In those cases with either signs of systemic illness,
complications (e.g., abdominal pain, hematochezia), and/or a lack of
response to therapeutic approaches within the first 2-4 weeks, a
more extensive diagnostic work-up is warranted, as described below.

Additional Laboratory Tests
Uremic toxins have the potential to cause colitis. Whenever there is
an elevated blood urea nitrogen and/or serum creatinine
concentration(s), it is important to differentiate prerenal azotemia
due to dehydration from primary renal disease. Liver dysfunction
can be responsible for GI signs, due to portal hypertension, changes
in GI motility, inadequate removal of toxins, and imbalance of
hormones. However, increased hepatic enzyme activities should be
interpreted cautiously in patients with intestinal disease because
increased translocation of small molecules and bacteria due to
barrier dysfunction can cause a reactive hepatopathy. However, in
patients with reactive hepatopathy, hepatic enzyme activities are
typically only increased < 3× the upper limit of the reference interval
while hepatic function parameters (e.g., serum bile acids and
bilirubin concentrations) are within the reference interval. Following
successful treatment of a primary enteropathy (e.g., food allergy,
parasites) the serum hepatic enzyme activities should return into the
reference interval. Serum bile acids are useful to rule out
portosystemic shunts, which can be present in older dogs and be
responsible for chronic GI signs.50 Also, pancreatitis can cause
inflammation of the anatomically adjacent colon. Measurement of
pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity (PLI) may be indicated if
pancreatitis is suspected (chs. 277, 278). Hyperkalemia and
hyponatremia are typically associated with hypoadrenocorticism but
have also been documented in whipworm infestations and other
enteropathies. In general, serum basal cortisol concentration should
be determined in every dog with unexplained GI signs, followed by
adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-stimulation testing if the

baseline cortisol concentration is <2 mcg/dL (<55 nmol/L) (ch.
296). The prevalence of hypoadrenocorticism among dogs with
chronic GI signs is much higher (4%) than the reported prevalence in
the general dog population (0.06-0.28%) and it is not possible to
reliably differentiate dogs with hypoadrenocorticism from those with
other causes of chronic GI signs based on history, physical
examination, or routine blood work alone.51 Measurement of serum
T4 concentration should be performed in any diarrheic cat older than
8 years, as well as in younger cats with additional signs suggestive of
hyperthyroidism, such as a palpable thyroid nodule, polyphagia, and
weight loss (ch. 287).

Fecal Examination (ch. 80)
Commercial veterinary diagnostic laboratories offer various fecal
enteric panels for the diagnosis of patients with intestinal disease. To
diagnose intestinal parasites, fecal flotation of 3 consecutive fecal
samples, preferably using a centrifugation technique, with a flotation
solution of adequate specific gravity, is recommended. However,
some parasites responsible for large intestinal disease, especially
Trichuris vulpis, are only shed intermittently and can be easily
missed on flotation.52,53
Giardia spp. (ch. 196) can be involved in colitis and documenting
a high number of cysts on flotation or motile trophozoites on a direct
fecal smear indicates an active infection. In contrast, Giardia antigen
tests are so sensitive that a positive test result, especially in chronic
cases, does not always mean that Giardia is responsible for the
diarrhea.
T. foetus (ch. 196) is an intestinal pathogen in cats causing
chronic large bowel diarrhea, especially in young, purebred cats. T.
foetus infection can be diagnosed by microscopic evaluation of a
fresh fecal sample mixed with one drop of saline, by fecal culture
systems, or by PCR.54-61 The latter is considered the gold standard
and is far more sensitive than a direct smear or fecal culture pouch.
The sensitivity of PCR testing can be further increased if antibiotics
are stopped for several days before testing and by a specific colonic
flush technique (Video 263.1

).

Fecal bacterial cultures are rarely useful unless there is evidence of
involvement of multiple individuals in the same environment or
there are signs of systemic illness.28,62 Primary enteropathogenic
bacterial infections are rare in dogs and cats (ch. 195). Furthermore,
interpretation of a positive culture result is difficult because of the
similar isolation rate of potential enteropathogenic bacteria from

healthy individuals. Therefore, antimicrobial therapy should not be
based on a fecal culture. Fecal cultures as well as PCR testing for
potential enteropathogenic bacteria (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni/coli,
Salmonella spp.) should be restricted to patients with colitis and
signs of systemic inflammation, to outbreaks of acute diarrhea in a
specific population and after histologically documenting a type of
mucosal inflammation suggestive of infectious enteritis (e.g.,
neutrophilic or granulomatous colitis [GC]). In cases of mucosal
invasive bacteria (e.g., enteroinvasive E. coli causing GC), a mucosal
culture might be superior to a fecal culture.43,63,64 Fecal cultures to
identify dysbiosis will not differentiate dogs with chronic
enteropathies from healthy dogs. Novel molecular genetic-based
tests have been developed to assess the composition of the
microbiota, and rapid PCR-based methods are promising tools
already available for the assessment of intestinal dysbiosis (e.g.,
DI).34,37,65
Fecal PCR testing for parvovirus infection should always be
performed in a young dog with acute intestinal signs, especially if it
is neutropenic and/or inadequately vaccinated (ch. 201). Feline
enteric coronavirus (FCoV; ch. 200) infection is associated with the
occurrence of diarrhea in cats, but FCoV can frequently be detected
by fecal PCR in both healthy and diarrheic cats from catteries with a
prevalence of 59% and 87% respectively.66

Rectal Cytology
A rectal scrape can be obtained by gently moving a cotton-tipped
applicator or cytology brush against the rectal wall. The applicator or
brush is then rolled onto a glass slide, dried and stained. Nucleated
cells other than epithelial cells should only rarely be seen, and any
number of inflammatory cells should be considered significant.
Neutrophils and a pyogranulomatous inflammatory response are
usually seen in primary large-intestinal infections (e.g.,
Campylobacter spp., enteroinvasive E. coli, histoplasmosis,
protothecosis). In some cases, infectious agents (e.g., Histoplasma
capsulatum [ch. 262: Figure 262.15], Prototheca spp.) may be
visualized. Fungal elements from Aspergillus, Candida spp., or
Saccharomyces spp. should always be considered pathogenic. The

presence of potential enteropathogenic bacteria (e.g., C. perfringens
endospores, Campylobacter spp.) should be interpreted in the
context of the clinical signs observed (e.g., fever) and the presence of
neutrophils on cytologic examination. Some colorectal tumors (e.g.,
lymphoma; chs. 262, 322) exfoliate well and can be diagnosed
cytologically; however, biopsies are usually necessary to confirm the
diagnosis.67,68

Imaging
Plain radiographs can be utilized to assess colonic distention in order
to diagnose obstipation and obstructive lesions. The maximal
diameter of the colon should be less than 1.5 times the length of the
fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) in cats and the seventh lumbar vertebra
(L7) in dogs, respectively.69-71 Survey radiographs are also useful to
detect pelvic canal stenosis and extraluminal causes of obstruction,
such as intraabdominal masses or prostatomegaly. In patients
presenting with an acute abdomen (ch. 126) and tenesmus or
hematochezia, abdominal radiographs are crucial to rapidly diagnose
or rule out mesenteric volvulus.69,72,73
Ultrasound has widely replaced contrast radiography of the
stomach and intestines, especially for assessing wall thickness and
layering. In addition, lymphadenomegaly and extramural masses
compressing the large intestine can be visualized sonographically.
Contrast radiographs are sometimes useful to diagnose focal
intraluminal lesions, to assess the exact length of the colon (e.g.,
congenital short colon; Figure 263.3) and to recognize motility
disorders (e.g., constipated colon after ruling out anorectal
obstruction).
Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) are useful to visualize and assess the extension of intrapelvic
mass lesions and to examine the spinal cord and cauda equina in
patients with neurologic deficits.

Contrast Radiography
Contrast procedures should be performed under general anesthesia,
and the colon should be completely cleaned to avoid artifacts. A
“negative contrast pneumocolonogram” can be performed by

insufflating the colon with air (10 mL/kg) using a balloon-tipped
catheter (Figure 263.4). By gently pulling at the catheter while
insufflating the colon, leakage of air can be prevented (Video 263.2
). Lateral and ventrodorsal radiographs should be obtained
immediately. The colon should be completely filled and distended. A
pneumocolonogram can be useful to differentiate between small and
large intestinal lesions and to identify strictures and intraluminal
masses, which might be missed using other imaging modalities or
even during direct visualization using endoscopy. Positive contrast
studies can be performed using a barium enema (1 part barium and 2
parts water; 10 mL/kg) and double-contrast studies involve
insufflation with 10 mL/kg air, after draining the barium enema.
However, these studies are contraindicated in patients with
suspected colonic perforation and are rarely performed because
pneumocolonography in combination with colonoscopy is usually
easier to perform and usually sufficiently sensitive to show lesions,
such as intussusception, cecal inversion, diverticula, herniation, and
mucosal changes.

Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography is useful to assess colonic wall thickness and
layering and to document focal lesions, such as neoplastic infiltration
and intussusception. Due to the much thinner wall of the colon
compared to the small intestine, the layering can only be defined
clearly when a high-resolution transducer is used. All layers
contribute equally to the total colonic wall thickness, which varies
between 1-2 mm in dogs and 1-1.7 mm in cats, depending on the
degree of distention. In cats with chronic, infiltrative, large intestinal
disease, the right colic lymph node is frequently enlarged and can
usually be visualized at the ileocolic junction (Video 263.3

). In

patients with diffuse, infiltrative, infectious, or neoplastic diseases,
the colonic wall is frequently thickened with an irregular mucosa
(Figure 263.5). A loss of layering in the colon of a patient with a
thickened colonic wall is most often indicative of neoplastic
infiltrative disease; less commonly, this may also be seen in severe
inflammatory mucosal reactions due to infiltrative infectious
diseases such as pythiosis, lagenidiosis, zygomycosis and E. coli-

associated GC. Abdominal ultrasound can also be used for guiding
percutaneous aspiration and transrectal biopsies of colonic wall
lesions (Video 263.4

). Ultrasound-guided aspiration of enlarged

lymph nodes is an easy and fast way to diagnose metastatic
neoplastic infiltrates, large-cell lymphoma, and translocated bacteria
and other infectious agents.74-77

Colonoscopy
Colonoscopy is a minimally invasive modality to examine the entire
mucosal surface of the large intestine and to collect biopsies for
histologic examination and culture (Videos 263.5-263.8

).

Colonoscopy is always preceded by a thorough digital exam to rule
out rectoanal strictures or masses. In select cases,
pneumocolonography prior to colonoscopy is useful to obtain an
overview of the colon and to localize focal lesions prior to
colonoscopy. Strictures can be missed if the colon is inadequately
distended by air insufflation or if a small diameter endoscope readily
passes through a narrowed lumen. Indications for colonoscopy
include chronic large intestinal signs not responsive to well-designed
treatment trials with different diets and anthelminthic agents,
intestinal signs in breeds with a predisposition for E. coli‐associated
GC, hematochezia on several occasions, and the identification of
bowel wall changes on ultrasound/imaging (e.g., loss of layering) or
other suspicion of neoplasia.78-82 For successful colonoscopy to take
place, patient preparation is essential (Box 263.1). The equipment,
procedure, and possible complications of colonoscopy are described
in ch. 107.

Diseases of the Large Intestine
CONGENITAL DISORDERS
Colonic Vascular Ectasia (Angiodysplasia)
Angiodysplasia is a very rare disease in young dogs. It is
characterized by fragile dilated vessels with a single layer of
endothelial cells that easily rupture, leading to hemorrhage and

chronic, prominent, and intermittent hematochezia. Microcytic
hypochromic anemia may occur. The dilated vessels in the tunica
mucosa and submucosa of the colon are seen exclusively on
colonoscopy, not on laparotomy from the serosal side. The colonic
vascular malformations can be seen histopathologically. Partial
colectomy is the treatment of choice, but argon plasma laser
coagulation of the vascular bundles can be attempted. Oral estrogenprogesterone therapy has also been described and seems to be
efficacious according to a few case reports; long-term treatment was
well tolerated without signs of bone marrow toxicosis.83-86

Short Colon Syndrome
In dogs and cats, individual cases of a shortened colon have been
described (Figure 263.3). During diagnostic imaging, the cecum

may then be visible on the left side of the body. Loose stool may be
present, or this can be a subclinical finding that does not cause
clinical signs.87

DISEASES CAUSING OBSTRUCTION
Intestinal Intussusception
In patients with an intestinal intussusception, typically the proximal
part of the intestine with its attached mesentery (the
intussusceptum) is invaginated into the lumen of the distal portion
of the intestine (the intussuscipiens). Intussusception occurs most
commonly in young animals of either sex and any breed, although
dogs and cats of all ages can be affected. Maine Coon cats may be
more commonly affected.77 Trigger factors may include an acute
intestinal infection (e.g., parvoviral enteritis, bacterial infections
such as leptospirosis, endoparasites), mechanical or structural
changes (e.g., foreign bodies, neoplasia), or severe diarrhea.76,88-91
Idiopathic intussusception in young animals may also be more
common due to abnormal muscular activity with an immature
enteric nervous system. Most commonly, the intestine invaginates at
the ileocecocolic junction, and cecocolic, ileocolic (most common), or
ileocecal intussusceptions have all been described. The
intussusception results in intestinal dilatation and stasis of contents
proximal to the lesion. Entrapment of blood and lymphatic vessels in
the intussusceptum disturbs the vascular supply of the affected
intestinal segment and results in focal edema, intramural
hemorrhage, and ultimately ischemia and necrosis.
Typical clinical signs are acute vomiting, anorexia, signs of
abdominal pain, and bloody mucoid diarrhea. Subacute or chronic
courses are rare. It is often possible in young or thin animals for the
veterinarian to be able to palpate the intussusception as a thick
cylindrical mass. Abdominal radiographs with or without contrast
usually show evidence of an obstruction. Ultrasound is the diagnostic
modality of choice and characteristically shows a target-like lesion
with 5 or more contiguous hyper- and hypoechoic, concentric bands
or rings in cross-section (Figure 263.6; ch. 262 [Figure

262.10]).76,77 In the longitudinal section, the invaginated portions
may be visible as hyper- and hypoechoic parallel lines. Intestinal wall
edema may make it difficult to distinguish the wall layers. Changes
consistent with local peritonitis and free abdominal fluid may also be
found. Rarely, in patients with an ileocolic intussusception, the
intussusceptum protrudes anally and is impossible to visually
distinguish from a rectal prolapse. Inserting a blunt probe between
the prolapsed segments can help distinguish a prolapse from an
intussusception as the probe can be inserted further than the edge of
the pelvis with an intussusception. This distinction has value in
terms of treatment approach.
Immediate surgery is the treatment of choice for intussusception,
but electrolyte shifts, dehydration, and acid-base imbalances must be
corrected prior to surgery (ch. 119). If the intussusception cannot be
reduced, resection and anastomosis is necessary; the ileocecal
junction should be preserved whenever possible. Postoperative
complications have been reported to occur in 35% of cases, 14% of
which were severe and life-threatening (e.g., septic peritonitis).
Postoperatively, food should not be withheld and feeding soon after
surgery is associated with a better prognosis.88,89,92,93

Colonic Torsion
Intestinal torsion (rotation along its longitudinal axis) or volvulus
(rotation around the mesenteric pedicle) are uncommon but lifethreatening conditions that can lead to ischemia/necrosis of the
affected segment of bowel and subsequent sepsis, circulatory shock,
and death. Early recognition is important to enable prompt
laparotomy. Risk factors include increased motility of the intestinal
tract, high-fiber diets, chronic constipation, colonic obstruction or
dilatation, and chronic intestinal inflammation. There are some case
reports describing strangulation with additional colonic torsion at a
gastropexy site. Primarily young to middle-aged, medium- to largebreed dogs are affected. Clinically, the dogs present with vomiting as
the most common clinical sign, typically associated with abdominal
distention and evidence of severe pain. Some dogs leak frank blood
from the anus. Hypovolemic shock is seen less frequently than in
patients with small bowel mesenteric volvulus or gastric dilatation

and volvulus (GDV). The diagnosis is initially based on radiographs.
A study including 14 dogs with surgically confirmed colonic torsion
showed segmental distention of the colon (14/14), focal narrowing of
the colon (11/14), displacement of cecum (11/14), and displacement
of descending colon (14/14).94 A barium contrast enema can
substantiate the diagnosis by showing the so called “torsion signs”
(narrowing of the colon and longitudinal striations that form a
helical pattern). An immediate exploratory laparotomy should be
performed if clinical signs and plain radiographs lead to a suspicion
of colonic torsion. A higher survival rate can be expected with rapid
surgical intervention.69,95-99

Other Non-neoplastic Obstructions
Foreign bodies, postoperative complications, inflammatory chronic
intestinal disease, and congenital changes are other non-neoplastic
causes of colonic strictures. Although postoperative complications
are the most common cause of colonic strictures in both dogs and
cats, they are rare and occur more frequently in the rectal region.
Clinically, a stricture should be suspected with the presence of
constipation proximal to a focal lesion. Endoscopy or negative
contrast imaging with air may help to establish a definitive diagnosis
(Figure 263.4). If a stricture is suspected or already diagnosed,
further diagnostics should focus on differentiating benign from
malignant strictures by ultrasound (e.g., increased wall thickness
and/or loss of layering in malignancy; Figure 263.5) and histologic
evaluation of tissue. Therapeutically, dilation with a balloon catheter
(benign stricture; ch. 116) or surgical removal of the lesion may be
attempted.

INFLAMMATORY DISEASES
Acute Colitis
Acute colitis is typically a self-limiting, sudden onset of largeintestinal diarrhea characterized by frequent defecation, tenesmus,
and substantial amounts of mucus in feces. The most important
causes of acute colitis include transient, uncomplicated protozoal,

bacterial, or viral infections; dietary indiscretion; adverse reactions
to food; and endoparasites. Fecal flotation is always indicated to
detect protozoal organisms and endoparasites as the inciting agents
or possible co-infection (ch. 80).
Differentiating acute colitis from acute hemorrhagic diarrhea
associated with toxic C. perfringens strains causing a severe acute
necrotizing and neutrophilic enterocolitis (so-called acute
hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome [AHDS]) can be difficult, especially
if dogs with AHDS are presented early in the course of the disease.
Toxigenic C. perfringens strains are found in healthy dogs, their
increase is only transient, and although proliferation of clostridial
strains (e.g., C. perfringens) and toxin release have been observed in
cases of canine acute colitis, it remains unclear if these are causative.
Consequently, documenting toxicogenic clostridial strains by fecal
PCR or by immunoassays for clostridial toxins by enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assay (ELISA) is not helpful.100-103 The most
important clostridial enterotoxin that has been reported to occur
frequently in dogs with bloody diarrhea is NetF enterotoxin.104
However, to date the implications of diagnosing NetF-related
diarrhea are unclear and showing the presence of this enterotoxin
does not constitute a necessity for starting antibiotic therapy. As
acute colitis is usually a self-limiting disease of short duration,
positive test results do not influence treatment decisions. Bacterial
cultures and PCR testing for other potential enteropathogenic
bacterial strains are also of limited value.62

Treatment
Dogs with acute uncomplicated diarrhea usually recover within a few
days with supportive treatment alone. Antibiotics are not beneficial
in most cases that respond well to dietary modification (e.g., low-fat,
highly digestible diet with fermentable fiber), toxin binding agents
(e.g., kaolin, charcoal, bismuth subsalicylate), and pain management.
Some dogs with severe tenesmus might benefit from anti-diarrheal
medications such as diphenoxylate or loperamide and from local
(e.g., budesonide rectal foam) or very short-, but systemically-acting
injectable corticosteroids. Long-term treatment with corticosteroids
should be avoided unless infectious colitis has been ruled out. Multi-

strain high dose probiotics and/or fecal microbiota transplantation
(FMT; ch. 106) might be effective to normalize the intestinal
microbiota.105
When acute colitis fails to respond to supportive, nonspecific
treatment within 7-10 days, a short-term trial with antimicrobials
(e.g., amoxicillin, tylosin, or metronidazole) might be performed,
especially if a neutrophilic inflammation is detected cytologically on
rectal scraping.106-113 Drugs containing anti-inflammatory 5aminosalicylic acid, such as sulfasalazine, are not routinely used in
acute colitis because of their delayed onset of action and potential for
severe adverse effects (e.g., anorexia, vomiting).

Chronic Inflammatory Enteropathy of the Large
Intestine
In patients with chronic inflammatory enteropathy (ch. 262),
clinical signs are present for longer than 3 weeks and there are
architectural changes of the mucosa, notably with an inflammatory
infiltrate (e.g., lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils, macrophages,
and/or neutrophils).114-117 Chronic inflammation can be triggered by
immune responses to intraluminal antigens (e.g., food allergens),118
infectious agents (e.g., parasites, enteropathogenic bacteria), and
commensal microbiota (e.g., dysbiosis) or may be due to a primary
dysregulation of the immune system.119-121 In many cases, the
etiology appears to be multifactorial.105,122-128 The term (idiopathic)
inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) implies that known causes of large
intestinal inflammation have been ruled out, trials with different
diets, anthelminthics and modulation of the intestinal microbiota
have failed, and the focus of treatment is on immunosuppression.

Idiopathic Chronic Inflammatory Enteropathy of the
Large Intestine
Idiopathic inflammation may involve any part of the GI tract. If the
colon is primarily affected, patients show chronic diarrhea, typically
with mucus and sometimes with fresh blood, urgency to defecate,
and tenesmus. In both major forms of IBD in humans—Crohn’s

disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC)—only specific parts of the
intestinal tract are affected. Granulomas (CD) and ulcerations (UC)
are consistent findings, and complications such as strictures and
fistulae (CD) may occur. In contrast, small animal patients with
chronic idiopathic inflammation demonstrate a diffuse infiltration,
predominantly with lymphocytes and plasma cells, and without
major mucosal defects. Eosinophilic inflammation can be the result
of an immune response to food antigens or parasites, or represent a
specific type of IBD. When inflammation is predominantly
neutrophilic or granulomatous inflammation, a primary infectious
etiology (e.g., E. coli-associated GC, Prototheca spp., H. capsulatum,
or Pythium insidiosum) should always be suspected; a very severe
form of idiopathic inflammation associated with colonic barrier
dysfunction and a secondary mucosal bacterial colonization also
could be possible.114,129

Etiology and Pathogenesis
The etiology of idiopathic chronic colitis appears to be multifactorial,
involving barrier dysfunction, an inappropriate immune response to
commensal bacteria and dietary components, intestinal dysbiosis,
and genetic susceptibility.

Barrier Dysfunction
The intestinal barrier is comprised of a mucus layer, the epithelial
lining, and the underlying lamina propria with its immune cells. In
the large intestine, the mucus layer is much thicker compared to the
small intestine and it forms 2 layers: an inner sterile layer and a
loosely adherent outer layer, which is heavily colonized by bacteria.
This mucus layer and the intestinal epithelium separate the luminal
microbiota from the mucosal immune system. A breach of this
barrier allows a close contact of the luminal microbiota and the
mucosal immune system and can trigger a sustained inflammatory
response. In addition, disruption of the colonic epithelium by acute
intestinal injury facilitates the translocation of dietary substances
and bacterial components and may lead to a loss of oral tolerance
against them. Acute enteritis is a well-recognized trigger of IBD and
irritable bowel syndrome in humans. Similarly, dogs with an episode

of acute, severe intestinal damage have an increased risk for
developing long-term intestinal disease later in life. Thirty of 71
(42%) dogs surviving a canine parvovirus infection showed chronic
diarrhea compared to only 8 of 67 control dogs (12%; P < 0.001).124
There was also a higher prevalence of chronic intestinal signs in dogs
with a previous episode of idiopathic acute hemorrhagic diarrhea
(22/80; 28%) compared to an age-and breed-matched control group
(9/71; 13%; P = 0.003).130 Thus, barrier dysfunction during an
episode of acute enteritis might represent an important mechanism
for inducing chronic inflammatory enteropathy in dogs.

Intestinal Microbiota
In an immunocompetent individual there is no inflammatory
response to the commensal colonic microbiota. In an experimental
study in mice, specific populations of bacteria were responsible for a
tolerogenic immune system and for the protection against
sensitization to food allergens. Further, the colonic mucosa of
germfree mice was deficient in regulatory T cells (Tregs). Specific
components of the microbiota are responsible for the induction of
colonic Tregs. Bacterial products bind to toll-like receptors, which
induce the production of interleukin (IL)-10 by macrophages in the
lamina propria, supporting Treg expansion and IL-10 release locally
and contributing to oral tolerance of harmless bacteria and food
components.128,131,132
The intestinal microbiota can influence the mucosal inflammatory
response via 3 main mechanisms: the presence of a true intestinal
pathogen, close contact of commensal bacteria and the intestinal
mucosal immune system due to intestinal barrier dysfunction (e.g.,
directly attached bacteria), and intestinal dysbiosis leading to a
proinflammatory intestinal environment. A specific role of bacteria
in the pathogenesis of IBD is supported by experimental studies in
rodents, which have shown that genetically susceptible individuals
do not have intestinal inflammation if they are germ-free; then, the
same rodents develop intestinal inflammation after bacterial
colonization. In addition, clinical improvement during antibiotic
therapy (so called antibiotic-responsive diarrhea [ARD]) can be

observed in about 10-20% of dogs with a chronic enteropathy.120,133
The treatment success is very likely due to the reduction of total
bacterial density and, potentially even more importantly, of
mucosally attached bacteria. After stopping antibiotics, bacterial
growth expands and patients usually show a relapse of clinical signs,
if the underlying disease process is not resolved (e.g., barrier
dysfunction, chronic inflammation). Thus, ARD should not be seen
as a distinctive disease, but rather 1 component of a multifactorial
disease.
Intestinal dysbiosis has been consistently described in humans
with IBD and companion animals with chronic enteropathies. Based
on a new validated assay to assess the intestinal microbiota in dogs,
the DI (ch. 260), up to 70% of dogs with chronic (inflammatory)
enteropathies are dysbiotic. Dysbiosis and mucosal inflammation are
interrelated as dysbiosis can be the cause or the consequence of
intestinal inflammation. States of dysbiosis are characterized by a
reduced diversity of the resident microbiota, including those that
affect intestinal barrier function and the regulation of mucosal
immunity. There is also a reciprocal signaling between the intestinal
microbiota and the immune system; thus, substances produced by
the host cells, such as defensins, shape the composition of the
intestinal microbiota. Disturbances in host-microbiota signaling may
adversely influence the inflammatory response in patients with a
chronic enteropathy.109

Genetic Susceptibility
A clear genetic susceptibility to IBD has been demonstrated in
humans, with an 8-10× higher risk among first-degree relatives
compared to the general population. So far, >150 gene loci associated
with an increased risk have been identified. Some are involved in
defective sensing of intracellular bacteria, indicating a connection
between disease susceptibility and host interactions with microbes.
In dogs, an increased prevalence of chronic inflammatory
enteropathies has been reported for German Shepherd Dogs, Great
Danes, Labrador Retrievers, Rottweilers, Boxers, and Rough-Coated
Collies, suggesting genetic susceptibility in these breeds. In humans,
a genetic predisposition for chronic intestinal inflammation is
primarily found in the major histocompatibility complex genes. In

addition, an alteration of the so-called NOD2-CARD15 gene is
frequently identified. This gene locus synthesizes products that
activate NF-kappa-B, a proinflammatory transcription factor, in
response to bacterial lipopolysaccharides. A polymorphism of the
NOD2 gene has been identified in various dog breeds. For example,
alterations in exon 3 of the NOD2 gene have been reported in
German Shepherd Dogs with IBD.124,134 Similarly, in some dog
breeds, certain genetic alterations increase activation of toll-like
receptors (TLR4 and 5).134 An alteration of TLR5 leads to an
increased sensitivity to bacterial flagellin. In addition, some dog
breeds show a mutation of the neutrophil cytosolic factor (NCF2)
gene. NCF2 is important for synthesis of a subunit of neutrophil
nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate hydrogen (NADPH)
oxidase that is necessary for intracellular autophagy. A mutation of
this gene has been reported in Boxers with histiocytic UC. Other
breeds are susceptible to lymphangiectasia and protein-losing
enteropathy (e.g., Rottweiler, Yorkshire Terrier, Norwegian
Lundehund, Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier), food intolerance (e.g.,
gluten hypersensitivity in the Irish Setter), or allergies (e.g., West
Highland White Terrier) (ch. 262).

Treatment of Chronic Colitis (Table 263.4)
Dietary Trials
Dietary trials should always be the very first step in patients with
chronic (inflammatory) enteropathies whose clinical signs persist
after anthelmintic treatment. Approximately 50% of patients will
respond to diet changes with partial or complete remission of clinical
signs. Different dietary strategies may be attempted: 1) high-fiber
diets (fermentable fiber to act as a prebiotic or non-fermentable fiber
to act as a bulking agent; ch. 165), 2) highly digestible, low-residue
diets (ch. 152), or 3) elimination diets (ch. 160). Several
consecutive diet trials of 2-3 weeks’ duration are often needed to
determine which food type works best for an individual patient.
Hydrolyzed diets or single protein/carbohydrate diets are useful to
identify adverse food reactions, which should be confirmed by
subsequent re-challenge with the previous food.
