Prebiotics and Fiber
Some dogs that are being presented for veterinary attention due to
typical signs of colitis and no histopathologic changes respond well
to fiber supplementation, but not all types of fiber have similar
effects. Different types of fibers should be used and gradually
increased in diet trials. A response should be assessed after 2 weeks
(ch. 165).135

Probiotics
Probiotics are live microorganisms which, in adequate numbers, may
confer a health benefit to the host. The positive effects are based on
the displacement of enteropathogens, immune modulation, and
strengthening the intestinal barrier function. Since every bacterial
strain has its specific functional properties, products with several
different bacterial strains are believed to be superior to single-strain
products. In animal models of colitis, probiotics can lead to
improvement of colonic disease. One study in dogs with IBD showed
a significant decrease in clinical severity scores in dogs that were
treated with a combination of prednisone and metronidazole (n=10)
as well as those on a high-dose probiotic (n=10), containing 8
different bacterial strains. An enhancement of regulatory T-cell
markers (FoxP3+ and TGF-beta+) and normalization of dysbiosis
after long-term therapy were specifically observed in the probiotictreated group. A second study including 30 dogs with chronic large
bowel diarrhea reported a rapid improvement of clinical signs in all
dogs after administration of a high dose of a probiotic mixture
combined with a high-fiber diet. Current data from only a few
controlled treatment trials in dogs and cats point toward a minor
clinical effect of probiotics in dogs and cats with colitis. If high dose
multi-strain probiotics are used, it should be in combination with
dietary intervention.120,121,136-138

Fecal Microbiota Transplantation
In fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), feces from a healthy
donor is transferred to the GI tract of a recipient. FMT can aid in
rapid restoration of the normal microbiota. As this increases the
diversity of the microbiome, metabolic capabilities are also
enhanced, and pathogenic bacterial groups are displaced. In patients
with acute GI disorders, such as parvovirosis and acute diarrhea, a
positive effect of a single rectal FMT, in addition to standard therapy,
has been documented. In patients with chronic intestinal disorders,
FMT only transiently improves dysbiosis if the underlying disease is
not resolved. Thus, repeated FMTs every 2-3 weeks may be used as
adjunctive treatment to standard therapy in dogs with chronic
enteropathies.105,109,111,132,139-143 The technique is described in ch.
106.

Antimicrobials
Antibiotic treatment should be restricted to patients with systemic
inflammatory signs and used only as a last choice in patients with
chronic enteropathies because they permanently damage the
resident microbiota and contribute to the development of resistant
bacteria. Metronidazole (mainly effective against anaerobic bacteria;
10 mg/kg PO q12h) or tylosin (broad-spectrum; 20 mg/kg PO q12h)
may improve clinical signs by reducing total and mucosa-adherent
bacteria. However, in studies of IBD, only 8-16% of dogs responded
to antibiotic treatment.120,133 Antibiotic trials should only be
considered after ruling out extraintestinal disorders, intestinal
parasites, and mucosal infiltration with fungi and algae and after
appropriate dietary trials in combination with modulation of the
intestinal microbiota by probiotics or FMT have failed. Also, patients
with moderate to severe lymphocytic-plasmacytic colitis will more
likely respond to anti-inflammatory medication than to
antimicrobials.129,144

Anti-inflammatory Drugs
Besides the classical immunosuppressants (ch. 144), there are also
local anti-inflammatory drugs that act primarily in the intestinal

tract (budesonide) or specifically in the colon (sulfasalazine).
Sulfasalazine is a prodrug in which the active ingredient, 5aminosalicylic acid (mesalamine), is combined with a
sulfapyridine.145 The anti-inflammatory effect only occurs in the
large intestine because the resident bacteria metabolize the prodrug,
leading to the release of mesalamine; this results in decreased
prostaglandin and leukotriene synthesis in the colonic mucosa. Full
anti-inflammatory efficacy should not be evaluated before 10-14 days
of treatment. Possible adverse effects include keratoconjunctivitis
sicca (KCS), acute pancreatitis, and acute vomiting.126 Thus,
adequate tear production must be confirmed by a Schirmer tear test
before and during treatment. KCS is reversible if treatment is
stopped immediately. Salicylates may cause toxicosis in cats and
should be used cautiously with a reduced dosage. New products have
been developed to overcome these adverse effects: olsalazine consists
of two 5-aminosalicylic acid molecules, which are released in the
large intestine in a pH-dependent fashion.
Budesonide is an orally administered, very potent glucocorticoid
(15 times more potent than prednisolone) with high local but low
systemic activity, due to high hepatic clearance. It has only weak
mineralocorticoid effects. Budesonide, given as coated granules, is
designed for a targeted release in the ileum and ascending colon in
humans and appears to be clinically effective in some dogs with
mixed or large intestinal inflammation. However, individual
treatment efficacy and systemic glucocorticoid side-effects are not
predictable, and a significant suppression of the hypothalamicpituitary-adrenal axis has been described in some dogs.

Immunomodulation/Immunosuppression
If dietary changes, modulation of the resident microbiota, and, in
dogs, the administration of sulfasalazine do not lead to an
improvement of clinical signs and if infectious colitis has been ruled
out (i.e., histopathologically with/without special stains), the next
step is anti-inflammatory and/or immunosuppressive medication.
The immunosuppressive drugs most commonly used for treating
colitis include predniso(lo)ne, cyclosporine, and chlorambucil.46,110
Adequate education of the pet owner is required.

Glucocorticoids
Systemic glucocorticoids are usually the first treatment and oral
predniso(lo)ne in dogs or prednisolone in cats is the drug of choice.
In cases where maintaining clinical remission requires a
glucocorticoid dosage that causes unacceptable adverse effects, the
authors combine corticosteroids with other antiinflammatory/immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., sulfasalazine,
cyclosporine, chlorambucil; ch. 169).

Cyclosporine
Cyclosporine is potent inhibitor of cell mediated immunity, which it
does by decreasing IL-2 production (ch. 144). Studies have shown
efficacy of cyclosporine in small animal patients with IBD,
specifically in cases refractory to corticosteroids. Various dosing
protocols are being used and the authors prefer to start at 2 mg/kg
PO q24h and gradually titrate the dose up to a target dosage of 5
mg/kg q24h to minimize GI side-effects. Other authors have treated
with dosages as high as 5 mg/kg PO q12h. The authors use
cyclosporine in combination with low-dose prednisolone (e.g., 0.25
mg/kg PO q24h), which usually keeps dogs with chronic immunemediated inflammatory enteropathies in remission. This
combination is usually well-tolerated. Dosages should always be
tapered to the lowest effective dosage of both drugs.146-148

Chlorambucil
Chlorambucil is a cytostatic alkylating agent that inhibits the
proliferation of rapidly growing cells. It has been used successfully in
dogs and cats with chronic IBD as well as in cats with feline
alimentary lymphoma (ch. 262). Chlorambucil appears to be potent
in the reduction of infiltrating inflammatory cells of the intestine. A
combination of chlorambucil and low-dose glucocorticoids is usually
well tolerated. Regular monitoring of bone marrow function (i.e.,
CBC) is recommended, specifically to rule out neutropenia.

INFECTIOUS COLITIS

Infectious diseases of the large intestine are less common than
immune-mediated inflammatory processes. The most common of the
many described pathogens in the dog appear to be E. coli causing GC
in predisposed breeds (French Bulldog and Boxer), and Prototheca
spp., H. capsulatum, and Pythium insidiosum in endemic areas. In
the cat, infections with T. foetus should always be considered in cases
of chronic large intestinal diarrhea, especially in cats with
hematochezia.

Bacteria (ch. 195)
The role of enteropathogenic bacteria in dogs with diarrhea has been
debated for many years. Campylobacter spp., Salmonella spp., and
enteropathogenic and enterotoxigenic E. coli may play a pathogenic
role in mixed or large bowel diarrhea. Similarly, cases involving
Anaerobiospirillum spp., Brachyspira pilosicoli, Yersinia
enterocolitica, C. perfringens, and C. difficile have been described.
However, these potential pathogens can also be detected in the GI
tract of apparently healthy dogs. Also, antibiotics should not be used
solely based on fecal culture. Unnecessary antibiotic treatment
destroys the protective intestinal microbiota, and resistant
enteropathogenic bacteria may gain a growth advantage, leading to
patients becoming permanent shedders of these resistant pathogens
(e.g., Salmonella spp.).62,149-153
Indications for antibiotics in dogs with diarrhea are patients with
immunosuppression and/or those with signs of sepsis/systemic
inflammatory response (Figure 263.7, Table 263.5) and
potentially those with an inflammatory pattern (i.e., primary
neutrophilic or granulomatous) on large intestinal biopsies that is
suggestive of bacterial mucosal invasion. Neutropenia represents a
high-risk factor for the development of sepsis. Immunosuppressed
dogs should be monitored closely for signs of a systemic
inflammatory response. In patients with E. coli-associated GC, a
specific diagnostic workup and antibiotic treatment must be
performed (see below). Caution and vigilance for sepsis should also
be exercised in animals in which adequate clearance of translocated
bacteria from the intestine cannot occur in the liver. This has been
the case in studies of dogs with high-grade hepatic dysfunction and
patients with congenital portosystemic shunts.

Sepsis or systemic inflammatory response syndrome criteria
adapted from human medicine are useful in the decision for or
against antibiotic treatment (ch. 128), but they must be assessed in
the context of the patient’s general clinical condition and hydration
status. For example, dehydrated patients may show clinical changes
that are similar to those of septic patients. At least 2 of the 4 criteria
listed in Table 263.5 should be met to warrant the use of
antibiotics.154,155
In septic patients, hypoalbuminemia, hypocalcemia, and
hyperbilirubinemia may also occur, as well as prolonged clotting
times due to a consumptive coagulopathy (ch. 171). Patients with
severe diarrhea and any systemic complications that have initially
been classified as non-septic should be closely monitored (e.g.,
hourly collection of vital signs, blood pressure, glucose
concentration).
If the decision for antibiotic therapy is made based on the
aforementioned criteria, a bacterial culture, including antibiotic
susceptibility, should be performed prior to treatment. Blood culture
is desired in septic patients, but it must be performed correctly (ch.
184). Evidence of lymphadenitis (e.g., hypoechoic areas suggestive of
microabscesses) or cholecystitis (e.g., thickened gallbladder wall with
an irregular mucosal surface) are indications for culture of aspirated
lymph node material or bile, respectively. Fecal culture for
enteropathogenic bacteria may help identify a specific
enteropathogen. Antibiotics effective only against obligate anaerobic

bacteria (e.g., nitroimidazoles, such as metronidazole) are generally
insufficient to treat enteric infections with systemic effects. Empiric
therapy with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid or ampicillin plus sulbactam
(both 10-25 mg/kg IV q8h), possibly in combination with
marbofloxacin (2-4 mg/kg IV q24h), can be given until the culture
and sensitivity results are available.
Finding a potentially pathogenic bacteria in the feces of dogs or
cats with diarrhea but without signs of systemic inflammation is
considered indicative of a microbial shift/dysbiosis. For example,
overgrowth of C. difficile in the feces of dogs is associated with a
reduction of protective and benign clostridial strains, such as C.
hiranonis. Intestinal dysbiosis is usually transient in patients with
acute enterocolitis, but persistent in those with chronic diarrhea
until the underlying enteropathy is resolved and the dysbiosis is
addressed. Detecting some enteropathogens (e.g., C. difficile) in the
feces in the absence of a systemic inflammatory response might be
an indication to try to shift the microbiome using dietary
modification, administration of probiotics, and/or fecal
transplantation.156,157

E. coli-Associated Granulomatous Colitis
GC, formerly histiocytic UC, is a chronic inflammatory large
intestinal disease, which primarily occurs in Boxer dogs and French
Bulldogs.43,63,64,114,116,129,144,145,158-163 The hallmark of this
disease is the presence of large, foamy, periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)positive macrophages infiltrating the colonic mucosa. A direct causal
role of enteropathogens is supported by detecting intramucosal E.
coli by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) in samples from
Boxer dogs and French Bulldogs with GC, but not in healthy controls.
Moreover, eradication of these invasive E. coli has been associated
with long-term clinical remission.

Etiopathogenesis
GC-associated E. coli invade the intestinal epithelial cells and are
then phagocytosed by the locally residing macrophages. A single
nucleotide polymorphism has been identified in the gene encoding
neutrophil cytosolic factor (NCF) 2. This gene region specifically

encodes for subunits of the multiprotein complex NADPH oxidase,
responsible for producing microbicidal, reactive oxygen species
within macrophages. Mutations in this gene are also known to cause
chronic granulomatous disease in humans with CD. There is strong
evidence that E. coli can invade and persist intracellularly in
intestinal epithelial cells, and macrophages trigger the chronic
inflammatory process in susceptible dogs.129,160

Diagnosis
Affected dogs are typically young and show clinical signs of chronic
colitis. In severe cases, they can even show weight loss. Infections are
more commonly associated with colonic disease rather than small
bowel disease. Colonic biopsies and histopathologic evaluation
should generally be performed earlier in the diagnostic workup.
Before any invasive diagnostic procedures (i.e., colonoscopy with
biopsy) are performed, a rectal examination to rule out obstructive
disease (e.g., anorectal stricture and neoplasia; ch. 3) and routine
clinicopathologic testing, including CBC, biochemistry profile,
abdominal imaging, and fecal flotation as well as antigen-testing for
Giardia and Cryptosporidium spp. (chs. 196, 262), should be
performed. A rectal scraping for cytologic analysis might be helpful
to detect other infectious agents such as Prototheca spp., H.
capsulatum, and Pythium insidiosum. A positive Giardia antigen
test should not postpone further diagnostic work-up since these
protozoa do not typically cause chronic large intestinal signs. Every
dog with chronic diarrhea should undergo routine deworming with
fenbendazole (50 mg/kg PO once daily over 3-5 days). Abdominal
radiographs can help distinguish obstructive (impacted large
intestine) from inflammatory (empty large intestine) disorders.
Abdominal ultrasound can identify focal structural changes such as
intussusception or neoplasia. In patients with chronic GC, the
colonic mucosa is usually thickened and irregular, and sometimes a
loss of layering of the wall can be seen (Figure 263.5).
Other differential diagnoses of chronic nonobstructive large
intestinal disorders include food responsive diarrhea and chronic
idiopathic diseases. Nevertheless, prolonged feeding trials and
immunosuppressants are not appropriate in breeds predisposed to
GC. Antimicrobials are contraindicated before performing a

complete work-up, including colonoscopy, colonic biopsies for
histologic evaluation (hematoxylin and eosin [H&E] and PAS stains;
FISH or immunohistochemical staining [IHC] for documentation of
mucosally invasive E. coli), and culture of the colonic mucosa. Since
lesions might show a patchy distribution, a minimum of ten
endoscopic biopsies should be collected. In financially limited
circumstances, ultrasound-guided or blind colon wall biopsies may
also be sufficient to obtain an accurate diagnosis; however, the owner
must be informed about the increased risk for complications. Typical
histologic lesions are mucosal ulcerations, infiltration with
histiocytes/macrophages and lymphocytes, and loss of goblet cells.
Based on signalment, characteristic histologic lesions, and
macrophages that stain positive with PAS, a tentative diagnosis of E.
coli-associated GC can be made. Ideally, invasive E. coli are
demonstrated in the mucosa by FISH or IHC (Figure 263.8). For
targeted antimicrobial usage, a culture of the colonic mucosa and
susceptibility testing for E. coli are necessary.43,63,64,129,159

Treatment
A successful outcome depends on the eradication of invasive E. coli.
Antimicrobials must be effective against the causative strains,
achieve an adequate intracellular concentration to eradicate the
bacteria in macrophages, and must be given long enough (e.g., 6-8
weeks) to eradicate all intramucosal bacteria. Although some dogs
with E. coli-associated GC respond within days to antimicrobials,
treatment should be continued strictly for 6-8 weeks. Treatment of
inadequate duration with enrofloxacin might be one of the main
reasons for widespread fluoroquinolone resistance. Recent studies
have shown fluoroquinolone resistance in ∼50% of dogs with GC,
making susceptibility testing mandatory. With adequate
antimicrobial treatment, positive long-term outcomes might be
expected in >80% of cases. In case of insufficient clinical response to
antimicrobials, repeated biopsy with histopathologic examination,
FISH/IHC, and culture can guide further treatment. Ongoing GI
signs despite eradication of E. coli can raise the clinician’s suspicion
of other conditions, such as food allergy. Treatment trials with
hydrolyzed diets might additionally be indicated.43,63,64,129,159

AlgaeProtothecosis
Prototheca spp. are unicellular achlorophyllous algae that exist
ubiquitously but are mainly found in such biologic niches as sewage,
stagnant waters, on plants, in soil, and in feces. After oral ingestion,
Prototheca spp. can cause severe disease in immunoincompetent
humans, dogs, cattle, and rarely in cats. There are 3 clinical forms of
protothecosis: the cutaneous/subcutaneous form, the systemic
disseminated form (i.e., various internal organ systems affected),
and the hematopoietic form (i.e., hematogenous or lymphatic system
affected).164-166

FIGURE 263.8 Fluorescence in situ hybridization
(FISH) and immunohistochemical staining (IHC) for
E. coli performed on a colonic biopsy from a male
Boxer with granulomatous colitis. A, FISH-positive
E. coli (white circles). B, IHC for E. coli, showing
abundant red immunolabeling throughout the
specimen with visualization of E. coli in the
cytoplasm of macrophages (black arrow). Courtesy
Patricia E. Ishii, Gastrointestinal Laboratory, College
of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences,
Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas.
Humans and cats mainly develop the cutaneous form, whereas in
dogs, the systemic or disseminated form is more common. The
systemic or disseminated form most commonly affects the GI tract,
especially the large intestine; the central nervous system and the
eyes; the kidneys; and bone, causing osteomyelitis. Affected dogs

often present with chronic large intestinal diarrhea, hematochezia,
blindness due to chorioretinitis and/or retinal detachment, and
seizures or ataxia. The Rhodesian Ridgeback has been reported to be
a predisposed breed.164-166 For mammals, P. wickerhamii and P.
zopfii are pathogenic. Humans are mainly infected with P.
wickerhamii and dogs with P. zopfii genotype 2. In a retrospective
study, 14/18 dogs were diagnosed with P. zopfii and 4/18 with P.
wickerhamii.167-169
CBC and serum biochemistry profile results are usually
unremarkable. A diagnosis can be made by cytologic evaluation of a
rectal swab (using a cytology brush), histopathologically on biopsy
specimens, or by culture. Prototheca spp. are only partially stained
by H&E, while PAS, silver, or Giemsa stains also stain their cell wall,
enabling easier detection. The organism may also be found in feces,
urine, and cerebrospinal fluid. An indirect ELISA for specific
antibodies against P. zopfii genotype 2 has demonstrated a
sensitivity and specificity of 100%. The disseminated form of the
disease, which affects mainly dogs, progresses over weeks to months
and is usually fatal. Response to treatment trials for several months
with amphotericin B and/or itraconazole can be difficult to predict
because there is a large discrepancy between the in vitro and in vivo
antimicrobial susceptibility. In a retrospective evaluation of 17 dogs
with systemic/disseminated protothecosis, 16 animals died or were
euthanized, with a median survival of 4 months. Although
Prototheca spp. have zoonotic potential, direct transmission is
unlikely if proper hygiene is prac-ticed.44,153,164-166,170-174

Fungi and Oomycetes
Almost any systemic mycosis can also affect the GI tract and colon.
These infections are discussed in more detail in their respective
chapters (chs. 207–209, 211). H. capsulatum and Pythium
insidiosum are particularly important in some regions (ch. 9).

Histoplasmosis
H. capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that grows in warm, moist, and
nitrogenous environments (e.g., water contaminated with bat or bird
excrement). Its epidemiologic and general clinical features are

described in ch. 209. Dogs may develop granulomatous
inflammation with ulceration of the GI tract. Infected dogs tend to be
young, large-breed dogs. The severity of clinical signs can range from
mild to severe, depending on the immunocompetency of the host.
Although GI tract infections primarily affect the colon, small
intestinal involvement with melena, watery feces, and intestinal
protein loss can occur. In cats, the GI tract is uncommonly affected.
The diagnosis and treatment are detailed in ch. 209. In addition,
supportive care with dietary modification, administration of
probiotics and fecal transplants, and locally acting anti-inflammatory
drugs (e.g., 5-aminosalicylate) can be provided. The prognosis
depends upon the severity of the disease. Animals with
histoplasmosis that have received glucocorticoids for “presumptive
IBD” may develop such advanced disease as to be fatal.45,153,175-182

Oomycoses
Pythium insidiosum, Conidiobolus spp., Basidiobolus spp. and
Lagenidium spp. are oomycetes found in aquatic environments.
Although caused by a phylogenetically diverse group of pathogens,
pythiosis, lagenidiosis, and zygomycosis share similar clinical and
histologic features. Young, male, large-breed dogs with access to
standing water appear to be predisposed. GI infections occur by
penetration of the mucosa. The zoospores that come in contact with
the (preinjured) mucosa encyst on the surface. The encysted
zoospores secrete an amorphous glycoprotein that mediates
zoospore adhesion to the tissue before they enter the tissue. In the
mucosa, the encysted zoospores develop hyphae that extend into the
tissue.
Dogs present with large intestinal or mixed small-large intestinal
diarrhea, weight loss, vomiting, and possibly fever. Abdominal
masses, which may produce obstruction, are sometimes palpable.
Cats are rarely affected. Ultrasonographically, severe segmental
thickening of the gastroduodenal and ileocolic portions of the GI
tract may be seen. Any segment of the GI tract can be affected.
Changes in mesenteric lymph nodes, blood vessels, the pancreas,
uterus, and prostate have also been described. The diagnosis is made
by histologic examination of deep wedge biopsies of the affected
areas. The predominant inflammatory pattern is eosinophilic and

pyogranulomatous in the submucosa and muscularis. A silver or PAS
stain is often needed to identify the nonseptate hyphae. PCR for P.
insidiosum can be performed from a fungal culture of biopsies and
antibody determinations (i.e., by ELISA or Western blot) are also
available. Mass lesions should be thoroughly resected, with 3-4 cm
wide margins in all directions. Postoperatively, itraconazole (10
mg/kg PO q12-24h) and terbinafine (5-10 mg/kg PO q24h) should be
prescribed for 2-3 months. Additional therapy with other antifungal
drugs (mefenoxam) or glucocorticoids has been reported. With
complete surgical excision, the prognosis is guarded; without it, it is
poor.183-185

Helminths
Schistosomiasis
Heterobilharzia americana is a schistosome that primarily affects
dogs in the southeastern and Gulf Coast regions of the USA.
Raccoons are known reservoir hosts and they excrete H. americana
eggs into water. Vectors (e.g., freshwater snails) excrete cercariae,
which in turn penetrate the skin of the dog and migrate through the
lungs and liver, growing into adult flukes. The flukes then migrate
into the mesenteric venules, resulting in severe granulomatous
inflammation of the intestinal wall and/or chronic hepatic fibrosis.
Clinically, dogs often show vomiting, blood admixed in feces, and
large intestinal diarrhea. Hypoalbuminemia and hyperglobulinemia
are common. Hypercalcemia may occur due to granulomatous
inflammation. Eggs in a fecal smear or upon fecal flotation, or in a
biopsy specimen from the liver or GI tract, are diagnostic. An antigen
ELISA test exists that can be performed on feces. A specific fecal PCR
for H. americana is the most sensitive and specific diagnostic test for
this disease in dogs.186
Recommended treatment involves high-dose praziquantel (25
mg/kg PO q8h for 2 days using tablets for use in humans) and
fenbendazole (50 mg/kg PO q24h for 10 days and repeated after 3
weeks). As long as the dog is not in liver failure due to cirrhosis, the
prognosis for affected animals after treatment is good to guarded.187193

Feline Strongyloidiasis
Strongyloides tumefaciens, the feline threadworm, is a rarely
diagnosed parasite of cats in warm regions of the USA near the Gulf
Coast and in tropical and subtropical regions. Larvae penetrate the
oral or esophageal mucosa or skin, migrate to the lungs, burst
through the alveoli, and are in turn coughed up and swallowed. Adult
worms then settle in the colon where they can create distinct 1-2 mm
nodules that can be visible during colonoscopy. They are the result of
an encapsulated, chronic, mixed inflammatory infiltrate in the
submucosa with eggs, larvae, and adults. Often times, affected cats
show no clinical signs. In young cats, however, severe large intestinal
diarrhea may occur. Observation of specific eggs during fecal
flotation is diagnostic. Larvae can be found by the Baermann
technique (ch. 80). Therapy includes fenbendazole (50 mg/kg PO
q24h) for 5 days. The prognosis is generally excellent.53,153,194,195

Whipworm Infection
Trichuris vulpis is a whipworm that frequently causes large
intestinal diarrhea in dogs. In cats, infection is rarely caused by T.
campanula and T. serrata. Trichuris is transmitted by ingestion of
ova, which develop in the small intestine into larvae and then
migrate to the ileum and colon. Adult worms tunnel their thread-like
bodies into the mucosa of the colon (and sometimes cecum),
producing severe colitis and typhlitis, respectively. Dogs of all ages
can become infected.
Clinical signs may be acute, intermittent, or chronic and include
classic large intestinal diarrhea with mucus, fresh blood, and
tenesmus, but subclinical infections do occur. In cases of severe
colonization, anemia, hypoproteinemia, and eosinophilia may also be
documented. Sometimes pseudo-hypoadrenocorticism (i.e.,
hyponatremia, hyperkalemia) may occur, but these dogs show
normal adrenal response to ACTH stimulation testing. The diagnosis
is made on routine fecal flotation (ch. 80). A negative result does
not rule out infection because eggs may be shed intermittently or
missed during flotation and whipworm infection is one reason
routine deworming should precede an intensive workup of colonic
diarrhea.

Effective treatments include fenbendazole, milbemycin,
moxidectin, and febantel, which is metabolized to fenbendazole and
oxibendazole (ch. 142 and textbook’s inside covers). Larval stages,
which may be present for 70-107 days, are less sensitive to therapy
and thus therapy should be repeated after 3 weeks and 3 months.
Eggs can survive in the environment for a long time, and intensive
environmental management is advisable. The prognosis is excellent
with adequate treatment.52,53,196-199

Protozoa (ch. 196)
Trichomoniasis
T. foetus is a flagellated protozoan with 3 anterior flagella and an
undulating membrane. Trichomonads may inhabit the GI tract (and
the genitourinary tract in people and cattle). They do not form cyst
stages; they divide by binary fission, and trophozoites are directly
transmitted from host to host. T. foetus is an important infectious
agent in cats, mainly causing large intestinal diarrhea. Cats usually
present with bloody diarrhea with associated weight loss or
inadequate weight gain. Sometimes fecal incontinence or rectal
prolapse due to tenesmus occurs. Cats usually appear alert and
maintain a good appetite. The infection occurs mainly in young cats,
especially those in multi-cat households or in animal shelters. Any
breed or mixed-breed cat can be affected. However, one study
described a breed predisposition for the Norwegian Forest Cat. In
some areas, the prevalence of T. foetus infestation is relatively high:
up to 20-31%. T. foetus mainly colonizes the distal ileum and colon
on the mucosa or in the lumen of the crypts; however, subepithelial
invasion also occurs. The infection results in plasmacytic,
neutrophilic, and lymphocytic inflammation.
Establishing a diagnosis of infection with T. foetus can be
challenging. Several methods have been described, but none shows
100% sensitivity, especially in antibiotic-pretreated animals. The
diagnosis can be made by direct saline fecal examination, selective
protozoan culture, specific PCR, or identification in colonic biopsies.
Notably, the sensitivity of routine fecal examination for diagnosis is
very low (2-14%), and T. foetus is often mistaken for Giardia. It is
also difficult to distinguish T. foetus from nonpathogenic

trichomonads. Cats with a previous diagnosis of giardiasis and no
improvement with fenbendazole therapy should be tested for T.
foetus. Microscopically, T. foetus trophozoites, in contrast to
Giardia, are conspicuous for their faster, erratic movement. Special
saline washes of the colon improve the detection of T. foetus (
Video 263.1). The collected fluid should be centrifuged promptly
(within a few minutes) and examined directly. However, sensitivity is
described as only 14%, even with immediate examination. Culturebased detection from feces can be attempted with a specific culture
medium (In Pouch TF, Biomed Diagnostics, White City, OR), but this
is relatively time consuming, requiring up to 12 days of incubation. A
real-time PCR using feces or the aforementioned colonic saline
swabs for T. foetus is currently the test of choice; however, a negative
PCR should not be overinterpreted. Cats may also be subclinical
carriers and have a negative PCR result. The feces should be fresh
because sensitivity decreases with prolonged cooling of the
specimen. Cat litter in the specimen may inactivate the PCR reaction.
A histopathological diagnosis of T. foetus is only conclusive in a
positive case. If there is a high-level of suspicion of a T. foetus
infection in a young cat with colonic diarrhea, the tests should be
combined or repeated if the result is negative.
Treatment of T. foetus consists of ronidazole. The recommended
dosage is 30 mg/kg PO q24h for 14 days. Neurotoxicosis, although
reversible in most cases, is common enough that therapy should be
initiated only with a confirmed diagnosis. If diarrhea persists for >2
weeks despite therapy, a repeated real-time PCR should be
performed and repeat treatment with ronidazole at 30 mg/kg PO
q12h should be considered. If untreated, cats usually recover within 5
months to 2 years. The time to obtain complete treatment response
is longer in cats in multi-cat households and in cats that had
previously received various antibiotics. It is important to note that
the absence of clinical signs is not equivalent to the absence of the
pathogen. In dogs, T. foetus plays no role as a colonic infectious
agent.54-61,153,194,200,201

adenoma of the colon in an 8-year-old Sheltie

Giardiasis
Dogs and cats with giardiasis may present with mixed diarrhea but
Giardia spp. are regarded as small intestine parasites (ch. 262). The
diagnosis and other aspects are discussed in ch. 196. Importantly,
infection should be treated only when clinical signs are present, in
which case fenbendazole and strict environmental hygiene is the
therapy of choice. In order not to cause long-term, severe dysbiosis,
metronidazole should not be used initially, especially in young
animals with giardiasis. Interestingly, case reports have shown
eradication of Giardia in dogs by fecal transplantation (ch. 106).202

Balantidiasis
Balantidium coli is primarily a parasite of pigs. Dogs can become
infected accidentally, leading to UC, when they are in contact with
pigs. Therapy with tetracyclines and metronidazole is used
successfully in humans. Coinfection with T. vulpis is common and
some animals respond well upon eradication of T. vulpis.203

Amoebiasis
Entamoeba histolytica primarily infects humans and leads to
amoebic dysentery. Animals usually become infected from diseased
humans. Although E. histolytica is present in the intestinal tract of
healthy dogs and cats, there are case reports of this organism causing
severe colitis. The diagnosis can be made by fecal smear.
Metronidazole (30 mg/kg PO q12h for 3 weeks) is the drug of choice
for treatment. However, neurotoxicosis is well-documented at this
high dosage (ch. 248).204-208

Viruses
Feline Infectious Peritonitis
Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) is caused by a mutated form of the
enteric feline coronavirus and is usually a disease that affects
multiple organ systems (ch. 200). When manifesting in the
intestinal tract, the colon may also be affected. Affected animals
show ultrasonographic bowel wall thickening either diffusely or as
focal nodules/masses. Associated lymph nodes may also be enlarged.
The diagnosis is made by IHC detection of the FIP virus in biopsy
specimens. Recent experimental studies showed remission of
clinical, laboratory, and ultrasonographical signs after
administration of a nucleoside analogue, GS-441524 (ch. 200).209212

NEOPLASIA
Etiology

Colonic neoplasms are uncommon in dogs and cats, but in dogs the
colon is the most common site for GI neoplasia. Affected dogs
typically are 7-11 years old, while cats have a median age of 12.5 years
at presentation. Adenocarcinoma (

Video 263.7) is the most

common (43% and 46% in dogs and cats, respectively) and
lymphoma is second (41% and 19% in dogs and cats, respectively;
ch. 322).70,78 Less frequent are mast cell tumor (ch. 327),
leiomyosarcoma or other stromal tumors (GI stromal tumor [GIST];
ch. 324) and plasmacytoma (ch. 322).213-216 Most tumors
originate in the descending colon or rectum, but leiomyosarcomas
commonly arise in the cecum.217 German Shepherds, West Highland
White Terriers, and Collies are overrepresented with
adenocarcinomas. Neoplasia with benign behavior (i.e., polyps [
Video 263.8], adenomas [

Video 263.5], leiomyomas) also do

occur (Figure 263.9). The Miniature Dachshund appears to be
predisposed to adenomatous colonic polyps. As in humans,
adenomas and polyps can rarely transform into adenocarcinomas in
dogs.70,78,218
In the cat, lymphoma occurs as the second most common tumor
type of the large intestinal tract (alimentary lymphoma; chs. 262,
322). Dependent on the type of therapy, response and median
survival time (MST) differ. Small cell lymphoma has the most
prolonged survival (MST, 18-30 months) and large granular
lymphoma the shortest (MST, 21 days).219-223 Alimentary
lymphomas are usually T-cell lymphomas and, unlike mediastinal
lymphoma, are not associated with feline leukemia virus infection.
Rare case reports of fibrosarcoma, ganglioneuroma,
hemangiosarcoma, and neurofibrosarcoma, or indolent follicular
lymphoma do occur.213

Physical Examination
Clinical signs of all these tumors include hematochezia, tenesmus,
possible bowel obstruction, and occasionally perforation. Local

neoplastic changes can lead to increased intestinal wall permeability,
translocation of intestinal bacteria, bacteremia, and possibly sepsis.
The differential diagnoses always include other structural changes
such as intussusception, FIP in cats, granulomas, strictures, foreign
bodies, hematomas, or fungal granulomas. A comprehensive workup
should always be done early in the disease course in older animals
with fresh blood in their feces. As leiomyosarcoma and leiomyoma
do not infiltrate the mucosa, hematochezia is less common.214,215,224
Paraneoplastic disorders include hypoglycemia due to insulin-like
substance secretion from GIST tumors (especially leiomyoma, ch.
324) and hyperglobulinemia in patients with plasmacytoma, due to
monoclonal antibody production leading to hyperviscosity syndrome
(ch. 331). In patients with diffuse alimentary lymphoma, there may
be anorexia and vomiting. Lethargy, signs of abdominal pain, and
weight loss may also occur. If a tumor ruptures spontaneously, acute
onset of lethargy, fever, signs of abdominal pain, vomiting, and even
collapse may occur.

Diagnosis
Rectal masses can be palpated in about 70% of cases with colonic
neoplasia.225 In cats, a mass is identifiable during abdominal
palpation in about 50% of cases.226 Larger masses and associated
lymph node enlargement might be detected radiographically
(Figure 263.4). However, ultrasound is the most helpful tool for
visualizing neoplasia of the colon, often revealing focal thickening of
the intestinal wall with complete loss of normal wall layering. In cats,
ultrasound is diagnostic in 85% of cases of malignant colonic
neoplasia.226 Fluid accumulation cranial to the obstruction may be
visible in large tumors. Regional lymphadenomegaly may be due to
metastatic infiltration or translocation of intestinal bacteria through
the permeable intestinal wall (Video 263.3

).70 In cats, care must

be taken when interpreting intestinal thickening
ultrasonographically, since chronic enteropathies may cause
thickening of the cecal wall and thus mimic neoplasia. In one study,
benign typhlitis associated with intestinal wall thickening was

described histopathologically in 13/18 animals.227 In dogs, focal
large intestinal wall thickening or a mass effect is frequently seen
with leiomyosarcomas.224
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of focal masses may be
helpful, but histopathologic evaluation of an endoscopic biopsy is
usually required for a definitive diagnosis (Videos 263.5, 263.7,
263.8

). Focal changes, with a mass effect, mucosal bleeding,

increased mucosal friability, erosions, and ulcers can be present.
Samples from the tumor itself can sometimes reveal only tumor
necrosis. It is crucial to collect multiple deep biopsy samples not only
from altered tissue, but also from adjacent healthy tissue, and the
transition zone between the two. Colonic perforation during
colonoscopy is a rare complication.80 Cross-sectional imaging (CT
and MRI) can be valuable in assessing lesion dimensions and
detecting metastatic lesions.

Treatment
Treatment depends on the tumor type, the presence of metastases,
and tumor size. Tumor staging should include thoracic radiographs
or CT and fine-needle aspiration of regional lymph nodes.
Obstructive tumors (e.g., adenocarcinoma, leiomyosarcoma) must be
completely excised with an endorectal pull-through excision for
distally located tumors or pelvic osteotomy for colorectal
adenocarcinomas. In cats with adenocarcinomas, local metastases
are often widespread and subtotal colectomy is recommended
instead of local excision. Better survival rates are described when
surgery is combined with carboplatin chemotherapy. In patients with
large cell lymphoma, initial excision is controversial, but 1 study
showed better survival rates with chemotherapy with prior removal
of the primary intestinal tumor. Various chemotherapeutic protocols
have been described for lymphoma (ch. 322).223
In some dogs with large intestinal neoplasia, upregulation of
cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) has been described and COX-2 inhibitors
(piroxicam, meloxicam) have also been used in non-lymphoma
colonic tumors.228-230 In patients with plasmacytoma, excision with

adjuvant chemotherapy (prednisolone, melphalan) has been
described (ch. 322).216 When removing polyps via colonoscopy,
recurrence should be expected if the stalk remains. An attempt
should be made to gently loosen the mucosa surrounding the polyp
with Allis forceps to be able to also remove the stalk. Additional
argon plasma coagulation can be applied.

Prognosis
The prognosis after excision for polyps and leiomyomas is excellent
but for most malignant colonic tumors it is guarded to poor. After
excision, dogs survive a median of 22 months and cats a median of 15
months without adjuvant chemotherapy. For patients with
adenocarcinoma, the MST in dogs is 1.6 months and cats that
received subtotal colectomy survived longer than those with only
mass removal (138 versus 66 days).226,231,232

CONSTIPATION
Etiology and Pathophysiology
Constipation is defined as the difficulty with defecation leading to 3
or fewer bowel movements per week. It is usually associated with an
increased mass of stool in the rectum and colon. Acute constipation
does not necessarily progress to chronic disease if treated adequately
and promptly because transient dilation of the large intestine does
not necessarily cause permanent loss of function. Chronic
constipation is defined as infrequent defecation for at least 3
consecutive weeks. Obstipation is a more severe form of constipation
associated with permanent loss of colonic function and it is not
reversible even with medical treatment.

Many different risk factors and secondary causes of constipation
have been described and should be considered. First, an obstruction
(i.e., extramural, intramural, or intraluminal) should be
distinguished from nonobstructive causes (i.e., inflammation or
neurogenic, metabolic, pharmacologic, environmental, or behavioral
factors) (Table 263.6). In hospitalized animals, constipation may
occur as a multifactorial problem (e.g., decreased physical activity
plus colonic hypomotility due to the underlying disease [e.g.,
pancreatitis] or treatment with opioids). Such secondary risk factors
should be addressed early to avoid long-term complications.
In a retrospective study of cats with chronic constipation, 62% had
idiopathic disease. Extraluminal obstruction (e.g., pelvic canal

stenosis) was the second most common cause (23%). Neurologic
(6%) and specific breed-related changes (e.g., spinal cord lesion of
the Manx cat, 5%) were described less frequently. Few cases were
caused by neoplasia or were iatrogenic (e.g., colopexy).
Hypo-/aganglionosis was suspected in 2% of cats. In one young cat
with feline megacolon, aganglionosis was diagnosed histologically.
The differential diagnoses for chronic feline constipation are listed in
Table 263.6.
Megacolon is the end stage of colonic dysfunction and it primarily
occurs in cats. There are 2 pathogenic mechanisms at play: dilation
and hypertrophy. Dilation most frequently occurs as the end stage of
an idiopathic colonic motility disorder with permanent loss of
microscopic colonic structure and function. Drug treatment may be
attempted, but most cats require subtotal colectomy. Animals with a
hypertrophic megacolon secondary to obstruction may respond to
early intervention (e.g., osteotomy for obstructive bony lesions).
Hypertrophic megacolon will evolve into a dilated, irreversible form
if intervention is not undertaken promptly. Nonobstructive
idiopathic feline megacolon may begin in the descending colon and
progress to the ascending colon. In vitro measurement of isometric
strain has shown less intense smooth muscle response to various
neurotransmitters (i.e., acetylcholine, substance P, cholecystokinin)
and less membrane depolarization.233-238

History and Physical Examination (Box 263.2)
Constipation, obstipation, and megacolon can occur in animals of
any age, either sex, and any breed. In cats, males are overrepresented
(70%). It is most common in Domestic Shorthair cats (46%),
Domestic Longhair cats (15%), and Siamese cats (12%).233-235,238

History
Affected cats typically exhibit absent, decreased, or painful
defecation over days, weeks, or months. Often, the animals have
been pretreated with home remedies by the pet owner. Cats may
experience increased and prolonged sitting in the litter box. Cats
tend to present later in the disease course compared to dogs because
defecation often is not observed by owners. Hard feces will
distinguish constipation from tenesmus due to diarrhea. However,
the defecation stimulus triggered by constipation can sometimes lead
to episodes of diarrhea, even in animals that are obstipated.
Tenesmus ani (GI disease) must be differentiated from tenesmus
vesicae (urogenital disease) through careful history-taking and, if
possible, observation of tenesmus by the veterinarian in person or
via videorecording (ch. 51). Clients may mistakenly believe their
anorectic dog or cat is constipated because it has not produced stool

with its usual frequency, without realizing that fecal output is also
reduced when food intake is reduced. The history must include
questions regarding possible underlying orthopedic and neurologic
disorders. Additional clinical signs may include blood stains during
defecation from chronic large intestinal irritation, anorexia causing
weight loss in chronic cases, and vomiting due to the stimulation of
stretch receptors in the colon.

Physical Examination
On physical examination, abdominal palpation may reveal evidence
of constipation, especially in small dogs and cats but less so in obese
animals or large dogs. Attention should be paid to signs of
dehydration, weight loss, and evidence of abdominal pain. The
anogenital region should be carefully examined for painful lesions
that may explain why an animal refuses to defecate, and a rectal
examination should be performed on all animals with constipation
(with sedation if needed) (ch 3). Rectal examination is essential to
identify rectal canal obstructions. The osseous pelvic ring should be
palpated carefully to detect a possible stenosis. Rectal examination
may also reveal foreign bodies, bone impactions, fecal consistency,
diverticula, strictures, perineal hernias, or neoplasia. It may be
necessary to repeat the rectal examination using different body
positioning to identify dynamic strictures.
Careful neurologic (ch. 241) and orthopedic (ch. 31)
examinations should be performed to evaluate the caudal spinal cord
reflexes and the autonomic nervous system (e.g., lack of urine
output, bradycardia, hypersalivation, mydriasis, decreased
lacrimation, or nictitating membrane prolapse).

Laboratory Changes and Diagnostic Imaging
The general laboratory workup for animals with constipation is often
unremarkable. Nevertheless, CBC, serum biochemistry profile, and
urinalysis are recommended to identify possible metabolic
disturbances (e.g., hemoconcentration, electrolyte disturbances such
as hypercalcemia or hypokalemia). Thyroid function (T4, TSH)
should be evaluated because constipation is a common clinical sign
of hypothyroidism, especially in cats with congenital hypothyroidism
(ch. 286). All animals with constipation must have abdominal

radiographs (minimum 2 orthogonal views) to investigate
obstructive causes of constipation, both intraluminal (e.g., foreign
bodies, mineral-opacity feces) and extraluminal (e.g., osseous
changes) (Figure 263.10; Box 263.2). Radiography with negative
contrast after evacuation of the colon may identify a stricture
(Figure 263.4,

Video 263.2). Ultrasound of the abdomen may

reveal enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes (chronic inflammatory
colonic irritation)71,239 (Video 263.3

). Focal masses of the

colonic wall may be visible (neoplasia), in which case the next step
may be colonoscopy with collection of biopsies for histopathologic
examination (ch. 107). Endoscopy can also help detect diverticula,
strictures, or inflammation of the colonic mucosa. In animals with
neurologic changes, additional cross-sectional imaging (i.e., CT and
MRI) may be performed (ch. 112). Anorectal manometry and
histopathologic examination of tissue specimens are necessary to
diagnose congenital aganglionosis.236

Treatment (Table 263.7)
A single episode of constipation does not necessarily require therapy.
However, recurrent episodes are an indication for medical treatment.
If the condition is not idiopathic, the underlying disease should be
identified and addressed. Often, mild to moderate constipation can
be treated on an outpatient basis with dietary modification and the
administration of laxatives and/or enemas. Prokinetics may also be
administered. In cases of severe constipation, initial inpatient
therapy consisting of enemas given under anesthesia with manual
fecal removal followed by outpatient treatment is usually necessary
to prevent recurrence. In cats with megacolon, subtotal colectomy is
indicated if drug therapy does not lead to adequate improvement.
Osteotomy must be considered for patients with a pelvic canal
stenosis.

Removal of Impacted Feces
Impacted feces can be removed with rectal suppositories, enemas,
and manually (ch. 108). Rectal suppositories of glycerol (lubricating

laxative) or bisacodyl (stimulant laxative) can only be used in
compliant animals and can be administered alone or with oral
laxatives. Enemas are more common and are administered using
warm water (in large dogs) or physiologic saline (in small dogs and
cats) at a dosage of 10 mL/kg, infused through a soft rectal catheter.
Mineral oil and lactulose may be added. Enemas containing sodium
phosphate should never be used in cats or small dogs because they
can cause severe or even fatal electrolyte shifts (i.e., hypernatremia,
hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia) and life-threatening
dehydration. Manual evacuation of stool from the colon may also be
required in conjunction with administration of an enema.

Oral Laxatives
The mode of action of laxatives is based on stimulating fluid
accumulation in the colon, thereby increasing motility.

Bulk-Forming Laxatives
Fiber preparations usually consist of polysaccharides and psyllium
that are poorly absorbed (ch. 165). They can either be a dietary

ingredient or a supplement (e.g., psyllium 1-4 teaspoons [5-20 mL]
per meal or pumpkin 1-4 tablespoons [15-60 mL] per meal). These
are only effective if the animal is well-hydrated and eating. In
patients where megacolon has already developed, fiber supplements
should be avoided, and a low-residue diet should be fed instead to
reduce the amount of fecal material produced.

Hyperosmotic Laxatives
These include indigestible polysaccharides (e.g., lactose, lactulose),
magnesium salts (e.g., magnesium citrate, magnesium hydroxide,
magnesium sulfate), and polyethylene glycols. Lactulose (0.5-2
mL/kg PO q8-12h) is the most potent and frequently used laxative in
this group.

Stimulant Laxatives
These are characterized by their ability to induce propulsive motility
(e.g., bisacodyl, phenolphthalein, castor oil). Bisacodyl (5 mg per cat
PO q24h) is the most effective laxative in the cat. It acts via nitric
oxide-mediated epithelial cell electrolyte secretion and myenteric
neuronal depolarization. Since there is evidence that continuous
daily administration of bisacodyl irreversibly damages the myenteric
plexus, it should only be used for short periods.

Lubricating Laxatives
These facilitate defecation and interfere with the absorption of water
from the colon. Mineral oil is the most commonly used lubricating
laxative. As aspiration can easily occur during oral administration,
these substances should only be used in compliant and fully mentally
responsive animals.240-242

Prokinetic Agents
Prokinetics may help improve colonic motility in mild recurrent or
first time moderate to severe constipation. However, in the presence
of definitive megacolon, no significant clinical improvement can be
expected from the administration of prokinetics.

These agents stimulate motility throughout the GI tract and have
relatively few adverse effects. The most commonly used preparations
contain serotonergic 5-HT4 agonists. Prucalopride (0.01-0.2 mg/kg
PO q12h) is currently recommended for use in these patients.
Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analog that is used as a
gastroprotective agent to prevent nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory
drug-induced gastric ulceration. However, faster GI transit time and
diarrhea have been described as adverse effects. Misoprostol is an
effective anti-constipation agent in humans, and it may be useful in
animals with refractory constipation. In vitro studies in dogs and
cats also show a beneficial effect on intestinal smooth muscle. While
ranitidine, an H2 receptor antagonist, has shown a prokinetic effect
in in vitro studies, this effect has not been confirmed in vivo and this
class of drugs should not be used for constipation.238,243-247

Surgery
In cats with megacolon, medical therapy is usually unsuccessful, and
colectomy appears to be the only reasonable treatment. The
prognosis for cats that survive the postoperative period after
colectomy is good, especially if the ileocecal valve is preserved.
However, self-limiting diarrhea can be expected for a few weeks after
surgery.237,248-250

CLIENT INFORMATION
Diseases of the Large Intestine
The colon represents the main part of the large intestine with a
length of approximately one-fifth of the entire gastrointestinal tube.
The main function of the colon is the absorption of water and
electrolytes. The colon is also responsible for storage and processing
indigestible food material after most nutrients have been absorbed in
the small intestine. Approximately half of the weight of the feces in
the colon consists of bacteria (intestinal microbiota), which are
essential for the production of various substances, including some
vitamins. The resident microbiota is also crucial in suppressing
specific organisms that can cause disease, plays a significant role in
the immune response, and can have pro-inflammatory and antiinflammatory effects on the intestinal tract.
The most commonly diagnosed chronic large bowel diseases
causing diarrhea are food responsive enteropathy, parasites, and
idiopathic chronic colitis. Much less common are chronic infectious
colitis, anatomic abnormalities, and cancer of the large bowel.
Patients with large intestinal disease usually show a high defecation

frequency (i.e., ≥5 defecation episodes per day), straining to defecate,
urgency to defecate, and mucus and/or blood coating the feces. Acute
symptoms are frequently self-limiting and usually do not require an
in-depth evaluation. Fecal flotation is always indicated to detect
certain types of intestinal parasites. Dogs with acute uncomplicated
diarrhea usually recover within a few days with symptomatic
treatment (i.e., treatments that are directed at the symptoms your
pet shows rather than the underlying cause). These treatments may
include a highly digestible diet that is lower in fat, pain medication,
or a probiotic. Antibiotics are usually not indicated. Chronic diarrhea
(i.e., diarrhea that persists >2-3 weeks) usually necessitates a
systematic diagnostic work-up of your pet. A thorough history is an
important first step in the diagnostic work-up and should include the
following information:
• Onset and duration of clinical signs
• Travel history (lived or traveled in a region with potential
exposure to certain infectious organisms)
• Previous deworming
• Dietary history (current diet; any improvement upon a
previous diet trial)
• Drug history (current treatment; medication prior to the onset
of gastrointestinal signs; any improvement on previous
treatments)
• Information about disease severity (e.g., activity, appetite,
vomiting, stool consistency/frequency, weight loss)
Further diagnostics are guided by history and physical
examination findings. In chronic uncomplicated diarrhea, a
minimum database including fecal flotation, assessment of the
intestinal microbiota (e.g., Dysbiosis Index), complete blood count
(CBC), serum biochemistry profile, and serum cobalamin and folate
concentrations should be performed to rule out extraintestinal
diseases, and assess the involvement of the small intestines and the
severity of the disease. Therapeutic trials may be beneficial in these
cases, including deworming for parasites that have evaded detection
previously, multiple dietary trials with restricted antigens (i.e., novel
protein source, hydrolyzed protein), or the supplementation with
fermentable fiber, modulation of the intestinal microbiota (e.g., high

dose multi-strain probiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation) and
local anti-inflammatory drugs. In those cases with signs of systemic
illness, complications (e.g., abdominal pain, hematochezia), a
predilection for bacterial invasion of the colonic mucosa (e.g., Boxer
dogs and French Bulldogs), and/or a lack of response to therapeutic
approaches within the first 2-4 weeks, a more extensive diagnostic
workup is warranted (e.g., special laboratory tests, imaging,
colonoscopy and histological evaluation of mucosal biopsies).
Stefan Unterer (Zürich, Switzerland) and Melanie
Werner (Zürich, Switzerland)
