Rectoanal disease, defined as a structural or mechanical
abnormality of the rectum and/or anal canal, can pose a significant
source of pain and discomfort for any patient. Possible consequences
of rectoanal disorders include dyschezia, tenesmus, potentially fecal
incontinence, and often a reduction in quality of life (ch. 51). A
thorough history (ch. 2), physical examination (PE) (ch. 3), and
diagnostic plan are key in the identification and treatment of
rectoanal disorders. Failure to resolve the disorder can be distressing
for both the pet and the owner, and might result in unnecessary
euthanasia.

ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF
DEFECATION
The most distal portion of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract is the
rectoanal canal, beginning with termination of the colon into the
proximal rectum. The rectum is delineated from the descending

colon by the pelvic inlet, is approximately 5 cm in length depending
on patient size, and is surrounded by the perineum. Termination of
the rectum marks the beginning of the anus. Both rectum and anus
have a mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, and serosa, similar to other
parts of the alimentary tract. The serosa and muscularis of the
rectum are continuous with that of the colon. The rectal epithelium is
columnar, and contains a large amount of mucus-secreting goblet
cells to help facilitate the passage of feces. The epithelium transitions
to squamous in the anal canal, which is also where the internal anal
sphincter (IAS) begins. The remaining epithelium of the anal canal is
divided into columnar, intermediate, and cutaneous zones.1 The
columnar zone connects rectum to anal canal. The intermediate
zone, otherwise known as the anorectal line, denotes separation of
the columnar from cutaneous zones.
The muscles that surround the rectum are the ventral
sacrococcygeal muscles dorsolaterally and levator ani muscle
laterally. The levator ani and coccygeal muscles together make up the
pelvic diaphragm (Figure 264.1). The rectococcygeus muscle is
responsible for elevating the tail during defecation, and originates
from the longitudinal muscularis layer of the distal rectum.1
Important structures in the anal canal include the IAS and external
anal sphincter (EAS). The IAS originates from the circular layer of
the rectal muscularis, is comprised of involuntary smooth muscle,
and serves only as a landmark with virtually no role in maintaining
fecal continence. In contrast, the EAS is a ∼1-1.5 cm band of
voluntary striated muscle that acts as the main determinant of fecal
continence. The innervation of the rectum, muscles of the pelvic
diaphragm, IAS, and EAS (Figure 264.1) includes parasympathetic
nervous system (PSNS), sympathetic nervous system (SNS), and
somatic fibers that work together to facilitate storage (i.e.,
continence) or expulsion (i.e., defecation) of feces. Parasympathetic
fibers of the pelvic nerve innervate the rectum which, when
activated, stimulate rectal motility. Sympathetic fibers of the
hypogastric nerve course via spinal cord segments L1-L4 and L5, and
are inhibitory to the rectum and facilitatory to the IAS. Somatic
fibers of the pudendal nerve innervate the EAS. Because these same
nerve fibers also innervate the urinary bladder, problems with
urinary storage and voiding are sometimes observed concurrently

with rectoanal disorders. Dysfunction of any part of these nerves can
result in fecal incontinence.
Successful defecation occurs when the urge to defecate is deemed
“appropriate” in the cerebral cortex, and coordination of the PSNS
and somatic nervous systems contract abdominal muscles while
simultaneously relaxing the EAS. Somatic fibers from the sacral
plexus and the pudendal nerve function to either contract (i.e.,
storage phase) or relax (i.e., defecation) the EAS (Figure 264.1).
Sacral nerves also act to contract muscles of the pelvic diaphragm via
the PSNS.
A series of subconscious reflexes occurs in between bowel
movements in order to ensure that the rectum can maximize storage
of feces in order to reduce frequency of defecation. The gastrocolic
reflex is initiated secondary to ingestion of food, and refers to
movement of feces from the distal large intestine (LI) into the
rectum. If the rectum is able to expand in order to accommodate the
feces, it will do so via relaxation of the IAS. The conscious urge to
defecate will be suppressed. This expansion of the rectum via
relaxation of the IAS is called the rectosphincteric inhibition reflex.2
Feces will then be stored until another fecal ball moves into the
rectum and increases intrarectal pressure. The storage phase of
defecation refers to the recurring act of rectal accommodation (i.e.,
relaxation of the rectum in response to increased intraluminal
pressure from feces) so that a greater volume of stool is stored with a
lower intraluminal pressure.3 As fecal matter in the rectum increases
and rectal luminal pressure rises, the urge to defecate becomes
stronger. Once the intraluminal pressure of the rectum reaches its
maximum threshold, the rectosphincteric inhibition reflex is
suppressed and EAS striated muscle tone increases. This increased
tone sends a signal to the brainstem via afferent fibers in the rectal
wall.4 When defecation is deemed appropriate by the cerebral cortex,
an impulse is transmitted via the brainstem to lower motor neurons
(LMNs) of the pelvic nerve, which stimulates colonic and rectal
motility. A series of colonic giant migrating contractions (CGMCs)5
provides the force necessary for expulsion of feces from the rectum.
As the CGMCs propel feces aborad, somatic fibers via the pudendal
nerve relax the EAS as abdominal and diaphragmatic muscles

contract to increase intraabdominal pressure. The combination of
the increased intraabdominal pressure and the force of the CGMCs
allow for successful defecation.

FIGURE 264.1 Neural control of defecation.
Sympathetic, parasympathetic, and somatic nervous
system pathways are denoted by red, blue, and black
nerves, respectively. Created with Biorender.com.
The most external structures of the distal alimentary tract include
the perineum, anal sacs, and surrounding skin. The skin of the
perineum is drained by superficial inguinal lymph nodes, while
deeper soft-tissue structures drain via the large medial iliac lymph
node. The anal sacs are located bilaterally at approximately 4 and 7
o’clock ventrolateral to the anal canal. Also called the paranal
sinuses, these sacs are open structures containing apocrine,
sudoriparous, and some sebaceous glands. Anal sac orifices are
visible if the skin flanking the anus is gently rotated ventrolaterally.
Cats have anal sacs with fewer apocrine glands as well as slightly
more laterally positioned orifices compared to the dog.6 Other
important glandular regions in the anal canal and sacs are the anal
and paranal sinus glands. The anal glands are tubuloalveolar glands
that open into the anal canal via the columnar and intermediate

zones and produce fatty secretions. The function of these glands
remains largely unknown. The paranal sinus glands are hepatoid
glands that open into the anal sacs, and produce pasty secretions
thought to be important for territorial marking. These glands
continue to grow in intact male dogs secondary to circulating
androgens, and might develop into perianal adenomas later in life.

HISTORY AND PHYSICAL EXAM
The clinical history of patients with rectoanal disease varies in
severity and chronicity depending on underlying etiology, but often
includes tenesmus, increased urgency to defecate, dyschezia, and/or
constipation (i.e., reduced frequency of defecation) (ch. 51). Owners
frequently mistake clinical signs of rectoanal disorders with those of
colonic disease. Most LI disorders will have a component of
constipation, diarrhea, or both. This can be a helpful feature in
differentiating strictly LI versus rectoanal diseases. If tenesmus is the
chief concern, the clinician must differentiate intestinal from lower
urinary tract (LUT) disease (chs. 54 and 263). This is because the
same nerves that innervate the rectum also innervate the bladder,
and can disrupt normal micturition.
Common clinical signs of rectoanal disease include increased
frequency of licking the anus and/or perianal skin, vocalization
during defecation, hematochezia, and potentially “scooting” (a dog
pulling itself forward by its forelimbs, with hindlimbs extended
forward and tail extended backward, to rub the perineum on the
ground) if the anal sacs are involved. Systemic signs are uncommon
except in cases of infectious or neoplastic disorders. Patients might
develop hyporexia if there is discomfort from fecal impaction and/or
local tissue inflammation. Rectoanal masses and strictures often
cause luminal narrowing, resulting in flattened or “ribbon-like” feces.
Disorders commonly diagnosed from a PE alone include atresia
ani (AA), perineal hernia (PH), and perianal fistula (PAF; i.e., anal
furunculosis) (ch. 3). A rectoanal mass or foreign body (FB) is often
palpable on abdominal palpation and/or digital rectal examination.
Anal sac abscesses or masses are similarly often visible on inspection
of the perianal region or palpable upon rectal examination. A

superficial inguinal lymphadenopathy is commonly seen with
perineal inflammation.

DISEASES OF THE RECTUM
PROCTITIS
Proctitis is an inflammation of the rectum and anus, and often
develops secondary to colitis, PAF, or perineal inflammation. Local
trauma, rectal FBs and local radiation therapy can also cause
proctitis. No sex or age predispositions have been identified, but
breeds predisposed to colonic or perianal diseases might be
overrepresented (e.g., German Shepherd Dogs [GSDs] for PAF;
Boxers and French Bulldogs for granulomatous colitis [GC] [see ch.
263]). Common clinical manifestations of proctitis often mirror
those of LI disease (chs. 51 and 263), with the exception of
constipation. Instead, increased frequency and urgency of defecation
is a hallmark of proctitis. Infectious etiologies, such as protothecosis,
should be suspected if there are concurrent ocular abnormalities
(e.g., uveitis) (ch. 13).7

Diagnosis
A thorough rectal examination is imperative in order to rule out
rectal or anal masses and FBs (ch. 3). Visual inspection of the
perineal region is important to look for perineal herniation, fistulas,
and anal sac abnormalities. Fecal examination for parasites (ch.
80), empirical deworming (ch. 142 and textbook’s inside covers),
highly digestible (i.e., altered fiber) or elimination diet trials (ch.
152, especially if there are concurrent dermatologic abnormalities
[ch. 160]), and potentially colonoscopy or proctoscopy (ch. 107)
are often necessary in the diagnostic workup. Rectal scrapes are
often successful in diagnosing protothecosis (ch. 263).7 Proctoscopy
is especially indicated if the pets’ clinical signs have been chronic,
unresponsive to initial therapies and/or are worsening. A diagnosis
of immune-mediated inflammation is made based on either
histopathologic confirmation of lymphoplasmacytic or eosinophilic

inflammation or a favorable response to immunosuppressive
therapy.

FIGURE 264.2 Severe colorectal prolapse in a
Domestic Shorthair cat (A) and a French Bulldog
(B). Courtesy Drs. Katee Adair and Cassie Lux,
University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN.

Treatment
Therapy is specific to the underlying cause, and varies depending on
whether the proctitis is acute or chronic. The diagnostic decisionmaking process for proctitis is similar to that of LI disease (ch. 263).
Immune-mediated and food allergic cases might require lifelong
dietary, anti-inflammatory, and/or immunosuppressive
management. Local anti-inflammatory suppositories (i.e.,
budesonide, hydrocortisone, or tacrolimus foams) might be useful
for short-term palliative care, while waiting for more chronic
therapies to take effect.

Prognosis

The prognosis depends on the underlying cause. If the etiology is
correctly identified, clinical disease can often be controlled if not
entirely resolved.

Rectal Prolapse
Rectal prolapse (RP) refers to partial or complete protrusion of the
rectum through the anus. A partial RP comprises the herniation of
mucosa only, whereas a complete RP implies that all layers of the
rectum are involved. Complete prolapses are the most common. Both
cats and dogs can be affected, with no sex or breed predilections
reported.

Pathogenesis
Specific factors contributing to the development of RP remain largely
unknown. In most cases, an underlying mechanical or functional
disorder is present. These include dyschezia and proctitis (e.g., LI
enteropathies, parasites, anal sac disorders), colorectal and rectoanal
tumors, any condition causing tenesmus, LUT disorders, PHs, and
dystocia (ordered based on frequency).1 Congenital conditions such
as colonic duplication8 and colorectal polyposis with
ganglioneuromatosis9 have been associated with RP in young dogs.
As some cases have no identifiable underlying condition, an
individual predisposition might also exist.

Diagnosis
Visual confirmation of a cylindrical mass protruding from the anus is
often diagnostic. In rare, severe cases, parts of the distal colon might
also prolapse (Figure 264.2). Accompanying perineal erythema
and swelling are common. Ileocolic intussusceptions (ch. 263),10,11
while rare, are an important rule-out to consider. Tritrichomonas
foetus must be a differential for cats with chronic LI diarrhea,
especially those which are younger, purebred and reside in densely
housed environments (ch. 196). T. foetus is one of the more
common causes of RP in the cat.12,13 A minimum database is often
unremarkable in patients with RP, but investigation for diseases
causing stranguria, colitis, and proctitis is important. This includes

fecal flotation in all cases (ch. 80), diagnostic imaging of the
abdomen, and potentially endoscopic biopsies (ch. 107).

Treatment
Gentle manual reduction with or without placement of a pursestring
suture around the anus might be sufficient for partial RP, or patients
presenting for the first or second time that also have healthy rectal
tissue. The anal orifice should be large enough for softened feces to
pass through, but small enough to prevent another prolapse.
Placement of a red rubber catheter through the anus during
placement of the pursestring can help prevent suture
overtightening,14 and the catheter is removed after completion of the
procedure. For recurrent or chronic cases, surgical correction of the
prolapse via colopexy15 is recommended. Rectal resection is
sometimes necessary if the prolapse is chronic, with identifiable
tissue ischemia and necrosis. Identification and management of
underlying conditions such as LI enteropathies (ch. 263), intestinal
parasites (ch. 142), or LUT conditions (chs. 307-315) is indicated.

FIGURE 264.3 Rectal pull-through procedure in a
dog with rectal adenocarcinoma. Courtesy Dr. Vanna
Dickerson, Texas A&M University, College Station,
TX.

Prognosis
The long-term prognosis is variable depending on the extent and
chronicity of prolapse at presentation, with a better prognosis given
to acute and/or partial cases. Any prolapse requiring rectal resection

has a worse prognosis due to the risk of postoperative stricture
formation.14

RECTAL NEOPLASIA
Colorectal tumors comprise up to 60% of all GI neoplasms in dogs
and cats.16 They include benign polyps and adenomas, with a lower
percentage of adenocarcinomas, lymphomas, leiomyosarcomas,17
hemangiosarcomas, and plasmacytomas.18 Colorectal follicular
lymphoma, a rare indolent lymphoma, has recently been reported in
dogs.19 It is common for adenomatous polyps to undergo
transformation into carcinoma in situ and eventual malignancy20
over time. Collies and Miniature Dachshunds are predisposed to
inflammatory rectal polyps.21,22 Siamese cats are overrepresented
for alimentary lymphoma (chs. 262, 322),23,24 but it is unclear if
this includes rectal tumors.

Diagnosis
Rectal masses are often identified via digital palpation on rectal
examination (ch. 3). Hematochezia (ch. 50) is the most common
clinical sign of colorectal neoplasia, including benign polyps,20 but
tenesmus, dyschezia and/or a change in stool shape are also
reported. It is rare that cytologic findings from a rectal scrape are
diagnostic, as many of these tumors exfoliate poorly. Definitive
diagnosis usually requires histopathologic evaluation of tissue, which
can be obtained from biopsies either via colonoscopy or, in many
cases, by proctoscopy (ch. 107). Rectal masses are variable in
conformation (e.g., pedunculated, polyploid, or annular) and size. A
large retrospective study reported that out of 82 dogs with multiple
rectal masses, including those located at the colorectal junction, no
concurrent colonic masses were identified.25 While colonoscopy
remains the gold standard to rule out additional proximal masses,
this study implies that proctoscopy might preclude the need for
colonoscopy in financially restricted cases. Full staging including

thoracic radiographs, and abdominal ultrasound (AUS) is ideal for
all patients, as these pets are often older and might have metastases
or unrelated neoplasms that could alter the diagnostic plan.

Treatment
Surgical resection of locally invasive rectal masses is recommended.
A rectal pull-through (RPT) technique26 (Figure 264.3) is one of
the most common approaches. Other surgical approaches include
open abdominal, transpelvic, or mucosal eversion depending on the
extent of the mass. Mass location and invasiveness usually dictate
surgical technique, with the ideal procedure maximizing a chance for
complete surgical resection. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories, such
as piroxicam, might help alleviate inflammation and discomfort,
especially in patients with nonresectable disease.27

Prognosis
Short- and long-term prognoses are variable, depending on tumor
type, invasiveness at the time of diagnosis, and therapeutic plan (i.e.,
surgery, radiation therapy, or both). Annular masses (ch. 263) have
a worse prognosis than polyploid or pedunculated tumors,28 which
is likely related to the ease of complete resection. Adverse effects
from surgery are variable and patient dependent, but must be
discussed with the owners prior to surgery. A large study of
postoperative complications from RPTs26 found that while nearly
80% of patients had complications, the median survival times
(MSTs) for dogs with carcinoma and carcinoma in situ were
approximately 700 and 1000 days, respectively. Commonly reported
complications include fecal incontinence (56% of all dogs, with 53%
of those permanently incontinent), diarrhea, tenesmus, stricture
formation, dehiscence, constipation and local infection.26
Adenocarcinomas, lymphoma, and plasmacytomas reportedly recur
more frequently.1

RECTAL AND ANAL STRICTURES

Rectoanal strictures develop secondary to a variety of neoplastic and
nonneoplastic conditions. These include colorectal FBs,29 congenital
malformations,30,31 recent colorectal surgery,31 and
inflammatory29,32 and infectious (i.e., histoplasmosis [ch. 209],
protothecosis [ch. 263], pythiosis [ch. 263]) etiologies.31 Purebred
kittens29 and GSDs31 might be overrepresented, given their
predisposition for congenital malformations and PAF, respectively.
Though one smaller study found a predisposition for male dogs,31 a
sex predisposition has not been consistently identified.

Diagnosis
While most strictures are palpable on digital rectal examination,31 a
definitive diagnosis relies on direct visualization with contrast
radiography (ch. 263; Figure 263.4) or colonoscopy (ch. 107).31
The most common clinical signs include tenesmus and constipation
(ch. 51), followed by hematochezia (ch. 50), dyschezia, and
diarrhea (ch. 49).29,31 Strictures are variable in length and can
range from a focal narrowing to a longitudinally strictured area. Pets
with strictures secondary to FB ingestion often have a grossly and
histologically normal colon, aside from the stricture itself, which is in
contrast to patients with diffuse, infiltrative colonic disease. While
colonoscopy is ideal to evaluate for LI disease, it is most important in
confirming that the balloon or bougienage for treatment spans the
length of the stricture and that triamcinolone injections are
appropriately placed.

Therapy
Many dogs and cats with nonneoplastic etiologies have done well
long term with balloon dilatation,32 local triamcinolone
injections,31,32 and even digital bougienage.29 It is common for cases
to require more than 1 balloon or bougienage procedure,29,32 which
should be communicated clearly to the owner at the time of
diagnosis. Analgesics, stool softeners, fiber supplementation and

prokinetics might be necessary for variable periods of time,31
potentially lifelong. In a retrospective study of inflammatory
strictures in dogs and cats, all cats were placed on psyllium-enriched
diets following bougienage and maintained clinical improvement for
the duration of the study.29

Prognosis
Most animals with benign strictures have a good long-term
prognosis if owners can afford multiple, repeat dilatations.31
Complications associated with dilatation procedures include
colorectal perforation, abscess formation, and hemorrhage.29 Pets
with strictures secondary to neoplasia have a worse prognosis,
although palliative options such as stenting (ch. 116)33 are available
to improve the quality of life in the short term.

RECTOANAL MALFORMATIONS
Atresia ani (AA) and rectovaginal fistula (RVF; ch. 313) are the most
common congenital malformations in puppies and kittens. They can
occur together34-36 or as separate entities. A prevalence of 0.007%
has been reported for AA in dogs.37 Females might be
overrepresented for both conditions,36,37 as well as Boston Terriers
and Toy Poodles.37,38

Pathogenesis
Both AA and RVF arise from problems with embryonic development.
Because of this, affected pets commonly have concurrent urogenital
malformations (ch. 313). Four different types of AA exist, depending
on the specific developmental arrest. A grading scheme categorizes
AA into types I-IV37 (Figure 264.4); only types I-III have been
reported in cats and dogs.

Diagnosis

The diagnosis is often made based on visual inspection of the anus
and perineal region. Abdominal distention (ch. 21) and tenesmus
(ch. 51) are commonly reported clinical signs, with perineal swelling
and a stenotic or absent anal orifice often seen on PE (ch. 3).38 Pets
with an imperforate anus are unable to defecate. Sometimes,
additional extraintestinal congenital defects (e.g., cleft palate,
hydrocephalus, open fontanelle, skeletal malformations) are present.
Female puppies and kittens with urogenital malformations are more
likely to have secondary vulvar dermatitis and/or cystitis. Moderate
to severe megacolon is often present on plain-film abdominal
radiographs.38 Iodinated contrast material can be used for
confirming the exact type of defect(s) present. A complete blood
count (CBC) and serum biochemistry profile are often normal for
young animals, with the exception of a urinalysis, which might show
an active sediment if there is communication between the urinary
and GI tracts.

Treatment
Surgical correction via anoplasty is the treatment of choice for AA
types II-III,38 with or without ballooning of the stricture. Many
puppies with type I AA do not require anoplasty, as ballooning is
sufficient. Prior to proceeding with anoplasty, owners should be
made aware that fecal incontinence is a common postoperative
complication.38 A “fistula flap” technique might offer the best chance
at preserving continence as it reportedly causes the least amount of
damage to the EAS.39 Postoperatively, puppies and kittens should
receive a low-residue diet (ch. 152), stool softeners (ch. 108), and
analgesics (ch. 6). Some patients may require stool softeners and
dietary modification for life.

Prognosis
Correction of type I and II AAs usually results in favorable long-term
survival (MST, 41 months) with a perceived good quality of life,
whereas patients with a type III AA often do poorly in comparison.38

PERINEAL HERNIA
Perineal hernias (PHs) are one of the most common acquired
rectoanal disorders seen in dogs. A PH results from failure of the
muscles of the pelvic diaphragm to function properly, causing
abdominal contents to inappropriately “push through” the perineum.
The levator ani and coccygeus are the most commonly affected
muscles, with dysfunction of only 1 muscle being enough to allow
herniation. Structures most likely to herniate are the prostate,
bladder, rectum, and/or abdominal fat. Hernias can be unilateral or
bilateral, although a higher incidence of right-sided hernias has been
documented.40 Predisposed breeds include the Boston Terrier, the
Miniature Poodle, and the Pekingese.41 Brachycephalic dogs are
overrepresented. Cats develop PHs infrequently compared to dogs.

FIGURE 264.4 Schematic for grading of atresia

Pathogenesis
Various anatomic and functional abnormalities are thought to
contribute to PH development. Male dogs are overrepresented,42,43
which is attributed to both thinner levator ani muscles and a possible
hormonal influence.43 Hormones and proteins that have been
implicated in the pathogenesis of muscle atrophy include relaxin,44
epidermal growth factor,45 and estrogen. Relaxin, produced by
placenta and prostate, likely plays a significant role as hormone
concentration and muscle weakening are positively correlated.44
There is conflicting evidence about the role of estrogen in this
disease.46,47 Any disorder causing increased intra-abdominal
pressure (e.g., stranguria, constipation, colorectal masses,
prostatomegaly) increases the risk for herniation.48 Comorbidities
(e.g., trauma, chronic cough)43 are commonly identified in female
dogs with PH. Cats are underrepresented compared to dogs, but
when they are diagnosed with PH, cats often have comorbidities,
such as megacolon or historical perineal urethrostomy.49-51

Diagnosis
Most PHs are diagnosed based on history, visual inspection of the
perineum, and rectal palpation. Tenesmus and perineal swelling are
the most common clinical signs for both dogs and cats, followed by
constipation, dyschezia, and erythema of the anus.41,49 Deviation of
perineal tissues to the side of the hernia is evident in unilateral cases,
with generalized subcutaneous “ballooning” of the tissues in
bilaterally affected dogs (Figure 264.5, A and B). Only about 20%
of cats have visible perineal swelling.49 Some hernias are not visually
apparent, and require palpation of the defect on rectal examination.
Rectal palpation is also important in differentiating between
reducible and non-reducible hernias, with a non-reducible PH
necessitating surgery. A subset of these patients presents as surgical
emergencies due to herniation and entrapment of the bladder,
known as urinary bladder retroflexion (UBR), or other abdominal

organs.41,52-54 UBR occurs in ∼18-25% of dogs with PH.52-54
Complications associated with UBR include diminished blood flow to
the bladder wall, resulting in ischemia and necrosis41,53 (Figure
264.6), with potential postrenal azotemia secondary to urinary tract
obstruction. Entrapment of the bladder or intestinal loops results in
an acute abdomen (ch. 126).
CBC and serum biochemistry profile results are often
unremarkable, unless a systemic disorder (e.g., colorectal neoplasia,
prostatic disease) or organ entrapment is present. In these cases,
clinicopathologic evidence of acute kidney injury (AKI) (e.g.,
azotemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperkalemia; ch. 300) and/or
systemic inflammation (e.g., leukocytosis, hyperglobulinemia; ch.
128) might be present. Diagnostic imaging is often necessary to
determine the severity of complications and/or underlying
comorbidities not evident on PE. Plain radiographs (Figure 264.5,
C), perineal ultrasonography, and contrast radiography might be
necessary to assess for organ entrapment, confirm uni- or bilateral
herniation, and screen for predisposing comorbidities. These include
colorectal masses (ch. 263), prostatic (e.g., prostatitis, benign
prostatic hypertrophy [BPH], neoplasia; ch. 314) and LUT disease
that might cause stranguria with secondary PH (ch. 54).

FIGURE 264.6 Urinary bladder retroflexion and
entrapment pictured intraoperatively in a dog with a
perineal hernia. Courtesy Dr. Whitney DeGroot,
Veterinary Emergency Clinic, Toronto, Ontario,
Canada.

FIGURE 264.7 Perianal fistulae in 2 different
German Shepherd Dogs. The tracts can form a
trajectory that is either parallel (A) or perpendicular

(A) and/or purulent discharge (B). Courtesy Dr.

Station, TX, and Dr. Linda Frank, University of
Tennessee, Knoxville, TN.

Treatment
Smaller patients and minor hernias can sometimes be managed
medically with stool softeners, enemas, and intermittent manual
extraction of feces. If UBR or other organ entrapment exists, manual
decompression via emergency cystocentesis and immediate surgery
are mandatory. The primary goal of surgical repair always involves
reconstruction of the pelvic diaphragm. Traditional surgery refers to
a herniorrhaphy, often with an internal obturator muscle
transposition.55-57 Herniorrhaphy is usually sufficient for most
uncomplicated PHs, but further steps to strengthen the pelvic
diaphragm might be necessary. Additional measures include
polypropylene mesh reinforcement,58 semitendinosus muscle flap
transposition,59 and/or biological membrane implantation.60,61
Repositioning or pexy of entrapped organs might be necessary prior
to herniorrhaphy.53 Colopexy is not the recommended repair of
choice unless RP is also present.15,52 For intact males, castration is
recommended given that intact status is considered a risk factor
(e.g., increased relaxin, enlarged prostate compressing pelvic wall).

Prognosis
The prognosis varies depending on whether underlying
comorbidities and organ entrapment are present. While some studies
have cited UBR to predict a worse prognosis (e.g., a 30% mortality
rate in a large study of 100 dogs41), a case series of 41 dogs with PH
found no increase in mortality between dogs with and without

UBR.52 The most common short-term postoperative complications
include incisional infection, RP, and tenesmus, in order of
occurrence.41,62 Postoperative tenesmus is a risk factor for
recurrence with an internal obturator muscle transposition.55

PERIANAL FISTULA/CANINE ANAL
FURUNCULOSIS
Perianal fistulas (PAFs), which are synonymous with canine anal
furunculosis, are characterized by ulceration, draining tracts,
purulent discharge, and necrosis of perianal tissue (Figure 264.7).
The disease is most similar to fistulizing Crohn’s disease in humans,
although communication between draining tracts and the rectal
lumen is rarely seen in dogs. Severe cases might develop rectoanal
stenosis, structuring, or PH. GSDs are overrepresented, comprising
up to 85% of some PAF populations.63 A genetic component is
suspected to be part of the underlying pathophysiologic mechanism
in this breed.64-66 Other recognized breeds include the Australian
Shepherd, Beagle, Border Collie, Bouvier des Flandres, English
Bulldog, Irish Setter, and Labrador Retriever.67-69

Pathogenesis
Factors that might play a role in the development of PAF in GSDs
include canine major histocompatibility complex (MHC) immune
response genes, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and certain matrix
metalloproteinases (MMPs).64,70,71 A study looking at 107 GSDs
with PAF in the United Kingdom versus healthy breed-matched
controls found that dog leukocyte antigen (DLA)-DRB1∗00101 was
positively associated with the presence of PAF.64 Homozygous dogs
also tend to develop PAF at a younger age (< 8 years).64,65 Further
evidence for a genetic basis in GSDs is the positive association of
ADAMTS16 and CTNND2 gene regions with the presence of PAF,
determined from a large genome-wide association study.66

Importantly, the CTNND2 gene has been linked to Crohn’s disease
and ulcerative colitis in people. mRNA expression of proinflammatory cytokines (i.e., interleukins 1-beta, 2, 6, and 8, and
tumor necrosis factor [TNF]-alpha)70 and MMPs-9 and 1371 is
increased in the tissue of PAF dogs compared to healthy controls.
The MMPs are produced by macrophages, and might signify type 1
helper T-cell dysfunction as an important contributing factor. While
these findings suggest that pro-inflammatory cytokines contribute to
PAF development, the anti-inflammatory IL-10 has also been
identified as increased,70 making it challenging to decipher whether
the altered cytokines contribute to or are a result of PAF. It has been
determined that TNF-alpha is likely elevated due to a linkage
disequilibrium with an abnormal DLA-DRB1∗0010165 due to the
close proximity of the 2 genes in the MHC. These associations point
towards a dysregulation in T-cell immunity, especially considering
that biopsies from dogs with PAF have shown increased aggregates
of CD3+ lymphocytes63 and type 1 T helper cell mRNA expression.70
Other conditions that might contribute to PAF development
include a high moisture environment from low tail carriage,
preexisting bacterial infection, an increased density of perianal
apocrine glands,72 and potentially cutaneous adverse food reactions
(CAFRs, ch. 166).73,74 A recent study investigating the intestinal
microbiota of dogs with PAF identified some clinically affected dogs
as dysbiotic (i.e., increased abundances of Bacteroides vulgatus and
Escherichia coli and decreased abundances of Megamonas sp. and
Prevotella copri), while others had a normal microbiota.75

Diagnosis
Middle-aged, adult dogs (mean age: 4-7 years)76 most commonly
develop PAF. Presenting clinical signs often include excessive
grooming, tenesmus (ch. 51), hematochezia (ch. 50), purulent
discharge from beneath the tail (Figure 264.7, B) and in some
cases, fecal incontinence. Because there is an established association
between PAF and colitis,77 dogs might also present with signs
indicative of LI disease (ch. 263). Differential diagnoses should

include ulcerated perianal tumors (e.g., adenomas,
adenocarcinomas), abscesses, FBs or, less commonly,
mucocutaneous lupus erythematous (MCLE; ch. 178).78 PAFs and
MCLE can usually be differentiated based on differences in lesion
distribution. With MCLE, lesions usually appear slightly merged
together rather than divided into distinct “tracts” as seen with PAF.78
Visual inspection of the perianal region is often sufficient to
definitively diagnose PAF, especially in predisposed breeds. Careful
assessment of the anal sacs, digital rectal examination, and
expression of the anal sacs should be performed. Sedation is often
necessary to accomplish these tasks due to extreme discomfort of
that region. Further imaging such as fistulograms might be necessary
for select cases in order to assess for rectocutaneous fistulas (i.e.,
communication with the rectal lumen). Biopsies are often
unnecessary, but can be performed if concurrent colonic disease is
suspected or if PE alone does not differentiate PAF from MCLE.

Treatment
PAFs pose a therapeutic challenge, as remission cannot be achieved
in all cases. The goals of treatment, which should be emphasized to
owners, are to slow disease progression and ideally induce clinical
remission. Medical management is standard, and surgery should
only be pursued if comorbidities (e.g., abscessation) exist at the time
of diagnosis or if 6 weeks of medical therapy fails to induce
remission.67 The cornerstone of medical management is
immunosuppression, including calcineurin inhibitors (i.e.,
cyclosporine A [CsA], tacrolimus), steroids, and nonsteroidal
immunosuppressive agents (e.g., azathioprine, mycophenolate
mofetil [ch. 144]). Calcineurin inhibitors are preferred as they
specifically inhibit T-cell-mediated immunity. A randomized,
controlled trial comparing single agent CsA with placebo in 20 GSDs
found that all dogs in the CsA group (n=10) showed improvement in
lesions after 4 weeks of therapy, with 85% achieving remission by 16
weeks.69 None of the control group dogs achieved remission. The
dosage and formulation of CsA are also important to consider. While
various dosages and dosing frequencies (i.e., once79,80 or twice81

daily) have successfully induced remission,69,79,81 higher dosages
are associated with an improved chance of success.80 Ketoconazole
(KZ) is commonly used in conjunction with CsA to reduce the dosage
of CsA (chs. 139, 141). This helps reduce the cost of treatment as
well as potential side-effects associated with CsA. Controlled studies
assessing the efficacy of combination CsA-KZ have documented 65100% of dogs achieving remission 3-16 weeks into therapy.82-84 All
dogs have maintained remission throughout the duration of the trial.
A dosage range of 2-4 mg/kg/day CsA combined with 5-10
mg/kg/day KZ is a currently acceptable starting regime,67 with
recommendations to escalate the dosage if no improvement is seen
in the first 4-5 weeks.80 Once there has been substantial clinical
improvement, the dosage of CsA should be slowly tapered (e.g., ∼25%
reduction every 4-8 weeks), if appropriate based on clinical status.
Microemulsified or modified formulations are preferred due to
increased bioavailability (ch. 169). The CsA should be administered
on an empty stomach (i.e., ≥2 hours before and after a meal) to
maximize absorption. Controlled studies evaluating topical
tacrolimus are lacking. In one published study, 50% of dogs treated
with tacrolimus twice daily achieved clinical remission.85 Topical
tacrolimus is reportedly irritating to tissues,67 and therefore might
be more suitable for smaller lesions.
While prednisone is preferable to no therapy, the remission rates
are not as favorable as with CsA (only ∼33% in 1 study77 using
prednisone in conjunction with a novel protein diet), and long-term
side effects can affect quality of life, especially considering many
affected dogs are large-breed dogs. Remission rates with
azathioprine treatment of PAF are variable,86,87 and one report
investigating MMF showed no response.88
A new therapy, which has been successful for people with
fistulizing Crohn’s disease, is local mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)
therapy. One veterinary study documented improvement in a small
group (n=6) of dogs with PAF given local human embryonic MSC
into their fistula sites.89 These dogs had failed at least 6 months of
standard CsA therapy, and all showed resolution of their draining

tracts 3 months post-injection. The dogs were followed for 6 months,
and 2/6 dogs had recurrence of PAF by the end of the monitoring
period. Thus, while MSC treatment appears promising, further
studies are necessary before it can be recommended for routine
management of PAF.
Given the concern that cutaneous adverse food reaction might be a
factor in development of PAF, many clinicians recommend a strict
novel or hydrolyzed protein diet as part of medical management
(chs. 160, 166).67 It is unknown how many dogs might be wellcontrolled with long-term dietary therapy alone, given the lack of
controlled studies. Additional therapies such as stool softeners and
analgesics might be necessary in some dogs. Decisions regarding
starting these should be made on a case-by-case basis.

Prognosis
The prognosis is variable based on whether or not remission can be
achieved. Dogs with concurrent PHs or draining tracts
communicating with the anal canal have been shown to have a worse
prognosis in regards to both recurrence and postoperative
complications.90

DISEASES OF THE ANAL SACS
ANAL SAC IMPACTION, SACCULITIS, AND
ABSCESSATION
Non-neoplastic anal sac disease (ASD) refers to impaction,
inflammation, or infection of the anal sacs. The incidence and
prevalence of non-neoplastic ASD in companion animals are largely
unknown. However, one English study cited anal sac impaction as
the third most common reason that dogs were presented to primarycare facilities.91 No sex predispositions have been identified for ASD,
although Cavalier King Charles Spaniels,92 Labrador Retrievers,92
Chihuahuas and Miniature Poodles are overrepresented. Cats
develop ASD much less frequently than dogs do.

Pathogenesis
The underlying etiology of most cases of ASD remains unknown, but
altered composition of anal sac secretions might contribute. These
secretions usually possess antimicrobial peptides that, if altered in
concentrations, could predispose to bacterial infections.93
Differences in the anatomical location of the sacs as well as type of
glands in the cat versus the dog might be the reason why cats rarely
develop ASD.1,6 Other predisposing factors include an anatomically
smaller duct opening, chronic diarrhea, seborrhea, and poor muscle
tone in small and obese dogs.94 Dogs with PAF are also more likely
to develop ASD.67

Diagnosis
The most common clinical signs of ASD are scooting, licking or
chewing at the anal region (up to 80% of dogs), followed by licking
under the tail (75% of cases).95 Conditions with similar clinical signs
include anal sac neoplasia, flea allergy dermatitis, rectoanal FB,
fungal disease, PAF, proctitis, trauma, and vaginitis.94 It is
important that the clinician distinguish between these and ASD.
Most dogs with anal sac abscessation or anal sacculitis will have an
erythematous and sometimes painful perianal region, with or
without discharge from the sacs. Cytologic evaluation alone is nondiagnostic, given that a large, blinded study comparing clinically
normal dogs to those with non-neoplastic ASD found no significant
differences in anal sac leukocyte populations or bacterial counts
between groups.95 It is well documented that the anal sacs of healthy
dogs contain variable numbers of white blood cells and intracellular
bacteria.96,97
Anal sacculitis and abscesses are painful upon sac expression, and
a severe sacculitis can develop into an abscess. The two can be
difficult to differentiate prior to anal sacculectomy. Impaction is
defined by enlargement of the anal sacs without accompanying
inflammation or pain.94 A large amount of pressure must be applied
in order to express an impacted sac, and the secretions usually take
on a thin, “ribbon-like” appearance.

Treatment
The type and severity of ASD will determine if medical management
alone is sufficient, or if surgery is necessary. Most impactions
respond well to thorough flushing of the affected sac(s) and warm
compresses, local antibiotic instillation, and topical corticosteroids
along with identification of the underlying cause. The animal must
also be prevented from licking at the area. Oral or injectable
antibiotics are necessary if systemic disease (e.g., fever, hyporexia) is
present. The presence of abscessation or sacculitis that is refractory
to medical management requires surgical excision of the affected
sac(s) via anal sacculectomy. Open and closed techniques exist, with
the closed method potentially resulting in fewer complications.98
Animals with ASD secondary to food allergies (ch. 160) or flea
allergy dermatitis or other parasitic diseases must receive treatment
for these conditions (ch. 142 and textbook’s inside covers).

Prognosis
The long-term prognosis depends on identification and control of
underlying causes. Complications reported secondary to anal
sacculectomy include fecal incontinence if the pudendal nerve is
damaged, tenesmus, anal stricture, seromas, and fistula formation
following incomplete excision.92,94,98 Smaller dogs (<15 kg) might
be more likely to develop postoperative complications compared to
larger dogs,92 though a large retrospective study found no
association between body weight and adverse events.98

ANAL SAC NEOPLASIA
Although apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinomas (AGASACA)
comprise <20% of perianal tumors in dogs and cats,99 the aggressive
behavior and high metastatic rates associated with this tumor
underscore the importance of early detection. Multiple studies have
found metastasis in up to 50-90% of dogs at the time of
diagnosis.100-102 The most common site of metastasis is to regional
lymph nodes, followed by the lungs and abdominal organs. Older,

female dogs might be overrepresented,100,103 but this has been an
inconsistent finding.101,102 Cats develop AGASACA infrequently
compared to dogs, though the Siamese might be predisposed.104 The
English Cocker Spaniel is at a higher risk for developing this
tumor.105 Animals with AGASACA are at risk of paraneoplastic
hypercalcemia secondary to upregulation of parathyroid hormone
related protein (PTHrP; chs. 69, 331). Hypercalcemic dogs might
have a shorter MST compared to normocalcemic dogs with
AGASACA.100,106

Pathogenesis
These tumors arise from the epithelium of the lining of the anal sac,
and can be unilateral or bilateral.100,103 An association between
AGASACA and an MHC haplotype (DLA-DQB1 allele) has been
reported for the English Cocker Spaniels, implicating a genetic
component to tumor formation in this breed.105

Diagnosis
Most pets clinical for AGASACA exhibit tenesmus, dyschezia, or
discharge from the anal sacs, or develop abnormally shaped stools.
Flattened or “ribbon-like” stools can develop secondary to
concurrent sublumbar lymphadenopathy. Animals with
hypercalcemia might be presented for evaluation of
polyuria/polydipsia. While a definitive diagnosis requires
confirmation either via fine-needle aspiration (FNA) or biopsy,
tumors are commonly palpated on rectal examination (ch. 3).102 A
minimum database including CBC, serum biochemistry profile and
urinalysis are warranted to identify existing hypercalcemia or
evidence of AKI. Due to the aggressive nature of this neoplasm, full
staging should be performed as soon as possible after diagnosis in
both cats and dogs. This includes thoracic radiographs and AUS, or,
at a minimum, thoracic and abdominal radiographs.

Treatment

A variety of single and multi-agent treatment modalities exists for
pets with AGASACA. Surgical excision of the tumor with or without
chemotherapy is the preferred treatment, with studies showing
benefits to surgery alone in prolonging survival time despite the
presence of metastasis.107-109 Dogs with early-stage AGASCA do
quite well with surgery alone, with a MST of ∼1200 days (40 months)
reported in 1 study.107 These dogs lacked both clinical signs and the
presence of metastasis at initial presentation. Seven (21%) and 9
(26%) of 34 dogs developed either tumor recurrence or metastasis at
350 and 600 days postoperatively, respectively. Radiation can be
palliative or definitive,110 with definitive radiation being used for
treating remaining microscopic disease following tumor excision.
The most common chemotherapeutic agents used are
carboplatin,101,111 cisplatin,101 doxorubicin,111 mitoxantrone,112 and
more recently, tocerbanib,106,113 a tyrosine kinase inhibitor. One of
the first studies evaluating toceranib in dogs with stage 4 AGASACA
found that although dogs improved clinically, these improvements
did not meet the criteria for a complete or partial response.113
Another study found toceranib to be successful both as a primary
and adjunct therapy in 36 dogs with AGASACA,106 with nearly 70%
of dogs experiencing a clinical benefit. This study was retrospective
and multiple different adjunct treatments were used. A prospective,
controlled study with a larger number of dogs assessing the efficacy
of toceranib compared to other treatments for AGASACA is still
lacking. The presence of preoperative hypercalcemia influences the
treatment plan. If hypercalcemia (ch. 69) and subsequent AKI (ch.
300) are present, appropriate therapy should be initiated prior to
surgery or chemotherapy. A recent report documented that two dogs
with AGASACA developed biochemical and clinical evidence (e.g.,
facial rubbing, muscle fasciculations, collapse;

Videos 69.1,

284.1, 284.2) of hypocalcemia postoperatively.114 Thus, careful
monitoring of postoperative serum calcium concentrations is
necessary for any patient with pre-operative hypercalcemia.

Prognosis

Despite the locally aggressive nature and high metastatic rate, the
MST for most dogs with AGASACA is 1-2 years102 with surgery,
chemotherapy, radiation, or combination therapy. Sublumbar
lymphadenopathy,108 lymph node extirpation,108 pulmonary
metastasis,102 and tumor size102 are negative prognostic indicators.
Side-effects can be local following surgery and radiation therapy, or
systemic with chemotherapy (ch. 321). Because there are few
reports of cats with AGASACA, accurate survival times are unknown.
Published studies suggest a less favorable outcome (e.g., overall
survival of 89-169 days)115 compared to dogs.

PERIANAL NEOPLASIA
Perianal adenomas are the most common perineal neoplasm in the
dog. Adenocarcinomas are rare, comprising only up to 12% of
perianal tumors.116 Because cats lack the same perianal glands that
dogs have, feline perianal tumors are exceedingly rare. Adenomas,
unlike adenocarcinomas, are hormone-driven and are
overrepresented in intact male dogs, with some studies citing >80%
prevalence in this population.117 Adenomas are slow growing and
non-painful, whereas adenocarcinomas tend to be larger in size and
might present as firm, ulcerated, and potentially irritating to the
patient.

Pathogenesis
Adenoma formation is driven by testosterone, and thought to be
suppressed by estrogen. This is why intact males are overrepresented
for this tumor, and if females are affected, they are usually spayed.
One report describes a spayed female dog with perianal adenomas,
which was suspected to occur secondary to testosterone secretion
from adrenal-dependent hyperadrenocorticism.118

Diagnosis

A definitive diagnosis usually requires histopathologic examination
of tissue, as FNAs might not distinguish benign versus malignant
tumors. While the rate of metastasis for adenocarcinomas is low
(<15%), complete staging with thoracic radiographs and AUS is
recommended prior to surgery.

Treatment
The recommendation for adenomas is surgical resection with
castration, which has been reported to be curative in 90% of
published cases.119 It is important to note that adenocarcinomas
must be resected with adequate margins, as margin invasiveness is a
defining feature.117 Minimally invasive techniques such as carbon
dioxide laser and cryotherapy are feasible,120,121 but do not allow for
assessment of margins and are thus infrequently performed.
Incisional biopsies are helpful in cases where an adenocarcinoma is
suspected, as this allows for planning of wider surgical margins and
minimizes local recurrence.

Prognosis
The prognosis is good to excellent for adenomas with surgical
resection, whereas patients with adenocarcinomas have a shorter
MST.117,119 Metastasis and tumors >5 cm in diameter carry a worse
long-term prognosis (<1 year).116

FECAL INCONTINENCE
Fecal incontinence refers to the conscious or unconscious leakage of
feces from the anorectum (ch. 51). Broad mechanisms of
dysfunction leading to incontinence include either diminished
storage capability (i.e., reservoir incontinence) or weakened anal
sphincter tone (i.e., sphincter incontinence). Reservoir incontinence
often develops secondary to inflammation of the rectum and/or anal
canal, resulting in an inability to appropriately store feces (i.e.,
abnormal rectal accommodation). These patients often have an
increased frequency and urgency to defecate, but might not be able

to hold their feces until it is appropriate to defecate. This is in
contrast to sphincter disorders, where the pet is unaware of the need
to defecate despite frequent dribbling or leaking of feces. Both dogs
and cats develop neurogenic and non-neurogenic causes of
incontinence. The most common neurologic etiologies include
intervertebral disc disease (IVDD), discospondylitis, spinal tumors
or arachnoid cysts, cauda equina syndrome, and degenerative
myelopathy (chs. 250 and 251). Diffuse LMN disorders and/or
junctionopathies (chs. 252 and 253) might also reduce anal tone.
Non-neurogenic causes include reservoir incontinence, aging
changes to the anal sphincter, trauma, neoplasia, and behavioral
disorders. Reservoir incontinence is the most common nonneurogenic cause of fecal incontinence in the dog and cat.

PATHOGENESIS
Any cause of dysfunction to the caudal lumbar and sacral PSNS, SNS,
or somatic nervous system can cause neurogenic incontinence
(Figure 264.1). Incontinence can also result from RPT,26,122 anal
sacculectomy,92 or herniorrhaphy procedures. Reservoir
incontinence commonly ensues secondary to severe colitis (ch. 263)
or proctitis. Patients with severe PAF might develop incontinence
either secondary to disease pathogenesis or as a postoperative
complication.123

DIAGNOSIS
Thorough neurologic (ch. 241) and rectal (ch. 3) exams, along with
visual inspection of the perineum, help in prioritizing differentials in
patients with fecal incontinence. Pets with neurogenic sphincter
incontinence often exhibit altered reflexes, ataxia, and potentially a
reduced tail carriage. Sacral nerve dysfunction typically results in
reduced to absent perineal reflex and anal tone. Urinary
incontinence is especially common with degenerative lumbosacral
stenosis (DLSS, cauda equina syndrome; ch. 250). Concurrent

tenesmus, LI diarrhea, hematochezia, and fecal mucus increase the
likelihood of colonic disorders (ch. 263).
Plain-film radiographs might identify vertebral or pelvic fractures,
discospondylitis, and narrowed intervertebral disc spaces, but
advanced imaging (e.g., CT or MRI, ch. 112) is often necessary for a
definitive diagnosis of these conditions. MRI is more sensitive than
CT for detection of compressive IVDD.124 Sampling of cerebrospinal
fluid (CSF, ch. 109) is required if inflammatory or infectious spinal
cord disorders are suspected (ch. 250). Results of a CBC and serum
biochemistry profile are often unremarkable except in cases of
infectious or neoplastic etiologies. Reservoir incontinence
necessitates fecal examination for GI parasites (ch. 80), often 1 or 2
diet trials (e.g., highly digestible, novel, or hydrolyzed protein diets;
ch. 152) and potentially proctoscopy or colonoscopy (ch. 107) to
visualize the LI mucosa and collect biopsies.

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
The long-term prognosis depends on identification of the cause of
fecal incontinence and response to therapy. Conditions that are best
treated surgically include IVDD and DLSS, with ∼6% of dogs with
IVDD developing permanent incontinence postoperatively.125 A
large retrospective study found that ∼50% of the dogs with fecal
incontinence secondary to RPT remained permanently
incontinent.26 Other, smaller studies have found incontinence to be
a rare complication with this surgery.122 Therapies and prognosis for
reservoir incontinence secondary to colorectal inflammation vary
depending on etiology. High-fiber or highly digestible, low-residue
diets can significantly reduce the frequency of defecation (ch. 165).
If incontinence is refractory to therapy, humane euthanasia is a
reasonable option given that fecally incontinent pets and their
owners often experience a diminished quality of life.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Rectoanal Disease
CAUSES OF RECTOANAL DISEASE
The rectum and anus make up the last part of the intestinal tract in
both dogs and cats. The job of the rectum is to store feces until a
bowel movement is necessary, and the job of the anus is to either
stop or allow passage of fecal material. The most common diseases to
interfere with normal rectal function are: 1) inflammation, usually
from large intestinal parasites, food allergies or immune mediated
intestinal disease, 2) an abnormal “protrusion” of certain parts or all
of the rectum through the anus (referred to as rectal prolapse), 3)
rectal masses or foreign material, and 4) stricturing or “narrowing”
of the rectum and/or anus. Trauma causing damage to the spinal
cord or nerves that help maintain normal rectoanal function and
tone can lead to leakage of feces (fecal incontinence). Both dogs and
cats also have a paired set of anal sacs (sometimes inaccurately
referred to as anal glands). The most common diseases affecting the
anus and anal sacs are: 1) infection, inflammation, and blockage of
the anal sacs, 2) both non-aggressive and aggressive anal sac masses,
and 3) problems with normal development prior to birth in puppies
and kittens which result in either an incomplete or absent anal
opening.
Sometimes the skin around the anus becomes severely inflamed
and develops draining tracts, also known as fistulas. This condition is
known as “anal furunculosis” or “perianal fistulas,” and is primarily
caused by a dysfunctional immune system. German Shepherd Dogs
commonly develop this condition. Another problem is weakening of
the muscles that support the diaphragm, which causes organs in the
abdomen to inappropriately herniate or “push through” under the
skin around the anus where they should not be. This condition is
called a perineal hernia.

SIGNS OF DISEASE
Common abnormalities that owners might note are straining or
vocalization during bowel movements, frank blood or mucus in the
stools, licking under the tail base, and pets “scooting” their rear end.

Young animals with congenital problems might be unable to produce
a bowel movement when transitioned from liquid to solid food, or
develop an abnormal shape to their stools. Animals with masses
might also develop a “pencil or ribbon like” shape of their stools.
Some pets with severe disorders develop fecal incontinence, which is
the inability to consciously void. These animals might be aware or
unaware that they are defecating, and might also have urinary
incontinence.

TREATMENT
Options depend on the underlying disease process, and include
medical or surgical management, or a combination of both. Rectal
inflammation is usually treated with de-wormers, special diets
designed to minimize or stop food allergies, and sometimes oral antiinflammatories or immunosuppressive agents. Some animals also
respond very well to increased amounts of fiber (mostly insoluble
fiber) in the diet. Most rectoanal masses, including cancer of the anal
sacs, should be surgically removed and then potentially treated with
chemotherapy. Rectal strictures and some congenital abnormalities
require gradual widening or dilation of the narrowed area, or
surgical correction. Some problems are unable to be fully corrected.

CHRONIC CARE
Animals with inflammation of the rectum and anus from either food
allergies or immune disease often require a strict diet for life. This
includes no treats or other dog foods unless they are hypoallergenic
(meant to minimize food allergies) or approved by a veterinarian.
Perineal hernias often require surgical repair, as do cases of rectal
prolapse. Dogs with perianal fistulas might never go into remission,
and require medications for life. Severe cases sometimes require
surgical removal of draining tracts. Certain rectoanal disorders cause
a poor quality of life for both pet and owner, and humane euthanasia
is understandable if long-term control of signs is impossible.
Emily N. Gould (College Station, Texas)

ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF THE
PERITONEUM
The peritoneum is a serous membrane that lines the abdominal
cavity and intraabdominal organs. The abdominal cavity is bordered
by the diaphragm cranially, the lumbar vertebrae and sublumbar
muscles dorsally, the oblique and transverse abdominal muscles plus
a small portion of the ilial wing laterally, and the rectus abdominis
muscles ventrally.1 The parietal peritoneum covers the abdominal

wall and diaphragm while the visceral peritoneum covers the
abdominal organs.2 Some abdominal organs are covered by
peritoneum on one surface and are thus considered retroperitoneal
organs, including the kidneys, most portions of the ureters, adrenal
glands, aorta, caudal vena cava, and lumbar lymph nodes.
The peritoneum’s primary function is to decrease friction of the
abdominal organs. The peritoneum is composed of a single layer of
surfactant-producing mesothelial cells attached to a fibroelastic
basement membrane. The basement membrane contains
glycosylated proteins, mast cells, macrophages, lymphocytes, and
adipose cells. It is absent in parts of the diaphragm, omentum, and
mesentery.2,3 Gaps in the basement membrane, called stomata,
facilitate absorption of fluid and particulate matter, which is taken
up by local lymphatics through lacunae. The peritoneum is a
semipermeable membrane allowing absorption, exudation, and
transudation of fluid. It has a very large surface area, which allows
for a high degree of communication with blood and lymphatics.1,3
Under normal circumstances, animals have a small amount of
peritoneal fluid present, with juvenile animals having a slightly
larger volume than adult animals.
Regardless of the cause, the peritoneum responds to injury in a
similar fashion. Vascular permeability increases, resulting in fluid
accumulation followed by leukocyte recruitment. Fibrin is produced
in order to wall off the offending agent. This results in free
abdominal fluid, which becomes richer in protein and cell count over
time. Fibrin can cause adhesions, reducing the ability of abdominal
contents to move freely. Additionally, fibrin clogs the stomata,
resulting in reduced lymphatic drainage and further increases in the
volume of free fluid within the abdomen.4

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS FOR
PERITONEAL DISEASE
PERITONITIS
Peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum. Peritonitis can be
caused by infectious etiologies, chemical irritants, foreign

material/substances, neoplasia, or trauma (Table 265.1).
Peritonitis can be subclassified into primary, secondary, and tertiary
causes. Primary peritonitis is defined as infection/inflammation
within the peritoneal cavity without an inciting intraperitoneal
cause.3,5-7 Most cases of primary peritonitis are thought to occur via
hematogenous spread, and feline infectious peritonitis (ch. 200) is
the most widely recognized form of primary peritonitis in small
animals.
Most cases of peritonitis in veterinary species are categorized as
secondary peritonitis.5 Secondary peritonitis refers to an
infection/inflammation in the peritoneal cavity caused by an inciting
intraperitoneal disease or condition, such as gastrointestinal (GI)
tract rupture or direct inoculation of the abdomen from a
penetrating wound. Persistent or recurrent peritonitis following
appropriate treatment is considered tertiary peritonitis.6
Infectious causes of peritonitis can be subdivided into those that
are likely to cause septic peritonitis and those that arise from
systemic disease and spread to the peritoneum hematogenously.
Sources of septic peritonitis can be categorized by the organ system
from which the infection arose. GI sources include perforation of the
GI tract from a foreign body, ulceration, neoplasm, trauma, or
torsion. Hepatobiliary sources include rupture of a liver abscess, liver
lobe torsion causing ischemia with bacterial colonization, or leakage
of infected bile.7 Pancreatitis is usually sterile (Figure 265.1; chs.
277, 278) but a ruptured infected pancreatic abscess or
peripancreatic fluid accumulation (ch. 279) could result in septic
peritonitis.7 Lymphoid organs such as the spleen and intraabdominal
lymph nodes can develop abscesses. Additionally, similarly to the
liver, splenic torsion with ischemia and bacterial colonization can
result in septic peritonitis. Genitourinary sources for septic
peritonitis could include leakage of infected urine from anywhere in
the urinary tract, pyometra, uterine rupture, uterine torsion with
bacterial colonization, traumatic breeding, prostatic abscess, or,
uncommonly, testicular infection that results in bacterial migration
through the inguinal canal into the abdominal cavity. Septic
peritonitis can also result from a penetrating wound/foreign body or
through iatrogenic contamination.5-7

Common causes of chemical peritonitis include bile peritonitis,
uroperitoneum, and pancreatitis. All of these substances—bile, urine,
and pancreatic digestive enzymes—can cause irritation of the
peritoneum, and injury is compounded if these fluids are septic. Bile
peritonitis causes a severe inflammatory reaction. Bile salts are
directly toxic to the mesothelium, acting as a detergent and possibly
directly damaging lipids. Additionally, bile reduces host immune
function, reducing phagocytosis and functional capabilities of
leukocytes in the peritoneal cavity.8,9 Bile peritonitis is most
commonly reported in conjunction with an obstructive biliary
mucocele (ch. 273; 21% prevalence of gallbladder rupture10),
bacterial gallbladder infection (ch. 272), trauma, or necrotizing
cholecystitis.10-12 Uroabdomen (ch. 127) is most frequently caused
by blunt trauma to the abdomen or pelvis and the urinary bladder is
the most common site of rupture.13 Urine in the peritoneum can
cause direct irritation; however, more importantly, it can cause
hyperkalemia due to an inability to excrete potassium and
nitrogenous wastes (ch. 68). This can result in life-threatening
cardiac arrythmias. Other, less common causes of chemical
peritonitis include barium sulfate peritonitis,14 and sclerosing
encapsulating peritonitis.15

The reported survival rate for dogs and cats with secondary
peritonitis in veterinary medicine is variable and often depends on
the cause and the treatment. Survival rates of 32% to 54% have been
reported in cases of secondary peritonitis in dogs.5,7,16,17 Survival
rates in cats with septic peritonitis have ranged from 44-70%.5,18

NEOPLASIA
Several neoplastic conditions have been associated with the
peritoneal cavity in dogs and cats including lymphoma (ch. 220),
carcinomatosis, or sarcomatosis. Carcinomatosis can originate from
carcinomas of the small intestine, kidneys, lungs, thyroid gland,

liver, bile duct, pancreas, and ovaries, while sarcomatosis can
originate from splenic hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325), soft-tissue
hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325), and osteosarcoma (ch. 326).35
Mesothelioma, a neoplasm arising directly from mesothelial cells,
affects the pleura (79%; ch. 220) and pericardium (64%; ch. 235)
more so than the peritoneum (7%) in dogs.36 Transformation over
time from idiopathic benign inflammation to mesothelioma has been
documented in dogs.37 Chronic body cavity effusions that
accumulate slowly are common.36,37 Leiomyomatosis, a benign
neoplasm, has been described in a dog.38 In general, the prognosis
for malignant disease of the peritoneum, whether primary or
metastatic, is quite poor.35,39

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH
HISTORY AND CLINICAL SIGNS
The history of an animal with peritoneal disease depends on the
etiology. Signalment is often helpful in prioritizing differentials.
Certain breeds may make some causes more likely; for example,
Miniature Schnauzers are predisposed to pancreatitis, Shetland
Sheepdogs have a predisposition to gallbladder mucoceles, and
Golden Retrievers have a predisposition to neoplasia. Historical
variables that may be helpful include the animal’s environment,
exposure to other animals, recent trauma, recent surgery, dietary
indiscretion or possibility of foreign body ingestion, drug and toxin
exposure (of importance would be a history of nonsteroidal antiinflammatory or corticosteroid use), and the presence of other
disease conditions.
The most common clinical signs associated with peritoneal disease
are evidence of abdominal pain and/or abdominal effusion. The
clinical manifestation depends on the etiology and severity of illness.
Peritonitis is generally painful; however, pain may be difficult to
assess on physical examination (ch. 3). Dogs exhibit signs of pain
associated with peritoneal disease more frequently than do cats, who
frequently only exhibit anorexia.18,35 Other clinical signs that can be

associated with peritonitis include depression, lethargy, anorexia,
vomiting, diarrhea, alterations in urine production, or other
nonspecific signs of illness. The physical exam may reveal abdominal
distention, a palpable fluid wave (ch. 21;

Videos 21.1, 182.1), a

palpable mass, arrythmias, and/or changes consistent with
hypovolemia or shock such as slow capillary refill time (CRT),
tachycardia, or tachypnea (ch. 121). Systemic inflammation may
result in a fever, excessively fast CRT, or hyperemic mucous
membranes. An animal with uroabdomen may have a
bradyarrhythmia associated with hyperkalemia.

FLUID ANALYSIS (CH. 71)
The history (ch. 2) and physical exam (ch. 3) are helpful to localize
the disease to the abdominal cavity. A basic approach can be applied
(Figure 265.2), and further steps should then be modified based on
clinical judgement and findings (Figure 265.2). In general,
clinically significant peritoneal disease causes peritoneal effusion.
Therefore, in animals where peritoneal disease is suspected, a search
for free fluid should be performed (

Video 21.2). Abdominal

focused assessment with sonography for trauma (AFAST) is an ideal
initial screening tool for early recognition of intraperitoneal fluid.
The principles of this method to identify free fluid are useful for all
causes of peritoneal disease and are not limited to trauma, as the
name implies. The AFAST examination is rapid, noninvasive, safe,
portable, and can be repeated easily (ch. 73).40

FIGURE 265.2 Algorithmic approach to
peritoneal disease. This is a general algorithm. The
reader is referred to the text for more information.
Also of note, there are many clinical nuances that are
not included in this general overview. AFAST,
Abdominal focused assessment with sonography for
trauma; BFG, blood-to-fluid glucose ratio; BFL,
blood-to-fluid lactate ratio; creat, creatinine
concentration; CT, computed tomography; K,
potassium concentration; NSAID, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug; PCV, packed cell volume; TG,
triglyceride concentration.
Once fluid has been identified in the peritoneal cavity,
abdominocentesis should be performed (ch. 86). This may be done
with ultrasound (US) guidance or blindly if a large volume is present.
Although peritoneal lavage or 4-quadrant sampling have been

recommended historically for small amounts of peritoneal fluid that
are difficult to reach, these methods are more cumbersome and
many clinicians find equivalent or superior yields with US-guided
centesis. It can be helpful and is most time efficient to collect the
fluid for cell counts, total protein concentration, biochemistry
profile, bacterial culture, cytologic examination, and packed cell
volume (PCV) (if hemorrhagic) at the time of initial fluid collection.

General Fluid Characteristics (ch. 71)
The macroscopic characteristics of the fluid can be very helpful for
narrowing the differential diagnosis list. Normal peritoneal fluid is
generally straw-colored and clear. The more opaque the fluid is,
generally, the more cellular and/or proteinaceous it is. If fluid is
brown, green, or orange, bile peritonitis should be prioritized. Red
fluid is consistent with a hemorrhagic effusion. White or milky fluid
should increase the suspicion of chyle.
Once obtained, the effusion can be characterized as a transudate or
exudate. This differentiation, and associated disorders, are discussed
in detail in ch. 71. Recently, a simplified classification scheme was
proposed that was more effective for prioritizing differential
diagnoses.41 For this classification, fluid is first classified as a
transudate or an exudate based on its total nucleated cell count
(TNCC). If the TNCC is <3,000/mcL the fluid is considered a
transudate and if the TNCC is >3,000/mcL it is considered an
exudate. The fluid is then further characterized as low-protein or
high-protein based on a total protein cut-off of 2.5 g/dL (25 g/L).
This categorization is helpful because many patients can have
exudates that are low in protein, including patients with septic
peritonitis or uroperitoneum. The most common causes of lowprotein transudates were severe liver disease and protein-losing
enteropathy. In contrast, heart failure was the most common cause
of high-protein transudates. Septic abdomen was the most common
cause of exudates, but all animals with peritonitis had exudates,
including those caused by pancreatitis. Neoplasia was common in all
groups. Similarly, in this study, uroabdomen fell into all groups. This
study also found that protein-poor transudates were common in dogs
with an albumin <1.8 g/dL (<18 g/L) and no other known cause for
effusion. This contradicts the popular thought that the serum protein

must be <1.5 g/dL (15 g/L) to result in effusions due to low oncotic
pressure.42
