If septic peritonitis is a differential, cytologic evaluation and
measurements of glucose and lactate concentrations should be
performed on the effusion fluid. A diagnosis can be made if
intracellular bacteria are seen cytologically (Figure 265.3).
However, the diagnosis can be challenging when bacterial numbers
are low. Low bacterial counts can occur secondary to proximal GI
perforation (gastric or proximal small intestine), low volume of
effusion, or when antimicrobials have already been administered.43
In dogs with septic effusions, peritoneal fluid glucose concentration
is consistently lower than the blood glucose concentration. A bloodto-fluid glucose (BFG) difference >20 mg/dL (>1.1 mmol/L) was
100% sensitive and 100% specific for septic peritonitis in dogs, and

86% sensitive and 100% specific in cats, in 1 study.44 A blood-tofluid lactate (BFL) difference < –2.0 mmol/L was also 100%
sensitive and specific for a diagnosis of septic peritoneal effusion.

Special Fluid Characteristics of Different Causes of
Effusion (ch. 71)
Hemorrhage
Hemorrhagic effusions have a PCV ≥25% of the PCV of peripheral
blood. Hemorrhagic effusions should not clot, even in a clot tube.
Cytologically, they may contain reactive macrophages with
phagocytized erythrocytes or intracytoplasmic hemosiderin and/or
hematoidin. Platelets are not usually observed.45

Bile
Most commonly, bile in abdominal fluid appears cytologically as
golden-green granular pigment. However, there are multiple cases of
bile peritonitis where bile was not observed and instead, acellular
mucinous fibrillar material was the predominant cytologic finding.
Bile leakage is confirmed if the abdominal fluid bilirubin
concentration is >2 × the concurrent serum bilirubin
concentration.29 Bile peritonitis is associated with an intense
inflammatory response (Figure 265.4). As such, a fluid that is rich
in neutrophils is common.8

Urine
Uroabdomen (ch. 127) can be high or low in cell count or protein. If
a uroabdomen is suspected, time-matched comparisons of serum
and abdominal fluid creatinine and potassium concentrations can be
confirmatory. In health, urine creatinine concentration should be at
least twice that of serum and the urine potassium concentration to
serum potassium concentration ratio should be greater than 1.4.41,46

Neoplasia

Effusions caused by neoplasia can be high-protein or low-protein
transudates or exudates because the potential effusive mechanisms
vary between neoplasms, although the vast majority lead to a highprotein effusion. Neoplastic cells can be identified on cytologic
evaluation of the effusion; however, changes in the vasculature that
result in a transudate or hemorrhagic effusion are common, and
therefore, lack of cytologic evidence of neoplastic cells within the
effusion cannot be relied upon to rule out cancer. Effusions may be
inflammatory, especially if the tumor is associated with
inflammation or necrosis. In one retrospective study, carcinoma was
the most common diagnosis when neoplastic cells were present in
the effusion.41

Lymph
Chylous peritoneal effusions are not common in dogs. They often
have a characteristic milky appearance. A definitive diagnosis of a
chylous effusion is made by demonstrating that the triglycerides
concentration in peritoneal fluid is greater than that in serum.47
There are also lymphatic effusions that are non-chylous. Increased
hydrostatic pressure within or increased permeability of lymphatic
vessels can lead to lymphatic leakage from vessels, as can physical
damage to the vessels.41

IMAGING
Radiography
Radiographs can be helpful for identifying some surgical disease
states. Radiography is less sensitive than US for identifying free
fluid, as small amounts of fluid may not be detected using
radiography but can be readily detected using US (ch. 73;

Video

182.1).48 Free fluid results in decreased serosal detail
radiographically. If peritoneal fluid is suspected on radiographs, it
can be useful to compare the contrast of the peritoneal versus
retroperitoneal spaces. Normally, the contrast of these spaces should
be the same. Many peritoneal diseases do not affect the

retroperitoneal space and therefore, there could be better contrast in
the retroperitoneal space compared to the peritoneum in patients
with peritoneal diseases. Radiography is more sensitive than US for
identifying free gas in the peritoneum, which would indicate a
surgical emergency. The left lateral and lateral horizontal beam
(patient in dorsal recumbency, horizontal beam) projections are
more sensitive than either the ventrodorsal or ventrodorsal
horizontal beam (patient in lateral recumbency, horizontal beam)
projections for identifying free gas.49 Radiographs can also be
helpful in identifying patterns consistent with GI obstruction, foreign
bodies, and mass effects.48

Ultrasonography
Ultrasound (US) can be helpful in prioritizing differentials and
assisting with sampling. Organ-associated masses or nodules,
aggregated bowel, and peritoneal thickening are more commonly
associated with peritoneal neoplasia, whereas localized or severely
complex fluid collections are more commonly associated with
inflammatory peritoneal disease. A cytologically interpretable yield
of 72.3% for US-guided fine-needle sampling has been reported in
dogs and cats.50Although some findings on US can be very helpful, it
is important to recognize its limitations. When US findings are
compared to surgery or necropsy in dogs with non-traumatic
hemoabdomen, US has a high sensitivity for identifying splenic
masses (87.4%,) but a low sensitivity (0/6, 0%) for identifying
peritoneal diffuse nodular metastasis.51 The hepatic veins should be
examined, because hepatic venous engorgement is associated with
high central venous pressures52; therefore, normal hepatic venous
diameter means peritoneal effusion is more likely to be due to an
intra-abdominal disorder and less likely to be due to right-sided
congestive heart failure (ch. 229), cardiac tamponade (ch. 235), or
a caudal vena caval abnormality (ch. 239).
Computed tomography (CT) has been shown to be a valuable
modality for assessing the peritoneum. CT is more sensitive for
assessing GI ulcerative disease than radiographs or US: sensitivities
of radiography, ultrasonography, and CT have been reported to be

30, 65, and 67% in dogs with non-perforated ulcers and 79, 86, and
93% in dogs with perforated ulcers, respectively. CT was a sensitive
modality for both the ulcer and signs of perforation.22 The utility of
CT has also been assessed for neoplastic conditions of the
peritoneum. The appearance of nonparenchymal hemangiosarcoma
with CT has been evaluated recently. The presence of intense foci of
contrast enhancement was found in 13 of the 17 tumors (76%).53
Additionally, CT and US features were assessed comparing
carcinomatosis and sarcomatosis in dogs and cats. Peritoneal lesions
were observed in the majority of both canine carcinomatosis cases
(78.5%) and sarcomatosis cases (85.7%) with nodules observed
remote to the primary tumor in all cases. In cats with
carcinomatosis, all had multiple peritoneal lesions, most of which
were on the visceral peritoneum. This study also found that
peritoneal effusion was more frequently observed in dogs with
carcinomatosis compared to dogs with sarcomatosis.35

MANAGEMENT
MEDICAL MANAGEMENT OF PERITONITIS
The treatment of peritonitis largely depends upon the cause. If sepsis
is a concern, IV broad-spectrum antimicrobials should be initiated as
soon as possible (ch. 140). A conscientious decision should be made
regarding what bacterial species are most likely. In most cases, the
source is from the GI tract so coverage for Gram-negative and
anaerobic bacteria is warranted. Septic peritonitis is a surgical
disease (ch. 128).
Most patients with peritonitis are dehydrated and/or hypovolemic
due to alterations in vascular permeability and reduced venous
return due to decreased lymphatic function. Additionally, these
patients may be vomiting or have diarrhea, further contributing to
volume losses. Most are hyporexic/anorexic and may not be
drinking. It is imperative that their volume status be assessed and
reassessed at regular intervals and that a dynamic fluid plan is in
place. If large volumes of peritoneal effusion are present, shifts in
electrolyte osmolalities may occur. A serum biochemistry profile or
blood gas analysis that assesses electrolyte concentrations should be

performed early in management and electrolyte derangements
should be corrected. Additionally, these patients may be
hypoalbuminemic, further contributing to their effusion. All of these
variables must be taken into account when choosing fluid type and
volume to be administered (ch. 120).

SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
The overall goals of surgery are: to prevent continued contamination
by eliminating the source of contamination, debridement of necrotic
tissue, and reduction of the bacterial load via lavage.
The type of surgery indicated for management of peritoneal
disease/peritonitis depends on the cause. Based on diagnostics
performed, including fluid analysis and imaging, the surgical team is
likely to be directed to a particular organ or organ system for surgical
intervention.
Septic peritonitis is always an indication for surgery, performed on
an emergency basis (

Video 265.1). The most common cause of

septic peritonitis is rupture of the GI tract. Occasionally, multiple
abnormalities are present. Most frequently, necrotic bowel with
perforation is the source of contamination. Possible causes of bowel
necrosis include intraluminal foreign material and bowel
obstruction, trauma, torsion, and ischemia. Regardless of cause, the
viability of affected tissue must be assessed and necrotic bowel
removed. Postoperative risk factors for developing tertiary septic
peritonitis include preoperative septic peritonitis, low preoperative
serum albumin and plasma protein concentrations, and
intraoperative hypotension.21
Treatment of bile peritonitis involves repairing the defect from
which bile is leaking. Often, surgical treatment involves
cholecystectomy. Biliary rerouting procedures may be required, e.g.,
if the gallbladder is healthy and the common bile duct is damaged
and leaking. Other options such as bile diversion with a
cholecystostomy tube can be considered, typically for temporary
management of biliary obstruction.54

Uroperitoneum is not always a surgical disease. The location of the
tear or rupture, and whether the urine is infected, influence the
decision on whether to proceed with surgical or medical
management. Preoperative detection of the site of leakage based on
imaging studies is important as some areas of leakage cannot be
visualized during a routine exploratory celiotomy and some surgical
procedures may be facilitated with specialized surgical equipment. A
non-septic uroabdomen is not a surgical emergency; it can be lifethreatening and requires emergency medical management, most
often of hyperkalemia (chs. 68, 296).13 Patients should be stabilized
prior to attempted surgical repair (chs. 119 and 121) and urethral
unblocking (ch. 99) or urinary diversion (via catheterization [ch.
98] or interventional techniques [ch. 117]) can be performed. Tube
cystostomy is another option for urinary diversion in patients with
disease of the bladder or urethra. Tubes can be placed for temporary
or permanent urine diversion.13 Once patients are stabilized and
imaging has been performed to identify the site of rupture, the need
for surgical intervention can be reassessed.

FIGURE 265.5 A torsed abdominal cryptorchid
testicle. Note the twisted vascular pedicle.
Organ torsions are uncommon in small animals, but are an
important differential when assessing a patient with evidence of
abdominal pain (ch. 126). The organs most commonly displaced
are: stomach (gastric dilatation and volvulus, ch. 261), spleen (ch.
182;

Videos 182.5, 182.6, 182.7), colon (ch. 263), mesentery,

reproductive (uterus or cryptorchid testicle, Figure 265.5), and
urinary bladder.55,56 Surgical intervention is needed for treatment.
When possible (spleen, testicle), the organ is removed without

derotating it, in an effort to prevent the release of thrombi, cellular
breakdown products and vasoactive compounds.1
Lavage is an important part of the surgical management of
peritonitis. The purpose is to remove debris, reduce bacterial load,
eliminate blood clots, and reduce inflammatory cell numbers and
mediators.1 Lavage should be performed after the source of
contamination has been addressed and necrotic tissue has been
resected. Copious amounts of warm, sterile, physiologic saline are
recommended. A volume of 200-300 mL/kg in veterinary patients
has been recommended, as well as continuing the lavage until the
returning fluid is clear.1

OVERVIEW: SIGNS ARE VARIABLE AND MAY OCCUR
LATE IN DISEASE

Hepatocytes synthesize and metabolize a vast array of compounds. Dogs and cats with liver
disease or liver failure may exhibit a wide range of clinical signs which can initially appear
unrelated. Since the liver has enormous reserve and regenerative capabilities, clinical signs
often are not observed before a large amount of hepatic parenchyma has been lost. Thus,
signs themselves can be a poor prognostic indicator in some scenarios. Common clinical
signs attributable to hepatic disease are encephalopathy, coagulopathies, portal
hypertension (PH), and ascites. As the liver has a key role in activation, metabolism, and
excretion of many compounds, clinicians should carefully evaluate therapeutic drug choices
in dogs or cats suspected of having liver disease, as pharmacokinetics may be unpredictable.

HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY (HE)
DEFINITIONS
HE is a clinical diagnosis. It is based on the presence or suspicion of hepatic disease and
compatible neurological signs for which other causes have been excluded (ch. 44). The
neurological disturbances associated with severe hepatic insufficiency or failure are due to
marked loss of hepatic parenchyma or function. HE is also seen in pets with vascular
abnormalities that cause portosystemic shunting (PSS) of blood, circumventing the liver
(ch. 267). Combinations of both PSS and loss of parenchyma or function have been
diagnosed (Table 266.1). In dogs and cats, Category B conditions are most common due to
the high prevalence of congenital portosystemic shunt (cPSS) in dogs.

CLINICAL SIGNS
HE may be an isolated clinical sign of liver disease or one of many, particularly in dogs and
cats with acute hepatic failure or cirrhosis (chs. 269 and 270). Features of HE can vary
dramatically between and within individuals depending on the underlying nature of the liver
disease as well as on the complex interplay between all potential triggers. Hyperammonemia
re-enforces suspicion of HE but absence does not exclude it. A grading scale may be of value
(Table 266.2). HE signs can be subclassified as the more common episodic or less common
continuous.1,2 Higher grades are easier to objectively measure while lower grades may be
ambiguous or missed by both owners and veterinary professionals. Grades ≤2 are often
unrecognized by owners of dogs with chronic liver disease (CLD) or acquired portosystemic
shunt (aPSS). Changes can be mistaken for aging or degenerative joint disease. New owners
may believe their puppy to be quiet and normal when the dog has a cPSS and grade I HE.
When hepatic disease is diagnosed the possibility of HE should be considered in explaining
“quiet” pets. If chronic episodic HE is possible, then owners should be educated as to
potential signs and to be aware that they may be more likely to occur and obvious 1-2 hours
after a meal.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Multiple factors combine to precipitate HE.3 The relationship between these “triggers” is
complex, including additive and synergistic effects that help explain why some pets acutely
deteriorate without appreciable deterioration in hepatic function or standard laboratory test
results, e.g., the dog with cPSS that shows no clinical signs for years and then suddenly
becomes profoundly encephalopathic. There is no laboratory test that accurately predicts the
presence or severity of HE; it remains a clinical diagnosis.4,5 Since the pathogenesis of HE is

identical in human disease and experimentally induced HE in animals, it is assumed that
important triggers are similar in dogs and cats,6,7 but their relative importance may differ
due to differences in trigger prevalence, e.g., people with cirrhosis are often depleted of
potassium (K+) whereas in cPSS dogs it is uncommon.5,6

Ammonia and High Protein Diets
Over 100 years ago, Nencki and co-workers described a “meat intoxication syndrome” that
occurred after dogs with surgically-created PSS were fed a meat diet which produced
progressive encephalopathy, coma, and death.8 They elegantly identified reduced urea
formation and hyperammonemia in the systemic circulation at levels comparable with portal
blood. CNS ammonia was also found to be increased. From these findings, they concluded
that the liver converted ammonia to urea and that high CNS ammonia was the cause of the
neurological deterioration. Ammonia has a central role in HE pathogenesis, although HE
can be diagnosed despite modest or even normal venous plasma ammonia concentrations

due to the complex interplay between triggers.5 The ammonia in portal blood is generated in
the gastrointestinal (GI) tract via 2 main methods.9
• Enterocyte metabolism: acidic amino acids are an important energy and precursor
source for enterocytes, resulting in deamination and ammonia generation, e.g.,
glutamine, the most abundant free acidic amino acid is converted to glutamate by
glutaminase in enterocyte mitochondria, releasing ammonia.
• Intestinal microbiome: bacteria metabolize intralumenal protein and amino acids,
generating ammonia. In addition, many species of intestinal bacteria produce
urease, hydrolysing urea to ammonia.

Ammonia in Health
In healthy animals, the portal vein can contain high concentrations of ammonia relative to
the systemic circulation and hepatocytes efficiently remove this delivered ammonia via 2
mechanisms.10 In the periportal area, hepatocytes convert ammonia to urea via the urea
cycle, using a high capacity, low affinity system resulting in the relatively non-toxic urea
being released into the systemic circulation; most is excreted by the kidneys. Some urea
returns to the GI tract to be converted to ammonia again by diffusion, active transport, or
urease bacteria in saliva. As blood travels through hepatic sinusoids, hepatocytes gradually
switch to a low capacity, high affinity conversion of glutamate to glutamine using the enzyme
glutamine synthetase, removing ammonia in the process. This is a high capacity system,
easily coping with variations in delivered ammonia concentrations and maintaining low
systemic release until the point of hepatic failure or where there is a physical bypassing of
hepatic blood supply as in cPSS or aPSS. Other organs have a role in ammonia metabolism
and in buffering systemic concentrations, which is relevant in clinical management of
hyperammonemia.

Kidneys and Ammonia
The kidneys excrete hepatocyte-derived urea, a crucial final step in ammonia removal, and
generate ammonia from glutamine metabolism to produce 2 molecules each of ammonium
(NH4+) and bicarbonate, contributing to acid/base balance.11 Ammonium can be excreted
into urine with the net effect of removing protons and generating bicarbonate or it can be
released into the systemic circulation and detoxified by the liver via the urea cycle,
consuming bicarbonate and resulting in no net change. Renal ammonia production is
influenced by many factors, most importantly pH, but K+ concentrations and hormonal
controls are involved. Ammonia-genesis and subsequent renal excretion has been shown to
increase in hyperammonemia.12

Skeletal Muscle and Ammonia
While skeletal muscle contains low levels of glutamine synthetase, as the largest tissue mass
in the body it provides an important route of ammonia removal.13,14 The glutamine
produced in muscle is released back into the systemic circulation and, in turn, likely releases
ammonia again when catabolized. The glutamine may be an important buffer when systemic
ammonia concentrations rise and, therefore, this is one reason for maintaining muscle mass
in pets with HE.15

Central Nervous System (CNS) and Ammonia

Astrocytes are the most common cell in the CNS and they contribute up to 50% of brain
volume.16 They are key in HE pathogenesis as they contain glutamine synthetase. They
mitigate increasing ammonia concentrations by converting glutamate to glutamine,
consuming 1 molecule of ammonia in the process.17 Both glutamate and glutamine are
neurotransmitters. There is shuttling of these compounds between astrocytes and neurons,
where neurons contain glutaminase and reconversion to glutamate occurs.

Inflammation
In human grades 3 and 4 HE (Table 266.2), infection and inflammation had the strongest
association with HE, not ammonia.4 In rats with surgically induced PSS and HE, the use of
anti-inflammatories restored learning abilities, highlighting the importance of
inflammation.18 Dogs with cPSS and clinical encephalopathy have higher C-reactive protein
concentrations than do dogs without encephalopathy.19 A study in dogs with cPSS suggested
both ammonia and systemic inflammation were predictive of HE.5 Tumor necrosis factoralpha and interleukin-6 values correlate with HE in humans. Although the blood-brain
barrier is impermeable to cytokines and other proinflammatory mediators, systemic
inflammation induces microglial activation.20,21 Some areas lack a blood-brain barrier and
allow direct access, e.g., the circumventricular organs. Active transport and signalling via
afferent nerves can also transmit a CNS proinflammatory process causing microglial
activation. Cytokines affect CNS blood flow and increase blood-brain permeability to
compounds such as ammonia.22 Experimentally induced hyperammonemia has been shown
to activate microglia.23

Manganese (Mn) and Ammonia
An essential trace element, Mn is almost ubiquitous in diets, but has the potential to be
neurotoxic.24 Portal blood concentrations of Mn are almost 100-fold higher than those in
systemic blood, demonstrating how efficiently the liver removes almost all Mn.20 Mn
concentrations in the blood of dogs and cats with PSS can be extremely increased.25,26 In
humans with CLD a correlation has been demonstrated between blood Mn, brain magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) changes, and HE grade.27 There have been reports of dogs and
cats with identical MRI changes and increased CNS concentrations of Mn, but without
association with HE.28

Electrolyte, Acid/Base Disturbances, and HE
Alkalosis and low sodium (Na+) and K+ concentrations are risk factors for HE in people but
not in dogs or cats.29 This likely reflects species prevalences rather than differences in HE
pathogenesis. The dogs studied had cPSS, but those with CLD would have better matched
the human condition.5,30 Electrolyte and acid/base derangements should be corrected, as
they likely potentiate HE in dogs and cats. Hypokalemia (ch. 68), common in ill cats, may
be an important risk factor.31

PATHOGENESIS of HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY
(HE)
Astrocytes
In all species, astrocytes have a pivotal role in the progression of HE.32,33 Increasing
intracellular ammonia concentrations impact metabolism by inhibiting the tricarboxylic acid
cycle, favoring anaerobic respiration, increasing lactate concentrations, and shifting
neurotransmitter buffering in favor of glutamine.34 Astrocyte mitochondria catabolize
glutamine, re-releasing ammonia which causes oxidative damage and further disrupts cell
respiration.34 Disrupted cell metabolism and intracellular accumulation of osmotically
active glutamine leads to cell swelling.35 If this occurs rapidly, e.g., fulminant acute hepatic
failure in people with hepatotoxicosis, there can be dramatic and fatal consequences. As
astrocytes expand within the restricted space of the skull, cerebral pressure increases that
can lead to herniation, coma, and death.36 In dogs and cats, HE is usually a more chronic
process, e.g., in PSS. Astrocyte swelling still occurs, but is less dramatic.37 Histologically,
swollen astrocytes are known as Alzheimer Type II astrocytes.38,39 Both glutamate and
glutamine are neurotransmitters; changes in their ratio affects neurotransmission with
glutamate being excitatory and glutamine converted to the inhibitory gamma-aminobutyric
acid.

Manganese (Mn) Excess
Excess Mn has similar effects on astrocytes, which have a high affinity transport mechanism
for Mn leading to high intracellular concentrations, especially within mitochondria.40 Mn, a
transition metal, leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and disrupts glutathione production,
both potentiating oxidative damage.41 In pure Mn intoxications, astrocyte changes identical
to those of hyperammonemia (Alzheimer Type II neurons) are recognized
histopathologically.42 This convergence of ammonia and Mn on mitochondrial dysfunction
is an example of synergy in HE development. Elsewhere in the CNS, the oxidative damage
due to Mn releases pro-inflammatory cytokines, potentiating a pro-inflammatory
environment.42 In the CNS, Mn appears preferentially deposited in basal ganglia, producing
MRI changes in location and hyperintensity which are pathognomic for Mn toxicosis.

MANAGEMENT OF HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY (HE)
Underlying Disease
Correcting the underlying cause has the best chance of resolving HE. This may or may not be
achievable, depending on cause. Regardless, medical management is of value, even if
surgical attenuation of a cPSS is planned (ch. 267).

HE Crisis
HE is one of many clinical and metabolic derangements, particularly in acute liver failure
(ALF), that require management (ch. 269). Other causes of neurological signs should be
excluded (chs. 44 and 45). Hypoglycemia, sometimes seen in hepatic failure, should be
identified and treated (ch. 61). Since inflammation and/or infection are important
contributors to the pathogenesis of HE, identifying and treating either can be lifesaving.

Urinary tract infections (ch. 307), a potential trigger, anecdotally are common in cPSS.
Increases in intracranial pressure have been recognized in dogs and cats with ALF, causing
stupor or coma. Monitoring and appropriate therapies should be employed (chs. 44, 125,
and 267-269). Electrolyte abnormalities, especially deficiencies in K+ and Na+, should be
corrected with IV fluids that can simultaneously dilute some trigger concentrations.
Correcting dehydration and restoring glomerular filtration rates enhance renal excretion of
urea and ammonia. Lactated fluids should be avoided, as lactate requires hepatic
metabolism (ch. 120). Physical removal of colonic contents with warmed isotonic fluid
enemas (ch. 108) will remove urease-producing bacteria and sources of nitrogen. This may
be particularly important after any GI hemorrhage because hemoglobin is a ready source for
bacterial degradation and ammonia release. Once the colon is completely cleansed, a
retention enema is often used (Table 266.3). Since colonic stimulation may induce
vomiting in cats, securing the airway is strongly advised if mentation is altered.

Chronic HE Management; Use of Non-absorbable Disaccharides
Based on clinical experience, non-absorbable disaccharides are commonly used in managing
HE (Table 266.3).43 Lactulose and lactitol are metabolized by colonic bacteria into shortchain fatty acids (SCFAs) with their potential for lowering systemic ammonia
concentrations.44 SCFAs are an energy source for bacteria that shifts the microbiome to
have fewer urease-positive bacteria and favors more bacteria that utilize ammonia.45 SCFAs
can acidify colonic content, trap ammonia as non-absorbable NH4+, and provide an
ammonia “sink.” SCFAs act as osmotic laxatives, speeding removal of trapped ammonia,
urease-producing bacteria, and nitrogen present in colonic content and in bacterial protein.
Since lactulose is sweet, when treating cats with HE, use of powdered lactitol or adding
lactose to the diet via milk or natural yoghurt improves compliance.46 The effect of lactose in
any individual requires lactase deficiency and it is unclear how prevalent or severe this may
be in cats.47

Chronic HE Management; Nutrition (ch. 154)
Historically, protein restriction was used for long-term HE management because protein is
an excellent source of nitrogen and decreasing dietary amounts would reduce systemic
ammonia concentrations. This strategy is no longer recommended in people with liver
disease. Young growing dogs with cPSS have the same protein requirements as healthy
dogs.48 Protein malnutrition encourages tissue, particularly skeletal muscle, catabolism in
individuals already at high risk of having poor muscle mass. Further dietary protein
restriction can slow growth and increase the risk of metabolic bone disease (ch. 162),
particularly in larger breeds. In mature animals, administering glucocorticoids to control an
inflammatory hepatopathy can induce a catabolic state and sarcopenia (ch. 151). Any
reduction in skeletal muscle mass reduces its ability to act as a buffer to hyperammonemia.
Hypoalbuminemia, common in pets with liver disease, can be exacerbated by protein
restriction with potential for disastrous consequences. Subtle shifts in colloid oncotic
pressure may lead to ascites in pets with PH. Albumin contains a multitude of binding sites
for exogenous and endogenous compounds and is highly biologically active,49 with multiple
antioxidant and immune-modulating properties. Since inflammation has a role in the
pathogenesis of HE, albumin concentrations should be keenly conserved.
As excess dietary protein is broken down, ammonia is released. Feeding useable proteins
rather than proteins digested by intestinal microbes reduces ammonia production. It is
crucial that species, life-stage, and underlying cause be considered when recommending
diets for pets with HE (ch. 154), e.g., cats have higher protein requirements than dogs and
those with hepatic lipidosis require high-protein diets (ch. 154). Intuitively, intake should
match protein requirement for life-stage, be of high biological value, and contain all
essential amino acids for the species (e.g., arginine in the cat; chs. 145-149).
In the short-term management of high-grade HE, protein restriction may be necessary.
Once the patient is stabilized, protein intake should be titrated up towards life-stage

requirements and only kept below this if HE cannot be sufficiently controlled. In pets with
cPSS, it may be desirable to feed a high-quality standard life-stage diet rather than
expensive, protein-restricted “hepatic diets.” There is evidence that vegetable-protein–
source diets may be advantageous compared to meat-based diets.1,50 Before recommending
any restricted diet for a pet with HE, a veterinary nutritionist should be consulted (ch. 154).

Chronic HE Management; Antibiotics
Although not proven, the rationale for antibiotic use is to reduce bacterial numbers in the
intestinal microbiota and reduce microbial ammoniagenesis (Table 266.3). If a systemic or
localized infection is present, antibiotics are indicated to control this HE trigger. Some
dramatic responses to antibiotics in pets with HE may be the result of resolving an occult
infection. Non-absorbable antibiotics are preferred if purely targeting intraluminal bacteria,
but expense and availability limit their use. Routine use of antibiotics in pets with HE is not
correct, and their use should be carefully considered and withdrawn as soon as possible (chs.
7 and 140). Some pets clinically improve while on antibiotics and deteriorate upon their
withdrawal, despite otherwise appropriate management.

PORTAL HYPERTENSION (PH)
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Categorizing the Sources of PH
Most blood (∼80%) delivered to the liver is via the low-pressure portal vein. The liver
contains a high capacitance, low resistance sinusoidal venous network that permits
unimpeded flow. In health, this system can function with minimal change in resistance
despite large fluctuations in portal blood volume.51 Sinusoidal epithelial cells (SECs)
monitor blood delivery and release nitric oxide to allow vasodilation.52 Various liver
diseases alter hepatic resistance and capacitance, which can lead to PH that can be classified
by location as pre-hepatic, hepatic or post-hepatic.51 Hepatic diseases can be further divided
into pre-sinuoidal, sinusoidal, or post-sinusoidal. Hepatic sinusoidal PH is most common in
inflammatory/fibrotic hepatopathies. This occurs due to a combination of architectural
increase in resistance and altered dynamic sinusoidal tone.

Architectural Increases in Resistance
Physical disruption of sinusoidal networks can follow inflammation, connective tissue
deposition, and/or regeneration. Sinusoidal endothelium may develop reduced numbers of
fenestrae and form a basement membrane, a process termed capillarization.53 Healthy SECs
are thought to inhibit stellate cell activation, an ability lost during capillarization. This allows
stellate cell contraction, perpetuating extracellular matrix formation and further
contributing to PH.54 Capillarization of the endothelium reduces oxygenation of
surrounding cells, causing release of angiogenic platelet derived growth factor and vascular
endothelial growth factor, both of which further promote angiogenic remodelling and
hypertension.

Dynamic Increases in Sinusoidal Resistance
Due to oxidation, inflammatory mediators, and physical changes to sinusoidal endothelium,
SECs become less able to compensate for increases in portal blood flow, producing fewer

vasodilatory substances and more vasoconstrictors such as endothelin-1 and angiotensin
II.55 As a result, sinusoidal relaxation and capacitance are decreased.

Splanchnic Response to Portal Hypertension (PH)
As PH increases, splanchnic arteries dilate due to local release of vasodilators in response to
shear stress and GI endotoxin adsorption. Vasodilation increases splanchnic and portal flow,
exacerbating hypertension, pooling blood in the splanchnic bed, and reducing effective
systemic circulating blood volume. These factors increase cardiac output, activate the renin
angiotensin aldosterone system (RAAS), lead to release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), and
ultimately increase blood volume. Increases in plasma renin and aldosterone have been
documented in dogs with chronic hepatitis and aPSS.56 The expanding blood volume
worsens PH. Increased portal pressure and release of angiogenic mediators such as vascular
endothelial growth factor open and develop aPSSs causing portal blood to directly enter the
systemic circulation.51

ASCITES
Physiology
In hepatic disease, ascites occurs when the rate of fluid leaving the splanchnic vascular bed
overwhelms the rate of lymphatic uptake (ch. 21). This can occur due to the increased
hydrostatic pressure from PH and expansion of the systemic blood volume that follows
activation of RAAS and ADH release. If there is reduced plasma colloid oncotic pressure due
to hypoalbuminemia, fluid is lost from the vascular space. Ascitic fluid due to PH is typically
a protein-poor or protein-rich transudate (ch. 71), dependent on the disease process, serum
albumin concentration, and subclassification of the PH. In dogs with both chronic and acute
liver disease, the presence of ascites is a poor prognostic indicator.57,58

Clinical Signs and Diagnosis
Often, the first sign of PH is ascites, detected by owners as abdominal swelling, during
physical examination, or imaging (ch. 21). Ascites usually occurs in the later stages of PH.
Significant ascites is likely to be uncomfortable and severe ascites can interfere with
respiration. Indications of PH as a cause of ascites include increased portal vein to aorta
ratio [PV/Ao] on computed tomography (CT) angiography, reduced portal velocity via
Doppler ultrasound (US), hepatofugal flow, and the presence of aPSS. It is likely that aPSSs
reduce PH and decrease PV/Ao ratios. Alterations in splanchnic blood flow can have
consequences for other intra-abdominal organs, e.g., predisposing to GI dysfunction.
Administering glucocorticoids to dogs with chronic hepatitis and PH may increase the risk of
GI ulceration. In cirrhosis, PH can reduce portal blood velocity and induce a
hypercoagulable state which can lead to portal vein thrombosis (PVT) and worsening PH.59

Management of Portal Hypertension (PH) and Ascites
Ideally, the cause of PH should be resolved. While this may be achievable in some pets with
hepatic arteriovenous malformation (ch. 267) or thrombotic occlusion, the vast majority
have non-resolvable CLDs. Medical management of PH in pets without ascites has not been
well studied. In people with PH, treatment is reserved for those actively bleeding or at high
risk of bleeding from esophageal varices. Beta-blockers and nitrates are used
prophylactically to dilate the splanchnic vasculature and reduce portal pressures.

Vasopressin and somatostatin analogues are used in people with active bleeding, but variceal
bleeding is extremely rare in dogs and cats. In humans, where there is interest in reducing
intrahepatic vascular tone, statins and tyrosine kinase inhibitors can reduce portal pressure
in those with CLD by reducing angiogenesis and sinusoidal capillarization.60,61 There is no
information on whether management of PH in the dog or cat is beneficial prior to overt
clinical signs.

Managing Chronic or Refractory Ascites
Restricting Na has been recommended for people and pets. However, decreasing Na reduces
calorie intake and promotes malnutrition in people.62 Avoiding malnutrition is critically
important (chs. 151 and 154). The aldosterone antagonist spironolactone is often used to
counter the effects of RAAS activation (1-2 mg/kg PO q24h). Full effect may require 1-2
weeks. Experimentally, spironolactone has also been shown to mitigate hepatic fibrosis and
sinusoidal capillarization which would provide a rationale for use early in the disease
process, before ascites develops to prevent worsening of PH.63 If the response is insufficient
or a rapid reduction is required, furosemide may be added (1-2 mg/kg q12h). When these
drugs are used, especially furosemide, daily monitoring of body weight, abdominal girth,
PCV, total solids, creatinine and electrolytes are advised while the goal is reducing body
weight 0.5-1.5% per day.64
In refractory ascites or with abdominal tension, therapeutic drainage in conjunction with
diuretic use should provide relief (ch. 86). When removing a large volume, heart rate, blood
pressure, and serum albumin concentrations should be closely monitored during and after
the procedure. Albumin is given IV to people when large volumes are removed, providing
circulatory and colloid support.64

COAGULOPATHY
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Hepatocellular Contributions to Coagulation
Hepatocytes synthesize almost all pro- and anticoagulants, the compounds that promote and
inhibit fibrinolysis (Table 266.4), and they are responsible for vitamin K-dependent
activation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X. Uptake of fat-soluble vitamin K depends
on bile production. Factor VIII is produced by non-hepatic sites, but clearance depends on
hepatic function. In people with cirrhosis, endothelial dysfunction associated with increased
von Willebrand factor (vWF) and decreased vWF cleaving enzymes has been reported. Dogs
with CLD have upregulated vWF expression in sinusoidal endothelial cells, which may offset
decreases in platelet numbers.65,66 Finally, the liver is an important site of thrombopoietin
production.67

It is recognized that most people with cirrhosis have a rebalanced hemostatic system less
able to maintain equilibrium when challenged.59 There is higher risk of thrombosis in
people with cirrhosis than hemorrhage, which may be true in hepatic fibrotic diseases of
dogs and cats. A retrospective study of 102 dogs undergoing US-guided hepatic biopsy found
42% experienced a ΔPCV ≥6%; however, only 2 required intervention.68 There was no
significant difference in coagulation parameters comparing those that did or did not
hemorrhage. Splanchnic thrombosis is increasingly recognized with advanced imaging
techniques in dogs with hepatopathies. In one retrospective study using CT angiography,
42% of dogs with PVT (ch. 239: Figure 239.12) had hepatic disease. PVT has also been
reported in cats with a variety of hepatopathies, both acute and chronic.69
Most routine coagulation testing concentrates on specific procoagulant pathways and is
less reliable for assessing the holistic effect of disturbances in both pro- and anticoagulants
(chs. 170 and 171).70 Use of thromboelastography (TEG) should better predict clinical
outcomes as it captures the dynamic process of clot formation and fibrinolysis (ch. 170).
Testing coagulation status in animals with liver disease provides information to assist with
diagnosis and prognosis, e.g., 1 criterion for defining ALF is a prothrombin time (PT) >1.5
upper reference interval, which carries a grave prognosis.71 Protein C testing can help
separate cPSS from primary portal vein hypoplasia.72

Coagulation in Acute Hepatopathies
Since coagulation is often abnormal in pets with acute liver disease, identifying the
underlying cause is always helpful, e.g., leptospirosis (ch. 192) causes thrombocytopenia as
well as acute hepatic insult.73 Dogs with acute hepatopathies commonly have
mild/moderate thrombocytopenia, increases in PT and activated partial thromboplastin
time (aPTT), and decreases in fibrinogen, antithrombin (AT), and protein C. From TEG
analysis, dogs with acute liver disease can be normal or hypocoagulable and/or
hyperfibrinolytic.74 Bleeding and thrombosis have been reported (chs. 170 and 171).58

Coagulation in Chronic Hepatopathies
Mild to moderate thrombocytopenia (ch. 59), common in dogs with a chronic hepatopathy,
has been associated with survival.75 Primary hemostasis in 18 dogs with CLD was examined

by platelet count, PFA-100 analyser closure time, buccal mucosal bleeding time (BMBT, ch.
79), and plasma vWF antigen.65 When compared with healthy dogs, no difference was found
in platelet count, closure time, or vWF. Although increased BMBTs were noted, all were
within reference ranges and all 18 had a hepatic biopsy without complication. In general,
risk of hemorrhage requiring intervention after liver biopsy in dogs with CLD appears low.76
It is possible that dogs with a chronic hepatopathy are at risk of thrombosis rather than
bleeding. Giving glucocorticoids to decrease inflammation to dogs with CLD increases risk of
thrombosis if there is aPSS and reduced portal flow velocity due to PH.76,77

Coagulation in Pets With Congenital Portosystemic Shunts (cPSS)
Platelet counts are lower than those of control populations, although overt
thrombocytopenia is uncommon. Factor VIII and vWF concentrations are increased, aPTTs
are mildly increased, and protein C concentrations are decreased. TEG analysis
demonstrated a hypercoagulable state in a subgroup who were also more likely to have HE,
likely reflecting underlying inflammation driving both. Clinically relevant bleeding or
thrombosis due to underlying coagulopathy appear to be rare.78-80

Coagulation in Cats With Liver Disease
In cats with liver disease, primary hemostatic abnormalities are less common and vitamin K
deficiencies more common than in dogs (ch. 171). This is likely a reflection of the higher
prevalence of biliary disease and concurrent pancreatic and intestinal diseases affecting lipid
digestion in cats (ch. 225), rather than failure to synthesize pro- and anti-coagulant factors.
Reduced vitamin K increases the PT, reduces factors II, VII and X, and increases proteins
induced by vitamin K’s absence (PIVKA). In one study, 44 of 45 cats with liver disease had
an abnormality in at least 1 hemostatic parameter.81 Factor XIII deficiency, frequently
reported, would cause clot fragility and re-bleeding. Cats with biliary obstruction (ch. 273)
requiring surgery have high risk of bleeding and often require transfusion.76 In 1 study, 17 of
30 cats undergoing US-guided liver biopsy had major bleeding and 2 required transfusion.
However, an automated biopsy device was used which may have contributed to the high rate
of complications.82,83

MANAGING COAGULOPATHIES
Testing Prior to Elective Interventions
While it is considered essential to test coagulation prior to hepatic biopsy,84 abnormal
coagulation test results are not an absolute contraindication for surgery or hepatic biopsy,
but are to be considered part of the risk/benefit analysis.70 In people, coagulation times do
not predict risk of significant bleeding after liver biopsy.85 The American College of
Veterinary Internal Medicine consensus statement on chronic hepatitis suggests values
placing dogs at high risk: platelets <50,000 mcL, PT or aPTT >1.5 times upper limit,
fibrinogen <100 mg/dL (<1 g/L), vWF activity <50%, or a BMBT >5 minutes.86 A PCV
<30% is also “high risk” due to the effect of anemia on platelet function and decreased
resilience against hemodynamic instability if there is hemorrhage. The consensus statement
recommends close monitoring post-procedure (up to 24 hrs) and having blood products
available (ch. 124).

As with any hepatic disease, resolving or mitigating the underlying condition decreases
risk of bleeding. For example, dogs suspected of having chronic hepatitis with coagulation
abnormalities that prevented biopsy were treated with prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) and this
was associated with normalized profiles, permitting safe biopsy.87 However, steroids may be
contraindicated (with infectious disease), may make diagnosis more difficult (with
neoplastic infiltration), or may lead to deterioration in clinical signs and/or life-threatening
GI hemorrhage in dogs with PH. In cats with hepatobiliary disease, before surgical
intervention or biopsy, vitamin K administration is advised even if PT and aPTT are within
reference ranges, as these are insensitive indicators of deficiency.76 If no intervention is
planned in a dog or cat with no evidence of bleeding, treating the clinical pathology
abnormalities is not indicated. It is unknown if pre-treatment when there is
clinicopathological evidence of hemostatic disorders prior to any invasive procedure will
reduce the likelihood of postoperative bleeding.

Managing Active Bleeding
If a dog or cat with hepatopathy is actively bleeding, administering a wide variety of factors
is recommended, as coagulation abnormalities are nonspecific (ch. 124).76 Fresh frozen
plasma can be an excellent source of coagulation factors. Cryoprecipitate is a source of
fibrinogen and factors VIII, vWF, and XIII. As laboratory results are not predictive of clinical
outcome, treatment is continued to clinical effect rather than to a numerical endpoint. If
hyperfibrinolysis is present, based on viscoelastic testing or re-bleeding, aminocaproic acid
has efficacy in people with cirrhosis. There are data supporting use of this drug in dogs,
although not specifically for those with hepatic disease.88,89

Managing the Hypercoagulable State
There is no evidence that prior treatment will mitigate or prevent thrombus formation in
dogs and cats with liver disease. Treatment options are limited. Nonsteroidal medications
are metabolized by the liver and their use is associated with risk of GI ulceration.
Anticoagulant medications all carry the risk of GI hemorrhage, especially in the presence of
PH, necessitating risk/benefit analysis. Clopidogrel, a prodrug, requires hepatic activation.
Rivaroxaban is albumin-bound, largely inactivated by hepatic metabolism, and eliminated
by both liver and kidney.90,91 Drug pharmacokinetics in hepatic insufficiency/failure are
unpredictable, further cautioning against use for prophylaxis.

Managing Portal Vein/Splanchnic Thrombosis
Thrombosis may be severely obstructive and can be acute or chronic. Acute PVT (ch. 239:
Figure 239.12) may cause abdominal pain and/or hypovolemic shock.92 Chronic PVT
increases resistance and may lead to PH. If aPSSs have developed, PVT may be clinically
silent.59 Treating dogs with acute PVT using heparin or warfarin for 6 months has been
recommended.93 In one retrospective study, a wide variety of treatment modalities was used
for dogs with PVT and an association between anticoagulant use and survival was noted.92
In people with cirrhosis and PVT, anticoagulation with heparin decreased mortality. Since
heparin has antifibrotic and portal antihypertensive effects, improvement may be unrelated
to PVT benefit.59 Humans with PVT given anticoagulants are more likely to re-cannulate.59
Low-molecular-weight heparin and fondaparinux are the standard of care in human PVT.

Thrombolytic medication is not recommended in human cirrhotics with PVT due to the high
risk of bleeding.59

JAUNDICE (ICTERUS; CH. 28)
DEFINITIONS
Jaundice, or “icterus,” is yellow discoloration of skin, sclera, and mucous membranes caused
by high systemic bilirubin concentrations. Concentrations above which jaundice becomes
clinically detectable depend on pre-existing pigmentation, hematocrit, and lighting.
Generally, jaundice becomes detectable first in separated plasma at bilirubin concentrations
>1 mg/dL (>17 micromol/L) and then the sclera when >1.5 mg/dL (>26 micromol/L). The
sclera, quite pale in color, also has high content of avid-bilirubin-binding elastin. At
concentrations >2.0-2.5 mg/dL (>34-43 micromol/L), jaundice becomes detectable in the
mucosa. Jaundice is neither specific nor sensitive in indicating hepatic disease.94

CLASSIFICATION
Pre-hepatic Jaundice
This jaundice is caused by systemic red blood cell destruction (hemolysis) which exceeds the
liver’s capacity for uptake (ch. 174).

Hepatic Jaundice and Jaundice of Sepsis
Hepatic jaundice is caused by reduced capacity in hepatocyte bilirubin uptake and
conjugation. Often, there is a significant component of intrahepatic biliary system
obstruction due to architecture disruption, usually secondary to the swelling caused by
inflammation or lipidosis. In canine chronic hepatitis, jaundice is often an end-stage
development. Hyperbilirubinemia can occur in people with genetic mutations in bilirubin
transporters, a condition not described in dogs or cats.95
Jaundice of sepsis is a form of intrahepatic jaundice, but without concomitant hepatic
disease. Bacterial toxins may directly inhibit hepatic and biliary canalicular membrane
transport and indirectly affect this process via pro-inflammatory cytokines.96 This
condition, anecdotally recognized in dogs and cats, may explain the isolated
hyperbilirubinemia seen in some dogs and cats with severe infections and some cats with
feline infectious peritonitis (FIP, ch. 200), where hepatobiliary enzyme activities are within
reference intervals.97-99

Post-hepatic Jaundice
Extrahepatic partial or complete bile duct obstruction causes bilirubin retention and
jaundice (chs. 272, 273). Obstructions can be intraluminal (bile sludging, cholelithiasis) or
extraluminal (e.g., neoplasia, pancreatitis).

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Bilirubin is formed from breakdown of hemoglobin, myoglobin, and cytochrome enzymes.
Hemoglobin produced during erythrocyte breakdown by macrophages in the spleen, liver

and bone marrow is responsible for most circulating bilirubin.94 During red blood cell
destruction, hemoglobin is converted to biliverdin by heme oxygenase, then to bilirubin by
biliverdin reductase. This “unconjugated” bilirubin is insoluble in water and binds to
circulating albumin for transport to the liver. Hepatocytes, in turn, bind bilirubin to
glutathione S-transferase where it is “conjugated” to glucuronic acid by uridine diphosphate
glucuronyltransferase (UDP-GT) to produce the water-soluble mono- and diglucuronide
forms. Conjugated bilirubin is then actively transported across the hepatocyte biliary
canalicular membrane into the biliary system. When excreted into the GI tract, microbes
mainly in the large intestine convert conjugated bilirubin to urobilinogen and then
stercobilinogen. Most water-soluble urobilinogen undergoes enterohepatic recirculation
while a small percentage is metabolized by the kidneys to the renally excreted urobilin.

INVESTIGATING THE CAUSE OF JAUNDICE (CH. 28)
Although assessing unconjugated and conjugated bilirubins would intuitively seem to be a
useful discriminator between jaundice types, it is not reliable and not recommended.94
Demonstrating moderate/severe anemia is key to diagnosing pre-hepatic jaundice. Serum
hepatobiliary enzyme activities are frequently increased in all 3 conditions: in pre-hepatic
jaundice, increases are due to the hypoxemic impact of severe anemia on the hepatocytes; in
intra-hepatic jaundice, increased enzyme activities are caused by the parenchymal disease,
although it is important to remember that with end-stage liver disease, there may be so few
hepatocytes that enzyme activity may be only modestly increased or even normal; and in
extra-hepatic jaundice, cholestasis often increases both biliary (marked) and hepatocellular
enzyme activities (ch. 65). Hypercholesterolemia is more frequently seen with extra-hepatic
obstruction. Complete extrahepatic biliary obstruction causing pale chalky (acholic) feces
due to the lack of stercobilinogen is uncommon in dogs and cats. Urine negative for urobilin
also is noted but is also normal. Abdominal imaging, most commonly with US, but also CT
or MRI, is most useful in confirming an extrahepatic jaundice cause.100
With time, conjugated bilirubin becomes covalently bonded to albumin and other
proteins, a product termed “delta-bilirubin.”101 Delta-bilirubin is neither taken up by
hepatocytes nor excreted in urine. Removal from the system is dependent on albumin’s halflife (∼2 weeks). In extra-hepatic jaundice, after resolving the obstruction, bilirubin
metabolism returns to normal quickly. However, jaundice and hyperbilirubinemia can
persist for days without being clinically significant if all other parameters are improved.

CLINICAL CONSEQUENCES AND MANAGING
JAUNDICE
Hyperbilirubinemia is a negative prognostic indicator in dogs with gallbladder mucoceles
(ch. 273) and those with acute liver disease (ch. 269) or CLD (chs. 270, 271). Jaundice is
also one of the parameters used to define canine ALF.57,58,102 Extremely high amounts of
lipid-soluble unconjugated bilirubin are able to cross the blood-brain barrier, accumulate in
the basal ganglia, and cause neurological signs similar to HE.103 This condition, seen in both
dogs and cats, is termed kernicterus or bilirubin encephalopathy.104-106
Bilirubin is not just a waste product to be excreted; it is a functional compound with
hormonal activities. People with mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia appear to be at
reduced risk of many chronic disease processes.107

Treatment should be directed towards the primary disease process. Therapeutic plasma
exchange has been described in 2 dogs with hyperbilirubinemia due to immune-mediated
hemolytic anemia (IMHA, ch. 174), which rapidly reduced circulating bilirubin
concentrations.108,109 The choleretic ursodeoxycholic acid may improve bilirubin excretion
in hepatic and extra-hepatic cholestasis, but does not specifically increase bilirubin biliary
excretion, nor reduce circulating bilirubin concentrations in healthy dogs.110,111 S-adenosylL-methionine (SAMe) has been shown to reduce circulating bilirubin concentrations in
humans with a congenital defect in bilirubin conjugation, but there are no specific data on
the effect of bilirubin metabolism or transport in dogs or cats.112

CLASSIFICATION OF HEPATIC
VASCULAR ANOMALIES
Classification of hepatic vascular anomalies includes 3 congenital
categories (Box 267.1): (1) congenital intrahepatic portosystemic

shunts (IHPSSs) and extrahepatic portosystemic shunts (EHPSSs);
(2) disorders associated with abnormal hepatic blood flow or portal
hypertension, currently termed “primary hypoplasia of the portal
vein” (PVH); and (3) disturbances in outflow. The second category,
PVH, remains confusing and includes processes that may or may not
cause portal hypertension, termed “PVH with portal hypertension”
(noncirrhotic portal hypertension [NCPH]/hepatoportal
fibrosis1/idiopathic hepatic fibrosis2/veno-occlusive
disease3/idiopathic chronic liver disease/nonfibrosing liver disease4)
and PVH without portal hypertension (formerly termed
microvascular dysplasia [MVD]).5,6

PORTOSYSTEMIC SHUNTS (PSSs)
DESCRIPTION
Normal vs Abnormal Development
Portosystemic shunts (PSSs) are congenital or acquired vascular
anomalies connecting the portal vein with the systemic circulation,
bypassing the hepatic sinusoids and liver parenchyma.7-12 They are
the most common hepatobiliary congenital abnormality, including a
number of different anatomic variants.13-15 Normally, venous blood
draining the spleen, pancreas, stomach, and intestine enters the
portal vein, perfuses the liver through the intricate sinusoidal
network, and drains to the hepatic veins, ultimately entering the
caudal vena cava (CVC).9 Portal blood carries many substances to
the liver, including trophic hormones (intestinal, pancreatic),
nutrients, bacterial products, and intestinal-derived toxins.7,8,12

Fetal Ductus Venosus
The fetal liver has limited function to process such products. Fetuses
have a large shunting vessel, the ductus venosus, which bypasses the
liver as a protective mechanism.9,12 This fetal blood vessel, located
on the left side of the liver, normally closes by 3-10 days of
age.9,10,16,17 This process is initiated by blood pressure changes after
umbilical venous flow ceases. Thromboxane or adrenergic
compounds can stimulate contraction of ductus venosus
musculature, likely aiding closure.9,11,12,16,18 If the ductus venosus
remains patent, or other congenital communications exist, a
congenital portosystemic shunt (cPSS) results. When blood bypasses
the liver, oxygen supply to the liver is reduced and trophic factors
(particularly insulin and glucagon) are not available to support
hepatic growth, resulting in poor hepatic development, deficient
protein production, reticuloendothelial dysfunction and altered fat
and protein metabolism.

PSS Blood Volume vs Clinical Signs

Clinical signs correlate with the volume and origin of blood
bypassing the liver. PSS can cause hepatic encephalopathy (HE),
chronic gastrointestinal (GI) signs, lower urinary tract signs
associated with cystolithiasis and/or bacteriuria, coagulopathies,
and/or delayed growth.8,9,11,12,19,20 These issues are caused by an
accumulation of exogenous and endogenous toxins that are normally
metabolized or eliminated by the liver, as well as the failure of
normal hepatic function (e.g., gluconeogenesis, urea cycle, uric acid
cycle, glycogenolysis).8,12,20-23

EMBRYOLOGY
The veins in the abdomen are derived embryologically from the
umbilical, vitelline, and caudal cardinal veins (Figure 267.1). The
paired vitelline veins originate at the yolk sac and form the left
hepatic vein, the hepatic sinusoids, the hepatic portion of the CVC,
the prehepatic portal vein, and its tributaries.16 The vitelline and
umbilical systems combine to form the ductus venosus and the left
branch of the portal vein. The nonportal abdominal, renal, and
gonadal veins are derived from the cardinal venous system. The
caudal cardinal veins form the CVC caudal to the liver, and the
azygos vein.9,16,24 In normal animals, the prehepatic and
intrahepatic segments of the CVC join at the communication between
the cardinal and the vitelline systems. Numerous nonfunctional
portocaval and portoazygos communications are present in the fetus
but are not patent in the adult unless portal hypertension occurs,
forming multiple acquired extrahepatic shunts (aPSSs). When
developmental errors create abnormal communications between
these two systems, congenital extrahepatic portosystemic shunts
(cEHPSSs) result.16 Abnormal vessel patency, or other abnormal
development in the vitelline venous system, results in congenital
intrahepatic PSS (cIHPSS). Most IHPSSs do not develop due to a
patent ductus venosus, and the cause of other left, right, and central
divisional IHPSSs or EHPSSs is currently unknown.

NORMAL ANATOMY
The portal vein is formed by the confluence of the cranial and caudal
mesenteric veins, providing up to 80% of the blood and 50% of the
oxygen content to the liver, with the remainder being supplied by the
hepatic arterial blood.9,11,12,25 Blood from the GI tract, spleen, and
pancreas is drained by their respective veins, which join the portal
vein. In the dog, the portal vein enters the liver, branching into left
and right vessels that supply the various liver lobes. The main right
branch supplies the right lateral and caudate process of the caudate
lobe, and the main left branch supplies all other lobes, giving off a
central branch that supplies the right medial lobe.9,25 In the cat, the
portal vein separates directly into left, central, and right
branches.9,11,25 The portal vein branches into smaller venules where
the blood enters the parenchyma via the portal triads. That blood
travels through the hepatic sinusoids, is cleansed by the
reticuloendothelial system, then drains into central veins that form
larger hepatic venules and ultimately hepatic veins that empty into
the CVC. When the path is interrupted by an anomalous vessel, blood
is diverted away from the liver and along the path of least resistance,
reaching the systemic circulation without having traversed the
hepatic circulation. PSSs also reduce portal venous perfusion
pressure (often close to central venous pressure), further limiting
hepatic perfusion through whatever diminutive portal vessels may be
present.
