CONGENITAL PORTOSYSTEMIC
SHUNTS (cPSSs)
Congenital PSS, reported in 0.18% of all dogs and 0.05% of mixedbreed dogs,26 most commonly occurs as a single vessel that provides
direct vascular communication between the portal venous supply
and the systemic venous circulation (CVC or azygos veins) (ch.
268). This commonly occurs as a single intrahepatic or extrahepatic
communication (80%). Rarely, a dog or cat has two or more
congenital communications.27 There are several types of cPSS found

in both dogs and cats, including intrahepatic portocaval shunts,
extrahepatic portocaval shunts, extrahepatic portoazygos shunts,
portal vein atresia with resultant multiple portocaval anastomoses,
hepatic arteriovenous malformations (HAVMs) causing portal
hypertension-induced acquired extrahepatic PSS, and
microintrahepatic PSS (PVH without portal hypertension, formerly
MVD).8,11,28-32 Approximately 25-33% of cPSSs are IHPSSs in dogs;
the condition is less common in cats. Single EHPSSs, with a major
solitary portocaval shunt being the most common, constitute 66-75%
of congenital single PSSs in both species.7-10,32 Most IHPSSs occur
in larger-breed dogs, whereas most EHPSSs occur in smaller
breeds.32 Some EHPSSs, e.g., splenocaval shunts, may be associated
with less severe clinical signs because splenic blood is not of GI
origin and less portal blood is shunted away from the liver. Dogs with
IHPSSs generally have the largest volume of diverted portal blood,
causing earlier or more severe clinical signs.7,8,33,34

ACQUIRED PORTOSYSTEMIC SHUNTS
(aPSSs)
Causes
aPSSs (20% of all PSS) most commonly occur secondary to chronic
portal hypertension that can open fetal vestigial blood vessels. These
open blood vessels have also been seen as a congenital abnormality
(ch. 268). These vessels provide an outlet for hypertensive portal
blood. aPSSs usually are multiple, tortuous, extrahepatic, and
located near the kidneys.28-30 The most common causes of acquired
extrahepatic shunts are hepatic fibrosis (cirrhosis), PVH with portal
hypertension (congenital NCPH),29 congenital ductal plate
abnormalities in dogs and less commonly cats, or HAVMs.30

PVH With Portal Hypertension, or NCPH
This condition has been described in various dog breeds,29,35 and is
diagnosed when intraabdominal portal hypertension, a patent portal

vein, and a noncirrhotic liver are present. Affected dogs have
incompletely developed smaller portal vein branches resulting in a
“pollard willow” abnormality. They have marked reduction in
parallel circulation and increased resistance that results in portal
hypertension and multiple EHPSSs.

PVH Without Portal Hypertension, Formerly MVD
This condition is a microscopic malformation of the hepatic
vasculature,31,34 characterized by small intrahepatic portal vessels,
portal endothelial hyperplasia, portal vein dilation, random juvenile
intralobular blood vessels, and central venous hypertrophy and
fibrosis. These lesions allow abnormal communications between the
portal and systemic circulation at a microvascular level, thus
avoiding the increase in portal pressure seen in NCPH. This can
occur as an isolated disease, or in combination with macroscopic
PSS. Fifty-eight percent of dogs and 87% of cats with PVH have
concurrent congenital macroscopic PSS.5 Clinical signs in dogs with
PVH can be similar to those of PSS; however, when PVH exists
without a macroscopic shunt, signs are often less severe, occur later
in life, and result in a better long-term prognosis with medical
management alone.

Hepatic Arteriovenous Malformation (HAVM)
HAVM is a rare congenital condition in dogs and cats of multiple
high-pressure arterial and low-pressure venous communications.
This condition, previously termed hepatic arteriovenous fistula, is
more appropriately named a malformation because most are
composed of numerous communications (malformation) rather than
a single communication (fistula).30,36 Usually, a branch of the
hepatic artery communicates directly with the portal vein via
multiple (dozens to hundreds of) aberrant shunting vessels. The high
pressure causes hepatofugal blood flow, portal vein arterialization,
and portal hypertension which opens multiple extrahepatic shunts to
decompress this system, often causing ascites. The long-term
prognosis for HAVM has been inferior to the more common PSS or
PVH but good outcomes can still be achieved.8,9,30

HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY (HE; CH.
266)
Most of the clinical signs associated with PSSs are due to HE, a
neuropsychiatric syndrome involving a number of neurologic
abnormalities that occurs when more than 70% of liver function is
lost and/or portal blood bypasses the liver.21-23,37-43 Infection and
inflammation play a role in development of HE in humans and Creactive protein is increased in dogs with HE. HE can be complicated
by GI bleeding, hypoglycemia, hypokalemia, and high-protein meals.
Typically, HE is not seen in dogs with PVH without portal
hypertension, but can be seen in other forms of cPSS, HAVM, and
aPSS.

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
Signalment
cEHPSSs are most common in small/toy-breed dogs.11,26,32 In one
series, Yorkshire Terrier, Havanese, Maltese, Dandie Dinmont
Terrier, Pug, and Miniature Schnauzer breeds had an odds ratio >19
for this condition.26 cPSS is likely hereditary in Yorkshire Terriers,
with an odds ratio for PSS >35.9 times than for all other breeds
combined.26,44,45 In the Maltese, a recessive, partially-penetrant
mode of inheritance is suspected for both macroscopic PSS and
PVH.46 In cats, EHPSSs are more common9,44 than IHPSSs.47-48
Domestic Shorthair, Persian, Siamese, Himalayan, and Burmese
breeds are overrepresented.10,48-51 IHPSSs are overrepresented in
larger breed dogs, including the Irish Wolfhound, Retrievers
(Labrador, Golden), Australian Cattle Dogs, and Australian
Shepherds.9,10,52-54 Left divisional IHPSSs are likely to be heritable
in Irish Wolfhounds,55,56 and right divisional IHPSSs have been
overrepresented in the Australian Cattle Dog and male dogs in
Australia.54,57 Cairn Terriers are likely to have an autosomal
inherited PVH.34 The Yorkshire Terrier was overrepresented with

MVD/PVH in a report.31 In a report58 on dogs with cPSS or aPSS,
those with aPSS were older, heavier, in poorer body condition, more
likely to have ascites, and less likely to have central nervous system
(CNS) signs than those with cPSS. HAVMs do not have breed
predispositions. Extrahepatic arterioportal fistulas have only been
reported in unrelated Pembroke Welsh Corgis.59 Evaluation of gene
expression in dogs with PSS revealed that 26 genes were altered in
both EHPSS and IHPSS when compared to liver samples from
control dogs.60

History
Most dogs and cats with cPSSs have signs (acute or chronic) before 12 yrs of age, though some have been older than 10.32,61 PSS is far
more common in dogs than cats. Multiple acquired EHPSSs in dogs
are diagnosed at a median age of 3 yrs (range: 7 months-7 yrs),28 and
the median age of dogs diagnosed with PVH is 3.25 yrs (range: up to
10 years).8,31 There is no clear sex predisposition for cPSS in dogs,
but male cats may be overrepresented.7,32 The history typically
suggests the pet has “failed to thrive” since birth, is small in stature
(or the runt of the litter), has weight loss (11% of cases) or failure to
gain weight, has anesthetic intolerance, is dull or lethargic at times,
and displays “bizarre behavior” (41-90% stargazing, head pressing,
staring into walls or corners, random barking, intermittent
blindness, pacing or aggression).7,8,11,32,62 Some pets have a history
of dysuria or hematuria.8,63 Polyuria and polydipsia (PU/PD) is
common in dogs with cPSS, likely due to a reduced renal medullary
concentration gradient caused by low blood urea nitrogen (BUN),
increased renal blood flow, increased adrenocorticotropic hormone
(ACTH) secretion and associated hypercortisolism, and psychogenic
polydipsia from HE.9,11,12,64 Ascites occurs in 75% of dogs with
HAVMs30 and can be seen with venous-venous PSSs if
hypoproteinemia is severe (ch. 21). This complication is seen with
concurrent protein-losing enteropathy, often associated with GI
ulceration/bleeding (ch. 261) or inflammatory bowel disease ±

lymphangiectasia (ch. 262) in IHPSS dogs and may also be seen
with excessive dietary protein restriction in growing dogs. Ascites is
not typically seen with PVH without portal hypertension but can be
seen with PVH with portal hypertension.

Clinical Signs/Physical Examination (PE)
The CNS, GI, and urinary systems are commonly affected.8,9,11,32
Signs of HE can be obvious or quite subtle and typically are
associated with aberrant behavior (ch. 266). More obvious CNS
signs include ataxia, unresponsiveness, pacing, circling, blindness,
seizures, random barking, and coma (chs. 43, 44;

Videos 267.1

and 267.2).9,16,11,62 Onset of signs correlating with meal ingestion
has been reported in only 30-50% of pets, supporting postprandial
GI enterocyte glutamine metabolism as a major source of ammonia
in the portal blood.11 GI signs (vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, pica,
and/or GI bleeding/melena/hematemesis) occur in about 30% of
dogs but are less frequent in cats.11,27,32,48 Ptyalism (ch. 46),
thought to be a manifestation of HE or GI upset, is common in cats
(75%).11,12,48,62,65 GI hemorrhage occurs more often in large-breed
dogs with IHPSS prior to repair (∼30%) than in dogs with EHPSS.66
Some pets (20-50%) have signs of lower urinary tract disease:
hematuria, stranguria, pollakiuria, or urethral obstruction (chs. 54,
55).8 Due to decreased urea production, increased ammonia
excretion, and decreased uric acid metabolism, formation of
ammonium urate calculi or debris is common (30-75.7% of pets with
PSSs, less common in cats than dogs19,67) and can be associated with
bacteriuria (chs. 307, 309).32,63,67 In a study of dogs with cPSS,
24% had positive urine cultures, 75.7% cystic calculi or debris, 39%
had hematuria, and 19.7% had bacteriuria on urine sediment.19 Cats
with PSS and urate urolithiasis tend to be younger (2 versus 7 years)
than those with urate urolithiasis without known PSS.67

Shunt Morphology and Associated Clinical Signs

In one series, preoperative clinical signs occurred in 88% of dogs
with portocaval cPSSs, and in 58% with portoazygos cPSSs.68
Clinical signs also were more common if the shunt inserted caudal to
the liver (91%) than if it inserted between the liver and diaphragm
(67%).68 CNS signs were most frequent with splenocaval cPSSs, and
urinary signs were more common with right gastric vein than
gastrosplenic vein origin.68 With EHPSS, older dogs have been
found to have splenophrenic and splenoazygos shunts more
commonly than right gastrocaval or splenocaval.69 Splenosystemic
shunts in cats are associated with older spayed females with a
concurrent hepatopathy, potentially associated with portal
hypertension.70

Concurrent Congenital Defects in Dogs and Cats
With PSS
Common concurrent defects include cryptorchidism (30% of male
cats in one study71 and 50% of male dogs in another72), heart
murmurs (incidental flow murmurs in young pets or congenital
cardiac defects)9,11,62,71 and copper-colored irises that are
inappropriate for the breed, particularly in cats.73

Dogs and Cats With PVH Without Macrovascular
Shunts
These pets have similar signalments and clinical signs (mild to
nonexistent) to those described and are usually older.11,31 PVH with
portal hypertension is diagnosed when there is intra-abdominal
portal hypertension with a patent but small to normal portal vein
and a noncirrhotic liver. Purebred dogs are overrepresented,
particularly Doberman Pinschers (27% of cases). Most dogs are <4
yrs of age and weigh >10 kg.29 Signs are similar to PSSs or to hepatic
cirrhosis with concurrent portal hypertension, resulting in ascites
(60% of cases), PU/PD, GI upset, HE, and weight loss, in association
with multiple EHPSSs. Dogs with portal hypertension secondary to

PVH tend to be brighter than dogs with end-stage liver failure and
cirrhosis without the other signs of end-stage chronic hepatitis.

Clinical Signs in Pets With HAVMs
Most affected pets are diagnosed in the first few years of life and
signs (acute or chronic) are due to multiple EHPSSs from portal
hypertension or ascites. All sizes of dogs and a small number of cats
have been reported.11,30 GI signs are common, and many dogs have
stunted growth and lethargy.30 Ascites has been documented in
about 75% of dogs, less than previously suspected, presumably due
to decompression of the portal system by the acquired shunts in the
remaining 25%. Heart murmurs (ch. 38) were documented in 20%
of dogs with HAVMs.30 Signs of HE are less frequent with HAVMs.
In some animals, the sound of turbulent blood flow (bruit) can be
auscultated over the liver.

Routine Laboratory Tests
Complete Blood Count (CBC)
CBC changes with PSS often include a mild to moderate, microcytic,
normochromic, nonregenerative anemia (chs. 57 and 173).
Erythrocyte target cells in dogs, and poikilocytes in cats, are
common.74 Studies suggest the microcytic anemia may be due to a
defective iron-transport mechanism, decreased serum iron
concentrations, decreased total iron-binding capacity, and/or
increased hepatic iron stores in Kupffer cells (possible iron
sequestration).75,76 Microcytosis, reported with or without anemia in
60-72% of dogs and in ∼30% of cats,9,75,76 usually resolves after
shunt correction, and is not common in dogs with PVH/MVD.11,31
Leukocytosis due to inadequate hepatic endotoxin and bacteria
clearance from the portal circulation has been associated with a poor
prognosis.7,8,32,52,77 Monocytosis and elevated C-reactive protein
concentrations are more commonly associated with HE.42

Serum Biochemistry Profile

Serum biochemical abnormalities are common in dogs and cats with
PSSs. Most are due to decreased hepatic synthesis: low albumin
(50%), low BUN (70%), hypocholesterolemia, and hypoglycemia. In
cats, hypoalbuminemia is uncommon but low BUN and creatinine
are common.49,65 Mild to moderate increases (2-3 X) in alkaline
phosphatase (ALP) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) activities are
common (ch. 65), typical of any hepatic vascular anomaly.74 Serum
ALP activities are typically higher than ALTs in dogs with PSSs, likely
due to contributions of bone isoenzyme in growing animals or
hepatic organelle injury and increased release or decreased
elimination of canalicular ALP.11,74 Dogs with aPSS are more likely
to have a lower hematocrit, higher mean corpuscular volume (MCV),
and higher ALT than dogs with cPSS.58 Eighty-one percent of dogs
with cPSS had abnormally increased renal volume and glomerular
filtration rates prior to shunt attenuation, which decreased
significantly after ligation,64 explaining, in part, the low BUN and
creatinine concentrations.64 High hyaluronic acid levels in dogs with
cPSS, suspected to be caused by reduced hepatic clearance, improve
with shunt attenuation,78 suggesting these levels reflect liver
function and may be used for evaluating success of shunt attenuation
in dogs with cPSS. Dogs with cPSS, HAVM, and PVH (with and
without portal hypertension) typically do not have increased serum
bilirubin concentrations, whereas dogs with other types of cirrhotic
portal hypertension or hepatopathy may.

Urinalysis (UA)
Common abnormalities in cPSS are low urine specific gravity (USG;
>50% are hyposthenuric or isosthenuric) and ammonium biurate
crystalluria (ch. 70).9,11,18,62 Low USGs are likely due to PU/PD and
the reduced medullary concentration gradient that occurs with low
BUN subsequent to a deficient urea cycle (chs. 53, 62).
Hyperammonuria, also resulting from the blood bypassing the
hepatic urea cycle, combined with hyperuricacidemia due to a
deficiency in hepatic purine and pyrimidine metabolism (uric acid
cycle), result in excessive urine ammonia and urate that can

precipitate into crystals or stones in the kidney or bladder (stones or
debris seen in 30-75% of cases) (chs. 308, 309).18,19,23,32,63
Ammonium biurate crystalluria is common and can be seen in 2675% of affected dogs and 16-42% of affected cats.19,63,67,72,79,80
Males, older age, history of medical management prior to evaluation,
but not shunt morphology, appear to be associated with urolithiasis
in dogs with cEHPSS.63 Proteinuria is common in dogs with PSSs,
perhaps secondary to glomerulopathy (e.g., glomerular sclerosis,
glomerulofibrosis, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis; ch.
302).81 The link between severe liver disease and immune-mediated
glomerulonephritis, seen in people, may follow antigens reaching the
kidneys that the liver normally clears.82

Liver Function Testing
Serum Bile Acids (SBAs)
Bile acids are synthesized in the liver from cholesterol and, following
conjugation, are secreted into the bile canaliculi and stored in the
gallbladder until postprandial release into the duodenum. They aid
lipid absorption via intestinal fat emulsification and metabolism, are
reabsorbed from the ileum, transported into the portal system, and
extracted by hepatocytes for recirculation.83-86 Production,
excretion, and enterohepatic recirculation are all evaluated when
measuring SBAs. Fasting (12-hr) and 2-hr postprandial SBAs are
tests of choice for evaluating liver function when suspecting PSSs.
These measurements can be affected by the timing of gallbladder
contraction, the rate of intestinal transport, the degree of bile acid
deconjugation in the small intestine, the rate and efficiency of bile
acid absorption in the ileum, portal blood flow, and the function of
the hepatocyte uptake and canalicular transport.
Increased postprandial SBAs have been reported as being 100%
sensitive for detecting PSSs in dogs and cats.83-86 Others suggest
paired samples are 100% sensitive, but not individual
measurements. A small subset of affected pets has normal
postprandial SBAs and elevated fasting samples while some have
normal fasting and elevated postprandial SBAs.32,84 Unaffected

Maltese dogs can have elevated SBAs without evidence of liver
dysfunction.57 Other false-positive results unrelated to PSSs are due
to inappropriate sample timing, other hepatobiliary
diseases/cholestasis (SBAs are unreliable in animals with hepatic or
posthepatic jaundice), glucocorticoid or anticonvulsant therapy,
tracheal collapse, seizures, and GI disease.12,74,85,87
Falsely low results can occur with delayed intestinal absorption,
lack of gallbladder contraction, inadequate food intake/delayed
gastric emptying, or malabsorption or maldigestion. Gallbladder
contraction occurs between meals during normal fasting due to
migrating motility complexes (MMCs), particularly in dogs, resulting
in higher preprandial than postprandial bile acid levels if the fasted
blood sample was obtained at the time of an MMC. The persistently
increased SBAs identified in pets with PSSs are due to the shunting
of reabsorbed SBA to the systemic circulation.12,74,85 SBAs can
remain elevated after attenuation of cPSSs and should not be used
solely to assess surgical outcome in dogs.88

Blood Ammonia
When SBA results are suspected to be falsely negative, serum
ammonia can be tested or an ammonia tolerance test (ATT)
performed. Increased ammonia is suggestive of hepatic insufficiency
but is not diagnostic for PSS. Serum ammonia is the only
biochemical test for PSS in a dog with cholestatic jaundice. In most
animals, the primary source of blood ammonia is GI absorption, both
from small intestinal enterocyte metabolism and from bacterial
metabolism (ch. 266)12,23,62 Portal blood delivers ammonia to
hepatocytes for conversion to urea via the urea cycle. This conversion
does not occur efficiently in pets with PSS, largely because blood
completely bypasses hepatocytes, resulting in increased blood
ammonia concentrations. Plasma separation and laboratory analysis
must be completed within 20 minutes of sample collection, making
this test difficult in most clinical settings. In cats with increased
ammonia and HE, an inborn error in ammonia metabolism due to an
enzyme deficiency (ornithine transcarbamylase) in the urea cycle has
been reported.89 Other causes of hyperammonemia in young

animals not associated with PSS include congenital cobalamin
deficiency, methylmalonic acidemia, other urea cycle enzyme
deficiencies, and urethral obstruction–induced
hyperammonemia.11,89 Baseline ammonias are not as sensitive (6288% of PSS abnormal) as SBA, especially after prolonged fasting or
with effective medical management of HE.12,32,57,72 Both falsepositive (Irish Wolfhound puppies) and false-negative baseline
ammonias have been documented.32,90,91
The 6-hr postprandial blood ammonia has been reported as more
sensitive (91%) than fasting concentrations (62%) in dogs with
PSS.92 Arterial, venous, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) ammonias
were higher in dogs with cEHPSS or cPSS than in control dogs.93 In
this study, dogs with cPSS had abnormally high arterial and venous
blood ammonia concentrations, and there was a positive correlation
between blood and CSF ammonia concentrations. This suggests that
the permeability of the blood-brain barrier to ammonia may be high
in dogs with EHPSS. Another study compared the value of rectal
ATT, fasting plasma ammonia level, and fasting plasma bile acids in
dogs with cPSS.94 In this group the ATT and the fasting SBAs had
the highest sensitivity (100% and 98%, respectively) and negative
predictive value (100% and 96%, respectively) for PSS. The
combination of increased fasted SBAs and fasting ammonia had the
highest specificity (97%) and had a positive predictive value of
97%.94

Additional Laboratory Tests
Coagulation Profiles
Prolonged coagulation times (ch. 170) are common in dogs with
PSSs, although prevalence varies in studies. Spontaneous bleeding is
rare and excessive bleeding does not usually occur during surgical
intervention.95-97 In one study, postoperative mortality increased in
those dogs that had a dramatic worsening of coagulopathy after
surgery.98 Liver parenchymal cells synthesize most clotting factors
(I, II, V, IX, X, XI, XIII [and VIII via the liver vascular
endothelium]), but also anticoagulant factors (ch. 266). Thus, the

effect of reduced liver function on coagulation, as seen in PSSs, is
unpredictable.97 Prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and/or activated
partial thromboplastin time (PTT) occur after loss of ∼65-80% of
factor activity.12,23,95 The liver also regulates coagulation via
clearance of activated factors, so that regeneration of inactivated
factors and fibrinolytic factors can occur.96,99,100 The prolonged
PTT reported in some studies of cPSSs is likely due to impaired
hepatic synthesis, qualitative abnormalities, and clearance of
coagulation factors.95,96,98 Interestingly, deficient factors include
those involved in the common (II, V, and X) and extrinsic (VII)
pathways, leading one to expect the PT to be prolonged as well,
which it may not be. One possible explanation is a factor XII
deficiency that can cause prolongation in PTT alone without overt
bleeding. Protein C, an anticoagulant protein reduced in dogs with
cPSS, might help explain the hypercoagulable state found on
thromboelastography (ch. 170) in a large number of dogs with
cPSS.97,100
In one study, platelet counts were normal in 87% of dogs with PSS.
In another study, dogs with PSS had abnormally low platelet counts
preoperatively, which worsened postoperatively (mean:
161,000/mcL).95,96 Platelet counts are rarely low enough to cause
clinical bleeding. This may be supportive of a postoperative
consumptive coagulopathy. Overall, coagulation status (PT, PTT, and
platelet count) returned to normal in one study by 6 weeks after PSS
surgical correction, but not in animals that had persistent
shunting.95 In some dogs with cPSS, coagulation parameters and
thromboelastography reveal hemostatic abnormalities consistent
with markers for coagulopathy and a hypercoagulable state.101 In
this study, the presence of a hypercoagulable state was found to be
40 times more likely to be associated with clinical HE.101

Plasma Cytokine Concentrations
Studies have shown an association between inflammation and HE,
with increases in pro-inflammatory cytokines. Various cytokines
were measured in healthy dogs with cPSS and controls, including

interleukin (IL)-2, IL-6, IL-8 and tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFalpha). Only IL-6 was increased in dogs with cPSS.102

Abdominal Effusion
Ascites is rarely seen in dogs with a single cPSS, unless there is
severe hypoproteinemia, severe GI bleeding causing
hypoproteinemia, or portal hypertension associated with HAVM,
NCPH, or acquired multiple EHPSS (chronic liver disease/cirrhosis).
Typically, the fluid (ch. 71) for any of these conditions is a clear,
relatively acellular pure transudate with a total protein <2.5 g/dL
(<25 g/L), specific gravity <1.017, and <1000 nucleated cells/mcL.74

Histology
Most dogs with a cPSS have hypoplasia or absence of intrahepatic
portal tributaries, typical of portal vein hypoperfusion but not
pathognomonic for cPSS. Arteriole profiles are increased as they
become swollen, more tortuous, and may proliferate. There may be
smooth muscle hypertrophy, increased lymphatics around central
veins, and Ito cell and Kupffer cell hypertrophy.12,103-106
Microscopic bile duct proliferation and hepatocellular atrophy may
be seen. Some animals have evidence of mild fibrosis around the
central veins and a few have signs of necrosis or inflammation.12,103
In an evaluation of histopathologic data versus prognosis in dogs
with cPSS, there was no significant association between histologic
features and survival times.103 Historically, histologic features
associated with a poor prognosis included fibrosis, biliary
hyperplasia, and necrosis.11,12,104 Many dogs with PSS have focal
lesions consisting of Kupffer cells and/or macrophages with
cytoplasmic brown pigments (ceroid and hemosiderin) and lipid
vacuoles called lipogranulomas,106 changes inconsistently
associated with prognosis.103,106,107
Another study assessed hepatic histopathologic lesions in relation
to clinical findings and ability to completely attenuate the cPSS in
dogs.108 The lack of identifiable portal veins (36% of dogs) was
associated with increased hepatic arteriolar proliferation, decreased

tolerance to complete surgical attenuation, and decreased
opacification of intrahepatic portal vessels on portovenography
(PVY). Surgical cPSS attenuation resulted in significant clinical,
biochemical, and portovenographic changes indicative of improved
liver function, but only subtle changes on hepatic histologic reexamination.108
In a study of dogs with cEHPSS, larger liver volumes were
associated with fewer lipid droplets per tissue point
histopathologically.107 The number of lipogranulomas was positively
associated with age, but the presence of hepatic lipidosis and
lipogranulomas had no demonstrable effect on development of
acquired shunts or the magnitude of increased liver volume after
shunt attenuation.107 In a study of 40 cats with cPSS evaluated
before and after surgical attenuation, histopathologic analysis
showed portal vein hypoplasia and arteriolar hyperplasia in all
samples.109 Hepatocyte swelling with microvesicular vacuolar
change (50%), fibrosis (42.5%), hepatocyte swelling with
macrovesicular vacuolar change (30%), biliary hyperplasia (20%),
and hemosiderin within Kupffer cells (5%) were seen in variable
amounts. Cats with macrovesicular vacuolar changes were
significantly older (median age 18.5 months versus 8.5 months). On
follow-up biopsy samples after partial attenuation, there were no
significant differences in histopathological features, though
intrahepatic vasculature was improved on PVY.109 In another
study,110 the livers of dogs with cPSS had 12 times the lipid content
of the livers of control dogs. Involvement of lipid-related genes in
steatosis in PSS was corroborated with gene-expression profiling.
Lipid analysis demonstrated different triglyceride composition and a
shift toward short-chain and omega-3 fatty acids in dogs with PSSs.
Dogs with PVH without MVD or with NCPH share hepatic
histopathologic changes with macroscopic cPSS. These syndromes
can, therefore, be confused histologically if correct history and
signalment are not provided.29,31,35 Dogs with NCPH often have
more significant fibrosis that extends into the parenchyma,
particularly along the portal tracts or even bridging to other portal
areas or central veins.29

Dogs with HAVMs that have had biopsies taken from liver lobes
not involved in the arteriovenous communication often have similar
histopathologic findings to those with venous-venous shunting.
Tissues close to malformations often have largely dilated portal
venules, marked arteriolar hyperplasia, muscular proliferation, and
sinusoidal capillarization. Some portal veins have evidence of
thrombus formation and recanalization.11,30
Dogs with HE can have histopathologic changes in the CNS that
include polymicrocavitation of brainstem, cerebellar nuclei, or
cerebral cortex, and hypertrophy and hyperplasia of cerebral cortical
protoplasmic astrocytes.9,18

MicroRNA Expression in PSS
MicroRNA biomarkers are being evaluated in humans and dogs for
hepatobiliary diseases. Serum cfa-miR-34a and 21 were expressed in
dogs with IHPSS and splenocaval or gastrocaval EHPSS, but were
not overexpressed in dogs with splenophrenic or splenoazygos
shunts.111 Interestingly, miR-34a is a potent regulator of
steatohepatitis progression and miR-21 is involved in the progression
of hepatic damage leading to fibrosis.

Diagnostic Imaging
Survey Radiographs
Survey abdominal radiographs often demonstrate microhepatica
(60-100% of dogs, 50% of cats) and bilateral renomegaly.9,11 In dogs
with PVH, liver and kidney size can be normal radiographically.11,31
Marginally radiopaque calculi may be seen in the bladder, urethra,
ureters, and/or kidneys, but some are radiolucent. The calculi are
usually ammonium biurate with associated calcium salt or struvite
shells (chs. 308, 309). To definitively diagnose a macroscopic shunt
requires advanced imaging.

Abdominal Ultrasonography (US)
US is the most widely used diagnostic tool for PSS (Figure 267.2).
It is noninvasive, does not require anesthesia (though sedation often

makes finding EHPSSs more reliable), and does not require special
licensing/handling (vs scintigraphy). Decreased numbers of hepatic
and portal veins, a subjectively small liver, and an anomalous vessel
are most often seen with cPSS. EHPSSs generally are more difficult
to diagnose via US due to small patient size, small vessel size,
variable location, and presence of gas in the bowel and lungs.
Multiple EHPSSs are often difficult to identify; they are typically
located near the left kidney. Sensitivity for detection of shunts has
ranged from 74-95% and specificity from 67-100%.112-114
Correct distinction of IHPSS from EHPSS was possible in 92% of
cases in one study. Sensitivity is higher for IHPSS (95-100%) than
EHPSS due to the presence of liver parenchyma surrounding the
shunting vessel, and the typically large diameter of the intrahepatic
shunting vessel and associated portal vein.112 Results are operatorand experience-dependent. Color-flow and pulsed-wave Doppler
imaging are useful for identifying changes in flow direction because
HAVMs (Figure 267.3) classically have hepatofugal flow and
venous-venous shunts have hepatopetal flow through the portal vein.
Portal flow velocity was increased or variable in 53% of dogs with
EHPSS and in 92% with IHPSS.11 Dogs and cats with EHPSS have
been documented to have reduced portal vein-to-aorta size ratios. US
also is useful for detecting uroliths in dogs and cats with hepatic
vascular anomalies because these stones often are
radiolucent.112,115,116

Ultrasound Contrast Venography (USCV)
USCV is an US-guided percutaneous splenic injection of agitated
saline mixed with 1 mL autologous heparinized blood.117 When
visualizing the vena cava, portal vein, and right atrium in dogs with
cPSS, it is possible to differentiate intrahepatic from extrahepatic
shunts depending on the entry point of microbubbles into the CVC.
Portoazygos and portocaval shunts also can be differentiated.117
Hepatic microvascular perfusion was evaluated in dogs with EHPSS
using intravenous (IV) perfluorobutane.118 It revealed changes in
hepatic microvascular perfusion including hepatic artery, portal vein,
and hepatic parenchyma when compared to controls. The rapid

hepatic arterial and hepatic parenchymal enhancement could reflect
a compensatory increase in hepatic arterial blood flow due to a
decrease in portal vein perfusion to the liver. HAVMs have also been
evaluated using USCV.119

(CVC).

Computed Tomographic Angiography (CTA)
CTA, the gold standard for evaluating the portal venous system in
people,120 is noninvasive, fast, and it images all portal tributaries
and branches after a single peripheral venous contrast injection. It
can be used in any species and any size of animal with accuracy,
allowing for further image manipulation after completing a study.

Dual-phase CTA provides a complete evaluation of portal and
hepatic vasculature and is considered superior to single-phase
CT.13,121 This type of study is most valuable in animals with
suspected IHPSS or HAVM, or for which US is not diagnostic and
more invasive imaging such as portography is not desired. CTA is
helpful in preprocedural planning for both surgical and
interventional radiologic (IR) approaches to IHPSS or HAVM (ch.
116) by reducing excessive liver dissection or manipulation during
surgery and minimizing contrast load during IR procedures. In a
study of canine EHPSS, CTA provided an excellent overview of shunt
anatomy and provided information about tributary vessels that could
be overlooked during surgery.122

Scintigraphy
Transcolonic scintigraphy utilizing the radioisotope technetium
(99mTc) pertechnetate is a useful, noninvasive method for detecting a
PSS.116 A bolus is infused into the colon, per rectum, and the pet is
imaged with a gamma camera. The isotope normally, in order, is
absorbed and drained through colonic veins and then the caudal
mesenteric vein, portal vein, liver, and heart. In a PSS, the isotope
reaches the heart, bypassing the liver, and then returns to the liver
through the arterial circulation.116 If a shunt is present, a calculated
shunt fraction provides an estimate of the percentage of portal blood
bypassing the liver. A fraction <15% is considered normal whereas
most dogs with PSS have fractions >60-80%. Some cats with PSS
(52% in one study) have lower fractions than dogs.123 There is
considerable variation (variable colonic absorption, operator
variability, fecal matter in the colon), so comparisons at different
time points are difficult and should not be used for assessing
postoperative success.124
If the isotope is administered “too high” into the rectum,
absorption directly into the CVC can occur, falsely elevating shunt
fractions. Since the half-life of pertechnetate is 6 hrs, animals must
be isolated for at least 24 hrs. Scintigraphy does not provide
morphologic information regarding shunt type or location, cannot
distinguish IHPSS from EHPSS, and cannot differentiate single from

multiple shunts. Scintigraphy can be normal or abnormal in dogs
with MVD/PVH. Shunt fractions can be lower in dogs with MVD
than macroscopic PSSs. Shunt fraction estimation is inexact and
prone to interoperator and intraoperator variability. Use of
transsplenic portal scintigraphy for diagnosis of a PSS, using
99M
TCO4−, has helped distinguish single from multiple shunts but
not IHPSS from EHPSS, and is not used routinely.125

A recent study correlated liver volume, portal vascular anatomy on
CTA, hepatic perfusion, and scintigraphy in dogs with cPSS before
and after attenuation with an ameroid constrictor (AC).126
Decreased hepatic arterial perfusion and portal shunt fraction, on
scintigraphy, correlated with liver volume. These were indicators of
successful shunt attenuation. Dogs that did not have visible portal
vasculature on CTA preoperatively had visible vasculature
postoperatively.126

Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) and CTA
MRA provides three-dimensional preoperative shunt images that can
aid in preprocedural planning. Images from dual-phase CTA
(Figure 267.4) are relatively easy to interpret, provide superior
detail (particularly with newer multi-slice CT scanners), and are less
costly and time consuming than MRA. MR imaging without
gadolinium-enhanced angiography is less promising, with
sensitivities ranging from 63 -79%, though specificity may be as high

as 97%.11 Contrast enhanced MRA (CE-MRA; Figure 267.5) can
identify both EHPSS and IHPSS,127 and was diagnostic of a portal
vascular anomaly in 16/17 dogs, including IHPSS (n = 13), EHPSS (n
= 2), HAVM (n = 1), and no shunt (n = 1).128 A recent study
evaluating ferumoxytol-enhanced MRA was shown to provide a
comparable vascular anatomy determination to CTA in dogs with
IHPSS.129 Ferumoxytol offers a long-acting IV contrast agent which
can make MRA easier to execute, reaching improved sensitivities
that are comparable to those obtained with gadolinium. This
technique is still in its infancy in veterinary medicine.

Portovenography (PVY)
Portography/PVY is not commonly performed due to availability of
the less invasive US, scintigraphy, and/or CTA/MRA. Surgical
mesenteric portography is the most commonly performed
angiographic test done intraoperatively for documenting PSSs in
dogs and cats. It allows visualization of a shunting vessel but requires
a laparotomy, fluoroscopy, and IV contrast material. The sensitivity
of intraoperative portography is 85-100% and is dependent on
patient positioning and digital subtraction of fluoroscopic images.9-11
Classically, differentiation of IHPSS from EHPSS on PVY is based on
where a shunt diverges from the portal vein. If this point is cranial to
the 13th thoracic vertebra, the shunt is typically intrahepatic, and
caudal to the 13th thoracic vertebra, the shunt is usually
extrahepatic.

Splenic and Mesenteric Angiography
Under US guidance, a bolus of ∼2-4 mL/kg of iohexol (240-360
mg/mL) is injected into a splenic vein. Fluoroscopy or radiography is
used to image splenic venous drainage through the portal vein, and
hepatic or systemic venous flow is identified. Caudally located
EHPSSs can be missed with this technique if the portal branch
communicates with the CVC caudal to the splenic vein.130 Injection
of contrast material into the mesenteric artery, cranial mesenteric
arteriogram via the femoral or carotid artery, is not commonly
utilized for standard PSS due to many less invasive alternatives. This
technique can be useful for HAVM interventional treatment
techniques (ch. 116).

Differential Diagnosis
If an animal is suspected of having a cPSS, conditions causing similar
clinical signs (e.g., GI parasitism [chs. 9, 262], hypoadrenocorticism
[ch. 296], protein-losing enteropathy [ch. 262], other primary
hepatopathies [chs. 268-271], MVD/PVH, NCPH, and HAVM
congenital CNS disorders [ch. 244]) should be ruled out. If SBA
concentrations are suggestive of PSS, differentiating MVD, NCPH,
HAVM, and PSS is necessary, usually with the diagnostic imaging
modalities mentioned above. Plasma protein C activity has been
documented to help differentiate MVD from PSS (protein C levels
were >70% in 88% of dogs with MVD and low in dogs with PSS).97 If
a macroscopic PSS is not identified but remains suspected, then
advanced imaging or PVY with the measurement of portal pressures
could be obtained to diagnose various forms of PVH. If an HAVM is

not found in a young dog with ascites and clinicopathologic evidence
of hepatic dysfunction, then PVH with portal hypertension (NCPH)
is possible and histologic examination of liver tissue is indicated to
rule out other severe hepatopathies and to guide treatment. Other
liver diseases (chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or leptospirosis) can
produce similar signs but are more common in older dogs, often
associated with hyperbilirubinemia and progressive increases in
serum ALT activity. If hyperammonemia and HE are detected in an
animal without evidence of PSS, serum cobalamin should be checked
and a urine metabolic screen should be evaluated for evidence of
ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, methylmalonic acidemia, or
other urea cycle metabolic abnormalities.89

MEDICAL TREATMENT
Aims
Medical management (Table 267.1) should begin in all animals
with portovascular anomalies at the time of diagnosis. Medical
management is aimed at controlling clinical signs associated with
shunting but does not treat the underlying diminished hepatic
perfusion.

Hepatic Encephalopathy (HE)
When a dog or cat has HE, rapid stabilization is required and
intensive efforts should be implemented to decrease ammonia levels
to near normal (chs. 119, 125, and 266). Nothing should be given
orally until the pet is alert and aware. IV fluid therapy to replace and
maintain hydration can be necessary, especially if an animal is
unable to drink or is dehydrated (ch. 120). Lactated Ringer’s
solution often is avoided due to the need for hepatic conversion of
lactate to bicarbonate. Potassium supplementation often is necessary
due to depletion from chronic diarrhea or decreased intake (ch. 68).
Hypokalemia can also contribute to HE.21,62
Metabolic acidosis (ch. 128) can contribute to HE and should be
corrected slowly with fluid therapy and, rarely, sodium bicarbonate.
It is important to verify that concurrent respiratory acidosis does not

exist prior to sodium bicarbonate therapy. Blood glucose
concentration (ch. 61) should be carefully monitored and
supplemented in IV fluids, particularly in young puppies with PSS,
where glycogen stores and gluconeogenesis are minimal. Therapy for
acute, severe HE includes nothing by mouth (NPO), administering
cleansing enemas with warm water and/or lactulose (ch. 108), oral
lactulose therapy, antibiotic therapy (metronidazole, ampicillin, or
neomycin), and anticonvulsants if needed (Table 267.1). Gammaaminobutyric acid (GABA) and its receptors have been implicated in
the pathogenesis of HE, with many other substances.21 Using a
benzodiazepine antagonist like flumazenil (0.02 mg/kg IV to effect)
has been beneficial in humans with HE-induced comas. Mannitol
should be considered in pets with severe HE or after seizures (ch.
246).21 In people, there is an association between HE and cerebral
edema.8,21
