Seizure Control
Low-dose midazolam is a benzodiazepine preferred over diazepam
due to its lack of propylene glycol as a carrying agent, which requires
liver metabolism. Once seizures are controlled, loading with either
phenobarbital, potassium bromide, sodium bromide, or
levetiracetam (Keppra) should be considered (Table 267.1; chs. 45
and 247). In one study, significantly fewer (0/42) dogs
preoperatively treated with levetiracetam (20 mg/kg PO q8h for a
minimum of 24 hr) experienced postoperative seizures after
attenuation of cPSS, whereas 4/84 (5%) of dogs not pretreated with
levetiracetam had seizures.131 More recent studies, however, did not
identify a protective effect of pre-operative levetiracetam.132,133 In 3
dogs with status epilepticus after PSS attenuation, a propofol bolus
and constant rate infusion (CRI), combined with phenobarbital, led
to recovery and discharge over 7-9 days, without recurrent CNS
signs.134 Medetomidine has also recently been reported for
treatment of postoperative refractory seizures in a dog.135

Lactulose and Antibiotics

Lactulose is a disaccharide metabolized by colonic bacteria to organic
acids, given by enema or PO (ch. 266). It promotes acidification of
colonic contents, trapping ammonia in the form of ammonium;
decreases bacterial numbers; and eliminates ammonium and
bacteria in the feces by preventing systemic absorption. The osmotic
effect results in catharsis, reducing fecal transit time and exposure to
bacteria for proliferation and ammonia production. Antibiotics, such
as metronidazole, neomycin, or ampicillin, decrease GI bacterial
numbers, further reducing ammonia production. Metronidazole and
ampicillin also decrease the risk of bacterial translocation and
systemic infections. In pets with signs of bleeding or anemia,
transfusion of packed red blood cells, whole blood, or fresh frozen
plasma may be of benefit (ch. 124). If there is evidence of HE, fresh
whole blood is preferred, as stored blood contains a decreased
concentration of clotting factors and elevated ammonia levels,
potentially worsening HE.

Nutrition (chs. 154 and 164)
Nutritional management is important, particularly in young animals
with poor body condition. Diets should be readily digestible, contain
a protein of high biologic value (enough to meet the animal’s needs,
but not to encourage HE), supply enough essential fatty acids,
maintain palatability, and meet the minimum requirements for
vitamins and minerals. Milk and vegetable (e.g., soya) proteins are
lower in aromatic amino acids (tyrosine and phenylalanine) and
higher in branched-chain amino acids, such as valine, leucine, and
isoleucine. These sources are less likely to precipitate HE.8,21 Protein
content of 18-22% for dogs and 30-35% for cats (dry matter basis)
should be the goal, with dairy or vegetable proteins preferred (ch.
266). Excessive protein restriction should be avoided because of the
risk of negative nitrogen balance, muscle breakdown and reduced
serum albumin.

Gastric Bleeding/Ulceration
GI bleeding is usually treated with a proton pump inhibitor
(omeprazole) and sucralfate. Misoprostol is used to enhance gastric
mucosal turnover, although there is no evidence of its efficacy in

dogs and cats with PSS. Animals with IHPSS are predisposed to GI
ulcerations.66,136 Use of lifelong gastric acid suppressant therapy in
dogs with IHPSS decreases morbidity associated with GI bleeding.
Nonsteroidal, and steroidal, antiinflammatory drugs should be
avoided in any dog with liver disease, but particularly those with
IHPSS, as this could perpetuate GI ulceration.

Ascites and Fibrosis
Ascites and fibrosis can occur in pets with HAVM or NCPH but are
rare in cPSSs unless there is severe hypoalbuminemia. If ascites is
due to poor oncotic pressure, colloidal therapy may be of value and
dietary protein content should be investigated (chs. 120 and 154). If
ascites is due to portal hypertension, diuretic therapy and low
sodium diets should be considered (chs. 157 and 229). Additional
sodium sources (particularly treats) can exacerbate ascites and
should be avoided. Spironolactone is the initial diuretic of choice
because of the importance of activation of the renin-angiotensinaldosterone system (RAAS) in portal hypertension and for its
potassium-sparing effects. Furosemide may be needed but should be
used with caution; it potentiates further RAAS activation and
hypokalemia. In some, therapeutic abdominocentesis is necessary to
make breathing easier and make the pet more comfortable (ch. 86).

Nutraceuticals
While recommended for a variety of liver diseases, nutraceuticals are
not necessary in portovascular anomalies that can be repaired
surgically or interventionally. Surgical or interventional therapies are
not used and nutraceuticals may have value for MVD, NCPH,
multiple EHPSS, or when shunts remain patent (e.g., HAVMs, many
IHPSSs; Table 267.1). S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAMe) has
hepatoprotective, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory properties. It
is important in membrane structure, fluidity, and function. It also
aids in the metabolism of glutathione, which is involved in many
metabolic processes and plays a critical role in detoxification
mechanisms of the cell. Depletion of hepatic glutathione can
indirectly cause toxic effects in these cells by increasing oxidative
stress, particularly in cats.

Vitamin E is an antioxidant which may prevent or minimize lipid
peroxidation within hepatocytes. Ursodeoxycholic acid is
recommended for most inflammatory, oxidative, and cholestatic liver
diseases and often is used in NCPH. It has anti-inflammatory,
immunomodulatory, and antifibrotic properties, as well as increasing
fluidity of biliary secretions, promoting choleresis and decreasing the
toxic effects of hydrophobic bile acids on hepatocytes. Silymarin is
the active extract in milk thistle. There is an abundance of data in
both in vivo and in vitro experimental animal models showing the
antioxidant and free radical scavenging properties of silymarin.21
Specifically, it has been shown to inhibit lipid peroxidation of
hepatocyte and microsomal membranes and protect against gene
damage by suppression of hydrogen peroxide, superoxide, and
lipoxygenase. Silymarin also increases hepatic glutathione content,
appears to retard hepatic collagen formation, and has
hepatoprotective effects through inhibition of Kupffer cell function.
Milk thistle has low toxicity and few side-effects, although its efficacy
in chronic liver disease is unproven.

Sodium Benzoate and/or Sodium Phenylbutyrate for
Dogs With cPSS
Neither agent controlled hyperammonemia in dogs with cPSS in a
study of efficacy. Neither should be part of the medical management
plan for dogs with cPSS.137

Outcomes With Medical Management Alone
In humans with cPSSs, their long-term prognosis without surgery is
excellent. cPSSs in humans are often not recognized until older age.
However, there is high risk of hepatocellular neoplasia when infants
are diagnosed with cPSS. Surgery is indicated in infants because
ligation causes regression of benign tumors. In 27 dogs with cPSSs
evaluated after long-term medical management alone, 14/27 (51.8%)
had been euthanized (median: 20 months after diagnosis) with a
median survival time (MST) of 9.9 months; 4/27 (14.8%) were lost to
follow-up; and 9/27 (33%) survived long-term with an MST of 56.9
months (4.7 years; range 5 months to >7 years) with many alive at

the time of publication.52 Of the 27 dogs, 9 had EHPSS, 17 had
IHPSS, and 1 was complex. This distribution is reflective of
veterinarians hesitant to perform surgery on IHPSS vs EHPSS due to
reported complications and technical difficulty. Some dogs with
IHPSS treated only medically continued to have CNS signs, GI signs,
and urinary tract signs. In contrast, dogs with EHPSS had clinical
signs occur with similar or lower frequency once medicated.52 Dogs
treated medically had a significant decline in total protein, ALP, and
ALT levels. Bile acids, BUN, albumin, and MCV did not show
significant changes long-term. Eleven of 17 (64.7%) dogs with IHPSS
were euthanized, usually due to uncontrolled signs of HE, and 3/9
(33%) dogs with EHPSS were euthanized.

Prognostic Indicators for Medical Management of
Dogs With cPSS
Medically managed dogs that are older at the onset of clinical signs
and dogs with higher BUNs have longer survival times. There are no
correlations with survival time among bile acids, serum protein,
albumin, ALP, ALT, or MCV. Overall, >50% of dogs treated
medically can be expected to be euthanized, usually due to persistent
HE, within 10 months of diagnosis and ∼33% can survive long-term
with medical management alone, though clinical signs do not
necessarily resolve. Euthanasia in some is due to progressive hepatic
fibrosis leading to portal hypertension.73 Another prospective study
of dogs with cPSS found that 24/27 dogs (88%) treated only
medically died or were euthanized, compared to 21/97 dogs (21.6%)
treated surgically.138 Survival in this study was not affected by age or
shunt morphology and all dogs were showing clinical signs at the
time of enrollment. Considering consistent results in the literature
and the experience of many, surgical or interventional attenuation,
when possible, is the treatment of choice for cPSS patients showing
clinical signs. If attenuation is not possible, a minority survive longterm with medical management.138,139 A study suggested better
survival times in surgically or interventionally treated HAVM as
compared with dogs managed medically.140

SURGERY
Preoperative Management
Many pets with PSSs are debilitated, in poor body condition, and not
neurologically stable when diagnosed. Intensive medical care, as
described, should be routine, even in animals that are not showing
clinical signs (chs. 119 and 125). After diagnosis, the pet may be
discharged, to return for surgery in weeks to months. There is no
ideal time for surgery, but surgeons usually prefer pets be treated
medically to minimize clinical signs, control HE, and gain weight
before intervening. Medical management likely reduces the risk of
postoperative seizures. Smaller debilitated pets are at risk for
perioperative hypothermia, hypoglycemia, and intraoperative
hemorrhage. Preoperative anticonvulsant therapy is controversial,
and is often used in pets with HE. Evidence that levetiracetam
pretreatment decreases risk of postoperative seizures and improves
survival is not clear.131-133,141 More broadly, it is not clear whether
anticonvulsants should routinely be employed preoperatively while a
pet is receiving appropriate medical therapy. Hypothermia during
abdominal surgery should be anticipated and forced warm air or
fluid blankets with or without warm water bottles should be used.
Water bottles should be changed regularly. For interventional
procedures, both jugular veins (IHPSS) or the femoral/carotid
arteries (HAVM) should be clipped of fur for access.

Anesthesia/Colloids
General anesthesia for pets with liver disease has been described.142
Briefly, anesthetic agents that are highly protein-bound or dependent
on liver metabolism are avoided. IV dextrose is often given during
anesthesia because the pet is often thin, debilitated, and fasted.
Colloidal support often is used (particularly in IHPSS) during
anesthesia (ch. 120). Although relatively less expensive plasma can
be used in small pets, the authors prefer synthetic colloids (1-2
mL/kg/h IV) which reduce risk of transfusion reactions and
perioperative thrombosis of the manipulated PSS that could
theoretically result from excessive plasma administration. There are
various colloidal support protocols. Since these pets are not usually

“hypocoagulable,” use of plasma for colloidal support should not be
routine. Blood type and coagulation screens are not usually obtained,
particularly in IHPSS, regardless of bleeding risk.

Antibiotics
Many are young and immunologically incompetent. Implants are
often used and there is systemic bacterial translocation from the GI
tract that is normally cleared by the liver, but instead shunted
systemically. Many already receive antibiotics as part of the
preoperative medical management regimen.

Goals of Surgery
The goal of surgery for PSSs is to attenuate the abnormal vessel to reestablish hepatic parenchyma blood flow from the portal system.
Complete shunt attenuation is the goal because partial shunt
occlusion has a worse prognosis.105,143 Unfortunately, the most
affected pets have insufficient portal development to permit
complete acute shunt ligation; 32-52% of dogs with EHPSS and
<15% with IHPSS have tolerated complete acute shunt
attenuation.105,143-145 A delicate balance must be addressed: shunt
attenuation to increase portal blood pressure sufficient for
developing portal perfusion without causing excessive portal
hypertension. If portal hypertension occurs acutely, pets could
develop ascites, GI congestion, diarrhea, hypoxemia, and possible
bowel ischemia. If portal hypertension occurs chronically, when the
portal vasculature fails to develop, multiple aPSSs may develop.

Surgical Technique
Progressive occlusion devices can reduce the risk of acute portal
hypertension, but it is unclear if these devices reduce development of
chronic portal hypertension and subsequent multiple acquired
shunts. Reportedly, 40-50% of dogs redevelop clinical signs
following partial ligation of EHPSS, months to years after surgery
(not including gradual occlusion devices).32,143,146 It is not clear if
the worse prognosis is due to partial attenuation or to reduced portal
vascular development at the time of surgery that prevented complete

acute attenuation. Further, it is often unclear whether these dogs had
persistent shunting or developed aPSSs.105
Following identification, careful dissection, and isolation of the
shunt, an encircling suture is placed as close as possible to the
systemic circulation (shunt termination) side. Shunt attenuation in
this location ensures no portal vessels join the shunt distal to the
attenuation site.146-154 Following temporary shunt attenuation,
intraoperative portal pressures >9-10 cm water above resting (preligation) or absolute pressures >17-24 cm water have been associated
with greater postoperative complications.105,155,156 Clinical signs
also have been used for determining if complete acute shunt
occlusion can be tolerated. In one study, 11 of 12 nonencephalopathic dogs with clinical signs attributable only to
ammonium biurate urolithiasis tolerated complete occlusion
safely.157 Animals with portal aplasia likely survive due to hepatic
arterial perfusion, often indicated by liver biopsies demonstrating
arteriolar proliferation.103,104 It is also likely that a wide spectrum of
shunt size and portal vascular development is encountered. This
explains how some pets with a PSS have minimal clinical signs and
live with or without medical therapy.
Complete abdominal exploration is always indicated because
animals with one congenital abnormality often have others. The
urinary bladder should be carefully palpated to identify calculi that
should be removed. Spay or castration is recommended. Liver biopsy
has been recommended, though one study reported no ability to
predict prognosis based upon pre-ligation biopsy results.103 The
authors do not perform liver biopsies routinely; however, liver biopsy
may be indicated when a macroscopic shunt cannot be identified
with surgery or portography.

Extrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt (EHPSS) Surgery
With Ameroid Constrictors (ACs)
Following identification of an EHPSS, the surgeon must decide if
complete attenuation is possible, using portal pressure
measurements, portal venography, and/or visual inspection.
Complete acute shunt attenuation is recommended, but complete

attenuation may increase the risk of the procedure.105,143 Gradualocclusion devices, e.g., ACs, cellophane bands (CBs; also called “thin
film bands” [TFBs]), have altered the management of most EHPSSs.
It was believed that hygroscopic casein in ACs gradually absorbed
peritoneal fluid, resulting in concentric expansion due to the
surrounding stainless steel ring. This produced complete shunt
attenuation in 6/12 dogs at 1 month and an additional 3/12 dogs by 7
months after surgery.151 However, partial occlusion and thrombosis
have been noted with ACs placed on dog iliac veins.158 Furthermore,
if shunt occlusion is too rapid or if occlusion is affected by the
amount of dissection needed for AC placement, the weight of the AC
on the thin-walled PSS vessel, repeated re-sterilization of an AC,159
AC size, or extent of tissue reaction surrounding the AC,160 multiple
aPSSs (17% of dogs) could follow.150,151
Reported complication rates are 7-20% and mortality rates are 017% following AC placement for EHPSS, with good to excellent
outcomes in up to 94% of dogs and estimated MSTs of 152
months.32,150,151,161,162 Dogs with incomplete shunt attenuation can
still have a good prognosis; in one study, continued flow through the
shunt after AC placement was identified in 21% with good to
excellent outcomes.161 Compared with suture ligation, ACs reduce
surgery times and intraoperative complication rates.161,163 With AC
placement for EHPSS in dogs, CTA and perfusion scans have
demonstrated smaller preoperative liver volumes to have the largest
subsequent increases in volume. Hepatic arterial perfusion and
portal scintigraphy both have correlated with successful shunt
attenuation.126

Extrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt (EHPSS) Surgery
With Cellophane Bands (CBs)
CBs use inexpensive material derived from plant cellulose, often
cigarette or giftwrap packaging. CBs are inflammatory, causing
progressive fibrosis around vessels. The material is easily sterilized
and stored, lightweight (will not kink the PSS), and requires less

shunt dissection. Most available “cellophane materials” are not
actually cellophane, the latter being distinguished by visible
striations (and confirmed using infrared spectroscopy).164 The more
progressive attenuation achieved with a CB149 is hypothesized to
reduce the incidence of aPSS. Following shunt dissection and
isolation, a three-layer folded piece of cellophane ∼3-4 mm in
diameter is placed around the shunt and secured with hemoclips.
Complete shunt occlusion appears to be possible without initial
shunt attenuation during placement. Partial attenuation at the time
of CB placement could be associated with development of aPSSs.165
Complication rates are ∼10-13% and mortality rates 3-9% following
CB of EHPSS, with good to excellent outcomes in ∼84% of
dogs.165,166 However, multiple aPSSs were demonstrated in 3/16
dogs (19%) with elevated shunt fractions 6 weeks following CB
placement.167 In general, clinical signs in many dogs with PSSs may
resolve despite persistent shunting.144,161,162,167 More recent
comparisons of EHPSS treated with AC or TFB suggest good
outcomes can be expected with both techniques; however, there may
be more persistent shunting and need for additional procedures
when TFB is performed initially.168-171

Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt (IHPSS) Surgery
IHPSSs are usually much larger, located within hepatic parenchyma,
and often not readily apparent to the surgeon. A soft spot can
occasionally be felt within the lobe with a large IHPSS, but does not
help identify the ideal location for dissection. Also, as many as 25%
of dogs with IHPSS have more than one shunt, as demonstrated by
intrahepatic venous collaterals on CT or portography.172 When
treated surgically, left divisional shunts are commonly approached
posthepatically (cranial to the liver) because these often enter the left
hepatic vein that enters the CVC at the level of the diaphragm. For
right and central divisional shunts that often enter the CVC
intrahepatically, the surgical approach is often performed
prehepatically (caudal to the liver) in order to dissect the
contributing portal vein branch (which typically is much larger than

the left portal branch). Various preoperative (CTA, MRA) and
intraoperative (PVY) methods can help identify shunt anatomy.
Surgical options include surgical dissection and attenuation with
suture, AC, CB, or hydraulic occluder (HO). Other options include
complete IHPSS occlusion with jugular venograft creation of an
EHPSS, temporary hepatic inflow occlusion with IV dissection, and
percutaneous transvenous coil embolization (PTCE) via the jugular
vein (ch. 116).8,66,155,166,173-179
Surgical complication rates are substantially higher in IHPSS (2977%) compared with EHPSS, and most (82%) only tolerate partial
attenuation.146,180,181 Mortality rates are 6-23% following suture
attenuation or 0-9% following placement of an AC, with good to
excellent outcomes in ∼75-100% of dogs following suture attenuation
and ∼70-90% following AC placement.175,182,183 Good to excellent
outcomes were reported in only 50% of dogs that underwent CB with
a 55% perioperative complication rate and 27% perioperative
mortality.166 A recent study comparing CB or PTCE for canine
IHPSS reported similar outcomes with the two techniques; however,
fewer minor and major complications occurred in the PTCE
group.184
Persistent shunting and unreliability of progressive occlusion
devices led to investigating HOs, an adjustable silicone cuff placed
around the IHPSS and attached to actuator tubing, and a vascular
access port placed subcutaneously at the time of surgery. This device
can be manually inflated with saline using a Huber needle placed
transcutaneously into the port in the awake dog weeks to months
after placement, as needed, to slowly inflate the cuff and
progressively occlude the shunt.185 Immediate survival was 100% for
10 dogs undergoing HO attenuation of IHPSS with a 20%
intraoperative complication rate. Surgical revisions were needed in 3
of 10 dogs before device modifications were made. Resolution of
clinical signs, and long-term survival, were documented in 8 dogs,185
but persistent shunting, aPSSs, and/or hepatic dysfunction was
suspected based on persistently elevated bile acids (4/8) and positive
scintigraphy scans (5/8) 2 weeks following complete HO
closure.27,175,185,186

COMPLICATIONS FOLLOWING PSS
ATTENUATION
Overview
Intraoperative complications typically are associated with anesthesia
or hemorrhage during shunt dissection. Postoperative complications
associated with PSS usually include neurologic abnormalities, acute
portal hypertension, and/or persistent shunting (either through the
original shunt or via the development of aPSSs).

Seizures
Postoperative seizures not associated with HE or hypoglycemia have
been reported in up to 12% of dogs.141 Preoperative phenobarbital
appeared to reduce severity but not incidence of neurologic sequelae
following shunt surgery.141 In another study, levetiracetam (20
mg/kg PO q8h for ≥24 hr preoperatively) significantly reduced the
incidence of postoperative seizures in dogs with EHPSS, but more
recent studies question this protective effect.131-133 Postoperative
seizures occur in dogs and cats, are independent of the type of
attenuation procedure, can occur days later, and are not associated
with the original HE. Reports are conflicting as to whether older
animals are at increased risk.141,187,188 Possible explanations include
the acute removal of endogenous benzodiazepines or changes in
brain amino acid concentrations or ratios.21,22,189
After surgery for PSS, all dogs and cats should be monitored for
neurologic signs. There is no agreed-upon algorithm for treatment,
but intensive management should be instituted immediately with
anticonvulsant therapy and/or propofol boluses (1-3.5 mg/kg IV)
followed by propofol IV CRIs (0.1-0.2 mg/kg/min or higher) (ch.
125).190 Phenobarbital loading is preferred because therapeutic
plasma levels can be achieved rapidly and levels can be readily
monitored. There should be less concern over using a potentially
hepatotoxic medication when planned for short-term use.
Recumbent, sedated, or comatose pets are difficult to load with
potassium bromide. Levetiracetam (Keppra) levels are not yet well

understood. Medetomidine has been reported to have been
successful in managing a dog with post attenuation seizures.135
Ventilation may be necessary in some pets and others can take
weeks or longer to recover. Acepromazine has been reported to help
decrease seizure activity in dogs with PSS, contrary to the previous
concern of acepromazine decreasing the seizure threshold.191 It has
been used at low dosages (0.005-0.01 mg/kg IV) for postprocedural
seizures. In general, the prognosis is considered poor; however,
many can recover with time and aggressive supportive care.
Recovery may never be complete and some continue to have some
long-term neurologic dysfunction. Reports have described 6 of 10
dogs and 9/11 dogs recovering following postligation neurologic
dysfunction, albeit some incompletely.141,166 In one recent study on
post-attenuation seizures in PSS dogs, only 32% survived to 30 days,
and positive predictors of short-term survival included a history of
pre-operative seizures and focal (rather than generalized)
seizures.192

Portal Hypertension
Some degree of portal hypertension can occur following acute partial
or complete shunt attenuation, causing mild ascites with or without
incisional drainage. Life-threatening conditions are uncommon,
particularly after introduction of progressive attenuation devices.
Worrisome postoperative signs, e.g., vomiting, abdominal
distension, progressive ascites, abdominal pain, and hypotension can
lead to shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
Immediate removal of the attenuating device is recommended in
those dogs and cats that do not respond to initial intensive
supportive care; however, once clinical signs have been recognized,
recovery is uncommon. Use of anticoagulants and/or thrombolytics
postoperatively to prevent or manage these conditions is not well
evaluated. Portal hypertension has not been a problem with the
IHPSS PTCE technique,27 likely due to the shunt attenuation being
located post-sinusoidally at the shunt orifice on the CVC. Increased
pressures generated at this location seem to be relieved through
intrahepatic venous collaterals before (at lower pressures) pre-

sinusoidal portal hypertension develops, reducing risk of portal
hypertension complications while also reducing the likelihood of
restoring complete hepatic portal flow without some degree of
shunting. This may be a reasonable trade-off between risk and
benefit and likely occurs with any type of IHPSS attenuation at this
location. This phenomenon also likely explains the persistence of
abnormal clinical, biochemical, and scintigraphic evaluations
following what was considered a complete shunt occlusion at the
time of surgery using any of a variety of shunt attenuation
techniques.27 Intrahepatic venous collaterals are identified in up to
25% of IHPSS in dogs before treatment172 but also can develop
iatrogenically post-attenuation.

Postoperative Hypoglycemia or Hypothermia (chs.
61, 130, and 289)
These complications can usually be prevented with appropriate care.
Forty-four percent of dogs were hypoglycemic after EHPSS surgery
and ∼33% did not respond to dextrose. Some respond to
supraphysiologic glucocorticoid doses (dexamethasone 0.1-0.2
mg/kg IV once) as well as to hastened anesthesia recovery. A relative
glucocorticoid insufficiency has not been documented.193

Persisting or Recurring Clinical Signs
While many reports do not have sufficient long-term follow-up to
know their true incidence, persisting or recurring clinical signs
suggest that the original shunt has remained patent, another shunt
was present originally, an incorrect vessel was attenuated, multiple
acquired shunts have developed, concurrent hepatic parenchymal
disease is present, or concurrent neurologic disease is present.
Serum biochemistry and liver function test results can confirm the
PSS; imaging is usually needed to identify the cause. If imaging
confirms shunt occlusion without aPSSs, a presumptive diagnosis of
PVH/MVD can be made.

Severe GI Bleeding

Dogs with IHPSS have a separate but important potential
complication: severe GI ulceration and bleeding, the most common
cause of long-term morbidity and mortality in one case series.27 Use
of lifelong gastric acid-suppressing drugs in IHPSS dogs has reduced
mortality from GI ulceration, in the authors’ cases, from 25% to
3.2%. There are many theories as to why GI ulceration occurs so
commonly in dogs with IHPSS (e.g., hypergastrinemia, abnormal GI
blood flow, hypoprostaglandinemia, poor mucosal integrity,
abnormal mucus production, abnormal cell turnover).
Hypergastrinemia does not seem to be the cause.

SURGERY FOR PORTOSYSTEMIC
SHUNTS IN CATS
Preoperative Management and Surgery
Perioperative management is similar to dogs; however, a higher
frequency of neurologic signs both preoperatively and
postoperatively in cats, despite appropriate medical treatment, has
resulted in use of anticonvulsant therapy preoperatively in all.
Levetiracetam or phenobarbital can be used. Potassium bromide is
avoided due to associated respiratory complications in this species.
Surgical management of PSSs in cats is technically similar to dogs in
terms of shunt identification and methods of attenuation. Although
some surgeons use suture ligation, most use AC or CB in cats even
though there are some concerns regarding the feline inflammatory
response to such devices consistently causing progressive fibrosis
and occlusion of a shunt. A recent case report documented
recanalization of a cPSS previously attenuated with CB in a cat.194
Regardless, successful TFB of feline cPSS has been reported with
83% 6 month survival rates and 89% having normal bile acid
concentrations after surgery.195

Complications
Complications are common, including a 24% postoperative seizure
rate.195 Like in dogs, the perioperative mortality rate for feline

EHPSS is low.65,196,197 Two critical PSS management differences in
cats (compared with dogs) are their high perioperative complication
rates and their worse long-term outcomes, particularly due to
persistent neurologic sequelae. Reported complication rates have
varied from 24-62%. Post-attenuation neurologic signs including
seizures following suture ligation have ranged from 8-77% following
AC placement, and in 1/5 cats and 3/9 cats following use of
CB.65,166,195-199,200 Neurologic signs include seizures in 8-33% of
cats and central blindness (usually transient) in up to 44%.61,166,195198
Lower intraoperative mesenteric portography scores (reduced
portal perfusion) are associated with a higher incidence of postattenuation neurological complications.199 One study on postattenuation neurological signs following PSS attenuation in cats was
unable to identify an association with the use of preoperative
levetiracetam, preoperative HE signs, age, shunt type, or degree of
shunt attenuation performed.200 A more recent, separate
classification of splenosystemic shunts in cats has been described,
predominantly identified in older spayed females often with
concurrent hepatopathies that may have been associated with portal
hypertension. Treatment for this different population of PSS cats will
vary accordingly.70

Outcomes
Reports must be interpreted with caution due to different follow-up
durations; however, fair to excellent outcomes have been reported in
75% of cats following suture ligation, 25-75% following AC
placement, and 66% and 100% (5/5) following CB
placement.61,166,196-198 Many cats have a good clinical outcome
despite persistently abnormal biochemistries: about 33-66% of cats
have had abnormal liver function testing and 57% have had
persistent shunting postoperatively.166,196,197 The contrary is also
true because some cats with persistent CNS dysfunction show
normalized liver function test results.65 In that same report, ∼33% of
cats were euthanized within 1 year due to persistent CNS dysfunction
following AC placement, despite most having normalized liver

function test results.65 IHPSSs are rare in cats, making predictions
on outcome difficult. Feline IHPSS can be treated similarly with
suture, AC, CB, or transvenous coil embolization.65,166,173,196,197

SURGICAL AND INTERVENTIONAL
THERAPIES: HEPATIC
ARTERIOVENOUS MALFORMATIONS
(HAVM)
Description of HAVMs
These are rare vascular anomalies involving multiple arterial
communications to the portal vein (Figure 267.5). Because they
usually involve multiple, rather than single, communications with a
central nidus, or “nest,” the term malformation rather than fistula is
appropriate. These communications are usually from the hepatic
artery but also have involved the gastroduodenal, left gastric, and
phrenic arteries. Angiography, CTA, or MRA helps identify the origin
and course of these numerous vessels. Based on CT angiography,
communications have been classified.201 The arterial blood shunting
to the portal vein is high in pressure, causing severe, chronic portal
hypertension often with subsequent massive ascites that results in
multiple aPSSs, as discussed. Multiple aPSSs have been observed in
every animal with HAVM except those with concurrent IHPSS.

Treatments
Liver lobectomy, ligation of the nutrient artery, fluoroscopicallyguided glue embolization of abnormal arterial vessels, and dominant
outflow vein (DOV) occlusion have been employed (ch. 116).30,202
Most HAVMs are located in the left or central liver lobes, and 25%
have involved two lobes. Lobectomy can be challenging because of
vascularity and proximity to the gallbladder and CVC. Temporary
occlusion of the portal vein and celiac artery (and often the cranial
mesenteric artery) is recommended during partial lobectomy to
reduce intraoperative hemorrhage.202 Lobectomy may be

contraindicated if the HAVM involves most of the liver parenchyma;
the liver mass after arteriovenous malformation (AVM) resection
might not provide sufficient hepatic function. Glue embolization is
described in ch. 113.
More recently the authors have been investigating venous
occlusion of HAVM, as these vascular anomalies resemble the large
pelvic AVMs in humans that can benefit from a venous (rather than
arterial) embolization. The concept is that a single, proximal
draining vein (DOV) immediately distal to the AVM nidus will
provide occlusion and such occlusion could be safer and more
effective than attempting to embolize the innumerable small arterial
feeding branches just proximal to the nidus. In one study,
conservative management, arterial embolization, or DOV occlusion
for HAVMs showed favorable outcomes and a reduced need for a
subsequent procedure when DOV was performed.140

Complications
Complications of surgery include hemorrhage, portal hypertension,
systemic hypotension, bradycardia, and portal or mesenteric vein
thrombus formation.30 Perioperative survival was 100% in dogs
undergoing glue embolization, with or without partial hepatectomy,
and 75-91% of dogs undergoing surgery alone.30 Long-term outcome
was fair or good for 38-57% of dogs treated with surgery alone and
100% for a small number of dogs treated with glue embolization.
Overall, 75% of dogs continue to require dietary or medical
management of clinical signs due to patent acquired EHPSS.30
Recurrence of arteriovenous communications can occur and
recurrence of clinical signs has been seen requiring additional
embolization procedures. Long-term survival is considered fair to
good with these interventional techniques, but too few cases have
been performed to be certain.30,140

POSTOPERATIVE CARE
General

After surgery or IR treatment, patients are maintained on IV fluids
until they are eating and drinking. Dextrose is added to the fluids
when blood glucose is <80 mg/dL (<4.4 mmol/L). Pets must be
monitored for hypothermia, delayed anesthetic recovery,
hemorrhage, seizures, and signs of portal hypertension (chs. 124,
125, 130, 247, and 289). Animals usually require opioid analgesics
such as buprenorphine for 1 to 3 days after surgery, although no
analgesic has been necessary following PSS coil embolization.
Sedation with a low dosage (0.005-0.02 mg/kg IV) of acepromazine
might be necessary if dogs are vocalizing or showing abdominal
splinting, as these activities will increase portal pressure.
Acepromazine does not seem to precipitate seizures in dogs with
shunts (and may even prevent them) but is never used in
hypotensive animals.191

Nutrition (ch. 154), Antibiotics, Lactulose, and
Weaning
A high-quality digestible vegetable or dairy protein diet, antibiotics,
and lactulose are continued after surgery until liver function
improves. Often, oral antibiotics are prescribed for 7-14 days when
an implant has been placed, although this varies. Weaning protocols
vary and no ideal protocol for reduction of medications has been
demonstrated. Weaning may be further delayed for gradual
occlusion devices, particularly the CB that has the slowest
attenuation rate. Biochemical panels are evaluated 1 month after
surgery. If liver parameters are normal, medical management is then
weaned over 2-4 weeks. At 3 months, SBAs are evaluated in EHPSS
dogs and cats. This is not routinely done in IHPSS dogs, or dogs with
HAVMs, particularly if they are doing clinically well and are able to
be weaned off medical management because persistent shunting is
common; instead, in these patients, preprocedural and
postprocedural protein C levels have been monitored along with
routine CBC and biochemistry values.97 If bile acid concentrations
are moderately increased in EHPSS, animals are rechecked 5 to 7
months after surgery. Some clinicians recommend supplementation
with silymarin (milk thistle) or S-adenosyl-L-methionine because of
their hepatoprotective and antioxidative effects (Table 267.1);

clinical studies of efficacy in animals with cPSSs or PVH are
lacking.203
Patients are weaned off medical therapy, typically 1 month after IR
treatment, and this weaning process takes approximately 2-3 weeks
starting with metronidazole, then lactulose, then transitioning to an
adult maintenance food (ch. 154). IHPSS patients are maintained
on proton-pump inhibitors for life. If this is all well tolerated, blood
count and serum protein C and biochemical parameters improve
(MCV, hematocrit, albumin, BUN), and no return of clinical signs
occurs, then the outcome is considered good, regardless of bile acids
test results. It has been shown repeatedly that return of bile acids to
normal after IHPSS attenuation is not necessarily correlated with
long-term outcome.32,95,143,180

INTRODUCTION
Whereas canine and feline hepatic vascular abnormalities (ch. 267)
are commonly reported, congenital biliary disorders have received
far less attention. Ductal plate malformations (DPMs) represent a
complex spectrum of pathological abnormalities arising from
abnormal development of the biliary ductal system.1-4 Normally,
highly orchestrated remodeling of a periportal sheet of embryonic
biliary precursor cells, known as the ductal plate, ultimately gives
rise to a complex network of bile ducts and ductules. Disturbances of
this delicate process can result in a continuum of pathological
abnormalities, collectively referred to as DPMs. Depending on the
level and extent of the biliary tree affected, the resulting disease
entities may exist as individual conditions or in combination.1,4-6
Although DPMs are well described in people, the occurrence of such
conditions in animals is less well studied. Nonetheless, their
importance may be underestimated considering that resulting
clinical and histopathological features bear similarities with other
etiologies of chronic hepatobiliary disease.6

EMBRYOLOGY OF THE BILIARY TRACT
Although the development of the biliary tract has been largely
determined from studies of humans and rodent embryos, the process
is considered to be relatively well-conserved across species.7-9 In the
embryo, the liver and biliary tract arise from the hepatic
diverticulum or “liver bud” which originates from the endoblastic
epithelium of the ventral wall of the cranial foregut.2,8-11 As this
hollow structure grows in size, it divides into a cranial part (pars
hepatica) and caudal part (pars cystica), which will ultimately give

rise to the liver parenchyma and extrahepatic biliary tree,
respectively. Sprouts of endodermal cells from the cranial part
extend from its outer surface into the adjacent mesoderm of the
septum transversum, which divides the pericardial and peritoneal
cavities. These liver-precursor cells grow between endothelium-lined
spaces connected with the capillary plexus of the vitelline veins,
thereby forming the characteristic architectural structure of the liver
with cords of hepatocytes alternating with hepatic sinusoids.2,8,9,11
The caudal bud of the hepatic diverticulum progressively grows in
length, giving rise to the primitive gallbladder, cystic duct, and
common bile duct (ductus choledochus).2,8-11 As the portion between
the cystic duct and the gut lengthens, a further bud forms from the
dorsal wall of the developing common bile duct, which gives rise to
the ventral pancreatic bud. By contrast, the hepatic ducts arise from
the cranial part of the hepatic diverticulum, forming initially as a
single, broad, funnel-like hepatic duct which later subdivides into
several separate channels as a result of rapid cellular proliferation in
the portion adjacent to the porta hepatis.10-12 Despite originating
from different parts of the hepatic diverticulum, all parts of the
developing extrahepatic biliary tree have been shown to maintain
luminal continuity from the start of organogenesis to its
completion.10,12
Compared to the extrahepatic biliary system, intrahepatic biliary
development is believed to occur somewhat later in gestation,2,10
although the exact timing in dogs and cats is unknown. Based on
changes in cytokeratin expression and other immunohistochemical
studies evaluating markers for parenchymal and bile duct cell
phenotypes in human and rodent embryos, intrahepatic biliary ducts
are postulated to arise from developing hepatoblasts,10,13,14 with
biliary cell differentiation induced by a periportal gradient of
activin/transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) signaling and
other influences such as hepatocyte nuclear factor 6 (HNF6) and
Notch and Wnt signaling.10,11,15 Consequently, the portal veins
become surrounded by a cuff of biliary cells, which duplicates to
form a double layered sleeve known as the “ductal plate” (Figure
268.1). As gestation further progresses, this slit-like structure

undergoes extensive remodeling, with short segments of its
perimeter developing ‘‘tubular’’ dilatations lined by taller, keratinrich cells, that become incorporated into the surrounding periportal
mesenchyme as individualized bile ducts.2,10,11 Although most of the
redundant epithelial components of the ductal plate not involved in
tubule formation subsequently involute or differentiate into
periportal hepatocytes,10,16 the primitive ducts remain connected to
the ductal plate and its adjacent parenchyma by thin epithelial
channels which communicate with the developing canalicular
network located between the hepatocyte precursor cells.10
Development and remodeling of the ductal plate occurs in a
predictable and organized fashion, beginning around the larger
portal vein branches in the region of the hilum and later spreading
centrifugally to smaller vessels at the periphery of the liver.2,10,15 In
humans, this process is thought to continue into the neonatal period
with full maturation of the most peripheral biliary tree not occurring
for several weeks postpartum.2,10,13 Although the regulatory factors
underlying intrahepatic bile duct development remain incompletely
defined, numerous transcription factors and genes are likely key in
influencing cellular differentiation, proliferation and apoptosis,
adhesion molecule expression, and cell polarity and
orientation.2,10,11,15 In addition, the portal mesenchyme is thought
to be crucial for inducing the biliary differentiation of bipotential
hepatoblasts and subsequent ductal plate remodeling.2 In turn, the
ductal plates are believed to influence the development of
neighboring intrahepatic arterial vessels, which are themselves
presumed to have a reciprocal facilitatory role in biliary tubule
formation and maturation.10,11 Thus, the portal vein appears to be a
key instigating factor not only in the evolution of the intrahepatic
biliary tree but also in the development of the portal triads and the
characteristic lobular microarchitecture of the hepatic parenchyma.

FIGURE 268.1 Illustration of normal
development of the ductal plate (A-C) and ductal
plate malformation (D and E). During early
embryogenesis, a single layer of biliary precursor
cells forms around the developing portal vein (A)
which later differentiates into a double-layered
ductal plate with a slit-like primitive bile duct lumen
(B). Under normal circumstances, highly
orchestrated remodeling of the ductal plate results in
a peri-portal network of fine bile ducts (C).
Abnormal remodeling and resorption of ductal plates
can, however, lead to large, dilated bile duct

structures surrounding the central portal vein (D) or
irregularly shaped proliferating bile ducts with
abnormal branching (E).

PATHOGENESIS OF DUCTAL PLATE
MALFORMATIONS (DPMs)
In its simplest sense, DPM refers to a lack of remodeling of the ductal
plate, resulting in the persistence of embryonic bile duct
structures.2,3,10,17 Thus, DPM can be considered an umbrella term
encompassing a wide range of developmental abnormalities of biliary
development.1,5 Whereas DPMs were originally described as a
microscopic abnormality, diagnostic imaging modalities have
demonstrated concurrent involvement of larger branches of the
intrahepatic biliary tree. Some also consider abnormalities of
extrahepatic biliary tract development, such as choledochal cysts, to
fall under the DPM umbrella spectrum of disorders.6,18-21
Histologically, the appearance of DPMs may depend on the level of
the biliary tree affected and the extent of ductal plate remodeling
that has occurred.1-3,5 With complete lack of remodeling, biliary
vessels, in cross section, appear as dilated ring-like luminal
structures surrounding a central fibrovascular axis, whereas Cshaped structures or interrupted circles of curved bile duct lumina
may occur with incomplete remodeling (Figure 268.1). Progressive
dilation may also result in the development of cyst-like lesions.2,3,10
In addition, aberrant ductal plate remodeling is frequently
accompanied by abnormal portal vein development, where the
vascular tree, rather than forming a regular system of branching
vessels, develops as a dense network of narrow and closely-spaced
ramifications, the appearance of which has been previously likened
to a pollarded willow tree.2,10 Consequently, although portal tracts
may appear subjectively enlarged on histologic examination, these
areas in fact result from the fusion of several adjacent portal tracts,

each containing several hypoplastic portal vessels surrounded by
incompletely remodeled ductal plates and biliary tubules.2,5,10
Although defective formation and function of primary cilia on the
apical cholangiocyte membrane and abnormalities in various
transcriptional regulators (e.g., HNF6, HNF1B and SOX9), and
signaling pathways (e.g., TGF-beta, Notch and Wnt) are suspected to
play a key role in the development of DPM, the exact genetic and
molecular pathogenesis remains ill-defined.11,15,16 Based on studies
in rodent models, it is likely that DPM may represent a common
endpoint caused by a variety of genetic or biochemical defects.17
Consequently, although recent studies have indicated potential for
future classification schemes based on distinct pathogenic
mechanisms, DPMs have traditionally been classified according to
histological appearance and the location of the level of the biliary
tree affected.1-3,6,18,19 Disease entities are therefore often broadly
subcategorized as those resulting in malformation of the extrahepatic
or large intrahepatic bile ducts (e.g., choledochal cysts, Caroli
disease), medium-sized ducts (e.g., polycystic liver disease [PLD]), or
small intrahepatic ducts (e.g., congenital hepatic fibrosis or Von
Meyenburg complexes [VMCs]). Although each can occur in
isolation, it is common for different DPMs to co-exist, and some
authors have consequently suggested that “DPM” be used to describe
all phenotypes within this spectrum, with specific disease
terminology reserved for characteristic histological abnormalities.13,5

DISEASES OF EXTRAHEPATIC AND
LARGE INTRAHEPATIC DUCTS
CHOLEDOCHAL CYST
Background and Etiopathogenesis
Choledochal cysts (CCs) are defined as segmental dilatations of
extrahepatic and/or intrahepatic biliary ducts, although the term
cyst is arguably a misnomer since continuity with the biliary system

is invariably maintained.22-24 They have been best described as
uncommon biliary anomalies in humans but have also been reported
to occur in cats and experimentally in canine and rodent models.2228
CCs are typically subclassified into 5 major types based on
anatomical appearance, of which types I and IV are further divided
(Figure 286.2).22,29 Based on the reported cases, most CCs in cats
are fusiform extrahepatic dilatations of the extrahepatic bile duct
(i.e., type I CCs) measuring up to 10 cm in diameter and often
containing biliary sludge or calculi.24,26-28,30 However, as reported
in humans, concurrent cystic pathology of the intrahepatic ducts
(i.e., type IV), and co-existence with other DPMs can also occur (
Video 268.1).24
Despite considerable debate, the exact etiology remains
uncertain.22 Whereas some believe CCs to be one of the spectrum of
DPMs resulting from disordered biliary morphogenesis and
remodeling, others propose that an anomalous proximal union of the
pancreatic and common bile duct results in a long common channel,
leading to reflux of pancreatic secreta, chronic inflammation, and
progressive bile duct dilatation.19-23,31 A similar phenotype has also
been produced experimentally in dogs following curettage of the
common bile duct wall and sustained increases in intraluminal
biliary pressure.25 Furthermore, considering the variability in CC
morphology, it is also suggested that the etiology, pathophysiology,
and natural course of disease may differ between subtypes.22

Presentation and Clinical Signs
Unlike in humans, where 80% of CCs are diagnosed in infants and
children, of the limited number of feline cases reported, most cats
have presented between the age of 5 and 11 years.24,26–28 Although a
female predisposition has been reported in humans,22 no sex or
breed predilections have yet been reported in other species. Clinical
signs in affected cats often relate to ascending cholangitis and
choledochitis and include vomiting, lethargy, anorexia and weight

loss24,26,27; however, it is possible that CCs may also be discovered
as incidental findings in patients undergoing abdominal
imaging.20,32 Pancreatitis and, rarely, cystic rupture are also
reported as potential sequelae in humans.19,30,32-34 Physical
examination findings are variable but may include hepatomegaly, a
cranial abdominal mass, icterus, and fever.24,26,27

Diagnosis
Nonspecific elevations in alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate
aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), gammaglutamyl transferase (GGT) and bilirubin; leukocytosis; and mild
normocytic, normochromic, nonregenerative anemia may be noted
on routine clinicopathological investigation.24,26-28,30 Diagnosis is
often based on ultrasonographic (US) appearance and surgical
exploration; however, CT, magnetic resonance cholangiography
(MRCP), and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
(ERCP) are also used for diagnosis in humans.19,20,34 Care must be
taken to rule out extrahepatic biliary tract obstruction, the main
differential diagnosis. Aspiration from the cyst can be considered to
confirm biliary origin (e.g., by comparison of cystic fluid and serum
bilirubin concentrations) and obtain samples for cytologic evaluation
and culture but must be weighed against potential risks of bile
leakage and peritonitis.24,27

Treatment and Prognosis
Optimal treatment is dependent on CC morphology.32,35 Septic
complications relating to bacterial cholangitis and choledochitis
should be managed with intravenous (IV) fluid therapy and
antibiotics. In stable animals, CC involving the extrahepatic bile
ducts may be amenable to complete or partial excision with or
without biliary stenting or diversion.24,26,27,32,35 When present,
concurrent infection should be treated postoperatively based on bile
culture and antibiotic sensitivity testing.35 For poor surgical
candidates, such as those with concurrent intrahepatic duct

involvement, medical management with antibiotics, hepatic
antioxidants, and choleretics has been attempted.24 Prognosis is
considered guarded due to the risk of postoperative complications or
recurrent biliary infection as a result of duct dilation and bile stasis.
However, good outcomes have been reported with either surgical or
medical management with follow-up times of 7 months to 5
years.24,26,27 Malignant transformation is a significant concern in
humans, occurring in approximately 6-30% of patients and
particularly those with type I, or IV CCs; it is unclear if the same risk
also exists in other species.32

CAROLI DISEASE AND CAROLI
SYNDROME
Background and Etiopathogenesis
Multifocal segmental dilatation of large intrahepatic bile ducts was
initially characterized by French physician Jacques Caroli in 1958.36
Caroli described two distinct variants: a less common form, known
as Caroli disease, with bile ductular ectasia in the absence of other
hepatic abnormalities, and a more common variant, referred to as
Caroli syndrome, in which bile duct dilatation was associated with
congenital hepatic fibrosis.2,36,37 The former is also classified as type
V CC using the Todani classification (Figure 268.2).20,22 Both
syndromes are recognized as rare causes of hepatobiliary disease in
humans and have also been described in other species including
dogs, cats, and rats.5,37-44 DPM is suspected to underlie both
phenotypes with disordered ductal plate remodeling restricted to the
earlier forming, large intrahepatic bile ducts in Caroli disease, and
Caroli syndrome arising from a combined dysmorphogenesis of both
the large and, later developing, small intrahepatic ducts.1-3,37 The
molecular pathogenesis is incompletely understood. In people, most
cases are inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion and a genetic
cause is therefore suspected.2,37,44 Due to the high frequency of
coexisting autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD), it

has been suggested that mutations in polycystic kidney and hepatic
disease gene 1 (PKHD1)—which encodes fibrocystin, a protein of
primary cilia—may also be responsible for Caroli disease and Caroli
syndrome.45,46 Nonetheless, whether this association equates to
causation, and whether other etiologies may result in the same
phenotype is not known. Interestingly, concurrent cystic renal
disease also appears to be common in dogs; however, no genetic
investigations of affected animals have so far been performed.39,41,42

FIGURE 268.2 Todani’s classification of
choledochal cysts.

Presentation and Clinical Signs
As described in humans, dogs with Caroli disease and Caroli
syndrome may present at a young age or show no clinical signs for
several years. Reported ages at diagnosis range from 6 months to 6

years.5,39,41-43 Although men and women are reported to be equally
affected, sex and breed predilections remain unknown in other
species.44 The clinical presentation is variable depending on the
extent and severity of biliary dilation and hepatic fibrosis, and the
coexistence of other conditions such as chronic kidney disease
(CKD). Vomiting, polyuria/polydipsia, ascites, anorexia, weight loss,
jaundice, and neurological signs have been commonly reported in
affected dogs; most have had significant concurrent fibrosis
consistent with Caroli syndrome.39,41-43 On physical examination,
hepatomegaly, icterus, ascites, and/or fever are variably present.
Recurrent cholecystitis (ch. 272) and cholelithiasis (ch. 273) are
common complications and reasons for presentation in humans but
are less common in dogs.41 Instead, clinical signs in dogs are
suspected to relate to portal hypertension and hepatobiliary
dysfunction, both of which are also recognized sequelae of Caroli
syndrome in people.41,43,47,48 The clinical picture in cats remains
poorly defined, having only been described in a 4-month-old kitten
where Caroli disease was incidentally identified during investigation
of a concurrent extrahepatic portosystemic shunt (PSS, ch. 267).40

Diagnosis
Variable increases in ALP, GGT, ALT, AST, bile acids, and bilirubin
have been reported in affected dogs, as well as leukocytosis and nonregenerative anemia.39-43 Azotemia and isosthenuria may be noted if
CKD is also present. Multiple cystic dilations of intrahepatic bile
ducts, which communicate with the biliary tree (Figure 268.3), are
typically documented on abdominal ultrasound (US) or computed
tomography (CT). Calcification of the cysts and evidence of portal
hypertension or other comorbidities (such as renal cysts, PSS, or
cholelithiasis) may also be noted.40-44 On CT, the presence of a
contrast-enhanced structure, corresponding to the central
fibrovascular bundle within the dilated intrahepatic bile ducts
(central dot sign), has been suggested to be pathognomonic in people
and has been described in dogs.37,43,44 MRCP, ERCP or
percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography are considered the

diagnostic modalities of choice in humans but are rarely employed in
animals.19,20,37,44 Although signs of portal hypertension may
increase suspicion of Caroli syndrome, definitive diagnosis and
distinction from Caroli disease ultimately requires liver biopsy
histology to confirm concurrent congenital hepatic fibrosis.4,5,41

FIGURE 268.3 B-mode ultrasound image with
color Doppler of the hepatic parenchyma of a dog
with suspected Caroli syndrome. The dilated
intrahepatic bile ducts are seen as anechoic tubular
structures which do not show any Doppler
flow. Image courtesy Marie-Aude Genain, Diagnostic
Imaging, Department of Veterinary Medicine,
University of Cambridge, UK.

Treatment and Prognosis
The prognosis and optimal treatment strategy for affected dogs and
cats is unknown, as most reported cases have been euthanized at the
time of diagnosis. Both are however likely to be influenced by the
extent and severity of biliary malformation and hepatic fibrosis, and
by the presence of secondary complications or other concurrent

disease. Ursodeoxycholic acid and antibiotics are often used in
managing people to treat and prevent future episodes of
cholelithiasis and cholangitis.37,44 Successful conservative
management has also been reported in dogs and cats over a followup period of 2-5 months.40,41 However, due to the risk of severe
secondary complications such as recurrent cholangitis, cholelithiasis,
and malignancy, surgical resection or liver transplantation is often
recommended in affected people.37,44,48 It is unclear if these same
sequelae occur in dogs and cats; however, partial hepatectomy or
liver lobectomy may be a feasible and curative option for dogs or cats
with localized disease.48 Management of animals with diffuse
disease is usually supportive, including symptomatic treatment of
portal hypertension and other secondary complications as
indicated.41,43

DISEASES OF MEDIUM-SIZED
INTRAHEPATIC DUCTS
POLYCYSTIC LIVER DISEASE
Background and Etiopathogenesis
Polycystic liver diseases (PLDs) are a group of genetic disorders
characterized by progressive expansion of fluid-filled cysts that
gradually replace liver parenchyma.15 Although best described in
humans, they have also been reported in cats, dogs, goats, lions, and
rodents.49-57 The cysts are suspected to result from DPM of the
medium-sized intrahepatic bile ducts due to loss of heterozygosity of
ductal plate cells which, rather than involuting following
disconnection from the biliary tree, continue to proliferate.15,19
Concurrent congenital hepatic fibrosis or other DPMs may also occur
if other stages of duct development are affected.2 Although the exact
mechanisms underlying this process remain elusive, disordered
formation or function of the primary cilium, an important regulator
of normal tubulogenesis, may be a key factor.15 Numerous

ciliopathy-causing mutations have been implicated in humans and
some also cause cystic abnormalities in other organs.15,45
In humans, PLD most commonly occurs as an extra-renal
manifestation of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
(ADPKD), caused by mutations in PKD1 or PKD2 genes which
encode polycystin, a transmembrane protein essential for normal
ciliary function.15,45,58 PKD1 mutation (C>A transversion resulting
in a stop codon) is also recognized as a cause of ADPKD in Persian
cats and related breeds which, as in humans, is reported also to cause
cystic abnormalities in the liver and other organs.59-61 Although
uncommon, PLD occurring alone or in combination with renal cysts
is also described in dogs and other feline breeds and it is therefore
possible that other etiologies in humans (e.g., autosomal recessive
polycystic kidney disease, caused by PKHD1 mutation, or autosomal
dominant polycystic liver disease) also occur in animals.
Nonetheless, the causative mutations in these cases has not been
investigated.49,51,54-56

Presentation and Clinical Signs
Clinical consequences of PLD are dependent on the number, size,
growth rate, and location of the hepatic cysts, and the presence of
concurrent pathologies in the liver and other organs. Persian cats or
related cross breeds are most commonly affected given the 36-49%
prevalence of ADPKD in this breed.53,55,60-62 Unlike in human
ADPKD where PLD is reported to occur in up to 75% of cases, the
frequency of cysts is lower in cats, affecting less than 10%.60
Although ADPKD has also been described in Bull Terriers,
concurrent PLD has not yet been reported.63 In most affected cats,
PLD does not appear to cause clinical signs and morbidity is mainly
related to the development of progressive CKD in adulthood.53,55,60
While dogs with PLD may show no clinical signs, severe and diffuse
polycystic liver and renal disease has been described in Cairn
Terriers and White Highland White Terriers, culminating in
organomegaly and hepatic failure by 6 weeks of age.51,54,56 Since the
genetic basis in animals is ill-defined, this varied presentation may

reflect different underlying etiologies. Considering its uncertain
pathogenesis, it has therefore been proposed that PLD in animals
should be subclassified into juvenile or adult forms based on age at
presentation.4

Diagnosis
Thin-walled, anechoic or fluid filled cysts are readily identified
within the hepatic parenchyma on US examination which, unlike in
Caroli disease, do not communicate with the biliary tract.56 CT or
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are also frequently used to
establish the diagnosis in people.18,19 The number and size of cysts
may vary considerably, and other lesions may also be noted in the
kidneys and other organs.51,53-56 Variable elevations in
hepatocellular and cholestatic enzymes, or evidence of liver
dysfunction may be noted on serum biochemistry profiles in affected
dogs and cats.53,55,56 In Persian cats or related breeds, evaluation of
PKD1 gene status is recommended; however, it should be noted that
5% may lack the mutation.62 Although the diagnosis is often based
on imaging findings in patients who are not showing clinical signs,
histopathologic evaluation of tissue is required to definitively exclude
other differentials (e.g., parasitic or neoplastic disease) and to
determine if PLD coexists with congenital hepatic fibrosis or other
DPMs.2,4 Cyst aspiration is generally unhelpful and increases risk of
infection or rupture.53

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatment is only indicated in clinically affected patients. In cats and
dogs, treatment is supportive, including management of CKD if
indicated (ch. 301). In humans, somatostatin analogues are
suggested to reduce cyst growth rate; however, their value in dogs
and cats has not been evaluated.58 Percutaneous drainage of cysts is
normally impractical and ineffective; however, hepatic resection or
cyst fenestration may be feasible if cysts are localized and causing
biliary or vascular compression.58 Prognosis is variable depending

on the severity of PLD, age, rate of cyst expansion, and presence of
concurrent diseases (e.g., congenital hepatic fibrosis or renal
disease).51,53-56 Although complications such as cyst infection,
rupture, torsion, and hemorrhage occur in humans, these sequelae
have not yet been reported in cats or dogs with PLD and many have a
relatively benign disease course.51,55,58 Nonetheless, given the risk of
familial transmission, breeding animals with PLD—particularly cats
with ADPKD—is not recommended.59,62 Conversely, the prognosis
for those presented with severe PLD and hepatic failure at a young
age is likely to be poor.54,56

DISEASES OF SMALL INTRAHEPATIC
DUCTS
CONGENITAL HEPATIC FIBROSIS
Background and Etiopathogenesis
Congenital hepatic fibrosis is the result of aberrant ductal plate
remodeling of the small interlobular bile ducts. It is characterized
histologically by variable periportal fibrosis and numerous small
irregular bile ducts.1,2,4 In addition, portal vein branches are often
hypoplastic, which may suggest concurrent malformation of the
portal vascular tree.1,2,64,65 The fibrosis is generally progressive and
portal hypertension occurs commonly in affected patients.64,65 In
humans, congenital hepatic fibrosis is considered rare. It is often
inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder.18,19,65 As with other
DPMs, reports in the veterinary literature are comparatively limited;
however, congenital hepatic fibrosis has been described in dogs, cats,
Swiss Freiberger foals, other horses, calves, and an African green
monkey.5,64,66-76 Although a genetic etiology remains ill-defined, in
common with other DPMs, mutations adversely affecting formation
and function of the primary cilium are suspected.5,65 In support of
this theory, in both humans and animals, congenital hepatic fibrosis
may coexist with other DPMs (e.g., Caroli disease or PLDs) or

ADPKD, suggesting a common causative link.2,5,37,60,65,67 The
inheritance in dogs and cats, however, remains unknown.

Presentation and Clinical Signs
Of the limited number of reported cases, most cats and dogs have
presented at a young age (2 months to 2 years) with signs relating to
portal hypertension: ascites, anorexia, vomiting, and neurological
signs.5,64,67,69 A firm liver may be noted on abdominal palpation.64
Clinical presentation may also be complicated if concurrent DPMs or
other conditions are present.5 In humans, latent and cholangitic
forms are described, although it is unclear whether these occur in
dogs and cats.65 Hepatic fibrosis resembling congenital hepatic
fibrosis has been reported in 22-48% of cats with ADPKD and
clinical signs associated with liver disease rarely occur in these cases;
however, a congenital basis for this disorder has not been
established.55,60,67

Diagnosis
Although elevations in cholestatic and hepatocellular enzymes may
be noted, clinicopathological abnormalities are often mild and nonspecific. Most cases are not hyperbilirubinemic; however, increased
serum bile acids and ammonia are expected if acquired
portosystemic shunting (APSS) is present (ch. 267).5,64,67,69 On
abdominal US, ascites and evidence of APSS may be noted but the
liver may appear normal. Liver size may be increased or decreased
with variably hyperechoic or heterogeneous parenchyma.18,64,67,69
CT and MRI are considered valuable diagnostic aids in people and
permit better characterization of vascular anatomy, but hepatic
changes in cats and dogs with congenital hepatic fibrosis have not yet
been described.18,19 Consequently, definitive diagnosis requires
histopathology which typically documents diffuse and often severe
periportal to bridging fibrosis containing numerous small and
irregular bile ducts, diminished portal venous vasculature, and
hyperplastic arterioles (Figure 268.4).4,64,65,67,69 The numerous
bile duct profiles and lack of inflammatory changes, cholestasis, or

nodular regeneration assist in differentiating congenital hepatic
fibrosis from cirrhosis, congenital hepatic vascular abnormalities,
and extra-hepatic biliary obstruction.4,64 Other DPMs or renal cystic
disease may also be noted.5,65,67,69 The histological appearance of
congenital hepatic fibrosis in animals may be less distinct than in
humans, as has been reported in a population of young, unrelated
Boxer dogs which displayed a diverse spectrum of DPM
phenotypes.1,5 Although marked fibrosis with increased numbers of
small bile ducts and reduced portal vein profiles were documented in
all cases in this study, variable saccular dilation of segmental,
interlobular, and intralobular ducts was also present in a proportion
of dogs and only 37% fulfilled criteria for congenital hepatic fibrosis
and 7% for Caroli syndrome.5

Treatment and Prognosis
No antifibrotic agents have been shown to stop or reverse congenital
hepatic fibrosis and treatment of affected dogs and cats is limited to
supportive, nonspecific treatment of secondary complications
including hepatic encephalopathy and ascites (chs. 266,
267).6,65,69 The value of hepatic antioxidants and choleretics is
unknown. The prognosis is variable depending on the severity and
progression of congenital hepatic fibrosis and presence of concurrent
disease but may be poorer if clinical signs of portal hypertension are
already present.5,67,69 Nonetheless, long survival times have been
reported in Boxers with a spectrum of DPM phenotypes including
congenital hepatic fibrosis, irrespective of the presence or absence of
APSS (median survival of 7.5 and 8.8 years, respectively).5 Humans
with advanced disease or signs of liver failure are managed with liver
transplantation.65

VON MEYENBURG COMPLEXES
Von Meyenburg complexes (VMCs), also known as biliary
hamartomas, are rare benign nodular lesions suspected to arise from
abnormal remodeling of peripheral interlobular bile ducts in the
latter stages of biliary development.2 They have been reported in a
variety of species including humans, other primates, rabbits, calves,
lions, and rarely in dogs and cats.18,19,51,68,77-79 When they occur,
VMCs are typically diagnosed as incidental imaging or necropsy
findings, appearing as variably sized nodular cystic lesions which
may occur multifocally or in isolation. In humans they most
commonly exist as multiple, uniformly distributed lesions of
relatively similar size (typically <1.5 cm)19; however, their
appearance in dogs and cats appears to be more variable and has not
been extensively described.18,19,51 As with other malformations, they
may exist as a distinct entity or in combination with other DPMs
such as Caroli disease/syndrome or congenital hepatic fibrosis.1,2
Histologic evaluation of tissue samples is required for definitive
diagnosis of VMC and exclusion of other differentials (e.g.,
metastasis, primary neoplasia, abscesses, and simple liver cysts) and
typically reveals focal disorderly collections of irregular and
frequently dilated bile ducts embedded within a dense fibrous
stroma.1,2,4,51 As VMCs are considered benign lesions, no specific
treatment is required and an excellent prognosis is expected;
however, rare instances of malignant transformation have occurred
in people and US monitoring might therefore be considered.6,80

CLIENT INFORMATION
Congenital Ductal Plate Abnormalities
INTRODUCTION
Under normal circumstances, the biliary tract forms as a branching,
tree-like network of vessels which transports bile from the liver,
where it is produced, to the small intestine. In dogs and cats, it also
includes a pear-shaped sac, known as the gall bladder, which
functions as a storage center for bile and typically empties around
the time of eating to aid digestion.
Ductal plate malformations are a collection of rare diseases which
result from abnormal development of the biliary tract. They are best
described in people but are also known to occur in dogs and cats.
Specific forms of ductal plate malformation include choledochal
cysts and Caroli disease which are characterized by dilations of the
large bile ducts either within or outside the liver, and congenital
hepatic fibrosis and polycystic liver disease where abnormal
development of the smaller bile ducts leads to the development of
fibrosis and/or cysts within the liver tissue. It is however common
for different types of ductal plate malformations to exist together
depending on how the normal biliary development has been
interrupted. Particularly in dogs and cats, the resulting changes in
any individual patient can therefore be quite variable.

SYMPTOMS
The symptoms caused by ductal plate malformations are variable
depending on type of abnormality present and the degree to which
the liver and biliary tract are affected. Despite being developmental
abnormalities, clinical signs often only develop after a variable
period of months to years. Animals with mild disease which does not
impact on normal function may display mild or no symptoms.
Conversely, ductal plate abnormalities which adversely affect liver or
biliary function may cause a variety of signs such as loss of appetite,
vomiting, diarrhea, excessive thirst or urination, a pot-bellied
appearance, jaundice of the skin, gums, and eyes, abnormal
behavior, and rarely seizures. In general, these are more likely to
occur in cases where the ductal plate malformation has led to the
development of a large amount of fibrous tissue or cysts within the
liver, or if infection is present. Unfortunately however, most of these
signs are nonspecific and it is unlikely that your vet will be able to
diagnose a ductal plate malformation without further investigation.

DIAGNOSIS
It is possible that your veterinarian may suspect that your pet may
have a disease of their liver or biliary tract based on their signs and
abnormalities on examination; however, further investigations are
required to determine the underlying cause. It is important to be
aware that ductal plate abnormalities are rare diseases and not
straight-forward to diagnose; consequently, a number of different
tests may need to be employed and each can have value. Although
blood tests cannot diagnose a ductal plate malformation, your
veterinarian may recommend performing these to confirm their
suspicion of liver or biliary disease and to assess liver function. An
ultrasound scan or advanced imaging (e.g., by computed tomography
[CT] or magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]) of the abdomen is also
likely to be required in order to evaluate whether structural
abnormalities are present. This may for instance identify dilations of
the bile ducts in casts of choledochal cysts or Caroli syndrome, or
multiple cystic structures in animals with polycystic liver disease. A
liver biopsy may also be recommended to determine whether
microscopic ductal plate malformations, such as congenital hepatic
fibrosis, are also present.

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Treatment depends on several factors including the type of ductal
plate malformation and the severity of the disease. Unfortunately,
because ductal plate malformations have been rarely reported in
animals, optimal treatment and expected outcomes are not well
established.
As ductal plate malformations are developmental abnormalities
often affecting a large proportion of the biliary tract, curative
treatment is often not possible. Although surgical treatment may be
feasible if lesions are localized or confined to the bile ducts outside
the liver (e.g., choledochal cysts), ductal plate abnormalities often
affect a large proportion of the liver and biliary system making
surgery impossible. Consequently, medical management, such as
antioxidants and supportive treatment for impaired liver function, is
often recommended when clinical signs arise.
The prognosis for many ductal plate malformations is also very
variable depending on a variety of factors such as the type of ductal
malformation, the extent of the biliary tract affected, and the speed
of progression. Whilst some animals with mild disease display no
clinical signs or do well with medical management for many years,
others may rapidly succumb to liver failure within a relatively short
time. In general, those with a large amount of fibrous tissue or
numerous cysts within the liver often tend to have a worse outcome.
