DEFINITIONS
Acute liver injury (ALI) is defined as an acute hepatic injury with
sustained hepatic function and normal conventional coagulation
times.1,2 Acute liver failure (ALF) is rare, even in people, in whom it is
defined as severe liver dysfunction with evidence of both coagulopathy
and hepatic encephalopathy (HE) in a patient with a short duration of
illness and without pre-existing liver disease.3,4 Extrapolating from
human guidelines, the definition of ALF in dogs and cats is defined as

development of acute clinical signs of severe hepatocellular injury with
concurrent hyperbilirubinemia and coagulopathy. Coagulopathy is
defined as a prothrombin time (PT) >1.5 times above the limit reference
interval. The presence of encephalopathy is not required for this
diagnosis, due to the challenges in defining the early stages of HE in
dogs and cats. This is also why HE evaluation is omitted from ALF
diagnostic criteria in human pediatric patients.4-6 For the purpose of
this chapter, acute liver disease (ALD) encompasses both ALI and ALF.

ETIOLOGY
The main reported causes of ALF in people are toxic, viral, metabolic
(Wilson’s disease), vascular (ischemia, Budd-Chiari syndrome),
heatstroke, and malignant infiltration.4 With advances in diagnostics,
the cause is not determined in as few as 5% of cases.7 Drug-induced liver
injury (DILI), especially acetaminophen, is the most common cause of
ALF in industrialized countries, whereas viral hepatitis predominates in
developing countries.4 In a retrospective study of 49 dogs with ALF, an
etiology was determined in 18/49 (37%) dogs: neoplasia (13/49; 27%),
leptospirosis (4/49; 8%) and ischemia (1/49; 2%). Thirty-one of fortynine (63%) had no identifiable cause, although 15 had exposure to
potential hepatotoxins (Table 269.1).5

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
ACUTE LIVER FAILURE
The liver has extensive reserve. Clinical signs and biochemical
manifestations often do not develop until >70% of functional hepatic
mass is lost.2 ALF culminates in sudden massive hepatocyte necrosis or
apoptosis which overwhelms the regenerative capacity of the liver.8
Release of material from dying hepatocytes is associated with the innate
immune response (Kupffer cells and circulating monocytes) causing
increased production of inflammatory mediators (tumor necrosis factoralpha, interleukin [IL]-6, IL-1-beta) and development of the systemic
inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS, ch. 128). A parallel
compensatory immune response develops involving cytokines IL-4 and

IL-10 which serve to modulate pro-inflammatory responses, limit the
degree of hepatocellular injury, and promote liver regeneration. When
these cytokines are released into the circulation, they are associated with
a predisposition to infection due to impaired innate immunity
(complement deficiency, functional impairment of circulating
monocytes and phagocytosis by Kupffer cells) leading to sepsis and
multiorgan failure. Regenerative processes are triggered leading to
hepatocyte replication in attempt to restore architecture and function.8,9

HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY (HE) AND
CEREBRAL EDEMA
Hyperammonemia and Systemic Inflammation
HE is categorized into types A-C according to the underlying disease
process. “Type A” HE is associated with ALF; in one retrospective study,
57% of dogs with ALF had signs of HE.5 Hyperammonemia plays a
central role in the pathophysiology of HE (ch. 266). Ammonia is
produced in both the small intestine from glutamine metabolism and in
the colon via the cleavage of urea to ammonia by urease-producing
bacteria. Ammonia diffuses into the portal circulation. In health,
circulating ammonia is converted to urea (via the urea cycle) or
glutamine in the liver. These mechanisms are impaired in ALF.10 HE is
potentiated by systemic inflammation as studied in dogs with congenital
portosystemic shunts (cPSS, ch. 267). The presence of SIRS is
predictive of HE in dogs with cPSS.11 Circulating inflammatory markers
(C-reactive protein and monocyte counts) are increased in dogs with
cPSS and HE. They decrease following shunt attenuation.14,15 The
magnitude of SIRS and infection correlate strongly with progression of
encephalopathy and mortality in people with ALF.12,13 A
neuroinflammatory response occurs due to pro-inflammatory cytokines
that are released following hepatic necrosis. These cytokines alter
cerebral endothelial permeability to neurotoxins and potentiate
ammonia toxicity. Cytokines also cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB),
activating microglia and resulting in local cytokine release. This process
causes cerebral vasodilation and hyperemia due to loss of cerebral
autoregulation.16-19

Cerebral Edema
Cerebral edema and intracranial hypertension (ICH) are sequelae of
acute HE that develop due to a combination of astrocytic swelling and
cerebral hyperemia.18 Cerebral edema is associated with increased
likelihood of compromising cerebral perfusion pressure leading to
hemorrhage, ischemia, or death due to brain herniation (ch. 44).20 Risk
factors for cerebral edema include severity of HE and high blood
ammonia concentrations. Approximately 20% of people with ALF have
ICH. This is a challenge when evaluating dogs and cats, as it requires
intracranial pressure monitoring methods not routinely performed in
our patients.21-23

SEQUELAE OF ACUTE LIVER FAILURE
Multi-organ dysfunction can develop as a sequela to ALF.
Cardiovascular dysfunction can resemble vasodilatory septic shock with
low systemic vascular resistance, increased cardiac output and
hypotension (ch. 121).8 An abnormal response to adrenocorticotropic
hormone stimulation has been reported in 62% of people with ALF
suggestive of relative adrenal insufficiency (ch. 296) but has not been
evaluated in dogs.24 Acute kidney injury (AKI; ch. 300) can occur due
to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC, ch. 171), sepsis,
dehydration, hypovolemia, or direct nephrotoxicosis (hepatotoxins or
leptospirosis).3,23 Respiratory involvement can occur due to leptospiral
pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome, acute respiratory distress syndrome
(ARDS; ch. 123), atelectasis due to recumbency, pulmonary
thromboembolism (PTE, ch. 219), aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217) as a
result of HE, or pleural effusion (ch. 220) secondary to low oncotic
pressure.2 The development of acute intrahepatic portal hypertension
can lead to formation of acquired portosystemic shunts (aPSS, ch. 267)
which can exacerbate HE.

CLINICAL FEATURES and COMMON
CLINICOPATHOLOGIC ABNORMALITIES
HISTORY AND CLINICAL PRESENTATION
History-taking should involve a careful review of toxin exposure,
medication history (including exposure to recognized hepatotoxic drugs,
nutritional and herbal supplements; Table 269.1), travel history (ch.
9), vaccination status (ch. 185), and diet history (ch. 145), including
snacks. Pets with ALD can have a spectrum of signs, ranging from
subclinical increases in liver enzymes to HE, seizures, and death.
Clinical presentations of ALD can be vague, nonspecific, and include an
acute history of vomiting, diarrhea, polyuria/ polydipsia (PU/PD),
anorexia, lethargy, abdominal pain, and/or jaundice. There may be
evidence of a bleeding diathesis (petechiae, hematemesis, melena).1,2
Signs of HE may manifest as behavioral changes, apathy, dull
mentation, obtundation, circling, head pressing, acting blind, tremors,
ataxia, ptyalism, delayed menace and pupillary light reflexes, anisocoria,
conscious proprioceptive deficits, stupor, seizures

, and coma (ch.

266; Videos 267.1, 269.1).2,5,10 Subclinical (covert) HE in people is
diagnosed by psychometric tests due to normal mental and neurological
examinations; it is likely underdiagnosed in veterinary patients.10

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (CH. 3)
Pets with ALD can be dehydrated or have signs of hypovolemic or
distributive shock due to SIRS (ch. 121). Those with hyperbilirubinemia
may be visibly jaundiced (ch. 28) and uremic oral ulceration can occur
if there is concurrent AKI (ch. 300). Tachypnea and dyspnea are seen
with respiratory compromise (ch. 37). Abdominal palpation may reveal
evidence of cranial abdominal pain, alterations in liver size, and/or
ascites (ch. 21). Ascites is usually mild, unless there is significant portal
hypertension, hypoalbuminemia, or excessive vascular leak due to
vasculitis, peritonitis, SIRS, or neoplasia.5 Pyrexia may be noted in
septic pets or those with an infectious disease. A baseline neurological
examination (ch. 241) is worthwhile to assess for subtle mentation
changes suggestive of HE. Patients with cerebral edema and ICH can
develop mydriasis, papilledema, decerebrate posturing (ch. 44),

seizures, or clinical signs consistent with a Cushing reflex (concurrent
acute arterial hypertension, altered respiratory pattern, and
bradycardia).1,8

SERUM BIOCHEMISTRY PROFILE
Serum Alanine Transferase (ALT), Aspartate
Transferase (AST), Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP),
Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT)
The serum biochemistry profile typically demonstrates marked
increases in activites of the hepatocellular leakage enzymes ALT and
AST with variable increases in activities of the inducible enzymes ALP
and GGT. ALT is a liver-specific cytosolic leakage enzyme. Activities
increase after centrilobular hepatocellular damage, with levels
increasing to >100-fold within 12-24 hours of injury, peaking within 2448 hours.25 The half-life of ALT averages 40-61 hours in the dog and 3.5
hours in the cat; therefore, a decline in sequential ALT activities by 50%
within 1 half-life is a good prognostic indicator in pets with ALD as it is
suggestive of recovery.26 However, exceptions to this are diminished
ALT activity in end-stage ALF (due to significant loss of hepatic
functional parenchyma) or impaired gene transcription due to certain
toxins (e.g., blue-green algae, cycads, aflatoxins) which can mask the
diagnostic utility of detecting hepatic injury.2,27AST is found within
hepatocellular mitochondria. Increased activities may reflect severity of
hepatic injury but AST is also derived from brain, skeletal muscle, and
erythrocytes, making increases less specific than ALT. AST activities
generally parallel those of ALT after hepatocellular injury.25
ALP increases occur as a result of de novo synthesis and/or elution
from cell membranes. Increases can be delayed in ALD. Activity usually
increases 2- to 5-fold following acute severe hepatic necrosis and then
gradually declines.1 ALP and GGT can also be increased due to
extrahepatic and intrahepatic cholestasis.25

Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN), Cholesterol,
Albumin, Bilirubin, Glucose (BG), Bile
Acids, Ammonia
Pets with ALD may show evidence of hepatic dysfunction on serum
biochemistry profiles, e.g., low BUN, cholesterol and albumin are classic
findings due to reduced hepatic production. Low albumin
concentrations may be exacerbated by gastrointestinal (GI) hemorrhage
or third-space losses due to ascites. Hyperbilirubinemia in ALD is due to
hepatocyte dysfunction and intrahepatic cholestasis.25 Hypoglycemia
follows impaired gluconeogenesis and glycogen storage, decreased
hepatocyte insulin uptake, and with xylitol intoxication (chs. 61,
134).1,8,26 A bile acid stimulation test (ch. 267) can be performed to
assess liver function in non-icteric animals. Ammonia is a relatively
insensitive marker of liver function due to the large reserve capacity for
the conversion of ammonia to urea in the liver. Hyperammonemia was
reported in 63% of dogs with ALF in one study.5 Whereas
hyperammonemia can be utilized to confirm a diagnosis of HE in a pet
with ALF, normal levels do not exclude HE and levels are unreliable at
predicting HE severity in the individual patient.28

Electrolytes and Acid-Base
Derangements include hypokalemia (secondary to PU/PD, reduced
intake, GI loss; ch. 68), hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia,
hypophosphatemia, hypernatremia, hyponatremia (which can
exacerbate cerebral edema), and metabolic acidosis. Increases in
creatinine may be prerenal due to dehydration or hypovolemia or reflect
concurrent AKI. Increased lactate is likely due to hypovolemia but
ongoing hyperlactatemia could reflect the severity of liver disease due to
inability to metabolize lactate.1,29

COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT (CBC)
Anemia may be due to inflammatory disease, acute hemorrhage (GI,
lungs), or DIC. Leukocytosis or leukopenia may occur with infectious
disease or sepsis. Eosinophilia may be seen in pets with DILI-associated
hypersensitivity. Thrombocytopenia may be due to impaired

thrombopoietin production by the liver, decreased platelet survival (e.g.,
increased platelet clearance due to SIRS), immune-mediated
destruction, splenic sequestration (a consequence of portal
hypertension), consumption (hemorrhage, thrombosis, DIC), or a direct
result of the causative agent (e.g., leptospirosis, xylitol, cycads,
aflatoxins).30,31 Thrombocytopenia has been reported in up to 92% of
dogs with ALF and less commonly in cats with ALF and suspected
DIC.5,32,33

URINALYSIS (UA)
Decreased urine specific gravity (due to PU/PD or concurrent AKI) is
common. Icteric pets may have bilirubinuria, although this can be a
normal finding in male dogs. Proximal renal tubular damage (seen with
leptospirosis, lomustine, carprofen, cycads, blue-green algae, Amanita
and copper toxicosis) may manifest as glucosuria (acquired Fanconi’s
syndrome), granular casts and proteinuria (ch. 303).2,27 Ammonium
biurate crystals may be seen in ALF as the liver fails to process ammonia
and to convert uric acid into allantoin.

COAGULATION TESTING and
THROMBOELASTOGRAPHY (TEG, CH.
170)
All clotting factors, except factor VIII, are synthesized in the liver, as are
anticoagulant proteins (antithrombin, protein C, protein S) and the
fibrinolytic proteins plasminogen, tissue plasminogen activatorinhibitor 1 (TPAI-1), and alpha-2 antiplasmin.30,34 Vitamin K deficiency
can occur in ALD due to cholestasis, decreased oral intake and antibiotic
treatment (which decreases bacterial vitamin K production). Vitamin K
is responsible for carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X, proteins C
and S. Deficiency can lead to factor dysfunction and depleted
concentrations.30 Subclinical vitamin K deficiency has been reported in
more than 25% of people with ALF and is commonly reported in cats
secondary to cholestatic diseases, e.g., hepatic lipidosis.32,35 The liver is
also responsible for the clearance of activated pro- and anticoagulants,

fibrin degradation products (FDPs), and D-dimers. Coagulation
abnormalities due to ALF can be difficult to differentiate from DIC (ch.
171) as both can cause increased PT, activated partial thromboplastin
time (APTT), decreased antithrombin and increased D-dimers and
FDPs.30
People and pets with ALF usually have balanced proportional
deficiencies in procoagulant and anticoagulant clotting factors. This can
shift to bleeding tendencies or hypercoagulability.5,36,37,38 Prolongation
in conventional PTs and APTTs are common. PT prolongation is
included in the definition of ALF.34 However, these tests only detect
procoagulant proteins and, therefore, fail to detect the complex changes
in coagulation seen in ALD patients, nor do they reliably predict risk of
bleeding in people or pets with ALF.5,37 Bleeding complications are seen
in ∼10% of people with ALF, with most occurring from the upper GI tract
and often deemed clinically insignificant.38 Evidence of spontaneous
hemorrhage, including GI, was reported in over 50% of dogs with ALF in
one case series.5 Factors impairing hemostasis include
thrombocytopenia, thrombocytopathia, vitamin K and clotting factor
deficiencies, hypofibrinogenemia, and hyperfibrinolysis.1,6,25 Factors
that promote hypercoagulability include increased factor VIII and von
Willebrand factor due to endothelial dysfunction as a result of SIRS,
decrease in anticoagulant factors (proteins C and S, antithrombin), and
production of pro-thrombotic microparticles.6,38 Evidence of
thrombosis was seen in 4/49 dogs with ALF in a retrospective case
series, including hepatic, splanchnic and PTE.5
TEG provides information about the global coagulation status,
including speed of clot formation, clot strength, and clot lysis (ch. 170).
In people with ALF, TEG typically reflects preserved hemostasis and is
considered more sensitive for predicting bleeding and guiding
transfusion requirements. TEG has led to reduced blood product
requirements.37-40 Conventional coagulation testing may overestimate
hypocoagulability compared to TEG in about 25% of dogs with early
ALD and sustained hepatic function. However, as liver dysfunction
progresses, both conventional coagulation times and TEG indicate
hypocoagulability and hyperfibrinolysis.6 The cause for
hyperfibrinolysis is unclear and whether this equates to an increased
bleeding tendency (delayed bleeding) but may be due to decreased

clearance of plasminogen activators or production of TPAI-1 by the
liver.6

IMAGING
Thoracic radiographs may document pleural effusion, metastasis, or an
alveolar pattern due to ARDS, aspiration pneumonia (ch. 217),
atelectasis, hemorrhage, or PTE (ch. 219). Abdominal radiographs
allow liver size and serosal detail estimations.2,5 Abdominal ultrasound
(US) allows assessment of the liver parenchyma and can be used to
guide needle biopsy sampling. However, US has poor accuracy in
diagnosing diffuse hepatic parenchymal disease and can be normal even
in the presence of severe ALD.41-43 Hepatic US abnormalities include
decreased liver volume (massive hepatocyte loss), hepatomegaly
(malignant infiltration, ischemic hepatitis), variable diffuse echogenicity
changes, and ascites.2,5,44 Other findings include GI ulceration, acute
pancreatitis, evidence of thrombosis, and renal changes (increased renal
cortical echogenicity, renomegaly, renal pelvic dilation, peri-renal fluid),
the latter may be seen in patients with leptospirosis or AKI.5,45
Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging may show
evidence of cerebral edema, although this doesn’t always correlate with
development of ICH. The principle value of advanced imaging is to
exclude other intracranial disease processes, e.g., spontaneous
hemorrhage, but is likely under-utilized due to the risk of sedating or
anesthetizing a critically ill pet.20

LIVER CYTOLOGY, BIOPSY, AND
HISTOPATHOLOGY
CYTOLOGY
There are four main methods of obtaining a sample of liver tissue: fineneedle aspiration (FNA), US-guided percutaneous needle biopsy, or
wedge biopsies obtained via laparoscopy or laparotomy (ch. 85). FNA
for cytologic evaluation of the liver has utility in diagnosing vacuolar
hepatopathy, infiltrative neoplasia, and even parasitic infections.5,46-48
Cytology has a lower sensitivity for inflammatory diseases and

fibrosis.49 Cytology does not always agree with histopathology and, in
one study, agreement with histology occurred in only 30.3% dogs and
51.2% cats.48,50 The advantages of cytology include low cost and ability
to sample multiple regions using only mild sedation. This enables tissue
sampling (and potentially exclusion of infiltrative disease and lipidosis)
in pets deemed unstable for a general anesthesia. Limitations include
risk of hemorrhage, small sample size, hemodilution (challenging to
ascertain inflammatory hepatitis), and inability to assess hepatic
parenchymal architecture.1,48

BIOPSY
Advantages and Disadvantages
Since tissue biopsy is associated with greater risk of hemorrhage, a prior
coagulation profile is recommended. A study of risk factors for bleeding
after percutaneous needle organ biopsy identified thrombocytopenia,
increased PT in dogs, and increased APTT in cats.51 However, a more
recent study assessing cats undergoing needle liver biopsies documented
major bleeding (defined as change in packed cell volume ≤−6%) in
nearly 60%, but conventional coagulation times did not predict this
risk.52 Although needle biopsy samples do not always correlate with
biopsies obtained surgically or at necropsy due to their smaller size,
advantages include shorter anesthetic times and limited tissue
trauma.53 Surgical and laparoscopic biopsies are more invasive but
allow direct visualization for hemorrhage and obtainment of larger
tissue samples.

Indications for Biopsy
Indications for a liver biopsy include establishing cause, severity (e.g.,
focal versus diffuse necrosis), reversibility, and/or prognosis. Indicators
of chronicity include fibrosis, biliary hyperplasia, and cirrhosis. Since
liver transplantation is the treatment of choice in severe cases regardless
of etiology, the role of biopsy is less clear in people.54 Further, in people
accurate drug/toxin history is usually established and tests are available
for common viral causes. However, in one study, biopsy results did

confirm disease in >80% of people and alter the initial diagnosis in 19%
of people, suggesting a diagnostic benefit.55

Histology
Hepatic necrosis is the most common diagnosis made in ALD. Necrosis
is divided into centrilobular, periportal, or panlobular (massive).
Hepatocytes are arranged in 3 zones around their blood supply: Zone 1
hepatocytes are located in the periportal region, those in Zone 2 are
transitional midzone, and in Zone 3 they are periacinar (centrilobular).
Centrilobular necrosis is the most common sequela of ischemic, viral,
and toxic etiologies.56 The centrolobular region is furthest away from
the blood supply, rendering it more susceptible to hypoxic injury. Since
this area also contains active hepatic biotransformation pathways (such
as cytochrome P450 enzymes), it is the region where reactive
metabolites are produced.2 Hematogenous infections demonstrate
random multifocal areas of hepatic necrosis and neutrophilic
infiltration. Viral causes, e.g., herpesvirus and canine adenovirus-1
(CAV-1), may have inclusion bodies. Direct visualisation of tachyzoites
and bradyzoites within cysts may be seen in Toxoplasma cases.56,57 In a
retrospective study of 49 dogs with ALF, histopathology was obtained
from approximately one third of cases either at antemortem biopsy or
post mortem. Aside from neoplasia, results did not often confirm a
specific etiology. The predominant findings were necrosis in 47%
(diffuse 47%, centrilobular 20%, multifocal 33%), neoplasia in 40%,
degenerative (lipidosis 40%, vacuolar 19%), inflammation in 21%
(lymphoplasmacytic/pyogranulomatous), biliary proliferation in 8%,
bile duct necrosis in 2% and gallbladder inflammation in 2%.5 A limiting
factor of liver biopsy is sampling variation due to histopathological
heterogeneity, e.g., regional areas of necrosis co-exist with inflammation
or residual normal liver.53,58 Furthermore, histologic findings can be
nonspecific, with extensive hepatic necrosis and varying degrees of
cholestasis simply reflecting the common final stages of ALF.54

COMMON CAUSES OF ALD IN DOGS AND
CATS

OVERVIEW OF INFECTIOUS ETIOLOGIES AND
DIAGNOSTIC TECHNIQUES
Although a multitude of infectious diseases have been associated with
acute hepatitis, determining causality can be challenging. In one study
of 98 dogs with hepatitis (of which nearly 30% had acute or subacute
hepatitis), infectious etiologies were not confirmed in the majority of
cases despite extensive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) screening for
infectious diseases (hepatitis viruses, adenovirus, parvovirus,
Helicobacter, leptospirosis and Borrelia). Only 2 dogs with acute
hepatitis were positive for parvovirus, which was deemed a secondary
reactive hepatitis.59 Bacterial hepatitis can be diagnosed by liver and
bile culture, histopathology, PCR, and fluorescence in-situ hybridisation
(FISH). Bile cultures are more often positive than liver culture and
should be obtained in pets undergoing liver biopsy. Escherichia coli
spp., Enterococcus, Bacteroides spp. and Clostridium spp. infections are
most commonly isolated in association with hepatobiliary infections.60
Since the development of FISH, a culture-independent means of
bacterial identification, the association of hepatitis with Salmonella and
leptospirosis infections have been more frequently reported. FISH has
also been able to confirm bacterial co-localization with inflammation in
dogs with inflammatory hepatitis.61-63 Other diagnostic techniques for
infectious causes include bile cytology, serology, histopathology,
immunohistochemistry, and PCR.64

Infectious Canine Hepatitis (CAV-1)
CAV-1 is a significant cause of fatal ALD in unvaccinated dog
populations. Wild carnivores, particularly red foxes in Europe, act as a
subclinical reservoir.65 The disease usually affects young dogs and is
both endotheliotropic and hepatotropic. Transmission occurs via the
oronasal route. Viral replication usually begins in the tonsils followed by
lymphatic and hematogenous spread. Non-hepatic clinical signs include
anterior uveitis, bronchopneumonia, and lymphadenopathy.66,67
Histopathologic findings include centri- to panlobular hepatic necrosis
with large basophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies.67
Immunohistochemistry, viral isolation, and PCR techniques can be
employed for diagnosis on histological sections. PCR techniques can also

be utilized on ocular swabs, feces, and urine. Serological testing is also
available.1,66,67 The prevalence of disease has decreased with
widespread vaccination (with modified live CAV-2) in Western Europe,
although recent outbreaks in Italy and Switzerland raise concern for reemergence of this disease in susceptible dogs.68,69 Studies have shown
that dogs are immune for at least 3 years after an initial vaccination
course. Long-term immunity in these animals may partly be due to
natural exposure to vaccination and/or field virus.70 Mortality can reach
30%. Complications in those recovering include corneal edema (“blue
eye”) and interstitial nephritis due to immune-complex deposition and
viral persistence in the kidneys.68 There is no specific treatment for
CAV-1.

LEPTOSPIROSIS
Pathogenesis
Leptospirosis, caused by the spirochete bacteria belonging to the genus
Leptospira, is a systemic zoonotic disease characterized by renal and
hepatic dysfunction, pulmonary manifestations, and reproductive failure
(ch. 192). Serovars are maintained in nature by subclinically affected
wild and domestic mammalian reservoir hosts that serve as potential
sources of infection for incidental animal hosts. Clinical leptospirosis in
cats is rare.45,71 Leptospires enter the susceptible host directly via
mucous membranes following contact with infected urine,
venereal/placental transmission, ingestion of infected tissues, bite
wounds, or indirectly from contaminated water, soil, and mud.
Leptospires spread hematogenously during a bacteremic phase, then
localize in the proximal renal tubules and are excreted in the urine.
Leptospiral factors produced by the spirochetes contribute to vasculitis
due to endothelial damage potentially resulting in both a bleeding
tendency and pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome.71 Leptospiral liver
damage is characterised by hepatocellular necrosis and cholestasis.
Liver enzyme activities are usually elevated, but ALP activity and
bilirubin are elevated more often than ALT activity.

Diagnosis (ch. 192)

A strong index of suspicion for leptospirosis is integral to the diagnosis
as specific testing should be performed at an early stage. The presence of
concurrent ALI, AKI, thrombocytopenia, and evidence of proximal
tubular damage (glucosuria) warrants further testing, regardless of
vaccination status due to lack of vaccinal cross protection. Leptospirosis
is diagnosed using microscopic agglutination test (MAT) serologic
testing which provides an estimate of the antibody titer against different
Leptospira serovars present in the blood. In acute cases, paired sera
over a 2-4 week interval are assessed, with a 4-fold increase in antibody
titers consistent with a diagnosis. A 4-fold increase in antibody titer is
consistent with a diagnosis. A single titer >1:800 raises the suspicion of
leptospirosis but does not confirm the diagnosis, especially in vaccinated
dogs (ch. 185).45 There is individual variation in serum titers due to
vaccination and, although they are usually <1:800, values of >1:3200
can be occasionally observed but do not usually persist for more than 3
months.71 It is often assumed that the highest titer reflects the causative
serovar; however, high titers to a specific serovar may not definitively
identify the causative serovar because antibodies to serovars within the
same serogroup cross-react.45 Serovars Icterohaemorrhagiae and
Pomona have been reported to induce the most severe hepatic
involvement; however, no clear distinction has been made between the
infecting serovar and clinical disease.45,71 PCR can detect leptospiral
DNA in blood and urine with positive results obtained before
seroconversion and it has utility in the diagnosis of seropositive
vaccinated animals; however, PCR does not identify the infecting
serovar and is affected by antibiotic treatment. Culture is impractical for
early diagnosis because leptospires are slow growing and require 3-6
months incubation.45 In patients with acute hepatic manifestations of
leptospirosis, histopathologic changes can range from mild vacuolar
hepatopathy in subclinical cases to diffuse mild to moderate hepatic
necrosis, neutrophilic periportal hepatitis and intrahepatic cholestasis in
severe cases.71 Cases of chronic leptospiral hepatitis often without
prominent renal involvement have been reported.45,62

Treatment
Antibiotics are the mainstay of treatment for leptospirosis to both treat
leptospiremia and to eliminate renal excretion. Parenteral potentiated
amoxicillin is recommended during initial hospitalization followed by a

2-week course of 10 mg/kg PO q24h doxycycline to prevent a long-term
carrier state.

NEOPLASIA
ALF can develop with malignant intrahepatic biliary infiltration,
obstruction of hepatic venules progressing to ischemic injury and
necrosis, and rapid replacement by malignant cells leading to a critical
mass of hepatocyte destruction.72 In one study of ALF in dogs, 85% of
neoplastic ALF cases were round cell malignancies (lymphoma, poorly
differentiated round cell tumors, mast cell tumors) with carcinomas also
being represented.5

COPPER STORAGE DISEASE (CH. 270)
Acute necrosis associated with copper storage disease has been reported
in dogs.73 Diagnosis of Wilson’s disease in people is confirmed by
demonstration of high serum and urine copper, and excess copper
staining on liver biopsy. Increased centrilobular copper staining has
been documented in dogs with acute hepatitis which could suggest a role
of excess copper in the pathogenesis of ALD.44 However, copper
staining was not evaluated in a large case series of dogs with ALF. The
role of copper toxicosis in the pathophysiology of ALD warrants further
evaluation.5 Treatment includes chelation therapy, dietary copper
restriction, and antioxidant treatment.

DRUG-INDUCED LIVER INJURIES (DILI)
OVERVIEW
Direct Drug-Induced Liver Injury (ch. 134)
The liver is the site of first-pass clearance of many drugs. The parent
drug or reactive metabolites generated by hepatic enzymes (e.g.,
cytochrome P450 metabolism) can lead to hepatocellular injury (hepatic
necrosis) or cholestasis (inhibition or downregulation of biliary
transporter pumps or mitochondrial injury with resulting steatosis).74,75
DILI can be direct or idiosyncratic. Direct DILI is predictable, usually

hepatocellular and dose-dependent (high or supra-therapeutic doses)
with a short latency period which typically responds to a reduction in
drug dose. Cessation of the drug is rarely required.75 Therapeutic drug
monitoring is useful to monitor for drug reactions.

Idiosyncratic Drug-Induced Liver Injury
Idiosyncratic DILI is caused by agents with minimal or no intrinsic
toxicity. Toxicosis is usually the result of reactive metabolite formation
which can covalently bind proteins to form drug-protein adducts that
exert direct toxic injury (oxidative stress and mitochondrial injury) or
trigger an immunological response.76 These reactions have a variable
latency period (usually within 4 weeks) and can occur after drug
discontinuation.8,75 Idiosyncratic reactions are difficult to predict and
only lead to toxicosis in a small percentage of patients at therapeutic
doses. Occasionally there is increased risk with higher doses in
susceptible individuals. Drug discontinuation is recommended, and it
should be borne in mind that structurally related drugs may cause
similar reactions. Due to the low incidence and abrupt onset of
idiosyncrasy, routine liver enzyme monitoring is not recommended.
Destructive cholangitis associated with intrahepatic bile duct loss has
been reported as a suspected idiosyncratic reaction in a dog receiving
milbemycin oxime, potentiated amoxicillin and amitraz, or to
potentiated sulfonamides reported in an older case series.77,78

Risk Factors of DILI
In people, there are genetic predispositions to DILI determined by
human leukocyte antigen polymorphisms supporting an immune basis.
Other risk factors include pre-existing liver disease, co-medications,
drug lipophilicity and increasing age. Autoantibodies can develop with
chronic drug exposure and, in a subset of people (<10%), drug-induced
autoimmune acute liver failure (AI-ALF) develops.76

Diagnosis of DILI
DILI is a diagnosis of exclusion as there is usually a lack of
immunological or allergic features at presentation, patients are often
receiving multiple drugs, and there are no blood tests available to
confirm a suspicion. DILI may be accompanied by hypersensitivity

reactions, e.g., pyrexia, rash, joint pain, eosinophilic leukocytosis.75
There is usually a temporal relationship between drug exposure and
hepatic injury. Some drugs are known hepatotoxins which will enhance
the index of suspicion (Table 269.1).5 In people, biochemical patterns
of DILI are classed as cytotoxic, cholestatic, or mixed depending on R
value (ALT/ALP) with >5: cytotoxic, <2: cholestatic, 2-5: mixed,
although the clinical utility of this system in dogs and cats is unclear.75
Histopathologic changes associated with cytotoxic DILI are those of
acute hepatic necrosis with minimal inflammation. Cholestatic DILI
demonstrates bile duct injury and cholestasis. Mild-moderate steatosis
may accompany DILI with associated mitochondrial injury.75 Response
to drug withdrawal and positive re-challenge are criteria used to
establish a diagnosis.5 However, re-challenge has ethical implications as
repeat exposure may be associated with a more rapid and severe return
of ALD due to adaptive immune responses; therefore, the diagnosis is
usually presumptive.79

Treatment of DILI
Treatment of DILI involves drug withdrawal of all but essential
medications (de-challenge) with serial monitoring of liver enzymes until
they normalize. Steroids may have a role in idiosyncratic cases
associated with hypersensitivity reactions or drug-induced AI-ALF.
Fewer than 10% of people develop ALF (in which there may be no
response to drug withdrawal) and approximately 20% progress to
develop a chronic hepatopathy.76,79

ACETAMINOPHEN-INDUCED LIVER
INJURY (CH. 134)
Acetaminophen (paracetamol), an antiinflammatory and antipyretic
drug, is licensed for use in dogs (but not cats) in the UK and may be
used in dogs in other countries. Accidental ingestion of human tablets is
also possible in both species. At therapeutic doses, the majority of
acetaminophen is metabolized by phase II conjugating enzymes with
glutathione (GSH) or cysteine and converted to non-toxic compounds
with subsequent renal excretion. Less than 10% is metabolized by

cytochrome P450 enzymes to the highly reactive intermediate
metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI). When intracellular
mechanisms to detoxify NAPQI are overwhelmed due to excessive
production, there is depletion of intrahepatic GSH stores. NAPQI binds
to intracellular proteins leading to hepatocellular necrosis and also
causes severe oxidative red blood cell (RBC) stress, which in turn leads
to methemoglobinemia and Heinz body formation.74,80,81 Dogs are
more predisposed to hepatotoxicosis than humans are, due to
intrinsically low hepatic GSH levels. Cats are more susceptible due to
absent expression of the enzyme UGT1A6 which glucuronidates
acetaminophen.82,83 Acetaminophen toxicosis can result in clinical
signs including brown/cyanotic mucous membranes, facial and paw
edema.
Doses in excess of 100 mg/kg can lead to hepatotoxicosis and 200
mg/kg can lead to methemoglobinemia in dogs. There is no safe dosage
reported for cats and hematologic effects are most common.
Decontamination can be undertaken with emesis and activated charcoal
(ch. 132); the latter is most effective within 1 hour but may be of benefit
for as long as 3-4 hours.3 N-acetylcysteine (NAC) replenishes GSH to
limit excessive NAPQI formation, thereby limiting liver damage. NAC
should be administered as soon as possible after ingestion and can
prevent or decrease the severity of hepatic damage if given up to 48
hours after ingestion.3,84,85 In cats, a combination of oral NAC and
silymarin was found to protect against liver oxidative stress due to
acetaminophen intoxication.86 The antioxidant S-adenosyl methionine
(SAMe) decreased acetaminophen-induced RBC and hepatic damage in
cats and dogs.81,87 Ascorbic acid (30 mg/kg SQ/IV q6-8h) can be used
in patients with methemoglobinemia to reduce methemoglobin to
hemoglobin.80

ANTIEPILEPTIC DRUG-INDUCED LIVER
INJURY
Phenobarbital
Phenobarbital can result in the development of increased liver enzyme
activities without hepatocellular damage, dose-dependent ALD or

chronic hepatopathy.88 Clinical signs, when apparent, usually develop
after >1 year of cumulative treatment. The extent of hepatic injury has
been associated with duration of administration.74 Although serum drug
concentrations were not found to correlate with the development of
hepatic dysfunction in epileptic dogs, improvement has been seen in
dogs after dose reduction. This suggests a dose-dependent mechanism
of toxicity associated with cytochrome P450 enzyme induction with
secondary bioactivation, and concurrent hepatotoxicity due to coadministered drugs, environmental toxins, or dietary components.74
Histopathological findings include bridging portal fibrosis, nodular
regeneration and biliary hyperplasia.88

Zonisamide
Zonisamide, a sulfonamide-based antiepileptic medication, has been
associated with idiosyncratic hepatotoxicosis in 2 dogs within 3 weeks of
beginning treatment. Histopathologic evaluation of liver tissue in one
dog showed severe, subacute, massive panlobular hepatic necrosis.89,90

AZATHIOPRINE-INDUCED LIVER INJURY
Azathioprine, a purine nucleoside analogue, has been associated with a
reversible dose-dependent DILI ranging from mild, asymptomatic, selflimiting increases in liver enzyme to, less commonly, clinical
hepatotoxicosis and jaundice.91,92 Hepatotoxicosis has been reported in
15% of dogs after a median of 2 weeks of treatment and has been
attributed to accumulation of the metabolite 6-methyl mercaptopurine
(6-MMP). Monitoring serum biochemistries in the first 4 weeks of
treatment is recommended. German Shepherd Dogs have been reported
as over-represented. Hepatotoxicity can be exacerbated by GSH
depletion so there may be a role for SAMe or NAC treatment.91

AZOLE ANTIFUNGAL DRUG-INDUCED
LIVER INJURY
Ketoconazole (dogs only), itraconazole, and fluconazole can cause
subclinical liver enzyme increases. Uncommonly, clinical

hepatotoxicosis has been reported. Increased ALT was seen in 17 and
26% of dogs receiving fluconazole and itraconazole, respectively, for
treatment of blastomycosis.93 Elevated ALT and ALP correlate with
plasma itraconazole concentrations, supporting a dose-dependent
mechanism of toxicosis.94 Azoles produce an oxidative metabolite (Ndeacetyl ketoconazole) which leads to covalent binding to liver proteins
and subsequent GSH depletion. Fluconazole is the least hepatotoxic
drug. Therefore, transitioning to this drug may be an option in patients
that develop hepatotoxicosis with the former drugs.74

AMIODARONE-INDUCED LIVER INJURY
Amiodarone is a class-III antiarrhythmic used in treating ventricular
tachyarrhythmias in dogs (ch. 230). Dose-dependent toxicosis,
manifested as vomiting, anorexia, and increased liver enzyme activities,
has been reported in up to 45% of dogs after 6 days to 8 months of
treatment.95,96 Toxicosis typically resolves following drug
discontinuation, but time to liver enzyme normalization can be
protracted. Toxicosis attributed to 2 oxidative metabolites—mono-Ndesethylamiodarone (MDEA) and di-N-desethylamiodarone (DDEA)—
which generate reactive oxygen species that lead to mitochondrial
injury.74

ANTIBIOTIC-INDUCED LIVER INJURY
Potentiated Sulphonamides
Potentiated sulphonamides/sulfonamides are associated with
idiosyncratic hepatotoxicosis mainly in dogs and uncommonly in cats.
The N-acetylation detoxification pathway is absent in dogs which
contributes to toxicity as sulphonamides are oxidized by cytochrome
P450 to reactive nitroso metabolites that act as haptens. Only 50% of
dogs develop sulfonamide serum adducts and anti-sulfonamide IgG
antibodies, suggesting other non-immune-mediated mechanisms are
likely involved.97,98 Samoyeds, Miniature Schnauzers and female
neutered dogs were overrepresented in one study. Although
hepatotoxicosis occurs at therapeutic doses, dogs that developed overt
hepatopathy were given higher doses. Clinical signs develop in 5-36 days

(mean 12 days) after exposure, including fever, polyarthropathy,
dermatologic lesions, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, hematologic dyscrasias
(thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, hemolytic anemia, eosinophilia),
hepatotoxicosis and uveitis.99 Hepatotoxicosis is associated with acute
parenchymal damage with moderate to severe increases in ALT, acute
cholestasis with jaundice, or a mixed pattern. The predominant
histopathological lesion is diffuse hepatic necrosis although severe
cholestasis and lymphoplasmacytic inflammation were also noted in
some.97 Hepatopathy was associated with decreased survival (46%
recovery) compared to sulfonamide hypersensitivity without
hepatopathy (89% recovery).95 Drug discontinuation usually leads to
resolution.

Tetracyclines
Tetracyclines cause mitochondrial dysfunction and subsequent steatosis
from inhibition of fatty acid beta oxidation in people but this has not
been reported in dogs. However, doxycycline has been associated with
subclinical increases in ALT and ALP in nearly 40% of treated dogs. The
clinical significance of this is unknown.100 Tetracycline administration
has been associated with clinical hepatotoxicosis in a cat.101

LOMUSTINE (CCNU)-INDUCED LIVER
INJURY
Lomustine is a nitrosurea alkylating agent used to treat canine round
cell neoplasia. The hepatotoxic mechanism is not fully understood but is
thought to involve GSH depletion and lipid peroxidation by reactive
metabolites. Increased liver enzyme activities are reported in up to 86%
of dogs receiving therapeutic doses; however, clinical hepatotoxicosis
only occurs in 3-6% of dogs.102 Hepatotoxicity is associated with higher
cumulative doses and number of doses, occurring after a median of 4
doses with a median of 11 weeks duration.103 Histopathologic evaluation
of tissue documents multifocal sinusoidal and portal aggregates of
hemosiderin-laden Kupffer cells, hepatocellular vacuolization, biliary
hyperplasia, minimal necrosis and bridging fibrosis.102 The
hepatotoxicosis is reversible in most dogs following discontinuation of

treatment; however, a subset of pets can develop a chronic hepatopathy
3 months to over 3 years after diagnosis.103 Median survival time is
reported as 15 weeks with over 60% dying or being euthanized due to
progressive hepatotoxicosis.103 A combination of SAMe and silymarin
has been shown to decrease the incidence and severity of
hepatotoxicosis and should be administered concurrently.102

DIAZEPAM-INDUCED LIVER INJURY
Diazepam is a benzodiazepine derivative prescribed for anxiolytic,
muscle relaxant, sedative, anticonvulsant, and appetite-stimulating
effects. Diazepam metabolism occurs in the liver via glucuronidation.
Clinical toxicosis, reported in cats, occurs via an unknown mechanism
but may be related to low capacity for glucuronidation in cats, leading to
the accumulation of reactive metabolites.104 Toxicosis has not been
reported with parenteral formulations. In idiosyncratic hepatotoxicosis,
repeated oral administration led to clinical signs (anorexia, lethargy,
jaundice, HE) within 4-11 days. Biochemical derangements include
increased ALT, mild-moderate increased ALP, and hyperbilirubinemia.
Histopathologic changes are consistent with centrilobular-to-panlobular
hepatic necrosis, biliary hyperplasia and suppurative cholangitis.
Prognosis is poor with 16 out of 18 reported cats dying or being
euthanized within 15 days of initial drug administration.33,104,105

METHIMAZOLE-INDUCED LIVER INJURY
About 2% of hyperthyroid cats (ch. 287), within the first month of
being given methimazole via oral or transdermal routes develop a
reversible idiosyncratic cholestatic hepatopathy.106 The mechanism of
toxicity in cats is unknown. Animal models suggest hepatic necrosis in
combination with GSH depletion are attributed to the oxidative
metabolite, N-methylthiourea, generated by flavin monooxygenases.74
Biochemical derangements include increased transaminases, ALP, and
hyperbilirubinemia and should be differentiated from the increased liver
enzymes seen with untreated hyperthyroidism which tend to resolve
with establishment of euthyroidism.

CARPROFEN-INDUCED LIVER INJURY
Carprofen, a nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug (NSAID), is associated
with idiosyncratic hepatocellular hepatotoxicosis of variable severity in
dogs, usually within the first month of treatment. Labradors have been
reported to be over-represented but this may simply reflect breed
popularity. The predominant histopathological finding is bridging
hepatic necrosis. Hepatotoxicosis tends to improve within a few weeks
of discontinuation. It is unclear if pre-existing liver disease is a risk
factor for toxicosis, nor whether chronic inflammatory liver disease
develops as a sequelae.107

ENVIRONMENTAL TOXINS
Overview
Environmental toxins are more commonly diagnosed in dogs than cats,
likely due to their scavenging nature. Confirmation can be difficult if the
exposure is not witnessed as there are no pathognomonic clinical
features. Antemortem analysis of serum, urine, gastric contents, and
antemortem/necroscopic analysis of tissue can be useful, but cannot
always be performed retrospectively. Only a few veterinary laboratories
offer testing and there can be a delay with obtaining results.5,56 Toxins
can be identified by bio-assays, liquid chromatography-mass
spectrometry (LC-MS), or enzyme linked immunosorbent assay
methods.108-111 Decontamination with emesis, gastric lavage, and
activated charcoal is recommended (ch. 132). The latter may disrupt
enterohepatic recirculation in Amanita intoxications. Due to the rapid
absorption of xylitol, there is a narrow window for safe decontamination
with emesis due to the risk of aspiration and activated charcoal has
limited benefit in preventing xylitol absorption.112 For toxins
undergoing enterohepatic recirculation, use of cholestyramine may be
used to bind and eliminate toxins, e.g., microcystins (blue-green
algae).113

Aflatoxins (ch. 134)
Mycotoxins may be found in cereal ingredients contained in
contaminated pet food formulations or mouldy foodstuffs (due to

improper storage). Aflatoxins are mycotoxins produced by Aspergillus
flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus and consist of aflatoxins B1, B2, G1
and G2.27 Aflatoxin B1 is the most hepatotoxic and undergoes hepatic
biotransformation mediated by cytochrome P450 enzymes to the
reactive metabolite AFB1-8-9-epoxide which covalently binds structural
proteins leading to hepatic necrosis. Secondary GSH depletion results in
further decreases of aflatoxin detoxification, exacerbating oxidative
hepatocyte injury. In dogs, the reported lethal dose is 0.5-1 mg/kg, with
levels as low as 0.06 mg/kg reported as toxic.27,114 Toxicosis occurs after
a median of 45 days; therefore, a detailed dietary history (ch. 145)
should be obtained. Interestingly, some dogs exhibit aversion to
contaminated food.115 Sporadic outbreaks have been reported, usually
as a result of accidental contamination of commercial dog food. Whereas
some dogs are subclinically affected, clinical signs include anorexia,
lethargy, vomiting/hematemesis, jaundice, diarrhea, ascites, peripheral
edema, bleeding diathesis, HE and sudden death.27,114 Histopathologic
changes in subacute cases include diffuse cytoplasmic lipid vacuolation,
biliary duct hyperplasia, scattered individual hepatocyte necrosis and
varying degrees of fibrosis. Chronic low grade exposure can result in
marked diffuse bridging portal fibrosis with regenerative nodules and
aPSS.27,114,115 Aflatoxin M1 metabolites can be measured in serum,
liver, and urine but are not detectable after 48 hours due to rapid
metabolism and excretion. Urine is most useful if analyzed while the dog
is still consuming the diet and food can also be analyzed for toxins.114,115
Mortality ranges from 64-100%.27,114,115

Sago Palms (ch. 134)
Sago palms are ornamental cycad plants and part of native flora in
subtropical and tropical regions. All parts of the plant contain toxins,
but the seeds contain the highest concentrations.116 The responsible
toxin is cycasin, metabolised by the gut bacterial enzyme betaglycosidase to methylazoxymethanol, causing hepatotoxic, carcinogenic,
GI, and teratogenic effects. Most dogs have GI signs, with hepatic
damage occurring within 24-48 hours of ingestion. Neurological signs
are seen in >50% of dogs. Histopathologic changes are consistent with
centrilobular coagulative necrosis, hydropic degeneration, and

sinusoidal congestion due to centrilobular collapse. Mortality is seen in
32-50% of dogs.116,117

Xylitol (ch. 134)
Xylitol is a sweetener found in chewing gum, baked goods (typically
formulated for diabetics), toothpastes and some medical products, e.g.,
nicotine gum. Xylitol intoxication at dosages over 100 mg/kg in dogs
leads to acute hypoglycemia due to insulin release followed by
hepatotoxicosis. Hypoglycemia may be delayed due to gradual depletion
of hepatic glycogen stores following ALF development.118,119
Experimentally, cats do not appear to develop xylitol hepatotoxicosis.112
The mechanism of hepatotoxicosis in dogs is thought to involve
adenosine triphosphate depletion during xylitol metabolism leading to
hepatic necrosis or the production of ROS. Acute hepatic necrosis with
increased liver enzyme activities occurs 9-72 hours after ingestion.118 In
a retrospective study of 192 dogs that consumed xylitol, none developed
liver failure. However, in an earlier study, 5/8 dogs died or were
euthanized due to ALF after xylitol intoxication.118,119 Histopathologic
changes are consistent with severe acute centrilobular and midzonal
hepatic necrosis.118 The development of ALF is thought to be
idiosyncratic and doesn’t appear to correlate with dosage of the
ingestion.118
The onset of clinical signs is variable but can occur in as little as 30
minutes after ingestion. Clinical signs include vomiting, lethargy,
weakness, ataxia and seizures.112 Diagnosis is based on history of toxin
ingestion. Laboratory toxin analysis is unreliable as xylitol is rapidly
absorbed and does not accumulate. Dextrose may prevent hypoglycemia
in mild intoxications and may be hepatoprotective. Dextrose should be
considered even in pets that are not hypoglycemic, especially if large
amounts were ingested. Treatment with SAMe and NAC should be
considered.118

Blue-Green Algae (Microcystins)
Cyanobacteria, also known as blue-green algae, are produced in shallow,
stagnant water sources which are nutrient-rich. Microcystis aeruginosa
or Nodularia spumigena cyanotoxins (cyclic peptides microcystins and

nodularins, respectively) are released as algae cells die and the bloom
appears as a blue-green scum floating on the water surface.111,113
Cyanotoxins in dogs disrupt the hepatocyte cytoskeleton leading to
hepatic necrosis and accumulation of blood in the sinusoids. Exposure
occurs through ingestion of contaminated water by drinking, swimming,
or licking contaminated fur. Light microscopy can identify toxins in GI
contents and in the water source.111,113 Pathologic changes include gross
hepatomegaly due to massive centrilobular to midzonal hepatocellular
hemorrhagic necrosis and acute tubular necrosis.120

Amanita phalloides
A. phalloides (also known as the “death cap”) is a species of mushroom
toxic to people, dogs and cats. It contains 2 heat-stable toxins:
phallotoxin which damages cell membranes of intestinal simple
columnar epithelium and alpha-amanitin (amatoxin) which is
hepatotoxic.109,121 Amatoxin reversibly binds RNA polymerase in
metabolically active cells, e.g., hepatocytes, GI crypt cells, and renal
tubular cells, leading to necrosis.109,110 There are 4 phases of toxicosis;
the first is a subclinical lag phase. The GI phase (phase 2) occurs 6-12
hours post-consumption and is associated with nausea, vomiting,
diarrhea, and abdominal cramping. Phase 3 is one of apparent recovery
(lasting about 12-24 hours) with subclinical increases in liver enzyme
activities. Phase 4 includes ALF and AKI (36-84 hours).109,110
Histopathologic changes are consistent with panlobular hepatic
necrosis. A. phalloides can be identified by a mycologist.109 Amanitin
concentrations are highest in urine within the first 24 hours so this is
the preferred antemortem sample for testing.109,121 Penicillin and
silymarin are accepted antidotes in people and act by inhibiting
hepatocyte amatoxin uptake during primary and enterohepatic
circulation. Silymarin has been shown to prevent hepatic injury in dogs
with experimental A. phalloides intoxication at higher doses (50 mg/kg
IV administered at 5 hours and 24 hours after intoxication).122 Survival
in dogs in one case series was 26%.110

AUTOIMMUNE ACUTE LIVER FAILURE
(AI-ALF)
AI-ALF is not yet recognized in dogs; however, the presence of
lymphoplasmacytic inflammation on ALF hepatic biopsies5 and the
acute presentation of a proportion of dogs with AI hepatitis are
suggestive. There are no pathognomonic clinicopathological features of
AI-ALF in people; however, the presence of high gamma-globulin and
auto-antibodies may aid diagnosis.8 AI-ALF histopathology typically
demonstrates severe centrilobular hepatic necrosis and interface
hepatitis, with an eosinophilic predominance in drug-induced cases.8
Treatment with steroids may be beneficial if given early in the disease
course, although their role once the disease has progressed to ALF is
unclear and can be associated with significant infection risk.54

TREATMENT
GENERAL SUPPORTIVE CARE
Liver transplantation is the treatment of choice in people with ALF and
supportive care bridges the gap until transplantation. In dogs and cats,
where the etiology of illness is usually unknown, the goal is to support
liver function until recovery. It is important to note that complete
recovery is possible, and transplant free survival rates continue to
improve in people.123 Patients with ALD are at risk of dehydration and
volume depletion due to vomiting, poor intake, and vasodilatory
hypotension.8 IV fluid therapy is recommended to rehydrate, replace
volume, increase ammonia excretion, and support pets with concurrent
AKI (chs. 120, 300). It is important to avoid over-hydration because
increased right-sided pressures may lead to deterioration of ARDS,
cardiac dysfunction (in cases of ischemic hepatitis), and exacerbation of
portal hypertension and cerebral hyperemia.1,29 Measuring central
venous pressure (CVP) can guide therapy (persistent CVP >10 mm Hg is
suggestive of volume overload; ch. 75). Hypotension and poor systemic
microcirculation can lead to hyperlactatemia. Theoretically, lactated
Ringer’s is poorly tolerated due to the lack of hepatic metabolism which
may worsen lactic acidosis and aggravate cerebral hyperemia. 0.9%
sodium chloride (saline) is preferred, plus it is less likely to lead to hypo-

osmolality and exacerbate HE.23 Colloids can be considered in
hypoalbuminemic pets to maintain oncotic pressure but care must be
taken as these can be associated with a risk of AKI and exacerbation of
bleeding tendencies (ch. 120).2 Refractory hypotension can be treated
with vasopressors (norepinephrine, vasopressin). Hydrocortisone can be
used to treat critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency (CIRCI)
and has been shown to reduce vasopressor requirements in people.2,7
However, steroids increase risk of GI ulceration and thrombosis.
Hypoglycemia should be treated with dextrose. Antiemetic treatment
(e.g., maropitant 0.5 mg/kg SQ q24h) can be considered in nauseated
and vomiting pets.

HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY (CH. 266)
Precipitating factors for HE should be addressed in the treatment plan
and include metabolic alkalosis (facilitates ammonia diffusion into the
brain), hypokalemia (stimulates renal ammoniagenesis), hyponatremia,
hypoglycemia, inflammation, infection (due to pyrexia and increased
protein metabolism), sedation/anesthesia (interaction amongst
neurotransmitters), increased systemic ammonia generation (blood
transfusions, protein calorie malnutrition, poor quality protein diet),
and increased ammonia production (high protein diet, GI hemorrhage,
azotemia, constipation).10,16 Treatment of acute HE is not well
established. Lactulose was shown in one study in people to increase
survival but led to no overall difference in outcome.3 Warm water
enemas can be used to physically reduce the numbers of ureaseproducing colonic bacteria and aid constipation (ch. 108).10 These are
usually followed by lactulose retention enemas. Due to the risk of
aspiration with oral treatment in pets with HE, oral lactulose is given
only when stable. Lactulose is a nonabsorbable disaccharide that
decreases ammonia due to decreased colonic transit time, decreasing
ammonia absorption. Lactulose also acidifies colon content which
converts ammonia to nonabsorbable ammonium (resulting in increased
fecal excretion) and also reduces urease-producing ammoniagenic
bacteria.10 The rationale for using antibiotics is to prevent production
and absorption of gut-derived ammonia. Neomycin and rifaximin are
minimally absorbed antibiotics. Oto- and nephrotoxicosis are seen with
significant systemic absorption of neomycin. Rifaximin is commonly

used in humans, is well-tolerated in dogs although use in HE has not
been assessed, and is likely cost-prohibitive.124 Amoxicillin 10-15 mg/kg
IV/PO q8-12h or metronidazole 7.5 mg/kg PO q12h (this is a lower
dosage due to hepatic metabolism) should be considered in animals with
acute HE with the added benefit that it can be used to treat leptospirosis
after obtaining diagnostic samples.10
Treatment of cerebral edema and ICH includes sedation or anesthesia
with intubation and ventilation in pets with high grade HE to minimize
stimuli that can exacerbate cerebral edema. Propofol has been
demonstrated to decrease ICH, has a short half-life, and has
anticonvulsant properties that reduce risk of subclinical seizure
activity.29 Short-term hyperventilation could be considered to promote
cerebral vasoconstriction and reduce intracranial pressure, but can
cause cerebral ischemia and should only be considered in pets with
imminent herniation.10,20 The head should be elevated to facilitate
venous drainage and decrease intracranial pressures. Blood pressure
should be monitored to optimize cerebral blood flow. Hypertonic saline
boluses may reduce intracranial pressure by increasing extracellular
osmolality leading to cellular dehydration.125 Mannitol (0.5-1 g/kg IV
over 20 minutes) decreases intracranial volume by drawing fluid into
the intravascular space and has been shown to reduce episodes of
cerebral edema and improve survival in people with ALF. However,
multiple doses can cause hyperosmolality so should be avoided.126
Dexamethasone has shown no benefit for controlling edema or
improving survival in people with ICH but has not been evaluated in
dogs.126 Seizures should be treated as they may exacerbate ICH and
cause cerebral hypoxia.3 Propofol or levetiracetam are reasonable
choices for seizure management. Diazepam should be used with caution
as it undergoes hepatic metabolism and increased endogenous
benzodiazepine receptor ligands may play a role in the pathogenesis of
HE. Phenobarbital can be considered for short-term emergency seizure
management, despite it being a recognised hepatotoxin.2,10

NUTRITION FOR ACUTE LIVER FAILURE
OR HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY (ch. 154)

ALF causes a hypermetabolic state with increased energy
expenditure.127 Protein restriction can lead to hyperammonemia due to
muscle catabolism, increases susceptibility to infection, and impairs
immunocompetence. Maintaining muscle mass is important because it
enables ammonia detoxification.128 Pets with acute HE may benefit
from short-term protein restriction as they may be unable to tolerate
protein. Early introduction of feeding minimizes muscle catabolism and
reduces risk of stress-induced GI hemorrhage, ileus, or bacterial
translocation.3,29 Consideration should be given to feeding tube
placement and antiemetic treatment to encourage return to voluntary
feeding. Naso-esophageal tubes are preferred in these critically ill pets
as no anesthesia is required and there is a low risk of hemorrhage (ch.
81). Although enteral feeding is preferred to maintain gut integrity,
aspiration is a risk if the pet has progressive HE and a large gastric
residue. Parenteral nutrition may be considered in these patients.29
Patients with ALD should be fed a high quality, digestible protein diet
given in small frequent portions if possible. Ideally the protein for dogs
should be from a dairy or vegetable source as they have been shown to
significantly reduce ammonia concentrations compared to meat
diets.129 Diets formulated for liver disease may be moderately protein
restricted and should be supplemented with high quality protein, e.g.,
cottage cheese. Cats have increased protein requirements as they don’t
downregulate their protein requirements even in catabolic and anorexic
states. Protein restriction should be avoided in cats. Cats with hepatic
lipidosis, for example, require relatively high protein diets to reduce
hepatic lipid accumulation.130

HEPATOPROTECTANTS AND
ANTIOXIDANTS
NAC (140 mg/kg IV once followed by 70 mg/kg IV q6-8h) is a thiol
donor that replenishes intracellular cysteine and GSH levels and acts as
a free radical scavenger with a well-established role in acetaminophen
intoxications.131 It may be useful in non-acetaminophen intoxications
and hepatic lipidosis due to improved microcirculatory function,
peripheral oxygen tissue delivery, antioxidant effects and amelioration
of cytokine storms.9,85 In people, it is associated with improved

transplant-free outcome in ALF patients with low-grade
encephalopathy.132 GI side effects limit oral administration, but no
adverse effects are reported with IV use in animals.131 Ursodeoxycholic
acid (UDCA; 10-15 mg/kg PO q24h) is a cytoprotective hydrophilic bile
acid which acts to replace hydrophobic toxic bile acids, stimulates
choleresis, stabilizes mitochondrial function, and has antiapoptotic and
immunomodulatory effects. UDCA can be used in ALD to treat any
aspect of extra- or intrahepatic cholestasis and it may have a role in
aiding biliary elimination of infectious organisms or toxins.131 Silymarin
(10 mg/kg PO q24h in combination with phosphatidylcholine) is an
extract of milk thistle plant seeds, Silybum marianum, and contains
several flavonoids, including silybinin (which is the predominant active
compound).131 It is recommended in hepatotoxic ALD and its
hepatoprotective properties include activity against lipid peroxidation,
cytochrome P450 inhibition, free radical scavenger and decreased
fibrosis.131 SAMe (20 mg/kg PO q24h) is used in the treatment and
prevention of toxin-induced hepatopathy, e.g., acetaminophen and
lomustine.81,87,102 SAMe augments hepatocyte GSH levels (an
endogenous antioxidant), improves membrane fluidity, modifies
cytokine expression and modulates apoptosis.131 Vitamin E (10-15 U/kg
PO q24h) inhibits lipid peroxidation of cell membranes, thereby
decreasing oxidative injury and should be considered in inflammatory,
toxic and copper-associated causes of ALD.131

MANAGING COMPLICATIONS
Infection
In people, infections develop during hospitalisation in up to 80% of ALF
cases. The infections most commonly affect lungs, urinary tract, and
bloodstream.133 Despite this, prophylactic antibiotics are not
recommended as they do not reduce the incidence of bloodstream
infections or mortality within 21 days of ALF.134 Rather, surveillance for
infections is important to recognize sepsis in critical patients and is
accomplished through urine and blood cultures on admission,
monitoring IV catheters, and obtaining thoracic radiographs if
pneumonia is suspected. Empiric treatment should be considered if

persistent hypotension, worsening encephalopathy, or development of
SIRS is diagnosed.7

Coagulopathies
In humans, prophylactic administration of clotting factors is not
recommended because they alter coagulation times (which can be a
useful prognostic factor to monitor), because clinically significant
bleeding is not common (including spontaneous intracranial bleeding),
and they have not been shown to decrease the risk of significant
bleeding.7,38,40 Consideration can be given to using TEG (ch. 170) to
guide replenishment prior to liver biopsy as this has been associated
with a decrease in blood product administration and mortality in dogs
and humans.39,54 Bleeding in people is usually upper GI, caused by
gastric mucosal ischemia proportional to the severity of underlying
illness rather than defective hemostasis.38 There may be a benefit of
sucralfate, histamine-receptor antagonists and proton pump inhibitors,
although these have not universally been shown to decrease incidence of
bleeding in people and there is limited evidence for their use in animals
in this context.1,3 Fresh frozen plasma (5-15 mL/kg) is a preferred firstline treatment if there is active hemorrhage or a planned invasive
procedure, e.g., liver biopsy. Criteria for administration prior to biopsy
include the presence of thrombocytopenia, prolonged coagulation times
or a hypocoagulable TEG. Prophylactic vitamin K1 0.5-1.5 mg/kg IM/SQ
q12h for 3 days should be considered in all patients with evidence of
cholestasis or increased bleeding tendencies. Cats are particularly
susceptible to vitamin K deficiency as a result of hepatobiliary
disease.30,32,35 Side-effects of transfusions include volume overload
which may aggravate bleeding risk or worsen ICH, potentiation of portal
hypertension, transmission of infectious agents, transfusion reactions,
transfusion-associated acute lung injury, and exacerbation of a preexisting hypercoagulable state.4,30,38 Treatment should be aimed at
resolution of bleeding and not at reversing abnormal coagulation times
which are unlikely to provide accurate assessment of
bleeding/thrombotic risk.30

PROGNOSIS

The literature available to enable clinicians to estimate survival and
outcome in pets with ALD is limited. Due to the remarkable regenerative
capacity of the liver, animals that survive the acute phase of ALD/ALF
can recover completely without permanent hepatic injury and with
normalization of liver enzymes and function.44,56 However, in one case
series, 5/12 dogs with acute hepatitis that underwent a repeat liver
biopsy were identified as developing chronic hepatic disease.44 In the
largest case series of ALF dogs, 14.3% survived to discharge but there
was limited follow-up data, suggesting a guarded prognosis.5
Transplant-free survival in people has improved over the years and is
56.1% at 3 weeks compared to 96.3% in patients undergoing a liver
transplant.123
In people, the main causes of death in ALF are sepsis, multi-organ
failure, and ICH.123 Etiology is a major prognostic factor in people.
Acetaminophen intoxication is associated with the highest rate of
spontaneous (transplant-free) recovery despite greater initial severity of
illness, which may reflect rapid hepatocyte regeneration and resolution
of hepatic damage.123 Spontaneous recovery can be as low as 33% for
indeterminate causes.7 Negative prognostic indicators in people include
hyperlactatemia, hyperbilirubinemia, prolonged PT, the presence of
SIRS, cerebral edema, HE grade, hyperammonemia,
hyperphosphatemia, extent of hepatic necrosis, adrenal insufficiency,
and time to onset of encephalopathy.13,20,24,54,55,135-137
Hypophosphatemia, on the converse, is a positive prognostic indicator,
likely reflecting an intracellular shift due to hepatic regeneration.131
Negative prognostic indicators in dogs include indicators of hepatic
dysfunction (hyperbilirubinemia, hypoalbuminemia,
hypocholesterolemia, hypoglycemia) and evidence of a bleeding
diathesis (elevated PT and APTT, decreased protein C and antithrombin,
thrombocytopenia and hypofibrinogenaemia). Evidence of a bleeding
diathesis is more often associated with evidence of spontaneous
bleeding.5,27,30,114,116,118,138 Other factors include hyperphosphatemia
(due to suboptimal hepatic regeneration or the direct result of
phosphate release from hepatic necrosis), ascites development and the
presence of granular cylindruria, particularly in toxic ALF.5,27,112 High
serum ALT at presentation and >50% decrease over several days were
good prognostic indicators with speculation that survivors had more

viable hepatocytes with subsequent greater ALT leakage or due to the
fact that toxic etiologies that inhibit ALT were more likely in nonsurvivors (e.g., aflatoxins, microcystins).5

CLIENT INFORMATION
Toxic Causes of Acute Liver Disease in Dogs and
Cats
Acute liver disease occurs relatively uncommonly in small animals and
is usually due to infectious, toxic and cancerous causes. Dogs are likely
to be affected by toxic causes due to their scavenging nature but it can be
challenging for your veterinarian to ascertain the cause, particularly if
the exposure was unwitnessed. If you or your veterinarian suspects a
toxic cause, please consider carefully whether your pet has had access to
any medications (human or veterinary) and provide clear information
about any nutritional or herbal supplements that they are receiving as
these can also be associated with toxic liver disease. Providing a
complete anti-parasiticide and dietary history can also help your
veterinarian to narrow down causes of acute liver disease.

ENVIRONMENTAL TOXINS
• Blue-green algae: blue-green algae forms in shallow, stagnant
water sources. Please inform your vet if your dog has been
swimming in suspect water.
• Amanita phalloides: the “death cap” mushroom.
• Xylitol: this is a sweetener found in chewing gum, diabetic foods,
toothpastes and some medical products, e.g., nicotine gum.
• Aflatoxins: these are toxins found in contaminated feeds. Please
inform your vet if your other pet is unwell as this may be helpful.
• Sago palms: these are ornamental plants and are part of the native
flora in subtropical and tropical regions.

DRUGS
• Anti-inflammatories (e.g., paracetamol and carprofen)
• Anti-fungal drugs (e.g., ketoconazole and itraconazole)
• Antibiotics (e.g., potentiated sulphonamides and tetracyclines)
• Anti-epileptics (e.g., phenobarbital and zonisamide)
• Chemotherapy drugs (e.g., lomustine)
• Appetite-stimulants (e.g., diazepam)
• Anti-thyroid drugs (e.g., methimazole)
• Nutritional and herbal supplements

CLINICAL SIGNS
• Gastrointestinal (vomiting and diarrhoea, with or without fresh
blood)
• Lethargy
• Reduced appetite
• Drinking and urinating excessively
• Jaundiced skin
• Discoloured urine
• Neurological signs (dull, circling, head pressing, behavioural
changes, seizures)

INVESTIGATIONS
• Blood tests will assess the degree of liver damage and dysfunction.

• Clotting tests will assess the liver’s ability to produce clotting
factors and can aid in prognostication.
• Urine analysis may suggest kidney damage or dilute urine due to
liver disease.
• Imaging may help to assess the liver size and structure but is
unlikely to provide a definitive diagnosis.
• Liver biopsy for cytology: this can provide assessment of liver cells
but is less useful for toxic causes.
• Liver biopsy and tissue sampling: this will provide information
about the type and degree of liver damage.
• Toxicology: your veterinarian may take samples of vomit, urine,
blood and/or tissue for analysis for specific toxins.

TREATMENT
Decontamination
if toxicity is known in your pet, your veterinarian may choose to
decontaminate your pet by inducing vomiting, lavaging their stomach
and treating them with medications which absorb ingested toxins.

Supportive
• Fluids
• Anti-vomiting medications
• Treating neurological signs with enemas, antibiotics, anti-seizure
medications and medications to lower pressure in the brain (in
severe cases)
• Nutrition, e.g., placing a feeding tube if your pet is not eating
• Liver supportive medications

PROGNOSIS
Unlike people, there is no option to treat our pets with liver
transplantation so treatment is supportive and aims to support the liver
while it regenerates. Despite our best efforts, recent studies have shown
that the cause of acute liver disease was unknown in two-thirds of
patients which can make treatment and prognostication much more
challenging. Although the prognosis can be poor, particularly when liver
failure develops, complete recovery is possible in our pets.
Katie Elizabeth McCallum (Cambridge, United Kingdom)

DEFINITION AND HISTOLOGIC FEATURES OF A
CHALLENGING DIAGNOSIS
Chronic hepatitis (CH) is histologically characterized by hepatocellular apoptosis or necrosis, variable
mononuclear or mixed inflammatory infiltrates, regeneration, and fibrosis.1 CH, rare in cats, is an
important cause of morbidity and mortality in dogs. For example, in one study, CH was identified in
12% of all dogs undergoing necropsy for any reason.2 CH can be a diagnostic challenge because dogs
may have no or mild and nonspecific clinical signs early in its course, increased liver enzyme activities
and imaging results are nonspecific, and the integration of hepatic histopathological findings into a
therapeutic plan is not always straightforward. If diagnosed at an early stage, CH can be rewarding to
manage. Delay in diagnosis and treatment can negatively affect outcome. CH must be discriminated
from nonspecific reactive hepatopathy (Table 270.1).

ETIOLOGY
There are many potential causes of CH in dogs but even with a thorough diagnostic evaluation,
including histopathologic evaluation of liver tissue, an underlying cause is not often identified. Since
some underlying conditions are treatable, diagnostics are worthwhile.

DRUGS AND TOXINS
Since a variety of drugs and toxins can cause liver injury, it is important to identify any toxin exposure
and all medications given to the dog (chs. 15, 134, and 269). Owners should be specifically asked if
herbal remedies are given to their dog, as some cause liver injury in humans.3 Drug- and toxininduced liver injury is often acute and followed by resolution or death, rather than causing chronic
inflammation. However, some drugs (particularly those that are administered daily) and toxins have
the potential to lead to CH (Box 270.1).

INFECTIOUS AGENTS
Viruses are an important cause of CH in humans, but have not been identified as a cause of CH in dogs
(ch. 183).4 A novel hepadnavirus was associated with CH and hepatocellular carcinoma in cats.5
Several infectious agents have been shown to cause CH in dogs as part of
granulomatous/pyogranulomatous multisystemic disease processes (e.g., Leishmania [ch. 197],
Histoplasma [ch. 209], Heterobilharzia americana; [ch. 262]; Box 270.1).6-12 Bacterial cultures of
liver and bile from dogs with CH are usually negative and eubacterial DNA was not found in archived
liver tissue from 11 dogs with granulomatous hepatitis.13 However, not all bacteria capable of
chronically infecting the liver and potentially causing CH are easy to grow in vitro. Leptospiral
organisms were identified using florescence in situ hybridization in 10 dogs with granulomatous
hepatitis but without obvious renal involvement (ch. 192).7

COPPER
Hydroxyl Radical Formation
Copper accumulation is a common cause of CH in dogs, seen in about a third of primary hepatitis
cases in one study.14 The liver is the principal recipient of copper absorbed from the gastrointestinal
(GI) tract. An essential trace element, copper in hepatocytes is bound to proteins, such as glutathione
or metallothionein. When hepatocyte copper binding proteins are saturated, harmful free copper ions
are released that can form hydroxyl radicals capable of causing oxidative liver damage.

Breed Predisposition
Copper can accumulate in the liver of dogs with genetic defects in its biliary excretion and/or due to
increased dietary intake. The following breeds are proven or suspected to be predisposed to copperassociated CH: Bedlington Terrier, Labrador Retriever, Doberman Pinscher, Dalmatian, and West
Highland White Terrier.15-20 It is also important to recognize that copper-associated CH can develop
in other breeds or mixed-breed dogs.

Genetic Basis
In Bedlington Terriers, autosomal recessive deletion mutations of exon 2 of the COMMD1 gene (that
may indirectly downregulate the cellular copper exporter ATP7B) have been identified.15,21 The
prevalence of copper-associated CH in Bedlington Terriers has been dramatically reduced after testing
and selective breeding. Dogs homozygous positive for the COMMD1 mutation are still present in the
population, however. Discordant Bedlington Terriers with copper storage disease but without this
deletion and other potential genetic predispositions are being investigated.22 A genetic basis for
copper-associated CH is also suspected in Labrador Retrievers and an association between increased
hepatic copper concentrations and a mutation of the Wilson’s disease gene (ATP7B) has been shown.
A mutation affecting another copper transporting protein, ATP7A, seems to attenuate copper
accumulation with a more marked effect in males, likely explaining the female predisposition in the
breed.23 However, environmental factors are also likely to play a role in this breed. A mutation of the
ATP7B gene has also been found to be associated with copper-associated CH in Doberman
Pinschers.24
