Excess Dietary Copper
Changes were made to dietary guidelines from the National Research Council and Association of
American Feed Control Officials in the 1990s. At this time, a switch was made from supplementing
commercial diets with copper oxide to the more bioavailable copper chelates, likely contributing to the
apparent increase in the prevalence of copper-associated CH in Labradors and other breeds at that
time.25,26

Chronic Cholestasis
Chronic cholestasis in people can lead to impaired bile excretion of copper with resultant periportal
copper accumulation. Copper accumulation after experimental common bile duct obstruction was not
marked unless dogs were also loaded with intravenous copper.27 Copper accumulation is not seen in
spontaneous cholestatic disease in dogs.28 Thus, genotype and dietary copper are likely to be more
important in the development of copper-associated CH.

Fanconi Syndrome
Fanconi syndrome has been reported in dogs with copper-associated CH. These dogs had glycosuria in
the absence of hyperglycemia, low urine specific gravity, and proteinuria caused by proximal renal
tubule injury (chs. 303 and 305).29

IMMUNE-MEDIATED CHRONIC HEPATITIS
Despite thorough diagnostic evaluations, an underlying cause is not identified for about 60% of dogs
with primary hepatitis.14 Some of these dogs are designated as having idiopathic CH, likely secondary
to an immune-mediated etiology. Evidence supporting an immune-mediated etiology includes: 1) a
female predisposition in Doberman Pinschers, English Springer Spaniels, and other breeds of dog,3032

2) an association with certain major histocompatibility haplotypes in Doberman Pinschers and

English Springer Spaniels,30,31 3) positive titers for autoantibodies that target hepatic proteins in
Doberman Pinschers and other breeds of dog,33,34 and 4) a positive response to immunomodulatory
drugs in some.35-37 Although none of these findings provides definitive proof of an immune-mediated
etiology, in combination they are compelling. It is not possible with histology to definitively diagnose
immune-mediated CH in dogs and tests for autoantibodies against hepatic proteins are not
commercially available. A predominant lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, often with interface hepatitis
(destruction of hepatocytes at the limiting plates), is expected. Therefore, a presumptive diagnosis is
usually made by ruling out other known causes, typical histopathologic findings, and documenting a
positive response to immunomodulatory therapy.

LOBULAR DISSECTING HEPATITIS
Lobular dissecting hepatitis, an uncommon form of CH often seen in younger dogs, is histologically
characterized by bands of myofibrocytes and thin strands of extracellular matrix between individual
and small groups of hepatocytes.38 This form of CH progresses quickly to cirrhosis/end-stage liver
disease but likely represents a pattern of liver injury rather than a distinct disease process.

PATHOGENESIS
CHRONIC INFLAMMATION LEADING TO FIBROSIS
Regardless of the underlying cause of chronic hepatocellular injury, recruitment of inflammatory cells
(i.e., lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, macrophages, or eosinophils) occurs. This inflammatory
infiltrate is usually seen in the periportal regions but may co-localize with (primary) copper

accumulation in centrilobular zones. Decreased hepatic glutathione concentrations indicative of
oxidative stress have been documented in dogs with necro-inflammatory liver diseases (including
CH).39 Regardless, oxidative stress perpetuates hepatocellular injury. Chronic inflammation leads to
activation of myofibroblasts, including hepatic stellate cells and portal fibroblasts. This results in an
increase in extracellular matrix deposition relative to its removal with resultant hepatic fibrosis.40
Hepatic fibrosis diminishes liver function, as hepatocytes are replaced by fibrous tissue.

PORTAL HYPERTENSION, ASCITES
Hepatic fibrosis also leads to increased intrahepatic resistance to blood flow with resultant hepatic
(sinusoidal) portal hypertension. Dynamic obstruction due to increased portal vascular tone also
occurs.41 Portal hypertension in dogs with CH leads to imbalances of Starling’s forces in hepatic
sinusoids, promoting formation of ascites (typically a protein-rich transudate [chs. 21, 71]).
Splanchnic vasodilation and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system exacerbate this
increase in vascular hydrostatic pressure. Dogs with CH often have hypoalbuminemia leading to low
oncotic pressure, also contributing to ascites formation (ch. 266).41,42 Hepatic portal hypertension
can cause development of acquired portosystemic collateral blood vessels, portosystemic shunting
(PSS) of blood, ammonia dysmetabolism, and hepatic encephalopathy (HE). This process, often
attributed to aging by owners, is more subtle than in dogs with congenital PSS (ch. 267).

HEMOSTASIS, GASTROINTESTINAL (GI) TRACT
The liver synthesizes thrombopoietin, nearly all the coagulant and anticoagulant factors involved in
the hemostatic system, and recycles vitamin K. Hemostasis is often abnormal in pets with advanced
liver disease, potentially leading to bleeding or thrombosis (chs. 170 and 171).43 Spontaneous
bleeding is rare in dogs with CH but can occur in end-stage disease and may contribute to GI bleeding.
Risk of bleeding increases during and after invasive procedures in these pets. Portal vein thrombosis, a
potential complication of CH in dogs, can contribute to portal hypertension (ch. 266).44
GI signs are common in dogs with CH26 and gastroduodenal ulceration has been a purported
complication of CH. However, the prevalence of GI ulceration in dogs with CH has not been
determined and hypergastrinemia does not appear to play a role in its development.45

SIGNALMENT AND CLINICAL FINDINGS
CH can occur in any breed or mixed breed dog. In dogs from the UK undergoing necropsy, increased
risk for developing CH was demonstrated in American Cocker Spaniels, Cairn Terriers, Dalmatians,
Doberman Pinchers, English Cocker Spaniels, English Springer Spaniels, Great Danes, Labrador
Retrievers, and Samoyeds.46 Breeds at risk of copper-associated CH or suspected to be at risk of
immune-mediated CH have been discussed. Some breeds, such as Doberman Pinschers, can develop
either copper-associated or idiopathic CH. In 983 dogs with CH, the median age at diagnosis was 7.2
years; however, the reported range was wide.26
In 983 dogs with CH, the most common clinical signs were decreased appetite (61%),
lethargy/depression (56%), icterus (34%), ascites (32%), polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD; 30%), vomiting
(24%), diarrhea (20%), HE (7%), and melena (6%).26 It is important to remember that early in CH,
dogs may not exhibit any clinical signs and the earliest are often nonspecific, e.g., decreased appetite
and lethargy. Liver specific signs, e.g., icterus, ascites, or HE, tend to occur later in the course of
disease.

DIAGNOSIS
LABORATORY TESTING

CBC and Liver Enzyme Activities (ch. 65)
Dogs with CH may have nonspecific hematological changes, such as a mild to moderate
thrombocytopenia or a mild normocytic normochromic non-regenerative anemia (ch. 57). The
earliest and most common biochemical change in dogs with CH is increased serum alanine
transaminase (ALT) activity, which was 71% sensitive for subclinical CH in one study.47 Some dogs
with histologically documented CH have normal ALT activities.47 Serum alkaline phosphatase
activities are also commonly increased (35% sensitive for subclinical liver disease) but usually of lower
magnitude and occur later in the course of disease than those of ALT.47 Serum aspartate transaminase
and gamma glutamyl transferase activities are less consistently increased. Hepatocyte derived
microRNA-122, a sensitive serum marker of hepatocellular injury, is increased early in the course of
CH, but is not specific.48

Bilirubin, Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN), Albumin, Cholesterol, Bile Acids,
Coagulation Factors
Many dogs with CH have normal serum bilirubin concentrations. Hyperbilirubinemia typically occurs
late in the course of CH and is a negative prognostic factor.49 Decreases in serum concentrations of
BUN, albumin, and/or cholesterol also occur late in the course of CH. Measuring paired pre- and
postprandial serum total bile acids is sensitive for identifying acquired PSS, but lack sensitivity for CH
and other liver diseases in the absence of PSS. In dogs with hyperbilirubinemia, serum bile acid
concentrations are predictably increased and in this context their measurement does not help
diagnosing PSS. Decreased plasma protein C activity, prolonged coagulation times (prothrombin time
and activated partial thromboplastin time), hypofibrinogenemia, and decreased plasma antithrombin
activity may be noted.50 Thromboelastography results (ch. 170) indicate that dogs with CH may be
hypocoagulable, hypercoagulable, or normocoagulable and that hyperfibrinolysis is common.51

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
No diagnostic imaging modality allows a definitive diagnosis of CH. Abdominal radiographs of dogs
with CH are often normal but may reveal microhepatica. Abdominal ultrasound (US) is the preferred
imaging modality as the biliary tract and hepatic parenchyma can be assessed. US changes consistent
with CH include a diffusely hyperechoic liver (due to fibrosis and/or glycogen deposition). With
advanced liver disease/cirrhosis, US reveals nonspecific changes: mixed echogenicity, subjective
microhepatica, and/or small nodules.52 Absence of changes on US does not rule out CH. Acquired
portosystemic collateral blood vessels (often multiple anomalous vessels caudal to the kidneys;
Video 270.1; ch. 267) or evidence of portal hypertension (reduced or reversed portal blood flow; ch.
266) may be appreciated with US. Where available, computed tomography (CT) angiography also
allows the detection of these complications of CH.53

CYTOLOGY
Fine-needle aspiration of the liver is straightforward and of relatively low risk. However, CH cannot be
definitively diagnosed cytologically (ch. 85). Cytologic findings consistent with hepatic fibrosis
include an increased spindle cell to hepatocyte ratio and mast cells.54 The presence of hepatic copper
granules on rhodanine stained cytologic smear is consistent with copper accumulation but their
absence does not rule this out.55

LIVER BIOPSY/HISTOPATHOLOGY
Techniques

Definitive diagnosis of CH and subsequent treatment planning requires histologic assessment of liver
tissue. The 3 techniques for liver biopsy in dogs are percutaneous needle biopsy (usually with US
guidance; ch. 85), laparoscopic biopsy, and biopsy during laparotomy. Each technique has
advantages and disadvantages but the latter 2 techniques generally result in better quality liver
specimens and were recommended in a recent expert consensus statement.26,56

Risk of Bleeding
Liver biopsy is invasive with a risk of hemorrhage. Thus, risk assessment should be performed (i.e.,
packed cell volume, platelet count and blood smear examination, prothrombin time, activated partial
thromboplastin time, ± fibrinogen concentration, ± buccal mucosal bleeding time [ch. 79]).43 Testing
is recommended in all cases but there is no direct link between hemostatic abnormalities and bleeding
risk (chs. 170, 171, and 266).

Culture, Copper, Histology, Copper Quantification
Multiple liver lobes should be sampled to reduce risk of sampling error.57 A specimen of liver (and
where possible a sample of bile) should be submitted for aerobic/anaerobic bacterial culture and
another stored or submitted for copper quantification using atomic absorption spectroscopy, which is
best expressed on a dry weight basis. Less preferably, inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry
allows measurement of hepatic copper on a wet weight basis from which the dry weight concentration
is estimated. It is important to provide the pathologist with sufficient clinical history. CH is
histologically characterized by hepatocellular apoptosis or necrosis, a variable mononuclear or mixed
inflammatory infiltrate, regeneration, and fibrosis (Figure 270.1).1 The presence of hepatocyte
apoptosis/necrosis and fibrosis helps distinguish CH from nonspecific reactive hepatopathy (Table
270.1). To maximize the value of biopsy, sections of liver should be stained for copper, iron,
connective tissue, and lipofuscin in addition to routine staining with hematoxylin & eosin.

INFECTIOUS DISEASE TESTING
Liver tissue and bile should be submitted for aerobic/anaerobic bacterial culture, but results are
usually negative in dogs with CH. If histologic assessment reveals granulomatous/pyogranulomatous
hepatitis with no apparent etiology, further testing for geographically relevant infectious agents is
indicated (ch. 9). Fluorescent in situ hybridization for eubacteria can also be helpful (Box 270.1).

MANAGEMENT
GENERAL SUPPORT
In confirmed CH and in cases of suspected CH where biopsy has not been performed, pets should be
fed a high-quality diet (ch. 154). Support with cytoprotective agents and treating any complications of
CH, as discussed below, are indicated. Copper chelators and immunomodulatory therapy should be
reserved for histopathologically confirmed cases.

COPPER-ASSOCIATED CHRONIC HEPATITIS
Indications for Chelation
Chelation should be initiated when hepatic copper concentrations exceed 1000 mcg/g dry weight and
considered when between 600 and 1000 mcg/g dry weight, depending on the presence, grade, and
localization of histologic copper staining.26 Occasionally histologic copper staining and copper
quantification are discordant due to sampling variation. In this case, additional liver biopsy specimens
can be retrieved from the paraffin-embedded block and submitted for quantification or image based
estimation of copper concentration can be performed.58 Regenerative nodules contain less copper
than the remaining liver, contributing to this problem.59 In the absence of copper quantification, the

histologic assessment grade of copper accumulation can be used as a surrogate, e.g., a copper score of
≥3 out 5 typically supports chelation initiation.60 Accurate digital quantification can also be
performed from histological sections.58 This technique typically provides slightly higher estimates of
hepatic copper content than spectroscopy-based methods possibly because the latter tends to
underestimate copper due to its uneven distribution.60

FIGURE 270.1 Histological sections of liver from dogs with chronic
hepatitis. A, Hepatic copper accumulation in a 5-year-old female spayed
Doberman Pinscher with chronic hepatitis. Abundant red/brown copper
granules are present in hepatocytes on this rhodanine-stained histologic
image. This dog also had chronic hepatitis which in this breed may also have
an immune-mediated etiology. B, Severe hepatic fibrosis in a 6-year-old
female spayed Bulldog with idiopathic chronic hepatitis. Severe hepatic
fibrosis with nodule formation is present on this picrosirius–red-stained

Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory.)

Chelating Agents: Actions, Options, Side Effects
Chelating agents remove hepatic copper by making it soluble. It is then excreted in the urine. Dpenicillamine, the chelating agent of choice for dogs (10-15 mg/kg PO q12h before feeding) is not
licensed for use in small animals. It commonly causes GI side-effects, e.g., vomiting, diarrhea, and
anorexia which are managed by giving it with a small amount of food, starting an antiemetic drug,
and/or reducing the dose at least temporarily. Glomerulonephropathy and dermatological lesions are
possible but uncommon side-effects, either of which dictates that the drug be promptly discontinued.
Trientine (10-15 mg/kg PO q12h before feeding) may be used if D-penicillamine is not tolerated. There
is less published experience with this drug and it was not recommended in a recent expert consensus
statement.26 Ammonium tetrathiomolybdate has been shown to reduce hepatic copper concentration
in dogs and appears to be reasonably well-tolerated, but further studies are needed before its routine
use can be recommended.61

Diet and Other Supportive Care
Dogs with copper-associated CH should be given a copper-restricted diet, such as a commercial liver
support diet (ch. 154). Some recommend concurrent vitamin B6 (pyridoxine; 10-25 mg per dog PO
q24h) as used for people with Wilson’s disease (although the racemic form of penicillamine that
interferes with pyridoxine action is no longer used).26,62 D-penicillamine and zinc should not be given
at the same time. When D-penicillamine is discontinued, giving zinc acetate (5-10 mg/kg PO q12h) is
suggested because it decreases copper absorption from the GI tract. Plasma zinc concentrations

should be measured to avoid toxic concentrations (ch. 138). Copper-restricted diets should be
continued throughout treatment.
The most important aspect of treating copper-associated CH is to treat the underlying cause.
Corticosteroids and other anti-inflammatory medications are not generally needed but may be
beneficial in dogs that are hyporexic at the time of diagnosis. As accumulation of copper causes
oxidative stress, there is a rationale for supplementing with antioxidant agents such as S-adenosyl
methionine and/or vitamin E (Table 270.2).

Chelation Duration
The optimal duration of chelation therapy has not been determined and knowing when to discontinue
therapy is challenging. Since D-penicillamine chelates slowly, treatment usually takes months.
Although rare, prolonged therapy can result in copper deficiency manifested by microcytic
hypochromic anemia, anorexia, vomiting, and weight loss. A study in Labrador Retrievers suggested
6-10 months of chelation should be adequate for most dogs, but there was considerable interindividual
variation.63 Monitoring the dog’s clinical signs and liver enzyme activities, especially ALT, can provide
indirect information regarding the efficacy of treatment. Usually it takes several months for ALT
activity to return to normal and it is advisable to treat for at least a month after this. At this point a
second hepatic biopsy procedure with hepatic copper quantification can be considered. Some dogs
require repeated intermittent therapy with D-penicillamine and Bedlington Terriers may need lifelong
therapy. The decision to restart therapy is usually made based on an increasing ALT activity.

IMMUNE-MEDIATED CHRONIC HEPATITIS
Trial Immunomodulatory Therapy
As a subset of dogs with idiopathic CH likely have immune-mediated disease it is reasonable to start
immunomodulatory drugs on a trial basis and to then assess response. Other causes of CH, such as
copper, toxins, drugs, and infectious agents, must be carefully eliminated first (Figure 270.2).
A retrospective study of 151 dogs with CH of various causes found dogs treated with corticosteroids
survived longer than those that were not. These results must be interpreted with caution as the
retrospective design, the relatively large number of Doberman Pinschers (19%), and the exclusion of
the 37% of dogs that died within 7 days of starting treatment from outcome analysis means that study
results were susceptible to bias.36 The results of a retrospective uncontrolled study of 36 dogs with
idiopathic CH found hepatic inflammation decreased after 6 weeks of prednisolone treatment.
However, the majority had a recurrence of clinical signs or residual disease at the end of treatment.64
An uncontrolled prospective study of prednisolone in 12 English Springer Spaniels documented
clinical and biochemical improvement.35 Typically, prednisolone (1-2 mg/kg/day PO) is begun and
then gradually tapered. It should be noted that high dosages of prednisolone often cause vacuolar
hepatopathy (ch. 274) and other adverse effects, such as increased risk of ascites, GI bleeding,
PU/PD, polyphagia, or muscle wasting. After starting treatment with prednisolone, serum liver
enzyme activities may improve but often do not return to normal.35 Some have recommended a
second liver biopsy after 6 weeks of treatment,65 but this should not be routine.

Other immunomodulatory drugs that are sometimes used in place of prednisolone include modified
cyclosporine (5 to 10 mg/kg/day PO), mycophenolate mofetil (10 mg/kg PO q12h), or azathioprine (2
mg/kg PO q48h) (chs. 144, 169). An uncontrolled retrospective study of 48 dogs with CH treated
with modified cyclosporine and cytoprotective agents documented a 79% remission rate (defined as a
return of ALT activity to the normal range). The median cyclosporine dose at remission was 7.9
mg/kg/day, the median time to remission was 2.5 months, and adverse events included GI signs (38%
of dogs) and gingival hyperplasia (25% of dogs). These results are promising but further studies are
needed.

CYTOPROTECTIVE AGENTS
As oxidative damage plays a role in the pathogenesis of many hepatic diseases, including CH, there is
rationale for antioxidant therapy, such as S-adenosylmethionine, silybinin, or vitamin E (Table
270.2). There is no evidence suggesting improved outcomes in dogs with CH that receive these
treatments, but they are usually well-tolerated. Ursodeoxycholic acid is a hydrophilic bile acid believed
to have beneficial properties, including a choleretic effect, displacement of other more toxic bile acids
from the circulating pool, an antiapoptotic effect, and an immunomodulatory effect.66 This drug has
not been proven to improve outcomes in dogs with CH but is well-tolerated. It is most clearly

indicated in dogs with cholestasis (except those with complete extrahepatic biliary obstruction) or
those with concurrent biliary infections (ch. 272).

MANAGING THE COMPLICATIONS OF LIVER DISEASE
Ascites
Avoiding high sodium diets is the first step in treating ascites in dogs with CH (ch. 154). For diuresis,
the aldosterone receptor antagonist spironolactone is preferred because the mechanism of ascites
formation in chronic liver disease involves renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activation (ch. 266).
If 1 mg/kg PO q24h is ineffective, the dosage may be incrementally increased to 2 mg/kg q12h, and if
still ineffective, furosemide can be added starting at a low dose (1 mg/kg PO q12h). Furosemide can
lead to hypokalemia and metabolic acidosis, both of which may precipitate HE. The dog’s general
condition, hydration status, abdominal circumference, serum electrolytes, renal values, and serum
protein concentrations should be carefully monitored during diuretic therapy. Diuretics can be
tapered to effect once the ascites has resolved. Occasionally paracentesis is used if a concern exists for
dyspnea due to cranial displacement of the diaphragm and/or high intra-abdominal pressures causing
inappetence and discomfort (ch. 86). Removing a large volume may decrease serum albumin.

Hepatic Encephalopathy (HE): Nutrition
It is important to identify and address any precipitating factors for HE, such as systemic inflammatory
response syndrome, hypokalemia, or alkalosis (ch. 266). Severe protein restriction is not
recommended for humans with HE as it contributes to muscle wasting and worsening of neurological
signs.67 A non-meat diet (soy protein) resulted in lower ammonia concentrations than a poultry based
diet with a similar protein content in dogs with congenital PSS.68 Once signs of HE are controlled with
a commercial hepatic support diet, the author considers adding non-meat protein (e.g., soy protein) to
the diet to help prevent protein malnutrition. Alternatively, a high quality digestible diet designed for
GI disease can be used (ch. 152).

Hepatic Encephalopathy (HE): Medications
Lactulose (1-3 mL/10 kg of body weight PO q6-8h) is given initially and the dose adjusted until the dog
has 3 to 4 soft stools/day. Neomycin, a poorly absorbed aminoglycoside antibiotic, is sometimes used
to treat HE in dogs. Its GI absorption is very low but increases in dogs with decreased GI motility or
bowel wall damage. Substantial systemic absorption can cause ototoxicosis and nephrotoxicosis. Thus,
the author no longer recommends this drug for treating HE. Metronidazole, which is metabolized by
the liver and which, at higher dosages, can cause neurotoxicosis (ch. 248), is usually given at a lower
dosage in dogs with HE: 7.5 mg/kg PO q8-12h. Ampicillin, amoxicillin, or amoxicillin clavulanate have
been used to treat HE. Aside from uncommon GI side effects, they are usually well-tolerated. If
possible, dogs should eventually be tapered off antimicrobials and managed on diet and lactulose
alone.69

Managing GI Signs
There is only weak evidence to support the prophylactic use of gastric acid suppressing medications in
dogs with liver disease (including CH).70 However, when gastroduodenal ulceration is documented or
suspected, treatment with a gastric acid suppressing drug is indicated. Proton pump inhibitors, such
as omeprazole (1 mg/kg PO q12h), are more effective than histamine-2 receptor antagonists.71 In dogs
that are actively vomiting or appear to be nauseated, antiemetic therapy (e.g., maropitant 1 mg/kg
IV/SQ/PO or ondansetron 0.2 mg/kg IV q12h or 0.5-1 mg/kg PO q12h) is indicated.

PROGNOSIS
Left untreated, CH progresses to end-stage liver disease/cirrhosis and eventually leads to euthanasia
or death of the dog. However, if the underlying cause of liver injury can be identified and treated at an

early stage, many dogs will have a prolonged survival. The mean survival time of 364 dogs with CH
was 561 days.26 Lobular dissecting hepatitis has a worse prognosis and median survival time in one
study was only 0.7 months.14 Negative prognostic factors identified in the literature include
ascites,14,72 advanced hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis,14,36,73 prolonged bleeding times,36,74 and
icterus.14,49

CLIENT INFORMATION
Chronic Hepatitis
BACKGROUND
Chronic hepatitis (CH) is a common liver disease in dogs that is characterized by inflammation and
fibrosis (scarring) of the liver. Early in the course of disease, dogs may not have any symptoms or their
symptoms may be those also caused by other diseases. CH cannot be diagnosed by blood tests, X-rays,
or ultrasound scans and microscopic examination of liver biopsy specimens is required for an accurate
diagnosis. When diagnosed at an early stage, this condition can be successfully managed (although
sometimes not cured) but delayed diagnosis can negatively affect outcome.
Excess accumulation of copper in the liver is a common cause of CH in dogs. Copper accumulation
can occur because of decreased excretion of copper from the liver in the bile, excess dietary intake, or a
combination of these. Excess copper in the liver leads to oxidative damage. Certain breeds are
predisposed to this problem (Bedlington Terrier, Labrador Retriever, Doberman Pinscher, Dalmatian,
and West Highland White Terrier) but dogs of any breed or mixed breed dogs can also be affected.
Certain drugs or toxins may cause liver injury in dogs. However, these typically cause acute disease
and are not common causes of CH. Certain fungal, bacterial, or protozoal infections or parasites may
occasionally cause CH. An infectious cause is more likely for dogs with a subcategory of CH called
granulomatous/pyogranulomatous CH. For some dogs with CH, despite undergoing a thorough
diagnostic evaluation, an underlying cause is not identified. It is likely that for a proportion of these
dogs their immune system is malfunctioning and inappropriately attacking their liver. These patients
may respond to medications that suppress the immune response.

DIAGNOSIS
Dogs can develop a wide range of liver diseases and an accurate diagnosis is needed in order for your
veterinarian to treat your pet’s liver disease most effectively. Common symptoms in dogs with CH
include: decreased appetite, decreased activity, yellow discoloration of the whites of the eyes and gums
(jaundice), abdominal swelling due to fluid accumulation, increased thirst/urination, vomiting, and
diarrhea. Initial diagnostic testing, such as blood and urine tests, are helpful in identifying if there is a
problem with the dog’s liver, but rarely lead to a final diagnosis. Abdominal ultrasound can provide
further information and is useful for detecting structural changes, such as a liver mass or enlargement
of the liver. However, microscopic examination of a liver biopsy specimen is needed to accurately
diagnose CH and to help identify its underlying causes. Liver biopsy may be performed by inserting a
needle through the body wall into the liver with ultrasound guidance, by a traditional open abdominal
surgery, or by key-hole surgery (laparoscopy). Liver biopsy is a relatively safe procedure but it is
associated with a slight risk of bleeding. Because of this your veterinarian may recommend blood tests
to make sure your dog’s blood can clot normally beforehand. It usually takes several days before the
results of microscopic examination of the liver biopsy specimens are available.

TREATMENT
Dogs with CH are often treated with a combination of several different medications. Often these need
to be given at different times in relation to their meals. Therefore, it is important to make sure you that
understand the instructions that are given to you regarding their use. These medications can
occasionally cause side effects. Therefore, it is important that you know what problems to look out for
and that you let your veterinarian know if your pet does exhibit these signs. If your dog is difficult to
give medications to, it can help if you ask your veterinarian to let you know which medications are
most important to give and which are non-essential.

Medications Used to Treat Copper Accumulation in the Liver
If your veterinarian believes that copper is the underlying cause of CH, they will likely prescribe a
copper chelating drug. These drugs help remove copper from the liver by increasing the amount of
copper that is excreted in the urine. A drug called D-penicillamine is the first choice of copper
chelating drug in dogs. It is better absorbed when given between meals. However, as it causes
vomiting, diarrhea, or loss of appetite in about a quarter to a third of dogs, your veterinarian may
suggest giving it with a small amount of food. Sometimes it is necessary to also give a medication that
helps prevent vomiting and nausea or to use a reduced dose of D-penicillamine. In extreme cases this
drug may need to be stopped. Let your veterinarian know if your dog develops any new skin problems
while he/she is receiving D-penicillamine. Most dogs do not require lifelong treatment with these
drugs and typically 6 to 10 months of treatment is enough. Prolonged treatment can lead to copper
deficiency. Therefore, your veterinarian will monitor your dog’s blood liver values during treatment
and may advise a second liver biopsy procedure to allow measurement of your dog’s liver copper
concentration.
Feeding a low copper diet is also essential during this process. There are several commercial low
copper “liver support” diets available and it is important that these are fed exclusively. It may also be
advisable to have the copper content of the water in your house measured.
Once your veterinarian thinks your dog’s liver copper concentration is nearly back to normal,
maintenance treatment with zinc may be started. Zinc supplements can be irritating to the stomach
and may lead to vomiting. Therefore, although zinc is ideally given between meals it may be necessary
to give it with a small amount of food. Sometimes repeated treatment with D-penicillamine is needed.
The low copper diet is usually continued for the rest the dog’s life.

Anti-inflammatory Drugs
In dogs with confirmed CH, where another underlying cause cannot be identified despite complete
diagnostic evaluation, anti-inflammatory drugs may be started on a trial basis. Anti-inflammatory
drugs are also sometimes used as supportive treatment in dogs with a known cause of CH. The
corticosteroid prednisolone is a commonly used anti-inflammatory drug for the treatment of CH in
dogs. This drug can be effective at reducing inflammation but often leads to side effects including
increased appetite, increased thirst, increased urination, panting, loss of muscle, development of a
“pot-belly,” skin changes, and loss of hair. A higher dose is often used initially to control the
inflammation and then the dose is gradually decreased to reduce the severity of these side effects.
These side effects are reversible if it is possible to sufficiently reduce the dose or stop this medication.
However, it is important not to suddenly stop giving prednisolone or other corticosteroids to a dog as
this can lead to an acute corticosteroid deficiency, which could make them very sick. It is also very
important not to withhold water from pets receiving corticosteroids as this can quickly lead to
dehydration or to give non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, such as aspirin, meloxicam (Metacam)
or carprofen (Rimadyl) at the same (this can lead to severe gastric ulcers). Cyclosporine is another
immunosuppressive agent that can help dogs with CH. Cyclosporine is best given at least 1 hour before
or 2 hours after meals. Make sure your veterinarian knows which kind and brand of this drug you are
giving as some are much better absorbed than others. Cyclosporine may cause vomiting or diarrhea in
dogs. If either occurs, your veterinarian may recommend giving this drug with a small amount of food
or freezing the capsule for 30 to 60 minutes before administration. Cyclosporine may also cause your
dog’s gums to get thicker. However, this is usually not a major problem and is usually not a reason to
stop administration. By their very nature these drugs suppress the pet’s immune system to some
degree. Because of this it is prudent to discuss the possible need to modify the dog’s lifestyle to reduce

their exposure to infectious agents with your veterinarian. For example, this may involve your dog no
longer being allowed to swim or wade and reducing contact with dogs outside of your household.

Nutritional Supplements
Nutritional supplements are often used as part of the supportive care provided to dogs with liver
disease. These agents are not classified as drugs and so do not have to undergo the rigorous testing to
prove that they are effective and safe that an approved drug would have to. For many of them the
current evidence to support their use in dogs is somewhat limited. On the other hand they rarely cause
side effects, there are theoretical reasons why they should be beneficial, and for some of them there is
evidence to suggest that they are effective at treating human patients with certain liver diseases.
The liver is very susceptible to oxidative damage, whereby reactive chemicals called oxidants or free
radicals are generated, which subsequently cause damage. Therefore, antioxidants that are believed to
help prevent this process are often used as part of the treatment for liver disease in dogs. Examples of
antioxidants include S-adenosyl methionine (SAMe), silymarin (milk thistle extract), and vitamin E
(alpha-tocopherol). Often these supplements are used in combination because they are believed to
exert their antioxidant effects in different ways. These nutritional supplements are widely available
from a variety of sources but there can be variation in how well different products are absorbed from
the gastrointestinal system. Therefore, where possible, it is recommended that products that have
been shown to be well absorbed in dogs be used. Several products that are marketed for use in dogs
meet this requirement and they are also formulated to make it easy to give the correct dose. Some
contain a mixture of several different hepatoprotective agents, which can mean that you have fewer
pills to give to your dog each day. It is also important that these supplements are given in the correct
way. For example, SAMe is best given at least 1 hour before a meal whereas vitamin E is best given
with food. Therefore, it is very important that you carefully follow the directions given to you by your
veterinarian.
The drug ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol) is a manufactured form of the traditional Chinese remedy
Yutan. This drug may aid the flow of bile and reduce inflammation of the liver. Although clinical trials
to prove that this drug is effective in dogs with CH have not been performed, it is sometimes used as a
supportive treatment and other than occasionally causing diarrhea it seems to be well-tolerated.

OUTLOOK
Left untreated, CH progresses to end-stage liver disease/cirrhosis and eventually leads to euthanasia
or death of the dog. However, if the underlying cause of liver injury can be identified and treated at an
early stage, dogs may have a prolonged survival. In one study, the average survival time of dogs with
CH was 561 days. Dogs diagnosed at a later stage of disease, with signs of liver failure or cirrhosis,
have a worse outlook.
Jonathan Andrew Lidbury (College Station, Texas)

OVERVIEW
This chapter describes histologically-defined chronic forms of feline
cholangitis and chronic hepatic parenchymal diseases. The large
functional reserve of the liver means that chronic progressive
diseases may remain subclinical for life. In those cats that show signs
of chronic hepatopathy, the clinical consequences range from varying
degrees of hepatic insufficiency to collapse or sudden death from
hemoabdomen in cats with hepatic amyloidosis. Chronic hepatic
disease (CHD) may be underdiagnosed in cats because the condition

may be subclinical, limiting diagnostic investigation. If suspected,
results of fine- needle aspirates (FNAs) or biopsy may not be
representative of abnormalities elsewhere in the liver (ch. 85).

LYMPHOCYTIC CHOLANGITIS
DEFINITIONS AND PREVALENCE
The World Small Animal Veterinary Association (WSAVA)
committee responsible for standardizing the diagnosis of canine and
feline liver diseases recognizes three forms of cholangitis in cats:
neutrophilic, lymphocytic, and chronic cholangitis, the latter
associated with liver flukes.1 Lymphocytic cholangitis is a chronic
progressive inflammatory process centered on the biliary tree,
characterized by the infiltration of small lymphocytes into portal
areas with variable portal fibrosis and biliary hyperplasia.1 The true
prevalence of lymphocytic cholangitis is not known but it seems to be
a common clinical diagnosis, accounting for 6.8% and 20% of feline
liver biopsy diagnoses in the UK and New Zealand, respectively.2,3
While not well understood, lymphocytic cholangitis may have an
immune-mediated etiology based on lymphocyte markers and
histological features, e.g., bile duct destruction.4,5 Bacterial infection
has been suggested as a trigger for progressive immune-mediated
hepatic inflammation, although prevailing evidence does not support
a role for infectious agents in most cats.4,6,7

CLINICAL SIGNS, LABORATORY TESTS,
ULTRASONOGRAPHY (US)
A chronic progressive clinical course over months to years is
typical.5,8-10 Cats of any age can be affected. No age, sex, or breed
predisposition has been identified. Owner observations are typically
non-specific and inconsistent: gradual weight loss, polyphagia or
anorexia, vomiting, lethargy, polydipsia and polyuria
(PU/PD).5,8,9,11 Poor body condition is common and, in contrast to

neutrophilic cholangitis, cats with lymphocytic cholangitis are often
bright on physical examination. Jaundice (ch. 28), hepatomegaly, or
ascites may be present (ch. 21).5,8,9,11 Marked hyperglobulinemia
and modest elevations of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and
alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity are frequent findings (chs. 60
and 65).8-12 Ascites typically has a high protein content with
increased globulins, small lymphocytes, non-degenerate neutrophils,
and other inflammatory cells (ch. 71).8-10 Hence, feline infectious
peritonitis (FIP) may be a differential in cats ultimately diagnosed as
having lymphocytic cholangitis (ch. 200). On abdominal US,
ascites, hepatomegaly, and/or lymphadenomegaly may be identified.
Liver echogenicity may be normal, increased, decreased, or
heterogeneous.13 Gallbladder and extra-hepatic biliary tree
abnormalities are uncommon, in contrast to neutrophilic
cholangitis.9 Normal abdominal US does not exclude a diagnosis of
lymphocytic cholangitis.8-10

DIAGNOSIS
Liver biopsy is required for the definitive diagnosis of lymphocytic
cholangitis (ch. 85). The most consistent histologic features include
infiltrating aggregates of small lymphocytes into the portal region,
portal fibrosis, and biliary ductular proliferation (Figure 271.1).14
In some cases, ductopenia occurs secondary to infiltration of the
biliary epithelium or even the lumen by lymphocytes.5,8 Where
lymphocyte infiltration is marked, well-differentiated lymphoma is a
major differential diagnosis. In contrast to lymphoma, the
histopathologic features of lymphocytic cholangitis often include bile
duct targeting, ductopenia, peribiliary fibrosis, portal B-cell
aggregates, portal lipogranulomas, and polyclonal T-cell receptor
rearrangements.15 Controversy remains regarding the classification
of lymphocytic cholangitis, and reports published since the last
WSAVA consensus statement provide additional information on
histopathological heterogeneity, immunophenotyping and

lymphocyte clonality, suggesting that an updated classification may
be required.4,7,16,17

marked chronic lymphocytic cholangitis. There is

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
While the optimal treatment is not defined, immunosuppressive
doses of prednisolone (ch. 144) and/or ursodeoxycholic acid (10-15
mg/kg PO q24h) are commonly used together with supportive care
e.g., therapeutic abdominocentesis.8-11 In one small study,

prednisolone treatment alone (1-2 mg/kg q24h) led to longer
survival times and a greater reduction of hepatic inflammation when
compared to ursodeoxycholic acid treatment alone.11,12 Treatment
with antibiotics is not indicated unless supported by bacterial culture
and sensitivity testing. The prognosis with treatment is good in some
reports, e.g., resolution of ascites and median and mean survival
times of 26 to 36 months. Long-term follow-up from a large number
of cats is needed.8-11

CHRONIC CHOLANGITIS ASSOCIATED
WITH LIVER FLUKES
FLUKES (TREMATODES)
Fluke Families and Their Distribution
Liver flukes from two families can infest the biliary systems of cats,
sometimes causing chronic cholangitis: Dicrocoeliidae
(Platynosomum spp.), and Opisthorchiidae (Opisthorchis spp.,
Clonorchis spp., Metorchis spp. and Amphimerus spp.).
Classification of individual species awaits consensus.1820
Platynosomum spp., in tropical and subtropical regions, may be
found in >80% of free roaming adult cats.18 Opisthorchiidae are
found in as many as 30-50% of free-roaming cats; they are rare in
Northern Europe; they have not been reported in the UK.21 The
Opisthorchiidae family also infests humans via consumption of
undercooked fish. Cats, and other mammals, may act as reservoir
hosts.22
Platynosomum spp. infections are responsible for most liver flukerelated clinical disease in cats. Commonly called “lizard poisoning,”
the flukes occupy the biliary ducts and gallbladder. This can lead to
chronic inflammation and obstruction, although most cases are
subclinical.1,18,19 Disease associated with Opisthorchiidae infestation
is rarely reported and clinically mirrors that of Platynosomum spp.21

Fluke Life Cycles
Trematodes have complex, often incompletely described life cycles
involving 2 to 4 hosts and many larval stages (e.g., redia, cercaria).
The proposed life cycle for Platynosomum spp. (Figure 271.2)
involves18,23:
• First intermediate host: land snails ingest eggs and shed
sporocysts into the environment.
• Second intermediate host: terrestrial isopods (crustaceans)
ingest sporocysts.
• Paratenic host: lizard and amphibian spp. are infected by
eating isopods.
• Definitive host: cats are infested by eating lizards. The flukes
migrate to the liver and eggs are shed in feces.
Opisthorchiidae fluke life cycle involves19:
• First intermediate host: aquatic snails ingest eggs and shed
redia into the environment.
• Second intermediate host: fish of the family Cyprinidae are
infected when cercaria penetrate their epithelium.
• Definitive host: cats are infested by eating raw fish. The flukes
migrate to the liver, and eggs are shed in feces.

CLINICAL SIGNS, LABORATORY TESTS,
IMAGING RESULTS
Clinical signs of liver fluke infestation include jaundice, dehydration,
hepatomegaly, abdominal pain, ascites, inappetence, lethargy,
vomiting, diarrhea and weight loss.21 Disease severity and prognosis
may be dependent on parasite burden, chronicity, and development
of extrahepatic biliary obstruction.24 Laboratory abnormalities may
include: mild nonregenerative anemia, eosinophilia, lymphocytosis,
hyperbilirubinemia, and increased ALT, aspartate aminotransferase
and ALP activities.21,25 Abdominal radiographs and US are often
unremarkable. Non-specific findings may include: distended and

tortuous common bile ducts, periductal hyperechogenicity,
intrahepatic biliary dilation, hyperechoic and thickened gallbladder
wall, gallbladder “sludge,” gallbladder distention, hepatomegaly,
irregular liver margins, hyperechoic and heterogenous hepatic
parenchyma, and diffuse cystic liver changes.24-26

DIAGNOSIS
Fluke eggs can be identified by fecal analysis but eggs are shed
intermittently, some cats have low parasite burdens, and fecal
analysis methods vary (ch. 80).27 Formalin-ether sedimentation
and double centrifugation with Sheather’s sugar flotation solution
are sensitive, but repeated analyses may still be required.27 Bile
obtained by percutaneous US-guided cholecystocentesis is reported
to contain significantly higher fluke egg counts than fecal analysis.25
Histopathological features of chronic cholangitis associated with
liver fluke infestations may include: periductal and portal
inflammatory infiltrates which may extend into the liver parenchyma
(lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells, eosinophils and
neutrophils), dilation and hyperplasia of biliary ducts, periportal and
periductal fibrosis, and hyperplastic adenomatous or ulcerative
cholecystitis.24,25 Adult liver flukes or eggs are not often identified.

TREATMENT (INCLUDING BACTERIAL
INFECTION), PROGNOSIS
Praziquantel is effective for treatment of liver flukes. There is no
consensus regarding dosage and intervals. Dosages used range from
20-40 mg/kg SQ, IM or PO as a single dose, or q24h for 3-5
days.18,24,28,29 Bacterial cholangitis (E. coli) associated with liver
fluke infestation has been reported in feline immunodeficiency virusinfected cats.25 The incidence of clinically significant bacterial
cholecystitis requires further investigation. Liver fluke infestations

have rarely been associated with biliary cystadenoma and
cholangiocarcinoma in cats.30,31

HEPATIC AMYLOIDOSIS
THE SYSTEMIC AMYLOIDOSES AND FELINE
AMYLOIDOSIS
Systemic amyloidoses are a group of clinical syndromes affecting
humans and animals that result from the extracellular deposition of
amyloid in multiple organs. Precursor proteins precipitate as a betapleated sheet forming the core of the amyloid fibril. Clinical signs
vary according to the pattern and extent of tissue dysfunction, but
most systemic amyloidoses manifest as renal dysfunction.
Hepatic amyloidosis is an uncommon systemic amyloidosis that
results in spontaneous hepatic rupture in young cats.32,33 The
amyloid precursor amyloid A is a fragment of the acute-phase
protein, serum amyloid A (SAA). Extracellular deposition of amyloid
occurs predominantly in the liver. The condition causes sudden
death or episodic signs attributed to intra-abdominal hemorrhage.
Involvement of other organs is usually subclinical, although
concurrent chronic kidney disease (CKD) has been described. Cases
can occur as clusters within the same unit or sporadically. Of ∼40
cases reported, >90% involve Siamese and related breeds. Affected
cats are usually <5 years old. Hepatic amyloidosis is considered to be
familial in Siamese-type cats with a complex genetic basis.34 Other
breeds and mixed-breed cats can be affected, and chronic immune
stimulation resulting in acquired amyloidosis has been suggested as
a potential trigger in non-Siamese cats.33

FIGURE 271.2 Proposed life cycle of P. fastosum.
IH, Intermediate host. From Basu AK, Charles RA. A
review of the cat liver fluke Platynosomum
fastosum Kossack, 1910 (Trematoda:
Dicrocoeliidae). Vet Parasitol. 2014;200:1-7.

DIAGNOSIS
Despite the dramatic underlying pathologic changes, hepatic
amyloidosis can be challenging to diagnose in cats that survive
repeated hepatic bleeds because clinical signs, laboratory changes,
and the hemoabdomen can resolve rapidly and completely. Signs are

usually non-specific (anorexia, lethargy, vomiting). On physical
examination, most cats are in good body condition. Signs caused by
hypovolemia and the presence of hypothermia will raise suspicion
for hemorrhage. Anemia, thrombocytopenia, and marked (5- to 10fold) elevations in ALT are seen, but not consistently, and can be
cyclical.35 On US, the liver is diffusely enlarged with a heterogeneous
echotexture and irregular borders, echogenic (“sparkling”) areas and
hypoechoic foci (Figure 271.3).13,33 Differential diagnoses include
vascular neoplasia, peliosis hepatis (a disorder characterized by
multiple, intraparenchymal blood-filled cysts), and telangiectasis. US
findings can be useful in suspecting a diagnosis and to screen cats at
risk for hepatic amyloidosis.
Definitive diagnosis requires cytologic assessment or
histopathologic evaluation of a liver biopsy. Apple-green birefringence on Congo-red-stained sections viewed with polarized
light is pathognomonic for amyloid. The risks associated with biopsy,
particularly hemorrhage, and whether FNA or open liver biopsy is
better, must be evaluated on a case-by-case basis and discussed with
owners.

FIGURE 271.3 Ultrasonographic appearance of
hepatic amyloidosis. This 3-year-old female neutered
Oriental Shorthair cat was referred for investigation
of anemia and suspected hemoabdomen. The liver is
enlarged and markedly heterogeneous due to the
presence of both hyper- and hypoechoic areas of

TREATMENT, PROGNOSIS
The prognosis for cats with hepatic amyloidosis is poor, with survival
of days to weeks; rare cases have survived for months. Supportive
care including cage rest and vitamin K1 supplementation are
indicated. Specific treatments are not available. Colchicine, which
reduces SAA release from hepatocytes and has been used to treat
familial amyloidosis in humans, has been used in cats but its safety
and efficacy are uncertain and it must be used with caution.33,35
Once the diagnosis is established, ethical considerations may limit
the use of blood transfusion.

COPPER STORAGE HEPATOPATHIES

ETIOPATHOGENESIS
Metabolism and homeostasis of copper, an essential dietary trace
element and enzyme cofactor, involve the liver. Dietary copper is
stored in hepatocytes, protein-bound for export, and excreted in bile.
The liver may be the main copper storage site in cats; liver levels
better reflect dietary intake than do blood levels.36 Any process that
causes excess hepatic copper accumulation can, in turn, precipitate
oxidative injury leading to hepatic inflammation, fibrosis, necrosis,
and can progress to cirrhosis. Copper hepatopathies are better
understood in dogs than cats (ch. 270). Hepatic copper
accumulation can be a primary condition, due to inborn errors of
metabolism, or more commonly can occur secondary to other
hepatobiliary diseases, including extrahepatic biliary tract
obstruction and chronic lymphocytic cholangitis.37

PRIMARY COPPER-ASSOCIATED
HEPATOPATHY (PCH)
Incidence and Causes
PCH is reported infrequently in cats.39-42 A presumptive diagnosis is
made on the basis of high hepatic copper concentrations with
centrilobular copper accumulation in the absence of other cholestatic
disorders. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms in feline ATP7B, which
encodes a copper transporting enzyme, have been reported in cats
with PCH.39,43 In humans, familial mutations in ATP7B are a
component of the autosomal recessive disorder Wilson’s disease
where copper accumulates in the liver and other tissues.41

Clinical Features
PCH affects cats <5 years of age with no sex or breed
predispositions.39-43 Clinical signs may progress slowly for more
than a year or cats can develop acute hepatic failure without
antecedent illness.40-42 History may include weight loss, vomiting,
diarrhea, lethargy and poor appetite. Observations on physical

examination may include jaundice, evidence of bleeding, and/or
ascites.37,39,40-42 Acute hemolytic anemia with Heinz body
formation and methemoglobinemia secondary to severe diffuse
hepatic necrosis and systemic copper release has been reported in 1
cat.41 Moderate to marked increases in liver enzyme activities, in
particular ALT, and hyperbilirubinemia are common in cats with
PCH but do not distinguish PCH from other hepatobiliary
disorders.37,39,40,41 Prolonged coagulation times (prothrombin time
and/or activated partial thromboplastin time; ch. 170) have been
documented in some cats with PCH.41 Abdominal US findings are
not specific. In 10 cats with presumed PCH, US identified
microhepatica in 1, hepatic nodules in 4, and coarse hepatic
echotexture in 2.41

Histopathology
Histopathologic findings from cats with PCH include inflammation
and fibrosis with variable degrees of multifocal mixed neutrophilic,
lymphocytic, and histiocytic centrilobular hepatitis; eosinophilic
cytoplasmic granules in zone 3 hepatocytes; and hepatocyte
vacuolation.39,40,41 Masson trichrome staining may identify variable
levels of hepatic fibrosis.41,43 Severe diffuse hepatic necrosis may be
seen in cats with acute hepatic failure.41 Histopathologic evaluation
alone cannot differentiate primary from secondary hepatic copper
accumulation.

Diagnosis
Ideally both copper staining and copper concentrations should be
assessed to diagnose and discriminate primary from secondary
hepatic copper accumulation.44 Liver sections stained for copper
with rhodanine or rubeanic acid can be characterized by the amount
(quantified by a scoring system) and location (centrilobular,
midzonal, periportal, panlobular) of the copper deposition.44 Cats
with PCH typically have higher copper accumulation in the
centrilobular region than in periportal hepatocytes (Figure

271.4),37,41,43 which progresses to a panlobular distribution. In
secondary copper storage hepatopathies, copper accumulates in
periportal hepatocytes adjacent to inflammatory infiltrates, with
minimal accumulation in centrilobular regions.41 Hepatic copper
concentrations can be measured on fresh or deparaffinized liver
biopsy samples using flame atomic absorption spectroscopy.44 Cats
with PCH have higher median hepatic copper concentrations
compared to cats with other hepatic disorders, however there is
overlap between groups.41 In one study, all cats with PCH had
hepatic copper concentrations >700 mcg/g dry matter basis (DMB)
while all cats without hepatobiliary disease and several cats with
non-PCH hepatic disorders had hepatic copper concentrations <190
mcg/g DMB.41

(PCH). Photomicrograph of a section of a liver

dense red-orange staining specific for copper in the

Treatment and Prognosis
Treatments reported for cats with PCH include combinations of
chelation therapy with penicillamine (10-15 mg/kg PO q12h),
elemental zinc (2-4 mg PO q12-24h), and antioxidants (Sadenosylmethionine, silybin or vitamin E).39,41,43 While dietary
modification for hepatic insufficiency and/or a reduced copper diet
may be indicated, dietary copper requirements are unknown (ch.

154).41 Penicillamine-induced hemolytic anemia, which resolved on
discontinuation, was reported in a cat treated for PCH.41 Additional
medical treatments for hepatic insufficiency may be indicated (chs.
266-270). In cats with secondary copper hepatopathy, treatment
should focus on the underlying disease process. Follow up and
survival times for cats treated for PCH are variable. Survival for
several years with reduced clinical signs, hepatic enzyme activities
and histopathological changes are reported.37,39,41,43 Successful
treatment may depend on early diagnosis. The prognosis for cats
with secondary copper hepatopathy is dependent on the underlying
disease process.

VITAMIN A TOXICOSIS
Ingesting excessive quantities of vitamin A (ch. 162) causes new
bone formation, primarily of the cervicothoracic vertebrae (Figure
162.3). This causes pain, restricted movement, and soft tissue
calcification from hypercalcemia.45,46 Vitamin A toxicosis is also
reported to cause hepatic changes in cats, as in other species. Severe
hepatic fibrosis and stellate cell lipidosis are described in a cat with
dietary and radiographic evidence of hypervitaminosis A.47
Experimental supplementation induced similar, but less severe liver
lesions in cats ingesting vitamin A at close to the reported upper safe
limit, suggesting that dietary guidelines may need to be revised.48,49
Whether vitamin A-induced hepatic fibrosis can result in clinical
manifestations has not yet been established (ch. 154).

CHRONIC VIRAL HEPATOPATHIES
Viral infection in people, including hepatitis-B virus (HBV) and
hepatitis-C virus, can cause chronic relapsing hepatitis that can
progress to cirrhosis and/or liver cancer. A hepatitis-B-like virus
infecting cats, domestic cat hepadnavirus (DCH), was discovered in
2018 (ch. 206).50 The potential for DCH to cause chronic hepatitis
and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in cats is under investigation.

Epidemiologic data show that <1% to >18% of cats tested are viremic
for DCH, with retrovirus infection and increased ALT both identified
as risk factors for DCH DNA detection.51 DCH DNA has been
detected by in situ hybridization in chronic hepatitis and HCC
lesions in cats with a distribution similar to that seen in HBVassociated lesions (Figure 271.5). Chronic hepatitis is uncommon
in cats, being reported in 2.4% of all hepatic biopsies.52 HCC is
reported at a frequency of 27% of all feline hepatic neoplasms,52 with
primary hepatic neoplasia estimated to account for 1-2.9% of all
feline cancers.52,53 If DCH does prove to be a feline pathogen, then
strategies developed to combat HBV in humans, including
vaccination, may have reverse-translational potential for cats.
Viruses closely related to hepatitis-C virus, so-called non-primate
hepaciviruses, are reported in an increasing number of species,
including dogs, horses, bats and rats, but not yet in cats. A role for
the canine hepacivirus in canine chronic hepatitis has been
effectively ruled out with neither viral sequences nor exposure
detected in large numbers of cases.54,55 This serves as a reminder
that the pathogenesis of closely-related viruses in different hosts is
difficult to predict.

The main diseases of the canine and feline biliary tracts with
potential for an infectious etiology are neutrophilic cholangitis (NC)
and cholecystitis (CC). Bacterial infections are the most common
infectious etiology for both.1 NC is the most common of the 4
recognized subtypes of cholangitis, occurring commonly in cats and
less commonly in dogs.1-4 This is thought to reflect differences in
their biliary tract anatomy.5 Some cats with immune-mediated

lymphocytic cholangitis (ch. 271) can have secondary bacterial
involvement.

BACTERIA AND THE BILIARY TRACT
HUMANS
The human gallbladder (GB) and bile, once considered sterile in
health, is now understood to have a complex microbiota.6 This
microbiota has homeostatic mechanisms, similar to those in the
gastrointestinal (GI) tract: protective against both pathogen invasion
and aberrant immune responses to commensal organisms.6 The
default setting of the hepatic immune system is one of tolerance,
driven largely by the innate immune system through production of
anti-inflammatory cytokines in response to bacterial proteins.
Secretory IgA and mucus help prevent bacterial adhesion and
colonization with further protection afforded by mechanical
mechanisms, including the flow of bacteriostatic bile and prevention
of reflux by the sphincter of Oddi.5 Disruption of this homeostatic
balance, rather than any one abnormality alone, can result in biliary
colonization and/or inappropriate inflammation. For example, GI
dysbiosis, biliary stasis, altered biliary tract anatomy, and/or
increased biliary pressure all predispose to symptomatic biliary
infection. Biliary inflammation can also result from dysregulated
immune responses to commensal bacteria/bacterial molecules, or
alterations in the microbiome, rather than overt infection.6

DOGS AND CATS
Dogs and cats, while less studied, likely have similar GB and biliary
microbiota. In the absence of disease, bacteria are not typically
identified using standard microbiological culture methods or
cytologic examination of specimens.5 Bacteria most commonly
identified in dogs and cats with biliary tract disease, regardless of the
underlying disorder, are the enteric organisms Escherichia coli,

Enterococcus spp., Bacteroides spp., and Clostridium spp. (ch.
195).5,7

NEUTROPHILIC CHOLANGITIS (NC)
AND CHOLECYSTITIS (CC)
DESCRIPTION
Acute NC in both dogs and cats is characterized by neutrophilic
periportal and intrahepatic bile duct inflammation with neutrophils
in bile duct walls and lumina.1 The distribution and severity of
inflammation vary considerably both within and between cases, with
the inflammatory infiltrate extending into the hepatic parenchyma in
some (cholangiohepatitis). Chronic NC is characterized by a mixed
inflammatory cell population, bile duct proliferation, and varying
degrees of fibrosis.1 Acute CC is also commonly characterized by
neutrophilic inflammation within the wall, epithelium, and lumen of
the GB, which becomes mixed inflammation with chronicity.1 In
acute CC, erosion or ulceration of the mucosa may occur. The less
common severe CC can result in necrosis of the GB wall or
emphysematous CC.1,5,8 Historically, detailed information about the
clinical presentation of dogs and cats with CC or NC has been
limited2-4,9-12; recent case series provide additional information on
NC.3,4,12a Most information regarding CC is from reports of
surgically managed biliary disease.8,13 CC may be identified in cases
of pets with NC2-4 or other GB diseases14 with few case series
specifically focused on the diagnosis of CC.10,15

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
NC is often thought to involve bacterial infection,1 although
hepatobiliary culture and/or eubacterial fluorescence in situ
hybridization (FISH) confirm bacteria in only about 50% of

cases4,12a,16 (69% in a recent case series12b). The predominance of
enteric bacteria in culture/FISH-positive cases supports the theory
that the bacteria either translocate from the portal circulation or
ascend from the GI tract.3,5,7,16 The role of bacteria in culturenegative cases is less clear; false negative results can be due to
antimicrobial therapy or a dysregulated immune response to
bacteria, or bacterial products, without colonization. CC may also
have a bacterial etiology,1 often occurring with cholelithiasis or other
GB diseases, e.g., GB mucocele (ch. 273).5,14 The prevalence of
culture positive cases is not well known, but 80% were positive in 1
surgical case series.16
Cats with NC frequently have concurrent pancreatitis (5090%),12a,17 inflammatory bowel disease (IBD; 40-90%),12a,17 or both
(30-50%).17 This is reported but less well explored in dogs.3,4 Dogs
with NC commonly have CC.2-4 This combination occurs in cats but
has been less frequently reported in that species.10,12a It is not
known which condition predisposes to the other. Situations that
result in cholestasis, disrupt normal biliary anatomy, provide a nidus
for infection (abnormal tissue/choleliths), alter the gut/biliary
microbiota, or alter immune function all have the potential to result
in NC and/or CC.5

CLINICAL SIGNS AND CLINICAL
LABORATORY TESTS: DOGS AND CATS
WITH NC, CC, OR BOTH (Table 272.1)
The most frequent clinical signs in dogs and cats with NC are
anorexia/hyporexia, lethargy and vomiting.2-4,9-12a Weight loss is
more common in cats (50%) than in dogs.2-4,9-12a Fever is reported
in 30-40%,2-4,9-12a icterus in 39% of dogs and 63% of cats,2-4,9-12a
and evidence of abdominal discomfort is seen in 32% of dogs3,4 and
24% of cats.10,12a Clinical laboratory test results can be vague; an

inflammatory leukogram, hyperbilirubinemia, and increased liver
enzyme activities should prompt consideration of NC in either
species (chs. 28, 65, and 266). Absence of these abnormalities does
not exclude NC. Confirmation requires exclusion of other causes.
Dogs and cats with CC in two case series exhibited clinical signs
similar to those described for NC, although many have both
conditions concurrently.2-4,10,12a,15

DIAGNOSIS USING ULTRASOUND (US)
AND CHOLECYSTOCENTESIS (TABLE
272.1)
US examination of the biliary tract for obstruction is valuable.
Increased GB wall thickness (

Video 272.1), irregularity, or

echogenicity are consistent with CC and US-guided percutaneous
cholecystocentesis may be indicated (

Video 272.2). Coagulation

testing before biopsy or aspiration is indicated (chs. 170 and 266).
Submitting bile for both cytology and microbiological culture
(aerobic and anaerobic) increases the chance of identifying bactibilia
(chs. 85 and 86).7,18 The complication rates for cholecystocentesis
range from 2-7% (dogs and cats); the lowest numbers were in reports
with larger case numbers.18-20 One report of cats with hepatobiliary
disease reported higher complication rates but those cats also had
liver and spleen biopsies.21
Complications, usually transient, include mild bile leakage or
hemorrhage. Less common but more worrisome bile peritonitis, GB
rupture, or cardiopulmonary arrest have been reported.20
Complications are more common in pets with biliary mucoceles or
those sampled multiple times due to progressive ongoing disease,
suggesting caution be used in these scenarios. Definitive diagnosis of
NC requires histologic evaluation of tissue, ideally from multiple
sites.1 While histologic evaluation is required for definitive diagnosis
of CC or acute NC, presumptive diagnoses can be based on US

findings and identification of bactibilia where there is no specific
indication for surgical management (e.g., biliary obstruction or
cholelithiasis). Treatment of bactibilia, guided by culture and
sensitivity results, may be sufficient and biopsy may not be needed.

MANAGEMENT
Antimicrobials
Broad spectrum antimicrobial therapy is the primary treatment for
both NC and CC, particularly when bactibilia is confirmed.5
Amoxicillin-clavulanate with or without metronidazole is a good
initial choice. Since antimicrobial resistance is common in biliary
isolates, aerobic and anaerobic culture and sensitivity testing should
be done.2,3,7 Treatment is currently recommended for 6-8 weeks,5
but should be based on response to treatment through monitoring of
US, serum liver enzyme activities and bilirubin (ch. 65). If serum
biochemistry or GB abnormalities persist or worsen despite
administration of appropriate antibiotics, prompt repeat
cholecystocentesis should be recommended to exclude antimicrobial
resistance.2,3

Other Treatments
Supportive care, e.g., IV fluids and alimentation (chs. 81 and 120)
should be dictated by clinical needs. Good theoretical arguments are
made for giving ursodeoxycholic acid (choleretic and
immunomodulating agent) and antioxidant agents (vitamin E, Sadenosylmethionine and silybin)5; however, no data confirm their
providing benefit. Cholecystectomy is indicated for cholelithiasis and
should be considered with severe or progressive GB changes.2,5
Management of underlying conditions such as pancreatitis (chs.
277, 278) and IBD (ch. 262) is extremely important.

Treating When Bactibilia Is Not Confirmed
Without confirmed bactibilia, management strategies for chronic NC
are not clear. Assessing response to antimicrobial therapy is prudent

initially, with ursodeoxycholic acid and antioxidants theoretically
indicated. Corticosteroids have been suggested in cats with refractory
disease, based on the theory that biliary inflammation reflects
ongoing, up-regulated immune responses to bacteria/bacterial
proteins. However, clinical trials are lacking. Less is known about
chronic NC in dogs, although it is likely to be similar.

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis for NC and uncomplicated CC is good with reported
survival times of several years in cats and dogs that are discharged
from hospital.2-4,9-12a The condition most commonly linked with
poor outcomes is biliary tract rupture and resultant bile peritonitis
which can occur with severe CC or GB diseases such as mucoceles or
cholelithiasis.3,4,8,13 Some chronic NC cases may prove refractory to
treatment with data in dogs and cats suggesting cholecystectomy is
linked to improved survival times.4,12a

UNCOMMON BILIARY TRACT
CONDITIONS AND ORGANISMS
Uncommonly, Toxoplasma gondii (chs. 196, 197) has been
diagnosed in immunosuppressed cats with CC.24 Helicobacter
pylori-specific DNA fragments have been detected by PCR analysis
of bile from cats with lymphocytic cholangitis; however, there is
currently insufficient information to determine if the organisms are
pathogenic in this setting.25 Feline liver fluke infections are
discussed in ch. 271.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Infectious Biliary Tract and Gallbladder Disease
The biliary tract refers to the parts of the liver involved in the
production, transport and delivery of bile (an important digestive
juice) to the gut. The gallbladder is a tear-shaped sac associated with
the liver and responsible for storing bile before it is released. Bile is
important for the breakdown and digestion of fats in the upper part
of the intestine and is released each time an animal eats by
contraction of the gallbladder. Infectious diseases affecting the
biliary tract and gallbladder are typically caused by bacteria and
result in inflammation of these structures and obstruction of the flow
of bile. Cholangitis is the term used for inflammation of bile ducts, or
the tubes through which bile flows, whereas cholecystitis refers to
inflammation of the gallbladder. These conditions can make some
animals become very unwell quite quickly and require rapid
veterinary attention, although there is a wide spectrum of possible
severities.

SYMPTOMS
The most common symptoms of these conditions are a reduction in
appetite, lethargy and vomiting, possibly diarrhea. Weight loss is also
a common sign in cats. However, the overall severity can vary widely
with some animals becoming dull and listless, others just showing
more mild, waxing and waning signs. If there is blockage to bile flow
the animal may become jaundiced (yellow in color), with this most
apparent on examination of the whites of the eyes, skin or the ears.
You may also note a darkening of the urine color even before the skin
changes. In addition, your veterinarian may note your pet to have a
fever or seem painful on examination of its belly.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTS
After thoroughly examining your pet, your veterinarian is likely to
want to run blood tests and perform an ultrasound. The blood tests
are likely to show elevations in the markers of liver disease and will
allow confirmation of the severity of the jaundice (if present). They
may also identify a high white cell count and changes suggesting
there is a biliary infection. Liver ultrasound is extremely useful for
evaluating the biliary tract and will help your veterinarian to look for
the likely cause of the blocked bile flow if there is jaundice. They will
also look at the appearance of the liver and gallbladder to assess for
clues that your pet has cholangitis (bile duct inflammation) or
cholecystitis (gallbladder inflammation) or both. They will also look
for the presence of other biliary abnormalities such as gall stones,
mucus accumulation in the gallbladder (mucocele) or bile leakage
that might indicate your pet requires surgery to manage their
condition. Inflammation of the pancreas (another organ involved in
food digestion), or pancreatitis can occur in combination with biliary
tract disease, so a thorough examination of the pancreas will also be
performed along with evaluation of the gut for any abnormalities.
The next steps in the diagnostic process are highly dependent on
what has been found on the ultrasound and to a lesser extent the
bloods. If there are concerning features on the ultrasound, your
veterinarian may want to perform surgery to investigate further and
obtain a liver biopsy, bile sample and maybe remove the gallbladder.
If they are less concerned, they may recommend obtaining a liver
biopsy and bile sample which can be performed using ultrasound

guidance, keyhole surgery with a laparoscope (camera) or surgically;
they will discuss the relative merits of each with you in order to make
a decision. If the suspicion is solely bacterial infection of the bile,
cholecystitis, sampling of bile using ultrasound guidance may be the
only test recommended. The aim with all of these tests is to make a
clear diagnosis to guide specific treatment. The risks are small but
there is a small risk of complications including bile leakage which the
veterinarian will explain to you before any procedure.

TREATMENT
The main treatment for both cholangitis and mild-moderate
cholecystitis is treatment of the bacterial infection thought to cause
them. The most appropriate antibiotics to choose are best selected
based on culture results from the bile sample as certain bacteria
respond better to particular antibiotics and some strains may show
antibiotic resistance. Medication to manage nausea and pain and
improve bile flow may also be required. Specific management of any
concurrent illnesses such as pancreatitis or gut disease may also be
required.
If there are any signs that there may be more severe cholecystitis,
gall stones or a blockage of bile flow, then surgery is likely to be the
most appropriate course of action. Removal of the gallbladder is
often the best option and animals can live normal lives following this
procedure. Any situation where there may be a risk of biliary tract or
gallbladder leakage or rupture is a cause for significant concern. This
is an emergency requiring rapid surgery and can be life-threatening,
typically necessitating intensive case hospitalization after the
surgery. However, animals that do well during the initial few days
and in which the underlying cause has been managed (for example
gall stones) can do extremely well long-term. After surgery, animals
are likely to require antibiotics, medication to manage pain and
nausea along with drugs to improve bile flow.

WHAT TO WATCH FOR AT HOME
Your veterinarian will give you specific instructions based on the
management that has been selected for your pet, however important
things to watch for are any sudden deterioration in your pet’s general
demeanor, any signs they may be uncomfortable in their belly or the

persistence of vomiting. It is always better to seek advice if you are at
all concerned.
Emma J. O’Neill (Dublin, Ireland)

INTRODUCTION
The hepatobiliary system is composed of a complex network of
“channels” essential for the transportation and formation of bile
containing components needed for fat digestion and absorption as
well as elimination of catabolized compounds. Derangements in this
system can have life-threatening sequelae. This chapter will focus on

clinically relevant non-infectious biliary tract and gallbladder
diseases: gallbladder mucocele (GBM), cholelithiasis, biliary
neoplasia, gallbladder agenesis, and destructive cholangitis.

GALLBLADDER MUCOCELES
CHARACTERIZATION AND
ETIOPATHOGENESIS
GBMs are characterized grossly by their accumulation of thick,
inspissated, immobile mucus, and bile (Figure 273.1).
Histologically, such gallbladders display proliferated mucosa with
fronds that project into the lumen as well as multifocal mucus-filled
cysts.1 GBM was considered rare, but over the past 2 decades it has
become the most common extrahepatic biliary disease in dogs. The
emergence of GBM could be related to the evolution of triggers
(parasiticides or high-fat commercial dog foods) that are directly or
indirectly involved with its pathogenesis.

FIGURE 273.1 Macroscopic images of gallbladder
mucoceles. A, Cross-section of gallbladder with
lumen filled by a firm, concentrically layered mass of
rubbery to gelatinous content that transitions from
tan (peripherally) to dark green (centrally) material.
B, Diffusely enlarged gallbladder with lumen filled
with layered tan to green/black gelatinous
material. Images courtesy Jason D. Struthers DVM,
MVetSc, DACVP, Midwestern University College of
Veterinary Medicine.
GBM typically affects older dogs (median 10 years) but has been
diagnosed in dogs 1.5-17 years of age without sex predisposition.2-9
There is a predilection for purebred dogs with Shetland Sheepdog,
Cocker Spaniel, Miniature Schnauzer, Border Terrier, Pomeranian,
and Beagle being most common.6,8,10 GBMs are extremely rare in
cats with only a few cases reported, possibly due to cats having fewer
mucous glands in their gallbladder.11-13 The specific etiology for
GBM formation is unclear. Affected dogs have a high incidence of
concurrent endocrinopathies (chs. 285, 293) and hyperlipidemia
(ch. 156).8,14 These observations regarding GBMs plus age and
breed predilections implicate a multifactorial process that includes
genetic, metabolic, and environmental contributions. GBMs are
associated with an acquired well-differentiated mucin hypersecretory
phenotype, increased gel-forming mucin content, altered mucin
profile, and abnormal unpacking of mucin granules.5 While reasons
for the observed phenotypic transformation remain a mystery,
proposed theories are related to gallbladder motility, bile fraction

composition, or an interplay between the two (Box 273.1).
Hydrophobic bile acids stimulate mucin secretion, induce cytotoxic
effects, and inhibit smooth muscle contraction of the gallbladder in
dogs.15,16 Gallbladder hypomotility causes supersaturation of bile
constituents which could incite a cycle of mucin hypersecretion,
epithelial cytotoxicity, and hypomotility. Hyperlipidemia,
endocrinopathies, hyperleptinemia, and decreased serum vitamin D
concentrations have been proposed to directly or indirectly
contribute to GBM formation.17-20 A potential link between
imidacloprid administration and GBM formation in Shetland
Sheepdogs has been suggested (Box 273.1).21

PRESENTATION AND CLINICAL SIGNS
Dogs with a GBM can have no obvious clinical signs or signs that
range from mild-to-severe illness and death. Some dogs have
intermittent biliary tract signs (e.g., vomiting, lethargy, diarrhea,
decreased appetite, evidence of a painful abdomen, and jaundice) for
months to years, but most have an acute onset (∼4 days).8 Chronic,
intermittent, transient biliary tract signs, which do not commonly
include jaundice, could be related to biliary colic, chronic
cholecystitis, or cholangitis/cholangiohepatitis (ch. 272). Acute
signs can be the result of partial or complete extrahepatic bile duct
obstruction (EHBDO), cholecystitis, gallbladder mural thrombosis
and necrosis, or cholangitis. A common misconception is that
emergent clinical signs in dogs with GBM are solely the result of
EHBDO, but a recent study failed to identify EHBDO via computed
tomography (CT) scans, cholangiography, nor visualized
intraoperatively in any dog requiring surgical intervention. Thus,
other causes for acute emergent GBM disease in dogs should be
considered.22
