Cholecystitis

DIAGNOSIS
GBMs, typically, are readily diagnosed with abdominal
ultrasonography (US) (Video 273.1

). A classification scheme has

evolved over the past 20 years. Classically, GBMs were described as
having a “kiwi-fruit” appearance with gravity-independent
hyperechoic material and a hypoechoic rim sign. Six types of GBMs
are now described based on their US appearance (Figure 273.2).4,17
There is a lack of long-term longitudinal studies to show if echogenic

sludge progresses to form a GBM or if developmentally immature
GBM types (e.g., lower GBM types, I-III) evolve to more advanced
and mature GBM types (e.g., higher GBM types, IV-VI). However, it
is clear that lower GBM types can be just as clinically significant as
higher types.4,9,17 Gallbladder rupture occurs in about 20% of dogs
with clinical signs due to GBM, a negative prognostic indicator. Dogs
with GBM should be managed surgically before rupture can
occur.3,4,6,9 Conventional US has a record of poor sensitivity and
moderate-to-good specificity in identifying gallbladder
rupture.4,6,9,23 Contrast-enhanced US has a reported 100%
sensitivity and specificity in detecting gallbladder wall rupture in
dogs but this tool is not widely available in veterinary medicine.23 CT
scans are superior to US in identifying gallbladder perforation in
people but this has not been investigated in dogs. When imaging
results are inconclusive, cytologic evaluation of peritoneal fluid
and/or bilirubin or bile acid concentrations can be useful for
diagnosing biliary rupture (ch. 71).

FIGURE 273.2 Ultrasonographic images of the six
gallbladder mucocele types. A, Type I: organized,
gravity independent, echogenic debris comprising
>30% of the gallbladder lumen. B, Type II:
combination of organized echogenic debris with
partial stellate strands adhered to the gallbladder
wall. C, Type III: stellate pattern. D, Type IV:
combination of stellate and kiwi pattern. E, Type V:
kiwi pattern with echogenic debris. F, Type VI:

classic kiwi pattern. Images courtesy Eric T. Hostnik,
DVM, MS, DACVR, Ohio State University College of
Veterinary Medicine.

TREATMENT
Surgery
Dogs can be treated medically or surgically. Cholecystectomy is
recommended in dogs that have had biliary tract signs (e.g.,
vomiting, lethargy, diarrhea, decreased appetite, painful abdomen,
jaundice) as well as in those that have moderate-to-severe
clinicopathologic derangements (e.g., total bilirubin, cholesterol,
liver enzyme activities) (chs. 28, 63, 65), or if there is suspicion of
EHBDO or gallbladder wall necrosis. Delaying surgery has potential
to result in life-threatening complications such as biliary tract
rupture, bile peritonitis, sepsis, multiple organ dysfunction
syndrome, and death. A recent study demonstrated that dogs with
mild clinical signs could have a good outcome if treated medically.10

Medical Therapy
Dogs with mild clinical signs should be fed low-fat diets (ch. 154)
and can be treated with choleretics, e.g., ursodeoxycholic acid
(UDCA) and S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe). The choleretic effects of
SAMe are based upon glutathione (GSH)-mediated bile salt
independent canalicular bile formation.24 Since bile stasis
predisposes to infection, consideration can be given to broadspectrum antimicrobials, although routine antibiotic administration
is not indicated without reasonable suspicion of infection (ch. 7).
About 16% of dogs with GBM that had ≥1 sample submitted for
bacterial culture had positive results.3,5-7,9,10,25-27 However, this is
likely an underestimation as the majority of dogs with GBM are given
antibiotics prior to obtaining samples for culture.6

Subclinical GBM

Treatment recommendations for subclinical dogs is less clear,
especially with respect to recommending cholecystectomy. There are
no published data indicating the likelihood of a dog without signs
eventually developing acute disease that requires emergent surgery.
There is also a lack of evidence that medical therapy alters disease
progression. It is recommended that subclinically affected dogs be
treated with UDCA, SAMe, a low-fat diet, and be screened for
concurrent endocrinopathies. Rigorous management of concurrent
endocrinopathies could slow progression or occasionally aid in
complete resolution of GBM. A single report of two dogs with GBM
and hypothyroidism highlights the possibility of complete GBM
resolution with medical therapy.28 Prophylactic cholecystectomy is
recommended if the GBM fails to resolve within 2-4 months of
medical therapy and adequate control of concurrent
endocrinopathies. If prophylactic cholecystectomy is not pursued,
then serial US examinations should be performed every 3-6 months
to monitor disease progression.

PROGNOSIS
Generally, dogs with GBM undergoing cholecystectomy have a good
prognosis if they survive the immediate postoperative period. Inhospital mortality rates in dogs with GBM (clinical or subclinical at
the time of cholecystectomy) are approximately 20% and <5%,
respectively.3,6-8,17 Negative prognostic indicators for survival in
dogs with GBM that undergo cholecystectomy include higher US
GBM type, increased alkaline phosphatase activities, postoperative
hypotension, increasing postoperative serum lactate concentrations,
owner recognition of jaundice, concurrent hyperadrenocorticism,
Pomeranian breed, increasing age, increasing bilirubin
concentrations, and the presence of clinical signs or gallbladder
rupture.3,6-9

CHOLELITHIASIS

PREVALENCE, CHARACTERIZATION AND
ETIOPATHOGENESIS
The prevalence of cholelithiasis in dogs is low, estimated at 0.9713%.29,30 Prevalence studies have not been reported in cats but are
likely similar. Choleliths are most commonly identified in the
gallbladder or common bile duct (CBD), but are occasionally
diagnosed within the liver.29,31 Dogs and cats with cholelithiasis can
be of any age but tend to be >9 years with no sex or breed
predilections.29,31,32 The majority of choleliths in dogs and cats are
“pigment stones,” in contrast to cholesterol based choleliths in
humans.30,32,33 Pigment stones are predominantly composed of
calcium bilirubinate with variable amounts of carbonate calcium salt,
phosphate, and free-fatty acids. The pathogenesis of cholelith
formation in dogs and cats is not known and proposed mechanisms
have either been extrapolated from human medicine or based on
results from experimental dog studies, that collectively, included
gallbladder hypomotility, inflammation, infection, mucus
hypersecretion, and altered composition of bile.30,32,34-36

PRESENTATION AND CLINICAL SIGNS
Most dogs and cats are subclinically affected when diagnosed with a
cholelith. These are usually an incidental finding during an
abdominal US screening for an unrelated condition.29,31 The
presence and severity of clinical signs are related to complications
that can manifest as a result of cholelithiasis such as EHBDO, biliary
rupture, bile peritonitis, cholecystitis, and cholangitis.29,32,37,38 Cats
can develop pancreatitis with choledocholithiasis due to their unique
common pancreaticobiliary duct. Choledocholiths can become
lodged at the sphincter of Oddi, inciting pancreatitis. This
phenomenon has been recognized clinically but is poorly
documented in cats. Biliary tract signs are generally nonspecific and
include vomiting, decreased appetite, lethargy, diarrhea, evidence of
a painful abdomen, and jaundice. Biliary colic is a disorder in
humans characterized by episodic pain that results from increases in

intraluminal gallbladder pressure following contraction against a
transient cystic duct obstruction (e.g., sludge or choleliths). Biliary
colic likely occurs in dogs and cats but the subtle, nonspecific, and
episodic clinical signs could easily be overlooked.

DIAGNOSIS
Choleliths are usually diagnosed with abdominal US.29,31,33
Choleliths exhibit distal acoustic shadowing on US that becomes
more pronounced as size and calcium content increase. Extrahepatic
choleliths can be more difficult to identify with US in the absence of
concurrent bile duct dilation because of interference from bowel
gas.39 Intrahepatic choleliths appear as multiple discrete
hyperechoic foci, which are accompanied by varying amounts of
distal acoustic shadowing.29,31 Intrahepatic bile duct wall
mineralization is recognized in some dogs but appears to be a
separate entity to cholelithiasis: branching mineral opacities in the
intrahepatic bile ducts are most commonly found in Cavalier King
Charles Spaniels and appear to be of no clinical significance,
although some have concurrent intrahepatic choleliths.40
Radiography is not recommended as a first-line imaging choice to
diagnose choleliths because of poor sensitivity (50-59%).29,33
Choleliths may not be visible on radiography because of small size,
limited calcium content, or interference caused by content in the
gastrointestinal tract.

TREATMENT
Surgery
Surgical intervention is recommended when there are clinical signs
and clinicopathologic abnormalities related to complications of
cholelithiasis, e.g., partial or complete EHBDO, biliary rupture, or
cholecystitis.29,32 Cholecystectomy is recommended for both
cholecystolithiasis and choledocholithiasis in dogs or cats with a
patent CBD.37,41 Cholecystotomy to remove choleliths is avoided

because of risk for recurrence as well as unabated short- and longterm complications (e.g., cholecystitis, biliary rupture).41 Biliaryenteric diversion procedures may be required when patency of the
CBD cannot be established.

Medical Therapies
Medical therapies in conjunction with surgery are dictated by the
severity of illness and comorbid disorders but typically include
intravenous fluids (ch. 120) supplemented with electrolytes,
antimicrobials, analgesics, antiemetics, UDCA, and SAMe.
Antimicrobial therapy should be based on culture and sensitivity
results; however, effective empiric antimicrobial options include
potentiated amoxicillin followed by combination of a
fluoroquinolone and metronidazole if refractory. Medical therapy
alone is an option in cases with cholecystolithiasis and mild-tomoderate clinical signs in which surgery is not an option. Pigment
stones are unlikely to be dissolved with medical management,
although one case report did demonstrate successful resolution of a
cholelith.42 Treatment of subclinical cases should also be aimed at
correcting suspected contributory disorders associated with
gallbladder hypomotility and bile acid hydrophobicity that may
mitigate risk of additional cholelith formation or complications (see
Subclinical GBM).

PROGNOSIS
Survival data for dogs and cats undergoing surgery for cholelithiasisassociated complications are limited. Generally, pets surviving the 7day postoperative period have a good long-term prognosis.29,33,43
There is even less information regarding outcomes in pets that
required choledochotomy, cholecystoenterostomy, or primary repair
of the CBD. Results of a case series suggest that outcomes may not be
as poor as once thought.29,32,37,44 Long-term outcome in pets with
no signs and an incidental diagnosis is unclear. A cohort study in
humans found that 20% develop complications related to
cholelithiasis in a 20-year follow-up.45 Results from 2 recent studies

with relatively short follow-up periods suggest that the likelihood of
eventual complications could be low in dogs and cats that were
subclinical at diagnosis.29,31

BILIARY NEOPLASIA
PREVALENCE, CHARACTERIZATION AND
ETIOPATHOGENESIS
Primary hepatobiliary neoplasia is uncommon in dogs and cats,
representing <2.0% of all cancer types (ch. 275).46,47 Most dogs and
cats with biliary neoplasms are older (>10 years).46-50 Intrahepatic
malignant cholangiocarcinomas predominate in dogs.47,48 One
retrospective survey found that 94% (61/65) of dogs with
intrahepatic biliary neoplasia had intrahepatic
cholangiocarcinoma.48 Extrahepatic neoplasms in dogs occur much
less frequently, with the gallbladder most commonly diagnosed with
neuroendocrine tumors (i.e., carcinoids) and, less frequently,
carcinomas.1,48,51 A predilection for Labrador Retrievers and female
dogs has been proposed.48 Brachycephalic breeds, specifically
Boston Terriers, were overrepresented in a series of dogs with
gallbladder neuroendocrine tumors.50 Cats have a relatively equal
distribution of intrahepatic and extrahepatic tumors; however, a
slight extrahepatic predominance may exist.46,49 In contrast to dogs,
bile duct adenomas (also named biliary cystadenomas due to their
cystic appearance) are common in cats, accounting for >50% of all
feline hepatobiliary tumors.46,49 No sex predilection has been
established for cats. Biliary trematode infection is a known risk
factor for cholangiocarcinoma in humans and a potential link has
been proposed in dogs and cats, but evidence demonstrating
causation is lacking.

PRESENTATION AND CLINICAL SIGNS

Dogs and cats with clinical signs due to biliary neoplasia are more
likely to have malignant lesions. Biliary tract signs are often vague
and nonspecific: vomiting, decreased appetite, lethargy, weight loss,
diarrhea, jaundice, and/or peritoneal effusion. Acholic feces can
occur with complete EHBDO. Bile duct adenomas in cats usually do
not manifest with clinical signs until they reach a large size and
compress adjacent organs.51

DIAGNOSIS
Radiographs, US, and CT imaging can be used to facilitate diagnosis,
staging, and potential surgical planning of biliary tumors. Thoracic
radiographs are suitable for staging; however, US or triphasic
(arterial, venous, and delayed contrast phases) CT of the abdomen
are recommended. Radiology lacks the sensitivity and specificity for
identifying lesions in the biliary system. The distribution of bile duct
adenomas in dogs can be single (i.e., massive) or multifocal lesions
limited to 1-2 lobes.52 Cholangiocarcinomas in dogs can be single
(37-46%), multifocal (up to 54%), or diffuse (17-54%), with or
without metastases.52 There is a relatively equal distribution
between single and multiple lesions in cats with bile duct
adenomas.52 Diffuse intraperitoneal metastasis and carcinomatosis
occurs in about 70% of cats with bile duct carcinomas.46,49
Inspissated mucus/bile and GBM can be adhered to the gallbladder
wall and appear similar to a neoplastic mass. Color-flow Doppler
analysis can be used to detect blood flow within any suspicious
structure. US-guided fine needle aspiration and cytologic
examination of biliary neoplasms has a fair-to-good specificity and
positive predictive value; however, cytology alone cannot be relied
upon to exclude the potential for neoplasia (ch. 85).53 Moreover, it
is difficult to differentiate metastatic adenocarcinoma from primary
bile duct carcinoma. Histology is the gold standard criterion for a
diagnosis of biliary neoplasia.

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS

Curative-intent surgery is indicated in dogs or cats with focal biliary
tract neoplasms. The type of surgical procedure depends on tumor
type and location. Liver lobectomy for bile duct adenoma has a good
prognosis. Cholangiocarcinomas are biologically aggressive and
associated with high rates of regional and distant metastasis in dogs
(88%) and cats (80%), precluding surgery.52 Surgical intervention
for CBD neoplasms resulting in an EHBDO are associated with high
perioperative mortality and a grave long-term prognosis. Dogs with
neuroendocrine tumors or carcinomas of the gallbladder can have
good survival after cholecystectomy. The median survival time of
dogs after cholecystectomy for gallbladder neuroendocrine tumors,
including those with metastasis, was 1358 days (range, 432-1834
days).50

GALLBLADDER AGENESIS
PREVALENCE, CHARACTERIZATION AND
ETIOPATHOGENESIS
Gallbladder agenesis is a rare congenital disorder in dogs that has
not been reported in cats. Aberrations in embryological development
result in development failure of the pars cystica and agenesis of the
gallbladder and cystic duct, with or without other hepatobiliary
anatomical anomalies. Most dogs with gallbladder agenesis have ≥1
developmental biliary disorder, e.g., ductal plate malformations
(DPMs) and hypoplasia of liver lobes (ch. 268).54,55 Cause for the
malformation in dogs and humans is unknown. Gallbladder agenesis
is most commonly reported in small breed dogs with Chihuahuas
overrepresented.54,56-59 Most dogs are young at the time of
diagnosis (2 years; range: 0.7-7.4 years) and there is a female
predominance.54,56-59

PRESENTATION AND CLINICAL SIGNS
Approximately 50% of dogs with gallbladder agenesis are
subclinically diagnosed.54,56-59 When present, clinical signs include

vomiting, anorexia, ascites, lethargy, diarrhea, and seizures.54,56-59
Most dogs with gallbladder agenesis had histologic evidence of DPM
(ch. 268), which can manifest with gastrointestinal signs, ascites,
and seizures (ch. 268).54,55 Symptoms in humans with gallbladder
agenesis alone are uncommon. Signs are usually associated with
choledocholithiasis, ascending cholangitis, or biliary dyskinesia.

DIAGNOSIS
Diagnosis in dogs is generally made when the gallbladder is not
visualized on abdominal US, but this is not pathognomonic. The
gallbladder can be difficult to identify in pets with contracted
gallbladders due to chronic cholecystitis. Many cases of gallbladder
agenesis in humans are diagnosed intraoperatively after an
erroneous preoperative US diagnosis of cholecystitis or gallbladder
rupture. Confirming a diagnosis is recommended in humans using
endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, hepatobiliary
scintigraphy, cholangiography, CT, or magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) cholangiography. Abdominal CT with and without
cholangiography has been used in dogs to confirm gallbladder
agenesis.54,58

TREATMENT
There are no specific treatment guidelines for dogs or humans.
Treatment recommendations in asymptomatic humans with
gallbladder agenesis alone consist of avoiding high-fat foods.
Management of humans with symptoms is conservative (e.g.,
antibiotics, smooth muscle relaxants, non-steroidal antiinflammatories) unless obstructive choledocholithiasis is identified.
Empiric therapy with UDCA, SAMe, and diet modification (low-fat)
has been used in dogs; however, evidence supporting this regimen is
lacking.54 Additional, more targeted therapies are indicated for dogs
with liver dysfunction and complications of portal hypertension that
can occur secondary to concurrent DPM (ch. 268).54 Dogs with
gallbladder agenesis alone should have a normal life-span; however,

the presence of concurrent congenital diseases like DPM could affect
prognosis. The gallbladder is not a required organ as its primary
function of interprandial bile storage can be supplanted by storage in
the CBD and hepatic ducts.

DESTRUCTIVE CHOLANGITIS
PREVALENCE, CHARACTERIZATION AND
ETIOPATHOGENESIS
Destructive cholangitis is rare in companion animals and
characterized by destruction and loss of the bile ducts in the portal
region with inflammation and eventual fibrosis.60 In humans, this
disorder comprises several conditions with atypical features that can
be a component of congenital DPM or as an acquired disorder that is
characterized by destruction and loss of interlobular bile ducts in
≥50% of small portal tracts.61 Only 9 cases in dogs have been
reported in the last 20 years.62-64 This disease has been recognized
in cats clinically, but has not yet been reported. The specific
pathogenesis in dogs is unknown and often idiopathic; however,
postulated causal mechanisms include idiosyncratic drug reactions
(e.g., sulphonamides, amoxicillin-clavulanate), viral infections, and
immune-mediated.62-64 Causal mechanisms in humans include
immunologic disorders (small-duct primary sclerosing cholangitis,
primary biliary cholangitis, graft-versus-host disease), viral
infections (hepatitis C virus, hepatitis B virus, and Epstein-Barr
virus), neoplasia (Hodgkin lymphoma, histiocytosis X), and druginduced.

PRESENTATION, CLINICAL SIGNS,
DIAGNOSIS, TREATMENT, PROGNOSIS
Clinical signs generally consist of vomiting, lethargy, weight loss,
diarrhea, decreased appetite, and jaundice. Destructive cholangitis is
the only known cause of intrahepatic cholestasis in companion

animals that can result in acholic feces.60 The length of time clinical
signs are observed by the owner before diagnosis varies from daysto-months owing to the heterogeneity of diseases that can cause
destructive cholangitis. Abdominal imaging results are often
nonspecific or unremarkable because injury is directed at small bile
ducts.63,64 Histopathologic examination of liver tissue obtained from
multiple lobes is required for a diagnosis. Specific treatment options
have not been established outside of discontinuing all possible causal
drugs. In humans, therapy commonly includes supportive care to
mitigate clinical signs, high-dose UDCA, and immunosuppression.
This strategy was used in a single case report of a dog with success.64
Humans either endure progressive, irreversible bile duct loss leading
to biliary cirrhosis or biliary epithelial regeneration and clinical
recovery over months to years. Prognosis in dogs cannot be
ascertained from limited reports, but recovery is possible.64

CLIENT INFORMATION
Non-infectious Biliary Tract and Gallbladder
Disease
There is a wide array of diseases specific to the bile duct system in
dogs and cats. Some of these disorders are associated with obvious
clinical signs and others remain clinically silent (i.e., asymptomatic).
Clinical signs that can be seen with biliary tract disease include
vomiting, diarrhea, decreased to absent appetite, weight loss,
lethargy, as well as distended and/or painful abdomen. If your pet
demonstrates these signs they should be evaluated by a veterinarian.
Two clinical signs that should prompt emergent evaluation by a
veterinarian include jaundice and acholic feces. Jaundice is a yellow
discoloration of tissue most commonly appreciated in the sclera of
the eye, ear tips, and mucous membranes in the mouth (e.g., gums or
tongue) or prepuce/vulva. Acholic feces looks like very pale beige or
cream colored feces that lacks normal pigment because of a complete
obstruction of the biliary system.
One of the most common biliary disorders in dogs is gallbladder
mucoceles. This condition is characterized by excessive mucus

secretion that can become rock-hard and cause inflammation in the
gallbladder, rupture, or obstruct the bile ducts. It usually occurs in
older-aged (>10 years) and purebred dogs like Shetland Sheepdogs,
Cocker Spaniels, Miniature Schnauzers, Border Terriers,
Pomeranians, and Beagles, but can happen in dogs of any age or
breed. Dogs can be asymptomatic or sick and can experience lifethreatening complications that require emergent surgery to remove
the gallbladder. If your dog is asymptomatic and has a gallbladder
mucocele then medical therapies can be instituted to try and dissolve
it, but ultimately, prophylactic removal of the gallbladder could be
recommended if medications do not work. Gallstones occur
uncommonly in dogs and cats. They usually do not cause clinical
signs unless they result in a complication like inflammation of the
gallbladder (cholecystitis) or an obstruction of the biliary system.
Both of these complications can make pets very sick and surgery is
typically needed. Gallstones in pets cannot be dissolved with
medication. The likelihood of eventual complications in
asymptomatic pets is not known. Therapy is aimed at managing
potential underlying triggers for stone formation. Cancer of the
biliary system in pets is uncommon, representing <2% of all cancer
types in dogs and cats. Some biliary tract cancers can make pets very
sick while others remain asymptomatic. Similarly, some biliary
cancers can be treated with surgery while others cannot. Your
veterinarian will guide you in appropriate recommendations.
Gallbladder agenesis is a condition only identified in dogs that
represents a congenital abnormality that results in the absence of a
gallbladder. Fortunately, pets do not need a gallbladder to have a
normal life and so, clinical signs occur, but are uncommon. Some
dogs can be born with more than one congenital disorder in the
biliary system, and those other disorders could cause clinical signs
and affect long-term prognosis. Typically, dogs with gallbladder
agenesis alone can live a normal life. The benefit of medical therapy
in these dogs has not been clearly established. Destructive
cholangitis is a very rare inflammatory disorder of the tiny bile ducts
inside the liver. It may be caused by drug reactions or viral
infections, but many times a known cause is not identified.
Treatment and long-term prognosis have not been established in
pets. Your veterinarian will guide you in treatment options and
management over time.

VH vacuolar hepatopathy

DEFINITIONS AND OVERVIEW
Vacuolar hepatopathy (VH) is a general term to describe vacuolated
hepatocytes, the most common metabolic liver disorder in dogs and
cats. Hepatocellular vacuoles may result from fat, glycogen, or water
(hepatocellular swelling or cloudy swelling). Water can accumulate
when injured hepatocytes are unable to maintain fluid homeostasis.
Vacuolar hepatopathies are often secondary to other diseases, e.g.,
diabetes mellitus (DM, chs 290-292) or hyperadrenocorticism
(hyperA, chs. 293-294). VHs can also result from toxicoses,
congenital cobalamin deficiency (ch. 262), hepatic congestion,
inflammatory hepatobiliary diseases (chs. 269-271), portosystemic
shunting (ch. 267), and dyslipidemias (ch. 156).1,2 Some lysosomal
storage diseases can cause hepatocyte vacuolation and
hepatomegaly, but the predominant clinical signs are usually
neurologic (ch. 244) and skeletal (ch. 162). An exception is the
cholesterol ester storage disease reported in one family of Fox
Terriers in Germany and in which the predominant abnormalities
are hepatosplenomegaly due to accumulation of lipid and cholesterol
crystals in the liver and spleen.3 The prognosis for affected dogs is
unclear but this is a benign disease in humans. Table 8.1 in the
WSAVA Standards for Clinical and Histological Diagnosis of
Canine and Feline Liver Diseases4 lists lysosomal storage diseases
causing changes in hepatocyte morphology in dogs and cats.
Vacuolar hepatopathies may be benign, but progression to hepatic
dysfunction and predisposition to hepatocellular carcinoma have
been reported.5,6 Therefore, a diagnosis of VH should instigate a
search for a primary disease, with appropriate treatment and

monitoring. Box 274.1 summarizes the primary and secondary
causes of vacuolar hepatopathies in dogs and cats.

CONDITIONS ASSOCIATED WITH
VACUOLAR HEPATOPATHY IN DOGS
GLYCOGEN-ASSOCIATED VACUOLAR
HEPATOPATHY (VH): “STEROID
HEPATOPATHY” (SH)
SH, the most common form of VH in dogs, is associated with
endogenous overproduction of steroid hormones or treatment with
glucocorticoids (GCs; chs. 293, 294).6 A variety of acute and
chronic diseases can result in glycogenic VH, presumably as a
normal physiological response to chronic stress-induced
hypercortisolemia. Dramatic increases in serum alkaline
phosphatase (ALP) activity are common. A cautious approach is
recommended in attributing VH and increased ALP activity to
hyperA, and cortisol assays are only recommended when clinical
signs (e.g., polyuria and polydipsia) and other changes are noted in
the serum biochemistry profile (e.g., hypercholesterolemia).
Typically, hepatocytes are vacuolated, with marked increases in
cytoplasmic (some may be nuclear) glycogen.4 Vacuolation begins in
the centrilobular region (zone 3) but becomes generalized when
chronic.7 SH has been considered benign in dogs. However,
considering the reported association between glycogen-like
hepatopathy in Scottish Terrier dogs and hepatic remodeling and
carcinoma, it would seem wise to take all canine vacuolar
hepatopathies seriously, particularly when chronic and severe.

GLYCOGEN-LIKE VACUOLAR
HEPATOPATHY OF THE SCOTTISH
TERRIER

A predisposition for glycogen-associated VH is reported in Scottish
Terriers, characterized by a moderate to marked elevation in serum
ALP, a milder increase in alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and
increased risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma.5,8 The
median age of dogs of either sex developing a carcinoma is ≥8 years.
The pathogenesis is not well understood and while clinical signs
suggestive of hyperA are noted in nearly half the dogs, low-dose
dexamethasone suppression testing and urine cortisol:creatinine
ratios are usually normal (ch. 293). The most consistent endocrine
abnormalities in affected dogs are increases in progesterone and
androstenedione post-adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation.
Adrenal glands are enlarged on ultrasound (US) in a minority (26%)
of cases. Hepatic changes, common on US, include mottled or coarse
hepatic parenchyma. Presence of hypoechoic nodules may indicate
progression to a degenerative lesion and occasionally malignant
transformation.5 Gallbladder mucocele is diagnosed in 16% of cases
(ch. 273). A minority of dogs have small nodular livers and signs of
portal hypertension. Thus, the disease phenotype is variable, ranging
from subclinical disease to liver failure or malignancy. The extent of
liver enzyme increases was neither discriminating nor predictive of
specific phenotype (ch. 65). Monitoring is recommended, as
increases in ALP and US changes may be consistent with malignant
transformation or mucocele development, necessitating surgical
intervention. Further supporting the lack of hyperA in affected dogs
is their poor response to treatments for hyperA, with severe sideeffects reported with mitotane or ketoconazole and lack of efficacy of
trilostane. Current treatment recommendations are therefore
unclear. Apart from regular sonographic monitoring, treatment with
S-adenosylmethionine may be beneficial, given the reduction in
glutathione reported in other VH in dogs.9,10

HEPATIC STEATOSIS
Buildup of fat within hepatocytes, termed “steatosis,” is also
commonly referred to as “lipidosis” or “fatty change.” “Steatosis” is
preferred, as it is the term used in human medicine and toxicology
textbooks, plus it avoids confusion with the clinical syndrome of
hepatic lipidosis in cats.4 Accumulation of fat within hepatocytes is
associated with DM (ch. 291) and hypothyroidism (ch. 285) in
dogs.1 Other causes include hepatocyte injury (e.g., aflatoxicosis),
congenital portosystemic shunts, or primary and secondary disorders
of fat metabolism. A characteristic feature of microvesicular steatosis
is multiple vacuoles that are smaller than the cell nucleus; this is
typical of DM. Larger vacuoles which often displace the nucleus to
the periphery of the cell are termed “macrovesicular steatosis.”

NON-ALCOHOLIC FATTY LIVER
DISEASE (NAFLD)
NAFLD is common in people. The condition varies from benign
hepatic steatosis to steatohepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular
carcinoma.11 The pathophysiology of NAFLD is primarily associated
with overnutrition, obesity, and the metabolic syndrome (insulin
resistant type 2 DM, hypertension and dyslipidemias).11 NAFLD has
not been demonstrated in dogs. Obesity in dogs can induce insulin
resistance, hyperlipidemia, and increased liver enzyme activities, but
secondary fat accumulation in the liver is not well documented.12-15
Obesity-related metabolic changes in dogs are likely more benign
compared to those of humans.16

FAMILIAL HYPERTRIGLYCERIDEMIA
(FHTG) OF MINIATURE SCHNAUZERS
In a study of 192 Miniature Schnauzers, 32.8% had increased serum
triglycerides and >75% were >9 years of age.17 Pancreatitis (ch.
277), hepatic steatosis, and gallbladder mucoceles (ch. 273) are
common sequelae of FHTG.1 In one study, delayed hepatic clearance
of dietary fats is the result of reduced expression of genes involved in
hepatic cholesterol trafficking and worsens with age.18 However, a
study of mutations in lipoprotein lipase (LPL) and apolipoprotein CII genes did not distinguish affected from unaffected dogs.19

DIAGNOSIS OF CANINE VACUOLAR
HEPATOPATHIES
Increased ALP activity is the most common finding in dogs with
glycogen-associated VH, with or without evidence of GC excess.6 It
has been suggested that delayed clearance of the ALP intestinal
isoenzyme occurs due to steroid-induced hepatic hyperglycosylation,

although it is not known why this occurs uniquely in dogs.8 Other
clinical and laboratory abnormalities are caused by the primary
underlying disease. Although nonspecific on US, a diffusely
hyperechoic liver or presence of many hypoechoic hepatic nodule(s)
<3 cm in diameter is moderately predictive of VH.20 Combining
serum biochemistry and US findings had a poor diagnostic accuracy
(50%) for VH.21 Cytologic evaluation of aspirates has moderate to
high sensitivity in detecting VH. Mild vacuolation of a minority of
hepatocytes is normal, representing physiologic metabolic activity.2
Well delineated clear cytoplasmic vacuoles usually represent lipids
while indistinct vacuoles may represent glycogen. Cytologic results
can be falsely negative if there are focal liver lesions and falsely
positive if subtle changes are overinterpreted.22 Histological findings
include cellular distention, increased fragility, and ballooning
degeneration, but special stains may be required to differentiate
between lipid and glycogen accumulation, e.g., periodic acid–Schiff
for glycogen and oil red O for fat.4 Lipid is lost in routine formalin
fixed section processing, causing fat to appear as clear cytoplasmic
vacuoles. Demonstrating fat with special stains requires frozen
sections. Severe VH may cause diffuse hepatic remodeling due to
hepatocellular necrosis, inflammation, and possible cirrhosis, portal
hypertension, hepatic insufficiency, or malignancy.5,6

FELINE HEPATIC LIPIDOSIS (FHL)
OVERVIEW
In contrast to the mostly benign hepatic steatosis in dogs,
hepatocellular fat accumulation in FHL can progress to acute liver
failure and death (ch. 269). FHL and cholangitis/cholangiohepatitis
are the most common causes of liver disease in cats.23,24
Geographically higher prevalences of FHL may be associated with
diet and outdoor access, both influencing risk of obesity.23,25
Anorexia for any reason lasting >2-14 days is the primary initiating
event, leading to negative energy balance (NEB) and FHL.23 The

duration of anorexia before development of FHL is affected by any
underlying disease (secondary FHL) and may be longest in primary
(idiopathic) FHL, when decreased food intake occurs in an otherwise
healthy cat (e.g., secondary to stress).23,24

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
The primary metabolic abnormalities leading to triacylglycerol (TAG)
accumulation in hepatocytes are not completely understood but
consist of alterations in free fatty acid (FFA) metabolism. Marked
steatosis interferes with hepatocyte function, leading to liver failure
and cholestasis secondary to compression of intrahepatic
cholangioles. Increased secretion of diabetogenic hormones (e.g.,
cortisol) and decreased insulin secretion follow NEB.23,26
Consequently, hormone-sensitive lipase activity increases, and LPL
activity decreases, collectively causing accelerated lipolysis of fat into
FFAs, which are transported to hepatocytes.16,23,26,27 Obesity (ch.
150) is a predisposing factor for FHL because obese cats have larger
quantities of FFAs that can be rapidly released from fat stores.
Increased adipose-derived pro-inflammatory adipokines (e.g., tumor
necrosis factor alpha) and leptin resistance have been reported in
cats with FHL.28,29 Obese cats do have some components of the
human metabolic syndrome (e.g., insulin resistance, dyslipidemia),
making it tempting to draw a connection between human NAFLD
and FHL. However, NAFLD in people typically develops due to
overnutrition rather than anorexia, with increased rather than
reduced insulin concentrations, and usually with less severe or acute
implications. The necro-inflammatory component of human
steatohepatitis, the severe form of NAFLD, is absent in cats with liver
lipid accumulation.30
Due to their carnivorous metabolism, cats have a limited ability to
adapt protein and fat metabolic pathways for conserving nitrogen
(ch. 148). Thus, deficiencies in essential fatty and amino acids
rapidly develop during anorexia.31 Decreased levels of mitochondrial
oxaloacetate and L-carnitine hinder the hepatocyte’s ability to utilize
FFAs as an energy source through beta-oxidation in the tricarboxylic

acid cycle. This leads to production of ketone bodies (i.e.,
acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate [BHBA]).32 Cats with FHL
are deficient in n-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs),
important for FFA hydrolysis and oxidation and favoring TAG
storage in hepatocytes.31 Cats with FHL have increased serum
concentrations of very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), suggesting
that its secretion is enhanced, but not sufficient to prevent FHL with
its dramatic concentrations of FFAs being transported to the
liver.20,31

DIAGNOSIS
Signalment, Comorbidities, History
Hepatic lipidosis is most common in middle-aged to elderly cats
(median 7 years; range, 1.5-16.0 years) of any breed, with a possible
overrepresentation of females.23-25,33 In one study, neutered females
had higher plasma TAG and lower long chain PUFA liver
concentrations compared to intact females. Omega-3 PUFAs favor
FFA oxidation over TAG storage, perhaps increasing FHL risk in
neutered females. Specifically in one study, neutered indoor cats
consuming dry diets were at increased risk for FHL, likely associated
with obesity.25 Searching for a primary comorbidity that may have
initiated anorexia is important; 50-95% of cats with FHL have had a
relevant concurrent condition, e.g., DM (ch. 292), pancreatitis (ch.
278), inflammatory hepatobiliary disease (ch. 271), gastrointestinal
(GI) disease (ch. 262), kidney disease (ch. 301), or neoplasia (ch.
225).23-25 In a recent study, as many as 20% of cats with FHL had a
history of recent stress (e.g., change of residence). However, as many
as 28% had no underlying cause of anorexia identified.25

Clinical Signs, Physical Examination (PE) and
Routine Laboratory Findings
Common clinical signs in FHL include anorexia, weight loss,
vomiting, and decreased activity (chs. 16, 18, and 48).23-25 Diarrhea

or constipation were less frequent.25,34 Ptyalism, which may be a
manifestation of hepatic encephalopathy (HE) or nausea, was rare.25
PE findings commonly include jaundice (ch. 28) and dehydration.25
Ventroflexion of the neck (

Video 68.1) may be due to muscle

weakness or secondary to hypokalemia and/or thiamine deficiency.31
Mild to moderate anemia, with poikilocytosis, Heinz bodies,
microcytosis, and anisocytosis were reported in 24% of cats with
FHL.25 Common serum biochemistry abnormalities included
increased serum ALP activity (100%) and hyperbilirubinemia
(97.2%), reflecting severe intrahepatic cholestasis (ch. 65).25
Increased ALP activity in anorectic cats usually precedes increased
total bilirubin and should prompt early diagnosis and intervention.35
Other common abnormalities included hypertriglyceridemia (84.6%)
and mild to moderate increases in ALT (88.7%), aspartate
aminoransferase (87.1%), and creatine kinase (CK) (48.2%). Serum
gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) activity, a post-hepatic
cholestatic marker in cats, is commonly within reference intervals
(74.6%).25 Certain patterns of enzyme activities, e.g., greater change
in ALT compared to ALP, with or without increased GGT activity is
reason to search for a primary hepatobiliary disease.34
Liver function test abnormalities consistent with liver failure, e.g.,
hypoalbuminemia, hypocholesterolemia, hypoglycemia, decreased
serum urea (blood urea nitrogen [BUN]) were documented in 40% of
cats with FHL (ch. 266).25 Hypoalbuminemia also occurs with
inflammation, overhydration, GI loss, and third space protein loss
(ch. 60). Decreased BUN and hyperammonemia can be caused by
arginine and cobalamin (ch. 262) deficiencies, or hepatic failure
(ch. 62).25 Increased cholesterol may be due to cholestasis and lipid
mobilization to peripheral tissues. Low cholesterol (noted in 26% of
cats with FHL) is consistent with liver failure or inflammation and
was reportedly a risk factor for death (ch. 63).25 Serum electrolyte
alterations at presentation or after giving intravenous fluids include
low chloride, potassium, magnesium, and/or phosphate

concentrations (chs. 67-69 and 120).25,33 Concurrent increases in
BHBA concentrations were common.25,36

Coagulation Testing
Abnormalities in coagulation testing are common (i.e., prothrombin
time, activated partial thromboplastin time, fibrinogen, fibrin
degradation products, and proteins invoked by vitamin K absence)
(ch. 170). These issues, caused by impaired vitamin K absorption
and decreased factor synthesis, only rarely result in clinically
relevant bleeding.24,33,34,37 Vitamin K supplementation with other
coagulation factors is indicated before invasive procedures. Severe
bleeding during biopsy procedures was seen with thrombocytopenia
(<80,000 platelets/mL), but this is not common, and with the more
common finding of an activated partial thromboplastin time >1.5
times the upper limit of the reference interval.31,38

Ultrasound (US)
US of cats with FHL usually reveals an enlarged, diffusely
hyperechoic liver with an echogenicity greater than that of falciform
fat. Seventy percent of cats with FHL have typical, but nonspecific,
abdominal US findings. Other causes of these hepatic observations
include obesity, cholangiohepatitis, fibrosis, and lymphoma.21,39 US
is most valuable in identifying features consistent with underlying
comorbidities.

Cytology, Histology
Diagnosis of FHL can only be confirmed via cytologic or
histopathologic evaluation of the liver, demonstrating vacuolar
changes typical of lipid accumulation in >50-80% of the hepatocytes
(ch. 85).24 Secondary intrahepatic cholestasis and distinct
structural changes are also common histologic findings.40 Histologic
evaluation may be required to confirm some underlying liver
diseases. Cytologic evaluation using fine-needle aspirates (FNA) has
been less reliable, even leading to incorrect diagnoses of FHL in cats

with lymphoma or cholangitis.41,42 These cats probably had FHL,
but secondary to an underlying severe liver disease. Considering that
cats with FHL are poor anesthetic candidates and have increased risk
for bleeding,34 initial diagnosis is usually based on cytology. Liver
biopsy should only be considered when cats fail to improve despite
treatment or if diagnostic findings are suggestive of an underlying
hepatic disease.31

TREATMENT
Enteral Feeding and Pharmacologic Strategies
Early enteral feeding, providing the required protein and calorie
needs, is the mainstay of HL treatment (chs. 17, 151, 164).23-25
Placement of a feeding tube is usually necessary to ensure effective
treatment (ch. 81). Assisted feeding lowers the mortality rate in
affected cats from up to 90% to ≤40%.25,33 Use of pharmacological
appetite stimulation is not effective and is not recommended.31,34
“Force feeding” should be avoided as it carries significant risk of
aspiration pneumonia, food aversion, and/or stress.34 Cats with FHL
commonly present with dehydration, electrolyte imbalances,
coagulopathies, and underlying diseases. These issues increase the
risk of anesthesia and invasive procedures. A temporary nasogastric
feeding tube can be placed until anesthesia is deemed safe, when an
esophageal or a gastric feeding tube is preferred to allow non-liquid
diets, medication administration, and no interference with the
natural return to voluntary food intake, which can take 12-16 days or
longer. Benzodiazepines should be avoided in anesthetic regimens
because they may worsen HE.

Dietary Recommendations
High-protein, high-caloric-density diets, supplemented with Lcarnitine (250 mg/day PO), are used (ch. 154).25 Although Lcarnitine deficiencies were not noted in tissues of cats with FHL,
supplementation lowers plasma FFA concentrations.32,43,44 In a

feline liver organoid model, lipid accumulation decreased with FFA +
carnitine supplementation compared to FFAs alone, and organoid
viability increased.45 Possibly, in a catabolic state, available Lcarnitine is insufficient to meet demand and supplementation is
beneficial.31 Veterinary commercial cat diets formulated for recovery
meet the protein requirements. There is no proven benefit for other
(i.e., taurine and arginine) supplementations. Initially, the calories
needed to meet resting energy requirements (RERs) are supplied.
The use of an “illness factor” is not recommended, because it may
lead to overfeeding, hyperglycemia, GI and hepatic dysfunction.46
Gradual feeding regimens are recommended, to prevent the
“refeeding syndrome” and to allow GI tract adaptation to meal
volumes. Refeeding syndrome is caused by insulin release, inducing
a massive shift of potassium, magnesium, and phosphate into cells.
Starting with 25-33% of the RER, divided into frequent meals or
given by an infusion gradually reaching the RER over 3-4 days, is
recommended. FHL is associated with lengthy hospitalizations
(median 5 days; range 1-18) in a recent report.25 Worsening
ptyalism, regurgitation, or vomiting were reported in 38% of cats,
may delay feeding, and carries fatal implications.25

Supportive Therapies
Supportive therapy with fluids and anti-emetics (e.g., maropitant
and ondansetron) may be beneficial in managing dehydration,
nausea, and vomiting.34 Monitoring and correcting electrolyte
abnormalities is crucial. Hypokalemia can increase the
encephalopathic effects of ammonia and cause muscle weakness and
ileus. Hypomagnesemia can cause refractory hypokalemia.
Hypophosphatemia can cause severe hemolysis.23-25,31
Supplementing with vitamin B12 (cobalamin; 250 mcg/cat q7 days
SQ) and thiamine (100 mg/day PO or SQ) is advised. Vitamin K (1
mg/kg, SQ, q24h for 3-5 days) is indicated to reduce bleeding risk.
Supplementing antioxidants (e.g., S-adenosylmethionine 20mg/kg
PO q24h on an empty stomach and vitamin E 100IU PO q24h) is
recommended for systemic and hepatic oxidant injury.31

Ursodeoxycholic acid is unlikely to be beneficial and should probably
be avoided.47 Omega-3 PUFA supplementation is reasonable due to
common deficiencies, but has not been widely studied. In cats with
HE, a reduced-protein diet is not recommended; instead, reducing
the amount fed, feeding in smaller, frequent meals, and adding
treatment for HE (i.e., lactulose), are preferred (ch. 266). If ileus
develops, prokinetics (e.g., ranitidine and cisapride) are indicated.
Dosage corrections are indicated with drugs metabolized in the liver
(e.g., maropitant). It is important to identify and treat any
underlying disease.

PROGNOSIS
Reported mortality rates range from 12% to almost 70% and was
38% in one recent study.23-25,33 Negative prognostic markers at
presentation include older age. Low serum protein and/or
cholesterol plus increased CK activity were moderately accurate in
predicting mortality.25 During hospitalization, worsening
hypoalbuminemia, hyperammonemia or hyperbilirubinemia, and
development of electrolyte depletion, hypotension and neurological
abnormalities, were associated with death.25 A decrease in serum
BHBA and bilirubin concentrations during hospitalization was
associated with survival.24,25

SUPERFICIAL NECROLYTIC
DERMATITIS
OVERVIEW
Superficial necrolytic dermatitis (SND) is an uncommon
hepatopathy associated with decreases in circulating amino acid
concentrations and excess loss of amino acids via the urine.
Synonyms include hepatocutaneous syndrome, metabolic epidermal
necrosis, necrolytic migratory erythema, and aminoaciduric canine
hypoaminoacidemic hepatopathy syndrome. The condition is usually

accompanied by severe skin lesions (ch. 12).48-51 SND is associated
with glucagon-secreting tumors and concurrent DM in humans.
Glucagonomas, usually metastatic, have been reported in a few dogs
and insulinoma in 1 dog with SND.52,53 SND was reported in 11 dogs
treated with phenobarbital and a heritable component was suspected
in 31 affected Shih Tzus.54,55 However, in most dogs with SND, the
cause remains obscure.48 The disease has been rarely reported in
cats, mostly in conjunction with pancreatic cancer.56 The underlying
pathogenesis of the skin lesions is poorly understood but appears to
involve amino acid, zinc, fatty acid, and B vitamin deficiencies.50,53
The deficiencies may develop due to glucagon-driven upregulated
hepatic metabolic activity or an unidentified stimulus in dogs with
normal glucagon concentrations.

CLINICAL PRESENTATIONS
SND has been reported most commonly in older small-breed dogs
with a median age of 8-10 years.48,54 Affected dogs usually have
hyperkeratotic, erythematous, crusting skin lesions, particularly on
the extremities (paw pads, nose, periorbital, and perianal regions),
around the genitals, and on pressure points (Figure 12.13). The
lesions, sometimes with fissures and secondary infections, often
appear painful. Presence and severity of skin lesions vary, with
severe skin lesions noted in 54% of dogs at presentation, and later
skin involvement in 73% of dogs, reported in a recent study.48 Thus,
SND is sometimes diagnosed based on hepatopathy-associated
clinicopathologic and US findings. Of dogs with SND, 25-40% may
also show signs of DM (ch. 291), although the DM often develops
later in the disease. Increased glucagon secretion is thought to cause
marked insulin resistance and DM, but in dogs with normal glucagon
concentrations, the cause of DM is unclear (although in the context
of hypoaminoacidemia, normal blood glucagon concentrations are
likely inappropriate).48 Clinical signs that are associated with liver
disease are uncommon. In the cases with glucagonoma, dogs may
also present with clinical signs of metastatic neoplasia but this is

uncommon. Dogs with SND associated with phenobarbital
treatment, which was administered for a median duration of 6 years
prior to the development of lesions, had a median age of 10 years.

DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT
Diagnosis is made on the basis of skin and/or liver histopathologic
findings combined with the typical appearance of the liver on
imaging.51 Plasma and urine amino acid profiling provides a noninvasive method for disease confirmation. Elevations of ALP and
ALT activities are common, and hypoalbuminemia is reported in
approximately half of cases, suggestive of negative nitrogen balance.
Hyperglycemia and glucosuria are present in cases with DM. Anemia
and microcytosis were reportedly associated with skin lesions
presence and severity.48 Hypoaminoacidemia was present in all dogs
with SND when measured, with significant deficiencies in plasma
concentrations of alanine, glutamine, glycine, lysine, proline, and
threonine.48 Complementary aminoaciduria is also a key feature of
SND.49 US of the liver demonstrates a “honeycomb” or “Swiss
cheese” appearance, with variably sized, hypoechoic nodules
surrounded by hyperechoic borders.57 This corresponds
histologically to nodular areas of normal hepatocytes surrounded by
zones of collapsed parenchyma with vacuolated hepatocytes. Skin
biopsies show parakeratotic hyperkeratosis with inter- and
intracellular edema, which results in a “red, white, and blue”
appearance on hematoxylin and eosin–stained skin sections. A
primary pancreatic mass and metastases may be visible on US, but
histology and immunohistochemistry are necessary to classify the
tumor type.

PROGNOSIS
SND carries a poor prognosis in most dogs, with death or euthanasia
often reported within 6 months of diagnosis. Treatment of a primary
cause (e.g., removal of a pancreatic tumor, octreotide injections and
replacement of phenobarbital with a different antiepileptic) is

important, but in most cases, where no underlying cause is
identified, treatment is supportive. Ample supply of amino acids to
replenish associated deficiencies is provided by a high-quality,
digestible, high-protein diet, such as a food designed for GI disease
or convalescence (chs. 151, 152, 154, 164). Supplementation with
zinc and essential fatty acids is also recommended. Administering
weekly parenteral amino acid treatment was reported, but the
efficacy of this approach was not widely investigated.58 Addition of
daily egg yolk was beneficial in one case report.59
Supportive treatment of skin lesions should include appropriate
antibiotics and antimycotics for secondary infections, topical
shampoos, and analgesia. The use of corticosteroids should be
avoided because of the risk of precipitating DM.

PREVALENCE

Tumors of the liver and the biliary tree in dogs and cats may be
primary or metastatic. Primary tumors are relatively uncommon,
representing 0.6-1.5% of all tumors in dogs.1-3 Primary liver tumors
represent 1-3% of all tumors in cats, but up to 7% of
nonhematopoietic tumors.4,5 Metastatic tumors are approximately 3
times more frequent than primary liver tumors in dogs, and more
commonly originate from the spleen, gastrointestinal (GI) tract and
pancreas.3 Primary tumors are more common than metastatic
tumors in the cat.4 Benign tumors are more common in cats, but in
dogs are usually malignant.1,3,5,6 Although peak incidence of primary
hepatobiliary cancer occurs at 10-12 years of age in both species, cats
develop malignant hepatic tumors at a younger age than benign
tumors.3,6-9

TISSUES OF ORIGIN AND
MORPHOLOGY
TISSUE TYPES
There are four general tissue types from which primary hepatic
tumors may be derived: hepatocellular, bile duct, neuroendocrine
and mesenchymal. The morphological types of primary hepatic
tumor are massive, nodular and diffuse.1 “Massive” is defined as a
large solitary mass confined to one liver lobe (

Video 275.1);

“nodular” tumors are multifocal and may involve multiple lobes (
Video 275.2); and “diffuse” includes multifocal or coalescing
nodules affecting all lobes or diffuse effacement of the hepatic
parenchyma (Video 275.3).4,10 The liver can also be involved in other
neoplastic processes, including lymphoma (ch. 322), systemic
mastocytosis (ch. 327) and malignant histiocytosis (ch. 328).5,10

Dogs

The most common primary hepatic tumors in dogs are the
hepatocellular adenoma and carcinoma. Bile duct adenoma and
carcinoma are observed less frequently.1 Fibromas, fibrosarcomas,
hemangiomas and hemangiosarcomas are relatively uncommon
primary hepatic neoplasms in dogs. In one study, 106 canine primary
hepatic neoplasms were classified into morphologically well-defined
groups on the basis of histopathologic features and
immunohistochemical stains for markers representative of
hepatocytic and cholangiocytic (bile duct) lineages.11 This
demonstrated 77% hepatocellular tumors, 9% bile duct tumors and
3% hepatic neuroendocrine tumors.11 Tumors accounted for 29% of
4600 canine liver histopathology submissions, and of those,
hepatocellular tumors (45%) were the most frequent primary tumor,
followed by those of hemopoietic (8%), mesenchymal (5%) and bile
duct (2%) tissues.12
