Cats
Bile duct adenomas are frequently reported to be the most common
(>50%) primary feline hepatobiliary tumor,6,8,13,14 although a study
of nearly 1500 feline liver biopsies in the UK reported hematopoietic
tumors to be most common, followed by those of hepatocellular
origin, with biliary tract tumors seen in about 17% of cats.15 In a
report of 61 feline primary liver tumors, classified into well-defined
groups based on histopathological and immunohistochemical
examination, there were 41% bile duct tumors, 34% hepatocellular
tumors and 13% hepatic neuroendocrine tumors.16 In this latter
study all the bile duct tumors were carcinomas, and no bile duct
adenomas were identified.

Nodular Hyperplasia: An Important Differential
Diagnosis for Any Liver Mass
Hepatic nodular hyperplasia is relatively common and is identified in
15-60% of older dogs.5 Nodular hyperplasia also occurs in cats, and
was reported in around 1% of histopathology submissions.15 It is
often identified as an incidental finding during laparotomy or at
post-mortem examination. Nodular hyperplasia is often diffuse with
a “classic appearance” of liver cancer (Figure 275.1, A). Thus,
histology must be performed before condemning a dog or cat.

PATHOLOGY
HEPATOCELLULAR TUMORS

Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)
Hepatocellular tumors include HCC; hepatocellular adenoma, which
is also referred to as hepatoma; and hepatoblastoma. HCC is the
most common primary hepatic tumor in dogs, accounting for >50%
in some studies. It is the second most common tumor in
cats.1,4,5,6,8,10,11,13 The average age of affected dogs is 12 years; 80%
of dogs are >10 years of age.1,2,17 Although most studies fail to
identify a breed or sex predisposition, 16% of the affected dogs in one
report were Miniature Schnauzers.1,2,11,17 Etiological factors
implicated in the development of HCC are largely unknown,
although a link between progressive vacuolar hepatopathy and HCC
has been proposed in Scottish Terriers (ch. 274), with HCC
diagnosed in 35% of Scottish Terriers with progressive vacuolar
hepatopathy.18 Morphologically, 53-83% of HCCs are massive
(Figure 275.1, B;
Video 275.1), 16-25% are nodular and up to
19% are diffuse.1,10 The left lateral and medial lobes and the caudate
lobe are involved in over two-thirds of dogs with massive
HCC.1,2,17,19 Metastasis is more common in dogs with nodular or
diffuse HCC; common sites include the regional lymph nodes,
peritoneum and lungs.1,10,13 The metastatic rate varies from 0-37%
for dogs with massive HCCs and 93-100% for dogs with nodular or
diffuse HCCs.1,2,6,8,10,13,17,19

Hepatocellular Adenomas (Hepatomas)
Hepatomas are often an incidental finding at necropsy in dogs, and
only rarely cause clinical signs unless they rupture and
hemorrhage.10 In cats, hepatocellular adenoma occurs more
frequently than HCC.13 In dogs and cats, adenomas can be
encountered as palpably obvious abdominal masses or sometimes as
pedunculated masses. Care must be taken to distinguish benign from
metastatic diseases. Solitary adenomas can become quite large and
encroach on other organs. Hepatoblastoma is a rare tumor and has
only been reported in 1 dog.20

Tumor Lineages
In humans, primary liver tumors are classified according to the
presence of hepatic progenitor cells (HPCs) and
immunohistochemical markers to differentiate hepatocytic and
cholangiocytic lineages. When using this method of classification in
dogs, hepatocellular tumors could be divided into three subgroups,
each with specific morphologic and immunohistochemical
characteristics.11 By far the largest subgroup is hepatocellular tumors
with 0-5% positivity for keratin 19 (K19), likely derived from mature
hepatocytes. These were well-differentiated and had no evidence of
metastasis.11 A second group contained tumors with >5% positivity
for K19, which were poorly differentiated and had intrahepatic
and/or distant metastasis. These exhibited characteristics of HPCs
without further differentiation towards cholangiocytic or
hepatocellular lineages and may have been derived from HPCs or
through dedifferentiation of mature hepatocytes. A final small group
had an intermediate position with regard to K19 staining and
malignancy. In a similar study in cats, histopathology and
immunohistochemistry classified 21 of 61 primary hepatic tumors as
being of hepatocellular origin, and these were subdivided into
adenomas (n = 18) and carcinomas (n = 3).16 All of the HCCs had
evidence of intrahepatic and/or distant metastases.16

BILE DUCT TUMORS
Bile Duct Carcinoma (Cholangiocarcinoma)
There are two bile duct tumor types in dogs and cats: bile duct
carcinoma and adenoma. Previous studies report that bile duct
carcinoma, or cholangiocarcinoma, is the most common malignant
non-hematopoietic hepatic tumor in cats, and second most common
in dogs (Figure 275.1, C).1,6,8,10,13 In a recent study where feline
primary hepatic tumors were classified based on histopathologic
features and immunohistochemical stains for markers representative
of hepatocytic and cholangiocytic lineages, bile duct tumors (100% of
which were malignant) were most common.16 Previous reports

suggested bile duct carcinomas account for 22-41% of all malignant
liver tumors in dogs.1 In one study, there was a relatively low
frequency (9%) of bile duct tumors in dogs.11 In this study, all canine
bile duct carcinomas were positive for immunohistochemical
markers suggestive of derivation from differentiated mucinproducing cholangiocytes normally present in larger bile ducts.11
A breed predilection for Labrador Retrievers,21 and a sex
predisposition for females has been suggested for canine bile duct
carcinoma.1,22 There are no apparent breed or sex predispositions
for bile duct carcinomas in cats, in whom 37-46% are massive, up to
54% are nodular and 17-54% diffuse.1,10,21,22 Bile duct carcinomas
can be intrahepatic, extrahepatic or within the gallbladder.
Intrahepatic locations are more common in dogs, whereas an equal
distribution of intrahepatic to extrahepatic tumors has been reported
in cats.1,13 Bile duct carcinomas behave aggressively, and metastasis
is very common, often to the regional lymph nodes and
lungs.1,6,8,13,21,22 In dogs, metastatic rates of 90% are reported. In
one study, all feline bile duct tumors had infiltrative growth or
vascular invasion together with intrahepatic and/or distant
metastases. Three tumors were associated with adult-type congenital
hepatic cystic disease.16 In cats, 67-80% had diffuse intraperitoneal
metastasis and carcinomatosis.6,8

Bile Duct Adenoma (Cystadenomas)
Benign adenomas of the bile duct, due to their cystic appearance, are
also called biliary or hepatobiliary cystadenomas. They can be single
or multiple, and usually do not cause clinical signs until they become
large and compress adjacent organs.14,23 They have accounted for
more than 50% of all feline primary hepatobiliary
tumors.5,6,8,13,14,23 However, in a more recent study using
histopathologic features and immunohistochemical stains for
markers representative of hepatocytic and cholangiocytic lineages,
none of 61 primary feline hepatic tumors was an adenoma.16 In other
reports, male cats appear to be predisposed, although no clear breed

predispositions have been reported.14 In a similar study using
histopathologic features and immunohistochemistry, no biliary
adenomas were noted among 106 dogs with primary hepatic
tumors.11 Malignant transformation occurs in humans, and may also
occur in some feline tumors.

NEUROENDOCRINE TUMORS
Neuroendocrine tumors, also known as hepatic carcinoids, arise
from neuroectodermal cells, and are infrequently reported in dogs
and cats.1,8,10,11,13,14,24 In one study, the frequency of
neuroendocrine carcinomas in dogs (3%) and cats (13%) was
relatively low.11,16 Immunohistochemical stains used in the
identification of human neuroendocrine tumors are useful in
determining cell origin.11,16,24 They are usually intrahepatic,
although neuroendocrine tumors of the gallbladder have also been
reported.24,25 Morphologically, carcinoids are nodular in 33% and
diffuse in the remaining cases. They tend to occur at a younger age
than other hepatobiliary tumors, with a mean of 7 years.1,25 Primary
hepatic neuroendocrine tumors are biologically aggressive and due
to their diffuse nature not usually surgically resectable.1,24,25
Frequent sites of metastasis include the regional lymph nodes,
peritoneum, and lungs, with other reported sites including the heart,
spleen, kidney, adrenal glands and pancreas.25

MESENCHYMAL AND OTHER TUMORS
Primary tumors of mesenchymal origin, or sarcomas, are rare in cats
and dogs.1,6,8,10,13,26 In two studies of 106 primary hepatic tumors
in dogs and 61 in cats, no mesenchymal tumors were identified.11,16
In other published reports, hemangiosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma and
fibrosarcoma are more frequently identified. Although the liver is a
very common site for metastatic hemangiosarcomas in dogs (Figure
275.1, D; ch. 325), only 4-6% of hemangiosarcomas occur primarily

in the liver. Other reported sarcomas include rhabdomyosarcoma,
liposarcoma, osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma and malignant
mesenchymoma.27 Hemangiosarcoma is the most frequently
reported primary hepatic mesenchymal tumor in cats and
leiomyosarcoma (ch. 324) the most common in dogs. Massive and
nodular morphology have been reported in 33% and 67% of cases,
respectively.1,26 Males appear predisposed to mesenchymal tumors
with no known breed associations.1 Hepatic mesenchymal tumors
are biologically aggressive, with pulmonary and splenic metastasis
reported in 86-100% of dogs. 1,26 Dogs with disseminated histiocytic
sarcoma (ch. 328) often have hepatic involvement.
Myelolipomas are a benign hepatobiliary tumor of cats and can be
single or multifocal.4,5,28 Histologically they are composed of
adipose tissue intermixed with normal hematopoietic elements and
are usually benign in behavior.

CLINICAL SIGNS AND PHYSICAL
EXAMINATION FINDINGS
Clinical signs of hepatic neoplasia are usually vague, nonspecific, and
they include lethargy, inappetence, weight loss, vomiting,
polyuria/polydipsia, pyrexia and ascites.5 Uncommonly, neurological
signs may develop due to paraneoplastic hypoglycemia (ch. 61),
hepatic encephalopathy (ch. 266) or central nervous system
metastasis (ch. 245).1,24,29,30 Weakness due to myasthenia gravis
associated with an HCC has been described in 1 dog.31 Icterus (ch.
28) is more common in dogs with bile duct carcinomas and diffuse
neuroendocrine tumors.1,10,22 Clinical signs are of relatively little
value in differentiating primary or metastatic liver tumors from
nonneoplastic hepatic disease. Approximately 50% of cats and 25%
of dogs with hepatobiliary tumors show no clinical signs. Many are
diagnosed with a liver tumor only during investigation of increased
liver enzyme activities (ch. 65).5 Physical examination is often
unrewarding, aside from palpating a cranial abdominal mass or

hepatomegaly in up to 75% of dogs and cats with a liver tumor.
Paraneoplastic alopecia has been reported in 1 cat with an advanced
HCC.32

DIAGNOSIS
CLINICAL PATHOLOGY
Complete Blood Count and Coagulation Testing
Clinicopathologic features are usually nonspecific. Complete blood
count may reveal a mild nonregenerative anemia due to anemia of
chronic disease (ch. 57), red blood cell (RBC) sequestration, RBC
destruction or iron deficiency.5 Neutrophilic leukocytosis may be
seen with neoplasia-associated inflammation or necrosis.1,2,17,19
Thrombocytosis is seen in approximately 50% of dogs with massive
HCC (ch. 59).19 Primary or metastatic hepatic hemangiosarcoma
may result in a regenerative anemia and thrombocytopenia.5
Prolonged coagulation times are a potential consequence of any liver
disease, although they are rarely clinically significant unless liver
failure has occurred as a consequence of diffuse disease. About 20%
of dogs with extensive or advanced HCC have prolonged coagulation
times (ch. 170Chapter 170Chapter 171).17,19 Animals with
hepatic hemangiosarcoma are at risk of developing disseminated
intravascular coagulation (DIC, ch. 171).

Serum Biochemistry Profile
Liver enzyme activities are commonly increased in dogs and cats
with hepatobiliary tumors, indicative of hepatocellular or biliary
epithelial damage or biliary stasis (ch. 65).5,33 However, increased
hepatic enzyme activity is not specific for hepatic neoplasia and does
not reflect degree of hepatic neoplastic involvement. Compared with
metastatic hepatic tumors, primary hepatic tumors are more likely to
result in hypoproteinemia, hypoglycemia and increases in serum
alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
activities. They are less likely to cause hyperbilirubinemia.3,33 In

dogs, an aspartate aminotransferase (AST) to alanine
aminotransferase (AST:ALT) ratio of <1 was consistent with an HCC
or bile duct carcinoma in one study, whereas a higher ratio was more
likely with neuroendocrine or mesenchymal tumors.1

Hepatic Function Testing
Elevated serum bile acid concentrations, a nonspecific abnormality,
have been reported in 50-75% of dogs and 33% of cats with liver
tumors. In a study which included 42 dogs with a histopathological
diagnosis of hepatic neoplasia, median resting serum bile acid
concentrations were 4.8 mcg/mL (11.7 mcmol/L), with a range of
0.4-156 mcg/mL (1-381 mcmol/L).34 In this same study, median
postprandial serum bile acids were 9 mcg/mL (22 mcmol/L), with a
range of 2-355 mcg/mL (5-868 mcmol/L). While biliary neoplasia is
more common in cats, only 33% have icterus. Other biochemical
changes may include hypercalcemia, hyperglobulinemia, and
hypoglycemia.1 Hypoglycemia may be seen as a paraneoplastic effect
due to a large tumor mass consuming glucose, or reflect production
of an insulin-like substance (chs. 61, 289, 331).29,30
Hypoalbuminemia, more common in dogs than cats, may reflect a
negative acute phase response, catabolism and poor nutritional
intake, or hepatic insufficiency. Increased serum pancreatic lipase
(PL) activity was reported in 6 dogs with either pancreatic or hepatic
neoplasia.35 Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), a glycoprotein produced by
fetal, neoplastic, and regenerating hepatocytes, is increased in about
75% of dogs with HCC and 55% with bile duct carcinomas.36

IMAGING
Radiology
Imaging is valuable for the diagnosis, staging and surgical planning
of animals with hepatobiliary tumors. Abdominal radiographs may
identify a cranial abdominal mass with caudal and lateral
displacement of the stomach, although sonographic, CT or MRI
examination is usually required for confirmation of its exact location.

Ascites may interfere with visualizing a mass.5,17 Occasionally,
dystrophic mineralization of mass lesions or the biliary tree is
identified.4 Assessment of thoracic radiographs is considered
critically important to exclude metastatic disease.

Abdominal Ultrasound (US)
Abdominal US offers several advantages over abdominal radiographs
in animals with hepatic disease. It can be used for determining
presence of a hepatic mass and for identifying if it is massive (
Video 275.1), nodular (Video 275.2) or diffuse (Video 275.3).5,37,38 In
focal disease, US can be used to determine mass size, location, and
its relationship to surrounding structures. For the detection of mass
lesions, however, sensitivity varies widely and is dependent on
operator skill, equipment, and tumor type.38,39 Diffuse tumors are
usually seen as having hypoechoic, heterogeneous, or multifocal
parenchymal nodules or masses. Less commonly, mass lesions
appear diffusely hyperechoic or, occasionally, normal.40 A cystic
component may be seen in biliary cystadenomas or hepatic
hemangiosarcomas. However, one must be cautious with hepatic
masses seen on US since a study demonstrated marked variability in
US appearance for all types of liver disease in dogs, with no
associations between US appearance and histologic diagnosis.40 The
sonographic appearance of hepatic nodular hyperplasia and
metastatic disease is similar, and in one study 36% of dogs with
ultrasonographically detectable focal hepatic lesions were diagnosed
with nodular hyperplasia.41 Biopsy and histopathology of lesions is
crucial for a definitive diagnosis. The most prevalent US features
were multifocal hepatic lesions in 63% of dogs with
hemangiosarcoma and 43% with HCC. Target lesions associated with
malignancy were identified in 67%.40 Doppler (color flow)
assessment of mass lesions may demonstrate vascularization
patterns helping to distinguish tumors from other benign
processes.5,42 The Doppler perfusion index can be of value in
assessing lymph nodes and liver for metastases.43 Contrast-

enhanced US can help differentiate benign from malignant lesions.44
US is also very valuable to determine local extension and regional
metastasis.

Computed Tomography (CT) or Magnetic Resonance
Imaging (MRI) Scans
Advanced imaging techniques can be useful for diagnosis and staging
of liver tumors and are used in preference to US in humans. In
addition, unlike US, imaging appearance may provide an indication
of tumor type. MRI provides superior soft tissue contrast and is
likely to provide better lesion detection, quantification and
localization when compared to CT. MRI of focal hepatic or splenic
lesions in dogs was reported to have high sensitivity (100%) and
specificity (90%) in differentiating malignant from benign masses.
MRI results correctly identified HCC in one study.45 Triphasic CT
had more than 90% accuracy in differentiating benign from
malignant masses in 44 dogs and was superior to US, but could not
differentiate the histologic type of malignant tumor.46 In humans,
CT and MRI are excellent for detecting small hepatic lesions and
determining the relationship of liver masses to surrounding
structures.47

FINE-NEEDLE ASPIRATION (FNA) AND
BIOPSY
Results of diagnostic imaging and clinicopathologic tests do not
typically provide definitive diagnoses in patients with liver neoplasia.
Obtaining samples for cytologic and/or histologic analysis can be
vital in providing additional information and, in many cases, a
definitive diagnosis. Exceptions may be made for solitary and
massive hepatic masses, when surgical resection is performed
without a preoperative histologic diagnosis because surgery can
provide both diagnosis and treatment. Samples can be collected by
FNA or biopsy via US-guided needle core biopsy, laparoscopy (

Video 275.4) or laparotomy (Video 275.5). Coagulation profiles are
advised prior to any biopsy (ch. 170). Mild to moderate hemorrhage
is a relatively frequent complication (about 5%).37,38,39 General
anesthesia or heavy sedation should be used to avoid patient
movement during needle biopsy.
The main disadvantage of FNA for cytologic evaluation is its
limited diagnostic accuracy. In one study, agreement between
cytology and histopathology was about 30% in dogs and 50% in cats
(ch. 85).48 With focal lesions, FNA can prove useful and may negate
need for biopsy. In dogs with focal hepatic lesions, sensitivity of USguided FNA versus biopsy for the identification of neoplasia was
52%. Cytology had the highest positive predictive value when the
lesion was neoplastic (87%).49 FNA for the diagnosis of diffuse
hepatic neoplasia is generally more reliable. More invasive
techniques, such as laparoscopy and laparotomy, can also be used to
obtain tissue for definitive diagnosis or staging. Follow-up US several
hours after biopsy should also be performed to assess the biopsy site
for bleeding. Careful postoperative monitoring, ideally for 24 hours,
is also advised.

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
SOLITARY HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA
(HCC)
Surgical resection, usually lobectomy, is recommended for most
solitary primary hepatic tumors that have not metastasized,
especially in dogs with a massive HCC.19 Surgery is rarely an option
for most nodular or diffuse hepatobiliary tumors, as complete
resection is impossible. However, localized resection of primary or
metastatic nodules is sometimes considered if likely to provide
palliation of clinical signs, such as reducing potential for lifethreatening hemorrhage. Surgical techniques for liver lobectomy
include surgical stapling, mass ligation, finger fracture, mattress
sutures, and bipolar vessel sealing devices, with surgical stapling
usually preferred. Histopathologically confirmed complete excision
of massive HCCs is associated with significantly better local tumor

control and survival times. Biliary tree diversion (biliary enteric
anastomoses) should be considered for obstructive lesions involving
the extrahepatic biliary structures because long-term palliation is
possible and chronic biliary tree occlusion results in cirrhosis.
Advanced imaging prior to surgical resection of liver tumors can
accurately assess tumor location and extent. In 42 dogs with massive
HCC treated by liver lobectomy, intraoperative mortality rate was
about 5% and the complication rate almost 30%.19 Complications of
surgical resection include hemorrhage, vascular compromise,
reduced hepatic function and hypoglycemia.4,19
Traditional radiation therapy (RT, ch. 318) has little place in the
management of hepatic tumors, although 3-dimensional conformal
RT, which enables very targeted high-dose RT, has been described in
6 dogs with non-resectable massive HCC.50 This resulted in partial
response in 5 of the 6 dogs, with a median survival time (MST) of 567
days.
HCC is usually considered chemoresistant, and adjunctive,
postoperative chemotherapy generally does not provide significant
benefit in dogs or cats with primary liver tumors. However, singleagent gemcitabine therapy has been used in dogs with HCC, and
although the overall MST was 983 days, dogs with massive HCC had
a MST of 1339 days.51 In another study, 1 of 4 dogs with massive
HCC treated with mitoxantrone had complete resolution.52 No
comparable information is available on the use of gemcitabine or
mitoxantrone in cats.
The prognosis for dogs and cats with massive HCC is good,
primarily because it is more likely they can be completely resected.
Local tumor recurrence is reported in 0-13% of dogs with massive
HCC after liver lobectomy,19 although local recurrence has been
reported in 12% of dogs with complete histological excision.53
Prognostic factors for dogs with massive HCC include tumor
location, serum ALT and AST activity, and ratios of ALP to AST and
ALT to AST.19 Histopathologic subtype of HCC and anaplastic
characteristics may also influence prediction of metastasis and
prognosis. The MST of 42 dogs with massive HCC managed by liver
lobectomy was not reached after more than 1460 days of follow-up.19

In comparison, the MST was only 270 days for dogs managed
conservatively, and these were about 15 times more likely to die of
tumor-related causes than dogs treated surgically.19 While location
of a massive HCC may increase surgical risk, location has no impact
on outcome for dogs that survive surgery. The prognosis for dogs
with massive HCC is good, with local tumor recurrence reported in
0-13% following lobectomy.17,19 However, metastatic disease to
other parts of the liver or other organs has been reported to be as
high as 37%.17,19

Nodular or Diffuse HCC
Surgical resection, which is the mainstay of treatment for solitary
HCC, is not usually possible in dogs with nodular and diffuse HCC,
and therefore the prognosis is poor. RT also has no place in their
management, primarily because the liver cannot tolerate the
significant doses required. However, there is limited evidence for the
use of chemotherapy in the management of nodular and diffuse
HCC. When dogs with nodular and diffuse HCC were treated with
single-agent gemcitabine therapy for 5 weeks, the MST was 983 days
and 113 days, respectively.51
Although liver transplantation, directed delivery of
chemotherapeutic agents (intraarterial chemotherapy), transarterial
chemoembolization, and immunotherapeutic regimens using tumorspecific antigen have been used in humans with HCC, these have not
been explored extensively in animals. Blind embolization and
chemoembolization have been reported in treating a limited number
of dogs with non-resectable HCC (ch.118).54,55 In a recent study of
16 dogs with non-resectable HCC managed with drug-eluting bead
transarterial chemoembolization, stable disease or partial response
was documented in 85%, with a MST of 337 days (range 22-1061
days).56

BILE DUCT TUMORS

There is no known effective management option for animals with
nodular or diffuse bile duct carcinomas. Surgical resection is not
possible and these tumors are not sensitive to radiation or
chemotherapy.5 Liver lobectomy is recommended for cats with a
single bile duct adenoma or multiple lesions confined to one or two
lobes.6,8,14,23 Lobectomy is also recommended for cats and dogs
with a massive bile duct carcinoma.
The prognosis for cats with surgically resectable bile duct
adenomas is excellent, with no reports of local recurrence or
malignant transformation.6,14,23 However, survival times for cats
and dogs with massive bile duct carcinoma managed by surgical
resection are poor, with the majority dying within 6 months due to
local recurrence or metastatic disease.5,6

NEUROENDOCRINE TUMORS
As most neuroendocrine tumors are nodular or diffuse, and behave
aggressively, they are generally not amenable to surgical resection.
There are no reports of the use of RT or chemotherapy for this tumor
type in dogs or cats. The prognosis for primary hepatic
neuroendocrine tumors is therefore poor, and metastasis to regional
lymph nodes, peritoneum and lungs has usually occurred by the time
of diagnosis.1,25

MESENCHYMAL AND OTHER TUMORS
Lobectomy is recommended for solitary and massive mesenchymal
tumors, although many have metastasized at the time of
diagnosis.1,26 RT is usually of limited efficacy and there are few
reports of chemotherapy for the management of these hepatic
cancers. Based on the response to chemotherapy for mesenchymal
tumors at other sites, it is likely that primary mesenchymal hepatic
tumors will respond poorly. However, adjunctive chemotherapy may
be considered for visceral hemangiosarcomas (ch. 325). Despite
surgical resection being an option for some primary hepatic

mesenchymal tumors, as metastatic disease is often present at the
time of diagnosis, the prognosis is poor.1,26 However, this strategy
may provide palliation of space-occupying effects of the tumor, or
prevent life-threatening hemorrhage from occurring.
There are few reports on management options for unusual primary
hepatic tumors, although liver lobectomy is recommended for cats
with a single primary hepatic myelolipoma.5 The prognosis for cats
with primary hepatic myelolipoma is excellent, with prolonged
survival times and no reports of local recurrence.4
Hepatic lymphoma (ch. 322), systemic mastocytosis (ch. 327)
and malignant histiocytosis (ch. 328) may all be managed by
systemic chemotherapy.

ACUTE PANCREATITIS

Acute pancreatitis (AP) is a reversible inflammation of the pancreas
characterized by edema, infiltration of neutrophils, and necrosis. AP
can be local but can also be associated with systemic inflammatory
response syndrome (SIRS; ch. 128) with possibly fatal multiple
organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS).1,2

ETIOLOGY
Etiologic factors for AP include pancreatic ischemia or hypoxia,
oxidative stress, bacterial toxemia, hyperlipidemia, retrograde influx
of bile or other substances into pancreatic ducts, or pancreatic duct
obstruction. In dogs and cats, however, the etiology of AP remains
mostly idiopathic but several risk factors need consideration.1,2 In
dogs, breed predisposition has been documented in terriers,
nonsporting breeds, and Miniature Schnauzers.3,4 However, genetic
mutations documented in humans failed to show an association with
canine AP (cationic trypsinogen and cystic fibrosis transmembrane
conductance regulator) or study results were controversial (serine
protease inhibitor Kazal-type 1 [SPINK1] gene variants in Miniature
Schnauzers).4-6 Neutered dogs, both male and female, seem to carry
a higher risk for AP.3 Obesity (ch. 150) and hypertriglyceridemia
(ch. 156) have been associated with an increased risk of AP in dogs.
In Miniature Schnauzers with idiopathic hypertriglyceridemia,
serum canine pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity (cPLI)
concentrations correlate with serum triglyceride concentrations.7
Diets that are rich in fat have been proposed but not definitively
proven as a risk factor for AP in dogs. However, dogs with
hypertriglyceridemia might have a higher risk of developing AP when
receiving a high fat meal. Dietary indiscretion, access to trash, and
table scraps are regarded as risk factors for canine AP.8 Infections
linked to canine AP include babesiosis (ch. 197), where AP appears
to be a negative prognostic factor.9 Canine monocytic ehrlichiosis
(ch. 193) does not cause AP in experimentally infected Beagles but
spontaneously diseased dogs can have increased serum cPLI
concentrations.10 Pancreatic abscesses with bacterial infections have

been reported in dogs, but are considered rare and are believed to be
sequelae to severe pancreatitis.11 Drug reactions are idiosyncratic
rather than true risk factors for AP as proposed for potentiated
sulfonamides.12 Drugs mentioned in occasional case reports of
canine AP include azathioprine, l-asparaginase, meglumine
antimonate, N-methyl-glucamine, and clomipramine.
Phenobarbital/potassium bromide treatment has been associated
with AP and elevated serum cPLI concentrations in dogs. Cerulein
and cholecystokinin 8 injections can induce AP in dogs. Intoxications
appear to be rare causes of canine AP and reports include zinc
intoxication and bites of Vipera xanthina palestinae. Concurrent
disorders linked to canine AP include hyperadrenocorticism (ch.
293), hypothyroidism (ch. 285), and diabetes mellitus (ch. 291),
but a true cause-and-effect relationship has not been explored.3,4
Surgery carries an increased odds ratio for AP in dogs, and this is
presumed to be due to anesthesia-associated hypotension rather
than mechanical manipulation of the pancreas.9 Collecting
pancreatic biopsies does not increase the risk for AP.13 Endoscopic
retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) can induce AP in
humans. Dogs can have transiently elevated serum pancreatic
enzyme values after ERCP without clinical signs of AP, possibly due
to subclinical inflammation.14 In cats, associations of breed, sex,
obesity, and hypertriglyceridemia with AP have not been reported so
far.2 Bacterial colonization of the pancreas was documented with
fluorescence in situ hybridization in cats with spontaneous
pancreatitis, but the clinical implications of these findings are
unclear.15,16 Bile duct obstruction might exacerbate AP and impair
the ability to clear bacteria in cats due to their joint termination of
common bile duct and main pancreatic duct.15 Pancreatic abscesses
with bacterial infections are rare in cats.17 Infections with parasites
(e.g., Toxoplasma gondii, Eurytrema procyonis and Amphimerus
pseudofelineus) or viruses (corona-, parvo-, herpes- and
caliciviruses) also are considered rare causes of AP in cats.2 Drugs
have not been associated with feline AP except for one report about
topical fenthion. Experimental acute hypercalcemia led to AP after

local arterial calcium gluconate infusion but, in contrast to humans,
there have been no reports of AP in cats with spontaneous
hypercalcemia. Feline AP can be associated with diabetes mellitus,
chronic enteropathies (ch. 225), hepatic lipidosis (ch. 225),
cholangitis, nephritis, and immune-mediated anemia.2 Traumatic
AP in cats can result from pancreatic ischemia due to road accidents
or falling from high buildings.2 Cats can have transiently increased
serum feline PLI concentrations after ERCP without clinical signs of
AP.18

PATHOGENESIS
The pathogenesis of AP has been studied extensively in experimental
models and human medicine.18 It is divided into intracellular and
tissue-related events. Intracellular trypsinogen activation can be
initiated by pancreatic ischemia, hypoxia, and/or oxidative stress
due to hypotension or vascular thrombus formation or by bacterial
toxemia.1,2 Another cause is the apical block of acinar cell secretion
due to retrograde influx of bile into pancreatic ducts or abnormal
Ca2+ signaling. Retrograde bile influx can occur either due to the
joint anatomic structure of both duct systems, as is present in a
majority of cats and a subset of dogs, or to duodenal obstruction that
sends bile, chyme, and bacteria into the pancreatic ducts (Figure
276.1, Video 276.1

).1,2 Normally, the Golgi apparatus of the

acinar cells separates pancreatic proenzymes and lysosomal enzymes
by producing distinct zymogen granules and lysosomes. SPINK1, an
intracellular pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor, completes this
protective mechanism against intracellular enzyme activation. When
an apical block of acinar cell secretion occurs, zymogen granules and
lysosomes accumulate at the cell apex and fuse. This leads to an
intracellular activation of trypsinogen to trypsin. The binding of
trypsin by SPINK1 is overwhelmed when >10% of intracellular
trypsinogen is activated or if SPINK1 mutations occur. Free trypsin

activates all other proenzymes of the zymogen granules, which leads
to acinar cell apoptosis (

Video 276.1).1,2

Pancreatic tissue-related events after the escape of activated
digestive enzymes include local inflammation with extravasation of
neutrophils. The shift from apoptosis to necrosis is probably caused
by neutrophils along with endothelin-1 and phospholipase A3.1
Reduced pancreatic microcirculation, increased vascular
permeability of capillaries, and disturbed lymphatic drainage
contribute to pancreatic edema. At that early stage of AP, fluid
resuscitation is considered to improve microcirculation. Neutrophils
aggregate with intercellular adhesion molecules of the vascular
endothelium. This interaction is mediated by lymphocyte function
associated antigen-1 (LFA-1), which plays also a key role in the
emigration of neutrophils from blood to tissue. Therefore, using
LFA-1 antagonists might be of benefit for treating AP.19 Neutrophil
aggregation eventually leads to neutrophil plaques, obstructing
capillaries with the consequences of capillary stasis, hemorrhage into
pancreatic tissue, and acinar cell necrosis. At that late stage of AP,
the lymphatic drainage of affected pancreatic tissue is blocked and
the capillaries cease to respond to fluid resuscitation.1 In rodent
models and humans, leakage of pancreatic triglyceride lipase into the
peripancreatic adipose tissue leads to visceral fat lipolysis, with the
severity of AP being dependent on the amount and composition of
visceral fat. Lipolysis of visceral fat generates unsaturated fatty acids
and their increased concentration in serum has been associated with
AP severity and SIRS (

Video 276.2).20 Lipase inhibitors are

considered a promising option to reduce the severity of human AP,
but have not been explored in dogs or cats yet.20

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Pathophysiologic consequences of AP include local and systemic
inflammatory responses. The local response includes pain, swelling,
reddening, heat, and disturbed function. Abdominal pain is a key
clinical sign of AP in humans and signs of pain have been reported in

∼50% of canine patients. Cats often just show changes in behavior,
which can respond to pain medication. Neurokinin-1 receptors
appear to mediate pancreatic pain and medications that block those
receptors are increasingly advocated for dogs and cats with AP.2
Swelling of the pancreas can cause extrahepatic biliary obstruction,
resulting in icterus. Reddening of pancreatic tissue in AP is patchy
and visible in vivo during laparoscopy or surgery. Increased organ
temperature cannot be determined per se, but fever can occur as a
systemic sign. Disturbed endocrine pancreatic function can result in
diabetes mellitus (chs. 291 and 292). Transient exocrine pancreatic
insufficiency (EPI) after AP has not been described in dogs and cats
so far but has been documented in humans and correlates with the
extension of pancreatic necrosis. Local complications after AP
include pancreatic fluid accumulation, pseudocysts, and areas of
necrosis. Case reports in dogs and cats have described both sterile
and infected fluid accumulations, which have both been previously
described as a pancreatic abscess. AP can be fully reversible but also
can result in chronic pancreatitis and focal or extensive adhesions of
the pancreas to surrounding organs.

FIGURE 276.1 Etiologic factors (A-C) and
pathophysiological consequences (1-4) of acute

2021;35:703-723.
A systemic inflammatory response results from an upregulation of
a large variety of proinflammatory mediators and chemokines.1,9
This so-called “cytokine storm” overwhelms the effects of antiinflammatory mediators and results in SIRS. In addition, lipolysis of
visceral fat and the complement, kinin-kallikrein, and reninangiotensin-aldosterone systems are involved in SIRS.1 The
development of systemic complications can be summarized as the
following chain of events: AP causes a cytokine storm, leading to
SIRS, which in turn results in MODS. In turn, MODS can include
acute lung injury, acute kidney injury, disseminated intravascular
coagulation, and cardiac arrhythmia, ultimately possibly leading to
multi-organ failure and death (ch. 128).1,2,9

CHRONIC PANCREATITIS

Chronic pancreatitis (CP) is characterized by continuing
lymphocytic/lymphoplasmacellular inflammation with irreversible
fibrosis and atrophy.21 CP can be subclinical or recurrent with
episodes of more or less severe illness. Pancreatic tissue loss can lead
to decreased exocrine or/and endocrine function.22

ETIOLOGY
The etiology of CP can be either AP or immune-mediated
inflammation but it remains largely idiopathic.2,22 CP seems to
disproportionately affect Cavalier King Charles and English Cocker
Spaniels, Boxers, and Collies.22 Autoimmune pancreatitis has been
reported in English Cocker Spaniels and dogs of other breeds, with
histologic features of human autoimmune pancreatitis type 1, a
multisystemic fibro-inflammatory disease.23 In cats, autoimmune
pancreatitis has been suggested, but not proven so far.2

PATHOGENESIS AND
PATHOPHYSIOLOGIC CONSEQUENCES
The pathogenesis of CP is linked to the activation of pancreatic
stellate cells (PCSs) in the interstitial space of the pancreas.2 Acinar
cells and tissue-associated pathways are involved in PCS activation
(Figure 276.2). Acinar cell-associated events include sensitization
of acinar cells to injury and necrosis by cholecystokinin and oxidative
stressors, abnormal Ca2+ signaling, and collapse of mitochondrial
membrane potentials. The resulting continued low-grade
inflammation mediates PCS activation. Tissue-associated events
include acidosis, lipopolysaccharides from endotoxemia, damage to
the pancreatic duct epithelium, and ductal obstruction. The outcome
of both pathways is ongoing PCS activation, resulting in periacinar
fibrosis and chronic inflammation (

Video 276.3).2

The pathophysiologic consequence of CP is a gradual replacement
of functional exocrine and endocrine tissue by fibrosis. This can
remain subclinical throughout life or can lead to a variety of clinical
signs, ranging from recurrent episodes of acute-on-chronic
pancreatitis to functional disorders such as EPI (ch. 279) and/or
diabetes mellitus (chs. 291, 292).2,22 In cats, CP is considered to be
the overwhelming cause of EPI. In dogs, EPI has been associated
mainly with immune-mediated pancreatic acinar atrophy, a disorder
unrelated to CP. The proportion of CP in canine EPI is currently
unknown. Acute-on-chronic pancreatitis might occur due to
increased pancreatic duct pressure. Pancreatic duct abnormalities
are a feature of human CP and have also been documented with
magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography in cats.24 Concurrent
inflammation of the pancreas, liver, and intestine has been
documented as triaditis in cats, but a cause-and-effect relationship
has not been demonstrated to date (ch. 225).25

INTRODUCTION
Pancreatitis is considered to be a common disease in dogs.
Historically, acute pancreatitis was considered to be much more
common than chronic pancreatitis, but more recent data suggest
that, similarly to cats, chronic disease is by far more common in dogs
than acute disease.1 However, acute disease is often clinically more
severe than chronic disease and may thus be more readily diagnosed.

DIAGNOSIS
CLINICAL PRESENTATION
It is now recognized that dogs with pancreatitis can have subclinical
disease or present with a wide variety of clinical signs, ranging from
mild hyporexia with no apparent gastrointestinal (GI) signs to severe
systemic signs, cardiovascular shock, and disseminated intravascular
coagulation (DIC). There is no single clinical sign or combination of
clinical signs that is pathognomonic for canine pancreatitis.
In many studies, the most commonly reported clinical signs for
acute pancreatitis include lethargy, anorexia, vomiting (with or
without blood), diarrhea, and signs of abdominal pain.2,3 In 1 recent
study, clinical signs included lethargy (88%), anorexia (86%),
vomiting (83%), and evidence of abdominal pain (59%; Figure
277.1).4 Selection bias should be considered: for most clinical
studies, inclusion criteria for dogs with pancreatitis typically include
at least 1 of these clinical signs (i.e., they are inherent to the
definition of clinical pancreatitis). Therefore, dogs with pancreatitis
but without those clinical signs would have been excluded. Also,
many studies reporting on clinical signs rely on necropsy findings
and thus typically include many dogs that died of pancreatitis and
likely represent more severe cases. Therefore, the true spectrum of
the clinical presentation of dogs with pancreatitis is unknown. Some
of the clinical signs are likely to be the result of complicating or
concurrent diseases rather than pancreatitis per se (e.g., polyuria
and polydipsia are more likely to be the result of concurrent diabetes
mellitus).

The most common physical examination findings in dogs with
severe acute pancreatitis include evidence of dehydration (97%),
signs of abdominal pain (58%), fever (32%), and icterus (26%) (ch.
3).3 It should also be noted that while the combination of vomiting
and abdominal pain is suggestive of pancreatitis, it can also be seen
with other diseases (e.g., GI foreign bodies, peritonitis). Some dogs
with severe abdominal pain (of any cause) present with the so-called
prayer position (Figure 277.1, Video 277.1

). Other possible

findings include shock, hypothermia, heart murmur, tachycardia,
bleeding diathesis, ascites, a palpable abdominal mass, and harsh
lung sounds.3

FIGURE 277.1 Prayer position. This image shows
a dog with pancreatitis displaying a prayer position,
which is believed to result from severe abdominal
pain.

Patients with less severe or chronic pancreatitis are typically
presented with less-profound clinical signs (e.g., anorexia and
depression), or might even be subclinical. In a study of 61 dogs with
histopathologically confirmed chronic pancreatitis, clinical signs
included lethargy (80%), decreased appetite (70%), vomiting (63%),
diarrhea (36%) and evidence of abdominal pain (27%).5 Therefore, it
is important to keep in mind that many dogs with pancreatitis may
not present with vomiting and abdominal pain, but less specific
clinical signs.

ROUTINE CLINICOPATHOLOGIC TESTS
A complete blood count (CBC), serum biochemistry profile, and
urinalysis should always be performed in dogs suspected of having
pancreatitis: they are useful for the diagnosis and for exclusion of
other differential diagnoses, and they give important information
about the general condition of the patient. These tests also help to
recognize specific abnormalities (e.g., electrolyte abnormalities), the
correction of which is crucial for the management of the patient.
The results of the CBC, serum biochemistry profile, and urinalysis
are often within normal limits in dogs with pancreatitis, especially in
those dogs with mild pancreatitis.3 However, dogs with pancreatitis
may present with almost any hematological or biochemical
abnormality.3 Different combinations of increases in liver enzyme
activities (i.e., alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase,
alkaline phosphatase; ch. 65) and hyperbilirubinemia are common
and, when present, should raise the suspicion for pancreatitis.3 In
some cases, these findings might be associated with extrahepatic
biliary tract obstruction (chs. 272, 273). Increases in serum
creatinine, urea nitrogen, and/or symmetric dimethylarginine
concentrations (ch. 62) are variably present and most often
associated with dehydration, but may also point to secondary kidney
injury. Other possible findings include hypertriglyceridemia,
hypercholesterolemia (ch. 63), hypoalbuminemia (ch. 60), and
hyperglycemia (sometimes associated with diabetes) or
hypoglycemia (ch. 61).3,6 A variety of electrolyte abnormalities may

also be present in dogs with pancreatitis, with hypokalemia being the
most common (ch. 68).

LABORATORY TESTS FOR
PANCREATITIS
Pancreatic Lipase Immunoreactivity (PLI)
PLI is currently considered the most sensitive and specific serum test
for the diagnosis of pancreatitis in dogs. The main advantage of PLI
assays over traditional lipase activity assays is specificity. In contrast
to traditional assays for lipase activity, which indiscriminately
measure the activities of lipases of multiple cellular origins,
immunoassays exclusively quantify lipase of pancreatic origin based
on its unique 3-dimensional structure.7,8 Therefore, PLI assays have
inherent advantages over the traditional serum lipase activity assays
that make them more suitable for specific evaluation of the exocrine
pancreas in dogs and cats.

Available Assays
The originally developed and analytically validated immunoassays
for the specific measurement of serum pancreatic lipase in dogs
(canine PLI [cPLI])9 have been replaced by a more widely available,
fully validated assay (Spec cPL) that demonstrates a similar clinical
performance to the original PLI assays and is available through
IDEXX Laboratories and the Gastrointestinal Laboratory at Texas
A&M University.10 The reference interval for Spec cPL is 0 to 200
mcg/L. Concentrations ≥400 mcg/L (Spec cPL) are considered
highly suggestive of pancreatitis.
A rapid, in-clinic, semiquantitative assay for the estimation of
canine pancreatic lipase in serum (SNAP cPL) is also available.11 The
results of this rapid assay are considered either normal or abnormal.
Dogs with a “normal” result are unlikely to have pancreatitis,
whereas those with an “abnormal” result might have pancreatitis or a
Spec cPL in the equivocal range.11 However, the two cannot be
differentiated without quantitative evaluation by measurement of a

Spec cPL in the laboratory. Three other assays for the measurement
of PLI in dogs are available. Laboklin Laboratories in Europe offers a
PLI assay for dogs, but this assay has been reported to have failed
analytical validation.12 The assay lacked dilutional parallelism and
results were different from Spec cPL, even though the reference
interval and cut-off values reported are the same as the Spec cPL
assay. An additional paper has since been published that utilizes this
assay in a clinical study, but no information is available on how the
assay has been revised since previously failing analytical validation.13
Another assay is a point of care assay available through Zoetis
(Abaxis VetScan cPL). A partial analytical validation study of this
assay showed that the assay’s results were not linear and it showed
poor repeatability and reproducibility with many repeat
measurements having results in different diagnostic bins (i.e.,
normal vs. equivocal vs. pancreatitis).14,15 Another in-house assay
(VCheck cPL, Bionote, Hwaseong, Korea) is available in parts of Asia.
This assay has also failed analytical validation for use in dogs.15

Performance of PLI Assays
Original PLI and Spec cPL Assays
Both clinical16 and histopathological13,17-19 studies concerning cPLI
for canine pancreatitis have been published and all generally agree
that serum cPLI is the most sensitive and specific serum marker for
pancreatitis in dogs to date. In a large clinical study that included 84
dogs, the sensitivity of cPLI as measured by Spec cPL was reported to
range between 72% and 78%.16 In a recent necropsy study, the
sensitivity of the cPLI was reported at 91% for moderate or severe
pancreatitis.13 Three older necropsy studies have also determined
the sensitivity of cPLI.11-13 In these studies, the sensitivity of cPLI
ranged from 21% for mild and potentially clinically insignificant
pancreatitis to 71% for histopathologically moderate to severe
pancreatitis.
Serum cPLI concentration is also considered to have the highest
specificity for pancreatitis compared to any other serum test

currently available, with specificities ranging between 81% and
100%.2,8,13,18 In the clinical study mentioned above, the specificity of
cPLI was reported to range between 81% and 88%.16 In two necropsy
studies that included dogs that died or were euthanized for a variety
of reasons and had a normal pancreas on histopathology, serum Spec
cPL showed a specificity of 100%18 and 90%.20 In another necropsy
study, the specificity of Spec cPL using the recommended cut-off of
400 mcg/L was 98%.7 Experimentally induced chronic renal
failure21 and long-term prednisone administration22 were not found
to have any clinically significant effect on serum cPLI concentration.
Also, pancreatic sampling by ultrasound-guided fine-needle
aspiration (FNA) or surgical biopsy did not cause any increases in
serum cPLI concentrations in healthy dogs.23
Finally, in a recent study, it was suggested that serum cPLI
concentrations can be used as objective markers for disease
progression in hospitalized dogs with acute pancreatitis.24

SNAP cPL
One study showed that there is a 90-100% agreement between the
SNAP cPL and the reference Spec cPL.11 Another study reported that
SNAP cPL has a sensitivity for pancreatitis of 91-94% and a
specificity of 71-78%.16 However, the main use of this diagnostic tool
is to rule out pancreatitis (i.e., a normal result makes a diagnosis of
pancreatitis very unlikely) and thus, the sensitivity of the SNAP cPL
is more important than its specificity.
There have been limited studies evaluating the clinical
performance of the other serum cPLI assays. One histopathologic
study reported a sensitivity of 90.9% for the Laboklin cPL with a
specificity of 92.5%.13 Another study evaluated the clinical
performance of the VetScan cPL and reported a sensitivity of 73.983.3% and a specificity of 76.9-83.8%.25 However, it should be noted
that the analytical validation of either assay has not been
demonstrated to date and thus the above studies should be

interpreted with caution. Also, to date, no studies have investigated
the diagnostic performance of the VCheck cPL.

Trypsin-Like Immunoreactivity (TLI)
TLI assays are immunoassays that measure trypsinogen and trypsin
concentrations in serum. They have been shown to be of only limited
usefulness for the diagnosis of canine pancreatitis. The sensitivity of
serum canine TLI (cTLI) for the diagnosis of spontaneous
pancreatitis is low (36-47%), possibly due to the short half-life of
trypsinogen and trypsin in serum.2,8,17,26 In addition, although there
is strong evidence that while trypsinogen is exclusively of pancreatic
origin in healthy animals, serum cTLI concentration can be increased
in dogs with kidney disease. This is likely due to the fact that
trypsinogen and trypsin are small, positively charged molecules that,
at least in part, get filtered by the glomerular membrane.

Serum Amylase and Lipase Activities
Serum amylase and lipase activities have long been used as markers
for pancreatitis in dogs. Although serum activities of these 2 enzymes
increase during experimental canine pancreatitis, several studies
have shown that these markers, when measured using traditional
assay methodologies, are not useful for the diagnosis of spontaneous
canine pancreatitis due to their low sensitivity and specificity.2 Many
tissues other than the exocrine pancreas synthesize amylases and
lipases and both the reported sensitivity and specificity for the
diagnosis of pancreatitis in dogs are low.2,3,17,27
More recently developed colorimetric lipase activity assays (such
as those based on 1,2-o-dilauryl-rac-glycero-3-glutaric acid-[6′methylresorufin] ester [DGGR] as a substrate) have been reported to
show better performance than traditional catalytic assays. It has
been claimed that DGGR-based assays are more specific for
pancreatic lipase than traditional catalytic assays; some studies have
compared DGGR-based assays with PLI assays and have suggested
similar performance between the two.28 A study of 142 dogs found
high agreement between a specific DGGR-based lipase assay and the
Spec cPL assay, with the best agreement (kappa=0.80) for a cutoff of

this DGGR-based lipase activity assay of >216 U/L.28 However, it
should be noted that an agreement of 0.80 is not very high for 2
assays that supposedly measure the same analyte. Also, there are
various DGGR-based assays for the measurement of serum lipase
activity and they differ dramatically due to changes in added
compounds (e.g., colipase, bile acids), assay conditions (e.g., pH),
and also the analyzer being used. Regardless, none of the currently
available DGGR-based assays has been shown to be consistently
more specific for the measurement of pancreatic lipase than more
traditional serum lipase activity assays. For example, a recent
experimental study showed that DGGR is not only hydrolyzed by
pancreatic lipase but also by lipoprotein lipase, hepatic lipase, or
both.29 Therefore, further studies are needed before DGGR lipase
assays can be recommended for the routine diagnosis of pancreatitis.

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
Radiography
In the majority of cases of pancreatitis, abdominal radiographs are
normal or only show nonspecific changes. Despite that, abdominal
radiography remains a logical initial approach for patients suspected
of having pancreatitis, because it is useful to rule out other
differential diagnoses.

Abdominal Ultrasound (

Videos 277.2 and 277.3)

Abdominal ultrasound is currently the imaging modality of choice for
the diagnosis of pancreatitis in dogs. Both the quality of ultrasound
machines and expertise have greatly advanced over the last 2
decades and ultrasonography is now routinely used for the
investigation of dogs suspected of having pancreatitis. However,
abdominal ultrasonography is highly dependent on the skill and
experience of the ultrasonographer and the equipment available. An
older study reported a sensitivity of 68% for detecting fatal acute
pancreatitis.3 In a recent study that included both healthy dogs and
dogs with clinical pancreatitis, it was shown that the sensitivity and

specificity of ultrasound for pancreatitis depend on the definition of
ultrasonographic evidence of pancreatitis.30 If only one criterion was
applied (e.g., pancreatic enlargement or changes in peripancreatic
echogenicity), the sensitivity was 89% but the specificity was only
43%. In contrast, if stringent criteria were applied (i.e., pancreatic
enlargement, hypoechoic areas within the pancreas due to pancreatic
necrosis, increased echogenicity of the surrounding mesentery due to
peripancreatic fat necrosis; Figure 277.2), the sensitivity decreased
to 43% and the specificity increased to 92%.30 Therefore, when
stringent ultrasonographic criteria for pancreatitis are applied, the
diagnosis is likely to be accurate when all criteria are met (high
specificity), but at the expense of sensitivity: the ability to meet those
stringent criteria can be low and pancreatitis cannot be excluded
based on a normal ultrasound examination.
It should also be noted that there may be a delay in the appearance
of imaging findings in comparison to the actual disease process,
which may require repeat ultrasonography 24-48 hours later.31 In 1
study of 38 dogs suspected of having acute pancreatitis in which
abdominal ultrasound was performed at presentation and again 4052 hours later, 12 (32%) had no ultrasonographic changes at either
examination (

Video 277.2), 14 (37%) only at the second

ultrasonographic examination, and only 12 (32%) at both
ultrasonographic exams.31 Currently, there is no convincing evidence
that repeated ultrasonography is useful for disease monitoring and
response to treatment. Finally, it should be noted that
ultrasonographic changes in dogs with chronic pancreatitis (Figure
277.3) are far less obvious than in those with acute disease.

FIGURE 277.2 Ultrasound image of the right lobe
of the pancreas from a 13-year-old female spayed
Springer Spaniel with signs of cranial abdominal
pain. The right pancreatic lobe (arrows) is thick and
diffusely hypoechoic. There is also a hyperechoic
peripancreatic area. These findings are suggestive of

FIGURE 277.3 Ultrasound image of the right lobe
of the pancreas from an 11-year-old male castrated
Cocker Spaniel with possible chronic pancreatitis.
The right lobe of the pancreas (between calipers)
appears as a thick, hyperechoic, mildly

Mantis.
The most important ultrasonographic findings suggestive of
pancreatitis in dogs include hypoechoic areas within the pancreas,
increased echogenicity of the surrounding mesentery (because of
necrosis of the peripancreatic fat), and enlargement and/or
irregularity of the pancreas (Figure 277.2, Video 277.3

).2,30

Abdominal ultrasonography is also very useful for the diagnosis of
local complications of pancreatitis such as pancreatic or
peripancreatic fluid accumulations or extrahepatic bile duct
obstruction (EHBDO).
In summary, while ultrasound can be useful for the diagnosis of
pancreatitis, it has limitations, does not always provide a definitive
diagnosis of pancreatitis, and should not be used in isolation for the
diagnosis of pancreatitis.30
Several other imaging modalities are routinely used for diagnosing
or evaluating pancreatitis in human patients and, in recent years, in
dogs as well. Contrast-enhanced ultrasonography in dogs has been

reported to be superior to regular ultrasonography.32,33 Contrastenhanced abdominal computed tomography is the diagnostic tool of
choice for evaluation of people with suspected pancreatitis and some
reports show promising results in dogs.34 Other imaging modalities
(e.g., endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, endoscopic
ultrasonography, magnetic resonance imaging) have also been
reported. However, because of the lack of standardized criteria for
the diagnosis of pancreatitis, the complexity of these modalities,
their limited availability, and the cost of the equipment, they are
currently not routinely used for the diagnosis of pancreatitis in dogs.

pancreatitis. There is mild to moderate neutrophilic
inflammation. A cluster of normal acinar cells can

Pancreatic Cytology
FNA of the pancreas and cytological examination of the aspirated
material is a minimally invasive technique that can be used for the
diagnosis and differentiation of pancreatitis and other exocrine
pancreatic diseases in dogs. It is usually performed either under
ultrasonographic guidance or during laparotomy. In the only
published study in dogs, ultrasound-guided pancreatic aspiration
was described retrospectively in 92 dogs and was found to be safe
and the aspirated material was reported to be diagnostic in 74% of
the samples obtained.35 In the same study, there was a 91%

agreement with histopathologic findings in the small number of dogs
for which histopathologic results were available.35 Pancreatic acinar
cells constitute the majority of the cells found in FNA smears from a
normal pancreas. In animals with acute pancreatitis, the cytological
picture is mainly characterized by the presence of intact and
degenerate neutrophils and degenerate pancreatic acinar cells
(Figure 277.4).35 In animals with chronic pancreatitis, small
numbers of lymphocytes are usually present, and the specimen is
often characterized by low cellularity, possibly due to replacement of
the normal pancreatic tissue by fibrotic tissue.35 It should be
highlighted that, as for histopathologic evaluation, localized lesions
might be missed. Thus, negative FNA cytologic results are not
sufficient to rule out pancreatitis.

Macroscopic Pathology and Histopathology
Certain macroscopic pathologic lesions of the pancreas identified
during surgery, laparoscopy, or necropsy are highly suggestive of
pancreatitis and are preferred sites for collecting a biopsy. Lesions
suggestive of pancreatitis may include peripancreatic fat necrosis,
pancreatic hemorrhage and congestion, and a dull granular capsular
surface (Figure 277.5), but macroscopic lesions are not always
present.17
Historically, histopathologic evaluation of pancreatic tissue has
been considered the gold standard for diagnosis and differentiation
of pancreatitis (i.e., acute vs. chronic vs. other exocrine pancreatic
diseases).2 The presence of permanent histopathologic changes (e.g.,
fibrosis and acinar atrophy) is considered suggestive of chronic
pancreatitis.1 Acute pancreatitis is characterized by absence of
permanent histopathologic changes and the presence of neutrophils,
edema, and necrosis (Figure 277.6).1 The predominant
inflammatory infiltrate (i.e., neutrophils or lymphocytes) is often
used for describing pancreatitis as suppurative or lymphocytic,
respectively, and a significant degree of necrosis characterizes the
pancreatitis as necrotizing. However, determining the clinical
significance of histopathologic findings may be challenging and what
constitutes normal pancreatic histologic features is still debated.

Although the presence of certain histopathologic findings confirms
pancreatitis, exclusion of pancreatitis based on normal histologic
findings is difficult because inflammatory lesions of the pancreas are
often highly localized and can easily be missed.1 Therefore, multiple
sections of the pancreas must be evaluated to increase the likelihood
of finding microscopic lesions; this is not always feasible in clinical
cases. Finally, although pancreatic biopsy per se is considered a safe
procedure, it requires invasive approaches that are expensive and
potentially detrimental to patients that are hemodynamically
unstable.

FIGURE 277.5 Macroscopic appearance of the
pancreas from a dog with pancreatitis. The pancreas
appears hemorrhagic, edematous, and granular, and
there is some peripancreatic fat necrosis. These
changes are highly suggestive of pancreatitis.

MANAGEMENT OF PANCREATITIS
MANAGEMENT OF SEVERE ACUTE
PANCREATITIS
Treatment of the Cause
The etiology of pancreatitis remains unknown in most cases and
treatment is almost exclusively supportive and nonspecific. The
presence of possible risk factors should always be investigated. If any
of these factors are present, they should be managed where possible.

Fluid and Electrolyte Therapy
Early and adequate fluid administration is the cornerstone of
management of acute pancreatitis (ch. 120).36 Dogs with severe
pancreatitis often have various degrees of dehydration, hypovolemia,
or both at the time of presentation, due to ongoing anorexia,
vomiting, diarrhea, and/or third space losses. Close monitoring is
required in order not to overhydrate the animal; in humans overly
aggressive fluid therapy may be associated with an increased risk of
acute kidney injury and/or acute respiratory distress syndrome
(ARDS).37 Crystalloid fluids are usually the preferred choice of fluid.
In humans, lactated Ringer’s solution is preferred over normal
saline.36 Administration of synthetic colloid fluids might be
indicated in cases of severe hypoalbuminemia or hypotension. Freshfrozen plasma (FFP) might also be used in cases with
hypoalbuminemia (it also contains protease inhibitors and
coagulation factors). However, limited data are available on the
usefulness of FFP in dogs. Studies in humans show no benefit of
plasma administration in the clinical outcome of patients with acute
pancreatitis.38,39 In a retrospective study, dogs with pancreatitis that
received FFP had a worse outcome than dogs that did not receive
FFP.40 Thus, the actual value of plasma administration is highly
questionable in dogs with pancreatitis.
Hypokalemia is often present as a result of potassium loss due to a
combination of diarrhea, vomiting, fluid therapy, and anorexia.
Therefore, serum potassium concentration should be monitored
throughout hospitalization, and potassium must be added to
intravenous (IV) fluids where necessary. Other electrolyte and any
acid-base disturbances should also be identified and corrected.

Nutritional Support (ch. 153)
There is mounting evidence that most humans and dogs with acute
pancreatitis benefit from early nutritional support.36 Studies have
also shown that enteral nutrition is superior to total parenteral
nutrition in the treatment of acute pancreatitis in both humans and
animals.36,41 Lack of enteral nutrition adversely affects intestinal

motility and GI barrier function, disrupts the normal intestinal
microbiota, and can cause villus atrophy.
In a pilot study, early enteral nutrition in 5 dogs with naturally
occurring, severe, acute pancreatitis delivered proximal to the
pylorus was well tolerated and resulted in fewer complications than
parenteral nutrition.42 In another study of 34 dogs with pancreatitis,
feeding within 48 hours of hospitalization had a positive impact on
return to voluntary intake and reduced the incidence of GI signs.43
In general, dogs with pancreatitis that do not vomit should be fed
orally as soon as possible. In dogs that do not vomit but are
anorectic, some form of a feeding tube should be used. In dogs with
severe vomiting, feeding tube placement should be delayed.
There is currently no evidence to support the use of postpyloric
feeding in either humans or animals with acute pancreatitis.36,42-44
A nasoesophageal tube is easily placed and does not require general
anesthesia (ch. 81). Placement of an esophagostomy tube requires a
short general anesthesia and represents an excellent option for dogs
with pancreatitis (ch. 81).45 Complications are uncommon.
Gastrostomy and jejunostomy tube placement require more invasive
procedures and might be associated with more complications.
There is currently no evidence-based information regarding the
appropriate diet that should be fed to dogs with pancreatitis.
Traditionally, feeding a low-fat diet is generally recommended,
although the ideal fat content of the diet has not been determined. It
is also recommended that feeding be introduced gradually over 3-4
days until resting energy requirements (RER) are met.

Analgesic Therapy
Although pain is reported to occur in only a fraction of dogs with
pancreatitis,3,4 it is believed to be present to various degrees in
virtually all dogs with pancreatitis. Pain induces several physiologic
changes, including decreased appetite, decreased GI motility,
decreased regional blood flow to several abdominal organs
(including the pancreas), and it may induce a catabolic state (ch. 6).
Thus, analgesic therapy should be an important component of the
management of dogs with pancreatitis, even when pain is not
clinically apparent.

Manifestations of pain in dogs with pancreatitis can range from
mild to severe. Pain management in dogs with pancreatitis is
typically achieved by opioid administration. Administration of an
injectable opioid such as buprenorphine (0.01-0.03 mg/kg, IV, IM,
or SC q4-8h), fentanyl (0.005-0.01 mg/kg, IV, IM or SC q2h;
constant rate infusion [CRI] 0.002-0.006 mg/kg/h), or meperidine
(2-5 mg/kg, IM or SC q2-4h) is effective and provides fast results.
Butorphanol (0.2-0.4 mg/kg, IV or SC, q4-6h) can be used in cases
with mild to moderate pain. Fentanyl patches (patch size is based on
patient size, every 3 to 4 days) are safe and practical, but they should
be used only after analgesia has been achieved by use of injectable
opioids, because it takes longer for transdermal application to
achieve analgesia. Multimodal analgesic therapy may be indicated in
some cases with severe pain (ch. 6). The effectiveness and safety of
nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) is questionable in
dogs with acute pancreatitis and this class of drugs ideally should be
avoided as these patients are often dehydrated or hypovolemic and
therefore at risk for GI ulceration or renal injury.

Antiemetic Therapy (ch. 48)
Antiemetic therapy is indicated in the majority of dogs with acute
pancreatitis. The need for antiemetic therapy is obvious in cases
where vomiting is present, but antiemetic therapy may also be
indicated in patients that are anorectic. Nausea is believed to
contribute to anorexia and weight loss and may lead to prolonged
hospitalization and a worse prognosis.
Maropitant (1 mg/kg, PO or SC q24h), a neurokinin-1 receptor
antagonist, is a very potent and safe antiemetic that is often used as a
first-line antiemetic in dogs with pancreatitis. There is also evidence
that maropitant has analgesic properties, making this drug very
attractive for use in pancreatitis patients. Furthermore, recent
evidence in experimental models of pancreatitis have suggested that
maropitant may also have anti-inflammatory properties.46 Other
good antiemetic choices include 5-HT3 antagonists such as
ondansetron (0.1-0.2 mg/kg, slow IV, q6-12h). Dopaminergic
antagonists (e.g., metoclopramide 0.2-0.5 mg/kg, IV, IM, SQ, or PO,
q6-8h) are considered less effective in treating nausea and vomiting,
but might be useful in enhancing upper GI motility; a constant-rate

infusion of metoclopramide (1-2 mg/kg/day IV) may be more
effective than intermittent dosing. In cases of intractable vomiting,
combinations of different antiemetics can be used.

Appetite Stimulants
Dogs with acute pancreatitis often have a reduced appetite. Many of
these animals have nausea, leading to anorexia (ch. 17). Thus,
treatment with an antiemetic may have a positive impact on appetite,
but many patients remain hyporexic. These patients may benefit
from an appetite stimulant. In hospitalized patients, capromorelin is
likely the most effective treatment option for dogs (3 mg/kg PO
q24h).47 Mirtazapine (0.5-1.5 mg/kg PO q24h, not to exceed 30
mg/dog/d) may also be effective and might also have antiemetic
properties but is less commonly used in dogs than in cats.

Antibiotic Therapy
Many veterinarians routinely treat dogs with pancreatitis with
antibiotics, but there is little scientific evidence for such practice.
There is currently very limited information regarding the role of
bacteria in canine pancreatitis. In rare cases, clinically important
infectious complications of pancreatitis may occur (e.g., aspiration
pneumonia [ch. 217], cystitis [ch. 308], infected pancreatic fluid
accumulation) and can be associated with a poor prognosis.
Therefore, broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., cefotaxime,
enrofloxacin, marbofloxacin) are recommended in cases where
infectious complications have been identified or are highly
suspected.

Glucocorticoids
Glucocorticoids were once believed to cause pancreatitis in both
humans and dogs.48,49 However, the scientific basis for this
hypothesis is weak and in humans, glucocorticoids are no longer
considered a risk factor for pancreatitis.50 A recent, non-controlled
study in 45 client-owned dogs suggested that 1 mg/kg prednisolone
SC q24h, given from diagnosis to discharge, decreased
hospitalization time, time for decrease of serum C-reactive protein

concentration, and 1-month survival.51 However, further studies are
needed before routine use of corticosteroids in dogs with severe
acute pancreatitis can be recommended.

Surgical Treatment
Experience with surgical treatment of pancreatitis in dogs is limited.
In general, surgical treatment is not indicated in most dogs with
pancreatitis. Surgery might be indicated in cases where pancreatitis
is complicated by an infected fluid accumulation. In addition,
surgical treatment may be indicated in some cases with a suspicion
for complete EHBDO (ch. 273) due to pancreatitis. However, in one
study, the majority (94%) of dogs with EHBDO due to pancreatitis
survived without surgical intervention, suggesting that medical
management alone may be sufficient in most patients.52

Other Management Strategies
No studies have evaluated the benefit of gastric acid suppression in
dogs with pancreatitis. The 2018 American College of Veterinary
Internal Medicine consensus statement on the use of gastric acid
suppressants in dogs and cats states that “There is no evidence that
acid suppression treatment is beneficial or indicated in the
management of dogs or cats with pancreatitis, unless the animal has
concurrent evidence of gastroduodenal ulceration and erosion.”53
Fuzapladib is a leukocyte function-associated antigen 1 antagonist
that prevents the extravasation of neutrophils from the capillaries
and thus the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps and ARDS.
Fuzapladib has received full approval in Japan and conditional
approval in the USA for the treatment of acute pancreatitis in dogs.
In an unpublished proof-of-concept study, fuzapladib dramatically
decreased mortality in dogs with experimentally induced
pancreatitis. Two other randomized clinical trials, also yet
unpublished, confirmed this beneficial effect of fuzapladib in dogs
with severe pancreatitis. Publication of these studies in the primary
literature and further randomized clinical trials in both dogs and cats
will be crucial before fuzapladib can be recommended for standard
therapy.

A plethora of other therapeutic agents, including but not limited to
dopamine, H1 histamine receptor antagonists, octreotide, NSAIDs,
somatostatin, anticholinergics, and antioxidants, could potentially be
useful for the management of canine pancreatitis. However, there is
currently no clinical evidence that any of these agents are beneficial
in spontaneous cases of pancreatitis in dogs. Thus, the authors
currently do not recommend the use of any of these agents until
more evidence on their efficacy and safety is available.

MANAGEMENT OF MILD CHRONIC
PANCREATITIS
Chronic pancreatitis is usually considered to be mild and it can be
managed on an outpatient basis in most cases. As for severe
pancreatitis, the presence of possible risk factors, such as
hypertriglyceridemia or hypercalcemia, should be evaluated and
managed accordingly if identified. Many dogs with chronic
pancreatitis show hyporexia or even anorexia. These patients may
benefit from an antiemetic, such as a NK1-antagonist (e.g.,
maropitant) or 5-HT3 antagonist (e.g., ondansetron). Also, an
appetite stimulant, such as mirtazapine (0.5-1.5 mg/kg PO q24h, not
to exceed 30 mg/dog/d) or capromorelin (3 mg/kg PO q24h) may be
useful.47 Analgesic treatment (e.g., tramadol, buprenorphine,
gabapentin) may be indicated in patients that appear to have
abdominal pain (ch. 6). Finally, the use of an ultra-low-fat diet (i.e.,
a diet containing less than 20 g of fat per 1000 kcal) is generally
recommended.
Many dogs with chronic pancreatitis have concurrent chronic
inflammatory enteropathy (ch. 262), hepatitis (ch. 270), and/or
diabetes mellitus (ch. 291), which need to be properly diagnosed
and managed accordingly.
In dogs, as in humans, there is some evidence that an autoimmune
mechanism might play a role in patients with chronic pancreatitis.
One report identified positive IgG4 staining of plasma cells in
English Cocker Spaniels, but also in some other breeds.54 In a case
report, a dog with chronic pancreatitis, poorly-regulated diabetes

mellitus, and atopy showed a swift response to cyclosporine
treatment.55 Therefore, some dogs with chronic pancreatitis may
benefit from immunosuppressive therapy with corticosteroids or
cyclosporine. However, this approach should probably be reserved
for patients that do not respond to other management strategies.

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis for dogs with pancreatitis depends on the severity of
the disease. Mild cases usually have a good prognosis, and if
recurrent episodes of pancreatitis do not occur, these animals
typically live for long periods of time. In contrast, the prognosis for
dogs with severe pancreatitis is usually guarded. The mortality
associated with severe acute pancreatitis is high and the
development of systemic or pancreatic complications (e.g.,
pancreatic fluid accumulation) or concurrent diseases (e.g., diabetes
mellitus or kidney disease) further contributes to a worse outcome.
Mortality rates in patients with more severe forms of acute
pancreatitis have been reported to be 20% to 42%.49,56
It is unknown if dogs that have a single episode of pancreatitis are
at risk for developing chronic or recurrent acute pancreatitis. The
prognosis for dogs with chronic or recurrent acute pancreatitis is
difficult to predict and depends on the severity of each acute
exacerbation of the disease. Unfortunately, no accurate method has
been reported to date for the prediction of the outcome of dogs with
spontaneous pancreatitis, and the prognosis should be evaluated on
an individual basis. Recently, the canine acute pancreatitis severity
scoring system has shown promise in some studies in dogs with
severe acute pancreatitis.57,58
