CLIENT INFORMATION
Pancreatitis in Dogs: Diagnosis and
Management
Pancreatitis is an inflammation of the pancreas. Unlike humans, the
cause of this condition is usually unknown in dogs, although in some
cases, consumption of high-fat foods or severely increased lipid
concentrations in the blood can cause pancreatitis. The symptoms in
dogs with pancreatitis can vary greatly depending on the severity of
the disease. While some dogs may not show any clinical signs, others
may show mild signs, such as not consistently wanting to eat or not
willing to play, and others may show more severe clinical signs, such
as vomiting, reduced appetite, and abdominal pain. The latter group
of patients should be considered an emergency and should be
brought to a veterinarian as soon as possible as life-threatening
complications can develop quickly and treatment success often
depends on an early diagnosis. Also, while vomiting and abdominal
pain could be due to severe pancreatitis, they could also be due to
other diseases, and it is crucial for the veterinarian to definitively
diagnose or rule-out pancreatitis so that the dog can receive the most
effective treatment possible.
While there is no specific therapy that is proven to treat such
patients with acute severe pancreatitis, your veterinarian will quickly
establish supportive measures that will prevent pancreatitis from
worsening and complications from developing. Typically, dogs with
acute severe pancreatitis need to be hospitalized and treatment
includes intravenous fluids, nutritional support, pain medications,
and drugs that will stop vomiting. Other measures or medications
will be necessary depending on the condition of your dog.
There is also no specific treatment for milder forms of chronic
pancreatitis, but your veterinarian will first make a definitive
diagnosis, then evaluate your dog for any potential risk factors, and
determine whether your dog has any concurrent conditions (such as
an inflammation of the liver or the gut, or diabetes mellitus). If any
of these are identified there may be special treatments that become
necessary.
Dogs that recover from acute pancreatitis or dogs that have
chronic pancreatitis typically need to be fed an ultra-low-fat diet,

which your veterinarian can recommend and prescribe for you. It is
important to note that in addition to exclusively feeding this
prescription diet you will also need to pay close attention to anything
else your dog maybe ingesting, such as treats from you or food items
picked up from other individuals. These all must be low in fat, such
as vegetables, fruits, or low-fat treats. You can even prepare
homemade low-fat treats using recipes your veterinarian or a
veterinary nutritionist can provide for you. You should expect to see
your veterinarian regularly to make sure he/she can monitor the
progress of your dog’s condition. Rechecks depend on disease
severity, but generally they are initially scheduled every 2-3 weeks,
and become less frequent as your dog’s condition improves. In some
patients with chronic disease, additional measures, such as
immunosuppression, will be needed and unfortunately, there are
some dogs that will slowly progress despite the best efforts of your
veterinary health care team and yourself.
Panagiotis G. Xenoulis (Karditsa, Greece; College Station, Texas;
Athens, Greece) and Jörg M. Steiner (College Station, Texas)

PREVALENCE

Pancreatitis in cats, previously considered rare (with a prevalence
<3.5%), is now recognized as a moderately frequent condition
following development of serologic testing, imaging modalities, and a
necropsy study.1,2 The overall prevalence of pancreatitis was 67%
(chronic 76%, acute 9%, acute and chronic 15%) among necropsied
cats regardless of cause of death. Since 45% of the necropsied cats
with pancreatitis were apparently healthy, using the histopathologic
definition of pancreatitis may have been too broad, causing some
cats with insignificant changes to be included.1 Regardless, the
prevalence is noteworthy.

DEFINITIONS AND DIAGNOSTIC
CHALLENGES
Acute pancreatitis, after resolving the inciting cause (Figure 278.1),
is an entirely reversible inflammatory condition.1 Chronic
pancreatitis is characterized by irreversible histopathologic changes
to exocrine pancreatic tissue, such as atrophy or fibrosis.1 Although
both forms can range from mild to severe, acute pancreatitis is
associated with more severe clinical signs, a worse short-term
prognosis,3-7 but a more favorable long-term prognosis with
appropriate management.2 Despite advances in pancreatic
biomarker testing, imaging, and histology, no single test has
excellent sensitivity and specificity, particularly in cats with lower
grade or early pancreatitis. However, combining clinical signs,
physical examination (PE) findings, biomarkers, imaging, absence of
an alternative disease, cytologic and/or histopathologic findings
increases the ability to make an accurate diagnosis. Pancreatitis in
cats, however, is often associated with comorbid diseases (ch. 225).2
It may be easier to identify etiopathogenetic factors not associated
with pancreatitis in cats than those which are.

FIGURE 278.1 Diagram depicting the unique
anatomy of the pancreas in cats, with a shared entry
of the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct into

ETIOPATHOGENESIS
Pancreatitis in cats has no age, sex, or breed predisposition.1 There is
no correlation with body condition score, high-fat meals, or drugs
(including steroids).1 Pancreatic intraoperative manipulation, with
or without biopsy or needle aspiration, was suggested to increase the
risk for pancreatitis but a study has indicated this to be unlikely.8,9
Pancreatic cancers have been associated with pancreatitis.10

Pancreatic cyto-histopathology may aid in detecting these cases.
Gastrointestinal (GI) foreign bodies may be associated with
pancreatitis; however, whether this is a comorbidity or a cause is
unknown. Abdominal trauma has been established as a cause.11
Hypercalcemia, organophosphate cholinesterase inhibitor
intoxication (topical fenthion), and idiosyncratic adverse drug
reactions can cause acute pancreatitis.12 Pancreatitis in cats has been
associated, but causality has not been determined, with several
parasite and viral infections13-15 and non-infectious diseases,
including diabetes mellitus, inflammatory bowel disease, hepatic
lipidosis, cholangitis, nephritis, and immune-mediated hemolytic
anemia.16-19 In people, autoimmune pancreatitis is recognized.20
Although initial studies have not confirmed a similar process in cats,
this mechanism is considered likely and may explain why some cats
respond to immunosuppression. Currently, >95% of acute or chronic
pancreatitis cases are idiopathic, a percentage likely to decrease with
further research.2

CLINICAL SIGNS AND PHYSICAL
EXAMINATION (PE)
Clinical signs and PE findings in cats with acute or chronic
pancreatitis are commonly nonspecific. Abnormal findings
potentially due to pancreatitis can also be caused by frequently
diagnosed comorbid disease(s) or complications. The most common
clinical signs include lethargy (incidence: 51-100%) and inappetence
(62-97%). Vomiting (35-52%) and weight loss (30-47%) are frequent.
Diarrhea (11-38%), dyspnea (6-20%), and polydipsia/polyuria
(PU/PD; 20%) are less common and often caused by non-pancreatic
conditions. Dehydration (37-92%), hypothermia (39-68%), and/or
hyperthermia/fever (7-26%) are common. Fever is more common
with acute pancreatitis or pancreatic complications. Apparent
abdominal pain is only reported in 10-30% of cases, but identifying
pain in cats is challenging.8,21 Resistance to direct pancreatic
palpation or to transducer pressure during ultrasound (US)
examination may be indicative of pain. Icterus (6-37%) and/or

cranial abdominal mass/organomegaly (4-23%) in cats with
pancreatitis can lead to a non-pancreatic disease being
prioritized.3,8,12,22-24 The clinical signs of pancreatitis are based on
retrospective studies in cats with severe forms of acute pancreatitis.
Thus, the clinical signs in less severe or more chronic pancreatitis are
likely even less specific and more obscure.

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT (CBC), SERUM
BIOCHEMISTRY PROFILE, URINALYSIS (UA)
After obtaining a medical history, including drug history, and
performing a PE, results of a CBC, biochemistry profile, and UA are
valuable for cats with clinical signs consistent with pancreatitis.
These test results permit screening for differential diagnoses,
pancreatic complications, and comorbidities.2 Abnormalities are
unpredictable. Hemoconcentration (17% of cats) secondary to
dehydration and an inflammatory leukogram characterized by
neutrophilia (46%) with a left shift or neutropenia (15%) may be
present, particularly with severe acute pancreatitis. Non-regenerative
anemia (38%) can be present, particularly with chronic pancreatitis.
Thrombocytopenia is rare in cats with severe acute pancreatitis
associated with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).2
Increases in liver enzyme activities (alanine transaminase 57%;
alkaline phosphatase 49%) and hyperbilirubinemia (58%) may be
present due to cholangitis, extrahepatic bile duct obstruction (ch.
273), and/or hepatic lipidosis (ch. 274).2 Hyperglycemia (45%),
associated with relative or absolute insulin deficiency, and, less
frequently, hypoglycemia (associated with a poor outcome),4 can be
seen with acute necrotizing pancreatitis.4,12 Increases in blood urea
nitrogen, creatinine, and symmetric dimethylarginine can be
secondary to dehydration, but when persistent or associated with
inappropriate urine concentration, may indicate acute kidney injury
(AKI). AKI has been linked to progressive pancreatic disease and a
poor prognosis.4 Hypoalbuminemia (36%), potentially associated

with an acute-phase protein decrease, is not frequent.
Hypercholesterolemia (72%) is common. Association between
pancreatitis and hypertriglyceridemia, as occurs in humans and
dogs, has not been identified in cats.2 Electrolyte abnormalities,
noted more commonly with severe forms of pancreatitis, may include
hypokalemia, hypochloridemia, hyponatremia, and hypocalcemia.2
Ionized hypocalcemia has inconsistently been associated with a poor
prognosis.3,25

PANCREAS-ASSOCIATED TESTING
The Ideal Biomarker
Biomarkers should be specific for pancreatitis, synthesized only by
pancreatic acinar cells, not present in non-pancreatic tissue, stable,
detectable in an easily obtained biologic sample (e.g., blood or
urine), and cost-effective. Pancreatic acinar cells secrete a variety of
digestive enzymes (e.g., amylase, lipase, DNAse, and RNAse) and
inactive pre-forms of digestive enzymes (i.e., zymogens, e.g.,
trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, and
prophospholipase).2 However, only small amounts of these
chemicals reach the vascular space, are stable, and not scavenged by
inhibitors.

Amylase, Trypsin-Like Immunoreactivity (TLI)
Increases in serum amylase activity in cats with acute pancreatitis
were not common in one study of cats with spontaneous
pancreatitis,2 with poor diagnostic sensitivity and tissue specificity.2
A species-specific immunoassay for feline TLI (fTLI), which
measures trypsinogen, trypsin, and likely some trypsin bound by
protease inhibitors, was developed and analytically validated.
Although increased serum fTLI concentrations were associated with
acute pancreatitis in cats, this finding is nonspecific (sensitivity: 3086%). Increases in fTLI have been identified with chronic
enteropathy, GI lymphoma, and decreased glomerular filtration
rates.2,25 Since trypsinogen is produced by pancreatic acinar cells,

the primary utility of fTLI is screening for exocrine pancreatic
insufficiency (ch. 279), which can be secondary to chronic
pancreatitis and subsequent pancreatic insufficiency. Results of
urinary trypsinogen activation peptide, a byproduct of trypsinogen
activation, are inconsistent and lack commercial availability.

Pancreatic Lipases
Lipases are present in large quantities, not rapidly cleared, and have
been evaluated. However, in addition to pancreatic lipase, gastric,
hepatic, and lipoprotein lipases, as well as pancreatic lipase-related
protein 2 can be present and influence results. Despite use of various
substrates, including 1,2-diglycerides, triolein, and 1,2-o-dilaurylrac-glycero glutaric acid-(6′-methylresorufin) ester (DGGR;
Precision PSL, Antech Laboratories, Fountain Valley, CA), none are
specific for pancreatic lipase.26 In a study of 12 cats with acute
pancreatitis, none had increases in serum lipase activity when
measured using 1,2-diglyceride as a substrate.27
Several species-specific immunoassays for serum feline pancreatic
lipase (fPL) immunoreactivity have been developed. The “Spec fPL”
has been validated as specific and sensitive for the diagnosis of
pancreatitis2,28 with higher sensitivity for moderate to severe
pancreatitis (100%) than for mild (54%).25 The Spec fPL has higher
positive predictive values (90%) than negative predictive values
(76%).29 At least 2 in-clinic assays are commercially available: SNAP
fPL (IDEXX Laboratories, Westbrook, ME) and VCheck fPL
(Bionote, Hwaseong, Korea). The SNAP fPL has been shown to
correlate well with the Spec fPL, as either “normal” or “abnormal.”2
As in dogs, other inflammatory conditions (e.g., chronic enteropathy,
peritonitis) may be associated with pancreatic inflammation and an
increase in serum fPLI concentration.
Studies have compared results of pancreatic biomarkers, US,
and/or histologic features. Agreement between DGGR-lipase (cutoff,
26 U/L) and Spec fPL (cutoff, >5.3 mcg/L) has a reported kappa of
0.681 and 0.7032, “good” for subjective diagnostic modalities but
considered less than ideal for objective modalities.28 Using the same
cutoff values, there was poor agreement comparing pancreatic

histologic findings and DGGR-based catalytic assay results or Spec
fPL (kappa = 0.06 and kappa = 0.10, respectively).28 There was poor
agreement comparing US “diagnosis” of pancreatitis and DGGRlipase (cutoff, 26 U/L) or Spec fPL (cutoff, >5.4 mcg/L), kappa =
0.221 and kappa = 0.264, respectively.28 In that study, the best
agreement was between increased DGGR-lipase or Spec fPL with
hypoechoic or heteroechoic pancreatomegaly.28

IMAGING
Abdominal US
US is the most commonly used imaging modality for evaluating the
pancreas of cats, also allowing visualization of the GI tract, liver, and
biliary system. A non-pancreatic condition may be diagnosed and
prioritized for treatment.30 Using high-frequency transducers (>7.5
MHz), patient compliance, and ultrasonographer experience likely
influence imaging results and value (

Video 278.1). Normal

pancreas is similar in echogenicity to the liver and isoechoic or
hypoechoic to surrounding mesentery, with a uniform, homogenous
echotexture, and smooth capsular margin. US findings in cats with
pancreatitis are likely dependent on multiple variables, e.g., presence
of acute, chronic, or acute-on- chronic pancreatitis, duration of
disease (i.e., imaging early in the onset), distribution of pancreatitis
(focal vs. diffuse), and complications of pancreatitis (e.g., regional
duodenal inflammation).
A single or combination of minimal US findings are not sufficient
for diagnosing pancreatitis. Based on a correlation study,28
hypoechoic or heteroechoic pancreatomegaly (>0.6 cm right lobe, >1
cm left lobe and body) is associated with increased serum lipase
activities (i.e., as measured by DGGR-lipase and Spec fPL) and is a
likely US finding of pancreatitis (

Video 278.1).2 Additionally,

hyperechoic peripancreatic mesentery and peripancreatic effusion,
pancreatic lymph node enlargement, and duodenal corrugation or
distention may be observed in cats with acute pancreatitis.2 Some

cats with acute pancreatitis have a normal pancreatic US; however,
US repeated over time often detects abnormalities.
Irregular pancreatic capsular margins, dilation of the pancreatic
(normal 0.7-2.5 mm) or common bile duct, and/or hyperechoic
pancreatic echogenicity are observed in cats with chronic
pancreatitis22,28,34 (Figure 278.2); however, positive or negative
predictive values for these findings have not been established and
such changes may be age-related (i.e., dilation of the pancreatic duct
occurs in older cats) or secondary to previous disease. US is a poor
diagnostic tool for assessing chronicity.22 Sterile pancreatic fluid
accumulation (previously termed pancreatic pseudocyst) and
nodules (from nodular hyperplasia) can be incidental findings in
older cats.2 However, they may also be present in cats with infected
fluid accumulations or pancreatic cancer, even though these
conditions are considered far less common than pancreatitis.
Cytologic evaluation of US-guided fine-needle aspirates (FNAs) or
histologic evaluation of tissue samples are needed to discriminate
these conditions.2 Results of US sensitivity in diagnosing pancreatitis
in cats have ranged between 11-67%, with a specificity of 73%, a
negative predictive value of 57%, and a positive predictive value of
80%.2 Considering advancements in US technology and training, the
accuracy is likely higher.

FIGURE 278.2 Longitudinal plane abdominal
ultrasound image of the right pancreatic lobe
(arrows) in a cat with chronic pancreatitis. The
ultrasound was performed with a high-resolution
linear array transducer. The pancreas is enlarged (1.1
cm; yellow line), diffusely heteroechoic, and with an
irregular capsular margin, but a relatively normal
peripancreatic echogenicity.

Radiology
Abdominal radiography has low sensitivity and specificity and
provides limited value in diagnosing cats with pancreatitis.2
Radiographs are commonly used to evaluate cats with acute vomiting
and suspected of a GI foreign body. Although not specific, loss of

abdominal detail in the cranial abdomen or a mass effect should
raise concern for pancreatitis and lead to further diagnostics.2

Computed Tomography (CT), Magnetic Resonance
Imaging (MRI)
Multiphase contrast-enhanced CT is often used in people with
suspected pancreatitis and has been evaluated in normal and
suspected pancreatitis cats (

Video 278.2).2 The normal pancreas

enhances homogenously on arterial, portal, and delayed-phase scans
and is hypo- or isoattenuating to the liver and spleen on pre-contrast
scans.2 The diagnostic accuracy of CT is not superior to US. MRI
scans were evaluated in normal cats and those with suspected
pancreatitis.2 The normal pancreas is T1 hyperintense and T2
isointense to hypointense, while in pancreatitis, T1 hypointensity and
T2 hyperintensity of the parenchyma, pancreatomegaly, pancreatic
duct dilation, contrast enhancement, or peripancreatic
hyperintensity have been reported.2 Neither CT nor MRI are
commonly used for diagnosing pancreatitis in cats.

CYTOLOGY (CH. 85)
US-guided pancreas FNA is minimally invasive, cost-effective, and
safe to screen for etiologies of pancreatitis, including cancer or
complications, e.g., secondarily-infected necrosis. Quick and gentle
sample smearing is essential since pancreatic acinar cells are fragile
and deteriorate quickly. In one study, diagnostic samples were
obtained in 67% of cases.31 Cytologic evaluations from a cat with
acute pancreatitis can reveal pancreatic acinar and ductal cells,
inflammatory cells (predominantly neutrophils with variable degrees
of degeneration), amorphous necrotic debris, and refractile
crystalline material.2 Peripancreatic fluid accumulation and ascites
often reveal a high-protein transudate (modified transudate) or
exudate. Screening for intracellular organisms is important, and an
aerobic bacterial culture is beneficial for organism identification.

Cytologic preparations from cats with chronic pancreatitis are often
poorly cellular due to pancreatic fibrosis and may not be diagnostic;
however, they may reveal lymphoplasmacytic inflammation.
Limitations of pancreatic cytologic evaluations include limited
sample size, missing a localized pancreatic lesion or disease process,
and the challenge of distinguishing dysplastic epithelial cells
associated with pancreatitis from an inflamed pancreatic
carcinoma.2

HISTOLOGY
Surgical or laparoscopic pancreatic biopsies are low-risk procedures
for obtaining tissue that overcome the diagnostic limitations of
cytology. Histologic evaluation of tissue is considered the gold
standard for diagnosing pancreatitis.1,22 Since acute and chronic
pancreatitis can have a multifocal, patchy distribution1,2,12 and the
macroscopic appearance of the pancreas does not always correlate
with histologic findings, obtaining multiple biopsies is ideal.1,2 If
only a single biopsy is obtained, the left lobe has provided the highest
yield for diagnosing pancreatitis.1 A semiquantitative histopathologic
scoring system for pancreatitis in cats, describing inflammatory cell
infiltration, edema, necrosis, fibrosis, amyloid, and/or cystic acinar
degeneration/acinar atrophy has been proposed and modified.1,2
However, correlation with clinical findings and prognosis remain
unclear,7 especially with mild/low-grade histologic findings.2 With
neutrophilic inflammation and edema, acute pancreatitis has been
classified as “acute necrotizing pancreatitis” with significant necrosis
and “acute suppurative pancreatitis” without necrosis, based on the
classification in humans.1,2,12 Chronic pancreatitis is characterized
by lymphocytic or lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, mild fibrosis
(Figure 278.3), and acinar atrophy. Potentially, there are retention
cysts (i.e., microscopic intraparenchymal cysts) or extensive
periductal fibrosis, leading to localized stenosis and cyst formation,
with squamous metaplasia of the ductal epithelium.1,2 As with
pancreatic cytology, neoplasia or infectious causes can be associated

with pancreatitis.10 Despite the apparent benefits of obtaining
pancreatic histologic results, it is rarely performed as a diagnostic
test for pancreatitis since most cases can be diagnosed in a less
invasive manner.

TREATMENT
GENERAL STRATEGIES (CH. 119)
Initial management considerations are often dependent on the
duration and severity of clinical signs, suspected or known
comorbidities, hydration status, and apparent abdominal pain. Many
cats with mild to moderate clinical signs can be managed as
outpatients, recognizing that deterioration may occur. Concurrent
management of comorbidities, if present, is important to avoid
treatment failure. For idiopathic pancreatitis, management is
predominantly supportive and nonspecific,2,8,24,32 with
recommendations extrapolated from humans, dogs, expert opinion,
and/or experimentally-induced pancreatitis in cats.2,14,33 Hydration,
nutritional support, pain management, and control of vomiting and
apparent nausea are central tenets of management.2

FLUID THERAPY (CH. 120)
Dehydration and secondary hypovolemia are common in cats with
severe acute pancreatitis. The duration of illness before presentation
to the hospital is directly proportional to odds of death, in part due to
hypovolemia.4 Subcutaneous or intravenous crystalloid fluid therapy
reverses dehydration and can be used to correct electrolyte
imbalances. No ideal crystalloid fluid or rate of administration is
recognized for cats. Early aggressive achievement of hydration with
lactated Ringer’s solution in humans is reported to expedite clinical
improvement.2 Establishing normovolemia may limit pancreatic
damage by improving perfusion and oxygen delivery. Avoiding
overhydration is prudent, and close monitoring is important (e.g.,
body weight rechecks, thoracic auscultation, thoracic US). Fluid

therapies chosen must consider and be adjusted for comorbidities
(ch. 223).

FIGURE 278.3 Histopathologic image of normal
feline pancreas (left) and that of a feline pancreas
with chronic pancreatitis (right). The overlay shows
scores based on a suggested histologic pancreatic
grading system for cats. Scale bar = 50 microns.

NUTRITION (CHS. 81 AND 153)
Inappetence is one of the most common clinical signs in cats with
acute or chronic pancreatitis and can result in dehydration,
malnutrition, an impaired GI barrier, and compromised immune
function. Prolonged inappetence can lead to hepatic lipidosis (ch.
274), further increasing morbidity and mortality. Nutritional
support plays a central role in managing acute pancreatitis in
humans and cats.2 In people with severe acute pancreatitis, early
(within 24 hours of admission) enteral nutrition is recommended to
reduce risk of infected pancreatic necrosis and the incidence of
multiple organ failure.2 Prolonged fasting or parenteral nutrition is
not routinely recommended in people, dogs, or cats.2

Appetite stimulants are often effective in restoring voluntary food
intake in cats with mild to moderate clinical pancreatitis.
Mirtazapine (oral, transdermal) and capromorelin (oral) are the
most commonly prescribed appetite stimulants. “Older” therapies,
including cyproheptadine, are occasionally beneficial.2 Mirtazapine,
evaluated in healthy and inappetent cats, is generally well-tolerated
(particularly the transdermal formulation and dosing), efficacious,
and may have antiemetic activity. However, adverse effects (e.g.,
vocalization, agitation, vomiting, abnormal gait/ataxia,
tremors/trembling, hypersalivation, tachypnea, tachycardia, and
lethargy) have been reported with higher dosages. Capromorelin oral
solution has also been evaluated in healthy and inappetent cats, is
generally well-tolerated and efficacious, and is approved for cats with
chronic kidney disease in the USA.2 Reported adverse reactions
include vomiting and hypersalivation; both have been more frequent
in males.
If inappetence persists for >48 hours despite multimodal medical
therapy (including appetite stimulants), enteral nutrition with a
feeding tube should be instituted (ch. 81).2,6 In people, nasojejunal
and nasogastric feeding tubes have not changed outcomes; however,
similar studies have not been performed in cats. Nasoesophageal,
nasogastric, esophageal, less commonly gastric, and rarely
nasojejunal feeding tubes are utilized in the author’s practice.
Nasogastric tubes have the added benefit of permitting gastric
suctioning in cats with gastric ileus and fluid accumulation, which is
often used and beneficial. While there have been no studies in cats,
suctioning in people with pancreatitis has worsened gastric
distension, gastroesophageal reflux, pain, and nausea.
Dietary requirements of cats with acute pancreatitis are unknown.
The focus is encouraging an inappetent or anorectic cat to eat, rather
than offering an “ideal” diet. Highly digestible “GI diets” are
recommended. Diets for cats with pancreatitis should contain
adequate arginine and methionine to help avoid hepatic lipidosis
(ch. 148). Diets should provide adequate protein to prevent proteinenergy malnutrition and lean muscle loss (chs. 151-153).2

PAIN MANAGEMENT (CH. 6)
Cats with pancreatitis may exhibit signs of pain. Inappetent cats
without clear indicators of pain should undergo pain management.2
Opioids are often first-line analgesics for cats with pancreatitis,2 with
oral/transbuccal buprenorphine, gabapentin, and, less commonly,
tramadol, used for mild to moderate clinical pancreatitis and
methadone or fentanyl reserved for severe pain.

CONTROLLING VOMITING (CH. 48)
Antiemetics should be given to vomiting cats and inappetent cats
without clear indicators of apparent nausea to encourage voluntary
eating before tube feeding. Maropitant citrate is efficacious,
commonly used, and has additional benefits, e.g., potential visceral
analgesic and anti-inflammatory activities.2 Ondansetron has been
used as a first-line antiemetic or combined with maropitant. Despite
these drugs, some cats with pancreatitis continue to vomit,
potentially secondary to functional gastroparesis or ileus, but other
causes (i.e., GI foreign bodies) need to be considered. Prokinetics can
improve GI motility. Erythromycin and cisapride are efficacious and
have a gastric prokinetic effect in cats.2 Metoclopramide, particularly
given as a constant rate infusion, increases gastric emptying and
decreases gastric atony.34

ANTIBIOTICS
In humans, dogs, and cats, antibiotic therapy is not recommended in
non-complicated cases of pancreatitis.2 This recommendation is
based on understanding that mild to moderate pancreatitis does not
have a bacterial etiology in most cats, antibiotic usage may be
associated with side-effects (i.e., vomiting and inappetence), and the
potential for development of multi-drug resistance (ch. 7). With
infectious comorbidities (i.e., cholangitis, urinary tract infection, and
aspiration pneumonia), complications of pancreatitis (pancreatic

abscess, infected pancreatic necrosis in 35% of cats with moderate to
severe pancreatitis by fluorescence in situ hybridization), or CBC
findings suggestive of sepsis, antibiotic therapy, ideally guided by
bacterial culture and sensitivity testing, should be provided.
2,8,32,35,36

GLUCOCORTICOIDS, CYCLOSPORINE
Routine corticosteroid therapy is also not recommended in cats with
non-complicated pancreatitis.2 However, it is indicated in treating
sterile comorbidities (e.g., chronic inflammatory enteropathy or
cholangitis; ch. 225). Glucocorticoids have been shown to improve
outcomes in humans and dogs with acute pancreatitis, potentially by
treating critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency.37-39
However, their routine use in cats, considering the risk of enhancing
peripheral insulin resistance, congestive heart failure, and
immunosuppression, is not recommended.2 Initial evaluation of
cyclosporine treatment in cats with chronic pancreatitis was
associated with a decrease in Spec fPL concentrations; however,
additional work is needed to determine a clinical benefit.40

OTHER THERAPIES
Although beyond the scope of this chapter, in cats with severe
pancreatitis, management of vascular complications (e.g., fluidrefractory hypotension, electrolyte and acid-base imbalances,
hypocoagulability, and hypercoagulability), respiratory
complications (e.g., volume overload, congestive heart failure,
aspiration pneumonia, pulmonary thromboembolism) and in rare
cases, pancreatic surgery, can be critical to a successful recovery.2,4046

EXOCRINE PANCREATIC
INSUFFICIENCY
INTRODUCTION AND DEFINITIONS
Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) describes a syndrome that is
characterized by the insufficient synthesis and secretion of digestive
enzymes by the exocrine pancreas. The most common cause of EPI is
an absolute lack of pancreatic acinar cells that is due to destruction
of acinar cells secondary to chronic pancreatitis (both dogs and cats)
or depletion of acinar cells due to pancreatic acinar atrophy (PAA;
likely only in dogs). In either case, pancreatic digestive enzymes are
lacking in patients with EPI. In rare cases, a single enzyme may be
lacking, but lack of a single enzyme, even if complete, may not lead to
any clinical signs as digestion of most macronutrients is
characterized by redundancy and a great functional reserve.
However, isolated pancreatic lipase deficiency has been reported as a
cause of clinical signs of EPI in humans and in 1 dog and was highly
suspected in a few other dogs.1-3 Another infrequent cause of EPI is
an obstruction of the pancreatic duct by either a tumor, surgical
damage, or trauma, which can lead to lack of digestive enzymes in
the small intestinal lumen, despite normal acinar production.
Exocrine pancreatic aplasia or hypoplasia could also lead to clinical
signs of EPI. This could be suspected in patients diagnosed with EPI
at a very young age, but to date no case has been described in the
literature and the author of this chapter has only encountered a
single case in a kitten to date.

PHYSIOLOGY
The process of digestion of macronutrients is characterized by
redundancy and a large functional reserve. Redundancy is achieved
by each macronutrient being able to be digested by at least two and
sometimes even more independent processes. For example, dietary
fat can be broken down by pancreatic lipase or pre-duodenal lipase,
which in dogs and cats is gastric lipase. While in healthy humans and
dogs it has been estimated that approximately one-third of all dietary
fat is digested by gastric lipase, this value can vary among

individuals.4 This degree of redundancy translates into some animals
not showing any clinical signs of maldigestion even if one digestive
pathway is insufficient. Also, digestion is characterized by a large
functional reserve and it has been estimated in humans that >90% of
exocrine pancreatic function has to be lost before clinical signs of
maldigestion will ensue.5 These numbers are based on averages and
there may be a wide interindividual variability, but they do
demonstrate the large functional reserve of exocrine pancreatic
function.
The exocrine pancreas plays a central role in the digestion of all
macronutrients (

Video 279.1). While acinar cells synthesize and

secrete some enzymes in their active forms, such as amylase, lipase,
RNase, and DNase, others are synthesized as an inactive preform or
zymogen, such as trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase,
prophospholipase, procarboxypeptidase, and others. While
trypsinogen is activated to trypsin in the small intestine by
enteropeptidase, the other zymogens are in turn being activated by
trypsin. However, the impact of pancreatic secretions on digestion
reaches far beyond secretion of enzymes and zymogens. Acinar cells
also synthesize and secrete colipase, which is necessary to overcome
the lipase-inhibiting properties of bile salts. Also, the pancreatic duct
system secretes large amounts of pancreatic juice, which has
buffering capacity and thus is a crucial source of buffer for gastric
acid; without it, the gastric acid would irreversibly inhibit many of
the digestive enzymes and destroy the intestinal mucosa and
microbiome.

ETIOLOGY
The most common cause of EPI in both dogs and cats is chronic
pancreatitis, which is suspected to be the cause of EPI in nearly
100% of cats and in approximately slightly more than 50% of dogs
with EPI. In dogs, the majority of the remainder of EPI cases are
caused by PAA, which is almost exclusively seen in German
Shepherd Dogs, Rough-Coated Collies, and Eurasians.6,7 In addition,
an increased risk for EPI has been described for Cavalier King

Charles Spaniels, Shar Peis, and West Highland White Terriers.8
Interestingly, the age of onset is young adult for German Shepherd
Dogs, Rough-Coated Collies, and Shar Peis, while the age of onset in
other dog breeds is usually later in life. This suggests that Shar Peis
also may have PAA, but this has not been studied further as of yet.8,9
Several studies have suggested that PAA is inherited as an
autosomal recessive trait in German Shepherd Dogs and
Eurasians.10-12 However, the search for a definitive genetic marker
for this disease has been largely unsuccessful, even though scans of
the entire canine genome using a set of microsatellite markers and
single nucleotide polymorphisms revealed several regions that
appear to be associated with this condition.13 Interestingly, a test
breed of an affected male and an affected female German Shepherd
Dog only resulted in 2 of 6 of the offspring being affected through
their entire life, strongly suggesting against inheritance as a simple
autosomal recessive trait.14 Thus, this condition is likely polygenic
with the major histocompatibility complex on chromosome 12 being
of special interest.15 Another study has identified a DLA-DQB1
duplication as a risk allele.16
Other, less common causes of EPI in dogs and cats are obstruction
of the pancreatic duct due to neoplasia, parasites, or trauma,
pancreatic hypoplasia, or isolated lipase deficiency, but all of these
causes are exceptionally rare. Severe acute pancreatitis with
pancreatic necrosis has been described as causing EPI in humans.
The hypothesis that has been proposed is that pancreatic necrosis
leads to irreversible damage of acinar tissue, but this has not yet
been described in either dogs or cats.17,18 Other proposed causes of
EPI in people are type I or type II diabetes mellitus (DM),
inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, pediatric intestinal
transplantation, human immunodeficiency virus infection, total
gastrectomy, Sjögren’s syndrome, aging, tobacco usage, critical
illness, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, or somatostatin analog therapy,
but the possible pathogenesis as well as a true cause-and-effect
relationship for most of these proposed causes is unclear.19-21 Also,
with the exception of DM and inflammatory bowel disease, none of
these has been suspected as a cause of EPI in small animals. More

importantly, many, if not most, of these proposed causes may be a
reflection of the poor positive predictive value of elastase 1,
commonly used as a diagnostic test for EPI in humans, rather than a
true association of EPI with these conditions.22 Finally, an
association of these conditions and EPI does not equal causality. For
example, both EPI and DM could be a result of chronic pancreatitis
without one causing the other.

PATHOGENESIS
As mentioned above, digestive enzymes and zymogens secreted by
pancreatic acinar cells are crucial for the digestion of all
macronutrients. When pancreatic acinar cells are lacking, regardless
of the cause, maldigestion ensues. Maldigestion leads to undigested
food components in the intestinal lumen, which can lead to loose
stools or diarrhea, and weight loss. Maldigestion also leads to
secondary intestinal dysbiosis (ch. 260), characterized by a decrease
in diversity and changes in abundances of various bacterial
species.23 Interestingly, these changes, while improving, did not
completely normalize with enzyme replacement therapy.23 Thus,
modulation of the intestinal microbiome may be a therapeutic option
for patients that do not respond to pancreatic enzyme replacement
therapy (PERT) and cobalamin supplementation alone. Also, rare
cases of EPI have been described with dogs and cats showing
neurologic signs. One cat was diagnosed with D-lactic acidosis, which
was hypothesized to be due to small intestinal dysbiosis and which
improved with PERT.24 Other patients have been hypothesized to
have neurological signs secondary to cobalamin deficiency.25
However, it has been suspected that clinical signs are not only due
to maldigestion, but that EPI also leads to malabsorption. This has
been hypothesized to be due to a lack of trophic factors normally
secreted by the exocrine pancreas that help maintain a normal
gastrointestinal (GI) mucosa.
The exocrine pancreas is the major source of intrinsic factor in
both dogs and cats (ch. 257).3,26 This is in sharp contrast to
humans, where intrinsic factor is mainly secreted by the gastric

mucosa. Since intrinsic factor is required for ileal cobalamin
absorption, EPI is frequently associated with cobalamin
malabsorption and hypocobalaminemia in dogs and cats. Indeed, in
one study, 82% of dogs with EPI had a decreased serum cobalamin
concentration, with 36% having marked hypocobalaminemia.27
Similarly, a retrospective study of 119 cats with EPI documented
hypocobalaminemia in 77% of them.28
As mentioned above the majority of both cats and dogs with EPI
are believed to develop the disease due to chronic pancreatic
inflammation (chs. 277, 278). Since pancreatic damage due to
inflammation does not spare the islets of Langerhans, DM can
develop concurrently. While some patients develop DM before EPI,
others develop them at the same time, and yet others develop EPI
before developing DM.29 This means that canine (ch. 291) or feline
(ch. 292) patients with DM should be screened for EPI if they are
losing weight and owners of patients with EPI should be educated on
the clinical signs of DM.

CLINICAL PRESENTATION
EPI can be subclinical and two large case series of German Shepherd
Dogs identified several dogs with severely decreased serum trypsinlike immunoreactivity (TLI) concentrations that did not have any
clinical signs.11,30 Some of the dogs underwent exploratory
laparotomy and pancreatic size was found to be severely
decreased.30 This is suspected to be due to the redundancy of
digestion of macronutrients mentioned above but is clinically of no
significance as animals with subclinical EPI do not need to be
diagnosed or treated. The most common clinical sign reported in
both dogs and cats with EPI is weight loss (Figures 279.1 and
279.2).28,31 Loose stools are also commonly observed (Figure
279.2, C), but watery diarrhea is less common.28,31,32 Often times,
patients have a poor hair coat and dogs with EPI are commonly
reported to have borborygmus and increased flatulence.28,32 Many
dogs and cats with EPI will show an increased appetite, while dogs

may even show coprophagia or pica.18,28 Thus, dogs that repeatedly
ingest foreign bodies and are thin should be investigated for possible
EPI. In cats, a greasy soiling of the hair coat in the perianal area can
be observed, but this is not a common finding.31 Some dogs and cats
with EPI have a decreased appetite that is believed to be due to
concurrent chronic inflammatory enteropathy (ch. 262) and has
been reported as a negative prognostic factor in dogs.28,33

DIAGNOSIS
Measurement of serum TLI concentration is the diagnostic test of
choice for both dogs and cats suspected of having EPI. Serum TLI
concentration is measured by species-specific assays. The TLI assay
measures the concentration of cationic trypsinogen, cationic trypsin,
and some cationic trypsin molecules bound to proteinase inhibitor
molecules. Under physiologic conditions, a certain amount of
trypsinogen is released into the vascular space and is detected by the
TLI assay. In patients with EPI, regardless of the cause, the amount
of trypsinogen released into the blood stream is severely decreased
(current cut-off values for a diagnosis of EPI: 2.5 mcg/L in dogs and
8.0 mcg/L in cats) to undetectable (

Video 279.1). In general,

serum TLI concentration is highly sensitive and specific for the
diagnosis of EPI in both dogs and cats. There are two special
scenarios, however, where serum TLI can be normal despite the
patient having EPI. The first is isolated pancreatic lipase deficiency,
which has been described in a single dog and suspected in 3
others.2,3 The second scenario is a patient with an obstructed
pancreatic duct. Such cases have not yet been described in the
literature, but a single dog with this condition has been identified (S.
Hill, personal communication, 2007). Pancreatic inflammation may
slightly increase serum TLI concentrations, but there have been no
cases of dogs and only few in cats where a diagnosis of EPI was
missed due to suspected residual pancreatic inflammation (P.
Xenoulis, personal communication, 2021).

There are other tests that have been recommended for the

turbidity test, the para-amino benzoic acid test, and fecal proteolytic
activity; however, none of them is considered useful for a diagnosis
of EPI for dogs or cats.34 Also, a fecal assay for the measurement of
pancreatic elastase is being marketed in Europe for the diagnosis of
EPI in dogs only. Initial studies showed an acceptable sensitivity and
specificity of this assay, but the estimated positive predictive value
was less than 60%.35,36 In another study, fecal elastase
concentration was shown to be associated with a high number of
false positive test results (23%).37 A follow-up study demonstrated
that dogs with a low fecal elastase concentration but a normal serum
canine TLI concentration had decreased serum cholecystokinin
(CCK) concentrations, suggesting that intestinal disease might be
associated with a decrease of CCK release from intestinal
enterochromaffin cells, leading to a false positive result.38 In
humans, fecal elastase is commonly used for the diagnosis of EPI.
However, it is widely recognized that this assay has a low positive
predictive value with many false positive diagnoses.22 Thus, a

suspected diagnosis of EPI based on a severely decreased fecal
elastase concentration must be verified by measurement of serum
TLI concentration to prevent a misdiagnosis. This is especially
important because management of EPI can be costly and despite the
good prognosis for patients with this disease, some owners
unfortunately elect euthanasia.

THERAPY
PERT is the mainstay of therapy for EPI.39,40 Pancreatic enzymes
can be replaced by several different products, a wide variety of which
is listed at epi4dogs.com.41 Dried pancreatic extract from pork
pancreas is by far the most common and effective means of PERT in
North America. Therapy is started with 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of dried
extract per 10 kg body weight and meal. After the patient completely
responds to therapy, the dosage can be slowly decreased until a
minimally effective dose has been reached. However, pancreatic
enzymes must be added to every meal. It is important to note that
the content of enzyme activity in the product may vary from
container to container and thus the minimally effective dose may
vary slightly over time. In Europe, micropelleted forms of pancreatic
enzyme supplements, which are considered state of the art treatment
for humans with EPI world-wide, are also commonly used in
veterinary patients.42 The capsules contain the micro-pelleted
product that protects pancreatic lipase from being irreversibly
inhibited by the low pH in the stomach, allowing a much lower dose
per meal. Recent studies have shown that these formulations work as
well as uncoated powder.43,44 Pancreatic enzymes are also available
as tablets and capsules but studies in humans and dogs have shown
that powder is preferable to these other formulations.40,45
Complications of enzyme supplementation are rare, but one study
reported 3 of 25 dogs being treated with pancreatic enzyme
supplements developing oral bleeding.46 When this occurs, a
coagulation profile should be evaluated (ch. 170) to exclude a
vitamin K-responsive coagulopathy, which has been reported in 2
cats with EPI.47 In case of a normal coagulation profile, the dosage of

pancreatic enzymes should be lowered. Two dogs in the study cited
above continued to do well on the lower dosage, but in 1 of the dogs
clinical signs did return.46 Also, switching the patient to a
micropelleted or other enzyme product may be an option. If a patient
refuses to consume the pancreatic powder mixed into the food, if
owners do not wish to feed pork products, or in the rare case of an
allergy to the porcine pancreatic powder, fresh raw pancreas from
various species can also be used.40 Beef, pork, sheep, and game
pancreas have all been used. One to 3 ounces (approximately 30 to
90 g) of raw pancreas replace 1 teaspoon of dried pancreatic extract.
The pancreas should be finely chopped, divided into portions for one
meal each, and immediately frozen. Frozen pancreatic tissue
maintains its enzymatic activity for long periods of time. Concerns
have been raised about the potential threat of infectious
contamination of such raw frozen pancreas. Theoretically, raw
bovine and ovine pancreas carries the risk of bovine spongiform
encephalopathy transmission and raw porcine pancreas carries the
risk of transmission of pseudorabies (Aujeszky’s disease). However,
these risks are more or less academic, as dried pancreatic powder
would carry the same risk. Game and ovine pancreas can be infested
with Echinococcus spp. and infestation with this parasite could
potentially cause significant disease and even death. This risk should
thus be discussed with the owner before initiating therapy with raw
pancreas from these sources. Preincubation of the food with the
pancreatic extract does not appear to be necessary to achieve a
therapeutic response, regardless of formulation or type of extract.
Some authors have recommended feeding a low-fat diet. However,
experimental studies have shown that in dogs with EPI treated with
pancreatic supplements, fat digestibility does not return to normal,
suggesting that fat restriction would only increase the risk of
deficiencies of fat-soluble vitamins and essential fatty acids.48 One
study did not find any benefit of feeding fat-restricted diets in dogs
with EPI.27 Also, two other studies did not reveal a significant effect
of diet on treatment success in dogs with EPI.49,50 However, this
does not mean that diet does not play a role in the optimal
management of dogs and cats with EPI. Instead, it means that the
optimal diet is not the same for each canine or feline patient with EPI

and several different diets may need to be trialed (ch. 153).51
However, diets with a high insoluble fiber content should be avoided
as dietary fiber may interfere with fat absorption.
As mentioned above, many patients with EPI are cobalamindeficient and thus every dog and cat with EPI should be evaluated for
possible cobalamin deficiency. While the measurement of serum
cobalamin concentration cannot provide an estimate of cobalamin
status on a cellular level, measurement of methylmalonic acid
(MMA) in serum is more expensive and only available on a limited
basis, and thus measurement of serum cobalamin concentration is
considered the routine tool for assessment of cobalamin status in
both dogs and cats. Based on the measurement of both cobalamin
and MMA in large numbers of dogs and cats, it is currently
recommended to provide cobalamin supplementation to any patient
with EPI if the patient has a serum cobalamin concentration <400
ng/L (which is in the low-normal range). Traditionally, cobalamin is
supplemented by weekly subcutaneous injections of cyanocobalamin
(250 mcg in cats and 250-1500 mcg in dogs, roughly based on body
weight). Hydroxocobalamin or methylcobalamin may also be used.
Doses are given weekly for 6 weeks, then one more dose after a
month, and a recheck of serum cobalamin concentration 1 month
later. However, daily oral cobalamin supplementation is equally
effective with 250 mcg in cats and 250-1500 mcg in dogs, roughly
based on body weight and given daily for 120 days, with a recheck 23 weeks after the last dose.52 Many formulations of oral cobalamin
supplements are commercially available, including tablets for human
use and one chew specifically made for use in dogs and cats, which is
flavored with a hydrolyzed chicken protein and can thus be used as a
treat. Many patients with EPI that have been treated appropriately
will have a normal or even supranormal serum cobalamin
concentration at the time of re-evaluation and cobalamin
supplementation can be discontinued, but many others need lifelong
supplementation. Serum concentrations of most fat-soluble vitamins
have also been shown to be decreased in dogs with EPI and can also
be assumed to be decreased in cats with this disease.49,53 However,
systematic vitamin supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins has not
been investigated in these patients and over-supplementation with
fat-soluble vitamins may cause side-effects. Anecdotal reports of

vitamin E supplementation (400-500 IU PO q24h for 1 month) are
available, but the beneficial effect of such therapy has not been
evaluated. Finally, blood taurine concentrations have been found to
be reduced in a subset of dogs with EPI and this might also hold true
for other amino acids.54 However, the clinical importance of this
finding remains to be determined. EPI is not a recognized
predisposing cause for taurine-deficient myocardial dysfunction (ch.
233).
Many patients with EPI will respond well to PERT and cobalamin
supplementation, if indicated. However, some patients may not
respond adequately to standard therapy. Potential causes of
treatment failure should be evaluated. The type, formulation, and
dosage of the enzyme supplement should be reviewed and if there is
any suspicion that enzyme replacement may be insufficient, the
protocol should be adjusted accordingly. Also, patients should be
evaluated for concurrent conditions, such as chronic inflammatory
enteropathy (chs. 225 and 262), DM (chs. 291 and 292), or small
intestinal dysbiosis (ch. 260). If there is no evidence of any
concurrent disease, a therapeutic trial with an antimicrobial agent
can be attempted. The treatment of choice is tylosin (Tylan powder,
25 mg/kg PO q12h for 6-8 weeks).
If patients still do not respond to treatment, a trial course of a
proton pump inhibitor can be administered. A large portion of
pancreatic lipase supplemented orally is irreversibly destroyed by the
low pH in the stomach.55 By increasing the pH in the stomach this
portion may decrease and the therapeutic response may improve.56
However, it must be noted that while an increase in gastric pH will
decrease the amount of pancreatic lipase being destroyed during
passage through the stomach, it also will increase the amount of
gastric lipase being irreversibly inactivated by the neutral pH with no
significant improvement in fat digestibility. However, a trial with
omeprazole at 0.7-1 mg/kg PO q12h can be attempted and may be
associated with significant improvement.
If none of these measures leads to control of the clinical signs, a
decrease in the dietary fat content may be effective. However, as
mentioned above, feeding a low-fat diet may be associated with
complications and should only be viewed as a last resort.

PROGNOSIS
EPI has traditionally been considered a lifelong condition, as
pancreatic acinar cells were generally considered to not be able to
regenerate. However, there are experimental data that suggest some
regenerative capacity of pancreatic acinar cells.57 Also, there are
anecdotal reports of isolated patients with EPI that do improve and
no longer require PERT.
One study has evaluated prognostic factors for dogs with EPI.27
The only factor associated with a poor outcome was marked
hypocobalaminemia, which was associated with a median survival
time of 1346 days compared to dogs without such marked
hypocobalaminemia of 2709 days (p = 0.012).27 In another study, a
serum cobalamin concentration <350 ng/L, being male, a decreased
appetite at diagnosis, or not receiving PERT were described as
independent risk factors for a decreased survival, though none of
these should be considered impactful enough to sway against
treatment.33 In general, most dogs and cats with EPI can be
successfully managed and will have a normal quality of life and a
normal life expectancy.

RARE CONDITIONS OF THE EXOCRINE
PANCREAS
EXOCRINE PANCREATIC NEOPLASIA
As is the case for any organ, the pancreas can also be affected by
neoplastic conditions; however, this is quite rare in dogs and cats.
Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAC) is one of the leading causes of
cancer death in humans worldwide. Conversely, it is rare in both
dogs and cats, though it appears to occur slightly more commonly in
cats than in dogs. Clinical presentation for dogs and cats with a
pancreatic adenocarcinoma is not distinguishable from that of
patients with chronic pancreatitis and patients often have subclinical
disease until late in the course. Clinical signs may include weight
loss, anorexia, vomiting, lethargy, diarrhea, and sometimes signs of
abdominal pain. Some cats with PAC have been reported to develop

paraneoplastic alopecia (ch. 12).58,59 Serum feline and canine
pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity concentrations are often
increased in cats and dogs with PAC as the tumor is often associated
with acinar cell damage and secondary inflammation.60,61 However,
since PAC is rare in both dogs and cats the impact of this is not
clinically relevant. Since abdominal ultrasound or computed
tomography (CT) in dogs and cats with pancreatitis is often
associated with a visible enlargement of the organ, imaging is often
not definitive in differentiating chronic pancreatitis from a
pancreatic adenocarcinoma, though imaging with contrast-enhanced
abdominal CT can identify the mass lesion as being wellvascularized, a hallmark feature of pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Both
cytological evaluation of a fine-needle aspirate as well as
histopathological evaluation of a pancreatic biopsy can confirm a
diagnosis of pancreatic adenocarcinoma. The prognosis for dogs and
cats with a PAC is poor and treatment is often supportive. Surgical
removal of an isolated pancreatic mass can be undertaken, but this is
rarely curative as diagnosis usually happens late in the course of the
disease. Chemotherapy and radiation therapy are largely
unsuccessful in treating PAC in dogs and cats. However, a single cat
with pancreatic adenocarcinoma was successfully managed with
surgical resection and toceranib phosphate and was reported to have
a progression-free interval of 1148 days62; this compares with an
overall mean survival of 97 days reported for cats with PAC,63 but it
remains to be studied whether this promising result can be achieved
in other patients.
Neoplastic diseases of the pancreas are not limited to PAC. Various
neuroendocrine tumors have been described and they carry a far
better prognosis than PAC (ch. 297). Also, GI lymphoma (ch. 322)
can involve the pancreas and various neoplastic lesions of other
abdominal organs can metastasize to the pancreas.

PANCREATIC AND PERIPANCREATIC
FLUID COLLECTIONS

Pancreatic and peripancreatic fluid collections can occur as a
complication of pancreatitis. In veterinary medicine, no consistent
nomenclature has previously been agreed upon, but in humans these
fluid collections are classified based on whether they contain any
necrotic material, whether they are infected, and whether they are
walled-off or not.64 Acute peripancreatic fluid collections commonly
develop during the early stages of acute pancreatitis, do not contain
any necrotic material, are often self-limiting, and thus don’t require
any intervention. In contrast, a pancreatic pseudocyst contains nonnecrotic material that is enclosed by a wall of fibrous or granulation
tissue. These fluid collections only require intervention if they
continue to grow in size and fail to regress over time or if there is any
evidence that the contents are infected. Acute necrotic fluid
collections occur during necrotizing pancreatitis when necrotic
debris liquifies. At least in human medicine, exploration of these
fluid collections should ideally be delayed until the lesion has been
walled-off. A walled-off necrosis represents well-encapsulated
necrotic tissue that can be infected. If patients are showing related
clinical signs, surgical or minimally-invasive intervention to drain
the walled-off necrosis should be considered. If the contents are
infected, the patient must be treated with antimicrobial therapy,
ideally based on bacterial culture and sensitivity testing.

PANCREATIC PARASITISM
Several systemic parasitic diseases can involve the exocrine pancreas.
For example, systemic schistosomiasis in dogs (ch. 262) or systemic
toxoplasmosis in cats (ch. 197) can involve the pancreas.65,66
Clinical signs are indistinguishable from those of patients with
chronic pancreatitis. Schistosomiasis can be diagnosed by a fecal
polymerase chain reaction, while toxoplasmosis can be diagnosed
based on a fecal smear combined with serologic titers.
In cats, the liver fluke Amphimerus pseudofelineus can lead to
pancreatitis.67 The diagnosis can be made based on fecal
examination by formalin-ethyl acetate sedimentation. Similarly, the
feline pancreatic fluke, Eurytrema procyonis, can lead to
obstructions of the pancreatic duct system, chronic pancreatitis, and

secondary pancreatic fibrosis and atrophy, ultimately leading to
clinical signs of EPI.68

CLIENT INFORMATION
Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency
Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) is a condition that is caused
by insufficient release of digestive enzymes by the pancreas. In most
cats and in about half of the dogs with this condition, chronic
inflammation of the pancreas, pancreatitis, is the underlying cause
for the destruction of the pancreas. In the remainder of dogs, the
underlying cause is a condition where the pancreatic tissue vanishes
without any previous inflammation, a condition referred to as
pancreatic acinar atrophy (PAA). This condition is believed to be
inherited as it almost exclusively occurs in German Shepherd Dogs,
Rough-Coated Collies, and Eurasians. While the exact mode of
inheritance in these breeds remains unknown, owners of affected
dogs of these breeds are encouraged to not breed their animal.

Dogs and cats with EPI usually will show weight loss and
voluminous soft stools that may be clay-colored (suggesting a large
amount of undigested fat in the feces). In contrast to dogs and cats
that have loose stools due to intestinal disease, patients with EPI
usually maintain a good appetite, with many of them even showing
an increased appetite, or even reports of ingestion of feces or foreign
bodies. Dogs and cats with above clinical signs should receive a
systematic work-up aimed at ruling out any obvious causes of the
signs from the clinical history and the physical examination. Also,
intestinal parasitism must be ruled out. Basic blood work will help
the veterinarian to rule out most diseases that are located outside the
gastrointestinal tract that could cause similar clinical signs. Once this
has been achieved, a blood sample is collected for measurement of a
highly species-specific test that estimates the amount of digestive
enzymes that are made by the exocrine pancreas, trypsin-like
immunoreactivity (TLI). This test should be combined with the
measurement of cobalamin and folate in the serum as many dogs
and cats with EPI are also cobalamin deficient. While EPI is usually
life-long in both dogs and cats, most patients can be managed
successfully by enzyme supplementation. Standard therapy is based
on dried pancreas extracts from pigs, but raw pancreas from a
variety of animal species can also be used. The pancreatic powder is
mixed with the food right before feeding. The minimum amount of
enzymes for supplementation may change over time and pet owners
can gradually decrease the dose added to each meal to a minimally
effective dose, that is a dose where the patient maintains a normal
body weight and has a normal stool quality. Also, many patients
require cobalamin (vitamin B12) supplementation either by
subcutaneous injection or by oral supplementation. There is no diet
that is universally optimal for dogs and cats with EPI and the pet
owner is encouraged to try a variety of high-quality foods to see
which the patient tolerates best. Generally, diets formulated for
patients with gastrointestinal disease or maintenance diets should be
well-tolerated. Patients that do not respond can be treated with an
antibiotic, tylosin, for 6 weeks. If the patient still does not respond to
therapy, further work-up for concurrent intestinal disease should be
undertaken. Also, a trial therapy with an antacid (omeprazole; trade
name Prilosec) can be attempted. Ultimately, most patients have a

good quality of life and a normal life expectancy, but exocrine
pancreatic function is not restored and measurement of serum TLI
concentrations remains subnormal (thus re-evaluation of serum TLI
concentration is not necessary). The website epi4dogs.com
provides valuable information for pet owners of dogs or cats with
EPI.
Jörg M. Steiner (College Station, Texas)

HYPOSOMATOTROPISM (HypoS)
PREVALENCE
Growth hormone (GH) deficiency during the early growth phase of life
causes dramatic pathological consequences. Fortunately, congenital
HypoS (“pituitary dwarfism”) seems rare, with only a small number of
cats described (ch. 22).1,2 Acquired non-traumatic feline HypoS is also

quite rare. GH deficiency follows hypophysectomy, but the clinical
importance of this adult-onset iatrogenic GH deficiency is unclear.

CAUSES
Congenital HypoS in dogs develops after failure of Rathke’s pouch
craniopharyngeal ectoderm to differentiate into a normally functioning
anterior pituitary (ch. 281). The cause(s) in cats is/are unknown,
although it may be similar to the process in dogs. An association between
HypoS and congenital hydrocephalus has been implied in 1 cat.2 Acquired
HypoS could follow any process impairing normal production and
secretion of GH in the anterior lobe of the pituitary, including any
inflammatory, infectious, immune-mediated, traumatic (including
iatrogenic, i.e., hypophysectomy), or neoplastic process.1

CLINICAL PRESENTATIONS
Congenital Hyposomatotropism
Abnormalities in a cat with congenital GH deficiency would begin as a
kitten, although they appear normal at birth. Stunted growth is typically
obvious by 1 to 2 months of age and even easier to observe if a healthy
litter mate is available for comparison (Figure 280.1). Initial post-natal
growth is mostly genetically determined and therefore, seems normal.
Problems only become apparent when the second GH-driven phase does
not materialize.1 In isolated GH deficiency, “short stature” will be
proportional (“proportionate dwarfism”) (ch. 22). Kittens deficient in
other anterior pituitary hormones, particularly thyroid stimulating
hormone, may grow disproportionately, with the square chunky contour
seen in dogs and cats with congenital hypothyroidism1 (ch. 286). Other
findings in cats with isolated congenital HypoS might include prolonged
retention of deciduous teeth, a dry and dull coat with retention of
secondary hairs, deficiency of primary or guard hairs,1,2 bilateral corneal
edema (ch. 13) due to reduced corneal endothelial cell density and
corneal epithelial cell layers (reported in 1 cat that may have been
hypothyroid),2 general weakness, lethargy, and signs associated with
hypoglycemia. Predisposition to hypoglycemia could be associated with
increased insulin sensitivity caused by lack of diabetogenic GH or it could

be associated with the limited gluconeogenic capacity commonly seen in
small juvenile kittens.

Acquired Hyposomatotropism
Acquired clinical GH deficiency has not been described.1 After the growth
phase has been completed, the clinical ramifications of GH deficiency are
likely too subtle to be noticed by owners or veterinarians. Severe
deleterious clinical consequences have thus far not been encountered
after hypophysectomy despite the documentation of subnormal serum
insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) concentrations in most cats and
evidence of morbidity and quality of life issues in people.3 Abdominal
adiposity has been noted in cats and proactive dietary intervention can be
beneficial (ch. 150).

FIGURE 280.1 Two sibling Domestic Shorthair cats
of 5 months of age; the cat on the right was presented for
stunted growth, displayed proportionate small stature
and was subsequently diagnosed with congenital
hyposomatotropism, through documentation of an
undetectable serum insulin-like growth factor-1 and
exclusion of more common causes for stunted growth.

DIAGNOSIS
Assay of Growth Hormone (GH)
Diagnosis of congenital HypoS is initially based on a suggestive clinical
picture, exclusion of inappropriate growth expectations, ruling out the
more common causes of proportionate dwarfism (e.g., malnutrition,
hepatic disease [particularly portosystemic shunt, ch. 267],
gastrointestinal disease, renal, cardiovascular disease), and
demonstration of a pathological GH deficiency. Demonstrating a GH
deficiency is difficult since feline GH assays are rarely available to

clinicians; even when they are available, overlap might exist between
“normal” and “abnormal” values, partially explained by GH being
secreted in a pulsatile manner.7 Gold standard stimulation or provocative
tests for diagnosis of a GH deficient state in humans and dogs have not
been validated for cats.

Insulin-Like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1) Assay
A more accessible alternative to GH-based testing is documenting low or
undetectable serum IGF-1 concentrations. Hepatic IGF-1 production is
primarily induced by GH; its secretion is non-pulsatile, and a single value
reflects the amount of GH secreted over the previous 24 hours. Clinicians
should bear in mind that certain diseases and medications can influence
the outcome of GH and IGF-1 testing, falsely implying a deficiency, e.g.,
IGF-1 is mainly produced by the liver and liver dysfunction could impact
its circulating concentrations. Moderate lowering of IGF-1 has also been
reported with a range of other diseases, including lymphoma,8 newly
diagnosed diabetes mellitus (DM),7 and renal disease. In these
conditions, however, IGF-1 is measurable, rather than undetectable or
severely decreased, as is seen with true HypoS. Serum IGF-1 has also
been shown to be positively correlated with body size, which could be
particularly relevant to a kitten of small stature. A 7-month-old male
kitten with retarded disproportionate growth was diagnosed as having
congenital hypothyroidism.9 That kitten had moderate decreases in
serum IGF-1 which normalized after 6 weeks of thyroid hormone
replacement therapy.9

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Growth Hormone and Other Pituitary Hormone
Therapies
GH replacement therapy has been anecdotally described for cats and
follows the protocols described for dogs (ch. 281). The lack of feline GH
products leaves only porcine or human exogenous GH, which may be
antigenic and could lead to antibody formation. Concurrent pituitary
hormone deficiencies, if present, should be treated if possible. If GH
replacement is deemed too expensive or undesirable (a major potential
adverse effect is development of DM), treatment of concurrent pituitary
hormone deficiencies could be the sole strategy.

Progesterone
Administration of progestins to induce GH secretion from mammary
tissue (ch. 281) has not been shown to raise circulating GH or IGF-1
concentrations in cats, despite expression of the feline GH gene in
mammary gland tissues undergoing progestin-induced fibroadenomatous
changes.10,11

Acquired Hyposomatotropism
Due to a lack of significant clinical consequences, acquired HypoS, as
occurs after hypophysectomy, is not treated.3

General Treatment
An adjustment in the daily caloric intake seems appropriate in cats with
documented low IGF-1 or GH concentrations, given their tendency to
amass abdominal fat. Lack of reports preclude a full assessment of
success rates and prognosis when congenital HypoS is treated. Left
untreated, these cats have a poor prognosis with shorter lifespans and
development of infectious, degenerative, or neurological complications.1,2

HYPERSOMATOTROPISM
(HyperS)/ACROMEGALY
While HypoS is primarily a disease of kittens and young cats, HyperS is a
condition most commonly diagnosed in middle-aged to older cats (Box
280.1). Over the past several decades, HyperS has been diagnosed most
frequently in cats initially diagnosed as having DM, likely a group of cats
with chronic and/or severe HyperS. As the profession becomes more
familiar with feline HyperS, its various and inconsistent non-DMassociated effects, it is anticipated that more HyperS cats without DM will
be reported and a clearer clinical picture will develop.

PREVALENCE OF
HYPERSOMATOTROPISM IN CATS WITH
DIABETES MELLITUS
HyperS is a relatively common underlying cause for “secondary” DM in
cats, with prevalence rates ranging from 18-32% (Figure 280.2; Box
280.2).9-12 These prevalence rates may be indicative of geographic
differences and/or they may reflect varying recruitment or screening
methods. The largest screening study, conducted in the United Kingdom,
included cats with DM recruited by offering a free fructosamine
determination. Spare serum was used to measure IGF-1 and if >1000
ng/mL (>131 nmol/L), confirmatory tests were offered, including free
contrast-enhanced pituitary computed tomography (CT). 1221 samples
were submitted. The randomly obtained IGF-1 concentrations suggested
possible acromegaly (>1000 ng/mL [>131 nmol/L]) in 319 cats (26.1%)
and confirmed in 95% of that subpopulation.12 These results suggested a
prevalence rate of HyperS among UK cats with DM of 24.8% (95%
confidence interval: 21.2-28.6%). Only 24% of clinicians attending to the
cats with an ultimate diagnosis of HyperS indicated a strong pre-test
suspicion, suggesting in most cases, it is not possible to phenotypically
recognize its presence. It is generally recommended that every newly
diabetic cat be screened for a urinary tract infection, a complication with
a prevalence estimate of 12%. On the basis of HyperS prevalence data, it
is therefore also recommended that a serum IGF-1 be obtained to screen
every newly diagnosed diabetic cat for HyperS. Screening each cat with
DM gains importance when considering that treatment of HyperS can
improve quality of life for owner and cat, especially if there is diabetic
remission (ch. 292).

PREVALENCE OF
HYPERSOMATOTROPISM IN NONDIABETIC CATS
The incidence of HyperS in non-diabetic cats is unknown. Similar to the
condition in humans, underdiagnosis is suspected. HyperS should be
considered in cats exhibiting some or all the signs of HyperS (Box
280.3), e.g., a cat with progressively louder upper respiratory sounds
(ch. 213) or one with myocardial thickening (ch. 234).13 In a screening
study, 6.7% of cats with clinical evidence of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
(HCM) (heart murmur or heart failure) had an IGF-1 level >1000 ng/mL
(>131 nmol/L; 95% confidence interval 1.8-16.2%).14 Using the >1000
ng/mL assay cut-off result for IGF-1 provides a minimum positive
predictive value of 95%. These results suggest that about 1-of-6 to 1-of-50
non-diabetic cats with myocardial hypertrophy have HyperS. HyperS
should be considered in middle-aged to older cats with respiratory stertor
and weight gain (chs. 20, 37).

CAUSES
Natural Progression of HyperS
HyperS follows hyperplasia or neoplastic transformation of acidophils
(somatotrophs) in the anterior pituitary. The normal pulsatile secretory
pattern associated with normal pituitary activity is retained by tumors but
with increases in both frequency and amplitude. Adenomas are common
and a few carcinomas have been described. Surprisingly, 10 of 37
pituitaries from cats with HyperS, assessed using reticulin staining (gold
standard classification method in humans), exhibited non-neoplastic
hyperplastic changes, a prevalence greater than in humans.12,15 It has

been proposed that hyperplastic change can precede adenomatous
transformation. Somatotroph hyperplasia has been shown to progress to
somatotroph adenoma formation in hypothalamic growth hormone
releasing hormone-overexpressing mice. The prevalence of pituitary
hyperplasia might be even greater if progression from mild non-clinical
hyperplasia to adenoma occurs in cats. Mixed GH and prolactin secreting
adenomas (mammosomatotroph adenoma) are diagnosed in as many as
30% of acromegalic people. Prolactin-positive-staining cells accounted for
<10% of cells in the pituitary glands from cats with HyperS and these
adenomas seem rare in cats.

Environmental Causes
Organohalogenated contaminants (OHCs) have been implicated in
enhancing endocrine oncogenesis in various species, including cats.16,17
OHCs are bio-accumulative chemicals that include organochlorine
pesticides found in food, industrial chemicals, (e.g., polychlorinated
biphenyls [PCBs]) and brominated flame retardants (BFRs, e.g.,
polybrominated diphenyl ethers [PBDEs]) found in household furniture,
floor coverings, and bedding. Both cats and humans are continuously
exposed to these chemicals via direct contact and indirect (dust)
contamination. Both direct and dust exposure is especially relevant
considering the time spent indoors and the grooming behavior of cats.
One study found significantly higher levels of all contaminants assessed
in cats with HyperS when compared to cats with primary DM and those
without an endocrinopathy.17 Data also suggested that cats with HyperS
have less capacity to metabolize persistent chemicals.

Genetic Causes
Human pituitary adenomas can be monoclonal in origin, suggesting that
they arise from an acquired single cell somatic mutation. Adenomas may
also develop after germline mutations cause inactivation of tumor
suppressor genes. Mutations of the tumor suppressor aryl hydrocarbon
receptor interacting protein (AIP) gene have been associated with up to
40% of isolated familial and naturally occurring human GH-secreting
tumors. The AIP tumor suppressor protein activates xenobiotic
metabolizing enzymes, making the link with exposure to and
accumulation of environmental OHCs even more concerning. In cats, a
nonsynonymous single nucleotide polymorphism was identified in exon 1

(AIP:c.9T > G) of 2 HyperS cats, 2 HyperS siblings, and none of the
control cats.18

CLINICAL SIGNS
Overview
Clinical signs of HyperS are determined, in part, on how early in the
disease process the cat is seen by a veterinarian, the strength of the cat’s
pancreatic beta cells, and clinician awareness (Box 280.3). It is likely
that a non-diabetic period precedes the overt DM. Some cats with HyperS
have been described that never became overtly diabetic.

Clinical Signs in HyperS Cats With DM
To date, most cats with HyperS have signs compatible with DM (Tables
280. and 280.2). Initially, treatment for DM can lead to amelioration of
clinical signs in some cats and temporary diabetic remission has been
observed. The DM can be successfully managed over time in some, while
in others it is difficult to attain good glycemic control (ch. 292).

In one large study of 323 cats with DM suspected to have HyperS, 70%
were neutered males, their mean age was 11.3 years (range: 4-19), and
87% were Domestic Shorthair cats. A variety of breeds was affected and
Maine Coon cats may be over-represented.12,16 Body weight and
fructosamine concentrations were significantly higher in the cats with
abnormally increased IGF-1 concentrations despite also receiving
significantly higher insulin dosages. However, the cats suspected to have
HyperS had a range of body weights and insulin requirements (from
modest to high). It was not possible to rule out HyperS on clinical signs.
The lack of definitive clinical signs together with the disease prevalence
underscores and validates the recommendation to routinely screen newly
diagnosed diabetic cats for HyperS. If the owner indicates no interest in
definitively treating their cat for HyperS, knowing the complete
physiologic status of any diabetic is still beneficial. Documenting an IGF-1
concentration consistent with HyperS may alter expectations and
prognosis with regard to long-term DM care. Further, owners may change
an initial decision about treating HyperS. HyperS-induced DM is quite
rightly classified separately from other forms of feline DM, with different
treatment response patterns and prognosis.18 Current information
implies that HyperS be considered in any poorly controlled cat with DM
gaining weight, exhibiting severe polyphagia, or having difficulties with
insulin resistance (ch. 292).
