Hypersomatotropism in the Non-Diabetic Cat
Healthy pancreatic beta cells are able to counteract the effects of excess
GH and IGF-1 to avoid or delay development of DM. Cats with “classic”
feline DM (as in people with type 2 DM) are suspected of having inherent
beta-cell dysfunction. Non-diabetic cats with HyperS are inherently
difficult to identify unless clinicians appreciate all the effects of excess GH
and IGF-1 with time. The most common clinical signs and changes are
summarized in Box 280.3.
The relatively high incidence (53%) of upper respiratory stertor (ch.
37) in the history of cats with HyperS (often reported as “snoring” by
owners) is caused by narrowing of the nasopharynx.16,19 Increased width
of the head and broad facial features (Figure 280.3) might be the most
readily identifiable changes on physical examination, but facial changes
secondary to excesses in GH and IGF-1 occur gradually and will only be
obvious in cats with longer-standing disease.19 Polyphagia (

Video

280.1) and weight gain could be the primary owner concerns.20
Neurological signs due to an expanding pituitary tumor have been
reported. HyperS should be considered as a relatively infrequent, yet
clinically relevant, underlying cause of myocardial thickening.13,14 A
diagnosis of “idiopathic” HCM should only be made after excluding
HyperS (ch. 234). As the profession gains more information about feline
HyperS, the number of diagnoses will increase. The term
“hypersomatotropism” is preferred over “acromegaly” because the latter
implies a syndrome with characteristic phenotypical changes that are
inconsistently observed (Box 280.1).

FIGURE 280.3 An 11-year-old Domestic Shorthair cat
suffering from hypersomatotropism-induced diabetes
mellitus. Broad facial features can be seen, though had
not been noted by the cat’s owner. These facial changes
tend only to be present when hypersomatotropism has
been present for a longer period of time.

DIAGNOSIS
Assessing Serum IGF-1

Serum total IGF-1 assays are a readily available and excellent screening
test for HyperS in cats with DM. Serum IGF-1’s positive predictive value
when >1000 ng/mL (>131 nmol/L) with one radioimmunoassay was
95%12 (Figure 280.4). Recently, an IGF-1 enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assay (ELISA) has been validated.21 One weakness
identified is that hepatic IGF-1 production is dependent on presence of
sufficient portal insulin, which can be deficient in cats newly diagnosed
with DM. This can lead to false-negative IGF-1 results in approximately
9% of untreated cats. Further, increased IGF-1 results have been reported
in non-HyperS diabetic cats.22 Finally, differences in the performance of
IGF-1 assays exist.22 All these factors should be considered when
screening cats with DM for HyperS (Figure 280.5). Serum IGF-1 has
also proved useful as a marker for treatment success posthypophysectomy.3

Growth Hormone (GH) Assays
Commercially available GH assays are not available, despite evidence that
all tested HyperS cats have had results above reference intervals.4 GH
suppression tests (often using oral glucose), considered a gold standard
for confirming the diagnosis of human HyperS, have not been useful in
cats; GH remains pulsatile even with HyperS present (Figure
280.6).7,16

Type III Procollagen Propeptide (PIIIP) and Serum
Ghrelin
HyperS is associated with tissue growth and the median serum PIIIP
concentration, a peripheral indicator of collagen turnover, was 5 times
higher in cats with HyperS-induced DM when compared to non-HyperS
diabetic cats. 23 Serum ghrelin, a GH secretagogue, was shown to be
sensitive but not specific, with lower results in HyperS cats when
compared with healthy controls but similar to results in cats with DM.24
Serum ghrelin may prove sensitive in assessing treatment response as
significant increases have been documented in radiation-treated HyperS
cats while IGF-1 changes were not significant.

Computed Tomography (CT) and Magnetic Resonance
Imaging (MRI) Scans
Identifying pituitary enlargement or a pituitary mass using either
contrast-enhanced CT (Figure 280.7) or MRI further confirms the
diagnosis of HyperS. Absence of any pituitary enlargement does not
exclude the diagnosis of HyperS (Figure 280.4). Microadenomas and
acidophil hyperplasia which cause no visible changes to the pituitary area
on imaging scans are more likely when the disease is in the early phases.
In more chronic disease, advanced imaging can provide additional
support for the diagnosis of HyperS by identifying prognathia inferior,
temporomandibular-joint malformations, and increased thickness of
subcutis, skin, and calvarium bone.19 CT usually requires less anesthesia
time and is therefore preferred.

TREATMENT (TABLE 280.3) AND
PROGNOSIS
Hypophysectomy
Successful hypophysectomy is associated with the highest DM remission
rates, longevity, and quality of life. As in humans, it is the best treatment
option.3,25 Contraindications include risk-averse owners, extremely large
tumors, and comorbidities that could interfere with anesthesia and
postoperative recovery (particularly significant renal or cardiovascular
disease). Anesthetic complications identified in a multi-disciplinary
hospital setting included hypothermia, hypotension, bradycardia and
airway obstruction.26 Administering alpha-2 agonists was associated with

a lower incidence of hypotension. Fentanyl infusion was associated with
higher incidences of airway obstruction when compared with
remifentanil. The initial financial commitment can be a major obstacle.
Owners should be educated to understand that a year of ineffective
insulin therapy or radiotherapy could have similar cost implications but
with poorer results.
In the author’s hypophysectomy clinic, pituitary tumors are excised via
the skull base, with the surgeon operating via the cat’s mouth and
nasopharynx (transsphenoidal approach, soft palate is incised). In one
study, 58 of 68 cats with HyperS-induced DM (85.3%) were alive 4 weeks
postoperatively, with 10 (15%) postoperative deaths.3 Complications
included hypoglycemia (n = 9), electrolyte imbalances (n = 9), and
transient congestive heart failure (n = 5). 95% of surviving cats had
improved DM control and remission was documented in 41 (71%). Insulin
administration was able to be discontinued after a median of 9 days
(range, 2-120). The postoperative 4-week serum IGF-1 concentration
nadir was significantly lower in cats achieving DM remission (Figure
280.8). After surgery, all cats received oral levothyroxine and oral
hydrocortisone long-term. Conjunctival desmopressin was needed in 72%
of the cats. DM recurrence occurred in 12% after a median of 248 days.
Median survival time of all cats was 853 days (range 1-1740). Myocardial
thickening reduced in all cats treated effectively.13 GH replacement
therapy is not considered necessary (see above: feline
hyposomatotropism).

Radiotherapy
Radiation therapy was considered the best option for treating HyperS.
However, even stereotactical or gamma-knife radiotherapy (ch. 245)
does not rival the positive results of hypophysectomy.27-30 Radiotherapy
has proven particularly unpredictable in terms of clinical improvement
regarding a) whether improvement will occur; b) when it will occur; c)
how much change in insulin requirement will be noted; and d) how long
the effects of radiotherapy last. Lack of attaining normal IGF-1
concentrations puts further doubt on the efficacy of radiation therapy,
even in cats that experience reduced insulin requirements. Indeed,
HyperS changes and excessive collagen turnover have been shown to
continue even if DM improvement or resolution is achieved.23,30
Myocardial hypertrophy, which can resolve after surgery, remains
abnormal after radiotherapy.13 Radiotherapy can reduce the size of large

tumors that increase risk of surgery, or can be used when
hypophysectomy is declined.

Medical Management: Somatostatin (SST) Analogues
and Dopamine Agonists
SST analogues and dopamine agonists are largely ineffective, possibly
explained by somatotrophinoma, SST, and dopamine receptor profiles.15
Further research is needed to explain the inconsistent responses to
dopamine agonists. Variable dopamine-receptor expression may be a
partial explanation.15
Pasireotide (Signifor, Novartis, Basel, Switzerland), a novel multireceptor ligand SST analogue with high binding affinity for SST receptor
subtypes 1, 2, 3 and 5, has been shown to effectively inhibit
somatotrophinomas in cats with DM, demonstrated by significant
decreases in serum IGF-1, average 12-hour blood glucose, fructosamine,
and insulin requirements.31,32 Short-acting q12h injectable and oncemonthly long-acting injectable forms have been tested. About 25% of cats
with DM treated with the once monthly form entered diabetic remission.
Disadvantages include mild transient loose stools or diarrhea and cost of
the drug in most countries. Lower and less frequent dosages than
reported in the literature can be tried to help reduce costs.

Cabergoline

Cabergoline is less expensive and has been effective in some people with
HyperS. While one prospective study failed to demonstrate a beneficial
effect in cats with HyperS,33 3 separate cats have been reported in which
cabergoline treatment (10 mcg/kg PO q48h) resulted in long-term
diabetes remission with significant decreases in serum IGF-1.34 Given
that cabergoline is more affordable, widely available, has few serious sideeffects, and has an easy-to-follow protocol, it is worthwhile to recommend
this drug when definitive treatment with hypophysectomy is declined.

Treating Diabetes Mellitus Complicated by
Hypersomatotropism
While the discussed treatment options are being considered or if they
have been declined, the only remaining option is solely treating the
secondary DM. Initial treatment is no different than is recommended for
uncomplicated DM. It can be anticipated that high insulin dosages are
often required to achieve an acceptable quality of life (ch. 292). Some
have suggested a limit to insulin dosages but experience indicates that
limitations do not address the reality: extremely high insulin dosages are
sometimes the only way to assure acceptable quality of life. Use of high
dosages of insulin requires that owners be well-informed about insulin
needs in HyperS cats and that episodes of iatrogenic hypoglycemia may
occur, although these are relatively rare.
Most functioning pituitary tumors retain their pulsatile secretory
nature (Figure 280.6). Thus, GH secreted from these tumors can
fluctuate from extremely high to extremely low concentrations. This may
explain that during rare periods of low circulating GH concentrations,
insulin sensitivity increases. Insulins which usually lack sharp peak
effects are preferred, e.g., protamine zinc insulin, glargine, detemir. The
insulin dosage required to control clinical signs of DM should be
determined gradually. Rarely should a dosage increase by more than 1
unit/injection/cat/week. Use of continuous glucose monitoring systems
like the Freestyle Libre (Abbott, Chicago, USA) can prove useful,
alongside, of course, a thorough evaluation of the clinical picture (chs. 78
and 292). HyperS diabetic cats can be accurately monitored by using the
widely accepted standardised ALIVE Diabetic Clinical Score.35
Negative sequelae of progressive acromegaly should be treated as
necessary, including arthropathies (ch. 256), congestive heart failure
(ch. 229) and chronic kidney disease (ch. 301). Central nervous system
signs (e.g., seizures, blindness, dull behavior) due to an expanding

pituitary mass are rare because these tumors tend to be slow-growing.
However, signs caused by a large tumor can occur and could warrant
additional palliative treatment strategies (chs. 14, 45, and 245). Regular
quality of life assessments should be planned, and euthanasia considered
if these prove unsatisfactory. This is especially important in those cats
whose DM becomes clinically uncontrolled and/or those cats suffering
from GH-induced extreme polyphagia. Fluoxetine has been used by the
author to attempt amelioration of the latter, with mixed success. Quality
of life measurement tools could help in the objective and structural
assessment of these patients (and their owners).36

GROWTH HORMONE OVERVIEW
GROWTH HORMONE DESCRIPTION AND
REGULATION OF GROWTH HORMONE
SECRETION

Growth hormone (GH), secreted by the anterior pituitary, is a rather
large single-chain polypeptide containing 190 amino acids. The
amino acid sequence of GH varies considerably between species, but
GH in dogs and pigs is identical.1 Anterior pituitary hormones,
including GH, are secreted in rhythmic pulses of high concentrations
separated by troughs of low levels. Pituitary GH secretion is
regulated mainly by the opposing actions of the stimulatory
hypothalamic peptide GH-releasing hormone (GHRH) and the
inhibitory hypothalamic peptide somatostatin (Figure 281.1). The
GH pulses reflect the pulsatile delivery of GHRH, whereas the
concentrations between pulses are primarily controlled by
somatostatin. GH synthesis and secretion can also be stimulated by
non-GHRH secretagogues, which exert their effect via receptors
different from those for GHRH. The endogenous ligand for these
receptors is ghrelin, synthesized and secreted from the stomach.2 In
young dogs, ghrelin is more potent than GHRH in stimulating
synthesis and secretion of GH.3 Ghrelin also stimulates food intake
as well as gastric and intestinal (GI) emptying. Fasting and food
intake are associated with higher and lower circulating ghrelin
concentrations, respectively.4
In dogs, GH is synthesized in both the pituitary and the mammary
gland. Administration of progestins (PGs) can increase plasma GH
concentrations in dogs but this secretion is not pulsatile, not
sensitive to GHRH, and not inhibited by somatostatin. Moreover,
PG-induced plasma GH concentrations do not decrease after
hypophysectomy, supporting an extra-pituitary source. This GH is
synthesized by foci of cells in hyperplastic mammary ductular
epithelium.5 Mammary GH is biochemically identical to pituitary GH
and the gene encoding mammary GH is identical to that in the
pituitary gland.6
The typical pulsatile secretion pattern of GH changes during the
luteal phase (diestrus) of healthy bitches, with higher basal
concentrations and less GH secreted per pulse during stages with a
high PG concentration.7 This can be explained by partial suppression
of pituitary GH release by PG-induced mammary GH secretion.
Thus, diestral mammary GH synthesis is normal in healthy bitches,

likely promoting mammary tissue preparation for lactation via local
autocrine and paracrine effects.7 Significant GH concentrations have
been identified in canine mammary gland secretions and,
particularly, in colostrum.8 Colostrum GH may promote neonatal GI
development. The PG-induced mammary GH production may also
play a role in mammary gland tumor development or tumor
progression.

PHYSIOLOGICAL EFFECTS
GH has two distinct effects: rapid catabolic actions and slow, longlasting anabolic actions (Figure 281.1). The rapid actions are
primarily associated with insulin antagonism which enhances
lipolysis, increases gluconeogenesis, interferes with glucose transport
across cell membranes, and raises blood glucose (BG). Slow anabolic
effects are mediated by insulin-like growth factors (IGFs) that are
produced in various tissues and have about 50% sequence similarity
with insulin. These IGFs have local paracrine or autocrine growthpromoting effects. The main source of circulating IGF-1 is the liver.
In contrast to insulin, IGFs circulate attached to binding proteins
(IGFBPs), which prolongs plasma half-life and is consistent with
long-term growth-promoting actions. IGFs are important
determinants in the regulation of body size by stimulating protein
synthesis, chondrogenesis, and growth.
The opposing biologic effects of GH are neither strict nor absolute.
There is evidence that GH exerts its growth-promoting effect not
only via IGFs but also directly on target cells. GH may be the major
determinant of body size. It appears that young large-breed dogs go
through longer periods of high GH release (i.e., juvenile
hypersomatotropism) than do young small-breed dogs.9 There is a
strong linear correlation when plasma IGF-1 concentrations and
body size. Furthermore, an IGF-1 single-nucleotide polymorphism
haplotype has been reported as a major factor in the final body size
of dogs.10 IGF-1 directly inhibits pituitary GH secretion and
indirectly inhibits secretion by stimulating release of somatostatin.
GH also suppresses GHRH synthesis and secretion at the
hypothalamic level (Figure 281.1).

ACROMEGALY
PATHOGENESIS
Acromegaly is a syndrome of bony and soft-tissue overgrowth and
insulin resistance due to chronic and excessive GH secretion. In
middle-aged and elderly dogs, either endogenous PG (luteal phase of
the estrous cycle) or exogenous PGs can increase mammary GH
secretion. Acromegaly has also been reported in dogs with a GHproducing mammary tumor.11 Hypothyroidism, in dogs, is associated
with increased plasma concentrations of GH and IGF-1 (ch.
285).12,13 Pituitary somatotroph adenomas may cause acromegaly in
dogs, but are rare. In cats the condition may be “common” (ch.
280).14

FIGURE 281.1 The pituitary secretion of growth
hormone (GH) is under inhibitory (somatostatin)
and stimulatory (GH-releasing hormone [GHRH])
hypothalamic control and is also modulated by
negative feedback control of insulin-like growth
factor-1 (IGF-1) and GH itself. The direct catabolic
(diabetogenic) actions of GH are shown on the left
side of the figure, and the indirect anabolic actions
are shown on the right.

FIGURE 281.2 The mouth of a 4-year-old Beagle
dog with progestin-induced growth hormone excess.
Note the hyperplasia of the gingiva, the widening of
the interdental spaces and the relatively large
tongue.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS AND
LABORATORY RESULTS
Signs of GH hypersecretion tend to develop slowly and often include
soft-tissue swelling of the head, neck and abdomen. In some
acromegalic dogs, severe hypertrophy of oral and pharyngeal soft
tissues can cause snoring and even dyspnea (Figure 281.2).
Articular cartilage proliferation, periarticular periosteal reaction, and
spondylosis deformans may result in stiffness, difficulty in rising,
and neck rigidity. Affected dogs often have polyuria, polydipsia, and
polyphagia (PU/PD/PP). The urine does not usually contain glucose,
but diabetes mellitus (DM) can develop due to insulin resistance.
Physical examination may reveal thick skin folds, especially in the
neck; prognathism; and wide interdental spaces (Figure 281.2).

Chronic GH excess may also lead to generalized increase in organ
size and subsequent abdominal enlargement. Laboratory
investigation often reveals hyperglycemia. Increased serum alkaline
phosphatase activity may be the result of the intrinsic glucocorticoid
activity of PGs. German Shepherd Dogs appear predisposed to
acromegaly.15 Acromegaly secondary to hypothyroidism tends to be
quite subtle (ch. 285). Large compressive somatotroph adenomas
may cause central nervous system signs.

DIAGNOSIS
Basal plasma GH concentrations in acromegalic dogs often exceed
the reference range but may not be abnormal by chance, if the
condition is mild, or early in its course. Increases in GH, alone, may
be incidental if samples are obtained soon after a GH pulse in a
normal dog. The diagnosis of acromegaly is supported if GHRH (1
mcg/kg IV) fails to stimulate GH secretion or if somatostatin (10
mcg/kg IV) fails to suppress GH. Because the amino acid sequence of
GH varies among species, GH should be determined by a speciesspecific homologous assay. Commercial GH assays are not widely
available.
Since plasma IGF-1 is bound to plasma proteins, its concentration
does not fluctuate as widely as does GH. Since the amino acid
sequence of IGF-1 is less species-specific, it can be measured with
heterologous (human) assays. Because of the strong linear
correlation between plasma IGF-1 concentrations and body size,
breed-specific reference ranges are required.16 If GH excess is noted
in a dog not given PG or PGs, hypothyroidism should be considered
(ch. 285). Advanced imaging of the pituitary area rarely reveals a
somatotroph adenoma.

TREATMENT
PG-induced acromegaly in dogs can be treated effectively by
ovariectomy. If chronic excesses of GH did not cause complete
exhaustion of pancreatic beta cells, eliminating the PG source by
ovariectomy may prevent or reverse DM. Dogs with PG-induced GH

excess should have PG drugs discontinued. Administration of PG
receptor blockers, such as aglepristone, significantly decreases
plasma concentrations of GH and IGF-1 in dogs with PG-induced
acromegaly.17 Treatment of dogs with primary hypothyroidism with
levothyroxine results in normalization of plasma concentrations of
GH and IGF-1 (ch. 285).12
In dogs with acromegaly due to a somatotroph adenoma,
treatment should be directed at the pituitary tumor. Therapeutic
options include medical management, radiation treatment, and
hypophysectomy. Medical treatment with (expensive) long-acting
somatostatin analogues (e.g., octreotide, lanreotide) can decrease
signs, normalize plasma IGF-1 concentrations, and reduce tumor size
in about 50% of acromegalic people. GH-receptor antagonists
developed for human use, e.g., pegvisomant, are not effective in dogs
because the canine GH receptor differs. Radiation therapy (ch. 318)
may shrink pituitary tumors but excesses in GH secretion often
persist. Radiation is not widely available and requires
hospitalization, frequent anesthesia, expense, and possibility of
relapse should an initial response be seen. Transsphenoidal
hypophysectomy has been performed successfully in dogs with
hypercortisolism due to corticotroph adenomas and in cats with
acromegaly due to somatotroph adenomas (chs. 280 and 293).18
Experience in dogs with acromegaly is limited.

PITUITARY DWARFISM
PATHOGENESIS
Any defect in pituitary gland organogenesis may cause an isolated or
combined deficiency of pituitary hormones. Congenital GH
deficiency, pituitary dwarfism, is a striking example of pituitary
hormone deficiency. Congenital GH deficiency has been described in
several dog breeds, such as Shepherd Dogs, Czechoslovakian
Wolfhounds, and Saarloos Wolfhounds, but only rarely in cats.
Dwarfism usually results from a simple autosomal recessive
inherited abnormality in German Shepherd Dogs. Genealogical
investigations suggest the recessive gene mutation occurred around

1940, with several champion carrier dogs identified.19,20 German
Shepherd Dog dwarfs typically have combined GH, thyroidstimulating hormone (TSH), and prolactin deficiencies, impaired
release of gonadotropins, and normal adrenocorticotropic hormone
(ACTH) secretion (Figure 281.3).21
Congenital GH deficiency was thought to result from pressure
atrophy of the anterior pituitary due to cyst formation in Rathke’s
pouch. While pituitary cysts exist in most German Shepherd Dog
dwarfs, young dwarfs may have no or only a small cyst without
evidence for pressure atrophy.21 Further, preservation of ACTH
secretion argues against cyst formation in Rathke’s pouch as the
primary cause of pituitary dwarfism.
Genetic studies have demonstrated that pituitary dwarfism in
German Shepherd Dogs is due to a mutation in LHX3.22 LHX3 is a
member of the LIM homeodomain protein family of DNA-binding
transcription factors. Molecular defects in the LHX3 gene in humans
and mice result in deficits of all anterior pituitary hormones except
ACTH. These findings are identical to the endocrine phenotype of
German Shepherd Dog dwarfs. Analysis of intron 5 of LHX3 revealed
that dwarfs have a deletion of one of six 7 base pair (bp) repeats,
reducing the intron size to only 68 bp, resulting in defective LHX3
splicing.22 This genetic defect is also the cause of pituitary dwarfism
in Saarloos Wolfdogs and Czechoslovakian Wolfdogs; German
Shepherd Dog–wolf cross-breeds.23 Screening clinically healthy
Saarloos and Czechoslovakian Wolfdogs demonstrated that 31 and
21%, respectively, had the defect, indicating that pituitary dwarfism
due to an LHX3 mutation is relevant and screening these breeds is
emphasized.
Congenital GH deficiency may also be due to genetic defects other
than an LHX3 mutation. Recently, a 6-month-old female Chihuahua
was reported with proportionate dwarfism, retained puppy hair coat
and hypoglycemia. The GH deficiency in this Chihuahua was
ascribed to a 6-bp deletion in exon 5 of GH1.24 Pituitary dwarfism
and associated DNA defects are often incompatible with life,
explaining why the condition is uncommon.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS
Pituitary dwarfism can lead to a wide range of clinical
manifestations.25 During the first weeks of life, pituitary dwarfs may
be of normal size, but then they grow more slowly than their
littermates. Pituitary dwarfs are usually brought to a veterinarian
between 2 and 5 months of age because of proportionate growth
retardation, retention of lanugo or secondary hairs, and lack of
primary or guard hairs (Figure 281.4). The lanugo hairs are easily
epilated. Truncal alopecia may gradually develop beginning at points
of wear, sparing the head and extremities. The skin becomes
progressively hyperpigmented and scaly. Secondary bacterial
infections in the skin are common. The dwarfs usually have a pointed
muzzle, resembling a fox. Due to impaired gonadotropin release,
male dwarfs often have unilateral or bilateral cryptorchidism and
females commonly fail to ovulate. The LHX3 mutation is also
associated with malformations of the atlantoaxial joint, which can
lead to instability and dynamic compression of the cervical spinal
cord.26 Physical examination may reveal the continuous heart
murmur of a patent ductus arteriosus (ch. 231).21 Pituitary dwarfs
are usually active and alert, but inappetence and decreased activity
usually develop by about 2-3 years of age due to secondary
hypothyroidism and impaired renal function.

DIAGNOSIS
Overview
Although the clinical signs of pituitary dwarfism may be obvious,
other endocrine and non-endocrine causes of growth retardation
and/or alopecia must be excluded. No abnormalities, aside from
increases in serum creatinine, are noted on routine laboratory test
results from dogs with naturally occurring pituitary dwarfism.21 GH
deficiency and (secondary) thyroid hormone deficiency cause
abnormal glomerular development and impaired renal function. Low
plasma IGF-1, TSH, and serum T4 concentrations are common, but

low IGF-1 concentrations do not provide a definitive diagnosis of
pituitary dwarfism.

Stimulation Tests
Because basal plasma GH values may be low in healthy animals, a
definitive diagnosis of GH deficiency should be based on results of a
stimulation test using GHRH (1 mcg/kg) or alpha-adrenergic drugs
(clonidine 10 mcg/kg or xylazine 100 mcg/kg). Plasma for GH should
be obtained immediately before and 20 to 30 minutes after
stimulation. In healthy dogs, plasma GH concentrations increase at
least twofold after stimulation. In dogs with pituitary dwarfism there
is no significant response (Figure 281.3). A plasma GH
concentration more than 5 mcg/L, 20 minutes after IV 2 mcg/kg
ghrelin, excludes pituitary dwarfism.27 Supra-pituitary stimulation
with corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), thyrotropin-releasing
hormone (TRH), or gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) may
reveal the presence of other pituitary hormone deficiencies.21

Pituitary Imaging
Diagnostic imaging of the pituitary area with computed tomography
(CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans (ch. 112) often
reveal pituitary cysts in dogs with congenital GH deficiency.21
Despite the cysts, most young dogs with pituitary dwarfism have a
small pituitary, compatible with pituitary hypoplasia (i.e., a lack of
endocrine cells in the pituitary anterior lobe). Cyst size gradually
enlarges during life.28 When cysts are large, pituitary size may also
increase. Because healthy dogs may also have pituitary cysts,
definitive diagnosis of pituitary dwarfism cannot be based solely
upon the presence of pituitary cysts.

Genetic Testing
A DNA test has been developed to aid in identifying the LHX3
mutation.22,23 Use of this test not only allows a proper diagnosis of
congenital GH deficiency, but it enables breeders to prevent dwarfs

from being born by testing the carrier status of potential breeding
animals and applying a correct breeding program.

TREATMENT
Porcine GH
Canine GH is not available. Attempts have been made to treat dogs
with congenital GH deficiency using heterologous GH. Antibody
formation precludes the use of recombinant human GH.29
Administration of porcine GH does not result in antibody formation,
because the amino acid sequence of porcine GH is identical to that of
canine GH.1 The recommended subcutaneous (SQ) dosage for
porcine GH, 0.1 to 0.3 IU/kg 3 times per week, may result in GH
excess and side-effects, such as DM. Therefore, monitoring of plasma
GH and glucose concentrations is recommended at 3-week intervals.
Long-term dosages should be determined based on measurements of
the plasma IGF-1 concentration. Whether administration of porcine
GH will lead to linear growth is dependent on the status of the
growth plates when treatment is initiated. A beneficial response in
the skin and lanugo hair growth usually occurs within 6 to 8 weeks of
starting therapy, but growth of guard hairs is variable.

Progestins (PGs)
Demonstration of PGs’ ability to induce expression of the GH gene in
the canine mammary gland, with subsequent secretion of GH into
the systemic circulation, has raised the possibility of so-treating
congenital GH deficiency. Treatment of young German Shepherd
Dog dwarfs with SQ medroxyprogesterone acetate (2.5-5 mg/kg),
first at 3-week intervals and then 6-week intervals, resulted in some
increase in body size and development of an adult hair coat. Parallel
with the physical improvements, plasma IGF-1 concentrations rose
sharply, with subtle increases in plasma GH that remained below the
upper reference range limit.27 Treatment of pituitary dwarfs with

proligestone has also been reported to result in the development of
an adult hair coat, increased body weight, and elevated plasma IGF-1
concentrations.30 However, administration of PGs may cause
recurrent periods of pruritic pyoderma and skeletal malformations.
PGs can also lead to development of mammary tumors, acromegaly,
DM, and/or cystic endometrial hyperplasia. As with porcine GH,
monitoring plasma concentrations of GH, IGF-1 and glucose is
important. Bitches should be ovariohysterectomized before starting
PG treatment. Treatment with levothyroxine should be started as
soon as there is evidence of secondary hypothyroidism (ch. 285).

PROGNOSIS
The long-term prognosis of German Shepherd Dog dwarfs is usually
poor without treatment. By 3 to 5 years of age, these dogs usually
become dull, thin, and bald due to progressive loss of pituitary
functions, expansion of pituitary cysts, and progressive renal failure.
At this stage, owners usually request euthanasia. Although the
prognosis improves considerably when dwarfs are properly treated
with levothyroxine and either porcine GH or PGs, their prognosis
remains guarded.

ACQUIRED GH DEFICIENCY (AGHD)
In addition to dogs and cats who develop AGHD following elective
hypophysectomy to remove a pituitary tumor and those who develop
AGHD following traumatic brain injury (ch. 246),31 there are
reports of mature dogs developing naturally occurring GH
deficiency. GH deficiency may explain some forms of alopecia in the
Pomeranian, Miniature Poodle, Chow Chow, Keeshond, and other
breeds. The alopecia, in dogs of either sex, neutered or sexually
intact, and of any age, is most common in dogs 1 to 3 years of age.
Their alopecia and darkly pigmented skin usually involves the trunk,
caudal thighs, perineum, and neck. The alopecia is not attributable to
any endocrine disease known to result in skin atrophy and hair loss
(i.e., hypothyroidism, hypercortisolism, or hyperestrogenism).

Treatment with heterologous GH32 or medroxyprogesterone
acetate33 has had poor to moderate results. Even so, the condition
has been given names such as “adult-onset GH deficiency” and “GHresponsive dermatosis.”
Uncertainty about the role of GH in this condition is further
illustrated by its other names: “castration-responsive alopecia,”
“biopsy-responsive alopecia,” and “alopecia X.”32,33 About one-third
of afflicted dogs have normal GH response to stimulation. Yet in
some with a normal response to stimulation, treatment with GH was
reported to be effective. In others, seemingly unrelated measures
such as castration or administration of testosterone were followed by
the appearance of a new hair coat.34 When GH stimulation tests
were performed on Pomeranians with alopecia and a control group
without alopecia, mean circulating GH concentrations failed to
increase significantly in either group.35 Thus, the association
between some forms of this adult-onset alopecia and decreased GH
secretion is poorly supported. Moreover, true GH deficiency is not
likely since plasma IGF-1 concentrations have invariably been within
reference ranges.32

CLIENT INFORMATION
Acromegaly (Growth Hormone Excess) in Dogs
INTRODUCTION
Acromegaly is characterized by bony and soft-tissue overgrowth and
insulin resistance due to excessive growth hormone secretion. In
middle-aged and elderly dogs, either the hormone progesterone,
produced by the ovaries after ovulation for about 2 months, or
progestins, drugs used for the prevention of an estrous cycle, may
give rise to hypersecretion of growth hormone. In addition,
acromegaly may be due to a hypofunction of the thyroid glands or,
very rarely, a pituitary tumor.

CLINICAL SIGNS

Acromegaly tends to develop slowly and is characterized initially by
soft-tissue swelling of the head, neck and abdomen. In some
acromegalic dogs, severe hypertrophy of soft tissues of the mouth
(with widening of the interdental spaces), tongue, and pharynx
causes snoring, and even dyspnea can be observed. Acromegalic dogs
often drink a lot and have a good appetite. Diabetes mellitus can
develop due to the insulin resistance induced by the growth hormone
excess.

DIAGNOSIS
The growth hormone concentration in the blood of acromegalic dogs
is often elevated. However, if the disease is mild or just beginning,
the blood growth hormone concentration may still be within the
reference range. A suppression test, showing that the growth
hormone levels in the blood cannot be suppressed, proves
acromegaly. Unfortunately, in many countries a commercial caninespecific growth hormone assay is not available. In this situation, an
elevated blood insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) concentration in
combination with typical clinical signs can be used to diagnose
acromegaly. If the growth hormone excess cannot be related to
exposure to progesterone or progestins, it has to be investigated
whether the growth hormone excess is associated with
hypothyroidism or is due to a pituitary tumor.

TREATMENT
If the acromegaly is due to the exposure to progesterone, the dog can
be treated effectively by surgical removal of the ovaries. Elimination
of the source of progesterone may prevent persistent diabetes
mellitus. Dogs with progestin-induced growth hormone excess
should have those drugs discontinued. Administration of
progesterone receptor blockers has been shown to result in a
decrease in blood concentrations of growth hormone and IGF-1 in
dogs with progestin-induced acromegaly. Treatment of dogs with
primary hypothyroidism with levothyroxine results in normalization
of plasma concentrations of growth hormone and IGF-1. In dogs with
acromegaly due to a pituitary tumor, treatment should be directed at
the pituitary lesion.
Hans S. Kooistra (Utrecht, The Netherlands)

CLIENT INFORMATION
Pituitary Dwarfism in Dogs
INTRODUCTION
Pituitary dwarfism is due to insufficient hormone secretion from the
pituitary gland, a small but important hormone-producing organ
located just beneath the brain. In most cases, pituitary dwarfism is
due to congenital growth hormone deficiency. However, there may
also be insufficient secretion of other pituitary hormones. The
condition is encountered most often as an inherited abnormality in
German Shepherd Dogs, but the disorder is also well known in
Saarloos Wolfdogs and Czechoslovakian Wolfdogs. In these breeds,
German Shepherd Dogs have been used in the breeding. The cause of
pituitary dwarfism in German Shepherd Dogs and related breeds is a
mutation in a gene (LHX3) that is important for the development of
the pituitary gland. This mutation results not only in insufficient
growth hormone secretion but also in a deficiency of the hormones
that regulate the thyroids and the gonads. When a dog is born with
pituitary dwarfism, it is clear that both parents are carriers of the
mutation.

CLINICAL SIGNS
Pituitary dwarfs are characterized by growth retardation, retention of
puppy hairs, and lack of guard hairs. The hairs are easily epilated
and there is gradual development of alopecia. The skin becomes
progressively hyperpigmented and scaly, and bacterial infections are
common.

DIAGNOSIS

The combination of growth retardation and an abnormal hair coat,
especially in Shepherd dogs, points to pituitary dwarfism, but this
suspicion has to be proven. Routine laboratory examination usually
will not reveal abnormalities, except for an impaired kidney function
and a hypofunction of the thyroid glands. A low concentration of
insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) in the blood strongly supports
the diagnosis, but the definitive diagnosis growth hormone
deficiency is based upon the results of a stimulation test.
Identification of the underlying mutation causing pituitary dwarfism
in German Shepherd Dogs has resulted in the development of a DNA
test. The availability of this diagnostic DNA test not only allows a
proper diagnosis of dogs with pituitary dwarfism due to this
mutation, but also enables breeders to prevent dwarfs from being
born by testing the carrier status of potential breeding animals and
applying a correct breeding policy.

TREATMENT
Canine growth hormone is not available for therapeutic use, but dogs
with pituitary dwarfism can be treated with porcine growth
hormone. Whether administration of porcine growth hormone will
lead to linear growth is dependent on the status of the growth plates
when treatment is initiated. A beneficial response in the skin and
hair coat usually occurs within 6 to 8 weeks of the start of therapy.
Treatment with levothyroxine should be started as soon as there is
evidence of hypothyroidism.

PROGNOSIS
The long-term prognosis of German Shepherd Dog dwarfs is usually
poor without treatment. Initially, pituitary dwarfs are usually lively
and alert. By the age of 3 to 5 years the animal has usually become a
bald, thin, and dull dog. These changes may be due to progressive
loss of pituitary functions and progressive renal failure. Although the
prognosis improves considerably when dwarfs are properly treated
with levothyroxine and porcine growth hormone, their prognosis still
remains guarded.
Hans S. Kooistra (Utrecht, The Netherlands)

PHYSIOLOGY
SYNTHESIS OF ARGININE VASOPRESSIN (AVP)

The principal hormonal regulator of water balance, AVP (antidiuretic
hormone [ADH]), is a 9-amino-acid peptide synthesized as part of
the prohormone preprovasopressin in the magnocellular neurons of
the hypothalamic paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei (Figure
282.1).1,2 The prohormone is packaged in neurosecretory granules,
axonally transported through the hypothalamic-neurohypophyseal
tract, and stored within the posterior pituitary. Enzymatic cleavage
into the constituent molecules, AVP, neurophysin-2, and copeptin,
occurs during transport and storage. When stimulated, all 3 products
are released into circulation. Stimulation of magnocellular neurons
leads to increased synthesis of AVP, but it takes several hours for
newly formed AVP to be ready for release. For this reason, relatively
large quantities of AVP are stored within the posterior pituitary.

SECRETION OF VASOPRESSIN
Circumventricular osmoreceptor cells within the organum
vasculosum of the lamina terminalis and subfornical organ, which lie
outside of the blood brain barrier, can detect a 1-2% increase in
osmolality (loss of water) and stimulate AVP secretion (to conserve
water). Entry of AVP into the systemic circulation is rapid through
fenestrated capillary vessels. As the half-life is short (5.9 minutes in
the dog3), plasma concentrations fall rapidly once the stimulus for
release subsides. Blood volume is primarily controlled by the reninangiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). High-pressure arterial
baroreceptors (in the carotid sinus and aortic arch) and low-pressure
volume receptors (in the atria and pulmonary venous system) can
inhibit AVP secretion via the glossopharyngeal and vagal nerves.2 A
10-15% decrease in blood volume or pressure stimulates AVP
secretion. Other stimulatory factors include stress, nausea, pain,
certain drugs, hypoglycemia, exercise, and ingestion of dry food.

ACTIONS OF VASOPRESSIN
Conservation of Water

In the absence of AVP, principal collecting duct cell luminal surfaces
in the kidneys have minimal water permeability. Binding AVP to
basolateral V2 receptors leads to fusion of intracytoplasmic vesicles
(aggregophores) containing aquaporin-2 with the apical cell
membrane, creating water permeability (Figure 282.1). Water
passes through the principal cell along an osmotic gradient
established between the hypotonic tubular luminal fluid within
nephrons and the hypertonic renal medullary interstitium. Urine
concentration (urine specific gravity [USG]) increases and urine
volume decreases in proportion to the amount of water reabsorbed.
Once receptor stimulation has ceased, aquaporins are internalized
and reincorporated into aggregophores.

FIGURE 282.1 An illustration of the mechanism
underlying the short- and long-term regulations of
aquaporin-2 (AQP2). Arginine vasopressin (AVP)
released from the posterior pituitary binds to the V2
receptor (V2R) present on the basolateral membrane

of principal cells in the renal collecting duct.
Activation of the receptor stimulates adenylate
cyclase (AC) activity, resulting in the production of
cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), which in
turn activates protein kinase A (PKA), and this
protein kinase phosphorylates aquaporin-2.
Subsequently, AQP2 accumulates on the apical
surface membrane through vesicular trafficking from
intracellular storage vesicles expressing AQP2.
Thereafter, water molecules flowing into the
collecting duct cells through AQP2 are able to flow
out to the interstitium via the basolateral water
channels aquaporin-3 (AQP3) and/or aquaporin-4
(AQP4). Aquaporins can be re-internalised in the
absence of AVP stimulation. The PKA also
phosphorylates CRE-binding protein (CREB), and
the phosphorylated CREB then stimulates
transcription of the AQP2 gene. ATP, Adenosine
triphosphate; P, phosphate.

Additional Actions of AVP
Binding to endothelial V2 receptors can release von Willebrand
factor (ch. 175) and tissue plasminogen activator while increasing
synthesis of nitric oxide and circulating concentrations of
coagulation factor VIII. Activation of V1a receptors stimulates
vascular smooth muscle contraction, platelet activation, and hepatic
glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Binding to V1b receptors
stimulates adrenocorticotropic hormone release from the anterior
pituitary in synergy with corticotropin releasing hormone and
increases insulin or glucagon secretion from the pancreas. In
addition, AVP has been identified as an important neurotransmitter
involved in learning, aggression, anxiety and social behavior.4,5

THIRST, ANGIOTENSIN-2,
NATRIURETIC PEPTIDES

Thirst is inextricably linked with the actions of AVP. Osmoreceptors
of the circumventricular organs stimulate thirst as well as AVP
secretion. Consuming water rapidly decreases both thirst and AVP
secretion prior to any change in plasma osmolality, a response
mediated in part by pharyngeal receptors to protect against
overhydration which could otherwise occur due to the inherent delay
between fluid intake and normalization of plasma osmolality.
Increased concentrations of angiotensin-2 stimulate both AVP
release and thirst.6,7 Natriuretic peptides have inhibitory effects on
renin, aldosterone and AVP release. AVP and angiotensin-2 have
stimulatory effects on atrial natriuretic peptide release.8 These
multiple mechanisms allow balanced, integrated control of water and
electrolyte balance.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF DIABETES
INSIPIDUS
OVERVIEW
Diabetes insipidus (DI) is associated with decreased production or
action of AVP. Although rare in dogs and cats, the condition is welldescribed, and is an important differential for polyuria and
polydipsia (PU/PD) (ch. 53). Animals incapable of drinking, or from
whom water is withheld, can rapidly develop life-threatening
hypernatremia (hyperNa).

CENTRAL DIABETES INSIPIDUS
Post-Trauma or Post-Surgery
Central diabetes insipidus (CDI) is characterized by complete or
partial deficiency of AVP. In dogs and cats, CDI is most commonly
due to structural defects within the hypothalamus, posterior
pituitary, or both. Pituitary neoplasia is most common in dogs and
trauma in cats. Several other causes have been described (Box
282.1).9,10 In people, traumatic or surgical transection of the
pituitary stalk may lead to a pattern known as the “triphasic

response.”11 Initial axon shock impairs release of AVP causing CDI.
Phase 2 is a period of antidiuresis due to unregulated and excessive
release of AVP stores from the posterior pituitary. Phase 3 is the
return of temporary or permanent CDI once AVP stores are depleted.
Temporary CDI reflects recovery of secretory function from the
stump of the transected pituitary stalk. This is more likely to occur
with distal injuries, below the level of the median eminence.12
Permanent CDI occurs if the initial injury or retrograde axonal
degradation causes death of 80-90% magnocellular neurons.
Although the triphasic pattern has not been specifically described in
dogs or cats, evidence of transient water retention or temporary
resolution of polyuria (PU) has been described in pets with CDI
following acute injury.9,13,14
CDI occurs in about 15% of severe traumatic brain injuries in
people, usually in the first 2-3 days.15 This acute post-traumatic form
of CDI is less commonly described in dogs and cats,16-18 but severe
hyperNa has been described in about 7% of dogs within the first 24
hours of head trauma19 (ch. 246). Hypophysectomy (to treat
pituitary-dependent hyperadrenocorticism) leads to CDI lasting >2
weeks in 53% of dogs and permanent CDI in 22%12 (ch. 293).
Sodium (Na) concentrations increase within hours and PU/PD
develops within days of surgery unless AVP is supplemented for
several postoperative weeks.20 Long-term CDI is more likely in dogs
with pituitary enlargement and in 72% of cats following
hypophysectomy.12,21-23 Hypophysitis or hypothalamitis can also
result in CDI. Inflammation can be sterile or associated with
infection (toxoplasmosis, migrating nematodes).10,24-26 Idiopathic
CDI has been reported in dogs and cats, but many did not undergo
advanced imaging of the pituitary area.

Other Causes of CDI
In humans, CDI is associated with mutations of the AVP gene
affecting the signal peptide or neurophysin-2.2 Mutations have not
been characterized in dogs or cats, but congenital CDI has been
reported in two 4.5-month-old Afghan Hound littermates.27
Individual cases of partial and complete CDI in young dogs and cats
are also described.10,28-31

NEPHROGENIC DIABETES INSIPIDUS
(NDI)
NDI is a diagnosis applied to a condition in which individuals with a
healthy hypothalamus and healthy pituitary produce normal AVP
that has reduced or no effect within the kidneys. Secondary NDI is a
feature of several diseases, including hyperadrenocorticism (chs.
293, 294), pyometra, and liver disease (chs. 53, 266). Primary
(familial) NDI is a rare genetic disorder in people with specific gene
mutations affecting the V2 receptor (AVP2R) and aquaporin-2
(AQP2) genes.32 More than 90% are sex-linked, due to the Xchromosomal location of AVP2R, and of these, about 10% are
believed to develop de novo. Autosomal AQP2 mutations are less

common. In dogs, primary NDI was suspected in a litter of Siberian
Huskies.33 Three of four male puppies had normal V2 receptor
numbers, but a 10-fold lower binding affinity for AVP in comparison
to healthy controls. All affected dogs were male, suggesting
involvement of the AVP2R gene. Isolated cases have been reported in
other breeds, but not in cats.34-36

SIGNALMENT AND CLINICAL
FEATURES
CDI can occur in dogs or cats of either sex, neutered or intact, at any
age, and in any breed or mixed-breed. Signalment depends on the
underlying cause. Primary NDI is congenital and signs become
obvious when attempting to house-break a puppy or when large
amounts of urine are observed in the litter box of a kitten. As the
AVPR2 gene is sex-linked, affected dogs are more likely to be male.
Secondary NDI, with its many causes (ch. 53), can occur at any age
and in any breed.
Diabetes insipidus (DI) causes severe polydipsia (PD), with
estimated water intakes up to 5-20 times normal (normal: <90-100
mL/day [dogs], <50 mL/day [cats]; ch. 53). Clinical signs may
develop acutely or gradually over several weeks or months. Animals
can display continuous thirst and select water over food, leading to
weight loss. Ingestion of large water volumes can lead to vomiting.
PU is also typically marked, with nocturia and urinary overflow
incontinence being common. Neurological findings are common in
dogs with structural pituitary or hypothalamic disease. In one study,
7 of 17 dogs with CDI developed neurological signs (seizure,
obtundation, behavioral changes, tremor) 2 weeks to 12 months after
the initial diagnosis, most commonly due to pituitary neoplasia (ch.
245).10 Neurological abnormalities can also develop if water is
withheld too long or if the animal fails to drink. In such cases,
cellular dehydration can lead to anorexia, weakness, ataxia, seizures,
and/or death. In animals with recent head trauma (ch. 246), these
signs can be difficult to distinguish from those due to brain injury.
However, neurological deficits may not be apparent at the time of
injury, and post-traumatic CDI may develop either soon or months

after the traumatic event. Neurological signs may also develop in
pets given free access to water after a period of water restriction due
to rapid decrease in their plasma osmolality leading to cerebral
edema.
Given the diverse endocrine functions of the pituitary gland, it is
not surprising that additional hormonal abnormalities are common
in pets diagnosed as having CDI. Functional pituitary tumors may
cause signs relating to hormone excess. Likewise, hypothalamic or
pituitary structural disease or hypophysectomy can lead to central
hypothyroidism (chs. 285, 286) or less commonly, secondary
hypoadrenocorticism (chs. 293, 294).37 Deficiencies of growth
hormone and gonadotropins can occur but are usually only clinically
evident in immature animals. Multiple persistent endocrine
deficiencies are common in people following head trauma and may
be under-recognized in dogs38 (ch. 246).

DIAGNOSIS
OVERVIEW AND ROUTINE TEST RESULTS
It is essential to exclude all causes of PU/PD before pursuing a
diagnosis of CDI, NDI, or primary polydipsia (PP) to avoid an
erroneous diagnosis. There is no single test to confirm a diagnosis of
DI and multiple diseases are known to alter AVP release or action.
Hyposthenuria is the only consistent clinicopathological finding in
pets with complete CDI or NDI, provided water intake is not
restricted and no other endocrinopathies are present. In partial
(non-absolute) CDI, isosthenuria or minimally concentrated USG
may be observed. Decreased blood urea nitrogen (BUN) may be
present due to renal medullary washout and decreased AVPdependent reabsorption. If water intake is decreased, changes
indicative of dehydration can develop rapidly, including increased
hematocrit, hyperNa, hyperproteinemia, hyperchloremia, prerenal
azotemia, and increased serum osmolality. In animals with head
trauma, monitoring serum electrolyte concentrations, urine volume,
and USG is necessary to ensure such changes are identified early,
and that neurological consequences are not attributed to brain injury
(ch. 125).

CONFIRMATORY TESTS
Background
Primary NDI can usually be excluded based upon signalment.
However, distinguishing between CDI and PP can be challenging as
the boundary between the 2 disorders may be obscure. Disorders of
AVP secretion are recognized in some people with PP, including
altered set-point for AVP release.39 Similarly, the AVP responses in
dogs with suspected PP have been characterized as exaggerated,
subnormal, or non-linear.40,41 This is further complicated by the
pulsatile and variable nature of AVP secretion and potential effects of
chronic over- or underhydration on AVP secretion and action.42

The Modified Water Deprivation Test (MWDT)—
Purpose and Protocol for Dogs
The MWDT is designed to distinguish CDI, primary NDI, and PP
(Figure 282.2).28 The test is time-consuming and should only be
considered if the dog can be assessed continuously. Accurate Na,
potassium, BUN, and urine test results must be rapidly available onsite. The first stage of the test consists of a 3-to-5-day period of
progressive water restriction. In theory, this allows for partial reestablishment of the renal medullary concentration gradient in dogs
with medullary solute washout. Dry food should be fed, and the
calculated total volume of water offered should be divided into
aliquots to avoid prolonged total deprivation. Although often
performed at home, it is possible for hypertonic dehydration and its
associated signs to develop rapidly during this stage. Owners must be
educated regarding potential adverse effects and to monitor their
dog’s demeanour carefully. As hypertonic dehydration is more likely
to occur in dogs with severe PU, it may be prudent to hospitalize
such cases for observation during this stage.
Water is completely withdrawn to begin the second stage, usually
early in the morning when most convenient for planned close
observation throughout the day. Stage 2 ends when 5% of body
weight is lost or when the USG is ≥1.025. The test should be
abandoned immediately if the pet becomes lethargic, azotemic, or

severely hypernatremic. In most pets with complete CDI or primary
NDI, 5% body weight is lost within 3-10 hours. However, in pets with
partial CDI or PP, it can take considerably longer. If USG increases to
>1.025, CDI and NDI are ruled out. A diagnosis of PP remains
possible. The third and final stage begins after 5% of body weight is
lost and with administering desmopressin (1-deamino, 9-D-arginine
vasopressin [DDAVP]), a synthetic analogue of AVP. At this time,
small volumes of water (2.5-3 mL/kg/hr total, but not at once)
should be offered to prevent continuing dehydration. Offering only
small volumes of water is meant to avoid the vomiting that often
follows ravenous consumption if given free access after becoming
dehydrated. USG is monitored every 30 minutes for 2 hours, hourly
for 8 hours, and after 12 and 24 hours if needed. The maximal
response to DDAVP is typically observed 4-8 hours after
administration. Stage 3 ends with a USG ≥1.015 or after 24 hours.
Water continues to be offered in larger volumes over time.

The Modified Water Deprivation Test—
Interpretation
Interpreting results can be challenging. PP is characterized by an
increase in USG >1.025 in response to water restriction. Failure to
concentrate urine during stage 2 followed by increased USG after
giving DDAVP is consistent with CDI. A failure to both concentrate
urine and respond to DDAVP is consistent with NDI. However,
failure to adequately restore some renal medullary concentration
gradient during stage 1 diminishes any response to DDAVP. Pets
with partial CDI classically show slight urine concentration in
response to water restriction, with further increases following
DDAVP. However, dehydration can induce maximal secretion of AVP
in some cases, with no additional response to desmopressin.

Testing Cats
The MWDT is of questionable value in cats. Only a single cat with PP
has been described. In addition, urinary catheterization and frequent
blood sampling can be difficult. It is wiser to consider trial therapy
with DDAVP in CDI-suspect cats.

Response to Trial Desmopressin Therapy as a
Diagnostic Aid
A simple alternative to the MWDT is a therapeutic trial. Average
daily water intake is determined prior to starting 5-7 days of DDAVP
therapy. In dogs with CDI, dramatic decreases in water intake and
increases in USG are typical. Dogs with primary NDI or PP fail to
respond. In animals with traumatic brain injury that cannot drink,
response to DDAVP can be assessed by measuring serum Na and
USG. Advantages of trial therapy include eliminating risk of
iatrogenic life-threatening hypertonic dehydration, decreased need
for intensive monitoring, and the ability to conduct the trial at home
which is extremely cost-effective. Although adverse effects associated
with DDAVP are rare, animals with PP can develop neurological
signs due to dilutional hyponatremia.43

Other Biochemical Tests
Due to the pulsatile and variable nature of its secretion, measuring
AVP concentrations is of little value. Further, samples for AVP
require meticulous handling and validated assays are not widely
available. The hypertonic saline infusion test was once considered
the gold standard method for differentiating between CDI, NDI and
PP. The test is based on measuring the AVP response to a 20%
sodium chloride infusion. A decreased AVP response is consistent
with CDI, a normal or exaggerated AVP response without a
corresponding increase in USG with NDI, and a normal AVP
response with appropriate rise in USG with PP. However, as
discussed, AVP assays are not widely available, and altered patterns
of AVP release can be a feature of PP. Urinary aquaporin-2
expression has been shown in healthy dogs to closely reflect changes
in AVP; however, further studies are necessary in a clinical setting.
Plasma copeptin concentrations correlate with AVP secretion in
people and are of value in diagnosing DI, but this marker has not
been evaluated in dogs or cats.44

Imaging
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT)
are used to identify structural pituitary and hypothalamic lesions
that may alter therapy or prognosis. In people, a hyperintense MRI
signal within the sella turcica is believed to represent phospholipid
or secretory granules within the neurohypophysis, and is absent in
the majority of people with CDI.45 Similarly, neurohypophyseal
intensity on T1-weighted MRI in dogs is proportional to AVP
content. This test has not been investigated clinically.46

TREATMENT
CENTRAL DIABETES INSIPIDUS

Treatment is not necessary if free access to water can be assured at
all times and the PU/PD are not distressing to the animal or owner.
Dogs and cats with partial or complete CDI, by definition, respond to
DDAVP. Although DDAVP is a potent V2 receptor agonist, negative
side-effects, such as excessive volume expansion or hyponatremia,
have not been reported. DDAVP has minimal effects on V1a
receptors and hypertension has not been reported. DDAVP
successfully controls PU/PD in almost all cases. Failure to respond is
most likely due to failure to administer the DDAVP or to the use of
tablets which are less effective than the liquid product. Dosage and
frequency are based on individual response.
DDAVP is available as an intranasal solution for human use. This
is commonly given at empirical dosages, ranging from 1-4 drops
(approximately 1.5-4 mcg/drop) into the conjunctival sac or nose q824h in dogs. Injectable DDAVP can be given at doses of 2-5 mcg.
Oral DDAVP (100 mcg, q12-24h) tablets can be given, but response
has been variable and often poor, likely due to low bioavailability
and/or interactions with food.47 In cats, oral (25-50 mcg q8-12h), SQ
(4 mcg q24h), conjunctival, and nasal (1 drop q12h) administration
have been described. The response to treatment is rapid and PU
returns rapidly if discontinued. Some owners may elect to treat only
at night to decrease the likelihood of nocturia.

NEPHROGENIC DIABETES INSIPIDUS
Primary NDI is extremely rare in dogs and cats; therefore, most
treatment recommendations have been extrapolated from humans.
In a minority of people with NDI, partial antidiuretic effects may be
seen in response to high doses of DDAVP. Thiazides decrease Na
absorption in distal renal tubules. The resultant diuresis leads to
decreased blood volume and glomerular filtration rate (GFR),
thereby increasing Na and water reabsorption in the proximal tubule
and reducing water loss. Additional effects may include a
tubuloglomerular feedback response-mediated reduction in GFR and
upregulatory effects on aquaporin-2 and distal renal Na transporter
expression.48-50 To further decrease the urinary solute load, a lowNa and low-protein diet is recommended. Nonsteroidal anti-

inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may have a synergistic effect in
reducing renal blood flow and GFR; however, adverse effects are
common.51 The sulfonylurea antidiabetic drug chlorpropamide may
be added. This drug, whose antidiuretic mode of action is not
understood, is more commonly used for managing partial CDI. It
may upregulate AVP receptors and unmask constitutive receptor
signalling.52 Use of thiazide diuretics in dogs with primary NDI has
been described with variable results; about 50% have reduced urine
production.34-36 The recommended dosage of hydrochlorothiazide is
2.5-5 mg/kg orally q12h in both dogs and cats.

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis for dogs with CDI is variable depending upon the
cause. Idiopathic and traumatic cases can be successfully managed
for several years while those with progressive hypothalamic or
pituitary neoplasia have a poorer prognosis. In one case series, 7 of
17 dogs were alive 18-72 months after diagnosis.10 The remaining 10
dogs died or had been euthanized 1 week to 2 years after diagnosis,
most commonly because of developing neurological signs.

CALCIUM HOMEOSTASIS IN DOGS AND
CATS
CALCIUM FUNCTIONS
Calcium (Ca), the most abundant element in the body due to its presence in
skeletal bone, is necessary for diverse processes, such as transmitting many
signals received on cell surfaces to intracellular locations, nerve conduction,
neuromuscular transmission, muscle contraction, blood coagulation,
hormone secretion and hepatic glycogen metabolism. Adverse effects on
organ systems are noted when Ca homeostasis is disrupted. The skeleton
acts as a Ca reservoir, used for correcting decreases in serum Ca
concentrations ([Ca]). Ca can be excreted or absorbed in the kidneys and the
small intestine. The Ca sensing receptor (CaSR), responsible for ensuring
that circulating [Ca] is maintained within a limited “normal” range, is a Gprotein present in parathyroid glands, kidneys, cartilage and bone.1
Interactions between the CaSR and parathyroid hormone (PTH),
synthesized and secreted by the parathyroid glands, can lead to direct or
indirect effects on skeletal bone, the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, and
kidneys.2

CALCIUM MEASUREMENT AND ITS SERUM
REGULATION
Ca, in common with other important electrolytes, is regulated to maintain
narrow reference intervals. Total serum [Ca] ([TCa]) is usually about 2.3-2.8
mmol/L (9.2-11.2 mg/dL) in dogs and 2.1-2.5 mmol/L (8.4-10.0 mg/dL) in
cats. Reference intervals vary between laboratories. When concerned about
Ca, it is recommended that both TCa and ionized Ca concentrations ([iCa]),
the biologically active form of the electrolyte, be assessed (ch. 69). About
50% of the [TCa] is iCa, about 40% is protein-bound (albumin plus a small
amount of globulin), and <10% is complexed with anions, such as

bicarbonate or citrate. Spectrophotometric methods are used to measure
TCa in serum or heparinized plasma. Blood anticoagulated with EDTA or
oxalate cannot be used because they chelate Ca. Hemolysis and lipemia can
falsely increase measured [TCa]. Hypoproteinemia lowers measured [TCa]
but does not affect measured [iCa]. Clinically, the [iCa], measured with an
ion-specific electrode, is most important. However, the proportion of iCa in
a sample can be altered by sample handling. When samples are stored, red
cell metabolism increases lactic acid concentrations, pH decreases, and the
iCa fraction increases. Conversely, when samples are exposed to air, CO2 is
lost, the pH rises, and the iCa fraction decreases.

CONTROL OF SERUM CALCIUM
CONCENTRATION [Ca]
Overview
Circulating [Ca] is under control of 4 important hormones: PTH, PTHrelated protein (PTHrP), vitamin D (calcitriol, 1,25-[OH]2-cholecalciferol),
and calcitonin. The CaSR senses extracellular [Ca]. Hypercalcemia activates
the CaSR, reducing PTH synthesis and secretion. Hypocalcemia inactivates
CaSR, increases PTH secretion, enhances PTH gene expression, and
promotes parathyroid gland cellular proliferation. Ca homeostasis is
disrupted when CaSR activity is abnormal or when pathological processes
interfere.

Parathyroid Hormone (PTH): Description, Function,
Assays
PTH is an 84 amino acid polypeptide hormone synthesized and secreted by
the parathyroid glands. Dogs and cats have 4 parathyroid glands (2 pairs).
One pair is either embedded within or closely associated with each thyroid
lobe (Figure 283.1). Cranial, “external,” glands are usually situated outside
the thyroid capsule and caudal, “internal,” glands are usually located within
thyroid tissue. Parathyroid glands consist of cords or nests of cells around
capillaries (Figure 283.2). Parathyroid chief cells continuously synthesize
PTH, which increases both TCa and iCa and decreases serum phosphate
(PO4) concentrations either directly or indirectly via activity in 3 major
target organs: bone, kidney, or GI tract (Figure 283.3). PTH is
metabolized quickly. Secretory granules within chief cells contain intact
active hormone, including the 34-amino-acid, biologically active N-terminus
and the carboxy-terminus portions required for PTH activity.2-4 When the

serum [Ca] is low, the secretory granule rate of degradation is reduced.
Conversely, when serum [Ca] is increased, the degradation rate is enhanced.
There is an inverse sigmoidal relationship between Ca and PTH; the setpoint of Ca homeostasis is the [Ca] that suppresses PTH secretion 50%. PTH
cannot be suppressed completely and low level production is continuous, so
the set-point is midway between this low-level production and maximum
PTH production. An altered Ca set-point characterizes many hypercalcemic
conditions, resulting in a drive to generate a higher [Ca] through the
synthesis and release of PTH. Increased concentrations of vitamin D slow
PTH gene transcription and reduce the rate of synthesis of the hormone.
High PO4 concentrations slow PTH breakdown and increase hormone
secretion.

PTH and its fragments cleaved from the prohormone circulate.
Biologically active intact PTH (amino acids 1-84) must be measured for
reliable assessment of parathyroid function.5,6 Assays developed for PTH
are sensitive and specific. Older PTH assays used antibodies directed at both
the C-terminal (amino acids 39-84) and N-terminal (amino acids 12-24, or
26-32). However, such assays also measured some of the fragments cleaved
between amino acids 1-12. Current (usually enzyme-linked immunosorbent
assay [ELISA]) assays use antibody combinations that only measure intact
hormone.7 A canine-specific ELISA, which has also been validated for cats,
is available. Some laboratories have validated human-specific PTH testing

kits for use in the dog and cat.8,9 Since assay availability changes, new
methods should be validated for the species being tested. EDTA plasma
samples are preferred for assaying PTH. Since PTH is labile, samples should
be immediately separated and frozen until assayed. The laboratory should
provide handling information, and many also provide freezer packs for
sample submission. The reference interval for PTH is approximately 20-65
pg/mL (2.1-6.9 pmol/L) in the dog and <25 pg/mL (<2.7 pmol/L) in the cat
but may differ depending on the laboratory and assay system used.

Parathyroid Hormone–Related Protein (PTHrP):
Description, Function, Assays
PTHrP is integral to Ca homeostasis in the fetus but after birth, it becomes
virtually undetectable in healthy animals. Increases in PTHrP are the cause
of humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (HHM).10 PTHrP has the same
physiologic effects as PTH, increasing TCa and iCa while decreasing PO4.
Measuring PTHrP is important when evaluating hypercalcemic dogs and
cats, since a neoplasia-related cause is always a possibility (ch. 69). Normal
or low PTHrP concentrations do not definitively exclude the possibility of a
neoplastic process, whereas increases are usually associated with a
malignant cancer (ch. 331). PTHrP can be reliably measured using 2-site
immunoradiometric assay (IRMA) or N-terminal radioimmunoassays
(RIAs). Several circulating forms of PTHrP, in addition to the intact 1-141
amino acid hormone, have biological activity. These include an N-terminal
1-36 amino acid fragment and a 1-86 amino acid N-terminal-and-midregion
fragment. Roles of these different forms are not completely understood.
Like most proteins, PTHrP is not stable, is measured preferentially in EDTA
plasma, and samples should be handled as described for PTH. The reference
interval for PTHrP is generally <0.5 pmol/L in both dogs and cats.

Vitamin D (Calcitriol, 1,25-[OH]2-Cholecalciferol)
Dietary cholecalciferol, hydroxylated once in an unregulated process by the
liver to produce 25-OH-cholecalciferol (25-OH vitamin D, calcidiol),
produces a reservoir pool of inactive vitamin D ready for activation to 1,25(OH)2-vitamin D, calcitriol. This step, which occurs in the kidneys, is
regulated: its synthesis is stimulated by PTH via alpha-1-hydroxylase and
suppressed by increases in PO4. 25-OH-cholecalciferol can also be
catabolized by 24-hydroxylation, then excreted. Vitamin D (25 and 1,25[OH]2 D) can be measured in cats and dogs by veterinary specialist
laboratories.

Calcitonin
Calcitonin, a peptide synthesized by thyroid gland C cells, reduces serum
[Ca] and aids in limiting postprandial hypercalcemia. Though calcitonin can
counteract the effects of PTH, its role is relatively minor. Following total
thyroid and parathyroidectomy, the clinical consequence is hypocalcemia
due to hypoparathyroidism, not hypercalcemia due to calcitonin deficiency.
Similarly, when there is neoplasia of the C cells (medullary thyroid
carcinoma) and excessive production of calcitonin, Ca homeostasis is not
disrupted. In people, release of calcitonin by Ca-stimulated CaSR activity is
unlikely to contribute to Ca homeostasis. Calcitonin is not usually assessed
in patients with Ca disorders, and no assays are commercially available.

How Do These Hormones Act Together to Maintain
Calcium Homeostasis?
PTH is the primary regulator of Ca homeostasis, increasing serum [Ca] by
increasing the number of osteoclasts on bone surfaces, increasing renal
tubular Ca absorption from distal convoluted tubules and thick ascending
loops of Henle, and increasing the hydroxylation of 25,OH vitamin D to
1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D, which increases Ca absorption from the small
intestine.2,3

FIGURE 283.3 Calcium homeostasis. The release of
parathyroid hormone (PTH) causes increased uptake of
calcium in the kidney and gut and mobilization from the
skeleton.

THE DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS FOR
HYPERCALCEMIA IN DOGS
Hypercalcemia can be caused by access to exogenous agents that alter Ca or
it can be the result of abnormalities in 1 of the endogenous homeostatic
mechanisms (Table 283.1; ch. 69). The approaches used in the systematic
workup of clinically stable or ill hypercalcemic dogs are reviewed in Figure
283.4.

PRIMARY HYPERPARATHYROIDISM
(PHPT) IN DOGS
DEFINITION
PHPT is an uncommon condition in dogs and is rare in cats. It should be
considered among the possible causes of hypercalcemia, particularly in
older dogs showing few or no clinical signs (ch. 69).12-14 PHPT is defined
by hypercalcemia and inappropriately increased PTH concentrations
(within or above reference intervals), with no other identifiable underlying
cause (Figure 283.5).

CAUSE
PHPT develops when 1 or more parathyroid glands function autonomously.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism develops after nonendocrine disruption of
Ca homeostasis associated with chronic kidney disease (CKD) or chronic
dietary Ca deficiency (ch. 162). PHPT is usually caused by a solitary
adenoma, carcinoma, or adenomatous hyperplasia of 1 parathyroid gland.
PHPT due to autonomous function of more than 1 gland has been diagnosed
in <10%. In a case series of dogs that went to surgery, 87% had a solitary
adenoma, 8% had hyperplasia and 5% had carcinoma.15 Functional
metastatic parathyroid tissue has been reported in only 1 of hundreds of
dogs with PHPT in the veterinary literature.16
The pathological change in 1 or more parathyroid glands causes persistent
excess secretion of PTH, independent of serum [Ca]. When
hyperparathyroidism is primary, usually 1 affected gland is the source of
autonomous PTH secretion. In the secondary condition,
hyperparathyroidism is usually due to hyperplasia of more than 1
parathyroid gland (classically all 4) in response to nonspecific stimuli to
produce PTH. Discriminating primary from secondary hyperparathyroidism

can be difficult. Histologic evaluation of extirpated parathyroid glands
seldom exhibits definitive evidence of being benign or malignant.
Hyperplasia may not affect each gland uniformly and, though most
frequently associated with secondary disease, has been described as a cause
of PHPT in cats and dogs.14,17,18

HUMAN PHPT AND COMPARISONS WITH
DOGS
PHPT is diagnosed in people who have increases in [TCa] and [iCa] together
with elevated or inappropriately normal PTH concentrations. PHPT most
commonly affects older women (>50 years) but may be identified in
younger individuals serendipitously when an asymptomatic individual has
blood-work in preparation for a routine procedure, similar to the experience
in dogs. It is managed using both surgical and non-surgical therapies.
Surgery is most appropriate for symptomatic people, such as those suffering
loss of bone density and bone fractures, or urolithiasis.
Hyperparathyroidism in people can occur sporadically or follow a familial
pattern either as part of a syndrome or as an isolated condition. Sporadic
PHPT can be caused by somatic MEN1 mutations (the gene mutated in
multiple endocrine neoplasia [MEN]) in about 35% of cases whilst other
mutations occur at low frequencies.19,20 Non-sporadic disease includes
familial isolated hyperparathyroidism (OMIM:145000), but PHPT has been
identified in other syndromes including MEN1 (OMIM:131100) and MEN
type 2A (OMIM:171400) and hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome
(HPT-JT, OMIM:145980). The main differential diagnosis for familial
isolated hyperparathyroidism/PHPT is the much rarer familial
hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH, OMIM:145980), identified using a Ca to
creatinine clearance ratio (CaCrCR). People with FHH have very low urinary
Ca clearance (80% have a CaCrCR <0.01) and normal or slightly elevated
PTH concentrations.21 This tool has yet to be used in dogs or cats.
The molecular genetics of familial conditions have been investigated
thoroughly in people where familial isolated hyperparathyroidism has been
associated with mutations in 3 genes associated with other phenotypes: the
genes coding for the CaSR, MEN1, and HRPT2.22 A diagnosis of familial
isolated hyperparathyroidism is reached if the criteria for diagnosing any of
the other phenotypes are not met when using standard, non-molecular
genetic tests. When people with familial isolated hyperparathyroidism are
investigated using molecular genetics, the CaSR and MEN1 genes are
assessed initially, as HRPT2 is a less common cause of isolated PHPT.23-26

The major differential diagnosis, FHH, overlaps with familial isolated
hyperparathyroidism in people and has not been recognized in dogs or cats.
The conditions tend to be somewhat benign over time and are often
managed medically. Two thirds of FHH cases are caused by mutations in the
CaSR gene as well as mutations in 2 more recently discovered genes
(adaptor protein-2 [AP2S1] and G-protein subunit alpha11 [GNA11]). These
genes code for proteins that are necessary for the functioning of the CaSR,
reflecting its G-protein-coupled structure.27-29 In people, PHPT is an
unpredictably progressive disease. One study documented disease
progression to end-organ lesions in only 25% of affected individuals30 and
end-organ lesions could not be predicted by severity of hypercalcemia. This
makes it difficult to make informed decisions about appropriate therapy in
asymptomatic patients and whether surgery is justified.

The Keeshond is the only dog breed identified to have a familial
predisposition to PHPT. Keeshonden have been studied using a candidate
gene approach.31,32 MEN1, CaSR and HRPT2 mutations were ruled out as

causative mutations leading to PHPT in the Keeshond. Despite using
genome-wide association analysis, the causative mutation has yet to be
defined.

SIGNALMENT
PHPT is a disease of older dogs (mean age 11.2 years; range 6-17 years) with
no apparent sex predisposition.15 In 1 review, Keeshonden were found to
have the highest breed-associated odds ratio, at 50.7.31,33,34 Cats of any
breed are infrequently affected. Neonatal PHPT has been reported in a litter
of German Shepherd Dog puppies, but this seems to have been an isolated
event.17

HISTORY AND CLINICAL SIGNS
Overview
PHPT does not cause dramatic clinical signs. Rather, it is slowly progressive,
insidious, and subtle (Box 283.1). Since affected dogs tend to be older,
many clinical signs are attributed to simple aging by owners who may not
seek veterinary advice until later in the course of the disease. Hypercalcemia
is often a serendipitous finding when blood chemistry is obtained for other
reasons. In one large retrospective study of 210 dogs with PHPT, 42% were
identified as having hypercalcemia when presented for other reasons, such
as a routine geriatric check, or when preanesthetic blood testing was
performed for procedures such as dental treatment.33 An association
between owners concerned about their dog having jaw pain or difficulty
eating hard foodstuffs and PHPT may exist, particularly in the Keeshond.
The most common reasons for seeking veterinary advice were clinical signs
related to urolithiasis (pollakiuria, stranguria and hematuria) or urinary
tract infection (50% of the 210 cases).33 Urolithiasis can cause acute urinary
outflow obstruction in dogs with PHPT (chs. 99 and 308).
