Polyuria and Polydipsia (PU/PD) and Other Signs (Box
283.1)
PU/PD was a concern of <10% of owners of dogs with PHPT, a surprisingly
small number given that increases in Ca antagonize effects of vasopressin
(antidiuretic hormone, ADH) in the collecting ducts of the kidneys and
hypercalcemia inhibits tubular uptake of sodium (Na) and chloride (Cl),
further inhibiting urine concentrating mechanisms. Affected dogs are
polyuric (PU) with secondary compensatory polydipsia (PD). This clinical
sign may be overlooked by dog owners because it progresses gradually and,
perhaps, nocturia and incontinence in these older animals is simply
tolerated. Dogs with PHPT often have reduced activity levels, appear listless
and may seem depressed. Again, these signs may be attributed to aging and

sometimes are not mentioned until after successful treatment, when dogs
are often described as having been “rejuvenated.”
In people, the signs of PHPT are remembered using the mnemonic
“stones, bones, abdominal groans, thrones, and psychiatric moans.” Some
people with PHPT are depressed and/or debilitated by bone pain. The
“thrones” in the mnemonic refers to the constipation commonly noted in
people with PHPT. However, recent literature suggests this classic view is
changing, as more people are diagnosed with PHPT and few or no
symptoms. The disease usually progresses in a benign manner, even without
treatment.35,36 Whether this is also true in dogs and cats is unclear, as there
are no large-scale animal studies. In contrast to the canine experience,
people with PHPT are at risk of an uncommon and potentially lifethreatening hypercalcemic crisis. This syndrome is associated with rapid
multiorgan functional deterioration and, if untreated, carries a 100%
mortality rate.37 There are no veterinary reports of this syndrome, but there
is a spectrum of disease severity and progression among dogs diagnosed as
having PHPT. The risk vs. benefit of treatment must be determined
separately for each dog. GI signs include inappetence, vomiting and
constipation. These signs can be secondary to Ca-induced gut smooth
muscle hypoexcitability and dysmotility.

Kidneys and Urinary Tract Stone Formation
In addition to causing PU and compensatory PD, the hypercalcemia of
PHPT may increase risk of CKD. CKD affects some dogs with PHPT, but not
others. PO4 concentrations should be at the low end or below reference
intervals in dogs with PHPT. If this were not the case, CKD would develop in
most dogs. In these dogs, closer monitoring and a more guarded prognosis
should be given. It has been suggested that calculating the Ca × PO4 product
may help predict the likelihood of CKD; dogs with PHPT, low PO4, and a
relatively low Ca × PO4 product may have lower risk. In a study of 210 dogs
the risk of CKD was deemed to be low.33 In a smaller study (29 dogs), about
25% developed CKD. In that study, the Ca × PO4 product was a poor
predictor of renal impairment.38 The genetically homogeneous Keeshond
population allows investigation of CKD in those carrying the mutation
linked to PHPT. If untreated, some PHPT dogs continue to have normal
renal function despite having prolonged, and in some cases severe,
hypercalcemia (TCa >4.0 mmol/L). Other PHPT dogs succumb to renal
failure with much more modest Ca elevations. Some dogs develop
nephroliths and urolithiasis. One dog with PHPT died with a large
nephrolith and renal failure after disease management had seemingly been
successful (Figure 283.6). It is therefore clear that predicting long-term
outcome with or without treatment is fraught with problems. Erring on the
side of caution when managing hypercalcemia is recommended and delays
to treatment should be avoided to protect renal function.

FIGURE 283.6 Ventrodorsal (A) and lateral (B)
abdominal radiographs showing a large nephrolith in the
left kidney and multiple smaller urocystoliths.
Uroliths are common in dogs with PHPT, due in part to increased [Ca]
filtered by the kidneys and lost in urine (ch. 308). Although PTH increases
Ca uptake from renal tubules, in PHPT there is also overt hypercalciuria;
reuptake is not likely able to match the amount of Ca filtered. Dogs with
PHPT also have increased PO4 excretion, creating urine supersaturated with
both Ca and PO4, enhancing chances of precipitation and stone formation.
Dietary oxalate uptake from the gut is reduced when there is abundant
intraluminal Ca, because Ca oxalate is not absorbable from the intestine. If
intestinal Ca absorption increases, oxalate absorption also increases. In this
scenario, the kidney filters more Ca and oxalate, again leading to urine
supersaturation. In hypercalcemic people, evaluation of the quantity of Ca
lost into urine is commonly assessed via urinary Ca:Cr clearance ratios;
however, these have not been widely used in animals.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (PE)
Relevant findings on PE (ch. 3) are few and nonspecific (Box 283.1). They
may include stiffness and gait abnormalities, dull mentation, weakness, and
muscle wastage. There are anecdotal reports of manic behavior in Keeshond
dogs with hypercalcemia, though this may reflect a response to discomfort
rather than implying a neurological component to the disease. While
parathyroid masses are usually too small to be palpated, careful
examination of the neck is indicated to assess the thyroid lobes and other
tissues.

ROUTINE CLINICOPATHOLOGIC TESTS
Total Calcium (TCa) and Ionized Calcium (iCa)
When hypercalcemia is identified, one should also assess iCa, PO4, PTH and
PTHrP. The hallmark of PHPT is an increase in both TCa and iCa while PTH
concentrations are within or above reference intervals (ch. 69). In the
series of 210 dogs with PHPT, mean TCa concentration was 3.6 mmol/L
(14.5 mg/dL).33 There was a range in severity of hypercalcemia: “mild”
increases in 52% of dogs (>3.0 to ≤3.5 mmol/L, >12 to ≤14.0 mg/dL),
“moderate” increases in 30% (>3.5 to <4.0 mmol/L, >14.0 to <16.0 mg/dL),
“serious” increases in 12% (>4.0 to ≤4.5 mmol/L, >16.0 to <18.0 mg/dL),
and “severe” hypercalcemia (>4.5 mmol/L, >18 mg/dL) in 6%. iCa
paralleled TCa concentrations in the 210 dogs. The mean plasma iCa
concentration was 1.71 mmol/L (range 1.22-2.41 mmol/L, reference range
1.12-1.41 mmol/L).
Severity of hypercalcemia is likely dependent on disease duration.
Keeshonden from families with PHPT generally begin exhibiting mild
hypercalcemia (<3.5 mmol/L, <14 mg/dL) when 6-8 years of age, which
gradually worsens over years. Some untreated dogs continue to experience
increased Ca concentrations until serious hypercalcemia is reached (>4.0 to
<4.5 mmol/L, >16 to <18.5 mg/dL). After this point some stabilization
occurs and concentrations do not continue to rise inexorably, similar to the
condition in people. Untreated Keeshonden with serious hypercalcemia
have lived with few or no clinical signs until their deaths at 13-15 years of
age. As the genetic basis for PHPT in other breeds is not known, it is not
clear if this pattern occurs in other breeds. Regardless, the disease is so slow
and insidious, affected dogs are often not considered ill by their owners.

Phosphate (PO4)
The hypercalcemia of PHPT, in individuals with normal renal function,
causes hypoPO4, an unusual finding in dogs (Box 283.2). PTH inhibits
renal PO4 resorption, commonly causing low-normal or low serum
concentrations. In the series of 210 dogs with PHPT, the mean serum PO4
was 2.8 mg/dL (0.9 mmol/L; range 1.3-6.1 mg/dL, 0.4 to 1.9 mmol/L;
reference range 3.0-6.2 mg/dL, 0.9-2.0 mmol/L).

Results of Other Serum Biochemistry Tests, Complete
Blood Count (CBC), Urinalysis (UA)

Serum biochemistries, other than Ca and PO4, are usually unremarkable in
dogs with PHPT. Since hypercalcemic dogs may be at risk for kidney
damage, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), PO4, and creatinine should be
assessed. Increases, due to pre-existing renal damage or prerenal factors,
may complicate making a diagnosis since changes associated with PHPT
with secondary CKD can mimic those of primary CKD and secondary
increases in PTH and TCa (Table 283.2). Serum alkaline phosphatase
(ALKP) may be elevated reflecting increased bone turnover. CBC
parameters show no consistent changes, although anemia of chronic disease
may be identified if the hypercalcemia is chronic. Since hypercalcemia
causes secondary nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, urine specific gravity
(USG) is expected to be <1.020 and some are hyposthenuric. Hematuria,
proteinuria, bacteriuria, pyuria and crystalluria are common.

FIGURE 283.7 Ultrasonographic image showing the
typical appearance of a parathyroid adenoma. The arrow
points to the thyroid gland and the calipers delineate the
parathyroid adenoma.

SPECIFIC ASSAYS

Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)
Circulating PTH concentrations should be assessed in hypercalcemic dogs
once increases in TCa and iCa have been confirmed and more obvious
causes ruled out (lymphoma). If a hypercalcemic dog has a PTH
concentration within the upper half or above the reference range (i.e., in the
upper half of the reference interval >35 pg/mL for dogs, reference range 2065 pg/mL), it is abnormal and consistent with PHPT. In most cases of
hypercalcemia not caused by PHPT, TCa and iCa concentrations may be
increased but PTH concentrations are low or undetectable.

Parathyroid Hormone–Related Peptide (PTHrP)
PTH is usually measured in conjunction with PTHrP (reference interval
generally <0.5 pmol/L in dogs and cats). If PHPT is not the cause of
hypercalcemia, PTHrP results may aid in narrowing the differential list to
include unidentified malignancies. Diseases such as multiple myeloma need
to be differentiated from PHPT since either can cause bone pain as well as
increases in TCa and iCa. Diagnosis of multiple myeloma is suggested by
hyperproteinemia and osteolytic lesions in bone identified on radiographs.
To further complicate the differentiation, there is 1 report of a dog with
PHPT and an unexplained and apparently associated monoclonal
gammopathy.39

IMAGING
Ultrasonography (US) of the ventral neck is the most useful imaging
modality when investigating the cause of hypercalcemia. About 90-95% of
dogs have a parathyroid nodule identified on US by experienced
radiologists.33 A high-frequency transducer of 7.5-10 MHz is required for
adequate resolution. In healthy dogs and cats, the parathyroid glands are
usually <3 mm in greatest diameter, seen only with excellent facilities and
expertise. When they are either hyperplastic or enlarged and adenomatous,
or when there is a parathyroid carcinoma, the parathyroid glands are
identified as nodules 2-20 mm in diameter, round to oval, hypoechoic,
within or near thyroid tissue (Figure 283.7).40 Thyroid nodules were
identified incidentally on US in 14 of 91 (15%) dogs being evaluated for
hypercalcemia.41 The finding of a thyroid nodule may complicate the
diagnosis because it may not represent the origin of hypercalcemia but may
indicate multiple concerns. Scintigraphy using technetium-99m sestamibi
has been tried in dogs as an aid to parathyroid identification, but unlike in
humans, it lacks sensitivity and specificity and is not recommended.42 Plain
abdominal radiographs or US is recommended to search for any
abnormalities, including calcium-containing renal or cystic calculi. Rarely,
extensive renal calcification is noted.

GENETIC TESTING
A genetic test for familial PHPT in the Keeshond is available. The test is
used to identify Keeshonden that carry the mutated allele responsible for or
linked to the autosomal dominant disease and is available through the
Animal Health Diagnostic Center at Cornell University, and details are
available at:
https://ahdc.vet.cornell.edu/Sects/Molec/PHPTtesting.cfm. Since
the molecular basis for this test has not been peer-reviewed, sensitivity and
specificity are not known. It is recommended that Keeshond breeders know
the genotype of their breeding lines and test the progeny of untested dogs.
The UK Kennel Club states that breeders are allowed to claim 2 generations
of negative by descent before they must retest their dogs, in response to
uncertainties about the accuracy of the test. Keeshonden at risk should be
monitored periodically to identify hypercalcemia, usually noted by 6-8 years
of age. However, PHPT can develop earlier or later, or indeed may never
manifest in the dog’s lifetime.

PRETREATMENT MANAGEMENT OF
HYPERCALCEMIA
Overview

Since PTH and PTHrP assays are usually performed by specialist
laboratories, there may be a delay between making a presumptive diagnosis
of PHPT and having that diagnosis confirmed. Emergency therapy for
hypercalcemia is rarely required in dogs with PHPT unless the Ca
concentration is in the “serious” to “severe” range. Some believe that
virtually no dog with PHPT requires therapy of any kind prior to specific
treatment of the PHPT, regardless of the degree of hypercalcemia. Others
suggest that serious to severe hypercalcemia be treated to lower serum [Ca]
while awaiting confirmatory results. Renal damage caused by persistent
hypercalcemia due to PHPT is quite uncommon but impossible to predict
(ch. 300). All affected animals must be considered at risk if significantly
hypercalcemic.

Fluid Therapy
Fluid therapy, the cornerstone of managing hypercalcemia, should aim to
correct any dehydration or volume deficit and expand the extracellular fluid
volume. This should increase glomerular filtration rate, urine output, and
renal Ca excretion while minimizing bone resorption. Diuresis using 0.9%
NaCl (saline) at rates of 5-10 mL/kg/hr should lower serum [Ca]. Saline is
the fluid of choice because Na ions compete with Ca ions to reduce tubular
reuptake. When an animal is considered optimally hydrated, furosemide (2
mg/kg PO, q8-12h) can further enhance renal Ca excretion. When giving
NaCl at high rates, particularly coupled with furosemide, one must avoid
inducing hypokalemia. If fluid therapy fails to lower serum Ca
concentrations, bisphosphonates, or much more rarely, calcitonin or
plicamycin may be used.

Glucocorticoids
Glucocorticoids do not have much effect on serum [Ca] in dogs with PHPT,
rarely lowering measured values, and their use is not recommended. The
use of glucocorticoids (about 1 mg/kg prednisolone or equivalent) to
decrease the serum [Ca] should be restricted to dogs clearly diagnosed but
in whom there will be a delay in treatment. Glucocorticoids are most
effective in HHM (ch. 331) by causing rapid tumor lysis and reducing
synthesis and secretion of PTHrP. Glucocorticoids increase renal Ca loss
and decrease both intestinal Ca uptake and bone resorption. When used in
undiagnosed pets, there is risk of masking and complicating the diagnosis of
neoplasia.

Bisphosphonates

Bisphosphonates decrease bone resorption by inhibiting osteoclastic activity
and inducing osteoclast apoptosis. Those used most include oral
(clodronate, etidronate, alendronate) and intravenous (IV) (pamidronate)
drugs. Although oral preparations are convenient for owners, this route is
not very effective, with <1% of a dose being absorbed.43 An IV infusion of
pamidronate is more reliable (1.3-2 mg/kg in 150 mL of 0.9% saline, given
over 2 hours). Pamidronate, approximately 100 times more potent than
etidronate, has effects that can last up to 3 weeks. Dosing can be repeated as
required. This drug is generally well tolerated44 but can cause GI sideeffects and hypocalcemia, particularly if overdosed. Pamidronate has been
used frequently to treat people with HHM, but a more potent
bisphosphonate, zoledronate, is now the drug of choice (ch. 331).
Zoledronate (0.1-0.22 mg/kg diluted in 45 mL normal saline and given over
30 minutes) is more than 100-850 times more active than pamidronate, can
be infused more rapidly, but has not been used much in dogs.45

Calcitonin
Salmon calcitonin is commercially available and, like bisphosphonates,
inhibits osteoclastic activity. It also inhibits renal reabsorption of Ca. It is
useful as an emergency treatment to decrease Ca concentrations but carries
the disadvantage that after the initial IV infusion (4 IU/kg), treatment must
continue daily (4-8 IU/kg, subcutaneous [SQ], q12-24h).46 Calcitonin can
cause anorexia and vomiting, is expensive, and is rarely used. Animals may
become resistant to the effects of calcitonin after a few days of treatment.

Plicamycin (Mithramycin)
There are few reports of this drug being given to dogs. A dosage of 25
mcg/kg, IV, in 5% dextrose over 2-4 hours every 2 to 4 weeks has been
suggested.47

Cinacalcet
This drug is a calcimimetic that interacts with the CaSR directly and can
control Ca, phosphate and PTH concentrations in human dialysis patients.
It has been suggested that this drug may be useful in dogs and cats with
hypercalcemia, particularly cats with idiopathic hypercalcemia, but there
are no data to support its use.

DEFINITIVE TREATMENT OPTIONS

Surgical Parathyroidectomy
Surgery is the treatment of choice at many referral institutions, especially if
the parathyroid nodule is large (>10 mm in greatest diameter).48 Good
visualization of each thyroid lobe is essential during surgical exploration of
the neck, achieved using a ventral midline approach. Parathyroid adenomas,
carcinomas or hyperplastic glands are usually easily discriminated from
normal parathyroid glands, often looking darker and larger (Figure
283.8). When the internal parathyroid glands are affected, they can be
identified by palpation and may be visible through the ventral or dorsal
aspect of the thyroid gland. Identification of the solitary, autonomously
functioning, abnormal parathyroid tissue can be aided greatly if its location
has been previously identified with US.
Parathyroid adenomas can be removed either by dissection of the
enlarged gland from the adjacent thyroid tissue or by partial thyroidectomy,
where the parathyroid nodule and part of the thyroid gland are removed en
bloc. In dogs with PHPT, usually 1 gland is affected. If more than 1 gland is
enlarged, then up to 3 glands may be removed at surgery. At least 1
parathyroid gland should be left in situ to maintain Ca homeostasis. When
multiple glands are enlarged, it is more likely that they are hyperplastic
rather than adenomatous, and therefore secondary rather than primary
hyperparathyroidism should be suspected.

FIGURE 283.8 Intraoperative pictures taken during the
removal of a parathyroid adenoma. A, The thyroid gland is
exposed. B, The cotton bud tip rests against the enlarged
parathyroid gland. Photos courtesy Ed Friend.
Techniques to determine if all functional abnormal parathyroid tissue has
successfully been removed intraoperatively have been described.49 In 1
study, samples were taken pre-, intra-, and postoperatively (20 minutes
after adenoma removal) to evaluate PTH concentrations and to confirm that
all functional tissue had been removed. All dogs in this study showed a

significant decrease in PTH concentration from pre- to postoperative
samples with an increase in PTH at times when parathyroid gland
manipulation was taking place. This may help with surgical identification of
parathyroid tissue, but only retrospectively, as analysis of samples in most
veterinary centers is not done on site and inevitably involves a delay of
several days.

Percutaneous, Ultrasound-Guided Ethanol Ablation
If parathyroid nodules are confidently identified by US, they should be
amenable to ethanol injection ablation. Nodules must be >3 mm in greatest
diameter, allowing accurate insertion of a 27-gauge needle. Animals must be
under general anesthesia for ablation. Ethanol causes coagulation necrosis
and thrombosis in the parathyroid nodule.50 Success is operator-dependent,
in that skill is needed for accurate needle placement and injection so that
the closely associated carotid artery and vagosympathetic trunk are not
compromised. When 3 techniques for treating PHPT were compared,
ethanol ablation was the least successful, with a positive outcome achieved
in 13/18 procedures (72%), compared with 45/48 (94%) for surgery and
44/49 (90%) for heat ablation.48 However, only a small number of cases
had been treated by ethanol ablation and in a subsequent report, a success
rate of >90% in 30 dogs was reported.51

Percutaneous, Ultrasound-Guided Heat Ablation
This therapy is infrequently used because few institutions have the
necessary equipment. The technique involves inserting a 20-gauge over-theneedle catheter, which acts as insulation, into the affected parathyroid
nodule. The needle is attached to a radiofrequency unit producing wattage
adjusted to achieve visible thermal necrosis at the needle tip.52 The dog is
anesthetized and positioned on an electrocautery ground pad. Usually, the
initial radiofrequency is applied at 10 watts and slowly increased as needed
until the entire gland becomes hyperechoic (

Video 283.1).

HISTOPATHOLOGIC EVALUATION OF
EXCISED PARATHYROID TISSUE
Differential diagnoses of enlarged parathyroid glands include adenoma,
hyperplasia, and carcinoma, but absolute diagnosis can be difficult.
Carcinomas can usually be separated from benign adenomas by features of

malignancy: capsular invasion, mitosis >5-10/high power field, cell atypia,
and tumor necrosis. Non-malignant parathyroid masses are frequently
reported as adenoma, hyperplasia, or adenomatous hyperplasia,
emphasizing the difficulty sometimes encountered in differentiating these 2
parathyroid processes.

PRE- AND POST-TREATMENT
CONSIDERATIONS
Vitamin D
Presence of autonomously functioning parathyroid tissue causes normal
glands to atrophy, making them unable to immediately support Ca
homeostasis after abnormal tissue is removed. This effect may be more
pronounced if more than 1 parathyroid gland is removed. When PHPT is
treated successfully, serum PTH and [Ca] should decrease rapidly and, in
some circumstances, a hypocalcemic crisis may be encountered because
remaining parathyroid tissue is atrophied. This usually happens if the Ca
has been “seriously” or “severely” elevated chronically, but knowing
duration of hypercalcemia and predicting those dogs at greatest risk for
worrisome hypocalcemia is difficult.53,54 Generally, hypocalcemia is more
likely if the pretreatment TCa is >3.5 mmol/L (14 mg/dL) or the iCa >1.80
mmol/L for more than a few months. Also possibly pivotal to the
development of clinical signs is the rate at which the iCa concentration
decreases. Rarely, clinical signs of hypocalcemia (panting, muscle
fasciculations, vocalization, and tetany; ch. 284;

Videos 69.1, 284.1,

284.2) can be seen in animals whose iCa is dropping sharply but is not yet
within or below the reference range.
Such a crisis can be averted by administering vitamin D ± oral Ca in the
immediate post-treatment period or, when the [Ca] is “moderately” to
“severely” elevated, by starting Ca and vitamin D supplementation 12-24
hours before surgery or ablation treatment. One study failed to identify a
clear indication for vitamin D supplementation in dogs with varying preoperative TCa concentrations. There was no difference in postparathyroidectomy outcome in dogs given no vitamin D versus those that
received 2 different doses in 1 study.55 Another study, however, found there
was a significant, though moderate, association between higher pretreatment iCa and the proportion of dogs with ionized hypocalcemia <1.00
mmol/L (P = .014) post-treatment.56 The prospective arm of this latter
study was abandoned because it was not considered ethical to withhold Ca

and vitamin D treatment in dogs that clinicians considered to be at risk of
postoperative hypocalcemia.
Vitamin D is available in several different preparations. It is valuable to
use a vitamin D preparation with a relatively rapid onset of action;
otherwise, treatment needs to be started earlier. The 2 preparations most
frequently recommended are calcitriol and alfacalcidol. Calcitriol (1,25dihydroxycholecalciferol) is active vitamin D and does not require
metabolism to become active. It has a rapid onset of action (1-4 days) and a
short half-life. Toxic effects would be expected to resolve in 2-7 days.
Calcitriol is available as capsules of 0.25 or 0.5 mcg and as a 1 mcg/mL oral
solution. Initial dose is 20-30 ng/kg PO q12h.57 Alfacalcidol requires
hepatic 25-hydroxylation to become active, which occurs rapidly in a
relatively unregulated fashion. There is no significant difference vs. calcitriol
in the time required to reach maximal effect. Alfacalcidol is available as
0.25, 0.5 and 1 mcg capsules and as liquid (2 mcg/mL). The dose is 0.010.03 mcg/kg PO q24h. However, these dosages are flexible and must be
titrated up or down as needed by the individual animal; additionally,
dividing doses for twice-daily administration can improve outcomes.

dog that had received intravenous calcium gluconate using

Calcium
Vitamin D may be given with or without oral Ca supplementation using Ca
gluconate, Ca lactate, or Ca carbonate. The dosage is calculated on the basis
of elemental Ca in each preparation (10-20 mg/kg PO q8-12h), not on the
mg tablet content. Thus, dosages are the same once the elemental Ca
content is calculated (e.g., 1 mg elemental Ca = 11.2 mg Ca gluconate, 7.7 mg
Ca lactate, or 2.5 mg Ca carbonate). Often, (particularly when postoperative
hypocalcemia has been severe and causing clinical signs), Ca
supplementation is used for short-term patient stabilization. In the longer
term, it is rarely necessary to use Ca supplementation because most pet
foods contain more than adequate amounts. Vitamin D dosage is quite
important, as it allows dietary Ca to be absorbed.

Recombinant 1-34 and 1-84 PTH
Recombinant PTH has been available for studies in people. Recombinant
PTH products are used in people with poor bone density and for those with
hypoparathyroidism. Please see ch. 284 for a discussion on these products,
use of which has not been reported in dogs.

Emergency, Short-Term Treatment of Hypocalcemia; IV
Ca Supplementation
IV Ca may be required for dogs that become seriously hypocalcemic after
treatment for PHPT, whether or not they are showing clinical signs. The
clinical signs of hypocalcemia are listed in Box 283.3 and further described
in ch. 284. Dogs hospitalized and not being exercised or unduly stressed
may be stable with [Ca] below the reference interval, but they are best
supplemented and carefully monitored in an attempt to avoid a
hypocalcemic crisis. When a hypocalcemic crisis is encountered, IV 10% Ca
gluconate can be given: 0.5-1.5 mL/kg, IV, slowly over 20-30 minutes or
until clinical signs have subsided and the dog is stable. Ideally, an
electrocardiogram (ECG) is used to monitor the heart during the infusion
and stopped if ST segment elevation, QT shortening, or arrhythmias
develop. Less sensitive pulse monitoring can be used if necessary.
Thereafter, a continuous rate infusion of 10-15 mg/kg/hr (10-15 mL/kg over
24 hr) should be employed until oral therapy can be safely started.
Calcium salt solutions are caustic vascular irritants that can cause
thrombophlebitis if the infused Ca concentration is high and if given for a
protracted period (more than 1-2 days). IV catheters should be repeatedly
inspected for patency and efficacy in an attempt to avoid extravasation of
Ca-containing fluids which can cause extensive tissue damage (Figure
283.9).

There are varying opinions regarding use of SQ Ca supplementation.
Sterile abscess formation and skin sloughing have been reported in some
dogs after Ca salts were given SQ.13 However, some authors recommend Ca
gluconate be given SQ, as it is much less likely to cause a problem. Although
Ca gluconate may be given SQ with no adverse effects, it can cause dramatic
skin sloughing. For this reason, only IV and oral routes of administration
are recommended (Table 283.3). When the pretreatment TCa
concentration is >3.5 mmol/L (>14 mg/dL) or the iCa >1.8 mmol/L and
particularly when the pre-treatment TCa or iCa is severe (TCa >4.0 mmol/L,
16 mg/dL; iCa >2.0 mmol/L), it is advisable to begin vitamin D
supplementation 24-36 hours before treatment to slow the decrease in [Ca]
after treatment and avoid severe hypocalcemia. This treatment is always
something of a balancing act, as it is not advisable to exacerbate the preexisting hypercalcemia. Given the delay in vitamin D’s onset of activity,
starting a day before definitive treatment for PHPT is safe.

PROGNOSIS
The short- to mid-term (<2 years) prognosis for PHPT is excellent in all
breeds. In all breeds except the Keeshond, the long-term prognosis also
appears to be good.

RECURRENCE OF PRIMARY
HYPERPARATHYROIDISM
Hyperparathyroid people are defined as “cured” when normocalcemic for 6
months after the date of surgery.58 Recurrences in people are known to
depend on whether they have a familial form of the disease or a
spontaneous sporadic disease. Recurrence is considered inevitable in
individuals with familial hyperparathyroidism, though the time to
recurrence is variable.59 Interpretation of data about the incidence of
recurrence is complicated by the different genetic and clinical
manifestations, with early reports unclear because clinical entities were not
separated using molecular techniques. Inherited forms of PHPT are now
known to recur predictably, whereas FHH does not respond well to
parathyroidectomy and treatment failure is more common than disease
recurrence. In a recent study of 261 patients with sporadic PHPT and
follow-ups ranging from 3-17 years, the recurrence rate was 10.7%.60 The
rate of recurrence of PHPT in dogs after curative surgery (>6 months postsurgery) is unknown across all breeds aside from Keeshonden. In the only
study of recurrence in dogs, involving 12 Keeshonden and 15 nonKeeshonden dogs, the Keeshond had a recurrence rate of 50%, whilst only 1
other dog breed, a Border Terrier, was documented to have recurrence.61
Confidently predicting possible recurrence in both people and dogs is
difficult.62 It is wise in all dogs, but particularly in Keeshonden, to
recommend yearly rechecks of TCa and iCa.

∗

Recurrence rates raise the question: When is the best time for
parathyroidectomy? In Keeshonden, the natural development of the disease
takes many years and early signs of mild-to-marginal hypercalcemia
associated with high PTH concentrations can be identified in some. It may
not be appropriate to surgically resect the affected gland in a relatively
young (<8 years) dog suffering from only mild hypercalcemia as there are
many remaining years ahead during which another gland can become
adenomatous and the risk of chronic kidney injury, urolithiasis and other
complications are low. There are currently insufficient data to suggest cutoffs for TCa or iCa above which surgery should be pursued, and certainly
there are multiple factors involved in determining the pathogenicity of
hypercalcemia over and above the absolute value.
An alternative approach would be to remove all but 1 parathyroid gland at
the time of the first surgery in Keeshonden with inherited PHPT. In this
author’s experience, this can result in severe postoperative hypocalcemia,
which in some cases requires lifelong supplementary Ca therapy to control.
One Keeshond, first successfully treated at the age of 10 years, became
hypercalcemic again at 11.5 years of age and had a second surgery removing
1 gland. Although 2 parathyroid glands remained, this dog was never again
able to maintain normal serum [Ca] without being given vitamin D. The
variability in response to surgery and requirement for supplementary Ca
makes successful perioperative management complex in Keeshonden.

FELINE HYPERCALCEMIA
FELINE IDIOPATHIC HYPERCALCEMIA

Although most causes of hypercalcemia in the dog can be identified
relatively easily, feline idiopathic hypercalcemia (FIH) is defined as a
“diagnosis by exclusion” (Figure 283.10) (ch. 69). Unexplained
hypercalcemia in cats was observed in the 1990s, with 20 affected cats then
described.63 Since that report, FIH remains an obscure condition, variably
reported as being the most common64 or among the top 3 causes of
hypercalcemia in cats.65 About 50% of cats with FIH show no related
clinical signs66 but in other cats, the condition has been associated with an
array of subtle clinical signs that include inappetence, anorexia, vomiting,
weight loss, constipation and urolithiasis. PU/PD are only observed in cats
with concurrent kidney disease as, unlike in dogs, hypercalcemic cats are
able to maximally concentrate their urine despite hypercalcemia.
Hypercalcemic cats are diagnosed with FIH when their PTH, PTHrP, and
vitamin D metabolite results are normal or below the reference intervals
and survey imaging of thorax and abdomen are normal. Cats not showing
clinical signs are often not treated.
Treatment of cats showing clinical signs usually begins with a change of
diet (high fiber, renal or calcium oxalate urolith preventative diets) (chs.
155, 159). If diet alone is not successful, bisphosphonates have fewer longterm side-effects than glucocorticoids. Alendronate has most frequently
been recommended (5-30 mg/cat PO, once weekly to be given with water on
an empty stomach and followed by a gap of 2 hours before food; tablets
should not be split).67 Bisphosphonates commonly cause esophageal
irritation and should be given with water to ensure esophageal transit.
Rarely, bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw may occur in
cats.68 For cats not tolerating oral medication, IV pamidronate can be used,
but it is more difficult to tailor for each cat and hypocalcemia is a potential
side-effect. More esoteric treatment regimens include use of chia seeds in
the diet. The rationale suggests FIH is caused by increased Ca binding and
uptake in the gut, a process impeded by fiber-rich chia.69

FIGURE 283.10 Algorithm to diagnose and manage
idiopathic hypercalcemia in cats. FNA, Fine-needle
aspirate; iCa, ionized calcium; PTH, parathyroid
hormone; PTHrP, parathyroid hormone–related protein;
TCa, total serum calcium concentration.

PRIMARY HYPERPARATHYROIDISM IN
CATS
PHPT has been reported in a few middle-aged to older cats. Clinical signs
described have included vomiting, PU/PD, weight loss and a palpable
cervical mass.70 Although the abnormal parathyroid gland may not be
palpable, similar to dogs, parathyroid disease is often associated with cystic
structures that make the mass more noticeable. Since hyperthyroidism is
the most common cause for a palpable cervical mass in cats, this condition
must be ruled out. PU/PD may be more subtle in cats and urine specific
gravity may not be significantly altered unless the cat is suffering from
concurrent renal insufficiency.14 Cats, like dogs, may also suffer from Ca
urolithiasis.71 The treatment of choice for PHPT in cats is removal of
abnormal parathyroid tissue.12 As in dogs, treatment success is greatly
enhanced when US is used before surgery to identify the parathyroid mass
or masses. Long-term prognosis is good post-surgery. Other treatment
techniques have not been reported in cats. Treatment with Ca and vitamin D
analogues may be necessary in cats due to the development of hypocalcemia
after parathyroid gland removal. There is less information available in cats
about when to prescribe calcium and vitamin D to pre-empt a postoperative
hypocalcemic crisis, but the same principles apply that have been outlined

for dogs. Again, it is difficult to predict which patients will need
supplementation and for how long.

BACKGROUND
The parathyroid glands were first discovered in the Indian
rhinoceros by Richard Owen in 1850. Ivar Sandstrom was the first to
name and describe them in 1880 while, in 1900, Giuilo Vassale and
Francesco Generali reported that complete parathyroidectomy
resulted in tetany.1 Naturally occurring hypoparathyroidism was first
described in dogs in 1966 and cats in 1990.2,3 Idiopathic primary
hypoparathyroidism remains an extremely uncommon disease in
both dogs and cats.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Normal parathyroid physiology is reviewed in ch. 283. Loss of
parathyroid hormone (PTH) or its activity results in hypocalcemia
and hyperphosphatemia through a combination of mechanisms:
decreased resorption of calcium (Ca; ch. 69) from bone causing
decreased release of Ca and phosphorus (PO4) into the circulation,
decreased absorption of Ca and PO4 from the small intestine, and
decreased reabsorption of Ca and decreased excretion of PO4 via the
renal tubules. Renal effects of PTH have the greatest impact on
serum PO4 concentration. Lack of PTH leads to hyperPO4. In health,
Ca stabilizes neuronal membranes by limiting sodium (Na)
permeability and membrane depolarization. In hypoCa, however,
both peripheral and central nervous system neurons become
hyperexcitable, leading to the common signs of tetany: seizures,
muscle tremors/fasciculations, stiff gait (muscle pain and/or muscle
tetany), and changes in behavior (likely due to painful tetany).

ETIOLOGY
Severely hypoCa dogs and cats with hypoparathyroidism and no
history of neck surgery or trauma may be classified as having
“idiopathic” primary hypoparathyroidism. An immune-mediated
etiology is suspected in some. Histologic examination of their

parathyroid glands reveals markedly decreased numbers of
parenchymal cells, infiltration with lymphocytes and, to a lesser
degree, plasma cells and neutrophils.4-6 However, parathyroid
histopathologic information has not been commonly obtained in
dogs or cats with apparent PTH deficiency. Resolution of
hypoparathyroidism in 1 dog given immunosuppressive therapy
supports an immune-mediated process as cause in some.7 There’s
one report of a dog that developed transient (<6 months)
hypoparathyroidism following a bite wound injury of the neck.8

CLINICAL FEATURES IN DOGS
SIGNALMENT
Dogs with primary hypoparathyroidism, at the time of diagnosis,
have ranged in age from 6 weeks to 13 years (mean: about 6 years) of
age. Females, Miniature Schnauzers, Poodles, German Shepherd
Dogs and Terriers are predisposed.4,5,9,10 Saint Bernards are
overrepresented in Australia and New Zealand.9,11

CLINICAL SIGNS
Most clinical signs associated with hypoparathyroidism are related to
neuromuscular “tetany” or “hyperexcitability.” Seizures, muscle
tremors, muscle fasciculations (

Video 284.1), and a stiff gait are

reported in most dogs, and jaw “champing” is seen in about half of
the dogs with fasciculations.4,9 Panting, facial rubbing (

Videos

284.1, 284.2), biting at the paws, and behavior changes (such as
restlessness, anxiety, and aggression) are often identified on careful
owner questioning. These signs may be explained either by reactions
to muscle cramping and pain or to a tingling sensation in the muscles
(ch. 31).4,9 Rarely, ataxia, circling, or synchronous diaphragmatic
flutter has been observed.12 Nonspecific signs include inappetence,
vomiting, “weakness” (pain and stiffness may be seen as weakness),

lethargy, and diarrhea. The duration of clinical signs preceding
diagnosis ranges from a few hours to a year or more (median: about
2 weeks).4,9 Neuromuscular signs (

Video 284.3) typically

become more severe with time, are episodic, and are exacerbated by
exercise or excitement. Virtually every clinical sign associated with
hypoparathyroidism resolves with therapy.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Dogs with primary hypoparathyroidism are often hyperthermic,
tense, anxious, nervous, and stiff-gaited. They may growl or snap at
being touched or palpated because touching can cause painful
muscle cramping. For example, a tense abdomen may be due to pain
in the abdominal muscles, pain elsewhere, or the dog may be
anticipating pain because petting may have caused muscle cramping
and pain in the past. Dogs may sometimes be aggressive or resist
petting, particularly on the head. Some have tachyarrhythmias.
Lenticular cataracts, appearing as small punctate to linear opacities
in the anterior and posterior cortical subcapsular region, may be
noted at initial presentation or following initiation of therapy (ch.
13). The mechanism of cataract formation is unclear, but they do not
appear to impair vision.4,9,13

CLINICAL FEATURES IN CATS
Primary hypoparathyroidism is most common in male cats. Clinical
signs are similar to those in dogs; cats have lethargy and a poor
appetite more often. Lenticular cataracts and/or prolapse of the third
eyelids have been observed.3,13-15A cat with myocardial failure and
echocardiographic findings consistent with dilated cardiomyopathy
had resolution of cardiac changes after treatment for
hypoparathyroidism.16

DIAGNOSIS (FIGURE 284.1)

ROUTINE TESTING
Total Calcium (TCa) and Ionized Calcium (iCa)
Concentrations
At diagnosis, hypocalcemia is present in all pets with
hypoparathyroidism and almost all are hyperPO4. Rechecking the
serum TCa is recommended in pets with severe hypoCa, because the
condition is uncommon. Rechecking gains importance if clinical
signs are not consistent. Using blood from an EDTA (“purple top”)
tube or even contaminating the needle with EDTA prior to injecting
blood into another tube can artificially decrease measured Ca due to
its EDTA binding. Since iCa is the biologically active Ca, its
measurement may provide a more accurate representation of the
pet’s status. In hypoparathyroidism, decreases in TCa and iCa tend to
be similar in severity. In the absence of hypoalbuminemia, if
measurement of iCa is not possible, repeatedly demonstrating low
TCa concentrations in a pet with compatible clinical signs is
generally adequate to confirm hypocalcemia. Clinical signs of hypoCa
are not usually observed until the TCa concentration is <7 mg/dL
(<1.75 mmol/L) or the iCa concentration <0.8 mmol/L. Signs quite
uncommonly occur at higher values if acute. Pets with
hypoparathyroidism often have profound decreases in TCa (as low as
2.7 mg/dL [0.68 mmol/L]).4,9 Since some dogs and cats do not
exhibit clinical signs, it is assumed that their disease has progressed
slowly, allowing some physiologic adaptation.13

Magnesium (Mg)
Only 1% of body Mg is located within extracellular fluids, taking
some credibility away from serum concentrations ([Mg]). HypoMg
(ch. 68) has been documented in Yorkshire Terriers with concurrent
hypoCa and protein-losing enteropathy (ch. 262). Low [Mg] may
interfere with PTH secretion.17 However, Mg concentrations have
been within reference limits in most dogs with primary
hypoparathyroidism and only mildly to moderately decreased in a
few. Since these dogs appear to recover without Mg
supplementation, the significance of their low [Mg] is unknown.4,13

Other Serum Chemistry, Complete Blood Count
(CBC), and Urinalysis (UA) Results
Most serum biochemistry panel results (other than calcium and
PO4), CBCs, and UAs are unremarkable in pets with primary
hypoparathyroidism. Increased creatine kinase activity has been
reported in a cat and dog and would be expected in any animal with
excess muscle activity (ch. 66).16,18

various causes of hypocalcemia. BUN, Blood urea
nitrogen; PO4, phosphorus (phosphate); PTH,
parathyroid hormone. From Feldman EC, Nelson
RW, Reusch CE, et al. Canine and Feline
Endocrinology. 4th ed. Saunders; 2015.

Electrocardiogram (ECG)

HypoCa prolongs the duration of myocardial muscle action
potentials, causing prolongation of S-T segments and QT-intervals
(chs. 69 and 96).9

PARATHYROID HORMONE (PTH)
MEASUREMENT
Diagnosis of primary hypoparathyroidism requires documenting low
serum TCa and/or iCa concentrations with concurrently
inappropriately low PTH concentrations ([PTH]). Due to tight Ca
regulation, [PTH] should be above the reference range in healthy
animals with hypoCa. Serum [PTH] in dogs and cats with primary
hypoparathyroidism may be low or in the low end of the reference
range.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES
The differential diagnosis of hypoCa includes a few common
conditions and a variety of uncommon causes (Figure 284.1). The
parathyroid gland-related conditions include immune-mediated
destruction, idiopathic destruction, surgical removal, and rare
conditions in people not yet reported in dogs or cats (ch. 69).
Conditions uncommonly associated with hypoCa are hypoMg, acute
kidney injury (AKI, ch. 300), chronic kidney disease (CKD, ch.
301), pancreatitis (chs. 277, 278), diabetes mellitus (chs. 291, 292),
eclampsia, malabsorption syndromes (ch. 262), urinary tract
obstruction (chs. 99, 308-312), and use of phosphate-containing
enemas. Hypoalbuminemia usually causes non-worrisome decreases
in TCa but not iCa, even though decreases can appear significant.
Other causes are uncommon (ch. 69).

TREATMENT
ACUTE TREATMENT
Intense IV

Dogs with severe hypoCa (

Video 284.3) should be treated

initially with an intravenous (IV) bolus of Ca gluconate and
maintained using a constant rate infusion (CRI) of Ca gluconate
(usually added to the IV fluids). Oral Ca supplementation can also be
provided until calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3;
dihydroxycholecalciferol; active vitamin D3) takes effect for longterm management. Initially, a tetanic dog or cat should be given IV
10% Ca gluconate, 0.5-1.5 mL/kg (5-15 mg/kg) slowly, over 10-15
minutes (note: 10% Ca gluconate contains 9.3 mg Ca/mL). ECG
monitoring is important, and the infusion discontinued if
bradycardia, premature ventricular complexes, or shortening of the
Q-T intervals develops. Once the ECG normalizes, the infusion
should begin at a slower rate. Ca chloride should not be used in dogs
and cats; it is extremely caustic and can cause tissue sloughing if
extravasated (see section below on subcutaneous [SQ] Ca
administration; see ch. 283). Following initial Ca gluconate bolus,
the serum TCa or iCa concentration should be rechecked. Clinical
signs in most pets improve significantly, well before the Ca
concentrations normalize.
After stabilization, Ca gluconate can be added to any maintenance
IV fluid (2.5-3.5 mg/kg/h; 0.3-0.4 mL/kg/h), remembering that
there is 9.3 mg of Ca/mL.19 Repeated boluses are only recommended
for continuing or recurring signs of tetany. [Ca] should be rechecked
several times during and after the infusion to determine if IV Ca is
needed and at what dosage. When oral Ca and calcitriol can be given,
and the serum [Ca] is stable, most pets can be weaned off IV Ca
because in addition to oral Ca supplementation, food contains
adequate amounts.

Subcutaneous (SQ) Conservative Therapy
SQ Ca gluconate therapy has been used as an alternative to IV CRIs.
While uncommon, SQ Ca can cause significant morbidity due to
tissue damage (resulting in death in 1 dog) and is no longer
recommended. If for any reason a CRI is not possible, the owners
should be counseled on the potential complications of SQ Ca
administration. Calcinosis cutis has been reported in 2 dogs and a cat

after each received SQ Ca gluconate.9,18,20 One protocol for SQ
therapy involves giving the same dose SQ as was given in the initial
IV bolus, diluted 1 part Ca gluconate to 1 part crystalloid, q6-8h.
Frequency and dosage are decreased as oral Ca and calcitriol begin to
take effect.19

LONG-TERM THERAPY
Background
Patients with primary hypoparathyroidism cannot obtain Ca from
skeleton or diet, nor is it reabsorbed and conserved by the kidneys.
Synthetic PTH formulations require parenteral administration and
are expensive. Use of oral vitamin D analogues remain key in the
long-term treatment of hypoparathyroidism. Supplementation with
oral Ca may be needed early in therapy but can usually be
discontinued after a few weeks if the dog or cat is eating well,
because the amount of Ca in commercial diets should be adequate.
Options for vitamin D supplementation include calcitriol and
ergocalciferol (vitamin D2). The synthetic vitamin D analogue
dihydrotachysterol is no longer commercially available.

Calcitriol
Calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D3, has shorter time to maximal
effect (1-4 days) and less time required to resolve toxicosis (1-7 days)
than ergocalciferol (5-21 days and 1-18 weeks, respectively).
Calcitriol is preferred over ergocalciferol unless financial limitations
preclude its use (ch. 283 for alternatives to calcitriol).13 Initial dose
of calcitriol (20-40 ng/kg/day; 0.02-0.04 mcg/kg/day) is usually
given for 2 to 4 days and then decreased to 10-20 ng/kg/day (0.010.02 mcg/kg/day). Dosing calcitriol using commercially available
formulations can be challenging since gel capsule sizes are limited
(0.25 and 0.5 mcg, Rocaltrol), which are not convenient for use in
dogs and cats. Based on clinical observation, not all compounded
formulations have provided consistent products. Thus, for each
patient, the product should be purchased from the same experienced

compounding pharmacy and not be used past the marked expiration
date.

Ergocalciferol
The initial dose of ergocalciferol is 4000-6000 U/kg/day. Once
serum [TCa] stabilizes between 8 and 9.5 mg/dL (2-2.38 mmol/L),
the dosage can usually be decreased to q48h. From the point, the
dosing frequency depends on the patient’s need, which is best
determined via regular monitoring. [Ca] should be monitored weekly
and the dosage adjusted as necessary.13 Frequency of long-term
monitoring is dependent on the owner, but it can almost never be too
often.

Oral Calcium
Oral Ca supplementation should be provided initially but can usually
be tapered and discontinued within a week of starting calcitriol (cats:
0.5-1 g/day, divided; dogs: 1-4 g/day, divided). Ca gluconate and
lactate can be used, but Ca carbonate is most frequently chosen due
to its availability. It is important to dose based on the amount of
elemental Ca. Ca carbonate, gluconate, and lactate are 40%, 9%, and
13% elemental Ca, respectively (40% means that 1 g of Ca carbonate
contains 400 mg elemental Ca).21

PTH
While PTH is an 84-amino acid polypeptide, its biological activity
resides in the first 34 amino acids. SQ-administered recombinant
human PTH (1-84) is approved for the treatment of
hypoparathyroidism in people in the U.S.22,23 In Europe and Asia,
but not the U.S., 1-84 PTH is approved for the treatment of
postmenopausal osteoporosis in women. Human recombinant 1-34
PTH has been approved in virtually every country for treatment of
postmenopausal osteoporosis in women.24 It not only increases bone
mass, but it decreases fracture rates. Similar attributes regarding
bone mass were noted with treatment in men with osteoporosis.25
Both oral and injectable formulations of the recombinant 1-34 PTH

have been shown to effectively increase [Ca] in people with
hypoparathyroidism.26,27 However, there are no reports of using
either the 1-34 nor the 1-84 amino acid recombinant human PTH
products in dogs.

TREATMENT GOALS
The goal is to maintain serum [Ca] just below the low end of the
reference range (about 8-9.5 mg/dL [2-2.38 mmol/L]). These values
are high enough to prevent clinical signs of hypocalcemia and to
decrease calciuresis due to the lack of PTH. These values are low
enough to prevent vitamin D toxicosis: hyperCa, hyperPO4, and AKI.
Once serum [Ca] increases to 7.5-8 mg/dL (1.88-2 mmol/L) on oral
vitamin D and Ca, and the pet is eating and drinking, the pet is
returned to the owner. Rechecks initially should be every 2-3 days.
As serum [Ca] stabilizes, recheck intervals can be progressively
prolonged, up to once every 2-3 months. Owners should be
instructed to return if any signs of hypoCa or hyperCa occur.
HyperCa should be treated by discontinuing vitamin D
administration until it normalizes; additional therapy, including IV
fluids and furosemide, is infrequently necessary (ch. 283).

PROGNOSIS
Hypoparathyroid dogs and cats with dedicated and capable owners
have an excellent prognosis. Owners must be reminded that this
disease requires lifelong therapy and frequent monitoring to help
prevent hypocalcemia or hypercalcemia. Most dogs and cats die of
causes unrelated to hypoparathyroidism if appropriate therapy is
pursued.4,9,13

CLIENT INFORMATION
Hypoparathyroidism
Your pet has primary hypoparathyroidism (hypoPT), a disease that
causes very low blood calcium concentrations. With proper
treatment and monitoring, your pet can live a normal life. This will
require daily medication, watching for signs of too much or too little
calcium in the blood, and monitoring blood calcium concentrations.
The parathyroid glands (PT glands) are 4 structures located on the
thyroid glands, in the necks of dogs, cats, humans, and other
animals. They release parathyroid hormone (PTH), which helps
control blood calcium concentrations. Without PTH, the body is
unable to keep calcium levels high enough for normal activity. Low
calcium levels can cause decreased appetite, trembling, muscle
twitching, stiff gait, restlessness, pawing at the face, chewing at paws,
and, potentially, seizures.
The exact cause of hypoPTH is usually unknown. Rarely, it is
caused by trauma to the neck, but most cases are probably caused by
the patient’s own immune system attacking the parathyroid glands.
It is important to note that, since we do not know what triggers this
disease, there is nothing that could have been done to prevent it from
happening in your pet. Some breeds, such as Miniature Schnauzers
and Poodles, are more likely to get the disease, so genetics may play a
role in the development of hypoPTH.

Dogs with hypoPTH must take medications to increase their
calcium levels. Unfortunately, dog and cat versions of PTH are not
available. Instead, we use calcitriol (a form of vitamin D) and
calcium supplements (such as Tums). Calcitriol helps the body
absorb calcium from the intestines, but it takes several days for it to
reach full effect. Once the calcitriol takes full effect, your vet may
wean your pet off the calcium supplement. Your veterinarian will
check your pet’s blood calcium level frequently while the proper dose
of calcitriol is being determined. After that, it will only need to be
checked every 2-3 months unless there are problems.
Calcitriol is commercially available in only a few sizes. Since your
pet will need an exact dose of calcitriol, your vet may order a form
from a specialized pharmacy (“compounding” pharmacy) so that an
accurate dose can be given. Make sure to check the label each time
you receive this medication to ensure that it is what your
veterinarian told you. Additionally, it is important that you do not
use this medication past the expiration date, since it may become less
effective and result in low calcium levels, resulting in emergency
veterinary care.
Calcium levels fluctuate during treatment of hypoPTH, especially
when medication doses are being adjusted. Your pet may experience
signs of either high blood calcium (hypercalcemia) or low blood
calcium (hypocalcemia) levels, and it is important that you let your
veterinarian know if they occur. Keeping a daily journal of your pet’s
behavior (including appetite and energy level) may be helpful. Signs
of low calcium include the same things you observed when your pet
was diagnosed: decreased appetite, trembling, muscle twitching, stiff
gait, restlessness, pawing at the face, chewing at paws, and,
potentially, seizures. These are serious and may require emergency
veterinary attention. Signs of excess calcium may include lethargy,
decreased appetite, weakness, and excessive drinking and urination.
Pets with hypoPTH have a great prognosis if they are properly
treated and monitored. Make sure to give medication as directed,
watch your pet for any signs of low or high calcium levels, and to
contact your veterinarian if you have any questions.
Patty Lathan (Baton Rouge, Louisiana)

INTRODUCTION AND ANATOMY
Hypothyroidism is the most common thyroid disease and one of the
most common endocrine disorders in dogs. Its prevalence has been
estimated between 0.2 and 0.8%.1-3 A survey on insured dogs from
Sweden, however, suggested a lower prevalence (0.07%) despite
including a large number of pedigree dogs more likely to have
hypothyroidism.4,5 Breed predisposition can be significant. A
prevalence as high as 15% has been recognised in Swedish Giant
Schnauzers and Hovawarts.6The thyroid gland of dogs has two
separate lobes, one on either side of the trachea (ch. 283, Figure
283.1). Each lobe is composed of microscopic follicles lined by a
single layer of thyroid epithelium. The lumen of each follicle contains
“colloid,” a thyroglobulin storage material secreted by follicular cells.
Thyroglobulin is a large glycoprotein containing iodotyrosines,
precursors of thyroid hormones.

PHYSIOLOGY
THYROID HORMONES
The thyroid gland synthesizes and secretes the hormones 3,5,3′,5′-Ltetraiodothyronine (thyroxine [T4]) and 3,5,3′-L-triiodothyronine
(triiodothyronine [T3]) (Figure 285.1). Several steps in thyroid
hormone synthesis are catalysed by thyroid peroxidase (TPO).
Thyroid hormones are highly protein-bound in the circulation.
Approximately 60% of T4 and T3 are bound to thyroxine binding
globulin, 17% to transthyretin, 12% to albumin, and 11% to various
lipoprotein fractions. Since binding affinities are lower in dogs than in
people, total concentrations in dogs are lower, free fractions higher
(estimated at approximately 0.1-0.3% for T4 and 1% for T3), and
serum half-lives shorter (10-16 hours for T4 and 5-6 hours for T3).
Only the free fraction is metabolically active. The protein-bound
moiety serves as a passive reservoir to buffer hormone delivery to
tissues. T3 is approximately 3-5 times more potent than T4. Up to 60%
of T3 is produced not by the thyroid gland but by peripheral outer ring
mono-deiodination of T4, a step that may be autoregulated. Inner ring
deiodination results in the formation of metabolically inactive reverse
T3 (rT3). Thyroid hormones affect most body tissues by interacting
with specific nuclear receptors to modify the expression of a diverse
array of genes. Thyroid hormones influence multiple metabolic
processes from regulation of mitochondrial oxygen demand to control
of protein synthesis.

REGULATION OF THYROID HORMONE
SYNTHESIS AND FUNCTION
Thyroid hormone production is controlled by the hypothalamus and
pituitary (Figure 285.2). The hypothalamus secretes thyrotropin
releasing hormone (TRH) that acts on the anterior pituitary to
promote synthesis and secretion of thyroid stimulating hormone
(thyrotropin; TSH). TSH promotes thyroid gland iodide trapping,

synthesis, and release of thyroid hormones. The secreted circulating
free T4 and T3 provides negative feedback to the hypothalamus and
anterior pituitary, decreasing TRH and TSH synthesis and release
and, subsequently, thyroid hormone production.
Thyroid hormones have numerous functions. Their major influence
is on metabolic rate, growth, development of the neurological system,
and tissue turnover. They have positive inotropic and chronotropic
effects on the heart, are necessary for lipid synthesis and metabolism,
and can stimulate erythropoiesis. When deficient, the spectrum of
possible abnormalities is extensive.

PATHOGENESIS OF HYPOTHYROIDISM
OVERVIEW
Clinical signs of hypothyroidism are the result of decreased T4 and T3
production due to an abnormality in any part of the hypothalamicpituitary-thyroid axis. Hypothyroidism is categorized by lesion
location. Primary hypothyroidism implies an abnormality with the
thyroid gland, secondary disease involves the pituitary gland and
tertiary disease implies abnormalities with the hypothalamus.
Distinguishing between secondary and tertiary disease is not always
possible and the term central hypothyroidism may be used to describe
either. Hypothyroidism can also be described as congenital or
acquired.

CONGENITAL HYPOTHYROIDISM
Congenital is less common than acquired hypothyroidism.7 It results
from thyroid hypoplasia or aplasia, dysgenesis or dyshormonogenesis.
Congenital hypothyroidism may be more prevalent than currently
recognized because some die at birth or shortly thereafter without a
definitive diagnosis. Central hypothyroidism (resulting from TSH or
TRH deficiency) has been reported sporadically and in one family of
Giant Schnauzers and related Miniature Schnauzers.8 TSH deficiency
is also a feature of pituitary dwarfism, although signs of
hypothyroidism are variably present and may be delayed. There are a

few reports suggestive of thyroid dysgenesis. Congenital
hypothyroidism with goiter as a result of dyshormonogenesis and
TPO deficiency has been reported sporadically and as an autosomal
recessive disorder in French Bulldogs, Spanish Water Dogs and,
Tenterfield, Toy Fox and Rat Terriers; breed-specific genetic tests are
commercially available.9-11 Congenital hypothyroidism with goiter has
also been anecdotally reported in Papillons7 and in Shih Tzus caused
by a mutation in the sodium iodide symporter.12 Congenital
hypothyroidism may develop in pups born to dams fed an iodinedeficient diet, dams given a variety of drugs or alternatively because of
iodine deficiency or excess in early life.

ACQUIRED HYPOTHYROIDISM
Central
Central disease is rare, accounting for <5% of hypothyroid dogs.
Pituitary neoplasia and surgical hypophysectomy account for most.
Secondary hypothyroidism arising from trauma (ch. 246),
nontraumatic intracranial hemorrhage (ch. 243), and
adenohypophysitis has been described.13-15 Tertiary hypothyroidism
is extremely rare. Secondary hypothyroidism is an uncommon feature
of glucocorticoid excess that is reversible. Central hypothyroidism
results in atrophic degeneration of the thyroid gland, characterized by
follicles distended with colloid and flattening of the follicular
epithelium, changes readily distinguishable from primary thyroid
abnormalities.

Primary
Acquired primary thyroid disease accounts for most of the diagnoses
of hypothyroidism in dogs. Histologically, lymphocytic thyroiditis or
thyroid atrophy are described with about equal frequency.
Hypothyroidism is a rare consequence of diffuse thyroid neoplasia,
occurring in <5% of cases.16 Hypothyroidism is a common
consequence of treating thyroid neoplasia by radiotherapy, bilateral
thyroidectomy, or high dose radioactive iodine therapy (ch. 288).1719

Hypothyroidism can also develop following administration of
potentiated sulphonamides and, possibly, toceranib.20-22
Lymphocytic thyroiditis is a destructive autoimmune process
characterized by multifocal or diffuse thyroid infiltration by
lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells. This leads to progressive
replacement by fibrous connective tissue. It is associated with
systemic inflammation that is primarily a cellular immune
response.23 By contrast, idiopathic atrophy is described as a
degenerative process with minimal inflammation and gradual

replacement of thyroid tissue by adipose connective tissue. It is
unclear whether idiopathic atrophy is truly a distinct entity or simply
an end stage of lymphocytic thyroiditis, as it is associated with similar
markers of inflammation.23
Thyroid biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis of lymphocytic
thyroiditis but can be inferred by finding circulating autoantibodies to
thyroid antigens such as thyroglobulin, T4, T3 and TPO. Thyroglobulin
autoantibodies (TgAAs) are most common; T3 autoantibodies (T3AA)
and T4 autoantibodies (T4AA) rarely occur in isolation.24,25
Approximately 50% of hypothyroid dogs have circulating TgAAs,
corresponding to the frequency of lymphocytic thyroiditis.
Lymphocytic thyroiditis is a slowly progressive disease with overt
signs of hypothyroidism only developing after about 75% of the
glandular tissue has been destroyed. Its progression can be divided
into four different stages (Table 285.1). The rate of progression
through the different stages is variable and only approximately onethird of TgAA positive euthyroid dogs eventually develop functional
hypothyroidism.26
There is evidence that TgAA-positive hypothyroid dogs become
negative with time supporting the concept that thyroid atrophy
represents an end stage of lymphocytic thyroiditis. Theoretically, the
complete destruction of all thyroid tissue leads to a reduction in
immune stimulation, absence of histologic thyroiditis, and conversion
to autoantibody negativity. Histologic progression from lymphocytic
thyroiditis to follicular atrophy has been described. Moreover, it has
been shown that TgAA-positive euthyroid dogs are younger than
TgAA-positive and negative hypothyroid dogs, but the proportion of
TgAA-positive hypothyroid dogs varies with breed.27 This may reflect
a difference in rate of progression of the disease or in susceptibility to
the different forms of hypothyroidism, if they are distinct diseases.
The cause of lymphocytic thyroiditis and thyroid atrophy is not
known. Primary hypothyroidism is particularly common in purebred
dogs.28,29 Reported breed predispositions and the familial nature of
hypothyroidism are consistent with a strong hereditary component to
the condition. Certain breeds with a high prevalence of TgAA
positivity are at significantly increased risk for the development of
hypothyroidism. These breeds include but are not confined to:

English Setter, Gordon Setter, Golden Retriever, Doberman Pinscher,
Old English Sheepdog, Rhodesian Ridgeback, Cocker Spaniel and
Boxer.25,27,30,31 In addition, the familial nature of hypothyroidism is
recognized in Great Dane, Beagle, and Borzoi colonies, and recently in
Swedish Hovawarts and Giant Schnauzers.6,32-34 Heritability of
hypothyroidism is moderate to high in Finnish Hovawarts.35
Using a candidate gene approach, certain major histocompatibility
(MHC) dog leukocyte antigen (DLA) class II alleles have been
identified as conferring increased susceptibility for hypothyroidism in
Doberman Pinschers, Rhodesian Ridgebacks, English Setters, Gordon
Setters and Giant Schnauzers.30,36-39 This association is not
surprising as DLA genes play an essential role in the immune
response. Genome-wide association studies have identified a risk
locus, shared by Gordon Setters, Hovawarts and Rhodesian
Ridgebacks, in a separate region of CFA12 and a protective locus on
CFA11 in Giant Schnauzers.40,41 Further genomic and functional
characterization of these loci is required to understand their
association with hypothyroidism. The complexity of genetic
associations and their use in selective breeding is highlighted by
certain haplotypes that protect against hypothyroidism but increase
susceptibility to other diseases such as symmetrical onychomadesis in
some breeds.39
The role of environmental risk factors in canine hypothyroidism are
unclear. Anecdotally, a link between intensive vaccination protocols
and development of autoimmune diseases in general and thyroiditis
in particular has been suggested but remains scientifically
unsupported. Season of the year (summer versus fall) and geography
(different states within the USA) have been suggested to marginally
influence prevalence.27 There is increasing concern that
environmental contaminants play a role in the development of human
and feline thyroid disease. Only one study has evaluated this in dogs
but found no association in serum concentration of polybrominated
diphenyl ethers (PBDEs) and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and
hypothyroidism.42

CLINICAL OBSERVATIONS
SIGNALMENT
Hypothyroidism can occur in any breed but typically affects purebred
animals as listed above. The mean age at diagnosis is about 7 years,
with a range of 0.5 to 15 years and few diagnosed at <2 years of age.
Predisposed breeds tend to develop hypothyroidism at an earlier age.
Neutered animals, particularly neutered females, are at greatest
risk.43

CLINICAL SIGNS
Overview
Hypothyroidism causes a variety of clinical signs (Table 285.2). The
onset of disease is insidious and the number, type, and severity of
signs vary widely. There are no pathognomonic features, making
hypothyroidism a differential for many common and uncommon
problems. The most common signs relate to metabolic and
dermatological abnormalities that occur concurrently in about 70% of
affected dogs. Less commonly, cardiovascular, neuromuscular,
reproductive, ophthalmic, and/or gastrointestinal (GI) signs are
described. For some presenting problems, a causative link with
hypothyroidism is unproven.

Metabolic Features
A decline in metabolic rate is classic, with associated clinical signs in
>80% of dogs that include lethargy, weight gain, exercise intolerance,
mental dullness, cold intolerance, generalized weakness, and
shivering.1,3,44 Approximately 40 to 50% of hypothyroid dogs are
classified as overweight or obese. However, obesity is a common
problem in the general dog population and hypothyroidism accounts
for only a minority of cases (ch. 20).

Dermatological Features
Thyroid hormones play an important role in the maintenance of hair
growth and in immune responses. Dermatological abnormalities that
include hair thinning, dry coarse hair coat, frank alopecia usually
involving the flanks and thighs, or failure to regrow hair after
clipping, occur in up to 80% of hypothyroid dogs and can be
extensive.1,3,45 Hypothyroidism is classically associated with an
“endocrine alopecia”: nonpruritic, bilaterally symmetric, with a
tendency to spare the head and extremities (ch. 12). Alopecia is often

noted in areas of friction such as the neck in dogs that wear collars,
the lateral extremities in large dogs, and the tail, resulting in the so
called “rat-tail” of hypothyroidism. Focal, multifocal and asymmetric
alopecia can occur. While alopecia involving the nasal planum is
thought to be highly associated with hypothyroidism, it is nonspecific
and occurs with other endocrine diseases. In a few selected breeds
such as the Irish Setter and Boxer, retention of the coat occurs. In
these, it becomes dull and often lighter in color because of
environmental bleaching. Other signs of hypothyroidism include dry
scaly skin, seborrhea, otitis and hyperpigmentation. Hypothyroidism
may predispose to secondary bacterial infections, but pyoderma is
reported in <10%. Malassezia has also been reported. Either
condition can cause pruritus. Although hypothyroidism should be
suspected if standard treatment of these disorders is ineffective, it is
diagnosed in <10% of dogs with recurrent pyoderma.46
Hypothyroidism is also associated with the development of adultonset demodicosis.47
