In people, hypothyroidism is associated with accumulation of
hyaluronic acid in the dermis (myxedema) resulting in a puffy
appearance to the skin that is pale, cool to the touch, but nonpitting.
Myxedema also occurs in dogs and is most noticeable over the head
and gives rise to a “tragic facial expression” characterized by
thickening of the lips and the skin over the forehead and drooping of
the eyelids. Rarely, mucinous vesiculation may develop.
Common histological changes associated with hypothyroidism are
shared by other endocrine disorders: a predominance of hairs in
telogen and hairless telogen follicles (kenogen follicles). Whereas
hyperpigmentation, atrophic, and dystrophic follicles are also
described they are less common as compared with other endocrine
disorders. A thickened dermis and vacuolated erector pili muscles are
more specific for hypothyroidism. Inflammatory changes in dogs with
secondary infection may obscure these findings.

Cardiovascular Features
Thyroid hormones have direct positive inotropic effects, stimulate
myocardial function, and increase responsiveness to adrenergic
stimulation. Theoretically, hypothyroidism could significantly impair
cardiac function but whether this is clinically important is
controversial. In large case series of hypothyroid dogs, cardiac
abnormalities are rarely diagnosed apart from apparently subclinical
bradycardia in ∼15% of dogs.1,3 However, electrocardiographically,
hypothyroidism is associated with reduced heart rate, low-voltage R
and P waves, sinus bradycardia and occasionally first- or more rarely
second-degree atrioventricular blo
ck.48 Echocardiographically, hypothyroidism is associated with a
reversible decrease in left ventricular fractional shortening and mild
increases in left ventricular end systolic diameter suggestive of

reduced myocardial function (chs. 97, 233).48 There are a few case
reports of congestive heart failure and myocardial dysfunction with
atrial fibrillation, partially or fully responsive to appropriate cardiac
and/or thyroid hormone supplementation.49-51 However, it is unclear
whether hypothyroidism is causative, coincidental, or capable of
exacerbating an underlying subclinical cardiomyopathy. Larger
studies have focused on breed-specific dilated cardiomyopathy. There
is little evidence of a causative role for hypothyroidism in Doberman
Pinschers with dilated cardiomyopathy (ch. 233).52,53 The value of
routinely testing for hypothyroidism in dogs presenting with dilated
cardiomyopathy is questionable.
Atherosclerosis is a known complication of the
hypercholesterolemia and lipid abnormalities induced by
hypothyroidism in people. Atherosclerosis is rare in dogs presumably
because of differences in their lipoprotein composition and
metabolism (ch. 63), but if seen is often associated with
hypothyroidism. Cholesterol concentrations are consistently highest
in those dogs that develop atherosclerosis. The clinical consequences
of atherosclerosis are not clear, but it has potential effects on the
cardiovascular system. There are a few reports of aortic
thromboembolism and severe atherosclerosis associated with
hypothyroidism.49,54 A cholesterol-based pericardial effusion has also
been described in a hypothyroid dog.55

Neurological Features
Various neurological disorders have been associated with
hypothyroidism, although neurological dysfunction is rare after
experimental radioactive iodine thyroid ablation.56 However,
experimental induction of hypothyroidism does not accurately reflect
the insidious nature and more prolonged duration of the naturally
occurring disease nor does it account for any contribution from
immune dysregulation in lymphocytic thyroiditis. Hypothyroidism
can result in neuropathies through accumulation of
mucopolysaccharides in nerves, by compression of nerves through
their respective foraminae, or because of impaired axonal transport
leading to degeneration (ch. 14). An association between
hypothyroidism and peripheral polyneuropathy is possible although

uncommon.57 A demyelinating and axonal pattern of polyneuropathy
has been demonstrated in hypothyroid dogs with a positive clinical
response to T4 supplementation.58 Associations between Horner’s
syndrome, facial nerve paralysis, or laryngeal paralysis and
hypothyroidism are questionable. Hypothyroidism has been
diagnosed in <5% of dogs with facial nerve paralysis or peripheral
vestibular disease, not all of which resolved with T4
supplementation.59,60 An association between hypothyroidism and
megaesophagus is also questionable. Whereas hypothyroidism is
described as a cause of acquired megaesophagus in approximately
10% of affected dogs, hypothyroidism is not considered a significant
risk factor for its development.61,62 Additionally, only a minority of
cases with hypothyroidism and megaesophagus exhibit a discernible
clinical and radiographic response after T4 treatment. Megaesophagus
(ch. 259) could also be related to concurrent development of
myasthenia gravis (ch. 253).
Reports of central nervous system (CNS) disease in hypothyroidism
are less common but perhaps less tenuous. Potential mechanisms
include atherosclerotic vascular disease (ch. 243), brain infarction,
and/or functional metabolic derangements arising directly from
thyroid hormone deficiency. Central vestibular dysfunction is a rare
but reversible sequela of hypothyroidism even if other signs are
absent (ch. 248). Seizures are a rare but potential complication of
atherosclerosis, but hypothyroidism is only diagnosed in 3% of dogs
with metabolic or toxin-associated seizures.63 Hypothyroidism rarely
causes myxedema coma, a life-threatening sequela characterized by
profound mental dullness and stupor, severe weakness, hypothermia
(often without shivering), hypoventilation, bradycardia and
hypotension (ch. 44). Many have evidence of a precipitating factor:
prior surgery, cardiac failure, drug therapies, or overwhelming sepsis
that may not be related to thyroid disease.In conclusion, there is
evidence that hypothyroidism is associated with peripheral
polyneuropathy and CNS disease and should be considered
particularly if other features of hypothyroidism are present or other
more likely causes are eliminated. Routinely testing for
hypothyroidism in dogs with cranial nerve disease (chs. 248, 249),

laryngeal paralysis (ch. 214), and megaesophagus (ch. 259) is not
justified.

Behavior Changes
Associating hypothyroidism with behavior issues is controversial (ch.
11). The implication that hypothyroidism results in aggressive
behavior is believed by many but with little supportive evidence.
Thyroxine supplementation of hypothyroid dogs was not associated
with any notable change of behavior.64 In a double-blind placebo
controlled trial, adequate T4 supplementation had no effect on ownerdirected aggression in dogs treated for suboptimal thyroid function
(defined as a free T4 [fT4] concentration <20% of the lower reference
interval and a total T4 [TT4], total T3 [TT3], or free T3 [fT3] <30% of
the lower limit of their respective reference intervals or the presence
of any anti-thyroid autoantibody).65 In reality, the prevalence of
hypothyroidism in dogs with behavior problems is low and no greater
than in dogs without hypothyroidism.66,67

Muscular Features
It can be difficult to distinguish clinical signs of neuropathy from
those related to myopathy and electromyography changes suggestive
of axonal neuropathy (ch. 111) can occur in myopathies.
Hypothyroid-induced myopathy is a potential cause of gait
abnormalities, weakness, and exercise intolerance (ch. 23).
Experimentally, hypothyroidism is associated with exercise-induced
hyperkalemia, which may contribute to decreased contractile
performance and endurance.68 Additionally, where experimental
hypothyroidism did not result in neuropathy, it did result in
subclinical, biochemical, electrophysiologic and morphologic evidence
of myopathy.69 Histologically, hypothyroid-induced myopathy is
characterized by nemaline rod inclusions, a predominance of type I
myofibers, a decrease in type II fiber area, abnormal mitochondria,
and myofiber degeneration with substantial depletion of skeletal
muscle free carnitine.69

Ophthalmic Features
The hyperlipidemia caused by hypothyroidism can result in arcus
lipoides, particularly in German Shepherd Dogs (ch. 13).70
Hypothyroidism is an uncommon (<10%) systemic cause of lipemic
uveitis that occurs secondary to hyperlipidemia and possibly
atherosclerotic damage to the uveal vessels.71 Any association
between keratoconjunctivitis sicca and hypothyroidism is
speculative.72 However, reduced tear production has been reported in
hypothyroid dogs that could exacerbate any other underlying ocular
disorder.73

Reproductive Features
Various reproductive abnormalities have been ascribed to
hypothyroidism and many breeders, particularly of large and giant
breeds, remain convinced of a link between hypothyroidism and
reduced fertility or infertility. Short-term (median 19 weeks)
experimental induction of hypothyroidism in bitches resulted in
prolonged parturition and reduced pup survival without affecting the
interestrus interval, fertility, litter size, or duration of gestation.74
More chronic hypothyroidism (at least 40 weeks) resulted in
decreased fertility, increased periparturient mortality, and lower birth
weights without affecting interestrus interval, gestation duration, or
breeding behavior.75 Experimentally induced hypothyroidism does
not affect male reproductive indices (sperm count, scrotal width,
sperm motility/morphology, libido) over a 2-year period.76 A
preliminary survey of five breeds (Great Dane, Dogue de Bordeaux,
English Mastiff, Leonberger, Golden Retriever) identified no
association between infertility and hypothyroidism.77
Hypothyroidism accounted for only 5% of cases of infertility in
another series.78 A hypothyroid bitch with hyperprolactinemia and
galactorrhea has been reported.79 Pituitary function tests in
hypothyroid dogs suggest that hyperprolactinemia is only likely in
intact bitches.80

Gastrointestinal (GI) Features
Anecdotally, constipation, vomiting, and diarrhea have been
associated with hypothyroidism but are unusual.1,3 In humans,
constipation is not unexpected because of decreased GI peristaltic
activity and it could theoretically occur in dogs. Diarrhea associated
with GI bacterial overgrowth (ch. 260), possibly due to reduced
intestinal motility, has been suspected but never confirmed.81 There
is one report of a dog with acute hepatopathy associated with
hypothyroidism and atherosclerosis.82

Gallbladder Mucocele
The association between gallbladder mucocele (ch. 273) and
hypothyroidism is important.83-85 About 25% of dogs with
gallbladder mucoceles are hypothyroid.86 The cause is unknown but
could be related to dyslipidemia, gallbladder dysmotility, altered bile
acid composition, decreased bile flow, or biliary stasis (ch. 273). A
prior diagnosis of hypothyroidism has limited impact on outcome
following surgical cholecystectomy.87 Medical management of
gallbladder mucocele is possible but with shorter long-term survival
when compared with surgical cholecystectomy.88 It is not yet known
whether a better response is possible in hypothyroid dogs adequately
treated with T4 together with standard gallbladder mucocele medical
management.

Renal Features
Hypothyroidism is not associated with either acute kidney injury,
chronic kidney disease, or polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD) except in the
rare case of thyroiditis-associated glomerulonephritis. Nevertheless,
decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of unknown significance
has been demonstrated in hypothyroid dogs.89,90

Congenital Hypothyroidism
Dogs affected early in life can develop any of the signs noted in adult
hypothyroid dogs. However, congenital hypothyroidism induces

disproportionate dwarfism. Affected pups appear normal at birth but
signs usually become evident at 8 weeks of age. They have
disproportionately wide skulls, macroglossia, delayed dental eruption,
a square trunk and short limbs.7 These features help differentiate this
condition from the proportionate features of pituitary dwarfism (ch.
280). Constipation may be noted, and mental impairment is usually
obvious. Goiter may or may not be evident depending on the
underlying cause. When present it can result in dysphagia/dyspnea as
a result of mechanical obstruction. Radiographically, delayed skeletal
maturation and epiphyseal dysgenesis are found and may result in
lameness or degenerative joint disease and vertebral physeal fractures
if thyroid hormone supplementation is delayed.91

Immuno-endocrinopathy Syndromes
Most autoimmune endocrine disorders occur in isolation but there are
instances when two or more immune-mediated disorders occur
concurrently or sequentially. Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome
type 1 (APS-1) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder l associated with
mutations of the autoimmune regulator gene (AIRE). It is
characterized by a triad of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis,
hypoparathyroidism, and adrenal insufficiency and less commonly
with autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes mellitus
(DM). Autoimmune polyendocrine disease type II (APS-II) is more
common but less well defined. Previously known as Schmidt’s
syndrome, it is characterized by hypoadrenocorticism occurring with
hypothyroidism (69% of people) or with type I DM (52% of patients);
other combinations are rare.
Such disorders are less well defined in dogs and, in most, unproven.
Single case reports and case series have described potential
combinations that mimic the human condition including
hypothyroidism and DM1-3,92-94; hypothyroidism and
hypoadrenocorticism2,95-106 with adenohypophysitis107;
hypothyroidism, hypoadrenocorticism, DM, and
hypoparathyroidism100; hypothyroidism and myasthenia
gravis1,108,109; and occasionally with other autoimmune diseases.110
The prevalence of DM in hypothyroid dogs has been reported as

between 1.2%2 and 10%3 while the prevalence of hypothyroidism in
diabetic dogs is estimated at 4% (ch. 291).94 The prevalence of
hypoadrenocorticism in hypothyroid dogs ranges from 1%2 to 3%1
while the prevalence of hypothyroidism in dogs with
hypoadrenocorticism is approximately 4% (ch. 296).100
Hypothyroidism should be suspected in dogs with
hypoadrenocorticism particularly if there is a poor response to
mineralocorticoid therapy, persistent hyponatremia or bradycardia,
inappropriate hypercholesterolemia, or other supportive clinical
signs.99 In a study of 35 dogs with two or more concurrent endocrine
disorders, the combination of hypothyroidism and DM (29%) was
more common than hypothyroidism and hypoadrenocorticism
(23%).111 Confirming a diagnosis of hypothyroidism in dogs suffering
from other illnesses is difficult. The combinations described are all
potentially immune-mediated and may be genetically related, but
other causal possibilities exist. Clinically, hypothyroidism has been
recognized as an uncommon cause of insulin resistance in diabetic
dogs.93 Hypothyroidism is known to induce substantial insulin
resistance in experimental dogs (ch. 290).112,113 Whereas obesity
may play a partial role, other direct and indirect factors may be
important. Naturally occurring and experimental hypothyroidism has
been associated with growth hormone (GH) or insulin-like growth
factor type 1 (IGF-1) excess (ch. 281).80,112,114-117
Transdifferentiation of somatotrop pituitary cells to thyrotrops is
possible.117 GH excess is highly diabetogenic.118

CLINICOPATHOLOGY
OVERVIEW
Various hematological and biochemical changes have been described
in hypothyroid dogs but none is specific. Their presence provides
supportive evidence of hypothyroidism but more importantly they
serve to include or exclude significant non-thyroidal illness (NTI).
NTI could account for the dog’s presenting signs or may indicate the

presence of a concurrent disease that may affect interpretation of
thyroid function tests.

COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT (CBC)
Anemia
Classically, the anemia in hypothyroid dogs is mild,
normochromic/normocytic, and is seen in up to 50% of dogs (ch. 57).
Hematocrit values are rarely below 0.25L/L and the dogs do not have
pale mucous membranes. Often termed a “physiological anemia,” it is
caused by decreased erythropoietin production and a lack of a direct
stimulatory effect of thyroid hormones on bone marrow. Most nonanemic hypothyroid dogs have a red cell count in the lower quartile of
the reference interval. Red cell distribution width (RDW) is higher in
hypothyroid vs healthy dogs, but with overlap.119 Increased white
blood cell count is extremely unusual in hypothyroid dogs.

Platelets and von Willebrand Factor
Hypothyroidism is associated with increased platelet counts and small
platelet size that may reflect an inverse relationship between
thrombopoiesis and erythropoiesis (ch. 59). Easy bruising,
anecdotally associated with hypothyroidism, was believed related to a
decrease in plasma von Willebrand factor antigen (vWf:Ag). However,
hypothyroidism is not associated with a prolonged buccal mucosal
bleeding time or significant change in vWf:Ag.120,121 Concentrations
actually decrease with thyroid hormone treatment.121 Any putative
link between hypothyroidism and von Willebrand disease likely
reflects common breed predispositions to these conditions. Previously
unrecognized congenital von Willebrand disease was diagnosed in a 7year-old hypothyroid dog with nasal hemorrhage associated with
factor VIII deficiency or complicated by loss of vessel integrity
because of atherosclerosis.122

SERUM BIOCHEMISTRY PROFILE

Cholesterol
Hypercholesterolemia occurs in about 75% of hypothyroid dogs, often
with hypertriglyceridemia. The higher the cholesterol concentration,
the more likely a dog is to have hypothyroidism (ch. 63). Thyroid
hormones stimulate almost all aspects of lipid metabolism including
synthesis, mobilization, and degradation. However, degradation is
severely affected in hypothyroidism resulting in lipid accumulation.
Plasma concentrations of low-density lipoproteins, very low-density
lipoproteins and high-density lipoproteins are usually increased in
hypothyroid dogs.123

Other Parameters
Increased creatine kinase activity occurs in 18 to 35% of hypothyroid
dogs but is usually less than twice the upper limit of the reference
interval (ch. 66).1,3 Believed to result from decreased metabolism or
excretion, hypothyroid-induced myopathy may also contribute.69
Fructosamine concentrations (ch. 291) are increased in 36-82% of
hypothyroid dogs, presumably due to reduced protein turnover rather
than chronic hyperglycemia.3,124 Although the increases are not
clinically relevant, they may impact treatment monitoring in dogs
with DM and hypothyroidism. Mild increases in liver enzyme
activities, particularly alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl
transferase, have been described in up to 30% of hypothyroid dogs
(ch. 65).1,3 This may be due to mild hepatic lipid deposition but if
markedly increased another underlying disorder should be
considered. Serum concentrations of creatinine and symmetric
dimethylarginine (SDMA) are higher in hypothyroid vs euthyroid
dogs and are mildly increased in approximately 30 and 50% of
affected dogs, respectively,125 presumably due to the hypothyroidrelated decrease in GFR (ch. 62).89,90 Total homocysteine
concentrations are about 75% higher in hypothyroid dogs, perhaps
related to decreases in clearance, metabolism, or folic acid
concentrations.126 Its consequences are unclear. Hypothyroidism
increases GH, IGF-1, and adiponectin concentrations.80,112-117

THYROID FUNCTION TESTING
Overview
Accurately diagnosing hypothyroidism can be challenging. Several
tests are available and recommendations for their use and
interpretation vary. Not all tests directly assess thyroid function but
may simply provide indirect evidence of thyroid abnormalities. No
single test has 100% diagnostic sensitivity or specificity. Knowledge of
factors that can influence test results is essential for accurate
interpretation.

ASSAY METHODOLOGIES
“Total” Thyroid Hormone Assays
Total thyroid hormone assays measure circulating protein-bound and
free concentrations. Radioimmunoassays (RIAs) are considered the
standard reference technique for assaying TT4 and TT3, are relatively
inexpensive, and require small sample volumes. These assays are
subject to radiation regulations, cannot be fully automated, and with
some exceptions, are no longer commonly used. Non-isotopic
methods can be fully automated (preferred by commercial
laboratories) or developed for in-house use. These assays use
enzymes, chemiluminescence, or fluorescence. Quantitative assays are
preferred over semi-quantitative. Liquid chromatography-tandem
mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) assays tend to be used for research.
There is reasonable agreement across the different total T4 and T3
assay methodologies even when human RIAs are used, providing they
are modified for the lower values of dogs. Results vary with different
assays, emphasizing need for method- and laboratory-specific
reference intervals and consistent use of one assay type and
laboratory in individual animals.127 Anecdotally, erroneous values are
more likely with enzyme or fluorescence methods.128
Both TT4 and TT3 results can be affected by autoantibodies. Falsely
increased or decreased values are possible depending on the
particular assay and separation system used. If the assay system uses
the antibody-bound portion for estimating hormone concentration,
the effect of autoantibodies is to increase measured values. This

applies to most commonly used total T4 assay systems. T4AAs cause
measured values to be within or above the reference interval. If the
estimation of hormone concentration is based on the unbound
hormone fraction, autoantibodies falsely decrease results. Some TT3
results are thus affected and become undetectable. One study found
no difference in TT4 concentrations estimated by chemiluminescence
vs high performance liquid chromatography (theoretically free from
interference with autoantibodies) in T4AA-positive samples.129
However, only two samples were evaluated and the thyroid status of
each dog was unclear. Increased TT4 values were reported in 1 of 13
TgAA-positive hypothyroid dogs.130 Others suggest that TT4
concentrations are below, within or above the reference interval in
approximately 54%, 34% and 12% of T4AA positive hypothyroid dogs
(P. A. Graham, personal communication).

Free (Unbound) Thyroid Hormone Assays
Circulating fT4 concentrations are similar in dogs and humans. Assays
that employ equilibrium dialysis (ED) or ultrafiltration to separate
free from bound T4 and then use a highly sensitive RIA are preferred.
Assays employing ED are commonly used and considered the gold
standard for measuring fT4 concentrations. These assays are
laborious, expensive, and usually only offered by large commercial
laboratories. Ultrafiltration followed by LC-MS/MS has been
validated for dogs but is not widely available.131
Accurate measurement of fT4 concentrations by other methods is
controversial. Popular assays use hormone analogs with similar T4
molecular structures and claim to be non-reactive with thyroid
hormone binding proteins; they directly compete with fT4 within the
sample. In people these assays are thought to merely “estimate” fT4
concentrations with minimal advantage over TT4 assays. They are
most problematic in accurately measuring fT4 in disorders associated

with abnormal thyroid hormone binding proteins, NTI, and thyroid
hormone autoantibodies. Older fT4 analogue assays tended to
underestimate fT4 concentrations in dogs, particularly in dogs with
NTI.132 Assay specificities have been improved, although use of
human assays remains limiting.133 A veterinary-specific
chemiluminescent fT4 assay (Immulite 2000 Veterinary Free T4,
Siemens Healthcare Diagnostics) is widely used. It is reported to have
high diagnostic specificity (97%) for canine hypothyroidism but it is
unclear whether healthy euthyroid dogs or dogs with NTI were used
for comparison.134 Another study suggested fT4 results decrease with
the severity of NTI, similar to TT4.135 Indeed, combined measurement
of TT4 and fT4 by analog methods adds little diagnostic information to
either measurement alone, suggesting that the assays may not be truly
measuring free T4 concentrations.135,136 These assays are influenced
by the presence of T4AAs.130

Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) Assays
TSH assays must be species-specific. Canine-specific TSH (cTSH)
chemiluminescent and immunoradiometric assays are widely
available, but do not distinguish low from reference interval results.
This limitation should have less importance in dogs with primary
hypothyroidism with, theoretically, increased cTSH values. However,
it can have implications when attempting to diagnose central
hypothyroidism or when assessing over supplementation in treated
dogs.

Thyroid Autoantibody Assays
Canine-specific TgAA assays are available, although presence of
T3AAs and T4AAs may be suspected if discordant total hormone
results are detected in TgAA-positive dogs. They can also be
specifically measured in some laboratories.

Sample Handling and Interferences
Most thyroid hormones and cTSH are stable in storage. However,
concentrations of fT4 significantly increase if stored at room
temperature. Thus, sample separation, refrigerated transport, and
expediently run assays are indicated. RIAs are generally resistant to
the effects of hemolysis, lipemia and hyperbilirubinemia. Use of nonisotopic methods may be affected. Severe lipemia may falsely increase
ED fT4 results.

PHYSIOLOGICAL FACTORS
Sample Timing, Age and Sex
No circadian rhythm in thyroid hormone secretion has been
identified. Episodic fluctuations can result in occasional subnormal
values. TT4 and fT4 values decline with age; results are often below
reference intervals in old dogs.137,138 cTSH concentrations increase
with age.137,138 Conversely, dogs <3 months old have TT4 values 2-5
times higher than those of adults. Sex, stage of estrus, and season
have been variably reported to affect thyroid hormones
concentrations but are not clinically significant.

Breed and Exercise
Breed is important when assessing thyroid status, but the hormone
and magnitude of change does vary. Sighthounds are known to have
low circulating thyroid hormone concentrations: TT4 values below
standard reference intervals are seen in about 90% of Greyhounds,139
75% of Basenjis,140 65% of Sloughis,141 55% of Salukis,142 25% of
Whippets,143 but only 5% of Scottish Deerhounds.144 In many,
concentrations are so low (at or below limit of detection of assay) that
breed-specific reference intervals cannot be calculated. Low TT3
values are found in Salukis142 and Irish Wolfhounds145 but not
Greyhounds.139 fT4 concentrations can be low in Greyhounds,139
Irish Wolfhounds,145 and Salukis,142 but not Whippets.143 TT4 results

are also low in the Dogue de Bordeaux and Giant Schnauzer.146,147
Breed variability can be so great that breed-specific reference
intervals have been recommended.138 TSH concentrations appear to
be less affected by breed. Intense training and exercise are associated
with decreases in thyroid hormone concentrations, but short-lived
exercise has limited effect.

Non-Thyroidal Illness (NTI)
Illness can profoundly alter thyroid hormone concentrations (Table
285.3). The term “NTI syndrome” describes the continuum of
changes in thyroid function secondary to acute or chronic illness.
There are numerous potential mechanisms: reduced peripheral
conversion of T4 to T3, reduction in binding affinity or concentration
of thyroid hormone binding proteins, altered thyroid hormone
metabolism, change in thyroid hormone receptor expression or
function, or changes in hypothalamic-pituitary function.
In humans, the most common abnormality associated with NTI is
suppression of circulating T3 and maintenance of reference interval
TT4 results.148 As diseases progress in severity, suppression of both
T3 and TT4 occurs and is associated with a poorer outcome. fT4 and
TSH concentrations are less affected, at least initially. In severe
illnesses, both fT4 and TSH may be suppressed. Occasionally,
transient increases in fT4 are noted while circulating TSH values may
increase during the recovery phase of illness.
Decreased thyroid hormone concentrations have been reported in
dogs with a wide variety of illnesses or infections involving most body
systems.147-167 In the most comprehensive study of NTI in dogs,
reductions in TT3 alone and in both TT3 and TT4 were documented,
but isolated decreases in TT4 were not common.152 Greater decreases
in TT4 and TT3 occur in the more severe illnesses and those with a
poorer prognosis.150-152,162,164-166,168 fT4 concentrations (by ED) are
usually maintained within reference interval in all but the most severe

illnesses151,152 or hyperadrenocorticism.169 Occasionally an increase
in fT4 is noted although this is poorly defined.167,170 Assessing the
influence of illness on canine TSH concentrations is hampered by the
poor sensitivity of the available assay, which does not allow
differentiation between normal and reduced values. Increased values
are not a feature of NTI168 except in hypoadrenocorticism where low
TT4 is uncommon but increased cTSH concentrations occur in about
35% of dogs.171 The increases in cTSH could be caused by a lack of
cortisol feedback to the pituitary. Increased cTSH concentrations
occur in the recovery phase of illness.167,170 Alterations in thyroid
hormone concentrations should not be expected in minor illnesses
without systemic involvement and if present, other reasons should be
investigated. Hypothyroidism is not associated with osteoarthritis,
recurrent seasonal flank alopecia, atopic dermatitis, or pyoderma.
Mechanisms causing the NTI syndrome in dogs have not yet been
elucidated. Albumin is a negative acute phase protein that decreases
in many diseases. Transthyretin concentrations are also lower in dogs
with NTI than in hypothyroidism.172 However, major modifications in
these proteins would be required to substantially alter T4
concentrations based on their capacity and the estimated proportion
of T4 that they bind. Recombinant interleukin-2 infusions have been
shown experimentally to induce changes to similar to those observed
with NTI.173

Drug Therapy
Several drugs are known to affect thyroid hormone concentrations
ranging from an isolated effect on TT4, to a state mimicking primary
hypothyroidism (Table 285.4).21,22,174-178 The drug, dose, and
duration of therapy dictate the magnitude of effect. A 15% decrease in
TT4 is expected in ill dogs treated with thyroid-suppressive
medications,152 but some drugs have limited effect.174,178 If a drug
has not been specifically evaluated in dogs it should be considered as
having the potential to affect thyroid hormone concentrations. If
thyroid hormone concentrations are affected, values should normalize
(often requiring as long as 6 weeks; longer after sulphonamides) when
the drug is withdrawn. Experimentally, thyroid function normalizes
within 1 week of short-term (up to 16 weeks) T4 treatment.179
However, this may not reflect the consequences of more prolonged
treatment especially in dogs with NTI.

DIAGNOSIS OF HYPOTHYROIDISM:
BASAL ENDOCRINE TESTS (TABLE
285.5)24,153,156,158,180-183
Total T 3 (TT 3 )
Measuring the TT3 is of limited value for diagnosing hypothyroidism
because of its low diagnostic sensitivity. TT3 values are within or
above reference intervals in up to 90% of hypothyroid dogs, perhaps
due to enhanced secretion of T3 from the thyroid or increased
peripheral conversion from T4.156 These processes may have transient
benefit, as T3 is the most potent thyroid hormone. Depending on the
assay, the presence of T3AAs may falsely increase measured TT3.
T3AAs are present in >5% of samples from dogs suspected of having
hypothyroidism25 and in >40% of TgAA-positive hypothyroid dogs.27
Specificity of TT3 in diagnosing hypothyroidism is poor. Low values
are common in many breeds, in NTI, and with many drugs. The only
value of measuring TT3 is in breeds, e.g., Greyhounds, known to have
low TT4 but TT3 concentrations within reference intervals.139

Total T4 (TT4)
Circulating TT4 concentrations are decreased in most hypothyroid
dogs. Its diagnostic sensitivity is excellent, and it is the most
frequently recommended screening test. Results within reference
interval are often used to rule out hypothyroidism but caution is
advised as T4AAs can falsely increase measured values. T4AAs are
present in <2% of dogs suspected of having hypothyroidism,25 but are
found in 14% of TgAA-positive hypothyroid dogs,27 decreasing
diagnostic sensitivity. Thus, hypothyroidism cannot be ruled out by
results in or above the reference interval. The greatest concern with
TT4 is its poor diagnostic specificity. There are myriad non-thyroidal

factors that can decrease TT4 in euthyroid animals: breed, age, NTI,
and drugs. TT4 should never be used as the sole diagnostic test for
canine hypothyroidism.142

Free T4 (fT4)
fT4 concentrations are below reference intervals in most hypothyroid
dogs. A small number have fT4 values in the low end of the reference
interval, negatively impacting diagnostic sensitivity. fT4
concentrations (using assays with a separation step, e.g., ED) are less
affected by extrathyroidal factors that could alter TT4 concentrations.
Thus, fT4 has excellent diagnostic specificity. fT4 is the single most
accurate test for diagnosing hypothyroidism in dogs.182

cTSH
Dogs with primary hypothyroidism should be expected to have
increases in cTSH, because of their lack of pituitary negative feedback.
However, cTSH has only moderate test sensitivity because a
significant proportion of hypothyroid dogs maintain cTSH in
reference intervals. Explanations suggest that some dogs have central
rather than primary hypothyroidism, but this would not explain all
the results. Random fluctuation of cTSH concentration to the
reference interval does occur in hypothyroid dogs but is an unlikely
explanation for all the low values.
In both experimental and naturally-occurring hypothyroidism,
pituitary secretion of TSH decreases as a result of TRH-receptor
desensitization, which can take years.80,114,115,117 Perhaps high cTSH
values are suppressed in hypothyroidism because of concurrent NTI
or drug therapies.182 The current cTSH assays may not measure all
possible isomers of TSH in the dog. Although diagnostic sensitivity of
this test is poor, measurement of cTSH concentration offers relatively
good diagnostic specificity. Increased values are less commonly
encountered in euthyroid dogs as cTSH is largely unaffected by NTI or
most drugs, but hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296) and recovery from

NTI are exceptions. High values are seen in silent and subclinical
hypothyroidism.27

Thyroglobulin Autoantibodies (TgAAs)
Positive TgAA results are associated with lymphocytic thyroiditis and
may be present long before an animal becomes clinically
hypothyroid.26,27 As such, TgAAs provide no information on thyroid
function but support the existence of underlying disease. Positive
TgAA results are uncommon in dogs with NTI.24,184,185 As a
consequence measurement of TgAA is an insensitive indicator of
thyroid disease but its specificity confers some benefit in supporting a
diagnosis of hypothyroidism.

Basal Endocrine Tests in the Context of Clinical
Information
The sensitivity and specificity issues in each of the diagnostic test
options create difficulties in reliably confirming a diagnosis of
hypothyroidism. Diagnosis should never rely solely on test results.
Rather, testing should be reserved for dogs strongly suspected as
having hypothyroidism: those with supportive clinical and
clinicopathological features without significant NTI or recent thyroid
suppressive medications (Figure 285.3). Then, a combination of

tests with high sensitivity/low specificity and high specificity/low
sensitivity should be chosen to minimize the shortcomings of either
alone. Choosing TT4 and cTSH provides a cost-effective and widely
available combination. fT4 should be reserved for dogs whose TT4 is
likely to be affected by concurrent NTI or drug therapies, or where
cTSH results are within reference interval. TgAAs can be used to
indirectly screen for T4AA while providing information on
pathogenesis and evidence of thyroid disease.

DIAGNOSIS OF HYPOTHYROIDISM: TRH
AND TSH STIMULATION TESTS
TSH and TRH stimulation tests, once routinely used in confirming
hypothyroidism, are now reserved for dogs when a diagnosis cannot
be confirmed using basal hormone tests in association with clinical
signs. TSH stimulation test results using bovine TSH were considered
the “gold standard” for diagnosing hypothyroidism, but that product
is no longer available. Comparable results are obtained using human
recombinant (rh) TSH, intravenous (IV), 50-75 mcg/dog, or 100 mcg
for dogs >20 kg, with samples taken before and 6 hours after
administration. A high dosage of 150 mcg/dog is no longer considered
needed to more accurately distinguish hypothyroidism from NTI.186
There are no adverse reactions, even when repeated. It is expensive,
but reconstituted rhTSH can be stored at 4°C for 4 weeks or −20°C for
up to 12 weeks without loss of activity. Criteria for interpretation of
results vary and dosage must be taken into consideration. A study
using 75 mcg/dog and a post rhTSH TT4 <1.7 mcg/dL (22 nmol/L)
suggested a high diagnostic sensitivity (100%) and specificity (>90%)
for hypothyroidism, but some results are vague.186
The TRH response test is less reliable than most available baseline
tests. At best, a good response to TRH can confidently exclude
hypothyroidism but lack of T4 response to TRH is not confirmatory.
The cTSH response to TRH administration can be assessed.114
Relatively low dosages (10 mcg/kg) of TRH cause pituitary TSH
stimulation with few side-effects. Circulating cTSH peaks

approximately 20 minutes following IV TRH. There is a limited TSH
response to TRH in hypothyroid dogs but results add little to basal
thyroid hormone analyses. Primary hypothyroidism is associated with
increased GH concentrations that increase further after similar doses
of TRH, allowing its use as a diagnostic test for hypothyroidism, if GH
assays become available.114 This test may be most helpful in
distinguishing dogs with NTI from hypothyroid dogs without an
increased cTSH concentration.187 Samples should be taken before and
45 minutes after TRH.

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
Overview
Investigating hyperthyroidism in cats and thyroid neoplasia in dogs
with imaging is well-established.188,189 Although theoretically less
affected by NTI or drugs, some imaging techniques only identify gross
abnormalities, not thyroid function.

Ultrasonography (US)
Reliable US results are highly dependent on the skill of the operator.
In euthyroid dogs, individual thyroid lobes are described as fusiform
in longitudinal section (Figure 283.7), triangular in cross section,
with a smooth capsule. Echogenicity is homogeneous and isoechoic or
hyperechoic to adjacent sternothyroid muscles. The thyroid lobes of
hypothyroid dogs have decreased echogenicity and are nonhomogeneous, irregular in outline, reduced in size, and more rounded
in shape.190,191 Any of these changes may be present and the
abnormalities may differ between the two lobes. By contrast, the
appearance of thyroids in healthy dogs are similar to those with NTI.
However, there may be wide breed differences that requires
consideration.192

Computed Tomography (CT) and Magnetic
Resonance Imaging (MRI)

CT and MRI thyroid findings in healthy dogs have been
described,193,194 but comparisons with hypothyroid dogs have not
been made. Given the need for anesthesia and expense, the risk-tobenefit ratio is small.

Thyroid Scintigraphy
Use of technetium-99M (as pertechnetate [99MTcO4−]) for
quantitative calculation of technetium thyroid gland uptake (TCTU)
has been suggested as the most accurate technique for distinguishing
primary hypothyroidism from NTI in dogs.195 Uptake values in
hypothyroid dogs range from 0.03-0.26% and in euthyroid animals
with low TT4 concentrations from 0.39-1.86%. This differential is
questioned, as glucocorticoids decrease TCTU and produce equivocal
results.196 Evaluation of TCTU has shown promise in confirming
euthyroidism in Greyhounds.197 It can also be useful in investigating
central hypothyroidism and differentiating dysgenesis from
dyshormonogenesis in congenital hypothyroid cases.189

TREATMENT
OVERVIEW
Hypothyroid dogs require thyroid hormone replacement therapy
(THRT) for life. Synthetic T4 is the treatment of choice as it is the
principal secretory product of the thyroid gland and is the
physiological prohormone for the more metabolically active T3. While
giving T3 would circumvent this normal physiological process, it
increases risk of thyrotoxicosis, has a shorter half-life requiring

multiple daily doses, and may result in T4 deficiency within organs
such as brain and pituitary gland—although its consequences are
unclear. Products containing a combination of T4 and T3 are used in
humans but are not recommended in dogs as the ratio is
inappropriate, resulting in excess T3. T4 is widely available in generic
and licensed proprietary tablet and liquid oral formulations. The
prognosis for treated hypothyroid dogs is excellent.

T4 SUPPLEMENTATION
Bioavailability
Total daily T4 secreted by healthy dog thyroids is about 2.5 mcg/kg,
but 4 times that amount, IV, is needed to normalize T4
concentrations. An even higher dosage is required for oral T4, in part
because GI absorption of T4 is poor, estimated at 10-50% and likely
influenced by intraluminal contents, dietary components, and GI
bacteria that bind orally administered T4 and reduce its availability.
Bioavailability of T4 is almost halved when given with food. Timing
feeding and oral dosing must be standardized, particularly on the day
of monitoring. Bioavailability also depends on the T4 product used.
Greater variation in bioavailability occurs with generic products but
there is also variability with proprietary products. The bioavailability
of oral tablet and liquid formulations may vary and thus not all
products can be used interchangeably.

Dosage and Frequency
The pharmacokinetics of oral T4 are similar in hypothyroid and
healthy euthyroid dogs, whether given q24h or q12h. T4 is rapidly
absorbed, reaches peak concentrations after 3 to 6 hours, and has a
serum half-life of 9 to 15 hours. Higher dosages have shorter halflives, suggesting a degree of dose-dependent kinetics. Steady-state
concentrations develop rapidly, allowing evaluation as early as 2

weeks after initiating therapy. Total daily T4 dosages ranging from 20
mcg/kg to 40 mcg/kg body weight administered q8h, q12h, or q24h
have been recommended for hypothyroid dogs. A dosage of 20
mcg/kg, q24h is widely accepted. This dosage is based, in part, on the
premise that the serum half-life of T4 does not necessarily reflect its
duration of biological effect. This dosage has been successful in about
65% of treated dogs while about 35% benefit from a higher dosage or
standardization of dosing to feeding. Dosage reductions are
uncommonly needed (<10% of dogs). Lower dosages may be required
in breeds that naturally have low TT4 concentrations.198 Dosages
required of pregnant bitches are similar to those given to all dogs.199
q12h dosing causes lower peak concentrations and less fluctuation of
circulating total T4. While 20 mcg/kg q12h is successful, it may not be
necessary or superior to q24h or 10 mcg/kg q12h. There was no
difference in 6-month outcomes in hypothyroid dogs given 20 mcg/kg
once or divided q12h.200
It is important to note that the effect of a given dose of T4 in
individual hypothyroid dogs is variable; clinical, clinicopathological
and hormonal monitoring is mandatory to ensure optimal effect. This
may require one or more dosage adjustments or moving from q24h to
q12h dosing or vice-versa. A practical advantage of q24h dosing is
greater owner compliance as therapy is lifelong. It has been
recommended to give dogs with concurrent illnesses 25-50% of the
usual starting dose, but 20 mcg/kg q24h has not been associated with
adverse effects in such dogs, conferring another advantage to this
regimen. The vaccination response in T4-treated hypothyroid dogs is
no different than in healthy dogs, suggesting alterations in vaccine
regime need not be made (ch. 185 and textbook’s inside covers).201

Clinical Response
Adequately treated hypothyroid dogs should exhibit no clinical signs
of hypothyroidism. Clinically obvious improvement, however, can
take weeks to months. Generally, metabolic changes such as dullness
and lethargy improve within days of commencing therapy and
increased activity is noted within 6 weeks.64 An expected 10% loss of

weight occurs within the first few months of therapy. Dermatological
improvements usually begin within a month of starting treatment, but
can take 2 to 3 months to normalize, often with a phase of increased
hair loss preceding hair regrowth. Neurological improvement may
take up to 6 months.

Clinicopathology
Circulating cholesterol and triglyceride values decrease dramatically,
while red blood cell values continue to increase during at least the
first 3 months of THRT.202 Fructosamine concentrations decrease
significantly following the start of THRT as protein turnover
increases.124,202 T4 treatment also rapidly reverses the hypothyroidinduced changes in creatinine, SDMA, adiponectin, leptin, and
GFR.90,125,203

Monitoring TT4
Therapeutic monitoring is aimed at achieving a satisfactory clinical
response and identifying the peak circulating TT4 concentration. Dogs
successfully treated q24h have a median peak TT4, 6 hours after
administration, of about 4 mcg/dL (50 nmol/L).44,202 Values <2.7
mcg/dL (35 nmol/L) are usually associated with an inadequate
clinical response and an increase in dosage is indicated. Markedly
increased peak TT4 of 7.0-7.8 mcg/dL (90-100 nmol/L) or greater
occasionally occur. Although dogs are usually resistant to clinical
thyrotoxicosis, such values should prompt a dosage decrease. Using
q12h dosing, TT4 values should be at the high end or just above the
reference interval 4-6 hours after administration and remain within
the reference interval prior to the next dose. Doubling the dose of T4
administered increases peak circulating TT4 concentrations by
approximately 50-60%. A more precise dosage adjustment may be
possible using the liquid rather than tablet formulation.

Monitoring TSH

Measurement of cTSH provides a longer-term assessment of the
adequacy of treatment, unlike TT4 which only provides information
for that moment in time.202 Measurement of cTSH can help identify
poor owner compliance where a particular effort to administer the
medication is made on days corresponding to the monitoring visit.
Unfortunately in the proportion of hypothyroid dogs that do not have
increased pre-treatment cTSH values, measurement during THRT is
of no additional value. Additionally, circulating cTSH can be highly
sensitive to the effects of THRT such that suppression of cTSH may be
achieved without also achieving optimal clinical control. The
limitations of the current cTSH assay do not allow identification of
over-supplementation. Monitoring cTSH concentrations can be
valuable in assessing those breeds that have low total T4
concentrations and require lower T4 dosages.198

Adverse Effects and Failure to Respond to T4 Therapy
Dogs appear to be particularly resistant to the thyrotoxic effects of
excessive T4 supplementation. Up to 10 times the standard dosage (20
mcg/kg/day) is well tolerated in healthy dogs.204 Clinical signs
include PU/PD, polyphagia, panting, weight loss, hyperactivity,
tachycardia, and hyperthermia. Most of these resolve within a few
days of withdrawing therapy. Corresponding total T4 concentrations
are usually >7.4 to 7.7 mcg/dL (95-100 nmol/L). Failure to respond to
therapy usually arises because of a failure to achieve appropriate
circulating hormone concentrations and usually responds to dosage
adjustment. However, the use of T3 may be required in dogs with
concurrent GI disease and impaired T4 absorption. A failure to
achieve the expected clinical response when T4 concentrations are
adequate should prompt investigation of another underlying disease.
Daily but not every other day anti-inflammatory doses of
prednisolone in treated hypothyroid dogs decrease TT4
concentrations; however, dosage adjustments are not required as fT4

concentrations are unaffected.205 An idiosyncratic skin reaction has
been reported against the inactive ingredients in the preparation.206

Myxedema Coma
In myxedema coma, T4 should be administered IV (5 mcg/kg) q12h.
Once the dog’s condition is stabilized, oral administration can be
substituted. Resolution of abnormal mentation, ambulation and
systolic hypotension should be expected within 30 hours.

Additional Uses of T4 Supplementation
T4 has numerous pharmacological effects unrelated to its
physiological effects when supplemented in thyroid-deficient states.
As a consequence there are anecdotal but rarely proven accounts of
using T4 for various situations, including use of these drugs to
improve coat condition. THRT has been used in dogs with ownerdirected aggression and borderline low thyroid hormone
concentrations without any significant effect.65 In humans T4
treatment of patients with NTI syndrome is controversial; there is
limited persuasive evidence that it improves outcome and the same is
likely in dogs.

CLIENT INFORMATION

Hypothyroidism
BACKGROUND
Hypothyroidism is a common endocrine disorder in dogs and results
from a failure of the thyroid gland to produce adequate amounts of
the thyroid hormones, T4 and T3.
Any breed or age of dog can develop hypothyroidism but it is more
common in early to late middle age. It is also more common in
purebred animals and certain breeds including English Setters,
Retrievers, Spaniels, Ridgebacks and Doberman Pinschers. Some
breeders test their dogs for thyroglobulin autoantibodies (a marker of
one type of hypothyroidism) to assess the risk of impending
hypothyroidism either in the dam or sire or their offspring.

CLINICAL SIGNS
Thyroid hormones have widespread effects in the body but their
major action is in controlling metabolic rate. As metabolic rate
declines your dog will slow down, be less eager or unwilling to
exercise and uninterested in the surroundings. Appetite is
uncommonly affected but because metabolic rate declines, the dog is
likely to gain weight. Hypothyroidism takes time to develop and it
may be many weeks to months before any significant changes are
noted.
The skin and haircoat are also typically involved. The coat becomes
dull and dry and usually fails to regrow after clipping. Patches of hair
loss usually develop and whilst often on either side of the flank it may
become noticeable in areas of friction such as the neck in dogs that
wear collars, the lower limbs and the tail. When these clinical signs
are present, testing for thyroid disease will be recommended.
However, when deficient, thyroid hormones have other far more wide
reaching consequences and it is not unusual for testing to be
recommended in the absence of these signs and in the presence of
others.

DIAGNOSIS
The diagnosis of hypothyroidism can be made by measuring T4 and
also TSH which is a hormone that controls T4 production. Relying on

T4 alone is not optimal as many breeds of dog (especially sight
hounds), sick dogs and those on various drug therapies can have low
values without being hypothyroid. However demonstrating a low T4 in
the presence of a high canine-specific thyroid stimulating hormone
(cTSH) is a more accurate indicator of hypothyroidism. Occasionally
test results are equivocal and it is not possible to confirm a diagnosis
of hypothyroidism. In such cases other hormone measurements or
thyroid imaging may be recommended.

TREATMENT
Treatment of hypothyroidism is relatively straightforward but is
required for life. A proprietary T4 preparation will be recommended to
be administered either once or twice daily. Food and various other
drugs potentially interfere with absorption of T4 and it is therefore
commonly recommended that treatment be given on an empty
stomach. However, if this is not possible, it is not a significant
problem providing that the drug is given in the same manner (either
with or without food) on a daily basis.

MONITORING THERAPY
Within days of instituting therapy, a clinical response is likely to be
noted. Dogs quickly become more active and less lethargic but it can
take weeks to months for their skin and haircoat to normalise. In the
meantime, it is important to ensure that the appropriate drug dose is
being administered and this is usually done by taking a blood sample
4 to 6 hours after administration to measure T4 concentrations. It is
not unusual for one or more dosage adjustments to be made over the
course of the treatment.

ADVERSE EFFECTS
Adverse effects to T4 supplementation are rare. Dogs appear very
resistant to the development of signs (hyperactivity, increased
appetite, weight loss) associated with excess supplementation.
Otherwise adequately treated, the disorder has an excellent prognosis.
Carmel T. Mooney (Belfield, Dublin, Ireland)

Chapter 286: Feline
Hypothyroidism
J. Catharine Scott-Moncrieff

A C RO N YM S

fT4 free T4
LT4Na levothyroxine sodium
NTIS non-thyroidal illness syndrome
TSH thyrotropin (thyroid-stimulating hormone)
TT4 total thyroxine
T3 triiodothyronine

Naturally occurring hypothyroidism in cats is a rare clinical entity.
A small number of cats with congenital or adult onset
hypothyroidism have been reported in the veterinary literature.1-9 In
contrast, iatrogenic hypothyroidism following treatment for
hyperthyroidism is common.11-15 The most common cause of a low
serum total thyroxine (TT4) concentration in cats is non-thyroidal
illness syndrome (NTIS).

ETIOLOGY
ADULT-ONSET HYPOTHYROIDISM
While only 4 case reports and one case series of 7 cats with primary
adult-onset hypothyroidism have been published, the disorder is
likely more common. Reported causes included lymphocytic
thyroiditis, diffuse follicular hyperplasia, and idiopathic.6-10 Diffuse
follicular hyperplasia causing goiter was documented in 2 cats and
suspected in a further 5 based on scintigraphic findings.10 The
underlying cause of follicular hyperplasia in cats with adult onset
hypothyroidism is unknown. Exposure to goitrogens or imbalances
in dietary iodine have not been documented. Adult cats with a mild
form of congenital hypothyroidism (dyshormonogenesis) is a more
likely explanation, but is not proven. Secondary hypothyroidism was
reported in an 18-month-old cat with stunted growth and a history of
head trauma at 8 weeks of age.3

CONGENITAL HYPOTHYROIDISM
Overview
Congenital primary hypothyroidism is recognized more frequently
than the adult-onset condition in cats. Cats with congenital
hypothyroidism are likely under-recognized because screening for
hypothyroidism is not routine in kittens and some likely die without
a diagnosis. Causes of congenital hypothyroidism include thyroid
dyshormonogenesis, thyroid hypoplasia or aplasia, thyrotropin (TSH
[thyroid-stimulation hormone]) resistance, and thyroiditis.1,2,4,16,17

Dyshormonogenesis
Dyshormonogenesis is the most common form of congenital
hypothyroidism in cats and is a condition caused by inborn errors
that interfere with synthesis of thyroid hormone, e.g., thyroid
peroxidase deficiency and iodide transport defects. Severity of
clinical signs varies and their onset may be delayed because some
defects are incomplete. Dyshormonogenesis is usually associated

with the development of goiter (enlarged thyroid) secondary to
sustained TSH stimulation. Both functional transduction of signal
via the TSH receptor and a block in the synthesis of thyroid
hormones must be present. A specific mutation was not identified in
the reported cats. Two kittens with congenital hypothyroidism due to
defective organification of iodide were diagnosed based on in vivo
discharge of accumulated labeled iodide by perchlorate.1 The defect
was complete in 1 cat and partial in another. No membrane-bound
peroxidase activity could be demonstrated in the cat with the partial
deficiency and it was suspected that “loose enzyme anchoring”
decreased peroxidase availability and decreased capacity for organic
binding of trapped iodide. An inherited autosomal recessive defect in
iodine organification was suspected in a family of Abyssinian cats
with congenital hypothyroidism and goiter.2 Congenital
hypothyroidism with goiter due to thyroid peroxidase deficiency was
reported in a family of Domestic Shorthair cats, also thought to have
an inherited autosomal recessive trait.18 Thyroid dyshormongenesis
was suspected in a series of 6 cats with congenital goitrous
hypothyroidism from a single veterinary hospital in Chile.5

Thyroid Gland Agenesis or Hypoplasia
Defects in development causing thyroid gland agenesis or hypoplasia
(dysmorphogenesis) have been described. The molecular genetic
defect has not been established. In other species, defects in genes
encoding thyroid transcription factors 1 and 2, the TSH receptor, and
signal transduction pathways downstream of the TSH receptor have
been described.4

TSH Resistance
TSH resistance was the proposed cause of inherited primary
hypothyroidism in a colony of Japanese cats, none of which had a
goiter.16 The defect was inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.

Thyroiditis

A colony of cats had severe signs of hypothyroidism and thyroiditis
that developed at 40 to 60 days of age.17 The severity of thyroiditis
was decreased by early treatment with thyroid hormone.

Iodine Deficiency
Rarely, iodine deficiency has been reported to cause hypothyroidism
in kittens fed a strict all-meat diet.

IATROGENIC HYPOTHYROIDISM
Iatrogenic hypothyroidism is most often the result of treating
hyperthyroidism and is the most common cause of the condition in
cats (ch. 287). Iatrogenic hypothyroidism has also been reported
following stereotactic radiation therapy for acromegaly.19 Iatrogenic
hypothyroidism may follow radioactive iodine treatment, bilateral
thyroidectomy, or administration of anti-thyroid drugs (ch. 287).
Depending on the mode of treatment, plasma TT4 may decline to
subnormal concentrations within hours (surgery), days (anti-thyroid
drugs), or weeks-to-months (radioactive iodine). The prevalence of
iatrogenic hypothyroidism following radioactive iodine treatment
ranges from 3 to 79%, a wide range that likely reflects differences in
criteria used for diagnosing iatrogenic hypothyroidism and use of
different radioactive iodine dose protocols.20,21
Diagnosis of iatrogenic hypothyroidism relies on clinical signs (see
below) in conjunction with low total TT4 (overt hypothyroidism). It is
now recognized that some cats with iatrogenic hypothyroidism do
not have overt clinical signs and may have serum TT4 concentrations
within the low end of the reference range (sub-clinical
hypothyroidism).13,15 The clinical consequences of sub-clinical
hypothyroidism are unclear but azotemia in some cats resolves with
thyroid hormone supplementation.
In two recent studies of cats treated with 2 to 6 mCi of radioactive
iodine, the reported prevalence of overt hypothyroidism after 6
months ranged from 1 to 40% and prevalence of subclinical
hypothyroidism ranged from 13 to 46%.13,14 The prevalence of overt

and subclinical hypothyroidism was lower in cats treated with lower
dosages of radioactive iodine. Iatrogenic hypothyroidism may also
occur in cats treated with anti-thyroid drugs. In a study of 80 nonazotemic hyperthyroid cats treated with methimazole for 6 months,
35% became hypothyroid, as defined by a TT4 below the reference
range and a serum TSH concentration above the reference range.12
Cats that became hypothyroid following therapy for
hyperthyroidism were more likely to become azotemic than those
that became euthyroid. Cats that became both hypothyroid and
azotemic had shorter survival times than the euthyroid azotemic
cats. Azotemia was presumed to be due to a decrease in glomerular
filtration rate in cats with underlying chronic kidney disease (CKD,
ch. 301) and concurrent hypothyroidism. Prolonged iatrogenic
hypothyroidism should be avoided, especially in cats with known
concurrent CKD. In 125 methimazole-treated hyperthyroid cats,
about 20% had decreased free T4 (fT4) and/or TT4 and increased
TSH concentrations, consistent with iatrogenic hypothyroidism.22
Hypothyroidism is not expected after unilateral thyroidectomy, but
approximately 50% of cats become hypothyroid after bilateral
thyroidectomy.23

CLINICAL SIGNS
Adult-Onset Hypothyroidism
Clinical signs of adult onset feline hypothyroidism vary in severity
and include lethargy, inappetence, mental dullness, dermatologic
abnormalities, obesity, polyuria, and polydipsia (Figure 286.1;
Video 286.1). In a report of 7 adult cats with spontaneous
hypothyroidism, only 2 were evaluated for hair loss, lethargy or
obesity, 3 had no signs but had abnormal results on annual thyroid
testing, and 2 had a palpable goiter. The goiters ranged in size from
2.5 to 8 times the upper reference of thyroid volume.10 Dermatologic
signs are quite variable (ch. 12). Affected cats may develop a dull,
dry, unkempt hair coat with matting, increased shedding, dandruff,
and seborrhea. Easily epilated and poor hair regrowth may lead to

alopecia affecting the pinnae, pressure points, and the dorsal and
lateral tail base region.6,7 Asymmetric or bilaterally symmetric
alopecia involving the lateral neck, thorax, and abdomen also occur.
Myxedema of the face, causing a “puffy” appearance, was reported in
1 cat with naturally acquired adult-onset hypothyroidism.6
Bradycardia and mild hypothermia may be additional findings on
physical examination.

CONGENITAL HYPOTHYROIDISM
Kittens with congenital hypothyroidism typically appear normal at
birth but their slow growth usually becomes evident by 6 to 8 weeks
of age. Disproportionate dwarfism develops over the ensuing
months, with affected kittens developing large heads, short wide
necks, short body and short thick limbs. Facial dysmorphism results
in a broad head and flat face (Figure 286.2). Additional findings
include palpable bilateral goiter, obesity, lethargy, mental dullness,
constipation, hypothermia, bradycardia, retention of deciduous teeth
and/or delayed eruption of adult teeth.1,2,4 Their hair coats consist
mainly of the undercoat with primary guard hairs scattered thinly.
Two littermate kittens with hypothyroidism had concurrent seizure
disorders but whether the seizures were related to hypothyroidism
was unclear.4 Radiographic abnormalities include delayed
epiphyseal ossification, epiphyseal dysgenesis, shortened vertebral
bodies, and constipation. An adult cat with suspected congenital
primary hypothyroidism had bilateral femoral capital physeal
fractures.24 In a case series of 6 cats with congenital goitrous
hypothyroidism, the age at diagnosis ranged from 4 to 19 months; a
diagnosis of congenital hypothyroidism has also been made in older
cats including a 3-year-old with severe constipation and
megacolon.25-27

IATROGENIC HYPOTHYROIDISM
In cats with overt iatrogenic hypothyroidism the clinical signs are
usually mild decreased activity and weight gain. Such signs are not
usually worrisome to an owner of a previously hyperthyroid cat. In
cats with subclinical hypothyroidism, increased risk of azotemia
remains a concern (ch. 287).

DIAGNOSIS
OVERVIEW
Scintigraphy and the TSH stimulation test are considered gold
standard tests for confirming a diagnosis of hypothyroidism. Neither
test is commonly performed in veterinary practices. The diagnosis of

hypothyroidism is more commonly based on history, clinical signs,
physical examination findings, low serum thyroid hormone
concentrations, and increased serum TSH concentrations. A
complete blood count (CBC), serum chemistry profile and urinalysis
should be evaluated to identify changes supportive of
hypothyroidism and assess for the presence of non-thyroidal illness.
Most hypothyroid cats have normocytic normochromic anemia,
hypercholesterolemia, and an increased creatine kinase (chs. 57, 63,
66). Azotemia was reported in 5 of 7 cats with adult-onset primary
hypothyroidism.10 Decreased hepatic function tests and a low
insulin-like growth factor 1 concentration have been reported in a cat
with congenital hypothyroidism.28 These abnormalities resolved
with treatment for the hypothyroidism.
Hypothyroidism is much more likely in cats that have had a
thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine treatment or a kitten with
disproportionate dwarfism. Naturally occurring adult-onset
hypothyroidism is rare and NTIS should be carefully considered.
Low serum TT4 concentrations in conjunction with an increased TSH
concentration support the diagnosis of primary hypothyroidism.
Further diagnostic testing to confirm the diagnosis and localize the
location of the defect includes scintigraphy with perchlorate
discharge and TSH stimulation testing. Response to trial therapy
with levothyroxine sodium (LT4Na) also supports the diagnosis but
is nonspecific and does not, by itself, prove the diagnosis.

SERUM TT4 CONCENTRATION
Cats with hypothyroidism typically have baseline serum TT4
concentrations below the lower limit of the reference range and
sometimes the TT4 concentration is undetectable. The TT4 in 6 cats
with goitrous congenital hypothyroidism ranged from 0.4 to 1.0
mcg/dL (5.2 to 12.9 nmol/L).5 In 7 cats with adult onset
hypothyroidism, 6/7 had low TT4 concentrations and 1 was at the
low end of the reference range.10 A TT4 concentration well within the

reference range excludes a diagnosis of spontaneous
hypothyroidism, but cats with subclinical hypothyroidism due to
radioactive iodine treatment may have a serum TT4 concentrations
within the reference range. Non-thyroidal illness and administration
of drugs such as glucocorticoids can lower serum TT4 concentrations
into the hypothyroid range; a low serum TT4 concentration alone
does not confirm hypothyroidism.

SERUM FREE T4 (fT4) CONCENTRATION
As with serum TT4, a low serum fT4 concentration does not, by itself,
confirm hypothyroidism since NTIS and some drugs can also lower
serum fT4 concentrations into the hypothyroid range. Serum fT4 may
be less influenced by NTIS or administration of drugs than serum
TT4: serum fT4 concentrations have been reported to increase rather
than decrease in some euthyroid cats with NTIS.29 The sensitivity
and specificity of serum fT4 and TT4 for thyroid gland function in
cats with suspected hypothyroidism is unknown. In 7 cats with adultonset hypothyroidism, both TT4 and fT4 were low in 6 of 7 cats and at
the low end of the reference range in 1 cat.10 In cats receiving
methimazole, the TT4 and fT4 concentrations were positively
correlated, but fT4 did not identify more cats with iatrogenic
hypothyroidism than did the TT4.22 In 118 cats treated with
radioactive iodine, 22% became hypothyroid.15 In the hypothyroid
cats, TT4 was low in 19% while fT4 was low in 88%. In the 71
euthyroid cats only 1 cat had a low TT4 while 5 cats had a low fT4,
suggesting that fT4 is more sensitive but less specific for diagnosis of
iatrogenic hypothyroidism in radioactive iodine-treated cats.

SERUM TSH CONCENTRATION

A canine TSH assay (Immulite canine TSH assay, Siemens
Healthineers USA) has been validated for use in cats.30 Although its
sensitivity is suboptimal, a high TSH concentration in a cat with a
low TT4 is highly specific for a diagnosis of hypothyroidism.
Increased TSH concentrations have been documented in cats with
congenital hypothyroidism, spontaneous adult-onset
hypothyroidism, and iatrogenic hypothyroidism. In 6 cats with
goitrous congenital hypothyroidism, serum TSH concentrations
ranged from 2.7 to 12 ng/mL.5 In 7 cats with adult onset
hypothyroidism, all had increased TSH concentrations (2.1-20
ng/mL).10 In 26 cats with iatrogenic hypothyroidism, 85% had an
increased TSH concentration, while only 14% of euthyroid cats had
an increased TSH.15

SERUM T3 CONCENTRATION
Measurement of serum triiodothyronine (T3) concentration is not
recommended in cats. Reported T3 concentrations have been
variable in cats with hypothyroidism.

TESTS FOR LYMPHOCYTIC
THYROIDITIS
Tests for the presence of circulating thyroglobulin and microsomal
antibodies were reported to be positive in a colony of cats with earlyonset thyroiditis. However commercial assays for feline thyroid
antibodies are not currently available.17

TSH STIMULATION TEST
The indications, protocol, and interpretation of the TSH stimulation
test are similar for cats and dogs, except that a lower dose of TSH (25
mcg IV) is used in cats.31,32 Euthyroid cats exhibit a 2 to 3 fold

increase in TT4 6-8 hours after TSH administration. There are few
studies reporting changes in TT4 after TSH administration in cats
with NTIS or hypothyroidism. In one small study, TT4 increased 111
to 300% after TSH administration in healthy cats and 146 to 414% in
cats with NTIS.32 Cats with iatrogenic hypothyroidism after
radioactive iodine treatment had increases in TT4 ≤11%, suggesting
that the TSH stimulation test may be useful for diagnosis of
hypothyroidism. TSH expense, however, limits its use.

SCINTIGRAPHY
Scintigraphy results using technetium99m can be evaluated
qualitatively or quantitatively (ch. 287, Figure 287.4).
Radionuclide uptake in normal thyroid lobes closely approximates
the update in the salivary glands with an uptake ratio of 1:1. In cats
with goitrous hypothyroidism the thyroid lobes are bilaterally
enlarged with homogenous uptake of radionuclide. In cats with
atrophic hypothyroidism, no thyroid tissue can be identified by
scintigraphy. Diagnosis of secondary hypothyroidism in a young cat
with head trauma was made by documentation of low TT4, low TSH,
and no increase in TT4 or TSH after administration of thyrotropinreleasing hormone. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
revealed an almost empty sella turcica and a small pituitary gland.3

TREATMENT
OVERVIEW
For cats with iatrogenic hypothyroidism due to thyroidectomy or
radioactive iodine treatment, transient hypothyroidism is expected
with a return of euthyroidism 2-3 months later. Treatment for
hypothyroidism is indicated when clinical signs are present,
azotemia is present, or if hypothyroidism does not resolve within 3-6
months of treatment. In cats treated with oral anti-thyroid drugs that
become hypothyroid, the dose should be decreased.

LEVOTHYROXINE SODIUM (LT4Na)
LT4Na is the recommended supplement for cats with spontaneous
hypothyroidism and for cats with iatrogenic hypothyroidism that
require treatment using an initial dosage of 10-20 mcg/kg PO q1224h. A minimum of 4 to 6 weeks should elapse before critically
assessing clinical response to treatment. Subsequent reevaluations
should include history, physical examination (including body weight
and body condition score, ch. 72 and textbook’s inside covers) and
measurement of serum TT4 and TSH. Goals of therapy are resolution
of clinical signs while avoiding hyperthyroidism. LT4Na dosage and
frequency of administration should be adjusted to maintain both
serum TT4 and TSH concentrations within reference ranges.
If serum thyroid hormone concentrations and TSH concentrations
are within the reference range after 4-6 weeks of treatment without a
positive clinical response, the diagnosis should be reassessed. In 6
cats with congenital goitrous hypothyroidism, all improved with
doses ranging from 10-20 mcg/kg PO q12h (median 13.5 mcg/kg).5
Haircoat and activity improved after 8 weeks and all had normal
physical appearance and dentition after 4 months. The final dosage
of LT4Na required to normalize serum T4 and TSH concentrations
was 14-20 mcg/kg (median 16 mcg/kg) PO q12h. The thyroid goiters
shrank markedly in all cats but remained palpable. In 7 adult cats
diagnosed with spontaneous hypothyroidism, the median LT4Na
dosage used for treatment was 200 mcg/cat PO q24h (32.7 mcg/kg
q24h), with a range of 100-200 mcg/cat/day. Clinical signs, azotemia
and anemia resolved in all cats and the goiters also decreased in size.
Thyroid gland size and radionuclide uptake failed to completely
normalize in most cats.10

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis for feline hypothyroidism depends on the underlying
cause and the age of the cat at the time clinical signs develop. With
appropriate therapy, the clinical manifestations should resolve

following thyroid hormone supplementation and the life expectancy
of an adult cat with primary hypothyroidism should be normal. The
prognosis for kittens with congenital hypothyroidism depends on the
severity of skeletal changes at the time treatment is initiated and
neurologic status. Although many of the clinical signs resolve with
therapy, musculoskeletal and neurologic problems may persist. In
cats with iatrogenic hypothyroidism the prognosis depends upon
whether the hypothyroidism in appropriately treated. The median
survival time for azotemic cats with untreated hypothyroidism was
456 days (range 231-1869) compared to 905 days (range 316-1869)
that of euthyroid azotemic cats.12

CLIENT INFORMATION
Feline Hypothyroidism
Your veterinarian suspects that your cat may have hypothyroidism
(an underactive thyroid gland).
There are several causes of hypothyroidism in cats. In kittens and
very young cats, congenital hypothyroidism is possible but is rare.
Affected kittens are born with this disease but it can take weeks or
months before symptoms are noticed. In older cats, hypothyroidism
usually develops as a complication of treatment for hyperthyroidism
(an overactive thyroid gland). This is called iatrogenic
hypothyroidism. Naturally occurring hypothyroidism also occurs in
adult cats but it is rare. An accurate diagnosis of hypothyroidism is
necessary so that veterinarian can determine whether treatment will
be in the best interest of your pet.
Clinical signs of hypothyroidism most commonly include lethargy
and weight gain. In adult onset hypothyroidism skin abnormalities

are common. In congenital hypothyroidism, constipation and
dwarfism (failure to grow, small size) are also present. In some cases
of congenital and adult onset hypothyroidism an enlarged thyroid
gland can be palpated in the neck. Because the clinical signs of
hypothyroidism are nonspecific, further testing is required to make a
diagnosis.
Diagnosis of hypothyroidism requires a routine blood analysis
(complete blood count and biochemistry profile) to rule out other
disorders, and measurement of thyroid hormone concentrations. In
young cats with failure to grow, radiographs are recommended.
Hypothyroidism is easily treated with synthetic thyroid hormone
usually given as a daily or twice daily pill. The treatment is life-long
but in most cases the clinical signs completely resolve with
treatment. If the thyroid gland was enlarged it will shrink with
treatment but may not completely return to normal. If you have any
further questions, please contact your veterinarian.
J. Catharine Scott-Moncrieff (West Lafayette, Indiana)
