INTRODUCTION
Hyperthyroidism is the most common feline endocrine disease, affecting about 10% of
senior cats, and one of the most common geriatric diseases of cats.1 Hyperthyroidism is a
progressive disease with disastrous consequences if untreated. Early diagnosis has been

facilitated by the inclusion of serum total thyroxine concentrations (TT4) in routine
screening panels for older cats. Affected thyroid nodules contain single or multiple
hyperplastic and/or adenomatous tumor nodules resembling toxic nodular goiter seen in
humans (i.e., Plummer’s disease).2 Pathologic changes are bilateral in about 70% of
affected cats and unilateral in about 25%.3 Ectopic disease is the least common form,
occurring in around 4%. Although most cats have an adenoma, carcinomas are diagnosed
in about 1-2%. Some benign thyroid tumors may transform into malignant carcinomas if
untreated or after chronic oral anti-thyroid drugs.4 Histologic evaluation of feline thyroid
tumors is rarely available, and carcinomas are indistinguishable from adenomas on
thyroid scintigraphy. A classification scheme was developed for more aggressive tumors
that require a different therapeutic approach. Some thyroid tumors cause severe
hyperthyroidism, may become huge thyroid masses, some are intrathoracic in location or
multifocal with resistance to anti-thyroid drugs (SHIM-RAD tumors).4 These are usually
best managed with high dosages of radioactive iodine (131I).

PATHOGENESIS
Evidence of an immune-mediated cause as observed in humans with autoantibodies
activating thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) receptors (i.e., Graves’ disease) has not
been identified in cats.5,6 Although the etiology is unclear, diet (i.e., iodine or selenium
deficiency) or chronic exposure to thyroid-disrupting compounds (i.e., bisphenol A,
polybrominated diphenyl ethers [PBDEs]) in food, water, and the environment may
contribute to the pathogenesis of feline hyperthyroidism.7-9 In some hyperthyroid
humans, activating mutations mostly in the TSH receptor gene and less commonly in the
adenylate cyclase stimulation protein Gαs subunit (GNAS) have been identified.10 In cats,
recent work has identified Met-452-Thr and GNAS mutations.11,12

CLINICAL FEATURES
HISTORY
Most hyperthyroid cats are ≥9 years of age with a mean of about 13. Occasionally, the
disease is diagnosed in younger cats.13-15 Common clinical signs (Table 287.1) include
weight loss, polyphagia (PP), gastrointestinal (GI) signs (especially vomiting),
hyperactivity, polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD), panting (

Video 287.1), poor grooming,

and behavioral changes. Despite their age, some hyperthyroid cats become hyperactive
and/or aggressive. Due to increased awareness and routine screening, the diagnosis of
hyperthyroidism is often made in cats with subtle (or absent) clinical signs. Occasionally
hyperthyroid cats are hypo- or anorexic and lethargic, which is sometimes referred to as
“apathetic” hyperthyroidism. Most of these “apathetic” cats, however, have
hyperthyroidism and a concomitant disease.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (PE)

Body Weight, Body and Muscle Condition Scores (BCS and
MCS), Thyroid Palpation
A palpable thyroid nodule(s) and muscle wasting are the most common findings on PE.
The weight loss typical of hyperthyroidism decreases skin elasticity, causing some
hyperthyroid cats to appear dehydrated when they are not. Good thyroid palpation
technique (

Video 287.2) is important. Losses in weight, BCS, or MCS (see textbook’s

inside covers) in middle-aged and senior cats are key clues for early detection of
hyperthyroidism. Thyroid lobes are not palpable in healthy cats. One or more thyroid
nodules are palpable in most hyperthyroid cats.16 Thyroid palpation is sensitive but not
specific for hyperthyroidism since small thyroid nodules can occasionally be palpated in
euthyroid cats and some “nodules” are not thyroid.17 A scoring system has been
described.18-20 Hyperthyroid cats tend to have larger goiters (large thyroids) than those
without the disease. In general, goiter sizes are tending to be smaller nowadays than in the
past, reflecting earlier diagnosis.21 Presence of no palpable thyroid nodule in hyperthyroid
cats has been seen with ectopic thyroid masses, identified anywhere from under the tongue
to being intrathoracic and as low as the base of the heart.

Cardiac and Blood Pressure (BP) Abnormalities
Thyroid hormones directly have positive inotropic and chronotropic effects and indirectly
cause peripheral vasodilation.22 Hyperthyroid-induced tachycardia, heart murmurs
(29%), and/or arrhythmias are common.16 Myocardial changes (ch. 234) are common
and often reversible with adequate therapy for hyperthyroidism (

Video 287.3). The

prevalence of cardiac abnormalities increases with severity of hyperthyroidism.23 About
10-30% of hyperthyroid cats have secondary hypertension (ch. 236).24 In some, systemic
hypertension develops following successful treatment of hyperthyroidism, regardless of
the treatment modality.25 Hence, BPs (ch. 91) and fundic examinations (ch. 13) should
be monitored before, during, and after treatment of hyperthyroidism.

ROUTINE LABORATORY FINDINGS
Overview
A variety of hematologic, biochemical, and urinary changes have been observed in
hyperthyroid cats. While many of these changes are nonspecific and mild, assessing these
parameters is important. Test results may be consistent with hyperthyroidism (e.g.,
increased liver enzyme activities in an older cat), they may aid in identifying other
explanations for some signs (e.g., PP due to diabetes mellitus), or they can help assess for
any concurrent disorders (e.g., chronic kidney disease [CKD]) that could affect prognosis
and choice of therapy (Table 287.2).

Complete Blood Count (CBC)
Mild erythrocytosis in a non-dehydrated cat should alert the clinician to consider
hyperthyroidism. The erythrocytosis likely follows direct thyroid hormone stimulation of
the bone marrow and/or erythropoietin synthesis stimulated by increased oxygen
consumption. Anemia is not typical and should alert the clinician of the possible presence
of concurrent disease.

Serum Biochemistries
More than 80% of hyperthyroid cats have increased alanine aminotransferase activities
and >50% have increased alkaline phosphatase activities.13,26 The cause for these
increases are multifactorial and presumably related to metabolic hepatic stress, passive
congestion, and a direct effect of thyroid hormone excess. Increased liver enzyme activities
in an older cat should prompt investigation for hyperthyroidism. In an untreated
hyperthyroid cat with expected clinical signs (e.g., PP, weight loss), mild to moderately
increased liver enzyme activities can be assumed to be secondary to the hyperthyroidism.
However, in presence of hypo- or anorexia, icterus, or disproportionate increases in
hepatic enzyme activities, concurrent liver disease is possible. Liver enzyme activities
rapidly return to normal once permanent euthyroidism is restored, but oral anti-thyroid
drugs may cause increases in liver enzyme activities. Lower concentrations of fructosamine
and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) are expected in hyperthyroid cats,27,28 which can

complicate diagnosing acromegaly and/or monitoring of diabetes mellitus (chs. 280 and
292). A tendency for hyperthyroid cats to have hypercoagulability has been reported,
although its clinical relevance remains unknown.29

Urinalysis (UA)
There are no UA findings specific for hyperthyroidism. Isosthenuria and mild proteinuria
are common.30 In contrast to earlier reports, the prevalence of subclinical bacteriuria
(∼5%) is low.31,32 Urine culture is not routinely recommended unless clinical signs of
urinary tract disease are present and subclinical bacteriuria is not an indication for
therapy.33

CONFIRMING THE DIAGNOSIS
HORMONE TESTING
Total Thyroxine (TT4)
A randomly obtained serum TT4 concentration is the most common first-line screening
test for hyperthyroidism. Assays are readily available, inexpensive, and results are similar
across laboratories. Results are abnormally increased in 90-95% of hyperthyroid cats on a
single randomly obtained blood sample, with the balance having TT4 results in the middleto-high end of the reference interval. The occasional “normal” TT4 value in these cats is
probably due to TT4 values that fluctuate from high-normal to high. The presence of nonthyroidal illness may decrease TT4 results. Reference interval or borderline results are
more common in cats with mild disease.34,35 The clinical severity of hyperthyroidism
correlates with the magnitude of TT4 increase. Hence, very high values are expected in
severely hyperthyroid cats. If normal TT4 results are obtained from a cat strongly
suspected to have hyperthyroidism, the TT4 should be repeated after several days to weeks.
Alternatively, measuring free T4 (fT4) and/or thyrotropin (TSH) as well as obtaining
thyroid scintigraphy should be considered. Basal serum total tri-iodothyronine (T3) results
are not often useful because of the overlap in results among normal cats, hyperthyroid
cats, and cats with non-thyroidal illness.34

Free Thyroxine (fT4)
Measurement of serum fT4 can be of value in diagnosing hyperthyroidism, if the
indications and pitfalls are understood. Overall, fT4 is abnormal in about 98% of
hyperthyroid cats, which is better sensitivity than the TT4. Interestingly, in mild
hyperthyroidism, 85-95% of cats have an abnormal fT4 versus “only” 60-80% with an
abnormal TT4.35 This particular setting, namely a clinical suspicion of hyperthyroidism
and a TT4 within reference interval (upper half of the reference interval), is when the fT4

has most value. Important limitations prevent using the fT4 in cats as the first-line
screening test for hyperthyroidism. Increases in fT4 are not specific for hyperthyroidism.
False positives are obtained from 10-30% of euthyroid cats without evidence of concurrent
disease and false positives can be obtained from cats with systemic illness.34-37 Further,
the methodology and reference intervals used are important. Most studies in cats assess
fT4 with the “gold standard” equilibrium dialysis assays. Results cannot easily be
extrapolated to other methodologies.38

Thyrotropin (TSH) Measurement
Almost all hyperthyroid cats have undetectable serum TSH concentrations, using a
commercial canine assay. The diagnostic sensitivity is about 98%.35 Thus, detectable TSH
in a suspected hyperthyroid cat renders the diagnosis as unlikely. Many healthy cats and
those with non-thyroidal illness also have undetectable TSHs, resulting in poor specificity
(∼70%) and negating its use as a sole diagnostic test for hyperthyroidism. A feline specific
TSH assay will be welcome. The canine assay may help detect iatrogenic hypothyroidism,
although its value in this context remains to be clarified.39-41

The T3 Suppression Test
The T3 suppression test was used to evaluate cats suspected of having hyperthyroidism
despite having TT4 results within reference limits. Although test results were rather
reliable, it was time-consuming. Readers are referred to older textbooks for protocols.

THYROID SCINTIGRAPHY
Results of thyroid gland pertechnetate (99mTcO4−) scans are extremely sensitive for
diagnosing feline hyperthyroidism. Thyroid-to-salivary gland ratios provide excellent
sensitivity and specificity (Figure 287.1).42 Thyroid scintigraphy requires special
licensing and facilities. In most cats, appropriate clinical signs and increased TT4
concentrations suffice to confirm the diagnosis, meaning scintigraphy is not needed.
However, scintigraphy has numerous positive attributes. Thyroid scintigraphy scans can
provide clarity regarding diagnosis of hyperthyroidism in cats with equivocal TT4 results;
can discriminate cats with unilateral hyperthyroidism from those with bilateral disease
before surgery (Figure 287.2); can identify cats with abnormal ectopic or intrathoracic
thyroid tissue (Figure 287.3); can determine if there is evidence for thyroid carcinoma
(Figure 287.4); can help identify cats “suspected of thyroid carcinoma” (SHIM-RAD
tumors); and can help determine an optimal 131I treatment dose while decreasing the
incidence of iatrogenic hypothyroidism. A classification system has been developed from

clinical and scintigraphic criteria to identify cats with SHIM-RAD tumors since they may
benefit from unique treatment strategies.4

TREATMENT
THE 4 OPTIONS
Hyperthyroid cats can be treated with anti-thyroid medication (oral or transdermal), an
iodine-restricted diet, thyroidectomy, or radioactive iodine (131I). Surgery and 131I are
definitive (permanent) treatment options. Anti-thyroid medication and diet are reversible.
Each of the 4 options can resolve hyperthyroidism and each has advantages and
disadvantages (Table 287.3). Owners should be fully educated regarding each option and
the choice that might be best for their cat. The recommended treatment should be based
on parameters that include age, overall health, concurrent disease, financial constraints,
surgical skill, availability of 131I, and the owner’s goals.

thyroid:salivary (T:S) ratio. The T:S ratio is calculated by dividing the
mean counts per pixel in the thyroid region by the mean counts per
pixel in the salivary gland region. Values ≤1.5 are normal whereas a
ratio >1.5 is diagnostic for hyperthyroidism. From Broome MR,
Peterson ME. Thyroid imaging. In: Feldman EC, Fracassi F, Peterson
ME, eds. Feline Endocrinology. Edra; 2019:169-197. Used with
permission.

FIGURE 287.2 Thyroid scintigraphy in 4 cats with multinodular

2019:169-197. Used with permission.
Initially, use of diet or anti-thyroid drugs can result in some or total resolution of the
metabolic and cardiac consequences of hyperthyroidism while permanent treatment
options are considered. This is especially important before surgery because resolving the
hyperthyroid state decreases anesthetic and surgical risks. It is important to underscore to
owners that the anti-thyroid medication and dietary options do not treat the thyroid
tumor, they “only” block thyroid hormone synthesis. This can resolve hyperthyroidism but
also “allows” the thyroid tumor to continue growing, sometimes becoming huge and
invasive.43 Veterinarians and owners should be aware of the potential for this disease
progression. Palpation of the cervical area is important, not only at the time of diagnosis
but also at every follow up examination. A gradual increase in thyroid tumor size over time
is expected in cats treated with an anti-thyroid drug or diet. However, a marked increase in
thyroid nodule(s) size is of concern and, if such a large nodule is palpated, thyroid
scintigraphy is indicated to rule out suspected carcinoma and to better define the
condition prior to surgery or 131I.

POTENTIAL LONG-TERM CONSEQUENCES IN
UNTREATED HYPERTHYROIDISM
Untreated, hyperthyroidism is a chronic, progressive, and relentless disease. The
prevalence of severe signs, large thyroid masses, multifocal disease, intrathoracic thyroid
masses, and thyroid malignancy all increase over time. In a study of cats referred for 131I
therapy, many of which had been treated with anti-thyroid medication for years, some had
benign thyroid tumors transform to malignant thyroid carcinomas.4

EVALUATION FOR CONCOMITANT DISEASE
A complete history and thorough PE should be completed in any cat suspected of or
diagnosed with hyperthyroidism since concomitant diseases are common. Thoracic
radiographs and abdominal ultrasound are always indicated if a concomitant disease is
suspected. In one study, almost 20% of cats examined prior to 131I therapy had at least one
comorbidity.44 Most clinician-researchers agree that a “minimum database” includes a
CBC, serum biochemistry profile, UA, and BP (ch. 91). Unless clinical signs of lower or
upper urinary tract disease are present, urine culture is not indicated.31 A recent
retrospective study demonstrated that thoracic radiography commonly reveals
abnormalities, but only about 5-10% had abnormalities that led to a change in treatment
plan.45

TREATMENT OBJECTIVES AND MONITORING

Treated hyperthyroid cats may improve clinically despite TT4 concentrations just above or
in the upper reference range. Such results likely indicate an underdosage, but overzealous
therapy also needs to be avoided (see iatrogenic hypothyroidism). Therefore, adequate
monitoring during treatment is essential. Careful detection and management of any
concomitant disease is also important to optimize the cat’s health. Weight gain, improved
body and muscular condition score (see scoring charts on textbook’s inside covers),
improved hair coat, resolving tachycardia/heart murmur, behavioral changes and liver
enzyme activities are expected.

ANTI-THYROID DRUGS
Overview and Precautions
The anti-thyroid medications methimazole and carbimazole are the most common
treatments for hyperthyroid cats worldwide; in some cases they are used lifelong and
others for a short period to identify masked CKD, to prepare for thyroidectomy, or to
resolve signs while awaiting 131I. No traces of anti-thyroid drugs were found in the urine of
owners pilling their cat daily with anti-thyroid drugs.46 Regardless, owners should be
instructed to handle these drugs carefully because they are as effective in humans as in
cats. Pregnant women should not administer these drugs (oral or transdermal) and should
avoid contact with the litter box. Anti-thyroid tablets should never be crushed or divided
and veterinarians MUST tell owners who plan to administer transdermal anti-thyroid
drugs that they MUST use appropriate gloves or finger protection.

Mechanism of Action (Figure 287.5)
Anti-thyroid drugs do not prevent the thyroid gland from “trapping” iodide. Instead, they
block thyroid hormone synthesis by inhibiting the actions of thyroid peroxidase, the
enzyme essential for oxidation of iodide to iodine, incorporation of iodine into
thyroglobulin (organification), and coupling of tyrosine residues to form the two major
thyroid hormones: tri-iodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4). Each enzymatic step must be
completed to manufacture thyroid hormones. Anti-thyroid drugs do not prevent secretion
of thyroid hormone synthesized prior its administration. Their actions over a period of
several weeks result in depletion of follicular cellular stores of hormone and, ultimately, in
decreasing circulating concentrations of T3 and T4. This explains the delay of 2 to 4 weeks
before normalization of circulating TT4 concentrations.47 Since these drugs have no
cytotoxic action and do not prevent tumor growth, thyroid tumors usually continue to
grow, most slowly.43

Oral and Transdermal Anti-thyroid Drug Formulations

Carbimazole is considered a “pro-drug” as it is rapidly converted to methimazole after
administration. A slightly higher dose of carbimazole is required to gain the effect of
methimazole: 5 mg of carbimazole is equivalent to 3 mg of methimazole.48 In humans
(and presumably in cats), methimazole accumulates within the thyroid gland, explaining
why the biological half-life is longer than the serum half-life. Should methimazole
administration be discontinued, serum TT4 concentrations usually rise to pretreatment
values within 48 hours.
Transdermal formulations of methimazole or carbimazole are available in several
countries through compounding pharmacies (ch. 139). Transdermal application to the
inner pinna of the ear is an appealing alternative when medication is difficult to administer
orally, or when a cat exhibits GI side-effects to the oral formulation (see below). Quality
and stability of compounded transdermal formulations must be ensured. A pharmacy with
a history of high quality is important.

Methimazole Dose
The recommended initial dose of methimazole is 1.25 to 2.5 mg PO q12h. Euthyroidism is
usually attained a few weeks faster when starting with q12h administration.49 This could
be of particular importance in hyperthyroid cats with severe metabolic or cardiac
complications requiring rapid resolution of hyperthyroidism. In cats difficult to pill or for
owners reluctant to commit to a q12h dosing plan, 5 mg PO q24h can be used. If the cat is
severely hyperthyroid with extremely elevated TT4 concentrations, a higher dosage of 5 mg
PO q12h can be considered if pre-treatment renal function is normal.

Carbimazole Dose
A starting dosage for the registered “slow release” carbimazole tablets is 15 mg PO q24h.
One may choose 10 mg q24h if TT4 results are only mildly increased.

Transdermal Dose
Transdermal formulations have lower bioavailability and delayed efficacy (few weeks) as
compared with oral administration. Therefore, the initial TT4 recheck in cats treated with
transdermal medication is recommended around 4 weeks after initiation therapy.
Compared to oral therapy, a higher daily dose may be needed to restore euthyroidism.
Various dose regimens of transdermal methimazole (2.5 to 10 mg q12h) resulted in
normalization of TT4 concentrations in 7/8 hyperthyroid cats.50 In a randomized
controlled trial, 66% of 27 hyperthyroid cats given 2.5 mg q12h became euthyroid after 4
weeks.51 In another study, 5 mg q12h resulted in clinical improvement and normalization
of TT4 concentrations in 10 hyperthyroid cats.52 As noted above, owners must wear gloves
or finger cots (to avoid absorption through the owner’s skin). Since some cats treated with
transdermal medications develop crusting and erythema of their pinnae, owners should
alternate applications between ears and keep the ears clean, gently removing any crusty
material with cotton moistened with warm water about 30 minutes after each application.

Non–Life-Threatening Adverse Reactions to Anti-thyroid Drugs
(Table 287.4)
Anti-thyroid drugs can cause mild to life-threatening adverse reactions.48,53 The
occurrence, frequency, and severity of side effects to methimazole and carbimazole appear
independent of dose.49,54 Adverse reactions are typically observed within the first 4 to 8
weeks of therapy. The most common non–life-threatening side effects (up to 25% of cats)
are anorexia, vomiting, and lethargy, which are usually transient and do not necessitate
discontinuation of methimazole.47,48 Depending on severity, owners can continue
treatment for several days, since many cats develop a tolerance to the drug and the adverse
signs resolve spontaneously. If signs persist, a 50% dosage reduction for a few days is
recommended. If adverse signs continue despite reducing the dosage, the drugs should be
stopped until signs resolve, usually a few days. Sometimes adverse reactions persist or
recur regardless of dosage; in these cats, oral anti-thyroid drugs should be permanently
discontinued and another treatment chosen. Transdermal administration of methimazole
or carbimazole is associated with fewer GI side-effects than oral administration. The

incidence of other side-effects (e.g., facial excoriations) are similar for both oral and
transdermal formulations.
Mild hematological abnormalities (mild leukopenia, eosinophilia and lymphocytosis) are
common in methimazole- and carbimazole-treated cats, regardless of administration route
and usually do not require discontinuation of therapy. The CBC should be monitored every
2 weeks to assess for more worrisome developments. Facial and/or neck excoriations are
not life-threatening but are serious, and anti-thyroid drugs should be permanently stopped
(Figure 287.6).

Life-Threatening Adverse Reactions (Table 287.5)
A severe but uncommon adverse reaction to anti-thyroid drugs is a toxic hepatopathy,
often accompanied by icterus and marked increases in serum liver enzyme activities. Other
worrisome and severe adverse complications include marked neutropenia,
agranulocytosis, or thrombocytopenia (ch. 176).48,54 With suspicion of a serious
hepatopathy or blood dyscrasia, anti-thyroid drug administration should be discontinued
at once. With appropriate support, complete resolution of these conditions can be expected
within a few days (blood dyscrasias) to weeks (hepatopathy). If any of these severe, lifethreatening side-effects develops, anti-thyroid drugs can no longer be given.
In addition to thrombocytopenia, other bleeding tendencies (epistaxis, oral hemorrhage,
excessive hemorrhage during surgery) can rarely develop in methimazole-treated cats (ch.
171). One of the documented mechanisms is a drug-induced interference with synthesis of
vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X. This can cause prolongation of
prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), and proteins
induced by vitamin K absence or antagonists (PIVKA) clotting times (ch. 170).55 If a
hyperthyroid cat is initially proteinuric or if the cat becomes azotemic, monitoring the UA
is important. Proteinuria usually resolves with treatment.30,56 Anecdotally, adverse
reactions to carbimazole appear less common than to methimazole. However, carbimazole
has been studied in fewer cats, which could explain the slight differences. Since
carbimazole is metabolized to methimazole, similar adverse reactions are expected with
both anti-thyroid drugs. When adverse reactions follow administration of one, there is no
value in switching to the other.

Dosage Adjustments
The goal of anti-thyroid drug therapy is for the cat to have serum TT4 concentrations well
within reference intervals. If the TT4 is high-normal-to-improved but still increased after 2
to 4 weeks of treatment, if adverse reactions have not been observed, and if the PE reveals
no new problems, the dosage should be increased by 1.25 to 2.5 mg/day for methimazole
and 5 mg/day for carbimazole.14,48 Dosages should continue to be increased every 2 weeks
until the TT4 has decreased to the desired levels, until values are too low, or until adverse
reactions develop. Many clinicians monitor CBCs every 2 weeks during the first month or 6
weeks, but need for frequent monitoring has been questioned as severe hematological side
effects are uncommon and they can occur when testing is not scheduled.48 Although
seemingly prudent, monitoring CBCs is not cost effective and can be eliminated if there are
owner budgetary concerns. On days when blood is to be sampled for TT4, anti-thyroid
drugs must be administered as usual. Timing blood collection relative to anti-thyroid drug

administration is not important, since the thyroid-blocking effect of anti-thyroid drugs
lasts for over 12 hours.48

Overdose: Iatrogenic Hypothyroidism
One reason for monitoring the serum TT4 is to recognize and avoid iatrogenic
hypothyroidism, which can worsen renal function, lead to azotemia, and shorten survival
time.56 However, diagnosis of iatrogenic hypothyroidism is not always straightforward
(ch. 286). Hypothyroid cats may have signs of lethargy, poor appetite, weight gain, and
dermatologic issues, but slowed activity, decreased appetite, and weight gain are goals of
treating hyperthyroidism. Therefore a combination of decreased TT4 and an increased
serum TSH (currently with a canine kit) can be used to confirm a diagnosis of iatrogenic
hypothyroidism and the anti-thyroid drug dosage decreased by 25-50% (decrements of
1.25 to 2.5 mg/day). The TT4 and kidney values should be rechecked after 1 week.14,48,57

Beta-Blocking Agents
Beta-blocking agents (e.g., propranolol, atenolol) have no direct effect on thyroid gland
function or on circulating thyroid hormone concentrations. However, these drugs can
reduce polypnea and hyperexcitability. Beta-blocking agents can also be helpful when
managing hypertension (ch. 236), tachycardia (ch. 230), or arrhythmias related to the
hyperthyroidism (Table 287.6).

Angiotensin Converting Enzyme Inhibitors (ACE-i), Angiotensin
Receptor Blockers (ARBs), and Amlodipine
The reported prevalence of hypertension in hyperthyroid cats ranges from about 5% to
>20%. In some, hypertension resolves with treatment of hyperthyroidism, whereas other
cats develop hypertension after euthyroidism has been restored. Hence, measuring BP at
every visit is important.14,48 One benefit of repeated BP measurements is that cats become
accustomed to the procedure, providing more credible results (ch. 91).
Often, direct management of moderate to severe hypertension is indicated in
combination with anti-thyroid drug administration (ch. 236). Amlodipine is usually
chosen for moderate to severe hypertension. Although ACE-i or ARBs are not as effective
for moderate to severe hypertension, they can be useful when a renal-protective effect
(reducing intra-glomerular pressure) is desired in cats with persistent proteinuria after
resolution of hyperthyroidism.14,48,58

LOW-IODINE DIETS
Iodine is a necessary component of thyroid hormones. Strict chronic restriction of dietary
iodine will reduce thyroid hormone concentrations. Feeding a low-iodine commercial diet
has the advantages of being initially less expensive, easy, and requires no anesthesia,
surgery, or hospitalization (ch. 155). Drawbacks are a lack of palatability in ∼25% of cats,

the need for strict adherence to the diet with absolutely no access to other food and
understanding that sub-optimal control of the hyperthyroidism is common. Several studies
have shown some improvement in TT4 concentrations, but body weight and tachycardia
did not resolve. Serum TT4 decreases to reference intervals in only 55% and 72% of cats fed
the diet for 30-60 days and 60-90 days respectively.59-65 While iodine restricted diets
offer some advantages, they should only be recommended if other treatment options (131I,
thyroidectomy or anti-thyroid drugs) are not possible. Normal adult cats fed the limited
iodine diet for 2 years did not show obvious side-effects.66 As with pharmacologic therapy,
adequate monitoring is important. The clinician should not be satisfied with a cat that
improves somewhat but continues to have TT4 values at the upper end or above reference
intervals.
To maximize diet acceptance, a slow transition over at least 7 days is recommended. The
first recheck is recommended after 4 weeks of feeding the low-iodine diet exclusively.
Monitoring should be similar to that recommended for anti-thyroid drugs. In cats that are
not clearly euthyroid within 3 to 6 months of feeding the low-iodine diet, another
treatment should be advised. Giving anti-thyroid drugs and an iodine restricted diet is too
potent and is not recommended. The combination can induce a dramatic fall in TT4 to
severe and even life-threatening levels. Only in cats with longstanding and severe
hyperthyroidism, where definitive treatment is excluded and anti-thyroid drugs are
insufficient, can this combination be tried.

RADIOACTIVE IODINE (131I) THERAPY
Overview
131

I therapy is simple (one injection suffices), effective, and safe. It almost always results in
a permanent “cure” for hyperthyroid cats and is the treatment of choice, especially in
younger cats and in the absence of significant concurrent disease. Although the treatment
itself is simple and relatively cat-friendly (except for the hospitalization in isolation), it
does require specially licensed facilities, nuclear medicine equipment, and a need to
comply with government protective regulations. The mandatory length of hospitalization
(i.e., usually around 3-14 days) varies between countries and within countries.67 Once
returned to the owners, the cat will still excrete small amounts of 131I, especially in the
urine but also in feces and saliva, for 2 to 4 weeks. Owners must be well-instructed about
radioprotective measures.

Patient Selection and Preparation
Cats should be relatively stable before 131I treatment because their radioactivity restricts
diagnostic and therapeutic interventions for several weeks. Mainly because of waiting lists,
hyperthyroid cats are often pre-treated with anti-thyroid drugs. It is common to
recommend discontinuing anti-thyroid medication at least 1 week prior to therapy to allow
thyroid hormones to rise into the hyperthyroid range and suppress TSH concentrations.68
As TSH is needed for uptake of iodine by thyrocytes, suppressed TSH levels are thought to
help “protect” normal or atrophic thyroid cells.

Dosage
Cats are susceptible to iatrogenic hypothyroidism following 131I therapy. It is a challenge to
determine the dosage of 131I which will cure the disease without causing hypothyroidism.
With experience, radioiodine dose recommendations have progressively decreased.69,70
One group using low doses (<2 mCi) takes pretreatment TT4, thyroid size based on thyroid
scintigraphy, % pertechnetate uptake, and % 24-hour thyroid 131I uptake to determine an
individualized optimal dose.68,70 The scintigraphic scan prior to 131I treatment is not
mandatory but results may confirm a diagnosis in equivocal cases, identify ectopic thyroid
tissue, provide staging and prognostic information, and aid in individualizing the 131I
dose.68 Cats with suspected thyroid carcinoma or SHIM-RAD are given much higher
dosages of 131I. In these cats, the treatment goal is total ablation of all thyroid tissue which
usually leads to iatrogenic hypothyroidism.68,71

Adverse Reactions
Adverse reactions to radioiodine therapy, aside from iatrogenic hypothyroidism, are
extremely rare (<0.1%). Radiation thyroiditis can lead to transient dysphagia or fever
within the first few days after treatment and are self-limiting.72 A permanent voice change
is possible.73 Treating hyperthyroidism always impacts renal function. Monitoring for
post-treatment renal azotemia allows rapid implementation of management strategies.
Owners should notice gradual improvement and resolution of hyperthyroidism within the
first month. After treatment, besides clinical evaluations (body weight, BCS, MCS), TT4
and TSH should be monitored after 1, 3, 6 and 12 months. Thereafter, monitoring at least
once a year is recommended.

SURGERY (THYROIDECTOMY)
Preoperative Testing and Treatment
Experienced surgeons consider thyroidectomy to be relatively simple. Bilateral
thyroidectomy leads to permanent euthyroidism in >90% of cats.74,75 Most owners who
have both options for a permanent cure often choose the less invasive 131I. As general
anesthesia is required and since these are invariably older cats, a pre-anesthetic evaluation
is imperative to establish the cats’ current health status and to attempt identification of
any concurrent disease. Most are given anti-thyroid drugs for 2-4 weeks, until the morning
of surgery, allowing some or total resolution of the metabolic and cardiac consequences of
hyperthyroidism.

Scintigraphy and Post-operative Hypocalcemia
As noted above, preoperative scintigraphy offers identification of unilateral versus bilateral
disease as well as ectopic thyroid disease. It is extremely useful for selecting appropriate
surgical candidates and in choosing uni- versus bilateral thyroidectomy. As hypocalcemia
due to iatrogenic hypoparathyroidism is the most severe life-threatening complication
after a bilateral thyroidectomy, the surgery can be staged, with the second lobe removed
about 4 weeks after the first. The 4 weeks, theoretically, is time for parathyroid tissue

associated with the first surgery to revascularize or recover from surgical trauma. After a
bilateral thyroidectomy, circulating calcium (preferably ionized) should be monitored in
hospital q12h for 2 to 3 days. If hypocalcemia develops, treatment with calcium and
vitamin D supplementation is initiated. Hypocalcemia is nearly always transient (ch.
284).74

SURVIVAL AND SUCCESS RATES (TABLE 287.7)
Most cats with hyperthyroidism, when treated and monitored appropriately, have a good
prognosis (Table 287.7). However, if untreated (or undertreated), the disease can be
severely debilitating.14 Serum TT4 concentrations start declining within a week of
initiating pharmacological anti-thyroid drug treatment, but good clinical control usually
takes 2-6 weeks after biochemical euthyroidism is restored. Longer median survival times
are reported after 131I therapy as compared with results of anti-thyroid drug treatment.76
However, these results are likely biased, at least in part, since the most motivated owners
might be more inclined to choose 131I treatment. Further, the age at which cats are treated
with 131I is progressively becoming younger. Thus, they are being treated earlier than their
predecessors 20 to 30 years ago. In addition, progression of the disease and lack of
monitoring undoubtedly contributes to different survival statistics in cats treated with
anti-thyroid drugs versus 131I.

THE KIDNEYS AND HYPERTHYROIDISM
Renal function is profoundly influenced by thyroid status. Hyperthyroidism leads to
increased cardiac output, intra-renal vasodilatation, decreased muscle mass, increased
glomerular filtration rate, and a decline in serum creatinine.77,78 Hence, these may lead to
overestimating renal function. Thus, with effective treatment of hyperthyroidism, “decline”
of renal function is expected. It probably would be more appropriate to use the term
“normalization” of renal function after treatment of hyperthyroidism instead of “decline.”
The true impact on renal function can usually be fully assessed at least 3 months after
resolution of hyperthyroidism. Clinicians can be confronted with 2 different scenarios
concerning the presence or development of azotemia. In the first scenario, pre-existing
azotemic kidney disease is diagnosed in an untreated hyperthyroid cat and these cats have
a more guarded prognosis.48,79 In the second, azotemia only develops after treatment of
hyperthyroidism (the hyperthyroid cat was initially non-azotemic) and their prognosis is
similar to cats remaining non-azotemic after treatment of hyperthyroidism.80 Appropriate
management of CKD, following the International Renal Interest Society (IRIS) guidelines,
is important in both scenarios (ch. 301). There is no parameter, including the symmetric
dimethylarginine (SDMA), that allows one to predict the cats most likely to become
azotemic after resolution of hyperthyroidism.78,81-85 Cats developing post-treatment renal
azotemia carry a similar prognosis to that of cats not developing post-treatment azotemia.
Kidney parameters are unlikely to increase more than 1 IRIS stage.86 Nevertheless,
predicting cats most likely to develop serious kidney issues is difficult. Thus, clinicians
should inform the owners of the importance of managing CKD while also closely
monitoring cats for iatrogenic hypothyroidism.

CONCLUSION
Early detection is important. In most cats, diagnosis can be confirmed with an increase in
TT4 concentration. In middle-aged to senior cats, the presence of comorbidities is
common. Treatment with anti-thyroid drugs is the most commonly used medical
management (either short term or long term). 131I therapy is the treatment of choice in
many cats as it is noninvasive, permanent, and addresses the underlying disease. Adequate

monitoring of hyperthyroid cats is the key to success. While monitoring TT4 serum
concentrations is essential to detect under-treatment, overtreatment (iatrogenic
hypothyroidism) should be avoided too and warrants monitoring of T4 and TSH values.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Hyperthyroidism in Cats
Hyperthyroidism is a very common disease in the older cat. It is usually the result of a
benign tumor of one or both thyroid glands. This tumor secretes excessive thyroid
hormones, raising the cat’s metabolism to an unhealthy high level. That is why most cats
with hyperthyroidism lose weight despite continuing to eat well (or even very well). Typical
symptoms include, besides this weight loss, drinking and urinating more, a very good
appetite, hyperactivity and gastrointestinal complaints. But, by no means are all symptoms
present or equally pronounced in every cat.

DIAGNOSIS
The diagnosis is made on the basis of one or more symptoms of hyperthyroidism and a
blood test in which the thyroid hormone, thyroxine or T4, is increased. The disease is so
common in older cats that measurement of the thyroid hormones is often included in the
routine blood screening recommended in older cats. Only in exceptional cases is the
diagnosis more challenging and a specialist examination should take place.

TREATMENT
Once the diagnosis has been made, it is important to choose the ideal treatment option for
your cat. With appropriate treatment and adequate follow up, most cats can be treated
very well. There are several options available, each with its advantages and disadvantages.
It is always necessary to treat your cat as left untreated hyperthyroidism is a life
threatening disease.

Anti-thyroid Medication
This is a very effective treatment, which is often used. The medication is generally well
tolerated. A common side effect of a transient nature is the occurrence of gastrointestinal
symptoms. In addition, a number of rare, but serious side effects, may warrant
discontinuation of treatment. Depending on the country, the medication exists in the form
of tablets or syrup. An ointment is also available in some countries. This treatment needs
to be administered daily and lifelong (unless another treatment is planned).

Radioactive Iodine

The treatment is very effective and is definitive in 95% of cases. Radioactive iodine not
only suppresses the disease, but also targets the tumor (in contrast to iodine-deficient diet
and anti-thyroid medication, which do not). In most cases, no further medication needs to
be given after treatment. In rare cases a second treatment is needed or the thyroid gland
functions too slowly after this treatment. Precautions should be taken for several weeks
due to the presence of residual radioactivity. This is a very elegant treatment as it “only”
requires 1 injection. However due to the use of radioactive material your cat must be
hospitalized for a certain period (ranging from days to weeks depending where you live).
Radioactive iodine is also a potential treatment option if the thyroid cancer in your cat is
suspected to be malignant.

Surgery
The thyroid gland(s) can also be removed surgically. This may be an option if your cat will
not take or does not tolerate medication/food well, and if radioactive iodine is not an
option. Nowadays radioiodine treatment is usually preferred over surgery as it is less
stressful for the cat and usually does not require anesthesia. This can also be a good option
for large tumors with cyst formation. However, if both thyroid glands are removed, lifelong
supplementation with thyroid hormones is necessary. If the parathyroid glands cannot be
spared, lifelong supplementation with vitamin D and temporary calcium is also necessary.
In exceptional cases overactive thyroid tissue can again be observed in other places such as
the thoracic cavity (ectopic thyroid tissue).

Low Iodine Diet (Hill’s Y/D)
Through this diet, the thyroid gland will produce fewer hormones since the raw material
for this, iodine, is limited in the diet. However, it is very important that your cat eats only
this food (no snacks, table scraps, ...). This option is “easy” for you but some cats will not
eat this diet and not all cats will respond sufficiently to this option (they improve but are
still mildly hyperthyroid). Therefore monitoring is very important.

OTHER DISEASES
Some hyperthyroid cats are also facing other diseases; most often either kidney or cardiac
problems.

Kidney Problems
The function of the kidneys and thyroid go hand in hand. A fast thyroid can potentially
mask kidney problems. This can cause kidney disease to manifest itself when the thyroid
problem is treated. Because of this, it is always important to monitor kidney function along
with thyroid function.

Heart Problems
A fast acting thyroid gland can lead to a thickened heart muscle. This can have serious
consequences if the hyperthyroidism is left untreated. The effect of hyperthyroidism on the
heart can be completely reversible if the treatment is properly adjusted.

PROGNOSIS
The outlook is good for most cats with a benign tumor of one or both thyroid glands. Good
treatment options are also available for cats with a malignant tumor but these can be more

challenging. An individualized and optimal treatment and monitoring plan should be
designed for each hyperthyroid cat.
Sylvie Daminet (Ghent, Belgium)

Hyperthyroidism is an uncommon condition in dogs that almost always arises from a
functional, malignant, thyroid tumor that secretes excessive thyroid hormone.
Thyroid tumors are usually easily palpable cervical masses. Uncommonly, feeding
uncooked diets containing thyroid gland tissue may cause clinical hyperthyroidism.

PATHOGENESIS
NATURALLY OCCURRING THYROID CANCER
Thyroid cancer represents 1-4% of neoplasms in dogs and is their most common
neuroendocrine tumor. Canine thyroid tumors are usually malignant, with only 1030% benign adenomas.1 Adenomas, typically small and nonfunctional, are usually
not diagnosed until noted as an incidental necropsy finding, although 3 Boxer dogs
that presented for palpable cervical masses were subsequently found to have benign
thyroid cystadenomas.2 With increased use of cervical ultrasonography (US),
incidentally discovered thyroid masses have been noted more frequently.3 Size is not

a predictor of malignancy. Most clinically significant thyroid tumors are carcinomas,
either follicular cell or medullary cell in origin; the latter also are termed
parafollicular cell or C-cell carcinomas. About 70% of canine thyroid tumors are
follicular cell carcinomas that arise from thyroid follicular cells and stain for
thyroglobulin immunohistochemically. Medullary thyroid carcinomas, about 30% of
tumors, arise from parafollicular cells that produce calcitonin and stain for calcitonin
antibodies immunohistochemically.4,5 Functional thyroid adenomas resulting in
clinical hyperthyroidism have been rarely reported.6

IATROGENIC HYPERTHYROIDISM

Clinical signs of hyperthyroidism can be seen in dogs that have no primary thyroid
gland disease, although dogs seem resistant to exhibiting signs of hyperthyroidism.7
Iatrogenic hyperthyroidism may result when a dog is over supplemented with Lthyroxine treatment for hypothyroidism or when given raw foods containing thyroid
tissue. Reports have implicated raw food or dried uncooked diets that contain thyroid
tissue as a cause of thyrotoxicosis in dogs, especially beef-based diets.8 The dogs
described in these studies had clinical signs of hyperthyroidism that resolved when
the dogs were no longer given the suspect diets.

THE ROLE OF THYROID STIMULATING
HORMONE (TSH) IN TUMOR DEVELOPMENT
The etiology of canine thyroid carcinoma is unknown. In people, risk factors include
exposure to radiation and lack of dietary iodine intake. Individuals who lack dietary
iodine or who consume iodine-blocking foods have decreased pituitary negative
feedback and increased TSH secretion (ch. 285). Excess TSH directly stimulates
thyroid cell mitogenesis, hormone synthesis, and may be involved in thyroid
neoplastic transformation (Figure 288.1). Excess TSH activity can cause mutations
in the TSH receptor that can lead to benign toxic nodular goiter in humans. Increases
in TSH have also been shown to induce angiogenesis in thyroid cancer cell lines, a
process possibly relevant to thyroid tumor development in dogs.9 About 50% of
Beagles with induced untreated lymphocytic thyroiditis and increased TSH
concentrations developed thyroid tumors, with carcinomas being more common than
adenomas.10 Thus, chronic exposure to excess TSH can cause unregulated cell growth
and function in dogs. A familial relationship in the development of thyroid carcinoma
was also demonstrated in the colony of Beagles by sibling pair analysis.

GENETIC ETIOLOGIES OF TUMOR
DEVELOPMENT
Several genetic cell-signal-transduction protein abnormalities have been described as
causative agents for human thyroid carcinoma, including point mutations in the ras
gene and abnormalities in the PI3K/Akt pathway (Figure 288.1). These signal
transduction pathways are coupled to cell surface receptor tyrosine kinases and G
protein–coupled receptors such as the TSH receptor. In human follicular cell
carcinoma, abnormalities in the PI3K/Akt pathway have been implicated. Important
genes in this pathway are the vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGFs) VEGFR-1
and VEGFR-2. VEGF is a target for TSH activation of angiogenesis in thyroid cancer
cell lines.11 In 74 dogs with thyroid neoplasia, immunohistochemical staining
revealed VEGF in follicular cell and medullary carcinomas, supporting its role as an
angiogenic factor in development of thyroid carcinoma.12 As canine thyroid
carcinoma cells bind TSH in a normal fashion, this may explain the effect of chronic

excess TSH exposure contributing to the neoplastic transformation seen in the Beagle
colony dogs.10,13

Studies of genetic signaling molecular abnormalities in canine cancer cells have
been limited. Point mutations of p53, a tumor suppressor gene, were found in only 1
of 23 dogs with canine thyroid carcinoma.11 In 59 dogs with canine thyroid
carcinoma, mRNA expression of several genes in the PI3K/Akt pathway were greater
than those in normal canine thyroid tissue.14 In addition, missense mutations of KRAS that would cause unregulated activation were documented. Microarray analysis
comparing thyroid tumor versus normal thyroid gene expression in dogs identified
differential expressions of osteopontin, a protein overexpressed in human follicular
cell carcinomas and implicated in activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway. This was
found in all 5 dogs with thyroid tumors, but also in 4 euthyroid dogs.15 Molecular
abnormalities in mitogenic pathways are a likely component of canine thyroid
carcinoma pathogenesis. A recent study has identified expression of the components
of the Janus kinase (JAK)-signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT)
cellular signaling pathway in thyroid carcinomas, although relationship to metastasis
or etiology is unclear.16

SIGNALMENT
The mean age of dogs with thyroid carcinoma is about 9-11 years, with one study
suggesting a slightly older 10-15 years.1,17 There is no sex predilection. Breeds
possibly predisposed to thyroid carcinoma include Labrador Retrievers, Golden
Retrievers, Beagles, Boxers, Shetland Sheepdogs, and Siberian Huskies.1,17 Medullary
thyroid carcinoma in a family of mixed breed dogs with Alaskan Malamute influence
on the pedigree has been reported.18

HISTORY and PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
The most common owner concern in dogs ultimately diagnosed with thyroid
carcinoma is a cervical mass. Most diagnoses are made within 1 to 2 months after
recognition of such a mass; however, there may be delays of 1 to 2 years.19 On
palpation, thyroid masses are usually firm and nonpainful. They can be freely
movable or fixed. Mass “movability” is an important factor in tumor staging and for
predicting surgical success (Table 288.1). Tumors arise in the right and left thyroid
lobes in equal frequency. Less commonly, tumors are bilateral.20,21 Sedation may
improve one’s ability to fully palpate the area, but usually is not needed. Regional
peripheral lymph nodes should also be palpated carefully for increased size or pain.22
Ectopic thyroid carcinoma may be suspected if a non-painful swelling is noted in any
location from the base of the tongue to the base of the heart.23

Most thyroid carcinomas are nonfunctional, with clinical signs usually caused by
the space-occupying mass. Signs include difficulty swallowing (chs. 47, 259),
dysphonia, coughing (ch. 34), or upper-airway dyspnea (ch. 37). Some masses cause
head or forelimb edema.17,24 Lower-airway dyspnea can occur because of metastatic
tumor spread to the lungs. Thyroid carcinomas have been reported to invade major
blood vessels causing local or thoracic hemorrhage.25 Ectopic thyroid carcinomas
have been reported in the mediastinum (ch. 222), heart base (ch. 235), and
sublingually (ch. 258); therefore, clinical signs may relate to tumor size in these
areas or invasion into these tissues.26-28 Thyroid hormone status can vary in dogs
with thyroid carcinoma; approximately 10% are hyperthyroid.17,19 Hyperthyroid dogs
often show classic signs of vomiting, diarrhea, weight loss, hyperactivity, panting,
polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD), and systemic hypertension17 (Figure 288.2; ch.
287).

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Most dogs with thyroid carcinoma are brought to a veterinarian after an owner
recognizes a cervical mass. However, signs of hyperthyroidism may be the first
concern seen by some owners.17 In those dogs, a palpable cervical mass is usually
noted on physical examination. Differential diagnoses of a cervical mass include an
enlarged lymph node, salivary gland, granuloma, abscess, or foreign body. Thus, a
complete diagnostic work up should be pursued and further examination of the
cervical mass attempted.

DIAGNOSIS
LABORATORY TESTING
Serum biochemistry profiles may reveal paraneoplastic hypercalcemia (ch.
331).29,30 Urine specific gravity is often <1.020 if the dog is hypercalcemic and/or
hyperthyroid. To determine tumor function, serum total T4 (TT4), free T4 (fT4) by
equilibrium dialysis, and canine TSH (cTSH) concentrations should be evaluated.
Anti-T4 antibodies should also be assessed. If a functional thyroid tumor is present,

usually both TT4 and fT4 are increased. The cTSH should be decreased due to
negative feedback caused by the excess thyroid hormone (ch. 285). A complete
thyroid profile should include T3, which has been reported to cause functional
thyrotoxicosis in a dog.31

IMAGING
Radiology, Ultrasonography (US), Computed Tomography
(CT), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) Scans
Plain radiographs often confirm the presence of a soft-tissue mass deviating or
compressing the trachea, larynx, and/or esophagus. US is a rapid, noninvasive, and
reliable screening modality for identifying thyroid tumors and can provide additional
detail regarding vascularity and/or invasion of other structures (Figure 288.3).32
Clinicians should interpret US findings cautiously, however, as clinically insignificant
thyroid masses can be identified. Fourteen of 91 hypercalcemic dogs (15%) without a
palpable cervical mass had a total of 15 thyroid masses identified on US examination;
2 were thyroid adenocarcinomas and 13 masses were likely insignificant cysts or
benign nodules.3 CT can provide further information regarding the nature of thyroid
masses, especially invasion of surrounding tissues (Figure 288.4).23,33 In a study of
23 dogs with suspected thyroid carcinoma, CT had the highest specificity (100%) and
MRI had the highest sensitivity (93%) in diagnosing thyroid carcinoma.32 In a recent
study of 4520 dogs, 96 had unilateral or bilateral thyroid masses of which 82% were
malignant.34 CT also allows the lungs to be assessed for metastases. It is
recommended that CT or MRI be performed for tumor staging and prior to surgery.

Scintigraphy
Scintigraphy is an effective imaging modality to aid in the diagnosis and staging of
thyroid carcinoma. 99mTc-pertechnetate (99mTcO4) uses the relatively specific
sodium-iodide transporter present in thyroid and salivary glands. Since the
transporter protein is upregulated as thyroid gland activity increases, levels of
radionuclide uptake can be correlated with thyroid function. Therefore, scintigraphy
is sensitive for identifying some thyroid carcinomas and, potentially, ectopic and/or
metastatic tissue (Figures 288.5 and 288.6).27 The pattern of radionuclide uptake
does not correlate with tumor histology, but it can predict the degree of capsular
disruption and local tissue invasion.21,35 This information can be helpful in
predicting surgical resectability and long-term prognosis, as invasive thyroid
carcinomas carry a poorer prognosis.36 Scintigraphy is not sensitive in identifying
pulmonary metastases and is inferior to plain thoracic radiographs and CT for
staging. 21,35 123I may be superior to 99mTcO4 for scintigraphy since the target-tobackground ratio favors specific uptake by thyroid tissue. However, lower

radioactivity of the compound requires longer image acquisition times, so it may not
be practical.21

FINE-NEEDLE ASPIRATION (FNA) CYTOLOGY
Definitive diagnosis of thyroid adenoma or carcinoma requires histologic evaluation
of tissue. Identification of malignant cells in a cytologic or, preferably, a histologic
sample can be suggestive. While cytologic examination of FNA samples can be used
for definitive diagnosis of thyroid carcinoma in humans, its use for canine thyroid
carcinoma is less reliable (ch. 85). Since thyroid carcinomas are highly vascular,
samples obtained by FNA often contain few cells but large amounts of blood.
However, depending on owner or patient restrictions, FNA cytology can provide an
inexpensive and noninvasive means of diagnosis. US guidance is recommended for
FNA to avoid highly vascular areas.

HISTOLOGY
Histologic examination of the tumor is the gold standard for diagnosing thyroid
carcinoma. For small and noninvasive tumors, excisional biopsy may provide
diagnosis and be curative. Usually, canine thyroid tumors are moderately to welldifferentiated.1 Malignancy is defined by the presence of capsular or vascular
invasion. Unlike people, histologic subtype does not appear to carry prognostic
significance in dogs with well-differentiated thyroid tumors.19 Therefore, it is crucial
to determine the invasive qualities of the tumor for prognosis. Since thyroid tumors
are highly vascular, a hypothesis has been promoted that identifying microvessels is
prognostic. However, microvessel density was not shown to help predict metastasis
or survival.20 Immunohistochemical staining is essential for determining origin of
thyroid carcinomas.

STAGING
Canine thyroid tumors are staged based on the size of the primary tumor and whether
spread to regional lymph nodes or distant metastases is identified (Table 288.1).
Full staging of dogs with thyroid carcinoma is recommended so appropriate
treatment options and prognoses may be presented to the owners.

TREATMENT
SURGERY
Solitary Thyroid Masses
Surgical excision is recommended for the solitary, well-encapsulated, freely movable,
functional or nonfunctional thyroid carcinoma (Figure 288.2).24,37 Mass removal
not only reduces tumor burden but also may relieve compression of surrounding

tissues. Invasive nonmovable tumors are less amenable to surgical excision. Adjacent
structures invaded by thyroid tumors include the recurrent laryngeal nerves, carotid
artery, jugular vein, larynx, trachea, and/or esophagus. These structures could be
further damaged if surgical excision is attempted. Additionally, thyroid carcinomas
are highly vascular and extensive hemorrhage is commonly encountered, whether or
not the surgery is well-planned. Advanced imaging should be employed prior to
surgery to determine extent of invasion. Other potential complications of surgery
include hypocalcemia from removal of parathyroid glands or disruption of their blood
supply, although this is quite rare if a unilateral thyroidectomy is performed (chs.
69, 284). In a recent study of 156 dogs undergoing unilateral thyroidectomy the
complication rate was 19.9% and the perioperative mortality rate was 1.9%.38

Bilateral Thyroid Masses, Ectopic Thyroid Masses, and the
Parathyroid Glands
Bilateral thyroidectomy may be attempted in unusual cases in which discrete
movable carcinomas are present in both lobes. In these dogs, parathyroid glands
must be preserved by the surgeon or removed parathyroid tissue should be minced
and re-implanted in a location other than the neck.39,40 Most dogs undergoing
bilateral thyroidectomy require lifelong thyroid hormone replacement to manage the
iatrogenic hypothyroidism (Table 288.2). If no parathyroid tissue is preserved, dogs
can be successfully treated with long-term calcitriol therapy to correct
hypoparathyroidism (chs. 283 and 284). Long-term treatment of
hypoparathyroidism is difficult and should be avoided if possible. Median survival
time for dogs after unilateral or bilateral thyroidectomy is approximately 3 years.39
Removal of ectopic thyroid carcinoma is also recommended if possible. A surgical
technique has been described involving partial resection of the hyoid apparatus
during surgical excision of ectopic cervical thyroid carcinomas in 5 dogs, 4 of whom
survived at least 20 months after surgery.28

EXTERNAL BEAM RADIATION
Surgery is usually not a reasonable option for dogs with a “fixed” (non-movable)
thyroid tumor due to extensive local invasion. Radiation therapy should be
considered as either a primary therapy for local control or as a means for reducing
tumor size so that surgery may be a future option (ch. 318). External beam radiation
is most commonly used in dogs with thyroid carcinoma.20,41,42 In 25 dogs with non-

resectable thyroid carcinoma and no visible metastases, the mean progression-free
interval was 45 months after radiation therapy.20 The 1- and 3-year progression-free
survival rates were 80% and 72%, respectively. The time to maximal tumor reduction
was a highly variable 8 to 22 months. In 8 dogs, the median survival time was 24.5
months after radiation therapy; none had primary tumor regrowth, but 4 died from
metastatic disease.41 In a more recent study of 20 dogs in which stage IV disease was
overrepresented, the median survival time was 170 days, suggesting that more severe
disease may not respond as well.43
Acute side-effects of radiation therapy include inflammation of the esophagus,
trachea, or larynx resulting in dysphagia, cough, or hoarseness. Inflammation,
erythema, or alopecia of the skin over the radiation site occurs in about half of treated
dogs. Most signs resolve within 2 to 3 weeks. Late side-effects including permanent
alopecia, chronic dry cough, and skin fibrosis may occur.20 Hypothyroidism is a
common side effect and thyroid function should be monitored following
radiotherapy.44 Iatrogenic hypothyroidism readily responds to thyroid hormone
supplementation (ch.285). In dogs with metastatic disease, external beam radiation
therapy may provide palliation of the slow-growing primary tumor. A variety of
tumor-burden-reduction procedures can be beneficial. In 13 dogs with metastatic
disease receiving weekly fractionated radiation, tumor growth was halted in all dogs
and 10 of the tumors decreased in size by at least 50%.42 Median survival time was
approximately 8 months, including the dogs with previously identified pulmonary
metastases.

RADIONUCLIDE THERAPY
Radioiodine (131I) therapy is commonly used postoperatively in humans with thyroid
carcinoma. It is effective at delivering high dosages of beta-emitting radioactivity to
the thyroid gland and is used to destroy microscopic carcinoma tissue anywhere in
the body. Uptake of 131I is enhanced by treatment with TSH, usually given
immediately prior to 131I.131I has been shown to be taken up by thyroid carcinoma
cells, although at lower levels than by normal thyroid cells. 131I has been effective in
treating dogs with stage II to IV thyroid carcinoma.36,45 Direct comparison of studies
is difficult due to differing 131I dosing protocols, the absence or presence of
concurrent treatment with TSH, a variety of adjunctive therapies, and differing pretreatment hormone evaluations. However, in 100 dogs, median survival times ranged
from 12 to 34 months and were longest in dogs given 131I as an adjunct to
surgery.36,45,46 Effectiveness of 131I treatment was not correlated to thyroid status in
these studies. A serious side-effect of 131I therapy includes irreversible bone marrow
suppression, seen in dogs given doses ≥0.2 GBq/kg or 5.5 mCi/kg.45
Although 131I shows some promise in the treatment of thyroid carcinomas,
especially as an adjunct to surgery, handling large amounts of radioactivity and

providing appropriate isolation areas to house radioactive dogs remains problematic.
In humans, TSH is routinely given with 131I in order to decrease the dose of iodine.
The use of recombinant human TSH on the uptake of radioactive iodine in 9 dogs
with thyroid tumors was reported using the isotope 123I, with a shorter half-life than
131
I. TSH administration had no effect on thyroid 123I uptake in the 9 dogs.47

CHEMOTHERAPY
There are few studies on using chemotherapeutic agents for treating canine thyroid
carcinoma, probably because initial results were disappointing. Doxorubicin,
cisplatin, and mitoxantrone have been used in small numbers of dogs with thyroid
malignancy. Of these, cisplatin was demonstrated to have the greatest effect, with a
median survival of 11 months. The greatest effect of these drugs is likely against
microscopic metastatic disease. More recently, toceranib phosphate (Palladia) alone
and in addition to carboplatin have shown promise.48,49

SUPPORTIVE MEDICAL THERAPY
Approximately 10% of canine thyroid carcinomas secrete excess thyroid hormone,
causing classic signs of hyperthyroidism that include PU/PD, hyperactivity, weight
loss despite polyphagia, systemic hypertension, and tachycardia. Thyrotoxicosis
should be controlled before a dog undergoes anesthesia for advanced imaging or
surgery. Furthermore, the hyperthyroidism in dogs with nonresectable functional
thyroid tumors should be treated to enhance longevity and quality of life.
Hyperthyroidism can be managed with methimazole, similar to its use in cats (dosage
= 2.5 to 5 mg/dog PO q24h or q12h; ch. 287). Serum T4 should be monitored 1 to 2
weeks after starting therapy and suitable adjustments made. This treatment should
effectively control clinical signs with negligible side-effects. In hyperthyroid dogs
undergoing anesthesia or surgery, a beta-adrenergic blocker, such as atenolol, should
be considered the night before and the day of the procedure to prevent tachycardias
related to potential thyroid storm (Table 288.2).
Hyperthyroid dogs may have significant systemic hypertension (ch. 91). Although
removal of a functional thyroid tumor may return blood pressure to normal, systemic
hypertension should be managed in dogs with non-resectable tumors or in those with
functional metastatic thyroid carcinoma (ch. 236). Anti-hypertensives such as an
angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor and/or amlodipine may be used for
such patients. Paraneoplastic hypercalcemia may also occur in rare cases of thyroid
carcinoma (ch. 331).29 Calcium-lowering drugs such as pamidronate or alendronate
may be used to manage such cases if the tumor burden cannot be lowered (Table
288.2; chs. 283 and 284).

INTRODUCTION
“

Insulinoma” is a neoplasm of pancreatic beta cells that synthesizes
and secretes excessive quantities of insulin, often causing clinical
signs of hypoglycemia. It is an uncommon condition in dogs and rare
in cats. Insulinoma was first described in the dog in 1935 and in the
cat in 1974.1,2 Subsequently, approximately 360 canine cases have
been described as compared with merely 10 well-documented feline
cases. Consequently, this chapter will focus on canine insulinoma
and conclude with a short section on the comparative aspects of
feline insulinoma.

PATHOLOGY
THE PRIMARY TUMOR
Insulin-secreting pancreatic beta cells comprise approximately 70%
of the cells of the islets of Langerhans which, in turn, comprise only
1-2% of pancreatic volume. Most canine insulinomas are malignant.
In one report utilizing immunocytochemical staining, 17 of 18 were
carcinomas, 1 was an adenoma.3 About 80% of insulinomas are
solitary, located in either limb rather than the body of the pancreas
(Figure 289.1).4-6 Occasionally no discrete nodule is seen or
palpated during gross pancreatic examination because some of these
tumors are microscopic in size. In these, histologic examination is
required to locate the tumor within a section of surgically removed
pancreatic tissue or at necropsy.

METASTASES
The rate of detected metastatic lesions in dogs with insulinoma
ranges from 45-64%, higher in necropsy-based studies than those
using surgically-obtained samples.6-8 Clinical staging of pancreatic
tumors defines stage I as T1N0M0 (presence of a primary Tumor and
absence of regional lymph Node or distant Metastases), stage II as
T1N1M0, and stage III as T1N1M1 or T1N0M1 (ch. 316). A majority of
dogs with an insulinoma have stage II or III disease at diagnosis. The
most common sites of metastases are regional lymph nodes and
liver, but they have an unlimited distribution.9

GROWTH HORMONE INVOLVEMENT
The etiology of insulinoma is not known, but local growth hormone
(GH) production, not associated with changes in circulating
concentrations, has been documented in primary and metastatic
canine insulinoma. This GH is postulated to promote islet cell
proliferation via paracrine or autocrine mechanisms.10

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Neoplastic proliferation of pancreatic beta cells causes autonomous
and excessive secretion of insulin with resultant episodes of
hypoglycemia. The most important compensatory mechanisms for
hypoglycemia are inhibition of insulin secretion and concurrent
stimulation of counter-regulatory hormone secretion. Glucose is the
primary regulator of insulin secretion. Glucose enters beta cells and
is metabolized to adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which closes ATPsensitive K+ channels. Closure of these channels decreases K+ efflux,
causing build-up of K+ ions inside beta cells, resulting in their
depolarization and the opening of voltage-sensitive Ca2+ channels.
The inflow of Ca2+ through these opened channels increases
cytoplasmic Ca2+ which is the primary driver for the fusion of
insulin-containing vesicles with the cell membrane. Rupture of the
external cell membrane allows insulin exocytosis into the
extracellular environment and blood in equimolar amounts to Cpeptide (“connecting” peptide: the chain of amino acids cleaved from
within proinsulin’s single amino acid chain. Cleavage of C-peptide
from the chain simultaneously creates insulin: 2 amino acid chains
connected by 2 disulfide bridges). In healthy animals, insulin
secretion is completely inhibited when blood glucose is <80 mg/dL
(<4.4 mmol/L). In contrast, insulin secretion from neoplastic beta
cells often persists despite low blood glucose concentrations. The
biochemical hallmark of insulinoma is a normal or increased blood
insulin concentration despite concurrently low blood glucose
concentration. Interestingly, insulinomas are notorious for their
unpredictable but often excess response to feeding or glucose
administration. The four counter-regulatory hormones secreted in
response to hypoglycemia are glucagon, catecholamines, GH, and
glucocorticoids. Glucagon and catecholamines are most important in
the short-term response to hypoglycemia (ch. 298).

FIGURE 289.1 Solitary insulinoma surrounded by
pancreatic tissue. Courtesy Dr. Lillian Aronson.

CLINICAL FEATURES
SIGNALMENT
The mean age of dogs with insulinoma is 9 years, with a range of 3 to
15 years. Although any breed of dog can develop insulinoma, it
appears most common in medium- to large-breed dogs. Canine
breed risk and sex predilection for insulinoma have not been
established.

CLINICAL SIGNS
Neuroglycopenia and Counter-Regulation
Glucose is the most important source of energy for the brain. Brain
cell function is dependent on a continuous glucose supply because
the brain’s ability to store carbohydrate and utilize other fuels is
limited. Clinical signs of hypoglycemia usually result from its effects

on the central nervous system (neuroglycopenia), or to
hypoglycemia-induced counter-regulatory release of catecholamines.
Clinical signs attributable to neuroglycopenia include mental
dullness, disorientation (

Video 61.1), weakness, ataxia

(staggering as if drunk;

Video 61.2), visual disturbances (acting

blind), collapse and seizures (

Video 61.3). Clinical signs related

to catecholamine release and its stimulation of the sympathetic
nervous system include nervousness and hunger.
Severity of clinical signs is partly correlated to the blood glucose
nadir. Severe hypoglycemia can ultimately result in coma and death.
However, clinical signs may also be related to the duration and the
rate at which hypoglycemia develops. Gradual decreases in blood
glucose concentration are less potent stimulators of catecholamine
secretion. Insulin secretion from insulinomas and resulting clinical
signs are episodic. Secretion of counter-regulatory hormones
increase blood glucose concentrations and can transiently resolve
neuroglycopenic signs. Similarly, eating raises blood glucose and can
resolve signs. However, while feeding can transiently resolve signs of
hypoglycemia, that same feeding can in turn exacerbate a rebound in
clinical signs by stimulating further insulin secretion. Moreover,
fasting, exercise, or excitement can worsen clinical signs by
decreasing blood glucose concentration or increasing sympathetic
stimulation. The clinical signs of canine insulinoma are summarized
in Table 289.1. Although most dogs have more than one of these
clinical signs, some dogs have none. Some dogs may be overweight
due to the anabolic effects of insulin.

Post-ictal Changes and Paraneoplastic Weakness
Post-ictal changes may be apparent if there has been recent seizure
activity. A peripheral polyneuropathy (ch. 252) characterized by
hind limb paresis or tetraparesis and decreased or absent
appendicular reflexes has been described in 13 dogs with
insulinoma.9,11,12 The etiology of this insulinoma-associated
peripheral neuropathy has not been firmly established, yet it is most

likely a paraneoplastic immune-mediated disorder, unrelated to the
metabolic changes associated with insulinoma (ch. 331).11

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES
The differential diagnoses for confirmed hypoglycemia (ruling out a
spurious result or insulin administration to a diabetic dog) may be
classified into those caused by excess secretion of insulin or insulinlike factors, those caused by decreased glucose production, those
caused by excess glucose consumption, and those due to various
drug-associated scenarios (ch. 61). Disorders causing excess
secretion of insulin or insulin-like factors include insulinoma, extrapancreatic tumors (i.e., hepatic tumors) or beta cell hyperplasia
(nesidioblastosis). Conditions associated with decreased glucose
production, aside from the hypoglycemia occasionally diagnosed in
neonates and juvenile toy breeds, include liver insufficiency (ch.
266), hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296), hypopituitarism, GH
deficiency (chs. 280, 281), and glycogen storage diseases (ch.
244). Fasting, malnutrition, or pregnancy may cause hypoglycemia.
Excess glucose consumption may occur secondary to sepsis or
extreme exercise (especially in hunting dogs). Artefactual
hypoglycemia may occur when blood cells are not promptly
separated from serum or in animals with severe polycythemia or
leukocytosis (Figure 289.2).
