DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
MINIMUM DATABASE, SERUM GLUCOSE AND
INSULIN CONCENTRATIONS

Complete blood count (CBC), serum chemistry screen and urinalysis
are usually unremarkable in dogs with insulinoma, aside from
hypoglycemia.4,8 Mild hypokalemia and increased alkaline
phosphatase and/or alanine aminotransferase activities have been
documented in some.5,8 Clinical suspicion of insulinoma results
from the documentation of appropriate clinical signs, persistent
fasting hypoglycemia (blood glucose concentration <60 mg/dL [<3.3
mmol/L]), and concurrent normo- or hyperinsulinemia (serum
insulin concentrations within or above reference intervals).13
Although hypoglycemia is observed on randomly obtained blood
from most dogs with insulinoma, especially if repeated, it is
important to note that blood glucose concentrations do fluctuate,
explaining why some dogs are euglycemic when tested.8,14

FIGURE 289.2 An algorithm delineating a
diagnostic approach to hypoglycemia.

FIGURE 289.3 Abdominal ultrasonography of a
rounded hypoechoic insulinoma surrounded by
pancreatic tissue. Above the pancreas, the duodenum
is visualized. Courtesy Dr. Wilfried Mai.
When a dog suspected of insulinoma is euglycemic, fasting and
close monitoring for hypoglycemia can be considered. Blood glucose
concentrations are measured every 30 to 60 minutes. Point-of-care
analysers are adequate. In most dogs with insulinoma, hypoglycemia
(blood glucose <60 mg/dL [<3.3 mmol/L]) develops within 12 hours
of the previous meal. When hypoglycemia is documented, serum
from that sample should be assessed for its insulin concentration.
Rarely, a dog with an insulinoma does not exhibit hypoglycemia even
with repeated measurements or after a prolonged fast (48-72
hours).8 In such cases, reassessment of this diagnosis should be
considered. Low fructosamines have been used to strengthen clinical
suspicions of insulinoma.14 Glycosylated hemoglobin A1c
concentrations have been less sensitive.15 Repeated serum insulin
measurements may also aid in the diagnosis. In one study, 76% of

insulinoma dogs had increased serum insulin concentration when
measured once and 91% when measured twice.8
Other tests have been described for the diagnosis of insulinoma in
euglycemic dogs with normal serum insulin concentrations. Insulinto-glucose, glucose-to-insulin, and the “amended” insulin-to-glucose
ratios are not sensitive and not used. “Tolerance” and “stimulation”
tests have been described, but are not advocated because of
questionable usefulness, unnecessary complexity and/or potentially
fatal side-effects due to hypoglycemia.

IMAGING
Radiographs and Ultrasonography (US)
Identification of a pancreatic mass with imaging studies strengthens
the suspicion of insulinoma, but the diagnosis can only be confirmed
histologically or after immunohistochemical staining of pancreatic
tissue. Most dogs with insulinoma have unremarkable abdominal
and thoracic radiographs.4,7,9,16 When combining results of studies
in which abdominal US was performed, 49 of 87 (56%) dogs had a
pancreatic mass identified and abdominal metastases were identified
in 17 (19%).5,6,9,16 While abdominal US may be helpful in supporting
clinical suspicion of a pancreatic mass and metastases, both falsepositive and false-negative results have been described (Figure
289.3). Contrast-enhanced US successfully discriminated
insulinoma from pancreatic carcinoma.17,18

Advanced Imaging
High-quality, dual-phase, thin-section multidetector computed
tomography (CT) of the pancreas is effective in identifying a
pancreatic mass in most people with an insulinoma.19 In people,
intraoperative, intra-duct US is more sensitive than CT in detecting
small (≤3 mm diameter) insulinomas.19 Use of CT has been reported
in a small number of dogs with insulinoma, but its sensitivity has yet
to be determined.20-22 One study compared results from 14 dogs
with an insulinoma imaged with US, CT, and single-photon emission

CT. The CT scan results were most sensitive: 10/14 identified
(71%).22
In another study, each of 3 dogs with insulinoma had a mass
detected with dual-phase CT angiography (CTA), 2 of whom did not
have a pancreatic mass detected on US.21 Two of these dogs had
strong insulinoma enhancement identified during the arterial phase
of the study only, underscoring the value of dual-phase CTA (Figure
289.4, A-C).21 Intravenous (IV) administration of radioactively
labelled synthetic somatostatin, followed by whole-body
scintigraphy, is of limited value in visualizing insulinomas in people,
likely because the number of somatostatin receptors expressed in
human insulinomas is low.19 Somatostatin-receptor-scintigraphy has
been reported in a small number of dogs with insulinoma.23,24
Abnormal foci of activity were observed 1 to 24 hours after
administration of the radioligand, but accurate localization of the
tumor was achieved in only 1 of 5 dogs.23

TREATMENT
ACUTE HYPOGLYCEMIA AT HOME
Many owners learn to recognize signs of impending severe
hypoglycemia and treat their dog at home. It is rare for an owner to
have time to bring their dog to a veterinary hospital once signs are
observed. Some seizures occur without warning. When possible, the
dog should be fed a small meal that does not contain sugar (ch. 155).
If the dog does not eat or if severity of signs precludes feeding, the
owner should be instructed to pour a sugar-containing solution (e.g.,
Karo syrup) onto their fingers and then rub that syrup inside the lips
and onto the outer gums of the dog. In most dogs, signs resolve
within seconds to a minute. Owners should NEVER put their hand
inside the dog’s mouth, where they could be inadvertently bitten.
Owners should NEVER pour a sugar solution down the dog’s throat,
as aspiration is likely. Owners can be taught to partially fill a 6-cc
syringe with syrup. Using the syringe to slowly drip syrup onto the
gums and inner lips is easier to control, safer, and less messy. After

giving oral sugar, feeding a small meal upon recovery is essential to
avoid rebound hypoglycemia.

ACUTE HYPOGLYCEMIA IN-HOSPITAL
During an acute in-hospital hypoglycemic crisis, 50% dextrose
should be given as a slow IV bolus (0.5 g/kg IV, diluted at a ratio of
1:3 in 0.9% sodium chloride to avoid phlebitis). The bolus is followed
by an IV continuous rate infusion (CRI) of 2.5-5% dextrose, using the
lowest amount of glucose needed, remembering that glucose
unpredictably stimulates insulin secretion from insulinomas, which
can cause rebound hypoglycemia and a subsequent vicious cycle that
may be difficult to break. For this reason, dextrose administration
should be discontinued when clinical signs resolve, even if mild
hypoglycemia persists. In most dogs, neuroglycopenia will resolve
quickly with IV dextrose.
If a dog fails to respond to dextrose administration alone,
dexamethasone (0.1 mg/kg IV q12h) and/or a somatostatin analogue
(10 to 50 mcg SQ q8-12h) may be administered. The anti-insulin
gluconeogenic effects of dexamethasone can be beneficial for 6 hours
or longer. Dogs with severe hypoglycemia and seizures should be
sedated with diazepam or pentobarbital for several hours. Prolonged
seizures may induce cerebral hypoxia that may lead to cerebral
edema (chs. 125, 246). If suspected, edema can be treated with
mannitol (1 g/kg IV given as a 20% solution at 2 mL/kg/h) and
furosemide (1 to 2 mg/kg IV q4h).25 A CRI of glucagon (5 to 13
ng/kg/min with or without concurrent 10% dextrose) can be given.
In 1 dog with insulinoma-associated hypoglycemia, clinical signs
resolved within 20 minutes and hypoglycemia resolved within an
hour of starting a glucagon CRI. Glucagon increases blood glucose
concentrations by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis,
but it also stimulates insulin secretion. Dogs so-treated require close
monitoring for worsening or rebound hypoglycemia.26

LONG-TERM CARE
Surgery
The long-term treatment of choice for insulinoma is surgical
resection of both the tumor and any obvious metastases.5 If
metastases are identified ahead of surgery, surgery may not be
efficacious. Most primary tumors are readily discernible or palpable
by the surgeon. Two dogs have reportedly undergone successful
resection of tumor thrombi that had extended into the pancreaticoduodenal veins.27 One dog had a prolonged disease free interval after
primary tumor resection, despite presence of metastases.28 Surgical
exploration and biopsy of a pancreatic mass can confirm a diagnosis
and may help in estimating survival time.29 When postoperative
hyperglycemia develops, it is usually transient and resolves once the

normal beta cells, which have been suppressed by autonomous
insulin secretion from neoplastic cells, regain function. About 10% of
dogs with insulinoma develop diabetes mellitus after tumor removal
and require exogenous insulin for an unpredictable length of time (1
to 37 months).7,8,29 Other postoperative complications include
pancreatitis, diabetic ketoacidosis, delayed wound healing, cardiac
arrhythmias or arrest, hemorrhage, sepsis, and leukopenia.5,6,8

Medical Therapy
Overview
Medical treatment is indicated until surgery can be scheduled,
postoperatively if needed, and in dogs in which surgery is not
performed. Medical therapy can be divided into cytotoxic treatment
directed at destroying insulin-secreting beta cells and treatment
aimed at relieving frequency and severity of hypoglycemic attacks.

Cytotoxic Therapy
Streptozocin, a nitrosourea antibiotic, selectively destroys beta cells
in pancreatic or metastatic locations. The drug is nephrotoxic in
dogs, but diuresis with saline decreases drug contact time with renal
tubular epithelial cells and may reduce nephrotoxicity. In one study,
17 dogs, most of whom had surgery with incomplete resection of
gross lesions, were treated with 0.9% sodium chloride (18 mL/kg/h
IV) for 3 hours prior to, 2 hours during, and 2 hours following
streptozocin infusion (500 mg/m2 given every 3 weeks for a total of 5
treatments). Butorphanol (0.4 mg/kg IM) was administered
immediately following streptozocin therapy as an antiemetic but
vomiting was still observed in approximately one-third of
treatments. Other side effects included diabetes mellitus; transient
hypoglycemia and seizures; transient hyperglycemia; transient
increase in alanine aminotransferase activity; azotemia; mild
thrombocytopenia; or mild neutropenia. Median duration of
normoglycemia in streptozocin-treated dogs was 163 days, not
significantly different than dogs treated surgically or medically.9 In a
subsequent study, the same protocol was used but at an intensified

2-week interval in 19 dogs. The median progression time was similar
(196 days), 8/19 dogs developed diabetes mellitus, and 2/19
exhibited nephrotoxicosis.30 Further studies are necessary before
streptozocin therapy can be recommended.

Diet
The main modes of relieving hypoglycemia include dietary
modification and treatment with prednisone, diazoxide or synthetic
somatostatin. Small, frequent meals (every 4 to 6 hours) of a diet
high in proteins, fats, and complex carbohydrates are recommended
(ch. 155). Feeding simple sugars (e.g., soft moist dog foods) MUST
be avoided.

Prednisone
The least expensive and most commonly used drug, prednisone
increases blood glucose concentrations via gluconeogenesis and
glucose 6-phosphatase activity while decreasing blood glucose
uptake into tissues and stimulating glucagon secretion.
Glucocorticoids in the form of dexamethasone can be administered
IV during an acute hypoglycemic crisis. Oral prednisone is preferred
when a dog is stable, given at an initial dose of about 0.5 mg/kg/d.
Try to begin with as low a dose as needed, since more is invariably
required until it is no longer beneficial in decreasing hypoglycemic
episodes or intolerable signs of iatrogenic hyperadrenocorticism
(polyuria/polydipsia [PU/PD]) develop and doses must be
curtailed.13,25

Diazoxide
Diazoxide is a benzothiadiazine derivative whose main action is to
inhibit closure of pancreatic beta cell ATP-dependent K+ channels
preventing cell depolarization and inhibiting opening of voltagedependent Ca2+ channels. Decreased Ca2+ influx causes decreased
exocytosis of insulin-containing secretory vesicles. Diazoxide also
increases blood glucose concentration by increasing glycogenolysis
and gluconeogenesis and by inhibiting cell uptake of glucose.31
About 70% of dogs respond to doses of 10-40 mg/kg/day PO divided

q8-12h. As with prednisone, initial doses of diazoxide should be as
low as possible, gradually increased as required.8 Side effects
(ptyalism, vomiting, anorexia) are uncommon.

Octreotide
Octreotide, a long-acting synthetic somatostatin analogue, primarily
inhibits insulin secretion through its binding affinity to any of five
somatostatin receptor subtypes present in insulin-secreting tumors.
Dogs show a variable response to octreotide, likely because
octreotide variably inhibits glucagon and GH secretion.32 If the
suppression of glucagon and GH secretion is of greater magnitude
and duration than octreotide’s suppressive effects on insulin
secretion, octreotide may worsen hypoglycemia. Some canine
insulinomas may lack somatostatin receptors. A single 50 mcg/dog
SQ octreotide dose given to 12 insulinoma dogs (median weight 23
kg) decreased plasma insulin concentrations, yet concentrations of
glucagon, GH, and adrenocorticotropic hormone remained
unchanged.33 No adverse side-effects were reported with the use of
octreotide. Side-effects in people include mild pain at the injection
site (which is lessened if the preparation is warmed before
administration), nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, or
steatorrhea. Further studies in dogs are warranted.

PROGNOSIS
Median survival time of 142 dogs that underwent partial
pancreatectomy, reported in different studies, was 12 to 14 months
with a range of 0 days to 5 years.4-6,8,29 Dogs with clinical stage I
disease have a significantly longer disease-free interval and
approximately 50% are expected to be normoglycemic 14 months
postoperatively, compared to only 20% of dogs in clinical stage II or
III.7 Young dogs and those with persistent postoperative
hypoglycemia have a poorer prognosis.7 In contrast, dogs with
postoperative hyperglycemia or normoglycemia have a significantly
better prognosis.6

One study reported a median survival time of 785 days in 19 dogs
with insulinoma that underwent partial pancreatectomy, which
improved to 1316 days in the subgroup of dogs that also received
prednisone.34 These survival times are most likely attributable to
earlier detection, more radical tumor resection protocols, and
continued medical therapy following relapse. Tumor size and mitotic
rates, as depicted by the Ki67 index (a proliferation marker), can
provide prognostic markers.35 This was followed by a tissue
microarray immunohistochemistry study which corroborated the
findings in 32 insulinoma samples. Multivariate analysis showed that
tumor size and Ki67 index retained predictive power for survival
time, as did tumor size for disease free interval.36 Conversely, age,
sex, body weight, clinical signs and their duration, US detection of
pancreatic mass, tumor location, gross presence of metastatic
disease, and blood glucose or insulin concentration have not been
significantly associated with prognosis.

FELINE INSULIN-SECRETING ISLET
CELL NEOPLASIA
To date, 16 cats with pancreatic islet cell tumors have appeared in the
English literature; 10 had detailed signalment, clinical, biochemical
and/or histopathological descriptions.37-46 The 6 cats described in
limited detail include the first cat in the literature, included in a
pathology survey.2 Two cats were described in a textbook chapter,25
2 cats had their tissues used for immunohistochemical staining,47
and 1 cat had tissue used for gene expression.48 Of the welldescribed 10 cases, 3 were Siamese, 4 Domestic Shorthaired, 2
Domestic Longhaired, and 1 Maine Coon cat(s). The cats were 9 to 17
years of age. There were 8 males and 2 females. One of these 10 cats
had an insulinoma as part of a “multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1”
syndrome that included an adrenocortical adenoma and a
parathyroid adenoma. Resection of all 3 functional masses resulted
in full clinical recovery and the cat was reported to be free of clinical
signs 6 months postoperatively.42 Six cats mentioned in the non-

English literature were referred to as “pancreatic islet cell tumors,”
but not documented as being “functional” and can thus not be
assumed to have been insulin secreting.49-54
Clinical signs associated with insulinoma are wide-ranging and
depend on the severity of the hypoglycemia and other concomitant
disorders and include: anorexia, weight loss, episodic
weakness/falling, mental dullness, lethargy, hypothermia,
bradycardia, limb and facial twitching, and seizures.
As in the dog, diagnosis of insulinoma is made by documenting
hypoglycemia in concert with inappropriately normal or elevated
serum insulin concentrations. In the first 3 cats described, 1 mass
was identified on abdominal US and 2 at exploratory laparotomy.40
In 10 cats described later, a mass was in the left pancreatic lobe of 6,
the right lobe in 3, and the angle of the pancreas in 1. Tumor size
varied (0.4 to 3 cm). More recently, a pancreatic mass was identified
on US in 3.44-46
Prompt surgical extirpation is the mainstay of treatment. Cats
should be monitored for transient post-operative diabetes mellitus,
secondary to suppressed insulin secretion from remaining atrophied
pancreatic beta cells.39 If surgery is declined, small frequent meals
and oral prednisolone therapy (0.5 mg/kg q12h) are recommended
(ch. 155). Glucocorticoids increase hepatic gluconeogenesis and
glycogenolysis and reduce tissue utilization of glucose. Prognosis
depends on stage at time of diagnosis, malignant nature of the mass,
and success of surgical excision. Enhanced glucose sensitivity and
insulin secretion, through the overexpression of glucokinase 1 by
neoplastic beta cells might also explain the varying prognosis.48
Earlier cats had survival times as short as 1 day to approximately 18
months, yet 2 later cats were alive 32 months post-surgery.43,44

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and the “hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state” (HHS) are two acute, severe,
potentially life-threatening complications of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (DM). Their clinical signs
overlap. Morbidity and mortality are usually a consequence of the underlying precipitating cause or the
result of complications derived from lack of therapy or improper therapy and monitoring rather than a
result of hyperglycemia. Prompt diagnosis, use of standardized treatment protocols respecting the
unpredictable nature of these conditions and responses to treatment, and the ability to resolve or
manage the underlying cause, affect outcome.

DEFINITIONS
DKA is defined by the triad of hyperglycemia (or previous diagnosis of DM), metabolic acidosis, and
ketonemia. The term HHS has been recommended by the American Diabetes Association for the
syndrome characterized by severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and dehydration in the absence of
significant ketosis. Compared to previously used nomenclatures (hyperosmolar coma, hyperosmolar

non-ketotic syndrome), this new title emphasizes that not all patients are comatose and that mild
degrees of ketosis and acidemia may be present.1,2 Although there are important differences in their
pathogenesis, both DKA and HHS result from a decrease in the net effective action of circulating insulin,
due to an absolute or relative insulin deficiency complicated by increases in circulating concentrations of
counterregulatory stress hormones: glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, and growth hormone (Figure
290.1).3-5

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS
A State of Starvation
Insulin, a peptide hormone produced by beta cells within the pancreatic islets, allows blood glucose (BG)
to be transported from the blood into cells throughout the body, fueling metabolic processes. Insulin
deficiency dramatically reduces glucose availability for cells and creates a physiologic state of
“starvation.” Without glucose, the body must utilize its alternative energy source: ketone bodies (KBs).
These include beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), acetoacetate (AcAc), and acetone. KBs are molecules
deriving from oxidation of nonesterified or free fatty acids (FFAs) by hepatic mitochondria. Their
synthesis is regulated by the amount of FFAs mobilized from adipose tissue and the shift in hepatic
metabolism from fat synthesis to fat oxidation and ketogenesis.6,7 Since insulin is a potent inhibitor of
lipolysis and FFA oxidation,8 its deficiency “permits” increased activity of hormone sensitive lipase in
adipocytes that increases the availability of FFAs for ketogenesis (Figure 290.1).

Consequences of Ketone Excesses
In short-term starvation, KBs provide an energy source for cells that can be lifesaving until food
becomes available. In DM, hyperketonemia (and hyperglycemia) becomes deleterious, leading to
acidemia, water loss, electrolyte depletion, and hypotension; a self-sustaining vicious circle responsible
for the clinical manifestations of DKA. During hepatic ketogenesis, the number of hydrogen ions
equivalent to the number of KBs synthesized are released into the bloodstream. When the concentration
of hydrogen ions overwhelms the body’s buffering system, metabolic acidosis develops, causing nausea,
vomiting, inappetence. When plasma BG and KB concentrations exceed the renal tubular threshold for
complete reabsorption, they spill into urine and induce an osmotic diuresis. Therefore, the anionic
charge on the KBs obligates the excretion of positively charged ions (e.g., sodium [Na], potassium [K],
calcium [Ca], and magnesium [Mg]) to maintain electrical neutrality (chs. 67-69). Chloride (Cl) and
phosphorus (PO4) are also lost. This process invariably predisposes to electrolyte and water depletion,
exacerbated by vomiting, diarrhea, and the inability to drink and retain water as the metabolic acidosis
worsens.

Counter-Regulatory Hormone Excess
Insulin deficiency is not the sole physiologic cause for development of DKA. Some pets with DKA are
insulin-treated diabetics with serum insulin concentrations within reference ranges when DKA develops,
although inappropriately low for the severity of hyperglycemia.9 Some pets newly diagnosed with DM
and DKA have “some” endogenous insulin. These pets have a “relative” insulin deficiency. They are likely
to have a small number of functioning beta cells. Insulin resistance (impaired sensitivity to insulin) is
caused and worsened by increases in circulating glucose-counterregulatory hormones: glucagon,
catecholamines, cortisol, and growth hormone.10,11 These hormones are produced as a defense
mechanism in a wide variety of diseases or stressful conditions (e.g., starvation, pancreatitis, infection).
However, their activity as insulin antagonists has the effect of worsening the hyperglycemia and
ketonemia in DM (ch. 224). Concurrent diseases can trigger or coexist with DKA and can contribute
clinical issues that alter both prognosis and treatment strategies; therefore, their recognition and
treatment is essential for achieving therapeutic success. Absolute or relative insulin deficiency together
with excess glucose counter-regulatory hormones also stimulate hepatic glycogenolysis and protein
catabolism providing substrate for gluconeogenesis.12 Increased glucose and KB production together
with their reduced peripheral utilization lead to accumulations of both in the blood. Most of the glucose
in severely hyperglycemic pets with DM is derived from the liver, not from diet.

FIGURE 290.1 Pathogenesis of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and
hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS). Both DKA and HHS result from an
insulin deficiency together with an increase in glucose counterregulatory
hormones (i.e., glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, and growth hormone). In
HHS, the presence of a small amount of insulin is able to inhibit the activity of
hormone sensitive lipase in adipocytes, thus decreasing the availability of free
fatty acids (FFAs) for ketogenesis and preventing metabolic acidosis and
systemic clinical manifestations. Hyperglycemia and hyperosmolarity
progressively worsen as a result of increased gluconeogenesis, accelerated
glycogenolysis, and inadequate utilization of blood glucose by peripheral tissues.
On the contrary, in DKA, the absolute insulin deficiency does not allow the
inhibition of hormone sensitive lipase and FFAs are mobilized by the adipocytes,
reach the liver and are used for ketogenesis. The synthesis of ketone bodies is
associated with the release of hydrogen ions in the bloodstream, resulting in
metabolic acidosis and associated systemic clinical signs. Adapted from French
EK, Donihi AC, Korytkowski MT. Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar
hyperglycemic syndrome: review of acute decompensated diabetes in adult
patients. BMJ. 2019;365:1114.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF HYPEROSMOLAR HYPERGLYCEMIC
STATE
The pathogenesis of HHS and DKA are similar. The lack of ketosis is usually explained by these patients
having a small amount of insulin to inhibit lipolysis but not enough insulin to prevent hyperglycemia.13
Hyperglycemia is due to increased gluconeogenesis, accelerated glycogenolysis, and inadequate use of
BG by peripheral tissues (Figure 290.1). Hyperglycemia together with hypernatremia can severely
increase plasma osmolality, resulting in an osmotic gradient that draws water out of cerebral cells and
contributes to progressive alterations in consciousness. Rapid correction of dehydration can cause water
to flow into cerebral cells leading to cerebral edema. Glomerular filtration is initially increased in HHS,
and the resulting glucosuria and osmotic diuresis prevent development of severe hyperglycemia. As
plasma volume contracts, glomerular filtration is impaired, limiting renal glucose excretion and
contributing to worsening hyperglycemia. The higher circulating ratio of insulin/glucagon in patients
with HHS, compared to patients with DKA, is consistent with little to no KB synthesis.14 Reduced renal

function, impaired renal glucose excretion, and low or undetectable concentrations of KBs slow
development of overt clinical signs. This prolongs the course of the disease and may explain why
hyperglycemia is generally more severe in HHS than in DKA. Concomitant diseases, especially those that
most compromise the ability to maintain adequate water intake (e.g., kidney failure, congestive heart
failure [CHF], pancreatitis, pulmonary disease, infection), contribute to progressive deterioration and
negatively affect prognosis.

SIGNALMENT, HISTORY AND PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
DKA and HHS occur most frequently in dogs and cats with undiagnosed DM, but either condition can
occur in insulin-treated DM pets. The latter group may have issues related to the insulin treatment
regimen (inadequate dosage, errors in the administration or storage procedure) and/or development of
another disorder causing insulin resistance (e.g., infectious, inflammatory, hormonal, cancers). The
signalment of pets with DKA and HHS is similar to that of pets with uncomplicated DM: middle-aged
and older dogs and cats without breed predisposition, most common in female dogs and male cats. The
history for pets with DKA can range from the classic polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD), polyphagia and
weight loss (sometimes unnoticed or considered insignificant by the owner), to the more worrisome
systemic signs of severe lethargy, anorexia, and vomiting. Severity of signs correlate with degree of
metabolic acidosis, hyperosmolality, dehydration, and the concurrent disorder. Physical examination
(PE; ch. 3) is used to assess mental status, strength, hydration, cardiac function, and respiratory status.
Sometimes slow deep breathing (i.e., Kussmaul respiration) with a strong odor of acetone on the breath
is noted.
Thorough history and PE considered in the context of laboratory and other diagnostic test results can
often help identify concurrent disorders. Successful management of concurrent conditions while treating
the DKA improves likelihood of therapeutic success. In dogs, the most common concurrent disorders
include acute pancreatitis (ch. 277) and bacterial pneumonia (ch. 217).15 In cats, common concurrent
diagnoses include acute pancreatitis (ch. 278), hepatic lipidosis (ch. 274), cholangiohepatitis (chs. 271,
272), urinary tract infection (UTI, ch. 307), acute kidney injury (AKI, ch. 300) and chronic kidney
disease (CKD, ch. 301).16,17
The history and PE in pets with HHS commonly reveal anorexia or inappetence, lethargy, vomiting,
PU/PD, behavioral changes, diarrhea, severe dehydration, abnormal mentation (dull, depressed
mentation, coma), and respiratory abnormalities.18,19 The most common concurrent diseases diagnosed
in dogs with HHS are UTI (ch. 307), acute pancreatitis (ch. 277), and hyperadrenocorticism (ch.
293)19; in cats they include CKD (ch. 301), infection, CHF (ch. 229), neoplasia (chs. 322-330), and
gastrointestinal disease (chs. 261-264).18

DIAGNOSIS
DEFINITIONS of DKA AND HHS
Although the diagnosis of DKA and HHS can be suspected clinically, confirmation requires laboratory
tests. Recently, the European Society for Veterinary Endocrinology (ESVE) established the Project
ALIVE (Agreeing Language in Veterinary Endocrinology) to clarify terminology and definitions used in
veterinary endocrine diseases. Their diagnostic criteria for DKA included (i) diagnosis of DM according
to ALIVE criteria; (ii) ketonemia: increased BHB concentrations, ketonuria, and/or detectable AcAc
(using nitroprusside test strips); (iii) metabolic acidosis defined as a venous/arterial blood pH <7.35 and
decreased bicarbonate. If blood gas analysis is unavailable, an ill pet whose condition meets the above
criteria should be suspected of suffering from DKA.
Diagnostic criteria for HHS have not been uniformly defined and vary slightly in the literature.
Usually, criteria for HHS include severe hyperglycemia (BG >600 mg/dL; >34 mmol/L), serum
osmolality >325-330 mOsm/kg in dogs19,20 and >330-350 mOsm/kg in cats,18,20,21 dehydration, and
absence of significant ketoacidosis.

IDENTIFYING KETONE BODIES

Recognition of KBs in urine is the basis of diagnosing DKA in most pets. Ketone test squares are
included in routine urine reagent strips. Less commonly, plasma can be checked for KBs.22,23 This test,
using the nitroprusside reaction, provides a semiquantitative estimation of AcAc and acetone
concentrations. It does not detect BHB, the predominant KB produced during DKA.24 Thus, urine and
blood results may underestimate the degree of ketosis. Direct measurement of blood BHB using a
quantitative enzymatic assay or portable blood ketometers is available and provides an accurate
indication of ketoacidosis.25-31

TEST RESULTS REQUIRED FOR DKA MANAGEMENT
Results of blood gas analysis, complete blood count (CBC), serum biochemistry panel that includes
electrolyte concentrations, and urinalysis (UA) are required to understand patient status and to identify
issues that need to be monitored or treated. Other tests (e.g., urine culture, thoracic radiographs,
abdominal ultrasound, serum pancreatic-specific lipase, antigen testing for feline leukemia virus, and
antibody testing for feline immunodeficiency virus in cats) may be indicated. Results of BG, serum
electrolytes, acid-base, and urea nitrogen (BUN) should be available within minutes of obtaining blood
and must be available for frequent rechecks.

THERAPY OF DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS
OVERVIEW
Classically, the goals of treating DKA are to replace fluid and electrolyte deficits, provide adequate
amounts of insulin to normalize intermediary metabolism, correct acidosis, identify and treat concurrent
diseases, and to provide carbohydrate substrate when required. Acidosis is usually managed adequately
through fluid resuscitation, restoring electrolyte balances, and by giving insulin to inhibit lipolysis,
ketogenesis and gluconeogenesis. The quest to identify any concomitant disorder should never delay
initiating treatment for DKA.
It is appreciated that dogs and cats recovering from DKA or HHS need to eat as soon as possible.
Prolonged anorexia can be associated with worrisome complications, especially in obese cats at risk for
hepatic lipidosis (chs. 269 and 271). Low-carbohydrate foods are preferred, but any reasonable food can
be offered initially to encourage voluntary food intake. Force feeding is discouraged. Tube feeding is
uncommonly necessary. Diabetics are notoriously hungry. Anorexia or inappetence is almost always
explained by unresolved DKA, concurrent illness, or iatrogenic conditions (e.g., hypokalemia). Overly
aggressive therapy can have dangerous consequences while slow and progressive improvement in
abnormal parameters (over a period of 24 to 48 hours) increases the likelihood of therapeutic success.

FLUID THERAPY
Benefits of Intravascular (IV) Fluids
Ill pets with DKA are invariably dehydrated and unable to meet their fluid needs. While IV fluids are
essential for any severely dehydrated pet, fluids alone do not suppress ketogenesis (ch. 120).32,33 Fluids
should be administered for 1 to several hours before starting insulin therapy to limit complications
exacerbated by initiating fluids and insulin together (i.e., hypoglycemia [ch. 61], hypokalemia [ch. 68],
hypophosphatemia [ch. 69]). Appropriate fluid therapy restores IV volume, lowers BG, raises blood
pressure, improves tissue perfusion, facilitates resolution of metabolic acidosis, and can begin to correct
electrolyte deficiencies while limiting further imbalances induced by insulin therapy.

Fluid Choice
Because animals with DKA have interstitial space and intracellular dehydration, crystalloid fluids are
indicated (ch. 120). Although 0.9% saline solution could be used for water and Na replacement, it is an
unbuffered solution which in humans is associated with hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis that can
prolong recovery from acidosis.34 Until evidence in dogs and cats is developed on this matter, balanced
crystalloids with a buffer are recommended for fluid resuscitation (e.g., Ringer’s solution, Plasma-Lyte

148, Normosol-R). These fluids contain trivial amounts of K. Hypotonic fluids (e.g., 0.45% saline) are
rarely indicated, even when severe hyperosmolality is present. Hypotonic fluids are unsuitable for
correcting Na and water deficits and increase the risk of decreasing extracellular fluid (ECF) osmolality
too quickly which could result in cerebral edema.

Rate of Administration
Fluid rates should be based on assessment of hydration, degree of shock, and the presence of concurrent
diseases which may limit the rate of infusion (ch. 120). Dogs and cats with DKA receiving IV fluids
require close monitoring subjectively and objectively to avoid complications resulting from giving
excessive or insufficient fluid volumes. Too much can lead to overhydration, pulmonary edema, or other
third-space fluid loss. Too little prolongs poor tissue perfusion, hypoxia, and prerenal azotemia. The
formula used to calculate the fluid deficit, based on estimation of dehydration (with % dehydration
expressed as decimal, e.g., 10% = 0.1), is:
Fluid deficit (mL) = % dehydration × body weight (kg) × 1000 mL/kg
This deficit should be gradually restored over 24 hours (about 60-80% within the first 12 hours and
the remaining 20-40% in the next 12 hours) while also supplying maintenance fluid needs and matching
ongoing losses due to PU, vomiting and diarrhea (Figure 290.2). When the patient is no longer
critically ill, the rate of IV fluids should be adjusted to meet the pet’s hemodynamic and electrolyte
needs. Fluid rates 1.5 to 2 times maintenance (i.e., 60 to 100 mL/kg/24 h) are usually used initially. If
the patient is in shock (ch. 121) at the time of admission, boluses of fluids are to be administered at 5-10
mL/kg in 20 minutes until the heart rate and blood pressure are adequate (chs. 120 and 121).

ELECTROLYTES
It should be assumed that all pets with DKA are K+-depleted. Their “total body depletion” is often
masked initially by translocation of K+ from intracellular to extracellular spaces due to acidosis.
Therefore, K+ should be added routinely to fluids according to serum concentration (Table 290.1),
except when renal function is impaired and urine production is inadequate. If resuscitative boluses are
needed, it is essential not to exceed 0.5 mEq/kg/h of K+. Since changes in serum electrolytes and blood
gases are unpredictable during the first 24 hours of treatment, frequent assessments (q2-4h) and
adjustments in treatment should be made accordingly (Table 290.1; chs. 120 and 121).

FIGURE 290.2 Principles of care for the diabetic ketoacidotic patient. DKA,
Diabetic ketoacidosis.

Blood Glucose (BG)
BGs should be monitored every hour for the first 24 hours of therapy. When the BG decreases ≤250
mg/dL (<14 mmol/L) or when the decrease is >50-75 mg/dL/h (>2.8-4.1 mmol/L/h) and the ketosis is
still marked, dextrose must be added to the IV fluid solution. A 2.5% glucose solution can be used
initially and this or a 5% solution is usually sufficient. One may need to use higher concentrations to
maintain BG concentration between 150 and 300 mg/dL (8.3-16.7 mmol/L), rather than decreasing the
dose of insulin. It is important to remember that IV glucose can cause phlebitis; catheter sites should be
monitored carefully and the risk is lower when a central venous catheter is used (ch. 75). While counterintuitive, adding dextrose to the IV fluids is crucial for providing a carbohydrate substrate which allows
continued insulin infusion at a rate sufficient to inhibit lipolysis and ketogenesis and to resolve
ketonemia. The dextrose helps to avoid hypoglycemic episodes and dramatic osmotic shifts. Use of

factory-calibrated flash glucose monitoring systems (FGMSs, FreeStyle Libre, Abbott) can provide
valuable data on dogs with DKA (ch. 78).35,36 They can continuously measure interstitial glucose
concentrations which reflect circulating BG concentrations.37-44 The FGMS provides results in real time,
does not require calibration, and can be used as long as 14 days. Glucose monitors are being improved
and changed frequently.

Acidosis
Fluid therapy and insulin administration are usually effective in slowly resolving the metabolic acidosis
of DKA over the first 12 to 24 hours. Insulin enhances KB utilization, important since metabolism of a
mEq of KB produces a mEq of bicarbonate. Sodium bicarbonate therapy can be counterproductive when
considering the risks associated with too rapid correction of acidemia (exacerbation of hypokalemia,
reduced dissociation of oxygen from hemoglobin, worsening of central nervous system function). For
these reasons, sodium bicarbonate treatment is strictly reserved for pets in DKA with plasma
bicarbonate concentrations ≤11 mEq/L despite several hours of fluid therapy. Even then, bicarbonate
should be given in conservative doses. The formula used to calculate the bicarbonate deficit (i.e., the
mEq of bicarbonate initially needed to correct acidemia to the critical level of 12 mEq/L) is:
bicarbonate deficit (mEq) = body weight (kg) × 0.4 × (12 − patient’s bicarbonate)
To avoid the adverse effects of Na bicarbonate treatment, only half of this deficit must be administered
over a period of 6 hours, after which the acid-base state should be re-evaluated, and a new dosage
calculated until plasma bicarbonate concentrations are ≥12 mEq/L.

INSULIN THERAPY
Physiology
Insulin administration is the cornerstone of treating DKA. Insulin inhibits lipolysis which, in turn, slows
mobilization of the FFAs necessary for hepatic ketogenesis. Insulin suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis,
promotes glucose utilization, and enhances KB metabolism.6,45 Reductions in BG, urine glucose, and KB
concentrations after insulin is given reduces osmotic diuresis and renal electrolyte losses, helping to
correct acidosis. As glucose moves from the extracellular space into cells, it is accompanied by water, K,
and PO4. Serum electrolyte changes are unpredictable and worrisome changes can occur rapidly. Their
concentrations must be monitored regularly early in treatment (q2-4h). Life-threatening hypokalemia,
hypophosphatemia, hyperkalemia, or hypernatremia occur, representing some of the challenges that
require management when treating DKA.

Goals of Insulin Administration
The goal of insulin therapy is to slowly lower the BG concentration <250 mg/dL (<14 mmol/L) while not
allowing it to approach 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L). This should take place over 6 to 10 hours. Hourly
decreases of 50-75 mg/dL/h (2.8-4.1 mmol/L) are ideal.46 Fluid therapy alone lowers BG via dilution.
Insulin doses that decrease BG are invariably effective at suppressing KB production. Once the BG
decreases to about 250 mg/dL, it is advisable to keep glycemia near this range by supplementing the IV
fluids with dextrose. This approach allows insulin to be given safely and continuously until DKA
resolves. One of many challenges in treating a critically ill dog or cat with DKA is using insulin correctly.
One wants to provide enough insulin to restore normal cellular utilization of glucose while avoiding
adverse effects. Adverse issues are avoided by appropriate use of fluid therapy, frequent monitoring of
serum electrolytes and BG, and delaying initial insulin administration for several hours while fluid
resuscitation is started. One should delay insulin for a minimum of 2 hours if serum K+ concentrations
are within the normal range, but up to 4 hours if hypokalemia persists. If hypokalemia seems resistant to
being resolved, it is essential to check that adequate K+ is being supplemented. Commercial IV fluids, in
general, contain little or no K+ (ch. 120). One may consider low initial insulin doses to limit
intracellular shifts of K+ and PO4, which can worsen their serum deficits.47 In one study, starting insulin

within 6 hours of admission was associated with faster resolution of DKA but no difference in
complication rate compared to starting insulin >6 hours after admission.48
The switch to long-acting insulin cannot take place until ketosis and acidemia are resolved, hydration
status is adequate, serum electrolytes are normal or near-normal, and appetite returns without
vomiting. In pets with concurrent insulin-antagonistic disease, insulin may be less effective. While the
dog or cat ultimately determines their insulin needs, an underlying disease in some determines ability to
resolve DKA and may be the major cause of morbidity and mortality.

The Ideal Insulin
The ideal insulin begins to work within moments and is metabolized quickly. These attributes allow
quick assessment of dosage enabling rapid adjustments in treatment. It is fair to suggest that choosing a
dosage of insulin for an ill dog or cat with DKA is, at best, an educated guess, an “experiment.”
Monitoring the effect of that first dose on BGs determines if too much or too little was given. Since pets
with DKA are critically ill, quick identification of insulin over- and underdosing can be lifesaving. The
clinician can adjust insulin dosage within minutes if it is being given IV continuously or within an hour if
short-acting insulin was given intramuscularly (IM) or subcutaneously (SQ). For decades, Regular®
crystalline insulin was the only preparation available with immediate activity and an extremely short
duration of action. Various dosages given IV, IM, or SQ have been recommended and used with some
success.49-52 When technology allowed continuous rate IV infusions (CRI), periodic injections of insulin
were generally replaced with low-dose continuous Regular® insulin, if facilities were available. Among
the advantages of the CRI is avoiding the potentially erratic absorption of insulin given IM or SQ,
especially in dehydrated pets with compromised tissue perfusion. In addition to hydration and
perfusion, absorption of insulin can be affected by the structural properties of the insulin molecule.
Regular® insulin is a solution of zinc-insulin hexamers, whose absorption requires dissociation
following IM or SQ injection. The process of dissociation can delay insulin’s onset of action and prolong
its duration of effect, resulting in a more variable time-action profiles. The less predictable changes in
BG increase the risk of hypoglycemic events. Rapid-acting insulin analogs (lispro, aspart, and glulisine)
have been developed with structures that differ from the original molecule by one or two amino acids,
hindering hexamerization and speeding absorption and metabolism following SQ injection. These
features ensure rapid onset and a short duration of hypoglycemic activity.53 In people, intermittent SQ
injections of insulin analogs were as effective as IV Regular® insulin in the treatment of mild-tomoderate DKA.54-56

Low-Dose IV Constant Rate Infusion (CRI) of Insulin
The decision to employ a CRI protocol (ch. 77) is based on clinician preference and availability of
technical support and infusion pumps. The initial dose of Regular® insulin (2.2 U/kg [dogs]; 1.1 U/kg
[cats])51 should be added to 48 mL of 0.9% saline and administered via a line separate from that used
for fluid resuscitation with an infusion pump. The initial dose should be about 2 mL/hour, using the 48
mL solution over 24 hours. Adjustments in the infusion rate should be based on BG concentrations
(Figure 290.2). Dextrose should be added to the IV fluids (generally a 2.5% solution) once BG drops
≤250 mg/dL (≤13.9 mmol/L). Since insulin binds to plastic, the 48 mL insulin solution should be left in
the infusion syringe and line for about 30 minutes.57-59 The entire 48 mL should then be discarded, and
a fresh insulin solution used.
The efficacy and safety of 3 Regular® insulin dosages (1.1 U/kg/24 h, 2.2 U/kg/24 h, and increasing
the dosage from 1.1 to 2.2 U/kg/24 h) were compared in cats with DKA.52 No significant difference was

identified between groups in the time required to reach a BG of 250 mg/dL, in serum K+ and PO4
concentrations, in the time required to resolve ketonuria, or the duration of hospitalization. The efficacy
and safety of an IV lispro insulin CRI in dogs and cats and of an IV aspart insulin CRI in dogs were
compared to IV CRIs of Regular® insulin.60-63 All protocols were equally effective and safe.

Intramuscular (IM)/Subcutaneous (SQ) Protocols
Regular insulin can be given in a loading dose of 0.1-0.2 U/kg IM followed by 0.1 U/kg IM every 1-2
hours (Figure 290.2).47 The insulin dosage should be reduced by 25-50% in the first hours of
treatment if hypokalemia is a concern. When the BG concentration approaches 250 mg/dL (13.9
mmol/L), the insulin can be administered at a dose of 0.1-0.3 U/kg IM every 4-6 hours if the pet is
dehydrated but can be given SQ every 6-8 hours if hydration status is adequate. A 2.5-5% dextrose
solution should be administered to maintain BG concentration between 150 and 300 mg/dL (8.3-16.7
mmol/L) until DKA resolves.
A study investigated the use of IM/SQ lispro insulin in dogs with the aim of simplifying the
management of DKA while exploiting the advantages associated with its molecular structure.64 The dogs
received IM lispro insulin at an initial dosage of 0.25 U/kg. If a drop of at least 10% in BG during the
next hour was not achieved, the insulin dose was repeated hourly; otherwise, the insulin dose was
repeated q3h. When the BG reached 250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L), the insulin dosage was reduced to 0.125
U/kg IM or SQ (based on hydration status) q3h and glucose was added to the IV fluids to create a 2.5%
solution. The median time to resolution of ketosis was significantly shorter in dogs treated with this
protocol compared to dogs treated with an IV CRI of Regular® insulin. No differences were noted in
frequency or severity of adverse events.64 The efficacy of IM insulin glargine (1-2 U/cat, q2-22h) with or
without concomitant SQ glargine (1-3 U/cat q12h) was evaluated in cats.65 This protocol was associated
with successful resolution of DKA in all 14 cats studied.

PROGNOSIS
Therapeutic success depends on the clinician’s ability and owner willingness to implement one of the
treatment strategies described for DKA. One cannot overemphasize the importance of constant
supervision, frequent monitoring of vital parameters, hydration, tissue perfusion, BG, K+, Na+, PO4, and
acid-base status. It is important to quickly identify parameters that require attention and adjusting
treatment to manage those issues (e.g., hypokalemia or hypoglycemia). Any underlying disease should
be identified and treated, especially those causing insulin resistance (ch. 224). These measures have
reduced mortality from 25-35%15-17,51 to <10%.52,60,62-66 Severe underlying medical disorders (e.g.,
pancreatitis, hormonal disorders, sepsis, AKI, CHF) or client financial constraints account for most
deaths, rather than the metabolic complications of DKA. In cats, remission of DM is possible following
resolution of DKA, especially in cats with concurrent pancreatic disease or cats being treated with
glucocorticoids at the time DKA is diagnosed.65,67

THERAPY AND PROGNOSIS OF HYPEROSMOLAR
HYPERGLYCEMIC STATE
Animals with HHS are critically ill and many have acute kidney failure causing death or euthanasia.
Treatment of HHS requires slow restoration of dehydration deficits (24-48 hours) and correction of
severe hyperglycemia to minimize iatrogenic cerebral edema. Despite severe hyperosmolarity, the initial
fluid of choice is isotonic 0.9% saline. Serum K+ and PO4 concentrations must be closely monitored and
supplementation based on adjusting their serum concentrations in the context of kidney function and
urine production. Initial supplementation with 20 mEq/L of KCl is recommended. Early insulin therapy
is not critical with HHS and should be delayed until plasma volume is restored. To avoid the risk of
cerebral edema, BG concentration should not drop by more than 50 mg/dL/h (2.8 mmol/L/h). The
insulin protocols are the same for HHS as those discussed for DKA, but the initial insulin dosage should

be reduced by 50% to avoid rapid decreases in ECF osmolality. Creating 2.5-5% dextrose IV fluids is
recommended when BG is <250 mg/dL (14 mmol/L). The prognosis of HHS is guarded to poor.18,19

CLIENT INFORMATION
Diabetic Ketoacidosis and the Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) are serious metabolic
emergencies that have potential for adverse outcomes when not promptly recognized and treated. DKA
is characterized by the triad of hyperglycemia (or a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus), metabolic acidosis,
and ketonemia; HHS is characterized by hyperglycemia (usually more severe than that encountered
during DKA), hyperosmolarity, and severe dehydration, in the absence of significant ketoacidosis.

The fundamental pathogenic mechanism is a decrease in the net effective action of circulating insulin,
in the presence of elevated counterregulatory stress hormones such as glucagon, epinephrine,
norepinephrine, cortisol, and growth hormone. These hormones, produced in a wide variety of diseases
or stressful conditions, are responsible for the stimulation of lipolysis and the generation of free fatty
acids (FFAs) leading to ketogenesis, for the stimulation of hepatic glycogenolysis, and for the stimulation
of protein catabolism providing substrate for gluconeogenesis. In HHS, the lack of ketosis would be
justified by the presence of a small amount of insulin that would be able to limit lipolysis by inhibiting
the activity of hormone sensitive lipase in adipocytes, thus preventing the availability of FFAs for
ketogenesis. In ketoacidotic patients, hyperketonemia is responsible for the clinical manifestations,
causing acidemia, water and electrolytes depletion, and hypotension, in a self-sustaining vicious cycle. In
patients with HHS, the low or undetectable concentration of ketone bodies, that hinders obvious clinical
signs prolonging the course of the disease, explains why hyperglycemia, hyperosmolarity and
dehydration are generally more severe than in patients with DKA.
In addition to timely identification of the precipitating cause, the first step in acute management of
these disorders includes administration of intravenous fluids with appropriate replacement of
electrolytes, primarily potassium. In patients with DKA, this is always followed by administration of
insulin, usually via an intravenous insulin infusion that is continued until resolution of ketonemia, but
potentially via the intramuscular/subcutaneous route, although the unpredictable insulin absorption
from the site of injection in dehydrated patients makes the constant rate infusion the procedure of
choice. Because insulin inhibits lipolysis thereby reducing the mobilization of FFAs necessary for hepatic
ketogenesis, suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis, and promotes glucose and ketones metabolism by
tissues, one of the goals of treatment is to continuously and consistently administer insulin as long as
possible until ketonemia is present. For this reason the administration of dextrose plays a crucial role
when blood glucose concentrations drop to values that put the patient at risk of hypoglycemic events. It
is the author’s opinion that this therapeutic strategy is not sufficiently understood and exploited during
the management of ketoacidotic dogs and cats, perhaps because the dextrose administration may seem a
contradiction in patients in hyperglycemic crises.
Careful monitoring by experienced clinicians is needed during treatment for DKA and HHS. Common
pitfalls in management derive from an incomplete knowledge of the pathogenetic mechanisms and
adverse effects induced by the therapy itself (hypoglycemia, hypokalemia, and hypophosphatemia).
Mortality is usually a consequence of the underlying precipitating cause(s) and/or of the possible
complications derived from improper therapy rather than a result of the metabolic changes of
hyperglycemia. Effective standardized treatment protocols, as well as prompt identification and
treatment of the precipitating cause, are important factors affecting outcome.
Eleonora Malerba (Ozzano dell’Emilia, Italy)

INTRODUCTION
Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a heterogeneous group of diseases with multiple etiologies characterized by
hyperglycemia resulting from inadequate insulin secretion, inadequate insulin action, or both.1 The
prevalence of DM in dogs has been estimated from about 0.3% in first opinion practices to about 1% in

referral institution practices.2-5 The reported incidence of DM in a population of 182,087 Swedish
insured dogs was about 13 cases per 10,000 (0.13%) dog-years at risk.6

CLASSIFICATION AND ETIOLOGY
“TYPES” OF DIABETES MELLITUS
There are two predominant forms of DM in people, one involving a permanent and absolute loss of
insulin and the other involving insulin resistance that may not be permanent. These 2 conditions were
referred to as “juvenile-onset” and “adult-onset” DM, respectively, then updated to “insulin-dependent
DM” (IDDM) and “non-insulin-dependent DM” (NIDDM). The terms type 1 and type 2 DM are now
employed, with about 10% of diabetic people worldwide having type 1 disease and about 90% with type
2, a condition almost identical to the previous NIDDM.7 Several classification systems for canine DM
have been proposed based on the underlying cause of their beta-cell dysfunction.8,9 More recently, the
European Society of Veterinary Endocrinology’s project (Agreeing Language in Veterinary
Endocrinology) proposed a common terminology (Box 291.1).1 The most common form of DM in dogs
resembles type 1 DM in people. It is characterized by permanent hypoinsulinemia, no increase in
endogenous serum insulin or C-peptide concentrations following administration of an insulin
secretagogue (e.g., glucose, glucagon, amino acids), and an absolute need for exogenous insulin to
control glycemia, avoid diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA, ch. 290), and survive.10 With rare exceptions, all
diabetic dogs require exogenous insulin therapy to manage their hyperglycemia.

HISTOLOGY AND POSSIBLE PRIMARY CAUSES
Common histologic observations in pancreatic tissue from dogs with DM include reduced size and
number of pancreatic islets and reduced number of beta cells within islets. Beta-cell vacuolization,
enlargement, and degeneration are common.11,12 The cause of pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction or
destruction in dogs has not been established. Genetic predisposition to DM is recognized and based on
familial associations, pedigree analyses of Keeshonden and several other breeds, and genomic studies to
identify susceptibility and protective major histocompatibility complex (MHC) haplotypes.2,13-15 A
number of genes linked to susceptibility to DM in people are also associated with increased risk in
dogs.14-16 Canine DM has been associated with MHC class II genes (dog leukocyte antigen; DLA).17
Similar haplotypes and genotypes have been identified in the most susceptible breeds.
The American Diabetes Association has recommended sub-categorizing human type 1 DM (T1DM)
into types 1A (immune-mediated) and 1B (idiopathic severe insulin deficiency).18 Type 1A DM is
characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of the islets, known as “insulitis,” and by the presence of serum
autoantibodies to pancreatic components (e.g., insulin, intracellular glutamic acid decarboxylase 65
[GAD65] or insulinoma antigen 2 [IA-2]) prior to the development of hyperglycemia.19 There is
evidence that a small percentage of diabetic dogs have an immune-mediated component contributing to
the beta cell loss, leading to insulin deficiency. However, studies are conflicting, and pancreatic
lymphocytic infiltration is rare in diabetic dogs.11,20-22 Also, circulating serum antibodies to beta-cell
autoantigens, such as GAD65, IA-2 and insulin, were only rarely identified in affected dogs at
diagnosis.11,21,23 Thus, autoimmunity may not be a contributory factor in most dogs. A few dogs with
juvenile-onset DM (i.e., onset <1 year of age) have been reported, with higher prevalence in some breeds,
e.g., Labrador Retrievers.24,25 Most reports describe various pancreatic histopathologic abnormalities in
diabetic dogs, but no clear etiology. Congenital hypoplasia of islet beta cells has been described in
Keeshond puppies and other breeds.26-28

EXOCRINE PANCREATIC DISEASE
DM may occur secondary to disease of the exocrine pancreas or any process that diffusely injures the
pancreas, most notably pancreatitis (chs. 276, 277), a recognized cause of human diabetes.29 The
incidence of histologically identifiable, often severe pancreatitis in diabetic dogs ranges from 30-40%. It
is a likely contributor to the development of DM and DKA (ch. 290).30-32 Any inflammatory process
involving exocrine pancreatic tissue could negatively impact beta-cell viability because beta cells are
particularly sensitive to the action of proapoptotic mediators, such as tumor necrosis factor alpha.33-35

INSULIN-RESISTANT DM
Progesterone
Insulin-resistant DM can follow the antagonistic effects of the progesterone (Pg)-dominated phase of
diestrus or pregnancy (see Females in Diestrus, below). Following estrus, all normal bitches (pregnant or
not) enter the luteal, PG-dominated phase (diestrus) of their ovarian cycle. Diestrus lasts 60 to 90 days,
every 6 to 12 months. Pg stimulates growth hormone (GH) secretion from mammary tissue and both
hormones antagonize insulin action.36 Older females are frequently diagnosed with DM while in
diestrus (whether or not pregnant), when serum Pg and GH concentrations are increased.37-39
Treatment with ovariohysterectomy removes the source of Pg and, in turn, the stimulus for GH
secretion. If an adequate population of functional beta cells is still present in the pancreas,
hyperglycemia may resolve without insulin treatment. Failure to quickly correct insulin resistance often
results in progressive loss of beta cells and a greater likelihood of permanent insulin dependency.38

Glucocorticoids

Glucocorticoids cause insulin resistance and decrease insulin secretion directly by reducing the incretin
effect and by direct cytotoxic effects (ch. 293).40-43 DM had been documented in about 10% of dogs
with hypercortisolism.44,45 In 1 study, 38% of dogs with hypercortisolism had moderate
hyperglycemia.46 Sustained hyperglycemia has been shown to damage canine islets and lead to DM.47 It
is possible that hypercortisolism merely exposes pre-existing pancreatic damage that has otherwise
remained subclinical, which can explain the progression of DM in some but not all dogs.

Obesity
Despite the increasing prevalence of obesity in dogs, there is no evidence that insulin resistance
unmasks beta-cell dysfunction resulting in type 2 DM as in people and cats (chs. 20, 150). Obese dogs
show evidence of insulin resistance but compensate appropriately through increased insulin secretion.48

“HONEYMOON PERIOD”
A “honeymoon period” occurs in some dogs with newly diagnosed DM, characterized by excellent
glycemic control in response to small doses of insulin (<0.2 U/kg/injection), presumably due to residual
beta-cell function. Glycemic control in these dogs usually becomes more difficult (the honeymoon ends),
requiring increasing insulin doses within months of beginning treatment, as the residual functioning
beta cells die and fail to be replaced.49

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
DM is the result of a relative or absolute insulin deficiency. Insulin deficiency causes decreased tissue
utilization of glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids, accelerated hepatic glycogenolysis and
gluconeogenesis, and accumulation of glucose in the circulation, causing hyperglycemia.50 Intestinal
glucose absorption and glucose entry into erythrocytes, kidney or brain is not affected. As renal tubular
capacity for glucose reabsorption is exceeded, usually when blood glucose (BG) concentrations are >180
to 220 mg/dL (>10-12.2 mmol/L), glycosuria occurs. Glucose-induced osmotic diuresis causes polyuria
(PU), water loss, and activation of the thirst mechanism leading to polydipsia (PD). The negative calorie
balance resulting from an inability to utilize glucose, loss of calories in urine, and tissue catabolism leads
to polyphagia (PP).
The physiological consequences of DM are similar to those of starvation. Protein metabolism shifts
from synthesis to proteolysis and available amino acids increase hepatic gluconeogenesis. These are
short-term protective mechanisms. But, in DM, enhanced glucose synthesis exacerbates hyperglycemia,
creates negative nitrogen balance, decreases muscle mass, and eventually leads to cachexia (ch. 151).51
The continuing lack of insulin prevents glucose from entering cells, accelerates lipid catabolism,
mobilizes triglycerides, and causes increased levels of plasma free fatty acids (FFAs). FFAs are
transported to the liver where they undergo beta-oxidation to acetyl coenzyme A (CoA), which may
exceed the need for adenosine triphosphate production via oxidation in the Krebs cycle. Excess acetyl
CoA is metabolized into ketones. In starvation, ketones are an acceptable short-term source for energy
but after prolonged starvation or in DM, excessive production of ketones can lead to ketosis and, in DM,
DKA. Increased hepatic concentration of FFAs also increases hepatic synthesis of both triglycerides and
very low density lipoproteins (VLDLs), causing hyperlipidemia (chs. 63, 156) and hepatic lipidosis (ch.
274).

SIGNALMENT
DM is most commonly diagnosed in middle-aged and older dogs, 5 to 12 years of age.1-6 Rarely, DM is
diagnosed in a juvenile dog.26-28 Peak prevalence is 7 to 10 years; most studies place females at a greater
risk.2-6 Regional differences in breed popularity or variation in neutering practices may influence sex
predispositions within a population, although associations identified between neutering and diagnosis of
DM also vary. Genetic predisposition for or against the development of DM in dogs has been suggested

(Table 291.1), e.g., Boxer dogs are seldom reported in epidemiologic studies on DM. Genetic
differences within the same breed due to different blood-lines also impact predispositions, e.g., Swedish
and Norwegian Elkhounds, Australian Terriers, and Samoyeds have the highest incidence of DM in
Sweden while English Setter dogs are overrepresented in Italy.6,52

ANAMNESIS
Dogs with DM almost always have the classical clinical signs of PU/PD/PP and weight loss. PU/PD are
constant in diabetic dogs. PP may be diminished by a concurrent condition that decreases appetite (e.g.,
pancreatitis, ketosis, DKA; chs. 277 and 290). Weight loss may not be noticed in dogs that have only
recently become diabetic. The most common reasons for dogs with undiagnosed DM to be brought to
their veterinarian are their need to urinate at night or because they urinate in the home. In the event
that a dog has free access to urinate out-of-doors, owner concerns often include weight loss, ravenous
appetite, sudden blindness caused by cataract formation (Figure 291.1), or signs associated with DKA
(e.g., lethargy, anorexia, vomiting, weakness) (ch. 290). Time from onset of clinical signs to
development of DKA is unpredictable, ranging from days to months, and may be dependent on type and
severity of concurrent disorders causing insulin resistance and/or stimulating ketone production.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Physical examination (PE) findings depend on the duration of DM, presence of concomitant disorders,
and whether DKA has developed. A thorough PE (ch. 3) is critically important, especially for identifying
any concomitant disease. Dogs with “uncomplicated” DM are usually in good condition and their PE
may be unremarkable. Diabetic dogs can be of normal weight, underweight or obese. Lethargy may be
evident. The haircoat in newly diagnosed or poorly controlled diabetics may be dull. Hepatomegaly due
to diabetes-induced hepatic lipidosis is commonly palpable. Cataracts are also common (ch. 13).
Anterior uveitis and keratoconjunctivitis sicca may be present. The neurologic signs commonly observed
in diabetic cats (e.g., weakness in the hind limbs, ataxia, plantigrade stance) are uncommon in dogs.

DIAGNOSIS
Diabetes Mellitus and Ketoacidosis (DKA)
The diagnosis of DM is confirmed in a dog with classic clinical signs (with no other plausible cause) and
random (fasted or unfasted) BG >200 mg/dL (>11.1 mmol/L).1 In some, clinical signs may not be
reported by owners. If there is uncertainty regarding clinical signs, the diagnosis of DM can be
confirmed by finding persistent hyperglycemia over several days and/or documentation of increased
glycated proteins and/or glycosuria.1 To diagnose DM in dogs with fasting BGs >130 mg/dL but ≤200
mg/dL (>7.2 mmol/L but <11.1 mmol/L), persistent fasting hyperglycemia on separate days or increased
glycated proteins must again be documented.1 Testing for disorders that cause insulin resistance is
indicated if a stable unstressed dog has mild but persistent fasting hyperglycemia. Concurrent evidence
of ketonuria establishes a diagnosis of diabetic ketosis (DK), whereas illness, ketonuria, and metabolic
acidosis with increased anion gap confirms DKA (ch. 290).

Complete Diagnostic Evaluation
Once DM is diagnosed, it is extremely important to thoroughly evaluate the dog’s overall health in an
attempt to identify clues for conditions that may have contributed to DM development (e.g., Cushing’s
syndrome [ch. 293], hypothyroidism [ch. 285], pancreatitis [chs. 276-277]) or conditions resulting
from DM (e.g., weight loss, weakness, urinary tract infection [ch. 307]). Minimum laboratory
evaluation in dogs with newly diagnosed DM should include a complete blood count (CBC), a serum
biochemical profile that includes a serum fructosamine concentration, and urinalysis (UA) with bacterial
culture. Serum Pg concentrations should be assayed in any intact diabetic female. Abdominal ultrasound
(US) is an excellent tool to search for evidence of pancreatitis, adrenal enlargement or masses,
pyometra, ovarian cysts, and other concerns. Because of the prevalence of pancreatitis in DM, canine
pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity (cPLI) could be considered, especially if US is unavailable. Other
tests may be indicated (Box 291.2).

SUCCESSFUL MANAGEMENT STRATEGIES
INITIAL PLAN AND THERAPEUTIC GOALS
The Team Approach
Successful treatment of DM in a dog requires excellent owner compliance and owner/veterinary team
interaction. The “owner” may be one person or several. The veterinary members of the team who will be
involved in the long-term care of these dogs should include veterinarians, technicians, and non-technical
personnel. The owner should be thoroughly educated regarding DM, how it is managed differently in
dogs when compared with people, and the goals of therapy. Caring for a dog with DM can have a
negative impact on the dog’s owner. The veterinarian must be able to communicate with the owner in
the most appropriate way and should try to modify therapeutic strategies as much as possible to achieve
success as defined by the dog’s owner (ch. 1).

FIGURE 291.1 Bilateral cataracts causing blindness in a diabetic dog.

Understanding and Responding to Common Owner Concerns
Establishing and agreeing on the definition of “successful management” is extremely important (ch. 1).
For most veterinarians, their primary goal in the long-term management of DM should be to have the
owner pleased with the health of their dog. This is usually achieved if PU can be eliminated or
significantly reduced, body weight is stable and acceptable, and PP is tolerable. If the dog is dull at
diagnosis, it is important for the dog to interact “normally” with others in the home. Open dialogue
provides the best chance for owner adherence and will help avoid cessation of therapy or euthanasia. A
survey of 1192 veterinarians reported that a median of 1 in 10 pets with DM are euthanized at diagnosis
and another 1 in 10 are euthanized within 1 year of due to “lack of success or compliance.”53 One study
described the social and psychological impact of DM on the quality of life of both dogs and owners.54
Aspects reported as most negatively impacting the owners’ quality of life included: general worry about
DM, difficulties in leaving the dog with friends or family, worry about the dog becoming blind, boarding
difficulties, concerns about hypoglycemia, changed social and working life, costs of treating a diabetic,
worry about future care, and owners wanting more control. Knowing these concerns can help
veterinarians address key issues and concerns to adapt a treatment and monitoring protocol specific for
each owner, e.g., one can introduce intensive glucose monitoring (i.e., the use of continuous glucose
monitoring devices) for owners who want control. Alternatively, the clinician can simplify treatment for
owners worried about their social or working life. Reviewing expenses carefully can address a top

priority for owners concerned about costs. Avoiding tight glucose regulation is an approach that can
allay concerns for owners who are worried about hypoglycemia. While these measures may be imperfect,
they can be ways of prolonging the life of the pet, with a good quality of life, via finding an approach that
is sustainable for individual owners (and not triggering a decision to euthanize).

WHEN TO BEGIN INSULIN THERAPY AND AVOIDING
HYPOGLYCEMIA
Once diagnosed, treatment for DM should begin. Dogs in good condition and with an excellent appetite
can be managed as “uncomplicated diabetics,” even in the presence of ketonuria. The goals of therapy
are to reduce or resolve clinical signs, prevent short-term complications (e.g., hypoglycemia, DKA),
achieve the previously discussed areas of clinical improvement, and have good quality life. In DM dogs,
this can be accomplished with exogenous insulin therapy, an appropriate diet, exercise, prevention or
control of concurrent inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic or hormonal disorders, and avoidance of
insulin-antagonistic drugs (ch. 224). Aiming for normal or near-normal BG concentrations is not
recommended, as it increases risk of hypoglycemia, a common, serious, and potentially life-threatening
complication. Hypoglycemia is usually the result of overzealous insulin therapy. Most DM dogs are
described as doing well if their BGs are maintained between 80 to 250 mg/dL (4.4-13.9 mmol/L).

ITEMS TO INCLUDE WHEN EDUCATING OWNERS
General Concepts
Owners should be aware of changes in water intake, urine output, appetite and body weight caused by
DM. Poor appetite, vomiting, diarrhea or unusual lethargy is always worrisome and worth veterinary
consultation. It should be emphasized that consistency in timing of injections, meals, type and amount
of food, and exercise will make control of DM easier. Owners must learn the signs of hypoglycemia and
DKA. Unfortunately, many dogs with DM become blind from cataract formation within 12 to 18 months
of diagnosis (Figure 291.1). Treatment should follow a precise and understandable protocol (Box
291.3). While owners are the key to good DM control, decisions regarding insulin, dose and frequency
of administration must always be made by the owner/veterinary team.
