per year. Re-evaluation should include history, physical examination, body weight, review of
owner’s log, fructosamine.
Adjustment of insulin dose as described above.
Re-evaluations in Dogs That Are Using the FGMS
• The owner should relate well-being, clinical signs of diabetes, and results of weekly measurement
of body weight. The veterinarian should evaluate the results of the glucose graphs on the cloud
(LibreView). Recommendations with regard to insulin dose change should be given after a
thorough evaluation of data. Adjustment of insulin dose as described above.
• Re-evaluation in the hospital approximately 8 and 12 weeks after diagnosis, thereafter 1-2 times
per year. Re-evaluation should include history, physical examination, body weight, review of
owner’s log, fructosamine.
Goals of Therapy
• Clinical signs: resolution of polyuria/polydipsia and polyphagia, normal body weight
• Blood glucose concentration: ideally between 250 mg/dL (before insulin administration) and 80
mg/dL (nadir)

• Fructosamine concentration: ideally slightly above the reference interval (please note:
fructosamine concentration is the least important variable for evaluation of metabolic control)

The Insulin
Insulin should be stored in a refrigerator in an upright position. Insulin must be mixed correctly.
Vetsulin/Caninsulin should be shaken, some insulins do not require mixing, and some insulin products
should be gently rolled. Owners must use appropriate syringes (40 U/mL for veterinary insulin products
and 100 U/mL for human insulin products), learn to eliminate air bubbles, and administer the insulin
subcutaneously (SQ) over the lateral wall of the chest. The confusing use of nonmatching syringes based
on conversion tables for U40 and U100/mL or the owner’s calculation should be avoided. Often U40
insulin syringes have scales in both mL and Units; the owner must be instructed to use the Units scale.
The injection technique should be demonstrated until the owner is comfortable. If an insulin pen device
is used for administration, owners must be specifically trained. Written instructions are useful. Owners
of DM dogs should be encouraged to keep detailed records of their dogs’ BG, urine glucose, urine
ketones, and any change in other parameters.

DIETARY RECOMMENDATIONS (CH. 155)
Goals and General Content
Food given to DM dogs must be palatable, nutritionally complete, and be consistent in composition,
ingredients, and calories. These factors improve the chance for consistent insulin requirements and
response. Ideally, near optimal body condition should be achieved and maintained. A dog with DM may
be overweight or underweight. In either, near ideal weight is a reasonable goal. Insulin is an anabolic
hormone and insulin-treated diabetics gain weight easily, making weight loss in an obese dog with DM
difficult. Weight loss diets should be considered for obese DM dogs as they are typically rich in insoluble
fiber, low in fat, and have decreased caloric density. Such diets should not be fed to underweight DM
dogs. Once glucose control is established and a near-normal body weight attained, owners should
provide a consistent calorie-dense and lower-fiber diet designed for maintenance.50 Several commercial
prescription diets are available for DM dogs. To minimize postprandial hyperglycemia, no diet should
contain significant amounts of simple sugar. Calories should be derived primarily from complex
carbohydrates and proteins. The amount of fat in the diet should be minimized to avoid increasing
circulating cholesterol, triglycerides, free glycerol, and FFAs.55 Dietary fat should be particularly
restricted in any dog with a history of pancreatitis or persistent hyperlipidemia.

Fiber Content
Several, but not all, studies evaluating the role of high-fiber diets in the management of DM dogs
demonstrated improved glycemic control.56-58 One study failed to demonstrate benefit from feeding
normal weight DM dogs a high-fiber diet.55 Most diets for DM contain a blend of soluble and insoluble
fibers. Common complications of feeding high-fiber diets include increased frequency of defecation,
constipation, and obstipation (insoluble fiber); soft to watery stools and excessive flatulence (soluble
fiber).50 Problems with palatability can result from switching diets too quickly and can be avoided by
gradually transitioning from one diet to another. With time, dogs may become less interested in fiberrich diets. Their palatability can be improved by adding minced boiled meat. Concurrent conditions may
take priority over DM in diet choices (i.e., inflammatory bowel disease, chronic kidney disease, food
allergy/intolerance).

Feeding Frequency
To simplify management, most DM dogs should be fed 2 equal-sized meals daily, about every 12 hours.
In dogs with a consistently good appetite, food can be given immediately after the insulin injection,
helping the dog associate the unpleasant injection with the more pleasurable meal. In dogs with poor
appetite, food can be given immediately prior to giving insulin to avoid having dog the refuse to eat after

receiving a full dose of insulin. Ad libitum feeding is not recommended, but finicky eaters should be fed
at the time of insulin administration and have any uneaten food available throughout the day.

EXERCISE
Consistent exercise usually makes DM management easier and should be encouraged. Physical activity
decreases BG concentrations by increasing absorption of insulin from its injection site, increasing blood
flow and insulin delivery to exercising muscles, stimulating translocation (i.e., upregulation) of glucose
transporters (primarily GLUT-4) in muscle cells, and increasing glucose disposal without need for more
insulin.59,60 Sporadic strenuous exercise can induce hypoglycemia and should be avoided. When the
occasional intense exercise (i.e., hunting) is planned for a DM dog, reduce the morning dose of insulin
50%. The percent reduction needed to prevent hypoglycemia is not predictable and adjustments should
be based on experience, e.g., symptomatic hypoglycemia or PU during or after exercise. Owners of DM
dogs should always have a glucose source readily available in case signs of hypoglycemia are observed
during physical activity.

INSULIN CHOICES
OVERVIEW
Various types of insulin are used to treat DM long-term. Based on duration of action and potency, they
include intermediate-acting (porcine lente, neutral protamine Hagedorn [NPH]) and long-acting
insulins (protamine zinc insulin [PZI], insulin glargine, insulin detemir) (Table 291.2). Lente (Vetsulin,
Caninsulin) is a porcine-origin zinc 40 U/mL insulin consisting of 30% short-acting amorphous insulin
and 70% long-acting, microcrystalline insulin. NPH (100 U/mL; Humulin N, Novolin N) is recombinant
human insulin, usually administered q12h. A long-acting veterinary PZI 40 U/mL insulin is made with
recombinant human insulin (ProZinc). This insulin may be useful for some dogs in whom duration of
intermediate-acting insulins is too short.64 Glargine and detemir are synthetic long-acting insulin
analogues designed to maintain basal insulin concentrations in diabetic people. Their use in dogs is
increasing. An ultra-long-acting novel SQ insulin formulation given once weekly, not yet approved,
controlled BG concentrations in 4 diabetic dogs.68 The efficacy and safety of this novel formulation must
be further assessed in larger clinical trials.

INSULIN ANALOGUES
Glargine
Insulin analogues are synthetic modified human insulin peptides with similar physiologic effects. They
are commonly used in treating cats and dogs with DM.69 The amino acid asparagine in human insulin is
replaced with glycine at position A21 and 2 positively charged arginine molecules are added to the Cterminus of the B chain to create insulin glargine (Lantus).70 This structure results in low aqueous
solubility at neutral pH but complete solubility at a pH of 4. The acidic glargine solution injected into the
pH-neutral milieu of the SQ forms insulin-analogue-microprecipitates that slow absorption and delays
onset of action. The result is a relatively constant, peakless, basal supply of insulin.70 Due to the
importance of pH, glargine should never be diluted or mixed with any solution that could alter pH. In
dogs, insulin glargine has been shown to be safe and efficacious for good to moderate glycemic
control.55,56
Insulin glargine is also available in a 300 U/mL (Toujeo) formulation. Given the high concentration, it
can only be administered using an insulin-dosing pen. Glargine 300 U/mL was compared to insulin
detemir in 8 dogs and it was found to have a longer duration of action and a relatively peakless timeaction profile.70a Glargine 300 U/mL is now one of the author’s first-choice insulin for treating dogs
with DM. The initial dose should be 0.5 U/kg once daily. In one study 54% of dogs remained on oncedaily insulin requiring a median final dose of 1.9 U/kg (0.2-5.2) once daily. Forty-six percent remained
on this insulin, but the insulin was given q12h.70b The decision for q12h is based on glucose

concentrations not being controlled for 24 hours. When switching from once daily to q12h dosing, it is
recommended that the dose is decreased by about 30% per injection (i.e., the total daily dose is
increased by 40%). A small percentage of dogs are best managed by adding NPH (0.25 U/kg SC) insulin
after meals to the Toujeo. The decision to add pre-meal NPH is based on a substantial period of high
glucose >300 mg/dL (>16.7 mmol/L) that consistently occurs for several hours following 1 or more
meals, while there is otherwise good glycemic control.70b

Detemir
Removing the amino acid threonine from position 30 of insulin’s B chain and then adding a 14-carbon
fatty acid (myristic acid) to the amino acid lysine at B chain position 29 creates insulin detemir
(Levemir). These modifications permit reversible binding to albumin, slowing absorption and
prolonging its consistent metabolic effect for as long as 24 hours in people.71 In dogs, insulin detemir is
about 4 times more potent than other insulin preparations. Insulin detemir, given SQ q12h, has been
used to treat dogs with DM. Due to the higher potency of this insulin in dogs, lower dosages are
required. A starting dose of 0.1 U/kg q12h is recommended. Detemir should be used with caution,
especially in small dogs.57 Use of diluent specifically designed for this insulin allows safer delivery of
small doses.

STORING, MIXING AND DILUTING INSULIN
Freezing or heating inactivates insulin. While storing insulin at room temperature is acceptable, it is
safest for owners to store insulin inside the refrigerator door. This maintains a consistent storage
environment, bottle to bottle. Some veterinarians recommend replacing insulin monthly to avoid
inactivation or contamination. However, the “shelf-life” of commercially produced insulin, stored and
handled appropriately, is far longer. Problems with loss of insulin potency or sterility are extremely rare
and monthly replacement is not recommended. While shaking rather than gentle mixing was thought to
inactivate insulin, recent studies again demonstrate that insulin is resistant to being destroyed in this
manner. For consistency, however, gentle rolling is suggested for most insulin products.
Vetsulin/Caninsulin should be “shaken thoroughly” until a homogeneous, uniformly milky suspension is
seen (

Video 291.1). Diluting insulin can be quite useful in small dogs, particularly when using the

potent detemir. Only diluent solutions provided by the manufacturer should be used. It is important to
emphasize that insulin glargine is pH-dependent and should not be diluted.

INSULIN PEN DEVICES
Dosing pens, designed for use by diabetic people, are also used in diabetic dogs and cats. In humans,
insulin dosing pens have been shown to decrease anxiety, discomfort, and social embarrassment
associated with insulin administration.72 Pens must be stored without needles attached to prevent air
from entering and “diluting” the insulin, also explaining the need for “priming” the pen before each use.
One or 2 units must be loaded and then ejected while keeping the pen in an upright position. Lente
porcine insulin is the only veterinary insulin product marketed with pens. Pens are available in 2 sizes: a
maximum 8 U/dose VetPen (0.5 to 8 U) with 0.5 U dose increments and a maximum 16 U/dose VetPen
(1 to 16 U) with 1 U increments. The insulin pen-injectors [e.g., VetPen (0.5 to 8 U)] were more accurate
at lower dosages (≤2 U) and syringes were more precise for higher dosages in 1 study.73 A prospective
study reported that half of DM dog owners preferred using syringes and half preferred insulin pen
devices.74 In humans, it is recommended that the needle be kept in the SQ for 10 seconds during dosing.
For the low insulin doses typically used in dogs, the injection requires a few seconds and a 5-second wait
is considered sufficient. Pen needles are usually between 29 and 32 gauge and come in different lengths,

ranging from 4 mm to 12.7 mm. Longer needles are recommended for dogs to avoid intradermal
injections. Owners choosing to use insulin dosing pens must be trained in their assemblage (

Video

291.2) and use (Video 291.3).

INITIAL INSULIN RECOMMENDATIONS
The first insulin preparations recommended for dogs with newly diagnosed DM are from the
intermediate-acting group, such as porcine lente (Vetsulin, Caninsulin) or recombinant human NPH.
With either, one should begin with about 0.25 U/kg SQ q12h. This conservative approach should be
sufficient to prevent DKA or symptomatic hypoglycemia, either of which might be quite distressing to an
owner. It is not recommended to increase insulin dose in these initial days if glucoses remain high,
because insulin action may improve after a few days (so-called equilibrium).51 Insulin therapy is usually
started on an outpatient basis, which is less expensive than hospitalization. As discussed under the
heading “Glargine,” the 300 U/mL formulation is becoming a first-choice insulin.

FEMALES IN DIESTRUS
Intact bitches diagnosed with DM should undergo ovariohysterectomy as soon as feasible, ideally 1 to 3
days after starting insulin.51 Ovariohysterectomy is most important if the bitch is in diestrus and under
the influence of Pg, because removing the ovaries should reduce insulin resistance by eliminating Pg
and, in a few dogs, remission of DM may occur after a few days or weeks.75 All intact bitches with DM
should be spayed, even if no obvious relationship is established between diestrus and onset of DM. After
spaying, glycemic control should be closely monitored with appropriate adjustments in insulin dosage.
Although spaying does not lead to remission of DM in most dogs, it does prevent Pg-induced secretion of
mammary-derived GH in subsequent cycles, insulin resistance, and worrisome decompensation. If
spaying is not possible, administration of the Pg receptor antagonist aglepristone may reduce insulin
resistance.76

CONCURRENT CONDITIONS
Concurrent inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic and metabolic conditions are common in dogs newly
diagnosed with DM. Many of these conditions interfere with cellular responsiveness to insulin,
negatively impacting DM management (ch. 224). Concurrent disorders and diabetogenic drugs can
cause insulin resistance by altering insulin metabolism (pre-receptor issues), decreasing concentration
or binding affinity of cell membrane insulin receptors (receptor issues), interfering with the insulin
receptor signaling cascade (post-receptor issues), or any of these in combination.50 Insulin resistance
can be mild (e.g., obesity) to severe (e.g., Cushing’s syndrome) or may fluctuate (e.g., recurring
pancreatitis). Thorough evaluation (history, PE and in-hospital testing) of dogs newly diagnosed with
DM is extremely important. Identification and treatment of concurrent diseases are integral to
successful management of DM. Some conditions (e.g., chronic pancreatitis) are, like DM, never
permanently resolved and require long-term management. Owners should be informed that treating DM
alone can be challenging. Concurrent conditions can make successful therapy even more difficult.
Frequent monitoring and dosage adjustments are almost always required. Administration of
glucocorticoids or Pgs should be discontinued and alternative medications used if possible (ch. 224). If
glucocorticoids are absolutely required, dosage and frequency should be kept as low and consistent as
possible.

MONITORING DIABETES MELLITUS
OVERVIEW
Long-term care of diabetics and insulin dose adjustments should be based, primarily, on owner
observations supplemented by periodic in-hospital examinations. The in-hospital assessments should
include body weight, PE, BG, and fructosamine concentrations. Glucose levels and glucose curves should

initially be carried out in-clinic. Subsequently, if appropriately trained, most owners are able to perform
home monitoring by measuring capillary BG with a portable BG meter (PBGM). Motivated owners with
a quiet dog can learn about the flash glucose monitoring system (FGMS) (FreeStyle Libre).

FREQUENCY OF IN-HOSPITAL EVALUATIONS (BOX 291.3)
Veterinary team members must inform owners that most dogs require a minimum of 1 to 2 months to
achieve reasonable and stable glycemic control. In some, the process is straightforward and takes little
time. In others, adjustments in insulin and other factors never cease. Periodic monitoring is used to help
ensure safe and effective treatment. Initially, reevaluations are recommended at 1, 2 to 3, 3 to 4, and 8 to
10 weeks after diagnosis. Dogs are then usually examined about every 4 months, or as needed.

REPEATED HISTORIES AND PHYSICAL EXAMINATIONS
The most important parameter for assessing glycemic control is owner opinion, specifically status of
their dog’s PU/PD/PP, body weight, and general health. Body weight is emphasized since insulinunderdosed diabetics tend to lose weight and insulin-overdosed diabetics tend to gain weight. Wellcontrolled diabetics have stable, near ideal, body weight. Objective findings on PE should be considered
in the context of owner observations. If the owner is satisfied, body weight stable, and PE consistent with
good glycemic control, further testing is only directed at avoiding overdose. Owners should specifically
report any possible hypoglycemic episodes (e.g., weakness, ataxia, “acting intoxicated”). Persistence or
recurrence of clinical signs or unwanted change in weight are suggestive of poor glycemic control and/or
presence of a concurrent disease. A serum fructosamine and BG curves (BGCs) may help characterize
the issue, guide changes in treatment, or indicate need for additional testing.

SERUM FRUCTOSAMINE AND GLYCATED HEMOGLOBIN
(HbA1c)
Background
Serum fructosamine and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) are glycated proteins synthesized from
irreversible non-enzymatic binding of glucose to serum proteins or hemoglobin in red blood cells
(RBCs), respectively. In dogs, serum fructosamine reflects the mean BG concentration over the
preceding 1 to 2 weeks, while HbA1c provides an index of the average BG concentration over the
preceding 2 to 3 months.77,78 Serum fructosamine and HbA1c are not affected by acute changes in BG.
Higher average BG concentrations result in greater amounts of blood fructosamines and HbA1c.
Hypoproteinemia, azotemia, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and hemolysis can decrease measured
fructosamine, independent of BG concentrations.79,80 Increased serum fructosamines have been
observed in hypothyroidism and in 2 dogs with hyperglobulinemia caused by multiple myeloma.81,82
HbA1c may be decreased in conditions that shorten RBC lifespans or increase erythrocyte turnover.83,84
Falsely increased HbA1c values might occur with extreme hypertriglyceridemia and hyperbilirubinemia,
under conditions that prolong erythrocyte lifespan, or that are associated with decreased erythrocyte
turnover (e.g., iron deficiency anemia and splenic disorders).83,84 Each laboratory should generate its
own reference range for serum fructosamine and HbA1c.

How to Best Use Results
It is important to remember that neither normoglycemia nor normal fructosamine or HbA1c results
should be therapeutic targets when treating dogs for DM. BGs in well-controlled DM dogs fluctuate
between normal and slightly above renal threshold. Well-controlled dogs usually have some glycosuria
and are moderately hyperglycemic throughout the day. Thus, serum fructosamines or HbA1c within
reference intervals (especially in the lower half) are more suggestive of prolonged episodes of
hypoglycemia due to insulin overdose than of excellent control. Serum fructosamine or HbA1c should
be, ideally, slightly above the reference range. In a study comparing serum glycated protein
concentrations with glycemic control in 46 dogs with DM, serum fructosamine and HbA1c correctly

identified the level of glycemic control in only 50% and 44%, respectively, confirming the poor
performance of both glycated proteins in classifying glycemic control.85 For these reasons, serum
fructosamine or HbA1c should never be used as the sole indicator of glycemic control and should
always be interpreted in context of owner opinion, clinical signs, body weight, and BG concentrations.
Establishing a baseline glycated protein concentration for each dog and then monitoring trends rather
than absolute changes is the most appropriate use of glycated protein measurements in diabetic dogs.

URINE GLUCOSE MONITORING
Daily owner monitoring of urine for sugar and ketones can be useful. Most diabetics have varying
amounts of glucose present in virtually every urine sample, with an occasional negative. Persistent
absence of sugar may be indicative of insulin overdosage or excellent control. Owners should not adjust
insulin dosage on the basis of morning urine glucose because this commonly leads to overdose and
increases likelihood of insulin-induced hypoglycemia.
Ketonuria suggests inadequate control and decompensation. Upon seeing ketones in the urine of a pet
who rarely has them, the owner should contact the veterinarian (ch. 290).

RANDOMLY OBTAINED SINGLE BLOOD GLUCOSE
A single BG is rarely useful in monitoring DM unless the result is quite low, which always indicates
overdose. Single glucose measurements may be sufficient when an owner believes the dog to be
asymptomatic, the PE is unremarkable, and serum fructosamine concentrations indicate good glycemic
control (e.g., <100 mcmol/L above the laboratory upper reference range). In such dogs, BGs of 180-250
mg/dL around the time of the insulin injection are consistent with good glycemic control and additional
BG measurements are not usually necessary.

PORTABLE BLOOD GLUCOSE METERS (PBGMs)
During the initial adjustment phase and in subsequent long-term management phases of therapy, if
signs of DM persist, signs recur, or fructosamine concentrations are high, single BGs should be avoided
and a BGC obtained. Serial BGCs can guide rational adjustments in insulin therapy. BGs are typically
determined by a hand-held PBGM. To avoid multiple venipunctures, one may collect capillary blood
from the ear (

Videos 291.4 and 291.5; ch. 78).86 Several PBGMs are commercially available. The

accuracy of PBGMs designed for people varies considerably when used in dogs, but some are sufficiently
accurate and precise to monitor BGs in dogs.86-91 Most devices give lower results than laboratory
reference methods. This bias may result in an incorrect diagnosis of hypoglycemia or the misconception
that the animal’s glycemic control is better than it actually is. The AlphaTRAK PBGM (Abbott Animal
Health) was designed for use in dogs and cats and is more accurate and precise in dogs than devices
designed for human use.88,90,91 Additional advantages of the AlphaTRAK are the small volumes of
blood needed (0.3 mcL) and the extended measurement range (20-750 mg/dL). The AlphaTRAK PBGM
tends to overestimate BG values, potentially missing hypoglycemia. The meter is less accurate in dogs
with hematocrits <30% or with erythrocytosis.92,93 VetMate, another veterinary PBGM, is accurate and
requires 0.4 mcL of blood for BG measurement.91 If there is any doubt regarding accuracy, BGs can be
compared with laboratory results.

BLOOD GLUCOSE CURVES (BGCs) AND INSULIN DOSAGE
ADJUSTMENTS
Protocol
When conducting a BGC, the dog should be seen early in the morning and BGs sampled every 1 to 2
hours throughout the day. One should begin just prior to the first insulin dose and continue until the
next dose is due. Most dogs respond similarly to insulin morning and evening.94 If different day vs night

BGs are suspected (e.g., good BGC and control of clinical signs during the day but presence of PU/PD
during the night), a 24-hour BGC or use of a continuous blood glucose monitoring (CGM) device should
be considered.50 When performing a BGC, the owner’s insulin and feeding schedules should be
maintained. Poor appetite limits the value of any BGC. Food and insulin can be administered at the
clinic after the first BG measurement. If a dog refuses to eat in the clinic, the BGC should be abandoned.
Subsequently, the owner should feed the dog at home, administer insulin, and then bring the dog to the
clinic as soon as possible to begin the BGC.

Interpreting Blood Gluose Curves
BGCs are used to determine whether the administered insulin lowers BG effectively and to identify the
glucose nadir, time of peak insulin effect, duration of insulin action, and degree of fluctuation in BGs. In
well-controlled DM, BGs are between 80 and 250-300 mg/dL (4.4 and 13.9-16.7 mmol/L). Insulin
efficacy is evaluated, in part, by determining the difference between highest and lowest BGs. A small
difference (e.g., 50 mg/dL) is acceptable if the highest BG is <220 mg/dL but not acceptable if it is >300
mg/dL.51 The most important parameters are the BG nadir and the duration of the insulin effect.
Ideally, the BG nadir should be 80-150 mg/dL. A lower nadir can be caused by insulin overdose,
excessive overlap of the insulin action (common if long-acting insulin analogues are used), prolonged
periods without food (the dog refused to eat in-hospital), or strenuous exercise. A BG nadir >160 mg/dL
can be due to an insufficient insulin dose, insulin resistance, or owner technical problems. In a dog
already treated with high dosages (e.g., >1.5 U/kg per injection), owner error and insulin resistance are
the main differential diagnoses.

Duration of Action
Duration of insulin action can be determined if the BG nadir is within the desired range. Duration is
defined as the time from injection through the glucose nadir until the BG exceeds 250 mg/dL. When
duration is too brief (e.g., <8 hours), signs of DM are usually exhibited. When duration is too long (e.g.,
>14 hours), risk of hypoglycemia increases. Poor duration of action may be altered by changes in diet.
One may need to choose an insulin product with a different action profile.

Reproducibility
Performing BGCs on consecutive days is not recommended and they should never be assumed to be
reproducible. Day-to-day variables and DM itself are rarely static. Variables include the amount of
insulin drawn into the syringe, the amount of insulin absorbed after each injection, and the interactions
between insulin, diet, exercise, stress, excitement, presence of concurrent disorders, gastric emptying,
and secretion of the counterregulatory hormones (e.g., glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol, GH). All these
factors fluctuate and prevent reproducible BGCs. Lack of consistency in BGC results can create
frustration unless expected. It is better to view lack of consistency as common and caused by any
variable that could alter glucose concentrations. When dose change appears appropriate, the change
should not exceed 10-25%. In documented or suspected hypoglycemia, the dose should be decreased by
about 50%. Insulin doses should not be changed more frequently than every 5 to 7 days, except when
hypoglycemia is documented.

HOME MONITORING
Owners should be encouraged to assess their dog’s DM on a daily basis (see earlier section). Initially,
body weight should be measured and recorded every week. Glucose measurement with PBGM using
capillary blood is usually easy and acceptable for most owners and should be recommended as more
accurate and less expensive. Capillary blood can be obtained using lancing devices on various sites: the
inner aspect of the pinna is a good site for capillary sampling (Video 291.5; ch. 78); good alternatives
are the buccal mucosa (

Video 291.6)95 or the paw pad (Video 291.7). Owners must be thoroughly

familiar with their PBGM and access to veterinary support should be available. In general, a good time
for introducing the concept of home monitoring is after the first 3 to 4 weeks of treatment, when the
client is somewhat familiar with DM, will understand the time that DM requires, and appreciate the
value of credible BGs. Once familiar with the procedure, the owner can perform a BGC by measuring the

morning BG before giving insulin and food, and then every 2 hours until the next injection is due or even
thereafter if a nadir is not obvious. Interpretation of home BGCs should be the same as those performed
in-hospital. Veterinarians should anticipate that some owners become overzealous, monitoring BGs too
frequently. Some interpret results and adjust the insulin dosages without veterinary consultation, a
practice that frequently leads to poorer control of DM, increased risk of overdose, confusion, and
frustration.

CONTINUOUS GLUCOSE MONITORING SYSTEMS (CGMSs)
CGMSs are routinely used for monitoring people with DM and are beginning to be used in DM dogs.96
The CGMSs allow glucose to be monitored without need for repeated blood sampling. The CGMS
measures interstitial glucose (IG) rather than BG. Interstitial fluid is easily accessible and results are
virtually the same as BG.96-98 Many CGMS devices (e.g., Guardian REAL-time) have some limitations.
They need to be calibrated 2 to 3 times daily, which requires blood sampling. Sensors are quite
expensive and can be used only for days. The monitor displays IGs from 40 to 400 mg/dL;
concentrations outside this range are correctly recorded but need to be downloaded to be seen.
A new human CGMS (Freestyle Libre [Abbott]; FGMS) consists of a small, round, disposable, waterresistant sensor that continuously measures IG by means of a small (5 mm long × 0.4 mm wide)
filament inserted SQ. The FGMS generates information every minute, and the readings are
automatically stored in 15-minute intervals for up to 14 days. IGs are displayed when the sensor is
wirelessly scanned (or “flashed”) with a reader device or smartphone on demand. The reader device then
displays the past 8 hours of IG information, including current IG, a trend graph, and a trend arrow
which indicates the direction of the patient’s current glucose concentration with respect to previous
results. The data are transferred in cloud to create an easy-to-read report for the owner that can be
shared with the veterinarian (LibreView; Figure 291.2). In dogs, the FGMS application is seemingly
painless, well-tolerated, and easy to use (

Video 291.8, Figure 291.3). Mild erythema at the site of

the application might be observed at the end of the wearing period. Good correlation between dog IG
and PBGM results (rho = 0.94) have been found.99 The FGMS readings are less accurate for glucose
concentrations <90 mg/dL (<5 mmol/L).99 Accuracy seems to be affected by the skin thickness; dogs
with thicker skin have more accurate measurements than dogs with thinner skin (<5 mm).100 In DM
dogs, the FGMS detects IG nadirs and hypoglycemic episodes more frequently than PBGMs.102 A CGMS
measuring IGs for up to 180 days (Eversense XL) has been developed for humans and will likely be
studied and available for diabetic dogs.

PERSISTENCE OR RECURRENCE OF CLINICAL SIGNS
OVERVIEW
Persistence or recurrence of clinical signs are frequent issues in any diabetic. Recurrence of signs,
especially PU/PD, can be noted at any time and common causes include technical issues in
administering insulin, use of the incorrect (for this patient) insulin type, and less than ideal dosage or
frequency of administration. Other common problems are insulin unresponsiveness caused by
concomitant inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic, or hormonal disorders (Table 291.3).

TECHNICAL ISSUES
Common reasons for poor glycemic control are errors in handling or injection techniques: specifically,
failure to mix the preparation correctly; use of an improper diluent; use of insulin that has been frozen,
heated, or is out of date; incorrect injection technique using a syringe or insulin dosing pen, or
inappropriate insulin dose or syringe size (U-40/mL vs. U-100/mL). These problems can be identified
by carefully evaluating the history and asking the owner to bring their insulin and syringes or pen device
to every appointment. If concerns arise, the veterinarian or technician can observe the owner’s entire
injection procedure. If needed, assistance should be provided until the owner is able to master the
technique.

INSULIN UNDERDOSE
Most dogs are well controlled with insulin doses ≤1 U/kg/injection SQ q12h. If the insulin dosage is
considerably less than 1 U injection/kg and the dog is receiving insulin q12h, underdosing can explain
poor glycemic control. In this scenario, the dose should be gradually increased by 10-25% per week.

EXPECTED GLYCEMIC VARIABILITY
In healthy dogs there is little BG variation within a day or from day to day (Figure 291.2, dog 1). In
contrast, within day and day-to-day glycemic variability is commonly observed in DM dogs, even in
“well-controlled” dogs (Figure 291.2, dogs 2 and 3). BG variability has been documented even if the
food, insulin dose, and environment in which the monitoring takes place (at home or in the clinic) are
kept constant.101 Glycemic variability refers to wide glycemic excursions, including episodes of
hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia during a single day or on different days.102 Since CGMSs have been
increasingly used, glucose variability has been recognized commonly, but its cause cannot consistently
be identified or resolved. In humans, high glycemic variability is considered a risk factor for
hypoglycemia, microvascular complications, neuropathy, retinopathy, stroke and all-cause mortality.103
No consensus gold-standard method has been identified for assessing the significance of glycemic
variability. Several indicators have been proposed. Mean and standard deviation (SD), which describes
the dispersion of values around mean BG, or percentage of the coefficient of variation [%CV = (Standard
Deviation of BGC values/Mean of BGC values) ∗ 100] are used in diabetic people and may have value in
DM dogs. High glycemic variability is a characteristic of poorly controlled diabetic dogs. Investigations
for strategies to reduce the glycemic variability are the same as those recommended for investigating the
causes of diabetic instability (Table 291.3, Figure 291.4). When it is not possible to identify a clear
cause for glycemic variability, a change in insulin should be considered, e.g., a dog that is treated with
lente porcine insulin can be switched to insulin detemir, or another insulin analogue (e.g., glargine
insulin). In humans, the use of insulin analogs (e.g., insulin detemir) can reduce glycemic variability in
comparison with other insulin preparations (e.g., NPH).104 If glycemic variability cannot be reduced,
insulin doses should be low enough to avoid worrisome hypoglycemia.

REBOUND HYPERGLYCEMIA (SOMOGYI RESPONSE)
The Somogyi response is defined as rebound hyperglycemia due to the hypersecretion of
counterregulatory hormones (e.g., glucagon and epinephrine) during a hypoglycemic episode. In human
diabetics, inadequate insulin action (often associated with low duration of insulin action) is considered
to be responsible for the majority of these episodes of hyperglycemia following hypoglycemia as opposed
to true rebound hyperglycemia associated with counterregulatory hormones. A recent study observed no

significant increase of circulating plasma glucagon concentration during insulin-induced hypoglycemia
in 13 diabetic dogs. Their epinephrine concentrations during insulin-induced hypoglycemia were lower
than those observed in healthy dogs.105 These observations contrast with the theory of rebound
hyperglycemia due to counterregulatory hormones. Additional studies may help understand the causes
of dramatic glycemic variability, but it is probable that the Somogyi phenomenon is not a special entity
but part of the glycemic variability complex.

SHORT DURATION OF INSULIN ACTION
In some diabetic dogs, the effect of NPH and porcine lente insulins may last <8 hours. As a result,
hyperglycemia to levels above the renal threshold (∼175-225 mg/dL [9.7-12.5 mmol/L]) may continue for
hours each day. Owners of dogs whose insulin is not lasting long enough usually report PU/PD. The

issue may be demonstrated on a BGC or with the use of a CGMS. Treatment involves switching to a
longer-acting insulin q12h (i.e., PZI, glargine or detemir; see Table 291.2).

PROLONGED DURATION OF INSULIN EFFECT
Prolonged duration of action is usually defined as exogenous insulin lasting >12 hours. Insulin given
q12h would overlap with the previous dose and increase risk of hypoglycemia. Prolonged duration of
insulin action is usually observed when the glucose nadir occurs ≥10 hours after injection. Treatment
options include decreasing the frequency of administration from q12h to q24h when using detemir or
glargine insulin. One may also consider changing insulin to one with a shorter duration of action.

ANTI-INSULIN ANTIBODIES
Canine, porcine and human insulin are similar. Development of significant insulin antibodies has been
reported but is uncommon in DM dogs treated with porcine or recombinant human insulin.106

CONCURRENT DISORDERS CAUSING INSULIN RESISTANCE
Most DM dogs can be regulated with insulin doses ≤1 U/kg q12h. In dogs with higher insulin
requirements, concurrent disorders should be suspected after “technical” issues or short duration of
insulin action have been ruled out. No insulin dosage clearly defines “insulin resistance.” It has been
proposed that insulin resistance be suspected when glycemic control is poor despite insulin doses >1.5
U/kg q12h, when high doses (>1.5 U/kg) are needed to maintain BGs <300 mg/dL (<16.7 mmol/L), or
when glycemic control is erratic and insulin doses continuously adjusted.50 Any inflammatory,
infectious, neoplastic or endocrine disorder can cause insulin resistance, as does obesity and a variety of
drugs, especially glucocorticoids and progestagens. Insulin resistance is most commonly caused by
glucocorticoid administration, diestrus, hypothyroidism, chronic pancreatitis, chronic kidney disease,
infection, neoplasia, hyperlipidemia, severe obesity, and Cushing’s syndrome. The most common sites of
infection are oral (dental) and urinary tract. Other less common causes of insulin resistance are
pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, cardiac disease, liver insufficiency, glucagonoma and
pheochromocytoma (see Table 291.3). Anamnesis and PE are the most important first “tests” in
identifying concurrent disorders. In most, a complete diagnostic work-up, including CBC, serum
biochemical profile, UA with bacterial culture, abdominal US and thoracic radiographs should be
considered as initial “screens” for concurrent illness. When indicated, one may consider a low-dose
dexamethasone suppression test, serum Pg concentration measurement (in intact females), thyroid
function tests, serum canine pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity (cPLI), serum trypsinlike
immunoreactivity (TLI) and computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging (pituitary mass).

LONG-TERM COMPLICATIONS OF DIABETES MELLITUS
HYPOGLYCEMIA
Hypoglycemia, rarely fatal, is an extremely common complication of insulin treatment.107 Hypoglycemia
may follow a large increase in insulin dose, sudden increase in insulin sensitivity due to treatment or
improvement of concurrent disorders (e.g., treatment of hypothyroidism), inadvertent insulin overdose,
overly stringent attempts at glycemic control, excessive overlap of the insulin action in dogs receiving
insulin q12h, excessive exercise, and inappetence resulting in relative insulin overdose. Signs of
hypoglycemia include lethargy, weakness, ataxia and increased appetite (chs. 61, 289). If hypoglycemia
is allowed to progress, seizures, coma and death can occur. Symptomatic hypoglycemia should be
treated with a glucose-rich food. If unable to eat, glucose can be applied to the dog’s oral mucous
membranes in the form of glucose gel or glucose solution, from which it is directly absorbed (ch. 289).
After recovery, the dog should be fed. Collapsed dogs should be given IV dextrose immediately as an
initial IV bolus of 1 mL/kg of 33% dextrose followed by a 5% dextrose infusion (ch. 289). Rates can be
changed if necessary. After symptomatic hypoglycemia, owners should be instructed to stop insulin until
glycosuria recurs and then give 25-50% less. Subsequent insulin doses should be adjusted to avoid

hypoglycemia and increase BG measurements.50 Treatment of asymptomatic hypoglycemia also
requires insulin dosage reductions of about 10-20%, or that insulin should be replaced with one that has
a shorter duration of effect.

OCULAR COMPLICATIONS
Cataract formation is the most common long-term complication in diabetic dogs (Figure 291.1) (ch.
13). A retrospective-cohort study on 132 DM dogs referred to a university referral hospital found
cataract formation in 14% at the time of diagnosis. In that study, the time interval for 25%, 50%, 75%,
and 80% of the study population to develop cataracts was only 60, 170, 370, and 470 days,
respectively.108 Cataracts are thought to occur as a result of altered osmotic relationship in the lens
induced by intra-cellular accumulation of sorbitol and galactitol following the metabolism of excess
glucose and galactose by enzymes within the lens. The accumulation of sorbitol and galactitol in lens
cells increases intracellular osmolality, increases intracellular fluid volume, ruptures lens fibers, and
causes cataract development.109 Once cataract formation begins, it is irreversible. They can evolve quite
rapidly. Complete blindness may be avoided by removing the abnormal lens. Vision is restored in 8090% of DM dogs that undergo cataract removal.110,111 Other ocular complications of diabetes can
include uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, bacterial conjunctivitis and diabetic retinopathy.

DIABETIC NEUROPATHY
Diabetic neuropathy has been described in dogs, although its prevalence is unknown.112-115 Subclinical
neuropathy seems to be most common. Clinical signs of diabetic neuropathy (weakness, muscle atrophy,
hyporeflexia, hypotonia) are most commonly recognized in dogs that have been diabetic for 5 years or
longer.50,115 Diabetic neuropathy in dogs is primarily a distal polyneuropathy, characterized by
segmental demyelination and axonal degeneration.

DIABETIC NEPHROPATHY
Diabetic nephropathy has occasionally been reported in dogs, but its clinical relevance remains
unknown. Microscopic changes can include membranous glomerulonephropathy with fusion of the foot
processes, glomerular and tubular basement membrane thickening, increase in the mesangial matrix
material, presence of subendothelial deposits, glomerular fibrosis, and glomerulosclerosis.116,117 In most
DM dogs, chronic kidney disease is thought to develop as an independent condition.50

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis for dogs diagnosed with DM depends, in part, on the owner’s commitment to treating the
disorder, ease of glycemic regulation, presence and reversibility of concurrent disorders, and avoidance
of chronic complications associated with the diabetic state. In a large study involving insured dogs in
Sweden, 347 dogs survived at least 30 days after the first DM claim. The proportion of those surviving 1,
2, and 3 years was 40%, 36% and 33%, respectively.6 A recent study reported a median survival time of
964 days in a population of dogs with DM treated in a referral center.118 A relatively high mortality rate
exists during the first 6 months of treatment due to concurrent diseases such as ketoacidosis,
pancreatitis or infections. It is a common opinion that well-controlled diabetic dogs that survive the first
6 months of treatment and have motivated owners have a life expectancy similar to that of non-diabetic
dogs of the same age, sex and breed.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Diabetes Mellitus in Dogs
Dear Madam/Sir _____________
Your dog has been diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, a disorder of glucose metabolism. The cause of
this disease is a deficiency of insulin, a hormone produced by the pancreas, which leads to an increase in
blood sugar. The main symptoms of diabetes mellitus are excessive thirst, increased urination, increased
appetite and weight loss. Treatment consists of subcutaneous insulin injections. The aim is to achieve
good glycemic control, which is reached when clinical signs improve or even disappear.
Since the amount of insulin can be different from dog to dog, it is very important to perform regular
re-checks of your dog.
• Inject your pet under the skin twice a day (every 12 hours) with:
_________units of ___________________________
• Feed your pet with ___________________ twice daily at the time of the insulin
administration

RE-CHECKS IN THE CLINIC
Blood Glucose Curve
During follow-up visits, your dog must stay a whole day at the clinic, as at 2-hour intervals we measure
blood glucose concentration in the blood to assess the trend during the day (blood glucose curve). Based
on the blood glucose curve, we can judge whether the daily insulin therapy is adequate or whether it is
necessary to change the dosage. On the day of the visit you should come to the clinic immediately after
administering insulin and food to your pet.

Fructosamine
Although the blood glucose curve allows us to verify whether the insulin treatment is appropriate, it is
not a method of retrospective investigation; this means it does not provide information on blood glucose
levels in the previous days. Therefore, it may be useful to assess blood fructosamine concentrations—
proteins that bind irreversibly to glucose and are therefore an excellent indicator of blood glucose in the
2-3 weeks prior to collection (“glycemic memory”).

Dates for Re-evaluations
• First re-evaluation: 1 week after discharge
• Second re-evaluation: 2-3 weeks after discharge
• Third re-evaluation: 3-4 weeks after discharge
• Fourth re-evaluation: 10-12 weeks after discharge
After completing these re-checks, we should perform re-evaluations about every 4 months.
When the dose or type of insulin is changed, a re-evaluation should be performed after 7-15 days.

INSTRUCTIONS FOR STORAGE, MIXING AND INJECTING INSULIN
• Keep the insulin in the refrigerator, in a vertical position. When your dog is with you on
vacation, the insulin bottle can be stored outside the fridge for 3 weeks (room temperature).
On your return you will have to use a new bottle.
• If your pet is treated with insulin named Vetinsulin/Caninsulin: take the insulin vial from the
refrigerator and shake it thoroughly until an homogeneous, uniformly milky suspension is
obtained.

• With other insulins (e.g., ProZinc, Humulin N, Novolin N), the insulin should be mixed by
rolling the bottle on the palm of the hands without shaking vigorously.
• If your pet is treated with insulin Lantus or Levemir insulin, no mixing is required.
• Fill the syringe with the insulin dose using only the proper syringes:
• U100/mL syringes for Humulin N, Novolin N, Lantus and Levemir
• U40/mL syringes for Vetinsulin/Caninsulin and ProZinc
In case you need to buy other syringes, make sure they are the right ones.
• Do not disinfect the skin.
• Remove any air bubbles in the syringe by gently stroking the syringe with your fingers, pointing
the needle upward, gently push the plunger to expel the air.
• Move the hair of your dog until you highlight the skin.
• Lift a fold of skin gently upwards, for example in the region left or right of the chest, and with
the index finger form a small dimple. The site of the injection should be different every time.
• Place the needle in the dimple and push it gently through the skin. Release the skin.
• Firmly push the plunger in the syringe, emptying its contents.
• Do not massage or rub the skin after injection.
In case you have problems with the insulin injection, do not hesitate to contact us.
During the injection minor inconveniences may occur to which you must be prepared: normally the
injection is not painful; however, you can inadvertently hit a small nerve that will cause the dog to move
as a reaction to the pain. Sometimes it is possible to hit a blood vessel and small traces of blood can be
visible at the injection site. In such cases there is no need to do anything.
If accidentally the injection is not performed correctly, it is possible that part of the insulin comes out
wetting the skin. In these cases do not administer more insulin, to avoid an overdose (insulin underdose
is better than insulin overdose). The next injection should be done as usual without increasing the dose.

DIET AND EXERCISE
A regular and consistent diet is very important and is complementary to insulin therapy. Your dog
should eat the same amount of food twice daily at the same time. Some dogs may not accept dietary
changes willingly. If your dog refuses to eat the diabetic diet, to improve its palatability mix some
minced boiled meat (i.e., chicken or turkey) to the commercial diet.
Exercise is important in the management of canine diabetes mellitus and, especially in overweight
dogs, it is recommended. As for food and insulin, consistency is of utmost importance. The amount of
exercise and the time of the day in which it is carried out should be constant. It is not appropriate for a
diabetic dog to do little or no exercise during the week and a lot of exercise during the weekend.
Strenuous and sporadic exercise can induce hypoglycemia and should be avoided.

HYPOGLYCEMIA
Hypoglycemia is a common complication of insulin treatment. It most commonly happens a few hours
after the insulin injection. Depending on the severity of a hypoglycemic episode, your dog will react
showing an increased appetite, agitation, or weakness and dizziness; in severe cases, loss of
consciousness and seizures may occur. In case of mild clinical signs of hypoglycemia, it is necessary to
feed the dog immediately; should food intake be impossible, give your dog sugared water, jam or honey
directly into the mouth. If the dog is not even able to swallow, rub the gums with glucose gel, glucose
solution or honey, where it can be directly absorbed. As soon as the animal shows signs of recovery, feed
it immediately with small amounts of food.
There is often a fast recovery; should that not happen, bring the dog immediately to a veterinarian.
After a hypoglycemic episode, the insulin dose should be modified, so please get in touch with us.
Federico Fracassi (Ozzano dell’Emilia, Italy)

DEFINITION AND DIAGNOSIS
Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a syndrome characterized by hyperglycemia due to defects in insulin
secretion, insulin sensitivity, or both.1,2 Regardless of the pathogenic cause, relative or absolute
deficiency in insulin action on target tissues leads to myriad abnormalities in carbohydrate, fat, and
protein metabolism. The criteria for the diagnosis of DM in cats developed by an international
consensus committee are provided in Box 292.1.3
Prediabetes is a state of abnormally increased blood glucose (BG) concentrations (either fasting or
after a glucose load) that do not yet meet the criteria of DM. Prediabetes is a risk factor for development
of DM.4 Multiple studies have described cats with abnormal BGs in various clinical and experimental
contexts5,6; however, no study has shown that a defined state of abnormal glucose in cats confers a risk
for developing DM.1 Therefore, criteria for diagnosis of prediabetes in cats have not been established.

ETIOLOGY AND CLASSIFICATION
Multiple etiologies can lead to DM.1 Feline DM is mostly considered analogous to type 2 DM in people,
characterized by beta cell dysfunction of unknown etiology, usually with concurrent insulin resistance.
This leads to either permanent or temporary states of exogenous insulin requirement.
Recent studies suggest that up to 25% of diabetic cats suffer from DM secondary to
hypersomatotropism (DM-HS; ch. 280).7 However, most studies on etiology, pathophysiology, and
epidemiology of feline DM were published before HS was commonly recognized. Thus, most cats with
DM-HS were probably misdiagnosed as having uncomplicated type 2 DM.
Other types of diabetes resulting from processes that cause beta cell dysfunction or loss occur in a
minority of affected cats. Pancreatitis can destroy beta cells (chs. 276, 278). Histopathologic evidence of
beta cell deficiency associated with lymphocytic infiltration (consistent with type 1 DM) has been
described rarely. With the exception of the serum insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) assay for
identification of DM-HS, there is no ante mortem test to classify the other etiologic types of feline DM.
From a clinical perspective, virtually all cats with DM are handled similarly. Importantly, many cats that
survive an episode of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA, ch. 280) can later achieve diabetic remission.8
BOX 2 92 .1 A LIV E ∗ C rit e r ia for D iagnos is of D iab e te s Me llit u s in C ats
The potential for stress hyperglycemia warrants caution in interpretation of hyperglycemia of any
magnitude in cats. Diabetes mellitus in cats is diagnosed:
1. In a patient with a random (fasted or unfasted) blood glucose concentration ≥270 mg/dL (≥15
mmol/L) with classic clinical signs of hyperglycemia (with no other plausible cause) or
hyperglycemic crisis AND at least one of the following criteria:
• increased glycated proteins
• glucosuria on more than one occasion on a naturally voided sample acquired in a home
environment at least 2 days after any stressful events.
In some cases clinical signs may not have been reported by the owner.
2. In a patient with random (fasted or unfasted) blood glucose concentration >125 mg/dL to ≤270
mg/dL (>7 mmol/L to ≤15 mmol/L) and at least two of the following:
• classic clinical signs of hyperglycemia (with no other plausible cause) or hyperglycemic
crisis
• increased glycated proteins
• glucosuria on more than one occasion on a naturally voided sample acquired in a home
environment at least 2 days after any stressful events.
Applying the above ALIVE criteria permits the possible existence of a subpopulation of cats where
diabetes mellitus or stress hyperglycemia cannot be confidently confirmed or excluded; if concerns
over presence of diabetes mellitus persist, periodic re-evaluation is warranted.

Project ALIVE (Agreeing Language In Veterinary Endocrinology) was founded by the European
Society of Veterinary Endocrinology in 2016 and endorsed by the Society for Comparative
Endocrinology in 2017. It focuses on creating agreement over the definition of common
terminology in veterinary endocrinology.

EPIDEMIOLOGY
The prevalence of DM in cats ranges from 0.5-2% depending on the population studied.9-11 Numbers are
steadily increasing due to the increasing frequency of predisposing factors, e.g., obesity and physical
inactivity.12-14 This is similar to human type 2 DM. Importantly, DM in cats is generally diagnosed later
in the disease process than in people, in whom diagnosis of DM is based on fasting hyperglycemia >126

mg/dL (>7 mmol/L).10 In contrast, the diagnosis in cats is often delayed until BGs exceed the renal
threshold (>270 mg/dL, >15 mmol/L)15,16 and clinical signs (polyuria/polydipsia/polyphagia
[PU/PD/PP], weight loss) are evident.17,18 This delay in diagnosis may explain why most cats are
insulin-dependent at diagnosis and why diet changes and oral hypoglycemic drugs are not typically
sufficient to control DM early after diagnosis.18
DM is most common in Domestic Long- and Shorthair cats. Most pure-breed cats are
underrepresented.12,19 However, in the UK, Australia, and New Zealand, Burmese cats are overrepresented.11,19-21 DM appears to be an autosomal, partially penetrant, dominant trait in Burmese cats
with about 4 times higher frequency than other breeds.20,21 Genome-wide association studies have
identified polymorphisms in genes related to beta cell function and lipid metabolism.22,23 Other
susceptible breeds include Tonkinese and Norwegian Forest in the UK, and Maine Coon, Russian Blue,
and Siamese in the USA.19,20,24
Increasing age is a risk factor; most cats are diagnosed at >8 years of age with peak incidence at 10-13
years.9,10,12 Neutered male cats are at greater risk than neutered females, even when controlled for body
weight.9,12 Other risk factors include indoor confinement and little physical activity.25 Obesity (ch.
150), increasingly prevalent in pet cats, causes insulin resistance, interferes with glycemic control, and
confers a high risk of DM in cats.9,12-14,26-29 In the USA, it has been estimated that 25-35% of pet cats
are overweight or obese.13,27,30 Environmental factors (e.g., living indoors, diet) predispose cats to
obesity.27,30 The risk of obesity is highest among middle-aged, neutered male cats, the same group that
is at increased risk of DM.27,30

FEATURES OF TYPE 2 DM IN CATS
Type 2 DM is a diagnosis of exclusion in cats—one to be considered only after ruling out HS. The
etiology of feline type 2 DM is unknown but likely similar to type 2 DM in people.1 Similarities include
risk factors, clinical presentation, epidemiology, and association with amyloid deposition in the islets of
Langerhans.1 Periods when exogenous insulin is not required are common and genetic predisposition
has been demonstrated in both cats and people.31 Type 2 DM is a progressive disease that can have a
prolonged preclinical period. It is characterized by the combination of impaired insulin secretion and
insulin resistance. Impaired secretion results in insulin deficiency, which is usually relative (rather than
absolute) to the overall increased insulin requirement resulting from insulin resistance. Although
obesity itself causes some degree of insulin resistance, it is not the cause of type 2 DM. Instead, obesity
leads to a compensatory increase in insulin secretion. Obese diabetic individuals have impaired beta cell
function whereas obese non-diabetics do not (ch. 150).
The melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R), expressed in the hypothalamus, mediates satiety when there is
positive energy balance.31 It is also expressed in intestinal L cells and mediates the secretion of the
incretin hormone glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1).32 In human obesity and DM, MC4R is a major
susceptibility gene. Polymorphism in the MC4R gene was demonstrated in obese diabetic cats but not in
obese non-diabetic cats.31 Thus, cats with this gene polymorphism may be predisposed to reduced
incretin effect when obese, and so be more likely to develop DM.

FACTORS ASSOCIATED WITH DM REMISSION
REMISSION IS NOT A “CURE”
There is no known cure for type 2 DM and remission of DM in cats is defined as a state of euglycemia
with no insulin therapy for at least 4 weeks when insulin was previously administered.33 Achieving
remission does not imply that the underlying disease has been cured but that endogenous insulin
secretion is meeting or exceeding requirements. Cats in remission usually continue to display impaired
glucose tolerance.34 Remission is a temporary state (although it might last for years) and, therefore,

efforts to maintain it and treat any underlying disease should be considered. One possible exception is
DM remission in cats treated for HS. In these cats, surgical removal of the growth-hormone secreting
tumor might be curative. Because it is by definition temporary, some question whether remission should
be a treatment goal in all cats with DM. That also raises the question of which cats are more likely to
achieve remission. Answers to these questions are not available, but remission is associated with longer
survival in some studies.35 Here we discuss the available evidence and pathophysiologic background.

PHYSIOLOGY OF REMISSION
Overview
For a cat with type 2 DM to achieve remission, beta cell capacity to synthesize and secrete insulin must
meet or exceed insulin requirements. Insulin requirements decrease with decreased insulin resistance
and decreased carbohydrate load. Insulin resistance can be reduced with weight loss, resolution of
inflammatory conditions, pharmacological intervention (insulin sensitizers, discontinuing
glucocorticoids and any drug that causes insulin resistance), and resolution of stress. Carbohydrate load
can be decreased by reducing dietary carbohydrates or reducing carbohydrate digestion (e.g., with
acarbose), by suppressing hepatic glucose output with pharmacological interventions (e.g., metformin,
glucagon receptor antagonists), or by enhancing glucosuria, e.g., sodium-glucose cotransporter-2
(SGLT-2) inhibitors.
While the cause of underlying beta cell dysfunctions that lead to type 2 DM is unknown, some
metabolic derangements that cause further beta cell dysfunction are somewhat reversible. Reversing
metabolic derangements such as glucotoxicity, lipotoxicity, and impaired incretin effect can lead to
substantial improvement in beta cell function that could make the difference between whether or not
remission is achieved.

Glucotoxicity and Lipotoxicity of Beta Cells
Longstanding hyperglycemia and hyperlipidemia are both toxic to beta cells, causing dysfunction and
eventually beta cell death. Glucotoxicity causing beta cell dysfunction occurred within 48 hours of IV
glucose infusion in healthy cats.36 After 10 days of hyperglycemia, beta cell dysfunction and markedly
reduced cell numbers persisted for some time after discontinuation of glucose infusion. Hyperlipidemia
does not have as dramatic an effect although it did seem to affect the cats’ ability to regulate BG.36 The
effect of lipotoxicity on feline beta cells may have been underestimated since mostly unsaturated fatty
acids were infused. In other species, saturated fatty acids are more injurious than unsaturated fatty
acids.37

Glucolipotoxicity and the Incretin Effect
Glucolipotoxicity can cause beta cell dysfunction by interrupting the incretin effect.38 Incretin hormones
(glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide [GIP]; GLP-1) are secreted from the intestine in response
to glucose and other nutrients in the gut lumen (but not in the blood).39 In a glucose-dependent
manner, incretins stimulate synthesis and secretion of insulin and inhibit glucagon secretion. Incretin
hormones also prevent beta cell apoptosis in response to injurious toxins (such as glucocorticoid drugs)
and enhance beta cell differentiation and proliferation.40,41 Incretin hormones are responsible for about
75% of postprandial insulin secretion in healthy people and abnormalities in incretin hormone secretion
or action lead to substantial beta cell dysfunction.
In people with type 2 DM, GIP secretion is normal or increased but beta cells become resistant to its
effects. This resistance can be partially reversed by treating DM. In contrast, GLP-1 secretion is
suppressed in type 2 DM but it retains effect on beta cells, at least at pharmacological levels. GLP-1
receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are useful for people with type 2 DM and can delay the need for insulin
therapy by years. Generally, the physiology of GLP-1 and the pharmacology of its analogs are similar in
cats and people.42 The role of GLP-1 analogs in inducing and maintaining DM remission or in treatment
of prediabetes in cats has not been established. In one study, newly diagnosed DM cats were treated with
insulin glargine U100 in addition to either the GLP-1RA exenatide-extended-release (ER) or placebo.43
Exenatide-ER caused no significant adverse effects, improved metabolic outcomes, but did not increase

remission rates. Studies in cats are hampered by the lack of a practical method of assessing pretreatment residual beta cell function. It is likely a proportion of cats in this cohort was not capable of
responding, diluting its perceived effect. Until practical beta cell function tests become available, it is not
possible to identify good candidate cats with DM for GLP-1RA treatment. Similarly, there is potential for
GLP-1RAs to maintain the prediabetic state in some cats, delaying or preventing progression to an
insulin dependent state.

PRACTICAL CONSIDERATIONS IN ACHIEVING REMISSION
Key Questions to Be Answered
The key questions that need answers pertaining to DM remission in cats are: 1) Can cats most likely to
achieve remission be identified? 2) Which treatment strategies are most likely to result in remission? 3)
Once achieved, how can remission be maintained? For all 3, there is little or no evidence on which to
base recommendations. Considering the pathophysiologic mechanisms, it is likely that tight glycemic
control, reduced carbohydrate load, and/or resolution of insulin resistance are needed. These treatments
should be implemented as early as possible in the course of the disease, before beta cell loss. The relative
importance of each of these components is mostly unknown for the general population, let alone for the
specific patient. Currently, all studies evaluate remission in cats that first present with DM at the time
clinical signs are evident. With earlier diagnosis, the medications and dietary manipulations may have
had more success in inducing remission.

Cats Likely to Achieve Remission
The likelihood of achieving remission is an important question to consider after diagnosing DM because
it affects choice of treatment and monitoring strategies. In a systematic review published in 2014,44 all
available studies were ranked based on objective criteria for scientific validity. Remission was more
likely in cats with “milder” or earlier DM when BGs are relatively low, hyperlipidemia not present, and
the reported disease duration is shorter. Remission is also more likely in older cats, potentially
representing a different disease etiology or slower progression of the same disease, and in cats with a
history of glucocorticoid therapy if discontinued when DM was diagnosed. Remission rates vary widely
in studies (0-100%). Remission rates of 30-50% were most common. Most studies were conducted at
academic institutions where cats received relatively intensive monitoring. Remission rates of only 13%
were identified from medical records of 524 cats diagnosed and treated by general practitioners in the
UK.45 Testing for HS was not consistent and this low remission rate may reflect the high prevalence of
unrecognized HS as a cause of DM. Another study of data from general practices reported much higher
remission rates, although DM was diagnosed without measuring glycated proteins and the criteria for
remission were relatively lax.35

Insulin Treatment and Monitoring Strategies Most Likely to Achieve Remission
In the 2014 systematic review, remission was reported in cats that had been treated with various insulin
formulations, including older insulins (e.g., protamine zinc insulin [PZI], lente) and newer formulations
(e.g., glargine, detemir), oral hypoglycemic drugs (acarbose, glipizide), and a variety of diets.44
However, there were few side-by-side comparisons to better understand the efficacy of diets,
medications, or treatment strategies, in the same clinical setting and using the same diagnostic criteria.
Thus, insufficient evidence was found to suggest that any particular insulin formulation was more likely
to lead to remission.44 In the only prospective randomized clinical trial, no difference in remission rates
was found between insulin glargine U100 and PZI in 46 cats fed a “low carbohydrate diet.”46

Diets Most Likely to Aid in Achieving Remission (ch. 155)
One prospective randomized clinical trial comparing 2 diets on the rate of DM remission in cats with
similar body weights47 showed higher remission rates (68% versus 41%) in cats fed a canned low
carbohydrate (3.5 g/100 kcal), low fiber (0.1 g/100 kcal) diet (N = 31; Science Diet Feline Growth, Hill’s
Pet Nutrition) when compared with cats fed a canned moderate carbohydrate (7.6 g/100 kcal), higher
fiber (3.1 g/100 kcal) diet (N = 32; Hill’s Prescription Diet Feline w/d, Hill’s Pet Nutrition). These 2 diets

had similar protein content from different sources, but fat content was 20% higher in the lowcarbohydrate, low-fiber diet.

Monitoring Strategies Most Likely to Achieve Remission
One retrospective, non-randomized study compared monitoring strategies in the same clinical setting on
remission rates.48 Cats with newly diagnosed DM fed a “low carbohydrate” diet (Purina DM and Hill’s
MD, dry vs. canned not specified) and treated with insulin glargine U100 to maintain near-euglycemia
(target BG 60-160 mg/dL, 3.3-8.9 mmol/L) as measured with a human point-of-care glucose meter
designed to overestimate hypoglycemia had a higher remission rate (78%) when compared to a group
managed with a traditional paradigm in which changes in insulin dose were based mainly on clinical
signs (14% of 36).48 The frequency of biochemical and clinical hypoglycemia was similar in both
treatment groups.

Maintaining Remission
Remission does not equal cure and most cats in remission continue to display impaired glucose
tolerance.34,49 Disease progression, increased carbohydrate load, and/or increasing insulin resistance
can over time lead to recurrence of a transient or permanent insulin-dependent state. Currently, no
studies have evaluated specific interventions for the maintenance of remission or the rate of relapse with
no treatment. Based on the pathophysiologic mechanisms, it is likely that the same interventions that
might lead to induction of remission would also help maintain it. These include minimizing insulin
resistance, minimizing carbohydrate load, and optimizing beta cell function.

INSULIN THERAPY
THE CHALLENGES
Insulin therapy is associated with many inherent challenges that must be overcome for treatment to be
safe, effective, and sustainable. These challenges relate to the complex nature of glycemic control,
pharmacological limitations of available insulin formulations, and the lifelong burden on caregivers.
These issues have been significantly diminished in human medicine with the shift from traditional
insulin suspensions that require the use of syringe and needles, to the use of recombinant insulin
analogues, novel application methods such as injection pens, and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM)
systems (Box 292.2).

INITIATING EXOGENOUS INSULIN THERAPY
Most cats require exogenous insulin therapy when diagnosed with DM. Alternatives should only be
considered when insulin is not possible. In a cat with clinical signs, delaying insulin therapy, even while
implementing hypoglycemic drugs, weight loss, and/or dietary carbohydrate restriction, increases risk of
glucolipotoxicity and decreases chance of remission. Low doses of insulin should be used in cats with
mild hyperglycemia and no clinical signs. In such cats, euglycemia and remission might be achieved with
alternative treatments, but there is risk of continuing beta cell injury from glucolipotoxicity if alternative
treatments fail.

GENERAL PRINCIPLES; THERE IS NO PERFECT INSULIN
There is little evidence that any one insulin formulation is superior for treating cats with DM. Insulin
formulations vary in their average time-action profile, day-to-day variability, cost, and methods of
administration. Currently, there are 2 insulin formulations specifically for cats but more than 10 human
formulations commercially available, some of which are routinely used in cats. The choice of an insulin
formulation depends on many factors which differ cat-to-cat and may differ in one cat at different times.
Factors include disease pathophysiology (including concurrent diseases), insulin-related factors
(including insulin pharmacology, cost, regional prescribing regulations), pet and owner compliance, diet
(composition and feeding frequency), monitoring strategy, and goals of therapy for that cat, taking into
account risk of hypoglycemia and likelihood of remission (Figure 292.1).
