Physiologic bolus insulin secretion in cats typically has a longer duration and a later and much lower
peak than in people or dogs. In many cats, insulin requirement is sustained with no clear bolus phase.
Note that this is a rough guide only as there is large individual variability depending on meal
composition, quantity consumed, and frequency of feeding.
The insulin chosen should best fit the specific clinical situation. Often, opposing needs will result in
compromise. For example, for a fractious cat or for an owner struggling to give injections, minimizing
the number of injections by using a long-acting insulin formulation once-daily might be a necessary
compromise even if glycemic control is not optimal. In contrast, an insulin formulation that is shorter in
duration of action but less expensive might be ideal for an owner that can easily administer insulin but
has cost constraints.

INSULIN PHYSIOLOGY: PEOPLE VS. CATS
In healthy people, a physiologic post-eating “bolus” of insulin secretion lasts 2-4 hours with 5-fold
increases in insulin peak concentrations from baseline,50 depending on the type and quantity of food. In
healthy cats, bolus insulin secretion has a longer duration (6 to >12 hr), occurs later, and has a much
lower peak (1.5-3 times baseline) at 1-8 hours, depending on the diet fed (Table 292.1).26,51,52 These
data may be misleading since cats in these studies were fasted for relatively long periods before being fed
a single meal. When once daily feeding was compared to 4 feedings per day in healthy cats, insulin
increased as described above with the single meal, but when the daily caloric intake was fed as 4 meals,
the increase in plasma insulin was minimal and sustained for the 24 hour period.53 This sustained
insulin requirement with no clear bolus phase is likely more representative of clinical insulin
requirements of cats.

COMMERCIALLY AVAILABLE INSULINS

SUSPENSIONS: LENTE, NEUTRAL PROTAMINE HAGEDORN (NPH),
PROTAMINE ZINC INSULIN (PZI)
Insulin’s natural tendency to crystallize is enhanced in these suspensions by adding either zinc (lente),
protamine (NPH), or both (PZI) to the formulation, causing precipitation in the vial and in tissue after
being injected.54 Slowing insulin absorption by enhancing its crystallization leads to slower onset and
longer duration of action. These insulins must be evenly resuspended before each use by gently rolling
and inverting the vial or, in the case of Vetsulin/Caninsulin (Merck/MSD Animal Health), to vigorously
shake the vial until the insulin is completely mixed. Resuspension can be inconsistent and lead to
inaccurate dosing.55 Breakdown of the precipitate at the injection site is highly variable and
unpredictable, altering insulin absorption patterns.56-58 These formulations do not have time-action
profiles that mirror a cat’s insulin requirement. Onsets of action may be too slow or durations of action
too long to mimic a cat “bolus” phase or their time-action profiles are too peaked and duration of action
too brief to mimic “basal” secretion.54,58

RECOMBINANT ANALOGUE INSULIN SOLUTIONS
Overview
These long-acting insulin analogues were developed as “basal” formulations for use in people. Since they
do not need resuspension their effects are more consistent because the unpredictable resuspension
process is bypassed. The vial or pen does not require rolling or shaking prior to drawing a dose. In
addition, absorption from the subcutaneous (SC) depot is less erratic. Because of superior predictability
(low day-to-day variability), these formulations are associated with lower risk of hypoglycemia.
Pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and guidelines for frequency of administration of specific insulin
formulations are presented in Table 292.2.

Insulin Glargine
Insulin glargine is soluble at pH 4.0 (in which it is supplied) but in neutral pH (such as SC tissue) it has
a strong tendency to precipitate, slowing its absorption.59 The precipitation-deprecipitation process
does introduce a component of variability in absorption but glargine is more predictable than NPH and,
likely, other suspensions, but might be less predictable than other insulin analogs.57,60 Insulin glargine
U300 (Toujeo, Sanofi) is biochemically identical to insulin glargine U100 (e.g., Lantus, Sanofi), but 3
times more concentrated.61 The concentrated glargine U300 delivers any dose in a smaller droplet with
smaller surface area, its absorption is slower, its duration is longer, its time-action profile is flatter, and
it is associated with less day-to-day variability when compared to insulin glargine U100.60-63 Emerging
evidence from several small studies and clinical experience suggests that insulin glargine U300 provides
better control of DM than insulin glargine U100, although its duration of action is often insufficient for
once daily administration (Table 292.2).64,65

Insulin Detemir
In contrast to insulin glargine U100 and insulin suspensions, the actions of insulin detemir are highly
predictable in people, with minimal inter- and intra-subject variability, key to minimizing hypoglycemic
events (Table 292.2).66-70 Detemir inhibits hepatic glucose output more effectively than other basal
insulin products, decreases adipose tissue lipogenesis, and weight gain is minimized.68-71 Preferential
insulinization of the liver and low day-to-day variability have yet to be demonstrated in cats. The
duration of action of insulin detemir is usually too brief for once-daily basal use.72
Because of its low potency in people, insulin detemir is formulated at a concentration 4 times higher
(2400 nmol/mL, 100 U/mL; Levemir, Novo Nordisk) than other insulin formulations, e.g., Lantus, 600
nmol/mL, 100 U/mL. Low potency is likely explained by most insulin detemir molecules being bound to
albumin in plasma, allowing only a fraction to be biologically active.73 This is likely true in cats
considering that the dose range required for achieving good glycemic control is similar (median of about

2 U/cat q12h) for insulin detemir and insulin glargine U100.74,75 Insulin detemir should be started
using the same dose used for other formulations in cats. Insulin detemir (or any insulin) should not be
diluted.

Insulin Degludec
Insulin degludec, originally formulated for every-other-day use in people with DM, is now usually given
once-daily without need for rigid injection schedules, improving patient compliance (Table 292.2). In
people, it reaches steady state within days and has minimal inter-day fluctuation even when the time of
injection is inconsistent,76 making it an ideal basal insulin in people. In cats however, the duration of
action of insulin degludec is limited to about 12 hours and it has a pronounced peak.65

“INTERMEDIATE”-ACTING INSULIN FORMULATIONS
Overview
Commercially available insulin suspensions (NPH, NPH/regular mixes, lente, and PZI), insulin glargine
U100, and detemir are categorized as “intermediate”-acting formulations that require q12h
administration for best results in cats (Table 292.2). These insulins are often associated with different
required vs delivered doses, causing fluctuation in intra-day BGs. This may be less obvious in cats with
residual beta cell function, because their endogenous insulin can “close the gap” between required and
delivered insulin. In contrast, cats with no residual beta cell function are more prone to substantial
glycemic variability.

Goals With Intermediate-Acting Insulins
The usual goal when using q12h “intermediate”-acting insulin protocols is alleviation of DM-associated
clinical signs. Since BG fluctuates each day and there is substantial inter-day variability, the goals should
be BGs that range from normal (80-100 mg/dL; 4.5-5.5 mmol/L) at their lowest and 250-350 mg/dL
(14-19 mmol/L) at their highest each day. Although uncommonly realized,77,78 the “ideal” curve would
begin with BGs at the high end just prior to giving insulin and lowest (nadir) about 6 hours later.79,80
Glycated protein concentrations remain above reference intervals using this approach and absence of
PU/PD may indicate good glycemic control, over-dose if episodes of hypoglycemia, or remission of DM.

Durations of Action, Induction of Remission
In cats, porcine lente and NPH insulins tend to have shorter durations of action compared with PZI,
glargine U100, detemir, and degludec.72,81,82 Once-daily high doses of PZI, glargine U100, or detemir
can achieve acceptable levels of clinical control, especially in cats with residual beta cell function, but
with increased risk of hypoglycemia. Insulin glargine U100 has been touted as advantageous in inducing
remission in cats with DM but the studies were uncontrolled, non-randomized, and there is little
compelling evidence to support this claim.44 In a small clinical study, q24h insulin glargine U100 was
compared with q12h porcine lente in cats.83 Both treatment groups experienced improved glycemia, 4 of
13 cats achieved remission of DM, but only 1 of these was in the glargine U100 group. Other studies
comparing glargine U100 to either PZI or detemir found no differences in remission rates.46,74,75

LONG-ACTING “BASAL” INSULIN FORMULATIONS
Commercially available basal insulins have time-action profiles evenly distributed from soon after
injection until metabolized, usually effective for 8-24 hours without a distinct peak. Basal formulations
are appropriate for most cats with DM, since most do not have a postprandial bolus insulin requirement
(Table 292.2). They have slow food transit times, should be fed multiple times a day, and/or fed a low
carbohydrate diet.84 Use of basal insulin may negate need for timing insulin administration to a meal.
For a basal insulin to be effective and safe as a once-daily injection, it should provide relatively constant

action throughout each 24-hour period. From experience and studies, insulin glargine U300 (Toujeo)
comes closest to meeting these standards in cats.64,65

COMPLIANCE, ADHERENCE, CONVENIENCE, COST
Owner Quality of Life
Owners’ response to surveys about administering insulin injections to their cats with DM85 revealed that
one great concern was the effect of this responsibility on the owners’ quality of life, rather than that of
the cat (Box 292.2). Worries about who would care for their cat if the owner was unavailable were
common. It is surmised that veterinarians must be flexible and offer insulin treatment options that are
client focused, particularly with respect to injection timing. It is unknown how the act of injection affects
cats’ compliance and the owners’ short- and long-term decisions to treat with insulin. It is reasonable to
assume that the high euthanasia rate (40%) upon diagnosis of DM is associated, at least in part, with
compliance.86

Factors in Adhering to Insulin Protocol
Studies on diabetic people show that adherence declines with increasing dosing frequency,87 if
injections are painful, due to forgetfulness or other priorities or regimen complexity (more than 1
medication, need to draw up insulin doses), and cost.88,89 For cats and cat owners, strategies that
reduce these barriers would likely result in greater treatment success, improved quality of life for pet and
owner, and an increase in percent of DM cats treated. In this context it is important to consider not just
the treatment choice per se, but also how it affects monitoring intensity and cost. For example, giving a
human recombinant basal insulin q24h using a convenient stress-free insulin pen may achieve
reasonably good glycemic control with minimal day-to-day variability, low risk of hypoglycemia (another
owner concern), and less need for intense monitoring. Cost and availability vary by geographic location,
e.g., veterinary formulations are relatively more expensive than human formulations in some countries
(Australia, Brazil) but the opposite is true in the USA. In the UK and parts of Europe, regulation requires
that veterinary products be used first in the prescribing cascade.

FIGURE 292.2 “Priming” the needle (“air shot”) with 1-3 U is recommended
prior to every injection. This potentially makes use of pens less economical for
cats, since their doses are usually small. From Feldman E, Fracassi F, Peterson

SYRINGE VS PEN FOR INSULIN ADMINISTRATION
Attributes of Pens
Multiple studies have identified advantages to using insulin dosing-pens rather than multi-dose insulin
vials and syringe-needles. Advantages include improved patient adherence,90,91 less frequent
hypoglycemic events,92,93 and overall healthcare cost-savings.93,94 Most people preferred the pen over
vial-syringe and consider it easier to use. Insulin pens are especially easier to use by those with visual
impairments or dexterity problems. They result in better patient satisfaction and improved quality of
life.90,91 Also, injection pens are consistently shown to be more accurate and precise compared to

insulin syringes,95-97 especially with small doses (<5 U). The relative imprecision of vial-syringe method
can be critical in causing day-to-day variability, which subsequently makes monitoring more
complicated and more expensive.
When using a traditional insulin syringe, for a target dose of 1 U, 50% of drawn doses were >20%
different than the target dose and most syringe-measured doses exceeded the intended dose.98,99
Currently, one insulin dosing pen is produced for Vetsulin/Caninsulin (VetPen, MSD Animal Health) (
Videos 291.2, 291.3). Initial pilot studies have shown the device to be easy to use in dogs, well
tolerated under real-life conditions, more accurate, wastes less insulin, and is preferred by a majority of
owners.100-102 Other available insulin dosing pens were designed for use in humans. Used as directed by
the manufacturer, such pens may be too expensive for common use in some countries (e.g., USA).

Delivery of 0.5 Unit Increments
Most pens are limited to deliver 1 U increments with no 0.5 U option. While a disadvantage when
compared with vial-syringes, the latter is also associated with low accuracy at 0.5 U dose increments.98

Practical Modifications to Insulin Injection Pen Protocols
Clinical experience suggests that with some modifications to the standard protocol of injection pen use,
substantial cost reductions can be achieved without significant compromise. Modifications should be
used with caution however, considering the lack of supportive clinical research. Insulin dosing pens are
tested for short-term stability (<42 days) without refrigeration. Keeping pens refrigerated between
dosing likely reduces the likelihood of bacterial contamination, allowing use until the insulin vial has
been completely emptied. Some pens have been used for months, substantially reducing cost. In contrast
to reports from people, injection of cold insulin does not seem painful to cats.
“Priming” the insulin dosing pen (“air shot”) with 1-3 U is recommended prior to every injection,
potentially making use of pens less economical for cats (Figure 292.2). A new pen should be primed to
verify that it works, but one USA-based author (CG) does not recommend further priming. Without
regular priming, air bubbles in the pen might interfere with accurate dosing or a pen becoming faulty
might not be noticed. These possibilities must be considered and the pen checked if a cat does not
respond to insulin as expected. It is also advisable to regularly check the insulin reservoir visually and
then eject any air bubbles. The problem of air bubbles can also be avoided by tilting the pen during
injection so that the plunger is higher than the needle tip, allowing the air bubbles to move away from
the needle. In people, it is recommended to keep the needle of the pen under the skin after injection for
at least 3 seconds to allow the dose to be completely delivered. This does not seem to be necessary with
the small doses used in cats with DM. A more comprehensive review of the use of insulin injection pens
can be found elsewhere.103

TIMING INSULIN ADMINISTRATION WITH FEEDING OR
WITH PRE-INSULIN BGs
It is not necessary to match food ingestion with insulin injections in cats, regardless of insulin used. In
cats treated with basal insulin, there is usually no need to adjust insulin dose for a specific meal based on
amount of food consumed. It is not necessary or effective to change an insulin dose based on preinjection BGs, as a substantial effect of any administered dose is achieved many hours after injection.

NON-INSULIN HYPOGLYCEMIC AGENTS
OVERVIEW AND SCENARIOS FAVORING THEIR USE
Non-insulin hypoglycemic agents include a variety of drug families with an array of pharmacological
targets.103 Most have not been rigorously studied in cats (Table 292.3). Commercially available noninsulin drugs may be useful as sole therapy when sufficient beta cells are present, usually early in the
disease process before BGs exceed renal threshold, preventing or postponing the need for insulin
therapy. Such drugs may be used together with insulin, to improve glycemic control and potentially

reduce dose or frequency of insulin injections. Non-insulin therapies are not usually sufficient for
managing later stages of DM.

SPECIFIC AGENTS (TABLE 292.3)
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists (GLP-1RAs)
GLP-1RAs, the most promising family of non-insulin hypoglycemic drugs, stimulate insulin while
inhibiting glucagon secretion only during hyperglycemia, making them exceedingly safe. By slowing
gastric emptying, GLP-1 slows digestion and absorption of carbohydrates, curbing postprandial
hyperglycemia. GLP-1RAs also decrease appetite and promote weight loss. Limited data suggest the
effects of GLP-1RA in cats include weight loss, insulin stimulation during hyperglycemia, and slowing
gastric emptying rates.104-107 The GLP-1RA exenatide was shown to curb weight gain, lower insulin
requirement, and decrease glycemic variability in diabetic cats.43,108,109 The duration of action of
exenatide-ER is longer than 30 days in cats, with few side-effects.43

Glipizide
Glipizide, a second-generation sulfonylurea, requires some functioning beta cells to have effect. When
50 newly diagnosed cats with DM were given 5 mg/cat q12h, 56% deteriorated within the first 22 weeks
and left the study.110 The remaining 44% improved, with 6 of the 50 cats (12%) achieving remission.
Side-effects were mild and transient (hypoglycemia in 6 cats, anorexia and vomiting in 8 cats, and
transient icterus with abnormal liver enzyme activities in 4 cats). There was no mortality.

Acarbose
Acarbose, an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor, decreases glucose absorption from the gastrointestinal tract.
Twenty-four cats with DM were given acarbose in addition to insulin and a canned low carbohydrate

diet.111 Remission was associated with weight loss but not with acarbose. No side-effects were described,
but diarrhea and flatulence occur in other species.

SGLT-2 Antagonists
SGLT-2 antagonists cause increased renal excretion of glucose. Short-term clinical trials in diabetic cats
have reported that bexagliflozin and velogliflozin are well tolerated in people and effectively decrease BG
concentrations.112,113 Long-term studies are required to assess the safety, survival and quality of life of
cats treated with these drugs compared to insulin. These agents do not require dose titration nor
increase the risk of hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy, so less intensive glycemic monitoring is
required compared with insulin therapy. However, ketosis occurs in a proportion of cats treated with
SGLT-2 antagonists, especially in the first 7 days. Ketosis can progress to either euglycemic or
hyperglycemic ketoacidosis. Therefore, treatment with SGLT-2 antagonists is only recommended for
cats that are well. Ketones in blood or urine should be closely monitored for at least the first week of
treatment and whenever the cat becomes unwell. Prompt insulin treatment is required if there is ketosis.

MONITORING
MONITORING BASED ON GOALS OF THERAPY
Tight Control vs Risk of Hypoglycemia
It is not known if remission of DM in cats is proportional to their level of hyperglycemia, related to a
certain threshold of hyperglycemia, to glycemic variability, or other factors. Regardless, there is scarce
evidence supporting tight glycemic control to improve likelihood of DM remission,48,75 but it may be
associated with increased risk of clinical hypoglycemia.114 There is abundant evidence from other
species that over time, hypoglycemia (even when subclinical and/or intermittent and sporadic) and high
glycemic variability lead to impaired counterregulatory responses and increased risk of fatal insulininduced hypoglycemia. Multiple well-established mechanisms explain this issue in people, rodents, and
dogs.115-118 Because it is potentially fatal, avoiding “hypoglycemia” is critically important, but there are
no guidelines for cats defining unacceptable levels of hypoglycemia (both in terms of absolute
concentrations or duration), or how they translate to low interstitial glucose concentrations (IGcs).
Heavier cats appear to be at greater risk of hypoglycemia, suggesting an association of insulin overdose
with obesity.119 Increased glycemic variability appears to be more common in cats with concurrent
diseases and those that fail to achieve DM remission, although causality has not been established.108,120

Potential for Long-Term Attrition in Owner Adherence and/or Pet Compliance
What may seem to be an ideal treatment and monitoring plan in the short term can result in problems
over time if owners reach the limit of their resources (financial and others). This is especially true if
concurrent diseases develop (ch. 224). With some cats and owners, minimalist treatment and
monitoring approaches might be preferable. It may help to identify goals that improve chances of
survival and quality of life for both cat and owner (Box 292.2).

MONITORING BASED ON CLINICAL SIGNS
Using Only Clinical Signs
With any DM monitoring strategy, assessment of clinical signs is crucial. In many cats, it is possible to
achieve reasonably good control when monitoring only clinical signs. While subclinical hypoglycemia
cannot be ruled out, careful and strategic dose alterations based on clinical signs can minimize that risk
without measuring BGs.

Body Weight
After ruling out other causes, weight loss in a cat with DM is a sign of overall insulin deficiency while
excessive weight gain might be a sign of overdosing. However, even in an animal that is losing weight,

hypoglycemia is a real possibility if insulin duration is too short and the dose is increased to compensate
for its short duration.

Water Intake and Urine Output
Severity of PU/PD can reflect glycemic regulation. Quantification of a diabetic cat’s water intake is ideal
but not always feasible. Water bowls that measure and report individual water intake (e.g., Felaqua) are
available. If exact quantification is not feasible, when questioning owners it is important to inquire about
changes since the last time therapy was altered and not focus only on absolute values. Some owners
report no change as “normal” because they have become accustomed to some degree of PU/PD.

Initial Low-Dose Insulin and PU/PD
Changes in BGs might not be reflected in water intake or urine output, especially when BG
concentrations fluctuate below the renal threshold. Thus, over-regulation cannot always be
distinguished from good glycemic control. One way to differentiate the 2 is to begin insulin at a dosage
likely to be insufficient and then increase the dosage gradually every 2-4 weeks while carefully
monitoring clinical signs. When a dosage is reached without further improvement in PU/PD, it should
be assumed that no better control can be achieved without significantly risking hypoglycemia. At that
point, it is recommended to decrease the dosage of insulin (by about 20-25%) and to continue reducing
it gradually (every 2-4 weeks) until PU/PD worsens. If no clinical difference is observed between 2
dosages, it is always safer to choose the lower.

Changing Insulins
If no improvement is observed when an insulin dose is increased and the level of control is unacceptable
to an owner (weight loss, other signs), it is important to determine if the owner observations are reliable
and be certain that insulin injection technique is appropriate, the insulin formulation is correct and not
mishandled, and concurrent diseases have been excluded. Then, the formulation of insulin can be
changed and the process should start over.

Suspected Hypoglycemia
Some have incorrectly suggested serial BG monitoring to be “mandatory” when hypoglycemia is
suspected.16 However, BG curves are not sensitive for detecting hypoglycemia and there is usually a time
gap between observing suspicious clinical signs and performing a curve, especially when performed in
the hospital. During this gap in time, the cat remains at risk of hypoglycemia. An alternative safe
approach is to reduce the insulin dosage by at least 20-25% without measuring any BG. This approach
effectively ensures use of a dosage previously considered safe and potentially even too low. If the clinical
signs of suspected hypoglycemia resolve, even if PU/PD worsens, the dosage of insulin should not be
increased again. The cat may benefit from a different insulin formulation at this point or remain on the
lower dosage of insulin. The choice depends on how intolerable the clinical signs are to the owners. If the
clinical signs of suspected hypoglycemia (chs. 61, 289) do not resolve, either the dosage needs to be
decreased further, or the clinical signs were not caused by hypoglycemia. Depending on the clinical
context, more diagnostic tests, including use of a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) and/or BG curve,
may be indicated.

Remission Desired
Monitoring DM cats using clinical signs when clinical remission is desired is often best accomplished by
adding fructosamine and/or daily urine glucose testing. Insulin dosage can be increased gradually as
described but with goals of normalizing clinical signs, having the fructosamine within the reference
interval, and/or persistently negative glucosuria. Then, the insulin dosage can be decreased gradually
about every 1-4 weeks if clinical signs do not recur, fructosamine concentrations remain normal, and/or
urine remains negative for glucose.

MONITORING BASED ON GLYCATED PROTEINS
Attributes and Disadvantages of Glycated Protein Measurements

Glycated proteins, usually fructosamine or hemoglobin A1c, are produced over time and are not affected
by within-day, day-to-day, or acute BG fluctuations on the day of testing (stress, feeding). Use of
glycated proteins is convenient for assessing long-term treatment response trends. Measuring protein
glycation is especially useful when clinical signs are not apparent or when owners are unable to
accurately report clinical signs. The main advantage of measuring protein glycation is also its main
disadvantage: short-term hypoglycemic episodes are not captured and high concentrations of glycated
proteins do not rule out episodes of hypoglycemia.

Inaccurate Glycated Protein Results
Use of glycated proteins assumes no abnormality in protein concentrations or half-lives. Fructosamine
values increase when the half-lives of serum proteins increase (e.g., hypothyroidism) and decrease when
the half-lives decrease (e.g., hyperthyroidism, protein-losing enteropathies). Results from lipemic
and/or hemolyzed samples are not reliable.

Fructosamine
Serum fructosamine concentrations are determined by BG concentrations over the previous 2 to 3
weeks. Fructosamine reference values for various degrees of glycemic control are not well-established
for cats with DM, do not consistently reflect its range of biological variability, and results do not always
match clinical observations. Comparing results from 1 cat over time are more useful. One should obtain
a baseline result to compare with any result after a treatment change, using the trends rather than the
absolute numbers.

Hemoglobin A1c
Glycosylated hemoglobin has been validated in cats and is commercially available (A1Care, Baycom
Diagnostics). It is marketed worldwide, requiring a few drops of dried blood on a test card to be mailed
to the laboratory. The inter-day assay coefficient of variation is ≤5% (within 3 weeks of testing) and the
laboratory complies with the National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program (NGSP.org).
Hemoglobin A1c reflects average BG concentrations over the previous 70 days in cats and therefore will
not be useful for monitoring if frequent changes in therapy are made. It is useful when serum
fructosamine cannot be interpreted with confidence. There is anecdotal evidence that it could be useful
for diagnosis and monitoring of prediabetes in cats. Chronic anemia falsely increases A1c values but,
unlike serum fructosamine, A1c is not affected by hemolysis or abnormalities in serum protein turnover
rate. Also, in contrast to fructosamine, a recent study established the reference interval (1.9-3.1%) for
A1Care in 48 healthy cats.120a

DIRECT MONITORING OF BLOOD GLUCOSE (BG) OR URINE
GLUCOSE
Blood Glucose Curves
BG curves fluctuate considerably hour-to-hour and day-to-day in DM cats treated with insulin. These
fluctuations are caused by many factors, only one of which is the insulin dose. Therefore, treatment
decisions based on BG curves are not often successful. In one study, hypothetical insulin dosage
recommendations frequently differed when based on BG curve results that were performed within days
when conditions were otherwise equivalent (including insulin dosage, feeding, apparent stress levels,
etc.).121 The most valuable and reliable finding on any BG curve is hypoglycemia, which should always
warrant a change: either a decrease in insulin dosage or a change in formulation. However, because of
day-to-day variability, and especially when a BG curve is performed in the hospital or under other
stressful conditions, hypoglycemia cannot be ruled out based on a single curve even if all BGs were
increased. Hypoglycemia aside, other BG curve-derived parameters, including perceived duration of
insulin action, time of nadir, “insulin resistance,” etc., cannot be estimated with confidence based on a
single BG curve completed over the expected duration of a single insulin dose, especially with insulin
formulations known to have marked day-to-day variation. These parameters can be better estimated
based on CGM over a few days (ch. 78).

Glucosuria
Glucosuria in a cat with DM indicates that the BG concentrations have exceeded renal threshold during
the time the urine was formed. Thus, measuring glucose in a single urine sample has limited value.

However, because measuring urine glucose can be done by owners on a regular basis, they may warn
when increased risk of hypoglycemia is suspected. If no glucose is detected in the urine over e.g. 3-5
consecutive days, the insulin dosage should be decreased.

CONTINUOUS GLUCOSE MONITORING (CGM; ALSO SEE CH.
78)
Interstitial Glucose Concentrations (IGcs) Are Not Blood Glucose
Concentrations
Available CGM systems (CGMs) are similar in accuracy and differ mostly in cost and convenience. Since
CGMs measure IGc, not BG, results often differ both in absolute values and timing. There is a delay of a
few minutes (at least) between changes in BG concentration and changes in IGc. Depending on the rate
and direction of BG change, changes in BG are not always fully reflected in IGc. Comparing CGM
absolute values to BG concentrations might not be relevant.

Scenarios for Using a CGM
CGMs might be used exclusively as a less invasive method for cats that otherwise require traditional BG
curves, an approach that underutilizes this technology. The authors use the FreeStyle Libre (Abbott)
when starting a cat on a new insulin formulation or investigating a challenging case. The use of a CGM
can shorten time for determining an insulin dose, conserving owner resources. When the insulin
formulation has low day-to-day variability (insulin detemir or glargine U300), we are aggressive in
changing doses, not waiting 2-3 weeks to assess clinical response. Instead, insulin dosage can be
increased by as much as 20-25% every day, if the IGc readings are consistently >350 mg/dL (19
mmol/L).
Once IGcs are <350 mg/dL (19 mmol/L), dosing changes are made after waiting to determine the new
insulin’s full effect and a consistent pattern is apparent. If owners can follow a strict daily routine, the
interval between dosing changes might be only 2-3 days. If owners are less consistent, or if a less
consistent insulin formulation is used, dosing changes are made less frequently, allowing the CGM to
display the different day-to-day glycemic fluctuations.

Long-Term Home Use of CGMs
When clinical signs have largely resolved, 1 of 2 strategies can be considered. Many owners are
interested in using CGMs permanently, they are shown how to apply the sensor, and communications
are continued by sharing data online with visits to the clinic only as needed. In this scenario, fine tuning
insulin doses can be ongoing, responding to transient changes in glycemia. Many owners do not want to
use a permanent CGM and less intense monitoring of clinical signs as described previously may be
employed. CGM sensors may also be applied periodically, replacing periodic fructosamines or BG
curves.

CGMs and a Goal of Euglycemia
In people with DM, CGMs aid in maintaining long-term near euglycemia. This should slow progression
of long-term complications. It is not known if using a CGM improves remission rates. While increasing
the safety of tight glycemic control protocols in the short term, the long-term use of CGM should be
assessed in terms of risking attrition in owner compliance and overall survival.

COMPLICATIONS OF FELINE DM
There is no evidence that specific glucose targets should be maintained in cats with DM to avoid shortor long-term complications.

DIABETIC NEUROPATHY

Neuropathy in diabetic cats is exhibited as a plantigrade and less commonly a palmigrade stance and
gait that interferes with walking and jumping (Figure 292.3). Irritability when touching the paws has
been reported.122,123 Conduction deficits can be identified in motor, sensory, and mixed nerves, with
decreased postural reactions and tendon reflexes. Structural nerve injury involves endoneurial
microvascular abnormalities affecting Schwann cells and neurons, similar to the neuropathy in some
people with DM.122 The condition is thought to result from a combination of chronic hyperglycemia,
insulin resistance, and hyperlipidemia.124 Signs of neuropathy are often reversible with 2-3 months of
DM treatment (

Video 292.1), but specific glycemic or other targets to optimize chances of resolution

are not known.

URINARY DISEASES
Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) (ch. 307)
DM is considered a predisposing factor for UTIs secondary to systemic immune suppression125 and
glucosuria providing a substrate for microorganisms. UTIs are more common in diabetic people treated
with SGLT-2 inhibitors that increase glucosuria.126 UTIs were reported in 12-13% of DM cats. Lower
urinary tract signs are a good predictor for a positive urine culture.127,128 However, a more recent study
did not identify DM as risk factor for subclinical bacteriuria, with 0 UTIs of 22 cats examined. DM was
significantly associated with candiduria in cats.129

Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD, ch. 301), Protein-Losing Nephropathy (PLN, ch.
302)
Type 2 DM is a leading cause of nephropathy in people. The prevalence of microalbuminuria and
proteinuria is high in diabetic cats130 and an association between CKD and DM was recently
observed,131 but 2 other studies suggest that DM might decrease risk of CKD in cats.132,133 Symmetric
dimethylarginine (SDMA), a marker of early CKD, was lower in DM cats than in healthy controls.133 The
risk of CKD was about 20% lower in cats with DM based on a large epidemiological study of primary
care data.132

POORLY CONTROLLED DM
DEFINITION, INCLUDING DKA
Poor diabetic control implies that an individual with DM is experiencing excessive hyperglycemia,
hypoglycemia, and/or glycemic variability. Poor control suggests presence of continuing PU/PD,
polyphagia, weight loss, failure to gain weight, weakness, and/or gait abnormalities. Transient
hypoglycemia often causes no clinical signs, but neuroglycopenia should always be avoided or treated
immediately. DKA (ch. 290) is usually the result of a concurrent disease and should be treated as an
emergency. Importantly, even small doses of insulin are sufficient to prevent DKA in an otherwise stable
diabetic with no concurrent diseases. Therefore, avoiding DKA does not require fine-tuning of insulin
therapy.

EXCESSIVE HYPERGLYCEMIA
Failure to curb hyperglycemia might be related to use of a short-acting insulin (which might also be
associated with episodes of hypoglycemia), improper insulin administration, or an underlying disease
that causes insulin resistance or increases glycemic variability (Box 292.3). Insulin resistance is usually
relative and clinical improvement should be observed as the dose of insulin is increased. In contrast,
improper insulin administration is usually associated with no response or an erratic response that is not
dose dependent.

INSULIN RESISTANCE
Definition and Differential Diagnosis
Insulin resistance is defined as reduced sensitivity to insulin or impedance of insulin’s action in target
tissue(s). Insulin resistance is suspected when BG concentrations are perceived to be insufficiently
lowered by insulin therapy. Resistance should be considered after other causes have been ruled out (Box
292.3). From a clinical perspective, potential causes of insulin resistance include inflammatory diseases
such as obesity (ch. 150) or pancreatitis (ch. 278), bacterial infections due to periodontal disease (ch.
258) or UTI (ch. 307), major organ failure, and concurrent endocrinopathies such as HS (ch. 280),
hyperthyroidism (ch. 287), hypercortisolism (ch. 294), hypothyroidism (ch. 286), or obesity (ch.
150). Iatrogenic causes include giving any form of progestagen or glucocorticoid. About 10% of cats
treated with prednisolone, particularly at high dosages and for long durations, develop DM.134

Pancreatitis (ch. 278)
Pancreatitis poses a diagnostic challenge, especially in a cat with DM. There is some evidence that
pancreatitis can precede DM, be the cause of DM, be the consequence of DM, or present as an unrelated
comorbidity.1 Feline pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity (fPLI) is often used as a screening test for
pancreatitis in cats with vomiting, abdominal pain, or decreased appetite; however, results are
frequently increased in DM cats with no clinical signs. Acute pancreatitis is a systemic inflammatory
disease that can lead to insulin resistance, but it is unclear if the situation is similar for chronic or
subclinical pancreatitis.

Endocrine Diseases

Endocrine diseases causing insulin resistance usually cause clinical and clinicopathologic changes
distinguishable from those of DM. Some overlap occurs. HS is a diagnostic challenge since many
affected cats only have signs of DM. Further, the insulin deficiency of DM suppresses IGF-1. Concurrent
hyperthyroidism can be a difficult diagnosis because of overlap in clinical signs, stress hyperglycemia in
hyperthyroid cats, high rates of protein turnover that can falsely decrease fructosamine concentrations,
and the euthyroid-sick syndrome in DM.135

Obesity
Obesity results in predictable insulin resistance but does not increase insulin requirement as markedly
as do other endocrinopathies (ch. 150). Weight gain should be expected when giving insulin and should
not prompt increases in dose “to correct for insulin resistance.”

HYPOGLYCEMIA AND GLYCEMIC VARIABILITY
Short- and Long-Term Consequences of Hypoglycemia
If not for hypoglycemia, patients with DM could have normal glycemic control throughout a lifetime.136
Hypoglycemia should be avoided whether or not it is associated with clinical signs, not only because
severe hypoglycemia is life-threatening but also because of the long-term consequences of milder
hypoglycemia. Repeated episodes of mild hypoglycemia in people lead to impaired counterregulatory
responses to hypoglycemia, hypoglycemia-unawareness (absence of systemic clinical signs of
hypoglycemia before neuroglycopenia ensues), and increased risk of future more severe hypoglycemia.
Although these long term consequences have not yet been documented in cats, they have been well
documented in humans and other species.137 In people, signs of hypoglycemia, e.g., hunger, shaking,
and trembling, are caused by activating the central and autonomic nervous systems. Episodic
hypoglycemia (as well as hyperglycemia) leads to progressive dysfunction in activation of these systems
and is manifested as progressively lower hypoglycemia thresholds of activation.137 This leads to a
decrease in the frequency and severity of the warning signs of hypoglycemia and eventually results in
sudden onset of seizures, coma, or death due to neuroglycopenia. If the same phenomenon exists in cats,
it might explain the variability in threshold for appearance of clinical signs. Although some cats have
clinical signs with BGs <60 mg/dL (<3.3 mmol/L), others are not clinical despite BGs <40 mg/dL (<2.2
mmol/L).138 Similarly, while the majority of cats that have BGs <20 mg/dL (<1.1 mmol/L) are comatose
or stuporous, about a third only exhibit mental dullness, lethargy, weakness, and/or ataxia.138 Other
clinical signs reported in hypoglycemic cats include vocalizing, twitching, seizures, bradycardia,
hypothermia, vomiting, panting, decreased appetite, inappropriate urination, diarrhea, and drooling.138
Importantly, BG concentrations in the above study were measured with a glucose meter designed and
calibrated for feline BGs (AlphaTrak, Zoetis) and might not apply when other methods are used to
measure BGs and certainly not when IGc is measured. We routinely observe cats with IGc <40 mg/dL
(<2.2 mmol/L) for hours that have no clinical signs. As is the case for BG meters designed for humans,
CGMs that measure IGc might have a negative bias in the hypoglycemic range, i.e., they report values
that are lower than the BG concentration.139

Impaired Counter-Regulatory Responses and the “Somogyi” Hypothesis
In people, dogs, and rodents, counterregulatory responses are often impaired in DM.118,137 Frequency
and severity depend on etiology, stage of disease, and glycemic control. The impairment results in
decreased activation of counterregulatory hormones. The Somogyi hypothesis that hypoglycemia leads
to exaggerated secretion of counterregulatory hormones with resultant hyperglycemia and insulin
resistance is not likely. There was no evidence of insulin-induced hyperglycemia based on lack of
correlation between hyperglycemic events and preceding hypoglycemia, in one study.114 Yet, clinical
experience suggests that in some cats, lowering insulin doses results in improved glycemic control. This
might happen in cats in which counterregulation is still not impaired. In such cats, increasing insulin
doses cause the BG to decrease below the threshold for activation of counterregulatory hormones sooner
with the result that the glucose-lowering effect of insulin is masked sooner and for a longer time.

High Glycemic Variability
High glycemic variability is a risk factor for hypoglycemia and other DM complications in people. This is
probably because it captures both the occurrence of hypo- and hyperglycemia excursions that separately
lead to autonomic dysfunction and impaired counterregulation.140 In cats, increased glycemic variability
is associated with a decrease in glycemic control but it is unknown whether it is an independent risk
factor for hypoglycemia or other complications.141 In diabetic cats treated with exenatide-ER, reduced
glycemic variability was associated with higher rates of remission.108

THE HISTORY OF
HYPERADRENOCORTICISM AND
DEFINITIONS
The most common manifestation of hyperadrenocorticism
(hypersecretion of adrenocortical hormones) in dogs is hypercortisolism
(HC). Chronically increased circulating glucocorticoids can be caused by
long-term glucocorticoid administration (iatrogenic) or it can be
naturally occurring, caused by excessive endogenous cortisol production.1
The clinical condition associated with chronic cortisol excess is often
referred to as Cushing’s syndrome, after the eminent neurosurgeon
Harvey Cushing. Cushing’s clinical description of his patient Minnie G.,
published in his monograph in 1912, incorporated all the features that are
now considered classic for HC. He speculated that the disorder may be
related to the adrenal gland (hyperadrenalism). In his later survey,
published in 1932, he associated the condition with a basophil adenoma
of the pituitary gland. The description of this fascinating discovery makes
Harvey Cushing one of the greatest figures in endocrinology.2 In
veterinary medicine the first mention of HC appeared in 1939, when
Verstraete and Thoonen reported the first 2 dogs with “pituitary
disorders.”3
Naturally occurring HC is usually the result of inappropriate excess
secretion of pituitary adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) or due to

autonomous adrenal glucocorticoid secretion. These are classified as
ACTH-dependent HC and ACTH-independent HC, respectively. ACTHdependent HC includes pituitary-dependent HC (PDH; Cushing’s
disease) and the ectopic ACTH syndrome. ACTH-independent HC
includes functional adrenocortical tumors (ATs) and primary ACTHindependent adrenocortical hyperplasia, such as food-induced HC. While
PDH and functional ATs are well-recognized, reports of primary ACTHindependent adrenocortical hyperplasia and ectopic ACTH syndrome are
limited to individual case reports.4

PHYSIOLOGY: HYPOTHALAMUSPITUITARY-ADRENOCORTICAL AXIS
(HPAA)
HYPOTHALAMUS AND PITUITARY GLAND
The hypothalamus is a part of the diencephalon located dorsal to the
pituitary gland and ventral to the thalamus (ch. 241). The hypothalamus
is intimately related to the pituitary gland through a portal vascular
system and an anatomic link, as the pituitary is attached to the ventral
part of the hypothalamus (median eminence) via part of the
neurohypophysis, the infundibular stalk.5 In dogs, the pituitary gland is
divided into 3 functional units: the anterior lobe, the neurohypophysis or
posterior lobe, and between them, the pars intermedia. The mature
anterior lobe is populated by at least 5 distinct endocrine cell types
distinguished by the tropic (stimulating) hormone each synthesizes:
somatotrophs: growth hormone (GH); lactotrophs: prolactin;
thyrotrophs: thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH); corticotrophs: the
precursor molecule pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), which is broken
down to ACTH and related peptides; and gonadotrophs: luteinizing
hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). The pars
intermedia contains 2 distinct cell types that can synthesize POMC:
predominant “A” cells are similar to corticotrophs and the less common
“B” cells in which ACTH is cleaved into alpha-melanocyte stimulating
hormone (alpha-MSH) and corticotropin-like intermediate-lobe peptide
(ACTH18-39 or CLIP).5
Secretion of ACTH from the anterior lobe is regulated by the
hypothalamus and central nervous system via neurotransmitters that
release corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) and vasopressin (VP).

CRH is released from small neurons in the paraventricular nucleus in
response to neural signaling. VP is primarily released from CRHcontaining neurons and is distinct from the VP involved in water
homeostasis. When CRH and VP are released, the ACTH precursor,
POMC, is secreted from the anterior lobe.6 The POMC is cleaved to
produce ACTH. The pars intermedia is poorly vascularized and is
predominantly innervated by dopaminergic nerve fibers from the
hypothalamus.7 The POMC-producing cells of the pars intermedia are
resistant to glucocorticoid suppression due to an absence of
glucocorticoid receptors.

ADRENAL CORTEX
The adrenal cortex consists of three functional and morphological layers:
the outermost zona glomerulosa (zG), the middle zona fasciculata (zF)
and the inner zona reticularis (zR). The zG is responsible for the
production of the mineralocorticoid aldosterone, regulated by plasma
concentrations of potassium (K) and angiotensin-II. Acute increases in
circulating ACTH also induce aldosterone secretion. The zF and zR
function together as a unit and are the sole source of glucocorticoids,
strictly regulated by the HPAA. The zR also produces androgens, e.g.,
dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and androstenedione.4
Adrenal steroidogenesis is initiated by ACTH, which binds to the Gprotein alpha subunit (GNAS)-coupled melanocortin 2 receptor (MC2R),
assisted by the melanocortin 2 receptor accessory protein (MRAP), and
activates the cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) and protein kinase
A (PKA) pathways. Cholesterol is the precursor molecule for all
adrenocortical hormones and its availability is the limiting step for
adrenal steroidogenesis. Cholesterol is converted to adrenocortical
hormones in several steps, each catalyzed by enzymes (Figure 293.1).
Each zone in the adrenal cortex expresses a different set of
steroidogenic enzymes. Dog steroidogenesis is unique with only one 11beta-hydroxylase enzyme (CYP11B1). Canine adrenals lack aldosteronesynthetase (CYP11B2), a specific enzyme involved in the last step in
aldosterone synthesis in humans and many other species. This implies
that in dogs the expression of the 17-alpha-hydroxylase enzyme
(CYP17A1) in the zF is crucial for cortisol synthesis, while lack of CYP17A1
in the zG restricts steroidogenesis to mineralocorticoid production.8
Activation of several transcription factors and steroidogenic enzymes in

adrenocortical cells increase cortisol production, which in turn exerts
negative feedback suppressing hypothalamic CRH and VP while also
suppressing ACTH secretion from the anterior lobe. Adrenal cortisol
secretion has no effect on ACTH secretion from pars intermedia. ACTH
and cortisol secretion are pulsatile and there is no circadian rhythm.9

PATHOGENESIS
ACTH-DEPENDENT HYPERADRENOCORTICISM
Pituitary-Dependent Hypercortisolism (PDH)
PDH, diagnosed in 80-85% of dogs with HC, is the most common
naturally occurring form. PDH is caused by a functional, autonomous,
ACTH-secreting, pituitary tumor that causes bilateral adrenocortical
hyperplasia and chronic excessive secretion of glucocorticoids (Figure
293.2).1 Pituitary tumors may arise from the anterior lobe or the pars
intermedia. Tumors in the pars intermedia tend to grow larger and are
resistant to dexamethasone suppression. Endocrine testing is often not
discriminative, as large tumors from the anterior lobe may also be
dexamethasone-resistant.9 Most of these pituitary tumors are
histologically classified as adenoma (well delineated from adjacent
parenchyma). Invasive adenomas (exhibiting local invasion of brain
parenchyma or adjacent structures), carcinomas (with distant
metastasis), and pituitary hyperplasia have also been described.10
Not much is known about the genetic background of canine HC. An
activating mutation in the corticotropin releasing hormone receptor gene
(CRHR1) was detected in just 1 Poodle from a series of 50 dogs, failing to
support the theory that ACTH-secreting adenomas develop after chronic
increases in positive feedback signals by constitutively activated CRH
receptors.11 The research on oncogenesis of canine pituitary tumors has
predominantly focused on candidate genes involved in pituitary
tumorigenesis in humans. The high prevalence of HC in dogs and
similarities in clinical presentation make the dog a suitable animal model
for studying Cushing’s disease in humans, but more molecular studies are
needed. The gain-of-function of the Ubiquitin Specific Peptide 8 gene
(USP8) is a main driver behind the formation of corticotroph adenomas
in humans. This peptide was not identified in dogs.12 Mutation of a T-box

transcription factor (Tpit), obligate for the expression of POMC in
humans and dogs, is not present in canine pituitary tumors.13,14

Ectopic ACTH Syndrome
Various tumor types, from well-differentiated and indolent carcinoids to
highly aggressive small-cell carcinomas, can secrete ACTH which, in turn,
leads to HC. Dogs with resistance to dexamethasone, negative pituitary
imaging, severely elevated endogenous ACTH (eACTH) concentrations,
severe hypokalemia, and obvious clinical signs are candidates for the
diagnosis of ectopic ACTH syndrome. A neuroendocrine tumor
originating in the pancreas has been described as source of ectopic ACTH
in dogs (Figure 293.2).15,16 Ectopic ACTH syndrome is rare and likely
underdiagnosed in dogs. Ectopic ACTH-secreting tumors are usually
small, difficult to visualize, and only identified after extensive diagnostic
imaging. Furthermore, treatment targeting the adrenal glands will
resolve clinical signs of HC regardless of the ACTH source. Although
typically slow-growing, most ectopic ACTH secreting tumors are
malignant. The prognosis is unpredictable.

ACTH-INDEPENDENT
HYPERADRENOCORTICISM
Autonomous Cortisol-Secreting ATs
Such tumors occur in about 15-20% of dogs with naturally occurring HC,
causing “adrenal-dependent” HC (AHC). Excessive production of cortisol
by the AT negatively feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary gland,
suppressing CRH and ACTH secretion. This causes atrophy of cortisolsecreting cells within the contralateral adrenal gland and the nonneoplastic cortisol-secreting cells of the affected adrenal gland (Figure
293.2).1 One of the mechanisms behind ACTH-independent cortisol
secretion is an activating mutation in the G-protein alpha-subunit gene
(GNAS), described in about one-third of investigated cases.17 An
activating GNAS mutation constitutively induces the PKA pathway, which
can lead to continuous and uncontrolled cortisol production, can
stimulate proliferative activity, and may be responsible for AT growth.
This mutation is present in both benign and malignant ATs.
The histological criteria for differentiating adrenocortical adenomas
from carcinomas include tumor size, peripheral fibrosis, capsular

invasion, a trabecular growth pattern, hemorrhage, necrosis, single-cell
necrosis, hematopoiesis, fibrin thrombi, cytoplasmic vacuolation, and the
Ki67 proliferation index.18 In the largest case series of functional ATs,
most were carcinomas (63% and 75%).18,19 The differentiation, however,
is challenging and the most reliable criterion of AT malignancy remains
metastases. Histopathological parameters can also serve as prognostic
indicators after adrenalectomy. Three parameters were significantly
associated with survival: the percentage cells with clear/vacuolated
cytoplasm, the presence of necrosis, and the Ki67 proliferation index.
Together, they comprise the Utrecht score, an easy-to-use
histopathological scoring system that can help to assess post-surgery
prognosis (Figure 293.3).20

Non–Cortisol-Secreting Adrenocortical Tumors
Some adrenocortical carcinomas secrete hormones other than cortisol
(ch. 295). Most of these dogs have clinical signs of HC. Excessive 17alpha-hydroxy-progesterone secretion and subnormal response to
exogenous ACTH were demonstrated in published cases.21,22 Secretion of
cortisol-precursors, instead of end-product cortisol, is presumably a
result of malignant dedifferentiation of the adrenocortical cells. In this
process, a highly specialized adrenocortical cell loses its hormonal
capacity and gains proliferative characteristics. Also loss of MC2R may be
ascribed to the process of malignant transformation of an AT.4

Unilateral vs Bilateral Masses
Functional ATs are usually solitary and unilateral. Bilateral ATs have
been diagnosed and may be difficult to distinguish from bilateral
adrenocortical hyperplasia in dogs with PDH.23,24 Concurrent pituitary
and adrenal-dependent HC has been reported in 5% of all dogs with HC
and in 10% of dexamethasone-resistant dogs.25

ACTH-Independent Adrenocortical Hyperplasia
ACTH-independent adrenocortical hyperplasia results from expression of
ectopic receptors in the adrenocortical cell or from overactivity of eutopic
receptors.26 In normal canine adrenal cortices and in a subset of ATs, the
expression of LH and gastric-inhibitory polypeptide (GIP) receptors has
been documented (Figure 293.2). These G-protein receptors bind with
its ligand to induce cAMP and PKA pathways leading to steroidogenesis.
Ectopic GIP receptor expression underlies food-induced HC, which is the
only documented form of ACTH-independent adrenocortical hyperplasia
in dogs.27 Suspicion of food-induced HC is based on negative endocrine
test results in a dog with strong clinical suspicion of HC and in which
there is no AT present. The major characteristic is direct and indirect (via
CRH) suppression of eACTH concentration by excess circulating cortisol
concentrations ([cortisol]) secreted after binding of GIP to its receptor at
the membrane of the adrenocortical cell. Food-induced HC is a rare but
likely underdiagnosed form of HC. Dogs with sub-diagnostic HC (see
below) represent a potential category of food-induced HC, because
endocrine testing will be negative if performed in fasted dogs. In foodinduced HC, cortisol excess can only be documented after food intake,

because food consumption induces GIP secretion which binds to the GIP
receptor and results in hypercortisolemia.

Sub-Diagnostic HC (Replacing “Atypical” or “Occult”
HC)
Dogs with clinical signs of HC but with “normal” endocrine test results
are categorized as sub-diagnostic HC, a term introduced by the ALIVE
group (http://esve.org). Dogs with sub-diagnostic HC have relatively
high [cortisol] and adrenal size that is comparable to the hyperplastic
adrenals of dogs with PDH.28 The most likely explanation for nondiagnostic endocrine tests may be testing too early in the disease, or
chance. Since HC is a chronic and progressive disease, repeating a
screening test or tests 2-3 months later confirms the diagnosis of HC in
most of these dogs. Among possible explanations for those with
persistent sub-diagnostic HC are increased sensitivity to the
glucocorticoid receptor, aberrant expression of adrenocortical receptors,
intra-adrenal ACTH production, and others.29

FIGURE 293.2 Multiple pathogenic mechanisms of

PREVALENCE AND SIGNALMENT
HC is relatively common, but its true prevalence is not known. The
incidence of new cases of HC is 1-2 per 1000 dogs per year, and the
prevalence of PDH is estimated around 0.2% based on several studies.3032
HC is a disease of middle-aged to older dogs. The age at diagnosis
ranges from 6 months to 20 years, but the mean is about 11 years. A
predisposition for HC has been shown for several breeds, including the
Miniature Poodle, Dachshund, Terriers, Boxer, and Standard
Schnauzer.31,33,34 “Blanket statements” about breeds can be misleading
because of varying breed distribution and popularity in different
geographic areas. HC affects both males and females. A potential
predisposition for females has been suggested, but lack of control groups
weakens any conclusive relationships. Neutering of either sex seems to be
associated with increased risk for HC. This could be related to the
expression of the LH receptor in the adrenal cortex.35 If eutopic activity
of this receptor is responsible for the development of HC, it remains to be
elucidated. Another explanation could be that neutered dogs develop HC
because they live longer than intact dogs.34

HISTORY AND PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
(PE)
COMMON SIGNS
Overview
The most common clinical signs of HC are a consequence of the
combined gluconeogenic, immune-suppressive, anti-inflammatory,
protein catabolic, and lipolytic effects of glucocorticoids.1,4 Clinical
manifestations usually progress slowly and owners often correlate health
with appetite: the better the appetite, the better the health. Dogs with HC
have excellent to ravenous appetites. Signs can be subtle and mistaken
for aging, especially when dogs are diagnosed at an earlier stage of

disease. Clinical signs, however, appear similar to those published in
earlier studies that included many dogs with more chronic disease.34,36

Polyuria/Polydipsia (PU/PD), Urinary Tract Infections
(UTIs)
The first step in gaining a suspicion of HC should always be based on the
history. PU/PD and polyphagia (PP) are the most common owner
concerns. Potential causes of PU/PD (ch. 53) include cortisol-induced
inhibition of VP action at the renal tubular level, an increased
neurohypophysis VP release threshold, or central diabetes insipidus
(CDI) if a large pituitary tumor compresses and/or invades the
neurohypophysis (ch. 282).37 Severe PU may lead to urine leakage,
especially when sleeping, i.e., owner-perceived urinary incontinence.
UTIs (ch. 307) are common and most likely due to cortisol-induced
immunosuppression and/or decreased bactericidal properties of dilute
urine.38

Polyphagia (PP), Potbelly, Panting
Most dogs with HC have an “excellent appetite” or PP (ch. 19), a direct
and unique effect of glucocorticoids in dogs. Other common clinical signs
include abdominal distension and panting. Abdominal distension
(potbelly, ch. 21) is believed to occur because of hepatomegaly (due to
glycogen deposition), fat accumulation within the abdomen, and an
enlarged bladder. Together, these increase the weight of the abdominal
contents and together with decreased muscle tone (a result of protein
catabolism) HC dogs often have a pot belly. Panting is attributed to
decreased pulmonary compliance, respiratory muscle weakness, or
pulmonary hypertension.39

Dermatologic Signs

Skin changes typical for HC include alopecia, hyperpigmentation,
comedones, thin skin, poor hair regrowth, and calcinosis cutis (ch. 12).
Chronic glucocorticoid excess commonly induces follicular atrophy
resulting in bilateral symmetrical truncal “endocrine alopecia.” Some
dogs only retain coat on their head and distal extremities (Figure
293.4). Thin skin may be due to the anti-proliferative effects of
glucocorticoids on fibroblasts and inhibition of collagen synthesis,
causing epidermal atrophy. The thin skin and suppressed immune system
predispose dogs to pyoderma. Calcinosis cutis, pathognomonic for HC, is
characterized by irregular plaques in or under the skin due to dystrophic
calcium (Ca) deposition40 (

Video 293.1).

PSEUDOMYOTONIA, LIGAMENT
RUPTURE, TESTICULAR ATROPHY,
ANESTRUS
A myopathy characterized by persistent active muscle contractions after
cessation of voluntary effort, known as Cushing’s pseudomyotonia, can
affect the pelvic or all 4 limbs, causing a stiff gait, but not pain (

Video

293.2).41 When severe, dogs are unable to walk. Electromyography is
characteristic (ch. 111) and muscle histology reveals noninflammatory
degenerative myopathy. Uncommonly in larger breed dogs, HC can result
in ligament laxity and tearing, causing lameness. Testicular atrophy in
males and persistent anestrus in females are less commonly mentioned.
Cortisol negative feedback to the pituitary suppresses synthesis and
secretion of FSH and LH.
