“SPACE-OCCUPYING” SIGNS (SIGNS DUE
TO LARGE MASSES COMPRESSING OR
INVADING ADJACENT TISSUES)
Clinical manifestations may develop secondary to the space-occupying
effect of a pituitary tumor or AT. Large pituitary tumors have been
associated with dull mentation, circling, aimless wandering, pacing,
ataxia, and behavior alterations (

Videos 293.3 and 293.4).42,43 While

inappetence or anorexia are common owner concerns for dogs with large
pituitary tumors, poor appetite is extremely atypical for a dog with HC.
Poor appetite is always a concern in a dog with HC and should be taken
seriously.
Large ATs may invade the phrenicoabdominal vein, caudal vena cava,
or both. Such tumors have caused retroperitoneal hemorrhage, blood
loss, abdominal pain, or formation of a tumor thrombus in a vein that
leads to blockage and subsequent ascites or hind limb paresis (

Video

293.5; ch. 238).44 The clinical manifestations of HC are usually chronic
and progressive, but rupture of an AT or major vessel can result in acute
life-threatening illness.

CLINICOPATHOLOGIC FINDINGS
OVERVIEW
Clinicopathologic abnormalities must be interpreted in the context of the
history and PE. Various alterations are common; none is pathognomonic.
An absence of common abnormalities should decrease suspicion of HC.
Conversely, failure to identify abnormalities does not, by itself, rule out
HC. When clinical suspicion is strong, endocrine tests should be
performed45 (Table 293.1).

COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT (CBC)
Common CBC findings include eosinopenia (54-81% of dogs with HC),
thrombocytosis (37-78%), lymphopenia (14-80%), neutrophilia
(approximately 24%), monocytosis (approximately 30%), and
erythrocytosis (10-14%).45 These white blood cell changes are referred to
as a “stress leukogram” (ch. 58). Lymphopenia is likely due to steroidinduced lympholysis, eosinopenia to bone marrow sequestration, and
neutrophilia and monocytosis to steroid-enhanced capillary
demargination. Erythrocytosis (chs. 57, 173) and thrombocytosis likely
result from direct bone marrow stimulation. Erythrocytosis may be due
to hypoxemia in some dogs with HC as a result of hypoventilation caused
by muscle weakness and obesity (Pickwick syndrome) or pulmonary
thromboembolism (PT, ch. 219).39

SERUM BIOCHEMISTRY PROFILE
Liver Enzymes, Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN), Blood
Glucose (BG)
Common biochemical findings in dogs with HC include increased
alkaline phosphatase (ALP; 76-100%) and alanine aminotransferase
(ALT; 80-95%) activities, hypercholesterolemia (73-90%), decreased
BUN (34-56%), and mild increases in BG (20-57%). Increased ALP
activities are the most consistent laboratory abnormality and can be
severe (>10 times above reference intervals), but these results remain
nonspecific. There is no correlation between ALP activity and severity of
HC, response to therapy, or prognosis. The increase of ALP is due to
steroid-induced expression of an ALP isoenzyme unique to dogs and to
vacuolar hepatopathy (ch. 274).45 Healthy-appearing dogs with no
owner concerns, regardless of increases in ALP measured for screening
purposes, are extremely unlikely to have HC. Increased serum cholesterol
(90% of HC dogs) is caused by steroid-induced lipolysis. Hyperglycemia
due to increased hepatic gluconeogenesis and decreased peripheral
glucose utilization is caused by glucocorticoids interfering with insulin
action at the cellular level (receptor and post-receptor defects).
Carbohydrate tolerance, maintained by hyperinsulinemia, is not
sufficient to completely normalize BGs in some dogs. Mild fasting
hyperglycemia is common, but their BGs usually remain below the renal
threshold (175-224 mg/dL [9.7-12.4 mmol/L]).46 When diabetes mellitus

(DM, ch. 291) occurs in a dog with Cushing’s syndrome, it is often
insulin-resistant. Decreased BUN is caused by increased renal clearance
due to the PU.

Phosphate (PO4), Calcium (Ca), Sodium (Na),
Potassium (K)
HyperPO4 occurs frequently in dogs with PDH while circulating Ca is
largely unaffected. Both intact and whole parathormone (PTH)
concentrations are increased.47 The combination of these seemingly
contradictory findings is called adrenal secondary hyperparathyroidism
and is proposed to be a consequence of lower urinary PO4 secretion and
increased renal Ca excretion. Mild hyperNa and hypoK can be seen in
dogs with HC. High [cortisol] saturates the protective 11-betahydroxysteroid dehydrogenase and enables cortisol to access the type I
mineralocorticoid receptor. HypoK is a result of cortisol-induced
mineralocorticoid effect and may reflect the severity of
hypercortisolemia.36

Canine Pancreatic Lipase Immunoreactivity (cPLI) and
Bile Acids
Dogs with HC may have increased cPLI, supporting the diagnosis of
pancreatitis in a few dogs, but the results should be interpreted with
caution to avoid an incorrect diagnosis (ch. 277). Lipase activity
measured by the 1,2-o-dilauryl-rac-glycero-3-glutaric acid-(6′methylresorufin) ester (DGGR) or 1,2-diglyceride (1,2-DiG) assays lacks
specificity in aiding the diagnosis of pancreatitis in HC dogs and is not
recommended.48,49 The cause of increased serum pre- and postprandial
bile acids, reported in 12% and 37% of dogs with HC, respectively, is not
known but is not indicative of clinically significant liver dysfunction.36

URINALYSIS (UA) AND URINE SPECIFIC
GRAVITY (USG)
Most dogs with HC have USG <1.020; a USG >1.030 is rare in the
absence of glucosuria.49 Proteinuria is common. A urinary protein :
creatinine ratio >1 has been reported in about 45%, and >0.5 in about

70%, of dogs with HC. Proteinuria decreases with successful treatment
and should be monitored.50 Bacteriuria or positive urine bacterial culture
was identified in 10-50% HC dogs, whose predisposition for UTI is likely
due to immunosuppression, dilute urine, and urine retention. Less than
5% of HC dogs with a positive urine culture exhibit lower urinary tract
signs (chs. 70, 184, 302, 307).

COAGULATION PARAMETERS
A hypercoagulable tendency (ch. 171), defined as finding of at least 1
abnormality in a coagulation panel, has been observed in >80% of dogs
with HC. The most common abnormalities include shorter prothrombin
time, higher fibrinogen concentrations, and increased thrombinantithrombin complexes.51,52 Thromboembolism, however, is not
common (see below).

THYROID FUNCTION TEST RESULTS
About 40-60% of dogs with HC have decreases in basal serum total
thyroxine (TT4) and/or triiodothyronine (T3) (ch. 285). About 24% have
decreased free thyroxine (fT4).53 Decreased thyroid hormone
concentrations in dogs with HC are caused by alterations in serum
thyroid hormone binding or peripheral hormone metabolism. Circulating
TSH concentrations are normal in HC dogs with a low TT4. Clinical signs
and routine laboratory changes associated with hypothyroidism and HC
overlap and differentiation may be challenging. If a dog is suspected to
have both, HC should be treated and thyroid replacement postponed.
Once HC is controlled, thyroid function should be reassessed.

MACHINE LEARNING
Models aimed at predicting individual likelihood of HC are being
developed and utilized in humans to aid clinical decision-making.
Machine-learning-based classification algorithms include risk factors and
estimate probability that a disease is present. A sufficiently large dataset
is necessary to ensure reliability.54 A machine-learning tool to predict HC
in dogs was introduced based on age, weight, sex, breed, clinical signs,

USG, and ALP. The tool provided a good predictive performance and
could be used in first-line practice to support decision-making and
increase confidence in the diagnosis of HC in dogs.34,55

ENDOCRINE TESTING
INDICATIONS FOR TESTING
The initial suspicion of HC begins with the history and PE. Any continued
suspicion should be supported by expected changes on routine blood and
urine test results. If HC remains likely, the diagnosis should be confirmed
by endocrine testing. Incidental identification of an adrenal mass on
imaging performed for a problem initially not related to HC (ch. 295)
and/or documenting a large pituitary mass on computed tomography
(CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to evaluate neurologic signs
are additional indications to test for HC. Testing should be avoided if a
dog is seriously ill, but concurrent illness must be considered.45

“CONFIRMING” A DIAGNOSIS OF HC AND
DISCRIMINATING PITUITARY FROM
ADRENAL HC
Confirming a diagnosis of HC requires demonstration of both increased
cortisol production and decreased sensitivity of the HPAA to negative
glucocorticoid feedback in a dog with clinical signs consistent with HC.56
The diagnosis of HC is a two-step procedure: first, “screening” tests are
used to distinguish dogs with HC from dogs without HC. Second,
“discrimination” tests are used to differentiate pituitary from adrenal HC,
which is essential for choosing the optimal treatment for each dog. Some
test results can be used for both screening and discrimination, e.g., the
low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (LDDST). Results of the urine
cortisol to creatinine ratio (UCCR) when combined with the oral highdose dexamethasone suppression test (HDDST) can also be used for both
screening and discrimination. The ACTH stimulation test (ACTHst) only
screens for HC.
No test is 100% accurate; each has advantages and disadvantages.
Testing depends on laboratory facilities and preferences of owner and
veterinarian. Recent administration of glucocorticoids or progestagens

may suppress the HPAA and alter endocrine test results. The cortisol
assay used for plasma, serum, or urine is of utmost importance as
reference ranges cannot be used interchangeably. Various methods of
cortisol measurement generate variations in [cortisol], and ideally,
reference ranges for each laboratory method should be established and
periodically re-evaluated.45

THE LOW-DOSE DEXAMETHASONE
SUPPRESSION TEST (LDDST)
Healthy vs HC Response to LDDST
The LDDST is commonly used to “confirm” a diagnosis of HC.49 In
healthy dogs, dexamethasone circulates throughout the body including to
the hypothalamus and pituitary where, within minutes, it suppresses
secretion of CRH and ACTH. Absence of ACTH leaves the adrenal
cortices with no stimulus to synthesize and secrete cortisol. Thus, after
giving dexamethasone, endogenous adrenal-source [cortisol] decreases to
negligible amounts within an hour or so, and remains suppressed as long
as the dexamethasone is active. Dogs with HC are abnormally resistant to
dexamethasone suppression, i.e., their [cortisol] does not decrease as in
the healthy dogs. The reported sensitivity and specificity of the LDDST
range from 85-100% and from 44-73%, respectively.49,56

Protocol
Serum or plasma samples for [cortisol] are collected before, 4- and 8hours after IV administration of 0.01 mg/kg dexamethasone. The test can
begin at any time of the day. If some dexamethasone extravasates from
the vein, the test is likely to remain reliable. Feeding should be avoided
because lipemic serum can influence cortisol measurements.

Interpretations
The basal and 8-hour post-dexamethasone cortisol results are used as the
“screening” test to distinguish dogs with HC from dogs without HC. In
healthy dogs, the plasma [cortisol] 4- and 8-hours after dexamethasone
decrease to or below the detection limit of assays. Complete suppression
rejects the diagnosis of HC. [Cortisol] consistent with HC is above the
laboratory cut-off of 1 or 1.4 mcg/dL (28-39 nmol/L), 8-hours post-

dexamethasone. In dogs with HC, several patterns in [cortisol] response
have been identified. Suppression of >50% from the basal [cortisol] at 4
or 8-hours, in dogs with confirmed HC, is compatible with PDH, i.e.,
“partial suppression pattern.” An “escape” pattern is when [cortisol] at
4-hours post-dexamethasone is below and the [cortisol] at 8-hours above
the laboratory cut-off. The definition of “no suppression” after an
LDDST: cortisols at 4- and 8-hours above the laboratory cut-off and
>50% of basal [cortisol]. No suppression is consistent with a diagnosis of
HC but does not help in discriminating pituitary from adrenal HC. Lack
of suppression is suggestive of an AT or a large pituitary tumor and
further evaluation with imaging is warranted. When the [cortisol] at 8hours is below the laboratory cut-off, it should exclude HC. But if the
[cortisol] at 4-hours post-dexamethasone is increased, an “inverse”
pattern is diagnosed. This result should be considered “equivocal” and
further testing for HC pursued by diagnostic imaging (Figure
293.5A).56 The “lack of suppression pattern” had the highest positive
predictive value for diagnosing HC (94%). The “partial suppression
pattern” (68%) and “escape or inverse pattern” (37%) had lower
predictive values.49

THE URINARY CORTISOL TO CREATININE
RATIO (UCCR) AND ORAL HIGH-DOSE
DEXAMETHASONE SUPPRESSION TEST
(HDDST)
The UCCR represents an integrated measure of corticoid production over
time (usually 1 night), smoothing the effects of short-term fluctuations in
plasma [cortisol]. Determination of basal UCCRs can be performed in
tandem with an oral HDDST. The combination has the advantage of
potentially demonstrating both increased cortisol production and
decreased sensitivity to glucocorticoid feedback, i.e., to differentiate
pituitary from adrenal HC. Reported UCCR sensitivity and specificity for
HC diagnosis ranges from 75-100% and 20-25%, respectively.45
The urine for a UCCR should always be obtained at home by the
owners, at least 2 days after a visit to a veterinary clinic. The owner is
instructed to collect 1-2 teaspoons (5-10 mL) of urine from the suspect
HC dog on 2 consecutive mornings for baseline UCCR. After collecting
the second urine sample, dexamethasone is administered PO in a dosage

of 0.1 mg/kg, at 12:00, 18:00 and 24:00 hours. The next morning, about
8 hours after giving the last dose of dexamethasone, the third urine
sample is collected.4 The reliability of the UCCR test depends also on the
availability of a trustworthy assay and the method specific reference
ranges and cutoffs.57

THE ACTH STIMULATION TEST (ACTHst)
Sensitivity, Specificity, Interpretation
The ACTHst assesses adrenocortical reserve. Its use is based on the
concept that dogs with HC have excess response to ACTH. It is the gold
standard test for diagnosing hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296) and
iatrogenic HC but does not assess the sensitivity of the HPAA to negative
glucocorticoid feedback. Results provide no information for
differentiating pituitary from adrenal HC.45 The sensitivity of the
ACTHst for naturally occurring canine PDH ranges between 80-83% and
57-63% for adrenal-dependent HC. The low sensitivity of the ACTHst in
adrenal-dependent HC is likely explained by downregulation of the
ACTH-receptor (MC2R) in adrenocortical carcinomas; specificity ranges
from 59-93%.56

Protocol
The ACTHst requires an hour and can be performed at any time of the
day. Plasma [cortisol] is measured before and 1 hour after administration
of synthetic ACTH; peak cortisol secretion occurs at 60-90 minutes.
Synthetic ACTH is commercially available in liquid, lyophilized, or
aqueous porcine ACTH gel forms. Liquid synthetic ACTH is given IV or
IM at a dosage of 5 mcg/kg, or 250 mcg/dog >10 kg or 125 mcg/dog <10
kg. After 5 mcg/kg IV, no difference was detected between 60- and 90minute [cortisol].45 The use of 1 mcg/kg of synthetic ACTH is not
recommended since results caused a different interpretation in about
25% of dogs suspected of HC. No difference in response following liquid
(250 mcg/kg IV) or lyophilized (250 mcg/kg IM) solutions were detected
in healthy dogs. Synthetic ACTH gel formulation is administered IM at a
dosage of 2.2 IU/kg. Use of compounded ACTH preparations is
discouraged because they may contain variable concentrations of ACTH,
may lead to lower post-ACTH [cortisol], and could lead to an incorrect
clinical interpretation. Because of its low sensitivity for adrenal-

dependent HC and the inability to differentiate pituitary from adrenal
HC, the diagnostic usefulness of the ACTHst is inferior to the LDDST
(Figure 293.5B).

ENDOGENOUS ACTH (eACTH)
ACTH is secreted from the pituitary gland in an episodic, pulsatile
fashion. Random measurement of circulating eACTH concentrations
overlap considerably between healthy dogs and those with PDH. Thus, its
measurement is not useful to screen for HC but it is the most accurate
stand-alone biochemical test for discriminating pituitary from adrenal
origin in dogs with proven HC.56 In dogs with adrenal-dependent HC,
the eACTH is expected to be low or undetectable. Low eACTH is
characteristic of food-induced HC. The accuracy for discriminating
pituitary from adrenal HC depends upon the analytical sensitivity, the
working range of the assay, and proper sample handling. eACTH is
rapidly degraded by proteases if samples are not cooled. Blood should be
collected into chilled, silicon-coated glass or plastic tubes containing
EDTA, centrifuged within 15 minutes (ideally in a cooled centrifuge), and
the plasma transferred to plastic tubes and frozen immediately.45

THE HIGH DOSE DEXAMETHASONE
SUPPRESSION TEST (HDDST)
The IV-HDDST is used to help differentiate pituitary from adrenal HC
when results of the LDDST demonstrate no suppression. The protocol is
the same as for the LDDST except that the dosage is 0.1 mg/kg IV. When
suppression is >50% in a dog with HC, it is of pituitary origin. However,
in dogs exhibiting no suppression on LDDST (the indication to obtain a
HDDST), the HDDST provides differentiation in only 12% additional
dogs and is no longer recommended. Instead, diagnostic imaging and
eACTH measurements are advised to differentiate pituitary from adrenal
HC in dogs with non-suppressible LDDST.45

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
INDICATIONS
Diagnostic imaging should be performed after HC has been confirmed
with endocrine testing. Diagnostic imaging, preferably of both pituitary
and adrenal glands, should be included in the diagnostic evaluation of
dogs with naturally occurring HC to differentiate pituitary from adrenal
HC, to choose the most optimal treatment, and to estimate prognosis.58
Finding a normal pituitary and normal adrenal glands on diagnostic
imaging does not rule out HC.

PITUITARY: COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY
(CT) OR MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING
(MRI)
Estimating Pituitary Enlargement
The pituitary gland area can be visualized with CT or MRI (chs. 112, 245)
and enlargement can be estimated using the ratio of pituitary height vs
the area of the brain (P/B value), measured through the midline of the

pituitary on an axial image. A P/B value >0.31 mm/mm2 indicates
pituitary enlargement.9 The P/B value can be used regardless of head
dimension, breed, or size of the dog. Pituitary tumors in dogs with PDH
range from microscopic nests of cells to large masses. Small pituitary
masses may not cause enlargement of the pituitary gland (normal P/B
value) but may still be identified with contrast-enhanced CT and MRI.59

Dynamic Contrast-Enhanced CT
The blood supply of the posterior pituitary gland is direct (arterial)
whereas that of the anterior pituitary gland is mainly indirect via the
pituitary portal system. Dynamic contrast-enhanced CT takes advantage
of this difference. In healthy dogs given IV contrast medium, the
posterior pituitary gland is identified before the anterior pituitary: the
“pituitary flush.” Its absence can indicate atrophy of the posterior
pituitary due to compression by an anterior pituitary tumor.
Displacement or distortion of the flush can be used to identify and
localize pituitary tumors60 (

Video 293.6).

Classifying Tumor Size
Classifying canine pituitary tumors as microadenomas (<10 mm height)
and macroadenomas (>10 mm height), adapted from humans, is not
useful and should be avoided. Pituitary adenomas 6-10 mm in height
enlarge the gland of small breeds and can result in neurological signs.
Such masses cannot be classified as microadenomas.61 The P/B value has
the highest discriminatory power for distinguishing enlarged from nonenlarged pituitaries. Pituitary enlargement is detected in 64% of dogs
with dexamethasone-resistant HC. Imaging may provide additional
information on the prognosis and quality of life of dogs with HC.25
Advanced imaging with a CT/MRI scan is indicated not only in dogs
intended to be treated by surgery or radiation, but also before starting
medical treatment.

ADRENALS
Abdominal Ultrasonography (US)

Abdominal US is an excellent tool for evaluating the symmetry, size,
shape, and echogenicity of the adrenal glands. US is also valuable in
identifying vascular or local soft tissue invasion of an AT. Adrenal
thickness is the most reliable indicator of enlargement, considering breed
and body size differences.62 Using separate upper limits of “normal” for
left and right adrenal gland thickness, obtained from healthy dogs,
results in high sensitivity (96%) for identifying adrenomegaly in dogs
with HC (

Video 293.7).23

In dogs with PDH, bilateral symmetrical enlargement of the adrenal
glands is expected; however, normal-sized adrenals and mild asymmetry
are common. Moderate to severe asymmetry with contralateral
adrenocortical atrophy (adrenal thickness <4-5 mm) is consistent with an
AT (

Video 293.7).63 Measuring the smaller adrenal gland may best

differentiate HC dogs with functional unilateral AT from dogs with PDH.
Equivocal adrenal asymmetry occurs in about 40% of dogs with HC,
making discrimination of pituitary from adrenal HC difficult. Also,
concurrent conditions such as non-functional AT or pheochromocytoma,
and bilateral ATs may also result in adrenal asymmetry in dogs with HC.
Some adrenal structural features can increase suspicion for
malignancy.64,65 A heterogeneous appearance, reflecting destruction of
normal tissue architecture with necrosis and hemorrhage, is suggestive of
AT rather than adrenocortical hyperplasia. Vascular invasion and adrenal
size >2 cm are the 2 most reliable criteria consistent with a malignant
AT.18

Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasonography (C-EUS)
C-EUS is a non-invasive method for quantifying adrenal gland vascular
patterns. In C-EUS, a contrast agent is administered IV and timeintensity curves are generated for the adrenal cortex, adrenal medulla,
and ipsilateral renal artery of both adrenals. Peak perfusion contrast
intensity, adrenal blood flow, and blood volume in hyperplastic adrenals
of dogs with PDH was twice that of healthy controls. Further studies are
needed to evaluate its usefulness as a differentiating test between
adrenocortical hyperplasia and bilateral ATs as well as between different
types of ATs.66,67

Adrenal Gland CT

CT imaging of the adrenal glands is a sensitive tool for assessing size,
structure, and symmetry. It is more sensitive than US for identifying
vascular invasion. In dogs with an AT intended for surgery, CT imaging is
extremely valuable to screen for metastases in abdomen and thorax. CT
imaging of an AT commonly shows a heterogeneous pattern of contrast
enhancement on late phase CT images.68,69 Studies on intra-tumoral
contrast attenuation with regular and triple-phase helical CT scans
showed more rapid excretion of contrast medium from adrenocortical
adenomas than carcinomas; however, diagnosis of malignancy based on
CT imaging alone is unreliable due to overlapping characteristics between
different tumor types.68,70
CT imaging of the adrenals and pituitary is advised in dogs with HC.25
CT imaging, particularly using reformatted images, is 100% sensitive and
98% specific in calculating the adrenal diameter ratio (maximal diameter
of the larger gland/minimal diameter of the smaller gland). This can be
helpful for discriminating pituitary from adrenal HC or for identifying
dogs with concurrent pituitary and adrenal HC.69 Lack of advanced
imaging to allow diagnosis of concurrent pituitary and adrenal HC may
lead to unsuccessful control of HC and an unrealistic estimate of the
prognosis and quality of life.25

TREATMENT
GOALS AND TREATMENT OF CHOICE
Ideally, treatment of HC would eliminate the source of either ACTH or
autonomous cortisol excess, normalize cortisol, eliminate clinical signs,
reduce long-term complications, decrease mortality, and improve quality
of life.58 Surgical removal of the causal tumor and radiotherapy are the
only treatment options with the potential to eliminate the source of either
ACTH or autonomous cortisol excess but these options are not widely
available and not suitable for every dog. Medical therapy is commonly
used to eliminate clinical signs of HC. Various combinations of radiation,
medical, and surgical treatments are possible. Since treatment choice
depends on the form of HC, discriminating pituitary from adrenal HC is
essential. Other important factors are the severity of the condition,
presence of concurrent disease, age, breed, and client preferences.
Without treatment, dogs with PDH have a median survival time of 359

days (95% confidence interval [CI], 271-829)71 to 506 days (95% CI, 292564).72 There are no survival data for untreated dogs with an AT.

TREATMENT AT THE PITUITARY LEVEL
Hypophysectomy (Removal of the Entire Pituitary)
Hypophysectomy in dogs is performed using a transsphenoidal
approach.73 In a recent study of 306 dogs with PDH that underwent
hypophysectomy, 91% were alive after 4 weeks, and remission was
confirmed in 92% of survivors.74 Of the dogs that went into remission,
disease recurrence was observed in 27%. The median survival time was
781 days (range, 0-3808 days) and the median disease-free interval of the
dogs in remission was 951 days (range, 31-3808 days). Replacement
therapies after hypophysectomy include life-long glucocorticoids and
thyroxine. Desmopressin, a synthetic VP analogue, is needed temporarily
in all dogs and permanently in about 10%. The tissue removed via
hypophysectomy includes the posterior lobe which stores and secretes
VP.75 Transient CDI (ch. 282) occurred more frequently (62%) in dogs
that had enlarged pituitary glands as compared with the non-enlarged
(44%).76
The most common complications of hypophysectomy are perioperative
death, transient mild postoperative hypernatremia, prolonged or
permanent CDI, recurrence of HC, and transient reduction or cessation of
tear production. Factors that negatively influence the prognosis include a
high P/B value, old age, increased preoperative eACTH and UCCR, and
dexamethasone resistance on endocrine testing.74,77 An early diagnosis
of corticotroph adenoma is expected to have the best outcome when
hypophysectomy is the first treatment for dogs with a non-enlarged or
moderately enlarged pituitary. Although a high P/B value is a negative
prognostic indicator, hypophysectomy remains a good treatment option
(Figure 293.4).74,78
The main limitation of hypophysectomy is availability, being limited to
large veterinary centers with an established team of experienced
surgeon(s), anesthetist(s), critical care specialist(s) and
endocrinologist(s). Prior to hypophysectomy, dogs must have a thorough
work-up to ensure they are acceptable anesthetic and surgical candidates.
After hypophysectomy, excellent owner compliance is mandatory to

successfully manage hormone replacements. The owner needs to follow
medication schemes tightly and learn to anticipate extremely stressful
situations. In the long term, screening for recurrence is recommended by
checking a UCCR twice yearly.75

Pituitary Radiotherapy
Pituitary irradiation can cause gradual reduction in tumor size over a
period of 1-16 months but does not usually eliminate the autonomous
hypersecretion of ACTH or clinical signs. Temporary or permanent
trilostane therapy may be required to manage HC.61,79 Usually a total
dose of 36-48 Gy is administered in 3-4 Gy fractions, requiring 12
anesthesias. Factors predictive of outcome for dogs with PDH treated
with radiation therapy include tumor size and severity of neurologic
signs. Dogs with severe neurologic signs have a poorer prognosis than
dogs with mild or no signs.61,71
The most common acute adverse effects (i.e., occurring within 4
months of completing radiation therapy) include anorexia and
depression due to pituitary hemorrhage. The most common late-onset
adverse effect is chronic otitis media, which does not usually cause the
typical clinical signs of head tilt, nystagmus, and/or pain. Some develop
hearing impairment. The reported median survival time of dogs with
PDH following radiation therapy ranges from 539 to 1405 days.71,79
Radiotherapy can be used as an adjuvant treatment after
hypophysectomy for recurrence or if surgical mass debulking was
performed to relieve neurological signs.42

Stereotactic Radiotherapy
This involves the precise delivery of highly conformal dose-intense
radiation to well-demarcated tumors. This unique biological mechanism
distinguishes stereotactic radiation therapy from other forms of external
beam radiotherapy (ch. 318). Stereotactic radiation therapy has emerged
as an attractive treatment for various canine brain tumors due to the
shortened treatment course and fewer anesthesias as compared with
standard radiation therapy.80 Studies on stereotactic radiation therapy
for canine pituitary tumors have been limited and have included dogs
with ACTH-secreting tumors and dogs with nonfunctional tumors. Dogs
with PDH received 24 Gy in 1 dose or divided into 3 fractions. Median
overall survival was 245 days (range 2-626 days), shorter than reported

with conventional radiation therapy.81 The small number of treated dogs
precludes detailed survival analysis but a trend towards shorter survival
in dogs with larger tumors was observed.82 Dogs with nonfunctional
masses had longer medial overall survival than dogs with HC.

Stereotactic Radiosurgery
This precise image-guided targeted form of radiotherapy is delivered in a
single high-dose session using the “Gamma Knife.” It is well tolerated in
humans with pituitary tumors and may require less time for a response
than after conventional radiation therapy. The same technique has
recently been applied to dogs with pituitary tumors and showed
promising results in reducing tumor volume.83,84

TREATMENT AT THE ADRENAL LEVEL
Adrenalectomy: Treatment of Choice for a Solitary
Tumor
Complete tumor removal is curative, resolving current or future issues
related to mass compression or tumor invasion. Successful surgery
resolves clinical signs of HC without need for lifelong replacement
medication. Glucocorticoid-producing cells in the opposite adrenal are
usually atrophied at the time of surgery due to chronic cortisol excess
suppressing CRH and ACTH secretion. Thus, temporary glucocorticoid
replacement should be anticipated.4 After bilateral adrenalectomy, dogs
require both glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids lifelong. Dosages are
monitored according to the treatment protocol for Addison’s disease (ch.
296).

Adrenalectomy: Laparoscopic vs Open Surgery
Adrenalectomy is commonly performed via ventral or paracostal open
laparotomies but laparoscopic adrenal tumor removal is gaining
popularity.85,86 Its advantages over open surgery include reduced
manipulation of other abdominal organs, an excellent view of abdominal
structures, decreased surgical wound complications, improved
postoperative comfort, shorter hospital stays, and shorter recovery
periods. The two major selection criteria for choosing a modality are
tumor size and presence of vascular invasion. When an AT is >5 cm in

diameter and/or invasion of the caudal vena cava is recognized, the open
technique is preferred to laparoscopy by many surgeons.

Adrenalectomy: Complications and Survival Times
Perioperative mortality rates are as low as 6-8% in dogs with a small AT
without evidence of vascular invasion87 to 24% with invasive ATs.88 The
main perioperative complications include minor to severe hemorrhage,
hypotension, hypertension, bradycardia, tachycardia, and death.87,89,90
The tumor capsule can rupture, possibly more often in laparoscopic than
in open adrenalectomies, but does not necessarily lead to tumor
regrowth. The main complications that can occur postoperatively include
pancreatitis and thromboembolism. Reported HC recurrence rates vary
from 12-30%. Recurrence of HC can be due to AT regrowth, functional
metastases, or development of PDH. Median survival times for dogs with
adrenal-dependent HC undergoing adrenalectomy range from 778 days91
to 953 days.89 AT diameter was significantly associated with survival,
while venous invasion, capsule rupture, surgery duration, or medical
treatment before surgery had no influence on survival. Dogs with an AT
diameter <3 cm had significantly better survival times after
adrenalectomy than those with a tumor ≥3 cm.20 Adrenalectomy is not
recommended in dogs with metastasis, underscoring the importance of
presurgical imaging. Vascular invasion does not necessarily exclude
adrenalectomy. Some studies indicate that AT with vena cava invasion
does not affect perioperative mortality since techniques to remove tumor
and tumor thrombus have improved (

Video 293.5).24,92 However,

when vascular invasion extends beyond the hepatic hilus, perioperative
mortality rates increase.88,93 Forty percent of dogs with a thrombus
extending beyond the diaphragm survived surgery as compared with 7381% when the thrombus terminated before the diaphragm, suggesting a
poorer prognosis for dogs with a tumor thrombus that extends beyond
the diaphragm.88

Stereotactic Radiotherapy
Hypofractionated stereotactic volume-modulated radiotherapy was
reported in 9 dogs with invasive ATs.94 The dogs received 30-45 Gy in 3
or 5 consecutive daily fractions. Their median survival time was 1030

days. The diameter and volume were reduced 32% and 30%, respectively.
These encouraging results may provide a feasible and effective
therapeutic option for dogs that have an AT with vascular invasion.

TRILOSTANE MEDICAL THERAPY
Description and Mechanisms of Action
Trilostane is a synthetic steroid analogue that competitively inhibits the
steroidogenic enzyme 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, required for
synthesis of all steroid hormones (Figure 293.1).95 Trilostane inhibits
cortisol and mineralocorticoid production. Inhibiting cortisol synthesis
decreases negative feedback to the pituitary, leading to increases in
ACTH. Inhibiting aldosterone causes a compensatory increase in plasma
renin activity.96 Additionally, trilostane possibly also affects other
enzymes in the steroidogenesis cascade, such as 11-beta-hydroxysteroid
dehydrogenase.97

Dose
Trilostane is registered for the medical management of both pituitary and
adrenal HC, but most studies have been limited to dogs with PDH.
Trilostane is absorbed rapidly from the gastrointestinal (GI) tract and
should always be given with food. There are marked variations in
individual trilostane dose requirements. Current recommendations are to
start with much lower doses than was originally recommended by the
manufacturer. Lower doses have been effective and induce fewer adverse
effects.98,99 Larger dogs generally need a lower dose/kg body weight
than smaller dogs. Because the duration of cortisol suppression is (far)
less than 12 hours in most dogs, giving the drug q12h improves the
clinical response, keeps the total daily dose relatively low, and
significantly reduces incidence of adverse effects. The initial
recommended dosage is 0.5-1 mg/kg PO q12h for dogs with PDH and
0.2-0.5 mg/kg for dogs with adrenal-dependent HC (Figure
293.6).100,101

Time to a Clinical Response
Within weeks, an adequate dose of trilostane can increase the dog’s
activity and reduce PU/PD/PP. Several months may be needed to observe

notable improvements on the skin and hair coat. The haircoat can
sometimes initially appear to worsen, due to shedding of telogen hairs
and dry skin scales.102

Adverse Effects
Trilostane is usually well tolerated. A significant number (>10%) of
trilostane-treated dogs fail to respond. The most common adverse effect
is transient hypocortisolism (insufficient glucocorticoids), possibly
combined with or followed by complete hypoadrenocorticism (shortage
of both glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids). One study suggested
that dogs have a 15% chance of at least 1 episode of clinical
hypocortisolism within the first 2 years of trilostane treatment.103 In
most dogs, adverse effects resolve quickly after trilostane is withdrawn.
In such dogs, continuing treatment with a lower dose is recommended
when clinical signs of HC recur. However, hypoadrenocorticism can be
permanent or fatal in some dogs, possibly the result of adrenal
necrosis.104,105

The “Best” or “Key” Monitoring Aid
There has been much frustration in identifying a consistent and reliable
monitoring tool when treating a dog with trilostane. Ideally, test results
identify proper dose, frequency, and would reliably indicate if a dog is
over dosed or under dosed. No available blood or urine test meets these
criteria. The only “test result” that has been consistent and reliable is
owner opinion. Regardless of any in-hospital test chosen to monitor
trilostane treatment, it is imperative to understand the owner’s opinion.
The value of owner opinion is enhanced dramatically through owner
education and by assuring owners that their observations are extremely
important.

Monitoring with the ACTHst
Results of the ACTHst reflect adrenocortical reserve capacity for
secreting cortisol (Figure 293.7).106 Since trilostane has its main effects
for only a few hours after administration, timing the start of the ACTHst
is crucial.107,108 Thus, the ACTHst should be started 2-4 hours after
trilostane administration. Despite its widespread use, ACTHst results
have never been validated as a monitoring tool for trilostane therapy and
several reports have indicated their lack of reliability. Results can be

completely altered by starting the test earlier or later, rather than
indicating level of control.109,110 Possibly overdosed dogs with baseline
and post-ACTHst [cortisol] <2 mcg/dL (<55 nmol/L), 3-6 hours after
trilostane, had much higher cortisols if the test was repeated 6 hours
later. Continuing trilostane therapy without reducing the trilostane dose
did not lead to clinical hypoadrenocorticism and seemed safe. Failure to
respond adequately to ACTHst at a time when trilostane is at its peak, is
not the same as a trilostane overdose.

FIGURE 293.6 Pre-pill algorithm for monitoring
dogs with hypercortisolism (HC) treated with trilostane.
ACTH, Adrenocorticotropic hormone. Cortisol unit
conversion: 1.5 mcg/dL = 41 nmol/L; 5 +/- 15% mcg/dL
= 138 +/- 15% nmol/L.

Monitoring with Pre-Pill Cortisols
A proposed alternative to using the ACTHst is to measure the pre-pill
[cortisol] and compare it with the clinical signs observed by owners. The
pre-pill cortisol was found to better reflect clinical control than ACTHst

results.110 The question remains, however, whether a single cortisol
measurement in trilostane-treated dogs with HC is sufficiently reliable.
Cortisol fluctuates and is influenced by various factors, e.g., stress.
Indeed, the agreement between two pre-pill [cortisol] taken 1 hour apart
and 11-13hours after the last trilostane application is only moderate.
Stress during any evaluation can influence [cortisol]. When using pre-pill
[cortisol] to monitor trilostane therapy, one should note any stress during
handling of the dog to more confidently interpret test results.111 In dogs
in which pre-pill [cortisol] is below the target range, a trilostane dose
reduction should be considered, because it is possible that the adrenal
reserve is not optimal. In unwell and possibly overdosed dogs, pre-pill
cortisol should be replaced by the ACTHst (Figures 293.6 and 293.7).
The principle of pre-pill cortisol is not comparable to that of the ACTHst:
it is not a measure of adrenocortical reserve. This is relevant, because
dogs with excellent clinical control and an adequate pre-pill cortisol can
have insufficient adrenocortical reserve capacity. This can become
clinically relevant in stressful situations (illness).103 This leaves the
ACTHst superior in evaluating the safety of trilostane therapy.

on the adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
stimulation test performed 2 to 3 hours after
administration of trilostane. Evaluation of clinical signs
is the first and crucial step in the interpretation of the

Other Monitoring Tools
Among other monitoring variables, the UCCR, cortisol/ACTH ratio, serial
serum cortisols after trilostane administration, and USG have not been

reliable for monitoring trilostane therapy in dogs with HC. None
consistently correlated with owner opinion and none reliably
discriminated dogs receiving an adequate trilostane dose from dogs that
might benefit from an increase in dose or frequency.100,101,112
Haptoglobin (Hp), a moderate acute phase protein, has been
demonstrated to increase in dogs with hypercortisolemia and a reduced
Hp concentration is detected during trilostane treatment.113 Measuring
serum Hp in dogs with HC provided additional information on the
response to the therapy with trilostane.114 However, the Hp is a positive
acute-phase protein, and the results could be biased if a dog has a
concomitant inflammatory condition (i.e., UTI). For this reason, it is
advisable to interpret Hp concentrations individually and to consider the
concomitant comorbidities as well.

Prognosis
In dogs with PDH, trilostane effectively controls HC clinical signs but
does not affect the pituitary tumor. Continued tumor growth should be
expected, even in dogs with non-enlarged pituitary glands at the time of
diagnosis (i.e., P/B value <0.31 mm/mm2). In healthy dogs, the P/B
value significantly increases following trilostane therapy, but this has not
been studied in dogs with PDH.115 Nonetheless, especially in younger
dogs, a CT or MRI scan after 1 year of treatment should be considered to
re-evaluate pituitary size (ch. 112). The reported median survival times
of dogs with PDH treated with trilostane range from 549 to 662 days
when treated once daily,116 and about 852 days when dogs were on once
or twice daily regimens.117 In dogs with a cortisol-secreting AT, trilostane
is only palliative. It can reduce clinical signs but does not affect AT
growth or development of metastasis. The reported median survival
times of dogs with ATs treated with trilostane range from 353 to 596
days.118,119

MITOTANE MEDICAL THERAPY
Description and Mechanisms of Action
Mitotane (o,p′-DDD) is an adrenocorticolytic agent derived from the
insecticide DDT that causes progressive adrenocortical necrosis and
atrophy in dogs. Mitotane inhibits the steroidogenic enzymes cytochrome

P450 cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme (CYP11A1) and CYP11B1,
which contribute to inhibition of cortisol synthesis and the activation of
other cytochrome P450 enzymes such as cytochrome P450 enzyme 3A4
(CYP3A4), which leads to increased metabolic clearance of
glucocorticoids. Although mitotane has been used to treat HC in dogs for
decades, the exact mechanism of action was poorly understood. A recent
study identified inhibition of sterol-O-acyl-transferase 1 (SOAT1), an
enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of free cholesterol to cholesterol
esters, as one of its actions. Inhibition of this conversion increases the
amount of free cholesterol in adrenocortical cells, which can lead to
endoplasmic reticulum stress and cell apoptosis.120

Indications and Dose
Use of mitotane to treat PDH in dogs has largely been replaced by
trilostane. Trilostane is as effective, safer to handle, and causes fewer
adverse effects. However, in dogs with an AT, mitotane remains a good
option because it can destroy AT cells.58 The goal of mitotane therapy in
AT is not only to reduce cortisol production but also to destroy the
neoplastic cells. A non-selective protocol that affects the entire adrenal
cortex is recommended using daily doses of 50 to 75 mg/kg PO for 5 days
and then q48h for 40 days.4 For dogs of small breeds, a higher dosage of
up to 100 mg/kg PO may be required. Daily doses should be divided into
3 or 4 portions. For sufficient absorption, mitotane should be given with
food. Replacement therapy starts on day 3, consisting of daily
glucocorticoids (e.g., 2 mg/kg cortisone acetate), mineralocorticoids (e.g.,
0.0125 mg/kg fludrocortisone acetate), and salt (0.1 g/kg NaCl), all
divided q12h. After completing the initial course of mitotane, the
glucocorticoid dose can be reduced (e.g., 0.5-1 mg/kg cortisone acetate)
but doubled for 1 or 2 days in the event of injury, severe physical stress,
or anesthesia. To prevent recurrence, mitotane should be administered at
the initial daily dose once weekly for at least 6 months, or even
lifelong.121

Adverse Effects, Monitoring, Prognosis
Adverse effects of mitotane include anorexia, lethargy, weakness and
diarrhea. If seen, mitotane must be temporarily discontinued, but not the
substitution therapy. To evaluate whether the AT has been destroyed
completely, the UCCR can be measured after the initial course of
mitotane (i.e., after day 45) and every 6 months thereafter. In addition to

UCCR, regular blood Na and K assessment is important to help
determine the dose of mineralocorticoids. The median survival times of
dogs with ATs treated with mitotane range from 102 to 476 days and did
not differ significantly from the survival times for dogs treated with
trilostane.118,119 However, these studies used only partial adrenocortical
destruction and did not use the mitotane protocol as described herein
(aimed at complete adrenocortical destruction).

NEW MEDICAL ADRENAL-TARGETED
TREATMENTS
Concerns regarding current medical adrenal-targeting treatment options
include low selectivity for specifically decreasing cortisol, possibility of
overdosage, and occurrence of disruptive changes in the adrenal cortex
which necessitate careful dosing schemes and regular check-ups. Current
research is exploring therapeutic candidates that might have superior
selectivity, effectivity, and/or tolerability. These candidates include
MC2R antagonist, steroidogenic factor 1 inverse agonists, and novel
formulations of SOAT1 inhibitors.

PHARMACOTHERAPY: DRUGS
TARGETING THE PITUITARY
Overview
Medical management of PDH would ideally target the pituitary tumor.
Because dopamine (DA) and somatostatin (SST) both have inhibitory
functions in the pituitary gland, research on pituitary-targeting drugs
focuses on 3 receptor subtypes: DA receptor subtype 2 (DRD2), SST
receptor subtype 2 (SSTR2), and SST receptor subtype 5 (SSTR5). In
canine corticotroph adenomas, the primary receptor subtype expressed is
SSTR2, while DRD2 and particularly SSTR5 are expressed, but at much
lower levels.122 There are currently no pituitary-targeted drugs that are
registered for use in canine PDH.

Cabergoline
Cabergoline is a DA agonist that binds to DRD2. In line with the
moderate DRD2 expression in canine corticotroph adenomas, canine

corticotroph cells responded only modestly to cabergoline in vitro.123
However, in vivo experiments demonstrate that 43% of dogs with PDH
responded to cabergoline therapy with fewer clinical signs, smaller
pituitary adenomas, and lower UCCRs. This observed difference in
efficacy could possibly be explained by the different durations of
treatment. Pro-apoptotic and anti-proliferative effects on the pituitary
gland, potentially reducing tumor size, make cabergoline an interesting
option.

Pasireotide
Pasireotide is a multiligand SST analog that binds to the SST receptors 1,
2, 3 and 5. In 20 PDH dogs, pasireotide decreased plasma eACTH and
improved clinical signs, while no severe adverse effects were observed.124
In a recent study, pasireotide plus trilostane or mitotane was given to
PDH dogs with large pituitary tumors. Pituitary tumor volume decreased
in 6/9 dogs and increased in 3. No neurologic signs or grossly apparent
adverse effects were observed.125

Octreotide
Octreotide, an SST analog, binds to SSTR2 with high affinity and to SST
receptor subtype 3 (SSTR3) and SSTR5 with moderate affinity. In line
with the high SSTR2 expression in canine corticotroph adenomas,
octreotide inhibited ACTH release from corticotroph cells in vitro more
effectively than either pasireotide or cabergoline.122 In humans,
octreotide can cause GI side effects, but this is less well documented for
dogs. For other cancers, e.g., insulinoma, octreotide is sometimes used as
adjunctive treatment to inhibit insulin secretion (ch. 289). Due to the
high SSTR2 expression in canine corticotroph tumors, the availability of
oral octreotide treatment could be an interesting treatment approach for
dogs with PDH.

COMPLICATIONS AND COMORBIDITIES
SYSTEMIC HYPERTENSION (CH. 236)
Hypertension, defined as a systolic blood pressure (BP) >160 mm Hg, has
been diagnosed in 37-86% of untreated HC dogs and nearly half had
severe hypertension (>180 mm Hg). Routine BP evaluation is advocated

in all dogs with HC (ch. 91). Dogs with thrombocytosis, hypokalemia,
and/or proteinuria have the highest risk of target organ damage
recognized in eyes, kidneys, brain, heart, and blood vessels. Proposed
pathophysiological mechanisms for the hypertension include increased
mineralocorticoid activity, decreased nitric oxide concentrations, and
increased renal vascular resistance.126,127 Systemic hypertension
warrants treatment. Prevalence and severity of systemic hypertension are
not correlated with clinical control of HC and some develop hypertension
only during medical treatment with trilostane. Therefore, continuous
monitoring of BP during treatment for HC is recommended.126

DIABETES MELLITUS (DM, CH. 291)
DM is one of the most common comorbidities of HC.33,45 Cortisol excess
induces a state of insulin resistance and favors hepatic gluconeogenesis,
but it also affects beta-cell function by decreasing insulin secretion,
blunting the incretin effect, and by direct cytotoxicity.128 This
combination commonly causes mild hyperglycemia in dogs with HC,
changes that resemble feline diabetes more than canine, and changes that
resolve with successful management of HC (chs. 291 and 292).
Restricting the diagnosis of DM to BG concentrations which exceed renal
threshold (175-225 mg/dL [9.7-12.5 mmol/L]) causing persistent
glucosuria in dogs with pre-existing HC is usually straightforward.
However, diagnosing HC in a dog with poorly controlled DM can be
challenging because of overlapping clinical and clinicopathological
features. Further, uncontrolled DM can result in false-positive adrenal
function test results and therefore diagnostic imaging is needed to
confirm the diagnosis.45 Trying to obtain reasonable management of DM
before testing for HC is usually advised. Management of dogs with
concurrent DM and HC should take into consideration both conditions.
Adequate control of DM is unlikely if HC is not properly managed.

GALLBLADDER MUCOCELE (CH. 273)
Gallbladder mucocele has been reported in 1.6-23% of dogs with HC (
Video 293.8).33,129 HC is reported in 3.4-23% of dogs with
gallbladder mucocele.130 Concurrent diagnosis of HC at the time of

cholecystectomy in dogs with gallbladder mucocele is associated with
about a 2-fold increase in odds of death-in-hospital than dogs without
HC.131 The association between gallbladder mucocele and HC is thought
to be due to significantly higher concentrations of unconjugated bile acids
within the extrahepatic biliary tree resulting from steroid excess.
Unconjugated bile acids are more hydrophobic and may lead to injury to
the biliary epithelium and subsequent mucinous hyperplasia, one of the
defining histological features of mucoceles. Recent work with adrenal
testing in dogs with both HC and mucocele showed increased basal and
post-ACTHst concentrations of DHEA, suggesting that these dogs have
impaired secretion of DHEA. Altered transport or increased androgen
synthesis by the adrenals is also possible.132 In dogs with HC and
mucocele, higher dosages of trilostane were required to control HC. Since
trilostane is a lipid-soluble drug, the higher dose requirement may be the
result of decreased ability to secrete bile, similar to what happens with
lipid-soluble nutrients known to be decreased when an extrahepatic
biliary obstruction is present.132

UROLITHIASIS (CH. 308)
Urolithiasis was reported in about 3% of dogs with HC.33 Hypercalciuria
appears to be a predisposing factor for Ca oxalate urolith formation. In
dogs with HC, a 10 times higher predisposition for Ca-containing uroliths
has been reported compared to control dogs.

PULMONARY THROMBOEMBOLISM (PT,
CH. 219)
PT is extremely uncommon in dogs with HC. When present, it may cause
acute tachypnea, orthopnea, and dyspnea. This complication is likely a
consequence of the hypercoagulability that occurs in dogs with HC.
Increased fibrinogen concentrations, decreased fibrinolysis, and/or
thrombocytosis have been suggested to be the cause of hypercoagulability
in affected dogs. Also, changes in thromboelastography consistent with a
hypercoagulative status can be observed.51,133

CLIENT INFORMATION
Hyperadrenocorticism (Cushing’s Syndrome) in
Dogs
WHAT IS CUSHING’S SYNDROME?
Cushing’s syndrome or hypercortisolism is a condition caused by
excessive secretion of the hormone cortisol, a glucocorticoid hormone
that is necessary for life and it is normally secreted in response to stress.
The chronic excess of cortisol leads to clinical signs, such as drinking and
urinating excessively, increased appetite, weakness and fatigue, excessive
panting even at rest, dull and dry hair coat, hair loss, or a distended
abdomen with potbelly appearance. These clinical signs might progress
slowly and, in some dogs the disease may remain unnoticed for some
time.
There are two main causes of this disease in dogs. The most common
cause of the disease (85% of the cases) is a benign tumor in the pituitary
gland, a small hormone secreting gland located in the base of the brain.
High amounts of a hormone (ACTH or adrenocorticotropin hormone)
secreted by the pituitary tumor stimulate cortisol production in adrenal
glands located in the abdomen. The disease is called pituitarydependent hypercortisolism (PDH).
In approximately 15% of the dogs with the disease, a tumor in one or
both adrenal glands produces the excess of cortisol, independently of the
pituitary gland. This is called adrenal-dependent hypercortisolism.
Adrenal tumors in dogs causing Cushing’s syndrome are malignant or
benign.

DIAGNOSIS
Diagnosis of Cushing’s syndrome requires routine blood and urine tests
and hormonal tests. Diagnostic imaging will also be needed to confirm
the disease and to differentiate between the pituitary and adrenal-

dependent hypercortisolism, but also to choose the most optimal
treatment.

TREATMENT
In PDH caused by a small pituitary tumor the treatment of choice
is the administration of the drug trilostane (Vetoryl), which reduces
the synthesis of cortisol in the adrenal glands. In most dogs trilostane will
be needed to be administered for life, since its effect is reversible, and it
will disappear some hours after its administration. You are going to
notice the effect of trilostane during the first days of treatment; your pet
will drink less water and urinate less, the appetite will be reduced, and
probably she/he will feel better. Other issues such as hair loss, skin
problems, weight gain and pendulous abdomen, as well as some of the
common blood test findings (increased liver enzymes), may take 3 to 6
months to resolve. The hair coat may worsen before it improves.
Trilostane may produce adverse effects, which are associated with
shortage of cortisol. The side effects can be subtle: reduced appetite and
thirst, and soft feces; or moderate to severe, including reduced appetite
or anorexia, nausea or vomiting, diarrhea, and weakness. If you observe
any of these signs, even if they are subtle, YOU SHOULD STOP GIVING
THE TRILOSTANE. These clinical signs will usually disappear after 1 to 2
days of drug withdrawal, since cortisol secretion is restored. However, in
a small number of patients, clinical signs of hypocortisolism might persist
and some dogs might require steroid supplementation.

Initial Dose and Monitoring
In most patients, the initial dose must be adjusted during follow up
(>70% of patients), and thus, it is essential to carefully monitor your pet
during the treatment with trilostane. The checkups must be done after 2
weeks of treatment, a month after the first recheck, and about every 3
months afterwards until the dosage is stable. In well-regulated dogs, after
the first year of the treatment, checkups can be done every 6 months.
Trilostane therapy should be monitored with either ACTH stimulation
test or pre-pill cortisol method; your veterinarian will discuss this with
you. Your veterinarian will ask you about the restoration of the clinical
signs, perform physical exam as well as blood analyses, in order to
evaluate whether the dose is adequate or should be modified.
In PDH caused by an enlarged pituitary tumor radiotherapy
or hypophysectomy might be a better choice. Large pituitary tumors can
cause reduced appetite, behavioral signs, reduced consciousness and

central nervous system signs and therefore treatment with trilostane is
not sufficient to provide a good quality of life. Trilostane does not affect
the pituitary tumor at all.
In dogs with adrenal-dependent hypercortisolism the
treatment of choice is surgery, because successful removal of the adrenal
tumor will cause the complete remission of the clinical signs and avoid
complications of uncontrolled tumor growth. Adrenalectomy should be
done by an expert at a specialized referral institution. Adrenal tumors
might also be treated with mitotane, since at high doses the drug may
cause tumor necrosis; however, at such doses, the risk of adverse effects
is also elevated. An alternative treatment in dogs with adrenal-dependent
hypercortisolism is the administration of trilostane, which reduces the
levels of cortisol and improves the clinical condition of the dogs. This
treatment does not reduce or eliminate the tumor; its goal is to help
reduce symptoms.
Sara Galac (Utrecht, The Netherlands)

INTRODUCTION
Feline hyperadrenocorticism (fHAC; Cushing’s syndrome; hypercortisolism) is less common, has more
worrisome consequences, and poses greater challenges to diagnose and treat than canine
hyperadrenocorticism (cHAC). fHAC has a worse prognosis than the condition in dogs. Unlike in dogs,
fHAC is commonly associated with diabetes mellitus (DM), a skin hyperfragility syndrome, and other
conditions that can complicate management. Basic pathophysiology and other aspects of fHAC are
similar to cHAC (ch. 293). This chapter focuses on the clinical condition in cats caused by chronic
exposure to excess cortisol or other steroid hormones with cortisol-like action. For example, cats with
progesterone-secreting adrenocortical tumors, with or without aldosterone secretion, may have clinical
signs similar to fHAC (ch. 295).1-3 Importantly, insulin-resistant DM in cats is more commonly
associated with hypersomatotropism (HS; feline acromegaly) than with fHAC (ch. 280).

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Naturally occurring fHAC is a multi-systemic disorder resulting from excessive production of cortisol by
the adrenal cortices. There are single case reports and several case series of cats with fHAC that together
total only about 100 cases.4-25 Pituitary-dependent hyperadrenocorticism (PDH) affects about 85% of
cats with fHAC, most commonly caused by an autonomous adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)secreting adenoma. Adrenal-dependent hyperadrenocorticism (ADH) affects about 15% of cats with

fHAC, usually caused by an autonomously functioning adrenocortical adenoma or carcinoma.5 A small
number of cats have a pituitary tumor that secretes more than 1 hormone.19,26-29 Iatrogenic fHAC has
been described after glucocorticoid or progestogen administration,30-32 either of which can severely
suppress endogenous cortisol and cause adrenocortical atrophy.33

CLINICAL SIGNS
OVERVIEW
Early reports of cats with fHAC described obvious clinical signs, often present for months before
diagnosis. As subtleties and variations in signs and associated biochemical disorders are better
appreciated, fHAC is being diagnosed in cats with fewer clinical signs (Table 294.1).6 Early diagnosis
and treatment may avoid development of severe clinical signs or DM.34

AGE, BREED, SEX
fHAC is most common in middle-aged to older cats (median age in the various studies was 9.5 to 13
years; range from 3 to 15 years) with no apparent sex or breed predilection.

PHYSICAL CHANGES
Skin
Cutaneous manifestations of fHAC include truncal and abdominal alopecia, but far less frequently than
in cHAC. An unkempt hair coat and cornification defects/seborrhea are common. Their thin skin is
prone to tears, bruising, and secondary infection (Figure 294.1). The hyperfragile skin is particularly
distressing to owners and unwary clinicians. Cats with fHAC should always be handled with great care.
Calcinosis cutis has not been reported in naturally occurring nor iatrogenic fHAC. Recurrent sebaceous
cysts have also been seen.

Other Physical Examination Findings
Cats with fHAC often have a pendulous abdomen, muscle wasting, hepatomegaly, and weight gain. A
minority lose weight. Some have softened tongue barbs or tongue ulcers.

METABOLIC ALTERATIONS
Diabetes Mellitus (DM)
Polyuria, polydipsia (PU/PD) and polyphagia (PP) are the most common metabolic signs of fHAC but
are almost always secondary to DM with its consequent glycosuria and osmotic diuresis (ch. 292) or to
chronic kidney disease (CKD) with its consequent inability to concentrate urine (ch. 301). Most cats
with fHAC have insulin resistant DM; in 1 case series, 27 of 30.11 Several other series have indicated that
a majority, but not all, cats with hyperadrenocorticism (HAC) have concurrent DM.7,10 Insulin
resistance is reflected in large daily insulin doses often required (∼2 units/kg) to control their
hyperglycemia and glycosuria.4,7 However, clinicians should not exclude the possibility of HAC in a wellcontrolled diabetic on a typical dose of insulin. PU/PD is not common in fHAC in the absence of DM or
CKD.

Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD, ch. 301)
PU/PD in fHAC can also be associated with CKD, a rare concomitant condition in cHAC. There is no
evidence of a direct correlation between the two nor that presence of one makes the other more difficult
to manage.11 Most cats with fHAC and a urine specific gravity (USG) <1.020 have CKD.

Infection
Many cats with HAC develop infections, sometimes with unusual organisms, that are frequently difficult
to resolve.4,9,11,17 This apparent predisposition to infection suggests that cats with fHAC are either quite
immunosuppressed or their fragile skin, DM, and other concurrent conditions increase susceptibility to
severe infection.

Pancreatitis (ch. 278)
Cats with fHAC have been described as having pancreatitis, but fHAC is a severe anti-inflammatory
condition, making this an unlikely pairing of conditions. Feline pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity
(fPLI) may not be reliable in cats with fHAC.11,35

Systemic Hypertension (ch. 236), Blindness (ch. 13)
About 20% of cats with fHAC are hypertensive, a lower prevalence than in cHAC.11,36 Acute blindness
due to bilateral retinal detachment was reported in a hypertensive cat with HAC.23

IMAGING
SERUM BIOCHEMISTRY PROFILE, COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT (CBC),
URINALYSIS (UA)
Hyperglycemia, seen in about 80% of cats with fHAC, is common. Most but not all of these cats have
overt DM (Table 294.2; Figure 294.2). About 50% of cats with fHAC have hypercholesterolemia,
probably related to poorly controlled DM and increased lipolysis (ch. 63). In 1 review, >50% of cats with
fHAC had increases in blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and >25% had increases in both BUN and creatinine
concentrations, consistent with CKD (ch. 62).37 Cats lack a steroid-induced isoenzyme of alkaline
phosphatase (ALP) and only ∼30% of cats with fHAC have even mild increases in ALP and/or alanine
aminotransferase (ALT) activity, likely secondary to DM (ch. 65). The “stress leukogram”
(lymphopenia, eosinopenia and neutrophilia) is not common in cats with fHAC (ch. 58). Cats with
fHAC that do not have DM or CKD usually have USG >1.020. In comparison to dogs with HAC, cats tend
to have more dramatic physical changes and less dramatic clinicopathological changes.

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
Overview
Diagnostic imaging allows identification of pituitary and adrenal size (large or small) and can provide
evidence of masses, local vessel or organ invasion, or metastases, aiding in choosing individualized
treatment strategies. Seeing a mass does not indicate function. Images should be interpreted in the
context of clinical signs and endocrine test results.

Radiography
Radiographic examination of the thorax and abdomen is advisable in all cats suspected or proven to
have fHAC. Survey radiographs of the thorax and abdomen uncommonly reveal an adrenal mass
(Figure 294.3, A), but also may identify concurrent abnormalities that alter a treatment plan and/or
prognosis. Abdominal contrast is enhanced by the marked intra-abdominal fat seen in cats with fHAC.
Steroid-induced osteopenia, calcium containing uroliths, and parathyroid hormone values have not been
reported for fHAC.38 Adrenal calcification can be a benign incidental finding in older cats (Figure
294.3, B).

FIGURE 294.2 Diagnostic approach to a cat suspected of having
hyperadrenocorticism (HAC). (Note on cortisol unit conversion: 400 nmol/L =
14.5 mcg/dL and 40 nmol/L = 1.4 mcg/dL.) ACTH, Adrenocorticotropic
hormone; ADH, adrenal tumor dependent hyperadrenocorticism; GI,
gastrointestinal; PDH, pituitary dependent hyperadrenocorticism; USG, urine
specific gravity.

Abdominal Ultrasonography (US)
Both adrenal glands can usually be seen in healthy cats. The right adrenal gland, due to its location
under the ribs, may be more difficult to identify. Normal cat adrenal glands (∼4.5-13.7 mm in length,
2.9-5.3 mm in width) are oval to bi-lobed, hypoechoic to surrounding tissue, and the medulla can be
slightly hyperechoic.39 The challenge is distinguishing normal from hyperplastic or neoplastic adrenals.
Adrenals of cats with PDH are symmetrically enlarged and of normal conformation, but the enlargement
is variable and subjective. Hyperplastic adrenals have normal homogeneous hypoechoic patterns. Seeing
1 large irregular adrenal while the other appears small is consistent with a functioning adrenal tumor.
Bilateral adrenal tumors are rare.2,4 Malignant adrenal tumors may invade local blood vessels and
surrounding tissues. If an adrenal mass is identified, liver, spleen, and kidneys should be carefully
examined for evidence of metastasis.

Computed Tomography (CT) and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) Scans
CT and MRI scans are useful in identifying adrenal tumors, adrenal hyperplasia, and pituitary tumors.
Contrast abdominal CT may help identify tumor invasion of the caudal vena cava, invasion of other
blood vessels, or adhesions in the area of the mass: important considerations before planning

adrenalectomy. Correlation between pituitary tumor size and presence or development of neurological
signs is not clear. Large pituitary masses are readily identified on MRI or CT (ch. 112).

ENDOCRINE TESTING TO “SCREEN” FOR fHAC
OVERVIEW
There is no “best test” for confirming a diagnosis of fHAC. Basal cortisol concentrations are of little use.
Dynamic testing is essential (Table 294.3). Measuring cortisol concentrations in cats has not been
studied in as much detail as it has been in dogs and reference ranges from different laboratories using
different machines cannot be used interchangeably.40,41 Clinicians should use reference ranges
generated from their laboratory and should consult with their laboratory personnel before using values
from other laboratories or the literature in test interpretation.

FIGURE 294.3 A, A right lateral abdominal radiograph of a 12-year-old
neutered male Domestic Shorthair with hyperadrenocorticism due to an adrenal
mass (black arrows). B, A lateral radiograph of a 10-year-old Domestic
Shorthair with calcified adrenal glands. This is an incidental finding in older
cats and is not associated with abnormal adrenal function.

ACTH STIMULATION TEST (ACTHst)
The ACTHst may be useful for diagnosing fHAC. However, the peak response in cats is variable in both
timing and magnitude. Samples should be obtained before and 60 and 90 minutes after giving 5 mcg/kg
or 0.125 mg/cat tetracosactrin IV.42,43 Reported test sensitivity varies from 56-80%.4,7,9,11 Normal cats
and cats with chronic disease rarely have a post-ACTH cortisol >400 nmol/L (>14.5 mcg/dL).44
However, some conditions, e.g., hyperthyroidism, can result in post-ACTH cortisol concentrations as
high as 600 nmol/L (21.7 mcg/dL). Cortisol results >600 nmol/L (>21.7 mcg/dL) are very suggestive,
and values between 400 and 600 nmol/L (14.5 and 21.7 mcg/dL) are supportive of fHAC in a cat with
appropriate clinical signs. Cats with fHAC rarely have post-ACTHst cortisol concentrations >800
nmol/L (>29 mcg/dL). An ACTHst result within the reference interval does not rule out fHAC.

DEXAMETHASONE SCREENING TESTS (DSTs)
Both the degree and duration of adrenocortical suppression produced by dexamethasone varies among
healthy cats. Generally, the “low dose” DST uses a higher dosage (0.1 mg/kg) in cats than for dogs.
Serum cortisol concentrations in healthy cats are reliably suppressed with this dose and the test can be
used as a screening test to identify cats with fHAC. The test is also used to aid in discriminating ADH
from PDH, although there is little evidence to justify this.4,6,42 Importantly, cortisols are suppressed
after giving 0.1 mg/kg dexamethasone in cats with DM but not those with fHAC and DM, independent of
glycemic control.45 The 0.1 mg/kg DST has good specificity. Serum cortisols fail to suppress 3, 4 or 8
hours post-DST in cats with adrenal tumors while some, not all, with PDH do suppress, reducing
sensitivity.
The canine low dose of dexamethasone (0.01 mg/kg IV) should NOT be used to “screen” for fHAC,4
since 20% of healthy cats do not suppress.46 The increased sensitivity is offset by a lack of specificity.
This “low-dose DST” may be useful in certain circumstances since “normal suppression” would make the
diagnosis of HAC quite unlikely. Equally, if a cat showing clinical signs of HAC has a “normal response”
on the 0.1 mg/kg DST, then the 0.01 mg/kg test may be indicated. Four cats in 1 study had both
dexamethasone tests performed, but their results did not alter the diagnosis.10

URINE CORTICOID:CREATININE RATIO (UCCR)
Urine collected in the hospital is not reliable, as stress may alter results. Almost all cats with fHAC will
be positive (good sensitivity), but false-positive test results may be seen in cats with non-adrenal illness
(poor specificity).47 Importantly, hyperthyroid cats (ch. 287) often have increased UCCR results.44,48
Assay results may vary. Using published reference ranges from different laboratories is
discouraged.49,50

OTHER TESTS
A suggested combined DST/ACTHst protocol is not recommended. Thyroid hormone concentrations are
usually normal in fHAC, important since hyperthyroidism may be considered in any cat with PU/PD and
weight loss. In 1 study, 4 of 25 cats with fHAC had low T4 concentrations.11 It has been suggested that
endogenous ACTH precursors (pro-opiomelanocortin [POMC] and pro-ACTH) may be useful in
identifying cats with PDH,51 but these assays are not widely available.

ENDOCRINE TESTS TO DISCRIMINATE PDH FROM
ADRENAL TUMOR HAC
No test to discriminate cats with PDH from those with adrenal tumor fHAC has been assessed.
Endogenous plasma ACTH concentrations should be normal or increased in cats with PDH and low or
undetectable in cats with an adrenal tumor. This test appears to be useful for distinguishing PDH from
ADH, once the diagnosis of feline HAC has been confirmed.52 However, it is essential that any assay
used be validated for cats.10,11,52 Radiography, US, CT, and MRI (ch. 112) can be extremely helpful in
distinguishing PDH from ADH.4,7,8,51

TREATMENT
INDICATIONS
Cats with fHAC, whenever possible, should be treated. Control of DM will likely improve with successful
treatment and risk of serious adverse consequences of chronic fHAC reduced, e.g., skin hyperfragility
and unusual or difficult to treat infections.

SURGERY
Unilateral Adrenalectomy
Before surgery (laparoscopy or laparotomy), diagnostic imaging (US, CT, MRI) should be used to assess
for major vessel or tissue invasion. There should be no evidence of distant metastases. Some surgeons
can remove tumor thrombi from vessels. Post-operative hypoadrenocorticism is common and requires
management (ch. 296). Prednisolone, needed initially, is usually tapered over time. Diabetic cats may
go into remission in the months following surgery. Those that remain diabetic often require much lower
insulin doses.6 Successful laparoscopic adrenalectomy has been reported and should be considered for

the treatment of unilateral functional adrenal neoplasia in cats when diagnostic imaging has ruled out
intravascular invasion and metastatic disease.53

Pituitary Surgery
Surgical options for PDH include trans-sphenoidal hypophysectomy (ch. 280).6,8 Trans-sphenoidal
hypophysectomy is the only definitive treatment for PDH. The first report of 7 cats with PDH
undergoing trans-sphenoidal hypophysectomy included 2 dying within weeks and 5 that did well. With
greater surgical and management experience, success rates will improve.8,54 Post-operative treatment
for central diabetes insipidus (ch. 282) is needed. Mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid replacement
are usually required for several weeks. Despite high initial remission rates in dogs with PDH following
hypophysectomy, recurrence was documented in ∼25%.55 Similar rates of recurrence may be seen in
cats.

Bilateral Adrenalectomy
Surgical options for PDH include bilateral adrenalectomy.6,8 Morbidity and mortality appear less for
cats than dogs but complications are still frequent.6,7 Resolution or improvement of DM may be seen in
the months following surgery, but long-term prednisolone and fludrocortisone are required. Surgery is
not an option for cats that are difficult to medicate orally.

MEDICAL TREATMENT
Trilostane
Trilostane, a competitive inhibitor of 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, is effective for treating
fHAC.9,10 Of 20 cats in 2 series, 17 survived for more than 3 months and many survived more than 1
year. There have been no pharmacokinetic studies of trilostane or its metabolites in cats. In 1 cat,
suppression of cortisol production was rapid and the duration of action was <12 hours.9 Manufacturers
do not recommend trilostane be used if concurrent hepatic or renal disease is present. Trilostane (1-2
mg/kg q24h or 0.5-1 mg/kg q12h) can be given when insulin is given. Reformulation is often necessary.
Trilostane seems well tolerated; improvement is often noted within weeks.10 In a series of 9 cats with
fHAC and DM treated with trilostane, insulin dose decreased by an average of 36% in 6 cats, 1 needed
more insulin, none went into DM remission.10 One cat was reported to have DM remission after
trilostane.56 Important possible complications of trilostane include anorexia, lethargy, hypernatremia,
and/or hypokalemia.
There are no published criteria critically evaluating any method to monitor treatment response. The
ACTHst is often used with target cortisol concentrations and test timing extrapolated from dogs9,10
(target post-ACTHst cortisols 4 hours after trilostane: 40 nmol/L [1.4 mcg/dL] to 140 nmol/L [5
mcg/dL]). However, ACTHst results are unreliable predictors of clinical status in dogs. Pretrilostane
cortisol levels are still under investigation. One must closely monitor history and physical examination
as these are the most important criteria.

o,p′-DDD (Mitotane, Lysodren)
Mitotane, well tolerated by cats despite their sensitivity to chlorinated hydrocarbons,12 is not effective in
fHAC in cats.4 One cat given 50 mg/kg/day for 1 week then 50 mg/kg weekly was controlled for 40
weeks before developing signs compatible with hypoadrenocorticism.13

Metyrapone
Metyrapone, an inhibitor of the 11-beta-hydroxylase enzyme that converts 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol,
proved effective at least transiently in controlling clinical signs and suppressing cortisol production in 1
cat (oral dose: 65 mg/kg q12h).15 Whether or not long-term therapy with metyrapone can control fHAC,

or whether rising ACTH concentrations eventually break the blockade, has not been determined. It
would, however, appear to be potentially useful for presurgical stabilization.14

Cabergoline, Ketoconazole
There is a single case report of a cat treated with cabergoline that had sustained DM remission and
reduced clinical signs of fHAC.57 Ketoconazole, an antifungal imidazole, is an inhibitor of
steroidogenesis in humans and dogs, but is ineffective in cats. It can cause anorexia, weight loss,
vomiting, diarrhea, hepatotoxicosis and/or thrombocytopenia.58,59 Ketoconazole, no longer available in
some areas, has been replaced by itraconazole. There are no reports of the use of itraconazole for fHAC.

PITUITARY IRRADIATION
For cats with neurologic signs associated with a large pituitary tumor, pituitary radiation therapy can
prove beneficial (chs. 245, 318). In one report, neurologic signs and endocrine signs improved following
radiation therapy in 7 cats with either fHAC or acromegaly caused by large pituitary tumors,60 with a
median survival of 17.4 months. Pituitary irradiation has been associated with improved DM control in
acromegalic cats, but not in fHAC.55

TREATING SKIN HYPERFRAGILITY
Severe spontaneous skin lacerations can be challenging to treat. Staged wound closure may be
necessary.61 Suturing of smaller lesions risks causing further traumatic lesions so the edges of small,
recent lesions may be better joined with tissue glue after routine cleaning (which is also less painful for
the cat).

PROGNOSIS
fHAC is a progressive disorder with a poor prognosis. Cats with fHAC are at risk of severe infection and
uncontrolled DM, often leading to euthanasia. With appropriate therapy, cats with adrenal adenomas or
PDH may have a good to excellent prognosis. Cats with fHAC require less insulin to manage DM.
Complete remission of DM may occur in those cats undergoing successful definitive treatment for HAC.
