UACR urinary aldosterone-to-creatinine ratio
US ultrasonography
Due to the routine use of abdominal ultrasonography (US) and
increased availability of advanced imaging modalities (computed
tomography [CT] and magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]), non–
corticol-secreting adrenocortical tumors are being recognized more
frequently. Importantly, an adrenal mass is not necessarily a primary
adrenal tumor (AT), not all ATs are adrenocortical, and not all
adrenocortical tumors secrete cortisol. Non-tumor possibilities
include nodular hyperplasia, cyst, abscess, hematoma, and
granuloma. In one study, 27% of canine and 60% of feline ATs were
metastatic lesions.1 Pulmonary, mammary, prostatic, gastric, and
pancreatic carcinomas and melanoma had the highest rates of
adrenal gland metastasis in dogs. Primary ATs can be benign or
malignant and may or may not be functional, i.e., secreting a
hormone. Myelolipomas or lipomas can occur in the adrenal cortex.
If functional, adrenocortical tumors synthesize steroid hormones
(chs. 293, 294); medullary neuroendocrine tumors are called
pheochromocytoma (ch. 298). Of primary ATs, approximately 75%
are adrenocortical and the remainder are neuroendocrine.2

INCIDENTALOMA
CLINICAL PRESENTATIONS
Abdominal US is used routinely for evaluating soft-tissue structures
and the unexpected finding of a seemingly “incidental” adrenal gland
mass (IAGM), defined as a focal enlargement of the adrenal gland in
pets with no suspicion of adrenal gland disease, is common (Figures
295.1 and 295.2). An AT should be suspected when there is loss of
the typical shape of an adrenal gland (regardless of size), asymmetry
in shape and size between the affected and contralateral adrenal
gland, or the mass has infiltrated the phrenicoabdominal vein,
caudal vena cava, or surrounding soft tissues. The incidence of IAGM
identified with US is estimated at about 4% in dogs; most are

middle-aged or older.3,4 With CT, about 9% of dogs had an IAGM
(Figure 295.3). Bilateral incidentaloma can also occur.5 Incidence
of adrenal incidentalomas in cats is unknown.
As the first step, abdominal US should be repeated to be sure an
adrenal mass is consistently identified (Figure 295.4). Once an
IAGM is confirmed, several differentials, as discussed above, need to
be considered. Many factors determine the aggressiveness of the
diagnostic and therapeutic approach to an IAGM, including the
severity of concurrent problems, the original reason for performing
abdominal US, pet age, the likelihood the mass is hormonally active
and/or malignant, the size and invasiveness of the mass, and the
client’s desires.

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH
History, Physical Examination (PE), Routine
Testing
The history, PE, and results of routine blood and urine tests should
be assessed for evidence of hypercortisolism, hyperaldosteronism,
excess sex hormone concentrations, or a pheochromocytoma.
Appropriate tests should be performed to determine the nature of
the mass (chs. 293, 294, and 298). Potential malignancy should be
assessed since 14-30% of IAGMs are malignant.3 It can be a
challenge to determine if an IAGM is neoplastic and if so, whether it
is benign or malignant, without histologic evaluation. Cytologic
evaluation has 90-100% accuracy for differentiating cortical from
medullary origin, but cannot be used to determine if a mass is benign
or malignant (ch. 85).6

Imaging
Imaging may be helpful in identifying an adrenal mass but must be
interpreted carefully. Characteristics that do not help differentiate
adrenal adenoma and carcinoma are mineralization or US
echogenicity. Both adenomas and carcinomas can contain mineral
densities or appear as “a mass” cranial to the kidney. While diffuse

ill-defined mineralization usually is associated with adrenal
neoplasia, discrete well-marginated mineralization can develop in
clinically healthy animals.7 One study suggested contrast-enhanced
US could be useful, but the study involved a small number of dogs
and this diagnostic aid is not widely used.8
Some US findings can be highly suggestive of malignancy.
Suspected metastases to abdominal organs, especially the liver, can
be visualized and confirmed by US-guided biopsy (ch. 85). If a dog’s
AT is >2 cm maximum diameter, chances of malignancy and growth
are increased.3,9 Evidence of invasion into surrounding tissues
and/or the caudal vena cava is suggestive of carcinoma.10 Of 34 dogs
with 36 ATs in one study, US was 100% sensitive and 96% specific
for identifying the presence of a tumor thrombus within the caudal
vena cava. However, when all forms of vascular invasion were
evaluated, including vascular wall invasion with no concurrent
thrombus, sensitivity and specificity were 76% and 96%,
respectively.11 The presence of tortuous vessels and heterogeneity of
contrast enhancement on contrast-enhanced US may also indicate
malignancy.12 Metastases to the lungs may be identified on thoracic
radiography.
Poor glandular demarcation, irregular contrast enhancement, and
a non-homogenous texture on CT scans are suggestive of
malignancy.13 Vascular invasion can be confirmed with CT with high
accuracy.14-16 In one study, vascular invasion was identified correctly
in 11 of 12 dogs using contrast-enhanced CT. Sensitivity and
specificity of ultrasonography both compare favorably with surgery
and with necropsy. In 1 dog, invasion of the phrenicoabdominal vein
was not identified on CT images.14 Conversely, enlarged adrenal
glands may adhere to or compress the caudal vena cava, incorrectly
suggesting invasion.13 Triple-phase helical CT may be able to
differentiate tumor type.17

TREATMENT AND FOLLOW-UP
If a malignant IAGM is suspected, adrenalectomy is the treatment of
choice. A more conservative approach should be adopted if there is
no evidence of malignancy, no worrisome clinical signs or findings
on PE, routine blood/urine tests are not indicative of a functional
AT, and the mass is <2 cm in diameter. Monthly US monitoring can
document the mass’s rate of growth and/or change in appearance
(Figure 295.4). Growth of IAGMs is unpredictable. Of 7 dogs with
an IAGM, 3 lesions were not found when US was repeated after >4
months. No growth occurred after >6 months in 2 dogs. In 2 dogs

with larger tumors, growth was observed. In one, the mass grew from
1.6 to 2.5-cm diameter and invaded the caudal vena cava within 10
months; in the other, the mass grew from 2.5 to 3.1-cm diameter
within 8 months.3 In 9 dogs with non–cortisol-secreting AT followed
for 12 months, no change was seen in 7 and 2 (originally 2.0 and 2.5
cm in length) did grow.9
If the IAGM has not increased in size after 3 months, the time
interval between US rechecks can be lengthened. However, if the
IAGM is enlarging, changing in appearance, or compressing or
infiltrating surrounding blood vessels or soft tissues, or if clinical
signs affiliated with excess hormone secretion develop,
adrenalectomy is warranted. For non–cortisol-secreting AT, median
survival without surgery in 14 dogs was 29.8 ± 8.9 months (range
1.0-96.0 months). Larger tumor size was associated with shorter
survival.9

approach to an incidentaloma. PE, Physical
examination.

ALDOSTERONE-SECRETING ADRENAL
TUMORS
PHYSIOLOGY AND DEFINITIONS

Aldosterone is the principal mineralocorticoid synthesized and
secreted by the zona glomerulosa, the outermost of 3 adrenocortical
zones. Its primary functions are regulation of serum sodium (Na)
and potassium (K) concentrations and intravascular fluid volume.
Increases in serum K concentration directly stimulate aldosterone
secretion. Decreases in blood pressure, primarily sensed within the
kidneys, stimulate synthesis and release of renin which, through
angiotensin II, stimulates aldosterone secretion, i.e., the reninangiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Aldosterone acts on the
distal nephron to promote Na reabsorption and excretion of K and
hydrogen. In conserving Na, aldosterone indirectly conserves water,
raising blood volume and, in turn, blood pressure. It also directly
increases blood pressure via enhancement of total peripheral
resistance. Aldosterone is also synthesized in heart, brain and
vasculature, where it may have paracrine or autocrine actions.18
Hyperaldosteronism can be primary or secondary. Primary
hyperaldosteronism (PHA) is defined as autonomous aldosterone
secretion by adrenocortical cells and characterized by circulating
aldosterone excess and, through negative feedback, renin
suppression. Secondary hyperaldosteronism is the result of a
condition, e.g., heart failure or chronic kidney disease (CKD), which
stimulates the RAAS and is associated with increased renin
concentrations.

FELINE ALDOSTERONE-SECRETING
ADRENOCORTICAL TUMORS
Background
PHA caused by an adrenocortical carcinoma in a cat was first
reported in 1983.19 A 2011 review identified only about 40 cats, not
all with confirmed PHA.18 In the past decade, however, PHA has
been identified as the most common feline adrenocortical disorder,
caused by either idiopathic (bilateral) micronodular hyperplasia or
adenoma or adenocarcinoma.20 The tumoral form is the bestdefined form of PHA, usually due to a solitary tumor, but bilateral

adrenal adenomas can occur.21 Adrenocortical carcinomas occur
more frequently than adenomas or bilateral micronodular
hyperplasia.18 This differs markedly from people, in whom bilateral
hyperplasia of the zona glomerulosa accounts for 60-65% of cases
and aldosterone-producing adenomas for 30-35%; unilateral
hyperplasia is uncommon, and functional adrenocortical carcinomas
are rare.22 This section focuses on PHA caused by adrenocortical
tumors (ATs). Non-tumorous PHA, i.e., bilateral zona glomerulosa
hyperplasia, is discussed in chs. 294 and 301.

FIGURE 295.5 Cat showing typical clinical
features of primary hyperaldosteronism: cervical
ventroflexion (muscle weakness due to hypokalemia)
and mydriasis (due to arterial hypertension). From
Kooistra HS. Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s

eds. Feline Endocrinology. Edra; 2019:386. With
permission.

Pathophysiology and Clinical Features
PHA is most commonly diagnosed in cats >10 years of age (median
about 13 years) but one was 5.23 No sex or breed predisposition has
been identified. Pathophysiologic consequences of excessive

aldosterone secretion include moderate to severe hypokalemia
(hypoK) and/or systemic arterial hypertension, due to retention of
Na and water. HypoK is more common than hypertension in cats
with an AT. The opposite is true of cats with PHA due to
hyperplasia.24 K depletion, due to increased renal K excretion, leads
to neuromuscular abnormalities: nerve and muscle membranes
become hyperpolarized which causes progressive and persistent
weakness, i.e., “hypokalemic polymyopathy.” Muscle weakness is
likely to occur at K concentrations <2.5-3 mmol/L (<2.5-3 mg/L).
Cervical ventroflexion (

Video 68.1), hindlimb weakness

(sometimes plantigrade stance), difficulty jumping, listlessness, and
ataxia are common owner concerns (Figure 295.5). Forelimb
stiffness, collapse, and dysphagia may result from nerve or muscle
effects.21 Weakness can be acute in onset or chronic and
episodic.21,25 Two cats collapsed due to intra-adrenal hemorrhage.26
Respiratory failure can occur with profound hypoK.27,28
Polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD) may be present. Hypertension can lead
to acute blindness and/or a sudden change in eye color due to retinal
detachment and/or intraocular hemorrhage.

Additional Hormone Abnormalities
Adrenocortical tumors may excessively secrete more than one
hormone. The “other hormone(s)” may cause additional clinical
signs, e.g., excess cortisol causes hyperadrenocorticism (ch. 294);
excess progesterone can cause polyphagia, PU/PD, weight loss,
and/or a sparse hair coat.29-31 One cat with PHA and excess
progesterone had weakness but also ataxia, agitation, vocalization,
and compulsive pacing due to a left forebrain meningioma.32 In
humans, progesterone can cause rapid growth of meningiomas
because their tumor cells can express progesterone receptors. In the
affected cat with excess progesterone, immunohistochemical staining
of the meningioma revealed strong positive labelling for
progesterone receptors.

Physical Examination (PE)

PE abnormalities are usually related to hypoK (weakness) or
hypertension. Ocular abnormalities attributed to hypertension
include intraocular hemorrhage, increased retinal vessel tortuosity,
retinal edema, and retinal detachment (chs. 13, 236). Clinical signs
due to progesterone or glucocorticoid excess include skin fragility,
alopecia, muscle atrophy, and a pendulous abdomen (ch. 294). A
cranial abdominal mass may be palpable if the AT is large. Systemic
hypertension can be associated with left ventricular hypertrophy,
systolic heart murmurs, and/or cardiac arrhythmias.

Routine Laboratory Features and Blood Pressure
PHA should be considered in any cat with hypoK (the most common
abnormality), especially if refractory to treatment (ch. 68). Most
cats with PHA have moderate to severe hypoK at the time of
diagnosis, possibly because concurrent non-adrenal disease such as
CKD may divert the clinician’s focus and the diagnosis is not sought
until later in the disease process.24 About 50% of PHA cats have
increases in urea (blood urea nitrogen), creatinine, and creatine
kinase (CK) concentrations.18 Increases in CK can be quite severe; an
activity >100,000 U/L was reported in one cat.33 As aldosterone
excess favors increased acid excretion, a mild metabolic alkalosis can
occur. Either hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia, or both may
develop. A low normal or low serum phosphorus concentration in an
azotemic cat should raise suspicion of PHA, since
hyperphosphatemia would be expected (ch. 69). Although
aldosterone causes Na retention, cats with PHA are not usually
hypernatremic. Water retention dilutes Na and circulatory volume
expansion caused by PHA may increase Na excretion. Hyperglycemia
or concurrent diabetes mellitus (DM) should raise concern for an AT
producing excess progesterone or cortisol in addition to aldosterone.
About 85% of affected cats are persistently hypertensive.18 PHA
should be strongly considered in a cat with unexplained
hypertension, particularly if accompanied by hypokalemia (ch.
236).

Imaging

Radiology is not helpful in diagnosing PHA unless an AT is large
enough to be seen or to displace adjacent organs. Adrenal
calcification is present in about 33% of aged healthy cats and should
not be over-interpreted (ch. 294, Figure 294.3). Pulmonary
metastases are not common and some metastases are too small to be
seen. Lung metastases from an aldosteronoma, each lesion ≤3 mm in
diameter, were not seen on thoracic radiographs but were identified
on necropsy in 1 cat.34 CT scans may be more sensitive for detection
of metastases. US, CT, and MRI can be used to visualize adrenal
abnormalities and, in cases of neoplasia, possible vascular invasion
and evidence of metastases. Imaging findings never confirm a
diagnosis. Non-functional adrenocortical tumors may be large and
not cause clinical signs. Conversely, a tumor causing PHA may be too
small for detection, although sensitivity approaches 100%.21 Thus, if
the decision to pursue surgery is based on diagnostic imaging alone,
a cat may be inappropriately selected or excluded.20

Aldosterone Concentrations
Confirmation of a functional aldosteronoma relies primarily on
demonstrating abnormally increased plasma aldosterone
concentrations (PACs). PACs have been increased in all reported cats
with PHA due to an AT. However, the PACs reported for primary and
secondary hyperaldosteronism overlap, with concentrations >1000
pmol/L (>36 ng/dL) in some secondary PHAs, especially in cats with
CKD. While other diseases associated with secondary
hyperaldosteronism must be excluded, PHA and CKD often coexist
(ch. 301). As suspicion for PHA becomes stronger due to its
increasing prevalence, testing will occur earlier in disease course,
when the PACs may be in the upper end of the reference interval.
Monitoring and repeat testing may be needed.

FIGURE 295.6 Diagnostic approach to
hyperaldosteronism in cats when a plasma renin

Plasma Renin Activity (PRA)

Ideally, PRA is measured on the sample submitted for PAC, as an
increase in PAC is not 100% specific for diagnosing PHA. In PHA,
the PRA should be within or below the reference range. In
hyperaldosteronism secondary to CKD, advanced heart disease, or
hepatic failure, PRA should be increased. Plasma aldosterone-torenin ratios (ARRs) are sensitive initial screening tests in humans
suspected as having hyperaldosteronism.22 The same seems true for
cats with PHA.25 The combination of high-normal or elevated PAC
and a low PRA indicates autonomous aldosterone synthesis despite
little or no RAAS stimulation. However, validated feline PRA assays
are not widely available, require large (4 mL) blood samples, need to
be quickly separated, and the plasma frozen. Further, there is no
accepted PRA reference range for cats. In addition, measurement of
a single ARR within the reference interval does not exclude PHA in
cats (Figure 295.6).18,25

Urinary Aldosterone-to-Creatinine Ratio (UACR)
The UACR reflects aldosterone secretion over time versus blood, that
reflects a concentration at a specific moment in time. Samples do not
require special sample handling or cooling and the urine can be
obtained by owners at home. Unfortunately, multiple disadvantages
exist. Urinary aldosterone can be difficult to measure in cats as
compared to dogs or humans, the reference range is wide, and basal
concentrations do not consistently identify cats with PHA.35,36 In a
study of 9 cats with PHA, only 3 had an elevated basal UACR.37
Commercially available UACR assays are not widely available.

Fludrocortisone Suppression Testing
Oral fludrocortisone, a synthetic mineralocorticoid, suppresses
serum aldosterone concentrations in healthy adult cats.36-38 Also,
oral fludrocortisone (0.05 mg/kg q12h for 4 days) given to healthy
cats suppressed the UACR by a median of 78%.36 The 4-day protocol
was evaluated in 19 client-owned cats with arterial hypertension
caused by PHA (n=9) or other causes (n=10).37 In all cats without
PHA, fludrocortisone suppressed the UACR >50% while

fludrocortisone resulted in <50% suppression in only 6 of the 9 cats
with PHA. Given the difficulty of administering oral medications to
cats, potential hardships in obtaining urine, and lack of a clear
diagnostic utility, this test is not recommended.

Confirming a Diagnosis of PHA
Suspicion of an aldosteronoma should arise in any cat with hypoK
and hypertension (Figure 295.6). Suspicion is greater if azotemia is
present with a normal or low serum phosphorus concentration.
Documentation of an elevated PAC and identification of an AT are
required for diagnosis. Histological confirmation of tumor type,
resolution of clinical signs, and normalization of PAC following
adrenalectomy further confirm the diagnosis.

Surgical Treatment
Surgery should be undertaken only by experienced surgeons in a
hospital with a well-equipped intensive care unit and 24-hour
observation and care. Unilateral adrenalectomy is the treatment of
choice for cats with a confirmed aldosteronoma, assuming there is no
evidence of obvious metastases. Although presence of a tumor
thrombus in the caudal vena cava (

Video 293.7) indicates

surgical removal may be difficult, failure to detect vascular invasion
by diagnostic imaging is no guarantee of its absence nor does it
predict an uncomplicated adrenalectomy.21,29,30 Adrenalectomy can
be performed via ventral midline celiotomy33 or laparoscopy.39,40
Laparoscopic adrenalectomy may become the procedure of choice in
veterinary medicine but can be technically challenging and
conversion to open celiotomy may be required.40 Open celiotomy
provides maximal exposure of the adrenal glands and blood vessels
and is required by some surgeons if an aldosteronoma extends into
the vena cava.41 With complete removal of a unilateral nonmetastasized aldosteronoma, prognosis is excellent, after surviving
the short-term post-operative period. Long-term medication is rarely
needed.18

Perioperative Complications
The most common perioperative complications are intraoperative or
postoperative intra-abdominal hemorrhage.21,23,34 Logical risk
factors for hemorrhage have been sought, including tumor type,
vascular invasion, or arterial hypertension, but none have been
identified. Additional postoperative complications include acute
kidney injury, thromboembolism, and sepsis.18 Recent studies report
encouraging results: 8 of 10 cats surviving to discharge following
open adrenalectomy for PHA in one study and 10 of 11 cats surviving
to discharge after laparoscopic adrenalectomy (8 of 11 had PHA) in
another.33,40 In the first study, the median survival time was 1297
days (range 2-1582 days) with no significant difference in survival
comparing cats with an adenoma versus adenocarcinoma.
Preoperative hypoK should be corrected with oral and/or parenteral
K. Pre-surgical imaging to assess for tumor thrombi and metastases
is imperative. Although unsubstantiated, the presence of metastases
is likely to decrease survival, and surgery would not be curative.
Survival can still be >1 year even if metastases are present, as these
tumors can be slow growing.
Tumors producing aldosterone may produce other adrenocortical
hormones, thus adrenalectomy could cause acute hypocortisolemia if
the tumor was synthesizing and secreting glucocorticoids (ch. 294).
Theoretically, autonomous aldosterone secretion from an AT should
suppress function of zona glomerulosa cells within the contralateral
gland. Since acute and transient hypoaldosteronism could occur
postoperatively, serum electrolyte concentrations must be monitored
frequently with intravenous fluid therapy adjusted to maintain
serum K and Na concentrations in or near reference intervals.
Exogenous mineralocorticoids are usually not needed
postoperatively.

Medical Treatments
Surgery may be contraindicated if a tumor is considered
nonresectable, if distant metastases have been identified, or if
comorbid conditions are present. Owner limitations are common.
Cats can be treated medically with a mineralocorticoid receptor
blocker (spironolactone, 2 mg/kg PO q12h), plus K supplementation

and antihypertensive drugs as needed (ch. 236). The dosage of
spironolactone can be changed as needed to control hypoK but
gastrointestinal side-effects (anorexia, vomiting, diarrhea) may be
seen with higher dosages. K supplementation (2-6 mEq q12h) has
been effective in managing hypoK. Amlodipine besylate (0.625-1.25
mg/cat PO q24h) is the treatment of choice to control arterial
hypertension. Medical management has yielded survival times of 7
months to 984 days in 4 cats; another survived only 50 days due to
poor owner compliance.24

CANINE ALDOSTERONE-SECRETING
TUMORS
Etiology and Clinical Signs
PHA, rare in dogs, is usually caused by a solitary adrenal adenoma or
carcinoma, although bilateral idiopathic adrenocortical hyperplasia
has been reported.42-45 Dogs with PHA, usually middle-aged to
older, have owner concerns similar to those observed in cats with
PHA: lethargy, anorexia, weakness, and PU/PD. Similar to cats with
PHA, clinical signs and routine testing can be consistent with
glucocorticoid excess, since some tumors secrete glucocorticoids as
well as mineralocorticoids, in excess (ch. 293).43-45

Diagnosis
Presence of hypoK in a dog with an AT identified on abdominal
imaging should raise suspicion of PHA. However, aldosteronesecreting tumors can be too small to be visualized with US. Failure to
identify a mass does not rule out either tumor or idiopathic
adrenocortical hyperplasia. Other findings consistent with a
diagnosis of PHA include systemic hypertension and a metabolic
alkalosis. Confirmation of an aldosteronoma requires documentation
of increased baseline aldosterone concentrations and suppressed
PRA in conjunction with exclusion of other causes of hypoK (ch.
68). Most dogs with an aldosteronoma have had aldosterone
concentrations >3000 pmol/L (>108 ng/dL), but canine PRA assays

have not been commercially available. Urine tests, such as the UACR,
have not yet been evaluated. Tumors secreting non-aldosterone
mineralocorticoids, e.g., desoxycorticosterone, occur rarely.46-48
Clinical findings are the same as with PHA but aldosterone
concentrations are low. Since no desoxycorticosterone assay is
commercially available, a diagnosis would be presumptively based on
the constellation of diagnostic test results.

Preoperative Management
Unilateral adrenalectomy is the treatment of choice for a solitary
adrenal mass, especially if there is no evidence of distant metastasis,
vascular invasion, or infiltration into the kidney or body wall. Oral K,
mineralocorticoid receptor blockers (e.g., spironolactone), and
antihypertensive drugs (e.g., amlodipine) should be given as required
until surgery. Medical therapy is indicated for long-term
management of PHA when adrenalectomy is not performed and for
dogs with suspected idiopathic adrenocortical hyperplasia.

Postoperative Management
Serum electrolyte concentrations should be monitored frequently
post-operatively and intravenous fluid therapy adjusted accordingly
(ch. 120). If hypoK persists, oral K supplementation can be initiated
when appropriate. Serum ionized magnesium concentrations should
be checked, and hypomagnesemia treated, especially if hypoK is
refractory to intravenous fluid therapy. Mineralocorticoid treatment
(i.e., oral fludrocortisone acetate or injectable desoxycorticosterone
pivalate [DOCP]) should be administered if hyperK and hypoNa
persist >72 hours (ch. 296) but this is rare. Usually, one dose of
DOCP is given and then daily oral fludrocortisone acetate can be
tapered and discontinued within a week.

Systemic Hypertension (ch. 236)
Systemic hypertension usually improves or resolves within 48 to 72
hours after adrenalectomy. Antihypertensive medications should be
initiated if hypertension persists. Tapering antihypertensive
medications should begin over the ensuing month. Glucocorticoid
therapy is usually not needed post-operatively unless the tumor was

secreting a glucocorticoid. An adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
stimulation test can be performed 6 to 8 hours after adrenalectomy
to assess the function of the remaining adrenal gland (ch. 296). If
the tumor was known pre-operatively to secrete a glucocorticoid, the
same precautions and recommendations apply as when removing a
cortisol-secreting tumor (ch. 293).

Prognosis
Successful surgical extirpation of an adenoma carries an excellent
prognosis but the prognosis is guarded for a carcinoma. If metastatic
sites exist, hyperaldosteronism, hypoK, and associated clinical signs
either persist or recur. Since these are slow-growing tumors,
recurrence may not occur for months or longer following surgery.
Management of recurrence with metastasectomy can be successful.45
The prognosis for idiopathic adrenocortical hyperplasia is unknown
and depends on the effectiveness of medical therapy. Bilateral
adrenalectomy, in theory, should offer a cure, but the dog would
require glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid treatment for life.

SEX HORMONE-SECRETING ADRENAL
TUMORS
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Adrenocortical tumors have the potential to synthesize and secrete a
variety of steroids other than cortisol and aldosterone (ch. 293,
Figure 293.1). Excess secretion of sex hormones by tumors may be
associated with aberrant biosynthetic pathways and/or enzyme
deficiencies. Progestins may either bind glucocorticoid receptors49
or displace cortisol from its binding protein, increasing serum free
cortisol concentrations.50 In dogs, progestins suppress endogenous
pituitary ACTH secretion and can cause adrenocortical atrophy, an
action suggestive of glucocorticoid activity.51

FELINE SEX HORMONE-SECRETING
ADRENOCORTICAL TUMORS
Clinical Presentation
A small number of middle-aged to older cats with sex hormonesecreting AT has been described.29,30,52-58 A 14-year-old, female
spayed Domestic Shorthair cat with bilateral adrenal enlargement
and excessive estradiol and testosterone production has been
reported.59 Excess production of a progestin, e.g., progesterone or
17-hydroxy-progesterone, may cause signs typical of cortisol excess,
such as a poor haircoat, dermal atrophy, and cutaneous fragility.
Most cats with a progesterone-secreting tumor also had difficult-toregulate DM.29,30,52,53 Excess androgen production can cause urine
odor to change, urine spraying behavior, aggression, and
development of penile spines.54,56,57,59 Hyperestrogenemia may
cause estrous behavior and vulvar enlargement in females55,57,59 or
mammary development in males.57 Malignant tumors predominate
over benign.

Diagnosis
Suspicion of a sex hormone-secreting tumor depends on recognition
of clinical signs, since complete blood count, routine serum
biochemistry profiles, and urine testing have no “typical” results.
Identifying an AT on US further increases suspicion. In 1 cat,
however, a tumor had replaced the normal adrenal and only mild
enlargement and a round shape were noted on US.55 Signs of
malignancy should be sought and thoracic radiographs taken to
assess for metastatic disease.
Definitive diagnosis of tumor functionality and type of hormone
secreted has usually been based on cortisol and sex hormone results
before and 1 hour after ACTH stimulation (125 mcg cosyntropin/cat
IV). If a progestin is secreted but not cortisol, cortisol concentrations
are usually at or below the low end of the reference range. Thus, if a
cat appears to have hypercortisolism but does not have the
diagnostic test results, one should consider a sex hormone disorder.

Estradiol does not increase with ACTH injection. In cats with an
estrogen-secreting tumor, the basal estradiol concentration was
elevated but the ACTH-stimulated concentration was not.55,57

Treatment and Prognosis
Surgical or laparoscopic removal of an AT is the treatment of choice.
Prognosis is influenced by preoperative health of the cat, presence of
metastases, and successful tumor removal. If the tumor has
suppressed cortisol secretion, glucocorticoid replacement must be
given post-operatively. Hyperprogesteronism can result in fragile
thin skin that makes surgery problematic. While 1 cat died 3 days
after surgery,29 survival for months to more than a year has been
reported. Aminoglutethimide was given in an attempt to control sexhormone secretion in a cat with an adrenal tumor, but it provided
only a transient response.53 Trilostane was used to control secretion
of sex hormones in a cat with bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, but after
about 6 months clinical signs returned and no further assessment or
treatment were sought.59

CANINE SEX HORMONE-SECRETING
ADRENOCORTICAL TUMORS
Clinical Presentation
A small number of dogs with sex hormone-secreting AT has been
reported,60-63 but none with clinical signs of hyperestrogenemia or
hyperandrogenemia. Two dogs with AT, an 11-year-old spayed
female Labrador Retriever and a 9-year-old castrated male Miniature
Poodle, had clinical signs of hyperadrenocorticism despite markedly
suppressed ACTH-stimulated serum cortisol concentrations.62
Clinical signs were believed due to hyperprogesteronemia. Both dogs
had polyphagia and PU/PD. One had changes in coat color, weight
gain, increased panting, and abdominal enlargement. Signalment
and clinical signs in other dogs with sex hormone-secreting tumors

were not delineated but presenting complaints were stated to be
consistent with hypercortisolism.60,61,63

Diagnosis
Initial suspicion of a sex hormone-secreting AT depends on clinical
signs. The primary reason for measuring sex hormones is cortisol
concentrations below the reference range in a dog suspected as
having hyperadrenocorticism (ch. 293).62,63 Low cortisols in dogs
with signs of Cushing’s syndrome are often the result of iatrogenic
corticosteroid administration. Once iatrogenic disease is ruled out, a
sex hormone-secreting AT may be considered. US identification of a
possible AT further supports the diagnosis, but some tumors are too
small to be seen.
To document sex hormone elevations, they should be measured
before and 1 hour after ACTH stimulation (ch. 293). However, sex
hormone concentrations must be interpreted cautiously. For
estradiol, a wide range of variability exists within and between dogs;
random, basal estradiol concentrations in individual dogs often
exceed the reference range.64 Many dogs without
hyperadrenocorticism can have elevated sex hormone
concentrations, potentially up to 40-50%.65-67 In 6 dogs with a
pheochromocytoma or a non-functional AT, androstenedione,
progesterone, 17OHP, testosterone and/or estradiol concentrations
were elevated.68

Treatment and Prognosis
Adrenalectomy, in theory, is the treatment of choice if the patient is
an appropriate surgical candidate. However, detailed information of
treatment of only 2 dogs with sex hormone-secreting ATs is
available. One dog with a sex hormone-secreting AT had an
adrenalectomy and did well for at least 13 months after surgery. A
second was treated medically with mitotane for approximately 20
days at a dose of 47 mg/kg daily with no response, and the owners
declined further therapy; given the resistance of AT in general to
mitotane, lack of response is not surprising given the dosage and
short duration of treatment (ch. 293).

INTRODUCTION
In 1855, Dr. Thomas Addison published a case series of 11 individuals, each described as having a
disease of the supra-renal capsule (adrenal cortex).1 Hypoadrenocorticism (HA) is, therefore, often
referred to as “Addison’s disease.” The adrenal cortex synthesizes and secretes glucocorticoids and
mineralocorticoids that are essential for life. The cortex is divided into 3 layers: the outermost
zona glomerulosa, the widest middle zona fasciculata, and the innermost zona reticularis.
Hypofunction or dysfunction of the cortex, such as that seen in HA, can be life threatening. Since
HA is common in dogs and rare in cats, the discussion that follows pertains to dogs and is followed
by a short discussion of the condition in cats.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
AUTO-ANTIBODIES AGAINST STEROIDOGENIC ENZYME: 21HYDROXYLASE
Glucocorticoids are secreted from all 3 layers of the adrenal cortex. The mineralocorticoid
aldosterone is synthesized and secreted from the zona glomerulosa, the only cortical layer which
contains the enzyme aldosterone synthase (adrenal physiology is discussed in ch. 293; see
Figure 293.1). In humans, HA is a rare autoimmune disorder. Most people with HA have
antibodies against the steroidogenic enzyme 21-hydroxylase, present in all 3 cortical layers but its
lowest concentrations are in the zona glomerulosa.2 Antibodies directed at the 21-hydroxylase
enzyme are believed to cause autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex.3 Although 21hydroxylase antibodies have not been identified in dogs with HA, P450 enzyme antibodies, more
common in females than males, have been documented in 24% of dogs with HA vs 1% in non-HA
dogs.4 A longitudinal study demonstrated these antibodies do not persist over time in most dogs
with HA.5 Lymphoplasmacytic adrenalitis characterized by CD4+ T-cell inflammation has also
been documented in some dogs with HA, further supporting this being an immune-mediated
disease in most affected dogs.6

GENETIC PREDISPOSITION TO POLYGENIC IMMUNEMEDIATED HYPOADRENOCORTICISM
The specific dog breeds at increased risk of developing HA provide strong evidence of the etiology
having a genetic component. Familial HA has been reported in Leonberger and Pomeranian dogs
while Great Danes, Standard Poodles, and Bearded Collies are also at increased risk.7-10 A
genome-wide association study of HA in Bearded Collies revealed their mode of inheritance is
polygenic, consisting of a single nucleotide polymorphism on canine chromosome 18 plus 3 other
smaller effect loci.10 The mode of inheritance of HA in Standard Poodles is also likely to be
polygenic.11 Several genetic studies have linked HA to immune function genes. The cytotoxic Tlymphocyte-associated protein 4, a T-cell regulator, has been associated with HA in 3 other
predisposed breeds: Portuguese Water Dogs, Cocker Spaniels, and Springer Spaniels.12,13 Another
important immune function gene, the major histocompatibility complex, is associated with HA in
numerous breeds and is sex specific in Standard Poodles.13-18 However, the methodologies
employed in some studies identifying an association between HA and the major histocompatibility
complex have come under question and further studies are needed.19 Allelic variation in the
immune function gene, PTPN22 is also linked to HA in Cocker Spaniels.20 Neutered dogs appear
to be at increased risk.21 Importantly, it is not clear if any genetic differences are functionally
responsible for formation of anti-adrenal autoantibodies that destroy the adrenal cortex.

FIGURE 296.1 The pituitary-adrenal axis in normal dogs (A); in dogs
with loss of adrenocortical function and excess adrenocorticotropic
hormone (ACTH) secretion due to a lack of negative feedback (the most
common form of hypoadrenocorticism) (B); in dogs with failure to secrete
ACTH and secondary atrophy of the adrenal cortex, specifically the zona
fasciculata and zona reticularis (C); and in dogs that are chronically
overtreated with exogenous glucocorticoids, causing insufficiency in
pituitary ACTH secretion and secondary atrophy of the adrenal cortex
(D). A, Adrenal; CRH, corticotropin-releasing hormone; P, pituitary. Solid
lines represent “normal” hormone concentrations; bold solid lines
represent increased concentrations; dashed lines represent decreased
concentrations. From Feldman EC, Nelson RW, Reusch CE, et al. Canine
and Feline Endocrinology and Reproduction. 4th ed. Saunders; 2015.

CLASSIFICATION
PRIMARY HYPOADRENOCORTICISM
Naturally occurring primary failure of the adrenal cortex is the most common form of HA,
classically characterized by decreases in both glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids. “Atypical
primary HA” describes a syndrome in which glucocorticoid secretion is absent but serum sodium
concentration ([Na]) and potassium concentration ([K]) are normal.22,23 Some dogs initially
diagnosed as having atypical primary HA develop hyponatremia (hypoNa) and hyperkalemia
(hyperK) with time.7,22-24 Others maintain normal electrolyte concentrations for years.22-24

Interestingly, some dogs with documented depletion of glucocorticoids and normal [Na] and [K]
have low aldosterone concentrations, suggesting that maintaining normal [Na] and [K] may not be
completely dependent on aldosterone, that serum electrolyte concentrations may not be indicative
of “active” hormone at receptors levels, or that the assays employed have limitations.24 If HA in
dogs develops secondary to anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies, it is possible that destruction of the
zona glomerulosa, the layer in which aldosterone is produced, could lag behind because the
concentration of 21-hydroxylase in this layer is lower than in the other 2 cortical layers.
Primary HA, whether typical or atypical, develops as a result of adrenal cortex atrophy or
destruction (Figure 296.1). Rarely, primary HA results from a destructive infiltrative disease,
such as neoplasia, the most common cause of this rare presentation. Tuberculosis, fungal diseases,
other granulomatous or infectious diseases, hemorrhage, and infarcts are possible causes of HA,
but are not well documented in dogs.25-30 Transient ketoconazole- and phenobarbital-induced HA
have been reported as has a rare HA dog with aldosterone depletion preceding glucocorticoid
depletion.31-34 Primary transient or permanent iatrogenic HA can be caused by administration of
o,p′-DDD (mitotane) or trilostane (ch. 293). Isolated hypoaldosteronism (without glucocorticoid
deficiency) has been reported but is extremely rare.

SECONDARY HYPOADRENOCORTICISM
Secondary HA is rare and involves pituitary or hypothalamic failure secondary to neoplastic
infiltration, inflammation, infection, infarct, or trauma, which can lead to impaired secretion of
pituitary adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) or hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone
(CRH).35-38 Neurologic clinical signs and other hormonal deficits in these dogs are inconsistent.
Enigmatic idiopathic secondary HA has been reported in dogs without neurologic signs, with longterm survival when given only glucocorticoid supplementation. Since the renin-angiotensinaldosterone system (RAAS) is independent of pituitary or hypothalamic control, these uncommon
diseases involve only glucocorticoid deficiency and normal [Na] and [K]. Unlike atypical primary
HA with normal [Na] and [K], in secondary HA ACTH concentrations are low (Figure 296.1).
Iatrogenic secondary HA is expected after hypophysectomy or abrupt withdrawal of long-term
steroid administration and is not usually a diagnostic challenge.39 Exogenous steroids suppress
ACTH secretion (Figure 296.1) and time is required for atrophied cells to regain function after
abrupt stoppage, explaining recommendations for always tapering glucocorticoid therapy.

SIGNALMENT, HISTORY, SIGNS, PHYSICAL
EXAMINATION (PE)
AGE
HA is a disease of young to middle-aged dogs; median age at diagnosis is 3-4 years. But dogs as
young as 2 months and as old as 12 years have been diagnosed (Table 296.1). Females are at
increased risk.7,40,41 HA can develop in any breed but specific genetic breed predispositions are
recognized, as previously discussed.41,42 The overall incidence of HA is 2.3 cases per 10,000 dog
years at risk.41

HISTORY AND CLINICAL SIGNS
Clinical signs can be mild, vague, wax and wane over time, or seem to develop in mere hours into a
life-threatening crisis. Sometimes stressful circumstances such as surgery or boarding can push a
borderline compensated dog with HA into a crisis. Dogs with HA exhibit 1 or more of the following
clinical signs with variable degrees of severity: anorexia, weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy,

weakness, polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD), shaking, and in extreme cases, collapse (Table 296.1).
Glucocorticoids are important for maintaining the mucosal gastric barrier responsible for
providing protection from its acidic contents. Glucocorticoids are also needed for healthy gastric
mucosal blood pressure, temperature, and glucose concentrations.43 When the mucosal barrier is
rendered ineffective, anorexia, vomiting, diarrhea, and weight loss become common.44 Bloody
vomiting and diarrhea are not “hallmarks” of HA (Table 296.1) but are noted in some. One such
dog required a blood transfusion due to gastrointestinal (GI) hemorrhage.45 Hematemesis,
melena, and hematochezia were less common in dogs with HA than dogs without HA requiring
emergency intravenous (IV) fluid resuscitation (ch. 119).40 Uncommonly, hypoglycemia
secondary to glucocorticoid deficiency causes lethargy, weakness, shaking, and/or collapse.
Glucocorticoids mediate catabolism of glycogen to glucose and synthesis of glucose via
gluconeogenesis. Weakness and lethargy are more common in dogs with HA than non-HA dogs
requiring emergency IV fluids (Table 296.1).40 PU is attributed to the lack of mineralocorticoids
causing osmotically active sodium (Na) loss in urine and hypoNa, leading to PU and compensatory
PD.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (PE)
The PE in dogs with HA can reveal mild to severe illness, including dehydration, hypotension,
bradycardia, weak pulses, weakness, underweight body condition, abdominal pain, and in extreme
cases, hypovolemic or hypotensive shock and/or seizures (ch. 121). Dehydration in dogs with HA
is due to vomiting, diarrhea, and urinary loss of Na and water while nausea interferes with water
consumption. Dogs with HA can have severe decreases in systolic blood pressure; the median in 53
HA dogs was 90 mm Hg (range 40-150 mm Hg; Table 296.1).40 Hypotension follows lack of
glucocorticoids, urine losses of free water, vomiting, diarrhea, and lack of oral intake.46
Bradycardia is attributed to hyperK. When [K] in the extracellular fluid is abnormally high, the
concentration gradient between cardiac intracellular and extracellular compartments is small,
causing potassium (K) retention and interference with the outward K current needed for the phase
3 final rapid repolarization of cardiac action potentials, slowing conduction. Abdominal pain may
be caused by the lack of glucocorticoids diminishing GI mucosal protection, as discussed above.

DIAGNOSIS
OVERVIEW
Suspicion of HA begins with evaluating history, clinical signs, and PE findings. When
clinicopathologic findings are also consistent, an ACTH stimulation test (ACTHst) is indicated to
confirm the diagnosis. Careful interpretation of complete blood count (CBC), urinalysis (UA), and
serum biochemistries is helpful in deciding when to pursue more costly adrenal axis testing.

COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT (CBC)

In a study of 53 dogs with HA and 110 ill non-HA dogs, those with HA had lower neutrophil counts
and higher lymphocyte and eosinophil counts (Table 296.1).40 A lymphocyte count ≥2.0 cells ×
103/mcL in ill dogs has an HA diagnostic specificity of 85%.40

ROUTINE SERUM BIOCHEMISTRY RESULTS
Overview
Serum chemistry results in dogs with HA are inconsistent. Abnormalities, mild or severe, usually
resolve within a few days of treatment. Severe biochemical anomalies do not necessarily indicate
that the condition is irreversible or that another illness is more likely; this is important when
discussing prognosis upon admission to the emergency room or before a definitive diagnosis has
been established. Unlike other diseases, severe azotemia, hypoalbuminemia, or increased liver
enzyme activities are usually completely reversible in dogs with HA.

Kidney, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base Results
Azotemia is common in dogs with HA, usually prerenal secondary to dehydration. Severe
dehydration can lead to acute kidney injury, but azotemia resolves with treatment in most HA
dogs. More than 80% of dogs with HA have hypoNa and/or hyperK (ch. 68) due to aldosterone
deficiency.7,42,47 Aldosterone facilitates hydrogen ion secretion into urine and its deficiency leads
to acidemia.7,42,48,49 Hypochloremia is observed in 40-60% of dogs with HA, probably because Na
and chloride are co-transported from blood to urine.7,42,49,50 Hypercalcemia, both total and
ionized, is poorly understood but relatively common. It does not appear related to altered
parathyroid hormone, parathyroid hormone-related protein, or serum 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D
concentrations.51-53 Since glucocorticoids facilitate calciuresis, their deficiency may contribute to
hypercalcemia. Acidemia may also increase ionized calcium concentrations as an excess of
positively charged hydrogen ions compete for albumin binding and displace positively charged
calcium ions from albumin.

Glucose, Cholesterol, Albumin, Liver Enzymes
Hypoglycemia, usually mild, develops in <20% of dogs with HA (ch. 61). Rarely, hypoglycemia
can be severe, causing life-threatening seizures.54 Hypoglycemia develops because
gluconeogenesis and the catabolic effects of glucocorticoids on glycogen are diminished, not due to
increases in insulin concentration.55 Increases in alanine aminotransferase and aspartate
aminotransferase activities are attributed to poor perfusion of the liver, ischemic damage to the
hepatocytes, and leakage of cytosolic enzymes. Hypoalbuminemia and hypocholesterolemia, which
are noted less commonly than the increases in liver enzyme activities, can mimic protein-losing
enteropathies and are probably due to the acute effects of GI hypoperfusion rather than to liver
dysfunction.7,42,56

Na:K Ratio
Use of the Na:K ratio as a screening diagnostic aid for HA has been scrutinized because it
encourages use of 2 results instead of 1 when deciding whether to pursue testing for HA (chs. 67,
68). When a Na:K ratio of 27 or 28 is used as a cutoff, about 95% of dogs are identified as either
having or not having HA.7 In dogs with a Na:K ratio of 24 or less, the likelihood of confirming a
diagnosis of HA with an ACTHst is high.7 The combination of the Na:K ratio (reflecting
aldosterone) and the lymphocyte count (reflecting glucocorticoids) is thorough and can aid in
determining the need for an ACTHst.40

URINALYSIS
Isosthenuria or relatively dilute urine, despite dehydration, is due to hypoNa reducing the renal
concentration gradient, limiting renal capability to concentrate urine, and to the osmotic effect of
increased Na concentration in the urine (ch. 70). In dogs with HA and hypoNa, urine Na
concentration is usually ≥30 mmol/L (>30 mEq/L).57

TESTING FOR NON-ADRENAL DISEASES
The extent and focus of other testing depends on clinical signs. In dogs with mild waxing and
waning lethargy, occasional lack of appetite, and thin body condition, testing is often less
aggressive as compared with testing a dog with acute severe disease. Additional testing may be
performed to exclude other major differential diagnoses in dogs with GI signs or PU/PD. In dogs
with HA, urine cultures are typically negative and no GI parasites or pathogenic fecal bacterial
growth are noted.

RADIOGRAPHS AND ULTRASONOGRAPHY
Megaesophagus (ch. 259) has been reported anecdotally in humans with HA, but a clear
association between megaesophagus and HA in dogs has not been established. Microcardia is most
commonly due to hypovolemia (Figure 296.2). If acute pancreatitis is suspected (ch. 277),
abdominal US and pancreatic lipase quantification are warranted. Abdominal imaging may be
used to exclude a GI foreign body or other condition. Abdominal US is not a test of adrenal
function, but the thickness of adrenal glands in dogs with HA is usually less than 3 mm.58

ELECTROCARDIOGRAM (ECG)
In dogs with bradycardia, a weak pulse (ch. 39), or a suspicion of HA, an ECG may reveal changes
consistent with hyperK and provide an incentive to consider HA: short-to-absent P waves,
prolonged P-R intervals, wide QRS complexes, short R waves, tall T waves, and ectopic beats
(Figure 296.3).

ADRENAL AXIS TESTING
ACTH Stimulation Test (ACTHst; Figure 296.4)
Confirming a diagnosis of HA requires adrenocortical testing. Functions of glucocorticoids and
mineralocorticoids are investigated separately. The ACTHst is the gold standard for diagnosing HA
via assessment of glucocorticoid function. In dogs with HA, the ACTHst is performed by
measuring serum cortisol concentration before and 1 hour after IV administration of 1 mcg/kg
synthetic short-acting ACTH.59 The required volume of ACTH is small and care must be taken
during administration since ACTH erroneously administered subcutaneously (SQ) in a severely
dehydrated animal may not reach the circulation to stimulate the adrenal glands. In hydrated
dogs, route of ACTH administration is irrelevant.60 Synthetic ACTH is expensive, and any
reconstituted volume remaining in a vial can be refrigerated or frozen. Synthetic ACTH
refrigerated (4-8°C) for as long as 60 days retains activity in humans, although it is recommended
not to refrigerate longer than 14 days.61 Reconstituted synthetic ACTH can be stored frozen (at
−20°C) in plastic syringes for up to 6 months.62
In a dog with normal adrenal function, ACTH administration should cause a surge of
glucocorticoid secretion from the adrenal glands. In non-HA dogs, serum cortisol concentrations
before and after ACTH administration are expected to be between 0.5-6 mcg/dL (14-166 nmol/L)

and >2 mcg/dL (>55 nmol/L), respectively. In a dog with HA the adrenals are atrophied and
unable to mount an appropriate response to ACTH. In most dogs with HA, serum cortisol
concentrations before and after administration of ACTH are <1 mcg/dL (<28 nmol/L) (Figure
296.4). A small number of dogs with HA have a serum cortisol concentration between 1-2 mcg/dL
(28-55 nmol/L) after ACTHst; however, a diagnosis of HA in a dog with serum cortisol
concentration >1 mcg/dL (>28 nmol/L) after ACTH stimulation should be made with caution.

Alternatives to the ACTHst
The cost of synthetic ACTH and its lack of availability in some countries have led to studies
investigating other options for diagnosis of HA. Although most dogs with a basal serum cortisol
concentration <1 mcg/dL (<28 nmol/L) have HA, this is not true for all. Resting cortisol alone
cannot be used to diagnose HA.63 However, basal cortisol concentrations are a useful tool for
excluding the diagnosis. Dogs with a basal cortisol concentration >2 mcg/dL (>55 nmol/L) are
unlikely to have HA.63 This test is particularly useful in dogs in which the Na:K ratio is normal and
only glucocorticoid dysfunction is suspected. The cortisol-to-endogenous-ACTH ratio has been
investigated as a possible diagnostic tool for HA. Although ratios are low in dogs with HA,
individual ratios may be of little value.64 A protocol using intramuscular (IM) long-acting depot
formulation of synthetic ACTH for diagnosis of HA has been reported in 10 dogs with suspected
HA.65

Mineralocorticoids
Assessing [Na] and [K] generally suffices for recognizing aldosterone function or absence. The
ratio of plasma aldosterone concentration to plasma renin activity in dogs with HA was lower than
in healthy dogs, with no overlap.66 It remains to be seen whether this ratio can be useful in
differentiating dogs with HA from other dogs with other illnesses.

Secondary HA

Rarely, a dog might be suspected to have secondary HA. Their endogenous ACTH concentrations
should be low in contrast to the extremely increased concentrations in most dogs with primary
HA. [Na] and [K] are expected to remain normal, as their regulation is controlled mainly by the
RAAS, independent of pituitary or hypothalamic control.

Isolated Hypoaldosteronism
In isolated hypoaldosteronism, cortisol concentrations before and after ACTHst are normal. Such
dogs are expected to have hyperK, hypoNa, low plasma renin activity and low aldosterone
concentrations before and after ACTHst (ch. 122).67,68

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES
The term “pseudo-Addison’s disease” has been used for ill dogs whose clinical and laboratory
results (especially [Na] and [K]) resemble HA. Some dogs with any severe GI disease (including
trichuriasis [ch. 263] and salmonellosis [chs. 195, 262]), ill pregnant dogs, and those with
chylothorax (ch. 220) may mimic HA.69-73 The only way to distinguish these conditions from true
HA is assessing results of an ACTHst. Differential diagnoses for PU/PD (ch. 53), azotemia,
isosthenuria, eosinophilia, hyperK, hypoNa, hypercalcemia, hypoglycemia, increased liver enzyme
activities, hypocholesterolemia, hypoalbuminemia, and acidemia are discussed in chs. 57-71.

TREATMENT
ACUTE ADRENAL CRISIS
Overview and Fluid Therapy
Treatment of an acute HA crisis consists of IV fluids and SQ desoxycorticosterone pivalate
(DOCP), and occasionally IV glucose and insulin. Dexamethasone is rarely administered in the
acute stages and bicarbonate treatment is not indicated. Fluid therapy is the single most important
treatment for an acute crisis and is vital. Although no studies guide the choice of a specific
crystalloid IV fluid therapy, 0.9% NaCl is recommended because it contains more Na and chloride
and less K than other crystalloids (chs. 120, 121).

FIGURE 296.3 Serial electrocardiogram (ECG) segments obtained from
2 dogs with hypoadrenocorticism and hyperkalemia. A and AA both
illustrate the effect of severe hyperkalemia, with the dog in A having a
serum potassium concentration of 8.6 mEq/L and the dog in AA a

measurement of 9.4 mEq/L. Note the lack of visible P waves, the short and
wide QRS complexes, and the T waves, which are not of excessive
amplitude. The ECG in A also reveals two instances of a bizarre-looking
QRS complex following a more normal-appearing QRS complex at a shorter
R-R interval (i.e., 2 wider, more bizarre-looking premature beats). These
represent premature ventricular complexes that could be the result of
acidemia, myocardial hypoxia, or other metabolic imbalances. B and BB
are ECGs from the same dogs as in A and AA, respectively. They were each
obtained approximately 1 hour after institution of intravenous normal
saline as the only treatment. The serum potassium concentrations had
decreased to 7.6 mEq/L and 7.9 mEq/L, respectively. Two important
factors to note: (1) improvement is seen in each case with the return of P
waves, a more rapid heart rate, and disappearance of premature ventricular
complexes; and (2) abnormalities are still present, most obviously the
prolonged P-R intervals (first-degree heart block), which alone suggest
hyperkalemia, especially when associated with a widened QRS complex and
a short Q-T interval. There are numerous other causes of P-R interval
prolongation. In C and CC, the serum potassium concentrations are
considerably lower, 6.2 mEq/L and 5.9 mEq/L, respectively. The P-R
interval and P, QRS, and T waves are of shorter duration, and the R waves
are taller. D, ECG from the dog in A; the serum potassium concentration is
5.6 mEq/L and a more spiked T wave is seen. Unit conversion for K+: 1
mEq/L = 1 nmol/L. From Feldman EC, Nelson RW, Reusch CE, et al.
Canine and Feline Endocrinology and Reproduction. 4th ed. Saunders;
2015.

Sodium (Na) and Potassium (K)
Acute and profound hypoNa can cause brain edema. However, hypoNa corrected too quickly can
cause potentially fatal brain osmotic fluid shifts. In hypoNa treatment in humans, it is
recommended that serum [Na] should not increase more than 1-2 mEq/L (1-2 mmol/L) during the
first 2-3 hours of emergency treatment and not more than 8-12 mEq/L (8-12 mmol/L) in the first
24 hours.74 Initially, serum [Na] and [K] should be monitored every 2-6 hours, depending on the
status of the dog and the severity of electrolyte abnormalities. HyperK typically resolves with IV
0.9% saline.

Glucose, Insulin, DOCP, Bicarbonate
If severe hyperK persists following 6-8 hours of fluid therapy or if bradycardia is profound, IV
glucose can be given to stimulate insulin secretion. Insulin shifts K from the extracellular fluid into
cells, decreasing extracellular [K]. If glucose administration alone fails to decrease [K], shortacting IV insulin can be safely added if the blood glucose (BG) concentration is >200 mg/dL (>11.1
mmol/L). When insulin is administered, BG must be measured at least every 2 hours to ensure
that the dog does not develop hypoglycemia. If the dog has severe hypoglycemia (BG <60 mg/dL
[<3.3 mmol/L]) at admission or after insulin administration, 5% dextrose or a dextrose bolus
(0.25-0.5 g/kg, diluted 1:3) can be given IV. Importantly, as glucose is administered,
hyperglycemia can cause artifactual decreases in measured [Na]. As BG concentration increases,
intracellular fluid flows into the extracellular compartment resulting in Na dilution. In humans,
there is a measured decrease of 1 mEq/L (1 mmol/L) in [Na] for every 62 mg/dL (3.4 mmol/L)
increase above 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) in BG concentration. If a rehydrated dog remains hyperK
and hypoNa, if the ACTHst has been performed, and if other major differential diagnoses have
been excluded, a SQ injection of DOCP (1.5 mg/kg) should be administered. DOCP appears to be
benign if administered to a dog not in need. Treatment with hydrocortisone sodium succinate
(0.5-0.625 mg/kg/hr) has been reported.75 Concerns have been raised over the lower pH of 0.9%

saline compared to other crystalloid fluids, however, the importance of correcting the hypoNa and
hyperK associated with HA far outweigh the risk of iatrogenic acidosis. HA-associated acidosis is
usually mild and corrects within 12-24 hours of IV 0.9% saline treatment. If acidosis is severe (pH
<7.1) and does not correct with fluid therapy, bicarbonate can be administered at increments of
1/4 (0.3 × base deficit × body weight in kg) every 20 minutes while monitoring venous pH.

FIGURE 296.4 Radioimmunoassay plasma cortisol concentrations
before and after exogenous adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation from
normal dogs and those with hypoadrenocorticism. The ranges are means ±

nmol/L. From Feldman EC, Nelson RW. Canine and Feline
Endocrinology and Reproduction. 3rd ed. Saunders; 2004.

Glucocorticoids
Usually, it is not necessary to administer glucocorticoids in the acute stages of treatment because
IV saline, alone, is lifesaving. IV fluids allow completion of the ACTHst. Unnecessary treatment
and monitoring of HA has adverse side-effects and is costly. A definitive diagnosis based on
ACTHst results is imperative. Once begun, glucocorticoid therapy should be discontinued
gradually. Oral prednisone should not be given for at least 48 hours before an ACTHst is
performed.
It is best to delay glucocorticoid treatment until after completing the ACTHst. If glucocorticoids
are deemed necessary before an ACTHst is performed, dexamethasone should be given because it
can be given IV, has rapid onset of action, and does not interfere with a cortisol assay if an ACTHst

is subsequently performed. While dexamethasone is not detected by cortisol assays, it may
suppress secretion of ACTH/CRH and impact results.

LONG-TERM (MAINTENANCE) THERAPY
Overview
Long-term treatment of HA begins once the dog is rehydrated, has normal electrolyte
concentrations, and is no longer vomiting, having diarrhea, or anorexia. This usually begins 24-48
hours after admission for a crisis or on an outpatient basis if the dog was never hospitalized. Longterm treatment usually includes giving a mineralocorticoid and a glucocorticoid. Dogs with normal
[Na] and [K] might only be given glucocorticoids.

Glucocorticoids
Glucocorticoids can be supplemented as prednisone or fludrocortisone (Florinef). Prednisone and
prednisolone are the most commonly used glucocorticoids for long-term management of HA.
Immediately following an acute crisis, prednisone can be administered at a relatively high dosage
of 0.5 mg/kg q12h for 2-3 days. Following this short course of intensive replacement, the dosage
can be decreased quickly to a physiologic dose of 0.1-0.2 mg/kg q12-24h. From there, many dogs
require even lower doses. Doses should be low enough to prevent PU/PD, polyphagia, weight gain,
and other adverse side effects. Finding the perfect prednisone dosage is based on trial, error, and
owner opinion. If lethargy, anorexia, vomiting, and diarrhea recur, a dose may need to be
increased. Owners should have an extra supply of prednisone in case of a crisis or in anticipation
of a stressful situation (travel, kennel, house guests). The owner can administer a higher than
usual dosage of prednisone (0.5 mg/kg), as needed.

Fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone contains both glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids. It can be difficult to
determine the dosage that provides appropriate levels of both hormones. Some dogs develop
clinical signs of iatrogenic hyperadrenocorticism on dosages required for healthy serum electrolyte
concentrations. Others require prednisone plus the fludrocortisone to prevent GI signs of HA.

Mineralocorticoids
Mineralocorticoids can be supplemented using injectable DOCP or oral tablet-form
fludrocortisone. The initial dosage of fludrocortisone is about 0.01 mg/kg q12h and can be
confidently adjusted by measuring [Na] and [K] 5, 14 and 30 days after the first dose. Often the
dosage needs to be initially increased to attain a Na:K ratio well above 27 (about 30).76 DOCP is
labeled for dogs at a dose of 2.2 mg/kg SQ every 25 days, but an initial dose of about 1.5 mg/kg is
now recommended. Young growing dogs require a slightly higher initial dose (about 1.7 mg/kg).
Most dogs ultimately require dose reductions.77,78 Dosing interval can also usually be safely
increased to about once monthly and in some dogs treatment is required only every 2 or even 3
months.77-80
If the Na:K ratio is above 32 on day 15, the subsequent dose of DOCP can be decreased by about
10% (from 1.5 mg/kg to 1.3 mg/kg). If the Na:K ratio is above 32 on day 30, the following DOCP
injection can be postponed for at least 5 days. If on day 35, the Na:K ratio is still above 32, the next
DOCP injection can be postponed for at least another 5 days. If the interval between injections is
increased, the Na:K ratio can be measured in the middle of this new interval, to make sure the
ratio is not >32. If high, the dose can be decreased further. For example, if the dosing interval has
been increased to 40 days, [Na] and [K] can be checked on days 20 and 40. This process can be
repeated over the course of several months until an appropriate dose and injection interval are
identified (Figure 296.5). For this protocol of treatment monitoring the owner must agree to
have [Na] and [K] checked frequently. Although there is expense involved with this approach, the

cost of the drug is also high and ultimately it is less expensive to give a smaller dose, less
frequently, despite the initial cost of repeatedly measuring serum electrolytes. Owners must keep
in mind that a perfect dosage one year may not be the perfect dosage the next year, and [Na] and
[K] rechecks are warranted every few months even in well-regulated dogs. Treatment of dogs with
DOCP and prednisone allows for successful supplementation of glucocorticoids and
mineralocorticoids, separately. DOCP is reportedly more effective than fludrocortisone in
decreasing plasma renin activity, increasing [Na], and decreasing [K] in dogs with HA.81

desoxycorticosterone pivalate (DOCP) treatment of a hypothetical
Addisonian dog.

MONITORING
Once a dog with confirmed HA begins therapy, ACTHst is no longer of value. Glucocorticoid dose
is determined by subjective owner opinion. The ideal dose resolves signs of poorly regulated HA
(vomiting, diarrhea, poor appetite, or weight loss) and avoids signs of iatrogenic
hyperadrenocorticism (PU/PD, polyphagia). Monitoring mineralocorticoid treatment is objective
and precise, based on Na:K ratios, as described. The Na:K ratio should be about 30, no lower than
28 and no higher than 32. Owners should monitor the dog’s clinical signs carefully, and report if
they note any worrisome signs, especially those that can be observed with under- or oversupplementation of glucocorticoids.
PU/PD (ch. 53) can develop in dogs treated for HA for several reasons. Identifying the cause
can be challenging. DOCP can cause PU/PD without increased [Na]. Glucocorticoids are a classic
cause of iatrogenic PU/PD. Poorly regulated HA also causes PU/PD. Finally, with time, an HA dog

can develop a second cause of PU/PD. Therefore, this relatively common problem must be
evaluated carefully, using all clinical signs and test results.
Remember that dogs diagnosed with atypical HA can progress to a state in which they are
mineralocorticoid deficient, so [Na] and [K] should be monitored in these dogs.

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis for HA is excellent, provided that the acute crisis is treated successfully and a
diagnosis established. Most dogs with HA that require IV fluid therapy are discharged from the
hospital about 48 hours after admission (Table 296.1).

FELINE HYPOADRENOCORTICISM
HA is extremely rare in cats. Cats with HA have similar clinical signs, PE findings, and
clinicopathologic abnormalities to those exhibited in dogs with HA.82 Spontaneous typical and
atypical HA, iatrogenic HA associated with withdrawal of steroids, and neoplastic invasion of
adrenals, have all been reported.83,84 Pseudohypoadrenocorticism with hypoNa and hyperK has
been documented in 4 cats with peritoneal effusion (chs. 21, 71).85 Feline HA should be suspected
if other common disorders, which can explain the classic clinical signs observed with HA, have
been excluded, and clinicopathologic findings are supportive of the diagnosis. The protocol for an
ACTHst in cats is different than the protocol in dogs (ch. 294). Treatment is based on
glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid supplementation after the acute crisis is overcome. The
prognosis for cats with HA appears to be worse than the prognosis of dogs with HA.82

CLIENT INFORMATION
Hypoadrenocorticism (Addison’s Disease)
WHAT IS ADDISON’S DISEASE?
Addison’s disease is a fairly common hormonal disease that affects mainly dogs. It involves failure
of the adrenal glands, small hormone secreting glands located near the kidneys. It is not known
exactly why the adrenal glands stop functioning, but it is possible that they are destroyed by the
immune system. The hormones that the adrenal glands normally secrete are steroids (also called
glucocorticoids) and aldosterone (also called a mineralocorticoid). These hormones are essential
for life. Therefore, if Addison’s disease is not treated it can be fatal. However, the good news is that
it can be treated, by simply giving your dog the hormones that the adrenal glands should normally
be making. Your dog is in good company. John F. Kennedy also had Addison’s disease, and it did
not kill him!

HOW WOULD I KNOW MY DOG HAS ADDISON’S DISEASE?
Classic chronic clinical signs are gradual loss of appetite, weight loss, perhaps some vomiting or
diarrhea, and maybe some lethargy. These signs can be mild and chronic or acute, and not all of
these signs must be present to confirm a diagnosis. Sometimes the initial clinical signs are not
noticeable, and the dog develops a clinical crisis, which involves hospitalization and intravenous
fluid care, as well as hormone supplementation.

HOW IS ADDISON’S DISEASE DIAGNOSED?
Addison’s disease is diagnosed based on clinical signs and some testing, which will depend on your
dog’s specific clinical signs. Ultimately, an adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation test,
which is a one-hour blood test, must be performed to confirm a diagnosis. Other tests will likely be
performed, to make sure this is the only problem that your dog has.

HOW IS ADDISON’S DISEASE TREATED?
Long-term treatment involves supplementing the hormones that would otherwise be produced by
the adrenal glands. We usually treat with desoxycorticosterone pivalate (DOCP) to supplement for
the missing aldosterone, and prednisone for the missing glucocorticoids.
DOCP is given as an injection under the skin, and your veterinarian can teach you how to give it
at home. If you prefer, you can come into the clinic to have one of the nurses or veterinarians give
your dog the injection. Initially we give the injection every 30 days, but we like to perform a blood
test (measure sodium and potassium) at days 15 and 30 and then every 5 days thereafter, to
determine if we can prolong the interval between injections and also to determine if we can give a
smaller dose of DOCP in the future. This testing may seem costly at first, but it saves resources in
the long run.
Prednisone is given orally, on a daily basis, and the dose of this medication will also be adjusted
as time goes by. Prednisone can never be discontinued abruptly. It is paramount that you notice
when your supply is diminishing and call for a refill in a timely fashion. Abrupt discontinuation of
prednisone can be fatal.
Your veterinarian may also give you some prednisone for special instances in which you think
your dog may experience more stress than usual. Such instances may include travel, kenneling,
company, or large family gatherings. In such instances your veterinarian may instruct you to give
more than the usual dose of prednisone.

Another treatment option is fludrocortisone, which includes both glucocorticoids and a
mineralocorticoid.

NOW THAT MY DOG HAS BEEN DIAGNOSED WITH ADDISON’S
DISEASE, IS THERE ANYTHING IN PARTICULAR I SHOULD BE
WATCHING FOR?
Yes! Please let your veterinarian know if you notice decreased appetite, vomiting, diarrhea, weight
loss, or lethargy. These signs may suggest that an increase in prednisone is warranted. Please also
notify your veterinarian if you notice increased drinking, increased appetite, or panting. These
signs may suggest that the dose of prednisone has to be decreased. Please be mindful of any
stressful situations that may arise, and discuss with your veterinarian the need to increase the dose
of prednisone for a day or two during such events. Please avoid deviating in any way from the
treatment protocol, without discussing this first with your veterinarian. Finally, be sure never to
run out of prednisone, because abrupt discontinuation of this drug can be life threatening.

WILL MY DOG BE OK?
Yes! Close and constant communication with your veterinarian, careful adherence to the treatment
protocol, and regular checkups will guarantee that your dog has a happy and long life, with
successfully treated Addison’s disease.
Rebecka S. Hess (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania)

INTRODUCTION

The gastrointestinal (GI) tract is considered the body’s largest endocrine
organ. Endocrine functions of the pancreas and GI tract are diverse,
involve more than 30 hormones, and are responsible for integrating and
coordinating physiologic processes that regulate appetite, digestion, and
energy metabolism.1 These substances are true hormones, entering the
bloodstream to act at target tissues distant from their site of origin. Some
GI hormones circulate in 1 of several isoforms, which may produce
different actions depending on the target tissue; others serve paracrine
or neurotransmitter functions. The biochemical diversity of the
hormones produced by the GI tract and pancreas is as broad as the
functions they regulate, resulting in a complex clinical endocrinology.
In some hormone families, such as gastrin and glucagon, functional
diversity is conveyed by specific genes to produce alternatively spliced
mRNAs and preprohormones that undergo various post-translational
modifications to produce a variety of structurally-related but functionally
distinct proteins. Thorough exploration of the genetic, biochemical, and
physiologic mechanisms that regulate these complex hormones is
beyond the scope of this chapter, but a brief review allows discussion of
clinical syndromes associated with abnormalities of gut hormone
production. Many GI and pancreatic hormones share biochemical and
structural similarities that permit classification into various hormone
families (Table 297.1). Clinically, the secretin, insulin, and gastrin
families are among the most relevant. Other hormones, such as
serotonin that cause defined syndromes in humans, have less defined
roles in animals. Some, such as ghrelin and glucagon-like peptide-1
(GLP-1), may have emerging roles in the treatment of endocrine
disorders (chs. 280, 291, and 292).

ENTERIC CELL HORMONES: THE
PANCREATIC AND GUT HORMONES
In addition to secretin, the clinically important members of this hormone
family include glucagon, glucagon-like peptide (GLP), and gastric
inhibitory peptide (GIP). Other hormones in this group include gastrin,
cholecystokinin (CCK), somatostatin, motilin, ghrelin, and serotonin.
Insulin, a major islet hormone, is not produced by enteric cells and is
discussed elsewhere (chs. 289, 291).
