SECRETIN
Secretin, a peptide hormone produced by S cells located principally in
the duodenum, is released in response to the presence of hydrogen ions
(H+) in gastric secretions.2 Like some other gut hormones (e.g., CCK),
secretin circulates in one of several isoforms (27-, 28-, 30-, and 71-amino
acid polypeptides have been described). Each polypeptide may have
slightly different functions. Secretin acts to stimulate release of
bicarbonate-containing fluid and bile, respectively, from pancreatic
ductal cells and biliary epithelium. Other effects include inhibition of
gastrin secretion, gastric acid production, and GI motility. Expression of
secretin or its receptor has been reported in central nervous system
(CNS) neurons, heart, and lung, but further study is needed to define its
role(s) in these non-enteric sites.

GLUCAGON, GLUCAGON-LIKE PEPTIDE
(GLP), AND GASTRIC INHIBITORY
PEPTIDE (GIP)
Glucagon from pancreatic islet alpha cells and enteroglucagons from GI
L cells are products of the same gene. Diversity within this peptide family
arises from tissue specific processing of primary gene transcripts. In islet
alpha cells, primary mRNAs encode glucagon while in L cells, mRNAs
derived from the same gene encode GLP, GIP, enteroglucagon and
glicentin.3 Glucagon, a vital hormone in energy homeostasis and nutrient
metabolism, has actions that generally counter the anabolic actions of
insulin. Glucagon is the principal hormone stimulus for hepatic
glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, actions opposite those of insulin.
GLP (GLP-1 and glucagon-like peptide-2 [GLP-2]) and GIP are
enteroglucagons known as incretins because their actions enhance
nutrient-induced insulin secretion. GLP-1, the most potent insulin
secretagogue, has been evaluated as a therapeutic aid for Type II
diabetes mellitus (DM). GLP-1 and GLP-2 are released from L cells in
response to intraluminal nutrients and they modulate intestinal glucose
absorption via inhibition of gastric motility and GLP-2 mediated
upregulation of glucose transporters.4,5

GASTRIN
Gastrin, synthesized and secreted by neuroendocrine G cells in the
stomach antrum and duodenum, is stimulated by ingested protein and
gastric distention and inhibited by low intraluminal pH (<3). Gastrin
circulates in several different molecular forms that vary in molecular
weight (e.g., gastrin-34, -17, and -14), which bind on target tissue
surfaces.6 Gastrin-34 is the major circulating gastrin, but the less
abundant gastrin-17 is more potent in promoting gastric acid secretion,
the primary biologic action of this hormone. Gastrin acts in concert with
acetylcholine from autonomic parasympathetic nerve endings and
histamine to regulate H+ secretion from gastric parietal cells. Other
biological effects of gastrin include trophic action on gastric epithelium
and stimulation of mucosal blood flow, pepsinogen release, and antral
motility. Gastrin also influences pancreatic enzyme production and has
trophic effects on pancreatic and duodenal tissue.

CHOLECYSTOKININ (CCK)
CCK, synthesized by duodenal and jejunal I cells, is released in response
to a variety of substances entering the duodenum, especially H+, fatty
acids, and amino acids.7 During synthesis, the CCK transcript undergoes
processing that results in a multitude of circulating isoforms. Of the 7
CCK isoforms identified, CCK-33, CCK-39, and CCK-58 are responsible
for the principal GI effects. CCK-8, expressed in neurons, serves as a
peptide neurotransmitter in the enteric nervous system. Other isoforms,
such as CCK-5, CCK-12, and CCK-63, have less importance. Major CCK
actions include stimulating gallbladder contraction and pancreatic
enzyme secretion, both mediated via presynaptic cholinergic neurons.
CCK also serves to coordinate overall digestive function including
stimulation of pancreatic fluid secretion (in the presence of stimulatory
levels of secretin), inhibition of gastric emptying, sphincter of Oddi
relaxation, and stimulation of pancreatic growth.

SOMATOSTATIN
The peptide somatostatin is synthesized in the hypothalamus, pancreatic
islet delta cells, GI D cells, and subsets of neurons in the CNS and enteric
nervous system. Intestinal D cells release somatostatin in response to
nutrients (fats and protein) and bile entering the gut. The endocrine,
paracrine, and neurotransmitter effects of somatostatin are principally
inhibitory: inhibition of gastric acid and pepsinogen secretion,
gallbladder contraction, insulin secretion, pancreatic exocrine function,
GI motility, and nutrient (amino acids and glucose) absorption.8

MOTILIN
Motilin, a peptide hormone synthesized in GI cells, is structurally related
to ghrelin. Its major endocrine actions occur during fasting when motilin
initiates and coordinates migrating motility complexes (MMCs), which
serve to clear the intestine in interdigestive states. After eating, motilin is
released in response to stomach acid (H+) or lipid entering the small
intestines. In the fed state, motilin serves to coordinate gastric,
pancreatic, and biliary secretions.9

GHRELIN
The hormone ghrelin, synthesized and secreted in the stomach, is
structurally related to motilin and is important as an appetite stimulant
and in energy metabolism.10 It stimulates adipocyte growth and pituitary
growth hormone (GH) synthesis and secretion. Ghrelin provides a link
between dietary nutrients, caloric energy, and the pituitary-GH axis that
is vital for growth regulation.

SEROTONIN
Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine [5-HT]) is a neuropeptide and hormone
located within enteric neurons and enterochromaffin cells distributed
throughout the GI tract. 5-HT acts in an endocrine and paracrine
manner to stimulate GI smooth muscle contraction and intestinal
secretions.11

CLINICAL DISORDERS ASSOCIATED
WITH GI HORMONES
INSULINOMA (CH. 289)
Insulinoma is both uncommon and the most common neuroendocrine
tumor in dogs. It is rare in cats.12-15 The pancreas is the most frequent
location for insulinoma, but it can also be found in mesenteric, splenic,
and hepatic locations. Non-pancreatic insulinomas may be primary or
metastases. Insulin release by insulinoma is not under precise
physiologic control and inappropriate increases in serum insulin cause
episodic hypoglycemia (ch. 61).

GASTRINOMA
Overview
Gastrinoma is an uncommon tumor of dogs and cats16-20 and no largescale studies of canine or feline gastrinoma have been published. Gastrin
overproduction caused by gastrinoma may lead to the Zollinger-Ellison
syndrome, clinically associated with gastric antral hypertrophy,

hyperacidity and ulceration.21 Treatment is surgical removal of the
tumor. Supportive treatment is directed at suppressing gastric acid
production.

Signalment and Clinical Signs
The veterinary literature includes fewer than 50 cases of gastrinoma,
most in dogs and a few in cats. Mean age at diagnosis in dogs is about 8
years and cats have been slightly older. Frequent owner observations
include vomiting, diarrhea, and weight loss. Less frequent concerns
include apparent abdominal pain, GI bleeding, polydipsia, and
constipation. Gastrin-induced hyperacidity can lead to reflux esophagitis
with resultant regurgitation, and esophageal colic (ch. 259). Disease in
the stomach is characterized by mucosal hypertrophy, mucosal
ulceration, and, in severe cases, outflow obstruction, vomiting and
weight loss. Diarrhea may develop due to the inhibitory effects of gastrin
on intestinal water absorption. Gastrinomas, usually quite small, are
rarely detected on abdominal palpation. Physical examination (PE)
findings depend on the stage of disease. Signs, if any, are not specific.
Early in the disease, the PE is often unremarkable. Animals with
esophagitis, gastric ulceration or gastric perforation exhibit signs of pain
on esophageal or abdominal palpation, evidence of dehydration, fever,
and signs of shock.

Laboratory Findings
Gastrinoma is not associated with specific abnormalities on complete
blood count (CBC) or serum biochemistry panels. Nonspecific findings of
leukocytosis, neutrophilia with left shift, anemia, and
panhypoproteinemia caused by inflammation and blood loss may be
seen secondary to gastric ulceration. Other reported biochemical
abnormalities include hypoalbuminuria, hypokalemia, hypochloremia,
hyponatremia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperbilirubinemia, and increased
liver enzyme activities. Biochemical changes may not be caused by
gastrinoma per se, but may develop secondary to consequences of
hypergastrinemia, such as chronic vomiting, diarrhea, or hepatic
metastasis. Some dogs with gastrinoma have concurrent disorders
(myelofibrosis, bile duct obstruction) that contribute to clinicopathologic
disturbances. Some gastrinomas may produce and secrete hormones in
addition to gastrin; concurrent secretion of insulin and
adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) have been reported.

Routine Diagnostic Imaging
Ultrasonography (US) is more efficient in detecting a pancreatic mass
than is radiography. Changes associated with gastrinoma include the
gastric wall being altered by ulcerations, hypertrophy of the mucosa, and
thickened rugal folds and gastric walls. US may detect metastases to
extrapancreatic sites such as liver or lymph nodes. Plain radiography
generally reveals nonspecific changes. The use of contrast radiography,
described in several case reports, identified gastric rugal fold
hypertrophy, narrowing of the antrum due to hypertrophy, and mucosal
defects caused by ulceration. Endoscopy, of limited value in obtaining a
definitive diagnosis, may provide useful information regarding
esophageal inflammation and ulceration, prominent gastric folds, antral
hypertrophy, gastric and duodenal ulceration, and hypersecretion of
gastric fluid (ch. 107). Endoscopic biopsy may permit histologic
characterization of GI changes but is not likely to provide definitive
diagnosis of gastrinoma.

FIGURE 297.1 Necrolytic migratory erythema lesions
on the foot and footpad of a dog with glucagonoma.

Assay of Basal Serum Gastrin Concentrations and/or
Gastric pH
An array of testing options is available, including measuring serum
gastrin concentrations, basal acid production, secretin- and calcium
(Ca)-stimulation of gastrin secretion, and tumor imaging using a labeled
somatostatin for scintigraphic localization. In dogs and cats, none of
these studies is common. In people, a serum gastrin level >1000 ng/L
together with a gastric pH <2.5 are diagnostic for gastrinoma. This
pairing of gastrin and gastric acid measurements has not been used
extensively in veterinary medicine.
Serum gastrin concentrations in dogs with confirmed gastrinoma have
been well above control values, but no specific cutoffs discriminating
between normal and abnormal have been established. Increased serum
gastrin concentrations are not specific; thus, gastrin results alone cannot
be used to confirm a diagnosis. Gastrin concentrations may be increased
in dogs and cats with kidney disease, gastropathies, hepatopathies, and
with use of drugs that inhibit gastric acid production. Measurements of
pH and/or gastric acid secretion, reported in a few dogs with gastrinoma,
have noted low gastric pH. Results can be helpful when the clinical
suspicion for gastrinoma is high and other disorders that might cause
hypergastrinemia have been ruled out.

Provocative Testing With Secretin
Provocative tests measure gastrin release in response to secretin or Ca,
neither of which alters gastrin concentrations in healthy individuals.
Either causes gastrin release from gastrinoma. The secretin stimulation
test is the most frequently employed provocative test in people, but
experience with this test in animals is limited. The test principle relies on
the enhanced responsiveness of gastrinoma tissue to secretin. In 1
protocol, serum samples were obtained before and 2, 5, 10, and 20
minutes after intravenous (IV) injection of secretin in dogs (2 to 4
U/kg).22 An alternative protocol suggests samples be obtained before
and 2, 5, 10, 30, and 60 minutes after IV injection of 2 U/kg secretin.23
Samples taken 2 and 5 minutes after giving secretin are most useful for
diagnosis, since tumor response to injected secretin is typically rapid and
short-lived. Humans with gastrinoma have about a 2-fold increase in
gastrin following secretin injection. While reports of secretin stimulation
tests in dogs are scarce, results have been similar. However, not all dogs

with gastrinoma have demonstrated an increase in gastrin
concentrations more than 2-fold above baseline.22

Provocative Testing With Calcium (Ca)
The Ca stimulation test is inexpensive and widely available. Adverse
cardiac effects during infusion are a potential disadvantage, requiring
appropriate precautions (ch. 284). One protocol includes obtaining
serum samples before and 15, 30, 60, and 90 minutes after IV Ca
infusion (2 mg/kg IV, given over 1 minute).24 Maximum gastrin
secretion was detected at 60 minutes. Humans with gastrinoma typically
have a 2-fold increase in serum gastrin concentrations, as did the few
dogs with confirmed gastrinoma.

Pathology
Gastrinomas are usually solitary masses within the pancreas, but cases
involving multiple masses have been reported. In dogs, gastrinomas have
been reported more often in the right limb or body of the pancreas and
metastases are common at the time of diagnosis. Metastatic lesions have
been identified in lymph nodes, mesentery, peritoneal surfaces, spleen
and/or liver in about 85% of dogs. Microscopically, gastrinomas are
carcinomas of endocrine cell origin, staining positively for gastrin using
immunohistochemistry. On ultrastructural studies, identification of
specific intracellular granules may permit definitive diagnosis of
gastrinoma. Although rarely performed, hormone measurements on
extracts of tumor tissue may also be used to confirm gastrin production.
Hypertrophy of the gastric wall and GI ulcerations are common, affecting
esophagus, stomach, and/or intestine. Perforations and peritonitis (ch.
265) have been seen. Additional endocrine disorders noted in some dogs
include thyroid carcinoma and adrenal hyperplasia.

GLUCAGONOMA
Overview
Glucagonomas are rare, reported in only a few dogs25-27 and a single
cat.28 Glucagonoma arises from neuroendocrine alpha cells in pancreatic
islets. Excess glucagon concentrations follow autonomous secretion that
induces hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, insulin resistance,

glucose intolerance, and in some, overt DM. Definitive treatment is
accomplished by surgical removal of the tumor. Necrolytic migratory
erythema (NME; superficial necrolytic dermatitis), a dermatologic
condition characterized by crusting and a rash, is considered
pathognomonic for glucagonoma in people.29 In dogs, the skin condition
has been seen with glucagonoma but is more commonly associated with
liver diseases (chs. 12 and 274).30

Signalment and Clinical Signs
The few dogs diagnosed as having glucagonoma were middle-aged or
older and the cat was 6 years old. Along with nonspecific signs (lethargy
and decreased appetite) a few dog owners were concerned about nonhealing skin erosions and ulcers. The distribution of lesions and
involvement of mucocutaneous sites in dogs with glucagonoma suggest
the possibility of an autoimmune component. Lesions have been
reported to involve lips, nose, ears, muzzle, paws, the ventrum, inguinal
region, and extremities (Figure 297.1). Dogs with uncontrolled DM
have classic signs, but insulin therapy is relatively ineffective in
controlling the hyperglycemia, requiring high doses.

Laboratory Findings
Numerous nonspecific laboratory abnormalities have been noted in the
dogs with glucagonoma: increased serum alanine aminotransferase
(ALT) and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activities plus decreases in
albumin, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and cholesterol. The abnormal liver
parameters in glucagonoma mimic those caused by primary liver disease,
a more common cause of NME in dogs. Liver function tests, such as bile
acids and blood ammonia levels, have been normal in dogs with
glucagonoma but may be important when investigating the possibility of
liver disease.

Diagnostic Imaging
Abdominal US is more sensitive than radiography in detecting pancreatic
masses, but masses have not been detected in most dogs with
glucagonoma. Computed tomography (CT) was used to identify a
pancreatic mass in 1 dog. Abnormalities in the US appearance of the liver
were frequently observed, but no consistent pattern was noted. Dogs

with NME and an abnormal hepatic US are much more likely to have
primary liver disease than glucagonoma.

Diagnosis
Definitive diagnosis of glucagonoma relies on demonstration of
hyperglucagonemia. When measured, serum glucagon in dogs with
confirmed glucagonoma has ranged from approximately 1.5 to 15 times
the upper limit of the reference range. No serum concentration is
diagnostic of glucagonoma in the dog but serum glucagon >1000 ng/L is
considered diagnostic for glucagonoma in humans. Since serum
glucagon may increase in disorders other than glucagonoma, the
diagnosis is made only when hyperglucagonemia occurs in association
with clinical signs of hormone excess. Diagnostic efforts may be
complicated by lack of commercially available serum assays for canine
and feline glucagon. Measurement of plasma amino acids may provide
support for a diagnosis of glucagonoma. Hyperglucagonemia stimulates
hepatic gluconeogenesis, accelerates amino acid turnover and lowers
plasma amino acid concentrations. Concentrations of arginine, histidine,
and lysine were reduced in all dogs with glucagonoma in which these
measurements were performed.

Pathology
Pancreatic glucagonoma is usually a solitary neoplasm that can arise
from any region of the pancreas (limbs, body). When metastasis occurs,
the liver is most likely to be affected, although lymphatic metastasis has
been seen. Metastatic nodules may be functional (liver metastasis was
the only site where glucagon production was documented in 1 dog with
glucagonoma), suggesting incomplete surgical removal of metastases
could result in persistent signs. By convention, these tumors have
positive immunohistochemistry staining for glucagon. Most dogs with
glucagonoma have exhibited positive cellular staining against multiple
hormones, although it is not clear whether these tumors secrete
hormones other than glucagon.

CARCINOID
Neuroendocrine tumors that secrete vasoactive substances such as 5-HT
(also known as serotonin) or kinins are referred to as carcinoid tumors,
usually arising from neuroendocrine cells in the epithelium of the

bronchial tree, lung, biliary system, GI tract, or other sites. In people, the
“carcinoid syndrome” is characterized by watery diarrhea, abdominal
discomfort, abdominal cramps, bronchoconstriction, and hyperemia of
the face (“facial flushing”). Carcinoid tumors are rare in dogs and cats.
Most information about these tumors has come from single case
descriptions.31 In dogs, carcinoids have been found in the stomach,
duodenum, jejunum, ileocolic region, colon, and rectum.32-36 In a few
reports on cats, locations included liver, pancreas, and GI tract.37,38
Metastasis to lymph nodes and other sites, including lung, was common.
The majority of carcinoids reported in dogs and cats cause signs
related to the physical presence of the tumor and are not functional. The
carcinoid syndrome has not been reported in cats. The 1 dog reported to
have carcinoid syndrome did not have elevated concentrations of
vasoactive substances 5-HT or kinins.39 Diagnosis of carcinoid is often
made postmortem but when identified antemortem, surgical removal of
the carcinoid is recommended to resolve mass-related signs: intestinal
obstruction, for example. The high frequency of metastases, however,
makes complete tumor removal unlikely. In the sole case report of
suspected carcinoid syndrome in a dog, tumor removal resulted in
improvement or resolution of the dog’s clinical signs.39 Serum
concentrations of 5-HT and other vasoactive substances may be
measured to confirm suspected carcinoid in people but these tests have
not been performed in animals. Histologic examination of tumor tissue is
required to confirm the diagnosis.

PANCREATIC POLYPEPTIDOMA
Pancreatic polypeptidoma is a poorly understood neuroendocrine tumor
that occurs as part of the multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndrome
in humans but can also occur sporadically as an isolated cancer.
Pancreatic polypeptidoma has been reported in the dog.24 Many
functional neuroendocrine tumors of pancreatic islet origin stain
positively for several peptide hormones, including pancreatic
polypeptide (PP). Thus, pancreatic polypeptidoma is only suspected
when PP is the principal protein hormone expressed. Excess PP secretion
causes few clinical signs and most pancreatic polypeptidomas are
considered non-functional.40 A minority of human pancreatic
polypeptidomas has been suspected of producing clinical signs related to

excess release of PP. Signs reported with PP excess include abdominal
pain and diarrhea. Some have had pancreatitis. In a dog, increased
plasma PP concentrations were associated with chronic vomiting,
duodenal ulcers, and evidence of hypertrophic gastritis. The dog also had
a pancreatic adenocarcinoma, which stained positively for PP and insulin
but not other peptides typically produced by canine pancreatic
neuroendocrine tumors (gastrin, glucagon, or somatostatin).24

DEFINITIONS

Pheochromocytoma (PCC) is a neuroendocrine neoplasm arising
from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal gland medulla. Non-adrenal
chromaffin cell tumors in sympathetic and parasympathetic
paraganglia are “paragangliomas” (PGLs).1 Chromaffin cells are
modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons devoid of axons and
dendrites which arise from neural crest cells within the autonomic
nervous system in the early stages of prenatal development.
PCC accounts for approximately 0.01-0.1% of all canine tumors,
but many PCCs are undiagnosed due to nonspecific and often
episodic clinical signs which leave the diagnosis not considered.
Necropsies are not often performed.2

TUMOR SIZE, INVASIVE NATURE,
METASTASES
PCCs have an average diameter of 5 cm (up to 15 cm) at diagnosis
and >90% are unilateral. Local invasion and metastases are reported
in 66% and 20% of dogs with PCC, respectively. Invasion into the
caudal vena cava has a frequency of up to 56%, usually with rightsided PCC.3 Invasion of the vena cava causing thrombosis may be
preceded by invasion of the phrenicoabdominal vein. Right atrial
thrombosis and aortic thromboembolism (ch. 238) have been
described in association with PCC in 1 and 2 dogs, respectively.4-6
There appears to be no association between tumor size and vascular
invasion. Canine PCCs have metastasized to many organs, including
the regional lymph nodes, liver, spleen, kidneys, pancreas, lungs,
heart, bones, and central nervous system (CNS).

PHYSIOLOGY
Chromaffin cells are the main source of the 3 catecholamines found
in the blood: epinephrine (adrenaline), norepinephrine
(noradrenaline), and dopamine. In chromaffin cells, the tyrosine
hydroxylase enzyme catalyzes the conversion of tyrosine into
dihydroxyphenylalanine, which is decarboxylated into dopamine,
hydroxylated into norepinephrine, which is then converted into

epinephrine via the enzyme phenylethanolamine-Nmethyltransferase (PNMT). This process is also stimulated by
cortisol.7
Catecholamines are stored in intracellular vesicles together with
other substances (e.g., chromogranin-A) and are released
intermittently into the bloodstream after stimulation by sympathetic
preganglionic nerve fibers. The metabolism of catecholamines occurs
mainly in chromaffin cells by monoamine oxidase and catechol-Omethyltransferase enzymes; epinephrine and norepinephrine are
converted into metanephrine and normetanephrine, respectively,
and then into vanillylmandelic acid. Unlike catecholamines,
secretion of metanephrine and normetanephrine (collectively known
as metanephrines) is continuous and stable. Catecholamines and
their metabolites are either free in the circulation or conjugated to
sulphate and are excreted in urine. Catecholamine activity in cells
throughout the body follows their binding to alpha- and betaadrenergic receptors located in cell membranes. Catecholamines
increase heart rate and contractility, raise blood pressure, decrease
gastrointestinal motility, and increase blood glucose and fatty acid
concentrations.1 This biological pathway is shared by normal and
neoplastic adrenal medullary cells. However, adrenal medullary
tumor secretion of catecholamines is not mediated by nerve impulses
and occurs autonomously by diffusion. Healthy chromaffin cells
preferentially secrete epinephrine, but human PCCs predominantly
secrete norepinephrine (alone or with epinephrine), and rarely only
epinephrine or dopamine. From studies on urinary catecholamines
and metanephrines, it seems likely that canine PCCs also
predominantly secrete norepinephrine.7

PATHOGENESIS
Approximately 70% of human PCC and PGL are associated with an
inherited or acquired genetic syndrome: 40% have germline
mutations and 30% somatic mutations. More than 20 susceptibility
genes have been identified in various functional classes, including
kinase signaling regulators (e.g., RET, NF1, and TMEM127),
constituents of the cellular response to hypoxia (e.g., VHL), and

components of energy metabolism (e.g., SDH, especially SDHB and
SDHD).8 Tumor behavior varies substantially depending on the gene
carrying the mutation. A mutation in the RET, NF1, and TMEM127
genes is associated with high expression of the PNMT enzyme and a
low rate of malignancy. A mutation in VHL has a greater risk of
malignancy if it causes deficiencies in SDH and PNMT. Highest risk
of malignancy is associated with a mutation in the SDH gene.
Human PCC and PGL are recognized components of multiple
endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes in which several endocrine
tumors coexist or subsequently develop in autosomal dominant
inheritance.9
In dogs and cats, the pathogenesis of PCC and PGL has been
investigated in 2 studies. A germline or somatic mutation in the SDH
gene (i.e., in SDHB, p. Arg38Gln, and in SDHD, p. Lys122Arg) was
identified with high frequency in both series of dogs with PCC or
PGL. Thus, dogs may share some of the genomic alterations seen in
human PCCs, suggesting common interspecies pathways.10,11 A total
of 8 dogs with multiple PCC and/or PGL have been identified to date,
but no genetic screening has been performed and it is not known if
they share specific germline mutations.2 The same inherited MEN
syndromes described in humans have not yet been documented in
dogs.

SIGNALMENT, HISTORY, PHYSICAL
EXAMINATION
SIGNALMENT AND INCIDENCE
No breed, sex, or age predisposition has been identified in dogs with
PCC. While PCC has been described in dogs 2 to 18 years of age, it is
most common in middle-aged and old dogs.12-14

CLINICAL SIGNS
Episodic Signs

The most common signs of PCC are caused by excess circulating
catecholamines. Since expression of adrenoreceptors is ubiquitous,
excess catecholamines impact multiple organs and create varied
signs. Importantly, catecholamine secretion from PCC is episodic
and unpredictable with signs noted as often as several times a day or
at intervals of weeks or months. Most dogs with PCC have
paroxysmal episodes and are healthy between episodes. At the time
of physical examination, clinical signs are rarely present. Their
severity varies from mild to life-threatening and may progress with
time.1

Nonspecific Signs
In most dogs with PCC, nonspecific clinical signs include lethargy,
anorexia, weight loss, diarrhea, and vomiting. Excess circulating
catecholamines can cause panting, collapse, seizures, and even
sudden death due to a severe arrhythmia; e.g., supraventricular or
ventricular tachycardia. Rarely, bradycardia and atrioventricular
block occur due to myocardial damage, ischemia, and fibrosis caused
by the prolonged exposure to catecholamines. Arterial hypertension
(ch. 236) is reported in 50% of dogs with PCC which can cause
epistaxis, retinal bleeding or detachment, and acute blindness (ch.
13). Seizures are likely due to catecholamine-induced vasospasms
and/or CNS bleeding (chs. 45, 243). Polyuria and polydipsia
(PU/PD) (20% of PCC) could be a result of catecholamine release.
The PU/PD could also be due to a form of a secondary tumorinduced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.2 Less frequently, clinical
signs are caused by tumor size, invasiveness, or rupture.

Signs due to Size, Vessel Occlusion, Distant
Metastasis
Large PCCs have been associated with necrosis, bleeding, and
hemoabdomen. Both size and the invasive nature of PCCs can cause
partial or total occlusion of the caudal vena cava via mural
compression or thrombosis, causing abdominal pain, abdominal
enlargement, ascites, and hind limb edema. Aortic involvement can
cause reduced or absent femoral pulses, cold/painful hind limbs, and
proprioceptive deficits. In dogs with neuromuscular metastases,

para- or tetra-paresis (ch. 43), lameness, seizures (ch. 45), and
other neurologic signs may be seen, depending on location. In
humans, PCC metastases are often norepinephrine-secreting, but
data are not available for dogs. PCC rupture is rare but if it occurs,
can cause life-threatening retroperitoneal hemorrhage.2

Incidentalomas
In 25-50% of dogs with PCC, an adrenal mass is an incidental finding
(“incidentaloma”) during imaging examination for unrelated
problems or at necropsy (ch. 295). PCC is not considered because
most clinical signs can be attributed to more common diseases.
Moreover, about 50% of dogs with PCC have a second endocrine or
nonendocrine tumor. Endocrine neoplasms such as glucocorticoidproducing adrenocortical tumors or adrenocorticotropic hormone
(ACTH)-producing pituitary tumors often coexist with PCC, making
the diagnosis of PCC difficult as clinical signs, laboratory
abnormalities, and imaging results can overlap (ch. 293).1

FIGURE 298.1 Algorithm for diagnosis and
treatment of pheochromocytoma (PCC) in dogs.

DIAGNOSIS
ROUTINE BLOOD AND URINE TEST RESULTS
There are no unique features of PCC on routine blood and urine test
results. If present, laboratory abnormalities are nonspecific and may
not be due to PCC. Abnormalities noted in 25-50% of dogs with PCC
are mild-to-moderate anemia, leukocytosis, increased liver enzyme
activities, azotemia, decreased urine specific gravity, and
proteinuria.12-14

BLOOD AND URINE TESTS SPECIFIC
FOR PCC (FIGURE 298.1)
Overview
Diagnosis of PCC is dependent on results of high-performance liquid
chromatography assays that measure catecholamines or
metanephrines in plasma or urine. In dogs, urinary catecholamines
and metanephrines are expressed as ratios to creatinine
concentration. Generally, assays of metanephrine are preferred
because they are secreted continuously while catecholamines are
secreted episodically. Results of normetanephrine are preferred over
metanephrine due to its higher sensitivity in both plasma and
urine.15,16

Urinary Normetanephrine
Urinary normetanephrine has been the only parameter significantly
higher in dogs with PCC than in both healthy dogs and dogs with
adrenocortical or pituitary tumors. It is also the only test result that
appears unaffected by stresses due to veterinary manipulation during
sample collection.16,17 For both plasma-free and urinary
normetanephrine, using a cut-off value equal to 4 times the upper
limit of the reference range enables PCC to be detected with almost
no overlap with other diseases (excellent specificity), but some cases
would be missed (poor sensitivity). A cut-off value of 2-3 times the
upper limit of normal balances sensitivity and specificity.16 To
ensure the reliability of biochemical test results, samples must be
stored properly, urine acidified to a pH of 2 or less after sampling,
and stored frozen at −20°C (−4°F) until analysis. Plasma and urine
should be delivered to the laboratory on dry ice.

Assay Interference
Some medications can affect the plasma and urinary concentrations
of catecholamines and metanephrines. Specifically,
phenoxybenzamine and dexamethasone can lead to increased levels
and either one may be administered after the detection of an adrenal

mass on imaging, especially phenoxybenzamine for PCC (see below).
In contrast, trilostane used to treat hypercortisolism (ch. 293) does
not cause a significant decrease in the urinary levels of
catecholamines and metanephrines.18

Other Tests
In humans, the clonidine suppression test, measurement of
chromogranin-A in blood, and assay of vanillylmandelic acid in urine
have been used. The urinary vanillylmandelic acid-to-creatinine ratio
has moderate to high sensitivity and specificity in discriminating
dogs with from those without PCC.19 Measurement of serum inhibin
concentration can help differentiate PCC from adrenocortical
tumors, as it is usually undetectable in the former and detectable in
the latter, but only in neutered dogs.20

FIGURE 298.2 Pheochromocytoma of the right
adrenal gland in a dog; the mass invades the caudal
vena cava. Three-dimensional computed tomography
reconstruction. (Courtesy Dr. Edoardo Auriemma.)

IMAGING
Useful Imaging Modalities
Ultrasonography (US), computed tomography (CT), and magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) are useful for assessing tumor location,
shape, size, boundaries, architecture, and invasion into extra-adrenal
structures, as well as for defining prognosis and planning
adrenalectomy. Imaging may follow clinical suspicion and positive
biochemical tests, but often accidental visualization of an abnormal
adrenal gland is the first indicator of PCC.

Radiography
Radiographs are of limited use in diagnosing canine PCC mainly
because of low sensitivity in detecting small-to-medium sized masses
and low yield in identifying tumor invasiveness. Abdominal
radiographs may reveal a perirenal mass of soft-tissue opacity or a
partially calcified mass with or without displacement of adjacent
structures. Evidence of renal distortion, caudal vena cava
enlargement, ascites, or retroperitoneal hemorrhage is possible.
Thoracic radiographs are used to detect pulmonary metastases and
other abnormalities that can result from PCC, such as generalized
cardiomegaly.1

Ultrasonography (US)
US is widely available, does not require anesthesia, and enables good
visualization of small masses and/or tissue invasion in the region of
the adrenal glands. Credibility of an US examination is correlated to
the skill of the operator and the facilities available. PCC can appear
as a nodule or a mass: hypoechoic, isoechoic, or hyperechoic with
respect to the kidney, homogeneous or heterogeneous in
echogenicity, solid to cystic in consistency, and with or without a
change in the shape of the adrenal gland. Small tumors tend to be
solid and relatively homogeneous, whereas larger tumors often
appear to have foci of necrosis or hemorrhage causing a
heterogeneous echogenicity (see Figures 295.1 and 295.2).21,22
US has 80% sensitivity and 90% specificity for detecting a thrombus
within the vena cava, but phrenicoabdominal vein invasion by a PCC
is likely to be missed.23

Computed Tomography (CT) and Magnetic
Resonance Imaging (MRI)
Contrast-enhanced CT is usually the preferred imaging technique for
studying canine PCC and is superior to US for defining tumor shape,
size, architecture, and in detecting vascular invasion (even in smaller
vessels, such as the phrenicoabdominal vein), for which 92%
sensitivity and 100% specificity have been reported (Figure 298.2,

Figure 295.3, and

Video 298.1). In vascular occlusions, CT may

differentiate tumor thrombus, blood clot, and mural
compression.24,25 PCC is found in the mid-dorsal abdomen as a
mass of soft tissue, with irregular margins, a heterogeneous
appearance, and multiple foci of low attenuation in hyperdense
tissue.21 No complications from contrast media have been described
in dogs. Nonionic media are preferable, as several episodes of
hypertensive crisis due to catecholamine release following
administration of ionic media have occurred in humans.26 The
combination of abdominal and thoracic scans can be helpful in
finding metastases. MRI is particularly useful for defining vascular
invasion. PCC usually appears isointense or slightly hypointense in
T1, and slightly or markedly hyperintense in T2 compared to the
normal adrenal gland, due to high vascularization and low lipid
content. Any hemorrhagic, cystic, necrotic, or calcified changes result
in greater image heterogeneity.27

Imaging Limitations
No imaging modality has consistently discriminated PCC from other
adrenal masses. Dogs with unilateral PCC usually have a normal
appearing contralateral adrenal. Glucocorticoid-producing
adrenocortical tumors suppress ACTH, resulting in contralateral
adrenal atrophy (ch. 293). Mineralization is rare in PCC while about
50% of adrenocortical tumors are mineralized. Contrast-enhanced
US (CEUS) has 90% accuracy in differentiating cortical from
medullary adrenal tumors. However CEUS has yet to be studied in
large groups of dogs.28,29 Functional imaging may revolutionize the
diagnosis of PCC by defining the hormones produced by a tumor and
confirming the source of increased catecholamine production.
123
Iodine-metaiodobenzylguanidine scintigraphy and 18Ffluorobenzylguanidine positron emission tomography have been
performed in 4 dogs with suspected PCC, demonstrating 100%
sensitivity and specificity.30,31

CYTOLOGIC EXAMINATION
Canine PCCs have cytopathologic features of a neuroendocrine
tumor: cells arranged in epithelial-like aggregates, bare nuclei with
inconsistent nucleoli, and cytoplasm with fine chromatin granules.
Cytologic evaluation is 90-100% accurate in identifying PCC as a
neuroendocrine tumor, but cannot predict biological behavior (ch.
85).32 While cytology can be valuable in evaluating adrenal masses,
if PCC has not been ruled out caution is required. In humans,
percutaneous fine-needle aspiration (FNA) or biopsy of a
catecholamine-secreting neoplasm is contraindicated because as
many as 70% of these procedures have caused serious complications:
hemorrhage, hypertensive crisis, tumor seeding, and/or death.33
FNAs of canine PCC have had complication rates of about 10%,
including mild-to-moderate hemorrhage, ventricular tachycardia in 1
dog with pericardial effusion and episodes of tachycardia before
sampling, and death from acute respiratory distress syndrome the
day after sampling in 1 dog with laryngeal paralysis.34,35 Serious
complications were more likely in dogs with severe concurrent
diseases rather than being triggered by the sampling procedure.
However, studies on a larger number of dogs with PCC are needed.

BLOOD PRESSURE MEASUREMENT
AND OTHER INVESTIGATIONS
Given the multiple effects of catecholamines on the cardiovascular
system, cardiac US, Holter-monitored electrocardiogram, and (ch.
96), blood pressure measurement (ch. 91) should be considered in
dogs with PCC to assess for cardiomegaly, arrhythmias, and/or
hypertension. Neurologic examination can assess for deleterious
effects of excess circulating catecholamines and/or CNS metastasis
(ch. 241). Fundic examination is particularly useful for identifying
retinal damage (ch. 13).

TREATMENT

ADRENALECTOMY
Benefit vs Risk
Adrenalectomy is the only definitive treatment for PCC, permanently
eliminating the source of excess catecholamines and resolving
clinical signs. However, some PCCs are malignant and metastasis
may precede diagnosis. Surgery should be performed as soon as
possible to minimize risks of metastasis or tumor rupture. With
anesthesia, intubation, surgical incision, and tumor manipulation,
life-threatening catecholamine-induced complications can develop,
including hypertension, tachycardia, arrhythmias, and hemorrhage.
Significant hypotension can follow tumor removal due to the sudden
decrease in catecholamine levels.1 Utmost attention must be paid to
all vital parameters by the surgeon, anesthetist, and the intensive
care team throughout the perioperative period to improve chances of
a successful outcome.

Laparotomy vs Laparoscopy
Adrenalectomy can be performed by laparotomy or laparoscopy.
Choice of procedure depends on tumor size, invasiveness, and the
preference of the surgeon. Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is performed
more frequently in dogs with a small to medium-sized PCC without
invasion of the caudal vena cava or adhesions to surrounding tissues.
Laparoscopy requires less time than surgery, shorter hospitalization
periods, fewer wound complications, and better postoperative
recovery. Sternal positioning improves access and visibility of PCCs,
further reducing surgical time.36 Laparotomy can be performed via
celiotomy or flank incision. If the caudal vena cava is invaded,
experienced surgeons can perform thrombectomy and
adrenalectomy without significantly increased risk.23,37

Preoperative Phenoxybenzamine
Stabilization before adrenalectomy reduces risk of intraoperative and
postoperative complications. In humans, alpha-adrenergic receptor
blockade is initiated at least 2 weeks prior to surgery using a selective
alpha-1 blocker or a non-selective blocker, e.g., phenoxybenzamine.
Phenoxybenzamine may improve perioperative survival for dogs with

PCC.38 One study on dogs undergoing surgery for PCC found that
phenoxybenzamine-treated dogs were 6 times more likely to survive
than untreated dogs,39 but another study questioned the value of
phenoxybenzamine in decreasing the perioperative mortality rate by
reporting a number of dogs in which the short-term perioperative
outcome was favorable despite the absence of preoperative
treatment.40 However, based on humans and current knowledge
regarding phenoxybenzamine pharmacology in dogs, treatment prior
to adrenalectomy is recommended.
Phenoxybenzamine is a noncompetitive, nonselective, long-acting
alpha-adrenergic blocker which covalently binds to alpha-1 and
alpha-2 adrenoreceptors, inhibiting their activity. It blocks the
alpha-adrenergic response to circulating epinephrine and
norepinephrine.38 Dose titration is needed to reduce side-effects,
e.g., hypotension (manifesting as lethargy, inappetence, vague signs
of ill thrift [ch. 10]), vomiting, and tachycardia. Treatment is
initiated at 0.25 mg/kg PO q12h, gradually increasing every 2-3 days,
until reaching 1-1.5 mg/kg PO q12h. Treatment in both hypertensive
and normotensive dogs should continue for 10-14 days before
surgery. Ideally, dose is adjusted until blood pressure is within a
desired range, but this is rarely feasible due to side-effects. Owners
should be informed about side-effects. If owners see side-effects,
they should stop giving the medication and promptly contact their
veterinarian.

Additional Medications
If catecholamine-induced complications persist after several days of
phenoxybenzamine treatment, adding a beta-adrenergic blocker,
preferably a selective beta-1 blocker (e.g., atenolol) rather than a
non-selective blocker (e.g., propranolol), can help with preoperative
stabilization. Concurrent treatment with a calcium-channel blocker
(e.g., amlodipine, ch. 236) may improve tolerability as lower doses
of phenoxybenzamine would be needed, but this attribute
demonstrated in humans has not been assessed in dogs.1

Postoperative Monitoring

General anesthesia, needed for adrenalectomy, can lead to
intraoperative complications, e.g., hypertensive crises and
arrhythmias.23,37 Continuous electrocardiogram and blood pressure
monitoring throughout the procedure and for 48 hours after can be
lifesaving if worrisome changes are managed.

MEDICAL MANAGEMENT
Surgery for PCC is not always possible due to its size, invasiveness, or
metastases. Severe concurrent disease or owners who decline surgery
also can negate the surgical option. Long-term treatment with an
alpha-adrenergic blocker is recommended for these dogs together
with monitoring clinical signs, heart rate, and blood pressure. If an
alpha-adrenergic blocker alone is not sufficient, adding a calciumchannel blocker or a beta-adrenergic blocker may help control
hypertension and tachycardia. Phenoxybenzamine is the most widely
used drug for the chronic medical management of canine PCC.38

Alternative Therapies
There are no studies on the use of chemotherapy in dogs with PCC. A
few chemotherapeutic agents have been used in humans, including
temozolomide, and a combination of cyclophosphamide, vincristine,
and dacarbazine, but with little success. Treatment with sunitinib
(i.e., an inhibitor of tyrosine kinase) or metyrosine (i.e., an inhibitor
of tyrosine hydroxylase) do not slow tumor progression or reduce
clinical signs.41 Recently, toceranib (i.e., a twin compound of
sunitinib) was used off-label in a small number of dogs with
confirmed or suspected PCC; however, the study failed to clarify its
benefits.42 Radiotherapy with 123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine in
humans usually leads to only partial remission; this treatment was
given to 1 dog and resulted in clinical stability for 5 months.43
Neither chemotherapy or radiotherapy requires general or long
periods of anesthesia. Neither involves tumor manipulation, but
studies on their use have failed to demonstrate effectiveness.
Compared to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, adrenalectomy

enables a more rapid and radical intervention which helps to avoid
metastasis and tumor rupture.

HISTOPATHOLOGY
Definitive diagnosis of PCC is achieved only by histopathologic
evaluation of tissue with immunohistochemial stains. On histologic
examination, cells are typically large, round to polygonal, with a
nested, trabecular, or solid arrangement. Nuclei are round to oval
with possible pleomorphism, and nucleoli are prominent. Cytoplasm
has pigmented granules and occasional vacuoles.44 PCCs will be
positive with several neuroendocrine markers: synaptophysin,
inhibin, neuron-specific enolase, protein gene product 9.5, and
chromogranin-A. Chromogranin-A is used for diagnosing canine
PCC and differentiating it from adrenocortical tumors, although
sufficient secretory granules are required to show
immunopositivity.45
In humans, increased proliferation rate assessed by Ki-67;
increased expression of COX-2, p53, BCL-2, c-erbB-2, and VEGF;
and the decreased expression of S100 seem to be associated with a
worse prognosis. The multiparameter scoring system
“Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal gland Scaled Score (PASS)” can
be used to help differentiate benign from malignant PCC based on
tumor invasiveness, histologic growth patterns, cytologic features,
and mitotic activity.46 However, these immunohistochemical
markers and PASS are not able to predict survival or invasiveness of
canine PCC. The definition of malignancy in dogs with PCC is based
on the presence of local invasion and distant metastasis.47 In
humans, the World Health Organization suggests considering only
distant metastasis for the definition of malignant PCC.

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis of canine PCC is mainly related to the tumor size,
secretory activity, and invasiveness. If left untreated, PCC can
progress to life-threatening complications from excess

catecholamines, tumor invasion into surrounding structures,
metastasis, or tumor rupture. Factors such as age, general condition
of the patient, and presence of serious concurrent diseases worsen
the prognosis.1 Adrenalectomy is the treatment of choice. The lack of
intraoperative arrhythmias and the short duration of surgery
significantly improve perioperative survival. In contrast, tumor
location, duration of anesthesia, and perioperative hypertension do
not seem to affect survival.39 Right-sided tumors may be more
difficult to remove due to their proximity and greater likelihood of
invading the vena cava, but no significant differences in
postoperative survival have been reported between right- and leftsided tumors.39,48 It is not yet clear whether tumor size, vascular
invasion, and/or hemorrhage have definite prognostic significance,
as study results are conflicting.3,23,37,39,48,49 These factors may
affect perioperative, but not long-term survival.3 In general, if the
PCC is removable and there is no evidence of metastases or other
concurrent diseases, and perioperative complications are avoided,
long-term survival from months to several years can be expected.
Dogs undergoing chronic medical treatment with phenoxybenzamine
without adrenalectomy can live for more than a year after diagnosis.1

FELINE PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA
PCC appears to be extremely rare in cats. To date, only 6 confirmed
and 2 suspected cases have been described, and PCC accounts for
less than 10% of all feline adrenal neoplasms.50-55 There is currently
only information on clinical signs and laboratory abnormalities for 3
cats with confirmed PCC, all of which were Domestic Shorthaired (2
males, 1 female; aged 7, 11, and 15 years). Nonspecific and vague
clinical signs are comparable to those reported in dogs.50-52 To date,
only 1 study has investigated the diagnostic utility of metanephrines
in feline PCC. Circulating free normetanephrine, but not
metanephrine, was found to be markedly higher in the cat with
suspected PCC compared to healthy cats and cats with nonadrenal
diseases. Although histologic examination was consistent with a

neuroendocrine tumor, there was no definitive diagnosis of PCC. The
cat with suspected PCC did not undergo a full endocrine workup to
rule out other adrenal tumors.53 Based on US examination, the
tumor had a maximum diameter ranging from 8 to 22 mm, was
normal to hypoechoic, and had heterogeneous echogenicity.50-52 No
tumor thrombosis has been reported in association with PCC in cats.
Adrenalectomy is the treatment of choice, but no detailed
information on perioperative management is currently available.

PARAGANGLIOMA (PGL)
PGL is a tumor arising from extra-adrenal chromaffin cells in
sympathetic and parasympathetic paraganglia and accounts for
approximately 0.2% of all canine tumors. Age at diagnosis ranges
from 2 to 12 years with no sex or breed predisposition aside from the
suggestion of a link between chronic hypoxia and high incidence of
PGL in brachycephalic breeds (ch. 235).2 Feline PGL is extremely
rare.56 PGL can develop in many regions of the body, including the
head, neck, and abdomen. Sympathetic PGL has only been described
in a few dogs, and has mainly been found in the posterior
mediastinum, abdomen, and pelvis. Parasympathetic PGL (also
called glomus tumor, chemoreceptor tumor, or chemodectoma) is
more common and usually arises from the aortic or carotid body.1
Unlike PCC, PGL can present with clinical signs resulting from mass
effect, local invasion, and metastasis, but not from excess
catecholamines. Sympathetic PGL is known in humans to be active in
norepinephrine secretion but clinically silent. No endocrine activity
has yet been demonstrated in dogs. Parasympathetic PGL is both
biochemically and clinically silent, possibly due to the lack of
tyrosine hydroxylase. Clinical signs such as dysphagia, dyspnea,
circulatory disturbances, and neurologic deficits (e.g., Horner’s
syndrome, paresis, paralysis) may be observed depending on the
location and invasiveness of the tumor. Canine PGL is generally
larger at diagnosis than PCC, with an average diameter of 6 cm (up to
16 cm). Local invasion and metastasis have been found in 56% and
18% of dogs with PGL, respectively.2

KIDNEY FUNCTION IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
HEALTHY KIDNEY FUNCTION
The function of the kidneys is to regulate the volume and composition of extracellular fluid by forming
urine. Urine is the result of nephrons creating an ultrafiltrate of plasma across the glomerular filtration
barrier that includes solutes, small proteins, and other non-cellular constituents of the blood. The
volume of ultrafiltrate formed is primarily determined by the number of functioning nephrons but is
also affected by the hydrostatic pressure within the glomerular capillary tuft. Following filtration, the
composition of this fluid is altered by the secretion and reabsorption of solutes and water as it passes
along the nephron. In a healthy animal, under normal physiological conditions, less than 1% of the fluid
that is filtered by the glomerulus is eventually excreted as urine.

KIDNEY FUNCTION IN DISEASE
Most commonly, kidney disease is diagnosed when glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is decreased (usually
recognized as azotemia) due to chronic kidney disease (CKD) or acute kidney injury (AKI) (chs. 300 and
301). Kidney disease may also be diagnosed in pets with proteinuria caused by a damaged glomerular
filtration barrier (ch. 302). Renal tubular defects may alter urine (and plasma) composition (ch. 303)
or cause urolithiasis (chs. 308 and 309). The kidney also has vital endocrine functions and is integral in
maintaining blood pressure (ch. 236).

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH TO KIDNEY DISEASE
HISTORY
Investigation of a dog or cat for renal disease is often initiated by owner concerns of polyuria/polydipsia
(PU/PD; ch. 53), uremia, abnormal renal palpation, edema (ch. 30), or ascites (ch. 21). Less
commonly, kidney disease may be suspected only after performing routine “wellness” blood work and
urinalysis (UA) or in a pet with nonspecific signs, e.g., depression and anorexia. Polydipsia (PD) has
been defined as water intake >100 mL/kg/day in dogs (and perhaps half this amount in cats). Even if
this threshold is not exceeded, observed increase in thirst may be significant. The volume of urine
produced is rarely quantified precisely, although some owners notice that the urine appears more clear
or dilute. It is important to differentiate polyuria (PU) from pollakiuria (with small volume), dysuria, or
urinary incontinence, which are generally problems of the lower urinary tract rather than the kidneys
(chs. 53, 54). It is also quite common for disease in the lower and upper urinary tracts to co-exist, e.g.,
PU worsens urinary incontinence, pyelonephritis usually results from ascending urinary tract infection
(UTI), and obstructive lesions may cause postrenal azotemia. Azotemic CKD may cause nonspecific
signs, e.g., poor appetite and/or weight loss. Ocular signs of hypertension (hyphema, mydriasis,
blindness; ch. 13) are more common in cats with CKD than dogs, even though prevalence is
comparable.1,2 Dogs and cats with AKI often have a history of recent nonspecific signs (lethargy,
inappetence; ch. 300). Occasionally pets with AKI have a history of known toxin ingestion or of being
given prescribed, potentially nephrotoxic, medications (ch. 135).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (PE)
A complete PE should be performed in any pet with kidney disease (ch. 3). The kidneys should be
assessed for size, contour, and evidence of pain on palpation. The kidneys of cats are easily palpated but
in dogs they are often difficult to identify conclusively. The size of the bladder may be important: a large
bladder in a pet that urinated recently suggests PU, bladder turgidity may indicate obstruction, and an
empty bladder in a pet that has not urinated may indicate oliguria. Hydration status can be abnormal in

pets with renal disease. Dehydration and/or hypovolemia can follow PU or contribute to development of
AKI. Edema and/or ascites are features of the nephrotic syndrome but can also develop with
overhydration in oligo-anuric dogs and cats (chs. 21, 30, 120). Cats are particularly vulnerable to
developing pleural effusion and dyspnea (ch. 37) with overhydration.
Pets with CKD may be in poor body condition. When CKD occurs in young growing animals,
deformity of the maxilla and mandible (“rubber jaw” due to fibrous osteodystrophy;

Video 162.1)

can occur, although this is uncommon. Older animals occasionally suffer pathological fractures due to
CKD-mineral and bone disorder (MBD). Mucous membranes may be pale in CKD due to anemia.
Uremic ulceration of the oral mucosa (Figure 299.1) and tongue tip necrosis can be present if azotemia
is severe but does not differentiate between acute and chronic disease.

BLOOD PRESSURE, FUNDIC EXAMINATION
Blood pressure should be measured in all pets with kidney disease (ch. 91). Fundic examination should
also be performed, particularly when systolic pressure is >160 mm Hg (ch. 13).

DIFFERENTIATING ACUTE FROM CHRONIC DISEASE
Definitions and Common Features
It is vital to differentiate pets with CKD from those with AKI. Pets with AKI may recover (ch. 300)
whereas CKD is an irreversible condition present ≥3 months. Despite permanent loss of functioning
nephrons in CKD, remaining nephrons may hypertrophy and hyper-filtrate circulating blood.
Differentiating acute from chronic disease is usually based on history and PE: longstanding history of
PU/PD, weight loss due to poor appetite, poor body condition, and poor coat quality are common
features of CKD. These features are not invariable and may have other causes. Kidney size and shape
may provide valuable clues to whether the azotemia is acute (normal or enlarged size, normal shape,
occasionally abnormal turgid feeling, evidence of pain) or chronic (small and/or irregular in shape),
especially in cats. Diagnostic imaging can provide further information permitting objective assessment
of renal size and contour, together with evaluation for mineralization and loss of internal architecture,
consistent with chronicity.

FIGURE 299.1 Uremic ulcers at the labial commissure in a cat with acute
kidney injury (AKI). These ulcers healed when the cat’s azotemia, which
occurred as a result of lily ingestion, improved. Courtesy Helen Wilson.

Routine Blood and Urine Testing
Nonregenerative anemia may be present in CKD (ch. 172) but anemia may also occur in pets with AKI,
e.g., with overhydration (ch. 120), leptospirosis (ch. 192), or hypoadrenocorticism (ch. 296).
Hemorrhage or hemolysis can cause hypoxia/hypotension, which may serve as an inciting cause for AKI.
Anemia is not always caused by chronic disease, particularly regenerative anemias (chs. 57, 174).
Hyperkalemia is most often associated with AKI and particularly with postrenal causes of azotemia.
Hyperkalemia may, however, develop in dogs with CKD fed “renal diets” especially if they are
concurrently treated with angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor
blockers.3
Complete UA is mandatory when investigating azotemia in a dog or cat. UA results may provide
valuable clues (ch. 70), e.g., pyuria, bacteriuria, and white cell casts are consistent with pyelonephritis;
calcium oxalate monohydrate crystals suggest ethylene glycol poisoning; euglycemic glucosuria indicates
proximal tubular dysfunction. Pyelonephritis and proximal tubular dysfunction can be either acute or
chronic. Large numbers of granular casts, and renal epithelial tubular cell casts, are indicative of acute
tubular necrosis.

Imaging
Uncommonly, discriminating acute from chronic disease remains unclear after reviewing routine blood
and urine test results. In this situation, radiographs of the mandible/maxilla evaluating for loss of the
lamina dura,4 ultrasound (US) examination of the parathyroid glands to detect hypertrophy consistent
with chronicity,5 and in theory, measurement of carbamylated hemoglobin (reflective of prevailing urea
concentration; not commercially available) may be useful.6 Renal biopsy is also occasionally used to
differentiate acute and chronic disease.

DIFFERENTIATING PRERENAL, RENAL, AND POSTRENAL
AZOTEMIA
Renal vs Prerenal Azotemia
Discriminating prerenal from renal causes of azotemia can be aided by measuring the urine specific
gravity (USG; chs. 62 and 70). If the USG is >1.030 in dogs or >1.035 in cats, azotemia is usually
prerenal in origin, with certain caveats. Some cats with CKD retain urine concentrating ability (>1.0351.040) despite azotemia.7 Azotemic dogs and cats with primary glomerular disease may also retain
concentrating ability. Conversely, pets with prerenal azotemia are only able to concentrate urine if
tubular/collecting duct mechanisms are intact. If there is minimal medullary hypertonicity,
concentrated urine cannot be produced, e.g., hyponatremia in hypoadrenocorticism, consuming a very
protein-restricted diet, interference with tubular or collecting duct function (diuretics, primary or
secondary diabetes insipidus; chs. 53 and 282). Prerenal azotemia is confirmed by administering
intravenous (IV) fluids (or reducing the dose of diuretics) and documenting the resolution or
improvement in azotemia.

Postrenal Azotemia
Postrenal azotemia is usually suspected from the history and PE, with signs referable to lower urinary
tract obstruction or rupture (chs. 54 and 127). Diagnostic imaging may be required to diagnose partial
or unilateral ureteral obstructions. If fluid is present in either the retroperitoneal or peritoneal cavity, a
sample should be collected for analysis (ch. 85); creatinine concentration greater than twice that in the
blood is consistent with urinary tract rupture. Since urine is a chemical irritant, nonseptic neutrophilic
inflammation is common but the amount of associated hemorrhage and inflammation is variable.8

ASSESSING DISEASE SEVERITY
The International Renal Interest Society (IRIS) has developed a staging scheme for CKD and a grading
scheme for AKI, which are widely used (chs. 300 and 301).

LABORATORY DIAGNOSTICS OF KIDNEY FUNCTION
GLOMERULAR FILTRATION RATE (GFR)
Key Factors and Indications

Direct assessment of GFR is the gold standard for assessing filtration and excretion kidney functions.9,10
Global GFR is the sum total of single nephron GFRs from both kidneys. Key factors determining GFR
include oncotic and hydrostatic pressures of plasma and ultrafiltrate within Bowman’s space together
with the capillary surface area for filtration and permeability. The result is the “ultrafiltration
coefficient” (Box 299.1). Markers of GFR have key characteristics: they must be freely filtered, not
circulate bound to plasma proteins, not undergo reabsorption or be secreted by the tubules, and must
not themselves alter GFR or be toxic to the kidneys.
GFR can be beneficial for evaluating renal function in pets suspected to have non-azotemic kidney
disease, screening for incipient renal disease (e.g., breeds with known juvenile or adult onset
nephropathies), or before administration of potentially nephrotoxic medications where dose adjustment
can be made.11,12 There is no reason for GFR assessment in pets with azotemic CKD, where creatinine is
an appropriate marker.
Several methods have been evaluated and validated in both dogs and cats for direct estimation of
GFR.

Renal/Urinary Clearance (R/UC) of Markers
R/UC is the rate at which a filtered substance is cleared from a given volume of plasma by the kidneys
into the urine, providing information about the amount of marker appearing in the urine per unit of
time. Assessment of R/UC requires that the amount of substance, either exogenous or endogenous, is
assayed both in the plasma and in the urine over a given time period (Box 299.2), usually necessitating
urinary catheter placement. Clearance markers include inulin, creatinine (endogenous/exogenous), and
iohexol. Whereas R/UC of inulin has long been considered a gold standard, endogenous/exogenous
creatinine or iohexol are more commonly used.13,14
