Plasma Clearance of Markers

Plasma clearance of a marker is calculated as per Box 299.2. The area under the curve (AUC) is
determined by obtaining the plasma concentration of the marker at multiple timed intervals for a
predetermined duration. Different pharmacokinetic models can be used to determine the AUC
depending on the analyte and sampling frequency (Figure 299.2).15 Analytes include contrast agents
(i.e., iohexol, gadolinium), exogenous creatinine, radioisotopes (i.e., [125I] Na iodohippurate), 51Crethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), and 99mTc-diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid (DTPA). Since
using radioisotopes carries limitations, plasma clearance of creatinine or iohexol are the most commonly
used methodologies in clinical practice. Contrast agents such as iohexol have been associated with AKI
in humans but in dogs this risk is considered to be very low.16

Radioisotope Administration with Scintigraphy
Using DTPA or 51Cr-EDTA,17-19 offers the potential for estimation of individual kidney GFR, useful for
planning partial or complete nephrectomy. Assessment does not provide information on recoverable
GFR, e.g., after relief of obstruction.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) or Computed Tomography (CT)
Radiocontrast agents (iohexol or gadolinium) and advanced imaging have been used to provide both
global and individual kidney estimation of renal uptake, similar to scintigraphy.20,21

Novel Techniques
These include 1) plasma clearance of fluorescent labelled markers, e.g., sinistrin,22 2) transcutaneous
assessment of fluorescent labelled markers,23 and 3) fiberoptic radiometric fluorescence.24

Estimated GFR (eGFR)
In humans, GFR is routinely estimated from plasma creatinine concentration or cystatin C using
equations which include age, sex, race, and measurements of body size that reflect muscle mass.25 To
date only 1 study has attempted to formulate such an equation for cats but the eGFR did not offer
substantial benefit over the use of creatinine alone.26

Reference Values
Before interpretation, GFR measurement, regardless of method, requires standardization to mitigate
effects of body weight, breed, sex, and age. GFR is therefore commonly expressed in terms of body
weight, assuming the relationship between body weight and GFR is linear.27 Although exact values vary
depending on method used, and direct comparisons should only be made between identical methods,
GFR is typically 3.5-4.5 mL/min/kg for dogs and 2.5-3.5 mL/min/kg for cats.

FIGURE 299.2 Models used for calculation of glomerular filtration rate
(GFR) from plasma clearance. A, One-compartment models consider the
patient as a single compartment and assume immediate distribution of the
substance used as the marker of GFR throughout the body and that the marker
is excreted from that compartment only. The plasma concentration of the
chosen marker (dots) is plotted against time. A linear slope is constructed
(dashed line) and area under the slope is calculated by dividing the zero time
intercept (A) by the slope of the exponential (alpha). Clearance of the marker is
determined by dividing the dose of marker by the area under the curve (AUC).
Using this model, the plasma concentration of the marker immediately after
injection exceeds that estimated by the one-compartment model, which may
lead to overestimation of GFR. B, The two-compartment model assumes
that the marker is initially distributed from the vasculature (central
compartment) to the extracellular fluid volume (ECFV; peripheral component).
A subsequent second elimination phase from the body allows slow
redistribution of the marker back to the plasma from the interstitial fluid as the
marker undergoes renal clearance. The log plasma concentration of the chosen
marker (dots) is plotted against time. The AUC is calculated from two straight
lines (dashed lines) representing an initial steep redistribution (alpha) from
plasma to ECFV and the second terminal elimination (renal clearance) phase
(beta). The AUC is calculated using the following equation: [A/alpha + B/beta],
where A and B represent the zero time intercepts of the first (distribution) and
second (elimination) phase, respectively, and alpha and beta represent the slope
of their respective exponentials. Multi-compartmental models are similar
to the two-compartment model except that each component is resolved to a
series of straight lines providing a theoretically more accurate representation of
the AUC but with the limitation that a more frequent sampling protocol would
be required. C, In a non-compartmental model the AUC is calculated by
adding the area of trapezoids defined by the curve. Unlike compartmental
models, a non-compartmental model is free from assumptions regarding the
redistribution and elimination phases. Errors in GFR calculation from this
approach may arise because the terminal phase of elimination from the last
sample to the time of theoretical zero must be estimated and also when early
ending of plasma sampling means that a greater proportion of the curve must be
estimated. D, Slope-intercept technique for estimation of GFR. The
slope-intercept technique can be used for estimation of GFR using a limited
number of samples (red dots) from only the elimination phase. Exclusion of the

distribution phase will lead to an overestimation of GFR (orange triangle) as the
AUC will be underestimated. This overestimation will be proportionally larger
for patients with near normal GFR compared to patients with low GFR as the
distribution phase in such patients contributes to a greater extent of the overall
AUC. A correction formula is applied to adjust for this.

Surrogate Plasma/Serum Markers of Glomerular Filtration Rate
Practical Assessment
For pets, renal function is usually assessed with USG and a surrogate GFR marker, e.g., urea, creatinine,
symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA). The relationship between surrogate markers and GFR is only
valid in pets with steady state renal function. Isolated evaluation of these markers does not determine
whether azotemia is prerenal, renal, or post-renal in origin, or whether it is acute or chronic, nor does it
predict potential for reversibility.

Urea
Urea is produced from ammonia derived from amino acids, originating from either endogenous or
exogenous protein sources, as part of the ornithine cycle within the liver. Urea is filtered at the
glomerulus but undergoes passive reabsorption within the tubules. The degree of reabsorption increases
with slower tubular flow rates, e.g., hypovolemia, dehydration. Plasma/serum urea concentration is
commonly reported as blood urea nitrogen (BUN) in the U.S. and as “urea” elsewhere. Two conversion
steps are required, first from BUN to urea, and then from traditional (mg/dL) to SI (mmol/L) units. A
main limitation of urea is that production and excretion are not constant and can be influenced by
several factors. Fasting for 8-12 hours is recommended to avoid effects of dietary protein. Conditions
associated with increased protein catabolism (e.g., fever, burns, infection, starvation, hyperthyroidism)
and upper gastrointestinal (GI) hemorrhage increase urea.28,29 Conversely, reduced hepatic function,
portosystemic shunting, and low protein diets may reduce urea concentrations.

Creatinine
Creatinine, freely filtered by the glomerulus, is the most widely used surrogate marker of GFR in clinical
practice. It is produced from dehydration of creatine and dephosphorylation of phosphocreatine in
muscle. If muscle mass remains stable, creatinine is produced at a constant daily rate but concentrations
are affected by lean body mass and as such, young animals and those with sarcopenia have
proportionally lower creatinine concentrations than mature or well-muscled individuals.30 Biological
variability occurs with impact of age and breed, e.g., Birman, Greyhounds.31-34 There is no apparent
effect of sex on plasma creatinine in cats or dogs, which is very weakly secreted in renal tubules in dogs,
especially males, but this is of negligible clinical significance.35 Creatinine is less influenced by recent
protein ingestion than urea but testing when fasted (8-12 hours) is recommended.36 Creatinine (and
other surrogate markers) has an exponential relationship with GFR; e.g., when GFR is near normal,
creatinine is less sensitive at indicating change (Figure 299.3).37 Use of creatinine in early renal
disease can be enhanced by serial trending using the same laboratory analyser.38-41

FIGURE 299.3 Creatinine demonstrates an exponential relationship with
glomerular filtration rate (GFR) (purple line) when plotted directly, while the
relationship between the reciprocal of creatinine plotted against GFR
approximates a straight line (inset).

Symmetric Dimethylarginine (SDMA)
SDMA, synthesized by all nucleated cells, is a dimethylated derivative of arginine produced from
intranuclear methylation of L-arginine residues by protein-arginine methyltransferase.42,43 Since it is
primarily excreted via renal filtration, it has characteristics required for an endogenous marker of renal
function. These include an exponential relationship with GFR that is almost identical to that of
creatinine, good correlation with creatinine, and a linear relationship between the reciprocal of SDMA
(1/SDMA) and GFR.40,44,45 SDMA is promoted to have greater sensitivity than other markers for
detecting early renal disease. In some studies, this advantage is less apparent and may result in lower
specificity.40,46-49 It has been incorporated into the IRIS staging system (ch. 301) being particularly
important for identification of IRIS stage 1 and more accurate classification of sarcopenic patients (ch.
151).42,43
A potential advantage of SDMA over creatinine is that it is not influenced by body muscle mass30,46 or
recent food ingestion, although fasting is still recommended.46 Age and breed (e.g., Birman and
Greyhounds) may influence SDMA.40,42,50,51 Certain disease conditions may affect results, e.g., thyroid
status, neoplasia, and diabetes mellitus.52-59 Inexplicably, some cats with normal kidney function have
markedly increased SDMA concentrations.42,59

Cystatin C
Cystatin C, a low molecular weight (LMW) (13 kilodalton [kDa]) protein, acts as a proteinase inhibitor
and is produced at a constant rate, freely filtered, but is reabsorbed and catabolized in the proximal
tubules of nephrons.60,61 It has been proposed as a more sensitive marker of GFR than plasma
creatinine in people.62 Numerous studies have evaluated the potential use of cystatin C in dogs and cats
but to date these have not demonstrated consistent superiority over creatinine and confounding factors
limit its use.49,60,63

PROTEINURIA
Definition and Sources
Proteinuria describes increased protein within the urine. If pre-renal (e.g., Bence Jones proteins) and
postrenal (lower urinary tract inflammation) causes are excluded, proteinuria can be considered renal in
origin. The glomerular filtration barrier limits the passage of medium- and high-molecular-weight
proteins from the blood into the glomerular filtrate, e.g., albumin (69 kDa) and larger proteins are too
large to be filtered. Filtered smaller proteins, in health, are so effectively reabsorbed within the proximal
tubular cells that the amount of proteinuria is normally low. If proteinuria develops after a change in
structure or function of the glomerular filtration barrier, it is “glomerular proteinuria.” If proteinuria
develops due to reduced capacity of the proximal tubular cells to reabsorb proteins, it is “tubular
proteinuria.”

Indications for Diagnostics
Proteinuria should be evaluated in all pets with CKD as part of the IRIS staging scheme (ch. 301).
Proteinuria also may be further investigated if a positive result is obtained on a urine dipstick or if
protein-losing nephropathy (PLN, ch. 302) is a concern.

Methods
Proteinuria is usually first assessed with a colorimetric biochemical reagent urine dipstick (ch. 70).
Dipsticks have reasonable sensitivity (>80%), but poor specificity.64,65 If there is concern about
proteinuria, further assessment with a urine protein to creatinine ratio (UPCR) is warranted.65 The
sulfosalicylic acid (SSA) test can be used as a confirmatory test after dipstick evaluation.64 Albuminuria,
quantified with species-specific enzyme linked immunosorbant assay or electrophoretic methods, is
reported as the urine albumin to creatinine ratio (UACR).66,67 Epidemiological studies have not
documented superiority of UACR to UPCR and use of UACR is largely restricted to research.

Urine Protein to Creatinine Ratio (UPCR)
The most common test for quantifying proteinuria is the UPCR; persistent values >0.4 in cats and >0.5
in dogs are considered abnormal.68 UPCRs >2.0 are strongly suggestive of underlying glomerular
disease although other etiologies cannot be excluded without renal biopsy.69 Spot UPCR correlates well
with 24-hour urine protein quantification.70 Since variation between laboratories can occur, the same
laboratory should be used for serial monitoring.71-73 Method of urine collection (free-catch, mid-stream,
cystocentesis) and type of container have little effect on UPCR. Although not confirmed in all studies,
values from in-hospital obtained samples may be higher.74-79 The impact of hematuria on UPCR results
are variable; some studies suggest no effect unless gross hematuria is identified (>250 red blood cells
[RBCs]/hpf). The effect of pyuria is minimal in most studies, although others suggest there can be an
impact.80,81 Clinical resolution of hematuria and pyuria is preferable prior to UPCR evaluation.
Considerable day-to-day individual variability in UPCR is reported, particularly in proteinuric pets.
UPCR must change by 35% for patients with UPCR ∼12 and by 80% for those with UPCR ∼0.5 for this to
reflect a true change in UPCR rather than day-to-day variability.82 Whereas 1 sample may be sufficient
for dogs with UPCR <4.0, more than 2 samples should be checked when there is marked proteinuria
(UPCR >4.0). They can be averaged to provide a credible assessment of proteinuria.82 Pooling an
equivolume of urine from 3 samples (e.g., collected in a 48-hour period) is a more cost-effective and
comparable way to evaluate proteinuria in pets with UPCR >4.0.83

RENAL BIOPSY (
ASPIRATION (FNA)

Video 299.1) AND FINE-NEEDLE

Indications
Current IRIS guidelines suggest that biopsy be considered for pets with persistent substantial
proteinuria (UPCR >3.5), in pets where proteinuria is unresponsive to anti-proteinuric therapy, or pets
with progressive worsening proteinuria or decline in renal function despite therapy. Biopsy results help
determine if immunosuppressive therapy is indicated (ch. 302). Biopsy does not often identify a cause
for AKI, although it may be useful to indicate if irreparable damage is present.

Contraindications
Contraindications for renal biopsy include IRIS stage 4 CKD, primary tubulointerstitial disease,
evidence of hydronephrosis, pyelonephritis, hemostatic disorders, and/or renal abscessation. There is
little to gain with biopsy results in a pet likely to have either amyloidosis or a hereditary nephropathy
given that, to date, there is no evidence that these dogs or cats will respond to immunosuppressive
agents.

Pre-biopsy Testing
Comprehensive diagnostic investigation should always precede renal biopsy to identify underlying
conditions contributing to proteinuria, e.g., neoplasia or infection, to document that the proteinuria is
persistent, and to ensure that it is renal in origin (ch. 302).68 Key considerations include control of
systemic hypertension (chs. 91 and 236), discontinuing anti-thrombotic therapy at least 72 hours before
the procedure (ch. 171), and assessment of hemostasis (ch. 170). Assessing hemostasis prior to biopsy
should be patient-specific but usually includes a platelet count with consideration for blood typing,
coagulation profile, thromboelastography (TEG, ch. 170), and buccal mucosal bleeding time (ch. 79).

Fine-Needle Aspiration
FNAs are rarely rewarding in pets with glomerular disease, although amyloid fibrils may be identified.
For suspicion of underlying inflammatory, primary, or metastatic neoplastic disease, FNA may be a lowrisk alternative to biopsy. It provides a diagnosis in 78% of canine renal lymphoma cases (ch. 85).84
Further information on procurement of renal biopsies can be obtained from ch. 302.85,86

COAGULATION STATUS IN A DOG OR CAT WITH PROTEINLOSING NEPHROPATHY (PLN)
In a dog or cat with PLN, hypoalbuminemia (ch. 60) is a concern. It is also one of the features of the
“nephrotic syndrome” along with hypercholesterolemia (ch. 63), proteinuria, and either cavitary
effusion (chs. 21, 220) or peripheral edema (ch. 30). Development of a hypercoagulable state (ch. 171)
in pets with glomerular disease was attributed to antithrombin (AT) loss, since AT has a comparable
molecular weight to albumin and can therefore be lost via the urine with PLNs. However, the association
between proteinuria and concentrations of AT is weak. Based on TEG studies, up to 89% of dogs with
PLN are hypercoagulable (chs. 170 and 171), but there is no association with serum albumin, UPCR, or
AT activity.87-89 All dogs and cats with PLN are at risk for thrombotic complications (chs. 219, 238,
302). Pets with AKI (ch. 300) are at risk for thrombosis and/or bleeding disorders.90 Coagulation
status is an integral part of managing any pet receiving extracorporeal therapies for renal disease (ch.
103).

GENETIC TESTING
Several breeds of dogs and cats have genetic mutations causative for renal diseases, including hereditary
nephropathy in Cocker Spaniels, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis in Wheaten Terriers, and various
tubulopathies (e.g., cystinuria, hyperoxaluria and hyperuricosuria) (ch. 305). For some of these
conditions, genetic tests are available from commercial laboratories (chs. 303 and 308).

URINE TESTING (CH. 70)
Indications for Urinalysis (UA)
Comprehensive reviews on performing complete UA include pre-/postanalytical factors that may
influence results and sediment evaluation.91-93 Collection of urine is reviewed in ch. 98. UA is
important for assessing renal function and evaluating for renal disease, particularly in terms of urine
concentrating ability, glomerular and tubular function, and identifying presence of bacteria. UA in all
pets with known or suspected renal disease should include biochemical evaluation (dipstick), USG, and
urine culture or UPCR as indicated.

Osmolality, Isosthenuria, Hyposthenuria
Normally, urine contains predominantly LMW molecules (e.g., electrolytes and urea). Urine osmolality
(Osm/kg), defined as the concentration of osmotically active molecules dissolved in urine, is dependent
only on the number of molecules in solution and is not altered by their molecular size or weight (ch.
70). It is measured using freezing depression point osmometers, based on the principle that each mole
of dissolved solute will depress freezing by 1.86°C. Since the relationship between osmolality and USG is
linear, USG measured by hand-held refractometer is used as an approximation of osmolality (ch. 70).
“Isosthenuria” is the term for USGs 1.008-1.015 (∼urine osmolality 300 mOsm/kg), usually indicating
that the urine has about the same solute concentration as the glomerular filtrate and plasma.
“Hyposthenuria” is defined as a USG <1.008 (UOsm <300 mOsm/kg), which indicates active tubular
dilution. “Hypersthenuria,” an infrequently used term, is a USG >1.015 (UOsm >300 mOsm/kg). Urine
dipsticks are not reliable for assessing USG.94

Urine Specific Gravity (USG)
USG is defined as the ratio of the weight of a volume of liquid to the weight of an equal volume of
distilled water, dependent on the number, size, and weight of the particles in the urine. Feline urine was
thought to have a higher refractive index than human or canine urine and that refractometers designed
for human urine might produce factitiously high results.95 Recent studies, however, indicate that results
from digital and optical analogue refractometers are comparable in dogs and cats.96-98 Proteinuria and
glucosuria have minimal impact on USG, e.g., 1 g/dL (10 g/L) protein (>3+ on dipstick) increases USG
by 0.003-0.005 and 1 g/dL (55 mmol/L) glucose (3+) increases USG by 0.004-0.005.99,100
Exogenously administered substances can have greater impact, e.g., colloids, mannitol and iohexol.

Urine Concentration in Health and in Kidney Disease
Normal urine concentrating ability is achieved from 8 weeks of age in kittens and 4 weeks in puppies.
Dogs and cats with normal renal function have variable USGs (1.015-1.050, dog; 1.030-1.060, cat). In
healthy cats, 91% had USG >1.030 and 88% >1.035 on spot assessments, demonstrating greater
consistency and ability to concentrate than dogs.101 A dog or cat with normal renal function that is
dehydrated or has prerenal azotemia should have maximally concentrated urine (USG >1.030 in dogs,
>1.040 in cats) as part of physiologic conservation of blood volume. For cats and dogs with either AKI or
CKD, identifying sub-maximally concentrated urine together with azotemia supports a renal etiology.
Isosthenuria (USG 1.008-1.012) is seen in health, AKI, and CKD and implies the kidneys are neither
concentrating nor diluting tubular filtrate. Hyposthenuria (USG <1.008) indicates active dilution in the
tubules and, therefore, non-renal causes of PU/PD should be investigated.

Water Deprivation Test (WDT)
The WDT can be used to test tubular response to arginine vasopressin (AVP) in pets with PU/PD after
all causes have been excluded apart from nephrogenic or central diabetes insipidus and psychogenic PD.
Some suggest that the WDT never be performed, due to attendant risks (ch. 282). Any dog or cat that is
azotemic or has a prerenal azotemia and inappropriately dilute urine (USG <1.030) has already failed a
WDT and should never have further water restriction.

MARKERS OF TUBULAR DYSFUNCTION/DAMAGE
Glucose in Urine
Glucosuria is most commonly identified in hyperglycemic dogs and cats after the renal threshold and
tubular maximum for glucose reabsorption has been exceeded (>180 mg/dL, 10 mmol/L in dogs; >280
mg/dL, 15.5 mmol/L in cats; chs. 61 and 70). Glucosuria in a euglycemic dog or cat is indicative of
altered renal tubular function, called renal glucosuria, and can be either a single or complex renal
tubular disorder. In the latter, increased excretion of other molecules (e.g., amino acids, phosphate,
bicarbonate and electrolytes) may occur and the disorder can be either inherited (e.g., Fanconi
syndrome; ch. 305) or acquired (ch. 303).

Fractional Excretion (FE) of Solutes, e.g., Electrolytes
FE is the percent of a filtered solute excreted into urine. Determination of FE requires collection of urine
over a protracted time (∼24 hours) with the dog or cat, ideally, in a metabolic cage or catheterized to
ensure complete urine collection. This can be clinically impractical and spot assessment FE of a solute is
therefore more commonly used. Spot evaluation of FE can be calculated using the following formula:

Non-protein bound electrolytes are freely filtered at the glomerulus and reabsorbed from the tubules.
For conserved solutes (e.g., amino acids and glucose) reabsorption within the proximal tubule is
virtually complete (>99%) such that FE in health is <1%. For solutes such as sodium (Na) and potassium
(K), about two-thirds is reabsorbed from the proximal and distal tubules and loop of Henle regardless of
body requirements. The remaining solute is either excreted or reabsorbed depending on homeostatic
hormonal regulation (e.g., aldosterone). Calcium (Ca) reabsorption (proximal and distal tubules) is
tightly regulated by parathyroid hormone (chs. 69, 283, 284). Phosphorus reabsorption (proximal and
distal tubules) is controlled by the combination of parathyroid hormone and fibroblast growth factor 23
(FGF23)/alpha-Klotho complex (chs. 69, 283, 284). Numerous exogenous and endogenous factors
influence the FE of electrolytes, such as age, breed, food intake, dietary composition, exercise,
ultrafiltration rate, the individual’s solute and volume status, renal function, and drug
administration.102
Calculation of FE of electrolytes from a spot sample is, at best, a crude assessment of 24-hour urinary
excretion of electrolytes. There are inherent inaccuracies when using creatinine as a marker of GFR and
fluctuations in urine electrolyte concentrations are common due to dietary change and circadian
rhythms.102 There are no clearly defined reference intervals for FE of electrolytes, although “normal
values” are reported. FE of electrolytes is rarely used clinically in veterinary medicine due to marked
inter- and intra-patient variability. When quantification of FE of electrolytes is being considered, it has
been suggested that a standardized diet be fed for a minimum of 1 week and that the patient be normally
hydrated for several days.103 FE of most electrolytes increases as GFR decreases, which severely limits
the value of this test in clinical patients with renal dysfunction. Serial evaluation of FE of Na has been
reported as a potential prognostic indicator of AKI outcome.104

Aminoaciduria
When amino acids, which in health are effectively and completely (>99%) reabsorbed by the proximal
tubule cells, are identified in urine, it is due to excess circulating concentrations exceeding the tubular
maximum for reabsorption, due to an intrinsic defect in the tubular resorptive mechanism or a failure of
intracellular processing or transport mechanisms on the basolateral surface of the proximal tubular cell.
Aminoaciduria may be an isolated finding due to a defect in an individual transport protein, e.g.,
cystinuria, although other amino acids may be involved (lysine, glycine, ornithine and arginine) or
hyperuricosuria (ch. 308). It may be part of a complex renal tubular disorder, e.g., Fanconi’s syndrome
or AKI (chs. 303 and 305).

Acid-Base Evaluation and Urine pH
The kidney is intrinsically involved in acid-base homeostasis. Evaluation of acid-base status via blood
gas analysis can be important in managing pets with either CKD (ch. 301) or AKI (ch. 300) where
metabolic acidosis is common. In addition, renal tubular acidosis is a rare group of disorders that leads
to metabolic acidosis where evaluation of both acid-base status and urinary pH are important (chs. 70
and 303).

Urine Sediment: Cells, Bacteria, Crystals, Casts
Excessive numbers of RBCs in the urine is referred to as hematuria (ch. 70). Hematuria originating in
the kidney is associated with nephrolithiasis (ch. 301), pyelonephritis (ch. 304), and is occasionally
idiopathic (ch. 117). RBC casts on UA confirm a renal origin of hematuria. Pyuria refers to the presence
of increased white blood cells (WBCs) in urine (ch. 70). Pyuria cannot be used to determine source:
whether inflammation is in the lower or upper urinary tract (e.g., pyelonephritis) unless WBC casts are
identified (Figure 299.4), or the sample has been obtained by pyelocentesis. Transitional epithelial
cells (ch. 70) are derived from urothelium and are typically smaller with tapered ends (caudate cells)
when originating from the renal pelvis (Figure 299.5) or they may form epithelial cellular casts, which
are indicative of renal injury (Figure 299.6). Bacteria on UA should always be linked to presence or
absence of clinical signs referable either to the upper or the lower urinary tract to differentiate
pyelonephritis (ch. 304) from subclinical bacteriuria or sporadic bacterial cystitis (ch. 307). Bacteria
in urine obtained from the renal pelvis is indicative of pyelonephritis.

Crystalluria is seen with some alterations in tubular function. They may be indicative of stone type in
pets with nephrolithiasis (chs. 70, 301, 308, and 309). Cylindruria implies kidney damage because
casts are typically formed within the ascending limb of the loop of Henle and the collecting duct, where
tubular flow rates are slowest (ch. 70). Rare hyaline or granular casts may be normal in dogs and cats,
but high numbers of cellular casts are always abnormal. Casts can be classified as hyaline, granular,
waxy, fatty, cellular (epithelial, WBC, RBC), may contain crystals and/or microorganisms, or can be
mixed in origin. Rarely, parasitic ova from Stephanurus dentatus, Capillaria plica (Figure 299.7),
Capillaria felis, or Dioctophyma renale may be identified in urine. Microfilariae of Dirofilaria immitis
(ch. 237) may rarely be observed in canine urine sediment.

Biomarkers for Renal Disease (Table 299.1)
Indications
Biomarkers for renal disease may be quantified from plasma/serum, urine, or occasionally
both.38,103,105-109 Those quantified in urine are usually standardized to the volume of urine produced,
and this is usually achieved by expressing the biomarker as a ratio to urine creatinine or USG of 1.010.
Biomarkers hold particular interest for the early identification of CKD where they may permit
identification of declining renal function in advance of increases in traditional renal function markers
(e.g., SDMA, creatinine). Biomarkers may improve our understanding of metabolic derangements,
bringing new targets for therapy. For AKI, biomarkers of cellular injury offer promise for early
identification and treatment. Knowledge of how markers are handled by the kidney (i.e., filtration and
reabsorption versus excretion) and site of synthesis can help localize specific areas of renal damage (i.e.,
glomerular versus tubular).

presenting with clinical signs of pollakiuria. Reproduced by kind permission of
Alice Hughes.

Differentiation of Proteins
Analyzing proteins in urine by molecular weight may provide information about functional change at the
glomerular filtration barrier versus change in tubular resorptive capacity. In glomerular disease,
alteration in the filtration barrier can lead to increased overall protein filtration and increased
concentrations of high molecular weight (HMW) proteins (>100 kDa, e.g., IgG). If tubular resorptive
capacity is overwhelmed, LMW and medium molecular weight proteins (<35 kDa) will be present.
Conversely, when altered renal function is primarily tubular, the distribution of proteins present in the
urine will be predominantly LMW, e.g., retinol binding protein (RBP). Distribution of proteinuria can be
captured by proteomic methodologies such as urine protein electrophoresis or through direct
quantification of specific characteristic proteins where molecular weight is known (Table 299.1).110

Urinary Enzymes
Enzymes are located on the brush border and in intracellular locations within tubular cells. Since
enzymes are usually medium- to high-molecular-weight proteins (>100 kDa), enzyme activity identified
in urine is most likely of renal origin. Knowledge of the location of urinary enzymes within the nephron
and alteration in either urine enzyme concentration or activity can be used to indicate either damage or
an alteration in activity of cells from that region of the tubule (Table 299.1).108,109 Urine gamma
glutamyl transferase (GGT)/creatinine ratio has been used for the monitoring of gentamicin
nephrotoxicosis.111

Proteins of Renal Origin
Proteins can be released or upregulated and detected in urine after tubular or glomerular damage. They
include the tubular markers neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), kidney injury molecule 1
(KIM1),112 clusterin,113-117 and cystatin B (Table 299.1).38,107 Serum/plasma concentrations of some
molecules, including KIM1 and cystatin B, are also being studied.107,115,118 NGAL has received the most
attention but all are only used in research. NGAL, a 25 kDa protein, is expressed by neutrophils and
epithelial cells, specifically the proximal tubular cells (PTCs) within the kidney.119-121 Given the
expression of NGAL by neutrophils, the presence of urinary tract inflammation and/or infection impacts
urinary NGAL concentrations.119,122 As such, urinary NGAL can be considered a marker of either renal
or lower urinary tract disease and the presence of lower urinary tract inflammation and/or infection is a
confounding factor in its interpretation.

Biomarkers of Inflammation, Hypoxia, Fibrosis
Some biomarkers can indicate that pathological processes are active and may be contributing to disease
development or progression (Table 299.1). These include markers of inflammation (e.g., interleukins),
hypoxia (vascular endothelial growth factor [VEGF]), or fibrosis (transforming growth factor-beta [TGFbeta]). Markers may be quantified in blood to indicate their systemic effect while quantification within
the urine may be indicative of a localized pathophysiological response. The ability to link these
inflammatory markers to clinical outcome is important, as they have the potential to indicate both renal
injury and regenerative response.

Biomarkers of Metabolic Abnormalities
Biomarkers can enhance our understanding of the metabolic derangements that may be occurring in
renal disease or injury. For example, serum inosine is produced during deamination of adenosine, a
breakdown product of ATP, in the basolateral membrane of proximal tubular cells by adenosine

deaminase. Rapid reduction in serum concentrations of inosine has been reported to occur during acute
nephrotoxic insult.107 Another example of altered metabolism (altered phosphate homeostasis) would
be increases in FGF23 as an early indicator of non-azotemic CKD (ch. 301).123 Other markers studied
are those which link the microbiome to CKD, e.g., straight versus branched short chain fatty acids.124
Indoxyl sulfate (IS) and p-cresol (pCS) are 2 further colonic-derived uremic toxins which may be
increased with intestinal dysbiosis in association with CKD.124-126 Urinary exosome microRNAs have
been explored recently and hold promise for novel biomarker discovery.127-130

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
RADIOLOGY AND COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY (CT)
Plain radiographs can be used to provide information about renal size, contour, and presence of
radiopaque calculi. Excretory urography (IV urography) may provide additional information about the
renal collecting system (renal pelvis, ureters, ureterovesicular junction), which can be of value when
evaluating a dog or cat suspected of urinary tract obstruction, rupture, or urinary incontinence (chs.
306, 310, and 313). IV urography has largely been replaced by US and CT. CT imaging of the kidneys
may be selected in preference to other imaging modalities when the focus of interest is the renal pelvis
and ureter (usually due to concern for ureteral obstruction or ectopia)131,132 or when a mass is present
in, or close to, the kidney.

ULTRASONOGRAPHY (US)
Kidney Size
US can provide important anatomical information about kidney size, shape, and internal architecture.
Remember that some significantly diseased kidneys can appear completely normal. In dogs, the
relationship between body weight and renal length is not linear, making it difficult to determine if
kidneys are increased or decreased in size.133 Methods for indexing renal length to the aortic
diameter,134 or to the length of vertebral body L5,135 are described but are not widely used. Normal
renal length in cats is about 3.0 to 4.5 cm (5 cm is not usually worrisome).136,137 Diffuse renal
enlargement with relatively normal internal renal architecture may occur with compensatory
hypertrophy, AKI of various causes (ch. 300), amyloidosis (ch. 302), lymphoma (ch. 322),
portosystemic shunts (ch. 267), and acromegaly (chs. 280, 281).138-140 Small kidneys are found with
congenital renal hypoplasia or dysplasia (ch. 305), chronic end-stage renal disease of many etiologies
(ch. 301), and as a sequela of chronic ureteral obstruction (ch. 306).138,141 Renal cortex thickness may
be a better indicator of CKD than total renal dimensions.142

Echogenicity
Kidneys are usually less echogenic than liver or spleen, but echogenicity may vary with the frequency of
the transducer being used. In addition, fat vacuoles in the renal tubular epithelium are thought to
increase the echogenicity of feline kidneys.143 Diffuse increase in cortical echogenicity is a nonspecific
indicator of renal disease and only weakly correlates with histologic findings.144 Lack of
corticomedullary definition is also a nonspecific finding commonly associated with CKD, whatever the
underlying etiology.

Focal Lesions
Usually easy to identify with US, focal lesions include cysts with round to oval contours, echo-free
contents, thin walls, and strong distal acoustic enhancement. Single, simple cysts are usually an
incidental finding. Multiple small cyst-like lesions may be seen throughout the cortex and medulla with
end-stage kidney disease. Multiple small cysts limited to the cortex or cortico-medullary junction may be
seen with familial forms of glomerulocystic disease.145,146 Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney

disease (PKD) is commonly found in Persian and related cat breeds,147 and occasionally in dogs (ch.
305). If cystic lesions have thick or irregular walls, internal septations, or if the contents are not
completely anechoic, then other disorders, such as hematoma, abscess, and tumor should be
considered.138,148,149

Solid Kidney Masses
Solid masses are often neoplastic and may be hypoechoic, isoechoic, or hyperechoic to the surrounding
renal parenchyma, or may have a mixed pattern.84,149,150 The appearance of most solid masses is nonspecific and aspiration cytology or biopsy is required for identification. Granulomas or calcified
hematomas or abscesses are potential differential diagnoses for this type of lesion but are much less
common. An acute renal infarct may initially appear isoechoic or hypoechoic and could be confused with
a mass lesion, but more typically these are diagnosed long after the original insult, resulting in
hyperechoic wedge-shaped lesions that are widest toward the outer surface of the kidney.

Subcapsular or Perirenal Fluid
Fluid surrounding the kidney may be difficult to localize. Small volumes of fluid may be urine, blood,
transudate, or exudate. Such fluid may be seen with urine leakage, AKI, ureteral obstruction, renal
abscessation, hemorrhage or neoplasia.151-153 Presence of a large volume of anechoic fluid is likely to
represent a perinephric pseudocyst which is more common in cats than dogs and usually in cats with
CKD. They may be unilateral or bilateral.154 Hypoechoic subcapsular thickening mimicking fluid
accumulation is a relatively common appearance of renal lymphoma in cats.155

Medullary Rim Sign
Sometimes a distinct hyperechoic line is present parallel to the corticomedullary junction: the so-called
medullary rim sign. The significance of this line has been debated. It may be a normal finding in both
dogs and cats.143,156,157 A diffuse band of hyperechoic tissue within the inner medulla has been reported
in some dogs with acute leptospirosis151 (Figure 299.8; ch. 192).

Pyelectasia
In normal dogs and cats, urine cannot be visualized within the renal pelvis; however, mild pyelectasia
may be visible during diuresis.158 This may be asymmetric. The differential diagnosis for renal pelvic
dilation therefore includes all polyuric renal diseases (ch. 53), as well as obstructive lesions (chs. 117,
306) and possibly pyelonephritis (ch. 304).159 US changes are not always present in dogs or cats with
pyelonephritis; however, changes that have been reported, in addition to pyelectasia, include increased
echogenicity of the medulla and/or renal cortex, and hyperechogenicity of the mucosal lining of the
renal pelvis.138,159 When the reason for pelvic dilatation is uncertain, US-guided percutaneous
antegrade renal pyelography may be useful to identify an obstruction (ch. 306).160-162

FIGURE 299.8 Long-axis sonographic images of kidneys from three different
dogs. A, Hyperechoic outer medulla of a non-azotemic Cocker Spaniel. B,

Pulsed-Wave Doppler Examination
Examination of blood flow in the interlobar or arcuate arteries can be used to measure its velocity and to
calculate the resistive index (RI). RI may increase with many tubulointerstitial renal disorders (acute
and chronic), ureteral obstruction, and renal allograft rejection.163 In clinical practice there are many
limitations to the interpretation of RI since it may also be affected by sedation and non-renal disorders.

DEFINITIONS, PHASES, AND
CATEGORIZING ACUTE KIDNEY
INJURY (AKI)
DEFINITIONS AND THE 4 PHASES
The term “acute renal failure” has been replaced with “acute kidney
injury” (AKI) to better describe the importance of mild-to-moderate
damage that does not result in overt kidney failure, as well as
emphasizing the maintenance and recovery phases of kidney injury.
There are 4 phases of intrinsic AKI: induction, extension,

maintenance, and recovery.1 The induction phase begins with an
ischemic or nephrotoxic insult and continues until a change in renal
function occurs, such as decreased urine output (UOP) or glomerular
filtration rate (GFR). The duration of this phase is variable,
depending on the nature and severity of the insult. During this stage
early intervention may prevent progression; however, clinical signs
are often not apparent, which makes recognition of AKI difficult.
During the extension phase the kidney is further injured via
alterations in renal perfusion, continued hypoxia, secondary
inflammation, and ongoing epithelial and endothelial injury. The
maintenance phase occurs after a critical amount of damage has
been established. The resulting decreased GFR and renal
hypoperfusion manifest as azotemia and clinical signs of uremia.
Elimination of inciting factors at this phase will not decrease existing
damage nor expedite the rate of recovery. The recovery phase is the
period where renal tissue undergoes regeneration and repair with
varying restoration of renal function.

GRADING AKI
The International Renal Interest Society (IRIS) has provided a
categorization scheme for both chronic kidney disease (CKD) and
AKI (Table 300.1). Each grade can be sub-graded by UOP (nonoligoanuric vs. oligoanuric) and the need for renal replacement
therapy. The trend of increasing serum creatinine in a hospitalized
dog or cat should increase concern for active kidney injury, even if
the patient is not azotemic. Monitoring serum creatinine is
recommended for hospitalized dogs and cats. Dogs with IRIS Grade I
AKI have a higher in-hospital mortality (58%) than those without
AKI (16%).1,2 Recognition of non-azotemic AKI should allow earlier
intervention with the potential to minimize the magnitude of
developing AKI.

STRUCTURE-FUNCTION
CATEGORIZATION OF AKI

AKI is a clinical syndrome of varying severity initiated by a multitude
of causes that can be accompanied by rapid decline in GFR and renal
function. Injury may occur to the nephron, however, while GFR is
preserved. Many injuries are reversible (at least partially); however,
the recovery phase of AKI may take days to months. Traditionally,
AKI is divided into categories based on the underlying etiology:
1. Prerenal (hemodynamic) AKI: renal hypoperfusion; the renal
parenchyma is not damaged.
2. Intrinsic Renal AKI: ischemia or a nephrotoxin damages the
renal parenchyma.
3. Postrenal or Obstructive AKI: acute obstruction of the urinary
tract.

KIDNEY INJURY CATEGORIZED BY
BIOMARKERS
The prerenal/renal/postrenal categorization of AKI can be
incomplete, since injuries develop on a continuum. Prolonged
prerenal and postrenal AKI can progress to intrinsic AKI. Since the
term “prerenal” is often assumed to mean “hypovolemia,”
inappropriate IV fluid therapy may ensue. Development of kidneyspecific biomarkers has helped create a new categorization of AKI.3,4
Biomarkers such as creatinine, blood urea nitrogen (BUN),
symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA), and serum cystatin C (CC)
provide information on GFR (ch. 62).4,5 Serum creatinine does not
rise immediately following renal injury; it may take 72 hours after
renal injury for increases to be detected and another 2-3 days are
required for increases to reach equilibrium.6 Other biomarkers
(Table 300.2; ch. 299, Table 299.1) provide evidence of injury
and dysfunction of various parts of the nephron. Fractional excretion
of sodium (FeNa; ch. 299) represents the percent of sodium (Na)
reabsorbed by the tubules, which should be 99% (FeNa <1% is
normal). Tubular injury often reduces the ability to reabsorb Na,
increasing the FeNa. Dogs surviving AKI had improvement in GFR
and lowering FeNa throughout hospitalization, whereas the non-

survivors had no improvement in GFR and increases in FeNa.7
Increased availability of validated kidney-specific biomarker assays
facilitates an updated categorization of AKI, using both functional
and structural assessments (Table 300.3).8 This structure/function
relationship allows for the assessment and monitoring of broader
kidney status. Renal injuries may be identified even when GFR is
preserved. Structural changes can be assessed with decreases in
GFR.

REPEAT VS SUSTAINED AKI
Following an episode of AKI, dogs and cats may continue to have
active kidney injury due to the inciting cause. Ischemia and
inflammatory changes may perpetuate or exacerbate injury. If such
injury is not stopped, renal recovery may not occur, which could
progress to CKD (ch. 301). Other pets may recover from 1 AKI
episode, only to have a second distinct AKI event shortly after. It is
challenging to differentiate sustained kidney injury with partial
recovery from multiple episodes of AKI within a short timeframe. In
humans, a minimum of 48 hours of sustained improvement is
needed between AKI events to characterize them as separate
episodes.9 Patients with partial improvement in kidney function for
<48 hours before subsequent worsening should be evaluated for a
second injury, but continued kidney dysfunction from the initial
cause of AKI is possible. Owners of pets with repeated episodes of
AKI should be asked to provide a detailed review of medications to
identify any with potential for nephrotoxicity (chs. 135 and 139).
Medication review may reveal failure to account for decreased kidney
function when determining doses. Evaluating each pet for
hypoperfusion or overhydration is critically important. Hospitalacquired pyelonephritis should be considered (chs. 186, 304),
particularly in pets with indwelling urethral catheters and those that
have undergone other urologic procedures (intermittent
catheterization, cystoscopy, interventional urology, etc.). An older
study suggested that most dogs with hospital-acquired AKI had
exposure to nephrotoxic medications (e.g., aminoglycoside

antibiotics) within 2 weeks of the AKI.10 Older dogs and dogs with
kidney or heart disease were most common.

ACUTE KIDNEY DISEASE (AKD)
DEFINITIONS
In people, AKI is defined as kidney injury that occurs over ≤7 days.9
AKD is defined as a persistent decrease in kidney function that
persists >7 days. Both human and veterinary medicine define CKD as
a decrease in kidney function that persists ≥3 months (ch. 301).
IRIS grading of AKI does not define duration of injury and does not
define AKD in dogs or cats. Persistent decrease in kidney function
extending beyond 7 days is frequently encountered. The median and

range of serum creatinine observed 30 days after the final dialysis
treatment for AKI in dogs was 1.8 mg/dL (1-4.9 mg/dL [159
mcmol/L; 88-433 mcmol/L]) and in cats it was 2.0 mg/dL (1-5.7
mg/dL [177 mcmol/L; 88-504 mcmol/L]).11 It is likely these pets
have a condition analogous to AKD in people, not matching the
criteria for diagnosis of either AKI or CKD.

Staging
The staging system created for people with AKD9 is modified for
veterinary use in Figure 300.1. Serum creatinine can be used to
grade AKD, proposed to be equivalent to the tiers used for IRIS AKI
grading. Identifying an AKI initiating event is not always possible. It
may be helpful to view AKD as a post-AKI state, but when complete
recovery is not achieved, the condition may also be early CKD. Pets
with AKD should be monitored and treated like those with AKI:
prudent assessment for volume needs to prevent hyper- or
hypovolemia, evaluation of medications for possible nephrotoxicity
(ch. 135), and adjustment of drug dose or frequency to account for
the decreased GFR and avoid drug accumulation.

AKD Subtype 1
Stages of AKD are stratified by serum creatinine concentration, as in
the IRIS AKI grading. Stage 1 AKD is further divided into 3 subtypes:
• 1C: the patient’s serum creatinine remains above baseline 7
days after diagnosing AKI. This patient has not had
demonstrable recovery and renal function should be closely
monitored for evidence of further loss.
• 1B: creatinine normalizes, but biomarkers suggesting renal
injury persist. These biomarkers can include newly developed
or worsened proteinuria or hypertension. Dogs or cats may be
classified as AKD grade 1C/B if they have persistently
increased creatinine and a new biomarker of kidney injury.
• 1A: dogs and cats with renal “recovery” and no evidence of
active renal injury.

AKD Renal Recovery

Renal “recovery” refers to GFR biomarkers (creatinine, SDMA, BUN)
that become normal following an episode of AKI. Normalizing these
values does not indicate full kidney recovery because these tests are
not sensitive for identifying mild decreases in GFR (chs. 62 and
299). Thus, “recovery” may only indicate 25-50% improvement in
GFR. Quantifying a pet’s GFR is unlikely to be helpful as a pre-AKI
GFR is usually not known. People fully recovered from AKI remain at
increased risk for major adverse cardiac and kidney
complications.12,13 Dogs and cats have not been evaluated for long
term consequence of AKI.

ETIOLOGY OF AKI
HEMODYNAMIC/PRERENAL AKI
Decreased GFR, Normal Injury Biomarkers
Prerenal AKI, which begins as an appropriate physiologic response
to hypoperfusion, is the most common cause of AKI in people.14
Characterized by normal renal parenchyma and a decreased GFR,
the hallmark of prerenal AKI is rapid correction of GFR following
restoration of renal perfusion. Prerenal AKI can result from a
variety of conditions (Box 300.1); hypotension is not required to
develop prerenal AKI.15 Normotensive ischemic renal damage can
occur in the presence of normal systolic blood pressure. In response
to hypovolemia or hypotension baroreceptors initiate neural and
humoral pathways to normalize effective circulating blood volume
via activating the sympathetic nervous system, stimulating the reninangiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and secretion of antidiuretic
hormone (ADH). The net effects are systemic vasoconstriction and
efferent arteriole vasoconstriction. Aldosterone stimulates thirst and
ADH increases water resorption within the kidney. These
compensatory changes preserve GFR and increase kidney filtration
fractions, e.g., the volume of plasma filtered through the kidney.
These compensatory mechanisms are adequate for mild states of
renal hypoperfusion. Persistent or severe hypoperfusion reduces
renal perfusion pressure below levels of autoregulation causing
endogenous vasoconstrictors to increase afferent arteriolar

resistance, decreasing renal blood flow and GFR. If this state is not
corrected, intrinsic renal ischemia will cause acute tubular necrosis,
tubular obstruction, and adenosine triphosphate depletion of tubular
epithelial cells, i.e., AKI (ch. 303).

Drugs and Conditions Contributing to AKI
Drugs that inhibit these compensatory mechanisms can contribute to
intrinsic renal damage, e.g., nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
(NSAIDs) inhibit production of vasodilatory prostaglandins and
kinins which during prerenal hypoperfusion can result in renal
ischemia and subsequent tubular damage. Administration of
carprofen to hypovolemic dogs caused 20% reduction in GFR.16
Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE-Is) can prevent
adequate tubuloglomerular feedback to increase GFR in states of
decreased tubular flow. Diuretic therapy decreases effective
circulating volume and can lead to RAAS stimulation.

Administration of NSAIDs and ACE-Is during a hypovolemic state is
contraindicated. Intrarenal vasoconstriction can be caused by
hypercalcemia, bacterial endotoxin, radiocontrast agents, and
cyclosporine.14,17-19

INTRINSIC AKI
Decreased GFR, Injury Biomarkers
Damage to the renal parenchyma can occur due to 4 different
processes14:
1. Diseases of large renal vessels (renal artery thrombosis,
vasculitis, renal vein compression)
2. Diseases of the renal microvasculature and glomeruli
(glomerulonephritis, vasculitis, hypertension, etc.)
3. Ischemic and nephrotoxic acute tubular necrosis (renal
hypoperfusion, endogenous and exogenous toxins)
4. Other processes involving the tubulointerstitium (neoplastic
infiltration, oxidative injury, infectious disease)
Hypovolemia or dehydration make differentiating prerenal from
intrinsic renal AKI difficult. Prerenal AKI should resolve after
restoring renal perfusion. Persisting clinical signs and biomarker
abnormalities following restoration of renal perfusion indicates
intrinsic renal damage. Biomarkers of GFR typically lag behind
kidney injury biomarkers. Use of biomarkers allows earlier
identification of AKI and may lead to earlier diagnosis and
treatment. Occlusion of large renal vessels is an uncommon cause of
AKI in dogs and cats; most of their thromboembolic disease involves
the lung and distal aorta.20,21 Glomerulonephritis can cause
inflammation and tubular obstruction that eventually can result in
tubular epithelial cell injury (chs. 302 and 303). Hypertension (ch.
236), hyperviscosity, and vasculitis (ch. 181) can decrease renal
perfusion.
A thorough history should be obtained with specific inquiries into
potential nephrotoxin exposure (ch. 135). The patient’s current drug
therapy as well as possible exposure to other nephrotoxic drugs

should be reviewed (ch. 139). Ethylene glycol, lily, grape, and raisin
exposure should all be determined. Few cat owners know that lily
plants can be toxic to cats.22
Numerous systemic diseases may result in AKI or tubular
dysfunction (Table 300.4; ch. 303).

Sepsis and Intrinsic AKI
Sepsis (ch. 128) often produces generalized arterial vasodilation,
decreased systemic vascular resistance, production of reactive
oxygen species, and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (ch.
171) with consumptive coagulopathy, thrombosis, and eventually
hemorrhage. One study found 12.3% of dogs with sepsis and multiple
organ dysfunction syndrome had renal dysfunction; only 14%
survived to hospital discharge.23 A review of the pathophysiology,
diagnosis, and treatment of veterinary AKI in sepsis has been
published.24

Heatstroke and Intrinsic AKI
The pathogenesis of heatstroke-associated AKI most likely includes
hypoperfusion, direct thermal injury, pigment nephropathy from
myoglobinemia, and systemic inflammatory response
syndrome.25,26 Based on IRIS grading, 63% of dogs with heatstroke
have developed AKI at presentation or during hospitalization. AKI is
associated with both glomerular and tubular injury (chs. 302 and
303); respective biomarkers are significantly increased even in nonazotemic dogs with heatstroke; however, biomarkers were not
predictive of outcome.26

Nephrotoxins (ch. 135)
Nephrotoxic AKI can be caused by a multitude of endogenous and
exogenous agents, each of which has different mechanism of injury.
However most cause renal injury through a varying combination of
intrarenal vasoconstriction, tubular cell toxic injury, and intratubular
obstruction.14 Because the kidney receives approximately 25% of
cardiac output, it is inherently vulnerable to toxins.

Nephrotoxic Contrast Agents
Contrast agents, e.g., iohexol, can cause contrast-associated AKI
(caAKI).27 Contrast agents cause renal vasodilation followed by renal
vasoconstriction, resulting in medullary ischemia. This, combined
with contrast-mediated oxidative damage, causes tubular epithelial
cell toxic injury (ch. 303).28 Risk factors for development of caAKI
include preexisting renal disease; increases in serum creatinine
parallel risk of nephropathy. However, risk of AKI due to contrast
agents is controversial.29,30 Most reports of caAKI in people occur
after intra-arterial administration. Risk of giving contrast IV is
debatable.31 There is not adequate evidence to suggest that contrast
studies be withheld in pets with AKI if indicated to help determine
cause of their illness.32

Myoglobin, Hemoglobin Toxicoses
Both can cause neph-rotoxic injury due to scavenging nitric oxide, an
important vasodilator. The resulting vasoconstriction leads to renal
ischemia. Myoglobinemia may be the result of trauma,
hyperthermia, seizures, or metabolic disorders, including
hypokalemia (hypoK) and hypophosphatemia.14 There is a case
report of anuric renal failure due to rhabdomyolysis in a dog after
red-bellied black snake envenomation.33 This dog had marked
tubular necrosis and tubular obstruction.

Nephrotoxic Drugs (chs. 135, 139)
Aminoglycosides
Aminoglycosides are bactericidal time- dependent antibiotics, long
recognized as causing nephrotoxicosis. The exact toxic mechanism is
unknown; however, intracellular accumulation of aminoglycosides
within lysosomes is thought to interfere with normal cellular
function, e.g., protein synthesis, mitochondrial function, eventually
leading to cell death. Toxicosis is typically seen as an increase in
BUN and creatinine 5-10 days after administration. Monitoring
trough drug levels can help limit, but not eliminate risks of

nephrotoxicosis. Toxic effects can be reversible in humans, but
dialysis may be required to achieve this goal (ch. 103). Urine
specific gravity (USG) and sediment evaluation should be assessed
daily to evaluate for casts or isosthenuria (ch. 170). Aminoglycoside
treatment should be discontinued immediately if these should occur.

Amphotericin B
Amphotericin B is an antifungal drug that binds ergosterol in the
fungal cell membrane to form channels that cause cell lysis (ch.
141). Nephrotoxicity is due to renal vasoconstriction and direct toxic
effects on tubular epithelial cells. Newer lipid-based formulations of
amphotericin B are thought to be less toxic. The availability of other
antifungal drugs has largely supplanted the use of amphotericin B
except in severe fungal infections.

Cyclosporine, Tacrolimus, Albumin, and Others
Cyclosporine and tacrolimus, calcineurin inhibitors, cause intense
constriction of afferent and efferent renal arterioles and are reported
to cause AKI in people.34 They increase vasoconstrictor factors
(endothelin, thromboxane), activate the RAAS, and reduce
vasodilator factors.18 In people, chronic use of calcineurin inhibitors
may lead to renal fibrosis, a complication that is not recognized in
dogs or cats. AKI was reported in a dog with acute overdose.35
Delayed type-III hypersensitivity reactions causing AKI, proteinuria,
and skin lesions have been observed after giving human albumin to
dogs.36 Other nephrotoxic drugs include cisplatin, methotrexate,
and sucrose-containing human IV immunoglobulins.34

Grape, Raisin, Currant Intoxication (ch. 135)
The cause of AKI, reported in dogs after eating grapes, raisins, or
currants,37-39 is unknown. Tartaric acid may be the nephrotoxic
agent in grapes.40,41 Affected dogs have moderate to severe diffuse
renal tubular degeneration, worse in the proximal tubules. While
severe AKI has been documented,42 retrospective studies have

shown AKI to be rare after dogs ingest these fruits.43,44 The amount
ingested to induce AKI ranges from 2.8-19.6 g/kg, but about 35% of
dogs ingesting this amount did not develop azotemia. The most
common signs are vomiting (typically seen within 24 hours of
ingestion), anorexia, lethargy, and diarrhea. Most affected dogs are
azotemic, hypercalcemic, and hyperphosphatemic. Of 43 dogs
reported with grape and raisin intoxication, there was a 53% survival
rate. Most of the surviving dogs had a return to normal renal
function.

Lily Intoxication (ch. 135)
Lily consumption can be nephrotoxic in cats.45-47 Easter lily
intoxication is frequently fatal, with most cats presenting in the
maintenance phase of AKI. Lily toxins are in the aqueous fractions of
leaves and flowers, providing potential for dialysis removal but most
cats are seen too late for dialysis.46 At least 16 different steroidal
glycoalkaloids have been identified in lily plants,48 compounds that
are cytotoxic to renal tubular epithelial cells in vitro. Further
evaluation is required to confirm these glycoalkaloids as the
nephrotoxins. Common clinical signs include vomiting and
polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD). Disorientation, ataxia, facial and paw
edema, head pressing, and seizures are less common. Azotemia,
glucosuria, proteinuria, and isosthenuria are seen. Increased liver
enzyme activities are not typical but have been reported. Pancreatitis
is possible. Acute tubular necrosis is commonly observed
histopathologically. Successful treatment with hemodialysis has been
reported.49 A retrospective report showed only 9% of cats with
presumed acute lily exposure became azotemic after gastric
decontamination and 48 hours of IV fluid diuresis.50

Ethylene Glycol Intoxication (ch. 135)
Ethylene glycol in automotive antifreeze, heat exchange fluids, and
some photographic fluids has a reported lethal dose of 1.4 mL/kg in
cats and 4.4 mL/kg in dogs. The conversion of ethylene glycol to
glycoaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting step.
Other major metabolites include glycolic acid, glyoxylic acid, and

oxalic acid. Most oxalic acid is excreted in urine; however, some may
be retained as calcium (Ca) oxalate. Ca oxalate and hippuric acid
crystals often precipitate in renal tubules and in vessels within other
organ systems. Tubular epithelial necrosis causes AKI secondary to
Ca oxalate crystals in the tubular lumen.51 Diagnosis can be made by
identifying Ca oxalate crystals in the urine, or with portable tests that
identify ethylene glycol in serum. A high anion gap metabolic
acidosis is typical due to exogenous anions (glyoxylic acid).
There are 3 phases of ethylene glycol toxicosis.51 Within 1 hour of
exposure, the animal can appear ataxic or “drunk,” followed by a
relatively asymptomatic period. Then, 12-24 hours after ingestion,
cardiopulmonary involvement inconsistently develops (e.g., heart
failure). Third, 1 to 3 days later, animals commonly develop oliguric
AKI, renomegaly, and signs that include obtundation, anorexia,
vomiting, evidence of renal pain, hypothermia, coma, and ultimately
death. Unfortunately, many animals are not seen before the third
phase.
Initial laboratory results may show hypocalcemia and increased
anion gap metabolic acidosis. Some blood gas machines falsely
record glycol as lactate, yielding spurious severe
hyperlactatemia.52,53 Ultrasound (US) shows enlarged and markedly
hyperechoic kidneys (

Video 300.1). Initial treatment should be

aimed at prevention of gastrointestinal (GI) absorption. Emesis
should be induced and activated charcoal administered to animals in
phase 1 (ch. 132). Hemodialysis can remove nearly all absorbed
ethylene glycol from the bloodstream.54 IV fluids may be helpful in
maintaining renal tubular flow (ch. 120). If discovered in the early
stages, 4-methylpyrazole (4-MP, fomepizole) can prevent
metabolism of ethylene glycol by effectively inactivating alcohol
dehydrogenase in dogs, preventing formation of oxalic acid and its
renal toxicity. It does not cause the side effects of ethanol and is the
treatment of choice.55-57 Alternatively, IV ethanol is given to
competitively inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase. 4-MP and ethanol are
of little benefit once renal damage has occurred. The prognosis at
this stage is guarded to poor.58-60

Melamine Intoxication (ch. 135)
In March of 2007 several brands of pet food were recalled in the
United States due to melamine contamination. Affected animals
developed anorexia, vomiting, lethargy, PU/PD and AKI.61
Toxicology studies identified 2 contaminants: melamine and
cyanuric acid. When these compounds are co-ingested, they form an
insoluble precipitate in kidney tubules that causes renal failure via
physical blockage, as confirmed in studies on rats.62 Melamine, a
compound used in fertilizer and soft plastics, was probably added to
the dog food to increase the reported protein content.63
Histopathologic examination of affected kidneys revealed
intratubular crystalluria, tubular necrosis with regeneration, and
subcapsular perivascular inflammation.64 Many affected animals
either died or were euthanized. Those that survived did eventually
have recovery or improvement in renal function. More recently
(2007-present) dogs that had received jerky or sweet potato treats
manufactured in China have developed various acquired renal
dysfunctions. These maladies include oligoanuric AKI, Fanconi
syndrome, and other tubular defects (ch. 303).

Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D) Intoxication (ch. 135)
Vitamin D3 is used as a rodenticide. Ingestion results in
hypercalcemia and AKI. It is absorbed from the GI tract and
metabolized in the liver and kidney to calcitriol. Calcitriol increases
serum Ca through increased GI Ca absorption, increased resorption
from bone, and decreased excretion in urine.65 Signs of toxicosis
(anorexia, weakness, depression, PU/PD, vomiting) occur 12-36
hours after ingestion.66 Laboratory results include hypercalcemia,
hyperphosphatemia, azotemia, and hyperproteinemia. Soft-tissue
mineralization may be seen in kidneys and lungs. Treatment is
directed at correcting enhancing calciuresis with furosemide and
prednisone. IV bisphosphonate therapy reversed hypercalcemic AKI
in children, suggesting bisphosphonates should be the primary
treatment in this type of intoxication.19

Infectious Causes
Leptospirosis
Leptospira (ch. 192) are Gram-negative spirochetes that can result
in renal and hepatic dysfunction. Leptospira serogroup Pomona
caused more severe renal disease and was associated with worse
outcomes when compared to disease due to other serogroups.67
Infection with Leptospira sp. produces a generalized inflammatory
state during the period of tissue invasion. Leptospiremia directly
injures kidneys as the organism replicates and persists in renal
tubular epithelial cells, resulting in interstitial nephritis, intracellular
Ca accumulation, and cell death. Cells and tubular debris are
sloughed into the tubular lumen.68 Increased liver enzyme activities
and thrombocytopenia increase suspicion of leptospirosis. Kidneys
may be enlarged with hyperechoic parenchyma and perirenal
effusion (

Video 300.2). Serologic titers are only 50% sensitive in

identifying leptospirosis in dogs with AKI.69 Ideally, blood and urine
polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing should be considered
concurrently. Urine polymerase chain reaction PCR has been
demonstrated to have 100% sensitivity and 88% specificity for
leptospirosis.70 When samples were submitted days after starting
antibiotics, blood and urine PCR were falsely negative.69 Treatment
consists of antibiotics and supportive care for AKI (ch. 192).

Pyelonephritis (ch. 304)
Pyelonephritis (an infection of the renal interstitium) is caused more
often by ascending bacteria than hematogenous spread. It was
identified as the cause of AKI in only 5.7% of dogs and cats,71 but this
may be falsely decreased because localizing the site of infection can
be difficult.72,73 Clinical signs are often the nonspecific poor
appetite, lethargy, vomiting, and diarrhea.74 While fever,
renomegaly, and renal pain upon palpation are reported, such signs
were observed in only 6-21% of dogs. About 80% of dogs with
experimental pyelonephritis had renal pelvic dilatation on US,
usually with proximal ureteral dilatation and a hyperechoic mucosal

margin line within the renal pelvis, proximal portion of the ureter, or
both.75 Bacterial culture of urine should be performed and the most
appropriate antibiotic chosen using soft-tissue breakpoints. While
ideal duration of treatment is not known, 2 weeks are
recommended.76 IV antibiotics should be administered empirically
for most intrinsic renal AKI patients until culture results are
available.

POSTRENAL AKI
Normal/Decreased GFR, Increased Injury
Biomarkers
Isosthenuria and azotemia typically do not occur until 66% and 75%
of nephron function is lost, respectively. Unilateral nephroureteral
obstruction does not lead to biochemical abnormalities if the
remaining kidney is normal. These pets have decreases in GFR that
may be identified via increased SDMA or progressive increases in
serum creatinine. Measurement of GFR could be done, but
reductions are nonspecific. Urethral or bilateral ureteral obstructions
cause postrenal azotemia. Unilateral obstruction with concurrent
CKD typically causes “acute on chronic” illness.

Uroabdomen (ch. 126)
Uroabdomen, either uroperitoneum or uroretroperitoneum, usually
following trauma, is a relatively common cause of postrenal azotemia
and uremia. If the kidney was traumatized when the uroabdomen
was caused, intrinsic AKI may occur. Uroperitoneum generally
develops from disruption of the distal ureters, bladder, or proximal
urethra whereas uroretroperitoneum results from injury to a kidney
or proximal ureter with the peritoneum remaining intact.
Uroabdomen is usually caused by bladder rupture after blunt
abdominal trauma. Pets with a full bladder are at greatest risk for
rupture when traumatized and male dogs, due to their long narrow
urethra, are also commonly diagnosed with uroabdomen.
Diagnosis of uroabdomen is based on history of trauma, physical
examination (PE), laboratory test results, and imaging studies (chs.

126 and 127). Bruising is often present in trauma cases. Pets may
present in shock (chs. 119 and 121). The urinary bladder may or may
not be palpable during PE. A palpable urinary bladder does not rule
out urine leak or rupture within the urinary tract (including the
bladder). Voiding urine that is not grossly hematuric does not
exclude a diagnosis of bladder rupture. Urine leakage into the
abdomen causes hyperkalemia (hyperK, ch. 68) and azotemia.

Ureteral (chs. 117, 306) and Urethral (chs. 99, 312)
Obstructions
Diagnosis of ureteral obstruction is best accomplished by combining
results of abdominal radiographs and US.77 Obstructive uroliths or
debris may not be apparent in 1 imaging modality but visualized with
the other. Suspicion of obstruction is often based on the US
appearance of the renal pelvis and proximal ureter (Table 300.5). A
combination of renal pelvis dilation, blunting of diverticuli, and
proximal ureteral dilation should raise concern for obstruction (
Video 300.3). Most obstructions result in the renal pelvis being
dilated to >7 mm and in 1 study, dilation >13 mm was only caused by
obstruction.78 Cats with an obstruction may have minimal pelvic
dilation; 26% of cats with nephroureteral obstructions had a renal
pelvis <4 mm in diameter in 1 study.79
Ureteral dilation begins at the ureteropelvic junction and proceeds
distally until reaching the obstruction. This process may take several
days, which may account for the inability to initially identify some
obstructions. Proximal ureteral dilation is observed in most cats with
ureteral obstruction. If nephroureteral obstruction is suspected but
unable be confirmed with US and radiographs, contrast studies may
be helpful. Percutaneous antegrade pyelography in dogs and cats has
a 94% diagnostic rate with only 2% major complication rate.80
Alternatively, pyelography can be performed intraoperatively as part
of ureteral stent or subcutaneous (SQ) ureteral bypass placement
(ch. 117). Once diagnosed, attempts to relieve nephroureteral
obstructions should be prompt. Medical management is reported to
be effective in <13% of cases.81 Interventional procedures are needed

in most obstructed pets. Ureteral stents, SQ ureteral bypass, and
percutaneous nephrostomy tubes may all provide relief from the
increased hydrostatic pressure occurring proximal to the
obstruction, which is the primary means of nephron injury (ch. 117).
Ureterotomy and ureteral rerouting may be considered. The
American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine consensus
guideline recommends subcutaneous ureteral bypass (SUB) or a
ureteral stent as first-line therapy.82 Ureterolithotomy was
associated with a 21% mortality rate in cats,83 ureterotomy (9%),84
ureteral stent (7.5-8%),84,85 and SUB placement (6%).86

DIAGNOSIS OF ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY
CLINICAL SIGNS, PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
FINDINGS, BODY TEMPERATURE, BLOOD
PRESSURE
Clinical signs associated with AKI vary and are dependent, in part,
on the severity of the injury. Pets with IRIS Stage I AKI may have no
signs and are only identified by monitoring kidney function. By
contrast, pets with IRIS Stage V AKI may have profound uremia
resulting in significant morbidity and mortality. Nearly every organ
system is affected by uremia with GI, neurologic, and cardiovascular
issues most frequent.87 Hypothermia was present in 21% and 38% of
nonspecifically uremic dogs and cats, respectively.88 Systemic
hypertension (ch. 236) due to various factors was identified in 3755% of dogs with AKI at the time of hospital admission, increasing to
75-81% during hospitalization.89,90 Hypervolemia (ch. 120) due to
excess IV fluids was noted in 42% and ventricular premature
complex arrhythmias (ch. 230) in 79% of dogs with AKI; none
required antiarrhythmic therapy.91 Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea,
anorexia, and GI and oral ulcerations may be seen in uremia. Pets
with marked uremia may be obtunded, comatose, or develop seizures
(chs. 44, 45).

Complete Blood Count (CBC) and Serum
Biochemistries
Nonspecific leukocytosis or evidence of hemoconcentration may be
noted on CBC as many pets with AKI have some degree of
hypovolemia or dehydration. This can make differentiation between
prerenal and intrinsic renal AKI difficult. Prerenal AKI should
resolve after restoration of renal perfusion (chs. 119-121) and
persisting biochemical abnormalities indicate intrinsic renal damage.
Increases in serum creatinine, BUN, and phosphorus concentrations
are typical. Creatinine is an insensitive marker of GFR in AKI
because of the time lag before creatinine accumulates in plasma (ch.
299, Figure 299.3),92 typically peaking days after the initial
ischemic event. Prerenal AKI is characterized by mild to moderate
increases in BUN and creatinine. BUN typically increases to a greater
magnitude than creatinine, resulting in an increased BUN/creatinine
ratio (>20; SI units, >0.64). Approximately 40-50% of BUN
resorption occurs passively in proximal tubules. In prerenal
hypoperfusion increased Na and water reabsorption occurs in the
proximal tubule and BUN passively follows. This increased BUN is
unrelated to GFR.92 Plasma phosphorus concentration may also
increase.
Postrenal AKI may be accompanied by marked azotemia, but
unilateral obstruction may not increase serum creatinine
concentrations. Some cats with AKI due to lily intoxication or
nephroureteral obstruction have marked azotemia (serum creatinine
>15 mg/dL [>1326 mcmol/L) and BUN >250 mg/dL [>98 mmol/L])
but, for unknown reasons, maintain an appetite with only minimal
signs. Such clinical presentations should prompt inquiry about
possible lily exposure. Uroabdomen typically causes azotemia,
metabolic acidosis, and electrolyte abnormalities including mild
hyponatremia, hyperphosphatemia, and hyperK. Azotemia and
hyponatremia often develop within 24 hours of uroabdomen; hyperK
may not develop for >48 hours.

Urine, Urinalysis (UA), Casts
Urine volume is not helpful in identifying the cause of AKI, due to
varying degrees of prerenal hypoperfusion initially present. UA (ch.

70) often reveals isosthenuria. USG may be less reliable in
oligoanuric pets. Casts may be seen microscopically (chs. 70 and
299). White blood cell casts are seen with acute tubular necrosis,
glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, or in the nephrotic syndrome.
Red blood cell casts are suggestive of vasculitis or
glomerulonephritis. Epithelial casts represent tubular damage,
typically seen in acute tubular necrosis or an acute
glomerulonephritis. Granular casts are cellular casts that have
undergone degradation. Waxy casts are degenerated granular casts
and typically seen in advanced renal disease. Casts are absent in 2030% of pets with intrinsic AKI.14 Casts often dissolve within several
hours after urine collection; therefore, urine sediment examination
should be prompt.
In hypoperfused states, UOP decreases due to RAAS and ADH
activity, with urine USG >1.018 (often >1.030) and an increased
osmolarity (UOsm; >500 mOsm/L). The urine sediment is usually
benign; however, hyaline casts may be present. Hyaline casts are not
indicative of renal disease, but are typical in concentrated urine.92
Urine culture (with soft-tissue breakpoints) should be performed to
rule out pyelonephritis. Urine cultures are positive in >90% of
people with pyelonephritis and should be performed in dogs and cats
prior to giving antibiotics. Screening tests for leptospirosis (ch. 192)
should be performed when this disease is suspected.
