IMAGING
Radiographs can be useful to determine kidney size and for
visualizing radiopaque calculi. US, the screening modality of choice
in AKI,14 can determine cortical thickness, cortical-medullary
densities, renal pelvis dilation, and identify radiolucent calculi.
Imaging usually reveals kidneys with normal size, shape, and
architecture in hypoperfused (prerenal) AKI. The presence of
perirenal effusion has been associated with AKI, but is nonspecific.93
IV pyelography may be necessary to diagnose ureteral obstruction,
but may not be reliable when kidneys are completely obstructed.
Antegrade pyelography can be performed if US fails to confirm a
nephroureteral obstruction.80 When present, peritoneal or
retroperitoneal effusion samples should be obtained for fluid
analysis, including cytologic evaluation (chs. 71, 85, and 86).
Effusion creatinine and potassium (K) should be measured and
compared to serum concentrations to investigate for uroabdomen
(Table 300.6).94 Retrograde cystourethrography may be required
to confirm urine leakage if the defect is small.

CYTOLOGY OF EFFUSIONS, KIDNEY
BIOPSY
Urine in the peritoneal cavity can be a protein-poor transudate,
protein-rich transudate, or exudate, depending on hemorrhage or
inflammatory cells present (ch. 71). Urine, a chemical irritant, can

cause nonseptic neutrophilic inflammation with a cell count
>5000/mcL and total solids of >3.0 g/dL (>30 g/L). Renal biopsy
(ch. 299; Video 299.1) may be considered if the cause of AKI is
unclear or if there is suspected concurrent glomerulonephritis.

RENAL INJURY BIOMARKERS AND
OTHER SPECIFIC TESTS
Increased cardiac troponin-I concentrations have been documented
in dogs with AKI and ventricular arrhythmias but are not necessarily
associated with outcome.91 Uremic thrombocytopathy due to
decreased platelet aggregation has been reported in dogs with AKI;
however, buccal mucosal bleeding time did not correlate to platelet
function testing.95 Numerous studies have evaluated renal injury
biomarkers and their utility in diagnosing AKI.26,96-104
Understanding the role of active injury biomarkers in the diagnosis,
monitoring, and management of AKI is limited by lack of commercial
availability.

EARLY AND CONTINUED MONITORING
OF PETS WITH AKI
Any hospitalized pet is at risk of developing AKI and should be
monitored. Critically ill patients and those with oligoanuria require
frequent assessment (chs. 119 and 121). Hydration and health status
should be monitored with serial body weights, PEs, hematocrit,
serum total protein, blood pressure, and serum electrolytes.
Hypoperfusion may accompany hypotension, hypovolemia,
dehydration, tachycardia, and/or hemoconcentration. Mucous
membrane moisture may mislead, as uremic pets can have
xerostomia which can cause overestimation of dehydration (ch.
119). Overhydration due to IV fluid overload is a frequent concern
and should be avoided (ch. 120). Signs of overhydration can include
serous ocular and nasal discharges, SQ edema, cavitary effusions,

and/or pulmonary edema. Hypertension is common in
hypervolemia. Central venous pressure measurement is not typically
required for evaluation of hydration status. Monitoring UOP with an
indwelling urinary catheter and closed collection system may be
helpful in identifying oligoanuria (ch. 98). While not needed in most
pets with AKI, monitoring UOP can guide fluid therapy in
hypervolemia. Serum electrolyte concentrations, acid-base status,
and renal parameters must be assessed as indicated, at minimum
once daily.

TREATMENT
FLUID THERAPY (CH. 120)
Goals
Derangements of Na and water balance, including dysnatremia,
dehydration, and hypervolemia, are common in kidney failure.
Abnormalities can be exacerbated by using an inappropriate type of
fluid or giving an excessive amount. Fluid therapy is used to correct
dehydration, hypovolemia, acid-base, and electrolyte disturbances. It
is assumed that nutritional requirements will be provided separately
(ch. 164). Fluid therapy is essential for maintaining cardiac output,
renal perfusion, systemic oxygen delivery, and promoting diuresis.
Reduced cardiac preload often results in a “prerenal” azotemia,
characterized by decreased renal plasma flow and GFR. IV fluids can
increase cardiac preload and stroke volume, improve systemic blood
pressure, and rapidly correct azotemia. The kidney functions to
conserve >97% of filtered Na, but altered Na reabsorption occurs in
AKI. The kidneys can easily be overwhelmed by chronically giving
too much Na, eventually leading to salt and water accumulation.

Crystalloids
Isotonic replacement crystalloids are recommended for volume
replacement and to maintain water balance. Although there are some
conflicting results, studies of hospitalized humans have generally
shown 0.9% NaCl to be associated with increased risk of AKI and
need for renal replacement therapy compared to people given
chloride (Cl)-restricted fluids (lactated Ringer’s, Plasmalyte, etc.).

When administering both isotonic and hypotonic crystalloids to meet
water requirements, Na and Cl inadvertently can be given in excess
of daily requirements. The initial fluid choice for most dogs and cats
with AKI should be an isotonic crystalloid. Correction of
hypovolemia should be performed rapidly, dehydration should be
corrected over the first 6 to 24 hours. After fluid deficits have been
replaced, the pet should be transitioned to a maintenance fluid with
lower concentrations of NaCl.

Colloids
There is controversy regarding use of synthetic colloids in humans,
dogs, and cats due to their causing hypocoagulability.
Hydroxyethylstarch given to critically ill humans is associated with
increased risk of mortality, AKI, and need for dialysis when
compared to giving crystalloids or albumin. Some studies have
shown an increased risk for developing AKI or progressive worsening
of AKI grade throughout hospitalization when dogs or cats are given
hydroxyethyl starch (HES).105,106 Until data show HES
administration leads to improved survival in humans and animals
with AKI, it should be used cautiously, but preferably avoided.

Fluid Volume and Sodium (Na) Levels (ch. 120)
The rate of giving IV fluids and the volume should be sufficient to
provide maintenance water requirement to meet metabolic water
demands and insensible losses, match ongoing sensible losses (which
can be significantly increased in polyuria [PU]), and correct volume
deficits. Most formulae for canine and feline maintenance fluid
requirements are based on studies in healthy animals. These
formulae yield varying fluid volumes and many deliver electrolytes
(particularly Na and Cl) at daily rates 15 to 25 times greater than
requirements recommended by the National Research Council.107
The kidneys must respond to this salt load by increasing rates of Na
excretion but pets with kidney disease who are unable to excrete
excess Na may develop hypervolemia (ch. 120), systemic
hypertension (ch. 236), and/or edema (chs. 30, 229).

Fluid Rate (ch. 120)

Prescribing fluid rates exceeding the pet’s water requirement is
commonly called “aggressive fluid therapy” and used “to induce
diuresis,” but this approach is not evidence-based and not supported
by renal physiology. Diuresis (the promotion of urine production)
does not necessarily improve GFR; this is shown by diuretics, which
increase urine production by decreasing renal tubular Na
reabsorption but simultaneously decreasing GFR.108 Fluids should
be administered to maintain renal perfusion, which may increase
UOP by reduced RAAS activity. No evidence supports the idea that
giving excess intravenous (IV) fluids has any beneficial effect on
renal function. Excessive fluid administration decreases serum
creatinine concentration via increased volume of distribution,
misleading clinicians to think AKI is improving, delaying recognition
of AKI, or underestimating disease severity. Conservative rates of
fluid administration are associated with lower incidence of AKI in
people compared to those who received liberal volumes. A study of
anesthetized healthy dogs showed no improvement in GFR after
giving 10 mL/kg/hr of lactated Ringer’s solution.109 Similarly, 6
mL/kg/hr of IV 0.9% NaCl produced no change in GFR in healthy
cats.110 Pharmacologically inducing PU, using IV fluids or diuretics,
does not reduce mortality or need for dialysis in humans or dogs
with AKI. Critically ill dogs had increased risk of death when fluid
overloaded.111 Appropriate fluid prescriptions consider the pet’s
water and electrolyte needs, minimize excessive NaCl, and are given
at rates that meet water demands.

MEDICAL THERAPIES (Table 300.7)
Hyperkalemia (hyperK) Overview (chs. 68, 120,
122, 296, and 299)
Most dogs and cats with AKI and hyperK are oligo-anuric because
the kidneys are the main site for K elimination. The major
complication of hyperK are life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias.
Certain electrocardiographic (ECG) abnormalities occur in
association with hyperK, notably disappearance of P waves (atrial
standstill) and, with critically high serum [K], idioventricular

rhythms and cardiac arrest (chs. 68 and 296).112 Paradoxically,
tachycardia has been reported in some hyperK cats.113 It is notable
that ECGs have poor sensitivity in detecting hyperK and clinicians
cannot reliably predict hyperK from an ECG tracing.114,115
Emergency management of hyperK includes cardiac stabilization and
correcting electrolyte abnormalities (chs. 68 and 296). Ca gluconate
can be administered to transiently restore cardiac action potentials
and correct arrhythmias caused by hyperK, but effects last ∼20-30
minutes and serum K still needs to be corrected. Relieving a urethral
obstruction (ch. 99) may lead to normoK with no other intervention,
but severe hyperK with ECG changes should be managed with
additional therapies.

Therapies That Shift Potassium (K) Into Cells (chs.
68, 120, 122, 296, and 299)
IV regular insulin given with dextrose can shift K from extra- to
intracellular spaces, decreasing K by ∼1 mmol/L/hr.116 Dogs and cats
should be monitored for hypoglycemia. A dextrose constant rate
infusion (CRI) should be adjusted to maintain euglycemia.
Albuterol, a beta-agonist, can shift K to intracellular spaces.
Albuterol can be administered via nebulization for
bronchoconstriction (180 mcg) but the dose for treating hyperK is

markedly higher. Albuterol can be delivered via nebulization over 10
minutes in people: 400 mcg to neonates <2 kg, 2.5 g to pediatrics
<2.5 kg, 5 g to pediatrics >2.5 kg, and 10-20 g to adults.117-119 It
likely begins working within minutes and can decrease K by ∼0.50.75 mmol/L within 60 minutes.
It has been suggested that Na bicarbonate helps correct hyperK by
translocation of K, but this is not supported by research. Studies
have failed to demonstrate that Na bicarbonate infusions reduce
serum K concentrations.116 Rather, because Na bicarbonate is
hypertonic, it may dilute K by drawing water into the IV space. Due
to efficacy of other therapies, Na bicarbonate alone should not be
administered to correct hyperK.

Therapies That Increase Urine Potassium (K)
Excretion
Patients producing urine may benefit from therapies that enhance
renal K excretion but not in oligo- or anuria. Combining 0.9% NaCl,
furosemide, and fludrocortisone may help correct hyperK (personal
observation) by increasing Na delivery to the distal nephron where it
is absorbed by principal cells, enhancing K excretion. Na bicarbonate
may enhance K elimination by increasing Na delivery to distal
tubules and increasing urinary pH.120 When given with a diuretic,
Na bicarbonate can increase kaluresis.

Therapies That Enhance Potassium (K) Removal
Dietary K should be evaluated in hyperK pets (ch. 158). Feeding
diets low in K (commercial or home prepared) may improve modest
hyperK. Na polystyrene sulfonate, a K exchange resin, binds K from
the GI capillaries and enhances fecal elimination but may require
days and has no value in emergency management of hyperK. Newer
drugs, e.g., Na zirconium cyclosilicate (Lokelma) and patiromer
(Veltassa), are more effective, work within hours, and may be
effective for emergency management of hyperK, but have not been
evaluated in animals. Extracorporeal renal support therapy (ch.
103) can quickly remove K and normalize hyperK but may not be

available. Dogs and cats may require some stabilization of their
hyperK before being referred for extracorporeal therapy.

Hypokalemia (HypoK)
HypoK can occur in pets with polyuric AKI. Supplementing IV fluids
or giving K orally can resolve hypoK (ch. 68). Supplementation
should be used extremely cautiously in oligoanuric pets that can
quickly shift from being hypoK to hyperK.

Sodium (Na) Abnormalities (Dysnatremias)
Hypernatremia is most often associated with free water deficits but
also with hypertonic fluids or excessive Na administration.
Hyponatremia is often associated with hypervolemia due to excessive
IV fluids and can also follow excessive urinary or GI losses (chs. 67,
68, 120, and 296).

Calcium (Ca) Abnormalities (chs. 69, 283, and 284)
Measuring the biologically active ionized Ca (iCa) is preferred over
total Ca (tCa), which does not accurately predict iCa in azotemic dogs
or cats.121 Dogs and cats with AKI are more likely to be hypoCa while
hyperCa is more common in CKD (ch. 301).122 HypoCa was
associated with worse survival rates in dogs with AKI.123 Treatment
of hypoCa should be initiated when clinical signs are observed, e.g.,
muscle tremors or fasciculations (

Video 69.1), ataxia, pain,

lameness, facial rubbing (Videos 284.1, 284.2), abnormal mentation,
or acute behavioral changes. Slow bolus IV Ca can be given in acute
hypoCa, followed by a CRI. There are concerns of increasing the risk
of tissue mineralization when Ca is given to hyperphosphatemic pets,
but these are outweighed by the acute risks of severe hypoCa.
HyperCa may cause renal vasoconstriction and decrease renal
perfusion. Pets with AKI and hyperCa should be evaluated for
primary causes of hyperCa (chs. 69 and 283) which may cause
secondary AKI. Severe hypercalcemia may be corrected with IV
calcitonin or bisphosphonate therapy.

Hyperphosphatemia
Most dogs and cats with AKI are hyperphosphatemic due to reduced
GFR. Acute hyperphosphatemia may lead to hypoCa with more
significant consequences. Hyperphosphatemia may be managed with
reduced phosphorus diets (ch. 158) and enteric phosphate binders
(ch. 301).124

METABOLIC ACIDOSIS
An increased anion gap metabolic acidosis is common in dogs and
cats with AKI due to retained uremic acids and, possibly, diminished
bicarbonate resorption and reduced H+ elimination. Na bicarbonate
may be considered after correcting hypoperfusion and
hyperlactatemia, if the pet’s venous pH <7.2 and serum bicarbonate
<12 mEq/L, but it should be given slowly to prevent paradoxical
central nervous system acidosis and alkalemia. Na bicarbonate may
be given IV after it is diluted to be isotonic (hypertonic bicarbonate
may be administered through a central catheter) to slowly replace
calculated deficits. Benefits and risks of bicarbonate have not been
evaluated in dogs and cats and there is some controversy over its
administration.125

ANTI-EMETICS
GI complications are common in the uremia. Anti-emetics and
prokinetics may help reduce nausea, anorexia, and ileus, usually
using a combination of maropitant and ondansetron (ch. 48).
Metoclopramide, not a potent anti-emetic, has prokinetic effects that
may help resolve ileus.

GASTRIC ACID SUPPRESSANTS
Anecdotally, pets with AKI have uremic GI (and oral) ulcerations
more often than those with CKD. PE may identify lingual ulcers,
abdominal pain, and melena. Giving a proton pump inhibitor PO

q12h or an IV CRI of famotidine are the most effective means of
neutralizing gastric pH, which improves ulcer healing time in people
(ch. 48).

NUTRITION (chs. 158 and 164)
Most dogs and cats with AKI do not voluntarily consume adequate
calories and require supplemental feeding assistance during
hospitalization. Many will benefit from placement of a feeding tube
(ch. 81). Esophagostomy tubes are often placed because they can be
used with inpatients and outpatients. Nasoesophageal tubes may
provide temporary assistance but require liquid diets and are not
suitable for at home usage. Appetite stimulants can be used with
antiemetics but most pets still fail to consume adequate calories.126

ANTI-HYPERTENSIVES (chs. 91 and 236)
Systemic hypertension is common during hospitalization.89,90 Blood
pressure should be measured twice daily. Amlodipine is an effective
therapy for systemic hypertension and can be given rectally if
needed. Use of ACE-I or angiotensin receptor blockers should be
avoided in AKI due to their effect on GFR.

ADJUSTING MEDICATION DOSAGES TO
ACCOUNT FOR AZOTEMIA
Many drugs undergo renal elimination, tubular reabsorption, or
biotransformation. Kidney disease leads to aberrations in all aspects
of drug pharmacokinetics (adsorption, distribution, metabolism, and
elimination). Any medication to be given to a dog or cat with renal
disease should be evaluated for its potential nephrotoxicity, the
degree of renal elimination, and window of safety (ch. 139). When
possible, medications with potential nephrotoxicity should be
avoided and drugs with wider margin of safety or those primarily
metabolized or excreted by the liver should be used. Drugs
eliminated by the kidneys have prolonged serum half-lives when

GFR is reduced, leading to increased plasma drug concentrations
unless the administered dose or schedule is adjusted. The
pharmacokinetics of most drugs have not been evaluated in dogs or
cats with kidney disease. Adjusted drug dosing for humans with
kidney disease is based on their estimated GFR but such formulae
have not been validated for dogs or cats. Serum creatinine, BUN, and
SDMA are surrogate markers of GFR, with limitations to their
accuracy. If GFR needs to be confidently known, direct measurement
should be performed (creatinine, inulin, or iohexol clearance, etc;
ch. 299). In the absence of GFR measurement, serum creatinine
may serve as a rough estimate for GFR and can be used to compare
the recommended change in drug dosing in people with similar
reductions in kidney function.

OLIGURIA AND ANURIA
Definitions
UOP is 1-2 mL/kg/hr in healthy dogs and cats.127-129 Abnormal
tubular solute reabsorption, seen with kidney disease, results in
solute diuresis and PU (>2 mL/kg/hr). Several definitions have been
used for anuria and oliguria in dogs and cats. Because most pets with
renal disease are PU, UOP <2 mL/kg/hr indicates relative oliguria.
UOP <1 mL/kg/hr is defined as absolute oliguria; anuria as 0-0.5
mL/kg/hr. Dogs and cats with oligoanuric AKI have higher mortality
rates, as much as 20-fold increased risk of death compared with PU
pets.7,10

Evaluations
Oligoanuric patients should be evaluated for SQ edema (ch. 30),
increased respiratory rate and effort, presence of abdominal
distention or pain, as well as urinary bladder size (ch. 3).
Intravascular volume and hydration status should be assessed
serially. Initial diagnostics should include imaging to document the
size or volume of the urinary bladder (often achievable with portable
US machines), packed cell volume/total solids, serum chemistry with
electrolytes, and acid-base analysis. Thoracic radiographs and/or US

should be assessed when there is concern of pulmonary edema or
pleural effusion.

Treatment
The therapeutic approach to the oligoanuric patient is dependent on
their current volume and hydration status (Figure 300.2).
Hypovolemic patients should be treated with boluses of isotonic
replacement solutions, given rapidly IV (chs. 119-121). Dogs and cats
with decreased renal perfusion have appropriate reductions in UOP
secondary to activation of the RAAS and should be adequately
hydrated to achieve normal IV volume before definitively declaring
an oliguric or anuric state. Dogs and cats with stable cardiac function
but dehydrated should have their degree of dehydration estimated
via PE. The dehydration volume is calculated and replaced over 6-8
hours.130 Once rehydrated, appropriate UOP is >2 mL/kg/hr
depending on the rate of IV fluid administration. A UOP <2
mL/kg/hr would be considered oliguria in a hydrated pet receiving
IV fluids. Normally hydrated pets should be given isotonic
crystalloids at a volume equal to 3-5% of body weight, since
dehydration of <5% cannot be detected clinically. If UOP fails to
reach an appropriate magnitude (2-5 mL/kg/hr), pharmacologic
conversion to PU may be attempted.

Converting Oligoanuria to Polyuria (PU) With
Mannitol
Pharmacologic conversion from an oligo-anuria to a PU state is
commonly attempted. Studies in dogs and cats are lacking, but it
should be noted that numerous studies in people have demonstrated
that successful pharmacological induction of PU has no effect on
mortality.131 Hypervolemia in an oligoanuric patient is an indication
for extracorporeal renal replacement therapy, and referral for this
treatment should be considered early. In people, increasing UOP
after giving diuretics can delay referral for dialysis, potentially at the
expense of worse clinical outcomes.132 Mannitol (IV, 0.25-1 g/kg,
given over 15-20 minutes), an osmotic diuretic that decreases
cellular swelling, may help wash out obstructive casts and debris

from tubules and also may work as a free radical scavenger. If an
increase in UOP is achieved, mannitol can be given q4-6h or as a CRI
(60-120 mg/kg/hr). Mannitol should not be given to dehydrated
patients because it can further exacerbate intracellular dehydration.
It is contraindicated if overhydration is present and may worsen
pulmonary edema. Due to lack of evidence showing mannitol can
help prevent AKI and potential risks of hypervolemia secondary to
administration, consensus guidelines in people suggest that mannitol
not be used in patients with AKI.133 While used in euvolemic dogs
and cats, no study has reported its efficacy.

Converting Oligoanuria to Polyuria (PU) With
Furosemide
Furosemide is a loop diuretic which inhibits the Na-K-2Cl
transporter in the thick ascending loop of Henle. Experimental
models have shown potential benefits including decreased renal
oxygen consumption and less ischemic damage. It should be noted
that it is the concentration of furosemide within the tubular filtrate
and not the blood that determines effect.134 It enters the tubular
filtrate via active secretion in the proximal tubule and is filtered as
non-protein bound furosemide across the glomerular filtration
barrier. Anuric dogs and cats with minimal to no tubular flow are
unlikely to have furosemide reach the site of activity. Thus, it is often
ineffective in increasing UOP. Humans who fail to respond to
furosemide are more likely to have disease progression and greater
severity of AKI.135 Furosemide is usually given as an IV bolus or IM
at doses of 1-4 mg/kg. If an increased UOP is observed, the dose may
be repeated every 6-12 hours if needed or given as a CRI. The
function of the CRI is to maintain serum concentrations sufficient to
allow continuous accumulation within the tubular filtrate. Dogs and
cats who fail to respond to a furosemide bolus are unlikely to
respond to a CRI, as they likely have adequate serum concentrations
for several hours following bolus administration. Consensus
guidelines for human use suggest furosemide only be used in early or
established AKI for management of fluid balance, hyperK, and
hypercalcemia, but any putative role in amelioration of the AKI
course is unproven.136

Converting Oligoanuria to Polyuria (PU) With
Dopamine
Renal-dose dopamine, advocated for managing oliguric AKI due to
its effects on renal vasodilation, has shown limited to no
improvement in morbidity, mortality, or need for dialysis. Even at
low doses, dopamine is potentially toxic in critically ill patients. It
can induce tachyarrhythmias and myocardial ischemia.14 Dopamine
is not currently recommended in treating AKI in humans or
animals.137

Converting Oligoanuria to Polyuria (PU) With
Fenoldopam
Fenoldopam, a selective postsynaptic dopamine receptor agonist,
causes more potent renal vasodilation and natriuresis than
dopamine. However, it can also promote hypotension by decreasing
systemic vascular resistance. Fenoldopam increased UOP in healthy
cats,138 and it increased GFR and fractional exertion of Na in healthy
dogs.139,140 A retrospective study of fenoldopam use in dogs and cats
with AKI demonstrated no improvement in survival or length of
hospitalization.141

FIGURE 300.2 IV, Intravenous; PRN, pro re nata
(i.e., as needed); UOP, urine output.

Converting Oligoanuria to Polyuria (PU) With
Diltiazem
Diltiazem, a Ca channel blocker, may improve renal blood flow via
afferent arteriolar vasodilation, increasing GFR and UOP.142 It may
also be reno-protective by preventing intracellular Ca accumulation,
which can trigger cellular necrosis. Diltiazem given to dogs with AKI
secondary to leptospirosis did not improve rates of reducing serum
creatinine, recovery of renal function, or survival.68

EXTRACORPOREAL RENAL SUPPORT
THERAPY
Peritoneal Dialysis
Indications for renal support therapy include symptomatic uremia,
acidosis, hyperK, or volume overload refractory to medical
management.143 Peritoneal dialysis is relatively “low tech” but
requires intense and continuous monitoring. Peritoneal dialysis
temporarily replaces renal excretory function by using the
peritoneum as a semipermeable membrane across which unwanted
solutes are eliminated (ch. 102). It is contraindicated in patients
with abdominal wall trauma and/or peritoneal infections. Peritoneal
dialysis is also contraindicated in severe catabolic states in which
marked hypoalbuminemia exists because large amounts of protein
can be lost through the peritoneum during dialysis. The most
frequent complications are the development of peritonitis (22% of
dogs and cats), catheter occlusion, excessive protein loss, pleural
effusion, and dialysis disequilibrium syndrome (DDS). It is believed
that DDS is due to rapid removal of urea and other osmotic products,
which causes influx of water into brain cells. In turn, this causes
subsequent neurologic dysfunction.

Hemodialysis and Continuous Renal Replacement
Therapies (CRRTs)
These treatment options are becoming more widely available (ch.
103). They more efficiently remove uremic toxins. Treatment is
performed through a dedicated large-bore dual-lumen catheter and
blood is passed through a semipermeable device to remove uremic
toxins via a specifically designed machine. The 30-day survival for
dogs and cats was 42% and 48%, respectively, for those requiring
intermittent hemodialysis to manage AKI11; 1-year survival was 38%
in cats and 33% in dogs.

PROGNOSIS

There are limited studies of survival in veterinary AKI. AKI mortality
rate in humans is approximately 50%, changing little over the past
30 years, even with the availability of dialysis. Mortality rates differ
depending on the underlying cause. A meta-analysis of AKI
survival73 showed a pooled mortality rate of 45% in dogs and 53% for
cats. Animals with infectious etiologies of AKI had superior survival
to non-infectious causes. Retrospective studies of feline AKI show a
mortality rate of 47-64%.144,145 In one study all non-oliguric cats
survived, and all cats that died were oliguric or anuric. A canine
retrospective study showed a 56% mortality rate.123 Canine hospital
acquired AKI had a 62% mortality rate.10 This study showed that
dogs that were initially oliguric had a 20-fold greater risk of death
than non-oliguric dogs.
Justification for aggressive treatment of AKI lies in the possibility
of recovery of renal function following an insult. Renal tubular
epithelial cells are destroyed in AKI. After the initial insult, the
remaining viable tubular cells differentiate and proliferate leading to
restoration of the normal epithelium. Of dogs who survived AKI only
19% had serum creatinine concentrations return to within the
normal reference range. This occurred within 13 days for 75% of
these dogs. Approximately 55% of these dogs eventually developed
CKD.123 Only 25% of cats with AKI were discharged with plasma
creatinine concentration within reference range. About half of the
survivors had persistent azotemia.
In the limited veterinary literature 20-25% of AKI patients were
shown to have full recovery of renal function. Of those survivors who
never regained renal function or those who progressed to develop
chronic renal failure the survival times often exceeded 2 years. The
management of CKD can be promising and allow a good quality of
life for affected patients.

OVERVIEW OF CHRONIC KIDNEY
DISEASE (CKD)
DEFINITIONS AND CO-EXISTING CONDITIONS
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is defined as structural and/or
functional abnormalities of one or both kidneys that have been
continuously present for ≥3 months. CKD is usually irreversible and
progressive, even with treatment. It is common for prerenal or
postrenal azotemia, or for active kidney diseases, e.g., “acute-onchronic kidney disease,” to co-exist with CKD. In contrast to CKD,
many complications are reversible (e.g., pyelonephritis, ureteral

obstruction, dehydration, etc.). Therefore, appropriate diagnostic
workup and assessment of all contributing factors is important (ch.
299). After correcting reversible primary diseases and/or prerenal or
postrenal conditions, further improvement in kidney function may
not occur because compensatory and adaptive mechanisms designed
to sustain kidney function have largely already occurred, promoting
progressive loss of remaining nephrons and kidney function.

PREVALENCE AND AFFECTED
POPULATIONS
Recent prevalence estimates of CKD in primary care practice range
from 0.5-3.74% in dogs and 1.2-3.6% in cats.1-3 Age strongly
influences prevalence; CKD is often considered a disease of older
animals, particularly in cats. It was estimated that 15-30% of cats >15
years old had evidence of CKD,4 but a more recent study suggested a
prevalence of 80%.5 In that study, the prevalence was significantly
higher than previously reported even in younger cats (37.5% 0-4.9
years; 40.9% 5-9.9 years; 42.1% 10-14.9 years). In another study of
cats >9 years of age, 30.5% of cats developed azotemia within 12
months.6 A “renal disorder” was the most common cause of death in
cats >5 years old and the most common cause of death in Swedish
insured cats dying before the age of 12; incidences increase with
age.7,8 Dogs from the United Kingdom ≥12 years of age had 5.5 times
greater risk of having CKD than dogs 7 to 12 years old.3

CAUSES OF CKD
A DIAGNOSIS USUALLY MADE LATE IN THE
DISEASE PROCESS
CKD in dogs and cats is usually diagnosed late in the disease course,
not until azotemia is present. Typically, these kidneys are small
because lost nephrons are replaced by fibrosis and chronic
inflammation. Surviving nephrons have undergone compensatory

modifications, and progression due to maladaptive processes may
have occurred. As these lesions are non-specific, they fail to provide
much insight into the etiologic origin of injury. Thus, the initial
inciting cause of CKD is not usually determined, and likely may be
attributable to a series of renal insults over the life of the pet as
opposed to one specific cause.

DOGS
Canine CKD may begin due to any of a variety of familial, congenital,
or acquired conditions. Juvenile nephropathy (renal dysplasia) is
most likely in young animals (ch. 305). Tubulointerstitial nephritis
tends to be found in older dogs, similar to cats (ch. 303).
Glomerular disease appears to be significantly more common in dogs
than cats, likely accounting for the majority of CKD (ch. 302). The
proportion of dogs with CKD attributable to glomerular disease is
not known since renal biopsy is necessary for diagnosis and there is
inherent bias in dogs selected for biopsy. In a retrospective study of
501 dogs with proteinuria, immune-complex mediated glomerular
nephritis (ICGN) accounted for 48.1% of dogs biopsied and
amyloidosis for 15.2%. The remaining dogs had non-ICGN
conditions: 20.6% had focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS),
9% had non-ICGN glomerulopathy, 4.8% had non-ICGN
nephropathy, and 2.4% had tubulointerstitial disease.9 Glomerular
diseases may result from infectious diseases, e.g., borreliosis (ch.
187), ehrlichiosis (ch. 193), anaplasmosis (ch. 193), babesiosis (ch.
197), and leishmaniasis (ch. 197).10

CATS
Features seen histologically in cats with CKD most commonly
include tubulointerstitial inflammation, tubular atrophy, and
fibrosis, with secondary glomerulosclerosis. These features are often
described as the final common pathway after any one of many
possible renal insults. Specific renal diagnoses were made in only
∼16% of postmortem tissues from cats with CKD at first opinion

clinics.11 Various etiologies for tubulointerstitial nephritis have been
proposed, e.g., age, viral infection (feline immunodeficiency virus
[FIV] [ch. 198], feline morbillivirus [ch. 206]), extrarenal disease
(hyperthyroidism [ch. 287], dental disease [ch. 258], systemic
hypertension [ch. 236], heart disease [ch. 234]), environmental
factors (stress, vaccines [ch. 185], diet [chs. 148, 149, 158]),
ischemia, hypoxemia, and others.12,13 The majority of cats with CKD
never have a definitive cause identified. Their disease likely results
from a combination of factors that varies among individuals.12
The role that tubular lipid may have in causing disease appears to
be unique to cats.14,15 Once tubular damage and cell death occurs,
lipid released into the interstitium may serve as a nidus of
inflammation and subsequent fibrosis. Since the incidence of feline
CKD substantially increases with age, this process merits special
consideration. Not only does this substantiate the theory that
multiple small injuries to the kidney over the lifetime of the cat
culminate in clinical disease, but the aged kidney has increased
susceptibility to injury; changes within the kidney such as senescence
and loss of telomere length, which have been documented in feline
CKD, mean that recovery and repair after injury are less
effective.16,17

STAGING CKD
OVERVIEW
Once the diagnosis of CKD has been confirmed and the dog or cat is
stable, International Renal Interest Society (IRIS) staging should be
performed. This four-tier system in cats and dogs is based on renal
function (Table 301.1). The system further subclassifies pets
according to the magnitude of their proteinuria and/or arterial blood
pressure (BP), facilitating application of appropriate guidelines for
developing management strategies and establishing prognosis.3,18,19

ASSIGNING IRIS CKD STAGE

Staging CKD is based on serum creatinine concentrations (Table
301.1), the most commonly used estimate of glomerular filtration
rate (GFR) in dogs, cats, and humans. Since creatinine has limited
specificity and sensitivity, staging should be based on a minimum of
2 results obtained several weeks apart when the dog or cat is fasted
and well hydrated. Clinical status should be considered when
interpreting creatinine, other laboratory tests, and when planning
treatment strategies. Variability in results from different
laboratories, patient-specific characteristics (e.g., breed, age, sex,
body condition and lean body mass), and transient prerenal or
postrenal events can influence the creatinine. Reduced muscle mass,
a common manifestation of advanced CKD (muscle condition score
charts are found inside the covers; ch. 151), may substantially
reduce creatinine concentrations relative to true GFR, particularly in
cats. IRIS therefore suggests that symmetric dimethylarginine values
may be used to modify IRIS CKD staging in dogs and cats where
body muscle mass is markedly reduced (www.iris-kidney.com).

SUBSTAGING IRIS CKD
Because it may be useful therapeutically and prognostically, the IRIS
staging system further subclassifies CKD using the magnitude of
proteinuria and/or arterial BP. Systemic arterial BPs and urine
protein should be determined several times over a period of weeks
(ch. 91). Before determining the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio
(UPCR), urinalysis (UA) and urine culture should be checked to rule
out infection, hemorrhage, or inflammation as a cause for increased
UPCR. The urine sediment should be inactive before performing a
UPCR. Unless markedly elevated or <0.2, it is recommended that the
UPCR be rechecked 2 to 3 times over at least 2 weeks, using the
average to classify the pet as proteinuric, nonproteinuric, or
borderline (Table 301.1). Urine collected at home has lower UPCR
values than samples collected in-hospital (ch. 299).20,21 Pets with
borderline proteinuria should be reevaluated after 2 months. In
some pets, classification of proteinuria may change as their disease
progresses or in response to therapy (ch. 302).

CLINICAL CONSEQUENCES AND
MEDICAL MANAGEMENT OF CKD
OVERVIEW AND GOALS IN MANAGEMENT
In general, dogs and cats with CKD have three major areas of
biologic dysfunction: (1) disturbed excretion of electrolytes and
water, (2) reduced excretion of organic solutes (i.e., uremic toxins),
and (3) impaired renal hormone synthesis. Impaired renal function
is correlated with degree of tubulointerstitial inflammation, tubular
atrophy, and tubulointerstitial fibrosis.11,14 CKD is a progressive
disease; no treatment short of renal transplantation has been shown
to reverse or halt declining renal function and only a few cats with
CKD are acceptable transplantation candidates. Medical
management, therefore, is the treatment mainstay and can help
minimize metabolic complications and work to slow progression
(Box 301.1).

The first step in developing a feasible long-term management plan
for dogs and cats with CKD is understanding owner goals and their
ability to administer medications. Treatment recommendations
should be individualized and based on each pet’s clinical and
laboratory status, and the likelihood of a medication being of
benefit.22 Treatment plans are unlikely to be followed if too involved,
time consuming, expensive, or perceived as negatively affecting
quality of life or disrupting the human-animal bond. Given the sheer
volume of medications that may be employed for CKD and knowing
that feeding tubes are not always used, treatments may need to be
ranked in order of importance. Owner education is a top priority (ch.
1). Adherence improves when owners understand why a medication
is being recommended and its potential outcome. Because CKD is
progressive and dynamic, serial clinical and laboratory assessments
allow informed therapy modifications. Fostering a strong
relationship between the veterinary care team and the pet owner
facilitates chances of the pet receiving the best care through the
stages of CKD.

CKD–MINERAL BONE DISORDERS
(CKD-MBD)
Pathophysiology
Phosphorus (PO4) in Early CKD
As kidney disease progresses, appropriate processing of calcium
(Ca), phosphate (PO4), and magnesium (Mg) declines, causing
parathyroid hormone (PTH), fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23),
and calcitriol to become dysregulated. Together with their associated
clinical manifestations, this is referred to as CKD-MBD.23-26
Mechanisms involved in CKD-MBD are different between early and
late stages of CKD. In early disease, as GFR and PO4 excretion starts
to decline, PO4 retention becomes a key mediator in CKD-MBD if
intake is not decreased. PO4 retention leads to production of the
phosphaturic hormone FGF23 which acts to decrease PO4 by

downregulating transporters responsible for PO4 regulation in
proximal tubules (NPT2a, NPT2c), decreasing PO4 absorption from
the gastrointestinal (GI) tract indirectly by inhibiting renal 1-alphahydroxylase activity which converts calcidiol to calcitriol, and by
inhibiting PTH secretion. In early CKD when nephron mass is
sufficient to excrete PO4 adequately these actions are able to control
PO4 retention.

Phosphorus (PO4), PTH, and FGF23 as CKD
Progresses
As CKD progresses, FGF23 no longer adequately mitigates PO4
retention due to the low number of functioning nephrons,
stimulating PTH synthesis and leading to renal secondary
hyperparathyroidism (RSHP). PTH primarily regulates Ca but
secondarily controls PO4. PTH, similar to FGF23, increases renal
excretion of PO4 by downregulating NPT2a transporters. PO4
concentrations do not need to be above the reference range to initiate
these processes. In one study of dogs with Stage 1 CKD, 36% had
RSHP but only 18% were hyperPO4.27 Therefore elevations in FGF23
or PTH are likely indicative of subclinical PO4 retention, referred to
as the “trade-off hypothesis.” Here, PO4 concentrations can only be
controlled with elevated FGF23 and PTH concentrations, with
deleterious consequences.
FGF23 continues to be increased as CKD progresses because a) it
is freely filtered at the glomerulus and susceptible to declining GFR,
b) hyperPO4 becomes more prevalent in later stages, continuing to
stimulate FGF23 secretion, and c) downregulation of receptors on

target organs leads to FGF23 resistance and decreased ability to
inhibit PTH.25 PTH stimulates Ca and PO4 efflux from bone and
normally stimulates calcitriol to increase GI Ca and PO4 absorption.
In CKD, however, calcitriol synthesis is no longer adequate due to
decreased renal mass and it is inhibited by increasing concentrations
of FGF23. Relative and absolute calcitriol deficiency, worsening with
disease stage, has been described in dogs with CKD and is thought to
play a pivotal role in RSHP as calcitriol is a major inhibitor of PTH
synthesis.28,29 Impaired GI absorption of Ca due to low serum
calcitriol and subsequent hypocalcemia (hypoCa) further drives
RSHP. Due to downregulation of Ca receptors on the parathyroids,
they become resistant to feedback from calcitriol and FGF23 (chs.
68, 283).25 The sum result of these mechanisms is hyperPO4,
hypoCa, and calcitriol deficiency, despite markedly increased PTH
and FGF23. Chronically elevated PTH leads to demineralization of
bone (Figure 301.1) and, in combination with hyperPO4, soft tissue
mineralization results in non-renal clinical manifestations of CKDMBD (ch. 162).

CKD-MBD in Dogs and Cats
FGF23
FGF23 concentrations were increased in cats with early nonazotemic CKD and were higher in cats that went on to develop
azotemia within a year, indicating it may be useful as a marker of
early disease.30 When cats of the same IRIS stage were compared,
FGF23 was found to be higher in cats with hyperPO4.26 FGF23
increases with IRIS stage and is positively correlated with serum
creatinine concentrations.26,30 In dogs, FGF23 is significantly higher
in Stage 3 and 4 disease when compared with Stages 1 and 2, but
increases still occur early in disease.31 Increased FGF23 was more
frequent than increases in PTH or PO4 in one study, providing
evidence for the initiating role of FGF23 in the sequence of events
leading to RSHP.29,31,32 In both species FGF23 is correlated with

PTH concentrations.26,31 Also, increased FGF23 is associated with a
high risk of disease progression and death.32,33

Renal Secondary Hyperparathyroidism (RSHP; ch.
162)
Prevalence of RSHP increases with IRIS stage in both cats and dogs.
In cats, the overall prevalence of RSHP was 84% in 1 study, with all
cats in end-stage CKD affected.34 Although RSHP can occur in cats
prior to the development of azotemia and mineral abnormalities, it is
more common in cats in Stage 4 disease vs Stage 2.26,35 RSHP was
documented in 75.9% of dogs with CKD. The prevalence and severity
increases with IRIS stage (36.4% Stage 1, 50% Stage 2, 96% Stage 3,
100% Stage 4).27,31,32 Although PTH has been claimed to be a
uremic toxin responsible for many clinical signs of uremia,36 a
correlation with prognosis has not been established and clinical
benefits of reducing PTH have not been conclusively documented.

Clinical Consequences of CKD-MBD
Hyperphosphatemia
PO4 retention and subsequent development of hyperPO4 is a main
factor in disease progression. HyperPO4 is associated with poorer
survival in humans, cats, and dogs with CKD.18,19,32 Higher plasma
PO4 concentration has been shown to predict progression in cats: a 1
mg/dL (0.32 mmol/L) increase was associated with a 41% increase
in risk of progression.19 In people with CKD, every 1 mg/dL increase
in serum PO4 is associated independently with increased risk of
kidney failure and mortality.37 Mortality risk associated with
hyperPO4 appears independent of increases in PTH, which alone
appeared to have only a weak association with survival.32,33 Ca ×
PO4 product is also important as it increases with disease severity in
both species and is associated with decreased survival in

dogs.29,32,38,39 This is consistent with data in humans where Ca ×
PO4 products >72 ([mg/dL]2) were associated with decreased
survival.40 Ca × PO4 product may be an indicator of dystrophic
mineralization associated with CKD-MBD.23,25

Hypercalcemia (HyperCa), Hypocalcemia (HypoCa)
Concentrations of total (tCa), ionized (iCa), and complexed Ca
(bound to PO4, bicarbonate, citrate, or lactate) vary widely in pets
with CKD (ch. 69).41 The prevalence of increased tCa was 10-32% in
cats with CKD, which increases with disease severity.34,42,43 In a
study assessing risk of hyperCa, 31.4% of cats with CKD developed
increases in tCa within a median of 175 days of CKD diagnosis.44
When iCa was assessed in 47 cats with various stages of CKD,
increases were identified in 6% and decreases in 26%. iCa was
significantly lower in cats with CKD than in healthy cats: >50% of
cats with advanced CKD had decreases in iCa.34 In another study,
iCa was increased in 29.4% and decreased in 9.8% of cats with CKD
but disease stage was not assigned.42 Dogs with Stage 1 or 2 CKD
uncommonly have abnormal tCa or iCa concentrations; none had an
increased Ca. However, 16% of dogs in CKD Stage 3 and 12.5% in
Stage 4 had increased tCa. Decreases in iCa were documented in 40%
Stage 3 and 87.5% Stage 4 CKD dogs.27

FIGURE 301.1 Light microscopy images of
tranverse cross-section of feline femur in (A) cat
with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and (B) healthy

One. 2014;9:e110057.
Serum tCa concentrations do not reliably reflect iCa
concentrations, particularly in dogs and cats with CKD.41,44,45 In 1
study, the majority of cats with increases in tCa also had increases in
iCa, but tCa was normal in a number of cats with low iCa.44 They
concluded that ionized hyperCa should be considered if iCa is within
the upper half of the reference range. Lower serum bicarbonate was a
risk factor for failure of tCa to predict iCa, implying a role for
metabolic acidosis.
In dogs, tCa results tend to overestimate iCa45 and metabolic
acidosis does not explain this discrepancy.41 Increased tCa despite
normal to reduced iCa concentrations is likely explained by increased
concentrations of complexed Ca.41 Because of these effects, formulas

developed to “correct” for variations in serum albumin are not useful
in dogs and cats with CKD, and iCa should be measured directly for a
more accurate assessment of CKD-MBD. Abnormal Ca has not been
associated with prognosis, but hyperCa does raise the Ca × PO4
product.

Magnesium (Mg)
Mg is essential for many intracellular processes and may have a
significant role in CKD. Actions of Mg include inhibition of vascular
calcification, release of profibrotic cytokines, and, possibly, a role in
regulating FGF23. Mg appears to modify risks associated with
hyperPO4. Increased serum PO4 was only associated with higher risk
of CKD progression and death in people with hypoMg and the same
may be true in cats46,47; 12% of CKD cats had total hypoMg (Stage
II: 9%; Stage III: 18%; Stage IV: 10%). The hypoMg was associated
with higher FGF23 concentrations and independently associated
with systemic hypertension and an increased risk of death.47 Low
plasma Mg was also associated with increased FGF23
concentrations. HyperMg is more common in cats with Stage IV
disease because renal excretion is compromised in later
stages.34,47,48 In a study of CKD cats with nephrolithiasis, 38.1% had
hyperMg and 14.3% had hypoMg, both linked to higher mortality
and imply a role for Mg in CKD-MBD.48 Incidence data have not
been published in dogs.

Renal Osteodystrophy
Chronic increases in PTH may cause leaching of mineral from bone
due to osteoclast activation resulting in a spectrum of bone disorders
referred to as renal osteodystrophy. In dogs this most commonly
manifests as fibrous osteodystrophy of the maxillae and mandibles
and is usually seen in younger pets. Bones of the skull and mandible
may be so demineralized that the teeth are moveable and fibrous
changes obvious, particularly in the maxilla (

Video 162.1).

Marked proliferation of connective tissue in the maxillary area may
distort the face. This condition is rarely reported in cats.23 In

contrast, significant bone fragility due to increased bone resorption,
decreased bone mineral density and decreased thickness has been
described in cats with CKD, and to a lesser extent in dogs.49,50 These
studies confirm the pathophysiologic effects of CKD-MBD on bone in
this patient population.

Soft Tissue Mineralization and Nephrolithiasis
Renal mineralization and nephrolithiasis are considered
manifestations of CKD-MBD and are common in CKD, particularly
in cats. In a study assessing renal histopathologic findings of cats
with CKD, 21% of non-azotemic control cats had mineralization. In
comparison, in cats with CKD, renal mineralization was documented
in 54% of Stage II, 50% of Stage III, and 58% of Stage IV cats.11
Tubules with mineralization had greater interstitial fibrosis,
inflammation, and glomerular obsolescence. It is not known if
mineralization is a cause or an effect.
Nephroliths are usually composed of Ca oxalate (98% of
ureteroliths in 1 study51). In that study, 62% of cats with ureteral
calculi also had renal calculi. In a case-control study of 14 CKD cats
in Stage II or III, nephrolithiasis unassociated with urinary
obstruction was not associated with increased mortality rates or rate
of disease progression.52 However, it is not always clear from
diagnostic imaging whether mineralization is embedded within
kidney parenchyma or the pelvis, where it could dislodge. Dislodged
material poses the greatest risk because ureteroliths can cause lifethreatening acute-on-chronic crises that require prompt intervention
for the best outcome (chs. 117, 300 and 306).

Non-Renal Mineralization
Soft tissue and/or vascular wall calcification has been widely
documented in people with CKD, but there is less evidence in dogs or
cats.23,24 A few case reports have documented soft tissue
calcification in cats, including footpads, interdigital tissues, and
radiographic evidence of mineralization within the gastric wall and
aorta (thoracic and abdominal). Affected cats had a Ca × PO4

product >70 mg2/dL2. In another study, gastric wall mineralization
was described in 38% of CKD cats at necropsy but only in cats in
Stage 3 and 4.38 Three cats in this study also had evidence of
vascular mineralization. Cats with gastric mineralization had higher
Ca × PO4 products.

Parathyroid Gland Enlargement
RSHP may be associated with enlarged parathyroid glands (ch.
283).34 In one report, hyperplastic parathyroid glands were palpable
as paratracheal masses in 11 of 80 cats with CKD.53 This is of clinical
importance in cats because hyperthyroidism is also common and
palpation of a cervical mass logically may raise suspicion of thyroid
rather than parathyroid disease. Care should be taken to confirm
either condition prior to starting treatment.

Treatment of CKD-MBD and RSHP
Dietary PO4 Restriction (ch. 158)
To compensate for decreasing PO4 excretion as CKD progresses,
dietary intake of PO4 must be reduced. Most maintenance diets
contain substantial quantities of PO4, with protein typically
contributing significantly to its content. It is a common
misconception that the main purpose of renal diets is protein
restriction. There is little consensus on how much protein should be
in renal diets, but there is significant evidence regarding the
importance of PO4 restriction.25,54 Renal diets are typically
formulated to have reduced amounts of PO4, modified amounts of
high-quality protein, increased caloric density, added soluble fiber
and B vitamins, increased omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid and
antioxidant content, and to have a neutral effect on acid–base
balance. Renal diets for cats should be supplemented with potassium
(K). “Early-stage PO4-restricted renal diets” that are less protein
restricted are available for cats.54 Recent evidence also suggests that

both PO4 amount and its form are important.54 PO4 from inorganic
sources (e.g., Na or K salts) are more bioavailable than PO4 from
organic sources (e.g., meat, bone meal, grains). Additionally, dietary
Ca:PO4 ratios are important. Feeding highly bioavailable PO4 salts
together with too little Ca has been documented to lead to renal
damage in previously healthy cats.55-57 Studies have demonstrated
efficacy in treating CKD and improved outcomes by decreasing
serum concentrations of PO4, PTH, and FGF23.58-60 Evidence also
suggests that even if serum PO4 is normal, PO4-restricted diets are
potentially beneficial by decreasing FGF23.60 A detailed review of
this evidence can be found elsewhere.25
The therapeutic goal for managing serum PO4 concentrations is
based on the IRIS CKD stage of the pet. The goal may be within the
“normal” reference range (Table 301.2). Evidence from clinical
trials supports these therapeutic goals, suggesting that maintaining
PO4 <4.5 mg/dL (<1.45 mmol/L) for Stage 2 and <5.0 mg/dL (<1.6
mmol/L) for Stage 3 improves survival and palliates CKD-MBD.25
Recommendations are unclear for pets with IRIS Stage 1 CKD.
Serum PO4 concentration should be assessed after a 12-hour fast to
avoid post-prandial variability. Dietary therapy may take several
weeks to have a discernable effect; in cats with CKD, full dietary
effect required 28 to 49 days.58 Thus, serum PO4 concentrations
should be rechecked 4-6 weeks after initiating a new diet. If in the
target range, the diet should be continued and the PO4 rechecked
every 3 to 4 months (every 4-6 months may be adequate for IRIS
CKD Stage II dogs and cats). Control of PO4 is more likely achieved
with a renal diet alone in patients with Stage 2 and 3 CKD. If diet
alone fails to achieve the PO4 target after 4-6 weeks, an intestinal
binding agent should be added.

Phosphate Binders and Diet

Actions
PO4 is absorbed from the small intestine by both passive diffusion
and active transport, the latter of which is mediated by the NPT2b
transporter. The goal of treatment is to bind PO4 within the GI tract
before it can be absorbed. Owner education is critical because these
drugs must be given at or around meal time to accomplish this goal.
PO4 binders should be dosed “to effect”; adjusted from the starting
dosage, as needed every 2 to 4 weeks, to achieve a targeted serum
PO4 concentration. If a dosage substantially exceeds the
recommended range, it is best to add a binding agent with a different
mechanism of action rather than risk overdosage. PO4 binders are
likely ineffective in anorexic pets. Since they are often unpalatable,
management of anorexia (ch. 17) should address appetite and
appropriate renal diets before using PO4 binders.
Giving PO4 binders to a dog or cat being fed a maintenance diet
will not be effective. The high PO4 content of maintenance diets may
greatly limit the effectiveness of binding agents or will require
substantially higher doses to attempt efficacy, potentially resulting in
more side-effects. Administration of 1500 to 2500 mg of aluminum
carbonate to dogs with moderate CKD failed to consistently correct
hyperphosphatemia when dogs were fed diets containing greater
than 1% PO4 on a dry matter basis.61 When sucralfate was given to
normal cats ingesting maintenance diets, there was no change in
serum PO4 concentration.62

Selecting a PO4 Binder
Several different PO4 binders are available (Table 301.3). Before
selecting a binder, the iCa concentration should be assessed and if
increased, Ca-based PO4 binders are contraindicated. Aluminum
hydroxide based agents; available, effective, inexpensive; are a
common first-line choice in dogs and cats.23,63 Although typically
well tolerated and safe in dogs and cats, they are poorly palatable and

can cause constipation.62,63 Aluminum toxicosis (neurologic and
neuromuscular signs, microcytosis) has been reported in dogs with
advanced CKD given high doses (126-200 mg/kg/day) via feeding
tube.64 The level of risk is unknown when these drugs are given
orally because most pets would refuse to eat such quantities.
Ca-based binders are effective, but have lower PO4 binding affinity
than aluminum, may require larger doses,63 and are not
recommended in hyperCa or with evidence of calcification.23,63 Cabased PO4 binders may cause hyperCa, especially if co-administered
with calcitriol. This combination should be avoided. iCa should be
monitored in dogs and cats given Ca-based PO4 binder.
Lanthanum salts can be quite effective in binding PO4 and are
common second or third tier options.23,63 Lanthanum causes few
side-effects because it has minimal systemic absorption, reducing
risk of toxicosis when compared to aluminum salts. It is accepted
and tolerated by cats. Lanthanum carbonate inhibits GI oxalate
absorption, preventing nephrocalcinosis in a rat model.65,66
Sevelamer hydrochloride, an organic polymer not commonly used in
dogs or cats, has been reported to exacerbate metabolic acidosis.
Sevelamer carbonate is preferred because of its carbonate buffer and
it is less likely to cause GI upset.63 Lanthanum and sevelamer are
generally far more expensive than aluminum or Ca-based PO4
binders and tend to not be available in formulations appropriate for
dogs or cats, limiting their use.

Cinacalcet
Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic drug that acts directly on Ca sensing
receptors in the parathyroid gland to reduce PTH secretion and
lower the serum Ca. While not used often in dogs or cats, it is widely
used in humans to combat CKD-MBD. Dosages extrapolated from
people are 0.5 mg/kg once daily. Starting low helps avoid hypoCa
and the dosage can be increased every 2-3 weeks until PO4 and Ca
are controlled or a maximum dose of 3 mg/kg is reached.23

Anecdotally the medication appears well tolerated with nausea and
vomiting as the most common side-effect.

Calcitriol (Vitamin D3)
Calcitriol has a rapid onset of action (about 1 day) and brief half-life
(<1 day), which allows rapid correction of overdose when the drug is
stopped (ch. 284). Calcitriol increases GI absorption of both Ca and
PO4, which should suppress secretion of PTH. The benefits of giving
calcitriol to dogs or cats with CKD are unclear. Results of 1 clinical
trial indicated that calcitriol reduced mortality in dogs in CKD Stages
III or IV by slowing disease progression.67 However, despite
anecdotal reports of improved demeanor in both cats and dogs,
calcitriol failed to decrease PTH in cats with CKD.36,68 Studies did
not confirm or refute drug-related improvement in clinical signs.
Calcitriol should not be given to dogs or cats with increases in either
serum PO4 or iCa. It is unclear whether nephroliths are a
contraindication; caution is recommended. Calcitriol dose, initiated
at 2.0-2.5 ng/kg daily, should not exceed 5 ng/kg/day and it should
be given on an empty stomach. Administration with food increases
Ca absorption and risk of hyperCa. Cost may be a concern for many
owners as the drug and required monitoring can both be costly;
careful monitoring of iCa, PO4, and PTH levels is required to avoid or
identify calcitriol-induced hyperCa. If hyperCa is identified, calcitriol
should be immediately discontinued. HyperCa is more likely to occur
when calcitriol therapy is combined with Ca-containing PO4 binding
agents.
