UREMIA AND UREMIC TOXINS
Definitions and Pathophysiology
Uremia, literally defined as “urine in the blood,” refers both to the
accumulation of substances as a result of declining renal function
and their clinical manifestations. Uremia globally includes abnormal
electrolyte, organic solute, and hormonal balances. Creatinine and
blood urea nitrogen (BUN), the best known organic solutes excreted
by the kidneys, are but 2 of about 146 recognized organic solutes that
are putative uremic toxins.69 Importantly, many of these substances
are not actively regulated; their levels progressively increase with
declining GFR. Although abnormally increased circulating
concentrations of a substance do not equal disease, numerous
uremic toxins that accumulate in CKD are known to have deleterious

effects. The waste products of protein catabolism (e.g., indoxyl
sulfate, p-cresyl sulfate) are of particular interest because they are
thought to have negative pathophysiologic effects and also contribute
to the clinical syndrome of uremia. Problematically, some uremic
toxins are not amenable to removal by hemodialysis (ch. 103).69
The accumulation of indoxyl sulfate and p-cresyl sulfate contributes
to the progression of CKD by promoting renal fibrosis, inducing
inflammation which damages renal tubular cells, and by stimulating
continued glomerular sclerosis.70-74 Uremic toxins contribute to
morbidity and mortality by impairing the neurologic system,75
lowering erythropoietin (EPO) synthesis,76 decreasing bone
turnover, and increasing the risk of cardiovascular disease.77-79
Uremic toxins are produced in the colon via protein
fermentation.80-82 Uremia associated with CKD negatively impacts
the GI microbiome in humans and rats, causing GI dysbiosis (ch.
260).83,84 This dysbiosis enhances production of colonic-derived
uremic toxins such as indoxyl sulfate and p-cresol sulfate, initiating a
vicious cycle.81,82,85 There is relatively limited information
regarding uremic toxins, the microbiome, and their link to kidney
disease in dogs and cats. Cats with CKD have been documented to
have fecal dysbiosis, decreased fecal microbial diversity and richness
based on 16S ribosomal rRNA gene sequencing.86 Indoxyl sulfate
concentrations increase in cats and dogs with CKD and are
associated with disease progression.87,88

Management
Diet
Due to the potential negative effects of uremic toxins and the
inability of dialysis to completely remove them, human medicine has
focused on strategies to decrease their production. Strategies include
modulation of bacterial growth in the colon with diet,89 prebiotics,
probiotics, and targeted adsorption of uremic toxins.81,84,90
Decreasing uremic toxin concentrations and clinical signs of uremia

through decreasing dietary protein has been a central tenet in
veterinary renal diets (ch. 158). However, there is no strong
evidence demonstrating that limiting protein intake decreases
uremic toxins or clinical signs of uremia, hence the debate,
particularly in cats, regarding protein content in renal diets.91-93
Current recommendations for restriction of protein center more
around palliating proteinuria in dogs, with a delicate balance
between the treatment goal and maintaining lean body mass.54 A key
concept for success is the maintenance of adequate caloric intake
when feeding a modified protein diet.

Medications to Decrease Gut-Derived Uremic Toxins
There is little literature on additional strategies to decrease gutderived uremic toxins in dogs or cats with CKD. Therapies targeting
“enteric dialysis” (e.g., Azodyl, Porus One) are available and may be
beneficial, but clinical trials are lacking. Given the wealth of rodent
and human literature in this area, further exploration of potential
therapeutic targets seems warranted.

DYSREXIA, NAUSEA, VOMITING
Clinical Presentation
Clinical signs of nausea, vomiting (ch. 48), and/or poor appetite
(ch. 17) causing weight loss (ch. 18) and poor muscle mass are
common in CKD.3,43,53 Appetite may be selective for certain foods,
may wax and wane, and behaviors associated with eating may
become abnormal. In a survey of owners of cats with CKD, 43% of
respondents reported abnormal appetite in their cat necessitating
77% of those owners to coax the pet to eat more than 50% of the
time.94 Adequate caloric support is crucial for chronically ill pets,
especially as there is evidence that CKD is an increased metabolic
state, making adequate nutrition even more of a challenge.95 In
addition to dysrexia, nausea, vomiting, and reduced nutrient intake,
other factors promote weight loss and cachexia (ch. 151). These
include hormonal changes, metabolic derangements, and catabolic

factors related to uremia, particularly acidosis. Poor body condition
score (inside covers) is associated with a poorer prognosis in dogs
and cats with CKD.96,97 Cats often have lost weight before CKD is
diagnosed and then continue to lose weight.97 A study assessing
quality of life parameters in cats with CKD revealed lower scores
than healthy young or geriatric cats in the categories of “appetite”
and “liking food.”98 Poor appetite is perceived as a significant quality
of life concern and can cause significant emotional distress to
owners.99

Pathophysiology
It has long been thought that uremia has effects on the GI tract, e.g.,
hyperacidity, uremic gastritis, and ulceration that lead to further
unwillingness to eat. Understanding this pathophysiology in cats and
dogs is evolving. Cats with CKD have increases in serum gastrin
concentrations that parallel CKD severity,100 but relationships
between gastrin, gastric acid secretion, and gastric pathology have
not been fully described. Since gastrin is renally excreted, it is
hypothesized that as renal function declines, hypergastrinemia and
gastric hyperacidity develop.100 Cats with gastrin-secreting tumors
and hypergastrinemia at concentrations similar to those in cats with
CKD have significant gastric disease (ch. 297), but this has not been
demonstrated in cats with CKD.101,102 In human CKD the
development of gastric hyperacidity appears to be inconsistent and
may be related to the presence of Helicobacter spp. infection.103
Gastric fibrosis and mineralization are more prominent alterations in
cats with CKD than are uremic gastropathy lesions previously
described in dogs and humans (uremic gastritis, ulceration, vascular
injury, edema).102 Additionally, uremic gastropathy has not been
reported as severe in dogs as in humans. Positive fecal occult blood
tests have been documented in dogs and cats with CKD, but the
mechanism of GI bleeding and responses to treatment have not been
assessed.104,105 GI hemorrhage in cats and dogs with CKD may be
more attributable to factors such as uremic thrombocytopathia

rather than the relatively rare overt ulcerative lesions.106 Thus,
giving gastric protectants may not be justified without clinical
evidence of GI hemorrhage.
Uremic toxins, sensed by the chemoreceptor trigger zone of the
area postrema in the brain, stimulate emesis via the vomiting center.
Experimental ablation of the area postrema inhibits uremic vomiting
in dogs after total nephrectomy, illustrating the involvement of this
structure.107 In addition to build up of uremic toxins and GI tract
alterations, the physiology of appetite regulation may be significantly
abnormal in pets with CKD. Appetite regulation is a complex system
involving many signaling compounds. As a refined summary:
regulation is comprised of orexigenic hormones that activate the
hunger center (i.e., ghrelin) and anorexigenic hormones that activate
the brain’s satiety center (i.e., leptin, cholecystokinin, obestatin, desacyl ghrelin).108 People with CKD accumulate anorexigenic
substances secondary to decreased GFR without concomitant
increases in orexigenic substances such as ghrelin. Anorexigenic
substances have also been demonstrated to be significantly higher in
CKD patients with poor body condition.108 Thus there is likely a
diminished signal to support appetite in the CKD patient.

Management
Assessment
Serial evaluations of nutritional status are key to CKD patient
management. An individualized nutrition plan should be developed
for each pet (chs. 145 and 158). Nutritional assessment includes
body weight, body condition score (ch. 72; textbook’s inside covers),
muscle condition score (textbook’s inside covers), adequacy of
caloric intake (including open-ended questions about how the pet is
eating, ch. 1), and a complete dietary history (including pet food,
treats, supplements and items used to give medications, ch. 145).
Assessment of muscle mass is particularly important in CKD, as it
can have a profound effect on serum creatinine and affect the
interpretation of the severity of disease, as well as have notable
implications for the nutritional status of the patient.

Gastric Acid Suppressants
There is little evidence that gastric ulceration and hyperacidity are
common in dogs and cats with CKD. The prophylactic use of H2blockers (e.g., famotidine, ranitidine), proton pump inhibitors
(omeprazole, pantoprazole, esomeprazole) and sucralfate is not
recommended in pets with IRIS Stage I-III disease.109 Additional
studies are needed before recommendations are made for those with
IRIS Stage IV disease. In general, gastric acid suppression should
only be given to dogs or cats with a clinical suspicion of GI
ulceration. Chronic administration of these medications may not be
benign. Use of proton pump inhibitors in people has been linked
with acute kidney injury (AKI). Chronic use may cause derangements
in Ca, PTH, and bone health in people, but no similar conclusion has
been drawn in cats.109-112 If utilized, it should be noted that
omeprazole (1 mg/kg q12h) is more effective at acid suppression than
famotidine,113 and tolerance to famotidine quickly develops when
given q12h.114

Antiemetic Therapy
Antiemetic therapy may be useful in managing uremic nausea and
vomiting (ch. 48). Antiemetic drugs may not directly improve
appetite unless they also target nausea, but they may minimize loss
of food and fluids via emesis. Maropitant (NK-1) and ondansetron
(5-HT3) act on the chemoreceptor trigger zone as well as in the gut.
Oral maropitant (4 mg/cat/day for 2 weeks) has been an effective
antiemetic for cats with IRIS CKD Stages II and III.115 Maropitant
can be used in dogs and cats with CKD (1-2 mg/kg/day PO or 1
mg/kg/day SQ or IV). It is commonly used for longer than the 5-day
recommended treatment period, specific to the label indication for
acute vomiting. While ondansetron has been documented to be
effective in uremic humans, pharmacokinetic studies have indicated
comparatively poor bioavailability when given orally with a short
half-life in cats and dogs.116,117 Parenteral ondansetron (0.5-1 mg/kg
SQ) has better bioavailability and a longer half-life in cats than oral
administration.117

Appetite Stimulation Therapy in Cats
Oral mirtazapine is an effective appetite stimulant in cats with CKD
and can increase body weight (ch. 17).118 Mirtazapine also appears
to have antiemetic properties in cats with CKD.115 Hyperactivity and
vocalization are side-effects and are generally dose-dependent. As
the drug is eliminated through the kidneys, smaller doses are
recommended (1.87 mg orally q48h) in cats with CKD.118
Mirtazapine can be administered transdermally and has been
demonstrated to achieve appropriate serum levels, appetite
stimulation, and weight gain in cats.119-121 The appetite effect of
transdermal preparations is much more subtle than oral mirtazapine
due to a flatter drug concentration curve that causes fewer sideeffects.119,120 The transdermal ointment is FDA approved for
unintended weight loss (Mirataz; 2 mg applied to inner ear pinna
q24h) and efficacy has been documented in pharmacokinetic and
pharmacodynamics studies.119,121 CKD cats do not appear to require
less frequent dosing with transdermal application of this product,
but each cat should be considered individually.

Appetite Stimulation Therapy in Dogs
Anecdotally mirtazapine is less effective in dogs than cats. A study in
6 Beagles indicated that dogs may have a different pharmacokinetic
profile compared to cats and humans, with a much shorter half-life
for oral mirtazapine.122 A starting dose of 0.6-1 mg/kg PO q12h may
be more appropriate.

Ghrelin Agonist Appetite Stimulation in Dogs and
Cats
The ghrelin agonist capromorelin is an FDA-approved appetite
stimulant for dogs (Entyce) and cats (Elura) that targets
pathophysiology of regulation, appropriate given the dysregulation
that likely exists in CKD. Studies in cats (2 mg/kg PO q24h) and dogs
(3 mg/kg PO q24h) have demonstrated that capromorelin increases
appetite and weight.123,124 The most common adverse effects

reported in a pivotal clinical trial in dogs were diarrhea (7.0%),
vomiting (6.4%), polydipsia (4.1%) and hypersalivation (2.3%).123 A
pivotal field study assessing a cat-specific formulation (2 mg/kg
orally) for managing weight loss in CKD did result in significant
increases in weight.124 The most common adverse events were
vomiting, hypersalivation, and lethargy.124,125 Use in cats with
acromegaly is contraindicated, and caution should be used in cats
with diabetes as hyperglycemia has been documented.124,126
Transient bradycardia and hypotension have also been documented
in cats. This medication should not be used in patients with
significant systemic compromise, likely precluding its use in dogs
and cats hospitalized for uremic crisis.124

Esophagostomy Feeding (ch. 81)
Failure to stabilize a pet at an acceptable body condition score is
likely to adversely affect long-term outcome. Esophagostomy tube
feeding can be quite beneficial for dogs and cats that continue to lose
weight despite all efforts to achieve adequate nutrition.
Esophagostomy tubes are an effective and convenient route for
delivering food, water, and medications to dogs and cats with CKD,
and can be a useful means of stabilizing or improving nutrition,
clinical signs, longevity, and owner satisfaction.54,127 In general,
tube placement is less likely to be effective when the decision to
proceed is delayed until advanced uremia and malnutrition have
developed.

WATER BALANCE
Clinical Presentation
As kidney disease progresses, the ability to concentrate urine is lost.
Polyuria/polydypsia is among the earliest and most common clinical
signs of CKD (chs. 53 and 70). While urine specific gravity (USG)
values from cats with CKD are usually <1.035, some retain urine
concentrating ability (i.e., USG >1.035), especially early in the course
of their CKD.

Pathophysiology
Decreased urine concentrating ability is the result of several factors:
increased solute load per surviving nephron (solute diuresis),
impaired genesis of the hypertonic gradient of the renal medulla due
to disruption of the renal medullary architecture and counter-current
multiplier system, and impairment in renal responsiveness to
antidiuretic hormone (ADH). If fluid intake fails to keep pace with
urinary losses, dehydration is likely because of the inability to
conserve water by concentrating urine. Dehydration is a common
complication of CKD and can lead to inappetence, lethargy,
weakness, constipation, and increased susceptibility to uremic crisis.
It may also exacerbate stone formation and urinary tract infections
(UTIs).128 Dehydration may precipitate pathophysiologic responses
that have negative effects on the kidney (e.g., activation of reninangiotensin-aldosterone system [RAAS], chronically increased ADH,
compromised perfusion causing renal hypoxia). Cats with CKD
appear particularly susceptible to chronic dehydration, perhaps since
their compensatory PD is inadequate. Lack of access to good
drinking water, concurrent illness, and some environmental
conditions can all limit fluid intake or promote fluid loss (e.g.,
pyrexia, vomiting, diarrhea) and lead to dehydration. Owners should
be aware that concurrent illness, vomiting and diarrhea, household
changes/stress or inadequate water sources promote dehydration
with serious effects in pets with CKD; potentially precipitating a
uremic crisis.

Management
Correcting dehydration may benefit the kidneys by reducing ADH
secretion, suppressing or blocking the RAAS, and optimizing
perfusion. In people, beneficial effects of therapeutic water intake
include reduced copeptin (a marker of ADH), reduced prevalence of
CKD, and slower progression of CKD.129 Dry oral membranes and
decreased skin elasticity are common in dehydration, but can be
misleading. Xerostomia (dry oral membranes) may result from
uremia. Loss of skin elasticity is common in dogs and cats that have
lost weight, are older, or in poor nutritional health. Thus, combining

PE, evidence of hemoconcentration, and stool quality should be used
to assess hydration status.
Feeding canned instead of dry food, or adding water to food are
simple strategies to increase water consumption (

Video 159.1).

Having fresh, accessible water is also key. Supplementing with free
water (orally or with a feeding tube) is preferred to avoid the Na load
in SQ electrolyte solutions. However, maintaining hydration with SQ
balanced electrolyte solutions appears, anecdotally, to improve
appetite, activity, and quality of life while reducing incidence of
constipation.22,130 SQ fluids can be a very helpful tool for owners,
but may not always be necessary or possible. Recommendations
regarding SQ fluids should be made on a case-by-case basis. While
many cats with CKD appear to benefit from SQ fluids, it is less often
needed in dogs. The best candidates for SQ fluid therapy (75-150 mL
SQ every 1-3 days depending on IRIS stage and clinical need) are cats
that subjectively benefit, are prone to secondary complications of
chronic dehydration such as constipation, and do not suffer quality
of life concerns from the procedure. After instruction, many owners
find SQ fluids to be feasible and tolerated by their pet.131 Possible
detriments of SQ fluid therapy include stress on the human-animal
bond and the unknown effect of Na on the RAAS. Response to longterm SQ fluid therapy should be assessed by frequently checking
hydration status, clinical signs, BP (ch. 91), kidney function, and,
possibly, electrolyte values. If detectable improvement in clinical
signs and/or renal function does not accompany fluid therapy, the
need for long-term therapy should be reassessed.

CONSTIPATION (CHS. 108, 263)
Both overt and subclinical constipation appear to be common
complications of CKD, particularly in cats.132,133 The etiology of
constipation is likely associated with water balance issues since water
is reabsorbed from the colon to compensate for systemic
dehydration. HypoK and PO4 binders may contribute to
constipation.62,63,134 Clinical history is important when assessing a

constipated CKD patient. Important answers needed include
frequency of defecation; time spent defecating; and degree of
difficulty, straining, or vomiting associated with defecation.
Assessment and recording hydration status is crucial. PE may reveal
small hard feces in the descending colon with a build-up of fecal
material anterior to the pelvic inlet, or, in more severe cases, a large
amount of hard fecal material in the colon. As CKD pets are typically
older, assessing for osteoarthritis may also be helpful as posturing
during defecation could be more difficult.
Hydration and hypokalemia (hypoK) should be corrected first in
any constipated CKD pet. Although the efficacy of prophylactic K
supplementation has not been evaluated, pets with constipation may
benefit from maintaining serum K >4 mEq/L (>4 mmol/L). After
correction of dehydration and hypoK, oral osmotic stool softeners
can be used, but because these therapies act by drawing water into
the colon they may exacerbate systemic dehydration. Polyethylene
glycol 3350 (Miralax), an osmotic assessed in normal cats, was
effective in softening stool.135 Although its efficacy in CKD patients
has not been evaluated, it is commonly prescribed (1/8 tsp q12-24h)
and is thought by some to be more effective than lactulose which is
processed by intestinal microflora and may lead to bloating.135 Also,
polyethylene glycol comes as a powder that appears to be well
tolerated. Promotility agents (cisapride 1 mg/kg PO q8h) are a
second tier for medical management of constipation associated with
CKD. Inherent colonic motility has not been assessed in dogs or cats
with CKD. Medical management of osteoarthritis may also be an
important adjunctive treatment for constipation in CKD patients to
facilitate appropriate posturing during defecation.

HYPOKALEMIA (HypoK) (ch. 68, 296)
Frequency
HypoK is common in cats with CKD (∼20-30% of cats affected).43,53
It is most common in IRIS Stages 2 and 3 CKD but appears less
common in Stage 4 due to markedly decreased GFR.22 Many cats
with CKD and systemic hypertension (ch. 236) have been reported

to also have hypoK.136 Additionally, the antihypertensive agent
amlodipine may promote hypoK in cats with CKD.137 HypoK is less
common in dogs with CKD, likely due to species differences plus they
are often prescribed an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor
(ACEi) or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) therapy for
proteinuria, which can increase serum K.

Clinical Signs and Consequences
Severe hypoK (<2.5 mEq/L) may induce signs of myopathy, e.g.,
cervical ventroflexion (

Video 68.1) and plantigrade stance in

cats. Moderate hypoK (2.5-3.0 mEq/L) usually causes more subtle
muscle weakness, lethargy, inappetence, and constipation.22,132 Mild
hypoK may not cause obvious clinical signs, but based on studies in
other species, the detrimental effects are probably under
appreciated. In rodent models, hypoK impairs renal angiogenesis
and is associated with capillary loss and decreased vascular
endothelial growth factor.138 In healthy adult cats, experimental
diets with inadequate K cause development of renal
dysfunction.139,140 Interestingly, renal function was also shown to be
adversely affected in normal cats when fed an acidified, K-restricted
diet, the two possibly being additive.82 K depletion may lead to
reduced renal blood flow and GFR as a consequence of angiotensin II
and thromboxane-mediated renal vasoconstriction.141 In addition,
hypoK may promote PU by impairing renal responsiveness to ADH
(chs. 53, 54, and 282) and by stimulating brain thirst centers via
angiotensin II. HypoK of varying severity is associated with
constipation, particularly in cats with CKD.132 In humans with
kidney disease hypoK <4 mEq/L (<4 mmol/L) is associated with
increased risk for end stage renal disease and mortality.142,143
Surprisingly, hypoK has not been shown to be a risk factor for
disease progression or outcome in CKD cats.19,144

Pathophysiology

The mechanisms causing cats with CKD to become hypoK are not
well understood. HypoK likely follows a combination of increased
urinary K loss due to PU that reduces reabsorption, inadequate
dietary intake, dietary Na restriction, and activation of the RAAS.
95% of K, the major intracellular cation, is in muscle.145 Chronic
metabolic acidosis associated with CKD encourages intracellular K
depletion due to intracellular influx of excess hydrogen ions and
concomitant efflux of K.146 Thus, serum K may not reflect
intracellular levels; normokalemic cats with CKD have lower muscle
K concentrations than normal controls.145

Diet (ch. 158)
Diets formulated for cats with CKD are usually supplemented with K,
containing an average of 0.7-1.2% K on a dry matter basis. Diets
formulated for dogs with CKD are not usually supplemented with K
(typically 0.4-0.8% dry matter basis).147 Anecdotally, cats with CKD
eating K-supplemented diets appear to develop clinically profound
hypoK less commonly.

Oral K Supplementation
K given orally appears to be the safest route in stable cats. Based on
the possible deleterious effects of hypoK and the questionable value
of serum K,145 some advocate prophylactic supplementation even
when the serum K is in the low reference range, with a goal of
maintaining serum levels >4 mg/dL (>4 mmol/L). K
supplementation is particularly important for CKD cats with
constipation, given the role of K for GI motility. However, the value
of prophylactic K supplementation has not yet been established. Oral
K gluconate and K citrate are available in various forms, including
pill, powder and gel. Recommended starting dosage for K gluconate
are 1-4 mEq/cat/day PO (divided as needed). The dosage of K citrate
is 40-75 mg/kg PO q12h (about 2-6 mEq/cat/day) and adjusted as
needed.130,148,149 Many cats achieve normal K after treatment with
the lowest dosages; in a recent study, doses of 0.25-1.6 mEq/kg/day
were sufficient.149 K citrate has the added advantage of being an

alkalinizing agent; however, its effectiveness for treating metabolic
acidosis has not been sufficiently evaluated.149 K chloride (KCl) is
not recommended as an oral supplement; it is acidifying and
unpalatable. It may be added to SQ fluids at concentrations up to 30
mEq/L (higher concentrations can be associated with irritation when
delivered via peripheral IV catheter).146

Hypokalemic Myopathy and Cats in Acute-onChronic Uremic Crisis
These cats are best treated with IV fluids supplemented with KCl to
normalize K before the cat is transitioned to oral supplementation at
home. Once normoK is achieved, IV supplementation can be slowly
decreased; if IV supplementation is acutely stopped, hypoK usually
recurs. It may be necessary in some cats to start oral
supplementation while weaning IV supplementation to prevent
relapse. After correcting hypoK myopathy, K supplementation
should be adjusted based on clinical signs and serum concentrations.
In more stable and more mildly affected cats, K should be rechecked
7-14 days after initiating supplementation and dosing titrated
accordingly. Clinical impressions suggest that most CKD cats benefit
from long-term K supplementation.150 If hypoK appears particularly
refractory to supplementation, medical conditions such as
hyperaldosteronism should be considered (ch. 295).
Intensive IV fluid therapy during uremic crises, particularly with
K-deficient fluids, may promote hypoK in cats or dogs not previously
deficient. Therefore, serum K concentrations should be monitored
during fluid therapy and maintenance fluids should be supplemented
with KCl to prevent iatrogenic deficiency (concentrations of 13 to 20
mEq/L are appropriate for maintenance fluids). IV K should not be
given at rates exceeding 0.5 mEq/kg/hr (chs. 68 and 120).

HYPERKALEMIA (HyperK; CHs. 68, 296)
HyperK occurs more commonly in dogs with CKD and it may be
exacerbated by giving an ACEi or ARB. HyperK can be managed by
reducing dietary K or by preventing GI uptake.151 Polymer resins

(e.g., Na polystyrene sulfonate) may be somewhat effective but are
associated with hypoCa, hypoMg, and GI necrosis in people.152
Zirconium cyclosilicate, a highly selective cation exchanger that traps
K within the GI lumen, is effective in mitigating hyperK in people,
but little is known about its use in veterinary medicine.152

ARTERIAL HYPERTENSION (CHS. 91
AND 236)
Clinical Presentation
Systemic hypertension is common in cats and dogs with CKD; its
pathophysiology is likely secondary and multifactorial, but not well
described.153-155 Hypertension is important to identify and treat due
to its numerous deleterious effects, e.g., progression of CKD,
worsening proteinuria, left ventricular hypertrophy and subsequent
cardiac impairment, ocular disease that includes retinal vascular
tortuosity and hemorrhage, hyphema, blindness due to retinal
detachment, and neurologic sequelae including encephalopathy (ch.
243), vascular events, seizures and death (ch. 236).153,154,156-159
All dogs with renal proteinuria and/or azotemia should be
assessed for hypertension. Cats should be routinely screened for
hypertension after 9 years of age, at initial CKD diagnosis and then
monitored thereafter. About 17% develop hypertension later in the
course of disease.160 A fundic exam should be included at each
assessment (ch. 13). Dogs and cats can be classified according to
their risk of hypertension-induced target organ damage (TOD) via
the IRIS CKD BP substaging system (Table 301.1). Once situational
hypertension has been ruled out, the decision to initiate therapy is
based on its severity and other clinical information (fundic exam, BP
trends, etc.). When BP is >200 mm Hg and/or evidence of TOD is
seen, therapy should be initiated. CKD patients with BP consistently
>160 mm Hg are candidates for treatment.22,161

Treatment

General guidelines are to reduce BP to <150 mm Hg.156,162
Aggressive reduction of BP is only necessary in pets with ocular
and/or neurologic complications. Usually it may take weeks,
particularly in dogs, to achieve adequate BP control.130 Treatment
strategies for cats and dogs differ slightly based on the efficacy of
currently available anti-hypertensive medications (ch. 236).
Amlodipine (a Ca channel blocker) and telmisartan (an ARB)
effectively lower BP in cats and monotherapy is typically
effective.162-166 Telmisartan has not been assessed for cats with TOD
or BP >200 mm Hg; amlodipine is indicated in these circumstances.
ACEis have not been demonstrated to adequately reduce BP in cats
when used as a sole therapy.167 In dogs, monotherapy is not usually
sufficient and some combination of ACEi, ARB, and a Ca channel
blocker is typically used.168 Since many dogs with CKD also have
protein-losing nephropathy (PLN), ACEis and ARBs are considered
first-line medications to address both proteinuria and hypertension
(chs. 236 and 302).169-171

Monitoring
BP should be rechecked within 7-10 days of initiating therapy in
stable mildly hypertensive pets and the dose adjusted accordingly
(ch. 236). Unstable dogs and cats, those with TOD, and those in late
stage disease should be rechecked earlier (∼1-3 days). In cats given
telmisartan, BP should be monitored over 3-6 months to determine
if dose decreases are needed to prevent hypotension.165,166
Monitoring renal values and electrolytes is also important; ACEis
and ARBs can decrease GFR and result in worsening azotemia: dose
and/or continued therapy should be reassessed.170,172 Care should
be taken when prescribing for pets in later stages of CKD or in
uremic crisis. In these instances, amlodipine may be a safer
alternative; if ACEi or ARB must be used, lower starting doses are
prudent. As previously mentioned, hyperK is also a common sideeffect of ACEis in dogs and may limit the dose that can be
administered.168

PROTEINURIA (chs. 70,302,303)
Origins of Protein Loss
The origin of proteinuria in dogs and cats in CKD can be glomerular
or tubular. In normal kidneys, small proteins freely pass through the
glomerulus and are reabsorbed by the proximal tubular epithelial
cells via megalin-cubilin mediated endocytosis.173 Pets with
tubulointerstitial CKD have proteinuria because there are fewer
tubules available to reabsorb small proteins and as disease
progresses, factors such as hyperfiltration and hypertension can
result in glomerulosclerosis, permitting additional protein loss via
the filtration apparatus.11,14 In primary glomerular disease, large
proteins (>∼65,000 daltons) can also leak through the damaged
glomerular apparatus and quickly exceed the reabsorption capacity
of tubular epithelial cells. Uptake of protein, subsequent processing,
and lysosomal storage is damaging to proximal tubular cells as it not
only increases their metabolic load, but results in oxidative stress
and ultimately may trigger apoptosis as overburdened lysosomes
burst.173,174 It is unsurprising therefore that proteinuria is associated
with poorer prognosis in several species.19,32,175,176 Measurement of
UPCR allows quantitative assessment of the condition (chs. 70 and
299).

Indications to Treat Proteinuria
Reducing proteinuria has been demonstrated to slow disease
progression in people. Studies in dogs and cats have documented
that ACEi and ARB decrease proteinuria, but results have only
“suggested” long-term benefit.175,177-179 Nonetheless, it is considered
standard of care that dogs and cats with CKD with UPCRs >0.5 and
0.4, respectively, be treated with antiproteinuric drugs such as ACEi
or ARB (ch. 302).169 Antithrombotic therapy is also considered
standard in managing glomerular disease (ch. 302). Systemic
hypertension exacerbates proteinuria and should be treated (ch.
236).

Diet for Proteinuria (ch. 158)
IRIS consensus recommendations include renal diets for proteinuric
CKD. However, no study has documented an ideal amount of dietary
protein for these pets, nor has the long-term benefit of dietary
protein restriction been demonstrated. Most studies have only
assessed a total “diet effect.”

Kidney Biopsy
In addition to diet and medications for pets with glomerular disease,
renal biopsy should be considered. About 50% of dogs and 75% of
cats with glomerular disease have immune mediated disease.9,180
Renal biopsy is contraindicated with any evidence of a bleeding
disorder, uncontrolled hypertension, chronic end-stage disease, and
in very small pets (cats and dogs <5 kg). The goals of biopsy are to
identify immune-mediated subtypes of glomerular disease to
determine best appropriate therapy and assess prognosis (ch. 302).

ANEMIA (CHS. 57 AND 172)
Clinical Presentation
Anemia, common in dogs and cats with CKD, increases in incidence
and severity with IRIS stage.53,144,181 The anemia of CKD is
classically normochromic, normocytic, and nonregenerative. Clinical
signs of anemia may include mucous membrane pallor, fatigue,
listlessness, lethargy, weakness, and anorexia.

Pathophysiology
The anemia of CKD is usually multifactorial in origin. The primary
cause is inadequate production of EPO, which regulates red blood
cell (RBC) production. Hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs), in
particular HIF-2, have emerged as transcription factors that regulate
EPO synthesis in the peritubular fibroblasts of the kidney. HIFs also
have a critical role in regulating intestinal iron uptake.182 EPO
stimulates RBC production in the bone marrow by binding to a
receptor on erythroid progenitors that stimulate those cells to

differentiate into normoblasts and then mature erythrocytes. With
CKD and renal fibrosis, peritubular fibroblasts become
myofibroblasts which produce little EPO. This phenomenon is likely
responsible for the relative EPO deficiency that occurs increasingly
with disease severity.
Other factors contribute to the anemia of CKD, e.g., excessive
blood taken for testing, spontaneous bleeding, poor nutrition
(including protein, iron, folate, and perhaps others), chronic
inflammation/infection, and reduced RBC life span. Cats in CKD
have a relative iron deficiency and excess hepcidin.183 Hepcidin, a
key regulator in iron homeostasis, is upregulated in inflammatory
environments and leads to sequestration of iron in cells. In addition
to the activities of hepcidin, pro-inflammatory cytokines also inhibit
erythropoiesis in inflammatory states. The histology of CKD often
includes inflammatory infiltrates, consistent with CKD being a
chronic inflammatory state contributing to the anemia. In cats
hepcidin concentrations positively correlate with serum
creatinine.184 Although gastric ulceration is less common in dogs
and cats than humans, chronic low-grade GI hemorrhage from
mucosal friability and uremic thrombocytopathia may also
contribute to anemia. Iron deficiency may be noted.38,106 Lastly RBC
life span may be shortened due to the deleterious effects of uremic
toxins.

Consequences of Anemia
The moderate to severe anemia associated with CKD in dogs and cats
negatively affects quality of life, causing weakness, lethargy and
inappetence. Anemia triggers adaptations that can be detrimental
including increased RAAS activity and release of norepinephrine,
which can lead to increased heart workload and hypertension.
Anemia may also cause left heart enlargement, predisposing pets to
heart failure and fluid overload.106
Through its contribution to hypoxia, anemia could exacerbate
progression of CKD. Renal tubular epithelial cells have compromised
access to peritubular capillary blood supply due to inflammatory
infiltrates and expansion of the interstitium. If delivered blood has
poor oxygen carrying capacity due to anemia, cells are further

starved of nutrients and oxygen. Hypoxia drives fibrosis, tubular cell
transdifferentiation, and activation of fibroblasts that exacerbate the
disease state.185

Treating Underlying Conditions
Treating the anemia of CKD includes correcting underlying factors,
blood transfusion, and giving erythrocyte-stimulating agents (ESAs).
GI hemorrhage, infection, or chronic inflammation are common
underlying conditions that should be treated as soon as possible.
Treating systemic infections, UTIs, and/or pyelonephritis is
particularly relevant in CKD. Chronic GI hemorrhage should be
suspected when melena, increased BUN to creatinine ratio, iron
deficiency, anemia disproportionate to level of azotemia, or any
combination of these abnormalities is noted. Treatment with proton
pump inhibitors with a subsequent increase in hematocrit supports
the diagnosis.

Erythrocyte-Stimulating Agents (ESAs)
Background
Administering ESAs is the most effective means of correcting the
anemia of CKD. Absent factors that impair their effectiveness, ESAs
induce dose-dependent increases in packed cell volume (PCV). Two
ESAs are currently available: epoetin alfa (Epogen, Amgen; Procrit,
Centocor Ortho Biotech Products; Eprex, Janssen) and darbepoetin
alfa (Aranesp, Amgen).106 These products differ in their degree of
glycosylation, which affects their renal clearance and, therefore,
influences their duration of action.

Available ESAs and Antibody Development
Available ESAs are based on human EPO, of which dogs and cats
share 81.3% and 83.3% homology, respectively,106 allowing these
drugs to be effective in stimulating substantial PCV increases in both
dogs and cats. However, there is risk of developing anti-EPO
antibodies, primarily with epoetin alfa. About 25-30% of cats and up
to 50% of dogs receiving epoetin develop neutralizing anti-EPO

antibodies. Not all cases with anti-EPO antibodies develop
anemia.186 These antibodies cross-react with all ESAs including the
pet’s endogenous EPO. Development of anti-EPO antibodies can
markedly suppress erythropoiesis and result in a pure red cell aplasia
(PRCA; ch. 172). Many pets with PRCA become transfusiondependent. If they live long enough, a response to endogenous EPO
may return. Although controlled studies on development of
antibodies directed at the ESA darbepoetin are not available, it
appears that this product is much less immunogenic.187,188 It is
suggested that the longer half-life of darbepoetin may reduce the
antigen load administered compared to epoetin, thereby reducing
the risk of antibody formation.106

Indications and Protocol
ESAs are indicated in dogs and cats with: (1) advanced CKD (IRIS
CKD Stages III and IV), (2) PCV values below 25%, and (3) those
with clinical signs attributable to anemia. While epoetin and
darbepoetin are both available, darbepoetin is preferred for dogs and
cats. The advantages of darbepoetin over epoetin include seemingly
lower risk of anti-EPO antibodies and need for weekly
administration. Darbepoetin is initially given SQ (1 mcg/kg, weekly)
and continued until the PCV reaches the low end of the target range
(cats: 28-35%; dogs: 37-42%). Once achieved, the frequency of
dosing is decreased to once every 2 weeks. The maintenance dose can
then be adjusted monthly, as needed, to keep the PCV within the
target range. Since excessive ESA has been linked to adverse
outcomes in humans, it is recommended that abnormally high PCVs
be avoided.189

Iron and Vitamin B
Erythropoiesis increases iron use. Due to the functional iron
deficiency associated with CKD,183,184 iron supplementation is
recommended when ESA treatment is initiated, as well as every few
months through the course of therapy. Iron injections (iron dextran
50 mg/cat IM, 10-20 mg/kg dogs IM) are usually well tolerated
except for rare anaphylaxis and are considered superior to oral

supplementation. Oral iron tends to be bitter and may further
decrease an already poor appetite and it is poorly absorbed from the
GI tract.106 B vitamins are necessary for RBC synthesis and the
degree to which they are deficient in CKD pets is poorly understood.
Given their benign nature supplementation is unlikely to be harmful.
B vitamins are not considered appropriate as a sole therapy for
anemia.106

Monitoring and Treatment Response
Initially, PE, PCV, and BP assessments should be obtained weekly
until the target PCV is achieved. Rapid rates of increase should be
avoided because of an association with hypertension. Once stable,
recheck examinations should be conducted every 1 to 3 months. It is
essential that regular follow-up examinations continue as long as
darbepoetin therapy continues. In 1 study, 56% (14/25) of cats given
darbepoetin achieved the target PCV (25%). The cats reaching the
target survived significantly longer than cats that did not respond
(mean of 238 days for responders; 83 days for nonsurvivors).187 Cats
in this study, on average, were significantly azotemic and anemic.
Based on more recent anecdotal experience response rates are better
in more stable dogs and cats. In another study, 7 of 7 cats with CKD
reached the target PCV (30%), and none had evidence of anti-EPO
antibodies.188 In dogs, 1 study reported that 85% achieved a PCV
>30%.194 In both species, increasing the PCV to the low end of the
normal range takes about 2 to 8 weeks, depending on initial PCV and
dose administered.187,190 As the anemia is corrected, most pets have
increases in appetite, body weight, energy, and sociability.186

Side-Effects and Failure to Respond
Hypertension may develop or increase in severity due to increased
peripheral vascular resistance secondary to improved oxygen
delivery and reversal of the vasodilation induced by chronic hypoxia.
Increased blood viscosity due to the increased PCV is thought to be
minor. Seizures, reported in dogs and cats being treated with ESAs
are not directly caused by the therapy, but rather related to

compensatory adaptations to increases in RBC mass.186 Other
reported side effects include polycythemia, injection site reactions,
vomiting, arthralgia, fever, iron deficiency, and PRCA.187,190
Treatment failure may stem from a variety of causes including
inadequate dose, owner noncompliance, GI bleeding, iron deficiency,
B vitamin deficiency, concurrent infection or inflammation,
aluminum toxicosis, inhibition of erythropoiesis by ACEis, or bone
marrow dysfunction. Typical trouble-shooting steps include
increasing the dosage, stopping ACEi or aluminum-based therapies
(aluminum hydroxide, sucralfate), treating for GI bleeding or
infection, and additional supplementation of iron and B vitamins. If
no response is seen, bone marrow assessment is indicated (ch.
84).106 If the anemia corrects with ESA therapy, but then PCV
values again decline, development of anti-EPO antibodies should
also be considered. If no other cause is found and anti-EPO
antibodies are suspected, ESA therapy should be stopped. If ESAs
are stopped early, antibody titers may decline and suppressed
erythropoiesis may reverse.

METABOLIC ACIDOSIS
Clinical Presentation
While data are not available for dogs, metabolic acidosis is reported
to affect about 15% of cats with IRIS CKD Stage III and about 53% of
cats with IRIS CKD Stage IV.191 Cats with earlier stage disease are
rarely affected. Although metabolic acidosis has not been found to be
a prognostic factor in cats or dogs with CKD, it is recognized to
promote CKD progression in humans.192,193 Chronic acidosis can
cause muscle wasting, signs of uremia, renal osteodystrophy,
hypoalbuminemia, activation of RAAS, oxidative stress, and
inflammation.192,193 Acidosis can result in protein malnutrition even
when dietary intake is adequate by promoting increased muscle
protein degradation without a change in synthesis, compromising
adaptation to dietary protein restriction.194 Dietary acidification in
cats can cause negative Ca balance, bone demineralization, hypoK,

renal dysfunction, and taurine depletion.195 In humans, alkalization
therapy effectively reverses acidosis-associated protein breakdown,
decreases muscle wasting, improves bone disease, and slows
progression of disease.192,193 Beneficial therapeutic effect has been
found even in subclinical acidosis (i.e., eubicarbonatemic metabolic
acidosis).192,193

Pathophysiology
The kidneys have a large role in acid-base homeostasis primarily by
reabsorbing bicarbonate, synthesizing bicarbonate, and excreting
acid. Bicarbonate is freely filtered by the glomerulus and then the
majority is reabsorbed by the proximal tubule and the rest by the
more distal segments of the nephron. Net acid excretion occurs by
two processes: excretion of hydrogen ions with ammonia, and
excretion of titratable acids which refers to the excretion of protons
with urinary buffers (primarily PO4).196 As renal function declines,
hydrogen ion excretion is maintained largely by increasing the
quantity of ammonium excreted by surviving nephrons. Eventually,
the capacity to enhance renal ammonia production is lost and
metabolic acidosis ensues. Decreased medullary recycling of
ammonia due to structural renal damage may impair ammonium
excretion.191 Decreased filtration of titratable acids such as PO4 plus
impaired renal tubular proton secretion may also contribute.
Impaired renal tubular reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate is not
typical of dogs and cats with CKD but may occur in selected tubular
disorders such as Fanconi syndrome (ch. 303).

Indications for Treatment
Data suggest that only a minority of dogs and cats with clinically
stable IRIS CKD Stages II and III are overtly acidotic. Thus, the
decision to add alkalization therapy should be based on a laboratory
assessment of acid-base status. No studies in dogs or cats have
identified treatment goals but in people, oral therapy for acidosis is
considered when blood gas analysis confirms plasma bicarbonate
values <16 mmol/L (goal 16-24 mmol/L). Parenteral intervention

should be considered for patients with metabolic acidosis and a
blood pH <7.10 to increase the value >7.20.197 It remains to be seen
if subclinical metabolic acidosis should be addressed in dogs or cats.

Treatment Options
Treatment options for alkalization include renal diets, K citrate, and
Na bicarbonate. Most renal diets are neutral to slightly alkalinizing.
If diet fails to ameliorate acidosis, alkalization therapy should be
considered. K-citrate solution provides both K and alkalization and is
usually more palatable than Na bicarbonate. Dosing is “to-effect,”
starting at 40 to 60 mg/kg PO q8-12h, with a goal of maintaining
reference range blood bicarbonate concentrations. Na bicarbonate
(initial dosage: 8 to 12 mg/kg PO q8-12h) is often not palatable
except when given by tablets. These medications should be given in
small doses frequently to minimize blood pH fluctuations. Response
to therapy should be assessed after 10 to 14 days, before the drug is
given, and dosage adjusted accordingly. The potential negative effect
of Na administration (i.e., RAAS activation) has not been assessed.

MONITORING DOGS AND CATS IN CKD
Response to treatment should be monitored at appropriate intervals
and individualized to the specific and often changing needs of the
pet. In general, evaluation every 2 to 4 weeks is suggested until the
initial response to therapy can be established. However, the
frequency of evaluation varies depending on severity of renal
dysfunction, complications, treatments applied, and response to
treatment. Dogs and cats in Stage I CKD may require evaluation as
infrequently as every 6 to 12 months. After the initial response to
therapy has been established, cats in Stage II CKD are usually
monitored about every 3 to 6 months. Dogs in Stage II CKD and dogs
and cats in Stage III CKD should be evaluated about every 2 to 4
months, depending on stability of their renal function. Pets given
EPO or calcitriol require frequent monitoring life-long.

PROGNOSIS OF CKD

A Variably Progressive Disease
While CKD classically causes slow but inexorably progressive decline
in function, predicting prognosis in CKD can be challenging as
disease progression can vary substantially and no single variable
predicts duration of survival (Table 301.4). Less tangible factors do
influence CKD prognosis, e.g., the quality of medical care, owner
commitment, pet compliance, and perceived quality of life. In some,
declining kidney function follows an almost linear pattern while
others have periods of relative stability punctuated by episodes of
precipitous renal function decline. Some in CKD have multiple
periods of stable renal function broken by a series of uremic crises
before succumbing. In 1 study, only 101 of 213 (47%) cats with CKD
had progressively worsening serum creatinine values.19 CKD usually
progresses much more slowly in cats than in dogs but CKD may
progress more slowly in dogs with congenital or familial
nephropathies not characterized by proteinuria (ch. 328). Many
such dogs appear resistant to developing clinical signs of uremia
despite substantial serum creatinine concentrations.

Median Survival Times
In order to more accurately determine prognosis in CKD, prerenal,
postrenal, and active complications (e.g., pyelonephritis) should first
be treated. Once the patient has reached a stable disease state,
applying the IRIS CKD staging system can guide estimating
prognosis. Survival varies significantly in dogs and cats based on the
serum creatinine and IRIS stage at the time of assessment.3,18,32 In a
retrospective study, cats with IRIS CKD Stage IIb (creatinine 2.3-2.8
mg/dL [203-248 mcmol/L]) had a median survival time of 1151 days
with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 1014 to 1565 days. Because
these data only included a subset of IRIS CKD Stage II cats, survival
durations might have been longer had all Stage II cats been included
(1.6-2.3 mg/dL [141-203 mcmol/L]). Median survival time for cats
with IRIS CKD Stage III was 679 days (95% CI: 445-910 days) and 35
days for cats in IRIS CKD Stage IV (95% CI: 21-99 days).18 In 228
dogs diagnosed at a first-opinion practice as having CKD, the overall
median survival time from diagnosis was 226 days (95% CI: 112-326

days).3 Compared to IRIS CKD Stages I and II, dogs with IRIS CKD
Stage III had 2.6 times and IRIS CKD Stage IV had 4.7 times the
mortality. A more recent smaller study in 27 dogs reported median
(range) survival time of 14.8 months (9.1-37.4) for Stage II, 11.14
months (0.46-38.4) for Stage III and 1.98 months (0.32-12.8) for
Stage IV dogs.32

SURGICAL INTERVENTIONS
ASSOCIATED WITH CKD
PERINEPHRIC PSEUDOCYSTS
Perinephric pseudocysts occur when transudate or modified
transudate accumulates between the renal cortex and the renal
capsule, or less commonly between the renal capsule and the
retroperitoneal lining.198,199 The term “pseudocyst” is used because
these have no epithelial lining. This condition appears to be specific
to cats and is commonly associated with CKD.198 Ultrasound (US) is
usually sufficient for diagnosis. Perinephric pseudocysts can be space

occupying, contribute to abdominal discomfort, and may decrease
GFR. Treatment should be considered.199,200 Although the cysts can
be drained using percutaneous US guidance, they commonly recur
and continue to accumulate fluid over time.198 Permanent
breakdown via surgery or laparoscopy is most effective for
permanent resolution.198,201 In 1 cat, GFR improved after
laparoscopy was used to fenestrate for permanent drainage.200
Prognosis is determined based on the degree of underlying renal
disease.199

KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION
Background
Renal transplantation was first introduced as a therapeutic option
for cats with CKD in 1984. An overview of considerations before
renal transplantation is provided. The emphasis is on cats because
kidney transplants in dogs are rarely successful.202 Detailed
protocols for screening and transplantation protocols should be
obtained from the transplant program if this therapeutic option is
being considered.

Recipient and Donor Selection
Candidates for renal transplantation are ideally stable with late Stage
3 or early Stage 4 CKD. Early non-clinical CKD likely does not
warrant the risks associated with transplantation. Cats with endstage uremia are not ideal and may not be suitable candidates, as
significant azotemia is associated with a poorer outcome. Age is also
associated with a shorter survival time, therefore younger recipients
are ideal, but older cats may qualify and do well. Cats with Ca oxalate
urolithiasis may undergo transplantation, but allograft
nephrolithiasis is a risk.203 A systemic diagnostic workup is required
to assess for candidacy (Box 301.2). Definite exclusion criteria
include feline leukemia virus/FIV infection, moderate to severe heart
disease (ch. 223), neoplasia, recurrent bacterial infections, fractious
nature, other significant comorbidities, or an inability to medicate

the cat or obtain medical care. If latent infection (bacterial or
protozoal) is a concern, a 1-3 month cyclosporine trial prior to
transplantation may be prudent.202

Cats selected to be kidney donors are typically young and healthy
(1-2 years), obtained from shelters or purpose-bred facilities.
Internationally, renal transplantation from living donors is not
universally accepted, as unlike human donors, the cats do not choose
to donate. However, transplant programs require that donor cats be
adopted by the owner, and retrospective data indicate that donor
cats may be minimally affected by donation. In a study with a
median follow up time of 10 years, 84% of donor cats for which
follow-up was available had no long-term effects.204 In a second
study, kidney disease occurred in 17.8% of donor cats for whom
medical records were available.205 It is important that both donor
and recipient candidates for transplantation be rigorously screened

to ensure the best possible outcome and ensure the donor’s kidney is
not wasted.

Immunosuppressive Therapy (chs. 144, 169, 227)
Immunosuppressive therapy begins prior to transplantation and
continues for life. An oral liquid microemulsified formulation of
cyclosporine (Neoral 100 mg/mL) is used to allow individual dose
titration (liquid can be placed in a gelatin capsule before
administration to hide the taste). Monitoring of serum cyclosporine
concentrations is performed to ensure dosing is within the
therapeutic range. Prednisolone is also started at the time of surgery
and gradually tapered over the course of several months. However,
recipients must remain on cyclosporine for life to prevent allograft
rejection. Long-term monitoring of serum cyclosporine
concentrations is necessary.

Surgery
Detailed information about surgical technique and peri- and postoperative management can be found elsewhere.202 Briefly, the
timing of the surgeries to harvest the donor kidney and transplant
into the recipient are coordinated to minimize time of ischemic
injury to the donor kidney. The donor kidney is implanted directly
behind the native kidney (which is typically not removed). After
securing perfusion to the transplanted kidney, the ureter of the
transplant is then connected to the bladder via one of several
techniques.202 The donor kidney is attached to the abdominal wall to
prevent torsion. An operating microscope is necessary for surgical
manipulations and the techniques require uro-microsurgery
expertise. Important aspects of immediate post-operative care
include minimizing stress and handling due to the delicate nature of
the transplant and small suture size, and managing pain, nutrition,
and fluid balance. Other aims include preventing hypothermia,
hyper/hypotension, seizures, or electrolyte abnormalities.
Cyclosporine levels must be regulated. A blood sampling catheter
and a feeding tube are generally placed at the time of surgery and
hospitalization of 10-14 days is anticipated if there are no
complications. After leaving the hospital, cats may have weekly

rechecks for the first 6-8 weeks and then every 3-4 months for long
term monitoring.

Acute Complications
The major peri-operative complications of renal transplant include
hemorrhage, uroabdomen, and thromboembolism. Immediate postoperative complications include hypertension, seizures, delayed
allograft function, and acute rejection reaction.202,206 Delayed
allograft function refers to dysfunction in the transplanted kidney
that is otherwise receiving adequate blood flow and does not have
evidence of post-renal obstruction. This may be the result of injury to
the kidney in the peri-operative period (intraoperative ischemia or
post-operative complications). Typically, the allograft will develop
normal function after a period of recovery, but there is increased risk
of allograft loss. Acute rejection reaction can occur at any time after
transplantation if immunosuppression is insufficient and should be
suspected in cats with malaise, poor appetite, worsening azotemia,
leukocytosis, hyper- or hypothermia and palpable enlargement of
allograft. Swift recognition and action are necessary to have the best
chance of controlling/reversing the reaction by interceding with IV
immunosuppression and supportive care. Frequent monitoring of
cyclosporine levels can help palliate the chances of a rejection
reaction.

Chronic Complications
These include chronic allograft nephropathy, infections secondary to
immunosuppression (ch. 227), retroperitoneal fibrosis, and
increased risk of neoplasia and diabetes mellitus.202 Chronic
allograft nephropathy is the gradual loss of function of the
transplanted kidney and is a major problem in human renal
transplantation. It is thought to occur in ∼70% of feline allografts.207
Retroperitoneal fibrosis is a condition where the transplanted kidney
and ureter become encased in fibrosis which results in ureteral
obstruction. This condition may occur in up to 21% of renal
transplant cats and can be addressed by debridement but can
subsequently recur. Risk factors to prevent this outcome are

currently poorly understood. Due to lifelong immunosuppression,
renal transplant patients are at risk for secondary infection,
including bacterial, viral, fungal, protozoal and mycobacterial
infections. Rigorous screening can help reduce the incidence; in the
case of toxoplasmosis this is crucial as treatment of active disease in
immunosuppressed patients is rarely successful. A 6-fold increased
risk of development of cancer and 5-fold increased risk of
development of diabetes mellitus have also been reported in feline
renal transplant patients.202

Outcome
Compared to survival times for cats with late stage CKD treated
medically, renal transplant undoubtedly improves survival. However,
the ability of a cat to tolerate the needed interventions necessary for
success is important. In 2 studies, survival to hospital discharge was
77.5-93% (which has improved from first reports with honing of
techniques and protocols), with 84% survival at 30 days, 65-76%
survival at 6 months, and 40% survival at 3 years. Median overall
survival time was 613 days (range 131-1095) in 1 study and 653 days
(range 2-4580 days) in the second.206,208 Factors such as age,
severity of azotemia, systemic hypertension and cardiovascular
disease may affect prognosis.206

Glomerular diseases are a leading cause of kidney disease in dogs.1
In randomly selected dogs, the prevalence of glomerular lesions is as
high as 43-90%,2 and it appears to increase with age.3 Glomerular
diseases also occur in cats, although less frequently.4,5 Immune
complex glomerulonephritis (ICGN), amyloidosis, and
glomerulosclerosis are the most common glomerular diseases of
dogs, comprising approximately 77-84% of the lesions described in
663 dogs that underwent renal biopsy for suspected glomerular
disease6 or renal disease (Box 302.1).7 In cats with renal biopsy
performed for investigation of proteinuric chronic kidney disease
(CKD), ICGN was the most common diagnosis.8 Progress has been
made in deepening our understanding of the varied glomerular
diseases that occur in dogs; fewer studies have been done in cats.
Consensus recommendations have been published regarding the
approach to the diagnosis, standard therapy, and
immunosuppressive treatment for dogs with suspected glomerular
disease.9-13

NORMAL GLOMERULAR STRUCTURE
AND FUNCTION
The glomerulus is a modified capillary bed that functions as a filter,
across which an ultrafiltrate of the plasma is formed.14,15 The normal
glomerulus contains several lobules, each composed of capillaries
supported on a centrilobular core of mesangial matrix (Figure
302.1).14,15 The filtration barrier is composed of 3 layers: a highly
fenestrated endothelium; the glomerular basement membrane
(GBM), a network of extracellular matrix proteins, including type IV
collagen, laminin, and heparan-sulfate-bound proteoglycans; and
visceral epithelial cells, or podocytes, with interdigitating foot

processes bridged by specialized cell junctions known as slit
diaphragms.16 On the luminal surface of the endothelium, a layer of
negatively charged glycoproteins, known as the glycocalyx, covers the
fenestrae.17 This complex structure is freely permeable to water and
small dissolved solutes, but retains cells and most macromolecules,
such as proteins. The passage into the filtrate is determined by
molecular size and ionic charge. Small molecules, such as inulin (5
kDa), pass freely through the filter. Substances are retained with
increasing efficiency as they increase in size to approximately 60 to
70 kDa; only small amounts of substances larger than this are
filtered. Albumin, a negatively charged protein with a molecular
weight of 69 kDa, is normally largely excluded from the filtrate,
though its filtration appears greater than previously determined.18
Although each layer is important for the selectivity of the filtration
barrier, the GBM is likely a primary determinant of size selectivity,
while the negatively charged glycoproteins in the glycocalyx, GBM,
and slit diaphragms promote charge selectivity.16,17 Despite this
complex filtration system, small amounts of albumin and other
proteins are normally found in the filtrate. Substantial degradation
of these proteins occurs, resulting in excretion only of peptide
fragments, which are not detected by routine total protein assays.
Proteins and peptide fragments may also undergo resorption in the
proximal tubule.18,19
