CLINICAL FINDINGS
SIGNALMENT
Glomerular diseases can develop at any age,7 but appear to be most
common in middle-aged to older dogs. The prevalence of
microalbuminuria, a marker of increased glomerular permeability,
increases as dogs age, with marked increases seen beyond 6 years of
age.20 The average age of 375 dogs with a variety of glomerular
diseases reported in 5 studies was 8.3 years.1,21-24 Dogs with
nephrotic syndrome (NS) may present at a younger age (mean, 6.2
years).25 Male and female dogs were equally represented. However,
the average age and sex predilection seen with specific glomerular
diseases vary from the overall averages. In cats, glomerular diseases
may be more common in young individuals, with 1 study reporting a
median age at diagnosis of 3.5 years for those affected by ICGN and
1.3 years for those affected by other glomerular diseases.8 Male cats
were overrepresented in the ICGN group in that study.
Glomerular diseases often occur secondarily to infectious (e.g.,
vector-borne diseases), inflammatory (e.g., chronic dermatitis),
immune-mediated (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus), or
neoplastic (e.g., lymphoma) diseases. Familial glomerular diseases
often are manifested at an early age. Several breeds of dogs are
known to have familial glomerular diseases; many of these are
discussed in detail in ch. 305. Labrador Retrievers and Golden
Retrievers may have a higher incidence of glomerular disease;
however, the possibility that this increased representation reflects
the popularity of these breeds requires further evaluation.7,21,26

HISTORY

The clinical signs associated with glomerular disease vary
considerably, depending on the severity of proteinuria and the
presence or absence of renal azotemia.21,22,27 Many affected animals
have no clinical signs, and proteinuria is detected during routine
health screening. Alternatively, specific signs related to an
underlying inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic condition may be
present. Signs of glomerular disease may be nonspecific (e.g., weight
loss, lethargy) or consistent with CKD or uremia (e.g., polyuria,
polydipsia, anorexia, vomiting, and malodorous breath). Acute
kidney injury (AKI; ch. 300) is not a common presentation in
animals with glomerular disease but does occur. When proteinuria is
severe, signs of fluid retention (e.g., abdominal enlargement
consistent with ascites [ch. 21], peripheral edema [ch. 30]) or
thromboembolism (e.g., dyspnea [ch. 219], loss of limb function
[ch. 238]) may be present. Hypertensive damage to the central
nervous system (ch. 243), eyes (ch. 13), or cardiovascular system
(ch. 236) may induce a variety of clinical signs.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION FINDINGS
The physical examination (ch. 3) is often unremarkable in dogs with
glomerular disease.21,22,27 Nonspecific evidence of systemic disease
(e.g., poor body condition or poor haircoat) or advanced kidney
disease (e.g., oral ulcerations, pale mucous membranes, or clinical
signs consistent with dehydration) may be present. Subcutaneous
edema, ascites, or both are sometimes noted (ch. 30). Occasionally
dogs have physical evidence of thromboembolic disease, such as
dyspnea or a decreased or absent peripheral pulse (ch. 238).
Evidence of a predisposing inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic
process may be noted. The kidneys of affected animals are variable in
size. Animals with CKD often have small, firm, irregularly shaped
kidneys (ch. 301), whereas those with acute disease often have
normal-sized or, occasionally, enlarged kidneys (ch. 300).

CLINICOPATHOLOGIC AND IMAGING
FINDINGS

Proteinuria is the hallmark of glomerular disease and is discussed in
ch. 70. Thorough assessment of proteinuria includes locating its
source and evaluating for persistence and magnitude.9,28 A urine
protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPC) >0.5 or 0.4 in a dog or cat,
respectively, is abnormal in a urine sample free of inflammation or
discoloration from hematuria. By itself, microscopic hematuria
appears to have negligible influence on UPC.29,30 The greater the
magnitude of proteinuria, the greater the likelihood that the animal
has glomerular disease.7,8,31 On average, dogs with ICGN have
higher UPCs than those with other glomerular diseases,7 while the
opposite appears to be true in cats.8 However, the overlap in
expected UPC ranges is too broad for it to be a clinically reliable
predictor of a specific diagnosis for an individual.7,31,32
In 3 studies of urine albumin in canine models of glomerular
disease, microalbuminuria was detected before increases in the UPC,
and the magnitude of microalbuminuria increased over time in dogs
that eventually developed an increased UPC.33-35 A dog with
persistent microalbuminuria of increasing magnitude may eventually
develop overt proteinuria and should be assessed as having an
injurious process to the glomerular filtration barrier. Glomerular
lesions also have been identified in dogs without proteinuria.36-38
Isosthenuria is a variable finding in dogs and cats with glomerular
diseases.7,8,31 The presence of renal azotemia and an intact
concentrating ability is indicative of glomerular disease. In 1 study,
37% of dogs with glomerulonephritis (GN) had urine specific
gravities in excess of 1.035, and isosthenuria was detected in only
29%.22 However, in dogs with amyloidosis, dilute urine (i.e., urine
specific gravity less than 1.016) occurred in 63% of individuals,
whereas only 5.1% showed evidence of being able to concentrate
their urine above 1.035.27 Cylindruria is common in dogs and cats
with glomerular disease; casts are most often hyaline but can be
granular, waxy, or fatty (ch. 70). Renal hematuria develops with
glomerular injury in humans with various specific diseases (e.g., IgA
nephropathy, thin basement membrane disease, postinfectious
GN),15 but it appears to be less common in dogs and cats with

glomerulopathies. Erythrocytes that have passed through the
abnormal glomerular capillary bed are often misshapen; the
morphology of urine erythrocytes can be used to differentiate
hematuria of glomerular origin from that resulting from other
causes.
Hypoproteinemia caused by hypoalbuminemia develops in many
dogs and cats with glomerular disease and is more likely in animals
with heavy proteinuria. Hypoalbuminemia occurred in 60% and 70%
of dogs with GN or amyloidosis,22,27 and 80% and 90% of cats with
ICGN or other glomerular diseases,8 respectively. Azotemia,
hyperphosphatemia, and metabolic acidosis, consistent with renal
failure, may be present in animals with severe disease (ch. 299). Of
dogs with GN or amyloidosis, 53% and 26%, respectively, were not
azotemic at the time of diagnosis.22,27 Nonregenerative anemia that
develops secondary to CKD or a systemic disease is observed in many
affected animals. Other hematologic abnormalities also may reflect
concurrent and possibly underlying systemic diseases.
Thrombocytosis and hyperfibrinogenemia are common findings in
dogs with glomerular disease.
The nephrotic syndrome (NS) of hypoalbuminemia, proteinuria,
hypercholesterolemia, and edema, although pathognomonic for
glomerular disease, was present in only 15% of dogs with GN in 1
study.22 Incomplete NS (i.e., without edema or ascites) was more
common, occurring in 49% of dogs.22 Though more likely to occur in
dogs with marked proteinuria, NS was not associated with any
specific histologic diagnosis in 1 study.25 The prevalence of NS in
cats is unknown, but it also occurs in that species.39-41
The nephritic syndrome is a term primarily used in people to
describe a constellation of signs that develop secondary to renal
inflammation, generally acute, that extends into the glomeruli. In
people, this syndrome is characterized by hematuria and red blood
cell casts with 1 or more of the following: subnephrotic proteinuria,
edema, hypertension, azotemia, and oliguria.42 Although the
nephritic syndrome has not been fully characterized in dogs, it is
possible that those with acute Lyme nephritis may have a “nephriticlike” syndrome (ch. 187).

Radiographically, the kidneys may appear normal or small and
irregular; some animals may have enlarged kidneys. Similar changes
in shape and size can be seen ultrasonographically; increased
echogenicity of the cortex and loss of corticomedullary distinction
may also be noted. The renal pelvis may be mildly dilated if polyuria
is present or fluids are being administered.
Consensus recommendations state that the diagnostic evaluation
should be more extensive for dogs with UPC above 3.5 and those
with more clinical abnormalities as a result of glomerular injury than
for dogs with only mild proteinuria.9 An extensive evaluation would
include tests for the detection of underlying infectious,
inflammatory, or neoplastic diseases. A thorough physical
examination should be performed; diseases of the oral cavity or skin
should not be overlooked as potential underlying disorders (chs. 12
and 258). Cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspirates should be
performed on all cutaneous and subcutaneous masses (ch. 83).
Serologic testing for regional infectious diseases should be
performed. Evaluation might include tests for autoantibodies (e.g.,
antinuclear antibodies) in animals with extrarenal abnormalities
(e.g., thrombocytopenia, polyarthritis; ch. 179). During radiographic
or ultrasonographic evaluation of the abdomen, attention should be
given to detecting extrarenal disease processes. Thoracic
radiographs, particularly in middle-aged to older dogs, should be
evaluated for evidence of neoplastic disease.

RENAL BIOPSY AND HISTOLOGIC
DIAGNOSES
Indications
Renal biopsy provides a definitive diagnosis of glomerular disease,
but may not be needed if treatment of a potential underlying disease
leads to resolution of the proteinuria or end-stage renal disease is
already present. Therefore, renal biopsy is typically recommended
for animals with substantial proteinuria, that fail to respond to or
whose disease progresses despite standard therapy (described
below), and when the kidney disease is not end-stage.9 When

evaluated appropriately, renal histologic features can provide
important clinical information about the type and severity of lesions
in dogs and cats with glomerular disease. In fact, obtaining an
accurate histologic diagnosis may be one of the more important
factors in the successful management of the dog or cat with
glomerular disease. Clinical decisions regarding the diagnosis,
treatment, and prognosis can be made from the information
obtained through renal biopsy.

Procurement and Processing of the Renal Biopsy
Specimen
The procedure used to obtain a renal biopsy specimen is discussed in
ch. 299 (Video 299.1).

The renal biopsy procedure requires

expertise and should be performed only by experienced personnel.43
Systemic arterial hypertension (ch. 236) and coagulation disorders
(ch. 170) should be controlled prior to biopsy. When a specimen is
to be used for evaluation of glomerular disease, only cortical tissue
should be obtained; biopsy of the medulla is not needed and is
associated with a greater risk of hemorrhage, infarction, and fibrosis.
The use of general anesthesia is associated with an ability to obtain
better-quality specimens. An adequate sample of cortex has a
minimum of 5 glomeruli when examined by light microscopy,
although 1 glomerulus may suffice to make a diagnosis in animals in
which the disease is diffuse and easily recognizable (i.e.,
amyloidosis).
If a percutaneous method is used to obtain a renal biopsy
specimen from an animal with glomerular disease, at least 2 quality
samples of renal cortex (i.e., each >10 mm long) should be obtained,
using either a 16- or 18-gauge needle. A dissecting microscope can be
used to verify that adequate biopsy samples have been obtained. One
sample should be placed in formalin, and the other should be divided
into 2 smaller pieces containing glomeruli. One piece is put into a
fixative suitable for transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (e.g.,
4% formalin plus 1% glutaraldehyde in sodium phosphate buffer),
and the other piece is frozen for immunofluorescent microscopy
(IFM). An alternative to freezing is to immerse the tissue in
ammonium sulfate-N-ethylmaleimide (i.e., Michel’s solution), which

preserves tissue-fixed immunoglobulins. Wedge biopsies should be
divided in a similar fashion. Tissue for TEM should be minced
appropriately and put into the fixative within 5 minutes of biopsy.
Renal biopsy kits containing the appropriate fixatives may be
obtained from centers that specialize in renal pathology, such as the
International Veterinary Renal Pathology Service.

Evaluation of the Renal Biopsy Specimen
Only pathologists who have expertise in renal pathology should
evaluate renal biopsy specimens. The inclusion of TEM and IFM is
required for determining the presence or absence of immunecomplexes and making an accurate and clinically useful morphologic
diagnosis.32 Limiting the evaluation to light microscopy alone often
allows for only a subjective interpretation of the glomerular lesion. A
standard classification system for the characterization of glomerular
lesions in dogs has been proposed.32 Information on complete
evaluation of renal biopsy specimens and images from dogs with
several of the glomerular diseases discussed below can be found at
https://ohiostate.pressbooks.pub/vetrenalpathatlas/.

URINE GEL ELECTROPHORESIS
Sodium dodecyl-sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis of urine,
performed by a renal pathology laboratory, can be used as a
noninvasive marker of glomerular injury. In a study of 207 dogs,
electrophoretic banding patterns had a sensitivity of 97% and
specificity of 100% for detection of glomerular damage, and
sensitivity of 90% and specificity of 100% for detection of
tubulointerstitial damage.44

GLOMERULAR DISEASES
Many glomerular diseases affect dogs; fewer appear to affect cats
(Box 302.1). The historical approach of grouping these under the
umbrella of “GN” has limited the advancement of our understanding
and management of these disorders. This section summarizes what is

known about the individual diseases in dogs and cats, with additional
information garnered from the wealth of knowledge on these
diseases in humans. Acquired glomerular injury is the result of
damage sustained after immune complex formation or deposition
(e.g., membranous nephropathy [MN]; membranoproliferative
glomerulonephritis [MPGN]) or damage caused by other systemic
factors that affect the glomerulus (e.g., amyloidosis). ICGN affected
48.1% of 501 dogs with suspected glomerular disease6 and 58% of 53
cats with proteinuric CKD, corresponding to 74% of cats with
glomerular diseases.8 Immune complexes that are deposited in the
glomerulus or that form in situ initiate glomerular damage.45 Cellmediated immune mechanisms also take part in the pathogenesis of
glomerular inflammation. Once glomerular damage has been
initiated, other processes contribute to glomerular injury, including
activation of complement and the coagulation cascade and resident
cells; influx of neutrophils, monocytes, and platelets; release of
proteolytic enzymes; synthesis of cytokines or growth factors;
generation of proinflammatory lipid mediators; and alteration of
hemodynamic factors. The mechanisms that determine whether
progressive renal damage or resolution of the process occurs are
unclear.

MEMBRANOPROLIFERATIVE
GLOMERULONEPHRITIS (MPGN)
MPGN is a pattern of glomerular injury diagnosed when both
thickened capillary loops and mesangial hypercellularity (more than
3 nuclei per mesangial region) are present.14,15,24,32 It is one of the
most common glomerular diseases in dogs and cats and was
identified in 26% of the 89 canine biopsies in 1 report.1,32,46
Prevalence of this disease is likely overestimated in early studies
because glomerular lesions are most likely to be called MPGN when
the evaluation has not included the use of IFM and TEM.
The mean age of dogs with MPGN in each of 2 studies was 6.7 and
10.5 years, respectively.7,24 Males and females appear to be equally
affected. In 1 study of dogs, MPGN was associated with the most

severe constellation of clinical abnormalities (i.e., highest median
UPC ratio and serum creatinine concentrations, lowest serum
albumin concentrations, and a higher frequency of hypertension
than any other disease cluster).32 In a different study, NS was
present in 36% of dogs with MPGN.25
MPGN has been identified as a familial disease in Bernese
Mountain Dogs.47 A unique, rapidly progressive form of MPGN that
is accompanied by tubular necrosis and interstitial inflammation and
is uniformly fatal has been reported in association with Borrelia
burgdorferi infection (Lyme disease; ch. 187) in dogs.26 The
average age of affected dogs was only 5.6 years. Labrador Retrievers
and Golden Retrievers were significantly predisposed to developing
this lesion.
The form of MPGN identified in dogs more closely aligns with type
I MPGN in people, which is often induced by infectious diseases and
is characterized by immune complex accumulation on the
mesangium and the subendothelial side of the GBM.14,15 MPGN has
been associated with a variety of infectious diseases in dogs. In
humans with MPGN, hypocomplementemia is common and this
disease is sometimes called hypocomplementemic
glomerulonephritis. Interestingly, type I MPGN also occurs in
Brittany Spaniels and humans with congenital C3 deficiency.36
Effective treatment of the underlying infectious, inflammatory, or
neoplastic disease is the cornerstone of treatment of MPGN.
Immunosuppressive therapy (chs. 144, 169) should be considered in
animals that have severe, persistent or progressive disease. Because
platelet activation appears to be involved in the pathogenesis of this
disease, antiplatelet drugs also should be given (chs. 219, 238).14
Specific data regarding the prognosis of MPGN in dogs and cats
are lacking. In people, azotemia, systemic hypertension, and marked
tubulointerstitial lesions at presentation are the most significant
predictors of an unfavorable outcome.15

MEMBRANOUS NEPHROPATHY (MN)

MN describes a loss of the normal lacy-appearance of the GBM,
which becomes uniformly thickened and more rigid due to the
deposition of immune complexes in the subepithelial spaces.14,24,32
MN is another common glomerular disease in dogs. While reported
in up to 45% of dogs in various studies, it was identified in 26% of
the thoroughly evaluated biopsies in a recent study.2,24,32,48-50 In
cats, MN is the most common glomerular disease, followed by
MPGN.8,51-53
MN appears to be more common in male dogs and cats
(approximate male to female ratios, 1.75:1 in dogs and 6:1 in cats).
The mean age of affected dogs from 5 studies was 6.8 years (range, 1
to 14 years).7,23,24,48,49 The disease is more common in younger
cats, with an approximate mean age of only 3.6 years (range, 1 to 7
years).51 There does not appear to be any breed predilection,
although a preponderance of Doberman Pinschers was seen in 1
report.49 Interestingly, 4 of 5 of those Dobermans were 3 years of age
or younger, which may suggest a familial pattern.
Proteinuria in animals with MN may be massive.7,38 In a study of
NS in dogs, 38% of dogs with MN had NS.25 Microhematuria is
reported in 30-40% of humans with MN,15 but has not been
systematically studied in dogs and cats. Animals with MN may
present with signs of advanced kidney disease. Many cats have
normal to enlarged kidneys at presentation.
MN has 4 ultrastructural stages (Figure 302.2) that correlate
with the temporal evolution of the disease and the clinical
presentation in dogs, cats, and humans. More advanced stages in
cats and dogs have been shown to correlate with more severe
azotemia, whereas animals with milder disease were more likely to
have NS.49,51 In some cases, lesions of different stages were found
within a single biopsy specimen.
Overall, MN is considered an ICGN. In human patients with
primary MN, the weight of evidence supports that immune
complexes form in situ, when unbound antibodies react with
antigens expressed on the podocyte’s surface (e.g., neutral
endopeptidase, NEP; or M-type phospholipase A2 receptor,

PLA2R).54 In this regard, primary disease seems to be a true
autoimmune disorder. Immune responses to non-glomerular
antigens adhered to the podocyte or circulating immune complexes
most likely play a larger role in patients with secondary disease.14

FIGURE 302.2 Ultrastructural stages in the
progression of membranous nephropathy. Stage I is
characterized by interspersed subepithelial deposits
without intervening glomerular basement membrane
(GBM) spike formation. In stage II, the subepithelial
deposits are more numerous and more closely
approximated with the intervening GBM spikes. In
stage III, the GBM spikes extend over and encircle
the deposits, incorporating them into the glomerular
capillary walls. In stage IV, the deposits lie within a
mottled, irregularly thickened GBM and appear
electron lucent, consistent with resorption. The
irregular thickness of the GBM is consistent with
extracellular matrix remodeling. Courtesy J.C.
Jennette, School of Medicine, University of North
Carolina, Chapel Hill, NC.
TEM should be used to confirm the location of the immune
deposits and characterize the stage of disease progression (Figure
302.2).14,32,49,51 Deposition of immune complexes, progressive
engulfment of the complexes by the surrounding GBM, and eventual
resolution of the deposits characterize the stages. Sometimes staging
is difficult because glomeruli at several stages of disease may be
present simultaneously.
In addition to the identification and treatment of potentially
inciting disease processes and nonspecific management of

proteinuria, immunosuppressive therapy may be warranted in dogs
or cats with severe, persistent, or progressive disease. Affected
humans with similar clinical pictures may respond to
immunosuppressive therapy.15 Even when treatment is effective,
relapses may occur. The use of immunosuppressive therapy in dogs
and cats with MN needs to be studied.
Although MN appears to be progressive in some dogs and cats, the
progression may be slow enough that many animals can lead
relatively normal lives. In a study of 24 cats with MN, 4 (17%)
survived 4 to 10 months, and 8 (33%) had long-term survival of 2.5
to 6 years; clinical remission occurred in 7 (29%) of the cats.
Corticosteroids were administered to 3 of the 8 long-term survivors.
However, 11 cats (46%) died or were euthanized because of NS or
advanced renal disease shortly after diagnosis.52 Long-term
survivors had only IgG deposition, C3 deposition, or both; cats that
also had deposition of IgM or IgA had a shorter survival period.
Stages III and IV MN, defined by the presence of intramembranous
deposits, were associated with a poorer prognosis.52
Survival data for dogs appear to be similar to what has been
reported in cats, with reported survival ranging from 4 days to
greater than 3 years.49 Spontaneous remission has been reported.
Spontaneous remission occurs in 20-30% of humans with MN,
whereas 20-40% of cases progress to CKD.15

PROLIFERATIVE
GLOMERULONEPHRITIS
Proliferative GN, an ICGN caused by endocapillary or mesangial
proliferation, accounted for 2-16% of glomerular lesions in dogs in 2
studies but none were identified in a recent pathologic study, most
likely because uncommon diagnoses were excluded.24,32,46 In
humans, a pathologic diagnosis requires both a morphologic
description (e.g., mesangial proliferative GN), and a specific disease
designation (e.g., IgA nephropathy, lupus GN).14,15 Mesangial
proliferative GN is characterized by mesangial cell hyperplasia (≥4

cells per mesangial area) that is often accompanied by increased
mesangial matrix.14,24 With the exception of IgA nephropathy,
proliferative GN in dogs has not included the specific disease
designation.55,56
Dogs with proliferative GN reported in 2 studies were on average
between 7 and 9 years of age.23,24 Proteinuria and renal azotemia
were the most common presenting signs. Azotemia may be mild or
moderate and acute or chronic. Although hematuria is associated
with this disorder in people,57 its presence in dogs is unknown.
Proliferative GN often develops secondary to systemic diseases.
The potential source of immune complexes should be removed, and
nonspecific management of glomerular diseases should be followed.
Immunosuppressive therapy may be warranted in animals with
severe, persistent, or progressive disease. While the prognosis has
not been fully evaluated in dogs, the presence of advanced azotemia
or crescents is likely associated with a poorer prognosis.

AMYLOIDOSIS
The term amyloidosis refers to a diverse group of diseases that have
in common the extracellular deposition of fibrils formed by
polymerization of proteins with a beta-pleated sheet conformation.58
The beta-pleated conformation is responsible for the characteristic
staining properties of the amyloid deposits, which include exhibiting
apple-green birefringence when stained with Congo red stain and
viewed with polarized light.14
Amyloidosis accounts for approximately 7-15% of the glomerular
lesions in dogs.6,7,31 Reactive amyloidosis is the most common form
of amyloidosis in dogs and cats, with the dog being the domestic
animal most commonly affected by amyloidosis. With the exception
of the Chinese Shar-Pei, amyloid is deposited primarily in the
glomeruli of affected dogs.27,59 Amyloidosis is relatively uncommon
in the cat, with the exception of Abyssinians and Siamese (especially
the Oriental shorthair color variant).60 In Abyssinians, amyloid is

deposited primarily in the renal medulla, although glomerular
involvement has been described.
Renal amyloidosis is more common in middle-aged to older dogs.
The mean age of affected dogs was 7.7 years in 1 study,7 and 9.2 years
in another study, in which 85% of affected dogs were 7 years of age
or older.27 In 1 report, females appeared to be affected more often
than males (male to female ratio, 1:1.7),27 though similar sex
distribution was reported more recently.61 Collies and Walker
Hounds may be at increased risk for amyloidosis; the disorder is
familial in the Chinese Shar-Pei and may be familial in Beagles and
English Foxhounds.27,62
Proteinuria associated with amyloidosis may be of high
magnitude, with NS reported in 10-56% of affected dogs.25,61
However, dogs with amyloidosis did not have higher UPC ratios or
serum creatinine concentrations or lower serum albumin
concentrations than dogs with other glomerular diseases.7,31,32 In
another study, 6 of 7 dogs with amyloidosis had nonselective
proteinuria, suggesting a marked loss of the size-selective properties
of the glomerular capillary wall.38 Although amyloid may be
deposited in other organ systems (e.g., liver, spleen, adrenal glands,
gastrointestinal tract), clinical signs associated with extra-renal
deposition are uncommon in dogs. Chronic infectious and
noninfectious inflammatory diseases and neoplasia have been
reported in association with reactive amyloidosis in 32-53% of
affected dogs; however, many affected animals do not have an
identifiable inflammatory process at the time of presentation.21,27
Renal amyloidosis in the Shar-Pei develops at an earlier age (mean
and median age, 4.1 and 4.8 years, respectively) than in other dogs
with amyloidosis.59,61 Like in other breeds, the disease might be
more common in females (male to female ratio, 1:2.5),62 though this
was not confirmed in a more recent publication.61 In Shar-Peis,
amyloid is most commonly deposited in the renal medulla; only 6479% of Shar-Peis had glomerular involvement and as few as 25-43%
had proteinuria.59,61 Affected dogs may have signs of involvement of

other organs, particularly the liver. Many Shar-Peis have a history of
recurrent fever and swelling of the tibiotarsal joints (commonly
called Shar-Pei fever or Shar-Pei swollen hock syndrome; ch. 177)
before the development of renal amyloidosis, suggesting that this
may be an animal model of familial Mediterranean fever.
The primary protein involved in the formation of amyloid deposits
in dogs and cats is amyloid A protein, which is formed by the
polymerization of the amino terminal portion of serum amyloid A
protein (SAA), an acute-phase reactant.58 SAA is synthesized and
released by hepatocytes after they have been stimulated by
macrophage-derived cytokines (e.g., interleukin-1 [IL-1], IL-6, tumor
necrosis factor). Because of the association of amyloid A with
inflammatory diseases, this form of amyloidosis has been termed
reactive, or secondary, amyloidosis. Humans with familial
Mediterranean fever, a disease similar to that reported in Shar-Peis,
have defective formation of pyrin, a protein involved in the downregulation of mediators of inflammation.63
SAA concentrations are increased during the predeposition phase,
before the appearance of tissue amyloid deposits; increases may
persist during the deposition phase. Abyssinians with renal
amyloidosis have increased SAA concentrations.58 Chinese Shar-Peis
with renal amyloidosis have increased serum concentrations of IL-6,
a cytokine that stimulates SAA synthesis and release.64
The beta-pleated sheet configuration of amyloid fibrils leads to
their insolubility and resistance to proteolysis, making specific
treatment relatively ineffectual. In humans with familial
Mediterranean fever, colchicine prevented the development of renal
amyloidosis even in patients who continued to have recurrent febrile
episodes.63,65 This led to the recommendation that colchicine be
used in the management of Shar-Peis with renal amyloidosis. Ideally,
this drug is administered during the pre-deposition phase, which in
Shar-Peis is presumably characterized by recurrent fevers and
swollen hocks. However, colchicine administration may lead to
remission of proteinuria even after the appearance of amyloid
deposits. No evidence supports the effectiveness of colchicine once
amyloidosis has resulted in persistent azotemia or
hypoalbuminemia. Although the effects of the drug in the treatment

of amyloidosis are not fully known, colchicine does impair the
release of SAA from hepatocytes by binding to microtubules and
preventing secretion. In addition, colchicine may prevent the
production of amyloid-enhancing factor. The dosage of colchicine
used is 0.01 to 0.03 mg/kg given orally every 24 hours.
Gastrointestinal upset is the primary side-effect. Colchicine use has
been recommended on occasion for people with renal amyloidosis
from causes other than familial Mediterranean fever and warrants
further evaluation in dogs.
Dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO) has been shown to be beneficial in a
limited number of dogs with renal amyloidosis,65 although the exact
benefit remains controversial. If given during the rapid deposition
phase, DMSO leads to a decrease in SAA concentrations and
resolution of tissue deposits. However, the amount of amyloid
deposited in the kidneys of humans was unchanged after DMSO
administration, which suggests that DMSO does not solubilize
amyloid fibrils. The anti-inflammatory effects of DMSO may account
for some of its benefits. DMSO has an unpleasant smell that may
cause poor owner compliance. Furthermore, this drug may
contribute to signs of nausea and anorexia seen in some dogs. The
recommended dosage is 90 mg/kg given orally or subcutaneously 3
times weekly. DMSO should be diluted 1:4 with sterile water before
injection to limit the pain associated with injection.
The prognosis for dogs and cats with renal amyloidosis is generally
poor. In 1 study of dogs with amyloidosis, 58% died or were
euthanized at the time of diagnosis. In the remaining dogs, survival
ranged from 2 to 20 months; survival of a year or longer was
reported in only 8.5%.58 The longest survival was observed in a dog
treated with DMSO.

HEREDITARY NEPHRITIS (HN)
The term hereditary nephritis (HN) refers to a diverse group of
inherited glomerular diseases that are the result of a defect in
basement membrane collagen (type IV).66 These diseases are
discussed in ch. 305. A brief discussion of HN is included in this
chapter because it should be considered as a differential diagnosis

for any dog presenting with proteinuric renal disease, particularly if
the dog is young.
HN has been reported in several breeds of dogs. HN is the result of
a genetic mutation or deletion in type IV collagen, the primary
protein constituent of the GBM.67,68 The presence of defective
collagen leads to premature deterioration of the GBM and
progressive glomerular disease. TEM is required to make the
diagnosis of HN. Multilaminar splitting and fragmentation of the
GBM are seen, often with intramembranous, electron-dense
deposits.
An autosomal recessive form of the disease occurs in English
Cocker Spaniels and English Springer Spaniels, whereas Bull Terriers
and Dalmatians develop an autosomal dominant form.66,69-72 An Xlinked dominant form of HN has been described in Samoyeds and
mixed-breed dogs; carrier females may have mild disease.69 The
report in Samoyeds is of a single kindred; the disease is not
considered to be common in this breed. HN is characterized by
proteinuria, renal hematuria, and progressive glomerular disease.
Concurrent hearing and ocular abnormalities, as described in
humans with HN, appear to be uncommon in affected dogs, with the
exception of anterior lenticonus, which occurs in some Bull
Terriers.70
No specific treatment is available for affected dogs. Standard
therapy (described below) has proved beneficial. Early detection of
HN through screening of dogs of relevant breeds for
microalbuminuria allows early therapeutic intervention, which may
slow disease progression.33
The rate of disease progression is predictable in Samoyeds and
English Cocker Spaniels, with terminal kidney disease generally
developing before 2 years of age.66 However, progression is more
variable in Bull Terriers and Dalmatians, with some dogs surviving
for 10 years.70,71

MINIMAL CHANGE DISEASE (MCD)

Although uncommonly described in dogs and cats, minimal change
disease (MCD) is a common cause of NS in humans, especially
children.15,73 There is a lack of light microscopic lesions in the
glomerulus, hence the name MCD.14 Because TEM is required for
diagnosis, the disease most likely is underdiagnosed in dogs and
perhaps in cats. In humans, this disease is sometimes referred to as
nil disease, lipoid nephrosis, or idiopathic NS. Previously, there were
only isolated reports of dogs that appeared to have MCD, and 1 welldescribed case report of MCD in a dog presenting with NS.73
However, in a recent study of thoroughly evaluated renal biopsy
specimens, MCD was eventually diagnosed in 11 out of 162 dogs.7
In humans, MCD is usually idiopathic, although disease secondary
to various causes (e.g., malignancy, infections, drugs, and other
kidney and systemic diseases) also occurs. The precise pathogenesis
of MCD is unknown: several pathogenic immunologic, podocyterelated, and epigenetic mechanisms are thought to interplay in
altering the integrity of the GBM.14,74 The resultant proteinuria is
highly selective; albumin is the primary protein lost.
An important reason to include MCD on the list of differential
diagnoses for dogs with NS is the disease’s seemingly exquisite
response to corticosteroids; the expected response rate in humans
with MCD is 70-90%, though one or more relapses are seen in up to
90% of affected individuals.15 The prognosis for MCD in dogs is
unknown.

GLOMERULOSCLEROSIS
Glomerulosclerosis accounted for approximately 20% of the
glomerular lesions of dogs in a large study.6 Glomerulosclerosis
often develops as an end-stage lesion in response to glomerular
injury. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) describes a
pattern of glomerular scarring that affects a subset of glomeruli and
involves only a portion of the glomerular tuft.14 The term FSGS
applies to a group of distinct diseases with diverse etiologies.
Regardless of the specific cause, glomerulosclerosis occurs as a

pathophysiologic response to podocyte injury and loss.75 In humans,
most cases of FSGS are considered primary or idiopathic, though
secondary causes of FSGS, including viral infections, drugs, toxins,
and adaptive responses to glomerular hypertension, also occur.14
Similarly, in dogs, primary FSGS appears to be more common than
secondary, affecting 22% (vs. 11%) of 162 dogs who underwent renal
biopsy included in a recent report.7 The prevalence of
glomerulosclerosis increases with age, although the expected
percentage of sclerotic glomeruli in dogs of advancing age has not
been fully characterized. Glomerulosclerosis is common in diabetic
nephropathy in humans. Although glomerulosclerosis and
proteinuria can develop in dogs with diabetes mellitus, the clinical
relevance of this is unknown (ch. 291). Glomerulosclerosis can also
develop after hypertensive renal damage.
FSGS was identified in 20-33% of the thoroughly evaluated
biopsies in recent studies, making it one of the more common
glomerular diseases in dogs.6,7,24,32 Primary FSGS is diagnosed in
the proteinuric patient that has segmental glomerulosclerosis in a
glomerulus that is otherwise normal, without other glomerular
lesions present to explain the sclerosis. IFM evaluation should be
negative in affected patients; however, nonspecific trapping of
immunoglobulins and C3 can occur in sclerotic areas.
In a report of 77 dogs diagnosed with FSGS, females were
overrepresented (1.5 : 1 ratio), and most dogs were not azotemic or
severely hypoalbuminemic at the time of biopsy.76 Systemic arterial
hypertension was common, though the median systolic blood
pressure was 153.5 mm Hg (range, 95-260). Both serum creatinine
and albumin concentrations were found to be significantly associated
with survival times in that study, with the overall median survival
time post-biopsy being 258 days (range, 26-1003).

TUBULOINTERSTITIAL LESIONS
ASSOCIATED WITH GLOMERULAR
DISEASE

Proteinuria induces tubular damage, leading to progressive nephron
loss.77 Chronic proteinuria can lead to interstitial fibrosis, tubular
atrophy and peritubular capillary rarefaction. The urine of
proteinuric humans shows mediators of renal inflammation and
fibrosis, some of which are produced by renal tubules exposed to
various proteins.77 However, albumin is likely not the culprit because
rats and humans with highly selective proteinuria appear to be at
lower risk of eventual tubulointerstitial damage.
Tubular fluid protein is resorbed by the proximal tubules and is
cytotoxic to the tubular epithelial cells.78,79 Additionally, the
increased workload leads to compensatory hypertrophy of the
tubular epithelial cells and, eventually, promoted cell death. Some
damage also occurs secondary to obstruction of the tubules by
protein casts.80 Glomerular injury also results in decreased
perfusion of the tubulointerstitium. A direct link between proteinuria
and progressive kidney damage in dogs has not been established, but
it certainly exists to some extent. Because proteinuria may be a major
factor for progressive kidney disease in animals with glomerular
disease, aggressive management of proteinuria should be considered
a cornerstone of the treatment of dogs and cats with glomerular
disease.

TREATMENT
STANDARD THERAPY OF GLOMERULAR
DISEASE
In addition to specific management that might be implemented with
the various glomerular diseases, standard therapeutic interventions
are considerations for all dogs with glomerular disease.10 Standard
therapy can be divided into 3 major categories: (1) treatment of
potential underlying disease processes, (2) reduction of proteinuria,
and (3) management of uremia and other complications of
generalized kidney disease (discussed in ch. 301).
ICGN or amyloidosis develop after a strong, potentially
malorganized, immune, or inflammatory reaction, respectively, that
has developed in response to a stimulus; a thorough evaluation for

underlying diseases is warranted. The inciting agent might not be
obvious at presentation if the offending disease is no longer present
or is occult. Continued observation and scrutiny are necessary,
because the causative disease process may become apparent in the
ensuing months after presentation. The initial step in the
management of a persistently proteinuric dog or cat is to treat and
eliminate, if possible, any potential predisposing diseases. Animals
that are seropositive for infectious diseases should be given specific
anti-infective treatment immediately, even when there is no direct
causal evidence, and consideration should be given for
immunosuppressive treatment using the same guidelines presented
in the following discussion.13 The animal should be subsequently
evaluated for resolution of the proteinuria, which may occur slowly
over a period of months. If proteinuria does not resolve or worsens, a
renal biopsy to determine the histologic diagnosis may be warranted.
Antiproteinuric agents should be considered when the UPC is
persistently above 0.5 in a dog or 0.4 in a cat. Through interaction
with the angiotensin II type 1 receptor, angiotensin II induces
systemic and renal vasoconstriction with preferential constriction of
the efferent arteriole, leading to increased glomerular transcapillary
hydraulic pressure,81 which augments glomerular filtration and
exacerbates proteinuria. Therefore, antagonism of the reninangiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) using angiotensinconverting-enzyme (ACE) inhibitors (e.g., enalapril, benazepril) or
angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs; e.g., telmisartan) is considered
standard of care for dogs and cats with renal proteinuria. RAAS
antagonists may reduce proteinuria and preserve renal function by
several possible hemodynamic and non-hemodynamic
mechanisms.82,83 In a prospective, randomized, masked,
multicenter, placebo-controlled clinical trial, enalapril significantly
reduced proteinuria and delayed either the onset or the progression
of azotemia in 29 dogs with GN.84 Similar observations were made
in Samoyed dogs with X-linked HN, although the number of affected
treated subjects (n = 5) was small.85 Prospective, randomized,
placebo-controlled studies in cats with CKD, though not specifically
glomerular disease, have also documented the antiproteinuric effects
of benazepril.86,87

Selective antagonist of the angiotensin II type 1 receptor by an
ARB also achieves efferent arteriolar dilation; however, unlike ACE
inhibition, the use of an ARB allows for continued interaction of
angiotensin II with the angiotensin II type 2 receptor, which
mediates afferent arteriolar vasodilation and might help preserve the
glomerular filtration rate.88 Further, as ACE-independent pathways
for generation of angiotensin II have been recognized, another
theoretical advantage of ARBs, relative to ACE inhibitors, is that the
effects of angiotensin II mediated by its type 1 receptor are
minimized, regardless of the source of angiotensin II generation.89
In a prospective, single-center, double-masked clinical trial
comparing the effects of enalapril and telmisartan in 39 dogs with
proteinuric CKD, treatment with telmisartan achieved a significantly
greater and faster reduction in UPC than that with enalapril, with no
significant differences in the safety profile of either drug noted.90
Antiproteinuric and antihypertensive effects of telmisartan were
additionally noted in retrospective studies, though comparing the
relative efficacy of the ARB with the ACE inhibitors evaluated is
difficult due to the selection bias in those samples.91-93 A
prospective, multicenter, controlled, randomized, masked clinical
trial evaluating 274 cats with CKD also showed significant
antiproteinuric effects of telmisartan, which proved noninferior to
benazepril.94
Typically, enalapril or benazepril is administered at a starting
dosage of 0.5 mg/kg PO q24h or q12h in dogs,84 with gradual uptitration ranging up to 1.5 mg/kg PO q12h being reported.90
Benazepril is administered at a dosage of 0.5 to 1 mg/kg PO q24h in
cats.94 For treatment of proteinuria, telmisartan is administered at a
starting dosage of 1 mg/kg PO q24h in dogs or cats,90,94 with
gradual up-titration ranging up to 3 mg/kg PO q24h being
reported.90 In azotemic animals, RAAS antagonist therapy is
initiated at one-half or one-fourth of the typical starting dosages. The
dosage can be gradually increased to achieve the therapeutic target of
UPC <0.5 (ideal target) or >50% reduction from baseline (alternate
target) (Figure 302.3). Serum creatinine concentration should be

closely monitored following any changes in therapy. It is uncommon
for dogs and cats to have dose-limiting worsening of azotemia (i.e.,
>30% increase in serum creatinine) at the starting dosages of an ACE
inhibitor or ARB as a monotherapy. Hyperkalemia can occur in dogs
with glomerular disease treated with a RAAS inhibitor and can be
controlled by feeding a potassium-reduced home-prepared diet that
has been formulated by a veterinary nutritionist.95 In humans,
hyperkalemia is less frequently observed following treatment with an
ARB relative to ACE inhibition.96 Though similar findings were not
observed in dogs,90 if severe hyperkalemia (i.e., serum potassium
>6.5 mmol/L) develops in animals treated with an ACE inhibitor, it
is reasonable to consider substituting therapy with an ARB instead.
Combination therapy with an ACE inhibitor and an ARB may lead to
a greater reduction in proteinuria than monotherapy with either an
ACE inhibitor or an ARB97,98; however, combination therapy is
associated with increased likelihood of substantial adverse effects,
including worsening azotemia and increased risk of hyperkalemia,
hospitalization, and AKI, in dogs and people.90,99 Therefore, dual
therapy is not advisable unless the magnitude of proteinuria is
contributing to life-threatening hypoalbuminemia that has not been
corrected with monotherapy.
Adequate blood pressure control of hypertensive individuals may
also lead to a reduction in proteinuria and slow the progression of
disease (ch. 236). While ACE inhibitors are relatively weak
antihypertensive agents, the ARB telmisartan is an efficacious
antihypertensive, albeit at higher dosages than those used to treat
proteinuria.100,101 Additional antihypertensive agents (e.g.,
amlodipine) may be needed if hypertension (i.e., systolic blood
pressure >160 mm Hg) persists after the initiation of ACE inhibitor
or ARB therapy.
Platelets and thromboxane may play an important role in the
pathogenesis of GN and thromboxane synthetase inhibitors have
been shown to decrease proteinuria in dogs with experimentally
induced GN.102 Additionally, dogs with glomerular disease and
protein-losing nephropathy (PLN) are at high risk for
thromboembolism, and thromboprophylaxis is recommended for

affected individuals (see below).10,103 Aspirin is a nonspecific
cyclooxygenase inhibitor that may be used to reduce glomerular
inflammation and inhibit platelet aggregation. In theory, low doses
of aspirin (0.5-5 mg/kg PO daily) may be used,10 though platelet
inhibition is inconsistent among individuals and the optimum
aspirin protocol for platelet inhibition in dogs is unknown.104,105
Clopidogrel (1.1-3 mg/kg PO q24h), an adenosine diphosphate
receptor inhibitor, may effectively reduce platelet activity in dogs
(chs. 219, 238).106,107
The International Renal Interest Society (IRIS) consensus
recommendation is to feed modified protein diets to dogs with
glomerular disease, and dogs or cats with proteinuric CKD (ch.
158).10,108,109 Dietary protein reduction reduces proteinuria and
slows progression of CKD.110,111 Egg white, casein, or whey protein
can be added to the diet when there is a concern for cachexia and
sarcopenia (ch. 151). Diets should not be supplemented with
protein, because this may aggravate urinary protein losses. The
enhanced omega-3 to -6 polyunsaturated fatty acid ratio and
restriction in salt and phosphorus found in renal diets might also be
of benefit to animals with glomerulopathies. Omega-3 fatty acid
supplementation has been shown to be renoprotective in dogs with
kidney disease and mitigate hypertension and reduce serum
triglyceride and cholesterol concentrations in humans with NS.112
These positive effects are in part mediated through generation of the
3-series prostaglandins. Sodium restriction is beneficial in the
control of hypertension and fluid retention.

IMMUNOSUPPRESSIVE TREATMENT OF
DOGS WITH GLOMERULAR DISEASE
The use of immunosuppressive drugs (chs. 144, 169) in the
treatment of dogs with glomerular disease has not been fully studied.
However, consensus recommendations are to treat dogs that have
severe, persistent, or progressive glomerular disease with evidence of
an active immune pathogenesis based on biopsy findings,11 which

would be expected in just under 50% of dogs with glomerular
disease.32 When renal biopsy results are not available it becomes
more difficult to make a decision about using immunosuppressive
treatment because approximately 50% of dogs with glomerular
disease would be expected not to have an immunopathogenesis of
their disease. Consensus recommendations are to consider
immunosuppressive drugs in the treatment of dogs with glomerular
disease when the source of proteinuria is clearly glomerular in origin,
the drugs are not otherwise contraindicated, the dog breed and age
of disease onset are not suggestive of a familial nephropathy,
amyloidosis has been deemed unlikely, and the serum creatinine is
>3.0 mg/dL (>265 mcmol/L) or progressively increasing, or the
serum albumin is <2.0 g/dL (<20 g/L).12
Dogs with more severe disease or rapid rates of progression should
be treated more intensively than those with more stable disease.
According to the IRIS consensus statement,11 single agent or
combination therapy for rapid onset of immunosuppression should
be considered in dogs with high magnitude proteinuria with
hypoalbuminemia, NS, or rapidly progressive azotemia.
Mycophenolate, or cyclophosphamide, with or without short-term
administration of glucocorticoids, was suggested as the first choice.
Glucocorticoids should be limited to short-term therapy because
proteinuria has been demonstrated in dogs with corticosteroid
excess and may induce glomerular lesions and prednisolone
administration was shown to reversibly increase proteinuria in dogs
with HN.22,113,114 Dogs with stable or more slowly progressive
disease that have only partial or no response to standard therapy
might be given drugs that have either a rapid or a more delayed onset
of action (chs. 144, 169), such as mycophenolate, chlorambucil or
cyclophosphamide. Cyclosporine was also suggested as a first choice
for stable or slowly progressive dogs; however, this is the only drug
that has been studied prospectively in dogs with glomerular disease
and was found to be of no benefit, although there were flaws in that
study.115 All dogs treated with immunosuppressive therapy for their
glomerular disease should be monitored closely. Treatment should
be discontinued or adjusted if adverse drug effects develop. In the
absence of adverse effects, 8-12 weeks of therapy should be provided

before changing the course of treatment. If the therapeutic response
is suboptimal at the end of 8-12 weeks, an alternate drug protocol
should be considered. However, if after 3-4 months a therapeutic
response has not been achieved, consideration should be given to
discontinuing immunosuppressive drug administration. If after this
time, a response has been noted, the drug dose or schedule should be
tapered to one that maintains the response without worsening of
proteinuria, azotemia or clinical signs.11

FIGURE 302.3 Making adjustments to reninangiotensin-aldosterone system inhibition therapy in

dogs or cats with glomerular disease. ACEI,
Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor; ARB,
angiotensin receptor blocker; BP, systolic arterial
blood pressure; K, serum or plasma potassium

for example, 2 mg/dL creatinine = 176 mcmol/L

PATIENT MONITORING
Following changes in therapy, dogs with stable glomerular disease
and IRIS CKD stage 1 or 2 should be evaluated within 3-14 days,
whereas those with unstable disease or IRIS CKD stage 3 or 4 should
be evaluated within 3-5 days. If therapeutic changes are not being
made and the dogs are seemingly stable, standard re-evaluations of
body weight, body condition score (ch. 72 and textbook’s inside
covers), systemic arterial blood pressure (ch. 91), serum albumin,
creatinine and potassium concentrations, urinalysis, and UPC should
be made every 3 months. Fundic examination is recommended to
monitor for the development of ocular hypertensive target organ
damage (chs. 13, 236). Because histologic lesions might not resolve
even though renal function may improve, repeat biopsies generally
are not needed.
Response to therapy has historically been focused on a reduction
in proteinuria. However, it is logical also to evaluate changes in
serum creatinine and albumin concentrations. A complete response
to therapy is defined as a reduction in UPC to <0.5, a reduction in
serum creatinine to <1.4 mg/dL (<124 mcmol/L), or a sustained
increase in serum albumin to >2.5 g/dL (>25 g/L); whereas a partial
response is defined as a >50% reduction in UPC, >25% sustained
reduction in serum creatinine or >50% sustained reduction in serum
albumin when compared with baseline values or an increase in
serum albumin to >2.0-2.5 g/dL (20-25 g/L).11 Day-to-day
variations in the UPC occur in most dogs with glomerular
proteinuria, with greater variation occurring in dogs with UPC >4.116

Consideration should be given to either averaging 3 serial UPC or
measuring a UPC in urine that has been pooled from 3 collections.117
Change in proteinuria is most accurately assessed by UPC trends
over time.

COMPLICATIONS OF GLOMERULAR
DISEASE
Complications of severe proteinuria include edema formation,
systemic hypertension, hypercoagulability and thromboembolism,
hyperlipidemia, increased risk for infection, altered
pharmacokinetics (ch. 139), malnutrition, muscle wasting (ch. 151),
and endocrine abnormalities.80

EDEMA FORMATION
Several factors contribute to the formation of edema in patients with
NS (ch. 30).80,118 In severe forms of NS, decreases in the plasma
oncotic pressure allow for transudation of fluid into the interstitial
spaces. The resultant decrease in effective plasma volume leads to
increased RAAS activity and retention of water and sodium and
worsening of edema. Primary renal sodium retention might also be
involved in the pathogenesis of edema in NS, and is believed to be
the most important determinant of edema formation in people until
the serum albumin concentration decreases below 2 g/dL (20 g/L).
Below this concentration, the plasma oncotic pressure is sufficiently
reduced to allow for transudation of fluid from the vascular
compartment into the interstitial space (chs. 219, 238, 300).80
Dogs may be more resistant to the formation of edema, which does
not generally occur until the serum albumin concentration is below
1.5 g/dL (15 g/L). Plasma volume may be reduced at this point,
making the use of diuretics in the management of edema relatively
ineffective and also dangerous because of the increased risk of AKI
and thromboembolism (chs. 219, 238, 300).80 Dogs with
glomerular disease should have a careful assessment of their

hydration status and vascular volume prior to and during fluid
therapy. This evaluation should be based on serial body weight
measurements, skin turgor, mucous membrane color and moisture,
capillary refill time, temperature of the extremities, heart rate, pulse
quality, and systemic blood pressure (ch. 119). The use of diuretics
should be limited to situations where cavitary effusion is critically
impairing organ function.10 When indicated, furosemide may be the
drug of choice for animals with pulmonary edema or hyperkalemia,
and spironolactone for those with cavitary effusion.10 Provision of
adequate exercise also may help reduce the formation of edema or
effusions.

SYSTEMIC ARTERIAL HYPERTENSION
Systemic arterial hypertension has been reported in up to 80% of
dogs and nearly 60% of cats with glomerular disease (ch. 236).8 The
frequency of hypertension in each form of glomerular disease has not
been fully established in dogs or cats but does vary in humans.
Preliminary findings suggest a higher frequency of hypertension
might be found in dogs with MPGN.32 The primary mechanism of
hypertension in association with NS is believed to be expansion of
the plasma volume in association with primary renal sodium
retention. However, generation of several vasoactive factors (e.g.,
renin, angiotensin II, endothelin) is increased in human patients
with NS and may contribute to hypertension. Nitric oxide deficiency
may also play an important role in the development of
hypertension.80 Systemic blood pressure should be measured in all
dogs and cats with glomerular disease, because uncontrolled
hypertension is a risk factor for progressive renal injury (see ch. 236
for complete discussion of systemic hypertension).

THROMBOEMBOLISM
Thromboembolism (chs. 219, 238), a serious complication of
glomerular disease, was reported in 5% of dogs with GN, 14% of dogs
with amyloidosis, and 13% of dogs with all forms of glomerular

disease.21,22,27 Because emboli may be difficult to detect, the
prevalence of thromboembolism in dogs with glomerular disease
may be higher than indicated by these studies. The risk of
thromboembolism is highest in dogs with nephrotic-range
proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia. Pulmonary thromboembolism is
most common, but emboli may also lodge in other arteries (e.g.,
mesenteric, renal, iliac, brachial, coronary) or the portal vein (ch.
239; see ch. 219 for complete discussion of pulmonary
thromboembolism).
Although urinary loss of antithrombin (AT) has gained the most
attention in veterinary medicine, the pathogenesis of the
hypercoagulable state is multifactorial (ch. 171).80 AT is a serine
protease inhibitor that modulates fibrin generation; heparin
catalyzes these reactions. AT (65 kDa) is similar in charge and size to
albumin (69 kDa); serum AT activity closely correlates with the
serum albumin concentration. Prior studies have suggested that this
close correlation can be used to predict thromboembolism when the
serum albumin concentration is <2 g/dL (<20 g/L), when expected
serum AT activity would be less than 75% of normal.21 However,
studies of thromboelastography (ch. 170) in dogs with glomerular
disease or PLN failed to demonstrate an association between
hypercoagulability and alterations in serum albumin concentration
or AT activity.119,120 This is because the pathogenesis of
hypercoagulability is complex. Albumin binds to arachidonic acid,
which, if unbound, would stimulate platelet aggregation through the
generation of prostaglandins (i.e., thromboxane B2);
hypoalbuminemia is associated with increased platelet
aggregation.80 Hypercholesterolemia contributes to platelet
hypersensitivity by influencing membrane-associated enzyme and
receptor activity through alteration of the membrane composition.
The role of platelet hypersensitivity in the development of
hypercoagulability may be enhanced by thrombocytosis, which
occurs in many animals with glomerular disease. Increased
fibrinogen concentrations (i.e., above 300 mg/dL [3 g/L]), which are
often present in patients with NS, lead to increased fibrin complex
formation and platelet hyperaggregation. The risk of
thromboembolism may be further enhanced by increased

concentrations of alpha2 macroglobulin; alpha2 antiplasmin;
procoagulant cytokines; coagulation factors V, VII, VIII, and X;
increased plasma viscosity and interstitial pressure; decreased
plasma plasminogen concentrations; decreased plasma volume and
blood flow; endothelial injury; and infections.80
Warfarin, aspirin and clopidogrel have been used in the prevention
of thromboembolism in at-risk dogs. Warfarin is highly proteinbound. It is very difficult to titrate the dose adequately to prolong the
prothrombin time appropriately (i.e., 150% of baseline) in dogs with
hypoalbuminemia, and its use is not recommended. Low-dose
aspirin is inexpensive and easy to administer. Clopidogrel is also easy
to administer and widely available, and might inhibit platelet
function more reliably in dogs. Lack of response to either aspirin or
clopidogrel, as assessed by platelet function testing, may occur in a
subset of dogs with PLN treated with these medications, though this
might be less frequent in clopidogrel-treated individuals.121 The
reader is referred to ch. 238 and elsewhere for an in-depth review of
the available literature and expert recommendations on the rational
use of antithrombotics in companion animals.104,122 In addition to
antiplatelet drugs, anticoagulants, such as low molecular weight
heparin (e.g., dalteparin) and direct Xa inhibitors (e.g., rivaroxaban),
have also been used in dogs with confirmed thromboembolism
secondary to PLN,123,124 though in theory, heparin would be
ineffective in dogs with reduced AT activity.

HYPERLIPIDEMIA
Hypercholesterolemia (ch. 63) was reported in 79% of dogs with
GN, 86% of dogs with amyloidosis, and 56% of cats with various
glomerular diseases (ch. 156).8,22,27 Cholesterol concentrations as
high as 749 mg/dL (19.4 mmol/L) have been reported, although the
mean concentration was 325 mg/dL (8.4 mmol/L) in 69 dogs with
GN and 350 mg/dL (9.1 mmol/L) in 23 dogs with amyloidosis.21,22
Increases in total plasma cholesterol, very-low-density lipoprotein,
and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) occur.125 Hyperlipidemia is

variably seen in humans with NS, and its pathogenesis is complex.125
Hypoalbuminemia stimulates hepatic protein synthesis, including
the synthesis of lipoproteins, leading to hypercholesterolemia.80 It is
unclear whether hypoalbuminemia or the decreased plasma oncotic
pressure, or both, induce the increased synthesis. Alterations in lipid
catabolism also contribute to the development of hyperlipidemia.
Orosomucoid, which plays an important role in the maintenance of
glomerular permselectivity, is lost in the urine of patients with
glomerular disease. Urinary losses of orosomucoid exacerbate
proteinuria but also contribute to hyperlipidemia by indirectly
causing decreased hepatic production of heparin sulfate, a cofactor
needed in normal lipoprotein lipase function.125
Some evidence supports the theory that uncontrolled
hyperlipidemia contributes to glomerular and tubulointerstitial
injury. LDL and oxidized LDL may alter mesangial cell function and
increase the synthesis of mesangial matrix, thereby promoting
glomerulosclerosis.80 Glomerular and tubulointerstitial lipoprotein
deposition and lipoprotein-induced cytotoxicity also contribute to
renal injury. Interestingly, glomerular lesions have been identified in
cats with lipoprotein lipase deficiency and Miniature Schnauzers
with hyperlipidemia.126,127

PROGNOSIS
The prognosis for dogs and cats with glomerular diseases is variable
and based on a combination of factors including the histologic
diagnosis. Although progressive disease can be expected to occur in a
large percentage of affected animals, spontaneous remission and
positive response to specific therapy can also occur. Furthermore,
disease progression can be slow enough for the animals to lead
relatively normal lives, especially when the diagnosis is established
early in the disease process. In humans, azotemia, severe
proteinuria, systemic hypertension, and marked tubulointerstitial
lesions at presentation are the most significant predictors of an
unfavorable outcome in most forms of glomerular disease. Clinical

impressions suggest that these same variables affect the prognosis in
dogs and cats.
The median survival of 53 dogs with GN and amyloidosis that did
not die or were euthanized shortly after presentation was only 28
days, although individual dogs survived for more than 3 years.21
Dogs with glomerular disease and NS had shorter median survival
than those without NS (12.5 vs. 104.5 days, respectively).25 Survival
of non-azotemic dogs (serum creatinine <1.5 mg/dL) with or without
NS (51 vs. 605 days, respectively) was longer.25 More study is needed
to characterize the natural history and prognosis of the various
glomerular diseases in dogs and cats.
