OVERVIEW
FUNCTION IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
Renal tubules control body fluid balance, drug secretion, acid-base
balance, and electrolyte regulation. While glomerular filtration rate
(GFR) is the main determinant of renal function, the tubules control
the final composition of the urine. Glomerular ultrafiltrate contains
all plasma solutes that are smaller than 69,000 Daltons; therefore,
all filtered glucose, amino acids, and electrolytes are delivered to the
tubules via the ultrafiltrate. The bulk of filtered substances are
reabsorbed. Tubular defects causing lack of function are uncommon
to rare. They can occur regionally or globally and are either
congenital or acquired. Indicators from biochemical profiles, blood
gas analysis, and urinalysis (UA) can be monitored to assess tubular
function.

FUNCTION AND ANATOMY
Renal tubules are described according to function and anatomic
location. The proximal tubule receives ultrafiltrate from Bowman’s
space and reabsorbs 60-65% of the ultrafiltrate, a proportion that is
maintained across a wide range of GFRs. This property prevents
distal nephron segments from being overwhelmed by excessive
solute delivery. Tubular absorption is accomplished by active
transport of sodium (Na) at the basolateral membrane, which in turn
promotes passive resorption of other solutes. The proximal tubule
also actively secretes some solutes (e.g., organic anions, cations, and
hydrogen ions [H+]).1 Solutes are not reabsorbed uniformly; virtually
all filtered glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed, with lesser
amounts of bicarbonate (HCO3−), Na, and chloride (Cl). The main
function of the loop of Henle is to reabsorb approximately 30% of
filtered NaCl against a concentration gradient to generate a
concentrated medullary interstitium and create an ultrafiltrate that
is hypo-osmolar to plasma.2 The distal tubules and the collecting
tubules and duct are responsible for fine control of electrolytes
including Na, potassium (K), and calcium (Ca); final regulation of

acid-base balance; and water resorption to produce concentrated
urine.3 Clinical manifestations of renal tubular disorders include
formation of urinary calculi, metabolic acidosis, glucosuria,
aminoaciduria, electrolyte disorders, and failure of urine
concentration.

CYSTINURIA
PREVALENCE IN DOGS AND CATS
Cystinuria is caused by inherited proximal tubular defects in which
resorption of particular nonessential amino acids fails. Of these
amino acids, cystine is relatively insoluble in urine, resulting in the
formation of cystine calculi in acidic urine (chs. 308 and 309).4-6
Cystinuria has been reported in 95 purebreed dogs and rarely in cats
and ferrets.7-12 Commonly reported dog breeds with increased risk of
cystine urolith formation vary somewhat with geographic location,
and include English Bulldog, Staffordshire Bull Terrier, Chihuahua,
Newfoundland, Dachshund, Welsh Corgi, Rottweiler, Miniature
Pinscher, and Jack Russell Terrier.9-11

TYPE 1 AND NON-TYPE 1
Type 1 cystinuria in people is characterized by an autosomal
recessive inheritance pattern, in which carriers have normal urine
amino acid concentrations. Non–type 1 is characterized by an
autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with incomplete
penetrance. In non–type 1 incidence of calculi formation is limited in
carrier individuals with cystinuria. Defects in the Slc3a1 and Slc7a9
genes account for most of the genetic defects associated with
cystinuria in people.4,13 Similar to people, cystinuric dogs have
different methods of inheritance, and a classification system
consisting of 3 types has been published.14 Newfoundland dogs,
Labrador Retrievers, and Landseers have been identified with a
severe form of type 1 cystinuria caused by a missense mutation in the
exon 2 of the Slc3a1 gene.13,15,16 Australian Cattle Dogs have been

identified with an autosomal dominant form of cystinuria caused by
a 6 base pair deletion removing 2 threonines in the Slc3a1 gene and
Miniature Pinschers have a missense mutation in Slc7a9.14 Type III
cystinuria has a sex-limited inheritance mode affecting intact male
dogs, although the genetic defect is undetermined.7 Genetic testing
for the mutation is available in Newfoundland dogs, perhaps
accounting for the decreased identification of cystine calculi in this
breed over time.10,16 Genetic testing is also available for other
affected breeds.14

CLINICAL FEATURES
The mean age of dogs diagnosed with cystine stones is 4.9 years
overall; however, Newfoundland dogs and Labrador Retrievers are
typically affected as early as 4 to 6 months of age (ch. 308).10 The
degree of cystinuria can vary among individuals and may decrease
with age.5 Cystine calculi submissions increased from 1.4% of all
calculi submission in 2006 to 8.7% in 2018 and >70% were
diagnosed in intact male dogs.17 Clinical signs associated with
cystine calculi formation include stranguria, pollakiuria, and
hematuria. Male dogs may develop secondary urethral obstruction.
Evaluation of urine sediment reveals cystine crystalluria in some
affected dogs, but a complete blood count (CBC) and serum
biochemical analysis do not aid diagnosis. Imaging studies may
identify calculi, but their size, shape, and radiopacity vary. The
radiopacity of larger calculi is similar to that of soft tissue, which
allows visualization on plain film radiographs. Digital radiography
improves visualization of cystine calculi.18

DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT
Treatment involves mechanical removal or medical dissolution of
calculi and long-term medical management to prevent recurrence.
Surgical management is indicated in animals with urethral
obstruction (chs. 99, 117). Quantitative calculi analysis provides a

definitive diagnosis. Bacterial urinary tract infection should be
resolved with appropriate antibiotic therapy (ch. 307). Dissolution
and prevention strategies include exclusive feeding of proteinrestricted diets (ch. 159). Cystine is twice as soluble at a pH of 7.8 as
at 6.5; therefore, urinary alkalization is desired.7 Some proteinrestricted diets (Prescription Diet Canine u/d, Hill’s Pet Nutrition)
result in the formation of alkaline urine, but if dietary therapy does
not maintain the urine pH at the desired level, oral K-citrate can be
used.19 Induction of diuresis by feeding canned low-protein foods or
adding water to dry food is likely to be beneficial.5,19
Drug therapies to reduce the formation of cystine calculi include
the thiol drugs D-penicillamine and 2-mercaptopropionylglycine (2MPG; tiopronin [Thiola, Mission Pharmaceuticals]).7 Cystine is
formed by a disulfide bond between 2 cysteine molecules. Thiol
drugs form a disulfide bond with cysteine to form a more soluble
cystine-thiol drug complex. Although both drugs are effective, metal
chelation and gastrointestinal (GI) side-effects of D-penicillamine
make it less desirable.6 2-MPG given orally (30 mg/kg PO q12h) is
the treatment of choice together with dietary modifications.

CARNITINURIA
Carnitine is a sulfur-containing nonessential amino acid that
functions as an enzyme cofactor necessary to transport energygenerating fatty acids from the cytosol to the mitochondrial matrix.
Continued deficiency, reported in dogs with dilated cardiomyopathy
(ch. 233), may result from defective biosynthesis, defective tissue
uptake or retention, or excessive renal excretion.20,21 Carnitinuria
has been reported in dogs with cystinuria.21 Although high-fat, lowprotein diets are used for managing cystinuria (ch. 159), high-fat
diets increase renal carnitine excretion in humans. Healthy dogs that
consume low- and high-fat diets excrete similar amounts of
carnitine; however, cystinuric dogs with altered amino acid
resorption might excrete an excessive amount of carnitine if they

consume a high-fat diet.21 Chronic, excessive carnitine excretion
eventually results in carnitine deficiency, leading to cardiomyopathy.

HYPERURICOSURIA
DEFINITION AND PHYSIOLOGY
Hyperuricosuria is defined as an excessive quantity of uric acid, an
intermediate product of protein metabolism, in the urine. The purine
portions of nucleic acids undergo metabolism to form hypoxanthine
and xanthine, oxidized to uric acid by xanthine oxidase (XO). In
most mammals, uric acid is further metabolized to allantoin (a more
soluble product) by hepatic uricase. In healthy dogs, allantoin is the
primary metabolic product excreted by the kidneys, while humans
excrete mostly uric acid.22 Certain naturally occurring diseases, such
as hyperadrenocorticism, cancer, and chronic kidney disease (CKD),
can alter excretion patterns for these metabolites, resulting in greater
excretion of xanthine or uric acid compared to allantoin.23

PREVALENCE AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Genetic Abnormalities
Abnormal purine metabolism or excretion accounts for
hyperuricosuria in dogs of certain breeds with a genetic
predisposition to formation of urate calculi, or those with underlying
hepatic disease. The most common affected dog breed with
hyperuricosuria is the Dalmatian; however, English Bulldogs and
Black Russian Terriers have also been identified.9,10 Dalmatians are
intermediate between dogs of other breeds and humans with regard
to purine metabolism, excreting approximately one-half to twothirds as much allantoin as urate.4 In humans, uric acid in
circulation can precipitate into the joints, causing gout; however,
Dalmatian dogs have serum uric acid levels more similar to those of
non-Dalmatian dogs than to those of people, and do not develop
gout.24 Differences exist between Dalmatians and non-Dalmatian

dogs in both hepatic and renal management of uric acid. The enzyme
uricase, which converts uric acid to allantoin, is stored in hepatic
peroxisomes. Uric acid must be transported into hepatocytes before
conversion to allantoin can occur. Dalmatians have the same amount
of uricase as non-Dalmatian dogs, but have abnormal uric acid
transport across hepatic membranes, limiting uric acid
metabolism.25 Uric acid passes through glomeruli and is reabsorbed
in proximal tubules; however, Dalmatians appear to have less
proximal tubular resorption than other dogs. All Dalmatians have
active distal tubular secretion of urates due to a membrane transport
defect inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.4,15,26 The defect is a
missense mutation in the Slc2a9 gene that encodes for a transporter
of uric acid.15 This gene has also been identified as abnormal in
English Bulldogs and Black Russian Terriers affected with
hyperuricosuria.27 Clinical manifestations occur in 25% of male
Dalmatians.

Primary Liver Disease
Dogs with primary hepatic disease (ch. 266) can have reduced
conversion of uric acid to allantoin and of ammonia to urea, causing
hyperuricuria and hyperammonuria.28 Portal vascular anomalies
and primary portal vein hypoplasia without portal hypertension
(formerly called hepatic microvascular dysplasia) have been most
commonly associated with urate calculi formation (chs. 267, 308),
although any severe hepatic dysfunction could cause calculi
formation.29 Cats have been reported with urate urolithiasis (ch.
309). While some cats with urate stones have been diagnosed with
portosystemic shunts, the cause is not apparent in other cats.30,31

CLINICAL FEATURES
Clinical signs of urate urolithiasis are consistent with lower urinary
tract disease (chs. 54, 55, 308, and 309). Male dogs can develop
urethral obstruction. Young to middle-aged dogs are most commonly
affected.9,10 In Dalmatians, males are more frequently diagnosed

with urinary calculi than females.10 Dogs with primary hepatic
disease have no sex predisposition for calculi formation; however,
older male dogs are more clinically affected.29 Cats diagnosed with
urate urinary calculi and with a hepatic vascular anomaly are
generally younger (<2 years) than cats that do not have hepatic
vascular anomaly (4-7 years), and are neutered.30,31 Definitive
diagnosis of urate calculi depends on calculi retrieval and
quantitative analysis (chs. 117, 308, 309). Urate calculi are
radiolucent on plain film radiography but can be visualized with
abdominal ultrasonography (US) or double-contrast cystography.
Hepatic function studies (e.g., pre- and postprandial bile acids,
ammonia evaluation) are appropriate for non-Dalmatian dogs and
for cats (chs. 266-268). Urate calculi are typically small and smooth
and vary in color from yellow to green to black.32

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
General
Treatment consists of calculi removal or dissolution, followed by
long-term medical management to prevent recurrence (ch. 308).
Dissolution therapy includes a calculolytic diet (ch. 159), medication
with XO inhibitors, urine alkalization, elimination of secondary
infections, and induction of isosthenuria.32 A purine-restricted diet
low in calculogenic minerals (e.g., Prescription Diet Canine u/d;
Hill’s Pet Nutrition, Topeka, Kan.) is recommended.22,26,33

Allopurinol
A synthetic XO inhibitor, allopurinol is used to treat and prevent
urate urolithiasis in Dalmatians. It can reduce serum and urine uric
acid concentrations by eliminating metabolism from hypoxanthine
and xanthine to uric acid. Allopurinol should be administered only to
dogs consuming a purine-restricted diet to avoid the formation of
hypoxanthine and xanthine calculi, and the dose should be adjusted
to reduce urine uric acid levels.22,32,34 Because their causes of urate

stones differ, allopurinol therapy is not recommended for dogs with
hepatic defects and should not be used in cats.34

Urine Alkalization and Dilution, Resolving Calculi
Alkalizing agents (e.g., oral NaHCO3 or K-citrate) should be given at
doses that maintain urine pH near 7.0 to 7.5.22,32,34 This reduces
renal tubular production of ammonia and diminishes production of
urinary ammonium ions that complex with urate to form calculi.
Dilute urine production is accomplished by feeding proteinrestricted diets that reduce renal medullary concentrating ability.
Mechanical calculi removal should be considered in urethral
obstruction or in those not responding to dissolution therapy. The
average time to dissolution of urate calculi is about 3.5 months
(range, 1 to 18 months).22 Dissolution may follow definitive repair of
a portovascular anomaly, but calculi do not resolve without
resolution of underlying hepatic defects.34

Prognosis
The prognosis is fair to guarded for calculi recurrence in Dalmatians
and long-term success depends on the owner’s commitment to
lifelong management. In dogs with underlying liver disease, the
prognosis is good if definitive therapy for the liver disease exists but
guarded to poor in dogs with irreparable liver disease.

HYPERXANTHINURIA
Xanthine calculi are rare (chs. 308 and 309). Xanthine, derived
from dietary purines, is metabolized to uric acid via XO (see above).
Reduced enzymatic conversion increases urinary excretion of
xanthine, which has urine solubility similar to that of uric acid. Most
dogs that form xanthine-containing calculi are receiving allopurinol
for urate calculi. Idiopathic xanthine calculi formation has been
reported.10,35 Xanthine uroliths are rare in cats and have been
reported in cats not receiving allopurinol.35-37 Congenital

xanthinuria has been reported in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels, and
in 1 Wirehaired Dachshund.38-40 Prevention consists of monitoring
for xanthine crystalluria in dogs receiving allopurinol to prevent
urate calculi, and tailoring allopurinol dosing to the patient.

RENAL GLUCOSURIA
Glucose is normally freely filtered at the glomerulus and reabsorbed
in the proximal tubules by facilitated diffusion in a cotransport
mechanism with Na. The transport mechanism has a maximum
capacity exceeded at a blood glucose concentrations >180-220
mg/dL (10-12.2 mmol/L) in dogs and >260-310 mg/dL (14.4-17.2
mmol/L) in cats.41 When blood glucose exceeds the renal transport
maximum (e.g., hyperglycemia from stress or diabetes mellitus),
glucosuria occurs. This is the most common explanation for
glucosuria. Rarely, proximal tubular defects caused by tubular
damage or inherited disorders can cause glucosuria in the absence of
hyperglycemia.41-44
Primary renal glucosuria is rare but has been reported in Scottish
Terriers, Basenjis, Norwegian Elkhounds, and mixed-breed
dogs.41,45,46 Persistent glucosuria causes an osmotic diuresis and
polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD, ch. 53), although some dogs show no
clinical signs. Evaluation of serial blood glucose measurements or
serum fructosamine concentrations should discriminate renal
glucosuria from hyperglycemia.47 There is no cure for primary renal
glucosuria, but the long-term prognosis is good with appropriate
fluid intake and control of concurrent urinary infections. In some
dogs, renal glucosuria is the initial sign of Fanconi syndrome.

FANCONI SYNDROME
DEFINITIONS, PREVALENCE
Inherited
In humans, Fanconi syndrome is an inherited proximal tubular
defect resulting in glucosuria, aminoaciduria, proteinuria,

phosphaturia, and hypophosphatemia. “Fanconi-like syndrome” has
been reported in dogs. Fanconi syndrome is inherited in 10-30% of
Basenjis.43,44,48,49 Genetic testing became available in 2011.50
Idiopathic and inherited Fanconi syndromes have been rarely
reported in other dog breeds.

Acquired Fanconi Syndrome
The acquired syndrome has been reported secondary to gentamicin
administration, to various intoxications causing acute tubular
necrosis (ch. 134), and primary hypoparathyroidism.42,51-53
Acquired Fanconi syndrome in dogs was identified in some dogs
after consuming chicken jerky treats manufactured in China (ch.
300).54-58 The first 4 cats with acquired Fanconi syndrome were
being treated with chlorambucil for GI lymphoma or inflammatory
bowel disease. Urine metabolic assays confirmed aminoaciduria and
glucosuria. Glucosuria stopped in 3 of the cats after chlorambucil
was discontinued.59

Pathophysiology
Fanconi syndrome causes abnormal fractional excretion of many
solutes.44 Abnormal glucose absorption, glucosuria, and PU/PD are
the most obvious findings. Amino acid resorptive abnormalities vary,
but generally include abnormal absorption of cystine. Abnormal
absorption of HCO3−, Na, K, and urate also occur. Isosthenuria
sometimes occurs prior to glucosuria, with the osmotic diuresis
secondary to nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (NDI).60

CLINICAL FEATURES, DIAGNOSIS,
TREATMENT, PROGNOSIS
Clinical Features
The onset of clinical signs in affected Basenjis typically occurs by 4 to
8 years of age, with no sex predilection.44 Clinical signs typically

include PU/PD, weight loss, poor hair coat, weakness, and
dehydration. Diagnosis prior to clinical signs is possible if
predisposed breeds are regularly evaluated for glucosuria.44
Diagnostic testing typically reveals glucosuria, euglycemia, and
isosthenuria. As the disease progresses, hyperchloremic metabolic
acidosis and renal failure may occur. Clinically significant
hypokalemia may contribute to muscle weakness. Progression is
variable; some affected dogs develop renal failure within months of
the onset of clinical signs, whereas others remain stable for years.44

Treatment
Since there is no treatment for tubular defects, supportive care and
monitoring for metabolic acidosis, urinary tract infections, and
azotemia should be performed regularly. A management strategy has
been developed by Basenji breed enthusiasts. The Gonto protocol44
involves rigorous monitoring and treatment of secondary electrolyte
disturbances and metabolic acidosis. The chronic proximal tubular
HCO3− loss that causes metabolic acidosis is managed by giving oral
NaHCO3, exacerbating bicarbonaturia. Alternatively, urinary
alkalization with K-citrate avoids bicarbonaturia while providing K
supplementation. The goals of alkalization are to maintain the serum
HCO3− concentrations >12 mEq/L and K between 4-6 mEq/L. CKD
and systemic hypertension should be treated (chs. 236 and 301).
Treatment for acquired Fanconi syndrome should be directed at
resolving the underlying cause and providing supportive care. In a
survey of owners and veterinarians, median survival time following
diagnosis was 5.25 years (range, 7 days to 9.8 years) and 86% of
owners reported “good” to “excellent” quality of life during long-term
management.44 Of 29 dogs, 17 died or were euthanized for reasons
unrelated to Fanconi syndrome.44

RENAL TUBULAR ACIDOSIS (RTA)

DEFINITIONS, PATHOPHYSIOLOGY,
DIAGNOSIS OF PROXIMAL RTA
Definitions
The renal tubules regulate acid-base homeostasis through 2
processes: resorption of 80-90% of filtered HCO3− in the proximal
renal tubule and excretion of acids via titration of urinary buffers and
excretion of ammonium in the distal renal tubule.61 RTA describes
rare tubular disorders that lead to hyperchloremic metabolic
acidosis. Several types of RTA have been described. Proximal RTA
(type II) is due to an inability of proximal tubules to prevent loss of
HCO3−. Distal RTA (classic, or type I) is the result of an inability of
distal tubules to excrete H. Type IV RTA is distal RTA and
hyperkalemia secondary to hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone
deficiency. Unique diagnostic criteria exist for each type of RTA
(Table 303.1).62

Physiology
A defect in the basolateral membrane NaHCO3 co-transporter, with
leakage of HCO3− into the tubular lumen, results in proximal RTA.63
This disorder can occur alone or as part of other clinical tubular
defects (e.g., Fanconi syndrome).62 Ongoing loss reduces HCO3−, but
the resulting metabolic acidosis is self-limiting due to the distal
tubule’s ability to excrete acid. If oral NaHCO3 is prescribed to
normalize the plasma concentrations, the amount accumulating at
the distal tubule increases and can overwhelm the distal buffering
system, resulting in marked bicarbonaturia.62

Diagnosis and Treatment
The diagnosis of proximal RTA is based on an acidic urine pH,
hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, normal GFR, increased urine pH,
and >15% fractional excretion of HCO3− after normalizing the

plasma HCO3− by giving alkali. Identification of concurrent proximal
tubular defects (e.g., euglycemic glucosuria, aminoaciduria) also
helps identify proximal RTA.62 HCO3− wasting in proximal RTA
interferes with treatment and alkali therapy can worsen K wasting.
K-citrate is preferred for chronic use.62 One 540 mg tablet of Kcitrate provides 5 mEq of K and 1.7 mEq of citrate. Its metabolism
yields 5 mEq of HCO3−.64

DEFINITIONS, PATHOPHYSIOLOGY,
DIAGNOSIS OF DISTAL RTA
Definitions, Pathophysiology
Distal RTA causes impairment of urinary acidification. As a result of
impaired H+ secretion in the distal tubule,61,62 the kidneys are
unable to maximally acidify urine in response to systemic metabolic
acidosis. Under normal conditions, the distal tubule is able to excrete
H+ ions against a steep concentration gradient because of a Hadenosine triphosphatase (H+-ATPase) pump. These tubular
segments have tight junctions that resist back leak of acid, and they
are able to generate ammonia to capture H+ ions by forming
ammonium ions, which are subsequently excreted.63
Type IV distal RTA is associated with hypoaldosteronism or
aldosterone antagonism. Acidosis most likely results from loss of
aldosterone stimulation of H+-ATPase and decreased distal Na
absorption. This syndrome has not been characterized in veterinary
medicine but should be considered in animals with hyperchloremic
metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia.61,62

Diagnosis and Treatment
Diagnosing distal RTA is based on finding a hyperchloremic
metabolic acidosis with a urine pH >6.0. In contrast to proximal

RTA, with relatively mild systemic metabolic acidosis, distal RTA can
have a more severe metabolic acidosis because the distal tubule does
not provide buffering ability. People with distal RTA have
nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, bone demineralization, growth
retardation, and hypokalemia.61,63 Distal RTA has been reported in
cats with pyelonephritis, 1 cat with hepatic lipidosis, 1 cat in which it
was idiopathic, 3 dogs with immune-mediated hemolytic anemia, 1
dog with leptospirosis, and 1 dog given zonisamide.65-68 The
diagnosis may be made by failure to acidify urine with an ammonium
Cl challenge test, performed by measuring the urine pH before and at
hourly intervals for 6 hours after oral administration of 100 mg/kg
once, to a maximum dose of 3000 mg of ammonium Cl. Normal dogs
should acidify to a urine pH of 5.0, and cats to a pH of 5.5. Treatment
consists of giving alkali. A combination of K- and Na-citrate (70-75
mg/kg PO q12h) is preferred over HCO3−.

NEPHROGENIC DIABETES INSIPIDUS
(NDI)
DESCRIPTION (ch. 282)
NDI describes any disorder in which urinary concentrating
mechanisms are unable to respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
ADH is produced in the hypothalamus, stored in the posterior
pituitary, and released into circulation in response to
hyperosmolarity or hypovolemia.69 Following release, ADH attaches
to receptors at the basolateral membrane of the collecting tubules
and collecting ducts, causing the tubular luminal surface to become
permeable to free water, promoting formation of urine more
concentrated than plasma.

ACQUIRED NDI
Acquired NDI is a common cause of PU because it can result from
receptor interference caused by toxins (e.g., Escherichia coli
endotoxin), drugs (e.g., glucocorticoids, chemotherapeutics),
metabolic conditions (e.g., hypokalemia, hypercalcemia), tubular
injury or loss (e.g., renal cystic disease, bacterial pyelonephritis), or
alterations in the medullary concentration gradient (e.g., medullary
washout).70 Acquired NDI has also been identified as the initial
presenting concern that occurred 11 days prior to development of
acute kidney failure from leptospirosis.71

CONGENITAL NDI
Congenital NDI is a rare disease caused by a deficiency of ADH
receptors. Clinical signs, apparent soon after birth, include severe
PU/PD and hyposthenuric urine (specific gravity of 1.001 to 1.005;
osmolarity <200 mOsm/kg). The diagnosis is based on failure to
concentrate urine after modified water deprivation testing, failure to
respond to exogenous ADH, and exclusion of more common causes
of NDI (ch. 282).69,72

TREATMENT
Treatment for acquired NDI should be directed at resolving the
underlying cause. Congenital NDI therapy consists of free-choice
water, dietary Na and protein restriction, and/or thiazide diuretics
(chlorothiazide, 20 to 40 mg/kg PO q12h; or hydrochlorothiazide, 2
mg/kg PO q12h). Dietary Na and protein restriction reduces the
amount of solute presented to the kidney that must be excreted in
the urine each day, further reducing obligatory water loss (ch.
158).72 Adding diuretics to dietary restrictions can result in mild
dehydration, increased fluid and Na uptake in the proximal tubules,
and 20-50% reduction of urine output.72 If medical management is
not an option and PU can be tolerated, the animal can be maintained
on free-choice water alone.

EVIDENCE OF ACUTE TUBULAR
INJURY OR CKD USING URINE
BIOMARKERS
Acute tubular injury (ATI) represents the initial phase of developing
structural and functional kidney damage, preceding clinical acute
kidney injury (AKI), since serum renal biomarkers are not typically
above reference limits. Initiation of ATI occurs from naturally
occurring disease (e.g., toxic insult, renal ischemia, infectious
disease) but can also occur secondary to systemic inflammatory
response or therapeutic intervention with nephrotoxic agents.73,74
Early identification of ATI allows therapy to be altered, avoiding
ongoing renal injury or as a prognostic indicator when counseling
clients. Serum biochemistry profiles, UA, and sediment evaluations
are relatively insensitive indicators of acute tubular necrosis. The
concept of urine biomarkers refers to the presence of biochemical
substances in the urine that might provide an indication of tubular
cell dysfunction and death.75,76 Novel biomarkers are being
evaluated for providing an earlier diagnosis compared to
conventional serum biomarkers for CKD in dogs and cats (chs. 299,
300).77,78
Examples of common urine biomarkers that are currently in use
include urine glucose and albumin. Novel biomarkers currently
undergoing investigation are in 3 categories: high molecular weight
protein biomarkers from systemic circulation, low molecular weight
protein biomarkers from systemic circulation or that are
constitutively expressed in various renal cells, and enzyme
biomarkers.75,76,78 Enzyme biomarkers are large (>80 kD) and only
in the urine after leakage of damaged tubular cells. These biomarkers
may prove to have greater clinical utility because enzymes become
elevated in urine prior to onset of overt dysfunction, analysis is often
easier than for proteins, and the quantity or ratio to creatinine of
certain enzymes may be able to predict the degree and severity of
injury.79-84 However, there appears to be long term within-dog
variability with some biomarkers.77 Biomarkers being studied for
early detection of CKD in cats can be influenced by other common

diseases, e.g., hyperthyroidism, lower urinary tract disease.78 In the
future, panels of biomarkers might be useful to localize the renal site
of injury, determine severity, and monitor progression (chs. 299,
300); however, urine biomarkers require further study to determine
sensitivity and specificity for particular diseases, and assay
standardization, prior to becoming available for clinical use (Table
303.2).

Chapter 304: Pyelonephritis
Ewan Wolff

A C RO N YM S
AKI acute kidney injury
CKD chronic kidney disease
ISCAID International Society for Companion Animal Infectious

UTI urinary tract infection

ETIOLOGIES
Pyelonephritis, an infection of the renal interstitium +/- renal pelvis,
can develop if the ureter fails to prevent retrograde seeding of
infection to the renal pelvis or via hematogenous spread. Structural
and functional abnormalities predispose to pyelonephritis (e.g., renal
dysplasia, hydronephrosis or hydroureter from renal obstruction,
ureteral stricture, ectopic ureters, ureteral papilla hyperplasia, or
neoplasia). Factors that lead to stasis of urine in the renal
pelvis/ureter may promote pyelonephritis. Innate defense
mechanisms which prevent ascending infection include the narrow

ureteral papilla, uretero-vesicular junction peristalsis, and the
uretero-pelvic junction. Pyelonephritis is always considered a
complex urinary tract infection.1

PATHOGENESIS
The 4 most common bacterial pathogens responsible for urinary
tract infections (UTIs) in dogs and cats (ch. 307) include Proteus,
Staphylococcus, Enterococcus, and Escherichia coli.2-4 In a study of
44 dogs with suspect renal infection, histopathologic evaluation of
tissue and bacterial culture demonstrated pyelitis in 28 and 18/28
had pyelonephritis. Most of the 18 dogs were infected with E. coli.5
In a more recent study of 1028 dogs with UTIs, 7.7% of complicated
UTIs were due to pyelonephritis.6 Of these, 58% had E.coli infection
and 9.3% had an Enterococcus infection. The organisms from these
dogs tended to be more resistant to trimethoprim-sulfa
combinations and amoxicillin-clavulanate. Proteus mirabilis was
associated with pyelonephritis in only 2 of 39 cats.7 In a study of
dogs and cats with Corynebacterium urealyticum UTIs, 3 out of 11
dogs had evidence of pyelonephritis due to renal pelvic dilation; 1
also had a mineralized renal pelvis.8 Virulence factors such as the
fimbriae of E. coli9 may contribute to the success of certain
organisms in the upper urinary tract. Evolving trends in multidrug
resistance genes in E.coli, Enterococcus and Staphylococcus10 may
further complicate treatment. Although rare, pyelonephritis caused
by fungi, including Cryptococcus,11 has been described in dogs12 and
in cats.13

HISTORY
The International Society for Companion Animal Infectious Diseases
(ISCAID) 2019 guidelines statement recognizes the challenges
inherent in diagnosing pyelonephritis, emphasizing that diagnosis
consists of interpreting a vague constellation of clinical signs,

laboratory results, urine output, and imaging findings.1 The medical
history (ch. 2) should include review of prior and current illnesses,
UTIs, cultures and sensitivities, urinary calculi, and/or incontinence.
Trends in creatinine, symmetric dimethylarginine, urine specific
gravity (USG), urine sediment, and urine protein should be assessed
(chs. 62 and 70).
Owner observations of dogs and cats with pyelonephritis vary.
Signs depend on presence or absence of lower urinary tract disease
that can cause pollakiuria, stranguria, hematuria, periuria, and/or
malodorous urine (chs. 54 and 307). Presence and severity of acute
kidney injury (AKI; ch. 300) and the acute or chronic nature of the
pyelonephritis affect signs. Common signs include fever,
polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD), vomiting, inappetence, and perirenal
discomfort. Anorexia (57%), lethargy (51%), vomiting (17%), diarrhea
(36%), dehydration (28%), and fever (21%) were listed in 1 report.14
Some dogs and cats have prior signs of fluid overload (ch. 120),
oliguria, anuria, hypotension, melena, severe diarrhea, declining
levels of consciousness, or death from AKI.
Clinical signs are also affected by comorbidities, e.g., congenital or
familial nephropathy, pancreatitis, endocrine disease (hypo- or
hyperadrenocorticism, diabetes mellitus), neoplasia, T3-L3
myelopathy, lower motor neuron disease in the hindlimbs, or
autoimmune disease. In a study of 47 dogs with pyelonephritis, 75%
had likely underlying causes. Immunosuppression either from nonurothelial cancer or medication was noted in 38%, changes to the
epithelium from inflammatory processes in 30%, and urinary
obstruction in 19%.14

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (PE)
The PE in some dogs and cats with pyelonephritis can be
unremarkable but also may reveal fever, dehydration, perirenal
discomfort, renomegaly, or irregular kidneys. Some have urine
scalding due to leakage, pooling, or vulvar recession (ch. 310). Some
males have prostatic discomfort, enlargement, or deformity (ch.
314). Prostate infection can be the source of bacterial seeding. The
presence of hindlimb weakness, decreased anal tone, “upper motor

neuron” or “lower motor neuron” bladder, incontinence, and/or
abnormal vulvar conformation may be indicative of pre-disposing
neurologic (ch. 241) or conformation factors.

DIAGNOSIS
OVERVIEW
Diagnosis of pyelonephritis can be relatively simple or quite a
challenge. Azotemia and isosthenuria may be present but are not
consistently identified. Some dogs and cats have lower urinary tract
signs. Some have AKI, defined by an increase of ≥0.3 mg/dL (≥27
mcmol/L) in creatinine above baseline. Some have minimally
concentrated urine (USG: 1.012-1.018) with an active sediment (ch.
70).

BIOMARKERS AND SPECIALIZED
TESTING
Biomarkers (ch. 299), pyelocentesis, urine cultures specified for
pyelonephritis to avoid standard urine breakpoint utilization, and
blood cultures may be used to help determine if a dog or cat has
pyelonephritis and testing for leptospirosis has been recommended.1
Recently identified urinary biomarkers of AKI, e.g., neutrophil
gelatinase-associated lipocalin and cystatin C,15 can be used to detect
incipient AKI in pets that may have infection. MicroRNA 16
upregulation showed some promise as a urinary biomarker of
pyelonephritis, but its specificity is poor.16

URINE CULTURE
Source of Urine
Urine for culture should be obtained via cystocentesis or ultrasound
(US)-guided pyelocentesis, which requires adequate renal pelvic
dilation. Pyelocentesis has inherent risks of causing urine leakage

and/or septic retroperitonitis, although a recent study17 identified
relatively few adverse events. In addition, once the needle is placed,
one can perform an anterograde pyelogram to identify partial or
complete obstructions. Fewer than 33% of patients suffered
complications from the procedure and most were minor.

Urine Culture
Urine culture results should be used to guide therapy. A rapid
culture, using 0.25 mL of urine, can be performed with some degree
of speciation based on colony growth in 12-24 hours (ch. 184).18
More than 33% of cats not suspected as having pyelonephritis
complicating acute on chronic kidney disease (CKD) had bacteriuria
and 29% had a positive urine culture.19 In cats with CKD, 20% with
positive urine culture results had pyelonephritis.20 In CKD dogs with
positive urine cultures, 40% had pyelonephritis.21 Despite positive
urinalysis (UA) and culture results, almost half of those with
pyelonephritis were not suspected and 21% of the dogs with positive
culture results had no clinical signs. There was no association
between presence or severity of azotemia and positive culture
results.14

IMAGING
Renal pelvis US (Figure 304.1) may demonstrate a range of
appearances. Some have no renal pelvic dilation, some have
“physiologic” dilation (∼1-1.5 mm), and others have dilation ≥2 mm.
Pyelectasia was visualized on US in 66% of dogs with pyelonephritis,
ureteral dilation in 41%, and urolithiasis in only 27%.14 In a study of
dogs and cats with renal pelvic dilation on US, dilation >1.3 mm was
non-specific for pyelonephritis vs. obstruction22 and dilation >13
mm was suggestive of obstruction. In pyelonephritis, the median
renal pelvic dilation in dogs was 3.6 mm and 4.0 mm in cats. For
dogs, median physiologic dilation was 2 mm and for cats, it was 1.6
mm. Median obstructive dilation was 15.1 mm in dogs and 6.8 mm in

cats.23 In a study of 66 cats with CKD, pyelonephritis could not be
differentiated from urinary obstruction on US.24 and the width of the
proximal ureter was not statistically different comparing those with
urinary obstruction and those with pyelonephritis.
Although AKI, CKD, and renal neoplasia cannot be separated on
US, dimension estimates can be helpful in renal pelvic evaluation
and in monitoring. Despite US limitations, narrowing the list of
possible conditions is still quite useful and can be performed with
point of care US equipment. These measurements can be taken in
transverse view (Figure 304.1, D, E), in which the renal pelvis
forms a “<” or a sideways “V.” The point of the “V” is the ureteral
outflow. The limbs are repeatable landmarks and transverse
measurements can be taken serially to monitor dilation during
hospitalization and at rechecks.

TREATMENT
THE CHALLENGES
Treatment of pyelonephritis involves 2 distinct clinical challenges:
successful targeted treatment of the infection (ch. 307) and
managing the AKI (ch. 300). In some, either no organism is
cultured, or the results show low to moderate counts of a bacterium,
e.g., Enterococcus, that might be opportunistic. In a study involving
pyelocentesis and urine culture from kidneys with some degree of
obstruction (mechanical vs. functional), cultures were negative from
30 kidneys,17 half of which were from pets that had received 1 or
more doses of an antibiotic.

ANTIBIOTIC ALTERNATIVES
Current treatment recommendations from ISCAID1 for patients with
suspected pyelonephritis include immediate antibiotic therapy with a
fluoroquinolone or 2nd/3rd generation intravenous cephalosporin.
Treatment for a suspected or confirmed ascending infection should
be based on urine culture, whereas systemic treatment for an
infection with a presumed or confirmed hematogenous origin should

be based on blood culture (ch. 184). If the dog or cat is able to be
treated with oral medication, treatment can be used if extrapolation
from human data is correct. Detailed treatment recommendations
based on culture results for complex cases are available in the
ISCAID guidelines. Consultation with a specialist may be beneficial.
The recommended treatment duration is 10-14 days for
pyelonephritis. Data regarding the type, efficacy, and duration of
antibiotic therapy is limited by factors including paucity of studies
and changing susceptibility trends.24 A consensus response from the
American Society of Veterinary Nephrology and Urology (ASVNU) to
these recommendations includes veterinary nephrology experience
with antibiotic therapy of pyelonephritis. Adjustment of antibiotic
therapy should be made with culture guidance. Newer therapies
include ureteral stent placement for obstructive pyonephrosis with
lavage and drainage of the renal pelvis (chs. 117, 306).25 As with
AKI, treatment of pyelonephritis should take into account the
underlying cause for the pet to become susceptible to infection. The
largest clinical challenge with pyelonephritis is in preventing
recurrence or persistence of infection.

PROGNOSIS
Issues that may commonly complicate treatment include ureteral
obstruction/partial obstruction, pyonephrosis, unresolved cystoliths,
congenital anomalies, incontinence, and congenital/structural
anomalies, e.g., ectopic ureter, paramesonephric remnants, or
recessed vulva (chs. 310, 313). In dogs with acute on CKD, twothirds of those suspected to have pyelonephritis survived to a median
all-cause survival time of only 130 days when their serum creatinine
concentration was 1.4-2.8 mg/dL (124-248 mcmol/L). Only 13%
survived to 1 year. There was no association between serum
creatinine concentration at presentation and long-term survival.26
For cats with acute on CKD (ch. 301), one-half of cats with
pyelonephritis survived with a median all-cause survival time of 233
days for Stage II IRIS (International Renal Interest Society) CKD
cats.19

CLIENT INFORMATION
Pyelonephritis

Regular lower urinary tract infections (cystitis/urethritis) in dogs are
characterized by increased frequency of urination, straining to
urinate, small urinations, urinary accidents, discolored and/or foul
smelling urine ± abdominal discomfort from bladder inflammation.
Pyelonephritis (which can be thought of as an upper urinary tract
infection with involvement of the kidney[s] and/or ureters) is
different in that it causes clinical signs beyond the urinary tract.
Patients with pyelonephritis frequently drink more/urinate more
(depending on the type of bacterial infection or the presence of acute
kidney injury), may develop fevers from spread of infection to the
local lymph nodes (urosepsis), and can have additional consequences
of decreased kidney function and acute kidney injury. Signs of acute
kidney injury are widely varied but can include vomiting, decreased
appetite or anorexia, diarrhea and/or melena/blood, foul smelling
breath, changes in urination, kidney pain, fluid overload which can
include fluid in the chest or abdomen, changes in neurologic status
and if severe enough, death. Pyelonephritis can be a very serious
condition and should be taken as such. The veterinary team will work
hard to try to identify the cause of the infection and typically provide
guided treatment. Pyelonephritis should never be considered simple
and routine, much in the same way that pneumonia is different from
hay fever. If at any time before or during treatment you notice that
your pet is producing little or no urine, becomes tired or
unconscious, or is looking more swollen than usual (large
face/paws/legs) you should your veterinarian for emergency
evaluation.

DIAGNOSTICS
Pyelonephritis is diagnosed after collection of several different pieces
of information. The presence of elevated kidney values (azotemia) at
the same time as changes in urine concentration, and evidence of
infection on urinalysis (e.g., high white blood cell count and bacteria)
is suggestive but not conclusive for pyelonephritis. Additionally, not
every case will have all of these changes. Other pieces of information
that can assist in making a definitive diagnosis include comparing
current to bloodwork and vital parameters to those taken prior to the
current illness, urine culture (sometimes with extended spectrum
antibiotic sensitivity panels if relapse is suspected) to confirm active

infection and choose appropriate antibiotics, and ultrasound to look
for the presence, character, and degree of renal pelvis dilation.
Pyelocentesis, or sampling directly from the renal pelvis, is
sometimes performed to provide a targeted urine sample for culture,
but may also be performed in order to inject contrast for
identification of ureteral obstruction. Some patients with
pyelonephritis may not have evidence of infection on a sterile urine
sample taken from the bladder (cystocentesis) because the infection
is secluded higher up in the urinary tract. Some patients may have
complex combinations of ureteral obstruction or partial obstruction
from stones that may complicate the treatment of pyelonephritis.

TREATMENT
In general, patients with pyelonephritis should be hospitalized and
given intravenous (IV) antibiotics with judicious IV fluid use.
Hospitalization times typically range from 2-4 days or more
depending on severity of initial kidney values. Patients with
pyelonephritis can have other major concerns like elevations in blood
pressure, high potassium, high calcium, low red blood cell levels,
vomiting and dehydration that are the result of acute kidney injury,
which require advanced care. Some patients whose cases are
complicated by the addition of ureteral obstruction may require
urologic interventional procedures or potentially dialysis in addition
to hospitalized care. Pyelonephritis is a condition that if not properly
addressed can lead to kidney failure and death, so early intervention
is of great importance.
There are differences of opinion regarding the type and duration of
antibiotic therapy to go home. In human medicine, antibiotic courses
are shorter and more standardized. In veterinary medicine,
anatomical specifics of smaller animals and differences in lifestyle
often compel longer treatment times. It is common for a patient to be
treated for 2-3+ weeks with antibiotics depending upon the
circumstances of the pyelonephritis case and at the discretion of the
attending clinician. It is important to remember that pyelonephritis
cases can have multiple other systemic problems that can complicate
care and many home care plans will include not only antibiotics and
hydration, but also other measures to combat acute kidney injury
and comorbidities.

There are some things that are not recommended initially. First is
any form of partially or severely limited protein kidney diet as this
can create food aversions, and such limitations may not be needed
longer term. Additionally, phosphorus binders such as aluminum
hydroxide can cause nausea and worsen kidney values in the short
term for patients with high phosphorus (this may be reversible as the
acute kidney injury improves). Finally, enalapril/benazepril and
telmisartan are frequently halted during acute kidney injury to
restore as much kidney function as possible, although they may be
restarted later once kidney values improve.

FOLLOW UPS
Pyelonephritis patients will require follow ups to monitor for
improvement of kidney values and clinical signs, and if possible,
evidence of resolution of infection. Since many patients with
pyelonephritis also have significant acute kidney injury, regular
appointments will determine initial kidney recovery followed by
evaluation of long term recovery (by checking renal and urine
concentration values at both 1 month and 3-4 months post initial
treatment). Relapse is possible, so a portion of future follow ups will
likely be devoted to examining comorbid conditions and other
possible underlying conditions such as urinary incontinence that
could have led to infection in the first place.

PROGNOSIS
Prognosis in pyelonephritis depends on 2 main items: 1) severity of
kidney values in the months following this episode; and 2) whether
underlying conditions can be managed to prevent relapse. If kidney
function returns to normal or near normal following an event, then
short term prognosis may be quite good, and it may be difficult to
predict the future outlook if the natural history of the infection is
unknown. For patients that are still producing urine at a normal to
increased rate at the time of diagnosis, it is always worth attempting
treatment. Even if a patient has severe acute kidney injury, those
with kidney infections or leptospirosis as the cause are more likely to
survive with good quality of life after treatment, which is a good
argument to try treatment. However, patients that have severely
reduced or lack of urine production may require dialysis (if they do

not have underlying kidney disease) and may have a poor prognosis.
Additionally, those patients that initially respond but then cease
responding with high kidneys values have a guarded to poor
prognosis for improvement.
Ewan Wolff (Portland, Oregon)

CONGENITAL, INHERITED, FAMILIAL
KIDNEY DISEASES
Congenital kidney diseases are either present at birth or develop
later in life due to a defect present at birth. Congenital diseases may
result from either a genetic disorder or abnormal organ development
during gestation. Therefore, congenital disorders are not necessarily
inherited. The causative defect and mode of inheritance are often

unknown in congenital diseases in veterinary medicine. These
diseases are collectively referred to as juvenile onset of chronic
kidney disease (CKD; ch. 301). This does not indicate a congenital
disorder, but rather is a loosely defined clinical term indicating
presence of CKD at a young age. Congenital diseases might manifest
as gross abnormalities in renal morphology as well as in histologic
changes, e.g., regions devoid of renal tubules, immature and fetal
glomeruli, tortuous arteries, metanephric ducts in the medulla, and
multiple other non-specific changes. None of these is pathognomonic
for congenital diseases. Each case requires thorough assessment
taking into consideration the type and extent of abnormalities
present in the histologic specimen. Familial diseases are present in a
relatively high prevalence in specific breeds, develop relatively early
in life, and are assumed to have an inherited basis. The inherited
basis in most, however, has not been proven. The term hereditary
nephropathy is used in cases where the inheritance pattern has been
determined.
Both congenital and familial diseases can cause clinical signs at
birth or signs that become apparent later in life (i.e., a late onset).
Due to their potential late-onset, congenital and familial diseases
should be suspected in animals that have signs of CKD at a relatively
young age (e.g., <5 years). Even so, the presence of a disease, even at
a very young age, is not proof of a congenital disease, since acquired
disorders, although less common, may also occur early in life. With
the exception of polycystic kidney disease (PKD), congenital and
familial kidney diseases are more prevalent in dogs compared to cats.
These diseases might affect each portion of the nephron (i.e.,
glomerulus, tubules, interstitium) and can cause a wide spectrum of
clinical signs. Consistent with other forms of CKD, congenital
diseases are often progressive in nature and ultimately fatal.
However, the rate of progression is highly variable.

DEVELOPMENTAL DISEASES
RENAL AGENESIS
Renal agenesis is defined as complete absence of 1 or both kidneys.
Bilateral agenesis has been reported but results in early death. Renal
agenesis is often associated with other congenital urogenital

abnormalities, e.g., ureteral agenesis. The etiology is unknown, but
familial predispositions have been suggested in few breeds including
Beagles, Doberman Pinchers and Shetland Sheepdogs.1-3 Unilateral
renal agenesis is clinically silent if the contralateral kidney is
functioning normally and, in the absence of concurrent urologic
abnormalities, animals with 1 healthy kidney are expected to have a
normal lifespan.

HYPOPLASTIC KIDNEYS
Hypoplastic kidneys are small, with a reduced number of functioning
nephrons. All components are mature and renal architecture is
normal. The condition should be differentiated from renal atrophy,
which might be secondary to other congenital disorders. Clinical
signs and prognosis depend on the degree of hypoplasia and the
overall kidney function.

RENAL DYSPLASIA
Renal dysplasia represents a group of developmental anomalies
defined as “abnormal differentiation of the renal parenchyma.”4
Grossly, the kidneys are indistinguishable from those of animals with
advanced acquired CKD. Histopathologically, the most consistent
finding is inappropriate differentiation (compared to the
development of the host) in various parts of the nephron, e.g.,
presence of immature (fetal) nephrons alongside normal nephrons.
Functioning nephrons undergo compensatory hypertrophy. Fetal
glomeruli and tubules are often present in radial segments,
extending from the surface of the kidney to the corticomedullary
junction. Additional findings include persistent immature
mesenchyme, persistent metanephric ducts, atypical tubular
epithelial proliferation, and dysontogenic metaplasia. Secondary
changes can include interstitial nephritis, fibrosis, mineralization,
cystic glomerular atrophy, cortical and medullary cysts, and
glomerular lipidosis. Histology of lesions from the neonatal period,
before secondary changes become dominant, allows thorough
assessment; this is rarely available in dogs or cats. Renal dysplasia

has been suspected histologically in many breeds; some are
extensively described but others may be limited to a single case
report or case series (Table 305.1).4-8 Some reports of congenital
nephropathy in several breeds (e.g., Great Dane, Yorkshire Terrier,
Keeshond) likely represented renal dysplasia, but were not
specifically recognized as such.

DIAGNOSIS
Developmental kidney disease should be suspected in any dog or cat
with an early onset of CKD. Clinical and clinicopathologic findings
are consistent with acquired CKD although some dogs with juvenile
onset CKD have stunted growth and/or rubber jaw (due to fibrous
osteodystrophy;

Video 162.1). The diagnostic work-up is similar

to animals with acquired CKD (ch. 301) and is based on history and
physical examination, laboratory findings, imaging, and kidney
biopsy if indicated (

Video 299.1). Ultrasonographic (US)

changes are highly variable depending on disease severity and are
not always symmetrical. In renal dysplasia, US changes are best
characterized compared with other congenital diseases, e.g.,
presence of multifocal hyperechoic speckles within the renal
medulla, along with generalized medullary hyperechogenicity and
decreased corticomedullary definition.9

STAGING, MANAGEMENT, PROGNOSIS
Staging and treatment guidelines for dogs and cats with juvenile
onset CKD are similar to those recommended for acquired CKD (ch.
301), with few modifications. Following diagnosis, staging is based
on serum creatinine or symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA)
concentration and sub-staging on presence of renal proteinuria and
systemic blood pressure. Treatment should be tailored to the stage of
the disease, based on the recommendations of the International
Renal Interest Society. The degree of dietary protein restriction must
be considered in growing animals (chs. 146 and 158).

A notable difference when comparing congenital CKD with
acquired CKD in dogs and cats is the clinical manifestation. Those
with juvenile onset CKD are often more resilient to azotemia and do
not exhibit clinical signs until late in the course of disease. Therefore,
diagnosis is often delayed in these animals until they are a few years
old. It would not be unusual for a dog with juvenile onset of CKD
Stage 4 to be showing no clinical signs whatsoever. Once the
diagnosis is confirmed, even in the absence of clinical signs,
complete staging and appropriate management should not be
delayed. One of the main therapeutic goals is preservation of kidney
function and slowing the rate of disease progression. Veterinarians
should always be conservative with prognostic projections of pets
with juvenile onset CKD, as their survival time is often longer as
compared with pets that have an acquired disease at the same
disease stage.

GLOMERULAR DISEASES
PROTEIN-LOSING NEPHROPATHY (PLN),
NEPHROTIC SYNDROME, SYSTEMIC
HYPERTENSION, EMBOLISM
Familial and congenital glomerular diseases have been recognized in
several breeds (Table 305.1; ch. 302). Amyloidosis and hereditary
nephritis are best understood. Clinical signs may be related to PLN
per se and hypoalbuminemia (e.g., edema, ascites; chs. 21, 30) or
due to azotemia. The nephrotic syndrome (i.e., proteinuria,
hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia, and edema/ascites) has
been documented in a subset of pets with profound proteinuria and
hypoalbuminemia, representing a more severe disease state.
Systemic hypertension (ch. 236) and thromboembolism (chs. 219,
238) are serious potential complications in pets with glomerular
disease and thus, these patients should be carefully evaluated for
physical signs of thromboembolic disease. The hallmark of
glomerular diseases in dogs and cats is proteinuria; therefore, in the
absence of specific genetic tests, suspected animals should be
screened for proteinuria to promote early detection.

AMYLOIDOSIS
Pathophysiology
Amyloidosis is a heterogeneous group of diseases characterized by
extracellular deposition of insoluble fibrillary proteins with a specific
beta-pleated sheet conformation.10 Hereditary amyloidosis is caused
by mutant genes encoding variant proteins whose structure makes
them amyloidogenic. Amyloid proteins may originate from various
precursors and their formation may be primary or secondary
(reactive). Secondary amyloidosis is the most common form in dogs
and cats, in which renal amyloid fibrils are composed of an Nterminal fragment of the acute phase protein, serum amyloid A.
Despite their diverse origins, all amyloid proteins possess similar
structural, physical, and chemical properties, e.g., formation of X-ray
diffraction patterns characteristic of beta-sheet aggregates, uniform
fibril morphology and fibril formation patterns, and specific staining
with Congo red and thioflavin T.11

Breed Predilections
Familial amyloidosis has been described in Chinese Shar-Peis
(CSPs), Beagles,12 and English Foxhound dogs,13 and in Abyssinian
cats.14 Amyloidosis is mostly reactive and has been relatively well
characterized in CSPs,15 where it has been associated with familial
Shar-Pei fever. The latter is a recurrent inflammatory disease,
characterized by recurrent episodes of fever and swollen hocks, and
is associated with an acute phase response and production of serum
amyloid A. This likely predisposes CSPs to systemic reactive
amyloidosis, similar to humans with familial Mediterranean fever.
Deposits are composed of the protein amyloid A, which is the aminoterminal fragment of serum amyloid A.

Chinese Shar-Pei vs Other Breeds and Cats

There are notable differences between amyloidosis in CSPs and other
dog breeds. First, in CSPs (as in Abyssinian cats), amyloid deposition
begins in the renal medulla; therefore, renal medullar lesions
predominate at the earlier stages of the disease. Yet, in later stages,
amyloid deposition appears in the cortex, eventually involving the
entire kidney. Conversely, in other breeds, amyloid deposition begins
in the glomerulus. Further, in CSPs amyloid deposition is common in
a variety of extrarenal organs including the spleen, liver, adrenal
glands, pancreas, gastric and intestinal submucosa, myocardium,
thyroid, prostate and lymph nodes, whereas in other breeds amyloid
deposition is predominantly renal and less common in extrarenal
tissues.10,16

Clinical Features, Diagnosis, Prognosis
Amyloidosis has a late clinical onset. Most dogs and cats are middleaged or older when first presented for medical care due to this
condition. However, the diagnosis is made in a wide range of ages.16
Most of the CSPs are presented due to severe azotemia and not due
to clinical signs associated with PLN. Nephrotic syndrome is not
common in CSPs, despite severe proteinuria.16 This is likely
explained by the amyloid being primarily deposited in the renal
medullary region, resulting in interstitial disease and nephron loss
prior to glomerular damage. Consequently, compared with other
breeds, the degree of proteinuria in CSPs is lower and the degree of
azotemia is higher. The disease is usually initially suspected on breed
predisposition, history, and persistent renal proteinuria. US changes
are non-specific. Confirming a diagnosis can only be based on a
kidney biopsy. The overall prognosis is poor16; however, survival
times vary substantially among dogs depending on the disease stage
and the degree of azotemia, emphasizing once again the need for
early diagnosis.

HEREDITARY NEPHRITIS (ALPORT
SYNDROME-LIKE NEPHROPATHY)

Pathophysiology
Healthy glomerular capillary basement membranes are composed of
collagen heteromers containing alpha-3–alpha-4–alpha-5 chains,
required for the assembly of the normal type IV collagen. Hereditary
nephritis is a well-studied congenital kidney disease, caused by a
genetic mutation resulting in abnormal formation of type IV
collagen. A mutation in 1 of the encoding genes COL4A3, COL4A4 or
COL4A5 results in improperly formed chains that are unable to
interact with the other chains to form the alpha-3–alpha-4–alpha-5
heteromer.

Breeds
Samoyeds
Various mutations and modes of inheritance have been described in
several dog breeds, including X-linked, autosomal recessive, and
autosomal dominant. X-linked hereditary nephritis was first
reported in the Samoyed, in which a single nucleotide substitution in
the COL4A5 gene is the origin of this mutation. It causes formation
of abnormal alpha-5 chains and abnormal assembly of the type IV
collagen, leading to splitting of the basement membrane which can
be detected via electron microscopy early in life. Proteinuria is the
first diagnostic indicator of the disease and in male dogs can be
detected as early as 3 months of age. Azotemia develops and
progresses over a few months until death at about 1 year of age.17
Carrier females develop mosaic expression of the alpha-3–alpha-4–
alpha-5 chains. As in males, proteinuria is detected early in life;
however, azotemia progresses at a much slower rate and is apparent
only at a few years of age.18

English Cocker Spaniels
In this breed, the disease is autosomal recessive and originates from
a single nucleotide substitution in the COL4A4 gene. Due to this
mode of inheritance, males and females are affected equally.
Proteinuria is detected at as early as a few months of age, and
azotemia progresses over the first and second years of life.19

Bull Terriers and Dalmatians
An autosomal dominant mutation has been described in Bull Terrier
and Dalmatian dogs, mostly from Australia.20,21 The underlying
genetic mutation has not been fully characterized. Affected dogs
invariably have PLN but the clinical presentation is highly variable.
Azotemia can become apparent from several months to as late as 7-8
years of age.21,22 Consequently, dogs with sub-clinical disease may
be bred, making the disease difficult to eradicate.

Diagnosis
Diagnosis of hereditary nephritis is based on kidney biopsy. In Xlinked hereditary nephritis, light microscopy reveals morphologic
features of membranoproliferative glomerulonephropathy (ch.
302). In X-linked and autosomal recessive disorders,
immunostaining of the glomerular basement membrane
demonstrates the abnormal pattern of the type IV collagen. However,
in Bull Terriers and Dalmatians, immunostaining shows a normal
pattern of type IV collagen. Thus, the diagnosis can only be made on
electron microscopic examination. For some of the hereditary
nephritis disease types, genetic testing is available.23

PODOCYTOPATHY
PLN with a complex mode of inheritance has been reported in 1015% of Soft Coated Wheaten Terriers (SCWT).24,25 Kidney biopsies
reveal glomerulonephritis, glomerulosclerosis, and evidence of
podocyte degeneration and loss. The disease has a late onset (mean
age: 6 years),25 and affected dogs are often bred before being
identified. Clinical signs are caused by PLN with or without
gastrointestinal (GI) signs. There is no currently recognized
biological marker for early identification. However, sequencing
candidate genes revealed single nucleotide changes in 2 closely
linked genes, NPHS1 and KIRREL2, which encode the slit diaphragm
proteins nephrin and Neph3/filtrin, respectively.25 This mutation
was also found in 2 Airedale Terriers.26

POLYCYSTIC KIDNEY DISEASE (PKD)
CATS
Pathophysiology
PKD is the most common genetic feline disease affecting Persian cats
and outcrossed breeds, with a prevalence of about 40% worldwide.
PKD is characterized by kidney, liver, and occasional pancreatic cysts
that gradually expand into the parenchyma (Figure 305.1).32,33
The mode of inheritance is autosomal dominant, originating from a
single nucleotide mutation (C to A transversion) in exon 29 of the
PKD1 gene, resulting in a premature stop codon.34 No homozygous
cats have been identified, supporting the suggestion that the
mutation is embryonic lethal.34 PKD has also been described in cats
lacking the PKD1 mutation; therefore, other mutations might also
occur and trigger PKD in cats.

Clinical Features
Clinical signs are consistent with acquired CKD and are usually
nonspecific. Common signs include decreased appetite, vomiting,
and weight loss. Physical examination is often suggestive, as severely
affected cats have variable degrees of renomegaly, while most cats
with acquired CKD have small kidneys. In extreme cases, especially
in cats in poor body condition, the kidney may be so enlarged and
irregular as to displace the body wall laterally (Figure 305.2).

Diagnosis
Early diagnosis of PKD relies on genetic testing and US results.
Affected kidneys have variable numbers of hypoechoic to anechoic
cysts from <2 mm to few centimeters in diameter. Cysts are present
in the cortex and medulla and are lined by cuboidal and flattenedcuboidal epithelial cells. Renal cysts grow slowly at the expense of
the normal renal parenchyma, resulting in a gradual decrease in
kidney function. Although the disease is congenital, it has a late, but
variable, clinical onset. The number of cysts and their size are highly
variable. Cats are presented for medical care at various ages, often
only as adults, when the kidney function declines to the point where

clinical signs become apparent. As the disease progresses, clinical
signs become more pronounced, e.g., decreased appetite, vomiting,
weight loss, and dehydration.
The disease should be staged when cats are at a steady state, based
on serum creatinine or SDMA, as well as sub-staged based on the
presence of renal proteinuria and hypertension. Cats with PKD are
often not proteinuric or hypertensive (ch. 91), but both should be
evaluated. Final diagnosis is usually made with US results (Figure
305.3) that demonstrate a variable number of cortical and
medullary round or oval hypoechoic to anechoic cysts, or by genetic
testing.35 US demonstrates renal cysts as early as 7 weeks of age,36
and their absence at 6 months of age is correlated with the absence of
PKD. Hepatic and pancreatic cysts are also present in some cats.

General Management
Cats with PKD should be evaluated and treated based on the current
available guidelines for animals with CKD (ch. 301). Treatment
guidelines of cats with PKD parallel the guidelines for cats with
acquired CKD. The primary aim, especially when the disease is
detected at early stages, is to slow progression and to preserve kidney
function, achieved by dietary modification (ch. 158) and addressing
factors associated with rapid progression, e.g., presence of
hyperphosphatemia (and secondary hyperparathyroidism),
proteinuria, and systemic hypertension. Other clinical signs and
clinicopathologic abnormalities, such as gastrointestinal signs,
weight loss, metabolic acidosis, and anemia should be treated as for
CKD (ch. 301).

Unique Management Considerations
Cats with PKD may have abdominal discomfort if the kidneys
become extremely enlarged and/or if 1 or multiple cysts become(s)
infected. Infected cysts are not commonly reported in cats, but about
30-50% of people with PKD have some form of kidney infection
during their lifetime.37 Therefore, infection should be considered in
any cat with PKD that is acutely systemically ill. Infected cysts should
be suspected when systemic inflammatory signs are noted, e.g., fever
and leukocytosis; however, their absence does not rule out the

presence of an infected cyst. The clinical suspicion is further
supported when 1 or few cysts appear hyperechoic (rather than
anechoic or hypoechoic) on US examination. Final conformation is
made by careful aspiration and analysis of the cyst content, using
cytologic evaluation as well as culture and sensitivity testing. Cats
with an infected cyst can be managed by careful aspiration of cyst
contents under US guidance and local antibiotic injection.38 This
procedure requires an experienced ultrasonographer and the risk for
cyst rupture resulting in septic peritonitis should not be overlooked.

Removal of Cats From Breeding
Due to the autosomal dominant mode of inheritance, the disease is
common in longhaired cats, specifically in Persian cats. Due to this
mode of inheritance and the availability of genetic testing, the
disease can be eliminated. Genetic screening tests and removal of
affected animals from colonies are recommended. US examination
can also aid in removing affected animals from breeding, as cysts are
apparent as early as few weeks after birth.

DOGS
PKD is uncommon in dogs. Affected dog breeds include the Bull
Terrier, Cairn Terrier, and West Highland White Terrier (WHWT). A
genetic mutation in the polycystin-1 (PKD1) gene,27,28 with an
autosomal dominant mode of inheritance has been suggested in Bull
Terriers.29 An autosomal recessive mode of inheritance was
suggested in Cairn Terriers and the WHWTs.30,31 Bull Terriers have
decreased kidney function by a few years of age and cysts are limited
to the kidneys. Cairn Terriers and the WHWTs typically have clinical
signs by a few months of age and multiple cysts can be identified in
the kidneys and liver.

TUBULAR DISORDERS

Renal tubular defects (ch. 303) are uncommon in dogs and cats and
may present as a sole disorder or they may accompany other renal
disorders (Table 305.1), some of which are hereditary or familial.
Tubular disorders include primary glucosuria, aminoaciduria (e.g.,
cystinuria), electrolyte disorders, acid base disorders (i.e., proximal
and distal renal tubular acidosis), and water metabolism disorders
(i.e., nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; ch. 28). In some, tubular
disorders coexist.
Fanconi’s syndrome (ch. 303) is a complex familial disorder in
Basenji dogs, with a reported incidence of at least 10%, and an
uncertain mode of inheritance.39,40 Renal tubular handling of
glucose, phosphate, sodium, potassium, uric acid, amino acids, and
bicarbonate may be impaired. On urinalysis, glucosuria, proteinuria
(usually mild), and dilute urine specific gravity are often present. In
dogs with advanced disease, azotemia, hypokalemia and variable
degrees of hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis are often present.
Clinical signs include polyuria and polydipsia, weight loss, and
weakness. Most affected dogs are diagnosed between 4 to 8 years of
age. The disease progression rate is highly variable with some dogs
having a normal life span.41

MISCELLANEOUS CONDITIONS
There are multiple other renal disorders that have been suggested to
have genetic basis. Some of these are limited to a very small number
of animals, are poorly characterized, and the genetic underlying
cause is not yet determined (Table 305.1).

CLIENT INFORMATION
Familial and Congenital Renal Diseases of Cats
and Dogs
Congenital diseases may result from a genetic disorder or abnormal
organ development during gestation; namely, congenital conditions
are not necessarily inherited. Familial diseases are present in a
relatively high prevalence in specific breeds, develop relatively early
in life, and are suspected to be genetically inherited.
In both congenital and familial diseases, clinical signs may be
present at birth or become apparent during different stages in life
(late onset). Many congenital and familial renal diseases are
progressive and irreversible in nature and ultimately fatal, but the
rate of progression varies among the different diseases, and some of
the animals may even have a normal life span, especially if treatment
is commenced early in life. Therefore it is of importance to recognize
the disease as early as possible and to slow down the progression rate
even before clinical signs become apparent.
Although very diverse in their origin and nature, most congenital
and familial kidney diseases result in a gradual decrease in kidney
function and retention of toxins in the body. In some animals protein
loss through the urinary tract is the primary disorder and might
manifest clinically as fluid accumulation in the abdomen or as
peripheral edema. In a subset of animals, the primary disorder is

associated with abnormal absorption and secretion of solutes,
electrolytes and water along the kidney tubules. Each one of these
disorders predisposes the animals to a specific disease (e.g., stone
formation, inability to concentrate the urine and acid base
imbalance).
Due to the congenital nature of the chronic kidney disease, dogs
and cats are often more acclimated to the retention of toxins in their
body, and therefore clinical signs may not be apparent during the
first stages of life (sometimes even years). The most common clinical
signs of animals with kidney diseases include excessive drinking and
urination (which may be the first indicator of the disease),
decreased/selective appetite, halitosis, stunted growth and weight
loss. Early signs as increased drinking and urination are often
overlooked by owners, as these are present from a very young age,
and are perceived as normal. Moreover, other clinical signs might be
initially subtle due to gradual accumulation of toxins, which allows
the animal time for acclimation.
When the disease is recognized, even if clinically silent, it is
extremely important to perform a complete set of diagnostic tests to
identify the underlying cause, if possible, as well as identifying
markers of rapid progression (e.g., increased blood pressure, protein
loss through the kidney, accumulation of phosphorus, etc.). The
treatment goals are to slow down the disease progression rate while
providing the best quality of life for the animal. The importance of
consuming a diet designed for animals with kidney disease cannot be
overemphasized, as these diets have been shown to slow down the
progression rate and to improve the animal’s quality of life. It is also
crucial to control the abnormalities identified on laboratory testing,
even if these are not clinically apparent. Neglecting to do so, might
enhance the decrease in kidney function as well as allow irreversible
kidney changes to occur.
With appropriate management and close follow up, animals with
congenital kidney diseases might have good quality of life and often
live beyond the life expectancy of animals with acquired kidney
disease at the same stage, provided the diagnosis was performed
early enough.
Gilad Segev (Rehovot, Israel)
