ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF THE
URETERS
The ureters are fibromuscular tubes that carry urine from the renal
pelvis to the bladder via a retroperitoneal course. The ureteral wall is
composed of an outer adventitial layer, a muscular layer, submucosa,
and a mucosa of transitional epithelium. The muscular wall of the
ureter consists of an outer longitudinal, middle circular, and inner
longitudinal muscle layer except at the ureterovesicular junction
(UVJ), where only longitudinal fibers are present. The maximum

ureteral luminal diameter in the dog is normally less than 2.7 mm
even with fluid diuresis.1,2 The normal ureteral luminal diameter in
cats is only 0.3 to 0.4 mm3; therefore, even small ureteroliths, blood
clots, or accumulations of cellular debris may occlude the ureter in
cats. The ureters enter the urinary bladder on the serosal surface and
tunnel though the bladder wall obliquely to the mucosal surface. The
oblique path of the intramural ureter results in a valve-like effect
termed the vesicoureteral valve. The vesicoureteral valve, along with
ureteral peristalsis and a compliant bladder, promotes unidirectional
flow of urine to aid in prevention of ascending infection or urine
reflux to the kidneys (vesicoureteral reflux). In both dogs and cats,
the intramural ureter has a j-hook conformation terminally turning
from a caudal to a cranial direction before entering the bladder. The
degree of curvature of the distal ureter at the trigone depends on the
degree of bladder distension, with greater distention of the urinary
bladder resulting in greater degree of curvature of the distal ureter.
Recognition of this curvature is important for interpretation of
excretory urography studies and for retrograde access to the ureters
during cystoscopy (ch. 117). Attempts to pass a guidewire and
ureteral catheter retrograde up the ureter via cystoscopic and
fluoroscopic guidance are impaired when the urinary bladder is
overdistended. The feline ureteral orifice is typically more caudal to
that of the canine, and is in the proximal urethra, just caudal to the
urethrovesicular junction.
Innervation to the ureter includes both sympathetic and
parasympathetic nerves; however, the sympathetic innervation
appears to be most important for neurogenically mediated ureteral
contraction.4,5 Alpha-1, alpha-2, and beta-adrenoceptors and
muscarinic cholinergic receptors exist in the canine ureter.5,6 Similar
studies are lacking in cats. The density of alpha-1 receptor binding
sites is significantly greater than that of the other receptor types in
dogs. However, ureteral innervation is not responsible for normal
ureteral peristalsis, which is myogenic in origin. Ureteral peristalsis
occurs when urine enters the ureter, initiating electrical impulses to
be conducted between smooth muscle cells. Normally peristaltic
activity is initiated in the renal pelvis and urine is propelled toward
the bladder. Because normal ureteral peristalsis is myogenic in

origin, ureteral peristalsis persists with transplantation. During
obstruction of the ureter, spasmodic contractions occur that are
mediated via sympathetic input and normal peristaltic activity is
inhibited. Stimulation of the ureter with alpha-adrenergic agonists
causes ureteral contraction and stimulation with betaadrenoreceptor agonists causes ureteral relaxation.4-6 Furthermore,
alpha-1 adrenergic antagonists inhibit basal ureteral tone, peristaltic
frequency and ureteral contractions.7 Given this innervation, drug
therapy to facilitate relaxation of the ureter for expulsion of
ureteroliths might include alpha-adrenergic antagonists or selective
beta-2/beta-3 agonists to relax the ureters and reduce ureteral
spasm.4,7

DIAGNOSTIC APPROACH TO DISEASES
OF THE URETERS
For dogs and cats suspected of having ureteral disease, the diagnostic
evaluation should include history, physical examination, complete
blood count, serum biochemistry profile, urinalysis, urine culture,
abdominal radiographs, and abdominal ultrasound. Abdominal
ultrasound examination of the urogenital tract (combined with
abdominal radiographs ± cystourethroscopy, ch. 100) has largely
replaced excretory urography and computed tomography (CT) for
evaluation of the ureters. Ultrasonographic indications of ureteral
obstruction include renal pelvic dilation, ureteral dilation and direct
visualization of an obstructive lesion, though this is not always seen
in cases of ureteral strictures, purulent debris or dried solidified
blood stones.3,8-16 Contrast CT scans can be useful for evaluating
ureteral disorders such as delineating the extent and location of
ureteral strictures, ureteroliths, ureteral neoplasia, extramural
compressive lesions that obstruct the ureter, or unique ureteral
anatomy,13 but CT is usually not necessary for interventional
procedures such as placement of a ureteral stent or subcutaneous
ureteral bypass (SUB) device. An antegrade pyelogram may be
performed during interventional procedures (ch. 117), but this is not

typically done preoperatively for diagnostic purposes alone for these
interventional techniques.14-16

URETERAL OBSTRUCTION
Clinical signs of ureteral obstruction may not be apparent unless
bilateral obstruction or unilateral obstruction in combination with
decreased function of the contralateral kidney occurs. Clinical signs
of ureteral obstruction include signs of abdominal pain or so-called
ureteral colic (less consistently observed than in humans with
ureteral obstruction), dysuria (especially with distal ureteral
obstruction in cats), and signs of renal functional impairment such
as anorexia, vomiting, and oliguria. Patients with complete, bilateral
ureteral obstruction show signs of severe oliguric acute kidney
injury. Complete bilateral ureteral obstruction may be fatal within
48-72 hours. Many ureteral obstructions are partial, especially those
associated with ureteroliths, and this seems to be more common in
cats compared to dogs, in the authors’ experience.
Ureteral obstruction may occur from intraluminal, intramural, or
extramural causes. Intraluminal obstruction may occur as a result of
ureteroliths, blood clots, neoplasia, strictures/stenosis, edema, or
other intraluminal debris.14-18 Extramural compression may occur
from circumcaval ureters, retroperitoneal masses, retroperitoneal
fibrosis, bladder neoplasia, or from accidental surgical ligation of the
ureter during ovariohysterectomy.19,20 Circumcaval ureter (or
retrocaval ureter) is a congenital anomaly characterized by ventral
displacement (or duplication) of the caudal vena cava, which crosses
over the ureter, resulting in potential compression of the proximal
ureter behind the vena cava. This is often concurrently associated
with a ureteral stricture that is proximal to the crossing blood
vessel.21,22 The right ureter is affected more commonly (80%) than
the left. In 1 study, circumcaval ureters were present in
approximately one-third of cat cadavers and were not associated
with obvious obstruction of the ureters.21 However, in clinical
reports of cats with ureteral obstructions, circumcaval ureters appear
to be associated with intraluminal ureteral stricture formation just

proximal to the location that the vena cava crossed the ureter.22 The
difference in these reports may be that the presence of circumcaval
ureters combined with even small ureteroliths may result in ureteral
stricture formation. The clinical signs and outcomes of cats with
obstruction associated with circumcaval ureters are similar to those
of other causes of ureteral obstruction.14,22 Ureteral strictures
associated with circumcaval ureters are more effectively managed by
SUB placement compared to surgery or ureteral stent
placement.14,15,22
In humans, ureteral stenosis at the ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) is
a commonly recognized disorder. Ureteral stenosis at the UPJ was
reported in 1 dog.23 The dog was successfully managed by retrograde
cystoscopic ureteral stent placement. UPJ stenosis has also been
reported in an adult cat resulting in severe renal failure from endstage hydronephrosis.24 Retroperitoneal fibrosis leading to
extramural ureteral obstruction was reported in 29 of 138 (21%) of
feline renal transplant recipients.25 All 29 cats had azotemia from
obstructive uropathy secondary to the retroperitoneal fibrosis.
Surgery was performed to relieve the ureteral obstruction in 25 of the
29 cats, and recurrence of ureteral obstruction occurred in 6 cats
(22%).25

URETEROLITHS
DIAGNOSIS OF URETEROLITHS
Ureteroliths result from migration of nephroliths or nephrolith
fragments into the ureter. Ureteroliths are typically diagnosed on the
basis of results from radiography or ultrasonography. Radiopaque
ureteroliths are often visualized in the retroperitoneal region on
abdominal radiographs (Figure 306.1), but should be confirmed by
other imaging modalities prior to surgical intervention.8,14,17 Some
ureteroliths are radiolucent (e.g., urate, cystine, or dried solidified
blood uroliths) and some radiopaque ureteroliths are too small to be
detected on abdominal radiographs. Ultrasonography is often useful
for detection of ureteroliths and aids in assessing renal pelvic or

ureteral dilation proximal to obstructive ureteroliths8,12,17 (Figure
306.2). Direct visualization of the ureteroliths is often possible with
ultrasonography, especially in dogs (Figure 306.2). In 1 older
study, ultrasonographic confirmation of ureteroliths was not possible
in 23% of cats with surgically confirmed ureteroliths.17 The presence
of a ureteral stricture has been documented in ∼17-25% of cats with
concurrent ureteroliths,14,15 and strictures occur alone as a cause for
obstruction, which are more difficult to diagnose
ultrasonographically.12,26 More recent studies indicate much higher
rates of direct ultrasonographic visualization of obstructive
ureterolithiasis on ultrasound, with a sensitivity of 98%, specificity of
96%, and positive predictive value of 98% in 1 study.12 These results
need to be interpreted in light of variables like study design; many
retrospective studies use the ultrasound diagnosis of ureteral
obstruction as an inclusion criterion, and sonographer skill can vary.
In the authors’ experience, the clinical sensitivity and specificity
probably lie between these 2 sets of results, considering that ureteral
strictures are common and often missed on ultrasound. While
marked renal pelvic dilation (>13 mm) was consistently associated
with ureteral obstruction in several studies, ureteral obstruction has
also been confirmed despite minimal renal pelvic dilation (<4 mm)
in many cats.3,9,10,27 In some studies, dilation of the proximal ureter
above the obstruction was a more consistent finding in cats with
ureteral obstruction than the degree of renal pelvic dilation.9,14
Recent studies indicate that a small renal pelvic diameter does not
exclude obstruction, and the size of the pelvis does not predict renal
recovery long-term.9-12,28,29 The presence of hydronephrosis with
concurrent hydroureter can be related to an obstructed renal outflow
tract even if an obstructive lesion is not visualized on ultrasound,
although pyelonephritis cannot be excluded. Without evidence of
infected urine, purulent material in the ureter or renal pelvis, or
ureteroliths, then ureteral stricture is often the cause of the
obstruction.
Ultrasound-guided nephropyelocentesis for antegrade
pyelography via injection of contrast media into the renal pelvis is a
minimally invasive option for documenting ureteral obstruction;

however, the technique requires that the renal pelvis be sufficiently
dilated to permit accurate needle puncture of the pelvis, and the
potential complications must be carefully considered.30-32 If there is
ureteral obstruction and nephropyelocentesis is performed,
uroabdomen may result if decompression is not also performed. If
the urine is infected, this could also result in septic uroabdomen
(chs. 126, 127).

FIGURE 306.1 Lateral and ventrodorsal
abdominal radiographs of a dog revealing
radiopaque ureteroliths in the right ureter (arrows)
and distal left ureter (arrowhead). A left nephrolith is
also present and the margins of the left kidney are
irregular. Ultrasonography revealed moderately
severe dilatation of the right ureter and renal pelvis
proximal to the ureteroliths. The distal left
ureteroliths passed into the urinary bladder within
24 hours with intravenous fluid therapy.

FIGURE 306.2 Ultrasonographic image of 2
obstructive ureteroliths with mild fluid distention of
the ureter proximal to the ureterolith. Note the
acoustic shadow created by the ureteroliths.
During nephropyelocentesis, urine is aspirated from the renal
pelvis, and then iodinated contrast material is injected into the pelvis
in a volume approximately equal to one-half the aspirated volume.
Fluoroscopy is used for monitoring the passage of the contrast from
the pelvis, down the ureter, and into the urinary bladder. Evaluating
the ureter filling with real time fluoroscopy is superior to
radiographs because ureteral peristalsis can falsely mimic an
obstructive lesion. This can help to document the severity and
location of ureteral obstruction.30 CT scans obtained before and after
intravenous (IV) contrast administration have been used for

confirmation of the number and location of ureteroliths in some
institutions.32 Rather than performing diagnostic studies separate
from interventional decompressive procedures, the authors prefer to
perform retrograde ureteropyelography in dogs (during endoscopic
retrograde ureteral stenting) and antegrade pyelography in cats
(during SUB device placement), at the time of decompression during
an interventional procedure (ch. 117).14,16 When treatment with
traditional surgery (e.g., ureterotomy or ureteral reimplantation) is
being considered, CT scan or antegrade pyelography to determine
location and number of ureteroliths prior to surgery can be helpful.

MANAGEMENT OF URETEROLITHS
Removal of ureteroliths is more difficult than removal of uroliths
from the lower urinary tract. Medical dissolution of ureteroliths is
typically not an option without placement of a ureteral stent, because
ureteroliths are not continually bathed in urine. In dogs, after
ureteral stent placement, dissolution of struvite ureteroliths has been
documented.16,31 In both dogs and cats, calcium oxalate is the most
common composition of ureteroliths; therefore, most ureteroliths are
not amenable to dissolution. Conservative medical management by
serial monitoring of ureteroliths along with administration of IV
fluids, diuretics (e.g., mannitol), and alpha-adrenergic blockade has
been recommended, provided there is minimal renal functional
compromise and no infection, renal colic, or progressive ureteral or
renal pelvic dilation.13,17 Typically, dogs and cats with evidence of
complete obstruction by the ureterolith, worsening azotemia,
anuria/oliguria, hyperkalemia, or evidence of pyelonephritis
(inflammation and infiltration of the renal parenchyma, calices, and
renal pelvis with bacteriuria) or pyonephrosis (distension of the
renal pelvis and calices with purulent debris, often causing an
outflow tract obstruction) should be treated by either minimally
invasive procedures, open surgical intervention, or shock wave
lithotripsy (SWL; in dogs only).13,14,16,33-35 Because of several
factors (size of the ureter, urolith susceptibility to SWL
fragmentation, differences in urolith composition), the treatment

approach for dogs and cats with ureteroliths is different for each
species, and may also vary based on size, sex and clinical stability.
Dogs and cats with pyonephrosis can become unstable due to
urosepsis (chs. 126, 127), necessitating immediate renal pelvic
lavage and decompression, which can be accomplished using
minimally invasive stent placement in dogs and SUB device
placement in cats (ch. 117).31,36

SPONTANEOUS PASSAGE OF
URETEROLITHS
Size and location of the ureterolith may help determine if
intervention is required. In humans, 68% of ureteroliths <5 mm in
diameter and 47% of ureteroliths 5-10 mm in diameter will pass
spontaneously.39 The majority of ureteroliths that pass
spontaneously will do so within 4-6 weeks. Most human ureteroliths
>10 mm in diameter require intervention with SWL or ureteroscopic
laser lithotripsy for removal.39 It is difficult to apply these specific
criteria to dogs and cats because of the wide variation in body weight,
ureteral diameter, and ureteral length, but the rate of spontaneous
passage of ureteroliths appears to be much lower in dogs than it is in
humans, and even lower in cats. In an experimental study of artificial
ureteroliths in hound dogs, solid spheres 2.8 mm in diameter or
larger became firmly impacted in the ureter; however, spheres 2.3
mm in diameter passed to the urinary bladder within 1 to 24 hours.37
However, this study may not apply to smaller dogs with spontaneous
ureteroliths because of their smaller ureteral diameter, the irregular
shape of uroliths, and variable urolith number. Likewise, the normal
cat ureteral luminal diameter of only 0.3-0.4 mm results in inability
to pass even <1-2 mm ureteroliths in most cats. In 1 study of cats
with ureteroliths, medical management for the treatment of cats with
obstructive ureteroliths was only reported to be effective in 13% of
cases, with only 8% of the cats having documented passage of the
ureteroliths into the bladder.17 Also, recent data indicate that 17-25%
of ureteroliths in cats are associated with concurrent ureteral
strictures; therefore, the success of medical management of

ureteroliths may be limited by concurrent strictures.12,14,15,27 The
presence of concurrent urinary tract infection (UTI, ch. 307) with
ureteral obstruction requires more intensive management such as
placement of ureteral stents or SUB devices (ch. 117) as opposed to
more conservative approaches.14-16

MEDICAL EXPULSIVE THERAPY
Medical expulsive therapy (MET) may have a role in management of
obstructive ureteroliths provided there is not concurrent UTI or
severe obstruction present. Suggested METs have included IV fluid
administration with diuretics (e.g., mannitol), and alpha-adrenergic
antagonists. In humans, the criteria for utilization of MET versus
interventional procedures include adequate well-controlled pain
during MET, no evidence of sepsis, and adequate renal reserve.7,39
The most common medical therapy for MET in dogs and cats is IV
fluid administration with diuretics to increase urine flow to facilitate
ureterolith passage with serial monitoring of the ureterolith position
by radiographs and ultrasonography, along with administration of
the alpha-adrenergic antagonists prazosin (cat: 0.25-0.5 mg/cat PO
q8-12h; dog: 1 mg/15 kg PO q8h) or tamsulosin (dog: 0.004-0.006
mg/kg PO q12-24h; may take 3 days to be effective).13 In humans, if
a ureterolith remains in the same location for 2 weeks, progressive
enlargement of the ureter or renal pelvis is observed, pain cannot be
effectively managed, or renal function is impaired by the obstruction,
interventional techniques are recommended over MET.39 This
information can also be applied to dogs and cats with ureteroliths. In
dogs and cats, non-obstructive ureteroliths that are not associated
with infection or azotemia may be managed conservatively using
MET for 1-2 weeks provided renal function is stable. However,
frequent monitoring for complications, such as progressive
enlargement of the ureter or renal pelvis, progressive azotemia,
oliguria, or evidence of UTI or sepsis, is required to prevent
permanent loss of renal function of the affected kidney. Over 95% of
cats and 50% of dogs with a ureteral obstruction have impaired renal
function, and therefore, these patients would not qualify as

appropriate candidates for MET.14-16,27,28 If an animal is monitored
for 2 weeks and the ureterolith is not moving distally despite MET,
some type of intervention should be considered. In dogs and cats, the
ureteroliths may also spontaneously move retrograde back into the
renal pelvis rather than passing distally towards the urinary
bladder.38
In humans, multiple clinical studies have confirmed that the
alpha-adrenergic antagonist tamsulosin facilitates passage of
ureteroliths more effectively than do other medications.7,39 In cats,
use of the alpha-adrenergic antagonist prazosin has been suggested
for MET as an alternative to tamsulosin, but clinical studies of
efficacy of MET in cats are lacking.32 Overall success in MET in cats
is low and concurrent ureteral strictures are present in 17-25% of
cats with ureteroliths; therefore, the authors only consider MET for a
limited time (usually 24-48 hours) and only for cats without evidence
of oliguria, severe azotemia, severe hydronephrosis, sepsis,
overhydration, or hyperkalemia.14,15

MANAGEMENT OF STRUVITE
URETEROLITHS IN DOGS
While the vast majority of upper tract uroliths in cats are calcium
oxalate, infection-induced struvite nephroliths and ureteroliths are
the second most common type of urolith in the upper urinary tract of
dogs. Clinical findings that would support struvite nephroureteroliths include UTI with urease-producing organisms
(Staphylococcus, Proteus, Klebsiella, Corynebacterium and
Mycoplasma), alkaline urine pH, moderately radiopaque uroliths in
the renal pelvis or ureter, and struvite crystalluria. While struvite
uroliths in the kidney and bladder may be medically dissolved in
dogs, obstruction of the ureter by ureteroliths often prevents
effective medical dissolution and causes obstructive pyonephrosis,
which frequently leads to urosepsis (chs. 126, 127).31 In dogs with
obstructive struvite ureteroliths, the obstruction should be corrected
prior to attempts at medical dissolution.31 In dogs, obstructive

pyonephrosis should be managed by a minimally invasive approach
of retrograde lavage of the renal pelvis using an open-ended ureteral
catheter combined with cystoscopic-guided ureteral stent
placement.31 Combined fluoroscopy and cystoscopy are required for
this approach (ch. 117). Once the initial pyonephrosis crisis is
effectively managed by drainage, ureteral stent placement and IV
antibiotic therapy, then medical dissolution of the ureterolith is
possible using a combination of antimicrobial therapy of the UTI
(guided by urine culture results) and struvite dissolution diets (chs.
159 and 308). Medical dissolution of struvite ureteroliths should
not be attempted without concurrent ureteral stent placement
because of the risk of obstruction, treatment failure, and urosepsis.
The diet and antibiotics should be continued until 2-4 weeks after
radiographs and ultrasound document complete dissolution of the
uroliths. The authors’ preference is to remove the ureteral stent by
cystoscopic retrieval once the ureteroliths are dissolved and monitor
for chronic UTI to ensure future struvite stone development is
prevented.

INTERVENTIONS FOR URETEROLITHS
If dogs and cats with obstructive ureterolithiasis require
intervention, options include ureteral stent placement, SUB
placement (ch. 117), SWL (in dogs only), ureterotomy to remove
ureteroliths, transection of the ureter and reimplantation of the
ureter into the bladder (ureteroneocystostomy), and modified Boari
flap.14,16,32-35,40 The relative success rates, indications and
complications of these different techniques vary by species.

Ureteral Stents
Resolution of ureteral obstruction by ureteroliths is possible by
placement of ureteral stents via cystoscopy or surgery to divert the
urine through and around the stent, bypassing the ureteral
obstruction. In dogs, ureteral stents are typically placed retrograde
up the ureter over a urologic guidewire via cystoscopy (Figure
306.3; ch. 117).16,31 In cats, ureteral stent placement usually

requires surgery for antegrade stent placement through
nephropyelocentesis, and the stent placement is much more difficult
compared to dogs. In addition, long-term complications associated
with dysuria are reported in about 38% of cats, which is not seen
with the SUB device.15 Therefore, the authors prefer to manage cats
with ureteral obstruction by placement of a SUB device rather than
ureteral stents.14,15,22,26

FIGURE 306.3 Abdominal radiographs showing
bilateral ureteral stents following retrograde
cystoscopic placement. This is the same dog as seen
in Figure 306.1. Note the right ureteroliths along the
outside of the right ureteral stent (arrow) and the left
nephrolith (arrowhead). The dog was subsequently
treated using shock wave lithotripsy to fragment the
nephrolith and ureteroliths, and then the stents and
urolith fragments were removed by cystoscopy.
Ureteral stents may be used temporarily or left in place long-term.
In dogs and female cats, if the ureteral stent is no longer needed to
bypass the ureteral obstruction, it can be extracted easily via
cystoscopy by grasping the distal end of the ureteral stent with a
grasper and providing gentle traction to withdraw the stent through
the ureter and urethra. In cats, although ureteral stents may be left
in the ureter long-term, stent exchange or SUB placement was

required in 27% of cats, most of which was due to re-obstruction
secondary to ureteral stricture ingrowth. This exchange rate is higher
than that reported for SUB devices.14,15 Indwelling stents can
develop mineral encrustation, resulting in occlusion of the ureter and
the stent, necessitating stent removal or exchange for either a new
stent or a SUB device (Figure 306.4).15
In dogs, ureteral stents are typically well tolerated and allow for a
minimally invasive approach for immediate and effective renal pelvic
lavage and decompression.16,31 Success rates for endoscopic
placement of ureteral stents in dogs approach 95% with training and
experience.
Complications with canine ureteral stents are uncommon, with
∼12% reported to need an exchange to a new stent or a SUB
device,16,41 most of which were due to ureteral strictures that
compressed or grew through the stent fenestrations, or the
development of ureteritis secondary to infection resulting in reobstruction of the ureter and compression of the stent lumen.
Another potential complication observed with ureteral stents is stent
migration, which may require stent repositioning or removal.42

Subcutaneous Ureteral Bypass (SUB) Devices
Surgical placement of a SUB device, which provides a route for urine
to bypass the obstructed ureter, has become one of the preferred
options for management of ureteroliths and ureteral strictures in
cats (ch. 117).10,14-16,22,29,43-45 Compared to traditional ureteral
surgery, SUB placement has a much lower reported perioperative
mortality rate, with 90-94% of cats having survived to discharge
following SUB placement.14,43 Long-term prognosis for cats with
SUBs correlates to the stage of residual chronic kidney disease (CKD)
following relief of ureteral obstructions, with cats having stage 1-2
CKD surviving significantly longer than cats with stage 3-4 CKD (ch.
301).14,29 An important concept to consider is that >30% of cats
have been reported to have a ureteral stricture as a cause of their
ureteral obstruction and therefore are not amenable to traditional
ureteral surgery like ureterotomy.14

FIGURE 306.4 Ureteral stent removed from a dog
because of encrustation with calcium oxalate
deposits, which are visible on the outside of the
stent. Mineral deposits inside the stent resulted in
partial obstruction of the stent, requiring stent
exchange.

Ureteral Surgery
Open surgical ureterotomy is one option for management of
ureteroliths in dogs and cats.13,17,46 In the authors’ opinion,
ureterotomy or ureteroneocystostomy are only appropriate for dogs
and cats with a single ureterolith without concurrent nephroliths or
an associated ureteral stricture, which is an uncommon sole cause of

ureteral obstruction based on multiple studies.14,22,26,35,43 Because
ureterotomy and ureteroneocystostomy have higher mortality and
surgical complication rates than ureteral stent placement followed by
SWL (dogs), a ureteral stent alone (dogs), or SUB placement alone in
dogs and cats, the authors prefer these minimally invasive
alternatives to ureterotomy or ureteroneocystostomy in the majority
of cases.14,17,34,46 A recent paper compared SUB device placement in
cats, with or without a concurrent ureterotomy, and found no benefit
of concurrent ureterotomy, accompanied by prolonged anesthesia
times for the ureterotomy cats compared to the placement of a SUB
device alone.44

Shock Wave Lithotripsy for Ureteroliths
SWL is a minimally invasive option for fragmentation and removal of
nephroliths and ureteroliths in dogs, but not cats.33,34 In SWL,
uroliths are fragmented using shock waves that are generated outside
the body and targeted at the uroliths using integrated fluoroscopy
(ch. 117). Approximately 80% of ureteroliths in dogs can be resolved
by SWL although up to 50% of dogs may require 2 or more SWL
treatments, which is a higher re-treatment rate than in dogs with
nephroliths.33,34 This is similar to observations in humans and in
research models that confirm impacted ureteroliths are more
difficult to fragment by SWL compared with nephroliths.47,48 This
difficulty in fragmenting ureteroliths compared to nephroliths is due
to the inability of cavitation bubbles to form and collapse on the
surface of the ureterolith if it is surrounded by the ureteral wall
rather than urine.49,50 The advantages of SWL include that the
procedure is non-invasive and complications occur in <10% of dogs,
with transient ureteral obstruction by urolith fragments being the
most common complication.33,34
Placement of ureteral stents is not essential for treatment of
ureteroliths by SWL, but there are advantages of ureteral stents that
facilitate SWL efficiency and patient management. Ureteral stents
allow urine to bypass ureteral obstruction at the site of the
ureterolith and prevent additional renal damage from obstructive

uropathy. Because ureteral stents are radiopaque, they facilitate
accurate targeting of ureteroliths during SWL. Ureteral stents also
induce passive ureteral dilation, thus increasing the diameter of the
ureter lumen by ∼3-fold.2 This dilation increases the efficiency of
urolith fragmentation through cavitation bubble formation and
collapse on the surfaces of smaller urolith fragments.49,50 Passive
dilation of the ureter also facilitates passage of nephrolith and
ureterolith fragments following ureteral stent removal. Placement of
a ureteral stent may also be used to prevent ureteral obstruction by
ureterolith fragments following SWL treatment of larger nephroliths
or ureteroliths in dogs (Figure 306.3).33
Unlike dogs, SWL is not effective for fragmentation and removal of
ureteroliths in cats.33 Because of the small ureteral diameter in cats,
even <1 mm fragments fail to pass down the ureter in cats, and in
other species, SWL typically results in urolith fragments of 1-2 mm
or larger. In addition to the smaller ureteral diameter, feline calcium
oxalate uroliths are resistant to fragmentation compared to calcium
oxalate uroliths from dogs.51 In research cats, kidney damage and
reduced renal function were routinely observed after <50% of the
normal therapeutic shock-wave “dose” used in dogs for SWL.33 In
combination, all of these factors result in the recommendation that
SWL should not be used for treatment of nephroliths or ureteroliths
in cats.

URETERAL NEOPLASIA
Primary ureteral neoplasia is rare in dogs and cats. Types of primary
ureteral neoplasia include urothelial carcinoma, leiomyoma,
leiomyosarcoma, sarcoma, hemangiosarcoma, mast cell tumor,
benign papillomas, and fibroepithelial polyp.52-57 Fibroepithelial
polyps are the most common type of primary ureteral neoplasia in
dogs.54 Ureteronephrectomy has been the most commonly reported
treatment for unilateral ureteral neoplasia, but SUB or ureteral stent
placement may be possible alternatives in some cases.54,58 In cases
where ureteral resection is required due to compression or

obstruction from a tumor, SUB device placement has been
effective.19
The most common neoplasm resulting in ureteral obstruction in
dogs is urothelial carcinoma located in the trigone of the urinary
bladder (ch. 330). Metastatic neoplasia may also result in ureteral
obstruction. Malignant ureteral obstructions can be bypassed using
palliative ureteral stent placement58 or a SUB device. Because it is
difficult to identify the ureteral orifice via cystoscopy in dogs with
extensive trigonal urothelial carcinoma, ureteral stents in these
patients must be placed either percutaneously antegrade through
nephropyelocentesis or via open surgery (ch. 117).58 The use of a
SUB device with radical cystectomy has also been performed for dogs
with trigonal neoplasia.

URETERAL TRAUMA
Trauma to the ureters has rarely been reported in dogs and cats.59,60
Ureteral injury can result from blunt abdominal trauma, penetrating
wounds, or iatrogenic damage during surgery such as inadvertent
ligation or transection of the ureter during ovariohysterectomy.60,61
Ureteral injury resulting from blunt trauma accounted for only
0.01% of canine hospital admissions in 1 report.59 In addition, in the
authors’ experience, ureteral rupture occurs as an uncommon
complication of ureteral obstruction due to either ureterolith
penetration or in association with overdistention.
Rupture of the ureter results in accumulation of urine in the
retroperitoneal space, post-renal azotemia, hyperkalemia and
metabolic acidosis. If the urine is infected, this can result in a
retroperitoneal abscess and urosepsis (ch. 127).31 If the
contralateral kidney and ureter are functioning normally, recognition
of ureteral rupture may be delayed for several days. If the ureter
ruptures near the UVJ or if the retroperitoneum is disrupted by the
trauma, uroabdomen may also occur.
The extent and location of ureteral injury and function of the
contralateral kidney determine treatment of ureteral injury.
Ureteronephrectomy has been reported as a treatment option for

unilateral ureteral rupture provided that the contralateral kidney and
ureter are functioning normally, although this is not the preferred
option.59 For dogs with distal ureteral trauma, implantation of the
healthy portion of the ureter above the damaged area
(ureteroneocystostomy) is an alternative to ureteronephrectomy.60
For incomplete tears of the ureter (<50% of the circumference),
conservative management via urine diversion often allows for
healing of the ureteral lesion. Ureteral stent placement via
cystoscopy or surgery is a minimally invasive option for urinary
diversion to allow for healing of partial ureteral tears to avoid
nephrectomy (ch. 117). The authors have managed dogs and cats
with ureteral rupture/trauma successfully with either SUB device
placement with ureteral ligation/resection or ureteral stent
placement.31
An uncommon consequence of ureteral trauma or ureteral
transection during ovariohysterectomy is the formation of a
paraureteral pseudocyst, or urinoma, which forms when urine that
has leaked from a ureter into the retroperitoneum becomes
encapsulated in a thick, fibrous wall.62,63 Urinomas may not need to
be treated as long as the ureter remains patent with or without a
ureteral stent.

ANATOMIC ABNORMALITIES
CONGENITAL URETERAL ABNORMALITIES
Congenital ureteral abnormalities include ectopic ureters,
ureteroceles, UVJ stenosis, ureteral agenesis, ureteral duplication
and ureteral atresia. These are discussed in ch. 313, Congenital
Lower Urinary Tract Disorders.

UTI urinary tract infection

INTRODUCTION
Urinary tract infection (UTI) development is multifactorial,
dependent on the interplay between the virulence of an organism
and alterations in anatomic, environmental, and immunological
competency of the host. Urinary bladders with normal urinary
defenses are inherently resistant to colonization and cystitis.1 It is
those bladders with compromised defenses that are at increased risk
for UTI development. Please refer to the 8th edition of this textbook

ch. 330 “Lower Urinary Tract Infections” for a review of “Natural
and Acquired Host Defenses” in Box 330-1.
The most common microbes invading the urinary tract are
bacteria. Other organisms like fungi account for only ∼1% of dog and
cat bladder infections. Infecting bacteria typically originate from the
enteric flora and ascend through the distal urogenital tract into the
proximal urethra and urinary bladder.2 When urinary tract
colonization results in lower urinary tract (LUT) inflammation and
clinical signs including caudal abdominal pain, pollakiuria,
stranguria, or dysuria, the term UTI or bacterial cystitis is
appropriate.3
Spayed female dogs have twice the risk of UTI when compared to
male dogs.4 Gram negative bacteria comprise >60% of positive
cultures, with Escherichia coli being isolated from 45-55% of
bacteriuric dogs. Other Gram negative organisms including Proteus
spp., Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Klebsiella spp. and Gram
positive bacteria that include Staphylococcus spp., Streptococcus
spp., and Enterococcus spp. are each cultured between 2-14% of the
time.5
In cats, E. coli is also the most common cause of bacteriuria
(37.3%); however, Gram negative and Gram positive infections each
occur roughly half the time with Gram positive Enterococcus faecalis
present in 27% of culture-positive urine samples.6 Overall, the
incidence of bacteriuria is much lower in cats than in dogs and a sex
predilection is variably reported.5,6

BACTERIURIA: CONTAMINATION,
SUBCLINICAL BACTERIURIA, AND
INFECTION
Quantitative aerobic culture is the gold standard for identifying
bacteriuria. However, the lower urinary tract is not a sterile
environment, and the microbiological documentation of bacteriuria
is not equivalent to diagnosing a UTI. Potentially benign

explanations for detecting bacteriuria include technical errors,
sample contamination, and subclinical bacteriuria (ch. 70).
Bacteriuria secondary to urine specimen contamination occurs
when the urine contacts non-sterile surfaces prior to analysis or
culture. Aseptic cystocentesis-collected urine is recommended to
obtain the most reliable sample for identifying true bacteriuria;
however, voided and catheter-collected urine samples are acceptable
when quantitative bacterial colony counts are provided. Using
>100,000 colony-forming units/mL as a diagnostic cut-off, voided
urine samples have a 94% sensitivity and specificity for noncontaminant bacteriuria (chs. 98, 184).7
Another form of benign bacteriuria is asymptomatic bacteriuria
(ASB). In human medicine, this term is used for describing
persistent bacterial urinary tract colonization that is not producing
symptoms or clinical signs. In veterinary patients, differentiating
non-clinical colonization from UTI is difficult because subtle clinical
signs are difficult to detect; hence, the term subclinical bacteriuria
(SCB) may be more appropriate.3
In people, the treatment of ASB is not recommended in many
circumstances. Eradication of ASB does not prevent future urinary
bladder re-colonization8 and the presence of ASB strains is
hypothesized to convey a degree of protection against urinary tract
colonization with more virulent bacteria.9 In veterinary medicine, a
similar approach has been recommended for the management of
SCB despite a lack of evidence demonstrating a protective benefit.
The decision of whether to treat a patient that has SCB is complex
and it requires the veterinarian to assess patient and bacterial
characteristics. For example, caution must be afforded when
managing dogs and cats with co-morbidities that may mask clinical
signs. Polyuric patients or immunosuppressed patients that are
unable to mount an appropriate inflammatory response require
special consideration as they may appear subclinical despite a
uropathogenic infection.
When deciding whether to treat bacteriuria, it is as important to
consider bacterial characteristics as to assess co-morbidities.
Bacteria contain genomic islands encoding fitness factors, which
promote commensalism and/or virulence factors that injure host

tissues. These fitness and virulence genes have tremendous
plasticity, which allows an organism to alter gene expression to adapt
to a changing environment.10 This means that clinically
nonpathogenic strains may contain unexpressed virulence genes and
the current bacterial phenotype is not necessarily predictive of future
pathogenicity as the urinary environment changes.11 At this time
bacterial genome sequencing to detect virulence genes is not a widely
available clinical diagnostic in veterinary medicine. Instead, patients
with untreated SCB are managed via vigilant observation of the
patient, and monitoring for subtle changes in clinical signs and urine
composition, including increases in urine concentrations of blood,
protein, and inflammatory cells.

URINARY TRACT INFECTION:
DIAGNOSIS
A definitive diagnosis of UTI requires concurrent evidence of
bacteriuria and cystitis. Aerobic urine culture alone will not
distinguish between SCB and UTI. Interpreting urinalysis, urine
sediment examination (ch. 70), clinical signs, and urine culture
results (ch. 184) together is essential, paying particular attention to
external factors that may alter results.
When interpreting aerobic urine culture results, the influence of
urine collection and storage methods must be considered (ch. 98).
Time to processing, storage temperature, and storage media all may
alter bacterial detection. At room temperature, bacteria may begin to
proliferate or die within 1 hour.12 Urine samples processed 2-24
hours after collection should be refrigerated at 4°C in a sterile
preservative-free tube. If urine culture submission is contingent on
pending diagnostic test results, storing urine in a preservative,
reducing media vial, or Amies transport media can extend the time
that bacteria will be viable for up to 72 hours.13
The growth of most uropathogens on culture media is apparent
within 18-24 hours of incubation, with 24-72 hours required to
obtain results. Some organisms such as Corynebacterium spp. and
Mycoplasma spp. can take 4 to 7 days. To improve the efficiency of

diagnosing UTI, in recent years, several point-of-care bacteriuria
screening tools have become available, with additional molecularbased diagnostic tests imminent. Two of these diagnostics tests
include a point of care rapid immunoassay (RapidBac Vet, Silver
Lake Research Corp, Monrovia, CA) and a catalase-based point-ofcare urine test (Accutest Uriscreen, Jant Pharmaceuticals Co,
Encino, CA). The immunoassay has a reported sensitivity and
specificity of 97.4% and 98.8%, respectively, when screening
cystocentesis-collected samples14; a sensitivity of 89% is reported
with voided samples.15 The catalase-based test is limited in its ability
to detect catalase-negative bacteria and also cross reacts with white
blood cells and epithelial cells, reducing its sensitivity and specificity
on samples obtained by cystocentesis to 89% and 71%, respectively.16

URINARY TRACT INFECTION:
TREATMENT
The standard therapy for UTIs is antimicrobials. Therapeutic plans
vary depending on previous UTI history, concurrent diseases,
neutering status, sex, and species. Broadly, treatment strategies for
UTI fall into 2 categories, depending on whether bacterial cystitis is
sporadic or recurrent.

SPORADIC BACTERIAL CYSTITIS
Sporadic bacterial cystitis is defined as a clinical bladder infection
occurring <3 times in a 12-month period, regardless of the patient’s
species, sex, neuter status or co-morbidities. The recently adopted
term sporadic bacterial cystitis focuses on the inflammation caused
by the bacteria and the infrequent nature of the episodes rather than
the presence or absence of a complicating risk factor for infection or
treatment.3 The treatment recommendations for sporadic cystitis
can be applied to all dogs (male and female) and cats provided that
bacteriuria is detected in the cat and a normal prostate is present in
the male dog. If these conditions are not met, then additional
diagnostic tests and treatment plans may be necessary. Please refer

to ch. 311 “Feline Idiopathic/Interstitial Cystitis” and ch. 314
“Prostatic Diseases” for more information.
Sporadic bacterial cystitis is associated with lower urinary tract
signs including dysuria, pollakiuria, and stranguria (ch. 54). In dogs
with limited previous antibiotic therapy, empiric antibiotic
prescriptions are justified; however, urine culture and sensitivity is
recommended, especially in cats. When choosing an antibiotic for an
infection of unknown bacterial susceptibility, selection should be
made with consideration of local community resistance patterns,
attainable urine antibiotic concentrations, risk of adverse events, and
cost. Veterinarians are encouraged to monitor antimicrobial
resistance patterns within their clinic to help further with selecting
an antibiotic with a spectrum and efficacy against the suspected
agent (chs. 7, 186). First-line antibiotics should have a local
resistance rate for sporadic bacterial cystitis cases of ∼10%.
Suggested first-line antibiotics to consider include amoxicillin,
cephalexin, or trimethoprim-sulfonamide.3
In some cases, the colonizing bacteria are found to be resistant to
the chosen antibiotic when antimicrobial susceptibility results
become available but clinically the patient has improved. In such
instances, the antibiotic course should be completed as prescribed,
with a follow-up urinalysis and culture performed 3-5 days after the
conclusion of therapy to ensure eradication of infection.
Alternatively, if the colonizing bacteria are resistant to the chosen
antibiotic and clinical signs remain, then the original antibiotic
should be discontinued and an appropriate antibiotic begun.
The current recommended treatment duration for sporadic
bacterial cystitis in veterinary medicine is 3-5 days.3 This
recommendation stems from studies demonstrating that
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or high-dose enrofloxacin for 3 days
yielded similar cure rates when compared to 10 days of cephalexin or
14 days of amoxicillin-clavulanic acid.17,18 Advantages of short
duration therapy include reduced patient side-effects, improved
adherence/compliance, reduced cost, and decreased antibiotic
resistance while maintaining clinical efficacy.17,19 Despite these
studies, the use of second line antibiotics such as fluoroquinolones
and cefovecin is not recommended for sporadic bacterial cystitis

treatment when first line antibiotics are options. When the treatment
course of sporadic bacterial cystitis is complete, additional
monitoring, diagnostic testing, or preventative therapies are usually
not required.
In recent years there have been some proponents of using
nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for managing
sporadic cystitis.3 The basis behind NSAID therapy is that the drugs
may limit lower urinary tract signs while the body’s innate defenses
and immune system clear the infection, thus limiting antibiotic use.
In people, NSAID therapy is not currently the standard of care, with
recent studies suggesting that NSAID therapy is inferior to
antibiotics and may be associated with increased occurrence of
pyelonephritis.20,21 In veterinary medicine, there are no studies that
assess NSAID therapy to manage UTI and given the challenges
veterinarians have identifying patients with pyelonephritis,22 UTI
treatment with NSAIDs as a sole therapy is not recommended by this
author. However, in an otherwise healthy dog with recurrent
infections, NSAIDs may be beneficial to reduce clinical signs while
awaiting culture and sensitivity results.3

RECURRENT BACTERIAL CYSTITIS
Recurrent bacterial cystitis or recurrent UTI is said to be present
when a dog or cat has 3 or more documented clinical infections
within 12 months. Recurrent infections indicate that an underlying
anatomic, functional, or metabolic abnormality or comorbidity is
present, either preventing the clearance of an infection (persistence
and relapse) or allowing for reinfection.

Persistence
Persistent infections occur when appropriate antimicrobial therapy
fails to sterilize the urine. Provided that the prescribed antibiotic was
administered at the appropriate dosage and for an appropriate
duration, persistent infections indicate that the infecting bacteria
developed resistance, the immune system of the patient is
compromised, or the mean urinary concentration (MUC) of

antibiotic was not 4× the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC)
for bacterial growth.23,24
Since measuring urine drug concentrations is not widely available,
recognizing when urinary drug excretion might be altered is
necessary to prevent persistent infections. Reduced MUC of an
antibiotic can occur with decreased intestinal absorption of oral
medications, altered perfusion of infected tissue, altered drug
metabolism, or reduced urinary concentrating ability. In short,
persistent infections require screening for systemic disease,
including an assessment of the function of the immune,
gastrointestinal, hepatic, and renal systems. If the disorder resulting
in a persistent infection cannot be corrected, then antibiotic dosages
should be adjusted to maximize the MUC or an alternative antibiotic
should be chosen.
Over the last few decades, as the incidence of resistant UTIs has
increased, there is a rising population of patients with infections that
are not susceptible to first- or even second-line antibiotics.
Alternative therapies have been proposed that are largely supported
by individual case reports and anecdotal evidence. The use of highdose amoxicillin/clavulanic acid is 1 technique that uses the urine
concentrating ability to treat infections that otherwise appear
resistant on susceptibility testing.25 Another approach bypasses the
steps of antibiotic absorption, metabolism and excretion by directly
instilling aminoglycoside antibiotics into the bladder.26
Occasionally, more invasive therapies may be indicated for the
treatment of persistent infections such as encrusted cystitis.
Associated primarily with Corynebacterium urealyticum UTI,
encrusted cystitis occurs when urease-positive bacteria form
mineralized plaques on the ulcerated and inflamed mucosa of the
urinary tract.27 Suspicion of encrusted cystitis should occur when a
urease-positive infection persists in combination with alkaline urine
containing struvite crystals. Diagnosis can be assisted by
ultrasonography and cystoscopy and treatment frequently requires
appropriate antibiotic therapy in conjunction with urine acidification
and surgical debridement.27

Relapse

A relapsed UTI differs from a persistent infection in that during
relapse, urine can be cleared of infection but bacterial reservoirs
remain. These allow for urine recolonization with the same organism
within a few days to weeks. Sites that may harbor bacterial colonies
include the kidneys (ch. 304), prostate (ch. 314), uroliths (dogs
[ch. 308], cats [ch. 309]), vagina, and possibly urothelial cells.
The treatment goal for relapsing infections is to identify the site of
infection and eradicate the bacterial reservoir. For suspected tissue
infections, bacterial sensitivities should be determined based on the
achievable plasma concentrations and tissue penetration of the
antibiotic and not the MUC. Usually, the course of therapy is
prolonged, although the optimal treatment duration to clear these
infections in veterinary medicine is largely unknown. It is possible
that in certain circumstances treatment duration could be safely
reduced depending on the site of infection. Recommendations for
treatment duration range from 7-14 days to 4-6 weeks.

Reinfection
Reinfection occurs when there is an alteration to host defenses that
allow new bacterial strains to colonize the urinary bladder weeks to
months after an initial UTI. In both reinfection and relapse, a time
period exists when the patient’s urine is sterile. This makes it
challenging to differentiate between the two when similar bacterial
species are isolated in subsequent infections. Comparing antibiotic
susceptibility patterns of prior and current infections is often used
for differentiating reinfection and relapse. The rationale is that
different patterns should indicate different bacteria, i.e., reinfection
rather than relapse. However, different bacterial strains can have
similar susceptibility profiles and the same infecting organism can
shift its antibiotic sensitivity, making this method unreliable.28
Genotyping using pulse field electrophoresis provides definitive
evidence of reinfection/relapse.29 Correctly categorizing infection as
reinfection or relapse is important, as the pathophysiologic
mechanism and necessary treatment are different.
If reinfection is suspected, a complete systemic evaluation of the
patient should be done. When possible, an evaluation of the
conformation of the external genitalia is performed (

Videos 3.17,

3.18, 3.19), including a digital exam and visual evaluation of voiding.
Urine retention should be assessed by measuring the post-void
bladder residual volume via catheterization or ultrasound
estimation30 (

Video 307.1). Residual volume should be low, with

common estimates ∼0.1-0.4 mL/kg. Advanced diagnostics including
radiographs/contrast studies, ultrasound, cystoscopy (ch. 100), and
urethral pressure profilometry can assist with identifying anatomical
and mechanical changes to lower urinary tract.
Treatment of reinfection requires a urine culture and sensitivity to
guide therapy (ch. 184). In both dogs and cats, prior antibiotic
administration is the leading risk factor for development of multidrug resistant infections and hence patients with histories of
reinfection will be at increased risk of treatment failure if antibiotics
are chosen empirically. If clinical signs are mild at the time of
diagnosis of a UTI, it is prudent to wait for antibiotic susceptibility
results before starting therapy. In instances where treatment must be
instituted immediately, a first-line antibiotic should be chosen as
described above for sporadic bacterial cystitis. Since reinfection is
caused by recolonization with a different bacterial strain each time,
treatment duration should be similar to what it would be if the
patient were having numerous single infections; therefore, long
courses of antibiotic treatment are usually unnecessary with
reinfections.

URINARY TRACT INFECTION:
PREVENTION
In a patient with reinfection, antibiotic therapy provides only
transient urine sterilization and does not prevent future infection.
While a treatment plan focused on UTI prevention would be a
superior option, there is little clinical evidence proving long-term
efficacy for nearly all preventative therapies. Most are based upon
theoretical ideas, in vitro studies, small case series, or anecdotal
reports.
The first step in any preventative plan begins with identifying and
eradicating the UTI. After sterilizing the urine, preventative
protocols can be divided into therapies that allow the bacteria to

remain viable and those that kill invading organisms. Successful
treatment with nonantimicrobial therapies is attractive because these
therapies do not apply bactericidal selective pressure (and therefore,
the development of resistance is reduced), and the normal flora
remains viable. Categories of nonantimicrobial prophylaxis include
adherence blockade and bacterial interference.

ADHERENCE BLOCKADE
The basis of anti-adherence therapeutics is to block the ability of
bacteria to adhere to the urothelium, allowing urination to flush
invading organisms from the urinary tract. The most commonly
referenced anti-adherence therapies include cranberries and
proanthocyanidins (PAC), D-mannose, and glycosaminoglycans
(GAGs).
PACs in cranberries have anti-biofilm properties and can prevent
pyelonephritis-inducing P-fimbriated uropathogenic E. coli from
binding to uroepithelial cells.31 In dogs, PAC consumption reduces
E. coli adherence in vitro but evidence of an in vivo clinical benefit is
lacking.32 Similarly, D-mannose aims to disrupt bacterial adhesion
to the urothelium by blocking the ability of lectins on the tips of type
1 fimbriae to interact with carbohydrate moieties located on
urothelial cells.33 Several rodent studies have demonstrated
decreased uropathogenic E. coli colonization after incubation of
bacteria with D-mannose,34 although it is unclear whether oral
administration of D-mannose achieves urinary concentrations
sufficient to provide a clinical benefit in dogs and cats. Finally, GAG
therapy theorizes that exogenously administered GAG may augment
the urothelial GAG layer or bind to invading bacteria, preventing
bacteria-induced injury. In people, several independent studies have
demonstrated that direct instillation of the GAGs hyaluronic acid and
chondroitin sulfate into the urinary bladder reduces UTI recurrence
rates.35 In veterinary medicine, the efficacy of GAG bladder
instillations to prevent UTI remains unproven. Studies measuring
urinary GAG concentrations after oral and intramuscular

administration were unable to achieve the urinary concentrations
deemed beneficial in human studies.36,37

BACTERIAL INTERFERENCE
The use of bacteria to prevent UTI attempts to establish colonies of
nonvirulent organisms that alter the urinary microenvironment,
preventing proliferation of virulent colonizers. In people with
disorders of urine retention causing reinfection, instilling the ASB
strain E. coli 83972 into the urinary bladder reduced reinfection by
up to 50%.38 In dogs, intravesicular instillation of a similar
biotherapeutic, E. coli 2-12, also resulted in near clinical cure in 4 of
9 dogs by day 14. However, a larger, long-term study is necessary
before making clinical recommendations.39
Probiotics may also be used for altering the urinary
microenvironment and to decrease the vaginal pH, thereby
inhibiting uropathogenic bacterial colonization. In people, oral and
vaginal administration of Lactobacillus has been shown to effectively
increase the population of lactic acid producing bacteria within the
vagina, reduce the number of uropathogenic bacteria isolated, and
reduce the recurrence of UTI.40 In female dogs, the importance of
Lactobacillus as a vaginal colonizer is not known and orally
supplementing female dogs with lactic acid producing bacteria has
failed to alter the vaginal population.41

MISCELLANEOUS NONANTIMICROBIAL PREVENTATIVES
The use of vaginally-applied estrogens helps prevent reinfection in
women by altering the urinary microenvironment. It does so by
promoting vaginal Lactobacillus growth, lowering vaginal pH, and
restoring atrophic urethral mucosa.42 It is unknown how this
treatment translates to dogs and cats, although patients with
subclinical urinary sphincter mechanism incompetence may benefit
from estrogen therapy (ch. 310).

Methenamine salts are bacteriostatic urinary antiseptics that are
converted to formaldehyde at a urine pH <5.5. These salts are coadministered with vitamin C or other urine acidifiers and should be
avoided when urease-positive UTI or conditions associated with
metabolic acidosis such as chronic kidney disease/uremia are
present.43 No veterinary recommendations for their use exist.
Additional therapies that appear promising for the future include
the development of anti-bacterial antibodies using various
vaccination strategies44,45 and targeted bacteriophage lysis of
bacteria.46 Some vaccination therapies have achieved modest
success in human clinical trials and may provide additional
prophylactic treatment options for preventing bacterial adherence
and colonization of the urothelium.

ANTIMICROBIAL PREVENTATIVE
THERAPY
In both human and veterinary patients, the use of long-term,
modified-dose antibiotic prophylaxis is controversial.3,47 In human
studies, active prophylaxis did reduce the recurrence of infection and
this therapy may be useful in some animals suffering from severe
clinical signs.43 This treatment will not prevent infection once the
antibiotics are discontinued and selective pressures applied to
bacteria via repeated courses of antibiotics may lead to the
development of multidrug resistant uropathogenic bacterial strains
and treatment failure.48-50
The basis of prophylactic antibiotic therapy is to provide one-third
to one-half of the total daily dose of an antibiotic usually at night
after the last urine void of the day. Antibiotics concentrate in the
urinary bladder overnight, preventing colonization of the urine. The
daily treatments are continued for 6 months, with monthly cultures
to ensure a breakthrough infection has not occurred. After 6 months,
if the urine remains sterile, the antibiotics can then be discontinued
and the therapy repeated as necessary.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Recurrent Urinary Tract Infection
Recurrent urinary tract infections occur when there is a structural or
mechanical abnormality in the urinary tract. Identifying and treating
the abnormality is essential to prevent future infections. Simple
antibiotic treatment may lead to short-term resolution of clinical
signs; however, long term this approach to therapy is usually
unsuccessful and infection will return within a few weeks to months.
The repeated cycle of infection and treatment is common and results
in owner frustration, pet discomfort, and increased expense.
In order to give your pet the best chance at resolution of infection,
a systemic evaluation must be performed. This may start with a more
specialized physical exam that includes a neurologic assessment,
exam of the external genitalia, and an assessment of the ability of
your pet to urinate appropriately and completely. Additional
diagnostics frequently include a biochemistry profile to identify
endocrine, kidney, and liver disease, a complete blood count to
identify a systemic inflammatory response, and a urinalysis to
identify dilute urine or cellular abnormalities that may hint at
problems with the kidneys and urinary bladder. If a cause of the
infections is not identified upon the initial screen, a second tier of

diagnostics may be performed including abdominal radiographs,
abdominal ultrasound, and/or cystoscopy. During cystoscopy a fiberoptic camera is used to visualize the lower urinary tract and
necessitates general anesthesia. These more complicated diagnostics
may require referral to an internal medicine specialist in your area.
In some pets the cause of the recurrent urinary tract infections
cannot be identified or treated, and long-term management is the
only option. To treat a current infection antibiotics may be used;
however, preventative measures to help stop future infections are
also often employed. Examples of these include the use of cranberry
extract, urinary antiseptics, and hormone therapies. These
treatments will not cure your pet. The goal is to increase the time
between symptomatic episodes.
As an owner of a pet with recurrent urinary tract infections the
most important thing that you can do to help your dog/cat and your
veterinarian is to be sure to give prescribed medications at the
appropriate dose and for the entire duration of the prescribed
therapy. Frequently pets feel much better after only a few doses of
the antibiotics, but they still need the entire treatment course to help
eradicate all of the infecting bacteria. It is also very important to be
aware of infections as they occur. Straining to urinate, urinating
small amounts frequently, painful urination, difficulty urinating, and
blood in the urine are all signs that indicate infection. Also watch for
signs of lethargy, changes in drinking or urinating habits, and/or
inappetence as these may indicate a more systemic problem. Should
you note any of these signs you should call your local veterinarian
immediately.
Michael Wood (Madison, Wisconsin)

PATHOGENESIS
GENERAL
In health, the urine exists in a metastable state, supersaturated with
solutes. Uroliths form when equilibrium is disturbed, resulting in the
precipitation of solutes into solid crystals that aggregate and grow in
a protein matrix. Multiple mechanisms can promote spontaneous
crystallization, including increases in solute concentrations (from
increased solute excretion and/or decreased urine volume),
decreases in excretion or function of natural crystallization
inhibitors, and urine pH changes, which alter mineral solubility.

Foreign material in the urinary tract can serve as a nidus for
crystallization; suture material is associated with 9% of cystolith
recurrences in dogs.1 The ability to void crystal aggregates before
significant growth has occurred is likely also important for stone
prevention; disorders that increase residual urine volume, such as
prostatic disease (ch. 314), are major risk factors for bladder stones
in humans.2

MINERAL-SPECIFIC
ETIOPATHOGENESIS
Common risk factors for specific urolith types are detailed below and
in Table 308.1.

Struvite
Struvite uroliths comprise 40-43% of canine urolith submissions to
urolith analysis centers.3,4 Most struvite uroliths form secondary to
urinary tract infections (UTIs, ch. 307).5 Staphylococcus spp.,
Proteus spp. and some other bacterial species produce urease, an
enzyme that converts urea to ammonia. When a hydrogen ion binds
ammonia, ammonium is produced, and the urine pH increases.
These effects increase precipitation of struvite (magnesium
ammonium phosphate). Rarely, canine struvite uroliths or plugs
(mineral mixed with proteinaceous debris) form in the absence of a
UTI.6,7

Calcium Oxalate
Calcium oxalate (CaOx) uroliths comprise 35-42% of canine urolith
submissions.3,4 Idiopathic hypercalciuria (increased urinary calcium
excretion despite normocalcemia) is a common underlying
disturbance.8-10 It is theorized to be caused by intestinal
hyperabsorption of calcium, possibly related to abnormalities in
vitamin D metabolism in some dogs.11 In <10% of cases, dogs with
CaOx urolithiasis have hypercalcemia due to primary

hyperparathyroidism (ch. 283) or malignancy (ch. 331).9 Genetic
factors contribute to CaOx urolith risk. Strong breed predispositions
are noted, with 58% of all CaOx urolith submissions coming from the
Miniature Schnauzer, Yorkshire Terrier, Shih Tzu, Bichon Frisé, and
Lhasa Apso.12 Specific genetic causes have not yet been identified in
these breeds and are likely complex (influenced by multiple genes
and environmental factors). Monogenic disorders exist in other
breeds but are rare.13,14

Calcium Phosphate
Calcium phosphate is the primary mineral in 1% of canine urolith
submissions.3 It is also frequently a component of mixed uroliths,
found in conjunction with struvite and/or CaOx.4 The combination
of alkaline urine and hypercalciuria likely contribute to its formation.
Primary hyperparathyroidism (ch. 283) is also a risk factor.15

Cystine
Cystine comprises 6% of canine urolith submissions.3 Cystinuria is a
hereditary disorder caused by mutations in genes encoding subunits
of a renal amino acid transporter (SLC3A1 and SLC7A9).16 The most
common form of cystinuria in dogs is androgen-dependent and thus
sex-limited, with 70-90% of cystine uroliths submitted from intact
males.4,12,17,18 An autosomal recessive form of cystinuria (ch. 303)
is common in male and female Newfoundlands,19 though prevalence
is declining likely due to incorporation of genetic testing into
breeding practices.12

Purine (Urate, Xanthine)
Urate comprises 5% of canine urolith submissions.3 Decreased
hepatic conversion of uric acid to allantoin results in hyperuricosuria
and urate stone risk. This occurs with congenital portosystemic
shunts (ch. 267) or hereditary hyperuricosuria (HHU, ch.

303).20,21 HHU is caused by a mutation in the uric acid transporter
gene, SLC2A9, and results in decreased hepatic uptake and renal
reabsorption of uric acid.21 Greater than 90% of Dalmatians have
HHU,21,22 and >90% of uroliths submitted from this breed are
composed of urate.12 HHU also occurs in Black Russian Terriers,
English Bulldogs, and >30 other breeds.23 Sex is important for urate
urolith risk; most submissions come from neutered males.12 Uric
acid is poorly soluble in acidic urine, and thus the risk of urate
urolithiasis is also affected by urine pH.24

Xanthine is a rare purine urolith (0.1% of submissions)12 caused
by a deficiency in xanthine dehydrogenase (XDH), the enzyme that
converts xanthine to uric acid. Most (75%) canine xanthine uroliths
are iatrogenic, caused by XDH inhibitor therapy (e.g., allopurinol)
for management of urate stones (see Treatment—Dissolution—Urate

below) or leishmaniasis (ch. 197), with the remainder attributed to
hereditary defects.25

Silica
Silica comprises <1% of canine urolith submissions.12 Approximately
90% form in male, primarily neutered, dogs.12 High dietary silica
intake is a risk factor, with corn gluten feed, rice or soybean hulls,
and intact grains as potential silica-rich sources.26 Breed
predispositions, such as the German Shepherd Dog, have also been
reported for silica uroliths.4,27

CLINICAL PRESENTATION
SIGNALMENT
Most dogs with bladder and/or urethral uroliths are middle-aged at
the time of diagnosis.28 In dogs ≥7 years old, 60% of uroliths contain
CaOx, 35% struvite, 9% urate, and 1% cystine.4 In contrast, in dogs
<7 years old, 58% contain struvite, 26% CaOx, 25% urate, and 5%
cystine. Note that totals are greater than 100%, as mixed uroliths are
included in multiple categories.
While near equal numbers of uroliths are retrieved from female
and male dogs,12 the most likely composition differs by sex. In
female dogs, 74% of uroliths are composed of struvite compared to
only 13% in male dogs,12 explained by the female predisposition for
UTI.29 In males, 73% of uroliths are composed of CaOx.12 Intact
males have an increased risk for cystine uroliths, due to androgendependent cystinuria.4,12,17,18
Certain dog breeds are predisposed to specific urolith types, as
described in the Pathogenesis section. The Minnesota Urolith Center
offers a free application (“MN Urolith”) that includes a CALCulate
function to predict the most likely urolith composition based on
signalment. Age, sex (including neuter status) and breed are
inputted, and the CALCulate function provides demographic data on

urolith compositions. The following CALCulate output from 2021
illustrates how composition differs based on signalment: 5-year-old
female spayed Labrador Retriever: 94% struvite; 8-year-old male
neutered Bichon Frisé: 91% CaOx; 6-year-old male neutered
Dalmatian: 94% urate; 3-year-old male intact English Bulldog: 70%
cystine.

CLINICAL SIGNS
Most dogs with uroliths have clinical signs secondary to irritation
and inflammation of the bladder and/or urethra. These “lower
urinary tract signs” consist of pollakiuria, periuria, and stranguria
(ch. 54). Hematuria is also common. In the case of urethral
obstruction, the dog might be unable to urinate, despite attempts
(Videos 54.1, 54.2, 54.3).

Dogs with partial obstruction might

have incontinence/dribbling. Dogs suffering from urethral
obstruction or ruptured bladder can have systemic clinical signs such
as vomiting, anorexia, and lethargy. If a UTI is present, the urine
might have a foul smell. When a congenital portosystemic shunt is
the underlying cause of urate uroliths, the dog might show signs of
delayed growth, gastrointestinal signs and/or abnormal mentation
(ch. 267). Upper urinary tract disease should be considered for dogs
with polyuria/polydipsia or persistent hematuria without lower
urinary tract signs (chs. 299-305).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Most dogs with bladder and/or urethral uroliths have a normal
physical examination. Large cystoliths may be palpable in lean and
small breed dogs. Palpation of the urethra can reveal the presence of
urethroliths. Bladder size is informative in dogs with
incontinence/dribbling; if the bladder is large, a partial obstruction
should be suspected.

DIAGNOSIS

DIFFERENTIALS
The following diseases should be considered in dogs with lower
urinary tract signs: bladder/urethral uroliths, bacterial cystitis (ch.
307), bladder/urethral neoplasia (ch. 330), urethritis (ch. 312),
and in males, prostatic disease (ch. 314). Patient signalment and
physical examination findings are helpful to rank differentials. For
example, 60% of females presenting with lower urinary tract signs
have bacterial cystitis compared to only 25% of males.29 If an
enlarged prostate is palpated in a male dog, prostatic disease should
be suspected (ch. 314). See Figure 308.1 for a diagnostic
algorithm.

URINALYSIS
A urinalysis is recommended for dogs presenting with lower urinary
tract signs (ch. 70). Expected findings with urolithiasis are
delineated below.

Urine Specific Gravity (USG)
Lower urinary tract urolithiasis does not affect the USG. However,
dogs with uroliths can have concurrent disease that affects urine
concentrating ability (e.g., portosystemic shunt [ch. 267], chronic
kidney disease [ch. 301], endocrinopathies).

pH
Some uroliths form more easily in acidic urine (e.g., urate uroliths)
versus alkaline urine (e.g., struvite uroliths). However, urine pH at
the time of presentation might not reflect the pH at the time of
urolith formation and can be affected by diet and postprandial
timing. Thus, it should not be the sole way of estimating the most
likely urolith type.

Proteinuria
Proteinuria is common with urolithiasis.30-33

Crystalluria
Neither presence nor type of crystalluria accurately predicts urolith
presence or composition. Struvite, amorphous phosphate, and CaOx
crystalluria can occur in healthy dogs without urolithiasis,32,33 and
in vitro crystal formation occurs with sample storage.33 Additionally,
the absence of crystals does not rule out the presence of uroliths.
Fewer than 10% of dogs with CaOx uroliths have CaOx crystalluria.32
Unlike other crystal types, cystine or urate crystalluria is
considered abnormal, as the urinary excretion of these solutes is low
in healthy dogs. These crystal types can indicate cystinuria and
hyperuricosuria, respectively (ch. 303), and help predict
composition in a dog with uroliths. However, not all dogs with
cystinuria or hyperuricosuria will form uroliths and not all dogs with
cystine or urate uroliths have crystalluria.

FIGURE 308.1 Algorithm illustrating a diagnostic
approach for dogs with lower urinary tract signs.

Blood/Erythrocytes
Hematuria is common with uroliths, regardless of composition.3032,34

Leukocytes
Pyuria is frequently observed with struvite urolithiasis, due to the
associated bacterial cystitis (ch. 307).30 It can also occur with urate
urolithiasis, again due to concurrent bacteriuria, but is uncommon
with other urolith types.31,32,34

Organisms
Bacteriuria is common in dogs with struvite urolithiasis and reported
in one-third of Dalmatians with urate urolithiasis.34,35 It is
uncommon (5%) with CaOx urolithiasis.32

URINE CULTURE
Urine culture with antimicrobial sensitivity testing is recommended
in patients with lower urinary tract signs and pyuria or bacteriuria on
urinalysis. It should also be considered for female dogs without these
sediment findings, given their predisposition for bacterial cystitis
and limitations of urine sediment analysis for detection of
bacteriuria.36,37

IMAGING
Imaging studies are used for identifying, counting, and measuring
uroliths. They can also help predict urolith composition. Uroliths
with a maximum diameter >10 mm, an ovoid shape, or a pyramidal
shape, have a >90%, 80%, and nearly 100% probability, respectively,
of a struvite composition.38 In contrast, a rosette-shaped urolith has
a 95% probability of having a CaOx composition. However, there is
great variation in urolith size and shape, and different minerals can
appear radiographically similar (Figure 308.2). In addition, the
inner composition of a urolith cannot be predicted by assessing the
outer layer, which determines shape. For this reason, stone
composition should be predicted based on a combination of
signalment, the presence or absence of major risk factors (Table
308.1), and urolith appearance.

Plain Radiography
Because of its availability and relatively low cost, plain radiography is
the preferred imaging technique to diagnose uroliths in dogs. It is
also the best method to estimate urolith size and number, and to
monitor dissolution of radiopaque uroliths. Greater than 90% of

CaOx and struvite uroliths are estimated to be visible with plain
radiography.38 In contrast, only 70-75% of urate and cystine uroliths
are estimated to be detected because of their relatively poor
radiopacity. These estimates might be outdated, as the use of digital
radiography has improved resolution compared to screen-film
radiography.39
A dog should have an empty colon and a full bladder when
radiographs are performed to optimize urolith detection. A lateral
abdominal view generally provides the best visualization of the
bladder. If the colon is overlaid with the bladder, a wooden spoon or
radiolucent paddle can be used to compress the abdomen and push
the colon dorsally, away from the bladder. The entire urethra should
be included. As most obstructing urethroliths localize to the penile
urethra, the pelvic limbs should be pulled cranially or caudally in
male dogs to prevent their overlay on this region.

FIGURE 308.2 Examples of how cystoliths with
different mineral compositions can have similar

Contrast Radiography

Contrast radiography techniques, such as pneumocystography and
double contrast cystourethrography, are highly sensitive for all
urolith types and sizes.38 Contrast cystourethrography is also the
preferred technique to detect intraluminal urethral disease when
cystoscopy is not available or feasible (narrow urethra or urethral
stricture; ch. 312).

Abdominal Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography can easily detect cystoliths (Video 309.1

),

bladder wall abnormalities (masses, thickening, hematomas), and
upper urinary tract uroliths; it is limited in its ability to detect
urethroliths because of pelvic bone superimposition.
Ultrasonography is more sensitive than radiography for uroliths ≤1
mm.38 However, it is difficult to accurately count uroliths using
ultrasonography. Ultrasonography also overestimates cystolith
size,40 which is relevant to decisions about urolith removal
techniques.

Computed Tomography
Computed tomography has advantages over plain radiography and
ultrasonography for urolith detection, such as greater quality of
visualization of the entire urinary tract. However, it requires general
anesthesia, is not as widely available, and is more expensive than
other routine imaging modalities.

UROLITH ANALYSIS
Urolith analysis is vital for delineating pathogenesis, clinical
management, and prognosis. After composition is determined,
additional diagnostic tests and therapy can be tailored to the specific
urolith type (Table 308.2). Conditions contributing to urolith
formation in an individual dog can change over time, depending on
environment, diet, and comorbidities. For this reason, it is essential
to submit uroliths for analysis with each recurrence, rather than
assume the composition based on previous urolithiasis events.

Similarly, if uroliths are removed from the upper and lower urinary
tracts, uroliths from both locations should be submitted.41 Uroliths
should be dry when submitted for analysis because wet or bloody
uroliths delay the analysis process; additionally, liquids such as
formalin can alter or dissolve some minerals.
