Methodology
Quantitative methods are recommended for urolith analysis. Several
quantitative techniques can be used, the most common being optical
crystallography (with polarizing light microscopy) and infrared
spectroscopy.42

Admixtures and Layers
Most uroliths contain a predominant mineral type (>70%). Discrete
layers of 1 or more mineral types might be present.42 A urolith is
referred to as “mixed” if no single mineral comprises greater than
70% of a layer or “compound” if 1 portion of the urolith comprises at
least 70% of 1 mineral type and 1 or more other layers are primarily
(>70%) of a different mineral.43 Factors that initiate urolith
formation (nidus/core) may be different from those that allow
urolith growth and subsequent layers (stone, shell, surface crystals).
Therefore, the urolith core can differ in composition from that of the
body.

TREATMENT
DISSOLUTION
Struvite, urate, and cystine uroliths are amenable to dissolution
using a combination of therapeutic diets (ch. 159) and medication.
Since urolith composition is often unknown at the time treatment is
selected, the available information from each patient should be
reviewed to estimate probable composition. The Minnesota Urolith
Center’s CALCulate application is helpful for this purpose. Since
struvite is the most common dissolvable mineral, it is critical to
consider whether or not this composition is likely when deciding
about whether to institute a dissolution trial. A diagnostic algorithm

is provided in Figure 308.3 for when to suspect struvite and how to
implement a dissolution trial.

Struvite
Struvite uroliths should be medically dissolved using a combination
of a therapeutic dissolution diet (ch. 159) and antimicrobial therapy
to clear the concurrent UTI (ch. 307; Figure 308.3). Struvite
dissolution eliminates the morbidity and risks associated with
surgical removal, such as incomplete urolith removal, incisional
complications, uroabdomen and anesthetic complications.44,45
There is no evidence to support faster resolution of clinical signs by
surgical removal. Dissolution trials should be considered in dogs
with urease-producing bacteriuria (e.g., Staphylococcus spp. and
Proteus spp.), dogs with a history of struvite urolithiasis, female dogs
that recently received antimicrobial therapy that could confound a
UTI diagnosis, and a radiographic urolith appearance supportive of
struvite (see above characteristics). Contraindications for a
dissolution trial include urethral obstruction and comorbidities that
prevent feeding of a therapeutic urinary diet.35,46 Success rates for
medical dissolution of suspected struvite uroliths are 50-60%, with a
median time to full dissolution of approximately 1 month.35,47 If no
dissolution is noted by 4-6 weeks or clinical signs fail to resolve
within 2 weeks, urolith removal should be considered (ch. 117).

FIGURE 308.3 Algorithm for when to suspect a
struvite composition in a dog diagnosed with uroliths
and how to implement a medical dissolution trial.
UTI, Urinary tract infection.

Calcium Oxalate

CaOx uroliths cannot be medically dissolved. Therapeutic diets for
CaOx uroliths are formulated to reduce risk of recurrence but will
not treat those that have already formed. In general, uroliths in adult
neutered male dogs are likely to be composed of CaOx. Notable
exceptions are dogs with confirmed or suspected urease-producing
bacteriuria (in which case struvite is likely), those with a congenital
portosystemic shunt or of a breed with a high prevalence of HHU (in
which case urate is likely), and intact male dogs that are at risk for
cystine uroliths.

Cystine
Cystine uroliths can be medically dissolved by feeding a therapeutic
diet low in animal protein (ch. 159) combined with administration
of tiopronin (synonym: 2-mercaptopropionylglycine), a cystine
chelating agent, at 20 mg/kg PO q12h.48 This therapy is successful in
60% of cases in a median of 2 months. Aggression, myopathy,
proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, and skin lesions can occur with
tiopronin therapy and resolve with a dosage decrease or
discontinuation. Potassium citrate (75 mg/kg PO q12h) can be given
as a urinary alkalinizer to increase cystine solubility.46 Cystinuria
resolves post-neuter in intact male dogs with the androgendependent form, but the probability of urolith dissolution without
other intervention is unknown.

Urate
Urate uroliths can be medically dissolved in dogs by feeding a
therapeutic low-purine alkalinizing diet (ch. 159) and treatment
with allopurinol, an XDH inhibitor, at 15 mg/kg PO q12h.46,49 In
dogs with HHU, full dissolution of urate uroliths is achieved in 3040% of cases in a median of 1 month; most failures are caused by
xanthine urolith formation.49 Success rates are not reported for dogs
with portosystemic shunts. Urate urolith dissolution can occur after
shunt attenuation, but success rates are thought to be low if the
shunt is left uncorrected.

Reasons for Dissolution Failure

A common reason for dissolution failure is a different urolith
composition than the one targeted with the dissolution therapy
(Figure 308.2). Other causes of dissolution failure are
noncompliance with diet or medication, premature discontinuation
of therapy due to a complication (drug side-effects, diet intolerance,
pancreatitis, urethral obstruction, etc.) or, in the case of struvite
uroliths, inappropriate antimicrobial selection.

REMOVAL
Uroliths should be removed when associated with clinical signs,
urethral obstruction, or recurrent infection.46 Removal should also
be considered for male dogs with uroliths close to the diameter of the
urethral lumen or if the uroliths are currently amenable to minimally
invasive removal techniques but would not be if further growth
occurred. Abdominal radiographs should ideally be performed a
week or less prior to removal to confirm persistence, size, number,
and location.
Minimally invasive procedures are encouraged because they are
associated with shorter hospitalization time and faster recovery for
the patient than cystotomy.46 Minimally invasive options include
voiding urohydropropulsion (VUH), basket removal (Video 308.1),
lithotripsy (Videos 308.2, 308.3

), and percutaneous

cystolithotomy, from the least to the most invasive. The type of
removal technique is dictated by the expertise of the clinician, size of
the dog, and equipment availability. An algorithm is provided in
Figure 308.4 for selection of urolith removal techniques. Incisionfree procedures are preferred, where possible, to prevent risk for
suture-induced urolith recurrence.1 Only VUH is described in this
chapter, and the other procedures are detailed in ch. 117.

VUH
During VUH, the bladder is filled with saline, agitated, and then
manually expressed while the dog is held vertically under general

anesthesia (male, traditional technique: Videos 308.5 and 308.6
; male, trough technique: Video 308.7; female, traditional technique:
Video 308.4). This technique requires minimal equipment: a urinary
catheter, saline, and syringes. Several factors can affect the success of
the procedure, such as the size and number of uroliths, size and sex
of the patient, urethral lesions (e.g., presence of a stricture), and
ability to palpate the bladder. A general guideline is that smooth
uroliths <5 mm in diameter can be voided in dogs that weigh >8
kg.50 Overall, female dogs are the best candidates for VUH because
of their short and wide urethra. In male dogs, the presence of the os
penis restricts urethral lumen distension. Large breed or obese dogs
are not ideal candidates for VUH due to difficulty palpating the
bladder. Passing a urethral catheter can be used for estimating the
urethral diameter and can guide the likelihood that uroliths can be
voided; for example, an 8 Fr catheter is 2.5 mm in diameter and a 12
Fr catheter is 4 mm in diameter.
VUH is well tolerated in dogs. Complications are generally minor
and self-limiting, such as hematuria. If a urolith gets lodged in the
urethra, it can be flushed back into the bladder by retrograde
urohydropropulsion and removed with other techniques (ch. 117).
Bladder rupture is a rare complication, only reported in a dog with a
recent urethral obstruction that compromised the bladder wall.50
Palpation of the bladder should be performed by an assistant as
saline is infused up to a total volume of 10 mL/kg.51 In female dogs,
catheterization under visualization with an otoscope (using a large
sterile cone) or cystoscope is recommended to decrease risk of
trauma from blind catheterization.

PREVENTION AND MONITORING
It is important to educate clients that urolith recurrence is common
in dogs, despite preventative measures.34,48,52 Frequent rechecks
including urinalysis (at 1 month and then every 3-6 months) and
bladder imaging (at 3-6 months and then every 6-12 months) are
recommended to guide preventative therapies and detect recurrence

early, when the urolith(s) might be amenable to removal with
minimally invasive techniques.

STRATEGIES
Increasing water intake is beneficial to reduce solute supersaturation
and minimize recurrence of all urolith types. The target USG is
≤1.020.46 Preventative therapies and diagnostic considerations for
common urolith types are listed in Table 308.2, with additional
details below.

Struvite
The most effective way to prevent struvite recurrence in dogs is
through prevention and early eradication of UTIs (ch. 307). A urine
culture is recommended at 1 month and any time there is recurrence
of lower urinary tract signs.46 If the dog has a history of recurrent
UTIs without a resolvable underlying cause, regular (e.g., every 3
months) urine cultures might be indicated. Subclinical bacteriuria
does not require therapy in most dogs.53 However, in the authors’
experience, clinical signs are not always present when struvite
uroliths first form. Thus, if urease-producing bacteria are cultured
from a dog with a history of struvite uroliths, treatment is
recommended, whether or not clinical signs are reported. A
therapeutic urinary diet is not sufficient to prevent infection-induced
struvite uroliths but might slow their growth.

Calcium Oxalate
Therapeutic urinary diets for CaOx prevention are formulated with a
low oxalate content, moderate calcium content (low calcium is not
recommended, as restriction increases oxalate absorption), and an
optimal calcium-to-phosphorus ratio (ch. 159). The optimal dietary
sodium content is questioned and varies among therapeutic diets.
Feeding a therapeutic urinary diet formulated for CaOx prevention
reduces hypercalciuria and estimates of urine supersaturation of
CaOx.54,55 Potassium citrate, an alkalinizer and crystallization

inhibitor, is also an ingredient of these diets and can be further
supplemented at 75 mg/kg PO q12-24h for dogs with persistently low
urine pH (<6.5). Potassium citrate supplements containing
cranberry extract should be avoided, as they might increase urinary
oxalate excretion.56

FIGURE 308.4 Algorithm for selecting the best
therapeutic options for dissolution or removal of
cystoliths in dogs.
It is important to set owner expectations that therapeutic urinary
diets do not totally eliminate the risk of CaOx urolith recurrence.
Rates are as high as 50% in 2-3 years, even on a therapeutic urinary
diet.52 Owners should also be informed that the impact of most
commercial diets on urine supersaturation of CaOx is not tested, and

some might increase urolith risk. For example, diets might be
acidifying (which increases hypercalciuria and decreases urine
citrate excretion), increase urine oxalate excretion (such as those
containing spinach, potato, or other high oxalate ingredients), or
could have other lithogenic effects.
Hydrochlorothiazide is a medical option for recurrent CaOx stone
formers at 2 mg/kg PO q12h. It reduces urine calcium excretion by
increasing its renal resorption.15 Blood or serum ionized calcium
concentration should be measured prior to starting
hydrochlorothiazide, as it might exacerbate hypercalcemia associated
with primary hyperparathyroidism.57

Cystine
Specific recommendations for cystine urolith prevention are a low
animal protein diet, low sodium diet, and alkalinization of the urine
with potassium citrate (target urine pH of 7.5).46 Quantification of
urinary cystine (high performance liquid chromatography) is
recommended in dogs with cystine uroliths. Urine creatinine should
also be measured on the same sample to allow for normalization
based on urine concentration by calculating a cystine-to-creatinine
ratio. Dogs with a cystine-to-creatinine ratio >178 micromol/g (or
nmol/mg) are cystinuric.16 Castration is recommended for intact
male dogs with cystine uroliths. With androgen-dependent
cystinuria, urine cystine-to-creatinine ratios return to normal within
2-4 months of castration. In dogs with persistent cystinuria despite
castration and dietary management, tiopronin 15 mg/kg PO q12h can
be administered.

Urate
A low-purine diet is recommended to prevent the formation of urate
uroliths (ch. 159). If the urine pH is acidic, potassium citrate
supplementation is recommended (target pH ≥7). In dogs with HHU
and persistent urate crystalluria despite these strategies, allopurinol
is advised at 5-7 mg/kg PO q12-24h.46 In dogs with portosystemic
shunts (ch. 267), surgical correction of the shunt should reduce
hyperuricosuria.

Mixed and Compound Uroliths
Since the nidus forms first, preventative strategies should be
prioritized based on the core mineral. One-third of compound
uroliths are composed of a CaOx nidus and a struvite outer layer.43
Because CaOx uroliths cannot be medically dissolved, prevention is
especially important and dietary and medical strategies for
prevention should be directed towards this mineral. For any urolith
containing a struvite admixture or layer, UTI detection and
treatment should be emphasized. In stones that are primarily
struvite with a small proportion of urate (<20%) without HHU (not
homozygous for the mutation) or a portosystemic shunt, the focus
should be on struvite prevention.
For combinations of urate and CaOx, struvite and calcium
phosphate, or calcium phosphate and CaOx, strategies to prevent the
formation of 1 type will also minimize the formation of the other.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Lower Urinary Tract Urolithiasis in Dogs
Urinary stones are common in dogs. They form for various reasons
including genetics, diet, and concurrent diseases.

WHAT TO LOOK FOR AT HOME?
Dogs with stones may show increased frequency of urination, urinary
accidents, bloody urine (which can appear red or pinkish), dribbling
urine, or straining when urinating. Urinary blockage is an emergency
because it can be life threatening. If a dog has not urinated for more
than 12 hours despite active attempts (posturing), it should be
examined by a veterinarian immediately.

WHAT WILL BE DONE AT THE VETERINARIAN?
Urine tests might be performed to rule out other diseases such as
infection but cannot diagnose stones. Note that crystals in the urine
are not the same as stones and can be normal in dogs. Bladder
imaging (x-rays or ultrasound) is needed to identify stones. Some
stone types can be dissolved with diet and medications, while others
require removal. Dissolvable stones are most common in female dogs
that have a urinary tract infection and are treated with diet and
antibiotics. In contrast, most stones in male dogs cannot be
dissolved. When stone removal is required, it is often achieved with
bladder surgery, after which the dog may have to be hospitalized for
1 to 2 days followed by a couple weeks recovery at home. If the stone
size and/or number is small, removal might be possible with nonsurgical techniques, though anesthesia is still required. You might be
referred to an internal medicine specialist for non-surgical
procedures that require special training and equipment. In all cases,
the stone(s) should be sent for analysis, as this determines the best
management plan to prevent new stone formation.

WHAT IS THE PROGNOSIS (OUTLOOK FOR
HEALTH)?
Stones are not life-threatening unless there is a blockage. However,
certain stone types reform frequently (e.g., 50% chance of recurrence
within 2-3 years for 1 of the most common types). For that reason, it
is essential to follow preventative instructions from your
veterinarian. Specific diets and medications can reduce the
likelihood that new stones will form, though none eliminate risk. If
your dog’s stone formed secondary to a urinary tract infection, the
priority will be to identify future infections early through regular
urine cultures. After stone removal, your dog will need rechecks of
their urine and bladder (x-rays or ultrasound) to check if the
preventative measures are working. If a stone is detected early
enough, removal might be possible without surgery. If additional
stone removal procedures are performed, stone analysis is important
for each episode, as the stone type can change.

WHAT SHOULD I FEED MY DOG TO PREVENT
NEW STONES?
Increasing water consumption is important for all stone types. This
can be accomplished by feeding canned food or by adding water or
low sodium broth to kibble. Some diets that are nutritious and
beneficial for healthy dogs could be problematic for a stone former.
Therefore, your veterinarian might recommend a prescription
urinary diet that was specifically formulated for prevention of your
dog’s stone type. If a home-prepared diet is desired, recipes should
be formulated by a veterinary nutritionist to ensure that it is
nutritionally balanced. See the American College of Veterinary
Nutrition directory: https://acvn.org/directory/

WHAT ABOUT TREATS?
Prescription treats are available that might be safe to feed your dog,
depending on their stone type. Information is lacking on the effect of
other commercial dog treats on stone formation. However, if treats
comprise <10% of your dog’s total calories, they are unlikely to
significantly increase risk for stones. Certain human foods might not

be advisable, depending on your dog’s stone type, and veterinary
advice should be sought prior to feeding them.
Alice Defarges (Guelph, Ontario, Canada) and Eva Furrow (St.
Paul, Minnesota)

Urolithiasis is the formation of calculi (uroliths, or stones) within
the urinary tract. Uroliths are characterized by their location within

the urinary tract, with this chapter focusing on stones in the bladder
(cystoliths) and urethra (urethroliths) in cats. Uroliths are varied in
composition, with the most common feline uroliths being struvite
(magnesium ammonium phosphate [MAP]) and calcium oxalate
(CaOx).1 The remainder of stones that occur in cats include purine,
cystine, calcium phosphate, compound, and mixed (Figure 309.1).

CLINICAL SIGNS
Lower urinary tract signs are one of the most common reasons that
cats are presented to their veterinarian’s office (chs. 54, 311), and
urolithiasis accounts for 10-23% of lower urinary tract signs.2,3
While cystoliths can be an incidental finding, some stones can cause
clinical signs such as hematuria, pollakiuria, periuria, stranguria, or
a combination of these. Clinical signs of urethral obstruction (chs. 99
and 312) may be seen when a stone moves into the urethra and
becomes lodged, causing secondary urethral obstruction. There is no
clinical sign specific to the presence of cystoliths, so other
differentials such as feline idiopathic cystitis (FIC, ch. 311), a
urinary tract infection (UTI, ch. 307), and neoplasia (ch. 330)
should be considered.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
When a cat presents with clinical signs of lower urinary tract disease,
a minimum database including a complete blood count (CBC) and
serum biochemistry panel should be performed. Most often these
values will be within normal parameters. However, in some instances
there could be an indication for a cause of urinary stones. Some
conditions that could predispose to urinary stone formation include
liver disease (such as portosystemic shunts, ch. 267), chronic kidney
disease (ch. 301), hypercalcemia (ch. 69), or diabetes mellitus (ch.
292). Thyroid hormone levels should be evaluated in older cats.
Urinalysis is a key component of a urolithiasis workup and it
should be performed prior to starting any therapy (ch. 70).4
Measuring urine specific gravity (USG) is important because creating

dilute urine, particularly in cats that have previously formed uroliths,
helps reduce crystal aggregation and ultimately stone formation,
while concentrated urine increases the risk of stone formation. The
presence of certain urinary crystals is abnormal and could indicate
the types of stones present. Urinary pH can affect crystal formation
and solubility. Acidic urine leads to reduced solubility of ammonium
urate, silica, and cystine crystals, whereas alkaline urine leads to
reduced solubility of struvite, calcium carbonate, and calcium
phosphate (apatite) crystals. Crystalluria should be evaluated with
caution. Urolithiasis can occur without the presence of crystalluria,
and the types of crystals seen may not accurately identify the type of
stone present. Urine samples should be analyzed within 1 hour
following collection to minimize crystal formation secondary to
temperature and in vitro time-dependent crystallization. Feline
urinary stones are typically sterile: in 1 study, only 8.8% (89/1007) of
uroliths submitted for culture showed bacterial growth. Most of
these were struvite. Due to these low numbers, stone culture is likely
of low yield and may not be warranted in every case.5

FIGURE 309.1 Mineral composition of feline
uroliths.
https://vetmed.umn.edu/sites/vetmed.umn.e
du/files/2020globaldata.pdf

FIGURE 309.2 Lateral abdominal radiograph
showing a mineral-opacity urocystolith.
Diagnostic imaging should be utilized to confirm the presence of
uroliths. Abdominal ultrasound is useful in identifying all types of
urolithiasis, including uroliths <3 mm in diameter (

Video

309.1). Abdominal ultrasound is not useful in identifying
urethroliths, in which case survey radiographs should be considered
(Figure 309.2; ch. 312). Mineralized stones that are most
commonly visualized with radiographs include CaOx, calcium
apatite, struvite, and silica.6 Most cystine and ammonium urate
stones are nonmineralized and therefore not typically visible on
radiographs; however, in rare instances these stones may be
visualized on radiographs when mixed with mineralized stones.
Abdominal ultrasound and contrast urethrography are commonly
necessary to visualize these stones in the bladder and urethra,
respectively.

TREATMENT OF UROLITHIASIS
Stones removed from the urinary tract should be submitted for
analysis, which helps with implementation of measures to prevent
future uroliths from forming. Various stone analysis methods are
available at a variety of laboratories (Box 309.1). Depending on the
type of urinary stone present, some can be medically dissolved while
others need to be removed. Stones that are moderately radiopaque
and suspected to be struvite, cystine, or urate based on signalment,
the animal’s history, and/or radiographic appearance within a
neutral pH urine should be medically dissolved.7,8
Contraindications to medical dissolution of suspected or
confirmed struvite, cystine, or urate stones include the inability to
medicate the cat, if the cat’s diet cannot be switched due to
comorbidities (ch. 223), the cat has a history of urethral
obstruction, or the stone is so large that it cannot be bathed in an
appropriate amount of urine.8
There are various other options available for stone removal if the
stones cannot be dissolved. Treatment is only required if the stones
have a high likelihood of causing urinary tract obstruction, have
already caused urinary tract obstruction, or are causing clinical
signs.7,8 A cystotomy has long been standard practice for stone
removal. Although commonly performed, it does carry the risk of
complications such as recurrence of cystoliths secondary to
intraluminal suture material, incomplete removal of cystoliths,
infection of the surgical site, UTIs, and uroabdomen.7,9 Less invasive
methods of stone removal are recommended to try to mitigate many
of these complications, including voiding urohydropropulsion
(VUH), cystoscopic basket retrieval, laser lithotripsy, and
percutaneous cystolithotomy (PCCL) (ch. 117).7

VUH (ch. 308) should be considered for stones <3 mm diameter
in female cats. This procedure is incision-less but requires general
anesthesia. The patient is placed in dorsal recumbency, a 3.5F or 5F
red rubber urinary catheter is aseptically placed, and the bladder is
distended with sterile saline until full, but not taut. The catheter is
removed, and the cat is then tilted at a 45- to 90-degree angle to
allow the stones to fall into the trigone and proximal urethra. The
bladder is expressed, and the urine collected in a container with a
filter to trap the stone(s). This procedure can be done on an
outpatient basis. Some complications seen with this procedure
include incomplete stone removal and potential urethral
obstruction.7 This procedure is not recommended when there are
large quantities of stones, if the stones are larger than 3 mm, or in
male cats that have not undergone a perineal urethrostomy.
If stones are not passing via VUH, cystoscopic-guided basket
retrieval can be considered. Laser lithotripsy can also be performed
via cystoscopic guidance and is recommended in cases of
urethrolithiasis or a small number of cystoliths that are too large to
pass with basket retrieval or VUH.10 For male cats, or when the
bladder stones are too large for VUH or cystoscopic-guided basket
retrieval, a transvesicular PCCL should be considered. Such
endourologic procedures carry very substantial advantages regarding
reduced invasiveness, completeness of stone removal, and reduction

of postoperative complications. They are described in detail in ch.
117.
Laparoscopic-assisted cystoscopy has been described as an
alternative method of stone removal. Some of its advantages include
reduced urine contamination in the abdomen, as well as better
visualization of the bladder and urethra compared to traditional
cystotomy.12 Its disadvantages include the need to convert to open
cystotomy if serious intraoperative complications occur, and the
need to create a pneumoperitoneum.11,13 All these procedures carry a
risk of bladder rupture or urine leakage, so all cats should have a
urine culture performed <2 weeks prior to the procedure.

DIETARY MANAGEMENT
There are many different veterinary diets available for treatment of
urinary stones, with some diets formulated for dissolution and others
formulated for prevention (Boxes 309.2-309.5; ch. 159). The
formulations and availability of these diets change often. It is
important to note that some dissolution diets are not nutritionally
balanced and therefore not recommended for extended feeding (>6
months). Dietary management for both prevention and dissolution is
most effective when strict adherence to the diet is undertaken with
no additional treats, toppings, or table scraps.

TYPES OF STONES
CALCIUM OXALATE UROLITHIASIS
Epidemiology

CaOx stones are one of the most reported types of cystoliths in cats.
In a recent report, CaOx monohydrate stones made up a majority
(57%) of CaOx stone submissions, while 43% of CaOx stones were of
mixed composition. Sole CaOx dihydrate stones are rare.5 Typically,
CaOx stones are found in middle-aged to older, male neutered cats.5
Burmese, Himalayan, and Persian breeds are predisposed to CaOx
stone formation.4,5,14

Clinical Signs
Clinical signs for CaOx stones are similar to signs discussed earlier in
the chapter. CaOx cystoliths may occur only in the bladder, or
concurrently with nephroliths and/or obstructive ureteroliths.
Affected male cats may present with urethral obstructions. There is
no clinical sign specific for CaOx stones, and other rule-outs for these
signs should be considered (such as FIC [ch. 311], UTIs [ch. 307]
and neoplasia [ch. 330]). Occasionally, cystolithiasis may be
identified without clinical signs.

Pathophysiology of Stone Formation
Urinary crystal formation is a complex process. The supersaturation
of urine with calculogenic materials is one of the biggest factors in
crystal and stone formation.14,15 Relative supersaturation (RSS) is
the concentration of a compound in a solution above its solubility
level.16 A computer calculates the interactions of substances that
promote stone formation with those that inhibit stone formation
(such as magnesium, pyrophosphates, citrate, and Tamm-Horsfall
mucoprotein [TMP]; ch. 159).6,16-18 To assess RSS, the relative
importance of urinary water content, calcium concentrations, and
oxalate concentrations have been examined. Increasing water intake
causes urinary dilution, reducing the overall saturation of
calculogenic materials, and helps increase the frequency of urination,
which reduces time for crystal aggregation.18,19 RSS is not available
for clinical use, however.
Urinary calcium and oxalate concentrations are a major factor in
CaOx stone formation. They depend on dietary intake, intestinal

absorption, and renal tubular excretion. Oxalic acid, a metabolite of
the combination of amino acids (such as serine and glycine) with
vitamin C (ascorbic acid), combines with calcium to form insoluble
salts of CaOx.20 Urinary oxalate concentrations are 15× more potent
than calcium concentrations in affecting CaOx saturation.19 Oxalic
acid absorption and excretion are affected by genetics, the amount of
oxalate present in the diet, nutritional deficiencies (such as vitamin
B6 in experimental settings), and intestinal flora. Oxalates are
present in varied quantities in differing foods, and once ingested,
they are degraded by an enteric bacterium, Oxalobacter
formigenes.19 Reduced numbers of O. formigenes in dogs can
predispose them to CaOx formation.20 While dietary oxalate
comprises 25-68% of oxalate contributions in people, there are no
corresponding data currently in cats. Oxalate absorption and
excretion have also been shown to be closely related to calcium
absorption, which is increased when calcium intake is low, and
reduced when calcium intake is high.21 Primary hyperoxaluria (PH)
due to endogenous overproduction has been found to be a primary
autosomal-recessive genetic condition in people and is an important
risk factor for CaOx formation.22 Few cases have been reported in
cats. Oxalate is produced primarily in the liver and is dependent on
glyoxylate, which is reduced to glycolate or transaminated to glycine
in the liver.19 Any remaining glyoxylate is oxidized into oxalate.
Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), an essential cofactor in the conversion of
glyoxylate into glycine, reduces endogenous oxalate formation.19
Vitamin B6 deficiency can lead to increased endogenous oxalate
production and subsequent hyperoxaluria. Urinary calcium
excretion, similar to oxalate excretion, also depends on dietary
intake, intestinal absorption, and renal tubular excretion. Acidic
diets have been shown to increase calciuria and decrease oxalate
excretion but not with significant effects on RSS and CaOx
formation.23 Hypercalciuria has also been shown to be induced by
metabolic acidosis, which promotes calcium release from bone into
serum. This increases urinary calcium excretion and decreases renal

tubular absorption of calcium.24 Hypercalcemia also leads to an
increased risk of CaOx stone formation. Although typically
uncommon in the general cat population, one-third of cats with
CaOx stones had idiopathic hypercalcemia.17,20 There have been
some thoughts that reducing dietary calcium supplementation could
lead to reduced calciuresis; however, on the contrary, this has been
shown to increase risk of CaOx formation.
Several substances have been identified as promoting or inhibiting
CaOx formation. Promoters include calcium, potassium, sodium,
phosphate, oxalate, ammonium, cellular debris, urinary proteins,
and other types of crystals.6,14,16,17,20,25 Inhibitors include
magnesium, citrate, and pyrophosphate, which form soluble
complexes with calcium in the urine and prevent crystal formation
with oxalate. Urinary citrate concentrations have been shown to play
a role in CaOx stones in people.26 Citrate chelates calcium and
prevents alkaline-induced calcium phosphate stone formation.19
Low citrate levels are correlated with increased risk of CaOx
urolithiasis in people, and acidifying diets have been associated with
lower urinary concentrations of citrate.
Urinary glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), also freely excreted in the
urine, can inhibit growth of CaOx crystals and form a part of the
extracellular matrix along the inner bladder wall to help defend the
bladder against crystal and microbe adherence.27 Cats with FIC (ch.
311) have reduced GAG concentrations in the urine.28 One study
showed that cats with CaOx stones fed a urinary stone prevention
diet have increased urinary GAG concentrations.29
Aciduria leads to increased risk of CaOx, urate, and cystine stone
formation in cats.24 The saturation of CaOx in urine is increased in
acidic urine and reduced when urine pH is >7. Cats that are fed a diet
that reduces urine pH to <6.2 are at a 3× greater risk of forming
CaOx stones compared to cats fed a diet that produces a urine pH of
6.5-6.9.25 In humans, a lower urine pH increases renal proximal
tubular citrate reabsorption, which results in lower urine citrate
concentrations and subsequently reduced calcium-citrate complex

formation.24 A lower urine pH can also affect the concentrations of
CaOx crystal inhibitors, which further increases risk.

Diagnosis
The initial evaluation for CaOx stones should include a thorough
assessment for underlying causes as previously stated. A urinalysis
should be assessed ideally within 60 minutes of collection to
minimize the effects of time and temperature on in vitro crystal
formation.30 The USG should be recorded, and reasonable goals
established to reduce urine concentration. Urinary pH is variable in
cats with CaOx stones, and CaOx crystals are not always present.
Serum ionized calcium concentration should be measured in any cat
that is suspected of having CaOx stones. If hypercalcemia is
confirmed, measurement of parathyroid hormone, parathyroid
hormone-related protein, and possibly serum vitamin D levels is
recommended (ch. 283). Imaging should include both abdominal
radiography and ultrasonography, as some stones may be missed if
only 1 modality is used. CaOx stones are typically seen on survey
radiographs due to their mineral opacity; however, very small stones
may require ultrasonographic evaluation. Radiographs are helpful in
assessing the urethra for evidence of urethroliths, as ultrasonography
cannot assess the pelvic urethra.

Management
CaOx stones cannot be dissolved with medical management.
Treatment via removal of lower urinary tract stones is described
previously in this chapter, and in ch. 117.

Dietary Management
As CaOx stones cannot be medically dissolved, prevention of stone
formation is very important. Increased water intake is thought to be
the most important factor in CaOx stone prevention.31 Increasing
water intake increases urination, which reduces the amount of time
crystals lie stagnant in the bladder and thus reduces the likelihood of
stone formation. Various studies have looked at water intake in cats
depending on their diet. Dry food diets lead to ∼30% less water

intake compared to high-moisture diets. Wet food diets with a
moisture content ≥73.3% significantly reduce CaOx RSS, increase
urine production, and reduce USG. Wet-food diets containing lower
moisture levels have not shown similar results.24 Feeding cats a
urolith-prevention diet reduces urinary CaOx supersaturation by at
least 59%, and feeding a wet version of the same diet lowers urinary
calcium concentration significantly without significant change in
USG.29 If feeding a wet food diet is not an option, water can be
added to the kibble (ch. 159) or alternative food options provided.30
The goal of increasing water intake should be to reduce the USG to
<1.030.8,30 Acidifying (urine pH-lowering) diets increase the risk of
CaOx formation in cats; therefore, treatment should aim to increase
the urine pH, which decreases the urine saturation of CaOx and the
risk of CaOx cystolith formation. However, it can then predispose to
struvite formation. Finally, owners must be thoroughly educated on
the benefits of feeding a strict urolith prevention diet.32 Owners may
try to feed varied treats, table scraps, and supplements without
considering their effects on their pet’s diet. Certain treats or
supplements may be high in oxalates and calcium, or they may alter
urine composition. There are several commercially available
prescription diets that have been designed to influence the RSS of
CaOx to reduce the likelihood of urolith recurrence. Additional
information on nutritional management of lower urinary tract stones
is available in ch. 159.

Medical Management
Several pharmacologic agents are available if dietary therapy is
insufficient to prevent CaOx formation. Potassium citrate (50-75
mg/kg q12h PO, titrated upwards ideally until urinary pH = 7.0) is a
urinary alkalinizing agent.32 It works by increasing urinary citrate
excretion. In humans, it does this by reducing intestinal calcium
absorption, increasing calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted
tubules, and decreasing bone resorption.36 These effects have not
been confirmed in cats, and hypocitraturia is not a known risk factor
for CaOx formation in cats. Serum potassium, bicarbonate, and

kidney values, and urine pH, should be closely monitored (every 7-14
days) when administering this medication.
Thiazide diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide are another
therapeutic option. Thiazide diuretics enhance renal tubular
reabsorption of filtered calcium in the proximal and distal renal
tubules by inhibiting the sodium-chloride cotransporter. A
significant decrease in urinary CaOx RSS was found in a study of
healthy cats that were treated with hydrochlorothiazide 1 mg/kg
q12h PO.40 Studies assessing safety and efficacy are currently
lacking.
In cats with hypercalcemia (ch. 69), managing the cause of the
hypercalcemia can help prevent the formation of CaOx stones (ch.
283).

Monitoring
The probability of CaOx urolith recurrence varies and is reported to
be as high as ∼7%.8,41 Recheck imaging is recommended 4 weeks
after the removal procedure, followed then at 3 and 6 months
following the procedure. If new stones are identified before they
become large, less-invasive therapies such as VUH may be used.

STRUVITE UROLITHIASIS
Epidemiology
Struvite stones are one of the most common types of stones
submitted for analysis in cats (Figure 309.1).1 Feline struvite
stones (MAP) are typically sterile, in contrast to canine struvite
stones, and are more commonly found in middle-aged female cats.5
Struvite crystals are often found in the urine of cats with lower
urinary tract disease; however, occasionally they can also be seen in
cats without evidence of urolithiasis.39 Domestic Mediumhair
(DMH) cats are at an increased risk compared to other breeds.5

Pathophysiology

In contrast to calcium urine RSS, struvite RSS can be reduced with
acidifying diets.5,14,25 As the urine pH drops, struvite becomes more
soluble.5 Increased moisture content in diet does not seem to reduce
the RSS of MAP as it does for CaOx.31 Cats fed diets higher in fat
content and reduced levels of carbohydrates, calcium, phosphorus,
magnesium, sodium, and potassium are at a lower risk of MAP
formation. Factors that may be associated with the formation of
alkaline urine, such as a low animal protein diet, distal renal tubular
acidosis, or a family history of struvite urolithiasis, should be
considered in cats with struvite stones.
Although most struvite stones in cats are sterile, 11% of submitted
struvite stones are positive for bacterial growth, and of that
percentage 64.8% have grown urease-producing
bacteria.5 Staphylococcus spp., Corynebacterium urealyticum, and
Proteus spp. are the bacteria that are most commonly cultured from
MAP, while the most commonly cultured bacteria from all submitted
urinary stones include Staphylococcus spp. (49.4%), Enterococcus
spp. (23.6%), and Escherichia coli (19.1%).5

Management
Sterile struvite stones in cats can be dissolved in 1-4 weeks with a
dissolution diet designed to acidify the urine, although some stones
may take up to 5 months for complete resolution.15,18 Struvite
dissolution diets increase urine volume, reduce urine pH to <7, and
adjust levels of magnesium and phosphorus minerals in the urine
(ch. 159).3,40 One proposed mechanism is that the phosphate group
changes with reduced urine pH. Phosphate is present in alkaline
urine in a trivalent state (PO43−), which is more readily available to
struvite crystal formation. When urine is acidified, the phosphate is
protonated (HPO42, H2PO4−, or H3PO4), which reduces its
availability.18 Commonly added dietary acidifiers include
methionine, calcium or sodium sulfate, and ammonium chloride.18
When feeding a dissolution diet, owners must be strict in feeding it
as a sole diet. Abdominal radiographs should be reevaluated 2-4

weeks after starting the diet, at which time the uroliths should be 33100% smaller. If there is minimal change in size, the most likely
reason is that the mineral composition of the urolith is not struvite,
the stone is of mixed composition, or the owners are not following
recommendations. The dissolution diet should be continued for an
additional 2-4 weeks following radiographic dissolution. In the rare
circumstance in cats when there is a concurrent UTI, an appropriate
antibiotic should be administered throughout the entire period of
dissolution. Dissolution diets have not been associated with urethral
obstruction as uroliths decrease in size.
VUH can be considered in female cats and in male cats that have
undergone perineal urethrostomy if the urolith burden is low and the
stones are <5 mm in diameter. In cases of high stone burden, or
stones >5 mm in diameter, PCCL is recommended.
To prevent struvite urolithiasis, treatment can be aimed at
increasing water intake by encouraging drinking or increasing
dietary water content. This promotes more frequent urinations to
increase excretion of stone-forming crystals. It is best to transition to
a diet that is low in magnesium and phosphorus and that reduces the
pH of the urine.8

PURINE UROLITHIASIS (URATE AND
XANTHINE)
Epidemiology
Urate stones are the third most commonly reported cystoliths in
cats.1 Ammonium urate is the most common form of naturally
occurring purine urolith observed in cats, with ammonium hydrogen
urate being the most commonly identified form of urate urolithiasis.
Urate stones often are mixed with other mineral components
(typically struvite and CaOx), whereas 49.3% of urate stones are
composed solely of urate.5 Males appear to be at an increased risk,
but this could be because more stones are submitted from the male
population due to lower urinary obstruction.41 Most affected cats are
4-10 years of age, with the mean age of urate stone formers being

younger than other types of stone formers.5,41,42 The Ocicat has been
found to have a higher risk of urate stones compared to the Domestic
Shorthair (DSH), and Siamese, Birman, and Egyptian Mau breeds
historically have been overrepresented.5,41,42 Egyptian Maus seem to
be significantly younger compared to the other breeds.41

Pathophysiology and Diagnosis
Any form of severe hepatic dysfunction can predispose cats to
forming purine stones (ch. 266). While portosystemic shunts and
microvascular dysplasia (ch. 267) are well-known predisposing risk
factors in dogs, these are uncommon in cats with urate urolithiasis.
Uric acid is one of several biodegradation products of purine
nucleotide metabolism. Purines are first metabolized into
hypoxanthine and then converted into xanthine via the enzyme
xanthine dehydrogenase (XDH) (Figure 309.3). Xanthine is
further broken down by XDH into uric acid, which is converted into
allantoin by hepatic uricase and excreted renally. Defects in purine
metabolism can lead to increased renal excretion of xanthine, which
is moderately insoluble at any urine pH, and xanthine stone
formation does not correlate with USG.41,43 Defects in purine
metabolism that cause xanthinuria are rare in humans, cats, and
dogs. Xanthinuria in humans is an autosomal recessive condition; in
animals it is not well understood but has been described in cats in
several reports.43-46 Iatrogenic xanthinuria can occur secondary to
allopurinol administration, which inhibits XDH action and can lead
to xanthine urolithiasis. The presence of urate urolithiasis in cats
should prompt a complete evaluation of liver function and hepatic
vascular abnormalities.

Management
Surgical removal is the treatment of choice as there are limited
studies assessing the safety and efficacy of medical dissolution of
urate stones in cats. A protein-restricted alkalinizing diet is
recommended for prevention of recurrence. Canned food is
preferred, to increase moisture content, and diets designed for liver
disease (ch. 154) or kidney disease (ch. 159), which are typically

protein restricted, are recommended.18 Periodic abdominal
ultrasonography is recommended. Abdominal radiographs are not
recommended as these stones are typically radiolucent unless mixed
with another mineral component.

Uricase; XDH, xanthine dehydrogenase.

CYSTINE UROLITHIASIS
Epidemiology and Pathophysiology
Cystine stones and cystinuria (ch. 303) are rare in cats.1,47,48 They
are a result of a hereditary disorder that causes a defect in proximal
renal tubular reabsorption with subsequent increases in urinary
excretion of the amino acids cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine
(COLA).47,48 Feline cystinuria is caused by a missense mutation in
SLC3A1 or SLC7A9, as in humans and dogs.47 SLC3A1 and SLC7A9
encode rBAT and bo,+AT subunits, respectively, leading to
cystinuria.47 Three cats were found to be homozygous for a point
mutation in SLC7A9 (the c.881T>A SLC7A9 point variant), including
a Maine Coon, a Sphynx, and a DMH. All 3 cats developed cystine
stones after 1 year of age.47 In dogs, cystinuria is classified as either
autosomal recessive (I) or dominant (II), and further classified by
which mutation is present (A for SLC3A1 and B for SLC7A9). Type
III cystinuria is considered androgen-dependent and has yet to be
identified in cats.

Diagnosis
Cats with cystinuria may present with lower urinary tract signs;
however, they may not have cystine crystals or calculi.48 Urinary
nitroprusside and COLA testing have shown success in diagnosing

cats with cystinuria without crystalluria or lower urinary tract stones.
Cats with cystinuria may also present with neurologic abnormalities
(such as hypersalivation, lethargy, behavior changes, or seizures)
that are thought to be secondary to arginine deficiency.47,48 Affected
cats are unable to synthesize arginine, and reduced levels are thought
to be a combination of increased renal arginine excretion with
reduced intestinal absorption.47,49

Treatment
Efforts are aimed at improving water intake, reducing certain
proteins, increasing urinary pH ≥7.5 to increase solubility of cystine,
and to improve the efficacy of thiol drugs.48,50 Reducing dietary
protein intake helps reduce intake of cystine and methionine (found
in high quantities in animal proteins), as well as improving urinary
pH which often acidifies with high-protein diets.51 Alkalinized urine
can be obtained by supplementing potassium citrate (75 mg/kg PO
q12h) to achieve a urine pH >7.5. If the urine pH is already >7.5, this
medication is not recommended. Cystine-binding drugs are often
used in humans to help lower risk of cystine stone formation.
In dogs, type III cystinuria (androgen-dependent) is cured with
castration. This form of cystinuria has yet to be reported in cats, but
if cystinuria is identified in an intact male cat, castration should be
considered.

OTHER TYPES OF LOWER URINARY
STONES
Calcium phosphate (CP) urolithiasis makes up <1% of annual urinary
stone submissions in cats. The most common forms seen in cats are
hydroxyapatite and carbonate-apatite. Other less common forms
include Brushite (calcium hydrogen phosphate dihydrate),
Whitlockite (tricalcium orthophosphate), and octacalcium
phosphate.52 Apatite uroliths make up a small proportion of urolith
submissions and are often mixed with other mineral types (primarily
struvite). Apatite stones are more common in middle-aged female

cats, with no known breed predilection.5 Conditions that lead to
hypercalcemia, such as idiopathic hypercalcemia and primary
hyperparathyroidism, have been implicated in the formation of these
stones. Management is similar to preventing other stone types (e.g.,
increasing water intake and feeding a dissolution diet).
Dried solidified blood (DSB) stones make up 1.8% of urolith
submissions and are more commonly seen in middle-aged male
(84.7%) versus female (15.3%) cats. Bengals, Persians, and Domestic
Longhair cats are at risk.5 The pathogenesis of DSB formation is not
well understood, but hematuria (macroscopic or microscopic) is
thought to be a predisposing factor.5
Silica stones are the least common type of urinary stone in cats. A
majority of silica-containing stone submissions are from DSH cats;
however, given the limited quantity, it is difficult to accurately say
that this breed is at a higher risk.5 Recommendations for prevention
of this urolith type are not well established. Diets containing high
quantities of grains and corn gluten feed (which are high in silica)
are thought to be contributors, and water from volcanic regions has
been implicated due to its high level of silica. These sources of silica
could be reduced or avoided. In dogs, a diet low in vegetables and
higher in animal protein and moisture is recommended.53

PHYSIOLOGY OF MICTURITION
The primary purpose of the lower urinary tract is to store urine and to facilitate its elimination at an
appropriate time. The bladder stores urine 99% of the time and is in emptying phase only 1% of the time.
Coordination of storage and emptying requires a complex interaction between the somatic and
autonomic nervous systems, as well as normal function of the organs and tissues involved.
All 3 components of the peripheral nervous system are involved in the micturition cycle (Table
310.1). In addition, conscious voiding involves the lumbar and sacral spinal cord as well as the
brainstem and cerebral cortex.
During filling and storage, activation of stretch receptors in the bladder wall leads to a reflex arc that
increases urethral tone and relaxing the detrusor muscle via sympathetic pathways (Figure 310.1).
During initiation of micturition, stretch receptors send afferent signals along myelinated fibers of the
pelvic nerve to the lumbar spinal cord and cranial to the pontine micturition center in the brain. If the
situation is appropriate for urination, parasympathetic pathways are activated to stimulate bladder
smooth muscle contraction and parasympathetic signals are inhibited to relax the urethra (Figure
310.2). There is also a local urethral reflex arc that causes somatically mediated contraction of the
striated muscle surrounding the urethra in response to a sudden increase in abdominal pressure and
movement of urine into the urethra, such as during a cough or sneeze.

In addition to normal neurologic mechanisms, several other factors are important for the normal
function of the micturition cycle in dogs and cats. The integrity of the smooth muscle of the urethra,
normal urethral mucosa, associated vasculature, and the support of connective tissues are also key.1,2 In
females, estrogen appears to have a significant impact on these tissues.3,4 Its decline after spaying
(ovariohysterectomy) appears to play a role in urethral sphincter mechanism incompetence (USMI).5,6

DISORDERS OF STORAGE
Storage disorders primarily occur due to an inability to maintain adequate urethral tone in the face of
normal bladder pressures. These may result from an anatomic or developmental abnormality or
acquired dysfunction in the spinal cord, urinary bladder, or urethra and surrounding tissues. Congenital
abnormalities (ch. 313) such as ectopic ureters or urogenital sinus malformation can result in the
unconscious loss of urine in juveniles, while acquired urinary incontinence disorders including USMI,
lower motor neuron (LMN) bladder, and over-active bladder (OAB), may develop later in life (ch. 54).

URETHRAL SPHINCTER MECHANISM INCOMPETENCE
USMI is the most common storage disorder and cause of urinary incontinence in dogs.7 The urethral
sphincter mechanism involves the smooth muscle of the urethra as well as the surrounding support
tissues, submucosal vasculature, and urothelium. There is recent evidence that the prostate and
bulbocavernosus muscles may also contribute to continence in male dogs.8 USMI is thought to result
from the breakdown in this complex through reduced muscular responsiveness and tone, and changes in
the periurethral tissues. In female dogs, these changes appear to be associated with a reduction in
estrogen and increases in follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone after spaying, which
explains the term “hormone-responsive incontinence.”9,10 The pathophysiologic mechanism of its
development in castrated male dogs is poorly understood; however, increases in follicle stimulating and
luteinizing hormone levels have been documented in response to decreased testosterone levels.11,12
USMI is most common among spayed female dogs. It is less common in castrated males and rare in
intact male dogs and cats.12 It appears to affect up to 20% of spayed females and particularly large-breed
dogs (weighing >20 kg). Several breeds have been found to have an increased risk of developing USMI

including the Doberman Pinscher, Giant Schnauzer, Old English Sheepdog, Rottweiler, Weimaraner,
and Boxer, but any breed can be affected.13 Several studies have demonstrated an increased risk of
development of USMI in dogs spayed before 3 months of age.14,15 A more recent study indicated that the
larger the dog as an adult, the higher the risk of developing urinary incontinence if the dog is spayed
early.16 In other words, the larger the dog will be, the later she should be spayed. The relationship to
estrous cycle and timing of spay is still unclear. However, allowing the bitch to reach sexual maturity
may improve the robustness of the urethral sphincter mechanism.
Predisposing factors such as a pelvic bladder, short urethra, or recessed vulva may also be associated
with an increased risk of developing USMI; however, the presence of any of these does not necessarily
lead to incontinence. A reduction in pressure transmission from the abdomen to the proximal urethra
has the potential to lead to urinary incontinence in animals with a short urethra or pelvic bladder by
setting up a negative pressure gradient from the bladder to the urethra. The leakage of urine seen with a
recessed or “juvenile” vulva may be related to pooling of urine in the vestibule during urination, which
leaks out at a later time.

Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis
Urinary incontinence due to USMI often appears within a few years of neutering, but has a wide range of
age of onset. Dogs with USMI usually have normal bladder capacity and are able to urinate normally
with complete emptying of the bladder. While most of these dogs are otherwise healthy, clinical signs
can worsen dramatically if comorbidities develop, especially those leading to polyuria. In patients with
polyuric conditions, the increased volume of urine in the bladder may lead to increased pressure on the
already weakened sphincter mechanism, and leakage. Lower urinary tract infection (UTI, ch. 307) can
also increase clinical signs. It is suspected that USMI, and urinary incontinence of any cause, are
associated with increased risk of UTI; however, no studies have been conducted to fully evaluate this.
Owners often seek veterinary care when the frequency becomes bothersome, although in the author’s
experience, the incontinence may have been present for months or years. It is essential to establish that
the animal is passing urine unconsciously. Many owners will complain of “incontinence” when the
animal is in fact demonstrating submissive urination or is otherwise consciously urinating in
inappropriate places (ch. 11). Dogs with USMI may leak urine when recumbent, sleeping, or after
exertion. Although the passage of urine is involuntary, dogs may increase grooming of the perivulvar or
preputial area. USMI is an adult-onset condition, so questioning of the owner regarding the onset of
clinical signs is important. Animals that have been incontinent from birth or prior to neutering should
be assessed for congenital malformations such as ectopic ureters (ch. 313) prior to making a diagnosis
of USMI.
The physical examination (ch. 3) of animals with USMI is often normal, with the exception of
perivulvar or preputial urine staining. The conformation of the vulva and condition of perivulvar skin
should be noted. The presence of perivulvar dermatitis may increase the risk of UTI. Rectal examination
and palpation of the urethra are usually normal. Urination is observed to be normal and complete, with
little or no residual volume. The assessment of residual urine volume is essential in male dogs with
urinary incontinence to differentiate USMI from detrusor urethral dyssynergia, a disorder of incomplete
bladder emptying (see below).
The presence of urinary incontinence in an otherwise healthy neutered female dog that was previously
continent is often adequate for presumptive diagnosis of USMI and a trial of empirical therapy. Due to
its lower prevalence, intact female dogs, intact or neutered male dogs, and cats with similar histories and
clinical signs require additional evaluation before making a diagnosis of USMI.
A urinalysis and urine culture should be performed (ch. 70). The presence of isosthenuria or
hyposthenuria may contribute to severity of incontinence and necessitates additional evaluation for an
underlying cause. As noted above, the risk of UTI in animals with USMI has not been evaluated, but its
presence may lead to worsening signs. A complete blood count and serum biochemistry panel are not
essential for diagnosis of USMI, although they may be helpful when making treatment decisions, and are
important in evaluating animals with polyuria.
If anatomic abnormalities are suspected, imaging such as contrast radiography, abdominal
ultrasound, or contrast computed tomography is indicated. Cystoscopic evaluation of the lower urinary
tract may also be necessary to assess conformation of the lower urinary tract and vagina (ch. 100).
Advanced diagnostics such as urodynamic studies are designed to quantify the pressure produced along
the urethra and the compliance and detrusor function of the urinary bladder. These are available at

some referral institutions and may be indicated in patients with equivocal signs and poor response to
therapy.

Medical Treatment
Medical therapy of USMI is generally considered the first line of management; only after failure of or
intolerance to medical therapy are surgical options considered. Medical treatment of USMI in the
neutered female dog consists of increasing number and sensitivity of alpha-receptors in the urethral
sphincter with estrogen, or by stimulating those receptors with an alpha-agonist (Table 310.2).
The most commonly used estrogens are diethylstilbesterol (DES) and estriol (Incurin, Merck Animal
Health, Madison, NJ). Diethylstilbestrol is not available commercially so it must be compounded. Estriol
appears to have a higher response rate among female dogs than DES (89% and 65%, respectively).17,18
Adverse effects associated with estrogen use are dose-related and include mammary gland development,
vulvar swelling, and attractiveness to males.17 These usually subside with dosage reduction. A more
serious adverse event associated with estrogen use is irreversible bone marrow suppression,19 although
the dosages associated with bone marrow suppression are much higher than those recommended to
treat USMI. The author recommends performing a complete blood count before starting treatment with
an estrogen compound, to establish baseline values.
Phenylpropanolamine (PPA, Proin, Proin ER, PRN Pharmacal, Pensacola, FL) is the most widely used
alpha-agonist for the treatment of USMI. The dosage and frequency needed for each animal vary widely
and may need to be increased over time to maintain continence. Adverse effects associated with PPA
include restlessness, aggression, changes in sleeping patterns, and gastrointestinal signs. These are also
usually alleviated by a reduction in dosage or frequency.20,21 Clinical response to PPA administration
ranges from 75-90%.21,22 Frequently, both an estrogen and PPA are used in the same patient for severe
or refractory incontinence. There are anecdotal reports of greater improvement when used together, but
there is little published evidence to support a synergistic effect.23
PPA is also frequently used in male dogs and cats with USMI. In addition, neutered male dogs may be
treated with testosterone cypionate as monthly injections; however, its efficacy is not well documented.
Although male dogs with USMI are most responsive to PPA, it is at a rate of only 43%, which is much
lower than in females.12 Estrogen compounds should not be used in males due to the risk of prostatic
metaplasia. They are rarely used in cats, and care should be taken to monitor the mammary glands for
neoplasia in cats receiving estrogens.
A recent retrospective report of 10 spayed female dogs with adult-onset USMI indicated a good
response to oral methyltestosterone at a median dosage of 0.9 mg/kg once a day with few side-effects in
9/10 dogs.24 Six of the dogs remained continent after medication withdrawal. Further investigation of
this treatment is needed before it can be recommended.

Surgical and Interventional Treatment
In patients that fail medical therapy, it may be necessary to consider surgical intervention. Several
surgical procedures have been used to treat USMI, many to increase abdominal pressure transmission to
the proximal urethra. These include colposuspension, trans-obturator vaginal tape, and urethropexy.
Outcomes are variable and they are considered to have poor long-term efficacy, particularly in animals
with normal bladder position.25 The most promising and commonly performed surgical procedure for
USMI is placement of an artificial urethral sphincter (AUS), which may be adjusted via a subcutaneous
port (ch. 117). Recent studies have shown a significant increase in continence in male and female dogs
that underwent placement of an AUS after having failed medical therapy for USMI.26-28
Injectable periurethral bulking agents, primarily bovine cross-linked collagen, have been used for
increasing urethral pressure and narrowing the urethral lumen (ch. 117). In addition to the collagen, a
cross-linked gelatin agent has also recently become available.29 The minimally invasive nature of the
procedure is the primary benefit; however, the durability of continence is variable with a median of 17
months.30

LOWER MOTOR NEURON BLADDER

Incontinence as a disorder of storage can also occur secondary to spinal cord injury or disease (chs. 250,
251). Lesions in the S1-S2 region will lead to weakness of the striated muscular sphincter. Disruption of
the local reflex arc at these segments leads to an easily expressible bladder which may empty with minor
increases in abdominal pressure. Animals with a LMN bladder are identified by decreased anal tone and
a poor perineal reflex as well as their easily expressible bladder (ch. 241). Most affected animals are
unable to voluntarily void and require intermittent catheterization or manual expression by the owner.
Correction of the underlying lesion may lead to some return to normal function. Because of the tendency
to have incomplete emptying of the bladder with manual expression, affected animals are at increased
risk of developing UTIs and appropriate surveillance must be in place. The muscarinic agonist
bethanechol has been used in these patients to increase detrusor contraction; however, the evidence for
its efficacy remains controversial.31,32

DETRUSOR HYPERREFLEXIA/OVER-ACTIVE BLADDER
Detrusor hyperreflexia/OAB is the most common form of urinary incontinence in people, but it has been
poorly characterized in companion animals. The true incidence of OAB and its importance as a cause of
urinary incontinence in dogs and cats is unknown. In people it is characterized by sudden urgency to
urinate and involuntary evacuation of urine associated with bursts of detrusor contractions at bladder
volumes far below capacity. In dogs it may manifest as loss of bladder compliance and capacity, causing
a need to urinate more often without polyuria or inflammation of the lower urinary tract. OAB may be a
cause of treatment failure in some dogs treated for presumed USMI, and should be considered in these
cases. The diagnosis of OAB in animals can be challenging and it is only definitively made using
urodynamic studies such as cystometrography. Response to therapy with anti-muscarinic drugs is often
used to presumptively diagnose OAB in animals. The most commonly used of these include oxybutynin
and imipramine, the latter of which also has alpha-agonist effects that potentially could increase
urethral sphincter tone. Adverse effects of these medications include gastrointestinal abnormalities such
as diarrhea and constipation, as well as parasympatholytic signs like tachycardia and hyposalivation.

DISORDERS OF EMPTYING
The inability to completely empty the bladder during a normal void can result from either a functional or
a mechanical obstruction of the outflow tract and urethra, or an abnormality of the detrusor muscle that
impairs its contraction. Overflow incontinence can result from the lack of complete emptying, often
when the animal is at rest. An owner may not be able to differentiate this from an animal with a storage
disorder (e.g., USMI), and it is up to the clinician to determine the underlying process so that
appropriate therapy can be instituted. Inability to completely empty the bladder is a risk factor for UTI,
and these animals should be monitored for infection.

DETRUSOR ATONY
Complete emptying of the urinary bladder is dependent on the normal contraction of the detrusor
muscle. In the normal animal, the bladder relaxes during filling with only small increases in intravesical
pressure. As the bladder continues to fill, the pressure increases to a threshold that triggers detrusor
contraction and emptying. Loss of adequate detrusor contraction can result from neurogenic or nonneurogenic abnormalities. Injury to the sacral spinal cord (S1-S3) or pelvic nerves can lead to bladder
atony, and is often associated with weakened urethral tone. Affected animals often have decreased
perineal reflexes and easily expressed bladders (LMN bladder). Treatment of the underlying lesion if
possible may lead to improved voiding function. However, until normal function returns, careful
management of urination must be followed. Male dogs are manually expressed or aseptically
catheterized (ch. 98) 2-4 times a day either in the hospital or at home, and cats and female dogs are
often manually expressed.
Direct damage to the detrusor muscle can occur from over-distension due to mechanical or functional
outflow obstruction of acute or chronic nature. The muscle fibers of the detrusor transmit action
potentials (that initiate contraction) via tight junctions. With over-distension, these tight junctions are
interrupted, leading to an absent or ineffective contraction. The over-distension may be acute, as with
obstructive feline idiopathic cystitis in a male cat, or chronic, as in a dog with a functional obstruction of
the urethra. Relief of the obstruction and maintenance of a small bladder volume for up to 2 weeks may
allow the junctions to reestablish and the return of coordinated detrusor function. This is usually
managed by either indwelling or frequent sterile catheterization of the bladder (ch. 98). Bethanechol
may be used in these patients to enhance stimulation of the detrusor contraction since the pelvic nerve is
intact. Other medications that have been shown to enhance detrusor function are cisapride and
metoclopramide, although the individual response varies widely.33,34 It is essential that relief of any
urethral obstruction, functional or mechanical, be attained before starting medical therapy to enhance
detrusor contraction.

FUNCTIONAL URETHRAL OUTFLOW OBSTRUCTION
Functional urethral outflow obstruction (FOO), or detrusor urethral dyssynergy, arises from an
abnormality in the reflex arc that should normally allow the urethral sphincter to relax at the initiation
of urination. The lesion is thought to be in the reticulospinal tract, Onuf’s nucleus, or the caudal
mesenteric ganglion, and likely involves the loss of inhibitory signals to the pudendal and hypogastric
nerves.35 It is unknown if injuries to peripheral nerves, neuromuscular junctions, or smooth or striated
muscular sphincters are also involved.36 Unlike the “upper motor neuron (UMN) bladder” seen in
animals with thoracolumbar intervertebral disc disease and other spinal cord lesions (chs. 250, 251),
these animals typically have an otherwise normal neurologic examination (ch. 241).
The disorder affects primarily middle-aged, large- and giant-breed male dogs, although female dogs
and cats can be affected. One case series of 22 dogs reported a mean age of 4.9 years.37 Clinical signs are
similar to those of mechanical obstruction. The animal often postures to urinate and is able to produce a
urine stream that quickly becomes attenuated or stops completely. The animal may continue to posture
to urinate or make several attempts without fully emptying the bladder (

Video 310.1). The retention

of large amounts of residual urine typically leads to overflow incontinence and may be mistaken for
USMI. This leakage can occur because the hypertonicity of the involved sphincter is often dynamic and
is triggered by the act of voiding. In chronic cases, bladder over-distension and subsequent atony may

develop. Unlike animals with mechanical obstruction, dogs with FOO are typically easy to catheterize
and contrast urethrography may be normal or reveal areas of narrowing of the urethra (urethrospasm).
A presumptive diagnosis of FOO is often made by observing the dog urinate with a typical interrupted
pattern, documentation of a large residual urine volume, easy passage of a urinary catheter, and ruling
out of a mechanical obstruction. Normal residual urine volumes in 48 normal dogs have been reported
to be 0.1-3.4 mL/kg body weight with a mean of 0.2 mL/kg.38 The author uses <1 mL/kg as a general
guideline. Ultrasonography is recommended to assess the ureters and renal pelves for dilation secondary
to chronic obstruction and ureterorenal reflux of urine.
Treatment of the hypertonic urethral sphincter generally consists of alpha-adrenergic blockade with
prazosin, an alpha1-specific antagonist with demonstrated effects on both the internal and external
urethral sphincters.39 Tamsulosin, which is specific for the alpha1A subtype found in the internal
urethral sphincter, has also been successful in these dogs. Some dogs will require additional therapy if
the striated muscle is more significantly affected. Benzodiazepines, such as diazepam, or other skeletal
muscle relaxants, including acepromazine and methocarbamol, may be more effective if the external
urethral sphincter is involved. Diazepam is typically administered 30 minutes before voiding to decrease
external urethral sphincter pressure. Dantrolene and baclofen have been used in the past as skeletal
muscle relaxants; however, the potential for adverse effects has decreased their use in small animal
patients.39,40 In severe and refractory cases, intermittent sterile catheterization by the owner at home
may be necessary (ch. 98). Medical therapy of associated bladder atony should only be started after
adequate relief of the functional urethral obstruction has been reached (Table 310.3). Close monitoring
of these patients for residual urine volume and UTI is needed to assess efficacy of treatment and prevent
complications.
The prognosis for recovery of normal voiding is good, but most dogs will require lifelong therapy for
FOO. Attempts to taper medications to the lowest effective dosage may be hampered by relapse of
clinical signs after months of normal voiding.37 The prognosis appears to be worse in patients with
bladder atony or UTI secondary to urine retention. Anecdotally, urethral stenting may improve clinical
signs; however, this is considered a salvage procedure with several potential complications, and is
indicated only in the most refractory of cases.

UPPER MOTOR NEURON BLADDER
Neurogenic functional urethral obstruction is generally caused by spinal cord lesions cranial to the
sacral segment (Figures 310.1, 310.2). This leads to loss of inhibitory signals to the hypogastric and
pudendal nerves, and this loss prevents sphincter relaxation upon voiding. This is the classic “UMN
bladder,” in which the patient is unable to urinate normally and where the bladder is difficult to express
manually. The most commonly affected dogs are those with intervertebral disc disease and associated
paresis or paralysis. These animals typically have additional neurologic deficits including paresis and
nociceptive loss (ch. 250). Treatment of the underlying lesion typically leads to partial or complete
return to normal voiding function after days to weeks. Until normal voiding resumes, the patients are
managed as for FOO, with alpha-adrenergic blockade and manual expression or catheterization.
Monitoring for over-distension and UTI is critical in these patients, as is nursing care since the overflow
incontinence that can accompany this process may lead to skin breakdown in these recumbent animals.
