INTRODUCTION
Feline idiopathic/interstitial cystitis (FIC) is the most common cause
of chronic lower urinary tract signs (cLUTS), which includes variable
combinations of straining, hematuria, pollakiuria, and periuria, in

domestic cats.1 Cats showing these signs have been referred to as
having “feline idiopathic/interstitial cystitis” only because of their
similarities to humans with interstitial cystitis (IC; now sometimes
referred to as bladder pain syndrome/interstitial cystitis). IC is
characterized clinically by difficult, painful, and frequent urinations
without a diagnosable cause, and often a variety of comorbid health
problems.2
FIC was once classified as a “feline lower urinary tract disorder”
(FLUTD)3 because cats present with cLUTS. FIC does not seem to
originate in the bladder, however. Just as jaundice can present as a
dermatologic or ophthalmic sign, it is neither a dermatologic nor
ophthalmic disorder. Research has identified genetic factors,
epigenetic effects, and environmental influences associated with risk
for (F)IC, documented that comorbid disorders often occur before
the onset of the lower urinary tract signs (LUTS), and demonstrated
how much systemic involvement can be present in these patients.1
One of us (CATB) has proposed the term “Pandora syndrome” to
describe the multiple health problems present in some of these cats
(as in people with chronic overlapping pain conditions), because it
does not identify any specific cause or organ, and tries to capture the
dismay and dispute associated with the identification of so many
problems outside the organ of interest of any particular
subspecialty.4
Regardless of the name eventually applied to this syndrome, we
urge clinicians and investigators to look beyond the bladder when
obtaining a history, performing physical examinations, and
considering pertinent diagnostics and treatments to manage the
clinical signs of their patients. To avoid confusion, we will refer to
this syndrome here as FIC, because it is the term used in most
published studies.
We currently perceive FIC to describe abnormalities resulting from
persistent activation of the central threat response system (CTRS).1
Persistent activation of the CTRS can occur when chronic perception
of threat exceeds the cat’s perception of control. This mobilizes
persistent activity in variable combinations of the nervous (sensory,
autonomic, and motor), endocrine, and immune systems, which can

eventually also affect the cat’s behavior, as well as bladder, skin,
gastrointestinal tract, and other organ function.5
The variability among individual cats’ responses to chronic
perception of threat may result from familial differences in organspecific vulnerability, and to the intensity of exposure to threatening
events that can durably sensitize the CTRS to the environment.
Sufficiently harsh events can sensitize the CTRS at any time of life,
but such events often occur early in life, even before birth, when the
CTRS is most plastic and vulnerable to the events via stress hormone
signals communicated to the fetus through the placenta by its
mother.6 Our current understanding of FIC is informed by
knowledge gained from studies of cats and people with the naturally
occurring disorder, and of induced models in rodents.

ETIOPATHOGENESIS OF FIC
RECENT STUDIES—CATS
A review of the pathophysiology and management of cats with cLUTS
was published in 2019.1 More recently, Kaul et al.,7 reported on the
recurrence rate and long-term course of 101 cats that were presented
for evaluation of cLUTS from 2010 to 2013 based on telephone
interviews using a questionnaire with cat owners. They reported that
52 cats were diagnosed with FIC, 21 with urolithiasis, and 13 with
bacterial urinary tract infection (UTI); no definitive diagnosis was
made for 15 cats. Of the 86 cats with a known diagnosis, the
recurrence rate, defined as recurrence of clinical signs following a
disease-free interval of at least 10 days after the previous episode,
was 58%. No significant difference in recurrence rate was identified
between the 3 groups (FIC, urolithiasis, or bacterial UTI). Twentyone cats (42%) had 1 relapse, 12 (24%) had 2 relapses, 10 (20%) had
3, and 7 cats (14%) had 4 to 8 relapses within a median observation
period of 38 months (range 0.5-138 months). Fourteen cats (28%)
suffered from different causes of LUTS during different episodes.
The mortality due to LUTS among all 101 cats was 5%.
Fourteen of the 50 cats (28%) with recurring LUTS episodes were
diagnosed with different etiologies at different episodes; the most
common combination of diagnoses in these cats was FIC and

urolithiasis. Although limited by recall bias and a lack of statistical
power, the study demonstrated that recurrent episodes of LUTS in
affected cats can occur commonly, and cannot be assumed to result
from the same etiology. It is worth recalling that Osborne et al., listed
some 30 possible causes of LUTS, from anatomical anomalies to
toxins, nearly 40 years ago.3

RECENT STUDIES—HUMANS AND
OTHER ANIMALS
Humans
IC in people recently has been classified as a “chronic overlapping
pain condition” by the National Institutes of Health,8 as
“nociplastic”9 and “chronic primary pain”10 by the International
Association for the Study of Pain, and as “centralized pain” by the
Multi-Disciplinary Approach to the Study of Chronic Pelvic Pain.11
All of these terms describe pain primarily originating from the
patient’s central nervous system (CNS).11 This change from a
“nociceptive” to a “nociplastic” perspective resulted from a paradigm
shift in understanding of chronic pain, which is now conceptualized
as resulting from variable combinations of nociplastic, neuropathic,
nociceptive, and mixed sensory input conveying danger (in the
presence or absence of tissue damage) to the CNS.12
CNSs receive constant input from external “envirosensors”
(auditory, gustatory, olfactory, somatosensory, and visual) and from
internal sensors throughout the body.13 Brodal14 recently suggested
the term homeoceptor rather than nociceptor to describe small
sensory fibers based on their response patterns to a variety of
environmental stimuli, and because nociceptive activity is neither
necessary nor sufficient to evoke pain (although it is required to
protect the body from injury15). Moreover, no innate properties of
nociceptive fibers endow them, and only them, with the capacity to
evoke pain.16

After variable excitatory and inhibitory processing in the spinal
cord,16 information from the periphery is transmitted to the brain.
Very early in life,17 animals begin to integrate these inputs with their
contexts to manage subsequent interactions with the world. This
integration permits the animal to develop some form of anticipation
of sensory input. The resulting system has been described as
“predictive processing (or coding)”18 and “interactivist.”19
Regardless of the process, sensory information reaching the brain is
integrated into a “decision” that forms the basis for subsequent
action, whether or not it is consciously perceived. At its most basic,
the CNS “decides” whether to continue with the present course of
interaction with the world, or to change course. Depending on the
salience of the message for the individual’s action and motivation,
threatening messages can change the course of behavior to
withdrawal and avoidance.20
Acutely dangerous, threatening situations can activate flight, fight,
or freeze reactions, which can suppress the pain of injuries in the
service of survival.21,22 In contrast, persistent exposure, particularly
to toxic levels of threat, can exacerbate rather than suppress chronic
pain symptoms.23 If the animal “learns” that withdrawal and
avoidance occur most efficiently in the presence of signals from a
particular source in the body, pain may be perceived to arise from
this source even when the threat is external to the body.4 Thus, pain
is a decision a brain makes to protect animals from threat, whatever
the source.23

Other Animals
FIC in cats has limitations as a model of IC in humans.24 Acquiring
affected cats depends on both veterinarian and owner cooperation,
and such cats are more expensive to maintain in laboratory animal
facilities than are rodents, are outbred, and lack many of the
molecular research tools available for rodents. For these reasons,
stress models of IC recently have been developed in rodents,
including water avoidance25 and early life stressors,26 to investigate

effects of environmental threats on visceral function, nociception,
anxiety, and depression.27
Water-avoidance stress (WAS) has been used for investigating
mechanisms of visceral pain associated with IC in adult rats.28-30
Briefly, WAS is induced by placing rats predisposed to anxiety on
pedestals in the center of tanks filled with water at room temperature
for an hour a day for 10 consecutive days. This stressor induces some
of the same histopathologic and clinical features of (F)IC, including
urothelial disruption, angiogenesis, mast cell infiltration, and
increased urinary frequency, but not in the frequency of non-voiding
contractions during cystometry under anesthesia. Lower hind paw
withdrawal thresholds and increased withdrawal responses to
suprapubic stimulation, which persisted for more than a month, also
have been reported.29
Adverse early life experiences appear to be more common in
people31 and cats32 with (F)IC than in healthy controls. Adverse
early life experience models, including maternal separation33 and
limited nest materials,33,34 recently have been used for investigating
effects of environmental threats on visceral function, nociception,
anxiety, and depression. After reviewing the effects of exposure of
healthy neonatal rodents to various stressors on chronic visceral
pain, Greenwood-Van Meerveld and Johnson33 concluded that
chronic stress early in life can result in gene × environment
interactions. Such interactions can induce epigenetically mediated
changes in neuronal circuitry, leading to neuroplasticity and
increased expression of pro-nociceptive neurotransmitters in the
CNS of affected individuals. This mechanism also has been described
for sensitization of the CTRS in patients with (F)IC.6

MANIFESTATIONS/SIGNS OF FIC IN
THE HOME ENVIRONMENT
As mentioned, FIC typically presents with a variety of LUTS,
including dysuria, stranguria, pollakiuria, hematuria and periuria.35

Cat owners may not be familiar with the signs of painful urination or
their cats’ normal urinary habits (e.g., frequency of urination,
amount of urine typically produced by cats). Some owners may
mistake FIC for spraying or marking behavior (ch. 11). Questions
about the frequency, location, positioning of urination (e.g., vertical
versus horizontal surface) can help rule out urine (spray) marking.36
Owners are often motivated to present the cat for medical
assessment when they observe blood in the urine or when the cat
starts urinating outside the litter box. Other signs associated with
stress, such as overgrooming (especially of the caudal ventral
abdomen and inner thighs), hiding, and biting or scratching, may be
overlooked.37 Because of FIC’s intermittent nature, with signs that
wax and wane, owners may mistakenly believe that the problem has
resolved, until another episode of FIC occurs, often triggered by
stressful situations in the environment.36

DIAGNOSIS1
We take several factors into consideration, including the number of
episodes the cat has had, the severity of the cat’s clinical signs
(including comorbidities), and the financial resources of the owner.1
No sensitive, specific, and clinically available test currently exists to
diagnose FIC, so the diagnosis rests on signalment; history,
including inclusion of cat and known environmental risk factors;
exclusion of other (common) causes of LUTS; and response to
therapy (Figure 311.1).

RESPONSE TO MEMO
Most middle-aged cats with cLUTS are eventually diagnosed with
FIC,38,39 so we often begin by offering multimodal environmental
modification (MEMO)40 for FIC and monitoring the cat’s response.
We watch carefully for a positive response to support the diagnosis of
FIC, particularly if the owner has financial constraints and declines
additional diagnostic testing (e.g., urinalysis, imaging).

ABDOMINAL RADIOGRAPHS
If the cat does not improve, or if clinical signs return within days to
weeks despite implementation of appropriate MEMO, we
recommend abdominal radiography because the next most common
differential in cats with cLUTS is urinary stone disease (ch. 309).
Abdominal radiographs that include the entire urinary system from
the cranial pole of the right kidney to beyond the end of the distal
urethra help detect radiopaque stones; approximately 20% of cats
with LUTS have bladder stones.7

URINALYSIS AND URINE CULTURE
A urinalysis (ch. 70) and bacterial culture and sensitivity of urine
should be evaluated at least once in cats with cLUTS if possible, but
most young, otherwise healthy cats do not have a true bacterial
cystitis. Furthermore, there is no evidence to support culture of the
urine after urinary catheter removal from cats with obstructive FIC
unless clinical signs have returned or progressed.41 We do not
recommend antimicrobial therapy unless the cat has LUTS in
association with a positive urine culture collected by cystocentesis.

FIGURE 311.1 A decision-making algorithm for
diagnosis and assessment of feline
idiopathic/interstitial cystitis (FIC) and treatment
protocols. CKD, Chronic kidney disease; LUTS, lower

urinary tract signs; PU/PD, polyuria/polydipsia;
USG, urine specific gravity; UTI, urinary tract
infection.

ADVANCED DIAGNOSTIC TESTING
Advanced diagnostic tests, such as contrast cystourethrography,
abdominal ultrasonography, and even cystoscopy (ch. 100), can be
performed in recurrent cases to assess for other diseases that could
account for recurrent clinical signs. These are rarely required or
performed in cats suspected of having an initial episode of FIC.

MANAGEMENT
EMPOWERING THE CLIENT
A diagnosis of FIC means that a potentially threat-responsive
disorder has been identified and, to whatever extent is possible,
other causes for the signs have been excluded. In the authors’
experience, the most important determinant of a successful outcome
for cats with FIC is effective client communication.42 Clinicians can
demonstrate empathy by listening carefully to the client’s description
of the history, and (often frustrated) story of the effects of having a
cat with FIC on clients’ lives, provide a satisfactory explanation for
the sources of the signs, express care and concern for the situation,
and enhance the client’s perception of control (ch. 1). Effective
doctor-patient interactions seem to enhance patient adherence to
treatments and quality-of-life outcomes of therapy.43 Any therapies
that are appropriate to the presenting manifestations can then be
prescribed, and when possible, the client can be introduced to a
trained technician or other staff member trained to care for cats with
FIC. These team members can coach the client to choose and
implement aspects of MEMO that are most likely to benefit the
patient. The formality of this introduction is intended to demonstrate
that the veterinarian understands the situation, intends to sustain
the partnership with the client through technical support staff to gain
control of the patient’s clinical signs, and maintain vigilance for
recurrences, which may occur due to different causes.

PHARMACOLOGICAL TREATMENT
To the authors’ knowledge, no studies to date have found that
medications commonly used for managing FIC (prednisolone,
chloramphenicol, pentosan polysulfate sodium, propantheline,
meloxicam, and prazosin) are effective in treatment or prevention (as
reviewed in44). There have been few randomized, double-blind,
placebo-controlled studies,38 and generally, research is lacking.
Many cats with FIC recover within a few days without such
treatment. Newer generation nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
such as robenacoxib are considered safer for cats, with fewer
concerns about kidney damage,45 but again, studies demonstrating
their efficacy in treating FIC are lacking. For welfare concerns, shortterm analgesia (e.g., buprenorphine46) is considered a critical part of
treatment for acute clinical signs of FIC (ch. 6). Otherwise,
treatment is best left to the clinician’s experience and judgment until
information from research provides stronger evidence.
Finally, it is worth noting that although there has been limited
testing for their use in cats with FIC, selective serotonin reuptake
inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressants are effective for some cats
exhibiting anxiety,47 and may be appropriate for cats having
frequent recurrence of FIC.48 The use of psychopharmaceuticals is a
complex issue, which should also factor in the risk of the cat losing
its home or life to euthanasia. Other considerations include the
owner’s ability to pay for ongoing medication, the ability of the
owner to medicate the cat without causing further stress, and the
efficacy of other treatments such as MEMO.

MEMO (MULTIMODAL
ENVIRONMENTAL MODIFICATION):
PREVENTION AND TREATMENT
The goal of MEMO is to address the underlying causes of FIC by
increasing a cat’s sense of control while decreasing its perception of
threat. An effective application of MEMO requires a thorough

assessment of an individual cat’s environment, considering a cat’s
history and temperament, and the resources available to the client
(Figure 311.2). An assessment can provide veterinary professionals
with a starting point for a discussion of the cat’s environment and
changes that may need to be made. Because MEMO may also be
effective in preventing health and behavioral problems, it is advised
to make this assessment part of the onboarding process for new
clients, which veterinary technicians can be trained to do. Clients can
also fill out the assessment at home prior to their appointment.
Multiple environmental and relationship factors can contribute to
a cat’s perception of threat, and therefore a potential diagnosis of
FIC. These factors can include such things as changes in a cat’s
routine, competition over resources, frustration, boredom, lack of
socialization, and lack of control during social interactions. There are
several guides available that describe the environmental needs of
domestic cats (especially those housed exclusively indoors). These
include the American Association of Feline Practitioners (AAFP) and
International Society of Feline Medicine Feline Environmental
Needs Guidelines, which include the Five Pillars of a Healthy Feline
Environment (a sense of safety, multiple and separated key
resources, play and outlets for predatory behavior, positive cathuman interactions, and a respect for a cat’s sense of smell; available
at https://catvets.com/guidelines/practiceguidelines/environmental-needs-guidelines).49 Other
publicly accessible resources include the AAFP’s Cat Friendly Homes
(https://catfriendly.com), Fear Free Happy Homes
(https://www.fearfreehappyhomes.com), and the Indoor Pet
Initiative (https://indoorpet.osu.edu/cats).

THE LITTER BOX
The litter box setup should be thoroughly explored with the client to
make sure it suits the cat’s needs. There need to be enough litter
boxes in the home for the number of cats (1 per cat plus 1), and boxes
should be in separate locations, not placed side by side. Boxes need
to be scooped at least once a day. Although some cats are tolerant of
various litter substrates, most cats prefer an unscented, sandy,

clumping-style litter.50 When non-traditional litters (e.g., pellets,
crystals, food-based litters) are used, they should be offered as a
choice and the cat’s preferences should be respected. Boxes should
be large, open, accessible, and easy to enter (Figure 311.3),
considering any cat-related factors (e.g., age, weight, mobility) that
might make modifications of the litter boxes necessary (e.g., lower
sides).
The potential stress of an inadequate litter box setup is often
overlooked. Litter boxes are often too few, small, and dirty, and not
placed in locations that provide the cat with a sense of safety. Litter
boxes in closets, basements, cabinets, and other enclosures are
popular with cat owners, but can be problematic for cats. As a
consequence, cats may forgo their use and retain urine for longer
than ideal, urinating larger amounts less frequently,51 or seek
alternative locations for elimination.52

FIGURE 311.2 An example of a questionnaire that
can be used with clients to assess a cat’s environment
and to help determine changes that may be
recommended.
Cats with a history of FIC may feel pain during voiding and can
quickly learn to associate that pain with the litter box. In some cases,
offering a novel litter box setup may be helpful, in addition to
appropriate pain control. Changes could include a new box, a
different substrate, or a different location, recognizing that any
change should be introduced as a choice, rather than immediately

replacing old litter boxes. If the cat prefers the new litter setup, other
boxes can be gradually switched or eliminated.
Because cats with FIC may be more affected by environmental
stimuli53 than other cats, they also may be less tolerant of dirty or
otherwise poorly maintained litter boxes. It is never appropriate to
assume that because a cat used the box before, the cat will do so in
the future. Just as stressful events may trigger a bout of FIC, they
may trigger changes in litter box behavior.

FURTHER AREAS TO EXPLORE WITH
CLIENTS
The answers to these questions, which are highly individual, may
provide clues to sources of stress that can be addressed as part of a
treatment/management plan.

FIGURE 311.3 A litter box made from a modified
storage bin (entry way added for accessibility)
provides cats with a space to eliminate that is large
and open.

General Temperament
Is the cat fearful or anxious in the home? Does the cat spend a lot of
time hiding (closets, under bed) or seeking refuge in elevated areas?
Conversely, is the cat overly demanding or needy for attention? Does
the cat engage in species-typical behaviors throughout the day (e.g.,
eating, eliminating, scratching, playing) or only at night when the
home is quiet?

History
Was the cat subjected to any potentially adverse early life
experiences, such as premature maternal separation,54 declawing,55
or rehoming/shelter stay?

Health Problems
Does the cat have any health problems that may contribute to its
stress? For example, obese cats or cats with degenerative joint
disease may have difficulty playing or accessing safe areas.

Safety
Does the cat have acceptable choices as to where it can retreat from
human activity, dogs, other cats, and children, if it likes? Do
resources allow the cat to have a vantage point to see if anyone is
approaching?

Resources
Are there adequate resources (feeding and watering areas, litter
boxes, scratching posts) to support the number of cats in the home?
Are the resources clumped or distributed throughout the house? If
necessary, the client can be asked to draw a rough map of the layout
of the home and the cat’s resources so the client and the veterinarian
can assess together whether there might be congested areas, or
challenges for the cat to safely access what it needs.

Household Routine
A lack of predictability in the environment and the owner’s daily
routine can be a source of stress for some cats. Activities such as
feeding, cleaning, play and social interactions should be offered as a
routine (to whatever extent is possible). Cats may need time to adjust
to changes.

FIGURE 311.4 An example of an enclosure (a
catio) designed to give indoor cats safe and
controlled access to the outdoors.

Social Relationships (Animal and Human)
Is the cat comfortable with every person or other animal in the
home? If not, who does the cat have a positive relationship with?
Who does the cat have an antagonistic relationship with? Who is the
cat neutral/indifferent toward? How do the humans in the home feel
about the cat? Does the cat enjoy being handled? If not, how do the
owners respond?

Enrichment/Cognitive Challenge
Is the cat’s environment adequately stimulating without being
overwhelming? What type of enrichment and activities is the cat
provided with? For example, can the cat be fed from food puzzles?56
Is enrichment provided that appeals to all of the cat’s senses (e.g.,
olfactory,57 tactile, auditory)?

Activity
Is the cat provided with any type of interactive play? Does the cat
enjoy playing on its own or with other animals in the home? Does the
cat have climbing opportunities (e.g., cat furniture or shelving)?

Safe Outdoor Access
Does the cat have access to safe, outside time, such as through
harness training, a stroller or a catio (enclosure, Figure 311.4)? If
the cat is allowed to roam outside, is the environment safe? Are there
other animals? Does the cat frequently get into confrontations or
fights with other animals? If the cat is indoors only, are outdoor
animals observed in the yard?

Provision of Choice
Are environmental changes (e.g., new food, new litter) introduced as
a choice? Does the cat have the option to avoid handling if it so
chooses? Does the owner understand basic feline body language that
indicates irritation or overstimulation from petting or other human
interactions?

Training and Use of Punishment
What methods does the owner use to attempt to modify or correct
undesirable behaviors? Punishment (physical, verbal, spray bottles,
etc.) should be avoided as it is associated with increased stress and
fear and decreased welfare.58,59 Does the owner engage in any type
of positive reinforcement training to reward desirable behaviors? For

cats who are easily frustrated, training may provide impulse
control60 and can be used for rewarding calm behaviors.58

Low-Stress Handling
Medical treatments can be stressful. Treatments and grooming
should be low-stress to whatever extent is possible. Owners should
be directed to (provided with?) appropriate resources, including the
use of compounded medication, gel caps, pre-veterinary visit
medication, and training cats to cooperate in their treatment
(“cooperative care”61).

AFTER THE ASSESSMENT:
APPLICATION OF MEMO
It is likely that almost every cat’s home environment could be
improved in some manner, but it is important to not provide clients
with a huge list of changes that they need to implement immediately.
Although research has found that environmental changes can
improve outcomes for cats with FIC,62 studies have not controlled
for any specific form of modification, meaning that
recommendations should be tailored to the cat and owner. We offer
clients a few suggestions for changes and encourage them to start
with one or two. This reduces the risk of overwhelming the cat or the
client with too many changes too quickly.42 Ideally, the initial
recommendations for change are made based on what is most likely
to impact a cat’s sense of threat/control, and on the owner’s time and
capabilities. The goals for MEMO should be to decrease the cat’s
perception of threat, increase its sense of control, and subsequently
increase the time that the cat is free of clinical signs. Recurrence in
FIC cats is common, but MEMO can reduce both the severity and
frequency of future episodes.62
Following up with the client on a regular basis (every few weeks
until improvement or resolution) is recommended for multiple
reasons:

• To provide the client with ongoing encouragement to continue
with the plan
• To answer any clarifying questions
• To troubleshoot or change the plan if there is no or little
improvement
• To use feedback to determine the feasibility and efficacy of
different recommendations for future clients
Additional support beyond an initial consultation will give the
client and cat the best chance of success. Support can be offered via
phone call, email, or text, depending on the preferences of the clinic
and client. In complex or refractory cases, referral to a specialty
hospital for advanced diagnostic tests, or to a veterinary behaviorist,
may be in the cat’s best interest.

ADDITIONAL APPROACHES TO FIC
Clients may inquire about alternatives to medications or MEMO for
FIC, such as nutraceuticals, cannabidiol (CBD), pheromone sprays or
collars, or dietary changes. To date, there are no studies
demonstrating the efficacy of nutraceuticals or CBD for cats with
FIC. A study evaluating the use of synthetic feline pheromone
analogue (Feliway) or placebo for 9 cats with a history of FIC found
no statistically significant differences between groups in days with
clinical signs.64 Data to support the efficacy of dietary changes or
veterinary diets in treating or preventing FIC are limited. Moreover,
a cat’s FIC signs improve without implementation of any diet
changes,62,65,66 and as 1 author recently concluded, “Given the
paucity of data, it is only possible to speculate about the ideal food
composition in the treatment and prevention of FIC.”67
Although not a treatment per se, there are several litters and litter
additives on the market that claim to provide early hematuria
detection (e.g., Blucare, Pretty Litter). When used properly, these
products may allow cat owners to seek treatment or identify triggers
for a recurrence of FIC, but empirical evidence of their efficacy and
accuracy is lacking.

TREATMENT AND OUTLOOK FOR CATS
WITH FIC
Environmental stressors (multi-cat households, lack of resources,
lack of a vantage point, use of non-clumping litter, dietary changes,
barren and threatening environments) and cat-related factors
(obesity, nervous disposition) have been associated with FIC and
sickness behaviors.65,68-71 Studies have also demonstrated that
making environmental changes (MEMO) to address the environment
and needs of an individual cat is effective in resolving FIC and litter
box avoidance (which may be undiagnosed FIC).62,66
A more recent study found that most cats with periuria who were
surrendered to an animal shelter were successfully adopted into
homes, and their return and euthanasia rates were low.72 These cats
were provided with a litter substrate trial in the shelter and all cats
successfully used the litter box before being placed for adoption. This
further demonstrates the sensitivity to context and the potential
effectiveness of environmental changes for cats presenting with
potential signs of FIC (although it should be noted that due to
constraints of shelter finances, diagnostic tests performed on the cats
in the study were minimal).
In short, for cats with FIC, the outlook is good if owners are
provided with support and are given information to help make
appropriate changes to improve their cat’s environment. When
presented with a cat who is suffering from FIC, the immediate goals
may be to provide appropriate pain relief and reduce the days a cat
has clinical signs. The long-term goals are to maintain the human-cat
bond, while improving quality of life for both the cat and owner.

Chapter 312: Urethral
Disorders
Julie K. Byron

A C RO N YM S
USMI urethral sphincter mechanism incompetence
UTI urinary tract infection

Urethral diseases are fairly common in dogs and cats and are often
related to, or an extension of, disorders of the bladder. There are
several types of disease that are specific to the urethra, however, and
they may or may not have impact on the rest of the lower urinary
tract. Clinical signs of urethral disease are similar to other lower
urinary tract disorders and include urinary incontinence, urine
retention, stranguria, pollakiuria, hematuria, poor urine stream, and
urgency (Box 312.1) (also see ch. 54). While these clinical signs are
often associated with bladder disease, the urethra must also be
considered as a primary site of disease.

DIAGNOSIS
Examination of a patient with suspected urethral disease includes
observation of the patient urinating, if possible, palpation of the
urethra through a rectal examination, retraction of the prepuce in

males, and digital vestibular palpation in females, size permitting
(ch. 3). A urinalysis with careful examination of the sediment may
be performed on both a free-catch and a cystocentesis sample to
evaluate for abnormal epithelial cells, microscopic hematuria, and
evidence of inflammation (ch. 70). Differences in the urinalysis
results between the two samples may assist in localization of the
lesions to the urethra rather than the bladder.
Imaging of the urethra can be useful in identifying spaceoccupying lesions. Radiography of the lower urinary tract should
include lateral views with the hind limbs extended caudally to expose
the neck of the bladder, as well as views with the hips flexed and hind
limbs drawn cranially to reveal the distal and perineal portions of the
urethra (Figure 312.1, A, B). Ideally, an enema or evacuation of the
patient’s bowels is performed prior to imaging to facilitate
visualization (ch. 108). Contrast urethrography, ideally using
fluoroscopy, or if unavailable, radiography or computed tomography,
is a useful means of visualizing areas that are difficult to ultrasound
and may be obscured by the pelvis. It is important to fill the bladder
sufficiently to allow for maximal urethral dilation.1 Fluoroscopy is
considered to be the ideal way to visualize the dynamic nature of the
lower urinary tract, but it is often unavailable. Computed
tomography can also be used for assessing the entire lower urinary
tract, provided the patient’s colon has been evacuated. The structures
within the pelvic canal are particularly well imaged in this manner
compared to ultrasound and radiography.
Urethroscopy allows for direct visualization of the luminal
structures of the urethra (ch. 100). Almost all female dogs and cats
have a urethra large enough to undergo rigid urethroscopy. Male
dogs with a large enough urethra can accommodate a flexible
urethroscope (>6.5 kg), or a rigid scope via a perineal approach (>7
kg). An antegrade cystourethroscopy approach can be used in
male/female cats or small male dogs. Some male cats with a perineal
urethrostomy may also accommodate a cystoscope; those without a
perineal urethrostomy generally cannot undergo the procedure. Most
uroendoscopy systems support tissue acquisition for histopathologic
analysis or culture, and a range of other instruments to assist in
diagnosis and treatment such as lasers, baskets, and stents (ch. 117).

CONGENITAL URETHRAL DISORDERS
Urinary incontinence (ch. 54) is a common consequence of
congenital urethral malformations. Ectopic ureters, urethral
hypoplasia, short/wide urethras, cloacal malformation, and
urethrovaginal, vaginovesicular, and urethrorectal fistulas have all
been reported in dogs and cats. Some animals, mainly female dogs,
may exhibit urinary incontinence since birth with no obvious
malformation. These patients are often characterized as having
“congenital” urethral sphincter mechanism incompetence (USMI),
resulting from some malformation of the collagenous, muscular, or
neurologic components that are responsible for urethral closure.
Congenital urethral disorders are discussed further in ch. 313.

URETHRAL SPHINCTER MECHANISM
INCOMPETENCE
Arguably, the most common urethral disorder in the dog is USMI.
This acquired disorder affects up to 20% of spayed female dogs,
particularly those over 20 kg.2 It is thought to be related to the loss
of estrogen’s influence on the functions and support structures that
maintain a closed urethra during bladder filling. Treatment is
lifelong and usually consists of estrogen compounds or alphaagonists to improve urethral closure. Surgical interventions,
including urethral bulking agents or the placement of an artificial
urethral sphincter, are available for those patients that fail medical
therapy. USMI is covered in detail in ch. 310.

URETHROLITHIASIS
Uroliths of any type can become lodged in the urethra, particularly of
male dogs and cats. Although they can lodge anywhere along the
urethra, in male dogs, the most common location is the narrowed
portion of the urethra at the proximal end of the os penis (Figure
312.1, A, B). There may be a single or multiple uroliths and they
may be lodged in place or move between the urethra and the bladder,
causing intermittent signs of obstruction. If the stone is in the pelvic
urethra, it may be palpated during rectal examination as a hard
lump. Twenty to 30% of male cat urethral obstructions are secondary
to uroliths (Figure 312.2).3
Imaging using radiography or fluoroscopy is the most common
method of diagnosis. Manipulation of the limbs as noted above and
evacuation of the colon may be necessary to visualize the entire

length of the urethra. A contrast urethrogram may also be helpful,
particularly when the urolith is composed of urate or cystine, which
tend to be more radiolucent than calcium oxalate and struvite
uroliths (Figure 312.3).
Direct visualization of urethroliths using cystoscopy (ch. 100)
may be necessary for very small or radiolucent stones. This has the
added benefit of allowing the operator to address them during the
procedure with laser lithotripsy, basket retrieval, or other methods.
Current recommendations for management are to remove
urethroliths using minimally invasive techniques such as flushing
them into the bladder for removal via cystotomy or percutaneous
cystolithotomy, or fragmentation using laser lithotripsy and basket
retrieval (ch. 117).4 The latter technique is particularly effective
when the urolith has lodged tightly in the urethra and is embedded
in the urethral wall. Urolithiasis is reviewed in depth in chs. 308
(dogs) and 309 (cats).

FELINE URETHRAL PLUGS
Twenty to 60% of male feline urethral obstruction is reported to be
caused by mucous and crystalline matrix plugs.3 These are often
associated with feline idiopathic cystitis, a partially understood
syndrome of altered sympathetic nervous system stress responses
leading to inflammation and lower urinary tract pain (ch. 311). The
plugs may be flushed into the bladder during the process of relieving
the obstruction, or passed through a catheter (ch. 99). Gentle
massage of the extended penis in the sedated cat prior to
catheterization may “milk” the plug out of the external urethral
orifice. There is controversy around the value of analyzing these
plugs, and currently the author does not do so.

FIGURE 312.3 Radiolucent uroliths (arrow) in the
urethra are revealed as gaps in the contrast column
during a urethrogram. (Image courtesy Dr. Amy
Habing.)

URETHRAL STRICTURE
Urethral strictures may occur anywhere along the urethra in male
and female dogs and cats. Common causes include trauma,
iatrogenic secondary to catheterization or surgery, erosive injury
secondary to urethrolithiasis, and neoplasia. Clinical signs include a
narrow or weak urine stream, prolonged urination, urine retention,
frequent need to urinate without emptying the bladder, and
stranguria (ch. 54). Rectal palpation may be normal or may indicate
an abnormal portion of the urethra (ch. 3).
If a stricture is suspected, a cystourethrogram with fluoroscopy,
radiographs, or computed tomography should be performed (Figure
312.4). Alternatively cystoscopy may be performed and the stricture

assessed under direct visualization. As noted above, it is important to
fully distend the urethra to avoid misinterpretation. A stricture may
be managed with balloon dilation under urethroscopic or
fluoroscopic guidance, broken down using a diode or holmium:YAG
laser, and/or treated via placement of a urethral stent. See ch. 117
for additional information.

FUNCTIONAL OUTFLOW OBSTRUCTION
(CH. 310)
In veterinary patients, functional outflow obstruction (FOO),
previously called detrusor-urethral dyssynergy, is suspected to arise
from an abnormality in the reflex arc which allows the urethral
sphincter to relax at the initiation of detrusor contraction and
urination. The disorder primarily affects young to middle-aged largebreed male dogs and clinical signs are similar to mechanical
obstruction. The diagnosis hinges on observation of an attenuated
urine stream and large residual urine volume, easy catheterization,
and no evidence of a mechanical obstruction (

Video 310.1).

Treatment involves smooth and skeletal muscle relaxation, and
potentially anti-anxiety therapy. Therapy may be life-long in some
dogs and stressful events may cause a relapse of clinical signs.

EXTRALUMINAL COMPRESSION
When evaluating a dog or cat for urethral obstruction, it is important
to assess the area around the urethra for sources of compression.
Benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatic neoplasia, severe sublumbar
lymphadenopathy, and peri-urethral sarcomas have been reported to
cause signs of outflow obstruction. Careful rectal palpation as well as
palpation of the perineum in male dogs is an important part of an
examination for urethral disease.

FIGURE 312.4 A stricture is shown (arrow) in the
pelvic urethra of a 9-month-old male neutered cat.
The stricture was resolved via fluoroscopic-guided
balloon dilation.

PROLIFERATIVE URETHRITIS
Proliferative urethritis is an uncommon condition that can lead to
partial or complete urethral obstruction. There is a circumferential
proliferation of tissue either focally or diffusely in the urethra with
bands and fronds that lead to narrowing of the urethral lumen
(Figure 312.5). Previous reports have referred to this disorder as
“granulomatous” urethritis; however, in recent reports, it is clear

that the histopathologic findings can be lymphoplasmacytic,
neutrophilic, eosinophilic, histiocytic, or a combination of these.
Thus, “proliferative” urethritis is the preferred term. It occurs most
commonly in female dogs, and may be associated with urinary tract
infection (UTI, ch. 307). There are no cases reported in the cat,
which may be due to the low incidence of UTI in cats. It is unclear
whether the UTIs seen in these patients are the inciting cause of the
proliferative reaction or secondary to it. In one study, >50% of dogs
with proliferative urethritis were positive for urethral bacteria by
fluorescence in situ hybridization, despite some being treated with
antibiotics and others having a negative urine culture at the time.5
Clinical signs are typical for lower urinary tract obstruction and
inflammation including stranguria, pollakiuria, urinary
incontinence, and evidence of abdominal pain (ch. 54). The patient
may make several attempts to pass urine and be unable to empty the
bladder. Affected dogs may have a history of UTI (ch. 307) or
urolithiasis (ch. 308). On physical examination, the bladder is often
distended and painful. Rectal palpation may reveal a thick or
irregular urethra (ch. 3). The lesions on cystoscopic and
ultrasonographic evaluation can look similar to transitional cell
carcinoma, although there are subtle differences with parallel
ipsilateral pale bands of tissue seen. Patients are rarely azotemic or
hyperkalemic. The diagnosis is made by histopathologic
confirmation and ruling out of neoplasia.
Treatment is aimed at relieving urethral obstruction and reducing
the inflammatory proliferation of tissue. A small retrospective study
found that dogs with the obstruction relieved by either a temporary
or permanent urethral stent had a longer time to relapse (843 days)
versus those treated with only balloon dilation (452 days). Dogs that
only had medical therapy relapsed after an average of 101 days.6
Medical therapy consists of a combination of antibiotic therapy for a
UTI if one is present, immunosuppressives, and anti-inflammatories;
however, no studies have been performed to evaluate the efficacy of
each of these treatments. Due to the limited understanding of the
pathogenesis of the disease process, much more work needs to be
done to develop targeted treatment protocols. The prognosis is good
if the obstruction can be managed with dilation or stenting.
Recurrence is common (∼70%), and owners must be prepared for the

potential need for multiple procedures over the dog’s life. Monitoring
for recurrent UTI and appropriate antibiotic therapy based on
culture and susceptibility testing may be a key part of follow-up and
prevention of recurrence.

FIGURE 312.5 Cystoscopic image of a female
spayed dog with proliferative urethritis. Note the
strands of tissue across the urethra.

URETHRAL NEOPLASIA
Neoplasia that originates in the urethra is rare in dogs and cats.
More commonly, it is an extension of disease from either the bladder

or the prostate in the form of transitional cell or prostatic
adenocarcinoma, respectively. While both bladder and prostatic
cancer are relatively common in the dog, they are very rare in the cat.
Although the urethra is not the primary site of disease, the impact of
spread of the tumor leads to urethral obstruction, which is often one
of the life-limiting consequences of disease (Figure 312.6). Urethral
stenting is a simple and minimally invasive intervention of choice,
although complications such as UTI and urinary incontinence may
occur (ch. 117). This topic is more thoroughly covered in ch. 330.

URETHRAL PROLAPSE
Urethral prolapse is a relatively uncommon condition primarily
occurring in male dogs, although it has been reported in at least 1 cat.
English Bulldogs are overrepresented, and Yorkshire Terriers are
frequently discussed in case reports. In a recent multicenter review
of 48 dogs with urethral prolapse, 77% were English Bulldogs and
4.1% were Yorkshire Terriers. Intact males were also found to be
more commonly affected, although outcome after treatment did not
appear to be affected by neuter status at the time of diagnosis.7
Sexual activity and arousal as well as urolithiasis and UTI have also
been associated with development of urethral prolapse. The distal
urethral mucosa protrudes through the external urethral meatus and
often becomes inflamed, edematous and engorged (Figure 312.7).
This can lead to bleeding from the tip of the penis and straining to
urinate. Other clinical signs include pollakiuria and self-trauma of
the prolapsed mucosa and penis.

FIGURE 312.6 Cystoscopic image of a transitional
cell carcinoma protruding from the urethra (U) into
the vestibule. The mass caused almost complete
obstruction of the urethra and the 13-year-old female
spayed mixed breed dog was unable to fully empty

FIGURE 312.7 Urethral prolapse in a 4-year-old
male intact English Bulldog. The dog had a 2-day
history of straining to urinate and licking the tip of
the penis. (Photo courtesy Dr. Mary McLoughlin.)
The diagnosis is based on signalment and identification of urethral
mucosa protruding from the tip of the penis. Treatment involves
surgical resection and anastomosis of the protruding urethral tissue
or urethropexy. Hemorrhage is a common postoperative
complication and can last for several days. Patients that were kept
sedated and had barriers to prevent self-trauma postoperatively had
less bleeding and a lower likelihood of recurrence than those that did
not, which was 38% and 71%, respectively.7 It is important to alert
owners to the high rate of recurrence.

URETHRAL FOREIGN BODY
Plant material, such as grass awns, make up the most common types
of urethral foreign bodies. These may migrate from the external

urethral orifice or transmurally from a penetration site in the skin
near the urethra. Other foreign materials have included broken or
chewed urethral catheters and vaginal cytology swabs. If the object is
known to be present, imaging and/or digital palpation may allow for
locating it. Some objects will require urethrocystoscopy to remove
using grabbing forceps or a stone basket (ch. 100). The advantage of
urethroscopy is that the magnified visual field allows careful
manipulation that reduces trauma to the urethral mucosa. If the
object is in the proximal urethra and protruding into the bladder, a
cystotomy may be performed to remove it. If an object is unable to be
retrieved via cystoscopy and is in the urethra, particularly of a male
dog, a urethrotomy over the object may be required (Figure 312.8).

CLIENT INFORMATION
Urethral Disease
Urinary diseases don’t just affect the bladder, they can also affect the
urethra which drains the bladder to the outside. The urethra of a
male or female dog or cat can become inflamed, have stones from the
bladder lodged in it, have benign or cancerous growth of tissue, or
become narrow from a stricture or external compression. Signs that
something is wrong with your pet’s urethra include straining to
urinate, needing to urinate frequently, painful urination, and over-

grooming of their genitals. In severe cases, the dog or cat may not be
able to urinate at all, which is a medical emergency. If you are
concerned that your pet may have a urethral problem, contact your
veterinarian for an evaluation.
Julie K. Byron (Columbus, Ohio)

Congenital lower urinary tract disorders are rare but important
conditions that occur in both dogs and cats. The most frequently
described, clinically significant abnormality is ectopic ureters (EUs,
ureteral ectopia). Clinical descriptions of many other anomalies are
limited to single case reports or small case series. Most reported
anomalies are anatomical and occur due to failure of normal

embryonic development of the urogenital tract, but at least 1
functional abnormality, congenital urethral sphincter mechanism
incompetence (USMI), is also recognized.

CONGENITAL DISORDERS OF THE
URETEROVESICULAR JUNCTION (UVJ)
ECTOPIC URETERS
Etiopathogenesis
Ectopic ureters (EUs) are a congenital abnormality in which at least 1
ureteral opening is located distal (caudal) to the bladder trigone.
Disruption of development of the metanephric and mesonephric
duct systems, or abnormal differential growth of the urogenital
sinus, are potential explanations for this more caudal ureteric
position. Faulty embryological development can occur either
unilaterally or bilaterally. Intramural and extramural phenotypes are
recognised; 86-100% of cases in dogs are reported to be intramural,14
whereas the majority of cats have extramural EU.5 The intramural
classification describes an EU that tunnels submucosally through the
wall of the bladder/urethra before opening into the urethra at any
point along its length. An extramural ureter is one that bypasses the
bladder and inserts directly into the urethra or more rarely into the
vagina or uterus. A third, intermediate classification likely also exists
according to anecdotal reports: extramural EU combined with an
intramural tunnel (Figure 313.1), but this has not yet been formally
described. The distal ureteric openings may be described as stenosed
or dilated, and more complex abnormalities such as multiple ureteral
openings or ureteral troughs have been observed.1,6,7 Concurrent
congenital urogenital tract abnormalities are commonly reported,
including renal dysplasia/hypoplasia/aplasia (ch. 305), ureterocele,
urethral hypoplasia and vestibulovaginal abnormalities (Figure
313.2).1,4-6 Secondary consequences of EU may develop in some
individuals, including hydronephrosis and hydroureter resulting
from increased resistance to outflow of urine, altered peristalsis

and/or vesicoureteral reflux, and bladder hypoplasia due to reduced
vesicular filling.1,2,4-6

FIGURE 313.1 Retrograde cystourethrogram
performed during cystourethroscopy (ventrodorsal

combined with an intramural tunnel in a 1-year-old

Signalment

In dogs, several breed associations are recognized for EU, including
the Golden Retriever, Labrador Retriever, Newfoundland, Siberian
Husky, Poodle and Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier,2,6,8 suggesting a
hereditary nature to this condition. This has only been confirmed in
the Entlebucher Mountain Dog.9 In cats, no breed predisposition has
been reported.5 Due to the congenital nature of EU, many affected
dogs present as juveniles at <6 months of age, but EU should remain
on the differential diagnosis list lifelong for any patient presenting
with compatible clinical signs and for male dogs, who are commonly
presented as older individuals.2,4 The mean age of cats presented for
investigation of EU is reported to be slightly older than dogs at 1.4
years.5 Females of both species are more commonly clinically
affected. This is likely due to their relatively shorter urethra
compared to males, although this difference is less pronounced in
cats.5

Clinical Features
The majority of animals affected by EU are presented for
investigation of urinary incontinence (ch. 54). However other
clinical presentations are recognized, such as recurrent urinary tract
infections (UTIs, ch. 307). Some affected individuals may show no
clinical signs because high urethral tone and retrograde flow of urine
into the bladder could allow normal storage and micturition. The
degree of incontinence reported is highly variable, ranging from
mild, intermittent incontinence to continuous dripping/pooling of
urine. The severity of incontinence has not been associated with
specific ureteral conformation or uni- versus bilateral disease.3,4,10,11
Hematuria, stranguria, or pollakiuria may be reported in addition to
incontinence, due to concurrent UTI, bladder hypoplasia, or a
ureterocele causing a partial outflow tract obstruction.
The physical examination (ch. 3) is often unremarkable, with the
exception of wet fur around the vulva, perineum and pelvic limbs.
Concurrent vulvar conformational abnormalities (e.g., hooded vulva)
may be observed in some dogs, although the significance of these
remains unclear, particularly in immature animals. Renomegaly
(uni- or bilateral) may be a palpable finding in older dogs presenting

with concurrent hydronephrosis. On rectal examination, a thick or
wide urethra can be palpated in some dogs as well as a bladder neck
located caudal to the pubis, suggesting a short urethra and
intrapelvic bladder.

Diagnosis
A minimum database of serum biochemistry profile, urinalysis and
urine culture are recommended for all patients presenting with
urinary incontinence and suspected to have EU. Renal compromise
is rarely diagnosed, but where present, indicates severe bilateral
secondary renal injury from recurrent pyelonephritis, chronic reflux,
or chronic hydronephrosis, or can be associated with congenital
renal disease. A history of UTI is reported in up to 83% of bitches
and 36% of cats presenting with EU, most commonly due to
Escherichia coli. UTIs must be treated and ideally resolved prior to
treatment, to reduce complications (ch. 307).5,11
Diagnostic imaging is key to identifying and classifying EU, which
in turn influences recommendations for treatment. Ultrasonography,
intravenous urography, retrograde urethrocystography, contrastenhanced computed tomography (CT) and cystoscopy have all been
described as diagnostic tools for this condition. The technique(s)
chosen in any specific case will depend on availability, cost, operator
expertise and other factors, but the key principles should be to
ensure thorough examination of both the upper and lower urinary
tracts in all cases to identify all urogenital abnormalities present and
to use the diagnostic test or tests with the greatest
sensitivity/specificity.
Ultrasonography is best utilised as an initial screening tool for
identifying EU, avoiding the need for sedation/anesthesia in most
patients (Figure 313.3). In addition, this modality provides good
structural information on the upper urinary tract. Ultrasonographic
abnormalities of the renal parenchyma are commonly observed, e.g.,
loss of corticomedullary definition; however, it is important to note
that these renal abnormalities rarely impact the clinical outcome of
patients with EU and thus should not adversely affect treatment
recommendations. Direct visualisation of the distal ureteric opening
or ectopic intramural pathway via ultrasonography may be
diagnostic for EU; observation of secondary changes commonly

associated with EU (e.g., hydronephrosis, hydroureter) may give a
high index of suspicion for this disorder.12 Observation of ureteric
jets can be improved using color Doppler ultrasonography (
Video 313.1), with or without administration of furosemide (1 mg/kg
IV or SQ).13 Diagnostic accuracy of ultrasonography for EU detection
in incontinent dogs was 95% in a recent study, but significantly lower
sensitivities and specificities have previously been reported,
demonstrating the main limitation of operator experience for this
technique.12
Computed tomographic excretory urography (CTEU) is a highly
effective, non-invasive diagnostic tool to identify and classify EU.
High quality, thin slice, transverse images are acquired that remove
superimposition of tissues and thus allow more confident
interpretation, compared to standard contrast radiographic
techniques.14,15 Positioning of the patient in ventral recumbency is
recommended to improve observation of the ureteral jets in the
dorsal area of the bladder trigone, but elevation of the pelvis has not
been shown to benefit image acquisition.16 The sensitivity of CT for
detection of EU is reported to be 73-100%, giving a high degree of
accuracy.14-16 This may be enhanced further by the administration of
furosemide, the use of post-processing techniques (e.g., analysis of
maximum intensity projection slices) or if available, using 4dimensional CT excretory urography (4D-CTEU).16-18 The use of 4DCTEU has recently been reported to achieve a sensitivity and
specificity of 97% and 94.6%, respectively, for detection of EU,
showing it to be mildly superior to standard CT technique.16 The
same study also reported the observation of an obtuse UVJ angle as
increasing the diagnostic accuracy of CT interpretation.16
Cystoscopy (ch. 100) is reported to have a 100% sensitivity for the
detection of EU in dogs, although false positive diagnoses are
occasionally reported in male dogs.3,14 Advantages of cystoscopy
over CT, or any other imaging modality, are the ability to identify
concurrent vestibular/vaginal abnormalities, as seen in up to 93% of
bitches with EU, and the ability to perform minimally invasive

treatment of the EU(s) at the time of diagnosis.11,19 The main
limitation is the inability to examine the upper urinary tract and this
necessitates its combination with an additional imaging modality
(e.g., ultrasound) to obtain a complete urinary tract assessment. In
male dogs, the technique is more challenging due to the reduced
visibility afforded by flexible endoscopy and the presence of multiple
prostatic ducts that can readily be mistaken for abnormal ureteric
openings by inexperienced operators.20
The imaging method of choice for diagnosis of EU in dogs is
currently considered to be cystoscopy in bitches and CTEU in male
dogs and cats.

Treatment
The principle of treatment of EU is to relocate the ureteral orifices
cranially to their normal position within the bladder trigone.
Appropriate treatment options vary according to the EU
classification as intramural or extramural. The preferred approach
for intramural EU is transurethral cystoscopic-guided laser ablation (
Video 313.2), a minimally invasive treatment that is associated
with low morbidity and short hospitalization times11,19-21 (ch. 117).
In clinics where laser surgery is not available, cystoscopic-guided
scissor transection has also been shown to have similar efficacy.22
Surgical correction of intramural EU is effective, but is associated
with increased morbidity compared with cystoscopic-guided laser
ablation.2,4 Both intravesicular (neoureterostomy) and
extravesicular (ureteral re-implantation) techniques have been
described, but intravesicular techniques are preferred due to a
reduced risk of major complications.2,23 Extramural EUs are
exclusively corrected surgically via ureteral re-implantation.2,23
Ureteronephrectomy could be considered only for patients
presenting with severe unilateral hydronephrosis/pyelonephritis.
This procedure is associated with few complications compared to
other open surgical techniques, but results in immediate nephron
loss, which should be avoided wherever possible.2

Outcome
Persistence of urinary incontinence has been reported to occur in 3563% of female dogs after treatment of EU2,4,11,21,24 and has been
largely attributed to concurrent USMI. This remains unproven,
although continence rates in all studies are improved with the
addition of medical management to improve urethral tone.4,11,21,24
Reported values for long-term outcome are broadly similar for both
surgically and endoscopically managed patients with intramural EU,
suggesting that one technique is not superior in resolving
incontinence.2,4,11,21,24 In male dogs, long-term outcome is
significantly better than in female dogs regardless of treatment type.
In a report of 4 male dogs treated by laser ablation, 100% continence
was achieved long term, and an 82% continence rate was reported in
a review of 16 male dogs treated with conventional surgery.20,25
Prognostically, no clinical features of EU have yet been associated
with outcome; breed, uni- versus bilateral disease, classification of
EU, age at presentation, position of the bladder/length of the urethra
and concurrent UTI have all been investigated, but have shown no
association with outcome in multiple studies.2,10,26

FIGURE 313.3 A, Ultrasonographic image of an
intramural ectopic ureter (between markers; 4 mm
diameter) tunnelling submucosally through the

Golden Retriever puppy. B, Ultrasonographic image
of a normal patient for comparison. University of
Cambridge, UK.
In patients with persistent incontinence, repeat cystoscopic
evaluation (ch. 100) is recommended to re-evaluate the ureteric
openings.11 If these are confirmed to be appropriately located,
medical management is initiated with alpha-1 adrenergic agonists
(e.g., phenylpropanolamine 0.8 mg/kg PO q8h or 1.2 mg/kg PO q12h
or 1.5 mg/kg PO q24h; duration of treatment is until the first estrus,
but could be lifelong if incontinence is persistent despite increased
postpubertal estrogen levels; see ch. 312). Additional surgical
management is reserved for those patients with persistent
incontinence despite medication. A significant increase in urethral
resistance and bladder capacity have been documented in sexually
immature Beagles over the first 2 estrous cycles27; therefore, a delay
in considering surgical procedures until after at least the first estrous
cycle is recommended. The use of an artificial urethral sphincter (ch.
117) in bitches remaining incontinent after laser ablation was
effective in 80% of cases in 1 study, suggesting that this is a
promising treatment for refractory incontinence in this subgroup.11

URETEROCELES

A ureterocele is defined as a cystic dilatation of the submucosal
portion of the distal ureter. It can be classified as either orthotopic
(the ureterocele and ureteric opening are located within the bladder)
or ectopic (if any portion of the ureterocele is located within the
urethra).28 Both types are reported to occur in dogs and a single
ectopic ureterocele has been reported in a cat.28,29 Ureteroceles can
occur uni- or bilaterally and may be associated with no clinical signs,
or with lower urinary tract signs such as stranguria, pollakiuria, and
urinary incontinence. Signs of abdominal pain may be a feature if
upper urinary tract obstruction or infection is present.28
Diagnosis is via ultrasonography, contrast-enhanced imaging
studies, or cystoscopy. Treatment of both ectopic and orthotopic
ureteroceles via endoscopic-guided laser ablation has been shown to
be safe and effective, with low morbidity, and is the treatment of
choice30 (ch.117). Surgical resection of ureteroceles is also described
with or without neoureterocystostomy, with similar results.31,32

CONGENITAL BLADDER DISORDERS
BLADDER HYPOPLASIA
Bladder hypoplasia may occur rarely as a primary entity, preventing
normal distension of the viscus and storage of urine; however, it is
more commonly observed secondary to other conditions causing
urinary incontinence in juvenile animals, e.g., EU or congenital
USMI.2 Insufficient bladder filling in animals with moderate to
severe incontinence may result in failure of bladder development.
Correction of the underlying cause should result in gradual return to
normal size and function in most patients. If loss of capacity/poor
compliance does not resolve, this may contribute to persistent
urinary incontinence.

URACHAL ANOMALIES
The urachus is an embryonic structure that allows transportation of
urine from the bladder to the allantoic sac in the developing fetus. At

birth, closure and atrophy of this structure occurs, with the remnants
merging into the median ligament of the bladder. Failure of this
postpartum process can result in 1 of 3 clinical urachal anomalies:
patent urachus, urachal cyst, or vesicourachal diverticulum.33
Patent urachus describes an ongoing open communication
between the bladder and the umbilicus, resulting in urine leakage
and subsequent urine scald dermatitis, omphalitis and ascending
UTI. Rarely, communication of a patent urachus with the abdominal
cavity may result in uroabdomen.34 A urachal cyst occurs if an
isolated section of the urachus retains an epithelial secretory lining,
resulting in subsequent fluid accumulation. A vesicourachal
diverticulum describes persistent communication of the proximal
portion of the urachus with the apex of the bladder, resulting in
either a macroscopic or microscopic outpouching of epithelial tissue
(Figure 313.4). A recent study reviewing 28,714 abdominal
ultrasound studies identified a prevalence of urachal anomalies of
0.93% in cats and 0.18% in dogs.35 Vesicourachal diverticulae
comprised 96.7% of the urachal disorders in cats and 89.5% in
dogs.35
A diagnosis is achieved with contrast imaging studies, cystoscopy
or ultrasonography, and urinalysis and culture should be performed
in all cases to identify any concurrent UTI. Resolution of a patent
urachus or urachal cyst requires surgical excision. Resection of
macroscopic vesicourachal diverticulae in dogs with recurrent lower
UTIs may be a beneficial addition to appropriate antimicrobial
therapy, but only weak evidence currently exists to support this.33
Microscopic vesicourachal diverticulae are likely to be clinically
silent and do not usually require treatment beyond that of any
concurrent lower urinary tract disease.34 Potentially of note, urachal
neoplasia is recognised as a rare sequel to untreated urachal
anomalies in humans and a single case report of urachal
adenocarcinoma has recently been reported in an 8-year-old
Labrador Retriever.36

FIGURE 313.4 Macroscopic vesicourachal
diverticulum in a 6-month-old, male neutered
Miniature Schnauzer. A positive contrast retrograde
urethrogram shows contrast filling the diverticulum
at the apex of the bladder (arrow). University of
Cambridge, UK.

BLADDER EXSTROPHY
Exstrophy of the bladder is a rare congenital abnormality reported in
dogs.37,38 It describes eversion of the bladder due to the absence of a
portion of the ventral abdominal wall. Other abnormalities of the
urogenital tract and surrounding organs are likely to be present.
Treatment involves anatomical reconstruction of affected
structures/organs and management of concurrent conditions.

URINARY BLADDER DUPLICATION
Duplication of the urinary bladder has been reported in dogs and 1
cat, in combination with other embryological failures of the hindgut
and urogenital tract.39-41 Only 1 dog is reported to have been treated
surgically. In this patient, the duplicate bladders were separated by a
median septum, which was ablated to achieve a single viscus. In
addition, the dog underwent left ureteronephrectomy; ligation of a
left, duplicate urethra; excision of a left, duplicate penis; and
castration.40

TRIGONAL DIVERTICULAE
Congenital vesicular diverticulae in the region of the trigone have
been reported in 3 German Shepherd Dogs.42-44 These result from
abnormal detrusor muscle development and subsequent herniation
of bladder mucosa. Stasis of urine within the diverticulae
predisposes to infection, struvite calculi formation, and potentially
urinary outflow tract obstruction or vesicoureteral reflux. Surgical
diverticulectomy is the recommended treatment for diverticulae
associated with clinical signs or giant (>5 cm diameter)
diverticulae.45 Given the location of this abnormality, ureter position
relative to the diverticulum must be known prior to resection.

CONGENITAL URETHRAL DISORDERS
HYPOSPADIAS AND EPISPADIAS
Hypospadias is a rare congenital abnormality that describes a failure
of fusion of the urogenital folds and thus incomplete formation of the
ventral aspect of the urethra. Boston Terriers are overrepresented
and males are more commonly affected than females.46
Classification of hypospadias is based on the location of the
abnormal urethral opening and glandular, penile, scrotal, perineal
and anal types are recognized. Concurrent cryptorchidism is
common.46

A diagnosis of hypospadias is usually based on physical
examination, which reveals an open communication between the
urethral lumen and the skin surface, combined with retrograde
urethrocystography. Abdominal ultrasound is advised to assess the
remainder of the urinary tract, and urine culture should be
performed to rule out UTI (ch. 307). Treatment, if required, is
surgical and most commonly involves creation of a urethrostomy
proximal to the affected urethral section.
Epispadias is very rarely reported. It results from a failure of
fusion of the dorsal urethra, such that in contrast to hypospadias, the
incompletely formed urethra is open dorsally rather than ventrally. It
may occur in conjunction with bladder exstrophy.38 Urethral
reconstruction or urinary diversion are required to treat this
condition in clinically affected animals.

URETHRORECTAL AND
RECTOVAGINAL FISTULAE
Failure of fusion of the urorectal fold, which separates the cloaca into
an anterior urethrovesical segment and a posterior rectal segment,
may result in a continued connection between the rectum and the
urogenital tract postpartum.47 In males, the resultant defect forms a
urethrorectal fistula, whereas in females a rectovaginal fistula is
created, the latter usually associated with concurrent atresia
ani.48,49 Fistulae have been reported in both dogs and cats.47-50 No
breed predilection is reported for rectovaginal fistulae, but an
increased prevalence of urethrorectal fistulae has been noted in the
English Bulldog.50
These disorders are commonly identified during the first few
weeks of life. Feces or urine may be seen to exit from the incorrect
orifice, or a bulging of the perineum may be observed if fecal
material cannot pass and constipation/obstipation occurs. UTIs are
common due to the connection with the gastrointestinal tract and
associated clinical signs such as hematuria, stranguria, and
pollakiuria may be observed.

The diagnosis of a fistula is usually suspected based on history and
clinical examination, and then is confirmed with positive contrast
retrograde urethrography (

Video 313.3), vaginourethrography or

fistulography. Abdominal radiographs additionally give information
on the degree of megacolon present in cases with concurrent atresia
ani. Urinalysis (ch. 70) and culture should be performed in all cases
to assess for UTI (ch. 307). Chronic UTIs may lead to secondary
struvite urolithiasis in some cases and medical or surgical
management may be required to address this (chs. 159 and 308).
Treatment with laxatives and feeding of a highly digestible diet prior
to surgery may reduce the build-up of fecal material in the
rectum/colon (chs. 108, 264).
Definitive treatment of a urogenital fistula is surgical. The fistula is
identified, transected, and ligated or sutured to prevent leakage of
urine/feces and to restore the normal outflow tracts. Atresia ani is
addressed surgically under the same anesthesic to provide an outflow
for fecal material. Neutering of affected animals is recommended due
to the likely hereditary nature of this condition.

CONGENITAL URETHRAL SPHINCTER
MECHANISM
INCOMPETENCE/URETHRAL
HYPOPLASIA
Congenital USMI describes a functional abnormality of the urethra
whereby muscular tone in this organ is insufficient to retain urine
within the bladder, particularly when the patient is recumbent and
abdominal pressure is increased. In some animals (particularly cats),
urethral hypoplasia or dilation of the proximal urethra may be the
primary underlying problem, but in others the anatomic structure of
the lower urinary tract appears normal.51 A diagnosis of urethral
hypoplasia or dilation can be made via retrograde
urethrocystography or cystoscopy (ch. 100). Functional
abnormalities are a diagnosis of exclusion in many cases.
Urodynamic testing, when available, can be used for assessing

urethral tone; however, normal values are not well established for
juvenile animals so pressure traces may be difficult to interpret.
Congenital USMI may be self-resolving in some animals as the
urogenital tract matures and hormonal influence changes following
estrus.27 In persistently incontinent animals, medical management
with alpha-1 adrenergic agonists is advised (ch. 310). Urethral
lengthening procedures have been described for cases with severe
urethral hypoplasia, improving continence in 8 female cats and 1
dog.51

URETHRAL DUPLICATION
Urethral duplication is a rare congenital abnormality reported in
dogs39,40,52 and 1 cat,53 for which the mechanism of embryological
formation remains unclear. The predominant clinical sign reported is
urinary incontinence, likely due to filling of the duplicate urethra
during micturition and subsequent slow drainage into the primary
urethra. Treatment is via surgical ligation of the accessory urethra, or
via a more recently reported alternative of minimally invasive
ablation using coil embolization and cyanoacrylate glue.52

URETHRAL DIVERTICULAE
While urethral diverticulae have long been recognised in human
medicine, they have only recently been reported in 1 dog and 2
cats54-56 (Figure 313.5). Diverticulae are lined with epithelium and
may have a wide connection to the urethra (a distension of a portion
of its length) or be connected via a narrow neck. Clinically these
result in urinary incontinence and UTIs. Surgical resection and
reconstruction of the urethra, or conversion to a perineal
urethrostomy have been described as successful treatments.54-56

CONGENITAL DISORDERS OF THE
VAGINA/VESTIBULE

VESTIBULOVAGINAL JUNCTION ANOMALIES
The point of fusion of the paired paramesonephric ducts is
associated with several congenital anomalies: vestibulovaginal
stenosis, vestibulovaginal septal remnant (VVSR) and a dual vagina.

Vestibulovaginal Stenosis
Vestibulovaginal stenosis describes an annular constriction at the
level of the vestibulovaginal junction. A presumptive diagnosis may
be made via digital vaginal examination; however, contrast imaging
techniques or cystoscopic evaluation are required for further
assessment. Contrast imaging affords calculation of the
vestibulovaginal ratio (ratio of the height of the vestibulovaginal
junction to the height of the vagina), but sources vary as to what
value constitutes stenosis and other congenital anomalies, such as a
septal remnant, can cause the vaginal orifice to look small on
contrast studies, making this diagnosis difficult. A figure of <0.33 is
commonly quoted, but <0.20 has been suggested as a more
significant value, as clinical signs better correlate to severe
stenosis.57 Vestibulovaginal stenosis has been postulated by some to
be a contributing factor to UTIs (ch. 307), chronic vaginitis, and
urinary incontinence in bitches, with treatment options of digital
dilation or surgical resection/vaginoplasty reported. There is little
evidence to support these theories, however. In 1 early observational
study of 99 bitches (42 continent and 57 incontinent), no statistically
significant difference was found in the prevalence of vestibulovaginal
stenosis between the affected and non-affected groups.58 This was
corroborated by a more recent study of 31 female spayed dogs that
reported a higher prevalence of vestibulovaginal stenosis in dogs
without lower urinary tract disease compared to those in the affected
group.59 These studies both suggest that vestibulovaginal stenosis is
an incidental finding rather than a clinical abnormality, although it
may cause reproductive issues for breeding females.

FIGURE 313.5 Urethral diverticulum in a 5month-old, male intact Domestic Shorthaired kitten.
This fluoroscopic image shows the dilated portion of
the urethra at the level of the ischium (white
