Vestibulovaginal Septal Remnants/Persistent
Paramesonephric Remnants, Dual Vagina
VVSRs (persistent paramesonephric remnants [PPMRs]) are a
vertical band of tissue resulting from retention of epithelium at the
point of mesonephric duct fusion (Figure 313.3). These septae
range from thin, likely clinically insignificant lesions, to thick bands

extending several centimeters cranially into the vagina. The term
dual vagina is used when the septum extends from the
vestibulovaginal junction to the cervix, completely dividing the
vagina into 2 compartments. The clinical significance of these latter
lesions is difficult to elucidate given the high prevalence of
concurrent urogenital tract abnormalities and thus the low number
of dogs treated solely for this condition. These lesions may
potentially be a contributing factor to lower urinary tract or
reproductive disorders in some patients. In a study of 36 female dogs
with PPMR, 89% had concurrent abnormalities.60 While some
PPMR lesions are palpable on vaginal examination, full endoscopic
examination of the lower urinary tract (ch. 100) is preferred to rule
out concurrent abnormalities such as EUs, a condition associated
with presence of a PPMR in 93% of dogs in 1 study11 (Figure 313.2).
Contrast imaging techniques will obscure the septa in most cases,
and thus these methods should not be relied upon for an accurate
assessment of this region. A further advantage of endoscopy is the
ability to treat the lesion using laser ablation or endoscopic scissors
at time of diagnosis. Endoscopic laser ablation has been shown to
result in effective, long-term resolution of PPMRs, although the
benefit of treatment remains unclear60 (ch. 117). Surgical resection
of a PPMR is an alternative but more invasive treatment approach,
usually requiring an episiotomy for access. This approach is difficult
to recommend until a clear benefit to treatment has been proven and
treatment should instead be focused on other lesions that are more
likely to be the cause of the clinical signs. In bitches being treated for
breeding purposes, inheritable diseases such as EUs must be ruled
out before proceeding to prevent perpetuation of these conditions.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Ectopic Ureters
WHAT ARE ECTOPIC URETERS?
The ureters are tubes that connect the kidneys on each side to the
bladder. The urethra is the tube leading from the bladder to the
outside, which is normally held closed to prevent urine passage, but

relaxes during urination. Ectopic ureter(s) is a congenital
defect where one or both ureters bypasses the bladder to
empty directly into the urethra (or occasionally the
vestibule/vagina/uterus in females). Ectopic ureters are the most
common cause of urinary incontinence in young dogs.
There are 2 types of ectopic ureters:
• Intramural (most common type in dogs)—where the ureter
enters the bladder in the normal position but then travels
within the bladder wall and opens into the urethra or
vestibule.
• Extramural (most common type in cats)—where the ureter
completely bypasses the bladder and instead enters the
urethra or vagina/uterus directly.

Current research suggests that there is likely to be a genetic basis
to ectopic ureters in dogs, and puppies/kittens that are born with the
condition can have other urinary or reproductive abnormalities.

BREED PREDISPOSITION
• Golden Retrievers
• Newfoundlands
• Siberian Huskies
• Labrador Retriever
• Poodles
• Soft Coated Wheaten Terriers
• Entlebucher Mountain Dogs

CLINICAL SIGNS OF ECTOPIC URETERS
• Urinary incontinence
• Involuntary dribbling of urine from the vulva or penis, or
pooling of urine when lying down
• Recurrent urinary tract infections

• Increased frequency of urination, blood in the urine or
straining to urinate
• Difficulty with housetraining
• Perivulval/peripreputial dermatitis and excessive licking
around these areas

DIAGNOSIS
Ectopic ureter(s) is the most likely diagnosis in young dogs/cats
presenting with urinary incontinence. This suspicion is confirmed
with a combination of imaging techniques, such as:
• Ultrasound scan
• X-rays or CT scan using contrast to highlight the urinary
tract
• Cystoscopy; a small camera is used to examine the lower
urinary tract directly to visualise any abnormalities.

TREATMENT
Treatment for ectopic ureters depends on whether they are
intramural or extramural.
• Intramural
• Transurethral cystoscopic laser ablation (TCLA)—a
minimally invasive procedure where a camera is used to
locate the ectopic ureteral opening and then a laser is used
to relocate the ureteral opening back into the correct
position in the bladder. After laser treatment, dogs can
usually be discharged as soon as they have recovered from
the anaesthetic and as there is no surgical skin wound there
is no need for strict rest or a buster collar afterwards.
• TCLA with a perineal approach—a modification to the
TCLA to enable access for the camera in male dogs.
• Surgical correction—an open abdominal procedure
which involves locating the ectopic ureter within the
bladder and opening the ureter internally to reposition the
ureteral opening into the correct place.
• Extramural

• Ureteral reimplantation—an open surgical procedure
where the abnormal ureter is ligated and cut at its point of
entry into the urethra, then re-implanted into the bladder.
• Ureteronephrectomy—complete removal (at open
surgery) of the ectopic ureter and associated kidney. This
procedure is reserved for cases where irreversible kidney or
ureter damage has been identified.

OUTCOME
Following appropriate relocation of the ureteric openings (with laser
or surgery), complete continence will be achieved in 37-65% of
female dogs and 82-100% of male dogs. The most likely cause of
persistent incontinence in the remaining patients is poor urethral
tone, usually referred to as urethral sphincter mechanism
incompetence (USMI).
Medical management for USMI will improve continence in many
patients; if successful this treatment would be expected to continue
lifelong. In patients that do not respond effectively to medical
management, further surgical treatment is recommended—usually
placement of an artificial urethral cuff device.
Affected animals must not be used for breeding purposes.
Neutering recommendations may vary from case to case.
Laura Owen (Cambridge, United Kingdom)

INCIDENCE AND FREQUENCY
Prostatic diseases may affect both dogs and cats. In dogs, prostatic disorders are the
most common problem associated with the reproductive system, especially intact
dogs >6 years of age.1 One retrospective study quantified the frequency of prostatic
diseases2 (Box 314.1). Prostatic cysts are usually secondary to other issues affecting
the gland or appear as paraprostatic cysts (PPCs), which can herniate. Perineal
herniation of the prostate and prostatic trauma are also possible (Figures 314.1 to
314.3). Large dogs are more commonly affected by prostatic disorders, except for
prostatic neoplasia.3 It has been estimated that 75% of prostate diseases are

subclinical. The prevalence of subclinical benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and
prostatic neoplasia increases with age while subclinical prostatitis is independent of
age.4 Prostatic diseases are exceedingly rare in intact or neutered cats; a few reports
describe cats with bacterial prostatitis, prostatic abscess, squamous metaplasia (SM),
PPCs, and/or neoplasia.5-7

BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA (BPH)
PREVALENCE
BPH is uncommon in dogs that were castrated when young. In geographic regions
where castration is not routinely performed, BPH is the most common prostatic
disease1 diagnosed in dogs, some as early as 2 years of age.8 Large breed dogs, e.g.,
Doberman Pinscher, German Shepherd Dog, Rhodesian Ridgeback, and Labrador
Retriever, may be predisposed.3,9,10 There is gross or microscopic evidence of BPH
in ∼80% of intact male dogs >5 years of age11 and >95% >9 years.12 Most of these
dogs do not develop clinical signs.1 Subclinical BPH was noted in almost 45% of dogs
with subclinical prostatic disorders, similar to the prevalence in humans,4
supporting the dogma that all males develop BPH if they live long enough.13,14

PATHOGENESIS
BPH is a benign disease that includes both an increase in cell numbers (hyperplasia)
and in cell size (hypertrophy).15,16 Etiopathogenesis is not clear, but 3 factors likely
contribute to BPH development: older age, functioning testes, and
dihydrotestosterone (DHT) that concentrates in hyperplastic prostatic tissue.8,17,18
BPH can be “glandular,” characterized by thickened epithelium with developed
“alveoli” especially in the periurethral area. BPH can also be “complex,” with
characteristics of the glandular form plus areas of atrophic epithelium and,
eventually, cyst formation. BPH can progress from glandular to complex.18,19

OWNER OBSERVATIONS, CLINICAL SIGNS,
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (PE)
A presumptive diagnosis of BPH can be based on history, signs (Box 314.2), PE,
routine laboratory results, and imaging. Although rarely recommended for BPH,
biopsy and histological examination can provide a definitive diagnosis.1 Owners may
observe blood dripping from the prepuce (due to increased prostatic
vascularization), hematospermia (1st and 3rd fraction of semen), and/or hematuria.
Tenesmus with thin tape-shaped feces, constipation, dyschezia, and less commonly
dysuria or urinary incontinence can be observed with large prostates or with large

cysts.10,16,20,21 Dogs with BPH are often “sub”-fertile (e.g., no offspring or small
litters) and are predisposed to prostatitis and cystic disease. On digital rectal
examination (ch. 3) of dogs with BPH, the prostate is large, symmetrical, mobile,
normally firm, and not painful. Cysts, if present, can make the prostate surface
asymmetrical or irregular with soft “fluctuant” areas.

DIAGNOSIS
Aside from hematuria, blood and urine (UA) test results from dogs with BPH are
usually unremarkable.10 While semen and urine cultures are usually negative,22
cultures can be useful when assessing for concurrent disorders.21 Radiographs can
provide the dimensions and position of the prostate, but ultrasound (US) is more
informative.23 Prostatomegaly with a uniformly echogenic parenchyma or with
nodular areas usually isoechoic or slightly different from surrounding parenchyma is
consistent with BPH.24 A dog may have 1 or more cysts, each with different shapes
and dimensions and well-defined margins (
Video 314.1).25 Advanced US
techniques allow visualization of the increased prostatic perfusion typical of
BPH.26,27 Cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspirates (FNAs) is normal, but may be
of value in detecting concurrent or other conditions (Figure 314.4; ch. 85).21,28
Serum canine prostatic specific esterase (CPSE) concentrations progressively
increase over time in dogs with BPH. When prostates were estimated to be >2.5
times normal size, CPSE concentrations were >90 ng/mL.9,29-32 There were no
differences among dogs suffering from BPH, bacterial prostatitis, or prostatic
carcinoma.33,34

TREATMENT RECOMMENDATIONS
Grading BPH: to Treat or Not to Treat?
Progression of BPH varies and its rate and extent are difficult to predict. Clinical
signs, when present, may remain static for years. Signs can be graded on severity,
frequency, and duration using an index validated for dogs (Table 314.1).20 This
classification system can objectively prioritize treatment recommendations for each
dog in the context of age, comorbidities, and owner preferences. Understanding the
pathophysiology of BPH is important.14 The decision to treat BPH should be based
on answers to 3 questions: is the BPH life-threatening?; is the BPH adversely
affecting the function of other organs?; is the BPH adversely affecting the dog’s
quality of life?14 No therapy, with q3 to q6 month monitoring, is recommended for
dogs with mild signs or with signs that do not appear to affect quality of life; a
“watchful waiting” approach often used in men (Figure 314.5).35 In addition to
“watchful waiting,” other options include medications or surgery (orchiectomy, cyst
management).36

FIGURE 314.2 Treatment approach for prostatic disease.
Green boxes are diagnoses. Black, green, and red arrows
represent treatment strategies, using the same color scheme
(disease categories) as described in Figure 314.1. BPH, Benign

FIGURE 314.3 Perineal prostatic hernia. Lateral (A) and

evident, consistent with congestion and ischemia.

Castration
Based on history, PE, and test results, BPH can be categorized as mild, moderate, or
severe and the most appropriate treatment can be recommended (Figure 314.2).
BPH treatment aims to suppress or prevent androgen synthesis or action. Castration
is common, easy, and definitive. It is always followed by resolution of BPH, with the
prostatic volume decreasing within 7-14 days (Figure 314.5).20

Medical Treatment
In breeding dogs and those in which castration is not desired or possible,
pharmacological options include 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (e.g., finasteride),
progestogens/antiandrogens (osaterone acetate), and gonadotropin releasing
hormone (GnRH) analogs (deslorelin acetate).1 Finasteride prevents conversion of
testosterone to DHT without reducing libido or sperm production. Several dosages
have been proposed,11,37,38 but a protocol with the lowest possible dose is
recommended (1.25 mg/day, PO) for 195 days regardless of weight or disease
severity.39 Osaterone acetate (0.2-0.5 mg/kg/day PO for 7 days) is a steroid similar
to progesterone with potent progestogen and anti-androgen actions that can lead to
significant reduction in prostate volume. Although some modifications in sperm
quality have been observed, this drug is not likely to affect fertility.40 Use of GnRH
agonist subcutaneous implants provide slow and constant release of the active agent
which supersaturates and downregulates pituitary receptors, leading to a drastic
reduction of testosterone synthesis (up to 90%). Deslorelin acetate also has been
shown to reduce scrotal circumference and decrease prostate volume >50% after
about 6 weeks.41 A decline in semen quality and an inability to collect semen were
observed 22 and 37 days after implant, respectively. Deslorelin effect is dosedependent and, using 4.7 mg implants, prostate volume returns to pre-treatment
values within 48 weeks.42,43

ACUTE AND CHRONIC PROSTATITIS, PROSTATIC
ABSCESSATION
CAUSATIVE BACTERIA
Prostatitis is most commonly diagnosed in mature intact dogs and is far less
common to rare in recently castrated dogs. Prostatitis has been diagnosed in
castrated dogs but is usually secondary to neoplasia. Aseptic prostatitis is rare. Septic
prostatitis, the most common inflammatory disease, can be acute or chronic, and
may be associated with prostatic abscesses (Figure 314.6).44 Multiple organisms
are usually demonstrated in dogs with septic prostatitis; infection by a single
bacterium is uncommon.45 Aerobic organisms are most common, e.g., Escherichia
coli, Staphylococcus sp., Streptococcus sp., Proteus sp., Pseudomonas spp., Brucella
canis, Klebsiella sp. Infections are often traced to bacteria ascending the urethra.
Local dissemination from urogenital organs or hematogenous spread is possible.36
Conditions that reduce normal defence mechanisms or that alter prostatic
architecture (BPH, cysts, metaplasia, neoplasia) can predispose to prostatic
infection.1,5

Quantitative cultures of prostatic fluid may help in understanding a positive
prostatic fluid culture (ch. 104). Definitive diagnosis of infection is made by growth
>10,000 bacteria/mL.46 It has been suggested that a 2-log difference between
prostatic and urine colony-forming unit counts is consistent with bacterial
prostatitis.47 When semen collection or prostate massage is not possible, US-guided
FNA (ch. 85) of parenchyma, cysts, or abscesses usually provides adequate material
for cytologic analysis, culture, and sensitivity (Figure 314.6). Value of a FNA must
be weighed against risk. One can drain a cystic or abscess cavity completely to reduce
risk of leakage into the abdomen. Cysts, especially those with urine, can become
infected secondary to prostatitis.

ACUTE PROSTATITIS (AP)
Common Signs, Physical Examination
A presumptive diagnosis of AP should be based on the history, signs (Box 314.2),
PE, laboratory findings, urine culture results, and prostatic imaging. AP may be
confirmed with prostatic cytologic examination of slides from aspirates, and
bacterial culture (ch. 104).45 Common clinical signs include fever, anorexia,
lethargy, vomiting, caudal abdominal pain, difficulty rising, painful stiff gait, low
sperm quality, poor libido, and subfertility. Some dogs have signs of peritonitis or
septic shock (ch. 128). Hematospermia, pyospermia, hematuria, pyuria, and/or a
constant or intermittent urethral discharge may be observed. Signs of prostatitis may
hide signs or evidence of other prostatic disorders. On PE, the prostate can be firm,

painful, normal or large in size and shape, and can feel asymmetric with an irregular
surface; fluctuant areas may be palpated if there are cysts or abscesses.

Test Results
Neutrophilic leukocytosis with left shift, increased alkaline phosphatase activity,
hematuria, and bacteriuria are common. On US, prostatic parenchyma and the
surrounding tissues may appear diffusely or focally hypoechoic. Sublumbar
lymphadenopathy can be present. Focal hypoechoic lesions can develop into
abscesses. Evidence of BPH, mineralization, cysts, or abscesses can be observed with
US. Cytologic evaluation of prostatic samples (fluid or tissue) show neutrophilia,
usually with degenerative changes and sometimes with intracellular bacteria. If
present, prostatic cells may be normal or damaged (Figure 314.4).

CHRONIC PROSTATITIS (CP)
Presumptive diagnosis of CP should be based on the history, signs (Box 314.2), and
PE. Laboratory findings are usually unremarkable; urinalysis may reveal pyuria,
hematuria, and/or bacteriuria. Cytologic evaluation of prostatic samples, culture and
sensitivity results can confirm a diagnosis (ch. 104). CP is often subclinical. Signs,
when present, include mild lethargy, urethral discharge, and poor semen quality.
Many dogs with CP have recurrent urinary tract infections (ch. 307)1 and
hypo/infertility. The prostate is not usually painful; is usually firm, with an irregular
surface; and its size and shape can be normal or small. On US, focal or diffuse
increases in prostatic echogenicity are often observed, areas of mineralization may
be present, surrounding tissue appears normal. Cytologic evaluation of prostatic
samples (fluid or tissue) usually shows macrophages, plasma cells, lymphocytes,48
and few prostatic cells. Presence of bacteria varies (Figure 314.4).

PROSTATIC ABSCESSATION (PA)
PA can occur as a primary condition, but more frequently as a sequela to AP. PA has
also been associated less frequently in dogs with squamous prostatic metaplasia or
neoplasia. PA can be suspected from the history, clinical signs (Box 314.2), and PE.
Neutrophilic leukocytosis is common with inflammation, sepsis, and/or
endotoxemia. PA can be confirmed with US, and prostatic cytology (Figure 314.4),
culture, and sensitivity results (ch. 104). Clinical signs, similar to those of AP, may
be complicated by tenesmus and dysuria when large abscesses compress the colon
and/or urethra. Peritonitis or septic shock has been seen after systemic spread of
infection or if the abscess ruptures (ch. 126).45 The prostate is usually large, painful,
and asymmetric. Some abscesses feel soft and fluctuant. Large abscesses can appear
on radiographs as prostatic enlargement with displacement of the colon and urinary
bladder. On US, foci of mineralization may be seen while changes are similar to
those in AP. Abscesses may be solitary or multiple, have varying sizes and shapes,
and are hypoechoic/anechoic with irregular internal surfaces (Figure 314.6).

Evaluation of urethral discharge (g) and hematuria (h) severity (0: absent; 1: mild; 2:
moderate; 3: severe) is based on mean value of their characteristics score (amount,
duration, and frequency) rounded up, if necessary. If dysuria and/or
dyschezia/tenesmus is/are present, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) grade is
always considered severe. If dysuria and dyschezia/tenesmus are absent, BPH grade

(1: mild; 2: moderate; 3: severe) is determined by the mean clinical severity score,
(i), rounded up if necessary. Treatment is recommended when BPH is graded
moderate or severe (see algorithm in Figure 314.5).

FIGURE 314.5 Treatment approach for benign prostatic
hyperplasia (BPH). Different therapeutic possibilities are
proposed in relation to severity.

TREATMENT
Supportive Care and Antibiotics
Supportive care (intravenous fluids [ch. 120], analgesics [ch. 6]) may be beneficial.
Antibiotics, the main treatment for bacterial prostatitis and PA, are ideally based on
review of prostatic and/or urine culture and sensitivity results as well as drug
pharmacokinetics (chs. 139, 140). It is recommended that antibiotics be given for 4
to 6 weeks in dogs with AP and 6 to 8 weeks in CP or PA. Castration may decrease
the need for long-term antibiotic use.47 Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be given
while awaiting culture and sensitivity results to reduce risk of the condition
worsening. Initial antibiotic chosen may need to be changed.45 Cultures should be
repeated 7-10 days after starting antibiotics and again in 30 days after antibiotics are
discontinued.
In contrast to dogs with CP, the blood-prostate barrier is often damaged in dogs
with AP or PA. Antibiotics that do not penetrate the prostate in healthy dogs can
easily pass into AP or PA prostatic parenchyma.49 Antimicrobials with good
penetrating capacity have high lipid solubility, low protein binding, high pKa
(trimethoprim, clindamycin, chloramphenicol) or zwitterion characteristics (also
called “inner salts,” these molecules contain an equal number of positively- and
negatively-charged functional groups; fluoroquinolones).

Drainage

Infected cysts and abscesses should be drained (Figure 314.6). Medical treatment
alone rarely resolves the condition. Surgical drainage can include use of Penrose
drains or marsupialization but omentalization is the treatment of choice.50 Nonsurgical US-guided percutaneous drainage (UGPD) should be followed with
percutaneous ethanol injection (PEI) to scar the inner tissue and help prevent
recurrence (ch. 104).51 PEI can be effective for treating small single cysts or
abscesses that are subcapsular, well surrounded by parenchyma, and not
communicating with the urethra. Abscesses often respond to this treatment but
cysts, probably due to their internal epithelial lining, are less sensitive to alcohol.51

Castration
Castration is strongly recommended for hormone deprivation and best results are
seen when coupled with antibiotics in dogs with prostatic infection. Castration is
recommended 5-7 days after antibiotics are started. In dogs with valuable breeding
potential, castration may be postponed and replaced with a medical treatment.

SQUAMOUS METAPLASIA
Male exposure to estrogen, usually due to an estrogen secreting testicular tumor,
causes prostatic squamous metaplasia (SM). Under the influence of estrogen,
prostatic columnar epithelial cells evolve into squamous cells that can exfoliate and
occlude the glandular ducts, leading to AP or PA. Diagnosis should be based on
clinical signs (Box 314.2). History, PE, preputial mucosa cytology (superficial cells
with >30% of keratinization), imaging of the testes and prostate, and prostate
histology or cytology (Figures 314.1 and 314.7) can all contribute to confirming the
diagnosis. Most clinical signs are related to femininization: nonpruritic symmetric
alopecia, skin hyperpigmentation, gynecomastia, penis sheath ptosis and erythema,
and attracting males. There are no pathognomonic US findings. The condition is
reversible by castration if there is a testicular tumor or by removing the exogenous
source.

PROSTATIC NEOPLASIA

Prostatic neoplasia, most commonly adenocarcinomas and undifferentiated
carcinomas, are rare in intact or neutered dogs (average age ∼10 years).1,45,52 A
higher prevalence has been reported in castrated males,52,53 and BPH is not
considered a predisposing factor.54 About 80% of prostatic neoplasms have
metastasized by the time of diagnosis. Common sites of metastasis include vertebral
bodies and lungs. Some of these neoplasms invade periprostatic tissues, including
urethra, urinary bladder, ureters, colon, and/or pelvic musculature. Secondary
infection can exacerbate lower urinary tract signs.45 There are no pathognomonic
signs (Box 314.2). Lameness, stiff gait, paresis of the hind limbs, lethargy, weight
loss, and caudal abdominal pain are common signs. Presumptive diagnosis should be
based on history, PE, laboratory findings, and prostatic imaging. The diagnosis can
be confirmed with cytologic examination of urethral samples (if neoplasia involved
the urethra), or prostatic FNA (ch. 85; Figure 314.4) or biopsy. The prostate is
typically painful, asymmetrically enlarged, and abnormally firm. Radiographic
findings include prostatomegaly, prostatic mineralization, regional
lymphadenopathy, and evidence of metastasis to the lungs and skeleton, especially
the ventral aspects of the lumbar vertebrae. US examination of the prostate often
reveals focal to diffuse hyperechoic areas with hemorrhage or necrosis,
mineralization, asymmetry, an irregular capsule outline, and loss of the normal
contour (Figure 314.8). US may identify sublumbar lymphadenopathy and visceral
metastases (liver, mesentery, spleen, heart, kidney). Prostatic neoplasia carries a
poor prognosis. Survival times of weeks to months are most common, since the
treatment frequently is not curative. Total and subtotal prostatectomy may increase
survival time, but is recommended only for dogs with no metastases. Treatment with
nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) alone 55 or in combination with
chemotherapy56 can improve quality of life and significantly prolong survival time.

PROSTATIC CYSTS
RETENTION CYSTS
Prostatic cysts are usually classified as “retention” cysts or PPCs (

Video 314.1).

Retention cysts are often seen in dogs with BPH and related issues. The inner surface
of the cysts is typically lined with atrophic glandular or ductal epithelium (Figure
314.6). Cysts are classified as large (≥3 cm in greatest diameter), medium (>1 to <3
cm), small (≤1 cm), or micro (≤1 mm), single or multiple. In our experience,
retention cysts are present in almost 75% of dogs BPH. Retention cysts can
communicate with the urethra, may contain urine, and can become infected.

PARAPROSTATIC CYSTS (PPCs)
Description

PPCs have been associated with remnants of the uterus masculinus. They are usually
single structures around the prostate, attached to its capsule. Large cysts can invade
the abdominal or pelvic cavity. Signs depend on size, number, location, and presence
of infected cyst fluid. Affected dogs may have no clinical signs or have signs similar
to those seen with BPH.

Diagnosis and Treatment
Large cysts may be detected via rectal or abdominal palpation and most cysts are
readily seen on abdominal US. When possible, the cyst contents should be sampled
with FNA for cytological, bacteriological and biochemical examinations (Figure
314.4). Based on the dogs’ condition and BPH grading,20 appropriate treatments
can be recommended. Specific treatments for cysts include surgical excision or
debridement, omentalization, marsupialization, or Penrose drain positioning.
Together with castration, medical treatment should reduce prostatic size and
minimize relapses. Castration alone or medical treatment alone may reduce the size
of small retention cysts. However, in dogs with large cysts, either treatment alone
reduces prostatic parenchyma but induces volume increases in the cysts.

INTRODUCTION
Medical disorders of the reproductive system are not limited to
“intact” male and female dogs and cats. Genitourinary disorders

occur in completely neutered dogs and cats of both sexes, and several
medical conditions can be traced to the presence of gonadal
remnants after incomplete neutering.

CLINICAL CONDITIONS
URINARY INCONTINENCE IN THE
OVARIECTOMIZED BITCH
Urinary incontinence (UIC) is a common and predictable
complication of ovariohysterectomy/ovariectomy in the bitch. It is
not appreciated in queens. UIC in older neutered male dogs is less
common and usually related to a myelopathy rather than
hypogonadism (ch. 54). UIC is uncommon in tom cats unless
associated with complications of urethral obstruction (chs. 54, 127,
and 309). Urethral sphincter incompetence (ch. 312) resulting in
UIC occurs most commonly in larger (>20 kg)
ovariectomized/ovariohysterectomized bitches >8 years of age; the
timing of surgery is not contributory unless the bitch was <12
weeks.1 Early age ovariectomy should be limited to animal shelters
where population control is prioritized. Important rule-outs include
overflow incontinence due to isosthenuria or hyposthenuria (ch.
53), urinary tract infection (UTI) (ch. 307), undiagnosed ectopia
(ch. 313), behavioral or submissive urination, and genitourinary
tract inflammatory or neoplastic disorders (chs. 54 and 310).

CHRONIC VESTIBULOVAGINITIS
Etiology
The etiology of chronic vestibulovaginitis is multifactorial. The
primary cause may be masked and/or exacerbated by long-term
antimicrobial use, traumatic douching, or self-mutilation. Vaginal
mucosal biopsy shows nonspecific lymphoplasmacytic inflammation,
sometimes neutrophilic (suppurative) or eosinophilic. Vaginal
cultures can show overgrowth of an atypical, often resistant, bacterial
species (pure Gram-negative cultures, Pseudomonas spp.).
Occasionally, yeast overgrowth is identified. Primary bacterial

vestibulovaginitis is rare. Vaginal strictures are commonly
implicated but rarely contributory. Neither previous juvenile
(“puppy”) vaginitis nor ovariectomy prior to the first estrous cycle
predisposes an adult to chronic vestibulovaginitis.2 Many are
classified as idiopathic (Box 315.1).

Signs, Physical Examination (PE), Laboratory
Testing, Imaging
Chronic vestibulovaginitis often causes a purulent or mucoid-tohemorrhagic vulvar discharge (ch. 56) and signs of discomfort
(licking, scooting, and pollakiuria). Perivulvar and vulvar dermatitis
is common and can be severe. The condition is seen in
ovariectomized bitches of any age, months-to-years post-neutering.
PE of the vulvovaginal area without sedation/analgesia may be
precluded due to pain or fear. Obtaining a complete blood count
(CBC), serum chemistries, urinalysis (UA; preferably acquired by
cystocentesis) and urine culture are advised. Ultrasound (US),

endoscopy and uroradiography of the entire genitourinary tract can
be helpful (chs. 306 and 313). US is advised initially as it does not
require anesthesia and evaluation of the entire abdomen can be
performed with focus on the genitourinary tract, including the
former ovarian sites and the uterine stump (Figure 315.1). Normal
values for uterine stump measurements have been standardized to
the distal aorta; as has the appearance of a stump under estrogen
influence.3,4

Endoscopic Examination
When abnormalities are not identified with US (i.e., uterine stump
granuloma, chronic cystitis, urolithiasis, trigonal lesions), thorough
vaginal examination under adequate sedation or anesthesia should
be performed with visualization of the external vulva, clitoral fossa,
vestibule, urethral papilla, ± urethra/urinary bladder,
vestibulovaginal junction, vagina, and caudal cervix (chs. 100 and
101) (

Videos 56.2, 101.2).5 Appearance of the mucosa, presence

of masses, foreign bodies, and source of any discharge should be
determined. If a vaginal stricture or marked narrowing of the
vestibulovaginal junction is identified, it is important to note if
vaginal inflammation secondary to retention of secretions is present
cranial to the stricture. If the cranial vagina is normal, the stricture
or narrowing is likely not contributory to vestibulovaginitis or urine
pooling (Figure 315.2).

Cytology, Biopsy, Culture
Cytology of vulvar discharge, vaginal mucosal cytology, aerobic
guarded vaginal cultures, and pinch biopsy of affected vaginal
mucosa may be helpful in better understanding this condition (ch.
101). Interpretation of vaginal cultures should consider previous
antimicrobial therapies that could impact normal vaginal flora
(mixed Gram negative and positive bacteria including Mycoplasma
spp.). Identification of any contributory anatomic abnormality is
important (mass lesions, redundant dorsal or lateral vulvar folds,
anomalous ureteral anatomy). It is helpful to have evaluated the
bitch in a normal standing position to accurately assess external

anatomy (vulvar folds?), after urination, and again after recumbency
(urine pooling and scalding?). This complete examination often can
only take place after a bitch is sedated or anesthetized (Figure
315.3, A and B). The presence of urine pooling in the vaginal vault
during anesthesia can be misleading. The presence of redundant
vulvar folds can be difficult to visualize if the bitch is positioned
dorsally.

FIGURE 315.1 Transverse ultrasound image of an
abnormal ovarian stump; arrowhead indicates an
echogenic foreign body (grass awn). Courtesy TW
Baker.

General Treatment Guidelines
Most dogs are managed by discontinuing any topical
irrigations/douching, prevention of self-mutilation with Elizabethan
collars, and initiation of antimicrobial therapy only when indicated
by proper interpretation of culture and sensitivity testing.

Antimicrobial therapy should be limited to dogs with pathogens that
have displaced normal flora (e.g., Pseudomonas spp.). Analgesia and
anti-inflammatory therapy are indicated. Non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs are superior to corticosteroids because the latter
increases risk of UTI. Tramadol (4-10 mg/kg PO q8h) or gabapentin
(10-20 mg/kg PO q8-12h) can be beneficial. Systemic probiotics have
not been shown to benefit vaginal floral normalization.

Specific Treatments
If a specific cause of chronic vaginitis is identified, resolution can be
straightforward (e.g., foreign body removal) (Figure 315.4).
Surgical correction with careful post-operative prevention of selfmutilation is indicated if anatomic abnormalities (redundant dorsal
or lateral vulvar folds, granulomatous uterine stump, os clitoris)
have contributed to or caused the condition (Figure 315.5).6-8
Appropriate management of chronic UTI should resolve associated
vaginitis. Surgery and/or chemotherapy may be indicated for
urogenital masses or neoplasia (Figure 315.6).

Idiopathic Estrogen-Responsive Vulvovaginitis
The condition is “idiopathic” if no anatomic, foreign body, infectious,
granulomatous, or neoplastic cause is identified. The term “estrogen
responsive vaginitis” is more accurate. Oral estrogen therapy is often
helpful in establishing normal mucosal integrity and eventual
normalization of the vaginal vault, similar to post-menopausal
estrogen-deplete vaginitis in women. Women improve with
intravaginal estrogen application, which can be challenging in dogs.9
Oral estrogen (estriol [Incurin; Merck] or compounded
diethylstilbestrol [DES]) is advised. The maintenance dose is empiric
and usually the same as used for UIC due to urethral sphincter
incompetence (estriol 2 mg/bitch PO q24h for 14 days, then tapered
to 1 mg daily × 7 days, 0.5 mg daily × 7 days, then 0.5 mg q48-72h as
needed to maintain normalcy; DES 0.1-1 mg/bitch PO q24h × 3-5
days, then tapered to lowest effective dose, typically 1-3 doses per
week). Several weeks of therapy may be required before
improvement is recognized. Side effects are uncommon;
myelosuppression is highly unlikely if the recommended dosage is

not exceeded. Analgesics and anti-inflammatories should be
continued until an estrogen effect with relief is established. Vaginal
cytology and vaginoscopy (ch. 101) can confirm the desired estrogen
effect (Figure 315.7;

Video 315.1).

EXOGENOUS ESTROGEN TOXICOSIS IN
THE NEUTERED BITCH OR QUEEN
Hyperestrogenism causes behavioral and/or physical signs of estrus
in a bitch or queen. Endogenous estrogen sources include functional
residual ovarian tissue (ovarian remnant syndrome [ORS] bitch or
queen ± malignant transformation) or adrenal gland disease (bitch).
Human hormone replacement transdermal products are the most
common source of exogenous estrogen, consumed or contacted
topically. Hyperestrogenism can also follow overdosage of veterinary
prescribed estrogen for UIC.10 Estrogen exposure in a neutered bitch
causes attraction of male dogs, swelling of the vulva, mucoid to
sanguineous vulvar discharge, passive interaction with male dogs,
flagging, and sometimes copulation (Figures 315.7 and 315.8).
Serosanguineous discharge is of uterine origin, indicating the

presence of uterine tissue or a uterine stump. Chronic estrogen
exposure can cause symmetric alopecia, myelosuppression,
gynecomastia, and/or lactation (ch. 314). The queen under estrogen
exposure exhibits head rubbing, vocalization, crouching of the
thoracic limbs with rigid extension and treading of the pelvic limbs,
lordosis, and a laterally deviated tail.

ENDOGENOUS ESTROGEN TOXICOSIS:
OVARIAN REMNANT SYNDROME (ORS)
Overview
ORS is responsible for about 17% of the complications noted postovariectomy/ovariohysterectomy. ORS is the result of failing to have
extirpated both ovaries completely. The presence of anatomically
abnormal ovarian tissue (fragmentation into the broad ligament or a
supernumerary ovary) is quite uncommon. Functionality can return
to ovarian tissue removed from its vascular supply and dropped onto
the abdominal wall; an omental ovarian remnant in a cat has been
reported.11,12

Signs
Signs of an estrous cycle can first occur days to years after
ovariectomy/ovariohysterectomy. Signs in the bitch are usually
cyclical (about every 5-8 months) rather than constant. Without
coital stimulation of ovulation, queens show estrus signs and then
progress into interestrus. Anovulatory queens will continue to
exhibit signs of estrus every 18 days providing they are exposed to
adequate day length. Stump pyometra causing a purulent vulvar
discharge can develop when a bitch or queen is under the influence
of post-ovulatory progesterone. Constant, noncyclical signs of
estrogen influence suggest an exogenous source, usually a
transdermal human hormone product. Remnant ovarian pathology
(follicular cyst, functional neoplasia), or rarely, adrenal gland
disease, are other possibilities (Box 315.2).

Diagnosis

Results of a CBC, biochemistry panel, and UA with culture are
usually unremarkable. Chronic blood loss has been seen in dogs with
ovarian neoplasia, follicular cysts, bleeding disorders, or other
systemic disease. Pancytopenia is possible from estrogen toxicosis
(chs. 57 and 59). Vaginal cytology will identify estrogen effect:
vaginal mucosal cornification is a bioassay for increased plasma
estradiol concentrations (Figures 315.7 and 315.8; ch. 101). Serum
progesterone concentrations >2 ng/mL (measured 1-3 weeks after
behavioral estrus) are consistent with functional luteal tissue and
ORS. A positive anti-müllerian hormone (AMH) result, now
commercially available (MOFA), in a bitch/queen >6 months of age
(post-pubertal) supports presence of ovarian tissue.13,14 MOFA is the
screening test of choice and more reliable than luteinizing hormone
(LH) results (Witness LH, Zoetis). Exogenous estrogen exposure will
not affect AMH results, permitting differentiation of ORS from
exogenous estrogen toxicity. Exogenous estrogen exposure in a
gonadectomized dog can cause the LH to become negative
misleadingly.15,16 US can be used to support a diagnosis of ORS
initially suspected on history, clinical signs, vaginal cytology, and a
positive AMH. Remnant ovarian tissue is most visible during the
follicular phase (anechoic cystic structures) or luteal phase
(hypoechoic or isoechoic cystic structures) (Figure 315.9;
Videos 315.2 and 315.3). The adrenal glands should be evaluated at
the same time (ch. 295).3

Surgical Treatment
Exploratory laparotomy to remove residual ovarian tissue confirms
the diagnosis and resolves the problem. Identification of residual
ovarian tissue is facilitated by the presence of active follicles or
resultant corpora lutea: surgery should be scheduled when clinical
signs are present. All visible ovarian tissue should be removed and
evaluated histologically. If no ovarian tissue is identified, all residual
tissue at the ovarian pedicles should be resected and submitted for
histopathology; this is important if neoplastic transformation has
occurred. A stump granuloma or pyometra should be removed.
Removal of functional luteal tissue may induce transient signs of

pseudopregnancy in bitches post-operatively, caused by increases in
prolactin following loss of progesterone. If profound, anti-prolactin
therapy (cabergoline; Galastop 2.5 mcg/kg PO q24h for 4-6 days)
can be given. Removal of remnant ovarian tissue should resolve
clinical signs of estrus. Feline mammary hyperplasia can result if the
remnant was luteal and progesterone levels decline precipitously.
Treatment with the progesterone antagonist aglepristone (where
available) is optimal.17,18

Medical Treatment
Medical therapy is often requested by clients reluctant to pursue a
second surgical procedure. Progestational or androgenic compounds
used to suppress follicular ovarian activity are not recommended
because of undesirable side effects (mammary neoplasia, diabetes
mellitus, undesirable behavior). Immunocontraception or
gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist administration offers an
alternative to laparotomy when commercially available. In dogs
being administered estrogen, lowering the dose is advised. In dogs
with accidental exposure, avoidance should lead to resolution of
clinical signs in 2-4 weeks.10

ESTROGEN TOXICOSIS IN THE
NEUTERED DOG: SQUAMOUS
PROSTATIC METAPLASIA
Etiology
Squamous prostatic metaplasia can develop due to hyperestrogenism
(ch. 314). The estrogen source may be endogenous (functional
Sertoli or Leydig testicular tumor, adrenal gland dysfunction) or
exogenous (inadvertent exposure to or consumption of owner
transdermal hormone medication). Prostatic epithelial squamous
metaplasia is accompanied by secretory stasis and the potential for
intraprostatic cysts.

Clinical Signs

Prostate palpation reveals an enlarged and firm gland, especially for
a neutered dog. Compression of the urethra and colon can cause
dysuria and/or tenesmus. Other findings typical of hyperestrogenism
can include: attractiveness to males, gynecomastia, symmetric
alopecia, hyperpigmentation, and a pendulous prepuce. Bone
marrow estrogen toxicosis can lead to anemia and pale mucous
membranes; thrombocytopenia and petechiation or hemorrhage;
and/or neutropenia and fever due to infection (chs. 57-59 and 138).

Testing and Diagnosis
A CBC, serum chemistry panel and UA/culture should be assessed
for myelotoxicosis and general health. Hematuria may occur due to
thrombocytopenia or prostatic bleeding. Squamous epithelial cells
exhibiting estrogen influence can be seen in the urine or recognized
in samples swabbed from the preputial mucosa. In a neutered dog
with no scrotal testes, abdominal US should be used to screen for a
malignant-transformed cryptorchid testis and to evaluate the
prostate. Benign prostatic hyperplasia (ch. 314) can occur due to
hormones synthesized by the retained testicle.3 A positive AMH
result supports the presence of testicular tissue.19 If an abdominal
testis containing a parenchymal mass or an enlarged prostate is
identified with US, fine-needle aspirate or biopsy sampling may
provide cytologic evidence of a functional testicular neoplasia and
prostatic squamous metaplasia (ch. 104).

Treatment
Therapy is dictated by the clinical findings: discontinuing estrogen
exposure if exogenous, or castration if cryptorchid. Concurrent
prostatic infection or abscessation can be present and should be
treated appropriately (ch. 314).

COMPLICATIONS OF OVARY-SPARING
NEUTERING
Etiology, Signs, Treatment

Clinicians responding to unsubstantiated client concerns about the
absence of ovarian function in ovariectomized middle to older aged
bitches sometimes perform a hysterectomy ± unilateral ovariectomy.
This results in sterility with intact ovarian function. The remaining
ovary is associated with an increased incidence of mammary and
ovarian neoplasia, cystic ovarian disease, and continuing estrous
cycles. Ovarian cysts in the bitch include follicular and luteal cysts
(producing estrogen and progesterone, respectively) and rete ovarian
subepithelial surface and para-ovarian cysts. Cystic
adenocarcinomas, papillary cyst adenomas, and granulosa-theca cell
tumors are common. Some ovarian neoplasias are functional.20
Bitches under the influence of estrogen and progesterone derived
from the ovary left in situ may experience estrus and breed. Acute
peritonitis secondary to deposition of semen into the abdominal
cavity can result if a breeding occurs. Because large volumes of
prostatic fluid, containing foreign antigens, are in the final fraction of
the ejaculate, semen can be forced into the abdomen through the
uterine stump or the vagina may tear during the copulatory lock.
Severe suppurative peritonitis and the systemic inflammatory
response syndrome are likely sequelae (ch. 265). Cytology of
peritoneal fluid can aid in the diagnosis (Figure 315.10).
Stabilization followed by exploratory laparotomy and extensive
lavage of the abdomen are indicated. This syndrome has high
morbidity and mortality for the bitch.

PRIAPISM
Definition and Etiology
Priapism, a persistent penile erection (primarily within the prepuce)
without sexual stimulation, is categorized as either nonischemic
(arterial, high flow) or ischemic (veno-occlusive, low flow). Priapism
occurs most commonly in neutered dogs (Figure 315.11).
Castration of a dog with priapism is not helpful; the condition is not
mediated by testosterone.21 Priapism should be differentiated from
paraphimosis (erect or partially erect penis unable to be returned
into the prepuce), which occurs more commonly in intact male dogs
after semen collection or masturbation and results from constriction

of the erect penis by the preputial opening (Figure 315.11, B).
Priapism should also be differentiated from other causes of penile
swelling, such as a hematoma, trauma, or mass lesions (Figure
315.11, C and D). Penile hematomas usually form as a result of
trauma or bleeding disorders. Visual inspection and palpation of the
penis are usually sufficient to differentiate the conditions, but US
and/or color-flow Doppler examination may further help
differentiate these disorders from priapism (Figure 315.12). US of
the perineum and the entire penile shaft may aid in identifying
neoplasia, os penis fracture, hematoma, or thromboemboli (
Videos 315.4 and 315.5).3 Priapism can be associated with vascular
disorders (efferent or afferent), neuropathy, or a myelopathy (L1-L4,
S1-S3). One hypothesis on the pathophysiology of priapism suggests
dyssynergic neurostimulation of inflow and outflow penile blood
vessels causing vasospasms or smooth muscle spasms, which may
occur at the level of the penis, the central nervous system (spinal
cord), or in the peripheral nervous system.22

FIGURE 315.10 Semen peritonitis. Arrow
designates phagocytized spermatozoa head.

Diagnosis and Treatment
Distinguishing ischemic (proceeds to gangrene) from non-ischemic
priapism is important, as is identifying and treating the underlying
cause. If determined to be ischemic, prompt aspiration of the corpora
cavernosa under sedation or anesthesia with or without irrigation
should be done. Intracavernosal injections of phenylephrine should
be considered, but carries some risk as appropriate dosages in dogs
and cats have not been determined. Therefore, starting with low
dosages (1-3 mcg/kg) and cardiovascular monitoring is important.
Providing lubrication is also important to limit tissue damage
secondary to exposure and excoriation. An Elizabethan collar is
indicated. If intracavernosal drainage and injections are not
successful or significant tissue damage has occurred, penile
amputation and perineal urethrostomy may be necessary.

Nonischemic priapism can resolve spontaneously but can take
hours to days. Conservative therapy using analgesia, protecting
penile integrity with lubrication, and use of an Elizabethan collar are
recommended. Sedation with a phenothiazine drug can be helpful.
Several systemic medications are of potential benefit, although little
controlled data exist regarding efficacy. Gabapentin (10-20 mg/kg
PO q8-12h), terbutaline (1.25-5 mg/dog PO q8-12h) or ephedrine (12.5 mg/kg PO q12h; discontinued commercially) should be tried.
Incrementally increasing dosage is advised. If detumescence is not
achieved after several days of treatment with one drug, switching to
another may be successful.

THE HALLMARKS OF CANCER/ORIGIN
OF CANCER
NOBEL LAUREATES HANAHAN AND
WEINBERG’S PROPOSED “HALLMARKS OF
CANCER”
A model for understanding the complexity of cancer, referred to as
the “hallmarks of cancer,” was proposed in 2000.1 One component of
the model was a cohesive structure which considers the complexity
and growing number of molecular changes identified in cancer cells

and how these events independently and collectively contribute to
the formation of a cancer. Briefly, despite the large number of
molecular alterations associated with cancer, cancer cells share 6
critical features: sustained angiogenesis, evading apoptosis, selfsufficiency in growth signals, insensitivity to anti-growth signals,
tissue invasion and metastasis, and limitless replicative potential. A
specific molecular alteration could contribute to cancer by providing
a cell with one or more of these hallmarks; however, it is the
acquisition of all 6 that yields the full cancer phenotype.

THE REVISED “HALLMARKS OF
CANCER”
In 2011, a revision was proposed to refine the features of cancer
progression and metastasis and include the “enabling features” of
cancer.2 This new 8-feature model considered deregulating cellular
metabolism and immune evasion as “emerging hallmarks” of cancer,
which have since become firmly established among the core
hallmarks of cancer (Figure 316.1). Hanahan recently proposed
additional enabling characteristics and prospective new hallmarks of
cancer,3 exemplifying the ongoing and complex nature of
understanding of cancer biology.

CLINICALLY APPLYING THE
“HALLMARKS OF CANCER”
The use of this model allows the clinician to focus on the critical
features of the cancer phenotype rather than a long list of genetic
molecular alterations. It also provides a simple framework to
characterize the contributions made by various molecular
alterations. Thus, it allows the simplification of thousands of genes
linked to the cancer phenotype to a simple set of “hallmarks” that
must be acquired in order to create cancer from a normal cell.

CANCER IS A GENETIC DISEASE
TUMOR PROMOTING AND TUMOR
SUPPRESSING GENES
Genetic Disease, Not Necessarily a Hereditary
Disease
It is clear from all points of evidence that cancer is a genetic
disease.4,5 Indeed, each of the 8 hallmarks required for a cancer can
be delivered via gene alterations. Suggesting that cancer is a genetic
disease does not indicate that cancer is a hereditary disease,
although there are familial, and therefore hereditary, risks associated
with cancer.6

Cancer and Genetics
The classical association between cancer and genetics involves
overactive tumor-promoting genes, “oncogenes,” or the loss of genes
that normally constrain 1 or more of the hallmarks of cancer,
referred to as “tumor suppressor genes.” The activation of oncogenes
often involves a mutation or other structural change that activates
the normal gene (a proto-oncogene) to become a cancer-associated
oncogene. The gain-of-function seen in an oncogene is a dominant
event, requiring the alteration of only 1 of a gene’s alleles.7,8
Conversely, the loss of a tumor suppressor gene is a recessive event
requiring the loss of both alleles.

FIGURE 316.1 Eight hallmarks and two enabling
core characteristics of cancer as outlined by Hanahan
and Weinberg in 2011. From Hanahan D. Hallmarks
of cancer: new dimensions. Cancer Discov.
2022;12[1]:31-46.

P53 Tumor Suppressor Checkpoint Genes
Loss of a tumor suppressor gene, P53, is believed to be the most
common genetic alteration seen across human cancers. Not
surprisingly, loss of P53 has also been described in a variety of
veterinary cancers.9-13 P53 is a member of a family of genes
described as “checkpoint genes.” P53 and other checkpoint genes
serve to “survey” the genetic landscape of a cell and determine if
there has been sufficient DNA damage to warrant halting the division
of the cell and its progress through the cell cycle (referring to a series
of steps that allows the cell to undergo mitosis). Halting the division

of the cell allows mechanisms to repair the identified DNA damage.
If the DNA damage is significant, genes like P53 will not only halt the
mitotic process but will shift the cell into a pathway of programmed
cell death (apoptosis). This allows elimination of this genetically
altered cell, therefore preventing it from potentially contributing to a
hallmark of cancer. Accordingly, the loss of P53 and its checkpoint
function will eliminate the ability of cells to enter this suicide/death
pathway, and therein increase the number of cells present with
genetically altered landscapes.

“Two Hits”
The loss of two alleles in a tumor suppressor gene will contribute to a
hallmark of cancer and often occurs as a result of a hereditary and
sporadic (“second hit”) event. In this scenario, the first loss of a
tumor suppressor gene is a familial risk and the second loss is
sporadic. The resultant loss of these two alleles, often described as
“two hits,” explains why there are families at increased risk for
specific cancers. This was first described by Knudson in the familial
and sporadic form of retinoblastoma (Rb) in humans, which results
from a two-hit loss of the Rb tumor suppressor gene.14

Epigenetics
It was believed that genetic alterations resulting in dysregulation of a
specific gene occurred as an alteration in the nucleic acids that
constitute that gene. It is now appreciated that these gene function
alterations can occur outside a specific change in the gene itself. This
concept is a component of cancer biology referred to as “epigenetics.”
Briefly, epigenetics largely refers to changes in the regulatory
elements of a gene (namely the promoter or enhancer of the gene).
Epigenetic alterations in gene function can be more common in
cancer-associated gene dysregulation than structural changes in a
gene (i.e., mutation). These epigenetic changes in gene function have
been aligned closely with various environmental and other acquired
risks for cancer.15,16

TELOMERASE AND ACQUISITION OF
LIMITLESS REPLICATIVE POTENTIAL
The acquisition of limitless replicative potential, a hallmark of
cancer, has been closely associated with the telomere and
telomerase. Telomeres are specialized DNA protein complexes that
cap the ends of chromosomes and maintain genomic stability by
preventing recombination or fusion with other chromosomes. Each
telomere consists of tandem repeats of TTAGGG and several
telomere-related proteins. In normal cells, telomeres shorten with
each cell division, referred to as telomeric attrition. Telomerase is a
reverse transcriptase capable of making the terminal telomeric
repeats, thus extending the telomere and compensating for attrition
during cell division.17 Low levels of telomerase are detected in
normal somatic tissues, but there are high levels in germline and
cancer cells, giving them long-term proliferative potential. Some
cancer cells are capable of maintaining telomere length and surviving
without telomerase.18 In these instances, alternative mechanisms are
used, referred to collectively as “alternate lengthening of
telomeres.”19,20 While the mechanisms are not fully understood,
uncovered novel therapeutic targets (i.e., ataxia telangiectasia and
Rad3-related kinase [ATR]) are being targeted in dogs by novel
anticancer drugs.21

TUMOR PROGRESSION AND
METASTASIS
THE METASTATIC CASCADE
For cancer cells to spread from their primary to distant secondary
sites, individual cells and groups of cells must accomplish discrete
processes associated with the metastatic cascade. A detailed study of
the metastatic cascade has defined critical steps, which appear to be
the most difficult for cancer cells to pass through successfully. These
steps represent unique periods of vulnerability during which cellular
stresses cause death of most cancer cells, especially non-metastatic

cells. The highest stresses appear when metastatic cells interact with
the microenvironment of the secondary sites. Only a minority of
cancer cells can adapt and survive these vulnerable states during the
metastatic cascade. Indeed, the metastatic phenotype now can be
defined by an ability of cells to adapt to stresses during these
vulnerable states.22-24

5 IMPORTANT STEPS IN TUMOR
METASTASIS
An understanding of stresses and the mechanisms by which cells
overcome them provides opportunities for development of
metastasis-specific therapies. Metastasis is a multistep process that
results in the dissemination of tumor cells from a primary site to
distant secondary organs, and the eventual progression of disease at
these secondary sites. This cascade can be broken down into 5
important steps: cellular basement membrane invasion and
migration, invasion of nearby vessels and lymphatics, survival in
circulation, extravasation into new tissues, and proliferation in the
new site.25 Metastatic cancer cells are unique in their ability to
endure and overcome cellular stresses associated with each step in
this process. Based on studies of the metastatic phenotype of
sarcoma cells in dogs, mice, and humans, a common determinant of
metastatic cancer cells is their ability to resist these stresses.26 Using
a comparative approach to the study of metastasis can hopefully be
translated rapidly to the clinic in the form of novel therapeutics.

ANGIOGENESIS AND THE TUMOR
MICROENVIRONMENT
ANGIOGENESIS
Tumor angiogenesis refers to the formation of blood vessels within
the tumor microenvironment through sprouting or intussusception
of pre-existing blood vessels. This is in contrast to vasculogenesis, or
formation of blood vessels de novo, during embryogenesis. The

vasculature within and surrounding a tumor is of critical importance,
as it supplies the nutrients, growth factors, metabolites,
inflammatory mediators, and oxygen for primary tumor cell
proliferation.27 Tumor blood vessels also provide a means for tumor
cells to enter the vasculature and spread to other parts of the body,
and play a vital role in the metastatic cascade. Normal angiogenesis
occurs in all tissues and is of particular importance in embryogenesis
and wound healing.
Hypoxia is the primary physiologic stimulator in the development
of vasculature. Hypoxia-sensing mechanisms in poorly perfused
tissues induce new vessel formation to satisfy the metabolic
requirements of cells. Cells respond by secreting proangiogenic
growth factors, including vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF),
platelet derived growth factor (PDGF) and basic fibroblast growth
factor (bFGF), among others. Briefly, these factors induce
endothelial cells from surrounding blood vessels to migrate towards
the angiogenic stimulus and organize new vessels. Generation of a
new blood supply to these tissues eliminates the hypoxic stimulus,
and VEGF production declines.28

THE TUMOR MICROENVIRONMENT
Many cancer cells are capable of inducing angiogenesis in the
absence of hypoxia, demonstrating that “normal” rules do not apply.
Multiple mechanisms have proven responsible for this phenomenon,
including the overproduction of VEGF and upregulation of other
vascular stimulating cytokines. This phenotype has been associated
with the activation of oncogenes, loss of function in a number of
tumor-suppressor genes, and downregulation of angiogenic
inhibiting mechanisms. The tumor microenvironment also lacks the
normal barriers present in non-cancerous tissues. For example, the
basement membrane and connective tissues often are compromised
in malignant tissues, creating an altered tumor-vascular interface,
which could influence metastatic potential, access to nutrients, and
access to other mediators.29

THERAPEUTIC AGENTS
In human medicine, many therapeutic agents have been developed
to target various steps in angiogenic pathways.30,31 In veterinary
medicine, small-molecular targeted therapies also have started to
emerge on the market. Palladia (toceranib), for example, is a
receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) inhibitor developed to target c-kit in
mast cell tumors.32 This drug also inhibits the RTKs of VEGF, and
other proteins, involved in angiogenesis with activity against a
number of cancer types, independent of c-kit.33 Indeed, many tumor
types overexpress VEGF or PDGF, or have aberrant VEGF signaling,
and reasonably could be targeted with this drug. More recent studies
have investigated other targeted inhibitors for animals with
cancer.34,35

THE CANCER STEM CELL HYPOTHESIS
It is recognized that within a cancer there are a variety of
subpopulations, including those that account for the rapid
recurrence of a cancer after initial response to therapy. The cancer
stem cell hypothesis proposes that a small but definable population
of cells within a tumor are able to self-renew and give rise to tumor
cells both at the primary tumor site and sites of metastasis. Within
this heterogeneous environment are a small number of slowly
dividing cells that differ from a majority of cancer cell populations
and are resistant to conventional treatment. These types of cells are
proposed as the cause for recurrent disease despite initial response
to treatment (e.g., chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery) or distant
metastasis to other sites in the body later in disease progression.36
Clinically, cancer stem cells (CSCs) have become a prominent area
of interest and research as potential targets in cancer treatment.
CSCs, first noted in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), were identified
by their ability to self-renew and repopulate the bone marrow of
severe combined immunodeficient (SCID) mice following
transplantation of human AML cells and administration of in vivo
cytokine stimulation.37 Later experiments identified a hierarchy

among these populations, and discovered specific cell markers,
present only on this small population of CSCs, capable of
differentiating into blastic leukemic cells.38 Various CSC markers
now have been identified on a number of solid cancers including
breast,39 colorectal,40-42 pancreatic,43 hepatocellular,44 ovarian,45
prostatic,46 and melanoma.47 Specific markers identified in these
tumor types have been associated with prognosis, metastatic rate,
and response to treatment in humans, indicating that these CSCs
could be a valid target for novel cancer therapies. Varying therapies
targeting altered cellular pathways in the stem-cell population have
shown promise in vitro and in some early clinical trials.48,49
Immunotherapy also has been used for targeting cell surface markers
unique to CSCs with varying efficacy in both the in vitro and in vivo
settings (ch. 319).50 Although new, targeted therapies towards CSCs
are not yet common practice in veterinary medicine, this approach
presents a new, exciting front that will likely benefit the veterinary
patient in the future.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Tumor Biology
Cancer is an incredibly complex set of disease processes. Over the
last 2 decades our understanding of tumor biology has increased
exponentially. This is in part through the identification of the
“hallmarks” of cancer that describe a number of features common
across cancers. Broadly, these hallmarks focus on the cancer’s ability
to act independently of the body’s normal feedback mechanisms,
allowing tumor growth and potential spread (metastasis). Unlike a
normal cell, cancer cells learn to evade the immune system, utilize
the tissue around them to feed tumor growth, and gain immortality
allowing them to replicate unchecked. This ability occurs in part
through the overactivation of tumor promoting genes known as
oncogenes, and/or the loss of function of genes that typically
constrain cellular proliferation, tumor suppression genes.
This understanding has also allowed for the development of much
more targeted cancer therapies towards these hallmarks. For

example, we know that cancer cells gain the capability to acquire
their own blood supply (angiogenesis), which has led to the
development of numerous therapeutics aimed at blocking this
ability. While targeted therapies are still limited for our animal
patients, ongoing studies continue to elucidate new treatment
options focusing on ways to address these known cancer hallmarks.
As our understanding of the complexity of cancer continues to
unfold, this will allow the clinician to more specifically tailor cancer
treatments to the unique nuances of each cancer patient.
Amanda Foskett (Washington, DC)
