Chemotherapy is the principal modality used to treat systemic
cancers such as hematologic malignancies and metastatic solid
tumors.

TUMOR BIOLOGY IN CHEMOTHERAPY
Understanding tumor biology is necessary in planning chemotherapy
(ch. 316), which is most effective against a small tumor burden. As
tumors grow, the growth fraction decreases, the cell cycle time
increases, cellular heterogeneity increases (leading to a higher
incidence of spontaneous resistance), and areas of poor perfusion
increase. It is difficult for chemotherapy drugs to reach cells in large
cancers at cytotoxic levels. Resistance to chemotherapy can occur
through spontaneous mutations that can occur during each cell
division. Cell divisions occur at a rate that is intrinsic to each tumor
and the likelihood of mutations causing drug resistance correlates
with the number of cell divisions. Chemotherapeutic cytotoxicity
follows fractional-kill kinetics, e.g., if a dose of drug kills 4 logs of
cells, then it will reduce a tumor of 1012 cells to 108 cells and a tumor
of 1010 cells to 106. The minimum clinically detectable mass is about
109 cells, so either outcome appears clinically as complete; however,
106 cells is obviously better. Therefore, it is most advantageous to
begin treatment with the smallest tumor, and in general,
chemotherapy will be most active either after early detection or after
a cytoreductive (“debulking”) procedure such as surgery or radiation
therapy.

APPROACHING CHEMOTHERAPY
Owner Communication (ch. 1)
Frank and compassionate communication between veterinarian and
pet owner/caregiver is essential. A number of diagnostic and
therapeutic matters should be considered in formulating
recommendations, and all options should be presented to caregivers
without preconceptions. A continuing, open dialogue allows an

owner to make informed decisions and will ultimately create a
“team” approach to treatment of the pet’s cancer.

Staging and General Health Evaluation
Definitive diagnosis of tumor type, clinical stage, and the pet’s
overall health are important in developing a prognosis and treatment
plan. Staging often carries prognostic significance that may assist in
making informed decisions about therapy. Most staging systems are
based on 3 major components of the malignant process: primary
tumor size (T), lymph node metastasis (N), and distant metastasis
(M). The staging system, appropriate tests, and prognostic
implications vary with tumor type. A general health screen is
directed at detecting other conditions that may affect life expectancy
(i.e., other systemic disease), issues that need to be resolved prior to
starting chemotherapy (e.g., urinary tract infection [UTI, ch. 307]),
or conditions that need to be taken into account in planning
chemotherapy (e.g., cardiac or renal disease, ch. 223).

Goal of Treatment, Cure vs Palliation
The goal of chemotherapy in human oncology is usually a cure. In
dogs and cats, palliation is sometimes more appropriate. Palliation is
aimed at improving quality of life (QoL), possibly extending life, but
without an expectation of cure. Palliative treatment is often
appropriate when there is a poor prognosis and significant toxicosis
is often not justified when only short-term survival is expected. For
many older animals, the diagnosis of cancer is made at a time when
other diseases may be more likely to limit survival than the cancer
will. Palliative care and choice of chemotherapy must be weighed
against the risks of toxic effects.
Cure is defined as eradication of all tumor cells, resulting in a
permanent disease-free state. Cure is an ideal, but not always
realistic, outcome. The limitations on chemotherapy doses to keep
side-effects within an acceptable range means that cure is only
realistic in a minority of dogs and cats, e.g., 15% of dogs with
lymphoma (ch. 322) and 20% of dogs with osteosarcoma (ch. 326),
given standard of care therapy. For dogs and cats in good health,
with no concurrent illness, and when chemotherapy may prolong
control of their cancer with little risk of toxic effects, curative intent

may be undertaken. It is rarely effective to begin with palliative
intent and then switch to a more definitive approach, but it is
common to begin treatment with curative intent and then later
switch to a palliative course.

Chemotherapy in Combination With Other
Treatment Modalities
In veterinary oncology, primary chemotherapy (chemotherapy as the
sole or main treatment) is usually reserved for hematopoietic tumors
(lymphoma, leukemias, multiple myeloma) (ch. 322).
Chemotherapy alone for dogs with solid tumors (carcinomas and
sarcomas) is rarely curative and is usually considered palliative.
Adjuvant (or adjunct) chemotherapy is used after resection or
radiation of a primary tumor to slow metastatic disease or possibly to
provide a cure when a dog or cat is at significant risk of local tumor
recurrence or metastasis, despite no evidence of spread, e.g., after
amputation in dogs with osteosarcoma. Adjuvant chemotherapy is
effective when used at the earliest stages of growth; after resecting a
primary tumor, micrometastatic foci of tumor cells have a high
growth fraction and low numbers of resistant cells. The potential
disadvantage or risk of adjuvant chemotherapy is a pet cured by the
surgery and then given chemotherapy unnecessarily. For tumors
such as osteosarcoma (ch. 326) and hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325) in
dogs and mammary tumors in cats (ch. 329), the percentage of
surgical cures is small; but for animals with some other tumors,
determining the risk/benefit ratio may be more difficult.
“Neoadjuvant chemotherapy” is used before localized treatment
modalities, e.g., surgery or radiation therapy, with the objective of
reducing the size of the primary tumor and reducing the scope and
side effects of other definitive treatments. “Chemoradiotherapy”
refers to the use of chemotherapy drugs primarily as radiation
sensitizers rather than for their direct antitumor effect.

CLASSES OF CHEMOTHERAPY DRUGS
AND DRUG COMBINATIONS

Many standard of care chemotherapy protocols use drug
combinations. Understanding combination chemotherapy requires
knowledge of the drug categories. Alkylating agents create crosslinks in DNA, causing strand breaks. A particularly useful feature of
this drug class is a low likelihood of cross-resistance between
different alkylating agents or with other classes of drugs. Commonly
used examples include cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, melphalan,
lomustine, dacarbazine and ifosfamide. Antitumor antibiotics
(anthracyclines) act by DNA intercalation, including interference
with topoisomerases. These highly useful drugs are substrates for the
multidrug resistance (MDR) pump. Cross-resistances are relatively
common with drugs in this and other classes, particularly mitotic
inhibitors, e.g., doxorubicin, epirubicin, mitoxantrone, dactinomycin
and bleomycin. Mitotic inhibitors block assembly (vinca alkaloids) or
disassembly (paclitaxel) of the mitotic spindle, e.g., vincristine,
vinblastine, and vinorelbine. Platinum drugs create cross-links in
DNA, similar to the action of alkylating agents, and no crossresistance with other classes of chemotherapeutic drugs is seen.
Commonly used examples include cisplatin and carboplatin.
Antimetabolites, which are analogs of normal metabolites that are
incorporated into DNA, interfere with enzyme activity, transcription,
or translation. With a few exceptions (rabacfosadine, gemcitabine),
these drugs often have significant toxic effects with low efficacy at
veterinary dosages and are not frequently used. Molecular targeted
agents are a new class of drugs, especially tyrosine kinase inhibitors
(TKIs). This class is rapidly expanding in human oncology and
represents the first chemotherapeutics developed specifically for
dogs (ch. 320).

CHEMOTHERAPY PROTOCOLS
Some veterinary chemotherapy protocols consist of using only one or
two agents, but others, especially for lymphoma, may be complex,
with many agents scheduled in combination. Although tempting to
consider chemotherapy protocols as “recipes” for treating cancer,
one must balance employing a strictly designed protocol and
tailoring treatment to the individual. Unnecessary variations from
the protocol should be avoided, but blindly following a standard

chemotherapy protocol without considering the pet’s metabolic
needs or treatment responses can lead to life-threatening adverse
effects or ineffective therapy and disease progression. Monitoring for
adverse effects, disease response, and being ready to adapt to
changes can be vital.
Chemotherapy protocol designs can be complex, requiring detailed
knowledge of drugs and their effects. The safest and most effective
protocols can be designed by veterinary oncologists. Tumor
resistance to individual drugs is common, and combination
chemotherapy may overcome some resistance by attacking different
tumor cellular metabolic pathways. Although combination
chemotherapy could become cumulatively more toxic, careful
scheduling of agents so their effects do not overlap can improve
tumor cell kill without compounding toxicity. The intervals between
treatments on a chemotherapy protocol are also carefully designed to
maintain the highest safe dose intensity.
To help avoid drug resistance, it is important to avoid giving
subtherapeutic doses. It is also important not to modify the planned
doses or dosing schedule in anticipation of a possible toxic event that
has not occurred, e.g., a dog that becomes neutropenic after receiving
doxorubicin is not at increased risk for myelosuppression from other
chemotherapeutics such as cyclophosphamide. Therefore, doses of
other drugs should only be reduced if they actually cause toxic
effects. Supportive care, e.g., antiemetics, also reduces need for
chemotherapy dose reductions. Likewise, if there is disease
progression, an alternative regimen of non–cross-resistant but
effective drugs should be used.

CHEMOTHERAPY DRUG CHOICES
Information on tumor sensitivity to chemotherapies is constantly
changing. Although good, published data are available for some of
the most common cancers in animals, information on other
malignancies often is unavailable or based on small case series. For
rare tumors that uncommonly metastasize, it is difficult to
demonstrate adjuvant efficacy. Since there is commonly a delay from
study completion to publication, the best resources for veterinarians
are the Veterinary Cancer Society (www.vetcancersociety.org),

and scientific literature databases, such as PubMed
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/). In addition to efficacy,
and possibly more important, the final choice of a drug (or protocol)
depends on its toxic effect profile, the owner’s tolerance for sideeffects, treatment goals, cost, and the veterinarian’s level of comfort
in delivering chemotherapy and supportive care.

CHEMOTHERAPY DOSING
Evidence in human and veterinary oncology suggests that optimal
dose intensity improves outcome. Dose intensity, defined as mg/m2
of drug/week of therapy, can be modified by adjusting dose,
intertreatment interval, or both. Because their desired effect is
cytotoxicity, many chemotherapy drugs have narrow therapeutic
margins; that is, the toxic dose is close to the effective dose.
Therefore it is important to be as accurate as possible when
calculating doses. For some drugs dosing is based on “metabolic
body size” (body surface area [BSA], m2) rather than weight.
Although imperfect, this is based on the generalization that smaller
animals have higher metabolic rates and should receive higher doses
on a body weight basis. For some drugs (e.g., doxorubicin) dosing
based on BSA is imperfect, and small dogs and cats should be dosed
at lower rates than larger dogs. Veterinarians should check the
dosing basis for any drug to be used and use a BSA conversion table
(see textbook’s inside cover for weight-surface area conversion
charts) when metabolic dosing is indicated. In human oncology,
dosing is tailored to the individual by monitoring drug levels or
based on patient characteristics, e.g., the appropriate dose of
carboplatin can be calculated from a formula based on the
glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and the desired area under the curve
(AUC). This type of calculation is not usually done in veterinary
oncology; however, similar principles are recognized: in patients
with reduced GFR (increased serum creatinine concentrations)
carboplatin dosing should be reduced.

ROUTES OF ADMINISTRATION

Intravenous (IV)
Most chemotherapy drugs are delivered IV or PO; less commonly,
SQ, IM, or other modes are used. For most IV administrations,
injection into a peripheral vein through an over-the-needle catheter
is safest, reducing the risk of extravasation even with small volumes
(ch. 321). For infusions lasting longer than 30 minutes, a throughthe-needle catheter is less likely to become dislodged. For long
infusions, e.g., timed drug delivery or diuresis with nephrotoxic
drugs, infusion pumps are recommended to ensure continued, even
administration. Vascular access may become a problem in small dogs
and cats receiving chemotherapy. Because the risk of extravasation is
greater in these animals, a SQ implantable vascular access port may
ease timely drug delivery and reduce stress. Ports for veterinary use
are available from Norfolk Vet Products, Skokie, Illinois
(www.norfolkvetproducts.com).

Oral
Most oral medications are administered as tablets or capsules.
Tablets must not be broken for personnel safety reasons, because
distribution of a drug may not be uniform throughout a tablet, or the
tablet may be enteric-coated (e.g., chlorambucil). For small animals,
reformulation of oral medications into smaller capsule sizes by a
reputable compounding pharmacy specially equipped for handling
cytotoxics can be considered.

Intracavitary, Intralesional, Topical, Intra-arterial,
Intra-thecal, Encapsulation
Platinum drugs may be delivered to dogs as an intracavitary infusion
into the pleural, pericardial, or peritoneal cavities, or intravesicularly
(into the urinary bladder). Intralesional chemotherapy usually
involves suspension of a chemotherapeutic agent in a vehicle.
Cisplatin, bleomycin, or 5-fluorouracil have been prepared in sterile
sesame oil or bovine collagen matrix for this purpose. Mixtures are
injected into a tumor, creating high drug exposure to tumor cells and
minimal systemic drug levels. This avoids the risk of systemic
toxicosis. Intralesional chemotherapy is used to treat small, easily
accessible tumors and great care must be taken to avoid exposure of

personnel; spillage occurs easily and drugs may leak from injection
sites. Electrochemotherapy uses permeabilizing high-intensity
electric pulses (electroporation) applied locally to the tumor to
enhance tumor-specific uptake of systemically or locally
administered chemotherapy drugs.
Topical administration (5-fluorouracil—dogs only) is rarely used
because of drug toxicity and risk of exposure to people applying the
medication or who interact with the dog.
Certain drugs can be given intraarterially or intrathecally for
specific treatment protocols; this is rare in veterinary medicine.
Encapsulation in liposomes can reduce or alter the toxicity of some
chemotherapy drugs. Conjugation of the liposome with polyethylene
glycol reduces clearance by the reticuloendothelial system, producing
“stealth” liposomes with greater circulating time. A liposomeencapsulated doxorubicin formulation has been reported to be less
cardiotoxic in dogs and cats but resulted in a cutaneous toxic effect.

CHEMOPROTECTION
Administering a second drug specifically to reduce host organ toxic
effects of a chemotherapy drug is termed “chemoprotection.”
Chemoprotectants used in human and veterinary oncology include
mesna and dexrazoxane (ch. 321). Mesna reduces risk of cystitis
caused by ifosfamide or cyclophosphamide by binding toxic
metabolites in the urine. Dexrazoxane protects against doxorubicinassociated chronic cardiotoxicosis and reduces severity of
doxorubicin-associated extravasation injury when used soon
thereafter.

SUPPORTING ANIMALS AND
ASSESSING CHEMOTHERAPY
RESPONSE
Nausea, Vomiting

Nausea and vomiting are usually mild when the drugs and dosages
recommended in veterinary protocols are used. However, given the
availability of safe and effective antiemetics and to maximize QoL,
proactive antiemesis should be considered (ch. 48). Veterinarians
may give antiemetics prophylactically (e.g., metoclopramide or
maropitant for 5 days, adding additional antiemetics for
breakthrough nausea), or dispense antiemetics which empowers the
owner to treat at the first signs of nausea (inappetence,
hypersalivation, or lip-smacking) and before vomiting is established.
Ondansetron sublingual wafers are also useful for pet owners to have
on hand, as these can be used at home if vomiting develops,
potentially avoiding an emergency hospital visit. Inappetence or
anorexia on chemotherapy may be a sign of nausea. Antiemetics
should be given before using appetite stimulants. Significant
vomiting is not considered an acceptable side-effect and would
warrant dose reductions.

Prophylactic Antibiotics
The greatest risk to dogs undergoing chemotherapy is febrile
neutropenia (FN)/sepsis. While some recommend prophylactic
antibiotics, antibiotic resistance is a world-wide problem (ch. 7). Use
of antibiotics is controversial (ch. 321). Since the mortality rate for
post-chemotherapy FN in dogs is nearly 9%,1 this complication
should be avoided. FN most commonly affected dogs with
lymphoma, smaller dogs, dogs not in remission (66%), during
induction phase of treatment (72%) and/or receiving a drug for the
first time (54%), and after doxorubicin or vincristine.2 Another study
of dogs with post-chemotherapy FN found primarily Gram-positive
bacteremia on blood cultures, most commonly Staphylococcus.
Organisms most commonly associated with death in humans are
Gram-negative bacteria (presumably entering from the
gastrointestinal [GI] tract). Prophylactic antibiotics tends to be
directed against these GI bacteria.3
A randomized, double-blind study showed that prophylactic
trimethoprim-sulfa given for 14 days from the start of doxorubicin
chemotherapy reduced risks of hospitalization and non-hematologic
toxicoses in dogs with lymphoma, but sepsis was rare.4 One study

found that dogs with neutrophil counts >750/mcL that were not
given antibiotics had low risk for sepsis, although dogs already on
antibiotics were excluded (ch. 321). It was recommended that
antibiotics only be administered to dogs without signs of sepsis if
they had neutropenia <750/mcL, but most veterinary oncologists use
a cut-off of <1000/mcL (Figure 317.1).5
In cats, post-chemotherapy FN is anecdotally uncommon. One
study of 20 cats with FN found most had lymphoma. Vinca alkaloids
and lomustine were the most common drugs associated with FN and
all recovered with supportive care.6

Definitions of Treatment Response
Evaluating treatment response regularly helps to avoid unneeded
expense, toxic effects, and/or tumor progression due to use of an
ineffective drug. Treatment responses are categorized as clinical
remission/complete response (CR), partial response (PR), stable
disease (SD), progressive disease (PD). “Overall response rate”
(ORR) is a combination of CR and PR and “clinical benefit” (CB) is
CR, PR, and SD combined. ORR and CB should not be confused or
considered the same. The Veterinary Cooperative Oncology Group
provides measurement criteria of both solid tumors and lymph
nodes.7,8

Drug Resistance
Resistance to chemotherapy may be either inherent or acquired.
Drugs may be physically unable to reach tumors in “sanctuary” sites
such as the central nervous system (CNS) or that are poorly perfused.
Some tumor cells inherently lack receptors for a drug or are not
susceptible in some other way, e.g., cells that have asparagine
synthetase are resistant to L-asparaginase. Tumor cells may develop
drug resistance spontaneously through mutation. With each cell
division comes the risk of a resistance mutation: the larger a tumor,
i.e., the more cell divisions it has undergone, the higher the
likelihood of resistance. Tumor cells can also develop drug resistance
specifically, e.g., exposure to sublethal drug concentrations can result
in gene amplification of detoxifying proteins.

FIGURE 317.1 Algorithm for interpretation of
neutrophil count after chemotherapy. CBC, Complete
blood count; GI, gastrointestinal.
The problem of cross-resistance to multiple unrelated
chemotherapy drugs is common. The transmembrane pump protein
(P-glycoprotein) is present at increased levels in some tumor cells,
and both the level and prevalence increase with exposure to
chemotherapy. This phenomenon of multiple drug resistance (MDR)
occurs between anthracyclines, mitotic inhibitors, and others. Since
alkylating agents are not substrates for the P-glycoprotein pump,
they become the mainstay of treatment in pets with this type of drug
resistance.

SAFE CHEMOTHERAPY DRUG
HANDLING (VIDEO 317.1 )
Healthcare Workers

People who handle chemotherapy drugs have been found to have
these drugs or drug-metabolites in their urine. Some healthcare
workers have had increased chromosomal aberrations which could
lead to reproductive complications. Studies and meta-analyses have
shown incremental increased risk of infertility and early pregnancy
loss with occupational exposure to chemotherapeutics. Exposure to
cytotoxic drugs can occur during handling, preparation, and/or
administration as well as by handling body fluids of treated patients.
Potential routes of exposure include skin or mucous membrane
absorption, inhalation of aerosols or drug particles, ingestion, and
needle stick injuries. Biologic safety cabinets (BSCs), closed-system
transfer devices (CSTDs), and personal protective equipment (PPE)
markedly decrease risk but do not always eliminate chance of drug
contamination. A National Institute for Occupational Safety and
Health (NIOSH) alert in 2004 and updated in 20169 classifies
handling cytotoxic drugs as an occupational health hazard.
Veterinarians contemplating using chemotherapy should check
local regulations. In the US, USP 800 addresses handling of
hazardous drugs in the healthcare setting; compliance entails
assessment of risk, containment strategies, careful labelling of drugs
as hazardous, facilities and engineering controls, e.g., use of
specifically designed controlled rooms for drug storage and handling,
BSC, CSTD, and PPE. PPE should include double-chemotherapy
gloves for most activities, hair and beard covers, impervious
disposable gowns, eye protection, respiratory protection if needed,
and double shoe covers. Environmental wipe tests are recommended
every 6 months, and competency of trained personnel re-assessed
every 12 months. Medical surveillance is recommended but not
required.
The American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine small
animal consensus statement on safe use of cytotoxic
chemotherapeutics in veterinary practice10 should be studied before
handling chemotherapeutics. Recommendations include designation
of a safety officer, preparation of written policies and procedures,
availability of (material) safety data sheet (SDS or MSDS);
alternative duties for workers who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or
attempting to conceive; restricting storage and use of drugs to
controlled and posted areas, use of PPE, BSC, and CSTD, ready

availability of spill kits, personnel training in use of all these, and
restricting handling hazardous drugs to personnel who have
completed the training.

Pet Owners
Although the greatest safety risk is to the workers who handle
cytotoxic drugs regularly, there is also a risk to pet owners. Family
physicians should be involved with answering the question of safety
or risk to members of a family (especially pregnant women and
young children). Veterinarians are not qualified to provide human
health advice. However, an information sheet on chemotherapy
safety should be provided to owners. Owners who plan to give
cytotoxic drugs orally should use provided gloves and waste (zip
style) bags.
Clear safety guidelines for pet owners handling bodily fluids of
chemotherapy patients are not well established. Some studies have
found drugs in urine for up to 21 days after treatment, although the
highest concentrations occur in the first 3 days. Recommendations
are to treat excreta as hazardous for a minimum of 72 hours after
injectable chemotherapy and for up to 7 days after oral. That said,
drug and metabolite excretion in bodily fluids should be treated with
respect but not panic. Most pet owners avoid contact with their pet’s
urine and feces as part of routine hygiene. Accidental one-time
contact is not cause for alarm if followed by washing. Animals should
relieve themselves in areas restricted from other animals and
children. When giving drugs known to be excreted in the urine, the
pet should urinate into soil with quick drainage. Urine and stool in
other areas should be handled and disposed of as cytotoxic.
Importantly, pet owners who are pregnant, attempting to conceive
or breastfeeding should consult their obstetrician before making a
decision about contacting their pet on chemotherapy, and should not
handle any chemotherapeutic agents.

RADIATION THERAPY IN VETERINARY
MEDICINE
OVERVIEW
The aim of this chapter is to provide a stepping-off point for
clinicians in navigating radiation therapy as a treatment option for
dogs and cats. Synopses are provided on radiobiology, radiation
physics, treatment planning, and a review of the canine and feline
cancers for which radiation can be effective. Radiation oncologists
should be involved early in discussions regarding treatment, as
surgical and medical approaches may influence efficacy and expected
normal tissue effects of radiation therapy.
Radiation therapy is considered one of the most effective ways to
treat cancer and is used in the treatment of around 50% of all human
cancers.2 Radiation therapy is likely underutilized in veterinary
oncology where surgery and chemotherapy have been predominant.
This is likely influenced by the high cost and limited availability of
radiation facilities. Radiation is most often utilized for the treatment
of localized disease, alone or in combination with other cancer
therapies, e.g., surgery, chemotherapy, and targeted therapies.
Radiation therapy is used in treating systemic human malignancies
such as lymphoma, but this is less common in dogs and cats.
Radiation has also been investigated for non-oncologic disease in
dogs, such as meningoencephalitis of unknown origin and
degenerative joint disease.3,4

INTENT OF RADIATION THERAPY
There are multiple techniques for delivering radiation therapy
(Table 318.1). The intent of a radiation protocol is independent of
delivery technique and is either definitive (curative intent) or
palliative. Definitive radiation protocols aim to control tumors as
long as possible with acceptable (low) levels of early and late toxicity.
Early toxicities are usually mild and resolve with supportive care. An
acceptable level of late toxicity has not been clearly defined for dogs
and cats, but a level of 10% has been suggested.5,6 Achieving low

levels of late toxicity relies on either utilizing low doses per fraction
to take advantage of the 4 R’s of radiation biology (e.g., low daily
doses of 2.5-4.2 Gy for 10-20 fractions) or careful geometric/physical
avoidance (as used with stereotactic techniques).

The intent of palliative protocols is relief from pain, bleeding, or
other signs, resulting in prolonged survival with minimal acute sideeffects. Such protocols often involve larger doses per fraction (e.g., 410 Gy) but longer inter-fraction intervals (weekly) or lower total
doses (daily) (4 Gy × 5 daily or 3 Gy × 10 daily).6a-6c Larger doses
per fraction carries risk of late radiation toxicity, but given the
shorter expected survival times, late side-effects are often not a
major clinical concern. Stereotactic protocols can also be successfully
used with palliative intent as has been reported in feline injection
site sarcomas and feline oral squamous cell carcinoma.7,8

EXPECTED ADVERSE EFFECTS IN
NORMAL TISSUES (CH. 321)
Early
Radiation therapy can adversely affect normal tissues near a tumor
or in the radiation path. Early radiation effects occur during or

shortly after therapy (Figure 318.1). Early effects usually occur in
tissues with high proliferative capacities caused by loss of more
differentiated cells, impaired cell production, and inflammation. The
tissues most sensitive to adverse effects are the oral mucosa, skin,
and internal organs with rapid cell turn-over, e.g., cells lining the
gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Supportive therapies for dogs and cats
include topical medications and oral antibiotics, but none have
proven efficacy.9 Prophylactic antibiotics did not decrease rates of
bacterial infection and led to higher rates of resistant infection.10
Despite the lack of strong data for other individual therapies, good
analgesia, prevention of trauma via E-collars, and limiting activity
are wise. Most acute radiation side-effects heal within 2-4 weeks of
completing treatment.

Late
Late effects tend to be irreversible and progressive, and are defined
arbitrarily as those occurring >90 days after radiotherapy in
humans. They tend to occur in tissues with low proliferative capacity,
e.g., heart, lung, muscle, bone, and nerves. Strategies to avoid late
adverse effects include reducing dose per fraction or geometrically
conforming dose to the tumor. Since larger doses are delivered per
fraction with palliative and stereotactic protocols, they have
increased risk of late side-effects. Some late effects (leukotrichia) are
cosmetic but others (osteoradionecrosis) can limit function and
affect quality of life (QoL). Cancer caused by radiation (“secondary”
cancer) is uncommon in dogs (<3.5%11) and can be a significant
concern in young patients. Late effects can be a consequence of
severe acute effects (“consequential late side-effects”) which result in
loss of barrier function and subsequent damage to connective tissues
or vasculature.12

RADIATION BIOLOGY
PRINCIPLES OF RADIATION BIOLOGY AND
FRACTIONATION
Radiation predominately acts by damaging deoxyribonucleic acid
(DNA) within cells.13 When photons are used, about one-third of
damage is due to ionization of DNA, considered a direct effect.
Conversely, two-thirds of damage occurs due to non-DNA molecule
ionizations, causing production of free radicals which in turn ionize
DNA, considered an indirect effect (Figure 318.2). Since cells are
80% water, it may be easiest to understand that ionized water
produces hydroxyl radicals (OH∗) which damage DNA; 1 Gy of x-ray
radiation induces about 40 double-strand breaks (DSBs), 1000
single strand breaks, >2000 base damages, and 30 DNA crosslinks.13 Most damage is repairable, but DSBs are the primary cause
of cellular mitotic death. Dividing large doses of radiation into
multiple smaller doses has been the most common treatment
method since the early 1920’s. Fractionation was based on noting

that rams were not sterilized after a single large dose of radiation
without inducing significant skin toxicity but when the total dose was
fractionated, sterilization occurred without excessive toxicity.13 The
observed benefits of fractionation can largely be attributed to the 4
R’s of radiation biology.

THE 4 (OR 5) R’s OF RADIATION
BIOLOGY
Repair
Radiation usually induces more repairable damage than nonrepairable. Most damage is readily repaired within 6-24 hours.13
Repair of sublethal damage is generally more efficient in normal cells
than in tumor cells. Fractionation takes advantage of this differential
repair,14 by allowing exploitation of a narrow therapeutic window in
which small doses of radiation damage tumor cells and early
responding tissues more than late responding tissues (Figure
318.3). As dose per fraction increases, the probability increases that
repairable DNA lesions will occur in close proximity to other
repairable DNA lesions.13 Multiple, closely spaced DNA lesions
behave like DSBs (i.e., less easily repaired). While this produces a
greater degree of tumor cell kill, large doses per fraction can also
cause greater late (chronic) normal tissue damage.
Physical/geometric avoidance with stereotactic delivery offers a
method to deliver large doses to tumor tissue while sparing normal
slowly dividing tissues and is largely the aim of most stereotactic
delivery techniques.13

FIGURE 318.2 Approximately two-thirds of
photon interactions (red arrow) in the cell result in
the ionization of water and production of the
hydroxyl free radical. This in turn results in damage
to DNA. Approximately one-third of the damage
induced by radiation is due to direct interaction of
radiation with DNA. Reproduced with permission
from Desouky O, Ding N, Zhou G. Targeted and nontargeted effects of ionizing radiation. J Radiat Res
Appl Sci. 2015;8(2):247-254.

Redistribution
Cell cycle phases have different sensitivities to radiation. Most cells
undergo a mitotic cell death, meaning cell death is triggered when
attempting mitosis.13 Cells in the M and G2 phases of the cycle are
most sensitive to radiation. Cells in the S and G0 phases are resistant.
Those in G1 are relatively resistant. Fractionated radiation delivery
allows cells to move from radiation resistant phases of the cell cycle
into more sensitive phases for subsequent fractions.13 The resistance
of cells to radiation is largely due to the availability of high-fidelity
repair (e.g., homologous recombination) during the S phase.
Irradiated cells will sometimes pass through mitosis carrying
damaged DNA (mutations) but then die at later mitoses. Radiation
can also cause cells to become senescent: reproductively dead (i.e.,
unable to replicate progeny). Effectively, senescent cells are not in
the cell cycle even though they are metabolically alive. Normal tissue
stem cells are generally in the G0 phase of the cell cycle and
considered more resistant to radiation, but loss of more
differentiated cells activates the stem cell niche. Cancer stem cells
are slowly proliferating and may be relatively spared by fractionated
radiation, resulting in treatment failures.13

FIGURE 318.3 In this diagram the y-axis shows
number of surviving cells decreasing towards the
bottom of the diagram, while the x-axis shows
increasing dose per fraction toward the right. At low
doses per fraction (x-axis), a greater number of
tumor or early responding cells will die when
exposed to radiation compared to late responding
cells. This is called the therapeutic window (red
arrow). Alternatively, protocols which use large
doses per fraction (e.g., stereotactic protocols) must
avoid late effects by physically avoiding late
responding tissues. Reproduced with permission
from Ahmed KA, Correa CR, Dilling TJ, et al. Altered
fractionation schedules in radiation treatment: a
review. Semin Oncol. 2014;41(6):730-750.

Repopulation

Repopulation of tumor cells during radiation therapy is one of the
most common reasons for treatment failure.13 Proliferation occurs
during radiation in both normal and tumor cells. While prolonged
inter-fraction intervals can reduce incidence of early normal tissue
effects, radiation may also cause stem cells to switch from
asymmetric to symmetric division (i.e., instead of dividing to
produce a stem cell and a progenitor cell they divide into two
progenitor cells).15 This may result in tumor growth rates faster than
in the untreated tumor (accelerated repopulation). In human head
and neck cancer, it occurs ∼21 days into therapy.13 For this reason,
radiation oncologists aim to avoid using protracted treatment
protocols while still giving enough time for repair between fractions
(typically 24 hours).

Re-oxygenation
When oxygen is present at the molecular level during radiation, it
interacts with induced free radicals to form organic peroxides which
cannot be reduced by interaction with sulfhydryl groups.13 In other
words, oxygen causes ionized DNA damage to be permanent and
prevents repair. Cells lacking oxygen are 2-3 times more resistant to
radiation. Tumors are heterogenous, with cells in regions of low
oxygen due to poor perfusion, consumption of oxygen by
surrounding cells (chronic hypoxia or diffusion limited hypoxia), or
cyclic closing of abnormal tumor vasculature (acute hypoxia or
perfusion limited hypoxia). Fractionation allows cells in regions of
low oxygen tension to gain greater access to oxygen as welloxygenated cells die. Furthermore, cells in regions of cyclic hypoxia
may have better perfusion at subsequent fractions. Methods used to
improve tumor oxygenation include oxygen mimetic agents,
hyperbaric oxygen, erythropoietin, or blood transfusions. These
methods have yet to be incorporated into standard of care treatment
protocols due to lack of consensus.13 A meta-analysis of hypoxic
modification for human head and neck cancer found a risk reduction
of 8% for local failure and disease related death.16

The 5th “R”—Radiosensitivity

Different cell types are inherently more or less sensitive to a given
dose of radiation, e.g., lymphocytes and canine mast cells17 are prone
to undergoing interphase (apoptotic) cell death and dying within
minutes to hours following a dose of radiation.13

THE INTERACTION OF RADIATION,
TUMOR MICROENVIRONMENT, AND
THE IMMUNE SYSTEM
The “linear quadratic model,” used to predict cell killing at lower
doses per fraction (2 Gy), may be inaccurate at larger doses per
fraction.18 Evidence suggests that the level of cell kill observed with
hypofractionated stereotactic protocols may be partially reliant on
the interaction of radiation, the tumor microenvironment, and the
immune system.18 The interplay between radiation and the immune
system is currently the topic of much investigation.

CHEMOTHERAPY AND BIOLOGIC
RESPONSE MODIFIERS (CHS. 317 AND
321)
Chemotherapy drugs are commonly given to people at the same time
as radiation therapy in some diseases, e.g., head and neck, rectal,
small cell lung, and other cancers.19 Despite known survival benefits,
increased early tissue responses also develop.13 Conclusions
regarding some agents given to dogs and cats have been conflicting.
Some agents are no longer recommended due to unacceptable local
and systemic toxicities, even after giving doses below maximally
tolerated dose, e.g., gemcitabine.20 Early management of
hematologic or GI side-effects is important to avoid radiation
treatment delays and inferior tumor control.

RADIATION PHYSICS
It is beyond the scope of this chapter to give an in-depth review of
Radiation Physics and The Treatment Planning Process. The
following was compiled with information from the following
sources.20a,20b

Definition of Gray
The most important underlying principle of radiation physics is the
deposition of dose within tissue. Radiation dose is measured in gray
(Gy; 1 joule/1 kilogram), essentially a measure of energy deposited in
a unit of mass.13 The more energy deposited, the more chemical
bonds broken, and the more damage is done. As discussed above,
increased dose of radiation increases the probability of a DSB within
DNA, which may result in cell death.

Generation of Photons or Electrons
Dose is deposited within tissues by high-energy photons or electrons
produced within the radiation machine (linear accelerator, Figure
318.4). Photons originate from the electromagnetic spectrum and do
not have mass or charge. High energy photons liberate electrons
from atoms within the patient. The electrons travel very short
distances via inelastic collisions, causing energy/dose deposition.
Producing photons within a linear accelerator is similar to diagnostic
X-ray machines. High-energy electrons are accelerated and directed
into a high atomic number target, e.g., tungsten. Linear accelerators
produce much higher energy photons than diagnostic X-ray
generators by accelerating electrons through a tube using high
frequency microwaves. Although the production of photons is very
similar between therapeutic radiation machines, the technique for
collimation and delivery varies greatly.

Use of Charged Particles
While photons are used for most veterinary radiation treatments,
charged particles such as electrons and protons are also used to treat
cancer. Because of their charge, their behavior and dose deposition

within patients vary as compared with photons. Charged particles
are directly ionizing, i.e., they deposit energy immediately upon
interacting with atoms within tissue. Electrons are commonly used to
treat superficial tumors, e.g., incompletely excised soft tissue
sarcomas. Protons and other large charged particles are rarely used
in veterinary medicine but are being used more in humans due to
their dose deposition patterns. Protons display a “Bragg peak
phenomenon”: they travel a specified depth into the patient and then
deposit dose within a very short distance of that point.

THE TREATMENT PLANNING PROCESS
IMAGING
As radiation delivery techniques have advanced, reliance on accurate
simulation computed tomography (CT) scans and planning has
increased. Diagnostic CT machines can be adapted using flat
tabletops for simulation, but other considerations must be made for
accurate patient repositioning. All devices used, e.g., vacuum
mattresses, bite blocks, head immobilization masks, and accelerator
couches, must be included in the radiation plan for accurate
calculation (AAPM 176).21 Some devices (couch tops) can attenuate a
radiation beam as much as 15% (AAPM 176)21 and if not accounted
for, could result in unpredictable tumor and tissue effects. CT
scanners must undergo routine quality assurance to ensure the data
generated during imaging are accurate in the radiation treatment
planning software. Then, correct calculations based on tissue
electron density or mass density can be performed. CT scanner data
used for radiation planning are unique to the facility in which they
are created.

FIGURE 318.4 Modern radiation delivery systems
are produced in different configurations and are
capable of delivering radiation therapy in various
ways. A, Accuray Radixact helical radiotherapy

POSITIONING
With the advent of imaging-based radiation dose calculation, patient
position in space becomes important. Accurate repositioning permits

smaller margins to account for error (planning target volume [PTV]).
This results in less normal tissue dose. Patient positioning needs to
be reproduced with as little variation as possible. Advanced accurate
treatment planning software calculates radiation dose assuming the
pet is in the exact same position for each treatment. There are many
different positioning aids used for this purpose (see imaging section
above).

CONTOURING
When creating a radiotherapy plan, a radiation oncologist must
define organs at risk (OAR) locations as well as the tumor, or target.
The International Commission on Radiation Units and Monitoring
Report 83 defines two anatomical volumes for radiation planning the
gross tumor volume (GTV) and clinical target volume (CTV) and a
third margin, the PTV to account for error (Table 318.1). Linear
accelerators are now designed to have fine tolerances for couch,
gantry, mechanical, and radiation isocenters. They often incorporate
3-dimensional on-board imaging (CT) to ensure accurate daily
patient positioning and delivery. No radiation system is completely
free from systematic error and physiologic motion cannot be
completely eliminated. In certain anatomical locations, internal
target volumes (ITVs) are used to account for motion such as that
caused by respiration. The ITV can be determined by special imaging
studies such as 4-dimensional CT or specialized techniques, e.g.,
abdominal compression, jet ventilation or breath holding.

PLANNING
Manual Planning
The simplest planning technique, manual planning, involves
calculating dose at a specified depth in the patient. It assumes each
patient has a uniform density of water, creating uncertainly in OAR
and target dose. Manual planning is commonly used when
performing palliative radiation for tumors such as osteosarcoma. It is
convenient because it does not require a CT scan, decreasing the
logistical and financial constraints for radiotherapy.

Computerized Planning
When using a computerized treatment planning system, radiation
oncologists calculate a radiation plan by forward or inverse planning.
Forward planning involves choosing beam angles and modifying
devices (e.g., wedges or blocks) and then examining the dose
deposited in the patient. The process is then repeated until a desired
dose deposition is achieved. Inverse planning relies on treatment
planning software to modify the intensity of the beams using the
multileaf collimator (MLC) to achieve predefined goals. All radiation
planning is a tradeoff between target and OAR dose, therefore
inverse planning also requires continual feedback from the planner
in an iterative manner to achieve the optimal plan (Figure 318.5).

Intensity Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT)
Modulating the intensity of the beam using the MLC results in
improved target dose conformity and increased sparing of OARs.
IMRT is a commonly implemented technique in both human and
veterinary radiation therapy. It is integral to many advanced
techniques, e.g., volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) and
helical radiotherapy (Tomotherapy), which have improved dose
conformity and treatment times.

Dose Volume Histogram (DVH)
After a radiation plan is completed, the quality of the plan can be
evaluated by investigating the DVH, a graphical representation of
target and OARs doses, and the isodose curves on the CT scan
(Figure 318.5). Both representations are needed to adequately
examine the quality of a plan, as they are complimentary, e.g., the
DVH may identify a “hot spot” within the plan, but its location can
only be identified when evaluating isodose curves on the CT scan. A
typical linear accelerator-based radiation therapy treatment is
depicted in

Video 318.1.

CLINICAL APPLICATIONS OF
RADIOTHERAPY
NASAL NEOPLASIA
The primary concern when treating nasal tumors is progression of
local disease, thus most studies have evaluated surgery and
radiation. Surgery has often resulted in short survival times and a
disproportionately high degree of morbidity.22 Thus, radiotherapy is
considered standard of care treatment for dogs with nasal tumors.
Most published radiation treatment protocols are definitive and
conventionally fractionated, with median survival times that average
about 14 months, but vary dramatically.23 Generally, clinical signs
resolve in most dogs and their QoL is very good for months. Tumor
stage is an important prognostic factor. Other prognostic factors are
age, presence of epistaxis, duration of clinical signs, metastatic
disease, and histologic subtype.24 In cats, radiation is considered the
treatment of choice, including for nasal lymphoma.25
Stereotactic (stereotactic radiation therapy [SRT]) delivery has
been utilized in treating nasal cancer in dogs with outcomes similar
to definitive radiation therapy. Additional studies are needed to
evaluate SRT and its adverse effects.26 Palliative radiation therapy is
a reasonable option in pets with locally or distantly advanced nasal
neoplasia. Most dogs exhibit either partial or complete resolution of
their clinical signs after palliative radiation.27
Acute expected normal tissue effects may include inflammation of
the gingiva (mucositis) and skin (desquamation) surrounding the
nasal cavity and reduced tear production. Chronic or long term
expected normal tissue effects should be rare (<10%) but can include
cataracts, chronic dry eye and oronasal fistula. Side-effects to the
central nervous system (CNS) are rare but possible.27b

ORAL NEOPLASIA
Surgery is considered the most aggressive and effective treatment
modality for oral tumors, but many oral tumors respond well to

radiation, including acanthomatous ameloblastoma, squamous cell
carcinoma, and melanoma.28-30 Fibrosarcoma is likely less sensitive
to radiation therapy.31 Response rates for melanoma are as high as
80-90%.30 Radiation can be used for microscopic disease after
incomplete resection of oral tumors or for palliation. Acute expected
normal tissue effects may include mucositis and desquamation.
Chronic or long term expected normal tissue effects should be rare
(<10%) but can include oronasal fistula and osteoradionecrosis.

CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (CNS)
NEOPLASIA
Brain Tumors
It is not known whether radiation, surgery, or both provides the best
outcome for dogs with brain tumors. Fractionated, curative intent
radiation therapy has consistently been shown to provide good
outcomes for dogs diagnosed with primary brain tumors with a
median survival time of about 19 months.32 Limited data suggest
radiation alone results in a similar outcome to surgery followed by
radiation.33 SRT survival outcomes appear similar to conventionally
fractionated radiation therapy,34 but the large dose per fraction may
increase risk of adverse effects (up to 36-77%).34,35 Adverse CNS
effects are usually steroid responsive.34,35

Pituitary Tumors
Surgical removal is likely the treatment of choice for small (less than
8-10 mm) pituitary tumors in dogs and cats (chs. 280 and 293).
While it is less common for dogs or cats with pituitary tumors to
exhibit complete resolution of their endocrine abnormalities after
radiation therapy, it is highly likely that radiation will result in the
resolution or marked improvement of neurologic signs caused by
surgically inaccessible tumors.36 In dogs, survival times are about 2
years with definitive radiation. SRT has not improved long-term
outcome.35-37 Cats diagnosed with acromegaly due to a pituitary
tumor can be treated with SRT, most require less insulin and their
median survival is about 35 months.38 However, as in dogs with
pituitary tumors, cats treated with radiation continue to exhibit
evidence of acromegaly and related issues following radiation.

CUTANEOUS AND SUBCUTANEOUS
NEOPLASIA
Soft-Tissue Sarcomas (ch. 324)
The most effective use of radiation in treating soft-tissue sarcomas is
in the microscopic disease setting, usually after incomplete or
marginal surgical excision. Three studies have reported long term
survival when definitive, conventionally fractionated radiation was
delivered after incomplete excision of soft-tissue sarcomas.39-41
Median survival times (MSTs) ranged from 60 months to not
reached, with a 17-31.4% risk of recurrence and a time to recurrence
of 23 months to >26 months. One study included dogs with oral
tumors, which may have artificially increased recurrence rates.39
Soft-tissue sarcomas can also be treated in the gross disease setting.
Most publications focus on palliative intent radiotherapy42 using
hypofractionated protocols. Overall response rates were 50% and
progression free survival (PFS) times were 5 to 13.7 months.42,43
SRT was reported to result in PFS of 17 months; however,
comparisons of retrospective studies are unreliable.44

Mast Cell Tumors (ch. 327)
Radiotherapy is commonly used in treating incompletely excised
mast cell tumors. In one study, the median disease-free interval was
not reached and the recurrence rate was 6.7% when definitive
radiation was performed after incomplete resection.45 Since mast
cells seem to be radiosensitive, palliative hypofractionated radiation
protocols provide robust, durable response rates when gross disease
is present, especially when combined with ancillary therapy such as
vinblastine, prednisone and/or toceranib phosphate.46,47 Acute
expected normal tissue effects involve the skin (desquamation)
surrounding the affected area, often the scar in the case of
incompletely excised tumors. Chronic or long term expected normal
tissue effects should be rare (<10%) and can include leukotrichia,
fibrosis or non-healing wounds.

BONE NEOPLASIA (CH. 326)
The use of radiation for primary bone tumors has historically been
focused on pain relief with the use of palliative, hypofractionated
radiation protocols.48 With palliative radiation, 80-90% of dogs
exhibit pain relief, usually lasting 3-4 months.48 SRT has the
potential to emulate the conventional curative-intent approach of
amputation and chemotherapy.49-51 Expected normal tissue effects
are generally mild; however, pathologic fracture rates of 41-63% have
been reported after stereotactic radiotherapy.49-51

MISCELLANEOUS
Many publications have investigated the use of radiation to treat
cancers that may be treated with another first line therapy, e.g.,
surgery or chemotherapy, or cancers that do not have a clear
standard of care. Long-term outcomes after radiation for nonresectable thyroid tumors may be seen with early disease, but
advanced stage thyroid tumors are less predictable.52,53 Thymomas
are generally radiation sensitive. Radiation is used in dogs, cats, and
rabbits if surgery is not possible, or after recurrence.54,55
Radiotherapy for heart-based tumors is available and being
investigated.56-58 Although chemotherapy is often used for the
treatment of urothelial carcinoma in dogs, definitive radiation has
resulted in long-term outcomes.59,60 Radiation may be used for
palliative or definitive treatment in dogs with anal sac apocrine cell
adenocarcinoma.61

PRINCIPLES OF CANCER IMMUNOLOGY
OVERVIEW
Clinical and experimental evidence provides the basis for our
understanding the immune system’s role in controlling initiation of
cancer, cancer progression, the nature of immune regulation in
cancer, and a complex mix of intersecting and often opposing innate
and adaptive immunological mechanisms. Key to cellular cancer
immunity are myeloid and natural killer (NK) cells (innate
immunity), and effector T and regulatory T cells (adaptive

immunity).1,2 Cancer immune responses are initiated and shaped
primarily by myeloid cells, particularly dendritic cells, which present
tumor antigens and regulate the development of effector and
memory T cells. The dendritic cell–T cell interaction is the key
process regulating the initial activation and expansion of effector T
cells, and ultimately the generation of memory T cells. Macrophages
and monocytes are important for modulating T cell responses
initiated by dendritic cells, rather than serving as the primary
initiating cells.

CD8 T AND NK CELLS
The 2 immune cells responsible for direct tumor killing are the
cytotoxic effector CD8 T cell and the activated NK cell. These cells
kill tumor cells by contacting tumor cells and secreting molecules
that cause membrane disruption and induction of apoptotic
pathways, leading to rapid cell death.3 An individual effector CD8 T
cell can kill up to 20 tumor cells per day, with tumor cell killing often
requiring the cooperation of multiple CD8 T cells. Thus, relatively
small numbers of effector CD8 T cells can eradicate tumors when
properly activated. While CD4 T cells do not kill tumor cells directly,
they have an essential role in initiating and sustaining tumor
immunity and supporting the activity of CD8 T cells. Effective cancer
vaccines induce the expansion and activation of both CD4 and CD8 T
cell populations. Unlike T cells, NK cells can be activated directly by
tumor cells without need of antigen presenting cells. Therefore, NK
cells cannot be generated by cancer vaccines.

REGULATORY T CELLS (TREGs)
Tregs, generated at the same time as effector T cells, have key roles
in downmodulating tumor immunity and serve as a check on
excessive T cell activation and development of autoimmunity.
Expanded populations of Tregs in blood, tumor tissues, and tumor
draining lymph nodes are often found in dogs with cancer, and are
associated with cancer immune suppression.4 Therefore, several

cancer immunotherapy strategies deliberately target Tregs for
elimination to relieve tumor immune suppression (see below).

MYELOID CELLS
Monocytes, neutrophils, and tumor macrophages potently suppress
tumor immunity. Their role is so critical that numerous strategies
include eliminating these cells from the tumor microenvironment
(TME) or to reprogram their immune suppressive pathways,5 e.g.,
depleting tumor associated macrophages using repurposed drugs to
block key chemokine signaling pathways can lead to spontaneous
tumor regression in dogs with metastatic osteosarcoma6 (Figure
319.1).

TUMOR SURVIVAL STRATEGIES
Tumors employ several strategies to avoid immune elimination (ch.
316), including both active and passive immune avoidance
strategies, e.g., tumors and infiltrating myeloid cells can secrete
potent immune suppressive molecules (e.g., interleukin [IL]-10,
tumor growth factor-beta) and produce enzymes that deplete key T
cell metabolites (e.g., arginase, indoleamine deoxygenase).7
Alternatively, particularly under immune selection pressure from T
cells, tumor cells can downregulate their expression of major
histocompatibilty complex (MHC) molecule, lose expression of
tumor antigens, and mutate key cytokine signaling pathways,
especially the interferon-gamma pathway.

IMMUNOTHERAPY BY ACTIVATION OF
INNATE IMMUNITY
Cancer immunotherapy, pioneered by the surgeon William Coley,
used bacteria and their secreted molecules to activate innate immune
responses to treat unresectable sarcomas (ch. 324). Our
understanding of key cells and molecules that regulate innate

immune response has advanced, but many principles established in
those early clinical trials still apply, e.g., innate immune activation
must be applied repetitively and sustained for relatively long periods
of time (months) for effective control of tumor growth and
metastasis. In addition, the innate immune system must be activated
to high levels, approaching immune toxicity, to induce anti-tumor
activity.
Specific ligands can now be used to activate selected innate
immune signaling pathways, including toll-like receptor (TLR) and
the Nod-like receptor (NLR) pathways. The best-known example of
an NLR agonist used for effective immunotherapy of canine cancer is
the immunotherapeutic liposomal muramyl tripeptide (MTP). This
drug has been shown to elicit effective tumor immunity, in part by
activating lung macrophages and suppressing tumor metastasis in
dogs with osteosarcoma (ch. 326).8,9 Activators of TLR signaling
pathways, including liposomal TLR agonists and, recently,
attenuated live Listeria monocytogenes, have also shown activity in
osteosarcoma in dogs.10

FIGURE 319.1 Cellular immune pathways in
cancer. NK, Natural killer; Treg, regulatory T cell.
Given the general immune suppressive properties of myeloid cells
(macrophages, monocytes, neutrophils) in cancer patients, removal
of these cells from the TME or modification of their immune
suppressive properties offers new targets for cancer immunotherapy.
Recent work with currently approved drugs and in vitro screens, has
identified 2 drugs (losartan and propranolol) with potent immune

modulatory activity in dogs. Both drugs target myeloid cells.
Losartan targets inflammatory monocytes. Propranolol targets
immune suppressive monocytes and neutrophils (known collectively
as myeloid derived suppressor cells [MDSCs]). Use of such drugs can
lead to depletion of tumor macrophages and inhibition of MDSC
mobilization and function.11,12 Toceranib (Palladia), a tyrosine
kinase inhibitor approved for treatment of mast cell tumors in dogs,
also has immune modulatory activity and induces depletion of both
Tregs and MDSC.13 Thus, these orally available drugs, with wide
safety margins in the case of losartan and propranolol, can be used to
deplete and reprogram macrophages and remove much of the
immune suppressive stromal cell burden in the TME, thereby
allowing existing anti-tumor T cells to generate renewed activity and
improved tumor control.

ANTI-CANCER VACCINES
The goal of vaccinating against cancer began decades ago and
continues to attract considerable interest in cancer immunotherapy.
However, there are few success stories in which vaccines alone
achieved meaningful cancer control in large numbers of patients.
Thus, current cancer vaccine trials now typically include additional
immune modulatory therapies, such as checkpoint targeted
antibodies. Cancer vaccines can consist of whole tumor cells or cell
lysates, tumor proteins or peptides, or tumor genes expressed as
DNA vaccines, or even tumor RNA. Vaccines in trials were delivered
using a variety of vector systems, including conventional vaccine
adjuvants, viral vectors, plasmid DNA vectors, or as RNA transfected
into dendritic cells. Nonetheless, vaccination alone is generally not
effective in eliminating existing tumors, especially larger tumor
masses.
Oncept, a canine vaccine targeting the melanoma antigen
tyrosinase, is approved for treatment of melanoma in dogs (chs. 258,
323). It has been evaluated in a number of trials, with conflicting
evidence of both success and failure.14 Other vaccines for cancers in
dogs are in later stages of development, including vaccines against
telomerase (lymphoma), GD2/3 (melanoma, osteosarcoma), CD20

(lymphoma), and Her2/neu (osteosarcoma) (chs. 258, 322, 323,
326).10,15-17 If past vaccine trials are instructive, it is likely that most
or all of these new cancer vaccines will need to be paired with other
immune modulating drugs to achieve successful cancer control.

CHECKPOINT MOLECULE-TARGETED
IMMUNOTHERAPIES
HUMAN TRIALS
The field of cancer immunotherapy underwent tremendous interest
and expansion beginning a decade ago. Immune therapies targeting
immune suppressive checkpoint molecules expressed by T cells and
antigen presenting cells demonstrated remarkable activity against a
number of advanced cancers in humans. These immune checkpoint
targeted antibody therapeutics initially focused on the CTLA-4, PD-1,
and PD-L1 checkpoint molecules, and were markedly effective in
removing the immune suppressive signals that held T cells in check
within tumors and prevented their full activity. T cells also express
many other checkpoint molecules, including both inhibitory
molecules (e.g., CTLA-4, PD-1) and stimulatory molecules (e.g.,
OX40, 4-1BB), and all are being targeted in ongoing human trials
(Figure 319.2).

CANINE TRIALS
Trials evaluating canine PD-1 and PD-L1 antibodies in dogs with
cancer did indicate some tumor responses.18 Notably, most
responses were observed in dogs with melanoma, including some
with advanced lung metastases. A canine CTLA-4 therapeutic
antibody is also nearing clinical trials in dogs.19 It is likely that a
canine checkpoint antibody will be available for treating dogs with
cancer in the near future. The human experience with checkpoint
antibodies predicts that the tumors most likely to respond to
immune checkpoint blockade are those with high numbers of
infiltrating T cells, including melanomas (chs. 258, 323),

uroepithelial cancers (ch. 330), and some high-grade sarcomas (ch.
324), whereas immunologically “cold” cancers such as osteosarcoma
(ch. 326) and glioma (ch. 245) are unlikely to respond.

ADOPTIVE CELL THERAPY
ADOPTIVE CELL THERAPY IN HUMANS
Cancers can be treated by expanding large numbers of activated T or
NK cells from blood, using bioreactors, and then infusing the cells
back into the patient to seek out and destroy tumor cells. A recent
approach, which has revolutionized the treatment of certain types of
leukemias and lymphomas in humans, is to expand the patient T
cells in vitro, and then transduce the cells to express a so-called
chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). These engineered CAR T cells are
targeted specifically to a tumor antigen, generally one expressed only
on tumor cells. Thus, CD19 and CD20 CAR T cells, targeting the
molecules CD19 and CD20 expressed by malignant B cells in acute
leukemia or lymphoma, can completely eliminate tumor cells and in
some cases induce sustained remissions. Indeed, a number of
patients have been effectively cured by a single administration of
CAR T cells. The CAR T cell technology is effective for treating
hematopoietic cancers but is less effective for treatment of solid
cancers such as glioblastoma and osteosarcoma, for reasons that are
still being elucidated.

FIGURE 319.2 Major immunotherapeutic
approaches employed currently in canine oncology.
CAR, Chimeric antigen receptor; NK, natural killer.

ADOPTIVE CELL THERAPY IN DOGS
Several small CAR T cell trials have been conducted in dogs with
lymphoma (ch. 322), using either CD19 or CD20 canine CAR T
cells.20 These studies have established the safety of CAR T cells in
dogs, but have not achieved long-term disease remissions, possibly
related to the number of CAR T cells infused or because the rapid
generation of antigen escape variants are no longer recognized by the
CAR construct. Other CAR targets are being considered in dogs,
including epidermal growth factor receptor and the checkpoint
molecule B7-H3, expressed by osteosarcoma and glioma cells.
Ultimately, the field is moving towards the development of
“universal” CAR T cells that can be administered to any patient,
regardless of MHC matching, which would provide a true off the
shelf cellular immunotherapy option.

Other adoptive cell transfer technologies are being explored in
dogs with cancer. Non-specific activation of T cells and in vitro
expansion, together with administration of a tumor lysate vaccine, is
being offered commercially for dogs with osteosarcoma, in either an
adjuvant or therapeutic setting (ch. 326).21 Canine in vitro
expanded NK cell therapies, together with inhaled IL-15
administration, are being developed.22

OUTLOOK FOR CANCER
IMMUNOTHERAPY IN VETERINARY
MEDICINE
The use of immunotherapy to manage cancer in dogs and cats is
likely to continue to expand, given the promise of non-toxic and
lasting therapies for many previously untreatable cancers. The
human experience suggests that most widely successful early
veterinary cancer immunotherapies will be checkpoint molecule
targeted antibodies and adoptive cell therapies. A successful
checkpoint antibody could be used alone, or more likely paired with
other cancer treatment modalities, including radiation therapy,
targeted therapies, and cytotoxics. We already have examples of
successful antibody therapeutics in dogs, including an IL-31
neutralizing antibody (CytoPoint, lokivetmab; ch. 227), and recently
in cats with the launch of a nerve growth factor neutralizing antibody
(Solensia, ch. 143). Cell therapy products such as CAR T cells are
much more expensive to manufacture than therapeutic antibodies,
but the upside is that only a single treatment is necessary, and has
the potential to cure cancers, especially hematopoietic cancers. Thus,
veterinary oncology is entering the age of effective immunotherapy,
which will undoubtedly transform how cancer is managed in our
canine and feline patients.

DEFINITIONS AND DRUG TYPES
Molecular targeted therapy is an innovative approach to target
specific molecules to cause functional changes. A principal
application in veterinary medicine is anticancer therapy. There are 2
major types of drugs: small molecules and antibodies (primarily
monoclonal antibodies). Small molecules act on cell membrane
surface protein targets and those in intracytoplasmic and
intranuclear locations. Antibodies act mainly on cell membrane
surfaces of target proteins. This chapter focuses on molecularly
targeted drugs approved or conditionally approved by the U.S. Food
and Drug Administration (FDA).

TOCERANIB (TOC; PALLADIA, ZOETIS)
IN DOGS
Mechanisms of Action
TOC is an orally administered small molecule drug designated a
multikinase inhibitor. It acts on multiple receptor tyrosine kinases
(RTKs), including KIT, vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2
(VEGFR2), and platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR)
beta.1,2 Launched in the U.S. and Europe in 2009 to treat recurrent
Patnaik grade 2 and 3 cutaneous mast cell tumors (MCTs, ch. 327),
TOC acts directly by inhibiting transmitting KIT signals with gain-offunction mutations and indirectly by controlling angiogenesis
through PDGFR and VEGFR inhibition. TOC also induces regulatory
T cell suppression, demonstrating immunomodulatory effects.3,4

Dosage

In a study of TOC efficacy in dogs with various malignancies, the
maximum tolerated dose was 3.25 mg/kg q48h.2 However, in a
Phase 3 study of dogs with MCTs using that dose, it was reduced in
19.5% of the dogs and the drug was suspended in 48.3% due to
adverse events (AEs).1 In a drug study of dogs with solid tumors
given TOC (2.4-2.9 mg/kg q48h), mean plasma concentrations 6-8
hours after administration were significantly higher than those at
which target inhibition occurs.5 Based on these results, many
oncologists administer TOC at a dose of 2.4-2.9 mg/kg q48h or 3
times a week (e.g., on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday).

Common Adverse Events (AEs) and Dosage
Reductions (Video 320.1

)

Common AEs associated with TOC in dogs include gastrointestinal
(GI) toxicosis (anorexia, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, GI
bleeding), myelotoxicosis (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia), and
musculoskeletal disorders (myalgia, lameness).1,2 GI AEs are most
common.5 With mild to moderate GI toxicosis, TOC can usually be
continued but supportive treatment is beneficial. If severe GI
toxicosis occurs, TOC should be discontinued, and supportive care
given until clinical signs improve. If AEs resolve and the quality of
life (QoL) improves, TOC therapy can be resumed; however, a dosage
reduction is usually required. In principle, TOC dosages should be
reduced by 0.25-0.5 mg/kg, but effective blood levels are likely
maintained if the dosage is adjusted to ≥2.4 mg/kg.5 A change in
dosing frequency from every other day to 3 times a week could also
decrease mild toxicoses. Co-administration of gastric acid secretion
inhibitors, e.g., H2 blockers or proton pump inhibitors, is often
effective in dogs with or at a high risk of GI bleeding. Ondansetron or
maropitant are often effective for anorexia, nausea, and vomiting,
and metronidazole and/or loperamide is usually effective for
diarrhea. However, it should be noted that any “AE” could in fact be
caused by cancer progression, which may not be obvious.

Uncommon Adverse Events (AEs) and Dosage
Reductions
Other less frequent TOC-related AEs include neutropenia, which
usually does not require a dose suspension or reduction unless
counts fall <1500/mcL. If neutropenia with a left shift is observed,
TOC-related neutropenia should be differentiated from neutropenia
associated with sepsis, such as seen with bacterial peritonitis and/or
GI perforation (ch. 265). TOC-related lameness is usually acute and
mostly reversible with TOC suspension and the administration of
analgesics, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
or tramadol (ch. 6). Other reported TOC-related AEs include
depigmentation,5,6 hypertension,7 and hypothyroidism with
prolonged TOC administration.8

Direct Actions of TOC
MCTs1,6 and GI stromal tumors (GISTs)9 are 2 of the few tumors
that respond to the direct actions of TOC (

Video 320.2). The

prevalence of c-KIT mutations in canine MCTs is 8-45%, and
mutations are commonly found in exons 11, 8, and 9.10 c-KIT
mutation rates are also high among highly malignant canine MCTs.
MCTs with internal tandem duplication (ITD) mutations in exon 11
are known for high recurrence and metastatic rates.10 In contrast,
MCTs with ITD mutations in exon 8 have recently shown possible
long-term survival.11
In a randomized, double-blind clinical study of 145 dogs with
grade 2 or 3 MCT (unresectable) treated with TOC, the response rate
(RR) at 6 weeks was 42.8% (complete remission [CR], n = 21; partial
remission [PR], n = 41), and the overall biologic RR was 60% after
adding 16 dogs with stable disease (SD) to the study.1 The RR of cKIT mutation-positive MCTs to TOC was approximately twice that of
c-KIT mutation-negative MCTs (69% vs. 37%), and the RR was
higher in dogs without lymph node (LN) metastasis than in those
with LN involvement (64% vs. 46%).1 Although the MCT grade did
not affect RRs, it did affect the period of non-progression. Grade 3

MCT cases also showed earlier recurrence than did the dogs with
grade 2 MCT.1

Indirect Actions of TOC (Off-Label Use)
TOC acts indirectly on many tumor cell types and tends to be more
effective in treating epithelial malignancies. Various malignant
tumors in dogs are sensitive to these indirect actions (Table 320.1).
The efficacy of TOC as an adjuvant therapy has not been established
in canine osteosarcoma or hemangiosarcoma.4 However, a
multicenter retrospective study of 92 dogs with various
adenocarcinomas suggested that TOC is potentially efficacious as an
adjuvant therapy.3

Combining TOC and Other Medical Therapies
The combined use of TOC with prednisone, NSAIDs, and/or
metronomic chemotherapy (including low-dose cyclophosphamide)
appears to be safe in dogs.6 If GI toxic effects due to TOC and NSAID
therapy are of concern, NSAIDs and TOC could be administered on
alternate days. Cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agent dosages should
also be reduced when administered with TOC.4

Combining TOC With Radiation Therapy (RT)
In a multicenter prospective study of 17 dogs treated with
hypofractionated RT (ch. 318), TOC, and prednisone to treat MCTs
with non-surgical macroscopic lesions, the RR was 76.4% (CR =
58.8%, PR = 17.6%) and the progression free interval (PFI) was 316
days.12 All RT-related dermatologic toxic effects observed in this
study were grade 1, and the favorable tolerability of the combined
therapy was confirmed. TOC and hypofractionated RT combination
therapy was tolerable in dogs with inflammatory mammary
carcinoma.13

TOC IN CATS (

Video 320.3)

Phase 1 TOC trials have not been performed in cats, but TOC has
been used at similar doses to those used in dogs (2.5-2.8 mg/kg,
q48h or 3 times/week).14,15 The AEs in cats are similar to those in
dogs; GI toxic effects are less common. Grade 3-4 hepatotoxicosis
was noted in a small number of cats.14,15 In a retrospective study, 55
cats treated with TOC for various malignancies (excluding those
treated with NSAIDs or chemotherapy), GI toxicoses (including
anorexia, 21.8%), thrombocytopenia (16.3%), neutropenia (9.7%),
azotemia (14.5%), and increased alanine aminotransferase activities
(7.2%) were noted.14 TOC has been shown to act directly in cats with
MCT15 (ch. 327); however, indirect actions have not been
demonstrated. In a retrospective study of cats treated with TOC ±
NSAIDs for oral squamous cell carcinoma (ch. 258), survival time
(ST) was significantly prolonged. Since NSAIDs can be associated
with prolonged ST, sole TOC efficacy needs to be assessed.16

IMATINIB (GLEEVEC, NOVARTIS);
MASITINIB (MAS; MASIVET, KINAVET,
AB SCIENCE)

Imatinib mesylate, an RTK inhibitor developed to treat chronic
myeloid leukemia in humans, has been used to treat MCTs and
GISTs in dogs and cats.17 Therapeutic doses are determined
empirically in dogs and based on Phase 1 results in cats; dogs and
cats are usually dosed at 10 mg/kg PO q24h (

Video 320.2).17

Compared with TOC, imatinib-related AEs are mild and infrequent
in dogs. GI toxicosis, myelotoxicosis, and increased liver enzyme
activities are rare in dogs. Nephrotoxicosis, GI toxicosis, and
increased liver enzymes have been seen in cats.17
In 2008, MAS, an RTK inhibitor, was marketed in Europe to treat
Patnaik grade 2 or 3 canine MCT (unresectable) (ch. 327). In 2010,
Kinavet-CA1 was conditionally approved in the U.S. to produce MAS,
but the approval was withdrawn in 2015. The therapeutic dosage in
dogs and cats is 12.5 mg/kg PO q24h; a 10-15 mg/kg dosage is
recommended to achieve adequate plasma concentrations.18,19
Imatinib and MAS act directly, but not indirectly, in canine and
feline MCT and GISTs.17,18

VERDINEXOR (KPT-335, LAVERDIACA1, ANIVIVE)
Verdinexor is a selective nuclear export inhibitor that inhibits the
function of exportin1 (XPO1),4 a nuclear export protein that
transports several major tumor suppressors and growth regulatory
proteins from intranuclear to extranuclear locations.4 A Phase 1
study confirmed tolerability and efficacy in about 65% of dogs with
lymphoma (LSA, ch. 322) with a good QoL.20 A Phase 2 study of 58
dogs with untreated or relapsed LSA showed a 37% RR overall and a
71% RR specifically for T-cell LSA.21 The most common AEs were GI
toxicosis (including anorexia and weight loss); however, 95% were
grade 1-2 AEs.21 In January 2021, the FDA conditionally approved
verdinexor as an oral treatment for canine LSA.
