CLIENT INFORMATION
Molecular Targeted Therapy
Your veterinarian has prescribed the following medication for your
dog or cat:
• Toceranib (Palladia)
• Imatinib (Gleevec)
• Masitinib (Masivet)
• Verdinexor (Laverdia)

TOCERANIB (PALLADIA)
1. What should I know about toceranib?
(a) Toceranib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is a medication
used to treat mast cell tumors and many other tumor types
in dogs and cats.
(b) Toceranib works in two ways:
• by blocking a specific biological pathway that inhibits
tumor growth (direct effect).
• by cutting off the blood supply to the tumor (indirect
effect).
2. What are the possible side effects of toceranib?
(a) Diarrhea
(b) Decreased/loss of appetite
(c) Vomiting
(d) Lameness
(e) Weight loss
(f) Blood in the stool

(g) Depigmentation of the skin, particularly around the face
and pads, mainly in dogs
(h) Decrease in the number of neutrophils (a type of white
blood cell in the blood)
(i) Elevated blood urea nitrogen (an indicator of kidney
function in the blood) and liver enzymes, especially in cats
(j) Increased blood pressure
(k) Possibility of decreased thyroid function with long-term
administration

IMATINIB (GLEEVEC) AND MASITINIB (MASIVET
OR KINAVET)
1. What should I know about imatinib and masitinib?
(a) Imatinib and masitinib, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, are
medications used to treat mast cell tumors or
gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) in dogs and cats.
(b) Imatinib and masitinib work by blocking a specific
biological pathway that inhibits tumor growth.
2. What are the possible side effects of imatinib or
masitinib?
(a) Diarrhea
(b) Vomiting
(c) Decreased/loss of appetite
(d) Weight loss
(e) Decrease in the number of neutrophils (a type of white
blood cell in the blood)
(f) Elevated liver enzymes
(g) Proteinuria (excessive amounts of protein in the urine)
(h) Kidney injury, especially in cats

VERDINEXOR (LAVERDIA)
1. What should I know about verdinexor?
(a) Verdinexor is a medication used to treat lymphoma in
dogs.
(b) Verdinexor works by blocking the transport of tumor
suppressor proteins, arresting the cell cycle, and inhibiting

growth of cancerous lymphocytes (lymphoma cells).
2. What are the possible side effects of verdinexor?
(a) Decreased/loss of appetite
(b) Weight loss
(c) Vomiting
(d) Lethargy (decrease in activity level)
(e) Diarrhea
STOP medications immediately and contact your
veterinarian if you notice:
(a) Refusal to eat.
(b) Vomiting or watery diarrhea, especially if more frequent
than twice in 24 hours.
(c) Black tarry stools.
(d) Bright red blood in vomit or stools.
(e) Or if your dog or cat experiences other changes that concern
you.

COMMON PRECAUTIONS FOR ALL MEDICATIONS
(a) These medications should be given to your dog by mouth
(orally). Follow your veterinarian’s instructions for how much
and how often to give medications.
(b) You should keep medication in a secure storage area out of
the reach of children.
(c) If you are pregnant, a nursing mother, or may become
pregnant, and you decide to give these medications to your
dog, you should be particularly careful when handling the
drugs.
(d) Anyone who administers medication to your dog should
wash their hands after handling tablets.
(e) Do not split or break the tablets.
(f) You must wear protective gloves when you clean up the stool,
urine, and vomitus.

OWNER OPINION, TREATMENT
OBJECTIVES, DETERMINING DOSE
Owner surveys about their dogs that underwent chemotherapy
indicate that complications were relatively common but that the
quality of life (QoL) of their pet was good; they had no regrets about
the decision to treat.1-3 The potential benefits of anticancer therapies
should outweigh risk of side-effects, but it is difficult to predict an
individual’s reaction to a specific drug. Drug dose may vary by the
cancer being treated, dog vs cat, breed, age, co-morbidities, pretreatment blood test results (organ function), and the user’s
experience. Common complications and side-effects of anticancer
therapy are generally classified by system and common terminology
criteria and grading schemes have been established.4
The primary objective of administering chemotherapeutic drugs is
to kill as many cancer cells as possible with each dose. Common
cytotoxic agents are dosed using maximum tolerated dose (MTD)
rather than standard pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD)
modeling (ch. 139).5 Expected side-effects are typically well
tolerated by a dog or cat dosed below the MTD. Tolerability is gauged
via grading severity of observed side-effects.4 Most cytotoxic drugs
are dosed by mg/m2. It is assumed that calculations based on body
surface area (BSA) are appropriate predictors of drug
pharmacokinetics. However, limitations have been demonstrated
and dosing all dogs and cats using BSA may cause smaller (<10-15
kg) pets to be overdosed and large dogs to be underdosed.6,7 Thus,
certain drugs, e.g., carboplatin and doxorubicin, may be best dosed
on a mg/kg basis in smaller pets (ch. 317). With the introduction of
novel classes of anticancer drugs, such as small molecule inhibitors,
therapeutic vaccines, or monoclonal antibodies (ch. 319), MTD may
not be the best method of establishing dose. For some newer agents,
in vivo “target inhibition” can be studied to help determine optimal
dosing, which, in turn, may be well below the MTD.8 This does not

always, however, translate to fewer side-effects. An expression long
used to describe the most common complications of anticancer
treatment is a “BAG” of side-effects: Bone marrow (suppression),
Alopecia, and Gastrointestinal (GI).

MYELOSUPPRESSION
ETIOLOGY
Traditional cytotoxic chemotherapy agents are myelosuppressive
because they kill rapidly dividing cells, e.g., bone marrow cells. It is
common for conventional chemotherapy drugs to cause varying
degrees of neutropenia and/or thrombocytopenia since those cells
have relatively brief bone marrow transit times and circulating halflives. Although red blood cells (RBCs) have a longer bone marrow
transit time and circulating half-life, anemia due to chemotherapy is
often observed, especially over the course of longer multi-agent
protocols. Cytopenias may also be present prior to anticancer
therapy secondary to invasion of the bone marrow by cancer.
Severity of cytopenias caused by anticancer therapy is graded from 1
to 4 (Table 321.1).4

NEUTROPHIL AND PLATELET COUNT
NADIRS (CHS. 58 AND 59)
The nadir, or lowest cell count after starting treatment, varies among
chemotherapeutics. Neutrophil nadirs occur 5-10 days (typically ∼7
days) after giving some common cytotoxic drugs, e.g., the vinca
alkaloids (vincristine, vinblastine, vinorelbine), doxorubicin,
mitoxantrone, rabacfosadine (RAB), and the alkylators
(cyclophosphamide, lomustine [CCNU]). Platelet nadirs occur 7-14
days after giving these drugs, although drugs like cyclophosphamide
are more platelet-sparing. Neutrophil and platelet nadirs after
carboplatin may occur later (14-21 days) in both dogs and cats.9,10
Nadirs post-CCNU are more variable and prolonged in cats,
occurring 7-28 days after and persisting as long as 14 days, especially

with higher doses.11 While any cytotoxic agent can induce
neutropenia, clinically significant neutropenias in dogs and cats are
most common after giving carboplatin, doxorubicin, CCNU,
mitoxantrone, vinblastine, and vinorelbine. Cyclophosphamide and
vincristine are less myelosuppressive, but either can cause severe
(grade 4) neutropenia with higher doses or in intrinsically sensitive
individuals.12 Although L-asparaginase is not considered
myelosuppressive, severe neutropenia may occur if it is coadministered with vincristine.13

BREEDS AT RISK
Dogs with the mutation of the ABCB1-1delta (MDR-1) gene have
higher risk of side-effects from some drugs, e.g., vinca alkaloids
(vincristine, vinblastine, vinorelbine), doxorubicin, mitoxantrone,
taxanes, and dactinomycin.14-16 Breeds most commonly affected
with this mutation are Collies (rough or smooth), Australian
Shepherds (miniature or standard), McNabs, Silken Windhounds,
Long-Haired Whippets, Shetland Sheepdogs, and German Shepherd
Dogs.16 Lists of breeds at risk, possible problem drugs, and
information on MDR-1 testing can be found at the Washington State
University Veterinary Clinical Pharmacology Laboratory website
(http://vcpl.vetmed.wsu.edu/). Commonly affected breeds
should be tested for their mutation status. Reducing dosages of
problem chemotherapy drugs is necessary for affected individuals. In
cats, ABCB1-1delta mutations are described that may affect their
chemotherapeutic and other drug sensitivities.17

MONITORING AND GENERAL
MANAGEMENT GUIDELINES FOR
SUBCLINICAL LOW CELL COUNTS
Complete blood cell counts (CBCs) should be rechecked serially
(typically 7 days ± 14 days) post-chemotherapy to identify any
alarming neutrophil nadir. CBCs are repeated prior to administering
a pulse dose of any cytotoxic agent. Generally, neutrophil counts
<1500 to 2000 cells/mcL and platelet counts <75,000 to 100,000
cells/mcL are thresholds. Counts below these thresholds are best
managed by delaying treatment for 2-7 days to allow bone marrow
recovery. A rebound neutrophilic leukocytosis is common after a
neutropenic event. There is risk of bleeding with platelet counts
<20,000-30,000 cells/mcL or systemic infection (sepsis) with
neutrophil counts <750/mcL. Prophylactic antibiotics are often
recommended in subclinically neutropenic pets.
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid,
enrofloxacin, and cephalexin are commonly used (chs. 7 and 140).
Owners should be instructed to monitor their pet for signs of septic
neutropenia, e.g., fever, inappetence, and lethargy. Dose reductions

of 10-25% should be implemented when more severe (i.e., grade 3 or
4) neutropenia develops. However, it is important to note that
neutropenia may indicate that the MTD has been reached or
approached, and may be associated with a better prognosis
(remission duration and survival times) in dogs and in people with
lymphoma.18 Therefore, attempts to completely avoid neutropenia
through conservative drug dosing may ultimately negatively affect
outcome, as it could theoretically precipitate drug resistance and
early relapse. All guidelines are general, since no true standard of
care exists and strategies vary. Cytotoxic drugs affecting both the GI
tract and bone marrow may be more likely to result in febrile
neutropenic episodes because of an increased risk of bacterial
translocation. Studies indicate that risk factors for developing sepsis
in dogs following chemotherapy included lower body weight, the
diagnosis of lymphoma, and the administration of doxorubicin or
vincristine.19,20

GENERAL GUIDELINES FOR PETS
SEPTIC DUE TO LOW CELL COUNTS
Clinical signs associated with chemotherapy-induced neutropenia
include fever, lethargy, and anorexia. Immuno-compromised pets
showing one or more of these clinical signs should be treated
intensively to prevent life-threatening complications. Treatment
usually includes in-hospital intravenous (IV) fluids, antibiotics, and
general support to minimize GI signs. Vital signs, blood glucose,
serum lactate, and electrolytes should be monitored (chs. 119 and
122). Sepsis is usually diagnosed on signs (ch. 128); blood cultures
are rarely necessary or rewarding as bone marrow recovery and
clinical signs associated with severe neutropenia often resolve
rapidly with intensive empirical therapy. A study of 70 dogs with
chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia reported an average
hospital stay of 3 days and a mortality rate of 8.5%.20

RECOMBINANT HUMAN
GRANULOCYTE COLONY STIMULATING
FACTORS (rhG-CSFs)
RhG-CSFs are of questionable benefit, since endogenous G-CSFs
have likely been released during neutropenic episodes. Use of rhGGSFs was associated with longer hospital stays and increased risk of
death, but rhG-GSFs were given to the most ill.20 RhG-CSFs may be
considered in pets with refractory neutropenia and/or chemotherapy
overdose. Cats develop true febrile neutropenia and neutropenic
sepsis less commonly than dogs, even though their nadirs are often
prolonged.21

THROMBOCYTOPENIA (CH. 59)
Transient thrombocytopenia often follows cytotoxic chemotherapy,
particularly with carboplatin, CCNU, dacarbazine, melphalan,
dactinomycin, cytosine arabinoside, and doxorubicin. Clinical signs
are rarely observed with platelet counts >25,000/mcL unless the
platelets are dysfunctional (chs. 171, 175). Pets with severe
thrombocytopenia should be monitored for ecchymoses, petechiae,
and overt bleeding from the GI tract, gingiva, or epistaxis. Trauma
and surgery should be avoided. Certain alkylating agents (CCNU,
chlorambucil, melphalan) may cause cumulative and even
irreversible thrombocytopenia if given chronically.22,23
Chemotherapeutics should be stopped if a downward trend in
platelet numbers is observed or if the count falls <100,000125,000/mcL. The use of thrombopoietic agents is of questionable
value.

ORAL TYROSINE KINASES (CH. 320)
Toceranib phosphate, masitinib mesylate, and imatinib are not
usually as myelosuppressive as traditional cytotoxic agents.
Neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia may occur secondary to

growth signal inhibition.24-27 These cytopenias are usually mild and
reversible but can be severe enough to warrant a treatment delay
(“drug holiday”), until cell counts return to normal. Cytopenias can
be more severe when toceranib is combined with traditional
chemotherapeutics.28-29

DERMATOLOGIC COMPLICATIONS
ALOPECIA AND PIGMENTARY CHANGES (CHS.
12, 320)
Chemotherapy-induced alopecias are common in people and
although cosmetic, they can carry negative psychological impact for
many. Alopecia after chemotherapy is not a common problem in
dogs or cats. Certain canine breeds that have continuously growing
hair may shed more than usual or may truly become partially or
completely alopecic, e.g., Maltese, Bichon Frisé, Poodles, certain
Terrier breeds, Shih-Tzu, and Old English Sheepdog. Alopecia does
not negatively impact QoL and is reversible. Cats most commonly
lose whiskers or facial hair due to chemotherapy. Transient
depigmentation, especially affecting the nose, footpads, lips, and less
commonly the entire hair coat, has been reported in dogs treated
with toceranib phosphate (Palladia) (

Video 320.1), and may

result from KIT protein inhibition in melanocytes.25
Hyperpigmentation and alopecia has been anecdotally seen in
certain breeds, particularly after doxorubicin.

DERMATOPATHY (CH. 12)
A unique and poorly understood dermatologic toxicosis, possibly the
result of drug distribution to the skin, can occur in up to 50% of dogs
given RAB.30-32 Lesions are usually focal to regional, erythematous,
alopecic, and pruritic. They are most common on the dorsum,
inguinal region, and ear canal (otitis). The dermatopathies are
typically low grade and manageable with dose delays and supportive

care, e.g., corticosteroids, antimicrobials, and/or topical
medications.30-32 A phase II study of RAB in dogs with cutaneous T
cell lymphoma (CTCL) reported an overall response rate of 45%,
including 1 complete response and 4 partial responses.33

ACCIDENTAL EXTRAVASATION OF
CHEMOTHERAPEUTICS OUTSIDE A
BLOOD VESSEL
Definitions and Management
Certain chemotherapeutics can cause tissue damage if given perivascular. Drugs are classified as either “irritants” or “vesicants”
depending upon type and degree of tissue damage they incite.
Prevention of extravasation injuries is key to safe and effective
chemotherapy. Ideally, chemotherapy should only be administered
through a long IV catheter placed via the “clean stick” technique (ch.
74) just before administration, in order to reduce the risk of
extravasation. Fluid pumps should be avoided. Simple gravity drip
and manual syringe push are favored. The few exceptions are for
drugs given as longer infusions (dacarbazine, cytosine arabinoside).
Minimal bandaging is recommended during chemotherapy to allow
visualization of the IV catheter site during an infusion. If
extravasation is observed, drug administration should be
immediately stopped. Gentle negative pressure can be applied to
remove as much drug as possible from the leakage site. Negative
pressure should be applied as the catheter is gently removed and
occlusive bandaging avoided.

Irritants
The platinum drugs (carboplatin and cisplatin), dacarbazine,
mitoxantrone, and the taxanes can cause local reactions if
extravasated. Usually there is mild to moderate erythema, edema,
and/or crusting, causing mild to moderate discomfort. Uncommonly,
extravasation of irritants may lead to more serious tissue damage

requiring surgical debridement.34 Analgesia should be provided with
nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or corticosteroids
(ch. 143) and adjuvant analgesic drugs (including antihistamines) as
needed (ch. 6). Antibiotics may be indicated for secondary bacterial
infections and self-trauma should be prevented.

Mild Vesicants
Mild vesicants include the vinca alkaloids. Anthracyclines
(doxorubicin, epirubicin), dactinomycin, and mechlorethamine are
worrisome vesicants. If a vinca alkaloid (vincristine, vinblastine,
vinorelbine) is extravasated, one should apply warm compresses for
15-20 minutes, q6h, for 2-3 days. Some clinicians instill sterile saline
(5-10 mL) around the site of leakage to dilute the vesicant. Other
supportive treatments, e.g., topical dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO),
corticosteroids, and local infiltration of hyaluronidase have been
reported but are of questionable value.35 Usually vinca alkaloid
extravasations cause mild to moderate tissue damage and completely
heal within 2-3 weeks.

Serious Vesicants
These drugs can cause severe local tissue damage, sometimes
progressing to dissecting necrosis in the deep tissues. Some require
surgical debridement or, when damage is irreversible, limb
amputation (Figure 321.1). Contrary to vinca alkaloid
extravasation, cold compresses are recommended after extravasation
of doxorubicin or other serious vesicants, typically for 15-20 minutes
duration, q6h, for 2-3 days. Importantly, IV dexrazoxane, an iron
chelator, may markedly reduce or even completely prevent local
tissue damage.36,37 Dexrazoxane (10 times the dosage of
doxorubicin) is given IV as soon as possible (ideally within 3 hours)
after extravasation and repeated 24 and 48 hours later.
Mechlorethamine extravasations can be treated with a 2.5% solution
of sodium thiosulfate, a sulfur group donor, injected IV and directly

into the extravasation site at the same volume as the volume of
mechlorethamine administered.

PALMAR-PLANTAR
ERYTHRODYSESTHESIA (PPES, “HANDFOOT SYNDROME”)
PPES is a common dermatologic toxicosis associated with IV
liposomal doxorubicin. In dogs it causes discomfort, erythema,
alopecia, and ulceration in the axilla, inguinal area, and/or skin
surrounding the footpads.38-42 Cats develop focal chin and limb
alopecia.38-42 Though self-limiting, PPES may warrant treatment
delay or discontinuation. Oral pyridoxine (vitamin B6; 50 mg PO,
q8h) with doxorubicin markedly reduces severity of PPES lesions in
dogs.39

GASTROINTESTINAL (GI)
COMPLICATIONS
MANAGING GI SIDE EFFECTS
GI side-effects from anticancer therapies are often the most feared
by human cancer patients and by owners of cancer-bearing pets, as
they negatively impact QoL. Common GI complications include
hyporexia, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation.
There are multiple mechanisms of the GI toxicoses caused by
chemotherapy. Clinical signs vary and their severity is graded from 1
to 4 (Table 321.2). Nausea and vomiting may result from
stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) in the medulla
oblongata. This occurs via neurotransmitters such as serotonin and
substance P binding to 5-HT3 and neurokinin 1 (NK1) receptors,
respectively. Vomiting from stimulation of the CTZ is an acute
phenomenon, often occurring within 24 hours of drug
administration. The most common agents causing vomiting include
cisplatin, dacarbazine, streptozotocin, doxorubicin, and

mechlorethamine. Poor appetite, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are
commonly caused by direct damage to the rapidly dividing immature
GI enterocytes, usually 1-5 days after administration. The drugs that
commonly cause these clinical signs include doxorubicin, epirubicin,
dactinomycin, mitoxantrone, dacarbazine, vinca alkaloids, RAB, and
taxanes. The tyrosine kinase inhibitors, toceranib, imatinib, and
masitinib, may cause direct GI irritation resulting in anorexia,
nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or hematochezia. Verdinexor, a novel
oral selective inhibitor of nuclear export conditionally approved for
canine lymphoma, has been associated with anorexia (50%),
vomiting (20%), and diarrhea (20%). The cause of these signs is
unclear, but they are mostly mild and self-limiting.43

FIGURE 321.1 Severe extravasation injury in a
Rottweiler with osteosarcoma treated with
doxorubicin 12 days earlier.
NSAIDs, commonly used in cancer-bearing pets for analgesia and
anticancer effects, can cause GI irritation, a complication amplified
when the non-selective drug piroxicam is combined with certain
cytotoxic chemotherapy agents.44,45 Vincristine can cause transient
ileus and constipation in the days following administration via a
neurotoxic effect on enteric motor function. Abdominal discomfort,
poor appetite, nausea, and vomiting may occur as a result.

NUTRITION AND APPETITE SUPPORT

Nutrition for pets with chemotherapy-induced anorexia and weight
loss is critically important (chs. 151 and 163). Pharmacologic
appetite stimulation may also be beneficial. Since a pet may be
hyporexic/anorexic and cachectic secondary to its cancer, poor
appetite and weight loss can be multifactorial and difficult to
manage. Canine and feline-specific drugs can help address this
distressing syndrome with negative impact on outcomes.46
Capromorelin, an oral appetite stimulant, is available in dog and catspecific dose formulations. It is a ghrelin receptor agonist
demonstrated to increase food consumption, body weight, and serum
insulin-like growth factor-1 concentrations, in healthy and
inappetent dogs and cats.47-49 The antidepressant mirtazapine,
available in both oral and transdermal formulations, is especially
effective in cats with anorexia and weight loss secondary to various
causes. The convenient transdermal formulation may improve owner
compliance.50,51 The efficacy of mirtazapine as an appetite stimulant
in dogs is less obvious. Other drugs occasionally used for poor
appetite, despite unknown efficacy, include cyproheptadine (cats),
cannabinoids, and megestrol acetate (dogs). Corticosteroids are
generally avoided as appetite stimulants due to their catabolic
effects, but may be used at low dosages for short durations if not
contraindicated.

NAUSEA AND ANTI-EMETICS
Nausea is a common cause of diminished appetite and ownerrecognition can be crucial. Signs of nausea may include loss of
appetite, hypersalivation, licking the lips, and food
avoidance/aversion. Mild nausea and vomiting may first be managed
by food restriction for 12-24 hours, followed by gradual introduction
of frequent small bland meals. Fasting dogs before giving vincristine
or doxorubicin reduced the frequency of nausea and vomiting.52,53
With most vomiting, use of antiemetics is warranted and IV
crystalloids may be indicated. The centrally acting antiemetic
maropitant, an NK1 receptor inhibitor that can be given to dogs and
cats, is approved to prevent vomiting after cisplatin in dogs and was
effective at reducing vomiting after giving doxorubicin.54-57 The 5HT3 antagonist ondansetron effectively mitigates cisplatin-induced
nausea in dogs.58 Metoclopramide was ineffective against cisplatininduced nausea but effective for vomiting from other causes and may
mitigate nausea secondary to vincristine-induced ileus.59
Mirtazapine not only improved appetite, but it had anti-emetic
effects on cats with renal disease.50

GASTRIC ACID INHIBITORS
The H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors do not have direct
antiemetic effects, but their use may be beneficial for pets with
nausea secondary to gastric acid hypersecretion and/or upper GI
erosion.60 However, prophylactic omeprazole given with the NSAID
piroxicam in cancer-bearing dogs was not protective and increased
risk of GI side-effects. This combination is no longer recommended
in the absence of known or suspected GI erosion.61 A unique aspect
of pets with macroscopic mast cell tumors is that GI signs may result

from hyperhistaminemia and hyperacidity after spontaneous
degranulation or from cytotoxic therapy.62,63 The histamine can
cause excessive hydrochloric acid secretion, low gastric pH, and
gastric irritation via the binding to H2-receptors on parietal cells.
One may consider giving the H1-inhibitor diphenhydramine and H2inhibitor famotidine, but efficacy data is lacking.

DIARRHEA
Mild diarrhea or soft stool can be initially managed by feeding a
bland, highly digestible diet (chs. 151, 152, and 163). With moderate
to severe chemotherapy-induced diarrhea, the antibiotic
metronidazole is often prescribed and is typically effective.64 A
canine-specific plant-based product, crofelemer, inhibits secretion of
chloride ions and water by GI epithelial cells. It is conditionally
approved for treating chemotherapy-induced diarrhea in dogs. The
use of the naturally occurring clay smectite is also beneficial in
treating chemotherapy-induced diarrhea in dogs.65 Probiotics are
often used in dogs and cats to treat acute or chronic diarrhea,
although efficacy data are lacking.66 A study evaluating the effect of
maropitant in preventing vomiting from doxorubicin serendipitously
found that it reduced the frequency and severity of diarrhea in
dogs.56 A study supporting prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfadiazine
(TMS) in dogs with osteosarcoma or lymphoma treated with
doxorubicin demonstrated reduced hospitalization rates and lower
frequency and severity of GI toxicosis.67 The antibiotic tylosin, rarely
needed for acute chemotherapy-induced diarrhea, may be used for
more chronic or refractory diarrhea.68

CHANGING ANTI-CANCER DRUG DOSE
Most mild GI side-effects do not require changing subsequent
chemotherapy dosages, but moderate to severe toxicoses may require
hospitalization for supportive therapy. This should lead to dosage
reductions of 10-25%, protocol modification, drug substitution,

and/or more intensive prophylactic supportive therapy. For example,
in pets with vincristine-induced effects on GI motility, prophylactic
coadministration of metoclopramide and/or replacing vincristine
with vinblastine may be valid options.69

CONSTITUTIONAL SIGNS (LETHARGY,
FATIGUE, WEIGHT LOSS)
Mild to moderate lethargy and fatigue are common after beginning
anticancer therapy but are typically self-limiting. It is important, and
can be challenging, to distinguish treatment-induced lethargy and
fatigue from cancer-induced signs. When lethargy is moderate to
severe, tests to assess for cytopenias, disease progression, or
concurrent disorders should be considered. Extreme lethargy in the
24-48 hours after the first intensive chemotherapy for lymphoma or
lymphoblastic leukemia could be secondary to the uncommon acute
tumor lysis syndrome (ATLS). Weight loss is common in dogs and
cats with cancer and when given chemotherapy. Varying degrees of
weight loss can be observed despite no change in caloric intake (chs.
151, 152, and 163). In this latter scenario, weight loss is likely
multifactorial, possibly due to cancer cachexia, or may reflect the
increased caloric demand in patients undergoing intensive and/or
chronic chemotherapy. Similar to lethargy and fatigue, it is
important to rule out weight loss from other causes. Appetite
stimulants, weight gain drugs, and nutritional support can be
critically important, even if the pet’s appetite is normal. Weight loss,
particularly loss of muscle mass, has been associated with poorer
outcomes in human cancer patients and can be distressing for pet
owners.70

CARDIAC TOXICOSIS
Cardiac toxicosis, acute or cumulative, is an uncommon but well
described issue in humans and pets given doxorubicin. Acute
toxicosis, during IV infusion, consists of transient ventricular
arrhythmias caused by release of histamine and catecholamines and

is not usually worrisome. One study showed no difference in cardiac
arrhythmias during doxorubicin infusion in dogs pre-treated with
diphenhydramine, but dogs with pre-existing cardiac disease were
excluded and the overall rate of arrhythmias during infusions were
low.71 The more serious cumulative cardiac toxicosis is the result of
permanent damage to the cardiomyocytes following oxidative injury
to the sarcoplasmic reticulum. This can lead to reduced contractility,
arrhythmias, and possible irreversible congestive heart failure (ch.
233). In dogs with no pre-existing heart disease, the risk of
permanent cardiac toxicosis is associated with cumulative doses
>180 mg/m2. However, a study on healthy dogs found that
doxorubicin caused decreases in fractional shortening and left
ventricular ejection fractions after cumulative doses as small as 30
mg/m2.72 Risk/benefit ratios must be considered before treating
dogs with either pre-existing heart disease or high cumulative doses.
Monitoring electrocardiograms (ECGs) and echocardiograms are
indicated for any dog being treated with doxorubicin, particularly
those with pre-existing cardiac disease.
In some dogs, doxorubicin must be avoided. Alternatives include
use of similar but less cardiotoxic agents, e.g., mitoxantrone,
dactinomycin, epirubicin, or pegylated doxorubicin. These drugs
may have less efficacy or increased risk of other side-effects.73-75
Another option is to co-administer IV dexrazoxane (10 times the
doxorubicin dosage), an iron chelator known to reduce the risk of
cardiotoxicosis from doxorubicin in people and potentially in
dogs.76,77 A recent study evaluating the cardioprotective benefit of
carvedilol in dogs receiving doxorubicin found some indexes of
diastolic function and electrocardiographic precordial chest leads
were less affected.78

HEPATOTOXICOSIS (CH. 135)
LOMUSTINE (CCNU)
CCNU is hepatotoxic in dogs. Serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
activities increase in up to 86% of treated dogs (ch. 65).79-85 CCNU

causes cumulative and often irreversible damage, with acute liver
failure rarely occurring after a single treatment. ALT activities should
be monitored before each CCNU dose and increases >3 times the
upper reference value indicate the need to delay or discontinue
treatment. The severity of liver enzyme activity and bilirubin
increases is graded from 1 to 4 (Table 321.3). A clinical trial
evaluated co-administering CCNU with 2 hepatoprotectants (Sadenosylmethionine and silybin), finding reduced rates and severity
of liver enzyme activities in dogs receiving the hepatoprotectants.85
In another study, dogs treated with CCNU were given the
nutraceutical alpha-lipoic acid as a hepatoprotectant, but lack of
controls negated any conclusion.86 In general, hepatoprotectants are
recommended for dogs given CCNU. Hepatotoxicosis in cats given
CCNU is less common.87

OTHER CHEMOTHERAPEUTICS
Increased serum ALT activities are reported after giving
streptozotocin to dogs with insulinoma and in dogs receiving
toceranib.88 The vinca alkaloids and doxorubicin are not necessarily
hepatotoxic but are at least partially eliminated via biliary excretion.
Use of these agents should temporarily be avoided or used at lower
doses in pets with hepatobiliary disease, particularly those with
marked cholestasis. Mild to moderate reversible liver enzyme
elevations are also reported with the tyrosine kinase inhibitors
toceranib and masitinib.25,89 Glucocorticoids increase serum
alkaline phosphatase activity in dogs, not cats (ch. 224, 293).

NEUROLOGIC TOXICOSIS (CH. 133)
Neurologic toxicosis is relatively uncommon in dogs and cats.
Vincristine causes ileus in cats and dogs due to a neurotoxic effect on
enteric motor function. The dose-limiting peripheral neuropathy
observed in people is rare.90 The risk of central neurotoxicosis from
vincristine is normally extremely low, but may be higher in dogs

homozygous for the ABCB1-1delta mutation.91 The antimetabolite 5fluorouracil (5-FU;150 mg/m2 IV) can, rarely, cause clinical signs of
neurotoxicosis in dogs.92 At higher doses, 5-FU can be extremely
neurotoxic in dogs. Cats should never be given 5-FU due to fatal
neurotoxicosis.93,94 The alkylator chlorambucil, especially in highdose pulse regimens, may rarely cause reversible myoclonus and
seizures in cats and dogs.95,96 Chlorambucil causes mood alterations
and seizures in people.97,98

NEPHROTOXICOSIS (CH. 134)
ANTI-CANCER DRUGS
Cisplatin (dogs), ifosfamide (dogs and cats), and streptozotocin
(dogs) are recognized nephrotoxicants. Prophylactically, this is
usually managed by intense saline diuresis to dilute their effect.88,99101
These drugs should be avoided in pets with pre-existing kidney
disease and kidney parameters monitored when they are used. Drugs
should be discontinued with increases in creatinine or blood urea
nitrogen (BUN), the severity of which is graded 1 to 4 (Table 321.3).
Doxorubicin has been described as a potential nephrotoxicant in
cats, if the dog dosage is given.102 The drug can be safe for cats at 2225 mg/m2. The extremely low dose that was recommended after the
initial toxicity study (1 mg/kg) may be overly conservative.103 Renal
parameters should be monitored in cats receiving doxorubicin and
the drug discontinued if signs of nephrotoxicosis are noted. CCNU
may be nephrotoxic in dogs, either with a high-dose pulse or lowdose metronomic protocol.23,84

ANTI-INFLAMMATORY DRUGS

Commonly given for their analgesic and potential anticancer
properties, NSAIDs (e.g., piroxicam, carprofen, deracoxib, firocoxib,
and meloxicam) can have toxic effects that are independent of their
cyclooxygenase (COX-2) selectivity. Serum biochemistries should be
monitored with chronic use, especially in pets with questionable or
decreased renal function. The combination of NSAIDs with cisplatin
is too toxic and should be avoided.104-106 Corticosteroids
consistently cause polyuria/polydipsia, negatively impacting both the
pets’ and owners’ QoL.

BISPHOSPHONATES
Bisphosphonates are generally well tolerated. They inhibit osteoclast
activity, which is beneficial in treating osteolytic bone pain and
hypercalcemia. Pamidronate and zoledronate are potent clinically
useful IV amino-bisphosphonates that exhibited possible
nephrotoxicosis in preclinical studies. Clinical studies in cancerbearing dogs showed that they can be safely given to dogs and cats,
alone or combined with other anticancer therapies.107-114 The
duration of infusion appears to play a role in their nephrotoxicity.
Pamidronate should be administered over 2 hours, zoledronate
requires a 15-minute infusion, and both should be diluted in 0.9%
saline.107-114

TYROSINE KINASE INHIBITORS,
CARBOPLATIN
The tyrosine kinase inhibitors toceranib phosphate and masitinib
mesylate can cause protein-losing nephropathy (PLN), which is
sometimes severe.26,27,115-117 Renal parameters, serum albumin,
urinalysis, and urine protein/creatinine ratios should be monitored
and the drug stopped if progressive proteinuria is seen. This druginduced PLN is usually reversible if identified early and the causative
agent is stopped.26,27,115 Carboplatin, unlike cisplatin, is not
nephrotoxic at dosages commonly used in dogs and cats. Carboplatin

is, however, subject to renal metabolism, and studies in cats
confirmed that optimal dosing may be individualized based upon
glomerular filtration rate and area under the curve.118-120

STERILE HEMORRHAGIC CYSTITIS
(SHC)
CAUSATIVE AGENTS
SHC, a recognized complication of cyclophosphamide or ifosfamide,
is caused by direct irritation by acrolein, an inactive metabolite. Risk
of SHC in dogs may depend on the dosing scheme of
cyclophosphamide, cumulative doses, and co-use of furosemide or
the thiol-based compound mesna.121-125 Cats appear be at lower risk
of developing SHC, but caution should be used when predisposing
factors are present, including feline idiopathic cystitis (ch. 311).126
Furosemide is commonly given to dogs treated with high doses of
cyclophosphamide. A study concluded that giving concurrent
furosemide significantly reduced likelihood of SHC (30.3% vs.
10.2%).127 In a study evaluating use of furosemide with metronomic
cyclophosphamide, the incidence of SHC was much lower (3.6%)
than historically reported with metronomic cyclophosphamide
alone.128 Mesna is recommended with ifosfamide and with highdose (myeloablative) cyclophosphamide. Without furosemide, both
have high rates of serious SHC.100,101,129 Ifosfamide also requires
saline diuresis to reduce the risk of nephrotoxicosis.

TREATMENT
Various treatment strategies have been described anecdotally for
SHC. It is imperative to discontinue the causative agent indefinitely
and to confirm SHC by ruling out urinary tract infection (ch. 307),
urolithiasis (chs. 308, 309), feline idiopathic cystitis (ch. 311),
bladder tumor (ch. 330), etc. Signs of SHC generally tend to abate
once the drug has been discontinued, but may take weeks or months

in severe cases. Early detection and drug discontinuation when
microscopic hematuria is observed may improve the chances of mild,
rapidly resolving SHC. Supportive therapy often includes the use of
NSAIDs to control discomfort and inflammation, oxybutynin to
reduce the severity of bladder and urethral muscle spasms, and
analgesics such as gabapentin (ch. 6). Some clinicians use
polysulfated glycosaminoglycan or pentosan polysulfate to help
restore the protective urinary bladder mucosa. In severe SHC,
instilling diluted formalin into the bladder has reduced clinical signs
in a few cases.130,131

HYPERSENSITIVITY REACTIONS
Hypersensitivity reactions are not common but may occur after
giving some chemotherapeutic agents. A true type I, IgE-mediated
anaphylactic reaction may occur after giving L-asparaginase, with
risk increasing with the number of doses (ch. 129). IV Lasparaginase is contraindicated in dogs and cats; IM or SQ routes are
recommended. Pre-treatment with diphenhydramine (1-2 mg/kg IM
or SQ) 15 minutes prior to repeated doses of L-asparaginase is
recommended.
Rapid IV doxorubicin can cause an anaphylactoid reaction caused
by histamine release from mast cells via non-IgE mediated
mechanisms (ch. 129).132 Histamine release can also cause cardiac
arrhythmias and hypotension. In general, doxorubicin is given in
brief infusions (15-30 minutes). If a reaction is noted, the infusion
should be stopped and the pet given diphenhydramine and
dexamethasone. If the reaction was not severe, the infusion can
generally be resumed at half the rate once the apparent reaction has
subsided.
Certain chemotherapy agents can cause relatively severe cutaneous
hypersensitivity reactions (pruritus, flushing, urticaria, facial
swelling) in pets, mediated by their inert vehicles.133-135 Reactions
were reported after either paclitaxel (cats and dogs) or etoposide
(dogs) caused by their carriers: Cremophor EL and polysorbate-80,
respectively, despite intensive pre-medication.132-135 Such reactions
can be minimized by using newer formulations or methods of

delivery, including micellar incorporation of paclitaxel and SQ
administration.136-138

MISCELLANEOUS TOXICOSES
Cisplatin given to cats IV can cause severe, fatal pulmonary edema.99
It is absolutely contraindicated apart from occasional locoregional
administration (electrochemotherapy) or intralesional placement
(impregnated beads).139 Pulmonary fibrosis can be a complication
associated with high cumulative doses of bleomycin in dogs, but is
uncommon.140 In cats, pulmonary hypertension and fibrosis has
been reported following high cumulative doses of CCNU.141
Pulmonary fibrosis is an uncommon complication in dogs treated
with RAB (Tanovea-CA1) but can be fatal.30,31,142
Streptozotocin is a chemotherapy agent that is especially toxic to
the pancreatic beta-cells and is used to treat insulinoma in people
and dogs. An expected potential complication is diabetes mellitus
resulting from complete beta-cell ablation and was observed in 42%
of treated dogs in 1 prospective study.88
Pancreatitis has been reported to occur in a low percentage of dogs
treated with toceranib phosphate.25 The cause-effect relationship
and underlying mechanism have not been established. Appropriate
diagnostic tests are recommended when a dog receiving toceranib
phosphate has clinical signs compatible with possible pancreatitis
and drug discontinuation may be indicated depending upon the
severity of the illness.
Lameness, most likely from muscular cramps, has been associated
with the administration of toceranib phosphate in dogs.25 The
lameness is most typically mild and weightbearing, and resolves with
a short (1-2 doses) drug holiday and an appropriate analgesic
approach. Interestingly, the lameness does not always recur upon reinitiation of toceranib administration.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Side Effects and Complications of Anticancer
Drugs

• Anticancer drugs are commonly used in pets and aim to
improve or maintain a good quality of life. We also can
improve the survival times of cancer-bearing pets with
anticancer therapy, as long as a good quality of life is present.
• Because of their mechanisms of action (attacking rapidly
dividing cells), anticancer drugs may cause side-effects or
result in complications, most of which are treatable or selflimiting.
• Common side-effects include:
• Lethargy/fatigue: self-limiting and not markedly impacting
quality of life.
• Gastrointestinal: self-limiting and generally tolerable, most
can be prevented or treated when present, to limit the
negative impact on your pet’s quality of life.
• Nausea in pets does not always mean vomiting, and may
present in various ways, including decreased appetite,
“turning the head” when offered food, hypersalivation
(drooling), “lip smacking.” When a pet is nauseated,
offering more palatable foods will not help and may
worsen the nausea.
• When the prescribed anticancer treatment is known to
carry a higher risk of gastrointestinal signs, medications
to prevent or reduce the severity of complications will
be used concurrently.
• Suppression of the bone marrow: the circulating white blood
cell and platelet numbers may temporarily decrease after
anticancer therapy.
• This is why repeating bloodwork on your pet is crucial.
Low cell counts need to be documented; this
information helps with future doses planning.
• With severely decreased white blood cell counts,
antibiotic therapy may be necessary.
• Hair loss is uncommon in pets, but may be observed in
certain dog breeds with continuously growing hair (ex:
Maltese, Bichon Frisé, Poodles, certain Terriers, etc.), and
cats may occasionally lose whiskers. When it happens, it
does not negatively impact their quality of life.
• Other less common side-effects are relatively specific to
certain drugs and may affect the heart, the kidneys, the

liver, etc.
• It is important to understand the potential toxicity profile of
each drug administered to your pet, mostly to recognize the
side-effects when they occur, and to report them to your
veterinarian in a timely manner.
• When bloodwork abnormalities are documented (ex: low white
blood cell count), your veterinarian may recommend to
monitor your pet at home (ex: observe for signs of lethargy,
take serial body temperatures, etc.) as part of the teamwork
efforts aiming to improve your pet’s health management.
• Remember that most side-effects observed with anticancer
treatments are tolerable and reversible and that, in general,
the potential benefits vastly outweigh the risks.

(Malvern, Pennsylvania)

DEFINITIONS
Hematopoietic tumors include lymphoid tumors (lymphoma [LSA;
historically, lymphosarcoma], lymphoid leukemia, and myelomarelated disorders [MRD]) and myeloid leukemias. Lymphomas arise
in lymphoid tissues outside of the bone marrow (BM). In dogs,
lymph nodes, liver, and spleen are affected most commonly; in cats
the gastrointestinal (GI) tract is affected most commonly. However,
in both species, LSA can involve almost any organ system, including
BM, peripheral blood, cranial mediastinum, skin, nasal cavity,
kidneys, and central nervous system (CNS).
Leukemias arise in the BM and occasionally the spleen. They can
be derived from lymphoid or myeloid cells. Myeloid leukemias are

usually neutrophilic or monocytic in origin, but can be derived from
other granulocytes, erythrocytes, or megakaryocytes. The word
“leukemia” sometimes is used to describe neoplastic hematopoietic
cells circulating in the blood, but this is imprecise and not
recommended. Not all primary BM cancers result in tumor cells
circulating in peripheral blood (so-called aleukemic leukemias).
Additionally, LSA can be associated with neoplastic cells found in
circulation due to secondary infiltration of the BM or occasionally
due to infiltration of extramedullary hematopoietic organs such as
the spleen. MRD includes multiple myeloma (MM) and several other
clinical syndromes all derived from plasma cells or immunoglobulin
(Ig)-producing B-lymphocyte precursor cells.

LYMPHOMA
PREVALENCE
LSA is one of the most common cancers in dogs and cats.1 Cancer
epidemiology studies in veterinary oncology are not as accurate and
thorough as those in human oncology and many studies are
outdated, particularly those in cats published before feline leukemia
virus (FeLV) assays and vaccines became available (ch. 199).2
Reported prevalence rates range from 13-114 per 100,000 dogs at
risk, and 44-200 per 100,000 cats at risk.1 The number of dogs and
cats diagnosed with LSA is increasing, but it is uncertain if this is a
true increase or an increase in diagnostic capabilities and willingness
of families to pursue diagnostic evaluation and therapy.1,2

ETIOLOGY (CHS. 198 AND 199)
In most dogs and cats diagnosed with LSA, an underlying cause is
not identified. No infectious etiologies have been identified in
affected dogs. In cats, FeLV is strongly associated with large-cell LSA
(usually T-cell) as well as lymphoid and myeloid leukemias,3,4
caused primarily by insertional mutagenesis where integrated
proviruses activate proto-oncogenes, such as c-myc.5 Cats with

progressive FeLV infection are 60 times more likely to develop LSA
compared to noninfected cats.3 Prior to FeLV testing and elimination
programs and widespread vaccination, 70% of cats diagnosed with
LSA were FeLV blood antigen positive. The most common FeLVassociated LSA is mediastinal, followed by multicentric and spinal,
and occasionally renal or ocular. More current studies report
progressive FeLV infection in cats with LSA with a prevalence of 0 to
21%.4 Regressive FeLV infections also can be associated with LSA.
Cats from FeLV cluster households have a 40-fold higher rate of
developing FeLV-antigen negative LSA than cats in the general
population.4 Additionally, proviral DNA has been detected in
neoplastic T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes of FeLV antigennegative cats.6,7
Cats infected with feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) are about 5
times as likely to develop LSA or lymphoid leukemia compared with
FIV-negative cats.3 FIV also has been linked to myeloproliferative
disorders. Unlike FeLV, FIV is not directly oncogenic;
immunosuppressive effects of the virus impede normal
immunosurveillance and elimination of neoplastic cells.3 FIVassociated LSA is usually B-cell in origin and typically arises in
extranodal sites. Other causes of chronic immunosuppression also
have been linked to LSA: ∼10% of cats on immunosuppressive drugs
after renal transplantation (usually cyclosporine; ch. 301) develop
mid- to high-grade diffuse large B-cell LSA.8 Non-cutaneous LSA has
been reported in dogs given oclacitinib (Apoquel, Zoetis), although
the prevalence was not significantly higher than the control
population.9
Exposure to tobacco smoke increases the risk of LSA in dogs and
cats.10,11 Herbicides, especially 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4D), have been implicated in canine LSA in some, but not all studies.1
Other reported risk factors reported in dogs include living in an
industrial area, exposure to paints or solvents, and exposure to
strong magnetic fields.1

HISTOPATHOLOGIC CLASSIFICATIONS
AND THEIR FREQUENCY
Definitions
There are several different forms of LSA that vary in clinical
presentation, response to therapy, and prognosis. Histopathologic
evaluations of tissues with immunophenotyping (determining
whether the tumor is of B- or T-cell lineage) remains the standard for
diagnosing and subclassifying LSA, although cytologic evaluation of
smears with or without immunocytochemical staining, flow
cytometry or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for antigen receptor
rearrangement (PARR) can be used (see Diagnostic Evaluation
below). Inappropriate use of terminology has confused classifying
LSA. “Lymphoblast” is often used indiscriminately to describe any
large lymphoid cell, but should be reserved for precursor or stem
cells. Lymphoblastic LSA and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)
are relatively uncommon, and are most reliably identified by being
CD34+ on flow cytometry.12,13

Dogs
The most common forms of LSA in dogs are diffuse large B-cell
lymphoma (DLBCL, ∼50% of cases) and peripheral T-cell lymphoma
(PTCL, ∼15% of cases).12,14 While derived from mature (peripheral)
lymphoid cells, both are characterized by large lymphoid cells
effacing lymph nodes and/or other affected tissues. LSA grade is
typically determined by mitotic index (MI), not cell size or LSA
subtype.14 Therefore, DLBCL and PTCL can be classified as low- (MI
0-5/400× field), intermediate- (MI 6-10/400× field), or high-grade
(MI >10/400× field). Other common forms of LSA in dogs include Tzone lymphoma (TZL, ∼10-15% of cases) and marginal zone
lymphoma (5-15% of cases).

Cats
In cats, GI LSA is most common (ch. 262), with 3 distinct
conditions recognized.15 Mucosal T-cell LSA (enteropathy associated

T-cell lymphoma [EATCL], type II) is characterized by small- to
intermediate-sized lymphocytes infiltrating small intestinal lamina
propria with or without epitheliotropism. Lesions can be patchy or
diffuse. Transmural T-cell LSA (EATCL, type I) is characterized by
large lymphocytes, often with eosinophilic granules typical of large
granular lymphocytes (LGLs). Tumor cells efface the mucosal lamina
propria, often exhibiting epitheliotropism, and heavily infiltrate the
submucosa. Lesions are focal or multifocal within the small intestine.
DLBCL is characterized by transmural infiltrates of large
lymphocytes that rarely exhibit epitheliotropism. Lesions commonly
involve the stomach (ch. 261), jejunum (ch. 262), and ileocecocolic
junction (chs. 262, 263). DLCBL also accounts for most feline nasal
LSA (ch. 213) and up to 33% of mediastinal LSA (ch. 222).12 About
10% of all feline LSAs are T-cell rich B-cell lymphoma (TCRBCL,
formerly Hodgkin’s-like LSA).12,16 As the name implies, this form of
LSA is characterized by small to intermediate-sized non-neoplastic
T-cells admixed with neoplastic large B-cells. T-cells predominate
initially, but B-cells gradually increase in proportion. Cats with
TCRBCL usually have 1 or more enlarged mandibular or cervical
lymph nodes.

CLINICAL SIGNS IN DOGS
Peripheral Lymph Node Lymphoma
Most dogs with DLCBL and PTCL have generalized
lymphadenopathy (Figure 322.1). Severity of lymphadenopathy
varies greatly and can be asymmetric. Concurrent liver and or/spleen
involvement is common. Occasionally other anatomic sites will be
affected as well, including but not limited to the BM or peripheral
blood. LSA can affect any breed at any age. Many dogs have no
clinical signs aside from peripheral lymphadenopathy with or
without cranial abdominal organomegaly. As the cancer progresses,
common clinical signs include inappetence, lethargy, vomiting, and
diarrhea. Mandibular lymphadenopathy rarely causes dysphagia or
dyspnea, but notably, if severe mandibular lymphadenopathy
impairs lymphatic drainage, pitting edema and associated clinical
signs result (ch. 239). Enlarged tonsils can cause respiratory stertor

and/or dysphagia. Other clinical signs depend on the organ
system(s) affected. Significant liver infiltration can lead to hepatic
failure. BM myelophthisis can lead to anemia and weakness,
thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy, and/or neutropenia and sepsis
(chs. 128, 176). Respiratory signs can result from tracheobronchial
lymphadenopathy, pulmonary infiltration, cranial mediastinal mass,
or pleural effusion. Almost any other organ system can become
infiltrated. Also, T-cell LSA can be associated with paraneoplastic
hypercalcemia, which can cause polyuria/polydipsia (PU/PD), renal
failure, anorexia, vomiting, and occasionally muscle twitching (chs.
69, 283, and 331).

FIGURE 322.1 Generalized lymphadenopathy in a
dog with large cell lymphoma. Calipers are
measuring the right superficial cervical lymph node.
About 75% of canine peripheral lymph node LSA are B-cell in
origin (DLBCL being the most common subtype), and 25% are T-cell
in origin (PTCL).14 There are significant breed differences.17 The
Basset Hound, Cocker Spaniel, Border Collie, and Doberman
Pinscher have higher prevalences of B-cell LSA. In contrast, the

Boxer, Shih Tzu, Cavalier King Charles Spaniel, and Airedale are
among the breeds with the highest prevalences of T-cell LSA.

Indolent T-Zone Lymphoma (TZL)
Most dogs with TZL have mild peripheral lymphadenopathy that can
be solitary, regional, or generalized,18-20 and is often stable to slowly
progressive over months. >50% of affected dogs have concurrent
peripheral blood lymphocytosis and are clinically healthy, although
concurrent demodicosis has been reported. Paraneoplastic
hypercalcemia is rare. Golden Retrievers account for ∼40% of cases,
and Shih Tzus about 8%. About 15% of dogs with TZL have
peripheral blood lymphocytosis and no concurrent
lymphadenopathy, indicating overlap between TZL and some chronic
lymphocytic leukemias (CLLs).20,21 ∼30% of Golden Retrievers >10
years old with no evidence of lymphoproliferative disease have
CD45− T-zone cells identified in their blood using flow cytometry,
referred to as T-zone like cells of undetermined significance.22

Cutaneous Lymphoma
Cutaneous lymphocytosis is a rare indolent skin LSA seen in older
dogs with rarely pruritic multifocal lesions of erythematous, scaly,
and alopecic macules, patches, or occasionally plaques.23,24
Transformation into cutaneous lymphoma has been reported (ch.
12).
Epitheliotropic cutaneous T-cell LSA includes mycosis fungoides
and pagetoid reticulosis. These conditions can only be discriminated
histopathologically: pagetoid reticulosis is characterized by
neoplastic infiltrates solely in the epidermis and adnexal structures,
whereas mycosis fungoides also has neoplastic lymphocytes in the
underlying dermis.24,25 Lesions include generalized exfoliative
erythroderma (generalized erythema, scaling, and pruritus),
mucocutaneous lesions with depigmentation, erosions or ulcers,
solitary or multiple cutaneous nodules or plaques, or infiltrative oral
mucosal disease (Figure 322.2). Concurrent mild to moderate
peripheral lymphadenopathy can be seen corresponding to the

location(s) of the skin lesions. Concurrent visceral involvement is
rare.
Nonepitheliotropic cutaneous LSA is histologically confined to the
dermis. Cutaneous lesions are similar to those seen with
epitheliotropic cutaneous LSA, but concurrent visceral organ
involvement is more common.

Other Sites
Since LSA can involve almost any anatomic site, clinical signs are
due to abnormalities in affected areas. GI LSA is associated with
anorexia, weight loss, vomiting, and diarrhea (ch. 262).26 Cranial
mediastinal LSA can cause respiratory distress due to the mass effect
and/or secondary to pleural effusion; concurrent paraneoplastic
hypercalcemia is common (ch. 222). Involvement of the CNS can be
recognized at time of diagnosis, but is more commonly identified at
relapse, presumably due the inability of many chemotherapy drugs
to penetrate the blood-brain barrier (ch. 245).27 Dogs with solitary
splenic LSA, usually marginal zone or mantle cell LSA, are often
asymptomatic, but can have lethargy, anorexia, abdominal
distension, or rarely hemoabdomen (ch. 182).28,29 In contrast,
hepatosplenic T-cell LSA is much more aggressive.30 Infiltration of
liver, spleen, BM and lung without peripheral lymph node
involvement is common. Affected dogs typically are clinically ill and
can present in hepatic failure.

FIGURE 322.2 Diffuse cutaneous T-cell
lymphoma (mycosis fungoides) in a dog.

CLINICAL SIGNS IN CATS
FeLV-Associated Lymphoma (chs. 198)
Recent studies have shown that FeLV-associated LSA, once thought
to occur mostly in young cats, is more likely in progressively FeLV-

infected adults.4 Males and cats with access to outdoor environments
are at greater risk for contracting both FIV and FeLV. Mediastinal
FeLV-associated LSA is most common (ch. 222), followed by
multicentric, spinal (ch. 251) (not brain), and occasionally renal or
ocular.3,4 Progressively FeLV-infected cats frequently have BM
suppression, especially anemia. LSA in the GI tract or nasal cavity
usually is not associated with FeLV.

Gastrointestinal (GI) Lymphoma
Cats with small cell mucosal T-cell LSA usually have some
combination of hyporexia, weight loss, vomiting, and diarrhea.31,32
Clinical signs typically persist for several months and occasionally 12 years before diagnosis. Concurrent involvement of intra-abdominal
lymph nodes, liver, and occasionally spleen or pancreas is reported;
rarely cats present with liver failure/icterus. Abdominal palpation
often is unremarkable, but in some, diffuse intestinal thickening,
mild mesenteric lymphadenopathy, and/or organomegaly is
appreciated. Discrete intra-abdominal masses are rare. Cats with
large cell GI LSA (transmural T-cell or DLBCL) usually have similar
clinical signs. However, clinical signs usually worsen quickly and
become more debilitating.31 Concurrent involvement of intraabdominal lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and other organs is common.
Cats with large cell GI LSA frequently have a palpable intraabdominal mass originating from the GI tract or severely enlarged
intra-abdominal lymph nodes. Occasionally they present with
hepatic failure/icterus or with peritoneal effusion.

Peripheral Lymph Node Lymphoma
<10% of cats with LSA have disease confined to peripheral lymph
nodes.2 Cranial and cervical lymph nodes are affected most
commonly, and the mass lesions are not always associated with
named lymph nodes (Figure 322.3) Cats with TCRBCL often have a
slow disease progression without overt clinical signs. In contrast,
cats with PTCL or DLBCL and peripheral lymph node involvement
usually have more rapid disease progression and usually exhibit
lethargy, anorexia, respiratory stertor, and/or dysphagia.

FIGURE 322.3 Enlarged cervical lymph nodes in
a cat with T-cell rich B-cell lymphoma. These
enlarged lymph nodes were located in between
palpably normal mandibular and superficial cervical
lymph nodes.

Other Sites
Since LSA can involve almost any anatomic site, clinical signs are
due to abnormalities in affected areas. Mediastinal LSA can cause
severe respiratory distress due to mass effect and/or secondary
pleural effusion (chs. 220, 222).33 Renal LSA is always bilateral,
although it can be asymmetric.34 Concurrent involvement of other
anatomic sites such as the GI tract is common. Cats commonly have
signs of kidney disease: PU/PD, hyporexia, weight loss (ch. 301).
Nasal LSA usually is confined to the nasal cavity with or without
regional lymph nodes.35 Cats can have nasal discharge, epistaxis,
sneezing, respiratory stridor, and/or facial deformity (ch. 213). LSA
involving the larynx, pharynx, or trachea usually is similarly locally
confined (chs. 214, 258). CNS LSA can cause neurologic deficits
corresponding to the anatomic site(s) affected in the brain, spinal
cord, and/or eye(s) (chs. 241, 245). Cutaneous LSA is uncommon in
cats and can present with lesions similar to those described above in

dogs (ch. 12). Cats may have subcutaneous LSA, a firm, painless SQ
nodule most commonly affecting the lateral thorax, lateral abdomen,
interscapular area, or tarsus.36

CLINICAL STAGING
The main goals of clinical staging are to confirm the diagnosis of
LSA, determine the extent of disease, and screen for other health
abnormalities that might affect treatment or prognosis. The
diagnostic tests most commonly required before initiating therapy
include lymph node cytology, complete blood count (CBC), and
serum biochemistry profile.37 Other tests commonly recommended
but not necessarily required include urinalysis (UA),
immunophenotyping, thoracic radiographs, abdominal ultrasound
(US), and BM cytology. The World Health Organization (WHO)
clinical staging for LSA in domestic animals is useful for
communicating the extent of disease in dogs with peripheral lymph
node LSA (Table 322.1). However, this system is not as useful for
the less common extranodal presentations, nor is it useful in cats.
Other staging schemes have been proposed for cats, but most
oncologists prefer using the anatomic site(s) affected. As additional
and more sensitive diagnostic tests are performed, additional lesions
might be identified and consequently dogs might be moved into
higher stages.38 This concept of stage migration makes it difficult to
compare dogs across and sometimes within studies and helps explain
the inconsistent prognostic factors seen with WHO clinical stage.

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
Physical Examination (PE; ch. 3)
Measure enlarged peripheral lymph nodes by longest diameter.39
For pets with cutaneous LSA, sentinel lesions should be measured;
photographs are helpful when lesions are diffuse. Mucous
membranes should be evaluated for pallor, petechiae, icterus, and/or
uremic ulcers. Thoracic auscultation can help suspect pulmonary
infiltration, a cranial mediastinal mass, or pleural effusion.
Abdominal palpation may identify organomegaly, intestinal wall
thickening, a GI mass, intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy, and/or
abdominal effusion. Ophthalmic examination can identify anterior
uveitis, retinal hemorrhage, and/or infiltrative disease (ch. 13).

Histologic and Cytologic Diagnosis
Histopathologic evaluation of tissue with immunophenotyping is
standard for diagnosing LSA.14,40 In addition to cell morphology,
histopathologic evaluation provides information about tissue
architecture, cell distribution, and mitotic rate. It is the most
accurate method for diagnosing LSA and determining specific

subtype, which can be crucial to both treatment and prognosis.
Biopsy samples should be large enough to fully assess tissue
architecture (ch. 88). Therefore, whenever possible, excisional
biopsy or an affected node or wedge biopsy of an affected site is
preferable to smaller core (e.g., Tru-Cut) samples. Full-thickness GI
biopsies are considered superior to endoscopic biopsies when trying
to differentiate mucosal T-cell LSA from lymphoplasmacytic
inflammatory bowel disease in cats, although the addition of
immunohistochemistry and PARR can improve the diagnostic
accuracy of the smaller, less invasive samples.41,42
Cytologic evaluation of smears is commonly used to diagnose LSA
due to ease of sample collection and rapid turn-around time (chs. 85
and 88). LSA can be reliably diagnosed cytologically when the
affected tissue has been largely effaced by large lymphoid cells
(Figure 322.4). This is common with DLBCL and PTCL, the most
common forms of LSA diagnosed in dogs and cats. Cytologic
assessments also can be useful for diagnosing large granular
lymphocyte LSA (Figure 322.5); the neoplastic lymphoid cells
contain characteristic azurophilic magenta granules that are readily
visualized with a Wright-Giemsa stain, but not Romanowsky-type
stains (e.g., Diff-Quik). However, when the neoplastic lymphoid cells
have not effaced nodal architecture, cytologic evaluation will often
yield a mixture of different types of lymphoid cells that can resemble
lymphoid hyperplasia. Similarly, when tumor cells are small, welldifferentiated lymphoid cells, they can be difficult to distinguish
from normal, non-neoplastic lymphocytes. Therefore, when LSA is
suspected clinically but not confirmed cytologically, histopathologic
evaluation is indicated. For example, in dogs with indolent T-zone
LSA, the neoplastic cells are small to intermediate in size, and they
do not efface normal nodal architecture. The diagnosis is often
suspected based on the presence of a uropod or “mirror handle”
cytoplasmic extensions (Figure 322.6), but histopathologic
examination of tissue and/or flow cytometry is needed for a
definitive diagnosis.21
BM aspiration or biopsy (ch. 84) is indicated when hematopoietic
cancer is suspected but cannot be identified elsewhere. Examples
include pets with aleukemic leukemia and pancytopenia or
hypercalcemia. BM evaluation also is recommended in LSA if

neoplastic cells are circulating in the blood and/or if significant
cytopenias are noted. Cytologic examination of CSF (ch. 109) can
help confirm CNS LSA, although the sensitivity in animals is
unknown and only ∼25% of people with CNS LSA have a positive
result.43 The use of PARR on CSF might improve sensitivity.27 CSF
analysis is not likely to be of benefit in cats with spinal LSA since
most lesions are extradural (ch. 251).44

Immunophenotyping and immunohistochemical staining can be
performed on biopsy samples. Some laboratories are also able to
perform immunocytochemical staining on unstained cytologic
preparations. Flow cytometry and PARR can also provide phenotype.

Flow Cytometry

Flow cytometry provides objective data about cell size and antigen
expression.13,20,21,45-48 Both lymphoid and myeloid markers exist,
useful for confirming a diagnosis of hematopoietic cancer and
prognosticating. Flow cytometry can be run on blood samples
preserved in EDTA, BM aspirates preserved in EDTA or citrate
phosphate dextrose adenine solution (CPDA-1), or tissue aspirates
preserved in tissue culture media or a 9:1 solution of saline and
serum. Cells must be viable at the time of analysis. Flow cytometry
can reliably determine LSA immunophenotype; agreement with
immunohistochemistry is almost 95%.49 Flow cytometry cannot
differentiate DLBCL from other B-cell subtypes.46 When evaluating
all B-cell LSAs together, large cell size, low levels of class II major
histocompatibility complex (MHC) expression, and high levels of
CD25 expression are negative prognostic factors.45,46

FIGURE 322.6 Fine needle aspirate cytologic
preparation of a peripheral lymph node in a dog with
T-zone lymphoma. The majority of the lymphoid
cells are small to intermediate in size, and several
have an asymmetric expansion of cytoplasm,
referred to as a uropod or “mirror handle” (Wright’s
stain, 500×). Original image obtained from

courtesy Dr. Tracy Stokol, College of Veterinary

Flow cytometry can be used to diagnose indolent TZL in dogs.20,21
TZL cells are positive for the pan-T-cell antigens CD3 and CD5, but
aberrantly do not express pan-leukocyte marker CD45. Expression of
class II MHC is high, and expression of CD4 and CD8 is variable.
PTCL is CD45+, and expression of class II MHC is low.47,48 The
majority of PTCL are CD4+ and CD8−, although some are CD4− and

CD8+ and others are dual negative.21,47 CD4 and CD8 expression
does not seem to impact prognosis. For CD4+ PTCL, loss of CD5
expression and small cell size are positive prognostic factors,
although the clinical impact for both is modest.47

Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) for Antigen
Receptor Rearrangement (PARR)
The antigen specificity of B- and T-lymphocytes results from somatic
DNA rearrangements in the Ig receptor and T-cell receptor (TCR)
genes, respectively. Recombination events cause nearly every
lymphocyte to have an Ig receptor or TCR that is slightly different in
size and sequence. PARR uses PCR to amplify the DNA in the
complementary determining region 3 that encodes part of the
antigen-binding portion of the Ig heavy chain and TCR gamma,
followed by size separation of the product.40,50,51 PARR of benign
lymphoid tissue typically yields a smear or ladder of PCR products
representing many different receptors. However, because neoplastic
transformation of lymphocytes typically occurs after the cells have
undergone receptor arrangement, PARR in patients with lymphoid
cancers usually yields a dominant band indicative of a monoclonal
population.
PARR can be run on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue,
blood, fluid samples, and air-dried (stained or unstained) cytology
slides.40,50,51 It is easy to perform this test on previously collected
samples, in contrast to flow cytometry, which requires viable cells.
Also, only about 50,000 cells are needed,40 making it a useful assay
with small samples of low cellularity such as CSF. PARR can only
give a positive or negative result regarding the presence of a clonal
expansion of lymphocytes. It cannot provide any information
regarding lymphoma subtype beyond B cell or T cell. Occasionally
cells test positive for clonal rearrangements in both Ig receptor and
TCR.49,51 Reported sensitivities in dogs are 70-85% and in cats 6065%.40,49-53 Specificity is high in both species (>95%), although
false positive results can occur in pets with certain chronic infections,
e.g., ehrlichiosis.40,51,52 Therefore, a positive result is strongly

supportive of LSA, but a negative result cannot be used to exclude a
diagnosis of LSA.

Complete Blood Count (CBC)
Anemia is reported in 30-40% of dogs and 45-60% of cats with LSA,
and is a negative prognostic factor in both.54,55 Anemia is usually
mild to moderate, normocytic, normochromic, and nonregenerative,
indicative of anemia of chronic disease (ch. 57). However, anemia
also can follow blood loss (e.g., GI ulceration in pets with GI
lymphoma), indirect BM inhibition (e.g., iron deficiency in pets with
chronic GI ulceration, erythropoietin deficiency in cats with renal
LSA, cobalamin deficiency in cats with GI LSA), myelophthisis (often
causing pancytopenia), or secondary immune-mediated hemolysis.
FeLV positive cats often have concurrent erythrodysplasia,
manifesting as a macrocytic anemia.
Thrombocytopenia, reported in 20-50% of dogs and 10-20% of
cats with LSA, is rarely clinically worrisome (chs. 59 and 175).54,55
Mechanisms include sequestration (especially in dogs with
significant splenomegaly), myelophthisis, and immune-mediated
destruction. Circulating atypical lymphocytes usually indicates BM
involvement, although occasionally this can result from infiltration
of extramedullary hematopoietic organs such as the spleen.

Serum Chemistry Profile, Cobalamin, FeLV, FIV
Hypercalcemia (35-55% of dogs with T-cell LSA) is usually caused by
ectopic production of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP)
by neoplastic cells (chs. 69, 283, and 331).54 Hypercalcemia is a
negative prognostic factor because it is associated with PTCL, and
PTCL is a more aggressive subtype. Hypercalcemia is less commonly
seen in cats with LSA. When present, hypercalcemia can be used as
an indirect biomarker to assess response to therapy. Other
laboratory abnormalities often reflect site(s) of involvement: liver
enzyme elevations or hyperbilirubinemia with liver infiltration,
azotemia and isosthenuria with renal involvement (or paraneoplastic
hypercalcemia), or hypoproteinemia with GI involvement. Serum
cobalamin should be assessed in all cats with GI lymphoma (ch.

262).32 FeLV and FIV tests are recommended in all cats with LSA
due to their impact on prognosis and husbandry (chs. 198, 199).

Imaging the Thorax
Thoracic radiographs can identify intrathoracic lymphadenopathy,
pulmonary infiltrates (usually interstitial and/or alveolar patterns,
rarely nodules), cranial mediastinal masses, and/or pleural effusion.
In dogs, the presence of a cranial mediastinal mass is most
consistent with PTCL, whereas in cats one-third are DLBCL.12
Significant pleural effusion (chs. 92, 220) can impact treatment,
quality of life (QoL), and prognosis.

Imaging the Abdomen
When imaging the abdomen, US is preferable to radiographs. In
substage-a dogs with peripheral lymph node LSA, it is common to
identify intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy with or without
involvement of the liver and/or spleen. Such changes rarely affect
prognosis, explaining why abdominal US is not absolutely needed
before starting therapy.37 Abdominal US is more important when
dogs have significant GI signs, since GI infiltration is a negative
prognostic factor.26 For dogs and cats, when most or all of the cancer
burden is internal, US is important to aid with diagnosis and
assessment of response to therapy. Abdominal imaging should be
routine in cats because the disease is often confined to the
abdomen.31 In cats with mucosal T-cell LSA, the intestinal wall
thickness typically is normal or mildly increased. Wall layering is
preserved, usually with thickening of the muscularis propria.
Concurrent mild mesenteric lymphadenopathy is common. US
cannot definitively distinguish mucosal T-cell LSA from
lymphoplasmacytic enteritis/chronic inflammatory enteropathy (ch.
262). In contrast, cats with large cell LSA often have concentric
transmural GI thickening with disruption of wall layering, with or
without mass effect. Concurrent involvement of lymph nodes and
other organs is common.
Computed tomography (CT) imaging is indicated for cats with
nasal or retropharyngeal LSA to guide biopsy procedures and plan

radiation therapy (RT). Magnetic resonance imaging is indicted
when CNS involvement is suspected (ch. 112).

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Overview
Chemotherapy remains the mainstay of treatment for LSA in dogs
and cats because most have multicentric disease.56 Specific
treatment protocol chosen depends on pet factors, e.g., LSA subtype,
LSA substage, paraneoplastic syndromes, and physical condition, as
well as client factors, e.g., time commitment, finances, tolerance for
risk of adverse events.

Surgery
Surgery can be considered in pets with solitary nodal or extranodal
LSA, e.g., cats with TCRBL16 or dogs with marginal zone LSA
confined to the spleen.28 With multicentric disease, surgery is
usually used to obtain tissue for histology, or to alleviate lifethreatening complications, e.g., GI obstruction or perforation in cats
with large cell GI LSA.

Radiation Therapy (RT; ch. 318)
RT is used primarily for dogs and cats with solitary or regional
involvement, e.g., cats with nasal or retropharyngeal LSA35 or dogs
with cutaneous LSA confined to the muzzle or oral cavity.57 It also
can be used in pets with CNS lymphoma since RT is not impacted by
the blood-brain barrier. Sequential cranial and caudal half-body RT
has been combined with chemotherapy in dogs with LSA,58 and
abdominal cavity RT has been combined with chemotherapy in cats
with GI LSA.59 Whole-body RT combined with autologous or
allogenic peripheral blood hematopoietic cell transplantation has
been evaluated in dogs.60-61a However, none of these half- or wholebody radiation protocols were clearly superior to standard CHOP-

based chemotherapy and adverse events were more common and
more severe.

Immunotherapy (ch. 319)
Immunotherapy is commonly combined with chemotherapy for
people with LSA. Rituximab, a monoclonal antibody directed at
CD20 on B-lymphocytes that is combined with CHOP for people with
DLBCL,62 does not bind to canine CD20.63 Alemtuzumab, a
monoclonal antibody directed against CD52 found on both B- and Tlymphocytes, is used in people with B-cell CLL and is being
investigated for cutaneous T-cell LSA and PTCL.62 Canine-specific
monoclonal antibodies directed against CD20 and CD52 have been
developed, but clinical trials did not show clear benefit over
chemotherapy alone (abstract data only). Similarly, a xenogeneic
DNA vaccine encoding human CD20 was developed, but efficacy
data was minimal (abstract data only). At the time of writing, there
are no approved, commercially available immunotherapies for the
treatment of LSA in dogs or cats.

Systemic Chemotherapy in Dogs With Intermediate
or Large Cell Lymphoma
NOTE: Weight-to-body-surface-area conversion charts can be found
on the inside covers of the textbook.

CHOP
Combining multiple chemotherapy drugs with different mechanisms
of action and dose-limiting toxicities improves overall protocol dose
intensity, resulting in higher remission rates and longer remission
durations. The most commonly used drug combination is often
referred to by the acronym “CHOP”: cyclophosphamide (C),
doxorubicin (hydroxydaunorubicin [H]), vincristine (Oncovin [O]),
and prednisone (P). Many combinations of these drugs have been
evaluated but small numbers of patients and varying entry criteria,
staging diagnostics, and responses evaluated make comparisons
among studies difficult. In general, CHOP-based chemotherapy
induces remission in 80-95% of dogs, with overall MSTs of 10-12

months and 2-year survival rates of 20-25%.1 Protocol lengths vary
from 12 weeks to 2 years; most oncologists use 19-25 week
protocols.37 Longer protocols with extended maintenance phases do
not improve prognosis.64 Shorter protocols are associated with
shorter remission durations or increased toxicoses.65,66 The protocol
used most commonly by the author is presented in Table 322.2.

L-Asparaginase
Retrospective studies have shown no differences in remission rate,
remission duration, or survival when L-asparaginase was omitted
from initial CHOP67,68; many oncologists now omit L-asparaginase
when patients appear clinically healthy (substage a).37 Since the drug
is not myelosuppressive and risk of adverse GI effects minimal, it is
an ideal first treatment for ill dogs (substage b), for dogs with
substantial BM involvement, or when clients are apprehensive about
chemotherapy-associated adverse events.
