Alkylating Agents
Immunophenotype is one of the most consistent prognostic factors.
When treated with CHOP, dogs with PTCL have similar remission
rates compared to dogs with DLBCL, but remission durations are
shorter and MSTs are only about 6 to 8 months.69,70 Some
oncologists routinely use different protocols for PTCL, usually
adding alkylating agents (e.g., lomustine [CCNU], mechlorethamine,
procarbazine) to the CHOP drugs or substituting them for
doxorubicin.37,71-74 MSTs for these protocols are comparable to
those reported with CHOP, but a small percentage of dogs have had
long-term survival (>2 years), indicating that a subset of dogs might
respond more favorably to alkylating agents. However, studies did
not require histologic confirmation or flow cytometry to definitively
rule out TZL. Further evaluation is needed.

Doxorubicin
Doxorubicin is the most effective drug for treating B-cell LSA in
dogs; it is effective in dogs with PTCL, but overall and complete
remission rates are lower.75 Doxorubicin (30 mg/m2 for dogs
weighing ≥15 kg, 25 mg/m2 for dogs weighing <15 kg, IV q3wk for 5
treatments) with tapering prednisone can be used as a less intensive
and less expensive protocol.76,77 Complete remission rate is 50-70%
overall, but 85% in dogs with B-cell LSA. MSTs are 6-8 months.

Rabacfosadine
Rabacfosadine (Tanovea, Elanco) is the only drug approved by the
U.S. Food and Drug Administration for treating LSA in dogs; all
other drugs are used extra-label. It has been evaluated as a single
agent in dogs with naïve or relapsed LSA.78,79 It also has been
evaluated when alternated with doxorubicin as well as when given
concurrently with L-asparaginase.80,81 Rabacfosadine (1 mg/kg IV
q3wk for 5 treatments) is used most commonly as a rescue agent, but
can be considered as a first-line treatment alone or in combination
with doxorubicin when clients prefer a protocol with fewer
treatments than CHOP. When rabacfosadine was used to treat naïve
LSA, complete remission was attained in about 60% of dogs with Bcell LSA and 25% of dogs with T-cell LSA.78 Median remission
duration was 6-7 months. As expected, remission rates and durations
are shorter when used in the rescue setting.

Lomustine (CCNU)
CCNU (70 mg/m2 PO q3wk) and prednisone, with or without Lasparaginase, can be used as first-line therapy or as a rescue
protocol.82-84 As discussed, CCNU can be used in a less-intensive
protocol for dogs with T-cell LSA. Some clients prefer this protocol
because CCNU is given orally. It is worth noting that oral does not
equate to safer: CCNU is one of the most myelosuppressive
chemotherapy drugs and it can cause cumulative hepatotoxicosis.
When used with prednisone for dogs with naïve LSA, about 35%
attained a complete remission, and an additional 15% a partial
remission.84 Median remission duration was brief (40 days), but
some have longer remissions. As expected, response rate and
duration improve when CCNU is combined with Lasparaginase.82,83

Glucocorticoids (Steroids)
When clients decline chemotherapy, single-agent prednisone (1-2
mg/kg PO q24h or 20-40 mg/m2 PO q24h) can be palliative, with

MSTs of 1 to 2 months.56 If steroid therapy is initiated before making
a definitive diagnosis, it can interfere with later diagnostics. They can
also select for LSA cells with a multidrug resistant phenotype,
resulting in shorter remission and survival durations with CHOPbased therapy.85

Indolent Lymphomas in Dogs
TZL is the most common indolent dog LSA. Marginal zone LSA,
mantle zone LSA, and follicular LSA are less common. Therapy is not
standardized. Because these have less aggressive biologic behavior,
less intensive therapies can be used. Some dogs with TZL can be
monitored and not treated.18-20 Chemotherapy is recommended for
indolent LSA when there is progression in lymph node size,
peripheral blood lymphocyte count >30,000 cells/mcL, significant
organ involvement beyond lymph nodes or spleen, or there are
clinical signs. The author usually uses chlorambucil (4 mg/m2 PO
q24h, but 20 mg/m2 PO q2wk has been reported) with prednisone.
Survival times of >2 years are common.18-20 Dogs with marginal
zone or mantle zone LSA confined to the spleen can be treated with
splenectomy alone.28,29 Survival times are often >2 years and can be
substantially longer in dogs that are free of clinical signs at the time
of surgery.

Cutaneous Lymphoma in Dogs (ch. 12)
Epitheliotropic cutaneous LSA is treated usually with CCNU (70
mg/m2 PO q3wk) and prednisone.24,25 Overall remission rates are
around 80%, but partial remissions are more common than complete
remission, and median remission duration is ∼3 months. Other drugs
used successfully include CHOP, rabacfosadine, L-asparaginase,
dacarbazine, and Doxil (liposome-encapsulated doxorubicin).
Concurrent treatment with retinoids improves prognosis.86 When
lesions are confined to the muzzle or oral cavity, RT can provide local
control for >2 years.57

There is no standard therapy for non-epitheliotropic cutaneous
LSA. The author typically begins with CCNU when lesions are
confined to the skin, and CHOP when there are substantial lesions
involving other organs.

Gastrointestinal (GI) LSA In Dogs
This form of LSA is aggressive in dogs and when treated with CHOPbased protocols, remission rates are ∼50-60%, MSTs are <3 months,
and 25% of dogs are alive 6 months after diagnosis.26 Severe (grade
3 or 4) GI adverse events are common. The combination of Lasparaginase, CCNU, and prednisone are reasonable since these
drugs tend to have lower incidences of GI toxicosis.

CNS Lymphoma in Dogs
When dogs have intra-axial CNS lesions, the blood-brain barrier
prevents many chemotherapy drugs from reaching lesions at
therapeutic concentrations (ch. 245). Drugs that can either cross the
blood-brain barrier or exert an effect across it include Lasparaginase, CCNU, cytosine arabinoside, and prednisone.27,87 RT
directed at a solitary lesion, or at the entire neuraxis can be used
because it is not impacted by the blood-brain barrier. MSTs for dogs
with CNS LSA are <6 months. The prognosis is especially grave when
CNS involvement is diagnosed at relapse rather than at initial
presentation.27,87

Systemic Chemotherapy in Cats With Intermediate
or Large Cell Lymphoma (ch. 317)
CHOP-based protocols are recommended for most cats with
intermediate or large cell LSA, regardless of anatomic site(s) affected
(author protocol Table 322.3). Most studies include LSA in a
variety of anatomic locations. Remission rates are 50-75%; MSTs ∼710 months.42,88,89 Response to treatment is one of the most
important prognostic factors. MSTs for cats only attaining partial
remission are ≤4 months. In contrast, cats attaining a complete
remission commonly survive 1-2 years. Anatomic site has not

consistently been shown to be a significant prognostic factor,
however FeLV positive status is a strong negative prognostic factor.
FeLV-associated LSA is more common in certain anatomic sites, e.g.,
cranial mediastinum and spinal cord. Immunophenotype is not a
prognostic factor in cats. However, large granular lymphoma is a
more aggressive variant with reported MSTs of 1-3 months.42,89,90

COP (cyclophosphamide, vincristine, prednisone) can be used as a
less aggressive alternative to CHOP. Some studies using COP have
reported remission rates and durations comparable to those seen
with CHOP,91 but studies have demonstrated benefit when
doxorubicin is included.42,89,92 Doxorubicin is not recommended as
single-agent therapy in cats; in past studies, only 25% of cats
attained a complete remission, and 15% a partial remission.93 Since
many cats are clinically ill at time of diagnosis, L-asparaginase is an
important induction drug, but response rate is only 30% when used
alone.94 Therefore, L-asparaginase usually is given concurrently with
vincristine at week 1. In cats too ill for vincristine, alternatives
include vinblastine or cyclophosphamide.95

CCNU (40-60 mg/m2 PO q3-6wk) can be used as first-line therapy
or as a rescue protocol. Cats with naïve LSA treated with CCNU and
prednisolone, with or without a single dose of L-asparaginase at
induction, have overall remission rates of 50% with roughly equal
complete and partial responders.96 While this response rate is lower
than that seen with COP and CHOP-based protocols, median
remission duration was 10 months. Cats treated with CCNU can have
delayed neutropenia, making it difficult to combine with other
myelosuppressive drugs or to quickly transition to other protocols if
ineffective.

Small Cell Mucosal T-Cell LSA in Cats
Commonly, chlorambucil and prednisolone are used32,42,89 with any
of various protocols. The author typically doses chlorambucil at 2 mg
PO q2-3d, aiming to achieve an average dose intensity of 4
mg/m2/day; others use 20 mg/m2 PO every 2 weeks. Prednisolone
typically is started at 1 to 2 mg/kg PO q24h and tapered based on
clinical signs. Treatment typically is continued for at least 1 year,
>75% of cats have resolution of clinical signs, and MSTs are 1.5-3
years.

Nasal LSA in Cats (ch. 213)
Nasal LSA can be effectively treated with CHOP-based protocols, as
described. Because this form of LSA usually is localized to the nasal
cavity with or without regional lymph nodes, RT can be considered in
place of or in combination with chemotherapy. In cats treated with
definitive intent RT (>32 Gy), MSTs are just over 1 year, and
complete remissions can persist for several years (ch. 318).35

TCRBCL in Cats
There is no standard of care for this form of LSA. When confined to
only 1 or 2 lymph nodes in the head and neck, surgical removal is
reasonable.16 Survival times of ∼1 year are reported with surgery
alone, although recurrence in lymph nodes is likely. When surgery is

not possible, RT or chemotherapy can be considered. Anecdotally,
chlorambucil/prednisolone or COP are used commonly.

General Supportive Care in Dogs and Cats
Treatment protocols are only a starting point. Many dogs and cats
with LSA are clinically ill at the time of diagnosis. Hemodynamic, GI,
and/or nutritional support are commonly needed (chs. 151 and 163).
Saline diuresis and/or other treatments might be needed for patients
with paraneoplastic hypercalcemia (ch. 331). Similarly, protocols
may be modified to account for comorbidities, e.g., doxorubicin must
be used cautiously in dogs with underlying heart disease or cats with
renal disease (chs. 317 and 321). Breeds at higher risk for ABCB1-1Δ
genetic mutation (Collies, Australian Shepherd Dogs) should
undergo genetic testing; dogs homozygous for this mutation
experience severe toxicosis if treated with vincristine, doxorubicin, or
other drugs that are a substrate of this transmembrane pump.97 To
treat safely and effectively, clinicians must have a thorough
understating of the chemotherapy drugs they are prescribing and
administering.

REINDUCTION AND RESCUE
CHEMOTHERAPY IN DOGS AND CATS
Not all dogs and cats attain remission with their first-line protocol,
and the vast majority of those that do achieve remission will relapse.
When disease progression is identified, treatment decisions depend
on where the pet is in its treatment regimen. If therapy had been
completed for at least 1 to 2 months before relapse, then re-induction
with that same protocol should be considered. Of dogs treated with
CHOP initially and restarted on CHOP at first relapse, 80% attained
a second complete remission and median second remission duration
was 5 months.98
If a pet relapses or progresses while undergoing treatment, then
the LSA is resistant to some or all drugs in that protocol. When using
a multi-drug protocol, it is crucial to confirm whether all of the drugs
in that protocol have lost benefit, e.g., about half of dogs started on

CHOP that failed to respond to vincristine or cyclophosphamide still
respond to doxorubicin and can be effectively maintained on singleagent doxorubicin.99As a rule, any drug given within 1 month of
relapse has lost clinical benefit and should be discontinued. Lasparaginase is an exception because it is not myelosuppressive and
typically does not cause GI toxicosis. Even short-lived responses can
be extremely beneficial when trying to bridge from a failed protocol
to a new rescue one. A variety of rescue protocols has been published
for dogs and cats.1

LEUKEMIA
DEFINITIONS
Leukemia is defined as the proliferation of neoplastic cells in the BM,
usually originating in the BM but occasionally in the spleen.
Neoplastic cells are usually, not always, circulating in peripheral
blood. Leukemias are first subclassified as lymphoid or myeloid.
Myeloid leukemias can be derived from granulocytic, monocytic,
erythroid, megakaryocytic, or mixed lineages. These
subclassifications reflect that the pluripotential stem cells in the
marrow give rise to lymphoid stem cells from which B- and Tlymphocytes originate, and myeloid stem cells from which
granulocytes, monocytes, erythrocytes, and megakaryocytes
originate.
Lymphoid leukemias are further subclassified as chronic
lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia
(ALL) based on neoplastic cell morphology. There are no
standardized criteria to distinguish leukemia from lymphoma with
blood infiltration, with the exception of CD34+ acute leukemias.21
Clinical judgements often are based on the severity of any concurrent
lymphadenopathy and degree of blood and BM involvement. For
many dogs and cats, this distinction does not substantially impact
treatment recommendations or prognosis.

CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKEMIA
(CLL)
Dogs
In dogs, at least 75% of CLL are CD8+ CD45+ T-cell in origin, and in
over half, the lymphocytes contain variable numbers of azurophilic
granules.21,100,101 This large granular lymphocyte morphology has
not been shown to have any prognostic significance in dogs with CLL
(in contrast to cats with large granular lymphocyte GI lymphoma,
above). CD21+ B-cell CLL is the next most common subtype. As
discussed, over half of dogs with CD3+ CD45− TZL have a concurrent
peripheral lymphocytosis, and 15% have peripheral lymphocytosis
and no lymphadenopathy, blurring the distinction between TZL and
leukemia.20 Over 60% of dogs with CLL have no clinical signs at
initial presentation. When clinical signs are observed, lethargy,
hyporexia, and weight loss are most common.102 Over half of dogs
have concurrent peripheral lymphadenopathy and/or splenomegaly.
About 25% of dogs with B-cell CLL will have concurrent
hyperglobulinemia.102,103

Cats
Almost all feline cases of CLL are CD4+ cell in origin104 and in about
half, the diagnosis is incidental on review of a routine CBC. Common
signs include weight loss, inappetence, lethargy, vomiting, and
diarrhea. Peripheral lymphadenopathy is uncommon. In some cats,
US identifies mild mesenteric lymphadenopathy, mild splenomegaly,
and GI wall thickening, possibly overlapping with mucosal T-cell
LSA.104 CLL is not associated with FeLV or FIV (chs. 198 and 199).

Diagnostics
In both dogs and cats with CLL, peripheral blood lymphocyte counts
can range from <10,000/mcL to >300,000/mcL (ch. 58).102-104
About 25-50% of dogs and cats are anemic; it usually is mild, and

regeneration is variable (ch. 57). Neutropenia and
thrombocytopenia are uncommon. Flow cytometry of peripheral
blood is recommended to confirm the diagnosis of CLL. Imaging of
the thorax and abdomen can be considered based on clinical signs
but are not always required. Aspirates of enlarged peripheral lymph
nodes are often interpreted as reactive hyperplasia, since the
neoplastic lymphocytes are morphologically similar to normally
present mature lymphocytes.102,104 Aspirates of the spleen or liver
rarely are useful; these samples usually contain blood contamination,
making it difficult to determine if neoplastic cells are derived from
tissue parenchyma or the blood circulating through. A BM aspirate
(ch. 84) for cytologic evaluation (ch. 85) is reasonable for all pets
with leukemia; specifically for those with CLL, it is strongly indicated
only when significant blood cell cytopenias exist suggesting advanced
disease and myelophthisis.

Treatment
Not all dogs and cats with CLL require immediate treatment.102,104
Chemotherapy is recommended if peripheral blood lymphocyte
count is ≥30,000 cells/mcL, if there is organ involvement beyond
mild lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly, if there are peripheral
blood cytopenias, or if clinical signs impact QoL. When monitoring,
one should begin with monthly PEs and CBCs and then frequency of
rechecks can be adjusted based on rate of disease progression. When
therapy is initiated, chlorambucil and prednisone/prednisolone is
recommended using the same dosing regimens provided above for
indolent LSA or small cell mucosal T-cell LSA. MSTs are ∼12 to 18
months in both dogs and cats.21,102,104,105 Immunophenotype has
not been shown to be prognostic in dogs, but MST for dogs with
CD8+ T cell CLL with a presenting peripheral blood lymphocyte
count <30,000 cells/mcL is 3 years.105

ACUTE LEUKEMIAS
Definitions

ALL is characterized by the proliferation of morphologically
immature lymphoblasts in BM. In addition to potentially resembling
stage V LSA, ALL resembles acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Older
studies used cell morphology to distinguish ALL from AML but
immunophenotyping has revealed that lymphoid and myeloid cells
were commonly misclassified.106 This underscores the importance of
molecular diagnostics, e.g., flow cytometry and cytochemistry on
blood and/or BM when evaluating a pet with acute leukemia.
A diagnosis of acute leukemia is based on >20% blasts in either the
peripheral blood or BM; some older studies used >30% blasts.106-109
Classically, acute leukemias can be distinguished from LSA by being
CD34+, but it is estimated that up to 25% of canine acute leukemias
are CD34−.21,101,106 Commercially available flow cytometry tests
have specific antibodies for lymphocytes and for
granulocytes/monocytes. However, about 20-25% of acute leukemias
cannot be definitively classified despite use of these markers (socalled acute undifferentiated leukemias).21,107 Additional
cytochemical or immunocytochemical stains are available through
some universities. PARR is not helpful because not all lymphoid
cancers test positive for a clonal rearrangement, and >60% of dogs
with AML test positive for clonal or biclonal rearrangements.110
When lineage can be determined, about 50-55% of acute leukemias
in dogs are ALL, and 45-50% are AML.100,106-108 In dogs with ALL,
there is not a consistent predominance of B- or T-cell.106-108 Both Band T-cell ALL have been reported in cats, but there are too few to
make meaningful comparisons.111

Clinical Signs
Most dogs and cats with acute leukemia are clinically ill at time of
initial presentation. Anorexia and lethargy are common108,109,111;
other clinical signs include vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, and
neurologic abnormalities. Mild lymphadenopathy is reported in over
half of dogs, but it is not reported in cats. Other PE findings include
cranial abdominal organomegaly, fever, pallor, petechia, and
epistaxis. T-cell ALL can cause paraneoplastic hypercalcemia,

causing PU/PD. FeLV (ch. 199) is associated with acute leukemias
in cats.3

Diagnostics
Greater than 90% of dogs and cats with acute leukemia have
neoplastic cells seen on peripheral blood smears (ch. 58). In some,
the number of neoplastic cells is small or they are not detectable at
all.106-109,111 Total white blood cell counts can be increased due to
neoplastic cells, normal, or even low in a pet with few neoplastic
circulating cells and concurrent neutropenia. Anemia and
thrombocytopenia are common (chs. 57 and 59). Many have
cytopenias in multiple cell lines due to neoplastic cells displacing
normal hematopoietic cells, termed myelophthisis. The percentage of
neoplastic cells circulating in the peripheral blood does not correlate
with the severity of concurrent cytopenias, emphasizing the
importance of BM cytology not only to assist with diagnosis but also
to assess normal hematopoietic function.106

Treatment, Support, and Prognosis
Treating acute leukemias is challenging. Most dogs and cats are
clinically ill and myelosuppressive drugs must be given to pets that
are already cytopenic and have impaired hematopoiesis. Severe
anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia are common. Even with
intensive supportive care, e.g., blood transfusions and broadspectrum antibiotics, clients must be prepared for life-threatening
treatment-associated adverse events (ch. 321).
When choosing a more intensive treatment approach, ALL is
commonly treated with L-CHOP, which consists of the CHOP
protocol with the addition of L-asparaginase. The inclusion of Lasparaginase at induction is strongly advised because it is does not
further impair normal hematopoietic function. Even with the most
intensive treatment approach, the prognosis is grave. Reported MSTs
in dogs and cats are <3 months and survival >6 months is
rare.105,107,108,111 There are no established chemotherapy protocols
for AML. Therapies used include L-asparaginase, CHOP, and
cytosine arabinoside.109 MSTs for dogs treated with aggressive

chemotherapy was <2 months, comparable to using only prednisone.
None of these afflicted pets lived beyond 6 months.

MYELOPROLIFERATIVE NEOPLASMS,
MYELODYSPLASTIC SYNDROME
Definitions and Diagnosis
Myeloproliferative neoplasms, previously termed chronic
myeloproliferative disorders, are characterized by excessive
production of differentiated BM cells, resulting in accumulation of
erythrocytes (primary erythrocytosis, also called polycythemia vera;
ch. 173), granulocytes and/or monocytes (chronic myeloid
leukemias [CMLs]), or platelets (essential thrombocythemia).
Because these cells are morphologically similar to their nonneoplastic counterparts, diagnosis centers around ruling out
physiologic or paraneoplastic etiologies for the increases in blood cell
counts (chs. 57-59).

Treatment and Prognosis
Primary erythrocytosis is reviewed in ch. 173. A subset of dogs with
CML have the same breakpoint cluster region-ABL (BCR-ABL)
chromosomal translocation (“Raleigh chromosome”) as the
“Philadelphia chromosome” translocation associated with CML in
people.112 Use of the tyrosine kinase inhibitor toceranib (Palladia,
Zoetis) has been successful in a dog with CML. Additional studies are
warranted. Historically, hydroxyurea (20-25 mg/kg PO q12h) has
been used to treat CML in dogs1 and continued until the leukocyte is
<15,000-20,000/mcL. The dose can then be reduced (10-15 mg/kg
PO q24h or to 50 mg/kg PO once every 2 or 3 weeks). Essential
thrombocythemia is rare in dogs and cats. There is no established
therapy in dogs or cats and in people it is controversial whether to
implement therapy in asymptomatic patients.1
Myelodysplastic syndromes (ch. 176) are uncommon in dogs and
cats. Patients have cytopenias involving multiple cell lines:
neutropenia with or without left shift, nonregenerative anemia,

and/or thrombocytopenia. Other blood abnormalities can include
macrocytic erythrocytes and metarubricytosis. The BM is usually
normocellular to hypercellular with dysplastic changes in multiple
cell lines. There usually are increased blast cells, but they constitute
<20% of all nucleated cells (a blast percentage >20% is diagnostic for
AML). Myelodysplasia is sometimes referred to as preleukemia
because in some it will progress to AML. There is no standard
therapy for myelodysplasia. Darbepoetin alfa, retinoic acid analogs,
1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D3, interferon-alpha, 6-thioguanine, and
cytosine arabinoside can induce differentiation of hematopoietic
cells.1

MYELOMA-RELATED DISORDERS
(MRD)
DEFINITIONS
MRD arise from neoplastic transformation of plasma cells or Igsecreting B-cell precursors,113 and include a variety of clinical
syndromes. Multiple myeloma (MM), the most common MRD, is the
systemic proliferation of malignant plasma cells arising as a clone of
a single cell with multifocal or diffuse involvement of the BM.114,115
These cells most commonly produce IgG or IgA immunoglobulins.
Production of IgM immunoglobulins is less common and is called
IgM macroglobulinemia (Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia)
because IgM normally exists as a high molecular weight pentamer,
and this larger size increases risk of serum hyperviscosity.54,116
Plasma cell tumors involving the BM can be seen as a solitary
osseous plasmacytoma, although most eventually progress to
MM.117 Plasma cell tumors also can arise outside of BM, either in the
skin (cutaneous extramedullary plasmacytoma, ch. 323) or
visceral organs (non-cutaneous extramedullary plasmacytoma).
Cats with MRD can have BM involvement, multicentric abdominal
organ involvement (most commonly liver and/or spleen), or both,
blurring distinction between MM and non-cutaneous

plasmacytoma.113,118,119 Lastly, MRD also includes Ig-secreting
lymphoma and leukemias (including plasma cell leukemia).

MULTIPLE MYELOMA (MM)
Prevalence
MM accounts for <10% of all hematopoietic tumors in dogs.114 In
cats, the relatively rare MM and multicentric noncutaneous
extramedullary plasmacytomas together account for <2% of all
hematopoietic tumors,1,119 with no FeLV or FIV association.

Pathophysiology
Because MM arises from a single clone of plasma cells or their
precursors, the neoplastic cells typically synthesize an
overabundance of 1 Ig component, referred to as the M component,
which can represent an entire Ig molecule of any class, or a
molecular portion, such as light or heavy chains (ch. 60).55 Biclonal
gammopathies also have been reported in both dogs and
cats.113,115,119 Nonsecretory MM with no M component is rare but
has been reported in dogs.120

Clinical Signs
In some dogs and cats, diagnosis is incidental, identifying
hyperglobulinemia on routine serum biochemistries. Clinical signs
vary widely, as they result from tumor infiltration of various organ
systems, from complications of excess M-component, and/or other
paraneoplastic syndromes, e.g., hypercalcemia.113-115,119 The most
common signs in dogs and cats are lethargy, weakness, and
decreased appetite. Tumor cells infiltrating BM can cause anemia,
thrombocytopenia, and less commonly neutropenia. Bone lesions,
classically discrete osteolytic painful lesions, occasionally with
concurrent pathologic fractures, occur most commonly in bones
engaged in active hematopoiesis: vertebrae, ribs, pelvis, and long
bones. Vertebral lesions also can secondarily compress the spinal

cord and cause neurologic deficits (Figure 322.7). Paraneoplastic
hypercalcemia (ch. 331), thought to arise more commonly due to
bone lysis than via PTHrP,114,121 can cause PU/PD, and renal failure
(ch. 69).
M components can interfere with coagulation primarily by coating
platelets, inhibiting platelet aggregation to damaged endothelial
surfaces, and release of platelet factor 3 (chs. 171, 175).54,55,116 The
resulting functional thrombopathy commonly causes epistaxis or
petechia. Intact Ig molecules are usually released by plasma cells, but
occasionally there is an imbalance in heavy and light chain
production. Excess free light chains excreted in the urine, called
Bence Jones proteins (ch. 70), can cause renal tubular casts,
interstitial nephritis and possibly renal failure.54,55,116 Despite
having a high serum globulin level, normal Ig levels can be severely
depressed, placing patients at risk for secondary infections.116
Hyperviscosity syndrome refers to a constellation of clinical signs
caused by an increase in blood viscosity. The clinical signs of
hyperviscosity result from sludging of blood in small vessels,
ineffective delivery of oxygen and nutrients, and coagulation
abnormalities. Reported neurologic abnormalities include stuporous
mentation, ataxia, and seizures.54,116,122,123 Ocular abnormalities
include enlarged and tortuous retinal vessels, retinal hemorrhages,
and retinal detachment, often resulting in acute-onset blindness (ch.
13).116,122,124 Bleeding diathesis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and
congestive heart failure also can occur.55,116,122,125

FIGURE 322.7 Midline sagittal T1-weighted
magnetic resonance image post gadolinium contrast
administration in a dog with multiple myeloma.
Brightly contrast-enhancing lesions are identified
throughout the lumbar vertebrae, most notably in
the vertebral bodies of L1, L3, and L4 (arrows), and
the dorsal laminae of L1, L2, and L3 (asterisks).

Diagnostic Evaluation
MM is diagnosed by identifying ≥2 of the following criteria: BM
plasmacytosis (>20%), serum monoclonal gammopathy, osteolytic
lesions, and/or Bence-Jones proteinuria.115 The author depends on
BM plasmacytosis and at least 1 other criterion. The diagnostic
criteria may be modified in cats because BM involvement is not as
consistent; thus, it includes plasma cell morphology and visceral
organ involvement.113,118,119 Identifying a monoclonal gammopathy
alone is not sufficient to diagnose MM. B-cell LSA, B-cell CLL, and
some chronic infectious diseases (e.g., ehrlichiosis, leishmaniasis,
feline infectious peritonitis) can also cause monoclonal
gammopathies. A benign monoclonal gammopathy not associated
with osteolysis, BM infiltration, or Bence-Jones proteinuria, has
rarely been reported in dogs.126
Any animal suspected of a plasma cell tumor should be assessed
with CBC, platelet count, serum biochemistry profile, and UA. Serum

electrophoresis discriminates proteins into distinct groups based on
electrical charge and size. A tall, narrow peak, due to a predominance
of same-size globulins, is consistent with a monoclonal gammopathy
(ch. 60). Spikes are usually in the gamma region of the
electrophoretogram (hence the term gammopathy), but occasionally
it can be seen in the beta-2 region.55 Routine electrophoresis cannot
determine Ig class; immunofixation is required if this information is
needed.127 Urine electrophoresis is needed to detect Bence Jones
proteins.128 In pets with bleeding disorders, platelet count, buccal
mucosal bleeding time (ch. 79), prothrombin time (PT) and partial
thromboplastin time (PTT) should be evaluated (ch. 170).
Thoracic radiographs are recommended, with careful inspection of
all bony structures. Additional radiographs may be indicated by
skeletal pain or other clinical signs. While whole-body CT is not
routinely indicated, it is more sensitive than radiography for
identifying bone lysis and can be useful to direct biopsy procedures
when standard BM sites are inconclusive. CT is helpful for
confirming focal disease in dogs thought to have solitary osseous
plasmacytoma. Abdominal US is recommended, especially in cats
because of the high prevalence of abdominal visceral involvement.
Definitive diagnosis usually requires BM aspirate or core biopsy.
Because MM can be multifocal, occasionally sampling multiple sites
might be needed to identify BM plasmacytosis. US-guided fine
needle aspiration of abnormal abdominal organs is also
recommended in cats since BM involvement is not as consistent (ch.
84).

Treatment
The initial treatment of choice is a combination of melphalan and
prednisone in dogs. Two different melphalan protocols have been
evaluated: 0.1 mg/kg PO q24h for 10 days and then 0.05 mg/kg PO
q24h indefinitely, or 7 mg/m2 PO q24h for 5 days repeated every 3
weeks.114,115 With both melphalan dosing protocols, prednisone is
given for 10 days (0.5 mg/kg PO q24h) and then 0.5 mg/kg PO q48h
for 60 days. A single dose of cyclophosphamide (200-250 mg/m2 IV
or PO) is sometimes given at the start of therapy in dogs with more

severe clinical signs in the hopes of inducing a remission more
quickly.1,114
In cats with MRD, melphalan has been used but is not routinely
recommended due to idiosyncratic severe and refractory
myelosuppression.113,129,130 Cyclophosphamide (200 mg/m2 IV of
PO q2-3wk, or 25 mg/cat PO twice a week) has been used in place of
melphalan with a comparable prognosis1,130 Prednisolone (1 mg/kg
PO q24h × 14 days, then 1 mg/kg PO every other day indefinitely).
COP protocols have been used,113 and are preferred by the author.
In both dogs and cats, long-term alleviation of clinical signs
depends on effective tumor control. However, more immediate
therapy might also be needed for secondary complications. Fluid
therapy is indicated for pets with hypercalcemia (chs. 283 and 331)
and/or renal impairment. Zoledronate can reduce
hypercalcemia,54,131 alleviate bone pain associated with lytic lesions,
and help prevent pathologic fractures.131 When fractures do occur,
surgical repair might be indicated depending on the location and
severity. RT also is highly effective for alleviating pain associated
with lytic bone lesions.117,132 Hyperviscosity syndrome is most
effectively managed with plasmapheresis.125,133

Monitoring
When assessing response to therapy, it is ideal to objectively
quantitate the tumor. However, when tumor cells are confined to BM
one must rely on indirect assessments: clinical signs,
clinicopathologic parameters, radiographs, and (in cats) abdominal
US. It is important to recognize that many of these parameters can
lag behind tumor control by several weeks. Radiographic
improvement in lytic bone lesions can take months and often is
incomplete. For routine follow-up, quantification of serum globulin,
Ig, or urine Bence Jones proteins is performed monthly until a good
response to therapy is verified, and then every 2 months. BM
reevaluation is indicated when peripheral blood cytopenias develop
during therapy. Drug-induced myelosuppression must be
distinguished from tumor progression/myelophthisis.

Prognosis, Dogs
About 85-90% have improvement in serum globulins, and reported
MSTs range from 1.5 to 2.5 years.114,115,134 Serial evaluation of
serum electrophoresis and immunofixation is more sensitive for
detecting minimal residual disease compared to measuring total
globulins.134 Dogs with ≥90% reduction in M-proteins have the best
prognosis. Hypercalcemia, excessive lytic bone lesions, and Bence
Jones proteinuria are negative prognostic factors.114

Prognosis, Cats
The prognosis for cats with multicentric MRD is more guarded.
About 50-85% of cats have a positive response to therapy, but MSTs
range from 8 to 13 months.113,129,130 One study anecdotally
suggested hypercalcemia, the presence of bony lesions with
pathologic fracture, anemia, Bence Jones proteinuria, azotemia, and
little to no improvement in serum protein levels 8 weeks after
starting therapy were all parameters associated with more aggressive
tumors and a poorer prognosis.129

SOLITARY OSSEOUS AND
EXTRAMEDULLARY PLASMACYTOMA
Solitary osseous plasmacytoma typically presents as a single lytic
bone lesion. Lesions in dogs and cats most commonly affect the
vertebrae, but in dogs they also have been identified in appendicular
skeleton, ribs, and skull.117,132,135,136 Patients usually present with
pain. Vertebral tumors also can cause neurologic deficits.
Hyperglobulinemia is uncommon, presumably because tumor cell
burden is not as high compared to MM. Full staging for MM is
strongly recommended to ensure the patient does not have systemic
disease. RT is highly effective for local tumor control and alleviating
pain.117,132,135,136 Surgery might be indicated to stabilize a
pathologic fracture or alleviate neurologic signs by decompressing
the spinal cord. Adjuvant chemotherapy has been used frequently,

but the benefit is uncertain.117,132,136 Most patients do progress to
MM, but this can take months to years.117,132,136 In people, there is
no benefit to starting chemotherapy prior to developing systemic
disease.1
In dogs, extramedullary plasmacytomas arise commonly in the
skin (limbs, trunk, and ears), followed by the oral cavity and lips, and
the GI tract (esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large
intestine).132,137-140 Cutaneous and oral plasma cell tumors in dogs
usually are benign, and prognosis is excellent with complete surgical
excision.137 When complete excision is not possible, RT is an
effective alternative.132 A small percentage of dogs will present with
multiple cutaneous plasma cell tumors, called cutaneous
plasmacytosis.141 Surgery typically is not an option for these dogs
due to the number of skin lesions as well as the higher prevalence of
systemic involvement. Melphalan and prednisone typically is used
(see above). About 75% of dogs have a positive response to
chemotherapy. Median time to progression is <6 months, but even
so median survival approaches 1.5 years.141 GI plasmacytomas are
more commonly associated with regional lymph node metastasis
than cutaneous tumors, but BM involvement and monoclonal
gammopathies are uncommon.138,139 There is some evidence that
colorectal plasmacytomas might be less aggressive than those arising
from other parts of the intestine, although regional lymph node
metastasis has been reported.139,140 Survival times of >1 year are
common with complete surgical excision. Adjuvant chemotherapy is
warranted for extramedullary plasmacytomas with confirmed
metastasis.
Feline noncutaneous extramedullary plasmacytoma is discussed
above with MM.
Cats with cutaneous extramedullary plasmacytoma can present
with a solitary mass but up to half will have multiple skin masses.113,118,119 Cats with cutaneous extramedullary plasmacytomas also
are more likely than dogs to have concurrent involvement in the BM
and/or abdominal visceral organs. There is limited information on
prognosis, but long-term survival (>1.5 years) is possible for cats

with disease that is confined to a local site when these cats are
treated with surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy.113

PREVALENCE, COMMON TUMORS,
ETIOLOGY

PREVALENCE
The skin is one of the most common tumor sites in dogs and cats,
and one often seen or felt by owners. The prevalence of skin tumors
in dogs and cats is vague due to inconsistent reporting and data
collection. It varies considerably from region to region, likely due to
differences in breed popularity and environment. Skin tumors
account for ∼25-45% of all canine1-5 and ∼20-30% of all feline
neoplasms.1,5-7 In dogs, most skin tumors (∼57-80%) are benign.24,7-12

In a recent study from Japan, ∼57% of skin tumors were

histologically malignant.13 In cats, most skin tumors (50-65%) are
histologically malignant.1,6,7,14

Common Skin Tumors
The 4 most common skin tumors in dogs (∼54% of all skin tumors)
are soft tissue sarcoma (ch. 324), mast cell tumor (MCT) (ch. 327),
lipoma, and histiocytoma (ch. 328).1,2,7,8,10-13,15-19 The prevalence
of the top 10 canine skin neoplasms compiled from 12 studies with a
total of 22,853 skin neoplasms is presented in Table 323.1.2,8,1013,15-19
The prevalence of lipomas, sebaceous gland adenomas, and
epidermal and follicular cysts are likely underreported, as they not
are often submitted for histologic evaluation. The 4 most common
skin tumors (∼65% total) in cats are basal cell tumor, fibrosarcoma,
squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), and MCT.1,6,8,9,14 The prevalence of
the top 10 feline skin neoplasms compiled from 4 studies with a total
of 9531 skin neoplasms is presented in Table 323.2.6,8,9,14

Classifications
Tumors of the skin can be broadly classified histologically according
to the tissue of origin: epithelial, mesenchymal, round, melanocytic,
and neuroendocrine. This chapter focuses on tumors of epithelial
origin, melanoma, and plasmacytoma (

Video 323.1). Anal sac

apocrine gland tumors (ch. 264), perianal gland tumors (hepatoid

gland tumors, ch. 264), mesenchymal tumors (soft tissue sarcomas
[ch. 324], and hemangiosarcoma [ch. 325]), round cell tumors
(MCT [ch. 327], lymphoma [chs. 12, 322], histiocytic disease [ch.
328], and transmissible venereal cell tumor [ch. 330]) are
discussed elsewhere. Merkel cell neuroendocrine carcinomas are
exceedingly rare tumors and not discussed.

Etiology
The cause of skin tumors is generally unknown, and likely
multifactorial. However, viral,20 ultraviolet (UV) radiation,21
ionizing radiation, immunosuppression,22 and genetic factors, likely
have roles.

HISTORY AND PHYSICAL
EXAMINATION (PE)
Tumors of the skin are usually easily observed by owners and the
veterinary health care team. Owners should be encouraged to seek
veterinary attention for any skin lesion or mass, even if present and
unchanged for months to years. Some tumors, e.g., MCTs (ch. 327),
have a highly varied range of appearances, and sometimes are
inadvertently mistaken for nonneoplastic lesions (e.g., skin infection)
or misdiagnosed clinically as a skin tag or lipoma. History should
include the rate of growth, duration, change in appearance, clinical
signs associated with the lesions or masses, and response to any
previous treatment. Benign tumors tend to have a history of slow
growth (i.e., months to years) whereas malignant tumors tend to
rapidly grow and change in appearance (i.e., days to weeks).
The PE (ch. 3) should include identifying and measuring all skin
lesions or masses (e.g., location, photographs, diagrams, and/or
caliper measurements), and accurately describing all measurable
lesions or masses (i.e., color, consistency, well-circumscribed versus
ill-defined, fixed versus movable). Locoregional lymph nodes should
be thoroughly palpated, and cytologic or histopathologic evaluation
performed on all palpably enlarged, asymmetric or firm lymph nodes
(ch. 88). However, lymph node size is not an accurate predictor of

metastasis. Nodes should always be sampled in dogs with MCT or
melanoma because metastasis may occur to palpably normal lymph
nodes.23,24 Although history and PE are important, they cannot
discriminate benign from malignant. Further diagnostic testing is
required to diagnose skin tumors.

DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
STAGING
Staging involves assessing potential sites of metastasis and may
include lymph node evaluation, radiography, ultrasonography (US),
computed tomography (CT), and/or magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI). The staging tests that are selected depend on tumor type and
clinical findings. CT or MRI may help delineate tumor borders to
facilitate surgical planning. A complete blood count and serum
biochemistry profile are not essential but recommended to assess
general health and identify any comorbidity that may affect
management. Some skin tumors are associated with paraneoplastic
syndromes (ch. 331).

CYTOLOGY
Fine-needle aspirates (FNA) or direct impression smears for
cytologic evaluation are recommended in all skin lesions and masses
(ch. 83). Cytologic evaluation can diagnose many common benign
skin tumors such as lipoma and sebaceous gland adenoma (Figures
323.1 and 323.2). However, for many skin tumors, cytology only
provides cell type (i.e., epithelial, mesenchymal or round cell tumor)
but not usually specific tumor type. For lesions that appear
malignant, equivocal or nondiagnostic cytologically, tissue sampling
with histopathologic assessment is recommended, and is the gold
standard diagnostic test required to obtain a definitive diagnosis.

BIOPSY
When performing a biopsy, it is crucial that representative tissue
samples are collected, properly preserved, and processed (ch. 83).
Excisional biopsy implies complete removal of the entire tumor and
is convenient because both diagnosis and treatment are
accomplished in one procedure. However, it is rarely the first best
step in confirming a diagnosis. Careful selection is required because
if the histologic margins are incomplete, a larger, more extensive
surgery may be required or not possible in some locations. Incisional
biopsy removes a portion of a tumor. This is often necessary in
difficult locations, e.g., masses or other lesions on distal extremities.
Applying India ink or other dyes to the excised surface of a biopsy
specimen can help the pathologist interpret surgical margins (

Video 323.2). Common incisional biopsy techniques include wedge,
punch, and core (Tru-Cut) needle biopsies (ch. 83).

EPITHELIAL TUMORS
PAPILLOMA
Description
Cutaneous papillomas (papillomatosis) are benign epidermal
proliferative lesions occasionally associated with papillomavirus
infection.20 They represent 3.4% of all canine skin neoplasms. They
usually affect older dogs (Table 323.1) but are rare in cats. They
usually grow in an exophytic pattern, protruding above the skin’s
surface.20,25 Some, usually in younger dogs, are “inverted,” i.e., they
grow into subcutaneous (SQ) tissues.20 In dogs, papillomas appear
as whitish, pedunculated, or cauliflower like masses, often referred
to as “warts” (Figure 323.3). In cats, papillomas have a plaque-like
appearance, white or pigmented, and scaly or greasy. They can be
single or multiple, and can occur anywhere on the body, but are most
common on the face, ears, and extremities.5,20

FIGURE 323.3 Typical appearance of multiple
papillomas around the mucocutaneous region in a 3year-old dog. Courtesy Dr. Zoe della Valle.

Clinical Presentation and Treatment
In dogs, many papillomas regress spontaneously. The length of time
between development of lesions and their regression varies from
weeks to months.20 However, for solitary lesions in both dogs and
cats, surgery is usually curative and the treatment of choice. In dogs
with multiple or persistent papillomas, oral azithromycin,25 oral
retinoids,26 or topical imiquimod cream,27 and treating the
underlying cause of the immunosuppression may be helpful. In rare
cases, papillomas can transform into SCC.20

Fibropapilloma is a variant of cutaneous papilloma seen in cats,
with similarities to equine sarcoids. Feline fibropapillomas have a
strong papillomavirus association and typically affect cats <5 years of
age. Lesions commonly occur on the head, neck, ventral abdomen,
and limbs, and recurrence may develop following surgery.28

CANINE SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA
(SCC)
Description
Canine dermal SCC is a malignant neoplasm of epidermal cells that
show differentiation to keratinocytes.5 Dermal SCC represent 4.3%
of all canine skin neoplasms (Table 323.1). Bull Terriers,
Dalmatians, Boxers, Beagles, Norwegian Elkhounds, Basset Hounds,
and Pointers are overrepresented.21 Dogs with nonpigmented thin
haircoats along the ventrum and flank, particularly dogs that spend
time in the sun, are at increased risk.21 Histologic solar-induced
actinic changes occur in approximately 40% of affected dogs.21

Clinical Presentation
Dermal SCC often starts as a precancerous lesion (dysplasia), which
progresses to in situ SCC (i.e., no invasion beyond basement
membrane layers), eventually forming an invasive SCC. Lesions may
be overlooked when in the form of dysplasia or in situ carcinoma,
often appearing as tenacious waxy debris that, when removed, may
reveal erythema and/or ulceration. In advanced cases, crusting,
ulceration, and invasion into surrounding tissues may be severe.
Skin lesions may be solitary (50%) or multiple (50%).21 Dermal SCC
is locally invasive, with a low metastatic rate of 5-22%.21 Metastasis
predominantly occurs to the regional lymph nodes, and rarely to the
lungs.21

Prognosis and Treatment

Negative prognostic factors associated with reduced survival
outcomes include non-actinic dermal SCC, non-predisposed breeds,
white-coated dogs, presence of nodal or distant metastasis, and
ventral cervical region location.21 Most dermal SCCs are well
differentiated with an excellent prognosis after adequate surgical
removal. Long term survival is expected in most dogs with dermal
SCC with complete surgical resection, even with non-actinic changes.
Cures are possible, especially with complete margins surgery and no
evidence of metastasis. Removing multiple tumors can be
challenging and some dogs develop new tumors throughout their
lifetime. There is high chance of recurrence after incomplete surgery.
The roles of chemotherapy and radiation therapy (RT) in treating
canine dermal SCC are unknown. However, chemotherapy (ch. 317)
or toceranib phosphate (ch. 320) can be considered in dogs with
unfavorable prognostic factors, such as metastasis. In dogs with too
many cutaneous lesions to consider resection, pre-neoplastic lesions,
or superficial SCC, oral piroxicam,29 oral retinoids,30 topical
imiquimod,22 strontium-90 plesiotherapy (ch. 318),31 and/or
intralesional chemotherapy32 may help. For dogs with solar-induced
dermal SCC, UV damage to the skin has already occurred, and will
likely lead to the development of new skin lesions during the dog’s
lifetime. Methods to reduce the risk of further cancer development
and delay disease progression include avoiding sun exposure,
applying sunscreen, and having dogs covered.

FELINE MULTICENTRIC SQUAMOUS
CELL CARCINOMA IN SITU
Description and Clinical Presentation
Bowenoid in situ carcinoma (BISC), also called Bowen’s-like disease
or multicentric SCC in situ, is a rare skin tumor of cats. BISC is a
variant of superficial SCC that does not penetrate past the basement
membrane of the epithelium.5,33 Most cases occur in domestic
shorthair cats.22 Devon Rex cats appear to be predisposed to
aggressive BISCs at a young age: some develop numerous and

rapidly progressive BISCs, systemic illness, metastasis, and undergo
humane euthanasia within a year.34
Cats usually present with multiple lesions.22 Solitary lesions are
uncommon. Lesions are typically crusty or waxy, well-demarcated,
erythematous plaques, but can be erosive, proliferative, coalescing
(Figure 323.4), and may be painful.5,22 Unlike most SCC, BISC is
not caused by exposure to sunlight, and may be caused by
papillomavirus infection. Lesions can occur anywhere on the body on
both haired and unhaired skin, and in areas with or without sun
exposure.22 BISC can be seen in conjunction with solar-induced SCC.
BISC’s behavior is similar to superficial solar- induced SCC, but often
slower in progression (i.e., grows over months). Around 20% of
BISCs progress into invasive SCC,33 and although uncommon, some
cats (particularly Devon Rex cats)34 will develop metastasis later in
the course of the disease, primarily to the lungs or regional lymph
nodes.

FIGURE 323.4 Bowenoid in situ carcinoma in an
11-year-old cat with a dark coat. This cat had
multiple, coalescing, crusty, proliferative lesions that
were not caused by exposure to sunlight.

Treatment
Treatment for BISC is primarily aimed at local disease control. Wide
surgical excision, the treatment of choice, is potentially curative.
However, >75% of cats develop new lesions at other sites over their
lifetime,22 which can be a nuisance or impractical to perform
surgery, particularly in cats that develop too many lesions over their
body. If surgery is not possible to remove all skin lesions, surgery can
still be considered for palliation on skin lesions that are bothersome
or not responsive to medical management. Even if the margins are
incomplete, some BISC lesions do not recur. Cats can exhibit
improved quality of life (QoL) after removal of painful and/or
infected lesions. Topical imiquimod,22 strontium-90 plesiotherapy

(ch. 318),31 photodynamic therapy,35 and oral piroxicam36 may
help.

FELINE SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA
Description and Clinical Presentation
Feline SCC is the third most common skin tumor, representing 11.5%
of all feline skin neoplasms (Table 323.2). In Australia and New
Zealand, feline SCC is their most common skin tumor, accounting for
about half of all feline skin neoplasms.37 This is likely associated
with chronic sunlight exposure, as SCC is believed to be actinically
(solar UV) induced. Cats have a predilection for developing SCC on
their heads (80-90%),5,6 particularly in lightly haired, and poorly
pigmented areas, e.g., the nasal planum, pinnae, and eyelids in white
or partly white cats (75-95%).5 Cats typically have multiple facial
sites affected. Most cases occur in Domestic Shorthairs.37 The
appearance and progression of feline dermal SCC is similar to dogs:
dysplasia to in situ SCC and eventually forming invasive SCC.37 SCCs
are locally invasive tumors, uncommonly spreading to regional
lymph nodes and rarely to the lungs.37 Metastasis is usually slow to
occur, usually later in the course of the disease (i.e., cats with
invasive or advanced SCC).37

Prognosis and Treatment
When a cat is left untreated, the prognosis is guarded. SCCs continue
to grow and locally invade tissue structures, impacting the cat’s QoL.
The course of disease may be slow or rapid (i.e., weeks to months).
Clinical stage is the most consistent and reliable prognostic factor for
feline facial SCC.37 Cats with nodal or distant metastasis have a
worse prognosis. If there is no evidence of metastasis, removal with
wide surgical margins is recommended. SCC is potentially curable,
particularly with small non-invasive lesions.
Although less likely, cats with invasive SCC can be cured with
adequate surgery, but the risk of local recurrence is much higher in

cats with more invasive lesions. RT (ch. 318) can be considered after
incomplete excision, or for large invasive/advanced SCC not
amenable to surgery. RT can be palliative to alleviate pain and
prolong survival.38 Chemotherapy or toceranib phosphate can be
considered in cats with unfavorable prognostic factors, e.g.,
metastasis. For cats with too many cutaneous lesions for surgery,
preneoplastic lesions, or superficial SCC, oral piroxicam,29,36 topical
imiquimod,22 strontium-90 plesiotherapy,31 photodynamic
therapy,39 or cryotherapy40 may help. Electrochemotherapy,41
intralesional chemotherapy,42 and high dose brachytherapy43 could
be used for unresectable tumors. Avoiding sun exposure is important
to reduce the risk of further cancer development, and delay disease
progression.

BASAL CELL TUMORS (BCTs; BASAL
CELL EPITHELIOMA)
BCTs are benign neoplasms that arise from the basal cells of the
epidermis with no epidermal or adnexal differentiation. BCTs are the
most common skin tumor in cats, representing 26.7% of all feline
skin neoplasms (Table 323.2), but are uncommon in dogs. BCTs
have confusing nomenclatures because of inconsistencies in
classification. Previously, BCTs included basal cell epithelioma, basal
cell carcinoma (BCC), trichoblastoma, solid cystic ductular sweat
gland adenoma, and adenocarcinomas. The latter three are no longer
considered BCTs. BCTs usually appear on the head as a solitary,
pigmented, firm, and well-circumscribed mass,44 that can be
misdiagnosed clinically as melanoma.5,6,44 Diagnosis is confirmed
via histology; they are likely underdiagnosed cytologically due to
their nonspecific and mixed cytologic features.45 Wide surgical
excision is usually curative. Metastasis has not been reported.

BASAL CELL CARCINOMA (BCC)

BCCs are uncommon low grade malignant counterparts of BCTs.
BCCs can have a similar appearance to BCTs. However, BCCs often
cause epidermal ulceration and extensively infiltrate the dermis and
SQ.5 The head and neck are the most common locations.5 Wide
surgical excision is usually curative. Metastasis and recurrence have
been reported in cats, but are rare.5,46,47 Recurrence has been
reported in dogs, but not metastasis.48

BASOSQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA
Basosquamous cell carcinomas are rare malignant skin neoplasms
that display characteristics of both BCC and SCC.5 Their biologic
behavior and prognosis are unknown. Systemic metastasis was
reported in a dog.49 Wide surgical excision is recommended.

PILOMATRICOMA
Pilomatricomas are rare (1-3% of all canine skin tumors) benign
tumors in dogs and cats.50 Pilomatricoma arise from hair follicles.50
They are usually firm, well-demarcated, solitary masses with a
predilection for the back, neck, and tail.5 Grossly, they appear as one
or several lobules of gray to white chalky tissue that may have areas
of pigmentation.5 Wide surgical excision is recommended. Malignant
pilomatricoma may occur in dogs (uncommon), and can metastasize
to unusual sites, e.g., bone.5,50

TRICHOEPITHELIOMA
Trichoepitheliomas are benign tumors with differentiation to all
three segments of the hair follicle. They are relatively common in
dogs and rare in cats.5 Wide surgical excision is recommended.
Malignant trichoepithelioma may occur in dogs (rare), and can
metastasize.5

TRICHOBLASTOMA
Trichoblastomas are common benign tumors derived from primitive
hair germ epithelium and considered distinct from BCTs. Most
trichoblastomas are solitary, firm, well-circumscribed, slow growing
masses, with a predilection for the head and neck.51 Multiple
trichoblastomas have been described in 1 dog.51 Wide surgical
excision is recommended and potentially curative if there is complete
excision.

INTRACUTANEOUS CORNIFYING
EPITHELIOMA
Intracutaneous cornifying epitheliomas (also called
keratoacanthomas, infundibular keratinizing acanthomas, and
squamous papillomas) are benign tumors derived from the outer
hair follicle.5 They are common in dogs but not reported in any other
domestic species. Most are solitary masses with a central pore filled
with inspissated keratinous material.5 However, multiple tumors
may occur, particularly in Norwegian Elkhounds.5,52 Digital pressure
often results in the expulsion of gray to white keratinous material
through the pore onto the skin surface. Rupture may produce a
severe inflammatory response from the keratin contents. Surgical
excision is recommended and considered curative.52 In one study,
treatment with oral retinoids caused partial and complete
responses.26 Isotretinoin can be used in dogs with multiple or
unresectable tumors.

SEBACEOUS GLAND ADENOMA
Sebaceous gland adenomas are benign glandular skin tumors derived
from sebocytes, that produce sebum (an oily white fluid). They are
common in dogs (4.9% of all canine skin tumors), but rare in cats
(0.2% of all feline skin tumors). Sebaceous gland adenomas typically
are cauliflower- or wart-like lesions, usually solitary and greasy. They

commonly occur on the heads of dogs, and the head and back in
cats.5 They are usually slow-growing and are cured by wide surgical
excision (Figure 323.2).

SEBACEOUS EPITHELIOMA
Sebaceous epitheliomas are low-grade malignancies characterized by
a preponderance of basal cells with few well differentiated
sebocytes.53 The incidence in dogs and cats is unknown, but they are
more common in dogs. Appropriate surgery is usually curative,
although they may recur in dogs. Lymph node and distant metastasis
are rare.53,54

FOLLICULAR STEM CELL CARCINOMA
Follicular stem cell carcinomas (formerly sebaceous gland
carcinomas) are uncommon malignant tumors in dogs, derived from
primitive epithelial cells capable of differentiating into different
portions of the hair follicle and apocrine gland.55,56 They have not
been reported in any other domestic species. They are usually
solitary on the head of intact male dogs.5 They are locally infiltrative
and can appear as a red, sometimes ulcerated, intradermal mass that
is indistinguishable from other intradermal carcinomas.5 Metastasis
to the draining lymph nodes and distant sites is rare,5,56 and may
occur many years after the primary tumor has been excised.56 Wide
surgical excision is the treatment of choice.

APOCRINE SWEAT GLAND TUMORS
Apocrine sweat gland tumors are relatively uncommon skin tumors,
representing 2.0%, and 3.6% of all canine and feline neoplasms,
respectively.57 They can be benign (adenoma) or malignant
(carcinoma). In cats, they commonly occur in the head, particularly

the perioral region.5 In dogs, they are most common in the
forelimbs.5,58 Adenomas are usually solitary, well-demarcated
nodules that are readily amenable to surgery,5 whereas carcinomas
are usually solitary, and nodular.58 Some carcinomas are firm,
poorly circumscribed masses diffusely infiltrating the skin,
producing an ulcerated, moist, and sometimes hemorrhagic skin
surface that may be misdiagnosed as an inflammatory skin disease.58
Carcinomas are locally invasive; therefore, wide surgical margins
surgery are required.58 Metastases to the regional lymph node and
distant sites have been reported,58 but are rare (<2% of affected
dogs); metastasis is possibly associated with invasion into the
vasculature.57,58 The incidence of distant metastasis is unknown in
cats but appears rare.

CERUMINOUS GLAND TUMORS
Ceruminous gland tumors are uncommon skin tumors derived from
modified apocrine sweat glands in the external ear.5 Dogs and cats
may have a mass, chronic otitis externa, aural discharge, odor,
pruritus, pain, or neurologic signs. Adenomas are usually an
exophytic pedunculated or nodular mass, whereas carcinomas tend
to be more infiltrative, erosive, and ulcerative growths.5 Although
carcinomas metastasize uncommonly, meticulous staging is
recommended before surgery. The treatment of choice for both
adenomas and carcinomas is surgery. However, a total ear canal
ablation and lateral bulla osteotomy (TECA-LBO) is recommended in
dogs and cats with carcinomas. TECA-LBO significantly lowers
recurrence rates and increases the median remission duration in
both dogs and cats, compared with lateral ear canal resection.59,60
RT can be helpful if histologic margins are incomplete.61

ROUND CELL TUMORS

PLASMACYTOMA
Cutaneous plasma cell tumors (cutaneous extramedullary
plasmacytomas) are rare skin tumors in companion animals (Figure
323.5). They comprise <1% of all neoplasms in dogs and are even
less common in cats.62 Most cutaneous plasmacytomas in dogs occur
on the head or limbs, and are solitary, benign, and unrelated to
multiple myeloma.63 The treatment of choice in dogs is surgery and
it is usually curative. The local recurrence rate is 5%, and metastatic
rate is 2%.64 Thorough staging for general health and to determine if
multiple myeloma is present should be offered for all dogs (ch. 322).
Plasmacytomas can transform to aggressive cutaneous plasma cell
leukemia65 or occur as part of multiple myeloma. Cutaneous
plasmacytosis is an uncommon syndrome of multiple cutaneous
plasma cell tumors in the absence of multiple myeloma.63 The
treatment of choice is melphalan or lomustine, and prednisolone.
There is a paucity of information available in cats. Most feline
plasmacytomas are cutaneous or SQ and are considered systemic
(ch. 327)66 or they progress into myeloma-related disorders.62
Testing for myeloma-related disorders is recommended in all cats
(ch. 322). Solitary cutaneous plasmacytomas should be excised.
Chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide or melphalan, and
prednisolone is recommended in cats with evidence of systemic
disease.67

MELANOMA
Description
Melanomas are common skin tumors derived from melanocytes
(Figure 323.6), representing 6.9% of all canine skin neoplasms
(Table 323.1). They are rare in cats. Golden Retrievers, Labrador
Retrievers, Doberman Pinschers, Miniature Schnauzers, and Vizslas
are overrepresented.68 Melanomas usually are pigmented, expansile
or infiltrative masses, but they can also be large, flat, wrinkled, or
pedunculated masses that are occasionally unpigmented
(amelanotic). The risk factors for canine melanoma are unknown,
but unlike humans, it is not associated with sunlight exposure.
Cutaneous melanomas in haired skin, not in proximity to mucosal
margins (except in the eyelids), often behave in a benign fashion.
Surgical excision is often curative. A subset of these tumors is more

aggressive locally and metastasizes, primarily to the regional lymph
nodes, and lungs.

Prognosis in Dogs
The prognosis for canine cutaneous melanoma is primarily based on
clinical staging and histologic features of the tumor. Negative
prognostic factors associated with reduced survival outcome include
advanced clinical stage,68 high mitotic count (≥3 or >20), high Ki-67
or MIB-1 proliferation index on immunohistochemistry (≥15%),
marked nuclear atypia, high tumor score, presence of inflammation,
necrosis, ulceration, and/or marked anisocytosis, deep (compared to
dermal only) location, lack of pigmentation, and/or junctional
activity, and older dogs (>9.4 years of age).68,69 Although
incomplete surgical margins are associated with a negative survival
outcome in dogs with melanoma in other locations, surgical margins
do not appear to be an important prognostic factor for survival in
dogs with cutaneous melanoma.

Treatment in Dogs
The treatment of choice for cutaneous melanomas in both dogs and
cats is surgery. Metastasis and recurrence occur in up to 22% and 8%
of dogs, respectively at a median of 9 months after surgery.68
Carboplatin chemotherapy, and/or a commercially available
xenogeneic DNA canine melanoma vaccine (Oncept Canine
Melanoma Vaccine, Merial), can be used in dogs with negative
prognostic factors, unresectable, or metastatic disease (ch. 319).
However, there are limited studies in dogs with cutaneous
melanoma. Coarse fractionated RT is useful in dogs with oral
melanoma, and could be considered in dogs with unresectable
tumors (ch. 318).

Prognosis and Treatment in Cats
The prognosis for cats with cutaneous melanoma is guarded. In one
study of 57 cats, metastasis was documented in 19% at
presentation.70 The mean survival after surgery was 4.5 months, and

48.9% developed local recurrence or metastasis. Coarse fractionated
RT can lead to short-term complete and partial remission in cats
with nasal planum and oral melanoma.71,72 RT should be considered
in cats with unresectable tumors (ch. 318). The role of
chemotherapy is unknown. The commercially available xenogeneic
DNA canine melanoma vaccine can be safely administered to cats
with minimal risk of adverse effects (ch. 319).73 Chemotherapy
and/or the canine melanoma vaccine can be considered for cats with
negative prognostic factors, unresectable or metastatic disease.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Tumors of the Skin
Skin tumors (also called skin cancer or skin neoplasms) are common
in dogs and cats. Skin cancer accounts for around 25-45% of all
cancers in dogs, and about 20-30% of all cancers in cats. Skin
cancers can be benign, where they do not invade nearby tissue or
spread to other parts of the body (i.e., metastasis). However, they can
be malignant, where they can potentially invade nearby tissue, and
spread to other parts of the body, such as the lymph nodes, lungs, or
internal organs. The majority of skin cancers in dogs are benign
(57.5-80%). Conversely, the majority of skin cancers in cats are
malignant (50-65%).
Dogs and cats of all ages are at risk of skin cancer. The cause of
skin cancer is generally unknown. However, viruses, ultraviolet (UV)
radiation, ionizing radiation, immunosuppression, and genetic
factors, likely play a role.
When a skin mass or lesion is detected, every attempt should be
made to obtain a specific diagnosis. Knowledge of the type of skin
cancer will assist your veterinarian in determining the prognosis, and
appropriate treatment recommendations for your pet.
A diagnosis is usually confirmed by sampling the skin mass or
lesion with cytology (fine-needle aspirate samples) or biopsy (tissue
sample). Cytology is usually the first step, and is performed by
directing a small needle into the skin mass or lesion, often without
the need for sedatives. Cytology will yield single cells or small sheets
of cells. Sometimes a specific diagnosis of tumor type can be
obtained with cytology. However, for many skin cancers, cytology is
usually only sufficient to determine if the cells are potentially a
benign cancer or malignant cancer. Often, a biopsy is required for
confirmation. Biopsy involves sampling of tumor tissue (e.g.,
surgery) that will usually require pets to undergo general
anaesthesia. The biopsy specimen is then assessed by a pathologist
under a microscope (i.e., histology) to try to determine the specific
skin cancer type. The pathologist can also evaluate the
aggressiveness of the cancer. In some situations, a diagnosis via
biopsy cannot be obtained, and further stains (i.e.,

immunohistochemistry) are required to try to obtain a diagnosis of a
specific skin cancer type.
In pets with suspected or confirmed malignant skin cancer, staging
to check if the cancer has spread is recommended. Depending on the
specific type of skin cancer, staging tests include lymph node
evaluation, chest x-rays, abdominal ultrasound, computed
tomography (CT) scan, and/or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
scan. In addition, blood and urine tests are often recommended to
assess your pet’s general health, and determine if any other diseases
or medical conditions (i.e., comorbidities) may affect management.
Treatment will depend on the specific type of skin cancer, and can
vary from leaving the skin cancer in place and monitoring it closely,
surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and/or immunotherapy.
Your veterinarian will discuss the individual treatment
recommendations available for your pet.
You can help monitor for new skin cancers by regularly running
your hands over your pet to check for any skin masses or lesions.
Once identified, no matter how small or insignificant you think the
skin mass or lesion may be, it is important to alert your veterinarian.
A body map can be performed by your veterinarian, and/or
photographs taken. These can help track the skin growths that have
been evaluated over time.
Catherine My-An Chan (Brisbane, Queensland, Australia)

SUBCUTANEOUS SOFT TISSUE
SARCOMA IN DOGS
Soft tissue sarcomas (STSs) present as subcutaneous (SQ) masses,
and are almost always skin-covered (Figure 324.1, A). A
histologically diverse group, tumor histological diagnoses include
fibrosarcoma (FSA), peripheral nerve sheath tumor (also
schwannoma or neurofibrosarcoma), perivascular wall tumors
(previously hemangiopericytoma), liposarcoma, myxosarcoma, and
undifferentiated sarcoma.1-11 A precise histological distinction is not
clinically important, however, because of similar biological behavior.
STSs can be discrete (mobile) or fixed to underlying tissues. They
do not grossly involve bone and are non-painful. Other than the
noticeable presence of a mass, they cause no clinical signs early in
the disease. Most STSs grow slowly over months or even years.
Eventually they can stretch and ulcerate skin, interfere with mobility
and cause discomfort (Figure 324.2). A recent burst of tumor
growth is often the reason for presentation. Tumors that develop late
in a dog’s life may never cause a clinical problem.3

DIAGNOSIS
Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) is recommended as a first diagnostic
step (ch. 85). Like other mesenchymal tumors, STSs can exfoliate
poorly. Samples may be non-diagnostic/poorly cellular or
misdiagnosed as lipoma if only SQ adipose tissue is collected.5,12,13
When cellularity is adequate, cytomorphologic characteristics are
often not distinctive enough to differentiate the tumor type, and a
generic diagnosis of STS or spindle cell tumor is made.3,13,14
Incisional biopsy can be performed by needle core (Tru-Cut),
punch, or wedge biopsy.15 Even if fixed to the underlying tumor,
intact skin does not need to be included in the sample; tumor tissue
can be collected through a small skin incision. Histopathologic
evaluation will provide a diagnosis of STS, identify the specific tumor
type, and propose a histologic grade for the tumor. Tumor grade is
an important prognostic indicator of local recurrence and

metastasis.1,3,4,9,16-19 However, the grade determined from
incisional biopsy is incorrectly estimated in almost half (41%) of
cases; it is usually underestimated rather than overestimated.15
Excisional biopsy (i.e., marginal removal of the entire tumor) will
provide more accurate tumor grading and prognostication. An
excisional biopsy is not curative. By removing and disrupting tissue,
a subsequent curative-intent surgery may be more difficult with
increased morbidity, cost and chance of failure. If a diagnosis of STS
is established by FNA, biopsy is rarely beneficial.3 Biopsy is
recommended if there is clinical suspicion for hemangiosarcoma
(ch. 325), histiocytic sarcoma (ch. 328), melanoma (ch. 323),
lymphoma (ch. 322) or other non-STS mesenchymal tumor, as the
management plan may be different.

HISTOLOGIC TUMOR GRADE AND
MITOTIC INDEX
Tumor grade, determined from histologic examination of the excised
STS, is the most important predictor of biologic behavior and patient
outcome (Table 324.1). Most canine STSs are classified as grade I
or II. Grade III tumors represent 5-17% of cases.3,5,9,17,20,21 Risk of
tumor recurrence is as follows (for histologic margins <1 mm): grade
I <10%; grade II 30%; grade III 75%.1,3,17,18 Risk of metastasis:
grade I 0-13%; grade II 5-20%; grade III 40%.4,9,16,19,22 Taken
together, this means that most grade I and II STSs do not recur or
metastasize. Grade III tumors have a higher risk of tumor recurrence
(at least 1 in 2 dogs with narrow margins), and while these tumors
are more likely to spread, less than half of dogs with grade III STS
will develop metastasis.
Mitotic index (MI), independent of tumor grade, also provides
prognostic information. MI <9 predicts a lower risk of recurrence
after a narrow or incomplete excision.1,17 MI >19 is associated with a
higher risk of metastasis4 and shorter survival.3,4

TUMOR STAGING AND METASTASIS
Tumor staging involves determining the extent of disease for optimal
treatment planning and prognostication. Locally, the extent and
resectability of the primary tumor can be evaluated by palpation
and/or advanced imaging, most commonly computed tomography
(CT). For mobile, discrete tumors that you can wrap your fingers
around, imaging is unlikely to inform the surgical approach (
Video 324.1). Metastasis at diagnosis is rare, affecting only about 5%
of dogs overall, but this increases to 12-15% for grade III tumors.19,22
Lungs and regional lymph nodes are the most common sites.4,9,12
Metastasis can be slow to develop, taking months to years. Liver,
spleen, kidney, omentum, mesentery, and skin involvement are less
frequent and more likely to occur later in the course of
disease.3,4,9,11,12 Tumor staging should include FNA of any enlarged
regional lymph node (nodes can be reactive, especially after a recent
surgery or biopsy)1 and thoracic imaging by 3-view radiographs or
CT. CT is more sensitive for detecting pulmonary nodules and can be
used to simultaneously evaluate the primary tumor, lungs and
regional lymph node, if the latter is not accessible by palpation.
Ultrasound is also an option to evaluate intra-abdominal regional
lymph nodes. Given the overall low rate of metastasis and cost of
diagnostic procedures, some pet owners may reasonably elect not to
investigate for distant metastasis. For grade III tumors or those with
a MI >19 where the risk of metastasis is higher, tumor staging is
more likely to impact clinical decision-making and outcome.3,4,22

TREATMENT
Surgery is the mainstay of treatment for SQ STS. A complete excision
predicts long-term local tumor control without recurrence.4 Thus,
the aim of surgery is to achieve a curative resection when possible.
However, since the recurrence rate for incompletely or narrowly
excised grade I and II STS is low (<10% and 30%, respectively), a
wide excision may not be necessary for long-term control of these
tumors.2,3 A reasonable surgical goal is to take gross normal-tissue

margins to the extent that perioperative morbidity and function are
not compromised (Figure 324.1, B). If margins are incomplete or
narrow, then the pet owner can decide, based on their risk tolerance
for recurrence, whether to pursue local adjuvant therapy.
Amputation is certain to achieve a complete excision for most
extremity tumors, but this may be overkill as first-line treatment
given the low recurrence rate of most STS. Complete excision or
adjuvant therapy is more important for grade III tumors given their
higher risk of recurrence. Inking specimen margins (

Video

323.2) at the time of surgery helps identify where residual tumor
cells remain along the surgical edge. This is useful for planning a reexcision in the event of incomplete margins. In addition, placing
hemoclips to mark the edges of resection before the surgical site is
closed will help radiotherapy (RT) planning if pursued.
