Histopathology reports should include the diagnosis with specific
tumor histologic characteristics, tumor grade, MI, and an assessment
of the margin of excision. If tumor cells do not extend to the surgical
edge, the report should indicate the distance to the closest cancer
cell. Most reports define a complete excision as a >3-5 mm histologic
margin and a narrow/marginal excision as <3 mm, without cancer
cells at the edge.

Adjuvant Local Therapy
Adjuvant treatment options to further reduce risk of recurrence after
a narrow or incomplete excision include scar revision (re-excision)
and RT. Re-excision is preferred over RT if it can be done with low
morbidity and if a meaningful (0.5 cm) gross margin of tissue can be
removed.5 Due to the limitations of histopathology, residual tumor
cells are sometimes not detected in resected scars. Rarely, recurrence
can occur following a scar revision if margins were deemed complete
or if there were no cancer cells identified in the resected tissue.5,16
RT offers a non-invasive option to sterilize or “clean up” residual
microscopic STS after surgery (ch. 318). RT involves multiple
anesthetic episodes, well tolerated by most dogs without significant
comorbidities. Multiple radiation protocols are published. Accurate
assessments of tumor control are difficult because of confounding
factors and non-standardized approaches. Furthermore, the low
recurrence rate of incompletely or narrowly excised STS makes it
difficult to assess the impact of radiation in studies without a control
group. Sarcomas are generally radioresistant and require high total
radiation doses. Since high doses are more safely delivered when
divided, or fractionated, into multiple low-dose treatments, the
standard approach to STS involves 15-25 radiation treatments (called

fractions) delivered multiple times per week (usually daily) to a total
dose of 50-60 Gy.13,23,24 This definitive approach minimizes the risk
of severe long-term side-effects because the radiation dose per
fraction is low, which is the most important determinant of tissue
necrosis after RT. While the risk of long-term complications is low,
definitive RT is associated with early (or acute) side effects that begin
towards the end of the protocol, affecting rapidly proliferating
epithelial tissues like skin. These unpleasant but self-limiting side
effects are managed at home with supportive medications and heal
2-4 weeks after RT (Figure 324.3, B and C). Other published
protocols, designed for convenience, include fewer fractions
delivered less frequently (e.g., 6 biweekly fractions of 5 Gy and 4
weekly fractions of 6-8 Gy).21,25,26 With the advent of highlyconformal radiation delivery systems that target tumors while
sparing normal tissue, high-dose-per-fraction (9-16 Gy) daily or
every other day short stereotactic protocols are being used by some
because of their convenience. The author avoids these protocols for
treatment of tumors in the microscopic disease setting because of the
risk of normal tissue necrosis as a long-term complication.

Radiotherapy for Macroscopic STS
When STS is unresectable or surgical morbidity is high due to large
size, difficult location, or fixation to surrounding tissues, RT can be
used alone (ch. 318). While definitive-intent RT delivered over
multiple weeks can be used for macroscopic disease, the long
treatment duration, high cost, and morbidity of acute radiation side
effects are generally not considered worth the limited benefit. In this
setting, only about 50% of tumors are controlled 1 year after RT and
tumor response worsens with increasing tumor size.27 Stereotactic
radiotherapy (SRT) has been recently reported for treatment of
macroscopic STS.28,29 These high-dose-per-fraction treatments
delivered for 1-5 days or every other day are considered by some as a
curative-intent option. Although convenient for the pet owner and
less invasive than surgery, SRT is associated with a risk of serious
long-term side-effects including skin and bone necrosis, is costly,
and has not proven advantageous over standard surgical approaches.
The author avoids these protocols for all but small, non-invasive

tumors (i.e., not STS) where the potential for successful tumor
control without long-term morbidity is good.

FIGURE 324.3 Orofacial fibrosarcoma (FSA) in a
5-year-old Irish Setter. Non-painful soft tissue
swelling on the lateral maxilla (arrows) with
osteolysis and osteoproliferation of the zygomatic
arch and extension into the retrobulbar space on
computed tomography (A). Staging was negative for
metastasis. Eye-sparing tumor resection was
performed. Histopathology confirmed FSA with
mitotic index of 1/10 hpf and incomplete margins.
Definitive radiotherapy (RT) was delivered daily over
4 weeks. Moist desquamation of the skin, an acute
radiation side effect, was present 2 weeks post-RT
(B). Resolved acute effects and radiation-induced
leukotrichia were present 3 months post-RT (C).
Four years later, the dog remained tumor-free.

Palliative-intent RT is less time-intense and less costly. Protocols
vary but usually involve 3-4 weekly fractions of 6-8 Gy or 5 daily
fractions of 4 Gy. The goal of these less aggressive protocols is to
temporarily slow growth and perhaps shrink the tumor with minimal
side effects. The total radiation doses are not high enough to have a
meaningful long-term impact. Published response rates are about
50% (partial response more likely than complete response) with a
median time to progression of 5-8 months and median survival of 811 months.30-32 Duration of benefit depends on tumor response,
stage of disease and degree of clinical signs at time of RT. When
highly-conformal RT is available, SRT protocols may be considered
for palliation, where the treatment goal is to prioritize sparing of
normal tissues over tumor coverage, thus reducing the risk of longterm radiation side effects.

Chemotherapy
The relatively low metastatic rate of grade I and II STS argues
against the use of chemotherapy to prevent or slow the progression
of distant spread. For grade III tumors or for MI >20 where the risk
of metastasis is higher, its use is controversial. In this setting, despite
lack of evidence of benefit,19 adjuvant doxorubicin-based regimens
are often recommended in combination with surgery ± RT to prevent
metastasis (ch. 317).13,29,30 Other agents, like carboplatin, are being
investigated. Adjuvant cytotoxic chemotherapy is almost never used
to try to prevent local recurrence, given the chemoresistant nature of
STS. It has been proposed, however, that local recurrence of
incompletely excised STS can be prevented with metronomic
chemotherapy (MC), which involves continuous administration of
low doses of cyclophosphamide (10 mg/m2 PO q24-48h) in addition
to standard doses of piroxicam (0.3 mg/kg PO q24h).33 MC is
believed to control tumors by inhibiting tumor angiogenesis and
suppressing regulatory T cells. In a non-randomized study that
included a historical control group, time to recurrence was
significantly prolonged with MC compared to no treatment after
surgery. Side-effects were notable with a 10% risk of sterile
hemorrhagic cystitis secondary to cyclophosphamide and

gastrointestinal (GI) toxicity, likely from piroxicam, in 40% of
dogs.33 Despite the appearance of efficacy, the use of MC remains
controversial. Questions remain about its true benefit because the
control group in this study had an unusually poor outcome (median
disease free interval of only 211 days). MC used with
hypofractionated RT (5 biweekly fractions of 6 Gy) improved survival
in dogs with macroscopic STS, but had no effect on time to tumor
progression.21
Electrochemotherapy (EC), a local technique that uses electric
pulses to enhance cellular chemotherapy uptake, produced tumor
responses in small STS and has been used for microscopic disease.34
More information about toxicity and efficacy is needed.

PROGNOSIS
Most dogs treated for STS do not die of the disease. Reported median
survival with surgery ± RT ranges from 2 to 6 years, with only about
one-third of dogs succumbing to tumor-related causes.1-4,911,13,18,19,23,24

Tumors that develop late in life may never cause a
clinical problem even untreated.2,3 Factors that increase the risk of
death include high grade (grade III), MI >20 and presence of
metastasis.3,4,13,18,23,29 Increasing grade and MI >9 predict
recurrence.3,13,17,18 Complete margins result in long-term local
tumor control, but even an incomplete or narrow excision can result
in a tumor-free life for many dogs. Thus histologic characteristics,
like tumor grade and MI, rather than tumor type or even extent of
excision are the principal determinants of outcome after surgery.
Local recurrence and metastasis when they occur can be slow, taking
months and often years to develop.3-6,9,11-12,18,19,23-25
Median survival for dogs that present with advanced STS,
including large or fixed tumors causing discomfort and mobility
issues where surgery is not feasible, is shorter, ranging from 8
months to 2 years depending on stage and clinical impact.28-32 Dogs
with clinical signs like discomfort, ulceration, or lameness are more
likely to be euthanized than are dogs without clinical signs.

ORAL SOFT TISSUE SARCOMA
DOGS
Fibrosarcoma (FSA) is the most common oral STS.24,35,36
Myxosarcoma and leiomyosarcoma (LMSA) are also reported.35,37
Medium- to large-breed middle-aged to older dogs are usually
affected, although younger animals are also at risk.35,37,38 Golden
Retrievers may be overrepresented for FSA and may have a worse
outcome.38,39 Bone lysis is common (>75%).36,37,40 These tumors
are more locally aggressive than conventional (non-oral) STS. They
can also present as less-aggressive swellings on the lateral maxilla,
resembling SQ STS, with minimal to no bone lysis, visible intraorally
under the lip as a mass covered by intact oral mucosa.41
Histologically, some FSA have a benign appearance resembling
proliferation of fibrous connective tissue (fibroplasia/granulation
tissue), yet they aggressively invade neighboring tissues; this variant
is called histologically low-grade, yet biologically high-grade FSA (hilow FSA).40
Wide surgical resection with the aim of a complete excision is the
mainstay of treatment. Surgery followed by definitive RT for narrow
or incomplete margins appears to result in the best outcomes.38
Head CT is needed to accurately assess the extent of the tumor
(Figure 324.3, A). Prognosis is considered worse than for SQ STS,
with median survival times after treatment of 1.5-2 years (compared
to 6 years for non-oral sites).24,38,39 Factors associated with more
favorable prognosis include small tumor size (<2 cm),36,38 lack of
bone lysis,36 complete excision,36,39 rostral location,36 and absence
of metastasis.36,38 Long-term survival of over 3-5 years is possible.36
Metastatic rate at diagnosis is low, but up to 12-25% of dogs may
eventually develop metastasis to lungs or lymph nodes.35,36,39,40
Death from tumor-related causes, occurring in 30-80% of dogs,36,38
is more likely due to local recurrence than metastasis.38-40

For dogs with unresectable tumors or when surgery ± adjuvant RT
is not feasible, palliative RT (ch. 318) results in good tumor
responses, including complete and partial remissions, in 64% of dogs
that last for a median of 6 months; median survival is 7-10
months.35,38 Definitive RT for macroscopic disease is controversial
and in 1 study does not improve survival compared to palliative RT
but has a similar response rate.35,40
Furthermore, when oral STS are considered collectively with
tumors on the head, location loses prognostic significance.2,5,21
Thus, it appears that only truly oral tumors may have a worse
prognosis, especially if grouped with hi-low FSA.

CATS
Oral FSA represents 12% of oral neoplasia and affects older cats.42
Occasionally, it invades bone or muscle. Surgery is standard of care,
albeit challenging given small head size. In a cohort of cats that
underwent maxillectomy (median tumor size 2 cm; no metastasis;
57% complication rate), ± RT and/or chemotherapy, 2-year survival
was 94% with only a 17% recurrence rate despite half the cats having
incomplete excision. Increased MI may predict recurrence and
shorter survival.42

FELINE INJECTION-SITE SARCOMA
Feline injection-site sarcoma (ISS) is an infrequent, iatrogenic tumor
caused most commonly by rabies and feline leukemia vaccines.43 It
affects 1-100 per 10,000 vaccinated cats.43 The term ISS is preferred
over vaccine-associated sarcoma because other injected materials
have been implicated, including steroids and certain antibiotics.43
The time to tumor development post-vaccination is months to as
long as 10 years. No single vaccine type or manufacturer has been
linked to ISS.44 The exact pathogenesis is not known, but the most
accepted hypothesis is that inflammation induced by injection

promotes neoplastic transformation of fibroblasts and
myofibroblasts in some cats.43
ISS are mesenchymal in origin, and FSA is most common. Other
histologic types include malignant fibrous histiocytoma,
osteosarcoma, myxosarcoma, liposarcoma, nerve sheath tumor,
chondrosarcoma, undifferentiated sarcoma and
rhabdomyosarcoma.43,45 Collectively, these are classified as ISS
because they share a common biologic behavior. ISS are extremely
locally invasive compared to their non-vaccine-associated feline STS
counterpart.43 Microscopic tumor extensions, extending far into
surrounding soft tissues, are the hallmark and therapeutic challenge
of ISS. Metastasis develops in 10-25% of affected cats, usually later in
the course of disease.46-49 Common sites of metastasis are lungs and
lymph nodes, but skin and viscera can be involved. ISS is fatal in 2050% of cats.47,48,50,51

DEMOGRAPHICS AND CLINICAL SIGNS
Cats with ISS are middle-aged to older, although cases in young
animals have been reported.46,47 There is no sex or breed
predilection. Cats typically present for a SQ mass that is skin-covered
and non-painful. As the tumor grows, it can stretch and ulcerate
skin, invade underlying tissues, compromise mobility and cause
discomfort.44 Tumors have become more common on the limbs and
caudolateral abdomen than in the interscapular region as
veterinarians aim to comply with changes in vaccination site
recommendations (Figure 324.4).52

DIAGNOSIS AND TUMOR STAGING
Cytologic evaluation of FNAs (ch. 85) should be performed to rule
out other differential diagnoses such as abscess, but it is rarely
definitive for ISS.43 This is because pleomorphic reactive fibroblasts
cannot be easily distinguished from malignant mesenchymal cells.

Instead, an incisional tissue biopsy using needle core, punch, or
wedge biopsy is recommended. Tissue sampling should be incisional
(vs. excisional) and performed prior to surgical excision to avoid
disrupting or contaminating surrounding tissues, as this could
impact the success of future surgery.

FIGURE 324.4 A small injection-site sarcoma
(arrow) on a distal limb has the best chance of being
cured with amputation because wide margins are
achievable. (Courtesy Dr. Sarah Boston.)

To differentiate self-limiting, benign postvaccinal inflammatory
reactions (granulomas) from ISS, recommendations to biopsy are
based on the 3-2-1 rule.44 This states that tissue biopsy should be
performed if the mass persists more than 3 months post-vaccination,
is larger than 2 cm in diameter and/or is increasing in size after 1
month post-injection.
Compared to non-vaccine-related STS, ISS is much more locally
invasive.43,53 Histologically, it is distinguished by the presence of an
inflammatory cell infiltrate and sometimes foreign material
(adjuvant).45 Non-vaccine STS are more likely to occur on the head
and neck; FSA is the most common histologic diagnosis and
peripheral nerve sheath tumors have been reported.45,54 To
differentiate ISS from non-vaccine-related STS, history of
vaccination, tumor location and histologic tumor changes
(inflammation) are important considerations.43,45 Unlike in dogs
with STS, tumor grade has not been shown consistently to correlate
with outcome.47,54-56
Tumor staging is important for treatment planning and
prognostication. Enlarged regional lymph nodes should be evaluated
cytologically. If regional nodes are located in the thorax or abdomen,
imaging (CT or abdominal ultrasound) should be considered. Lungs
can be evaluated by 3-view thoracic radiography or CT. Advanced
imaging of the primary tumor is key for optimal surgical and/or
radiation planning. Peritumoral projections, often unrecognized on
physical exam, are commonly detected by CT or magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI),57,58 and while they are not all neoplastic,58 they
should be included in the surgical or RT fields if curative-intent
treatment is desired (Figure 324.5). MRI may be more sensitive for
detecting neoplastic peritumor projections, but is more costly than
CT and not used for RT planning.58

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Due to the relatively low metastatic rate of ISS, treatment is aimed at
local tumor control. If gross and microscopic disease is excised, then

surgery in theory can be curative. Simple (marginal) excision
inevitably leads to recurrence, which is often more difficult to control
than the original tumor. This is due to the invasive nature of this
disease, which cannot be overstated. Median time to tumor
recurrence after conservative surgery is 3 months with recurrence
rates as high as 70%.46 When a more aggressive surgery is
performed, the median time to tumor recurrence is extended.46
Radical excision with 5 cm normal tissue margins around gross
disease and at least 2 fascial planes deep, including removal of bone
and body wall, has the lowest recurrence rate of all reports at 14%.48
However, radical surgery other than amputation requires expert
surgical skill, can be associated with greater risk of surgical
complications including perioperative death, and is less feasible for
tumors larger than 4 cm.48 With wide excision (3 cm lateral margins,
body wall resection and 2 fascial planes deep), median time to
recurrence is 1.75 years with a recurrence rate of 38%.51 Thus, even
with curative-intent surgery, many ISS will recur. Unfortunately,
excisions reported as histologically complete are associated with a
relatively high risk of recurrence.48,49,54 ISS located distally on a
limb or tail and treated with amputation or hemi-pelvectomy are
reported to have the best tumor control rates, because wide
histologic margins can be achieved (Figure 324.4).46,58a For other
cases, multimodal treatment with definitive-intent RT is
recommended to “clean up” residual microscopic disease left after
surgery (ch. 318). Hemoclips placed at the edges of resection before
the surgical site is closed will help with RT planning, if pursued.43

FIGURE 324.5 Computed tomography shows a
large, cystic injection-site sarcoma (arrows) in the
caudoabdominal region compressing the abdomen.
Soft-tissue projections, not appreciated on physical
exam, extend distally from the tumor.
Definitive RT is used preoperatively or postoperatively. Radiation
is delivered daily for about 4 weeks to a total dose of 48-57
Gy.49,50,59-61 The aim of preoperative RT is not necessarily to treat
the palpable tumor, but rather to “sterilize” residual microscopic
disease that may be left behind after subsequent curative-intent

surgery. Among the benefits of preoperative RT is the fact that the
radiation treatment field is smaller, exposing less surrounding
normal tissue to radiation. The treatment field is smaller because the
radiation margin (3-5 cm of normal tissue) is measured from gross
tumor, not from a postoperative scar which is inevitably larger than
the original tumor. Surgical excision, using a wide to radical
approach to remove as much microscopic disease as possible, is
performed 2-4 weeks after RT; the surgical approach should not be
conservative just because RT was used.49 The smaller radiation
treatment field of the preoperative approach makes it more feasible
to deliver an effective, tumoricidal radiation dose with low
morbidity. The primary disadvantage is the possibility of impaired
postoperative wound healing in tissues previously exposed to
radiation, which is rare.49 Preoperative RT can also be used after a
marginal first excision to increase the success of a scar revision. In
the author’s opinion, preoperative RT is the approach of choice when
curative-intent surgery is planned. Postoperative radiation is used by
the author when the cat presents already having had surgery and
when more surgery is not possible or desired.57,59-61 Radiation sideeffects in cats are generally mild and primarily include dry
desquamation of the skin,49 but depend on the dose delivered to
organs at risk. When surgery and RT are used in combination,
median time to recurrence is about 1.5 years, but can be as long as 5
years.49,50,59-61 Reported median survival is 1.5-3.5 years.49,50,59-61
Tumor size, location, extent of surgery, margins of excision and
number of previous surgeries influence outcome.46,49,50,59 In
general, best outcomes are achieved when aggressive treatment is
pursued as a first intervention soon after diagnosis and when tumors
are small.46,50,51,59 Median survival of cats that develop metastasis
ranges from 6 months to 1 year.47,48
RT also plays an important role in the palliation of cats with
advanced ISS. For growing tumors or those causing clinical signs,
when curative-intent treatment is not possible or desired,
hypofractionated RT can shrink tumors and bring about short-term
palliation. Palliative RT usually involves hypofractionated protocols
such as 4 weekly fractions of 8 Gy, 5 daily fractions of 4 Gy, or 3 daily

fractions of up to 10 Gy (stereotactic delivery). Tumor response rates
of 50-70%, including complete responses, have been reported with
median time to progression of 4-8 months.61-63 Median survival is 711 months.61-63 Pet owners of cats with newly diagnosed ISS for
whom a curative-intent approach is not feasible, should be made
aware that palliative RT is a future treatment option to extend good
quality of life as clinical signs develop.
The role of chemotherapy in ISS is poorly defined (ch. 317).
Measurable responses, including some complete remissions, can be
observed but are short-lived.43 Doxorubicin or carboplatin are most
commonly used.47,49,59-62 The low metastatic rate argues against
use of chemotherapy to prevent or slow metastatic disease,43 but
some advocate for a role in local control in combination with surgery
± RT.49 Most studies, however, have not shown a benefit.49,50,59-60
Tyrosine kinase inhibitor toceranib phosphate provides no clinical
benefit for macroscopic ISS.64 Electrochemotherapy as well as
combination local IL-2 immunotherapy and brachytherapy are novel
treatments and have been investigated in conjunction with
surgery.43,65,66 Recurrence rates are encouraging but more evidence
is needed before they can become mainstream, and few facilities
offer them.

VACCINATION CONSIDERATIONS (ch.
185)
The American Animal Hospital Association and American
Association of Feline Practitioners have issued a joint consensus
report on vaccination recommendations geared at minimizing the
risk of ISS.44 Key guidelines include: 1) Vaccine protocols should be
individualized based on age, lifestyle and environment to avoid
unnecessary vaccination. 2) Vaccines should be administered
subcutaneously (versus intramuscularly) for easier detection of
postvaccinal lumps. 3) There is still insufficient evidence to
recommend a particular vaccine type (recombinant versus

inactivated). 4) Recommended vaccination sites include below the
right elbow for feline panleukopenia virus, feline herpes virus type 1,
and feline calicivirus vaccines; below the right stifle for rabies
vaccine; below the left stifle for feline leukemia vaccine; distal tail
for any vaccine. This is because cats with tumors located distally on
limbs or tails may be excellent candidates for curative, complete
surgical excision by amputation (Figure 324.4). 5) Vaccination
between the scapulae and proximally on limbs is unequivocally
discouraged. 6) Pet owners should be educated about the risk of ISS
and advised to have lumps investigated immediately. 7) Accurate
record keeping for each patient including vaccine manufacturer, lot
number, as well as date, site and route of vaccine administration is
important to track development of ISS. Some vaccine manufacturers
provide funds to help cover the cost of treatment and may require
this documentation.

VISCERAL SOFT TISSUE SARCOMA
In dogs, most primary visceral sarcomas develop in the spleen and
GI tract.67 Other sites include liver and urinary tract.67 Since splenic
sarcomas are more aggressive,68 they are not conventionally
classified as STS and are addressed in ch. 182. LMSA, a cancer of
smooth muscle, occurs more commonly than FSA or sarcoma
without subtype.67 These visceral (non-splenic) STS are locally
invasive and have a low to moderate metastatic rate. Gastrointestinal
stromal tumors (GISTs) clinically resemble LMSA and also qualify as
visceral STS based on their similar biologic behavior. GIST arise
from the interstitial cells of Cajal, which are electrical pacemaker
cells that control peristaltic motility in smooth muscle. Visceral STS
is rare in cats.

GASTROINTESTINAL
LEIOMYOSARCOMA AND
GASTROINTESTINAL STROMAL TUMOR

These are uncommon tumors of older dogs that occur as discrete
masses in the GI tract wall. There is no breed predilection. GIST is
more frequent than LMSA.69,70 They can both affect any segment of
the abdominal GI tract, although cecal tumors are more likely to be
GIST.69-71 They have overlapping histologic features, but GIST can
also have a more benign histologic appearance, resembling
leiomyoma.71 GIST is characterized by expression of transmembrane
tyrosine kinase receptor c-KIT (CD117) and calcium-activated
chloride channel DOG1 (discovered on GIST1).69-71 Given their
similar histologic appearance, immunohistochemical staining (IHC)
is used to differentiate GIST from LMSA (GIST: CD117+, DOG1+,
SMA ± [smooth muscle actin]; LMSA: CD117−, DOG1−, SMA+).
Tumors negative for all markers are considered sarcomas without
subtype. The distinction is important, because c-KIT inhibitors such
as toceranib phosphate (Palladia, Zoetis) or imatinib can be used to
treat GIST. The best treatment option for GIST and LMSA is surgical
resection. Complete surgical excision can be curative; a 5 cm surgical
margin of normal GI tract on either side of tumor is recommended.72
For unresectable tumors or when gross metastasis is present,
toceranib (Palladia), given at 2.6 mg/kg PO on an every-other-day or
Mon/Wed/Fri schedule (with routine monitoring), can result in
clinical benefit in over 50% of dogs.73 Complete and partial
remissions are possible and the median time to progression after
clinical benefit based on a small group of dogs is 2 years.73 Median
time to progression in the setting of microscopic disease was 1.25
years, but without a control group the role of Palladia is uncertain.73
MI >10 or presence of metastasis predicted shorter time to
progression.73
Clinical signs are similar for GIST and LMSA. Dogs usually present
due to anorexia, lethargy, weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal
distension and/or abdominal pain.68,71-74 Rarely, tumors can be
found incidentally.71,73 GI bleeding (chs. 50, 261-263) can lead to
melena, hematochezia, hematemesis, and anemia69,71-73; blood
transfusions are occasionally indicated (ch. 124). Perforation can

cause hemoperitoneum or potentially fatal septic peritonitis.6971,73,74
Hypoglycemia (ch. 61) is a rare paraneoplastic syndrome
associated with intra-abdominal smooth muscle tumors.74 Dogs
present with systemic weakness, tremors, seizures or collapse.
Insulin levels are normal. Hypoglycemia and the associated clinical
signs resolve with tumor removal. The mechanism is unknown.
An abdominal mass is palpable in many cases, but not all.72
Abdominal ultrasound is more sensitive than radiography,71,72,74
and allows for evaluation of other viscera and lymph nodes for
metastasis. CT may improve detection of some tumors and/or
metastasis and inform surgical planning. Endoscopically, these
tumors appear as hard masses covered by normal mucosa.
FNA with cytologic evaluation, performed using ultrasound
guidance, can provide diagnostic information before surgery.
Cytologically, LMSA and GIST are usually not distinguishable, but
the presence of spindle cells can help rule out other tumors like
carcinoma or lymphoma. Histologic evaluation with IHC provides
the definitive diagnosis.
Metastasis at diagnosis is present in <15% of dogs with LMSA or
GIST,69,70,72 but up to 30-50% will eventually develop spread.70,7274 Intra-abdominal metastasis appears to be more common than
pulmonary. Sites include liver, mesentery/omentum, spleen, lymph
nodes, diaphragm, peritoneal cavity, kidney and/or lung.68,70,72-74
Tumor staging prior to treatment includes 3-view thoracic
radiography, abdominal ultrasound, or CT. Abnormal tissue,
including enlarged lymph nodes, can be sampled by FNA before
surgery or removed at time of surgery. If not extensive, excision of
focal intra-abdominal metastasis should be considered, as these are
relatively slow growing cancers and reducing tumor burden may be
of benefit.73,74 The role of chemotherapy is unclear, but doxorubicinbased protocols are sometimes used for unresectable or metastatic
tumors.67,69,70,74
Outcome appears to be similar for GIST and LMSA with reported
overall median survival ranging from 8 months to 2.8 years (range 08 years).68-72,74,75 Longer survival is predicted with complete

excision (no cells at the surgical edge) and MI <9-10 (3.5+ years
versus 6-10 months).67,70 For GIST, weak c-KIT staining may predict
shorter survival (8 months versus 3.8 years). Presence of metastasis
is a controversial prognostic indicator. Some studies suggest that
dogs with metastasis have a worse outcome,72,73 but others found no
impact on survival.70,74 Survival can be long (20-24 months) even
with metastasis.73,74

OTHER VISCERAL SITES AND
HISTOLOGIC TUMOR GRADING
Sarcomas of other visceral organs are rare. Liver and urinary tract
(bladder, kidney, ureters) tumors are reported and include LMSA,
FSA, and STS without subtype.67 Older dogs are affected and there is
no breed predilection.67
Diagnosis requires abdominal imaging (ultrasound or CT) and
histology for a definitive diagnosis. Cytology often suggests a
sarcoma or malignant neoplasia, or can be non-diagnostic. Tumor
staging is as for GI STS (see above).
Like for other STSs, surgery is the mainstay of treatment.67 The
role of chemotherapy is unclear, but doxorubicin-based protocols are
sometimes used for unresectable or metastatic tumors.67 When
considered in a case series that included a majority of splenic
sarcomas and GI LMSA, the median survival after surgery was 1.6
years (range 0->5 years).67 Interestingly, the histologic tumor
grading system used for prognostication in canine SQ STS (Table
324.1) predicted outcome in this setting as well.67 Grade III tumors
were more likely to develop metastasis and have shorter survival. In
contrast to SQ STS, more tumors were classified as grade III
compared to grade I and II. MI >9 and presence of metastasis at
surgery predicted shorter survival of 10 months and 2 months,
respectively. Rate of metastasis was 24% at time of surgery and 40%
overall. These results may be confounded by the inclusion of a
majority of splenic sarcomas (more aggressive biologic behavior) and

the exclusion of GIST. Application of the grading system to visceral
tumors with typical STS behavior should be evaluated further.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Subcutaneous Soft Tissue Sarcomas in Dogs
Soft tissue sarcomas (STSs) are slow-growing cancerous lumps
(tumors) that develop under the skin, usually on the trunk or limbs.
They have tendrils of microscopic cancer cells that extend beyond the
visible lump. STSs are differentiated from more common, noncancerous skin lumps, like lipomas, by a needle aspirate or a tissue
biopsy. The goal of treatment is to surgically remove the main tumor
and the microscopic cancer cells so the cancer cannot regrow or

spread. Most STSs do not spread to other parts of the body
(metastasize), but some aggressive tumors can.
Most dogs are not bothered by the STS in the earlier stages of the
disease. When tumors get large, they can break through skin, ooze,
get infected, interfere with mobility (if on a limb) and cause
discomfort, which sometimes leads to euthanasia. It can take many
months to years for STS to cause these problems. This means that
some elderly dogs that develop STS might never be symptomatic for
it in their lifetime, even without treatment.
Surgery is the treatment of choice. When STS is incompletely
excised (the main lump is removed but microscopic tendrils of
cancer cells remain at the tumor site), the tumor can grow back. The
likelihood of regrowth depends on the “grade” of the tumor. Tumor
grade is a score given by the pathologist based on microscopic
examination of the tumor. STSs scored as grade 1 grow back in <10%
of dogs. Grade 2 STSs grow back in <30% of dogs. This increases to
about 70% for grade 3 STS. Most STSs are grade 1 or 2, so the risk of
tumors coming back is usually low. For dogs with grade 3 STS,
removing all the cancer cells is more important because the risk of
regrowth is higher if excision is incomplete.
Radiotherapy (RT) can be used to “sterilize” microscopic cancer
cells left behind after surgery. RT makes it less likely that
incompletely excised tumors will regrow, which may be particularly
useful for grade 3 tumors. RT involves daily delivery of a low dose of
radiation targeted to the tumor site for multiple weeks using a
radiation device called a linear accelerator. The experience is like
getting an x-ray, except that a short period of anesthesia is required
so the patient does not move. Radiation side effects are temporary
and can include changes to the skin in the radiation field. These heal
within 2-3 weeks. RT does not make the dog radioactive. RT facilities
are available at many specialty veterinary practices.
When curative-intent treatment is not possible or desired, then RT
can be used in a palliative setting to temporarily improve the quality
of life of dogs symptomatic for STS. Palliative RT involves fewer
treatments, less time, and less cost. It shrinks most tumors for up to
several months and improves quality of life in the short term without
aiming to cure the disease. If an STS is not bothering a dog and other
treatment options are not feasible, then palliative RT can be
considered later when the tumor becomes problematic. Average life

expectancy after palliative RT is 8-11 months, compared to years for
curative treatment.
Metronomic chemotherapy (MC) is another therapy that can be
used after surgery, instead of RT. MC is low-dose chemotherapy
given by mouth at home daily or every-other-day. Its use is
controversial, and it comes with risk of complications that
infrequently are severe.
Grade 3 STSs are more likely to spread to other parts of the body
(40% risk). To slow or prevent this, standard (non-metronomic)
chemotherapy may be recommended. Whether chemotherapy
extends life expectancy is not clear, and some studies suggest that it
does not.
The takeaway: STSs are slow growing tumors that are rarely fatal
in dogs that undergo treatment. Surgery is the treatment of choice.
RT can be used to “clean up” cancer cells left behind after surgery to
prevent regrowth. The risk of regrowth depends on tumor grade,
which is the most important indicator of prognosis. Grade 3 tumors
are the most aggressive and more likely to recur and metastasize.
Chemotherapy is often recommended for dogs with grade 3 STS to
slow or prevent metastasis, although it is unclear if it works.
Michelle Turek (Madison, Wisconsin)

CLIENT INFORMATION
Vaccination Tips for Cat Owners and
Information About Feline Injection-Site
Sarcoma
Vaccination protects cats against feline infectious diseases and
prevents the fatal, zoonotic (transmissible to humans) disease called
rabies. Vaccines administered under the skin cause temporary
inflammation at the site of injection. Very rarely, this inflammation
can turn into a cancer called feline injection-site sarcoma (ISS). ISS
affects an estimated 1 in 1000 to 10,000 vaccinated cats. Even
though very few cats develop ISS, pet owners should be aware of
vaccination recommendations that minimize the risk and what to do
should a lump develop in an area where a vaccine was administered.

If your cat has developed ISS, refer to the “Feline Injection Site
Sarcoma” Client Information Sheet.
The following vaccination guidelines do not prevent ISS but make
it less likely and increase the chances of cure with treatment if a
tumor develops.1
1. Avoid over-vaccination: Avoiding over-vaccination reduces
the risk of ISS. Not all cats need the same vaccines. Your
veterinarian will make a customized vaccination plan for your
cat based on its age and lifestyle. The rabies vaccine is a
required vaccine; its use is mandated by state governments to
protect both animals and humans from rabies.
2. Where to inject: If your cat develops ISS, it is more likely to
be cured by surgery on a lower limb or on the tail. This is
because ISS is very invasive, even when tumors are small, and
microscopic cancer cells extend into tissues well past the
growing lump. Curative surgeries must be extensive.
Amputation of a limb or tail is more likely to be curative than
surgery near the trunk. Therefore, vaccines should be
administered low on the limbs or tail. This can be difficult
because cats are squirmy and can require special restraint
techniques.
3. Have lumps checked out immediately by your
veterinarian: Because ISS is so invasive, small tumors are
more often successfully treated than larger tumors. The
importance of having lumps checked out when they are small
cannot be overstated. It could mean the difference between a
cure and a shortened lifespan due to re-growth of ISS after
surgery. When a lump develops after vaccination, it is
necessary to distinguish it from a more common local
inflammatory reaction called a granuloma. Granulomas are not
cancerous and go away on their own. They cannot be
distinguished from ISS based on touch and feel alone. Your
veterinarian will recommend a biopsy based on the 3-2-1 rule:
biopsy the lump if it persists more than 3 months postvaccination; if it is larger than 2 cm in diameter; and/or if it is
still growing 1 month after the injection. These circumstances
make ISS more likely. Confirming the diagnosis is necessary
before pursuing treatment.

4. Documentation: Your veterinarian should maintain
thorough vaccination records for your cat, including vaccine
brands, lot numbers, and administration sites. This allows
vaccines to be tracked if ISS develops. The time between
vaccination and tumor development can be up to 10 years, so
records should be kept long-term. Some vaccine
manufacturers help cover the cost of treatment of ISS, and
vaccination records may be needed to support a claim.
Michelle Turek (Madison, Wisconsin)

CLIENT INFORMATION
Feline Injection Site Sarcoma
A very uncommon but serious complication of vaccination in cats is
feline injection site sarcoma (ISS), also called vaccine-associated
sarcoma. It is most associated with vaccines against rabies and feline
leukemia virus. Other injectable medications like steroids or certain
antibiotics have been implicated, but this is very rare and should not
impact medical treatment decisions for cats.
ISS develops as a lump under the skin in the area where a vaccine
was administered, anytime from months to years before. The masses
can be soft or firm and are not painful. Eventually, they can break
through skin and cause oozing, bleeding, infection and/or
discomfort. Most cats are not bothered by the lump until later in the
course of the disease. The goal of treatment is to remove the lump
and the tendrils of microscopic cancer cells that invade the tissues
around the lump so that the tumor does not have the opportunity to
grow big enough to cause unpleasant symptoms. Metastasis, or
spread of cancer to other parts of the body, is not common. Instead,
it is the main cancerous lump and its regrowth after surgery that
causes the demise of most cats.
The life expectancy of cats with ISS depends on the success of
removing the cancer cells from the body. When tumors are small,
aggressive surgery is more effective. In those cases, cats can be cured
and live a normal lifespan. For larger tumors or after conservative
surgeries or when ISS affects a part of the body where surgery is
difficult, microscopic cancer cells often remain after surgery. In those

cases, tumors may recur along or near the scar and the average life
expectancy is 1 to 1.5 years; survival is longer with more aggressive
surgeries when fewer cells are left behind. With each additional
surgery to remove regrowth of ISS, the tumor recurs faster. Thus, the
most effective approach to managing ISS is early diagnosis when the
tumor is small, followed by aggressive treatment. Curative-intent
surgeries must be extensive and may include amputation of
extremities.
Because there are limits to the success of surgery that depend on
the size and location of the tumor, radiotherapy (RT) is often used
before or after surgery. The decision of when and how to use RT
should be made at the time of diagnosis before any treatment is
pursued. RT involves daily delivery of a low dose of radiation to the
tumor site for multiple weeks, using a radiation device called a linear
accelerator. The experience is like getting an x-ray, except that each
treatment requires a short period of anesthesia, so the patient does
not move. RT and anesthesia are well tolerated by most cats. RT does
not make the cat radioactive. RT facilities are available at many
specialty veterinary practices. The most successful treatments are
those that are coordinated with multidisciplinary input at the time of
diagnosis. In other words, surgery and RT should be considered early
on and sequenced thoughtfully for each individual cat. Average life
expectancy for combination treatment is 1.5-3.5 years.
Treatment for ISS is expensive. Some vaccine manufactures will
help cover the cost of treatment if vaccination records link their
vaccine to the disease. When curative-intent treatment is not
possible or desired, then RT can be used in a palliative setting to
temporarily improve the quality of life of cats symptomatic for ISS.
Palliative RT involves fewer treatments, less time, and less cost. It
shrinks most problematic tumors and improves quality of life in the
short term without aiming to cure the disease. If a tumor is not
bothering a cat and other treatment options are not feasible, then
palliative RT can be considered later when the tumor becomes
problematic. Average life expectancy after palliative RT is 7-11
months.
Michelle Turek (Madison, Wisconsin)

GENERAL FEATURES
Hemangiosarcoma (HSA) is a highly malignant tumor diagnosed
more frequently in dogs than in any other domestic species. It
accounts for ∼2% of all canine tumors.1,2 HSA tends to affect older
dogs of either sex, with a median age of 10 years at diagnosis.
German Shepherd Dogs, Golden Retrievers, and other large/giant
breeds appear predisposed.1,2 The spleen, heart (right atrium or
auricle), skin or subcutaneous (SQ) tissue, and the liver are the most
common primary sites for HSA, but HSA can occur in any anatomic
location (Figure 325.1).1-5 Biologic behavior varies by tumor
location, with certain sites, e.g., the skin, being associated with a
more favorable prognosis when compared with visceral sites.
Generally, local infiltration and metastatic dissemination occur early
in the course of disease, either hematogenously or via local seeding
following tumor rupture and subsequent intracavitary implantation
(Figure 325.2). Metastasis can occur to any site, with the liver,
omentum, and lungs being the most frequent sites of
dissemination.1-5 Notably, HSA is the most common sarcoma to
metastasize to the central nervous system (CNS; ch. 245).5

PATHOLOGY AND BIOLOGIC
BEHAVIOR
Dogs
The spleen is the most common primary organ affected in dogs.
Based on pathology studies, the “rule of two-thirds” was informally
established: two-thirds of dogs with a splenic mass have a
malignancy and two-thirds of malignant splenic tumors are HSA.1,6-9
Other neoplastic differential diagnoses for a splenic mass include
malignant fibrous histiocytoma, histiocytic sarcoma, splenic stromal
cell tumor, leiomyosarcoma, fibrosarcoma,
anaplastic/undifferentiated sarcomas, and lymphoma. Common
non-neoplastic diagnoses include nodular hyperplasia,
extramedullary hematopoiesis, and splenic hematoma.6,9 HSA
represents the most common primary tumor of the canine heart,
often originating on the right atrium/auricle; however, other cardiac
sites have been reported (ch. 235).1,10,11 In 1 study, only 8.7% of
dogs with HSA had concurrent cardiac and splenic HSA.12

Cats
HSA is much less common in cats than in dogs, typically occurring in
older cats with no sex predisposition. The biologic behavior of HSA
in cats is similar to that in dogs, with the spleen, liver,
gastrointestinal (GI) tract, cutaneous/SQ tissue, and mesentery
being the most common primary sites. Common metastatic sites
include lungs, liver, and omentum.13-15 A study of spontaneous
hemoperitoneum in 65 cats noted that 46% had abdominal
neoplasia, 60% of which were HSA with the spleen the most common
site of origin.16 Another study evaluating 26 cats with visceral HSA
reported pulmonary metastasis and multifocal disease in 33% and
77% of cats, respectively.13

ETIOLOGY AND PATHOBIOLOGY

The definitive etiology of canine HSA remains unclear; however,
several risk factors have been reported. Chronic UV light exposure
along the ventral abdomen and conjunctival locations is implicated
in superficial (dermal) HSA in lightly pigmented, short-haired breeds
such as Salukis, Whippets, Italian Greyhounds, and Greyhounds (ch.
323).17 A few studies have suggested a variable link between
spay/neuter status and risk of HSA in dogs18,19 (ch. 315).
With evaluation of genome-wide gene expression, the specific
genes associated with HSA are being identified. One study found 3
distinct tumor subtypes in dogs with HSA: those associated with
angiogenesis, inflammation, and adipogenesis.20 This suggests that
tumors either can arise from single multipotent progenitor cells that
differentiate via multiple lineages as an adaptive process, or that
multiple progenitor lineages contribute to tumor formation. Studies
using multi-parameter flow cytometry have demonstrated that
canine HSA originates from a hematopoietic precursor with
commitment to the endothelial lineage.21 These data refute the longheld belief that HSA represents malignant transformation of mature
endothelial cells in the peripheral vasculature.20-22 Malignant
endothelial cells display increased expression of genes involved in
inflammation, angiogenesis, adhesion, invasion, metabolism, cell
cycle regulation, and cell signaling.23,24 This “signature” is not only a
cancer-associated angiogenic phenotype, but distinguishes HSA from
other cancers.25 Abnormalities in oncogenes and tumor suppressor
genes have been identified that could influence tumor
formation.26,27 Several cancer driver genes have been identified
associated with aberrant cellular signaling pathways, including
angiogenesis.20,25 Multiple angiogenic factors and their associated
receptors are overexpressed in HSA and increased levels of
angiogenic factors are present in the blood of dogs with HSA.28-33
There is considerable similarity between genomic abnormalities and
apparent driver mutations seen in canine HSA and its human
counterpart, angiosarcoma, which may aid in developing novel
therapies for both populations.34

HISTORY, CLINICAL SIGNS, PHYSICAL
EXAMINATION (PE)
Clinical presentation, history, and associated clinical signs are linked
to tumor location; most pets with HSA in spleen, liver, or heart are
seen as an acute emergency secondary to tumor rupture and internal
hemorrhage (chs. 121, 124, and 182). Some collapse and die before
emergency treatment can be provided or during treatment. Pets with
intra-abdominal or intrathoracic HSA commonly have histories of
acute weakness, collapse, and pale mucous membranes secondary to
blood loss anemia. Often, the initial presentation may not be the first
time that similar, albeit less severe, signs have occurred. A thorough
history often uncovers previous episodes. For splenic or hepatic

HSA, cessation of acute bleeding and blood resorption (autotransfusion) from the affected cavity may lead to temporarily
recovery until another bleeding episode occurs at an unpredictable
moment. Other observations include anorexia, weight loss, lethargy,
abdominal distension, vomiting, dyspnea, and vocalization.1,7-11
Similar clinical signs are noted with renal HSA, sometimes with
hematuria.3 Pets with cardiac HSA might require even more rapid
attention due to the development of life-threatening cardiac
tamponade (chs. 121 and 235).
On PE, severe weakness, pale mucous membranes, muffled heart
sounds, pulsus paradoxus (ch. 39), and secondary arrhythmias are
common in pets with pericardial effusions resulting from a bleeding
cardiac HSA.10,11 Clinical presentation with CNS HSA can vary
widely depending on tumor location; seizures and mentation
changes are common (chs. 245 and 247).5 Cutaneous HSA
presentations vary depending on whether the lesion is primarily
dermal or SQ (chs. 12 and 323). Dermal HSAs are typically small,
discrete, blood blister–like lesions, while SQ HSAs are deeper, often
larger and mass-like, with associated bruising.17,35-39 Intramuscular
(IM) HSAs are large masses that can produce mass effects, with
distal swelling and lameness when on or near a limb. Metastasis to
external and/or internal sites is much more common with SQ and IM
HSA compared to the dermal presentation.37-39

STAGING
Histologic evaluation of tissue is the gold standard for diagnosis. A
presumptive diagnosis of HSA is often based on history, signalment,
and PE. Often, when the clinical presentation is suggestive of HSA,
complete clinical staging is performed before a histologic diagnosis is
achieved. Results of clinical staging provide an assessment of HSA
progression (Box 325.1), which helps define prognosis and guide
therapy. Complete staging includes standard laboratory work
(complete blood count, serum biochemistry profile, urinalysis, and
coagulation profiles), 3-view thoracic radiographs, abdominal
ultrasound (US), and if applicable and available, multiple image-

plane echocardiography (Echo) (ch. 97). Advanced imaging and
novel biomarkers may aid in diagnosis and staging. A delay in
complete staging might be needed to allow for emergency
intervention.

CYTOLOGY AND HISTOLOGY

Depending on the specific lesion and clinical presentation, tissue can
be evaluated histologically after submission of a surgically removed
affected organ, excision of a localized external (i.e., dermal/SQ/IM)
mass, or an incisional, wedge, core needle/Tru-Cut biopsy of either
internal or external lesions, if deemed clinically safe. Grossly, intraabdominal HSA can be a solitary mass or may be characterized by
multifocal lesions that appear soft with a dark red appearance and
may be oozing blood constituents. Histologically, HSA is composed
of irregular, anastomosing vascular channels lined by pleomorphic
spindle cells with large multifocal cavities filled with blood. Areas of
necrosis are commonly noted within the tumor. Marked
anisokaryosis and anisocytosis are common, and a high mitotic index
is often observed (Figure 325.3).2,6,10,17,35
Most visceral HSAs tend to be classified as “high grade.” In 1
study, histologic criteria such as nuclear pleomorphism, mitotic
score, grade, and overall differentiation were prognostic for
survival.40 In a retrospective series, mitotic index was prognostic in
dogs undergoing surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy, where dogs
with a mitotic score of 0 (<11 mitoses/10 high power fields) had a
superior median survival time (MST).41 When histopathological
differentiation from other sarcomas is not possible,
immunohistochemical staining for von Willebrand factor (factor
VIII–related antigen) or CD31/platelet endothelial cell-adhesion
molecule can be used to demonstrate endothelial derivation to
support a diagnosis of HSA.42,43 Further, 1 study demonstrated high
(94.4%) immunohistochemical KIT expression in canine HSA,
whereas no benign hemangiomas showed KIT expression.44
Although cytologic analysis is a non-invasive and clinically valuable
technique for the diagnosis of cancer in general, the diagnostic yield
for HSA is typically low.45,46 However, in some SQ or IM tumors,
cytologic evaluation of smears may provide a diagnosis in lieu of
histopathologic analysis (Figure 325.4) (ch. 85).
