Given the highly metastatic nature of visceral HSA and the effect of
stage on prognosis, any suspicious lesions seen at surgery should be
sampled and examined histologically. A retrospective study
evaluated macroscopic appearance of hepatic lesions and the
corresponding histologic findings in 79 dogs undergoing laparotomy
for splenic HSA. All HSA-positive samples were obtained from
grossly abnormal livers; however, 59% of histologically benign
lesions also were obtained from grossly abnormal livers.
Furthermore, only 50% of grossly abnormal livers had HSA

metastasis; the livers that had multiple nodules and/or dark red or
black lesions were more likely to be consistent with HSA47 (Figure
325.5). Therefore, the presence of gross hepatic abnormalities was
associated with a high sensitivity but low specificity for HSA,
reaffirming the importance of histologic confirmation prior to
clinical decision-making. A study of 65 dogs that underwent
splenectomy, including 30 dogs (46%) with HSA, noted that larger
splenic masses (higher ratio of mass to splenic volume) and heavier
spleens (as a percentage of body weight) were more likely to be
benign and less likely to be HSA.48

LABORATORY EVALUATION
Anemia, common with HSA, is usually regenerative. Schistocytes,
acanthocytes, and nucleated red blood cells often are present,
consistent with microangiopathic-related damage secondary to
vasculitis, hepatic insufficiency, deficient reticuloendothelial system,
and/or acute hemorrhage (ch. 172).49 Neutrophilic leukocytosis is
common, postulated to be a paraneoplastic syndrome and/or due to
necrosis that occurs in large and/or rapidly growing tumors.11,50
Recent research suggests that this tumor-associated neutrophilia,
and often a monocytosis, could be partially composed of myeloid
derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), a subset of granulocytes
responsible for suppressing innate anti-tumor immunity and
associated with a poor prognosis in some cancers.51,52 In 1 study,
dogs with HSA and increasing post-splenectomy peripheral
monocyte counts had a poorer prognosis compared to dogs whose
monocyte counts decreased post-splenectomy.52 Thrombocytopenia
is noted in up to 75% of dogs with HSA and has been shown to be a
negative prognostic indicator.11,53 Thrombocytopenia can be a result
of tumor hemorrhage, destruction via fibrin crosslinks within the
tumor vasculature, or secondary to consumptive coagulopathies such
as disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC; ch. 171), reported
in up to 50% of dogs with HSA.49,54 As a result of DIC, abnormalities
can be present on coagulation profiles (prothrombin time, partial

thromboplastin time, fibrin[ogen] degradation products, fibrinogen,
d-dimers; chs. 170 and 171). The serum biochemistry profile and
urinalysis rarely aid in the diagnosis of HSA given their lack of
specificity, although in 1 study, 53% of cats with visceral HSA had
increased aspartate aminotransferase (AST) activities.16

FIGURE 325.6 Three-view thoracic radiographs
from a 12-year-old spayed female Labrador
Retriever. Numerous poorly- to well-defined, small,
soft tissue nodules are present throughout the lungs,
consistent with metastatic
hemangiosarcoma. Images and description courtesy
Chris Ryan, VMD, DABVP, DACVR.

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING
Radiology

Three-view thoracic radiographs are standard for detecting
metastatic disease. Pulmonary metastatic disease usually appears as
coalescing miliary patterns; however, either nodular or generalized
miliary interstitial patterns have been observed (Figure 325.6). In a
study comparing thoracic radiographic and postmortem findings in
dogs with histologically confirmed HSA, the radiographic sensitivity
was 78% and the negative predictive value was 74% for metastatic
pulmonary HSA.55

Abdominal Ultrasonography (US)
US is commonly used and readily identifies effusions, hepatic and
splenic lesions, as well as metastatic omental lesions, depending
upon the skill level of the operator. HSA can take on many different
echogenic characteristics (anechoic to hypoechoic to mixed) and
tumors often have areas of cavitation (Figure 325.7).56 More
advanced techniques, e.g., contrast harmonic US to evaluate tissue
perfusion dynamics, showed improved diagnostic yield for hepatic
HSA via detection of nodules not seen during traditional US
examination.57 Contrast-enhanced US studies have shown
hypoechogenicity of splenic lesions during early and late vascular
phases were highly associated with malignancy.58

FIGURE 325.7 Abdominal ultrasound image from
a 7-year-old male neutered mixed breed dog
presenting for acute collapse secondary to
hemoabdomen. There is a large, mixed-echogenicity
mass with multiple central cavitations effacing the
normal splenic architecture and occupying most of
the image. CT, Computed tomography. Images and
description courtesy Chris Ryan, VMD, DABVP,
DACVR.
The presence of acute hemoabdomen (chs. 21 and 124) and US
identification of a splenic mass are highly suggestive of HSA;
however, no patient with hemoabdomen should be euthanized based
on identifying a solitary splenic mass “consistent with HSA” via US.
Many nonmalignant splenic lesions, such as hematomas, appear
similar on US and carry a very good to excellent prognosis with
splenectomy alone.6 One group assessed a multivariable model and
online decision-support calculator to help predict, preoperatively,
likelihood of a splenic mass in dogs being benign or malignant. Using
clinical data obtained retrospectively from records of 422 dogs that

underwent splenectomy, the final multivariable model contained 8
clinical variables to estimate splenic malignancy probability: serum
total protein concentration, presence vs. absence of ≥2 nucleated red
blood cells (nRBCs)/100 white blood cells (WBCs), US measured
splenic mass diameter, number of liver nodules (0, 1, ≥2), presence
vs. absence of multiple splenic masses or nodules, moderate to
marked splenic mass inhomogeneity, moderate to marked
abdominal effusion, and mesenteric, omental, or peritoneal
nodules.59

Echocardiography (Echo), Arrhythmias
Echo is the best modality for identifying cardiac tumors. Pericardial
effusion, if present, improves the ability to detect such masses (ch.
235 and

Videos 235.2-235.5, 325.1).60 The use of Echo in

routine staging for HSA first identified in another location is
controversial since occurrence of concurrent lesions is low.12
However, Echo can be used as a screening tool to assess heart
function in breeds at risk for dilated cardiomyopathy prior to the
initiation of doxorubicin (DOX) chemotherapy, enhancing its value
for these HSA dogs.61
Perioperative ventricular arrhythmias occasionally occur in dogs
undergoing splenectomy for HSA. Many dogs with pre- and postoperative cardiac arrhythmias are asymptomatic and effective
treatment consists of controlling the triggers of the arrhythmias (e.g.,
treating anemia with blood transfusions, or correcting serum
electrolyte imbalances) rather than using antiarrhythmic therapy
(chs. 121 and 230). Peri-operative arrhythmias should be resolved
before discharging a pet to the owner and before employing adjuvant
treatments. Arrhythmias can occasionally occur as part of organic
cardiac dysfunction, a contraindication to DOX chemotherapy. In 1
study, dogs that developed intra-operative arrhythmias had an odds
ratio of death greater than twice that of dogs that did not.62

FIGURE 325.8 Computed tomography image of a
subcutaneous hemangiosarcoma in a 9-year-old
male Boxer dog. Transverse image through the level
of the pelvis demonstrates a large subcutaneous
mass in the left inguinal region (white arrowheads).
The mass is heterogeneously contrast-enhancing at
the periphery, non-enhancing centrally, and has
multiple thick, irregular, contrast-enhancing
septae. Image and description courtesy Chris Ryan,
VMD, DABVP, DACVR.

Computed Tomography (CT) and Magnetic
Resonance Imaging (MRI)
CT or MRI can be utilized to evaluate SQ, IM, cardiac, splenic, or
hepatic HSA. CT and MRI can aid in determining the anatomic
origin, invasiveness, and extent of disease. These data assist in
surgical and/or radiation therapy (RT) planning (Figure 325.8)
since both MRI and CT have high sensitivity and specificity for
discriminating benign from malignant splenic and hepatic lesions.63

CT has an increased sensitivity for detection of early pulmonary
metastasis in dogs with neoplasia.64 Imaging both the thoracic and
abdominal cavities is often recommended for dogs with HSA. CT has
identified skeletal muscle metastasis in dogs with visceral or IM
HSA, dramatically changing the recommended treatment course for
some of these patients.65

BIOMARKERS
Cardiac Troponin I (cTnI)
HSA-specific biomarkers could be clinically useful for early detection
and intervention as well as to monitor disease status during and after
treatment. cTnI is a highly specific and sensitive marker for
cardiomyocyte damage (ch. 228). The median plasma cTnI
concentration in dogs with cardiac HSA was significantly higher than
the median concentration in dogs with HSA at other sites, with other
neoplasms, and with pericardial effusion not caused by HSA (ch.
235). Increased cTnI concentrations were identified in dogs with
cardiac involvement and HSA at any site (sensitivity, 78%;
specificity, 71%) as well as identifying cardiac HSA in dogs with
pericardial effusion (sensitivity, 81%; specificity, 100%).66

Serum Collagen XXVII Peptide (CXP)
Serum CXP levels in dogs with HSA and in dogs with large metastatic
burdens were 9.5-fold higher than in healthy dogs.67 These increases
could be related to protein cleavage or degradation in surrounding
tissues or associated with invasive behavior or angiogenic processes.
Interestingly, CXP concentrations in dogs with other forms of
neoplasia (osteosarcoma, lymphoma, carcinomas) and inflammatory
diseases were also increased, but at consistently lower values than
those for HSA. Reductions in CXP levels after surgical resection of
HSA and subsequent increases with tumor recurrence demonstrate
its value as a HSA biomarker.67

The Cytosolic Enzyme Thymidine Kinase 1 (TK1)

TK1 activity is closely correlated with DNA synthesis and expression
is restricted to proliferating cells.68 One study demonstrated that
serum TK1 activity was significantly higher in archived serum of dogs
with HSA compared to that of healthy dogs. Serum TK1 then was
prospectively evaluated in 62 dogs with hemoabdomen secondary to
either a benign splenic mass or HSA. Statistically, there was no
difference in mean TK1 activity level, but differentiation of the 2
groups became possible when a specific 2-tiered cut-off system was
implemented.68

Flow Cytometry, Prostate-Specific Membrane
Antigen (PSMA), Nucleosomes, microRNAs
(miRNAs)
Other ancillary tests could aid in early detection of HSA, since most
patients have microscopic metastatic dissemination at the time of
histologic diagnosis. Early work with flow cytometry illustrated its
ability to identify an increased number of hematopoietic precursor
cells in the peripheral blood of dogs with HSA as compared to that of
healthy dogs or dogs that have had an HSA removed.21 Flow
cytometry, which assesses expression patterns of cell surface
markers in multipotential bone marrow–derived stem cells, can aid
in confirming the early diagnosis of HSA and possibly be useful in
the monitoring of minimal residual disease.21,23
PSMA, a transmembrane protein overexpressed by human
prostate carcinoma and tumor-associated endothelium of various
other solid tumors, has been studied in vitro and in vivo for canine
HSA. PSMA is overexpressed in HSA cell lines as compared to nonmalignant endothelial cell lines. It was also detectable in HSA tumor
tissues via immunohistochemistry (IHC) and, most importantly, in
hemorrhagic effusions collected from dogs with HSA or other PSMAexpressing cancers, raising the possibility for using such a test as a
screening method for microscopic disease burden in dogs with
known or suspected HSA.69
Use of a platform that measures circulating nucleosomes in the
blood showed a 6.6-fold increase in the median plasma nucleosome
concentrations in dogs with HSA as compared to that of control dogs.

Nucleosome concentrations increased with stage of disease. While
not specific to HSA, with better characterization of HSA-associated
nucleosomes and optimization of methods, such a platform may
become a valuable monitoring tool for dogs with HSA.70
There is interest in using miRNAs as biomarkers for cancer in
people and animals; research in canine HSA has shown
dysregulation of miRNAs related to angiogenesis and other critical
pathways involved in cancer development and progression. miRNAs
can be detected and measured in plasma using real time quantitative
polymerase chain reaction. These molecules could ultimately be used
for early disease detection and monitoring of disease burden during
and after therapy for canine HSA.71

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
SURGERY
General
Surgery is the treatment of choice for HSA, including splenectomy;
liver lobectomy; nephrectomy; excision of dermal, SQ, IM, or
retroperitoneal masses; and right auriculectomy, as appropriate
given the anatomic locations of mass lesions. The primary aims of
surgery are to remove all macroscopic tumors and prevent risk of
acute hemorrhage, DIC, and death. Postoperatively, the prognosis of
patients with HSA is associated with tumor location, stage,
completeness of excision, and use of adjuvant therapies.

Dermal, Subcutaneous (SQ), and Intramuscular
(IM) HSA
HSA limited to the dermis without hypodermal invasion (as opposed
to SQ/IM lesions) has a lower metastatic rate and often can be
controlled with surgery alone. MSTs of 780-987 days have been
reported for dogs after excision of dermal HSA.35,36 In 1 study of 94
dogs with cutaneous HSA, predisposed breeds with ventral tumor
location and histologic solar changes had longer MSTs, whereas
tumors with SQ invasion were more likely to metastasize. Even

though long-term survival was reported, locoregional recurrence was
observed in 77% of dogs.36 These survival data are in stark contrast
to those reported for tumors with SQ or IM involvement, where
MSTs of 172 and 307 days, respectively, were reported.35 For SQ or
IM HSA, surgical excision should be as aggressive as possible to
achieve wide margins. Sometimes, this necessitates limb amputation
or the use of adjuvant RT in the event of incomplete or narrow
excision, as the local recurrence rate for inadequately excised HSA is
substantial.36,37,39 Due to the higher risk of metastasis and poor
long-term survival associated with SQ/IM HSA, adjuvant systemic
therapy also is warranted. Cats with cutaneous HSA treated via
surgical excision have been reported to have MSTs of ∼9 months to 4
years.14,15 Similar to dogs, feline HSA with SQ involvement was
associated with incomplete excision, higher metastatic rate, and
tumor-associated euthanasia.14,15

Visceral HSA
Because of the high risk for metastasis, surgery for visceral (most
commonly primary splenic) HSA is considered palliative and
associated with MSTs of only 19 to 86 days for dogs undergoing
splenectomy alone, and 77 days for cats undergoing
laparotomy.1,13,72 Therefore, adjuvant chemotherapy, discussed
below, is recommended following surgery for essentially all forms of
visceral HSA. For dogs with cardiac HSA, surgical tumor excision
usually is not possible due to location or surgery is declined due to
risks and/or the expected poor to grave prognosis. However, a few
case reports and case series describe long-term survival after tumor
excision.73-75 Pericardiectomy via thoracotomy or thoracoscopy is
performed more commonly to alleviate risk of life-threatening
cardiac tamponade, but alone it is unlikely to significantly prolong
survival (ch. 235).76 Although an uncommon variant, primary renal
HSA without evidence of hemoperitoneum or metastasis may carry a
more favorable prognosis with surgery alone. In 14 dogs with renal
HSA, most had localized disease on presentation and 10 had surgery
alone with an MST of 286 days, but 10/14 dogs still died of effects

secondary to HSA.3 HSA is the most common histologic diagnosis
for retroperitoneal sarcomas in dogs and is extremely aggressive
locally, carries a high rate of local invasion and metastasis, and as
such, is associated with a poor survival time even when treated with
multimodal therapy.4

RADIATION THERAPY (RT)
Due to HSA’s predilection for inaccessible anatomic sites, its
frequently acute presentation, and its high metastatic rate, the use of
RT has been limited. A study of 20 dogs with measurable,
histologically confirmed non-splenic HSA treated with palliative RT
showed subjective reduction in tumor size in 14 dogs (70%), with 4
complete responses and an MST of 95 days.77 A small pilot study of
dogs with presumed cardiac HSA showed that conformal hypofractionated RT reduced the need for pericardiocentesis and had a
MST of 79 days.78

CONVENTIONAL CHEMOTHERAPY (CH.
317)
Visceral HSA
Doxorubicin (DOX) appears to be the most active chemotherapy
agent against HSA and has provided the best extension of postsurgical survival times. Common protocols include single agent
DOX; combination DOX and cyclophosphamide (Adriamycin
[doxorubicin]/cyclophosphamide [AC] protocol); combination
vincristine, DOX, and cyclophosphamide (vincristine/Adriamycin
[doxorubicin]/cyclophosphamide [VAC] protocol); and combination
DOX and ifosfamide.47,79-81 MSTs, related to stage of disease, are
typically in the 5-7 month range with DOX-based protocols. In a
prospective study comparing an AC with a DOX/dacarbazine (DTIC)
protocol in 27 dogs with HSA of various locations (20/27 splenic), an
overall MST of 142 days was reported for 18 dogs treated with an AC
protocol, while the MST for 9 dogs treated with DOX/DTIC was

>550 days,82 but the small number of dogs in the DOX/DTIC group
limits conclusions.
Attempts to improve on reported MSTs have used dose-intensified
single agent DOX protocols along with both intravenous (IV) and
intraperitoneal (IP) liposome-encapsulated forms of DOX (Doxil),
but have not significantly changed survival benefit.83-86
Interestingly, the IP-treated dogs had fewer serosal, mesenteric, and
omental metastases than historical controls treated with systemic
DOX.86 Epirubicin, a stereoisomer of DOX developed to decrease
cardiotoxicosis in people, has been evaluated in dogs with HSA; 18
dogs given epirubicin following splenectomy had an MST of 144
days.87 Epirubicin was associated with a higher rate of GI sideeffects, often necessitating hospitalization, than the rate of such side
effects commonly seen with monotherapy DOX. Regardless, this
agent could be an attractive alternative for pets with pre-existing
heart disease. In a small study, ifosfamide given to 6 dogs after
splenectomy for HSA resulted in comparable MSTs of 147 days.88
Recently, a small retrospective study compared the outcomes of dogs
undergoing adjuvant DOX versus carboplatin following splenectomy
for splenic HSA with similar MSTs (160 days for the carboplatin
group and 139 days for the DOX group, p = 0.82). These results
suggest that carboplatin could be considered as an alternative in
cases where DOX is contraindicated.52

SQ or IM HSA
For dogs with SQ or IM HSA, chemotherapy may be used
postoperatively to address the considerable metastatic rate.
Interestingly, the results of 2 retrospective studies evaluating dogs
undergoing local therapy followed by adjuvant DOX were quite
disparate. In the first study, a MST of 1189 days was reported for
dogs undergoing surgery and adjuvant DOX ± RT for non-metastatic
SQ HSA and 272.5 days for dogs receiving similar therapy for nonmetastatic IM HSA.37 The second study evaluated 71 dogs with SQ or
IM HSA and reported a MST of 246 days for dogs with adequate
local tumor control of smaller (<4 cm) tumors without metastasis.39

This discrepancy might be explained by the small number of dogs in
each study, as well as the terminology used for cutaneous and SQ
HSA. In the first study, it is possible that dogs with primary
cutaneous HSA with SQ extension might have been included,
whereas the second study excluded those with primary cutaneous
HSA.

Cardiac HSA
The MST for dogs with cardiac HSA (ch. 235) remains lower than
that achieved for the splenic presentation, likely due to the difficulty
in obtaining local control for cardiac tumors. However, when surgical
excision is feasible and combined with adjuvant chemotherapy,
survival times comparable to those achieved with splenectomy and
chemotherapy are possible. Specifically, 1 study evaluating 23 dogs
with cardiac HSA reported a MST of 42 days for dogs treated with
surgery alone versus 175 days for dogs receiving adjuvant
chemotherapy following surgery.89 A small study of 16 dogs with
right atrial masses that received DOX either alone or in combination
with cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, or DTIC, documented a MST of
140 days.90 A larger retrospective study evaluated 64 dogs with
presumptive cardiac HSA treated with a standardized protocol of
single-agent DOX. The objective response rate was 41% and the
biologic response rate (measurable responses plus stable disease), or
“clinical benefit,” was 68%. The MST for treated dogs was 116 days
and was significantly improved compared to the MST of 12 days for
the 76 untreated control dogs.11

Non-resectable or Higher Stage HSA
Pets with non-resectable and/or higher stage HSA represent a
therapeutic challenge; however, data exist to suggest that a subset
can respond to therapy. A study of 18 dogs receiving DOX-based
chemotherapy for non-resectable SQ HSA reported a response rate of
38% for a median duration of 53 days.38 This approach could
represent palliative therapy or neoadjuvant therapy to downsize
tumors to improve resectability. A more drug-intensive protocol
combining DTIC, DOX, and vincristine (DTIC/Adriamycin

[doxorubicin]/vincristine protocol) was evaluated in 24 dogs with
advanced stage inoperable HSA and a response rate of 47.4% was
reported, including 5 complete and 4 partial responses91; median
time to tumor progression was 101 days. Another retrospective study
evaluated 67 dogs with stage I/II or III HSA treated with a VAC
protocol. The overall MST for the 67 dogs was 189 days. There was
no significant difference between MST for the stage III (195 days)
and stage I/II dogs (189 days). Response data were available for 28
dogs and the overall objective response rate for these patients was
86%.92 In another study, a subset of dogs with stage III HSA treated
with DOX and deracoxib had a median survival of 149 days.79

METRONOMIC (LOW DOSAGE,
CONTINUOUS) CHEMOTHERAPY
Conventional chemotherapy typically involves cycles (“pulses” or
“bursts”) of chemotherapy given at the maximally tolerated dose
(MTD) with long breaks to allow normal cells to recover from
damage. Conversely, metronomic chemotherapy utilizes continuous
(typically once daily) chemotherapeutics at doses well below the
MTD, without prolonged drug-free breaks.93,94 A key feature of
metronomic chemotherapy is compression of the drug
administration schedule with the cumulative dose being significantly
less than with MTD-based chemotherapy. This should provide a
favorable toxicity profile and the potential for long-term
administration without interruption. Unlike MTD chemotherapy,
where the tumor cells are the primary targets of therapy,
metronomic therapy appears to target cells of the tumor
microenvironment, including the endothelial cells that support and
nourish the tumor. In this context, the chemotherapeutics act as
anti-angiogenic agents. The mechanisms of action include direct
apoptosis for dividing endothelial cells, suppressing mobilization of
circulating endothelial progenitor cells (CEPs) from the bone
marrow, and increasing production of the body’s own natural
angiogenesis inhibitors.93,94 Further, metronomic chemotherapy
has been shown to selectively inhibit and deplete T-regulatory

(Tregs) lymphocytes, thereby decreasing immune tolerance.95 A pilot
study evaluating metronomic chemotherapy used a protocol of
cyclophosphamide, etoposide, and piroxicam in 9 splenectomized
dogs with stage II HSA. The MST of 178 days compared favorably to
an MST of 133 days in 24 dogs with stage II HSA treated with
splenectomy and adjuvant DOX.96 Since then, several studies have
evaluated other chemotherapy agents given in metronomic fashion
as well as different combinations of low dose chemotherapy, MTD
chemotherapy, and other non-chemotherapeutic agents with mixed
results, where nearly half the studies noted a survival benefit and the
other half showed no improvement in outcome.96-103 Some studies
demonstrating a survival advantage with metronomic chemotherapy
included the use of thalidomide, a potent antiangiogenic
inhibitor.102,104,105

IMMUNOTHERAPY (CH. 319)
A small number of studies investigating immunotherapies in canine
HSA has been published. A novel tumor vaccine was combined with
DOX in 28 dogs with various presentations of HSA. Vaccinated dogs
were found to mount strong antibody responses against canine HSA
cells, but this response did not translate into improved survival.106
The combination of the AC protocol and the immunomodulator
liposomal-muramyl tripeptide-phosphatidyl ethanolamine (L-MTPPE) resulted in a significant increase in disease free survival and
overall survival time (277 days) compared to dogs receiving
chemotherapy with placebo liposomes, particularly dogs that
presented with stage I HSA.83 Unfortunately, L-MTP-PE is no longer
clinically available. Other published studies on immunotherapies for
HSA have yielded mixed results.107,108

MOLECULAR TARGETED THERAPY
Understandably, given the failure of chemotherapeutic and
immunotherapeutic approaches to significantly improve outcomes of

dogs with visceral HSA, more targeted therapies provide a new area
of study (ch. 320). Targeted small molecule inhibitors, e.g.,
masitinib, imatinib, and dasatinib, have demonstrated growth
inhibition and an ability to induce apoptosis in canine HSA cell lines
in vitro,30,109 but this has not translated clinically. In 1 study, there
was no significant improvement in median disease free interval or
overall survival for dogs with stage I or II HSA receiving
maintenance toceranib following splenectomy and single agent DOX
treatment.110 In another study evaluating the novel product
epidermal growth factor bispecific ligand targeted angiotoxin
(eBAT), a bispecific epidermal growth factor (EGF)-urokinase
angiotoxin, an improved MST and 6-month survival rate was noted
for dogs with HSA receiving eBAT prior to standard DOX
chemotherapy.111

NATURAL PRODUCTS
Alternative therapies using natural products have become a novel
source of investigation in HSA. An in vitro study evaluating the
effects of Yunnan Baiyao (YB) in 3 canine HSA cell lines documented
a dose- and time-dependent cell death via caspase-mediated
apoptosis112; however, 2 studies demonstrated no modulation of
coagulation parameters in healthy dogs receiving oral YB.113,114
Furthermore, a retrospective study evaluating a combination of YB
and epsilon aminocaproic acid in dogs with presumed cardiac HSA
found no benefit against bleeding and no associated survival
benefit.115 In a small case series (n=5 dogs), post-operative
administration of polysaccharopeptide (PSP), the bioactive agent
from the mushroom Coriolus versicolor, was associated with delayed
metastasis and improved survival time for dogs with HSA as
compared to surgery alone.116 A more recent prospective study
showed no survival benefit for dogs treated with this product either
alone or along with DOX post-splenectomy; in fact, dogs treated with
adjuvant single agent PSP had inferior outcomes compared to dogs
receiving DOX.117

PROGNOSIS
There is variation in the presentation and associated prognoses with
the different anatomic forms of HSA. Regardless, HSA remains one
of the most aggressive and lethal cancers in dogs and cats. Certainly,
surgical tumor removal followed by adjuvant DOX chemotherapy, as
is the current treatment of choice for splenic HSA, remains the
approach that is most likely to provide the longest survival benefit
for any anatomic presentation of this neoplasm. However, the
emergence of more novel therapies could hold promise for potential
improvements in historically stagnant survival times associated with
this cancer.

PRESENTATION
Most primary bone tumors in dogs are osteosarcoma (OSA), a
mesenchymal tumor of osteocyte origin1 that usually affects largeand giant-breed dogs.2 The age at diagnosis is typically about 7-10
years; the incidence increases as dogs become older, but the
diagnosis has been made in every age group over 1 year.2 Dogs with a
primary bone tumor typically have progressive lameness, an
observation that depends on tumor progression and owner
awareness. Lameness can begin as a mild and progressive issue or be
acute and severe. Some dogs may have an initial response to
nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and rest, but the
lameness invariably recurs and/or progresses. A small percentage of
dogs with OSA have acute non-weight bearing lameness due to
pathological fracture. OSA typically occurs at metaphyseal locations.
The distal radius and proximal humerus are the most common sites,
with the distal femur and proximal tibia less frequently affected.
Unless late in the stage of disease, physical examination (PE)
abnormalities are generally limited to the orthopedic issues. Dogs
typically exhibit moderate to severe pain on palpation of the affected
site and there may be evidence of a firm or soft-tissue swelling in
lean regions. A full orthopedic examination should be performed
with careful palpation of the other limbs and spine for potential
metastatic lesions. Evaluation of dogs’ orthopedic and neurological
(ch. 241) statuses is important to assess candidacy for limb
amputation.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
The most common type of OSA is endosteal, arising within the
medullary canal. Periosteal and parosteal OSAs arise from the
periosteum and are much less common. Periosteal OSA can invade
the medullary cavity from the periphery, cause bone lysis, have
reactive bone formation, and produce neoplastic bone. Parosteal
OSA also arises from the periosteum but differs from periosteal OSA;

it forms an expansive mass that surrounds but does not invade the
underlying cortex. Both periosteal and parosteal OSAs are relatively
rare.3 The cortical lysis seen in early cases of OSA can be mild and
may only involve the endosteum.

DIAGNOSIS
SIGNALMENT, HISTOLOGY, DIFFERENTIAL
DIAGNOSIS
A presumptive diagnosis of OSA is based on signalment, tumor
location, and radiographic and computed tomographic (CT) signs
that include cortical lysis, periosteal reaction, extension of
osteogenesis into adjacent soft tissues, loss of the fine trabecular
pattern of the metaphysis, areas of fine punctuate lysis, and lack of a
distinct border between normal and abnormal bone. A sharp
demarcation between normal and abnormal areas of bone is more
suggestive of an infectious process or bone cyst than neoplasia
(Figures 326.1-326.3). Histopathologic analysis of tissue samples is
necessary for a definitive diagnosis. Differential diagnoses for
primary bone tumors include sarcomas originating from the other
mesenchymal cells present in bone (chondrosarcoma [CSA],
fibrosarcoma, hemangiosarcoma), metastatic neoplasia, multiple
myeloma, lymphoma, bacterial or fungal osteomyelitis, and bone
cyst. Both CSA and hemangiosarcoma may be difficult to distinguish
from OSA until definitive surgical therapy and histopathologic
analysis is performed on an adequate tumor sample. Periarticular
histiocytic sarcomas have unique signalment and tumor locations.
Both histiocytic sarcoma and synovial cell sarcoma are centered on a
joint and may involve bone on both sides of the joint, not features of
OSA.

CYTOLOGY
Site Selection, Methods
Cytologic examination is a useful tool to confirm the cell type and
likely diagnosis for primary bone lesions and is recommended when

evaluating a dog suspected as having a primary bone tumor. Several
methods have been described, including ultrasound (US)-guided fine
needle aspirate (FNA),4 CT-guided aspirate,5 core aspirate, and
conventional FNA using an 18G needle and 6 cc syringe (ch. 85).6
Aggressive bone lesions are painful and manipulation for aspiration
will cause pain. Heavy sedation or general anesthesia with pure
opioids as part of the sedation protocol is recommended when
performing diagnostic sampling for cytologic evaluation of bone
lesions (ch. 6). Combining diagnostic staging tests during sedation
is prudent. Invasive procedures should be performed using sterile
technique. Results of radiographs and palpation are used to
determine needle location, with a goal of entering the cortex. Both
puncture and suction techniques can be employed to obtain a
sample, which should be evaluated in-house to ensure that
diagnostic material was obtained. Cytologic findings alone may not
provide a definitive diagnosis of OSA, but can help narrow the
differential diagnoses, with a reported sensitivity and specificity of
97% and 100% in 1 study.4 Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)-staining has
been reported to be useful in definitively diagnosing OSA with
cytology samples, with a sensitivity and specificity of 88% and 94%,
respectively, in 1 study6a and a sensitivity of 100% in another.4 ALPstaining is not available at all commercial laboratories. Accuracy of
cytologic results compares favorably with bone biopsies: 1 study
reported an accuracy of 83% and 82.1% for cytology and
histopathology, respectively.7 In another study, diagnostic accuracy
of cytologic analysis compared with histopathologic results was 71%
overall and 92% for neoplastic lesions.6

FNA vs Bone Biopsy
FNA is recommended initially because it is less invasive, less
expensive, and can yield a diagnosis quickly (ch. 85). However, bone
biopsy should be considered when cytologic evaluation fails to yield a
diagnosis, when results are not typical for a primary bone tumor,
where a periarticular histiocytic sarcoma is suspected due to breed or
location, in geographic areas with high rates of endemic fungal
disease, or when a bone culture is desirable. Bone biopsy may
increase the risk of pathological fracture and the biopsy tract should
be considered contaminated with tumor cells. If a surgical or
radiation-based limb salvage technique is being considered, the bone
biopsy should be performed after consulting with the specialist
performing the limb salvage procedure. Bone biopsy requires general
anesthesia and sterile technique. A Jamshidi needle is most
commonly used to obtain several core bone samples. Jamshidi
biopsy was reported to accurately discriminate tumors from nontumors in 91.9% of cases and to correctly identify specific tumor type
in 82.3% of dogs.8 If a bone biopsy is performed, the samples can be
used to produce slides for cytologic evaluation by rolling the cores on
slides prior to placing them in formalin. Samples should also be
submitted for bacterial and possibly fungal cultures (being mindful
of laboratory public health concerns around culturing dimorphic
fungi, e.g., Blastomyces, Histoplasma, Coccidioides). When

assessing a bone biopsy, one should remember the difficulty in
discriminating chondroblastic OSA from CSA. It is possible that a
bone biopsy initially diagnosed as CSA may be changed to
chondroblastic OSA after a pathologist reviews the entire sample and
observes osteoid production, which is definitive for OSA.

FIGURE 326.3 Bone scan image of the same dog
in Figures 326.1 and 326.2 showing increased
uptake of technetium in the distal radius (arrow).

STAGING TESTS—OSTEOSARCOMA
(OSA)
Thoracic Radiographs
Appendicular OSA is highly metastatic and dogs with confirmed or
presumptive OSA, which has a predilection for metastasis to lung
and other bone sites, should be staged prior to initiating treatment.
Most dogs have micrometastasis at the time of diagnosis. The
presence of obvious metastasis carries a worse prognosis for survival
and may change treatment recommendations. Palliative amputation
may still benefit the patient. Evaluation for metastasis to lung is
more straightforward than for metastasis to bone. Three-view
thoracic radiographs, a good screening tool, are often utilized to rule
out metastatic disease, but there is a chance of missing smaller
lesions or those superimposed over other structures. Lung lesions >7
to 9 mm in diameter should be visible on high-quality radiographs9
(Figure 326.4). Fewer than 10% of dogs with OSA are positive for
gross disease on thoracic radiographs at the time of initial staging.

Computed Tomography (CT) Scans
The imaging modality of choice for identifying lung metastasis in
humans with OSA is the CT scan.10,11 CT is highly sensitive, but not
specific, for diagnosing gross metastasis to the lung in humans.10,11
CT is reported to be a highly sensitive modality for identifying
pulmonary metastasis in dogs,12,13 with a threshold of >1 mm for
diagnosis of pulmonary metastatic nodules.9 A study comparing
thoracic radiography and CT in 39 dogs with appendicular OSA
found better detection of nodules on CT (5% via radiographs, 28%
via CT).14 The number of nodules diagnosed on CT negatively
influenced survival but the survival times (STs) of dogs with and
without nodules on CT scan were not significantly different.14
Further, only 22 dogs were treated with surgery and only 10 received
chemotherapy in that study.14

FIGURE 326.4 Lateral radiograph of the thorax of
a dog with osteosarcoma. The presence of several
soft-tissue opacity lung nodules of varying sizes is
consistent with pulmonary metastasis. Image
courtesy Dr. Mila Friere.

Stage Creep … Is the Cancer Progressing?
A patient’s stage may worsen with improved sensitivity of staging
tests, rather than due to actual disease progression. The prognostic
effect of stage creep for dogs that are radiographically negative but
CT-positive for thoracic metastasis is not known. Intuitively,
confirmation of metastasis by identifying lesions on CT scan would
suggest an increased tumor burden, resulting in a worse prognosis.

Radiographically Detecting Bone Metastasis
Detection of metastasis to bone before definitive therapy is initiated
is important not only for prognostic purposes, but also because it
usually precludes limb amputation and may make other treatment
options more practical. The probability of diagnosing gross bone

metastases at the time of diagnosis is similar to the probability of
finding gross pulmonary metastases.15 Of 399 dogs with OSA staged
with a bone scan, 7.8% were highly suspected as having metastatic
disease based on regions with increased uptake of a
radiopharmaceutical.15
Detection of metastasis to other bones begins with a complete
orthopedic examination, including palpation of the spine (ch. 31).
This is important in determining which dogs are candidates for
amputation and in evaluating for possible metastatic disease.
Focused radiographic evaluation should be performed on
particularly painful areas. Radiography of all long bones and the
pelvis has been used to survey for evidence of metastatic disease,16,17
but recent studies indicate that long bone survey radiographs have
low sensitivity for detecting metastasis.13 This low sensitivity may be
the result of single-projection (lateral) and not orthogonal views used
in long bone survey radiography and because bone lesions are not
usually detectable until there is >30% bone loss and lesions >2 cm in
greatest diameter.18

Nuclear Scintigraphy With Technetium-99m for
Bone Metastasis
Nuclear scintigraphy is a sensitive but nonspecific tool when
searching for metastatic disease. Technetium, administered
intravenously (IV), is preferentially incorporated into metabolically
active areas of bone. Relative uptake in different areas of the skeleton
is then evaluated by a gamma camera. These scans do not
discriminate bone tumor, infection, fracture, or some other
orthopedic conditions. Experienced radiologists are aware of this
dilemma and can generally determine the likelihood of metastatic
disease (Figure 326.5). Areas that appear abnormal on bone scan
should be evaluated radiographically and/or with CT to determine
the cause of the increased radioisotope uptake. In a study comparing
long bone survey radiography, bone scans, and whole body CTs in 15
dogs with appendicular OSA, bone scans were the only modality to
definitively identify bone metastasis on blinded independent
review.13 The overall rate of bone metastasis (27%) was higher than

previously reported and may be exaggerated due to the relatively low
number of cases, or it may suggest that aggressive staging using
multiple modalities improves and increases the rate of diagnosing
gross lesions. This study highlighted the benefit of combining the
inherent sensitivity of bone scan as a screening test with the
specificity of CT scan. In another study evaluating whole-body CT for
staging 50 dogs with appendicular OSA, no bone lesions were
detected.19 CT is a useful and sensitive staging modality for
evaluation of the lungs and to specifically assess regions of increased
uptake on bone scan but is not reliable for screening dogs for bone
metastases.

Positron Emission Tomography (PET)-CT
While not yet widely available in veterinary medicine, PET-CT
capitalizes on the sensitivity of bone scan and the specificity of CT. It
is now being used as a staging tool for humans with OSA20,21
(Figure 326.6). When available, bone scan followed by CT of areas
of interest is an optimal method for staging dogs with OSA13
(Figure 326.7).

OSA Soft-Tissue Metastasis
OSA spread to draining lymph nodes is rare, with a rate of 4.4% in 1
study.22 The prognosis in dogs with lymph nodes positive for OSA
was significantly shorter: median STs were 59 days for dogs with and
318 days for dogs without lymph node metastasis.22 Draining lymph
nodes should be palpated prior to surgery and aspirated if accessible
and/or enlarged (ch. 88). Practically, draining lymph nodes should
be evaluated histologically at surgery. Metastasis to abdominal
organs is extremely rare, being detected in 0-2.5% in dogs evaluated
with abdominal US.23,24 The chance of finding a second, unrelated
neoplasm was 5% in 1 study, although some of these dogs had a
palpable abdominal mass on PE.23 Abdominal staging may be
appropriate in some cases to rule out concurrent occult disease prior
to OSA treatment.

ETIOLOGY
The cause of OSA is generally not elucidated. The breed
predisposition supports genetic factors for spontaneous OSA. Two
known causes of appendicular OSA in dogs, fracture-associated and
radiation-induced, are both rare compared to spontaneously
occurring OSA. Fracture-associated OSA occurs most frequently in
dogs that have had a comminuted fracture with a history of
complicated healing, implant loosening, and/or infection, and it
tends to occur after a period of 5 years or longer following fracture
repair.25 The cause of fracture-associated sarcoma is not known.
Hypotheses include implant corrosion and/or inflammation at the
fracture site associated with complicated healing, chronic
inflammation, and infection.25-27 Histopathologically, fractureassociated sarcomas have inflammation not recognized with
spontaneously occurring OSA.25 The development of OSA at the site
of a tibial plateau leveling osteotomy (TPLO) has been described.28
Radiation-induced bone tumors are rare in dogs, with a lag period of
2.6-8.7 years posttreatment.29

TREATMENT
SURGERY
Primary and Secondary Goals
Pain management is the critical primary goal of surgery, with a
secondary goal of removing the primary tumor.

Limb Amputation
Limb amputation is recommended for OSAs of the humerus, radius,
femur, or tibia. Amputation has the advantages of completely
removing the cancer source of pain and carries low complication
rates. The obvious disadvantage is limb loss, but most dogs tolerate
limb amputation, even those with concurrent orthopedic issues.
Weight loss (ch. 226), physiotherapy (ch. 256), sling support, and
long-term medication for osteoarthritis (ch. 143) should be
considered to support dogs after limb amputation.

Limb Salvage for Distal Radial OSA
Surgical limb salvage is primarily performed for distal radial OSA.
The distal radius is removed with a 2-3 cm margin of normal bone
proximally, disarticulation distally, and the bone defect replaced with
an allograft or an endoprosthesis, spanning the carpus with a bone
plate. Although this technique has the obvious advantage of
preserving the limb, the complication rate is extremely high. In a
recent study evaluating endoprosthesis limb salvage for distal radial
OSA in dogs, the major complication rate was 64% and the overall
complication rate was 96%.30 The most common complications
noted with limb salvage include infection, local recurrence, and
implant failure.30,31 Some dogs (4-15%) treated with limb salvage
ultimately require limb amputation.30,31 The high complication rate,
costs associated with limb salvage and OSA treatment, and the high
metastatic rates have decreased recommendations of limb salvage
and driven innovative attempts to overcome complications and
improve outcomes. Some of these innovations include bone
transport osteogenesis, manus transposition or ulnar rollover, 3D
printing of custom prostheses, and limb-shortening limb salvage.3233b

FIGURE 326.7 Osteosarcoma staging algorithm.
CT, Computed tomography.

Limb Salvage for Non-distal Radial Primary Bone
Tumor
Primary bone tumors of uncommon sites, such as the scapula, ulna,
metacarpals, metatarsals, and digits, can be managed by resection of
the affected bone only. Because most primary bone tumors are
metaphyseal, managing the adjacent joint of many long bone sites
can be problematic, e.g., proximal humeral OSA, which is not
amenable for surgical limb salvage.34 While limb salvage has been
reported, the proximal femur poses similar challenges.35 For a
diaphyseal location in long bones, rare for a primary bone tumor,
resection of the affected bone and limb salvage with an intercalary
bone graft can result in good to excellent limb function and should be
considered.36 For lesions of the distal limb, partial amputation and
reconstruction with an intraosseous transcutaneous amputation
prosthesis has been reported.37

Surgery for Pelvic OSA

External hemipelvectomy, which involves removal of the affected
portion of the hemipelvis and corresponding limb, is most often
performed.87 Internal hemipelvectomy, which involves removal of
the affected portion of the hemipelvis and limb preservation, has also
been reported for primary bone tumors of the ilium and ischium and
may be appropriate in select cases.38-40

RADIATION THERAPY (RT; CH. 318)
Palliative Intent
RT can be administered with palliative or curative intent for primary
or secondary bone tumors. The goal of palliative RT is to reduce pain
and inflammation caused by the tumor. Generally, hypofractionated
protocols are employed with doses of 8-10 Gray (Gy) weekly for 2-4
treatments.41 Response rates vary from 74-93%, with durations of
53-180 days.41 Chemotherapy can be combined with palliative RT. In
a retrospective study, this strategy was shown to prolong ST in dogs
with primary bone tumors treated with palliative RT.42 These
responses should be interpreted with caution because most studies
reporting outcomes are retrospective and rarely include objective
measures of pain relief. They often rely on owner interpretation of
response and quality of life (QoL), which makes them open to
treatment bias.

Curative Intent
Curative-intent fractionated RT did not improve survival when
compared with hypofractionated protocols for dogs with OSA in 1
retrospective study.43 This is likely due to the low alpha to beta ratio
of OSA cells, which means that higher doses per fraction are required
to induce cell death than those typically administered in a full-course
fractionated protocol.44 As stereotactic radiotherapy (SRT) has
become available, curative-intent RT for OSA has become a viable
treatment option. SRT allows precise delivery of high radiation doses
to a focal tumor with minimal exposure to surrounding tissues. It has
been reported to be a method of nonsurgical limb salvage for OSA in

dogs.45 This technique has the distinct advantage of avoiding
amputation and/or the complications associated with limb salvage.
The disadvantages of SRT not only include limited accessibility and
cost, but the high rate of pathological fractures.
One study reported a median time to fracture of 4.2 months, with
fracture-free rates at 3, 6, and 9 months of 73%, 44%, and 38%.46 In
a large study of SRT for treating OSA, 123 dogs were retrospectively
evaluated and a fracture rate of 41% and median duration of
lameness improvement of 6 months were reported.47 Preoperative
aspirate or bone biopsy did not increase the rate of fracture, despite
earlier concerns.45,47 The median survival time (MST) was 233 days,
with longer survival in the cohort of dogs that received salvage
amputation (21%).47 Both repair of pathological fractures after
SRT48 and prophylactic plating at the time of SRT49 have resulted in
very high complications rates due to infection and/or implant
failures.48,49 These strategies are not recommended to manage or
prevent this complication. Improved strategies for determining the
risk of pathological fracture prior to treatment may help decrease
risk, but this potential complication remains the main drawback of
SRT for treating OSA. A recent retrospective study compared
conventional hypofractionated RT (palliative radiation) with SRT. It
was determined that dogs receiving concurrent chemotherapy and
SRT had longer STs than dogs treated with palliative RT and that
dogs with high pain scores prior to RT had decreased STs.50

Radiopharmaceuticals
Using radiopharmaceuticals with an affinity for OSA, e.g., samarium,
has provided mixed results.41 One of the primary advantages of this
strategy is the potential to treat both primary and metastatic lesions.
This treatment has provided inconsistent results and is not widely
available due to challenges with working with therapeutic
radiopharmaceuticals in veterinary medicine.

SYSTEMIC THERAPY

Chemotherapy
Because of the high rate of metastasis in appendicular OSA,
chemotherapy is recommended as part of curative-intent protocols
after local therapy with amputation, surgical limb salvage, or SRT.
Amputation followed by chemotherapy results in significantly longer
STs than amputation alone.51,52 Chemotherapy is also used in
palliative-intent strategies. Postoperative chemotherapy is usually
started at the time of suture removal. One must ensure that the
surgical site has healed without complication first, as an incisional
infection and chemotherapy-induced neutropenia can be
catastrophic (chs. 317 and 321).
Most chemotherapy protocols in dogs include either cisplatin or
carboplatin, and doxorubicin. Historically, cisplatin was the
platinum-based drug used more commonly in dogs due to the high
costs of carboplatin.53 However, giving cisplatin is cumbersome, as it
requires saline diuresis and has the potential for nephrotoxicosis
(chs. 317 and 321).54 Cisplatin was largely replaced with carboplatin
when its generic form became available in 2004. Current protocols
for chemotherapy in dogs with OSA include single-agent carboplatin,
single-agent doxorubicin, and alternating the two.51,55-59 The
reported MSTs with amputation and chemotherapy tend to be
similar across studies (10-11 months), with 1- and 2-year survival
rates of 36-48% and 18-22%.55,58,59 One notable exception to these
results can be found in a randomized, prospective study that
evaluated 6 doses of single-agent carboplatin compared with 3 doses
each of carboplatin and doxorubicin; STs were 425 and 135 days,
respectively.56 This result, combined with the lower rate of adverse
events reported with single-agent carboplatin compared with
alternating carboplatin and doxorubicin57 has led to single-agent
carboplatin being the preferred contemporary treatment for OSA.

Immunotherapy (ch. 319)
Harnessing the immune system in the treatment of metastatic
disease has long been a goal in treating canine OSA. The first
evidence that immunologic stimulation may improve STs was

published in 2005, when it was shown that dogs with infections
following limb-salvage had improved STs.60 Subsequent studies
have corroborated their findings.31 Similarly, dogs that have had
limb salvage that develop implant failure as a complication have also
been reported to have an improved ST.31,30 In a retrospective study,
infection at an amputation site did not have beneficial effects on
survival.61 However, there was a relatively small number of cases, so
type II error is possible.
In a more compelling evaluation of immunologic therapy for
canine OSA, an attenuated Listeria vaccine expressing Her2/neu was
administered to 18 dogs with spontaneous OSAs positive for
Her2/neu, a tyrosine kinase receptor that is overexpressed in 40% of
human pediatric and canine OSA. This phase I study reported MSTs
of 956 days and an overall survival at 1, 2, and 3 years of 77.8%, 67%,
and 56%, respectively. These were significantly longer compared
with historical Her/Neu positive controls, which had a MST of 423
days and an overall survival at 1, 2, and 3 years of 55%, 28%, and
22%.62 Most reported adverse events were mild and self-limiting.
This approach and its results generated excitement in the veterinary
and human oncology community, as canine OSA is an excellent
model of OSA in humans. This vaccine was briefly commercially
available under a conditional license in the United States. However,
recent reports of more significant adverse events and the ability to
culture Listeria from the joint, an incisional abscess, and urine in 3
dogs,63 and an incisional abscess in 1,64 raised concerns, as Listeria
is a zoonotic disease. Continued advances in vaccine development
and approaches to immunologic treatment of OSA will evolve and
hopefully improve long-term outcomes.

PAIN CONTROL
NSAIDs and Adjunct Analgesics
Pain control alone (ch. 6), without additional measures, is chosen by
some owners for various reasons, including presence of metastatic
disease and a guarded long-term outcome. One must educate owners
to appreciate that bone cancer pain in both humans and animals is

common, complex, and difficult to treat. In general, NSAIDs are the
cornerstone pain treatment if tolerated and not contraindicated (ch.
143). The addition of adjunctive analgesics, e.g., gabapentin, has
been advocated. However, a recent study prospectively evaluating
palliative treatment of OSA with cimicoxib, amantadine, and
gabapentin suggested that neither amantadine nor gabapentin
improved analgesia outcome measures and they may have worsened
with gabapentin.64 Studies of bone cancer pain in dogs and humans
are ongoing. Overall, this study highlighted the challenge of
managing bone cancer pain, especially in dogs that are stoic. Close
monitoring of QoL in these dogs is critical. Owners should be
counseled about euthanasia when QoL declines. The ST for these
dogs is short, with a MST of 43 days reported.65

Pamidronate (chs. 283 and 331)
Bisphosphonates decrease malignant and nonmalignant bone
resorption by inducing osteoclast apoptosis and may have a direct
negative effect on cancer cell viability.66,67 Pamidronate (1-2 mg/kg,
IV with saline, once monthly) is commonly used in dogs with OSA
and has been shown to decrease pain scores when included in
palliative treatment.68,69 When evaluated in combination with
palliative RT in a prospective clinical trial, pamidronate was not
shown to significantly effect duration of pain relief compared with
placebo but did decrease focal bone resorption.69 In a retrospective
study, the addition of pamidronate into a palliative RT protocol for
dogs with primary bone tumors, for unknown reasons, had a
negative effect on survival.42 Additional research into the efficacy of
this drug and the optimal timing of treatment is warranted.

Zoledronate
Zoledronate is used in human oncology and its use is increasing for
dogs because it is more potent, easier to administer, despite being
more expensive than pamidronate.67 Since the half-life in bone is
much greater for zoledronate compared to pamidronate, some cost
can be offset by less frequent administration. In people with osseous

malignancies, it is given every 3 months to manage.67 Optimal dose
and timing are not known, but it has been suggested that the
monthly intervals could be extended, while sustaining clinical effect.
Zoledronate decreased surrogate markers of bone turnover,
increased bone mineral density, and decreased pain in 5/10 dogs
with OSA for >4 months.66 The MST in that study, 75 and 76 days in
groups treated with placebo or pamidronate, was characteristically
short for palliative treatment of OSA.69 That study did not show a
significant difference in dogs treated with bisphosphonates but did
show that pamidronate was safe and improved objective measures of
bone density and bone resorption.

Palliative Amputation
Amputation can be employed with palliative intent to remove the
source of bone cancer pain. Although technically a major surgery,
this is a routine procedure and most dogs are discharged from the
hospital the following day. Postoperative pain control is
straightforward (ch. 6), whereas bone cancer pain management is
complicated, difficult to assess and treat, and generally should be
short-term to prevent patient suffering.

PROGNOSIS
OSTEOSARCOMA (OSA)
Several prognostic factors have been identified for both disease-free
interval (DFI) and overall survival time (OST). Two recent metaanalyses identified increased serum alkaline phosphatase (SAP)
activity as a negative prognostic indicator for both DFI and OST and
increasing age as a negative prognostic indicator for OST.70,71 Tumor
site has been shown to be significant for both DFI and OST; 1 study
suggested improved prognosis for the distal radius70 and the
proximal humerus carried a negative prognosis in another study.71
Chemotherapy after amputation has been shown to improve OST.
Total SAP should be assessed preoperatively. Although bone SAP
(BSAP) is not routinely evaluated, increases in both total SAP and

bone alkaline phosphatase (BALP) have been identified as an
indicator of poor prognosis in dogs with OSA.32,72 The correlation
between SAP and poor prognosis is likely a function of increased
tumor burden, resulting in an increased production of membranous
BALP, rather than an indication of tumorigenic or metastatic
phenotype.73

CHONDROSARCOMA (CSA)
When compared with appendicular OSA, appendicular CSA has
much lower metastatic rates, with the potential for much longer
OSTs and possibly even cure with amputation alone. In a
retrospective study of 25 large- or giant-breed dogs with CSA, the
mean age was about 6.5 years. The anatomic site distribution was
slightly different than that of OSA: 10 tumors in the tibia (6 proximal
and 4 distal), 5 in the femur (2 proximal and 3 distal), 4 in the
humerus (3 proximal and 1 distal), 2 in the distal ulna, 1 in the
metacarpals, and 1 in the calcaneus. Seven dogs had pulmonary
metastases. All dogs were treated with amputation alone, with an
overall MST of 979 days.45 When tumors were graded histologically,
an increased rate of pulmonary metastasis was seen with increased
grade: 0% for grade I, 31% for grade II, and 50% for grade III. This
difference was not statistically significant. A significant association
was noted between histologic grade and OST. MSTs were 6, 2.7, and
0.9 years with tumor grades of I, II, and III, respectively.45 The value
of chemotherapy for dogs with high-grade CSA is unknown, but such
treatment should be considered.

PRIMARY HEMANGIOSARCOMA (CH.
325) AND TELANGIECTATIC
OSTEOSARCOMA
Primary hemangiosarcoma of bone and telangiectatic OSA can have
similar histological appearances and be difficult to discriminate.74
Both have cystic blood-filled spaces, with hemangiosarcoma being

lined with endothelial cells and OSA being lined with malignant
osteoblasts.74 Although osteoid is often used to definitively diagnose
OSA, it is not a prevalent feature of telangiectatic OSA.74
Immunohistochemistry (IHC) accurately distinguishes these 2
conditions, using factor VIII-related antigen/von Willebrand factor
to identify endothelial cells.74 A retrospective study of
hemangiosarcoma of bone and telangiectatic OSA in dogs suggested
a universally poor prognosis and that treatment with amputation and
chemotherapy extended survival.75 Tumor site and signalment for
telangiectatic OSA was consistent with other OSA subtypes.
Hemangiosarcoma of bone had a predilection for the hind limbs (the
proximal tibia) and for relatively smaller breeds, with medium-sized
breeds and Border Collies identified to be at risk.75

HISTIOCYTIC SARCOMA AND
SYNOVIAL CELL SARCOMA IN DOGS
(CH. 328)
Tumors arising from the synovium include synovial cell sarcoma,
histiocytic sarcoma, synovial myxoma, and other sarcomas.76
Affected dogs present with lameness and either joint swelling or a
periarticular mass. Generally, large-breed older dogs have tumors of
the synovium. These tumors can have a similar clinical presentation
and histologic appearance. With tumors of synovial origin, an
incisional biopsy of affected bone and surrounding soft tissues
should be performed for histopathologic evaluation and IHC to
determine the tumor type. FNA for cytologic analysis may be helpful
to confirm malignancy but less apt to determine a definitive
diagnosis (chs. 83 and 85). Previously, this group of joint-associated
tumors was collectively referred to as synovial cell sarcoma, making
interpretation of some of the earlier literature problematic because
of the lack of a definitive diagnosis to distinguish synovial cell
sarcomas from histiocytic sarcomas. The radiographic appearance of
bone lesions secondary to histiocytic sarcoma are characterized
primarily by bone destruction, with osseous production being a less

common feature.77 A soft-tissue mass is variably present in
periarticular lesions.77 When the proximal humerus is affected, the
radiographic appearance is similar to OSA77 (Figure 326.8).
Breeds commonly affected with periarticular histiocytic sarcoma
include Rottweilers, Bernese Mountain Dogs, and Flat Coated
Retrievers.76,78-80 In a retrospective study of 35 dogs with a synovial
tumor, 51.3% were diagnosed with histiocytic sarcoma using CD18 as
an immunohistochemical marker76; 66% of these cases had been
misdiagnosed as other types of sarcomas.76 Rottweilers were
overrepresented among dogs with histiocytic sarcoma.76 An
apparent predilection for the stifle among dogs with histiocytic
sarcoma was noted, with a high proportion of dogs having evidence
of cranial cruciate ligament rupture, suggesting that chronic
synovitis could be a potential inciting cause of this disease.81 This
was also found in another study evaluating peri-articular histiocytic
sarcoma and previous joint disease in Bernese Mountain Dogs.79 In
that study, the odds ratio for developing a peri-articular histiocytic
sarcoma in a location with previous joint disease compared to a joint
free of disease was 5.4.79 Another study found a strong association
between joint disease and the development of periarticular
histiocytic sarcoma, with an odds ratio of 13.42. This was particularly
evident in the Rottweiler and dogs with prior cruciate ligament
injury.78 These findings suggest that both genetic predisposition and
chronic inflammation may contribute to the neoplastic etiology and
emphasize the importance of reevaluating dogs with chronic
progressive lameness, as some may have a chronic orthopedic
condition and a subsequent neoplastic process.
Dogs with histiocytic sarcoma had significantly shorter MSTs (5.3
months) compared with dogs with synovial cell sarcoma and synovial
myxoma, but not all dogs were treated.81 Periarticular histiocytic
sarcoma is a distinct clinical entity from disseminated histiocytic
sarcoma, which carries a much higher metastatic rate and a more
guarded prognosis (ch. 328).82 Dogs with periarticular sarcoma had
a MST of 391 days versus 128 days for the disseminated form with

treatment.82 In that study, dogs with periarticular histiocytic
sarcoma with and without metastatic disease at the time of diagnosis,
the OSTs were 980 and 253 days, respectively.82

FIGURE 326.8 Sagittal computed tomography
scan of a Rottweiler with a polyostotic lytic lesion
that involves the distal scapula and proximal
humerus. This patient was diagnosed with a
periarticular histiocytic sarcoma. Image courtesy Dr.
Meredith Gauthier.
True synovial cell sarcomas are rare and must be distinguished
from periarticular histiocytic sarcomas using IHC.76 It has been
suggested that this term is a misnomer and that cytokeratin-positive

joint-associated sarcoma is more appropriate.83 Synovial myxoma, a
differential diagnosis for a joint-based tumor, can be diagnosed on
the gross appearance (gelatinous nodules that fill the joint cavity),
histologic features, and IHC. This neoplasm is most commonly seen
in Doberman Pinschers and Labrador Retrievers and typically affects
the stifle and/or digits. Reported MSTs were 2.5 years with surgical
removal. Local recurrence has been reported but metastatic disease
has not.81
Treatment of synovial tumors depends on the tumor type. Full
staging with 3-view thoracic radiographs, lymph node palpation and
aspiration, and abdominal US or whole-body CT is recommended
prior to treatment. In general, amputation is the recommended
treatment for this disease if staging is negative for gross metastatic
disease, but RT can be considered in select cases. Chemotherapy is
recommended for periarticular histiocytic sarcoma. One study
comparing outcomes in dogs with periarticular histiocytic sarcoma
treated with chemotherapy and amputation or radiation, the MST
was 398 and 240 days, respectively.80 This difference was not
statistically significant. The decision to treat with amputation versus
RT will depend on stage, degree of pain associated with the tumor,
and the owner’s goals.

OSTEOSARCOMA (OSA) IN CATS
OSA is a rare tumor in cats but is their most common primary bone
tumor.84,85 The reported mean age at presentation for appendicular
OSA is 8-10.7 years.86-88 Most reports of feline OSA evaluate both
appendicular and axial OSA cases together.86,88,89 In a large,
retrospective study of 145 cats with OSA, 62% were skeletal and 38%
extra-skeletal. Of those that were skeletal in origin, 55% arose from
the appendicular skeleton and 45% from the axial skeleton.89 A
distribution of 65% appendicular and 35% axial OSA has been
reported in cats.88 No breed or sex predilection has been
identified.86,88,89

The metastatic rate at the time of presentation and during the
course of disease (10%) is much lower in feline OSA than in canine
OSA.88 In a study of 145 cases, only 2 of the 35 cats with
appendicular OSA that had thoracic radiography performed had
evidence of pulmonary metastasis during the course of treatment.89
Treatment of appendicular OSA with amputation or excision resulted
in postoperative STs of 16.789 and 64 months,86 respectively, with
no adjunctive therapy provided. Axial OSA carries a worse prognosis
for survival than appendicular OSA.86,89 This is primarily because of
the difficulty associated with achieving clean margins of excision in
axial locations, as clean margins have also been associated with
survival.88 In 1 study, the recurrence rate was 44%, highlighting both
the difficulty and the importance of attempting to achieve clean
margins in axial or appendicular OSA.88 The histologic grade and
mitotic index have been shown to have prognostic value in feline
OSA.88 The recommended treatment for appendicular OSA in cats is
amputation without adjunctive chemotherapy. Staging with thoracic
radiographs or CT should be performed prior to surgery. Some cats
will succumb to metastatic disease. However, the metastatic rate is
much lower than with canine OSA, and prolonged survival can be
expected in most cases if a wide or radical excision is achieved.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Osteosarcoma in Dogs
Your dog has been diagnosed (or presumptively diagnosed) with a
primary bone tumor. Although other types of primary sarcomas of
bone can occur that can look similar to osteosarcoma, osteosarcoma
is considered the most likely diagnosis. This tumor type is
definitively diagnosed by sending tissues for histopathology, but a
first step can be a needle biopsy (aspirate) for cytology.

STAGING
Unfortunately, at the time of diagnosis of osteosarcoma, spread of
tumor cells (metastasis) has likely already occurred. Staging tests are
performed to distinguish between microscopic spread, meaning that
there are cells that have spread that are undetectable, and gross
spread, meaning that there are cells that have spread to the extent
that new tumors have formed elsewhere in the body. The most
common sites for osteosarcoma to spread are the lungs and other
bone sites.
Treatment options:
1. Amputation – This is the most common treatment for
osteosarcoma. Most dogs will do well on 3 limbs and will feel
much better once the primary bone tumor has been removed.
2. Surgical Limb Salvage – In some cases, the bone tumor can be
removed and the limb can be preserved. This approach has the
obvious advantage of limb preservation, but the disadvantage
of higher costs and a higher potential complication rate
compared with limb amputation.
3. Radiation Therapy – Radiation can be used to control bone
cancer pain, which is called palliative radiation. Palliative
radiation is administered in 2-4 doses and will decrease pain in
most cases for an average of 4 months. In select cases,
radiation can be administered to give a high dose of radiation
that will provide long term control of the tumor. This is called
stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT). The primary advantage of
this approach is that tumor control is similar to amputation,
but the approach is nonsurgical. The primary disadvantage of

this approach is that approximately half of the dogs treated
with SRT will develop a fracture at the tumor site.
4. Chemotherapy – With all of the above treatment approaches
for local control of the tumor, systemic chemotherapy is
recommended to slow the progression of metastatic disease.
Chemotherapy is generally well-tolerated in dogs.
5. Palliative Treatment – Along with palliative radiation, pain
medications can be administered to help control pain and this
may be the only treatment that you decide to move forward
with. With this approach, it is very important to monitor your
dog’s quality of life closely and humanely euthanize them when
quality of life declines. Bone cancer pain is difficult to control
and most dogs will not exhibit pain overtly. Lack of limb use is
a sign of pain.
Sarah Elizabeth Boston (Guelph, Ontario, Canada)

CANINE MAST CELL TUMORS
INCIDENCE AND RISK FACTORS
Mast cell tumors (MCTs) represent the most common cutaneous malignancy in the
dog, accounting for 16-21% of all cutaneous tumors.1 Several breeds are at
increased risk for MCT, including brachycephalic breeds (English Bulldog, Boxer,

Pug, Boston Terrier), Schnauzers, retrievers, Cocker Spaniels, Beagles,
Staffordshire Bull Terriers, Rhodesian Ridgebacks, Weimaraners, and Chinese
Shar-Peis.1-3 MCTs in brachycephalic breeds are more likely to be low-grade.1,4 In
contrast, Shar-Peis anecdotally may develop more biologically aggressive MCTs.
The best characterized molecular alteration in canine MCT involves the receptor
tyrosine kinase (RTK) KIT. It is normally expressed on various cell surfaces,
including melanocytes, mast cells (MCs), hematopoietic stem cells, and others.5 In
contact with the growth factor ligand, stem cell factor (SCF), KIT dimerizes,
phosphorylation occurs at multiple intracellular sites, and intracellular signaling
promotes proliferation, differentiation, and maturation of normal MCs.5 The KIT
protein is expressed on canine and feline MCTs, and aberrant (cytoplasmic)
localization of KIT in MCTs can be associated with dysregulated function.6-8
Furthermore, 15-35% of intermediate and high-grade canine MCTs possess
mutations in the c-kit gene, which result in constitutive, SCF-independent KIT
activation.9-12

HISTORY AND CLINICAL SIGNS
Most MCTs in dogs are solitary in the dermis or subcutaneous (SQ) tissues; 11-14%
of dogs have multiple lesions and a visceral form has been described.13-19
Cutaneous MCTs have a variety of appearances and are sometimes inadvertently
mistaken for non-neoplastic lesions (ch. 12). The history and clinical signs of dogs
with a MCT may be complicated by signs caused by release of histamine, heparin,
and/or other vasoactive amines from MC granules, e.g., erythema, edema in
surrounding tissues, pruritus, or changes in mass size. Dogs with substantial tumor
burdens (i.e., large tumors, significant metastatic disease) are more likely to have
systemic signs, including vomiting, diarrhea, fever (ch. 16), melena (ch. 50),
peripheral edema (ch. 30), and rarely collapse. Histamine, released intermittently
and unpredictably from MCT granules, is thought to act on gastric parietal cells via
histamine H2 receptors, which can result in increased hydrochloric acid secretion
and gastric/duodenal irritation and/or ulceration.

FIGURE 327.1 Suggested diagnostic algorithm for canine
cutaneous mast cell tumors.

DIAGNOSIS
Most MCTs are readily diagnosed via fine-needle aspiration (FNA) and cytologic
evaluation of smears (ch. 85). MCs are small to medium-sized, round, and usually
contain numerous small uniform cytoplasmic granules that stain purplish red
(metachromatic).1,20 However, a small percentage of MCTs have granules that do
not stain readily with conventional Romanowsky (Diff-Quik type) stains. In these,
Wright-Giemsa or toluidine blue stains often reveal granules. In a small number,
histologic assessment of a tissue sample may be necessary. Highly anaplastic
agranular MCTs can be challenging to definitively diagnose histologically by H&E
staining and routine light microscopy. CD117 (KIT) immunohistochemistry can be
used to differentiate anaplastic MCTs from other round cell tumors.6

STAGING (Figure 327.1)
Before Surgery
Before surgery, staging should include a complete blood count (CBC), serum
biochemistry profile, cytologic evaluation of regional lymph node(s) (LN[s]),
abdominal ultrasound (US), cytologic evaluation of splenic or liver FNAs if
warranted (chs. 85, 88), and thoracic radiographs. Extensive staging is generally
not necessary for dogs that are node-negative and without negative prognostic
factors (see below). If negative prognostic factors are not identified and the MCT is

in a location that is amenable to wide surgical excision, testing beyond the
minimum database and cytologic evaluation of regional LNs is unnecessary.
Cytologic evaluation of LN FNAs, even with normal sized nodes, should be done
prior to wide surgical excision and biopsy for histopathologic assessment.

MCT Not Amenable to Surgery
If a MCT is at a site not amenable to wide surgical excision or if negative prognostic
factors exist, additional diagnostics are recommended prior to definitive therapy:
thoracic radiographs, abdominal US, +/− FNA cytologic evaluation of abnormal
organs.21,22 An incisional biopsy can be obtained to determine histologic grade, if
the results affect owner willingness to pursue therapy (ch. 88). Occasional solitary
MCs identified in LN cytologic preparations can be normal and are not diagnostic
of metastasis. MC clustering and aggregates are more worrisome.23 Disease in a
regional LN, but not beyond, should not be reason to avoid surgery; rather, the LN
should be excised and submitted for histopathologic evaluation at the time of
primary tumor resection. Histologic assessment may be necessary to accurately
determine whether LN MCs represent metastatic disease. A grading scheme has
been proposed to better quantify the degree of LN infiltration in canine MCT.24
With the exception of extremely rare cases of primary MC leukemia (ch. 322),
involvement of bone marrow or peripheral blood in the absence of visceral disease
is very rare.25 Therefore, buffy coat smears and bone marrow aspiration for
cytologic examination are rarely informative.

PROGNOSTIC FACTORS (Table 327.1)
Histologic Grade
One well-defined prognostic factor is tumor histologic grade. Pathologists often
utilize a numeric (Patnaik) grading scheme, where “Grade I” is well-differentiated
and “Grade III” is poorly differentiated.2 Some pathologists also assess masses as
low-, intermediate-, or high-grade, or well-, poorly, or intermediately differentiated
rather than a numerical scale. Completely excised Patnaik low- or intermediategrade MCTs without LN involvement usually require no further therapy, as the risk
of recurrence or metastasis is only about 10%. In contrast, completely excised highgrade MCTs have a low chance for recurrence, but a high chance for metastasis and
short postsurgical survival times.26,27
The Patnaik grading system may not detect a small percentage of grade I/II
MCTs that may behave aggressively, complicated by disagreement in tumor
grading schemes among pathologists. A grading system has been introduced which
separates tumors into “high” or “low” grade based on 4 fairly objective histologic
features (mitotic count, multinucleation, bizarre nuclei, karyomegaly), in an
attempt to minimize inter-pathologist disagreement and still provide helpful
prognostic information.28 In a series of dogs evaluated by both systems, the “2-

tier” system was somewhat better at predicting dogs more likely to die of MCT,28
and at least 1 follow-up study has confirmed the value of this 2-tiered system.29 It
is not entirely clear whether the 2-tiered system is truly “better” than the Patnaik
system for predicting the biologic behavior of MCTs. The author still prefers to
receive histologic grades according to both schemas on MCT pathology reports.
