Assessments of Tumor Cell Proliferation
There is substantial information that assessment of mitotic index (MI) or mitotic
count can be strong predictors of outcome, identifying intermediate grade tumors
at increased risk of metastasis and, potentially, high-grade tumors at reduced risk
of metastasis.30,31 This information should be provided on all MCT histopathology
reports. A variety of specialized histochemical or immunohistochemical tests for
assessment of proliferation (argyrophilic nucleolar organizer region [AgNOR] Ki67
and proliferating cell nuclear antigen [PCNA] among others) have been evaluated
for predictive value and correlate well with grade, MI, and postsurgical outcome.3238 However, it is not known yet if these cumbersome assessments provide any
prognostic information beyond that provided by simple assessment of MI/grade.
These assessments can be reserved for ambiguous histopathologic grades or
“borderline” MI.

c-kit Mutation Status and KIT Protein Localization
Studies have suggested that dogs with tumors with activating c-kit gene mutations
or with aberrant (e.g., non-cytoplasmic) KIT localization (via
immunohistochemistry) may have inferior postsurgical outcomes.9,11,35,38-43
Given the strong associations between c-kit mutation/aberrant KIT localization
and other known prognostic factors (e.g., grade, MI),35,43 the value of these
independent prognostic values is evolving. A consensus statement regarding the
use of KIT related diagnostics in canine MCT has been recently published by the
Oncology-Pathology Working Group.44

Cytologic Grading
Cytologic methods for assigning tumor grade, recently described,45-47 appear to
have fairly good correlation with those assigned histopathologically. Cytologic

grading may help identify more aggressive MCTs, for which thorough presurgical
staging may be warranted; however, assignment of cytologic grade should not be
considered a substitute for histopathology, e.g., MI and/or surgical margins cannot
be assessed.

Multiplicity of Lesions
As discussed, a small percentage of dogs have multiple cutaneous tumors at the
time of diagnosis or that develop over time. The clonal origin of these tumors is
unclear, e.g., are the masses the same neoplastic clone metastasizing in an atypical
fashion or are they multiple independent unrelated tumors? Assuming the MCTs
are relegated to the skin, these dogs have a favorable outcome following excision
alone. The same criteria (e.g., grade, margins, mitotic activity) appear to be
predictive of more aggressive behavior. Important for owner education, about 50%
of dogs with multiple cutaneous MCTs continue to develop others. Careful
monitoring is warranted.14,15,17 There is no known effective measure to prevent
additional tumors from occurring.

Cutaneous vs SQ Mast Cell Tumors
It has been suggested that MCTs arising from the SQ have different behavior from
cutaneous MCTs. Specifically, it appears that most SQ MCTs have a relatively
benign clinical course and that few recur, even with incomplete excision. The
conventional 3-tier and 2-tier grading schemas are not applicable to SQ MCTs;
however, some of the same criteria (MI, infiltrative growth and presence of
multinucleation) appear to be predictive of more aggressive behavior.48

TREATMENT
Surgery
Treatment decisions are based on presence or absence of negative prognostic
factors and on clinical stage. In tumors localized to the skin (+/− regional LN) in
areas where wide excision is straightforward, surgical excision of the primary
tumor (and affected/suspicious LN) is the treatment of choice. A 3 cm margin of
surrounding normal tissue has been recommended for MCT excision, but recent
evidence has suggested 1-2 cm lateral margins and 1 uninvolved fascial plane are
sufficient for complete excision of many MCTs, particularly when lower grade and
small.49-53 Importantly, inability to achieve desired margins should not preclude
surgery, if primary closure can be achieved. Rather, the owner should be prewarned about a higher potential for incomplete excision and the possible need for
additional postoperative therapies to address residual local disease. Surgical
margins should be evaluated histologically for completeness of excision. Routine
use of neoadjuvant corticosteroids to facilitate surgical resection is not
recommended, except in cases where even marginal excision is not possible due to
location or extent of disease.

Options for Incomplete Excisions
When margins are incomplete, local therapy is warranted to prevent recurrence5456

; however, not all MCTs with surgically incomplete margins recur.57,58 Reexcision of the previous surgical scar with wider margins should be performed
when possible. If additional surgery is not possible, adjuvant radiation therapy
(RT) can be effective (ch. 318). Two-year control rates of 85-95% are reported
following RT for incompletely resected MCTs of low or intermediate grade.59-61 A
less optimal alternative is a combination of surgery and chemotherapy (discussed
below).62,63 For MCTs where acceptable marginal excision is not possible, RT
alone,61,64,65 RT plus toceranib (TOC),66 or medical therapy alone (see below)
may be considered.

Postoperative Follow-Up
Regardless of therapies employed, dogs with low- and intermediate-grade MCTs
should be rechecked regularly for local recurrence +/− metastasis. Complete
physical examinations should include careful palpation of the local site and
regional LNs. FNA of any new cutaneous masses or enlarged LNs is recommended.
More complete staging including abdominal US should be included if the dog had a
MCT at high risk for metastasis.

Candidates for Medical Therapy
Treating “high-risk” MCTs remains challenging. This includes dogs with highgrade tumors, intermediate-grade tumors with regional or distant metastasis or
high proliferative activity as assessed by MI or special stains, as well as those
arising from a mucous membrane or mucocutaneous junction. Although some
studies suggest that low-/intermediate-grade tumors with only regional LN
involvement may have a better prognosis than high grade tumors,67-70 it is
recommended that such tumors be treated as having high capacity for metastasis if
the nodal involvement is substantial as assessed by “HN grading.”24

Medical Therapy Options
In addition to local therapy, adjuvant medical therapy should be offered for dogs
with high-risk MCT to try and delay or prevent further metastasis. Full clinical
staging should be performed, if not done preoperatively. Corticosteroids have been
reported to be of some benefit,65,71,72 but most responses are incomplete and brief.
Corticosteroids can reduce peritumoral edema/inflammation, which may interfere
with response assessment. Studies have reported objective response rates as high
as 64% when measurable canine MCTs were treated with various cytotoxic
chemotherapy protocols (ch. 317).56,73-79 Multi-agent protocols may have higher
response rates than single-agent therapy.56,73,75,77,78 The most commonly
employed first-line agents are vinblastine (VBL) and lomustine (CCNU), often with

concurrent corticosteroids.56,74,77,79 Importantly, the response of most bulky
MCTs to chemotherapy tends to be incomplete and short-lived, stressing the need
for local control of disease if at all possible prior to the institution of medical
therapy. VBL- and/or lomustine-based chemotherapy for “high-risk” MCT in the
postoperative setting tended to result in longer disease-free and overall survival
times than historical data employing surgery alone, with median survival times >2
years in most studies (ch. 317).40,68,75,77,80,81

KIT Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKIs)
Orally available TKIs can inhibit KIT protein signaling (ch. 320). Two TKIs are
approved for MCT treatment in dogs: TOC (Palladia, Zoetis) and masitinib (MAS;
Masivet, AB Science). Studies have also evaluated the human TKI imatinib
(Gleevec, Novartis).82 Following encouraging early-phase clinical trials,12 a
multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study assessed TOC
efficacy in dogs with recurrent, metastatic, intermediate or high grade MCTs.83
The TOC-treated dog response rate was 37.2% (7 complete response [CR], 25
partial response [PR]) versus 7.9% (all PR) in the placebo-treated dogs. The
median response duration and time to tumor progression were 12.0 and 18.1
weeks, respectively. Dogs whose MCT possessed c-kit gene activating mutations
had objective response rates higher than those with wild-type c-kit (69% vs 37%).
Gastrointestinal (GI) toxic effects (poor appetite, diarrhea, weight loss, and
occasionally vomiting or melena) were the most common adverse effects (AEs; ch.
321). AEs were usually manageable with supportive care, “drug holidays,” and/or
dosage reductions. Other AEs include mild to moderate leukopenia and occasional
muscle pain.83 Recent experience with TOC suggests that equivalent antitumor
activity and reduced AEs may be observed if doses lower than the label dosage are
employed. Doses of 2.4-2.75 mg/kg q48h or 3 days per week (Monday, Wednesday,
Friday) are commonly used.66,84
A similar study was completed using MAS (ch. 320) for dogs with recurrent or
unresectable MCT,85 with significantly improved time-to-progression in MAStreated dogs. Time to progression was improved in dogs with MCT harboring
activating c-kit mutations and in first-line treated dogs. Follow-up demonstrated
improved long-term disease control in the MAS-treated dogs (40% MAS-treated vs
15% placebo-treated alive at 2 years).86 GI AEs (vomiting or diarrhea) were usually
mild and self-limiting (ch. 321). Myelosuppression, usually mild, was also noted.
A small percentage of MAS-treated dogs developed a protein-losing nephropathy
(PLN, ch. 302) causing edema (ch. 30). Increases in blood urea nitrogen and
creatinine were observed in some and hemolytic anemia was rare (chs. 172 and
321).85

Combining TKI/Standard Therapies

A few studies have assessed combining TKIs with standard forms of therapy, e.g.,
RT or cytotoxic chemotherapy. Evidence of benefit when used postoperatively has
yet to be demonstrated. In 1 trial, a combination of TOC and VBL was assessed in
dogs with measurable MCTs. While significant VBL dose and frequency reductions
were necessary due to additive myelosuppression, encouraging results were
reported (71% objective response rate).87,88 The combination of TOC, prednisone
and hypofractionated RT was studied in dogs with non-resectable and/or
metastatic MCT with overall response rates of 76.4% (58.8% CR, 17.6% PR, overall
median progression free interval: 10.5 months).66

c-kit Mutation Status and KIT Localization in Predicting
Benefit From TKI Therapy
The value of c-kit mutation status in predicting outcome of TOC or MAS treatment
has been evaluated to some degree. In the TOC registration study and a
preliminary study, MCT dogs with c-kit gene mutations had objective response
rates twice as high as those without mutations (60% vs 30%), but long-term
outcome was not reported.12,83 In the MAS registration study, a significant
outcome improvement between MAS and placebo arms was observed only in dogs
with c-kit mutations. Dogs in the MAS arm of the study with c-kit mutations
appeared to have longer times to progression (230 d vs 83 d) and maintained
higher overall response rates at 6 months (20% vs 10%).85 However, 2 recent
studies have suggested no correlation between response to TOC and c-kit
mutational status.41,89
Interestingly, dogs with c-kit mutations had decreased progression free survival
times compared to those without c-kit mutations in a study of TOC and
hypofractionated RT.66 A recent comparatively large multicenter prospective study
suggested a similar negative correlation between c-kit mutation status and
outcome following TOC treatment.41 Thus, even if initial response rates are
increased in dogs with MCTs that possess c-kit mutations, this may not translate
into better long-term outcome, and certainly does not predict benefit if used
postoperatively.
Dogs without c-kit mutations may to respond to TKIs,12,41,83 perhaps due to
non-mutational activation of KIT (e.g., autocrine or paracrine signaling,
amplifications), the presence of activating mutations not screened for as part of
routine testing, or inhibition of other kinases (e.g., PDGFR, VEGFR2). The effects
of KIT localization on outcome following TKI treatment were assessed in 2 recent
studies,41,89 neither of which detected correlations between KIT localization and
objective response. In 1 study, aberrant KIT localization was associated with an
inferior progression free and overall survival time following TOC treatment.41

Tigilanol Tiglate (TT)

An alternative to surgery for focal, relatively small canine MCTs (total volume of
<10 cm3) is injecting lesions with the protein kinase C activating drug TT. TT can
be used for treating nonmetastatic cutaneous MCTs or nonmetastatic SQ MCTs at
or below the elbow or hock. In the randomized, placebo controlled trial, the CR
rate in TT-treated MCT was 75% after 1 injection and 88% after a second
injection.90 Eighty-nine percent of CR dogs were recurrence free 6 and 12 months
after injection.91 Tumor necrosis resulting in full-thickness cutaneous ulceration is
common, occurring 3 to 14 days post injection and requiring an average of 4 to 6
weeks to heal.92 It is important to note that incisional biopsy of MCT lesions to be
treated with TT is not recommended within 2 weeks of injection, due to concerns
regarding drug leakage from the biopsy site. Thus, histologic information is often
not obtained on TT-treated MCTs, making identification of dogs with “high risk”
MCT where adjuvant medical therapy should be offered, difficult. In this
circumstance, FNA cytologic grading should be performed.

Ancillary Therapies
Ancillary palliative therapy to address the systemic effects of MC mediators is
sometimes warranted in dogs with MCT (chs. 317 and 321), usually by giving both
H1 and H2 blockers (e.g., diphenhydramine and famotidine). The proton pump
inhibitor omeprazole may be more effective for diminishing gastric acid secretion,
particularly in dogs with bulky MC disease. These agents are particularly used for
dogs where: 1) systemic clinical signs are present; 2) the tumor is likely to be
extensively manipulated at surgery (i.e., cytoreductive surgery, incisional biopsy);
or 3) treatment is undertaken in the context of gross disease (e.g., RT or medical
therapy for large tumors that are not cytoreduced). There is no clinical evidence
that H1/H2 blockers or omeprazole have any antineoplastic effects.

FELINE MAST CELL TUMORS
Unlike MCTs in dogs, which are primarily cutaneous/SQ, MCTs in cats typically
occur in 3 distinct syndromes: cutaneous, splenic/visceral and intestinal. In 1
study, 67% of cutaneous and splenic/visceral MCTs had c-kit activating
mutations.93

FELINE CUTANEOUS MCT
Two Distinct Forms
MCTs are the second most common cutaneous tumor in cats, accounting for ∼20%
of cutaneous tumors (ch. 323).94,95 They are usually solitary, raised, firm, well
circumscribed, hairless, dermal nodules 0.5-3 cm in diameter. About 20% are
multiple, although 1 series reported multiple lesions in most.1 Two distinct
cutaneous MCTs have been reported: (1) the more typical “mastocytic” MCT,

histologically similar to MCT in dogs; (2) the less common histiocytic MCT, with
morphologic features characteristic of histiocytic MCs, and which may regress
spontaneously over 4 to 24 months.96,97 Oriental breeds appear to be predisposed
to both.94-97
The mastocytic form can be further subdivided based on histologic appearance:
previously referred to as compact (50-90% of all cases) and diffuse
(anaplastic).94,96 Well-differentiated compact tumors tend to behave in a benign
manner and metastasis is uncommon, while anaplastic tumors may have a high
MI, marked cellular and nuclear pleomorphism, and SQ infiltration. Clinical
behavior of these anaplastic tumors is variable.97-101 Recently, a histologic grading
scheme has been developed for feline MCT, which appears to have prognostic
value.102

Diagnosis
Most feline MCTs are usually easily diagnosed by cytologic examination of FNAs
(ch. 85). Cats with cutaneous MCT should be evaluated for evidence of additional
tumors and/or potential splenic involvement via abdominal US; some cats with
multiple cutaneous MCTs also have splenic disease.99 CBC, serum biochemistry
profile, urinalysis (UA), and careful examination of local LNs is recommended.

Surgical Management
Most cutaneous feline MCTs can be surgically excised. Local recurrence after
excision occurs in as many as 24%94,97-101 and reported metastatic rates range
from 0 to 22%.97-101 For histologically anaplastic/high grade tumors or those with
a high MI, systemic therapy as for canine MCT may be indicated, although
statistics regarding postoperative efficacy are lacking.101,103 Following biopsy
confirmation, conservative resection or active surveillance may be undertaken with
the histiocytic form, as these may spontaneously regress.94-96

RT and/or Medical Treatment
RT may be considered for incompletely excised “high-risk” tumors.104 Limited
information exists concerning the utility of chemotherapy in cats with MCT (ch.
317). Objective responses to lomustine (CCNU) have been reported in cats.105,106
Anecdotally, prednisone/VBL, as used in dogs, appears to be associated with
antitumor activity in some. Administration of imatinib has been associated with
PR in cats with MCT expressing activating mutations in c-kit,93,107 and a recent
report described an objective response rate to TOC of approximately 70%.108

FELINE SPLENIC/VISCERAL MCT

Description
MCTs represent the most common differential diagnosis for splenic disease in cats
(15% of submissions in 1 series) (ch. 182).109 Most cats with splenic MCT do not
have a history of cutaneous MCT, although recent evidence suggests that some cats
with multiple cutaneous MCTs may also have splenic involvement.99 While the
spleen is the primary site affected by this disease, other organs may also be
involved.94,110 Peripheral blood mastocytosis has been reported in the majority of
cases, with peripheral MC counts as high as 32,000 cells/mcL reported.94,111

Signs, Testing, Treatment
Cats with splenic MCT may have signs of systemic illness, e.g., vomiting,
hyporexia, and/or weight loss.94,110 Clinical signs associated with degranulation,
such as GI ulceration, hemorrhage, hypotensive shock, and labored breathing, may
also be noted. Abdominal palpation usually reveals marked cranial organomegaly.
Cats with suspected splenic MCT should have CBC, serum biochemistry profile,
UA, abdominal US, and thoracic radiographs performed. US-guided FNA cytology
or cytologic evaluation of effusions is usually diagnostic for splenic MCT (ch. 85).
Splenectomy is the treatment of choice for cats with splenic MCT, even if other
organ involvement is noted. Long-term survival with good quality of life is
common following splenectomy, even if there is significant bone marrow and/or
peripheral blood involvement; median survival times from 12 to 19 months have
been reported.94,112 As with high-risk feline cutaneous MCT, the utility of adjuvant
medical therapy is unknown.

FELINE INTESTINAL MCT
Intestinal MCT is the third most common primary intestinal tumor in cats after
lymphoma and adenocarcinoma (ch. 262),94 causing vomiting, diarrhea and
hyporexia in most afflicted cats. A palpable abdominal mass is often evident.94
Enlarged mesenteric LNs and/or hepatomegaly may also be identified. Peritoneal
effusion containing MCs and eosinophils may be present. Diagnosis is usually
made by FNA of the mass or involved organs (ch. 85). Since metastasis is common
at the time of diagnosis, cats with intestinal MCT should be staged with a CBC,
serum biochemistry profile, UA, thoracic radiographs and abdominal US. Cats with
intestinal MCT have a poor prognosis,94,113-115 although 1 recent case series
suggested a more favorable outcome with medical or surgical therapy, or a
combination of both.116 Surgery is the treatment of choice when possible and wide
surgical margins are necessary (5-10 cm) as the tumor typically extends
histologically well beyond the obvious gross disease.94,113 Postoperative
chemotherapy is reasonable to offer in all cases.

DEFINITIONS
Histiocytic diseases represent a diverse and potentially confusing spectrum of syndromes ranging from
solitary lesions that spontaneously regress (histiocytoma) to highly malignant tumors involving multiple
sites in the body (disseminated histiocytic sarcoma [HS]). Also included in this category are reactive
conditions associated with underlying immune dysregulation (cutaneous histiocytosis, systemic
histiocytosis).

CELL ORIGIN AND DEVELOPMENT OF HISTIOCYTES
Etiology
Histiocytes develop from CD34+ bone marrow (BM) stem cells, migrate from BM to blood as monocytes,
and enter various tissues where they undergo differentiation into macrophages and dendritic cells
(DCs). Under the influence of monocyte/macrophage-colony stimulating factor, blood monocytes
differentiate into macrophages, while granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor, interleukin-4,
and tumor necrosis factor-alpha lead to various DC lineages, including interstitial DC and Langerhans
cells (LCs). The latter are critically dependent on transforming growth factor-beta1 stimulation.1-3
Interstitial DCs occur in perivascular locations in many organs, LCs are mainly in the epidermis, and
recently identified populations have been identified in lymph nodes and other locations.4,5

Function
Histiocytes play a key role in immune function via phagocytosis (macrophages) and antigen processing
and presentation (DCs, LCs). DCs represent the most potent antigen-presenting cells (APCs), inducing

immune responses in naïve T cells. Cells are defined by their expression of molecules essential to their
function as APCs (Table 328.1).

Testing
Canine- and feline-specific monoclonal antibodies for these functionally important molecules aid
identification of macrophages, DCs, and LCs in tissues, and can be useful in distinguishing among
histiocytic diseases. Thus, collection of fresh snap-frozen tissue is often used in addition to more routine
sample collection for cytologic and histopathologic evaluation. Positive immunohistochemical (IHC)
staining for the macrophage scavenger receptor CD204 is highly specific for histiocytic malignancies and
provides another useful diagnostic tool distinguished by its applicability to both cytologic and formalinfixed tissues. Of interest, CD204 is macrophage-specific and raises questions regarding the historical
belief that most histiocytic malignancies arise from DCs.6

HISTIOCYTIC DISEASES
CANINE HISTIOCYTOMA
Canine histiocytoma is a common, benign skin tumor originating from LCs. It is usually diagnosed in
young dogs; the prevalence drops after 3 years of age. In a retrospective study of histologic tumor
diagnoses in dogs <1 year of age in the United Kingdom, cutaneous histiocytoma was the most common
diagnosis, representing 89% of the total.7 Lesions usually are solitary hairless dome- or button-shaped
masses on the head, although lesions can develop anywhere. Diagnosis requires cytologic evaluation
(ch. 83). Cytologic features typically consist of round cells with benign nuclear features, abundant
cytoplasm, and often a high mitotic index. Histiocytomas usually undergo spontaneous regression,
typically within 3 months. Recurrence is uncommon. Regression is mediated by CD8+ T-cells and
progressive lymphocyte infiltration is evident within tumors over time.8 Surgical or medical treatment
generally is not needed, but may be considered for lesions that are persistent, recurrent, or problematic
for the animal.

CANINE CUTANEOUS LANGERHANS CELL HISTIOCYTOSIS
(cLCH)
The uncommon presence of multiple histiocytomas in dogs can be included in the spectrum of
cutaneous LCHs, since the skin is consistently involved and is considered the site of origin.9 Lesions may
be limited to the skin, involve regional lymph nodes, and rarely, internal organs. Diagnosis requires
cytologic examination but biopsy with histologic evaluation and immunophenotyping are needed for
definitive diagnosis (chs. 83 and 85). Lymph node cytologic evaluation, thoracic radiographs, and
abdominal ultrasound (US) help in determining extent of disease. Spontaneous regression of lesions can

occur but may be delayed, with lesions persisting several months prior to regression. Lack of regression
and the challenges of managing extensive ulcerated lesions often lead to euthanasia. Limited
information exists on effective treatments, although 1 case report described transient improvement
following administration of CCNU (ch. 317).10

FELINE PULMONARY LANGERHANS CELL HISTIOCYTOSIS
(fLCH)
Proliferative LC disorders are rare in cats; 3 cats with primary pulmonary proliferative disease of LC
origin were described.11 The cats were older (10-15 years) with signs of respiratory disease and distress
ranging from 5 days to 7 months. Thoracic radiographs identified a severe, diffuse, bronchointerstitial
pattern in all 3 cats, with diffuse miliary to nodular opacities noted in 2. Glucocorticoids given to 2 cats
did not improve clinical signs. Euthanasia was elected in each due to progressive respiratory distress.
LCH was diagnosed postmortem through histopathologic, immunohistochemical, and electron
microscopic evaluations. Postmortem evaluation identified metastasis to distant sites: pancreas, liver,
kidneys and visceral lymph nodes. In another study of 4 cats (7-14 years of age), signs of respiratory
distress lasted from a week to 5.5 months.12 The thoracic radiographs in these cats identified mixed
pulmonary patterns, predominantly interstitial and alveolar. Supportive care did not improve clinical
signs and all cats died or were euthanized 1 day to 1 month after presentation.

CANINE REACTIVE HISTIOCYTOSIS (CUTANEOUS
HISTIOCYTOSIS, SYSTEMIC HISTIOCYTOSIS)
Definitions
Reactive histiocytosis consists of a group of non-neoplastic diseases of DC origin. Lesions in affected
dogs either can be confined to skin, subcutaneous (SQ) tissue, and draining lymph nodes (cutaneous
histiocytosis), or can involve skin and other sites including lymph nodes, liver, spleen, lung, BM, eye,
and/or mucous membranes (systemic histiocytosis). Cutaneous lesions are similar in both forms, and
progression from cutaneous to systemic histiocytosis is possible. The exact etiology and pathogenesis are
unknown, but dysregulation of immune response mechanisms has been proposed.

Cutaneous Histiocytosis
Cutaneous histiocytosis tends to occur in younger dogs. In a retrospective study of 32 dogs, median age
was 4 years; range, 1-8.13 Reported duration of signs prior to diagnosis is variable, with a median of 1.75
months and range of 0-30 months.13 Lesions are multifocal nodules, plaques, and crusts within the skin
and SQ tissue, often ulcerated. Diagnosis requires histologic assessment and immunophenotyping may
help. Lesions are characterized by histiocytic infiltrates with variable angiocentricity in the dermis and
SQ tissues. Lymphoid infiltration is common, comprising up to 50% of dermal infiltrates.13,14 Histiocyte
antigen expression patterns are consistent with DC origin.14 Lymph node evaluation (ch. 88), thoracic
radiographs, and abdominal US can be helpful in distinguishing cutaneous versus systemic forms of
disease. The disease course can be punctuated by remissions and relapses, especially early in the disease.
Given its diffuse nature, surgery is of limited use. Treatment typically involves systemic
immunomodulatory drugs (chs. 144 and 169). Variable responses were seen after giving corticosteroids
to 7 dogs.14 In another series, complete resolution of dermatologic lesions was reported in dogs
receiving a variety of immunomodulatory drugs for a median of 45 days (range, 14-162 days).13
Immunomodulatory drugs included prednisone alone or in combination with tetracycline/niacinamide
or azathioprine, tetracycline/niacinamide alone, and cyclosporine. Long-term maintenance therapy or
repeated treatment courses may be needed. Of the dogs with complete resolution of lesions, 30% had
recurrences and each dog responded to further treatment in 1 study.13 At the conclusion of that study,
with a median follow-up of 25 months, 26 of 32 (81%) dogs were alive with no lesions; 6 dogs had died
with no signs of cutaneous histiocytosis.

Systemic Histiocytosis
Systemic histiocytosis was initially reported in a group of closely related Bernese Mountain Dogs,
suggesting a genetic predisposition.15 A predilection in Rottweilers, Golden Retrievers, and Labrador
Retrievers has also been suggested.14 Systemic histiocytosis predominantly affects middle-aged dogs
(median 5 years; range, 1-9 years)14,15 causing nonspecific signs: depression, anorexia, and weight loss.
Other signs reflect the distribution and extent of lesions. Cutaneous and SQ lesions are similar, though
possibly more widespread, to those seen with cutaneous histiocytosis. Involvement of lymph nodes,
liver, spleen, lung, BM, eye (conjunctiva, sclera, orbit, third eyelid), and mucous membranes (gingiva,
nasal cavity) are variably present.14,16
Diagnosis requires histologic evaluation and consideration of immunophenotyping. Lesions are
identical to those described for cutaneous histiocytosis. Angiocentric infiltration with vascular invasion
may be more consistently seen with the systemic form of disease.14 Lymph node evaluation (ch. 88),
thoracic radiographs, and abdominal US may be helpful in determining extent of disease. These
collective features also are helpful in distinguishing systemic histiocytosis from malignant histiocytic
and non-histiocytic diseases.
As with cutaneous histiocytosis, the disease course can be punctuated by remissions and relapses.
Systemic medications with some efficacy include prednisone, cyclosporine, leflunomide, experimental
bovine thymosin fraction 5, and the chemotherapy drug doxorubicin.14,15 The clinical course can be
prolonged, although subsequent relapses often are associated with increased severity of signs and
diminishing response to treatment. A waxing and waning disease course and occasional spontaneous
remissions complicate assessing treatment efficacy. Nonetheless, repeatable responses to
immunomodulatory agents capable of inhibiting T-cell activation support the theory that reactive
histiocytosis is the result of disordered immune regulation arising from abnormal DC/T-cell interactions
and not a neoplastic process.

FELINE PROGRESSIVE HISTIOCYTOSIS
Histiocytic proliferative diseases, uncommon in cats, include feline progressive histiocytosis, a disease of
DC origin. Affected cats typically are older, with a median age of 10 years (range, 2-17 years).17 Afflicted
cats have solitary (16/26 cats in 1 study) or multiple (10/26) intradermal papules and nonpruritic
nodules or plaques in the skin (ch. 12), most commonly involving the extremities (73%).18 Similar to
reactive histiocytosis in dogs, lesion size waxes and wanes, although unlike canine histiocytosis,
complete spontaneous regression was not seen in 30 cats.17 Nodules progress in size over time; some
coalesce to form larger ulcerated and painful plaques. In most cats, lesions are confined to the skin for
extended periods. Occasionally, internal involvement is present at the time of diagnosis, as in 4 of 22
(18%) cats in 1 series.17 Lymph node evaluation, thoracic radiographs, and abdominal US may be helpful
in determining presence of internal sites of disease. The disease usually is progressive over months to
years (median 13.4 months) and in the advanced disease setting, spread to internal sites becomes more
common, as reported in 4 of 18 (22%) cats.17 Etiology is unknown, although lack of spontaneous
remissions and non-responsiveness to immunomodulatory drugs makes an etiology linked to immune
dysregulation unlikely. Instead it appears that feline progressive histiocytosis represents a neoplastic
process, initially indolent and ultimately more aggressive.
Diagnosis requires histologic examination and consideration of immunophenotyping. Microscopic
lesions consist of diffuse dermal histiocytic infiltrates, which may extend into the SQ tissue. Some
lesions manifest epitheliotropism. Cellular atypia and extension deep into the SQ tissue are more
notable in late-stage lesions.8,17 Histiocyte antigen expression patterns are consistent with DC origin.8,17
Given its diffuse nature, surgery is of limited benefit and is reserved for particularly bothersome lesions
causing morbidity. In 1 study, surgery was performed in 8 cats,17 but local tumor recurrence was seen in
4, and all 8 developed new lesions distant from the surgery site. In a study of 19 cats, 14 (74%) had
disease recurrence.18 Medical therapy, including corticosteroids, chemotherapy agents (L-asparaginase,
vincristine, vinblastine, cyclophosphamide, nitrogen mustard) and immune modulating agents

(corticosteroids, cyclosporine, leflunomide, interferon-gamma, retinoids) have met with disappointing
results.

MALIGNANT FIBROUS HISTIOCYTOMA (MFH)
MFH, a soft-tissue tumor originating from mesenchymal stem cells, can be included in the larger
category of soft-tissue sarcomas. Tumors most often arise in the skin as a single mass (historical reports
of splenic MFH have largely been reclassified as our understanding of histiocytic diseases has evolved).
In cats, MFH is a histologic variant of vaccine-associated sarcomas.19 Staging and treatment is as for
other types of soft tissue sarcomas (ch. 324).

HISTIOCYTIC SARCOMA (HS) COMPLEX
PREVALENCE, CLASSIFICATION, ETIOLOGY
Breed Prevalence
Malignant disease of histiocytic origin was first reported in dogs in the late 1970s,20 with 1 early report
describing HS in 11 Bernese Mountain Dogs; 9/11 were closely related, suggesting a genetic
predisposition.21 Flat-Coated Retrievers also exhibit a strong breed predisposition to HS. Histiocytic
malignancies are responsible for many deaths in these 2 breeds. Rottweilers, Golden Retrievers and
Labrador Retrievers also appear to be overrepresented.22,23 Pembroke Welsh Corgis (47% of cases) and
Shetland Sheepdogs are overrepresented for disease originating within the central nervous system
(CNS), but are not at-risk for HS in other body regions. Miniature Schnauzers may be overrepresented
in primary pulmonary HS.24-28 Affected dogs are typically middle-aged.

Classification
While classification continues to evolve, HS has become the term for this group of malignancies, with
two subcategories: localized HS and disseminated HS (formerly referred to as malignant histiocytosis).
Localized HS arises from a single organ. Disseminated HS is a multisystem disease. Both arise from DCs,
with characteristic positive staining for CD11c and CD18 antibodies. Hemophagocytic HS represents a
third subtype, unique in its macrophage origin, and characterized by positive CD11d and CD18 antibody
staining.
While microarray analyses have identified differences in gene expression comparing localized and
disseminated HS,29 they are morphologically and immunophenotypically identical. They are
distinguished by clinical presentation. Genetic sequencing may provide further insight. One study
reported recurrent PTPN11 mutations in both the visceral form of disseminated HS in dogs and in a
subset of human HS and may provide insight into identifying targeted therapies.30

LOCALIZED HISTIOCYTIC SARCOMA (HS)
Localized HS most commonly affects the skin and SQ tissue (ch. 12), usually involving the limbs and
periarticular tissues. Other reported sites include spleen, lung, brain, spinal cord, nasal cavity, bone, and
BM.22-25,31-34 Periarticular, splenic, CNS, and primary pulmonary forms have been described as unique
subsets of localized HS.24,25,31,34-36 Periarticular HS might be more common in Rottweilers.31
Lameness and/or periarticular soft tissue swellings are the most common signs, reported in 79% and
68% of dogs, respectively.34
The stifle joints are the most common location (37-61% of affected dogs).31,34 Interestingly, 55% of
dogs in 1 study had a history of cranial cruciate ligament (CCL) rupture in the joint that later developed
HS.31 A more recent study also reported association between prior joint disease and periarticular HS
(88% of dogs).37 Inflamed synovium following CCL rupture contains numerous DCs, although
relationship between inflammation and subsequent tumor development has not been well defined.38

Radiographs are indicated for dogs with suspected periarticular HS. Sixty percent of dogs in 1 study had
radiographic evidence of osteolysis or proliferation at the tumor site.34
HS of the CNS (ch. 245) can be localized, confined to a single site within the brain or spinal cord, or
multifocal, with signs reflecting location (ch. 241). Signs include seizures, altered mentation, behavioral
changes, postural reaction deficits, and paresis.24,25 Metastasis is present in 15-70% of dogs with
localized HS at the time of diagnosis. Fifty percent to 90% of affected dogs eventually develop metastatic
disease to lymph nodes, lung, and abdominal viscera.22,25,31,32,34,35 Signs of primary pulmonary HS
include cough, tachypnea, and dyspnea.35

DISSEMINATED HISTIOCYTIC SARCOMA (HS)
Disseminated HS involves multiple organ systems, suggesting either progression and metastasis from
the localized form of disease or a primary multicentric disease with tumors arising simultaneously in
multiple locations. Lungs, spleen, liver, lymph nodes, and/or BM are commonly affected.22 Diagnosis of
HS requires cytologic (ch. 85) or histopathologic evaluation and consideration of immunophenotyping.
After diagnosing HS, staging should include lymph node aspirates for cytologic evaluation or biopsy for
histologic analysis (ch. 88), thoracic radiographs, abdominal US, and possibly cytologic assessment of
BM aspirates (ch. 84).

TREATMENT OF HS
Limited reports document outcome after surgical excision; median survival time was 6 months in 5 dogs
with synovial HS treated with amputation alone.31 Chemotherapy should always be considered, either as
adjuvant therapy for localized HS or to treat metastatic or disseminated HS. CCNU appears to be the
most effective drug in dogs (60-90 mg/m2 PO q 21 days) with complete blood count monitoring and
hepatoprotectants, e.g., Denamarin (ch. 317). Response rates of 29-46% are reported when CCNU is
used for treating gross measurable disease, with a median response duration of 90 days (range, 29-805
days).35,39,40 The presence of metastatic disease is a negative prognostic factor.35,41 In 1 study,
thrombocytopenia (<100,000 platelets/mcL) and hypoalbuminemia negatively impacted outcome, with
survival <1 month when present. Importantly, these features suggest the hemophagocytic variant of
disease (see below).35 One study of Miniature Schnauzers had a higher response rate (5/6; 83%) to
CCNU, although median progression free survival remained short (117 days).26
An improved outcome can be achieved for localized HS when local therapy is combined with adjuvant
CCNU chemotherapy. In 1 series, 16 dogs with localized HS and no evidence of distant metastatic disease
were treated with intensive local therapy (surgery and/or radiation therapy) and CCNU
chemotherapy.42 Metastasis to regional lymph nodes was identified in 4 of 16 (25%) dogs at the time of
diagnosis; metastases were resected at the time of primary tumor removal. Median disease-free interval
was 8 months and overall median survival time was 18.6 months.42 In a more recent study, 49 dogs with
periarticular HS with both regional lymph node (70%) and distant (25%) metastasis were treated with
surgery (n=15) or radiation therapy (n=34) combined with adjuvant CCNU (n=31) or other (n=3)
chemotherapy/investigational agents. Overall median survival time did not differ between groups; 13
and 8 months for surgery and radiation therapy, respectively.41 A series of dogs with primary splenic HS
in which 12 of 14 dogs received adjuvant CCNU or CCNU/doxorubicin chemotherapy reported an overall
progression-free interval of 6.7 months and an overall median survival time of 14 months.36 A series of
dogs with primary pulmonary HS treated with surgery and adjuvant CCNU-based chemotherapy
reported an overall median survival time of 12.3 months.35
A more favorable outcome has been suggested for dogs with periarticular HS. One study reported a
median survival of 391 days (range, 48-980 days) for dogs treated with local therapy combined with
chemotherapy (47%), chemotherapy alone (42%), or local therapy alone (11%). This outcome was
achieved despite an overall metastatic rate of 68% at the time of diagnosis.34 Combination
chemotherapy may be superior to single-agent therapy, although ideal agents and combinations are not
defined. Based on limited information, doxorubicin, paclitaxel, vinorelbine, epirubicin, and dacarbazine

have shown some activity.34,43-47 A study reporting the use of alternating doxorubicin and CCNU
described an overall response rate of 58% and median time to progression of 185 days (range, 59-268) in
dogs with measurable gross disease.48
Another area of study has focused on the potential role of the bisphosphonate clodronate, which kills
osteoclasts and other macrophages via induction of apoptosis. When clodronate is incorporated within
liposomes, uptake by phagocytic cells is greatly enhanced, resulting in selective targeting of
macrophages. Susceptibility of HS cells to this approach has been demonstrated in vitro.49 A pilot study
of liposomal clodronate demonstrated regression of lesions in 2 of 5 dogs (40%) with HS.49 Combining
bisphosphonates with chemotherapy may prove beneficial. In vitro data suggest an increase in HS
cytotoxicity when selected bisphosphonates are combined with either vincristine or doxorubicin.50

HEMOPHAGOCYTIC HISTIOCYTIC SARCOMA
Pathogenesis and Signs
While DC origin is common among other histiocytic diseases, the neoplastic histiocytes in
hemophagocytic HS are of macrophage origin. Cells express a distinctive surface antigen profile
consistent with a splenic red pulp and/or BM origin. Hemophagocytic HS appears most common in
Bernese Mountain Dogs, Golden Retrievers, and Rottweilers.51 Its clinicopathologic features also are
unique; most striking is marked erythrophagocytosis by neoplastic histiocytes, resulting in a moderate to
marked regenerative hemolytic anemia (ch. 174). In 1 study, 94% of dogs had regenerative anemia
(median hct 22.6%, range 10.1-37%).51 Other findings included thrombocytopenia (88%),
hypoalbuminemia (94%), and hypocholesterolemia (69%).51 Splenomegaly with diffuse, ill-defined
nodular changes is consistently seen. Liver, BM, and lungs are often diffusely infiltrated and spread
occurs via insidious intravenous invasion with minimal mass formation.

Diagnosis
Diagnosis is made cytologically or histopathologically, with consideration of immunophenotyping. There
appears to be marked variation in the cytologic characteristics of neoplastic histiocytes, although
marked erythrophagocytosis accompanied by foci of extramedullary hematopoiesis are consistent
features.51 Not to be confused with immune-mediated hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia (chs.
174 and 175), dogs with hemophagocytic HS are Coombs-negative. Staging should include lymph node
evaluation (ch. 88), thoracic radiographs, abdominal US, and BM aspiration or biopsy (ch. 84).

Treatment and Prognosis
Hemophagocytic HS carries a poor prognosis; reports on effective treatments are lacking. In 1 study,
17/17 affected dogs died or were euthanized, with a median time (4 weeks, range 2-32 weeks) from onset
of clinical signs to death or euthanasia.51 Treatments used were not provided. Given reported activity
against other forms of HS, CCNU may be a reasonable consideration. In 1 study using CCNU, while the
diagnosis was not specifically identified as hemophagocytic HS, dogs with anemia, thrombocytopenia,
hypoalbuminemia, and splenic involvement were significantly less likely to respond. Further,
thrombocytopenia and hypoalbuminemia were associated with a significantly decreased median survival
of <28 days, compared with >163 days in the absence of these signs.34 Similarly, 10 Flat-Coated
Retrievers presumptively diagnosed with hemophagocytic HS and treated with CCNU had no
discernable benefit with overall median survival of 24 days (range, 4-67 days).52
HS rarely has been reported in cats. In 1 series of 3 cats, the disease closely resembled
hemophagocytic HS in dogs.53 Age at presentation was variable (1, 4, and 9 years). Anemia (packed cell
volume, 9-15%) and thrombocytopenia (31,000-94,000 platelets/mcL) were identified in all 3 cats. All
cats were euthanized shortly after the diagnosis. Postmortem evaluation identified malignant histiocytic
cells exhibiting erythrophagocytosis in the liver, spleen, and BM in each cat. Other sites of disease
included lymph node, lung, kidney, brain and urinary bladder.

PREVALENCE AND RISK FACTORS
Mammary gland tumors (MGTs) are the most common tumor in
intact female dogs and the second to third most common tumor

overall in cats.1-3 The incidence varies geographically, mostly due to
different attitudes about neutering. A common risk factor for both
species is advancing age. Dogs with malignant mammary gland
tumors (mMGTs) are older. mMGTs are rare in dogs <5 years of
age.4 In cats, the mean age at diagnosis is 10-12 years. One recent
study noted a trend in higher rates of mMGTs versus benign
mammary gland tumors (bMGTs) in dogs, similar to epidemiologic
trends in women.2
Exposure to ovarian hormones during the first 2 years of life is a
recognized risk factor for the development of MGTs, and
ovariohysterectomy (OHE) greatly decreases risk of MGT in both
species.5,6 Dogs spayed before their first estrus have a risk of 0.5%;
after the first estrus, the risk increases to 8%; and after a second
estrus, risk increases to 26%. After the third estrus cycle and/or
approximately 4 years of age, OHE provides only modest protection.
Some studies, however, show a decreased risk of developing new
tumors if OHE is performed at MGT removal. Additionally,
histologic progression with increasing tumor size has been reported
in dogs with multiple tumors, suggesting a continuous effect of
hormones throughout the dog’s lifespan.7 Studies suggest MGTs
progress not only from benign to malignant, but also from low to
highly malignant.8 Neutering before the first estrus in cats provides
91% risk reduction; before the second estrus, an 86% risk reduction;
and before the third estrus, an 11% risk reduction. After the age of 2
years, OHE provides no MGT protection.6 Exogenous hormone
exposure also increases risk of MGTs, more frequently benign than
malignant. Estrogen and progesterone receptors have been identified
in dog and cat MGTs; the less differentiated the canine tumor, the
fewer hormone receptors expressed. Male dogs and cats
uncommonly develop MGTs, usually benign in dogs (Figure 329.1)
but both bMGTs and mMGTs in cats.9-11 Small dog breeds may be
overrepresented. Breeds reported to be at risk include Siamese cats
and Poodles, English Cocker Spaniels, Brittany Spaniels, English
Setters, and German Shepherd Dogs. Breed predispositions tend to
vary by country.11,12 Obesity at a young age and high-fat diets have
been linked to an increased risk of MGTs in dogs, and tumors in

these dogs are associated with a higher grade and younger age of
onset.13

STAGING
Traditionally dogs with MGTs are staged according to the modified
World Health Organization (WHO) TNM system (T, size of tumor; N,
lymph node involvement; M, distant metastasis).11 This staging
system does not provide prognostic information regarding tumor
types or lympho-vascular invasion. Newer “bio-scoring” pathologic
staging systems have been proposed that more accurately predict
survival, although further studies are needed.14,15 Feline MGTs are
staged as are dog MGTs, using a modification of the original system.
In the modified system, stages increase from I (<2 cm in size), to II
(2-3 cm), to III (>3 cm).11 Use of newer histopathologic staging
systems have sought to refine prognosis assessment.16-18

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (PE) and
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES
Dogs and cats may have single or multiple nodules within the
mammary gland chain (ch. 3). Solitary tumors are more common in
cats; multiple tumors are more common in dogs (>50%).4,17 If more
than 1 MGT is recognized on PE, each mass could be different
(bMGT vs mMGT); therefore, histopathologic assessment of each
mass is recommended.19 bMGTs tend to be small, wellcircumscribed, and firm. The caudal mammary glands are the most
often involved in dogs and in cats,4,8,20 although some studies
describe MGTs in all glands of cats (Figure 329.2).11 MGTs may be
freely movable or adherent to the skin or abdominal wall (

Video

329.1). They may be ulcerated, inflamed, edematous, or have a
discharge from the nipple. Inflammatory mammary gland
carcinomas (IMGCs) are typically rapidly growing, painful, and can

occasionally cause edema of the extremities (Figure 329.3).
Differentials for MGTs include other skin neoplasms, mastitis,
lobular hyperplasia, and fibroepithelial hyperplasia in cats.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTING AND
TREATMENT
COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT (CBC), CHEMISTRY
PROFILE, URINALYSIS (UA), HISTOLOGIC
FEATURES
Evaluation of dogs and cats with a MGT should include a CBC, serum
biochemistry profile, and UA. These results are used to assess
general health, check for concurrent conditions, and to identify
paraneoplastic conditions (ch. 331). Histologic examination of the
mass(es) via excisional biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing
canine MGTs. Some studies have shown good correlation between
cytologic and histologic findings (ch. 85).11,21 Histologic evaluation
of tissue is needed to avoid underestimating malignant potential.1
Cytologic evaluation of aspirates is helpful in ruling out differentials,
detecting locoregional lymph node metastasis (Figure 329.4), and
when dermal extension is suspected (aggressive MGTs or IMGCs)
(Figure 329.5).

male dog.

FIGURE 329.2 Large inguinal mammary gland
tumor. Clinical presentation characteristics are
prognostic, including the growth pattern, fixation
and ulceration.

METASTATIC DISEASE RECOGNITION
Metastatic spread of mMGTs is usually via lymphatic vessels to
regional lymph nodes or hematogenously. The lungs are the most
frequent site of distant metastases.11 Thoracic radiographs must be
evaluated for metastases and/or lymph node histologic assessment is
required to definitively diagnose metastasis, which worsens the

prognosis. Detection of micrometastasis has not consistently been
associated with a worse outcome.22 Although sentinel lymph node
(SLN) mapping is standard in humans, it is rarely performed in dogs
or cats. A few studies have explored SLN mapping using various
tools, e.g., contrast-enhanced ultrasonography (US), computed
tomographic (CT) or radiographic indirect lymphography using
contrast agents/iodized oil and intraoperative dyes. Knowledge of
the lymphatic drainage of the neoplastic mammary glands, which
tends to vary and can even drain to contralateral nodes, is extremely
important. Decisions will need to be made during surgery in an
attempt to achieve complete MGT excision and for an accurate
postoperative prognosis. The size and shape of the lymph nodes are
less reliable criteria.11,23 Thoracic radiographs are important to
evaluate for metastatic disease or pleural effusion (common in cats).
Abdominal US can be used for staging by assessing locoregional
(superficial inguinal and axillary lymph nodes) or intra-abdominal
nodes for metastatic lymphadenopathy, especially when the MGT
involves caudal glands. US suspicion of metastasis should be
confirmed by cytological analysis via fine needle capillary sampling
(ch. 85). Mammary mass US has been reported but correlations
with histopathologic changes and the diagnosis of malignancy has
not been consistent.24

mix with an inflammatory mammary carcinoma.
These are generally rapidly growing and painful
tumors.

HISTOLOGIC FEATURES OF MAMMARY
GLAND TUMORS (MGTs)
Histologic Predictors of Biologic Behavior in
Dogs
The new classification of MGTs,25 replacing the Goldsmith 2011
system,26 is used worldwide for mMGTs.27 This system has given
pathologists a tool for accurate diagnosis and prognosis of canine
MGTs.28,29 In dogs, up to 60% of MGTs are benign,26 most often
fibroadenomas (benign mixed tumors). The most common
malignancies in dogs are solid carcinomas and then tubular
adenocarcinomas; only about 3-5% are sarcomas, and 1% are IMGCs.
Of the 50% mMGTs, 50% recur, metastasize, or develop after the
first surgical resection.2,30 Mortality related to canine invasive

mammary carcinoma is relatively high: over 40% of dogs and cats
with invasive MC die within a year of diagnosis.31 Ductal carcinomas,
carcinomas arising in mixed tumors, and complex carcinomas had
lower risks of lymphovascular invasion. In contrast, carcinosarcoma
(

Video 329.1), invasive micropapillary carcinoma, anaplastic

carcinoma, comedocarcinoma, solid carcinoma, adenosquamous
carcinoma, and lipid-rich carcinoma behave aggressively.11,12 Poorly
differentiated tumors, sarcomas, and inflammatory carcinomas also
have a worse prognosis. Despite the relevance of molecular
subtyping in human breast cancer, it is not commonly performed in
dogs or cats. Triple-negative tumors account for approximately half
of canine invasive MC (58.6%)31 and show a significantly shorter
disease-free interval (DFI) and overall survival (OS) in comparison
to luminal A tumors.32 Other factors associated with shorter survival
in dogs with MGTs include histologic grade, stage, tumor size greater
than 3 cm, lymph node involvement, histologic evidence of lymphatic
or vascular invasion, OHE status, lymphocytic infiltrate intensity,
expression of hormone receptors (estrogen receptors and
progesterone receptors), cyclooxygenase-2 expression, microvessel
density, proliferation markers, clinical behavior (growth pattern,
fixation, ulceration) and distant metastases.11,12,27-29,33,34

FIGURE 329.4 Cytologic image from an inguinal
lymph node in a dog with grade III metastatic
mammary gland tumor. A population of malignant
epithelial cells arranged in cohesive clusters and,
rarely, individualized, is present. These cells have
well-defined cell borders and scant clear blue
cytoplasm. Nuclei are round to oval with prominent
nucleoli. Nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio is high and
anisocytosis and anisokaryosis are mild to moderate.
In the background, moderate numbers of lysed cells
and remnant lymphoid tissue derived from small
lymphocytes and plasma cells can be seen.

Histologic Predictors of Biologic Behavior in Cats
Most (80-90%) feline MGTs are malignant, most often
adenocarcinomas.16-18 IMGCs have been reported in cats; they are
biologically aggressive with high rates of metastasis, but survival
times vary significantly. Tumor size, disease stage, histologic
grading,16-18 and the extent of surgical intervention have been shown
to influence prognosis. Tumors larger than 3 cm have been
associated with shorter survival times (4-12 months).35,36 Classical
histological grading by the Elston and Ellis system and new revised
grading systems have shown significant correlation with OS.16-18 The
type of surgery performed (see below) and histological completeness
of resection have been shown to be prognostic for both the DFI and
OS.37

SURGICAL TREATMENT
Most MGTs in Dogs
Surgical removal is the gold-standard treatment for MGTs in dogs
and cats. The goal of surgery is to remove the entire tumor by the
simplest procedure, e.g., a “lumpectomy” is acceptable for small (<1
cm) superficial mammary nodules since they are most likely benign.
MGTs 1-2 cm in diameter may be best managed with locoregional
mastectomy. If masses are present in multiple glands, they may be
resected individually or in a chain mastectomy. The surgery chosen
should be the easiest for removing all affected tissue and the draining
lymph node when possible. The lymphatic drainage of affected
glands should be considered when trying to include the draining
lymph node. This is especially true in those MGTs with poor
prognostic factors, for which surgery should include not only the
draining lymph node in order to stage the disease, but also the
underlying muscular fascia “en bloc.”

FIGURE 329.5 Dermal extension of an
incompletely excised grade III mammary
adenocarcinoma (A). Cytological analysis of
cutaneous lesions revealed pleomorphic glandular
epithelial cell clusters with several criteria of
malignancy (anisokaryosis, anisocytosis,
macrokaryosis, and, macronucleoli) (B).

Avoid Surgery in Dogs With IMGC
Surgery is not a good option for dogs with IMGC because of their
high rate of early regional and distant metastases and their high rate
of locoregional recurrence with surgery. Recurrence may be obvious
within days of surgery. Therefore, IMGC should be considered a
systemic disease, even if metastases are not identified.38

Ovariohysterectomy (OHE), Prophylactic
Mastectomy, Incomplete Excision
OHE does not increase morbidity or mortality and should be
recommended to prevent future ovarian or uterine disease and to
reduce risk (50%) of further MGT development.5,7,11,34,39
Prophylactic mastectomies of normal mammary glands, especially
when the tumor is located in the caudal mammary glands, could be
considered to prevent new MGTs. About 60% of dogs undergoing
removal of single mammary tumor are likely to develop new tumors
ipsilaterally, although benefit in terms of OS has not been proven.30
Bilateral MGT surgery does increase morbidity.34 Additional surgery
should be pursued if the tumor is incompletely excised.40

Surgery in Cats
In cats, lymphatic connections between individual glands and
potential connections between the left and right sides can exist due
to unusual lymphatic connections when a MGT is present. Therefore,
complete unilateral or bilateral mastectomies, including the
underlying fascia “en bloc,” are recommended (Figure 329.6). In a

large multi-institutional study, the outcome of cats having unilateral
or bilateral surgery for mammary carcinoma suggested that bilateral
mastectomy was an independent prognostic factor for survival
(median survival times of 1140 days versus 473 days for cats
undergoing unilateral mastectomy). Morbidity is usually higher in
cats with single-session bilateral mastectomy than for staged
bilateral mastectomies20,37 and usually a period of 2 or more weeks
should exist between surgeries. The SLN should be identified and
removed at the time of mastectomy when possible.

FIGURE 329.6 Regional mastectomy performed
after tumor reoccurrence with removal of abdominal
fascia “en bloc.” Oncologic surgery including
underlying fascia is recommended for canine tumors
presenting with negative clinical prognostic factors
and all feline mammary tumor patients. Courtesy

MEDICAL TREATMENT
Pharmaceuticals
In dogs with mMGTs considered at risk for metastasis or recurrence
—e.g., those with poor prognostic factors, locally advanced or
metastatic disease, or a biologically aggressive histologic type—the
use of chemotherapy may be beneficial. Unfortunately, little
information is available on the role of chemotherapy in the adjuvant
setting, with only small case series using doxorubicin, mitoxantrone
or carboplatin. These studies do not meet the highest scientific
evidence-based standards in order to show a clear benefit. Newer
formulations of paclitaxel have shown efficacy in the macroscopic
setting while being associated with fewer allergic reactions than
previously reported.11,12,41
Due to the increased expression of COX-2 in mMGTs as compared
with bMGTs or normal mammary tissues and its association with a
worse prognosis,11,12 COX-2 inhibitors have been included as single
agents or in combination protocols in the treatment of canine MGTs,
mainly in cases of IMGC as part of a multi-therapy treatment,
improving quality of life and increasing survival rate over
chemotherapy alone.33,38 Of the other 3 studies in non-IMGC MGTs,
1 included only 5 cases in which a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory
drug was combined with carboplatin, another included 7 cases in
which firocoxib was used as an adjuvant treatment following surgery,
and 1 included 9 cases in which a COX-2 inhibitor was used in a
metronomic chemotherapy protocol (combined with
cyclophosphamide) following conventional chemotherapy and

surgery.11,42,43 Further studies are needed before the use of COX-2
inhibitors can be routinely recommended as an adjuvant therapy.
Thalidomide, a drug with antiangiogenic and immunomodulatory
activity, although its exact mechanism of action as an antineoplastic
agent remains unknown, has been shown to be well tolerated in dogs
with advanced clinical-stage MGTs and IMGC. Additional studies are
warranted to investigate the therapeutic benefit of thalidomide in
canine MGTs and other neoplasms. Despite the guarded prognosis in
cases of IMGC, which ranges from 1 to 2 months, medical treatment
with chemotherapy or in combination with newer targeted therapies
or radiation therapy may improve the outcome of these patients.38,44

Radiotherapy With Medications
Although radiotherapy is commonly used in human breast cancer as
a locoregional treatment, only 1 study has been published on dogs
with IMGC. Patients treated with radiotherapy in combination with
piroxicam, toceranib (Palladia, Zoetis), and thalidomide showed
significantly longer time to progression than those patients treated
with the same regimen, but without radiotherapy.44

Desmopressin, Progesterone Antagonists
Other non-conventional treatments have also been tried, such as
perioperative administration of desmopressin, a synthetic analogue
of vasopressin that has shown mixed results, with older studies
finding improved DFI and MSTs in dogs, but a newer prospective
randomized trial in dogs with MGTs and a large study in cats have
failed to prove a metastasis-preventing effect.11,20,45 Specific drugs
targeting progesterone receptors have also been tried, with apparent
improvements in DFI in a specific subset of dogs receiving a
progesterone receptor antagonist (aglepristone).46

Adjuvant Chemotherapy for Cats
Based on the aggressive behavior and metastatic rate in cats,
adjuvant chemotherapy is often recommended, although its role in
prolonging survival is still unclear. Several adjunctive regimes have

been published retrospectively, including few cases using carboplatin
and mitoxantrone, among other drugs; however, doxorubicin is the
most commonly reported chemotherapy agent in cats,11,47,48 most
likely because of the reported moderate response rates in the
macroscopic setting (40-50%).11 Results with doxorubicin are mixed
but the latest studies suggest a potential benefit in terms of survival.
Cats with advanced metastatic disease typically have poor response
to treatment; however, adjuvant treatment with toceranib (Palladia,
Zoetis; ch. 320) or metronomic cyclophosphamide and meloxicam
helped some survive longer than 6 months.49

Need for Clinical Studies
Considering how common the disease is, little information is
available regarding the efficacy of chemotherapy for canine or feline
MGTs. Moreover, most of the treatments are still considered
experimental, especially those in the adjuvant setting after surgery.
There is a great need for well-planned large prospective randomized
clinical trials in dogs and cats with mammary cancer to obtain valid
results in order to allow widespread use of some of these treatments,
as well as to develop newer targeted therapies that could improve
treatment and prognosis of this disease.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Mammary Gland Tumors in Dogs
WHAT ARE MAMMARY GLAND TUMORS?
These are tumors originating from cells of the mammary glands
(breast tissue). They are one of the most common tumors in dogs

that are not spayed or were not spayed until later in life. The average
age of dogs at diagnosis is around 10 years. The risk for developing
mammary gland tumors is closely associated with exposure to female
sex hormones. Therefore, early spaying (i.e., spaying before the first
heat cycle) reduces the probability of developing this type of tumor to
almost nothing. Spaying before the third heat cycle will also reduce
the risk; however, spaying after that is not associated with any
reduction in the risk. Treatment with megestrol acetate (“the pill”) is
also strongly linked to the development of mammary tumors in dogs.

HOW DOES MAMMARY CANCER PRESENT?
Most dogs will present for a firm mass or swelling in the area of one
or more mammary glands. Dogs have a linear mammary system,
usually with 5 nipples (glands) on each side (10 nipples in all),
running from the groin area to the chest. Masses can occur at any
point, although the last 2 sets of glands (the fourth and fifth) are the
most commonly affected. Patients often present with several masses
at diagnosis and may have both benign and malignant tumors
concurrently. The tumors can be different sizes and may grow slowly
or quite fast. Rarely, mammary tumors can bleed or become infected.
The longer they stay, the higher the probabilities of transforming
from benign to malignant or from less aggressive malignant tumors
to more aggressive malignant tumors.

WHAT TESTS ARE NEEDED FOR THE DIAGNOSIS?
The diagnosis of a mammary gland tumor relies on clinical judgment
and evaluation of a biopsy. A reasonable rule of thumb regarding
mammary gland tumors is that about 50% of these tumors are
benign and 50% are malignant. Further, 50% of the malignant
tumors in dogs can be cured with just surgery, while 50% will likely
spread to other parts of the body. The smaller the tumor is at the
time of diagnosis, the better the prognosis.
In order to determine whether the cancer has spread, your
veterinarian will recommend further tests at the time of diagnosis.
This will help define your pet’s prognosis and treatment: chest xrays, abdominal ultrasounds, fine-needle cytology
sampling or biopsy of lymph nodes that drain the site of the

tumor, and blood work to evaluate your pet’s overall health
might be included in the initial evaluation.

WHAT TREATMENT IS NEEDED?
All dogs with benign mammary tumors can be cured with surgery.
As noted, 50% of dogs with malignant mammary gland tumors can
also be cured with surgical removal of the mass. There are several
types of surgeries for removing the tumor(s):
• Lumpectomy: removal of a small localized lesion.
• Unilateral mastectomy: removal of the mammary tissue on one
entire side (mammary chain).
• Bilateral mastectomy: removal of the mammary tissue on both
sides. This procedure is usually performed in 2 stages,
allowing the animal to recover from the surgery on the first
side before proceeding to the surgery on the second.
If the dog is not spayed, an ovariohysterectomy (OHE) should be
recommended at the time of mastectomy to prevent future ovarian or
uterine diseases, as well as to attempt to reduce the risk of further
mammary tumor development. For the 50% of dogs with malignant
tumors that cannot be cured with surgery, in which there is a greater
risk of the cancer spreading, chemotherapy or newer targeted
therapies may also be offered.
The following factors will help your veterinarian decide whether
your dog should be treated with chemotherapy rather than surgery
alone:
• The size of the tumor at the time of diagnosis
• Whether or not the tumor site is ulcerated, fixed to underlying
tissue or growing fast.
• The existence of evidence that the tumor has spread to the
lymph nodes, lungs, or other sites of the body
• Characteristics of the tumor on microscopic examination
(histologic grade, proliferation markers)
Doxorubicin, carboplatin, mitoxantrone, cyclophosphamide and
paclitaxel are some of the drugs that are commonly used to treat
dogs with malignant mammary gland tumors. Certain newer

targeted therapies have also shown promising results in preliminary
studies.

WHAT CAN I DO TO PREVENT THESE TUMORS?
Dogs should be spayed before their first or second heat in order to
significantly reduce the risk. If a dog develops a mammary tumor
and undergoes surgical excision, it is important for owners to
schedule regular follow-up appointments with their veterinarian,
typically every 3 months for the first year after surgery, so that
physical exams and chest x-rays can be performed. Owners should
also actively monitor the remaining mammary glands for the
appearance of any new masses, because even if a mammary tumor is
completely removed with surgery, your dog can develop another one
in the future.
Juan Borrego (Valencia, Spain)

CLIENT INFORMATION
Mammary Gland Tumors in Cats
WHAT ARE MAMMARY GLAND TUMORS?
These are tumors originating from cells of the mammary glands
(breast tissue). They are one of the most common tumors in cats that
are not spayed or were not spayed until later in life. The average age
of cats presenting with mammary tumors is 10-12 years. Siamese cats
appear to have a higher risk of developing this type of tumor. The
risk for developing mammary gland tumors is closely associated with
exposure to female sex hormones. Therefore, spaying early (i.e.,
before the second heat cycle) dramatically decreases the risk of
developing these tumors. Treatment with synthetic hormones (“the
pill”) is also strongly linked to the development of mammary tumors
in cats and should thus be avoided. More than 90% of these tumors
in cats are highly malignant and readily spread (“metastasize”) to
other parts of the body.

HOW DOES MAMMARY CANCER PRESENT?

Most cats will present for a firm mass in the mammary chain, usually
under the skin. Cats have a linear mammary system, usually with 4
nipples (glands) on each side (8 nipples in all). Masses can occur at
any point on or in between the glands, and patients often present
with several masses at diagnosis. Ulceration and bleeding can also
occur.

WHAT TESTS ARE NEEDED FOR THE DIAGNOSIS?
The diagnosis of a mammary gland tumor primarily relies on the
evaluation of a biopsy, and the vast majority of tumors are
malignant. The smaller the tumor is at the time of diagnosis, the
better the prognosis.
Because of the high rate of metastasis, chest x-rays, abdominal
ultrasounds, fine-needle cytology sampling or biopsy of lymph nodes
that drain the site of the tumor, and blood work to evaluate your
pet’s overall health might be included in the initial evaluation to
determine whether the cancer has spread. This will help define your
pet’s prognosis and treatment.

WHAT TREATMENT IS NEEDED?
Surgery, typically involving the entire affected chain or both chains
(“bilateral total mastectomy”), is the recommended treatment. It is
usually performed in 2 stages, allowing the animal to recover from
the surgery on the first side before proceeding to the surgery on the
second side but could also be planned in one single procedure
depending on each case. The more extensive the surgery is, the lower
the chances of local recurrence and better prognosis. Because of the
high metastatic rate, chemotherapy and/or targeted therapies are
usually recommended following surgery.
Survival times can vary significantly; however, the size of the
tumor, presence of metastasis, histologic grading (i.e., how
aggressive the tumor looks under the microscope), and extent of
surgery have all been shown to influence the prognosis.
Doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide are 2 of the most commonly
used drugs to show some efficacy in the treatment of malignant
mammary gland tumors. Certain newer targeted therapies have also
shown promising results in preliminary studies.

WHAT CAN I DO TO PREVENT THESE TUMORS?
Cats should be spayed before their first or second heat in order to
significantly reduce the risk. If a cat develops a mammary tumor and
undergoes surgical excision, it is important for owners to schedule
regular follow-up appointments with their veterinarian, typically
every 3 months for the first year after surgery, so that physical exams
and chest x-rays can be performed. Owners should also actively
monitor the remaining mammary glands for the appearance of any
new masses, as even if a mammary tumor is completely removed
with surgery, your cat can develop another one in the future.
Juan Borrego (Valencia, Spain)

KIDNEY
PREVALENCE AND RISK FACTORS
Primary renal neoplasia is estimated to account for 0.3-1.5% of all
canine neoplasms.1 Epithelial tumors, e.g., renal cell carcinomas
(RCC), are the most common primary tumor of the canine kidney
and must be differentiated from other primary epithelial neoplasms,
e.g., adenoma, oncocytoma, nephroblastoma, transitional cell
carcinoma (TCC), lymphoma (ch. 322), and sarcoma (ch. 324).1,2
The average age of dogs with renal tumors is around 9 years, and a
male predisposition has been reported in some studies,2,3 but an
equal male/female ratio in another.4 An unusual syndrome in female
German Shepherd Dogs is similar to Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome in
people: concurrent cystadenocarcinomas, nodular dermatofibrosis,
and uterine tumors.5
The most common kidney tumor in cats is lymphoma. Most
affected cats in the post-feline leukemia (ch. 199) era are not
infected with the virus. The median age at diagnosis is 9 years with
no breed or sex predilection.6-8 Other kidney-associated tumors
include tubular RCC, tubulopapillary RCC, sarcomatoid RCC,
adenoma, adenocarcinoma, TCC, hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325),
nephroblastoma, squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), leiomyosarcoma,
oncocytoma, and paraganglioma.1,2,8

SIGNS AND DIAGNOSIS

Dogs and cats commonly have nonspecific signs, e.g., inappetence,
weight loss, lethargy, vomiting, and/or hematuria. Physical
examination (PE, ch. 3) may reveal unilateral or bilateral kidney
enlargement, which may be painful. Renal cystadenocarcinoma may
be associated with firm, nodular dermal lesions (ch. 12) and benign
uterine growths in German Shepherd Dogs. Although histologic
examination is required for diagnosis, ultrasound (US)-guided fine
needle aspiration (FNA) with cytologic evaluation is often diagnostic
with lymphoma (ch. 85). The sensitivity and specificity of cytologic
evaluation for the detection of other renal neoplastic lesions are 78%
and 50%, respectively (ch. 85).2,6,9 Tumor tissue can be obtained by
US-guided percutaneous biopsy or at surgery. Ancillary tests such as
a complete blood count (CBC), serum chemistry profile, and
urinalysis (UA) may identify anemia or erythrocytosis secondary to
decreased or increased erythropoietin production (chs. 57, 173),
nonspecific serum biochemical changes (azotemia,
hypoalbuminemia), or rare paraneoplastic syndromes associated
with renal tumors, e.g., neutrophilic leukocytosis (chs. 59, 331).8
Clinical staging should include thoracic and abdominal imaging.
Pulmonary metastases have been reported in as many as half of dogs
with primary kidney tumors, although lower rates of pulmonary
metastasis at diagnosis have been reported in dogs with RCC (1118%).2,3 Abdominal US is integral to staging by assessing regional
lymph nodes, intra-abdominal structures, and can guide FNA of
suspicious areas.10 The combination of renomegaly, hypoechoic focal
lesions, and bilateral involvement are common US observations in
dogs with lymphoma.10 Bilateral involvement is rare with
carcinomas.2,8,10 Imaging cats with renal lymphoma often reveals
bilateral (>80%) irregular renomegaly with hypoechoic subcapsular
thickening (Figure 330.1),11 as well as the involvement of other
organs.7 Computed tomography (CT) scans might be more sensitive
in detecting metastases and useful in surgical planning in dogs with
RCC and caval invasion.4,12 Pre-surgical planning should include
evaluating function of the “healthy” kidney, e.g., excretory
urography, CT, determining glomerular filtration rate via
scintigraphy.

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Nephrectomy is the most effective treatment for dogs with unilateral
tumors, with median survival times (MSTs) of 16 to 24 months for
carcinomas, 9 months for hemangiosarcomas, and 6 months for
nephroblastomas.2,4,13 A mitotic index >30 and increased
cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) expression seem to be associated with a
worse outcome in RCC following surgery.4,8 The role of adjunctive
therapy for dogs with kidney tumors remains unclear, with some
studies suggesting no benefit.4 Treatment with chemotherapy is
indicated for cats or dogs with renal lymphoma (ch. 322). In
addition to being bilateral in most, the disease is typically systemic
and on rare occasions primary.7,10,14 Extension to the central
nervous system (CNS) has been reported in both cats and dogs with
rates as high as 40-50% (ch. 245).7,14 With treatment—typically
multidrug protocols with the addition, in older studies, of drugs that
reach the CNS (e.g., cytosine arabinoside)—the average survival time
in cats is 3 to 7 months with a minority of long term responders (>1
year).6,7,13 The prognosis for dogs with renal lymphoma receiving
treatment is poor, with short-lived responses to chemotherapy
usually under a month.14 Surgery is the treatment of choice for cats
with other renal tumors. Renal cystadenocarcinomas in German
Shepherd Dogs, although malignant and metastatic, progress slowly
and survival times may be longer.
