URINARY BLADDER AND URETHRA
PREVALENCE AND RISK FACTORS
Tumors of the urinary bladder are rare in cats and uncommon in
dogs. In dogs they account for only 1.5-2% of cancer diagnoses.15
Most bladder and urethral tumors are epithelial and malignant.
Intermediate to high-grade invasive urothelial carcinoma (iUC/TCC)
is by far the most common diagnosis in both species.1,15 Other

differentials include SCC, adenocarcinoma, rhabdomyosarcoma,
lymphoma, and other mesenchymal tumors.8 A trigonal location
with urethral and prostatic involvement is common, often leading to
urinary tract obstruction (Figure 330.2).8,15,16 Metastatic disease
is detected in 10-20% of dogs when first diagnosed and in up to 58%
at necropsy.8,15,16 Common metastatic sites of canine TCC include
lymph nodes, lung, bone, and skin.1,15,17 Feline TCC is uncommon,
occurs in geriatric cats, usually does not involve the bladder trigone
(27%), and metastatic disease is rare (20%).8,18,19
Several risk factors for TCC in dogs include age (9-11 years) and
sex, with a female-to-male ratio reported to range from 1.71:1 to
1.95:1.15 Small breeds, e.g., Scottish Terriers, are 21 times more likely
to develop TCC. Other breeds, e.g., West Highland White Terriers,
Shetland Sheepdogs, and Beagles, are 3-5 times more likely to
develop TCC than mixed-breed dogs.8,20 Other possible
predisposing factors in dogs include obesity, neutering status (with
the incidence being ∼2 times higher in spayed or neutered dogs), and
prior cyclophosphamide therapy.8 Exposure to older-generation flea
control products and lawn chemicals have been associated with TCC,
while newer spot-on flea control products, such as fipronil, appear
safer.8,15,20 Vegetable consumption has been reported to reduce the
risk of TCC in Scottish Terriers, which have a strong breedassociated risk for the disease.21

FIGURE 330.2 Transitional cell carcinoma in the
urinary bladder as visualized with abdominal
ultrasonography. Sagittal image of the bladder with a
lobulated mass in the trigone as delineated by the 4
“+” signs.

SIGNS AND DIAGNOSIS
Common clinical signs caused by neoplasia within the urethra or
bladder include stranguria, pollakiuria, hematuria, dysuria, and/or
urinary incontinence, signs that mimic bacterial cystitis and
urolithiasis (chs. 54, 55). Antibiotic treatment may transiently
resolve clinical signs since as many as 25% of dogs have a urinary
tract infection (UTI, ch. 307).22 If clinical signs do not completely
resolve with antibiotic treatment or if they reoccur, the presence of
stones or cancer should be investigated, especially in predisposed
breeds (Figure 330.3). In advanced cases, a mass might be
palpable in the caudal abdomen; abnormalities such as a thickened

urethra or enlarged sublumbar or intrapelvic lymph nodes may be
identified on rectal examination. Less commonly, dogs are lame due
to the pain associated with metastases to bone. Rare skin metastasis
can cause erythematous, ulcerated, or proliferative lesions.
A CBC, serum chemistry profile, and UA allow review of overall
health and may reveal paraneoplastic conditions. Due to the high
rate of infection, urine culture and sensitivity testing should be
performed and periodically rechecked during treatment.22 Thoracic
radiographs are used to screen for lung metastasis. Urinary tract
imaging, including abdominal US,8,23 is needed to locate and define
the cancer and monitor response to treatment. CT scanning may be
used to detect intrapelvic urethral TCC or lymph node and/or bone
metastasis.24 Ideally, when monitoring treatment response, the
same bladder volume, positioning and operator should be used,
especially with US.25 Tumor measurements with CT are reliable and
do not overestimate the size of irregularly shaped tumors.23,26 The
presence of abnormal epithelial cells in the urine sediment in a pet
with a mass or thickened bladder is suggestive of TCC; however,
other inflammatory conditions may also cause “reactive” epithelial
cells to be present (Figure 330.4).27 Histologic examination via
traumatic catheterization (

Video 330.1), surgical, or cystoscopic

biopsy usually provides a definitive diagnosis. US-guided cytology
sampling or biopsy is not recommended, as seeding of the biopsy
tract with viable tumor cells is a possible complication.28,29
Cystoscopic biopsy is an effective method to obtain biopsy samples in
dogs with TCC of the bladder/urethra and is more likely to produce
diagnostic samples in about 96% of females and 65% of males.30
Newer diagnostic tools include liquid biopsies, which enable the
detection of a BRAF V595E mutation found in more than 80% of
dogs with TCC but not in normal dogs or those with cystitis. The
sensitivity of these assays is >85% with a specificity of 100% when
used on free-catch urine from dogs with urothelial or prostatic
carcinoma (PC). The BRAF mutation test is a new tool for diagnosis,
screening high-risk breeds, monitoring disease progression or
treatment response, and identifying metastasis.31-33

TREATMENT
Most dogs with TCC are managed with drug therapy or, less
commonly, radiation or surgery. Surgery should be considered for
tumors located cranially in the bladder. Because the trigone region is
usually involved, complete resection with acceptable postoperative
bladder function is rarely feasible. Partial cystectomy can be
combined with COX inhibitors, with or without chemotherapy.
Survival times compare favorably to medical therapy alone; however,
there are no prospective studies comparing treatment modalities for
cranially located tumors.34,35 TCC, likely due to its highly exfoliative
nature, has been reported in the abdominal wall. Tumor cells were
likely implanted during surgery to obtain specimens, tumor removal,
tumor debulking, cystotomy tube placement, or FNA sampling.29
TCC located in the abdominal wall carries a worse prognosis, so
caution is warranted to avoid seeding the tumor into the abdomen or
along the surgery site during those procedures, especially surgery29
(Figure 330.5). Instruments and gloves that have contacted a
tumor should be replaced. More complex surgical approaches in dogs
with iUC have included total cystectomy36,37 and removal of the
bladder neck and trigone.38 For neoplasia confined to the urethra,
vaginourethroplasty and transurethral resection have been
described.39 Urinary diversion surgical strategies carry risk of high
morbidity, limiting the success of these approaches.8

FIGURE 330.5 Abdominal wall transitional cell
carcinoma tumor seeding (arrow) after a subtotal
cystectomy to remove the primary bladder tumor.
Transitional cell carcinomas located in the
abdominal wall carry a worse prognosis than those in
the urinary tract.
Chemotherapy, COX inhibitors, and combinations are the
mainstay for treating iUC in dogs. The goal of the treatment is to
reduce clinical signs and improve quality of life (QoL). Although
around 20% remission rates are obtained with single-agent therapy
(nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug [NSAID] or chemotherapy),
and rates of 35-50% when combined with a COX inhibitor, stable
disease (SD) is the most common result.8,16 Chemotherapy drugs
most commonly used, as sole agent or combined with an NSAID,
include vinblastine, carboplatin, mitoxantrone, doxorubicin, and
gemcitabine. Cisplatin is rarely used due to its high toxicity.8,16
MSTs in dogs with TCC treated with a single drug is about 130-220
days. Combination drug protocols achieve an overall 75% tumor
control rate and have resulted in MSTs of a year or more.8

Current single-agent recommendations include non-selective COX
inhibitors (piroxicam 0.3 mg/kg/24h) or a more selective COX
inhibitor (deracoxib or firocoxib).8,16,40 These drugs cause
gastrointestinal (GI) side effects in ∼30% of dogs. Since a cure is rare,
response to therapy should be evaluated (signs, imaging, QoL) every
4 to 8 weeks. Signs of UTI should prompt a UA and culture. If culture
negative or if antibiotics provide no benefit, the protocol should be
changed.8,16 Rescue protocols should include previously described
effective drugs used as single agents or metronomic administration
of chlorambucil (4 mg/m2/24h). Newer approaches include use of
targeted therapies, e.g., toceranib phosphate (Palladia, Zoetis), alone
or in combination. While not improving the progression-free interval
(PFI) or MST, it has achieved 80% SD and 6% partial response (PR)
rates. In combination with vinblastine and a COX inhibitor,
responses were not better than for other vinblastine protocols.41,42
Because TCC in cats is often in the cranial bladder, surgery is an
option. A retrospective study of 118 cats with lower urinary tract TCC
assessed partial cystectomy, NSAIDs, chemotherapy, radiation
therapy (RT), and urethral/ureteral stent placement. The MST for all
cats was 155 days. The MST for untreated cats, cats treated without
cystectomy, and cats treated with cystectomy were 46 days, 176 days,
and 294 days, respectively. Surgical excision (cystectomy) and
NSAIDs were associated with longer survival. COX inhibitors
(piroxicam and meloxicam) used alone or in combination may
provide palliation of TCC, with reported survival times of 261 to 311
days.8,18
Newer state-of-the-art RTs enable administration of a highly
conformal dose to a select target. This form of RT combined with
medical therapy has lower risk of damage to surrounding tissues.4345
Low-dose palliative RT combined with chemotherapy has also
been used with an overall response rate of 61% in dogs.46 This
technique is non-invasive, urinary continence is retained, and local
control can be achieved. The disadvantages are related to the cost
and availability of such radiation facilities.

PALLIATIVE PROCEDURES AND
PROGNOSIS
Most dogs with TCC die from urinary tract obstruction complications
before developing substantial metastatic disease. Prepubic
cystostomy catheters or low-profile cystostomy tubes have been used
as simple better-tolerated procedures to bypass urinary obstructions
while other therapies are instituted or as palliative procedures.
Complications are frequent but usually easily managed, e.g., urine
leakage, inadvertent tube removal, tube damage (due to chewing by
the dog), and infection.47
Minimally invasive treatment options such as palliative
urethral/ureteral stenting using interventional radiology and
interventional endoscopy for urologic disease have become more
common (ch. 117).48,49 While urinary incontinence affects 26-39%
of dogs, urethral stents are well tolerated and solve urinary tract
obstructions in 97% of all cases.45,46 While resolving urinary tract
obstructions, stenting remains palliative with short MSTs if it is not
combined with other therapies.49 Another palliative option is USguided endoscopic laser and carbon dioxide laser ablation. Welllocalized tumors are the best candidates for this procedure, which
debulks and removes obstructive and potentially obstructive TCC
lesions. Risks of this procedure are bladder perforation and, in some
cases, transient worsening of clinical signs.8,50

PROSTATE (CH. 314)
PREVALENCE, RISK FACTORS, AND SIGNS
Prostatic tumors have a prevalence of <1% in dogs. Median age at
diagnosis is 10 years. Neutered dogs and certain breeds (Shetland
Sheepdogs, Scottish Terriers, et al.) have increased risk.16,51,52 A
higher prevalence of PC is seen in castrated dogs, but both castrated
and intact develop PCs at about the same age, suggesting that
castration is not a cancer initiator but it favors tumor progression.53
Most prostate tumors are TCCs or adenocarcinomas that arise from

glandular epithelium, prostatic ducts, or prostatic urethra.. TCC of
the prostatic urethra commonly invades the prostate and may be
difficult to distinguish primary PC from secondary invasion of a
urethral tumor. Several histologic subtypes have been reported with
no impact on overall prognosis.55,56 Fibrosarcoma (ch. 326),
leiomyosarcoma (ch. 324), osteosarcoma (ch. 326), lymphoma
(ch. 322), and hemangiosarcoma (ch. 325) have also been
described.57 Other more common conditions causing prostatomegaly
include chronic prostatitis, prostatic abscessation, benign prostatic
hyperplasia (BPH), and prostatic cysts.54 Due to rapid growth and
high risk for metastasis (up to 80% in necropsy studies),16,58 dogs
seen late in the course of the disease have signs consistent with
metastatic disease (weight loss, rear limb lameness, pain,
neurological signs) rather than signs of urogenital disease
(stranguria, hematuria, pollakiuria). Skeletal metastases, affecting as
many as 40% of dogs, may cause signs of pain, gait abnormalities, or
lameness. Other clinical signs include those related to local
obstruction (dyschezia, tenesmus, constipation, altered stool shape)
due to an enlarged prostate or locoregional sublumbar lymph
nodes.16

DIAGNOSIS
Cancerous prostates, on rectal examination, usually feel asymmetric,
fixed, and firm (ch. 3). Digital exam may detect enlarged intrapelvic
lymph nodes. Many affected dogs have a non-regenerative anemia
and leukocytosis on CBC. Azotemia, on serum chemistries, may be
due to obstructive disease and paraneoplastic hypercalcemia can be
seen. Secondary bacteriuria is common.54,58 Neoplastic cells may be
seen in urine sediment, although differentiation between reactive
and neoplastic epithelial cells is difficult.16,58 With the high
percentage of distant metastases at diagnosis, complete staging is
recommended with 3-view thoracic radiographs and abdominal or
transrectal US used as general screens,59 to assess for prostate size,
locoregional lymph node metastasis, and/or bladder/ureter
involvement. CT and magnetic resonance imaging have been used,

but have not been extensively studied in dogs with PC.60 Prostatic
lymphoma is rare but should be included as a possibility when there
are hypoechoic lesions.57 Mineralization of the prostate on
abdominal radiographs or US is not pathognomonic for PC, but in
castrated male dogs, this finding is highly suggestive of neoplasia.60
Metastasis to bone occurs anywhere, but the ventral aspect of lumbar
vertebrae is most common, followed by the pelvis and femur.
Prostatic metastases appear as lytic, proliferative, or mixed lesions
on radiography (Figure 330. 6).60
Histologic examination remains the gold standard for diagnosis
and despite common secondary infections and inflammation,
cytologic and histologic agreement is excellent for PC.27,54 Samples
for cytologic examination are usually obtained via traumatic
catheterization, prostatic wash, or US-guided FNA. Cytology or
histology of any suspected metastatic lesion (e.g., lymph node, bone)
may aid with diagnosis and staging. US-guided aspiration or biopsy
should be used carefully to avoid tumor seeding.16,28,58 As with
bladder cancer, assays for BRAF V595E mutations can be used to
help diagnose urothelial (or prostatic) carcinoma.

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Most dogs with PC have a poor prognosis because metastasis has
occurred prior to diagnosis. Therapy is considered largely palliative,
focusing on controlling local and distant metastatic disease.
Surgeries to achieve local control are described but retrospective
studies suggest that prostatectomy as a single therapy is often
associated with high morbidity and MST <3-4 months. Subtotal
intracapsular prostatectomy may be used in dogs with early-stage
disease, since it can immediately palliate local clinical signs and is
associated with a lower rate of postoperative complications than total
prostatectomy (e.g., urinary incontinence, in 33-35% of dogs). Total
prostatectomy in dogs without extracapsular extension followed by
adjunctive treatment resulted in MST of 248 days.61 Urethral
obstructions can be managed with tube cystostomy or urethral
stenting (ch. 117). Palliative stenting can immediately alleviate
obstruction in most dogs. Incontinence and stent dislodging are the

most common complications.48 There is no consensus on standardof-care systemic therapy for PC; the possible benefits of
chemotherapy are being investigated. Most treatment options
include use of a COX-2 inhibitor. In 1 study, piroxicam or carprofen
were associated with increased survival rates when compared with
an untreated group. A retrospective study suggested increased
survival in dogs treated with a COX-2 inhibitor and chemotherapy;
however, prognosis was still poor, with an overall MST of 82 days
and a median time-to-progression of 63 days.62 Image-guided
intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) has shown promising
results in treating local disease with few side effects, a median eventfree survival of 220 to 317 days, and a MST of 563 to 654 days after
54 to 58 Gy or 48 to 54 Gy of radiation, respectively, delivered as
daily doses of 2.5 to 2.9 Gy.43,63

PENIS, PREPUCE, AND SCROTUM
Most tumors of the penile area are of soft-tissue origin, most
commonly transmissible venereal tumor (TVT). Uncommonly, a
cancer may originate in the os penis, e.g., ossifying fibroma,
chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, multilobular osteochondrosarcoma.
The prepuce and scrotum can be involved in any cutaneous cancer.
Mast cell tumors (ch. 327) account for >50% of scrotal tumors,
followed by mesenchymal and melanocytic tumors.64 Complete
staging with a CBC, serum chemistry profile, UA, and regional lymph

node evaluation (palpation, FNA cytology, biopsy, US) is
recommended prior to surgery. General recommendations for the
treatment of penile tumors depend on site and involve either a
partial penile amputation or ablation of the external genitalia with a
urethrostomy in the scrotal area if necessary.65 Scrotal and preputial
mast cell tumors have the worst outcomes compared to other
locations, requiring a multimodal approach that should include local
surgery/RT, castration with scrotal ablation, and systemic
chemotherapy/tyrosine kinase inhibitor treatment.66,67 TVT rarely
metastasizes, is readily diagnosed cytologically, and is a
chemosensitive and/or radiosensitive tumor usually curable with
vincristine (0.5-0.7 mg/m2 IV weekly).68 Lesion involution is
gradual, with complete remission in 90% of dogs after 2 to 8
injections. Therapy should be continued for 1 to 2 doses beyond
complete visible resolution. Lesions that are resistant to vincristine
may be successfully treated with doxorubicin or RT.68

TESTICLE
PREVALENCE, DIAGNOSIS, STAGING
Testicular tumors are the second most common tumor in intact male
dogs and the most common of canine male genitalia (ch. 314).
Middle-aged to older dogs (10 years) are affected.69 The 3 main
histologic types seen include interstitial (Leydig) cell tumor (ICT),
seminoma, and Sertoli cell tumor (SCT). Other histologic types are
rare.58 Recent studies indicate that about 50% of testicular tumors
are ICTs and 8-17% SCT.58,69-71 About 10-20% of dogs with a
testicular tumor have a second testicular tumor concurrently;
seminoma and ICT are the most common combination.58,69,72
Cryptorchid individuals have a higher risk of developing SCT or
seminoma, but not ICT. Right inguinal testicles are more commonly
affected than abdominal, and at a younger age than males with
descended testes.70 Most testicular tumors do not metastasize. SCTs
and seminomas have rarely (<15%) spread to regional lymph nodes.

ICTs rarely metastasize.58 Although most testicular tumors are an
incidental finding on PE, clinical signs may include decreased libido,
signs of prostatomegaly (stranguria, tenesmus), and inappetence
and/or weakness secondary to anemia. Asymmetric testicles, scrotal
or inguinal swellings, and prostatomegaly secondary to estrogeninduced squamous metaplasia may be detected on PE and/or rectal
exam. Signs of hyperestrogenism including alopecia, gynecomastia, a
pendulous prepuce, and a poor haircoat may be seen in up to 50% of
SCTs. Feminization signs are rare in seminomas and ICTs.
Complete staging should include a CBC to check for estrogeninduced anemia and abdominal US to evaluate regional lymph nodes
or detect a cryptorchid testicle. Thoracic radiographs should be
assessed for metastases. Testicular US may aid in ruling out nonneoplastic processes such as orchitis or testicular torsion, but
changes are not specific for tumor identification. Histopathologic
analysis provides a final diagnosis. Diagnosis prior to surgery can
usually be made cytologically via FNA.73 Bone-marrow suppression
is a rare but well-documented complication of hyperestrogenism.
This syndrome is characterized initially by neutrophilic leukocytosis,
which ultimately progresses into pancytopenia.

TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS
Bilateral orchiectomy with scrotal ablation is the preferred surgery
technique and is curative in most (Figure 330.7). If lymph node
metastasis is diagnosed, excisional biopsy should be performed. The
role of adjunctive chemotherapy, RT or novel targeted therapies in
dogs with metastatic disease is largely unknown, with only a few case
reports showing some degree of efficacy for these therapies,
including RT or cisplatin.58 If estrogen-induced myelosuppression
has occurred, the prognosis is guarded with aggressive supportive
care requiring months of hematologic support and antibiotics.

VAGINA AND VULVA

Tumors of the vagina and vulva most commonly affect older intact
nulliparous bitches and are rare in cats. Excluding skin tumors
arising on the labia of the vulva (melanoma, TVT, mast cell tumors),
the majority are benign smooth muscle tumors. Leiomyoma is the
predominant histologic type; polyps and fibromas are also frequently
diagnosed.74,75 Some benign tumors, e.g., lipomas and
hemangiomas, can cause vaginal bleeding.74 The most common
malignant tumor is leiomyosarcoma. A small number of spayed dogs
have had an adenocarcinoma affecting the clitoris. Urethral tumors
can extend into the urethral papilla.76 Tumors of the vestibule or
vagina may be intraluminal or extraluminal. Intraluminal tumors are
usually solitary, measure up to several centimeters in diameter, are
attached to the vaginal wall by a thin stalk, often cause stranguria,
and less often discharge (sometimes bloody), dysuria, or vulvar
licking. Owners may see a mass protrude during urination or
defecation (Figure 330.8). Extraluminal tumors appear as slowgrowing perineal masses.
Diagnostic evaluation should include vaginal and rectal palpation
and a vaginoscopic examination (ch. 101). Cytologic evaluation of
the mass via FNA can help in the diagnosis, although histopathologic
evaluation of a biopsy is often necessary (ch. 85). Complete staging
with thoracic radiographs and abdominal US to evaluate for lymph
node involvement should be obtained in dogs with non-pedunculated
masses. A CT scan of the caudal abdomen and perineum enables
assessment of the size and location of vaginal leiomyoma and
fibroma.60,76
Diagnosis of pedunculated intraluminal tumors usually requires
excisional biopsy transecting the pedicle. Local recurrence is rare.
For benign, hormonally responsive tumors, ovariohysterectomy
(OHE) performed at the time of tumor removal reduces risk of
recurrence even further and is usually curative. The cytological,
histological, and clinical features of the few canine clitoral
carcinomas described mimic those of neuroendocrine tumors.77
Unlike benign tumors, malignant vaginal masses tend to be broadbased and infiltrative, often requiring more extensive surgical
resection. Episiotomy alone, ventral median celiotomy, a
combination of ventral median celiotomy, episiotomy and pubic

osteotomy, and ostectomy have been reported. Surgical excision via
subtotal vaginectomy, vaginectomy or vulvovaginectomy have been
described for invasive benign and malignant vaginal cancers with few
complications and good outcomes.74,78 Radiation and/or
chemotherapy may be considered for the rare, malignant mass. The
prognosis for cats with vulvar adenocarcinoma appears to be poor; a
small number reported were euthanized for progressive local disease
or reoccurrence.79

UTERUS
Tumors of the uterus, including horn, body, and cervix, are rare in
dogs and cats. Leiomyomas account for 85-90% of canine uterine

tumors and leiomyosarcomas ∼10%. Fibroadenoma, lipoma,
adenocarcinoma, lymphoma (ch. 322), and mast cell tumors (ch.
327) are less common. Spayed females can develop tumors arising
from their uterine stump.74 Adenocarcinoma is the most common
uterine tumor in middle-aged-to-older cats but there have been
occasional reports of cats <1 year of age.74,76 German Shepherd Dogs
may have a hereditary condition characterized by concurrent renal
cystadenocarcinoma, nodular dermatofibrosis, and uterine
leiomyomas.60 Most uterine tumors in dogs are slow-growing,
noninvasive, and non-metastatic. In cats, uterine tumors are usually
biologically aggressive with widespread metastases.80
Uterine tumors in dogs are rarely associated with clinical signs,
although uterine enlargement with abdominal distension, vaginal
discharge, and urinary symptoms may be present. Cats may also
have signs related to metastatic disease. While no abnormality is
most common, bloodwork and thoracic radiographs should be
assessed. Abdominal radiographs may confirm the presence of a softtissue mass in the caudal aspect of the abdomen, but US is more
definitive for identifying the origin of the mass (uterine body or
cervical tumors). The appearance of uterine tumors on US in dogs is
variable. Usually, definitive diagnosis of uterine tumor requires
histologic examination of completely excised tissue (Figure
330.9).60 CT might help with surgical planning since larger tumors
invading the pelvic canal tend to be malignant.60,76 OHE is often
curative for dogs. OHE alone is unlikely to provide long-term control
for cats, due to the aggressive behavior of these tumors and has a
guarded prognosis. The efficacy of chemotherapy in both dogs and
cats remains largely unknown.

OVARY
TUMOR TYPES AND BIOLOGICAL BEHAVIOR
Ovarian neoplasms are rare, probably because a large portion of the
canine population is neutered at an early age. The prevalence in
intact females is 6.25%, affecting dogs with a median age of 10-12

years.74,81 Ovarian tumors are usually found incidentally during
routine OHE in older animals (Figure 330.10); however, ovarian
cysts may have a similar appearance. Other tumors may be larger
prior to detection, with clinical signs caused by the space-occupying
mass. Masses may be palpable or cause ascites. Rarely, ovarian
tumors secrete hormones. Based on the human World Health
Organization system, ovarian tumors are classified as epithelial
Mullerian origin, sex cord-stromal tumors, germ cell tumors, and
mesenchymal tumors.82 Most (80-90%) are epithelial or sex cordstromal tumors.74,82,83 Malignant tumors may metastasize to the
peritoneum and can cause a malignant effusion; metastases are also
seen in the lymph nodes, liver, and lungs. Feline ovarian tumor types
are similar to those of dogs with the exception of mesenchymal
tumors, which have not been reported to date.

FIGURE 330.9 Large uterine
leiomyosarcoma. Courtesy Manuel Jimenez Peláez,
LV, MRCVS, DECVS.
Epithelial ovarian tumors include the histologic diagnoses of
papillary adenoma, cystadenoma, papillary adenocarcinoma, and
undifferentiated adenocarcinoma. These tumors are typically
unilateral, rarely bilateral, usually non-functional, and have a
metastatic rate of approximately 50%.82 Epithelial tumors are rare in
cats.
Germ cell tumors (∼10% of canine ovarian tumors) arise from
primordial cells in the ovary and include dysgerminomas, teratomas,
and malignant teratomas (teratocarcinomas). Arising from
undifferentiated germ cells, dysgerminomas (ovarian seminomas)
are usually unilateral with a low rate of metastasis (10-30%).74,82
Teratomas comprise more than 1 germ cell layer (ectoderm,
mesoderm, and/or endoderm), and most are well differentiated.
Teratocarcinomas have differentiated and undifferentiated
components, and metastasis is noted in up to 50%.74,82 In cats,

about 15% of ovarian tumors are dysgerminomas with a similar
metastatic rate to that found in dogs.74
The granulosa cell tumor is the most common sex cord-stromal
tumor and the only tumor in this category that can metastasize. Less
common tumors include Sertoli-Leydig, thecomas, and luteomas.
They are rarely bilateral, ∼50% are functional, and their metastatic
rates are <20%.83 These tumors can produce estrogen and
progesterone with clinical signs related to estrogenic effects such as
vulvar enlargement, vaginal discharge, and cystic endometrial
hyperplasia. In cats, sex cord-stromal tumors make up roughly 50%
of ovarian tumors, and more than 50% are malignant. The most
common histologic type in cats is granulosa cell tumors, and
hyperestrogenism is commonly seen.
Tumors from residual ovarian tissue in dogs have a higher
prevalence (26.3%) than do tumors involving intact ovaries. All but 1
of the neoplasms of the ovarian fragment in 1 case series were
granulosa cell tumors; a single case was a cystadenoma.84

FIGURE 330.10 Ovarian granulosa cell tumor in a
9-year-old female mixed dog. Courtesy Manuel
Jimenez Peláez, LV, MRCVS, DECVS.

DIAGNOSIS, TREATMENT, PROGNOSIS
Diagnostic evaluation of dogs or cats with ovarian tumors should
include a minimum database, thoracic radiographs, and abdominal
US. If ascites is present, cytologic examination of the fluid may be
diagnostic for malignancy. US-guided aspirates for cytologic analysis
have a high correlation (94%) with histologic diagnoses (ch.
85).85,86 The risk of tumor seeding and tumor spillage, especially in
malignant cystic tumors, has not been evaluated. On US, ovarian
tumors in dogs range from solid to cystic. Malignant tumors tend to
be solid, whereas benign tumors tend to be cystic with smooth
borders. Cystic endometrial hyperplasia and pyometra are common
in dogs with sex cord-stromal tumors.60
Treatment of ovarian tumors relies primarily on OHE and careful
examination of the abdominal cavity for any potential metastatic

lesions. The prognosis is good for benign or localized malignant
tumors. Considering the good prognosis, aggressive treatment can be
recommended for dogs with malignant ovarian tumors, especially
early-stage cases.83 Despite metastasis being present at diagnosis,
50% of dogs with metastasis survived more than 1 year. Metastatic
disease carries a poor prognosis, and the role of conventional
therapies such as chemotherapy or RT has not been widely
investigated. Dogs with ovarian tumors with malignant effusion can
survive relatively long after intracavitary platinum-based
chemotherapy in addition to OHE, with a more favorable prognosis
for granulosa cell tumors than adenocarcinomas.74,87

DEFINITIONS
Paraneoplastic syndromes (PNSs) are defined as the signs and/or
biochemical alterations caused by indirect effects of a tumor’s
production and release of biologically active substances. While some
oncologists ascribe the term paraneoplastic syndrome only be used
when the compound released by the tumor is not normally produced
by the tumor cell of origin, this stringent definition would exclude
many commonly cited PNSs, e.g., hypoglycemia secondary to
pancreatic insulinoma. PNS signs are usually seen at sites distant
from the tumor location and may be the first evidence of neoplastic
disease. These signs often resolve with the successful treatment of
the underlying neoplastic process. Recrudescence of signs may
precede grossly detectable recurrence or relapse of the inciting
neoplastic process. Therefore, continued monitoring for these signs
is important.

ENDOCRINE-RELATED
PARANEOPLASTIC SYNDROMES (PNSs)
HYPERCALCEMIA OF MALIGNANCY (HM; CH.
69)
Mechanisms of HM
Cancer is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in dogs, whereas
non-neoplastic conditions predominate in cats.1 Abnormalities in
calcium (Ca) regulation may be caused by a wide variety of nonneoplastic diseases (chs. 69 and 283). About 66% of hypercalcemic

dogs and 33% of hypercalcemic cats have HM.1,2 There are 2
principal mechanisms that can lead to HM: humoral hypercalcemia
of malignancy (HuHM) due to tumor-produced factors and
hypercalcemia related to primary bone tumors or metastases with
local osteolytic bone resorption.2 HuHM is the primary mechanism
leading to HM via promotion of bone resorption by osteoclasts and
the subsequent release of Ca into the circulation. Factors released
from neoplastic cells may also affect the kidney and gastrointestinal
(GI) tract’s ability to modulate Ca concentrations. The most common
cancer produced “hormone” is parathyroid hormone-related peptide
(PTHrP).2 Other factors produced and released by neoplastic cells
that contribute to HM include receptor activator of nuclear factor
kappa-B ligand (RANkappaL), transforming growth factor-beta
(TGF-beta), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumor necrosis factor (TNF).2

Cancers Causing HM in Dogs and Cats
Lymphoma (ch. 322), anal sac adenocarcinoma (ch. 264), and
multiple myeloma (MM, ch. 322) are malignancies most commonly
associated with HM in dogs.2 This list is not exhaustive, and other
tumor types associated with HM in dogs include mammary gland
tumors, melanoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, squamous cell
carcinoma (SCC), thyroid carcinoma, and thymoma.2 HM in cats is
most frequently reported with SCC (chs. 258, 323) and lymphoma
(ch. 322). Other causes include MM, osteosarcoma (OSA), and
bronchogenic adenocarcinoma.2 Like dogs, PTHrP is considered to
be the primary factor driving HM in cats. Serum ionized calcium
(iCa) concentration should normalize rapidly with successful
treatment of the underlying cancer. Assessment of iCa should be
included with follow-up monitoring of any pet with HM. For pets in
which the inciting tumor is not amenable to complete removal or
refractory to treatment, other supportive measures for managing
hypercalcemia should be employed (ch. 283).

HYPOGLYCEMIA (CH. 61)

A paraneoplastic condition should be considered in any repeatedly
hypoglycemic dog or cat (chs. 61 and 289). This PNS is most
commonly caused by tumors of pancreatic beta cells (insulinomas).3
Other non-beta-cell tumors associated with hypoglycemia include
pulmonary adenocarcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma,
hemangiosarcoma (HSA), oral melanoma, and tumors of mammary
tissue, MM, plasma cells, kidneys, salivary glands, and smooth
muscle (leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma).4-8 Hypoglycemia due to
insulinoma is caused by overproduction of insulin by the primary
tumor. In contrast, hypoglycemia of the extra-pancreatic tumors has
been associated with insulin-like growth factors I and II, and
somatomedins.4 Other potential causes of paraneoplastic
hypoglycemia include the increased expression of insulin receptors,
glucose utilization by neoplastic cells, decreased hepatic
glycogenolysis or gluconeogenesis, and binding of insulin by M
proteins in MM. Paraneoplastic hypoglycemia is optimally treated by
the surgical removal of the neoplasm. However, it may be necessary
to supportively treat the hypoglycemia before surgery, or medically
manage the hypoglycemia if surgery is not feasible (chs. 155, 289).

ECTOPIC ADRENOCORTICOTROPIC
HORMONE (ACTH) SYNDROME
The ectopic production of ACTH or ACTH-like substances by
malignancies in animals is extremely rare. Case reports have
described this syndrome in dogs with primary lung tumors, an
abdominal neuroendocrine tumor, and a hepatic carcinoid.9-11

ESTROGEN EXCESS CONDITIONS
The most common neoplastic cause of hyperestrogenism is the
Sertoli cell tumor (chs. 314, 315, 330).12 Up to 50% of dogs with a
Sertoli cell tumor will display signs of hyperestrogenemia. Sertoli cell
tumors arising in cryptorchid testicles (vs. tumors in descended
testes) are more likely to produce excess estrogen.13 Not all dogs

with clinical signs of hyperestrogenemia have detectably high
estrogen concentrations. Decreased testosterone production,
reducing the testosterone : estrogen ratio, can contribute to clinical
signs.14 Clinical signs of hyperestrogenism include bilateral
symmetrical alopecia, cutaneous hyperpigmentation, epidermal
thinning (ch. 12), gynecomastia, galactorrhea, attracting males,
preputial atrophy, and atrophy of the nonneoplastic testicle.14
Pancytopenia may be detected on a complete blood count and bone
marrow evaluation may reveal a hypocellular marrow (ch. 176).12
Severe pancytopenia usually leads to lethargy, bleeding secondary to
thrombocytopenia, petechiae, and pale mucus membranes.12
Surgically removing the testicle with a Sertoli cell tumor is usually
curative, although recurrence of feminization was documented in a
dog with delayed-onset metastatic disease.15 Pancytopenic animals
may require pre-operative broad-spectrum antibiotics and blood or
red cell transfusions. Bone marrow recovery may take weeks to
months.

HEMATOLOGIC PARANEOPLASTIC
SYNDROMES
ANEMIA (CHS. 25, 57, AND 173)
Causes
Anemia is a common PNS in dogs and cats. Most paraneoplastic
anemias are likely secondary to anemia of chronic disease (ACD),
microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, immune-mediated hemolytic
anemia (IMHA), or blood loss. For blood loss anemia to be
considered a PNS, the blood loss must occur at a site distant from the
primary tumor, e.g., GI ulceration and bleeding secondary to
excessive histamine secretion from mast cell tumors (MCTs) or
excessive gastrin production by gastrinomas.

Anemia of Chronic Disease (ACD)

The chronic disease associated with many cancers is commonly
associated with anemia. ACD arises secondary to impaired iron
storage and metabolism, which suppresses erythroid progenitor cell
differentiation, decreases erythropoietin production, and reduces
survival of erythrocytes. ACD is usually mild/moderate, normocytic,
normochromic, non-regenerative, slowly progressive, and rarely
requires supportive measures.

Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia (ch. 174)
This PNS is often associated with microvascular solid tumors, e.g.,
HSA (ch. 325). However, it may occur with any tumor causing
disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC, ch. 171).16
Fragmentation of erythrocytes may occur as they pass through the
intravenous fibrin formed in DIC, or secondary to abnormal
vascularity within a tumor, pulmonary intraluminal tumor emboli, or
the narrowing of pulmonary arterioles.16 Successful treatment of the
underlying malignancy is considered the only effective therapy for
paraneoplastic microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.

IMHA (ch. 174)
While IMHA is a recognized PNS in people, most commonly in
association with hematopoietic tumors, a recent consensus
statement by the American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine
failed to identify a strong causal link between cancer and IMHA in
either dogs or cats.17 Cancer cannot be ruled out as a potential
trigger for IMHA in some dogs and cats (ch. 174). PNS is considered
a secondary IMHA because antibodies directed at tumor cellmembrane antigens can cross react with erythrocytes, resulting in
their early destruction. Signs commonly associated with IMHA are
lethargy, weakness, tachycardia, pallor, icterus, hepatosplenomegaly, hemoglobinuria, and anorexia. Removing the tumor is
the best treatment for paraneoplastic IMHA, but may not be feasible
in the short or long-term for some dogs and cats. Either transient or
long-term medical treatment can be helpful (ch. 174).

ERYTHROCYTOSIS (POLYCYTHEMIA;
CH. 173)
Polycythemia is an uncommon PNS in dogs and cats, most often
associated with primary or secondary tumors of the kidney.18-20
Other neoplasms that could cause erythrocytosis include lymphoma,
schwannoma, nasal fibrosarcoma, transmissible venereal tumor,
bronchioalveolar carcinoma, and cecal leiomyosarcoma.20-25 PNS
erythrocytosis is a form of secondary erythrocytosis, as the
underlying cause is excess erythropoietin (EPO) concentrations.20
Clinical findings may include erythema of mucous membranes,
polydipsia, and neurologic signs secondary to hyperviscosity or
hypervolemia, e.g., disorientation, ataxia, and/or seizures.

NEUTROPHILIC AND EOSINOPHILIC
LEUKOCYTOSIS (CH. 58)
Increased number of mature neutrophils in the absence of infection
or leukemia meets the criteria for PNS neutrophilic leukocytosis.
Renal carcinomas (transitional cell and tubular), lymphoma,
metastatic fibrosarcoma, pulmonary carcinoma, and rectal
adenomatous polyps have been associated with this PNS.26-30 PNS
neutrophilic leukocytosis is commonly observed in dogs with
hypertrophic osteopathy (HO),31 which can follow tumor production
of granulocyte and/or granulocyte-monocyte colony-stimulating
factors (G-CSFs, GM-CSFs).28,29 This PNS is most commonly an
incidental finding and resolves with successful treatment of the
underlying tumor.
Paraneoplastic eosinophilia, rare in dogs and cats, has been
reported in dogs with pericardial leiomyosarcoma, intestinal T cell
lymphoma, mammary carcinoma, and oral fibrosarcoma.32-34 In
cats, paraneoplastic eosinophilia has been reported with MCTs,
intestinal T cell lymphoma, acute leukemia and transitional cell
carcinoma of the bladder.35

THROMBOCYTOPENIA (CHS. 59 AND
175)
PNS thrombocytopenia has been associated with lymphoma,
melanoma, HSA, OSA, MCT, histiocytic malignancies, and various
carcinomas.36,37 Decreased platelet production may follow
myelophthisis induced by marrow-infiltrating malignancies or
estrogen-secreting testicular or ovarian tumors.38
Thrombocytopenia secondary to sequestration may occur with
splenic malignancies. Immune-mediated processes directed at
platelet destruction have been associated with lymphoma and MM.
Thrombocytopenia secondary to consumption may occur with
tumors that induce hemorrhage (HSA or MCTs) or coagulopathies,
e.g., DIC, multiple metastatic tumors, and HSA.36 Clinical signs of
thrombocytopenia, e.g., petechia (ch. 29), are not usually observed
if the platelet count remains >30 × 109/L. Treating PNS
thrombocytopenia depends on the inciting mechanism, although
resolution of the primary tumor is optimal.

THROMBOCYTOSIS (CHS. 59 AND 175)
PNS thrombocytosis is less common than thrombocytopenia. In
retrospective studies assessing cats and dogs with thrombocytosis,
neoplasia was the most common concurrent illness,39 seen with
OSA, gingival carcinoma, chronic myeloid leukemia, bronchoalveolar
carcinoma, metastatic SCC, and those undergoing
chemotherapy.39,40 PNS thrombocytosis is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Definitive causes include vinca alkaloid administration, splenectomy,
iron deficiency, and myeloproliferative disorders. Thrombocytosis
usually resolves with successful treatment of the underlying
malignancy.

PLATELET HYPERAGGREGABILITY,
HYPERCOAGULABILITY, AND DIC
(CHS. 170, 171)
Platelet hyperaggregation and hypercoagulability are common
hemostatic abnormalities in dogs with cancer.41 DIC is a complex
syndrome characterized by excessive activation of the coagulation
cascade, resulting in widespread microthombosis and multiorgan
failure. As a PNS, DIC has been associated with tumors of the
vasculature and solid tumors. Along with the mechanisms of DIC
common to other diseases, tissue factor is expressed on cancer cells
and complexes with factor VIIa to stimulate thrombin formation and
activate factors IX and X. Patients with paraneoplastic DIC generally
have a poor prognosis.

HYPERGLOBULINEMIA (CH. 60)
Hyperglobulinemia, a PNS commonly associated with MM, has also
been seen with lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and
plasmacytoma.42,43 Hyperglobulinemia is caused by excess
production of immunoglobulins by plasma cells or lymphocytes.43
Most pets with MM have an IgG or IgA monoclonal gammopathy.
Clinical signs relate to the hyperviscosity secondary to excess
globulins in circulation. In addition to hypertension and tissue
hypoxia, the decreased production of normal immunoglobulins
predisposes to infection. Hyperviscosity may cause cardiomegaly,
renal failure, ocular disorders (e.g., retinopathies), and neurologic
abnormalities.43 Bleeding tendency is common with
hyperglobulinemia and is caused by decreased platelet adhesion to
damaged endothelial surfaces, coating of platelets with
immunoglobulins, and release of platelet factor III. Confirmation of
hyperglobulinemia is via serum electrophoresis. Treatment of PNS
hyperglobulinemia depends on successful treatment of the inciting
tumor, usually with chemotherapy. The use of plasmapheresis may
be considered for cases of hyperglobulinemia that are not amenable
to quick resolution.

CUTANEOUS PARANEOPLASTIC
SYNDROMES (CH. 12)
FELINE PARANEOPLASTIC ALOPECIA
A unique PNS alopecia occurs in some cats with pancreatic or biliary
carcinomas.44 The acute, progressive, nonpruritic, symmetrical
alopecia occurs with easily epilated hair covering smooth shiny skin.
Palliation may be possible with resection of the primary tumor.

SUPERFICIAL NECROLYTIC
DERMATITIS (SND, CH. 274)
SND is a rare PNS most commonly associated with glucagonsecreting tumors in dogs (ch. 297). PNS SND has also been reported
in a cat with a glucagon-producing neuroendocrine carcinoma
(hepatic carcinoid).45 Hypoaminoacidemia is characteristic and may
be central to its etiology. The erythema, crusting, exudation,
ulceration, and nonpruritic alopecia is characterized histologically by
epidermal parakeratosis with laminar hydropic degeneration of the
stratum spinosum, hyperbasophilia of the deep epidermis, and
hyperplasia of the stratum basale. SND resolved after surgical
removal of pancreatic tumor and somatostatin therapy.46

NODULAR DERMATOFIBROSIS (ND)
ND is associated with renal cystadenoma or cystadenocarcinoma and
rarely with uterine leiomyoma or ovarian adenoma (ch. 330).47,48
This PNS in German Shepherd Dogs has been linked to mutations in
the chromosomal region overlapping the Birt-Hogg-Dubé locus.47

GASTROINTESTINAL PARANEOPLASTIC
SYNDROMES

CANCER CACHEXIA (CH. 151)
Weight loss and metabolic alterations in pets with cancer, despite
adequate nutrition, are termed cancer cachexia. In people this has
been associated with negative effects on strength, immune function,
wound healing, and survival.49 Similarly, poor body condition has
been associated with shortened survival times in feline cancer
patients.49

GASTROINTESTINAL (GI) ULCERATION
PNS GI ulceration is most common secondary to histamine release in
pets with mast cell disease. Excessive histamine stimulates gastric
H2 receptors, causing increased secretion of gastric acid (chs. 261,
297). As many as 75% of dogs with macroscopic MCT have increases
in plasma histamine, causing clinical signs in about 30%.50
Symptomatic therapies, e.g., proton pump inhibitors, H2 blockers,
misoprostol, or sucralfate may be of benefit; however, resolution of
PNS GI ulceration is expected only when the primary tumor is
adequately controlled. In addition to MCTs, gastrinomas have also
been associated with GI ulceration as a PNS.51

NEUROLOGIC PARANEOPLASTIC
SYNDROMES
MYASTHENIA GRAVIS (MG; CH. 253)
MG as a PNS most often occurs with thymoma, but it has been
described in association with cholangiocarcinoma, lymphoma, OSA,
and an oral sarcoma.52 Antibodies against the nicotinic acetylcholine
receptors are produced by the tumor, disrupting synaptic
transmission. Clinical signs of MG include weakness, dysphagia,
regurgitation, and aspiration pneumonia secondary to
megaesophagus. Removal of the primary tumor is recommended, but
MG may not resolve.

PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY (PN; CH.
252)
PNS PNs have been reported in dogs and cats with HSA, primary
lung tumors, leiomyosarcoma, mammary tumors, MM, lymphoma,
insulinoma, and undifferentiated sarcomas.53 PNS PN is likely
secondary to the production of antibodies targeting antigens shared
between the primary tumor and peripheral nerves. Removal of the
tumor is the only effective treatment for this PNS.

GLOMERULONEPHRITIS (CH. 302) AND
NEPHROPATHIES (CHS. 299-301)
Deposition of tumor-related immune complexes in glomeruli may
cause glomerular disorders (ch. 302). The prevalence of PNS
glomerulonephritis is unknown in dogs or cats. A dog with
lymphocytic leukemia developed immune complex
glomerulonephritis.54 Nephropathy in dogs and cats with neoplasia
may occur secondary to PNS hypercalcemia that can cause basement
membrane mineralization. Therapy for paraneoplastic
glomerulonephritis and nephropathy should be aimed at removal of
the inciting tumor.

MISCELLANEOUS PARANEOPLASTIC
SYNDROMES
HYPERTROPHIC OSTEOPATHY (HO)
The stimulation of afferent nerves is thought to increase blood flow
to the extremities and cause periosteal proliferation. Resolution of
signs following vagotomy supports this belief. HO is characterized by
periosteal proliferation along the shafts of long bones, typically in the
distal extremities, and soft tissue swelling of the limbs. HO initially
affects the distal aspect of all 4 limbs and progresses proximally. It is
most often associated with primary intrathoracic masses, though HO
has been reported in pets with renal, adrenal, metastatic Sertoli cell,

and urinary bladder tumors.35 While HO is most common in
neoplastic conditions, it has been diagnosed with
infectious/inflammatory pulmonary diseases (ch. 217), Spirocera
lupi esophageal granuloma (ch. 259), and bacterial endocarditis
(ch. 232).31 Dogs and cats affected by HO often have shifting-leg
lameness and/or they are reluctant to move (ch. 31). Typically, the
distal extremities are warm and swollen on palpation. A diagnosis of
HO is aided by radiography of the affected bones and subsequent
radiographic evaluation of the thorax. If thoracic radiographs are
negative for intrathoracic disease, additional diagnostics to evaluate
for infectious/inflammatory causes should be pursued. Successful
treatment of the primary mass usually resolves HO.31 Efforts to
manage the pain associated with HO should be attempted using antiinflammatory doses of steroids or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory
drugs (NSAIDs).

FEVER
Paraneoplastic fever occurs secondary to elaboration of pyrogenic
cytokines by either the tumor or by the host immune response to the
tumor (ch. 16). These pyrogens include IL-1, IL-6, interferons, and
tumor necrosis factor-alpha, which act on the thermoregulatory
center of the anterior hypothalamus. In addition to pyrogen-induced
fever, neoplastic infiltration into the hypothalamus may result in
fever. Therapy is dependent upon the underlying cause of the fever,
although symptomatic therapy with NSAIDs may provide some
palliation if the underlying cancer cannot be eliminated.

CLIENT INFORMATION
Paraneoplastic Syndromes
Paraneoplastic syndromes (PNS) are signs and symptoms arising
from the indirect effects of a tumor. It is important to note that not
all tumors are associated with paraneoplastic syndromes, though it is
possible that any tumor has the potential to be associated with these
signs. Tumors may produce and release a number of different
substances that have an effect on your pet’s body. These signs and
symptoms are not due primarily to the tumor, rather they are due to
the substances that are produced and released from the tumor. The
signs of paraneoplastic syndromes typically arise at sites away from
the tumor location and these signs may be the first evidence of a
tumor. These signs are often noticed on physical examination or

bloodwork performed by your veterinarian. Signs of a paraneoplastic
syndrome may range from changes in your pet’s urination frequency,
haircoat, or activity level that may be more obvious to changes that
may only be identified with tests performed on blood or urine. In
addition to the tumor itself, some paraneoplastic syndromes may
impact your pet’s health and should be treated, along with the tumor,
if your veterinarian believes these changes are potentially harmful to
your pet’s health. Often times the signs associated with
paraneoplastic syndromes will go away with the successful treatment
of the underlying tumor. Once a tumor has been treated successfully
and the accompanying paraneoplastic syndrome goes away, it is
important to very carefully monitor for the return of these
symptoms. The return of the signs associated with paraneoplastic
syndromes may be the first indication that a tumor has returned.
Timothy Stein (Austin, Texas)

A list was compiled of the top international destinations to which owners traveled with their pets in
2019. The information was provided by American Airlines, Air Canada, Delta Air Lines, KLM, and
United Airlines, which cumulatively transported approximately 170,000 companion animals via cargo in
2019. (NJ Bryant, personal communication, October 30, 2023). The chart provides the common entry
requirements; however, an in-depth review of the entry requirements can be found using the USDA Pet
Travel Website.

If FPV/FCV/FHV-1 begins at <8 wks of age, or interval between vaccines is <3 wks, the number of

First dose and protocol may change between products. See ch. 205.

Currently only available in Japan, Australia and New Zealand. Studies of efficacy vary widely, with

For FHV-1 and FCV: q 3 years for low-risk cats and annually for high-risk cats.

Revaccinate 12 months after last dose of initial series, then annually for cats at high risk of exposure
or q 2-3 years (depending on the vaccine’s DOI) for low-risk cats.

Bb, Bordetella bronchiseptica; CAV, canine adenovirus (infectious canine hepatitis); CDV, canine
distemper virus; CIV, canine influenza virus; CPiV, canine parainfluenza virus; CPV, canine parvovirus;
DOI, duration of immunity; IN, intranasal; MDA, maternally derived antibody; MLV, modified live
virus; revax, revaccinate; wk, week.
- core vaccine;

- can be considered core where the disease is prevalent;

- non-core vaccine.

If FPV/FCV/FHV-1 begins at <8 wks of age, or interval between vaccines is <3 wks, the number of doses
is increased so the last dose is given at ≥16 wks of age. Some kittens have MDA at 20 wks of age, so
primary series could be extended to 20 wks of age, with another vaccine given at 26 wks of age. See chs.
201 and 205.
(1)

If CDV, CPV and CAV protocol begins at <8 wks of age, or interval between vaccines is <3 wks, the
number of doses is increased so the last dose is given at ≥16 wks of age. The dose at 16+ wks of age is the
most important, when MDA may have waned and the puppy should respond to vaccination.

(2)

To confirm protective immunity for CDV, CPV and CAV in a puppy, it is possible to perform a gold
standard or a point-of-care (with high specificity and positive predictive value) serological test at least 4
wks after the vaccination given at 16+ wks. A seropositive puppy does not require the 26-wk vaccine and
can be revaccinated 3 years later. Seronegative puppies should be revaccinated and retested. If the
puppy again tests negative, it should be considered a non-responder that is possibly incapable of
developing protective immunity against this antigen.
(3)

Serologic testing for CDV, CPV and CAV can also be an alternative to routine triennial (q 3 years)
revaccination. A negative test result indicates that revaccination is recommended. Seropositive animals
are protected and don’t need to be revaccinated that year.
(4)

A single dose of MLV or recombinant vaccine will likely protect most dogs.

(5)

Use of CPiV as a mucosal vaccine in combination with Bordetella bronchiseptica may be preferable

(6)

Use of a mucosal vaccine may be preferable.

(7)

Vaccination can start as early as 3 or 8 wks of age, depending on the manufacturer.

(8)

There is some evidence that the intranasal route provides superior clinical outcomes compared to the
oral route.
(9)

Vaccination can start as early as 6 wks of age.

(10)

Vaccination can start as early as 9 wks for most vaccines, followed by annual revaccination,
preferably before the beginning of tick season. The use of this vaccine is controversial.
(11)

Depending on the licensed DOI.
